# Zevachim 2

## Intro: Seder Kodashim

### New masechet

We begin today a new *masechet* and a new *seder*, moving from Nezikin to Kodashim and opening with Zevachim — a large tractate of approximately 120 *daf* that will occupy us for four months.

### Three masechtos

Zevachim concerns the animal sacrifices. Following it comes Menachot, which deals with the grain offerings. After those two *masechtos* comes Chullin, known among the *rishonim* as *Shechitat Chullin* — the slaughtering of non-*kodshim* animals — which is the domain of the classical laws of *kashrut* of meat.

### Sources: Rishonim

An important practical note for the student: in Zevachim and Menachot one finds the standard Rashi and Tosafos, but virtually none of the other *rishonim*. In Chullin, by contrast, the full range of *rishonim* is available. In Kodashim generally there is very little *rishon* literature, though of course the Rambam and Ra'avad are present. There is also no *Yerushalmi* on Kodashim — and though the Rambam in his *Peirush Hamishnayot* alludes to one, and roughly 150 years ago a *Yerushalmi* on Kodashim was reportedly discovered, it proved to be a forgery. We therefore work essentially with the *gemara*, Rashi, and Tosafos.

---

## Kol hazevachim

### Shelo lishmah rule

The *masechet* opens with a sweeping principle: *kol hazevachim shenizbechu shelo lishman kesherim* — all sacrifices that were slaughtered not for their name, meaning not for the type of sacrifice they properly are, remain valid — *ela shelo alu laba'alim lesheim chovah* — except that they do not count for their owners toward the satisfaction of any obligation.

To appreciate this, one must understand the mechanics of the *avodah*. It is the *kohanim* who perform the slaughter, not the owners. One can easily imagine the practical complexity: vast numbers of people bring their animals, the *kohen* may lose track of which animal is which type of sacrifice, and slaughter a *chatat* with a *shelamim* in mind, or an *olah* with a *shelamim* in mind. The *mishnah* tells us that such an error, while it severs the connection between the sacrifice and the owner's obligation, does not render the animal itself invalid as a *korban*.

### Kesher vs. obligation

This distinction — between the validity of the sacrifice as an object and the satisfaction of the owner's personal obligation — is foundational and must be held clearly in mind from the outset. The owner may have brought a sacrifice because he sinned and owes a *chatat*, because he is undergoing a purification process, because he accepted a *neder*, or for any number of other reasons. Alternatively, he may have brought a sacrifice with no personal obligation at all — simply sanctifying an animal as an *olah* or *shelamim* without accepting any personal duty. If the animal is lost or something goes wrong, he owes nothing, because he has no personal *chovah*.

The validity of the *korban* as a *korban* is an entirely separate matter. When the *mishnah* says it is *kasher*, it means that all subsequent *avodos* — sprinkling the blood on the *mizbeach*, burning the fats, eating the meat — proceed in their normal course. The animal is not disqualified. The owner simply does not exit the sacrifice having fulfilled his obligation, and must therefore bring another. The *kohen*, separately, may face questions of liability — a discussion the *gemara* in Gittin takes up — but that is a different legal domain entirely.

One might further ask: if the sacrifice has been offered *shelo lishmah* and the owner therefore does not fulfill his obligation, yet the animal is still *kasher*, does the owner retain his status as *ba'alim* for other purposes — such as the *tenufa*, the waving ceremony for a *shelamim*, or the right to eat the meat? This is a genuinely interesting question. According to the view of Rabbi Yosi that *kodashim kalim mammon ba'alim hem*, the animal remains his property in *dinei mamonot* terms, and presumably those proprietary relationships would survive even if the obligation-fulfillment dimension does not. But it is worth flagging as a question that demands further investigation.

### Pesach, Chatat

The *mishnah* then identifies two exceptions: the *korban pesach* and the *chatat*. For these two, a *shechita* performed *shelo lishmah* does not merely fail to satisfy the owner's obligation — it renders the entire *korban* invalid.

The *pesach* rule applies *bizmano* — specifically during the window of the afternoon of the fourteenth of Nisan from midday until nightfall. Outside that window, an animal sanctified as a *pesach* and brought at the wrong time automatically converts to a *shelamim*, and the *pesach* rules do not apply to it. But within that window, a *pesach* slaughtered for the sake of another sacrifice is completely *pasul* and must be burned.

The *chatat* case is the more intuitive one. A *chatat* brought for a sin is highly specific: it atones for a particular sin of a particular person. Unlike an *olah* or *shelamim*, which can easily be imagined as a *nedava* — a gift with no personal obligation attached — a *chatat* is inherently bound up with its owner. Ownerless *shelamim* is a coherent concept. Ownerless *chatat* is not. A *chatat* is defined by the nexus of owner, sin, and atonement. Once that nexus is severed — because the *kohen* slaughtered it for some other purpose — the animal has no independent standing. It does not continue to live as generic *chatat* the way an *olah* or *shelamim* can continue as a valid *korban*. Divorced from its owner and its occasion, it must be burned.

### R. Eliezer, Yosi ben Cho…

Rabbi Eliezer extends this principle to the *asham* as well. His view — *af ha'asham* — follows directly from the same logic: an *asham*, like a *chatat*, is linked to a specific sin and a specific owner. Once detached from that owner, it has no independent standing. The *mishnah* states his position as: *haPesach bizmano, vehaChatas vehaAsham bechol zman* — *Pesach* in its time, *chatat* and *asham* at any time, are completely invalid when slaughtered *shelo lishmah*.

The Rabbis do not clearly answer this argument; the logic of Rabbi Eliezer appears strong. The question reduces to this: to what degree can a sacrifice maintain an identity independent of its owner?

Yosi ben Choni approaches the issue from a different angle entirely, driven by the desire for symmetry. He argues that the rules should be parallel in both directions. If a *chatat* slaughtered for an *olah* is *pasul*, then an *olah* slaughtered for a *chatat* should likewise be *pasul*. Similarly, within the applicable window, if a *pesach* slaughtered for another sacrifice is *pasul*, then another sacrifice slaughtered for a *pesach* during that period should also be *pasul*. He wants the schema to be fully reciprocal.

One should also note, as Tosafos emphasizes near the end of its extended discussion on this *mishnah*, that a crucial and separate question underlies this entire discussion: when we say the *kohen*'s wrong *machshavah* invalidates, must that intent be verbally articulated (*dibur*) or is even a silent mental thought sufficient? This debate between Rashi and Tosafos runs through all areas in which *shelo lishmah* is operative and will recur throughout the tractate.

---

## Gavo'ah vs. Namuch

### Higher vs. lower

Shimon Achi Azaryah — so called because his brother Azaryah supported him financially in a *Yissachar-Zevulun* arrangement — introduces a further refinement. He rules that if you slaughter a sacrifice for a *higher*-level sacrifice, it is *kasher*; if you slaughter it for a *lower*-level sacrifice, it is entirely *pasul* — not merely a failure of obligation, but a complete invalidity of the *korban*.

The word *kesherim* here, and correspondingly *pesulim*, must be read carefully. *Kesherim* in Shimon's formulation may carry even greater force than in the *tanna kamma*: there is a question in the *gemara* whether slaughtering upward toward a higher-level sacrifice not only preserves the *korban*'s validity but may even allow the owner to fulfill his obligation. *Pesulim*, by contrast, means the *korban* must be removed from the altar and burned — it has no standing at all as a sacrifice.

### Hierarchy examples

The *mishnah* then illustrates the hierarchy. *Kodshei kodashim* — the most holy sacrifices such as the *olah* — slaughtered *leshem kodashim kalim* such as *shelamim*: *pesulim*. *Kodashim kalim* slaughtered *leshem kodshei kodashim*: *kesherim*. Even within *kodashim kalim* there is an internal hierarchy: *bechor* and *maaser*, though functionally similar to *shelamim*, are considered a step below, because they lack several of the *avodos* associated with *shelamim* — the resting of the hand on the animal's head, the bringing of flour and wine, the waving of the thigh and breast. Because fewer ritual demands are made upon them, they are understood to occupy a lower rung of *kedushah*. Accordingly, *shelamim* slaughtered as *bechor* or *maaser* is *pasul*; *bechor* or *maaser* slaughtered as *shelamim* is *kasher*.

---

## Sanctity intact

### Language analysis

The *gemara* opens its analysis of the *mishnah*'s language with a precise grammatical observation. Why does the *mishnah* use the word *ela* — "except"? It could simply have said: they are *kesherim* and did not count for the owners toward their obligation. The word *ela* signals something additional. And the *gemara* answers: *leba'alim hu delo olu lesheim chovah, aval bekadushataihu kaimi* — the only deficiency is that the owners did not fulfill their obligation. But in all other respects, the sacrifices retain their full *kedushah*, intact and uncompromised.

### Rava's ruling

This is a striking ruling, and Rava draws out its practical implication. One might think: since the sacrifice was already slaughtered *shelo lishmah*, and since the owner will not fulfill his obligation regardless, the *kohen* might as well continue doing the remaining *avodos* with wrong intent too. Rava rejects this categorically. *Olah sheshachtan shelo lishmah, asur lizrok damah shelo lishmah* — just because the *shechita* of an *olah* was done *shelo lishmah* does not license the subsequent *zerikah* to be done *shelo lishmah* as well.

The reason is profound: the demands of proper *avodah* — thinking about what type of *korban* this is throughout each of the four key acts — are not merely instrumental toward achieving a *kasher* status. They are expressions of the *kedushah* of the *korban* itself. The *olah* still is an *olah* in every sense. Its *kedushah* still demands that every *avodah* be performed with the proper orientation. Just as one who fails to sprinkle the blood on all four corners of the altar has done something wrong even if it does not *pasul* the sacrifice, so too here: you are still obligated to do things properly, even though departing from propriety will not retroactively invalidate what has already been done.

The *gemara* offers two bases for this ruling — *iba'it eima sevara* and *iba'it eima kra*. The logical argument: just because you made one thing wrong, does that entitle you to keep making things wrong? The verse-based argument comes from Deuteronomy: *motza sefatecha tishmor ve'asita ka'asher nadarta lashem elokecha nedava ka'asher dibarta beficha.*

### Neder vs. nedava

The distinction between *neder* and *nedava* in the usage of *Chazal* is important here. In the Torah the terms are relatively interchangeable, but *Chazal* read them carefully: a *neder* is a personal obligation — *harei alai* — whereby one accepts upon oneself a duty to bring a *korban*. A *nedava* is a gift: one sanctifies the animal without incurring a personal obligation. If the animal is lost, one who brought a *nedava* owes nothing further.

The *gemara* reads the verse as follows: *ka'asher nadarta* — if you executed the sacrifice exactly as you vowed — *yehei neder*, it functions as a *neder* and discharges the personal obligation. *Ve'i lav* — if you did not execute it in exact accordance with your vow — *nedava yehei*. It becomes a *nedava*. The *kedushah* and validity of the *korban* as a sacrificial object are not undermined; it simply no longer functions to discharge a personal *chovah*. The *gemara* notes that while this verse was cited primarily to establish Rava's point about not continuing with wrong intent, it also provides an elegant scriptural foundation for the basic principle of the *mishnah*: a sacrifice offered *shelo lishmah* is still *kasher* — it continues as a *nedava* — but it does not satisfy the owner's *neder*.

---

## Zevachim vs. Get

### Ravina's question

Ravina addresses Rav Pappa, noting that he had missed Friday night's session at the *beis medrash*, where Rava had posed what seemed to be a contradiction between two rulings and then offered a brilliant resolution. What was this teaching of Rava?

The *mishnah* states: *kol hazevachim shenizbechu shelo lishman* — all sacrifices slaughtered *shelo lishman* are *kasher* but do not satisfy the owner's obligation. This prompted Rava to observe a tension with a parallel rule from the laws of *gittin*.

### Language nuance

Rava's analysis begins with a close reading of the *mishnah*'s language. There is a precise difference between saying *shelo nizbechu lishmam* — "that were not slaughtered for their proper purpose" — and *shenizbechu shelo lishmam* — "that were slaughtered for their non-proper purpose." The former formulation would imply that any sacrifice lacking the affirmative right intent is invalid. The latter implies that only a sacrifice actively slaughtered *for a wrong purpose* is affected; if the *kohen* simply had no particular thought — a blank mind — that does not constitute a problem.

The *mishnah* uses the latter formulation. Its implication, therefore, is: *ta'ama d'shelo lishmam* — the reason for the deficiency is the active wrong intent — *ha stama, alu nami leba'alim lesheim chovah* — but if the mind was simply blank, the sacrifice also satisfies the owners' obligation. *Alma stamei nami k'lishmam dami* — blank intent is treated as equivalent to proper intent.

### Blank intent

Against this, the *gemara* raises a contradiction from the laws of *gittin*: *kol get shenichtav shelo l'shem isha pasul* — any *get* written not for this woman is invalid. And we know — as the *gemara* will establish through evidence below — that this extends to the case of blank intent as well. A *get* written with no particular woman in mind is *pasul*, even though the analogous sacrifice would be *kasher*. How are these two regimes to be reconciled?

Rava's answer: *zvachim b'stam lishma omdim, isha b'stama lav l'geirushin omedet* — sacrifices, when their intent is unexplicated, stand as though properly designated; a woman, when unexplicated, does not stand as though designated for divorce.

---

## Stam leshmah omed

### Sanctity defines act

The conceptual basis of Rava's answer is this: an animal is sanctified. It carries the *kedushah* of an *olah* or a *shelamim* as part of its very identity. Therefore, any act performed upon it — *shechita*, *kabbalah*, *holachah*, *zerikah* — is automatically defined by what that animal is. The requirement for *lishmah* in the context of *zevachim* is not primarily about what thought happens to be passing through the *kohen*'s mind. It is about the *definition* of the act. Since the animal itself has the identity of an *olah*, any act done to it is an *olah*-act by virtue of what is being acted upon — unless something actively redefines it.

This has a striking implication: the relevant question is not whether the *kohen* is consciously thinking the right thought. The question is whether the act has been actively redirected toward a different purpose. As long as the *kohen* does not impose a different identity upon the act, the *kedushah* of the object does the definitional work. *Stam leshmah omed* — blank intent stands as proper designation.

One can test the logic with a borderline case. Tosafos raises the question of a *katan* — a minor — performing the *avodah*. Since minors lack halachically meaningful intent, does their *shechita* count? The answer, on this analysis, should be yes: the issue is not the *kohen*'s conscious thought; it is whether the act has been positively redefined. A minor who does nothing to redefine the act has not undermined it.

Similarly, Tosafos applies this principle to *brit milah*: *stam brit milah lishma omed* — an act of removing the foreskin is defined as an act of *brit milah* unless actively redefined as something else.

### Woman no default

A woman, by contrast, has no inherent designation toward any particular divorce. There is nothing in the nature of the object — the paper, the ink, the names written — that automatically defines this document as *the get* for *this woman*. Writing the name שרה בת רחל tells us nothing about which שרה בת רחל is intended. There may be countless women with that name, including multiple such women married to men with the same name. Nothing in the act of writing defines it as for *this* woman's *geirushin* rather than any other.

Rashi and Tosafos press this further: even if the woman is publicly known to be in the process of getting divorced, even if the husband has made his intention known, that context does not automatically define the *get* as being for her. The reason is that unlike the sanctified animal, the document has no intrinsic identity that would do the definitional work. Unless the scribe (*sofer*) has *her* specifically in mind, the act of writing remains unattached to any particular woman. *Isha lav stama lav l'geirushin omedet.*

---

## Evidence: stam works

### Mishnah language

Having established Rava's conceptual framework, the *gemara* now seeks evidentiary support for each part of the bifurcated rule — first, that blank intent is acceptable for *zevachim*, and second, that it is not acceptable for *gittin*.

The first attempt to prove that blank intent works for *zevachim* looks to the language of the opening *mishnah* itself — the same distinction we already noted between *shelo nizbechu lishmam* and *shenizbechu shelo lishmam*. But this attempt is deflected: the parallel *mishnah* about *gittin* uses the identical grammatical formulation, so one cannot derive a meaningful distinction from phrasing alone.

The *gemara* then turns to a later *mishnah* that discusses mixed-intent cases. *Keitzad lishmam v'shelo lishmam* — what counts as for the right purpose and for the wrong purpose? The example given is: the *shechita* was *leshem pesach* and the *kabbalah* was *leshem shelamim*. The *gemara* observes: the example of *shelo lishmah* is always an *actively wrong* identification — *shelamim* where *pesach* was intended — not the mere absence of right intent. This implies that blank intent would be fine.

But this is deflected as well. Perhaps, says the *gemara*, the reason blank-plus-right works in sequential cases is the principle that *kol ha-oseh al da'at rishonah hu oseh* — acts done without explicit redirection are presumed to follow the initial intent. So if you started with *pesach* and then had blank intent for *kabbalah*, the blank is defined by the opening *pesach* thought. That does not prove that blank at the outset, from the beginning, would work on its own.

The *gemara* then tries from the second half of the same *mishnah* — *shelo lishmam v'lishmam*: the *shechita* was *leshem shelamim*, the *kabbalah* was *leshem pesach*. The observation: the *shelo lishmah* example is actively naming a wrong sacrifice. But perhaps blank *shechita* followed by *pesach* at *kabbalah* would also be rescued by the final *pesach* thought — *yochiach sof al techilato*, the end retroactively defines the beginning. So again, the absence of blank intent at the outset is not proven from here.

### Six things; R. Yosi

The *gemara* then turns to a different *mishnah*: *leshem shisha devarim hazevach nizbach* — for six considerations a sacrifice is slaughtered. These are: *leshem zevach* (the type of sacrifice), *leshem zoveach* (the owner), *leshem Shem* (for God), *leshem ishim* (that the right portions be burned on the *mizbeach*), *leshem reiach* and *leshem nichoach* (the fragrant smoke ascending properly as an act pleasing to God — Rashi explains *nichoach* as referring not to the pleasant smell per se but to doing the *avodah* for God's *nachas ruach*, in fulfillment of His command). For *chatat* and *asham* there is an additional consideration: *leshem chet*, for the sake of the sin.

Rabbi Yosi then states: *af mi shelo haya belibo lesheim achas mikol elu — kasher* — even one who had none of these considerations in mind, the sacrifice is *kasher*. *She-tenai Beis Din hu* — it is a condition stipulated by Beis Din.

### Beis din rule

The phrase *tenai Beis Din* might naturally be read to mean that Beis Din has made an enactment that retroactively frames the *kohen*'s intent as though it were proper — analogous to declarations of *hefker* that apply to objects left in a defined context. On that reading, blank intent is validated only because of Beis Din's special framing, not because of any inherent principle.

But the *gemara* reads it differently. Beis Din, on this reading, instructed the *kohanim* not to try to articulate their intent. The reason: if they actively try to think *leshem olah* or *leshem chatat*, there will be occasions when they accidentally think or say the wrong sacrifice type. Better to keep a blank mind entirely. *Azkinhu Beis Din delo leima lishmo dilma asi leimei shelo lishmo* — Beis Din told them not to articulate *lishmah* lest they come to articulate *shelo lishmah*.

Now the *gemara* makes its proof: *ve'i salka da'atach stama pasul* — if it were true that blank intent invalidates a *korban* — *kaymi Beis Din u'masnu midi de'asi lidei pasul* — how could Beis Din give an instruction that would render every *korban* invalid? The fact that Beis Din could issue such an instruction presupposes that blank intent is perfectly valid. This is the clearest evidence that *stam* works for *zevachim*.

The *gemara* thus takes Rabbi Yosi's statement not as an independent enactment creating validity by fiat, but as evidence for the underlying *halacha* that *stam* is *kasher* — which then also explains why Beis Din could permissibly tell the *kohanim* to think nothing at all.

---

## Get requires lishma

### Marketplace get

Having established that blank intent is valid for *zevachim*, the *gemara* now seeks to establish the converse for *gittin* — that blank intent does *not* suffice for a *get*.

The first candidate: a man walking through a marketplace hears students (*sofrim*) reading aloud a sample *get* — "Reuven ben Shimon divorces Sarah bas Rachel from Tel Aviv" — and discovers that the names match his own and his wife's. *Pasul legaresh bo* — he cannot use it. But the *gemara* deflects this proof, citing Rav Pappa's explanation: *hacha b'sofrin ha'asuyim lilmod askinan, v'lo nichtav leshem krisus klal* — this case involves scribes practicing for educational purposes; the document was not written as a *get* at all. Its *get*-identity has not been established. So we cannot learn from this about a document written with the intent to serve as a *get* but with generic names.

### Generic names

The *gemara* therefore advances to a stronger case. A man wrote a *get* intending to divorce his wife, then changed his mind. A neighbor with identical names — same man, same wife's name — asks to use it. *Pasul legaresh bo*. But again the *gemara* deflects: the *get* was designated *l'geirushin d'hahi* — for the divorce of that specific first wife — not generically. It is not a case of blank, undirected intent; it is a case of intent that was positively directed at one woman and then redirected.

### Two wives case

The *gemara* then tries: a man has two wives with the same name. He wrote a *get* for the older one. He cannot use it for the younger one. *Lo yigaresh bo es hakatan*. But this too is deflected: the *get* was designated for the older wife's divorce, not the younger's. Again it is not a case of pure blank intent; it is a case of specific designation for one woman that cannot be transferred.

### Blank form gittin

Finally the *gemara* reaches a convincing proof. The *mishnah* discusses a scribe who writes *tufsei gittin* — boilerplate *get* forms. He must leave blank spaces for the man's name, the woman's name, the signatures of the witnesses, and the date. Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: he must also leave blank the line *harei at muteres le'chol adam* — "behold you are permitted to all men" — the declaration of release that must be written with the specific woman in mind. The necessity of leaving that line blank demonstrates that writing it generically — even in a document that is being prepared as a *get* — is invalid. The document only becomes *kasher* when that line is filled in with the particular woman in mind.

This establishes that for a *get*, even a document whose *get*-identity is established, specific *lishmah* — affirmative intent directed at *this* woman — is required. Blank intent does not suffice.

---

## Object vs. act

### Sanctified identity

The underlying conceptual distinction now comes into sharp focus. A sanctified *korban* carries its identity within itself. It is an *olah* or a *shelamim*, and that status is real, objective, and legally operative. Any act performed upon it is defined by what it is, not by what the performer is thinking. The definitional work is done by the object. *Stam lishmah omed* — blank intent stands as proper designation — because the *kedushah* of the animal itself assigns meaning to the act. Only active, positive redirection of that act toward a different purpose can override this inherent definition.

### No inherent woman

A *get*, by contrast, is a document without inherent identity. There is nothing in a piece of paper bearing a name that ties it to any particular person. The act of writing does not define itself. No woman is inherently designated to be divorced by any document. The document must *acquire* its identity through the explicit, directed intent of the one creating it. Without that intent, there is nothing to do the definitional work, and the document remains unattached — and therefore *pasul* as a *get*.

The difference, then, is not that the two legal domains of *zevachim* and *gittin* operate under different formal rules about intent. It is that the nature of the objects involved differs fundamentally. Where the object already *is* something — an *olah*, a *shelamim*, a sanctified animal with real *kedushah* — blank intent does no harm. Where the object must *become* something through the act of creation — a *get* for *this* woman — blank intent is simply insufficient to constitute that becoming.

---

# Zevachim 3

## Stam Kodshim

### Ravina & Rav Pappa

The daf opens with Ravina recounting to Rav Pappa a pair of contradictions and resolutions that Rava had presented the previous evening in the beit medrash. The first contradiction had pitted two domains against each other: the laws of *kodshim* and the laws of *gittin*. By *kodshim*, if a *kohen* performs *shechita* without any specific intent — neither for the right *korban* nor for the wrong one — the offering is valid. By *get*, however, a document written without specific intent for the particular woman is invalid, even if written in a generic fashion.

### Kodshim vs. Get

These two rulings appear flatly inconsistent. In both cases, a legally significant act is performed without directed intent. Why should *kodshim* be forgiving of generic performance while *gittin* is not?

### Kedusha Defines Act

The resolution, as Rava had explained, turns on a fundamental difference in the nature of the act. By *kodshim*, the animal arrives already endowed with *kedusha* — it has an identity. *Stam kodshim lishman hem omdim*: sanctified animals stand as already defined by their consecration. The act of *shechita* therefore does not require the officiant's intent to define it; the *kedusha* itself defines the act. One need only ensure the absence of a disqualifying thought, not the presence of a specifying one. By *get*, no such identity inheres in the raw materials. A piece of parchment and ink have no intrinsic relationship to any woman. Only the scribe's specific intent invests the document with its identity. Absent that intent, the *get* is unformed, and *stama* — generic performance — is disqualifying. This contrast — *stam kodshim lishman* versus the requirement of directed intent for a *get* — was the first major resolution of the previous session.

---

## Minah vs. Lo Minah

### Chatat: Olah vs. Chulin

With that recap established, the *gemara* turns to a second contradiction raised by Rava. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: a *chatat* that was slaughtered *leshem olah* — with intent that it be an *olah* — is invalid; but a *chatat* slaughtered *leshem chulin* — with intent that it be a non-consecrated animal — is valid. At first glance this is counterintuitive: an *olah* is at least a sacred offering, while *chulin* is entirely outside the domain of *korbanot*. One might have expected the more radical departure to be more disqualifying, not less.

### Principle Stated

The *gemara* draws the principle explicitly: *d'mina machriv bah, d'lo mina lo machriv bah* — something of its own kind can destroy it; something of a completely different kind cannot. The threat is always greatest from that which is closest. A thought about *chulin* is so far outside the world of *kodshim* that it has no traction, no purchase on the act. It is as irrelevant as a ruling that contradicts an explicit verse — it simply does not register. A thought about an *olah*, however, remains within the sacred domain and therefore has the power to displace the *chatat*'s identity.

### Get Challenge

This principle is immediately challenged from the laws of *get*. The rule there is that any *get* written *shelo lishmo* — not for the sake of this particular woman — is invalid. And the *gemara* presses: presumably, this applies even if the *get* was written for a non-Jewish woman, who has no place in the halachic world of *gittin* whatsoever. A non-Jewish woman would seem as irrelevant to *gittin* as *chulin* is to *kodshim*. So why does thinking of a non-Jewish woman still invalidate the *get*?

### Stama Pasul

The answer is a near-softball given what was established the day before. By *get*, thinking of a non-Jewish woman does not disqualify because of its content — it is indeed irrelevant. But its irrelevance means only that it is not a *positive* disqualifying thought. The problem remains that one lacked the *required* specific intent for the right woman. *Stama pasul* — generic performance is disqualifying for a *get*. The absence of a wrong thought does not help if the right thought was never present. By *kodshim*, as established, *stama keshera* — generic performance is acceptable, because the *kedusha* already defines the act. The two domains thus remain fully consistent with the principle: the structure of each domain determines what counts as disqualifying, and within *kodshim*, only something *minah* — of the same sacred genus — can destroy.

---

## Kli Cheres & Tocho

### Shratzim & Tumah

The *gemara* now introduces a new contradiction bearing on the same principle, drawing from the laws of *tum'ah*. The Torah states, concerning a *kli cheres* — a pottery vessel — that if a *sheretz* falls into its interior (*el tocho*), everything within it (*kol asher be-tocho*) becomes *tamei*. The critical feature of a *kli cheres* is that it conveys *tum'ah mei-aviro* — through its airspace — rather than through direct contact. The *sheretz* defiles the vessel's interior atmosphere, and that atmosphere in turn defiles whatever is suspended within it, even without physical touching.

### Tocho Concept

The *halacha* thus operates on two levels: the *sheretz* falls *el tocho*, into the airspace of the *kli cheres*, rendering the vessel *tamei*; and then *kol asher be-tocho yitma* — anything within that airspace becomes *tamei* as well, even without direct contact with the *sheretz*.

### Vessel Inside Vessel

The *gemara* cites a *beraita*: *tocho ve-lo toch tocho* — the airspace of the vessel, but not the airspace within the airspace. Moreover, *afilu kli shetef matzil* — even a non-pottery vessel placed inside the *kli cheres* saves its contents. To picture this: a drinking glass, open at the top, is placed inside a *kli cheres*, with the rim of the glass extending above the rim of the *kli cheres*. Food inside the glass is considered to be *within the glass*, not within the *kli cheres*, and is therefore not *tamei*. The glass need not be sealed; as long as its opening is above the rim of the outer *kli cheres*, the food is considered in its own separate airspace.

This raises the precise question the *gemara* has been building toward. A glass vessel is *lav mina* — not of the same genus as a *kli cheres*. Based on the principle that only something *minah* has a meaningful impact, one might argue that from the perspective of the *kli cheres*, the glass is irrelevant; the food should still be considered as residing within the *kli cheres*'s airspace, and *tamei*. Yet the *halacha* is that even a glass vessel saves. How does this square with *d'lo mina lo machriv bah*?

### Vessel vs. Wall

The *gemara* resolves this with a pointed analogy: *asu chulin etzel kodshim k'mechitzah etzel tannur* — *chulin* vis-à-vis *kodshim* is comparable to a partition (*mechitzah*) within an oven. A glass vessel is not truly *lo mina*. Whatever its material, it remains a vessel, a *kli*, and that is precisely the relevant category. The question of whether food is inside the *kli cheres* or in a separate airspace is a question defined by the world of *keilim* — vessels. A glass is still a *kli*. That is sufficient to create a distinct relational space: the food is in vessel B, not in vessel A.

The truly *lo mina* case is a wall dividing the oven. A wall is not a vessel at all. It is entirely irrelevant to the world of *keilim*. If one drives a plank through a *kli cheres* and places the *sheretz* on one side, the food on the other side is still *tamei* — the wall accomplishes nothing. Walls define separate spaces in the domain of *ohalim*, of buildings, but not in the domain of vessels. The *machloket* between type-*olah* and type-*chatat* maps onto the distinction between vessel-and-vessel; *chulin* vis-à-vis *kodshim* maps onto wall-within-vessel. The principle is intact.

---

## Tannur & Mechitzah

### Tannur Division

The *gemara* makes this concrete by citing a *mishna*: *tannur shechatzatzo b'nesarim* — an oven that was divided by planks, or by *biriyot* (curtains). If a *sheretz* is found in one section (*nimtza sheretz b'makom echad*), the ruling is *hakol tamei* — everything in the oven is *tamei*. A wall or partition does not create separate airspaces within a *kli*; only a separate *kli* does.

### Keiveret Case

The *mishna* then introduces the *keiveret* case. A *keiveret* is a large cylindrical vessel — its name suggests a beehive shape — that has been *pechutah u'pekukah b'kash*: it had a hole large enough to deprive it of vessel status, and that hole was stuffed with straw, a non-permanent repair. The result is that the *keiveret*, despite its vessel-like shape and enclosed interior, is not halachically a *kli*. It functions, for these purposes, as a *mechitzah* — a partition — not as a vessel. When this *keiveret* is suspended (*meshulshelet*) in the airspace of the oven, the question is whether it creates a protected inner zone. The ruling: if the *sheretz* is inside the *keiveret*, the oven is *tamei*; if the *sheretz* is in the oven and the food is inside the *keiveret*, the food is *tamei*. Since the *keiveret* is halachically not a vessel, it operates as a wall — and walls, as established, are *lo mina* in the world of *keilim* and have no separating power.

### R. Eliezer's Kal Vchomer

Rabbi Eliezer, however, disagrees and rules the food *tahor*. He advances a *kal v'chomer*: if a wall saves from *tumat hameis* — the most severe form of *tum'ah* — should it not certainly save within the more lenient domain of a *kli cheres*? The argument is compelling on its face. In the context of *ohel*, of houses and buildings, a wall is so powerful that it stops even *tumat meis* from spreading to the adjacent space. If walls can do that, why can they not divide an oven?

### Rabbis Respond

The *Rabbanan* reject the *kal v'chomer*. By *ohel* — houses — walls are the natural mechanism for defining separate spaces. It is entirely appropriate that a wall divides a house into distinct zones, and that is why it blocks *tumat meis*. But a *kli cheres* is a vessel, and the natural mechanism for defining a distinct interior space within the domain of vessels is another vessel, not a wall. *She'ein chalukin b'ohalim* — vessels are not divided by walls the way buildings are. Walls are *lo mina* vis-à-vis vessels; they are structurally irrelevant to the category and therefore have no force there.

### Both Positions

The *gemara* clarifies both positions in a precise formulation. The *Rabbanan* hold to the principle *d'lo mina lo machriv bah* — something of a different category simply has no impact — and apply it consistently: walls are not the mechanism of division for vessels, so they accomplish nothing. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, accepts the general principle in theory but is willing to deploy a *kal v'chomer* to override it. He agrees that walls are not the natural dividing mechanism for vessels, but argues that their demonstrated power against *tumat meis* is sufficient to import them into this domain by logical inference.

That imports a question. If Rabbi Eliezer uses a *kal v'chomer* to override *lo mina* in the case of walls within a *kli cheres*, why not deploy the same logic by *kodshim* and say that a thought about *chulin*, though irrelevant in principle, should still invalidate the *korban* via *kal v'chomer* — if *kodshim* can desecrate *kodshim*, surely *chulin* can? The *gemara* responds: *ata kra afkei mikal v'chomer* — a verse comes and removes us from the *kal v'chomer*. The verse in *terumah*, *v'lo yechalelu et kodshei b'nei Yisrael*, is read not only as a prohibition but as a structural statement: *chulin* simply does not have the power to *mechallel kodshim*. Only *kodshim* can desecrate *kodshim*. The verse blocks the *kal v'chomer* in that domain.

By *kli cheres*, one might similarly expect a verse to block the *kal v'chomer*. And indeed, the word *tocho* appears to be available. *Tocho* — the interior — could be read as limiting the *mechitzah*'s efficacy: only what is genuinely in a separate inner vessel is saved, not what is merely behind a wall. However, the *gemara* explains that this extra deployment of *tocho* is already occupied by a different *halacha* entirely: *ochlim shegibevam b'tit*. That case, and the *derashah* from *tocho*, is addressed in the next section.

---

## Food Wrapped

### Plaster Wrap

The word *tocho* that the *gemara* turns to in this context addresses the following scenario: food that has been encased in plaster — *ochlim shegibevam b'tit* — and brought into the airspace of a *kli cheres*. The food is entirely within the vessel's airspace, but it is wrapped and sealed. There is no separate vessel; it is simply food encased in a non-vessel covering.

### Touch vs. Air

One might have reasoned as follows: since a *kli cheres* does not transmit *tum'ah* by direct contact to the outer surface of the plaster — the plaster is not itself susceptible — perhaps the airspace mechanism also cannot reach through to the food within. *Ho'il u'venegi'ah lo metamei*, since touch does not reach the wrapped food, *be-avira nami lo metamu*, perhaps the airspace also does not defile it.

### Tocho Teaches

The *gemara* answers that the extra word *tocho* comes precisely to teach that even this food remains *tocho* — within the interior of the *kli cheres* — and is therefore *tamei*. The wrapping changes nothing. The *kli cheres* operates through airspace, not through contact, and wrapping the food in plaster does not remove it from the vessel's interior domain. It is emphatically still *tocho*. This is the purpose for which the extra *tocho* is expended — to include wrapped food — and it therefore cannot simultaneously serve to exclude *mechitzot* from saving, leaving Rabbi Eliezer's *kal v'chomer* without a scriptural counter.

---

## Shinui Kodesh

### Rav's Teaching

Rav Yosef bar Ami now presents a further contradiction. Rav has taught: a *chatat* slaughtered *leshem chatat* — even for a different kind of *chatat* than the one the owner is obligated in — is *kesherah*; slaughtered *leshem olah*, it is *pesulah*.

### Contradiction

This appears to invert the principle that has been guiding the analysis. The cases can be specified precisely. David is obligated in a *chatat* for eating *chelev*. The *kohen* slaughters it with intent for a *chatat* for eating *dam* — a different sin of the same type. That, says Rav, is valid. But if the *kohen* slaughters it with intent for an *olah*, it is invalid. Now, on the principle *d'mina machriv bah*, this is puzzling. A *chatat* for *dam* is closer to a *chatat* for *chelev* than an *olah* is. Closer proximity should mean greater destructive potential. Yet the closer change — *chatat* to a different kind of *chatat* — produces a valid offering, while the more radical change — *chatat* to *olah* — produces an invalid one.

---

## Shinui Be'alim

### Owner Change

Rav has taught a parallel rule for *shinui be'alim*: a *chatat* slaughtered *al mi shemechuyav chatat* — for someone else who is also obligated in a *chatat* — is *pesulah*; slaughtered *al mi shemechuyav olah* — for someone obligated only in an *olah* — is *kesherah*.

### Gloria vs. Dov

Two figures are introduced to clarify the cases. David has a *chatat* obligation. Gloria has no *chatat* obligation; she is donating a voluntary *olah*. Dov has a *chatat* obligation of his own. If the *kohen* performs *shechita* on David's *chatat* while thinking of Gloria — who is not in the world of *chatat* at all — it is valid. If he thinks of Dov — who is also obligated in a *chatat* — it is invalid.

### Relevance Levels

On first impression, this again seems to contradict the principle. Thinking of Gloria, who is completely outside the world of *chatat*, should be more threatening than thinking of Dov, who at least shares the same type of obligation. Yet it is the thought of Dov — the closer, more *minah* thought — that disqualifies, while the thought of Gloria, the *lo minah* thought, is harmless. This is entirely consistent with the principle. Thinking of Gloria is so irrelevant — she is not in the *parsha* of *chatat* at all — that the thought has no purchase on the act. It is like thinking about picking up one's children. It registers as nothing and the *shechita* proceeds as it should. Thinking of Dov, however, is a meaningful substitution: Dov is in the same category, is *mechuyav* in the same type of *kaparah*, and the intent to serve his obligation is a real displacement of the intent required for David.

---

## Shinui Kodesh (II)

### Precision Level

The apparent contradiction in *shinui kodesh* — why a *chatat* slaughtered for a different *chatat* is valid while one slaughtered *leshem olah* is invalid — is resolved by attention to what the Torah actually demands. The verse states *v'shachat osah l'chatat*: one must slaughter it *as a chatat*. The Torah specifies intent for a *chatat* generically — not for a particular type of *chatat*, not for the specific sin that generated the obligation. When the *kohen* slaughters David's *chatat* while thinking of a *chatat* for *dam* rather than *chelev*, he has in fact satisfied the Torah's demand. He intended a *chatat*. The specific variety is below the threshold of precision that the Torah requires.

This is not a case where proximity renders something less dangerous despite the principle. Rather, the Torah does not demand that degree of exactitude in the first place. The thought about a different kind of *chatat* is not a disqualifying thought at all — it satisfies the requirement. Only the shift to *olah* is a genuine violation of the requirement to intend a *chatat*.

---

## Shinui Be'alim (II)

### Vekipper Alav

The parallel resolution for *shinui be'alim* is drawn from a different verse. The Torah states *vekipper alav* — atonement must be effected *for him*, the specific owner. This creates an explicit demand for intent directed at the right person. The *kohen* must have in mind the correct individual. When he intends Dov rather than David, he has violated *vekipper alav* — he has directed the atoning act toward the wrong person, and both are within the world of *chatat* obligation. When he thinks of Gloria, however, the thought is so categorically irrelevant that it fails to constitute a redirection at all. Gloria is not *mechuyav kaparah* in a *chatat*, and the thought about her does not rise to the level of an alternative *vekipper alav*. It is simply noise. The act proceeds as if the thought never occurred.

---

## Rav Chaviva's Q

### Glass Vessel Q

Rav Chaviva now poses the final challenge of the daf, combining the *shinui be'alim* analysis with the *tocho* discussion. The question is elegant: Rav has ruled that slaughtering David's *chatat* while thinking of Gloria is valid, on the grounds that Gloria is *lo mina* — not in the world of *chatat* obligation — and therefore the thought is irrelevant. But if a thought about something *lo mina* is truly harmless, why does a glass vessel inside a *kli cheres* save the food? A glass vessel is equally *lav mina* relative to the *kli cheres*. If *lo mina* thoughts and entities are genuinely without impact, the glass vessel should not create a separate space; the food should still be *tamei*.

### True Distinction

The question is sharp, and Tosafot makes it sharper still. When the *gemara* earlier resolved the glass-vessel question, it answered that a glass vessel is still *minah* — it is still a *kli*, still in the world of vessels, even if not a pottery vessel. That answer worked when the comparison was between *kodshim* and *chulin*, or between a wall and a vessel. But here, the *lo mina* of Gloria vis-à-vis Dov is not like *chulin* vis-à-vis *kodshim*. It is more like the difference between an *olah* and a *chatat* — they are both *kodshim*, yet that difference suffices for the ruling. Similarly, Gloria and Dov are both human beings; the distinction is only that one is *mechuyav chatat* and the other is not. If that relatively small difference is enough for Gloria to be *lo mina* and harmless, why is the glass vessel — which differs from the *kli cheres* only in material — still considered *minah* enough to protect?

### Tocho Verses

The *gemara*'s answer draws on the multiplicity of the word *tocho* in the relevant passages. The word *tocho* appears, with its various forms, four times in the verses: *asher yipol meihem el tocho* and *kol asher be-tocho yitma*. Each appearance of *toch*/*tocho* yields two counts, producing four total. One is required to establish the basic *halacha* — that *tum'ah* operates through the interior airspace. A second serves as the basis of a *gezeira shava* establishing that not only is the food *tamei* but the vessel itself becomes *tamei*. A third teaches *tocho shel zeh ve-lo tocho shel acher* — that food inside an inner vessel is not considered inside the outer vessel's airspace. And the fourth — the apparently extra word — teaches that even a glass vessel, despite being *lav minei* a *kli cheres*, still functions to save the food within it. This extra verse is not an application of the *minah* principle but a specific *limud* that extends the saving power of inner vessels to all vessels, even non-pottery ones. The *gemara* thus affirms the principle while acknowledging that in the domain of *keilim*, the Torah has provided an additional verse to widen the category of what counts as a protecting inner vessel.

---

## Summary & Principle

### General Rule

The overarching principle that has animated the entire daf is *minah machriv, lo minah lo machriv* — closer things are more destructive, and entirely irrelevant things have no impact. This has been demonstrated consistently across the domains of *kodshim*, *gittin*, *kli cheres*, and *korbanot*: a thought or entity that belongs to the same category as the act in question has the power to displace or disqualify it; one that is categorically foreign does not register.

### Exception: Precision

The apparent exceptions are not genuine exceptions but rather applications of a complementary principle: the Torah does not always demand the maximum degree of precision. Where the Torah specifies only that one must intend a *chatat* — not the particular variety of *chatat* — the principle of *minah machriv* simply has no domain of application for intra-*chatat* distinctions. The Torah has defined the relevant category broadly, and staying within the broad category satisfies the requirement. This is not *lo mina* failing to cause harm; it is the Torah declining to recognize the distinction as halachically operative.

### Preview

Tomorrow the daf will move to address *lishmah* directly — the requirement of intent in *korbanot* and the sources from which it is derived.

---

---

# Zevachim 4

## Four Blood Services

### Mishnah Overview

The opening *mishnah* of *Masechet Zevachim* establishes the foundational principle governing the entire tractate: *kol hazvachim shenizbechu shelo lishmam kesherim ela shelo alu labaalim leshem chovah* — all sacrifices that were slaughtered not for their own sake are valid, yet they do not fulfill the obligation of the owner who brought them. This is the backdrop against which the Gemara on daf 4 operates. The task before us is to trace the textual proofs establishing that each of the four blood services must be performed *lishma* — with proper intent.

### Dimensions of Intent

The requirement of *lishma* operates along two distinct axes. The first concerns the *kodesh* of the offering — that is, the type of sacrifice. If a *kohen* sets out to bring a *korban shelamim*, the intent throughout must remain fixed on it being a *shelamim* and not drift toward some other category, such as an *olah* or a *chatat*. The second axis concerns the *ba'alei hakorban*, the owners of the sacrifice. The person for whom the offering is brought must be the one in whose name it is performed; one may not redirect the offering toward a different individual. Both dimensions of intent — *shinui kodesh* (change in the type of offering) and *shinui ba'alim* (change in the owner) — must be examined separately for each of the four services.

### Four Services

The four *avodot hadam* — the blood services — are *shechitah* (slaughter), *kabbalah* (collection of the blood), *zrikah* (sprinkling of the blood), and *holachah* (carrying the blood to the altar). Each service must be shown, through its own textual derivation, to require *lishma*. The services share certain features with one another, but each also possesses unique characteristics that prevent a simple inference from one to the others. The analysis of the *daf* proceeds through this comparison methodically, examining each service in turn for both the *kodesh* and *ba'alim* dimensions.

---

## Shechitah & Kodesh

### Vayikra 3:1 Proof

The Gemara opens with the question: *menalan d'ba'inan zvicha lishma?* — from where do we derive that the *shechitah* must be performed *lishma*, for the sake of the offering? The answer is drawn from Vayikra 3:1: *ve'im zevach shelamim korbano* — and if his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings. The verse contains what appears to be a redundancy: it might have said simply *ve'im shelamim korbano*, or alternatively *ve'im zevach korbano*. The presence of both terms — *zevach* and *shelamim* together — is the source of the *derashah*.

### Redundancy Analysis

From the double expression *zevach shelamim*, the Gemara derives *shetehei zvicha leshem hashelamim* — that the slaughtering must be performed for the sake of the *shelamim*. The word *zevach* is superfluous unless it comes to teach that the act of slaughter itself must be oriented toward the identity of the offering.

### Zevach as Name

One might object: perhaps *zevach shelamim* is simply the proper name of this category of sacrifice, just as we speak of a *korban olah* or a *chatat*. If so, there is no redundancy to analyze — the Torah is merely using the offering's full title.

### Not the Name

This objection is refuted by examining other verses. In Vayikra 7:33, the Torah writes *hamakriv et dam hashelamim* — the one who brings the blood of the *shelamim* — and in Vayikra 7:14, *hazorek et dam hashelamim* — the one who sprinkles the blood of the *shelamim*. In neither case does the Torah write *dam zevach hashelamim*. If *zevach shelamim* were truly the formal name of the offering, it would appear consistently whenever the offering is referenced. The absence of the word *zevach* in these parallel contexts demonstrates that it is not a fixed name.

### Shechitah Conclusion

Since *zevach shelamim* is not merely a title but a meaningful locution, the presence of *zevach* in the verse teaches something substantive: *shema mina shetehei zvicha leshem shelamim* — we derive from here that the *shechitah* must be performed for the sake of the *shelamim*. The first of the four blood services has been anchored in a textual proof.

---

## Kabbalah & Kodesh

### Learn from Shechitah?

Having established that *shechitah* requires *lishma*, the Gemara asks: *ve'chi teima leilaf mizvicha* — perhaps we can simply derive all the other services from *shechitah*? If slaughter must be *lishma*, surely collection, sprinkling, and carrying must be as well?

The Gemara introduces the principle that each service possesses its own unique stringencies that prevent a straightforward inference from one to another. The services are, in a sense, like a Venn diagram: they share certain features but not all, and these differences block the extension of any single derivation across the board.

### Pesach Limitation

The *shechitah* carries a special stringency that does not apply to the other services: *sheken nifsela shelo leshem ochlav bepesach* — it is disqualified in the case of the *Pesach* offering if it is not slaughtered with intent toward those who will eat it. If the person bringing the *korban Pesach* is somehow unable to eat the requisite amount — whether due to illness or any other incapacity — the offering is disqualified. This unique *chumra* of *shechitah* with regard to *Pesach* means that *shechitah* is not a neutral template from which we can simply derive the other services.

### Vayikra 7:33 Proof

A separate derivation is therefore required for *kabbalah*. The Gemara cites Vayikra 7:33: *hamakriv et dam hashelamim* — the one who brings near the blood of the *shelamim*. The verb *hamakriv*, from the root *karov* (to be near, to bring close), is understood as indicating the act of collecting the blood — *kabbalah*. From the fact that this verse specifically identifies the blood as being of the *shelamim*, the Gemara derives *shetehei kabbalah leshem shelamim* — that the collection of the blood must also be performed for the sake of the *shelamim*. In other contexts the Torah simply says *dam*, blood, without reattaching the identity of the offering; here the repetition of *shelamim* teaches that *kabbalah* must be intentional regarding the type of offering.

### Distinction Analysis

One might then ask: since we now have a verse for *kabbalah*, why not derive *shechitah* from *kabbalah* rather than the other way around? The Gemara addresses this by noting that the traffic of inference cannot simply be reversed. Each derivation is anchored in a specific textual excess, and the question of which service teaches which cannot be settled by reversing the direction of the argument. The Gemara's framing — *velichtov rachmana bakkabbalah veneilef shechita minnah* — presents this as a challenge: let the Torah have written the rule only for *kabbalah*, and we would learn *shechitah* from it. The response is *mishum deika lemeifrach* — because there is a refutation. The *kabbalah* has its own unique stringency: *sheken pesulah bezar ve'ishah* — it is disqualified if performed by a non-*kohen* or a woman. This stringency does not apply to *shechitah*, and therefore we cannot derive *shechitah* from *kabbalah* any more than we can derive *kabbalah* from *shechitah*. Each requires its own independent proof.

### Kohen Requirement

This last point warrants emphasis. While *shechitah* may be performed by virtually anyone — a *zar* (non-*kohen*), a woman, even in principle the owner of the animal — *kabbalah* is categorically restricted to a male *kohen*. This is a dimension of stringency entirely absent from *shechitah*, and it is precisely this difference that blocks the inference between them.

---

## Zrikah & Kodesh

### Learn from Others?

With *shechitah* and *kabbalah* both established, the Gemara proceeds to *zrikah*: *zrikah menalan?* — from where do we derive that the sprinkling of the blood must be *lishma*? And as before, the Gemara first considers whether we might simply derive it from the two already-established services.

### Location Distinction

The proposed derivation is rejected on familiar grounds. What is unique about *shechitah* and *kabbalah* that does not apply to *zrikah*? The Gemara notes: *mah hanni sheken te'unot tzafon* — these services are unique in that they require a specific location. For *kodshei kodashim*, *shechitah* and *kabbalah* must be performed in the northern section of the Temple courtyard. The *zrikah*, by contrast, may be performed from any position in the courtyard. This locational stringency that characterizes *shechitah* and *kabbalah* is absent from *zrikah*, and therefore we cannot extend the rule automatically.

### Vayikra 7:14 Proof

A fresh prooftext is therefore required. The Gemara finds it in Vayikra 7:14: *hazorek et dam hashelamim* — the one who sprinkles the blood of the *shelamim*. Just as with the *kabbalah* verse, the explicit attachment of *shelamim* to the act of *zrikah* teaches *shetehei zrikah leshem shelamim* — that the sprinkling must be performed with intent toward the *shelamim*.

### Death Penalty

Could we reverse the inference and derive *shechitah* and *kabbalah* from *zrikah* instead? No — because *zrikah* possesses its own unique stringency: *mah lezrikah sheken chayav aleha zar mitah* — a *zar* who performs *zrikah* is liable to death (or *karet*). This is a severity that does not attach to *shechitah* and is likewise absent from *kabbalah* in the same degree. The unique stringency of each service thus both prevents upward inference from it and justifies the need for its own independent derivation.

---

## Holachah & Kodesh

### Learn from Others?

Three services established, the Gemara turns to *holachah*, the carrying of the blood from the site of slaughter to the altar: *ashkacha kulhu holachah menalan?* — we have found sources for all the others, where do we derive *holachah*?

### Dispensability

The Gemara immediately anticipates the attempt to derive *holachah* from the other three, and preempts it: *mah lekulhu sheken avodah she-i efshar levatlah tomar beholachah she-efshar levatlah?* — what is unique about all the other services? Each of them is indispensable — the offering cannot be completed without them. *Holachah*, by contrast, is dispensable. If the *shechitah* takes place adjacent to the altar, there is nowhere to carry the blood — it is already where it needs to be. One does not perform *holachah* in such a case. An obligation that can be bypassed entirely under certain circumstances cannot automatically be assimilated to obligations that are always mandatory.

### Vayikra 1 Proof

The prooftext for *holachah* is derived from the first chapter of Vayikra, where the verb *vehikriv* — and he shall bring near — appears in the context of the *olah*. The Sages interpret *vehikriv hamizbecha* as referring to the carrying of the limbs up the *kevesh*, the ramp leading to the altar. The language of *lehakriv* — bringing close — generates the *derashah* for *holachah lishma*.

### Holachah & Kabbalah

A deeper connection emerges from the parallel usage. The same expression, *lehakriv*, is used for both *holachah* and *kabbalah* in adjacent verses: *vehikriv* refers to carrying, and *ve'hikrivu* is understood as *kabbalat hadam*. The Gemara derives from this parallel that *holachah* is linked to *kabbalah*: *ve'afik rachmana bilshon holacha lemeimra deholacha lo tafka miklal kabala* — the Torah expressed the collection of the blood using language associated with *holachah* to teach that *holachah* should not be excluded from the category of *kabbalah* in terms of the *lishma* requirement. The two are connected, and what is demanded of one is demanded of the other in this respect.

---

## Shechitah & Owner

### Owner Intent Source

Having established that all four blood services must be performed *lishma* with respect to the type of offering (*shinui kodesh*), the Gemara turns to the second dimension: the owner. *Ashkechan shinui kodesh, shinui be'alim minalan?* — we have found the sources for change-of-offering-type; from where do we derive the rules regarding change of owner?

### Todah Meat Law

Rav Pinchas brei deRav Ami cites Vayikra chapter 7: *uvasar zevach todat shelamav* — and the meat of the sacrifice of his thanksgiving peace offering. The *todah*, the thanksgiving offering, has a uniquely stringent eating restriction: it must be eaten on the day of the offering and the following night. The Gemara reads this verse as teaching two things. First, *shetehei zvicha leshem todah* — that the *shechitah* must be performed for the sake of the *todah*. Second, it raises the question: does the word *zevach* here come to teach the *shinui kodesh* requirement, or the *shinui ba'alim* requirement? Since the *shinui kodesh* requirement for *shechitah* has already been derived elsewhere, the Gemara applies the *im eino inyan* principle — if a teaching is unnecessary for one matter, apply it to another. Here, *zevach* is redirected to teach the *shinui ba'alim* requirement: the *shechitah* must be performed for the sake of the owner.

The purpose of this mechanism is worth pausing over. The *todah* offering is brought by someone in gratitude — for surviving illness, a sea voyage, imprisonment, or crossing a desert. Its meat must be eaten quickly, forcing the owner to invite others to share it, thereby publicizing his gratitude and, in turn, the *shem Hashem*. When the Torah says *zevach todat shelamav*, it is associating the act of slaughter with the identity and purpose of the owner's offering.

### Todah vs Shelamim

This leads to a teaching of Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, cited from a *beraita*: *todah she-shechatah le-shem shelamim, kesherah. Shelamim she-shechatan le-shem todah, pesulah.* A *todah* slaughtered with the intent of a *shelamim* is valid; a *shelamim* slaughtered with the intent of a *todah* is disqualified. The asymmetry is explained: *todah keruyah shelamim ve-ein shelamim keruyim todah* — a *todah* may be called a *shelamim*, but a *shelamim* may not be called a *todah*. The *todah* is a subspecies of *shelamim*, so directing it toward the broader category is permissible. The reverse, however, takes the *shelamim* outside its own category and into a more specific one it has not been designated for — and that disqualifies it. The relationship is one-directional, like a set and its subset.

### Zevach Teaches Both

A further nuance: the word *zevach* in this verse is also needed to extend the time restriction of the *todah* to other offerings, such as the *chatat* and *asham*. One might therefore argue that the word is already occupied and cannot be reassigned to teach *shinui ba'alim*. The Gemara responds that if the verse had wanted only to teach the eating restriction, it could have written *uvasar todat shelamav zevach* — placing *zevach* differently. Since it is written as *uvasar zevach todat shelamav*, the term *zevach* here carries multiple teachings. *Mah zevach? Shema mina tarti* — what does *zevach* teach? We derive two conclusions from it: both the *todah*'s extended rules and the requirement of *lishma* with regard to the owner.

---

## Owner Intent Others

### Learn All from Shechitah?

The Gemara now replicates the same analytical structure used for *shinui kodesh*, this time for *shinui ba'alim*. We have established that *shechitah* must be performed for the sake of the owner. Can we derive the same requirement for all four services from *shechitah* alone?

### Pesach Limitation

The answer is no, for the same reason encountered before: *mah lizevichah sheken posel shelo lishmo ochlim uvapesach* — the *shechitah* is uniquely stringent in the case of *Pesach*, where slaughtering with intent toward those who will eat it is critical. If the person who is to eat the *Pesach* is unable to eat the requisite amount at the time of *shechitah* — for instance, if the owner becomes *tamei* between the time of slaughter and the time of *zrikah* — the offering may be disqualified. This *chumra* is particular to *shechitah* and does not map onto the other services. Therefore *shechitah* cannot serve as a universal template for *shinui ba'alim* either.

### Four Differences

The Gemara then identifies four ways in which *shinui kodesh* (change of offering type) differs from *shinui ba'alim* (change of owner), each of which independently blocks the inference from one to the other: first, *sheken psulah begufah* — the *shinui kodesh* disqualifies the offering itself; second, *v'yeshno b'arba avodot* — the *shinui kodesh* applies to all four services; third, *v'yeshno l'achar mitah* — the *shinui kodesh* requirement persists even after the death of the owner; and fourth, *v'yeshno b'tzibbur k'veyachid* — the *shinui kodesh* applies equally to communal and individual offerings.

### Communal vs Individual

The fourth distinction bears elaboration. For communal offerings, the concept of an individual owner does not apply in the same way — the *tzibbur* as a whole is the owner. The *shinui ba'alim* concern is therefore relevant primarily to individual offerings and does not extend naturally to communal ones. The *shinui kodesh* requirement, however, governs all offerings regardless of whether they are individual or communal. This asymmetry is itself a reason we cannot derive *ba'alim* rules from *kodesh* rules.

### Animal vs Thought

The first distinction is elaborated further. When one asks whether *shinui ba'alim* disqualifies the animal itself — *psulah begufah* — or whether it operates only as a matter of thought, the Gemara notes: *machshava be'alma* — it is a matter of thought alone. The *shinui kodesh* also begins as a thought; however, once one entertains the wrong intent, the disqualification attaches to the animal itself. *Kevan d'achshava psala* — once the wrong thought arises, the offering is disqualified through that thought. The same logic applies to *shinui ba'alim*: once the intent is directed toward the wrong person, the disqualification is effected by thought. In this respect the two are more similar than they initially appear, which is why the Gemara acknowledges that this distinction may not be fully precise.

### Zrikah Primacy

The second distinction — that *shinui ba'alim* applies to *zrikah* specifically — reflects the centrality of *zrikah* in the sacrificial process as the act through which atonement is principally achieved. The *zrikah* is the culminating moment of the blood service, and the owner's intent at that stage is paramount. The rules of *shinui ba'alim* are therefore anchored in *zrikah* in a way that does not parallel the broader spread of *shinui kodesh* across all four services.

### After Death

The third distinction concerns what happens after the owner's death. The Gemara notes that *shinui kodesh* — the disqualification arising from performing the offering for the wrong type — continues to be relevant even posthumously, whereas *shinui ba'alim* is tied to the living owner. The Gemara cites Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi in connection with the verse *venirtza lo lekhaper alav*: the word *lo* — for him — is apparently superfluous, since the verse could have simply said the offering is accepted to atone. This extra word teaches *velo al chavero* — for him and not for another. The verse requires that the offering be performed for the benefit of its designated owner and not redirected to someone else.

A *beraita* further elaborates: Rabbi Shimon teaches that whoever bears responsibility for the offering — *et she'alav hayav be'achrayuto* — is obligated in its accountability, but whoever does not bear that responsibility is not. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi explains the logic: once a person says *alai* — this is upon me — it is considered as if the offering is loaded upon his shoulders. He carries it with him as an obligation until he discharges it through the actual sacrifice. Rav Ashi connects this specifically to the *zrikah*, deriving from *mi-venirtza lo lekhaper* that the *zrikah* must be performed for the sake of the specific owner — the extra *lo* excludes performance on behalf of another.

---

## Nazir Ram Proof

### Kabbalah Owner Source

The Gemara now returns to the structural question: *ashkachan zvicha u'zerika, kabbalah mina lan?* — we have found prooftexts for *shechitah* and *zrikah* with respect to *shinui ba'alim*, but where do we derive the same requirement for *kabbalah*?

The same reflexive challenge is posed: can we simply derive *kabbalah* from *shechitah* and *zrikah*? The answer is no — *mah le-zvicha u'zerika, sheken avodah she-chayavim alei b'choutz* — *shechitah* and *zrikah* are unique in that performing them outside the Temple carries the punishment of *karet*. The *kabbalah* does not carry this penalty for performance *chutz limkomo*, and therefore the inference cannot be made.

### Nazir Offering

Rav Ashi therefore seeks a different derivation. He points to the *eil Nazir* — the ram of the *Nazir* — whose offering is described in *Parshat Nasso*: *ve-et ha-ayil ya'aseh zevach shelamim* — and the ram he shall make into a sacrifice of peace offerings. From this verse Rav Ashi derives *she-tehei asiyato leshem shelamim* — that the performance of this sacrifice must be for the sake of the *shelamim*. Since the *shinui kodesh* requirement has already been established from other sources, this verse is superfluous on that count — and by the principle of *im eino inyan*, it is redirected to teach *shinui ba'alim*.

### Klal U'Prat

Rav Acha bar Abba then challenges Rava with a pointed objection rooted in the hermeneutical principle of *klal u'prat* — generalization and detail. The verse reads *ya'aseh zevach shelamim*. The word *ya'aseh* — he shall make/perform — is a general term; *zevach* is the specific detail. By the rule of *klal u'prat*, when a generalization is followed by a particularization, the law encompasses only what is specified in the detail. Here, *zevach* specifies *shechitah*. If so, the derivation would teach only that *shechitah* of the *Nazir's* ram must be *lishma* with respect to the owner — *zvicha in, midei achrina lo* — slaughter yes, nothing else no. The other services would remain unaddressed.

### Incomplete Generalization

One might respond that the order could be rearranged: had the verse written *ya'aseh shelamim zevach*, then *shelamim* would serve as the *klal* and *zevach* as the *prat*, and the derivation would function differently. But the verse as it stands reads *ya'aseh zevach shelamim* — and in this order, *zevach* interrupts before *shelamim* has been fully articulated. This renders the putative *klal* (*ya'aseh*) incomplete — *klal she'eino malei*. And the principle is: *kol klal she'eino malei, ein danim oto biklal u'prat* — a generalization that is not fully formed cannot serve as the basis for the *klal u'prat* interpretive method. Whether this ultimately resolves or merely displaces the difficulty — and how the Gemara eventually establishes the *ba'alim* requirement for *kabbalah* on firm ground — is where the *daf* breaks off, to be taken up in the continuation.

---

---

# Zevachim 5

## Lishmah Requirement

### Shelamim Lishmah Review

We pick up in the middle of the previous discussion, at the point where the *Tosafot* of *shkulin heim* appears on 4b, a few lines down from which we find the words *Ravina amar*. The discussion until now has established that one is required *lechatchila* to perform the *avodot* of a *korban* with *lishmah* — that is, for the proper sake of the offering — and that this requirement applies to all four primary *avodot*. The foundational case was *zevach shelamim*: the *zevichah* must be *l'sheim shelamim*, for the sake of it being a *shelamim*. We then sought to expand this to the other *avodot*, and further, to show that the *avodah* must be performed *l'sheim be'alim* — for the sake of the owners.

The primary *pasuk* establishing the requirement of *l'sheim be'alim* was *ve-nirtzah lo l'chaper alav*. The word *l'chaper* refers to the blood, and specifically to the *zerikat hadam*, while *alav* refers to the owner. It is important to keep in mind that the requirement of *l'sheim be'alim* is ultimately rooted in the *zerikah*. Even when we speak of the other *avodot* needing to be performed for the sake of the owner, what we mean is that at the time of *shechita*, one must have in mind on whose behalf the *zerikah* will ultimately be performed. If someone performs the *shechitah* without thinking at all about who the *zerikah* will be done for, that is not a problem. The *be'alim* requirement is intrinsically about the *zerikat hadam*; the other *avodot* can be invalidated only if one actively intends the *zerikah* for the wrong owner. *Sitmah* — the default, implicit state — is sufficient for *shechitah*, *kabbalah*, and *holacha* with respect to *be'alim*.

### Four Avodot Lishmah

The *Gemara* now turns to establishing that all four *avodot* must be performed *lishmah*. One *pasuk* available for this purpose is *es ha-ayil ya'aseh zevach shelamim l'Hashem*. The word *zevach* refers to *zevicha* — *shechitah* — and we would wish to expand the *lishmah* requirement from *shechitah* to the remaining *avodot*. However, reading *ya'aseh* as a *klal*, *zevach* as a *prat*, and *l'Hashem* as another *klal* raised the possibility of applying *klal u-prat u-klal*, which would allow expansion beyond the *prat* to other similar *avodot*.

### Zerika as Root

Before proceeding to Ravina's answer, a conceptual point warrants emphasis. The *lishmah* requirement as it relates to *be'alim* is specifically anchored in the *zerikah*. The *pasuk* of *ve-nirtzah lo l'chaper alav* — *l'chaper* meaning the blood, *alav* meaning the owner — fixes the *be'alim* consideration precisely at the moment of *zerikat hadam*. This is why, even as the *Gemara* extends the *lishmah* requirement to cover all four *avodot*, the conceptual center of gravity remains the *zerikah*.

### Ravina Klal Prat Klal

Ravina offers an answer to how the *lishmah* requirement is extended beyond *shechitah* alone. He reads *ya'aseh zevach shelamim l'Hashem* as a *klal u-prat u-klal*: *ya'aseh* is the first *klal* — any type of *avodah* — *zevach* is the *prat* — specifically *zevicha* — and *l'Hashem* returns as a second *klal*, again encompassing any *avodah* performed for Hashem. By the rules of *klal u-prat u-klal*, we expand beyond the *prat* to include other similar *avodot*, thereby requiring *lishmah* across all of them.

### Rav Achai Objection

Rav Achai mi-Difti raises an objection to Ravina's reading. He argues that the two *klalim* in this *pasuk* are not equivalent — *lo dami klala kama l'klala basra* — and that this asymmetry disqualifies a straightforward *klal u-prat u-klal* derivation. The first *klal*, *ya'aseh*, refers specifically to the *avodot* that constitute the act of bringing a *korban* — the four classic *avodot* of *shechitah*, *kabbalah*, *holacha*, and *zerikah*. This is exactly where we want to arrive. But the second *klal*, *l'Hashem*, is broader: it encompasses *kulo l'Hashem* — anything done in the service of the *korban* that is *l'Hashem* — which would include even *shefichat shirayim* (pouring the remainder of the blood on the base of the *mizbe'ach*) and *haktarat emurim* (burning the *emurim* on the *mizbe'ach*). These occur after the *korban* is already complete and valid. Because the two *klalim* are not coextensive — the first encompasses the four defining *avodot* while the second is far broader — this does not constitute a proper *klal u-prat u-klal*.

### Rabbi Yishmael Method

The *Gemara* responds that *hai tanna d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* — this *tanna* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael — applies *klal u-prat* in precisely this manner. Rabbi Yishmael's school is somewhat more flexible in its hermeneutical approach (*dibra Torah k'lashon bnei adam*), and it will accept a *klal u-prat u-klal* structure even where the second *klal* is broader than the first. The operative requirement remains that whatever is included must be similar to the *prat* in the middle: *mah haprat meforash avodah u-veinan lishmah* — the *prat* is *zevach*, which is *shechitah*, an *avodah* that must be done *lishmah* (here meaning *l'sheim be'alim*) — *af kol avodah beinan lishmah*, all *avodot* must similarly be *lishmah*.

### Expansion Principles

However, the *Gemara* presses further. Even granting *klal u-prat u-klal* via Rabbi Yishmael's school, the expansion from *shechitah* need not encompass all four *avodot*. The principle of *k'ein haprat* — similarity to the *prat* — could be applied in more than one direction, each pointing to a different subset of *avodot*.

On one reading, the defining characteristic of *shechitah* is that it is among the *avodot* for which one is liable if performed outside the *Beit HaMikdash* — the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*. Expanding *lishmah* to all *avodot* similarly prohibited outside the *Beit HaMikdash* would include *shechitah* and *zerikah*, but not *kabbalah* or *holacha*.

On another reading, the defining characteristic of *shechitah* is that it sometimes must be performed at the *tzafun* (northern) side of the *mizbe'ach*, and it also applies in the case of the *chatat ha-penimiyot* — the inner *chatat* whose blood is applied with a finger to the inner altar. Expanding *lishmah* to all *avodot* sharing these characteristics would include *shechitah* and *kabbalah* (since the blood of animals slaughtered at the *tzafun* is also caught at the *tzafun*, and both apply to *chatat ha-penimiyot*), but would exclude *zerikah* — which is not confined to the *tzafun* and does not apply to *chatat ha-penimiyot*, whose blood is placed with a finger rather than sprinkled.

### Shkulim Hem Principle

The *Gemara*'s resolution is elegant.
