Since both modes of expansion are equally valid — *ika lemaimar hachi ve'ika lemaimar hachi* — and there is no principled reason to prefer one over the other, the *Gemara* invokes the principle of *shkulim hem*: they are equivalent. When two directions of expansion are equally justified and neither can be ruled out, both are included. *Yavo'u shneihem* — both expansions apply. The first expansion covers *shechitah* and *zerikah*; the second covers *shechitah* and *kabbalah*. Together, they encompass *shechitah*, *kabbalah*, and *zerikah*. *Holacha* is subsumed under *kabbalah*, as it is consistently treated together with *kabbalah* in such derivations. Thus all four *avodot* are now covered.

An alternative formulation — *chada v'chada teki b'milsa*, each one becomes established in its own domain — conveys the same principle in different language: since you can go either way, each expansion is effectuated, and both are applied simultaneously.

There is an additional approach: *zrikah mid'Rav Ashi nafka* — we already know *zerikah* from the *pasuk* of *ve-nirtzah lo l'chaper alav*, which applies specifically to *zerikah l'sheim be'alim*. Since *zerikah* is already covered, the *klal u-prat u-klal* expansion is naturally directed toward *kabbalah*, and *holacha* follows along with *kabbalah*. The combination of these *pesukim* — *ve-nirtzah lo l'chaper alav* for *zerikah*, *ya'aseh zevach shelamim* for *shechitah*, and the *klal u-prat u-klal* for *kabbalah* and *holacha* — thus yields the requirement of *lishmah l'sheim be'alim* for all four *avodot*.

### Zot HaTorah Expansion

Having established the *lishmah* requirement for *shelamim*, the *Gemara* confronts the question of how to extend it to all other *korbanot*. One might suggest learning from *eil nazir*, but that is readily countered: *eil nazir* has special stringency because it is accompanied by other *korbanot* — an *olah* and a *chatat* — and so it cannot serve as a general source.

The *Gemara* then addresses why the word *shelamim* is written in the plural: *mai shelamim — lerabos kol hashelamim*, to include all *shelamim*. But we still need to extend the requirement to *korbanot* other than *shelamim* entirely. One might suggest learning from *shelamim* directly, but *shelamim* are in some respects the most demanding of *korbanot* — they require *semikhah*, *nesachim*, and *tenufah* of the *chazeh* and *shok* — and so their requirements cannot simply be extended outward. The fact that *shelamim* have these unique additional components means one might attribute the *lishmah* requirement specifically to those unique features.

The *Gemara* therefore turns to the *pasuk* of *zot hatorah la-olah v'la-minchah v'la-chatat v'la-asham v'la-miluim u-l'zevach ha-shelamim* — "This is the law of the *olah*, the *minchah*, the *chatat*, the *asham*, the *miluim*, and the *zevach shelamim*." This *pasuk* links all *korbanot* to *shelamim* via *hekesh*. Since *shelamim* appears last in the list, the *pasuk* is read as taking *shelamim* and expanding its requirements — including *bein shinuy kodesh bein shinuy be'alim* — to all the others: *af kol bein shinuy kodesh bein shinuy be'alim ba'inan lishmah*.

We now have three *pesukim* working together. The *shelamim* passages establish the *lishmah* and *l'sheim be'alim* requirements. *Zot hatorah* extends these requirements to all *korbanot*. And *motza sefatecha* — which will be developed shortly — establishes what happens when these requirements are not met.

---

## Shelo Lishmah Status

### Should It Be Invalid?

Having established that all *korbanot* require *lishmah*, the *Gemara* now asks: what is the status of a *korban* performed *shelo lishmah*? The *Mishnah* teaches that, with the exception of a *chatat* and a *pesach*, a *korban* slaughtered *shelo lishmah* is *kasher* — valid — but does not fulfill the obligation of the owners. The *Gemara* presses: *ema, heicha de-shachatei shelo lishmah lifselu* — why should a *korban* performed *shelo lishmah* not simply be rendered invalid entirely?

### Meakev Requirements

An important principle governs this question. By ordinary *mitzvot*, if the *Torah* establishes a requirement, its absence invalidates the act. A *lulav* that lacks *hadar* is *pasul*; an *esrog* that does not meet the criteria is *pasul*. One might assume the same applies throughout *halachah*. But in the domain of *kodshim*, a distinct rule applies: a requirement does not automatically render the *korban* invalid if unfulfilled unless the *Torah* repeats the requirement twice — *shanah alav ha-katuv le'akeiv*. Since there are so many requirements in the *avodah*, the default presumption is that not all of them are *me'akeiv*, and only explicit repetition signals that the absence of a given requirement invalidates the *korban*. *Tosafot* raises this question explicitly: given this principle, why does the *Gemara* assume that *shelo lishmah* should be *pasul* at all? The answer *Tosafot* offers is that by the case of *shinuy kodesh* — performing the *avodah* for a different type of *korban* — there were multiple *pesukim*, which is sufficient to raise the question of *pesul*.

### Motza Sefatecha Pasuk

The *Gemara* cites the *pasuk* of *motza sefatecha tishmor ve-asita ka-asher nadarta l'Hashem Elokecha nedavah* — "What comes forth from your lips you shall observe and do, as you vowed to Hashem your God, a *nedavah*." The surface reading is puzzling: if one made a *neder*, why does the *pasuk* call it a *nedavah*?

The *Gemara* resolves this by reading the *pasuk* as follows: *im ka-asher nadarta asita* — if you did it exactly as you vowed, performing all the *avodot* for the sake of the designated *korban* and its owners — *yehei neder*, it counts as a *neder* and satisfies your personal obligation. But *v'im lav* — if something went wrong, if the *avodah* was not performed for the proper sake — *yehei nedavah*: it still stands as a valid *korban*, functioning like a *nedavah* — a freewill offering — but it does not count as a *neder*. That is, it does not fulfill the owner's personal obligation.

A *neder* is an acceptance of personal obligation; a *nedavah* is the sanctification of an animal without a binding personal obligation. The *pasuk* teaches that when the *avodah* is not performed correctly — when it is *shelo lishmah* in some respect — the *korban* exists in an intermediate state: it is *kasher* as a *korban*, but it does not discharge the owner's obligation. It functions *k'nedavah* rather than *k'neder*.

### Three Pesukim Combined

The *Gemara* makes explicit that all three *pesukim* are necessary and each contributes something distinct. *Ve-itzterich motza sefatecha* — you need the *pasuk* of *motza sefatecha* to tell you what happens when the *avodah* is not done correctly, namely that the *korban* enters this intermediate state. *Ve-itzterich zot hatorah* — you need *zot hatorah* to tell you which requirements, when violated, trigger this intermediate state: it was *zot hatorah* that taught that all the *lishmah* requirements applying to *shelamim* extend to all *korbanot*. Had we only the *motza sefatecha pasuk*, we would not know which specific deficiencies it addresses. And had we only *zot hatorah*, we would have concluded that any violation of *lishmah* renders the *korban* invalid entirely, without the *motza sefatecha* *pasuk* to inform us that it results instead in this middle status of *kasher* but not *olu l'be'alim*.

The *Gemara* then raises a question about the *chatat*: *zot hatorah* includes the *chatat* in its list, yet the *Mishnah* teaches that a *chatat* performed *shelo lishmah* is invalid altogether. The resolution is that the special status of the *chatat* — that *shelo lishmah* renders it fully *pasul* — is derived from a different *pasuk*, as the *Gemara* will develop. For purposes of the present derivation from *zot hatorah*, that *pasuk* establishes the *lishmah* requirement across all *korbanot lechatchila*; the *chatat*'s unique rule of *pesul bedi'avad* comes from elsewhere.

---

## Asham Ownership Problem

### Reish Lakish Throws Self…

The *Gemara* now pivots from the *pesukim* to a fundamental conceptual question. The intermediate status — *kasher* but not working for the owners — is established textually, but can it be sustained conceptually? The *Gemara* introduces this question with a vivid image: *rami Reish Lakish al me'ohi bei midrasha u-makshi* — Reish Lakish threw himself on his stomach on the floor of the *beit midrash* and posed this question. The verb *rami* ordinarily introduces a contradiction between two Tannaitic sources; here it seems to capture instead a logical tension that Reish Lakish found so acute that it could not be contained in ordinary discourse.

His question: *im kesherim heim yirtzu* — if these *korbanot* are *kasher*, they should work for the owners. *Ve-im einam mirtzim lama ba'im* — and if they are not going to work for the owners, why should they be brought at all? The intermediate status seems logically unstable. It should be all or nothing: either a *korban* is fully valid and counts for the owner, or it is invalid.

### Olah After Death Example

Rabbi Elazar responds to Reish Lakish: *matzinu be-va le-achar misa she-hein kesherim ve-ein mirtzim* — we already find cases where a *korban* is valid but does not work for its owners, namely a *korban* that is brought after the owner's death. The *Gemara* cites a *Mishnah*: *ha-isha she-hevia chatasa u-mesa* — a woman who brought her *chatat* (associated with the *korban* brought after childbirth, the subject of *parashat Tazria*) and then died. *Yaviu yorshim olasah* — her heirs should bring her *olah*, if she had already designated it. An *olah* can be brought after the owner's death; a *chatat* cannot. This is the principle of *chatat le-achar misa*: a *chatat* designated by a deceased person is left to die, while an *olah* or *shelamim* that was sanctified is brought even after the owner's death. In that case, the *korban* is *kasher* — its blood is sprinkled, its meat or *emurim* may be consumed or burned as appropriate — yet there is no living owner for it to work for.

### Asham Not After Death

Reish Lakish is not satisfied. *Modeh ani lach be-olah de-asya le-achar misa* — he concedes the point regarding an *olah* or *shelamim* that comes after the owner's death. These are *korbanot* that can arise from a *nedavah*, a freewill offering, and are by their nature less tightly bound to the personal standing of the owner. It is intuitive, if not simple, that such *korbanot* can function without a living owner. But the *asham* is categorically different. An *asham* does not come after death. If a person designated an *asham* and died, the *asham* is not brought. It is entirely defined by its connection to a living obligated owner — it is a *korban* of atonement, rooted in a specific *chet* and a specific person. The phenomenon of an *olah* operating without an owner cannot serve as a precedent for an *asham*, because an *asham* never exists without its owner in any recognized form. The conceptual problem — how can an *asham* be *kasher* and yet be severed from its owner — remains unresolved.

Rabbi Elazar points out that Reish Lakish's position is exactly that of Rabbi Eliezer in the *Mishnah*, who rules that an *asham* performed *shelo lishmah* is invalid. But Reish Lakish dismisses this: *ka-amina ana mishnah shelemah* — he is troubled by the *stam Mishnah*, the accepted *halachah* that rejects Rabbi Eliezer's view and holds that the *asham* is *kasher* but does not count for the owner. The fact that a dissenting view shares his intuition does not resolve his question about the accepted *halachah*.

### Reish Lakish's Own Solut…

Finding no satisfactory answer from others, Reish Lakish declares *eftecha ana pitcha lenafshai* — he will open the door himself. He derives the intermediate status from the *pasuk* of *motza sefatecha*: *im ka-asher nadarta l'Hashem Elokecha nedavah* — if it was done as you vowed, it is a *neder*; if not, it stands as a *nedavah*. This *pasuk* establishes that a *korban* which was initiated as a personal obligation but whose *avodah* was not performed correctly can exist in a middle state, functioning *k'nedavah* — as a freewill offering not tethered to the owner's obligation.

A notable point about the chronology of this *sugya*: Rashi observes that the attribution of this reading of *motza sefatecha* to Reish Lakish suggests that it was Reish Lakish himself who first worked out this derivation. The *Gemara* had already cited the *pasuk* twice earlier in the *sugya* in the voice of the *stam*, without attribution — likely because once Reish Lakish's derivation became known, the *Gemara* incorporated it into the earlier discussions. When we read the earlier citations and wonder why Reish Lakish did not simply recall them, the answer is that he was the one who first found the *pasuk*; the earlier appearances are the *Gemara*'s retroactive integration of his contribution.

---

## Chatat Shelo Lishmah

### Gemara Challenges Soluti…

A group of Amoraim — Rav Zeira, Rav Yitzchak bar Abba, and Abaye — are sitting together and discussing Reish Lakish's dramatic question and the *motza sefatecha* solution he offered. They raise a challenge: *eima haba b'neder u-vindavah laysu ve-lo yirtzu, asham lo laysi klal* — the *pasuk* of *motza sefatecha* speaks the language of *neder* and *nedavah*, which is the conceptual world of *olah* and *shelamim*, *korbanot* that can originate from either a personal vow or a freewill designation. In that world, it is intelligible that something can shift from the status of a *neder* to that of a *nedavah* — it remains a *korban* but its tether to the owner's personal obligation is loosened. But an *asham* does not exist in that world. An *asham* arises only from a Torah-imposed obligation; it is never a *nedavah*. You cannot apply a *pasuk* about *neder* and *nedavah* to the *asham* and thereby establish a middle state for it. Reish Lakish's problem, they argue, remains unsolved.

### Otah Lechatas Source

Abaye offers an answer. He says that Reish Lakish did not ultimately derive the *asham*'s middle status from *motza sefatecha* alone. Rather, his foundation was a different *pasuk*: *ve-shachat osah le-chatat* — "and he shall slaughter *it* as a *chatat*." The word *osah* — *it* — introduces a limiting principle. *Osah lishmah kesherah, shelo lishmah pesulah* — doing *it* for the sake of a *chatat* renders it *kasher*; not doing it for the sake of a *chatat* renders it *pasul*. The word *osah* signals that this harsher consequence — invalidity *bedi'avad* when performed *shelo lishmah* — is unique to the *chatat*.

### Chatat Distinction

The derivation proceeds: *osah* specifies that the *chatat*'s demand that *lishmah* be *me'akeiv bedi'avad* is unique to the *chatat* alone. *She'ar kodashim*, all other *kodashim* — including the *asham* — are therefore *kasher bedi'avad* even if performed *shelo lishmah*. We now know from *otah le-chatat* that the *asham* is *kasher* when done *shelo lishmah*. The remaining question is whether being *kasher* means it also counts for the owner. For this, *motza sefatecha* becomes relevant: the *pasuk* teaches that even when a *korban* is *kasher*, it does not fulfill the owner's obligation if the *avodah* was not performed correctly — *yehei nedavah* rather than *yehei neder*. Together, *otah le-chatat* tells us the *asham* is *kasher*, and *motza sefatecha* tells us it does not count for the owner. The two *pesukim* together establish the *asham*'s intermediate status.

---

## Asham Owner Counting

### Asham Meratze Question

The *Gemara* now poses a further challenge. Even accepting that an *asham* performed *shelo lishmah* is *kasher*, perhaps it should be fully *meratze* — perhaps it should count entirely for the owner. After all, the *asham* is so tightly bound to the person who brought it, so thoroughly defined by its connection to a specific owner and a specific *chet*, that if it is *kasher* at all, it ought to count for the owner completely. The logic that *motza sefatecha* places it in an intermediate state may work for *olah* and *shelamim*, where the connection to the owner is looser, but perhaps for an *asham*, if it is valid, it must be *meratze*.

### Kal VaChomer Olah

Abaye offers a *kal va-chomer* to counter this. *U-mah olah she-einah mechaperet einah mirtzah* — an *olah* does not normally serve the function of *kaparah*, atonement, and yet when performed *shelo lishmah* it is not *meratze*, does not count for the owner. *Asham she-mechaper* — an *asham*, whose very function is *kaparah* — *eino din she-eino mirtzah* — is it not all the more so that it should not be *meratze* when performed *shelo lishmah*?

The logic here requires unpacking. The argument is not that the *asham* is weaker than the *olah* and therefore a *kal va-chomer* applies in the usual direction of strength to weakness. Rather, the point is precisely about the direct connection between purpose and person: an *olah* has no inherent *kaparah* function in the ordinary sense — it is a gift *korban*, an ascent offering, not primarily a means of atonement. And even so, when performed *shelo lishmah*, it does not count for the owner. An *asham*, by contrast, is entirely defined by its *kaparah* function — it is the most personally connected *korban* to the owner's obligation. If even the *olah*, with its looser connection to the owner, does not count when performed *shelo lishmah*, then the *asham*, so intimately bound to the owner's personal sin and atonement, certainly should not count when performed *shelo lishmah*. The tightness of the connection to the owner works against the *asham* being *meratze*, not in its favor.

### Comparing Korbanot

The *Gemara* challenges the *kal va-chomer* step by step. Perhaps an *olah* is distinctive because it is *kalil* — entirely burned on the *mizbe'ach* — and this unique quality, not the absence of *kaparah* function, is what explains why it is not *meratze shelo lishmah*. In that case, we cannot extend the rule to an *asham*, which is not *kalil*. The *Gemara* counters: *shelamim yochiachu* — a *shelamim* is also not *meratze* when performed *shelo lishmah*, and a *shelamim* is certainly not *kalil*. But then the *Gemara* objects to the *shelamim* side of the argument: *mah le-shelamim she-kein te'unim nesachim tenufah va-chazeh va-shok* — *shelamim* have greater weight due to their requirement of *nesachim*, *tenufah*, and the *chazeh va-shok*; perhaps these additional components explain why the rule applies to *shelamim* and does not extend to an *asham*.

The back-and-forth continues: *olah tochiah* — an *olah* also lacks *nesachim*, *tenufah*, and *chazeh va-shok*, and yet the rule applies to it. *Ve-chazar ha-din* — the argument goes in circles. Each *korban* has unique characteristics that could potentially explain the rule applying to it specifically, and none of those unique characteristics is shared by all the others.

### Common Denominator

The *Gemara* resolves this through the principle of *tzad ha-shaveh*: *lo rei zeh ke-rei zeh ve-lo rei zeh ke-rei zeh — hatzad ha-shaveh she-bahen she-hein kodshim ve-shachtan shelo lishmah kesherim ve-einam mirtzim*. The distinctive characteristics of each *korban* are not identical to those of the others. But the common denominator across all of them — *olah*, *shelamim*, and *todah* — is that they are all *kodshim*, and when slaughtered *shelo lishmah* they are *kasher* and yet not *meratze*. Through this *tzad ha-shaveh*, we include the *asham* as well: *af ani avi asham she-hu kodesh ve-shachto shelo lishmo kasher ve-eino mirtze*. The *asham* is *kodesh*, and when slaughtered *shelo lishmah* it is *kasher* and not *meratze*.

The *Gemara* raises one more objection. The common denominator of *olah*, *shelamim*, and *todah* is that they all can come as a *neder* or a *nedavah*, and they can exist even without the same tight tether to a living obligated owner. Perhaps it is precisely this quality — *she-hein ba'in b'neder u-vindavah* — that explains why the rule of *kasher ve-eino mirtze* applies to them, and not some general principle applicable to all *korbanot*. This returns us to the conceptual difficulty that has been present throughout: the *asham* is different in kind.

---

## Zot HaTorah Asham

### Rava's Zot HaTorah

At this point Rava provides the definitive answer: *ello amar Rava zot hatorah* — Rava derives the *asham*'s intermediate status from *zot hatorah*. The *pasuk* of *zot hatorah* equates all *korbanot* to *shelamim* via *hekesh*: just as *shelamim*, which are *kodshim* and when slaughtered *shelo lishmah* are *kasher ve-einam mirtzim*, so too all *korbanot* listed in that *pasuk* — including the *asham* — share the same rule. *Hekisho ha-katuv l'shelamim*: the *Torah* connected them all to *shelamim*, and *shelamim* have this intermediate status when performed *shelo lishmah*.

### Not Connected to Chatat

One might object: *mai chazis de-akish l'shelamim* — why connect the *asham* to *shelamim* and conclude it has this intermediate status? Perhaps instead we should connect the *asham* to the *chatat*, which is also listed in *zot hatorah*, and conclude that an *asham* performed *shelo lishmah* is fully invalid. If the *chatat* is *pasul* when performed *shelo lishmah*, and if the *asham* is comparable to the *chatat* in its tightness of connection to the owner, perhaps the *asham* should share the *chatat*'s stringency.

### Otah Exclusion

The *Gemara* answers: *ha mi'eit rachmana osah* — the word *osah* in the *pasuk* of *ve-shachat osah le-chatat* specifically and exclusively limits the harsher rule — invalidity *bedi'avad* — to the *chatat* alone. We cannot connect the *asham* to the *chatat*'s harsher rule because the *Torah* explicitly excluded everything other than the *chatat* from that rule via *osah*. With the *chatat* ruled out as a model, we must connect the *asham* to *shelamim* — and *shelamim* teach us the intermediate state of *kasher ve-eino mirtze*. The *chatat*'s inclusion in *zot hatorah* serves a different purpose: it establishes the *lechatchila* requirement of *lishmah* for the *chatat* along with all other *korbanot*. The *bedi'avad* consequence — *pesul* — comes from *otah*, not from *zot hatorah*.

---

## Asham Without Owner

### Three Rabbis Discussion

A second group of *Amoraim* — Rav Huna, Rav Nachman, and Rav Sheshet, who was sitting with them — reflect on the same problem that occupied Reish Lakish: *kasha lei le-Reish Lakish, asham de-lo asi le-achar misa* — Reish Lakish was troubled that the *asham* does not come *le-achar misa*, and therefore it seemed to lack any precedent for existing in a state severed from its owner. They consider what Rabbi Elazar could have said to Reish Lakish beyond citing the *olah* after death.

### Asham Reincarnated Form

Rabbi Elazar could have told Reish Lakish: *asham nami asi le-achar misa* — there is, in fact, a sense in which an *asham* does come *le-achar misa*. If a person designated an *asham* and then died, what happens to the animal? It is left to graze until it develops a *mum* (blemish), at which point its *kedushah* is transferred to money through redemption, and that money is used to purchase an *olah*, which is then offered on the *mizbe'ach*. The *asham* does not simply cease to exist. In a sense, its *kedushah* persists and is ultimately realized — in a reincarnated form, as an *olah* on the *mizbe'ach*. The *kedushah* migrates: the animal is redeemed, the money takes on the sanctity, and the *olah* purchased with that money is the final expression of the original *asham*'s consecration.

### Motaro Becomes Olah

Rav Sheshet clarifies the precise mechanics: *asham le-mai karev — le-motaro*. The *asham* itself is not offered *le-achar misa*; what is offered is its *motar* — the residual value of its *kedushah* realized through the chain of redemption and repurchase as an *olah*. One might object that the same could be said of a *chatat*: a *chatat* also has a *motar* in a very specific case — when someone designated two *chataot* as mutual guarantors (*hifrish shtei chataot le-achrayut*), was atoned for through one of them, and then died. In that unusual case, the second *chatat* can still be brought in some form. The *Gemara* responds: *chatat af al gav de-karva motara, mi'eit rachmana hu* — even though a *chatat* has a *motar* in that narrow case, the word *hu* (or *hi*, in the feminine, *hia*) in the *pasuk* about the *chatat* limits and excludes, establishing that the stringency of *pesul shelo lishmah* applies uniquely to the *chatat*. The *chatat*'s special treatment is grounded in that word, not undermined by the exceptional *motar* case.

### Precedent for Middle Sta…

This discussion provides an important conceptual foundation for the *halachah* that has been under examination throughout the *sugya*. The persistent difficulty with the *asham*'s intermediate status was this: an *asham* is so bound to its owner that it seemed impossible to conceive of it existing in a middle state — *kasher* yet not *meratze* — severed from the owner who brought it. The resolution offered here is that this is not entirely without parallel even within the world of *asham* itself. The *asham* can exist *le-achar misa* in a reincarnated form: its *kedushah* migrates to money, which becomes an *olah*. This is not a full answer to the conceptual question, but it provides a *sevara* — a rational basis — for understanding that even the *asham*, though tightly bound to a living owner, is not absolutely and unconditionally annulled when that connection is severed. The *halachah* that an *asham* performed *shelo lishmah* is *kasher ve-eino mirtze* thus gains not only textual support from *otah le-chatat* and *zot hatorah*, but also a measure of conceptual grounding from the reality that the *asham*'s *kedushah* can persist and find expression on the *mizbe'ach* even after the owner has died.

---

---

# Zevachim 6

## Asham vs. Chatas

### Reish Lakish Challenge

The daf opens in the middle of 5b, at the line beginning with the word *mosarah*. The subject is Reish Lakish's pointed observation about what seems to be a paradox: an *asham*, which is fundamentally bound up with its *ba'alim* — its owners — how can it be brought in a valid state when it is no longer connected to those owners? Specifically, the case at hand is one in which the animal was slaughtered *shelo lishmah*, not for its proper designation, and yet the *gemara* has been treating it as *kasher*. The challenge is to explain how a *korban* so intimately tied to its owners can function validly when that connection is severed.

### Asham Reincarnation

The *gemara*'s answer proceeds by way of analogy. Just as a *chatas* whose owners have died undergoes a kind of reincarnation — the money is transferred and ultimately used to purchase an *olah* — so too an *asham* whose owners have died can be similarly reincarnated and brought as an *olah*. There exists, therefore, a genuine and recognized phenomenon in which an *asham* is brought without being connected to its original owners. That is precisely what gives the *shelo lishmah* case its foothold: if an *asham* can in principle be brought entirely detached from its owners, then the fact that a *shelo lishmah asham* is brought without counting for the owners is not categorically impossible but simply an extension of a known reality.

A *chatas*, by contrast, presents greater difficulty. On the one hand, the *gemara* acknowledges that by the case of *mosarah* — where someone separated two animals as backup for each other — there is at least some theoretical analogue in which a *chatas* might be brought apart from its original purpose. So the possibility is not entirely impossible. Yet the Torah's own language — *chatas hi*, "it is a *chatas*" — places a limiting constraint: only when performed properly, in its intended manner, fully connected to the owners, does it count as a *chatas*. The *gezeiras hakasuv* forecloses any latitude. The *asham*, by contrast, has no such limiting *pasuk* — or so it seems momentarily.

### Hu Post-Emurim

At this point the *gemara* introduces a complication: the word *hu* — "it is" — does in fact appear by the *asham* as well. The verse reads *v'hiktiru hamizbeiach isheh lashem asham hu*, "they shall burn it on the altar as a fire-offering to God; it is a guilt offering." One might therefore think that the same logic applies — that *asham hu* restricts the *asham* to only its proper, owner-connected mode.

The *gemara* rejects this. The *pasuk* speaks of *asham hu* at the stage *le'achar haktaras emurim* — after the *emurim* have already been burned on the *mizbeiach*. At that late stage, there is nothing left that could possibly invalidate the *korban*; the *emurim* have already been offered. Thus the word *hu* at that juncture cannot be a limitation on *kashrus*, because by that point any defect in procedure is irrelevant. A *tanna* makes this explicit: the word *hu* by an *asham* is stated only with reference to the post-*emurim* stage, and a *shechita* of an *asham* without the *emurim* having been brought is nonetheless *kasher*. The limiting force of *hu* simply cannot be functioning as a restriction on *lishmah* when applied to a stage at which no such restriction could have any effect.

### Pasture Transition

This raises the natural follow-up: if *asham hu* is not limiting the *kashrus* of the *shechita*, what is it teaching? The *gemara* answers: it is the source for the ruling of Rav Huna in the name of Rav. When an *asham* has been *nitak l're'iyah* — put out to pasture, meaning the animal has been set aside to graze until it develops a *mum* and can be redeemed, its sanctity ultimately destined to fund an *olah* — and it is slaughtered *stam*, without explicit intent for any particular *korban*, it is valid. Since the animal's sanctity is headed toward that of an *olah*, a generic *shechita* at that transitional stage is treated as an *olah* and is *kasher*. However, if the animal has *not* yet been put out to pasture, this leniency does not apply. The word *hu* teaches that the *asham* identity has a certain stickiness; it does not simply dissolve on its own. Only once the formal transition to the *re'iyah* stage has occurred is the identity sufficiently shifted that an unspecified *shechita* can ride along with it. But a *shelo lishmah asham* is *kasher* and simply does not count for the owners — that much has been established.

---

## Heirs & Ownership

### Setup Discussion

The *gemara* now shifts to a new discussion. Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet were sitting together, with Rav Adda bar Matna also present among them, and they were analyzing Rabbi Elazar's response to Reish Lakish. Rabbi Elazar had pointed to the phenomenon of *korbanos* being brought after the owner's death — particularly *olah* and *shlamim* — as a precedent for why it should not be surprising that an *asham* can be brought in a valid state without being connected to the owners.

One might press back on behalf of Reish Lakish: granting that this phenomenon exists by *olah* and *shlamim*, why not simply argue that those too should be *mirtze* — that they should actually count on behalf of whoever brings them? If you insist that *korbanos* must be connected to someone, why not let the *yorsehim*, the heirs, receive some benefit from bringing them? What exactly is the nature of the *heir's* relationship to a *korban* they have inherited? This becomes the central question of the section.

### Yoledet Proof

Rav Adda bar Matna provides what he considers a decisive answer. Consider a *yoledet* — a woman who has given birth and incurred the obligation to bring an *olah* as part of her *tahara* process — who then dies before bringing it. Her children inherit the obligation and bring the *olah*. But the *olah* of a *yoledet* is specifically connected to childbirth. If we were to say the heirs receive some form of *kapara* or merit from bringing it, we would face an absurdity: the sons who are bringing it never gave birth. The *korban* is not an atonement for a general *mitzvat aseh* that they too might have violated; it is organically tied to a biological event that the heirs simply did not experience. Rav Adda bar Matna therefore concludes: *im hi yalda, baneha mi yaldu* — "if she gave birth, did her sons give birth?" The very impossibility of the *korban*'s purpose applying to the heirs demonstrates that there can be no assumption that the heirs receive *kapara* from it, and thus the phenomenon of a *korban* being brought without being *mirtze* for anyone is simply a settled *halacha*.

### Rav Ashi Counter

Rav Ashi, however, challenges this. Even the *olah* of a *yoledet*, he argues, carries within it a general atoning function. The *gemara* establishes elsewhere that an *olah* atones for *mitzvot aseh* — positive commandments — that one has failed to fulfill. This function belongs to the *olah* as such, regardless of the occasion for which it was brought. A *yoledet* who brings her *olah* would simultaneously achieve atonement for any *mitzvot aseh* she had neglected — that is simply what an *olah* does. If that is so, then even the sons who bring the *olah* on her behalf might gain some *kapara* for their own unfulfilled *mitzvot aseh*, since the *korban* carries that general atoning capacity regardless of whose name it is technically brought under. The argument of Rav Adda bar Matna is therefore not conclusive: even in the *yoledet* case one could in principle argue that the heirs receive secondary atonement.

### Ownership Core Q

This brings the *gemara* to the core question: do heirs actually *own* the *korban* they inherit? The suggestion that heirs might receive atonement from a *korban* implies that they must have some ownership stake — *kapara* is not something one receives from a stranger's *korban*. And if ownership is the criterion, then the question of whether heirs truly become the *ba'alim* of an inherited *korban* must be resolved before anything else can follow.

---

## Mincha-Temurah Tension

### Mincha No-Partnership

The *gemara* adduces the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan as a starting point. If a person sanctified a *mincha* and died, leaving it to his two sons, can that *mincha* be brought? The general *halacha* is that all *korbanos* may be owned and brought in partnership — *b'shutfut* — with one exception: a *mincha*. A *mincha* cannot be a *minchat shutafim*, a partnership meal-offering. The Torah's use of the word *nefesh* — "a soul" — in connection with the *mincha* is interpreted to limit it to an individual's offering, excluding any jointly-owned *mincha* from being valid. Rabbi Yochanan rules that when two sons inherit a *mincha*, it may nonetheless be brought, and it does not carry the disqualifying status of a *minchat shutafin*. The implication seems clear: the heirs do not become the owners of the *korban*. It remains, in some sense, their father's *mincha* — brought by them but not owned by them — and therefore the partnership concern simply does not apply.

### Behema Temurah Block

Yet the same Rabbi Yochanan says something that appears to cut in the opposite direction. If a person left a *behema*, an animal set aside as a *korban*, and died, leaving it to his two sons, Rabbi Yochanan rules that the *korban* may be brought — but neither son can perform *temurah* on it. *Temurah* is the act of substituting another animal for the *korban*, and the entire *parasha* of *temurah* is formulated in the singular, excluding jointly-owned *korbanos*. If the two sons collectively own the *korban* as partners, they are in the position of *shutafin* — joint owners — and *shutafin* cannot perform *temurah*. This ruling only makes sense if the heirs are considered the actual owners, with joint ownership that prevents *temurah*. But that directly contradicts the *mincha* ruling, which implies they are not owners at all.

### Contradiction Framed

The contradiction is now squarely before us. The *mincha* case indicates the heirs do not own the *korban* — otherwise it would be an invalid *minchat shutafin*. The *behema* case indicates they do own it — otherwise they should each individually be able to perform *temurah*, since two non-owners could not be blocked by the *shutafin* rule. How can both rulings be ascribed to the same Rabbi Yochanan?

### Hamir Yamir Include

The *gemara* resolves the tension through a careful reading of the verse governing *temurah*. The Torah's doubled language — *im hamir yamir* — is interpreted as a deliberate inclusion: it comes to include the *yoresh*, the heir, within the scope of those who can perform *temurah*. This is the operative principle that makes an heir's *temurah* possible at all. Once the inclusion of the heir is established through the *pasuk*, the *gemara* then applies the parallel rule: *v'ein shnayim m'mirin* — two people cannot jointly perform *temurah*. Just as two genuine joint-owners cannot do *temurah*, two heirs — even though they are not genuine owners — likewise cannot. The verse that includes the heir also implicitly carries the single-person limitation that accompanies *temurah*.

The *gemara* then addresses a further challenge from Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod, who asks whether the same logic should not apply to *maaser sheni*. By *maaser sheni* the *pasuk* similarly uses doubled language — *gaol yigal* — to include the heir in the obligation of adding a fifth when redeeming. Should we then say that two heirs cannot jointly redeem? The *gemara* dismisses this: *maaser* is fundamentally different, because even with genuine joint-owners by *maaser*, partnership does not affect the status of ownership. Partners in *maaser* add a fifth just like sole owners. Since the *shutafut* concern has no purchase by *maaser* even in ordinary cases of real ownership, it certainly does not affect the status of heirs. By *temurah* and *mincha*, on the other hand, partnership is definitionally relevant — those *halachot* are stated in terms that exclude joint-owners — and heirs track that structure accordingly.

---

## Ownership Definitions

### Multi-Halacha Principle

The *gemara* now develops a more precise conceptual framework. Rather than asking whether heirs do or do not "own" the *korban* in some univocal sense, it recognizes that different *halachot* within the laws of *kodshim* are keyed to different relationships one might have to the *korban*. Ownership, sanctification, and atonement are not always vested in the same person, and the *halacha* tracks each relationship independently.

### Sanctifier Add Fifth

The *gemara* cites Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on this point. Take a case where someone else sanctifies an animal on another person's behalf — your friend has the *korban* obligation, you own the animal, and you declare it sanctified for your friend's sake. Who adds a fifth when redeeming it, should it develop a *mum*? The Torah says *ve'im gaol yigal hamakdish* — if the *makdish*, the one who sanctified, redeems it, he must add a fifth. Thus: *hamakdish mosif chomesh* — the sanctifier adds the fifth, not the person whose *korban* it functionally is.

### Atone-for Temurah

In that same configuration, who can perform *temurah*? Here the rule runs the other way: *umitkapeir oseh tmurah* — the one for whom the *korban* atones has the power to perform *temurah*. There is a *pasuk* from which this is learned. The capacity to perform *temurah* belongs to the one for whom the *korban* has atoning function, not to the one who technically sanctified it. Additionally, a third *halacha*: if someone takes *terumah* from his own grain on behalf of his fellow's grain, the right to designate to which *kohen* that *terumah* goes belongs to the one who took it from his own produce — *tovat hana'ah shelo*.

### Heir Temurah Logic

This tripartite framework now creates a pointed logical problem. We have established that the *mincha* case demonstrates heirs do not genuinely own the *korban* — it remains their parent's. But if they do not own it and it does not atone for them in any direct sense, how can a single heir perform *temurah*? The power of *temurah* belongs to the one for whom the *korban* atones. If the *korban* does not atone for the heir — since it is fundamentally their parent's — then the heir should have no *temurah* power at all, regardless of whether there is one heir or two.

---

## Mikufya Atonement

### Hybrid Status

The *gemara*'s resolution is elegant and conceptually precise. It introduces the distinction: *mikiva lo mechapra, mikufya mechapra* — "from its fixed identity it does not atone, from what floats above it, it does atone." The heir occupies a hybrid status: not an owner, not the designated beneficiary of the *korban*'s primary function, and yet the recipient of a secondary, ripple-effect *kapara*.

### Fixed-Identity Ripple

What does this mean concretely? The *korban* was sanctified by the mother — call her the primary identity of the *korban*. It was designated to atone for her *mitzvot aseh*. That is *kiva* — its fixed, fundamental identity. She has since died. The heirs bring the *korban* because that is the *halacha* — an *olah* that was sanctified must be brought even after the owner's death. The *korban*'s core purpose remains keyed to her. Yet once the *korban* is brought, the heir who participated in bringing it gains something — a secondary atonement, a halo effect, a ripple from the act. It is not the primary function of the *korban*, but it is a genuine *kapara* that attaches to the heir by virtue of his role in bringing it.

### Non-Owner Temurah

This secondary level of atonement is sufficient, the *gemara* concludes, to vest in a single heir the capacity to perform *temurah*. The rule is that the one for whom the *korban* atones can do *temurah*. The heir receives atonement — not at the *kiva* level, but at the *mikufya* level — and that is enough. Two heirs, however, cannot do *temurah* together, because the *pasuk* of *im hamir yamir* includes only a single heir, and the structural exclusion of joint performance applies by analogy to the *shutafin* rule. The *mincha* remains perfectly coherent: since the heirs do not own it and it is not their *korban* at the *kiva* level, two heirs bringing an inherited *mincha* do not constitute a *minchat shutafin* and the *mincha* is valid. The entire system is now internally consistent.

---

## Shelo Lishmah Kippur

### Atone Question

Having established the parameters of when a *korban* is brought and for whom it functions, the *gemara* turns to a new question regarding *shelo lishmah*. We have already been told that if an *olah* was slaughtered *shelo lishmah*, the *korban* is *kasher* but does not fulfill the owner's obligation — *lo ala l'be'alim l'shem chova* — and the owner must bring another *korban* to discharge his *neder* or obligation. The new question is whether, setting aside the formal obligation question, the *korban* achieved any metaphysical effect at all. Did it *kippeir*? Did it accomplish the spiritual function of atonement, even if it did not discharge the formal *chova*?

### No Atonement Answer

Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi argues that it makes sense to say it did not atone — *mistavra d'lo kipro*. His reasoning is a *kal v'chomer*-style inference: if the *korban* did achieve atonement, then what is the purpose of bringing the second one? The owner has already been atoned for. To say that a *korban* both fully atoned and yet the obligation to bring a replacement remains is difficult to accept. The simpler conclusion is that no atonement was achieved, which is precisely why the replacement is necessary.

### Valid Start Logic

Rav Ashi reframes the question. He clarifies what Rav Sheshet's difficulty actually was: if the *korban* did not achieve atonement, one might wonder why it is brought at all — what is the point of completing a *korban* that accomplishes nothing? To this, Rav Ashi says: *shelo lishmo mikoach lishmo ka'ati* — the *shelo lishmah* korban comes from the strength of a *lishmah* korban. It began its life as a fully valid *korban* that was supposed to be brought. An error occurred in the process — it was slaughtered *shelo lishmah* — but you do not simply abandon something that began as a legitimate *korban*. You finish bringing it. The obligation to complete it derives not from any atonement it will achieve, but from the fact that it was properly sanctified and initiated as a *korban*. The *shechita* was a mistake, but the *korban* must nonetheless be brought to completion.

### Finish Obligation

The *gemara*'s conclusion is thus: no atonement is achieved by the *shelo lishmah korban*, but it must still be brought because it began as a valid *korban* and the process must be completed. The obligation to bring a second *korban* — to actually discharge the *neder* and achieve atonement — remains fully in force. The interesting conceptual point the *gemara* considered along the way is whether it is theoretically possible to separate the question of *kippur* from the question of *yotzei b'chova* — and the *gemara* shows that while they often track each other, they are in principle distinct questions, even if the conclusion here is that the *shelo lishmah korban* fails on both counts.

---

## Post-Separation Aveiros

### New Q Setup

The *gemara* now pivots to a question that stands entirely on its own, independent of *shelo lishmah*. It is a general question about when an *olah*'s atoning power is temporally defined. The principle is well known that an *olah* atones for *mitzvot aseh* — positive commandments one has failed to fulfill. The question is: which *mitzvot aseh* does it atone for? Specifically, if a person sanctified an animal as an *olah* and then, between the moment of sanctification (*hafrashah*) and the moment of bringing it, he failed to perform some *mitzvat aseh* — say he neglected to put on *tefillin* or failed to eat in a *sukkah* — does the *olah* atone for that post-*hafrashah* transgression?

### Chatas Comparison

One position reasons by analogy to the *chatas*. A *chatas* atones only for a sin committed before the *hafrashah*; it does not extend its atoning reach to sins committed after the animal was sanctified. One might therefore say the same about an *olah*: what was done before you set the animal aside is covered; what happens after is not.

### Olah Generic

The opposing position distinguishes the *olah* from the *chatas*. A *chatas* is inherently particular and concrete — every separate sin requires its own separate *chatas*. Because it is tied to a specific sin, its identity is fixed at the moment of sanctification in relation to that specific transgression. An *olah*, however, is generic. It is not linked to any particular *mitzvat aseh*; it works for *mitzvot aseh* generally, as a class. And precisely because it is not anchored to one specific act, *keivan de'ika kammah asei gabeih mechapera* — since any number of *mitzvot aseh* are potentially within its scope — it may well atone for those that come after the *hafrashah* as well.

### Vesamach Proof

To adjudicate between these positions, the *gemara* invokes a *beraisa*: *vesamach venirtza* — "and he shall lay his hands and it shall be accepted." The *beraisa* asks: does the *semichah* itself achieve atonement? Surely not — *ein kaparah ela bedam*, atonement comes through the blood, not the laying of hands. Rather, the juxtaposition of *vesamach venirtza* — the laying of hands alongside the acceptance — teaches that if one treats the *semichah* as a mere *shiyurei mitzvah*, an afterthought, then the *katuv* treats him *ke'ilu lo kibeir* — as though he did not fully achieve atonement. The phrase used is *ke'ilu lo kibeir vechibeir* — it is as though he did not atone, yet he did atone.

The *gemara* attempts to read this *beraisa* as bearing on the post-*hafrashah* question. Reading *lo kibeir* as referring to a specific failure and *kibeir* as referring to prior coverage, the *gemara* suggests: *lo kibeir* means the *olah* did not work for the *asei* of *semichah*, while *kibeir* means it did work for the *mitzvot aseh* committed prior to the *hafrashah*. If that reading is correct, it implies that the *olah* does not atone for the failure to do *semichah* specifically because *semichah* was omitted after the *hafrashah* — which would prove that post-*hafrashah* transgressions are generally excluded.

---

## Kailuah Reading

### Part Works Read

The initial reading of the *beraisa* thus proposes a clean split: the *olah* atones for *mitzvot aseh* committed before the *hafrashah*, but does not atone for the failure to do *semichah*, which occurred after the *hafrashah*. The phrase *ke'ilu lo kibeir vechibeir* is parsed as: part A was covered (*kibeir*), part B was not (*lo kibeir*) — not because *semichah* is uniquely excluded, but because it is paradigmatically a post-*hafrashah* failure.

### Rava Counter

Rava challenges this reading. He is willing to grant, in principle, that an *olah* works generically for post-*hafrashah mitzvot aseh* — that is exactly his position — but he insists that *semichah* is different and would be excluded even on that theory. Why? *Shani hatam de-chol kamma de-lo shachit be-amor ve-smoch ka'i* — as long as the animal has not yet been slaughtered, you can always still do *semichah*. The moment you transgress the *asei* of *semichah* is only the instant the *shechita* is performed — at which point it is too late. So the *asei* of *semichah* is not really a post-*hafrashah* transgression at all in the sense under discussion; it is a transgression that occurs at the very moment of *shechita* itself, or immediately after. The *beraisa* excluding *semichah* therefore tells us nothing about whether the *olah* covers sins committed in the period between *hafrashah* and *shechita*. Rava's conclusion remains: the *olah* atones generically for *mitzvot aseh*, including those violated after the *hafrashah*, with the one natural exception being the *asei* of *semichah* itself, which arises only at *shechita*.

### C-Minus Read

Huna bar Yehuda offers a simpler reading of the *beraisa* that eliminates the problem entirely. The phrase *ke'ilu lo kibeir vechibeir* does not mean the *olah* worked for some things and failed for others. It means: the person technically achieved *kapara* — *kibeir gavra* — but did not achieve *kaparah shleimah*, a complete and ideal atonement. He got a *kapara*, but not the way it was supposed to be done. As Rashi formulates it: *le-nachat ruach le-kono* — he did not bring satisfaction to his Creator. The *korban* was technically valid, but was not performed at its highest level. This reading makes the *beraisa* entirely irrelevant to the post-*hafrashah* question.

### Metzora Oil Case

To support this reading, Huna bar Yehuda points to a parallel case in the *tahara* process of the *metzora*. Part of that process requires the *kohen* to take the remaining oil and pour it on the head of the *metzora*. This oil is called *ha-notar* — the remainder — suggesting it is not the central act. Yet it is juxtaposed to the language *lechapper alav lifnei Hashem* — to atone for him before God. Rabbi Akiva reads the juxtaposition stringently: *im natan kipper ve-im lo natan lo kipper* — if the oil was poured on the head, it worked; if not, it did not. But Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says it is only *shiyurei mitzvah* — a supplementary part of the *mitzvah* — and therefore *bein nittan bein she-lo nittan kipper*: whether or not it was poured, the *tahara* is effective. Yet he adds: *u-ma'alin alav ke-ilu lo kipper* — we treat it as though it did not work.

### Akiva-Ben Nuri

The *gemara* asks: what does Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri mean by *ke-ilu lo kipper*? If it truly did not work, he would have to bring another *korban* — but he explicitly said it did work. *Ella kipper gavra lo kipper kaparah shleimah* — technically the *metzora* is *tahor*, but the *mitzvah* was not performed optimally. This is the same structure Huna bar Yehuda proposes for the *semichah beraisa*. The *beraisa* then uses the same language back in the *semichah* context: *ke'ilu lo kibeir vechibeir* simply means the *korban* was technically valid but suboptimal — a C-minus — with no implication about which category of sins was or was not covered.

The *gemara*, however, notes that the parallel is not perfectly clean. One could still read the *metzora* case as a split — the oil placement on the ear worked (*kibeir*), but the oil placement on the head did not (*lo kibeir*) — rather than reading it as a unified C-minus grade. The question of whether *ke-ilu lo kibeir vechibeir* always means suboptimality or can sometimes mean "worked for A, not for B" remains open, and Rashi and Tosafos debate the practical implications.

---

## Shavuot Two Goats

### Second Goat Tumah

The *gemara* now seeks a more direct proof from the *Shavuot* offerings. Rabbi Shimon teaches: the two *se'irei l'chatas* brought on *Shavuot* are both for *tumat mikdash v'kodashav* — for the ritual impurity of the sanctuary and its sancta. The question is: once the blood of the first *se'ir* is sprinkled, why is there a need to bring the second? Rabbi Shimon answers: *al tumah she'eira bein zeh l'zeh* — to cover any *tumah* that occurred between the bringing of the first *se'ir* and the second. He then elaborates: in principle, Bnei Yisrael should be obligated to bring a *korban* every few minutes, given how easily *tumat mikdash* occurs inadvertently. It is only the Torah's *rachamim* — its mercy — that does not burden us with that frequency, stretching the coverage from one *Yom Tov*'s *korban* to the next. Here on *Shavuot*, the Torah deliberately includes two *se'irim* to demonstrate this principle and cover even the brief interval between them.

### Post-Sep Implication

This teaching carries a significant implication for the question at hand. The *korban tzibur* of *Shavuot* is, in its nature, more analogous to the *atonement for mitzvot aseh* scenario than to a specific *chatas* for a specific sin. And critically, it appears that the second *se'ir* — which covers the *tumah* between the two offerings — atones for *tumah* that occurred *after* the *korban* was sanctified. If both animals were sanctified simultaneously at the outset, the *tumah* that occurred between the first and second offering would be post-*hafrashah* relative to the second one. If so, this is precisely the proof being sought: a generic *korban* can atone for transgressions occurring after its sanctification.

### Beit Din Retcon

Rav Pappa objects to drawing this conclusion. He argues that *korbanos tzibur* operate under special rules. *Beit din* — the rabbinic court that oversees communal *korbanos* — has the authority to stipulate regarding *korbanos tzibur* in ways that individuals cannot do for their own *korbanos*. Applied here: even if the two *se'irim* were sanctified simultaneously, *beit din* can retroactively stipulate that the sanctity of the second *se'ir* took effect only immediately before it was brought. Under that stipulation, the second *se'ir* is not really a post-*hafrashah* atonement at all — its *hafrashah* effectively occurs right before its *shechita*, after all the relevant *tumah* had already occurred. Therefore, nothing can be proven from *Shavuot* about whether individual *korbanos* atone for post-*hafrashah* transgressions.

This power of *beit din* is illustrated by the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *korbanos tzibur, sachin meshachtan l'ma shehein* — communal *korbanos* follow the designation determined at the moment of their *shechita*, meaning that through *beit din*'s authority, the identity and sanctity of a communal *korban* can be determined at the time of slaughter, not the time of sanctification.

### Shimon No Retcon

Rav Yosef the son of Rav Shmuel challenges Rav Pappa's recourse to *beit din*'s power. Can one really attribute to Rabbi Shimon — who is the source of this entire teaching about the two *se'irim* — the position that *beit din* has this authority? The *gemara* cites a ruling transmitted through a long chain: Rav Idi bar Avin, Rav Amram, Rav Yitzchak, all in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *temidin shelo hutzrechu l'tzibur* — if there were *temidin* that were left over from one year and now cannot be used with the new year's communal funds, may they be redeemed without a *mum*?

### Temidim Redemption

The answer depends on one's position regarding *beit din*'s power. *L'divrei Rabbi Shimon ein nifdin temimim* — according to Rabbi Shimon, they cannot be redeemed while still unblemished. For Rabbi Shimon, the ordinary rules apply: a *korban* can only be redeemed once it has developed a *mum*. *Aval l'divrei chachamim nifdin temimim* — but the *chachamim* permit redemption without a *mum* in this case, precisely because *beit din* can stipulate retroactively that the *korban* was never truly meant to be sanctified under these circumstances, effectively treating it as though it was never sanctified and allowing it to be redeemed as if unblemished. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, does not accept this *beit din* stipulation mechanism — the *korban* was sanctified and that sanctity is real and follows normal rules.

### Shimon Final

Since Rabbi Shimon does not hold that *beit din* can retroactively manipulate the *hafrashah*, Rav Pappa's defense cannot be invoked on his behalf. It was Rabbi Shimon who taught about the two *se'irim* of *Shavuot* in the first place, and since Rabbi Shimon rejects *lae beit din masneh aleihem*, the second *se'ir* truly does cover *tumah* that occurred after its sanctification — not by virtue of any retroactive *beit din* stipulation, but simply because it is a generic *korban* that atones for a generic category of *aveira*. The proof therefore stands: generic *korbanos* — analogous to the *olah* that atones for *mitzvot aseh* — do have the capacity to atone for transgressions occurring after the moment of *hafrashah*. The *gemara* leaves the discussion at this point, noting that the full resolution will be completed the following day.

---

---

# Zevachim 7

## Two Se'irim/Shavuot

### Why Two Se'irim?

The discussion opens at the end of Daf 6, in the context of the two different *se'irei chatat* brought on *Shavuot*. One *se'ir chatat* is brought as part of the regular *korban musaf*, and another is brought in connection with the *shtei halechem*. This raises a natural question: why are two distinct *korbanot chatat* necessary? One proposed rationale is that the second *se'ir* is needed to provide *kapparah* for *aveirot* that may have occurred during the interval between the *hafrashah* — the initial designation of the animal — and the actual *shechitah*.

### Designation at Shechitah

This explanation, however, is complicated by a teaching cited from the end of Daf 6: *de'amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel korbanot tzibbur tzrichin moshachtan lema shehen* — for communal sacrifices, it is the act of *shechitah* itself that finally designates them to their sacred status. If that is the case, there would be no meaningful gap period between the designation and the *shechitah*, and thus no window during which additional *aveirot* could occur that would require a second *chatat*.

### Beit Din Matneh/Challenge

This leads Rav Yosef the son of Rav Shmuel to challenge Rav Pappa: *u'mi it leh leRabbi Shimon lev Beit Din matneh aleihem?* — Does Rabbi Shimon actually subscribe to the principle that the *Beit Din* makes a conditional designation that only takes effect at the moment of *shechitah*? The answer turns on a teaching transmitted through a long chain of authorities.

### Temidin/Leftover Sheep

Rabbi Yochanan's teaching is introduced via Rav Iddi bar Avin, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak: the case of *temidin shelo hutzrechu latzibbur* — the sheep purchased and designated for the *korban tamid* of a given year that turn out to be surplus by the end of the year. Once *Rosh Chodesh Nisan* arrives, the *tamid* must be funded from the newly collected *shekalim*, and so the leftover animals become superfluous. The debate between Rabbi Shimon and the *Chachamim* concerns what happens to these animals: according to Rabbi Shimon, *ein nifdin temimim* — they cannot be redeemed while still unblemished; according to the *Chachamim*, *nifdin temimim* — they may be redeemed even in an unblemished state.

### Gap Period/Averot

The crucial inference is that Rabbi Shimon does *not* hold of *lev Beit Din matneh aleihem* — he does not regard the *hafrashah* as retroactively delayed until *shechitah*. Instead, Rabbi Shimon recognizes a genuine gap period between the time the *korban* is designated and the time it is actually slaughtered. It is precisely this gap that creates the theoretical need for a second *se'ir chatat* on *Shavuot* — to provide *kapparah* for *aveirot* that might occur during that window.

That said, the obvious answer remains that the *Torah* simply commands two *se'irim*, each accompanying a different element of the *musaf* structure of *Shavuot*, and there is no intrinsic need to find a further rationale. Indeed, it is worth noting that every *korban musaf* — with the exception of *Shabbat* — comes with a *chatat*. One might speculate that the *chatat* is not necessarily tied to some specific *cheit* but perhaps reflects a kind of trepidation about the act of bringing *korbanot* on the holidays themselves, or relates to the purifying function that *chatat* can also serve — as extensively discussed at the beginning of *Masechet Shevuot* — to cleanse the *mikdash* and the *mizbe'ach*.

---

## Se'irei Atzeret

### Question About 2nd Se'ir

The *sugya* continues with a question posed by Rabbi Yirmeyah to Rabbi Zeira: *she'irei Atzeret shekibel danam bishnei kosot, venizrak dam shel rishon — sheni lama hu ba?* If the blood of the two *se'irim* on *Shavuot* was collected in two separate vessels and the blood of the first was already sprinkled, why is the second *se'ir* still needed?

### Simultaneous Shechita

Rashi explains the premise: the two goats were slaughtered simultaneously — *shnei kosot nishchatin ke'echad* — so there was no opportunity for a *tumah* or *aveirah* to occur between the *shechitah* of one and the *shechitah* of the other. Given that, once the *zerikah* of the first is complete, what purpose does the second serve?

### Gap in Zerikat Hadam

The answer given is: *al tumah she'ire'ah bein zerikah shel zeh lazeh* — the second *se'ir* provides *kapparah* for *tumah* that might arise between the *zerikat hadam* of the first *chatat* and the *zerikat hadam* of the second. The window of concern has now shifted: it is not between *shechitah* and *zerikah* that we worry, but between the two acts of *zerikah* themselves.

This is a striking observation. It shows that *zerikat hadam* is not merely a procedural step but is itself a primary locus of *kapparah* — it is the blood, as the life-force of the animal, that effects the atonement. The fact that a gap between two *zerikos* can generate the need for an additional *korban* underscores the independent significance of *zerikah* as a time-point for *kapparah*.

### Unresolved Case

However, the *sugya* is left unresolved. As the *Gemara* itself notes with the phrase *dilma im timtzi lomar ka'amar*, the answer about the gap between the two *zerikos* does not fully address the question of what happens in the case of a *tumah* that occurred after *hafrashah* alone — that is, before *shechitah* had even taken place. The *sugya* is left open.

### Time Points/Kapparah

What emerges from this entire discussion is a clarification of the key time-points relevant to a *korban*: *hafrashah*, *shechitah*, and *zerikat hadam* each play a distinct and significant role. At the level of practical halacha, the real reason for the two *se'irim* on *Shavuot* is almost certainly simply the *Torah*'s requirement. But in probing *why* the *Torah* might have structured things this way, the *Gemara* opens a window into the internal logic of *kapparah* and the spiritual significance of each stage of the sacrificial process.

---

## Korban Todah

### Todah Intro/Short Window

The *sugya* now turns to the *korban todah*, which occupies the bulk of this *amud*. The *korban todah* is a subcategory of *korban shelamim*, but it differs from a regular *shelamim* in one critical respect: its eating window is dramatically shorter. A standard *shelamim* may be eaten for close to two full days; a *korban todah* must be consumed only until midnight of the night following the day it is brought. Moreover, the *korban todah* is a large animal — typically a cow — and is brought together with forty loaves of bread: thirty loaves of *matzah* of three varieties and ten loaves of *chametz*, making it one of only two *korbanot* brought in conjunction with *chametz*.

The shortened deadline to midnight is, in fact, a rabbinic stringency. The Gemara elsewhere records the position of Rabban Gamliel — cited in the very first *mishnah* in *Shas* — that the midnight limit was instituted as a *chumra*, and that *b'dieved* one has until *alot hashachar*.

### Todah/Todah Interchange

The central question that now arises from the *mishnah* is about the interplay between *korban todah* and *korban shelamim* when there is a *shelo lishmah* designation. The specific case introduced is: *todah sheshachatah leshem todat chaveiro* — what if a *kohen* performing the *shechitah* of one person's *todah* has in mind the *todah* of a different person?

### Shinui Kodesh

One might expect this to be analyzed as a case of *shinui ba'alim* — a change of owner — since two different people are involved. Yet Rashi explicitly rejects that framing. He writes: *lo sheshachatah al menat sheyitkaper bah mi she'eino ba'aleha* — this is not a case of *shinui ba'alim* at all. Rather, he classifies it as *shinui kodesh* — a change in the sacred designation of the offering. As he elaborates: the scenario is that Reuven has his own *todah* and Shimon has his own *todah* for different reasons, and the *kohen* slaughtered one with the designation of the other in mind — not intending that the wrong person be atoned for, but that the sacred character of one animal be transferred to the other. Rashi adds that the same analysis applies to a *kohen* who slaughters a *chatat chelev* with a *chatat dam* in mind.

Rashi's reading is admittedly difficult and somewhat counterintuitive — the plain sense of the case seems to involve *shinui ba'alim*. But Rashi deliberately avoids that categorization, and as will become clear from the subsequent *amoraic* debate, the underlying question turns on *shinui kodesh*.

### Rabba/Rav Chisda

The *amoraic* dispute is as follows: Rabba says the *korban* is *kesheirah* — and by *kesheirah* is meant not merely that the animal retains its sanctity but that it counts *alu l'ba'alim l'shem chovah*, it fulfills the owner's obligation. Rav Chisda says it is *psula* — the *korban* is technically valid but does not discharge the owner's obligation. The reasoning of each position is clear: Rabba holds that *todah leshem todah nishchatah* — it was designated as a *todah*, and that is sufficient. Rav Chisda counters — *leshem shelamim didei nishchatah ba'inan* — the *shechitah* must be oriented toward the specific *shelamim* that belongs to this particular owner.

### Todah/Shelamim

Rabba supports his position from a *Tannaitic* teaching. The pasuk *uvesar zevach todat shelamov beyom korbano yacheil* is cited, and Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer teaches: *todah sheshachatah leshem shelamim, kesheirah* — if a *todah* was slaughtered with a *shelamim* in mind, it is valid. Conversely, *shelamim shenishchatu leshem todah psulim* — a regular *shelamim* slaughtered with a *todah* in mind is disqualified. The asymmetry is explained: since *todah* is a subcategory of *shelamim*, having *shelamim* in mind when slaughtering a *todah* is simply thinking of a broader category that includes the *todah* itself — and that is permissible. But designating a *shelamim* as a *todah* means assigning it a more specific status it does not possess, which disqualifies it.

### Rava's Inference

From this *Tannaitic* discussion, Rava draws an inference: if *todah leshem todah kesherah* — meaning even if the *kohen* had in mind a *todah* that was not specifically the one being slaughtered — then this holds even where two different owners are involved. For if we have already learned that a *todah* being mentally exchanged with a *shelamim* is valid in one direction, and the case of *todah leshem todah* was left as an implicit conclusion of the *midrash*, then evidently *todah leshem todah* — even another person's — is *kesheirah*.

### Rav Chisda Response

Rav Chisda, however, rejects this inference. He argues that the reference to *todah leshem todah* in that *Tannaitic* teaching concerns only one person who designated multiple *todot* — not two different owners. The *limud* is thus necessary to teach something else entirely. One might have thought, argues Rav Chisda, that since the *Torah* itself calls a *todah* a *shelamim*, the terms are fully interchangeable — that a *todah* and a *shelamim* are legally identical in all respects, differing only incidentally in the length of the eating window and the accompanying loaves. The teaching therefore comes to negate that assumption: a *todah* and a *shelamim* are genuinely distinct categories. But it does not follow that two different owners' *todot* are interchangeable with one another.

Rav Chisda's final defense is compelling: had the *midrash* intended to teach about two different *todot* belonging to different owners, it should have stated *todah leshem todah* explicitly alongside *shelamim leshem todah*. Since it did not, the exclusion of that case is deliberate — and *Rabba*'s inference fails. The *halacha* regarding the interchange of two different people's *todot* thus remains the subject of unresolved *amoraic* dispute.

---

## Rava/Chatat Teachings

### Chatat/Chatat vs. Olah

The *Gemara* now turns to a series of brief, sequential teachings attributed to Rava. The first: *chatat sheshachatah leshem chatat, kesheirah; leshem olah, psula* — a *chatat* slaughtered with a *chatat* in mind is valid; slaughtered with an *olah* in mind, it is disqualified. This appears redundant given what the *mishnah* already stated, but the *Gemara* anchors it in a *pasuk*: the Torah says *veshachat otah l'chatat* — the *shechitah* of the *chatat* must be performed as a *chatat*. And so it follows directly that having an *olah* in mind invalidates it.

### Shinui Ba'alim Rules

The second teaching: *chatat sheshachatah al mi shemechuyav chatat, psula; al mi shemechuyav olah, kesheirah*. If I slaughter a *chatat* on behalf of another person who is likewise obligated to bring a *chatat*, it is disqualified. But if that other person is obligated only in an *olah* — meaning he has violated a *mitzvat aseh* rather than an *issur kareit* — then the *chatat* remains valid. The *Gemara* explains through the principle of *vekipper alav* — the *Torah* says the *chatat* must atone *for him*, which excludes others — but only *chavero hadomeh lo*, someone comparable to him in his obligation to bring a *chatat*. One who is not *mechuyav chatat* at all is outside that category and creates no disqualifying interference.

### Aino Mechuyav Klum

The third teaching: *chatat sheshachatah al mi she'aino mechuyav klum, psula* — a *chatat* slaughtered on behalf of someone who has no obligation whatsoever is disqualified. However, Rava immediately qualifies this: *she'ein lecha adam b'Yisrael she'eino mechuyav aseh* — there is no one in Israel who has not at some point violated a *mitzvat aseh*. Therefore, no one is truly *aino mechuyav klum*, and the case of disqualification is purely theoretical.

### Chatat/Aseh

The fourth teaching of Rava: *chatat mechaperet al chayavei aseh* — a *chatat* can provide *kapparah* even for violations of positive commandments, derived through a *kal vachomer*. Ordinarily, one would bring an *olah* in connection with a *mitzvat aseh* violation. But the *chatat*, which possesses greater atoning power, can also *mechapper*, at least partially — *mikupya mechapper* — for one who is *mechuyav aseh*. This follows directly from the preceding teaching that a *chatat* brought for someone *mechuyav olah* is *kesheirah*: since such a person's obligation is predicated on having violated a *mitzvat aseh*, the *chatat* retroactively provides at least partial *kapparah* for that *aseh* violation.

---

## Olah Shelo Lishmah

### Shelo Lishmah Rule

The *Gemara* now addresses the *olah* brought *shelo lishmah*: *olah sheshachatah shelo lishmah — asur lizrok dama shelo lishmah*. That is, if the *shechitah* of an *olah* was performed without the proper *lishma* intention, it is prohibited to then perform the subsequent *zerikah* also *shelo lishmah*. One must do the best one can to restore proper intention at each remaining stage of the *avodah*.

### Two Justifications

Two independent justifications are offered for this rule. The first is based on the *pasuk*: *motza sefatecha tishmor ve'asita* — one must take care to fulfill what has emerged from one's lips, and since you designated this as an *olah*, each action must be done with that *olah* designation in mind. The second is based on *svara* — sheer logic — *mishum de'shanya bah*: you should perform each step of the *avodah* as correctly as possible. It is notable that both the *kra* and the *svara* converge here, as the *Gemara* itself cross-references this rule to an earlier discussion at the beginning of the *masechet*.

### Olah/After Death

Another teaching of Rava: *olah haba'ah le'achar mitah sheshachatah beshinui kodesh, pesulah* — an *olah* brought after the owner's death, if slaughtered with a *shinui kodesh* (the wrong sacred designation in mind), is disqualified, and the heirs must bring another. But *beshinui ba'alim, kesheirah* — if brought with a different *ba'al* in mind, it is valid — *de'ein ba'alim le'achar mitah*. Once the owner has died, the very concept of *ba'alim* no longer applies in the same way. The heirs have an obligation to bring the designated *korban*, but the requirement that the *shechitah* be oriented toward the specific owner is dissolved by the owner's death.

This ruling opens a broader conceptual question about the nature of *hekdesh*. Two fundamentally different types exist: *kedushat damim*, where the animal's monetary value is consecrated to the *Beit HaMikdash* as corporate property, and *kedushat haguf*, where the animal itself is designated to be brought as a *korban* but continues in a meaningful sense to "belong" to the owner, who bears the obligation to bring it. The animal designated as a *korban* has *kedushat haguf* — it belongs to the owner even as he is obligated to bring it to the *mizbe'ach*.

### Owner/After Death

Rav Pinchas the son of Rav Ami dissents from Rava and holds *yesh ba'alim le'achar mitah* — the owner's designation remains legally operative even after death. Rav Ashi then presses Rav Pinchas for clarification: when you say *yesh ba'alim le'achar mitah*, do you mean *davka* that the heirs must bring a second *olah* if the first was slaughtered with a *shinui ba'alim*? Or perhaps you mean only that if the deceased had multiple *chiyuvei asei*, the heirs may bring additional *olot* to address them? Rav Pinchas responds *davka kamina* — he means it precisely: if the *olah* was invalidated through *shinui ba'alim* after the owner's death, the heirs are indeed obligated to bring another.

### Olah as Doron

Rava then offers what is perhaps his most conceptually striking teaching in this sequence: *olah doron hi* — the *olah* is, at its core, a gift to *Hashem*. Tosafot note an apparent tension: the *olah* does possess the capacity to provide *kapparah* for *mitzvat aseh* violations. Yet Rava's point is that this atoning function is secondary, not primary. The *olah* is fundamentally a *doron*, an act of giving.

The *Gemara* then explores what this means in practice. If there is no *teshuva*, the offering of a wicked person is *to'evah* — abominable. But if *teshuva* has been done, a *Tannaitic* teaching already states: *avar al mitzvat aseh veshav, lo zaz misham ad shemochalin lo* — one who violates a *mitzvat aseh* and repents is forgiven immediately, before taking a single step. Therefore, by the time one brings an *olah* for a *mitzvat aseh* violation, the *kapparah* has already been achieved through *teshuva*. The *olah*, then, is not needed for *kapparah* in any strict sense — it is a gift, a *doron*, brought after forgiveness has already been granted.

Rashi captures this precisely: *olah doron hi eina ba'ah lechapper al aseh kappara mamash ela achar shekapparah teshuva al aseh* — after *teshuva* has already achieved *kapparah* for the *aseh* violation, the *olah* is brought not as atonement but as an expression of gratitude and closeness.

### Chatat Before Olah

A *Tannaitic* teaching of Rabbi Shimon concludes this discussion and beautifully synthesizes the relationship between *chatat* and *olah*. Rabbi Shimon asks: why does the *chatat* always precede the *olah* — as seen throughout *Sefer Vayikra*, where those who must bring both, such as a *metzora* or a *yoledet*, always bring the *chatat* first? His answer: *leparaklit shenichnas, ritza paraklit nichnas doron acharav* — it is like a royal courtier who first enters to appease the king for an offense that was committed, and only once forgiveness has been granted does the gift follow. You first address what is wrong — *chatat* removes the sin — and only then may you offer a gift from a place of love and gratitude. The *olah* is the gift; the *chatat* is the appeasement.

This explains the profound pairing of *chatat* and *olah* throughout the *korbanot*: they are two sides of the same spiritual act. The *chatat* takes away something negative; the *olah* adds something positive. And the *chatat* always comes first.

---

## Pesach/Lishmah

### Pesach Exception

The *mishnah* stated: *kol hazvachim shenizbechu shelo lishmam kesherim, ela shelo alu l'ba'alim l'shem chovah — chutz min haPesach vehaChatat. HaPesach bizmano, vehaChatat bechol zman* — every sacrifice brought *shelo lishmah* remains valid but does not fulfill the owner's obligation, except for the *pesach* in its proper time and the *chatat* at any time. The *pesach* is unique in that if brought with a different *korban* in mind, it is not merely unfulfilling of the obligation — it is actually disqualified entirely.

### Pesach Source

The *Gemara* asks: *pesach minalan* — what is the source for this stringency? The *pasuk* cited is *shamor es chodesh ha'Aviv ve'asisa Pesach* — *sheyihyu kol asiyosav l'shem pesach*: every act performed for this *korban* must be done with the *korban pesach* in mind. This establishes a positive requirement of *lishmah* for all the *avodot* of the *pesach*.

### Shinuy Kodesh

The *pasuk shamor es chodesh ha'Aviv ve'asisa Pesach* addresses *shinui kodesh* — the requirement that the *shechitah* be designated for the *pesach* and not for some other *korban* such as a *shelamim* or *chatat*.

### Shinuy Ba'alim
