For *shinui ba'alim*, a separate *pasuk* is invoked: *va'amartem zevach pesach hu* — you must declare "this is the *zevach pesach*," which the *Gemara* interprets as requiring that the *zevichah* be designated for the *pesach* and for its proper *chaburah*. This is distinctive to *korban pesach*: not only must the owner have the proper intent, but all those who will be eating the *korban* — the entire *chaburah* — must have been designated in advance as part of the group on whose behalf this *korban* is brought.

### Rav Safra Challenge

Rav Safra challenges the derivation of *le'akeiv* from the *pasuk* *vezavachta Pesach l'Hashem Elokecha*. He argues: *hai miba'ei lei l'chidrav Nachman* — that *pasuk* is already needed to teach what Rav Nachman derived. Rav Nachman, in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha, learned from *vezavachta Pesach l'Hashem Elokecha tzon uvakar* that a leftover *korban pesach* animal — one that was designated as a *pesach* but was not brought in time — can be brought subsequently as a *shelamim*. The apparent difficulty is that the *pesach* can only be a sheep or goat, not cattle; yet the *pasuk* mentions *tzon uvakar*. Rav Nachman resolves this by saying the mention of cattle teaches that the leftover animal may become a *shelamim*, which can be brought from either sheep or cattle. Since the *pasuk* is already needed for this purpose, it cannot simultaneously serve as the source for *shinui ba'alim le'akeiv*.

### Sources/Responses

Rav Safra therefore restructures the derivations. *Shamor es chodesh ha'Aviv ve'asisa Pesach* teaches the *mitzvah* requirement of *lishma* as it concerns *shinui kodesh*. *Va'amartem zevach pesach hu* teaches the *mitzvah* requirement as it concerns *shinui ba'alim*. And *vezavachta Pesach* is reserved for Rav Nachman's teaching about *mosar pesach* becoming *shelamim*.

As for the requirement of *le'akeiv* — that violation actually disqualifies the *korban* — the *Gemara* derives this from the convergence of multiple *peshakim* that each mention *zevichah*: *bein hacha vehacha ashkechan zvicha*. All the relevant *pesukim* focus on the act of *shechitah*, establishing it as *me'akeiv*. For the other three *avodot* — *kabalah*, *holacha*, and *zerikah* — the principle of *ho'il vegalei galei* is invoked: once the *Torah* has revealed the requirement for *shechitah*, the same rule applies to all the *avodot*.

### Pesach/Shelamim

A further *Tannaitic* source establishes the broader framework. The *pasuk* *beyom tzavoto b'nei Yisrael l'hakriv et korbeneihem* refers specifically to *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *pesach* — the three *kodashim kalim* most intimately associated with their owners — and compares them through a *hekesh* to *shelamim*. From this comparison it follows: just as by *shelamim* there is no distinction between *zevichah* and the other *avodot* with respect to the requirement of *lishmah*, so too by *pesach*. And just as by *shelamim*, *shinui kodesh* and *shinui ba'alim* apply equally to all the *avodot*, so too by *pesach*.

### Word Hu/Me'akeiv

The word *hu* in the context of the *korban pesach* — *zevach pesach hu* — functions as a marker that the requirement is *me'akeiv*: if the *shechitah* is not performed *lishmah*, the *korban* is entirely disqualified. Notably, by contrast, the *korban asham* does not use the word *hu* in the relevant context. The *Gemara* derives from this absence that for the *asham*, if the *imurim* — the sacrificial fats — were not burned on the *mizbe'ach*, the *korban* remains valid *be'dieved*. The presence of *hu* signals indispensability; its absence signals that the step, while required, is not strictly *me'akeiv* in every dimension.

---

---

# Zevachim 8

## Chatas Pesukim

### Shechitah Source

The eighth daf of Zevachim opens by pivoting from the previous discussion — which established that most *korbanos* must be performed *lishmah* and *l'shem ba'alim* at least *lechatchila*, though failure to do so renders them *kasher* while denying the owners fulfillment of their obligation — to the exceptions enumerated in the *mishnah*: *chatas* and *pesach*. When either of these is performed *shelo lishmo*, the *korban* is entirely *pasul* and cannot be offered on the *mizbeach*. The *gemara* now undertakes the task of locating the scriptural basis for both the *lechatchila* requirement and the *me'akev* status of *lishmah* by *chatas*.

The *gemara* begins with the question *chatas minalan* — where do we learn the law of *chatas*? The relevant *pasuk* states *v'shachat osah l'chatat*, "and he shall slaughter it for a *chatas*." The phrase *l'chatat* — for the purpose of being a *chatas* — establishes that the *shechitah* must be performed *l'shem chatas*. The principle derived is *she'te'hei shechitah l'shem chatat*: the slaughter must be done for the sake of the sin offering. This covers the first of the four *avodos*.

### Kabbalah Source

At the top of 8a, the *gemara* turns to the *kabbalah* — the receiving of the blood in a vessel. The *pasuk* reads *v'lakach hakohen midam hachatat*, "and the *kohen* shall take from the blood of the *chatas*." The formulation *hachatat* — the *chatas* — is a doubling of reference that could have been expressed more simply; the Torah's choice to specify *hachatat* teaches that *she'te'hei kabala l'shem chatat*, the receiving of the blood must also be for the sake of the *chatas*. The term *lakach* is classically understood to encompass both the *kabbalah* and the *holacha*, the carrying of the blood toward the *mizbeach*.

### Zerikah Source

For the *zerikah* — the throwing of the blood on the *mizbeach* — the *gemara* cites *v'chiper alav hakohen michatato*, "and the *kohen* shall atone for him from his sin." The act of atonement is the blood service on the *mizbeach*, and the formulation teaches *she'te'hei kapara l'shem chatat* — the atonement, too, must be performed for the sake of the *chatas*.

### Shinui Kodesh

Having established from these *pesukim* that all the *avodos* must be performed *l'shem chatas* at least *lechatchila*, the *gemara* notes: *ashkachan shinui kodesh* — we have now established the requirement regarding *shinui kodesh*, the case where the *avodah* is performed with intent for a different type of *korban*.

### Shinui Ba'alim

The *gemara* then asks *shinui ba'alim minalan* — where do we learn that *lechatchila* one must also have in mind the correct owner? The answer is found in the word *alav* from the same *pasuk*: *v'chiper alav hakohen* — "and the *kohen* shall atone for him." The precision of *alav v'lo l'chavero* — for him and not for another — establishes that the *avodah* must be performed with intent for the actual owner. And the *gemara* concludes: *ashkachan l'mitzva* — all of this establishes the *lechatchila* requirement.

---

## Me'akev Requirements

### Shinui Kodesh Gap

Having established the *lechatchila* requirements for both *shinui kodesh* and *shinui ba'alim*, the *gemara* now confronts the harder question: *l'akev minalan?* How do we know that failure to comply renders the *korban pasul*?

The *gemara* reviews what has been established and what remains to be proven. The *pesukim* of *v'shachat osah l'chatat* and *v'lakach midam hachatat* establish *lechatchila* for *shinui kodesh* across the *avodos*. The *pasuk* of *v'chiper alav hakohen michatato* establishes both the *lechatchila* and the *me'akev* status — but only for *shinui ba'alim* by *zerikah*, because the word *michatato* ("from his *chatas*") reiterates the ownership requirement a second time in the same verse, and the doubling teaches that the *zerikah* with *shinui ba'alim* invalidates the *korban*.

The resulting picture is therefore incomplete in two respects. First, *shinui kodesh*: we know all the *avodos* must be performed *l'shem chatas*, but we do not yet know that failure to do so is *me'akev*. Second, *shinui ba'alim*: we know it is *me'akev* only by *zerikah*, but not by the other *avodos*. The question *l'akev b'chol avodos b'shinui kodesh*, and *b'she'ar avodos b'shinui ba'alim*, is therefore still open.

Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua had already made a *drasha* from the extra *vav* in the word *chatato* — the possessive suffix — arguing that the reiteration teaches that the ownership requirement is *me'akev*. The *gemara* notes that the same type of reasoning will be applied here: *hacha nami chatat chataso*, the expression *michatato* doubles down on the ownership requirement and teaches *me'akev* status. But this still only covers *zerikah*. The broader application to all *avodos* requires an additional source.

### Chatas Nazir

Rav Yona provides the answer: *atya m'chatat nazir* — one learns from the *chatas* of a *nazir*. The relevant *pasuk* states *v'hikriv hakohen lifnei Hashem v'asa et chatato v'et olato*, "and the *kohen* shall bring before God and perform his *chatas* and his *olah*." The word *v'asa* — "and he shall perform" — is generic and encompasses all the *avodos* at once. From *v'asa et chatato*, we learn *sheyaaseh kol asiyotav l'shem chatat* — all of the acts of the *avodah* must be performed for the sake of the *chatas*. This covers the *lechatchila* requirement for *shinui kodesh* across all *avodos*.

Regarding *shinui ba'alim*, the *gemara* adopts the *girsa* of Tosafot: since the *pasuk* of *v'asa et chatato* by *chatas nazir* is superfluous (the *lechatchila* requirement for *shinui kodesh* was already derived from the *pesukim* by *chatas chelev*), it is redirected — *im eino inyan l'shinui kodesh, tneihu inyan l'shinui ba'alim* — to teach that all the *avodos* must also be performed *l'shem ba'alim*.

### Doubling Teaches Me'akev

The *lechatchila* for *shinui ba'alim* across all *avodos* is now established, but *me'akev* remains elusive beyond *zerikah*. It is Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua who supplies the answer: the extra *vav* in *chatato* — appearing as *michatato* — reiterates the ownership requirement in a way that signals *me'akev* status. Once applied, this covers the *me'akev* requirement for both *shinui kodesh* and *shinui ba'alim* across all *avodos* of *chatas*.

---

## Me'akev Requirements (II)

### Chatas Chelev vs Nazir

At this point Ravina raises a sharp challenge. The entire structure rests on the assumption that one *chatas* can be learned from another — specifically, that the *pesukim* by *chatas nazir* can be applied to fill the gaps by *chatas chelev*. But this assumption does not go unchallenged. The *gemara* poses the question: *migmari mehadadi? chatas chelev mechatas nazir lo gamri* — can one really learn them from one another? Perhaps not.

---

## Chatas Metzora

### Ravina's Challenge

Ravina challenges the derivation: how can one learn *chatas chelev* from *chatas nazir*? Each *chatas* may have requirements unique to its own context. *Chatas chelev mechatas nazir lo gamri*, the *gemara* states, *sheken yesh immah damim acherim* — a *chatas nazir* comes together with other blood offerings, specifically an *olah*, and therefore one cannot assume that the demands applying to *chatas nazir* transfer to a standalone sin offering. Conversely, one cannot learn in the reverse direction either: *chatas nazir mechatas chelev lo gamar, sheken karet* — a *chatas chelev* is brought for a sin punishable by *karet*, which may entail heavier requirements. Each type of *chatas* carries a distinctive feature that might explain elevated demands, and therefore neither can be derived from the other.

### Minchah Nesachim

At this point the *gemara* notes that Ravina challenged specifically the *vav* of *olaso* — the *olah* of the *nazir* — asking: if you are going to use the *vav* in *chatato* to teach *me'akev*, what will you do with the extra *vav* in *olaso*, since the *me'akev* requirement does not apply to an *olah* the way it does to a *chatas*? Why did Ravina not similarly challenge the extra *vavs* found in *minchaso* and *nisko* — his *minchah* and wine libation?

The *gemara* explains that those *vavs* are not problematic because they are needed for a separate *drasha*. The *pasuk* by *Sukkos* teaches, from the possessive form of *minchasam veniskeihem*, that the *minchah* and *nesachim* accompanying a *korban* may be brought even at night or even on the following day. Applying the same reading to the *korban* of the *nazir*, *minchaso venisko* teaches that a *nazir*'s *minchah* and *nesachim* may similarly be brought on a subsequent night or day. Since those *vavs* serve that separate purpose, Ravina's challenge was rightly directed only at *olaso*. And the challenge about *olaso* — paired with the structural objection that one *chatas* cannot be learned from another — leaves the derivation incomplete.

### Rava's Solution

Rava proposes an alternative: *atya mechatas metzora* — learn not from *chatas nazir* but from the *chatas* of a *metzora*. The relevant *pasuk* states *ve'asah hakohen et hachatas*, "and the *kohen* shall perform the *chatas*." Once again the word *ve'asah* is generic and encompasses all the *avodos*, yielding the principle *sheyehu kol asiyosav leshem chatas* — all acts of the *avodah* must be for the sake of the *chatas*. And for *shinui ba'alim*, the *pasuk* adds *v'chiper al hamitaher* — he shall atone for the one becoming purified — from which one derives *al hamitaher zeh v'lo al mitaher chaveiro*: for this person and not for another's *metzora*. Combined with the *pesukim* already known by *chatas chelev*, the doubling would then signal *me'akev* status.

### Metzora Distinct

The *gemara* immediately raises the same objection against Rava's solution. *Chatas chelev mechatas metzora lo yalfei, sheken yesh imom damim acherim* — a *chatas metzora* comes alongside an *olah* and an *asham* and other *korbanos*, so its demands may be heavier and cannot be assumed to apply to a standalone *chatas chelev*. And in the reverse, *chatas metzora mechatas chelev lo gamar, sheken karet* — the demands of a *chatas* brought for a *karet* offense may be more stringent than those applicable to a *metzora*. Once again, the two *chatasos* are too distinct to allow learning one from the other.

---

## Tzad HaShaveh

### Learn One from Two

*Chada mechada lo asya* — one cannot be learned from the other alone, since each has a distinctive feature that might account for its requirements. But the *gemara* proposes a way forward: *teisi chada mitartei* — why not learn one from two? We now have three sets of *pesukim* requiring *lishmah* by *chatas*: by *chatas chelev*, by *chatas nazir*, and by *chatas metzora*. If any two of them together would suffice to establish the requirement in the third, then the *pesukim* by the third are superfluous — and that surplus teaches not merely *lechatchila* but *me'akev*.

The *gemara* tests each possible configuration. First: why not omit the *lishmah* requirement from *chatas chelev* and learn it from *chatas nazir* and *chatas metzora*? No — *mah lehanach sheken yesh imom damim acherim*, both of those come in a cluster of *korbanos*, and their combined demands might not transfer to a standalone *chatas chelev*. Second: why not omit it from *chatas nazir* and learn from *chatas chelev* and *chatas metzora*? No — *mah lehanach sheken ein lahem she'eilah*, a *nazir* can in principle approach a *chacham* to have the *nezirus* annulled, so the demands applying to the irreversible *chatas chelev* and *chatas metzora* might not apply to *chatas nazir*. Third: why not omit it from *chatas metzora* and learn from *chatas chelev* and *chatas nazir*? No — *mah lehanach sheken ein bam bedalut*, those two have no *oleh v'yored* option for the poor, while *chatas metzora* does allow a lesser offering for someone impoverished; perhaps that leniency means *chatas metzora* carries lighter requirements.

In every configuration, the third *chatas* cannot be learned from the other two, and therefore every one of the three needed its own *pesukim* to establish the *lishmah* requirement independently. This means none of the *pesukim* are superfluous, and therefore none of them can be used to teach *me'akev*.

### Shelamim Connection

The *gemara* resolves the impasse by returning to a *pasuk* cited earlier: *zos hatorah la'olah u'laminchah v'lachatat v'la'asham v'lamiluim u'lizevach hashelamim* — this is the teaching for the *olah*, the *minchah*, the *chatas*, the *asham*, the *miluim*, and the *zevach hashelamim*. *Hikishu hakasuv leshelamim* — the verse compares *chatas* to *shelamim*. Just as *shelamim* requires *lishmah* and *l'shem ba'alim* at least *lechatchila* for both *shinui kodesh* and *shinui ba'alim* — as established in earlier discussions — the same applies to *chatas*. This *hekesh* to *shelamim* is the foundation that all *korbanos*, including *chatas*, must be performed *lishmah* and *l'shem ba'alim* at least *lechatchila*. That is our starting point.

### Extra Pesukim Teach Me'a…

Once that baseline is established through the connection to *shelamim*, the individual *pesukim* by each *chatas* category — *chatas chelev*, *chatas nazir*, and *chatas metzora* — are no longer needed to teach the *lechatchila* requirement, since that is already known. Each of those sets of *pesukim* is now available to teach something additional: *hanach kra'ei l'akeiv* — those verses come to teach that the requirement is *me'akev*. If you fail to perform the *avodah* *lishmah* or *l'shem ba'alim* in any of these *chatas* categories, the *korban* is *pasul*.

### All Five Categories

The *gemara* now traces how all five categories of *chatas* are covered. *Chatas chelev* — the standard sin offering — has its own *pesukim* stating *l'chatat*, which now teach *me'akev*. *Chatas nazir* and *chatas metzora* similarly have their own *pesukim* teaching *me'akev*. *Chatas avodas kochavim* — the *chatas* brought for idolatry — can be learned directly from *chatas chelev*, since both involve a *karet*-level transgression; if it is *me'akev* by *chatas chelev*, it is likewise *me'akev* for the *chatas* of *avodas kochavim*.

The remaining category — the *chatas oleh v'yored* found at the end of *Parshas Vayikra*, covering cases such as a false oath, failure to testify, or *tumah* in the *Beis HaMikdash* — does not have its own explicit *pesukim* establishing *me'akev*. Here the *gemara* applies a *tzad hashaveh*: since across all the other *chatas* categories — *chatas chelev*, *chatas nazir*, *chatas metzora*, and *chatas avodas kochavim* — *lishmah* is *me'akev*, one can infer by logical equivalence that the same applies to the *chatas oleh v'yored* as well. *Kulhu asyan b'ma hatzad* — all of them together support the inference.

There is also an underlying logic to why *me'akev* applies specifically to *chatas*: the *chatas* is inherently bound to its owner and their particular sin. The mechanism of *lo olah l'ba'alim l'shem chovah* — which ordinarily allows a *korban* performed *shelo lishmah* to be offered even if it doesn't count toward the owner's obligation — has no meaningful application to a *chatas*, since a *chatas* disconnected from its owner and their transgression loses its essential character entirely. This is also the explanation behind the category of *chatasos meisos* — *chatasos* that must be left to die once atonement has been achieved through other means — and it explains why a *chatas* performed *shelo lishmah* is not merely unhelpful but fully *pasul*.

---

## Pesach Overview

### Pesach Mishnah

The *gemara* now turns to the second exception identified in the *mishnah*: the *pesach* offering. A *baraisa* is cited: *tanu rabbanan*, *pesach bizmano lishmo kasher shelo lishmo pasul* — the *pesach* slaughtered at its proper time, from *chatzos* on the fourteenth of *Nissan*, if done *lishmo* is *kasher*, and if done *shelo lishmo* it is *pasul*.

This parallels *chatas*: when the *pesach* is performed at the correct time but with the wrong intent — for a different *korban* — it is entirely invalid.

### Pesach Becomes Shelamim

But the *mishnah* introduces a further ruling that applies when it is *not* the proper time — any time other than the fourteenth from *chatzos* onward. *Uv'she'ar yemos hashanah lishmo pasul shelo lishmo kasher* — during the rest of the year, the reverse holds. If it is slaughtered as a *pesach*, it is *pasul*, since the *Torah* repeats multiple times that the *pesach* must be slaughtered on the fourteenth after *chatzos*, and bringing it as a *pesach* at the wrong time is simply invalid. But if it is slaughtered for something other than *pesach* — thereby *oker hashem*, uprooting its *pesach* status — then it is *kasher*, and it becomes a *shelamim*.

---

## Pesach to Shelamim

### V'Im Pasuk

The *gemara* asks: *minalan hanei mili* — where do we learn that when a *pesach shelo bizmano* is slaughtered *shelo lishmo* it is *kasher*? The father of Shmuel answers that the *pasuk* states *v'im min hatzon korbano l'zevach shelamim la'Hashem*, "and if from the sheep is his offering as a *zevach shelamim* to God." This appears at the beginning of *Vayikra* in the context of *shelamim* offerings. The *drasha* proceeds: *davar haba min hatzon* — a type of *korban* that comes exclusively from sheep — this is the *pesach*, which is restricted to *tzon* (sheep or goats). *Yehei l'zevach shelamim* — such a *korban* brought outside its proper time shall be a *shelamim*. Since a *pesach* cannot be a *shelamim* on the fourteenth of *Nissan* after *chatzos*, the verse must refer to a *pesach* brought at any other time of year.

### Kavana Scope

One might object: perhaps the verse means only that if one explicitly had *kavana* for *shelamim*, it becomes a *shelamim*, but not if one had *kavana* for something else entirely. If one slaughtered the *pesach* with intent for an *olah* or a *chatas*, perhaps it should be *pasul*?

This question is not merely technical. The underlying mechanism would be: intent for something other than *pesach* uproots its *pesach* status, and because of its fundamental *kedusha* as something eaten by the owners in *Yerushalayim*, it gravitates toward becoming a *shelamim*. But that mechanism is not obvious; one might assume that only explicit *kavana* for *shelamim* could produce this result.

### Grammar L'Zevach

Rav Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves this: *l'zevach l'rabot kol zavach* — the word *l'zevach* functions as a *ribuy*, an expansion, including any type of *zevach*. The full verse then reads: if it is a *korban* of sheep (*i.e.*, a *pesach*) — *l'zevach*, for any *zevach* — *shelamim*, it becomes a *shelamim*. Any form of *shelo lishmah* intent transforms the *pesach* into a *shelamim*.

However, the *gemara* presses further. If *l'zevach* is read as a *ribuy*, one might ask: why does it become specifically a *shelamim*? Why not become whatever *korban* the *shochet* had in mind — an *olah* if intent was for *olah*, a *chatas* if intent was for *chatas*? The *gemara* considers whether *l'zevach shelamim* should be read as *klal u'prat* — a general statement (*l'zevach*) followed by a specific (*shelamim*) — in which case the rule *ein baklal ella mah shebaprat* would restrict the result to *shelamim* only when one explicitly intended *shelamim*.

### Klal U'Prat

Rav Yaakov miNehar Pekod challenges the *klal u'prat v'klal* reading on its own terms. A valid *klal u'prat v'klal* requires that the two *klalim* be of comparable scope, but here they are not. The first *klal*, *l'zevach*, encompasses only *zvachim* — slaughtered mammals. The second *klal*, *l'Hashem*, is far broader, potentially including *olos ha'of*, *menachos*, and any form of *korban* brought to God. If the two *klalim* are of unequal scope, the *klal u'prat v'klal* analysis does not function properly.

The *gemara* responds that this *tanna* follows the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which takes a looser approach to *klal u'prat* and allows the inference even when the *klalim* are not precisely matched.

### Ribuy Resolution

Ultimately, the *gemara* sets aside the *klal u'prat v'klal* analysis and returns to the reading of *l'zevach* as a *ribuy*. As Rashi explains, whether a term functions as a *klal* or as a *ribuy* depends on the linguistic context and one's hermeneutical methodology. Here, reading *l'zevach* as a *ribuy* — as simply expanding the scope of which *zevach* intent suffices — the verse teaches that any *zevach* intent transforms the *pesach*. And *shelamim* specifies what it becomes.

The *gemara* asks one final question on this reading: if *l'zevach* is a *ribuy* and no longer part of a structured *klal u'prat v'klal* sentence, how do we still know that the result is *shelamim* rather than whatever *korban* the *shochet* intended? The answer to this question is provided in the next section.

---

## Why Shelamim

### Kodshim Kalim

Rav Avin supplies the principle: *dochin kodshim ne'echalim etzel kodshim ne'echalim v'ein dochin kodshim ne'echalim etzel kodshim she'einam ne'echalim* — *kodshim* that are eaten are pushed toward other *kodshim* that are eaten, and they are not pushed toward *kodshim* that are not eaten. A *pesach* is eaten by its owners; an *olah* is entirely consumed on the *mizbeach* and not eaten by people. Therefore, even if one had *kavana* for an *olah*, the *pesach* will not become an *olah* — it will gravitate toward something that is eaten, namely *shelamim*.

Rabbi Yose berebi Avin states the principle more precisely: *dochin kodshim kalim etzel kodshim kalim v'ein dochin kodshim kalim etzel kodshei kodshim* — items of *kodshim kalim* status (eaten throughout *Yerushalayim*) are pushed toward other *kodshim kalim*, and not toward *kodshei kodshim*. A *pesach* is *kodshim kalim*, and *shelamim* is *kodshim kalim*, and therefore the *pesach* becomes a *shelamim*.

### Maaser Objection

Rabbi Yitzchak berebi Svara raises an objection: *eima shachatei l'sheim Maaser l'havei Maaser* — why not say that if one slaughtered the *pesach* with intent for *maaser*, it should become *maaser*? *Maaser* is also *kodshim kalim*, eaten by the owners in *Yerushalayim*. And the distinction matters practically: if treated as *maaser*, it would not require *nesachim* — the accompanying wine libations — and one would receive *malkus* for selling it, given the specific *lav* against redeeming *maaser* improperly.

### Ha'Asiri Answer

The *gemara* answers by citing the *pasuk* *ha'asiri yihiyeh kodesh* — the tenth shall be holy. The *drasha* is: *zeh Maaser v'ein acher Maaser* — only the item that is literally the tenth in a sequence acquires *maaser* status. Something like a *korban pesach*, which does not emerge from a tithing process, cannot spontaneously become *maaser* regardless of the *kavana* at the time of *shechitah*. Therefore, the only available destination for the displaced *pesach* is *shelamim*.

---

---

# Zevachim 9

## Pesach Exception

### Mishna Review

The *mishna* established a fundamental *halacha* regarding the *korban pesach* and the *chatat*: unlike other *zevachim*, which if slaughtered with incorrect intent — either for the wrong *korban* or for the wrong owner — are at least *kosher* post-facto even if they fail to discharge the owner's obligation, these two offerings are exceptions. The *korban pesach* brought *shelo lishmah* is disqualified. This much was established early in the *sugya*, and the remainder of the discussion pivots to a second point: what happens when a *korban pesach* is brought outside its proper time.

### Sugya Outline

The governing principle under scrutiny is that a *korban pesach* brought *shelo lishmo shelo bizmano* — without correct intent and outside the proper season — reverts to being a *korban shelamim*, regardless of what other *korban* the slaughterer had in mind. The *sugya* has mounted a series of challenges to this principle, each framed by the word *eima* — "one might suggest" — proposing alternative *korbanot* to which the *pesach* might revert instead of *shelamim*. We now rejoin the discussion in the middle of the *ma'aser* challenge.

### Ma'aser Classification

*Ma'aser behema* is classified as *kodshim kalim*, like *shelamim*, but occupies a lower level of sanctity: it requires no *nesachim* and has only a single *matana* of the blood rather than the full *shtayim she'hen arba* of the *shelamim*. The *ma'aser behema* is designated by the owner, who drives the newborn animals of his flock through a narrow passageway and counts them — the tenth animal to pass through becomes *ma'aser*. It is precisely this counting process that underlies the rich imagery of the *Rosh Hashana* and *Yom Kippur* liturgy, which draws on the language of the shepherd tallying his flock.

---

## Reversion Alternatives

### Bechor Challenge

Having treated *ma'aser*, the *gemara* turns to the *bechor*, which shares a close affinity with *ma'aser*. Unlike *ma'aser*, which the owner designates, the *bechor* is *kadosh meirechem* — the firstborn animal of the flock or herd becomes sanctified automatically at birth. Notably, many *amoraim* hold that there is nonetheless a *mitzvah lehakedisho*, a positive obligation to actively designate and acknowledge the animal's sanctity — a concept structurally parallel to *kiddush* on *Shabbat*, where the day is made holy by the Almighty regardless of human action, yet we are nonetheless commanded to declare and acknowledge that holiness. Rav Soloveitchik develops this parallel at length in the *Shiurim L'zecher Abba Mari*.

The *gemara* proposes: *eima shachatei l'shem bechor* — perhaps if one slaughtered a *korban pesach* with the intent that it be a *bechor*, it should revert to a *bechor* rather than to a *shelamim*. The *halachic* import would be twofold: first, that the offering would not require *nesachim* (which a *korban shelamim* does require but a *bechor* does not); and second, that it would have to be given to the *kohanim* to eat, not to the owner. The *gemara* rejects this by invoking a *gezeira shava* linking *bechor* and *ma'aser*, which appear together at the end of *Parshat Bechukotai* in *Sefer Vayikra*.

### Ma'aser Challenge

The *gemara*'s rejection of the *ma'aser* reversion rests on the same textual proximity: *bechor* and *ma'aser* are linked by *gezeira shava*, and the same logic that dispenses with one applies equally to the other.

### Temurah Challenge

The *gemara* then asks: *ve'eima shachatei l'shem temurah* — what if one slaughtered the animal with intent that it be a *temurah*? All three of *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *temurah* appear together at the end of *Parshat Bechukotai*, which is itself a striking fact worth noting. *Temurah* is not an independent category of *korban* in the usual sense; rather, it is the prohibition against transferring the *kedusha* of a consecrated animal onto a different animal. The *halachic* consequences would be: *lemilka alei* — the slaughterer would be liable to *makkot* for having performed the prohibited exchange; and alternatively, *l'meikam alei b'lo yamir v'lo yiga'el* — the animal would be subject to the rule that once a *temurah* is made, the resulting animal can neither be sold nor redeemed.

Mar Zutra the son of Rav Nachman derives from the *pasuk* — *v'haya hu utmurato yihyeh kodesh*, "it and its exchange shall be holy" — that this applies only to a genuine *temurah*, not to the *korban pesach*. The reading is striking: the *pasuk* on its face affirms that the *temurah* takes effect, yet Mar Zutra uses it to limit *temurah* only to cases of *hu* — the paradigmatic case — excluding the *korban pesach*, which instead reverts to *shelamim*. The *pasuk* is, in effect, being read almost in the opposite direction from its plain sense.

### Toda Challenge

The *gemara* next raises the *toda*: *eima shachatei l'shem Toda* — perhaps the *korban pesach* should revert to a *korban toda*. The suggestion is admittedly strange from the outset, since a *korban pesach* must come from sheep or goats, while a *korban toda* must come from cattle. Any *machshava* to bring a sheep or goat as a *toda* is thus peculiar. Nonetheless the *gemara* entertains it: *d'lehavyei k'Toda*, that it should be treated as a *toda*, the practical consequence being *l'asuyei lechem* — an obligation to bring the forty loaves of bread that accompany the *korban toda*.

### Toda Rejection

The *gemara* rejects this sharply: *mi ika midei d'Pesach gufeih lo ba'ei lechem umotaro ba'ei lechem*? Can it really be that the *pesach* itself requires no bread, yet its *motar* — the leftover animal being brought at the wrong time — would require bread? This is wholly absurd. And notably, the absurdity runs even deeper here, since the *korban toda* includes among its forty loaves ten that are *chametz*, which cannot coexist with any *pesach* context whatsoever.

There is something philosophically interesting lurking beneath this rejection. The question of how much the mistakenly-offered sacrifice retains its original identity versus how much it becomes the new, intended *korban* runs throughout the *sugya*. Here the *gemara* suggests that the original identity is not entirely extinguished — it is absurd to say that a *korban pesach* should suddenly generate a *chiyuv lechem*. The original and the new cannot simply coexist in that way.

The *gemara* then tightens the reasoning further: *mi ika midei d'motar todah atzmah lo ba'ei lechem?* Even the *motar* of a *toda* itself — an animal left over from a *toda* that subsequently reverts to a *shelamim* — does not require bread. All the more so would something associated with a *toda* only by one degree of removal be free from any *chiyuv lechem*. This closes the door on the *toda* suggestion.

The *gemara* then notes the parallel objection regarding *nesachim*: the *pesach* itself does not require *nesachim*, yet once it reverts to *shelamim*, its *motar* does require *nesachim*. The answer offered is *anan hachi ka'amrinan* — this is precisely what we mean. The logic governing *toda* and its *lechem* is not parallel to the logic governing *shelamim* and their *nesachim*, and the two cases must be distinguished.

---

## Three Pesukim

### Asham Challenge

Rav Yeimar the son of Rav Hillel challenges the foundational proof itself. The *gemara* has been relying on the *pasuk* *ve'im min ha'tzon korbano le-zevach shelamim* as establishing that a *korban pesach* reverts to a *korban shelamim*. But Rav Yeimar asks: *u'mimai de-be-motar pesach ketiv* — how do we know that this *pasuk* is speaking about *motar pesach* at all? *Dilma be-motar asham ketiv* — perhaps it is speaking about *motar asham*, an animal designated as a *korban asham* that is being brought outside its proper context. The *korban asham*, after all, also comes exclusively from the flock — specifically, a male ram, an *ayil* — so the *pasuk*'s reference to *min ha'tzon* would fit the *asham* just as well as the *pesach*.

This is a genuinely interesting challenge, since the *korban asham* is in some ways a *korban* without a settled identity: it shares features with the *chatat*, the *olah*, and the *shelamim*, and is frequently in play when the *gemara* tries to determine to which category a *korban* is most closely related. The suggestion here is that the *asham* is most naturally compared to the *shelamim*, and that the *pasuk* might be teaching that a *motar asham* reverts to *shelamim*.

### Rava's Response

Rava responds by reading the *pasuk* more carefully: *ve'im min ha'tzon korbano le-zevach shelamim* — *davar ha-shaveh be-chol ha'tzon*. The *pasuk* must be speaking of something that applies equally to all types of flock, both sheep and goats. The *korban asham*, which can only be brought from a male ram — not from a goat — is far too restricted to fit this characterization. The *korban pesach*, by contrast, may be brought from either sheep or goats, and thus qualifies as something truly *shaveh be-chol ha'tzon*. The *pasuk* therefore cannot be speaking of the *asham*.

### Min as Inclusion

Rav Avin bar Chiya — and some say Rav Avin bar Kahana — raises a different challenge: throughout *halacha*, the word *min* in a *pasuk* serves *lehotsi* — to exclude, to narrow. Here, in *ve'im min ha'tzon*, we are being told that the word *min* serves *lerabot* — to include the *korban pesach* within the *din* of *shelamim*. This is a methodological inconsistency that troubles the *drasha*.

### Min Excludes Age

Rav Mani defends the *drasha*: *hakha nami min lehotsi* — here too, *min* is functioning as an exclusion. Specifically, it excludes *ben shtei shanim* — an animal that is two years old — and *nekevah* — a female animal. A *korban shelamim* may be brought from an older animal or from a female, but a *korban pesach* may not. This *halacha* of the *korban pesach* — that it must be a first-year male — is in fact being derived from this very *pasuk*, which ostensibly discusses *shelamim*. It is a remarkable hermeneutic move: the exclusionary force of *min* teaches a *din* about the *korban pesach* from a *pasuk* that appears to be about something else entirely.

### Rav Chana Challenge

Rav Chana of Baghdad presses a further challenge: if this *pasuk* is truly speaking about *motar pesach*, one must contend with another *pasuk* in *Vayikra* that addresses the *shelamim* by saying *im kesev im ez* — whether a sheep or a goat. The use of *im* in that context should signal that we are simply describing the normal *korban shelamim*, not any reversion from a *korban pesach*.

### Sheep/Goat Rules

The *gemara* resolves this by assigning independent *derashot* to each element. *Kesev* — sheep — teaches that if the *korban pesach* comes from a sheep, its *alyah* (the characteristic fat tail of certain breeds of sheep, which constitutes a form of *chelev*) must also be burned on the *mizbeach* as one of the *chalavim*, just as with any *korban* that comes from a sheep. The *gemara* notes that this is a *halacha* about the *korban pesach* derived from a *pasuk* that appears to be discussing *shelamim*. The word *im kesev* in a second context then teaches that a *pesach* that aged out — that is, became more than a year old — is disqualified. And *ushelamim ha-ba'im machmat pesach* — the *shelamim* that accompanies the *pesach*, namely the *korban chagigah* of the fourteenth of Nisan, the *chagigat arba'ah asar* — is included in all the obligations of a standard *shelamim*: *semikhah*, *nesachim*, *tnufat chazeh va'shok*.

*Im ez* — goats — then serves to break the passage and teach that goats, which lack the distinctive fat tail of sheep, are not subject to the requirement of *alyah* at all. This is a natural exclusion from the rule about sheep.

The *gemara* then notes a potential redundancy: this teaching — that whatever comes from the flock reverts to a *korban shelamim* — also appears to emerge from a teaching of Shmuel's father (*avuh d'Shmuel*), who derives from *ve'im min ha'tzon korbano le-zevach shelamim* that whatever comes from the flock becomes a *shelamim*, specifically including the *korban pesach*. And Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuh derives the same *halacha* from a *pasuk* in *Devarim* — *ve-zavachta pesach la-Hashem Elohecha tzon uvakar* — which says that the *korban pesach* may be from sheep or from cattle, even though in fact a *korban pesach* can only be brought from sheep or goats, not cattle. The *gemara* infers that the mention of cattle must be teaching that *motar ha-pesach* reverts to a *korban* that can be brought from cattle — namely, a *shelamim*.

### Three Cases

The *gemara* now notes that three distinct *pesukim* teach the same principle. Rather than treating this as redundancy, it concludes that each *pasuk* addresses a different scenario of *pesach* disqualification: *chad l'avar zemano* — one for the case where the appointed time has passed; *ve'avar shenato* — and the animal has also aged beyond its first year; *ve'chad l'avar zemano velo shenato* — one for the case where the time has passed but the animal has not yet aged out; and *ve'chad d'lo avar lo zemano velo shenato* — one for the case where neither the time has passed nor the animal has aged out.

### Case Breakdown

The necessity of all three is demonstrated through a *tzrichi* argument. Had the Torah written only the first case — time passed and the animal aged out — one might have thought that reversion to *shelamim* applies only where the animal is doubly disqualified (*tartei l're'uta*) and can serve no further *pesach* purpose whatsoever. Had the Torah written the first two cases together, one might still have excluded the third case: an animal that is still within its first year even after the *pesach* has passed remains eligible for *Pesach Sheni* and retains some connection to its *pesach* identity, so perhaps it does not revert to *shelamim*. And had the Torah addressed only cases where the time has passed, one might have thought that the rule does not apply when the animal is brought *before* the proper time for the *korban pesach* — for instance, on the twelfth of Nisan, when the animal could still be used as a *korban pesach* on the fourteenth. All three *pesukim* are therefore necessary.

Rashi explains that the third case — *d'lo avar lo zemano velo shenato* — refers precisely to a situation where the *korban pesach* animal is slaughtered before *Pesach* as a *shelamim*. The *kohen*, encountering the animal a few days early, brings it as a *shelamim* and it is valid. What the *mishna* means when it says that the *korban pesach* must be brought *lishmah* is therefore quite limited in scope: only on the fourteenth of Nisan must the *korban pesach* be brought with correct intent. At every other time, an animal designated as a *korban pesach* that is slaughtered *shelo lishmah* reverts automatically to a valid *shelamim*. The *halacha* is, in a sense, protective: bring your *pesach* on *Pesach* properly and you fulfill the *mitzvah*; bring it at any other time without the correct intent and it still counts as a valid *shelamim*. Either way the offering is not lost.

One might also ask about redesignation: an owner could simply perform *akirah* — uprooting the *pesach* designation — and formally redesignate the animal as a *shelamim*, a procedure discussed in *Pesachim*. If one was *tamei* and could not bring the *korban pesach* at the proper time, one may use that animal for *Pesach Sheni*, or alternatively bring it as a *shelamim* and bring a different animal on *Pesach Sheni*.

---

## Nesi'im Korbanot

### Nesi'im Problems

The *gemara* now pivots to a discussion prompted by the *korbanot* brought by the *nesi'im* — the tribal princes — during *Chanukat HaMizbeach*, as recorded in *Parshat Naso*. The twelve *nesi'im* brought their offerings on twelve consecutive days. Three difficulties trouble the *mefarshim* and *Chazal* alike. First: how could they have brought personal *korbanot* on *Shabbat*, since some of those twelve days must have fallen on *Shabbat*? Second: how could each *nasi* bring a *korban chatat* if he had not committed any sin obligating him to bring one? Third: how could an individual bring *ketoret* as a personal offering, when *ketoret* is a communal obligation brought twice daily and has no individual counterpart?

One approach — and a compelling *peshat* reading associated with Jacob Milgrom — is that *makriv* in this context means not that the offerings were actually sacrificed on those days, but that they were donated to the *Beit HaMikdash* to stock its stores for the *korbanot* that would follow. This resolves all three problems simultaneously. The word *makriv* usually connotes actual sacrifice, but the reading has considerable contextual merit.

The *gemara* here focuses specifically on the *korban chatat*, each *nasi* having brought one alongside his other offerings during the twelve days of *Chanukat HaMizbeach*. The question is: what is the nature of a *chatat* brought as a *nedava* — as a free-will offering — by someone who has no sin requiring atonement?

### Rav's First Teaching

Rav, quoting from Mavog — an otherwise obscure figure, apparently a city name, quoted by Rav who was himself a student of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — taught: a *chatat* that was slaughtered *leshem chatat Nachshon*, with intent that it be like the *chatat* of Nachshon ben Aminadav (the *nasi* of the tribe of Yehuda, who brought the very first such offering), is *kesheira*. The proof-text is *zot torat ha-chatat* — this is the law of the *chatat* — from which is derived *Torah achat le-chol ha-chata'ot*: a single law governs all *chataot*. On the face of this teaching, it would seem that a free-will *chatat* — not associated with any specific sin — is valid at least *bedi'avad*, and perhaps even beyond the exceptional circumstances of the desert.

---

## Mavog Attempts

### Menachot Parallel

Rav Mesharshiya challenges Rava, who was transmitting this teaching of Rav. He cites the parallel *mishna* in Menachot — which mirrors the opening *mishna* of Zevachim — where Rabbi Shimon rules that all *menachot* whose *kmitza* was performed *shelo lishmah* are *kesheirot* and even discharge the owner's obligation, precisely because *menachot* are not comparable to *zevachim*: *she-ein ha-menachot domot la-zevachim*.

### Menachot Distinction

The *gemara* explains the distinction: in *menachot*, the specific type of *mincha* being offered is identifiable from the *ma'asim* themselves — the actions taken. A *mincha machavat* (griddle-baked) versus a *mincha meracheshet* (pan-baked) are distinguishable by the manner of preparation; a dry *mincha* (*charivah*) versus one mixed with oil (*belulah*) is similarly self-evident from how it is made. Thus *ma'aseha mochi'chin aleha* — the actions testify to the nature of the offering, even if the stated intent was for a different type of *mincha*. In *zevachim*, by contrast, all animal sacrifices share the same *shechita*, the same *kabala*, and ostensibly the same *zrika* — and so the intent of the slaughterer governs in a way it does not for *menachot*. The *gemara* acknowledges — and this is somewhat difficult — that in practice different *zevachim* do have different *zrikot*, but the principle stands for purposes of this discussion.

The upshot of Rav Mesharshiya's challenge is that the *pasuk* *zot torat ha-chatat* parallels *zot torat ha-mincha*, and if the latter does not establish a blanket equivalence between all *menachot* (since we know there are *halachic* differences depending on intent), then the former cannot establish a blanket equivalence between all *chataot* either. The proof offered by Mavog is therefore flawed.

The *gemara* responds: *ela i itmar hachi itmar* — if this teaching was transmitted, it must have been transmitted in a different form. This introduces the second version.

### Wrong Owner

Second version: Rav, quoting Mavog, taught that a *chatat* slaughtered *al m'nat she-yitkaper bah Nachshon* — with intent that it effect atonement for Nachshon ben Aminadav — is *kesheira*. This is a case of *shinui be'alim* — the *kohen* had in mind the wrong owner. Here, crucially, the real owner is alive and has sinned, and the *kohen* during the *shechita* had in mind Nachshon ben Aminadav, who is long dead. Since *ein kapara la-metim* — the dead cannot achieve *kapara* — the intended *shinui be'alim* to a dead person is effectively no *shinui be'alim* at all, because the *ba'al* one is attempting to designate it for does not exist in any meaningful *halachic* sense. The offering therefore remains valid, though it does not achieve *kapara* for the actual owner, who must bring a new *korban chatat*. The *kohanim* may still eat it.

One might ask why Mavog did not simply say *met* — a dead person generally — rather than specifically Nachshon. The *gemara* explains: had he said *met* generically, one might have inferred that only in the case of a dead person does the *shinui be'alim* fail to disqualify, but that if the mistaken person were living — like Nachshon — the *korban* would be *pasul*. By specifying Nachshon, Mavog implies that the case parallels Nachshon in some way, which leads the *gemara* to ask: what makes someone *chai dumya d'Nachshon*? A living person who had no sin requiring a *chatat* — as was the case with Nachshon's offering. And if such a person were the intended (but erroneous) owner, it would also render the *korban pasul*. The examples of such a person are *chatat Nazir* and *chatat Metzora* — chataot that are not brought for a sin in the usual sense, but for a process of purification, and which the *gemara* accordingly characterizes as comparable to *olot* (*hanei olot ninhu*).

### Obligated Person

Third version: Rav, quoting Mavog, taught that a *chatat* slaughtered *al mi she-mechuyav chatat keNachshon* — on behalf of someone obligated in a *chatat* comparable to that of Nachshon — is *kesheira*. This formulation is difficult to parse: the whole premise of the discussion is that Nachshon was *not* obligated to bring a *chatat* in the conventional sense, having committed no sin. The text here is acknowledged to be obscure. What seems to be meant is that this version attempts to identify a person whose obligation in a *chatat* is structurally unusual — analogous to the nature of Nachshon's *chatat* — and teaches that bringing a *chatat* on such a person's behalf is nonetheless valid. The objection raised is that *chatat Nachshon olah hi* — Nachshon's *chatat* functioned like an *olah*, a gift rather than an atonement — and since *chatat Nazir* and *chatat Metzora* are similarly characterized as *olot*, one could have derived this ruling from those cases instead. The *gemara* responds that Mavog preferred to cite a paradigmatic *chatat* (*ikar chatat nakat*) rather than the unusual edge cases of Nazir and Metzora.

### Wrong Sin Type

Fourth version — and the *gemara* introduces this as *ika de'amri*, a variant tradition: Rav, quoting Mavog, taught the opposite — that a *chatat* slaughtered *leshem chatat Nachshon* is *pesulah*. This version resolves all the difficulties that burdened the previous three attempts. The *chatat* of Nachshon, having been brought as a free-will offering without an underlying obligating sin, is characterized as *chatat Nachshon olah hi* — it is functionally an *olah*, not a genuine *chatat*. An offering brought *leshem chatat* but for what is really an *olah* is *pasul*. This is clean and consistent, and dispenses with the need for the elaborate explanations required by the first three versions.

---

## Chatat Interchanges

### Chatat Categories

The *gemara* records a second teaching of Rav: *chatat cheilev she-shachatah l'shem chatat dam* — a *chatat* brought for the sin of eating forbidden fat, slaughtered with intent that it be for the sin of eating blood; or *l'shem chatat avodat kochavim* — for the sin of idolatry committed unwittingly (which obligates a *korban*) — is *kesheira*. Interchanging one sin-*chatat* for another sin-*chatat* does not disqualify the offering.

### Nazir/Metzora

However, *l'shem chatat Nazir v'chatat Metzora* — if one brought a *chatat cheilev* with intent that it be the *chatat* of a *nazir* or *metzora* — it is *pesulah*. This is because, as established, *hanei olot ninhu*: those *chataot* function like *olot*, not like sin-*chataot* in the full sense, and interchanging a real *chatat* with what is effectively an *olah* is a disqualifying *shinui kodesh*.

### Rava's Question

Rava poses a question: *chatat cheilev she-shachatah l'shem chatat d'tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* — what is the law if one brought a *chatat cheilev* with intent that it be a *chatat* for the sin of *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav* (entering the *Beit HaMikdash* or eating consecrated food while *tamei*)? The latter sin is atoned for by a *korban oleh v'yored* — a variable offering whose form depends on the owner's financial circumstances, as discussed in Masechet Shavuot. The question is: *mi amrinan karet k'motah* — do we say that since both *chatat cheilev* and *tumat mikdash* carry liability for *karet*, they are sufficiently equivalent that the interchange does not disqualify? Or do we say *ein kevua k'motah* — a fixed-form *chatat* and a variable *korban oleh v'yored* are structurally different enough that interchanging them constitutes a disqualifying *shinui kodesh*?

### Shinuy Be'alim

Rav Ashi asks Rav Acha the son of Rava how his father Rava's question was being transmitted. Rav Acha responds that when he taught the preceding material, he taught it entirely as a matter of *shinui be'alim* — change of owner — not *shinui kodesh*. That is, Rava's teaching about the various *chatat* interchanges concerned cases where the *korban* was brought on behalf of the wrong person, not cases where one *korban* type was substituted for another. Accordingly, Rava's question was also about *shinui be'alim*: if a *chatat cheilev* was brought *al mishum mechuyav chatat dam* or *chatat avodat kochavim* — on behalf of a person obligated in one of those *chataot* — it is *pesulah*; but if brought *al mishum mechuyav chatat Nazir ve-chatat Metzora* — on behalf of a person whose obligation is of the *olah*-like variety — it is *kesheira*.

### Karait Equivalence

Rava's question, reframed in terms of *shinui be'alim*, becomes: if a *chatat cheilev* is brought on behalf of someone obligated in a *chatat* for *tumat mikdash ve-kodashav*, what is the law? *Mi amrinan karet kevosah* — do we say that since both offenses carry *karet*, the persons obligated in each are sufficiently equivalent that there is no meaningful *shinui be'alim*? Or does the fact that one *chatat* is *kevuah* (fixed) and the other is not (*ein kevuah kevosah*) mean that even in terms of *be'alim* these persons are categorically different?

### Teiku

The question was left unresolved in the time of Rav Ashi. What the discussion does clarify is that Rav Acha the son of Rava reframed his father's question from *shinui kodesh* to *shinui be'alim*, and it is in that reframing that the *teiku* stands. Rabbi Linzer will continue from the *itmar* at the bottom of the *amud*.

---

---

# Zevachim 10

## Shelo Lishmah Overview

### Opening

Today's daf is daf 10. We pick up four lines from the bottom of 9b, in the midst of an extended exploration of what constitutes *shelo lishmah* and its various gradations.

### Previous Day Review

At the close of yesterday's discussion, the *Gemara* examined cases where the intent is directed toward the wrong person — specifically, where the *kohen* performs the service with a person in mind who is obligated not a *chatas* but an *olah*. In such a case, the intent is so irrelevant to the actual *korban* that it does not invalidate. The *Gemara* also considered intermediate cases — from one *chatas* to another *chatas*, from a *chatas* to an *olah* — probing the degrees at which *shelo lishmah* crosses from valid to invalid. With those degrees established, we now turn to a different dimension of the problem: not what kind of intent, but *when* the intent occurs relative to the *avodah* it concerns.

---

## Machshava Me'avodah L'av…

### Shechita for Zrika Shelo…

The *Gemara* introduces a new case: *shachata lishmo lizrok damo shelo lishmo* — one slaughtered a *chatas* with proper intent for the *shechita* itself, but with a plan that when the time comes to throw the blood, he will do so with the intent of an *olah*. The *shechita* is performed correctly in the present; the problematic intention is directed at a future *avodah*. The question is whether this forward-looking *machshavah*, held at the moment of *shechita*, invalidates the *korban*.

### R. Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *psulah* — it is invalid. His principle is *machshavim me'avodah l'avodah*: a *machshavah* formed during one *avodah* can be operative with respect to a different *avodah*. Therefore, thinking during *shechita* that one will perform the *zrikas hadam shelo lishmah* is sufficient to invalidate the *korban* at that moment. Rabbi Yochanan derives this principle from the model of *piggul*: the verse *lo yei'chashev lo piggul hu* is read by *Chazal* as centering on thought — when performing an *avodah*, one's intention to perform the *achilah* component (whether the throwing of the blood, the burning of the *emurim*, or human consumption of the meat) at the wrong time invalidates. This is precisely a case of a *machshavah* about a future *avodah* operating to invalidate the present act.

### Piggul as Model

Rashi is careful to clarify that the *vav* introducing this point connects rather than contrasts: Rabbi Yochanan's position and the *piggul* model are one and the same argument. The structure of *piggul* is instructive. Classic *piggul* cannot arise from performing an act at the wrong time — if one waits until the next day to throw the blood, the *korban* is already *nosar*. Rather, *piggul* operates precisely when the *avodah* is performed at the correct time, but the *kohen*'s intention is to perform a subsequent *achilah* act — throwing the blood, burning the *emurim*, or eating the meat — at the wrong time. It is an intention about a *future* act that retroactively defines the present one.

However, Rashi further notes a tension within this model that will become central to Reish Lakish's critique. The *machshavah* that generates *piggul* concerns acts that are not necessarily the critical *avodos* that render the *korban kasher* — it can concern the human eating of the meat, which is not itself one of the four essential *avodos*. Moreover, if one were to slaughter with the intent that the *shechita itself* be *shelo bizmano* — e.g., explicitly declaring "I am slaughtering this as a nighttime *shechita*" — that thought does not generate *piggul* and does not invalidate. *Piggul* is not created by a mistaken intention about the act being performed; it is created only by an intention about a *future* act.

### Reish Lakish Position

Reish Lakish rules: *kesherah* — it is valid. His principle is the mirror image: *ein machshavim me'avodah l'avodah* — a *machshavah* about one *avodah* does not import itself into and invalidate a different *avodah*. Accordingly, he rejects the *piggul* model.

### Piggul vs Shelo Lishmah

The basis of Reish Lakish's rejection is precisely the asymmetry Rashi identified. *Piggul* is a category unto itself: the problematic thought is specifically about a *future* act, and that future act need not even be one of the critical *avodos* — it can be the eating of the meat. The structure of *piggul* is therefore not analogous to *shelo lishmah*. In *shelo lishmah*, the question is whether thinking during *shechita* about performing *zrika shelo lishmah* — where *zrika* is itself an act that *shelo lishmah* would invalidate — should carry over. But *piggul* is defined uniquely: it is only operative when one performs a critical act at the proper time with an intention about a future consumption-type act. The fact that having a *machshavah* of *shelo bizmano* on the *shechita itself* does not invalidate shows that *piggul* operates in a manner entirely its own, not as a general precedent for *machshavah me'avodah l'avodah*.

---

## Avodas Zarah Parallel

### Shechita for Avodas Zarah

The *Gemara* presents a parallel case: *hashochet et habeheimah al menat l'hazrik damah l'avodas kochavim ulehaktir chelba l'avodas kochavim* — one slaughters an animal not with the present intention of offering it to *avodas zarah*, but with the plan that when he gets to the blood-throwing or the burning of the *chelev*, he will direct those acts as an offering to *avodas zarah*. The question is whether this plan, held at the time of *shechita*, constitutes sufficient *tikrovet avodas zarah* to render the animal forbidden in benefit — even if he never actually follows through.

As Tosafot notes, one might think the act of *shechita* itself with this intent already constitutes a performative act of *avodas zarah* for which one would be liable. But setting that aside, the distinct question here is whether the plan for the future *avodah* defines the *animal's* status at the moment of *shechita*.

### R. Yochanan Avodas Zarah

Rabbi Yochanan rules the animal is *asur* — forbidden. His reasoning: *machshavim me'avodah l'avodah*, and one may apply the *piggul* model across contexts, learning from what occurs inside the *Beis Hamikdash* to define the status of an act performed outside it (*chutz mipnim*). The intention for a future act of *avodas zarah* is sufficient to define the *shechita* as an act of *tikrovet avodas zarah*.

### Reish Lakish Avodas Zarah

Reish Lakish rules the animal is *muteres* — permitted. *Ein machshavim me'avodah l'avodah*, and one does not import rules of *avodas zarah* from the *piggul* model of the *Beis Hamikdash*. The categories are sufficiently different that the precedent does not transfer.

### Why Both Cases Needed

The *Gemara* establishes that both formulations of the dispute are necessary. Had only the *avodas zarah* case been stated, one might have said that Reish Lakish's leniency stems specifically from the fact that *avodas zarah* is not a *Beis Hamikdash* act — one would not learn it from *piggul*, a *pnim* principle, for a *chutz* context. But perhaps in the purely *Mikdash* context of *shelo lishmah*, Reish Lakish would concede to Rabbi Yochanan. Conversely, had only the *shelo lishmah* case been stated, one might have said that Rabbi Yochanan's stringency is specific to two *Mikdash* principles being compared, but he might concede to Reish Lakish in the *avodas zarah* case. Both cases must therefore be stated explicitly to establish that the dispute runs through both.

---

## Rav Yirmiya's Piggul Pro…

### Rav Dimi Report

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported that the debate had continued there with advocates taking sides. Rav Yirmiya brought a proof to support Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Ila brought a proof to support Reish Lakish.

### Rav Yirmiya Support

Rav Yirmiya's approach is to construct a *kal vachomer* from the *piggul* model rather than simply invoking it as a parallel. By examining the internal structure of *piggul*, he attempts to build an argument that is logically compelling independent of whether *piggul* is a perfect analogue.

### Piggul Kal V'Chomer

The *kal vachomer* runs as follows: in the case of *piggul*, if one slaughters and declares "I am slaughtering this as *shelo bizmano*" — treating the present *shechita* as though it were a night-time *shechita* — that declaration is meaningless and the *korban* remains valid. The thought about the present act in the wrong-time register does not invalidate. Yet if one slaughters *al menat lizrok damo chutz lizmano* — with the intent to throw the blood at the wrong time — that does invalidate, generating *piggul*. So: in the world of *piggul*, a *machshavah* about a future act is more powerful than a *machshavah* about the current act.

Now apply this to *shelo lishmah*: in the *shelo lishmah* world, if one slaughters and declares "I am slaughtering this as *shelo lishmah*," that *does* invalidate — the thought about the current act works. *A fortiori*, if a *machshavah* about a future *avodah* is in the *piggul* context more powerful than the thought about the current act, then in the *shelo lishmah* context — where the thought about the current act already invalidates — certainly a *machshavah* about the future *zrika shelo lishmah* should also invalidate.

---

## Piggul Weightiness Issue

### Kares Distinction

Rava bar Ahilai challenges this *kal vachomer*. The issue is not the uniqueness of *piggul*'s structure per se, but that *piggul* is a categorically weightier legal category. When one performs *shechita* with intent to do *zrika shelo bizmano*, he transgresses a *lav* by generating *piggul*. But more significantly, once the animal becomes *piggul*, one who eats its meat is *chayav kares*. By contrast, *shelo lishmah* invalidates the *korban* but eating it does not incur *kares*. Since the *piggul* world carries *kares* and is therefore weightier, its laws may be stricter — one cannot derive that what applies in the *piggul* context must equally apply in the comparatively lighter *shelo lishmah* context.

### Chutz Limkomo Alternative

The *Gemara* therefore proposes replacing *piggul* with *chutz limkomo* as the basis of the *kal vachomer*. *Chutz limkomo* follows precisely the same structural rules as *chutz lizmano* — a *machshavah* during an earlier *avodah* to perform a later *achilah* act in the wrong place renders the *korban pasul* — but without the *kares* consequence. If one performs *shechita* with the intent to sprinkle the blood outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, or to eat the meat outside its proper location, the *korban* is *pasul*, but eating it does not incur *kares*. The *kal vachomer* from *chutz limkomo* thus avoids the *kares* objection entirely.

---

## Rav Ashi's Chutz Limkomo…

### Chutz Limkomo Model

The refined *kal vachomer* proceeds: by *chutz limkomo*, if one performs *shechita* declaring "I am slaughtering this as *chutz limkomo*" — treating the present *shechita* as though it were being done outside its proper location — that is meaningless and the *korban* is valid. The *machshavah* about the current act in the wrong-place register does not invalidate. Yet if one slaughters with the intent to throw the blood in the wrong place, the *korban* is *pasul*. Again, a *machshavah* about a future act is more powerful than a *machshavah* about the current act.

### Chutz Limkomo to Shelo L…

Applied to *shelo lishmah*: since a *machshavah shelo lishmah* about the current act of *shechita does* invalidate, certainly a *machshavah* about performing the future *zrika shelo lishmah* should also invalidate — in parallel with what we observe by *chutz limkomo* where the future-directed thought is more powerful.

---

## Rav Pappa's Challenge

### All Korbanos Affected

Rav Pappa challenges this *kal vachomer* on grounds of comparative weight. *Chutz limkomo*, he argues, is a weightier category than *shelo lishmah* in a specific respect: *chutz limkomo* applies to and invalidates all sacrifices — *olah*, *shelamim*, across the full range of *korbanos*. The *parasha* of *piggul* is principally discussed in the context of *shelamim*, but the principle of wrong-place thought applies universally.

### Limited Application

*Shelo lishmah*, by contrast, only invalidates two specific *korbanos*: *pesach* and *chatas*. All other *korbanos* — *olah*, *shelamim*, *asham* — are valid whether performed *lishmah* or *shelo lishmah*. Because *shelo lishmah* is therefore a less pervasive and less weighty category, it does not necessarily follow that it must possess the same feature of *machshavah me'avodah l'avodah* that *chutz limkomo* possesses by virtue of its universal application.

---

## Shelo Lishem Baalim Model

### Baalim vs Lishmah

Rav Ashi reformulates the argument on entirely different grounds, drawing a model not from *piggul* or *chutz limkomo* but from within the *shelo lishmah* world itself — specifically from the category of *shelo lishmah baalim*. To understand this, one must recall the *drashos* earlier in the *masechta*: the *psukim* teaching *shelo lishem baalim* are built around the phrase *l'chaper alav* — to atone *for him*. The word *l'chaper* points to *zrikas hadam* as the central act of atonement, and *alav* points to the *baalim*, the owner. Since the verse anchors the *baalim* requirement in the *zrika*, what is invalidated by *shelo lishem baalim* at the earlier *avodos* is specifically a *shechita* — or *kabala* or *holacha* — performed with an *intention* directed at the *zrika*: I am doing this *shechita* now with the plan to do the *zrika l'shem Shimon* (when the *korban* belongs to Reuven). That, and only that, constitutes *shechita shelo lishem baalim*. A plain *shechita* for Shimon's name, without any intention about the *zrika*, does not invalidate.

### Baalim Machshava Pattern

This structural point is crucial: *shelo lishem baalim* at the earlier *avodos* is not simply a mislabeling of the current act. It requires a *machshavah* specifically about the *zrika* — I am doing this *shechita* now with the intention that the *zrika* will be for the wrong person. This is precisely the same formal structure as the question under debate regarding *shelo lishmah*: does a *machshavah* during *shechita* about performing the *zrika shelo lishmah* carry operative legal weight?

### Lishmah Kal V'Chomer

The *kal vachomer* is now formulated with precision. By *shelo lishem baalim*: if one declares at *shechita* "I am doing this *shechita lishem Shimon*" — wrong person, current act — the *korban* is valid. This mislabeling of the present act does not invalidate. Yet if one does the *shechita* with the intent to do the *zrika lishem ploni* — wrong person, future act — that does invalidate. So even in the *shelo lishmah* world itself, a *machshavah* about a future *avodah* carries more force than a *machshavah* about the current one.

Now: if a *machshavah shelo lishmah* on the *shechita* itself invalidates, and we know from *shelo lishem baalim* that a future-directed *machshavah* is even more powerful than a current-act *machshavah* — certainly a *machshavah* during *shechita* to perform the *zrika shelo lishmah* should invalidate. This *kal vachomer* operates entirely within the *shelo lishmah* framework, does not depend on *piggul* or *chutz limkomo*, and is not vulnerable to the objections of *kares* or universal applicability. It remains without a rebuttal.

---

## Rav Ila's Textual Defense

### Zrika Redundancy Question

Rav Ila mounts a textual defense of Reish Lakish. The *Gemara* notes that we have explicit *psukim* teaching *shelo lishmah* at *shechita*, at *kabala*, at *holacha*, and at *zrika*. The question arises: why did the Torah need to state *shelo lishmah* separately at *zrika*? Given that we already have *shelo lishmah* taught at *shechita* and *kabala*, one could have inferred *zrika* from a *kal vachomer*: if *shelo lishmah* invalidates at those earlier *avodos*, certainly it should invalidate at *zrika*, which is the more weighty act — it is the central act of *kapara* and carries the added *psul* of *shelo lishem baalim* and all that flows from it.

Note: why couldn't we have inferred *zrika* from *shechita* alone? Because *shechita shelo lishmah* has its own particular source in the *korban pesach* requirement (*le'ochlav*, etc.), which is unique to *shechita*. And why not from *kabala* alone? Because there would have been grounds to distinguish *kabala* in ways that would prevent the inference to *zrika*. But between *shechita* and *kabala* together, for a *shelamim* (which is the context of these *psukim*), one could certainly infer *zrika*. So why did the Torah state it explicitly?

### Limiting Interpretation

Rav Ila's answer: the Torah's explicit mention of *shelo lishmah* at *zrika* is not expansive but limiting. It comes to tell us that *zrika* has its own *shelo lishmah* requirement — meaning, the *machshavah* must occur *during* the *zrika* itself. The extra word by *zrika* teaches: *ein machshavim me'avodah l'avodah* — a *machshavah* about *zrika* held during an earlier *avodah* does not invalidate. Only a *machshavah* during the *zrika* itself counts.

### Expansion Challenge

The *Gemara* challenges this reading. Perhaps the Torah's explicit inclusion of *zrika* is not limiting but expanding. Perhaps it is teaching precisely the opposite: that a *machshavah* about *zrika* is operative even when held at an earlier stage, thereby *expanding* the scope of when *shelo lishmah* applies. On this reading, the extra word supports Rabbi Yochanan, not Reish Lakish.

### Limiting Conclusion

The *Gemara* responds: given the power of Rav Ashi's *kal vachomer* from *shelo lishem baalim*, it would have been natural — without any additional *pasuk* — to conclude that a *machshavah* during *shechita* to perform *zrika shelo lishmah* invalidates, in direct parallel with the established *halacha* of *shelo lishem baalim*. One would have reached Rabbi Yochanan's position as the natural inference. Since the Torah nevertheless went out of its way to state *shelo lishmah* by *zrika* explicitly, that cannot be mere confirmation of what was already inferrable. It must be a limiting statement: only the *machshavah* during the *zrika itself* invalidates; a *machshavah* about *zrika* held at an earlier *avodah* does not.

The *Gemara* then records the back-and-forth between the positions regarding whether the *psukim* of *shechita* and *kabala* were already sufficient to infer *zrika*. The counter-argument notes that *shechita* and *kabala* of a *chatas* are weightier in certain respects — they must be performed at the north of the *mizbeiach* (*te'un tzafon*), and these *avodos* apply even in the context of inner *chataos* brought in the inner sanctuary — whereas *zrika* on the outer *mizbeiach* has neither characteristic. One might therefore not have inferred *zrika* from *shechita* and *kabala* at all. The rejoinder: but we are discussing *shelamim*, not *chatas*, and in the world of *shelamim* there is no *te'un tzafon*. Therefore the Torah indeed could have remained silent about *zrika* and it would have been inferred. The Torah's explicit statement at *zrika* must therefore carry the limiting message Reish Lakish proposes: only a *machshavah* at the moment of *zrika* invalidates — not a *machshavah* about *zrika* imported from an earlier stage.

---

## Rav Nachman & Rava

### Rav Nachman Position

The practical *halacha* among the Babylonian *Amoraim* is then recorded. Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi Yochanan: *psula* — the *korban* is invalid.

### Rava Retraction

Rava initially rules like Reish Lakish — *kesherah* — but subsequently retracts and adopts Rav Nachman's position.

### Rava's Reason

The reason for Rava's retraction is the force of Rav Ashi's *kal vachomer* from *shelo lishem baalim*. The argument is straightforward and compelling: we see in the established *halacha* of *shelo lishem baalim* that a *machshavah* during *shechita* directed at the *zrika* invalidates, even though a *machshavah shelo lishem baalim* on the *shechita* itself does not. If this is true in the *baalim* dimension, it should be equally true in the *lishmah* dimension — certainly when a *machshavah shelo lishmah* on the *shechita* itself already invalidates, a *machshavah* about performing the *zrika shelo lishmah* at the time of *shechita* should invalidate as well. This *kal vachomer*, operating entirely within the existing *shelo lishmah* framework and requiring no external model, persuaded Rava to retract.

It bears noting: this principle applies specifically to *zrika*. The unique legal force of *zrika* — *lizrok damo l'chaper alav* — is what underlies *shelo lishem baalim*. It is not a general rule that any *machshavah* about any future *avodah* imports itself into the current one; it is specifically a *machshavah* about *zrika* that carries this power at the earlier stages.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Asham Proof

### Asham-Chatas Link

The *Gemara* now turns to the position of Rabbi Eliezer in the *Mishna*, who states that an *asham* is analogous to a *chatas*. The *Gemara* cites a *braisa* that elaborates.

### Rabbi Eliezer Argument

Rabbi Eliezer argues: *chatas* comes for sin and *asham* comes for sin; just as a *chatas shelo lishmah* is *pasul*, so too an *asham shelo lishmah* is *pasul*. The logic is intuitive — a *chatas*'s entire identity is bound up with atonement for a specific person's specific sin; once it is performed with a different identity in mind, it is disconnected from its purpose. Rabbi Eliezer maintains that the same is true of an *asham*, and he has the verse *kachatas ka'asham* as explicit textual support linking the two.

---

## Blood Location Distincti…

### Above vs Below Line

Rabbi Yehoshua responds to Rabbi Eliezer's initial argument by pointing to a distinction between *chatas* and *asham* regarding the placement of blood on the *mizbeiach*. The *mizbeiach* has a midpoint marker called the *chut hasikra* — the red line. Blood of a *chatas* is placed at the four *karnos* — the corners of the *mizbeiach* — which are above this line. Blood of most other *korbanos*, including *asham*, goes below the line. *Olas ha-of* goes above. The *chatas* is thus categorically distinct in its blood service, and perhaps it is precisely this distinction — reflecting the unique weightiness of *chatas* — that underlies its *shelo lishmah* invalidation. An *asham*, whose blood goes below, cannot simply be equated with it.

### Pesach Counterexample

Rabbi Eliezer counters: *pesach yochiach* — the *korban pesach* proves otherwise. A *pesach shelo lishmah* is also *pasul*, yet the blood of *pesach* goes below the line. Therefore, being above or below the line is not what determines whether *shelo lishmah* invalidates. You cannot use the blood-placement distinction to differentiate *asham* from *chatas*.

### Fixed Time Argument

Rabbi Yehoshua responds: *pesach* has a fixed time — it can only be brought at the appointed moment — and perhaps that unique characteristic accounts for the stringency of *shelo lishmah* by *pesach*, not the above/below distinction. An *asham*, which has no fixed time, cannot be derived from either *chatas* or *pesach*.

### Circular Reasoning

Rabbi Eliezer counters by returning to *chatas*: a *chatas* has no fixed time, so one cannot blame the *pesach* stringency on its fixed time. This is the classic *chozer hadin* — he wants to eliminate each distinctive characteristic through the other example, leaving a common denominator. Don't say it's about being above the line — *pesach* proves otherwise. Don't say it's about a fixed time — *chatas* proves otherwise. What remains must be the relevant factor.

### Common Denominator Need

Rabbi Yehoshua's response — *chozarni chalila*, "I have gone in a circle" — sounds, on the surface, like an admission of defeat. But the *Gemara* will explain that it is in fact a calculated move: by noting that the *chozer hadin* leads in a circle, Rabbi Yehoshua is flagging that no valid *tzad hashaveh* can be constructed from this pair.

---

## Hirhurim/Hu Proof

### Hu Word Proof

Rabbi Eliezer pivots to a textual argument. The Torah uses the word *hi* (or *hu*) in proximity to each of these three *korbanos*: *chatas hi* by the *chatas*, *zevach pesach hu* by *pesach*, and *asham hu* / *asham asham l'Hashem* by *asham*. The word *hu* or *hi* signals that the *korban* must be what it is — it must be performed as that which it is designated. The *Gemara* earlier established that *hi lishma kesherah shelo lishma psula* — only when the *korban* is done *lishmah* is it valid. Since all three *korbanos* carry this formulation, Rabbi Eliezer argues that all three should be invalid *shelo lishmah*.

### Timing Distinction

Rabbi Yehoshua distinguishes. By *chatas*, the word *hi* appears at the moment of *shechita* — the verse *shachato osah l'chatas* and *chatas hi* — so the *hu/hi* word applies precisely at the *avodah* that can be rendered *shelo lishmah*. By *pesach* as well, *zevach pesach hu* appears in the context of the *shechita*. But by *asham*, Rabbi Yehoshua argues, the word *asham hu* appears only after the description of the burning of the *emurim*.

### Too Late to Invalidate

By the time the *emurim* are burned, one has already passed through the four critical *avodos*. At that stage, *shelo lishmah* can no longer invalidate — the *korban* is already complete with respect to the blood service.
