Moreover, even if the *emurim* themselves were never burned, the *korban* would still be valid. The *hu* by *asham* therefore cannot serve as a source for *shelo lishmah* invalidation, because it appears at a point in the verse where such invalidation is no longer relevant.

---

## Explicit Verse Link

### Ka-Chatas Ka-Asham

Rabbi Eliezer offers a third and final proof. The Torah contains an explicit verse that links *asham* directly to *chatas* using the words *kachatas ka'asham*: just as a *chatas*, so too an *asham*. From this explicit equation, Rabbi Eliezer derives: just as *chatas shelo lishmah* is *pasul*, so too *asham shelo lishmah* is *pasul*. This is not an inferential analogy requiring one to navigate distinguishing characteristics — it is a direct textual linkage.

### No Response

The *braisa* records no response from Rabbi Yehoshua to this third proof. The structure of the *braisa* thus presents Rabbi Eliezer's position as prevailing by the third argument, even if the first two were successfully parried.

---

## Tzad Hashaveh Analysis

### Common Denominator Setup

The *Gemara* now unpacks what was happening in the back-and-forth between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. When Rabbi Yehoshua said *chozarni chalila* — "we have gone in a circle" — he was not simply complaining about circularity. He was strategically identifying that the *chozer hadin* Rabbi Eliezer was attempting requires a valid *tzad hashaveh*, and the *tzad hashaveh* here is vulnerable.

### Tzad Hashaveh Method

The *tzad hashaveh* method works by taking two cases, eliminating each one's distinguishing characteristics through the other, and identifying what they share in common. If that common denominator is what underlies the *halacha* in both, one can apply it to a third case. Rabbi Eliezer was using *chatas* and *pesach* as his two cases: don't blame the *shelo lishmah* stringency on being above the line (*chatas*), because *pesach* proves otherwise; don't blame it on a fixed time (*pesach*), because *chatas* proves otherwise. What remains is: both are *korbanos* that come for sin, and both are *shelo lishmah pasul* — therefore *asham*, which also comes for sin, should be *shelo lishmah pasul*.

### Kares Concern

Rabbi Yehoshua's real counterpoint was that the common denominator between *chatas* and *pesach* is not merely "comes for sin" — it is that both are connected to *kares*. A *chatas* atones for a sin punishable by *kares* (at least in the paradigmatic case), and failure to bring a *korban pesach* incurs *kares*. Their shared connection to *kares* may be what lends them the stringency of *shelo lishmah*. An *asham* carries no such connection to *kares*, and therefore cannot be derived from this *tzad hashaveh*. This is what Rabbi Yehoshua meant: by pointing to *kares* as the true common denominator, he shows that the *tzad hashaveh* cannot extend to *asham*.

---

## Blood Location Justifica…

### Location vs Other Factors

The *Gemara* now examines why Rabbi Yehoshua specifically chose the above/below-line distinction as his initial pushback against Rabbi Eliezer, rather than any number of other ways in which a *chatas* is demonstrably weightier than an *asham*. One might have thought: why focus on above and below the line? Is that really the most significant distinguishing feature?

The *Gemara* considers several alternatives. Why not say that a *chatas* is weightier because in certain cases (*chataos penimiyos*) its blood is brought into the inner sanctuary — *lifnai v'lifnim*? The answer: we are speaking of the *chatas hachitzonah*, the *chatas* whose blood is applied to the outer *mizbeiach*, and those *chataos* do not have that characteristic. Why not point to the *halacha* that if the blood of a *chatas* is brought into the *Heichal*, the *korban* is invalidated — *kol chatas asher yuva midamah el ohel mo'ed lachaper bakodesh lo te'achel ba'esh tisaref* — a stringency that does not apply to the blood of an *olah* or other *korbanos*? Here, however, the *Gemara* notes that Rabbi Eliezer, who consistently links *asham* to *chatas*, would himself say the same *halacha* applies to *asham* — if *asham* blood were brought into the *Heichal*, it too would be invalidated. So Rabbi Yehoshua could not use that as an asymmetric distinguishing feature.

### Alternative Distinctions

The *Gemara* continues to consider other potential distinctions. Why not say *chatas* is weightier because it is associated with sins of *kerisos* — atonement for sins punishable by excision? Rabbi Eliezer counters: there are *chataos* that come for non-*kares* sins — such as the *chatas* of *shemiat hakol* (oath relating to testimony), which is not a *kares* sin. So one cannot say the *shelo lishmah* stringency of *chatas* is rooted in its connection to *kares* sins.

Why not say *chatas* is weightier because it requires *arba matanos* — four separate applications of blood, one at each corner? The *Gemara* asks why Rabbi Yehoshua did not use this feature. The answer: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer holds like Rabbi Yishmael, who maintains that all blood applications — not just *chatas* — require four separate acts of throwing. If one follows Rabbi Yishmael's view, both *chatas* and other *korbanos* each receive four separate blood applications, so this feature would not differentiate *chatas* as uniquely weighty.

### Multiple Options Availab…

The *Gemara* concludes: there are indeed many ways one could demonstrate that a *chatas* is weightier than an *asham* — among them the four *karnos* (as opposed to two-that-are-four), the application with a finger (*etzba*), the placement at the *keren* specifically, the precise edge (*huda*) of the *keren*. Rabbi Yehoshua could have chosen any of these. He chose the above/below-the-line distinction as one example from among several available arguments. *Chada mi'trei tlas ta'ami nakat* — he selected one from two or three possible reasons.

---

## Asham Below Line Logic

### Expected Objection

The *Gemara* now raises a question about Rabbi Eliezer's silence. Given that Rabbi Eliezer consistently wants to make an *asham* equivalent to a *chatas*, why did he not simply respond to Rabbi Yehoshua's blood-placement argument by saying: I maintain that the blood of an *asham* should also go above the line? If *asham* is like *chatas* in matters of *shelo lishmah*, why not also in blood placement?

### Olah Kal V'Chomer

Abbaye explains that Rabbi Eliezer could not make this move, because a *kal vachomer* from *olah* precludes it. An *olah* is entirely consumed — *kalil* — the entire animal is burned on the *mizbeiach*, making it the most weighty *korban* in terms of its complete dedication to Heaven. Yet even the *olah*'s blood goes below the line. An *asham*, which is not *kalil*, most certainly should be below the line as well. This *kal vachomer* prevents Rabbi Eliezer from claiming the *asham* blood goes above.

### Not About Atonement

The *Gemara* questions whether one can push back against this *kal vachomer*: perhaps the reason *chatas* blood goes above the line is specifically because *chatas* atones, and an *olah*, which does not atone for a specific sin in the same way, naturally goes below. If so, the *olah* is not a good comparison for *asham*, which does atone. The *Gemara* counters with the *chatat ha-of*.

### Bird Chatas Counterexamp…

A *chatat ha-of* — a bird *chatas* — does atone, yet its blood goes below the line. So atonement alone does not place blood above the line. Therefore the *olah kal vachomer* stands: one cannot argue that an *asham*, which atones, must go above the line simply because it atones.

### Common Denominator

The *Gemara* then anticipates the counter: a bird is categorically different — *einah min hazevach*, it is not among the slaughtered large animals. Perhaps large animals that atone should go above the line. The *Gemara* responds by constructing a *tzad hashaveh*: between *olah* (large animal, not *kalil* in every sense, does not atone) and *chatat ha-of* (atones, but not a large slaughtered animal), the common denominator is that both go below the line.

### Kodshei Kodashim

This leads to the principle: *kodshei kodashim* — things of the highest sanctity — have their blood below the line. Both *olah* and *chatat ha-of* are *kodshei kodashim*, yet both go below. An *asham* is also *kodshei kodashim*. Therefore *asham damo l'mata* — the blood of an *asham* goes below the line — and Rabbi Eliezer had no basis to argue otherwise.

---

## Word Osah Limitations

### Asham Weightier

Rava from Pizka raises a challenge to the above analysis. He argues that an *asham* is in fact weightier than the comparison cases used above. Specifically, an *asham* has a minimum monetary value (*kitzvah*) — the Torah states *asham b'kesef shekalim* — whereas both an *olah* and a *chatat ha-of* have no fixed minimum worth. Therefore, the *tzad hashaveh* between *olah* and *chatat ha-of* is undermined: their common denominator of going below the line may be linked to their lesser weight in terms of monetary obligation. An *asham*, being weightier by virtue of its required minimum value, might be expected to go above the line, like a *chatas*.

### Osah Limits Chatas

The *Gemara* responds with a textual argument. The verse says *ha-Kohen ha-mechateh osah* — the *kohen* who makes it a *chatas* — in the context of the blood placement above the line. The word *osah* — "it," referring specifically and exclusively to the *chatas* — teaches: *v'ein damo shel acher l'ma'ala* — no other blood goes above the line. This *osah* is a limiting term that restricts the blood-above-the-line requirement to *chatas* alone, regardless of any comparative weightiness an *asham* might possess.

### Osah for Lishmah

The *Gemara* raises a further question: if *osah* is limiting, doesn't *osah* in the *lishmah* context also limit — teaching that only a *chatas* must be done *lishmah*, and nothing else? If so, Rabbi Eliezer's entire project of extending *shelo lishmah* to *asham* would be undermined by the same word.

### Pesach Exception

The *Gemara* answers: *osah* in the *lishmah* context cannot be fully excluding, because *pesach* is also *shelo lishmah pasul*. Since the *osah* does not exclude *pesach* from the *lishmah* requirement, it cannot be functioning as a strict exclusionary term in that context. It does not mean "only *chatas* and nothing else."

### Slaughtered Animals Only

By contrast, when *osah* limits blood placement above the line, it does function as a genuine exclusion. Among all *shechted* animals — large animals slaughtered in the conventional manner — only the *chatas* has blood above the line. The *olas ha-of* goes above the line as well, but that is a bird, not a slaughtered animal in the ordinary sense. So among *zevachim* — slaughtered animal offerings — *osah* limits the above-the-line placement exclusively to *chatas*. This is a genuine and operative exclusion, unlike the *lishmah* context where *pesach* already prevents *osah* from functioning as absolute exclusion.

---

## Separate Placement Doctr…

### Source Attribution

The *Gemara* offers an alternative explanation for why Rabbi Eliezer concedes that *asham* blood goes below the line, based on the position of Rabbi Eliezer b'Rebbi Shimon.

### Separate Places

Rabbi Eliezer b'Rebbi Shimon maintains that each *korban* requires its own distinct place on the *mizbeiach*. The different types of blood service are not simply categorized as "above" or "below" a line; rather, each type of *korban* has a specific location reserved for it, and those locations cannot overlap.

### No Space for Asham

Given this principle: *olas ha-of* has its specific location above the line; *chatas behemah* has the four *karnos* as its specific location. These two together account for the available space above the line. There is simply no remaining place above the line for the blood of an *asham* to go, since every position above the line is already occupied by the specific requirements of *chatas* and *olas ha-of*.

### Placement Constraints

Therefore, the blood of an *asham* must go below the line — not because of any inherent inferiority of *asham*, but because the spatial organization of the *mizbeiach* as understood by Rabbi Eliezer b'Rebbi Shimon leaves no available position above the line for it. Rabbi Eliezer thus concedes this point on structural grounds rather than because *asham* is categorically less weighty than *chatas*.

---

## Unresolved Tension

### Concession Explanation

With the analysis now complete, the *Gemara* has established why Rabbi Eliezer concedes the point about blood placement — whether through the *osah* limitation or through Rabbi Eliezer b'Rebbi Shimon's placement doctrine, the blood of an *asham* must go below the line, and this is not something Rabbi Eliezer can argue against.

### Maintains Position

Nevertheless, Rabbi Eliezer's concession on blood placement does not move him from his primary position. Even granting that *asham* blood goes below the line — making *asham* structurally different from *chatas* in that respect — Rabbi Eliezer maintains that *asham shelo lishmah* is *pasul*, just like *chatas*. The blood placement distinction, in his view, does not undermine the *shelo lishmah* equivalence established by the verse *kachatas ka'asham*.

### To Be Continued

The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on this point continues in tomorrow's daf.

---

---

# Zevachim 11

## Blood Invalidation

### Three Opinions

The daf opens by citing a *mishnah* from elsewhere in *Masechet Zevachim* — specifically from 91b — which records a three-way dispute concerning bloods that entered the *heichal*, the inner sanctuary. Rabbi Akiva holds that *kol damim shenichnasu laheichal l'chaper psulim* — any blood whatsoever that entered the sanctuary to effect atonement renders the offering *pasul*. The Rabbis restrict this rule to the *chatat* alone. And Rabbi Eliezer includes both the *chatat* and the *asham*, deriving this from the *hekesh* between them expressed in the verse *kachatat k'asham* (Vayikra 7:7).

### Rabbi Akiva's Logic

Rabbi Akiva draws his expansive position from a verse in *Parshat Tzav* (Vayikra): *v'chol chatat asher yuvah midamah el ohel moed lo teachal ba-esh tisaref* — every *chatat* whose blood is brought into the Tent of Meeting shall not be eaten but burned in fire. The double formulation — *v'chol chatat*, "and every sin offering" — reads to Rabbi Akiva as a kind of double plural, a linguistic amplification that extends the disqualification beyond the *chatat* itself to all bloods that enter the sanctuary.

### Rabbis vs. R. Eliezer

The Rabbis confine the rule to the *chatat* alone, while Rabbi Eliezer extends it to include the *asham* on the basis of the *hekesh* linking *chatat* and *asham*. The tension between these positions — when the *chatat* and *asham* are treated as equivalent and when they are not — runs as a central thread through much of the discussion that follows. As will become clear, the question of which direction legal inferences may travel between these offerings is not settled so simply.

---

## Rava's Reasoning

### Rava's Answer

The *Gemara* asks: *bishlama* Rabbi Eliezer, his reason is stated — but what is the Rabbis' reason for excluding the *asham*? Rava explains: we cannot derive from a *kal vachomer* from the *olah* that the *asham*'s blood entering the sanctuary renders it *pasul*.

### Failed Kal va-Chomer

The attempted *kal vachomer* runs as follows: if the *olah*, which is completely burned — *kalil* — and yet its blood entering the sanctuary does not disqualify it, could we not argue *kal vachomer* that the *asham*, which is not burned completely, would similarly not be disqualified when its blood enters? The argument collapses immediately on inspection, however: this proves the *asham* is *kasher* when its blood enters, not *pasul* — the exact opposite of what we were trying to establish.

### Refuting Olah Logic

A possible objection to the *olah* as the basis for this reasoning is then raised: *mah l'olah sheken einah mechaperet* — what is special about the *olah* is that it does not atone for a specific transgression. Since the *olah* is not an atonement offering in the way the *chatat* is, the comparison breaks down. The *olah* belongs to a fundamentally different category, and legal inferences across such a divide are suspect.

### Meal Offering Attempt

The *Gemara* therefore attempts to construct the argument from the *minchat choteh*, the meal offering of a sinner — an offering that, like the *chatat* and *asham*, does serve an atonement function. But this too is rejected: *mah leminchat choteh sheken einah min hazevach* — the *minchah* is simply not in the category of animal sacrifice (*zevach*), and the analogy therefore fails for a different reason. The *Gemara* briefly considers whether the *chatat ha'of*, the bird sin offering, might serve instead, but that too is rejected — the *chatat ha'of* follows the ruling of Rabbi Avin and involves a different process; the blood is collected differently, with a finger rather than through standard *shechitah* and *kabbalah*.

### Kal va-Chomer Fails

Having exhausted these alternatives, the *Gemara* reverts to the *olah*. Now both possible analogies have failed on their own terms. As the formulation goes: *lo rei zeh k'rei zeh v'lo rei zeh k'rei zeh* — this case is not fully like that one, and that one is not fully like this one. The *kal vachomer* cannot be constructed from either direction.

---

## Kodshei Kodashim

### Holiness Level

Since no single offering provides an adequate basis for a *kal vachomer*, the *Gemara* seeks instead the *tzad hashaveh* — the common feature shared by the *olah* and the *chatat* that might allow an inference to the *asham*. The answer: both the *olah* and the *chatat* are *kodshei kodashim*, offerings of the highest degree of sanctity. From this shared characteristic one might seek to derive: *af ani avi asham shehu kodesh kodashim* — I will similarly bring the *asham*, which is also *kodshei kodashim*, into the same legal category.

### Asham Classification

The *asham* does indeed qualify as *kodshei kodashim*. The attempt to group it with the *olah* and *chatat* on this basis initially seems promising. However, a distinction is then introduced that cuts against the inference.

### Asham's Minimum

Rava of Barnish points out to Rav Ashi: *mah l'tzad hashaveh shebahen sheken ein lahen kitzvah* — what is distinctive about the common feature of the *olah* and *chatat* is that neither has a prescribed minimum monetary value. *Tomar b'asham sheyesh lo kitzvah* — but you cannot make the same inference regarding the *asham*, which does have a minimum value (*kitzvah*). The Torah was more stringent with the *asham* in requiring a minimum, and this distinguishing feature prevents the inference from succeeding. This, the *Gemara* concludes, is the fundamental reason (*ta'amei d'Rabbanan*) underlying the Rabbis' position.

---

## Verse Interpretation

### Damah Pronoun

The *Gemara* now turns to the precise derivation from the verse itself. The relevant verse (Vayikra) reads: *v'chol chatat asher yuvah midamah el ohel moed* — every *chatat* from whose blood is brought into the Tent of Meeting. The word *damah* — "its blood" — is now subjected to close analysis. The *Gemara* first reads it as *damah shel zu v'lo damah shel acher*: the verse speaks of the blood of this specific offering and not the blood of a different one. That is, it is only the *chatat*'s own blood entering the sanctuary that disqualifies it; blood from another offering entering does not disqualify the *chatat*.

### R. Eliezer's Read

Rabbi Eliezer takes the word *damah* differently. For him, the reference to blood — *damah v'lo besarah* — teaches that it is the blood of the offering that triggers disqualification, not its flesh. He is not concerned with whether it is the blood of this offering or another's; his reading addresses a different question entirely.

### Rabbis' Limit

The Rabbis, by contrast, learn two separate lessons from *dam damah*. First, as Rabbi Eliezer does, that the verse speaks of blood and not flesh. Second — and this was already noted at the bottom of 10b — that the rule applies only to the *chatat* and does not extend to other offerings. The double formulation (*dam... damah*) yields both restrictions simultaneously for the Rabbis.

### R. Eliezer Differs

Rabbi Eliezer does not read the verse in this doubled fashion. Since the word *damah* is the grammatically correct form for "its blood," he treats it as a single, necessary term — not an amplification from which additional rulings may be derived — and uses it solely to teach that blood, not flesh, is the operative element. He therefore cannot draw from the same verse the Rabbis' limiting conclusion.

---

## Mincha Connection

### Asham Intent

Returning to the broader question, the *Gemara* notes: *bishlama l'Rabbanan d'amri asham sheshachato shelo lishmo kasher* — according to the Rabbis, an *asham* that was slaughtered *shelo lishmo*, not for its designated purpose, remains *kasher*. It does not fulfill the owner's obligation, but the offering itself is valid. This sets up the question of how the *minchah* is linked, by *hekesh*, to both the *chatat* and the *asham*.

### Mincha Dual Nature

The *Gemara* observes that the *minchat choteh* — the meal offering brought by a sinner — can in some respects resemble a *chatat* and in other respects resemble an *asham*, depending on the context. This dual character follows from a specific verse.

### Rabbi Shimon Quote

Rabbi Shimon cites the verse from *Parshat Tzav* (Vayikra 6:10): *kodesh kodashim hi kachatat v'ka'asham* — it is most holy, like the *chatat* and like the *asham*. This verse, he explains, is the source for the *minchat choteh* being treated as analogous to both.

### Two Mincha Types

The practical consequence runs as follows: *minchat choteh harei hi kachatat* — the *minchat choteh* is like the *chatat* — therefore, if the *kemitzah*, the removal of the handful, was performed *shelo lishmah*, not for its intended purpose, it is *psulah*, invalid. By contrast, *minchat nedavah harei hi ka'asham* — the voluntary *minchah* is like the *asham* — therefore, if its *kemitzah* was performed *shelo lishmah*, it remains *kasher*. The *asham* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* is still valid; so too the voluntary *minchah* whose handful was removed without the requisite intent.

---

## Four Blood Works

### Blood Services

The *Gemara* now identifies the four *avot ha-dam*, the four primary blood services performed in connection with animal sacrifices: *shechitah* (slaughter), *kabbalah* (collection of the blood), *holachah* (conveying the blood to the altar), and *zrikah* (sprinkling the blood).

### Mincha Parallels

Each of these four services has a parallel in the *minchah*. In place of *shechitah* stands the *kemitzah* — the removal of the handful. In place of *kabbalah* stands the placing of the *minchah* into a *kli sharet*, a sacred service vessel. *Holachah* corresponds directly to *holachah* — carrying the handful to the altar. And in place of *zrikah* stands the placing of the *kometz* upon the fire.

### Kemitza Role

The analogy between *kemitzah* and *shechitah* is worth pausing over. Just as *shechitah* is the initial act of preparation that enables all subsequent blood service, the *kemitzah* is the first act that sets the *minchah* service in motion. And just as any valid *shochet* may perform *shechitah* in the context of sacrifices that require a *kohen* for the blood service, the *kemitzah* must be performed specifically by a *kohen*. This shared requirement of priestly performance reinforces the parallel.

### Kli Sharet Need

The requirement that the *minchah* be placed into a *kli sharet* parallels the *kabbalah* of the blood into a vessel. There is a deeper principle at work here as well. Animal sacrifices possess an intrinsic *kedushat haguf* — a sanctity of the body — that attaches to the animal from the moment of designation. The *minchah*, however, acquires this sanctity of the body only through the act of placing it into the *kli sharet*. Without the *kli sharet*, the *minchah* has not yet received the full measure of *kedushah* that enables the subsequent service to be valid. The teaching recorded in the *mishnah* — *shelo bichli sharet psulah* — that a *minchah* processed without a sacred vessel is *psulah* — reflects this principle, though Rabbi Shimon disagrees and validates it.

---

## Rav Yehuda Explains

### Kodesh Kodashim

Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Chiyya explains the reason behind Rabbi Shimon's position. The verse states: *kodesh kodashim hi kachatat v'ka'asham* — most holy it is, like the *chatat* and like the *asham*. This single verse, he argues, contains within it two distinct teachings about how the *minchah* resembles each of these offerings in turn.

### Hand Distinction

The parallel to the *chatat* emerges from the right-handed performance of the *minchah*'s service: *ba le'ovda beyad, ovda be-yamin kachatat* — when it comes to performing the service by hand, performing it with the right hand makes it analogous to the *chatat*. The parallel to the *asham* emerges from the left-handed dimension: *ovda be-smol ka'asham* — when performed with the left hand, the service resembles that of the *asham*. This yields a coherent framework: the same offering may behave like a *chatat* in one register and like an *asham* in another, depending on the specific act being analyzed.

### Dual Extraction

Rabbi Shimon extracts both of these lessons from the single verse. The verse *kodesh kodashim hi kachatat v'ka'asham* is not redundant; each element of the comparison — *kachatat*, *ka'asham* — carries its own distinct legal meaning, and Rabbi Shimon deploys both.

---

## Kemitza Intent

### Purpose Requirement

The *Gemara* now specifies the conditions under which the *minchat choteh* is rendered invalid on account of improper intent. If the *kemitzah* — the removal of the handful — was performed *shelo lishmah*, not for the purpose of the *minchat choteh*, the offering is *psulah*. The requirement of *lishmah* is not merely aspirational; a deviation in intent at this stage invalidates the service entirely.

### Specificity from 'Hi'

The source for this ruling is the word *hi* — "it is" — appearing in the verse: *kodesh kodashim hi kachatat v'ka'asham*. The word *hi* is not syntactically necessary; the verse could have read *kodesh kodashim kachatat v'ka'asham* without it. Its presence teaches that the offering must be specifically what it is — *davka* this *minchah*, for this purpose. The word *hi* introduces a requirement of particularity: the handful must be removed with the *minchah choteh*'s own identity in mind.

### Chatat Parallel

The same word *hi* appears in the verse governing the *chatat* itself (Vayikra 4:24), and the Rabbis read it there identically: the *chatat* too must be slaughtered specifically for its own purpose. The parallel structure of the two verses — each containing the word *hi* in an apparently superfluous position — allows the *Gemara* to derive the same purpose requirement for both offerings from the same linguistic device.

---

## Semichah Requirement

### Hekesh Logic

The *Gemara* then asks how the Rabbis employ the *hekesh* linking *asham* to *chatat*, given that they reject Rabbi Eliezer's use of it to extend the blood-invalidation rule to the *asham*. The answer: *mah chatat te'unah semikhah af asham ta'un semikhah* — just as the *chatat* requires *semikhah* — the owner's leaning upon the animal's head prior to slaughter — so too the *asham* requires *semikhah*. This, and not the extension of blood-disqualification, is the legal lesson the Rabbis extract from the *hekesh* between the two offerings.

---

## Wrong Purpose

### Yosef & R. Eliezer

The *Gemara* now returns to the *mishnah* from the beginning of the tractate (2a), where Yosef ben Choni states: *hanishchatim leshem pesach v'leshem chatat psulim* — animals slaughtered with the intent of a *pesach* or a *chatat* are *psulim*. The reasoning is apparent: the *chatat* is an atonement offering tied to a specific sin and a specific individual; intent cannot be freely redirected between atonement offerings. And the *pesach* carries its own cluster of stringencies — a fixed time, a fixed group of designated eaters, a fixed sacrificial identity — that make it uniquely resistant to substitution.

### Yochanan Expansion

Rabbi Yochanan reads Yosef ben Choni's position as equivalent to that of Rabbi Eliezer, and goes further: the agreement between them, he argues, extends beyond *chatat* and *pesach* themselves. Not only are those specific offerings *pasul* when done *shelo lishmam*, but all *korbanot* performed for the sake of a *chatat* or *pesach* are likewise *pasul*.

### Raba's Limit

Raba offers a more restrained reading. He holds that Yosef ben Choni and Rabbi Eliezer agree regarding the *pesach* — an *olah* slaughtered for the sake of the *pesach* is *pasul* — but they diverge when it comes to other offerings slaughtered for the sake of a *chatat*. For Yosef ben Choni, such an offering is *pasul*; for Rabbi Eliezer, it is *kasher*, though it does not fulfill the owner's *chiyuv*. The sacrifice itself remains valid; only its capacity to discharge the obligation is lacking. This disagreement between Raba and Rabbi Yochanan — whether they are truly in agreement or differ on the question of *bacharim leshem chatat* — is noted as a matter of dispute, with the *Tosafot* on 11b arguing that Raba is not in fact disputing Rabbi Yochanan but elaborating upon him.

---

## Pesach Dispute

### Baraita Setup

A *baraita* is now introduced that sets out the positions of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua more fully. Two cases are considered together: (1) a *pesach* that passed its year — the animal designated for *pesach* grew older than one year before being brought, and is now slaughtered at the time of *pesach* with *pesach* intent; and (2) an animal that was not designated as *pesach* but is slaughtered at the time of *pesach* for the sake of *pesach*. In both cases, Rabbi Eliezer declares the offering *pasul* and Rabbi Yehoshua declares it *kasher*.

### Three Categories

Before entering the debate, it is important to note that the *Gemara* works with three distinct legal statuses, not two. An offering can be *kasher* — valid and accepted. It can be *pasul* — invalid. Or it can occupy an intermediate position: *kasher* but *lo yotzei hachiyuv* — valid as a sacrifice in that it may be eaten, but not fulfilling the owner's religious obligation. This third category is crucial to understanding the dispute. A *pesach* offering done with imperfect intent does not necessarily become forbidden; the question is whether it achieves anything beyond producing a meal.

### Yehoshua's Kal

Rabbi Yehoshua advances a *kal vachomer*. During the rest of the year, the *pesach* offering is not valid for its own sake — it cannot be a *pesach* when offered outside of its time — yet other animals offered for its sake are *kasher* (they become *shelamim*). How much more so, then, at the time of *pesach* itself — when the *pesach* is valid for its own sake — should other animals slaughtered for its sake also be *kasher*?

### Eliezer's Counter

Rabbi Eliezer refuses this *kal vachomer* and offers the reverse. During the rest of the year, the *pesach* offering is not *kasher* for its own sake, yet it is *kasher* for the sake of other offerings — meaning a *pesach*-designated animal offered outside its time becomes *shelamim* and is valid. If so, at the time of *pesach* itself — when it is *kasher* for its own sake — *kal vachomer* it should be *kasher* for the sake of other offerings as well. But this conclusion — that a *pesach* slaughtered on the fourteenth of Nisan *shelo lishmo* is *kasher* — directly contradicts established *halacha*. Since the reverse *kal vachomer* produces an absurd result, Rabbi Eliezer uses it to refute Rabbi Yehoshua's original reasoning.

### Yehoshua Responds

Rabbi Yehoshua pushes back sharply: if Rabbi Eliezer insists on this reading, then he has diminished the power of the *pesach* and artificially elevated the power of the *shelamim*. The argument Rabbi Eliezer is making would make the *pesach* — in some respects — weaker than the *shelamim*, which is a counterintuitive and legally uncomfortable result.

### One-Way Logic

Rabbi Eliezer then presents a different principle. *Matzinu motar pesach ba-shelamim v'ein motar shelamim ba-pesach* — we find that the surplus designated for a *pesach* offering may become a *shelamim*, but the surplus designated for a *shelamim* may never become a *pesach*. The *pesach* is a subcategory within the broader family of *kodashim kalim* — and like any subcategory, it can be absorbed upward into the general category (*shelamim*), but the general category cannot be pressed downward into it. If a person set aside funds for a *pesach* and had money left over, those surplus funds may be directed toward a *shelamim*; but funds designated for a *shelamim* cannot be redirected to acquire a *pesach*. From this asymmetry Rabbi Eliezer argues: *u'mah pesach shemotaro ba-shelamim shechato bizmano leshum shelamim pasul* — even the *pesach* whose surplus becomes *shelamim*, if it is slaughtered at its proper time with the intent of *shelamim*, is *pasul*. How much more so would *shelamim*, whose surplus can never become *pesach*, be *pasul* if slaughtered at the time of *pesach* for the sake of *pesach*.

### Chatat-Olah

Rabbi Yehoshua counters with a parallel case. *Matzinu motar chatat ba-olah v'ein motar olah ba-chatat* — we find that the surplus designated for a *chatat* may become an *olah*, but the surplus designated for an *olah* can never become a *chatat*. (The *olah* is completely burned; there is no surplus left to redirect, and furthermore the *chatat* is female while the *olah* is typically male — they cannot even be the same animal.) If the *chatat*, whose surplus goes to an *olah*, is nonetheless *psulah* when slaughtered for the sake of an *olah*, then by the same logic, the *olah*, whose surplus cannot come to a *chatat*, would certainly be *psulah* if slaughtered for the sake of a *chatat*. Rabbi Yehoshua is testing whether Rabbi Eliezer's framework yields consistent and defensible results when applied to other pairs of offerings.

### Time-Specific Rule

Rabbi Eliezer offers his final and decisive principle. *Lo, im amarta b'chatat sheken k'sheirah lishmah kol hashanah kulah, tomar b'pesach she'eino kasher lishmah ela bizmano* — you cannot reason from the *chatat* to the *pesach*, because the *chatat* is valid for its own sake throughout the entire year. The *pesach*, by contrast, is valid for its own sake only at its designated time. Since the *pesach* offering is *pasul* for its own sake during the rest of the year, it follows logically that other offerings done for its sake at its designated time are equally *pasul*. The *pesach*'s identity is inseparable from its time; only what belongs to that time may participate in it.

---

## Offering Hierarchy

### Hierarchy Rule

The *Gemara* now returns to the *mishnah* and the position of Shimon *achi* Azariah, which was cited at the opening of the tractate (2a). His rule: *shechatan l'shem gavoha meihen k'sheirim, l'shem namuch meihen psulim* — if lower-sanctity offerings are slaughtered for the sake of higher-sanctity offerings, they are *kasher*; if higher-sanctity offerings are slaughtered for the sake of lower-sanctity offerings, they are *pasul*. The hierarchy of sanctity operates as a one-way street: ascending is permitted, descending is not.

### Desecration Verse

The source for this rule is a verse in Vayikra 22:15: *v'lo yechalelu et kodshei bnei Yisrael et asher yarimu l'Hashem* — and they shall not desecrate the holy things of the children of Israel that they shall lift up (*yarimu*) for *Hashem*. The word *yarimu*, from the root of *terumah* — to lift up — is read to teach: what is desecrated (*mechullal*) is that which is brought downward (*namuch*); what is lifted upward (*gavoha*) is not subject to desecration. The verse is transmitted in two versions: Rav Ashi teaches it in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Acha son of Rava teaches it in the name of Rabbi Yannai.

### Shmuel's Use

The same verse, however, is also the basis for a teaching of Shmuel in an entirely different context. Shmuel derives from it that one who eats *tevel* — produce from which *terumot* and *ma'asrot* have not yet been separated — is liable to the death penalty. The verse reads: *v'lo yechalelu et kodshei bnei Yisrael asher yarimu l'Hashem* — the holy things of Israel which they *will* separate for *Hashem*. Shmuel reads *yarimu* as a future tense referring to what is *destined* to be set apart; the *tevel* is already designated in principle for *terumah*, and one who eats it before that separation has been made has desecrated something consecrated. The *Gemara* notes that the verse is needed for Shmuel's derivation and asks how it can simultaneously be available for Shimon *achi* Azariah's hierarchy principle.

### Tense Lesson

The resolution lies in the verb tense. The verse uses the future form *yarimu* — "they will lift up" — when, if it were speaking only of a past act, it should have said *hurmu*, "that which has been lifted." The use of the future tense is therefore intentional and carries extra meaning. *Shema mina tartei* — we learn two things from it: one governing past consecrated items (Shimon *achi* Azariah's hierarchy rule applied to offerings already sanctified) and one governing future ones (Shmuel's ruling about *tevel*, which is destined for sanctification but not yet separated). A single verb in a single tense is thus pressed into service for two distinct *halachic* domains.

---

## Valid Not Accepted

### Zeira's Query

Rabbi Zeira raises a pointed question regarding Shimon *achi* Azariah's position. When Shimon holds that lower-sanctity offerings slaughtered for the sake of higher-sanctity ones are *kasher*, does he mean they are *kasher v'ein mirtzin* — valid but not accepted, meaning the owner has not fulfilled his obligation — and that Shimon is disagreeing with the Rabbis on only one matter (the *kasher* status of such an offering)? Or does Shimon hold that such offerings are both *kasher u'mirtzin* — valid and accepted — meaning they fully discharge the owner's obligation, and Shimon therefore disagrees with the Rabbis on two matters?

### Two Positions

The question opens up a three-part logical space. An offering can be *kasher* and fulfill the obligation (*kasher u'mirtzin*); it can be *kasher* but not fulfill the obligation (*kasher v'ein mirtzin*); or it can be *pasul* entirely. Whether Shimon's leniency extends to acceptance and obligation-fulfillment, or only to the technical validity of the sacrifice, determines the full scope of his disagreement with the Rabbis.

### Bechor Example

Abaye — or, as some attribute it, Rabbi Zrika — brings a *ta shema* to probe the question. The *mishnah* teaches: a *bechor*, firstborn animal, or *ma'aser beheimah*, tithe animal, that was slaughtered with the intent of *shelamim*, is *kasher*. These are lower in the holiness hierarchy than *shelamim* proper, and slaughtering them for the sake of the higher offering is permitted.

### Reverse Invalid

The same *mishnah* continues: *shelamim* slaughtered for the sake of a *bechor* or *ma'aser* are *pasul* — the higher for the lower is disqualified, consistent with Shimon's rule. The *Gemara* then asks: if we were to entertain the possibility that the lower-for-higher case yields both *kasher* and *meratzeh* — fully acceptable — then is the *bechor* the kind of offering that can achieve *ritzuy*, acceptance? The *bechor* is not an offering chosen by the owner for the purpose of pleasing *Hashem* in the sense of fulfilling an elected obligation; it is an offering mandated by the firstborn status of the animal. It therefore does not function as a vehicle of *ritzuy* in the relevant sense. The conclusion follows: the *bechor* slaughtered for the sake of *shelamim* is *kasher v'ein mirtzin* — valid but not accepted.

### Hierarchy Only

From the concluding clause, the *Gemara* infers that the opening clause must be read consistently: the *bechor* slaughtered for *shelamim* is also *kasher v'ein mirtzin*. The principle that emerges is that the hierarchy rule governs validity (*kashrus*) but does not automatically generate full acceptance (*ritzuy*). Shimon *achi* Azariah's leniency, on this reading, concerns only whether the sacrifice is *pasul* — not whether it discharges the owner's obligation.

---

## Order Precedence

### Shelamim Priority

The *Gemara* then raises another *mishnah*, which teaches that *shelamim* take precedence over *bechor* and *ma'aser* when a *kohen* must decide which offering to perform first. The reason: *shelamim* require additional services that *bechor* and *ma'aser* do not.

### Shelamim Services

The services unique to *shelamim* are enumerated: *matan arba'* — the four applications of blood to the corners of the altar; *semikhah* — the leaning of hands upon the offering; *nesachim* — the wine libations; and *tenufat chazeh v'shok* — the waving of the chest and thigh. Because *shelamim* require this more elaborate service, they are given priority so that the *kohen* may complete their more demanding *avodah* while fully attentive.

### Hierarchy Primary

The *Gemara* notes that the primary and authoritative statement of the hierarchy principle between higher and lower offerings appears in the earlier *mishnah* addressed in the main discussion, not in this later one. The second *mishnah*, which addresses the order of precedence among offerings of comparable status, invokes the hierarchy principle only incidentally — in the course of explaining why *shelamim* precede *bechor* in the queue. The foundational rule, however, is the one derived from Shimon *achi* Azariah and grounded in the verse of *yarimu*, and it is to that earlier *mishnah* that the primary statement properly belongs.

---

---

# Zevachim 12

## Pesach Morning 14th

### Mishna Intro

The Mishna on 11b turns from the general laws of *shelo lishmo* to zoom in on a specific and puzzling case involving the *korban pesach*. The *pesach* has a designated time — *bein ha'arbayim*, generally understood as the afternoon beginning from *chatzot* — and if slaughtered *shelo lishmo* during that window, it is *pasul*. But what happens if the *pesach* is slaughtered in the morning of the 14th of Nisan, *shelo lishmo*?

The background rule is clear: a *pesach* slaughtered when it is *eino zmano* — not its time — and *shelo lishmo* is *kasher* as a *shlamim*. The question is whether the morning of the 14th counts as *zmano* or as *eino zmano*. If it is *eino zmano*, then *shelo lishmo* should render it *kasher* as a *shlamim*. If it is considered *zmano*, then *shelo lishmo* would *pasul* it, just as the Mishna already taught regarding a *pesach bizmano shelo lishmo*.

### Dispute Setup

The Mishna records a dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Ben Beteira. Rabbi Yehoshua rules *kasher* — *ke'ilu nishchat bishlosha-asar*, as if it had been slaughtered on the 13th. In his view, the morning of the 14th is *eino zmano* for the *pesach*, and since it was slaughtered *shelo lishmo* outside its time, it is valid as a *shlamim*. Ben Beteira rules *pasul* — *ke'ilu nishchat bein ha'arbayim*, as if it had been slaughtered in the afternoon. In his view, the afternoon of the 14th is close enough — or determinative enough — that the morning already carries the status of *zmano*, and therefore a *pesach* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* during this time is *pasul*.

A striking consequence of Ben Beteira's position, as was noted during the discussion, is that on the 14th in the morning, the *pesach* is invalid no matter what one does: *lishmo* it is *pasul* because the true *zman* has not yet arrived (*pesach kodem zmano*), and *shelo lishmo* it is *pasul* because the day is already considered *bizmano* and a *pesach bizmano shelo lishmo* is *pasul*. The morning of the 14th is, in effect, a complete blackout period.

### Ben Beteira Logic

The Gemara then cites Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, who offers a more radical reading of Ben Beteira's position: *machshir hayah Ben Beteira b'pesach sheshchato shacharit bearba'asar lishmo* — Ben Beteira actually holds that a *pesach* slaughtered in the morning of the 14th *lishmo* is *kasher*. In other words, Ben Beteira does not merely say that the afternoon *zman* is close enough to color the morning; he genuinely believes that the *zman* of the *korban pesach* begins in the morning. The entire day of the 14th is *zmano*. That is why *shelo lishmo* is *pasul* — not because the afternoon is approaching, but because the morning itself is a valid time. His phrase *ke'ilu nishchat bein ha'arbayim* was formulated in response to Rabbi Yehoshua's phrasing (*ke'ilu nishchat bishlosha-asar*), matching the structure of the debate — but the underlying position is that the morning is itself fully valid.

### Gemara Challenge

The Gemara immediately presses this reading: *ei demapligi be'shelo lishmah liflagi be'lishmah* — if this is the real dispute, why are they arguing about the *shelo lishmo* case, which is derivative? They should be debating the more fundamental question: can a *korban pesach* be brought *lishmo* in the morning?

### Resolution

The Gemara answers: had they debated *lishmo* directly, one might have concluded that even Rabbi Yehoshua — who holds the *pesach* is only valid in the afternoon — would nonetheless agree that *shelo lishmo* in the morning is *pasul*, on the grounds that *ho'il u'miktzat ra'uy*, since part of the day is its *zman*. The reasoning: even if the morning is not itself the true *zman*, perhaps the fact that the afternoon will be *zmano* is enough to make the whole day *bizmano* for purposes of *shelo lishmo*. By formulating their dispute specifically over *shelo lishmo*, the Mishna teaches us that Rabbi Yehoshua holds two things: first, the *pesach* itself is only valid in the afternoon; and second, even though the afternoon *zman* is coming later that day, the morning is still sufficiently *eino zmano* that *shelo lishmo* there is *kasher* as a *shlamim*.

---

## Bein Arbayim

### Bein Arbayim Meaning

The Gemara now interrogates the premise that Ben Beteira holds the entire day to be *zmano*. Doesn't the Torah say the *pesach* is brought *bein ha'arbayim* — between the evenings — which is universally understood to mean the afternoon? The Gemara raises an alternative reading offered in the name of the son of Rabbi Ilai: *bein shnei arvayim* — between two different "evenings." Sunrise, understood as the end of the prior night, is the first *erev*; sunset is the second. Between these two lies the entire day. On this reading, *bein ha'arbayim* means the whole day.

### Tamid & Menorah

The Gemara challenges this extended reading with a series of parallels. The *korban tamid* is also described as brought *bein ha'arbayim* — does that mean it could be offered at any point during the day? Clearly not. The Gemara answers that for the *tamid*, the Torah itself provides the corrective: *es hakeves echad ta'aseh baboker* — one lamb in the morning. The explicit morning-and-afternoon pairing of the two *tamid* offerings establishes that *bein ha'arbayim* for the afternoon *tamid* means the afternoon specifically, not the entire day. Even if one would otherwise read *bein ha'arbayim* expansively, the verse forces the narrow reading here.

The Gemara similarly asks about the *menorah*: it too is described as lit *bein ha'arbayim* — does that mean it could be lit anytime during the day? No, because the Torah says *me-erev ad boker*, from evening until morning — which establishes that the lighting is specifically in the late afternoon or evening, not throughout the day.

### Ketores Parallel

A related *braita* is cited: *me-erev ad boker, tein lah midasah shetehei dolekes ve-holeches me-erev ad boker* — the lamp must be given enough oil to burn through the night. The *braita* also adds: this is the only *avodah* in the *Beis Hamikdash* that begins during the day and continues through the night.

Turning to the *ketores* — also described as burned *bein ha'arbayim* — the Gemara similarly asks whether that could mean any time of day. No, because the Torah links it explicitly to the lighting of the *menorah* by Aharon: *u'vha'alos Aharon es haneros bein ha'arbayim yaktirenah* — when Aharon lights the lamps. Since the lighting of the *menorah* has been established to be in the afternoon, the *ketores* is similarly fixed to that time.

### Pesach Erev

Returning to the *pesach*, the Gemara notes that by *pesach* it also says *ba'erev*, in the evening — which should likewise restrict the *pesach* to the afternoon rather than the entire day. But the Gemara responds: *hahu l'ichar davar hu d'asa* — that word *erev* by *pesach* serves a different purpose: it teaches that the *pesach* must be the last sacrifice brought in the afternoon.

### Ordering: After Tamid

This is the subject of a *braita*: *ye'achar davar shene'emar bo ba'erev bein ha'arbayim* — a sacrifice described with both *erev* and *bein ha'arbayim* (namely, the *pesach*) comes after *l'davar shelo ne'emar bo ela bein ha'arbayim bilvad* — a sacrifice described only with *bein ha'arbayim* (namely, the *tamid*). The *halacha* is therefore that the *korban pesach* is brought after the afternoon *tamid*.

This produces an initially striking result: if one holds that the *pesach* is valid in the morning, then it could be brought anytime during the morning. But once the afternoon arrives, it must come *after* the *tamid*. The Gemara validates this asymmetry by analogy to Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on *tefillah*: if one forgot to daven *musaf* and realizes this in the afternoon, one should daven *mincha* first and then *musaf* — because *tadir v'she'eino tadir, tadir kodem*, the more frequent takes precedence. Even though *musaf* would normally precede *mincha* in terms of the day's sequence, in the afternoon the more frequent *mincha* goes first. Similarly, the *pesach* which in the morning can be brought at any point, must in the afternoon defer to the *tamid* which is *tadir*.

---

## Gemara Reinterpretation

### Rabbi's Challenge

Having developed all of the above, the Gemara introduces a *tosefta* in which *Rabbi* — standing in for Ben Beteira, as the Gemara puts it, *heishiv Rabbi tachas Ben Beteira l'divrei Rabbi Yehoshua* — challenges Rabbi Yehoshua's position. Rabbi argues: *im amarta bishloshah asar* — on the 13th, no part of the day is a valid time for the *pesach*, so one might accept that *shelo lishmo* there is *kasher*. *Tomar b'arba'ah asar* — but on the 14th, *shemiktzaso ra'uy*, part of the day — the afternoon — is indeed the *zman* of the *pesach*. Therefore, even the morning should be considered *bizmano* enough to *pasul* a *pesach* slaughtered *shelo lishmo*.

This version of Ben Beteira's argument is importantly different from the earlier one: it does not require Ben Beteira to hold that the morning is itself a valid time for the *pesach lishmo*. Rather, it says: since the afternoon is coming, the morning is already *bizmano* enough to *pasul* a *shelo lishmo*.

### Everyone Agrees

The Gemara therefore revises its understanding of the dispute entirely. Rabbi Yochanan states: *posel hayah Ben Beteira b'pesach sheshchato b'arba'ah asar shachris bein lishmo bein shelo lishmo* — Ben Beteira invalidates the *pesach* slaughtered on the morning of the 14th regardless of intent. Everyone agrees — both Rabbi Yehoshua and Ben Beteira — that the *pesach* is only truly valid *lishmo* in the afternoon. The question is never whether the morning is an independent valid time for the *pesach*.

### Shelo Lishmo Debate

The real and only dispute is: does *shelo lishmo* in the morning count as *bizmano* because the afternoon *zman* is coming later that day? Ben Beteira says yes — the halachic unit of time is the day, not the hour. Since the 14th is the *zman* of the *pesach*, the entire day carries that status, and a *pesach* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* anywhere on the 14th is *pasul bizmano*. Rabbi Yehoshua says no — the morning is genuinely *eino zmano*, and even though the afternoon *zman* is approaching, that is insufficient to make the morning *bizmano* for purposes of invalidating a *shelo lishmo* slaughter.

---

## Dichui Concept

### Abahu's Objection

Rabbi Abbahu now raises a sharp objection. Given Ben Beteira's position, how can there ever be a *kasher korban pesach* at all? The morning of the 14th is entirely invalid in both directions — *lishmo* it is *pasul* because the true *zman* has not arrived, and *shelo lishmo* it is *pasul* because it is already considered *bizmano*. This makes the morning a complete blackout. Any *korban pesach* that passes through this blackout period should be considered *dachui* — pushed off and permanently stigmatized.

### Dichui Mei'ikara

Rabbi Abbahu elaborates: *ha de-afrishei ba-tzafra, dachui mei-ikara hu* — if you sanctified the animal during the morning of the 14th, it was *dachui mei-ikara*, never valid from the moment of sanctification, since at that moment it could neither be brought *lishmo* nor *shelo lishmo*. And *ha de-afrishinhu me-etmol, nira ve-nidcha* — if you sanctified it on the 13th, that is even worse, because *nira ve-nidcha* — something that was once fit and then became unfit — is subject to an even stronger form of rejection. A candidate who was hired and then fired is in a worse position than one who never got the job. Either way, Ben Beteira seems to leave no path to a *kasher pesach*. Rabbi Abbahu therefore concludes: *tehei l-achar chatzot* — according to Ben Beteira, the only way to have a valid *korban pesach* is to sanctify it after *chatzot*, once the afternoon has already begun and the *pesach* can immediately be brought.

### Abaye's Response

Abaye rejects this constraint: *afilu teima mi-tzafra* — even if sanctified in the morning, it is fine. The principle is *ein mechusar zman l-vo bayom* — something that can be offered later today is not considered to be lacking in time. We do not measure halachic validity by the current moment; we measure in whole-day units. The same logic that makes Ben Beteira say the morning of the 14th is *bizmano* — because the *pesach* can be brought later today — equally prevents us from calling the morning a *dichui* period. Since the animal can be brought later today, it is not halachically entering an unfit time when it passes through the morning.

### Rav Papa's Response

Rav Papa goes further: *afilu teima mei-orta* — one could even sanctify the *pesach* the night before and it would not be *nidcha*. The principle is *layla ein mechusar zman* — the nighttime is not considered a period in which the *korban* is lacking its time. Night and day together constitute a single halachic unit, and since the *pesach* can be brought the following afternoon, the night before is already considered part of its time. This is not unlike any other *korban* that is sanctified at night — one never says such an animal is *nidcha* simply because *korbanot* are not brought at night; since it will be brought in the morning, the sanctification is entirely valid.

---

## Mechusar Zman

### Eighth Day Case

The Gemara now points out that the phrase *mechusar zman* has a more specific technical meaning beyond "can be done later today." It refers to an animal that has not yet reached its eighth day — the minimum age for a *korban*. An animal born seven days ago cannot yet be brought as a *korban*, even though tomorrow morning it will be eligible.

### Maaser Behema

The application of *lailah ein mechusar zman* in this more technical sense comes from a *braita* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *leil shemini nichnas ledir lehit'aser* — on the night of the eighth day, such an animal may enter the pen to be counted for *maaser behema*. When performing *maaser behema*, one counts the animals one by one and designates every tenth; this is done only with animals old enough to be brought as *korbanot*, i.e., at least eight days old. Yet the *halacha* permits including such an animal on the night of the eighth day, even though it is not yet morning and cannot actually be brought as a *korban* until then. Since in the morning it will be eight days old and fit, the nighttime of the eighth day is already treated as if it is fit.

### Lailah Ain Mechusar

This is the source for the principle that night is not considered *mechusar zman* — the night does not render an animal lacking in time when that time will arrive in the morning. We count in whole-day units, and the eighth day begins at nightfall.

### Rabbi Aptorikí

Rabbi Aptorikí notes an apparent contradiction. One verse says *vehaya shivas yamim tachas imo* — the animal must be seven days with its mother. Once seven days have passed, the night of the eighth arrives and the animal seems immediately eligible. But another verse says *miyom hashemini vahalah yeratze* — only from the eighth day onward is it fit to be brought. These two verses seem to conflict: the night of the eighth is after seven days have passed, yet it is not yet the eighth day itself.

### Lailah & Yom

The resolution: *laila lekeddusha, yom lehertza'ah* — the night of the eighth is fit for sanctification, while the actual bringing of the *korban* takes place only during the day. An animal sanctified on the night of the eighth is not *nidcha* and not considered to have been sanctified prematurely — it has reached the threshold of eligibility for sanctification even though the day has not yet begun. But it may only be physically offered once the day arrives. This framework — night for sanctification, day for offering — maintains internal consistency: we measure fitness for *keddusha* in whole-day units, while the actual *avodah* is restricted to daytime.

---

## Live Animals Dichui

### Zeira's Question

Rabbi Zeira raises a pointed question to Rabbi Abba: *leima kasvar Rabbi Yochanan baalei chayim nidchin?* The entire analysis just conducted concerning the *pesach* passing through an invalid period presupposed that it matters whether the living animal is considered *nidcha* or not. The very fact that we had to find a reason why such an animal is *not* pushed off implies that in principle live animals *can* be pushed off. Does Rabbi Yochanan hold that *baalei chayim nidchin* — that living animals are subject to *dichui*?

This question is theoretically significant. There is reason to think that a living being, precisely because it is dynamic and not static, cannot be permanently stigmatized the way an already-slaughtered sacrifice can. A living creature has, so to speak, the capacity for renewal. But the analysis of the *pesach* case seemed to take seriously the possibility that a live animal could become *nidcha*.

### Partnership Case

Rabbi Abba confirms that yes, Rabbi Yochanan holds *baalei chayim nidchin*, and cites a case Rabbi Yochanan himself discussed. Two partners own an animal together. One partner sanctifies his half. The *keddusha* does not spread throughout the animal because the other half belongs to someone else, so the animal is half-sanctified and cannot be brought as a *korban*. The partner then purchases the other half from his co-owner and sanctifies it as well. The animal is now fully sanctified. Nonetheless, says Rabbi Yochanan, the animal is *kedusha ve-eina kereiva* — it is holy but cannot be offered. Why? Because there was a period when it had *keddusha* but could not be brought — the half-sanctified state. That passing through a sanctified-but-unfit period is enough to render it permanently *nidcha*.

### Three Conclusions

The Gemara notes that three distinct principles can be derived from this case. First, *shma mina baalei chayim nidchin* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that live animals can indeed be *nidcha*. Second, *dichui mei-ikara havei dichui* — even if the animal was pushed off from the very beginning, having never been fully fit, that still constitutes *dichui*. Some might have argued that *dichui* only applies when something was once fit and then became unfit (*nira ve-nidcha*), but not when it was never fit from the start; this case demonstrates otherwise. Third, *yesh dichui be-damim* — even a sanctity that is merely *kedushat damim* (monetary sanctification of the animal's value rather than full bodily *kedushat mizbeach*) is sufficient to create *dichui* if the animal passed through a period when it had that sanctity but could not be offered.

---

## Dichui Cases

### Mumar Case

Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan presents a case that further illustrates *dichui* with living beings. Reuven ate *chelev* in error and then designated a *korban chatas* for that sin. He then became a *mumar* — rejecting that *mitzvah* or the Torah entirely — and in that state was unfit to bring a *korban*. In the language of the Gemara, a sacrifice brought by such a person is a *zevach resha'im*, unfit. He subsequently did *teshuvah*. Nevertheless — *ho'il ve-nidcha yidache* — since the *korban* passed through a period when it could not be brought, it remains *nidcha* and he must designate a new *korban*.

### Shoteh Case

A parallel case is reported by Rabbi Yirmiyah in the name of Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Reuven ate *chelev* in error, designated a *korban*, and then suffered a period of mental illness (*nishtateh*). He subsequently recovered (*nishtafa*). Here too — *ho'il ve-nidcha yidache* — the *korban* is *nidcha* because it passed through a period when the owner could not bring it.

### Why Both Cases

The Gemara explains why both cases must be taught. If only the *mumar* case were given, one might think: *mishum de-hu dachi nafshei be-yadayim* — he actively and willfully pushed himself out of eligibility, so *dichui* applies. But perhaps the *shoteh*, who did not choose his state, is different — *ki yashen dami*, he is like someone sleeping, in a temporary and natural state, and perhaps the *korban* is not *nidcha*. Conversely, if only the *shoteh* case were given, one might say: *mishum de-ein be-yado lachazor* — since he cannot will himself out of his illness, there is full *dichui*. But perhaps a *mumar*, who can choose to do *teshuvah* at any moment, is not considered to have pushed the *korban* away fully — *aval hacha de-yesh be-yado lachazor, eima lo*. Both cases are needed to establish that in either situation — voluntary rejection or involuntary incapacity — the *korban* remains *nidcha*.

This discussion also raises an interesting related question about a person in a coma. Unlike sleep, a coma is not a natural cycle one can expect to emerge from, and unlike the *mumar*, the person has no capacity to will himself out of the state. Such a person's status is at least as strongly subject to *dichui* as the *shoteh* case, perhaps more so.

### Horayos Case

Rabbi Yirmiyah then poses a more difficult question: someone ate *chelev* in error, designated a *korban*, and then *Beis Din* issued an erroneous ruling that *chelev* is in fact permitted. While this ruling stands, the *Beis Din* itself would have rejected this *korban* — the act is not considered a sin, so there is nothing to bring a *korban* for. *Beis Din* subsequently retracted its ruling. Is the *korban* now *nidcha*?

A *sava* — a certain elder — reports that when Rabbi Yochanan would begin teaching the laws of *dichui*, this was precisely the case he would open with, as his paradigmatic example.

### Horayos Explanation

This is surprising — one might think the *Horayos* case is *less* compelling than the *mumar* or *shoteh* cases. After all, *Beis Din*'s ruling was simply an error; retroactively, the act always was a sin. Why should the *korban* be pushed off?

The Gemara explains: *mai ta'ama — hasam gavra idchi, korban lo idchi* — in the *mumar* and *shoteh* cases, it is the *person* who became temporarily unfit to bring the *korban*, but there was never any period in which the concept of a *korban* for that sin was itself meaningless. The *korban chatas* always had a purpose; it was just the *gavra*, the individual, who was temporarily disqualified. Here, however, *hacha korban nami idchi* — during the period of the erroneous ruling, the very idea of a *korban* for this act was erased. The act was declared permissible; no *korban* was called for. The *korban* itself — not just the person — was pushed away. That is why Rabbi Yochanan found this to be the clearest and most forceful illustration of *dichui*.

---

## Ben Azzai Tradition

### Tradition Source

The Mishna records Shimon ben Azzai's statement: *mekubal ani mipi shivim u-shnayim zekenim* — I have received a tradition from seventy-two elders, on the day that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah was appointed head of the academy. The tradition was that all edible sacrifices slaughtered *shelo lishmo* are *kasher*, though the owners do not fulfill their obligation, with the exception of the *pesach* and the *chatat*. The significant word in Ben Azzai's formulation is *hane'echalim* — the edible sacrifices. The only sacrifice not included in that category (given that *chatat* is explicitly excepted) is the *olah*, which is entirely burnt.

### Olah Addition

The Mishna therefore concludes: *v'lo hosif Ben Azzai ela ha-olah* — the only thing Ben Azzai added beyond what was already known was the *olah*. The tradition as he received it implicitly included the *olah* among those for which *shelo lishmo* is *pasul*. However, *v'lo hodu lo chachamim* — the *chachamim* did not agree to this addition. In their view, the list is limited to *chatat* and *pesach*.

### Rav Huna Kal Vachomer

What is the reasoning behind Ben Azzai's position? Rav Huna offers a *kal va'chomer*: if a *chatat*, which is not entirely burnt (*eina kalil*) and retains portions for human consumption, is nevertheless *pasul shelo lishmo*, then an *olah*, which is entirely consumed on the *mizbeach* (*shehi kalil*) and thus embodies the highest level of dedication to God, should certainly be *pasul shelo lishmo*.

---

## Kal Vachomer Challenge

### Atonement Objection

The Gemara immediately challenges this *kal va'chomer*. A *chatat* has the special quality of *mechaperet* — it atones — and perhaps it is this quality that makes it especially sensitive to intent, requiring *lishmo*. One cannot necessarily extend that requirement to the *olah*, which does not perform the same atoning function.

### Pesach Proof

The response: *Pesach yochiach* — the *pesach* proves that *kaparah* is not the critical factor. The *pesach* does not atone for sins and yet *shelo lishmo* is *pasul* for it as well. The common denominator of *pesach* and *chatat* shows that the *lishmo* requirement is not specifically tied to *kaparah*.

### Fixed Time Objection

But then one could argue: *mah le-pesach sheken zemano kavua* — what is special about *pesach* is its fixed time. The *pesach* has a rigid, once-a-year *zman*, and perhaps that rigidity is what generates the heightened requirement of *lishmo*. One cannot extend from *pesach* to *olah* because *olah* has no fixed time.

### Common Denominator

The response: *chatat tochiach* — the *chatat* will prove that a fixed time is not the key factor, since *chatat* has no fixed time yet *shelo lishmo* is *pasul* for it. Then the *kal va'chomer* is reformulated as a *tzad ha-shaveh*, a common denominator: *shechein kodashim veshachtan shelo lishman pasul* — they are both *kodashim* for which *shelo lishmo* is *pasul*. Therefore, the *olah*, which is also *kodashim* and whose *shechita shelo lishmah* should likewise be *pasul*, is included.

### Denominator Problem

However, this common denominator proves too much. Once the *tzad ha-shaveh* is stated in these terms — they are *kodashim* for which *shelo lishmo* is *pasul* — there is no principled reason to stop at *olah*. All *korbanot* would appear to be *kodashim*, and all would then be subject to invalidity *shelo lishmo*. But the *chachamim* hold that the general rule is precisely the opposite — *shelo lishmo* is *kasher* for all *korbanot* except *pesach* and *chatat*. The *kal va'chomer* seems to be proving too broad a conclusion.

### Karet Objection

A further challenge: *mah lehatzad hashaveh shebahen, shechein yesh bahen tzad karet* — both *pesach* and *chatat* are connected to *karet*. Not bringing a *pesach* carries *karet*; a *chatat* atones for sins that involve *karet*. The *olah* has no such connection to *karet*, and therefore one cannot extend the rule to it.

### Tzibur Connection

The Gemara reports that Ben Azzai is not persuaded by the *karet* challenge. He responds with a different limiting principle: *shechein yeshnan betzibbur keveyachid* — both *pesach* and *chatat* are brought in a communal context as well as individually. A *chatat* is brought as a communal offering (as in the *Horayos* scenario or on *Rosh Chodesh*), and the *pesach*, though individually designated, is brought by the entire community together. The *olah* similarly has communal dimensions, whereas an *asham* does not — there is no communal *asham*. This connection to *tzibbur*, rather than the *karet* connection, is what Ben Azzai sees as the shared characteristic justifying the extension to *olah* but not to *asham*.

### Tradition Only

The Gemara ultimately steps back from the entire enterprise of constructing a *kal va'chomer*. As the objections multiply and interlock, it concludes: *u-ven Azzai gemara gmir lah* — Ben Azzai's position is not derived from a *kal va'chomer* at all. It rests on his received tradition from the seventy-two elders. That is exactly what he said at the outset: *mekubal ani*. Why, then, did Rav Huna present the *kal va'chomer*? *Lechadudei letalmidiah* — to sharpen his students. The *kal va'chomer* was offered as an exercise: can you construct a valid logical argument? Where does it break down? What objections can be raised? The entire elaborate back-and-forth was pedagogical — a workout for the analytic mind — not a genuine attempt to derive Ben Azzai's ruling from first principles, since that ruling ultimately rests on tradition alone.

---

---

# Zevachim 13

## Four Avodot & Lishmah

### Mishna: Pesach & Chatat

The thirteenth daf of Masechet Zevachim opens with a *mishna* that reads almost like a poem in its elegant comprehensiveness. The *mishna* states that a *pesach* offering and a *chatat* that were slaughtered *shelo lishmah* — not for their own sake — and whose blood was received, carried, and sprinkled either entirely *shelo lishmah*, or partly *lishmah* and partly *shelo lishmah*, or partly *shelo lishmah* and partly *lishmah*, are *pesulim*, disqualified. The underlying principle is striking in its strictness: it does not matter in what sequence the proper and improper intentions appear. Whether the *avodah* begins properly and deteriorates, or begins improperly and is later corrected, the result is the same — the offering is invalid. Proper intent must characterize each and every one of the four *avodot* throughout.

### Four Avodot Explained

The four *avodot* under discussion are *shechitah* (slaughter), *kabbalah* (receiving the blood), *holachah* (carrying the blood to the altar), and *zrikah* (sprinkling the blood). These four acts together constitute the complete sacrificial process, and the *mishna* teaches that the disqualifying intent — *machshavah shelo lishmah* — can take effect in any one of them.

The *mishna* then illustrates what it means to have mixed intent: *lishmah* for the sake of a *pesach* and *shelo lishmah* for the sake of a *shelamim*, or the reverse — starting with *shelamim* intent and redirecting toward *pesach*. Once the intent has been misdirected, there is no rectification. The sacrifice has been disqualified.

### R. Shimon on Holachah

Rabbi Shimon dissents on one point: he rules that the *holachah* does not require *lishmah* intent in the same way the other three *avodot* do. His reasoning is rooted in a distinction between the inevitable and the contingent. *Shechitah*, *kabbalah*, and *zrikah* are inherently unavoidable — there can be no sacrifice without each of them. The *holachah*, by contrast, is avoidable. If the *kohen* slaughters the animal directly adjacent to the altar, no carrying is required at all, and the blood can be sprinkled immediately. Since it is possible to perform the sacrifice without a *holachah* at all, Rabbi Shimon reasons that an improper thought during this dispensable act should not invalidate the offering.

### R. Eliezer's Distinction

Rabbi Eliezer introduces a further nuance. In his view, a *machshavah* is *poselet* — disqualifying — only when it occurs during a *holachah* performed in the place where walking is required. If, however, the *kohen* happens to be walking in an area where no *holachah* is obligatory — perhaps traversing a route that is not part of the required path — then a problematic thought arising in that context does not disqualify the offering. Improper intent is only operative when it attaches itself to a required act; when the act itself is unnecessary in the given circumstances, the errant thought has no surface on which to take effect.

At this point, the *Gemara* signals a transition that will define much of the daf. There are, in fact, two distinct categories of problematic intent in the realm of *korbanot*. The first, *machshavah shelo lishmah*, which the *mishna* has been discussing, concerns intent directed at a different offering than the one being brought. The second, *machshevat pigul*, concerns improper intent related to time — specifically, intending to eat or otherwise complete the offering outside its designated time. These two categories are not interchangeable, and much of the *Gemara*'s analysis will depend on keeping them carefully distinguished.

---

## Tarfon vs. Akiva

### Kabbalah Disqualification

The *Gemara* now raises a pointed question: does the *kabbalah* — receiving the blood — actually have the capacity to disqualify an offering through improper intent? The question arises from a *beraita* that appears to complicate matters, and the *Gemara* begins its inquiry by examining the biblical source for the four *avodot* themselves.

### Deriving from Vayikra 7

The *beraita* cites a verse from Vayikra (chapter 7) that serves as the scriptural basis for the four sacrificial acts. The verse reads: *ve'shachat et ben ha'bakar lifnei Hashem ve'hikrivu bnei Aharon ha'kohanim et ha'dam ve'zarku et ha'dam al ha'mizbeach saviv asher petach Ohel Moed* — "And he shall slaughter the young bull before God, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood near and sprinkle the blood on the altar all around, at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting." Three verbs emerge from this verse: *shachat* (slaughter), *ve'hikrivu* (and they shall bring near), and *ve'zarku* (and they shall sprinkle). Two of these verbs correspond directly to two of the four *avodot*: *shechitah* and *zrikah*. But what of the other two — *kabbalah* and *holachah*?

### Hikrivu = Kabalah

The *Gemara* identifies the middle verb, *ve'hikrivu*, as corresponding to *kabalat ha'dam* — receiving the blood. The question immediately follows: how do we know that *ve'hikrivu* refers to *kabbalah* and not to *zrikah*? The *Gemara*'s answer is straightforward: since *zrikah* is explicitly mentioned later in the same verse with the word *ve'zarku*, the term *ve'hikrivu* must refer to something else — and that something else is *kabbalah*.

The *Gemara* continues, noting that the verse specifies *bnei Aharon ha'kohanim* — that the act must be performed by a fit *kohen*, one who is not a *chalal* and not a *ba'al mum*, and moreover that it must be performed with *kli sharet*, meaning the *kohen* must be wearing his priestly vestments.

Rabbi Akiva then asks: what is the source that *kabbalah* requires a fit *kohen* and priestly vestments? He draws a comparison to a verse in Bamidbar at the opening of that book, which mentions *bnei Aharon ha'kohanim ha'meshuchim asher milei yadam l'khahen* — Aaron's anointed sons who were consecrated to serve. Since that passage refers to fit *kohanim* serving in their vestments, the same requirement extends to the *kabbalah* here.

### Rashi: Kabalah & Holachah

Rashi's comment on the identification of *ve'hikrivu* as *kabbalah* is particularly illuminating. One might ask: *ve'hikrivu* could refer equally to *holachah*, the act of bringing the blood near by carrying it to the altar — after all, *holachah* also involves coming close. How do we know it refers to *kabbalah* and not *holachah*?

Rashi explains that both *kabbalah* and *holachah* share the linguistic sense of drawing near. The root of *ve'hikrivu* — *karov*, nearness — captures both acts. *Kabbalah* involves receiving the blood as it pours from the slaughtered animal, a kind of passive encounter with what comes toward you. *Holachah* is active, a deliberate movement toward the altar. Rashi notes that the *svarah* underlying the *Gemara* is that *mah she'noheg b'kabbalah noheg b'holachah* — the same principles that govern *kabbalah* govern *holachah*, because they are intrinsically linked as two expressions of the same fundamental movement of drawing near.

There is something quietly profound in this linguistic observation. Both *kabbalah* and *halachah* — the reception of tradition and the path of practice — share this quality of approaching the Divine. One is receiving; the other is moving. Rashi sees them as of a piece.

The verse's phrase *bnei Aharon ha'kohanim* applies equally to the *kabbalah*, and Rashi further notes that the requirement of a *kli sharet* can be derived from the fact that Moshe himself received blood in a vessel at Sinai, establishing the vessel as an integral part of the act.

### R. Tarfon Affirms

What follows is one of the most emotionally charged exchanges in the *Gemara*. Rabbi Tarfon, the elder, cries out: *akapeach et banai im lo shamati l'havchin hefreish bein kabbalah l'zerikah ve'ein li l'fareish* — "By my sons' lives, if I have not heard a distinction between *kabbalah* and *zrikah*, yet I cannot now articulate it." He remembers that there is a difference, but the memory has escaped him. Rabbi Akiva, the younger, responds with perhaps a touch of audacity: *mah Rabbi Akiva, ani afareish* — "What is this? I, Rabbi Akiva, will explain it."

### R. Akiva's Distinctions

Rabbi Akiva proceeds to enumerate three distinctions between *kabbalah* and *zrikah*.

The first: *kabbalah lo asah bah machshavah kema'aseh* — in the context of *kabbalah*, a wrong thought does not have the same legal force as a wrong action. *Zrikah*, by contrast, operates under the principle that *machshavah kema'aseh* — intent is treated as equivalent to action.

The second: if the *kabbalah* is performed outside the Temple precincts, there is no liability for *karet*. If the *zrikah* is performed outside, the person is liable for *karet*.

The third: if *pesulim* — disqualified persons — performed the *kabbalah*, there is no capital liability. If *pesulim* performed the *zrikah*, there is.
