Rabbi Tarfon's response is extraordinary: *ha'avodah, at hitit yamin u'smol, ani shamati ve'ein li l'fareish ve'atah doreish u'mas'kim la'shmu'ah* — "By the Temple service, you have veered neither right nor left! I heard it and cannot explain it; you derive it and arrive at the same teaching." And then, in an act of profound tribute, he says: *kol ha'poreish mimcha ke'poreish mechayav* — anyone who separates from you is like one who separates from life itself.

The linguistic resonance is striking. The root *p-r-sh* appears throughout the entire passage: Rabbi Tarfon says he cannot *l'fareish*; Rabbi Akiva says *ani afareish*; and Rabbi Tarfon concludes that anyone who *poreish* from Rabbi Akiva is *poreish* from life. The word that signifies "to explain," "to articulate," "to separate" binds the entire drama together.

Yet this celebrated exchange creates a legal problem. The *mishna* stated that all four *avodot* must be performed *lishmah*, implying that a wrong thought in *kabbalah* is disqualifying. But Rabbi Akiva has just told us that *lo asah bah machshavah kema'aseh* — an improper thought in *kabbalah* is not as consequential as a wrong action. How do we reconcile the two?

---

## Pigul vs. Shelo Lish (II)

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves the contradiction with characteristic economy: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty at all. The two sources are simply discussing different categories of improper intent. *Kan be'machshevet pigul, kan be'machshavah shelo lishmah* — the *mishna* concerns *machshavah shelo lishmah* (intent directed at a different type of offering), while the *beraita* of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon concerns *machshevet pigul* (intent involving time-related impropriety). These are two distinct legal categories, and each has its own set of rules. The *Gemara* further notes that the *mishna*'s own language supports this reading: it describes the offering becoming *pasul*, disqualified, and does not use the language of *mitpagel*, becoming *pigul* — a precise linguistic signal that the *mishna* is not discussing *pigul* at all.

### Pigul Definition

*Pigul* is defined by its relationship to time and consumption. When a *kohen* performs one of the *avodot* with the intention of eating the offering, or completing a required act pertaining to the offering, after its designated time has elapsed, this intent renders the offering *pigul* — a category of disqualification that carries with it the penalty of *karet* for one who eats of the offering. *Machshavah shelo lishmah*, by contrast, means intending to bring the offering for the sake of a different sacrifice entirely — redirecting its identity rather than its timing. These two categories operate on distinct tracks, and Rabbi Akiva's teaching applies only to the domain of *pigul*, not to *shelo lishmah*.

---

## Pigul Source & Rules

### Vayikra 7:18 & Pigul

The *Gemara* now introduces the central scriptural source for *pigul*, a verse in Vayikra 7:18: *ve'im he'achol ye'achel mibesar zevach shelamav ba'yom ha'shelishi lo yeiratzeh ha'makriv oto lo yechashev lo pigul yiheyeh ve'ha'nefesh ha'ochelet mimenu avonah tisa* — "And if the flesh of his *shelamim* sacrifice shall indeed be eaten on the third day, the one who offered it shall not be accepted; it shall not be counted for him — it is *pigul*, and the person who eats of it shall bear his iniquity."

Several features of this verse arrest the rabbinic attention. The verb for eating appears twice — *he'achol ye'achel* — a grammatical doubling that the *Gemara* will exploit. The offering in view is the *shelamim*. The operative concept is *lo yeiratzeh* — it will not be accepted, which the *Gemara* identifies with the *ritzui*, the acceptance effected through *zrikah*. And the verse establishes *pigul* as the consequence of wrong intent regarding time of consumption.

The *Gemara* understands from this verse that *pigul* applies to everything connected with *devarim ha'mevi'im lidei achilah* — acts that bring the sacrifice toward consumption. The question becomes: which acts are included, and which are excluded?

---

## Pigul Source & Rules (II)

### Which Avodot = Pigul

The *beraita* begins from a position of maximal inclusion and then narrows. One might think that only *zrikah* can generate *pigul*, since it is the *zrikah* that constitutes the *ritzui*, the act of acceptance. But the *beraita* asks: from where do we include *shechitah* and *kabbalah*? The answer derives from the verse's language. Since the verse specifies that *lo yeiratzeh* — it will not be accepted — and since *ritzui* is the *zrikah*, the *zrikah* is taken as the paradigm. Every *avodah* that is *me'akevet kaparah* — that is indispensable for atonement, without which the atonement does not take effect — is included in the *pigul* framework.

The verse then serves to exclude two further acts: *shefichat shirayim* (pouring the remainder of the blood on the base of the altar) and *haktarat imurim* (burning the sacrificial portions on the altar). These are not *me'akevet kaparah*; the atonement is complete without them. Therefore, an improper time-related thought during these acts does not render the offering *pigul*.

The *ritzui* — acceptance — is thus identified specifically with *zrikah*, the sprinkling that finalizes the offering and creates the connection between the blood and the altar. Without *zrikah*, the *korban* does not atone. All four of the primary *avodot* — *shechitah*, *kabbalah*, *holachah*, and *zrikah* — share this quality of being indispensable to the completion of the sacrifice, and therefore all four are subject to *machshevet pigul*.

### Pigul Examples

The *Gemara* then works through specific cases to illustrate the boundaries. One sage poses a question to Rava: does a wrong thought regarding *shefichat shirayim* and *haktarat imurim* not disqualify the offering at all? A *beraita* had seemed to suggest that even these acts are covered by *pigul* — so how can we say they are excluded?

Rava resolves this by distinguishing between two different scenarios. In the first case: *hareini shochet al menat lekabel damah machar* — "I am slaughtering this animal with the intention of receiving its blood tomorrow." This is a wrong thought during *shechitah* about an act (*kabbalah*) that will happen the next day. This does not constitute *machshevet pigul*, since the *kabbalah* itself is not an act of consumption. In the second case: *hareini mekabel damah al menat lishpoch shirayim lemachar* — "I am receiving the blood with the intention of pouring the remainder on the altar tomorrow." Here, the intent during *kabbalah* concerns *shefichat shirayim*, and since *shefichat shirayim* is considered a form of *achilat mizbe'ach* — the altar's consumption — this intent does render the offering *pigul*.

The resolution of the further difficulty — where the *Gemara* cites a *mishna* suggesting that even thoughts about *shefichat shirayim* and *haktarat imurim* are covered — proceeds similarly. The verb *achol ye'achel* appears twice in the verse, corresponding to two types of consumption: *achilat adam* (human eating of the flesh) and *achilat mizbeach* (the altar's consumption of the blood and portions). A wrong thought during *zrikah* intending to pour the remainders the next day renders the offering *pigul*, because the *zrikah* itself is *me'akevet kaparah*. But a wrong thought during the *shefichat shirayim* itself, intending to burn the *imurim* the next day, does not render it *pigul*, since *shefichat shirayim* is not *me'akevet kaparah*.

In summary: two conditions must be met for *pigul* to apply. First, the improper intent must occur during one of the *avodot* that is *me'akevet kaparah* — indispensable for atonement. Second, the intent must concern the performance of an act of consumption — whether human eating of the meat or the altar's consumption of blood or portions — after the allotted time. If either condition is absent, the offering does not acquire *pigul* status.

---

## Pigul vs. Shelo Lish (II)

### Pigul & Eating Acts

The *beraita* thus establishes a coherent principle: *pigul* is generated only by thoughts that concern acts directly related to consumption — *devarim ha'mevi'im lidei achilah* — and only when those acts are themselves *me'akevet kaparah*. The *shefichat shirayim* and *haktarat imurim*, while they are acts of the altar's consumption in some sense, are not indispensable to the atonement and therefore fall outside the *pigul* framework when they are the object of an improper intent during a non-critical act. The verse's doubling of the verb of eating is the peg on which the *Gemara* hangs this entire structure.

---

## Inner Chatat Pigul

### R. Yehuda's Testimony

The discussion now shifts to a particularly intricate case: the *chatat pnimit*, the inner sin offering whose blood is sprinkled on the curtain separating the Sanctuary from the Holy of Holies. Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Chiyya reports: *shamati she'tevilat etzba mefagelet be'chatat pnimit* — I have heard that dipping one's finger in the blood of the inner *chatat* renders it *pigul* if done with improper time-related intent. The act in question is *tevilat etzba* — dipping the finger in the blood before sprinkling it on the curtain — which is the characteristic procedure of the inner *chatat*.

Ilfa heard this teaching and reported it before Rav Padda. Rav Padda raises an immediate objection.

### Learning Pigul from Shel…

Rav Padda's objection is pointed: *kelum lamadnu pigul ela mishlamim?* — Have we not derived all the laws of *pigul* from the *shelamim*, from the verse in Vayikra 7:18? And if all *pigul* law flows from that verse, then any application of *pigul* to other offerings must be derived by analogy to *shelamim*. But this creates a serious problem: in *shelamim*, there is no act of *tevilat etzba*, no dipping of the finger in the blood. The *shelamim*'s blood is collected in a vessel and sprinkled; the finger-dipping procedure simply has no parallel there. How, then, can we derive that *tevilat etzba* generates *pigul* in the inner *chatat* when there is nothing in *shelamim* with which to compare it?

This is reinforced by a further argument. If we truly learn everything from *shelamim*, then we should also learn: just as *shelamim* sacrificed *shelo lishmah* does not preclude it from becoming *pigul* — for an offering can be *shelo lishmah* and yet still be rendered *pigul* — so too a *chatat shelo lishmah* should not preclude it from becoming *pigul*. But this contradicts established *halachah*: a *chatat* sacrificed *shelo lishmah* is disqualified entirely and cannot become *pigul*. If we cannot fully learn the *chatat* from *shelamim* in this respect, how can we selectively apply the comparison only where it suits us?

The *Gemara* raises this question and notes that it requires derivation from *ribbui de'kra'ei* — an amplification drawn from multiple verses — rather than simple analogy.

The exchanges between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who reports having heard in a particular upper chamber that *tevilat etzba* does indeed render the inner *chatat pigul*, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who challenges this on precisely the grounds Rav Padda articulates, rehearse the same fundamental tension. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish insists: *kelum lamdu pigul ela mishlamim?* — everything we know about *pigul* comes from *shelamim*, and since *shelamim* has no *tevilat etzba*, there is no basis for saying that *tevilat etzba* creates *pigul* in the *chatat*.

### R. Yosi's Approach

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina proposes a resolution. He agrees that we learn everything from *shelamim*, but the comparison must be conducted through the lens of shared disqualifying factors. He states: *hoil ve'chutz limkomo posel be'shelamim ve'shelo lishmo posel be'chatat* — since the disqualification of *chutz limkomo* (consuming the offering outside the designated area) applies to *shelamim*, and the disqualification of *shelo lishmo* (offering not for its sake) applies to *chatat*, we can learn from one to the other through this parallel structure of disqualification.

The argument unfolds as follows: just as *chutz limkomo ha'posel be'shelamim motzi midei pigul* — the disqualification of *chutz limkomo* in *shelamim* precludes the offering from becoming *pigul* — so too *shelo lishmo ha'posel be'chatat motziah midei pigul* — the disqualification of *shelo lishmah* in *chatat* precludes the *chatat* from becoming *pigul*. The comparison works by identifying the structural parallel: each offering has a factor that disqualifies it and that, precisely because it disqualifies, removes the offering from the domain of *pigul*.

---

## Posel vs. Me'akev

### R. Yirmiyah's Framework

Rabbi Yirmiyah, however, challenges Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina's approach from within. He argues that the comparison is structurally flawed: *mah le'chutz limkomo ha'posel be'shelamim, she'ken noheg be'chol ha'zevachim* — what is distinctive about *chutz limkomo* as a disqualification in *shelamim* is that it applies universally, to all slaughtered offerings. Every *korban* is subject to the disqualification of *chutz limkomo*. By contrast, *shelo lishmo* does not apply universally; it applies specifically to *pesach* and *chatat* alone — as we saw at the very opening of the *mishna* with which this daf began. Because the two disqualifying factors do not share the same scope of application, the analogy is imprecise, and the derivation does not hold cleanly.

Rabbi Yirmiyah then proposes his own framework, one that proves to be among the most conceptually important principles of the daf: *davar ha'posel bahen motzi'am midei pigul; davar ha'me'akev bahen mevi'am lidei pigul* — something that disqualifies the offering prevents it from being rendered *pigul*; something that is indispensable to the offering's completion — that impedes the *kaparah* if absent — brings the offering within the domain of *pigul*.

The logic is as follows. A *davar ha'posel* is an element whose presence or improper performance renders the offering invalid from the outset. Because the offering is already disqualified, there is no valid offering remaining upon which *pigul* can operate. *Pigul* requires a valid offering as its substrate. But a *davar ha'me'akev* — an act that is essential to the completion of the atonement, without which the *kaparah* is not effected — is precisely the kind of act during which improper intent regarding time can create *pigul*. It is indispensable, which means the offering depends on it, which means an improper thought during it can determine the offering's ultimate status.

### Inner Chatat Ruling

Applying this framework to the inner *chatat*: *tevilat etzba* — dipping the finger in the blood — is it a *davar ha'posel* or a *davar ha'me'akev*? Rabbi Yirmiyah's framework would generate *pigul* from it only if it is a *davar ha'me'akev*. This becomes the question driving the remainder of the analysis.

---

## Meal Offering Avodot

### Rav Mari's Analogy

Rav Mari brings a *mishna* from Menachot to bear on the question, drawing an analogy between the four *avodot* of the *minchah* (meal offering) and the four *avodot* of the animal sacrifice. The *mishna* in Menachot enumerates: *kol ha'kometz ve'noten bikli ve'hamolich ve'hamaktir* — all who take the handful, place it in a vessel, carry it, and burn it. These four acts of the *minchah* parallel the four acts of the blood offering.

The parallels are largely transparent: *kometz* corresponds to *shechitah* (both prepare the essential sacrificial substance); *molich* corresponds to *holachah* (both involve carrying toward the altar); *maktir* corresponds to *zrikah* (both are the finalizing act of the offering upon the altar).

### Noten Bikli Parallel

The problematic parallel is *noten bikli* — placing the handful in a vessel. Rav Mari suggests this corresponds to *kabbalah*. But the *Gemara* challenges this: the cases are not fully comparable. In *kabbalah*, the blood flows into the vessel *memeilah* — on its own, spontaneously, once the animal is slaughtered. The *kohen* need not actively place anything; the blood comes to the vessel. In *noten bikli*, the *kohen* actively takes the *kometz* and places it into the vessel — it does not happen on its own.

The *Gemara* responds that this distinction is ultimately inconsequential: *keivan de'idi ve'idi matan kli hu* — since in both cases the defining feature is the placement into a vessel, whether it arrives there spontaneously or is actively placed makes no difference. *Mah li memeilah, mah li ka shakil ve'yahiv* — it is the same to me whether the blood flows in by itself or whether the *kohen* takes and places it. The vessel is the common denominator.

### No Pigul for Finger Dipp…

But this resolution, while it establishes the parallel between *noten bikli* and *kabbalah*, actually sharpens the problem regarding *tevilat etzba* in the inner *chatat*. The *noten bikli* of the *minchah* and the *kabbalah* of the blood offering can be compared because both involve the vessel as the defining element. *Tevilat etzba*, however — the dipping of the finger in the blood of the inner *chatat* — has no counterpart whatsoever in the *shelamim* procedure. There is no vessel, no spontaneous collection, no analogous act in the offering from which we derive all *pigul* law.

The conclusion therefore follows: since *tevilat etzba* in the inner *chatat* has no equivalent act in *shelamim*, and since all *pigul* law is derived from the *shelamim* verse, there is no basis for applying *pigul* to *tevilat etzba*. The dipping of the finger in the blood of the inner *chatat* does not render the offering *pigul*, because the act has no comparable *avodah* against which to measure it and from which the *pigul* status could be derived.

---

---

# Zevachim 14

## Four Avodos & Pigul

### Opening & Four Avodos

The daf begins in the middle of a substantive conceptual debate — a welcome breath of fresh air after the extended *drashot* of the earlier *pesukim*. The Gemara on the bottom of 13b opens with *leima k'tana'ei* and we are squarely in the world of the four *avodos* of sacrifice: *shechita* (slaughtering the animal), *kabbalas hadam* (receiving the blood), *holacha* (transporting it to the altar), and *zerika* (sprinkling it on the altar). A *machshava* — a disqualifying thought — during any one of these *avodos* carries legal consequences. For ordinary sacrifices, a *shelo lishma* thought means the sacrifice does not fulfill the owner's obligation. For a *chatas* or a *pesach*, such a thought renders the sacrifice entirely invalid. Similarly, a *pigul* thought — intending to eat the sacrifice outside its proper time — arises during these same *avodos* and is a regular subject of the Gemara's discussion.

### Piggul & Shelo Lishma

Against this backdrop, the Gemara raises a focused question: what is the status of dipping the finger (*tvillas etzba*) into the blood of the *chatas*? This act pertains both to the inner *chatas* (whose blood is applied on the inner altar, as on *Yom Kippur*) and to the outer *chatas* (whose blood is applied at the corners of the outer altar). Can a *machshava* during *tvillas etzba* invalidate — either by generating *pigul* or *shelo lishma*? And does a *pigul* thought directed at *tvillas etzba* render the act the content of the invalid intent? The Gemara frames this as a question of whether *tvillas etzba* possesses the halachic status of an *avodah*.

### Tvillas Etzba as Avodah

The Gemara categorizes *tvillas etzba* as a form of *holacha* — part of the process of conveying blood toward the altar — rather than as *zerika* (the actual placement). One might intuitively assign it to *zerika*, since blood is being moved toward the altar. The Gemara acknowledges this and seems to prefer *holacha* because the act is not the final placement but a necessary step in getting the blood ready for placement. More significantly, the framing as *holacha* is appropriate because *holacha* is precisely the *avodah* about which there exists a debate between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon: whether thought during *holacha* invalidates. Since *tvillas etzba* is a form of *holacha* that cannot be dispensed with — unlike ordinary *holacha*, which in principle can be avoided by slaughtering adjacent to the altar — it should arguably carry greater weight as a necessary *avodah* even by Rabbi Shimon's logic. A parallel question arises from *mincha*: the *kometz* of the *mincha* parallels *shechita*, placing it in a *kli* parallels *kabbala*, and burning it on the altar parallels *zerika*. But *tvillas etzba* has no exact parallel in the *mincha* framework, which raises the additional question of whether one can recognize an entirely new *avodah*, or incorporate a non-standard act into an existing category, even when it is explicitly mentioned in the *pasuk* and is halachically necessary.

---

## Tvillas Etzba Tannaim

### Baraita on Tvillas Etzba

The Gemara cites two conflicting *Baraisos*. The first states: *t'vilas etzba m'paggeles b'chatas* — dipping the finger can cause *pigul* in a *chatas*, meaning it is treated as a genuine *avodah* during which intent matters. The second *Baraita* states the opposite: *lo m'paggeles v'lo mitpaggeles* — it neither causes *pigul* nor is it subject to being the object of a *pigul* thought during other *avodos*. The *v'lo mitpaggeles* clause is of less interest here; what commands attention is the dispute over whether *tvillas etzba* is itself an *avodah* that can generate *pigul*. The Gemara initially proposes that this is a straightforward *machlokes Tannaim* — a dispute as to whether *tvillas etzba* counts as one of the recognized *avodos*.

### Rabbanan vs. R. Shimon

The Gemara then reframes the dispute. Rather than being a debate specifically about *tvillas etzba*, it may reflect the broader *machlokes* between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Shimon regarding *holacha*. For the *Rabbanan*, *holacha* is a full *avodah* during which *machshava* invalidates; for Rabbi Shimon, since *holacha* is an *avodah* one can in principle avoid, *machshava* during it does not invalidate. One might object that Rabbi Shimon is a *Tanna*, making this indeed a *machlokes Tannaim*. But the Gemara's point is that one need not say it is a debate specifically about *tvillas etzba*. Rather, everyone may agree that *tvillas etzba* counts as *holacha*, and the dispute is really about the broader question of *holacha* — which is a known debate.

### Inner/Outer Chatas

The Gemara then offers a resolution that avoids positing any *machlokes* at all. *V'lo kashya* — the two *Baraisos* are not in conflict. Each addresses a different case: one speaks of the inner *chatas*, the other of the outer *chatas*. By the inner *chatas*, the *pasuk* explicitly states *v'taval et etzba'o badam* — "he shall dip his finger in the blood." Since the act is both necessary and explicitly labeled by the Torah, it carries the full status of *holacha*, and *machshava* during *tvillas etzba* invalidates according to all opinions. By the outer *chatas*, while the act of dipping is halachically required, the *pasuk* does not explicitly say *v'taval*. Instead, it says *velakach b'etzba'o min hadam* — "he shall take from the blood with his finger." One might have supposed that since *velakach* implies taking with the finger — which is essentially dipping — it is equivalent to an explicit *pasuk*, and *machshava* should invalidate here as well. After all, if a monkey came and placed blood on the *kohen*'s finger, the *kohen* would still be required to dip his finger back into the blood (*ba'ei l'mitbal zimna achriti*), demonstrating that the act of dipping is genuinely required even by the outer *chatas*, not merely incidental.

### Monkey Example

The monkey case thus establishes that even for the outer *chatas*, the act of dipping is substantively obligatory and not merely the consequence of whichever method happens to get blood onto the finger. One might therefore conclude — since the required act is functionally identical to the inner *chatas* — that *tvillas etzba* should count as an *avodah* for the outer *chatas* as well, rendering it *k'man de'ksiv v'taval*, as if the *pasuk* had explicitly stated "dip."

---

## Scripture & Avodah

### Why Not Vtaval

The Gemara rejects this conclusion. The outer *chatas* is categorically different because the *pasuk* does not explicitly say *v'taval*. The word *velakach* carries dual interpretive weight: *Rashi* notes that one reading of *velakach* focuses not on the finger at all but on the blood itself — "*take the blood*," meaning the act of *kabbala*, catching the blood in a vessel from the neck of the slaughtered animal. Thus the word *etzba* is somewhat bracketed in that reading. The fact that the Torah chose *velakach* rather than *v'taval* signals that this act, though halachically required, is not being designated by the Torah as a central *avodah* of the *chatas* ritual.

### No Explicit = No Piggul

The Gemara states this as an operative principle: *lo ksiv v'taval — ka mashma lan*. The Torah deliberately avoided writing *v'taval* to indicate that while the act must be performed, it does not carry the status of an *avodah* for purposes of invalidation. If the *pasuk* had said *v'taval* explicitly, we would have treated *machshava* during *tvillas etzba* of the outer *chatas* as invalidating — *k'man de'ksiv v'taval dami*, as if it had been explicitly stated. But since the *pasuk* is ambiguous — *d'mashma hachi u'mashma hachi* — and does not explicitly designate this act, it remains a required step without the halachic weight that would make *machshava* during it operative.

### Inner/Outer Summary

The upshot is a clean distinction: for the inner *chatas*, where the *pasuk* explicitly labels *tvillas etzba*, the act is treated as a form of *holacha*, and *machshava* during it invalidates according to all views (including the *Rabbanan*). For the outer *chatas*, while the dipping is halachically required — and failure to dip renders the sacrifice invalid — it is not treated as a designated *avodah* for purposes of *machshava*, and thought during that moment does not invalidate. Both *Baraisos* are therefore consistent: one addresses the inner *chatas*, the other the outer *chatas*, and no *machlokes Tannaim* need be posited.

---

## R. Shimon & Holacha

### R. Shimon's Principle

Having resolved the tension between the two *Baraisos*, the Gemara now turns explicitly to Rabbi Shimon's position on *holacha*. The principle is stated clearly: *avodah she'efshar levatlah, lav avodah hi* — an *avodah* that can in principle be dispensed with does not carry the halachic weight of an *avodah* for purposes of *machshava*. Since one could in principle slaughter an animal right next to the altar and thereby eliminate the need for *holacha*, Rabbi Shimon holds that *machshava* during *holacha* does not invalidate.

### Inner Chatas Exception

The Gemara records that Rabbi Shimon himself acknowledges an exception: *modeh Rabbi Shimon beholachas chatas hapnimis shemachshava poseles bo*. For the inner *chatas*, even Rabbi Shimon concedes that *machshava* during *holacha* invalidates. The reason is *hoil ve'avodah she'eino yachol levatlah* — it is an *avodah* that cannot be dispensed with. Since the animal cannot be slaughtered inside the *heichal* or the *ulam*, it must be slaughtered outside, and the blood must then be transported inside. That *holacha* is therefore genuinely necessary — not merely incidental to where one happens to position oneself — and Rabbi Shimon agrees that *machshava* during a truly necessary *holacha* does invalidate.

### Temple Layout Diagram

Understanding why the *holacha* is unavoidable requires attention to the physical layout of the *Beis HaMikdash*. The outer altar stands in the *azarah*. Adjacent is the *ulam*, the vestibule, and beyond it the *heichal*, the inner sanctuary. The inner altar, on which the blood of the inner *chatas* is applied, stands within the *heichal*. The animal must be slaughtered to the north of the outer altar — in the *azarah* — since slaughtering inside the *ulam* or *heichal* is not halachically acceptable (and the Gemara implies it would be invalid, even though *Rashi* describes it only as inappropriate; for the Gemara's analysis to hold, the invalidity must be operative). The blood therefore must travel from the *azarah* into the *heichal*, making *holacha* genuinely unavoidable. This is why even Rabbi Shimon agrees that *machshava* during *holacha* of the inner *chatas* invalidates.

---

## Piggul/Shelo Lishma

### Piggul Problem

A difficulty now surfaces. If we are saying that *machshava* during *holacha* of the inner *chatas* invalidates — specifically a *pigul* thought — we encounter Rabbi Shimon's independent ruling that *kol she'ein al mizbeach hachitzon kishlamim, ein chayavin alav mishum pigul*: anything not offered on the outer altar as a *shelamim* is excluded from the laws of *pigul*. The inner *chatas* is by definition not brought on the outer altar. Therefore, according to Rabbi Shimon, *pigul* does not apply to the inner *chatas* at all. How then can we say that a *machshava* during *holacha* of the inner *chatas* would generate *pigul*? *Rashi* notes that the simpler answer would have been to say we are not talking about *pigul* at all — the *Mishnah* is fundamentally discussing *shelo lishma*, and a *shelo lishma* thought during *holacha* of the inner *chatas* would of course invalidate since it is a necessary *avodah*. However, since the Gemara framed the question around *pigul*, it answers within that framework.

### Piggul on Meat Only

The resolution is offered by Rebbi Yosi b'Rebbi Chanina: when Rabbi Shimon said *pigul* does not apply to things not brought on the outer altar, he meant specifically that the *status* of *pigul* does not attach to the *meat*. The significance of the *pigul* status on the meat is that one who eats it incurs *kares*. The meat of an inner *chatas* is already forbidden; one who eats it violates a *lav*, but even without *pigul* status one would not incur *kares* for eating it, since there is no *pigul* designation applicable. What Rabbi Shimon excluded, therefore, is specifically *kares* for eating the meat. He did not exclude the invalidation of the *korban* itself. A *machshava* of *chutz lizmano* during *holacha* of the inner *chatas* does invalidate the sacrifice — it simply does not confer the additional *kares* penalty on the meat. The same applies to *shelo lishma*: it invalidates the *korban*.

### Kal Vachomer

This resolution leads the Gemara to a *kal vachomer*. If *shelo lishma* — which does not invalidate a *shelamim* — nonetheless invalidates a *chatas*, then *chutz lizmano* — which *does* invalidate a *shelamim* (with *kares*) — should certainly invalidate a *chatas* as well. This is Rebbi Yosi b'Rebbi Chanina's logic: *umah shelo lishman shehuchshru bishlamim pasul bachatat, chutz lizmano shepasul bishlamim eino din sheyifsol bachatat*. The *chatas* is structurally easier to invalidate than the *shelamim*, and so whatever invalidates the *shelamim* certainly invalidates the *chatas*.

The Gemara then presses further: granted that *chutz lizmano* invalidates the inner *chatas* via this *kal vachomer*, what is the source for *chutz limkomo* — a thought of the wrong *place* — also invalidating the inner *chatas*? One might attempt a parallel *kal vachomer*: just as *chutz lizmano* invalidates, so does *chutz limkomo*. But the Gemara objects — *chutz lizmano* is weightier because it carries *kares*, and one cannot simply transfer that logic to *chutz limkomo*. Alternatively, one might derive *chutz limkomo* from *shelo lishma*: if the weaker (*shelo lishma*, which has no application to *shelamim*) invalidates a *chatas*, certainly *chutz limkomo* (which does invalidate a *shelamim*) should. But the Gemara objects here too: *shelo lishma* has broader scope in one sense — it applies even on a *bama* (a private altar during periods when *bamot* were permitted). *Chutz limkomo* is irrelevant on a *bama* because there is no fixed *makom*; it is not that *chutz limkomo* is halachically inapplicable, simply that the concept has no referent. But *shelo lishma* similarly has no real application on a *bama*, since only free-will offerings were brought on *bamot*, and *pesach* and *chatas* — the sacrifices where *shelo lishma* actually invalidates — were never brought on a *bama*. So neither can demonstrate the broader scope of the other, and the *kal vachomer* from *shelo lishma* to *chutz limkomo* is valid.

The ultimate source is a *hekesh* — an analogy derived from the same *pasuk*. The *pasuk* states: *im he'achol ye'achel bayom hashlishi pigul hu lo yeratzeh* — if it will be eaten on the third day, it is *pigul*, it will not be accepted. *Shlishi* — the third day — is *chutz lizmano*, a thought to eat it at the wrong time. *Pigul hu lo yeratzeh* would be redundant if it referred to the same thing; the Gemara reads *lo yeratzeh* as including *chutz limkomo* — the wrong place — thereby linking both categories in a single verse. Since the *pasuk* packages *chutz lizmano* and *chutz limkomo* together, whatever *din* applies to one applies to the other. Even according to Rabbi Shimon, therefore, a thought of the wrong time or the wrong place invalidates the inner *chatas*.

---

## Necessary Holacha

### Shechita Location

Having established that Rabbi Shimon agrees *machshava* during *holacha* of the inner *chatas* invalidates because the *holacha* is unavoidable, the Gemara now explores precisely *how much* of that *holacha* is truly necessary. This is where the discussion becomes particularly intricate. Rava opens with: *im timtzi lomar* — if you say that Rabbi Shimon holds like his son, who rules that the space between the *ulam* and the outer altar counts as "north of the altar." The requirement to slaughter the inner *chatas* to the north of the altar means, on the broadest reading, that *shechita* must occur directly adjacent to the altar's northern face. From that point, all the walking to the *heichal* would be necessary *holacha*.

### North Space

But Rabbi Shimon's son holds that even the airspace between the *ulam* and the outer altar — the open courtyard area that lies between them — counts as north of the altar. If so, one could slaughter the inner *chatas* anywhere in that space, including right at the door of the *ulam*. In that case, the only truly necessary *holacha* — the only portion during which *machshava* would invalidate — is from the door of the *ulam* inward. Walking prior to that point is not halachically required, because in principle one could have slaughtered right at the *ulam* doorstep. *Ein machshava mo'eles b'holachas chatas hapnimiyos ela mipisach ulam v'lifnim* — *machshava* is operative only from the door of the *ulam* and inward.

### Ulam Door Threshold

The Gemara continues with further refinements, now shifting to a different case — *siluk bezichin*, removing the incense (*levona*) from the *lechem hapanim* (the showbread) on the *shulchan*. This incense had to be brought out and burned on the altar, an act that functionally releases the bread for consumption. The question of necessary *holacha* applies here as well. If one holds that the floor between the *ulam* and the outer altar has the sanctity of the altar itself (a position attributed to Rabbi Yehuda — *toch azarah mekadesh*), then in principle one could burn the incense on that floor as soon as one exits the *heichal*. The only *holacha* that is truly necessary is from the door of the *heichal* outward. Any further walking, since the incense could have theoretically been deposited just outside the *heichal* door, is not required. In this scenario, *machshava* would be operative only from the *heichal* door and outward — *mipisach heichal velachutz*.

But why from the *heichal* door and not from where the inner altar actually stands? Because the inner altar could in principle be positioned right up against the *heichal* doorway, and from that position the incense could be burned on the floor immediately upon exiting. Any earlier movement of the altar within the *heichal* is not halachically mandated.

### Arm Stretch Only

The refinements continue. If one holds that the *heichal* and the *ulam* share a single level of sanctity (*kedushas heichal ve'ulam chada hi*), then the inner altar could theoretically be positioned anywhere within the combined space of *heichal* and *ulam*, up to the outer door of the *ulam*. Since the floor of the *azarah* already has the sanctity of the altar (in this framework), one could in theory place the *shulchan* right against the outer edge of the *ulam* doorway, take the incense, and burn it by merely extending one's arm to deposit it on the floor just outside. The doorway of the *ulam* had significant physical thickness — like a thick wall through which one walks. If the doorway itself (*toch petach*) shares the sanctity of the interior, then theoretically the *shulchan* could be at the very outer edge of that doorway, and the only necessary act would be stretching the arm to place the incense on the floor. Not even a full step would be required — only *bichedei lehoshit yado*, the distance of extending one's arm.

Taking this to its logical extreme: *ein machshava mo'eles afilu pesiah achas* — not even one step of *holacha* would carry *machshava* weight. The only operative moment would be the arm's extension from the threshold to the floor. And this introduces the next question directly: if the only "transport" is the stretching of an arm with no bodily movement of the feet, does that even qualify as *holacha* in a halachic sense?

---

## Holacha Beregel

### Hand-to-Hand Transfer

This brings the Gemara to a new question: *holacha shelo beregel, shemah holacha o lo shemah holacha* — if the blood is transported without any walking — for example, passed hand to hand among a line of *kohanim*, each standing in place — does that constitute a valid act of *holacha*?

The question is two-directional. If such passing does *not* constitute *holacha*, then the blood must be returned and transported again properly; but on the upside, since no *avodah* occurred, any *machshava* during that hand-to-hand transfer does not invalidate. Conversely, if hand-to-hand transfer *does* constitute *holacha*, then it was a valid *avodah* — but any disqualifying *machshava* during it would invalidate the blood. Similarly, if a *zar* performed this transfer: if it counts as *holacha* and *holacha* requires a *kohen*, the *zar*'s act would have invalidated the sacrifice; if it does not count as *holacha*, no act of consequence occurred and the blood may simply be transported again properly.

---

## Non-Kohen Holacha

### Abaye's Question

Abaye's question to the *amora* of Rav Chisda — relayed so that it could be posed to Rav Chisda at the next opportunity — is direct: *holacha bezar mahu*, what is the *halacha* if a non-*kohen* performs *holacha*? The background assumption is that ordinarily, a *zar* who performs an *avodah* invalidates it. But *shechita* is the well-known exception: a non-*kohen* may perform *shechita* and the sacrifice remains valid. The question is whether *holacha*, which follows *kabbala* (an act that unambiguously requires a *kohen*), is more like *kabbala* and *zerika* or more like *shechita*.

### Rav Chisda's Source

Rav Chisda responds that *holacha* performed by a *zar* is *keshera* — valid — and he supports this from a *pasuk* in *Divrei Hayamim*: *vayishchatu es hapesach vayizreku hakohanim es hadam miyadam* — the people slaughtered the *pesach* offering, and the *kohanim* sprinkled the blood *from their hands* — meaning from the hands of the Israelites who slaughtered. The implication is that after the *kohen* received the blood, a non-*kohen* carried it to the *kohen* who performed the *zerika*. *Rashi* notes that a *kohen* must have performed the initial *kabbala*, but once the blood was caught, a non-*kohen* brought it to the *kohanim* who threw it. This sequence suggests that the *holacha* portion was performed by a non-*kohen* without invalidating the *korban*.

### Rav Sheshes Counter

Rav Sheshes objects from an explicit *Baraita*: *zar ve'onen, shikor u'vaal mum — bekabbala, beholacha uvizrika pasul*. A non-*kohen*, a mourner (*onen*), someone intoxicated, or someone with a physical blemish — all of these disqualify the sacrifice if they performed *kabbala*, *holacha*, or *zerika*. The only exception is *shechita*. This *Baraita* is unambiguous. It goes on to note: *vechen yoshev vechen smol* — similarly, performing these *avodos* while seated or with the left hand is invalid, because service in the *Beis HaMikdash* must be performed while standing, as derived from *laamod leshares*. The contradiction between this *Baraita* and Rav Chisda's reading of the *Divrei Hayamim* passage requires resolution.

### Pedestal Solution

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the *Divrei Hayamim* passage is describing a situation where the non-*kohen* was not performing an act of *holacha* at all. Rather, *de'avid maaseh itztaba* — he acted as a pedestal. The *kohen* caught the blood, placed the vessel on the non-*kohen*'s outstretched hands (without the non-*kohen* moving), and another *kohen* then took it from the non-*kohen*'s hands and carried it to the *zerika*. The non-*kohen* in this scenario is functionally an inanimate stand — he holds the vessel without transporting it. The *pasuk*'s phrasing — the *kohanim* took the blood *from their hands* — supports this reading: the Israelites did not hand it to the *kohanim*; rather, the *kohanim* retrieved it from stationary Israelites. This was not an act of *holacha* by a *zar* but merely the use of a human pedestal.

### Machlokes R. Shimon

Rabba and Rav Yosef then offer an alternative framing: *holacha bezar machlokes Rabbi Shimon verabbanan* — the question of whether a *zar* can perform *holacha* is actually tied to the *machlokes* about the status of *holacha* as an *avodah*. For Rabbi Shimon, who holds *avodah she'efshar levatlah lav avodah hi* — that an *avodah* one can in principle dispense with is not treated as a full *avodah* — *holacha* is downgraded and can therefore be performed by a *zar*. For the *Rabbanan*, who maintain that *holacha* is a full *avodah*, a *zar* who performs it invalidates. The proposed correlation is thus: the weight assigned to *holacha* as an *avodah* determines both whether *machshava* during it invalidates and whether a *zar* performing it invalidates.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges this correlation. *Shechita* is an *avodah she'i efshar levatlah* — one that cannot be dispensed with; *shechita* is absolutely necessary for the sacrifice. Yet *shechita keshera bezar* — a non-*kohen* may perform it. So the proposed correlation — that an *avodah* one cannot avoid requires a *kohen*, while one that can be avoided does not — breaks down. The inability to dispense with an *avodah* does not entail that a *kohen* is required.

### Shechita Non-Avodah

The Gemara's response is pointed: *shechita lav avoda hi* — *shechita* is simply not an *avodah* in the technical sense. It is necessary, *machshava* during it can invalidate, slaughtering for *avoda zara* carries capital liability, and slaughtering outside the *Beis HaMikdash* carries liability for *shechutei chutz* — yet it is not classified as an *avodah* in the halachic sense that would require a *kohen*. The marker of its non-*avodah* status is precisely that a non-*kohen* may perform it. The Gemara acknowledges that the question of what exactly constitutes an *avodah* — and what cluster of *halachos* attach to that designation — is not fully resolved by a single criterion. Within the recognized *avodos* from *kabbala* onward, however, the correlation between *avodah* status and the requirement of a *kohen* does hold. *Shechita* is in a category of its own and should not be imported into this analysis.

An attempt is made to demonstrate that *shechita* is nonetheless an *avodah*, based on the ruling of Rav (cited by Rabbi Zeira) that *shechitas parah bezar psula* — slaughtering the *parah aduma* by a non-*kohen* is invalid. If the requirement of a *kohen* signals *avodah* status, and *shechita* of the *parah aduma* requires a *kohen*, then *shechita* must be an *avodah*. The Gemara even proposes a *kal vachomer*: if by *kadshai bedek habayis* — sanctified items that are not even sacrifices — *shechita* is treated as an *avodah* requiring a *kohen*, how much more so by *kadshai mizbeach*. But this is rejected: *shani parah, d'kadshai bedek habayis hi* — the *parah aduma* is anomalous, as it is not a *korban* at all and is not brought in the *Beis HaMikdash*. Its particular laws cannot be the basis for a *kal vachomer* about sacrificial *shechita*. Rav Sheshes the son of Rav Idi adds: the need for a *kohen* is not in itself a mark of *avodah* status, since inspecting *nega'im* (leprous afflictions) requires a *kohen* and is clearly not an *avodah*. So the inference fails, *shechita* remains a non-*avodah*, and the challenge from *shechita* to the correlation does not stand.

### Holacha Always Pasul

The Gemara ultimately concludes via Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *holacha bezar pesulah afilu Rabbi Shimon* — even according to Rabbi Shimon, a *zar* who performs *holacha* of the blood invalidates it. The Gemara's conclusion therefore assumes that even Rabbi Shimon's downgrading of *holacha* for purposes of *machshava* does not reduce *holacha* to such a degree that a *zar* may perform it. *Holacha* retains its status as an *avodah* — a *zar* performing it renders the sacrifice invalid — even if, according to Rabbi Shimon, *machshava* during a non-necessary *holacha* does not invalidate. The downgrading is specific and limited: it affects *machshava* for avoidable *holacha*, but not the fundamental requirement that the *avodah* be performed by a *kohen*.

---

## Holacha Beregel (II)

### Sitting/Left Hand

The Gemara now returns to the unresolved question of *holacha shelo beregel* — whether *holacha* requires actual bodily movement, i.e., traversing the distance with one's feet. The first source adduced is the *Baraita* cited earlier: *vechen yoshev vechen smol* — sitting or using the left hand invalidates *holacha*. If sitting invalidates *holacha*, this seemingly implies that standing while performing the same action (passing the vessel) is valid. That in turn would suggest that stationary hand-to-hand transfer — done while standing — constitutes valid *holacha*.

But the Gemara is not satisfied with this inference. Perhaps *yoshev de'kashif meishaf* — one who is sitting might be scooting along the ground, performing a form of bodily movement. If so, the invalidity of sitting is because sitting while moving is an inappropriate mode of service (*laamod leshares* requires standing); and the corresponding valid form — standing — would also involve some bodily movement (*ha'omed dumya deyoshev denayad purta*), a slight shifting while moving. On this reading, the *Baraita* does not tell us anything about whether pure hand-to-hand transfer without any movement constitutes *holacha*.

### Pesach Narrative

The Gemara then turns to the *pesach* narrative — precisely the passage raised earlier. *Shachat Yisrael, vekibel hakohen, nasan lechavero vechavero lechavero* — the Israelite slaughtered, the *kohen* caught the blood, and it was passed from one *kohen* to the next, until it reached the *kohen* who performed the *zerika*. This chain of hand-to-hand passing is familiar from the Gemara's earlier resolution of Rav Chisda's source, where it concluded that the Israelites functioned as pedestals. But here the question is different: does the chain of *kohanim* passing the blood to one another — without each necessarily walking — constitute a valid *holacha*? The narrative seems to present it as the proper procedure, suggesting it is valid. The Gemara responds again: *hatam nami denayad purta* — perhaps each *kohen* took a small step as he passed the vessel to the next, incorporating some bodily movement, however minimal, into the act of transfer.

### Pasul Recipient

This leads to a further nuance. The *Baraita* states: *kibel hakosher venasan* — if a valid (*kosher*) *kohen* received the blood and passed it to an invalid (*pasul*) *kohen* (or a *zar*), then *yachzir lakasher* — it must be returned to a *kosher* kohen. Now, this ruling might imply that the initial *kosher* *kohen*'s act of handing the blood to the *pasul* recipient was itself an invalid *holacha* — meaning no *avodah* took place, so the blood may be recovered and the *holacha* performed again. But it might also be read otherwise: another *kohen* can come and retrieve it from the *pasul*'s hands — *eima yachzor hakasher veykablah* — meaning the initial act of the valid *kohen* stretching his arm to hand the blood was a *holacha*, but since it landed in the hands of a *pasul*, it needs a valid *kohen* to retrieve it and continue. The ambiguity in the *Baraita*'s language — does *yachzir lakasher* mean "hand it back" or "let a valid *kohen* take it forward" — is genuine and unresolved.

### Unresolved Question

In the end, the Gemara does not reach a definitive resolution on whether *holacha shelo beregel* constitutes valid *holacha*. The question — whether the act of transporting the blood requires that the *kohen* physically traverse the distance with his feet, or whether stationary hand-to-hand passing suffices — remains open (*teiku*). Each attempted source either admits an alternative reading that preserves the possibility of bodily movement, or is ambiguous enough not to settle the matter. This unresolved question stands as the conclusion of the daf.

---

---

# Zevachim 15

## Holacha Shelo Baragel

### Intro: Holacha Shelo Bar…

The sugya opens in the middle of a discussion concerning the act of *holacha* — the conveying of the blood, after *kabbalah*, from the point of slaughter to the *mizbeach* for *zerika*. The preceding *mishnah* had focused on whether *machshava she-lo lishma* (an invalidating intent) during *holacha* disqualifies a sacrifice, and on Rabbi Shimon's position that since *holacha* is theoretically dispensable — the animal could in principle have been slaughtered right next to the *mizbeach* — a disqualifying thought during *holacha* cannot affect the sacrifice's status. Setting aside *machshava* for the moment, the *gemara* now turns to a distinct question: *holacha she-lo baragel* — conveyance accomplished not by walking but by passing the vessel from hand to hand. If the *mizbeach* is at point B and the blood is at point A, and the *kohen* hands it across rather than physically walking it over, does this constitute a valid act of *holacha*?

### Yochanan: Not Valid

The *gemara* cites an *itmar*: Ulla said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — *holacha she-lo baragel lo shema holacha*. Non-foot conveyance does not constitute *holacha*. The blood must be physically walked from point A to point B; merely handing it across does not fulfill the *avodah*.

### Efshar Letikuna Question

This ruling immediately raises a further question: *efshar letikuna o lo efshar letikuna?* Suppose the *kohen* handed the vessel to someone standing at point X, a midpoint between A and B — an act that, per Rabbi Yochanan, does not count as *holacha*. Is this a nullity that can simply be undone — bring it back to A and walk it over properly — or does this non-foot conveyance actively invalidate the *holacha*, rendering it beyond repair? Rashi notes that the same question applies when a *zar* (non-*kohen*) was involved, but the *gemara*'s primary focus is on the *she-lo baragel* case.

### Mishna: Reversibility

In search of an answer, the *gemara* invokes a *mishnah* cited earlier in the tractate: *kibel hachasher v'natan l'pasul, yachazir l'kasher* — a fit *kohen* received the blood and handed it to an unfit one; the unfit *kohen* then returns it to the fit *kohen*. The plain sense of this *mishnah* is that the fit *kohen* takes it back at point A and walks it properly to B. This seems to demonstrate decisively that the situation is *efshar letikuna* — it can be corrected.

The *gemara* initially deflects by invoking the alternative reading proposed the previous day: perhaps the *mishnah* envisions that the fit *kohen* walks to point X and retrieves the vessel from the unfit *kohen* there, so that the hand-off itself counted as *holacha* — a reading consistent with the view that *holacha she-lo baragel* is valid. But the *gemara* now reads the *mishnah* in its simple sense: the vessel must be returned to point A. Even so, a different version of the ruling now surfaces: *holacha she-lo baragel pesula* — non-foot conveyance is not merely null but actively invalid, which implies it cannot be corrected. The *gemara* then draws the logical inference: *alma lo efshar letikuna* — this language of *pesulah* indicates the act cannot be undone.

### Gemara: Direction Matters

But the *mishnah* of *kibel hachasher v'natan l'pasul* still seems to imply reversibility. The *gemara* resolves this by reframing the case: *mi savrat dekai zar gavai? — dekai zar barai*. Who said that the unfit *kohen* at point X is standing *between* A and B, i.e., closer to the *mizbeach*? Perhaps he is standing on the far side of A, further from the *mizbeach* than the starting point. In that case, the hand-off moved the blood in the wrong direction — away from the *mizbeach* entirely — which everyone agrees is simply nothing. It did not constitute *holacha* in the negative sense; it was zero. In that scenario, returning to point A and proceeding properly is an obvious corrective with no obstacle.

The *gemara* thus introduces a crucial distinction. If the blood is passed in the wrong direction — away from the *mizbeach* — the act is simply null, and a do-over is straightforward. If the blood is passed in the right direction — toward the *mizbeach* — but without walking, our question remains open: is it null or actively invalidating?

---

## Spilled Blood Issue

### Spilled Blood Case

A fresh challenge is brought. Rav Nachman challenges Ulla from the following ruling: *nishpach min hakli al haritzpa, ve'asfo kasher* — if the blood spilled from the vessel onto the floor during the *kohen*'s conveyance from A to B, one may collect it and continue. The sacrifice is not invalidated.

### Problem: Spillage Toward…

The difficulty is immediate. If the *kohen* spills the blood at point X — some midpoint between A and B — some of the spilled blood will naturally flow in the direction of the *mizbeach*, toward B. That forward movement is *holacha she-lo baragel*: the blood has been propelled toward the *mizbeach* not by deliberate walking but by the spillage. Yet the *mishnah* says we collect it and proceed — implying that this movement does not invalidate.

One might argue that spillage is categorically different, since it may not qualify as human conveyance in the meaningful sense. But there is a counter-argument: the *kohen*'s own energy caused the spill, so in some sense the blood was propelled toward the *mizbeach* through his act, even if not by walking.

### Gemara Solutions

The *gemara* first attempts to resolve this by limiting the case. Perhaps the *mishnah* is discussing a case where the blood spilled *away* from the *mizbeach* — *kesheyatza lachutz* — not toward it. The *gemara* finds this implausible: *levarai nafik legavai lo ayeil?* If it can spill outward, away from the *mizbeach*, can it really be that none of it spills inward, toward it? The *gemara* then offers three technical scenarios in which forward movement could be prevented: *bemakom midron* — a slight incline in the floor such that all the blood flows backward; *beguma* — a small indentation right at point X into which all the blood collected; or *besmicha* — the blood was thick and coagulated, landing exactly where it fell.

### Proof: Initial Kabbalah…

But the *gemara* then objects to this entire approach. Would the *tanna* really go out of his way to construct the ruling only for these narrow, specialized circumstances? Furthermore, the *gemara* adduces a proof from another *perek*: *nishpach al haritzpa ve'asfo pasul* — if the blood went directly from the neck of the animal to the floor, without ever being received into a vessel, and one then collected it, the sacrifice is invalid. The invalidity there is due to the absence of an initial act of *kabbalah*. Critically, the *gemara* points out: if forward spillage during *holacha* were itself invalidating, the later *mishnah* need not have gone to the extreme case of no initial *kabbalah* at all. It could have drawn the distinction internally within the *holacha* case: spillage toward the *mizbeach* is invalid, spillage away is not. The fact that it does not make this distinction proves that forward spillage does not invalidate.

### Conclusion: No Invalidat…

The *gemara* concludes: *tyuvta tyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation of the position that non-foot movement actively invalidates. Even if blood moves toward the *mizbeach* in a manner other than walking, it does not render the *holacha* *pasul*. It is simply null — zero — and the process can be corrected. Whether the blood was handed over or spilled forward, the answer is the same: it does not count as *holacha*, but neither does it destroy the *holacha*. One can return to point A and proceed properly.

---

## Reinterpretation Attempt

### Radical Proposal

The *gemara* now advances a startling proposal, which Rashi reads as follows. An *itmar* is cited: *holacha she-lo baragel, machloket Rabbi Shimon ve-Rabanan* — the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Rabanan* in the *mishnah* is not, as one would naturally read it, a dispute about ordinary walking-*holacha* and whether *machshava she-lo lishma* invalidates during such conveyance. Rather, what they are actually debating is the case of *holacha she-lo baragel* — non-foot conveyance. According to this radical reframing, when Rabbi Shimon says *holacha* lacks the power to be affected by disqualifying intent, he is talking specifically about a *holacha* accomplished by handing rather than walking. The *Rabanan*, who say it does invalidate, hold that *holacha she-lo baragel* is a valid *avodah* whose intent matters. This reading sits very awkwardly with the plain text of the *mishnah*, where Rabbi Shimon's stated reason — that the animal could in principle have been slaughtered next to the *mizbeach* — has nothing to do with the mode of conveyance. The *gemara* is aware of this difficulty and will ultimately reject the proposal.

### Large vs. Small Holacha

The *gemara* attempts to make this reframing work by introducing the distinction between *holacha rabta* — the large *holacha*, i.e., ordinary conveyance by foot from point A to the *mizbeach* — and *holacha zutrata* — a small *holacha*. According to Rashi, *holacha zutrata* refers not to a different category of non-foot conveyance but to the minor movement that takes place at the moment of *zerika* itself: even as the *kohen* stands beside the *mizbeach*, the act of extending his arm and propelling the blood forward toward the wall of the *mizbeach* involves a small degree of *holacha she-lo baragel*. The blood is being moved forward — not by foot — from where the *kohen* holds it to where it strikes the *mizbeach*. The *gemara* proposes that on this *holacha zutrata* Rabbi Shimon says *holacha* is not a real *avodah*, while the *Rabanan* say it is. On *holacha rabta*, everyone would agree.

This is difficult on multiple levels: why should the forward extension of the arm during *zerika* be classified as *holacha* rather than as *zerika* itself? And how does this interact with the explicit text of the *mishnah*? The *gemara* proceeds anyway.

### Chatas Ha'of Application

Those in Eretz Yisrael laughed at this proposal — *machu alah be-ma'arava* — and their objection is telling. If the debate of Rabbi Shimon and the *Rabanan* is only about *holacha zutrata*, the question arises: by a *chatas ha'of*, where is *holacha* ever a venue for invalidating *machshava* according to Rabbi Shimon?

In a *chatas ha'of*, the *kohen* uses his fingernail to cut the back of the neck of the bird right at the *mizbeach*, and the blood sprays directly onto the *mizbeach*. There is no separate *kabbalah* into a vessel and no extended conveyance. Now, the *Rabanan* can still find a *holacha* in the movement of the bird itself toward the *mizbeach* after the neck is cut — treating the blood still in the bird somewhat like blood in a vessel, and the arm's motion as the *holacha*. But for Rabbi Shimon, if that very arm-motion is *holacha she-lo baragel* and therefore not a real *avodah*, where can *machshava* invalidate during *holacha*? The *gemara* considers the possibilities: if one had the thought before the blood emerged, that is nothing; if after the blood emerged, that is already *zerika*. So the question is genuine: *depsula be-machshava l'Rabbi Shimon heichi mashkachat lah?*

### Hand-Cutting Hypothetical

The *gemara* responds by directing attention to a different moment: the blood in midair, after it has left the bird's neck but before it strikes the *mizbeach*. At this instant, one could have a *machshava* that invalidates. The proof is a famous *she'elah* posed by Rabbi Yirmeyah to Rabbi Zeira: *haya mazeh ve-nikte'ah yado* — if the *kohen* was in the process of squirting or sprinkling the blood and his hand was severed while the blood was in midair, has the *avodah* been completed by a whole *kohen* or does the cutting — which renders him a *ba'al mum* — invalidate the *zerika*? Rabbi Zeira answers: *pesulah* — it is invalid.

### Avodah Until Impact

The reasoning is derived from the verse, which implies a dual requirement: the act of squirting and the act of placement. *Ve-hizah ve-natan* — he shall sprinkle *and* he shall place it. This indicates that the *avodah* is not complete at the moment the blood leaves the *kohen*'s hand; it extends through the arc of the blood's flight until the moment of contact with the *mizbeach*. This principle has interesting structural parallels in other areas of *halacha* — such as the *melacha* of planting on *Shabbat*, where the act is only fully realized when the seed takes root, yet retroactively the placing of the seed in the ground is the definitive act. Here, however, the ruling goes the other direction: the entire arc of the blood's flight belongs to the *avodah*, so a disqualification occurring mid-flight retroactively contaminates the *zerika*.

Once this is established, a *machshava* during the blood's flight through the air — between neck and *mizbeach* — can also invalidate. And this is where the *gemara* locates the *holacha*-adjacent moment of *chatas ha'of* during which intent matters: not the walking, not the *kabbalah* (which does not exist in this *avodah*), but the blood in flight — which, while technically part of the *hazaya* process, still serves as the moment where *machshava* can take effect. Rashi essentially concedes that this is not quite *holacha* proper; rather, the *gemara* is saying that whatever moment one was positing for *machshava* in *holacha*, one can still find an equivalent moment — the blood mid-flight — that achieves the same invalidating effect.

### Rejection from E.Y.

When Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua returned from *bei rav* — from the academy — they reported that this is precisely why Eretz Yisrael found the entire reinterpretation laughable. The claim was that on *holacha rabta*, normal walking conveyance, everyone agrees — there is no debate. But this is manifestly false. The *mishnah* in front of us is plainly about ordinary *holacha*, and Rabbi Shimon and the *Rabanan* plainly disagree about it. Are they not in fact debating? Of course they are.

### Correction: Debate Scope

The correction is thus stated cleanly: *ela be-holacha zutrata kulei alma lo pligi depasla* — on the small *holacha*, the minor forward arm-motion during *zerika*, everyone agrees that it does invalidate (with the caveat that there is a *girsa* question here). *Ki pligi be-holacha rabta* — the debate of Rabbi Shimon and the *Rabanan* is precisely about the large, ordinary *holacha* by foot. The strange reinterpretation that attempted to relocate the entire dispute into the domain of *holacha she-lo baragel* is rejected, and the plain reading of the *mishnah* is restored.

---

## Zar's Holacha

### Zar Conveys

The *gemara* now transitions to a separate but parallel question concerning *holacha* performed by a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — rather than by a *kohen*. The *mishnah* cited near the top of 14b lists *holacha* done by a *zar* as *pasul*. The question now is the same structural question asked earlier by *she-lo baragel*: is this *pesul* correctable?

### Debate: Fixable?

The scenario: a *zar* conveys the blood from point A to point X. This is *pasul*. Can a *kohen* take the vessel, walk it back to point A, and then walk it properly to B? The *gemara* reports that the sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yanai debated this: *chad amar kasher, ve-chad amar pasul* — one said it is valid after the correction, one said it remains invalid. The *gemara* glosses this as a dispute about *efshar letikuna* versus *lo efshar letikuna*, exactly parallel to the earlier debate about *she-lo baragel*.

It is worth noting that *holacha* is peculiarly suited to this question of reversibility. Of the four *avodot*, *holacha* alone is non-transformative. *Shechita* by a *zar* cannot be undone; the animal is already slaughtered. *Kabbalah* of the blood by a *zar* cannot be undone; that blood cannot be re-caught. *Zerika* onto the *mizbeach* is final. *Holacha* alone leaves open the theoretical possibility of reversion — the vessel can be walked back, and the process begun again. This quality of *holacha* somewhat resembles the *melachah* of carrying on *Shabbat*, which is classified as a *melachah geru'ah* — qualitatively different in certain respects from the other principal *melachot*, though still fully subject to the *chiyuv*.

### Reverse Scenario

The *gemara* then presents the inverse case: a *kohen* begins the *holacha* and walks the blood from A to X. Then a *zar* picks it up from the *kohen*, walks it back to A, and walks it forward again to X. In absolute terms, the net result is identical to what the *kohen* accomplished on his own — the vessel is at the same point X. Has anything changed?

### Last Act Matters

Rav Shimi bar Ashi analyzes this: *ledivrei hamachshir pasul, ledivrei hapasul machshir* — the debate flips. The disputant who validated the correction when a *kohen* followed a *zar* was reasoning that we define the *holacha* by the last, most proximate act. Since the *kohen* acted last, the *holacha* is defined by him and is kosher. Applying that same logic to the reverse scenario: the *zar* acted last, so the *holacha* is now defined by the *zar* — *pasul*. Conversely, the disputant who invalidated even after the *kohen*'s correction was reasoning that the initial disqualified conveyance is definitive; subsequent acts are superfluous. Applying that logic to the reverse scenario: the *kohen*'s initial conveyance is definitive; the *zar*'s subsequent movement is superfluous — so it remains *kasher*.

### Rava: Ongoing Obligation

Rava rejects this symmetrical analysis: *af ledivrei hapasul, pasul* — even the authority who said it cannot be fixed in the original case (where the *zar* went first) would also say it is *pasul* in this reverse case. His reasoning is *tzarich le-amtuye* — there is an ongoing obligation to bring the blood to the *mizbeach*. Once the *zar* walks the blood back to point A, the blood now sits at A and must be conveyed forward to B. That obligation of *holacha* now rests on a *kohen*, and a *zar* cannot discharge it. It is not sufficient to say that zooming out, the *zar*'s interference was duplicative and the *kohen*'s prior act suffices. Once the blood is returned to A, the obligation of *holacha* from A to B is real and present, and a *zar* discharging it is *pasul*.

Similarly, when the *kohen* acts first: just because the *kohen* walked it to X does not mean the status is locked in permanently. The *zar* then takes it back to A. At that point, A to B must be walked by a *kohen*, and since the *zar* does it, it is *pasul*. In short, Rava's principle is: regardless of who acted first, once the blood arrives at any given point through a reversal, the obligation of *holacha* is freshly reconstituted at that point and must be fulfilled by a *kohen*.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer's View

### Eliezer: Necessity Requi…

Rabbi Yirmeyah, citing this to Rav Ashi, adds: the precise principle of *tzarich le-amtuye* — that at each stage the *holacha* obligation is freshly constituted and must be fulfilled by the appropriate person — is itself subject to a *machloket*. Specifically, it is the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim* as found in our *mishnah*. The relevant portion of the *mishnah* states: *Rabbi Eliezer omer, ha-mahalach mi-makom she-tzarich le-halech, machshavah poselet; makom she-ein tzarich le-halech, ein machshavah poselet* — if the *kohen* moved through a space he had to traverse in order to bring the blood to the *mizbeach*, *machshavah* invalidates. If he moved through a space he had no obligation to traverse, *machshavah* does not invalidate.

### Rava: Doubling Back

Rava steps in to clarify the precise contours of this debate. One might have assumed the debate is about moving in non-optimal directions — taking a circuitous route, going sideways rather than directly from A to B — such that some segments of movement are necessary and others are not. Rava rejects this. The debate is specifically about a case where the *kohen* moved from A toward B, then doubled back toward A, and then moved again from A toward B.

### Common Ground

Rava first establishes what is uncontested on both sides. *Hakol modim kibel be-chutz ve-hichniso be-fnim, zehu hilucha she-tzarich le-halech* — everyone agrees that catching the blood at point A and walking it toward the *mizbeach* at B is necessary *holacha*, and *machshavah* there invalidates. And *kiblo be-fnim ve-hotzio la-chutz* — if after catching it at A one then walks it in the wrong direction, *away* from the *mizbeach*, that is *hilucha she-ein tzarich le-halech*, and everyone agrees *machshavah* does not invalidate during that movement.

### The Real Debate

The dispute, says Rava, arises in the case of *she-hichniso ve-chazar ve-hotzio* — the *kohen* walked from A toward B (the right direction), then doubled back toward A (the wrong direction). Now he is going to proceed again from A toward B. The *Chachamim* say: right now, moving from A toward B is precisely what must be done — *ha-tzorech le-amtuye* — and therefore *machshavah* here invalidates. Rabbi Eliezer says: looked at in the aggregate, this entire segment of movement from A back to X (where you already were before you doubled back) is unnecessary; it is merely undoing a deviation you introduced yourself. Therefore, it has the status of *hilucha she-ein tzarich le-halech* and *machshavah* there does not invalidate.

In other words, the *Chachamim* look at the micro-level — at each step, is the current movement toward the *mizbeach*? Rabbi Eliezer looks at the macro-level — is this segment of movement, considered in context, genuinely necessary, or is it merely correcting a self-inflicted detour?

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rava's reading by pointing to a *braita* that elaborates on Rabbi Eliezer's position. The *braita* says: *kiblah be-chutz ve-hichnisah lifnim, zehu hiluch she-tzarich le-halech* — if one moved from outside toward the *mizbeach*, that is necessary *holacha*. *Kiblah be-fnim ve-hotziah la-chutz, zehu hiluch she-ein tzarich le-halech* — moving away from the *mizbeach* is unnecessary *holacha*. Then the *braita* continues: *chazar ve-hichnisah, zehu hiluch she-tzarich le-halech* — and if one then brought it back toward the *mizbeach*, that is also necessary *holacha*. Explicitly, Rabbi Eliezer considers this return movement to be *tzarich le-halech*. This directly contradicts Rava's reading, which had placed Rabbi Eliezer's innovation precisely in denying that the return movement is necessary.

### Resolution

Rava's response to Abaye is simply: *ei tanya, tanya* — if that is what the *braita* says, then so be it. If Rabbi Eliezer explicitly considers the return movement *tzarich le-halech*, then his position does not serve as a precedent for the principle that *tzarich le-amtuye* can be denied in any case. But then, what exactly is Rabbi Eliezer saying that differs from the *Chachamim*? According to Rashi's reading, the conclusion is that Rabbi Eliezer is not, in the end, making a substantive halachic distinction that differs from the *Chachamim* on any practical outcome. Rather, he is articulating a principle in contrast to his father — Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Shimon said that *holacha* can be theoretically dispensed with, and therefore *machshavah* during *holacha* is harmless even in the standard case. Rabbi Eliezer's response is: I do not reason by theoretical dispensability. I look at whether the movement is practically necessary right now. If it is, *machshavah* invalidates; if not, it does not. On that basis, Rabbi Eliezer agrees with the *Chachamim* about the practical result — once you are moving toward the *mizbeach*, even after a detour, *machshavah* matters — but he is fundamentally rejecting his father's theoretical framework.

With this, the *gemara* closes the first *perek* — *Kol HaZvachim* — which centered primarily on *machshava she-lo lishma* and its relationship to the four *avodot*, with this concluding dive into the nature and weight of *holacha* as an *avodah*.

---

## Person-Based Invalidatio…

### New Perek Overview

The *gemara* now begins a new *perek*: *Kol HaZvachim She-kiblu Daman*. Where the first *perek* focused on invalidation through improper *intent*, this second *perek* shifts to invalidation through the status of the *person* performing the *avodah*. The *mishnah* begins with *kabbalah* — not *shechita* — because *shechita* may be performed by a non-*kohen* without invalidating the sacrifice. Since we wish to list all the personal statuses that disqualify the *avodah*, including those specific to *kohanim*, we begin with the first act that must be done by a *kohen*.

### Invalidating Categories

The *mishnah* enumerates the following categories: if a *zar* (non-*kohen*) received the blood; if an *onen* (one whose immediate relative died that day and has not yet been buried) received it; if a *shikor* (one who is intoxicated) received it; if a *ba'al mum* (a *kohen* with a disqualifying blemish) received it; if a *tevul yom* — one who has immersed in the *mikvah* that day to purify from *tumah* but upon whom sundown has not yet arrived, rendering his purification incomplete — received it; if a *mechussar kippurim* — one who has completed his immersion and awaited sundown but has not yet brought his concluding *korbanot*, and who therefore remains in a quasi-*tamei* status resembling a *shelishi* — received it; if the *kohen* was *mechussar begadim*, not wearing the required *bigdei kehunah*; if he had not washed his hands and feet as required before the *avodah*; if he was *arel*, uncircumcised — Rashi explains this might apply even to a pious Jew whose family had a history of hemophilia, where circumcision was contraindicated; if he was *tamei*; if he was *yoshev*, sitting rather than standing during the *avodah*; if he was standing on a vessel, a rock, a carpet, or even wearing something on his feet rather than standing directly on the floor; if he was standing on an animal; or if he was standing on someone else's feet — in all these cases the sacrifice is *pasul*. Additionally, if the *kohen* received the blood with his left hand, the sacrifice is *pasul* — though Rabbi Shimon is *machshir* in that case, a dispute noted here and to be elaborated upon.

### Deriving from Pessukim

The *gemara* immediately asks: *za minailan* — from where do we derive that a *zar* who performs the *avodah* invalidates the sacrifice? The *gemara* notes that the prohibition itself is not yet in question — it asks specifically about the *chilul*, the invalidating effect. Levi cites the verse in Vayikra 22: *ve-yinazru mi-kodshei Bnei Yisrael* — they shall separate themselves from the holy things of *Bnei Yisrael* — and *ve-lo yechalelu et shem kodshi* — they shall not desecrate My holy name. The surrounding context is about *kohanim* and *tumah*, suggesting that a *kohen* who is *tamei* and touches *kodshim* brings about *chilul*. But the *gemara* questions what function the phrase *Bnei Yisrael* serves in this verse. Does it exclude women — suggesting that *korbanot* of women are not subject to *tumah* concerns? Obviously not; that would be absurd. Does it exclude non-Jews — implying that their offerings are not subject to *tumah* invalidation? Also implausible: in fact, when non-Jews bring sacrifices and there is a *tumah* problem, the *tzitz* — the golden plate worn by the *Kohen Gadol* — does not atone for it, unlike with Jewish sacrifices. The *gemara* cites the principle: *ovdei kochavim, bein be-shogeig bein be-mezid, lo hurtzah* — for non-Jews' sacrifices, whether the *tumah* was incidental or deliberate, the *tzitz* does not effect atonement. This is because the verse says *le-ratzon lahem lifnei Hashem* — the *tzitz* atones on behalf of *them* specifically. So non-Jewish sacrifices face a *more* stringent situation regarding *tumah*, not a more lenient one. The exclusion of *Bnei Yisrael* cannot therefore be teaching that their sacrifices are exempt from *tumah* concerns.

The *gemara* concludes: *ela hachi ka'amar* — rather, the verse is saying this: *Bnei Yisrael* must separate themselves from My holy things — meaning non-*kohanim* must distance themselves from performing the sacrificial *avodah*, lest they *mechalel* it. The phrase *Bnei Yisrael* is thus read as identifying the class of people — non-priestly Israelites — who must not approach the *avodah*, and the verse teaches that their doing so constitutes *chilul*.

### Kal V'Chomer Logic

The *gemara* then cites a second approach, from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: the *zar*'s invalidation can be derived by *kal va-chomer* from *ba'al mum*. From Vayikra 21:17–23, we learn that a *kohen* with a *mum* may not perform the *avodah*, and the verse applies the language of *lo yechalel* — desecration — to his doing so. Now: a *ba'al mum* is permitted to *eat* from *kodshei kodashim*; yet if he performs the *avodah*, he invalidates it. A *zar* is not permitted even to eat from *kodshei kodashim* — his exclusion is total. Does it not follow *a fortiori* that if a *ba'al mum*'s partial exclusion causes *chilul* when he performs the *avodah*, a *zar*'s total exclusion certainly should?

The *gemara* deflects: *mah le-va'al mum she-ken asah bo karev ke-makriv* — there is a unique feature of *ba'al mum*: the laws of *mum* apply not only to the *kohen* but also to the animal. An animal with a *mum* is also disqualified from being offered.
