This dual application of *mum* — to both the officiant and the sacrifice — might be what gives it the power to cause *chilul* when the blemished *kohen* officiates, and this extra dimension is absent by a *zar*.

### Common Denominator

The *gemara* then proposes the resolution through a *tzad ha-shaveh* — a common denominator argument. *Tamei* — the other person explicitly mentioned in the verse — is *muzhrar* and causes *chilul*, yet *tumah* does not apply to animals in the same dual manner as *mum* (live animals cannot become *tamei*). Conversely, *ba'al mum* may lack the spreading dimension of *tumah*, which *tamei* possesses. Neither *ba'al mum* alone nor *tamei* alone suffices for the *kal va-chomer*, but the shared feature — *she-muzharin she-im avdu chalelu*, that both are warned not to perform the *avodah* and if they do they invalidate it — is the operative principle. From this common denominator we derive: *af ani avi zar she-hu muzhar* — I will also include a *zar*, who is equally warned against performing the *avodah*, and conclude *ve-im avad chillel* — if he did so, it is invalidated. The *gemara* notes that the derivation of the *zar*'s prohibition itself — from which his *muzhar* status is established — will be the subject of the next discussion.

---

---

# Zevachim 16

## Intro & Ch. 2 Overview

### Opening & Topic Setup

Daf 16 opens at the beginning of the second *perek*, which moves beyond the discussion of *shelo lishma* and into a broader inquiry about the various circumstances — primarily relating to the personal status of the officiating *kohen* — that invalidate a sacrifice. This chapter presents a whole list of categories of persons who, if they perform the *avodah*, render the *korban* invalid.

### Kabbalat HaDam Review

Because *shechita* is technically valid even when performed by a non-*kohen*, the Mishnah focuses on *kabbalat hadam* as the first *avodah* under discussion, so that the full list of disqualifying statuses can be surveyed properly. The Gemara has established — through a *tzad hashaveh*, a common denominator argument — that just as a *kohen* who is *tamei* or a *baal mum* invalidates if he performs the *avodah*, so too does a non-*kohen*. The general principle emerging is: anyone who is prohibited from performing the *avodah* in a given state will, if he performs it anyway, invalidate the *korban*. The Gemara now examines each case to establish both the prohibition and the invalidation.

---

## Zar & Tzad HaShaveh

### Source of Zar Prohibition

With the general principle in place, the Gemara asks: where do we know that a non-*kohen* is prohibited from performing the *avodah* in the first place? The *tzad hashaveh* requires a proven prohibition as its starting point, so the source of the *zar*'s prohibition must be identified independently.

### Veyinnazru vs. Vezar

One might have thought the source is the verse *veyinnazru mikodeshei benei Yisrael* — "they shall be separated from the holy things of the children of Israel" — which could, on one reading, include a *zar*. But the Gemara immediately sets this aside: the plain sense (*pshat*) of that verse concerns a *kohen* who is *tamei*, not a non-*kohen*. More decisively, if we were to read the verse as referring to a *zar*, the verse itself already contains the word *yechalelu* — it would explicitly state both the prohibition and the invalidation, making the entire *tzad hashaveh* unnecessary. Since we are constructing a *tzad hashaveh* precisely because we need to derive the invalidation, we must be reading that verse as referring to *tumah* alone. The source for the *zar*'s prohibition is therefore the explicit verse *vezar lo yikrav aleichem* — "a stranger shall not come near you" — which plainly bars a non-*kohen* from performing the Temple service.

### Bamah Challenge

With the prohibition of the *zar* established, the *tzad hashaveh* from *tamei* and *baal mum* would seem to yield the rule that the *zar* also invalidates. But the Gemara raises a challenge: *mah letzad hashaveh shebahen sheken lo hutru bebama* — what is distinctive about the common denominator, the cases of *tamei* and *baal mum*, is that neither of them is permitted to perform sacrifices outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. A *tamei* person and a *baal mum* remain disqualified even at a private altar (*bamah*). But a *zar* is permitted to bring a *korban* on a *bamah* — he is only barred in the *Beit HaMikdash* itself, where the *kohen* functions as part of the Temple apparatus. Perhaps, then, the *zar*'s disqualification is categorically different: since he is sometimes permitted, maybe he does not rise to the level of invalidating the *korban*.

### Onen & Baal Mum Fix

To address this challenge, the Gemara introduces the *onen* — a *kohen* who has just suffered the death of an immediate relative — alongside the *baal mum*. Rather than using *tamei* and *baal mum* as the two poles of the *tzad hashaveh*, the Gemara substitutes *onen* for *tamei*. The critical question is whether an *onen* is prohibited on a *bamah*. Rav Samra son of Rava pointedly asks: *u'man leima lan de'onen assur bebama* — who says an *onen* cannot bring on a *bamah*? There is no explicit basis for that restriction. Since we have no evidence that an *onen* is barred from a *bamah*, we assume he is permitted there. This allows the *tzad hashaveh* to proceed: both *onen* and *baal mum* are prohibited in the *Beit HaMikdash* and invalidate — and crucially, at least one of them (the *onen*) may be permitted on a *bamah*, just like the *zar*. Therefore, the fact that a *zar* can bring on a *bamah* cannot be used to exempt him from the rule that prohibited persons invalidate.

### Common Denominator Accep…

The resulting *tzad hashaveh* is simply that both *onen* and *baal mum* are prohibited in a given state and, if they perform the *avodah* in that state, they invalidate. Since the *zar* is equally prohibited, he equally invalidates — and one cannot narrow the rule by pointing to the *bamah* permissibility of the *zar*, given that the *onen*, who shares in the common denominator, may himself be permitted on a *bamah*.

---

## Yoshev Kal VaChomer

### Yoshev Kal VaChomer

Rav Mesharshiya offers an independent derivation: a *kal vachomer* from the case of *yoshev* — a *kohen* who performs the *avodah* while sitting. The *kal vachomer* runs as follows: a *kohen* who sits is permitted to eat the *korbanot* — even *kodshei kodashim* need not be eaten while standing — yet if he performs the *avodah* while sitting, he invalidates it. A *zar*, who is not permitted to eat *kodshei kodashim* at all, should certainly invalidate if he performs the *avodah*.

### Yoshev Edus Challenge

The Gemara challenges this *kal vachomer*: *mah leyoshev sheken pasul le'edut* — sitting entails a disqualification for testimony as well. Perhaps sitting is a uniquely weighty category of invalidity, and therefore one cannot draw an inference from it to the case of a *zar*, whose disqualification does not extend to testimony.

### Talmid Chacham Exception

The Gemara deflects this challenge: *v'afilu teima yoshev talmid chacham* — there are cases where a *talmid chacham* is permitted to give testimony while seated, as a mark of respect accorded to him. Since there are instances of sitting that are valid for testimony, one cannot categorically characterize *yoshev* as more stringently invalid than other disqualified states. The Gemara states *shem yoshev lo parach* — the sitting-equals-testimony-invalidity objection does not hold, because the existence of cases where a sitting person's testimony is accepted means that *yoshev* cannot be bracketed as uniquely severe.

### Tzad HaShaveh Alternative

Even if one insists that the *yoshev* category is weightier because some *yoshev* cases are invalid for testimony, the Gemara offers an alternative: construct a *tzad hashaveh* from *yoshev* together with one of the other disqualified categories — *baal mum*, *tamei*, *onen* — and the common denominator of those cases will yield the same conclusion without relying on *yoshev* alone.

### Lifnei Hashem Source

The discussion of *yoshev* raises the question of how we know a *kohen* who performs the *avodah* sitting is *mutar* on a *bamah*, a point required to make the *tzad hashaveh* work properly (so that not all members of the common denominator are disqualified on a *bamah*). The source is the verse *la'amod lifnei Hashem lesharto* — "to stand before God to serve Him." The requirement of standing is derived from the phrase *lifnei Hashem*, which specifically designates the *Beit HaMikdash* as the place of the divine presence in this legal sense. A *bamah*, by contrast, is not *lifnei Hashem* in this technical sense — one may offer sacrifices there without the standing requirement applying. Therefore, *yoshev* is valid on a *bamah*, which is precisely what the *tzad hashaveh* needs.

### General Rule Established

The upshot is a broad general principle: any person who is in a prohibited status invalidates the *korban* if he performs the *avodah*, and one cannot escape this rule by pointing to the exceptions each category enjoys in certain contexts. *Baal mum*, *tamei*, *onen*, and *yoshev* all have situations in which they are permitted — yet all invalidate. The principle therefore extends uniformly: prohibition entails invalidation.

---

## Onen Invalidation

### Kohen Gadol Source

The Gemara turns to the *onen* specifically and asks: *onein minalan* — from where do we know that an *onen* invalidates? The first proposed source is a verse concerning the *Kohen Gadol*: *u'min hamikdash lo yetzei v'lo yechalel* — "and from the Sanctuary he shall not go out, and he shall not desecrate." The *Kohen Gadol*, even as an *onen*, must remain in the *Beit HaMikdash* and does not desecrate the sacrifices. The inference is: *ha'acher shelo yatza chillel* — an ordinary *kohen*, who is not commanded to remain, would invalidate if he stayed and performed the service while an *onen*.

### Hen HaKrivu Debate

Rabbi Eliezer derives the same principle from a different verse: *hen hikrivu* — the exchange between Moshe and Aharon following the deaths of Nadav and Avihu, recorded in the Torah. The Gemara presents a reading of that exchange in which Moshe raises the possibility that Elazar and Itamar, as *kohanim hedyotim* who were *onanim* after their brothers' deaths, may have brought the *chatat* — and if so, as *kohanim hedyotim* performing the *avodah* as *onanim*, they would have invalidated it. Aharon responds that it was he — the *Kohen Gadol* — who brought it, and the *Kohen Gadol* may perform the *avodah* as an *onen*. From this exchange one infers that had the *kohanim hedyotim* brought it, it would indeed have been invalidated.

### Nadav & Avihu Context

The underlying factual context is that Nadav and Avihu died, rendering Elazar and Itamar *onanim*. Aharon, as *Kohen Gadol*, is governed by the rule *kohen gadol makriv onein v'eino ochel* — the *Kohen Gadol* brings sacrifices as an *onen* but does not eat them as an *onen*. The *kohen hedyot*, by contrast, may neither bring nor eat as an *onen*. So Aharon's response — "I was the one who brought it" — serves to explain that no invalidation occurred, since the *Kohen Gadol* may perform the *avodah* in a state of *aninut*.

There is a secondary question about why the meat was burned at all, if Aharon's bringing it was valid. One answer: the verse's emphasis is *hen hayom* — "they brought it today." Being *onanim*, Elazar and Itamar could not eat the *chatat* during the day, and if one holds *aninus layla* applies through the night as well, the meat remained uneaten until it became *notar*, requiring burning. The burning was thus the consequence of the *onen*'s inability to eat, not of any invalidation of the offering itself.

### Gemara Rejects Both

The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Eliezer does not simply use the *min hamikdash lo yetzei* verse, and conversely, why the first opinion does not use *hen hikrivu*. The answer to the first question: *mi ktiv ha'acher shelo yatza chillel* — the verse does not explicitly state that a different (*hedyot*) *kohen* who stays would invalidate. The verse tells us only that the *Kohen Gadol* who stays does not desecrate. One might equally read the verse as saying the same is true of a *kohen hedyot* — just as the *Kohen Gadol*'s remaining does not invalidate, so too a *kohen hedyot*'s remaining does not invalidate. The negative implication (that the *kohen hedyot* would invalidate) is not logically entailed by the verse; it is a possible reading but not a forced one.

The answer to the second question: the reading of *hen hikrivu* as implying that the *kohanim hedyotim* would have invalidated is rejected by the second opinion because, on that opinion's reading, the reason the meat was burned was not *aninut* at all but *tumah*. If the meat became *tamei*, that explains the burning independently, and the inference from the exchange between Moshe and Aharon collapses. The *onen* issue becomes irrelevant to the burning on this reading, and therefore one cannot derive from the exchange that an *onen hedyot* invalidates. The derivation from *hen hikrivu* then proceeds through a *gezeirah shavah* rather than a direct inference from the *pshat* of the verse.

### Kal VaChomer Approach

The school of Rabbi Yishmael (*d'vei Rabbi Yishmael*) takes yet a different approach, deriving through a *kal vachomer* from *baal mum*: if a *baal mum*, who is permitted to eat the *korban*, nonetheless invalidates when he performs the *avodah*, then an *onen*, who is not permitted to eat, should certainly invalidate.

### Baal Mum vs. Zar

The Gemara challenges: *mah l'baal mum sheken asah bo korbanin kemakrivin* — perhaps the *baal mum* has greater disqualifying power because the concept of *mum* applies not only to the *kohen* but to the animal itself. An *onen* has no such extension of disqualification to the *korban*. The Gemara addresses this by introducing the *zar* alongside the *baal mum*: the *zar*'s disqualification does not apply to the animal at all, so the combination of *zar* and *baal mum* neutralizes this distinctive feature.

### Takana Challenge

A further challenge: *mah l'zar sheken ein lo takana* — a *zar* can never stop being a *zar*; his status is permanent. An *onen*, by contrast, has a *takana* — his status is temporary, lasting only through the day. Perhaps only permanent disqualifications generate invalidation. The Gemara responds: *baal mum yochiach* — the *baal mum* proves otherwise, since a *mum* can be temporary (*mum over*) and the *baal mum* nonetheless invalidates.

### Zar & Mum Tzad

The Gemara then brings the full *tzad hashaveh*: *lo rei zeh kirei zeh v'lo rei zeh kirei zeh* — each case has its own unique characteristic that the other lacks. The *zar* has no exceptions but his disqualification does not extend to the animal; the *baal mum*'s disqualification extends to the animal but may be temporary. Neither encompasses the other's distinctive feature. The *hatzad hashaveh shebahen* — the common denominator — is simply that both are prohibited from performing the *avodah* in their respective states and, if they do so, they invalidate. An *onen*, who is equally prohibited, therefore equally invalidates.

### Onen Prohibition Source

To deploy this *tzad hashaveh*, however, one must first establish the prohibition independently. Where is the *onen* prohibited? If we say it is from the *min hamikdash lo yetzei* verse, then the invalidation itself is already packaged in that verse (*chillul begufei ketiv bei*), and a *tzad hashaveh* is unnecessary. If we say the prohibition is derived from *hen hikrivu* — the exchange of Moshe and Aharon — then the *pshat* of that passage implies prohibition but not necessarily invalidation as its explicit content.

### Kohen Gadol Source Limits

The Gemara makes the point sharply: from *hen hikrivu* one can at most learn the *issur* — the prohibition on the *kohen hedyot* to perform the *avodah* as an *onen*. The actual rule that he *invalidates* if he does so is derived through the *gezeirah shavah*, not from the verse's plain meaning. This is why both derivations — from the *Kohen Gadol* verse and from *hen hikrivu* — are needed, each contributing a different element.

### Tamei Exception Analogy

The Gemara next confronts a challenge to the *tzad hashaveh* itself: *mah lehatzad hashaveh shebahen sheken lo hutru miklalan* — both *zar* and *baal mum* are never permitted in the *Beit HaMikdash* in their respective states; there are no exceptions. An *onen*, however, does have an exception — the *Kohen Gadol*. Perhaps the rule "prohibited entails invalidation" applies only where there is an absolute prohibition with no exceptions, and since the *onen* prohibition has an exception (the *Kohen Gadol*), it does not generate invalidation for the *kohen hedyot*.

The Gemara answers: *tamei yochiach* — throw *tamei* into the *tzad hashaveh*. *Tumah* has an exception: *tumah hutra betzibur* — ritual impurity is permitted for communal offerings. Yet a *tamei* person who performs the *avodah* when not permitted to (i.e., for a private offering) nonetheless invalidates. Since the exception does not eliminate the invalidation by *tamei*, the same logic applies to the *onen*: the existence of an exception for the *Kohen Gadol* does not mean that when the *onen hedyot* transgresses and performs the *avodah*, he fails to invalidate. *Hanakh yochichu v'chazar hadin* — combining all the cases, no single distinctive feature can be used to bracket the *onen* out of the general principle.

---

## Rava's Korban Yachid/Tzi…

### Rava's Position

Rava now proposes a significant qualification: the rule that an *onen* invalidates applies only to a *korban yachid* — a private individual offering. With respect to a *korban tzibur* — a communal offering — an *onen hedyot* who performs the *avodah* does not invalidate; rather, it is *meratzeh*, acceptable.

### Rava's Logic Grid

Rava's reasoning proceeds through a *kal vachomer* from *tumah*. The structure requires holding several parameters simultaneously. By *tumah*: a *Kohen Gadol* performing the *avodah* for a *korban yachid* in a state of *tumah* is not permitted — there is no exception for a *Kohen Gadol* with *tumah* by a private offering. Yet a *kohen hedyot* performing the *avodah* for a *korban tzibur* in a state of *tumah* is permitted — *tumah hutra betzibur*. Now by *aninut*: a *Kohen Gadol* performing the *avodah* for a *korban yachid* as an *onen* is permitted — the *Kohen Gadol* may bring even a private offering while an *onen*. The *kal vachomer* then argues: if *tumah*, which is not permitted even by the *Kohen Gadol* for a *korban yachid*, is nonetheless permitted by a *kohen hedyot* for a *korban tzibur*, then *aninut*, which is more lenient in that it is permitted by the *Kohen Gadol* even for a *korban yachid*, should certainly be permitted by a *kohen hedyot* for a *korban tzibur*.

---

## Rava Bar Ahilai Refutes

### Multiple QV Paths

Rava bar Ahilai challenges Rava's *kal vachomer* by demonstrating that the same grid of parameters admits multiple alternative inferences, each of which yields a different — and equally unacceptable — conclusion. The problem is that Rava's argument assumes certain cells of the grid as fixed and derives the unknown from them. But there is no principled reason why those particular cells should be the fixed ones; other assignments of fixed and variable yields contradictory results.

### Alt 1: Onen Limits

One could instead run the inference in the opposite direction regarding *oninut* by the *Kohen Gadol*: since *tumah*, which is permitted for the *kohen hedyot* by *korban tzibur*, is not permitted for the *Kohen Gadol* by *korban yachid*, perhaps *aninut*, which is not permitted for the *kohen hedyot* by *korban tzibur* (starting from that assumption), is also not permitted for the *Kohen Gadol* by *korban yachid*. In other words, rather than deriving that the *kohen hedyot* is permitted as an *onen* for *korban tzibur*, one could derive that the *Kohen Gadol* is *not* permitted as an *onen* for a *korban yachid* — which directly contradicts the explicit *pshat* of *min hamikdash lo yetzei*.

### Alt 2: Tumah Extends

Alternatively, one could argue in the opposite direction for *tumah* by the *Kohen Gadol*: since *aninut* is permitted for the *Kohen Gadol* by a *korban yachid* (which is a place where *tumah* is not permitted), and since *tumah* is permitted for the *kohen hedyot* by a *korban tzibur* (where *aninut* is not permitted), perhaps *tumah* should also be permitted for the *Kohen Gadol* by a *korban yachid*. This contradicts the well-established rule that *tumah* has no exception for private offerings regardless of who performs the *avodah*.

### Alt 3: Tumah Limits

A third alternative runs the *kal vachomer* so as to restrict *tumah* even by *korban tzibur*: since *aninut* is permitted for the *Kohen Gadol* by a *korban yachid* and yet is not permitted for the *kohen hedyot* by a *korban tzibur*, perhaps *tumah*, which is not permitted for the *Kohen Gadol* by a *korban yachid*, should equally not be permitted for the *kohen hedyot* by a *korban tzibur*. This would overturn the entire principle of *tumah hutra betzibur* as applied to ordinary *kohanim*.

### Pshat Conclusion

Since any of these inferences is logically as valid as Rava's original *kal vachomer*, and since each leads to a conclusion that contradicts established law, the Gemara concludes: *ika l'mifrach hachi v'ika l'mifrach hachi* — you can challenge in this direction and you can challenge in that direction. The grid-based *kal vachomer* reasoning breaks down entirely because there is no way to determine which parameter to hold fixed and which to derive. The Gemara therefore rules: *kocha d'hacha tichu b'duchtei* — let each law stand as it is, in its own place. The rule about *tumah* belongs to the category of *tzibur*; the rule about *onen* belongs to the category of *Kohen Gadol*. These are independently derived principles, not nodes in a logical grid from which further inferences can be pressed. Attempting to construct *kal vachomers* across these categories leads only to confusion, and Rava's proposed leniency for an *onen* by *korban tzibur* is accordingly rejected.

---

---

# Zevachim 17

## Tevul Yom Sources

### Tevul Yom Definition

We pick up two lines from the top of 17a, where the Gemara continues its enumeration of individuals whose status invalidates the *korbanot* if they perform the *avoda*. Having covered the cases of a non-*kohen*, and an *onein* — a *kohen* who has just suffered a bereavement — the Mishnah turns to the *tevul yom*: a person who was *tamei*, immersed in a *mikvah*, and is now waiting for nightfall to achieve complete *taharah*. This figure occupies an intermediate state — no longer fully *tamei*, but not yet fully *tahor*.

The baseline for invalidation of the *avoda* by a *tamei* person is derived from the *pasuk* (Leviticus 22:2), *veyinazru mikodeshei benei Yisrael velo yehallelu* — that the *Bnei Yisrael* shall separate from the holy things, lest they desecrate them. This source establishes that a fully *tamei* person who performs the *avoda* has desecrated it. But what of the *tevul yom*?

### Kedoshim Yihyu Source

The Gemara cites a *braisa* in the name of Rabbi Simai: *remez le-tevul yom she-im avad hillel minalan* — where is the textual basis for the principle that a *tevul yom* who performed the *avoda* has desecrated it? The answer is drawn from the *pasuk* in Leviticus 21:6: *kedoshim yihyu leloheihem velo yehallelu shem eloheihem ki et ishei Hashem hem makrivim vehayu kodesh* — they shall be holy unto their God, and shall not desecrate the name of their God, for they offer the fire-offerings of God and shall be holy.

The Gemara reasons: *im eino inyan le-tamei* — since a fully *tamei* person's invalidation is already derived from *veyinazru*, this verse cannot be read as addressing that case. Therefore the verse must be redirected — *tena-u inyan le-tevul yom* — to speak of someone who bears only a residual degree of *tumah*, having immersed but not yet waited for nightfall. The operative term is *kedoshim yihyu*: they must be holy, and someone in the state of a *tevul yom* has not yet arrived at full *kedushah*.

One might challenge this reading by noting that the preceding verse (Leviticus 21:5) addresses the prohibitions against making baldness on the head, shaving the corners of the beard, and making incisions in the flesh, and the phrase *kedoshim yihyu velo yehallelu* follows immediately. Could the verse be addressing a *kohen* who has violated those bodily prohibitions and thereby desecrates the *avoda*? The Gemara responds with a counter-question: *tevul yom de-im avad be-misah minalan* — from where do we know that a *tevul yom* who performs the *avoda* is deserving of death (understood here as *misa bidei shamayim*, death at the hands of Heaven)?

### Chalul Chalul Link

The answer is *de-gamir hillul hillul mi-terumah* — we derive it through a *gezeirah shava* from the word *yehallelu* appearing in the context of *terumah*. The relevant *pasuk* in *terumah* (Leviticus 22:9) reads *u-meisu vo ki yehallelu-hu* — they shall die thereby if they desecrate it — and this is understood to address, among other cases, a *tevul yom* who eats *terumah*, who is thereby liable to *misa bidei shamayim*. Since the word *challul* appears both in the *terumah* context and in the *kodshim* context, the Gemara links the two: just as a *tevul yom* who eats *terumah* is liable to *misa bidei shamayim*, so too a *tevul yom* who performs the *avoda* in the *Mikdash* is liable.

The Gemara then draws a further conclusion from this link: *d'pasul bi-terumah mechal avodah* — whoever invalidates *terumah* also desecrates the *avoda*, and *d'lo pasul bi-terumah lo mechal avodah* — whoever does not invalidate *terumah* does not desecrate the *avoda*. This is admittedly not a perfect equivalence. The *Shittah Mekubetzet* raises a sharper difficulty: it appears that a *tevul yom* does not himself *posel* in *terumah* in the conventional sense — which seems to directly contradict the operative principle being used here. The Gemara nonetheless proceeds with this framework, using the *chalul chalul* link to import the category of *tevul yom* into the *kodshim* context, thereby establishing that a *tevul yom* who performs the *avoda* invalidates it.

It bears noting that this *pasuk* — *kedoshim yihyu* — is being read in an extremely specific and concrete *halachic* sense. On the level of *peshat*, the verse is speaking about the conduct and moral bearing of the *kohanim* in relation to God's name, not about technical invalidation of *korbanos*. The Gemara's reading is a *halachic derasha* that moves well beyond the plain meaning of the text.

---

## Three Cases Needed

### Rava's Question

With the sources for *tamei*, *tevul yom*, and *mechusar kippurim* each established, Rava raises a question: *lama li d'chtav Rachmana tamei u-tevul yom u-mechusar kippurim* — why did the Torah need to specify all three of these states? If one person in a weaker state of *tumah* invalidates the *avoda*, surely one who is more *tamei* does as well. It should have been sufficient to mention the weakest case — *mechusar kippurim*, someone who has completed a seven-day purification process and immersed, lacking only the *korban* of the eighth day — and from there infer that the more *tamei* cases certainly invalidate as well.

### Tamei Baseline

The Gemara notes, and Rashi makes the point explicit, that the Torah could not simply have omitted *tamei* from the discussion. Since the Torah does not explicitly label the *tevul yom* as such, nor does it explicitly call out *mechusar kippurim* — these categories are derived through *derashot* and linkages — whenever an extra *pasuk* appears dealing with someone whose *tumah* compromises their status, the natural reading would be that it addresses a fully *tamei* person. The baseline is *tamei*, so the Torah must establish that case first, and only then can the additional *pesukim* be understood as extending the invalidation to the weaker cases.

The practical consequence is that once the *tamei* case is established as the necessary starting point, the real question is why all three were explicitly addressed rather than two. The Gemara therefore asks: *tzrichi* — all three are necessary, each for a different reason.

Had the Torah written only the case of a fully *tamei* person, one could not have inferred *tevul yom* or *mechusar kippurim*, because a fully *tamei* person *she-ken metameh* — he himself transmits *tumah* to others, a higher level of *tumah*.

### Obstacle Distinction

Had the Torah written only the case of a *tevul yom*, one could not have inferred *mechusar kippurim*. The reason: *she-ken posel bi-terumah* — a *tevul yom* retains sufficient *tumah* to invalidate *terumah*.

To understand this, consider the structure of *tumah* transmission. An *av ha-tumah*, such as a *zav*, transmits *tumah* to what he touches, creating a *rishon*. That *rishon* can render food a *sheni*. A *sheni* can only *metamei terumah* — causing it to become a *shelishi*. A *tevul yom* who has immersed occupies the level of a *sheni*: he can *metamei terumah* but not ordinary *chulin* food.

After nightfall on the day of immersion — the transition from *tevul yom* to *mechusar kippurim*, for someone like a *zav* who had undergone a seven-day process — the person's level drops further, to approximately that of a *shelishi*. He can only *metamei kodshim*; he can no longer *metamei terumah*. This is the weaker state.

Yet, counterintuitively, one cannot simply infer the *mechusar kippurim* case from the *tevul yom* case, even though the *mechusar kippurim* is weaker in *tumah*. The reason is that the *mechusar kippurim she-ken mechusar ma'aseh* — he still lacks an act, specifically the bringing of a *korban*. The *tevul yom*, by contrast, needs only to wait for nightfall; his transition to full *taharah* happens by itself. One might have thought that since a *mechusar kippurim* requires a positive *ma'aseh* to complete his purification — an act of *kaparah* — there is an ongoing obstacle before him of greater weight, and therefore he should perhaps not be compared to the *tevul yom*.

Similarly, had the Torah written only *mechusar kippurim*, one could not infer *tevul yom*: *she-ken mechusar ma'aseh* — the *mechusar kippurim* needs an active step (the bringing of the *korban*) to change his status, whereas the *tevul yom* needs merely the passage of time. One might have thought: the *mechusar kippurim* invalidates because his process has an outstanding obligation; the *tevul yom*, who simply needs to wait, might not invalidate.

### Residual Status

The Gemara then entertains whether one should have written only *tamei* and *mechusar kippurim* and derived *tevul yom* from the combination. The Gemara answers: *mai parchat mah lehannach she-ken mechusar ma'aseh* — one would counter that both *tamei* and *mechusar kippurim* require an active step to change their status (*mikvah* immersion and *korban*, respectively), and therefore one cannot infer the *tevul yom* who requires no act whatsoever.

The Gemara then counters this counter: *sof sof klishus tumasan* — but even granting that both require a *ma'aseh*, the *mechusar kippurim*'s *tumah* is so weak that one could have inferred *tevul yom* from these two cases. The *Shittah Mekubetzet* offers a clarification: the *ma'aseh* of immersion in the *mikvah* (required for the *tamei* person) is fundamentally different from the *ma'aseh* of bringing a *korban* (required for the *mechusar kippurim*). Immersion is an act that weakens the *tumah*; bringing a *korban* is an act of *kaparah* — atonement. These are qualitatively different acts, and therefore throwing both of them into the comparison does not yield a simple inference to the *tevul yom* who needs no act.

Why, then, is the *mechusar kippurim* case still necessary? *Kasavar mechusar kippurim de-zav ke-zav dami* — because a *mechusar kippurim* who was a *zav* retains the personal status of a *zav*. Even though his level of *tumah* has become highly residual — so residual that he can only *metamei kodshim* — the source of that *tumah* was something very potent. His *tumah* is, in a sense, residual radioactivity rather than residual germs. The *tevul yom*, by contrast, is someone whose original *tumah* was of a more ordinary kind. Just because the *tevul yom* invalidates the *avoda* does not mean we can infer that the *mechusar kippurim de-zav*, whose residual *tumah* carries the weight of a *zav*'s identity, equally invalidates. And conversely, just because the *mechusar kippurim* invalidates — weighty though his personal status remains — one cannot infer the *tevul yom*, whose *tumah* level is higher but whose personal identity is less weighty. All three cases must therefore be stated.

---

## Mechusar Kippurim Status

### Residual Identity

The Gemara has now invoked the principle *mechusar kippurim de-zav ke-zav dami* — that a *mechusar kippurim* who was a *zav* retains the personal status of a *zav*. This is a conceptually striking claim. The *mechusar kippurim* has completed his seven-day count, he has immersed, nightfall has passed — the only thing separating him from complete *taharah* is the bringing of a *korban* on the eighth day. His *tumah* in practical terms is extremely weak: it can only *metamei kodshim*, not *terumah*, not ordinary food. And yet the Gemara asserts that in some sense he retains the identity of a *zav*.

What does this residual identity entail? Two *nafka minot* are considered. The first — raised by *Tosafos* though *Tosafos* believes everyone actually agrees on it — concerns a person who is *mechusar kippurim* when a *korban pesach* is being brought in a state of *tumah*. The rule is that when the entire community is *tamei met* and the *korban pesach* is offered in *tumah* (*tumah hutrah betzibur*), a *zav* — someone whose *tumah* derives from the body itself (*tumah ha-yotzei mi-gufo*) — is nonetheless excluded and cannot bring the *korban pesach* together with them. The question is: if someone was a *zav*, completed his process, and is now merely *mechusar kippurim*, can he join the community in the *korban pesach* under *tumah hutrah betzibur*? If *mechusar kippurim ke-zav dami* — if his personal status is still that of a *zav* — he remains excluded.

A second, highly practical *nafka mina* concerns access to Har HaBayit. Those who advise visitors to ascend the Temple Mount in an *al-pi halacha* fashion note that ordinary *tamei met* status does not disqualify one from *Machane Leviyah* — the broader precincts of the Temple Mount — whereas *tumah ha-yotzei mi-gufo* (such as *ba'al keri*, *niddah*, *zav*) does. The common guidance is that men should immerse in a *mikvah* before ascending. But here is the subtlety: if someone was a *ba'al keri* and immersed that morning, he is now a *tevul yom*. If his *tevul yom* status carries with it the residual personal identity of a *ba'al keri*, he may still be disqualified from ascending the Temple Mount. *Rashi* considers this the relevant *nafka mina* of the debate; *Tosafos* disagrees with *Rashi* and believes that on this particular question all opinions agree that he is disqualified.

In any case, the conceptual question is clear: when a person has gone through most of a purification process but has not fully concluded it, does their personal identity (*b'gavra*) continue to reflect their former status? Or has that earlier identity dissolved, leaving behind only a weak, impersonal residue of *tumah*?

### Parah Adumah Case

The Gemara now presents a *braisa* that reveals this to be a dispute among *Tannaim*. The context is the *parah adumah*. A *braisa* states: *srefah onen u-mechusar kippurim kesherah* — if the *parah adumah* was burned by a *kohen* who was an *onein* or a *kohen* who was *mechusar kippurim*, the burning is valid. Yosef HaBavli disagrees in part: *onen kasher, mechusar kippurim pesulah* — an *onein* is valid, but a *mechusar kippurim* who burned the *parah adumah* has invalidated it.

The *parah adumah* is not a *korban* offered inside the *Beis HaMikdash*; it belongs to the category of *kodshei bedek ha-bayis* and is performed outside. For this reason, the standard disqualifications that apply to *avoda* inside the *Mikdash* — such as the disqualification of an *onein* — do not automatically apply. Nevertheless, the *parah adumah* does carry its own requirement: the *pasuk* describing it refers to the person performing it as *hatahor* — one who is *tahor*.

The initial reading of the *braisa* suggests that the debate between the first *tanna* and Yosef HaBavli tracks precisely the question of *mechusar kippurim ke-zav dami*: one holds that the *mechusar kippurim* retains the identity of a *zav* and therefore cannot be considered *tahor* for purposes of *parah adumah*; the other holds he has lost that identity and is sufficiently *tahor*.

### Vehizah Hatahor

The Gemara, however, rejects this reading of the dispute, and the reasoning is important. The *pasuk* describing the *parah adumah* (Numbers 19:19) reads: *vehizah hatahor al ha-tamei* — the *tahor* person shall sprinkle upon the *tamei* person. The Gemara reads this in a striking way: *michlal she-hu tamei* — the fact that the *pasuk* emphasizes that the person is *tahor* implies that he had recently been *tamei*. In other words, the *pasuk* is specifically referring to someone who was *tamei* and is now in the process of becoming *tahor* — a *tevul yom*. This tells us that a *tevul yom* is valid to perform the *avoda* of the *parah adumah*.

This reading, the Gemara notes, was not merely academic. The *Mishnah* elsewhere describes how the *Chachamim* would go to extraordinary lengths to frustrate the *Tzedukim* on this point. The *Tzedukim* maintained that a *tevul yom* was invalid for the burning of the *parah adumah*; the *Chachamim* would raise children from birth in conditions of strict *taharah* specifically to perform the *parah adumah*, and then on the very day of the burning they would render these children *tamei* and have them immerse, so that they would be *tevulei yom* — specifically to demonstrate, against the *Tzeduki* position, that *vehizah hatahor* includes and even highlights the *tevul yom*.

### Two Positions

The context of *vehizah hatahor* is explicitly *tumat meit* — the *tumah* of a corpse, which is the subject of the entire *parasha* of *parah adumah*. A person rendered *tamei met* does not need a *korban* to complete his purification; he requires the sprinkling of the *parah adumah* ashes on the third and seventh days, immersion in a *mikvah*, and nightfall. He is never *mechusar kippurim*. So when the *pasuk* states *vehizah hatahor* — implying the performer had just been *tamei* — it is straightforwardly referring to a *tevul yom* of a *tamei met*, and by *kal va-chomer* it includes the lighter forms of *tumah* (such as *tevul yom* of a *tamei sheretz* or *ba'al keri*).

The question is whether this allowance extends to a *mechusar kippurim de-zav*. Here the *parah adumah* context creates a genuine debate:

The first position (*tumah de-chol ha-Torah kulluh*) holds that the verse's allowance of someone who was recently *tamei* extends to all forms of *tumah* across the Torah — including a *mechusar kippurim* who was formerly a *zav*. Any person who was *tamei* and is now in an advanced stage of *taharah* may perform the *avoda* of the *parah adumah*.

The second position (*tumah de-hach parshah*) holds that the allowance is contextually limited to the *tumah* discussed in this specific *parasha* — that is, *tumat meit*. Since a *mechusar kippurim de-zav* derives from a different and in certain respects weightier form of *tumah* — specifically *tumah ha-yotzei mi-gufo*, *tumah* that issues from the body — it is not encompassed by *vehizah hatahor*. The *zav* is indeed weightier in certain respects: one who is *tamei met* may still enter *Machaneh Leviyah*, the precincts of Har HaBayit, whereas a *zav* or *ba'al keri* may not. And the *mechusar kippurim de-zav* also requires a *korban* to complete his purification — a more demanding threshold. Therefore, a *mechusar kippurim de-zav* who performs the *avoda* of the *parah adumah* has invalidated it.

### Resolution

The Gemara concludes its analysis by clarifying that the debate between the first *tanna* and Yosef HaBavli is *not* about the general question of whether *mechusar kippurim ke-zav dami* as a matter of personal status. Everyone may well agree that the *mechusar kippurim de-zav* retains the personal identity of a *zav* in general. The debate is specifically and only about the reach of the *pasuk* *vehizah hatahor*: does the allowance it extends to those who were recently *tamei* encompass even someone with the identity and history of a *zav*, or is its scope limited to the *tumah* of this *parasha*?

This distinction is important. Questions about ascending Har HaBayit, or about eligibility for *korban pesach be-tumah*, are separate *nafka minot* that depend on the general question of *mechusar kippurim ke-zav dami* as a personal status. The *parah adumah* debate, by contrast, is about a specific exegetical question: how far does the *pasuk*'s special leniency extend? These are two different discussions, and the resolution of the *braisa* does not resolve the broader dispute.

---

## Mechusar Begadim

### Bigdei Kehunah Source

The Gemara now turns to the case of *mechusar begadim* — a *kohen* who is not wearing the full complement of *bigdei kehunah*. Rav Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, transmitted also in the name of Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, derives the rule from the *pasuk* in Exodus 29:9: *ve-chagarta osam avnet Aharon u-vanav ve-chavashta lahem migbaos ve-hayesa lahem kehunah le-chukas olam* — and you shall gird them with the belt, Aharon and his sons, and put the miters upon them, and the *kehunah* shall be unto them an everlasting statute.

### Garments Create Status

The principle derived from this *pasuk* is: *bizman she-bigdeihem aleihem kehunasam aleihem, ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunasam aleihem* — when their garments are upon them, their *kehunah* is upon them; when their garments are not upon them, their *kehunah* is not upon them, and they are therefore like a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — performing the *avoda*.

This makes intuitive sense. The entire ritual of donning the *bigdei kehunah* — described both in *Shemos* and in the seven-day inauguration process (*miluim*) — was the mechanism by which the *kohanim* were incorporated into the apparatus of the *Mikdash*. Just as the *Mikdash* itself was anointed and sanctified, so too the *kohanim* were anointed and invested through their garments. The *kohen gadol*, when there is no *shemen ha-mishchah*, achieves his status through *merubeh begadim* — wearing the eight garments — as discussed in *Horayos*. The garments are not merely a uniform; they are constitutive of the *kohen*'s functional identity as part of the *Mikdash* service.

### Scope of Ruling

One should not misread the principle *ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunasam aleihem* as though it dissolves the *kehunah* status of a *kohen* for all purposes. Throughout *Shas*, the *Gemara* consistently applies the restrictions of *kehunah* — the prohibition against marrying a *gerushah*, the restrictions related to *tumat meit* — without any suggestion that these depend on wearing *bigdei kehunah*. The principle applies specifically to the *avoda* in the *Mikdash*.

An instructive illustration appears in the *Mordechai*, who cites a story involving Rabbeinu Tam. When a student challenged Rabbeinu Tam for asking a *kohen* to pour him a glass of water — invoking the *Yerushalmi*'s ruling that one who makes personal use of a *kohen* is as though he has committed *me'ilah*, trespass against sanctified property — Rabbeinu Tam responded with the principle of *ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunasam aleihem*. The point is precise: the *Yerushalmi* describes using a *kohen* for personal service as analogous to *me'ilah*, and *me'ilah* is a category that applies to the *kelim* of the *Mikdash*, its sacred vessels. A *kohen* who is wearing his *bigdei kehunah* functions as a *kli* of the *Mikdash*, part of its sacred apparatus — and in that context you may not make personal use of him. When not wearing his *bigdei kehunah*, that relationship to the *Mikdash*'s apparatus is suspended. The ruling is entirely about the *kohen*'s connection to *avodat ha-Mikdash*, not about his general status as a member of *shevet Levi* bearing the obligations and privileges of *kehunah*.

### Wine Pasuk Alternative

The Gemara then raises a challenge: *ve-ha me-hacha nafka, me-hasam nafka* — is this actually derived from the *pasuk* about *bigdei kehunah*? We could instead derive it from the *pasuk* about wine. The *pasuk* (Leviticus 10:9) states: *yayin ve-sheichar al tesht atah u-vanecha itacha be-vo'achem el ohel mo'ed ve-lo tamutu* — wine and strong drink you shall not drink, you and your sons with you, when you come to the Tent of Meeting, and you shall not die — and then *u-lehavdil bein ha-kodesh u-vein ha-chol* — that you shall distinguish between the holy and the profane. From this verse we learn that a *kohen* who is *shoteh yayin*, drunk, desecrates the *avoda*. A *braisa* then extends this by *gezeirah shava*: the *pasuk* by drinking uses the language *chukat olam*, and so too by the *bigdei kehunah* it says *chukas olam*, and by washing the hands and feet it also says *le-chukat olam*. From this linkage, all three cases — being drunk, not wearing the *begadim*, and not having washed the hands and feet — are treated in parallel.

### Two Lists of Avodot

However, the Gemara explains why the derivation from *ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunasam aleihem* is essential and cannot be replaced by the *gezeirah shava* from the wine *pasuk* alone. Had we relied only on the wine *pasuk*, we would have said: *hanei milei avoda de-zar chayav aleha misa* — this applies only to an *avoda* for which a *zar* who performs it is liable to the death penalty. The wine *pasuk* uses the language *ve-lo tamutu*, connecting it to a category of *avoda* that carries *chiyuv misa*. A *zar* who performs certain *avodot* is indeed liable to *misa bidei shamayim*, and those *avodot* are specified by the *pasuk* *va-avadetem* as *avoda tama* — a completed act: things like *zerika* (the sprinkling of blood), *haktara* (the burning of the sacrifice), *nisuch ha-mayim* and *nisuch ha-yayin* (the wine and water libations). These are the culminating acts.

The four central *avodot ha-dam* — *shechita*, *kabala*, *holacha*, and *zerika* — are a different list. Of these, *shechita* is *kesheira be-zar* and valid even when performed by a non-*kohen*. The remaining three — *kabala*, *holacha*, and *zerika* — are the *avodot* that can invalidate a *korban* if performed improperly. But the *chiyuv misa* attaches to the different, overlapping list of *avoda tama*.

Had we derived the rule about *mechusar begadim* solely from the *gezeirah shava* to the wine *pasuk*, we would have concluded that the disqualification of a *mechusar begadim* applies only to the *avodot* for which a *zar* incurs *misa* — that is, *zerika* and its associated acts. We would not have known that *kabala* and *holacha* are also disqualified when performed by a *kohen* without his *begadim*. It is precisely the derivation from *ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunasam aleihem* — the principle that without his garments the *kohen* is like a *zar* for all purposes of the *avoda* — that extends the disqualification to *kabala ve-eilach*, all the *avodot* from *kabala* onward that are reserved for a *kohen*. The derivation from the *bigdei kehunah pasuk* is therefore indispensable, establishing that the *kohen*'s status as valid for service depends entirely on the presence of his garments, for the full range of *avodot* rather than only those associated with the *chiyuv misa*.

---

---

# Zevachim 18

## Mechusar Begadim

### Introduction

Masechet Zevachim, daf 18a, opens by returning to the discussion of the *kohen mechusar begadim* — the kohen who is not properly attired in the priestly garments — and the consequences this has for his *avodah*. The previous session had examined two primary *pesukim*: one from Shemot 29 in Parshat Tetzaveh, addressing the priestly vestments, and another from Vayikra, following the incident of Nadav and Avihu, addressing the *kohen* who performs the *avodah* while intoxicated. A third passage, from Parshat Ki Tisa, concerns the washing of hands and feet. All three passages share the phrase *chok olam* or *chukat olam*, providing the basis for a *gezeirah shavah* that links them together.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The *gemara* now arrives at the word *ashkechan* — "I have found" — near the middle of the fourth line from the top of daf 18a. Having established the case of *mechusar begadim*, the *gemara* asks: *shtuyei yayin minalan* — from where do we derive that a drunk *kohen* invalidates the *avodah*? The answer is *atiah chuka chuka mi-mechusar begadim*: we learn it through a *gezeirah shavah* on the word *chukah*, drawing the laws of intoxication into parallel with those of improper dress. The passage from Vayikra regarding *u-lehavdil bein ha-kodesh u-vein ha-chol* is also invoked in this connection.

### Learning Direction

The *gemara* then probes the direction of the learning: does the law of *mechusar begadim* derive from *shtuyei yayin*, or the reverse? The resolution is that the *gezeirah shavah* was established first from the existing *pesuk*, and only afterward was the *gezeirah shavah* itself applied. The deeper point of the *gezeirah shavah* is this: *minayin she-lo nechelku bein mechusar begadim le-shtuyei yayin ve-she-lo rachutz yadayim ve-raglayim* — from where do we know that there is no distinction among these three categories: one who lacks the proper garments, one who has consumed wine, and one whose hands and feet are unwashed? The answer is: *talmud lomar chuka chuka le-gezeirah shavah* — all three are bound together under the same *chukah*, equally disqualifying the *avodah*.

### No Distinction

This raises the question: once we have the *gezeirah shavah*, why do we still need the independent *pesukim*? The *gemara* answers that one of those verses — the passage in Vayikra about *u-lehavdil bein ha-kodesh u-vein ha-chol* — carries its own independent legal function, beyond what the *gezeirah shavah* alone could teach. The point is that the *gezeirah shavah* unifies the three cases, showing that in each of these domains — garments, wine, and hand-washing — there is no internal distinction: all failures under each category are equally invalidating.

### Rav's Translator

The *gemara* notes an additional lesson derived from the *pasuk* regarding *shtuyei yayin*: *de-Rav lo mokim amora aleih mi-Yom Tov le-chavereih mishum shichrut* — Rav would not position his translator beside him from one *Yom Tov* to the next, lest it appear that he was teaching *halacha* while possibly under the influence of wine. Rav's teaching method involved having an intermediary who would explain and expand upon his words to the audience — a practice that naturally would be suspended on any day when drinking was obligatory or likely. The pedagogical irony here is rich: by conspicuously removing his translator on those occasions, Rav was in effect teaching his students, through action, that one must not deliver *halachic* rulings when one has been drinking.

---

## Garment Sources

### Vayikra 1:7

The *gemara* now turns to an independent source for the laws of *mechusar begadim*, examining several *pesukim* from the opening of Vayikra. The first is Vayikra 1:7: *v'natnu bnei Aharon ha-kohen ve-archu etzim al ha-esh* — "And the sons of Aharon the kohen shall place wood upon the fire." The *gemara* asks: why is the word *ha-kohen* necessary here? We already know that the sons of Aharon are *kohanim*. The answer is that the *gemara* reads *bekihuno* — "in their priesthood" — meaning while properly invested in their priestly vestments. This superfluous term is therefore understood as a deliberate textual signal that the *kohanim* must be in their garments when performing the *avodah*.

### Deficiency Implication

From this superfluous *ha-kohen*, the *gemara* derives: *bekihuno limed al Kohen Gadol shelavash bigdei Kohen Hedyot v'avad avodato psulah* — it teaches that a *Kohen Gadol* who donned the garments of a *kohen hedyot* and performed the *avodah*, his service is *pasul*. This is the case of *chisur* — deficiency — where the *Kohen Gadol* is wearing less than his full complement of eight garments. One might think that this applies only to *avodot* that are *meakev kapara* — those that are indispensable to the atonement process — but not to auxiliary acts of service. The verse in Vayikra 1:7, however, describes the placing of wood on the altar — an act that is *not* among the *avodot meakev kapara* — and yet the same requirement applies. This extends the *halacha* of *mechusar begadim* beyond the core acts of atonement to the full range of priestly service. It is worth noting that this derivation appears in a *beraita* in the Sifra, *Torat Kohanim*, lending it additional authoritative weight.

### Vayikra 1:8

The *gemara* continues: *ve-akati meihacha meihatam nafka* — but if we already have this source, can we not derive everything we need from it? It then introduces the next verse, Vayikra 1:8: *ve-archu bnei Aharon ha-kohanim et ha-netachim asher al ha-mizbeach* — "And the sons of Aharon, the *kohanim*, shall arrange the pieces upon the altar." Here again the word *ha-kohanim* appears, and again it is read as *ha-kohanim be-khunam* — the *kohanim* while in their priestly service.

### Excess Implication

From the second superfluous *ha-kohanim*, the *gemara* derives the opposite case: *mikan le-kohen hedyot shelavash bigdei kohen gadol v'avad avodato psulah* — a *kohen hedyot* who donned the garments of a *Kohen Gadol* and performed the *avodah*, his service too is *pasul*. This is the case of *yitur* — excess, wearing more than one's proper complement.

### Two Sources Needed

Why are two separate *pesukim* necessary? The *gemara* explains: if we had only the first source, we might conclude that the *halacha* applies only to *chisur* — deficiency in garments — but not to *yitur* — excess. A *kohen hedyot* wearing the *Kohen Gadol*'s garments is not missing anything; he has more than he needs. One might therefore think this would not be problematic. And conversely, had we only the second source, we might think only excess is addressed. It takes both *pesukim* together to establish that the principle is not one of quantity but of fitness: each *kohen* must wear precisely the garments designated for his level of service — neither more nor less.

---

## Rabbanan Position

### Condition List

A *tanna devei rabbanan* is now cited: *hayu merushalin mesulakin meshuchakim ve-avad avodato keshera* — if the garments were *merushalin* (too long, dragging), *mesulakin* (too short, raised), or *meshuchakin* (threadbare, worn), and the *kohen* performed the *avodah*, his service is nonetheless *kasher*. According to the *rabbanan*, these variations in the condition of the garments do not rise to the level of invalidating the *avodah*.

### Invalidating Conditions

The same *beraita* then enumerates what does invalidate the *avodah*: if the *kohen* wore two pairs of pants or two *avnetim* (belts); if he was missing one garment or added one beyond his proper complement; if he had a bandage (*retiyah*) on a wound beneath his garment, creating a *chatzitzah* — a separation between garment and body; or if the garments were *metushtashin* (soiled with mud) or *mekora'in* (torn). In all these cases, the *avodah* is *pesulah*.

### Mido Derivation

The source for the requirement that the garments fit the *kohen* precisely is the word *mido* in Parshat Tzav (Vayikra 6:3): *velavash ha-kohen mido bad* — the *kohen* shall wear his garment of linen. The word *mido* is read as *ke-midato* — according to his measure, his size. The garments must be made to fit the individual *kohen* precisely.

### Soiled and Torn

Rashi explains the cases of *metushtashin* and *mekora'in*: *metushtashin* means soiled with mud, and *mekora'in* means torn. Rashi comments on the torn garments: *ve-afilu einan chadashim, de-lav bigdo ha-ra'ui la-avodah, de-be'inan le-chavod u-le-tiferet* — even if they are not entirely new, what we require is that the garment be fitting for the *avodah*, and for that we need garments that reflect *kavod ve-tiferet* — honor and splendor. A threadbare garment that remains intact may still possess that dignity; a soiled or torn garment does not.

---

## Shmuel vs. Rav

### Shmuel's Position

The *gemara* now records the opinion of Shmuel, transmitted by Rav Yehudah: *merushalin kesherin, mesulakin pesulin* — garments that are too long are *kasher*, garments that are too short are *pasul*. This is immediately challenged: but the *beraita* cited above rules that *mesulakin* are *kasher*! The *gemara* thus presents a direct contradiction between Shmuel and the *beraita*.

### Rami's Resolution

Rami bar Chama resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — kan she-silkan al yedei avnet, kan de-litin nafish* — there is no difficulty. In one case, the garment appeared short because it was gathered up by the *avnet* (the priestly belt), and in the other case, the fabric itself is genuinely insufficient in length. When the garment is the proper length but has been bunched up by the belt, it is *kasher*; when it is genuinely too short — when there is simply not enough material — it is *pasul*. The *avnet* thus serves a dual function: as a required component of the priestly dress and as a practical tool for adjusting the garment's fit. A longer garment gathered by the belt remains valid; but a garment that lacks material cannot be remedied by the belt, since cinching it would only make it shorter still.

### Rav's Position

Rav takes a more stringent position: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh pesulin* — both too long and too short are *pasul*. This means that for Rav, the garments must fit correctly from the outset, and neither excess nor deficiency is tolerated. The underlying logic is consistent with the broader principle of *kavod ve-tiferet*: garments that do not fit properly are unworthy of the *avodah*, in either direction.

### Belt Function

Rashi's comment on Rav's position clarifies: *echad merushal ve-echad mesulakim yoter midai she-lo al yedei avnet* — whether too long or too short, when this is not a result of the *avnet*'s adjustment, it is *pasul*. This preserves the coherence of Rav's view: the *avnet* may play a role in fit, but only within limits. What the *avnet* cannot do is remedy a garment that is fundamentally the wrong size.

### Rav Huna Story

The *gemara* records that Rav Huna happened upon a place called *Argiza*, where the son of his host posed the apparent contradiction: Shmuel holds that *merushalin* are *kasher* and *mesulakin* are *pasul*, yet a *beraita* rules *mesulakin kasher*? Rav Huna responded: *bar mina* — leave us alone with this; it has already been resolved by Rami bar Chama. The *gemara* notes, however, that while Rami bar Chama's resolution settles the question for Shmuel, it still creates a difficulty for Rav. One might propose on Rav's behalf that what the *beraita* calls *merushalin* refers to garments raised by the *avnet*, and that the *avnet* itself compensates for the additional length — but the *gemara* notes that if the garment was too long to begin with and was shortened by the *avnet*, the *avnet* itself is now covering that excess. What remains problematic, even after Rami bar Chama's answer, is the case for Rav where the garment is *mesulakin* without any *avnet* adjustment — genuinely short fabric with no mechanism for remedy. The question of whether an *avodah* performed in imperfectly fitting garments is *pasul be-di'avad* or only problematic *le-chatchila* runs throughout this discussion.

---

## Tzitzit Parallel

### Four Corners Debate

The *gemara* now imports an analogy from the laws of *tzitzit* in order to shed light on the garment debate. The relevant verse is Devarim 22, which commands: *al arba kanfot kesutcha asher techaseh bah gedilim taaseh lach* — "On the four corners of your garment with which you cover yourself, you shall make *gedilim*." Two terms in this verse appear to point in opposite directions: the phrase *arba kanfot* ("four corners") suggests a specific, bounded requirement, while *asher techaseh bah* ("with which you cover yourself") suggests a broader, more expansive application. The *gemara* presents two competing readings of this tension.

The first *tanna* asks: does the phrase "four corners" mean four and not three, or four and not five? This question determines whether the verse functions as a *ribui* (expansion) or a *miut* (restriction). The *tanna* reasons: since the verse adds *asher techaseh bah* — anything with which you cover yourself — this phrase comes to include even a five-cornered garment in the obligation of *tzitzit*. Why? Because *marbe ani ba'alat chamesh she-yesh bi-khlal chamesh arba* — I can include a five-cornered garment since five inherently contains four. By contrast, I can exclude a three-cornered garment: *she-ein bi-khlal shalosh arba* — three does not include four. The better reading, then, is that *arba* means four and not three, while the *ribui* extends the obligation even to garments with more than four corners.

### Five Corners Included

A second *beraita* holds the opposite: *arba velo shalosh, arba velo chamesh* — four and not three, four and not five. Only a four-cornered garment is obligated; garments with three or five corners are entirely exempt. The *gemara* asks whether this dispute reflects the broader question of *yeter ke-man de-ita dami* — does excess count as present, or as absent? That is, does a fifth corner mean the garment still "has" four corners and is therefore obligated, or is it so different from the paradigm that the obligation does not apply?

The *gemara* ultimately rejects this framing: *lo, de-kulei alma yeter ke-man de-ita dami* — everyone agrees that what is present is present. You cannot ignore a fifth corner by pretending it does not exist. The disagreement between the two *tanna'im* on *tzitzit* is thus not a dispute about excess as such. Rather, the different readings stem from how each *tanna* interprets the term *asher techaseh bah*: one derives from it a *ribui* that includes all covering garments, including those with more than four corners; the other does not read that term as a *ribui* at all.

This matters for the *kohen's* garments as well: one cannot argue that an excess of garment fabric should simply be "ignored" as if it were not there. Just as a five-cornered garment cannot be treated as a four-cornered one, a garment that is too long or too short cannot be treated as if it were the proper fit.

### Visibility Requirement

The *gemara* turns to the other verse about *tzitzit*, from Bamidbar 15: *u-re'item oto ve-haya lachem le-tzitzit* — "And you shall see it, and it shall be a *tzitzit* for you." From the word *u-re'item* — "and you shall see" — the *gemara* derives a visibility requirement. This raises the question: does *u-re'item* exclude nighttime garments (since one cannot see at night), or does it exclude the garments of a blind person (since he cannot see at all)?

### Night vs. Blind

The *gemara* resolves the question: *asher techaseh bah* comes to include the garments of a blind person in the obligation of *tzitzit*, because a blind person's garments are visible to others even if not to himself. And *u-re'item* serves to exclude nighttime garments, because at night neither the wearer nor others can see the *tzitzit*. The principle is: *marbe ani kesut suma she-yeshna be-re'iyah etzel acherim* — I include the blind person's garments since they exist in the realm of visibility from the perspective of others; *umotzi ani kesut layla she-einah be-re'iyah etzel acherim* — and I exclude night garments since they are not visible to anyone. This is, as noted, what makes *tzitzit* a *mitzvat aseh she-ha-zman grama*, a time-bound positive commandment applicable only during the day.

One *tanna* derives the inclusion of five-cornered garments from the word *asher* in *asher techaseh bah*, reading it as a textual expansion. The other *tanna* does not treat *asher* as a source for *drash* at all — *asher lo darish* — and therefore draws no expansion from it.

---

## Linen Requirements

### Bad Qualities

The *gemara* cites a new *tanu rabbanan* enumerating the qualities required of the priestly linen. The word *bad* appears repeatedly in the Torah in connection with the priestly garments — once in Parshat Tetzaveh, twice in Parshat Tzav, and four times in Parshat Acharei Mot — and each repetition is taken to teach something. The *beraita* derives five requirements: *sheyihyu shel butz* — the fabric must be fine linen; *sheyihyu chadashim* — new; *sheyihyu shezurim* — twisted or woven; *sheyihyu chutan kaful shisha* — the threads folded sixfold; and *shelo yilbash chol imahem* — no secular garment may be worn together with them.

### New vs. Worn

Abaye raises a challenge to Rav Yosef: the requirement that the garments be *chadashim* — new — implies that worn garments are *pasul*. Yet we have the *beraita* cited earlier, stating that *meshuchakim kesherin* — worn garments are *kasher*! This is a direct contradiction.

### Bad Interpretation

Rav Yosef deflects the challenge by reframing it. He points out that the word *bad* itself, etymologically, suggests singularity — related to *levad* and *badad*, meaning alone or separate. *Bad bad chad chad le-chudei mashma* — each instance of *bad* denotes something single, individual, and non-splitting. This refers to the nature of the flax stalk: it grows as a single, discrete stalk, unlike wool, which splits and branches. The word *bad* thus characterizes the material's origin and structure, not a prohibition of worn garments. What the *beraita* is saying is: wherever the Torah uses the word *bad* in reference to priestly garments, it is specifying a material with these particular qualities — fine, new, twisted, sixfold thread, and worn without secular admixture.

### Chumra vs. Meakev

The *gemara* then distinguishes among these requirements: *yesh me-hen le-mitzvah ve-yesh me-hen le-akev* — some of these are ideally required (*le-mitzvah*, as a *chumra*) while others are *me-akev* — indispensable, such that their absence invalidates the *avodah*. The precise demarcation between the two categories is left to be worked out, but the overall point is that not every specification derived from the repetition of *bad* carries equal weight in *halacha*.

### Bad is Flax

The *gemara* then asks: how do we know that the term *bad* refers specifically to flax? The word in the Torah just says *bad*. From where do we know it is not wool or some other material? Rabbi Yosef b'Rabbi Chanina answers: *davar ha-oleh min ha-karka bad be-vad* — we need a material that grows from the ground with each stalk growing on its own, *bad be-vad*, not splitting into multiple strands. Flax naturally fulfills this criterion. Wool does not: *amra miftzal* — wool splits and branches. One might still ask: does not flax also split? The *gemara* answers: *al yedei lakuta miftzil* — flax only separates when beaten in processing, not naturally of its own accord. Its natural state is the single stalk, and that is what qualifies it as *bad*.

### Yechezkel Support

Ravina offers a further source for identifying *bad* as flax, citing Yechezkel 44:18: *pe'arei pishtim yihyu al rosham u-michnesei pishtim yihyu al motneihem ve-lo yachgeru be-yaza* — "They shall wear linen (*pishtim*) crowns upon their heads and linen pants on their waists, and they shall not gird themselves in a place of sweat." *Pishtim* — flax — is explicitly named in Yechezkel as the material of the priestly garments, and *pishtim* is unambiguously flax.

### Ravina Citation

Rav Ashi raises an objection to Ravina's proof: *ve-ha ad de-ata Yechezkel minalan* — but Yechezkel was written some 480 years after the *mishkan* was established and many centuries after the laws of the priestly vestments were given at Sinai. How could the earlier generations have derived this requirement from Yechezkel? The same question applies to Rav Chisda's teaching elsewhere in our *masechet*: *davar zeh mi-torat Moshe Rabbeinu lo lamadnu, mi-divrei Yechezkel ben Buzi lamadnu* — there are things we did not learn from the Torah of Moshe, but from the words of Yechezkel. The answer is: *ela gemara gemiri lei* — the practice was already known by tradition. Yechezkel did not originate the requirement; he provided a scriptural anchor (*asmachta*) for a practice that had been transmitted all along: *ve-ata Yechezkel ve-asmachei akra* — Yechezkel came and gave it a textual grounding, so that later generations would have a *pasuk* to point to, even though the practice itself predated his prophecy.

---

## Belt Placement

### Sweat Restriction

The *gemara* returns to the verse from Yechezkel: *ve-lo yachgeru be-yaza* — they shall not gird themselves with *yaza*. Abaye interprets: *lo yachgeru be-makom she-maziin* — they must not place the *avnet* in the part of the body where one sweats. This is the practical *halacha* derived from the verse: the belt must not be positioned at a spot where perspiration would accumulate beneath it, for this would compromise both the dignity and the physical integrity of the priestly garment.

### Elbow Height

A *beraita* elaborates: *ein chogrin lo le-mata mi-motneihem ve-lo le-mala me-atzileihem* — when the *kohanim* gird themselves, they must not do so below the waist and not above the height of the elbows. The area below the waist and the area above the elbows are places where folds of flesh may collect and cause sweating. *Ela ke-neged atzilei yedeihem* — the correct position is level with the elbows. This is where the *avnet* must sit.

### King Izgadar

Rav Ashi transmits a remarkable story in the name of Huna bar Natan. On one occasion, Huna bar Natan was standing before *Izgadar*, the Persian king, when his belt (*hemyani*) was not sitting properly. The king himself reached over and adjusted it for him. Then *Izgadar* said to him: it is written about you, before the giving of the Torah in Shemot 19, *mamlechet kohanim ve-goy kadosh* — "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." The implication is clear: the proper wearing of one's garments and the dignity of one's bearing are not merely requirements of the *kohen* alone, but of the entire Jewish people, who are themselves designated a *mamlechet kohanim*.

### Priestly Nation

Huna bar Natan then brought this exchange before Amemar, who said to him: *akayem becha* — fulfilled in you is the verse from Yeshayahu 49: *ve-hayu melachim omnecha* — "And kings shall be your foster parents," meaning kings will guide you and teach you who you are. It should be noted that Huna bar Natan was himself the *Reish Galuta* at the time of Amemar and Rav Ashi, which gives this story an added dimension: even the leader of the exile, standing before a gentile king, is reminded through that encounter of Israel's fundamental vocation. The entire extended discussion of priestly garments — their fit, their material, their proper placement — thus closes with a broadening of perspective: the dignity encoded in these precise requirements is not the exclusive province of those who serve in the *Beit Hamikdash*, but reflects the calling of an entire nation.

---

---

# Zevachim 19

## Begadim Fit & Coverage

### Invalid Service

The daf opens with the continuation of a broader discussion about the *bigdei kehuna* — the priestly garments — and the ways in which deficiencies in those garments render the *avoda* invalid. The Gemara had already explored a range of fitting questions: what happens if the garments are too long or too short, if they are held up by the belt so that they do not reach the proper position, or if they are the correct size only because they are being gathered. All of these scenarios bear on the fundamental requirement that a *kohen* must wear his prescribed garments in the prescribed manner. The *avoda* performed without the proper *begadim* — *chutz mibegadim* — is *pasul*.

### Bandaging on Shabbat

The Gemara cites a teaching: *kohen she'laka be'etzba'o* — a *kohen* who sustained a cut on his finger. We are not dealing with a *psul* of the service per se at the outset; the concern is more fundamental hygiene of the Temple rite. The *kohen* may wrap the wound with a *gemi* (a light cloth bandage) in the *Beis Hamikdash*, even on *Shabbos* — *bamikdash aval lo bamedina* — though not outside, where the prohibition applies. The reason this is an issue on *Shabbos* at all is that keeping a wound covered assists the healing process and constitutes a form of *refuah*, which is rabbinically prohibited on *Shabbos*. However, *ein shevus bamikdash* — the general principle that rabbinic restrictions are waived within the Temple — licenses the practice there. It is worth noting the apparent irony: the holiest place on the holiest day grants more latitude, not less. The explanation is that *kohanim* are presumed to be scrupulous regarding Torah-level prohibitions, and the rabbinic fence need not be extended into that domain.

The Gemara clarifies that if, while wrapping the wound, the *kohen* intends to squeeze out blood, this is forbidden in both locations — *kan vekan assur* — because that crosses into the category of *chavala*, causing a wound, which is an independent prohibition entirely unrelated to the rabbinic healing concern.

### Extra Garments Debate

The Gemara now pivots to the *begadim* issue raised by the case of the bandage. *Rav Yehuda brei deRav Chiya* teaches: *lo shanu ela gemi* — the ruling that the bandage is permissible applies only to a light cloth bandage. But *tziltzul katan havei yitur begadim* — if the item is something more garment-like, such as a small decorative band or bracelet-like object, it constitutes an extra garment — *yitur begadim* — and is therefore forbidden. A *kohen* may wear only the prescribed *bigdei kehuna*; anything additional, if it constitutes a *beged*, invalidates.

This naturally raises the question of whether a *kohen* could perform the *avoda* wearing a ring, eyeglasses, or other everyday items. The *Gemara* will develop these questions further, but the initial framework is that any item that qualifies as a *beged* creates a problem.

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees and introduces a critical distinction: *lo amru yitur begadim ela bemakom begadim* — the prohibition of wearing an extra garment applies only to those parts of the body where the *bigdei kehuna* are designed to cover. On parts of the body not covered by the priestly garments — such as a finger, or the face — *shelo bemakom begadim lo havei yitur*, wearing something there does not constitute an extra garment.

The Gemara then raises the obvious challenge: even granting *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position on *yitur begadim*, why isn't the bandage problematic as a *chatzitza* — an interposition between the *kohen*'s hand and whatever he is handling during the *avoda*? The principle that the service must be performed *be'itzumo shel kohen* — directly by the essence of the *kohen* himself, with direct skin contact — would seem to apply. The Gemara resolves this: *bismolo* — the wound is on the left hand, and the *avoda* is performed with the right. Alternatively, the bandage is positioned on the back of the hand, which *Rashi* notes is not the operative surface that contacts the vessels or blood. These answers point to two distinct categories of concern: *chatzitza* between the skin and the object of the *avoda*, and *yitur begadim* as a separate issue applying even where no direct *avoda* contact occurs.

## Chatzitza & Size Limits

### Single Thread Issue

*Rava*'s position sharpens the entire discussion considerably. He teaches — citing *Rav Chisda* — that *bemakom begadim afilu nima achas chotzetzes* — in the place where the priestly garments are worn, even a single thread constitutes a *chatzitza*. The rationale derives from the verse *michnesei vad yihyu al besaro* — the garments must rest directly upon the skin. Any intervening object, however small, violates this requirement. A loose thread, a hair that has separated from the body and settled on the skin — all of these are problematic.

It is worth pausing to note, as *Rashi* flags throughout this section, that the term *chatzitza* is used somewhat loosely in the Gemara. In its technically precise sense, *chatzitza* refers to interposition either between the garment and the skin, or between the skin and the object of the *avoda*. But sometimes the Gemara uses the term to describe what is functionally a *yitur begadim* problem. The reader must attend carefully to context.

### Three-by-Three Rule

*Rava* continues: *shelo bemakom begadim shalosh al shalosh chotzetzes, pachos mikan eina chotzetzes* — in a place on the body where the priestly garments are not worn, something constitutes a problem only if it is at least three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths in size. This measurement is the standard threshold in *hilchos tumah vetaharah* for a piece of cloth to be classified as a significant garment. Below that threshold, the item does not rise to the level of a *beged* and presents no concern of *yitur begadim*.

The positions can be mapped out as follows. According to *Rava*: where the *begadim* are worn, even a single *nima* is a *chatzitza*; where they are not worn, the threshold is three by three for *yitur begadim*. According to *Rabbi Yochanan* (in his initial formulation): where the *begadim* are worn, a genuine alternative *beged* would be required to constitute *yitur begadim*; where they are not worn, there is no concern at all. According to *Rav Yehuda brei deRav Chiya*: the determining factor for the second zone is whether the item is a functional *tziltzul* — something with genuine garment character — regardless of its size.

### Reconciling Positions

The Gemara asks whether *Rava* necessarily disagrees with *Rav Yehuda brei deRav Chiya*. The answer is that they need not be in conflict: *shani tziltzul katan dechashiv* — a small *tziltzul* is significant because of its inherent garment character. The two positions represent two independent criteria for classifying something as a *beged*: functional character (*tziltzul*) and minimum size (three by three). These are complementary rather than contradictory standards, and either one could render an item a *beged* for the purposes of *yitur begadim*.

The Gemara then presents a second formulation (*lishana acharina*) of the positions. In this version, *Rabbi Yochanan* himself takes a stance very close to *Rava*: *bemakom begadim* even less than three by three is problematic, while *shelo bemakom begadim* requires three by three — *ve'hainu de'Rava*, which the Gemara notes is effectively identical to *Rava*'s position.
