The difference between this version of *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Rav Yehuda brei deRav Chiya* is that *Rabbi Yochanan* rejects the *tziltzul* criterion as independently sufficient below the three-by-three threshold.

The Gemara raises a question: according to *Rabbi Yochanan*, why did the *Mishnah* in *hilchos Shabbos* specifically choose the case of a *gemi* rather than illustrating the rule with a small *tziltzul*, which would also be permitted? The answer is: *milta agav urchia kamashma lan de'gemi masi* — the *Mishnah*'s interest was in teaching the law of *Shabbos* healing; it chose the bandage specifically because it wanted to convey that this material actually promotes healing, which is why it is permitted in the *Beis Hamikdash* but not outside it. Incidentally teaching a *chiddush* in *bigdei kehuna* was not its purpose.

## Objects & Chatzitza

### Air Gaps & Normal Wear

Having established the framework, *Rava* proceeds to pose a series of open-ended questions about what precisely constitutes a *chatzitza*. The first: *nichnesa lo ruach bevigdo mahu* — if a wind lifts the tunic slightly off the leg, creating a momentary air gap between garment and skin, is this a *chatzitza*? The Gemara frames the question as: do we require *al besaro* to be understood literally at every point of contact, or does *derech levisha bekach* — the normal manner of wearing a garment — include the natural and unavoidable variation in contact? The logical answer is clearly the latter; no garment maintains uniform contact with every inch of skin at all times, and to demand otherwise would make the priesthood functionally impossible.

### Lice Status

The next question: *kinah mahu shetachlotz* — what is the status of a louse on the *kohen*'s skin between the garment and the body? *Metah lo tiba'i lach* — a dead louse requires no deliberation; it is clearly a *chatzitza*, as it is something unwanted on the body. *Chayah mai* — but a living louse? *Mi amrinan keivan de'azla ve'atya ravita hi* — perhaps since it moves about on its own, it is considered quasi-organic and not truly an interposition? *Rashi* notes that the argument would be analogous to something that is part of one's body — it comes and goes naturally. Or: *keivan dekapid aleih chotzetzet* — since one obviously objects to its presence, it is a *chatzitza*. The question is left open.

Similar unresolved questions are raised about fine dust (*avak afar*) on the skin and about the armpit area, where the structure of the garment necessarily creates a permanent air pocket.

### Hair as Barrier

*Mar bar Rav Ashi* poses the question: *yatza se'aro bevigdo mahu* — if the *kohen*'s hair exits through the garment and lies between the garment and the skin, what is the status? *Se'ar kegufo dami* — is hair to be considered an extension of the body, and therefore not an interposition, in the same way one might argue that inserting one's own hand into the fold of a garment (*hichnis yado letoch cheiko*) does not constitute *chatzitza* because *gufo michai*? Or is hair sufficiently separate from the body that it functions as a barrier? These too are left unresolved by the Gemara.

### Tefillin Issues

The Gemara raises the case of *tefillin*. *Rashi* clarifies that the question here is not primarily about *chatzitza* in the sense of interposition between the skin and the object of the *avoda*, but rather whether *tefillin* worn during the *avoda* constitute an extra *beged* — *yitur begadim* — or a *chatzitza* between the garment and the skin.

The Gemara distinguishes by opinion: *aliba deman d'amar layla lav zman tefillin* — according to the view that night is not the time of the *mitzvah* of *tefillin*, *lo tibay lach* — there is no question. At night, *tefillin* are worn without a *mitzvah* context, making them plainly a foreign garment. *Keivan de'layla chaitz yom nami chaitz* — since at night they constitute an extra *beged*, and the daytime *avoda* is presumably more weighty, they would remain a problem during the day as well. The real question arises *lema'an d'amar layla zman tefillin* — according to the view that *tefillin* may always be worn. In that case, are *tefillin* to be viewed as a perpetual *mitzvah* object — perhaps comparable in status to the body itself — or as a foreign *beged*? *Mitzvah degupei chaitz o lo chaitz?*

The matter reached *Rabbi Ami*, who ruled decisively: *talmud aruch hu beyadenu tefillin chotzetzet* — we have a longstanding teaching that *tefillin* do constitute a *chatzitza*.

A *braita* is then raised in apparent contradiction: when *kohanim* are performing their *avoda*, *levi'im* are on their platform, and *Yisraelim* are present at the *ma'amad*, they are *peturim* — exempt — from wearing *tefillin*. This implies they could wear *tefillin* without invalidating. The Gemara resolves this: the *braita* says *peturim* rather than *asurin* because the ruling applies equally to *levi'im* and *Yisrael*, for whom there is no question of invalidation; the language of exemption rather than prohibition accommodates all three groups, even though for a *kohen* performing the *avoda*, wearing *tefillin* would in fact invalidate.

The Gemara then reconciles an explicit *braita* stating that *im henicham einam chotzetzim* — wearing *tefillin* does not constitute a *chatzitza* — by distinguishing between *tefillin shel yad* and *tefillin shel rosh*. The *shel yad* is a *chatzitza*, since it is positioned where the priestly garment must rest directly against the skin. The *shel rosh* is not a *chatzitza* — there is no garment pressing against that part of the head — and does not constitute *yitur begadim* either, because the *mitznefet* does not cover the entire skull, and the space between the *tzitz* and the *mitznefet* is where the *kohen gadol*'s hair was visible, and it is there that *tefillin* are placed. *Tam searo hayah nir'eh bein tzitz lemitznefet vesham manichin tefillin* — and in that uncovered space, *tefillin* of the head may be worn without any concern of *chatzitza* or *yitur begadim*.

## Purification & Washing

### Mechusar Kippurim

The Gemara moves to another category of invalidation: *mechusar kippurim* — one who has completed the immersion process but has not yet brought the required *korban* that finalizes the *tahara* process. Such a person — whether a *zav*, a *yoledes*, or any other individual whose purification requires a concluding sacrifice — remains in a state of personal *tumah* until that offering is brought. *Rav Huna* derives this from the verse *vichiper aleha hakohen vetahera* — the *kohen* shall atone for her and she will become *tehorah* — which implies that until the atonement is effected, her status of *tumah* persists. Since a *tamei* person performing the *avoda* invalidates it, a *mechusar kippurim* doing so likewise invalidates.

### Morning Washing

The next item on the Mishnah's list: *shelo rachutz yadayim veraglayim* — a *kohen* who did not wash his hands and feet before beginning the service. This too renders the *avoda* invalid. The derivation proceeds by a *gezeira shava* — the word *chok* — linking the washing requirement to the requirement for *bigdei kehuna*, which is itself linked to a *chukas olam* formulation. Just as lacking the proper *begadim* invalidates, so too does lacking the morning washing.

## Yom Kippur Washings

### Teaching Overview

The Gemara now cites a *baraita* that defines the scope of the washing requirement with precision, particularly as applied to the *Yom Kippur* service. On *Yom Kippur*, the *kohen gadol* changes his garments five times and is required, as described explicitly in the Torah, to immerse in the *mikveh* and wash his hands before and after each change — potentially ten washings in total over the course of the day. The *baraita* rules: *kohen gadol shelo taval veshelo kidesh bein beged lebeged uvein avoda la'avoda ve'avad — avodaso kesheira* — if the *kohen gadol* omitted these intermediate immersions and washings between the garment changes, the *avoda* remains valid. By contrast: *ve'echad kohen gadol ve'echad kohen hedyot shelo kidesh yadav veraglav shacharis ve'avad — avodaso pesulah* — whether a *kohen gadol* or an ordinary *kohen*, if the initial morning washing was not performed, the *avoda* is invalid.

The *chiddush* is the first clause. One might have assumed — given that *Yom Kippur* is governed by the phrase *chukas olam*, meaning that every prescribed element of the service is indispensable — that missing an intermediate washing would also invalidate. The question is why it does not.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Drasha

*Rav Assi* poses this question directly to *Rabbi Yochanan*: the five immersions and ten washings are *de'Oraita*, and the word *chok* is written regarding *Yom Kippur* — which ordinarily signals that every detail is *le'akeiv*, preventing validity if omitted. Why then do the intermediate washings not invalidate?

*Rabbi Yochanan* responds with an exegetical reading of the verse: *verachatz es besaro bamayim velavasham* — "and he shall wash his body in water and wear them." The verse already listed the garments in full detail earlier; the repetition of *velavasham* — "and wear them" — following the mention of immersion conveys a specific message: *levisha me'akevet ve'ein davar acher me'akeiv* — wearing the garments is what prevents validity; nothing else mentioned in that verse — specifically the immersion — carries the same force. The word *velavasham* reasserts the centrality of *levisha* and implicitly limits the scope of *ikkuv* to the donning of the garments alone.

The reaction of *Rav Ashi* is telling: *tzahavu fanav* — his face lit up with admiration for the reading. Yet *Rabbi Yochanan* himself then challenges it: *vav aufsa kesivi lach* — an idiomatic expression of dismissal, roughly meaning "did I write you a fine letter on a log?" — indicating that the answer is not satisfactory. The objection: *ei hachi detzafra nami* — if that verse downplays the immersions, then by the same logic the morning washing should also not be *me'akeiv*. Yet the morning washing clearly is *me'akeiv*. The answer that *Rabbi Yochanan*'s *drasha* provides cannot distinguish between the morning washing and the intermediate ones, and therefore it collapses under scrutiny — even though, as one might note, the morning washing is a general requirement for all *kohanim* and the verse in question specifically addresses the *Yom Kippur* context. Nevertheless, *Rabbi Yochanan* finds the answer insufficient.

### Chizkiyah's Drasha

*Chizkiyah* offers an alternative source: *vehayesa lahem chok olam lo ulezaro ledorosam* — "it shall be for them an eternal statute, for him and for his descendants throughout their generations." This verse accompanies the commands regarding the *kiyor* and the morning washing. The *drasha*: *davar hame'akeiv bizaro me'akeiv bo* — a washing that applies to and prevents validity for ordinary *kohanim* likewise prevents validity for the *kohen gadol*. Conversely, *davar she'eino me'akeiv bizaro eino me'akeiv bo* — a washing that does not apply to ordinary *kohanim* — namely the intermediate *Yom Kippur* washings, which are unique to the *kohen gadol* — does not carry the force of *ikkuv* even for him. The morning washing is thus the only one that is *me'akeiv* universally; the *Yom Kippur* intermediate washings, while prescribed, do not prevent validity if omitted.

### Rabbi Yonatan's Drasha

*Rabbi Yonatan* arrives at the same conclusion from a different verse: *verachatzu mimenu Moshe ve'Aharon uvanav* — "and Moshe and Aharon and his sons shall wash from it." The parallel structure — *Moshe ve'Aharon* together with *vanav*, his sons — teaches the same principle. A washing that is *me'akeiv* for the sons is *me'akeiv* for *Aharon*; a washing that is not operative for the sons does not carry *ikkuv* for *Aharon* either.

The Gemara then asks why *Rabbi Yonatan* did not use *Chizkiyah*'s verse, and vice versa. *Rabbi Yonatan* does not use *Chizkiyah*'s verse because *hu ledoros hu dikesivi* — that verse is simply establishing the eternal applicability of the washing requirement for all generations; it does not specifically address the question of *me'akeiv*. *Chizkiyah*, for his part, could not use *Rabbi Yonatan*'s verse because he needs it for a different teaching: that of *Rabbi Yose beRabbi Chanina*, who derives from *Moshe ve'Aharon uvanav* that any *kiyor* must be large enough for four *kohanim* to wash from it simultaneously.

## Washing Procedure

### Washing Methods

Having established that the morning washing is *me'akeiv*, the Gemara now explores the proper method of performing it. The *baraita* teaches: *maniach yado hayemanit al gabei raglo hayemanit veyado hasmolit al gabei raglo hasmolit veshocheh u'mekadesh* — the *kohen* places his right hand on his right foot and his left hand on his left foot simultaneously, bends down, and sanctifies — that is, he washes — in this position.

*Rabbi Yose beRebbi Yehuda* offers an alternative: *maniach shtei yadav zo al gabei zo ushtei raglav zo al gabei zo u'mekadesh* — he places both hands together and both feet together and then washes. The response is *amru lo hiflagta* — "you have gone too far" — meaning this posture is practically untenable; standing with one foot on top of the other is physically impossible without support.

*Rav Yosef* resolves this: a fellow *kohen* may support him so he does not topple — *chavero mesay'o*. The disagreement then, as *Abaye* clarifies, is whether *amida min hatzad* — supported standing — counts as *amida* for halachic purposes.

### Standing Requirement

This raises the underlying question: why must the washing be done standing at all? The Gemara answers from the verse *la'amod leshareit* — "to stand to serve" — and the general principle that *sherut* in the *Beis Hamikdash* must be performed standing. Since the washing of hands and feet is classified as part of the Temple service, it must be done in a standing position.

*Tosafot* extends this principle: *amida min hatzad ke'amida* — whether supported standing counts as standing — is relevant beyond the Temple context. When receiving an *aliyah* to the Torah, one should not lean on the *bimah* for support, since the Torah reading requires standing, both because of the principle derived in *Megilla* that reading Torah requires *amida*, and because, as the Yerushalmi states, just as the Torah was given with reverence and awe, so it should be read with reverence and awe. This applies as a *lechatchila* requirement; for those who are unable to stand due to illness or disability, it is not *me'akeiv*.

### Night-to-Day Work

The Gemara turns to the question of when the washing must be repeated. *Tanu rabbanan*: *kidesh yadav veraglav beyom ein tzarich lekadesh balayla* — if a *kohen* washed in the day and then continued into the night, he need not wash again simply because night has arrived. But *balayla... tzarich lekadesh beyom — divrei Rabbi* — if he was working through the night and dawn breaks, *Rabbi* holds that the new day requires a new washing.

### Rabbi vs. Rabbi Elazar

*Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* disagrees: *ein lina mo'elet bekidush yadav veraglav* — the passage of the night has no effect on the washing; as long as the *kohen* did not leave the *Beis Hamikdash* and was not distracted (*hesech hadaat*), his original washing remains valid.

A second *baraita* presents a parallel case: a *kohen* who spent the entire night placing limbs on the altar, and at daybreak continues this same activity. *Rabbi* again requires a new washing. *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* holds that since the washing was performed at the outset of the *avoda* and the *kohen* has remained continuously engaged — *afilu mikan ve'ad asarah yamim* — even for ten days without interruption — *eino tzarich lekadesh*, no fresh washing is needed.

The Gemara notes that both cases are necessary to state (*tzericha*). If only the first case had been given, one might think that *Rabbi* requires a fresh washing only when the *kohen* shifts to a new *avoda* in the morning, not when he continues the same task through the transition. And one might think *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* concedes a new washing when the *avoda* itself is new. By stating both cases, we learn that *Rabbi* requires the morning washing even in mid-task continuity, and *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* exempts even when the task changes, as long as the *kohen* never departed.

### Textual Basis

*Rabbi*'s basis: the verse *bigishtam el hamizbeach leshareit* — "upon their approach to the altar to serve." The word *bigishtam* — a new encounter — points to the fact that at daybreak, when fresh wood is placed on the altar (*maaracha chadasha*), the altar has been renewed, and this constitutes a new *gisha*, a new encounter, requiring a new washing. *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*'s basis: the verse *bevo'am el ohel moed leshareit* — "upon their entry into the Tent of Meeting to serve." Entry into the sanctuary is the operative trigger; as long as there has been no new entry, no new washing is required.

Each *amora* must account for the verse invoked by the other. *Rabbi* reads *bevo'am* as limiting the *bigishtam* principle: without *bevo'am*, one might think a new washing is required every single time the *kohen* approaches the altar during the day. *Bevo'am* tells us that presence within the *Mikdash* is the baseline, and *bigishtam* adds only the one exception — the renewed altar at dawn. *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* reads *bigishtam* as teaching a different *halacha* entirely: that the washing must be juxtaposed with the actual approach to service (*bigishtam*), which leads to the ruling discussed below.

### Garment Change Order

The verse *bigishtam* is applied by *Rav Acha brei deRav Yaakov* to a different question: *hakol modim bekiddush sheni keshehu lavush mekadesh* — all agree that the second washing of the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur* — performed after changing from one set of garments to another — must be done while already wearing the new garments, not before donning them. The derivation: *mi sheino mechusar ella gisha bilvad* — the washing must be the final act before the *gisha*, the approach to service. If the *kohen* washes before dressing, the washing is not immediately contiguous with the encounter; he must still don the garments. Therefore, one must first put on the new *begadim*, and only then wash the hands and feet — so that the sole remaining step between the washing and the *avoda* is the approach itself.

This is framed as *kiddush sheni* — the secondary washing between garment changes — and all opinions agree on this point of sequencing, whatever their broader disagreements about which washings are *me'akeiv* and which are not.

---

---

# Zevachim 20

## Washing Hands & Feet

### Source Pasuk

The discussion opens at the very end of 19b and continues onto daf 20. The source text is Shemot 30:19–20: *verachatzu Aharon u-vanav mimenu et yedeihem ve-et ragleihem* — Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet from it — *bevo'am el Ohel Moed yirchatzu mayim velo yamutu*, when they come to the Tent of Meeting they shall wash with water and not die, *o begishtam el hamizbe'ach lesharet* — or when they approach the altar to serve — *lehaktir isheh laHashem*, to offer a fire-offering to Hashem. The earlier discussion on 19b turned on the two verbs describing the kohanim's entry: *bevo'am*, when they come, and *begishtam*, when they approach — whether the obligation of hand and foot sanctification is triggered by entering the sanctuary or specifically by drawing near to perform a service.

### Exegetical Question

The *gemara* opens daf 20 by asking: *lehaktir isheh lama li*? Why does the *pasuk* need to add the phrase "to offer a fire-offering to Hashem"? The verse would have been perfectly intelligible without it. The answer is that one might have thought the entire requirement of *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim* — hand and foot sanctification — applies only to an *avodah* that is *ma'akvet kaparah*, a service that is indispensable to achieving atonement, such as *zerikah* (blood dashing) or *kabalah* (blood reception). An *avodah* that is not *ma'akvet kaparah* one might have thought exempt. Therefore the *Torah* specifies *lehaktir isheh laHashem* — even the burning of the fire-offering, which is not *ma'akvet kaparah*, requires sanctification. This is the *ka mashma lan*.

### Rabbi vs R. Elazar

The *gemara* now recalls a dispute introduced on 19b that will run through the rest of this *daf* and must be kept clearly in view. *Rabbi* — Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi — holds that the water with which a kohen sanctifies his hands and feet becomes *nifsal be-linah*, invalidated by overnight passage. If a night passes, the kohen must sanctify again before resuming service. *Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon*, by contrast, holds that once a kohen has sanctified his hands and feet and entered the *mikdash*, he may continue serving for even ten consecutive days without repeat sanctification — the overnight does not disqualify. This dispute will animate everything that follows: the question of the *kiyor* water, the resolution attributed to Rabbi Yochanan, and the debate between Abaye and Rava over that resolution's proper attribution.

---

## Kiyor Overnight

### Ilfa's Question

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel, he taught in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Ilfa had posed a dilemma: *ledivrei ha'omer ein linah mo'elet be-kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim, mei kiyor mahu she-yifsalu* — according to the one who says that *linah* does not invalidate *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim*, what is the law concerning water left overnight in the *kiyor*? Does that water become *pasul*, disqualified?

### First Explanation

The first line of analysis is as follows: water in the *kiyor* is there *lekiddush yadayim ve-raglayim*. But once that sanctification has been performed, there is no more water on the hands and feet — the hands and feet themselves have no residual water that could become *pasul be-linah*. Since there is nothing left on the kohen's person to be disqualified, perhaps *linah* does not apply. The *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim gufeih lo pasal be-linah* — the sanctification itself, considered in isolation, is not subject to overnight disqualification.

### Alternative View

The alternative position is that the *kiyor* has the status of a *kli sharet* — a service vessel — and any water consecrated within a service vessel that remains overnight is subject to overnight invalidation on those grounds. *Kevan dekadosh kadosh hu be-khli sharet mipsali*: because it has been sanctified within a service vessel, the water is disqualified when morning comes after a night.

### Ravin's Teaching

A separate tradition arrives when Ravin comes from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel. He reports in the name of Rabbi Yirmiyah, in the name of Rav Ami, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, that Ilfa ultimately resolved his own dilemma: *kemachloket be-zo kach machloket be-zo* — just as we have the dispute concerning hand and foot sanctification between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon, so too the same dispute applies to the question of the *kiyor* water. Rabbi holds that the water left overnight in the *kiyor* is *pasul*, and Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon holds it is not disqualified.

### Objection Raised

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna objects before Rabbi Yochanan: you are answering the first question by introducing a second question that is itself unresolved. *Ata omer ken*? Is this really your intended resolution? The dilemma about the *kiyor* water remains exactly as difficult as the original question about *linah* in hand and foot sanctification.

### Rav Assi Teaching

The *gemara* then presents another teaching. Rav Assi, citing Rabbi Yochanan who heard it from Ilfa himself, rules: *kiyor shelo shik'o ba-erev, mekadesh mimenu la-avodat layla, u-lemachar eino mekadesh* — a *kiyor* that was not lowered into the spring overnight may nonetheless be used to sanctify hands and feet for night service, but the following morning the water in it is no longer valid for sanctification. The practice alluded to here is one we will encounter shortly: submerging the *kiyor* into a spring at night so that its water mingles with fresh water, thereby avoiding overnight disqualification.

### Rejection

The *gemara* rejects this teaching as a sufficient resolution of the underlying question. The ruling that *lemachar eino mekadesh* — the next morning the *kiyor* cannot be used — does not tell us why. Is it because the water remaining overnight in the *kiyor* is *pasul be-linah*? Or is it because the *kiyor* that was not lowered simply no longer needs sanctification the next day? *Ve-la pasht lan* — we have not received an answer — and the *gemara* dismisses this attempted proof: we did not receive resolution, and you think this constitutes one?

---

## Ben Kattin's Device

### Twelve Spigots

At this point the *gemara* introduces a *ta shema* drawn from a historical detail about the Temple. Ben Kattin, who served as *kohen gadol*, redesigned the *kiyor* from a vessel with two spigots to one with twelve — *Ben Kattin asa shenaim asar dad la-kiyor* — so that twelve kohanim could sanctify their hands and feet simultaneously rather than waiting in line.

### Pulley System

More significantly for our discussion, Ben Kattin also created a pulley mechanism — *mukhni* — that allowed the *kiyor* to be lowered each evening into the spring beneath it, so that its water would mingle with the fresh spring water. The purpose was explicit: *shelo yehu meimav nifsalim be-linah* — so that the water of the *kiyor* would not become *pasul* through overnight standing. This device addressed a problem that had apparently gone without a technical solution for the entire period of the *Mishkan* and much of the *Bayit Rishon*.

### Attribution Question

The *gemara* now asks: according to whom was this practice instituted? *Mai lav Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon?* One might have thought that since Ben Kattin went to the trouble of lowering the *kiyor*, he must have been concerned that the water would otherwise become *pasul* — which would suggest he followed the view of Rabbi, not Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon. Or one might argue the opposite: perhaps he follows Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *linah* does not disqualify, and the lowering was done for some other reason or as an added stringency.

### Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes: *lo, Rabbi hi* — this practice reflects the position of Rabbi, who holds that overnight does disqualify the water, and the *mukhni* was therefore constructed to prevent that disqualification. However, the *gemara* then notes that the reasoning can be inverted: one could have assumed from the earlier clause that this is according to Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon, and inferred the same for the later clause. Neither inference constitutes definitive proof. The question remains open on this front, and the *gemara* moves to a different avenue of discussion.

---

## Temple Geography

### Bull's Position

The *gemara* transitions to a distinct but related topic arising from the Yom Kippur service. The *par* — the bull brought by the *kohen gadol* on Yom Kippur — stood between the *ulam* (the entrance hall) and the *mizbe'ach*, with its head to the south and its face to the west, while the *kohen* stood to its east facing west. The reason the bull's body ran north-south rather than east-west is that if it faced east, this would be considered *lo kavod* — undignified — since it would be oriented toward the entrance through which the populace entered.

### Definition Tzafon

The positioning of the *par* in this location raises the broader question: what is *tzafon* — the "north" — for purposes of the laws requiring that *kodshei kodashim* (offerings of the highest sanctity) be slaughtered in the northern section of the *azarah*? The north is clearly designated as such, but its precise boundaries — how far the designation extends — is a matter of dispute. A *baraita* frames the question: *eizehu tzafon?*

### Tannaitic Dispute

Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda defines *tzafon* as extending from the northern wall of the *mizbe'ach* to the northern wall of the *azarah*, and spanning the full width of the *mizbe'ach* — *mi-kir mizbe'ach tzefoni ve-ad kotel azarah tzefoni u-keneged kol ha-mizbe'ach kulo*. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon extends this definition to include also the area between the *ulam* and the *mizbe'ach* — *af bein ha-ulam ve-la-mizbe'ach*. Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) extends it further still to include the area where the kohanim walk and the area where Israelites stand.

The *gemara* had initially suggested that the *mishna* describing the *par*'s position could serve as proof that the law follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon specifically, since the space between the *ulam* and the *mizbe'ach* is included in his definition of *tzafon* but not in Rabbi Yossi bar Rabbi Yehuda's. However, this proof collapses: since Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi's definition is the broadest of all, the area that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon designates as *tzafon* is entirely subsumed within the area that Rabbi designates as *tzafon*. Thus the *mishna* is equally consistent with Rabbi's position.

### Kohen Gadol Fatigue

A second approach is attempted: if the position of the *par* between the *ulam* and the *mizbe'ach* reflects Rabbi's expansive definition of *tzafon*, one might ask why the bull is not simply positioned closer to the entrance gate, which would also qualify as *tzafon* under Rabbi's view, and would spare the *kohen gadol* the exertion of walking further into the *azarah*. The *gemara* answers that the placement of the *par* near the *ulam* rather than at the entrance is not a legal ruling about what constitutes *tzafon* — it is a practical accommodation to the physical state of the *kohen gadol*. On Yom Kippur the *kohen gadol* is fasting, running repeatedly between different areas of the *mikdash*, and has been awake all night. The bull is positioned close to where he is working so as to reduce his burden. *Mishum chulsha de-kohen gadol* — because of the weakness of the *kohen gadol* — the bull is brought to him, not as a legal statement about the boundaries of *tzafon*. This resolves neither the question of the *kiyor* water nor the dispute about *tzafon*'s precise extent, and the *gemara* moves on.

---

## Terumat HaDeshen

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *kiddesh yadav ve-raglav le-terumat ha-deshen, lemachar eino tzarich le-kaddesh, she-kevar kiddesh mi-techilat avodah* — a kohen who sanctified his hands and feet for the *terumat ha-deshen*, the removal of the ash from the altar, does not need to re-sanctify the following day, because he already sanctified at the beginning of the service.

*Terumat ha-deshen* — the removal of the ashes — is the first service of each morning, performed by a kohen who comes before dawn and clears the residue of the overnight burnt offerings from the altar. It is the opening act of *Parashat Tzav*, and it carries a certain symbolic weight: before the new day's service can begin, the remnants of the previous day must be cleared. That this task — taking out, in a manner of speaking, what remains — should fall to a kohen and be treated as sacred service says something important about how even the clearing away of what is finished is elevated within the *mikdash*.

The question is: *lema'an mi* — according to whose opinion is Rabbi Yochanan making this ruling? The challenge is immediate. If this statement is according to Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a kohen need not re-sanctify even after ten days, then of course there is no need to sanctify the next day — that is obvious and requires no special ruling. The very modesty of Rabbi Yochanan's claim — that one need not sanctify again merely the *next day* — implies a more restrictive background position.

### Abaye's View

Abaye resolves the tension by saying that Rabbi Yochanan is following the view of Rabbi — who holds that *linah* does disqualify — but that Rabbi agrees *linah de-rabanan hi*: the overnight disqualification of *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim* is rabbinic in nature. And Rabbi concedes one exception: *mi-kri'at ha-gever ve-ad tzafra lo pasla linah* — from the *kri'at ha-gever* (the pre-dawn call, whether by rooster or appointed caller) until the break of dawn, the *linah* does not disqualify. A kohen who sanctified during this liminal period before dawn may continue to perform service into the following day, because that brief transitional interval does not constitute the kind of overnight separation that triggers the rabbinic disqualification. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, then, is addressed to a kohen who sanctified during that window: he does not need to sanctify again when the full day begins.

### Rava's View

Rava offers a competing interpretation. He maintains that Rabbi Yochanan's statement does follow Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon — but only in part. Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon's lenient view, says Rava, was acknowledged by Rabbi Yochanan for *techilat avodah* — the beginning of the service — but not for *sof avodah*, the end or continuation of the service. This is a striking position: Rabbi Yochanan, an *amora*, is essentially accepting Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon's ruling for one phase of service while declining to extend it to another.

### Chronology Problem

This raises a methodological puzzle that deserves explicit attention. Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, the redactor of the *Mishnah*, is roughly contemporaneous with the late *Tannaim* and flourished around 200 of the common era. Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon is a *Tanna* of the same period or somewhat earlier. Rabbi Yochanan, who studies and teaches in Tiberias, belongs to the first generation of *Amoraim*, working approximately 250–300 CE. Abaye and Rava belong to a later Babylonian generation, around 300–400. The *Amoraim* as a matter of general principle do not dispute *Tannaim* directly — they interpret, harmonize, and explain, but they do not simply overrule.

Yet Rava's reading of Rabbi Yochanan places him in a position of accepting one dimension of Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon's ruling while disagreeing with another. Moreover, the Babylonian *Amoraim* (Abaye and Rava) are attempting to determine what an earlier Israeli *Amora* (Rabbi Yochanan) meant when addressing a ruling of still-earlier Israeli *Tannaim* (Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon). The entire conversation reflects the urgency with which the later authorities felt pressed to resolve these laws — as though the *mikdash* might be rebuilt at any moment and clarity was essential.

---

## Tamid Mishna

### Scene Description

The *gemara* next introduces a *Mishnah* from Masechet Tamid. The brethren kohanim — *echav ha-kohanim* — see the kohen who has descended from the altar after performing the *terumat ha-deshen*. Seeing this is a signal that the new day has begun. *Hem ratzu u-va'u miharu ve-kidshu yedeihem ve-ragleihem min ha-kiyor* — they run and come quickly and sanctify their hands and feet from the *kiyor*. The image is vivid: kohanim hurrying to the laver at the moment the day's service is inaugurated.

### Interpretive Ambiguity

The question is what this *Mishnah* proves. The kohanim rush to sanctify — which implies they had not yet done so, or that the overnight had intervened and they must begin again. On the face of it, this seems to support Rabbi's position that overnight passage requires re-sanctification. But the *gemara* pauses: is that the only reading?

### New Kohanim

The *gemara* resolves: *le-olam ke-Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon, ve-hacha be-mai askinan? Be-Kohanei chadati* — in truth this *Mishnah* may be following the view of Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon, because the kohanim who are running to sanctify are entirely new kohanim — *kohanei chadashim* — who have never sanctified their hands and feet before and are coming to the *mikdash* for the first time. Even Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon agrees that a kohen sanctifying for the first time must do so *bevo'am*, when they enter. These are not kohanim who sanctified yesterday and need to decide whether to repeat — these are kohanim who have never yet sanctified for this service at all.

### Unresolved

The result is that this *Mishnah* proves nothing decisive for either side of the dispute. It is consistent with Rabbi's position and equally consistent with Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon's position. The *gemara* has not moved any closer to resolution, and both views remain viable.

---

## Yetziah Question

### Core Question

The *gemara* now turns to a new and related question: *ibayya lehu, yetziah mahu she-to'il be-kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim?* — what is the legal effect of *yetziah*, leaving the *azarah*, on prior sanctification of hands and feet? A kohen who has sanctified his hands and feet inside the temple and then exits — does his sanctification remain valid when he returns, or is it nullified?

A brief preliminary note is important here. From *de-oraita* there is no concept of *tumat yadayim* — partial impurity affecting only the hands. A person is either entirely *tamei* or entirely *tahor*. The notion that hands can be independently impure is a rabbinic enactment — *takanat Chachamim* — that the Sages applied in the context of kohanim who handled *piggul* (sacrifices with invalid intent) or *notar* (leftover sacrifices), which the Rabbis declared to render hands *tamei*. It is against this backdrop that the entire system of *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim* is being discussed.

### Two Approaches

Two frameworks are proposed for understanding whether *yetziah* disqualifies prior sanctification. The first is that the problem, if there is one, is *prishut* — the physical separation itself: the kohen has left the domain of sanctified service, and the departure constitutes a break. The second is that the issue is *hasachat ha-da'at* — a distraction or diversion of attention: if the kohen leaves but only to briefly retrieve something and immediately return, his mind (*da'at*) remains focused on his service and he has not truly disengaged. *Keivan de-veyado lachzor lo mesiach* — since it is within his power to return, his attention has not been diverted.

### Ta Shema 1

The *gemara* attempts to resolve the question with a *ta shema*: if a kohen sanctified his hands and feet and then became *tamei*, he immerses and does not need to re-sanctify — and if his hands and feet *left* (exited), they remain in their sanctified state. This seems to suggest that exiting does not nullify sanctification.

### Rejection 1

The *gemara* immediately dismisses this: *yatza'u yadav la ka miba'i lan, ki ka miba'i lan yatza kol gufo* — we were not asking about a kohen who merely extended his hands outside while his body remained within the *azarah*. That would be a trivial case. The question concerns a kohen whose entire body left the temple. This source does not address that situation.

### Ta Shema 2

A second *ta shema* is offered: if a kohen sanctifies his hands and feet *outside* the temple using a *kli sharet*, or inside using a *kli chol* (a non-sacred vessel), or by immersing in cave water, his service is *pasul*. The implication drawn is: *ta'ama de-kiddesh be-khli sharet ba-chutz, ha kiddesh bi-fnim ve-yatza, avodato kesherah* — the reason the first case is *pasul* is precisely that he sanctified outside; but if he had sanctified properly inside and then exited, the service would be valid.

### Rejection 2

The *gemara* rejects this as well: *dilma kiddesh be-khli sharet ba-chutz heichi dami* — perhaps the case of sanctifying outside refers to someone who extended his hands out the wall and sanctified in that position, with his hands outside but his body inside. That too would be *pasul*, and from that we might infer that if the hands left but the body remained it is *kasher*. But the case of the entire body exiting is still unaddressed.

### Ta Shema 3

Rav Zvid presents to Rav Pappa a third *ta shema*: *yatza chutz le-mechizat chomat ha-azarah, im lishhot ta'un tevilah, im le-fi sha'ah ta'un kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim* — if a kohen left outside the wall of the *azarah* for a significant stay (*lishhot*), he requires full immersion; if for just a brief moment (*le-fi sha'ah*), he requires only *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim*. This at least implies that a brief exit does not eliminate prior sanctification entirely — otherwise full immersion would be required in all cases.

### Rejection 3

Rav Pappa rejects this as well: *hacha be-mai askinan? Ke-gon she-yatza le-hasech raglav u-le-hatil mayim* — this source is dealing with a kohen who left the temple to use the bathroom. That is a specific case with its own rules, and it is in fact already taught in Yoma: *kol ha-mesi'ach raglav ta'un tevilah, ve-khol ha-matil mayim ta'un kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim* — one who goes to relieve himself completely requires immersion; one who urinates requires *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim*. The *braita* cited by Rav Zvid is simply restating and elaborating on this principle — *tani ve-hadar mefaresh* — and teaches nothing about the general case of a kohen who exits the *azarah* for an ordinary reason.

### Ta Shema 4

A fourth *ta shema* is introduced from the service of the *Para Aduma* — the red heifer — whose ritual takes place entirely outside the temple. Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef rules that the kohen performing the *Para Aduma* service sanctifies his hands and feet inside the temple using a *kli sharet* and then exits to perform the service outside. Rabbi Yochanan, however, rules more leniently: the kohen may sanctify his hands and feet even outside the temple, even with a *kli chol*, and even with a *mkida shel cheres* — an earthenware vessel — that would ordinarily be invalid.

### Pappa Analysis

Rav Pappa addresses this case: *shani Para, ho'il ve-khol ma'aseha ba-chutz, lo pasla bi-yetziah* — the *Para Aduma* is different, because the entire service takes place outside the *azarah*. Since the *avodah* itself is conducted outside, the act of exiting cannot disqualify the sanctification — there would be nothing left to perform if it did. This is a special case and cannot serve as a general proof about a kohen who exits during an otherwise interior service.

However, this very reasoning generates a counterquestion: *iy hachi, lama li de-mekadesh?* — if the service is entirely outside and exiting does not disqualify, why does the kohen need to perform *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim* at all for the *Para Aduma* service? The *gemara* answers: it is done *ke-eyn avodat pnim* — to mirror and approximate, as closely as possible, the procedures of the interior temple service. Even when the *avodah* takes place outside, the requirements of interior service are maintained where feasible.

### Suspended

Notwithstanding these four attempted proofs, the question of *yetziah* and its effect on prior *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim* remains entirely unresolved. Each *ta shema* has been dismissed without providing a definitive answer to the central dilemma — whether it is the physical act of separation from the *azarah* that matters, or whether it is *hasachat ha-da'at*, the diversion of the kohen's attention and intention, that is the operative factor. The *gemara* leaves the question suspended for continued study.

---

---

# Zevachim 21

## Tumah & Kiddush

### Kohen Becomes Tamei

The Gemara opens a new question within the broader framework of *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* — the hand and foot washing that *kohanim* must perform before the *avodah*. The *iba'ya lehu* asks: *tumah mahu she-to'il kiddush yadayim v'raglayim?* — if a *kohen* who has already washed his hands and feet becomes *tamei* in the course of the *avodah*, does the purification process he must undergo — immersing in a *mikvah* — count as a substitute for *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*, or must he wash his hands and feet again separately afterward?

The question is framed in a somewhat unusual way, which Rashi's explanation helps clarify. The Gemara presents two sides: *im timtzei lomar yetziah la pasla d'gavra chazi* — if leaving the *beis hamikdash* does not disqualify one's prior *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*, this is because the *kohen* who has left is still a *gavra chazi*, a person who remains fit to perform the *avodah*. His departure does not strip him of his capacity. But in our case, where the *kohen* has become *tamei*, he is entirely removed from the ability to perform the *avodah*, and thus one might argue that he has experienced a heightened form of *hesach hadaat* — a loss of mindful focus — since he is no longer in a state of readiness to serve.

### Hesach Hadaat

The question therefore turns on what generates *hesach hadaat*. Is it the sheer duration of the interruption, or is it the qualitative character of the interruption — specifically, whether the person's circumstances are such that he is no longer oriented toward performing the *avodah*? The counter-argument is *odilma keivan d'hadar chazi daklei v'lo masech datei* — perhaps the very fact that he can go to the *mikvah* and become *tahor* again means that he never fully disengages, and so the immersion does not constitute a disqualifying interruption requiring a new *kiddush*.

The difficulty with the question, however, is that if a *kohen* becomes *tamei* in his entire body — as opposed to merely his hands — he normally requires not only immersion but also *he'erev shemesh*, waiting until sunset, before achieving full *taharah*. During that intervening period he is a *tevul yom*, an intermediate status that is not fully *tahor*. This extended waiting period would seem to compound the concern about *hesach hadaat*, and it is this objection that naturally arises against the question.

### Hands Alone Tamei

The Gemara addresses a simpler case first. The *braita* states: *kidesh yadav v'raglav v'nitma* — if a *kohen* washed his hands and feet and then his hands became *tamei* (the Rabbis recognize that hands can become *tamei* through contact with certain things that would not render the whole body impure), *matbilan v'ein tzarich lekadesh* — he may immerse his hands in a *mikvah* and does not need to wash them again from the *kiyor*. The Gemara immediately clarifies: *nitma'u yadav lo miba'ya lan; ki miba'ya lan nitma kol gufo* — the case of hands alone becoming *tamei* is not the genuine question, since it is readily resolved by simple immersion of the hands. That case does not require the prolonged waiting that would generate serious *hesach hadaat* concerns. The real question is *nitma kol gufo* — where the person's entire body has become *tamei*.

### Tumah Near Sunset

Once the question is restricted to whole-body *tumah*, the objection arises that the *kohen* will be required to wait for *he'erev shemesh*, which would seem to guarantee an extended interruption. The Gemara therefore narrows the question further: *kegon de-itmei samuch li-shki'at ha-chamah* — the case under discussion is specifically one where the *kohen* became *tamei* shortly before sunset, went quickly to the *mikvah*, and the sun then set, rendering him fully *tahor* — potentially within minutes. In such a scenario, does the brief interlude of *tumah* constitute sufficient *hesach hadaat* to require a renewed *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*, or not? With the question properly framed, the Gemara has not yet provided an answer — it has only clarified the scope.

## Para Aduma

### Para Washing Location

The Gemara next attempts to resolve the open question by adducing a *braita* about *Para Aduma*, the red heifer. The *para aduma* represents a paradigmatic halachic borderline case: it bears many hallmarks of the *avodah* — it must be performed by a *kohen*, it requires *bigdei kehunah*, it demands *taharah* — yet it is performed outside the *beis hamikdash* and is not technically a *korban*. Its hybrid status means it is frequently cited as a comparison and just as frequently rejected as one, since its rules are so singular that lessons drawn from it are often inapplicable elsewhere.

*Rabbi Chiya berabbi Yosef* states that for the *para aduma*, a *kohen* may perform *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* using a *kli sharet* inside the *beis hamikdash* and then leave to perform the *para aduma* on *Har HaZeisim* — and the intervening time and distance are not considered a disqualifying interruption.

### Rabbi Yochanan's View

*Rabbi Yochanan* goes further: *afilu bachutz* — one may even wash his hands outside the *beis hamikdash*, *va-afilu b'kli chol* — even using an ordinary vessel rather than a *kli sharet*, *va-afilu b'makeira shel cheres* — even a low-grade earthenware basin. This is because the *para aduma* is not truly an *avodah*, and the act of hand washing preparatory to it is correspondingly less formal in its requirements. The implication seems to address the timing concern as well: if one may wash in an entirely ordinary vessel outside the Temple, time elapsed between washing and performance would seem not to be the issue.

### Tzadukim Dispute

At this point a striking *mishnah* from *Masechet Para* is introduced — one that has become a flashpoint in historical and polemical discourse. *Metammim hayu ha-kohen ha-soref et ha-parah* — the Rabbis would deliberately render *tamei* the *kohen* who was about to burn the *para aduma*, and then immediately immerse him in a *mikvah*, *lehotzi milibam shel Tzadukim* — in order to counter the position of the *Tzadukim*. The *Tzadukim* held that the *para aduma* must be performed at the highest possible level of *taharah*, and that a *tevul yom* — one who has immersed but not yet waited for sunset — is insufficiently *tahor* to perform it. The *Perushim* disputed this: a *tevul yom* is *tahor* enough for *para aduma*. To demonstrate this publicly, the Rabbis would make the *kohen* *tamei*, take him to the *mikvah*, and have him perform the burning while he was still in the status of *tevul yom*.

This is itself a remarkable practice, given the extraordinary stringencies surrounding *para aduma* in other respects: the extension of the normal gradations of *tumah* to fifth and even further degrees of remove, the care taken with the children who drew the water — who were born and raised on special platforms in Jerusalem to ensure they had never contracted *tumah* — the requirement for a double bridge to Har HaZeisim. All of this stringency coexisted with the deliberate use of a *tevul yom* for the burning, and that is precisely the *Perushim*'s point: *tevul yom* is a categorically different status, and *para aduma* is categorically different from the regular *avodah*.

### Why Washing Needed

From the above *mishnah*, the Gemara attempts to derive that *tumah* is not an interruption for *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*: *shema mina lo paslah bah tumah* — since the *kohen* was made *tamei* and then immersed, and yet performed the *para aduma* without a new *kiddush*, apparently the immersion sufficed and *tumah* did not invalidate the prior washing. But the Gemara immediately rejects this proof: *shani para ho'il ve-tevul yom lo pasil bah* — the *para aduma* is different, since a *tevul yom* is valid for it; one cannot draw ordinary conclusions from its rules. The retort is then raised: if *para aduma* is so anomalous, why is *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* required for it at all? The answer: *ke-ein avodah bayinan* — one must perform it in the manner of the *avodah*, even if it is not the *avodah* in the full sense. The *para aduma* walks the line — it resembles the *avodah* in some respects and not in others. The attempted proof from *para aduma* fails, and the original question remains unresolved.

## Kiyor Immersion

### Dipping Question

A new question is introduced: *mahu le-kadesh yadav ve-raglav be-kiyor* — may a *kohen* fulfill the requirement of *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* by dipping his hands and feet into the *kiyor* rather than having water poured from it over them? Rashi clarifies that without this precision, the question would not even arise. The Torah uses the expression *mimenu* in the context of *ve-rachatzu yadeihem ve-ragleihem* — "from it" — which may imply washing *from* the *kiyor* rather than immersing *into* it. The Gemara considers whether *velo betocho* — "and not inside it" — can be derived from *mimenu*, or whether *afilu betocho* — even immersing into the *kiyor* itself — might be permitted.

### Mei Me'arah Proof

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* attempts to resolve this by citing a *braita*: *o she-taval be-mei me'arah ve-avad avodato psulah* — if a *kohen* immersed in cave water (*mei me'arah*), essentially a *mikvah*, and then performed the *avodah*, the *avodah* is *pesulah*. Since the water of the *kiyor* resembles *mei me'arah* in being stationary — *ha-kiyor dumya de-mei me'arah* — perhaps immersing into it would similarly be invalid, and only having water poured from it would work. This would suggest that dipping hands and feet into the *kiyor* is prohibited.

### Exclusion Logic

The Gemara rejects this proof. The *braita* about *mei me'arah* was not written to exclude dipping in the *kiyor*; it was written to exclude something else entirely: *shelo tomar kol gufo tovel bahen yado ve-raglo lo kol sheken* — one might have thought that since a person immerses his whole body in a *mikvah* to achieve *taharah*, surely immersing only hands and feet would achieve *kiddush* for the *avodah*. The *braita* teaches that this is not so — immersion in a *mikvah*, even of the whole body, does not substitute for the formal *kiddush* from the *kiyor*, which must be performed with a *kli sharet*, in the *beis hamikdash*, with the proper intention. The *braita* therefore excludes dipping hands and feet into a *mikvah* — but it does not thereby settle the question of whether dipping hands and feet into the *kiyor* itself might be valid, since the *kiyor* is the designated vessel. The attempted proof of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak is not dispositive, and the question remains open.

## Kiyor Disqualification

### Rav Chiya's View

The Gemara turns to a related question: at what point does the water remaining in the *kiyor* become *pasul* for use the next day? The *kiyor* was equipped with a mechanism — a wooden crank or winch — that allowed it to be submerged into an underground cistern at night, keeping the water from becoming *pasul* through *lina* (overnight exposure). *Rav Chiya bar Yosef* offers a graduated rule: *mei kiyor nifsalin le-matirin ke-matirin, le-eivarim ke-eivarim*. The water becomes *pasul* in parallel with the *avodah* for which it is used. For *matirin* — the daytime *avodot* such as the *korbanot* that exempt a person from obligation — the water becomes *pasul* when those *avodot* become *pasul*, namely at sunset. For *eivarim* — the overnight burning of fats and limbs on the *mizbeach* — the water becomes *pasul* at sunrise. Rav Chiya bar Yosef thus has two distinct disqualification times: sunset for day-service, and sunrise for night-service.

### Rav Chisda's View

*Rav Chisda* disagrees: *af le-matirin ein nifsalin ela be-amud ha-shachar ke-eivarim* — even for the daytime *avodot*, the *kiyor* water is not disqualified until dawn. There is thus only one disqualification time for Rav Chisda: sunrise, regardless of which *avodah* the water is intended to facilitate.

### Rabbi Yochanan Reconciled

*Rabbi Yochanan* is cited with a statement that initially appears to posit a third, stricter position: *kiyor keivan she-shik'u shuv ein ma'alehu* — once the *kiyor* has been submerged in the evening, one may not raise it again until the next morning. This seems to imply that if the *kiyor* were raised during the night, the water would be disqualified — suggesting a disqualification time earlier than sunrise, and perhaps even applying to night-time *avodot*.

However, the Gemara then cites a second statement of Rabbi Yochanan, transmitted by *Rabbi Assi* in the name of *Ilfa*: *kiyor she-lo shika'o me-etmol, mikadesh mimenu la-avodat laila* — if they did not submerge the *kiyor* on the previous evening, one may still wash from it during the night. *U-le-machar eino mikadesh* — but once it becomes day, it is no longer valid. This second version places disqualification at sunrise, apparently agreeing with Rav Chisda rather than introducing a stricter position.

To resolve the tension between Rabbi Yochanan's two statements, the Gemara considers whether his ruling about not raising the *kiyor* once it has been submerged refers specifically to *avodat yom* — the daytime service — rather than to *avodat laila*. If the *kiyor* was put away for the night and one seeks to raise it for a nighttime *avodah*, perhaps that is not permitted for the daytime service afterward, but it would still be usable for night-service. Under this reading, Rabbi Yochanan would coincide with *Rav Chiya bar Yosef*: different times for day and night *avodot*. But if so, what distinguishes Rabbi Yochanan from Rav Chiya bar Yosef?

### Gezeirat Shikua Debate

The Gemara resolves this: *ika beiniyahu gezeirat shikua* — the real disagreement between Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Chisda is not about the practical consequence of leaving the water out overnight, but about whether there was a positive mandate — *gezeirat shikua* — requiring the *kiyor* to be submerged each evening. Rabbi Yochanan holds that there was such a mandatory requirement, independently of whatever halachic consequence might follow from leaving it out. Rav Chisda holds that there was no such formal decree; if the *kiyor* was left out and the water remained valid until sunrise, no obligation was violated by not submerging it.

A further complication arises from Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that if one washed his hands in preparation for *trumat ha-deshen* — the removal of ash from the altar that takes place before dawn — he need not wash again later, *she-kvar kidesh mi-techilat avodah*, since his initial washing before the previous day's *avodah* carries forward. This fits well with the opinion of *Rava*, who holds the *halacha* like *Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon* — that *ein layla ela be-kiddush*, nightfall alone does not invalidate a prior *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*, and so a washing performed the previous afternoon remains in effect through the night. But it creates a difficulty for *Abaye*, who rules like *Rabbi* — that sunset *does* constitute an interruption, requiring a new *kiddush* at the start of the night. Under Abaye's view, how could one perform *trumat ha-deshen* on the basis of a *kiddush* from the prior afternoon? The Gemara acknowledges this difficulty — *kashya d'Rabbi ad-Rabbi* — and considers whether the cases can be distinguished based on whether the *kiyor* was submerged, removed, and submerged again. Ultimately, the Gemara concludes that the underlying debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Chisda reduces to the question of *mitzvat shiku'a* — whether the nightly submersion was a formal obligation or merely a practical precaution against forgetting — and is connected to the broader *machlokes* between Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi regarding whether nighttime serves as an interruption for *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*.

## Kiyor Timing & Crank

### Crank Signal

The Gemara cites a *mishnah* from *Tamid* bearing on the timing of when the *kiyor* was raised and lowered. The *mishnah* states: *lo hayu ro'in oto ve-lo shom'im et kolo ad she-shom'im kol shel etz she-asa Ben Katin mochni la-kiyor* — they would not see it or hear it until they heard the sound of the wooden crank that *Ben Katin* had fashioned for the *kiyor*. Upon hearing that sound, the *kohanim* would say: the time has come for *kiddush yadayim ve-raglayim min ha-kiyor*.

### Raising vs. Submerging

The Gemara asks: *mai lav de-maslek lei* — does this *mishnah* refer to the moment when they were raising the *kiyor* (taking it out of the water in the morning), or *de-mishkale* — when they were submerging it (lowering it into the water in the evening)? On the plain reading of the *mishnah*, it sounds like a morning event: people hear the crank sound and know it is time to come wash. But the Gemara attempts to read it as an evening event, in order to establish that the proper time for *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* associated with the *kiyor* is at or around sunset.

The difficulty with reading it as submersion is: *mi mishtama kalei?* — if they are simply lowering the *kiyor*, why would the crank make a sound? Lowering would be aided by gravity, and could be accomplished without the noisy effort of the winch. The Gemara responds: *meshkale be-gilgala* — they would in fact lower it using the wheel, so it did produce sound. An alternative formulation clarifies: *demishkale be-chumratei ki heichi de-lishtama kalei* — they would lower it using the crank mechanism specifically so that the sound would be audible, and people would take note.

### Double Announcement

One might ask why such a sound signal was necessary at all, given that the *beis hamikdash* had *Gavini*, the official town crier, who would announce events and signal to the *kohanim* what time it was. The Gemara's answer is elegant: *bei terei hekeirei havu avdei* — they would make a double announcement. The crank sound and the human proclamation served as two independent signals so that no one would miss the notification — *de-shama me-hai atu, de-shama me-hai atu* — whoever heard one signal would come, and whoever heard the other would also come. The conclusion is that the *mishnah* in *Tamid* is understood as describing the evening submersion of the *kiyor*, and the crank sound together with the crier's announcement jointly marked the time of *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* for the night-service.
