# Zevachim 22

## Kiyor Capacity

### Minimum Basin Size

The *gemara* opens with a *gufa* — returning to an earlier statement to examine it closely. The passage in question appears four lines from the bottom of 21b, where Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina rules: *kol kiyor she'ein bo kidei lekadesh arba kohanim mimenu ein mikadshin bo* — any basin that does not contain sufficient water for four *kohanim* to wash their hands cannot be used for *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*. The proof text is the *pasuk*: *v'rachatzu mimenu Moshe v'Aharon u'vanav* — Moshe, Aharon, and his sons washed from it. Though in practice they did not all serve simultaneously, the verse is read to indicate that the basin must be capable of accommodating four *kohanim* at once.

It is worth noting the phrasing *kol kiyor* — "any basin." Since there was only one *kiyor* in the *Beis HaMikdash*, the formulation implies a general principle: whether describing the historical requirement of that vessel or establishing criteria for any future one, the minimum capacity is four *kohanim*. This also raises an immediate question: since a *kli shares* may also be used for the washing, does that requirement apply there as well? That question will unfold shortly.

### Kli Shares Alternative

The *gemara* immediately raises a *meitivei*: we have been taught that *kol hakelim mikadshin, bein sheyeish bahem revi'is bein she'ein bahem revi'is, u'vilvad sheyehu kli shares* — all vessels may be used for *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*, whether they contain a *revi'is* or not, provided they are *kli shares*. This is quite striking. We already know that the washing must be performed on the Temple grounds with a sanctified service vessel, but here the *braisa* states explicitly that the vessel's capacity is irrelevant — it may even hold less than a *revi'is*. Rashi notes that even for ordinary hand-washing performed today for *tumah* purposes, a *revi'is* is required. That a vessel holding less than that could be sufficient for the Temple's *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* is genuinely surprising. And of course it appears to contradict the requirement that the basin hold enough for four *kohanim*.

### Rashi's Kodach View

Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves the tension: *bikode'ach b'tocho* — the case is one where a hole is carved into the basin. According to Rashi, the procedure is as follows: one takes a large basin containing four *log* of water, carves a hole in its side, and inserts the *kli shares* into that opening. The *kli shares* then functions essentially as a spout — water flows from the basin, through the *kli*, and onto the hands of the *kohanim*. The vessel itself may be tiny, but because it draws from a source containing the requisite quantity, the washing is valid.

Admittedly, this construction is conceptually unusual. If the water is flowing from the basin through the *kli* like a spout, one might argue that the *kohen* is effectively washing from the basin, not the *kli*. But that, Rashi seems to suggest, is precisely the *chiddush*: the sanctified status of the *kli* remains conceptually relevant even in this configuration. Because the water emerges through the *kli*, one is considered to be washing from the *kli* — and since four *kohanim* could in principle wash from this arrangement given the water source behind it, the requirement is satisfied.

### Tosafos on Water Status

Tosafos reads the case very differently. In their comments on *kode'ach m'tocho* (the third Tosafos on the page), they explain that *kode'ach* does not mean literally carving a hole in the basin. Rather, it means that one removes water *from* the basin — one takes a smaller vessel, dips it into the larger basin, and then washes one's hands from that smaller vessel. There is no physical alteration of the basin; it is simply a matter of sourcing.

Under Tosafos's reading, the key criterion is not the vessel's capacity but the status of the water it contains. Water drawn from a source that held the requisite amount for four *kohanim* carries a kind of valid status with it. It is not the *kiyor* itself that must hold the full quantity in every configuration — rather, the water must originate from something that held the correct amount, whether that is the *kiyor* proper or some other sanctified vessel.

This also changes how Tosafos reads the *gemara*'s challenge from the word *mimenu* — "from it." Rashi understands the challenge as: how can we use a *kli shares* at all, given that the *pasuk* specifies *mimenu*, from the basin itself? Tosafos notes that we already know independently that the *Kohen Gadol* washed from a *kli shares* on *Yom Kippur*, so the ability to use a *kli shares* is not really in question. The challenge for Tosafos is instead this: since we know a *kli shares* may be used, must it replicate the *kiyor*'s requirements exactly? If the *kiyor* needed to hold enough for four *kohanim*, should not the *kli shares* be held to the same standard?

### Kal v'Chomer Argument

The *gemara* proceeds to explain why a non-sanctified vessel (*kli chol*) cannot be used, even though the word *yirchatzu* — the repeated mention of washing — appears to broaden the permissible instruments beyond the *kiyor* alone. Abaye provides the exclusion: *k'lei chol lo masis amart* — you cannot possibly say a non-sanctified vessel is valid — *mikkal vachomer mikkanno* — by means of a *kal v'chomer* derived from the pedestal (*kano*) of the basin.

The *pasuk* states: *va'asita kiyor nechoshet v'kanno nechoshet lerachtza* — make a copper basin and its copper pedestal for washing. The Torah explicitly mandates both the basin and its stand. Now consider the *kal v'chomer*: the pedestal was fashioned together with the basin as a single unit, was anointed with *shemen hamishcha*, and was consecrated as *kli shares* — if anything should function as a substitute for the basin, it would be this. Yet the pedestal cannot be used for *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim*. (Tosafos explains the physical scenario: imagine the pedestal as an inverted dome or hollowed base upon which the basin rested; in theory its hollow could be reversed and filled with water, yet this is prohibited.)

How do we know the pedestal is excluded? A *braisa* records this explicitly: Rabbi Yehuda raises the possibility that the pedestal might be valid just as the basin is, and then derives from the doubled word *nechoshet* — copper appearing twice — that the only common ground between the two is their material. They are not functionally equivalent and the pedestal may not be used for washing.

From the pedestal, then, the *kal v'chomer* runs: if the pedestal — which was co-consecrated with the basin — cannot be used, surely an ordinary non-sanctified vessel cannot be used either.

### Mar Zutra Challenge

Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari raises an objection to Ravina: *mah l'khanno she-ken ein asui l'tokho* — there is a distinguishing feature of the pedestal: its hollow is not designed to contain anything. The pedestal, understood as an upturned dome, has no functional capacity as a receptacle. One might therefore argue that it belongs to an entirely different category from a vessel specifically constructed to hold liquid. A non-sanctified vessel designed as a basin — *asui l'tokho*, made to hold contents — may be categorically superior to the pedestal and cannot be excluded on the basis of this *kal v'chomer*.

### Two Limiting Factors

The *gemara* therefore turns to a different resolution. We have two competing words in the verse: *yirchatzu* (the repeated form of washing) and *mimenu* (from it). The word *yirchatzu* broadens the scope — there are additional means by which one may wash, beyond the *kiyor* alone, including a *kli shares*. The word *mimenu* limits — suggesting only from the basin itself. This tension, rather than collapsing one word against the other, places us in the middle: a *kli shares*, which is anointed and consecrated like the basin and is fashioned as a receptacle, is close enough to the *kiyor* to be included by *yirchatzu*. A *kli chol*, however, falls outside that inclusion. As the *gemara* puts it: *mimenu l'ma'utei kli chol* — *mimenu* comes to exclude non-sanctified vessels.

When the *gemara* asks whether *mimenu* should then exclude *kli shares* as well, the answer is *ha ribbi rachmana yirchatzu* — the Torah's broadening term *yirchatzu* rescues *kli shares*. And when pressed — why is *kli shares* the beneficiary of the broadening and not *kli chol*? — the answer is: *zeh ta'un meshichah v'zeh eino ta'un meshichah kemoto* — a *kli shares* is also anointed with *shemen hamishcha*, making it sufficiently analogous to the *kiyor* that the broadening applies to it. A non-sanctified vessel, by contrast, lacks this quality and is excluded by *mimenu*.

---

## Liquids for Mikveh

### Reish Lakish Principle

The discussion now turns from the act of washing to the water contained within the *kiyor*. Reish Lakish formulates a general principle: *kol ha-mashlimin l'mei mikveh mashlimin l'mei kiyor* — anything that can complete (*mashlim*) the forty *se'ah* of a *mikveh* can also serve to complete the required quantity in the *kiyor*. The concept of *mashlim* refers to substances that, while not themselves water and insufficient to render a *mikveh* valid on their own, can supplement a *mikveh* that is already mostly water and bring it to the required forty *se'ah*.

### Revi'is Exception

Reish Lakish immediately qualifies his principle: *l'revi'is eino mashlim* — such substances cannot complete the measure of a *revi'is*. When the requirement is that small — the measure used for ordinary hand-washing — it must consist entirely of pure water; the supplementing substances that work for the mikveh's forty *se'ah* do not apply here.

Tosafos, as we will see, understands the reference to *revi'is* somewhat differently, but the basic contour of the ruling is clear: there is an asymmetry between the two contexts. The large quantity of water required in the *kiyor* admits of the same supplementing substances as a *mikveh*, while the small measure for hand-washing does not.

### Gemara Questions

The *gemara* immediately asks: *limutei mai* — what exactly is being excluded? Which specific substance does Reish Lakish have in mind when he says that something works for a *mikveh* but not for the *revi'is*? The *gemara* begins its search with *tit ha-nerok* — pourable plaster, a thin watery mixture — which appears in *Mishnah Mikva'ot* as something that can supplement a *mikveh*. But before confirming whether this is the case in point, the *gemara* tests the limits.

### Cow Drinkability Test

The *gemara* introduces a criterion: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? *I d'parah shochah v'shotah mimenu* — if a cow could bend down and drink from this substance, then it is sufficiently water-like that it works even for the *revi'is* of hand-washing. *V'i ein parah shotah v'shochah mimenu* — and if a cow could not drink from it, then it is not water-like enough to serve even as a *mashlim* for the forty *se'ah* of a *mikveh*.

This is a striking move. Tosafos points out that the tractate *Mikva'ot* provides various definitions for the consistency of *tit ha-nerok*, and none of them employ this "cow drinkability" standard. It is puzzling that the *gemara* treats this criterion as obvious, and equally puzzling that it assumes no middle ground exists — no consistency that would qualify for the *mikveh* but not for the *revi'is*. The *gemara* appears to take for granted that the line is binary: either it qualifies for everything, or it qualifies for nothing. Nevertheless, this is the framework the *gemara* is working with, so it concludes that pourable plaster cannot be what Reish Lakish had in mind.

### Water-Origin Criteria

The *gemara* then suggests: *ela limutei yavshushim adumim* — perhaps the excluded category is little red water bugs. These insects, which the *gemara* understands to originate in or from water, might be thought to carry enough water-status to count toward the forty *se'ah* of a *mikveh*, yet not enough to serve for ordinary hand-washing. But the *gemara* challenges this as well: *afilu beinhu nami* — even these should count fully as water. For indeed, a *braisa* records that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: *kol she-techilas bri'aso min hamayim matbilin bo* — anything whose original formation was from water, one may immerse in it. And Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi adds that one may even immerse in the liquefied contents of a fish's eye. If the water bugs are treated as fully water-equivalent to the point of permitting *tevilah* directly in them, they should work even for the *revi'is* — and so they, too, cannot be what Reish Lakish meant.

### Natan/Natal Se'ah

Rav Pappa resolves the question: *limutei natan sa'ah v'natal sa'ah* — Reish Lakish is referring to the case of adding and removing from a *mikveh*. The relevant *mishnah* in *Mikva'ot* establishes: *mikveh sheyesh bo mem se'ah mechuvvanot, natan sa'ah v'natal sa'ah, harei zeh kasher* — a *mikveh* containing exactly forty *se'ah* into which one adds a unit of some non-water liquid and then removes a unit of the mixture remains valid.

The classic illustration is fruit juice — apple juice or orange juice. Such a liquid would not on its own bring a *mikveh* up to the required forty *se'ah*; it is too unlike water for that purpose. But if a *mikveh* that already contains forty *se'ah* of valid water has a unit of fruit juice fall into it, and then a unit is removed, the *mikveh* remains *kasher*. Rabbi Yehuda bar Shila citing Rav Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan extends this: one may repeat this process again and again — adding a unit of juice and removing a unit — up to the point where the *mikveh* physically contains a majority of water. So long as the water remains the majority, the *mikveh* is valid. Each time juice is added to an already-valid *mikveh*, it becomes assimilated into the *mikveh*'s status and is treated as part of it.

This is the type of *mashlim* that Reish Lakish has in mind. Fruit juice does not render a *mikveh* valid on its own, and it does not get you to forty *se'ah* from scratch — it only maintains the validity of a *mikveh* already established. When the amount in question is as small as a *revi'is*, there is no pre-existing valid *mikveh* into which the juice can be absorbed; at that scale, everything must be pure water.

### Mikveh Crevice Case

Rav Pappa then introduces a closely related ruling that illuminates the earlier discussion of *kodach*. He states: *im kodach bo revi'is matbilin bo machten v'tzinoryot hoilei me'achsherei d'mikveh atya* — if one carves a small crevice in the wall of a *mikveh* and a *revi'is* of water flows into that crevice, one may immerse small objects such as needles and fine instruments in it, since that *revi'is* derives from the waters of a *kasher* mikveh of forty *se'ah*.

This use of *kodach* — carving a small space connected to a valid *mikveh* — illuminates Tosafos's reading of the earlier *gemara* about the *kiyor*. Just as water drawn from or physically continuous with a valid *mikveh* retains a valid status even in a tiny volume, so too water drawn from a valid *kiyor* containing the requisite quantity is valid for the *kohen*'s washing even if the immediate vessel is small. The structural parallel makes Tosafos's position considerably clearer.

---

## Water Sources

### Mikveh Waters Valid

Rabbi Yirmiah citing Reish Lakish now addresses a different question about the *kiyor*: from where did the basin draw its water? We know that the *kiyor* was lowered into a well each night so that its water would not become *pasul* through *lina* — overnight standing outside the Temple service. But what type of water was used? Rabbi Yirmiah in the name of Reish Lakish states: *mei mikveh k'sheirim l'mei kiyor* — the waters of a *mikveh* are valid for the *kiyor*.

### Mayim Chayim Dispute

This ruling carries an immediate implication: *l'maimra d'lo mayim chayim ninhu* — it asserts that *mayim chayim*, "living water" — water from a natural underground spring, flowing river, or ocean — is not required for the *kiyor*. *Mikveh* waters are typically rainwater collected in a pool, not living spring water, and if such water qualifies for the *kiyor*, then *mayim chayim* is not the criterion.

The *gemara* challenges this from a *braisa*: the verse *v'hakerev v'hakra'ayim yirchatz b'mayim* — the innards and the legs of the animal shall be washed in water — is expounded as follows: *b'mayim v'lo b'yayin* — water, not wine; *b'mayim v'lo b'mazag* — water, not a wine-water mixture; *b'mayim l'rabot she'ar mayim* — but "water" in the broader sense to include other types of water. The *braisa* then adds: *v'kal v'chomer l'mei kiyor* — and this is a *kal v'chomer* to the waters of the *kiyor*.

Rashi explains that "other types of water" here means rainwater. The verse is saying: rainwater may be used for washing the animal's limbs — and certainly it may be used for the *kiyor*. This *kal v'chomer* seems to presuppose that the *kiyor*'s water is held to a higher standard than rainwater — which would mean the *kiyor* requires *mayim chayim*, from a spring. If rainwater were sufficient for the *kiyor*, what would the *kal v'chomer* even mean?

### No Modifying Name

The *gemara* then considers a different way to read the *kal v'chomer*: perhaps "the waters of the *kiyor*" are valid for washing the animal's limbs because they have been sanctified — and the *kal v'chomer* is from the sanctification status, not the water type. If rainwater works, surely water that has been consecrated through the *kiyor* works all the more. But the *gemara* immediately challenges this: *v'kadishim alyusa hi* — is the sanctified status actually a benefit in this context?

A *braisa* is cited in which Rabbi Yishmael rules: *mayim she'ein bahem shem l'vay* — the verse requires water that carries no modifying name. Water called by a special designation — *mei kiyor*, sanctified waters, or any other appellation — is excluded. *Yatzu mei kiyor sheyesh lahem shem l'vay* — specifically the waters of the *kiyor* are excluded because they carry such a name. On this view, the *kal v'chomer* cannot be: "if rainwater, then certainly *kiyor* water" — because *kiyor* water itself is disqualified.

The *gemara* therefore reinterprets: the *kal v'chomer* means not that the actual *kiyor* water may be used, but that water of the *type* used for the *kiyor* may be used — namely, *mayim chayim*, spring water. The argument runs: if rainwater can wash the animal's limbs, spring water certainly can — and spring water is indeed the type appropriate for the *kiyor*. This reading, in turn, implies that the *kiyor* requires *mayim chayim*.

### Tannaim Dispute

The *gemara* concedes the point: *alma mayim chayim ninhu* — the *braisa* does seem to imply that the *kiyor* requires *mayim chayim*. But rather than overturning Reish Lakish's ruling, the *gemara* responds: *tanai hi* — this is a dispute between *tannaim*. Rabbi Yochanan records: *mei kiyor, Rabbi Yishmael omer mei mayim hein* — Rabbi Yishmael holds that the *kiyor* requires true spring water (*mayim chayim*); *v'chachamim omrim she'ar meimot hein* — but the *chachamim* hold that any water is valid. The *Rambam* rules in accordance with the *chachamim*, permitting any water for the *kiyor*.

In summary, the picture that emerges from this *sugya* is as follows: the *kiyor* must contain enough water for four *kohanim*; a *kli shares* may also be used, provided it is sourced from a valid supply; any water is sufficient (according to the *chachamim* and the *Rambam*), and the supplementing principles analogous to the *mikveh* apply to the quantity required in the *kiyor* as well.

---

## Arel Kohen

### Arel Definition

The *gemara* now moves to a new topic: *arel* — the uncircumcised *kohen*. After the lengthy analysis of *bigdei kehunah* and *rechitzas yadayim v'raglayim*, and the conclusion that performing the *avodah* without them renders the service *mechulal* — derived from the word *chalal* — the *gemara* turns to the next disqualifying condition.

Who exactly is this uncircumcised *kohen*? Rashi explains that we are dealing with someone who could not undergo *bris milah* for medical reasons — a family with a history of hemophilia, for instance — not someone who has principled objections to the *mitzvah*. Tosafos extends this to include someone who failed to be circumcised due to fear of pain, provided the omission is not an ideological rejection of the *mitzvah*. A *kohen* who actively rejects *bris milah* as a matter of principle would be in the category of *mumar* or *min* — and as we will see shortly, such a person is independently excluded by the category of *arel lev*. The *arel* under discussion here is someone whose physical status is the disqualifying factor, not his beliefs.

### Source in Yechezkel

The *gemara* asks the expected question: *menalan* — from where do we derive that an uncircumcised *kohen* may not perform the *avodah*, and that if he does, it is *mechulal*? The answer is striking. Rav Chisda states: *davar zeh miTorat Moshe Rabbeinu lo lamadnu, midivrei Yechezkel ben Buzi lamadnu* — this law we did not learn from the Torah of Moshe our teacher; we derived it from the words of Yechezkel son of Buzi. This is a genuinely surprising declaration. The general principle is that the Torah of Moshe is the ultimate source of law, and prophetic books are not normally the origin of halachic obligations. The *gemara* here is prepared to say outright that this particular law does not originate in the *Chamisha Chumshei Torah*, a position the *gemara* will address only obliquely.

### Yechezkel's Text

The relevant verse in Yechezkel reads: *kol ben neichar arel lev v'arel basar lo yavo el mikdashi* — any foreigner who is of uncircumcised heart or of uncircumcised flesh shall not enter My sanctuary.

### Lechalel = Mechulal

The *gemara* then establishes not just the prohibition but the invalidating effect: *umenalan demachli avoda* — from where do we know that such a *kohen*'s service is *mechulal*, rendered invalid? From the continuation of Yechezkel's prophecy: *behavi'achem benei neichar arelei lev v'arelei basar lihyot bemikdashi l'chalel et beiti* — when you brought foreigners of uncircumcised heart and uncircumcised flesh to be in My sanctuary *to desecrate* My house. The word *l'chalel* establishes that the service is *mechulal* — the same verbal root used in the earlier analysis of priestly garments and hand-washing.

### Ben Neichar Meaning

The *gemara* now parses the terms. A *braisa* is cited: *ben neichar* — one might think this refers literally to a non-Jew. But a non-Jew cannot serve as a *kohen* in the first place; there would be no *hava amina*. The *gemara* therefore explains that the term is glossed by the very next phrase: *arel lev*. The *ben neichar* is not a gentile but a Jew who has made himself foreign — *shenitnachru ma'asav l'aviv shebashamayim* — whose deeds have become estranged from his Father in Heaven, who has alienated himself from *Torah* and *mitzvos*. Rashi explains further: *nechshavim l'nochrim l'makom* — such a person is regarded as if he were a non-Jew in relation to God. This connects to the broader halachic concept — invoked frequently by the *Rambam* — of treating a *mechalel Shabbat* or similar transgressor as though he stands entirely outside the communal fold.

### Two Arel Categories

The *gemara* then asks: *v'ein li ela arel lev* — I have only derived the exclusion of someone who has rejected *Torah* and *mitzvos*; from where do I know that *arel basar* — someone physically uncircumcised — is also excluded? The answer: *talmud lomar v'arel basar* — the text continues with this phrase to exclude him as well.

The *gemara* then explains why both exclusions are necessary. *V'tzrichi* — both are needed, because one could not be derived from the other.

### Aesthetic vs. Intent

If the Torah had only excluded *arel basar*, one might have explained the reason as aesthetic concern — *mishum de'ma'is*, because it is repugnant. The Temple's standards of propriety extend to appearances even where no human observer is present; *mumin* that are invisible disqualify a *kohen* all the same. An uncircumcised *kohen* — particularly one from a family of hemophiliacs who bears no personal blame — is excluded not because of any spiritual deficiency but because the *Beis HaMikdash* demands a certain aesthetic wholeness. One might then have thought that *arel lev* — someone who has rejected God's will but whose body is physically whole — presents no aesthetic problem and should not be excluded. Hence the Torah must say both.

Conversely, if only *arel lev* were stated, the exclusion would be explained as *mishum d'ein libo lishmayim* — because his heart is not directed toward Heaven. One might then have thought that *arel basar*, whose heart is entirely *lishmayim* and whose omission of *bris milah* is medical or rooted in fear rather than ideology, should be valid. Hence again, both must be stated explicitly.

The *gemara* does not in this passage resolve the difficulty raised by Rav Chisda — that this law originates in Yechezkel rather than in the Torah of Moshe — beyond what was addressed earlier in the *sugya*, where the *gemara* indicated that the law was always a *masorah*, a tradition transmitted orally, and Yechezkel's prophecy made explicit what was already known from *Torah she'be'al peh*. Yet it is notable that the *gemara* is willing to state plainly that we cannot find the source in the five books of Moshe. The *gemara* will proceed in the next session to the category of *tamei*.

# Zevachim 23

## Tamei & Psul

### Mishnah: Tamei Psul

The daf begins on 22b, picking up the next case in the *mishnah*: *tamei pasul* — a *kohen* who is ritually impure renders the *avodah* invalid. Having already treated lesser degrees of impurity, such as *mechusrei kippurim* and *tevul yom*, the *mishnah* now addresses the general case of *tamei* itself.

### Ziknei Darom Position

The *mishnah*'s blanket rule is immediately qualified by a striking opinion. *Amru Ziknei Darom* — the elders of the South — teach: *lo shanu ela tamei sheretz, aval tamei meis, ho'il u-miratzeh betzibur, miratzeh nami beyachid.* The rule that a *tamei kohen* invalidates the *avodah* applies only when he is *tamei* through contact with a *sheretz* — a dead rodent or similar source of contact-based impurity. But if he is *tamei meis* — impure through contact with a human corpse — paradoxically the more severe *tumah*, the *avodah* is nevertheless *kasher*. The reason: since *tumah* of this kind is accepted, i.e., overridden, in cases involving the *tzibur*, it is also accepted *beyachid*, in the individual case.

Before proceeding to the Gemara's analysis, it is worth noting that the constant term of approval for a sacrifice — *ritzuy*, *miratzeh* — is the same root as *Retzei Hashem Elokeinu*, the blessing in *Shemoneh Esrei*. *Tefillah keneged korbanos*, prayer corresponds to sacrifices, yet *korbanos* are remarkably absent from *Shemoneh Esrei* except for the faintest allusion in *Retzei* — *ishei Yisrael u-tefillatam*, their fire offerings. That *ritzuy*, the key verb of sacrificial acceptance, is also the key verb of that blessing is worth pausing over.

## Tumah Hutra

### Ritzuy & Retzei

The *Ziknei Darom* position rests on the principle of *tumah hutra betzibur* — impurity is overridden for communal sacrifices. This is actually a slight misnomer, as both *Tosafos* and the *Rambam* point out: the principle is not strictly about communal sacrifices but about sacrifices that have a fixed time. Most such sacrifices are indeed *korbanot tzibur* — *korban tamid*, *yom tov musafim* — but the fixed-time requirement can apply to an individual offering as well, most notably *korban Pesach*, which is brought at a precise, fixed moment and cannot be deferred. Conversely, there are communal *korbanos* that do not have a fixed time, such as the *korbanos* of *horayos*, and those would not fall under this principle.

### Only Tamei Meis

The principle overrides *tumah*, but critically, not all *tumah* — only *tumei meis*, impurity derived from a human corpse. More severe forms — *zav*, *niddah*, *metzora*, and the like, which are *tumah yotzei m'gufo*, impurity originating within the body — are not overridden. And, strikingly, even less severe contact-based *tumot*, such as *tamei sheretz*, are also not overridden. The principle applies exclusively to *tamei meis*. This is not derived through logical inference but is a fixed *halacha*, and since it is *halacha lemoshe misinai* one does not apply *kal vachomer* to extend it.

### Conditions

Two further conditions govern the principle. First, it applies to a sacrifice with a fixed time. Second, in the case of *korban Pesach* specifically, it applies when the *rov* of the *tzibur* is *tamei*, since otherwise — when only a minority is *tamei* — those individuals are simply pushed off to *Pesach Sheni*. Outside of *korban Pesach*, the more usual application of *tumah hutra betzibur* is when the *kohanim* themselves are *tamei*, since their *tumah* is what prevents the *korban* from being brought.

### Hutra vs Dchuya

There is a significant debate whether *tumah hutra betzibur* — impurity is categorically permitted in this context, as though there were no prohibition at all — or *tumah dchuya betzibur* — impurity is merely overridden by necessity. The practical consequence: if *dchuya*, the override operates only when there is no alternative. If *tahor kohanim* are available from another priestly division, those *kohanim* must be called in and the *tamei kohanim* set aside. Only when no *tahor* alternative exists does the *avodah* proceed in a state of *tumah*. The operative rule, then, is that *tumah* is *dchuya*, overridden in the absence of alternatives, for sacrifices of fixed time, but only for *tamei meis*, and only when no *tahor kohen* is available to substitute.

## Meis vs Sheretz

### Reish Lakish Challenge

Against the *Ziknei Darom*, the *Gemara* presses a *kal vachomer*. *Amar Reish Lakish*: if *tamei meis* — the more severe *tumah*, requiring sprinkling of purification waters on the third and seventh day — yields a valid *avodah bedi'avad* for an individual *kohen*, then *tamei sheretz*, which requires no such seven-day process and is purified through simple immersion, should certainly yield a valid *avodah* by the same logic. Why limit the leniency of *Ziknei Darom* to *tamei meis*?

The *Gemara* responds on behalf of *Ziknei Darom*: *kasavri Ziknei Darom, mechapprim k'mitchapprim* — those who atone are compared to those who are atoned for. The basis of *tumah hutra betzibur* for *tamei meis* derives from the law of *korban Pesach*: when the majority of *Yisrael* is *tamei meis*, they bring the *korban Pesach* on the fourteenth of Nisan rather than being deferred to *Pesach Sheni*. This override applies for *tamei meis*, and emphatically not for *tamei sheretz*, even though *sheretz* is the lesser *tumah*. The *Ziknei Darom* argue: just as this asymmetric rule holds for the *Yisraelim* who are atoned for — *tamei meis* yes, *tamei sheretz* no — so too it holds for the *kohanim* who perform the atonement: *tamei meis* is within the scope of tolerance, *tamei sheretz* is not.

The irony is philosophically striking, as one of the students raised: why should the more severe *tumah* be the one that is overridden, while a lesser one is not? The *drasha* identifying *tamei meis* as the subject of the override derives from the very passage that gave rise to *Pesach Sheni*: *ish ki yihyeh tamei lanefesh* — *tamei lanefesh* means *tumaat meis*, and that is the *tumah* the *Torah* happens to be addressing in that context. It is less an explanation than a textual identification.

### Mechapprim Analogy

On a more reflective level, several dimensions of this asymmetry were explored. The cases in which the *Torah* imposes severe restrictions in the face of death — *Nadav v'Avihu*, the men who could not bring *korban Pesach* — all involve encounter with human death. There is, perhaps, a counterintuitive affirmation at work: precisely because so much of life closes down in the presence of death, the *Torah* creates an opening to bring *korbanos* when most of the community is engaged with death. According to *Chazal*, the men who were *tamei lanefesh* on the first *Pesach* were those who had buried *Nadav v'Avihu*, performing the highest act of *chesed* possible. One participant offered a further insight: if there were no override, people might hesitate to accompany the dying or tend to the dead, lest they forfeit their *avodah*. The override removes that hesitation. Whatever the precise rationale, the textual anchor is clear even if the philosophical explanation remains open.

### Individual Level Issues

*Reish Lakish* then sharpens his challenge further. The *Gemara* frames the problem at the individual level:

*Mai kasavar* — what exactly is the position of *Ziknei Darom* regarding *tamei sheretz*? If they hold *ein shochtin vezorkin al tamei sheretz* — that a *korban Pesach* cannot be slaughtered and its blood sprinkled for an owner who is currently *tamei sheretz*, even if he will be able to eat it that night — then *amay lo avdi tzibbur betumah*: why isn't *tumaat sheretz* overridden at the *tzibur* level? If the majority of the *tzibur* is *tamei sheretz*, one would expect the principle of communal override to apply and allow the *korban Pesach* to be brought for them.

The *Gemara* concludes that *Ziknei Darom* must hold *shochtin vezorkin al tamei sheretz* — one may bring the *korban Pesach* for an owner who is currently *tamei sheretz*, because he will in fact be able to eat it that night. Therefore *tumaat sheretz* was never a genuine obstacle for the *korban* to be brought; it never *needed* overriding at the *tzibur* level. And since it was never the subject of a communal override, no principle of tolerance for *tamei sheretz* was ever established — not for *Yisrael* and not for *kohanim*. Even if an entire generation of *kohanim* were *tamei sheretz*, since the principle of *tumah hutra betzibur* was never articulated for *sheretz*, there is no *heter* to draw upon. The *Ziknei Darom* therefore have a consistent framework: for *tamei meis*, the override was needed and established; for *tamei sheretz*, it was never needed and therefore never established, which is why the *bedi'avad* tolerance applies only to *tamei meis*.

*Reish Lakish* presses the point from a different angle. He notes that the *Torah* tolerates *tumah* more readily at the level of the *Yisrael* than at the level of the *kohen*: when a *Yisrael* is *tamei sheretz*, he simply does not enter the *Beit Hamikdash*, and a *kohen* brings his *korban* on his behalf. The *kohen's* own *tumah*, by contrast, is the obstacle. Therefore, *Reish Lakish* argues, we should reason from what is true at the *yachid* level: since *tamei meis* is worse for the *Yisrael* sending the *korban* — who cannot participate in *korban Pesach* even as an owner when *tamei meis* — so too the *kohen* who is *tamei meis* should not produce a valid *avodah bedi'avad*.

*Ziknei Darom* respond: *tamei meis nami meshale'ach korbanotav* — even an owner who is *tamei meis* can send his *korban* and have it brought for him. This is a radical position. The *Gemara* immediately objects: *ve'haktiv ish ish ki yihyeh tamei*, which implies that a *tamei meis* individual brings on *Pesach Sheni*, not the first *Pesach*. *Ziknei Darom* answer: *le'mitzvah* — that is the ideal, but *bedi'avad*, having it brought on the first *Pesach* even though the owner cannot eat it that night fulfills the obligation. The *Gemara* then raises the requirement of *ish lefi ochlo*, that the *korban Pesach* is slaughtered according to those who will eat it, and *bemichsat nefashot*, that only those enrolled can be the basis for the *shechita*. The *Gemara* derives that eaters and the enrolled group are *huksha* — compared — so if you cannot eat you cannot serve as the basis for the *shechita*. *Ziknei Darom* respond that they do not accept that *hekkesh* — they do not link the eaters requirement to the enrollment requirement.

The *Gemara* then presses further: even if *Ziknei Darom* escape the *hekkesh* objection, there remains an asymmetry. When the owners are *tamei sheretz*, the *korban* can be brought for them *lechatchila* — they simply don't enter the Mikdash and the *kohen* brings it. But when owners are *tamei meis*, even *Ziknei Darom* concede it is *lechatchila* not done on the first *Pesach*. So we still have a *lechatchila* distinction: *tamei sheretz* by the owner is preferable to *tamei meis* by the owner. By parallel, *tamei sheretz* by the *kohen* should be preferable to *tamei meis* by the *kohen*. And if *tamei sheretz* by the *kohen* is invalid *bedi'avad*, then *tamei meis* should certainly be invalid *bedi'avad* — against *Ziknei Darom*'s entire position. The *Gemara* leaves this question unanswered.

### Death & Tuma

The philosophical dimension underlying these discussions is the question of why *tumaat meis* specifically receives this unique status — neither the most severe *tumot* nor the lighter contact ones, but precisely *tumaat meis*. One suggested reading: the *Torah* is responding to a profound human reality. The encounter with death brings with it obligations — *chesed shel emet*, burial, the care of the dying — that are among the highest *mitzvot*. If the cost of performing those obligations were to permanently disqualify one from *avodah*, the community would face an agonizing conflict between human duty and religious service. The override dissolves that conflict, affirming that where the community is most deeply engaged with death, the *avodah* continues. *Aharon*'s standing at his post on the day of *Nadav v'Avihu* — maintaining public function in the midst of private grief — is the iconic expression of the same principle.

## Pesach Sheni

### Scripture Basis

The *Gemara* now focuses on the scriptural basis for when a *tamei meis* individual brings *korban Pesach* on *Pesach Sheni*. The verse *ish ki yihyeh tamei lanefesh o bederech rechoka* — a man who is *tamei lanefesh* or on a distant journey — establishes that the individual who is *tamei meis* defers to *Pesach Sheni*. The *Gemara's* *drasha* is that when an *ish* — an individual — is *tamei*, he defers; when *hatzibur* is *tamei*, the *korban* is not deferred but brought on time. And the *tumah* the *Torah* was addressing in that foundational passage was *tumaat meis*, which is why *tumaat meis* is the *tumah* identified with the override.

### Eaters Requirement

The *Gemara* raises the requirement *ish lefi ochlo tachossu al haseh* — that the *korban Pesach* is apportioned according to those who will eat it. From *bemichsat nefashot* we learn that the *korban Pesach* may be slaughtered only for those enrolled in a group; slaughtering for those not enrolled is invalid. The *Gemara* then reasons *va-hikish ochlim limnu'im* — eaters are compared to those enrolled — so that one who cannot eat from the *korban* that night is as though not properly enrolled, and the *shechita* on his behalf is invalid *bedi'avad*. This creates a direct problem for *Ziknei Darom*, who hold that an owner who is *tamei meis* can still have his *korban Pesach* brought for him even though he cannot eat it.

### Ziknei Darom Radical

*Ziknei Darom* respond by rejecting the *hekkesh* — they do not equate the eater requirement with the enrollment requirement. An owner who is *tamei meis* and who is enrolled in the group has his *korban Pesach* brought validly *bedi'avad*, even though he cannot eat from it that night. *Lechatchila*, the *Torah* directs him to *Pesach Sheni*; *bedi'avad*, having the *korban* brought on the first *Pesach* is sufficient for the obligation. This is described as a radical position — one that severs eating from participation in a way the standard *halacha* does not accept. The *Gemara* continues to mount challenges against this position, noting that even *Ziknei Darom* must concede the *lechatchila* distinction between owners who are *tamei sheretz* — for whom the *korban* is brought *lechatchila* — and owners who are *tamei meis* — for whom even they concede it is not *lechatchila*. If so, *tamei meis* is demonstrably worse at the owner level, and by analogy the *kohen* who is *tamei meis* should not produce a valid *avodah bedi'avad* — which is precisely the point *Reish Lakish* was making.

## Tzitz & Atonement

### Tzitz Function

As if the foregoing were not sufficiently complex, the *Gemara* now introduces another layer: the principle of the *tzitz*, the golden forehead-plate worn by the *kohen gadol*, inscribed with *Kodesh L'Hashem*. The *Torah* states: *ve-nasa Aharon et avon hakodashim asher yakdishu bnei Yisrael l'Hashem* — *Aharon* will bear the sin of the sacred offerings that *Bnei Yisrael* consecrate. *Chazal* understand this to mean that the wearing of the *tzitz* renders acceptable — *miratzeh* — certain *korbanos* that were brought in an irregular state. A *braita* states: *mipnei she-amru nazir ve-oseh Pesach, hatzitz meratzeh al tumat dam, ve-ein hatzitz meratzeh al tumat haguf* — for a *nazir* and one bringing the *korban Pesach*, the *tzitz* atones for the *tumah* of the blood (*dam*) of the sacrifice, but does not atone for the *tumah* of the person (*haguf*).

The reason these two — *nazir* and *oseh Pesach* — are specifically mentioned is that both require the owner to be *tahor* as a prerequisite: the *oseh Pesach* must be able to eat from the sacrifice, and the *nazir* brings his *korban* specifically to terminate his *tumah* and restart his *nezirut*, so he cannot bring it while still *tamei*. For other sacrifices, where the owner's personal *tumah* is not a direct obstacle to the sacrifice's validity, the framework is different.

### Dam vs Haguf

The distinction between *tumat dam* — impurity of the sacrificial blood — and *tumat haguf* — impurity of the person — is central to understanding the scope of the *tzitz*. When the blood of the sacrifice itself became *tamei* and was nonetheless sprinkled, the *tzitz* validates the sacrifice *bedi'avad*. But when the person — whether owner or *kohen* — is *tamei*, the *tzitz* does not remedy the situation.

The *Gemara* presses: how exactly is the person *tamei* in the scenario where *tumat haguf* is the problem? If it is through *sheretz*, then according to *Ziknei Darom* one may bring a *korban* for that person in any event — *shochtin ve-zorkin al tamei sheretz* — so the *tzitz* would be irrelevant. Therefore the case must involve *tamei meis*. And the *braita* then says the *tzitz* does not work — *ein hatzitz meratzeh* — which, if the case is *tamei meis*, would seem to demonstrate that when owners are *tamei meis* the *korban* is invalid even *bedi'avad*, directly against *Ziknei Darom*'s stated position.

The *Gemara* deflects this reading: the case is actually one where the *kohen* is *tamei sheretz*, not the owners. *Hacha be-mai askinan, ke-gon she-nitma kohen be-sheretz* — here we are dealing with a *kohen* who became *tamei sheretz*. When the owners are *tamei*, one does not need the *tzitz*; when the blood itself is *tamei*, the *tzitz* works; when the *kohen* is *tamei sheretz* — which *Ziknei Darom* themselves hold renders the *avodah* invalid — the *tzitz* does not help.

### Tumat Hatehom

The *braita* continues: *nitma tumat hatehom, hatzitz meratzeh* — if the *tumah* was of the variety called *tumat hatehom*, the *tzitz* does work. *Tumat hatehom* — literally the impurity of the depths — refers paradigmatically to walking over ground where a corpse may be buried deep underground, creating a doubtful *tumah*. By extension, *Chazal* apply the concept to other cases of *safek tumah* — doubtful impurity — provided there is a concrete, specific reason to suspect the *tumah* rather than a general theoretical possibility.

*Rabbi Chiya* teaches: *lo amru tumat hatehom ela le-meis bilvad* — the principle of *tumat hatehom* applies only to *tumaat meis*, not to *tumaat zav* or other severe *tumot*. An example of a *tumat hatehom* of a *zav*: if a person experienced a flow throughout *bein hashmashos* and cannot determine whether it began on one day or another, thus not knowing whether it counts as a one-day or two-day flow — that doubtful scenario is analyzed like *tumat hatehom*, though the paradigm remains tied to *tumaat meis*.

What does *tumat hatehom* limited to *meis* exclude? The *Gemara* considers: does it exclude *tumat hatehom de-sheretz* — meaning, a case of doubtful *sheretz*-type contact? Or does it exclude the more severe *tumat hatehom de-zivah* — doubtful *zav*-type impurity? The *Gemara* concludes the latter: the *tzitz* works for *tumat hatehom* of *sheretz* but not for *tumat hatehom* of *zivah*.

Pulling this together: for *tamei meis*, according to *Ziknei Darom*, the *bedi'avad* tolerance operates without needing the *tzitz*. For *tamei sheretz* — if certain, not doubtful — no tolerance exists and the *tzitz* does not help. For doubtful *tamei sheretz* — *tumat hatehom de-sheretz* — the *tzitz* does provide *bedi'avad* validity. And for *zivah*-type impurity, the *tzitz* does not operate even in the *tumat hatehom* form. This leaves the cases that remain fully invalid — certain *tamei sheretz* and *tamei zav* — as the hard boundaries.

One might ask whether the *tzitz* must actually be worn at the time for it to effect *ritzuy*. This is a good reason for the *kohen gadol* to remain consistently at his post. As for the nature of *ritzuy* itself: the verse uses the language of *nesi'at avon* — bearing sin — which in *Torah* usage always implies that something improper occurred but is being overlooked. *Chazal* understand the *tzitz* as actually validating the *korban bedi'avad* rather than merely atoning for the individual's sin while leaving the *korban* invalid. The *nisiat avon* does not mean the end justifies the means — which *halacha* does not accept, save for the narrow doctrine of *aveira lishmah* — but that the *korban* is retroactively rendered *nirtzeh*, acceptable.

### Rami Bar Chama

*Rami bar Chama* poses a pointed question: *kohen ha-miratzeh be-korbanoteihem* — when a *kohen* is bringing the *korbanos* on behalf of a *nazir* or *oseh Pesach* — *hutra lo tumat hatehom o lo hutra lo tumat hatehom?* — is *tumat hatehom* overridden for the *kohen* himself, or not? That is, we have established that *tumat hatehom* of the *nazir* or *oseh Pesach* does not disqualify the *korban* thanks to the *tzitz*. Does the same apply when it is the *kohen* bringing the *korban* who has *tumat hatehom*?

The significance of this question is that it assumes the normative position — against *Ziknei Darom* — that the *tzitz*'s function as discussed in the *braita* concerns the owners of the *korban*, not the *kohen*. *Rami bar Chama* is asking whether the *kohen* can benefit from the same leniency extended to the owner by the *tzitz*. The *Gemara* concludes: *de-Rami bar Chama vadai pligi* — *Rami bar Chama* clearly disagrees with *Ziknei Darom*, because *Ziknei Darom* held that the entire discussion of the *tzitz* in this *braita* was about the *kohen*, not the owner. According to the mainstream view that *Rami bar Chama* is working within, it is the owner's *tumah* that the *tzitz* addresses, and the question of whether the *kohen*'s *tumat hatehom* is remedied remains open.

## Tzitz Scope

### Excluding Pigul

The *Gemara* now turns to establishing precisely which sin the *tzitz* atones for. The verse *ve-nasa Aharon et avon hakodashim* — what *avon* does *Aharon* carry? *Im avon pigul* — if it is the sin of *pigul*, understood here in the sense of improper intention regarding place of consumption, *harei kvar ne'emar lo yeichashev* — the *Torah* already states it shall not be counted: no atonement is possible. *Im avon notar* — and here, following *Rashi*, *notar* refers to true *pigul*, the intention to eat at the wrong time — *harei kvar ne'emar lo yeiratzeh* — it already says it will not be accepted.

### Impurity Only

If the *tzitz* cannot atone for *pigul* in either of its forms, what is left? *Ela avon tumah* — only the sin of *tumah*. The *Gemara* asks: why leap to *tumah* specifically? There are other invalidities — *zar* performing the *avodah*, *onen*, and others discussed throughout this tractate. Why is *tumah* singled out?

### Logic Framework

The answer: *she-hutra miklala betzibur* — because we find that *tumah* is sometimes overridden entirely, namely in the communal sacrifice context. Since the *Torah* itself demonstrates a category of *tumah* that can be tolerated, and since the *tzitz* also makes acceptable things that would otherwise be invalid, we conclude that the *tzitz* operates in the domain of *tumah*. The logic is that because *tumah* has an internal exception — it is sometimes *hutra* — the *tzitz* can function within that same domain. *Pigul* and *notar* have no such internal exception; they are categorically rejected. *Tumah* alone has the characteristic of sometimes being tolerated, which is what makes it the domain where the *tzitz* can operate.

### Which Tumah

But which *tumah*? *Mai tumah, ileima mitumat sheretz* — if it is *tumaat sheretz*, there is a difficulty: *heichi ishtrei*, how was it ever permitted? We never apply *tumah hutra betzibur* to *tumaat sheretz*. *Ela tumat meis* — it must be *tumaat meis*, the only *tumah* for which we find a communal override. And the implication is *nitmeu ba'alim be-meis meshalachin korbanoteihem* — when the owners are *tamei meis* they can send their *korbanos*, which is the position of *Ziknei Darom*.

The *Gemara* complicates this reading: if it concerns a *nazir*, the *Torah* separately teaches that *nazir* who becomes *tamei* must begin his count again — *ve-chi yamut meit alav amar Rachmana* — suggesting the *korban* cannot be brought while he is *tamei*. So the case in the *braita* must concern *oseh Pesach*, and the *Gemara* reads it as support for *Ziknei Darom*'s position that an *oseh Pesach* who is *tamei meis* can still send his *korban*. The *Gemara* immediately pulls back: *le'olam besheretz* — one may say the *tumah* being discussed for the purpose of identifying *tumat hatehom* is actually *tumaat sheretz*, and the logic is merely that since the *Torah* tolerates *some tumah* in some context, the *tzitz* operates in the domain of *tumah* broadly — without requiring that the *specific tumah* being remedied by the *tzitz* be the same *tumah* that was overridden *betzibur*.

### Kodashim vs Makdishim

Some *rishonim* read the sources in the opposite direction, yielding a *kashya* on *Ziknei Darom* rather than a support. *Avon kodashim in, avon makdishim lo* — the *tzitz* bears the sin of the *kodashim*, the sacrifices themselves, but not the sin of the *makdishim*, those who consecrate and bring the sacrifices. *Mai tumah* — what *tumah* is this talking about? If it were *tumaat sheretz* it was never overridden *betzibur*, so it must be *tumaat meis*. But the *braita* says the *tzitz* works for the *kodashim* — the sacrifice itself — and not for the *makdishim*, the persons involved. This demonstrates that even when the *makdishim*, i.e., the owners, are *tamei meis*, the *tzitz* does not work for them — meaning the *korban* is invalid — directly against *Ziknei Darom*'s claim that *tamei meis* owners can have their *korban Pesach* brought for them.

The *Gemara* resolves: *le'olam tumas sheretz, ve-she'ein tumah ba'olam* — the *tumah* that the *tzitz* atones for is *tumaat sheretz* (for the *kodashim*), and the logic is simply that since there is *some tumah* in the world that is sometimes permitted, the domain of *tumah* in general is where the *tzitz* operates. The argument does not require the *same* type of *tumah* to be both the overridden *tumah* and the *tumah* the *tzitz* remediates.

The discussion at this point involves enormous *Tosafos* precisely because the principle throughout seems to turn on the *tzibur* rather than the *yachid* — yet the entire discussion of *Ziknei Darom* has been about individual cases. The interplay between the communal *tumah hutra betzibur* principle and the individual-level *bedi'avad* tolerances, mediated by the *tzitz* and its specific *ritzuy*, remains one of the most intricate topics on this *daf*, and the discussion continues into the following *daf*.

---

---

# Zevachim 24

## Standing During Service

### Standing Requirement

The Gemara on 23b opens with a discussion of *yoshev* — sitting — as one of the conditions that invalidates the *avodah*. The question posed is *minalan*: what is the scriptural basis for this rule?

### Scriptural Source

Rav Nachman, cited by Rava, points to the verse *la'amod lishareis* — "to stand and to serve" — which describes how God chose the *kohanim* from among all the tribes to stand before Him and perform the service. The Gemara derives from the framing of the verse — *la'amida bechartiv velo leyoshiva*, "I have chosen him when he is standing, not when he is sitting" — that a *kohen* performing the *avodah* while seated has not fulfilled the service. The verse could simply have stated *ein sheirus ela be'amida*, that the proper manner of service is standing. The specific language of *bechirah*, divine election, however, opens the door to a broader consequence, as we shall see.

### Repetition Principle

A *baraisa* observes that had the Torah stated *la'amod lishareis* only once, one might have concluded it is a mere *mitzvah* — a directive to perform the service while standing, but not a *me'akev* condition. However, the Torah repeats the concept in a second verse, *ha'omdim sham lifnei Hashem* — "those who stand there before God." The principle *shana alav hakesuv le'akev* holds that when the Torah doubles a requirement in this fashion, the repetition signals that the condition is indispensable even *b'dieved*: service performed while seated is retroactively invalid.

### Sitting = Non-Priest

Rava then poses a sharper formulation. If a *kohen* who is seated is, by virtue of the language of *bechirah*, no longer in the category of "the chosen" — then *yoshev kezari dami*, a sitting *kohen* is like a non-*kohen*. This has practical consequences: it means the *avodah* performed while sitting is invalid. But one might push the analogy further and argue that since a *zar* who performs the *avodah* incurs the divine death penalty, perhaps a sitting *kohen* should as well.

### Kezari Limitations

A *baraisa* forecloses this conclusion. It lists several categories — an *arel* (uncircumcised *kohen*), an *onen* (one in immediate mourning), and a *yoshev* (one sitting) — and states explicitly that these individuals do not incur the divine *misa* death penalty. They do invalidate the *avodah* and they do transgress a negative prohibition, but they are not liable to divine death.

Why not? If they are *kezari dami*, why not extend the full consequences of the *zar* comparison? The Gemara answers with the rule of *shenei kesuvim ba'im k'echad* — two explicit scriptural passages teach that specific comparable categories do incur *misa* (the *kohen* who serves without the complete *bigdei kehuna*, and the one who has not washed hands and feet). These two explicit cases establish themselves as exceptions, not as the basis for a general rule.

### Two Verses Rule

The principle *shenei kesuvim ba'im k'echad ein melamdin* holds that when two explicit verses establish a rule for particular cases, one cannot generalize from those cases to other situations. Rashi and Tosafos both note the difficulty here: the argument against applying the death penalty to a sitting *kohen* need not depend on generalizing from those two verses at all, since we are independently deriving his *zar*-like status from the language of *bechirah*. Tosafos resolves this by pointing to a parallel principle: just as by the *bigdei kehuna* — where we already say *ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunatam aleihem*, they are not true *kohanim* when not wearing the vestments — the Torah still needed to state the death penalty explicitly, so too here. The lesson is that even when someone is deemed *kezari dami*, that comparison does not automatically carry the death penalty unless the Torah says so. The practical conclusion stands: a *kohen* who performs the *avodah* while sitting invalidates it and transgresses a prohibition, but is not subject to divine death.

---

## Standing on Objects

### Invalid Positions

The Gemara now turns to cases enumerated in the Mishna. A *kohen* who performs the *avodah* while standing on top of a vessel (*al gabei keilim*), on top of an animal (*al gabei behema*), or on his fellow's foot (*al gabei raglei chaveiro*) — in all these cases the *avodah* is *pasul*. The implicit point of the Mishna is that there must be no *chatzitza* — no interposition — between the *kohen*'s feet and the floor of the *azarah*.

### Floor Sanctification

The Gemara cites a *baraisa* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *haritzpah mekadeshet ve-klei shareis mekadeshim* — the floor sanctifies and the *klei shareis* sanctify. There is a significant question regarding the correct *girsa* of this passage. If one reads *mekudeshet* and *mekudashim* — the floor has been sanctified, and the *klei shareis* have been sanctified — the passage simply describes the sanctity of these objects. If one reads *mekadeshet* and *mekadeshim* — the floor sanctifies, and the *klei shareis* sanctify — the passage describes an active role these objects play in elevating other things or persons that come into contact with them.

### Holy Vessel Analogy

Reading the passage in the manner of *mekadeshet*, which appears to be the approach of Tosafos, yields a richer teaching. The principle *ma klei shareis lo yehei davar chotzetz beino uvein klei shareis* — just as when the *kohen* holds the holy vessel there must be nothing interposing between his hand and the vessel — so too, *af ritzpa lo yehei davar chotzetz beino uvein haritzpa*, there must be nothing interposing between him and the floor.

Rashi reads the *klei shareis* of the analogy as the bowl used to catch the blood, and draws the following lesson: just as the *kohen* must hold the holy vessel directly — the principle *lekicha be'itzmo shel kohen* requires him to grip it without any intervening material — so too his feet must be in direct contact with the holy floor. The *kohen* must be directly connected to all the sanctified objects involved in the *avodah*, whether they are above him in his hands or below him underfoot.

Tosafos offers what is described as a more internally consistent reading of the *mekadeshet* version. If the *klei shareis* actively sanctify, one would expect this to mean that blood or other sacrificial material placed into the bowl is elevated to a higher degree of sanctity — and indeed the Gemara elsewhere teaches that the *klei shareis* do precisely this, raising what is placed in them from *kedushat peh* to a more intrinsic sanctity. But there is then no natural analogy between the *klei shareis* sanctifying the blood and the floor sanctifying the *kohen*. The two are not parallel.

Tosafos therefore proposes that *klei shareis* in this passage refers not to the vessels but to the *bigdei kehuna*, the priestly vestments. There is precedent for using the term *klei shareis* to encompass the sacred garments. On this reading, the *baraisa* draws a parallel between two sanctifying processes: just as the *bigdei kehuna*, worn directly against the skin, sanctify the *kohen* and render him fit for service — *ein bigdeihem aleihem ein kehunatam aleihem*, when they are not wearing the garments their priestly status does not apply — so too the floor of the *Beis Hamikdash*, when touched directly by the *kohen*'s bare feet, participates in this same transformative process. The *kohen* entering the *Beis Hamikdash* and standing barefoot on its floor becomes, in a sense, part of the *mikdash* itself. This reading resonates with the broader theme of the *miluim*, the inauguration of the *kohanim*, in which the anointing oil was applied both to the vessels of the *Mishkan* and to the *kohanim* themselves — transforming them, as it were, into *klei kodesh*.

### Garments Interpretation

The Tosafos reading — identifying the *klei shareis* in the *baraisa* with the *bigdei kehuna* — also illuminates why a *chatzitza* between the garments and the skin is prohibited. The garments do not merely cover the *kohen*; they sanctify him. Any interposition prevents this sanctifying contact from taking effect, just as a *chatzitza* in the bowl prevents the vessel from sanctifying the blood. The parallel holds elegantly if one accepts this identification of terms.

### Necessity of Cases

The Gemara asks why the Mishna needed to enumerate all three cases — the vessel, the animal, and the fellow's foot. The answer is that each case might have been considered permissible on its own grounds. One might have thought that a vessel, being inanimate and clearly distinct from human flesh, is obviously a *chatzitza*, but an animal — *de'mina d'basar hu*, being flesh like the *kohen* — might not be considered an interposition. And one might have conceded that an animal is not truly *min b'mino* since it is not of the same species, but a fellow human being — *d'adam hu*, of the same species — might be considered close enough to not constitute a *chatzitza*. The Mishna therefore had to specify all three cases to teach that in none of them is the *chatzitza* overlooked. By implication, standing on one's own foot is not mentioned — and is understood not to be a problem, both because of the *min b'mino* consideration and for reasons that emerge in the next section.

---

## Standing Without Support

### Eliezer's Test

The Gemara cites a *baraisa* in the name of Rabbi Eliezer addressing mixed cases: a *kohen* with one foot on a vessel and one foot on the floor, or one foot on an unattached stone and one on the floor. The operative test is: *roin* — one assesses the situation. If, were the vessel or stone removed, the *kohen* could still stand on the one foot that remains on the floor and perform the *avodah*, then *avodato keshera* — the service is valid. This implies that standing on one foot is in principle permissible for performing the *avodah*. This rule, it is noted, carries over into other halachic contexts where standing is required.

Conversely, if the *kohen* could not stand and perform without the support of the object, then *avodah pesulah* — the service is invalid, because he is in effect standing on that object.

### Loosened Stone

Rabbi Ami poses a more subtle question: what if one of the stones of the *azarah* floor has become loose (*nidaldelah even*) — no longer cemented in place, though it is still sitting in position? If a *kohen* performs the *avodah* while standing on it, what is the rule? The Gemara notes that if there is no intention to re-cement the stone, there is no question — *devadai chotzetz*, it is clearly considered something extraneous and the *avodah* is invalid. The question arises only when the intention is to re-cement it (*deda'ato lechabra*). In that case, one might argue *keivan deda'ato lechabra keman demachabra damya* — since it is intended to be reattached, it is treated as if it already is, and the *avodah* would be valid. Or one might say that right now it is in fact detached, and that is the operative reality. The Gemara leaves this unresolved.

### Missing Stone

A question attributed to Rabba Zuta addresses the adjacent case: *nikrah even* — the stone has been fully removed, leaving an indentation or hole in the floor. If a *kohen* stands in that hole to perform the *avodah*, what is the rule?

The Gemara first asks what is even at issue. If one assumed that David sanctified only the upper paving (*ritzpah elyona kadish*), then standing in a hole would mean standing on unsanctified ground, and the *avodah* would certainly be invalid. But if one assumes *ad ar'ah detehoma kadish* — that the sanctity extends all the way down through the earth beneath — then even the ground below the paving is sanctified floor of the *Beis Hamikdash*. The Gemara challenges this framing: if that is the question, one should simply ask whether a *kohen* standing on bare earth, with all the stones stripped away from the entire *azarah*, would be valid. That question is more straightforward and more general. The Gemara answers that in fact Rabbi Ami assumed the deeper earth *is* sanctified. His question is something else entirely.

### Hole Question

The actual question Rabbi Ami is raising is one of *derech sheirut*: if a *kohen* is standing in a hole — below the level of the surrounding floor — is that the *derech sheirut*, the proper manner of service? Even if the ground beneath him is sanctified, perhaps the dignified and proper mode of performing the *avodah* requires that the *kohen* be standing at floor level rather than sunken into a pit. The Gemara does not resolve this question, and it stands as *teiku*.

The broader upshot of this section is clear: the *kohen* must be directly in contact with the sanctified floor, and the precise parameters of what constitutes valid standing — one foot versus two, a loosened stone, a hole in the floor — generate a cascade of increasingly fine-grained questions.

---

## Left Hand Usage

### Rabbi Shimon View

The Mishna teaches *kibul b'smol pasul* — catching the blood with the left hand invalidates the *avodah* — and then states that Rabbi Shimon permits it. This is a focused position: Rabbi Shimon is not saying that any *avodah* may be performed with the left hand, but specifically the *kabbalah*, the catching of the blood.

### Etzba Evidence

The Gemara cites a *baraisa* that analyzes the verse *velakach hakohen midam hachatat b'etzbao venatan* — "and the *kohen* shall take from the blood of the *chatat* with his finger and place." The word *b'etzbao*, "with his finger," is the crux of the matter. Based on a *gezeirah shavah* with the *metzora*, where the Torah specifies *etzbao hayemanit* — his right finger — the Tanna Kamma reads *etzba* throughout the *avodah* context as indicating the right hand or finger. Accordingly, the Tanna Kamma reads *b'etzbao* as applying to both the *lekichah* (the catching of the blood) and the *netinah* (the placing of the blood on the altar horns): both must be performed with the right hand.

### Tanna Kamma View

The *baraisa* states it explicitly: *b'etzbao velakach* — the word *b'etzbao* teaches that the *kabbalah* must be with the right; *b'etzbao venatan* — the *netinah* must be with the right. The Tanna Kamma reads the word *b'etzbao* as modifying both the preceding act and the following act, *nidrash lefanav ule'acharav*.

### Shimon's Logic

Rabbi Shimon challenges this. He notes that the verse does not use the word *yad*, hand, in connection with the *kabbalah* — it only uses the word *etzba*, finger. Since you cannot catch the blood in a vessel using only your finger, the word *etzba* cannot be referring to the catching. It can only be referring to the placing of the blood on the altar horns, which is indeed performed with the finger dipped in the blood. Therefore *b'etzbao venatan* — the *etzba* term modifies only the *netinah*, not the *lekichah*.

The Gemara raises a difficulty with this explanation. Rav Sama the son of Rav Ashi points out to Ravina that one could in principle hold the vessel with a finger by fashioning an *ozen*, a handle, on the rim of the bowl — enabling the *kohen* to catch the blood while gripping the vessel through the handle with a single finger. This technical possibility undermines the argument that *etzba* cannot refer to the catching.

Abaye therefore reframes the entire dispute. He sets aside Rabbi Shimon's stated reason about *etzba* versus *yad*, and argues that the fundamental disagreement is about *bemikra nidrash lefanav ule'acharav* — whether a word in the middle of a verse is read both forward and backward. The Tanna Kamma holds that *b'etzbao* refers to both the preceding *lekichah* and the following *netinah*. Rabbi Shimon holds that it refers only to the following word, *venatan* — it is read forward (*lefanav*) but not backward. This is a clean and sufficient explanation of the disagreement, without requiring any argument about what the finger can or cannot do.

---

## Vessel Handle Objection

### Sama Objection

Rav Sama's challenge to Rava's reading of Rabbi Shimon — that *etzba* cannot refer to catching because one cannot hold a vessel with a finger — was that one could simply attach a handle (*ozen*) to the rim of the vessel and catch the blood that way. This objection is what drives the Gemara to set aside Rava's explanation and seek a better one.

### Abaye Reinterprets

Abaye's reinterpretation removes the entire argument from the domain of physical feasibility and places it in the domain of hermeneutics. The dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon is a pure *derasha* debate: does a word in scripture refer to what immediately follows it, to what immediately precedes it, or to both? The Tanna Kamma says *nidrash lefanav ule'acharav* — it refers in both directions. Rabbi Shimon says *nidrash lefanav* only — it refers only to what follows. This reinterpretation will be further developed as the Gemara examines the position of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

---

## Elazar's Position

### Elazar's Rule

Abaye notes that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon staked out a position that differs from both his father's and from the Tanna Kamma's. The *baraisa* states his view: *kol makom shene'emar etzba bekabbalah* — wherever the word *etzba* is associated with the *kabbalah* (the catching of the blood), then if one altered the *kabbalah* and used the left hand, it is *pasul*; but the *netinah* performed with the left hand would be *kasher*. Conversely, wherever *etzba* is stated in connection with the *netinah*, altering the *netinah* would be *pasul* while the *kabbalah* could be done with the left hand.

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon does not take a single uniform position on which act requires the right hand. Instead, he determines it case by case based on where in the verse the word *etzba* appears. He holds *mikra nidrash lefanav* — the word refers only to what immediately precedes it, to the immediately prior act. This is why in our verse, where *b'etzbao* comes after *velakach* and before *venatan*, he reads it as modifying only the *lekichah* — the *kabbalah* must be with the right hand, not the *netinah*. This is precisely the mirror image of his father Rabbi Shimon's position.

### Par Exception

Where does Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon derive the rule that there are cases where the *netinah* requires the right hand and the *kabbalah* does not? From the verse concerning the *par hamiluim*, the bull of the inauguration offering: *velakachta midam hapar venatatah al karnot hamizbeach b'etzbe'echa* — "and you shall take from the blood of the bull and place it on the horns of the altar with your finger." Here, *b'etzbe'echa* appears unmistakably after *venatatah* and not after *velakachta*. There is no grammatical ambiguity: the word *etzba* modifies only the placing, not the catching. For the *par hamiluim*, therefore, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon rules that the *netinah* requires the right hand and the *kabbalah* does not.

### Derash Principle

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's hermeneutical principle is *mikra nidrash lefanav velo lifnei fanav* — a word is read as modifying only the immediately preceding element, not what comes two positions back — *velo l'acharav*, and not what follows it. This stands in contrast to the Tanna Kamma (*nidrash lefanav ule'acharav*, both directions) and to Rabbi Shimon (*nidrash lefanav* only, meaning toward what follows). The result is a third, distinct position: by the standard *chatat* verse, the *etzba* term modifies the *kabbalah* and not the *netinah*; by the *par hamiluim* verse, it modifies the *netinah* and not the *kabbalah*. Each verse is read on its own terms.

This position is described as genuinely striking: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon assigns the requirement of the right hand to the *kabbalah* rather than the *netinah*, even though the *netinah* — the placement of blood on the horns of the altar — would seem to be the more significant act. One possible explanation is that the *kabbalah* in the *klei shareis* is itself part of the sanctifying of the blood, and so carries its own weight.

---

## Right Hand Tests

### Yochanan Principle

The Gemara now introduces a broader principle in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, cited by Rabbah bar bar Chanah: *kol makom shene'emar etzba u'kehunah einah ela yamin* — wherever the Torah uses the word *etzba* (finger) and/or *kehunah* (the language of priesthood, i.e., the word *kohen*), it indicates the right hand is required.

### Metzora Source

The Gemara initially assumes that *tarti ba'inan* — both terms are needed together. The basis is our verse from the *chatat*: *velakach hakohen midam hachatat b'etzbao*, which contains both *kohen* and *etzba*. This is then connected by *gezeirah shavah* to the *metzora* verse: *vetaval hakohen et etzbao hayemanit* — where the *kohen* dips his right finger — which makes explicit that the combination of *kohen* and *etzba* indicates *yamin*, the right side.

### Mincha Exception

The Gemara challenges this with the *kemitza* of the *mincha*. When the *kohen* takes the handful of flour, the verse states *vekamatz hakohen* — the *kohen* shall take — using the language of *kehunah* without the word *etzba*, since the act involves multiple fingers, not a single digit. Yet the *Mishna* rules *kamatz b'smol pasul* — if he used his left hand it is invalid. Thus the word *kohen* alone, without *etzba*, is sufficient to require the right hand. This forces a broadening of Rabbi Yochanan's principle.

### Rule Broadened

Rava accordingly reformulates: *o etzba o kehunah* — either the word *etzba* alone or the language of *kehunah* alone is sufficient to indicate that the right hand is required. One does not need both terms together.

---

## Kehuna Limitation

### Limbs Exception

Abaye immediately raises a difficulty. If the mere presence of the word *kohen* in a verse is enough to require the right hand, then the act of *holachat evarim lakevesh* — carrying the limbs of the sacrifice to the ramp — should also require the right hand, since the verse states *vehikriv hakohen et hakol*, using the language of *kehunah*. Yet the *Mishna* elsewhere describes how a *kohen* would carry the right foreleg of the animal in his left hand while holding the head in his right, and this is unproblematic. Clearly the left hand is permitted for bringing the limbs.

### Central Acts

The Gemara resolves this by introducing a limiting principle: *ki amrinan o etzba o kehunah bidvar hame'akev kapparah* — we say that either *etzba* or *kehunah* indicates the right hand only when the act is central to the atonement, *dumya demetzora*, comparable to the paradigmatic acts associated with the *metzora* ritual. The bringing of limbs to the ramp, while part of the service, is not itself an act without which the atonement is incomplete. When it is not a *davar hame'akev kapparah*, the presence of the word *kohen* in the verse does not impose the requirement of the right hand.

### Catching Test

The Gemara then applies this principle to the *kabbalah*, the catching of the blood. The *kabbalah* is clearly a *davar hame'akev kapparah*, and the verse uses the language of *kehunah* (*velakach hakohen*). By the newly broadened principle — *o etzba o kehunah* — the word *kohen* alone should suffice to require the right hand. Yet Rabbi Shimon rules that the *kabbalah* with the left hand is *kasher*. How can this be?

### Shimon Distinction

The Gemara answers: *Rebbi Shimon tarti ba'ei* — Rabbi Shimon requires both terms together. For Rabbi Shimon, the word *kehunah* alone is not sufficient to mandate the right hand; he needs the word *etzba* as well. And since *etzba* appears in the verse but (according to Rabbi Shimon's reading) refers only to the *netinah* and not the *kabbalah*, the *kabbalah* lacks the *etzba* requirement and may be performed with the left hand. The broadened rule — *o etzba o kehunah* — reflects the position of the *rabbanan*, not of Rabbi Shimon.

---

## Context Resolution

### Zerika Question

The Gemara now notices a further apparent problem. If Rabbi Shimon's entire position rests on the word *etzba* — and the word *etzba* appears in the verse only in connection with the *netinah* of the *chatat* — then by the same logic, the *zerika*, the throwing of the blood onto the altar, should also be permitted with the left hand. The verse describing *zerika* uses *kehunah* language but not *etzba*. Rabbi Shimon, who requires *etzba*, should therefore permit left-hand *zerika* as well. Yet the *Mishna* rules *zarak b'smol pasul* without attributing any dissent to Rabbi Shimon.

### Zerika Disagreement

Abaye resolves the difficulty: Rabbi Shimon does in fact disagree about *zerika* as well. A *baraisa* makes this explicit — *zarak b'smol pasul, Rabbi Shimon machshir* — if one threw the blood with the left hand it is invalid, and Rabbi Shimon says it is valid. The absence of Rabbi Shimon's dissent from the *Mishna* on *zerika* does not mean he agrees; the *baraisa* supplies the missing dissent.

### Etzba Locations

The complete picture of where the word *etzba* appears in the Torah in the context of blood service now clarifies the entire structure of the debate. The word *etzba* appears explicitly only in connection with the *netinah* of the *chatat* — the placement of blood on the altar horns. It does not appear by the *kabbalah* and it does not appear by the *zerika*.

### Final Framework

The final framework emerges as follows. The *rabbanan* hold that either the word *etzba* or the language of *kehunah* is sufficient to require the right hand, for any act that is a *davar hame'akev kapparah*. Since *kehunah* language appears by the *kabbalah* and by the *zerika*, both of these require the right hand according to the *rabbanan*, in addition to the *netinah* of the *chatat* where *etzba* appears. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, holds that only the word *etzba* is operative, and not *kehunah* alone. Since *etzba* appears only in connection with the *netinah* of the *chatat*, that is the only act for which Rabbi Shimon requires the right hand. The *kabbalah* and the *zerika* — where only *kehunah* language appears — may, according to Rabbi Shimon, be performed with the left hand without invalidating the *avodah*.

---

---

# Zevachim 25

## Right vs. Left Hand

### Rabbi Shimon & Kabbalah

Our daf begins at the bottom of 24b, continuing the extended discussion of when the right hand is required for *avodah*. The central figure in this debate is Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the right hand is not required for *kabbalas ha-dam* — the catching of the blood. His position turns on a careful reading of a *pasuk* containing the word *be-etzba'o* ("with his finger"): the question is whether that word governs the first half of the verse, which speaks of catching the blood, or only the second half, which speaks of placing it.
