For Rabbi Shimon, the determinative word is *etzba* — "finger." The right hand is required only where that word appears explicitly.

### Etzba vs. Kohen

The *Gemara*'s current position is that the *chachamim* derive the right-hand requirement from two distinct words: either *etzba* or *Kohen*. Wherever the *pasuk* uses the word *kohen* to describe an *avodah*, the *chachamim* read that as implicitly requiring the right hand. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, recognizes only *etzba* as a trigger for that requirement.

### Chatas, Olah, Mincha

The practical implications are as follows. By the *chatas*, everyone agrees that the placing of the blood on the *mizbei'ach* requires the right hand, since the verse says *be-etzba'o ve-natan* — the word *etzba* appears explicitly. The dispute concerns the catching of the blood, where the verse says *ve-lakach ha-kohen*: the *chachamim* say the word *kohen* demands the right hand; Rabbi Shimon says it does not. Similarly, by the *olah*, the throwing of the blood is described with *ve-zarak ha-kohen* — no mention of *etzba*. The *chachamim* again require the right hand; Rabbi Shimon does not.

One act that complicates Rabbi Shimon's position is the *kemitza* — taking the handful from the *mincha*. The verse there reads *ve-kamatz ha-kohen*, using the word *kohen* but not *etzba*, yet everyone, including Rabbi Shimon, agrees that the *kemitza* requires the right hand. How Rabbi Shimon knows this has not yet been explained at this point in the *Gemara*, and we proceed to investigate.

---

## Two Stages Kemitza

### Rava's Yad Yad

The *Gemara* now introduces a teaching of Rava. By the *metzora*, there is a *pasuk* that details the placement of blood on the right earlobe, the thumb of the right hand, and the toe of the right foot. The *Gemara* understands these references as superfluous in their immediate context and therefore reads them as establishing right-hand requirements for other *halachot* by way of *gezerah shavah*. Rava formulates this as follows: *yad yad le-kemitza* — the word "hand" (*yad*) by the *metzora* teaches that the *kemitza* requires the right hand; *regel regel le-chalitza* — "foot" teaches that *chalitza* must use the right foot; *ozen ozen le-retzi'ah* — "ear" teaches that the ear piercing of a slave who chooses to remain in bondage must be the right ear.

For Rabbi Shimon, who cannot derive the right-hand requirement for *kemitza* from the word *kohen*, this *gezerah shavah* of *yad yad* is in fact an elegant and necessary source. But for the *chachamim*, who already derive it from *kohen*, why is Rava's *yad yad* needed at all?

### Taking vs. Receiving

The *Gemara* answers: *chad le-kometz ve-chad le-kiddush kometz* — one derivation is for the taking of the handful itself, and the other is for a second, distinct stage of the process. The *kemitza* involves two acts. First, the *kohen* reaches into the *mincha* vessel and removes the *kometz* — the handful. Second, he places that *kometz* into a *kli sharet* — a service vessel — which sanctifies it and elevates it to the level required for the *mizbei'ach*. This second act, the placing of the *kometz* into the *kli sharet*, is structurally analogous to *kabbalas ha-dam*: just as the blood must be caught in a vessel, so too the *kometz* must be received into a *kli sharet*. And just as *kabbalas ha-dam* requires the right hand according to the *chachamim*, so too this receiving into the *kli sharet* requires the right hand — the *kohen* holding that vessel must hold it in his right hand.

### Extra Yad Needed

Thus, for the *chachamim*, the word *kohen* already establishes the right-hand requirement for the initial taking of the *kometz*. The extra *yad* from Rava's *gezerah shavah* is then needed for the second stage — the placing of the *kometz* into the *kli sharet*, which parallels *kabbalas ha-dam*. Neither derivation is redundant: each governs one of the two distinct acts that together constitute the *kemitza* process.

---

## Mincha & Vessel Logic

### No Kiddush Kometz

The *Gemara* now turns to Rabbi Shimon's position with greater precision. There is a separate *Gemara* teaching that according to Rabbi Shimon, the *kohen* does not require the stage of *kiddush kometz* — that is, he need not place the *kometz* into a *kli sharet* at all. Rabbi Shimon holds that the *kohen* may simply take the *kometz* directly from the *mincha* and walk it straight to the *mizbei'ach*, placing the entire handful on the altar without first depositing it into a vessel. The *shirayim* — the remainder of the flour — stays behind; the *kometz* alone goes on the altar, but it goes there directly from the *kohen*'s hand.

Even if one were to say that Rabbi Shimon does require this stage, a further point follows: since the placing of the *kometz* into the *kli sharet* parallels *kabbalas ha-dam*, and Rabbi Shimon explicitly permits the left hand for *kabbalas ha-dam*, he would equally permit the left hand for this act. The result is that for Rabbi Shimon there is at most one act within the *kemitza* process requiring the right hand: the initial taking of the handful. The second stage either does not occur at all, or, if it does, may be performed with the left hand.

### Kohen as Kli Sharet

This leads to a conceptually elegant and recurring principle in Rabbi Shimon's thinking: the *kohen* himself can function as a *kli sharet*. If a *kli sharet* is employed, it is the vessel that sanctifies the *kometz*; the act of placing it on the altar thereafter does not itself require the right hand. Rabbi Shimon is broadly lenient about acts that do not require the *etzba*, and for him the throwing of blood by an *olah* or the placing of a *kometz* on the altar does not demand the right hand in principle. But if no *kli* is used, something must sanctify the *kometz* — and that something is the hand of the *kohen* itself. When the *kohen*'s body substitutes for the vessel, his hand must be the right hand, functioning in place of the *kli sharet*. This is the unifying logic: the right hand is required precisely when the body of the *kohen* itself is doing the sanctifying work that would otherwise be done by a vessel.

### Kodesh Kodashim Drasha

The textual basis for Rabbi Shimon's position is derived from the verse that describes the *mincha* as *kodesh kodashim hi, k'chatas v'k'asham* — "it is holy of holies, like the *chatas* and like the *asham*." Why does the verse compare the *mincha* to both? Rabbi Shimon reads it as follows: *ba l'ovdah b'yad, ovdah b'yamin k'chatas* — if the *kohen* performs the service using his hand directly, it must be done with the right hand, as with the *chatas*; *ba l'ovdah b'kli, ovdah b'smol k'asham* — if he uses a vessel, it may be performed with the left hand, as with other *korbanot* such as the *asham*. The comparison to the *chatas* is not incidental: the *chatas* is the one *korban* where Rabbi Shimon unambiguously agrees the right hand is required, specifically for the placing of the blood with the finger. Since that act uses the body directly — *etzba* — the right hand is demanded. The *mincha* mirrors this: when the *kohen*'s own hand is the operative instrument, the analogy to the *chatas* kicks in and demands the right hand.

### Hand vs. Vessel

The practical upshot of this *drasha* is clear. If the *kohen* takes the *kometz* and brings it directly to the altar with his own hand — without using a *kli* — he must use his right hand, just as the *kohen* uses his right finger when placing the blood of the *chatas*. If, however, he places the *kometz* into a *kli* and then brings the *kli* to the altar, the same logic that permits the left hand for *zerikah* by an *olah* or *asham* applies here as well, and the left hand suffices. It is worth noting the elegant parallel: just as by the *chatas* the finger is the operative instrument — and it is precisely the word *etzba* that triggers the right-hand requirement — so too by the *mincha* when the hand is the operative instrument, it must be the right. The verse's dual comparison thus encodes a complete and consistent system.

Implicit in this *drasha* is also the basis for Rabbi Shimon's right-hand requirement for the initial *kemitza*. Since the verse teaches that whenever the *kohen* uses his hand directly it must be the right hand, the taking of the *kometz* — which is obviously and necessarily done directly with the hand — must be done with the right hand. This is how Rabbi Shimon arrives at his position on *kemitza* without relying on the word *kohen* and without needing Rava's *yad yad*.

---

## Mincha Chotei

### Sinner's Mincha

If Rabbi Shimon's *drasha* from *kodesh kodashim* already establishes that the *kemitza* requires the right hand, the *Gemara* asks: why is Rava's *yad yad* needed at all for Rabbi Shimon? The answer is that Rava's teaching is needed specifically for the *kometz minchas chotei* — the handful taken from the *mincha* of a sinner. The *minchas chotei* is described in Vayikra 5:11, the case of the *olah v'yored* offering for one who cannot afford an animal: a tenth of an *eifah* of fine flour is brought as a *chatas*, with no oil and no *levonah*. The Torah deliberately strips this offering of adornment because it is the *korban* of a sinner.

Rabbi Shimon, as a *ta'ama di-kra*, explains: the reason the *minchas chotei* lacks oil and frankincense is *she-lo yehei korbano mehudar* — so that his offering should not be beautified. This raises a *hava amina*: since the Torah deliberately degrades this *korban*, perhaps we would extend that degradation further and permit the *kemitza* even with the left hand. If the Torah is signaling that this *korban* is to be treated as second-tier, perhaps even the requirement of the right hand should be relaxed.

### Even Sinner Needs Right

The *Gemara* therefore says: *lo nitzrecha ela le-kometz minchas chotei* — Rava's *yad yad* is needed precisely to teach that even the *minchas chotei* requires the right hand for its *kemitza*. The Torah's downgrading of the offering in terms of its aesthetic quality does not extend to the manner in which the *avodah* is performed. This is what Rava's *gezerah shavah* comes to teach: *ka mashma lan* — it informs us that no inference from the *minchas chotei*'s diminished status may be drawn to relax the right-hand requirement.

---

## Summary Right Hand

### Chachamim Universal

By way of summary, the *chachamim*'s position is a comprehensive and consistent one. They require the right hand for virtually every major act of *avodah*: *kabbalas ha-dam*, *zerikah*, *kemitza*, and the receiving of the *kometz* into the *kli sharet*. They derive this from two separate hermeneutic triggers — the word *etzba* and the word *kohen* — which between them cover nearly every relevant act in the *korban* process. The one significant exception, which all agree on, is acts like bringing the limbs to the altar, which are not part of the core *kaparah* process involving the blood, and which therefore are not subject to the same requirements.

### Body vs. Vessel

Rabbi Shimon's position is more nuanced but equally coherent. He rejects the word *kohen* as a trigger for the right-hand requirement, insisting that only the word *etzba* demands it in the primary sense. His own *drasha* from *kodesh kodashim* — the comparison of the *mincha* to both the *chatas* and the *asham* — adds a second principle: wherever the *kohen*'s body itself is the operative instrument, it must be the right hand. The common denominator across all the acts Rabbi Shimon agrees require the right hand is precisely this: the direct use of the *kohen*'s body. The placing of the blood of the *chatas* uses the finger directly — right hand required. The taking of the *kometz* uses the hand directly — right hand required. If the *kohen* places the *kometz* on the altar directly with his hand and no *kli* — right hand required, because his body is standing in for the *kli sharet*.

By contrast, wherever a vessel intervenes — *kabbalas ha-dam* into a vessel, *zerikah* using the blood-vessel toward the *mizbei'ach*, placing the *kometz* into a *kli sharet* — the *kli* itself is doing the sanctifying work, and Rabbi Shimon does not demand the right hand. The *kohen* is acting as a *kli sharet* only when no actual *kli* is present; when a *kli* is present, the *kli* carries the operative halachic weight, and the *kohen*'s hand may be the left.

---

## Nishpach Dam

### Mishna Spilled Blood

The *Gemara* now shifts to the next *Mishnah*, which addresses what happens when the blood does not travel properly from the animal's neck into the vessel. The ruling is: *nishpach ha-dam al ha-ritzpa v'asfo, pasul* — if the blood was spilled on the floor and was then gathered up, it is invalid. This stands in contrast to a case where the blood was first properly caught in a *kli sharet* and then subsequently spilled; in that case, the blood may be gathered again and placed on the altar. The operative principle is that the blood must be caught directly by the *kli sharet* as it flows from the animal. Once it touches the floor, it cannot be reclaimed.

### Midam Hapar

The *Gemara* cites a *Baraita*: *ve-lakach ha-kohen ha-mashiach mi-dam ha-par* — the *kohen* should take from the blood of the ox. The *Baraita* derives several requirements from this verse. *Mi-dam ha-nefesh* — the blood must come from the life-blood, from the major arterial flow. *Ve-lo mi-dam ha-or* — not from blood that merely seeps from a cut in the skin. *Ve-lo mi-dam ha-tamtzit* — not from the *dam ha-tamtzit*, the blood that dribbles out in the aftermath of the *shechita*, after the initial forceful flow has subsided. The *dam ha-tamtzit* is chemically the same blood, but it no longer represents the full vital force of the animal's blood.

### Mem Derivation

The *Gemara* then addresses the requirement that the blood be caught directly from the animal. The textual mechanism is a *gezerah shavah* built on the letter *mem*. The verse reads *mi-dam ha-par*. The *Gemara* rearranges the letters by a technique known as *gorin u-mosifin ve-dorshin* — you remove a letter from one word and add it to another, then expound. Taking the *mem* from *dam* and attaching it to *ha-par*, the verse is read as *dam me-ha-par yekablenu* — the blood must be received directly from the ox. It must flow from the animal into the vessel without interruption; it cannot be collected off the floor.

One might object that the *mem* in *mi-dam* is needed to teach a different point: that only some of the blood — *mi-dam*, even a portion — need be caught. The *Gemara* addresses this by citing a teaching of Rav: *ha-shochet tzarich she-yekabel kol damo shel par* — ideally one must receive all the blood of the animal, as derived from *ve-et kol damo yishpoch*. Since the word *kol* — "all" — applies to the blood, the *mem* of *mi-dam* cannot be standing there to permit catching only a portion. The *Gemara* further resolves the verse *ve-et kol damo* by noting that this phrase, which speaks of spilling all the blood, cannot refer to the *shirayim* stage (where not all the blood remains), and must therefore be redirected to the act of *kabbalah* — teaching that ideally all the blood should be caught from the outset.

---

## Practical Requirements

### Raising Knife

The *Gemara* continues with a teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *ha-shochet tzarich she-yagbi'a sakin le-ma'alah* — after completing the *shechita*, the *kohen* must raise his knife away from the vessel that is catching the blood. The reason is straightforward: blood inevitably gets on the knife during *shechita*. If the knife remains positioned above the vessel, blood from the knife will drip into the vessel. That blood is invalid — *ve-lo mi-dam ha-par ve-davar acher* — because it did not travel directly from the animal's neck into the vessel. It went first to the knife and then into the vessel, which breaks the required direct path from animal to *kli*.

### Knife Contamination

The status of blood that drips from the knife into the *kli sharet* is analogous to blood spilled on the floor: both represent interruptions in the chain from animal to vessel. One might think the knife-blood is slightly more legitimate, since it at least came from the animal in the immediate sense and has not yet reached the floor. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* treats it as equally invalid, because the requirement is that the blood go *directly* from the neck to the vessel, without any intermediary — and the knife is an intermediary.

### Wiping Knife

Having established that the knife must be moved away, the *Gemara* asks: where does one wipe the blood off the knife? Abaye says: *bi-sfat mizrak* — on the outer lip of the *mizrak*, the *kli sharet* used to catch the blood. Rashi notes that the very word *mizrak*, which is cognate to *kiporei* (as in *kiporei zahav*), may itself carry a connotation of cleaning, suggesting that wiping the knife on the vessel's rim was indeed the intended practice. That said, the practical logic here is genuinely difficult to follow: it seems both halachically risky (the blood could accidentally fall back in) and physically inadequate (the outer lip is an imprecise surface for cleaning a blade). The *Gemara* does not elaborate further.

### Veins Positioning

Rav Chisda citing Rav Yirmiya bar Abba adds another requirement: *ha-shochet tzarich she-yitein v'ridin l'toch ha-kli* — the *shochet* must position the jugular veins directly over the vessel. This does not mean physically inserting the neck into the vessel, but rather ensuring that the severed veins from which the blood flows are positioned directly above the opening of the vessel, so that the blood flows straight down into it. Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states similarly: *v'ridin tzerichin she-yiru avir kli* — the veins must have a clear line of sight into the airspace of the vessel. The concern being addressed is that if the neck is positioned to the side, the blood may arc through the air horizontally before descending, meaning the vessel is collecting blood not from directly below the neck but from blood that has already traveled through the air at some remove. The vessel must be directly beneath the cut veins.

---

## Airspace Question

### Bottom Falls Out

Rav Assi posed the following question to Rabbi Yochanan: *haya mekabel ve-nifchetu shulei mizrak ad she-lo higi'a dam la-avir mahu?* — suppose the *kohen* is in the process of receiving the blood, the blood has left the neck and is traveling through the air toward the vessel, but it has not yet reached the airspace of the vessel — and at that precise moment the bottom of the vessel falls out. What is the status of that blood?

The underlying assumption of the question is that once the blood enters the *airspace* of the vessel — the hollow space above the floor of the vessel — it is already considered "received" by the vessel, even before it touches the vessel's base. This is because at any given moment, most of the blood is not hitting the floor simultaneously; the airspace functions as part of the vessel's domain. If that is so, is blood that is still in the air above, heading toward the vessel's airspace, already considered caught — or not?

The logical intuition leans toward saying it is not yet caught, since it never actually entered the vessel's airspace before the vessel ceased to exist as a valid *kli*. But the *Gemara* now considers what precedents bear on this.

### Water Para Aduma

The *Gemara* draws a comparison to a discussion about water for *Para Aduma*. Water used for *Para Aduma* must be *mayim chayim* — living water directly from a spring — and may not be water that has already sat in a vessel, which would lose its status as *mayim chayim*. A *Baraita* addresses the case of a barrel (*chavit*) positioned beneath a pipe (*zinuk*) through which spring water flows. Water already inside the barrel is invalid for *Para Aduma*. Water outside the barrel — that is, in the airspace above it, still in flight from the pipe toward the barrel — is also invalid. In a second case, the barrel's mouth is pressed flush against the pipe, eliminating any open airspace; in that configuration, water drawn from within the pipe itself (not yet in the barrel) is valid.

This parallel is instructive: water in the open airspace above the barrel is treated as though it were already inside the barrel. This is the principle of *avir kli* — the airspace of a vessel is legally equivalent to the vessel itself.

### Airspace Keshesofo Lanua…

The *Gemara* now examines this principle carefully, noting the distinction between two cases. The case of *avir she-sofo lanuach* — airspace above a vessel whose floor is intact, meaning the object (blood or water) will inevitably land in the vessel — is one thing. In that case, the *Gemara* is inclined to say *ke-munach dami* — it is treated as though it has already landed. But the original question was about *avir she-ein sofo lanuach* — airspace above a vessel whose floor has fallen out, so that the object will not in fact land in the vessel. Does the same principle apply?

Three Amoraim — Rav Yosef, Rav Kahana, and Rava — transmit the exchange between Rav Assi and Rabbi Yochanan differently. Rav Yosef teaches that Rav Assi's question was about the blood of a *korban*, and the answer was derived from the *Para Aduma* case. Rav Kahana teaches the reverse: the question and answer were entirely within the *Para Aduma* discussion. Rava teaches a third version: the question was about *Para Aduma* and the answer was derived from the *mizrak* — the case of blood — with the argument that blood traveling from the neck of the animal does not literally fall straight down but moves in an arc (*it could not travel otherwise, since the kohen cannot always position the vessel to catch blood in a perfectly vertical drop*). According to Rava, the very fact that blood caught in the *mizrak* is considered *midam ha-par* — from the animal — even though some of the blood traveled horizontally before descending, demonstrates that the airspace of the vessel is what matters: the blood entered the airspace of the vessel directly from the neck, and that counts as direct receipt, even though the floor of the vessel received it only after a change of direction.

### Indirect Vessel Entry

The resolution of the question follows from this analysis. *Avir she-sofo lanuach ke-munach dami* — airspace above an intact vessel is treated as the vessel itself. Blood or water that enters that airspace is considered received, even before reaching the floor. This explains why the *Baraita* about *Para Aduma* invalidates water in the open air above the barrel: it is treated as though already in the barrel, rendering it no longer *mayim chayim*. It also explains Rava's reading of the blood case: the blood enters the airspace of the *mizrak* in a direct line from the neck; the subsequent arc is only within the airspace, and that is sufficient. As for the original question — the case where the bottom falls out before the blood reaches the airspace — that would indeed be invalid, since the blood was never in the airspace of a valid vessel.

---

## Water Transport Validity

### Edible Items Invalid

The *Gemara* now cites a *Mishnah* that elaborates on the *Para Aduma* water requirements: *natan yado o raglo alei yerakot kedei she-ya'avru mayim le-chavit, pesulim* — if someone used his hand, his foot, or vegetable leaves to channel water from the spring into the vessel, the water is invalid for *Para Aduma*. The reason is that these are all items capable of receiving *tumah* — *mekabel tumah*. However, *alei kanim ve-alei egozim, kesherah* — leaves of reeds or nut trees, which are not edible and cannot become *tamei*, are valid transport media. The general principle: *davar ha-mekabel tumah*, anything that can become ritually impure, disqualifies the water when used to transport it.

### Tahara Source

The *Gemara* traces this to a verse: *ach ma'ayan u-vor mikveh mayim yihyeh tahor* — a wellspring or a cistern, a gathering of waters, shall be pure. The *Gemara* derives from *yihyeh tahor* that the creation (*havayatan*) of these ritual water gatherings must occur *al yedei taharah* — through means that are themselves in a state of purity, i.e., things incapable of receiving *tumah*. Anything *mekabel tumah* cannot serve as the conduit for water that is to be used in this context.

### Hand Transport Problem

This *halacha* connects back to the *avir kli* principle in a precise way. The question arises: if water traveled from one's hand into the vessel, why not argue that the hand was not the direct cause — rather, the water left the hand, passed through the open air, and the air then deposited it into the vessel? If the water went through the airspace before entering the vessel, one might say it was the airspace that delivered the water, not the hand, and the hand's status as *mekabel tumah* is therefore irrelevant. This is precisely where the principle of *avir kli* does its work: the airspace above the vessel is treated as the vessel itself. Water passing through that airspace is considered as though it passed directly into the vessel. Therefore, the hand's delivery into the airspace is a delivery into the vessel, and the disqualification applies.

### Passing Water Proof

The final proof for the *avir kli* principle in this context is provided by Rav Zeira, who challenges Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: perhaps the water went straight from the hand into the vessel proper, without going through the airspace — in which case no inference about *avir kli* can be drawn. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba responds: *tirdu — kedai she-ya'avru mayim le-chavit tenan* — the *Mishnah* uses the language "so that the water should pass into the barrel," implying a streaming or flowing motion through open air, not a drip directly onto the vessel floor. The word *ya'avru* ("pass") establishes that the water traversed open space before entering the vessel, and yet it is invalid — because that open space above the vessel is itself considered the vessel. *Avir kli ke-kli dami.* This is the final, conclusive statement of the principle: the airspace of a vessel is legally equivalent to the vessel itself.

---

---

# Zevachim 26

## Unblemished at Kabbalah

### Tzorem Ozen Parah

The daf begins with the final line of the previous *sugya*, which concerned the principle of *avir k'kli dami* — the halakhic status of the airspace directly above an open vessel as equivalent to the vessel itself. This principle was applied to the blood of sacrifices, which must flow directly from the neck of the animal into the receiving vessel, and was extended as well to the waters of the *parah adumah*. The concluding point of that *sugya* is a teaching of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the ruling regarding how the waters of the *parah adumah* may be directed into a vessel was established from the testimony of Rabbi Tzadok, as recorded in tractate *Eduyot*. Rabbi Tzadok testified that if the flowing waters were directed using the leaves of nut trees — which, being inedible, are not *mekabel tumah* — the gathering is valid. This case came before the sages in the *Lishkat HaGazit* and was ruled *kasher*. With that, the prior *sugya* is closed.

The Gemara now introduces a new teaching. Rabbi Zeira said in the name of Rebbe: if one pierced the ear of the animal (*tzorem ozen parah*) after the *shechitah* but before the blood was received (*kibel damo*), the *korban* is *pasul*. The reasoning derives from the verse *v'lakach midam hapar* — "he shall take from the blood of the ox" — where the definite article (*heh ha-yedi'ah*) indicates that the animal must be in the same state it was in before: unblemished, without a *mum*. Therefore, at the moment the blood is received, the animal must still be *tamim*.

One might find this ruling striking, even somewhat paradoxical. The animal has already had its neck severed — surely that is a far greater *baal mum* than a hole in the ear. But the Gemara's *drasha* operates within precisely defined parameters: bracketing the necessary wound of *shechitah* itself, the animal must otherwise remain unblemished at the time of *kabbalah*. If someone pierced the ear in that instant between the cut and the catching of the blood, that additional blemish invalidates the *korban*.

### Kodshim Kalim Extension

With Rabbi Zeira's ruling established for *kodshei kodashim*, the Gemara asks: *ashkachan kodshei kodashim* — we have found the source for the most sacred offerings, but from where do we derive the same requirement for *kodshim kalim*? Would one not readily assume the rule carries over? Tosafot raises this question explicitly: ordinarily, a ruling established for one category of *korban* would be assumed to apply to others without requiring a separate derivation. Tosafot suggests that perhaps because this particular ruling is so counterintuitive — requiring the animal to remain unblemished even after its head is severed — there was reason to think it might be a special stringency limited to *kodshei kodashim*, and therefore a separate source is necessary.

Rava answers from the verse concerning the *korban pesach* — a *kodshim kalim*: *seh tamim zachar ben shanah yihiyeh lachem*, "it shall be a perfect male lamb, one year old" (Shemot 12:5). The immediately preceding verse, *tachossu al haseh*, speaks of the *shechitah*. The subsequent verse then specifies that the animal must be *tamim* and *ben shanah* — indicating that even after the act of *shechitah*, the animal must continue to satisfy both conditions. So the requirement of *tamim* at the time of *kabbalah* is established even for *kodshim kalim*.

### Meat/Fat Remain

The Gemara then extends the discussion further. Rava reads the word *yihiyeh* — "it shall be" — as encompassing all stages of the sacrificial service: the *shechitah*, the *kabbalah*, the *holachah* (carrying the blood), and the *zerikah* (throwing the blood onto the altar). The *yihiyeh* means that throughout all these acts, the animal must remain *tamim* and *ben shanah*.

Abaye challenges this broad reading from the teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that for all sacrifices in the Torah, the throwing of the blood is only valid if at least a *kezayit* of meat or a *kezayit* of fat remains from the animal at the time of *zerikah*. Rabbi Yehoshua's view establishes that even if the majority of the meat or fat has been destroyed or rendered *tamei*, so long as a *kezayit* remains, the *zerikah* is valid. Now, if Rava's principle requires the animal to remain *tamim* — unblemished — all the way through *zerikah*, then a case in which most of the meat has been destroyed would present a contradiction: the animal is clearly no longer in its original state.

### Psul Limited to Kabbalah

The Gemara resolves this tension by drawing back the scope of Rava's ruling. The *yihiyeh*, it concludes, extends the ongoing requirement only with respect to the condition of *ben shanah* — one year old — not with respect to *tamim*. The requirement of *tamim* is limited to the moment of *kabbalah* alone, derived from *v'lakach midam hapar*. After the blood has been received, if the meat becomes damaged or destroyed, this does not retroactively invalidate the service with respect to the *tamim* requirement. What must remain valid at all stages is only the age qualification.

### Sha'ot Poslot

This resolution prompts a question from the Gemara itself: how is it even possible that an animal could be *ben shanah* at the time of *shechitah* and *ben shtayim* — two years old — by the time of *holachah* or *zerikah*? After all, the blood-throwing follows the *shechitah* by only moments. The Gemara answers with a ruling of Rava: *sha'ot poslot bekodshim* — in matters of sacrificial law, age is measured by the hour, not by the calendar day. This contrasts with, for example, *bar mitzvah* and *bat mitzvah*, where we measure by days: once the date of one's birth has come around again, one is considered to have entered the next year, regardless of the hour of birth. By *korbanot*, however, the calculation is precise down to the hour. It is therefore possible that an animal was *shechted* while still in its first year — say, an hour before the exact anniversary of its birth — and by the time of *zerikah*, it has entered its second year. Hence the requirement that it remain *ben shanah* through all stages is practically significant, and the ruling of *sha'ot poslot* is directly derived from this discussion.

The ultimate conclusion: the requirement of *tamim* applies specifically and only at the time of *kabbalat hadam*. If thereafter the meat is destroyed or blemished, the *korban* is not invalidated on that account. What must hold through all stages — *shechitah*, *kabbalah*, *holachah*, and *zerikah* — is the condition of *ben shanah*, measured by the hour.

---

## Animal Inside/Outside

### Raglah Bachutz

A small but essential ruling of Tosafot at the top of 26a sets the foundation for this entire section: a single drop of *pasul* blood that becomes mixed with valid blood is not subject to *bittul berov* — it is not nullified by a majority of valid blood. Whether by rabbinic enactment or by Torah law, any admixture of *pasul* blood invalidates the entire contents of the vessel. This principle, that invalid blood cannot be nullified, governs everything that follows.

With this in mind, the Gemara introduces the ruling of Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Elazar: if the animal's body was inside the *Azarah* but one leg extended outside (*hi bifnim v'raglah bachutz*), and one cut off that leg and then performed the *shechitah*, the *korban* is *kasher*. This requires explanation.

When the *shechitah* is performed, the blood in every part of the animal's body begins to flow toward the wound in the neck and out into the receiving vessel. Blood flowing from a limb that is positioned outside the *Azarah* is *pasul* — it is analogous to blood that has been taken out of its proper domain. Just as blood that is carried out of the *Azarah* after *kabbalah* becomes invalid (*psul yotzei*), so too blood pumped in from outside the *Azarah* at the moment of *shechitah* is invalid. Since even a single drop of such blood mixed into the vessel invalidates the entire reception, the presence of a limb outside the *Azarah* poses a serious problem.

If one severs that limb *before* the *shechitah*, no blood will flow from outside — the problem is solved. But there is an immediate difficulty: cutting off a limb creates a *baal mum*, and we have already established that the animal must be *tamim* at the time of *kabbalah*. Performing the *shechitah* on a blemished animal would be invalid.

The Gemara works through the possible solutions. Cutting the limb after *shechitah* but before *kabbalah* does not work either, because Rabbi Zeira's teaching states that the animal must remain unblemished at the time of *kabbalah*, and cutting off a limb between *shechitah* and *kabbalah* would introduce a *mum* before the blood is received. This is derived from *v'lakach midam hapar* — the animal must remain as it was.

Rav Chisda citing Rav Avimi provides the resolution: one may cut into the flesh of the limb down to the bone without severing the bone itself (*chotech ba-eivar ad she-magia la-etzem*). Cutting flesh without cutting bone does not constitute a *baal mum*, since the bone structure remains intact. Yet because all the soft tissue has been cut through, no blood will travel up through that limb. This procedure can therefore be performed before the *shechitah*, precluding the flow of outside blood without creating a disqualifying blemish.

The Gemara thus recasts the ruling: if one cut the limb after *shechitah* but before *kabbalah*, the *korban* is invalid on account of the *mum* created before *kabbalah*. If the blood was received and only thereafter the limb was severed, that too is invalid — though for a different reason, which the Gemara now addresses.

### Cutting Limbs

The Gemara reformulates the ruling: *chatach v'achar kach kibel* — if one cut (using the technique of cutting flesh to the bone, without severing it) and then received the blood, it is *kasher*. *Kibel v'achar kach chatach* — if one first received the blood and then cut — it is *pasul*. Why should the *kabbalah* be invalidated if the severing occurs only after the blood has already been caught? The Gemara says we must infer from this that the blood embedded in the limbs, *dam hamuvla ba-eivarim*, is halachically considered blood — blood that carries the capacity to invalidate. That capillary blood, present throughout the flesh, flows during *shechitah* and can enter the vessel, and if it comes from a limb positioned outside the *Azarah*, it renders the *kabbalah* invalid.

### Dam Hamuvla

The Gemara pauses to examine this assumption. Why should *dam hamuvla ba-eivarim* — the blood embedded within the meat, blood found in capillaries and soft tissue, not the primary life-blood used for the altar service — be treated as halachically significant blood? It is more akin to an irrelevant fluid. If water from outside the *Azarah* were somehow mixed in, it would not invalidate; why then should this embedded blood, which has no function on the *mizbe'ach*, invalidate?

The Gemara responds: *dilma mishum shamnunit* — perhaps the problem is not the blood itself but the *shamnunit*, the fattiness present within the meat. According to Rashi, what invalidates is not the embedded blood per se, which could indeed be treated as irrelevant liquid, but rather that this blood carries with it the fat content of the meat. That fattiness — unlike the *chelev* (the suet-like free-floating fat that is placed on the altar) — is the normal fat embedded within muscle tissue. When a portion of the animal is outside the *Azarah*, that meat and its embedded fat become *pasul* as a component of the sacrifice. When the blood from that limb enters the vessel, it carries with it that invalid fattiness, which mingles with and invalidates the blood in the vessel.

One might ask: why should invalid fat mixed into the blood prevent the blood from being thrown on the altar? The fat itself is not the blood. The prohibition regarding invalid fat is that it may not be burned on the altar — but why does its admixture with the blood prevent the blood from being dashed on the wall of the altar? The Gemara does not resolve this question explicitly, but proceeds on the assumption that such commingling does render the blood unusable.

### Basar Outside Azarah

The Gemara then draws a broader inference. Since the case of the animal with a limb outside was not limited by the Gemara to *kodshei kodashim*, it would seem to apply to *kodshim kalim* as well. This raises a question: *basar kodshei kalim she-yatza lifnei zrikat hadam, pasul?* — does meat of a *kodshim kalim* offering become invalid if it exits the *Azarah* before the blood has been thrown?

This question has practical significance. The relevant zones differ by category of sacrifice. *Kodshei kodashim* must remain entirely within the *Azarah* — meat, blood, and fat alike. *Kodshim kalim*, such as a *shelamim* or *korban pesach*, have a broader zone: once the blood has been thrown and the *korban* is accepted, the meat may be eaten throughout Jerusalem. But what is the status of the meat *before* the blood is thrown? Does the meat's expanded zone (*kol Yerushalayim*) apply from the moment of *shechitah*, or only retroactively once the blood is thrown? In other words, does the meat of a *shelamim* become invalid if removed from the *Azarah* in the period between *shechitah* and *zerikah*?

The Gemara attempts to derive an answer from the case of the animal with a limb outside the *Azarah*, but rejects the inference. *Dilma bekodshei kodashim* — perhaps the ruling in that case was specifically about *kodshei kodashim*, for which there is never any allowance to leave the *Azarah*, not even for meat. If the concern arose from the *shamnunit* — the fattiness — then for *kodshei kodashim* the fattiness of the meat is like the meat, and the meat of *kodshei kodashim* can never exit the *Azarah*. But for *kodshim kalim*, the fattiness of the meat might not be problematic even before *zerikah*, since the meat's ultimate zone is all of Jerusalem. 

Similarly, when the Gemara discusses a case where the animal after *shechitah* thrashed out of the *Azarah* entirely (*pirchasa v'yatzah*), the question arises: what is invalid? By *kodshim kalim*, the meat going outside the *Azarah* might not be the problem. The Gemara answers: *dilma b'alyah v'yoteret hakaved u-shtei haklayot* — perhaps what becomes invalid is not the meat at all, but the *chelev* and the other sacrificial portions — the fat-tail, the diaphragm, the kidneys — which must always remain in the *Azarah* for burning on the altar, and which are invalid if removed even from a *kodshim kalim* sacrifice. The meat, on the other hand, may still be eaten, since ultimately its zone is all of Jerusalem and it is not necessarily invalidated by exiting the *Azarah* before *zerikah*. The question of whether meat of a *kodshim kalim* becomes invalid if it exits the *Azarah* before *zerikah hadam* thus remains unresolved from this passage.

---

## Kodshei Kodashim Location

### Shechitah Batzafon

A *baraita* is introduced: *kodshei kodashim* — the *olah*, *chatat*, and *asham* — require *shechitah* in the north (*batzafon*) and the reception of blood with a *klei sharet* also in the north. To fix the relevant geography: the *Azarah* is divided along its northern boundary, and the area along the north of the altar — *al yerech hamizbe'ach tzafonah* — is where *kodshei kodashim* must be slaughtered. The *baraita* then poses a case: *amad badarom v'hoshit yado latzafon v'shachat* — the *shochet* was standing in the southern half of the *Azarah* but reached his hand into the northern zone and performed the *shechitah*. What is the ruling? *Shechitah zo kesherah* — that *shechitah* is valid. The determinative factor is where the animal is located, not where the *shochet* is standing. The person performing the *shechitah* need not be a *kohen* — *shechitah* may be performed by any Israelite — and therefore there are no requirements governing where the *shochet* must stand. As long as the animal is in the north, the *shechitah* is valid regardless of the *shochet*'s position.

### Kibel Batzafon

With respect to *kabbalah*, however, the rule is different. *Kibel kabbalato pesulah* — if the *kohen* caught the blood while standing in the south, the *kabbalah* is invalid. The *kabbalah* must be performed by a *kohen*, and from the stage of *kabbalah* onward, the *kohen* must himself be in the appropriate zone. By *kodshei kodashim*, not only must the vessel and blood be in the north; the *kohen* performing the *kabbalah* must also be situated in the north.

The *baraita* then addresses partial presence. If the *kohen* was standing in the south but leaned his head and the majority of his body across the line into the north (*hichnis rosho v'rubo*), this counts as though he were fully inside (*k'ilu nichnas kulo*), and the *kabbalah* is valid. One might have assumed that a person is defined by where his feet are planted, but the Gemara rules otherwise for the north-south threshold: the majority of the body, including the head, determines location.

After *shechitah*, if the animal thrashed and moved into the southern zone (*pirchasa v'yatza ladarom*), this does not invalidate — once the *shechitah* and *kabbalah* have been performed validly, the subsequent movement of the carcass within the *Azarah* is inconsequential.

### Kodshim Kalim Location

For *kodshim kalim*, the requirements are calibrated differently. *Shechitatan bifnim* — the *shechitah* need only be inside the *Azarah*, not specifically in the north. *Kibel damam bichlei sharet bifnim* — the blood must also be caught with a *klei sharet* inside the *Azarah*. If the person performing the *shechitah* was standing outside the *Azarah* but reached his hand inside and performed the *shechitah*, it is valid — *shechitato kesherah*. Since *shechitah* requires no *kohen* and imposes no requirement of sacred standing, the *shochet* need not be inside the *Azarah* at all. One could theoretically perform the *shechitah* from any distance, as long as the animal itself is inside the *Azarah*.

For *kabbalah*, however, the *kohen* must be inside the *Azarah*. Here a crucial distinction emerges. For the north-versus-south question within the *Azarah*, we said that if the *kohen* leans his head and majority into the north, he counts as being in the north even if his feet are planted in the south. But for the *Azarah*-versus-outside question, the rule is reversed: *hichnis rosho v'rubo k'ilu lo nichnas* — if his head and the majority of his body lean into the *Azarah* while his feet remain outside, it is as though he has not entered at all.

The reason for this distinction is conceptually significant. The *kohen*'s sanctified status as a servant of the Temple derives from his direct physical connection to its floor — he is barefoot and his feet touch the ground of the *Azarah*, making him part of the apparatus of the *Beit HaMikdash*. When we measure north versus south within the *Azarah*, both zones are already within the sacred precincts, and we may use the majority of the body to determine location. But when determining whether a *kohen* is "inside" the *Azarah* at all, what matters is whether his feet are planted on the sacred ground. A *kohen* whose feet are outside the *Azarah* — even if most of his body leans in — has not established the foundational connection required for the *avodah*.

### Pirchasa V'Yatzah

For *kodshei kodashim*, if the animal thrashed after *shechitah* and exited the *Azarah* entirely, then returned, it is *pasul*. The act of exiting invalidated it. The question raised is: if this is a *shelamim*, why does it matter that the meat exited the *Azarah*? The meat of a *shelamim* is ultimately eaten throughout Jerusalem. The answer, as discussed above, is that the problem lies not with the meat but with the portions that must always remain in the *Azarah* — the *chelev*, the *alyah*, the kidneys. These components of even a *kodshim kalim* sacrifice cannot exit the *Azarah*, and their doing so before *zerikah* renders them invalid for the altar.

---

## Animal/Priest Positioning

### Kula Bifnim

The father of Shmuel posed a question to Shmuel: if the animal was inside the *Azarah* but its legs were outside (*hayu bifnim v'ragleihen bachutz*), what is the ruling? One might have thought this question was already resolved by the earlier discussion — the blood from outside would flow in and render the *kabbalah* invalid. But the question here is framed differently. The father of Shmuel is asking whether the animal is considered halachically "presented before God" when not all of its body is inside, and whether there is an independent requirement that the entire animal stand within the *Azarah*, beyond the concern about blood or fat traveling from outside.

The answer: *v'yuvam laHashem, ad she-tihyeh kula bifnim* — "it shall be brought before God," meaning the entire animal must be inside. This establishes a distinct requirement from the earlier *shamnunit* discussion: not only is there a practical concern about blood or fat from outside invalidating the *kabbalah*, but there is a formal requirement that the entire animal be present within the *Azarah* — all four legs included. Even if one leg is outside, the animal is not considered to be "before God."

### Taluy V'Shachat

Shmuel's father then asked about a suspended animal: *tala v'shachat mahu* — if the animal was hoisted in the air within the *Azarah* and the *shechitah* was performed while it was suspended, what is the ruling? Shmuel answered: *kesherah* — it should be valid. His father replied: *ishtabashta* — you have erred. The verse says *al yerech hamizbe'ach tzafonah* — "by the side of the altar, northward" — and this implies that just as the altar is planted on the ground, so too the animal, at the time of *shechitah* of *kodshei kodashim*, must be standing on the ground. A suspended animal, even if positioned in the correct northern zone, does not satisfy the requirement of *al yerech*.

### Shochet Position

Shmuel then guesses that the next case — the *shochet* himself suspended in the air while performing the *shechitah* — is likewise invalid. His father again corrects him: *shechitah al yerech v'lo shochet al yerech* — it is the *shechitah*, meaning the animal's position, that must satisfy *al yerech*, not the *shochet's* position. The *shochet* need not be in the north, need not be in the *Azarah*, and need not stand on the ground — because *shechitah* does not require a *kohen*, and therefore imposes none of the positioning requirements that attach to a *kohen* performing *avodah*. The *shochet* could, in principle, be suspended in midair.

### Suspension Validity

The series of questions continues. Shmuel's father then asks: *nitla v'kibel mahu* — if the *kohen* himself was suspended in midair while performing the *kabbalah*, what is the ruling? Shmuel guesses invalid, reasoning from the last answer. His father corrects him again: *ishtabashta* — you erred. The problem is not that the *kohen* was physically off the ground in any geometric sense, but that this is not the normal manner of Temple service — *ein derech sheirut bekach*. From the stage of *kabbalah* onward, the *avodah* must be performed in the manner of dignified service to God. A *kohen* suspended in midair does not constitute *derech sheirut*, and the *kabbalah* is therefore invalid. This is distinct from the *shechitah* case, where *derech sheirut* is not required because *shechitah* is not confined to the *kohen*'s act.

The next case: *tala v'kibel mahu* — the animal was suspended and the *kohen* stood on the ground and received the blood. Shmuel guesses invalid, still working from the previous answer. His father again corrects him: *shechitah al yerech v'lo kabbalah al yerech* — the requirement that the animal be situated on the ground (*al yerech*) is derived from the verse about *shechitah*, and applies only to *shechitah*. For *kabbalah*, there is no such verse requiring the animal to be ground-level. The feet of the animal do not need to touch the ground at the time of *kabbalah*.

### Abaye's Stringency

Abaye formulates his own summary. For *kodshei kodashim*, all suspension scenarios are invalid except for the case where the *shochet* himself is suspended — because *shechitah* imposes no *kehunah* requirements on the person performing it. By contrast, Abaye is more stringent than Shmuel's father on one point: he holds that even at the time of *kabbalah*, the feet of the *animal* must be on the ground. He reads *al yerech* as applying both to *shechitah* and to *kabbalah*, not just to *shechitah* alone.

For *kodshim kalim*, Abaye holds that all cases are valid except the case where the *kohen* performing the *kabbalah* is suspended. There is no *al yerech* requirement for *kodshim kalim* — neither for the *shochet* nor for the animal. The only suspension that is invalid is that of the *kohen* during *kabbalah*, which violates *derech sheirut* and the requirements of *kehunah*.

### Rava's Lenient View

Rava challenges Abaye's stringency regarding the animal at the time of *kabbalah* for *kodshei kodashim*. If, for *kodshim kalim*, a suspended animal at the time of *kabbalah* is valid because *avir pnim k'pnim dami* — the airspace within the *Azarah* is halachically equivalent to the *Azarah* itself — then the same principle should apply for *kodshei kodashim*: *avir tzafon k'tzafon dami* — the airspace over the northern zone is halachically equivalent to being in the north. There is no verse requiring the animal's feet to touch the ground at the time of *kabbalah*; the verse *al yerech* is uniquely bound to *shechitah*. Therefore, Rava argues that suspension of the animal at *kabbalah* is not independently derived and should not invalidate.

Rava's conclusion: for both *kodshei kodashim* and *kodshim kalim*, all cases involving a suspended animal are valid — except for one: the *shechitah* of *kodshei kodashim* where the animal is suspended, which is excluded by *al yerech hamizbe'ach tzafonah*. And in every category of sacrifice, if the *kohen* performing the *kabbalah* is himself suspended, that is invalid on account of *ein derech sheirut bekach* — it does not constitute proper priestly service. This applies equally to *kodshei kodashim* and *kodshim kalim*.

### Tzitzit Outside

The daf concludes with a question posed by Rav Yirmeyah to Rabbi Zeira. If the *kohen* is standing fully inside the *Azarah* — his feet planted on the sacred ground — but his *tzitzit*, a strand of hair (literally, his forelock or ponytail), extends outside the *Azarah*, what is the ruling at the time of *kabbalah*?

Rabbi Zeira answers by referencing the principle already established regarding the animal: *v'yuvam laHashem, ad she-tihyeh kula bifnim* — "it shall come before God," meaning the entire entity must be inside. The same applies to the *kohen*: *bevo'am el ohel mo'ed* — "when they enter the Tent of Meeting" — implies that the *kohen* must be fully present, *kulo l'ohel mo'ed*, not merely his feet and the majority of his body. Even a single strand of hair outside the *Azarah* at the time of *kabbalah* would constitute a deficiency in that complete presence.

This stands in sharp contrast to *shechitah*, where the *shochet* can stand outside the *Azarah*, can be suspended in midair, and faces virtually no locational requirements. From the moment of *kabbalah* onward, however — where *kehunah* is required — the *kohen* must be entirely and completely present within the sacred precincts. There is, embedded here, a teaching that resonates beyond the narrow *halakha*: when one is engaged in the *avodah* that requires the full weight of *kehunah*, one must be wholly present — not physically divided between the sacred and the outside.

---

---

# Zevachim 27

## Shelo Bimkomo K'Bimkomo

### Mishnah Blood Placement

The *daf* opens by continuing a list of procedural defects that can invalidate a *korban*. An earlier *mishnah* had addressed the failure to catch the blood in a *kli shareit*; the present *mishnah* turns to invalid placements of the blood on the *mizbe'ach* itself. The cases enumerated are: placing the blood on the *kevesh* (the ramp leading up to the altar) rather than on the altar walls proper; placing it on the section of the altar wall opposite the southeast corner, which lacked a *yesod* (base) beneath it; placing blood that was designated for below the dividing line (*lemata*) above that line (*lemala*), or vice versa; and placing blood designated for the inner altar on the outer altar, or the reverse.

In all such cases the verdict is *pasul* — the sacrifice has been invalidated. The *mishnah* then adds the phrase *ve'ein bo karet*: one who eats the meat does not incur *karet*. This clause is not addressing any question about the *kohen*'s liability for mishandling the blood. Rather, it is clarifying that the meat does not acquire the status of *pigul*. *Pigul*, as will become relevant throughout the discussion, is the specific invalidity that results from a wrong-time thought during the *avodah* and that renders the meat subject to *karet* for one who eats it. The *mishnah* is telling us that although the *korban* has been invalidated, the meat is not *pigul* — whoever eats it does not incur *karet*.

### Shmuel's Position

The *gemara* opens with a striking statement from Shmuel: *pasul basar, aval be'alim nitkapru* — the meat is invalidated, but the owners have achieved *kaparah*. This is a surprising reading of the *mishnah*'s language of *pasul*. One would naturally assume that *pasul* means the entire *korban* is void. Shmuel, however, draws a distinction: when the blood reaches the *mizbe'ach* even in the wrong location, the *korban* does achieve atonement for its owners *bidi'avad*; it is only the meat that may not be eaten.

This introduces a novel conceptual model. Earlier in the *masechet* we encountered cases where the meat could be eaten but the *korban* had not atoned for the owners — a valid *korban* that was simply unconnected to the owners' obligation. Here we have almost the inverse: the owners are atoned for, the obligation is fulfilled, yet the meat cannot be eaten. It is as if the blood's work of *kaparah* is severed from the status of the meat. The *korban* functions on behalf of the owners but remains somehow incomplete in its own identity.

### Scriptural Source

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is Shmuel's reason? The answer is a *pasuk* (Vayikra 17:11): *ve'ani netativ lachem al ha-mizbe'ach lechaper* — "And I have given it to you upon the altar to atone." The verse speaks of blood placed "upon the altar" without specifying the precise location, implying that blood anywhere on the *mizbe'ach* achieves *kaparah*. Hence: *keivan she-higia dam la-mizbe'ach nitkapru be'alim* — once the blood reaches the altar, the owners have atoned.

It is worth noting that *Tosafot* flags two boundary questions. First, does this principle extend to the *kevesh* as well? Is the ramp considered part of the altar for this purpose? Second, does it apply to blood designated for the inner altar? When the *pasuk* says "upon the altar," it likely refers to the outer altar. So the scope of Shmuel's ruling — while certain at its core regarding above-and-below placements — may be subject to debate at the margins.

The *gemara* then presses: *ei hachi, basar nami* — if the *korban* worked, why not permit the meat as well? The *gemara* answers from the same *pasuk*: *lechaper netativ, velo le-davar acher* — "for atonement I gave it," and not for any other purpose. The *pesukim* that specify precise locations for the blood are what govern the *korban*'s full validity, including the permissibility of the meat. The broad verse enables *kaparah* in any location, but the specific directives are what render the meat edible. Without precise placement, the owners atone but the meat remains forbidden.

Shmuel's position is thus formulated by the *gemara* as: *shelo bimkomo k'bimkomo dami* — the wrong place on the *mizbe'ach* is treated as if it were the right place. The "as-if," however, is partial: it is sufficient for *kaparah* but insufficient to validate the meat. The wrong location is close enough to the right place for atonement to take effect, but the full identity of a valid *korban* — including the permissibility of eating the meat — requires precision.

### Challenge to Shmuel

The *gemara* challenges Shmuel from a *mishnah* quoted from a later *perek*: if blood was placed on the ramp and not opposite the *yesod*, or if it was placed above when it should have been below (or vice versa), or inside when it should have been outside, then — *im yesh dam ha-nefesh, yachzor ha-kasher ve-yekabel* — if there is remaining life-blood from the animal, a qualified *kohen* should re-catch the blood and perform the application properly.

This *mishnah* implies that the incorrect placement achieved nothing — it did not invalidate, but neither did it accomplish anything. If there is blood remaining, do it again properly. That reading sits comfortably with a view that the wrong placement is simply meaningless. But it directly challenges Shmuel: if the first application already atoned for the owners, why redo the blood? The *gemara* anticipates a possible answer — perhaps the redo is motivated by the desire to permit the meat — but immediately rejects it: *mi ika zrika d'lo mechaperes ve-sharya basar be-achilah?* Can there be an act of blood application that is not an act of *kaparah* and yet independently permits the meat? The eating of the meat is a byproduct of the *kaparah*; once the *korban* has atoned, no subsequent blood application can stand on its own to permit the meat. So according to Shmuel, the *mishnah*'s instruction to redo the blood proves that the first application achieved nothing — which contradicts Shmuel's position.

### Invalid Kohen's Role

The *gemara* resolves this by contextualizing the *mishnah*. The earlier *mishnah* from which this case is drawn was discussing an invalid *kohen* — and this is reflected in the language *yachzor ha-kasher*, "let the qualified one return," which implies the first application was done by an unqualified person. The *gemara* therefore answers: *ee d'avid kasher hachi nami* — if the first application was performed by a valid *kohen*, then according to Shmuel the deal is sealed. The *korban* has atoned, the meat cannot be eaten, and there is no further blood application that can be performed. The instruction to redo the blood applies only when the first application was done by a *pasul kohen* — in which case it was entirely meaningless, regardless of where on the altar it was placed.

This generates a further question: why is a *pasul kohen*'s action so completely without effect? The *gemara* explores whether a *pasul kohen*'s act of *zrika* should constitute a *deichuy* — a definitive rejection of the *korban* that forecloses any redo. The *gemara* cites a *mishnah*: if all the *pesulim* — invalid persons — caught the blood while entertaining a thought of the wrong time or wrong place, the instruction is still *im yesh dam ha-nefesh, yachzor ha-kasher ve-yekabel*. The wrong thoughts of a *pasul kohen* do not invalidate.

The *gemara* initially considers inferring from the phrase *kibla, in; zarka, lo* — that this rule (that the *pasul*'s actions are irrelevant) applies only to catching the blood, not to throwing it. Perhaps if the *pasul kohen* performs the *zrika*, that constitutes a *deichuy* and the *korban* cannot be redone. The *gemara* then considers and rejects several formulations, ultimately reaching Rava's principle.

## Invalid Kohen & Intent

### Thoughts & Kabbalah

The *mishnah* establishes that if invalid persons — those who are *pesulim* — performed the *kabbalat ha-dam* (catching of the blood) while entertaining a thought of the wrong time or wrong place, their thoughts do not invalidate the *korban*. The instruction remains: if life-blood is available, a valid *kohen* should re-catch it and proceed properly. This teaches that a *pasul kohen*'s mental intent during *kabbalah* is legally irrelevant.

### Redo Question

The *gemara* asks whether this principle — that the *pasul*'s action is irrelevant and permits a redo — applies equally to the *zrika* (the throwing of the blood onto the altar). The initial reading of the *mishnah* might suggest that only *kabbalah* is covered by the instruction to redo, and that *zrika* by a *pasul* would constitute a *deichuy*, a definitive invalidation that forecloses correction. The *gemara* entertains this reading and then challenges it.

If the *pasul kohen*'s wrong thought does not invalidate during *kabbalah*, why would it invalidate during *zrika*? The *gemara* considers answering that the two stages are different: *kabbalah* is not the act of *kaparah*, so a *pasul*'s participation there is truly null; *zrika* is the act of *kaparah*, and perhaps there the *pasul kohen*'s act carries enough weight to constitute a rejection. The *gemara* then attempts a different answer — that the combination of being *pasul* and having a wrong thought creates an invalidation — but this is rejected as internally inconsistent: since a wrong thought by a *pasul kohen* is irrelevant (as Rava will explain), the combination of the two cannot produce an invalidation that neither produces alone.

### Rava's Principle

Rava articulates the foundational rule: *ein machshava mo'eles ela be-mi she-ra'uy la-avoda* — intent is legally operative only when the person performing the act is qualified for the *avodah*. Rava adds two further conditions: the matter being performed must itself be appropriate to the *avodah*, and it must be performed in the right location. Since a *pasul kohen* is not *ra'uy la-avoda*, his thoughts — whether of *shelo bizmano*, *shelo bimkomo*, or anything else — have no legal traction whatsoever. They cannot invalidate, and they cannot create *pigul*.

### Mishnah Reading

With Rava's principle established, the *gemara* offers the correct reading of the *mishnah*. The clause referring to *kabbalah* onward is not meant to exclude *zrika* from the same leniency. Rather, the *mishnah* teaches that from *kabbalah* and beyond — through *zrika* — a *pasul kohen*'s thoughts are irrelevant. The *mishnah* is not creating a contrast between *kabbalah* and *zrika*; it is marking the point from which the *pasul*'s thoughts become entirely without effect.

The reason is grounded in Rava's principle: a *pasul kohen* does not belong in the role at all from *kabbalah* onward (since *kabbalah* and *zrika* are *avodot* requiring a valid *kohen*). His thoughts, therefore, are incapable of effecting *pasul*. What does remain meaningful even for an invalid person is *shechita*, which does not require a *kohen* at all. If the *pasul kohen* performed the *shechita* with a wrong thought of *shelo bimkomo*, that thought does carry legal weight — because in the act of *shechita*, he is in fact *ra'uy la-avoda*. The *mishnah*'s structure reflects precisely this: prior to *kabbalah*, his role is legitimate and his thoughts operative; from *kabbalah* onward, he is disqualified and his thoughts irrelevant.

## Wrong Place & Pigul

### Two Thoughts Scenario

The *mishnah* introduces a case involving two sequential thoughts during *shechita*. A *kohen* performs the *shechita* while first entertaining an irrelevant thought — such as planning to place the blood at the wrong location on the *mizbe'ach* today — and then entertaining a second thought of *chutz limkomo* (wrong place) or *chutz lizmano* (wrong time). The question is how each thought, and their combination, affects the status of the *korban*.

A thought during *shechita* of merely a different location on the same altar — intending to do it at the wrong place today — is by itself a neutral, legally inconsequential thought. Not every wrong intention invalidates; only the specific categories of *shelo bimkomo* and *shelo bizmano* in the relevant halakhic sense produce legal consequences. A vague plan to do the *zrika* at a slightly different location, intended for immediate execution, is treated as an irrelevant thought. Consequently, a subsequent second thought — of *chutz limkomo* or *chutz lizmano* — still has operative force, because the first thought did not disturb the *korban*'s validity. If that second thought is *chutz limkomo*, the *korban* is *pasul* but there is no *karet*; if it is *chutz lizmano*, the *korban* is *pigul* and *karet* applies.

The *mishnah* also presents the scenario of thinking during *shechita* that one will perform the *zrika* at the wrong place on the *mizbe'ach* tomorrow. This is *pasul* without being *pigul*, and a subsequent second thought — whether of *chutz lizmano* or *chutz limkomo* — cannot transform it into *pigul*, since the *korban* is already invalid.

### Pigul Question

This raises a sharp question that the *gemara* frames explicitly: *v'ee shelo bimkomo k'bimkomo dami* — if, according to Shmuel, the wrong place on the altar is treated as equivalent to the right place, then a thought during *shechita* of performing the *zrika* at the wrong place tomorrow should constitute a *pigul* thought. After all, you are planning to do the *zrika* in a way that, according to Shmuel, achieves *kaparah* — and you are planning to do it tomorrow. Why is this not *pigul*?

### Pigul Condition

Mar Zutra answers: *zrika de-sharya basar be-achilah mayti lidei pigul; zrika de-lo sharya basar be-achilah lo mayti lidei pigul*. A *zrika* that would render the meat permissible for eating can generate *pigul* when done at the wrong time; a *zrika* that would not render the meat permissible — even if it achieves *kaparah* — cannot generate *pigul*. The halakhic category of *pigul* is anchored in the *pasuk* (Vayikra 7:18): *im he'achol ye'achel mi-besar zevach shelamav pigul yihiyeh* — the entire framework is about eating the meat. Therefore, a thought during *shechita* about performing *zrika* in a way that will not make the meat edible is outside the *parsha* of *pigul* entirely. A *zrika* at the wrong place on the altar, even granting Shmuel's view that it achieves *kaparah*, does not permit the meat. A thought about such a *zrika* therefore cannot be a *pigul* thought.

### Scriptural Limit

Rav Ashi challenges Mar Zutra on his source: *minalach ha?* Where do you derive this? The *pasuk* states *im he'achol ye'achel mi-besar zevach shelamav pigul yihiyeh* — *mi she-pigulo garam lo*, the *pigul* thought must itself be the cause of the meat's prohibition. If it is something other than the *pigul* thought that renders the meat inedible — namely, the fact that the *zrika* was performed at the wrong location — then the *parsha* of *pigul* does not apply. Here, what makes the meat forbidden is the wrong-place *zrika*, not the wrong-time thought. Consequently, a thought about doing a wrong-place *zrika* tomorrow is not a *pigul* thought.

This being established, the *gemara* asks a further question: *ei hachi, ipsulei nami lo lipsol* — if the thought about a wrong-place *zrika* tomorrow is outside the *pigul* framework entirely, why does it invalidate the *korban* at all? The *gemara* answers, citing Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yehuda: it is comparable to a thought of *hinuach* — a plan simply not to throw the blood at all. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a thought to withhold the blood is itself a sufficiently significant *machshava* to invalidate the *korban*, even without producing *pigul*. Planning to perform the *zrika* at the wrong place tomorrow is treated as tantamount to planning not to perform the *zrika* at all, and that is enough to invalidate.

## Resh Lakish Position

### Resh Lakish Agrees

Resh Lakish now enters the discussion. His position is, at first glance, surprising: *le-olam pasul mamash* — when the *mishnah* says *pasul*, it means categorically invalid, not merely that the meat is forbidden while the *korban* still atones. The *korban* does not atone at all when the blood is placed at the wrong location. However — and this is the striking part — Resh Lakish does not disagree with Shmuel's underlying principle. He actually accepts that in general *shelo bimkomo k'bimkomo dami*: a wrong-place blood application does achieve *kaparah*. What Resh Lakish disputes is the reading of the *mishnah*. He holds that our *mishnah* is dealing with a specific scenario — one involving a wrong-time thought — and that in that scenario the *korban* is categorically invalid.

## Resh Lakish Position (II)

### Silent vs. Articulated

Resh Lakish resolves the apparent tension between his reading of the *mishnah* and his agreement with Shmuel's principle by distinguishing between two cases: *kan she-natan bi-sh'tika, kan she-natan bi-amira* — one case where the blood was placed silently (without a disqualifying thought), and one where it was placed with an articulated intent. When the blood is placed at the wrong location without any additional wrong thought, Shmuel's principle applies: *kaparah* is achieved, though the meat is forbidden. But our *mishnah* is describing a case where the *kohen* who placed the blood at the wrong location was simultaneously entertaining a *shelo bizmano* thought — a wrong-time intent.

### Pigul Analysis

The proof that the *mishnah* must be describing such a scenario is embedded in the *mishnah*'s own language. The *mishnah* concludes with the phrase *ve'ein bo karet*. This phrase requires explanation: the only circumstance in which eating forbidden sacrificial meat incurs *karet* is in the case of *pigul*. If the *mishnah* needs to explicitly tell us there is no *karet*, it can only be because we might have thought the meat was *pigul*. And the only way we would think that is if the case involves a *shelo bizmano* thought — a thought that would ordinarily create *pigul* — which the *mishnah* then tells us does not result in *pigul* here, precisely because the *zrika* was performed at the wrong location and therefore does not make the meat edible, placing it outside the *parsha* of *pigul* (as Mar Zutra explained). Resh Lakish thus reads the *mishnah* as: the *kohen* performed the *zrika* at the wrong place while thinking *shelo bizmano*; the *korban* is categorically *pasul*; and the *mishnah* specifies *ein bo karet* to tell us that this does not constitute *pigul*, because the wrong-place *zrika* is not the kind of act that can produce *pigul*.

Since Resh Lakish's substantive position mirrors Shmuel's, all the challenges previously mounted against Shmuel apply equally to Resh Lakish, and the *gemara* disposes of them with the same answers, compressing the repetition with the notation *ad midei de-hava a-machsheves hinuach ve-aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda ve-chulei*.

## Rabbi Yochanan

### Wrong Place Nothing

Rabbi Yochanan now presents the genuinely dissenting position: *idi va-idi bi-sh'tika* — whether done silently or with a wrong thought, *shelo bimkomo lav k'imkomo dami*. The wrong place on the *mizbe'ach* is simply not equivalent to the right place. There is no partial-*kaparah* model; the *korban* does not atone at all. The *mishnah*'s language of *pasul* means exactly what it says — total invalidity. Consequently, there is no novel conceptual model required, and the *mishnah* need not be read as addressing any special scenario of concurrent wrong-time thoughts. The *pasul* is absolute and unqualified.

However — and this is the defining feature of Rabbi Yochanan's view — the wrong-place *zrika* is so entirely without effect that it does not even invalidate the *korban* in the sense of foreclosing a redo. It is as if nothing happened. Therefore, if life-blood remains, a valid *kohen* may re-perform the *zrika* properly and the *korban* can yet be validated. The *mishnah*'s instruction to redo the blood flows naturally from this: since the wrong-place application was null, the blood can be done again.

The *gemara* notes the difficulty in Rabbi Yochanan's position regarding the phrase *ve'ein bo karet*. According to Resh Lakish, that phrase is necessary because the case involves a *shelo bizmano* thought and one might have assumed *pigul*. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds the wrong-place *zrika* is simply nothing — like not having thrown the blood at all — there would never have been any reason to suspect *karet*. The phrase is superfluous. The *gemara* marks this as *kasha* without resolving it.

As for Shmuel, the *gemara* harmonizes him with Resh Lakish: the *ain bo karet* clause informs us that even if one were to perform the *zrika* in the wrong place accompanied by a *pigul*-type thought, the wrong-place context prevents the meat from being rendered edible, and since *pigul* requires that the thought be about an act that would otherwise make the meat edible, no *karet* ever applies. Thus both Shmuel and Resh Lakish read the *mishnah* as: meat forbidden, *korban* atones (in the general case), and no *pigul* can ever attach to a wrong-place *zrika*.

### Reuse Question

Having established that according to Rabbi Yochanan the wrong-place *zrika* achieves nothing, the *gemara* presses a further question: *li-havei ki-nishpach min ha-kli al ha-ritzpah ve-yasfenu* — if the wrong-place application is truly nothing, it should be no different from blood that spilled from the vessel onto the floor. And we have learned that blood spilled onto the floor — if it was originally caught in a *kli shareit* — may be gathered and reused. So why does the *mishnah* require new blood (*dam ha-nefesh*) for the redo? According to Rabbi Yochanan, one should simply scrape the blood off the wrong section of the altar and reapply it correctly.

### Rav Chisda Distinction

The *gemara* answers in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *savar lah k'man de-amar lo yasfenu* — Rabbi Yochanan holds the position that even when a *zrika* achieves nothing, once the blood is on the altar, the altar "absorbs" it (*mizbe'ach kolet*) and it may not be reused. This is Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef's report of Rabbi Yochanan's view: everyone agrees that if blood was placed in the right location — even if the *zrika* was somehow defective — it cannot be gathered and reapplied. The debate is only whether blood placed in the wrong location on the *mizbe'ach* may be reused.

Rav Chisda then sharpens the picture. He reports in the name of Avimi that in fact everyone agrees: blood placed in the wrong position on the same *mizbe'ach* — above when it should have been below, or below when it should have been above — cannot be reused. This is not like blood spilled on the floor. Once on the altar, even at the wrong location, it cannot be gathered for reuse. The sole debate between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon concerns blood placed on the wrong *altar* entirely — blood designated for the outer altar that was placed on the inner, or vice versa. That scenario, involving a physically distinct object, may be more analogous to spillage onto the floor, and there the opinions diverge. Rabbi Yose holds it may be reused; Rabbi Shimon holds it may not. 

Rav Chisda adds a further observation about relative proximity: blood designated for above the line that was placed below is, in a sense, closer to its correct location than blood designated for below that was placed above, because blood naturally flows downward. Blood that should have been above would eventually drip downward, making below a closer approximation to the right place than above would be for blood meant to go below. This ranking, however, does not affect the operative ruling.

Our *mishnah*, which instructs the *kohen* to obtain *dam ha-nefesh* for the redo rather than gathering blood from the altar, aligns with the view that the blood on the altar cannot be reused — whether following the version of the debate attributed to Rabbi Yochanan (where the debate concerns wrong-position on the same altar) or Rav Chisda's version (where everyone agrees on the same-altar case and the debate is only about the wrong altar).

## Limbs on Altar Rule

### Al Mokdah Rule

The *gemara* now introduces Rav Nachman's observation that the very *mishnah* we have been analyzing provides independent support for certain conclusions about the reuse of blood. The *mishnah* cites the verse *Zot ha-Torah, hi ha-olah al mokdah al ha-mizbe'ach* — "This is the law of the *olah*: it shall remain on the altar's fire." From this verse the principle is derived: once the limbs of a *korban* have been placed on the altar to burn, they do not come down, even if the *korban* was in some respect invalid.

### Rabbi Yehudah Exceptions

Rabbi Yehudah, however, limits this rule. He interprets the repeated and seemingly limiting language in the verse — *zot, hi, ha-olah* — as exclusionary markers (*mi'utim*) teaching that certain severely invalid *korbanot* do not benefit from the *al mokdah* rule. Specifically, Rabbi Yehudah lists: an animal slaughtered at night (*she-nishchata ba-lailah*), one whose blood was spilled (*she-nishpach damah*), and one whose blood was carried outside the precinct of the *Mikdash* (*she-yatza damah chutz la-kela'im*).
