In these cases, if the limbs were placed on the altar, they must be removed, because the blood never properly performed its function and the *korban* was fundamentally broken from the outset.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon takes the more expansive position. His starting point is that only a valid *olah* is mentioned in the verse, which might imply that only a fully kosher *olah* may remain on the altar. But Rabbi Shimon reads the verse's additional language — *Torat ha-olah* — as an inclusive broadening: *Torah achat le-kol ha-olim, she-im alu lo yerdu* — one law for all that ascend, that once on the altar they do not come down.

Rabbi Shimon then proceeds to include in this leniency even cases that Rabbi Yehudah would have required removed: an animal slaughtered at night, one whose blood was spilled, one whose blood exited the precinct, *notar* and *yotzei* (meat left overnight or taken outside), *tamei* animals, animals slaughtered *chutz lizmano* or *chutz limkomo* (creating *pigul*), cases where invalid *kohanim* caught and threw the blood, and cases where the blood was applied at the wrong location on the altar.

Rabbi Shimon, however, does draw a line. He excludes: an animal used for bestiality (*ha-rovea ve-ha-nirba*), one set aside for idolatry (*muktzeh*), one worshipped as an idol (*ne'evad*), the *esnan* and *mechir* (a prostitute's hire or the price of a dog), *kilayim* (a hybrid animal), a *treifah* (an animal with a fatal defect), and an animal born by caesarean section (*yotzei dofen*). These must come down even after having been placed on the altar.

### Timing Criteria

The basis for Rabbi Shimon's distinction is: *marbeh ani et elu she-hayah psulan ba-kodesh* — I include those whose disqualification arose within the sacred precincts, i.e., during the course of the *avodah* itself. Whatever problem occurred after the animal entered the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* is an internal *avodah* failure, and the *al mokdah* principle still applies. But the excluded cases — bestiality, idolatry, *treifah*, hybrid species, and the like — are problems that predate the animal's entry into the *Mikdash* entirely. They are constitutional defects, unrelated to the performance of the *avodah*, and such animals are so fundamentally ineligible that even after being placed on the altar they must be removed.

### Wrong Place vs Spilled

The *gemara* draws a critical inference from this *mishnah*. Rabbi Shimon's list includes both the case of spilled blood (*nishpach damah*) and the case of wrong-location blood (*ha-nitnin le-ma'ala she-nasan le-mata, ve-ha-nitnin le-mata she-nasan le-ma'ala*), and in both cases he says the limbs may remain on the altar. But note that Rabbi Yehudah — who disagrees with Rabbi Shimon and says spilled blood requires the limbs to be removed — does not disagree with regard to wrong-location blood. That is, Rabbi Yehudah concedes that wrong-location blood is better than spilled blood: the limbs placed on the altar after a wrong-location *zrika* do not have to come down, even according to Rabbi Yehudah.

Now, if we follow Rabbi Yochanan's view that wrong-place *zrika* achieves nothing — is completely null — then the case of wrong-location blood should be indistinguishable from spilled blood. If Rabbi Yehudah requires the limbs to come down when the blood was spilled, he should equally require them to come down when the blood was placed at the wrong location, since both cases represent a failure of the blood to perform its *avodah*. Yet Rabbi Yehudah does not require removal in the wrong-location case.

The *gemara* concludes: *lav mishum d'kaltah mizbe'ach* — the explanation is that the altar "absorbs" the blood even when it is placed in the wrong location. Even if the wrong-place *zrika* achieves nothing in terms of *kaparah*, the blood has nonetheless reached the *mizbe'ach*, and that contact with the altar carries its own legal consequence. The altar's absorption of the blood — even at the wrong place — is sufficient to distinguish the case from spilled blood, and consequently: (a) the limbs placed on the altar need not come down, and (b) *shema mina lo yasfenu* — the blood may not be gathered from the altar and reused.

This confirms, even within Rabbi Yochanan's framework, that wrong-place blood is not simply equivalent to blood spilled on the floor. It is legally null for purposes of *kaparah*, but it is not null with respect to the altar itself. Once blood touches the *mizbe'ach*, even ineffectually, it is "absorbed" — it cannot be removed and reapplied, and the limbs placed above it are not subject to removal.

# Zevachim 28

## Inner Altar Sanctifies

### Rabbi Eliezer's View

The sugya opens with a statement attributed to Rabbi Eliezer near the beginning of 27b, just before the lines widen: *mizbeach hapnimi mekadesh psulim* — the inner altar sanctifies invalid offerings. This principle emerges in the context of a broader discussion about what happens when the *dam* of a sacrifice is applied to the wrong part or the wrong altar. As established in the preceding analysis, the question is whether misplaced blood accomplishes anything at all, or whether it accomplishes just enough to permit the limbs that have already been placed on the altar to remain there.

The specific application here is striking. If a *kohen* took the blood designated for the outer altar and instead brought it to the inner altar — an act that itself *invalidates* the blood — can the limbs placed on the outer altar subsequently remain? Rabbi Eliezer holds that yes, even this invalid application to the inner altar is sufficient to allow the limbs to remain. Crucially, this does not mean the *korban* has been validly offered, that anyone has fulfilled their obligation, or that the meat is permitted for consumption. It means only that the blood has reached *some* altar, and that threshold suffices to prevent the limbs from being removed.

### Blood Location Validity

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *mai kamashma lan tanina* — what novelty is Rabbi Eliezer introducing? This same point appears to be covered by the earlier *baraisa* attributed to Rabbi Shimon, which lists scenarios including inner blood applied to the outer altar and outer blood applied to the inner altar, in all of which the limbs may remain. The Gemara assumes Rabbi Yehuda concurs with these scenarios, since his dissent in that *baraisa* is limited specifically to the case where the blood was spilled entirely — only there does he require the limbs to be removed. So what *chiddush* does Rabbi Eliezer add?

The Gemara answers: *ei mehatam havah amina hani mili dam* — had we learned only from that earlier source, we might have restricted the principle to blood. Blood, after all, sometimes belongs on the inner altar, as on Yom Kippur. One could argue that blood placed on the inner altar retains some residual legitimacy because blood has a legitimate relationship with that surface. But what about a *komets* — the handful of a *mincha* offering — placed on the inner altar? A *komets* has no business there whatsoever. The verse states explicitly: *lo ta'alu alav ketoret zarah ve'olah u'mincha* — do not offer upon it foreign incense, an *olah*, or a *mincha*. Given this explicit prohibition, one might have thought that placing a *komets* on the inner altar accomplishes nothing, leaving it subject to removal. Therefore, *ka mashma lan*: even the *komets* on the inner altar is sanctified to the degree that it may remain and continue to burn — and this despite the fact that leaving it there appears to continue the violation of the *lo ta'aleh alav* prohibition. The *chiddush* is that *lechatchila lo ta'aleh alav* — one may not do this in the first place — but *bedi'eved*, once it is there, it may remain.

### Ketoret Zarah Issue

The Gemara now raises a challenge from a *baraisa*: *ketoret zarah she'alah legabei mizbeach tered* — foreign incense that was placed on the altar must be brought down. This is precisely analogous to the case of Nadav and Avihu, who brought incense they were not licensed to offer. If the *ketoret zarah* must be removed, why should the *komets* of a *mincha* be permitted to remain? Both appear in the same verse of prohibition.

The immediate reading of this *baraisa* seems to say: only the outer altar sanctifies invalid items; the inner altar does not. Perhaps the inner altar works for blood — since blood sometimes legitimately belongs there — but not for *mincha* or *ketoret*. This reading would directly contradict the position that the inner altar sanctifies even things not fit for it.

### Outer Altar Reading

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by rereading the *baraisa*. The correct reading is: *ketoret zarah she'alah lemizbeach hachitzon tered* — it is *ketoret zarah* placed on the *outer* altar that must be removed. Why? *She'ein mizbeach hachitzon mekadesh pesulim ela hara'ui lo* — the outer altar sanctifies only those things that are fit for it. *Ketoret* is not fit for the outer altar; therefore it does not become sanctified there and must be taken down.

This reading, far from limiting the inner altar, actually leaves it untouched by the *baraisa* entirely. The *baraisa* says nothing about the inner altar's inability to sanctify *ketoret* or *mincha*; it says only that the outer altar cannot sanctify *ketoret zarah*.

### Inner vs Outer Power

Once the *baraisa* is reread this way, the conclusion is the inverse of the initial impression: *ve'hapenimi bein ra'ui lo bein she'ein ra'ui lo* — the inner altar sanctifies both things that are fit for it and things that are not fit for it. The inner altar is actually *more* powerful than the outer one, not less.

What accounts for this? *Hai ritzpa v'hai kli shares* — the outer altar has the status of the floor of the *Beis HaMikdash*, something fixed and immovable, while the inner altar carries the additional status of a *kli shares*, a sacred vessel. While one might intuitively assume the permanent structure of the *Mikdash* would be more sanctified than its vessels, the Gemara holds otherwise: the *kli shares* status of the inner altar confers a higher degree of sanctity. As a result, even explicit violations of *lo ta'aleh alav ketoret zarah ve'olah u'mincha* — once accomplished — do not require removal. The inner altar's sanctity is so great that it absorbs even these misplaced items. This is a remarkable *chiddush*: the inner altar is not weaker than the outer one with respect to sanctifying invalid items; it is stronger, and its power extends even to things that flagrantly do not belong upon it.

---

## Piggul & Chutz

### Machsheves Chutz

Having concluded the extended digression into the laws of blood placement and altar sanctity, the Gemara now arrives at the *mishna* that introduces the thought-based invalidities of *piggul* — a subject the *masechet* has been circling for many pages and will continue to develop throughout. The *mishna* opens: *hashochet et hazevach lizrok damo bachutz* — if one slaughters a sacrifice with the intent to throw its blood outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. Like the invalidity of *shelo lishmo*, the thought invalidates beginning already at *shechita*. The *mishna* then enumerates parallel cases: even if one intends to throw only part of the blood outside; to burn the *imurim* outside; to burn only part of them; to eat the meat outside; to eat even a single *kezayis* of the meat outside; or even to eat a *kezayis* of the skin of the fat tail outside. In all these cases, the *mishna* rules *pasul ve'ein bo karet* — the sacrifice is invalid but carries no *karet* penalty for one who subsequently eats from it.

### Chutz Limkomo

This category — intending to perform an act in the wrong *place* — is *chutz limkomo*. It is the counterpart to true *piggul* but distinct from it: the invalidity arises not from a thought about the wrong *time* but about the wrong *location*. Because it is not genuine *piggul*, it does not carry *karet*.

Before proceeding to the stronger form of invalidity, it is important to appreciate what these thoughts have in common. The *mishna* is careful to list only thoughts whose content relates to acts of eating: either the eating of the meat by a person, or the "eating" of the altar, meaning the *dam* placed upon it and the fats and limbs burned upon it. A thought about the wrong time or place only invalidates when it concerns one of these four *avodos* — *shechita*, *kabala*, *holacha*, *zerика* — and when its content pertains to an act of eating. This principle will prove critical to the debates about the fat tail skin that follow.

### Piggul Proper

The second half of the *mishna* presents the stronger category. If one slaughtered with intent to throw the blood *tomorrow* (*lemachar*), or some of the blood tomorrow, or to burn the *imurim* tomorrow, or some of them, or to eat the meat tomorrow, or a *kezayis* of the meat tomorrow, or even a *kezayis* of the skin of the fat tail tomorrow — in all these cases the ruling is *piggul ve'chayavim alav karet*. This is true *piggul*, the wrong-time invalidity, and carries the full *karet* penalty for one who eats the meat afterward.

It is worth noting one nuance regarding the word *lemachar*: in the case of a *shlamim*, which is permitted for eating over two days, the wrong-time thought would need to contemplate eating on the *third* day, not merely the next day. The very paradigm case of *piggul* in the Torah involves a *shlamim*, precisely because its extended permitted eating period makes "the third day" the relevant threshold.

---

## Fat Tail Skin Debate

### Samuel's View

The Gemara's immediate focus is the repeated appearance of *or ha'alya* — the skin of the fat tail — in both halves of the *mishna*. *Savruha or alya k'alya dami* — the Gemara initially assumes that the skin of the fat tail is like the fat tail itself, meaning it is categorized as something burned on the altar rather than something eaten by a person. On this reading, the skin goes onto the *mizbeach* along with the fat.

### Challenge to Samuel

This assumption immediately generates a difficulty. If the skin of the fat tail is like the fat tail — an item that belongs to the altar's "eating" — then why does thinking about eating it at the wrong time or wrong place invalidate the sacrifice? Doing so would constitute *kamachashev me'achilat mizbeach l'achilat adam* — taking something belonging to the altar's consumption and redirecting the thought toward human consumption. Generally, such a cross-category thought is not a valid *piggul* thought. The thought must concern eating what is meant to be eaten by a person (at the wrong time/place) or burning what is meant to be burned (at the wrong time/place). Transplanting an item across these categories should not invalidate.

The Gemara answers: *amar Shmuel ha meni Rabbi Eliezer hi* — Shmuel explains that the *mishna* follows the minority opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that *machashev me'achilat mizbeach l'achilat adam u'me'achilat adam l'achilat mizbeach* — a cross-category thought *does* invalidate in both directions. A thought to burn something that should be eaten, or to eat something that should be burned, is still a *piggul*-type thought according to Rabbi Eliezer.

The source for Rabbi Eliezer's position is a *mishna* cited by the Gemara: if one slaughtered intending *le'echol davar she'ein darko le'echol* — to eat something not normally eaten (such as the blood or forbidden fat) — or *lehaktir davar she'ein darko lehaktir* — to burn something not normally burned — the ruling of the *rabbanan* is that such a sacrifice is *kasher* and the *piggul* invalidity does not apply. But *Rabbi Eliezer posel* — Rabbi Eliezer invalidates even in those cross-category cases.

This resolution, however, creates a striking internal problem within our *mishna* itself. Immediately following the cases of the fat tail skin, the next *mishna* (which the Gemara notes will be read on 29b) states: *zeh haklal* — this is the rule: *kol hashochait... le'echol davar shedarko le'echol ul'haktir davar shedarko l'haktir* — only thoughts about eating what is normally eaten or burning what is normally burned invalidate. This formulation is explicitly the *rabbanan's* position, not Rabbi Eliezer's. So the *reisha* of our *mishna* — which includes the fat tail skin case — would represent Rabbi Eliezer, while the immediately following *mishna* beginning with *zeh haklal* articulates the rabbanan's directly opposing rule. The Gemara acknowledges this tension and provides a weak but accepted resolution: *ein* — yes, the *mishna* is internally divided, the *reisha* following Rabbi Eliezer and the *zeh haklal* reflecting the rabbanan. The fact that the *mishna* presents these sequentially without flagging the discontinuity is noted as unusual, particularly since *zeh haklal* typically functions as a summary of the immediately preceding material.

### Rav Huna's View

Rav Huna offers a cleaner solution that avoids attributing the *mishna* to Rabbi Eliezer at all: *or alya lav k'alya dami* — the skin of the fat tail is *not* like the fat tail. The skin is categorically part of the meat that a person is permitted to eat, not part of what goes onto the *mizbeach*. On this reading, when one thinks about eating the skin of the fat tail at the wrong time or place, there is no cross-category problem whatsoever — one is simply thinking about eating human-consumable meat at the wrong time or place, which is a straightforward *piggul* or *chutz limkomo* thought.

The textual basis for Rav Huna's position is the verse *chelbo ha'alya temimah* — which specifies the *fat* of the complete fat tail. The possessive "its fat" indicates that only the *chelev* of the *alya* goes on the altar, *v'lo or ha'alya* — not the skin surrounding it.

### Rav Chisda's View

Rav Chisda takes yet a third approach: *le'olam or ha'alya k'alya dami* — the skin of the fat tail is indeed like the fat tail itself and is burned on the *mizbeach*. Yet he too avoids attributing the *mishna* to Rabbi Eliezer. His solution is: *v'hacha b'mai askinan b'alya shel gdi* — the *mishna* is not discussing a sheep's fat tail at all, but rather the tail of a goat. A goat, unlike a sheep, does not have a fat tail; its tail is simply an ordinary tail whose flesh is consumed. Therefore, when the *mishna* speaks of the skin of the "fat tail," it refers to the skin of the goat's ordinary tail, which is human-consumable meat — and thinking about eating it at the wrong time is a standard *piggul* thought, fully within the rabbanan's framework.

### Rejecting Goat Read

The Gemara notes, however, that this reading faces an inherent conceptual awkwardness: calling the goat's tail *alya shel gdi* — the "fat tail" of a goat — makes no sense, since a goat has no fat tail. Referring to it in these terms is as strange as speaking of the "fifth leg" of a goat. Nevertheless, Rav Chisda maintains this reading.

The Gemara then asks why Shmuel and Rav Chisda — both of whom hold that the skin is like the fat tail — did not adopt Rav Huna's position. The answer: *or alya ka'alya dami kamashma lehu* — both are committed to the view that the skin is categorically equivalent to the fat tail. Rav Huna's solution was not available to them.

Conversely, the Gemara asks why Shmuel did not follow Rav Chisda's goat reading. The answer: if the *mishna* is talking about the tail of a goat, then the only *chiddush* it would be conveying is that the skin of a goat's tail counts as edible — i.e., that it has the status of meat rather than bone or hoof. But that point is already implicit from the laws of *tumah*.

### Edibility Standards

This observation leads naturally to the *baraisa* dealing with *tumah*: *v'eilu she'oroteihen k'visran* — the following are cases where the skin of an animal is treated like its flesh, rendering it susceptible to *tumah*, since only edible matter contracts *tumah*. Among the items listed is the skin beneath the fat tail. If the *mishna* were limited to the goat case, its entire teaching would be that such skin is edible — but this is already derived from the *tumah* laws.

Rav Chisda responds: the *mishna* is still necessary. One might have thought that the skin counts as edible for *tumah* only because *d'rachich mitztaref* — it is soft and contiguous with the flesh, making it sufficiently flesh-like to combine with flesh for *tumah* purposes even if it is not truly edible on its own. But for the laws of *piggul*, the standard is higher. The *kohanim* must eat *korbanot* *l'moshchah*, *k'derech shehamelachim ochlim* — in a dignified manner, as kings eat. Would a king eat the skin of a goat's tail? Perhaps not, as it might be considered too difficult or undignified to consume. Therefore *eima lo* — one might have thought such skin is too lowly to qualify as "eating" for *piggul* purposes, and the *mishna* teaches us *ka mashma lan* that it does qualify.

---

## Tosefta: Olah Case

### Tosefta Reading

The Gemara now cites a *Tosefta* that bears directly on the question: *hashochet et ha'olah lehaktir kezayit me'or shetachat ha'alya* — if one slaughtered a burnt offering (*olah*) with intent to burn a *kezayis* of the skin beneath the fat tail outside its proper place (*chutz limkomo*), the sacrifice is *pasul ve'ein bo karet*; if the intent was *chutz lizmano*, it is *piggul ve'chayavin alav karet*. This Tosefta aligns directly with our *mishna* and speaks explicitly of the skin beneath the fat tail.

### Edible Parts List

The Tosefta continues with a broader statement from Elazar ben Yehuda ish Evelim in the name of Rabbi Yaakov, and similarly from Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda ish Kfar Ichus in the name of Rabbi Shimon. They enumerate multiple types of skin treated as flesh: the skin of the area around the hooves (*or beit haparsot*) of small animals; the skin of the skull of a young calf; the skin beneath the fat tail; and, in general, everything listed by the Sages in the context of *tumah* as cases where skin is like flesh — including the skin of the genital area (*or beit haboshet*). In all these cases, the rule is *chutz limkomo pasul ve'ein bo karet, chutz lizmano piggul ve'chayavin alav karet*. The Tosefta thus confirms that thoughts about eating any of these skins, at the wrong time or wrong place, carry the full *piggul* or *chutz limkomo* consequences.

### Olah Constraint

However, the Gemara points out a critical feature of the Tosefta's language: the case is introduced as *hashochet et ha'olah* — one who slaughters an *olah* — suggesting that this law applies specifically to a burnt offering and not to other sacrifices (*olah in aval zevach lo*). This is puzzling: if the skin beneath the fat tail is considered edible, why should the rule be limited to an *olah*?

The Gemara explains: *bishlama l'Rav Huna hainu d'katani olah* — for Rav Huna, this limitation makes perfect sense. Rav Huna holds that the skin of the fat tail is *not* burned on the altar together with the fat tail of a regular sacrifice; rather, it is consumed by people. Therefore, a thought about *burning* the skin at the wrong time or place only arises as a *piggul*-type concern in the case of an *olah*, where everything is burned on the altar. In an *olah*, even the skin beneath the fat tail is consigned to the fire; therefore, a thought about burning it in the wrong time or place is meaningful. But in other sacrifices, since the skin is eaten rather than burned, a thought about *burning* it would not arise in the relevant way.

The implicit difficulty with this analysis is that once we are dealing with an *olah* — where everything is burned — the reason to single out the skin beneath the fat tail (as opposed to hooves or other parts) must be to establish that this skin has the status of "meat" and not "hoof," thereby making a *piggul* thought about it meaningful. That appears to be the *chiddush*.

### Challenge to Olah

For Rav Chisda, however, the *olah* limitation is difficult. Rav Chisda holds that the skin of the fat tail is burned on the *mizbeach* together with the fat tail in *every* sacrifice, not only in an *olah*. If so, why does the Tosefta specifically invoke the *olah* case? Any sacrifice involving the fat tail would generate the same question.

Rav Chisda offers two responses. First: *i ba'is eima b'alya shel gdi* — one can say the Tosefta is speaking of a goat's tail, in which case the *olah* limitation makes sense: only in the case of an *olah* would the goat's tail go onto the altar entirely; in other sacrifices the tail would be consumed. Second: *i ba'is eima tani zevach* — alternatively, the limitation to *olah* in our text of the Tosefta may simply be a textual variant, and the Tosefta in fact applies to all sacrifices. Tosafot notes that this second resolution is actually supported by their own textual tradition of the *Tosefta*, which does not limit the ruling to an *olah*.

---

## Piggul Sources

### Long Pesuk Tzav

Turning from the particular laws of the fat tail skin, the Gemara now asks: *mina hanei mili* — what is the scriptural basis for the entire framework of *piggul* and *chutz limkomo*, including the differentiation that one carries *karet* and the other does not? *Amar Shmuel trei kraei ktivi* — Shmuel states that there are two relevant verses.

The first is the long verse in Vayikra 7:18 (*parshat Tzav*), which reads:

> וְאִם הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל מִבְּשַׂר זֶבַח שְׁלָמָיו בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי לֹא יֵרָצֶה הַמַּקְרִיב אֹתוֹ לֹא יֵחָשֵׁב לוֹ פִּגּוּל יִהְיֶה וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ הָאֹכֶלֶת מִמֶּנּוּ עֲוֹנָהּ תִּשָּׂא

This verse contains multiple key phrases. The reference to eating on the third day points to *chutz lizmano* — the wrong-time category. The word *lo yeratze* — it will not be accepted — is significant: once the blood is on the altar, eating from the meat cannot retroactively invalidate the offering. The acceptance or rejection of a *korban* is determined entirely by the blood. Therefore, the verse cannot be speaking of actually eating on the third day; it must be referring to thinking about eating on the third day. This is reinforced by *lo yeichashev* — "it will not be reckoned for him" — which the Gemara reads as *machashava*, thought. The word *piggul yihyeh* seems redundant after all the foregoing, and therefore carries additional information: it introduces the category of *chutz limkomo* as well.

### Raba's Division

*Amar Rava*: *shlishi zehu chutz lizmano* — the third-day reference is the source for *chutz lizmano*. *Piggul zehu chutz limkomo* — the apparently superfluous word *piggul* in the verse points to the second category, *chutz limkomo*. Strikingly, the word *piggul* — which gives its name to the wrong-time invalidity — is here being used as the source for the wrong-*place* invalidity. The Torah's own terminology is being deployed against its apparent meaning, in service of the exegetical need to source both categories from this verse.

### Karet Allocation

The verse concludes: *ve'hanefesh ha'ochelet mimenu avonah tisa* — the person who eats from it bears their sin. The word *mimenu* — "from it" — implies a single referent. Since both *chutz lizmano* and *chutz limkomo* have been read into the verse, the *karet* consequence (*avonah tisa*) applies to only one of them.

The Gemara asks: how do we know it is *chutz lizmano* that carries *karet* and not *chutz limkomo*? Perhaps *mimenu* refers to the *chutz limkomo* case. Several arguments are advanced. First: *mistabra chutz lizmano adif d'patach bei* — it stands to reason that *chutz lizmano* is the weightier category, since the verse opens with it. Counterargument: *adaraba chutz limkomo adif d'samich lei* — on the contrary, *chutz limkomo* is the most recently mentioned category and *mimenu* naturally refers back to the most proximate referent. The Gemara cannot resolve this from the verse alone.

### Short Pesuk Kedoshim

This leads to the second verse: Vayikra 19:7 (*parshat Kedoshim*):

> וְאִם הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי פִּגּוּל הוּא לֹא יֵרָצֶה

This is the short verse. It shares key language with the Tzav verse — *bayom hashlishi*, *piggul hu*, *lo yeratzeh* — but it omits the *karet* clause entirely. The Gemara, citing a *tanna* quoted by Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi in the name of Rav, proposes a complete reassignment: the long verse in Tzav is entirely about *chutz lizmano*, and the short verse in Kedoshim is entirely about *chutz limkomo*. Since the Kedoshim verse does not mention *karet*, this elegantly explains why *chutz limkomo* carries no *karet*: the verse that introduces it simply does not include that penalty. *She'ein talmud lomar* — there would be no need for the Kedoshim verse if both categories were already covered by the Tzav verse. Therefore: *im eino inyan lechutz lizmano tnehu inyan lechutz limkomo* — since the Kedoshim verse is redundant for *chutz lizmano*, apply it to *chutz limkomo*.

The next verse in Kedoshim (19:8) then reads:

> וְאֹכְלָיו עֲוֹנוֹ יִשָּׂא כִּי אֶת קֹדֶשׁ ה' חִלֵּל וְנִכְרְתָה

This verse follows the *chutz limkomo* verse and mentions *karet* (*ve'nichreta*). However, the Gemara argues, this *karet* applies not to *chutz limkomo* but to *nosar* — leftover meat that was not eaten in time. The *peshat* of the passage is indeed about *nosar*, and since the verse says *lo yeratzeh* (which, as established, signals that we are dealing with intention rather than actual eating), it must be that the *chutz limkomo* is embedded in it while the *karet* clause attaches to *nosar* alone. *Umi'et Rachmana gabi nosar ve'ochlav avono yisa lemi'utei chutz limkomo* — the Torah excludes *chutz limkomo* from *karet* through the *nosar* verse's formulation *ve'ochlav avono yisa*, which singles out one category (nosar) as bearing *karet* to the exclusion of the other (*chutz limkomo*).

---

## Nosar Connection

### Gezeirah Shavah

The Gemara, however, immediately questions the allocation: why say that *ve'ochlav avono yisa* refers to *nosar* and not to *chutz limkomo*? Maybe *chutz limkomo* is the one that gets *karet* while *nosar* is excluded. *Amar Abaye ki asa Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi*, citing a teaching by Rav: the resolution comes from a *gezeirah shavah* taught by Rabbi Yochanan — *atya kodesh kodesh*. The phrase *ki et kodesh Hashem chillel* in Kedoshim 19:8 contains the word *kodesh*, and another verse about *nosar* — in Shemot 29 — reads *hanosar ba'esh lo ye'achel ki kodesh hu*. Since both verses use the word *kodesh* in the context of *karet* consequences for eating sanctified matter, we establish a *gezeirah shavah* linking them. This proves that the *karet* in Kedoshim 19:8 refers to *nosar*, not to *chutz limkomo*.

### Karet Only Nosar

The logic is thus: the long Tzav verse is the source for *chutz lizmano*, and *karet* applies to eating from a sacrifice rendered *piggul* through that wrong-time thought. The short Kedoshim verse is the source for *chutz limkomo*, and it carries no *karet*. The following verse in Kedoshim does mention *karet*, but via the *gezeirah shavah* of *kodesh-kodesh* we know it refers to *nosar* — actual leftover meat — not to the *chutz limkomo* invalidity embedded in the same context.

### Zman & Bamah Link

But the Gemara still needs to justify why *ve'ochlav avono yisa* attaches to *nosar* rather than to *chutz limkomo*, given the *gezeirah shavah*. The deeper argument is: *mistabra nosar havei leh le'okmei be'karet lemimar avon avon mi'chutz lizmano de'dami leh be'zav*. The *zav* here is an acronym: *zayin* for *zman* and *vet* for *bamah*. Both *chutz lizmano* and *nosar* share two defining characteristics — they are both time-related concepts (wrong *time* of intent vs. actually leaving meat past its permitted time), and both apply on a *bamah* (a private altar). These shared features make it appropriate to derive *karet* for *nosar* through comparison with *chutz lizmano*: the word *avon* in the *nosar* verse is learned from the *avon* in the *chutz lizmano* context. *Chutz limkomo*, by contrast, is place-based and does not apply on a *bamah*, so it shares neither of these features with *nosar*.

### Juxtaposition Logic

The Gemara offers a counterargument: *adaraba aricha be'chutz limkomo* — perhaps the long verse in Tzav is actually about *chutz limkomo*, and the short Kedoshim verse is about *chutz lizmano*. In that case, the *karet* of the following verse would be applied via the acronym *mikdash* — *mem* for *machshava* (both are thought-based invalidities), *kof* for *ktzat* (both invalidate through a thought about even a portion), *dalet* for *dam* (both involve thoughts about blood), and *shin* for *shlishi* (both relate to the third day). These points of comparison between *chutz limkomo* and *nosar* are numerous — arguably more numerous than the *zav* comparison between *chutz lizmano* and *nosar*. Furthermore, it makes narrative sense for *chutz lizmano* to be juxtaposed to the *nosar* verse: they are conceptually similar (both time-related), and the juxtaposition would serve to compare and distinguish them — confirming that while both involve time considerations, only *nosar* (actual leftover meat) generates *karet* from the subsequent verse, not the mere thought of eating at the wrong time.

### Inconclusive End

The Gemara concludes that neither side can definitively prove its case. The question of which verse is the *chutz lizmano* verse and which is the *chutz limkomo* verse cannot be resolved through the arguments advanced. The shiur ends on this unresolved note — with the understanding that the following day will return to learn everything out from the first verse and demonstrate how both categories, and the differentiation in *karet*, are derived from that single source.

---

---

# Zevachim 29

## Piggul Sources

### Opening & Daf Overview

The daf begins at the bottom of 28b, eleven lines from the end, at the words *vekamei mai*, in the midst of a sustained effort to identify the *pesukim* from which the laws of *piggul* are derived. The central questions are where we learn that a *machshava* of *chutz lizmano* — an intent to consume a sacrifice outside its permitted time — renders the offering *piggul* and incurs *karet* for one who eats it, and, correspondingly, where we learn that a thought of *chutz limkomo* — intent to consume it in the wrong place — constitutes only a *lo ta'aseh*, a negative prohibition, without the penalty of *karet*.

### Long & Short Pesukim

The *gemara* works with two *pesukim*. The first, the longer one, appears in *Tzav* (Vayikra 7:18): *ve'im he'achol ye'achel mibsar zevach shelamav bayom hashlishi lo yeratzeh hamakriv oto lo yechashev lo piggul yihyeh venefesh ha'ochelet mimenu avonah tisa*. If one eats from the flesh of his *shelamim* on the third day, it will not be accepted; the one who offers it shall have it not reckoned to him; it shall be *piggul*, an abomination; and whoever eats of it shall bear his iniquity. The second, shorter *pasuk* appears at the opening of *Kedoshim* (Vayikra 19:7): *ve'im he'achol ye'achel bayom hashlishi piggul hu lo yeratzeh* — and it shall be *piggul*, it will not be accepted — followed by an explicit statement of *karet*: *venichreta hanefesh hahi me'ameha*.

Although the plain sense of both *pesukim* concerns *notar* — leftover sacrificial meat eaten after its permitted time — the *gemara* reads them as speaking of *machshava*, of intent, since a *korban* cannot logically be retroactively invalidated by what someone does with its meat two days after the fact.

---

## Rava's Derivation

### All from Tzav

The *gemara* had struggled to resolve precisely which *pasuk* addresses *chutz lizmano* and which *chutz limkomo*, and which carries *karet*. It had reached an impasse. Now, in a fresh approach: *ela amar Rava* — rather, Rava says — *kulu mikra arichta ati*, all of the fundamental laws of *piggul* are derivable from the single long *pasuk* in *Tzav*.

### Double Language

The *pasuk* opens *he'achol ye'achel*, a doubled verb. The *gemara* interprets this as speaking of two distinct types of eating: *achilat adam*, human eating, and *achilat mizbe'ach*, the consumption by the altar. Accordingly, a *piggul* thought may concern either the intent that a human will eat the meat of the *korban* at the wrong time or the intent that the *emurim* — the entrails — will be burned on the altar at the wrong time. The act of *zorek hadam*, throwing the blood, is both the act during which the *piggul* thought is formed and the subject around which the entire *avoda* turns. The focus of the double language, however, is on these two forms of consumption: the *basar* and the *emurim*.

---

## Rava's Derivation (II)

### Shelamim Paradigm

The *pasuk* specifies *mibsar zevach shelamav* — from the flesh of his *shelamim* sacrifice. The *gemara* asks: why are *shelamim* the paradigm for *piggul*? Because *shelamim maphalgin umitpalgin* — *shelamim* divide and are divisible. That is, in a *shelamim* there is both the act through which the *piggul* operates (the blood service) and the result that becomes permitted through that act (the meat). The *shelamim* thus has a clear *matir* on one side and a *muttar* on the other. This principle, *maphalgin umitpalgin*, is the basis for the rule that *piggul* applies to any *korban* that has both these features. What is thereby excluded? The *mincha* of the *Kohen Gadol*, which is burned entirely on the altar — there is no portion that becomes permitted to a human through the act of offering, and thus the structure of a *matir* and a *muttar* does not apply.

### Shlishi & Hartzaah

The *pasuk* then says *bayom hashlishi* — on the third day. This is the concept of *chutz lizmano*: the thought to consume the offering beyond its permitted time. The *pasuk* continues *lo yeratzeh* — it will not be accepted. From here the *gemara* derives: *k'hartzat kasher ken hartzat pasul* — just as a *kasher* sacrifice must go through the full process of *hartza'ah* to be accepted, so too even in the case of *piggul* the offering achieves the status of *piggul* only if the entire process is carried out properly. This is one of the genuine ironies of the laws of *piggul*: it is only when everything is done correctly that the *piggul* thought takes full effect.

### Matirim & Process

The principle is stated explicitly: *mah hartzat kasher ad she'yakrivu kol matirav* — just as an offering becomes accepted only after all of its *matirim* are brought, so too *hartzat pasul ad she'yakrivu kol matirav* — even by a *pasul* offering, specifically a *piggul*, one achieves the status of *piggul* only after all the *matirim* are properly offered. If the blood is spilled rather than properly thrown, there is no *piggul*. If the *zrikah* is performed *shelo lishmo*, the *piggul* thought is neutralized. Everything must be done in perfect conformity with *halacha* — the sole imperfection permitted, as it were, is the *piggul* thought itself. *Ad she'yakrivu kol matirav.*

### Time of Piggul

The *pasuk* says *hamakriv oto* — the one who offers it. From this the *gemara* derives: *b'hakrava hu nifsal v'eino nifsal bashlishi* — the *korban* becomes invalid at the time of its being offered, not on the third day itself. Contrary to the plain sense of the *pasuk*, the invalidation does not occur when the *notar* is actually eaten on the third day. It is the *machshava* at the moment of *hakrava* that renders the *korban piggul*.

### Lo Yechashev

The phrase *lo yechashev lo* — it shall not be reckoned to him — teaches: *lo ye'arev bo machshavot acherot*, other invalidating thoughts may not be mixed in. If, in addition to a *chutz lizmano* thought, there is also a thought of *chutz limkomo*, that additional thought removes the *korban* from the category of *piggul*. The *korban* remains *pasul*, but it is no longer *piggul*, and therefore one who eats from it does not incur *karet*. This flows directly from the same principle that requires *kol matirav* to be offered properly: a *piggul* can exist only when the sole flaw is the *piggul* thought. Any other invalidating thought compromises that exclusivity.

### Yihyeh & Combining

The word *piggul yihyeh* — it shall be *piggul* — teaches, by the word *yihyeh*, that *mitztarfin zeh im zeh*: different categories of improper intent combine with one another. If one had a thought to eat half a *kezayit* in the wrong place and half a *kezayit* at the wrong time, even though there is no full *kezayit* of a single type of *piggul* thought, and even though the presence of a *chutz limkomo* thought means it cannot be *piggul*, nonetheless both thoughts together constitute a *kezayit* of improper intent sufficient to render the *korban pasul*. Not *piggul*, but *pasul*.

### Mimenu Singular

The *pasuk* then reads *venefesh ha'ochelet mimenu* — the soul that eats *mimenu*, from it, singular. *Echad velo shnayim* — only one of the two types of improper thought carries the punishment of *karet*. Having established that *chutz limkomo* and *chutz lizmano* combine for *psul* but represent two different categories, the singular *mimenu* now tells us that only one of them — not both — incurs *karet*.

### Chutz Lizmano Karet

Which one is it? *Zeh chutz lizmano* — it is *chutz lizmano* that carries *karet*. The reasoning: *degmar avon avon minosar* — we derive it through a *gezeirah shavah* of the word *avon* appearing here (*avonah tisa*) and the same word appearing in the *pasuk* in *Kedoshim* (*avono yisa*), which speaks explicitly of *karet* and which, in its plain sense, concerns *notar*. Both *notar* and *chutz lizmano* are fundamentally about *zman*, about time — and the close conceptual and textual connection between them, *dedami lei bizman*, is what establishes that the *karet* flows to *chutz lizmano* and not *chutz limkomo*. Furthermore, *chutz limkomo* has no application by a *bamah*, a private altar — there is no fixed *makom* in such a context — whereas *chutz lizmano* applies there as well, reinforcing the alignment of *chutz lizmano* with the punishment derived from *notar*.

---

## Piggul Sources (II)

### Shelamim Paradigm

With all of the major laws of *piggul* now derived from the single long *pasuk* in *Tzav* through Rava's comprehensive *derasha*, the question naturally arises about the role of the shorter *pasuk* in *Kedoshim*. Before proceeding to Rav Pappa's challenge, it is worth noting again the underlying logic of the *shelamim* paradigm. The principle of *maphalgin umitpalgin* — that the *shelamim* divides and is divided — means that there is a clear structure in which an act of blood service on one side permits both the eating of the meat by the *ba'alim* and the burning of the *emurim* on the altar. Any *korban* that shares this structure, in which one set of acts (*matirim*) permits another set of resulting consumptions, is subject to the laws of *piggul*. What is excluded is precisely that which lacks this bilateral structure.

---

## Rav Pappa & Kedoshim

### Rav Pappa's Q

Rav Pappa challenged Rava: having derived all the laws of *piggul* from the long *pasuk* in *Tzav*, what does the *pasuk* in *Kedoshim* — *ve'im he'achol ye'achel bayom hashlishi* — come to teach that is not already known from *Tzav*?

### Makom Meshulash

Rava responds: the *pasuk* in *Kedoshim* is needed to teach the requirement of *makom meshulash* — a tripartite place. *Hu mibaei lei lemakom shemeshulash bedam bebasar uve'imurim*: the laws of *piggul* apply only where the relevant location is equally valid — or equally invalid — with respect to all three: the *dam*, the *basar*, and the *emurim*. This is a distinct and additional *halacha* that could not simply be derived from the *pasuk* in *Tzav*.

### Rashi Heichal

Rashi understands the requirement of *makom meshulash* as follows: a thought of *chutz limkomo* constitutes a valid *piggul* thought only if the place contemplated is invalid for all three — the blood, the meat, and the *emurim*. The *heichal* presents the relevant test case. The *heichal* is not a place where one eats the *basar* of *kodshei kodashim*, nor where the *emurim* are burned; however, the blood of certain inner *chataot* is applied there on *Yom Kippur*. Since the *heichal* is not uniformly invalid for all three, a thought to eat the *korban* inside the *heichal* does not qualify as a *chutz limkomo* thought that creates *piggul*. Rashi's reading thus focuses on whether the contemplated location is invalid in a uniform and tripartite manner.

### Tosafot Views

Tosafot offer alternative interpretations. One explanation holds that *makom meshulash* refers to the type of *korban* being brought: *piggul* applies only to offerings brought on the outer *mizbeach*, since the outer *mizbeach* is the place for the meat of the *olah*, for the blood, and for the *emurim*. By contrast, a *korban* whose blood is applied on the inner *mizbeach* — such as certain inner *chataot* — would not generate *piggul* since the inner *mizbeach* is not a place for all three elements. Tosafot itself notes the difficulty with this position, since evidence from elsewhere in the *gemara* indicates that *piggul* does apply to inner *chataot*. A second explanation offered by Tosafot shifts the focus entirely to the person performing the *avoda*: the *kohen* must be standing in a place that is *meshulash*, meaning in the *azara*, a location that is equally valid for blood, meat, and the burning of *emurim*. If the *kohen* is performing the *shechita* while standing outside the *azara* — which is in itself *kasher*, since a long knife can extend across the threshold — but has a *piggul* thought at that moment, the thought is not operative, since he is not standing in a place that qualifies as *makom meshulash*.

### Need for Kedoshim

One might ask why the *pasuk* in *Tzav* alone could not teach this requirement. The *gemara* explains: in the *pasuk* of *Tzav*, the word *shelishi* — third — appears, followed immediately by the word *piggul*. Had we tried to derive *makom meshulash* from *shelishi* in *Tzav*, we would have read *shelishi* as a *prat* narrowing the scope of *piggul* to a tripartite context, and then *piggul* immediately afterward would function as a *klal*, broadening it back out — resulting in a *klal mosif al haprat* that would expand *piggul* to apply even to non-tripartite locations. As Rav Ashi related in the name of Rav Masna: *im mehatam hava amina shelishi prat piggul klal venasa klal mosif al haprat veyisrebu shear mekomot* — I would have concluded that other locations are included, and the tripartite limitation would be lost. Therefore the separate *pasuk* in *Kedoshim* was necessary to anchor the requirement of *makom meshulash* without being subjected to such an expansive reading. That, and no more, is the function of the *pasuk* in *Kedoshim*.

---

## Baraitot Disputes

### R. Eliezer View

With the derivations from the *pesukim* now firmly established, the *gemara* turns to a *baraita* that examines the same *pasuk* in *Tzav* from a different angle. *Tanu rabbanan*: our Rabbis taught. Rabbi Eliezer opens: *kof oznecha lishmoa* — bend your ear and listen carefully, for this *pasuk* is being read against its plain sense. *Bemachshev le'echol mizivcho bayom hashlishi hakatuv medaber* — the *pasuk* is speaking of one who intends to eat from the sacrifice on the third day. He is not speaking of the case where someone actually ate the *notar*. The alternative — that the *pasuk* describes someone who literally consumed the meat on the third day, and that the *korban* is thereby retroactively invalidated — is untenable. *Achar shehuchshar yachzor viyepasel?* Can something that was already accepted retroactively become invalid? No: *lo yeratzeh* tells us the *korban* will not be accepted, and this cannot logically refer to a retroactive undoing of an offering that was already valid at the time of the blood service. The *pasuk* must therefore be read as concerning the *machshava* at the time of *hakrava*.

### R. Akiva Tzad

Rabbi Akiva pushes back: *hen* — yes, retroactive invalidation is not impossible. We find it in the case of a *zav* and a *zavah* and a *shomeret yom kineged yom*. A *zav* who has experienced three emissions and a *zavah* who has seen blood on three consecutive days outside her menstrual cycle must each count seven clean days before immersing. By the principle of *miktzat hayom k'kulo*, part of the seventh day counts as the whole, and they may immerse in the *mikvah* on the morning of that day. But if later on the seventh day a further emission or bleeding occurs, their entire count is retroactively annulled. Similarly, a *shomeret yom kineged yom* — a woman who saw blood one or two days outside her regular cycle and must observe one clean day — may immerse in the *mikvah* once the clean day has begun, but if she subsequently sees blood, her *mikvah* immersion is retroactively ruined and the count must begin again. Rabbi Akiva argues: we thus do have a recognized category of retroactive invalidation. *She'af al pi shehuchshar yachzor viyepasel* — even if something became *kasher*, it is possible for it to subsequently become *pasul* retroactively.

### R. Eliezer Response

Rabbi Eliezer replies that the cases of *zav*, *zavah*, and *shomeret yom kineged yom* are based on the specific principle of *miktzat hayom k'kulo* — we permit the person to immerse in the morning on the anticipation that the remainder of the day will proceed as it began. That is categorically different from the situation of a *korban* which is accepted at the time of the blood service, and then, two days later, someone eats from the *notar* and allegedly undoes the original *hakrava*. The two cases are simply not comparable. Rather, Rabbi Eliezer turns to the *pasuk* itself: *hamakriv oto* — the one who offers it — focuses us on the moment of *hakrava*. *B'sha'at hakravah hu nifsal v'eino nifsal bashlishi*: the invalidation occurs at the time of offering, not on the third day. This is derived not from logic alone but from the textual emphasis of *hamakriv* — pointing to the act of offering as the locus of invalidation.

### Ben Azzai Oto

Ben Azzai then introduces an entirely different reading of *oto*. *Oto mah talmud lomar?* What does the word *oto* — it, this — come to teach? Not the point that it is the *korban* and not the *kohen* that becomes invalid. Rather, Ben Azzai reads *oto* as limiting the scope of *lo yeratzeh*: only this *korban*, the one with a *piggul* thought, is subject to *lo yeratzeh*. *Oto belo yeratzeh ve'ein me'acher nidro belo yeratzeh* — it is this case that incurs *lo yeratzeh*, but one who is delinquent in fulfilling his vow through *bal te'acher* does not thereby render his *korban* invalid. Perhaps one might have thought that violating *bal te'acher* — the prohibition against delaying the fulfillment of a vow beyond the prescribed time — causes the *korban* itself to become unacceptable. *Oto* teaches otherwise.

### Acherim View

Acherim — others — take a different approach: *lo yechashev bemachshavah hu nifsal v'eino nifsal bashlishi*. Rather than deriving the primacy of *machshava* from *hamakriv*, Acherim ground it in the phrase *lo yechashev* — it shall not be reckoned. This is in truth the most natural textual anchor for the entire principle, since the very language of *lo yechashev* centers on thought and reckoning. The *korban* is invalidated through *machshava*, not through what occurs on the third day.

### Korban Not Kohen

The *gemara* then asks: Ben Azzai uses *oto* to exclude *bal te'acher* — but where does he learn that it is the *korban* that becomes invalid and not the *kohen* himself? Two answers are offered. First, from Acherim: the phrase *lo yechashev* tells us it is invalidated through *machshava* and not on the third day, which only makes sense if we are speaking of the *korban*, not the *kohen*. There is no imaginable scenario in which a *kohen* becomes personally invalid on the third day due to *notar*. Second, from the phrase *lo yeratzeh* itself: *ritzui* and *hartzaah* are terms that throughout the *korbanot* literature refer to the sacrifice being accepted, not to the standing of the *kohen*. Accordingly, Ben Azzai does not need *oto* to establish that it is the *korban* and not the *kohen* — *lo yeratzeh* already makes this plain — and *oto* is therefore free to teach the *halacha* of *bal te'acher*.

### Ben Azzai Source

The *gemara* presses further: does Ben Azzai actually derive the *bal te'acher* exemption from *oto* in our *pasuk*? Perhaps he derives it from elsewhere — from a different *pasuk* altogether. *Me'acharina nafka* — he learns it from another source. A *baraita* is cited: Acherim say that one might have thought a *bechor* that passed its first year — like other *kodashim* that are invalid if brought at the wrong age — is similarly rendered *pasul*. The *Torah* teaches otherwise by linking *bechor* to *ma'aser* in the *pasuk* of *ve'achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha ma'asar deganecha* etc. *Makish bechor lema'aser*: just as *ma'aser* is not invalidated by being consumed in a different year — since the whole point is that every three years one clears out the *ma'aser* — so too a *bechor* is not invalidated by the passage of years. *Af bechor eino nifsal mishanah lachaverta*. We thus have a source for the *bechor* case from the *hekesh*. Why then does Ben Azzai need *oto* from our *pasuk*?

### Rav Ashi Why Both

Rav Ashi explains: *itztarech* — both sources are needed. Without *oto*, one might have said: granted, a *bechor* is not invalidated by the passage of time — *d'lav bar hartza'ah hu* — because a *bechor* does not come to atone or to establish a relationship of *hartza'ah* between Israel and God. It is a recognition of divine ownership of the firstborn, not a volitional act of drawing close to God. *Aval kodashim d'vnei hartza'ah ninhu* — but other *kodashim*, which genuinely function as acts of *hartza'ah*, acts of seeking divine acceptance — an *olah* that atones for the violation of a positive commandment, *shelamim* that cultivate the bond between Israel and their Father in heaven — one might have thought that if the person violated *bal te'acher* with respect to these, the *korban* itself loses its validity. *Ka mashma lan* — therefore *oto* is needed to teach that even these *kodashim*, when offered after *bal te'acher*, remain *kasher*.

### Kodashim Hartza'ah

The broader principle now emerges clearly: Ben Azzai requires *oto* specifically because the *bechor* precedent, derived from the *hekesh* to *ma'aser*, would not have been sufficient to establish the rule for standard *kodashim* that are *bnei hartza'ah*. The conceptual distinction between a *bechor* — which lacks the quality of *hartza'ah* — and voluntarily offered *korbanot* is significant enough that without *oto*, we would not have been able to generalize from one to the other. *Oto* bridges that gap.

### Why Oto Needed

A further question presents itself: why does Ben Azzai need *oto* at all, given that the *pasuk* of *bal te'acher* itself states *lo te'acher leshalmo*, and the sequel reads *ve'haya becha cheit* — the sin shall be *in you*? The *drasha* seems obvious: *becha cheit v'lo b'korbanacha cheit* — the sin is in you, not in your *korban*; the *korban* is not invalidated. If so, *oto* is superfluous for this purpose.

### Wife Death Neder

The *gemara* explains that Ben Azzai requires *ve'haya becha cheit* for an entirely different *derasha*: *v'lo b'ishtecha cheit* — the sin falls upon you, not upon your wife. The point of departure is a teaching cited in the name of Rabbi Eliezer (and some say Rabbi Yochanan): *ein ishto shel adam meta ela im kein mevakshim mimeno mamon v'ein lo* — a man's wife dies only when Heaven demands payment from him and he has nothing with which to pay. Tosafot understands this specifically to refer to the case of *bal te'acher* — when a man has made a vow to bring a *korban* to the *Beit Hamikdash* and has delayed beyond the prescribed time. One might have thought that in such a case, the principle of collective familial consequence would apply, and his wife might suffer as a result. Ben Azzai therefore derives from *ve'haya becha cheit* that by *bal te'acher* specifically, the sin rests with him alone: *bechetecha v'lo be'ishtecha chetecha*. The *gemara* does not deny the general principle of familial consequence — it is referenced with respect to cases of *gezel* or other unpaid obligations — but it limits it so that *bal te'acher* is not among the causes that trigger such consequences.

### Malkaot Taught

The *gemara* then turns to an additional teaching cited by Rav Mari in the name of Rabbi Yannai. One reading of *lo yechashev* goes beyond its use in limiting the role of competing thoughts: *minayin lemachashev bekodashim shehu lokeh* — how do we know that one who entertains a *piggul* thought receives *malkaot*, lashes? *Talmud lomar lo yechashev* — the *pasuk* teaches that one may not have this thought; it is a negative prohibition, and the violator receives *malkaot*.

### Lav Lo Ma'aseh

Rav Ashi challenges Rav Mari: *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh hu* — this is a negative prohibition without a physical act. And the general rule is *kol lav she'ein bo ma'aseh ein lokin alav* — one does not receive *malkaot* for a prohibition that involves no physical deed. A *piggul* thought, being purely mental (or at most verbal), does not constitute a *ma'aseh*, and therefore *malkaot* should not apply.

### R. Yehudah Malkaot

Rav Mari responds: *Rabi Yehuda hi* — this follows the position of Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh lokin alav*, that even a prohibition with no accompanying physical act can incur *malkaot*. This is a known position of Rabbi Yehudah applied here to the case of the *piggul* thought.

---

## Mishnah Four Avodot

### Four Avodot

The *mishnah* now presents a comprehensive *klal* — a general rule — governing the laws of *piggul*. There are four acts of the blood service during which a *piggul* thought is operative: *shochet*, *makabel*, *mehalech*, *zorek* — slaughtering, receiving the blood, walking it to the *mizbeach*, and throwing it. A *piggul* thought formed during any one of these four acts can render the *korban piggul*.

### Kavana Requirements

Several conditions govern the efficacy of the *piggul* thought. The thought must concern *davar shedarcho le'echol* — something normally eaten, meaning the *basar* of the *korban* — or *davar shedarcho lehaktir* — something normally burned, meaning the *emurim*. A thought to eat the *emurim* or to burn the *basar* does not qualify. Furthermore, the thought must concern at least a *kezayit* — the minimum halachic measure of eating — since anything less is too insignificant to trigger *piggul*.

### Chutz Limkomo

If the improper thought is *chutz limkomo* — intending to eat or offer the *korban* in the wrong place — the *korban* becomes *pasul* and there is no *karet* for one who subsequently eats from it. *Pasul ve'ein bo karet*.

### Chutz Lizmano

If the improper thought is *chutz lizmano* — intending to eat or offer the *korban* at the wrong time — the *korban* becomes *piggul*, and one who eats from it is liable for *karet*. *Piggul vechayavin alav karet*.

### Matir Kemitzvato

A critical condition applies to both: *uvilvad sheyakriv hamatir kemitzvato* — provided that the *matir*, that which permits the *korban*, is brought in the proper manner. The *matir* refers to the act that makes the *korban* and its parts permissible — the blood service, or in the case of a *mincha* the *kometz* and the *levona*. *Kemitzvato* is the key word: not only must the physical acts be completed, but they must be performed without any additional invalidating thought.

### Kemitzvato Example

How is *kemitzvato* illustrated? If the *shechita* was performed silently and without any improper thought, and then the *kibbul*, the *halacha*, and the *zrikah* were all performed with a *chutz lizmano* thought, that is a case of *hikriv hamatir kemitzvato* — the *matir* was brought properly. Even if three of the four acts were performed with the *piggul* thought, as long as everything was otherwise valid and no other invalidating thought intruded, the *korban* is *piggul*. The presence of additional *chutz lizmano* thoughts in subsequent acts does not take it out of *piggul*.

### Lo Karav Examples

What are examples of *lo karav hamatir kemitzvato* — cases where the *matir* was not brought properly? If the *shechita* was performed with a *chutz limkomo* thought and then the remaining acts were performed with a *chutz lizmano* thought: since the first act introduced a different type of invalidating thought, the subsequent *piggul* thought is ineffective. Alternatively, even if the *shechita* was performed with a *chutz lizmano* thought — establishing a *piggul* intent from the very first act — if a later act, such as the *zrikah*, is performed with a *chutz limkomo* thought, the *piggul* is annulled. A *piggul* requires that all the *matirim* be brought without any invalidating thought other than the *piggul* thought itself. The same applies to *korbanot* for which *shelo lishmo* is disqualifying: a *pesach* or *chatat* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* renders the *korban pasul*, and if *shelo lishmo* appears in any subsequent act alongside or following the *piggul* thought, the *lo karav kemitzvato* condition is not met.

### Half Kezayit Mix

If one had a thought to eat a half *kezayit* in the wrong place (*chutz limkomo*) and a half *kezayit* at the wrong time (*chutz lizmano*), the *mishnah* teaches: *pasul ve'ein bo karet* — invalid but no *karet*. The *halacha* here combines two principles already derived. First, from *yihyeh*, we learned that *mitztarfin zeh im zeh*: thoughts of *chutz limkomo* and *chutz lizmano* combine to constitute a *kezayit* of improper intent. Second, since a full *kezayit* of *piggul* thought was never formed — and since the *chutz limkomo* thought is present — the *korban* cannot be *piggul*. The combination is sufficient for *psul* but not for *piggul* and *karet*.

### R. Yehudah First

Rabbi Yehudah disagrees. His principle: *kol she'machshavat zman kadma l'machshavat hamakom piggul vechayavin alav karet* — whenever the thought of time (*chutz lizmano*) precedes the thought of place (*chutz limkomo*), the *korban* is *piggul* and one who eats it is liable for *karet*. Rabbi Yehudah holds that once a *piggul* thought has been formed, a subsequent thought of *chutz limkomo* — whether during the same act or a later one — cannot undo what has already been established. Once the *korban* has been made *piggul*, it cannot be un-*piggul*'d.

### R. Yehudah Order

The order matters to Rabbi Yehudah in both directions. *Im machshavat hamakom kadma l'machshavat hazman* — if the thought of place preceded the thought of time, the *korban* was already rendered invalid before the *piggul* thought arrived, and it cannot subsequently become *piggul*. *Pasul ve'ein bo karet*. The asymmetry in Rabbi Yehudah's position is clear: *chutz lizmano* first yields *piggul* and *karet*, which are not dislodged by a later *chutz limkomo* thought; *chutz limkomo* first yields *psul* without *karet*, which cannot be converted into *piggul* by a later *chutz lizmano* thought.

### Chachamim View

The *chachamim* reject this asymmetry entirely: *zeh v'zeh pasul ve'ein bo karet* — in either order, the result is *psul* without *karet*. Whenever thoughts of *chutz lizmano* and *chutz limkomo* are intermixed, regardless of which comes first, there is no *piggul* and no *karet*.

### No Achila Haktara

A final distinction closes the *mishnah*: *le'echol kechatzi zayit lehaktir kechatzi zayit* — if one had a thought to eat half a *kezayit* of *basar* at the wrong time and to burn half a *kezayit* of *emurim* at the wrong time. Even though both thoughts are *chutz lizmano* thoughts, one pertaining to *achilat adam* and one to *achilat mizbeach*, they do not combine. *Klal she'ein achila vehaktara mitztarvin* — eating and burning are categorically distinct modes of consumption and do not join to form a *kezayit*. For the thoughts to combine and create *psul*, they must be of the same type. A half *kezayit* of human eating and a half *kezayit* of altar burning, even when both are directed to the wrong time, remain separate and do not constitute a *kezayit* of a unified *piggul* intent.

---

---

# Zevachim 30

## Piggul Intro

### Piggul Definition

We arrive at the heart of the *piggul* discussion, picking up from the *gemara* at the bottom of 29b, immediately following the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* established the basic framework: *piggul* requires an improper intention during one of the four blood *avodot* — *shechita*, *kabalah*, *holachah*, or *zerikah* — directed toward one of the two categories of *achilot*: either the *achilat ha-dam ha-ra'uy lo* or the *achilat mizbeach* of the blood or the *emurim*, with the intent to consume or offer them at the wrong time. A thought about the wrong place renders the sacrifice *pasul* but does not produce *piggul*.

### Avodot & Achilot

The *mishnah* thus requires both a specific type of *avodah* and a specific type of *achilah* to be implicated. The four *avodot* of the blood — *shechita*, *kabalah*, *holachah*, and *zerikah* — each serve as the locus during which an improper *machshavah* can operate, while the categories of *achilah* define what kind of disqualifying thought is involved.

### Tanna Kamma vs. R. Yehuda

The *mishnah* then presents the dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda. The *tanna kamma* holds that an invalidating thought of *chutz li-mkomo* or *shelo lishmo* by a *chatas* prevents the sacrifice from becoming *piggul* even if that bad thought arrives after an initial *piggul* thought. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: identity is established by the first thought. If the first thought was something other than *piggul* — such as *chutz li-mkomo* — the sacrifice is already *pasul* and can never become *piggul*. But if the *piggul* thought came first, a subsequent invalidating thought cannot strip it of its *piggul* status.

---

## Ilfa's Position

### Ilfa: Two Avodot

Ilfa opens the *gemara*'s analysis: *machloket bi-shtei avodot* — the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* is specifically about a case involving two separate *avodot*. For example, one had a *piggul* thought during *shechita* and a *chutz li-mkomo* thought during *zerikah*, or vice versa. In such a case, Rabbi Yehuda says the first thought establishes the sacrifice's identity and the second cannot override it, while the *chachamim* hold that any *pasul* thought undermines *piggul* status.

### One Avodah Not Piggul

But *aval be-avodah achat divrei ha-kol eiruv machshavot havei* — if both thoughts occurred during one and the same *avodah*, even Rabbi Yehuda concedes that this constitutes *eiruv machshavot*, a bundling of thoughts, which prevents *piggul*. Rabbi Yehuda's position is only operative when the *piggul* thought has clearly been established first, at which point a later bad thought cannot interfere. His claim is not that any sequence of thoughts during a single *avodah* can lock in *piggul* status; that more aggressive reading is rejected, according to Ilfa, by Rabbi Yehuda himself.

---

## R. Yochanan Position

### Sequential Within One

Rabbi Yochanan disputes Ilfa: *af be-avodah achat machloket* — even when both thoughts occur during a single *avodah*, the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* still applies. The reason is that even within a single *avodah* there can be a genuine sequential ordering of thoughts. As one is performing the *shechita*, one might first think *chutz li-zmano* and then, in the next moment, think *chutz li-mkomo* — both during the same act, yet one preceding the other.

### First Thought Locks

According to Rabbi Yochanan's reading, Rabbi Yehuda maintains that so long as the *piggul* thought came first — even if the next thought about *chutz li-mkomo* followed immediately and all of it occurred within the single act of *shechita* — the sacrifice is already established as *piggul* and cannot be dislodged from that status. The question of whether such sequential thoughts within one *avodah* can truly be treated as discrete thus becomes the crux of the Ilfa–Rabbi Yochanan dispute.

The *gemara* then raises a textual consideration: according to Ilfa, the latter section of the *mishnah* — which formulates the case of *le-echol kezayit ba-chutz kezayit li-machar* — parallels the opening section of the *mishnah* and therefore must likewise concern two separate *avodot*. This is coherent for Ilfa: the *mishnah* remains internally consistent, always discussing cases across distinct *avodot*. For Rabbi Yochanan, however, the opening section discusses two separate *avodot* while the later section can encompass thoughts expressed even within a single *avodah* — whether one or two *avodot*, Rabbi Yehuda's principle applies as long as the *piggul* thought came first.

The *gemara* then cites the formulation of Rabbi Yehuda's own *klal* in the *mishnah*: *im machshevet ha-zman kadmah le-machshevet ha-makom, piggul ve-chayavin alav karet* — if the thought about time preceded the thought about place, it is *piggul* and one is liable for *karet*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the phrase *zeh ha-klal* signals a broad generalization covering multiple scenarios, whether across two *avodot* or within one — all governed by the single principle that the first thought locks in the sacrifice's identity. According to Ilfa, however, the *zeh ha-klal* applies only to the case of two separate *avodot*, and there is nothing broader being stated. The *gemara* acknowledges this as a genuine difficulty for Ilfa's reading.

---

## Temurah Parallel

### Tmura Olah Shelamim

The *gemara* now draws a comparison to a case in *Temurah*: if one declared *harei zeh tmurat olah tmurat shelamim* — this animal is an exchange for an *olah* and an exchange for a *shelamim* — is it governed by the first word (*olah*), or is it a hybrid? This parallel is directly relevant to the question at hand: when one utters two distinct designations in sequence, do we treat the first as establishing identity or do we treat the combined utterance as a single packaged statement?

### Meir vs. Yossi

The *mishnah* in *Temurah* records the dispute: *harei zu tmurat olah — divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that the first words out of one's mouth establish its identity as an *olah*, and the subsequent mention of *shelamim* cannot alter that. Rabbi Yossi takes a more contextual approach: *im le-kach nitkaven techilah, ho'il ve-ee efshar le-hotzi shtei shemot ke-achat, devarav kayamin* — if the speaker's original intent was to create a hybrid *olah-shelamim*, and since it is physically impossible to pronounce two words simultaneously, we follow the intent and recognize it as a hybrid. However, if one genuinely changed one's mind after saying *tmurat olah* and then said *tmurat shelamim*, Rabbi Yossi agrees: it is an *olah* and the second statement is disregarded. Tosafot adds a further refinement within Rabbi Yossi's position: the presence or absence of a pause between the two declarations is a meaningful contextual clue — a pause within *toch kdei dibbur* suggests unified intent, while a longer interval suggests genuine reconsideration.

### Abaye: Packaged Case

The *gemara* poses a sharper case: *harei zu tmurat olah u-shelamim* — what if one said "an exchange for an *olah* and a *shelamim*," using the conjunctive *vav*? Or alternatively, *lachatzot* — declaring that both designations take effect simultaneously at a fixed moment, so that no sequential priority can be established. Abaye holds that in this case, Rabbi Meir would certainly agree that the designation is treated as a packaged hybrid: *be-ha vadai modeh Rabbi Meir*. When the speaker's words unambiguously signal that both are intended as a unified whole, even Rabbi Meir concedes.

### Rava: First Word

Rava disagrees: *adayin hi machloket*. Even when the formulation packages the two designations together, Rava maintains that since the word *olah* appears first and the two categories are mutually exclusive, we simply apply the *olah* designation. The first word takes precedence regardless of how closely the second was bundled with it.

### Shechita Process

The *gemara* now draws this dispute back into the *piggul* context. Rava challenges Abaye: according to you, if someone clearly packages two thoughts together at a single moment, Rabbi Meir agrees it is all one statement — so why does Rabbi Yehuda still maintain that a *piggul* thought takes priority during *shechita*? Is not *shechita* precisely such a case where everything is packaged together at the conclusion of the act?

The *gemara* explores this via the principle of *yeshna la-shechita mi-techila ve-ad sof* versus *ein la-shechita ela le-basof*. If *shechita* is only legally consummated at its final moment, then all thoughts entertained during the cutting — first one, then another — converge at that final instant, like saying both things take effect *lachatzot*. In that case, they would be treated as packaged together, and according to Abaye, even Rabbi Meir would concede there is no sequential priority. But the *gemara* counters: no, the correct view is *yeshna la-shechita mi-techila ve-ad sof* — the act of *shechita* is a process, operative throughout. The *mishnah* itself reflects this, discussing a case where one *siman* was cut with a *chutz li-zmano* thought and the second *siman* with a *chutz li-mkomo* thought. Each stage of the cutting constitutes a distinct moment within the *avodah*, and so the two thoughts are genuinely sequential, not packaged.

### Discrete Acts

This leads to the more precise formulation: it is only when the sub-acts within a single *avodah* are discrete and separately identifiable that we treat the associated thoughts as sequential. Tosafot makes this point explicitly: we do not say that moving the knife one millimeter and then another millimeter constitutes two distinct acts — the motion is continuous and undivided. By contrast, the two *simanim* of the *behemah* — the trachea and the esophagus — are each identifiable as a separate anatomical stage, and therefore the thoughts corresponding to each *siman* are treated as genuinely sequential.

The same logic applies to *holachah*: each individual step (*psi'ah*) is a discrete act. Therefore, one might hold a *piggul* thought at one step and a *chutz li-mkomo* thought at the next step, and Rabbi Yehuda would say the *piggul* is already established. By contrast, the act of *kmitza* — taking the handful — is treated as a unified act consummated at its endpoint, so any two thoughts held during the process of *kmitza* would be packaged together and would constitute *eiruv machshavot*.

The *gemara* raises the case of a *minchat chotei*, which has no *levonah*. Without the *levonah*, there is only a single discrete element — the *komatz* of flour — and so one cannot distinguish two separate discrete stages within the offering-up. The *gemara* initially wonders whether Rabbi Yehuda's rule even applies in such a case, and concludes: *lo peligi* — the debate is not stated for *minchat chotei*. Rav Ashi adds: *im timtza lomar peligi, peligi bi-fsi'ot* — if one were to insist they do debate even there, the scenario of debate would have to involve the steps of *holachah*, since that is where discrete, identifiable sub-acts occur within a single *avodah*.

The connection to Rabbi Meir's position is then drawn explicitly. Rav Dimi transmitted: *Rabbi Meir b'shitat Rabbi Yehuda amrah, d'amar tefos lashon rishon* — Rabbi Meir's rule in *Temurah* that the first word establishes identity is stated in the tradition of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *tefos lashon rishon* as his operative principle in *piggul*. Rabbi Yochanan, however — as transmitted by Rabba bar bar Chanah — notes that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi can be brought quite close to one another: the debate between them is not a sweeping philosophical disagreement about whether to follow the first word versus intent, but a narrow dispute about how to interpret an ambiguous declaration of *tmurat olah tmurat shelamim*. When the intent is explicit — either through the formulation *techol zo ve-achar kach techol zo* (clearly sequential) or *lo techol zo ela im ken chalah zo* (clearly simultaneous) — there is no dispute. The debate arises only in the middle case, where the formulation is ambiguous and the parties disagree about what to infer from it.

---

## Levi's Question

### One Kezayit Query

The *gemara* now presents a question posed by Levi to Rabbi: *chishav le-echol kezayit li-machar ba-chutz, mahu?* What if the *kohen* thought about a single *kezayit* with both a *chutz li-zmano* and a *chutz li-mkomo* intention simultaneously? According to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the first thought establishes identity, the *piggul* thought (*li-machar*) came first — does this constitute *piggul*? Or, since it is a single *kezayit* with a single unified thought about both violations, does Rabbi Yehuda agree that it is *eiruv machshavot* and not *piggul*?

### R. Shimon Inference

Rabbi Shimon b'Rabbi challenged Levi's question before his father: *lo mishnateinu hi?* Is this not already resolved by our *mishnah*? The *mishnah* lists cases of *le-echol kezayit ba-chutz kezayit li-machar* — with two separate *kezayitim* — and declares those cases *pasul ve-ein bo karet*, with Rabbi Yehuda disagreeing. If those cases, which are more discrete, are where Rabbi Yehuda says *piggul* is established, then a fortiori the case of one *kezayit* directed to both violations simultaneously would be *eiruv machshavot* by Rabbi Yehuda's own reasoning. Levi's question, Rabbi Shimon implied, is self-evident from the *mishnah* itself.

### Abbreviated Texts

Rabbi responded to his son: *hu she'al bi devar chochmah* — Levi asked me a question rooted in pure logical reasoning, without relying on the text. And *ve-atah amarta mishnateinu* — you answered by pointing to the *mishnah*. The reason Levi could not resolve his question from the *mishnah* is that the text he had received from Rabbi was abbreviated: Rabbi had taught Levi only the case of *kezayit kezayit* (two separate *kezayitim*, without the conjunctive *vav*), while the students in the *beit midrash* had received both *kezayit kezayit* and *kezayit ve-kezayit* (with the *vav*). Levi did not know whether his text was the complete text — in which case a more bundled formulation would obviously be agreed-upon *eiruv machshavot* — or whether the full list included the *vav* case as well, in which case Rabbi Yehuda disputes even that, and perhaps even the single *kezayit* case remains in dispute.

---

## Final Synthesis

### Established Status

The picture that emerges from Rabbi Yehuda's position across all these cases is consistent: once the *piggul* thought has been registered — whether across two *avodot* or, according to Rabbi Yochanan, within discrete stages of a single *avodah* — that status is established and cannot be undone by a subsequent *pasul* thought. The question "when are thoughts sufficiently bundled together that the *piggul* thought never gets to stand on its own?" is what drives the remainder of the analysis.

---

## Text Girsa

### Inferring Girsa
