The *gemara* now attempts to resolve the question of the *mishnah*'s correct *girsa*: was the text *kezayit kezayit* (without *vav*) or *kezayit ve-kezayit* (with *vav*)? The inference proceeds as follows: if the text Levi received was *kezayit ve-kezayit* and the students' text was *kezayit kezayit*, then Levi's text already implicitly covers the more discrete case — and what the students had would not represent any additional information. There would be nothing "abbreviated" about Levi's version. It must therefore be that Levi's text was *kezayit kezayit* and the students' text added the *kezayit ve-kezayit* case, since only then does it make sense that Levi was working from an abbreviated list and could not infer what Rabbi Yehuda would say about a more bundled formulation.

---

## Final Synthesis (II)

### Bundling Exception

The upshot is that *kezayit ve-kezayit* — two *kezayitim* connected by a *vav* — is indeed a case where Rabbi Yehuda maintains that the first thought establishes *piggul* status and the second thought does not override it. The *vav* is not sufficient to bundle them into a unified, packaged statement. The only configuration that would truly constitute *eiruv machshavot* and prevent *piggul* even according to Rabbi Yehuda is when the entire thought concerns a single *kezayit* — thinking about one portion of food with both a *chutz li-zmano* and a *chutz li-mkomo* intention at once.

### Separate Kezayitim

When two discrete *kezayitim* are involved — even with the conjunctive *vav* linking the two thoughts — Rabbi Yehuda treats them as separate, sequential thoughts. The first thought locks in the *piggul* designation, and the second thought, however closely attached in formulation, cannot dislodge it. Similarly, when two discrete stages within a single *avodah* are involved — such as the two *simanim* of *shechita* or consecutive steps in *holachah* — the same logic applies: the thoughts are sequential, not packaged, and the first thought governs.

---

## Text Girsa (II)

### One Q, Two Answers

Why, then, did Levi ask Rabbi about the single-*kezayit* case rather than going directly to Rabbi and asking about the *kezayit ve-kezayit* case? The *gemara* explains: *savar ibayei minei chada d'lishma tartei* — Levi calculated that by asking the single-*kezayit* question, he could learn the answer to both questions at once, depending not only on what Rabbi answered but on *how* Rabbi answered. If Rabbi said, "That's a good question — in that case Rabbi Yehuda agrees it is *eiruv machshavot*," Levi would know that the *kezayit ve-kezayit* case, being more discrete, is certainly a case where Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. If Rabbi answered the same content but with impatience — *mirtach ratach*, getting angry — saying "What kind of question is that? Rabbi Yehuda agrees even in the *kezayit ve-kezayit* case, so of course he agrees here!" — then Levi would know that even the *kezayit ve-kezayit* case is treated as *eiruv machshavot* by Rabbi Yehuda. By asking the more extreme question, Levi could extract both answers from a single inquiry.

### Conclusion: Vav Text

The *gemara* thus establishes, as Rashi summarizes: *shma minah kezayit ve-kezayit tnan* — the correct *girsa* of the *mishnah* is *kezayit ve-kezayit*, with the *vav*. The case where Rabbi Yehuda agrees — where *eiruv machshavot* prevents *piggul* — is exclusively the case of a single *kezayit* intended simultaneously for two violations. But with two separate *kezayitim*, even linked by *ve-*, Rabbi Yehuda holds that they are discrete intentions, the first of which establishes the *piggul* status irrevocably.

Rashi further notes that this *gemara* is cited in other places in *Shas* — in *Kiddushin* and in the *gemara* of *shevu'at ha-pikadon* — where the question arises whether a *vav* connecting two statements renders them a single unified declaration. The answer derived from here is that even within Rabbi Yehuda's framework, the *vav* alone is insufficient to merge two statements about different *kezayitim* into a single packaged thought. Only when everything refers to the same *kezayit* is true bundling achieved. As a final summary: according to the *chachamim*, even once *piggul* has been established, a subsequent invalidating thought at a later *avodah* can prevent the sacrifice from retaining *piggul* status. According to Rabbi Yehuda, once *piggul* is established, it cannot be undone — and the only way to prevent *piggul* from ever being established in the first place is to ensure the thoughts are so thoroughly packaged together, referring to a single *kezayit* with unified intent, that the *piggul* thought never stood alone.

---

---

# Zevachim 31

## Piggul w/ Intervening Th…

### Half-portions Case

The daf opens three lines down from the top, continuing the discussion of *piggul* thoughts and the effect of an intervening thought of *chutz l'mkomo*. As a brief orientation: the position of the *Rabbanan* is that any extraneous invalid thought interjected during the sacrificial service prevents the offering from becoming *piggul*. Rabbi Yehuda disagreed, holding that once *piggul* has taken effect, a subsequent bad thought cannot undo it — but if the bad thought came first, the offering is invalidated before *piggul* can form, and the later *chutz l'zmano* thought is therefore inoperative. With that context, the Gemara introduces the following case.

The case is: *chatzi zayis chutz lizmano, v'chatzi zayis chutz limkomo, v'chatzi zayis chutz lizmano* — the *kohen* entertains three consecutive thoughts: first, that he will consume half a *k'zayis* outside its designated time; second, that he will consume half a *k'zayis* outside its designated place; and third, that he will consume another half a *k'zayis* outside its designated time. This case is being analyzed within the framework of the *Rabbanan*.

The underlying conceptual issue requires some unpacking. A thought about a mere half-*k'zayis* is legally inconsequential — only a thought involving a full *k'zayis* carries halachic weight. Had the *kohen* thought about a full *k'zayis* in the wrong place, that would constitute a meaningful invalidating thought capable of preventing *piggul*. But a half-*k'zayis* thought of *chutz l'mkomo* is not significant enough to serve as an *eruv machshavos* on its own.

Now, consider the progression. The first thought — half a *k'zayis chutz lizmano* — is, taken alone, insufficient for *piggul*. When combined with the second thought — half a *k'zayis chutz limkomo* — the two halves together constitute a full *k'zayis* of disordered intent, and by the principle of *tzeiruf* established in our *Mishnah* (derived from the word *yihyeh*), the *korban* becomes *pasul*. So by the time the second thought has been entertained, the offering is already *pasul*. The question is whether the third thought — another half *k'zayis chutz lizmano* — can now interact retroactively with the first half-*k'zayis chutz lizmano* to produce *piggul*, or whether we say the offering is already *pasul* and cannot now become *piggul*.

One might argue: since the two *chutz lizmano* half-thoughts are more naturally aligned with each other, we should step back, reassess, and say that the dominant thought is a full *k'zayis* of *chutz lizmano*, rendering the offering *piggul*. The half-thought of *chutz limkomo* is not sufficiently weighty to disrupt that pairing. Alternatively, one might argue: by the time the third thought arrives, the *korban* is already *pasul* from the combination of the first two thoughts, and *piggul* cannot take hold in something already *pasul*.

### Rava: Piggul Wakes Up

Rava rules: *vayikatz k'yoshen ha'piggul* — "and the *piggul* wakes up, like a sleeping person." The *piggul*, though temporarily dormant due to the intervening half-thought of *chutz limkomo*, reasserts itself. We step back, assess the totality, recognize the more natural pairing of the two *chutz lizmano* half-thoughts, and declare the offering *piggul*.

### Tosafot on Thoughts

Rashi invokes a closely related phrase — *chozer v'nei'or*, "it wakes up again" — drawn from the domain of physical mixture. The classic case: sixty parts of chicken soup into which half a unit of forbidden matter (*chazir*) falls and is *batel*. If another half-unit of forbidden matter subsequently falls in, the question arises whether the first half "wakes up" — *chozer v'nei'or* — and combines with the second to form a full prohibited unit no longer subject to *bitul*. Rava's formulation borrows this imagery.

Tosafot, however, flags an important disanalogy. In the physical case, at the moment the second half-unit is added, both halves are *physically present simultaneously* — there is an actual full unit of forbidden substance co-existing in the mixture at one moment in time. In the case of *piggul*, we are dealing with thoughts that existed sequentially and have passed. There is no moment at which a full *k'zayis* of *piggul* thought exists simultaneously in any coherent sense. These are distinct mental acts distributed across time, not physical quantities occupying space together. Tosafot therefore regards Rava's analogy as illuminating but imperfect, and maintains that in the domain of thought, one should not so readily say the *piggul* "wakes up."

### Rav Hamnuna: Erev M'chav…

Rav Hamnuna takes the opposing position: *erev machshavos havei* — the thought of *chutz limkomo* constitutes an *erev machshavos*, an extraneous thought that invalidates the sequence, and the offering remains *pasul* rather than becoming *piggul*. His reasoning, it may be presumed, turns on the fact that by the time the third thought arrives, the *korban* has already become *pasul* through the combination of the first two half-thoughts, and once *pasul*, it cannot be reconstituted as *piggul*.

One might ask: what if the intervening thought had been only a quarter-*k'zayis* of *chutz limkomo* — insufficient, even in combination with the first half-thought, to render the offering *pasul*? Presumably Rav Hamnuna would agree that in that case *piggul* does take effect. The critical factor for Rav Hamnuna is not the mere presence of an intervening thought but whether that intervening thought succeeded in rendering the offering *pasul* before the *piggul* configuration could fully form.

---

## Tumah Analogy

### Rava's Tumah Proof

Rava now seeks a proof for his position from a *Mishnah* in the laws of *tumah*. The *Mishnah* states: *kebeitzah ochel rishon u'kebeitzah ochel sheni* — a *kebeitzah*-worth of food that is a *rishon l'tumah* and a *kebeitzah*-worth of food that is a *sheni l'tumah*. To set up the scenario concretely: imagine one lump of dough that came into contact with a *neveilah* — it is now a *rishon l'tumah*, first degree of contamination. A separate lump of dough touched the first lump and is now a *sheni l'tumah*, second degree of contamination.

These two lumps are then mixed together — *shebelalan zeh bazeh* — into one large two-*kebeitzah* piece of dough. Within that larger piece, there is a full *kebeitzah*-worth of *rishon l'tumah* distributed throughout. When this combined dough touches another food item, say an apple, the apple becomes a *sheni l'tumah*, because there is a full *kebeitzah* of *rishon* present capable of transmitting contamination. A *kebeitzah* of substance is required for food to function as a *metamei*, to render other things *tamei*.

Now the *Mishnah* continues: *chilkan* — if you divide the combined dough back in half, then *zeh sheni v'zeh sheni* — each half now operates only as a *sheni l'tumah*. Why? Because in each half there is only a half-*kebeitzah* of *rishon l'tumah* and a half-*kebeitzah* of *sheni l'tumah*. Since you need a full *kebeitzah* of *rishon* to render something else a *sheni*, and no single half contains that full amount, the halves each operate at the lower common level of *sheni*.

Then: *hechezir v'irvan* — if you recombine the two halves, *rishon havei* — it reverts to functioning as a *rishon*. And indeed the *Mishnah* makes this explicit in its *seifa*: if both halves fall separately on a loaf of *terumah*, each falling alone can only make the *terumah* into a *shlishi* (*terumah* can attain a *shlishi* status, which is called *pasul*). But — *im naflu shnehem ke'echad* — if both halves fall on the *terumah* simultaneously, or if one falls and remains while the second falls upon it, then at that moment there is a full *kebeitzah* of *rishon l'tumah* in contact with the *terumah*, and the *terumah* becomes a *sheni l'tumah*. *Asa sheni.*

How does this serve as a proof for Rava? The argument is as follows: when the dough was divided, each half was a mixture of half-*kebeitzah rishon* and half-*kebeitzah sheni*. Despite that internal mixture — despite the fact that the *rishon* component was thoroughly blended with *sheni* material — when both halves are reunited on the *terumah*, the *rishon* component within each half does not lose its identity. It reconnects with the *rishon* component in the other half, and together they form a full *kebeitzah* of *rishon* capable of transmitting *tumah*. The *rishon*, so to speak, wakes up. This is Rava's model for the *piggul* case: the *chutz lizmano* thought, though interrupted by the *chutz limkomo* half-thought, retains its identity and can combine with the other *chutz lizmano* half-thought to form a full *piggul*.

Tosafot's objection, noted above, applies here again: in the *tumah* case, at the critical moment when both halves lie simultaneously on the *terumah*, there is a physically present full *kebeitzah* of *rishon*. This is not an abstraction — both halves coexist at one instant. In the *piggul* case, however, the thoughts existed at different moments in time and are no longer present. Moreover, the temporal sequencing is itself part of what defines *piggul*. These differences render the *tumah* analogy genuinely strained.

### Rashi: Full Measure Start

The Gemara now records Rav Hamnuna's rebuttal: *hatam ika shiura, hacha leka shiura* — "there a *shiur* is present, here no *shiur* is present." But what exactly does this mean?

Rashi explains the distinction as follows: in the *tumah* case, *before* any mixing occurred, you began with a full *kebeitzah* of *rishon* and a full *kebeitzah* of *sheni*. Each component started at its full measure. Even after they were mixed and split, since the *rishon* began as a complete *kebeitzah*, it retains its identity more readily and can reconstitute itself as a full measure upon recombination. The identity of the *rishon* was never genuinely compromised — it simply passed through a stage of physical distribution. In the *piggul* case, by contrast, you never had a full *k'zayis* of *chutz lizmano* thought to begin with. You only ever had a half, and a half is not a full *shiur*. A half cannot wake up the way a temporarily dispersed full measure can.

### Tosafot: Tight Bonding

Tosafot offers a different reading. The phrase *leka shiura* does not mean that the *rishon* started at a full measure; rather, it refers to the *sheni l'tumah* present in the mixed dough. Because the *rishon* component is incomplete — only a half-*kebeitzah* — it bonds more tightly with whatever it is mixed with. Incompleteness creates a stronger attachment. In the *piggul* scenario, by analogy, the half-thought of *chutz limkomo* that falls between the two *chutz lizmano* thoughts forms a tight bond with the adjacent half-thought, making it harder for the *chutz lizmano* thoughts to reassert themselves and combine over that intervening thought. In the *tumah* case, the *rishon* component, when present at a full *kebeitzah*, does not need the *sheni* to complete it, and so the bond between them is weaker — allowing the *rishon* to separate out and reconstitute itself when the two halves are reunited. Tosafot thus focuses on the bonding dynamics of the intermediate component rather than the starting quantity of the dominant component.

### Rav Hamnuna: No Shiur

Rav Hamnuna himself brings a counter-proof from a parallel *Mishnah*: *ha'ochel she'nitma b'av hatumah* — food that became *tamei* through an *av hatumah* (such as a *neveilah*), rendering it a *rishon*, *v'shenitma b'vlad hatumah*, and food that became *tamei* through a derivative of *tumah* (a *rishon*), rendering it a *sheni* — *mitztarfin zeh im zeh l'tamei b'kala shebishneihem*, these combine to operate at the lower of the two levels, that of a *sheni*. This is the same basic scenario but now the two components start as halves from the outset — you never had a full *kebeitzah* of either *rishon* or *sheni* separately. You have half a *kebeitzah* of *rishon* and half a *kebeitzah* of *sheni*.

Rav Hamnuna wants to infer from the language of this *Mishnah* — which says simply that they combine to act as a *sheni* — that even if you then added a completing half-*kebeitzah* of *rishon*, the combined mass would still operate only as a *sheni*, because the *Mishnah*'s ruling is stated definitively without any qualification. This would parallel the *piggul* case: even if you add the third thought, the offering remains in its *pasul* state.

The Gemara pushes back: *lo dilma delo hadar malyei* — perhaps the *Mishnah* only means that at the stage described, the mixture operates as a *sheni*; if you were to subsequently add the remaining half-*kebeitzah* of *rishon*, it might well revert to operating as a *rishon*. The *Mishnah* is not ruling on the subsequent scenario at all. So the debate remains unresolved from this source.

---

## Half-portions Debate

### Rav Dimi's Case

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he formulated a related case. His case is: *chatzi zayis chutz limkomo, v'chatzi zayis chutz lizmano, v'chatzi zayis chutz lizmano* — first half a *k'zayis chutz limkomo*, then half a *k'zayis chutz lizmano*, then another half a *k'zayis chutz lizmano*. Rav Dimi states that this case is obviously *pasul* but not *piggul*.

His point is that the novelty he is presenting is not this case — which all would agree is *pasul* and not *piggul*, since by the time you reach the first full *k'zayis* (combining the *chutz limkomo* thought and the first *chutz lizmano* thought), the *korban* is already *pasul*. Rather, Rav Dimi's implicit claim is that even a case that seems more naturally inclined toward *piggul* — where the two *chutz lizmano* thoughts appear side by side — is nonetheless not *piggul*, because the first full *k'zayis* was reached at the *pasul* stage rather than the *piggul* stage.

### Bar Kappara Position

Bar Kappara disagrees. He holds that in the arrangement *makom, zman, zman* (i.e., the case with *chutz limkomo* first), the offering is *pasul* and not *piggul* — obviously, since the *chutz limkomo* intervened before the two *chutz lizmano* thoughts could combine. But in the reverse arrangement — where the two *chutz lizmano* thoughts appear consecutively, with *chutz limkomo* following — Bar Kappara says that is *piggul*. His ruling: *ein chatzi kezayis mo'il b'makom kezayis* — a half-*k'zayis* thought cannot function in place of a full *k'zayis* thought. Since at the moment when the first full *k'zayis* is completed you have a combination of two *chutz lizmano* halves, that constitutes *piggul*. The subsequent half-*k'zayis* of *chutz limkomo* is too small to disrupt what has already formed.

### Ravin's Formulation

When Ravin came, he presented yet another arrangement: *chatzi kezayis chutz lizmano, v'chatzi kezayis chutz lizmano, v'chatzi kezayis chutz limkomo* — that is, *zman, zman, makom*. Bar Kappara holds that this arrangement is *piggul*: by the time you have reached the first full *k'zayis*, both halves are *chutz lizmano*, giving you a complete *piggul* thought, and the subsequent half-*k'zayis* of *chutz limkomo* is insufficient to retroactively undo what has already taken effect. *Ein chatzi kezayis mo'il b'makom kezayis.*

The three arrangements can now be laid out clearly. The arrangement *makom, zman, zman* is agreed by all to be *pasul* and not *piggul* — the *chutz limkomo* half-thought combined with the first *chutz lizmano* half-thought to produce *pasul* before any *piggul* could form. The arrangement *zman, zman, makom* is *piggul* according to Bar Kappara, since the first *k'zayis* is reached through two *chutz lizmano* thoughts. And the arrangement *zman, makom, zman* — Rava's original case — is where the real dispute between Rava and Rav Hamnuna lies: Rava says *piggul* wakes up; Rav Hamnuna says it remains *pasul*.

### Rav Ashi Restructured

Rav Ashi presents a further restructuring of the case. His formulation is: *chatzi kezayis chutz lizmano u'kezayis chetzyo chutz limkomo v'chetzyo chutz lizmano* — one half-*k'zayis chutz lizmano*, followed by a full *k'zayis* that the *kohen* declares to be split: half *chutz limkomo* and half *chutz lizmano*. Bar Kappara rules: *piggul*. *Ein chatzi kezayis mo'il b'makom kezayis.*

In this formulation, when you combine the initial half-*k'zayis chutz lizmano* with the second *k'zayis* (itself internally divided half-*chutz limkomo* and half-*chutz lizmano*), you cannot draw a boundary anywhere that gives you a full *k'zayis* of *pasul* without simultaneously producing a full *k'zayis* of *piggul*. The moment the two *chutz lizmano* half-thoughts combine, you have a full *k'zayis chutz lizmano* — there is no stage at which the offering settles as merely *pasul* before *piggul* is constituted. The half-*k'zayis chutz limkomo* embedded within the second *k'zayis* is not independent enough to serve as an *eruv machshavos*; it is structurally bound within the whole.

One might have supposed that in Rava's original case — *zman, makom, zman* — the intervention of the *chutz limkomo* half prevents *piggul*, while in Rav Ashi's case, because no such intervention is possible, *piggul* results. But Rav Ashi's point (according to Bar Kappara) is that even in Rava's case, the *piggul* holds — and this case is an even more striking instance, because here one might have thought the internally combined *k'zayis* of *pasul* (half-*makom* plus half-*zman* bound together) should prevent the two *zman* halves from combining. The ruling is that they do combine.

### Rashi Correction

At this point a significant correction is in order, because Rashi reads these cases in precisely the opposite direction from an initial reading.

On reflection, Rashi understands Rav Ashi's formulation not as moving along a spectrum from clearer cases of *pasul* toward a single case of *piggul*, but in the opposite direction: all the cases are *piggul*, and Rav Ashi's *chiddush* is that even the most challenging configuration — where the intervening half-*chutz limkomo* is not a standalone thought but is structurally embedded within a full *k'zayis* combined with a half-*chutz lizmano* — is still *piggul*.

According to Rashi, the concern in Rav Ashi's case is that one could view the second *k'zayis* as a fully constituted *pasul k'zayis* (half-*makom* and half-*zman* forming a complete *pasul* unit), in which case one might argue: the first half-*k'zayis chutz lizmano* paired with this complete *pasul k'zayis* should yield only *pasul*, not *piggul*. The *chiddush* is that even so, we disaggregate: the two *chutz lizmano* halves find each other and combine, the embedded *chutz limkomo* half is insufficient to hold them apart, and *piggul* results. This is a greater *chiddush* than Rava's case, because in Rava's case the *chutz limkomo* half-thought was independent and free-standing, whereas here it is wrapped together with a *chutz lizmano* half — and even so, it cannot prevent the *piggul*.

---

## Dogs & Fire Thoughts

### Rav Yanai: Dogs Eating

Rav Yanai rules: *chishiv sheyocheluhu klavim l'machar, piggul* — if the *kohen* thought during the service that the meat would be fed to dogs tomorrow, this constitutes a *piggul* thought. The consuming act of dogs is considered *achilah* — eating. His proof is from the verse: *v'es Izevel yochlu haklavim b'chelek Yizreel* — "and Jezebel shall be consumed by the dogs in the plot of Jezreel" (Melachim I 21:23). The verb *yochlu* is used, demonstrating that the Torah treats the consumption of dogs as an act of eating.

Tosafot raises an objection: many verses speak of animals eating, so what is the *chiddush* here? The deeper question, Tosafot notes, is not merely about whether the verb *achilah* applies to dogs, but whether the conceptual structure of *piggul* can be satisfied by such a thought at all. The logic of *piggul* is that the *kohen* is redirecting the intended act — human consumption of the sacrifice — to the wrong time or place. *Piggul* is premised on a *thought about the natural, designated act of consumption*. Feeding meat to dogs is not the natural, intended act for sacrificial meat; it is closer to destruction than to the proper consumption that *piggul* addresses. Yet despite this conceptual difficulty, the ruling stands that it does constitute a *piggul* thought.

### Rav Ami Challenge

Rav Ami challenges: *ella me'ata, chishev shetochluhu esh l'machar* — if that is so, what about a thought that fire would consume the meat tomorrow? The verse states: *tochlu esh lo nopach* — "a fire not blown will consume it" (Iyov 20:26). The word *tochlu* — consuming — is used of fire. Should we then say that planning for fire to consume the sacrifice tomorrow constitutes *piggul*?

The answer, one might suggest, is yes. But then the following problem emerges from the *Mishnah*: *le'echol k'chatzi zayis u'lehaktir k'chatzi zayis kasher, she'ein achilah v'haktarah mitztarfin* — if one planned to eat half a *k'zayis* and to burn half a *k'zayis* on the altar, it is valid — these two half-*k'zayis* thoughts do not combine. If burning on the altar were simply another form of *achilah*, why would this *Mishnah* not allow the two halves to combine?

### Language Matters

The Gemara's resolution is that the answer depends entirely on precise verbal formulation. *Ei de'afkei belashon achilah, hacha nami* — if you expressed the thought about burning using the language of *achilah* — saying, for example, that the fire would *consume* it, using the eating idiom — then even fire-consumption might combine. *Hacha bemai askinan de'afkei belashon haktarah* — the *Mishnah*'s case involves the standard language of *haktarah* (offering on the altar), not *achilah*. And *lashon achilah lachud v'lashon haktarah lachud* — the language of eating and the language of altar-burning are distinct categories.

This resolution is, to say the least, striking. The entire framework of *piggul* is built on redirecting the natural act of the sacrifice to the wrong time or place. That feeding dogs or burning by fire — acts that would never satisfy the obligations of the sacrifice — should generate *piggul* based solely on the verbal category one uses in formulating the thought is a deeply counterintuitive position. And indeed it is strange that whether one says "I will burn it" versus "I will have it consumed by fire" should determine whether the thought is a valid *piggul* thought. The Gemara nonetheless resolves the question in precisely this way, leaving the reader with a sense that the formal structure of *piggul* is being operated at a level of abstraction quite removed from the practical realities of the service.

It is also worth noting, as Tosafot elsewhere points out, that this stands in stark contrast to the rule that a thought of *teme'im* eating the sacrifice is *not piggul* — because *teme'im* are categorically excluded from eating *kodashim*, and the thought therefore cannot redress the natural eating that should occur. If tamei persons do not constitute a valid eating thought, the question of why dogs should — given that neither dogs nor fire would ever satisfy the obligation — becomes all the more acute.

---

## Two People Eating

### Rav Ashi Question

Rav Ashi poses the following question: *chishev le'echol kezayis bishnei bnei adam mahu* — if the *kohen* thought during the service that a full *k'zayis* of the sacrifice would be consumed tomorrow, but split between two people, each eating half a *k'zayis*, what is the ruling? Does the thought constitute *piggul*?

The question divides on two framings. On one view: *batar machshava azlinan d'ika shiura* — we follow the thought, and the thought was about a full *k'zayis* being consumed. Since the *kohen*'s mental intent encompassed a full *k'zayis* of consumption, it should constitute *piggul*. On the alternative view: *batar ochlin azlinan v'leika shiura* — we assess each act of eating independently, and each person's act involves only a half-*k'zayis*, which is below the threshold of significance. Since no single act of eating reaches the required *shiur*, there is no valid *piggul* thought.

### Abaye's Proof

Abaye resolves the question by invoking the *Mishnah*: *le'echol k'chatzi zayis u'lehaktir k'chatzi zayis kasher, she'ein achilah v'haktarah mitztarfin* — half a *k'zayis* for human eating and half a *k'zayis* for altar consumption do not combine. The reason they do not combine is that human eating and altar-burning are categorically distinct acts. But this implies — *ha le'echol v'le'echol mitztaref* — that eating and eating do combine. If the half-*k'zayis* intended for the altar were instead intended for a second human being, the two halves of eating would combine to form a valid *piggul* thought.

Abaye states this as a near-explicit inference: *v'heichi dami b'shnei bnei adam, mitztaref* — when two human beings are each to eat half a *k'zayis*, that combines. What makes human-and-altar fail to combine is not the division of the act between two parties, but the categorical difference between human eating and altar burning. Two instances of the same category — human eating — do combine. *Shma mina.*

---

## Time Duration Issue

### Rava Slow Eating

Rava poses a further question: *chishev le'echol kezayis b'yoser m'kdei achilas pras, mahu* — if the *kohen* thought that he would eat a full *k'zayis* of the sacrifice tomorrow, but at an extremely slow pace, over a duration longer than *kdei achilas pras* (the halachically defined time unit for eating, roughly the time required to consume half a loaf of bread, often understood as approximately five to ten minutes) — does this constitute *piggul*?

The principle of *kdei achilas pras* governs many areas of halacha: for *matzah* on Pesach, eating *cheilev* or *chametz* — the forbidden act or the fulfillment of the *mitzvah* is defined by whether consumption occurred within this timeframe. Eating spread across a longer period is not considered a unified act of eating. Rava's question is whether the *piggul* thought must envision consumption within *kdei achilas pras* to be valid, or whether a thought of extended, slow consumption suffices.

### Altar vs Human Time

Two possible frameworks present themselves. *L'achilas gavoah madminan lah* — perhaps we compare the act to altar-burning, which by its nature takes far longer than *achilas pras*, and therefore a thought of extended consumption is still valid. *O l'achilas hedyot madminan lah* — or perhaps we compare it to ordinary human eating, in which case the thought must envision consumption within *achilas pras*. Logically, the answer would seem to depend on what the *kohen* was planning: if planning for his own consumption, it should be measured by human eating norms; if planning for the altar, by altar norms.

Abaye attempts to bring a proof from the same *Mishnah*: *le'echol k'chatzi zayis u'lehaktir k'chatzi zayis kasher, she'ein achilah v'haktarah mitztarfin*. He argues: *ha le'echol v'le'echol mitztaref* — if instead of an altar-half, there had been a human-eating-half, they would combine. But altar-burning takes longer than *achilas pras* — *v'haktar b'yoter m'kdei achilas pras hu*. This suggests that even when the act will take longer than *achilas pras*, it remains a valid *piggul* thought — which would seem to support the view that extended duration does not invalidate the thought.

The Gemara deflects this proof: *dilma b'hesek gadol* — perhaps the case of altar-burning being analogized involves a large fire, one that would in fact consume the sacrifice quickly, within the standard timeframe. If so, the inference fails, because we may be comparing only to a fast altar-burning case. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved. One might have expected the answer to depend naturally on the nature of the plan — human or altar — but the Gemara does not provide a clear resolution and leaves it as an open *teiku*.

---

## Non-Standard Parts

### Meat + Altar Split

The Gemara now focuses directly on the *Mishnah* that has been cited throughout: *le'echol k'chatzi zayis u'lehaktir k'chatzi zayis kasher, she'ein achilah v'haktarah mitztarfin* — a thought to eat half a *k'zayis* plus a thought to burn half a *k'zayis* on the altar: valid (*kasher*). The two half-*k'zayis* thoughts do not combine, since eating and altar-burning are two categorically distinct acts.

The Gemara now draws an inference from the precise subject matter of the *Mishnah*. What is being burned on the altar in this scenario? The *emurim* — the sacrificial innards and fats designated for the altar. And what is being eaten? The meat, which is the portion designated for human consumption. The *Mishnah* tells us that planning to eat half a *k'zayis* of meat plus planning to burn half a *k'zayis* of *emurim* does not combine. One might infer from this: but if instead of burning the *emurim* on the altar, one had planned to eat that half-*k'zayis* of *emurim* oneself, that would combine with the half-*k'zayis* of meat — yielding a full *k'zayis* of human eating-intent — and constitute *piggul*.

But this inference would be significant, because it would imply that a *kohen*'s thought to eat the *emurim* — the parts not designated for human consumption — constitutes a valid *piggul* thought. This is a matter of explicit dispute.

### R. Eliezer Dispute

Rabbi Yirmiyah identifies the position implied by this inference as that of Rabbi Eliezer: *ha meni Rabbi Eliezer hi* — this follows Rabbi Eliezer's view. For Rabbi Eliezer holds: *mechashvin me'achilat adam le'achilat mizbe'ach u'me'achilat mizbe'ach le'achilat adam* — we extend *piggul* thought from the domain of human eating to that of altar-consumption, and vice versa. A thought to eat what is normally burned on the altar, or to burn on the altar what is normally eaten, still constitutes a relevant *piggul* thought, because all parts of the sacrifice are united in the framework of *k'vod hakorban*.

The source for Rabbi Eliezer's position is the *Mishnah* later in the tractate: *ha'shochet et hazevach le'echol davar she'ein darko le'echol, le'haktir davar she'ein darko le'haktir, kasher* — if one slaughters the sacrifice with the thought of eating what is not normally eaten (e.g., hooves, or *emurim*), or burning what is not normally burned, it is valid (*kasher*) — meaning no *piggul* is created. *Rabbi Eliezer posel* — Rabbi Eliezer says it is invalid, meaning such thoughts do create *piggul*. Rabbi Eliezer takes the more expansive view that any consumption-related thought regarding any part of the sacrifice is relevant.

### Abaye Clarification

Abaye intervenes with a crucial clarification: *afilu teima Rabbanan* — even according to the *Rabbanan*, the Gemara's inference need not be read as implying that eating the *emurim* would combine. Abaye reframes the inference entirely.

The *Mishnah* says that eating half a *k'zayis* plus burning half a *k'zayis* does not combine. Abaye says: do not read the implied positive case as "eating the *emurim* would combine." Rather, read the implied positive as: if instead of burning the *emurim*, there was a plan to *eat* another half-*k'zayis* of meat — that is, the normal food portion — those two human-eating halves would combine. The *Mishnah*'s contrast is between *eating and burning* (which do not combine) versus *eating and eating* (which do combine). The combining pair must consist of two acts of the same natural category, each natural in its own domain.

The Gemara asks: but then what *chiddush* does the *Mishnah* add? If the answer to the positive case is simply that two halves of human eating combine, we already knew that from the *reisha* of the *Mishnah*, which teaches that a half-*k'zayis* eaten outside its place plus a half-*k'zayis* eaten the next day (*pasul* for being outside its time) combine and render the offering *pasul*. The Gemara responds: the *chiddush* of the *Mishnah* is precisely the negative — *she'ein achilah v'haktarah mitztarfin* — human eating and altar-burning do not combine, even though each is the natural act for its respective portion of the sacrifice. One might have thought: since eating the meat is natural and burning the *emurim* is natural, and each half represents the appropriate designated act for its part of the sacrifice, they should combine. The *Mishnah* tells us they do not.

*Salka da'atach amina hasam hu d'lav k'orchei kamachshev* — one might have supposed that the reason eating the *emurim* does not form *piggul* (per the *reisha*) is because it is not the natural act for the *kohen*. But here, where burning the *emurim* is the natural act for the altar, and eating the meat is the natural act for the human, one might have said they should combine — *eima litztaref*. The *Mishnah* teaches us otherwise: *kamashmalan*. Two natural acts in two different categories do not combine. For combination (*tzeiruf*) of half-*k'zayis* thoughts to yield *piggul*, both halves must be of the same type of act.

---

## Third Perek Opens

### Invalid Servers OK

*Hadrach alach kol hazvachim shekiblu damam* — we have completed the second *perek* and now begin the third. The new *Mishnah* opens: *kol hapesulim sheshachtu, shchitatam ksheira* — all persons who are normally disqualified from performing the Temple service, if they performed the *shechita* (the slaughter of the sacrifice), their *shechita* is valid. The list includes: one who is *tamei*, an *onen* (one in acute mourning), one who is not standing on the ground, a non-*kohen* (*zar*), and others. The reason is that *shechita* is inherently valid even when performed by persons who would be disqualified from other aspects of the *avodah* — *shehashechita ksheira b'zarim u'vnashim u'vavadim u'vtme'im* — *shechita* is valid when performed by non-*kohanim*, by women, by servants, and by *teme'im*.

The consequence follows: *lefikach hein poslim bemachshava* — therefore, because their *shechita* is valid, their *piggul* thoughts are legally operative. The law of *piggul* does not require a *kohen*; it requires only that the person performing the act be one whose performance is valid. Since all these individuals may validly perform *shechita*, their intent during *shechita* has halachic consequence, including the capacity to generate *piggul*.

### Women & Zarim OK

The *Mishnah* adds that this applies *afilu bekodshei kodashim* — even for offerings of the highest sanctity, *kodshei kodashim*, such as the *olah* and *chatat*, which must be slaughtered in the inner courtyard (*azarah*) near the altar. One might have thought that the heightened sanctity and the specific spatial requirements of *kodshei kodashim* would restrict *shechita* to qualified *kohanim*. The *Mishnah* tells us this is not so. The *Mishnah* adds: *u'vivlad shelo yehu tme'im nogim babasar* — the one condition is that *teme'im* must not come into physical contact with the meat and render it *tamei*.

### Tosafot on Women

Before proceeding to the next section of the *Mishnah*, Tosafot raises an important point: *hagemara muvchach denashim shochtot afilu lechatchila* — the Gemara demonstrates that women may perform *shechita* even *lechatchila*, not merely *b'diavad*. The *Mishnah*'s language of "if they slaughtered" (*sheshachtu*) in the past tense refers specifically to the *tamei* persons — for whom *lechatchila* is indeed inappropriate, since they risk contaminating the meat. But women are not subject to that concern, and thus the *lechatchila* permission for women is unrestricted.

Tosafot then cites this as a *teshuvah* — a formal rebuttal — to a ruling in a work called *Hilchos Eretz Yisrael*, which stated that women should not perform *shechita* because their minds are unreliable (*da'atan kalah*). Tosafot notes that this work, whose authority and provenance were questionable — likely originating from a pietistic or Kabbalistic circle — also contained the ruling that a *shechita* performed without reciting a *berachah* is *pasul*, and that if the *shochet* was unclothed at the time, the *shechita* is invalid. Both of these rulings are plainly contrary to accepted *halacha* — proper *shechita* remains valid regardless of whether a *berachah* was recited, and the physical state of the *shochet* does not affect the validity of the act. Tosafot concludes that the rulings in that work are merely personal *chumros* of whatever scholar composed it, not binding *halacha*.

This discussion reflects a broader phenomenon in the Tosafot literature: the *Rishonim* of Ashkenaz wrote in a social context where women were active participants in commerce and public life, and Tosafot frequently engages with *halachic* questions arising from that reality — whether women may be in circumstances of potential *yichud* due to business necessity, whether women may recite a *berachah* on time-bound positive commandments (*mitzvas asei shehazman grama*), and so on. Whether women were in practice actually serving as *shochatat* is a separate historical question, but Tosafot clearly feels the need to address the matter on principle.

### Tamei Access Problem

A logistical difficulty arises regarding *tamei* persons and *kodshei kodashim*. The *Mishnah* says that even *teme'im* may perform *shechita* of *kodshei kodashim* — but *kodshei kodashim* must be slaughtered inside the *azarah*, and a *tamei* person is prohibited from entering the *azarah*. How, then, can a *tamei* person perform this *shechita*?

Tosafot engages with this problem and notes that the solution depends on the precise *level* of *tumah* involved. Some categories of *tamei* persons can stand in the *Ezrat Nashim* but not in the inner *azarah*; others cannot enter even the *Ezrat Nashim*. For those who cannot enter the *Ezrat Nashim* at all, Tosafot suggests that perhaps they could stand just outside the boundary of the *azarah* near a small opening and position the animal close enough to the entryway that *shechita* could be performed — with a sufficiently long instrument and the animal placed right at the threshold. The *azarah*'s boundaries are defined by its structural walls, not by a surrounding radius. The *tamei* person need not be inside; the animal, however, must be inside for the *shechita* to count as performed in the proper location. Tosafot works through the geometry of this logistical difficulty without arriving at a fully seamless resolution, but the principle stands: somehow, the *shechita* can be accomplished by a *tamei* person without that person entering the prohibited space.

---

---

# Zevachim 32

## Psulim & Shechita

### Kol Hapsulim

The new *perek* opens with a sweeping declaration: *kol happsulim sheshachtu shechitatan kesherah* — any invalid person who performs the act of *shechita* has done so validly. The category of *pasul* here includes a non-*Kohen*, an *onen*, a *tamei* person, and others of similarly compromised status. The reason is fundamental: *shechita* requires no particular personal qualification. Even for *kodshei kodashim*, the holiest class of sacrifices, *shechita* is *kasher* performed by non-*Kohanim*, by women, by slaves, and by those in a state of *tumah* — *bezarim uvenashim uvavadim uvitmeim*, even *bekodshei kodashim*. The single operative restriction is *uvilvad shelo yiheyu tameim nogim babasar*: if the *shochet* is *tamei*, he must take care not to touch the meat and thereby transmit impurity to it.

### Machshava of Shochet

A direct consequence of this ruling concerns the role of intent. Because the act of *shechita* performed by a *pasul* person is itself legitimate, the *machshava* — the operative thought — of the person actually wielding the knife is legally meaningful. If any of these *psulim* performs *shechita* while entertaining a *piggul* thought, their thought has real halachic effect. The corollary is equally important: the thought of the owner is legally irrelevant to *shechita*. It is not ownership but the identity of the one performing the *avoda* that determines whose *machshava* counts.

### Shechita Fundamental

This principle flows directly from *shechita*'s status as one of the four foundational acts — *shechita*, *kabbalat dam*, *holachah*, and *zerikah* — that together render a *korban kasher*. For three of those four acts, a *Kohen* specifically must perform them, and so only a *Kohen*'s intent is operative. But *shechita* belongs to whoever does it. The act is not tethered to *kehunah* and is not conditioned on the performer being the owner. Therefore, whoever performs the *shechita* — *Kohen* or non-*Kohen*, owner or stranger — it is that person's *machshava* that matters.

### Tosafot on Women

*Tosafot* raises two important observations here. First, *Tosafot* emphasizes that women may perform *shechita* on *korbanot* even *lechatchila*, rejecting any *chumra* to the contrary suggested by a work called *Hilchot Eretz Yisrael*. Second, *Tosafot* addresses the practical difficulty posed by a *tamei shochet*. A *tamei* person, depending on the nature of the *tumah*, may be required to stand outside *Ezrat Nashim*. If so, how could such a person perform *shechita* at all? The answer lies in the fact — learned earlier in the first *perek* — that the *shochet* need not stand inside the *Beit Hamikdash* at all, since *shechita* is *kasher* performed by a non-*Kohen*. The *behema* stands on one side of the boundary line and the *tamei shochet* stands on the other side, cutting across with a sufficiently long knife. This works as long as the *tamei*'s *tumah* only requires exclusion from the *Azara* proper. If the *tumah* is of such severity as to require standing outside *Ezrat Nashim* as well, the practical arrangement becomes considerably more difficult to envision.

---

## Kabbalat Dam Rules

### Vechulan Shekiblu

The *Mishnah* continues: *vechulan shekiblu et hadam chutz lizmano vechutz limkomo* — all of these *psulim*, if they received the blood with a *machshava* of wrong time or wrong place, they do not render the *korban* *piggul* and they do not actively invalidate it. This is the key structural principle: because their act has no positive validity, their improper *machshava* equally lacks effect. They cannot make *piggul* and they cannot positively disqualify. The *korban* remains in an undetermined state — not rendered valid, but not actively ruined.

### Chutz Lizmano

From this principle follows a practical remedy: if the blood was received by a *pasul* person with an intent of *chutz lizmano* or *chutz limkomo*, the *korban* is not yet lost. *Im yesh dam hanefesh* — if the animal's lifeblood is still flowing from the neck — *yachazor hakasher veyekabel*: a *kasher* person should return and receive the remaining blood. If all the blood was already caught by the *pasul* person and none remains, then nothing further can be done. The *korban* cannot be rendered valid because no *kasher* person performed the *kabbalah*, but equally it was not affirmatively disqualified. The critical point is that nothing was accomplished — neither for good nor for ill — by the *pasul*'s act of reception.

### Psul No Active Stigma

This brings into sharp relief an important structural *halacha*: a *pasul*'s performance of an *avoda* act does not constitute an active *psul*. It is not that the act is done and then damages the *korban*; rather, the act simply fails to accomplish what a valid performance would have accomplished. There is no affirmative disqualification. Therefore, wherever there is an opportunity to redo the act validly — wherever more blood remains, wherever a *kasher* person can step in — one should do so. The contrast is instructive: if an animal was slaughtered incorrectly, there is no possibility of a second *shechita*. But if blood was caught by a *pasul*, that failure to constitute valid *kabbalah* is not a one-way door. If more blood is available, a *kasher* person may catch it and the *korban* may yet be saved. This same logic extends, at least in principle, to *zerikah* — throwing the blood — though the *Gemara* will examine whether that final act carries distinct complications.

---

## Nitenat Locations

### Kibel Kasher Natan

The *Mishnah* next addresses a case of handoff: *kibel hakasher venatan lapasul* — a *kasher Kohen* received the blood and then transferred it to a *pasul Kohen* for transport. The ruling: *yachzir l'kasher*, return it to the *kasher* person and redo the *holachah*. The same underlying logic applies — the *pasul*'s carrying did not validate the *holachah*, but it also did not destroy anything. (This connects to the broader *Gemara*ic debate about *holachah shelo b'regel* and what constitutes valid transport, but the simple force of the *Mishnah* is clear: no harm was done, so redo it.) This section thus reinforces the general rule: a *pasul*'s involvement is merely the absence of a valid step, not the presence of an invalidating act.

### Biyemino Bikli Kodesh

The *Mishnah* continues through a series of similar cases, each governed by the same principle. If blood was received in the right hand and transferred to the left hand — an invalid mode of transport — it should be returned to the right hand; this did not invalidate. If blood was caught in a *kli kodesh*, a sanctified vessel, and then poured into an unsanctified vessel (*kli chol*), from which it cannot validly be transported, the solution is equally straightforward: return it to the *kli kodesh*. It was not invalidated. Similarly, if blood spilled from the vessel onto the floor after having been properly caught from the neck of the animal — the *kabbalah* itself was performed correctly — one may gather it back up and the blood remains *kasher*. In none of these cases did the deviation constitute an affirmative act of disqualification. They simply represent valid acts yet to be completed, and wherever a correction is possible, it should be made.

### Shelo Bimkomo Rashi

The *Mishnah* then addresses what is perhaps the most significant set of cases: blood placed on the wrong location. The scenarios include: placing the blood on the *kevesh* (the ramp) rather than on the altar walls themselves; placing it at a corner of the altar where there is no projecting *yesod* (base) below, which is not a legitimate location; placing blood that was supposed to go below the *chut hasikra* (the dividing line on the altar) above it, or vice versa; and placing blood designated for the inner altar on the outer altar, or the reverse. In all these cases, if *dam hanefesh* remains, a *kasher* person should redo the *zerikah*.

This last ruling is the most striking *chiddush* of the *Mishnah*, because here we are dealing with the final act of the *avoda*. A separate Talmudic question — *zarika osa shirayim*, whether the act of *zerikah* itself renders any remaining blood as *shiyarei hadam* (remnant blood that may no longer be used for a redo) — bears directly on this case. The *Mishnah* nonetheless permits a redo, and Rashi presents two distinct interpretive pathways for understanding why.

### Rashi Derech Rishona

Rashi's first reading operates from the assumption that a *pasul* person who performs *zerikah* does *make* the blood into *shiyarim* — that is, even an invalid *Kohen*'s performance of the final act brings the *korban* to a point of no return if done in the right location. Given that premise, the fact that the *Mishnah* permits a redo must be teaching something else: *shelo bimkomo lav kimkomo dami* — placing the blood in the wrong location on the altar is not equivalent to placing it in the right location. Since it is as though nothing was done at all, the blood is not rendered into *shiyarim*, no terminal act has been completed, and therefore a *kasher* person may collect the remaining blood and redo the *zerikah* properly.

Under this reading, the distinction between a valid and invalid location on the altar is doing significant legal work. If a *pasul Kohen* threw the blood on the correct spot, that would end the matter — no further act is possible, and the *korban* is lost. But throw it on the wrong spot, even if you are a *pasul*, and it is as though no *zerikah* occurred at all; the process remains open.

### Rashi Derech Shniya

Rashi's second reading proceeds from the opposite premise: *shelo bimkomo kimkomo dami* — wrong-location *zerikah* is halachically equivalent to right-location *zerikah*. If that is true, then we cannot explain the *Mishnah*'s permission for a redo by virtue of the wrong location. Instead, the *Mishnah* must be teaching the converse: *ein pasul ose shirayim* — a *pasul* person's *zerikah*, even when performed in the correct location, does not render the blood into *shiyarim*. The *pasul*'s act accomplishes nothing, not even the terminal transformation of the remaining blood into remnant. Therefore, even after a *pasul* has thrown the blood — even onto the right place on the altar — if blood remains, a *kasher Kohen* may still perform a valid *zerikah*.

These two readings of the *Mishnah*'s end correspond to two distinct questions: whether location or personal status is the operative factor generating the permit for a redo. Under Rashi's first reading, location is the key; under the second, personal status is. And each reading implies a different *halacha* for the case not addressed by the *Mishnah* — either a *kasher Kohen* throwing blood in the wrong place, or a *pasul* throwing blood in the right place.

---

## Gemara: Non-Kohen

### Shachtu Bedieved

The *Gemara* now takes up the language of the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* says *shachtu* — they slaughtered — implying *b'diavad in, lechatchila lo*: one who is *pasul* may have slaughtered and the *shechita* stands, but such a person should not do so *lechatchila* in the first place. Yet this seemingly *b'diavad* framing sits in tension with other sources.

### Midrash on Shechita

The *Gemara* raises a *midrash halacha* from a *braita* that reads the relevant verse closely. The *pasuk* says *veshachat et ben habakar* — and he shall slaughter the ox — without specifying *veShachat haKohen*. The *Kohanim* are only introduced in the very next phrase: *vehikrivu bnei Aharon haKohanim et hadam* — the sons of Aharon the *Kohanim* shall bring the blood close. The Torah is thus deliberately careful to associate the *Kohanim* with the blood and all subsequent acts, but not with the *shechita* itself. The *braita* spells this out: *mikabbalah va'eilach mitzvat kehunah* — from the receiving of the blood onward, that is the *mitzvat kehunah*. The *shechita* is thereby taught to be *kesherah b'chol adam* — valid performed by any person. One might have thought otherwise, since the *pasuk* elsewhere says *vetishmeru et kehunatchem lechol dvar hamizbeach* — you shall guard the *kehunah* for all matters of the altar — suggesting the *Kohen* must perform even *shechita*. But the precise juxtaposition of *veshachat* (without specifying *Kohen*) followed immediately by *vehikrivu bnei Aharon haKohanim* (specifying *Kohanim* only from the blood onward) forecloses that reading.

### Havu Lei Hu Hadin

The language of this *braita* — *shechita b'zarim uvnashim* — makes no qualification at all; these persons may perform *shechita lechatchila* with no hesitation. Why then did the *Mishnah* adopt the *b'diavad* formulation? The *Gemara* answers: *hu hadin d'afilu lechatchila nami* — the same *din* applies even *lechatchila*. The *b'diavad* formulation in the *Mishnah* is not a restriction but a stylistic artifact.

### Tamei Gezeira

The reason for the *b'diavad* framing is practical: the *Mishnah* needed to include the case of a *tamei* person, and for a *tamei shochet*, *lechatchila* is indeed inadvisable — not because the *shechita* itself is deficient, but because of a Rabbinic concern. The restriction is a *gezeira shema yigu b'vasar*: there is concern the *tamei* person may come to inadvertently touch the meat and transmit *tumah* to it. As a precautionary measure, we say a *tamei* person should not perform *shechita lechatchila*. The *shechita* itself remains fully and unconditionally *kasher*.

### Tosafot Tamei Concern

*Tosafot* offers a noteworthy observation: one might have expected the concern about a *tamei shochet* to be the possibility of inadvertently stepping over the boundary line and entering the *Azara*. *Tosafot* dismisses this. A person who knows they are *tamei* is, precisely because of that awareness, on heightened guard about the boundary. The danger of crossing a line is actually greater for someone who does not perceive themselves as restricted. The analogy is apt: the risk of confusion between *kasher* and non-*kasher* food is greater when everything at the table appears permissible than when one item is clearly forbidden. Awareness of *tumah* status prevents inadvertent boundary crossing. The only genuine concern, therefore, is the possibility of physical contact with the meat.

---

## Shochet Location

### Utamei Dieved

Having established that even a *tamei* person's *shechita* is unimpeachable *b'diavad*, the *Gemara* now raises a sharper challenge. The prior discussion assumed that the *shochet* need not be physically situated within the *Azara* — only the animal must be there. But if a *shochet* must in fact stand in the *Azara*, then a *tamei* person could not perform *shechita* even *b'diavad*, since entry into the *Azara* in a state of *tumah* is a categorical prohibition.

### Samach V'Shachat

The challenge is mounted from a *braita* that juxtaposes *smicha* and *shechita*: *vSamach* — he shall lean [his hand on the animal] — and *vShachat* — and he shall slaughter. One *Tanna* reads this juxtaposition as a *hekesh*: just as *smicha* requires the person to be *tahor*, so does *shechita* require *tahor* status. But why would we ever have thought *smicha* requires *tahor* status in the first place? The *braita* points to the *pasuk*'s use of the phrase *lifnei Hashem* — the *someich* must perform the *smicha* in the presence of God, meaning within the *Azara*. And a *tamei* person cannot enter the *Azara*. But the *pasuk* equally places the word *lifnei Hashem* in immediate proximity to *vShachat* — and the *Gemara* observes that *lifnei Hashem* is actually more closely juxtaposed to the act of *shechita* than to *smicha*.

### Efshar Sakina Aruka

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty by arguing that *lifnei Hashem* refers not to the person performing the act but to the animal being slaughtered. The animal must be *lifnei Hashem*, within the *Azara*; the *shochet* may stand outside. This is practically realizable: *efshar d'avid sakina arucha v'shachit* — one can simply use a long knife and slaughter from beyond the boundary. Similarly, for *smicha*, if *lifnei Hashem* refers only to the animal, the *someich* could extend his arms across the line and press his hands upon the animal's head. The *Gemara* considers this possibility but notes that it depends on the question of *bia b'miktzat* — whether extending part of one's body across the threshold constitutes a prohibited entry for a *tamei* person.

### Bia Bimiktzat

This is the crux of a major debate. The question of *bia b'miktzat shma bia* — whether partial-body entry into a sacred precinct constitutes halachically cognizable entry — is not merely a technicality. If *bia b'miktzat shma bia*, then a *tamei* person who extends his hands across the line into the *Azara* has transgressed as fully as if he had walked in entirely. Under that view, *smicha* would be impossible for a *tamei* person, since pressing one's hands onto an animal standing within the *Azara* necessarily requires that the hands cross the boundary. *Shechita*, by contrast, requires no entry at all — the long knife crosses, but no part of the person's body does.

### Shimon HaTeimani

Against the dominant assumption that only the animal need be within the *Azara* for *shechita*, the *Gemara* presents the opinion of *Shimon HaTeimani*, who reads the *pasuk* differently. The verse *vShachat et ben habakar lifnei Hashem* — he shall slaughter the ox before God — is read by the majority as meaning the *nishchat*, the animal being slaughtered, must be *lifnei Hashem*. But *Shimon HaTeimani* holds that *vShachat* — the *shochet* — must be *lifnei Hashem*. The *shochet* himself must stand in the *Azara*. This reading is intuitive on the face of it: *shechita* is an act of *avoda*, and one naturally expects the performer of an *avoda* to be standing within the sacred precinct. The difficulty, of course, is that *shechita* does not require a *Kohen* at all — and once the personal status requirement is lifted, it becomes less obvious why a locational requirement should persist. *Shimon HaTeimani* nonetheless maintains it. Under his view, a *tamei* person cannot perform *shechita* even *b'diavad* because a *tamei* person cannot be present in the *Azara*.

---

## Bia Bimiktzat Ulah

### Tamei Yad Lokei

*Ulla* transmits in the name of *Reish Lakish* a striking ruling: *tamei shehichnis yado lifnim lokei* — a *tamei* person who inserts his hand into the *Azara* receives *malkot* (lashes). This is a full-fledged violation, not a mere rabbinic concern.

### Mikyash Bia Negiah

The source is a *hekesh* between *negi'ah* (touching) and *bia* (entry). The verse, in the context of a woman who has given birth, states *bechol kodesh lo tiga ve'el hamikdash lo tavo* — she shall not touch any holy thing and shall not enter the *Mikdash* until her days of purification are complete. The *Gemara* derives: just as *negi'ah* with a mere part of one's body — a finger, a hand — constitutes full halachic touching, so too *bia b'miktzat shma bia* — entry with a part of the body constitutes entry. Extending a hand across the boundary of the *Azara* is entry. Hence, lashes.

### Metzora Chamishi

*Rav Oshaya* challenges this ruling from the case of a *metzora* whose eighth day falls on *erev Pesach*.

---

## Metzora Baal Keri

### Yom Shmini Metzora

The case is as follows. A *metzora* reaches his eighth day of purification — the day on which he must appear at the *Beit Hamikdash* to bring his *korban* and complete his *taharah* process — and this day falls on *erev Pesach*. Under ordinary circumstances this presents no difficulty: he comes to the *Mikdash*, completes the eighth-day procedure, and is fully *tahor* in time to eat the *korban Pesach* that night. But this particular individual is also a *baal keri* — he has had a seminal emission. Now his situation is considerably more complicated.

### Machane Shechina Levels

The *Gemara* recalls the *pasuk*: *vayishalchu min hamachane kol tzaruah vechol zav vechol tamei lanefesh* — three categories of *tumah*, three separate zones of exclusion. *Tzaruah* is excluded from all three *machanot* — he must dwell entirely alone outside the camp. *Zav* — and this category includes *zavah*, *niddah*, and *baal keri*, all those who have *tumah yotzei migufo* — is excluded from *machaneh Leviyah* (the *Har HaBayit*) and *machaneh Shechina* (the *Azara* and *Ezrat Nashim*) but may be present in *machaneh Yisrael* (the rest of *Yerushalayim*). *Tamei lanefesh*, meaning *tamei meis* — along with those *tamei* from external sources such as *sheretz* or *neveilah* — is excluded only from *machaneh Shechina* itself.

Our *metzora* on his eighth day has completed the seven-day purification and may now enter as far as the *Har HaBayit*. What bars him from the *Azara* is not his *tzaraat* status — that he has effectively worked through — but only the fact that he has not yet completed the eighth-day procedure itself. He is a *mechusar kipurim*, lacking only the final *korban*. He stands at the *Nicanor Gate*, on the boundary between *Ezrat Nashim* and the *Azara*, and the *Kohen* applies the blood from the *korban metzora* to his thumbs. This physical procedure cannot be delegated; the *metzora* must be personally present.

His problem is that he is also a *baal keri*. As a *baal keri*, even if he immerses in a *mikvah*, he is a *tvul yom* — one who has immersed but whose *taharah* is not complete until nightfall. The question is whether a *tvul yom* of a *baal keri* retains a prohibition against entering *Har HaBayit* and *Ezrat Nashim* until nightfall.

### Tvul Yom Pesach

The *Chachamim* rule that in this case we allow the *metzora* who has immersed — now a *tvul yom* of *baal keri* — to enter nonetheless. The reasoning: *mutav sheyavo asei sheyesh bo karet* — let the positive *mitzvah* that carries *karet* if neglected, namely the obligation to bring the *korban Pesach*, come forward and push aside the positive *mitzvah* that does not carry *karet* — namely the *asei* of *vishilchu min hamachane* that keeps the *baal keri* off *Har HaBayit*. The argument is that the *tvul yom*'s presence does not violate the negative prohibition of *velo yitam'u et machaneihem*, since a *tvul yom* is no longer considered *mitamei* — he has already entered the *taharah* process and his residual impurity no longer causes defilement to the surrounding area. Therefore the only obstacle is the positive commandment, and that is overridden by the weightier positive commandment of *korban Pesach*.

### Rabbi Yochanan Tvul

*Rabbi Yochanan* goes further. He holds that *d'var Torah afilu asei ein bah* — even as a matter of Torah law, there is no positive *mitzvah* preventing a *tvul yom* from being in *machaneh Leviyah*. A *tvul yom* is, from the Torah's perspective, effectively *tahor* for purposes of *Har HaBayit* and *Ezrat Nashim*. His proof: the verse *vayaamod Yehoshaphat bikhal Yehudah viYerushalayim b'veis Hashem lifnei hahatzer hahadashah* — he stood in the House of God before the new courtyard. *Rabbi Yochanan* understands *hatzer hadashah* as *Ezrat Nashim*, and the "newness" refers to a rabbinic innovation: *sh'hiddeshu bah devarim*, they newly decreed that a *tvul yom* should not enter *machaneh Leviyah*. This shows that prior to the rabbinic decree, a *tvul yom* was permitted in this zone. The biblical prohibitions — both the positive *asei* and the negative *lo ta'asei* — apply only to a *tamei* person who has not yet immersed. Once immersion occurs, the Torah considers the person effectively *tahor* for these zones, and any remaining restriction is purely rabbinic. For *korban Pesach*, that rabbinic restriction is set aside.

### Amar Eli Bia Bonanot

But now the *Gemara* resurfaces the problem that *Rav Oshaya* was building toward. Even if we accept that this *metzora-tvul yom* is permitted in *Ezrat Nashim* — either because the *asei* is overridden or because there is no *asei* at all — a separate and serious difficulty remains. The *metzora* must have the blood from his *korban* applied to his thumbs. He stands on the *Ezrat Nashim* side of the *Nicanor Gate*. His thumbs must cross into the *Azara* proper. Everyone agrees that until his eighth-day procedure is complete, a *metzora* may not enter the *Azara* proper. So the only way his thumbs can be in the *Azara* is if he reaches them across the boundary line. That is precisely *bia b'miktzat*. If *bia b'miktzat shma bia*, how is this permitted? And all the more so for someone who is also a *baal keri*: even after immersing, he is not permitted in the *Azara* itself, and sticking his thumbs into the *Azara* would constitute *bia b'miktzat* — which on *Ulla* and *Reish Lakish*'s account would incur *malkot*.

---

## Metzora Hutrah

### Houil Vetuter

*Reish Lakish* responds: *matuncha* — the very challenge you pose is my answer. *Shani metzora, ho'il v'hutar l'tzara'ato hutar l'keryo* — the *metzora* case is unique, because the Torah itself, by prescribing the thumb-application as the mechanism of the *metzora*'s *taharah*, implicitly permits the *metzora* to extend his thumbs. There is an inherent *heter* embedded in the *taharah* procedure for *metzora*. Once that *heter* exists for the *metzora*'s status, it extends as well to the lighter *tumah* status of *baal keri* that the same individual carries. Since the dispensation already applies, and the *baal keri* status is the lesser *tumah*, the dispensation encompasses that as well.

### Rav Yosef Inference

*Rav Yosef* seizes on the logic of *Ulla*'s position to draw a broader inference. Since *Ulla* holds that a dispensation granted for one *tumah* extends to a lesser *tumah* in the same individual, *Ulla* must hold the following: if the majority of the *tzibur* consists of *zavim*, and those same people become *temei meitim*, then since they would receive a dispensation to bring the *korban Pesach* as *tamei meis* — under the principle of *tumah hutrah b'tzibur* — that dispensation would extend to cover their *zivah* status as well.

### Abaye Hazirah

*Abaye* objects: *mi dami?* The comparison does not hold. By the *metzora*, the dispensation came first — the *metzora* had the *heter* for his thumbs before he acquired the *baal keri* status. Here you have the sequence reversed: they were *zavim* first, which status is not covered by *tumah hutrah b'tzibur*, and only then did they become *temei meitim*. You cannot say that an override granted for a subsequent *tumah* reaches back to cover a pre-existing and heavier *tumah* that was never individually subject to an override.

### Dilma Hachi Kamart

*Abaye* then reconsiders and offers a corrected version of *Rav Yosef*'s inference: perhaps the *chiddush* works with the reverse order. The majority of the *tzibur* is *temei meitim* — already subject to *tumah hutrah b'tzibur*, the dispensation applies. Then they become *zavim*. Now the question is whether the already-active dispensation continues to cover them even in light of the new *zivah* status. This mirrors the *metzora* case: dispensation first, additional *tumah* second. *Rav Yosef* accepts the correction.

### Lo Dami Hutrah

Even so, the *Gemara* challenges the analogy. There is a fundamental difference between *metzora* and *tumah b'tzibur*. By *metzora*, the Torah prescribed the thumb-application as part of the *taharah* procedure itself. The implication is that for a *metzora*, the *bia b'miktzat* is not merely tolerated or overridden — it is simply not a problem at all. This is the distinction between *hutrah* and *dchuya*. *Hutrah* — the Torah's complete dispensation — means that no prohibition was ever in force here to begin with: sticking the thumbs in is simply part of what the *metzora* does, and the Torah never considered it a violation. *Dchuya* — the "pushing aside" model — means that there is a genuine prohibition, but it is overridden by a countervailing value. *Tumah b'tzibur* operates in the *dchuya* framework: the *tumah* is a real problem that is being overridden by the communal necessity of the *korban Pesach*. Under *dchuya*, since we are acknowledging a real problem and consciously overriding it, we are limited in how far that override reaches. It can cover *tamei meis*, which is the specific *tumah* the dispensation was articulated for. It cannot automatically sweep in *zivah*, which was never individually covered.

### Rava Adderaba

*Rava* disputes this reasoning directly. *Adderaba ipcha mistabra* — the reverse logic is more compelling. By *metzora*, if the correct understanding is *hutrah* — that the Torah simply never considered the thumb-extension to be any kind of violation — then what we have is a narrow, specific, self-contained dispensation. The Torah said: for a *metzora*, this is fine. That says nothing about any other situation. Apply it to *baal keri*? We never heard that. There is no principle of override in force that could logically extend. *Lehah ishtarei, lehah lo ishtarei* — to this it applies, to that it does not.

By contrast, under *dchuya* — the *tumah b'tzibur* model — we have articulated an affirmative principle: the communal obligation of *korban Pesach* is weighty enough to override *tumah*. That is a principle, not a narrow exception. And once you have established that such overrides are possible, *ma li chada dchuya ma li shtei dchuyos* — what difference does it make whether we are overriding one type of *tumah* or two? The power of override, once invoked, can reach further. *Hutrah* creates a specific carve-out. *Dchuya* creates a principle that can be extended. *Rava*'s logic is that the *dchuya* framework is therefore actually broader in its potential application than the *hutrah* framework — a counterintuitive but compelling argument.

### Metzora vs. Baal Keri

The conclusion that emerges from this discussion is that the question of how the *metzora* who is also a *baal keri* can extend his thumbs into the *Azara* admits of two resolutions. Under one view, *bia b'miktzat* is not a violation to begin with — *bia b'miktzat lo shma bia* — and there is therefore no problem to solve. Under the other view, *bia b'miktzat shma bia* is indeed a real violation, and the special *hutrah* that the Torah grants the *metzora* for his thumb-application extends to cover even the *baal keri* status that the same person carries simultaneously. What cannot work, according to *Rava*, is an explanation based on *dchuya* — for a *dchuya*-based dispensation, being inherently broader in principle, would only reinforce the thumb-extension, not limit it. It is therefore *hutrah* or nothing.

---

## Mikhlal Shecheihem

### Common Ground

Despite their disagreement over which framework is more logically expansive, both *Reish Lakish* and *Rava* share two foundational commitments. First, both agree that the *metzora*'s thumb-application is a case of *hutrah* — the Torah's complete dispensation, not a situation of overriding a prohibition. Second, both agree that *tumah b'tzibur* operates under the framework of *dchuya* — the communal *tumah* is a real problem that is being overridden, not a situation that the Torah simply defined as non-problematic. These two points of agreement — *metzora hutrah, tumah dchuya* — are *michlal*, established by inference from their very debate, and they set the stage for the next discussion.

### Next Discussion Intro

Tomorrow's *shiur* will take up the broader question of *tumah dchuya b'tzibur* and examine the logical scope of that principle: what precisely the *dchuya* framework permits, what it cannot reach, and how far the override of communal *tumah* extends when there are multiple competing considerations. That discussion picks up directly from the shared premise that both *Amoraim* have implicitly accepted here.

---

---

# Zevachim 33

## Tumah: Dechuyah Review

### Metzora & Tevul Yom

The daf opens with a brief recapitulation of yesterday's discussion. The *gemara* had been wrestling with the case of the *metzora* who inserts his hands into the *azarah* at the Gate of Nicanor in order to perform *smicha* on his *asham*. The complication arose when the *metzora* was simultaneously a *tevul yom* — one who had immersed in a *mikvah* after a seminal emission (*ba'al keri*) but whose purification would not be complete until nightfall. The *gemara* had offered multiple approaches: perhaps *bia'ah b'miktzat lo shemah bia'ah* — that entering only partially, with one's hands, does not constitute a halachically cognizable entry — or alternatively, that since the Torah had already overridden the prohibition (*hutra*) to permit the *metzora* to insert his hands as part of his purification ritual, that override extended as well to his status as a *ba'al keri*.

### Hutra vs. Dechuyah

The *gemara* then extended that question to the more general issue of *tumah* in the context of communal sacrifices. When a majority of the *tzibur* is *tamei meis* — impure from contact with the dead — and simultaneously *zavim*, would the same logic apply? This led to a broader discussion of whether the status of the *metzora* is one of *hutra* — meaning there was never any prohibition for him in the first place — or whether *tumah* in general is merely *dechuyah*, overridable under pressing circumstances but still intrinsically prohibited. The *gemara*'s concluding formulation is: *michlal d'travayhu svira lehu tumah dechuyah hi b'tzibur* — it can be inferred that both positions in the debate agree that *tumah* is *dechuyah*, not *hutra*, in the context of communal sacrifices. The practical consequence of this distinction is significant: if *tumah* is *dechuyah*, one must minimize the extent of the override and cannot treat the dispensation more expansively than necessary, even though a mechanism for override does exist.

## Bia'ah B'Miktzat at Gate

### Smicha/Shechita Verse

With that summary concluded, the *gemara* turns to the central theme of the day: whether *bia'ah b'miktzat* constitutes a genuine violation. The *gemara* introduces a potential proof: *kol ha-smichot she-hayu sham korei ani aleihem teichef lismicha shechita* — all the acts of *smicha* performed in the *Beis HaMikdash* are governed by the juxtaposition of *smicha* and *shechita* in the verse, which places the two acts in immediate sequence. This juxtaposition obtains for every *korban* — *chutz mizo*, except for the *asham* of the *metzora*, which was performed at the Gate of Nicanor. Because the *metzora* cannot fully enter the *azarah* to have his *smicha* juxtaposed to the *shechita*, the verse's requirement of *teichef lismicha shechita* cannot be fulfilled in his case.

### Gate Geography

To appreciate this fully, the geography of the *Beis HaMikdash* must be kept in mind. The Gate of Nicanor stood precisely at the threshold between the *Ezrat Nashim* — the women's courtyard — and the *azarah* proper, which is the *Ezrat Yisrael* leading into the *Ezrat Kohanim*. Crossing that gate constituted entry into the sanctified precincts of the *azarah*. The distinction between who was permitted where is important: a *mechusar kippurim* — one who has undergone immersion but has not yet brought his purification offering — is permitted in the *Ezrat Nashim* but is forbidden to enter the *azarah* itself. Mid'oraita, a *tamei meis* could likewise proceed as far as the *Ezrat Nashim*, though the rabbis restricted this as well. It is thus on the outer side of the Gate of Nicanor that the *metzora* stands.

### Metzora Restrictions

The verse mandates that the *metzora* cannot enter until the blood of his *chatat* and *asham* have been processed — *ad she-mazin alav midam chatato midam ashamo*. Rashi notes that this formulation is slightly imprecise: the blood of the *chatat* is not literally sprinkled upon him, but the verse is indicating that both the *chatat* and the *asham* must be brought first, and the blood of the *asham* is used in the purification ritual applied to his thumbs, big toes, and right ear. Until this process is complete, the *metzora* is not sufficiently *tahor* to enter.

The natural question presents itself: why not simply have the *metzora* stand at the gate, thrust his hands inside, perform *smicha* on the animal standing within the *azarah*, and then immediately proceed to *shechita*?
