The fact that the *gemara* does not entertain this solution — and instead indicates that the *smicha* cannot be juxtaposed to the *shechita* — implies that inserting one's hands constitutes a prohibited entry. This cuts against what had been assumed yesterday, when the *gemara* proceeded on the assumption that the *metzora* was permitted by the Torah to insert his hands as part of the ritual. Today's discussion entertains the alternative: that sticking one's hands in is a genuine problem, even for the *metzora*, and therefore the solution must be to bring the animal out to him into the *Ezrat Nashim* so that he can perform *smicha* there. This is itself a remarkable *chiddush*, since it implicitly assumes that *smicha* need not be performed *lifnei Hashem* — with the animal standing inside the *azarah*.

A student correctly noted that this cannot be the complete picture, because the application of the *asham*'s blood to the *metzora*'s thumbs and toes cannot be accomplished by bringing the blood out of the *azarah* — blood of a *korban* may not be taken outside. Therefore, for the blood-application ritual, there is no alternative: the *metzora*'s thumbs must go in, and the Torah implicitly granted that dispensation. The *smicha*, however, presents a different situation — there, we can bring the animal out to him, which is the approach the *gemara* pursues, provided the animal does not need to be physically within the *azarah* for *smicha* to be valid.

### Juxtaposition Problem

The implicit assumption that *bia'ah b'miktzat* is a problem — demonstrated by the fact that we do not simply have the *metzora* extend his hands inside to perform *smicha* — thus serves as a possible proof that *bia'ah b'miktzat shemah bia'ah*. The *gemara* states this directly: *v'im amarta bia'ah b'miktzat lo shemah bia'ah*, let him insert his hands and perform the *smicha* immediately adjacent to the *shechita*. The fact that the *halacha* does not permit this suggests that partial entry is itself a violation.

## Three Solutions

### Merchak Tzafon Answer

The *gemara* answers: *amar Rav Yosef*, this entire passage reflects the position of Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *merchak tzafon* — that the valid northern zone for *kodshei kodashim* is not the broad area generally north of the altar, but rather the area immediately opposite the altar wall itself, not at a distance from it. According to this view, the Gate of Nicanor, which sits roughly in the center of the complex, is too far from the immediate north of the altar. The *metzora* could theoretically insert his hands to perform *smicha* — since *bia'ah b'miktzat* is not the problem — but the animal would then need to be walked to the directly opposite northern zone of the altar for *shechita*, during which time the *metzora* cannot accompany it further into the *azarah*. Hence the *smicha* and *shechita* cannot be juxtaposed. This is not a statement about *bia'ah b'miktzat* at all.

The *gemara* then asks: if the *metzora* can insert his hands and the only obstacle is that the animal needs to be moved north before *shechita*, why not simply cut a small doorway (*pishpash*) at the northern wall of the *azarah*, allowing the *metzora* to stand there and insert his hands directly adjacent to the proper northern zone, thereby achieving *teichef lismicha shechita*? The *gemara* answers in the name of Abaye and Rava that the structure of the *Mikdash* cannot be arbitrarily altered: *ha-kol bi-chtav mi-yad Hashem alai hiskil* — everything was divinely prescribed. If such a doorway cannot be created, then the *mechak tzafon* problem remains even if *bia'ah b'miktzat* is permitted, and the proof fails.

### Kol Kocho Answer

A second version of Rav Yosef's statement offers an entirely different resolution. According to this version, *bia'ah b'miktzat lo shemah bia'ah* is perfectly valid — the *metzora* could in principle insert his hands without transgressing. The problem is a different one: *kol ha-somech rosho ve-rubo machnees* — one who performs *smicha* must lean in with his head and the majority of his body, because *smicha* requires *kol kocho*, one's full bodily weight and force. A mere gentle placement of hands from outside the threshold is insufficient; the person must genuinely press down, putting his back into it, which necessarily means that the greater part of his body crosses the line. And that constitutes a full *bia'ah*, not a *bia'ah b'miktzat* at all. Therefore it is not a question of partial entry — his entry would necessarily be complete, and that is what is forbidden.

### Rabbinic Override

Rav Adda bar Matnah raises a deeper challenge. If *smicha* for the *asham metzora* is biblically required (*d'oraita*), and *teichef lismicha shechita* is likewise a *d'oraita* obligation, then the very fact that the Torah requires both of these for the *metzora* implicitly licenses him to fulfill them — just as the Torah implicitly licenses the insertion of the thumbs for the blood-application ritual. If the Torah truly demands *smicha* followed immediately by *shechita* from this *metzora*, then presumably it also provides the means to do so. Why then is there any problem?

Rav Adda bar Matnah answers: in truth, *d'oraita* the *metzora* does have a license — either to enter with his full body to the north of the altar, or to perform *bia'ah b'miktzat*, or to lean in with *kol kocho*, depending on which obstacle one accepts. The rabbis, however, introduced a rabbinic override restricting this, out of concern for *gezeirah shema yarbeh bifsi'ot* — lest he take more steps than necessary into the forbidden zone. For a *metzora* to whom entry is otherwise categorically prohibited, even one extra step inside is a serious matter, and the rabbis restricted the license to its absolute minimum.

Yet even accepting this rabbinic restriction, a further question remains: if we resolve the problem by bringing the animal out to the *metzora* in the *Ezrat Nashim*, how has the obligation of *smicha* been fulfilled? The animal is outside the *azarah* — is that a valid *smicha* at all?

## Smicha Location

### Tahorim Derasha

The *gemara* now confronts this question directly by examining the scriptural basis for *smicha* requirements. The verse states *vesamach veshachat* — he shall lean and he shall slaughter — and from this juxtaposition the *gemara* derives: *mah smicha b'tehorim af shechita b'tehorim* — just as *smicha* must be performed in a state of *tahara*, so too *shechita* must be performed in a state of *tahara*. The premise of this *derasha* — that *smicha* requires *tahara* — itself presupposes that *smicha* must be performed inside the *azarah*, where only those who are *tahor* may stand. If the animal could simply be brought outside to an impure person for *smicha*, there would be no basis for requiring *tahara* as a precondition for *smicha*.

### Implications

The *gemara* draws out the full implication: if one were to say that *teichef lismicha shechita* is not *d'oraita*, then *smicha* could also be performed *b'temei'im* — with impure persons — by bringing the animal out to them in the *Ezrat Nashim*. But the *derasha* clearly presupposes both that *smicha* is performed inside the *azarah* (*lifnei Hashem*) and that it is immediately followed by *shechita*. Hence both the location requirement and *teichef lismicha shechita* are *d'oraita*. The solution of bringing the animal out to the *metzora* in the *Ezrat Nashim* is therefore in direct tension with these established requirements.

### Non-Obligatory Smicha

The *gemara*'s resolution is to reverse the assumptions entirely: *semikhat asham metzora lav d'oraita* — the *smicha* performed as part of the *asham metzora* ritual is not a biblical obligation at all. *Teichef lismicha shechita* is indeed *d'oraita*, but since *smicha* itself is not required for the *asham metzora*, the entire framework collapses. There is no biblical mandate being bypassed, and therefore no implicit license is created by the Torah.

Why is *smicha* not required here? Rashi explains that the *asham metzora* is unusual among sacrifices in that its entire purpose is instrumental — it exists to generate the blood that will be applied to the *metzora*'s thumbs, toes, and ear as part of his purification. Unlike an ordinary *chatat* or *asham*, where the owner brings the *korban* as an act of spiritual identification and atonement, the *asham metzora* is not truly being offered as an expression of the owner's religious act; it is a means to produce the purifying blood. Tosafot raises difficulties with this reasoning, but that is the *gemara*'s position.

The full picture can now be stated coherently. The *metzora* cannot insert his hands for *smicha* — whether because of *bia'ah b'miktzat*, or because *kol kocho* would make it a full *bia'ah*, or because of the *merchak tzafon* issue. He has no implicit license to enter for *smicha* because *smicha* is not actually required of him. The solution of bringing the animal out to him in the *Ezrat Nashim* is therefore not a bypass of a *d'oraita* obligation; since the *smicha* is not biblically required anyway, bringing the animal to him constitutes a rabbinic pseudo-*smicha*, performed in the spirit of the ritual even though it does not satisfy any biblical standard. The parallel is the well-known *gemara* about women performing *smicha* — the *tanna* records that the animal was brought into the *Ezrat Nashim* and women laid their hands upon it, *lo she-hasemicha banashim ella k'dei la'asot nachas ruach lanashim* — not because *smicha* is obligatory for women, but as a meaningful gesture. Similarly here, the *metzora* performs a symbolic *smicha* in the *Ezrat Nashim*, which suffices precisely because no biblical *smicha* is demanded of him. The thumbs-in ritual for applying the blood remains in a separate category: there, entry is unavoidable, the Torah implicitly licensed it, and the rabbis left that license intact.

## Ravina's Solution

### Lashes for Touching

The *gemara* now returns to the original question from yesterday's discussion with a fresh approach, attributed to Ravina. Recall the problem: even granting that the *metzora* has a general override permitting his hands to enter the *azarah* for purposes of his purification, why can he insert his thumbs when he is simultaneously a *ba'al keri* — a status that independently prohibits entry? Yesterday's answer was that the *ba'al keri* status is subsumed within the general *metzora* override. Ravina offers an entirely different answer.

The statement that *bia'ah b'miktzat* carries lashes — *le'inyan malkot itmar* — was specifically said in the context of touching a *korban* while impure. The question of *bia'ah b'miktzat* and lashes was never about spatial entry into the *azarah* as such; it was about the act of a *tamei* person making physical contact with a sacred object. When one extends a finger and touches a *korban*, that contact is the violation, and lashes follow.

### Malkot vs. Karet

The crucial implication of Ravina's reading is this: if *bia'ah b'miktzat* carries only *malkot* and not *karet*, then the *metzora* who is a *ba'al keri* and inserts his thumbs for the blood ritual incurs at most a prohibition punishable by lashes — not *karet*. A prohibition of *malkot* alone is capable of being overridden by the positive obligation to bring a *korban pesach*, which is an *asei she-yesh bo karet* — a positive commandment whose violation incurs *karet*. Therefore, the need to complete the *metzora*'s purification so that he can bring his *korban pesach* provides sufficient grounds to override the *malkot*-level prohibition associated with the *ba'al keri* status. Tosafot is troubled by this reasoning — since when does *korban pesach* override a *lav* that carries *malkot*? — but that is the structure of Ravina's answer.

## Ravin's Rejection

### Bia'ah Not Topic

When Ravin arrived from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted a tradition in the name of Rabbi Abba that fundamentally reframes the entire discussion: *le'inyan tamei she-nagah b'kodesh itmar* — the original statement about lashes was never about *bia'ah b'miktzat* at all. There was never a ruling that partial entry into the *azarah* with a limb constitutes a violation. The statement about *malkot* for using only part of one's body was always about something else entirely: a *tamei* person who physically touches a *korban*. That is the violation — *bia'ah b'miktzat* as an independent category does not exist.

### Reish Lakish Ruling

With this clarification, the *gemara* pivots to the underlying dispute. *D'itmar tamei she-nagah b'kodesh* — it was stated regarding a *tamei* person who touches a sacred object: *Reish Lakish amar lokeh* — Reish Lakish rules that one receives *malkot*. The verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga* — "you shall not touch any sacred thing" — explicitly prohibits a *tamei* person from touching a *korban*, and Reish Lakish takes this prohibition at face value as generating *malkot*.

### Yochanan Disputes

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *eino lokeh* — one does not receive *malkot* for touching a *korban* while *tamei*. In Rabbi Yochanan's reading, the verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga* is not referring to *korbanot* at all — *hu b'trumah ksiv*, it is written in the context of *terumah*. And moreover, Rabbi Yochanan maintains that even within that context, the verse's primary referent is eating *terumah* in a state of *tumah*, not mere touching. One might attempt a *kal va-chomer* from *terumah* to *korbanot*, but the principle *ein onshin min ha-din* — one does not derive punishments by logical inference — would preclude deriving *malkot* for touching *korbanot* from a verse about *terumah*.

## Touching Korban

### Touching & Eating

The *gemara* now elaborates the full positions of Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan. Reish Lakish, who reads *bechol kodesh lo tiga* as referring to *korbanot*, derives two distinct prohibitions from this single verse — a prohibition against *touching* a *korban* while *tamei*, and a prohibition against *eating* a *korban* while *tamei*. The verse's use of the language of *negiah* (touching) establishes a *lav* for the act of touching; simultaneously, the verse is also understood to generate a *lav* for eating. This requires explanation, since a single phrase cannot straightforwardly yield two separate prohibitions.

### Terumah Argument

Rabbi Yochanan's counterargument proceeds in two stages. First, the verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga* is not about *korbanot* at all — it is about *terumah*. Second, even regarding *terumah*, what the verse prohibits is eating while *tamei*, not mere touching. The prohibition against eating *terumah* in a state of *tumah* is indeed subject to *malkot*, but it is derived differently. Rabbi Yochanan does not generate his prohibition for eating *korbanot* while *tamei* from this verse; he derives it through a *gezeirah shavah* linking the phrase *v'tumaso alav* that appears in the context of *ochel kodesh* to the phrase *o tumaso bo* that appears in the context of *bia'at mikdash*. Just as entering the *Mikdash* while *tamei* incurs *karet* and is subject to a negative prohibition (derived from *v'lo yitamu es machneichem*), so too eating *kodesh* while *tamei* incurs *karet* and is subject to a negative prohibition — not from the *tiga* verse, but from this derivation. According to Rabbi Yochanan, then, one never receives *malkot* for merely touching a *korban*; that prohibition simply does not exist.

### Both Inferred

The *gemara* presses Reish Lakish: can he truly derive both touching and eating from this single phrase? He needs the verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga* to establish the *azhara* for *ochel basar kodesh* — the prohibition against eating sanctified meat while *tamei*. If the verse is generating a prohibition for eating, is it also simultaneously available to generate a prohibition for touching? The *gemara* answers on behalf of Reish Lakish: yes, it can do both. The verse prohibits touching (*tiga*), which gives a *lav* for *negiah*. But the verse is also implicitly about eating — and this is known not from the language of touching, but from the structural context of the verse.

### Karet Connection

The reasoning is as follows. The verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga v'el ha-mikdash lo tavo* juxtaposes touching sacred things with entering the *Mikdash*. We know that entering the *Mikdash* while *tamei* carries *karet*. We also know independently that eating *korbanot* while *tamei* carries *karet* — whereas touching does not. Therefore, when the verse says *lo tiga* in the same breath as *v'el ha-mikdash lo tavo*, the implicit referent of the prohibition must include eating, because that is the act associated with *karet*. Touching alone does not trigger *karet*, so the *karet*-bearing element of the verse must be pointing at eating. But since the verse uses the language of *negiah*, it is simultaneously generating a *lav* for touching as well. In this way, Reish Lakish extracts from a single verse a prohibition on touching (derived from the literal language) and a prohibition on eating (derived from the *karet* connection to *bia'at mikdash*).

Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, denies that this verse speaks of *korbanot* at all and therefore never concedes a *lav* for touching *korbanot* while *tamei*. His *lav* for eating *korbanot* while *tamei* comes from the *gezeirah shavah*, and the *karet* for eating is independently established by *v'tumaso alav venichratah*. The *gemara* cites a *baraita* that supports Reish Lakish's position: *bechol kodesh lo tiga asro le'ochal* — this verse prohibits eating, and the *baraita* then derives this through the very mechanism Reish Lakish employs, comparing *kodesh* to *mikdash* on the basis of the *karet* penalty and the juxtaposition of the two clauses.

The *sugya* thus concludes with the following structure. According to Ravin citing Rabbi Abba, the original statement attributed to Reish Lakish was never about *bia'ah b'miktzat* as spatial entry; it was about the *lav* for a *tamei* person touching a *korban*. Reish Lakish holds that such a *lav* exists and is derived from *bechol kodesh lo tiga*, and he further derives from the same verse a *lav* for eating. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the verse speaks only of *terumah*, that no *lav* exists for touching *korbanot*, and that the *lav* for eating *korbanot* while *tamei* is derived through the *gezeirah shavah* of *tumaso-tumaso* connecting *ochel kodesh* to *bia'at mikdash*.

---

---

# Zevachim 34

## Resh Lakish vs. R. Yocha…

### Verse Context

The daf opens three lines from the top of 34a, in the middle of an ongoing debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. The verse under examination is *bechol kodesh lo tiga v'el hamikdash lo tavo* — "do not touch anything holy, and do not enter the sanctuary" — a verse originally addressed to a woman after childbirth. This verse had previously served as the entry point into a broader discussion about *bi'ah b'miktzat*, namely whether partial entry into the *mikdash* by a *tamei* person constitutes a violation. That question was left unresolved. Now the Gemara turns to ask: setting aside that derivation, what else do we learn from this verse?

### Resh Lakish's View

Resh Lakish reads the verse at its most straightforward level. *Bechol kodesh lo tiga* — don't touch anything sanctified — constitutes a simple *lav*, a negative prohibition, and one who violates it receives lashes. But Resh Lakish goes further. Since the verse concludes with a reference to entering the *mikdash* — an act punishable by *kareis* — the context is clearly one of great weight. Mere touching of an object, absent any *kareis* connection, would ordinarily not rise to that level. Therefore Resh Lakish understands the verse as encompassing not only touching but also eating sacrificial food while *tamei*, an act that does carry *kareis*. Both prohibitions — touching and eating — are thus derived from this single verse.

### R. Yochanan's View

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. He holds that this verse is not speaking about sacrifices at all but about *terumah*. This is admittedly a striking position — it implies that one would receive lashes for touching *terumah* but not for touching a sacrifice — and the *Shita Mekubetzes* offers an alternative reading. Nevertheless, Rabbi Yochanan does not derive the prohibition against a *tamei* person eating *kodesh* from this verse. He arrives at it through a different route.

### Methodological Difference

The methodological contrast between the two *amoraim* is sharp. Resh Lakish derives the prohibition of a *tamei* person eating sacrifices from the verse itself; Rabbi Yochanan derives it instead from the fact that the act is punishable by *kareis*, drawing on the juxtaposition of two separate *pesukim*, each of which uses the word *tumaso*, through a *gezeirah shavah*. The verse *vetumato alav venichreta* (Vayikra 7:20) concerns eating sacrificial meat while *tamei*; the verse *o tumaso bo* concerns entering the *beis hamikdash* while *tamei*. Since the latter is accompanied by an explicit *lav* — *velo yetame'u es machanechem* — Rabbi Yochanan infers by a kind of transitive equivalence that a *lav* applies to eating *kodesh* while *tamei* as well. For him, the verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga* plays no role in this derivation.

---

## Tamei Before Zerika

### Third Derivation

With the methodological background established, the Gemara now presses Resh Lakish: having derived two things from the verse — touching and eating — is there yet a third? The answer is yes: the verse also teaches that a *tamei* person who eats sacrificial meat *before the blood has been placed on the altar* — before *zerikah* — is in violation.

This requires some unpacking. The pre-*zerikah* stage is one in which the meat has not yet become fit for human consumption. The *zerikah* — the throwing of the blood on the altar — is the act that renders the meat permissible to eat. Before that stage, no human being is permitted to consume the meat in any case. One might therefore argue that the prohibition against a *tamei* person eating *kodesh* applies only to meat that is in a state fit to be eaten, and that this prohibitory framework simply does not extend to meat that no one is yet permitted to consume. Perhaps, in other words, the prohibition is contingent on edibility.

### Baraita Dispute

The Gemara presents a *baraita* that directly frames the debate. A *tamei* person who eats sanctified meat before *zerikah*: Resh Lakish says he receives lashes; Rabbi Yochanan says he does not. Resh Lakish's reasoning is that the verse *bechol kodesh lo tiga* makes no distinction — *lo shana lifnei zerikah velo shana le'achar zerikah* — and the extra word *bechol* ("any") is precisely what broadens the prohibition to include circumstances in which the meat is not yet fit to be eaten. Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, draws his prohibition from the *gezeirah shavah* linking *vetumato alav venichreta* to the *bi'at mikdash* verses. As he reads it, the entire context of that verse — *vehabasar kol tahor yochal basar*, all that is *tahor* may eat the meat — presupposes meat that is already in a state of permitted consumption. The whole *inyan* of that verse postdates *zerikah*, and therefore his prohibition does not reach the pre-*zerikah* stage.

It is worth noting a recurring pattern. Throughout these two *dappim*, Resh Lakish is consistently prepared to assign lashes, while Rabbi Yochanan is more reticent. This is somewhat surprising: in tractate *Avodah Zarah*, the dynamic appears to be reversed, with Resh Lakish generally more lenient and Rabbi Yochanan more stringent. Whether the reversal is connected to the particular subject matter of *Kodshim* or to the specific question of *malkus* is unclear, but the pattern here is pronounced.

### Abaye's Interpretation

Abaye now enters to reframe the debate. The dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan, he says, concerns only *tum'at haguf* — the case where the *person* is *tamei* — and whether that person's *tumah* generates lashes when he eats pre-*zerikah* meat. But if we are speaking of *tum'at habasar* — the case where the *meat* itself is *tamei* — everyone agrees the person receives lashes, even if the blood has not yet been placed on the altar.

Why would *tum'at habasar* be different? Because there is a separate verse: *vehabasar asher yiga bechol tamei lo ye'achel* — meat that has come into contact with anything *tamei* shall not be eaten. And then there is an additional phrase: *vehabasar kol tahor yochal basar*, all that is pure may eat the meat. This extra phrase — and specifically the word *vehabasar* — is read as including things that are not literally meat at all: wood that goes on the altar, frankincense, items that are entirely inedible. If the verse extends its prohibition to frankincense and wood — objects no human would eat — then it certainly extends to meat before *zerikah*, whose only disqualification is that it has not yet reached the stage of permitted consumption.

### Vehabasar Inclusion

The inclusion of wood and frankincense through the word *vehabasar* is one of those arresting moments in the Gemara. The emphasis on the word "meat" is used precisely to include what is *not* meat. If one causes these inedible sanctified items to become *tamei* and then eats them — however bizarre that sounds — the prohibition applies. And if that is true for things that are inherently inedible, then *a fortiori* it applies to meat that will become edible once *zerikah* is performed, but happens not to be edible yet. So says Abaye: when the meat is *tamei*, the dispute vanishes and everyone agrees lashes apply even before *zerikah*.

A related question arises about whether wood susceptible to *tum'ah* is a *de'oraita* or *derabbanan* category — *Tosafot* engages with this — but the Gemara proceeds without resolving that point.

### Rava's Position

Rava takes the opposite position from Abaye. He agrees that the dispute of Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan concerns *tum'at haguf*, but he holds that when the meat is *tamei*, everyone agrees the person does *not* receive lashes — not merely before *zerikah*, but in any case of *tum'at habasar*.

His reasoning is rooted in the structure of the verses. The prohibition against a *tamei* person eating *kodesh*, which yields *kareis*, appears in the same context as the verse about *tum'at habasar*. Even Resh Lakish agrees that the *kareis* penalty for eating *kodesh* applies only when the meat is in a state fit to be eaten — that is, when the meat is *tahor* and the blood has been placed on the altar. If the sanctity of the meat has been compromised by *tumah*, the *kareis* no longer applies. And since the verse prohibiting a *tamei* person from eating *kodesh* is embedded in and contextually linked to the *kareis* framework, the *lav* likewise extends only to situations where the *kareis* would apply — i.e., when the meat is *tahor* and post-*zerikah*. If the meat itself is *tamei*, the negative prohibition simply does not engage, and therefore even Resh Lakish would agree there are no lashes.

### Matirim Principle

Having explained why Rava excludes *tum'at habasar* from lashes, the Gemara presses Rava with Abaye's argument: what about the wood and the frankincense? If those inedible items are included through the word *vehabasar*, why would *tamei* meat before *zerikah* be any less subject to the prohibition?

Rava's answer introduces the *matirim* principle. The inclusion of frankincense and wood through *vehabasar*, he explains, applies only *shekidash bicheili* — once the item has been sanctified by being placed in a *kli sharet*, a sacred vessel. The act of placing frankincense into a sacred vessel constitutes what one might call "stage two" in the sacrificial process. Physically, frankincense is no more edible after being placed in a vessel than before. But functionally, it has reached the stage at which it is ready to be offered on the altar — it has undergone its *matir*, the act that makes it fit for its purpose. For items that have a separate *matir* — like sacrificial meat, where the blood is the *matir* — that threshold is crossed only when the blood is placed on the altar. For items that have no separate *matir* — like frankincense or wood, where the object itself is what goes on the altar — the threshold is crossed when it is placed in a *kli sharet*.

The principle is then confirmed by the *mishnah*: *kol sheyesh lo matirin*, anything that has things that make it permissible — the obligation attaches once the *matirim* have been brought, *mishekerivu matirav*. *Kol she'ein lo matirin*, anything without a separate *matir* — the obligation attaches once it has been sanctified in a vessel, *mishekidsho bicheili*.

So Rava's conclusion is precise: you are not exempt from *tum'at basar* before *zerikah* because the meat is not edible. The meat of a *minchah*'s *levonah*, after all, is not edible by humans either. You are exempt because the sacrifice has not yet reached stage two. And for exactly the same reason, frankincense only enters the prohibition framework once placed in a *kli sharet* — not because it becomes edible, but because it has then reached its own stage two. *Tosafot* raises the independent question of how wood is ever sanctified in a *kli sharet*, since wood that is going to be burned on the altar does not obviously pass through a *kli* at all — an issue the Gemara leaves open.

---

## Behema Temeia on Altar

### Case Setup

The Gemara now introduces a new *itmar* — a reported dispute — also between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan, but on a different topic. The case: *hama'aleh eiverei beheimah temei'ah agabei mizbe'ach* — someone who takes the limbs of a non-kosher animal, say a pig or a horse, and places them on the altar. Note carefully: this is not about meat that has become *tamei*. This is about a *beheimah temei'ah* — a non-kosher species — whose limbs are brought up to the *mizbe'ach*. What has such a person violated?

### Resh Lakish's View

Resh Lakish says he receives lashes. The Torah states *min habakar umin hatzon takrivu es korbanchem* — from the cattle and the sheep you shall bring your sacrifices. Implicit in this positive command is: not from a horse, not from a pig. *Tehorah in, temei'ah lo* — a kosher animal yes, a non-kosher animal no. Resh Lakish further holds that *lav haba miklal asei lokin alav* — a negative prohibition implicit in a positive command still subjects the transgressor to lashes. This is a striking claim, one we have not encountered before in this context.

### R. Yochanan's View

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. He accepts the logical inference — *tehorah in, temei'ah lo* — but holds that *lav haba miklal asei ein lokin alav*. Since the prohibition is never stated explicitly as a "do not," but only exists as the implicit flip side of a positive command, it does not generate lashes.

### Kosher Animals Proof

Rabbi Yirmiyah challenges the version of the dispute that ascribes *lav haba miklal asei lokin alav* to Resh Lakish by bringing a *baraita* about kosher animals. The Torah states *kol mafereses parsa ma'alas geirah babeheimah osah socheilu* — anything with split hooves and that chews its cud you may eat, *osah tocheilu*, "this you shall eat." Implicit in that formulation is *velo beheimah temei'ah* — not the non-kosher animals. The *baraita* identifies this as a positive command whose flip side functions as a *lav*, and then notes that one would not receive lashes on that basis alone. Lashes come only because the Torah goes on to state explicitly *velo tochlu mehem* — an explicit negative prohibition. This *baraita* demonstrates, according to Rabbi Yirmiyah, that no one actually holds that an implicit negative prohibition generates lashes. How then can the dispute be presented as it was?

### Correction: Chaya Case

Rav Yaakov bar Yirmiyah bar Tachlifa corrects the record. The dispute was misattributed. Regarding a *beheimah temei'ah* — a non-kosher animal — there is actually no dispute at all. Everyone agrees you do not receive lashes, because the prohibition is only derived implicitly from a positive command. The real dispute, properly stated, concerns the *chayah* — a wild kosher animal such as a deer. The question there is not about lashes but about whether bringing a *chayah* on the altar violates even a positive command. That is where Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan actually disagree.

---

## Behema vs. Chaya

### R. Yochanan Position

With the case restated, the Gemara presents the corrected positions. Rabbi Yochanan holds *over be'asei* — one who brings a *chayah* on the altar transgresses the positive command of *bakar vaTzon*. The Torah specifies sheep and cattle; therefore, by implication, a deer falls outside the permitted category, and offering one violates that *mitzvah*.

### Resh Lakish Position

Resh Lakish holds *eino over belo klum* — one who brings a *chayah* does not transgress at all. The verse *min habakar umin hatzon takrivu* is, in his reading, expressing the ideal *mitzvah* — the normative, meritorious manner of bringing a sacrifice — but not a limitation that excludes all else. If the *spirit* should move someone to bring a deer, there is, in Resh Lakish's view, nothing technically wrong with doing so. It may not accrue *mitzvah* credit, but neither does it constitute a violation. The verse is read as prescriptive of the *mitzvah*, not prohibitive of alternatives.

This is, frankly, a remarkable position. It seems to suggest that there is a category of *reshut* — discretionary space — in the world of *korbanos*, in which one may bring offerings not mandated by the Torah as long as they are kosher animals.

### Nadav and Avihu

This is precisely where a powerful objection arises. The entire story of Nadav and Avihu — who brought *aish zarah* "which God had not commanded them" — is the Torah's most emphatic statement that in the *beis hamikdash*, discretionary initiative carries no shelter. The verse *asher lo tzivah osam* is itself the condemnation; they did something God had not specified, and they were punished with death. The very concept that there could be a category of *reshut* when approaching the altar runs directly against the message of that narrative. The notion that one could say "I feel like bringing a deer today, there is no prohibition" seems incompatible with what the Torah communicates through Nadav and Avihu.

### Baraita Clarity

The *baraita* brought by Rava settles the question. The verse says *min habeheimah min habakar umin hatzon takrivu es korbanchem*. If the Torah had simply said *korban l'Hashem beheimah*, one might have thought *beheimah* includes *chayah*, since elsewhere — in the context of the laws of permitted animals — *beheimah* is used to include deer and similar species. But the Torah specifies: *min habakar umin hatzon*, sheep and cattle specifically. This list is exhaustive.

### Rava's Refutation

The *baraita* then formulates two analogies. One might think: you're not supposed to bring a deer, but if you did, perhaps it is at least valid after the fact — like a student told to buy wheat who also brings barley; he exceeded the instruction but did not defy it. The *baraita* rejects this with a second analogy: the Torah repeated *bakar vaTzon* not once but twice in the opening chapters of Vayikra, and the repetition signals not "here is the preferred item" but rather "this is the exclusive list." The second analogy is that of a student told "bring nothing but wheat" — bringing barley in that case is not adding to the instruction, it is defying it. The *baraita* concludes: *pesul* — a *chayah* is invalid. This is a decisive refutation of Resh Lakish's position. *Tiuvta d'Reish Lakish, tiuvta.*

The Gemara's conclusion here carries its own weight. Even as we note the *tiuvta*, the underlying halachic point — that placing a pig on the altar technically violates only a positive command and not a negative one — remains striking. A fine piece of trivia: what is the prohibition involved in bringing a pig as a sacrifice? The answer the Gemara yields is that it violates the *asei* of *min habakar umin hatzon*, nothing more.

---

## Invalid Kohen & Shirayim

### Question Setup

The Gemara now returns to the framework of the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* had established that certain invalid persons — a *tamei kohen*, an *onen*, a non-*kohen*, and others — cannot perform the acts of *kabbalah* (receiving the blood), *holachah* (carrying the blood to the altar), or *zerikah* (placing the blood on the altar). Their thoughts at *shechitah* may generate *piggul*, but their invalid performance of subsequent acts does not. The Gemara now asks a specific follow-on question.

Resh Lakish posed the following question to Rabbi Yochanan: *pasul mahu she-ya'aseh shirayim?* — if an invalid person caught the blood and then placed it on the altar, does that make the remaining blood *shirayim*? In other words, after blood is placed on the altar, whatever blood remains cannot be used to repeat or supplement the *zerikah*; it becomes *shirayim*, leftover blood poured at the base of the altar. But does this "leftover" status depend on the *zerikah* having been performed validly? If an invalid *kohen* performed the *zerikah*, was that truly a *zerikah* — such that the remaining blood is now *shirayim* — or was the entire act null, leaving the blood still usable for a valid *kohen* to perform *zerikah* again?

### R. Yochanan's Answer

Rabbi Yochanan's answer is precise: *ein oseh shirayim ela chutz lizmano v'chutz limkomo, ho'il u'meratzeh l'piggulo.* The only invalidity that converts remaining blood into *shirayim* is a *piggul*-category thought — *chutz lizmano* (improper time-intention) or *chutz limkomo* (improper location-intention). Any other invalidity — including a *tamei* person or non-*kohen* performing the *zerikah* — results in nothing happening, and the remaining blood can still be used for a valid *zerikah*.

### Piggul Logic

The logic behind this ruling is one of the more elegant features of the laws of *piggul*. *Piggul* only takes effect when everything else in the sacrificial process is performed correctly. This creates a structural paradox: in order to assess whether *piggul* has occurred, we must evaluate the remainder of the service as if the *piggul* thought had not invalidated it — we must bracket the invalidity and ask whether, in a hypothetical valid world, the act would be complete. Since we are forced by the logic of *piggul* to view the *zerikah* through the lens of theoretical validity, we also conclude that blood has genuinely been applied to the altar. The remaining blood is therefore genuinely *shirayim* — it cannot be used again. In contrast, any other invalidity is simply null. Nothing happened. The remaining blood retains its status as blood available for *zerikah*, not as leftover *shirayim*.

---

## Invalid Person vs. Blood

### Rav Zevid's Challenge

Rav Zevid presents an alternative version of this exchange. Rather than asking whether an invalid *person* performing *zerikah* makes the remainder *shirayim*, Resh Lakish's question was actually about a *kos pasul* — invalid blood. Imagine that the blood itself has become *pasul* — say, a *tamei* person touched the blood in the vessel, or the blood was brought outside the *beis hamikdash* — and then a valid *kohen* takes that invalid blood and places it on the altar. Does the remaining valid blood in a separate vessel become *shirayim*, or can a valid *kohen* now use it?

### Equivalence Principle

Rabbi Yochanan's response in this version is telling. He pushes back on the framing of the question itself: *pasul gufei mai svira lach?* — what is your assumption about a *pasul* person? If you think a *pasul* person's *zerikah* makes the remainder *shirayim*, then the same would be true when the blood is *pasul*. If you think a *pasul* person's act is null and the remainder can still be used, the same would apply when the blood is *pasul*. There is no asymmetry between the two cases; Rabbi Yochanan sees them as governed by identical principles. He refuses to let the question about invalid blood stand as an independent inquiry separate from the question about an invalid person, insisting that whatever answer one gives to one, one must give to the other. Interestingly, Resh Lakish's reason for distinguishing the two cases — whatever it might have been — is left unexplained by the Gemara, and that remains an open question for the reader.

---

## Two Vessels Question

### Case Setup

The Gemara now records a third version of a related question, attributed to Rabbi Yirmiyah of Difti. Here the question is not one that Resh Lakish posed to Rabbi Yochanan, but one that Abaye posed to Rabbah. The case: an animal is slaughtered and its blood is caught in *two separate vessels*. Nothing is invalid — neither the person nor the blood. A valid *kohen* then takes the blood from vessel one and performs *zerikah* on the wall of the altar. What is the status of the blood remaining in vessel two?

### The Question

Two possibilities present themselves. One is that vessel two's blood is *dichuy* — pushed away and rejected. The *zerikah* has been fulfilled; vessel two's blood was a candidate for the altar and has now been displaced. As rejected blood, it is invalid, and it gets poured into the *amah*, the channel that carries invalid matter out of the *beis hamikdash*. The alternative is that vessel two's blood is *shirayim* — not rejected, but leftover in the same sense that the remnant in vessel one is leftover. Just as the small amount remaining in vessel one after *zerikah* is poured at the base of the altar, so too vessel two's blood is treated as *shirayim* and poured at the base. The question is not trivial; these two dispositions represent meaningfully different halachic statuses.

### Tannaim Debate

Rabbah informs Abaye that this is in fact a dispute of *Tannaim* — specifically, a debate between the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Shimon. A *baraita* presents the framework. The Torah uses two formulations in proximity: *et damo yishpach* — "its blood" — and *v'et kol damo yishpach* — "all of its blood." The former implies *some* blood; the latter emphasizes *all* the blood. How do these two phrasings interact?

### Sages' Position

The Sages read the two verses as governing two distinct cases. Take a *chatas* whose blood was caught in four vessels. If the *kohen* took blood from each of the four vessels and performed one of the four applications from each — *nasan matanah achas mizeh v'nasan matanah achas mizeh* — then all four vessels had blood that participated in the *zerikah*, and the remnant in all four is considered *shirayim*: *v'et kol damo yishpoch*, all the blood is poured at the base. But if the *kohen* performed all four applications from a single vessel — ignoring the other three — then only the remnant of that one vessel is *shirayim* and goes to the base. The other three vessels, whose blood never participated in any *zerikah*, are *dichuy*: *hein nishpachin l'amah*, they are poured out into the channel. Only the blood in the vessel that was actually used for *zerikah* achieves the status of *shirayim*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Shimon disagrees. Even if all four applications were performed from a single vessel, all four vessels' blood is considered *shirayim* and is poured at the base. He derives this from the verse *v'et kol damo yishpoch* — "all of its blood" — reading it expansively to include even blood that was never drawn upon in the *zerikah* process. Once *zerikah* has been performed, all blood caught in advance for the sacrifice is retrospectively treated as leftover, not as rejected.

### Resolution

The Gemara then asks: how does Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Shimon handle the verse that says *et damo* — "the blood," without *kol* — implying only *some* blood? Rav Yoshiya answers: that verse comes to exclude *shirayim shebitzavar habeheimah* — blood that was never captured in a vessel at all. Blood that remains in the neck of the animal after *zerikah* has already been performed, still spurting out and never caught, is not considered *shirayim* and is not poured at the base. The verse *et damo* — "its blood," a limited quantity — excludes that blood from the *shirayim* category. But any blood that was caught in a vessel before *zerikah* and then *zerikah* was performed — even from a different vessel — is *shirayim* according to Rabbi Eliezer, and goes to the base. The debate between the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer thus maps directly onto the question Abaye raised: whether unused vessels of blood are *dichuy* (the Sages' position) or *shirayim* (Rabbi Eliezer's position).

---

---

# Zevachim 35

## Psul Person & Dachuy

### Psul Thrower

The shiur picks up in the middle of daf 34b, continuing to work through the *mishnah*. The opening question concerned whether when a *pasul* person throws the blood, the remainder of the blood — the *shirayim* — loses its status and can no longer be used for *zrikat hadam*. The *mishnah* now moves on to a related but distinct scenario.

### Invalid Service

The *mishnah* establishes that if various invalid persons perform the *avodah*, the *korban* is not invalidated outright — one simply performs a redo. The case given is *kibbel hakasher venatan lapasul*: a valid *kohen* received the blood and handed it to an invalid person, and the invalid person then handed it back to the valid *kohen*. The ruling is that a redo is performed; it is as though the invalid person's action was a nullity, and the *korban* itself is not compromised.

### Multiple Scenarios

The *gemara* explains that all of the scenarios listed in the *mishnah* are necessary — *tzricha* — because each one might otherwise be read as categorically distinct. Had the *mishnah* given only the example of a *tamei* person, one might have thought the ruling is specific to *tumah*, because *tumah* carries a certain leniency: *tamei* persons may perform the service for communal fixed-time *korbanot* when the majority of the community is *tamei* — *d'chazi l'avodat tzibur*. One might therefore conclude that since *tumah* is sometimes permissible, an act performed in a state of *tumah* does not actively invalidate. But then one might say that using the left hand — *smolo* — would actively invalidate, since the left hand is virtually never permitted. Yet even there, one can point to *Yom Kippur*, when the *kohen gadol* carries the fire pan and incense with both hands — one in each — so that even the left hand has one context of validity. And if the *mishnah* had given only the case of a non-sanctified vessel — *kli chol* — one might assume that since the vessel can be instantly sanctified simply by declaration (*mishum d'chazi lakadishinhu*), it is likewise not an active invalidation, whereas *tumah* or the left hand, which are less trivially corrected, might genuinely invalidate. Each scenario is therefore necessary: whatever the nature of the invalidity, as long as it does not rise to the level of an invalid *zrika* itself, the *korban* is not rendered permanently invalid — one simply performs the service again.

### Dachuy Principle

Having established that these cases call for a redo rather than outright invalidation, the *gemara* presses further: why does *dachuy* not apply? *Dachuy* — the principle that something which entered a state of disqualification is considered "pushed away" and cannot return to valid status — is one of the foundational concepts in the laws of *kodshim*, as pervasive in this domain as *pigul* itself. If the blood passed through a *pasul* state — say, while it was in the left hand — it was at that moment unfit for *avodah*. Should it not be considered permanently rejected?

### Chanana Mitzri

*Ravina* addresses this to *Rav Ashi*, citing a statement of *Rabbi Yirmiah mi-Difti* in the name of *Rava*: the ruling follows the position of *Chanana HaMitzri*, who rejects the category of *dachuy* entirely — *d'leis lei dechuyin*. The *gemara* demonstrates this from a *braita*: *Chanana HaMitzri omer afilu dam b'kos mevi chaveiro u'mezaveig lo* — even if the blood of one of the two *Yom Kippur* goats has already been collected in a vessel and the paired goat is subsequently lost, one simply brings a replacement goat and pairs it with the existing blood, proceeding as normal. *Chanana HaMitzri* holds that even inanimate objects — blood already collected — do not become rejected merely because they entered a temporary state of unavailability.

To appreciate this position fully, it is worth noting the range of views on the question of the paired *Yom Kippur* goats. One opinion holds that even a living animal can be subject to *dachuy* — *dachuy b'ba'alei chayim* — so that if one goat is lost, the remaining living goat is also rejected and an entirely new pair is required. A second opinion holds *ein dachuy b'ba'alei chayim* — living things are not subject to *dachuy* — but once the goat has been slaughtered and the blood collected, if its pair is then lost, the blood must be discarded and the entire process restarted, since inanimate blood can be rejected. *Chanana HaMitzri* goes furthest of all, holding that there is no *dachuy* even by inanimate objects.

### Kol She'biyado

*Rav Ashi* offers an independent principle that avoids the need to invoke *Chanana HaMitzri*'s sweeping rejection of *dachuy* altogether. He states: *kol she'biyado lo havi dachuy* — anything whose correction is within one's power does not attain the status of *dachuy* in the first place. If something can be trivially remedied, it never truly entered a state of rejection; it was merely a momentary technical difficulty. Thus blood in the left hand, which can be immediately transferred back to the right hand, was never really "pushed away."

One might wonder: is going to fetch a replacement goat not also "within one's power"? The *gemara* implicitly distinguishes — the principle requires not merely that a fix is possible, but that the fix is essentially immediate and effortless. *Rashi* more or less spells this out: going to procure another animal is not sufficiently trivial to qualify as *kol she'biyado*, and therefore the blood in the *Yom Kippur* case is indeed considered *dachuy* by those who hold of that principle. Switching the blood from left hand to right hand, by contrast, is the paradigm of a trivial correction.

The *gemara* concludes that *Rav Ashi*'s principle is the more sensible one — *k'vashtei d'Rav Ashi mistabra* — and moreover that it can be demonstrated from the position of *Rabbi Yehuda* himself, who is elsewhere known to hold the most expansive view of *dachuy*, including *dachuy b'ba'alei chayim*. A *braita* shows that *Rabbi Yehuda* himself maintains *kol she'biyado lo havi dachuy*, because he rules that on *Erev Pesach* blood that had been spilled on the floor of the *azarah* can be scooped up and thrown on the altar. If it were truly *dachuy*, the spilled blood would be permanently rejected. The very fact that *Rabbi Yehuda* permits this fix demonstrates that when a correction is within one's power, the object never enters *dachuy* status. *Shema mina kol she'biyado lo havi dachuy — shema mina*.

---

## Pesach Blood Spill

### Mixed Blood Fix

Having cited *Rabbi Yehuda*'s ruling in passing, the *gemara* now turns to examine it in full. The *braita* is quoted directly: *Rabbi Yehuda omer, kos echad haya malei midam hata'aruvot* — on *Erev Pesach*, when hundreds of thousands of *korbanot* were being slaughtered in rapid succession, it was inevitable that some blood would be spilled before reaching the altar. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s solution is elegant: at the end of the day, before *Erev Pesach* concludes, one scoops up from the blood pooled on the floor of the *azarah* — where all the bloods have commingled — and throws it on the altar. Since the blood of any *korban* that was spilled will be present within that mixture, this throwing serves retroactively to place each *korban*'s blood on the altar. *Rabbi Yehuda* relies on the principle *ein dam m'vateil dam* — blood does not nullify blood — so that no individual blood loses its identity when mixed with other blood of the same substance.

### Vessel Question

The *chachamim* challenge *Rabbi Yehuda*: *v'halo lo nitkabel b'kli* — how does one know that the spilled blood was originally received in a valid vessel? Perhaps the blood went directly from the animal's neck onto the floor without ever being caught in a *kli sharet*, in which case gathering it now cannot fix the problem, and one might even be introducing invalid blood onto the *mizbeach*. *Rabbi Yehuda* responds — as the *braita* continues at the top of 35a — *af ani lo amarti ela b'nitkabel b'kli*: he concedes that he is addressing only the case where the blood was caught in a vessel and subsequently spilled. The *gemara* then asks how *Rabbi Yehuda* can know which scenario applies in practice. The answer is that this is a standard operating procedure performed at the end of every *Erev Pesach*: *d'kohanim zrizim hem* — *kohanim* are careful and meticulous, so we can assume that blood was always caught in a vessel — but *avdi hai*, they work with great speed, and accidents happen in the rush, so blood gets spilled. The procedure is designed to address those cases of spilled but properly received blood.

The underlying difficulty in the exchange — why there is any concern about throwing the mixture onto the altar even if it contains some blood that cannot be fixed — seems to rest on an assumption that there is some prohibition against placing invalid blood on the *mizbeach*, even in trace amounts within a valid mixture. That assumption drives the entire debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *chachamim*, though its precise basis is not made fully explicit by the *gemara* here.

### Invalid Blood Bittul

The *gemara* raises a further question: even granting *Rabbi Yehuda*'s solution, the blood pooled on the floor would inevitably include blood from animals whose slaughter was simply proceeding normally — valid blood that ended up on the floor but had already been thrown on the altar, as well as blood of doubtful status. This raises the concern of invalid blood causing *bittul* — annulling or erasing the presence of the valid blood that one needs to apply to the altar. Here, *Rabbi Yehuda*'s principle of *ein dam m'vateil dam* does the work: since all the substance in question is blood, no particular portion of blood loses its identity to any other, and the valid blood is considered fully present within the mixture.

### Dam Hatamtzit

A further difficulty is raised: the pooled blood on the *azarah* floor would also include *dam hatamtzit* — blood that flows from the animal after the primary life force has departed, which is not *dam hanefesh* and which does not go on the altar. Would the presence of this blood compromise *Rabbi Yehuda*'s procedure? The *gemara* answers: *Rabbi Yehuda l'ta'amei d'amar dam hatamtzit karuy dam* — *Rabbi Yehuda* consistently holds that even the non-life blood is called blood in the full halachic sense. A *braita* is cited to this effect: *dam hatamtzit b'azhara*, meaning one violates a negative prohibition for eating it; *Rabbi Yehuda omer b'karet* — *Rabbi Yehuda* goes further and says one incurs *karet*, treating it as fully equivalent to *dam hanefesh* for the purposes of the prohibition.

A complication arises, however, from a statement attributed to *Rabbi Elazar*: *modeh Rabbi Yehuda l'inyan kapparah she'eino mechaper* — even *Rabbi Yehuda* concedes that when it comes to *kapparah*, atonement, only *dam hanefesh* atones, as the verse states *ki hadam hu banefesh yechaper*. Blood through which the life force departs is what effects atonement; blood through which it does not depart does not. The *gemara* therefore reframes the concern: the problem is not that *dam hatamtzit* is being placed on the altar in an impermissible way, but rather that since *dam hatamtzit* does not effect *kapparah*, its presence in the mixture risks causing *bittul* — making the valid blood appear absent. And again, *Rabbi Yehuda*'s answer is *ein dam m'vateil dam*: since valid blood is present in the mixture, there is no *bittul*, and the throwing achieves its purpose.

### Drain Stopper

*Rabbi Yehuda* now turns the tables on his opponents. *L'divreichem lama pokekim ha'azarah?* — according to your view, why did the *azarah* have its drainage channel stopped up on *Erev Pesach*? The *azarah* had a channel through which blood and refuse could drain away; on *Erev Pesach* this channel was blocked, causing the blood to pool on the floor rather than drain out. If one cannot use the pooled blood to remedy spills — whether because of concerns about invalid blood or concerns about *bittul* — why would there be any purpose in stopping the drain? *Rabbi Yehuda* infers that the stopping of the drain was specifically intended to enable his procedure. The *chachamim* respond: *shevach hu livnei Aharon sheyelechu ad arkuvoteihem bedam* — it is a glory for the sons of *Aharon* to walk ankle-deep in blood during the *avodah*. This is a striking answer: the display of the sheer volume of *korbanot* offered, manifested in the depth of blood through which the *kohanim* wade, is itself considered honorable. The sensibility at work is entirely antithetical to modern instincts, which tend toward concealment of the physical realities of slaughter, but it appears to reflect an embrace of the sanctified nature of the *avodah* in its full, unfiltered reality.

### Kohanim Platforms

Once the *gemara* accepts that *kohanim* were in fact wading through blood on *Erev Pesach*, a series of practical difficulties presents itself. First: *veha kamitnafi manayhu* — their *bigdei kehunah* would become soiled, and a *mishnah* teaches explicitly that if a *kohen*'s garments were soiled — *hayu begadav metushtashim* — his *avodah* is invalid. One might suggest that the *kohanim* hiked up their garments, but a *braita* states *mado bad k'midato* — the priestly garment must be worn as tailored, and the *gemara* elsewhere indicates this requires wearing it down to the ankles. Second: would not the blood pooling between their feet and the floor constitute a *hatzitzah* — an interposition — that would invalidate their standing? The *gemara* resolves this: *lach velo havi hatzitzah* — a liquid does not constitute a *hatzitza*, as a *mishnah* establishes that blood, ink, honey, and milk only create an interposition when dried.

For the *begadim* question, the *gemara* offers the resolution: *beholachat evarim lakevesh* — the wading in blood would occur specifically during the carrying of limbs to the ramp, which the *gemara* initially suggests does not require full priestly garments. This is challenged, since a verse applies the term *kohen* to this very act, implying that *bigdei kehunah* are required. The *gemara* ultimately restricts the ruling to *beholachat etzim lema'aracha delav avoda hi* — carrying wood to the altar-fire, which is not a technical priestly *avodah* and does not require *bigdei kehunah*. The resulting picture is somewhat remarkable: for all other moments of the *avodah*, the *kohanim* would have moved about on a series of raised platforms built into the floor of the *azarah*, stepping between them to avoid walking in the blood, while the one occasion on which they would wade through blood — carrying wood — was chosen precisely because it does not involve a technical *avodah*. It is a curious architectural and logistical arrangement, constructed to make room for what the *chachamim* call a *shevach* for the sons of *Aharon*.

---

## Pigul Intro

### Abnormal Intent

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah* on *pigul*, a subject from which there is no escaping in *Kodshim*. The *mishnah* states: *hashochet et hazevach le'echol davar she'ein darko le'echol lehaktir davar she'ein darko lehaktir* — if one slaughters the sacrifice intending to eat something not normally eaten, or to burn something on the altar that is not normally burned, the *korban* is *kasher*. The "not normally eaten" could mean physically inedible, such as a hoof, or it could mean normally destined for the altar rather than for human consumption. Similarly, intending to burn the meat that is normally eaten, or to eat the *emurim* that are normally burned, does not create *pigul*. *Rabbi Eliezer* takes a stricter position — *Rabbi Eliezer posel* — holding that even misdirected intent between the domain of the altar and the domain of human consumption invalidates, though he does not go so far as to declare it *pigul* with its attendant *karet*.

### No Combination

The *mishnah* continues: if one intends to eat something normally edible or burn something normally burned, but the intended amount is less than a *kezayit* — *pachot mikezayit* — the *korban* remains *kasher*, since *pigul* requires intent involving a *kezayit*. A further case: if one intends to eat half a *kezayit* at the wrong time and burn half a *kezayit* on the altar at the wrong time, combining to a full *kezayit* between the two — the *korban* is still *kasher*, because *she'ein achila vehaktara mitztarfin* — eating and burning on the altar do not combine to constitute the requisite *pigul* intent. These two acts belong to categorically different domains and cannot be aggregated.

### Inedible Parts

The *mishnah* then lists a series of parts of the animal that are inedible and toward which a *pigul* intent therefore has no effect: *min ha'or* — the skin; *min harotav* — the broth or gravy produced when the meat is cooked; *min hakipa* — the sediment at the bottom of a pot; *min ha'alal* — the neck sinew, which is too tough to eat; *min ha'atzamot* — the bones; *min hagidim* — the sinews; *min hakarnayim* — the horns; and *min hatelafayim* — the hooves. Intending to eat any of these outside the proper time or place — *chutz lizmano* or *chutz limkomo* — leaves the *korban kasher* and creates no *pigul*. The principle is clear: *pigul* intent requires that the object of the intent be something that is genuinely eaten.

The *mishnah* adds: *ve'ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul notar v'tamei* — one incurs no liability for *pigul*, *notar*, or *tumah* in connection with these parts. If the animal became *pigul* because the *kohen* intended to eat the meat at the wrong time, one who eats the horns or hooves is not liable. If the animal became *notar* — left over past its permitted time — eating the hooves incurs no *notar* liability, because these parts are not considered meat in any halachically meaningful sense. This principle has well-known relevance to later discussions about the status of gelatin derived from bones and hooves.

### Fetus & Placenta

The *mishnah* addresses *mukdashim* — which *Rashi* explains consistently refers here to female consecrated animals, since the context always involves something unique to females. If one slaughters these female consecrated animals intending to eat *shalil* or *shilya* — fetus or placenta — outside the proper time, *lo pigel* — no *pigul* is created. The reason, as will be developed in the *gemara*, is that the fetus and placenta are not considered part of the *korban* proper; they are separate entities. An intent directed at a separate entity cannot make the mother *pigul*.

The *mishnah* similarly states that if one performs *melikah* on turtledoves intending to eat their eggs outside the proper time, this also does not create *pigul*. The eggs found inside the bird are, like the fetus, a separate entity from the bird itself.

### Milk & Eggs

A final clause is added: *chalav hamukdashim u'veitzei torin ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul v'notar v'tamei* — the milk of consecrated animals and the eggs of turtledoves do not carry liability for *pigul*, *notar*, or *tumah*. Even if the mother animal has become *pigul* — because the *kohen* intended to eat a *kezayit* of its meat at the wrong time — one who consumes the milk is not liable for *pigul*. The milk and eggs, although edible, are not part of the *korban* and are treated as separate entities.

What is conspicuously absent from this final section is any ruling about the *fetus* in the reverse scenario: when the intent was about the *mother*, does the *fetus* become *pigul*? The *mishnah* tells us that an intent about the milk and eggs does not make the mother *pigul*, and an intent about the fetus does not make the mother *pigul*. But what happens when the mother is made *pigul* — does the fetus become forbidden? The silence of the *mishnah* here is what the *gemara* will immediately investigate. The question also arises regarding the practical status of milk and eggs produced by consecrated animals: they are not *pigul*, not *notar*, not *tamei* — but are they simply *chullin*? If the animal is consecrated, whatever it produces is presumably still owned by the *beit hamikdash*, even if it lacks the specific *kedushah* of the *korban* itself. This touches on the broader question of *gidulei hekdesh* by *kodshei mizbe'ach*, a matter that would require separate investigation.

---

## Pigul Asymmetry

### Elazar Asymmetry

The *gemara* opens with the statement of *Rabbi Elazar*: *pigul b'zevach nitpagel shalil; u'vishalil lo nitpagel zevach* — if the animal is made *pigul*, the fetus becomes forbidden; but if one had a *pigul* thought about the fetus, the animal does not become *pigul*. This makes explicit what the *mishnah* left implicit by its silence. What is striking here is the asymmetry: the relationship between mother and fetus is not treated symmetrically for purposes of *pigul*.

### Rashi Explanation

*Rashi* explains the asymmetry as follows. In order to make an animal *pigul*, the intent must concern something that is normally eaten. The fetus is not normally eaten under ordinary circumstances — it is at most in the category of *ne'echal al yedei hadechak*, something consumed only in conditions of difficulty or extremity. Therefore, a *pigul* intent directed at the fetus lacks sufficient grounding in normal eating to make the mother *pigul*. However, once the mother has been made *pigul* through a properly directed intent — an intent about something normally eaten — then any part of the animal that is even somewhat edible becomes *pigul*. The fetus, marginally edible, falls within this broader sweep. The asymmetry thus turns on the distinction between what is edible enough to *generate* a *pigul* intent versus what is edible enough to *become pigul* once the animal is already so designated.

### Bird Parts

The same asymmetry appears in a parallel case involving birds. *Pigul b'alal nitpaglah mora* — if one had a *pigul* intent about the neck sinew (*alal*) of a bird, which in a bird is considered edible, even the *mora* — the crop or stomach — becomes *pigul*. But *bimora lo nitpaglah alal* — if one had a *pigul* intent about the *mora*, the rest of the bird does not become *pigul*. *Rashi* again explains this through the lens of *ne'echal al yedei hadechak*: the *mora* is edible only under duress, so it cannot serve as the source of a *pigul* intent, but it can become *pigul* once the bird has been so designated through a properly grounded intent.

### Tosafot View

*Tosafot* offers a cleaner explanation, though one that does not map as neatly onto the case of the fetus. *Tosafot* holds that *pigul* intent is only operative when it concerns a part of the animal that the Torah commands to eat or to burn on the altar. The *mora* — the crop of the bird — is neither commanded to be eaten nor commanded to be burned; what one normally does with it is discard it. Because even under proper circumstances the *mora* has no prescribed destination, a *pigul* intent directed at it is not a meaningful misdirection. *Pigul* is, at its core, the misdirecting of something heading toward the altar or toward human consumption — and the *mora* is heading neither place. However, once the bird has been made *pigul* through a genuine misdirection of something commanded, the *mora*, as a physically edible part of the animal, is swept up in the resulting prohibition.

### Burned Animals

The case of *parim hanisrafim* — the offerings whose blood is brought into the inner sanctum and whose meat is burned outside the *beit hamikdash* rather than eaten — illustrates *Tosafot*'s principle most sharply. *Pigul b'emurim nitpaglah paree* — a *pigul* thought about the *emurim* (the entrails that are burned on the altar) makes the meat *pigul* as well, even though the Torah commands that the meat be burned outside. But *pigul baparim lo nitpaglu emurim* — a *pigul* thought about the meat that is to be burned outside does not make the *emurim pigul*, because the meat of *parim hanisrafim* is not directed toward the altar or toward human consumption; it is neither to be eaten by people nor burned on the altar. A *pigul* thought about it is therefore categorically irrelevant — it is not misdirecting something heading to a commanded destination. *Lo asa velo klum* — one has accomplished nothing.

### Baraita Proof

*Leima mesayei lei* — the *gemara* now attempts to support this principle from a *braita*. The *braita* states: *veshavin she'hamachashev b'achilat parim u'visreifatan lo asa velo klum* — there is agreement that one who thinks about eating the meat of *parim hanisrafim* or burning it at the wrong time has accomplished nothing. This directly supports the principle that a thought about the meat that is commanded to be burned outside is not a *pigul* thought.

What the *braita* does not address directly is the corollary: what happens if a *pigul* thought was directed at the *emurim*? If the *chachamim* hold that there *is pigul* by *parim hanisrafim* — which they do, in contrast to *Rabbi Shimon* who denies *pigul* to any offering whose blood is not placed on the outer altar — then the only source of *pigul* for *parim hanisrafim* must be a thought about the *emurim*. So the *gemara* asks: does this prove the asymmetry — that a *pigul* thought about the *emurim* makes the meat *pigul*, but not vice versa? *Mai lav hachi ka'amar: b'emurim nitpaglu haparim?*

### Emurim Thought

The *gemara* declines the inference: *lo* — not necessarily. It is possible to read the *braita* symmetrically. The *braita*'s ruling about the meat may exhaust the discussion: when your thought concerns the meat, neither the animal nor the meat itself is made *pigul*. When your thought concerns the *emurim*, the *emurim* themselves become *pigul* — but perhaps the meat does not. *Hachi ka'amar: b'emurim nitpaglu emurim atzman* — the *emurim* become *pigul*, and if you eat them, you incur *karet* for *pigul* even though they are items normally destined for the altar rather than human consumption. But this does not necessarily mean the meat becomes *pigul* as well. The asymmetry that *Rabbi Elazar* describes — the *pigul* of the *emurim* sweeping in the meat but not vice versa — is not yet proven.

The *gemara* then attempts another avenue of proof. A *braita* dealing with *parim hanisrafim* states that *me'ila* — the prohibition of benefiting from consecrated property — applies from the time of sanctification; that once slaughtered, the meat becomes susceptible to *tumah*, *tevul yom*, *mechusar kippurim*, and *linah*; and that *me'ila* continues to apply until the meat completely chars. The *gemara* focuses on *linah* — the meat becoming *notar* by remaining overnight. If the meat of *parim hanisrafim*, which is commanded to be burned outside the Temple and is not eaten, can become *notar*, perhaps this proves that the meat can also become *pigul*, since *pigul* functions as a kind of conceptual projection of wrong-time thinking onto the reality of the act. This analogy is articulated as *migo depasla belinah pasla bemachshava* — since it is disqualified through *linah*, it is disqualified through [wrong-time] intent as well.

This jump from the world of action to the world of thought — treating *pigul* as a mental analog of *notar* — is taken almost entirely for granted by the *gemara*, which is itself striking. The *gemara* counters, however, that the *braita*'s reference to *linah* may concern only the *emurim*, not the meat. The *sof* of the *braita*, which speaks of *me'ila* applying until the meat chars, concerns the meat — but *reisha u'veseifa*, the earlier and later clauses can each operate in their own domain: *linah* applies to the *emurim*; *me'ila* until charring applies to the meat. The *gemara* acknowledges this is a somewhat strained reading — the more natural *pshat* would have the *linah* apply to the meat as well — but this is the formal resolution. The asymmetry proposed by *Rabbi Elazar* thus remains affirmed but not yet definitively proven from a *braita*. The *gemara* will continue to circle back to this question as the *sugya* develops.

---

## Non-Pigul Items

### Hair & Body Parts

The *gemara* now introduces a *braita* that catalogs items which neither create *pigul* nor become *pigul*: *tzemer sheberoshei kvasim* — the wool on the heads of sheep (which is not burned with the skin and is not edible); *se'ar shebezakan hatyashim* — the hair of the beards of goats; *ha'or* — skin; *harotav* — broth; *hakipa* — sediment; *ha'alal* — the neck sinew; *hamora'ah* — the crop of the bird; *ha'atzamot* — bones; *hagidim* — sinews; *hakarnayim* — horns; *hatalpayim* — hooves.

### Separate Entities

The *braita* then adds: *v'hashalil v'hashilya* — fetus and placenta; *chalav hamukdashim* — the milk of consecrated animals; and *beitzei torin* — the eggs of turtledoves. These items are treated as separate entities, neither making the animal *pigul* nor becoming *pigul* themselves.

### No Obligation

The *braita* concludes: *kullan lo mifaglin v'lo mitpaglin, v'ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul notar v'tamei* — none of these make the animal *pigul*, none become *pigul*, and one incurs no liability for *pigul*, *notar*, or *tamei* in connection with any of them. The *braita* further states that one who offers them outside the Temple — *hama'aleh meihen bachutz* — is *patur*, since these are not items normally sacrificed. The logic behind the exemption from *notar* for the fetus, even when the whole animal was left overnight, is that the *korban* is constituted only by the mother — the fetus is simply not part of the *korban*. It is viewed as analogous to the milk: just as the milk in the udder is not *korban* meat, the fetus is not treated as *korban* meat either, regardless of whether it is physically edible.

### Mother Thought

*Rabbah* now raises a challenge from this very *braita*. The *braita* states *kullan lo mifaglin v'lo mitpaglin* — all of these items neither make *pigul* nor become *pigul*. This appears to include the fetus in an absolutely symmetric statement: a *pigul* thought about the fetus does not make the mother *pigul*, and the mother being made *pigul* does not make the fetus *pigul*. This contradicts *Rabbi Elazar*'s asymmetry, according to which if the mother is made *pigul*, the fetus does become *pigul*.

### Baraita Intent

The *gemara* resolves this by restricting the scope of the *braita*'s statement. *Lo mifaglin v'lo mitpaglin machmat atzman* — the *braita* is addressing only the scenario in which the *pigul* thought is directed *at* these objects themselves. When the thought is about the fetus, it does not make the mother *pigul*, and it does not make the fetus *pigul* either. When the thought is about the hair or hooves, it neither makes the animal *pigul* nor the hair and hooves *pigul* themselves. The *braita* is not addressing the scenario in which the thought is about the mother: *Rabbi Elazar* would maintain his position that in that scenario, the fetus does become *pigul*. The apparent redundancy of the phrase *kullan lo mifaglin v'lo mitpaglin* is noted, but the *gemara* explains it as a throwaway construction — *aidie d'ba'i l'mitni notar v'tamei*, since the *braita* wanted to add the ruling about *notar* and *tamei*, it deployed the familiar trio of *pigul, notar, tamei* even though the *pigul* component was somewhat redundant in context. Similarly, since the *braita* wanted to state that one is *patur* for offering these outside the Temple, it packaged in the phrase about *pigul* as a formulaic accompaniment.

### Rava Inference

*Rava* offers a further support for *Rabbi Elazar*'s position directly from the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* tells us that a *pigul* thought about the fetus does not make the mother *pigul*, and that a *pigul* thought about the mother does not make the milk *pigul*. But the *mishnah* pointedly says nothing about what happens to the fetus when the mother is made *pigul*. *Af anan nami tenina* — we can infer from the *mishnah* itself: since the *mishnah* lists the milk and eggs as items that do not become *pigul* even when the mother does, but omits the fetus from this list in the parallel context, the implication is that the fetus *does* become *pigul* when the mother is made *pigul*. *Ela shema mina: kan machmat zevach, kan machmat atzman* — clearly there is an asymmetry, and it is well grounded in a close reading of the *mishnah*. When the thought is directed at the fetus, it neither makes the mother *pigul* nor itself *pigul*. When the thought is directed at the mother, the fetus — unlike the milk and eggs — does become *pigul*. *Shema mina*.

The underlying rationale, as noted earlier, divides between *Rashi* and *Tosafot*. For *Tosafot*, the principle is that *pigul* intent must misdirect something commanded toward the altar or toward human consumption, and the fetus has no such commanded destination. For *Rashi*, it is a matter of degree of edibility: the fetus is only *ne'echal al yedei hadechak* and therefore lacks the requisite centrality to serve as a source of *pigul*, but it is edible enough to be swept in when the mother is already *pigul*. The *emurim* thought case fits *Tosafot*'s framework more cleanly; the fetus case sits more naturally with *Rashi*.

---

## Blemished Animals

### Akiva Permits

The final section of the daf opens a new topic through a *mishnah* cited from elsewhere: the question of whether a blemished animal placed on the altar must be taken down. *Rabbi Akiva machshir b'va'alei mumim* — *Rabbi Akiva* holds that a blemished animal placed on the altar may remain. *Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *Rabbi Akiva*'s ruling applies only when the blemish did not involve a missing limb — *ela b'dukin sheba'ayin*, literally something like a cataract of the eye, though more broadly any non-disqualifying blemish. The reason is derived from the parallel to birds: among birds, no blemish invalidates except a missing limb. Since by birds a comparable blemish would not invalidate, and since by birds we already know the animal may remain on the altar, the same leniency extends to animals with non-limb-missing blemishes.

### Bird Parallel

The limiting principle from birds runs in both directions: it provides the basis for *Rabbi Akiva*'s leniency, and it defines its outer boundary. A missing limb remains disqualifying because even by birds a missing limb would invalidate.

### Female Olah
