*Rabbi Akiva* would also concede — *umodeh Rabbi Akiva b'olat nekeiva* — that a female animal consecrated as an *olah* must be taken down even if placed on the altar, because its disqualification is intrinsic from the moment of consecration. *D'keman d'kodam mum lehakdasha dami* — it is as though the blemish preceded the consecration: since the animal was never fit for the *mizbeach* as an *olah* even for a moment, it falls outside the scope of *Rabbi Akiva*'s leniency, which applies only when the animal was first consecrated in a fit state and subsequently became blemished.

### Zeira Challenge

*Rabbi Zeira* poses a challenge from the *braita* about the fetus. As established earlier, if one offers the fetus outside the Temple one is *patur*; the implication — *ha me'imurei iman chayav* — is that one would be *chayav* for offering the mother's *emurim* outside the Temple. But for one to be *chayav* for offering something outside the Temple, that thing must be something that would in some context be valid if offered inside. Since we are discussing a fetus born of a female *korban*, the mother is female. If the mother is an *olah*, a female *olah* — *olat nekeiva* — must come down from the altar according to *Rabbi Akiva*'s own concession. How then can one be *chayav* for offering the female *olah*'s meat outside the Temple, if even inside the Temple it would not be permitted to remain?

### Meat vs Emurim

The *gemara* resolves this by shifting the referent. Rather than reading the *braita*'s implication as *chayav* for the meat of the mother, the *gemara* reads it as *chayav* for the *emurim* of the mother. One is *chayav* outside the Temple for burning *emurim* on an external fire, and *emurim* are brought from any *korban* — including *shelamim* or *chatas* — which may be female. There is thus no need to invoke a female *olah* at all; the *braita*'s ruling applies to the *emurim* of a female *shelamim* or *chatas*, which are entirely permissible. The *gemara* does note the difficulty with this reading: *veha mehem katani* — the *braita* speaks of "them," referring to the fetus, with the contrast being the mother, implying the parallel is between the fetus's meat and the mother's meat, not the mother's *emurim*. The *gemara*'s final resolution is to read *hamale me'imureihen bachutz patur* — if one offers the *emurim of the fetus* outside, one is *patur* — while the implication for the mother concerns her *emurim*, not her meat. This is admittedly a difficult reading of the *braita*, and the straightforward *pshat* would be that the ruling concerns the meat of a female *olah* — in which case *Rabbi Akiva* would need to hold, contrary to his stated concession, that a female *olah* placed on the altar may remain. The *sugya* ends with this tension unresolved, and the daf closes here.

---

---

# Zevachim 36

## Machshava L'Haniach

### Daf 36 Overview

Daf 36 brings the third *perek* to its close, a chapter that has been devoted throughout to the laws of *pigul*. The *mishna* at the bottom of 35b launches the discussion that will occupy much of the daf, and the *gemara* that follows takes us deep into the logic of *Rabbi Yehuda*, the scope of invalidating *machshava*, and a series of important positions by the *amoraim*.

### Planning to Leave Over

The *mishna* opens with a case that sits at the edge of the classic *pigul* framework. The standard case of *pigul* or *chutz l'makomo* involves a *kohen* who, during one of the four *avodos*, intends to eat the meat, throw the blood, or offer the *emurim* at the wrong time or in the wrong place. But what happens when the *kohen* does not intend to perform any of those acts in the wrong time or place — he merely plans to leave the blood or the *emurim* over until the next day, or to bring them outside the *beis hamikdash*? The *mishna* states: *shachat al menat l'haniach et damo o emurav l'machar o l'hotzi l'chutz* — he slaughtered with the intent to leave the blood or the *emurim* until tomorrow, or to take them outside.

### Intent vs. Action

This is a fundamentally different category from standard *pigul*. In the classic case, the invalidating thought follows the structure of *he'achol ye'achel*, the eating-language of the *Torah*'s *pigul* verse — whether it is *achilas adam*, human consumption, or *achilas mizbeach*, offering on the altar. Here, there is no thought about eating or about *zerika* in a disqualified time or place. The *kohen* is simply planning on leaving the blood and *emurim* in place — committing the sin of *nosar* — or planning to bring them outside the precincts without any improper *zerika*. This is what the *mishna* calls *machshava l'haniach*.

### Rabbi Yehuda vs. Chachamim

*Rabbi Yehuda posel v'chachamim machshirim*. *Rabbi Yehuda* rules the *korban* is *pasul*, while the *chachamim* rule it is *kasher*. Importantly, neither side says this is *pigul* — since it does not meet the *he'achol ye'achel* criterion, it cannot carry the full *pigul* status. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that it occupies a middle ground: not *pigul*, but nevertheless *pasul*. The *chachamim* disagree entirely. In their view, if the *machshava* does not fall into the category of *chutz l'zmano* or *chutz l'makomo* as defined by the *Torah* — meaning a thought about an act of eating or offering at the wrong time or wrong place — then it has no invalidating power whatsoever, and the *korban* remains *kasher*. There is no intermediate state of *pasul* for a *machshava l'haniach* according to the *chachamim*.

### Non-Category Invalidations

The *mishna* continues by listing a series of improper intentions that everyone — including *Rabbi Yehuda* — agrees do not invalidate the *korban*. These include: *al menat l'nitnam al agav hakevesh shelo kineged hayesod*, intending to place the blood on the ramp or at the south-east corner that lacks a *yesod*; intending to place blood that belongs above the *chut hasikra* line below it, or blood that belongs below above it; and intending to place blood meant for the outer *mizbeach* on the inner *mizbeach*, or vice versa. These are all cases of *zerika* in the wrong place within the *beis hamikdash*, but they do not constitute *chutz l'makomo* in the technical *pigul* sense of outside the precincts.

The *mishna* further lists: intending that *tmei'im* eat the meat or offer the *emurim*; intending that *arelim* eat or offer; intending to break bones of the *korban Pesach*, which violates *etzem lo tishbru bo*; intending to eat the meat raw, violating *lo tochlu mimenu na*; and intending to mix the blood with invalid blood, which would render it unusable. All of these are intentions to commit an *aveira* with the *korban*, some of which could cause problems with the *korban*, yet none of them constitutes *chutz l'zmano* or *chutz l'makomo* in the relevant halachic sense.

### What Invalidates

The *mishna* concludes by articulating the principle of the *chachamim*: *she'ein machshava poselet ela b'chutz l'zmano u'b'chutz l'makomo* — the only *machshava* that can invalidate is one of *chutz l'zmano*, which produces *pigul*, or one of *chutz l'makomo*. Anything outside those categories is *kasher* and beyond the scope of the discussion. The *mishna* also recalls the opening case of the first *perek* — a *Pesach* or *chatas* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* — as another type of invalidating *machshava*, but again, only those specific categories carry weight. If the thought is of *chutz l'zmano* or *chutz l'makomo* but in the *l'haniach* form — planning to leave the material rather than to eat or offer it — that is the precise point of dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *chachamim*.

---

## Rabbi Elazar's Source

### Nosar Pesukim

The *gemara* opens by asking: *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Yehuda?* What is *Rabbi Yehuda*'s source for this middle category of *pasul* that is neither *pigul* nor fully *kasher*? The question is pointed: since the invalidating *machshava* does not fit the *he'achol ye'achel* framework, what entitles *Rabbi Yehuda* to invent a new intermediate category? *Rabbi Elazar* offers an answer. He says there are two *pesukim* regarding *nosar*, and the doubling is the key.

### L'Haniach Language

One *pasuk* says *lo sosiru mimenu ad boker* — do not leave it over until morning — using the standard verb of *nosar*, meaning leftovers. A second *pasuk* says *lo yaniach mimenu ad boker* — do not leave it until morning — but uses the different root *l'haniach*, meaning simply "to leave," not "to leave over as a remainder." *Tosafot* notes that these two *pesukim* address different *korbanot*, so in principle they might not be directly redundant. Nevertheless, the *gemara* works with the assumption that the *Torah* could have expressed both laws with a single formulation. Why then the change of language in the second *pasuk*? *Im eino inyan l'hinuach, tnahu inyan l'machsheves hinuach* — if the alternate language is not needed simply to state the *issur* of actually leaving it over, since we already learned that from the first *pasuk*, then the shift in language must be teaching a new category: even the *thought* of leaving it over.

### Pasuk Needed Elsewhere

The *gemara* challenges *Rabbi Elazar*'s derivation immediately. *Hai mibaei lei l'chid'sanya* — *Rabbi Yehuda* needs that *pasuk* for something else entirely, as demonstrated by a *baraita*. The *baraita* uses the *pasuk* beginning *u'vesar zevach todat shelamav* — the verse about the *todah* — which includes the phrase *lo yaniach mimenu ad boker*, to derive a vast range of halachos about how long various *korbanot* may be eaten. If that *pasuk* is consumed entirely by this *baraita*, *Rabbi Elazar* cannot simultaneously use it to derive the law of *machsheves hinuach*.

### Leviticus 7:15 Baraita

The *baraita* is built around Vayikra 7:15, *u'vesar zevach todat shelamav b'yom korbano ye'achel* — the meat of a *todah shlamim* shall be eaten on the day it is brought. The *baraita* proceeds to derive, from each word in the verse, additional categories that share the *todah*'s one-day eating limit. The word *basar* — "meat" — includes derivatives of the *todah* itself: a *chalifin* (a substitute animal designated when the original was lost, distinct from *tmurah*), offspring born from the *todah* animal, and *tmurah* proper (where *kedushah* is attempted to be transferred, and by *Torah* law both animals become *kadosh*). How do we know these derivative animals also have only one day? From the word *basar*, "flesh," which is more expansive than *zevach*, teaching that even things that derive from the *todah*'s flesh-category are treated like the *todah* itself.

### Extension to All Types

The word *zevach* — "sacrifice" — extends the one-day limit to *korbanot* that are neither *shlamim* nor *todah*, including *chatas* and *asham*. This is a striking observation, since the *Torah* nowhere states explicitly how long *kohanim* have to eat the meat of a *chatas* or *asham*. It is entirely derived from this *pasuk*. The word *shelamav* — "his *shlamim*" — extends the rule to special types of *shlamim* that are not the generic two-day *shlamim*: *shlomei nazir*, the ram a *nazir* brings upon completing his *nezirut*, and *shlomei pesach*, which *Tosafot* understands as a *Pesach* that became *shlamim* because it was not offered on the 14th of Nissan (as distinct from *Rashi*'s interpretation that it refers to the *chagigah* of the 14th). The word *korbano* — broader still than *basar* or *zevach*, extending beyond slaughtered offerings — includes the bread loaves that accompany the *todah* and the *chalot* and *rekikin* that the *nazir* brings with his *shlamim*. *Kulan korei bihen lo yaniach mimenu ad boker* — all of them may not be left until morning. So the *pasuk* is indispensable for this entire *baraita*; it cannot simultaneously serve as the source for *machsheves hinuach*.

### L'Haniach Teaches Machshava

The *gemara* resolves this by noting that while the *pasuk* is indeed needed for the *baraita*, the specific word *lo yaniach* — rather than *lo sotiru* — remains available to teach *machsheves hinuach*. Had the *Torah* simply wished to state the general prohibition and extend it to all *korbanot*, it could have used the standard language of *lo sotiru*. The deliberate shift to *yaniach* signals that beyond the act itself, there is a further teaching about *machshava*: *im eino inyan l'hinuach, tnahu inyan l'machsheves hinuach*. The content of the *baraita* — the extension to all *korbanot* — can be derived from the *pasuk* generally, while the choice of language specifically teaches about *machsheves hinuach*. The two teachings are complementary, not competing.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda's Logic

### Consequence to Thought

The *gemara* now presses further. Even granting *Rabbi Elazar*'s derivation for the *l'haniach* case — planning to leave the blood over — this only explains *chutz l'zmano* in its *l'haniach* form. What is the source for the parallel case of *chutz l'makomo* — planning to bring the blood or *emurim* outside the *beis hamikdash*? There is no comparable *pasuk* to derive it from. Moreover, the *gemara* notes, *taameh d'Rabbi Yehuda sevara hu* — *Rabbi Yehuda* is not actually basing himself on a *pasuk* at all; his reasoning is pure logic. This is evident from a *baraita*. In the *baraita*, *Rabbi Yehuda* addresses the *chachamim* directly: *ee atem modim she'im hinicho l'machar shehu pasul* — do you not agree that if you actually left the blood over until the next day, the *korban* is *pasul*? Once it becomes night, the blood can no longer be thrown, so the *korban* is invalidated. *Af chishev lehaniach l'machar pasul* — likewise, if you planned to leave it over, the *korban* is *pasul*. The same logic extends to *chutz l'makomo*: if you bring the blood outside the *beis hamikdash*, it becomes *pasul b'yotzei*, unfit for use, and so too planning to do so invalidates.

### Act vs. Thought Principle

*Rabbi Yehuda*'s underlying principle is now exposed: any act that, if performed, would invalidate the *korban*, invalidates equally when it is merely the subject of a *machshava* during the *avodah*. This is a broad abstraction — it is not limited to the specific *Torah* categories of *chutz l'zmano* or *chutz l'makomo*, but applies generically to anything that would disqualify the *korban* if done. But if this is the logic, says the *gemara*, *veniflog nami Rabbi Yehuda bechulhu* — *Rabbi Yehuda* should argue on every case listed in the *mishna*, since most of those cases involve acts that, if performed, would have some effect on the *korban* or its associated objects.

### Other Mishna Cases

The *gemara* works through the *mishna*'s cases methodically, asking for each one why *Rabbi Yehuda* does not dispute its *kasher* status. This analysis is what forces the *gemara* to clarify the precise contours of *Rabbi Yehuda*'s principle.

### Pesach Bones Case

The easiest cases to dispose of are breaking the bones of the *Pesach* and eating from it raw. The *gemara* asks: *zivcha gufeh mi mipsal?* Does the *korban* itself become *pasul* if you break a bone or eat from it raw? These are *aveiros*, but they do not invalidate the *korban*. Since performing the act would not invalidate the *korban*, a *machshava* to do so certainly would not.

### Tamei/Arel Eating

The cases of *tmei'im* or *arelim* eating or offering require more analysis. At first glance, one might think that if a *tamei* or *arel* person performs the *zerika*, the *korban* becomes *pasul* — and if the act invalidates, should not the *machshava* also invalidate according to *Rabbi Yehuda*? *Rashi* explains that *yakrivuhu* in the *mishna* refers specifically to the offering of the *emurim* on the *mizbeach*, not to the *zerika* of the blood. Neither a *tamei* nor an *arel* person offering the *emurim*, nor a *tamei* or *arel* person eating the meat, invalidates the *korban* itself. Only the *zerika* can invalidate, and these cases do not involve *zerika*. This reading is somewhat strained, as *Rabbi Yehuda*'s own case in the *mishna* involves a *machshava* about leaving the *emurim* over, and the *gemara* acknowledges the tension. An alternative explanation is offered — *ko k'minei?* — meaning that the *machshava* must be something within your control. Thinking that other people, *tmei'im* or *arelim*, will eat or offer is not under your control and therefore does not constitute a meaningful *machshava* capable of invalidating the *korban*.

### Mixing Blood

The case of planning to mix the blood with invalid blood is resolved by noting that *Rabbi Yehuda l'taimei* — *Rabbi Yehuda* follows his own reasoning that blood of *korbanot* is not *batel* when mixed with other blood. *Min b'mino* is not *batel* according to *Rabbi Yehuda* for various reasons, and therefore mixing the blood would not actually invalidate it. Since performing the act would not invalidate the *korban* according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, neither does the *machshava*.

### Makom Meshulasch

The cases of intending to place blood that belongs above the *chut hasikra* below it, or vice versa, are resolved by the principle of *shelo l'mkomo k'bmkomo* — according to at least one approach in the earlier *gemara*, placing blood in the wrong location on the *mizbeach* still counts, so it does not invalidate. Since the act itself would not invalidate according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, the *machshava* is similarly harmless.

More complex is the case of intending to bring blood that belongs on the outer *mizbeach* inside to the inner *mizbeach*, or vice versa. This does invalidate. So why does *Rabbi Yehuda* not say the *machshava* of doing so also invalidates? The *gemara* answers that *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *beinan makom shemeshulash bedam bebasar ba'imurim* — the relevant category of *makom* for purposes of *machshava* requires a place that is triply defined by blood, meat, and *emurim*. The inner *mizbeach*, the *heichal*, does not satisfy this criterion: the *emurim* are not offered there, and *basar* is not consumed there under normal circumstances. Therefore, a *machshava* involving the inner *heichal* falls outside the operative category of *makom* for these purposes, and does not invalidate. This is admittedly a surprising restriction on an otherwise broad principle, but it is what the *gemara* holds.

### Kol Davar Ra Contradiction

A *baraita* now creates a sharp contradiction. *Rabbi Yehuda* himself is cited as deriving from the *pasuk* *lo tizbach l'Hashem Elokecha... kol davar ra* (Devarim 17:1) that a *chatas* slaughtered in the south of the *azarah* rather than the north is *pasul*, and that this falls under the *lav* of the *pasuk*, implying one would receive *malkus*. Furthermore, the *baraita* implies that thinking about bringing the blood of an outer *chatas* into the *heichal* during the *shechita* would also invalidate the *korban* — *Rashi* explains this because the *pasuk* speaks at the moment of *lo tizbach*, which is at *shechita*, and *Tosafot* adds that *davar* may also suggest thought or speech rather than a physical act.

If *Rabbi Yehuda* truly says that a *machshava* about bringing the blood inside the *heichal* invalidates, then his position would be entirely consistent with the broad *sevara* — thought about an invalidating act is itself invalidating. But the *gemara* then immediately pulls in the other direction: *Rabbi Yehuda* elsewhere states *hechnis bishogeg kasher*, *ha b'meizid pasul* — bringing the blood inside by mistake leaves the *chatas* valid; only doing so intentionally invalidates. And *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that the invalidation occurs specifically at the moment of *zerika* inside the *heichal*, not at the moment of bringing it in. If even the act of bringing the blood in does not invalidate unless one performs *zerika* inside, then certainly a mere *machshava* to bring it in would not invalidate. A *kal vachomer*: *ilu ayeilei i kiper, in i lo kiper lo* — when you actually bring it in, the *korban* is only invalidated if you perform *zerika* there; *hacha dechashiv chishuvey lo kol shekein* — here, where you merely thought about bringing it in, certainly it would not invalidate.

*Tosafot* notes, incidentally, that this *kal vachomer* is strange on its face, since it would seem to undermine the entire institution of *pigul* — after all, eating the meat tomorrow also does not currently invalidate anything, yet a *machshava* to do so produces *pigul*. *Tosafot* attempts an answer, though it is not fully satisfying, and the *gemara* presses on regardless.

### Two Tannai'im

The *gemara* now resolves the contradictions by invoking the standard mechanism: *trei tannai v'aliba d'Rabbi Yehuda* — two *tanna'im* transmit *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position differently. One *tanna*, the author of the *kol davar ra baraita*, holds that *Rabbi Yehuda* says a *machshava* about bringing the blood of an outer *chatas* into the *heichal* does invalidate, consistent with the broad principle that a *machshava* about any invalidating act is itself invalidating. A second *tanna*, the author of the *mishna* who does not record *Rabbi Yehuda* as arguing about this case, holds that *Rabbi Yehuda* exempts thoughts related to the *heichal* due to the requirement of *makom meshulash*, and the *kal vachomer* from actual bringing-in-without-*zerika* further supports this exemption. Similarly, a separate contradiction exists in the *baraita* about whether *Rabbi Yehuda* includes a *chatas* slaughtered in the south under the *lav* of *kol davar ra* — one *baraita* includes it, another explicitly excludes it by limiting *kol davar ra* to an intrinsic defect in the animal itself, like a *mum*, rather than a procedural error in the *avodah*. Here too the *gemara* concludes *trei tannai aliba d'Rabbi Yehuda*.

---

## Rabbi Abba's Claim

### Piggul Still Applies

*Rabbi Abba* now advances a novel claim: *modeh Rabbi Yehuda she-chozer v'kovah l'pigul* — *Rabbi Yehuda* agrees that even where the *machshava l'haniach* has rendered the *korban pasul*, one can still subsequently create *pigul*. In other words, once a *machshava l'haniach* has invalidated the *korban*, a subsequent *machshava* of *chutz l'zmano* during the *avodah* would transform it into *pigul*. This is a striking claim, because the standard rule is that a *korban* already invalidated for another reason cannot then become *pigul*. *Rabbi Abba* argues that the generic *machshava l'haniach* of *Rabbi Yehuda* — which is not a formal *Torah*-category disqualification like *chutz l'makomo* — lacks the power to permanently remove the *korban* from the *pigul* framework.

### Piggul Before Zerika

*Rava* attempts to support *Rabbi Abba*'s position with an analogy. *D'basar lifnei zerika lav klum hi* — the meat before the *zerika* is not yet fit to be eaten. Nevertheless, a *machshava* of *chutz l'zmano* during the *zerika* produces *pigul* for that meat. *V'asya zerika v'kavah lah b'pigul* — the *zerika* comes and establishes *pigul* status, even though the meat was unfit beforehand. So too, *Rava* argues, even after a *machshava l'haniach* has made the *korban pasul*, a subsequent *machshava* of *chutz l'zmano* should be able to establish *pigul*.

### Two Machshavos Issue

The *gemara* rejects the analogy immediately: *v'lo hi*. The cases are not comparable. *Hasam hu chad machshava hi* — in the normal *pigul* case, there is only one *machshava*, the *machshava* of *chutz l'zmano* during the *zerika*. The meat was not yet fit to be eaten, but this was not because of any independent *machshava* that had actively invalidated it; it was simply not yet ready, waiting for the *zerika* to permit it. *Hacha trei machshavos* — here there are two distinct *machshavos*: one that actively invalidated the *korban*, and a subsequent one attempting to impose *pigul*. An active invalidating *machshava* removes the *korban* from the *pigul* category entirely; a subsequent *pigul* thought cannot restore it.

### Blood Tomorrow Invalidates

*Rav Huna* challenges *Rabbi Abba* directly from a *baraita*. The *baraita* addresses a sequence of thoughts during the *avodah*. If you intended to place the blood above when it should go below, or below when it should go above — intending it *la'altar*, immediately — then according to the *chachamim*, since it is neither *chutz l'zmano* nor *chutz l'makomo*, the *korban* is *kasher*. If you then had a thought of *chutz l'makomo* — intending a genuine wrong-place *zerika* — the *korban* is *pasul v'ein bo kares*, the standard *chutz l'makomo* result. And if you had a *chutz l'zmano* thought, the *korban* is *pigul v'chayavin alav kares*. So far, nothing surprising: the first thought was inert, and the subsequent *chutz l'zmano* thought created *pigul*.

Now the *baraita* introduces the *l'machar* variant. If your intention to place the blood in the wrong position was framed as doing so *tomorrow* — that is, you plan to place it in the wrong place not now but the next day — this is functionally equivalent to *machshava l'haniach*, planning to leave the blood over. And the *baraita* rules: *pasul* — this is *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position.

### Cannot Become Piggul After

The *baraita* then states its critical conclusion: *chozar v'chishev bein chutz l'zmano bein chutz l'makomo pasul v'ein bo kares* — if after this *machshava l'haniach* you then had a thought of *chutz l'zmano* or *chutz l'makomo*, the *korban* is *pasul* but carries no *kares*. It does not become *pigul*. *Tyuvta d'Rabbi Abba tyuvta* — this is a complete refutation of *Rabbi Abba*'s position. Once the *machshava l'haniach* has rendered the *korban pasul*, even *Rabbi Yehuda* agrees that no subsequent *machshava* of *chutz l'zmano* can elevate it to *pigul* status.

---

## Tamei Eating as Piggul

### Tamei Eating Tomorrow

*Rav Chisda* cites a ruling in the name of *Ravina bar Shila*: *chishev sheyachalu tmei'im l'machar chayav* — if during the *avodah* one had a *machshava* that *tmei'im* would eat the meat tomorrow, one is *chayav*, meaning this constitutes *pigul*. This is surprising on two counts. First, we discussed earlier that thoughts involving other people — *tmei'im* eating — are not under one's control and therefore do not invalidate. But here, the thought is structured as a *machsheva l'achila*, a thought of eating, directed toward the next day, which is the classic *pigul* framework. It is not a *machshava* about an external invalidating act; it is a *machsheva* of consumption framed in *chutz l'zmano* terms. The fact that the eaters are *tmei'im* might seem to take it out of the category of valid *achilas adam*, but *Rav Chisda* holds that since it remains a *machsheva* about eating, it is sufficient to produce *pigul*.

### Meat Before Zerika

*Rava* once again supports the ruling with an analogy. The meat before *zerika* is unfit to be eaten — *d'basar lifnei zerika lo chazi*. Nevertheless, a *machshava* during the *zerika* about eating it *chutz l'zmano* constitutes *pigul*. So too, a *machshava* of eating by *tmei'im* — even though the act of eating by *tmei'im* makes the meat unfit — should still qualify as a *machsheva l'achila* sufficient for *pigul*.

### Unfit vs. Unready

The *gemara* again rejects *Rava*'s analogy: *v'lo hi*. *Hasam zerika zorek u'michzi* — in the normal *pigul* case, the *zerika* is being performed, and through the *zerika* the meat will become fit to be eaten. The meat is not yet fit, but it is on its way to becoming fit; there is nothing about it that makes it inherently or permanently unfit. *Hacha lo michzi klal* — here, with a plan to have *tmei'im* eat it, the meat is not fit at all, and the very mode of eating one is contemplating makes the meat unfit rather than being a form of valid consumption. The *gemara* thus distinguishes between meat that is merely not yet ready and meat that is rendered unfit by the very contemplated act. *Tosafot* notes that this reasoning requires distinguishing the *tmei'im* case from the earlier discussions involving dogs or fire eating the meat, where *machsheva l'achila* was still recognized as potentially operative.

### Pesach/Toda Examples

*Rav Chanina bar Ravina* — cited by *Rav Chisda* — raises two additional cases. *Basar Pesach shelo hutzla* — the meat of a *Pesach* that has not been roasted. After the blood has been thrown, the meat is permitted from a *kodashim* perspective, but the *Pesach* specifically must be eaten roasted, and eating it raw violates *lo tochlu mimenu na*. If a *tamei* person were to eat this raw *Pesach* meat, would they be *chayav kares* for eating *kodashim b'tuma*? Similarly, *lachmei todah shelo hurmu* — the bread loaves accompanying a *todah*, before one out of every ten has been separated and given to the *kohen*, which functions like *terumah* and prohibits eating the rest. After the blood of the *todah* has been thrown, the bread is permitted from a *kodashim* standpoint, but prohibited from the *terumah* standpoint. If a *tamei* person ate this bread, would they be *chayav kares*? The ruling, cited by *Rav Chisda*, is *chayavin aleihem mishum tumah* — yes, they are *chayav*, since the *korban* dimension of the *kodashim* has been completed and the material is fit from that perspective, even though there is an additional prohibition making it currently forbidden.

### Emurim After Zerika

*Rava* attempts a third analogy in support of *Rav Chisda*'s ruling about *tmei'im*. The *baraita* cited by the *gemara* derives from the *pasuk* *asher la-Hashem* (Vayikra 7:21) that eating the *emurim* — the portions of the *korban* designated for the *mizbeach* — while *tamei* makes one *chayav kares*. This is remarkable because *emurim* are not food for human beings and are indeed prohibited from human consumption; they must be placed on the *mizbeach*. Yet once the blood has been thrown, eating them in *tumah* carries *kares*. So too, *Rava* argues, a *machsheva* about having *tmei'im* eat the meat should qualify, since we see that even non-food items can generate *chiyuv* in the *tumah* framework.

### Emurim Purpose

The *gemara* once again rejects this: *v'lo hi*. *Hasam imurei kodshi kalim chazu legavoah* — there, once the blood is thrown, the *emurim* have fully reached their intended purpose. They are completely fit for what they were designated to do — to be placed on the *mizbeach*. Even though they are not fit for human consumption, they have achieved their final halachic state. *L'afukei basar pesach shelo nitzla v'lachmei todah shelo hurmu* — as opposed to the roasted meat of *Pesach* and the *todah* breads, which in their current state are fit neither for *gavoah* nor for *hediot*: the *Pesach* meat is not yet roasted, and the breads have not yet been separated. These items have not fully completed their process, and therefore one could argue they remain outside the full *chiyuv kares* for *tumah*. The distinction is between something that has fully arrived at its purpose and something still in an intermediate state.

---

## Blood Placement Debate

### Minimal Placement

With the conclusion of *Perek Kol HaPsulim*, the *gemara* transitions into the opening *mishna* of the next *perek*. The subject shifts to a debate between *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* about how many *matanos* — applications of blood — are minimally required for the *korban* to be valid *bedieved*. The *mishna* enters this topic not for its own sake but because of its implications for *pigul*, as the word *l'fichach* ("therefore") indicates. *Beis Shammai* holds that for any *korban* whose blood is applied to the outer *mizbeach* — where the standard procedure involves two diagonal corner applications, effectively hitting all four walls — a single application suffices *bedieved*. The *pasuk* *kiper* implies that even one placement achieves atonement. For a *chatas*, where four finger applications at four corners are required, *Beis Shammai* requires two applications *bedieved*. *Beis Hillel* is more lenient: even a *chatas* is valid *bedieved* with a single application.

### First Valid, Second Invalid

The *mishna* draws out the *pigul* implications of this dispute. Suppose the first placement is done properly, *ketiknah*, and the second is done with a *chutz l'zmanah* thought. According to *Beis Hillel* — and for any non-*chatas* according to *Beis Shammai* — the first application alone was sufficient to establish the *korban*'s validity. The *korban* is therefore already valid at that point, and the subsequent *pigul* thought during the second application cannot retroactively invalidate it. *Im nasan et harishonah ketiknah vehashniyah chutz l'zmanah, kiper* — the *korban* is valid, and the additional applications, though a *mitzvah* to perform, are no longer definitionally constitutive of the *korban*. Once the minimum has been achieved, the *korban* is sealed.

### Both Invalid Remains Piggul

Conversely, if the first application was done with a *chutz l'zmanah* thought — making the *korban pigul* — and the second application was done with a *chutz l'makomo* thought, one might expect the second *machshava* to remove the *pigul* status, since ordinarily a subsequent invalidating *machshava* of *chutz l'makomo* takes the *korban* out of *pigul* and reduces it to the lesser status of *pasul* without *kares*. But here this does not apply, because after the first *matanah* the *korban* is already complete — whatever its status. The *pigul* is established by the first application, and the subsequent applications, being beyond what is needed, cannot alter the *korban*'s status in either direction. *V'im nasan et harishonah chutz l'zmanah vehashniyah chutz l'makomo, pigul v'chayavin alav kares* — it remains *pigul* with *kares*.

### Inner Mizbei'ach Rules

For *korbanot* whose blood is applied to the inner *mizbeach* — the *mizbeach hazahav* inside the *heichal*, used for *chatas hapenimit* — all four corner applications are essential. Unlike the outer *mizbeach*, where a single application suffices *bedieved*, the inner *mizbeach* requires all four, and *she'im chisar achas min hamatanos k'ilu lo kiper* — missing even one is as if no atonement was achieved. The *mishna* therefore rules: *nasan kullan ketiknah v'achas shelo ketiknah psulah v'ein bo kares* — if three applications were done correctly and one was done with a thought of *chutz l'zmano* or *chutz l'makomo*, the *korban* is *pasul* but carries no *kares*.

### Partial Invalid Not Piggul

This is the crux: why does even a *chutz l'zmano* thought during one of the four inner applications not produce *pigul*? The *mishna*'s *tanna* holds that since all four applications together constitute a single act of *kippur*, a *machshava* of *pigul* during only one of the four — only one quarter of the *matir* — is not sufficient to create *pigul*. This parallels the earlier *gemara* discussion of *mifaglin b'chatzi matir*: a *pigul* thought during only part of the *matir* does not create *pigul*. Here, since each of the four applications is an indispensable component of the single *matir* act, a *pigul* thought on one component alone is *machshava* on a fraction of the *matir*, insufficient to establish *pigul* and its *kares*. The *korban* is *pasul* — invalidated by the wrong thought — but *ein bo kares*. The discussion of the next *perek* will continue from here.

---

---

# Zevachim 37

## Pigul & Blood Apps

### Perek 4 Intro

We have just begun the fourth *perek* of Zevachim and pick up in the *gemara* two lines from the bottom of 36b. The discussion remains centered on *pigul*, but in order to address the more nuanced cases that arise in that context, the *gemara* introduced the debate between *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai*.

### Hillel vs Shammai

The question at issue is: what is the minimum number of *zrikot* — applications of blood — required for a *korban* to be valid? For all *korbanot* other than a *chatat*, even though the Torah prescribes *zorek saviv*, throwing the blood all around, which *Chazal* understand to mean two diagonally opposite corners (each corner serving two walls), *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* both agree that *bedi'avad* even a single *zrika* suffices — presumably even one wall. For a *chatat*, where the Torah prescribes placing the blood on the four corners of the altar with the finger — not throwing, but direct application — *Beit Shammai* requires a minimum of two *bedi'avad*, while *Beit Hillel* holds that one suffices there as well. With regard to the inner *chata'ot* applied on the inner *mizbe'ach*, all agree that all four applications are required.

### Kapara Status

This framework has direct consequences for *pigul*. Because *kapara* takes effect at the moment the first valid blood application is performed, the *korban* achieves its *kapara* status immediately. Any subsequent applications are no longer relevant to *pigul*: once the *korban* is valid, its *pigul* status is fixed, even though the remaining applications are still part of the *lechatchila* required *avoda*. Thus the entire *pigul* analysis turns on the first application — or, according to *Beit Shammai* in the case of *chatat*, the first two.

---

## V'Dam Zvachecha

### One App Suffices

The *gemara* now asks: from where do we derive that a single application on the outer *mizbe'ach* suffices? *Tanu Rabanan*: the rabbis taught — *minayin l'nitanim al hamizbe'ach hachitzon shenetanam b'matana achat shekiper?* — how do we know that if one placed them with a single *matana* it is effective? *Talmud lomar*: *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech al yesod mizbach ha'olah* — "you shall pour the blood of your sacrifices on the base of the *olah* altar," which is the outer *mizbe'ach*. The *pasuk* speaks in general terms — pour the blood of your sacrifices — and does not limit itself to any particular number of applications. It appears to be describing the fundamental act of *kapara* itself. From this we derive that even one application, even one pouring, suffices.

### Shirayim to Yesod

The *gemara* immediately challenges this reading. *V'hai l'hachi hu d'ata?* — is that really what this *pasuk* comes to teach? Perhaps the *pasuk* is needed for an entirely different *halacha*, as the *gemara* cites from a *baraita*: *minayin l'chol hadamim shete'unin matan dam l'yesod?* — from where do we know that the leftover blood of all *korbanos* must be poured at the *yesod*, the base of the altar?

The Torah explicitly states this only in the context of *chatat*; it is not stated for other *korbanos*. One might note — and this was a suggestion offered by Rabbi Yitzchak Aaron — that the reason the Torah omits this by other *korbanos* is that for those offerings the *p'shat* of the relevant *pesukim* suggests that all the blood is thrown around the *mizbe'ach* (*v'zarku bnei aharon et hadam al hamizbe'ach saviv*), leaving no *shirayim*. Only by *chatat*, where blood is applied to four specific points with the finger, is there obviously going to be blood left over. But the *gemara* still needs to know the source for pouring *shirayim* to the *yesod* for all *korbanos*. *Talmud lomar: v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* — pour the blood of your sacrifices. This would then be read not as describing the act of *kapara* but as referring to the remainder after the primary application: all leftover blood must be poured at the base. If so, the *pasuk* cannot simultaneously be teaching us that one application suffices.

### Chatas Ha'of

The *gemara* responds: the source for the *halacha* that *shirayim* of all *korbanos* go to the *yesod* can be derived instead from the *pasuk* concerning *chatat ha'of* — the bird *chatat* — where the blood is squeezed out against the wall of the *mizbe'ach* and runs down to the base. The *pasuk* there reads: *v'hanishar badam yimatze* — and what remains of the blood shall be squeezed out. The Torah could have written simply *v'hanishar*, "what remains," without the word *badam*, "of the blood." As Rabbi (Rebbi) teaches in a *baraita*: *she'ein talmud lomar badam, u'mah talmud lomar badam?* — the word *badam* was not needed and its presence must therefore be teaching something. Before the additional word is cited, the *baraita* notes that from the explicit text one might only have known that *nitanim matan arba*, those offerings requiring four blood applications and requiring *shirayim* to the *yesod*, are subject to this rule. *Sha'ar damim minayin?* — from where do we know it applies to all other blood offerings? *Talmud lomar: v'hanishar badam yimatze* — the extra word *badam* generalizes the principle beyond the bird offering. Thus *kol hadamim shete'unin matan damim l'yesod* — for all *korbanos*, any remaining blood must be poured at the base. The *halacha* of *shirayim* to the *yesod* can accordingly be derived from *chatat ha'of*, freeing the *pasuk* of *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* to teach that one application suffices.

### Multiple Teachings

The *gemara*, however, is still not satisfied. *V'akti l'hachi hu d'ata?* — even now, is that all *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* comes to teach? Perhaps it is needed for yet another *halacha*, as a further *baraita* states: *minayin l'nitanim b'zrika shenetanan b'shficha yatza?* — from where do we know that for offerings whose blood is supposed to be thrown (*zrika*), if one instead poured (*shficha*) it at the base, one has nonetheless fulfilled the obligation? *Talmud lomar: v'dam zvacheicha yishafech*. This is a considerable *chiddush*: the blood of a normal *korban* is to be thrown at the wall of the altar, yet if one poured it at the base instead, one is *yotzei*. One might argue that this makes sense given that the lower half of the altar and the base are both areas where blood goes, but nonetheless it is a significant ruling. If this is what *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* is teaching — that *shficha* serves as an alternative to *zrika* — then it is not available to teach that one application suffices.

---

## Shficha vs Zrika

### Shficha Alternative

The *gemara* addresses this by noting that *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* could hold *k'Rabbi Akiva*, who rules *lo zrika bikhlal shficha v'lo shficha bikhlal zrika* — throwing and pouring are mutually exclusive categories; each serves its own type of offering and cannot substitute for the other. According to *Rabbi Akiva*, there is no ruling that *shficha* works as an alternative to *zrika*, and therefore *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* need not be reserved for that teaching. It remains available to derive that one application suffices.

---

## Bechor Drashos

### Second Drasha

The *gemara*, however, continues to press the question. Even granting that *Rabbi Akiva*'s position removes one usage of the *pasuk*, the *gemara* cites yet another *baraita* that appears to need *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* for a different purpose. *Rabbi Yishmael* teaches: the *pasuk* in Parashat Korach — *ach bechor shor o bechor kesev o bechor ez lo tifdeh kodesh hem* — teaches us about the *bechor*, the firstborn animal, that its blood is thrown on the *mizbe'ach* and its *emurim* are burned, like any normal *korban*. But the Torah does not specify in other contexts what to do with the blood of *ma'aser* (tithe animals) or the *korban Pesach*. For *ma'aser*, the focus elsewhere is on it as a gift arrangement; for *Pesach*, the focus is on eating the meat. So from where do we know what to do with their blood and *emurim*? *Talmud lomar: v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* — "pour the blood of your sacrifices" — teaching that there are *korbanos* whose blood arrangements the Torah did not specify elsewhere, and this *pasuk* now tells us: pour it at the base.

This establishes the premise underlying the earlier discussion — that the *korban Pesach*'s blood is poured rather than thrown — but it also means the *pasuk* is occupied with teaching the *halacha* for *Pesach* and *ma'aser*, and cannot simultaneously teach that one application suffices.

---

## Shficha vs Zrika (II)

### Rabbi Akiva View

To resolve this, the *gemara* says: *savar lah k'Rabbi Yosi HaGelili* — the author of our *mishnah* would hold like *Rabbi Yosi HaGelili*, whose position we will now examine. But first, the *gemara* takes up the source for *Rabbi Akiva*'s ruling that *zrika* and *shficha* are mutually exclusive.

### Pesachim Mishnah

The *gemara* cites the final *mishnah* in Pesachim. After the full treatment of *hilchot* *Seder*, *Kiddush*, and related matters, the last *mishnah* addresses the question of whether the *bracha* recited over one offering can exempt the obligation to recite a separate *bracha* for another. The relevant offerings are the *korban Pesach* itself and the *chagiga* of the fourteenth of Nisan — the *chagiga* brought when a group is large and people would otherwise eat the *Pesach* while ravenously hungry, so an accompanying *shelamim*-like offering is brought to be eaten first. When eating the *Pesach* one recites *asher kidshanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu l'echol hapesach*; when eating the *chagiga* one recites *asher kidshanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu l'echol et hazevach*.

The first opinion in the *mishnah* rules: *birach birchat hapesach patar et shel zevach; shel zevach lo patar et hapesach* — if one recited the *bracha* for the *Pesach*, one need not make a separate *bracha* for the *chagiga*, but if one recited the *bracha* for the *chagiga*, that does not exempt the *Pesach* and a separate *bracha* is required. *Divrei Rabbi Yishmael* — these are the words of *Rabbi Yishmael*. *Rabbi Akiva* disagrees: *lo zo poteret zo v'lo zo poteret zo* — neither *bracha* exempts the other; each requires its own.

### Pesach/Chagiga

One might naturally understand this dispute as turning on the principle of *ikar* and *tafel*: *Rabbi Yishmael* holds that the *Pesach* is the *ikar* of the evening, and the *chagiga* is subordinate to it, so the *bracha* on the *ikar* covers the *tafel*, while the reverse does not hold. *Rabbi Akiva* would reject this framing, requiring separate *brachot* in any case. *Rashi* indeed entertains this reading. However, the *gemara*'s preferred understanding — and the one adopted in Pesachim — is that the dispute reflects the precise question of *shficha* versus *zrika*.

The assumption is that the Torah never specifies what to do with the blood of the *korban Pesach* because the *Pesach* is fundamentally about eating the meat; accordingly, its blood is poured (*shficha*). The *chagiga*, by contrast, is a classic offering whose blood is thrown (*zrika*). According to *Rabbi Yishmael*, since *shficha* serves as a legitimate alternative to *zrika* for any offering that normally requires *zrika*, the *chagiga* too can be done by *shficha*. Thus the *bracha* over the *Pesach* — which is a *shficha* offering — covers the *chagiga* as well, because the *chagiga* too can be performed by *shficha*. But the *bracha* over the *chagiga*, which is fundamentally a *zrika* offering, does not cover the *Pesach*, because the *Pesach* can only be done by *shficha* and not by *zrika*.

*Rabbi Akiva*, by contrast, holds that *shficha* and *zrika* are mutually exclusive: the *Pesach* is only *shficha* and the *chagiga* is only *zrika*. Neither can substitute for the other, and therefore neither *bracha* exempts the other.

---

## Bechor Drashos (II)

### Yosi HaGelili

The *gemara* continues. *Rabbi Yishmael*'s use of *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* both to establish that the *Pesach*'s blood is done by *shficha* and to teach that *shficha* serves as an alternative to *zrika* raises a difficulty: both inferences are attributed to the same *pasuk*, yet the *mishnah* in Pesachim seems to assume *Rabbi Yishmael* relies on both simultaneously. The *gemara* resolves this with the comment *trei tanna'ei aliba d'Rabbi Yishmael* — there are two different *tanna'im* who transmit *Rabbi Yishmael*'s position, each using the *pasuk* for a different teaching. *Rashi* recognizes, however, that this resolution is not entirely satisfying, since the *tanna* who speaks about the *bracha* still presupposes both that the *Pesach* is *b'shficha* and that *shficha* can work for *zrika* offerings — both derived from the same *pasuk*. *Rashi* therefore concludes that the debate over the *bracha* in the *mishnah* in Pesachim is really about *ikar* and *tafel* and has nothing to do with *shficha* and *zrika*. This does not fit perfectly with the language of *trei tanna'ei*, but *Rashi* accepts the difficulty in order to resolve the deeper logical problem. The bottom line is that a great many *halachot* are being derived from this one *pasuk*, and while the *gemara* seems to treat them as mutually exclusive candidates, *Tosafot* works through how the various *halachot* might in fact be derived from other *pesukim* as well.

The *gemara* now turns to *Rabbi Yosi HaGelili*'s interpretation, which offers an entirely different reading of the *bechor* passage. *Damo lo ne'emar ela damam* — the *pasuk* in Parashat Korach does not say *et damo tizrok*, "its blood shall be thrown," in the singular, but rather *et damam*, "their blood," in the plural. Similarly, *chelbo lo ne'emar ela chelbam* — it says *chelbam*, "their fat," not *chelbo*, "its fat." The simple reading of the plural is that the three types of *bechor* mentioned — *bechor shor*, *bechor kesev*, and *bechor ez* — are all collectively addressed. But *Rabbi Yosi HaGelili* argues that the Torah could have used the singular throughout, since they are all one category of *korban bechor*, and the plural is therefore a deliberate expansion. *Limed habechor ma'aser u'fasach* — it teaches that not only *bechor*, which the *pasuk* mentions explicitly, but also *ma'aser* and *Pesach* — offerings for which the Torah never specifies what to do with their blood and *emurim* — are governed by the same rule. For all three, the blood is thrown on the *mizbe'ach* and the *emurim* are offered.

Thus, according to *Rabbi Yosi HaGelili*, the *bechor pasuk* in Korach teaches *zrika* for *ma'aser* and *Pesach*, derived from the plural *damam* and *chelbam*. This leaves *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* free to teach its other lessons, and *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* who need to derive that one application suffices can accordingly use it for that purpose — or, as we will see, they may derive it from *chatat* instead.

### Textual Tensions

Having established *Rabbi Yosi HaGelili*'s reading, the *gemara* examines the rest of the *pasuk*. According to *Rabbi Yishmael*, the entire passage — *et damam tizrok al hamizbe'ach v'et chelbam taktir* — speaks only about *bechor*, with the plural reflecting the three species of *bechor* animal mentioned. The next *pasuk*, *u'vsaram yiyeh lach*, "and their flesh shall be yours," refers to the *kohanim* receiving the meat of the *bechor* — entirely coherent within a single-theme passage about *bechor* in the context of *matnot kehunah*.

According to *Rabbi Yosi HaGelili*, however, the passage addresses *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *Pesach* together. The following *pasuk*, *u'vsaram yiyeh lach*, then presents a difficulty, since *ma'aser* and *Pesach* are not eaten by *kohanim* — *ma'aser* is eaten by the owners, and *Pesach* similarly. The *gemara* resolves this: *mah u'vsaram yiyeh lach? echad tam v'echad ba'al mum* — the plural of *u'vsaram yiyeh lach* is teaching a different extension. In the first *pasuk*, the plural *damam* and *chelbam* extends the blood-and-*emurim* rules to all three offerings. In the second *pasuk*, the plural *u'vsaram* teaches something about *bechor* itself: the *kohanim* receive the meat both from a *tam* — an unblemished *bechor* brought as a *korban* — and from a *bechor ba'al mum*, a blemished firstborn animal.

This latter point is itself a striking *halacha*. *Shelo matzinu lo bechol haTorah kulah* — as *Rashi* notes, we do not find elsewhere in the Torah what to do with a *bechor ba'al mum*. It cannot be redeemed — *lo tifdeh* is explicit — yet it cannot be offered. *Tosafot* sharpens this further: not only is there no other *pasuk* about it, but there is no other phenomenon in the Torah quite like it — something that is *kadosh* yet may be eaten in its state of *mum* without redemption. You need the plural *u'vsaram yiyeh lach* to tell you that this bizarre category exists and that the *kohen* eats the meat both of a *tam* (brought as a *korban*) and of a *ba'al mum* (eaten directly in its *kedushah* state). Both the *kosher*-for-offering and the blemished *bechor* are included.

### Yishmael vs Yosi

Where then does *Rabbi Yishmael* learn the *halacha* of *bechor ba'al mum*, since he does not use the plural for this purpose? The *gemara* answers: *Rabbi Yishmael nafka lei milach yihyeh desifa* — he derives it from the doubled language at the end of the *pasuk*. After stating *u'vsaram yiyeh lach kachazeh hatenufah u'cheshok hayamin*, the *pasuk* adds *lach yihyeh*, a seemingly superfluous repetition. This extra phrase teaches that the *kohen* receives an additional category of *bechor* beyond what was already stated — namely the *bechor ba'al mum*.

The *gemara* then asks the reverse question. According to *Rabbi Yishmael*, who reads the entire *bechor* passage as referring only to *bechor*, with *Pesach* and *ma'aser* derived from *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* by *shficha*, where does *Rabbi Yossi HaGelili* learn the *halacha* that the *temura* of *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *Pesach* cannot be offered? According to *Rabbi Yosi HaGelili*, the *pasuk kodesh hem* — "they are holy" — is the source: since the *pasuk* refers to all three together, it is teaching *hem kreivim v'ein tmuratan kreivah* — they may be brought as *korbanos*, but their *temura* may not.

### Temura Laws

To ground this in explicit *halacha*, the *gemara* cites a *mishnah*: *tmurat bechor u'ma'aser* — if one makes a *temura* for a *bechor* or *ma'aser*, *hein u'valdeihen v'velad valdeihen ad sof kol ha'olam harei hen k'bechor u'ma'aser* — they and their offspring to all generations have the status of *bechor* and *ma'aser*. The consequence: *v'ye'achlu bemumam labe'alim* — they may only be eaten once they develop a *mum*; they cannot be offered as *korbanos*. They carry the *kedushah* of *bechor* and *ma'aser* but are never brought on the altar, only consumed after a blemish appears, like a *bechor ba'al mum*.

For *Pesach*, the *gemara* cites *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s statement: *shamati she'tmurat haPesach kreiva u'tmurat haPesach eina kreiva* — I have heard that some forms of *temurat haPesach* may be offered and others may not, *v'ein li l'faresh* — but I cannot explain the distinction. The *gemara* elsewhere resolves this: a *temura* of a *Pesach* made before Pesach — when the *Pesach* still retains its full *Pesach* identity — cannot be offered; a *temura* of a *Pesach* after Pesach — when the *Pesach* has effectively assumed the status of *shelamim* — may be offered as *shelamim*.

Now, where does *Rabbi Yishmael* derive these same *temura* rules for *ma'aser* and *Pesach*, since he reads *kodesh hem* as applying only to *bechor*? For *ma'aser*, the *gemara* answers: *gmar avara avara m'bechor* — a *gezeira shava*. The Torah uses a form of the root *ayin-beit-reish* (passing over) by *ma'aser* (*kol asher ya'avor tachat hashevet*) and by *bechor* (*v'ha'avarta kol peter rechem*). The *gezeira shava* links them and carries the *temura* rule from one to the other. For *Pesach*, the *pasuk* concerning *shelamim* states *im kesev hu makriv*, and the extra word *im* — whose necessity is not grammatically obvious — extends the rule: the *temura* of a *Pesach* after Pesach may be brought as *shelamim*. This implicitly establishes that the *temura* of a *Pesach* before Pesach — when *pesach hu*, "it is a *Pesach*," and only it may be brought — cannot be offered.

---

## Chatas Source

### Problem Setup

Having reviewed the full range of *drashot* drawn from *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* and the *bechor* passages, the *gemara* now poses the question in the other direction: *v'chol hanahu tanna'im d'mapkei lei l'hai dam zvacheicha yishapech l'drasha acharina* — all the *tanna'im* who use *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* to derive something else — where do they learn the fundamental *halacha* that a single *netina* suffices for the outer *mizbe'ach*? The *gemara* had raised this as a cliffhanger, and now addresses it directly.

### Chatas Solution

The *gemara* answers: *savira lahu k'Beit Hillel d'amri af chatat she'nitna matana achat kiper, v'yalfinan kuleihu m'chatat* — they hold like *Beit Hillel*, who maintains that even for *chatat* a single application suffices, and from *chatat* we derive the same rule for all other *korbanos* by means of a *binyan av* or *kal vachomer*: if a single *netina* suffices for *chatat* — which explicitly requires four — then it certainly suffices for all other offerings. This will of course require us to understand where *Beit Hillel* themselves derive that one application suffices for *chatat*, and the *gemara* now turns to that question.

Before doing so, the *gemara* notes that this approach is not available to *Beit Shammai*, who holds that *chatat* requires two applications *bedi'avad*. *Chatat* cannot serve as the source for the other *korbanos* when it itself demands two. It is therefore specifically for *Beit Shammai* that *v'dam zvacheicha yishafech* must bear the teaching that one application suffices for the outer *mizbe'ach*. *Tosafot* raises a conceptual point here: there may be a principled reason not to derive the rule for other *korbanos* from *chatat* even according to *Beit Hillel*, since by those other *korbanos* the Torah demands *zorek saviv*, "all around," and one might argue that this is not merely a number but a conceptual requirement — the blood must have reached all four walls. Anything less than that is not *saviv* in any sense; it is not one-out-of-four, it is simply zero. By *chatat*, which specifies four points, doing one of the four is at least genuinely one-of-four. The *gemara*, however, does not pursue this reasoning and proceeds on the assumption that the rule transfers from *chatat* to all other offerings.

---

## Shammai 2 Apps

### Six Corners

*Amar Rav Huna*: *mai ta'ama d'Beit Shammai?* — what is the reasoning of *Beit Shammai* that two applications of blood are required for *chatat bedi'avad*? The answer lies in counting the occurrences of the word *karnos* — corners — in the Torah's discussion of the *chatat* brought by individuals (in Parashat Vayikra, covering the *nasi* and the ordinary individual). The Torah says *karnos hamizbe'ach* in three separate places. Since each usage of *karnos* in the plural yields two, three instances of *karnos* yields six corners altogether. *Harei kan shesh* — here we have six.

### Shammai Math

From this number of six, *Beit Shammai* derives: *arba l'mitzvah u'shtayim l'akev* — four is the *mitzvah*, the standard requirement that is the full and proper performance of the *avoda*, and two is the *akeiv*, the minimum that is *me'akev*, without which the *korban* is invalid.

### Shina Principle

This analysis rests on a general principle in the laws of *kodshim*: *shina lo hakasuv l'akev* — if the Torah repeats an element of a procedure, that repetition signals that the element is *me'akev*. Absent repetition, even mandatory steps in the *avoda* are not necessarily *me'akev bedi'avad*. It would be counterintuitive to apply such logic outside of *kodshim* — one would never suggest that a *mitzvah* need not be fulfilled because the Torah mentioned it only once — but the principle is well-established in *kodshim*, where the elaborate multi-step procedures of the *avoda* lead the *gemara* to presume that not every step is absolutely indispensable unless it is expressly repeated. Given this background, *Beit Shammai* starts from the position that we cannot simply say all four are *me'akev*. With six total mentions, four serve as the *mitzvah* and two as the *akeiv*.

---

## Hillel 1 App

### Hillel Reading

*Beit Hillel* disagrees with how to count the corner-mentions. Where *Beit Shammai* reads all three occurrences of *karnos* as the full plural form — *karnos*, *karnos*, *karnos* — yielding two, two, two, for six, *Beit Hillel* focuses on the *masores*, the way the words are written in the *sefer Torah*. Two of the three instances are written without a *vav* — *karnat* — which, as a defective spelling, suggests the singular form in *smichus*, carrying a value of one each. Only one instance is written in the full plural *karnos*, giving two. According to *Beit Hillel*'s reading by the *masores*: *karnat*, *karnat*, *karnos* — one, one, two — yielding four altogether.

---

## Shammai 2 Apps (II)

### Gemara Q

The *gemara* raises an obvious question against *Beit Hillel*: *v'eima kuleihu l'mitzvah?* — why not say that all four are merely a *mitzvah*, the ideal performance, with nothing being *me'akev*? If the Torah did not repeat the requirement, why say even one is *me'akev*?

### Kapara Min

The *gemara* answers: *kapara b'chidi lo ashkechan* — we never find that *kapara* is achieved without any blood application whatsoever. While the principle of *shina lo hakasuv l'akev* would in theory lead us to say nothing is *me'akev*, we cannot conclude that the *korban* achieves *kapara* without any blood being placed at all. Something must be *me'akev*. Since the Torah did not repeat any specific number of applications as an absolute requirement, we set the floor at the minimum: one application is *me'akev*, and the remaining three are *mitzvah*.

---

## Hillel 1 App (II)

### Averaging Method

The *gemara* now presents an alternative formulation of *Beit Hillel*'s reasoning that is more elegant and arithmetically explicit. Rather than relying on the logical floor argument, *Beit Hillel* may be understood as follows: *hani mikra v'hani masoret* — we pay attention both to the *mikra*, the way the words are read aloud (*karnos*, *karnos*, *karnos*, giving six), and to the *masores*, the way they are written (*karnat*, *karnat*, *karnos*, giving four). Neither reading is simply discarded. The *mikra* adds one to the four, and the *masores* subtracts one from the six. The result: five. Arithmetically, we take both values (six and four), sum them, and divide by two, yielding five.

### Hillel Math

From the number five, *Beit Hillel* draws the same structural conclusion as *Beit Shammai* did from six: *arba l'mitzvah v'achas l'akev* — four is the *mitzvah*, and one is the *akeiv*. The *gemara* acknowledges that this is a more satisfying way to reach the conclusion, even if the arithmetic is unusual.

---

## Testing Method

### Tefillin Case

The *gemara* now stress-tests the averaging methodology. *Ela me'ata* — if we accept this approach, consider the case of *tefillin*. The Torah mentions *l'totafot bein einecha* three times. Two of the three occurrences are written without a *vav* — *l'totafet*, *l'totafet* — and one with a *vav* — *l'totafot*. By the *masores* this yields two, two, two — wait, more carefully: if we read the defective spelling as singular (value: one) and the full spelling as plural (value: two), we get one, one, two — four. If we read all three by the *mikra* as the plural form *l'totafot*, we get two, two, two — six. Adding four and six and dividing by two yields five. *Chamisha batei ba'ei l'me'avad* — should we say five compartments are required for *tefillin*?

### Totafot Etymology

The *gemara* answers: *savar lah k'Rabbi Akiva* — *Beit Hillel* can hold like *Rabbi Akiva*, who teaches *tat b'Katfi shtayim, pat b'Afriki shtayim* — the word *totafet* itself carries the meaning of four, because *tat* in one language means two and *pat* in another language (African) means two, making the word itself encode the number four. Since the word *totafot* inherently means four, the averaging method does not apply here. We do not need to count and average the individual occurrences; the meaning of the word itself settles the number at four.

### Sukkah Case

The *gemara* presses further. *Ela me'ata, basukat, basukat, basukot* — the Torah mentions *sukkot* three times in the relevant passage. By the *masores*, two of the three occurrences are written without a *vav* — *basukat* — suggesting a value of one each; the full spelling *basukot* gives two. That yields one, one, two — four. By the *mikra*, all three are read as the plural *basukot*, yielding two, two, two — six. Adding four and six, dividing by two: five. *Chamisha defanot ba'ei lemivnei* — should we require five walls for a *sukkah*? That is clearly not the *halacha*; three walls suffice.

### Sukkah Resolution

The *gemara* resolves this: *hatam chad kra kuleh legufeh* — one of the three mentions of *sukkot* is needed entirely for its plain meaning, simply to establish the basic *mitzvah* of dwelling in a *sukkah* (*basukkot teshvu shivat yamim*). That mention is consumed by the fundamental *pshat* of the text and does not enter the counting. We are left with *sukat* and *sukot* — the defective and the full spelling — giving four by the *masores* and two by the *mikra*... wait: *sukat* (one) and *sukot* (two): by the *masores*, three; by the *mikra*, *sukot* and *sukot*, four. Adding three and four gives seven, dividing by two gives three and a half. The *gemara* notes that you cannot work with a half. And in a sense this works out neatly: one for *sechach* and two-and-a-half for walls — a non-integer that cannot yield a clean requirement. The *halacha lemoshe misinai* then reduces one full wall to a *tefach*, yielding the familiar rule of two full walls and one *tefach*.

One might ask why the first mention is used up for *pshat* here but not in the cases of *karnos* or *totafot*. *Tosafot* raises precisely this question, acknowledging that it is difficult to determine with precision when the *gemara* regards the first mention as consumed by *pshat* and when it allows counting to begin from the first occurrence.

### Yoledet Case

The *gemara* raises one more case. *Ela me'ata, vetame'ah shevu'ayim* — by a woman who gives birth to a girl, the Torah states she shall be *tame'ah shevu'ayim*, for two weeks. But the word is written without a *vav* — *shivi'im* — which, taken as written, would mean seventy days. If we apply the averaging method: fourteen (two weeks) and seventy, summing to eighty-four, divided by two gives forty-two. *Ahni kra v'ahni mesoret, arba'im v'tarti ba'ei lemesav* — would this woman have to wait forty-two days?

### Yoledet Resolved

The *gemara* answers: *shani hatam d'chtiv kenidatah* — that case is different because the *pasuk* adds *kenidatah*, "like her *niddah*." Her *niddah* period is a week, and the comparison fixes the unit of counting: *shevu'ayim* means two of those weekly units, i.e., two weeks. The word *kenidatah* anchors the meaning of *shevu'ayim* and prevents any alternative reading from the defective spelling. The averaging method therefore cannot be applied here.

The *gemara* leaves us at this point with two accounts of *Beit Hillel*'s position on *chatat*: either the number four is derived from the *masores* alone and the floor argument (*kapara b'chidi lo ashkechan*) brings us to one *me'akev*; or, more elegantly, the averaging of *mikra* and *masores* yields five, which divides naturally into four for *mitzvah* and one for *akev*. For *Beit Shammai*, the derivation proceeds through three occurrences of the full plural *karnos*, yielding six, which divides into four for *mitzvah* and two for *akev*. We will continue from here tomorrow.

---

---

# Zevachim 38

## Beis Shammai vs Hillel

### Two vs One Corner

We pick up several lines into 38a, in the middle of a discussion concerning the debate between Beis Hillel and Beis Shammai regarding the placement of blood on the corners of the *chatas*. The Torah requires placing the blood of the *chatas* on all four corners of the *mizbe'ach*, yet both schools agree that *be'dieved* fewer than four suffice. The dispute is over precisely how few: according to Beis Shammai, two corners suffice *be'dieved*, while according to Beis Hillel, even one suffices.

### Karnos Derivation

Beis Shammai derives this position from the word *karnos* — the plural form used in the relevant *pesukim*. Reading *karnos*, *karnos*, *karnos* across the relevant passages yields a combined count of six, which, divided appropriately, produces four *lechat'chilah* and two *be'dieved*.

### Hillel's Corner Count

The more difficult derivation is Beis Hillel's. Establishing the *lechat'chilah* requirement of four corners is not the challenge, but arriving at one *be'dieved* from the counted corners has proven elusive, and several approaches have been attempted. The *gemara* now introduces an entirely new framework — a *baraita* that grounds Beis Hillel's position not in the corner-count at all, but in a different set of words in the *Torah* entirely.

---

## Vekiper Drasha

### Three Vekipers

At the end of *Parshat Vayikra*, in the passages concerning individual *korbanos* — whether of the *nasi* or of a private individual — each passage describing the placement of blood on the corners of the *mizbe'ach* concludes with the word *vekiper*, "and it will atone for him." The *tanna* of the *baraita* learns Beis Hillel's position from the fact that this word is repeated three times: *vekiper*, *vekiper*, *vekiper*. But first, the *baraita* must establish why a *pasuk* is necessary at all — why we cannot simply derive the same conclusion through logic alone.

### Logical Sufficiency

The *baraita* introduces the principle of *midrash halacha* by first presenting a logical argument (*din*) that might have made the *pasuk* unnecessary. *Neemru damim lemata veneemru damim lemala* — the Torah speaks of blood placed on the lower half of the *mizbe'ach* (as with all other *korbanos* that are not a *chatas*) and of blood placed on the upper half of the *mizbe'ach* (as with the *chatas*). Now, we know from a separate source — *vedam zevachecha yishapech* — that for all other *korbanos* on the lower half of the *mizbe'ach*, one application of blood suffices. If so, one might have argued by analogy: just as one *matana* suffices for blood placed below, so too one *matana* suffices for blood placed above, in the case of the *chatas*. Why, then, does the Torah need to repeat *vekiper*?

### Inner vs Outer

However, the *baraita* immediately counters this argument with an alternative logical path: *o kalach lederech zu* — one could equally well argue in the opposite direction. *Neemru damim bifnim veneemru damim bachutz* — the Torah also speaks of blood placed on the four corners of the inner *mizbe'ach*, in the case of the *chatas pnimit*, and it speaks of blood placed on the four corners of the outer *mizbe'ach*, in the case of the outer *chatas*. We accept, from the *mishna*, that by the inner *chatas* all four *matanos* are *me'akev* — if even one is missing, nothing has been accomplished. One might therefore analogize the outer *chatas* to the inner *chatas*: just as all four are *me'akev* on the inner *mizbe'ach*, so too all four should be *me'akev* on the outer *mizbe'ach*.

### Need for Pasuk

Since the logical arguments point in opposite directions, the *gemara* considers whether one analogy is stronger than the other. On one hand, one might prefer to compare the outer *chatas* to the other *korbanos* on the outer *mizbe'ach*, since they share the same location — *danim chutz michutz ve'ein danim chutz mibifnim*. On the other hand, one might prefer to compare the outer *chatas* to the inner *chatas*, since both involve a *chatas* with four corners — *danim chatas v'arba karnos michatas v'arba karnos* — whereas the other *korbanos* on the outer *mizbe'ach* involve neither a *chatas* nor four corners. Since each analogy has a compelling basis and the arguments are genuinely balanced, logic alone cannot resolve the question. Therefore, the *Torah* explicitly teaches through the repeated *vekiper*: even if not done perfectly, atonement will be achieved. The first *vekiper* teaches that atonement is achieved even if only three *matanos* were performed; the second, even if only two; the third, even if only one. Thus three *vekipers* successively reduce the requirement from four down to one, establishing that *be'dieved* a single *matana* suffices.

### Adda's Explanation

The *gemara* raises an immediate difficulty: perhaps the word *vekiper* is needed simply for its plain meaning — to inform us that the *korban* achieves *kapara*. Why assume it is available for this *drasha* at all? Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves this by pointing out that the *pasuk* actually uses two words in tandem: *vekiper venislach* — "and it will atone, and he will be forgiven." Since *venislach* already communicates that atonement and forgiveness are achieved, the word *vekiper* is freed from its simple function and becomes available to teach the *be'dieved* leniency. With that established, three iterations of *vekiper* progressively reduce the requirement: from four to three, from three to two, and from two to one.

---

## Vekiper Alternatives

### Three Above One Below

Having established that three *vekipers* teach a reduction in the number of *matanos*, the *gemara* asks whether those three *vekipers* might be teaching something different altogether — not a reduction in the number of corners, but a shift in the *location* of the blood on the *mizbe'ach*. Perhaps the first *vekiper* teaches that atonement is achieved even if only three applications were placed above and one below; the second, even if two were above and two below; and the third, even if none were above and all four below.

### Rejection: Eliminate Cor…

This reading is rejected: if the three *vekipers* are used to permit placing all the blood below the *chut hasikra* (the red line dividing the *mizbe'ach*), then the requirement to place blood on the corners — which are above — is entirely eliminated. One might respond that if the *Torah* teaches this, so be it; perhaps there is an alternative path of placing blood below, just as there are other variations in blood service. However, Rava rejects this: three *vekipers* are structurally suited to reduce a fourfold requirement by one step at a time, arriving at the number one. If the endpoint were "all four below," four *vekipers* would be required, not three.

### All Below Option

This logic clarifies the structure of the *gemara*'s argument: three *vekipers* drive the count from four to one. The alternative reading — which would have used those same three *vekipers* to arrive at "all four below, none above" — is therefore not numerically coherent with the available text.

### Need Four Vekipers

Rava's formulation makes this precise: *eizu drush she-tzarich shalosh havei omer elu karnos* — what type of *drasha* requires exactly three steps? The *karnos*, going from four down to one. If the intended conclusion were "everything below," four steps would be needed. Three *vekipers* cannot carry that weight.

### One Above Three Below

The *gemara* then raises a third alternative: perhaps the three *vekipers* teach that atonement is achieved even with one application above and three below. This is the middle option that the *gemara* had apparently passed over in the initial discussion.

### No Split Placement

This too is rejected, on different grounds. The objection is not numerical but structural: *lo matzinu damim she-chetzyan lema'ala ve-chetzyan lemata* — we have never found a *korban* in which the blood placement is fundamentally divided between the upper and lower halves of the *mizbe'ach* as a halachic requirement. Such a split cannot be an acceptable endpoint for *matan damim*. This, the *gemara* explains, is why this option was not considered earlier: the *gemara* was looking for a landing point that is halachically coherent, and "one above and three below" is not, because it requires a constitutive division of blood between two zones of the *mizbe'ach*.

### Yom Kippur Proof

The *gemara* challenges this principle with an apparent counterexample: the *mishna* regarding *Yom Kippur* states that the *Kohen Gadol* sprinkles one application above and seven below when facing the *Aron*. If taken literally, this would seem to require blood in two distinct locations — one above and seven below — directly contradicting the principle just established.

### Matzlif Meaning

The *gemara* resolves this by explaining that the phrase refers not to the physical location of the blood on the *Aron* itself, but to the direction of the flicking motion — *ke-matzlif*, like the motion of one who administers lashes. Rav Yehuda demonstrated this with his finger: the motion of the wrist determines whether a given sprinkling is counted as "above" or "below," but the blood is not being split between two physical locations on the *Aron*. The *Aron* is not functioning as a *mizbe'ach* here in the relevant sense.

### Taharo Sprinkling

The *gemara* continues with a related case: on *Yom Kippur*, after completing the service inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* and at the *paroches*, the *Kohen Gadol* proceeds to the *mizbe'ach ha-zahav* and sprinkles seven times on its *taharo*. The *gemara* asks what *taharo shel mizbe'ach* means. Drawing an analogy to the phrase *tiahra tiahra de-yoma* — the brightness or purity of the day, meaning midday, the midpoint of the day — one might understand *taharo shel mizbe'ach* as referring to the middle of the *mizbe'ach* wall. If so, those sprinklings are placed at a level distinct from the corners (which are above), and we would again have blood divided between two locations.

### One Place Clarified

Raba bar Shila rejects this interpretation. *Taharo* does not mean the middle of the wall but rather the exposed, uncovered part of the *mizbe'ach* — which is its roof. Since the corners are also on the roof, all the blood placements remain in one zone: above. The *pasuk* that compares it to the clarity of the heavens (*uke'etzem ha-shamayim la-tohar*) confirms this, as it denotes what is uppermost and open. Hence there is no division of blood between two physical regions of the *mizbe'ach*.

### Shirayim Exception

The *gemara* raises a further potential counterexample: for any *korban*, after the *matanos* of blood on the *mizbe'ach*, the *shirayim* — the remainder of the blood — are poured at the *yesod*, the base of the *mizbe'ach*. This is clearly a different location from the corners or the roof. Does this not constitute a required division of blood in two places? The *gemara* answers: *shirayim lo ma'akvei* — the pouring of the *shirayim* is not *me'akev*. The entire discussion concerns what is *me'akev* in the blood service, and the *shirayim* fall outside that category.

### Pnimiyim Shirayim

A sharper version of this challenge involves the *shirayim pnimiyim*: after the four *matanos* on the *mizbe'ach ha-zahav* in the service of an inner *chatas*, there is an opinion that the remainder of the blood must be poured at the *yesod* of the outer *mizbe'ach*, and that this is *me'akev*. Here we have two blood placements that are *me'akev*, and they occur not merely in different locations on one *mizbe'ach* but on entirely separate *mizbeachos*.

### One Altar Principle

The *gemara* resolves this with a limiting principle: *bechad makom kamina* — the rule that blood placement cannot require two fundamentally separate locations applies to blood service on a single *mizbe'ach*. When blood must be placed on two distinct *mizbeachos*, each *mizbe'ach* has its own independent role, and there is no paradox.
