Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin argues that when the *baraita* says a *piggul* thought at the "second" or "third" stage creates *piggul* for Rabbi Meir, it is referring to a case where that *piggul* thought occurred specifically at the moment of this new *shechita* — a discrete, fresh *matir* event — not at an ordinary blood application in the middle of a sequence. Since the new *shechita* is itself a complete *matir* unto itself, having the *piggul* thought there is indeed having it at a full *matir*, not merely at a *chatzi matir*.

The *gemara* does not resolve this cleanly, and the difficulty is palpable. The *baraita*'s language — speaking of the first, second, or third application of blood — reads naturally as referring to the sequential applications within a single, continuous process. Reading it as a reference to an interruption requiring a new *shechita* is a radical reinterpretation. The *baraita* appears to state plainly that for Rabbi Meir, *piggul* at any one of the applications is sufficient — a position that coheres naturally with *mefaglin b'chatzi matir* but sits uneasily with the *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona* framework. This is where the daf concludes, and the tension will carry forward into the next session.

---

---

# Zevachim 42

## Reish Lakish's Reading

### Meir vs. Chachamim

The daf opens by returning to the central debate between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* concerning *pigul* — the invalidation of a sacrifice through an improper intention expressed during one of the four key sacrificial acts. The question at stake is the concept of *mefaglin bechatzi matir*: whether a *pigul* thought expressed during only one component of a composite *matir* act is sufficient to create *pigul*, or whether the intention must accompany every component.

To appreciate the structure of this debate, it is necessary to understand what constitutes a *chatzi matir*. The *matir* acts are the four pivotal moments that render a *korban* valid: *shechita*, *kabbalah*, *holachah*, and *zerikah*. Within some of these acts, there are discrete sub-components — for instance, applying blood to one of four corners of the altar, or severing one of the two organs (*kaneh* or *veshet*) during *shechita*. Each such discrete component is a *chatzi matir*. Importantly, however, not every partial act qualifies. A single step taken while walking the blood toward the altar is not a *chatzi matir*, because it is not a discrete, bounded component of *holachah* — it is merely part of a continuous act. The concept of *chatzi* here does not mean exactly half; it refers to any discrete sub-unit within a composite *matir* act.

The *pshat* of the *mishnah* is clear: Rabbi Meir holds *mefaglin bechatzi matir* — a *pigul* thought on even one discrete component suffices to create *pigul*. The *chachamim* disagree, requiring *ad sheyefagel bechol hamatir* — the *pigul* intention must accompany every component of the *matir* act.

### First Act Only

It is in this context that Reish Lakish proposes a striking reinterpretation of Rabbi Meir. Reish Lakish argues that even Rabbi Meir does not truly hold *mefaglin bechatzi matir* in the broadest sense. Rather, Rabbi Meir's position is that a *pigul* thought expressed during the *first* component suffices — because the first act is understood to define and encompass all subsequent acts. Since every subsequent act is performed *al da'as* the first, the first declaration of intent retroactively covers the whole process. A *pigul* thought expressed in the middle of the process, by contrast, does not — according to Reish Lakish's reading of Rabbi Meir — create *pigul*.

Rashi notes that "thought" here means articulated thought — a verbalized intention — not a merely internal mental state.

### Yom Kippur Blood

To appreciate the full scope of the debate, the *gemara* catalogues the 43 blood applications of Yom Kippur. The *kohen gadol* performs one-and-seven applications on the *kaporet* and one-and-seven on the *parochet*, separately for the *par* (bull) and the *sa'ir* (goat), yielding 32 applications. He then mixes the bloods and applies four to the corners of the golden altar and seven across its top, yielding another 11 — for a total of 43. The same structure applies to the *par* of the *kohen hamashiach* and the *par he'alem davar shel tzibbur*, both of which involve 11 applications of blood.

The *baraita* states that Rabbi Meir says *pigul* applies whether the improper thought occurred during the first, second, or third set of applications. This is already a striking formulation — Rabbi Meir is *more stringent* here than by a standard outer-altar *chatat*, for which a *pigul* thought after the first application does not create *pigul*. By the inner-altar applications, since all are required, Rabbi Meir holds that a *pigul* thought on any one of them suffices. The *chachamim* are correspondingly *more lenient* than by the outer *chatat*: they require the *pigul* intention at every single application.

### Baraita Challenge

The *baraita* thus presents an immediate challenge to Reish Lakish. The text explicitly states that a *pigul* thought during the second or third set of applications — not the first — still produces *pigul* according to Rabbi Meir. The *gemara* presses the point: *katani miha* — it states plainly, *pigul bein berishona bein beshniya bein beshlishis*, "whether the first, or the second, or the third." This appears to directly contradict Reish Lakish's claim that Rabbi Meir limits *pigul* to a thought expressed during the first act.

Reish Lakish is therefore compelled to reinterpret. His proposal, attributed in the *gemara* to Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin, is that the *baraita* is not discussing a straightforward sequence of blood applications, but rather the unusual case where blood spilled partway through the Yom Kippur service and the *kohen gadol* performed a second *shechita* to obtain more blood. In Rashi's reading, for instance, blood might have spilled between the *kaporet* applications and the *parochet* applications. The *kohen* would then slaughter a second animal to obtain fresh blood and continue. When the *baraita* says the *pigul* thought occurred "during the second" or "during the third," it means the *pigul* thought was expressed *during the shechita* of the second or third animal — not during a middle blood application. Since *shechita* is itself a complete, discrete *matir* act, this is not *chatzi matir* at all. Even on Reish Lakish's reading of Rabbi Meir, a *pigul* thought during a full *shechita* suffices — and so the *baraita* is not a counterproof.

This reading is, as the *gemara* itself will acknowledge, extremely forced (*dachuk*). But it represents Reish Lakish's attempt to preserve his interpretation.

---

## Spilled Blood Scenario

### Rashi's Reading

Rashi's scenario, then, is this: the blood spills at some point mid-process on Yom Kippur — say, between the *kaporet* and the *parochet* applications. A second animal must now be slaughtered. The *baraita*'s reference to a *pigul* thought "during the second" or "during the third" refers to a *pigul* thought expressed at the moment of *shechita* of the second or third animal slaughtered to replenish spilled blood. In that case, the *pigul* thought is attached to a *shechita* — itself a full, unambiguous *matir* act — not to a mere component within a larger blood application process. Thus, Rabbi Meir can be read as requiring a *pigul* thought on a full act, and the apparent counterproof dissolves.

The *gemara* then asks the obvious follow-up: *ei hachi*, if that is so — if the *shechita* here is a full *matir* act — then why do the *chachamim* say it does *not* create *pigul*? If we accept the framework that *shechita* is always a full, discrete *matir*, what basis could there be for the *chachamim*'s leniency?

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* formulates this challenge precisely. If, as Reish Lakish insists, we are speaking of a *pigul* thought during *shechita* — which is a single, complete *matir* — then *mai ta'ama de-Rabbanan*? What is the rationale of the *chachamim* who would not recognize this as *pigul*? The scenario now seems to involve a straightforwardly valid *pigul* thought on a complete act, and yet the *chachamim* exempt. Something in the structure of this unusual case must give the *chachamim* grounds to distinguish it from the standard case.

### Rava Identifies

Rava resolves this by identifying: *man Chachamim? Rabbi Eliezer.* The *chachamim* in this unusual reading of Reish Lakish are none other than Rabbi Eliezer. The case has an inherent complexity: ordinarily, the entire Yom Kippur *avodah* requires only a single *shechita*. This second *shechita* is being performed solely because blood spilled — it is not the inaugural *shechita* of the *korban* itself, but rather a supplementary one, performed in the middle of an ongoing blood application process. Is this second *shechita* a full *matir* in the same sense as the first? Or is it somehow a partial *matir* — a *chatzi matir* — by virtue of the fact that it is contributing to a process already underway, stepping in where the first *shechita* left off?

This question — whether a *shechita* performed mid-process to replenish spilled blood is a full *matir* or a *chatzi matir* — is genuinely interesting and would have constituted a meaningful debate on its own. What makes the association with Rabbi Eliezer more complex, however, is the analogy the *gemara* now attempts to draw.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Analogy

### Eliezer Full Amount

The *mishnah* cited in this context enumerates items that are entirely consumed on the *mizbeach*: the *kometz* (the handful taken from the *mincha*), the *levonah* (frankincense accompanying the *mincha*), the *ketores* (incense burned on the inner altar), *minchas kohanim*, *minchas kohen mashiach*, and *minchas nesachim*. With respect to all of these, the general rule is that if one brings even a *kezayit* of any of them outside the *Beis Hamikdash* — the prohibition of *shechutei chutz* or *ha'alas chutz* — one is liable.

Rabbi Eliezer, however, exempts: *poter ad she-yakriv es kullan*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that one is not liable until one offers up the *entire* amount outside — a *kezayit* alone does not suffice. Rashi explains this as follows: if part of the item was already offered on the inner altar in the *Beis Hamikdash* and then a *kezayit* of the remainder was offered outside, liability may follow, because the act of bringing the partial amount outside can be connected to and measured against the prior inside offering. But if nothing was offered inside and someone brings only a *kezayit* outside, without ever having brought the full amount inside, then this *kezayit* is not a sufficiently meaningful act of *hakravah*. Since the normative requirement is to bring the entire *kometz* or *levonah* on the altar, a mere *kezayit* outside — disconnected from any inside offering — does not rise to the level of a culpable act of *ha'alas chutz*. One is liable outside only for an act of a type that would have generated liability inside, and since bringing a partial *kometz* on the inside altar accomplishes nothing definitive, a *kezayit* of it outside likewise does not.

### Tosafot Comparison

Tosafot draws an inference from this analogy that illuminates the broader relationship between *pigul* and *shchutei chutz*. Tosafot argues that the standards for creating *pigul* are, as a general rule, *higher* than the standards for liability in *shchutei chutz*. The evidence: according to the *chachamim* who hold *ein mefaglin bechatzi matir* — and, under Reish Lakish's reading, Rabbi Meir as well — a *pigul* thought about the *kometz* alone does not create *pigul*, because the *levonah* is a co-*matir* of the *mincha*. Both the *kometz* and the *levonah* are required to permit the remainder, and therefore a *pigul* thought on only one of them is insufficient. Yet by *ha'alas chutz*, one is liable even for a *kezayit* of the *mincha* — a fraction, not the full *kometz* let alone the full *mincha*. The threshold for *pigul* is thus demonstrably higher than for *chutz*.

The practical implication of this asymmetry, Tosafot argues, is a *kal vachomer*: if one is exempt from liability for *chutz* by bringing a partial amount outside, then one certainly cannot create *pigul* with a comparably partial act. Specifically, applying this to the *shechita*-in-the-middle scenario: if Rabbi Eliezer exempts from *chutz* liability because the *kezayit* of the *kometz* outside is insufficiently meaningful without the full amount — then, *kal vachomer*, Rabbi Eliezer would hold that the second *shechita* performed mid-process cannot create *pigul*. It is, in some sense, a partial *matir*, and by the *kal vachomer* from *chutz*, where even more is sometimes required, *pigul* would certainly not attach.

The analogy, however, is admittedly imprecise. A *kezayit* of the *kometz* is genuinely a *chatzi matir* — a partial unit of the permitting substance. The second *shechita* in the Yom Kippur spilling scenario is, by contrast, a complete act of *shechita* — a full discrete act — that happens to occur in the middle of an ongoing process. The comparison between these two cases is strained, and both Rashi and Tosafot do not fully articulate how the analogy holds. The *gemara* will ultimately abandon it.

### Blood Exception

The *gemara* then raises a complication that undermines the entire structure of the Eliezer analogy. Rava points out: *u-modeh Rabbi Eliezer be-damim* — Rabbi Eliezer concedes when it comes to blood. As a *mishnah* states, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon both hold *mi-makom she-pasak misham hu matchil*: if blood spills mid-process, one slaughters a new animal and resumes from the point of interruption rather than restarting the entire *avodah* from the beginning. This ruling reflects a view that each completed blood application inside the *Beis Hamikdash* accomplishes something meaningful in its own right — because if it did not, there would be no basis to "pick up where one left off." Since each application is not negated by the subsequent spilling, even a partial blood application has real and durable significance.

Given this, Rabbi Eliezer's exemption for a *kezayit* of the *kometz* outside cannot be extended by simple analogy to the blood. A *kezayit* of *kometz* offered inside accomplishes nothing identifiable — it does not "move" the *korban* forward in the way that a blood application does. But a partial blood application, even if incomplete, is considered to carry real weight. Therefore, by *ha'alas chutz*, Rabbi Eliezer would actually hold that even a small amount of blood brought outside generates liability. His exemption applies only to the *kometz* and like items, not to blood.

### Spilling Rule

This complicates the attempted analogy beyond repair. Tosafot draws the conclusion that one cannot extract from Rabbi Eliezer's position on *chutz* a clean, predictable rule about *pigul*. Rabbi Eliezer's rulings on *chutz* are internally differentiated: he exempts for a *kezayit* of *kometz* outside, but he would hold liable for a small quantity of blood outside. This asymmetry within his own view of *chutz* means that one cannot draw a straight line from his *chutz* position to whatever his *pigul* position might be in the second-*shechita* scenario. The *gemara* abandons the analogy.

What remains is a genuinely interesting underlying question: if the principle is *ein mefaglin bechatzi matir*, and if *shechita* is ordinarily a full *matir*, what happens when a *shechita* is performed in the middle of an ongoing blood-application process to replenish spilled blood? Is that *shechita* a full *matir* or a *chatzi matir*? This question would have constituted a real and meaningful debate. The difficulty is that linking it to Rabbi Eliezer's rulings about *chutz* introduces more confusion than clarity, and the *gemara* leaves this line of analysis behind.

---

## Meir's True Position

### Bracketing Problem

The *gemara* now returns to what is plainly the *pshat* of the *mishnah* — that Rabbi Meir holds *mefaglin bechatzi matir* without qualification — and puts aside the forced re-readings Reish Lakish has proposed. With this as the foundation, the *gemara* raises a fundamental structural problem about how *pigul* operates in the context of *chatzi matir*.

The general principle is: *kehartza'as kasher ken hartza'as pasul* — just as a valid *korban* requires all its *matirim* to be properly performed, so too a *pasul* (invalid) *korban* — including a *pigul korban* — requires that all the *matirim* apart from the *pigul* act itself be performed properly. One is only liable for *pigul* if the rest of the *avodah* was done correctly: *ad sheyikrevu kol matirav*. The *pigul* thought on one act "brackets" that act, but the rest must be kosher.

The *gemara* now asks: how does this work in a case of *chatzi matir*? Say the *kohen* has a *pigul* thought during the first of the blood applications on the *kaporet*. The blood is now *pasul* — the act of *keivas dam* on the *kaporet* is invalidated by the *pigul* thought. But now, when the *kohen* continues to the *parochet* and applies the same blood, he is applying *pasul* blood. How is this "doing the rest properly"? The blood applied to the *parochet* is, at this stage, no better than water — *mayim be'alma* — it cannot accomplish anything, because the blood itself has been invalidated. Therefore, the condition of *ad sheyakrivu kol matirav* — that all the *matirim* be performed correctly — seems to be violated, not by the *pigul* thought itself, but by the *pasul* blood that continues to be sprinkled after the *pigul* thought.

One might wonder: isn't this the same problem for any case of *pigul*? Even in the standard case, if a *pigul* thought occurs during *shechita*, the blood that comes from that *shechita* is *pasul*. Yet we routinely say that *zerikah* must be performed properly for *pigul* to take effect. This seems to present the same paradox: you are applying *pasul* blood, so how is the *zerikah* kosher?

The answer is that in the standard case, we "bracket" the *pigul* act — we treat the *shechita* as a self-contained event and assess the rest of the *avodah* separately from it. Bracketing the *shechita*'s *pigul* status, the *zerikah* was technically performed properly. This bracketing works because the *pigul* act is a complete, discrete unit: the *shechita* is a whole act, and the *zerikah* is a separate whole act. We can quarantine the *pigul* reality to one act and assess the others independently.

### Rashi Solution

Rashi argues that this bracketing breaks down in the *chatzi matir* case. When the *pigul* thought occurs in the middle of the blood-application process — say, at the first application on the *kaporet* — we cannot cleanly bracket that one application and assess the rest of the process separately. The reason is that all of these applications are part of a single composite act. We cannot label part of a single act as *pigul* and the rest as kosher; the entire act resists being given a single unitary label. Since the act as a whole is neither fully *pigul* nor fully kosher, we cannot bracket the *pigul* portion and say the rest was done properly. Instead, we must evaluate the whole act honestly: part of it was done with a *pigul* intention and part without. The result is not *pigul* — which requires the full bracketing operation — but simply *pasul*: the *korban* is invalid, not because of *pigul*, but because the act was partially compromised.

The *gemara*'s difficulty, on Rashi's reading, thus flows from the very definition of *chatzi matir*: because the *pigul* event is embedded within a composite act, the act cannot be unambiguously labeled *pigul* for purposes of the bracketing operation. Without successful bracketing, the condition of *ad sheyakrivu kol matirav* cannot be met, and the *pigul* status cannot be established. This, then, is what makes the case puzzling.

### Rava Final Answer

Rava resolves the difficulty by rejecting the premise that discrete acts are required for bracketing to work. He first suggests that the case in question involves multiple animals — four bulls and four goats — where spilled blood at various points necessitated additional *shechitos*, creating genuinely discrete stages. In those circumstances, the bracketing is unproblematic, since each stage is independently bounded.

But Rava then goes further and says: *afilu teima bepar echad use'ir echad* — even if one takes the case at face value, with a single bull and a single goat, the resolution is the same. The mechanism of *pigul meratzeh* — the principle by which *pigul* operates to "permit" the *korban* for purposes of liability — applies even to an intra-act *pigul* thought. Just as we bracket the *pigul* reality when it attaches to a discrete whole act, we bracket it equally when it attaches to a component within a composite act. The rest of the process is evaluated as if the *pigul* event is quarantined, and if the remainder was performed correctly, the *pigul* takes effect. There is no categorical distinction between bracketing a whole act and bracketing part of an act — the *gemara*'s proposed distinction between discrete and non-discrete scenarios does not hold, and Rava's final answer is that even within a single continuous process, *pigul* on one component can be bracketed and the rest assessed as properly performed.

---

## Blood Counts

### Mixing Question

Having established the framework for the 43 blood applications of Yom Kippur, the *gemara* notes that a *baraita* records a different count: 47. The discrepancy hinges on the question of when the bloods of the *par* and the *sa'ir* are mixed together. After the applications on the *kaporet* and *parochet* for each animal separately (yielding 32 applications in total), the *kohen* mixes the bloods and performs the remaining applications on the golden altar — four on its corners and seven across its top, for 11 additional applications, giving 43.

The debate is: *ha-keman de'amar me'arvin lekranot, ha-keman de'amar ein me'arvin lekranot* — one opinion holds that the bloods are mixed *before* the corner applications, yielding 11 applications with the combined blood and a total of 43. A second opinion holds that the corner applications are performed separately with each blood before mixing — *ein me'arvin lekranot* — which doubles the four corner applications to eight and yields 47. The relevant *pasuk* is noted: the phrase *mi-dam ha-par u-mi-dam ha-sa'ir* at the corners could be read as indicating separate applications of each, while the subsequent phrase *min ha-dam* for the seven upper applications indicates a unified blood. This textual evidence tracks the structural debate precisely.

### Sheirim Debate

A third *baraita* records yet another count: 48. The additional application arises from the question of whether the *sheirim* — the residual blood poured at the base of the outer altar — is *me'akev*, an indispensable prerequisite. If this final spilling is halachically required and not merely supplementary, it would count as an additional application and bring the total to 48 (or to 48 from 47, depending on which view of the mixing one follows).

This connects to a broader question about inner *chata'ot* generally: is the spilling of *sheirim* at the *yesod* of the outer altar indispensable to the *avodah*, or merely a desirable additional act that does not invalidate the offering if omitted? Our *mishnah* in *Eizehu Mekoman* states explicitly that omitting the *sheirim* does not invalidate — *ve-im lo natan lo ikev*. The *baraita* that yields 48 appears to represent the dissenting view that the *sheirim* is *me'akev* for the Yom Kippur *avodah*.

---

## Menachot Challenge

### Mincha Baraita

Having exhausted the main lines of challenge to Reish Lakish from the Yom Kippur *baraita*, the *gemara* raises yet another challenge from an entirely different domain — the *mincha* offering. The *baraita* discusses the case of two *matirim* in the *mincha*: the *kometz* and the *levonah*. Either one alone can create *pigul* according to Rabbi Meir, since each is a *matir* in its own right. The *baraita* then presents two sub-cases: a *pigul* thought during the *kometz* with silence during the *levonah*, and silence during the *kometz* with a *pigul* thought during the *levonah*. Rabbi Meir says *pigul* in both cases; the *chachamim* require both.

### Sequence Evidence

The *gemara* focuses on the second sub-case: silence during the *kometz*, followed by a *pigul* thought during the *levonah* alone. This is explicit evidence that a *pigul* thought occurring *after* a silent first act still constitutes *pigul* for Rabbi Meir. The *levonah* is not the first *matir* — the *kometz* was taken first, in silence. Yet Rabbi Meir says the *pigul* thought on the *levonah* alone suffices. This directly contradicts Reish Lakish's claim that Rabbi Meir requires the *pigul* thought to occur at the *first* act.

The *gemara* presents this challenge with the formula *katani miha*: "it states nonetheless" — the *baraita* explicitly gives a case where the first act was done in silence and only the second carried the *pigul* thought, and Rabbi Meir rules *pigul*.

### Rejection

Reish Lakish attempts his usual response: read *kvar natan et ha-levonah be-machshavah* — understand the *baraita* as saying that the *levonah* had *already* been given with a *pigul* thought (i.e., the *levonah* was first), and the subsequent mention of the *kometz* in silence is describing what came after. On this reading, the *baraita* is not describing a case of a first-act silence followed by a second-act *pigul* thought; rather, the *pigul* thought was on the *levonah* first, and the *kometz* in silence came afterward.

The *gemara* rejects this in two steps. First: *chada de-hainu reisha* — this reading would make the second case merely redundant with the first case already stated in the *baraita*. There is no reason to repeat the same scenario. Second, and more decisively: another *baraita* adds the explicit words *ve-achar kach* — "and afterward" — making the sequence unambiguous. First the *kometz* in silence, and *then* afterward the *levonah* with the *pigul* thought, and still Rabbi Meir says *pigul*.

The *gemara* ends with *kashya* — this is a difficulty for Reish Lakish. The editorial understatement is notable. The accumulated weight of evidence — from the Yom Kippur *baraita*, from the *mincha baraita*, and from the explicit sequential language of the supplementary *baraita* — makes it abundantly clear that Rabbi Meir's *pshat* position is straightforwardly *mefaglin bechatzi matir*: a *pigul* thought on any discrete component of a *matir* act, whether first or last, creates *pigul*. Reish Lakish's rereadings, for all their ingenuity, cannot be sustained against the textual evidence.

---

## Exempt from Pigul

### Matir Exempt

The *gemara* now transitions to a new *mishnah*. The *mishnah* opens: *ve-elu devarim she-ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul* — "and these are the things about which there is no liability for *pigul*." This requires some orientation. Once a *korban* has been successfully rendered *pigul*, eating a *kezayit* of it triggers *chiyuv karet*. But not every part of the *korban* is subject to this liability. The basic rule is that *pigul* liability applies to the parts of the *korban* that are "edible" in the relevant sense — that is, parts designated for eating, whether by human beings or by the *mizbeach* (*achilas mizbeach*). This includes meat, entrails, and the like.

However, a fundamental exception applies: the *matir* itself is not subject to *pigul* liability. The very item through whose agency *pigul* was created is exempt from the resulting prohibition. The logic is that the *matir* is the agent of the *pigul* status — it is the thing that "permits" the rest, and through which the improper intention operated — but the *issur* of *pigul* does not retroactively attach to it as an object of prohibition.

The blood, for instance: a *pigul* thought during *zerikah* (the blood application) does create *pigul* for the meat of the *korban*, because the intention expressed during blood application is an intention regarding the *achilas* of the meat. Yet the blood itself, being the *matir*, is not the object of the *pigul issur*. Separately, eating blood would carry its own prohibition — but not the specific prohibition of eating *pigul*.

### Blood Kometz

The *mishnah* enumerates the items that are exempt from *pigul* liability on these grounds: the *kometz*, the *levonah*, the *ketores*, *minchas kohanim*, *minchas kohen mashiach*, and the blood. Each of these serves as a *matir* — it is the operative instrument that renders other portions of the *korban* either edible (for humans) or acceptable on the *mizbeach*. Since they are *matirim*, they are exempt from the *pigul* liability that their own activity generates for others.

The *kometz* is the handful taken from the *mincha* and burned on the altar: it permits the remainder of the *mincha* flour to be eaten by the *kohanim*. The *levonah* similarly accompanies the *mincha* and functions as a co-*matir*. The *ketores* is the incense burned on the inner altar. The *minchas kohanim* and *minchas kohen mashiach* are fully consumed on the *mizbeach* — there is no remainder to be "permitted" for eating — and so they function as *matir atzman*, permitting themselves. Blood is the paradigmatic *matir* for animal sacrifices. All of these are therefore outside the scope of *pigul* liability as objects.

### Nesachim Issue

The *mishnah* then adds another category: *ve-hanesachim ha-ba'im bifnei atzman* — the wine and flour offerings (*nesachim*) when they are brought independently, not on the same day as the animal sacrifice with which they are associated. The normal model of *nesachim* is that the wine, flour, and oil are brought together with the *korban behemah* on the day of the animal sacrifice. However, the *halacha* permits these to be brought on a later day, independently. When they are brought *bifnei atzman* — on their own, without the animal — what is the *matir* for them?

In the independent case, there is no external *matir* — no animal whose *zerikah* permits something else. The *nesachim* themselves are fully offered on the *mizbeach*, and they are considered *matir atzman* in the same sense as *minchas kohanim*: the act of bringing them to the *mizbeach* is itself the full act, permitting nothing else since there is nothing else. They therefore fall into the category of *matir* items exempt from *pigul* liability.

### Meir Chachamim

*Divrei Rabbi Meir* — this is the position of Rabbi Meir. The *chachamim*, however, extend the exemption further: *ve-chachamim omrim af ha-ba'im im ha-behemah* — even when the *nesachim* are brought together with the animal on the same day, they are still exempt from *pigul* liability. The reasoning is subtle: since in principle these same *nesachim* could have been brought on a different day — independently — they are always considered to possess the character of *matir atzman*. Even when brought alongside the animal, they could have stood alone. This theoretical independence is sufficient to classify them as *matir*-type items and exclude them from *pigul* liability, even in the case where they are in practice accompanying an animal *korban*.

The *gemara* will examine this position more closely in subsequent discussion. Here we conclude the *mishnah* at this stage.

---

---

# Zevachim 43

## Pigul Exemptions

### Opening

Daf 43 of Zevachim opens on 43a, picking up in the middle of a *mishna* that addresses which items, when consumed, carry *kares* liability due to *pigul*. The *mishna* is built around a fundamental structural principle: an offering can only become *pigul* if there exists the relationship of a *matir* — something that renders the primary item permitted — and a *nittar* — the remainder that becomes permitted through that *matir*. Where this relationship does not obtain, the status of *pigul* cannot take hold.

### Matir & Nittar

The governing principle underlying *pigul* is that every offering subject to this disqualification must have two components: the *matir*, which is the element that enables the other part to become permitted — either for human consumption or for being burned on the *mizbeach* — and the *nittar*, the thing thereby rendered permitted. If something is offered straight, with no other element serving as its *matir*, and it does not itself render something else permitted, it falls outside the framework of *pigul* entirely. Items that lack this two-stage structure are exempt from *pigul* liability.

### Mishna Items

The *mishna* opens its list of things exempt from *pigul* with the following: *ve'elu devarim she'ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul* — the following things are not subject to *pigul* liability. One who eats them has not consumed *pigul* in the halachically consequential sense.

### Kometz & Frankincense

The *mishna* begins by listing: *hakometz*, the handful of flour taken from the *mincha* offering and burned on the *mizbeach*. This *kometz* functions as the *matir* that renders the *shirayim* — the remainder of the *mincha* — permitted to the *kohanim*. Since the *kometz* is itself the *matir*, it does not become *mutar* through something else; it has no *matir* of its own. Thus, even if the *mincha* becomes *pigul* and one who eats the *shirayim* incurs *kares*, eating the *kometz* itself does not carry *pigul* liability.

Similarly, *vehaktoret* — the burning of the *ketoret* — is burned straight and does not render anything else permitted in the two-stage sense. *Vehalevona* — the frankincense — functions identically: it is burned directly on the *mizbeach* without being rendered *mutar* through something else. *Uminchat kohanim* — any *mincha* brought by a *kohen* — is burned entirely on the *mizbeach*, and since the whole offering is consumed by the altar, there is no bifurcation of *matir* and *nittar*. *Uminchat kohen mashiach* — the daily *mincha* of the *kohen gadol*, half in the morning and half in the evening — likewise follows the rule that the entire offering is burned, so it too lacks the structure required for *pigul*.

### Blood & Nesachim

*Vehadam* — the blood of a *korban* — is also listed as exempt from *pigul* liability. Blood is the *matir* of the offering: it is through the sprinkling of the blood that the meat becomes permitted. But the blood itself never becomes *mutar* through anything else. Therefore, even if one's improper intention during the blood service rendered the *korban* into *pigul*, and even though one incurs *kares* for eating the meat, eating the blood of that offering does not carry *pigul* liability. This is separate from the prohibition against eating blood altogether, which is a distinct *issur*.

The *mishna* then introduces a dispute. *Vehanesachim haba'im bifnei atzman divrei Rabbi Meir* — wine libations brought independently, i.e., when someone takes a vow to bring wine to the *mizbeach*, are exempt from *pigul* according to Rabbi Meir. His view implies, however, that *nesachim* brought together with a *korban* are subject to *pigul*, because the blood of the *korban* serves as the *matir* — it is through the sprinkling of the blood that the meat, the accompanying *mincha*, and the *nesachim* all become permitted. Thus, when brought together with the animal, the *nesachim* fall within the *matir*-*nittar* framework, and Rabbi Meir holds they are subject to *pigul*.

*Vachachamim omrim af haba'im im habehemah* — the *chachamim* dispute this and maintain that even *nesachim* brought on the same day as the animal are not subject to *pigul*. Their reasoning is that the *halacha* permits one to bring the accompanying *nesachim* on a later day, after the *korban* has already been offered. Since it is possible to bring the *nesachim* the following day, the *korban*'s blood is not the *matir* for the *nesachim* — the *nesachim* stand on their own. And if the mechanism is that the *korban* does not make the *nesachim mutar*, then even when they are brought on the same day, the logic is identical. One may be obligated to bring the *nesachim* because of the *korban*, but the *korban* does not render the *nesachim mutar*. Consequently, the *nesachim* remain independent and do not fall within *pigul*.

A parallel dispute exists regarding the *log shemen shel metzora*. A *metzora* undergoing *tahara* on the eighth day brings an *asham* and, alongside it, a *log* — approximately twelve ounces — of *shemen*. This oil is applied to the *metzora*'s ear, thumb, and other places as part of the purification process, and the *gemara* elsewhere establishes that the remainder of the *log* is eaten by the *kohanim*. The question is whether the blood of the *asham* serves as a *matir* for the *log shemen*, rendering it subject to *pigul*.

*Rabbi Shimon omer ein chayavin alav mishum pigul* — Rabbi Shimon holds that one is not liable because of *pigul* for eating the *log shemen*. His reasoning mirrors that of the *chachamim* regarding the *nesachim*: since it is possible to bring the *log shemen* on a later day after the *asham* has been offered, the blood of the *asham* is evidently not the *matir* for the *log*. Therefore, even when brought on the same day, the *korban* is not rendering the *log mutar*, and *pigul* does not apply.

*Rabbi Meir omer chayavin alav mishum pigul shedahm ha'asham matiro* — Rabbi Meir maintains that one is liable, because when the *log* is brought on the same day as the *asham*, the blood of the *asham* does serve as a *matir* for it, just as he holds that the blood of any *korban* serves as a *matir* for *nesachim* brought on the same day.

### General Principle

The *mishna* concludes by articulating the positive formulation of the rule: *vechol sheyesh lo matirin bein le'adam bein lemizbe'ach chayavin alav mishum pigul* — anything that has a *matir*, whether it is rendered permitted for human consumption or for being placed on the *mizbeach*, is subject to *pigul* liability.

---

## Matir Examples

### Olah

The *mishna* now proceeds to enumerate cases where the *matir*-*nittar* relationship does obtain, establishing that *pigul* applies. Regarding the *olah*: *damah matir et besarah lemizbe'ach ve'orah lakohanim* — the blood of the *olah* makes the meat fit to be placed on the *mizbeach* (since the meat of an *olah* is not consumed by people but burned entirely on the altar), and it simultaneously renders the hide permissible to the *kohanim* as a benefit. Because the blood functions as a *matir* for both the meat on the *mizbeach* and the hide for the *kohanim*, one who eats from the meat of a *korban* that became *pigul* would incur *kares*. The *olat ha'of* follows the same logic: *damah matir et besarah lemizbe'ach* — the blood renders the bird's meat fit for the *mizbeach*, and since there is no hide involved with a bird, the equation is simpler but structurally identical.

### Chatat HaOf

The *mishna* proceeds to the *chatat ha'of*: *damah matir et besarah lakohanim* — its blood renders the meat permissible to the *kohanim*, who eat it. The same principle could have been stated about a regular *chatat* of a *behemah*, where the blood similarly renders the meat permitted to the *kohanim*. The *mishna* states the rule in terms of the bird offering, but the logic extends to the animal *chatat* as well.

### Parim HaNisrafim

The *mishna* addresses the *parim hanisrafim* and *seirim hanisrafim* — the bulls and goats whose blood is sprinkled inside the *heichal* and whose meat is then taken outside and burned. One might have thought that in these cases there is nothing being rendered *mutar*, since the meat is not consumed either by people or by the *mizbeach* in the usual sense. Yet the *mishna* teaches: *daman matir et emureihem lekarev* — even in these cases, the blood renders the *eimurim*, the innards and fats of the offering, fit to be burned on the *mizbeach*. The *eimurim* cannot be placed on the *mizbeach* until after the blood has been sprinkled. Therefore, the blood functions as a *matir* for the *eimurim*, and one who eats the *eimurim* of such a *korban* that became *pigul* incurs *kares*.

### Rabbi Shimon

*Rabbi Shimon omer kol she'eino kemizbe'ach hachitzon kishlamim ein chayavin alav mishum pigul* — Rabbi Shimon disagrees with the application of *pigul* to the *parim hanisrafim* and *seirim hanisrafim*. His position, which appears earlier in the tractate as well, is that the *Torah* discusses *pigul* in multiple places in the context of *shelamim*, and from this he derives that only offerings processed on the outer *mizbeach* are subject to *pigul*. Since the blood of the *parim hanisrafim* is sprinkled on the inner *mizbeach*, inside the *heichal*, the critical act of the *matir* — the sprinkling of the blood — takes place at the inner altar. Even though the *eimurim* are ultimately burned on the outer *mizbeach*, because the *matir* itself is performed at the inner altar, Rabbi Shimon excludes these offerings from the category of *pigul* entirely.

---

## Ulla on Kometz

### Pigul Removed

*Amar Ulla* — Ulla states: *kometz pigul she-he'alo al gabei mizbeach paka pigulo mimenu* — if a *kometz* of a *mincha* was offered with a *pigul* intention, rendering the *mincha* disqualified as *pigul*, and that *kometz* was then placed on the *mizbeach*, its *pigul* status departs from it. The *gemara* will interrogate both the logic and the precise halachic implication of this statement.

### Matir Not Pigul

Before identifying the specific halachic ruling Ulla is communicating, the *gemara* parses his underlying reasoning. Ulla frames his point as follows: *im acherim meivi lidei pigul, hu atzmo lo kol shekein* — if the *kometz* can bring other things to *pigul*, is it not all the more so the case that it itself must be regarded as not *pigul*?

This initially seems paradoxical: the argument appears to be a *kal vachomer* in the direction of making the *kometz* itself *pigul*, yet Ulla is claiming the opposite. The *gemara* therefore clarifies what Ulla means: *im eino mitkabel, heich mevi acherim lidei pigul?* — if the *kometz* were itself regarded as having been offered improperly (as *pigul*), then the *korban* would not have been properly brought, and the *shirayim* would not have become *pigul*. For an item becomes *pigul* only once all its *matirim* have been properly offered — *hikrivu kol matirav*. The fact that the *kometz* does make the *shirayim* into *pigul* demonstrates that at some level the *kometz* itself is viewed as having been properly offered, i.e., as if it were not itself *pigul*. The *kal vachomer* thus runs in the reverse direction from what might first appear: *if* it brings the *shirayim* to *pigul*, *then* we must be treating the *kometz* as not itself *pigul*, otherwise the mechanism could not operate.

### Gemara Challenge

Having established the logic, the *gemara* asks: *mai kamashmalan?* — what is Ulla actually informing us? If his intention is to rule that one does not incur *kares* for eating the *kometz* because it is regarded as not itself *pigul*, the *gemara* responds: *tanina* — we already know this from our *mishna*. The *mishna* at the bottom of 42b explicitly lists the *kometz* among the things for which one does not incur *pigul* liability: *hakometz vehaktoret vehalevona minchat kohanim uminchat kohen mashiach uminchat nesachim vehadam*. It is worth noting that the logic of the *mishna* is somewhat different from Ulla's logic. The *mishna*'s reasoning is simply that *pigul* applies to the *nittar* and not to the *matir*. Ulla's reasoning is that we regard the *matir* as if it were not itself *pigul*, because otherwise the whole mechanism of *pigul* in the *nittar* could not function. Perhaps Ulla's reasoning serves as the explanation for the *mishna*'s ruling, but in any case the practical ruling is already stated in the *mishna*, so the *gemara* presses for what new information Ulla is conveying.

### If Removed

The *gemara* then proposes: *ela de-im alu lo yardu* — perhaps Ulla is teaching that if this *pigul kometz* was placed on the *mizbeach*, the ruling is that it need not be removed, because we regard it as if the *kometz* itself were not *pigul*. The *gemara* again replies: *tanina* — this too is already taught. A later *mishna* in the tractate establishes that items such as *lan* (meat or blood left overnight), *yotzei* (carried outside its proper boundaries), *tamei* (ritually impure), and items offered *chutz lizmano* (with out-of-time intent, i.e., *pigul*) or *chutz limkomo* (with out-of-place intent) — all of these, though they should not be placed on the *mizbeach*, if they were placed on the *mizbeach*, one does not remove them. And as the *gemara* notes, that rule has nothing to do with Ulla's specific logic about the *matir* not being *pigul*; it applies to the full range of *pesulim* as a general principle.

The *gemara* then suggests: *ve-iba'is eima de-im yardu ya'alu* — perhaps the novelty is that if such a *pigul kometz* was removed from the *mizbeach*, it should be put back, since we regard it as if it were not *pigul* at all, and therefore the proactive obligation to offer it remains. But this too the *gemara* rejects with another *tanina*: a *mishna* explicitly teaches *keshem she'im alu lo yardu, kach im yardu lo ya'alu* — just as if they went up they are not taken down, so too if they were taken down, they are not put back up. This principle explicitly includes *pigul*. So that conceptually appealing inference — that if the *kometz* is regarded as not *pigul*, it should be restored to the *mizbeach* — is directly contradicted by an established *halacha*.

### Fire Takes Hold

The *gemara* resolves the matter: *lo tzericha she-mashlah bahen ha-ur* — Ulla is speaking specifically about a case where the fire of the *mizbeach* has taken hold of the *kometz*. Rashi explains this with the phrase *na'aseh lachmo shel mizbeach* — once the fire has truly seized the item, it is transformed, and is now regarded as belonging to and consumed by the *mizbeach*. Once that transformation occurs, even if the item is taken down, it is put back up, because it is no longer viewed as the same disqualified object it was before.

The *gemara* notes that even this principle — that once the fire takes hold, the item is restored even if removed — is not new from Ulla. Ulla himself had already stated elsewhere: *lo shanu ela she-lo mashlah bahen ha-ur* — the rule that disqualified items taken down are not replaced applies only before the fire has taken hold; *aval mashlah bahen ha-ur ya'alu* — once the fire has taken hold, they are put back up even if removed. That statement applied to all categories of *pesulim*.

What, then, is Ulla's novelty here? The *gemara* concludes that Ulla is teaching a specific refinement regarding the *kometz* of a *mincha*. One might have thought that the principle of *mashlah bahen ha-ur* — fire taking hold — applies to whole units, such as a limb of a *korban*, where once the fire consumes the majority of the limb, the entire limb is regarded as transformed. But a *kometz* of flour and oil is not a single firm unit; it can be separated into pieces. One might therefore have thought that even if the fire took hold of the majority of the *kometz*, the remaining portion that was not yet burned is to be regarded as a separate entity, and the transformation does not extend to it. *Ulla* teaches otherwise: since the *kometz* was placed on the *mizbeach* as a single unit, we always regard it conceptually as a single unit. Once the fire has consumed the majority of it, the entire *kometz* is regarded as transformed — *lachmo shel mizbeach* — and if any part of it is taken down, even the unburned portion, it is to be restored to the *mizbeach*. The *chiddush* is that the scattered or fractured nature of the *kometz* does not defeat the unifying logic of *mashlah bahen ha-ur berubo*.

It is important to emphasize that this conclusion has nothing to do with Ulla's earlier reasoning about the *matir* not being itself *pigul*. The principle of *mashlah bahen ha-ur* is a general principle applicable to all *pesulim* — a *mincha* that is *tamei*, a *mincha* that is *yotzei*, any category of disqualification — and its extension to a fractured *kometz* is a halachic point about the unity of an offering placed on the *mizbeach*, not about the unique logical status of a *matir* in the *pigul* framework.

### Rav Achai

*Amar Rav Achai* — Rav Achai (whose statements are sometimes understood as of Geonic provenance) draws a further inference from Ulla's ruling. He states: *hai kometz pigul de-palgei machis ara u-palgei askei amaaracha* — consider a case where a *pigul kometz* was divided in two, with one half left on the ground of the *Beis HaMikdash* and the other, larger half (say, sixty percent) placed on the *mizbeach* and burned. *Umashlaba beih or* — and the fire has now consumed that portion. Since Ulla teaches that even when the *kometz* is in separate pieces we regard it as a single unit once the fire has taken hold of the majority, Rav Achai reasons that *maskinei lei lekulei lechatchila* — we should place the remaining half on the *mizbeach* proactively, even though it had never been on the *mizbeach* at all.

This is a somewhat difficult ruling to follow. It is one thing to say that when the *kometz* is placed as a unit on the *mizbeach* and then breaks apart, we continue to regard it as one unit, so that the fire's transformation of the majority extends to the parts that come down. But if a portion was never placed on the *mizbeach* at all, it is harder to understand why it should be regarded as part of the transformed unit. Moreover, there is a practical puzzle: if the entire *kometz* has not been offered, then strictly speaking the *matir* of the *korban* has not been fully brought, and the *korban* may not have fully acquired *pigul* status. Would it not be wiser simply not to offer the remaining portion? This line of Rav Achai does not fit smoothly within the logical framework of the *sugya*, which is perhaps why some treat his statements as Geonic additions that occasionally stand somewhat independently of the preceding *amoraic* analysis.

---

## Status Change

### Status Removed

The *gemara* transitions to a related but broader statement. *Amar Rabbi Yitzchak amar Rabbi Yochanan: hapigul vehanotar vehatamei she-he'elo legabei mizbeach paka isur meihen* — Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that if *pigul*, *notar* (leftover sacrificial meat), or something *tamei* was placed on the *mizbeach*, the *issur* departs from them. This is a significantly more sweeping claim than what Ulla said specifically about the *kometz*: it applies to all three disqualifications and states that placing the item on the *mizbeach* actually removes its prohibited status.

### Rav Chisda

*Amar Rav Chisda* — Rav Chisda challenges this sharply: *mari de-hai, mizbeach mikveh tahara?* — the master of this teaching, is the *mizbeach* a *mikveh* for ritual purification? How does placing *tamei* meat on the *mizbeach* cause it to stop being *tamei*? What is the mechanism by which the *mizbeach* removes a status of *tumah*?

### Fire Transforms

*Amar Rav Zeira: she-mashlah bahen ha-or* — the answer, says Rav Zeira, is again the principle of *mashlah bahen ha-ur*. Once the fire of the *mizbeach* truly takes hold of the item, it is transformed. It is no longer viewed as *tamei* meat or *pigul* eimurim; it has become something else entirely — an object consumed by the *mizbeach*. For the same reason that an item once transformed by fire is restored to the *mizbeach* even if taken down, so too does it no longer carry the *issur* of *tumah* or *pigul* as an eating prohibition. One who eats from it would not be liable for having consumed *tamei* meat, because the object has changed its identity.

### Tamei Meat

*Metiv Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna* — Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna challenges this from a *braita*. *Acherim omrim: v'tumaso alav, mi she-tumah porachat mimenu; yatza basar she-ein tumah porachat mimenu* — others say in a *braita* that the verse *v'tumaso alav* (which we will analyze at length in the next section) must be referring to a person, because it implies the *tumah* is temporary and can depart; this excludes meat, because *tumah* does not depart from meat. But if the position of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yochanan and Rav Zeira is correct, that fire does cause the *tumah* to depart from the meat, then the *braita*'s exclusion collapses — *tumah* would after all be capable of departing from meat, just through a different mechanism.

---

## Tumah Pesukim

### Tzav Pasuk

The discussion of *tumah* departing from meat leads the *gemara* into a sustained analysis of a *pasuk* in Tzav (Vayikra 7). The verses there read as follows: *v'habasar asher yiga bechol tamei lo yei'achel ba'esh yisaref* — meat that touches anything *tamei* may not be eaten and must be burned; *v'habasar kol tahor yochal basar* — only someone *tahor* may eat the meat. Then: *v'hanefesh asher tochal basar mizevach hashelamim asher l'Hashem, v'tumaso alav, v'nichrasa hanefesh hahi mei-ameha* — the soul that eats from the *shelamim* offering of God, and its/his *tumah* is upon it/him, that soul shall be cut off from its people.

### Tumah On Whom

The question is: does *v'tumaso alav* refer to the *tumah* being on the person eating, or on the meat itself? The *halacha* is that *kares* is incurred when the *person* is *tamei* and eats *shelamim*, whereas eating *tamei* meat carries only a negative prohibition without *kares*. But how do we know that *v'tumaso alav* is not referring to the meat? Indeed, Rashi notes that there is a grammatical argument in favor of reading it as referring to the meat: the subject *nefesh* is feminine, and the passage uses feminine verb forms — *tochal*, not *yochal*; *v'nichrasa*, not *v'nichrat*. Yet *v'tumaso alav* uses masculine forms — *tumaso* and *alav* — which grammatically correspond to *basar* (meat), a masculine noun, rather than to *nefesh*, a feminine noun. So the grammar actually seems to support that *v'tumaso alav* refers to the *tumah* of the meat, not of the person.

How then does the *halacha* learn that this verse is speaking of the person being *tamei*?

The *braita* presents several answers. The first is a *gezeira shava*: *ne'emar kan tumaso v'ne'emar lehalan tumaso* — the word *tumaso* appears here and also in another context, where a *tamei* person enters the *Beis HaMikdash* and the verse says *o tumaso bo*, clearly referring to the person being *tamei*. By *gezeira shava*, *tumaso* here likewise refers to the person.

*Rabbi Yosi* offers a different reading: *ho'il v'ne'emru kodashim bilshon rabim v'ne'emar tumah bilshon yachid, bitumas haguf hakatuv medaber* — since *shelamim* is expressed in the plural while *tumah* is expressed in the singular, the *tumah* cannot be referring to the *shelamim*, which would require a plural form; therefore it must refer to the person. This is admittedly a difficult explanation to follow — *shelamim* as a word does carry a plural-looking ending, but it refers to a single sacrifice, and in any case the subject of the *tumah* would be the meat (*basar*), not the *shelamim* as such.

*Rabbi* (Rebbi) then states: *v'achal bitumas haguf hakatuv medaber* — the word *v'achal* in the immediately following verse indicates that this is about the person being *tamei*. The *gemara* will interrogate what exactly Rebbi means by this.

### Acherim View

*Acherim omrim* — others offer yet another derivation: *v'tumaso alav, mi she-tumah porachat mimenu; yatza basar she-ein tumah porachat mimenu* — the phrase *alav* (upon him/it) implies that the *tumah* is a temporary condition, something that can depart while the subject remains intact. This can only describe a person, since a person can go to the *mikveh* and be purified while remaining the same person. Meat, by contrast, cannot be rendered *tahor* — food that has become *tamei* has no mechanism for purification while remaining itself. Therefore, *v'tumaso alav* must refer to the person, not the meat.

It is at this juncture that Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna's challenge to Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yochanan's statement gains its force: if the fire of the *mizbeach* causes *tumah* to depart from meat, then the *Acherim*'s exclusion of meat (on the grounds that *tumah* does not leave it) would be undermined.

The *gemara* first records Rava's response: *al yedei mikveh ka'aminan* — Rava says that *Acherim* are referring specifically to removal through *mikveh*. The *mikveh* can remove *tumah* from a person but not from food; fire operating on meat placed on the *mizbeach* is a different mechanism. The *gemara* challenges this immediately: *midi mikveh ksiv?* — where does the verse mention *mikveh*? The derivation from *alav* is that the *tumah* is a temporary, removable status. If one accepts that the fire of the *mizbeach* removes the *tumah*, then meat would also qualify as something from which *tumah* can depart, and the exclusion would fail.

### Ravina

*Ravina amar* — Ravina offers a more precise formulation. *V'tumaso alav, mi she-tumah porachat mimenu ke-she-hu shalem; yatza basar, davar she-ein tumah porachat ke-she-hu shalem, ela ke-she-hu chaseir* — the word *alav* implies that the *tumah* is a temporary condition on this entity, and the entity itself remains the same entity after the *tumah* departs. That is, the *tumah* can leave it while it remains *shalem* — whole and intact. This fits a person perfectly: a *tamei* person goes to the *mikveh*, the *tumah* leaves, and the same person stands there, now *tahor*. But for meat, *tumah* does not depart from the meat while it remains the same meat. If anything departs from it, it is only when the meat has been transformed — when it has changed identity, as when it is consumed by the fire of the *mizbeach*. The *tumah* does not leave the meat as it is; only when the meat becomes something else does the question of its prior *tumah* cease to be relevant. Therefore, the verse's use of *alav* cannot be referring to meat, because meat lacks the property of being something from which *tumah* can depart while the thing itself remains *shalem*. The verse must be referring to the person.

This answer is elegant and also helps clarify the underlying logic of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yochanan's original statement. When he said the *issur* departs from *tamei* items placed on the *mizbeach*, the mechanism is not that the *tumah* left the meat in the sense *Acherim* are discussing — it is that the item transformed. Ravina's formulation is thus consistent with both the *gezeira shava* of *Acherim* and the principle of *mashlah bahen ha-ur*.

---

## Braita Analysis

### Emor Pasuk

The *gemara* now turns to a parallel passage in *Emor* (Vayikra 22), which addresses *tumah* and eating *kodashim* more broadly. The relevant verses establish that a *kohen* who is *tamei* — whether from *tzaraat*, a *zav* condition, contact with a *tamei* person, or contact with a *sheretz* — may not eat from the *kodashim* until he has immersed and the sun has set. The opening verse of this section states: *kol ish asher yikrav mikol zar'achem el hakodashim asher yakdishu vnei Yisrael l'Hashem v'tumaso alav, v'nichrasa hanefesh hahi milfanai ani Hashem* — any person of your seed who approaches the holy things that Israel has consecrated to God while his *tumah* is upon him, that soul shall be cut off before Me; I am God. *Chazal* understand the *kodashim* here to include not only *korbanot* but also *ma'aser sheni* and *terumah*.

### Braita Intro

The *gemara* presents a *braita* that is, as Rava previewed, quite difficult to understand without the explanation of Rav Zeira. The *braita* reads: *im ne'emru kalim, lama ne'emru chamuros; ve-im ne'emru chamuros, lama ne'emru kalos* — if the light cases were stated, why were the weighty cases needed? And if the weighty cases were stated, why were the light ones needed? The *braita* continues: had only the light cases been stated, I would have said that for the light ones there is a negative prohibition and for the weighty ones there is *misa* (death at the hands of Heaven). The *Torah* therefore stated the weighty cases to teach that they too carry only a negative prohibition, not *misa*. Conversely, had only the weighty cases been stated, I would have said that for the weighty ones there is a negative prohibition but for the light ones there is no prohibition at all. The *Torah* therefore stated the light ones as well.

### Light & Heavy

The *gemara* asks: *mai kalos u-mai chamuros* — what are the light cases and what are the heavy cases? The *braita*'s structure requires that the conclusion be: whether light or heavy, the punishment is only a negative prohibition and not *misa*. This will prove to be the key constraint on interpreting the *braita*.

### Maaser vs Terumah

The first suggestion is that *kalos* refers to being *tamei* and eating *ma'aser*, and *chamuros* refers to being *tamei* and eating *terumah*. The *braita* would then be saying: had the *Torah* only stated the light case (*ma'aser*) with a negative prohibition, I might have thought that *terumah* (the weightier *kedushah*) would carry *misa*; the *Torah* therefore tells you that *terumah* also carries only a negative prohibition. But this is impossible: the *halacha* is that a *tamei* person who eats *terumah* does incur *misa bidei shamayim*. So the *braita* cannot be saying the punishment for *terumah* is only a *lav*. Furthermore, even the logical structure fails: if I started from *ma'aser* with a *lav*, how would I ever have thought to reach *misa* for *terumah*? The rule of *dayo lavo min hadin lihyos kenidon* — a *kal vachomer* cannot produce a conclusion more severe than its premise — would prevent me from deriving *misa* from a case that itself carries only a *lav*. So this interpretation is doubly untenable.

### Sheretz vs Meis

The second suggestion is that *kalos* and *chamuros* refer to the degrees of *tumah* rather than the food consumed: *kalos* is *tumas sheretz* (the lighter *tumah* from contact with a creeping thing) and *chamuros* is *tumas meis* (the weightier *tumah* from a corpse). The *braita* would then be teaching that whether you have a light *tumah* or a heavy *tumah*, the punishment is only a *lav*.

The *gemara* then asks: with which food are we discussing this? If the *braita* is speaking about *terumah*, then again both cases actually carry *misa*, not merely a *lav*, which contradicts the *braita*'s conclusion. And if we are speaking about *ma'aser*, the logical structure again breaks down: my starting point would be *tumas sheretz* eating *ma'aser* — a *lav*. How would I have thought that *tumas meis* eating *ma'aser* could produce *misa*? The *dayo* principle would prevent me from constructing a *kal vachomer* that reaches beyond the original case of a simple *lav*.

### Rav Zeira

Here the *gemara* delivers on Rava's earlier promise: *amar Zeiri* — it is Rav Zeira who now provides the brilliant resolution. *Kalos tumas sheretz, chamuros tumas meis* — the degrees of *tumah* are indeed the axis of *kalos* and *chamuros*, as the second proposal suggested. But here is the precise reconstruction of the *braita*'s reasoning.

Had the *Torah* stated only *tumas sheretz* — the lighter *tumah* — in connection with both *ma'aser* and *terumah* (establishing that *tumas sheretz* with *ma'aser* produces a *lav* and *tumas sheretz* with *terumah* produces *misa*), I would have had a point of departure for a *kal vachomer*. The reasoning would run as follows: a *light* form of *tumah* (*tumas sheretz*) combined with a *heavy* form of eating (*terumah*) produces *misa*. By analogy, perhaps a *heavy* form of *tumah* (*tumas meis*) combined with a *light* form of eating (*ma'aser*) should also produce *misa*, since in each case one of the two variables is at its maximum weight. The *Torah* therefore needed to state the case of *tumas meis* explicitly, to teach that even in that case — even with the heaviest *tumah* eating the lightest *kedushahma'aser* — the punishment is only a *lav*, not *misa*.

Conversely, had the *Torah* stated only *tumas meis* (the heavier *tumah*) with *ma'aser* and established that as a *lav*, I would have thought that *tumas sheretz* (the lighter *tumah*) with *ma'aser* might carry no prohibition at all — the *kal vachomer* reasoning that a lighter *tumah* is less severe and perhaps not prohibited at all when eating *ma'aser*. The *Torah* therefore stated the lighter case of *tumas sheretz* eating *ma'aser* as well, to establish that even the lighter *tumah* carries a *lav* for eating *ma'aser*.

This is a genuinely elegant solution. The *braita* is comparing two different combinations of *tumah* and food: the *kal* combination is heavy-*tumah* with light-food (*tumas meis* eating *ma'aser*), and the *chamur* combination in the background is light-*tumah* with heavy-food (*tumas sheretz* eating *terumah*, which carries *misa*). The *chiddush* of stating the *kal* combination explicitly is that I might have thought the crossing of a heavy *tumah* with a light food would also escalate to *misa*, by analogy with the crossing of a light *tumah* with heavy food. The *Torah* tells us no: it is only a *lav*. And the *chiddush* of stating the *kalos* case (*tumas sheretz* with *ma'aser*) is that I might have thought the light combination carries nothing at all. The two explicit statements are thus mutually necessary, each preventing an erroneous inference that the other alone would leave open. The daf concludes here.

---

---

# Zevachim 44

## Piggul & Matirin

### Daf Overview

Daf 44a picks up approximately ten lines into the page, at the break in the text, continuing the *mishna* that identifies which parts of the various *korbanot* are subject to *piggul* and which are not.

### Matir Concept

The *mishna* states: *kol sheyesh lo matirin bein le'adam bein la'mizbe'ach, chayavin alav mishum piggul* — anything that has something else serving as its *matir*, meaning the element that renders it permitted, is subject to *piggul*. The paradigmatic case is an animal sacrifice: the blood is the *matir*, because once the blood is applied to the *mizbe'ach*, the meat and the *emurim* become permissible — either for human consumption or for burning on the altar. The blood makes the remainder of the *korban* valid.

### Piggul Not on Matir

*Piggul* does not apply to the *matir* itself. Even when a *korban* is rendered *piggul*, one who eats the blood does not incur *kares*. It is specifically the parts of the *korban* that have a *matir* — the meat and the *emurim* — to which *piggul* applies. The *matir* itself, because it is the enabling element rather than the element enabled, stands outside the scope of this prohibition.

---

## Deriving Scope

### Shelamim Question

The *Gemara* introduces a *baraita* that traces the derivation of *piggul*'s scope from the biblical text. The *pesukim* concerning *piggul* speak specifically about a *shelamim*, so the opening question is whether *piggul* applies only to *shelamim*. The verse in question is Vayikra 7:18: *ve'im he'achol ye'achel mibasar zevach shelamav bayom hashlishi lo yeiratzeh hamakriv oto lo yeichashev lo piggul yihyeh vehanefesh haochelet mimenu avonah tisa*. Perhaps *piggul* is limited to offerings similar to *shelamim* — specifically, those eaten for two days and an intervening night. The *baraita* then asks how we extend *piggul* beyond that narrow category.

### Basar & Zevach

The first extension comes from the word *mibasar*: the phrase *mibasar zevach shelamav* is parsed so that the word *basar* — meat — functions as a broadening term. Anything that has edible remains (*she'ayarim ne'echalim*) is included. But what of the *olah*, which has no meat that is eaten? For that, the *baraita* derives from the word *zevach*: the term *mibasar zevach shelamav* contains both *basar*, covering offerings with edible remnants, and *zevach*, covering all animal sacrifices including those wholly consumed. Together, these two words extend *piggul* to all animal *korbanot*.

### Kedoshim Inclusion

The *baraita* then asks how we know to include birds, *menachot*, and the *log shemen* of the *metzora* — a far broader category. The source is *asher hem makdishim li* (Vayikra 22), which speaks of anything they sanctify. The difficulty is that this verse concerns *tumah*, not *piggul*. The *baraita* resolves this through a double *gezeira shava*: the word *chilul* links *nosar* to the *tumah* verse, and the word *avon* links *piggul* to *nosar*. Since the scope of *kodashim* by *tumah* encompasses all *korbanot*, and *nosar* shares that scope, and *piggul* is equated to *nosar*, it follows that *piggul* likewise applies to the full range of sanctified items.

### Shelamim Emphasis

If the Torah ultimately includes everything through these expansions, why does it mention *shelamim* at all? The *baraita* answers: *lomar lecha* — to tell you, the mention of *shelamim* is not to limit the scope to *shelamim* alone, but to identify a structural principle.

### Limiting Principle

The principle derived from *shelamim* is this: *piggul* applies only to something that has *matirin*, whether for human consumption or for the altar — *mah shelamim meyuchadim sheyesh lahem mattirim bein la'adam uvein la'mizbe'ach, af kol sheyesh lo mattirim bein la'adam uvein la'mizbe'ach chayavin alav mishum piggul*. The word *shelamim* does not limit the scope to those *korbanot* resembling *shelamim* in their eating period; rather, it defines the structural requirement: there must be two components, a *matir* and that which the *matir* permits. Anything satisfying this structure, across all categories of *kodashim*, is subject to *piggul*.

### Excluded Items

The *baraita* then lists what this principle excludes: the *kometz*, the *levonah*, the *ketoret*, the *minchat kohanim*, and the *minchat kohen mashiach*. These are things that are themselves the *matir* for something else, or that are wholly consumed with no remainder dependent on them. *Tosafot* raises the interesting question of whether the *kometz* is the *matir* for the *levonah* or vice versa — but in any case, both are *matirin* themselves. Similarly, the *ketoret* burned on the inner altar, the free-will *mincha* of any *kohen* that is entirely burned, and the obligatory daily *mincha* of the *kohen gadol* all fall into this excluded category. The *dam* — the blood — is likewise excluded, as it is the *matir* itself.

### Nesachim Debate

The *baraita* also excludes *minchat nesachim* — the flour, oil, and wine accompanying a *korban*. The rationale is that *nesachim* can be brought independently, even days after the animal sacrifice, and therefore they function as their own *matir*. The *mishna* records a parallel debate about *nesachim* that will be explored further: when brought together with the *korban*, is the blood of the *korban* their *matir*, or are they considered *matir es atzman* even in that circumstance?

---

## Rabbi Shimon View

### Outer Mizbe'ach

Rabbi Shimon introduces an additional criterion derived from the comparison to *shelamim*: not only must there be *matirin*, but the *matir* must be applied to the outer *mizbe'ach*, just as it is by *shelamim*. He states: *mah shelamim meyuchadim she-yeshnam al mizbe'ach ha-chizon ve-chayavin alav, af kol she-yeshnam al mizbe'ach ha-chizon chayavin alav mishum piggul*.

### Parim Exclusion

By this reasoning, *parim hanisrafim* and *se'irim hanisrafim* are categorically excluded from *piggul*. Although their *emurim* are burned on the outer *mizbe'ach*, the blood — the *matir* — is applied to the inner altar. Since the *matir* does not go on the outer *mizbe'ach* as it does by *shelamim*, Rabbi Shimon rules there is no *piggul* liability for these offerings at all: *yatz'u parim hanisrafim use'irim hanisrafim ho'il ve-ein al mizbe'ach ha-chizon ke-shelamim ein chayavin alav mishum piggul*. This ending of the *baraita* is nearly word-for-word identical to our *mishna*, and the parallel is instructive — the *mishna* codifies the conclusion while the *baraita* exposes the derivation.

---

## Bechor & K-P-K

### Bechor Query

The *Gemara* now examines the opening move of the *baraita* more closely. The *baraita* raised the possibility that *piggul* applies only to offerings eaten for two days and an intervening night, like *shelamim*. The *Gemara* asks: what offering could possibly fit that description other than a *shelamim* itself? The answer: *bechor* — the firstborn animal, which is also eaten for two days and one night and is in many ways treated similarly to a *shelamim*, though it is technically a distinct category of *korban*. So the narrow reading of the *baraita* would limit *piggul* to *shelamim* and *bechor* alone.

### K-P-K Rule

The *Gemara* then asks: if one wanted to broaden beyond just *bechor* through a *binyan av* or *mah mazinu* analogy, could that work? No — because *shelamim* have distinctive requirements not shared by other *korbanot*: the laying on of hands (*semicha*), *nesachim*, and the waving of the breast and thigh (*tenufas chaze ve-shok*). Since *shelamim* are not sufficiently similar to other offerings, an analogical extension would be vulnerable to refutation. Instead, the *baraita* relies on the *klal u-prat u-klal* principle applied to the verse *im he'achol ye'achel mibasar zevach shelamav*: *he'achol ye'achel* is a *klal*, *zevach shelamav* is a *prat*, and the closing form of the verse provides a second *klal* — thus broadening the scope to anything similar in kind to the *prat*.

### Juxtaposed Klalim

One might object: both *klalim* — the doubled language *he'achol ye'achel* — appear together before the *prat* of *zevach shelamav*, not framing it on both sides in the classic *klal u-prat u-klal* structure. The *Gemara* answers by citing the principle stated by Rava in the name of the sages of *Eretz Yisrael*: *kol makom she-ata moza shnei klalim ha-smuchim ze la-ze, hatel prat beineihem ve-donehu be-klal u-prat u-klal* — wherever you find two *klalim* adjacent to each other with a *prat* immediately following, you may rearrange them and apply the *klal u-prat u-klal* rule. The double language of *he'achol ye'achel* is thus legitimately read as two *klalim* enclosing the *prat* of *shelamim*, enabling the standard *klal u-prat u-klal* derivation that broadens *piggul* beyond *shelamim*.

---

## Log Shemen Debate

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *Gemara* identifies which Tanna authored the *baraita* cited earlier — specifically the portion that includes *log shemen shel metzora* within the scope of *piggul*. The *Gemara* states: *ha mani Rabbi Meir hi*. A separate *baraita* confirms this: *log shemen shel metzora she-chayavin alav mishum piggul divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir holds that *piggul* applies to the *log shemen* of the *metzora*. Rabbi Meir's reasoning is that the blood of the *asham* accompanying the *metzora* serves as the *matir* for the oil, just as the blood of an animal sacrifice is the *matir* for the meat. Correspondingly, Rabbi Meir applies the same logic to *nesachim*: *nischei behemah chayavin aleihem mishum piggul mipnei she-dam ha-zevach matiran likarev* — since the blood of the animal is the *matir* that permits them to be offered, *piggul* applies to them as well.

### Rabbis Counter

The rabbis challenge Rabbi Meir on both counts. With respect to *nesachim*, they demonstrate that since a person may bring his animal sacrifice today and his *nesachim* up to ten days later, the blood of the *korban* cannot be the *matir* for the *nesachim* — they stand independently. Rabbi Meir acknowledges this: *af ani lo amarti ela be-ba'im im ha-zevach* — he limited his ruling to *nesachim* that are brought together with the *korban*. The rabbis, however, maintain that even when brought together, the fact that they could come separately means they are considered *matir es atzman* in all circumstances, and are therefore excluded from *piggul*. By the same logic, the rabbis argue, the *log shemen* should likewise be excluded.

This creates a problem for the *baraita*: it appears to include *log shemen* in *piggul* while excluding *minchat nesachim*. Since Rabbi Meir includes both and the rabbis exclude both, neither position can account for the *baraita*'s split verdict.

### Rav Yosef Answer

Rav Yosef resolves the difficulty by attributing the *baraita* to a third opinion: *ha mani Rabbi hi* — this is the position of *Rabbi* (Yehuda HaNasi). Rav Yosef explains that Rabbi holds *log shemen shel metzora matnosav sharu leih* — the sprinkling actions (*matanos*) of the *log shemen* are what render the remainder of the oil permissible. This means the *log shemen* itself has two components: the sprinkling (which functions as a *matir*) and the remaining oil (which the sprinkling permits). On this view, even when the *log shemen* is brought separately without any accompanying *korban*, it retains an internal *matir*-and-remainder structure.

The textual support for this position comes from a dispute about *meilah*. The rabbis hold: *mo'alin bo ad she-yizarek ha-dam* — the *log shemen* retains *meilah* status until the blood of the *asham* is sprinkled; once the blood is applied, *lo nehenin ve-lo mo'alin* — it may not be used for benefit but no longer carries *meilah*. Rabbi, however, holds: *mo'alin ad she-yiten matnosav* — *meilah* applies even after the blood is sprinkled, until the oil itself is sprinkled. Since the act of sprinkling the oil removes the *meilah* status, it follows that the sprinkling serves as a *matir* for the remaining oil. Accordingly, Rabbi holds that even when the *log shemen* comes separately, the oil has its own internal *matir* structure — the sprinkling — distinct from anything the blood provides.

This allows Rabbi to split the vote in a way neither Rabbi Meir nor the rabbis do: like the rabbis, Rabbi holds that *nesachim*, having no internal two-part structure, are excluded from *piggul*; but unlike the rabbis, Rabbi holds that the *log shemen* does have an internal *matir* — the sprinkling — and is therefore subject to *piggul*. This is a striking resolution.

### R. Yirmiah Object

When this answer of Rav Yosef was reported before Rabbi Yirmiah, his reaction was sharp: *gavra rabba k'Rav Yosef leima ki hai milta?* — would so great a scholar as Rav Yosef give such an answer? The objection is this: if the rationale for including *log shemen* in *piggul* is that the sprinkling of the oil is its *matir*, then even when the *log* is brought alone — completely separately from the *korban*, with no blood of an *asham* in the picture — the same reasoning should apply. The sprinkling still functions as the *matir* of the remaining oil in that case, since everyone agrees *matnosav sharu leih* — the sprinkling is what permits it even then.
