Yet the *baraita* unambiguously states that there is no *piggul* for *log shemen* when brought alone: *lo shemen shel metzora chayavin alav mishum piggul mipnei she-dam matiro lebehonot divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir says that when it comes with the *korban*, the blood permits it; and when asked about bringing them separately, he concedes *afilu lo amarti ela be-va'im im ha-asham* — I only said so when it comes with the *asham*. So even Rabbi Meir acknowledges there is no *piggul* when the *log* comes alone.

But that is precisely the problem with Rav Yosef's answer. When the *log* comes alone, the sprinkling is still the *matir* for the remaining oil — yet no one says *piggul* applies in that case. If the existence of an internal *matir* through the sprinkling were sufficient to create *piggul*, it should apply when the *log* comes alone as well. The failure of *piggul* to apply in that case suggests that the mere fact of the sprinkling being a *matir* does not suffice. The distinguishing factor, it seems, is that the *log* brought alone does not function as a genuine *korban* in the full sense — notably, none of the *log shemen* is placed directly on the *mizbe'ach*.

### Abaye Reconcile

Rabbi Yirmiah's preferred answer is to take the *baraita* as straightforwardly representing Rabbi Meir's position and simply to delete the exclusion of *nesachim* from the list: *ela amar Rabbi Yirmiah le'olam Rabbi Meir hi, ve-sami mikan nesachim* — erase that line. On this reading, the *baraita* is entirely consistent with Rabbi Meir: both *log shemen* and *nesachim* are included in *piggul* when brought with the *korban*.

Abaye, however, objects to any emendation: *le'olam lo tismi* — do not erase anything. Abaye instead proposes a reread of the *baraita*'s structure. The *baraita* is not drawing a distinction between *log shemen* (included in *piggul*) and *nesachim* (excluded). Rather, it is drawing a distinction between coming *with* the *korban* and coming *without* it. When it says there is *piggul* by the *log*, it means the *log* brought together with the *asham* — and the same applies to *nesachim* brought together with their *korban*. When it says there is no *piggul* by *nesachim*, it means *nesachim* brought separately — and the same applies to *log* brought separately. The *baraita* illustrates two cases of the same Tannaitic position: with the *korban*, the blood functions as *matir* and *piggul* applies; without the *korban*, there is no *matir* from the blood and no *piggul* — whether the item in question is *nesachim* or *log shemen*.

---

## Priestly Rights

### Chatas Ha-of

The *Gemara* notes that *chatat ha'of dama matir besarah la-kohanim* — the blood of the bird *chatat* renders its meat permitted to the *kohanim* — and asks: from where do we know that *kohanim* are entitled to eat the bird *chatat*? The Torah does not state this explicitly. The source is a *baraita* taught by Levi, derived from the concluding section of Parashat Korach. Rashi notes the aptness of the context: the challenge of Korach to the *kehunah* occasioned a comprehensive reaffirmation of all priestly entitlements at the end of that *parasha*. The verse (Bamidbar 18:9) states: *zeh yihyeh lecha mikodesh hakodashim min ha'esh — kol korbanam le-chol minchasam u-le-chol chatasam u-le-chol ashamam asher yashivu li kodesh kodashim lecha hu u-le-vanecha*. The *Gemara* proceeds to derive a series of priestly entitlements from the expansive language of this verse.

### Log in Kol

The word *kol korbanam* — "all their sacrifices" — is read as including the *log shemen shel metzora*. One might have thought the *log shemen* is excluded because *min ha'esh* — "from the fire" — implies that what the *kohanim* receive must be something placed on the *mizbe'ach*, and none of the *log shemen* goes on the *mizbe'ach* directly. The Torah therefore writes *kol korbanam* to include anything that is *nikrav* — brought near — and Rashi points out that the verse in the *metzora* passage explicitly uses the language *ve-hikriv oto le-asham ve-et log ha-shemen*, applying the root of *korban* to the oil itself.

### Minchas Omer

The phrase *le-chol minchasam* — "all their meal offerings" — is read to include *minchat ha'omer* and *minchat ha-kena'ot* (the *sotah mincha*). One might have excluded these because the eating of the *mincha* is normally justified by its being *asher kupar bahem* — something that achieves atonement — whereas *minchat ha'omer* comes to permit the new grain (*le-hatir*) and *minchat kena'ot* comes to clarify whether the woman sinned (*le-varer avon ka-atya*). Since neither achieves classic *kapara*, one might have thought the *kohanim* have no entitlement to them. The Torah therefore writes *le-chol minchasam* to include them.

### Chatasam Detail

The phrase *le-chol chatasam* includes *chatat ha'of* — the bird *sin-offering*. This is the case the *Gemara* began with. One might have excluded it on the grounds that it is technically a *neveilah*, since it is not slaughtered through a conventional *shechita* but through *melikat ha-oreph* — breaking the bird's neck from the back. The Torah nonetheless includes it within the *kohanim*'s entitlement.

### Asham Types

The phrase *le-chol ashamam* — "all their guilt offerings" — is read to include *asham nazir* and *asham metzora*. The *Gemara* notes that the entitlement to *asham metzora* is actually stated explicitly elsewhere; the function of *le-chol ashamam* here is therefore to equate *asham nazir* to *asham metzora*. The basis for possible exclusion: both are brought not for classical atonement but to change the person's halachic status — the *asham nazir* reinstates a new *nezirut* (the actual purification from *tumah* being accomplished through the *parah adumah*), and the *asham metzora* is part of the purification process. Since these are not standard *kappara* offerings, one might have thought the *kohanim* have no eating entitlement. The verse teaches otherwise.

### Gezel Ger

Finally, the phrase *asher yashivu li* — "that which they return to Me" — is identified as referring to *gezel ha-ger*: the principal and added fifth that must be returned when one steals from a convert who subsequently dies without heirs. Since a convert who dies without descendants has no one to receive restitution, the money goes to the *kohanim*. The *Gemara* emphasizes that this money is fully owned by the *kohanim* — *le-kohen hu she-yehei afilu ka-rishbasa isha* — it may even be used for *kiddushin*. This stands in sharp contrast to the meat of a *chatat* or other sacrificial portions, which the *kohanim* eat but do not own. As the *Gemara* elsewhere formulates it, the *kohanim* eating sacrificial meat are eating from *mishulchan gavoa* — God's table. The host permits them to partake; the food remains His. Accordingly, if a *kohen* were to use the meat of a *chatat* as the instrument of *kiddushin*, it would not take effect. The money of *gezel ha-ger*, by contrast, belongs fully to the *kohanim* and may be used freely.

---

## R. Eliezer Parim

### Outside Acts

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraita* containing the position of Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rabbi Yose HaGlili: *piggul b'davar hane'aseh ba-chutz* — *piggul* in the context of *parim hanisrafim* applies only when both the *avoda* being performed and the improper thought concern acts and elements of the *chutz*, meaning the *azara*, the courtyard — as opposed to the *pnim*, the inner *heichal*. This is a more nuanced position than that of Rabbi Shimon, who categorically excludes *parim hanisrafim* from *piggul* altogether. Rabbi Eliezer holds that *piggul* does apply to *parim hanisrafim*, but only under a specific structural condition.

### Examples

The *baraita* provides a series of cases. If a *kohen* was standing in the *azara* performing *shechita* and declared that he was slaughtering in order to sprinkle blood on the inner altar tomorrow — *lo pigel*. Although the *avoda* being performed (the *shechita*) is in the *chutz*, the improper thought concerns an act of the *pnim* (the inner sprinkling). Since the thought is about something done inside, no *piggul* results.

Conversely, if the *kohen* was standing in the *heichal* performing the inner blood sprinkling and declared that he intends to burn the *emurim* or pour the *shirayim* tomorrow — again, *lo piggul*. The improper thought concerns outer acts, but the *avoda* being performed is an inner act. The two elements must match: both the act and the thought must concern the *chutz*.

The positive case: if the *kohen* was standing in the *azara* performing *shechita* and declared that he intends to pour the *shirayim* tomorrow or to burn the *emurim* tomorrow — *pigel*, *shemachshava ba-chutz bidavar na'aseh ba-chutz*. Here the *avoda* is outer (*shechita* in the *azara*) and the improper thought concerns outer acts (the pouring of *shirayim* and the burning of *emurim* on the outer *mizbe'ach*). Both conditions are satisfied and *piggul* results.

One nuance worth noting: whether the pouring of *shirayim* itself counts as a qualifying outer *avoda* depends on whether *shirayim* are *me'akev* — indispensable — for *chataot ha-penimiyot*; if they are not *me'akev*, they do not constitute a *piggul*-generating *avoda*. But at minimum, the *shechita* itself is performed outside, as are *kabalah* and *holachah*, giving multiple outer *avodos* through which *piggul* could be generated during the processing of a *par hanisraf*.

### Makish Source

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks: what is the scriptural basis for this limiting condition? The answer lies in the verse by the *par kohen hamashiach*, one of the *parim hanisrafim*: *ka'asher yuram mi-shor zevach hashelamim* — the *emurim* are to be treated just as the *emurim* of a *shelamim*. This verse is puzzling: the *Torah* already listed all the *emurim* of the *par* in detail. After enumerating them, why does it add "just like the *shelamim*"? There is nothing left to teach about the *emurim* themselves. Therefore, the comparison must be doing something different. The *baraita* reads it as a *makish* — an analogy — connecting the *par kohen hamashiach* to the *shor zevach hashelamim*: just as by a *shelamim* the laws of *piggul* apply only when both the acts (*ma'asim*) and the thoughts (*machshavot*) concern the outer *mizbe'ach*, so too by the *par kohen hamashiach* — and by extension all *parim hanisrafim* — *piggul* applies only when both the *avoda* being performed and the wrongful intention concern acts on the outer *mizbe'ach*.

---

## R. Eliezer Parim (II)

### Halacha

Rav Nachman rules in the name of Rabba bar Avuha in the name of Rav: *halacha ke-Rabbi Eliezer she-amru mishum Rabbi Yose* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Eliezer. *Parim hanisrafim* are not categorically exempt from *piggul*, as Rabbi Shimon held; rather, *piggul* applies to them when both the *avoda* being performed and the improper intention concern matters of the outer *azara*.

---

## Pesak Theory

### Messianic Era

Rava immediately objects: *hilchesa le-mashiacha?* Is this a ruling on a law that can only become practically relevant in the messianic era, when the Temple is rebuilt? What is the force of pronouncing a definitive *halacha* on such a matter?

### Torah Study Value

Abaye responds: *ela me'atah kol shechitas kodashim lo lisni?* Should we abandon the study of the entire tractate of *Zevachim*? None of it is currently applicable. *Ela derosh ve-kabel sachar* — study it and receive the reward; *hachi nami derosh ve-kabel sachar* — here too, study it and receive the reward. Torah study is intrinsically valuable regardless of immediate practical application.

### Relevance Concern

Rava refines his objection: *halacha kamina* — what troubles me is not the study of these laws but the specific act of rendering a formal *psak halacha*. Issuing a definitive ruling implies practical relevance. When one says "the *halacha* is like Rabbi Eliezer," the natural implication is that this determination matters — that someone might rely on it or be affected by it. If there is no context in which it could ever be applied, what does it mean to issue such a ruling? The resolution offered — that one is simply studying and receiving reward — does not entirely satisfy, because it does not explain the *phrasing* of the *halacha* as a formal ruling rather than as a theoretical position.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* addresses this tension by cataloguing a number of places in the *Gemara* where *halacha le-mashiacha*-type rulings are issued on matters exclusive to *mikdash* practice, without the *Gemara* raising any objection. *Tosafot* observes that in most of those cases, a practical application can be identified that makes the ruling relevant even today. For the handful of cases where no such application can be found, *Tosafot* offers a distinct resolution: perhaps the particular concern in our passage is not merely that the law is Temple-era, but that *piggul* by definition only arises when a *kohen* has acted wrongly — has harbored an improper intention. Issuing a *psak halacha* about a law that presupposes transgression, which is itself applicable only in the time of the Temple, invites a sharper objection than ruling on a straightforward Temple-era procedure. That combination — inapplicable in practice and arising only through wrongdoing — may be what Rava finds difficult to justify as a formal *psak*, even if the study itself remains entirely worthwhile.

---

---

# Zevachim 45

## Non-Jewish Sacrifice (II)

### Mishna Setup

The daf opens with the *mishna*, which pivots from the foregoing discussion of *piggul* to a broader set of related topics — *nosar*, *tamei*, and the question of what *halachos* apply to a distinctive category of *korban*. The *mishna* asks: what is the legal status of *kodshei ovdei kochavim* — an animal sanctified by a non-Jew for the purpose of bringing a *korban*? It is an established principle that the *Beit HaMikdash* accepts *korbanos* from non-Jews, and indeed the verse supports this. But does such a *korban* carry the full halachic status of a Jewish sacrifice?

The *mishna* states: *ein chayavin aleihem mishum piggul, nosar, ve-tamei* — one does not transgress the prohibitions of *piggul*, *nosar*, or *tamei* in connection with such offerings. Furthermore, one who slaughters such an animal outside the *Beit HaMikdash* is exempt (*patur*). This is presented as *divrei Rabbi Shimon* — the position of Rabbi Shimon.

### Kedusha Concept

The *mishna*'s ruling raises a fundamental conceptual question. On one hand, if we permit the animal to be offered on the *mizbe'ach*, we might expect it to carry the full array of halachic statuses that apply to any *korban*. On the other hand, one might frame the question differently: to what degree does a non-Jew's act of *hakdasha* generate genuine *kedusha* — the kind that produces consequences such as *piggul*, *nosar*, *tamei*, and *me'ilah*?

Two distinct framings emerge. The first is territorial or relational: how much does a non-Jew's *korban* truly *belong* in our *Beit HaMikdash*? The verse *beiti yikarei le-chol ha-amim* suggests universal access, and historically non-Jewish authorities sent sacrifices to be offered in the Temple. But one might still ask whether such an offering is an accommodation — a kind of *hutra* — rather than a full expression of the *korban*'s essential function. This framing connects naturally to the rule that *chutz la-mikdash* liability attaches only to something that fundamentally belongs inside, which is why exemption from that prohibition serves as an indicator of diminished status.

The second framing concerns *kedusha* as a halachic construct. The various statuses that attend a *korban* — *piggul*, *me'ilah*, *nosar*, *tamei* — are not simply the natural human experience of bringing an offering. They are products of a legal system that defines sanctity from within a Jewish framework. The question then becomes: can someone outside that system create this halachic status? This is not a question about spiritual worth but about legal capacity. A fascinating edge case illuminates the issue: if a Jew were to be *makdish* an animal as an *olah* on behalf of a non-Jewish friend, has a Jew created the *kedusha*, or is it the non-Jew's *korban* regardless? The *gemara* does not pose this precise question, but it sharpens the underlying conceptual tension.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

According to Rabbi Shimon, the *korban* of a non-Jew is accepted but carries a diminished status. All the prohibitions enumerated — *piggul*, *nosar*, *tamei*, the liability for *shechita* outside the Temple — do not apply. This position implicitly treats the non-Jew's offering as something permitted but not fully integrated into the *halachic* structure governing Jewish sacrifices.

---

## Braita Exclusions

### Hana'ah & Me'ilah

The *gemara* proceeds to a *braita* — a *tosefta* — that expands on the *mishna*'s ruling while following the position of Rabbi Shimon. The *braita* states: *kodshei ovdei kochavim lo nehenin ve-lo mo'alin* — one may not derive *hana'ah* from them, but if one does, there is no violation of *me'ilah*. Rabbinically, deriving benefit (*hana'ah*) is prohibited; at the Torah level, however, the formal *me'ilah* prohibition does not apply.

### Pigul, Nosar, Tamei

The *braita* continues: *ve-ein chayavin aleihem mishum piggul, nosar, ve-tamei* — the prohibitions of *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* do not apply. Adding to what the *mishna* stated, the *braita* specifies further: *ve-ein osin temurah* — the laws of *temurah* do not apply, so that if one attempts to exchange the consecrated animal for another, the second animal does not become sanctified. The *braita* then addresses *nesachim*: non-Jews may not bring *nesachim* independently, though when their *korban* is offered, it must be accompanied by *nesachim*, just as any *korban* brought on the *mizbe'ach* would be. If the non-Jew provided funds for the *nesachim*, those are used; if not, public funds cover the requirement. These distinctions — some things excluded, others required — will each be linked to *pesukim* by the *gemara*.

---

## Non-Jewish Sacrifice (II)

### Rabbi Yose Position

Rabbi Yose takes the opposing view: *roni be-chulam le-hachmir* — in all of these matters, I would rule strictly that the full halachic status applies. His reasoning derives from the very verse that establishes non-Jewish participation. The *pasuk* in *Vayikra* reads: *ish ish mi-beis Yisrael u-min ha-ger be-Yisrael asher yakriv korbano le-chol nidreihem u-le-chol nidvosam asher yakrivu la-Hashem le-olah*. The phrase *ish ish* — "any person" — is taken to include non-Jews. Strikingly, the very *pasuk* that one might least expect to extend participation to non-Jews — one that begins with *mi-beis Yisrael* — serves as the textual source for their inclusion, by virtue of the doubled *ish ish*.

Rabbi Yose then reasons: since this *pasuk* ends with *asher yakrivu la-Shem* — that they bring it "to God" — the offering is fully consecrated *la-Shem*. If the *pasuk* itself declares the offering fully dedicated to God, Rabbi Yose argues it cannot simultaneously be treated as a second-class sacrifice. The logic is straightforward: if you include them, you include them fully.

---

## Braita Exclusions (II)

### Me'ilah Distinction

The *braita* then introduces a qualification: *bameh devarim amorim — be-kodshei mizbe'ach. Aval be-kodshei bedek ha-bayis mo'alin bahen* — this applies to sacrificial *korbanos*, but when it comes to property sanctified to the Temple treasury (*kedushas bedek ha-bayis*), the laws of *me'ilah* do apply even according to Rabbi Shimon.

Rashi reads this as a continuation of Rabbi Shimon's position — not Rabbi Yose's — and it is a logically compelling distinction. The *gemara* explains: *kasavar ki gamar me'ilah cheit cheit mi-terumah dumya de-terumah de-kadish kedushas ha-guf*. The *me'ilah* prohibition is derived from *terumah* via a *gezeira shava* on the word *cheit*, and *terumah* involves *kedushas ha-guf* — an intrinsic sanctity defined by the object's designated purpose. A *korban* is sanctified for the *mizbe'ach*; *terumah* is sanctified for the *kohanim*. In both cases, the sanctity is a function of what the object *is*, not who owns it. It is in this domain — sanctity of purpose — that Rabbi Shimon argues a non-Jew cannot generate the full legal status, because the *halachic* system defining that sanctity is specifically Jewish.

But *kedushas bedek ha-bayis* is different. This is *kedushas damim* — monetary sanctity, sanctity of value and ownership. When a non-Jew transfers ownership of his property to the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *kedusha* derives from the Temple's *ownership* of that asset, not from the non-Jew's ability to confer *kedushas ha-guf*. Once the Temple holds legal title, the *me'ilah* prohibition follows automatically, regardless of who originally owned the item. Thus even Rabbi Shimon, who limits the halachic status of non-Jewish sacrificial offerings, agrees that *me'ilah* applies to *kodshei bedek ha-bayis* of a non-Jew.

---

## Torah Derivations

### Hana'ah & Me'ilah Gezeira

The *gemara* now provides the textual underpinnings for each of these exclusions. Regarding *hana'ah*: the prohibition on deriving benefit is *mi-de-rabbanan* — rabbinic in origin. There is no Torah-level prohibition violated by deriving *hana'ah* from a non-Jewish *korban*; the Sages enacted the restriction. Regarding *me'ilah*: it is excluded by a *gezeira shava* from *terumah*. The *me'ilah* violation is described using the word *cheit*, and the same word *cheit* appears in the context of *terumah* — specifically in the phrase *velo yisu alav cheit*. Furthermore, *terumah* explicitly limits itself: *velo yechalelu et kodshei bnei Yisrael*. Since *terumah* is demonstrably the domain of *Bnei Yisrael*, and *me'ilah* is learned from *terumah*, it too is limited to *Bnei Yisrael*.

### Pigul Gezeira Shavah

The exclusion of *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* follows a chain of *gezeiros shavos*. The *pasuk* governing *tumah* states: *vayinazru mi-kodshei Bnei Yisrael* — separate yourselves from the sanctified items of *Bnei Yisrael*. This *pasuk* thus limits *tumah* to the *korbanos* of *Bnei Yisrael*. From *tumah*, *nosar* is derived via the shared keyword *chilul* (both violations are described as *chilul* in their respective *pesukim*). And from *nosar*, *piggul* is derived via the shared keyword *avon* (*piggul avon avon mi-notar*). The irony is notable: the same verse that uses the phrase *Bnei Yisrael* to include non-Jews in *korban*-bringing (*ish ish*) is also the source tradition that ultimately works to limit their inclusion in these various prohibitions. Rabbi Shimon reads the inclusion as partial and governed by the many verses that specify *Bnei Yisrael* explicitly.

### Temurah Hekesh

For *temurah*, the derivation is more complex. The *parsha* of *temurah* in the Torah opens with *maaser behema*, and the *gemara* notes that *maaser behema* and *temurah* are thus linked through a *hekesh* — a juxtaposition. Furthermore, the verse *aser te-aser* is read as linking *maaser behema* to *maaser dagan*, grain tithes, and *maaser dagan* explicitly states *Bnei Yisrael*. The apparent conclusion is: *maaser dagan* establishes *Bnei Yisrael* → *maaser behema* → *temurah*, and therefore *temurah* applies only to *Bnei Yisrael*.

However, the *gemara* pauses to raise a significant methodological problem: *vechi davar ha-lamed be-hekesh chozer u-melamed be-hekesh?* — can something derived through a *hekesh* itself turn around and teach through another *hekesh*? Unlike a *gezeira shava*, which carries a special hermeneutic power allowing multi-step derivations, a *hekesh* — which works through natural textual juxtaposition rather than a shared keyword — does not permit this kind of double jump in the domain of *kodshim*. The *gemara* answers that ordinarily the rule against double *hekesh* applies when the intermediate category is *kodshim*, but *maaser dagan* is *chulin* — non-sacred produce — which permits the double step. This, however, raises a further complication: does one determine the category by *the source* of the teaching (*batar melamed azlinan*), or by *the subject* of the teaching (*batar lamed azlinan*)? If the latter, then since *maaser behema* is *kodshim*, the double jump may again be impermissible for those who hold that view.

### Maaser Behemah

The *gemara* resolves this difficulty by sidestepping the *maaser dagan* link entirely. There is a direct and simpler reason to exclude non-Jews from *maaser behema*: it is an obligatory sacrifice (*chovah*), and non-Jews were only ever included in *nedarim* and *nedavos* — vows and free-will offerings. They were never included in obligatory sacrifices. Therefore, non-Jews are self-evidently excluded from *maaser behema* without any need for a chain of derivation. And since *maaser behema* and *temurah* are linked by *hekesh* within the same *parsha*, and non-Jews are definitionally excluded from *maaser behema*, they are likewise excluded from *temurah*. *Ve-chovah she-ein la zman kavua Yisrael maasiru, ovdei kochavim lo maasiru.*

---

## Nesachim Rules

### Ezrach vs. Non-Jew

The *gemara* now turns to the *nesachim* requirement, citing the relevant *parsha* in *Bamidbar* 15 — in *Parshat Shelach*, following the *chet ha-miraglim*. The *Torah* states that when one brings a *korban* — *olah*, *zavach*, *neder*, or *nedavah* — one brings the *nesachim* along with it. The *pasuk* continues: *ve-chi yagur itchem ger* — if a *ger* dwells among you and brings a fire-offering, he does likewise. And then: *Torah achat u-mishpat echad yihyeh lachem ve-lagger ha-gar*. Before that, the *pasuk* states: *kol ha-ezrach ya'aseh kachah et elleh* — the *ezrach* brings like this. The *braita* derives: *ezrach mevi nesachim ve-ein oved kochavim mevi nesachim* — the *ezrach* brings *nesachim*, but a non-Jew does not bring *nesachim* independently.

### Nesachim Attached

One might have inferred from this that even a *korban* brought by a non-Jew is exempt from *nesachim* requirements. The *braita* answers: *talmud lomar kachah* — the word *kachah* instructs that every *korban* on the *mizbe'ach* must come with *nesachim*. Rashi notes that *kachah* is parallel to the usage *kachah ye'aseh la-par ha-echad*, specifying the manner in which a *korban* is brought. The upshot is clear: a non-Jew cannot bring *nesachim* as a standalone offering, but when he brings an animal *korban*, the *korban* itself demands *nesachim* — whether funded by the non-Jew or by public Temple resources.

---

## Ritzuy Tzitz

### Blood Tamei Case

The *gemara* introduces a *braita* concerning a different topic with a parallel Jew–non-Jew distinction: the *ritzuy tzitz*, the capacity of the *Kohen Gadol*'s *tzitz* to render acceptable a *korban* whose blood became *tamei*. The *braita* states: *dam she-nitma ve-zarko be-shogeg — hurtzah; be-meizid — lo hurtzah*. If blood that had become *tamei* was sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach* unknowingly, the *korban* is accepted — that is the principle of *ritzuy tzitz*, rooted in the verse that the *tzitz* atones for *tumot Bnei Yisrael*. But if it was done knowingly, the *gemara* explains that while *mi-ikar ha-din* the *tzitz* might technically render the *korban* acceptable, the Sages ruled as a *kenas* that in the case of knowing transgression, the owner may not eat the meat. Importantly, it does not mean another *korban* must be brought — that would raise the issue of *chulin ba-azara* if the first in fact worked — but the practical consequence is that the meat is forbidden *mi-de-rabbanan*.

By contrast, for a communal *korban*, the *tzitz* is *meratze* both *be-shogeg* and *be-meizid* without restriction.

### Non-Jew Ritzuy

The *braita* then states: for a *korban* of a non-Jew — *bein be-shogeg bein be-meizid lo hurtzah* — neither knowingly nor unknowingly does the *tzitz* render it acceptable. The Rabbis raised this before Rav Pappa: is this ruling consistent only with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that non-Jewish *korbanos* lack full status? For Rabbi Yose, who grants them full status and rules strictly on all counts, the *ritzuy tzitz* should presumably apply. Rav Pappa responded: *afilu teima Rabbi Yose* — even according to Rabbi Yose the *tzitz* does not work here, because a distinct verse limits it: *le-ratzon lahem lifnei Hashem* — the *tzitz* creates *ratzon* for *them*, meaning *Bnei Yisrael*.

### Rav Ashi Resolution

Rav Huna son of Rav Nassan challenged Rav Pappa: if we use the word *lahem* to exclude non-Jews, we face a problem. The very *pasuk* that permits non-Jews to bring *korbanos* contains the phrase *asher hem makdishim li* — "that *they* sanctify to Me." If *hem* there does not exclude non-Jews from bringing *korbanos* in the first place, how can *lahem* elsewhere exclude them from *ritzuy tzitz*? One cannot simply invoke a pronoun as an exclusionary force in one context when the same grammatical structure is used inclusively elsewhere.

Rav Ashi provides the resolution: the exclusion of non-Jews from *ritzuy tzitz* does not rest mechanically on the word *lahem* as a pronoun. Rather, *le-ratzon lahem lifnei Hashem* expresses a substantive idea: the *ritzuy* achieved by the *tzitz* is grounded in a particular relationship — *lahem* — between *Bnei Yisrael* and God. The *gemara* articulates this as: *ve-ovdei kochavim lav bnei hartzah ninhu*. The concept of *ritzuy* — of the sacrifice being favorably received — is tied to the unique covenantal relationship expressed through the *avodah* of *Bnei Yisrael*. The *tzitz*, as part of the *bigdei kehunah*, and the entire apparatus of *ritzuy* it achieves, is anchored in that relationship.

It should be noted that one need not read this as a sweeping theological statement that God does not accept prayer or sacrifice from non-Jews — after all, *Noach* brings *korbanos* and they are clearly accepted. The more precise reading is that this specific mechanism of *ritzuy* — the formal *ritzuy* achieved by the *kohen gadol*'s *tzitz* as part of the Temple's *avodah* system — operates within the framework of *Bnei Yisrael*'s covenantal service and is not extended to non-Jewish *korbanos*. Nevertheless, the *gemara*'s language — *lav bnei hartzah ninhu* — is broader than this narrow reading strictly requires.

One additional conceptual observation is worth noting in this context. A student raised the question of whether the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yose might be understood as focusing on different axes: Rabbi Shimon focusing on the *gavra* — the person behind the offering — and Rabbi Yose focusing on the *cheftza* — the object, the animal itself. If Rabbi Yose treats the animal as simply an object that has been sanctified and placed on the *mizbe'ach*, then distinctions based on the offerer's identity become less operative. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, may be more attentive to who stands behind the act of *hakdasha* and whether that person's relationship to the *Beit HaMikdash* is such that they can generate the full legal status. This reading resonates with a broader observation about the halachic literature on *korbanos*: the Talmud tends to focus on the technical acts of the *kohanim* rather than on the identity and intent of the offerer, and the dispute here may partly reflect that tension.

---

## Piggul Mishna

### Piggul Exclusions

The *mishna* now addresses a different question: which items are excluded from *piggul*? The *mishna* states: *devarim she-ein chayavin aleihem mishum piggul, chayavin aleihem mishum nosar mishum tamei*. Things that are themselves *matirim* — such as the *kometz*, *levonah*, and *dam* — are not subject to *piggul* (this was established earlier). But one who eats them in a state of *tumah* or leaves them past their time (*nosar*) does transgress those prohibitions. The one exception is *dam*: *chutz min ha-dam* — blood is excluded from *nosar* and *tamei* as well, for reasons to be worked out in the *gemara*.

### Rabbi Shimon Edible

Rabbi Shimon adds a further qualification: *Rabbi Shimon mechayev be-davar she-darko le-echol* — Rabbi Shimon holds one liable only for things that are customarily eaten. He does not dispute the exclusion of *dam*, but he does dispute whether *tamei* and *nosar* apply to *levonah*, *ketoret*, and wood, which are not eaten. The *mishna* thus records his view: *aval etzim ve-levonah ve-ketoret ein chayavin aleihem mishum tumah* — one who is *tamei* and comes into contact with these non-edible sanctified items, or who retains them past their time, does not thereby transgress. The violations of *tamei* and *nosar* require that the object be of the kind normally consumed.

---

## Tamei Scope

### Kal VaChomer

The *gemara* now interrogates the scope of *tumah*. The *mishna* has implied that *tumah* applies even to items that are not subject to *piggul* — specifically, to *matirim* such as *kometz* and *levonah*. But the *gemara* asks: why not confine *tumah* to the same scope as *piggul*? A *kal va-chomer* is constructed:

*Piggul* is stringent in several respects: it requires a *korban chatas kevuah* (a fixed-value sin-offering), only one act of awareness is required (*yedia achas*), and it has no exceptions — it is never *hutar mi-kelalo*. Despite all this stringency, *piggul* applies only to something that has a *matir* — both a *matir* for human consumption and a *matir* for the *mizbe'ach* (*bein le-adam bein le-mizbe'ach*). If *tumah* is lighter — it requires a variable-cost offering (*oleh ve-yored*), demands prior and subsequent awareness (*shtei yedios*), and is sometimes suspended in public circumstances (*tumah hutrah be-tzibur*) — then certainly *tumah* should have no broader scope than *piggul*. By a *kal va-chomer*, *tumah* should likewise apply only to items with a *matir*.

### Asher Hem Makdishim

The *gemara* answers from a verse in the *parsha* of *tumah*: *vayinazru mi-kodshei Bnei Yisrael asher hem makdishim li* — separate from the sanctified items that they dedicate to Me. The phrase *asher hem makdishim li* is deliberately broad — "all things that they sanctify to Me." This overrides the *kal va-chomer* and expands the scope of *tumah* to include any sanctified item, regardless of whether it has a *matir* in the manner required for *piggul*.

### Yikrav Requirement

One might then think *tumah* applies from the moment of *hakdasha* — from the instant an item is sanctified. The *gemara* corrects this by citing a further verse: *kol ish asher yikrav mi-kol zarachem el ha-kodashim asher yakdishu Bnei Yisrael la-Hashem ve-tumaso alav* — the word *yikrav* indicates that liability attaches only when the item is *fit* to be offered, not from the mere moment of sanctification. Rabbi Elazar clarifies: *yikrav* cannot be read literally as "touching" (there is no known *kares* liability for merely touching a sanctified item while *tamei*). Rather, *be-muchshar basar li-krav ha-katuv medaber* — the verse speaks of when the item is fit to be offered on the *mizbe'ach* or consumed by those entitled to eat it.

### Matirim Threshold

For items that have a *matir*, the threshold is straightforward: *mi-she-yikrevu matiraiv*. The *korban*'s meat and entrails become fit for eating or the *mizbe'ach* only once the blood has been sprinkled. Correspondingly, one who is *tamei* and eats the meat is not liable until after the *zrikat ha-dam* has occurred. Before that point, the meat is not yet in the state of *muchshar li-krav*, and there is no *kares* liability for consuming it while *tamei*.

### Kli Sharet Threshold

For items that have no *matir* — such as *kometz*, *levonah*, *ketoret*, or *minchat kohanim* — there is no analogous act of *zrika* to render them fit. What makes these items fit for the *mizbe'ach* or for their proper use? The *gemara* answers: *mi-she-yikdash be-kli* — once they are placed in a *kli sharet*, a sacred service vessel. It is this act that renders them fully fit to be offered. Therefore, one who eats such an item while *tamei* is liable only once it has been sanctified through a *kli sharet*. This is the *yikrav* threshold for this category.

---

## Nosar Scope

### Chilul vs. Avon

The *gemara* now turns to *nosar* and asks whether it follows the broad scope of *tumah* or the narrow scope of *piggul*. The chain of derivation that excluded *piggul* and *nosar* from non-Jewish *korbanos* (discussed earlier) also implied that *nosar* and *piggul* are related — *nosar* was linked to *piggul* via the *gezeira shava* of *avon-avon*. Now the *gemara* raises the competing possibility: *nosar* appears in its *parsha* with the word *chilul*, and *tumah* appears in its *parsha* with the word *chilul*. Should we therefore link *nosar* to *tumah* via *chilul-chilul*, giving it the broad scope? Or should we link *nosar* to *piggul* via *avon-avon*, giving it the narrow scope?

This is a genuine *gezeira shava* conflict: *nosar* shares *chilul* with *tumah* and *avon* with *piggul*. How do we resolve which linkage governs? The *gemara* raises the possibility that there are more points of similarity between *nosar* and *piggul* than between *nosar* and *tumah*, which would argue for linking *nosar* to *piggul*. The common features of *nosar* and *piggul* include: neither is *hutar be-tzibur*; the *tzitz* works for *tumah* but not for either *nosar* or *piggul*; both *nosar* and *piggul* are time-related (one conceptually, one factually); and both apply to the *object* consumed, whereas *tumah* is a status of the *person*. On this count, the similarities tilt toward *piggul*. If so, *nosar* should have *piggul*'s narrow scope and not apply to *matirim*.

### Double Lamed

The *gemara* resolves the tension by appealing not to the *gezeira shava* comparison but to an internal reading of the *pasuk* governing *tumah* itself. Levi teaches: *minayin she-af be-psul zman ha-katuv medaber? Talmud lomar ve-lo yechalelu* — the doubled *lamed* in *ve-lo yechalelu* signals two forms of *chilul*. The *pasuk* does not merely govern *tumah*; it is formulated to encompass another category of *chilul* as well. That second *chilul* is *nosar* — *psul zman*, the disqualification through time. Accordingly, *nosar* is included within the same *pasuk* that establishes *tumah*'s broad scope, and derives its scope from there directly — not via the *chilul-chilul gezeira shava* from *tumah*, which would face the competing *avon-avon* derivation from *piggul*, but via the doubled *lamed* in the *pasuk* itself, which independently includes *psul zman*.

### Nosar Conclusion

The upshot is that *nosar* does not derive its scope by comparison to *piggul* or by a contested *gezeira shava*. Instead, the *pasuk* that establishes *tumah*'s broad scope — *velo yechalelu* — simultaneously establishes through its doubled *lamed* that *nosar* shares that same broad scope. Both *nosar* and *tumah* therefore apply to a wider range of items than *piggul*, including those without a *matir* in the *piggul* sense, subject to the *yikrav* threshold: the item must be fit for offering, whether through the completion of its *matirim* or through placement in a *kli sharet*.

---

---

# Zevachim 46

## Piggul Overview

### Daf Overview

Today's daf begins two lines from the top, continuing the discussion of the *Mishnah*'s treatment of categories that invalidate a *korban*. The organizing theme is *piggul* — the disqualification of a sacrifice through improper intent regarding the time of consumption or burning — alongside two related categories: *notar* (sacrificial meat left past its permitted time, the consumption of which carries *kares*) and *tumah* (the prohibition, likewise carrying *kares*, of eating *kodashim* while ritually impure). All three categories share the common feature that violating them subjects one to *kares*, the divine punishment of excision.

### Piggul vs Notar/Tumah

The critical distinction introduced here is one of scope. *Piggul* applies only to the body of the sacrifice — to what is eaten or burned — but not to the *matir*, the enabling agent that renders the sacrifice valid. The *dam* (blood), the *kometz* (the handful of flour), the *levonah* (frankincense), and similar items are *matirim*: they are what "permit" the remainder of the offering, whether for human consumption or for the altar. *Piggul* cannot apply to the *matir* itself. By contrast, *notar* and *tumah* have a broader application. They do apply to the *matir*, as we learned from yesterday's discussion, derived from the inclusive language of *asher yakdishu b'nei Yisrael* and *asher heim makdishim li*, which is read expansively to encompass these enabling elements.

### Blood as Matir

The blood, however, stands in its own category. Even though *dam* is itself the *matir* — the very thing upon which the entire *korban* rests — it is not included in the extended application of *notar* and *tumah*. If blood left over were eaten, there is certainly a *kares* for eating blood, but there is no additional *kares* for *notar* on account of the blood, and no additional *kares* for *tumah*. The practical *nafka mina* (legal difference) would manifest, for example, in whether one must bring multiple *korbanot chatat* for inadvertent violations, or incur multiple sets of lashes if warned. The question the *Gemara* now takes up is: what is the source for this exclusion?

---

## Three Verses on Dam

### Ulla's Drasha

*Amar Ulla amar kra*: the verse states, *v'ani nasati lachem al hamizbeach l'chaper* — "and I have given it to you upon the altar to atone" (Vayikra 17:11). The *drasha* reads *lachem* — "to you" — as implying *shelachem yehei*, it is yours. Since God declares the blood to be given over as it were to you, it does not fully belong to the sacred domain in the sense that would generate *me'ilah*. As *Rashi* notes, this *drasha* was originally articulated in a different context, to establish that there is no *me'ilah* by blood. The *Gemara* will show that we have three separate verses that exclude the blood from *me'ilah*, and from there the *Gemara* derives that all three exclusions are being put to work: one for *me'ilah*, one for *notar*, and one for *tumah*.

It is worth pausing to appreciate the striking theological irony here. The blood is not merely an element of the *korban* — it is, in the *Gemara*'s understanding, the sole agent of atonement. Rabbinic tradition insists, against what one might read from the narrative passages of the *Torah* with their emphasis on the *reiach nichoach* and the smoke rising heavenward, that the *korban* is fundamentally about the blood. The verse *v'ani nasati lachem al hamizbeach l'chaper* is itself the basis for that insistence. And yet it is precisely this verse that serves to remove the blood from the domain of *me'ilah* — to say that it is "yours," not fully consecrated in the technical sense. The one element without which the *korban* has no validity is the one element to which the most severe categories of sacred-property law do not adhere. Perhaps, as one might suggest, this connects to the idea of *ki hadam hu hanefesh*: if blood represents the life-force itself, it partakes of a different order than the merely physical components of the sacrifice, and therefore the technical statuses that adhere to physical sacred matter do not apply to it.

### Beis Yishmael

*Dvei Rebbi Yishmael tana amar kra*: a separate *drasha* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael is brought on the word *l'chaper*. The verse gives the blood *l'chaparah*, for atonement, but not for *me'ilah* — *l'chaparah nasativ v'lo l'me'ilah*. It is designated to achieve atonement; transgressing its sanctity through benefit (*me'ilah*) is simply not within its scope.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan offers a third approach, based on the verse *ki hadam hu banefesh yechaper* (Vayikra 17:11): *hu lifnei chaparah ke'achar chaparah* — the blood has the same legal status before it achieves atonement (i.e., before it is placed on the altar) as after it achieves atonement. Since after the blood is placed on the altar there is no *me'ilah*, the same is true before it is placed on the altar.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this reasoning: why does it follow that after the blood is on the altar there is no *me'ilah*? Why not read the equation in reverse — since normally items designated for a *korban* carry *me'ilah* before their function is performed, perhaps the verse is equating the two and saying that even after the blood is placed on the altar, *me'ilah* still applies? *Eima le'achar chaparah kelifnei chaparah: ma lifnei chaparah yesh bo me'ilah af le'achar chaparah yesh bo me'ilah.*

The *Gemara* answers with a general principle: *ein lecha davar shena'aseit mitzvato umo'alin bo* — there is nothing, once its *mitzvah* is completed (*ne'aseit mitzvato*), regarding which *me'ilah* still applies. This principle has a clear logic. *Me'ilah* by items designated for the altar — *kodshei mizbeach* — is not simply a matter of appropriating Temple property (which is the character of *me'ilah* by *bedek habayit*). It is rather a matter of diverting a sacred object from its designated purpose. Once that purpose is fulfilled, the object's sanctified designation is, as it were, exhausted, and the prohibition of *me'ilah* no longer applies. An analogous principle operates with respect to *chametz* that one has fulfilled the *mitzvah* of burning: once burned, it is no longer *asur behana'ah*, because *ne'aseit mitzvato* — its designated fate has been accomplished.

---

## Ne'asita Mitzvato

### Principle Explained

The general principle that once a *mitzvah* is complete *me'ilah* no longer applies is established here as the background rule. With respect to blood, once it is placed on the altar — *ne'aseit mitzvato* — there is certainly no *me'ilah*, and Rabbi Yochanan's verse establishes that the same is therefore true even before it reaches the altar.

### Three Exceptions

The *Gemara* immediately challenges the universality of the *ne'aseit mitzvato* principle: *ve-harei trumat hadeshen* — what about the removal of the ashes? The *Torah* prescribes that the *kohen* remove a portion of the ashes from the outer altar and place them beside the eastern side of the ramp (*vesamo etzel hamizbeach*). Once this act is performed, the *mitzvah* is complete. Yet the *drasha* derived from the word *vesamo* — "and he shall place them there" — establishes that they must remain there and may not be put to any other use. Here is a case of *ne'aseit mitzvato* where the prohibition endures afterward.

The *Gemara* answers: *mishum dehavah trumat hadeshen u'bigdei kehunah shnei ketuvim habaim ke'echad* — because we have two exceptional cases: *trumat hadeshen* and the priestly garments worn by the *kohen gadol* on *Yom Kippur*. Regarding the latter, the verse says *vehinicham sham* — "and he shall leave them there" — indicating that these garments may not be reused. The rule of *shnei ketuvim habaim ke'echad ein melamdin* applies: when the *Torah* needs to spell out a rule in two separate places, it signals that those are exceptions, not illustrations of a general principle. Thus the *ne'aseit mitzvato* rule stands for everything else, including blood.

The *Gemara* notes the substance of the *bigdei kehunah* case further: the standard rabbinic view is that the *kohen gadol*'s *Yom Kippur* garments require *genizah* (burial), which implies that *me'ilah* continues to apply to them even after the service. The dissenting view of Rabbi Dosa holds that they may actually be used by an ordinary *kohen*, provided they are not worn on another *Yom Kippur* — the restriction being that each *Yom Kippur* must be served with its own unique set of garments, a principle in its own right.

### Debate on Exceptions

The *Gemara* then considers: if one follows Rabbi Dosa and does not accept *bigdei kehunah* as an independent case of *ne'aseit mitzvato* where the prohibition endures, then we have only one exception (*trumat hadeshen*), and perhaps the principle of *ne'aseit mitzvato* is not well established enough to serve as the background rule from which we derive the status of blood. The *Gemara* responds that even according to Rabbi Dosa, there is a second exception: *eglah arufah*. By the calf whose neck is broken in the valley (*ve'arfu sham et ha'eglah banachal*), the *Torah* uses the same word *sham* to indicate that it must be left there and may not be used for any benefit. Though *eglah arufah* is not technically a case of *me'ilah* — it is not a *korban* — it is a case of a sacred act (*mitzvah*) whose completion does not dissolve the object's prohibited status. The *Gemara* broadens the principle accordingly: there are things where the *ne'aseit mitzvato* rule does not dissolve their prohibited status, but these are clearly marked as exceptional. Therefore, blood follows the general rule.

### Resolution via Extra Let…

The *Gemara* then addresses a further refinement. The principle of *shnei ketuvim habaim ke'echad ein melamdin* — that two isolated verses are not applied broadly — is itself debated. According to the view that *ein melamdin* requires two verses, the two we have (*trumat hadeshen* and *eglah arufah* under Rabbi Dosa) suffice to prevent generalization, and blood is confirmed as following the rule. But according to the view that three verses are needed before one stops generalizing (*melammadin* — two verses can still establish a rule), we need all three cases — *trumat hadeshen*, *bigdei kehunah*, and *eglah arufah* — to prevent the principle from being applied to blood.

The *Gemara* resolves this through *trei mi'utei ketivi* — there are two extra letters in the relevant verses that mark these cases as uniquely exceptional. By *eglah arufah* the verse writes *ha'arufah* (with the definite article *heh*), marking that broken-necked calf specifically. By *trumat hadeshen* the verse writes *vesamo* (with the full form *vav-shin-mem-vav*), not merely *vesham* — the fuller form signals exclusivity. These textual markers establish that those cases, and only those cases, retain their prohibited status after *ne'aseit mitzvato*. Blood therefore follows the general rule without exception.

We thus have three biblical sources establishing that there is no *me'ilah* by blood: (1) *v'ani nasati lachem* — it is given to you, implying *shelachem yehei*; (2) *l'chaparah nasativ v'lo l'me'ilah* — it is given for atonement, not for *me'ilah*; and (3) *hu lifnei chaparah ke'achar chaparah* — the equation of before and after the altar, combined with the *ne'aseit mitzvato* principle. These three verses in turn serve the additional purpose of excluding blood from *notar* and from *tumah*: one verse for each category.

It is worth noting that *Tosafot* here raises a genuine difficulty. There is a *Gemara* elsewhere that discusses the blood of sacrifices being channeled through a conduit out to *Nachal Kidron*, where it was sold as fertilizer, and that passage implies that *me'ilah* did apply to that blood before it was formally redeemed. *Tosafot* offers several answers — among them the possibility that that *me'ilah* was only *derabbanan* — but the tension is worth noting and the matter is not entirely resolved.

---

## Three Verses on Tumah

### Three Verses Purpose

Having established the three exclusions for blood, the *Gemara* now turns to a related set of three verses, cited by Rabbi Yochanan, dealing with *tumah* and *kares*. Why are three separate verses in the *Torah* needed to establish that one incurs *kares* for eating *kodashim* while *tamei*?

The relevant passages are: twice in Vayikra 7 (verses 20 and 21), and once in Vayikra 22 (verse 3), all relating to the *shelamim* and to *kodashim* more broadly. The verse at 7:20 — *v'hanefesh asher tochal basar mizevach hashlamim asher l'Hashem v'tumaso alav v'nichresa hanefesh hahi mei'ameha* — deals with one who is *tamei* eating from the *shelamim*. The adjacent verse at 7:21 — *v'nefesh ki tiga b'chol tamei... v'achal mizevach hashlamim asher l'Hashem v'nichresa* — similarly refers to a person who has come into contact with various sources of *tumah*. And the verse at Vayikra 22:3 — *kol ish asher yikrav mikol zar'achem el hakodashim asher yakdishu v'tumaso alav v'nichresa* — uses more general language about *kodashim*.

The answer given is: one verse establishes the principle for *shelamim*; one repeats the point by *shelamim* in a way that — following the rule of *davar shehayah bikhlal veyatza min haklal lilamed* — signals that the *halacha* applies to all sacrifices, not only *shelamim*; and a third verse establishes that the prohibition applies even to things that are *einam ne'echalim*, inedible items offered on the altar — the *ketores*, the *kometz*, and similar items. This last extension is a considerable *chiddush*: one would incur *kares* for eating in a state of *tumah* something that is itself inherently inedible.

### Rabbi Shimon Exemption

But the *Mishnah* we encountered yesterday included Rabbi Shimon's dissenting position: *mechayyev b'davar shedarko le'echol* — Rabbi Shimon holds that *kares* for eating *kodashim* while *tamei* applies only to things normally eaten, not to inedible items. So for Rabbi Shimon, the third verse cannot be serving to include inedible items. What then is the third verse teaching? The *Gemara* answers: *l'asuyei chatas hapnimiyot* — to include the inner *chatat*, whose blood is applied to the inner altar rather than the outer one. One might have thought that since Rabbi Shimon excludes the inner *chatat* from *piggul* (because its blood does not go on the outer *mizbeach* as the *shelamim*'s does), the same exemption would extend to *tumah*. The third verse therefore comes to establish that even according to Rabbi Shimon, one incurs *kares* for eating the inner *chatat* while *tamei*.

### Amoraim Debate

The *Gemara* now presents two versions of an *Amora'ic* debate — reported in one version by Rav Tavyumi and in another by Rav Kahana — concerning the exact scope of the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Chachamim*.

The debate turns on two distinct situations: *tumat haguf* (the person himself is *tamei*) and *tumat basar* (the sacrificial meat itself is *tamei*). For the latter case there is a separate verse — *v'habasar asher yiga b'chol tamei lo ye'achel* (Vayikra 7:19) — and the *drasha* reads the *vav* of *v'habasar* as inclusive, expanding the prohibition to cover even inedible items (*eitzim u'levonah*). There is therefore more textual basis to argue that the prohibition when the *basar* is *tamei* applies even to inedible things.

One position in the *Amora'ic* debate holds: *machloket b'tumat basar* — the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *Chachamim* is specifically about *tumat basar*, where the *drasha* might extend the prohibition to inedible items. But *b'tumat haguf divrei hakol ein loke* — when it is the person who is *tamei*, there is no textual basis to extend the prohibition to inedible items, and even the *Chachamim* would agree with Rabbi Shimon that one is exempt.

The other position holds: *k'machloket b'zo kach machloket b'zo* — the same debate applies to both scenarios. The reasoning is that the two *pesukim* are juxtaposed and interconnected: *keivan d'karinan bei v'habasar asher yiga b'chol tamei* to include inedible items, *karinan bei v'tumaso alav* — the adjacent verse about personal *tumah* is thereby linked, and the same extension follows in both directions.

The same structure appears in reverse in Rav Kahana's version, where the question is which case Rabbi Shimon — the one exempting — is speaking about. One version says Rabbi Shimon exempts only in the case of *tumat haguf*, while even he would agree that when the *basar* is *tamei* one incurs *malkot* because of the explicit *drasha* on that verse. The other version again holds *k'machloket b'zo kach machloket b'zo*.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava rules: *mistabra k'man d'amar k'machloket b'zo kach machloket b'zo* — it stands to reason that the two cases rise and fall together. His reasoning is the mirror image of the argument above: *keivan d'lo karinan bei v'tumaso alav v'nichresa, lo karinan bei v'habasar asher yiga b'chol tamei lo ye'achel* — since Rabbi Shimon reads the verse about personal *tumah* as not extending to inedible things, he similarly reads the verse about the *basar*'s *tumah* as not extending there. The two are textually linked, and Rabbi Shimon's exemption encompasses both.

The *Gemara* then raises a final difficulty: how can Rabbi Shimon exempt in the case of *tumat basar* given the classic *drasha* that *v'habasar* includes *eitzim u'levonah*? The answer: *psula b'alma* — that inclusion yields only a rabbinic-level prohibition, not a biblical one. Intrinsically, the idea of transgressing through eating something inedible is conceptually strained. One might suggest in passing that the framework borrowed from elsewhere in the *Gemara* — comparing *achilat mizbeach* with *achilat adam* — could be relevant: what the altar "consumes" might in some sense be considered "eaten" even if a human cannot literally eat it. But as the *Gemara* stands, Rabbi Shimon does not recognize a biblical-level prohibition in such a case.

---

## Six Intentions

### Six Intentions Listed

We now arrive at the *Mishnah* that opens a new section of the perek. One might argue that this *Mishnah* — or the entire following chapter of *Eizehu Mekoman* — ought to have come first in the tractate, as it lays out the basic affirmative framework for how a *korban* is properly offered. The placement of this foundational material after all the discussions of invalidity reflects the *Gemara*'s orientation toward the rabbinic class rather than the uninitiated: the interesting cases of disqualification are treated first, and the basic rules follow.

*Leshem shisha devarim hazevach nizbach* — the sacrifice is offered with six things in mind. The *Mishnah* lists: *leshem zevach* — that it should be sacrificed as the right type of *korban* (an *olah* should not be intended as a *shelamim*, which connects to the *Mishnah*'s opening discussion of *shinui shemo*); *leshem zoveach* — for the sake of the owner (*shinui be'alim*); *leshem Hashem* — with awareness that it is being offered to God; *leshem ishim* — with awareness that part of it will be offered on the fire of the altar; *leshem reiach* — with the intent that smoke will rise; and *leshem nichoach* — that it should be a pleasing offering.

The final two items on this list mark a notable shift in the texture of the discussion. The *Mishnah* here is operating in a different register than the technical-halachic discussions of blood, *piggul*, and *me'ilah*. These intentions speak to the relational dimension of offering a sacrifice: the consciousness of the offerer, the direction toward God, the desire that the offering ascend and please. The stories of sacrifice throughout the *Torah* — *vayarach Hashem et reiach hanichoach* — live here. The *Chachamim* acknowledge this dimension, even as they situate it as secondary to the strictly operative elements of *lishma* and *leshem be'alim*. The tractate has, in effect, kept the relational framing in reserve, and now presents it — but only briefly, before returning to the technical.

*Vechattat ve'asham leshem cheit* — and the *chattat* and *asham* must be brought with conscious intent toward the specific sin for which they atone.

### Rabbi Yose's Position

Rabbi Yose offers a broad qualification: *af mi shelo hayah belibo leshem echad mikol elu kasher* — even one who had none of these six things consciously in mind, the sacrifice is nonetheless *kasher*. The basis: *shehu tenai beit din* — it is a standing stipulation of the court (a *tenai beit din*) that this is so. And further: *she'ein hamachshavah holeches ela achar ha'oved* — the *machshavah* follows only the one performing the service.

The relationship between these two clauses is not immediately obvious, and *Rashi* reads the second clause as a somewhat independent addendum: not only is *stam lishmah* acceptable, but even if the owner had a wrong intent, that does not invalidate, because the operative *machshavah* is that of the *kohen*, not the owner.

### Alternative Readings

Two alternative readings are worth examining closely. The *Rambam* in his *Peirush HaMishnayot* suggests that the *Tanna Kamma* may have implicitly assumed that it is the owner's intent that governs — and that Rabbi Yose is therefore correcting this: even if the owner had none of these thoughts, the sacrifice is *kasher*, because the *machshavah* does not follow the owner but rather the one performing the *avodah*. On this reading, the *tenai beit din* is not simply about *stam lishmah*, but is making the more fundamental point that the owner's intent is legally inoperative.

A third reading — which may find support in the *Tosefta* — turns on the word *nizbach* in the opening phrase *leshem shisha devarim hazevach nizbach*. *Lizboach* is the act of *shechitah*, and *shechitah* does not require a *kohen* — anyone may perform it. The term *oved* in the final clause, by contrast, refers to the one performing the *avodah*, which is specifically priestly service (the *kabbalah*, *holachah*, and *zerikah* of the blood). On this reading, the *Tanna Kamma* may have held that the operative *machshavah* is that of the *shochet*, while Rabbi Yose holds it is only the *kohen* performing the blood service whose intent governs. This connects to the *Gemara*'s opening *sugyot* in the tractate, where we derived that the rules of *shelo lishmo* apply to each stage of the *avodah* in turn — which, on this reading, may have been resolving an actual historical debate rather than merely extending an agreed principle.

There is something additionally interesting about the *shochet* reading. In practice, the *shochet* at the Temple was often the owner himself, since *shechitah* did not require priestly status. Thus holding that the operative *machshavah* is that of the *shochet* is not entirely different from the position that the owner's intent governs — it situates the *machshavah* in the same person, but specifically at the moment of that person's act within the ritual framework. Rabbi Yose then removes that power from the *shochet-owner* entirely and locates it solely in the *kohen* performing the subsequent blood service.

In the end the accepted position is that *machshavah* governs at all stages — *shechitah* and the subsequent *avodot* — but this excludes the owner when not performing an *avodah*.

---

## Intent in Detail

### Chattat Intent Cases

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: first, a brief *drasha* on the six-part formula of *olah hi ishei reiach nichoach l'Hashem*. Each element of the phrase corresponds to one of the six intentions: *olah* — that it should be offered as an *olah*, to exclude *leshem shelamim* (the issue of *shinui shemo*); *ishim* — that it be burned on a proper fire, to exclude the intent of placing it on mere embers; *reiach* — that smoke should rise, to exclude *evarim she'tzla'an* (limbs that were pre-roasted before being placed on the altar, which is established by Rav Yehuda in Rav's name as failing to satisfy the requirement of *reiach nichoach*); *nichoach* — that it be *leshem nachat ruach*; *l'Hashem* — *leshem mi she'amar vehayah ha'olam*, for the sake of the One who spoke and the world came into being.

It is worth noting that the *Gemara* treats these elements — the relational, direction-toward-God aspects of the offering — efficiently and then moves immediately to the more technically operative material. The entire dimension of *reiach nichoach* as a framework for understanding what a *korban* is receives, in effect, a brief acknowledgment and is then set aside.

Now the *Gemara* turns to the more technically operative question. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: a *chattat* that was slaughtered with the intent that it be *leshem olah* — for the sake of an *olah* — is *psulah*. A *chattat* that was slaughtered with the intent that it be *leshem chulin* — for the sake of ordinary, non-sacred meat — is *kesheirah*.

### Why Intent Matters

Rav Elazar explains the reasoning: *velo yechalelu et kodshei b'nei Yisrael* — one category of *kodashim* desecrates another category of *kodashim*, while ordinary *chulin* cannot desecrate *kodashim*. The intent to make a *chattat* into a different *korban* is a relevant religious act of misdirection; the intent to make it into *chulin* is so categorically outside the domain of the sacred that it has no operative force. The thought simply has no traction.

### Rabba's Challenge

Rabba challenges from the *Mishnah*. Rabbi Yose ruled: *af mi shelo hayah belibo leshem echad mikol elu kasher* — even with no intent at all, the sacrifice is *kasher*. This is the principle of *stam lishmah*. Reading the implication: *ta'ama shelo hayah belibo klal* — the reason it is *kasher* is that there was no active thought at all. *Ha hayah belibo leshem chulin pasul* — this implies that if one did actively think *leshem chulin*, it would be *pasul*. So Rabba challenges Rav: Rabbi Yose seems to indicate that *leshem chulin* intent does invalidate.

### Abaye's Resolution

Abaye responds: *dilma lo hayah klal kasher u'meratzeh* — perhaps the reading is that with no intent at all, the sacrifice is both *kasher* and *meratzeh* (accepted on behalf of the owner, fulfilling the owner's obligation). *Ha hayah belibo leshem chulin kasher ve'eino meratzeh* — whereas if intent was *leshem chulin*, the sacrifice is still *kasher* (the meat remains permitted, no technical disqualification applies), but it is not *meratzeh*, not *olah l'be'alim leshem chovah*.

This establishes an interesting intermediate category specifically for *chattat*. Normally a *chattat shelo lishmo* is fully *pasul* — the meat cannot be eaten. But a *chattat leshem chulin* occupies a middle space: technically valid enough that the meat remains permitted, yet not fulfilling the owner's obligation. This distinction flows from Rav's original ruling and is now resolved by Abaye to be consistent with Rabbi Yose's *Mishnah*.

---

## Intent Distinctions

### Intentional vs Mistaken

Rav Elazar introduces a further qualification. A *chattat* shechted with conscious intent that it be *leshem chulin* — where the *shochet* knows it is a *chattat* but deliberately redirects his intent toward *chulin* — is *kesheirah* in the sense described above (not *meratzeh* but not fully *pasul*). However, if the *shochet* actually believed the animal to be *chulin* — if he labored under a mistaken assumption about what he was shechting — then it is *psulah*, entirely disqualified.

### Misyasek Problem

This distinction raises the question of *misyasek*: what is the status of one who is entirely unaware of what he is doing? The question posed — *minayin l'misyasek b'kodashim she'hu pasul* — asks for the source that one who performs the *shechitah* of a *korban* while not consciously aware that he is doing so has performed an invalid act.

The application here is instructive. If the *shochet* is in the precincts of the *Beis Hamikdash* and assumes that the animal before him is ordinary *chulin* — perhaps believing that someone brought him an ordinary cow — and shechts it without any awareness that it is a *korban*, that is *misyasek*. The act is not an act of *shechitat korbanot* in any meaningful sense. The one who intentionally directs his intent toward *chulin* but knows he is dealing with a *korban* is in a different position: his act is at least consciously directed, even if misdirected. The one who has no awareness at all that a *korban* is involved is performing an act that is halachically inert as a *shechitat korban*.

### Misyasek Source

The source is derived from the verse *v'shachat et ben habakar lifnei Hashem* (Vayikra 1:5). Shmuel asked Rav Huna for the source; Rav Huna said the verse implies *ad she'tehei shechitah l'shem ben habakar* — the *shechitah* must be conscious that it is being performed on a bovine, that one is at least aware of the nature of the act. Shmuel replied: that we already know; the question is the source that *be'diavad* it is invalid. Rav Huna responded with *lirtzonchem tizbachu*.

### Conscious Intent Required

The verse *lirtzonchem tizbachu* establishes that the act of *zevichah* must be performed *l'da'atchem* — with conscious awareness, with one's own will. The *ratzton* must be present: not just that God should receive the offering willingly, but that the one performing the act should be doing so with full, willing, conscious intent. An act performed in a state of unawareness — *misyasek* — lacks this quality entirely and is therefore invalid from the outset. This applies not just to the specific case of *chattat*, but to any *shechitat korbanot* performed without conscious awareness that one is engaged in that act.

To summarize the full spectrum of distinctions arrived at: a *chattat* slaughtered with intent *leshem olah* is *psulah* (*chattat shelo lishmo*); a *chattat* slaughtered knowingly *leshem chulin* is *kasher* but not *meratzeh*; a *chattat* slaughtered under the mistaken belief that it is *chulin* is fully *psulah* as *misyasek*; and a *chattat* slaughtered with no active intent at all (*stam*) is both *kasher* and *meratzeh*, by the principle of *stam lishmah* and the *tenai beit din* of Rabbi Yose.

---

---

# Zevachim 47

## Owner vs. Kohen Thought

### Rebbe Yose Introduction

The daf opens on 47a, picking up approximately four lines from the top, wrapping up the fourth *perek* before beginning the fifth. The final line of the *mishnah* had presented the position of *Rebbe Yose*, who argued that even when a *kohen* fails to maintain the proper intention during the *avodah*, the *korban* remains valid by virtue of *tnai beis din* — a standing condition established by the court. That much was clear. But appended to his ruling was a further statement that seemed to stand apart from *Rebbe Yose*'s main point: that *machshava* follows only the *oved*. The *Gemara* now turns to examine who this statement is directed against, and why.

### Rabbi Eliezer Opinion

The *Gemara* introduces the matter with the framing *masnisin delo ki hai tana* — our *mishnah* (and indeed, as will become apparent, the entire *masechta*) does not accord with a particular *tana*. A *braisa* is then cited: *amar Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Yose, shamati she'habalim mefaglin* — Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose testified that he had heard that the owners of a *korban* can render it *pigul*. The implication is striking. Normally the entire framework of *Masechet Zevachim* concerns what the *kohanim* do — the technical *avodos* performed in the *Beis HaMikdash*. But Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose introduces the possibility that the *ba'alim*, the owners, have their own role: since they are connected to the *korban* in a meaningful way, their thought carries independent weight.

### Machshava Follows Oved

Against this view, the final line of the *mishnah* asserts that *machshava* follows only the *oved*. This principle can be understood as the operative logic behind *Rebbe Yose*'s broader position: if the owner's *da'as* were to matter, the entire *korban* would be placed in the hands of non-experts whose intentions are unknown and uncontrolled. The condition of *tnai beis din* might itself be read as a legal mechanism for marginalizing the owner's intent — a way of saying that whatever the owner may be thinking, the court's standing presumption governs the *korban*'s status. Either way, the *Gemara*'s reading is clear: *machshava* is the province of the one performing the *avodah*, not of the one who brought the animal.

### Shechita vs. Dam

An alternative interpretation, grounded in the *Tosefta*, offers a different way of understanding the underlying debate. The *mishnah* opened with the phrase *lesheim shisha devarim hazevach nizbach* — the sacrifice is slaughtered. One might argue that the relevant mental state attaches to the act of *shechita* itself, and since *shechita* can be performed by a non-*kohen* — even by the owner — the owner's intention during *shechita* might be considered formative. Against this, the position that *machshava* follows the *oved* would insist that the *avodah* properly begins with the *kibbul ha-dam* and the subsequent blood rites, and it is there — performed exclusively by the *kohanim* — that intent is legally operative. While the *Gemara* itself reads the debate as being about the four *avodos* versus the owner, this alternative reading situates the disagreement in the contrast between *shechita* and *dam*, and between the act of the *zoveiach* and the act of the *oved*.

### Rava's Source Hikriv

The *Gemara* then asks: what is the textual basis for Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose's position? *Amar Rava: de'amar kra, yakriv hamakriv es korbano* — a verse in Bamidbar 15 reads *vehikriv hamakriv korbano la'Hashem*. The apparent redundancy — *hikriv hamakriv* — is taken to signal that the *makriv*, the one who brings the offering, refers not to the *kohen* performing the *avodah* but to the owner presenting the *korban*. In the ordinary idiom of *Zevachim*, the person designated as performing the *avodah* would naturally be the *kohen*; but here the *Torah* draws attention to the one whose *korban* it is. This provides the textual anchor for Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose's claim.

One might ask whether the owner's *machshava* in this framework would be effective at any moment, or only during the four *avodos*. This is a genuine question touching on a classic *chakira*: is it the thought alone that makes *pigul*, anchored to an act as a requirement of connectivity, or is it the *avodah* itself that is rendered invalid when framed by a particular intention? If the former, then in principle the owner's thought at any point during the *avodos* might suffice. The *Gemara* does not resolve this fully, but the implication is that the owner's *machshava* is still bounded by the period of the four *avodos* — it is not a free-floating invalidation.

### Rashi on Makriv

Rashi explains the derivation as follows: *ama be'alim bichlal makriv* — the *ba'alim* are included within the category of *makriv*. The doubling of the verbal root in *hikriv hamakriv* signals that the one "bringing" the sacrifice encompasses not only the *kohen* performing the sacred rite but also the owner in whose name the *korban* is offered. While it remains somewhat unclear why this *pasuk* more than others establishes this inclusion, the principle Rashi draws is that for purposes of *machshava* and its capacity to create *pigul*, the owner is recognized — at least by Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose — as a legitimate subject of *halachic* intentionality.

---

## Abaye's Three Tannaim

### Three Tannaim Intro

*Amar Abaye*: Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar — all three hold the principle that *ze machashev veze oved havya machshava*, meaning that even when one person thinks and a different person acts, that thought can nonetheless be *halachically* significant. Abaye is identifying a structural similarity across three otherwise disparate *halachic* domains, each involving the unusual case of a *machshava* that operates independently of the one performing the act.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

The first case — *Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose ha de'amran* — is what has just been discussed: the *ba'alim* are connected to their *korban* in a way that, according to Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose, gives their thought operative weight even though they are not performing the *avodah*.

### Shechita Avodas Kochavim

The second case involves a ruling of Rabbi Eliezer himself, found in a *mishnah*: *hashochet la'avodas kochavim shechitata kesheira, Rabbi Eliezer posel* — the standard ruling is that if one slaughters an animal intended for *avodas kochavim*, the *shechita* is valid; but Rabbi Eliezer holds it invalid. The scenario envisioned is one in which a *kohen* or Jew performs the *shechita* while the non-Jewish owner harbors the intention to offer the animal to his deity. The non-Jew is not performing the act — he is merely thinking. Yet Rabbi Eliezer holds that the owner's intention to dedicate the animal to *avodas kochavim* is sufficient to render the *shechita* problematic, making the meat the equivalent of *zivchei meisim*, an offering to idols, and thus forbidden. The parallel to the first case is clear: an owner, not performing the act, whose *machshava* nonetheless defines the character of what is being done.

### Shabbos Crumbs Case

The third case is a ruling of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar regarding *Shabbos*. A general principle governs *Shabbos* liability: one is not *chayav* for carrying out an object unless it meets the threshold of *lehatznia* — it must be the kind of thing that a normal person would set aside and preserve. This has two components. First, the object must be objectively suitable for preservation — something that has real use and value. An object forbidden in *hana'ah*, such as *chametz* on *Pesach*, fails this test objectively. Second, even an object that is in principle suitable must be of sufficient quantity that normal people would bother to preserve it; a crumb so tiny that people routinely let it be trampled fails the subjective threshold.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's case involves an object that fails one of these thresholds — say, a crumb too small for ordinary people to bother saving. But a particular individual, Reuven, decided that this crumb was significant to him and set it aside (*hitzni'o*). He thereby established its subjective importance. Subsequently, Shimon — a different person — comes along and carries that crumb out into *reshus harabim* on *Shabbos*. *Nischayav zeh bemachshava shel zeh* — Shimon is *chayav* by virtue of the *machshava* of Reuven. The significance that made the crumb legally cognizable was established by someone who did not perform the act of carrying; the one who actually carried it out performed the act without independently having established the object's importance.

In all three cases, the same conceptual structure is at work: one person's *machshava* defines or frames an act performed by another person. As Abaye notes, however, while these cases share this structure, they are not identical in *halacha*, and one does not automatically imply the other.

### Gemara Hierarchy

The *Gemara* now proceeds to analyze the hierarchical relationships among the three positions. It begins with the observation that *travayhu is lehu de'Rabbi Eliezer be'Rabbi Yosi* — the *tannaim* responsible for the latter two cases (*Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*) would certainly agree with Rabbi Eliezer beRabbi Yose's ruling about *pigul*. The argument runs as follows: *hashta bechutz amrinan* — if we say outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, where the *Torah* does not particularly emphasize *machshava* as a transformative legal force, another person's thought can define an act, then *bifnim mibaya* — inside the *Beis HaMikdash*, where the *Torah* explicitly emphasizes the power of *machshava* (as expressed in the special *parsha* of *pigul*, *lo yeichashev lo pigul yihyeh*), there is all the more reason to say that even one who is not performing the act can invalidate it through thought.
