Could the *chatas* and *asham* establish a paradigm for the *olah*? No — both achieve atonement, but the *olah* does not. Could the *olah* and *asham* establish a paradigm for the *chatas*? No — both are male animals (*zecharim*), while a *chatas* is typically a female. Could the *olah* and *chatas* be used because one appears as a communal offering and one as an individual offering? Every attempted pairing yields a distinguishing feature that would undermine the *binyan av*.

The result is that there was no way to establish *tzafon* for all three by derivation — each required explicit scriptural statement. Consequently, this case provides no proof one way or the other regarding whether a *binyan av* can be built on a *hekkesh*. The question remains unresolved. It is worth noting, as an observation about the internal logic of the system, that *kal vachomer* — which succeeded where *binyan av* is uncertain — is conceptually stronger: it does not merely assert similarity but argues from the logic of greater and lesser stringency. The uncertainty about *binyan av*, by contrast, tracks the fact that it is fundamentally a pattern-matching exercise, and pattern-matching is more easily disrupted by categorical distinctions.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah Column

### Todah from Ma'aser

The *gemara* now turns to the second column: derivations that begin with a *gezeirah shavah*. The first question is whether a law derived by *gezeirah shavah* can then serve as the basis for a *hekkesh*. Rav Pappa advances a proof from the case of a *todah* brought from *ma'aser sheni* funds.

The principle at stake is that when one redeems *ma'aser sheni* produce onto money and then spends that money in Jerusalem, one may use it to purchase an offering whose meat one eats. A *todah* — a thanksgiving offering — may be brought with such money, provided the person specified at the time of the vow that the offering would come from *ma'aser sheni* funds.

### Sham Sham Connection

The derivation works in two steps. We know that *shlamim* may be purchased with *ma'aser sheni* money. How do we know that? From a *gezeirah shavah* of *sham sham*: the verse describing *shlamim* uses the word *sham* ("there"), as does the verse about *ma'aser sheni* consumption — *ve'achalta sham* by *shlamim* and *ve'achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha bamakom asher yivchar leshaken shemo sham* by *ma'aser sheni*. This shared word links the two contexts and establishes that *shlamim* may come from *ma'aser sheni* funds (A to B via *gezeirah shavah*).

From there, the Torah's statement *vezot torat zevach hashlamim im al todah yakrivennu* — "this is the law of the *shlamim* if he brings it as a *todah*" — links the *todah* to the *shlamim*. This linkage (B to C via *hekkesh*) allows us to apply what is true of *shlamim* to the *todah* as well.

It is worth noting that calling the second step a *hekkesh* might seem overstated. When the Torah says "this is the law of the *shlamim* if he brings it as a *todah*," it appears to state directly that a *todah* is a species of *shlamim*, rather than merely linking the two by implication. Similarly, the statement *bimkom asher tishachat ha'olah tishachat hachatat* looks more like an explicit instruction than a *hekkesh*. Nevertheless, the *gemara* treats any move from B to C — even when fairly direct — as a *hekkesh* for purposes of this analysis.

### Rav Pappa Debate

Rav Pappa's proof establishes that *gezeirah shavah* followed by *hekkesh* is a valid derivation chain. However, the *gemara* does not let the matter rest.

### Chulin Source Issue

Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari challenges Rav Pappa: *ma'aser dagan chullin b'alma hu* — grain that is *ma'aser sheni* is, fundamentally, *chullin*. Even according to those who hold that *ma'aser sheni* has a degree of sanctity, it is certainly not in the category of *kodshim*. If the starting point of the derivation — the A in the A-to-B *gezeirah shavah* — is *chullin*, then the restrictions on chained derivations within *kodshim* simply do not apply. The case of *sham sham* tells us nothing about whether *gezeirah shavah* followed by *hekkesh* is permitted when the entire chain operates within the domain of *kodshim*.

### Restrictions Apply

Rav Pappa responds: the restrictions are not determined by where the derivation begins — the *melamed*, the source — but by what is being derived — the *lamed*, the application. Since the *shlamim* and *todah* (B and C) are *kodshim*, the relevant restrictions do apply, and nevertheless Rav Pappa holds the derivation is valid.

### Source vs Application

Rashi makes explicit the dispute implicit in this exchange. Rav Pappa holds *d'batar lamed azlinan* — we follow the derived case; so long as what is being derived is *kodshim*, the restrictions apply and must be reckoned with. Mar Zutra's implicit counter-position is *d'batar melamed azlinan* — we follow the source; if the original teaching is *chullin*, the restrictions of *kodshim* do not engage at all. This debate about whether the restrictions track the *melamed* or the *lamed* is embedded in, and clarified by, the passage before us.

### Gezeirah Shavah Chain

The *gemara* moves on to the next combination: *gezeirah shavah* followed by *gezeirah shavah*. Can a law derived by *gezeirah shavah* itself become the source for a further *gezeirah shavah*? Rami bar Chama cites a *braita* that appears to demonstrate exactly this.

### Bread Types Case

The *braita* concerns the breads that accompany a *todah*. A *todah* is brought with forty loaves: ten *chalos* (unleavened loaves), ten *rekikin* (thin wafers), ten *revuchah* (loaves prepared by first cooking in water and then frying), and ten *chamotz* (leavened loaves). The question is how we know that the *chalos* and the *rekikin* — in addition to the *revuchah* — must be made from *soles* (fine flour).

The *braita* teaches: for the *revuchah*, the requirement of *soles* is stated explicitly in the Torah. For the *chalos*, we derive it by a *gezeirah shavah* of *chalos chalos* — the word *chalos* appears both in the context of the *revuchah* and in the context of the standard *chalos*, establishing that the latter must also use *soles*. For the *rekikin*, we derive it by a *gezeirah shavah* of *matzos matzos* — the word *matzos* appears in the context of the *chalos* and in the context of the *rekikin*. Thus: *revuchah* to *chalos* via *gezeirah shavah* (*chalos chalos*), and *chalos* to *rekikin* via *gezeirah shavah* (*matzos matzos*) — a clear chain of *gezeirah shavah* upon *gezeirah shavah*.

### Direct Source Challenge

Ravina challenges this proof. He asks: *mimai d'matzos matzos me-chalos gmar* — how do we know that the *matzos matzos* derivation for the *rekikin* is drawing from the *chalos* (which was itself learned via *gezeirah shavah*)? Perhaps the *matzos* of *rekikin* is derived directly from the *mincha* baked in an oven (*maafeh tanur*) — a *mincha* brought as a *nedavah* — where the Torah explicitly uses the word *matzos* and also specifies *soles*. If so, the *matzos matzos* of *rekikin* is a direct derivation, not a *gezeirah shavah* built on a *gezeirah shavah*, and the *braita* proves nothing about chained *gezeirot shavot*.

### Cutting Up Case

Rava therefore proposes an alternative proof. He cites a different *braita* that describes the treatment of the inner *chatas* of the *kohen mashiach* — the *par* that is burned entirely outside the camp. The Torah states *v'kirbo u'firsho v'hotzi* — "its innards and its refuse he shall take out" — and the word *v'hotzi* implies a single act of removal, which in turn implies it is taken out whole rather than in pieces. Yet the Torah also says, by an *olah*, *rosho u'chrao* — "its head and its legs" — using a *gezeirah shavah* of *rosho u'chrao* (stated here by the inner *chatas* and stated there by the *olah*) to teach that the *chatas*, like the *olah*, must be cut into sections (*nitoach*) before burning. So from the *olah* to the *par kohen mashiach* is one *gezeirah shavah*.

Furthermore, the *gemara* notes, the verse also establishes that the *par* is not flayed (*hefshet*) before burning, since *v'kirbo u'firsho* indicates the innards remain enclosed — and just as the innards are not separated from the body cavity, the skin is not separated from the flesh. This is Rav Pappa's explanation of the verse *v'es or ha'par v'es kol besaro al rosho v'al kerav v'kirbo u'firsho v'hotzi* — everything is taken out as a unit, and just as the *pirsho* remains within the *kirbo*, so the skin remains on the flesh.

Then Rebbi, in a second *braita*, applies these same rules to the *par v'seir* of *Yom Kippur*. The verse there also says *or u'vasar u'feresh*, and by *gezeirah shavah* of *or u'vasar u'feresh* (stated here by *Yom Kippur* and there by the *par kohen mashiach*), we learn that the *Yom Kippur par* too is cut into sections but not flayed before burning. This is precisely *gezeirah shavah* built on *gezeirah shavah*: from *olah* to *par kohen mashiach* via one *gezeirah shavah*, and from *par kohen mashiach* to the *par v'seir* of *Yom Kippur* via a second *gezeirah shavah*. Rava's proof is thus established without any of the problems Ravina raised.

### Gezeirah Shavah → Kal Va…

With *gezeirah shavah* to *hekkesh* (debated by Rav Pappa) and *gezeirah shavah* to *gezeirah shavah* (established by Rava) now on the table, the *gemara* turns to the third combination in this column: *gezeirah shavah* followed by *kal vachomer*. May a law derived by *gezeirah shavah* serve as the basis for a *kal vachomer*?

### Strength Argument

The *gemara* employs a logical *kal vachomer* to resolve the question. We know two things: first, a *hekkesh* cannot support a further *hekkesh* (*hekkesh min hahekkesh* is forbidden), yet a *hekkesh* can support a *kal vachomer* (from *Tanna D'vei Rabbi Yishmael*). This shows that *kal vachomer* is strong enough to be built even on a weak foundation. Second, a *gezeirah shavah* is a stronger foundation than a *hekkesh*, because while you cannot build a *hekkesh* on a *hekkesh*, you can build a *gezeirah shavah* on a *gezeirah shavah* and — according to Rav Pappa — even a *hekkesh* on a *gezeirah shavah*. If the weaker foundation (*hekkesh*) permits *kal vachomer*, then certainly the stronger foundation (*gezeirah shavah*) permits *kal vachomer*.

The *gemara* notes a qualification: the first formulation of this argument relied on Rav Pappa's position that *gezeirah shavah* permits *hekkesh*, making *gezeirah shavah* demonstrably stronger than *hekkesh*. If one rejects Rav Pappa's position, that version of the argument fails. The *gemara* therefore offers an independent version: even without invoking Rav Pappa, we know that *hekkesh* cannot build on *hekkesh*, yet *gezeirah shavah* can build on *gezeirah shavah*. The capacity of a method to build on itself demonstrates its relative strength. Since *gezeirah shavah* is stronger than *hekkesh* by this measure, and *hekkesh* can still support a *kal vachomer*, *gezeirah shavah* certainly can.

### Conclusion

The *gemara* accepts this reasoning. Starting from a *gezeirah shavah* and then applying a *kal vachomer* is permitted without reservation.

### Gezeirah Shavah → Binyan…

The fourth and final combination in the *gezeirah shavah* column is *gezeirah shavah* followed by *binyan av*. The *gemara* offers no resolution: *teiku*. The question remains open.

To summarize the *gezeirah shavah* column: *gezeirah shavah* to *hekkesh* — Rav Pappa says yes, others dispute; *gezeirah shavah* to *gezeirah shavah* — yes, as proved by Rava; *gezeirah shavah* to *kal vachomer* — yes; *gezeirah shavah* to *binyan av* — *teiku*.

---

## Kal Vachomer Column

### Kal Vachomer → Hekkesh

The *gemara* now takes up the third column: derivations that begin with a *kal vachomer*. The first question is whether a law derived via *kal vachomer* may then become the basis for a *hekkesh*.

### Kal Vachomer → Gezeirah…

Simultaneously, the *gemara* addresses the second combination: *kal vachomer* followed by *gezeirah shavah*. Both are argued together through the same logical framework.

### Strength Comparison

The argument for *kal vachomer* to *hekkesh* proceeds as follows. We know that a *gezeirah shavah* cannot build on a *hekkesh* — that was established by Rabbi Yochanan from the case of *chatas* and *asham*. Yet even *gezeirah shavah*, despite this weakness, can when it is the *first* step support a *hekkesh* as the second step — that is Rav Pappa's position. A *kal vachomer* is demonstrably stronger than a *gezeirah shavah* as a second step, because a *kal vachomer* can build on a *hekkesh* whereas a *gezeirah shavah* cannot. If the weaker *gezeirah shavah* can, as a first step, support a *hekkesh* second step, then certainly the stronger *kal vachomer* — as a first step — can support a *hekkesh* second step.

### Buildability Logic

Similarly, for *kal vachomer* to *gezeirah shavah*: we know a *gezeirah shavah* cannot build on a *hekkesh*, but it can build on itself (*gezeirah shavah* to *gezeirah shavah*, from Rami bar Chama). Meanwhile, a *kal vachomer* is stronger than a *gezeirah shavah* because it can build on a *hekkesh* (from *Tanna D'vei Rabbi Yishmael*) while a *gezeirah shavah* cannot. If a *gezeirah shavah* — even the weaker method — can generate a further *gezeirah shavah*, then certainly a *kal vachomer* — the stronger method — can generate a *gezeirah shavah*.

### Rav Pappa Dependency

The *gemara* qualifies: the argument for *kal vachomer* to *hekkesh* depends on Rav Pappa's position. If one accepts that *gezeirah shavah* followed by *hekkesh* works, then *kal vachomer* (being stronger) certainly supports *hekkesh* as well. But if one rejects Rav Pappa — for instance, on the grounds that his proof case involved *ma'aser sheni*, which is *chullin*, and thus the restrictions of *kodshim* were never engaged — then we have no established instance of *gezeirah shavah* followed by *hekkesh* within *kodshim*, and the argument for *kal vachomer* followed by *hekkesh* also collapses. In that case, *teiku*.

### Kal Vachomer → Kal Vacho…

The third combination in the *kal vachomer* column is *kal vachomer* followed by *kal vachomer*. The *gemara* attempts to prove this is permitted.

### First Proof Attempt

The initial argument: we have shown that *gezeirah shavah* is a weaker method than *kal vachomer*, because a *gezeirah shavah* cannot build on a *hekkesh* while a *kal vachomer* can. Yet even *gezeirah shavah*, the weaker method, can support a *kal vachomer* as a second step — we established this earlier using a *kal vachomer* argument. If the weaker *gezeirah shavah* can support a *kal vachomer*, then certainly the stronger *kal vachomer* can support a *kal vachomer*.

### Circularity Problem

The *gemara* objects sharply: *v'zehu kal vachomer ben kal vachomer* — this argument is itself a *kal vachomer*, and moreover it is *ben beno shel kal vachomer* — the grandson of a *kal vachomer*. The problem is recursive. We are trying to establish whether *kal vachomer* can build on *kal vachomer*. The proof we offer is itself a *kal vachomer* — and the premise of that *kal vachomer* (that *gezeirah shavah* can support *kal vachomer*) was itself established by a *kal vachomer* in the earlier discussion. So we are using a *kal vachomer*, itself derived from a prior *kal vachomer*, to prove that *kal vachomer* can be derived from *kal vachomer*. The argument begs the question it is meant to answer.

It is worth noting that in the common *yeshiva* parlance, calling something a *kal vachomer ben beno shel kal vachomer* expresses that it is the most obvious possible inference — the "granddaddy" of logical arguments. But in its technical *talmudic* usage here, the phrase carries the opposite valence: it signals that the argument is derivative to the point of circularity.

### Non-Circular Proof

The *gemara* therefore constructs a non-circular proof. The established, uncontroversial facts — derived without any *kal vachomer* reasoning — are: *hekkesh* cannot build on *hekkesh* (*hekkesh min hahekkesh*), and yet *hekkesh* can support *kal vachomer* (from *Tanna D'vei Rabbi Yishmael*). These two data points are established from Tannaitic tradition directly, without any *kal vachomer* argument. From these two facts, we observe that *kal vachomer* is strong enough to be generated even from a weak foundation (a *hekkesh* that cannot even support another *hekkesh*). Now *kal vachomer* is a stronger foundation than *hekkesh* — we have already demonstrated this. Therefore, if the weaker *hekkesh* can generate a *kal vachomer*, certainly the stronger *kal vachomer* can generate a *kal vachomer*. This *kal vachomer* argument is genuinely first-order — it does not rely on any previously derived *kal vachomer* — and the *gemara* accepts it.

### Kal Vachomer → Binyan Av

The final combination in the *kal vachomer* column is *kal vachomer* followed by *binyan av*. Rav Yirmiah introduces a proof from the laws of *tum'ah* of birds.

### Melikat Tereifah Case

The case: a bird upon which *melikat* (*malikat*) was performed — the method of slaughter for bird-offerings, whereby the kohen cuts the back of the neck — and it was subsequently found to be a *tereifah* (mortally wounded prior to the act). Does such a bird convey *tum'ah* when swallowed (*beit ha-beli'ah*), like a *nevela*, or is it *tahor* like a properly slaughtered *tereifah* of a non-bird animal?

Rebbi Meir rules it is *tahor* and does not convey *tum'ah*. Rebbi Yehuda rules it does convey *tum'ah* — and indeed, Rebbi Yehuda holds that even an ordinary *shechitah* of a *tereifah* bird leaves it with *tum'ah*.

### Behemah Comparison

Rebbi Meir builds his case with a *kal vachomer*: a *nevela* of a *behemah* (domestic animal) is stringent — it conveys *tum'ah* both through touching and through carrying. Yet *shechitah* of that animal, even if the animal is a *tereifah*, removes it from *tum'ah*. A *nevela* of a bird (*of*) is comparatively lenient — it conveys *tum'ah* only through swallowing, not through touching or carrying. Is it not a *kal vachomer* that if *shechitah* removes *tum'ah* from the stringent *behemah*, it certainly removes *tum'ah* from the more lenient bird? This establishes that *shechitah* of a *tereifah* bird renders it *tahor*.

### Melikat Application

Building on that *kal vachomer*, Rebbi Meir then applies a *binyan av*: just as *shechitah*, which renders a bird fit for eating (*makhsheret be'akhilatah*), also purifies it from *tum'ah* (*metaheret tereifatah*) — so too *melikat*, which renders a bird-offering fit for consumption (*makhsheret me'akhilah*), should likewise purify it from *tum'ah*. This is a *mah matzinu* — a paradigm built directly on the *kal vachomer* that established *shechitah*'s purifying effect.

This appears to be a clean example of *kal vachomer* followed by *binyan av* — exactly what we want to establish.

### Chulin Caveat

The *gemara* declines to accept this as a proof: *v'lo hi* — this is not a demonstration of the rule for *kodshim*. There it is clear that the derivation starts from *chullin* — the *behemah* and the bird are both *chullin* cases. The *kal vachomer* begins entirely outside the domain of *kodshim*. When the derivation originates in *chullin*, the restrictions that govern chained derivations within *kodshim* never come into play. We therefore still do not know whether, within *kodshim* proper, a *kal vachomer* can serve as the foundation for a *binyan av*. The fourth combination in the *kal vachomer* column — like the fourth combination in the *gezeirah shavah* column — is left without resolution.

The *gemara* will address the final column — *binyan av* as the first step — in the following daf.

---

---

# Zevachim 51

## Drashot in Kodshim

### Four Methods Review

Today's daf is daf 51a, and we are wrapping up the meta-discussion of what types of doubly-derived *drashot* are legitimate in the area of *kodshim* — a domain in which more restrictions govern when one may apply certain hermeneutical methods. Two rules apply in *kodshim* that do not apply elsewhere. First, while in other areas of *halacha* one generally assumes that a stated requirement is binding — as with *u-lekachtem lachem pri etz hadar*, where no one debates whether a *pri* or an *etz* is truly indispensable — in the world of *korbanot* there are so many requirements that the default assumption is that unless something is explicitly repeated, it is not *me'akev*, meaning it does not invalidate the *korban* if omitted. Second, the question of "chaining" derivations — learning from A to B, and then from B to C — which is generally permitted in other areas of *halacha*, is restricted in *korbanot*, presumably because of the sheer proliferation of details that would result.

The *gemara* previously identified four methods by which connections between laws can be established: *hekesh* (juxtaposition), *gezeirah shavah* (verbal analogy), *kal va-chomer* (an a fortiori argument), and *binyan av* (paradigmatic analogy). It then proceeded through a 4×4 chart exploring which of these methods may serve as a starting point for a further derivation within *kodshim*. To recall the conclusions reached: *hekesh* to *hekesh* — no; *hekesh* to *gezeirah shavah* — no; *hekesh* to *kal va-chomer* — yes; *hekesh* to *binyan av* — left open. We now turn to the final row of that chart: what happens when one starts with a *binyan av*?

### Binyan Av Starting Point

The *gemara* poses the question on daf 51a: *davar ha-lamed be-binyan av, mahu she-yihei lamed be-hekesh u-ve-gezeirah shavah u-ve-binyan av* — when a law has been derived through a *binyan av*, may one then proceed to derive further laws from it via *hekesh*, *gezeirah shavah*, *kal va-chomer*, or another *binyan av*? Because all of these are asked together, the *gemara* addresses them in a fairly summary fashion. An additional layer of the question concerns how to determine whether one is even operating "within the world of *kodshim*": when you have three links in a chain — A, B, and C — which of them must be in *kodshim* for the restrictive rules to apply?

The *gemara* states: *pashat mi-achada* — we can at least resolve one of these. It proceeds to bring a proof.

### Dam Kasher Proof

The relevant *halacha* is as follows: if something *pasul* (disqualified) is placed upon the *mizbe'ach*, one is generally permitted to leave it there — with certain exceptions. According to Rabbi Yehuda's position, which defines a larger category of things that must be removed, items such as blood that was slaughtered at night, blood that was spilled, or blood that left the *Beit Hamikdash* must come down. The question is: where does one draw the line? What determines whether something *pasul* on the *mizbe'ach* may remain?

A *braita* addresses this through a series of comparisons arranged as a *binyan av*. The first link: why do we know that blood which has stayed overnight (*lan*) and is then placed on the *mizbe'ach* may remain there? *She-harei lan be-imurin kasher* — because we know that *imurim* (the sacrificial fats and portions designated for the altar) that have stayed overnight are valid if placed on the *mizbe'ach*. And how do we know *that*? *She-harei lan be-basar kasher* — because in the case of a *shelamim*, the meat is permitted for eating for two days. Thus, since the meat can be valid even a day later, we extend that principle to the *imurim* as well: if the *imurim* slept overnight, they too are still valid on the *mizbe'ach*. And since this is true of the *imurim*, we extend it further to the blood.

### Weak Comparisons

The *braita* continues with a series of additional comparisons, each establishing that another category of *pasul* material placed on the *mizbe'ach* may remain there.

*Yotze*: how do we know that something that has left the *Beit Hamikdash* and been placed on the *mizbe'ach* may remain? *Ho'il ve-yotze kasher be-bamah* — because on a *bamah* (a temporary altar outside the *Mikdash*), the concept of *yotze* does not apply; the correct location for the service is simply wherever one happens to be. So something that has gone outside the *Mikdash* can still remain on the *mizbe'ach*.

*Tamei*: how do we know that meat which is *tamei* and placed on the *mizbe'ach* may remain? *Ho'il ve-hutar be-avodat tzibur* — because there are occasions when *tamei* is permitted for communal service (*tumah hutrah be-tzibur*). This is admittedly an imperfect comparison, since *tumah hutrah be-tzibur* applies when the *people* are *tamei*, not when the *meat* is *tamei*. One could have invoked *ritzuy tzitz* (the atoning power of the priestly forehead-plate) instead, but that is a direct *halacha*, not a comparison.

*Chutz lizmano*: how do we know that *pasul* meat offered with the intent for the wrong time (*pigul* thoughts) may remain on the *mizbe'ach*? *Ho'il u-mratze le-pigulo* — because when *pigul* thoughts are entertained, the remainder of the *korban* is still treated as having been performed correctly in order to establish the *korban* as *pigul*. Since within the framework of *pigul*, those very *pigul* thoughts do not constitute an additional invalidation, the *korban* retains enough validity to remain on the *mizbe'ach*.

*Chutz limkomo*: an intent for the wrong place (*chutz limkomo*) is derived from its linkage to *chutz lizmano*, as they are compared to each other.

Finally, the case of *pasul kohanim* who received and threw the blood: *be-hanach psulim de-chazu le-avodat tzibur* — this applies specifically to the type of *psulim* who would be valid for a communal offering, which in practice limits this to kohanim who are *tamei*.

### Challenge: Kosher to Pas…

The *gemara* now raises a sharp objection — one that had been lurking throughout the *braita*'s entire presentation: *ve-chi danim davar she-lo be-hechsheiro mi-davar she-be-hechsheiro?* — how can one draw an inference from something that is fundamentally *kasher* (meat on the second day of a *shelamim*, or something outside the *Mikdash* by a *bamah*) to establish that something which is fundamentally *pasul* may remain on the *mizbe'ach*? The comparison is not genuinely analogous: one case is inherently valid, the other is inherently disqualified.

### Zot Torat Ha-Olah

The *gemara* responds by citing a *baraita*: *tanya mi-zot torat ha-olah ribah samuch lo* — we actually know from the verse *zot torat ha-olah* that anything which goes on the *mizbe'ach* is permitted to remain there: *torah achat le-chol ha-olim* — one rule for everything that ascends to the *mizbe'ach*.

This reframes the entire preceding discussion. The *braita*'s comparisons were never meant to serve as the *positive* basis for concluding that these *pasul* items may remain. We do not begin from the premise that everything must come down and then use weak analogies to carve out exceptions. Rather, we begin from the opposite premise: *zot torat ha-olah* establishes that everything which goes up remains on the *mizbe'ach*. The question is only which categories are so severely disqualified that they fall outside this blanket rule — those are the few things that must come down. And how do we establish that these problematic categories are not among the worst exceptions? By showing that in some loosely associated scenario, something similar would be *kasher*. The comparisons are not logically rigorous proofs; they are simply indicators that these cases are not egregious enough to be expelled from the general rule of *zot torat ha-olah*.

### No Proof of Binyan Av

This resolution carries an important implication for the meta-discussion. Once we understand that the real source for these laws is *zot torat ha-olah* — and not a chain of *binyan av* derivations — the *braita* no longer constitutes a proof that one can apply a *binyan av* on top of a *binyan av*. The *halacha* that *pasul* items may remain on the *mizbe'ach* is not actually being learned through a *binyan av* built upon a *binyan av*; it derives from the general principle of *zot torat ha-olah*, with the comparisons serving only a subsidiary function of classifying which cases fall outside the rule. It is therefore possible that the *gemara* has, in the end, not resolved any of the questions about what one may derive from a starting point of *binyan av*.

---

## Shirei Hadam

### Source Question

Having concluded — or at least set aside — the meta-discussion of hermeneutical methods, the *gemara* now turns to the next *halacha* of the *mishnah* concerning *chata'ot*: *shirei hadam* — the remnant blood. The *mishnah* states that the remnant blood of inner *chata'ot* is spilled on the western base of the outer *mizbe'ach*. To situate this: an inner *chatat* involves bringing blood into the inner precincts and applying it there — on the *paroches* or on the inner *mizbe'ach* — and the remainder of the blood is then brought back out and spilled on the base of the outer *mizbe'ach*, specifically the western base. The *gemara* asks: *shirei hadam mai ta'ama?* — what is the source for this *halacha*?

### Pesach Ohel Moed

The *gemara* answers: *amar kra, el yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah asher pesach ohel moed* — the verse says to pour it at the base of the *mizbe'ach ha-olah* which is at the opening of the *Ohel Moed*. Since the opening of the *Ohel Moed* faces west, this identifies the western base as the place for pouring the remnant blood.

Interestingly, there is a variant reading of the *gemara* where the answer is phrased as *mai ta'ama* — asking for a *reason* rather than a *pasuk* — and the response would be *hahu depaga bereisha*: as one exits the inner area, the first part of the base that one encounters is the western one. This alternative reading raises an important conceptual question, discussed at length by Tosafot: is the rule that *shirei hadam* goes on the western base a *gzeiras hakasuv* — a direct scriptural decree — or is it grounded in the principle of *ein ma'avirin al ha-mitzvot*, the rule that one does not bypass a *mitzvah* opportunity in order to do it elsewhere? Tosafot ultimately sides with the reading preserved in our *gemara* (as Rashi edited it), which bases the rule directly on the *pasuk*, setting aside the *hahu depaga bereisha* formulation.

Tosafot notes an important reason why *ein ma'avirin al ha-mitzvot* would be inapplicable here. That principle governs a situation where one encounters a *mitzvah* and is tempted to bypass it in order to perform a different *mitzvah*. But the question here is not whether to perform the *mitzvah* of spilling blood — one is going to do that regardless — but rather *where* on the base the *mitzvah* should be performed. The question of which location is the correct one is not answered by the principle of *ein ma'avirin al ha-mitzvot*.

### Outer Chata'ot Placement

This debate has a practical ramification for the outer *chata'ot*. When offering an outer *chatat*, the blood is applied to the corners of the outer *mizbe'ach* and the *kohen* descends. Where does he then pour the *shirayim*? If the rule is based on a *gzeiras hakasuv* — the explicit verse *pesach ohel moed* pointing to the west — then one would move to the western base. But if the rule is based on *hahu depaga bereisha*, the principle of taking the first base one encounters as one descends, then one would pour it on the southern base, since that is what one reaches first upon coming down from the corner of the outer *mizbe'ach*. This is thus a genuine *machlokes* with practical consequences.

### Pesukim Analysis

The *gemara* now cites a *baraita*: *tanu rabanan — el yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah*. Rashi notes that there are five passages in *Vayikra* dealing with *chata'ot*, each of which describes the spilling of blood at the *mizbe'ach* base. In three of these passages, the text reads explicitly *mizbe'ach ha-olah*; in the other two, it reads simply *el yesod ha-mizbe'ach* without the word *olah*. The *baraita* derives three distinct *drashot* from these three occurrences of *mizbe'ach ha-olah*.

### Rashi Classification

Rashi identifies the five *parshiyot* as follows: the *par mashiach* (the anointed Kohen Gadol's bull), the *par helam davar* (the communal sin offering for an unknowingly erroneous ruling), and the *se'ir nasi* (the prince's goat) — these three have the phrase *mizbe'ach ha-olah* in the context of spilling their remnant blood. The remaining two — the *kivsah shel yachid* (the individual's ewe) and the *se'irah shel yachid* (the individual's she-goat) — have only *el yesod ha-mizbe'ach*. Rashi classifies the first two (*par mashiach* and *par helam davar*) as inner *chata'ot* — *penimiyot* — and the latter two (*kivsah* and *se'irah*) as outer — *chitzoniyot*. The *se'ir nasi* presents a more interesting case that will figure in the *gemara*'s analysis below.

---

## Three Drashot

### First Drasha

The *baraita* states: *el yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah — ve-lo yesod mizbe'ach ha-penimi*. The first *drasha* derived from *mizbe'ach ha-olah* is that the remnant blood of inner *chata'ot* must be spilled on the base of the outer *mizbe'ach* — the *mizbe'ach ha-olah* — and not on the base of the inner *mizbe'ach*. This explains why the Torah specifically had to write *mizbe'ach ha-olah* by the inner *chata'ot*: to make clear that even though the blood service took place inside, the *shirayim* must be carried out and poured on the outer altar's base.

### Second Drasha

The *baraita* continues: *el yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah — ein lo yesod le-penimi atzmo*. The second *drasha* derived from the same phrase teaches that the inner *mizbe'ach* does not even have a *yesod* (a base) at all. Unlike the outer *mizbe'ach*, which has a protruding base around its lower perimeter, the inner *mizbe'ach* is a simple rectangular solid — no ledge, no protruding base. This is derived from the implication of *mizbe'ach ha-olah*: only the *mizbe'ach ha-olah* (the outer altar) has a *yesod*; the inner *mizbe'ach* does not.

### Third Drasha

The third *drasha* is the most complex and, frankly, the most difficult to pin down: *el yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah — ten yesod le-mizbe'ach shel olah*. The phrase is deliberately opaque — "give a base to the *mizbe'ach* of the *olah*" — and the difficulty of interpreting it is reflected in the extensive Tosafot on the following page, which does not represent the usual Tosafot trying to reconcile contradictory *sugyot* but rather a sustained effort to figure out the *pshat* of this single phrase.

According to Rashi, this third *drasha* teaches a general principle: all *korbanot* offered on the outer *mizbe'ach*, if there is any remnant blood (*shirayim*), must have that blood poured at the *yesod*. The Torah only explicitly mentioned spilling the blood at the base in the context of *chata'ot* — which makes sense, since with most other *korbanot* the blood is thrown (*zrikah*) in a manner that leaves little or nothing remaining. A *chatat* involves applying blood with a finger at the corners, leaving substantial remainder, but an *olah* or *shelamim* involves a broad throw, after which there is typically nothing left. Nevertheless, if there *is* remainder blood, one needs to know what to do with it. The Torah's silence on this point by other *korbanot* could leave one without guidance. The third *drasha* therefore establishes that the principle of *yesod* applies to the entire outer *mizbe'ach*: any remnant blood of any outer *korban* goes to the base.

Tosafot offers an alternative reading. According to Tosafot, the phrase *ten yesod le-mizbe'ach shel olah* means: whenever you throw blood on the *mizbe'ach ha-olah* — other than at the corners where a *chatat* is applied — it must be thrown opposite a place where there is a *yesod* below. The outer *mizbe'ach* did not have a *yesod* running along its entire perimeter; one corner was without a protruding base. The *halacha* is that blood thrown against the wall of the *mizbe'ach* must be thrown where there is a base beneath it. According to Tosafot, this is what the third *drasha* teaches. Notably, both Rashi and Tosafot agree on the underlying *halachot*; the question is only from which *pasuk* each is derived.

### Initial vs. Remnant

The *gemara* now raises a question about the third *drasha* itself. Before accepting that it teaches about the spilling of *shirayim* of all outer *korbanot*, perhaps the *drasha* is teaching something else entirely: that the initial application of blood for an *olah* must be placed where there is a base below it. This is itself a genuine *halacha*, and the *gemara* entertains the possibility that the verse *el yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah* is its source. Two Amoraim — Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva — will now argue that this is not what the verse is teaching, and in doing so will reveal a dispute between themselves.

---

## Yishmael vs. Akiva

### Yishmael Kal Vachomer

Rabbi Yishmael argues: *mah shirayim she-ein mechapperim te'unim yesod* — the remnant blood, which does not itself create *kaparah* (atonement), nonetheless must be poured at the base. *Techilat olah she-mechapperes — eino din she-te'una yesod?* — then certainly the initial blood of an *olah*, which *does* achieve atonement, must be applied where there is a base below it. This is a *kal va-chomer*: if the less significant act (pouring the remnant) requires a *yesod*, certainly the more significant act (the initial atoning application) requires one. Therefore, Rabbi Yishmael concludes, we do not need the verse to tell us that the initial blood of an *olah* goes opposite a base — we know that from a *kal va-chomer*. The verse *mizbe'ach ha-olah* must therefore be teaching us something else.

### Why Extra Drasha?

The *gemara* presses: if one can derive from a *kal va-chomer* that the initial blood must be placed opposite the base, why would I have thought otherwise? What was the *hava amina* (initial assumption) that required the *kal va-chomer* to dispel? And conversely, once the *kal va-chomer* suffices to teach us about the initial blood, what remains for the verse *mizbe'ach ha-olah* to teach?

### Mizbeach Principle

Rashi's explanation addresses both questions. Had the verse said only *el yesod ha-olah* (without the word *mizbe'ach*), one might have concluded that the initial blood of an *olah* goes on the base specifically — meaning on the *gag ha-yesod*, the top surface of the protruding ledge. The word *mizbe'ach* changes the focus: rather than speaking about a specific *korban*'s application of blood, the verse is making a statement about the *mizbe'ach* itself — that the *mizbe'ach* and its *yesod* are always a relevant destination for blood. This shifts the *drasha* from being about the initial application of blood to being a general principle about the *yesod* as a receptacle for all blood.

Because the word *mizbe'ach* introduced this ambiguity, one might still have thought the verse is teaching about initial blood application (only now understood differently — not about the top of the *yesod* but about the *mizbe'ach* and its base in a more general sense). Rabbi Yishmael therefore steps in with the *kal va-chomer*: since I already know from a *kal va-chomer* that initial blood must go opposite a base, the verse cannot be teaching me that. It must instead be teaching me that all *shirayim* of all outer *korbanot* go to the *yesod*.

### Counter-Interpretation

The *gemara* makes this logic explicit. *Mi kesiv al yesod ha-olah? Al yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah kesiv* — it does not say *el yesod ha-olah*; it says *el yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah*. The inclusion of the word *mizbe'ach* signals that the verse is making a statement about the *mizbe'ach* as an institution rather than about a particular *korban*. If the Torah had simply said *el yesod ha-olah*, one might have read it as: when offering an *olah*, the blood must go opposite the *yesod*. The word *mizbe'ach* instead conveys: the *mizbe'ach ha-olah* — the outer *mizbe'ach* in its entirety — has the quality that all blood remnants are poured at its base.

The *gemara* adds: had it said *el yesod ha-olah*, one might have thought the verse was telling me where to place the initial blood, and I would have interpreted it as meaning even on the *zkifa* — the vertical face of the *yesod* — or perhaps even on the *gag ha-yesod*, the top of the protruding ledge. Since *mizbe'ach* is written instead, it teaches us a principle about the *mizbe'ach* itself: the *yesod* of the *mizbe'ach* is always a destination for blood, referring to spilling the *shirayim*.

### Shirayim on Yesod

At this point, the *gemara* asks another question about the third *drasha*. One might have thought the verse is needed to teach not the *shirayim* of all outer *korbanot*, but something far simpler: that the outer *chatat* — namely the *se'ir nasi*, which is an outer *chatat* and for which the verse *mizbe'ach ha-olah* is written — has its *shirayim* poured at the outer base, just as the inner *chata'ot* do. After all, the first two *drashot* established the rule for inner *chata'ot*; perhaps the third *drasha* is simply confirming the rule for the outer *chatat* as well.

The *gemara* rejects this reading. If we only needed to know that the outer *chatat*'s *shirayim* go at the outer base, *no verse would be necessary* — it follows by *kal va-chomer* from the inner *chata'ot*. If the inner *chatat*, whose entire service was performed inside, still has its *shirayim* poured outside at the outer base, then certainly the outer *chatat*, whose service is entirely outside, has its *shirayim* poured at the outer base. Moreover, one might have supposed some chiasmic logic — that inner *korbanot* pour blood outside and outer *korbanot* pour blood inside — but this is impossible once the second *drasha* established that the inner *mizbe'ach* has no *yesod* at all. Since there is no base on the inner *mizbe'ach*, there is no possibility of pouring there; the *kal va-chomer* works perfectly and no verse is needed to establish the outer *chatat*'s *shirayim* on the outer base. Therefore, the third *drasha* must be teaching something new: that the *shirayim* of *all* outer *korbanot* — not just *chata'ot* — go to the *yesod*. This includes an *olah*, a *shelamim*, and any other *korban* offered on the outer *mizbe'ach*, if remnant blood remains.

### Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva's formulation sounds nearly identical to Rabbi Yishmael's, but the *gemara* discerns a meaningful difference in phrasing. Rabbi Akiva says: *mah shirayim she-ein mechapperim ve-ein ba'in le-chapper te'unim yesod* — the remnant blood neither achieves atonement (*mechapperim*) nor is it brought for the purpose of atonement (*ba'in le-chapper*), yet it still requires the *yesod*. *Techilat olah she-mechapperes u-va'ah le-chapper — eino din she-te'una yesod?* — certainly the initial blood of an *olah*, which both atones and comes for the purpose of atonement, requires the *yesod*. The conclusion is the same as Rabbi Yishmael's: we know the initial blood's placement from a *kal va-chomer*, so the verse teaches us about the *shirayim*. *Im kein mah talmud lomar yesod mizbe'ach ha-olah — ten yesod le-mizbe'ach shel olah*: all *shirayim* of all outer *korbanot* go to the *yesod*.

### Me'akev Debate

What, then, distinguishes Rabbi Yishmael from Rabbi Akiva if they reach the same conclusion? Rav Ada bar Ahava explains: *sheyariyim me'akvin ika beinaihu* — the *me'akev* status of the *shirayim* is the point of contention between them.

Rabbi Yishmael's formulation emphasizes that the *shirayim* are not *mechapper*. He does not say they are not *ba'in le-chapper*. This implies that while the pouring of *shirayim* at the *yesod* does not accomplish atonement in itself, the act of pouring is nonetheless *me'akev* — it is an indispensable element of the service whose omission would retroactively undermine the validity of the *korban's* atonement.

Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, adds the phrase *ve-ein ba'in le-chapper*: the *shirayim* neither atone nor even *come* for the purpose of atonement. By emphasizing this double negation — that the *shirayim* have no atoning function whatsoever, not even instrumentally — Rabbi Akiva implies that the pouring of *shirayim* at the *yesod* is not *me'akev*. It is a required act, but its omission does not invalidate the *korban*. *Mar savar me'akvin, u-mar savar lo me'akvin* — one holds it is *me'akev*, the other holds it is not.

This connects directly to the position of our *mishnah*, which assumes that *shikhfas shirayim* of inner *chata'ot* is not *me'akev*. The *gemara* will continue to explore the debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva and consider further ways of articulating their disagreement.

---

---

# Zevachim 52

## Rav Papa's Resolution

### Yesterday's Recap

Today's daf is 52, and we pick up in the middle of an ongoing discussion about the *halachot* of the *chatat* and the spilling of its blood at the outer *mizbeach*, including when dealing with an inner *chatat*. Yesterday's discussion centered on a debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael who appeared to be making essentially the same argument by way of a *kal vachomer*.

According to Rashi, the *kal vachomer* concerned the placement of blood for outer sacrifices. By an outer *chatat* one does not throw the blood; rather, one applies it to all four corners. But when one applies the blood of an *olah*, a *shlamim*, or other outer sacrifices, this must be done at corners that have a base opposite them — as opposed to the southeast corner, which does not have a base below it. The argument is that one does not even need a *pasuk* to establish this, because a *kal vachomer* suffices: if the remnant blood — which is not itself an act of atonement — must be spilled at the base, then certainly the initial application of blood, which is the act of atonement, must be placed at a corner that has a base beneath it.

The question then arose: given that Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael appeared to be saying almost exactly the same thing — that the spilling of the remnant blood is not *mechapeir* — what was the difference between them? The *Gemara* raised the possibility that although Rabbi Yishmael agrees the spilling of the blood of an inner *chatat* does not achieve atonement, he might nonetheless hold that it is *me'akev*, that is, that its omission invalidates the inner *chatat*. Our *Mishnah* in this *perek* stated that the spilling of the blood of an inner *chatat* is not *me'akev*. But the near-identical formulations of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael prompted the *Gemara* to suggest that their debate might hinge on precisely this point — whether the spilling, while not an act of atonement, is nonetheless required for validity.

### Rav Papa's Point

Rav Papa rejects this suggestion. He says that *dechulei alma shirayim ein me'akvin* — even Rabbi Yishmael would agree that the spilling of the remnant blood of an inner *chatat* is not *me'akev*. What then are Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael debating? Rav Papa explains: *ve-hacha be-mitzuy chatat ha-of k-miflagi* — their dispute concerns the *mitzuy chatat ha-of*, the squeezing of the blood of a bird *chatat*.

The procedure is as follows: after performing *melikah* on a bird *chatat*, the blood that flows from the neck is squeezed against the side of the altar and runs down. The question Rav Papa identifies is whether this squeezing is *me'akev*. That is what Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael are debating — not whether the spilling of the remnant blood of an inner *chatat* is *me'akev*, but whether the squeezing of the bird *chatat* blood is *me'akev*.

### Inner vs. Outer

One might ask whether the inner *chatat* is treated differently from the outer with respect to the question of *me'akev* status. The answer is that the possibility of the spilling being *me'akev* would apply only to an inner *chatat*, since by an outer *chatat* even one of the four applications suffices *bedieved*. If even one application is sufficient, clearly the spilling of the blood is not *me'akev*. The question of the spilling being *me'akev* arises only by an inner *chatat*, where every single application is *me'akev*.

---

## Shirayim Me'akev?

### Extra Word 'Par'

A *baraita* is now cited in support of Rav Papa's position. The verse in the context of the *par kohen mashiach* states: *ve-et kol dam ha-par yishapech* — all the remaining blood of the ox you shall pour out at the base of the altar. The *baraita* asks: why does the verse use the word *ha-par*, "the ox"? The context already makes clear we are dealing with an ox. The *baraita* answers — *limed al par Yom HaKippurim she-taun damim l'yesod*, divrei Rabbi — this extra word teaches that the ox of Yom Kippur, an inner *chatat* whose blood is applied to the *kaporet*, the *parochet*, and the *mizbeach ha-zahav*, also requires that the remnant blood be poured at the base of the outer altar. This is the view of Rabbi.

### Kal Vachomer Args

Rabbi Yishmael does not disagree with this conclusion but notes that one could have derived it from a *kal vachomer* without needing the extra word *par*. His *kal vachomer* is as follows: the *par kohen mashiach* — the ox brought when the *kohen gadol* sins — is not a *chova*, not a standing obligation, since one only brings it if the *kohen gadol* actually transgresses. And yet the Torah requires that its blood be poured at the base. The *par* of Yom Kippur, by contrast, is a fixed, recurring *chova*. Is it not all the more so that it should require the blood to be poured at the base?

Rabbi Akiva sharpens the *kal vachomer* further. He argues: *uma mi she-ein damo taun lifnai v'lifnim bein l'chova bein l'mitzva taun yesod* — the *par kohen mashiach* is weighty in two ways relative to other sacrifices, yet its blood does not enter the Holy of Holies for any purpose, neither as a *chova* nor as a *mitzva*, and yet it requires the base. The *par* of Yom Kippur is weightier in two ways: first, it is a standing annual obligation, and second, its blood is brought into the Holy of Holies. How much more so should it require the base?

### Doubling as Meakev?

Now the *baraita* raises a question. Since one could derive the requirement for the *par* of Yom Kippur from a *kal vachomer*, the explicit *pasuk* that uses the extra word *par* functions as a kind of doubling. The principle is that when the Torah repeats a requirement that could have been derived independently, this doubling may indicate that the requirement is *me'akev*. Accordingly, one might say: *yachol y'akeivenu* — perhaps the verse is teaching that the spilling of the blood at the base is *me'akev*, at least for Yom Kippur.

### Vichilah Mechapeir

The *baraita* rejects this possibility. The verse states: *v'chilah mikapeir et ha-kodesh* — "and when he has finished atoning for the Holy." Rabbi Yishmael derives from here: once all the *kaparot* — the atoning acts — are completed, one has fulfilled the obligation. What are the *kaparot*? The applications of blood on the *kaporet*, the *parochet*, and the *mizbeach ha-zahav*. The spilling of the blood at the base is not identified as an act of atonement and is not even mentioned by Yom Kippur explicitly. Therefore, when the verse says one is done once the atoning is complete, it means only the blood applications count. The spilling at the base is not *me'akev*. Even though the spilling is indeed required on Yom Kippur, its omission does not invalidate the *korban*. This is *divrei Rabbi Yishmael* — and it directly confirms Rav Papa's position that Rabbi Yishmael agrees the *shirayim* are not *me'akev*.

### Par Kohen Mashiach

Having established that the spilling is not *me'akev* for Yom Kippur, the *baraita* proceeds to make a parallel argument for the *par kohen mashiach*. A *kal vachomer* can be constructed from an outer *chatat*: if an ordinary outer *chatat*, whose blood does not enter the inner sanctum for any purpose — neither as a *chova* nor as a *mitzva* — requires the blood to be spilled at the base, then the *par kohen mashiach*, whose blood does enter the inner sanctum, certainly should require the base as well. And since one could have derived this from a *kal vachomer*, the explicit verse stating *ve-et kol dam ha-par yishapech* might be read as a doubling — and one might therefore argue it renders the spilling *me'akev*: *yachol y'akeivenu*.

The *baraita* responds by pointing to the style of the verse itself. The verse could have written simply *ve-shafach et ha-dam el yesod ha-mizbeach*, as one more verb in a sequential list — *ve-lakach, ve-hizah, ve-natan*, and so on. Instead, the verse shifts register and speaks of the blood in a more tangential, wrap-up manner: *ve-et kol dam ha-par yishapech*. It is not phrased as another step in the procedure but as a separate, secondary note. This, says the *baraita*, indicates the spilling is not central to the act and is not *me'akev*. The verse *nitka ha-kasuv le-aseh va-asahu shiyarei mitzva* — the Torah has detached this instruction and treated it as a residual *mitzva*, thereby signaling that the *shirayim* do not invalidate.

### Rashi's Grammar

This grammatical reading is developed by Rashi. He observes that the earlier verbs in the passage flow as a direct sequence of procedural steps. When the Torah arrives at the spilling of the blood, it could have maintained that rhythm. Instead, it breaks the pattern, addressing the blood separately in a way that distinguishes this act from the atoning applications. The stylistic disruption is itself interpretively significant: the Torah is indicating that the spilling of the remnant blood is secondary, not integral. This is how one knows that even though the spilling is obligatory, it is not *me'akev* — the manner in which the verse is formulated tells you so.

---

## Bird Blood Meakev?

### Rabbi Yishmael's Braita

With the *baraita* having confirmed that Rabbi Yishmael holds the *shirayim* of an inner *chatat* are not *me'akev*, the *Gemara* now examines whether Rabbi Yishmael really holds the *mitzuy chatat ha-of* — the squeezing of bird *chatat* blood — is *me'akev*, as Rav Papa suggested. A *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael is cited: *ve-ha-nishar ba-dam yimatze* — what remains of the blood you shall squeeze out. And: if there is blood remaining, squeeze it; if there is nothing remaining, do not squeeze it. This implies that the squeezing is done only when it is possible to do so. Since the procedure is sometimes not going to happen — there may simply be no blood left — this implicitly signals that the *mitzuy* is not *me'akev*. How then can one say Rabbi Yishmael holds it is *me'akev*?

### Two Tanaiim

The *Gemara* resolves this by saying *trei tanaei aliba de-Rabbi Yishmael* — there are two *tannaim* within Rabbi Yishmael's school who disagree about whether the *mitzuy* of a bird *chatat* is *me'akev*. The *baraita* just cited represents one view within his school, but another view within that same school holds it is *me'akev*.

---

## Rami's Tanna

### Osah Dispute

Rami bar Chama now identifies a *tanna* who holds that the *shirayim* of an inner *chatat* are *me'akev*. He does so by pointing to a *baraita* that deals with the word *osah* — "it," referring to the *chatat* — found in the verse *ha-kohen ha-mechate osah yochelenah*, the *kohen* who performs the *chatuy* of the *chatat* shall eat it.

The *baraita* derives from *osah* that only a *chatat* performed in the prescribed manner is valid. Specifically: if one applied the blood of an outer *chatat* in the upper half of the altar — at the horns — it is a valid *chatat*; but if one applied the blood in the lower half of the altar, it is invalid. The word *osah* — "it" — excludes a *chatat* whose blood was applied in the wrong zone.

The *baraita* then asks: why would one have thought the lower half could work, such that a *pasuk* was needed to exclude it? The argument would have been as follows. We know that by an outer *chatat*, even one of the four applications suffices *bedieved* — this is derived from the verse *ve-dam zevachecha yishapech al mizbeach yesod ha-olah ve-ha-basar tochal*, which teaches that any valid blood application at the *mizbeach* suffices. Given this latitude, and given that blood applied at the top naturally runs down to the bottom due to gravity — *shekein sofan lemata* — one might have thought that placing the blood at the lower half initially is also valid, since that is where the blood ends up anyway.

### Hava Amina Refuted

The *baraita* introduces a counter-argument to this *hava amina*, based on the principle of *shirayim pnimiyim*. The remnant blood of an inner *chatat* eventually ends up at the base of the outer altar. Yet if one were to place the blood of an inner *chatat* directly on the outer altar *lechatchila*, bypassing the inner service entirely, it would obviously be invalid. This shows that the fact that blood eventually reaches a certain destination does not permit one to begin there. Apply the same logic to the outer *chatat*: even though the blood from the horns eventually runs down, one may not begin at the bottom.

The *Gemara* pushes back. The cases are not parallel. When one says the inner altar does not "finish" the blood — *she-ein mizbeach ha-pnimi memarkan* — and the outer altar's horns do "finish" the outer *chatat* blood — *karnav memarkot otan* — this creates an asymmetry. Because the inner *chatat* blood is not finished at the inner altar, one might think more latitude exists for the outer *chatat*, whose blood is fully discharged with one corner application. Therefore, the word *osah* is still necessary to teach that even so, the outer *chatat* blood may not be applied at the lower half.

Rami bar Chama's point is that this entire argument, specifically the claim that the inner altar "does not finish" the blood, implicitly assumes that the *shirayim* of the inner *chatat* are *me'akev*. Because if the spilling at the base is still required and still *me'akev*, then the inner altar truly has not completed the process, lending the inner *chatat* greater stringency and limiting the *hava amina* accordingly. Thus, the *tanna* who authored this *baraita* holds that *shirayim* of an inner *chatat* are *me'akev*.

### Rava's Reading

Rava disagrees with this reading of the *baraita*. He argues that if the *baraita* were assuming *shirayim* are *me'akev* by an inner *chatat*, the *kal vachomer* would have run in the opposite direction entirely, and would actually have strengthened the case against the *hava amina* — not weakened it. If *shirayim* of the inner *chatat* are *me'akev* and the outer base is a required part of the process, and yet one may not simply begin with the outer base, then *a fortiori* for an outer *chatat* where the base is not *me'akev*, one certainly should not be permitted to begin there. The comparison, on that reading, would only fortify the prohibition, making the word *osah* unnecessary.

Rava therefore offers a different reading. The phrase "the inner altar does not finish them" does not refer to the *shirayim* and does not assume they are *me'akev*. Rather, it refers to the fact that the inner *chatat*'s blood service is not confined to a single location — it requires application both at the inner *mizbeach* and at the *parochet*. Because the inner *chatat* requires blood applications in two distinct locations, the overall process is more demanding and more constrained. This heightened stringency — not anything to do with the *me'akev* status of the *shirayim* — is what makes the inner *chatat* a poor basis for a *hava amina* about the outer. Rava thus concludes that this *baraita* does not in fact demonstrate that any *tanna* holds *shirayim* are *me'akev*.

---

## Akiva vs. Yehuda

### Akiva's Position

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* directly addressing the question. The verse *v'chilah mikapeir et ha-kodesh* — "and when he has finished atoning for the Holy" — is the subject of a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Akiva reads the verse as follows: *im kipeir chila* — if he has atoned, then he is done. The condition for completion is the performance of the atoning acts. Only those acts that are identified as acts of atonement — the blood applications — are *me'akev*. The *shirayim* spilling, which is not *mechapeir*, is therefore not *me'akev*.

### Yehuda's Position

Rabbi Yehuda challenges this reading. He asks: why not read the verse the other way — *im chila kipeir*, if he is done, then he has atoned? Rather than making atonement the condition for completion, one makes completion the condition for atonement. And he adds: *im chisair achas mi-kol ha-matanot lo asa ve-lo klum* — if one omitted even one of the blood applications, one has accomplished nothing. All applications are *me'akev* by an inner *chatat*.

### Amoraim's Debate

The *Gemara* asks: what exactly is the practical difference between their positions? Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi debate this question. One *amora* says: *mashmaus darshein ika beinaihu* — their dispute is purely hermeneutical, a question of which formulation better captures the verse's meaning, with no practical *halachic* difference between them. The other *amora* says: *shirayim me'akvin ika beinaihu* — their dispute is whether the *shirayim* are *me'akev*. According to Rabbi Akiva, only atoning acts are *me'akev*, and since the *shirayim* are not an act of atonement, they are not *me'akev*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who reads "when you are done you have atoned," completion of everything — possibly including the *shirayim* — is the condition, and therefore the *shirayim* may be *me'akev*.

The *Gemara* notes that it appears Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is the one who holds that this is the debate, since he explicitly entertains the practical consequences of the *shirayim* being *me'akev*: *l'divrei ha-omer shirayim me'akvin* — according to the opinion that *shirayim* are *me'akev* — if on Yom Kippur the remnant blood spilled accidentally before being placed at the base, the *kohen gadol* would face a problem. One cannot simply slaughter another animal and call that blood "remnant" — it is original blood, not *shirayim*. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi concludes that in such a case, one would be required to bring an entirely new *par* and repeat the inner blood service, so as to generate genuine *shirayim* to spill at the base.

### Final Conclusion

The *Gemara* objects: surely Rabbi Yochanan also acknowledges that some *tanna* holds *shirayim* are *me'akev*? Indeed, Rabbi Yochanan himself stated that Rabbi Nechemia — in the context of the law that one is liable for performing *avoda bachutz* with *shirayim* blood — holds in accordance with the opinion that *shirayim* are *me'akev*. If the remnant blood constitutes a required *avoda* within the *Beis HaMikdash*, then using it as an *avoda* outside incurs liability. This makes clear that Rabbi Yochanan too acknowledges such an opinion exists.

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent difficulty: *ela k'divrei ha-omer v'lav le-hani tannai* — both Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi agree that some *tanna* holds *shirayim* are *me'akev*. What they debate is whether that opinion is specifically the position of Rabbi Yehuda in his dispute with Rabbi Akiva. One *amora* identifies the debate of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda as hinging precisely on this question; the other says the dispute is merely stylistic, and the *tanna* who holds *shirayim* are *me'akev* is someone else entirely.

The conclusion is that both Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi concede the existence of at least one *tanna* who holds — at minimum for Yom Kippur, and possibly for all inner *chataot* — that the *shirayim* are *me'akev*. This is the *chidush* that the *Gemara* has been working toward. Whether that opinion belongs to Rabbi Yehuda specifically remains a point of dispute between the *amoraim*. And so, to summarize the complete picture of the inner *chatat*: all blood applications are *me'akev*, while whether the *shirayim* are *me'akev* is left as an unresolved debate among the *tannaim*, with a majority view — including Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael — holding they are not.

---

## Regular Chattaot

### Communal Chattaot

The *Mishnah* now transitions from the inner *chatat* to the regular outer *chatat*, addressing both communal and individual varieties. The *Mishnah* begins: *chataot ha-tzibbur ve-ha-yachid* — the outer *chataot* of the community and the individual. The communal outer *chataot* include, as the *Mishnah* specifies, the *se'irei roshei chodashim ve-shel mo'adot* — the goats of *Rosh Chodesh* and of the festivals, which form the *chatat* component of the *musaf* offering brought on each *Rosh Chodesh* and *Yom Tov*.

### Slaughter North

The *Mishnah* states: *shechitatan ba-tzafon* — slaughter is in the north. The *shechita* must take place in the northern section of the *azarah*. And further: *u-kibul damam bi-chli sharet ba-tzafon* — the reception of the blood must take place in a holy vessel, in the north. This means the catching of the blood, the vessel itself, and the person catching must all be in the north. By *shechita*, one notes, the person performing it does not have to stand in the north.

This raises an observation noted by Tosafos: why does the *Mishnah* mention *kli sharet* specifically in connection with receiving the blood, but not in connection with *shechita*? Tosafos explains that this may simply reflect the stylistic need to specify that both the act of catching and the vessel must occur in the north. By *shechita*, since the person and the knife can be in the south — it is sufficient that enough of the blade reaches the animal's neck — there is no reason to specify the knife's status. This leads Tosafos to raise the fascinating question of whether the knife used for *shechting* a *korban* must be a *kli sharet* at all, since *shechita* does not require a *kohen*, need not occur in the *Beis HaMikdash*, and carries no inherent restriction to standing in the north.

### Four Corners

The *Mishnah* continues: *ve-damam te'un arba matanot al arba kranot* — their blood requires four applications on the four corners of the outer altar. Unlike the inner *chataot*, which involve the *parochet*, the *mizbeach ha-zahav*, and the *kaporet*, the outer *chatat* involves the four corners of the outer altar. And as has been established, *bedieved* even one application suffices.

### Ramp & Circle

The *Mishnah* then describes the procedure: *oleh ba-kevesh* — the *kohen* ascends the ramp, which is on the south side of the altar. He then *poneh la-sovev* — turns onto the walkway that encircles the altar, known as the *sovev*, which allows him to reach the horns. He proceeds counterclockwise — always moving to his right — beginning at the southeast corner, then northeast, northwest, and finally southwest. This reflects the general principle that *kol pinos she-ata poneh lo yehei ela le-yamina* — whenever you turn, you turn to the right. This is the same principle that governs circling in other ritual contexts.

### South Base & Eating

After completing the four applications, the *kohen* descends. *Shiyarei ha-dam haya shofech le-yesod dromi* — the remnant of the blood was poured at the southern base. This is in contrast to the inner *chatat*, whose *shirayim* were poured at the western base — the base one encounters first when approaching from inside. For the outer *chatat*, having descended the ramp on the south side, the *kohen* is closest to the southern base, and that is where the *shirayim* are spilled.

*Ve-nechlaim bifnim min ha-klaim* — the meat of the *chatat* is eaten inside the curtains, meaning within the *azarah* proper. This formulation evokes the *Mishkan*, where curtains surrounded the courtyard. It excludes the *Ezrat Nashim* and the *Ezrat Yisrael*; the meat must be consumed within the inner courtyard of the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Eating Rules

The *Mishnah* specifies further: *le-zichrei kehuna* — it may be eaten only by male *kohanim*, even those who are *baalei mumim*. *Be-chol ma'achal* — it may be prepared and eaten in any form; unlike the *Korban Pesach*, it need not be roasted. *Le-yom ve-layla ad chatzot* — it may be eaten for that day and the following night, until midnight. In principle the *halacha* permits eating throughout the entire night, but the Rabbis established a cutoff at midnight to prevent people from being lax and missing the deadline, as the first *Mishnah* in *Brachot* teaches.

---

---

# Zevachim 53

## Outer Chattat Corners

### Opening Remarks

We continue in *Eizehu Mekoman*, the *perek* that many recite daily in *davvening* each morning. The chapter addresses the general *chataot* — specifically the outer *chattat* — and on daf 53a the Gemara turns to the precise mechanics of how blood was applied to the altar's corners.

### Mishna Description

The *mishna* describes the outer *chattat* procedure as follows: the animal was slaughtered in the north, blood was applied to all four corners of the altar, and the remnant blood was spilled at the base — here, at the *south* base rather than the west base, a point to which we will return. The inner *chataot*, by contrast, had their remnant blood spilled at the west base. The *kohen* ascended the *mizbeach* and proceeded counterclockwise, since one always turns rightward with one's face toward the center — the same principle by which a *kallah* circles the *chosson*, and by which a *Sefer Torah* is taken out and returned to the *aron*. The outer *chattat* was eaten by male *kohanim* within the *Beis Hamikdash*.

## Keren Definition Debate

### R. Yochanan Position

The Gemara opens with the question *heichi avid* — how exactly was the blood placed at the corner of the altar? The altar's four corners each had a horn (*keren*) measuring one *amah* by one *amah* at the top. The *kohen* would be standing on the *soveiv*, the walk-around, and applying the blood to the horns. Rabbi Yochanan holds: *nosen amah eilech v'amah eilech* — one may place the blood anywhere on the horn, an *amah* in one direction or an *amah* in the other. It need not be precisely at the outermost edge; anywhere on that horn counts. This is the position of one opinion.

### R. Elazar Position

The other opinion holds: *mechatei v'yored k'neged chodo shel keren* — one applies the blood in a downward motion directly opposite the actual edge of the horn. The downward motion is practical as well, preventing blood from soiling one's garments. The verb *mechatei* is drawn from the word *chatas* itself, echoing the verse's language about the *chattat* procedure. According to this view, the application must be at the corner's edge itself, not merely somewhere on the horn's surface.

### Debate Clarification

The Gemara clarifies that the precise terms of this debate depend on a further dispute — that of Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon and *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) — concerning what qualifies as *keren* when the application is made *below* the horn itself.

To understand the geometry: the *soveiv* runs at a lower level than the horns. The question is whether, when one is not applying the blood at the horn itself but rather lower on the altar wall, the zone directly below the horn — the full height of the altar section beneath it — is still considered the *keren*. Imagine projecting the horn straight downward: is any point along that imaginary vertical line still considered the corner?

Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon holds that the *chattat* must be performed *b'gufo shel keren* — at the horn itself. *Rebbi* holds that it can be performed anywhere directly below the horn, along that vertical line, within the upper section of the altar.

Given this framework, the Gemara explains the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar as follows: *aleyba d'Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon*, who requires the horn itself, everyone agrees — if you are at the horn, it matters not where on that *amah-by-amah* surface you place the blood; anywhere is acceptable. The debate concerns *aleyba d'Rebbi*, who permits the area directly below the horn. There, one opinion holds that an *amah* in either direction along the wall (directly below the horn) still counts as the *keren*; the other holds that below the horn, only the very edge itself qualifies as the *keren*. Outside that edge — even one *amah* to either side along the lower wall — would not be considered the corner.

## Braita Challenge

### Braita Procedure

A challenge is raised from a *braita*. The *braita* describes the proper procedure for the communal and individual *chattat*: the *kohen* ascends the ramp (*kivesh*), proceeds to the *soveiv*, and comes to the southeast corner (*keren dromit mizrachit*). He dips with his right hand — specifically with *ha-miyumenet shebayamin*, which Rashi explains as the most dexterous and effective finger, namely the pointer finger — into the blood held in the *mizrak* (the service vessel). He then uses his thumb and his pinky (*godlo* and *etzba ketana*) to assist. Rashi explains this means he scrapes the blood along his pointer finger to ensure that all of it is applied; Rambam understands it as using the thumb to support the pointer finger. Either way, these additional fingers help facilitate clean and complete application.

The *braita* then specifies: *umechatei v'yored k'neged hudo shel keren* — he applies the blood going downward, directly opposite the actual corner of the horn. He continues until *kol hadam shebe'etzba'o* — all the blood on his finger is used up. The same is done at each corner in turn. This appears to settle the question: the *braita* explicitly says the application is opposite the edge of the horn, not an *amah* in either direction.

### Ideal vs. Acceptable

The Gemara resolves this: *mitzvah b'chuda* — the ideal is indeed at the edge itself, as described in the *braita*. However, *i avid amah eilech v'amah eilech leit lan bah* — if one applied it an *amah* in either direction, *b'dieved* it is acceptable. The *braita* describes the *lechatchila* procedure; the dispute concerns what is still valid after the fact. All agree that at the horn itself, an *amah* in any direction is acceptable *b'dieved*. The debate is whether, when one is below the horn, placing blood an *amah* to either side along that lower wall still counts as a valid application of *keren*.

## Upper/Lower Blood Lines

### Blood Division Intro

The Gemara now introduces the fundamental division of *damim elyonim* and *damim tachtonim* — upper bloods and lower bloods. The blood of different *korbanot* is applied to different zones of the altar, divided at the *chut ha-sikra*, the red line that runs around the altar at its midpoint. The upper bloods, from the red line and above, include the *chattat behemah* — the animal sin-offering, applied specifically at the corners. All other large-animal *korbanot* — *ola*, *shelamim*, *asham*, and the like — are applied below the red line. By bird-offerings, the rule is reversed: the bird *chattat* goes below and the bird *ola* goes above.

### Altar Structure

To understand the red line's placement, the altar's structure must be described. At the bottom was a one-*amah* protruding *yesod* (base). Above that was a five-*amah* middle section. Above that was a three-*amah* upper section, and atop that were the horns, which were one *amah* tall — totaling ten *amot* overall, not counting the horns, with the horns bringing the full height to eleven. The red line would be at the midpoint, five *amot* up, which means it runs along the upper boundary of the middle section, at the point where the upper three-*amah* section begins.

When the *kohen* ascended the ramp, he could either continue all the way up to the top surface of the *mizbeach* to place the parts on the fire, or he could exit onto the *soveiv* — the walk-around created by the one-*amah* inset of the upper section — to apply the blood. Standing on the *soveiv*, which was roughly at the level of the upper section, the *kohen* would be at approximately the right height to reach the horns for the *chattat* application. A *chattat behemah* blood application was performed up here, near the top of the altar.

### Rabbi vs. R. Elazar

The *braita* records the dispute: *damim elyonim nitanim mechut ha-sikra ulema'alah* — the upper bloods are given from the red line and above; *damim tachtonim nitanim mechut ha-sikra ulematah* — the lower bloods from the red line and below. This is the view of *Rebbi*. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon then qualifies: when does the rule of "from the red line and above" apply? Only for a *olas ha'of* — a bird burnt-offering. But for a *chattat behemah*, the blood application must be *b'gufo shel keren* — at the horn itself. One cannot satisfy the requirement merely by applying anywhere in the upper section.

This is the operative difference between the two positions. *Rebbi* permits the entire zone from the red line upward for the *chattat behemah* as well; Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon confines the *chattat behemah* to the corner itself, while reserving the broader upper zone for the bird *ola*.

### Four Amot Derivation

Rabbi Abahu asks: what is *Rebbi*'s basis for permitting the entire upper zone, and not just the horn itself? The *pshat* of the verses refers to *karnos ha-mizbeach* — the corners of the altar — and the natural reading is that this means the horn itself. Rabbi Abahu cites a verse from Yechezkel: *ve-ha-har'el arba amos* — the *har'el* (a name for the altar or its upper section) is four *amot*. Rabbi Adda bar Ahava explains: this does not mean the altar as a whole is four *amot* — it is clearly much taller. Rather, it means *reshus ha-karnos arba* — the zone of the corners occupies four *amot*. That is, the effective territory of the corner extends from the horn downward four *amot* — encompassing the one-*amah* horn plus the three-*amah* upper section, bringing one all the way down to the red line.

The Gemara briefly questions whether the four *amot* should be counted from the top of the horn down (yielding horn plus three *amot* of upper section) or from the bottom of the horn down (yielding three *amot* of upper section alone). Rashi understands the four *amot* to extend from the bottom of the horn down to the red line — that is, the horn itself plus the three *amot* below it — such that the entire upper section from the red line upward constitutes the *reshus ha-karnos*. This is a striking reading: it means that in principle, one could apply the *chattat* blood quite far below the horn, as long as it is within this four-*amah* zone above the red line, and it would count as *keren*. The precise question of whether one must still be at the literal edge of the altar in this lower zone, or may be an *amah* to either side, remains to be clarified.

### Red Line Purpose

The Gemara then asks the foundational question: what is the conceptual basis for dividing the altar at the midpoint? The idea that certain blood goes on top and other blood goes below is clear from the *korbanot* themselves — but where does the notion of a dividing line at the precise midpoint come from? Rav Acha bar Rav Katina derives it from the verse *ve-haysa ha-reshes ad chatzi ha-mizbeach* — the grillwork (*reshes*, a lattice or grating) extended to the midpoint of the altar.
