Having established that Monday night is not a time of eating, the *beraita* considers whether it might nevertheless be the time to burn the remaining meat — perhaps immediately when the eating period ends at Monday's sunset. A *kal vachomer* from the *chatat* is proposed: by one-day offerings, the *sreifah* follows immediately upon the end of the eating period (the meat is eaten through the night and burned the next morning). Perhaps here too *sreifah* should follow immediately after the eating period closes — meaning burning Monday night. This is refuted from the explicit *pasuk*: *bayom hashlishi ba'esh yisaref* — on the third day it shall be burned. *Bayom atah sorfo ve'ee atah sorfo balaylah* — you burn it during the day, not at night. The *sreifah* is reserved for Tuesday's daytime only, leaving Monday night as a space in which the meat is neither to be eaten nor burned — the very liminal period at the heart of the Chizkiyah–Rabbi Yochanan debate.

---

## Bechor/Ma'aser/Pesach

### Bechor Rules

The *Mishnah* now turns to the final category: *habechor vehama'aser vehapesach* — the firstborn animal, the animal tithe, and the Paschal offering. All three are *kodashim kalim*. Their slaughter is permitted anywhere within the *azarah* — *shechitatan bechol makom ba'azarah*. Most significantly, their blood requires only a single application anywhere on the *mizbe'ach* — *vedaman ta'un matanah achat* — provided it is applied where the *yesod* (the protruding base of the *mizbe'ach*) runs beneath. This is a notably simpler blood requirement than those of other offerings, which typically require either two applications amounting to four or a specified manner and location.

### Ma'aser Rules

When it comes to eating, the three offerings diverge. *Habechor ne'echal lakohanim* — the *bechor* is eaten exclusively by the *kohanim* and their families, throughout Jerusalem, in the manner of the *chazeh* and *shok* of the *shelamim*: it is as if the entire animal is a priestly portion. *Vehama'aser lechol adam* — the animal tithe, by contrast, is eaten by any person. None of it is given to the *kohanim*; the owner brings the *ma'aser behemah* and eats it himself in Jerusalem. Both are eaten for two days and the intervening night throughout the city.

### Pesach Rules

The Paschal offering is more restricted in every dimension. *Vehapesach eino ne'echal ela balaylah* — it may only be eaten during the night following the slaughter; it does not carry over to the next day. *Ve'eino ne'echal ela ad chatzot* — even within the night, it is limited to *chatzot* (midnight). Whether this *chatzot* is the standard rabbinic provision applying to all night-offerings (a protective fence against inadvertent delay until morning) or a special limitation rooted in the verse *vayehi bachatzi halailah* is debated; in context, the *beraita* appears to treat it as the standard rabbinic *chatzot*. *Ve'eino ne'echal ela limnuyav* — it may only be eaten by those who pre-registered for that particular offering. *Ve'eino ne'echal ela tzali* — and it may only be eaten roasted, not boiled or cooked.

### Yose HaGalili

The Gemara asks: *man tanna?* — who is the *tanna* who rules that all three of these offerings require only a single blood application? Rav Chisda answers: it is Rabbi Yose HaGalili. The derivation works as follows. By *bechor*, the Torah writes: *ve'et damam tizrok al hamizbe'ach ve'et chelbam taktir* — throw their blood on the altar and burn their fat. The word *damam* — "their blood" — is plural, not "its blood" (*damo*); similarly, *chelbam* — "their fat" — rather than *chelbo*. Rabbi Yose HaGalili reads these plurals as encompassing *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *pesach* together: *limed al habechor uma'aser vapesach shete'unin matan damim ve'imurim legabei hamizbe'ach* — they all require blood application and burning of the *imurim* on the *mizbe'ach*. Since the Torah provides no further specification, a single application (*matanah achat*) suffices.

A striking observation: by *korban Pesach*, the Torah never explicitly states what is to be done with the blood at the Temple. This is particularly noteworthy given the nature of the offering. The *korban Pesach* is fundamentally oriented toward eating — it is referred to as *korban Hashem* but never as *korban laHashem*, and the phrase *lerei'ach nicho'ach* never appears in connection with it. In Egypt, the blood was placed on the doorposts rather than offered on an altar; to some degree, the offering is less about presenting something to God and more about sanctifying the meat for the purposes of the commanded meal. It is therefore quite significant that the *halachah* of what to do with the blood in the Temple is learned not from any explicit verse about *pesach* but by *gezerah shavah* from *bechor*.

### Yesod Requirement

How do we know that the single blood application must be *keneged hayesod* — in a location where the base of the *mizbe'ach* protrudes beneath? The Torah's verse simply says *tizrok al hamizbe'ach* — throw it on the altar — without specification. Rabbi Eliezer derives the *yesod* requirement via a *gezerah shavah*: *atya zerika zerika me'olah* — the same word *zerika* appears by the *olah*, and by the *olah* we know the blood must be applied *el yesod mizbe'ach ha'olah*. But how do we know that the *yesod* requirement for the *olah* does not also import the requirement of two applications that amount to four (*shetei matanot she'hein arba*)? If the *gezerah shavah* connects these offerings to the *olah*, perhaps it should bring along the *olah*'s fuller blood-application requirement.

### Abiay: One Matanah

Abaye resolves this. The Torah explicitly says *saviv* — "all around" — by the *olah* and also by the *chatat*. The rule of *shenei ketuvim haba'im ke'echad ein melamdin* — when the same teaching appears in two separate verses, it cannot serve as a basis for applying the rule elsewhere — limits *saviv* to those cases where it is explicitly stated. Since it is explicitly stated by *olah* and *chatat*, those two cases cannot be used as a model to import *saviv* into cases where the Torah was silent. Accordingly, the *gezerah shavah* from *olah* establishes only the *yesod* requirement, not the requirement of *saviv*.

### Hermeneutics

For those who hold that *shenei ketuvim haba'im ke'echad* do in fact teach elsewhere (the minority position), the Gemara notes that *saviv* appears in three cases — *olah*, *chatat*, and *asham* — and three cases (*sheloshah vadai ein melamdin*) certainly cannot serve as a basis for applying the rule elsewhere.

Rashi adds an observation that enriches the hermeneutic picture. Normally, the principle of *shenei ketuvim haba'im ke'echad* means that when a rule appears in two (or more) places, you cannot extend it further by analogy. Here, however, the principle is working in the opposite direction: the fact that *saviv* is explicitly stated in those cases restricts the scope of the *gezerah shavah* of *zerika zerika*. Even though the *gezerah shavah* would otherwise connect *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *pesach* to the *olah* and might seem to import all the characteristics of *olah*'s blood-service, the explicit limitation of *saviv* to *olah*, *chatat*, and *asham* signals that this feature is deliberately confined to those three. The *gezerah shavah* therefore carries over only the *yesod* requirement — a single application in a location where the base protrudes — and nothing more. The Torah's silence regarding *pesach* and *ma'aser* is thus deliberate, and the halachic result is both elegant and precisely calibrated.

---

---

# Zevachim 57

## Kodashim Kalim Categories

### Three Kodashim Types

The present daf — the last of the fifth *perek* — opens its discussion of *kodashim kalim* by examining three remaining sacrificial categories: *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *pesach*. All three share a common structural feature: a single application of blood *keneged hayesod*. Beyond that, however, they diverge considerably in the parameters governing their consumption. The *bechor* is eaten exclusively by *kohanim*; *ma'aser behema* is eaten by its owners and may be consumed anywhere within Yerushalayim; and the *pesach* is subject to a unique set of restrictions — it may only be eaten until *chatzot*, only roasted, and only by those who had been counted among its registered participants (*limnuyav*). Both *bechor* and *ma'aser* are eaten over two days and the intervening night, while the *pesach* is more severely limited. The Gemara now proceeds to derive the sources for each of these parameters.

## Bechor Two Days/Night

### Tannaim Bechor Source

The *Tanu Rabbanan* opens by asking: from where do we derive that a *bechor* may be eaten for two days and the intervening night? The *Torah* does not state this period explicitly for *bechor*. The answer lies in a verse that links the *bechor* directly to the *shelamim*: *uvesaram yihye lach kachazeh hatenufa ukeshok hayamin lach yihye* — "and their flesh shall be yours, like the breast of waving and like the right thigh" (Bamidbar 18:18). The verse compares the flesh of the *bechor* to the *chazeh* and *shok* of the *shelamim*. Just as *shelamim* is eaten for two days and one intervening night — a rule explicit in the *Torah* — so too *bechor* is eaten for two days and the intervening night. The reason the verse does not simply say "the *bechor* belongs to the *kohanim*" is precisely to create this *hekesh* and thereby teach the eating period.

### Yavneh Question

This question was put before the Sages in the *kerem* of Yavneh — the *yeshiva* that reconstituted Torah scholarship following the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The question posed was: for how long is a *bechor* eaten? Rabbi Tarfon answered directly: two days and the intervening night, though at this stage he did not explain the derivation.

### Yose HaGalili Challenge

A student who was attending the *beit midrash* for the very first time — later to become the celebrated Rabbi Yose HaGalili — pressed Rabbi Tarfon for his source. Rabbi Tarfon responded with a *ma matzinu* argument: *shelamim* are *kodashim kalim* and *bechor* is *kodashim kalim*; just as *shelamim* is eaten for two days and one night, so too *bechor*. Rabbi Yose HaGalili immediately challenged this reasoning: one could equally well categorize the *bechor* not alongside *shelamim* but alongside *chatat* and *asham*, for *bechor matana lakohen vechatat ve'asham matana lakohen* — the *bechor*, like the *chatat* and the *asham*, is given as a gift directly to the *kohen*. Just as *chatat* and *asham* are eaten for only one day and the following night, perhaps *bechor* should likewise be eaten for only one day and night.

### Tarfon Responds

Rabbi Tarfon acknowledged the logic but pushed back: one should compare things to what they most resemble, and there is a compelling reason to place *bechor* alongside *shelamim* rather than *chatat* and *asham*. Neither *shelamim* nor *bechor* comes as a result of any sin — *shelamim ein ba'in al cheit af bechor eino ba al cheit*. They are both *kodashim kalim*, freely brought and not sin-related. On those grounds, the two-day period of *shelamim* should apply to *bechor* as well.

### Yose Counter-argument

Rabbi Yose HaGalili was not persuaded. He countered that just as one should compare like to like, there remains an equally compelling reason to align *bechor* with *chatat* and *asham*: not only are all three given as gifts to the *kohen*, but there is an additional structural parallel — *chatat* and *asham* cannot be brought as a voluntary offering (*neder* or *nedava*); they arise from obligation. Similarly, *bechor* is not voluntary — the animal is automatically consecrated as *peter rechem*, and there is no act of will that creates it. Therefore, by this logic, *bechor* should be treated like *chatat* and *asham* and eaten for only one day and one night. The debate at this point reached an impasse, with two equally balanced analogical arguments on either side.

## Akiva-Yishmael Debate

### Akiva Explicit Text

At this point Rabbi Akiva entered the discussion — and Rabbi Tarfon stepped aside. Rabbi Akiva argued that the dispute need not rest on inferential analogy at all, because the *Torah* itself provides an explicit textual link. The verse *uvesaram yihye lach* directly compares the *bechor* to the *chazeh* and *shok* — and those portions belong specifically to the *shelamim*. Since the text has already performed the comparison for us, *bechor* is equated to *shelamim*, and the two-day eating period follows.

### Yose Toda Question

Rabbi Yose HaGalili, however, refused to concede. Yes, he agreed, the verse links the *bechor* to the *chazeh* and *shok* — but who says it is the *chazeh* and *shok* of a *shelamim* specifically? Perhaps it is the *chazeh* and *shok* of a *toda* (thanksgiving offering). And since a *toda* is eaten for only one day and one night, the *bechor* would correspondingly be limited to that shorter period as well.

### Akiva Lach Yihye

Rabbi Akiva offered a response: the verse begins *uvesaram yihye lach* and then concludes with *lach yihye* — the phrase "it shall be yours" appears twice. This repetition is superfluous if it merely restates the same point. The extra *lach yihye* at the end is therefore coming to teach something additional: the *bechor* is granted to the *kohanim* in an even more expansive way — *hosif hakatuv havaya acheret b'bechor* — pointing to the longer eating period of *shelamim* rather than the shorter period of *toda*.

### Yishmael Correction

When this entire exchange was reported to Rabbi Yishmael, he responded sharply: *ta'ita* — Rabbi Akiva had erred by conceding the initial point. The concession was that, absent the extra *lach yihye*, one might have thought the verse was linking *bechor* to the *chazeh* and *shok* of a *toda*. But this concession was fundamentally mistaken: from where do we know that a *toda* even *has* a *chazeh* and a *shok*? The *toda* is a form of *shelamim*, and it is only from the *shelamim* that we know the *toda* has these portions at all. The *toda*'s *chazeh* and *shok* are themselves derived through a *hekesh* connecting *toda* to *shelamim*.

### Heikesh Double-Apply

This is the principle of *davar halamad b'hekesh ein chozer u'melamed b'hekesh*: something that has been learned through *hekesh* cannot in turn go and teach through another *hekesh*. Since the existence of a *chazeh* and *shok* by a *toda* is itself known only through its connection to *shelamim*, one cannot use the *toda*'s *chazeh* and *shok* as the referent of the link in the *bechor* verse. The verse linking *bechor* to *chazeh* and *shok* must therefore be pointing to the *chazeh* and *shok* of *shelamim* directly — since only there does the rule exist independently. Rabbi Akiva should have maintained his original position from the outset, and the *lach yihye* is not needed for this purpose.

## Lach Yihye Mum

### Yishmael Mum Teaching

The Gemara now asks: since Rabbi Yishmael does not need *lach yihye* to establish the two-day eating period — that follows directly from the unambiguous *hekesh* to *shelamim* — what does Rabbi Yishmael do with the extra phrase? The answer is that *lach yihye* teaches an entirely different *halacha*: even a *bechor ba'al mum* — a firstborn animal with a physical blemish — is given to the *kohen*, and the *kohen* eats it without bringing it as a *korban*. This is an unprecedented rule (*shelo matzinu bechol haTorah*): Rashi understands this to mean it is not stated explicitly anywhere else in the *Torah* that a blemished animal goes to the *kohen*; Tosafot, cited elsewhere, interpret it more broadly to mean there is nothing else like it in the entire *Torah* — an animal that is not redeemed, not brought as a sacrifice, but simply eaten with its *mum* intact.

### Akiva Besaram

The Gemara asks: and where does Rabbi Akiva — who uses *lach yihye* to establish the two-day period — derive this rule about the *bechor ba'al mum*? Rabbi Akiva derives it from the plural form *besaram*, "their flesh." The word *besaram* (rather than *besaro*, "its flesh") indicates a plurality of cases: one for the *tam* (unblemished animal) and one for the *ba'al mum*.

### Yishmael Besaram

Rabbi Yishmael, by contrast, reads *besaram* as referring not to two categories of *bechor* (blemished and unblemished) but to the multiple species of *bechor* that have been mentioned — *shor*, *ez*, *kesev*, and so forth. For him, *besaram* simply aggregates the various animal types and does not extend to teach about the *ba'al mum*. That teaching comes instead from *lach yihye*, as stated above.

## Himenu v'Davar Acher

### Akiva Reasoning

The Gemara now turns to the underlying disagreement between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael — specifically, why Rabbi Akiva initially accepted Rabbi Yose HaGalili's challenge about learning from the *toda*'s *chazeh* and *shok*, when in principle this should be ruled out by *davar halamad b'hekesh ein chozer u'melamed b'hekesh*. The answer is that Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael dispute a more nuanced application of this principle. The principle states that something learned through a *hekesh* cannot in turn be used to teach through another *hekesh*. But what if only *part* of the relevant law was learned through *hekesh*, while another part was already present in the intermediate category independently? In that scenario — referred to as *himenu v'davar acher* — Rabbi Akiva holds that the restriction does not apply. The reasoning can be modeled as a three-step chain: law X is introduced in category A; through a *hekesh*, A teaches B, so X now applies to B; and then, from B to C through another *hekesh*, one wishes to extend X to C. The concern is precisely this double-step. But if category B already contained part of X independently — apart from anything derived from A — then, according to Rabbi Akiva, linking B to C carries with it the part that was already in B, and the derived portion can travel along. The rule against double *hekesh* does not block this.

Applied to our case: the law we wish to derive for the *bechor* from the *toda* is that it is eaten for one day and one night. The one-day rule is explicitly stated by a *toda* in the *Torah* — that is the "part already present in B." What was learned through *hekesh* from *shelamim* to *toda* is only the existence of a *chazeh* and a *shok* by the *toda*. So when the *bechor* verse links to *chazeh* and *shok*, and one argues it refers to the *toda*'s *chazeh* and *shok*, what we would be deriving is the one-day rule — but that was already present in the *toda* independently. This is why Rabbi Akiva thought the argument from *toda* was legitimate, and why he felt compelled to rebut it using the double *lach yihye*.

### Yishmael View

Rabbi Yishmael disagrees: even in a case of *himenu v'davar acher* — even when part of the relevant law already exists in the intermediate category — the principle of *davar halamad b'hekesh ein chozer u'melamed b'hekesh* still applies in full. The reason is that nothing can actually happen through the link from B to C unless the *hekesh*-derived element (the existence of *chazeh* and *shok* in the *toda*) is operative. The fact that the one-day rule is independently present in *toda* is beside the point: the vehicle of transmission — the *chazeh* and *shok* — only exists in *toda* because of the *shelamim* connection. Therefore the double *hekesh* remains blocked, and Rabbi Akiva's concession was unwarranted.

### Pesach Kapparah

The Gemara now brings a different case to test these positions. On Yom Kippur, the *kohen gadol* sprinkles blood in the *Kodesh Kodashim* — once above and seven times below — from both the *par* (the ox) and the *se'ir* (the goat). The *Torah* states explicitly by the *par* that there are seven sprinklings below but does not specify how many above; by the *se'ir*, the word *oto* ("it") implies one sprinkling above, but the seven below are not stated. Since the verse links the two — *ve'asitem ka'asher asa ledam hapar* — each is derived from the other, giving both animals one above and seven below.

The question then becomes: how many sprinklings are done in the *heichal* (outside the *Kodesh Kodashim*), on the *parochet*? The verse says *vechen ya'aseh le'ohel mo'ed* — "so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting" — indicating that the same pattern of one above and seven below applies there as well, for both the *par* and the *se'ir*. But the "one above" for the *par* was only learned from the *se'ir* via *hekesh*. Extending that knowledge to the *heichal* appears to be a second application of that *hekesh*-derived rule — a double step that would be problematic for Rabbi Yishmael.

The Gemara offers two resolutions for Rabbi Yishmael's position. First: *mekomos hu digemiri mehadadi* — the two *hekesh* applications here are not of the same type. The first *hekesh* links the *par* to the *se'ir*; the second links the *Kodesh Kodashim* to the *heichal*. These are distinct comparisons — one between animals, the other between locations — and that distinction means it does not constitute a problematic double-chain.

### Resolution

Second resolution, found at the top of 57b: *chutz mi'pnim b'chad zimna gamir* — the laws for the interior and the exterior are learned together at the same time, not sequentially. Rashi explains: the *par* already has seven sprinklings on the inside independently. The link from inside to outside carries the seven from the *par* on purely direct grounds — no *hekesh* is needed. Once that direct link is operative, one can piggyback and include the "one above" that was learned through the *par*-*se'ir* *hekesh*. This is crucially different from the *toda* case. In the *toda* case, the entire vehicle of transmission — the existence of *chazeh* and *shok* in the *toda* — depends on the *hekesh* from *shelamim*. Nothing moves without it. Here, by contrast, the seven-sprinkling rule travels on its own independent basis from inside to outside; the *hekesh*-derived element (the one above) merely rides along. For Rabbi Yishmael, this distinction is decisive: when there is a genuine independent anchor in the target category, the derived element may accompany it. It is only when *nothing at all* can move without first invoking the *hekesh*-derived component that the principle blocks the chain entirely.

## Shtei HaLechem

### Lechem Heikesh

The Gemara introduces another test case — this time regarding the *shtei halechem* brought on Shavuot. The verse states: *mi'moshvoteichem tavi'u lechem tenufa* — "from your dwellings you shall bring a wave-bread offering." By the *shtei halechem*, the *Torah* specifies *shnei esronim* — two *esronim* of flour for the two loaves, meaning one *issaron* per loaf. We now wish to derive that the ten *chametz* loaves of a *toda* also require one *issaron* per loaf — that is, ten *esronim* total for the *chametz* portion of the *toda*. This derivation is performed by linking the *shtei halechem* (category A) to the *toda*'s *chametz* loaves (category B), establishing one *issaron* per *chametz* loaf wherever *chametz* is brought.

### Matza Extension

But a *toda* also includes thirty *matzah* loaves. How do we know that the total flour for those thirty *matzah* loaves also equals ten *esronim*? The verse *al challat lechem chametz* teaches that the *matzah* corresponds proportionally to the *chametz* — *neged chametz havi matzah* — so the total weight of the *matzah* equals the total weight of the *chametz*, even though the *matzah* loaves are individually smaller (each being one-third of an *issaron*). The derivation thus runs: from the *shtei halechem* (A) to the *toda chametz* (B), one learns one *issaron* per loaf; then from the *toda chametz* (B) to the *toda matzah* (C), one learns ten *esronim* total. This is a two-step chain — and the question is whether it constitutes a prohibited *davar halamad b'hekesh chozer u'melamed b'hekesh*.

For Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *himenu v'davar acher* does not constitute a prohibited double-*hekesh*, this is straightforward: the number ten was already present in B (there were always ten *chametz* loaves), and only the *issaron*-per-loaf rule was learned through *hekesh*. Applying the total of ten *esronim* from *chametz* to *matzah* is anchored in that pre-existing element. But for Rabbi Yishmael, who prohibits even *himenu v'davar acher*, a problem remains — and the Gemara must explain how even his position permits this two-step learning.

### Taviu Direct Rule

The Gemara resolves this for Rabbi Yishmael's position: *taviu yeseira hu* — the word *tavi'u* in the verse is redundant. The verse did not need to say *tavi'u*; the text already established the *shtei halechem*. The extra *tavi'u* therefore functions not as a *hekesh* but as an independent, direct rule: whenever you bring *chametz* as a waved offering, one *issaron* per loaf applies — regardless of which sacrifice is involved. Because this rule is stated directly by the verse rather than derived through analogy, it is not subject to the restriction on double *hekesh*. The law applies to the *toda chametz* on its own textual authority, and from there the *matzah* derivation proceeds without any forbidden chaining.

## Pesach Chatzot

### Elazar ben Azarya

The discussion now turns to the final clause of the *mishnah*: the *pesach* is eaten only until *chatzot*. The Gemara identifies this position as that of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya — a figure familiar from the first *mishnah* of *Berachot*, where the same authority rules that the *afikoman* must be eaten before *chatzot* on *Pesach* night. The *baraita* records his argument: the verse states *balayla hazeh* regarding the eating of the *pesach*, and separately, God says *va'e'evor b'eretz Mitzrayim balayla hazeh* regarding the plague of the firstborn. Through a *gezerah shavah* on the phrase *balayla hazeh*, we link the eating of the *pesach* to the moment of *makat bechorot*, which occurred at *chatzot*. Just as the plague struck at midnight, so too the eating of the *pesach* is limited to until *chatzot*.

### Akiva Night Eating

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. He cites the verse *va'achaltem oto bechipazon* — "you shall eat it in haste." The *chipazon* — the hurrying and rushing — refers to the actual departure from Egypt, which occurred in the morning. Therefore the permitted eating window extends throughout the entire night, until the time of actual departure. The *pesach* is eaten the whole night.

### Akiva Balayla

Given his position, Rabbi Akiva must explain what the phrase *balayla hazeh* comes to teach. He argues: one might have thought that just like other *kodashim*, which are brought and may begin to be consumed during the day, the *pesach* should similarly be eaten during the day of the fourteenth. The verse therefore states *balayla* — no, the *pesach* is eaten specifically at night, not during the preceding day. The phrase *balayla hazeh* is not connecting the *pesach* to *makat bechorot* to establish a *chatzot* deadline; rather, it is simply excluding daytime eating.

### Abaye Question

Abaye raises a pointed question directed at Rav Yosef's attribution of the *mishnah* to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya. Why must we say the *mishnah* reflects Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's position — namely that the *chatzot* limit is *de'oraita*? Perhaps the *mishnah* accords with Rabbi Akiva's ruling that the *pesach* is permitted all night *de'oraita*, and the *chatzot* deadline stated in the *mishnah* is merely *derabbanan* — a rabbinic precaution to distance a person from potential transgression. This is precisely the principle stated in *Masechet Berachot*: even for *kodashim* that are permitted all night, the Sages decreed that they be completed by *chatzot* as a protective measure.

This is, as the lecturer acknowledges after a moment's reconsideration, actually a strong question — because in fact the *mishnah* in the earlier part of the *perek* does say *ad chatzot* regarding other *kodashim* such as *zivchei shalmei tzibur*, *ashamot*, *toda*, and *eil nazir*, which are technically eaten all night but are described with the *chatzot* deadline reflecting the rabbinic precaution. So when the *mishnah* says *chatzot* by *pesach*, why should that be treated differently — why not simply say it too is *derabbanan*?

### Deoraita Limit

The Gemara's answer is precise and telling. The *mishnah*'s phrasing regarding *pesach* is *ve'eino ne'echal ella ad chatzot* — "and it is not eaten except until *chatzot*." The critical word is *ella* — the formulation is one of absolute exclusion. Wherever else the *mishnah* says *ad chatzot*, it says simply *ne'echal ad chatzot*; here it says *eino ne'echal ella ad chatzot*. The *ella* construction indicates that *chatzot* is an absolute and definitive boundary — the language of something that simply cannot occur, not a rabbinic guideline reflecting an ideal cutoff. This phrasing marks the limit as *de'oraita*, not merely a precaution enacted *derabbanan*. The *mishnah* therefore follows the position of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who holds that the *pesach* is forbidden *mi'de'oraita* after *chatzot*.

With this, we conclude the fifth *perek* of *Zevachim*. *Hadran alach Eizehu Mekoman.*

# Zevachim 58

## Slaughtering at Altar Top

### Perek Opening

Daf 58 opens a new *perek*, *Kodshei Kodashim*. Having devoted the previous *perek* to laying out the rules for each *korban* — where it is slaughtered, where its blood is applied — the Talmud now turns to the consequences of deviation from those rules. One might have wished that every *masechet* began this way: one *perek* establishing the basic rules, followed immediately by a *perek* exploring what happens when they are not followed. As it happens, we had to wait until the fifth *perek* for this opening statement, and now the sixth *perek* takes up the question of deviation.

### North Slaughter Rule

The foundational rule with which this *perek* begins is well established: *kodshei kodashim* — sacrifices of the highest sanctity — must have their *shechita* performed in the north. This was set out in the previous *perek*. The present *perek* asks: what happens when the rules are not followed perfectly?

### Top of Altar Issue

The first case the *mishnah* takes up is: what if the *kodshei kodashim* were slaughtered not in the north of the *azarah* opposite the altar, but on top of the altar itself? The issue here is not whether the top of the altar counts as valid ground for the purpose of *shechita* — one can assume the altar, as an extension connected to the floor, carries the same status as the ground below, especially given that *kohanim* perform their *avodah* while standing on the altar. The real question is one of geometry: if the *shechita* must be performed *al yerech hamizbeach tzafonah* — on the north side of the altar — does "north" refer to the northern half of the *mikdash* or to the north side of the altar itself? And when the animal is brought to the top of the altar, which portions of that top surface count as valid?

## Yosi Positions

### Yosi: Whole Altar

*Rabbi Yosi omer: ke'ilu nishchetu batzafon* — Rabbi Yosi says that if *kodshei kodashim* were slaughtered on top of the altar, it is as if they were slaughtered in the north. The phrasing is immediately striking: he says "as if" (*ke'ilu*) they were slaughtered in the north — not that they actually were. This invites the question of what the qualification is. If Rabbi Yosi holds that the entire altar is situated in the north of the *mikdash*, why would he describe slaughter on top of it as merely "as if" in the north? One would expect him simply to say it is in the north.

### Yosi bar Yehuda: Half/Ha…

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda offers a different ruling: *mechatzi hamizbeach uledarom kadarom, mechatzi hamizbeach uletzafon katzafon* — from the midpoint of the altar southward, it is treated as the south; from the midpoint northward, it is treated as the north. This position reflects the intuitive assumption that the altar is centered in the *azarah*, straddling the dividing line between north and south. On that reading, the northern half of the altar lies in the northern hemisphere of the *mikdash* and is valid for *kodshei kodashim*, while the southern half is not.

### As If Analysis

The tension in Rabbi Yosi's language now becomes the *gemara*'s first point of inquiry. Rav Assi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, reports that Rabbi Yosi held *kulo mizbeach batzafon kai* — the entire altar stands in the north. On that understanding, the phrase *ke'ilu* — "as if" — is not conceding that the top of the altar falls short of the northern designation. Rather, it addresses a different concern: one might have thought that *al yerech hamizbeach* requires the *shechita* to take place specifically on the side of the altar, not on its top surface — much as a hole-in-one is not the same as getting the ball closest to the hole. The word *ke'ilu* therefore comes to teach us that slaughtering on the top of the altar itself is sufficient and counts as if it were performed along the side, provided the location falls within the northern zone of the *mikdash* opposite the altar (*kineged hamizbeach*).

## Yochanan's Approach

### Altar in North

The tradition reported by Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is therefore that Rabbi Yosi's position — that the whole top of the altar is valid — reflects his view that the entire altar stands in the north. The *ke'ilu* of the *mishnah* is not concessive but pedagogic: it comes to forestall the misreading that *al yerech* demands contact with the side rather than the top.

### Zeira Challenge

Rabbi Zeira challenges Rav Assi. His challenge is reasonable: if Rabbi Yosi's ruling that the whole altar top is valid reflects his view that the whole altar is in the north, then by the same logic, Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that only the northern half of the altar top is valid must reflect his view that the altar is positioned half in the north and half in the south. The debate in the *mishnah*, on this reading, is simply a debate about where the altar is situated. Rabbi Zeira presses this point: *v'chi teima hachi nami* — isn't that exactly the right inference?

### Below Altar Proof

Rav Assi responds by pointing to a tradition he himself had cited in Rabbi Yochanan's name: *modei Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda she'im shachtan kenegdan bakarka pesulah* — Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda concedes that if one slaughtered *kodshei kodashim* directly below the northern half of the altar at ground level, the *shechita* is invalid.

The challenge posed by this ruling is conceptual. To understand the ruling, one must first understand what scenario is being described, but let us begin with its implication. If Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda held that the altar is situated half in the north and half in the south — that is, if the north half of the altar is genuinely in the northern zone — then slaughtering directly beneath the northern half, at ground level, should be valid: one would be in the north. The fact that it is invalid suggests that the ground directly beneath the altar's northern half is not, in fact, situated in the northern zone. That can only be the case if the altar is not half-north, half-south at all, but is entirely situated in the south. The northern half of the altar top is valid only by virtue of a special scriptural dispensation — not because the altar occupies the north. And what is below the altar, absent any such dispensation, remains in the south and is therefore invalid.

One might have proposed a different explanation: that ground-level space directly beneath the north of the altar is invalid not because it is not in the north, but because it is not *al yerech hamizbeach* — it is neither the altar itself nor north of the altar in any meaningful sense. The airspace extends upward, but not downward. The *gemara*, however, does not accept this logic. It reads the invalidity of ground-level slaughter directly below the northern half as definitive evidence that that space is not in the northern zone — implying that the altar, for Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda, is situated entirely in the south.

### Verse Interpretation

With this, the *gemara* recasts the entire *mishnah* debate. Rabbi Yochanan's conclusion: *shneihem mikra echad darshu* — both Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda are debating the interpretation of a single verse, not staking out positions about where the altar is physically situated.

The verse in question is *vezavachta alav et olotecha ve'et shelamecha* — "and you shall slaughter upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings." The word *alav* — "upon it" — is read with unusual literalism: one may slaughter directly on top of the altar. This is striking, and Tosafos on the first *tosafos* of this *perek* notes explicitly that according to this verse, *lechatchila* one is permitted to perform *shechita* on top of the altar from Torah law. The only possible rabbinic restriction, Tosafos suggests, is that one should not bring a live animal to the top of the altar because of the concern that it will defecate there — but from the Torah itself, the top of the altar is a valid location.

The debate between Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda is then about how to read this verse. Rabbi Yosi holds *kulo le'ola v'kulo lishlamim*: the entire top of the altar may be used for an *olah* and the entire top for a *shelamim*. The verse permits using the full surface for either. The fact that it mentions both *olotecha* and *shelamecha* is not to divide them; it is simply because one might have thought the dispensation was granted only for the *olah*, which has limited space in the *azarah* during busy periods, and not for the *shelamim*, which has ample space elsewhere. The verse comes to teach that the *shelamim* may also be slaughtered anywhere on top.

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, reads the verse as dividing the altar top: *chatzi le'ola v'chatzi lishlamim* — half for the *olah* and half for the *shelamim*. The northern half is designated for the *olah*, the southern for the *shelamim*. This is structurally analogous to the debate about *Yom Tov* — whether it is entirely for God, entirely for oneself, or divided.

The upshot of Rabbi Yochanan's reformulation is decisive: the positions in the *mishnah* are about scriptural interpretation for this particular *halachah* of the altar top. They say nothing about where the altar is actually situated. In principle, Rabbi Yosi could hold that the entire altar is in the south and still permit the entire altar top by virtue of the verse. And Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda could hold that the altar is in the south and still divide the top in half based on the same verse. The question of where each *tanna* holds the altar to be situated must come from elsewhere — from some independent source or tradition — not from their positions in the *mishnah*. The tradition that for Rabbi Yosi the entire altar stands in the north must be grounded in some Tannaitic text.

## Below Altar Scenarios

### Ground Below Query

Having established that the invalidity of slaughtering directly beneath the northern half of the altar at ground level is part of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's position, the *gemara* turns to a pointed practical question: *mai kenegdan bakarka* — how does one actually get to ground level directly beneath the altar? The altar is sitting there. One cannot simply stand on the ground beneath it. Is this a hovering altar? A theoretical case with no real-world scenario?

### Sovev Solution

The first possibility: perhaps what the *gemara* means by "below the altar at ground level" is not the earth beneath the altar itself, but rather a position on the *sovev* — the walk-around ledge — or on the *yesod* — the base course. One would be at ground level in the sense of standing on an outer structural element rather than on the top of the altar. This is rejected: *hai gufa mizbeach hu* — that is itself the altar. The *sovev* and the *yesod* are integral parts of the *mizbeach*. A dispensation for slaughtering on the altar would encompass them as well. The case of slaughtering "below the altar at ground level" must refer to actual earth, not to architectural features of the altar structure. Moreover, the phrasing *kenegdan bakarka* — "opposite them on the ground" — plainly indicates actual ground, not a structural platform.

### Tunnels Rejected

The next possibility: perhaps one excavates tunnels (*mechilot*) or vaulted underground spaces (*kippin*) directly beneath the northern half of the altar, creating a cavity in which a person could stand on the ground while physically positioned beneath the altar's northern portion. But this is ruled out by a *beraita*: *mizbeach adama ta'aseh li* — "you shall make for Me an altar of earth" — is interpreted to mean the altar must be connected to solid ground. Specifically, *she-lo yivnennu agav mechilot ve-lo agav kippin* — one may not build the altar over tunnels or over vaulted underground spaces. The altar must rest on uninterrupted compressed earth; any cavity beneath it would compromise its status. The *gemara* takes this requirement to mean that there can be no hollow space anywhere beneath the altar's footprint — a stringent reading of *adama* as demanding that the altar be truly integrated with the ground beneath it.

### Reconfiguration

The *gemara* settles on a third scenario: *de-batzrei bitzurei* — the altar was reconfigured and reduced in size. In some circumstances it was apparently possible to alter the dimensions of the altar (the dimensions specified as *halachah le-Moshe mi-Sinai* are not the dimensions of the Second Temple altar), and if the altar was made smaller, a strip of the ground that previously lay beneath the northern part of the altar would be exposed. A person could stand there on actual ground, directly opposite where the northern half had been. The *gemara* confirms this is the intended scenario. And crucially, on this reading, the ruling that slaughtering there is invalid carries a clear implication: the ground that was formerly under the northern half of the altar, once exposed, is not in the northern zone — it is in the south. This means the altar in Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's view is situated entirely in the south, with the northern half of its top permitted only by scriptural dispensation, not because it occupies the northern zone.

## Second Pyre Tannaim

### Tamid Source

Rabbi Zeira, recognizing that the tradition of Rabbi Yochanan must have some basis in Tannaitic literature, goes and searches and finds the following *mishnah* in tractate Tamid. The *mishnah* there describes the selection of wood to place on the *ma'aracha*, the arrangement of logs on the altar fire. Specifically, the priests would select fine fig wood for the *ma'aracha shniya shel ktoreth* — the second pyre designated for the purpose of burning the incense. This second fire on the altar top was distinct from the main central fire on which the *korbanot* were consumed. From the second pyre, coals would be taken to the inner golden altar for the daily burning of the *ketoreth*. Rabbi Rashi notes that fig wood may have been preferred for its quality, and also suggests a connection to the fig leaves with which Adam covered himself after his sin, giving the wood a kind of redemptive association. Regardless, this second arrangement of wood was maintained specifically for the incense service.

### Four Amot Location

The *mishnah* in Tamid specifies where on the altar this second pyre was situated: *keneged keren maaravit dromit* — opposite the southwestern corner — *mashuch min hakeren klapei tzafon arba amot* — set back from the corner four *amot* in the direction of the north. In other words, at the southwestern corner of the altar top, four *amot* removed northward from the southernmost edge.

The pyre was sized to produce *be-omed chamesh se'in gechalim* — approximately five *se'in* of coals, sufficient for the coal-taking required for the daily incense offering. On *Shabbat*, the fire was built larger to produce approximately eight *se'in* of coals, since on *Shabbat* coals were also required to burn the frankincense of the *lechem hapanim* — the show-bread — on the outer altar.

The *mishnah* in Tamid adds: *ve-sham hayu notnim shenei bezikhei levonah shel lechem hapanim* — and it was there that they would place the two scoops of frankincense of the *lechem hapanim*. The fire at the southwestern corner therefore served a dual purpose: it supplied the coals for the daily *ketoreth*, and it was the place where the *levonah* from the *shulchan* was burned on *Shabbat*.

### Inside/Outside Principle

The *mishnah* in Tamid then poses the question: *u-mah simanah* — what is the identifying marker? That is, what is the *siman* that pins down this location? *Rabbi Yosi hi* — the *mishnah* is in accordance with Rabbi Yosi. And the *gemara* cites the relevant *beraita*: *kol ha-nital bifnim lenatan bachutz eino nital ela besamuch* — anything taken from inside (the *heichal*) to be placed outside (in the *azarah*) is taken out only adjacent to the exit. Symmetrically, anything taken from outside to be brought inside is taken only from the place nearest the entrance of the *heichal*.

This principle is attributed to Rabbi Yosi, and it is a principle rather than an explicit verse — which is why it serves as a *siman* rather than a derivation from *pesukim*. The *gemara* clarifies what kinds of acts fall under each half of this rule. One might have thought that the "inside to outside" half refers to the spilling of the remaining blood (*shirayim*) at the base of the altar — but that is explicitly stated in a verse: *el yesod mizbeach ha-olah asher petach ohel moed* — "at the base of the burnt offering altar which is at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting." No *siman* of Rabbi Yosi is needed there. Similarly, the "outside to inside" half might have referred to the coals taken on *Yom Kippur*, but that too is explicit: *velakach melo hamachtah gechalei esh me'al hamizbeach milifnei Hashem* — "and he shall take a pan full of burning coals from the altar before God" — meaning from the place nearest the *heichal*.

### Frankincense Evidence

The *gemara* therefore identifies the actual subjects of Rabbi Yosi's rule. For "inside to outside," the application is *shenei bezikhei levonah shel lechem hapanim* — the two scoops of frankincense from the *shulchan*. These are taken from inside the *heichal* and brought out to be burned on the outer altar, and no verse specifies where on the outer altar this is done. Rabbi Yosi's principle establishes that it must be done adjacent to where one exits — that is, at the western portion of the altar, the side nearest the *heichal* entrance. For "outside to inside," the application is *gechalim d'chol yoma v'yoma* — the coals taken daily for the burning of the *ketoreth*. These are taken from the outer altar to be brought inside to the golden altar, and while *Yom Kippur* coals are explicitly required to come from *milifnei Hashem* — the front of the altar, near the *heichal* — no verse specifies this for the daily coal-taking. Rabbi Yosi derives it by analogy.

The second pyre thus stands at the western side of the altar because both the frankincense and the daily coals must be handled adjacent to the *heichal* entrance, and the western face of the altar is the face nearest that entrance. It is specifically the southwest because when ascending the altar — which one does from the south — the southwestern corner is the first part of the western face that one reaches, making it the nearest practicable point. This *mishnah* in Tamid therefore reflects Rabbi Yosi's principle and is attributed to him.

## Four Amot Calculation

### All South Theory

Now that the *mishnah* in Tamid has been attributed to Rabbi Yosi, the *gemara* asks what the measurement of four *amot* from the southern edge tells us about where Rabbi Yosi held the altar to be situated. The logic is as follows: the second pyre must be positioned *keneged* — opposite — the opening of the *heichal*. It must fall within the zone of the doorway. The *gemara* considers three scenarios.

If Rabbi Yosi held that the entire altar stands in the south, the center of the *mikdash* and the center of the altar would not coincide. The door of the *heichal* is in the center of the *mikdash*, spanning ten *amot* — five to each side of the midline. If the entire thirty-two-*amah* altar is in the southern half, then only five *amot* of the altar's width fall within the zone of the door. To get the fire on the altar top to a position opposite the door, one would have to move it at least twenty-seven *amot* northward from the southernmost edge — and at that point one would not describe it as being at the southwest corner but at the northwest corner. Alternatively, if the sanctity of the *heichal* and the *ulam* are considered a single continuous unit, the door of the *ulam* was twenty *amot* wide, giving ten *amot* in the southern zone — but even then, one would need to move the fire at least twenty-two *amot* from the edge. In neither case does "four *amot* from the south" make sense.

### Half/Half Theory

If the altar is centered — half in the north, half in the south — then the midline of the altar aligns with the midline of the *mikdash*. The door of the *heichal* (ten *amot* wide) gives five *amot* in each hemisphere. The altar is sixteen *amot* into the southern hemisphere from its southernmost point to center. To reach the zone of the door, one would need to move at least eleven *amot* from the southern edge. If the *ulam* door suffices (twenty *amot* wide, ten in each hemisphere), one would need to move at least six *amot* from the edge. Still not four.

### All North Theory

If the entire altar is in the north, the problem is reversed. The door of the *heichal* lies in the center of the *mikdash*, but since the altar is entirely in the northern hemisphere, the fire must stay as far south as possible — within the five *amot* of the door that fall into the northern zone. One may not push the fire any further north than that without departing from the zone of the door entirely.

### Base Components

The critical question, then, is: how much of the altar's vertical structure must one traverse before reaching the surface where the fire can be placed? Counting from the base of the altar upward: one *amah* for the *yesod*, one *amah* for the *sovev*, one *amah* for the space of the corner projections, and one *amah* for the walkway space used by the *kohanim* to move around the altar top. That totals four *amot*. Before one has any open surface available to place the fire, four *amot* of the altar's southern face have already been accounted for. The fire therefore sits at exactly the first available position — the immediate southernmost opening on the top surface — which is four *amot* above the base. At five *amot* above the base, the zone of the door would end; anything beyond that would fall outside the range of the *heichal* opening. So the measurement of four *amot* is actually a maximum: put the fire at the first available spot on the surface, and you are exactly within the five-*amah* range of the door.

This reading only works if the entire altar is in the north. Any other configuration forces the fire further northward — well beyond four *amot* from the base — to reach the zone of the door. The attribution of this *mishnah* in Tamid to Rabbi Yosi thus provides the Tannaitic grounding for Rabbi Yochanan's claim that Rabbi Yosi held *kulo mizbeach batzafon kai*.

## Adda Bar Ahava View

### Yehuda Centered

Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges this attribution. He proposes that the *mishnah* in Tamid belongs not to Rabbi Yosi but to Rabbi Yehuda. *Detanya: Rabbi Yehuda omer: mizbeach memutza ve-omed be-emtza azara* — Rabbi Yehuda explicitly states that the altar is centered in the *azarah*, positioned exactly halfway between north and south. Furthermore, *u-sheloshim u-shtayim amah hayu lo* — and its measure was thirty-two *amot*. And Rabbi Yehuda adds: *eser amot keneged pitcho shel heichal, achat esrei amah mikan ve-achat esrei amah mikan* — ten *amot* opposite the door of the *heichal*, and eleven *amot* to each side. The result is that the altar is precisely aligned with the *heichal*: *nimtza mizbeach mechuvvan keneged heichal* — the altar is found to be perfectly opposite the *heichal*. Rashi notes that this alignment is exact in both directions: the inner width of the *heichal* was twenty *amot*, and with six-*amah* thick walls on each side, the total structure was thirty-two *amot* — identical to the altar — and both are centered on the same axis.

### Top Measurement

On the assumption that the altar is centered and half in the north, one would need to move the fire at least eleven *amot* northward from the southern edge to reach the zone of the *heichal* door, or at least six *amot* to reach the zone of the *ulam* door. How, then, does Rabbi Yehuda's position accommodate the "four *amot*" of the Tamid *mishnah*?

The *gemara* answers with a clarification that represents a much more natural reading of the measurement: *mi kasavrat hani arba amot bahadi amah yesod ve-amah sovev* — who told you we are measuring from the base of the altar? The four *amot* are not counted from the ground up. They are counted from the top surface of the altar downward — or rather, from the edge of the top surface as one's starting point, moving inward. *Arba amot bar mimmah yesod ve-amah sovev* — the four *amot* are in addition to, and separate from, the *yesod* and *sovev*. The base and walk-around structure add two *amot* below the top surface. So four *amot* from the edge of the top surface equals six *amot* from the base of the altar. And six *amot* inward from the southern edge, on a centered altar, brings the fire exactly to the zone of the *ulam* door — which is the minimum required, assuming that the *heichal* and *ulam* are treated as a unified sacred precinct for this purpose.

This is, as noted, a more intuitive way of reading the measurement. A priest ascending to place the fire would naturally count from the surface he is standing on, not from the ground far below. Four *amot* from the surface edge is six *amot* from the base — and six *amot* from the southern edge of a centered, thirty-two-*amah* altar puts the fire at the entry zone of the *ulam* door.

### Attribution Question

The *gemara* now presses Rav Adda bar Ahava: having shown that the Tamid *mishnah* works for Rabbi Yehuda's position of a centered altar, why not then challenge Rabbi Yochanan's attribution entirely? One could argue that the *mishnah* in Tamid is consistent with Rabbi Yosi as well — that Rabbi Yosi holds the altar is centered, not entirely in the north, and the four *amot* is measured from the surface, yielding the same arithmetic. Why attribute the *mishnah* specifically to Rabbi Yehuda rather than simply saying that Rabbi Yosi holds it is half and half?

### Yehuda Explicit

The answer given: *mishum de-Rabbi Yehuda shamana lei mimutza behedya* — because we hear explicitly from Rabbi Yehuda that he holds the altar is centered. Rabbi Yehuda states this position outright in his own words. Once Rabbi Yehuda has explicitly articulated the position of a centered altar, and the Tamid *mishnah* fits that position, it is most natural to assign the *mishnah* to Rabbi Yehuda. But this answer concedes a limitation: there is now no compelling proof that Rabbi Yosi holds the entire altar is in the north. If Rabbi Yosi could be read to hold the altar is centered — just as Rabbi Yehuda explicitly does — then Rabbi Yochanan's assertion that Rabbi Yosi holds *kulo batzafon* remains without direct Tannaitic support from this *mishnah*.

## Yosi HaGalili

### HaGalili Intro

Rav Sharvaya proposes yet another attribution: *ha mani Rabbi Yosi HaGlili hi* — the *mishnah* in Tamid belongs to Rabbi Yosi HaGalili. This is a distinct *tanna* from the Rabbi Yosi discussed throughout — the latter being Rabbi Yosi bar Chalafta, the standard referent of the unqualified name — and also distinct from Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosi HaGalili is a *tanna* of an earlier generation, and the *gemara* now introduces a *beraita* in his name that takes the position that the entire altar is in the north.

### Kiyor Evidence

*Detanya: Rabbi Yosi HaGalili omer: mitoch shenemar ve-natata kiyor bein ohel moed u-vein hamizbeach* — as it is written: "and you shall place the laver between the Tent of Meeting and the altar." Rabbi Yosi HaGalili derives the position of the altar from the placement of the *kiyor* — the laver. The verse specifies that the laver stands between the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and the altar. The analysis of exactly where this places the altar — and how the *kiyor*'s location implies that the entire *mizbeach* stands in the north — will be taken up in the next session.

---

# Zevachim 59

## Mizbeach Location

### Fire & Four Amot

The daf opens with an unresolved question carried over from the bottom of 58b: where precisely was the *mizbeach* located within the *azarah*? Was it entirely in the north, entirely in the south, or split evenly between the two halves? The half-and-half arrangement has considerable intuitive appeal, yet the Gemara has been examining a complicating datum — the fire used to light the *ketoret*. Twice daily, when the *kohen* brought fire into the *kodesh* for the *ketoret* offering, and when he carried it out on *Shabbat* for the burning of the *levonah*, that fire was positioned in the southwest corner of the altar's top, four *amot* removed from the edge. The question is what this placement implies about the altar's overall location: if the entire *mizbeach* was in the north, it means the fire could be no more than four *amot* from the southern ledge; if the entire *mizbeach* was in the south, it means the fire had to be at least four *amot* from that edge. The counting of that edge itself is also in dispute. The Gemara did not reach a conclusion on this basis, so it turns to other evidence.

### R. Yosi HaGlili

Rav Shravya introduces a different attribution and a different proof. The position that the *mizbeach* was entirely in the north, he says, belongs to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili — and the evidence comes not from the placement of the fire but from a *braita* that addresses the location of the *kiyor*, the laver.

### Kiyor Placement

Two verses create an apparent tension. One states: *venatata et hakiyor bein ohel moed uvein hamizbeach* — the *kiyor* is to be placed between the *ohel moed* and the *mizbeach*. A second verse states: *ve-et mizbeach ha'olah petach ohel moed* — the altar of the *olah* stands at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. From the juxtaposition, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili derives that while the *kiyor* must be in the space between the *mizbeach* and the *ohel moed*, it cannot itself stand *petach ohel moed*, because that position belongs exclusively to the *mizbeach*. The verse implies that only the *mizbeach* faces the doorway — not the *kiyor*.

This has a compelling logic beyond the mere textual inference. The entire zone designated as *petach ohel moed* represents a kind of access — an approach toward the *shechinah* residing within. One would not want anything interrupting that line of sight, even symbolically and metaphorically. At the same time, the verse distinguishes between the *ohel moed* as a structure and the *petach ohel moed* as its doorway, so the prohibition applies specifically to the opening, not the building's full extent.

To visualize this: the *heichal* is ten *amot* wide at its opening and the *ulam* is twenty *amot* wide. The *mizbeach* is thirty-two *amot* across at its base. If the *mizbeach* is centered, it extends eleven *amot* beyond the *ulam*'s walls on each side. Placing the *kiyor* somewhere between the *mizbeach* and the *ohel moed*, away from the direct line of the door, seems perfectly achievable — there is ample space in the *azarah* for such a placement.

### Mizbeach Petach

The Gemara cites the essential framing of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's *braita*: *mizbeach petach ohel moed velo kiyor petach ohel moed*. Where, then, was the *kiyor* placed? *Bein ha'ulam velamizbeach* — between the *ulam* and the *mizbeach* — *mashuch kima klafei hadarom*, drawn slightly southward. The Gemara's assumption is that "drawn southward" means drawn below the southernmost edge of the *mizbeach*. This raises an obvious question: why does it need to be pulled that far? There is clearly space between the *mizbeach* and the *ohel moed* without interfering with the doorway, regardless of whether the altar is positioned all in the north, all in the south, or split between the two.

### North Clear Only

The Gemara works through the possibilities systematically. If the entire *mizbeach* is in the south, there is obviously room in the southern portion of the *azarah* to place the *kiyor* between the wall of the *heichal* and the *mizbeach* without blocking the door. The same holds even if one considers the *kedushat ha'ulam* and the *kedushat ha'heichal* to be a single unified sanctity — so that the *kiyor* cannot stand opposite the door of the *ulam* either — because there are still six *amot* of wall on each side of the *ulam*'s opening, and room enough to position the *kiyor* there without interference.

Similarly, if the *mizbeach* straddles the midline, numerous positions remain available. The Gemara considers every combination: *kulei mizbeach bedarom kaei*, *chetzyo batzafon vechetzyo bedarom*, *kedushat heichal ve-ulam chada hi* — and in each case concludes that there would be room to place the *kiyor* appropriately without pulling it all the way below the southern edge of the *mizbeach*.

The only configuration that forces the *kiyor* to be drawn southward beyond the *mizbeach*'s southern edge is if the *mizbeach* is entirely in the north and there is a prohibition against placing anything else in the north at all. In that case, there is simply nowhere to put the *kiyor* in the northern zone, and it must be relocated entirely to the south. The Gemara concludes: *lav mishum dekasavar kulei mizbeach batzafon* — the reason the *kiyor* must be pulled south is that Rabbi Yosi HaGlili holds the entire *mizbeach* is in the north, and the north must remain clear.

But clear of what? The verse says *al yerech hamizbeach tzafona* — one slaughters to the north of the *mizbeach*. From the word *tzafona* the Gemara derives: *shetzafon panui miklum* — the north must be free of everything. One might ask: if the only valid location for *shechita* is directly to the north of the *mizbeach* itself, why does the space between the *ulam* and the *mizbeach* also have to remain clear? That is a genuine difficulty. Yet the Gemara does assume that this inner gap must also be free.

It is worth noting an important precision raised in discussion: the prohibition derived from the verse is not that the *kiyor* cannot stand *in front of the door*, but rather that it cannot interpose between the door and the *mizbeach*. If the entire *mizbeach* is in the north, the *kiyor* could technically be positioned just below the *mizbeach*'s southern edge and still be in front of the door without violating the rule — because it would not be standing between the door and the *mizbeach*. Practically speaking, one would still want to move it further south to avoid obstruction, but there is a halachic distinction worth preserving.

### Tosfot's Distinction

Tosafot engages with a complication. The verse says the north must be clear — *panui miklum* — yet in practice the north was not at all empty. There were tables, hooks, and posts there — the entire apparatus for *shechita*. If the *tzafona* verse demands total clearance, how can all that equipment be present?

Tosafot resolves this by clarifying the scope of the requirement. When the Torah demands that the north be clear, the purpose is to preserve adequate space for the *shechita* of *kodshei kodashim*. Since all *kodshei kodashim* must be slaughtered in the north and that is the only zone available for such sacrifices, the Torah insists that extraneous objects not crowd it out. But items that are themselves required *for* the *shechita* — tables, hooks, posts — are not extraneous at all. They serve the very act the verse is protecting space for, and therefore *tzorechei shechita* may be present. The prohibition applies to objects with no function in the slaughter process, like the *kiyor*.

On a related point, Tosafot notes that even if the *mizbeach* of Moshe was a portable vessel — a *kli* — rather than a fixed structure, and was itself in the north, that does not contradict the rule. The principle that the north must be clear of vessels refers to vessels other than the *mizbeach* itself. *Danin kli mikli ve-ein danin kli mibinyan* — one draws an analogy between a vessel and a vessel, not between a vessel and a permanent structure. The *mizbeach* in the *beit hamikdash* was a permanent structure and its presence in the north defines rather than violates the requirement.

### R. Eliezer ben Yaakov

Having established Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position — that the entire *mizbeach* is in the north — the Gemara asks: who holds the opposing view that the *mizbeach* is entirely in the south? That is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, as derived from a *braita*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov reads the word *tzafona* not merely as requiring clearance of vessels but as requiring clearance of everything — *afilu min hamizbeach*. The north must be free even of the *mizbeach* itself. Therefore the entire altar must be in the south. From a functional standpoint this actually has some appeal: if *kodshei kodashim* are slaughtered in the north, placing the *mizbeach* entirely in the south maximizes the space available for that slaughter rather than the *mizbeach* consuming part of that zone.

---

## Damaged Altar

### Rav's Rule

The Gemara now shifts to a related but distinct topic. Rav states: *mizbeach shenifgam kol hakodashim shenishchatu sham psulin* — if the *mizbeach* was chipped or damaged, any sacrifices whose *shechita* took place from the moment of the damage onward are invalid. The *shechita* itself is rendered *pasul*. The question of retroactivity — if the chip is discovered midday, whether earlier slaughterings of that day are presumed invalid — follows the usual rules of *chazakah*, and the Gemara does not pursue it here.

### Lost Verse

What is striking about Rav's statement is his candid admission: *mikra hu bi'yadeinu ve'shachachnuhu* — we have a verse that proves this, but we have forgotten it. The *halacha* has been retained in memory while the scriptural source that generated it has slipped away. There is something symbolically resonant about this. In the world of *kodashim*, we have held onto the practical rulings, the operational memory, while the living textual experience behind those rulings has become harder to access — much like the famous parable of successive generations losing first the words, then the melody, then the dance, until all that remains is the story about the story.

### Rav Kahana's Source

When Rav Kahana traveled to Eretz Yisrael — going back, as it were, toward the source — he found Rav Shimon the son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi the missing derivation.

### Ve-Zavachta Alav

The verse is: *ve-zavachta alav et olotecha ve-et shelammecha* — you shall slaughter upon it your *olot* and your *shelamim*. The Gemara asks: *ve-chi alav hu zove'ach?* Does one literally slaughter on the altar? This verse is, of course, cited elsewhere in our *masechta* as a basis for the ruling that *shechita* may be performed on the top surface of the altar — a hyper-literal reading. But the Gemara here recovers the more contextual reading: *alav* means in reference to it, in correspondence with it, in the context of its standing whole before you. The *shechita* is performed with the altar as its frame of reference. From this follows: *ella keshe'hu shalem ve-lo keshe'hu chaser* — the slaughter must occur when the altar is complete, not when it is deficient. An incomplete altar is, in a meaningful sense, not fully an altar, and the *shechita* performed in its shadow lacks what it requires.

### R. Yochanan Dichuy

Rabbi Yochanan extends the ruling further. He states: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh psulin* — both an animal slaughtered while the altar was chipped, and an animal that was merely sanctified during that period and slaughtered afterward once the altar was repaired, are invalid. The mechanism is the principle of *dichuy ba'alei chayim*: even a living animal can be "pushed away" from its sanctified status. If during the period when the *mizbeach* was chipped a sanctified animal existed and could not be offered, it acquired a stigma of rejection — *dichuy* — that persists even after the altar is repaired and the animal remains alive.

Practically, this would mean that whenever the *mizbeach* sustained damage, some form of notice would have to be given to everyone who had sanctified an animal prior to that moment, informing them that their *korban* is now invalid — much like the *eruv* notice in a community today.

### Rav vs. R. Yochanan

The Gemara identifies the root of the dispute: Rav holds *ba'alei chayim einam nidchin* — a living creature is not subject to *dichuy*. Because something living is dynamic rather than static in its identity, a period of disqualification does not permanently stigmatize it. As long as the altar is repaired before the *shechita* takes place, the animal may still be offered. Rabbi Yochanan holds *ba'alei chayim nidchin* — even a living sanctified animal can be pushed away by a period of disqualification.

---

## Damaged Altar (II)

### Before Altar Built

A *braita* is introduced that appears to support Rabbi Yochanan: all animals sanctified before the *mizbeach* was built, and offered after it was built, are *psulin*. This seems to confirm that sanctification followed by a period of inability to offer — even because no altar yet existed — permanently invalidates the animal.

### Emendation

The Gemara presses on the *braita*'s language. *Ad shelo nivneh hamizbeach* — before the altar was built — would represent *dichuy mei'ikara*, a case where the animal was never fit to begin with, which is potentially a less severe form of rejection than *nir'ah ve-nidcheh*, where the animal was once suitable and then disqualified. If the *braita* means animals sanctified before the Second Temple's altar was constructed, that is merely *dichuy mei'ikara*, and it is not obvious that even Rabbi Yochanan holds this invalidates them.

The Gemara therefore reads the *braita* differently: it must refer not to *ad shelo nivneh* — before it was built — but to *ad shelo nifgam* — before it was chipped. Animals sanctified before the altar was chipped and then the altar was chipped: that is *nir'ah ve-nidcheh*, the animal was once fit and was then pushed away. With this reading the *braita* supports Rabbi Yochanan's position that *ba'alei chayim nidchin*. However, since the Gemara has had to substantially emend the *braita*'s text, it concludes that the *braita* can no longer serve as a clean proof for either side — once editing begins, the other side can propose its own reading.

---

## Golden Altar Exception

### Mizbeach She-Ne'ekar

A further challenge to Rav's ruling: Rav Gidal teaches in the name of Rav himself that if the golden altar — the inner *mizbeach* used for the *ketoret* — was uprooted, one may still burn *ketoret* on the spot where it had stood. The floor of the *kodesh*, in other words, retains a sanctity sufficient to permit offering *ketoret* even without the physical altar present. This seems to undercut the very premise that the altar must be whole and present for a valid offering.

### Blood vs. Incense

Rava resolves the tension by invoking a distinction he draws in a different context: *modeh haya Rabbi Yehuda be-damim* — in matters of blood, different rules apply. The same principle operates here. When Rav rules that the *mizbeach* must be present and whole for a valid offering, he is speaking of the blood-related service — the *shechita* and the *zerikat ha-dam* on the outer altar — where the physical reality of the *mizbeach* is constitutive of the act. The *ketoret*, by contrast, is not blood-dependent; in that realm one can perhaps rely on the sanctity of the space rather than the physical object. Hence *modeh Rav be-damim*: Rav himself would agree that when it comes to blood, the *mizbeach* is indispensable, while for *ketoret* the floor may suffice.

---

## Temple Dedication

### Bayom Hahu Kidesh

The Gemara now turns to the source of Rava's invocation of Rabbi Yehuda's distinction between blood and *ketoret*, which emerges from a *braita* about Shlomo's dedication of the Temple. The verse states: *bayom hahu kidesh hamelech et toch ha'chatzer hapnimit ki mizbeach hanechoshet asher lifnei Hashem katan me-hachil* — on that day the king sanctified the inner courtyard, because the copper altar was too small to contain all the sacrifices he was bringing. Shlomo offered twenty-two thousand *shelamim* on the day of dedication. The *braita* records a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi about what this verse means and what Shlomo actually did.

Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse as written: Shlomo sanctified the courtyard itself — the ground of the *azarah* — to serve as a sacrificial surface, because even the new altar he had built was too small to handle the volume of offerings. On Rabbi Yehuda's reading, *mizbeach hanechoshet* refers not to Moshe's original copper altar but to its replacement, the new altar of Shlomo, which also fell short.

### R. Yosi Rebuttal

Rabbi Yosi challenges this reading by doing the arithmetic. He notes that at a different occasion the verse records Shlomo offering one thousand *olot* on the original copper altar of Moshe. Now at the dedication he offers twenty-two thousand *shelamim* — twenty-two times as many. Rabbi Yosi then computes the usable surface of each altar. The altar of Moshe is described in the Torah as five *amot* by five *amot*. Taking that literally, and subtracting an *amah* on each side for the corners and an *amah* on each side for the *sovev*, the usable space at the top is one *amah* by one *amah* — a single square *amah*. The new altar of Shlomo, by contrast, was thirty-two *amot* at its base, twenty-eight at its second ledge, and at its top — after subtracting similarly — approximately twenty by twenty *amot* according to Rashi, giving four hundred square *amot* of usable space. That is four hundred times the usable surface of Moshe's altar, far more than the twenty-two-fold increase in offerings. There was no need to sanctify the courtyard floor.

For Rabbi Yosi, then, the verse means that Shlomo sanctified the new altar — *toch ha'chatzer* refers to the new *mizbeach* that stood within the courtyard — and *mizbeach hanechoshet* refers literally to the original copper altar of Moshe, which genuinely was too small, necessitating the construction and dedication of the new one.

### R. Yehuda Too Small

The Gemara asks: given Rabbi Yosi's arithmetic, why does Rabbi Yehuda insist the new altar was not big enough? The answer is that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi have a deeper, prior dispute about the dimensions of Moshe's altar — a dispute that fundamentally changes the ratio.

### Dimensions Debate

The Torah describes the altar of Moshe as *chamesh amot orech ve-chamesh amot rochav* — five *amot* long and five *amot* wide — and *shalosh amot komaso* — three *amot* high — and adds the word *ravu'a*, square. Rabbi Yosi reads these numbers literally: five by five by three. The usable top surface is one square *amah* after accounting for the corners and the *sovev*, so the new altar of Shlomo at four hundred square *amot* is indeed four hundred times more capable.

### Measured from Center

Rabbi Yehuda invokes a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *ravu'a* appears here regarding Moshe's altar and also in the book of Yechezkel regarding the future altar. In Yechezkel, the measurements are taken *me'emtzi'ato* — from the center outward. The verse in Yechezkel specifies twelve *amot* in each direction; the additional phrase *al arba'at reva'av* — across all four sides — teaches that the measurement emanates from the center point, going twelve *amot* in each of the four directions, producing a twenty-four *amah* altar. Rabbi Yehuda applies this same principle to the word *ravu'a* by Moshe's altar: *chamesh amot* means five *amot* measured from the center in each direction, producing an altar ten *amot* by ten *amot*. After subtracting the corners and the *sovev*, the usable space is six by six — thirty-six square *amot* — compared to the one square *amah* of Rabbi Yosi's reading. Shlomo's new altar at four hundred square *amot* is approximately eleven times larger, not four hundred times. Since one thousand offerings were brought on a single square *amah* and twenty-two thousand offerings were needed, eleven times the capacity is insufficient. Hence Rabbi Yehuda's conclusion stands: the new altar was too small, and Shlomo had to sanctify the courtyard floor itself.

### Ravu'a Height Double

Rabbi Yosi now responds. He agrees that the *gezeirah shavah* from *ravu'a* in Yechezkel teaches something — but says it teaches something about the *height*, not the width. The *braita* records: Rabbi Yosi says the word *ravu'a* appearing here corresponds to the golden altar of the *mishkan*, where the dimensions are one *amah* by one *amah* by two *amot* — the height is double the other two dimensions. *Mah lehalon govah pi shnayim ke-arko* — just as there the height is twice the length and width, *af kan pi shnayim ke-arko* — so too here, the height of Moshe's altar is twice its five *amot*, making it ten *amot* high. The three stated in the verse does not represent the total height but the height of a particular section above the *sovev*.

### Exposure Concern

Rabbi Yehuda objects to this reading with a practical challenge: *efshar kohen omed al gabei mizbeach va'avodah beyado ve-chol ha'am ro'im oto mibachutz?* — is it possible that the *kohen* stands atop a ten-*amah* altar performing the service, and all the people outside can see him? The *kla'im* — the curtains surrounding the *chatzer* — are only five *amot* high. A *kohen* standing ten *amot* off the ground would be towering some fifteen feet in the air, fully visible to everyone outside. The entire purpose of the enclosure is to preserve the intimate character of the *avodah*, to prevent it from becoming a public spectacle. A ten-*amah* altar reduces those curtains to irrelevance. Rabbi Yehuda's altar — wide but only three *amot* high — keeps the *kohen* largely within the enclosure, with perhaps only the very top of his head visible above the curtains.

### Curtains Fifteen Amot

Rabbi Yosi responds: the same method that expanded the height of the altar from three to ten *amot* can be applied to the curtains. The verse describing the *mishkan* says that the *kla'im* surround both the *mishkan* and the *mizbeach* — and since the *mishkan* itself was ten *amot* high, the curtains surrounding it must have been at least ten *amot*.
