Furthermore, a verse explicitly mentions *kla'im chamesh esreh amah al hakatef* — curtains fifteen *amot* along the shoulder. Rabbi Yosi reads this not as a measurement of width but of height: the curtains are fifteen *amot* tall. When the same verse elsewhere says *chamesh amot*, that refers to the portion that rises five *amot* above the top of whatever they surround — five *amot* above the ten-*amah* *mizbeach*, giving fifteen *amot* total. Similarly, the three *amot* in the Torah's description of the altar's height means three *amot* above the *sovev*, the walkway partway up the altar's face.

On this reading, Rabbi Yosi has transformed three stated *amot* into ten, and five stated *amot* of curtain height into fifteen. Rabbi Yehuda, for his part, has transformed five stated *amot* of altar width into ten. Both positions involve departures from a plain reading, but in opposite directions — Rabbi Yehuda makes the altar wide, Rabbi Yosi makes it tall. These strikingly different proportions have direct implications for the capacity calculations that determine whether Shlomo needed to sanctify the courtyard floor, which in turn determines whether blood service could be performed on sanctified ground rather than on a physical *mizbeach* — the thread that connects this entire discussion back to the damaged altar and the distinction between blood and *ketoret* with which the sugya began.

---

---

# Zevachim 60

## Altar Dimensions

### Blood vs. Ketores

We pick up four lines into daf 60a, at the words *u'le'Rabbi Yehuda*. We are in the middle of a debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose, which was brought into the discussion in connection with the ruling that a chipped *mizbeach* prevents *shechita* of a *korban*. The question was raised: if the inner golden altar is absent, can the *ketoret* still be offered? The answer is that blood-related *avodah* is categorically different. The blood requires the *mizbeach*; the burning of incense does not. This distinction will now be connected to a parallel debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose regarding what happened in the time of Shlomo.

### R. Yehuda: Wide Altar

The debate concerns the relative size of Shlomo's altar compared to the copper *mizbeach* of the *mishkan*. Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse describing the *mishkan*'s copper altar — which states dimensions of five by five by three — as meaning ten by ten, with the five measured from the center outward, and only three *amot* in height. This makes the altar low and very wide. According to this reading, even the new altar built by Shlomo was not proportionally much larger than Moshe's, so when an enormous volume of sacrifices was required on a particular day, they had to sanctify the floor of the *azarah* to burn the *emurim* there. The burning of the *emurim* requires a large surface area, and that is precisely why the dimensions of the altar's top were the focus: you need room to burn a great many entrails. The blood work, by contrast, does not require the same expanse — you perform a *zerika*, step aside, and proceed. The *mizbeach* structure is therefore always sufficient for blood, even when it is insufficient for the *emurim*.

### R. Yose: Tall Altar

Rabbi Yose reads the very same verse differently. He holds that the altar was five by five, but ten *amot* tall — the "three" in the verse refers to the height of the latticed grating in the middle of the structure. On this reading the *mishkan* altar was narrow and tall, and Shlomo's new altar was therefore a substantial improvement in size. According to Rabbi Yose, the ground of the *azarah* was never sanctified to serve as an altar; the new altar was fully adequate.

This creates an immediate difficulty. If the altar was ten *amot* tall and a *kohen* is approximately three *amot* to his shoulders, the *kohen* standing atop the altar would have his shoulders at six *amot* off the ground — yet the surrounding curtains were only five *amot* high. The *kohen* would be visible above the curtains, and this was considered deeply inappropriate, a violation of the intimacy and sanctity proper to the *avodah*. Why would curtains be erected at all if they scarcely obscured anything?

### Privacy Resolution

Rabbi Yose's answer requires a rereading of the verse about the curtain height. Since the verse compares the courtyard curtains to those of the *ohel moed*, and the *ohel moed*'s own curtains reached ten *amot* to the height of its structure with an additional five *amot* extending beyond, these curtains too were not five but fifteen *amot* — ten up to the top of the altar and five beyond. This is how the *kohen* performed the *avodah* in privacy.

What then of Rabbi Yehuda's reading, where the curtains are taken literally as five *amot* and the altar is only three *amot* high? A *kohen* standing on a three-*amot* altar would have his shoulders at six *amot*, still above the five-*amot* curtains. The *Gemara* addresses this directly: *nihi dikohan mit'chazi, avoda d'beyado lo mit'chazi*. It is true that the *kohen* himself was visible from the chest up, but the actual *avodah* — the work of his hands, the arrangement of the limbs — could not be seen. The visibility of the person does not undermine the sanctity; it is the visibility of the sacred acts that matters, and those remained hidden.

### Solomon Context

Having resolved the internal difficulties of each position, the *Gemara* now returns to the event in Shlomo's time. The verse states that on that day the king sanctified the courtyard because the copper *mizbeach* was too small. The problem is that by Shlomo's time a new altar had already been built; why does the verse speak of the copper *mizbeach* as if it were still the relevant altar?

### Sanctification Interpret…

Two readings emerge, each reflecting the underlying position on altar dimensions.

According to Rabbi Yehuda, even the new altar that Shlomo built was insufficient for the scale of the sacrifices brought on that day. The verse refers to the new altar as "the copper *mizbeach*" because it was the copper altar's replacement — it stood in for it. But since even this substitute was too small, they sanctified the actual floor of the *azarah* to function as an altar. On Rabbi Yehuda's reading, then, *kidesh* means that the courtyard ground itself was consecrated to serve as a sacrificial surface, and *mizbeach hanechoshet* refers not to the original copper altar but to its stone successor.

According to Rabbi Yose, the courtyard was sanctified not to function as an altar but to provide a site for the construction of a new altar — *l'ha'amid bo mizbeach*. The old copper altar was too small, and Shlomo consecrated the courtyard space in order to erect something adequate. The word *kidesh* therefore means he prepared the space for the new structure, not that the floor itself became an altar.

The *Gemara* then works through the textual consequence of each reading. According to Rabbi Yose, the text's mention that the old altar was "too small" (*katan*) makes sense: the old altar was inadequate, so a new one was needed. But according to Rabbi Yehuda, the same word *katan* is puzzling, because even the new altar was too small — so the *Gemara* explains: *mizbeach avanim she'asa Shlomo tachat mizbeach hanechoshet katan hu*, the stone altar that Shlomo built as a substitute for the copper altar was itself too small, and that is why the courtyard had to be sanctified.

### Hermeneutical Basis

What underlies the disagreement about the altar's shape? The debate turns on which analogical connection one prefers for the word *ravua* (square) as it applies to the copper *mizbeach* of the *mishkan*.

Rabbi Yehuda holds *danim chutz michutz v'ein danim chutz mipnim*: we learn an outer altar from an outer altar. He links the *mishkan*'s copper altar to the altar described in Yechezkel, where *ravua* means measured from the center outward — yielding a ten-by-ten structure, low and wide.

Rabbi Yose holds *danim kli mikli*: we prefer to connect one vessel to another. The copper altar of the *mishkan* was movable and thus had the status of a vessel; it is therefore better compared to the golden incense altar, which was also a vessel. For the golden altar, *ravua* implied that the height was double the width. Applied to the copper altar, this yields a structure that is tall and narrow. Rabbi Yose adds *v'ein danim kli mibinyan*: one should not compare a vessel to a permanent structure, and therefore linking the copper altar to the altar of Yechezkel — which was a fixed architectural structure — is the less appropriate inference.

---

## Blood Requires Altar

### Rava: Blood Necessity

Having established the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose, the *Gemara* now addresses how far Rabbi Yehuda's principle extends. If the floor of the *azarah* can function as an altar for burning *emurim*, does the same apply to blood work? Rava states clearly: *modeh Reb Yehuda b'damim*. Whatever flexibility Rabbi Yehuda grants for the burning of entrails and incense, he concedes that the blood work — the *zerika* that gives the *korban* its validity — requires an actual *mizbeach*.

### Pesach Blood Proof

The proof comes from a *braita*. Rabbi Yehuda himself taught that on *Pesach*, when the volume of sacrifices was so great that blood inevitably spilled onto the floor, one would fill a vessel with blood gathered from the mixture on the floor — a mixture that might include blood from a *korban* whose vessel had been properly filled but then spilled before reaching the altar — and pour that collected blood onto the *mizbeach*. The reasoning: if someone's blood had been caught properly in a vessel but spilled before being thrown, this mixture, thrown on the altar, would validate it. *V'shofcho gabei mizbe'ach* — they would pour it on the base of the altar.

### Floor Theory Refuted

This teaching proves that the floor does not have altar-status for blood. The *Gemara* presses: *v'ei salka daitach savar Reb Yehuda kula Azara mikdasha* — if Rabbi Yehuda truly held that the entire *azarah* functions as an altar, why bother gathering the spilled blood and carrying it to the *mizbeach*? For the *korban Pesach* in particular, whose blood merely needs to be "spilled" (*v'damam shel zevachecha yishpach*), one who tripped and spilled the blood onto the *azarah* floor should have fulfilled the obligation right there, if the floor had altar-status. The fact that the *braita* prescribes gathering the blood and bringing it to the altar demonstrates that the floor does not function as a *mizbeach* for blood.

### Koach Adam Question

The *Gemara* attempts to deflect this proof: *v'dilma mishum d'kasvar shfichah mikoach adam beinan* — perhaps the floor does have altar-status for blood, but the reason one cannot simply leave the spilled blood on the ground is that the act of sprinkling must be performed through deliberate human agency. An unintentional spill, caused by tripping, does not constitute a valid *zerika* regardless of where the blood lands.

This raises a genuinely fascinating question about what constitutes *koach adam*. Even in other contexts — such as *netilat yadayim* — there is debate about whether water flowing through a faucet, where one's agency is indirect, qualifies as *koach gavra*. Here too: if one trips and the vessel tilts over, is that not still the *kohen*'s energy, even if unintentional? Perhaps the requirement is not intentionality per se but directed agency — the act must in some meaningful sense be *his* act, not the floor's.

The *Gemara* then presses further: if the only issue with the spilled blood was the absence of *koach adam*, why does the *braita* instruct one to gather the blood and pour it on the *mizbeach*? Why not simply gather it and re-pour it right back onto the *azarah* floor — this time intentionally? The *Gemara* responds: *v'dilma mishum d'bainan mitzvah min hamuvchar* — perhaps one simply prefers the better form of the *mitzvah*. If the floor had altar-status for blood, one could theoretically throw blood directly on the floor and satisfy the requirement, yet one chooses the altar for the superior manner of fulfillment.

### Tosafot: Blood Obvious

The *Gemara*'s willingness to entertain these alternative explanations is notable, because *Tosafot* register sharp surprise at the premise of the discussion. On the phrase *modeh Reb Yehuda b'damim*, *Tosafot* ask: *teima mai kasalka daiteich me'ikara* — how could one have imagined for even a moment that blood work does not require an actual *mizbeach*? The entire *masechet* has been replete with requirements of physical altar structure: *keren*, the horn of the altar; *arbuah*, its square shape; *yesod*, its base. All of these structural requirements — and the *Gemara* has repeatedly made clear that they are indispensable — make it inconceivable that blood could simply be thrown on the ground. The novelty of Rava's statement, says *Tosafot*, lies entirely in the other half of the principle: that the *emurim* and the *ketoret* do *not* require an altar. That is the *chiddush*; the blood's dependence on the *mizbeach* was never in question.

### Blood Theology

This principle — that blood is the exclusive focus of what makes a *korban* valid, while the burning of entrails and incense does not require a *mizbeach* — is a striking theological claim. The stories of *korbanot* throughout the Torah emphasize the burning, the ascending smoke, the *rei'ach nicho'ach*. Think of Noach building an altar, of Kayin and Hevel — it is what is placed on the fire and ascends that seems to carry the weight of the offering. Even in *Vayikra*, the Torah describes what is done with the blood, what is done with the *emurim*, what is done with the various parts, without obviously privileging one over the other.

Yet *Chazal* throughout this *masechet* have consistently placed blood at the absolute center. The conceptual foundation is a single *pasuk*: *ki hadam hu banefesh yechaper, va'ani netativ lachem al hamizbeach lechaper al nafshoteichem* — for the blood, through the life-force it carries, effects atonement, and it is for this reason that I have given it to you upon the altar to atone for your souls. Even this verse does not unambiguously establish blood as the *sole* vehicle of atonement; it could be read as identifying blood as one important component. Yet it is this verse that animates the entire *masechet*'s governing principle: it is the blood, and the blood alone, that is *me'akev*. One could, in theory, have burned the entrails on the ground of the *azarah*. All that elaborate burning — and the *Gemara* is prepared to say that none of it needed a structure. Only the blood required the altar.

---

## Chipped Altar

### Chipped Invalidates

The *Gemara* returns to the ruling of Rabbi Elazar: a *mizbeach* that has become chipped (*nifgam*) not only prevents valid *zerika* but also retroactively affects the *shechita*. This is derived from the verse *vezavachta alav* — the slaughtering must be performed while the *korban* is "upon" a valid altar, meaning the altar must be whole at the time of *shechita*. If the *mizbeach* was intact during *shechita* but became chipped before *zerika*, and one then repaired the altar, the *korban* remains invalid because the *shechita* and the altar's integrity must coexist.

Given that we have established blood work as the defining requirement of the altar, one might ask about related acts that are not themselves blood work but are connected to it. What, for instance, about eating the *shiyarei mincha* — the remnant of the *mincha* consumed by the *kohanim*? And beyond that, what about eating the meat of various categories of *korbanot*?

### Mincha Remnant

The *Gemara* rules: *mizbeach shenifgam ein ochlin bigino shi'arei mincha* — when the *mizbeach* is chipped, one may not eat the remnant of the *mincha*. This is not immediately about blood; it is about the consumption of the *mincha* by the *kohanim* after the *kometz* has been offered. That this eating should be connected to the altar's wholeness requires explanation.

### Mincha Verse Link

The source is a verse from the *milu'im*, where Moshe instructs Aharon and his sons: *ve'achlu hamatzot etzel hamizbeiach ki chen tzuveiti* — eat the unleavened bread beside the altar, for so have I commanded. Does this mean they literally had to stand next to the altar? Of course not — they had the entire *azarah* in which to eat. Rather, the verse's invocation of the altar is interpreted as establishing a conceptual and legal connection: the eating of the *mincha* remnant is contingent upon the altar's integrity, just as the *shechita* is contingent upon the altar's integrity. *Ella bizman shehu shaleim velo bizman shehu chaser* — only when the altar is whole, not when it is lacking.

This has an important implication for the taking of the *kometz* as well. If the eating of the remnant is tied to the altar's wholeness, then certainly the *kemitzah* — the act of taking the handful, which is the *mincha*'s parallel to *shechita* — is similarly dependent on an intact *mizbeach*. And note the striking scope: not only is the preparatory act (*kemitzah*) and the core act (burning the *kometz*) connected to the altar, but even the *kohanim*'s eating afterward is tied to it. Once the *korban* has been offered, one might assume the eating is simply a benefit unrelated to the altar's status. The *Gemara* says otherwise.

### Kodshei Kodashim

From the *mincha* the *Gemara* extends the principle to *kodshei kodashim* — offerings of the highest sanctity such as the *chatat* and the *asham*, whose meat is eaten by the *kohanim* within the *azarah*. The source is the continuation of the same verse: *ki kodesh kodashim hi* — for it is holy of holies. Anything classified as *kodesh kodashim* stands in this same relationship to the altar.

This is a significant claim about the nature of the *kohanim*'s eating. One might have understood their consumption of *kodshei kodashim* meat as simply their form of material support — God's generosity toward those who serve in the *Mikdash*, an instance of *mishulchan gavoah kazchu*, receiving from the divine table. But the *Gemara* draws on a deeper principle: *kohanim ochlim uba'alim mitkaprim* — the *kohanim* eat and the owners achieve atonement. The *kohanim*'s eating is not merely a benefit; it is an extension of the atonement process itself, a continuation of what the *mizbeach* accomplishes. Their consumption is, in a meaningful sense, the *mizbeach*'s consumption. It follows that just as the *mizbeach* must be whole for the blood and the burning, it must be whole for the eating.

This produces a striking and even counterintuitive result within Rabbi Yehuda's own framework: according to Rabbi Yehuda, the burning of *emurim* does not require an intact *mizbeach* — it can be performed on the *azarah* floor. Yet the eating of the meat does require an intact *mizbeach*. The eating is, on this analysis, more tightly bound to the *mizbeach* than the burning of entrails. That is genuinely surprising.

---

## Kodshim Kalim Need Altar

### Kodshim Kalim Scenario

If the above holds for *kodshei kodashim*, whose consumption takes place within the *azarah* in close proximity to the altar and involves the *kohanim* in their sacral role, one might consider it intuitive. But the *Gemara* now extends the principle to *kodshim kalim* — offerings of lesser sanctity eaten by the owners themselves anywhere within *Yerushalayim*. Here the connection to the *mizbeach* is far less obvious. Once the blood has been properly sprinkled and the *korban* validly brought, and one is sitting at home somewhere in *Yerushalayim* eating the meat — what possible relevance does the *mizbeach*'s physical integrity have?

The scenario the *Gemara* contemplates: the *korban* was brought properly, the blood was thrown, and subsequently the *mizbeach* was chipped. Must one stop eating the *kodshim kalim* meat? The *Gemara*'s answer is yes — even this eating requires the *mizbeach* to be whole.

### Abaye Source

Abaye derives this ruling from the same *drashah* of Rabbi Yose that transmits a teaching in the name of Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Yose is cited as having taught three things in the name of three different sages; the relevant teaching here was said in the name of Rabbi Yishmael.

### Ishmael Ma'aser

Rabbi Yishmael poses the following question: perhaps one should be permitted to bring *ma'aser sheni* to *Yerushalayim* and eat it there in the present era — that is, after the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The question arises because *ma'aser sheni* is not brought to the *Beit HaMikdash* itself; it is eaten in *Yerushalayim*. If the sanctity of the land of Israel for agricultural obligations (*terumot u-ma'asrot*) remains in force today — a position that itself requires a separate determination — then the sanctity of *Yerushalayim* might similarly persist, and one could theoretically bring *ma'aser sheni* to the city and eat it there even without a standing *Beit HaMikdash*.

Rabbi Yishmael proceeds to reject this possibility. The governing principle: *bekhor ta'un hava'at makom u-ma'aser ta'un hava'at makom* — both *bechor* and *ma'aser* require being brought to a specific place, namely *Yerushalayim*. Just as *bechor* can only be brought when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands — since it is a *korban* requiring *matan damim* and *emurim* on the *mizbeach* — so too *ma'aser* can only be eaten when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands.

### Bechor-Ma'aser Link

The obvious objection: *mah l'bechor shekein ta'un matan damim v'imurim legabei mizbeach* — the *bechor* obviously requires a *Beit HaMikdash* because it is a *korban*. Blood is thrown on the altar and *emurim* are burned there. *Ma'aser sheni* is not a *korban* at all; it is simply food eaten in *Yerushalayim*. Why should it require a *Beit HaMikdash*?

The *Gemara* attempts to rescue the analogy by invoking *bikurim*, which also requires the *Beit HaMikdash* — one brings the first fruits to the *Mikdash* and places them before the altar, as the verse states *v'hinachto lifnei mizbach Hashem Elokecha*. However, this too fails: *mah l'bikurim shekein te'unim hanacha* — *bikurim* requires placement before the altar, and *ma'aser* does not. And the attempt to learn from a *mah hatzad*, a common denominator of *bechor* and *bikurim*, is also rejected: *mah l'tzad hashaveh shebahen shekein yesh bahen tzad mizbeach* — both *bechor* and *bikurim* involve an altar-related act, so naturally both require a *Beit HaMikdash*. *Ma'aser sheni*, which has no altar-related act, cannot be included in the inference.

The only available source is therefore a direct verse. The *pasuk* in *Devarim* groups all of these together: *v'havasem shama olosaychem v'zivchaychem v'eis ma'asrosaychem v'eis trumas yedchem u-vchorot bkarchem v'tzonchem v'achaltem sham lifnei Hashem Elokechem* — bring there your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your *ma'asrot*, your *terumot*, your *bechorot*, and eat them there before the Lord your God. The verse packages *ma'aser* together with *bechor* in the same directive to come to *Yerushalayim*. From this shared context, *mekish ma'aser l'bechor*: *ma'aser* is linked to *bechor*, and just as *bechor* requires a *Beit HaMikdash*, so does *ma'aser*.

Conceptually, the connection makes sense. *Ma'aser sheni* must be eaten *lifnei Hashem* — in the presence of God. This is not merely a geographic requirement of being within *Yerushalayim*'s walls; rather, *Yerushalayim* derives its character of being "before God" from the presence of the *Beit HaMikdash* at its center. Being anywhere in the city is a way of being in the divine presence because the city's entire identity is defined by the *Beit HaMikdash* within it. Without the *Beit HaMikdash*, the designation *lifnei Hashem* loses its grounding.

### Kedusha vs. Structure

This raises a question that the *Gemara* addresses but does not fully resolve. What exactly is the obstacle to eating *ma'aser sheni* nowadays — is it the absence of the *Beit HaMikdash*'s physical structure, or is it the absence of the *kedushah* of *Makom HaMikdash*?

The *Gemara* frames this as a question about what Rabbi Yishmael assumes: *ei kasavar kedushah rishonah kidsah le-sha'atah ve-kidsah le-atid lavo* — if he holds that the original sanctification of *Yerushalayim* and the *Mikdash* was for all future times, then even today the place retains its sanctity and one could theoretically bring a *bechor*, since *makrivin af al pi she-ein bayit* — offerings may be brought even without a standing structure, as long as the place retains its sanctity (along with a *mizbeach*, since we have established that blood requires one). In that case the analogy between *ma'aser* and *bechor* would be undermined, because *bechor* can still be brought today.

The alternative is that Rabbi Yishmael holds the sanctity did not endure — *lo kidsah le-atid lavo*. In that case the question about *bechor* is not whether it requires a physical structure but whether the *kedushah* of the place exists at all.

*Ravina* clarifies: *le'olam kasavar lo kidsah le-atid lavo* — Rabbi Yishmael consistently holds that the *kedushah* of *Makom HaMikdash* does not persist after the *churban*. The question about *bechor* that the *Gemara* raises is therefore the following: the *Gemara* then focuses the discussion on a case where the *bechor*'s blood was sprinkled before the *churban* but the meat remained to be eaten afterward.

---

## Bechor Post-Churban

### Blood-Meat Timeline

The *Gemara* now investigates a hypothetical that is conceptually precise even if historically strained: *bebechor shenizrak damo kodem churban habayit vecharav habayit* — a *bechor* whose blood was sprinkled before the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*, after which the Temple was destroyed, and the meat still remained to be eaten. The *bechor* is eaten over two days and a night; imagine the blood was thrown on the eighth of *Av*, and on the ninth of *Av* the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed. The *kohen* is now somewhere in *Yerushalayim* with the remaining meat. May he eat it?

This case is parallel in structure to the scenario of a chipped *mizbeach*: the *korban* was validly initiated — the blood was properly sprinkled — but the condition that enables eating has subsequently been compromised. The question is whether the eating of the meat is so tightly bound to the altar's presence that its destruction terminates permission to eat, or whether valid *zerika* having already occurred, the eating may continue.

---

## Bechor Post-Churban (II)

### Bechor Linkage

The resolution comes from a verse. The Torah states regarding the *bechor*: *ve'es damam tizrok al hamizbeach ve'es chelbam taktir u-vsaram yiheyeh lach* — throw their blood on the altar, burn their fat, and the flesh shall be yours. The verse links blood, *emurim*, and flesh in a single sentence. From this, *ve'itkash besaro ledamo* — the flesh is made legally equivalent to the blood through *hekesh*.

### Meat Requires Altar

*Mah dam bemizbeach af basar bemizbeach* — just as the blood requires a *mizbeach*, so does the flesh. The eating of the *bechor*'s meat is not merely a benefit that flows from valid *shechita* and *zerika*; it is a continuation of the same *avodah* complex that is tied to the *mizbeach*'s presence. If the *Beit HaMikdash* is destroyed and the *mizbeach* is gone, the meat may not be eaten even though the blood was already validly thrown.

---

## Chipped Altar (II)

### Meat-Blood Link

This same verse — linking *emurim*, blood, and flesh together in the context of *bechor* — provides the exegetical foundation for the broader principle: the eating of meat parallels the blood work. The flesh's dependence on the *mizbeach* is not derived independently or by mere analogy; it is derived directly from the same verse that establishes the blood's requirement of the altar. Blood and flesh are thus presented as a unified legal unit, not as two separate requirements that happen to converge on the same object.

This point will become significant in the discussion that follows, where the *Gemara* confronts a structural problem in the chain of reasoning.

---

## Hekesh Resolution

### Hekesh Limitation

Having established that the flesh of the *bechor* is linked to the blood (*itkash besaro ledamo*), the *Gemara* proceeds to apply this to *ma'aser sheni*: the flesh requires a *mizbeach*, and therefore by analogy so does *ma'aser*. But the *Gemara* raises the classic objection: *v'chi davar halamed behekesh chozer umelamed behekesh* — a matter derived by *hekesh* cannot itself serve as the source for a further *hekesh*. If the *bechor*'s flesh-requirement is itself derived from the blood by *hekesh*, can that derived rule then teach us something about *ma'aser sheni* through a second *hekesh*? The principle prohibiting double *hekesh* inference would seem to block this.

### Unity Resolution

The *Gemara* answers: *dam u-vasar chad milsa hi* — the blood and the flesh of a *korban* are not two separate matters that happen to be linked; they are a single legal entity. The verse does not derive the flesh-requirement from the blood-requirement by *hekesh* in the traditional sense. Rather, it reveals that flesh and blood together constitute one unit, and it is this unified blood-and-flesh unit that stands in relation to *ma'aser sheni* through a single *hekesh*. There is accordingly no "double" inference: the connection from the blood-flesh unit to *ma'aser* is a single step, and the principle against chained *hekesh* does not apply.

---

## Moving Camp

### Yirmiya Critique

When Ravin went up from *Bavel* to *Eretz Yisrael* and presented this entire discussion — the *bechor* scenario, the *ma'aser sheni* derivation, the link between flesh and blood — before Rabbi Yirmiyah, Rabbi Yirmiyah responded with his characteristic phrase: *Bavla'ei tipsha'ei, deyasvi be'ara dechashocha, amri shemaysa demachshacha* — those foolish Babylonians, who dwell in a dark land, say murky teachings. He maintained that the Babylonian scholars had worked through an elaborate derivation to establish something that could have been learned directly from a straightforward *baraita*.

### Camp Sanctity

The *baraita* Rabbi Yirmiyah cites: *besha'at siluk masaot* — at the time the camp was in motion and the *mishkan* was being dismantled for travel — *kodshim nitzolim*, one could not eat the *korbanot*. Yet *vezavim u-metzoraim mishtalchim chutz lemechitzah* — the *zavim* and *metzoraim* were still expelled beyond the camp boundary. This last detail is critical: the expulsion of *zavim* and *metzoraim* outside the camp demonstrates that the camp retained its sanctity and its camp-status even while moving. The *machaneh shechinah*, the *machaneh leviyah*, and the *machaneh Yisrael* all remained legally constituted; a *zav* who wandered into *machaneh Yisrael* was still in violation, a *metzora* had to remain outside, and so on.

Yet *kodshim nitzolim* — the *korbanot* could not be eaten. The *kedushah* of the camp persisted, but eating was prohibited. The reason can only be that the eating of *korbanot* requires not merely the *kedushah* of the camp but the standing of the *mizbeach* in a fixed location. While the altar was in transit — disassembled, being carried — it was as though the *mizbeach* were absent, even though the camp retained its sanctity. This maps precisely onto the cases we have been discussing: it is the structure, not merely the *kedushah* of the place, that governs the eating of *kodshim*.

### Kodshei vs. Kodshim

However, the *Gemara* then raises a second *baraita* that states *beshnei mekomot kodshim ne'echalin* — that *kodshim* may be eaten in two distinct situations, which the *Gemara* interprets as including both when the camp is stationary and when it is in motion. This seems to directly contradict the first *baraita*.

The resolution: *mai lav hai bekodshei kodashim hai bekodshim kalim* — the first *baraita* refers to *kodshei kodashim* and the second to *kodshim kalim*. *Kodshei kodashim*, eaten within the *azarah* by the *kohanim* in the context of the *mizbeach*'s service, requires the *mizbeach* to be standing in place. When the camp moves and the *mizbeach* is in transit, the eating of *kodshei kodashim* is prohibited. But *kodshim kalim*, eaten by the owners throughout the camp (parallel to eating in *Yerushalayim*), does not require the *mizbeach* to be fixed in place. The owners may continue eating even as the camp moves.

### Ma'aser Parallel

This distinction maps naturally onto *ma'aser sheni*: eating *ma'aser sheni* in *Yerushalayim* does not require the *mizbeach* to be standing, in the same way that eating *kodshim kalim* does not require the *mizbeach* to be standing. What *ma'aser sheni* requires is not the physical presence of the *mizbeach* but the *kedushah* of *Makom HaMikdash* — the sanctity of the place as expressed through the verse *lifnei Hashem Elokecha*. On this analysis, the question of whether one may eat *ma'aser sheni* nowadays turns not on whether the *mizbeach* is standing but on whether *Makom HaMikdash* retains its *kedushah*. This is precisely the question that Charlie raised at the outset of the *ma'aser sheni* discussion, and which the *Gemara* here implicitly addresses by distinguishing between the altar-presence requirement applicable to *kodshei kodashim* and the *kedushah*-of-place requirement applicable to *kodshim kalim* and *ma'aser sheni*.

---

## Blood Spill Dispute

### Rav Papa Setup

The *Gemara* now presents an alternative version of the entire dispute. Rav Papa reframes where exactly the disagreement lies. According to this version, when the *mizbeach* itself is destroyed, there is no dispute: all authorities agree that one may not eat the meat. The eating is dependent on the *mizbeach*'s existence, and when it is gone, the permission to eat is terminated. The disagreement, says Rav Papa, arises only in a case where the blood was spilled — that is, the *shechita* was performed but the blood was not successfully sprinkled on the altar.

### Bavel Position

The scholars of *Bavel* hold that eating the meat is dependent on the blood having been sprinkled on the *mizbeach*. If the blood was spilled and never reached the altar, the meat is forbidden regardless of whether the *shechita* itself was valid. The act of valid *zerika* is a condition for the permissibility of eating, not merely a requirement of the *avodah* process.

### EY Position

The scholars of *Eretz Yisrael* hold otherwise: eating the meat depends on the validity of the *shechita*, not on whether the blood was ultimately sprinkled. Once the animal has been slaughtered in a valid manner, the meat is in principle permitted to eat, and the failure of the *zerika* — whether through spillage or some other cause — does not retroactively prohibit it.

This is the second version of the debate between *Bavel* and *Eretz Yisrael*. Where the first version concerned the presence or absence of the *mizbeach* as a structure, this version concerns the relationship between *zerika* and eating: is the *kohen*'s act of throwing the blood a prerequisite for the *bechor*'s meat, or is valid *shechita* alone sufficient to permit it?

---

---

# Zevachim 61

## Mizbeiach Whole

### Shechita Requirement

The daf opens at the bottom of 61b with a ruling that had been established: one must perform *shechita* while the *mizbeiach* is whole. A parallel question had been raised regarding the *ketores* — whether the incense offering also requires an intact *mizbeiach* — but the conclusion was that it does not. The *shechita* requirement, however, is firm. And further: just as *shechita* requires an intact *mizbeiach*, so too does the consumption of the meat, since the meat is linked to the blood. The same logic extends to the *mincha*: one must take the *komets* with the *mizbeiach* intact, and presumably one must eat the remainder under those same conditions as well.

### Kodshei vs. Kodshim Kalim

All of the above is straightforward with respect to *kodshei kodashim*, because the eating of *kodshei kodashim* takes place in the *azarah* and is therefore inherently referenced to the *mizbeiach* — it can be understood as something analogous to being burned on the altar. The question becomes more pressing with regard to *kodshim kalim*. Since *kodshim kalim* is eaten anywhere in Yerushalayim, and is consumed by the owners rather than the *kohanim*, there is a compelling reason to think it bears no intrinsic connection to the *mizbeiach* whatsoever.

### Rabbi Yishmael Bechor

The initial position was that, yes, even the meat of *kodshim kalim* requires the *mizbeiach* to be whole — derived from a teaching of Rabbi Yishmael concerning the *bechor*. Rabbi Yishmael linked the blood of the *bechor* to its meat: just as the blood of the *bechor* requires a *mizbeiach*, so too does the eating of its meat. This linkage was then read as extending even to *maaser sheni*, raising deeper questions about whether the operative factor is the *kedushah* of the *makom*, the *kedushah* of the *mikdash* as an institution, or the physical structure of the *mizbeiach* itself — a fascinating set of distinctions that we bracket here for its own discussion.

---

## Rabbi Yirmiyah Dispute

### Babylonians Criticized

When this teaching was reported to Rabbi Yirmiyah — *ki salik* Ravin and presented the discussion before him — his response was strikingly harsh. He said: *bavlayi tipshayi* — the foolish Babylonians — because they sit in a land of darkness they speak dark, unilluminated ideas. Could they really think that the eating of *kodshim kalim* requires the *mizbeiach* to be whole? Did they not hear the following *braita*?

### Camp Transit Pesul

The *braita* Rabbi Yirmiyah cites states: *bishat siluk masa'ot* — at the time the camp decamps and moves — *kodshim nifsalim*, sacrifices become invalidated. At the same time, *zavim* and *metzora'im* are still sent outside their respective boundaries, which demonstrates that the concept of *machaneh* as such continues to exist even in transit. The question therefore becomes: if the *machaneh* still exists in transit — and the proof is that *teme'im* are expelled from it — why should *kodshim* be invalidated?

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

This is where Rashi and Tosafot part ways in a genuinely illuminating dispute. Rashi holds that this *braita* supports precisely what we had been saying about the *mizbeiach*. Even in transit, the concept of *machaneh shechinah* continues to exist — the *machaneh* is intact — but the *Mishkan* has been deconstructed, and therefore the *kodshim* are invalidated because there is no *mizbeiach*. The *machaneh* is present; it is the *mizbeiach* that is missing.

Tosafot disagrees fundamentally. For Tosafot, even in transit one can speak of *machaneh Yisrael* and *machaneh leviyah* — the *Bnei Yisrael* marching in formation, the *Leviyim* in their procession — and it is precisely those camps that generate the expulsion of *zavim* and *metzora'im* from their respective zones. But what one cannot speak of during transit, says Tosafot, is *machaneh shechinah*. For *machaneh shechinah* to exist, the camp must be encamped and the *Mishkan* must be erected. When the *Mishkan* has been taken apart and is being transported, there is no *machaneh shechinah*. The *kodshim* are therefore invalidated not merely because there is no *mizbeiach*, but because the situation is analogous to the meat having been taken outside the bounds of the *azarah* — as if the *Beit HaMikdash* itself were destroyed.

The conceptual stakes are sharply drawn: one can have *Har HaBayit* and *Yerushalayim* without having *makom hamikdash*. So too here, one can have *machaneh Yisrael* and *machaneh leviyah* without having *machaneh shechinah*. For Rashi, *machaneh shechinah* persists in transit and the problem is solely the absence of the *mizbeiach*. For Tosafot, *machaneh shechinah* itself is absent in transit, and that absence is the primary disqualification.

### Two Eating Scenarios

A second *braita* is then cited: *bishnei mekomos kodshim ne'echalin* — *kodshim* may be eaten in two contexts. The assumption is that these two contexts are: when the camp is encamped, and when it is in transit. But this creates an immediate difficulty: the first *braita* said that *kodshim* are invalidated in transit, and now this *braita* says they can be eaten in transit. How are these reconciled?

The initial suggestion is: *mai lav ha bekodshei kodashim veha bekodshim kalim* — perhaps the first *braita* refers to *kodshei kodashim* and the second to *kodshim kalim*. The logic would be: in transit there is no *mizbeiach* and no *machaneh shechinah* (for Tosafot), so *kodshei kodashim* are invalidated. But *kodshim kalim*, which may be eaten throughout all of *machaneh Yisrael* — i.e., throughout Yerushalayim — do not require a *mizbeiach* and do not require *machaneh shechinah*; they require only *machaneh Yisrael*, which continues to exist even in transit. This reading, says the *Gemara*, supports Rabbi Yirmiyah's position: at least one *braita* shows that *kodshim kalim* does not need a *mizbeiach*.

### Ravina Reconciles

Ravina intervenes to defend the position that *kodshim kalim* does require a *mizbeiach*. He argues: *idi ve'idi bekodshim kalim* — both *braitot* are actually speaking about *kodshim kalim*. The first *braita* rules that even *kodshim kalim* cannot be eaten in transit, because *kodshim kalim* also requires a *mizbeiach*. So how does one explain the second *braita*, which seems to permit eating in transit?

*Velo kashya ha Rabbi Yishmael ha rabbanan* — this is a *machloket*. The second *braita* reflects the view that *kodshim kalim* does not require a *mizbeiach*, which is one opinion. Rabbi Yishmael's derivation from the *bechor* — linking the meat to the blood and requiring the *mizbeiach* for both — is what generated the position that *kodshim kalim* does require a *mizbeiach*. Rabbi Yirmiyah's citation proves only that there exists an opposing view; it does not demonstrate that Rabbi Yishmael's position is simply wrong. The Babylonians were not in error to follow Rabbi Yishmael — they were following a legitimate opinion.

### Two Places

There is a further resolution offered: *ve'ibais eima ha veha bekodshei kodashim* — both *braitot* can be read as speaking about *kodshei kodashim*, and the phrase *bishnei mekomos* does not refer to "while erect" versus "in transit" at all, but rather to two distinct partial-transit scenarios.

Specifically, *kodem she'ya'amidu Leviyim es hamishkan* — before the *Leviyim* erected the *Mishkan* — and *le'achar she'yifreku Leviyim es hamishkan* — after the *Leviyim* dismantled it. But this requires clarification, since taken literally it would mean they ate *kodshim* before the *Mishkan* was ever standing, which cannot be the intent.

### Shechinah Status

Rashi explains that the phrase "before they erected it" is *lav davka* — it is simply structurally parallel phrasing. The actual two scenarios are: first, the normal case where the *Mishkan* is fully erected; and second, a moment early in the dismantling process, when the curtains have already been taken down but the *mizbeiach* has not yet been moved.

To understand this concretely: when the camp would prepare to travel, the *Leviyim* responsible for the curtains and structural elements would take those down first. The *Bnei Kehat* would then come and transport the sacred vessels. So there was a window — after the curtains came down but before the *mizbeiach* was removed — during which the altar remained in place. Rashi holds that even in that transitional state, *machaneh shechinah* continues to exist, and since the *mizbeiach* is still in its position, *kodshei kodashim* can still be eaten in reference to it. That is the second of the two permitted contexts.

Tosafot disagrees. For Tosafot, once you are in any state of transit, there is no *machaneh shechinah* — you may have *machaneh leviyah* and *machaneh Yisrael*, but not *machaneh shechinah*. However, Tosafot reads the *Mishkan* very precisely: if one dismantles only the *Mishkan* proper — the inner structure housing the *aron* and related vessels — but the *kela'im*, the curtains forming the *chatzer*, remain standing, and the *mizbeiach* remains in place, that is the second permitted scenario. The *chatzer* with its curtains is what constitutes *machaneh shechinah*, not the inner *Mishkan* alone. So: curtains down, *mizbeiach* gone — you have lost *machaneh shechinah*. But: inner *Mishkan* dismantled, curtains still up, *mizbeiach* still present — *machaneh shechinah* persists and *kodshei kodashim* may be eaten.

This is a striking structural difference. For Rashi, the *chiddush* is that even fully in transit — even after the entire apparatus has been packed up — *machaneh shechinah* persists, and as long as the *mizbeiach* remains, one may eat. For Tosafot, once the curtains are removed and the camp is moving, *machaneh shechinah* is gone — but the inner *Mishkan* can be dismantled while the curtains and *mizbeiach* remain, and that still qualifies.

There is an additional subtlety here for Tosafot. Recall the earlier discussion about *petach ohel moed* — the *shechita* had to be performed *lifnei* the *Ohel Moed*, but the eating did not have to be specifically at the entrance. In the scenario Tosafot describes, there is no *Ohel Moed* per se — the inner structure is dismantled — and yet the *chatzer* with its curtains retains enough sanctity to constitute *machaneh shechinah* for the purposes of eating. That is Tosafot's position, and the debate between Rashi and Tosafot here is genuinely consequential.

### Ohel Moed Transit

The *Gemara* then raises a further challenge: *eima hachi nami* — perhaps one should say that once in transit the *kodshei kodashim* are invalidated like *psul b'yotze*, as if the meat had been taken outside the permitted area. For Tosafot this would have been answered by pointing to the curtains still being up; but the *Gemara*'s actual answer is a verse: *venasa ohel moed* — the *Ohel Moed* will travel. The verse teaches: *af al pi shenasa, ohel moed hu* — even while in transit and on the move, it retains the status of *Ohel Moed*. The simple reading of this verse lends itself naturally to Rashi's position — in transit there is still *machaneh shechinah*, so there is no *psul b'yotze* — and Tosafot would presumably read it as: the *Ohel Moed* is indeed in transit and dismantled, but the *ohel moed* status persists, while still requiring the curtains to remain in place to define *machaneh shechinah*.

---

## Mizbeach History

### Shiloh Stone Altar

The *Gemara* now transitions to a historical survey of the *mizbeiach* from Moshe through Shlomo and into the Second *Beit HaMikdash*. Rav Huna states in the name of Rav: *mizbe'ach shel Shilo shel avanim haya* — the altar at Shiloh, where the *Mishkan* was established after entering *Eretz Yisrael*, was made of stone. The copper altar of Moshe's era was replaced with a large stone altar.

### Three Avanim

A *braita* is cited to support this: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov asks, *ma talmud lomar avanim avanim avanim* — why does the verse about building the altar upon entering *Eretz Yisrael* repeat the word *avanim* three times? *Avanim shelemot tivneh et mizbe'ach Hashem Elokecha, lo tanif aleihem barzel* — you shall build the altar of God from whole stones, you shall not lift iron upon them. From the triple repetition, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives that there were three distinct stone altars: *echad shel Shilo* — one at Shiloh, where, even though the curtain-and-curtain *Mishkan* structure continued from Moshe's era, a new stone altar was built to accommodate the increased volume of the nation entering the land, and perhaps also to express a sense of greater permanence; *ve'echad shel Nov veGivon* — one at Nov and Givon, where even without the full *Mishkan* structure there was a *bama gedola*, a major altar, also of stone; and *u'veit olamim* — and the third is the *Beit HaMikdash* itself. By the time the nation entered *Eretz Yisrael*, the central altars were already stone.

### Fire on Copper

Rav Acha bar Ami challenges this. He cites a *braita* from *Seder Olam*: *esh sheyarda min hashamayim bimei Moshe lo nistalka me'al mizbe'ach hanechoshet ela bimei Shlomo* — the divine fire that descended in the time of Moshe (the fire we read about in *parshat Shmini*, which consumed the sacrifices at the inauguration) never departed from the copper altar until the time of Shlomo. And then: the divine fire that descended in the time of Shlomo similarly did not depart until *Menashe* the evil king caused it to be removed. If, as Rav Huna says, they replaced the copper altar with a stone altar as soon as they arrived at Shiloh, the divine fire should have left the copper altar at that point — or at minimum, the source should have described it as transferring. But it says explicitly that it remained on the copper altar. This implies the copper altar remained in active use straight through until the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Hybrid Altar

The *Gemara* responds: *hu de'amar k'Rabbi Natan* — Rav Huna is following the position of Rabbi Natan. As the *braita* records: *Rabbi Natan omer, mizbe'ach sheb'Shilo shel nechoshet haya, chalul umalei avanim* — the altar at Shiloh was made of copper but was hollow and filled with stones. It was not the same altar as Moshe's solid copper altar; a new one was fashioned, with a copper exterior shell and stones filling the interior. This is an interesting compromise — presumably because the rest of the structure retained the appearance of the *Mishkan*, they wished to preserve some visual continuity with the copper altar, while at the same time incorporating stone, perhaps as a marker that this was not yet the final resting place. According to this view, two *braitot* reflect two genuine opinions about the Shiloh altar.

### Coexisting Altars

Rav Adda bar Yitzchak offers a more elegant resolution that avoids positing a *machloket*. His answer: *mai lo nistalka? lo nistalka levatala* — when the source says the divine fire did not depart from the copper altar, it does not mean the copper altar remained the functional altar of use. Rather: *rabbanan amri shaviva hava meshadra* — the fire would send out bolts and sparks. The picture Rashi draws is striking: in Shiloh there were, in fact, two altars. The large stone altar was the one actively used for sacrifices. But the small copper altar from Moshe's era stood alongside it, and the divine fire resided on the copper altar. When sacrifices were offered on the stone altar, the divine fire would send out a bolt — a spark — from the copper to the stone, connecting the two.

This image carries a weight beyond the technical. The new, larger altar is where the work of *avodah* happens; but the genuine divine fire, the original heavenly presence, remains tethered to the older altar. The nation is doing its own thing, in a sense, but borrowing from the original source of sacred fire. It is a picture of continuity and transition simultaneously.

### Fire Rounds

Rav Pappa offers yet another reading: *ushpiza havei nakit, zimnin hacha zimnin hacha* — the fire would do its rounds like a host visiting different places. Sometimes it would be on the copper altar, sometimes on the stone. The contrast with Rav Adda's view is subtle but meaningful. Rav Adda pictures the fire permanently on the copper altar, sending out occasional bolts to the stone. Rav Pappa pictures the fire alternating, fully present at one and then the other. If Rav Adda's image suggests the old is the permanent and genuine source from which the new borrows, Rav Pappa's image of alternation conveys something different: a moment of genuine transition, where neither the old nor the new has exclusive claim on the divine presence — a hovering between one era and the next, appropriate to the liminal period before the *Beit HaMikdash* established a final and permanent home.

---

## Expansion Reasons

### Footprint Extended

The *Gemara* cites a *mishnah* from tractate *Middot*: *uchshe'alu Bnei Gola* — when the returnees from exile came up in the time of Ezra — *hosifu alav arba amot min hadarom ve'arba amot min hama'arav, k'min gamma* — they added four *amot* from the south and four *amot* from the west, in the shape of a gamma.

To understand the significance of these numbers, one must recall the earlier discussion of dimensions. The *mizbeiach* of Shlomo had a base of 28×28 *amot*. Going inward one *amah* for the *yesod*, one *amah* for the *sovev*, and then allowing for the *karnot* and the walkway — a total of four *amot* inward on each side — a 28×28 base yields a top surface of 20×20. The *Bnei Gola* extended the base: four *amot* added to the south and four to the west, bringing the footprint to 32×32. On a 32×32 base, the same four-*amah* reduction on each side yields a top surface of 24×24. This was not an addition to an existing structure — obviously one cannot simply attach to an existing *mizbeiach* — but the new *mizbeiach* was built with this larger footprint as its foundation.

### Population Reason

Rav Yosef offers an explanation for why the *Bnei Gola* enlarged the *mizbeiach*: *mishum d'lo sipaik* — the older dimensions were insufficient; they needed greater surface area to handle the volume of offerings.

### Abaye Counters

Abaye immediately challenges this. He points to the verse about the First Temple period, which describes the population of *Yehudah veYisrael rabim k'chol asher al hayam* — as numerous as the sands of the sea. With that enormous population, the 28×28 base was sufficient. The Second Temple began with *kol kahal ke'echad arba ribu* — the entire assembled community numbered a mere 40,000 people who made *aliyah*. How could a far smaller population require a larger altar?

### Divine Fire Speed

The response resolves the paradox: *hasam eish shel shamayim mesayasa, hacha ein eish shel shamayim mesayasa* — there the heavenly fire helped; here the heavenly fire did not help. The divine fire consumed offerings miraculously and instantaneously in the First Temple period — there was no waiting for things to burn naturally — so the surface area of the altar was effectively unlimited in its throughput. As soon as one sacrifice was placed, it was consumed, and the next could begin. In the Second Temple, the burning had to proceed naturally, requiring sacrifices to occupy the altar surface for extended periods. A note must be added here: Rashi, drawing on another *Gemara*, clarifies that there was indeed a heavenly fire in the Second Temple period — to say otherwise would raise severe theological difficulties about the validity of the *avodah* entirely — but that fire did not accelerate the consuming. It was present as a *siman* of divine presence but did not perform the miraculous rapid consumption of the First Temple's heavenly fire. Hence the need for greater surface area.

### Wine Libation

A second reason for the expansion is then offered: *shissin hosifu* — the addition was made in order to accommodate the *shittin*, the underground cavern that received the wine *nesachim*. The mechanism requires explanation.

### Hole Position

Rashi describes the situation as follows. In the First Temple, when wine *nesachim* were poured at the southwest corner of the altar, the wine would run down the sides of the altar and flow into an exterior pit — a *bor* — situated just outside and below the corner. In the Second Temple period, a different practice was desired: the wine should be absorbed into the altar itself, descending through an interior channel built into the structure and flowing down into the same underground well. However, for this to work, the base of the altar had to be positioned directly over the well, so that the corner of the altar — where the *shittin* opening was located — would be situated above it. Since the well was in a position slightly removed from where the First Temple footprint had placed the corner, the solution was to extend the base of the new altar southward and westward by four *amot* in each direction. This repositioned the southwest corner over the well, allowing an interior channel — a funnel — to carry the wine from the corner of the *mizbeiach* down into the underground *shittin*.

### Solid to Drinking

This practical adjustment rested on a conceptual shift. The earlier understanding of *mizbe'ach adamah* — the verse's requirement that the altar be of earth — had been interpreted to mean that the altar must be *atum be'adamah*, completely solid on the inside, with no hollow spaces. Under this interpretation, an interior channel was impossible. But a new interpretation prevailed: *shtiyah ke'achilah* — drinking is analogous to eating. Just as the sacrificial meat is consumed by the altar's fire, so too must the wine *nesachim* be consumed — not simply poured on the exterior and allowed to run away, but taken in by the altar itself. This conceptual equation of the altar's "drinking" with its "eating" justified — and indeed required — the interior cavity.

One might note a certain irony here: much of the earlier discussion had been oriented toward de-emphasizing the anthropomorphic dimensions of the *avodah*, stressing that it is God's fire that consumes, that the rising smoke is not literally food for God. And yet here the *Gemara* embraces the image wholeheartedly — the altar eats and the altar drinks. Whatever discomfort that imagery may occasion, the halachic point stands.

And then the *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: if *mizbe'ach adamah* prohibits any hollow interior, how could the *shittin* — the underground well — exist at all? After all, the *Gemara* in tractate Sukkah famously recounts that David built the *shittin*, drilling deep into the earth until he cracked open the *tehom*. Tosafot there addresses the question directly in a brief but pointed comment: *bor shel shittin lo hayah chashuv mechilah kivan de'tzorech mizbe'ach* — the pit of the *shittin* does not count as a *mechilah*, a forbidden void beneath the altar, because it serves a function of the altar itself. The prohibition is against constructing the altar over something extraneous — a vaulted room used for other purposes below. When the underground space is functionally integrated into the altar's *avodah*, it is part of the structure, not a disqualifying void beneath it.

---

## Ezra Dimensions

### Proper Dimensions

Rav Yosef then introduces a *braita*: *vayachinu hamizbe'ach al mechonav* — the verse about Ezra's generation describes how they established the *mizbeiach* on its foundation. The *braita* teaches: *she'higiyu lesof midotav* — that in the time of Ezra they arrived at the proper, correct dimensions of the *mizbeiach*, dimensions that had not been fully known in the time of Shlomo. This is why they built it differently — not merely for practical reasons, but because they genuinely understood something about the *mizbeiach*'s true dimensions that Shlomo had not grasped.

### Better Than Shlomo

This is a striking *Gemara*. Shlomo is famously described as *hachacham mikol adam* — wiser than any person. Moreover, the verse in *Divrei HaYamim* records David himself saying *hakol bichsav miyad Hashem alai hiskil* — everything was revealed to me in writing from God. If the very dimensions of the *Beit HaMikdash* and its altar were communicated by divine revelation, how could Ezra's generation claim to know better? How can those who returned from Babylonian exile — a far smaller and less distinguished generation — have a more accurate understanding of the proper altar dimensions than Shlomo, who received direct divine communication?

### Verse Derivation

Rav Yosef resolves this: *kra ashkach ve'daraish* — they found a verse and interpreted it. This very phrase is used in a parallel context elsewhere, regarding changes made in the Second Temple. Ezra's generation did not simply innovate or claim to know better through personal wisdom. They engaged in *drash* — they looked carefully at a verse and derived from it a new understanding.

### House Analogy

The verse is from *Divrei HaYamim*, where David says: *zeh hu Beis Hashem Elokim ve'zeh mizbe'ach le'olah le'Yisrael* — this is the house of God, and this is the *mizbeiach* for the *olah* for Israel. The word *ki bayit* — "like a house" — then provides the basis for a *gezerah shavah* or analogical derivation: *ma bayit* — what is the house, meaning David's palace — *shishim amah* — was 60 *amot* in one dimension; *af mizbe'ach shishim amah* — so too the *mizbeiach* has a dimension of 60 *amot*. Rashi clarifies that this does not mean the *mizbeiach* must be 60×60; it means the *mizbeiach* may be built within a zone of up to 60×60 *amot*. The 28×28 of Shlomo's altar was not invalid — but it was not the only legitimate possibility. The verse reveals that within a 60×60 space, there is halakhic room to expand.

What Ezra's generation discovered, then, was not that Shlomo had erred. They discovered that the existing dimensions had not been the only valid option. They were permitted — and, given the circumstances, wise — to build larger. The practical need for more surface area (absent the accelerating divine fire) and the desire to position the *shittin* properly under the altar both pointed in the same direction, and the verse confirmed that expanding within the 60×60 limit was entirely legitimate.

### Oral Torah Space

This conclusion resonates far beyond the technical question of altar dimensions. The entire episode is, in essence, a parable for the relationship between *Torah Shebe'al Peh* and the received tradition. The instinct would be to reconstruct the altar exactly as it had been — Shlomo built it as 28×28; who are we, returning from exile with a fraction of the population and none of the grandeur of the First Temple period, to do otherwise? The answer is *kra ashkach ve'daraish*: we looked at a verse and we interpreted. And that interpretation — a genuine act of *drash*, not mere innovation — revealed that there is more space than the received practice had utilized.

The keyword is *darash*. It is not a simple, literal reading of a verse. It is an insight, an act of interpretation that unlocks latent meaning. And that interpretive act reveals that the tradition, while binding, is not so rigid as to admit only one possible configuration. There is halakhic space, room to move, room to respond to changed circumstances. The First Temple had heavenly fire that made the smaller surface sufficient; the Second Temple does not, so more surface is needed. The First Temple poured wine on the exterior; the Second Temple wants the altar to drink it internally. These are genuine differences, and the tradition — properly interpreted — provides room for them.

*Af mizbe'ach shishim amah* — the *mizbeiach* can be up to 60 *amot*. That is the outer boundary. Within it, each generation works with what it has, interprets as it must, and builds accordingly.

---

---

# Zevachim 62

## Locating the Altar

### Question: Locating Mizbe…

The *gemara* on 62b opens with a question that follows naturally from a discussion a few lines earlier, where the *gemara* had been addressing how the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* knew how to construct the Second *Beit Hamikdash* and in what respects they modified the *mizbe'ach* from the one built by Moshe. The *gemara* now narrows its focus: *bishlama bayit minkar tzurato* — it is understandable how the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* knew where to locate the structure of the *Beit Hamikdash* itself, since the foundations of the first *Beit Hamikdash* were still visible. *Ela mizbe'ach mena yad'ei* — but how did they know where to place the *mizbe'ach*? The *mizbe'ach* itself was gone, and there was apparently nothing obvious to mark its precise location.

### R. Elazar: Michael's Vis…

Rabbi Elazar answers: *ra'u mizbe'ach banuy u-Michael haSar haGadol omeid u-makriv alav* — they had some form of prophetic vision in which they saw the *mizbe'ach* already built, and Michael, the great angelic *sar*, standing there and offering a sacrifice upon it. This is a striking passage. The image of Michael as *sar melitz* — the angelic advocate — bringing *korbanot* invites the question of what kind of offering an angel would bring, and to what end. One natural inference is that these were *olot*, which are not brought for sin, consistent with Michael's role as *melitz yosher*. More broadly, the vision suggests that when the earthly *Beit Hamikdash shel mata* does not exist, some sort of spiritual *Beit Hamikdash shel ma'ala* continues to operate at the level of the *malachim*, and the *Maharsha* connects this to the well-known idea that the heavenly Jerusalem is directly above its earthly counterpart, as discussed in *Taanit*. When *Yisrael* returns and reconstructs the *Beit Hamikdash shel mata*, they fill in the gap below. The *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* were shown the heavenly *mizbe'ach* as a kind of template — a divine blueprint — so they would know exactly where to build on earth. The analogy is evocative: what could not be recovered archaeologically was instead revealed spiritually.

This also bears on the relationship between *ruach hakodesh* and the act of building the *Beit Hamikdash*. One recalls that Moshe himself, when confronted with the construction of the *menorah*, did not know precisely how it should be made, and the Torah says *kazeh* — God showed him the form. Something similar seems to be at work here: when human understanding reaches its limit, divine assistance bridges the gap.

### R. Yitzchak: Ashes of Yi…

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha offers a second answer: *afro shel Yitzchak hu she-munach b'oto makom* — the ashes of Yitzchak are deposited in that very spot. This opinion draws on the imagery of the *Akeida* and the *olah*, connecting the *mizbe'ach* in Jerusalem to the binding of Yitzchak on that same site. The precise nature of the ashes is worth noting: the *efer* mentioned here is presumably from the ram that was sacrificed in Yitzchak's place, though certain *midrashim* develop this idea further, suggesting — in ways that may reflect later martyrological contexts — that Yitzchak himself was in some sense sacrificed and then revived. The ashes, whatever their precise nature, served as a physical marker — a trace of the primordial sacrifice that identified the exact location of the future *mizbe'ach*.

### R. Shmuel: Smell Distinc…

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani provides a third answer, which operates on an entirely different register: *mi-kol ha-bayit kulo herichu rei'ach ketoret, mi-sham herichu rei'ach evarim* — throughout the entire area of the *Beit Hamikdash*, which was recognizable from its foundations, the air smelled of *ketoret*, the incense. But from that one spot, the smell was different — it was the smell of *evarim*, of burnt animal limbs. The location of the *mizbe'ach* was thus distinguished by a distinct olfactory signature, the residual smell of centuries of animal sacrifice, as against the pervasive fragrance of *ketoret* that characterized the rest of the *chatzer*. This answer, like the others, points to a form of knowledge unavailable through ordinary architectural or archaeological investigation — whether visionary, physical, or sensory, the location had to be revealed.

### Three Prophets from Exile

Rabba bar bar Chana, citing Rabbi Yochanan, introduces a complementary tradition: *sheloshah nevi'im alu imahem min ha-golah* — three prophets came up with the people from the exile to rebuild the *Beit Hamikdash Sheni*. The first testified to them about the *mizbe'ach* — that is, regarding its permitted dimensions, namely that the *mizbe'ach* could be built as large as sixty *amot*, larger than either Moshe's or Shlomo's. The second testified about the *mekom ha-mizbe'ach* — where the *mizbe'ach* should be located, which stands as a fourth answer to the question with which the *gemara* opened. The third testified that sacrifices may be offered even when there is no *bayit* — *makrivin af al pi she-ein bayit*. This third ruling, as Rashi notes, is connected to the principle of *kedushat ha-bayit kidsheha l'shata v'kidsheha l'atid lavo* — that the sanctity of the *Beit Hamikdash* consecrated the site both for its time and for the future. This is, of course, a *machloket* that runs throughout *Shas*, and the *gemara* here does not develop it further; the *rishonim* are similarly brief on the matter.

### R. Elazar ben Yaakov

A parallel *baraita* is then cited: *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov omer*, similarly recording that three *nevi'im* came up from the *golah*. In this version, however, the three testimonies are configured differently. One prophet testified about both the location of the *mizbe'ach* and its permitted dimensions, combining what the first *baraita* split across two figures. The second testified that sacrifice may be offered even without the *bayit*. The third testified about something entirely outside the world of the *Mikdash* — *she-tikatev Ashurit*, that the Torah should be written in the *Ashurit* script. This refers to the transition, associated with the time of Ezra, from the ancient *Ketav Ivri* to the *Ketav Ashuri*, the square script familiar today. According to one view in the *gemara* in Sanhedrin 21b, discussed by both Rashi and Rambam, the *Ketav Ashuri* was the original script, subsequently lost, and restored by Ezra. The inclusion of this testimony alongside the testimonies about the *mizbe'ach* is striking: it suggests that the prophetic charge of those who came from exile encompassed not only the physical rebuilding of the *Beit Hamikdash* but also the transmission and accessibility of Torah itself — the dual revolution of Ezra's era.

---

## Mizbeach Components

### Me'akvin Components

The *gemara* now turns to a *baraita* enumerating what invalidates the *mizbe'ach*. *Keren v'kevesh v'yesod v'ribu'a me'akvin* — the four *keranot* at the top corners of the *mizbe'ach*, the *kevesh* or ramp, the *yesod* or foundation, and the *ribu'a*, meaning that the *mizbe'ach* must be a perfect square — all of these are *me'akvin*: if any of them is absent, the *mizbe'ach* is *pasul*. By contrast, *midato orko midato rochvo midato komato ein me'akvin* — the precise measurements of length, width, and height are not *me'akvin*. The *mizbe'ach* may deviate from its specified dimensions without being rendered *pasul*, as long as these four essential structural features are present.

### Pesuk Derivation

The *gemara* asks *mena hanei milei* — what is the scriptural basis for this distinction? Rav Huna points to the use of the definite form *hamizbe'ach* in several verses in Vayikra. The rule he derives is: *kol makom she-ne'emar hamizbe'ach le-akev* — wherever the Torah uses the form *hamizbe'ach*, it indicates that the element mentioned alongside it is *me'akev*. Rashi identifies three such verses: *keren hamizbe'ach* in Vayikra 4, making the *keranot* *me'akev*; *el yesod hamizbe'ach*, also in Vayikra 4, making the *yesod* *me'akev*; and *el pnei hamizbe'ach*, where *panim* — the face of the *mizbe'ach* — is understood to refer to the approach to it, i.e., the *kevesh* or ramp.

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge: if *hamizbe'ach* wherever it appears renders the adjacent element *me'akev*, then the verse *ve-natata oto tachat karchov hamizbe'ach mi-lemata* would imply that the *karchov* is likewise *me'akev*. What is the *karchov*? The *gemara* cites a *machloket tannaim*: *Rabbi omer ze kiyor* — Rabbi holds it is the *kiyor*, a decorative element at the top of the *mizbe'ach*; *Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehuda omer ze ha-sovev* — Rabbi Yose holds it is the *sovev*, a surrounding strip. The *gemara* accepts that yes, the *karchov*, whatever it is, is *me'akev*, since the verse uses *hamizbe'ach* in connection with it.

### Karchov Debate

The *machloket* between Rabbi and Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehuda about what the *karchov* actually is thus has direct practical consequence: according to Rabbi, it is a decorative feature — *kiyor*, a kind of ornamental element — placed atop the *mizbe'ach*; according to Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehuda, it is the *sovev*, a structural surrounding strip. Both agree it is essential to the *mizbe'ach's* validity.

### Broken Horn Story

The *gemara* supports its ruling with a *baraita* that describes a historically famous episode: *oto ha-yom nifgema keren hamizbe'ach* — on that day a *keren* of the *mizbe'ach* was broken. The story, elaborated in *Sukka*, involves the practice of *nisuch ha-mayim*, the water libation on *Sukkot*. This *mitzvah* is not stated explicitly in the Torah and was disputed by the *Tzadokim*, who were more literalist in their reading of scripture. On this occasion, a *Tzadoki Kohen* refused to pour the water onto the *mizbe'ach* — or poured it instead on his feet. The people, enraged, pelted him with their *etrogim* and also, according to the text, with stones. The debris struck the *mizbe'ach* and broke off one of its *keranot*. The *gemara* records that they brought a *bul shel melach* — a lump of salt — and stuffed it into the broken corner as a temporary repair, not because this made the *mizbe'ach* fit for use, but to preserve the dignity of the *mizbe'ach* so that it would not be seen as defective: *she-lo yeira'eh mizbe'ach pagum*. The *baraita* then concludes with the ruling that underlies the entire discussion: *she-kol mizbe'ach she-ein lo keren ve-kevesh ve-yesod ve-ribu'a pasul* — any *mizbe'ach* lacking a *keren*, *kevesh*, *yesod*, or *ribu'a* is *pasul*. Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehuda adds: *af ha-sovev* — also the *sovev*, consistent with his view that the *sovev* is the *karchov* which the verse renders *me'akev*.

### Two Karchov Functions

The *gemara* then refines our understanding of the *karchov* further, with a *baraita* that asks *eizehu karchov* — what is the *karchov*? The answer given is: it is the space *bein keren le-keren*, and in addition, *mekom hiluch raglei hakohanim amah* — a place one *amah* wide where the *kohanim* walk. The *gemara* objects: the *kohanim* could not literally walk *between* the *keranot*, since the corners would impede movement. The *baraita* must therefore mean that the *karchov* designates the space between the corners as one element, and the *amah* walkway for the *kohanim* as a separate, additional feature.

A further difficulty arises from the verse *tachat karkuvo mi-lemata ad chetzyo*, which implies the *karchov* was below — on the side — while the discussion of the *karchov* as an architectural feature placed it near the top. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by saying *trei havu* — there were two *karkovim*. *Chad le-noy*, one was decorative, corresponding to the feature described by Rabbi (the *kiyor*) or Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehuda (the *sovev*). *Ve-chad le-kohanim de-la nishtakedu*, the other served as a safety feature for the *kohanim* so they would not slip. Rashi explains this second *karchov* not as a fence projecting upward, but as a groove or indentation carved into the surface along the top of the *mizbe'ach*, giving the *kohanim's* feet traction. Whether one imagines it as a lattice engraving or as a narrow channel cut into the stone, the effect is the same: a recessed strip that prevented slipping, while the decorative *karchov* on the exterior side served an aesthetic and structural purpose. The two functions — beauty and safety — thus coexist in two distinct features, both sharing the name *karchov*.

---

## Mizbeach Dimensions

### Dimensions Not Me'akvin

Having established the four *me'akvin* elements, the *gemara* returns to the other side of the *baraita*: *midato orko u-midat komato ein me'akvin* — the precise length and height of the *mizbe'ach* do not constitute *me'akvin*. That is to say, variations in the overall dimensions of the *mizbe'ach* do not render it *pasul*, as long as the essential structural features are present.

### Rabbi Yosi's Size Limit

Rabbi Mani qualifies this ruling with an important caveat: *u-bilvad shelo yifchatenu mi-mizbe'ach she-asa Moshe* — provided one does not make it smaller than the *mizbe'ach* that Moshe built. While the upper bound extends to sixty *amot*, there is a floor below which the *mizbe'ach* may not be reduced.

### R. Yosef's Confusion

The *gemara* then asks how large that floor is: *kamah*? Rabbi Yosef answers *amah* — one *amah*. His colleagues laughed at this, and cited the explicit verse: *chamesh amot orech ve-chamesh amot rochav ravu'a yihiyeh ha-mizbe'ach* — the *mizbe'ach* should be five *amot* by five *amot* square. How could Rabbi Yosef say one *amah*? Rashi notes at the top of the *daf* that Rabbi Yosef suffered from memory difficulties in his old age, which explains why his students thought he had erred.

Abaye, his devoted student, intervened: *dilma mekom ha-ma'arachah ka'amar mar* — perhaps the master was referring to the middle square, the *mekom ha-ma'arachah*, the space where the actual pyre was arranged, which was indeed one *amah* by one *amah*. Rabbi Yosef responded gratefully: you, a great man, understood what I was saying. He then turned on those who had laughed at him and called them *bnei Keturah* — implying they were peripheral to the tradition, like the sons of Avraham who were sent away and did not inherit the covenant, almost sons of Avraham, but not quite.

This same epithet, *bnei Keturah*, appears shortly afterward in a story involving Rabbi Tarfon. The nephews of Rabbi Tarfon were sitting before him studying. He opened his mouth and deliberately misstated a *pasuk*, substituting a different name for Keturah. When they corrected him — *Keturah ketiv*, it says Keturah — he called them *bnei Keturah*. The technique was apparently a classic: a teacher feigns a mistake to test whether the students are paying attention. Rabbi Tarfon's use of the name Keturah in the deliberate misquotation is itself a kind of jest: the word he used to catch his sleeping students was the very word they had to supply to correct him, and his rebuke was then that they were *bnei Keturah* — knowing the surface but not the depth, or as one might put it, all fragrance and no substance.

### Gezirin Measurements

The *gemara* next addresses the dimensions of the *gezirin*, the wooden logs used as the base of the *ma'arachah*. Abaye bar Huna, citing Rav Chama bar Guria, states: *gezirin she-asah Moshe orchan amah ve-rochban amah ve-ovyan ke-machak godesh se'ah* — the wooden logs that Moshe made were one *amah* long, one *amah* wide, and as thin as the implement used to level a *se'ah* measure of grain. These two flat wooden squares, stacked one atop the other, formed the platform on which the *atzei ha-ma'arachah* and the fire rested. The thinness of the *gezirin* is notable: they were substantial in area but minimal in thickness, functioning essentially as a base rather than as a structural element.

### Amah Kduma Discussion

Rabbi Yirmiyah adds that the *amah* in question is an *amah gedumah* — a smaller *amah* of five *tefachim* rather than the standard six, appropriate for the constrained space at the top of the *mizbe'ach* where the *kohanim* were walking in a one-*amah* strip. Since that strip was already not wide, the middle *amah* of the *ma'arachah* should be minimally sized.
