Rav Yosef questions whether Rabbi Yirmiyah's deduction was even necessary, pointing to a *baraita* that derives the same principle from a verse: *al ha-etzim asher al ha-esh asher al ha-mizbe'ach* — the layered description of wood upon fire upon *mizbe'ach* teaches *she-lo yehu etzim yotzim min ha-mizbe'ach klum*, that the logs must not protrude beyond the *mizbe'ach* at all. They must fit exactly within the *mizbe'ach's* dimensions.

Rashi's commentary clarifies that Rabbi Yirmiyah and Rav Yosef may in fact be referring to two different types of reduced measurement — the *amah kedumah* of five *tefachim* on the one hand, and what Rashi calls *amah metumtemet* on the other — though the precise distinction between them is referenced elsewhere, in *Menachot*.

---

## Ramp Specifications

### Kevesh Dimensions

A *mishna* in *Masechet Midot* records the dimensions of the *kevesh*, the ramp ascending to the *mizbe'ach*: thirty-two *amot* long, sixteen *amot* wide, and nine *amot* high. The *gemara* now proceeds to derive and analyze the various specifications of the *kevesh*.

### Kevesh North Location

The *gemara* asks *mena hanei milei* — not about the measurements, but about the location: how do we know that the *kevesh* was on the south side of the *mizbe'ach*? Rav Huna cites the verse: *ve-shachat oto al yerech hamizbe'ach tzafonah* — one must slaughter the offering on the *yerech* of the *mizbe'ach* to the north. He derives from this: *she-yehe yerech ba-tzafon u-fanav ba-darom* — the *yerech*, the thigh or flank, should face north, and the face should be toward the south. The image evoked is of a person lying down, with his legs toward the north and his face toward the south. Since the *kevesh* is the face — the front — of the *mizbe'ach*, it follows that the *kevesh* was on the south side. The *mizbe'ach* is thirty-two *amot* in length (the long dimension), and sixteen *amot* wide; the person in this analogy is lying with his head to the south, his legs — his *yerech* — pointing north.

### Lying vs. Sitting Debate

The *gemara* challenges this interpretation. The verse says the *yerech* should be toward the north — but why does that require the face to be toward the south? One could equally imagine the *kevesh* on the north side, with a person sitting upright facing north, so that both the *yerech* and the face point in the same direction. In that case, the legs would still face north, satisfying the verse, yet the *kevesh* would be on the north, not the south.

Rava resolves this by invoking the word *ravu'a* — the verse says the *mizbe'ach* shall be *ravu'a*, and Rava understands this to imply lying down, consistent with the image of the *kevesh* being at the southern foot of the reclining figure. Abaye objects: *ravu'a* does not mean lying down; it teaches that the *mizbe'ach* must be square. Using *ravu'a* to also indicate a lying position is an overextension.

Rava responds: *mekhdiv meruba* — the word used is *ravu'a*, not *meruba*; had the Torah written *meruba*, that would only teach squareness. *Ravu'a* is deliberately chosen to convey both squareness and the orientation of the *kevesh*, since it carries connotations of both flatness and geometric perfection. Abaye counters: if *ravu'a* implied lying down, the Torah would have written *ravutz*. Rava's final answer is that *ravu'a* is the precisely correct word because it means both things simultaneously — *d'mashma hach u'mashma hach* — it teaches squareness and it conveys the image of a figure lying flat, which in turn establishes that the *kevesh* is on the south.

### Right Turns East

A second source for the *kevesh's* southern position comes from a *baraita* citing Rabbi Yehuda: the verse *u-ma'alotav pnot kadim* — the steps should turn to the east — establishes the rule that *kol pinot she-ata poneh lo yehu ela derech yamin la-mizrach*, all turns one makes should be right turns toward the east. If the *kevesh* is on the south, a *kohen* ascending and then turning would make a right turn that takes him eastward — toward the *kedushah*, toward the *kadim*. If the *kevesh* were on the north, the turn eastward would be a left turn. The requirement to turn right toward the east thus necessitates that the *kevesh* be on the south.

The *gemara* asks: perhaps the rule should be left turns to the east? The answer is derived from the *Yam shel Shlomo*, the great basin constructed by Shlomo. The verse describing the twelve cattle supporting the *yam* says that three face north, three face west, three face south, and three face east. The description proceeds from north to east by going around clockwise — right turns. The repeated use of *ponim* for each group of cattle is not merely to describe the basin; it establishes a general halakhic principle: *kol pinot she-ata poneh lo yehu ela derech yamin la-mizrach*. When approaching the *mizbe'ach*, one should always turn right to face east.

### Air Space Requirement

A question is posed to Rabbi Yosi in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: *avir yesh bein kevesh la-mizbe'ach* — there is an air space between the *kevesh* and the *mizbe'ach*. They were not flush against one another. Rabbi Yosi asks whether the questioner himself accepts this. He then offers a *pasuk*-based proof: *ve-asita olotecha ha-basar ve-ha-dam* — the verse juxtaposes *basar* (meat) and *dam* (blood) in connection with *olot*. The inference is *mah dam be-zrika af basar be-zrika* — just as the blood is applied through *zrika*, throwing, so too the meat must be thrown. Throwing implies that the *kohen* stands at some remove and sends the *basar* through the air onto the *mizbe'ach*, which implies an air space between the *kevesh* and the *mizbe'ach*.

The respondent pushes back: one could say the *kohen* stands on the top of the *ma'arachah* itself and throws from there — the air space traversed is within the *mizbe'ach*, not between the *kevesh* and the *mizbe'ach*. The reply: this argument fails because it is obvious that the *kohen* must throw, since the fire on the *ma'arachah* is already burning — no one places meat directly onto live flames with their hands. The throwing action is forced by the fire regardless. If the analogy between *basar* and *dam* is to teach us something beyond the self-evident, it must teach us that there is also an air gap between the *kevesh* and the *mizbe'ach* itself.

Rav Papa offers an alternative derivation that does not rely on the throwing analogy. He reasons logically: *ki dam mah dam avir karka mafsiko af basar avir karka mafsiko* — just as the *dam*, when thrown, traverses air space over the ground before reaching the *mizbe'ach*, so too the *basar* must traverse actual ground-level air space, not merely air space above the metal surface of the *mizbe'ach*. The analogy thus teaches that the *kohen* must stand on the ground — or equivalently, on the *kevesh* — and the *basar* must fly through open air between the *kevesh* and the *mizbe'ach*.

### Two Small Ramps

Rav Yehuda teaches that in addition to the main *kevesh*, there were *shnei kvashim ketanim yotzim min ha-kevesh* — two small ramps branching off from the main *kevesh*. One led to the *sovev*, and one led to the *yesod*, allowing the *kohanim* to access these elements of the *mizbe'ach* for the relevant *avodot*. Even these smaller ramps were *muvdalim min ha-mizbe'ach melo nima* — separated from the *mizbe'ach* by the width of a hair, not physically connected to it. The reason: *mishum she-ne'emar saviv* — because the verse says the *mizbe'ach* must be *saviv*, surrounding or encircled, which implies that the *mizbe'ach* must be a self-contained entity, completely surrounded by open space, even if only by a hair's breadth.

Rabbi Abahu provides an alternative derivation for the same gap, using the word *ravu'a* — the requirement that the *mizbe'ach* be square implies that it stand as an independent, self-contained structure. The *gemara* notes that both *limudim* are necessary. Had the Torah only written *saviv*, one might have thought the *mizbe'ach* could be round, merely requiring separation from adjacent structures; the word *ravu'a* teaches that it must be square. And had the Torah only written *ravu'a*, one might have thought it could be rectangular — elongated rather than perfectly square; the word *saviv* contributes the sense of perfect encircling, reinforcing the requirement for a proper square.

The *mishna* in *Midot* then records that the *kevesh* and the *mizbe'ach* together measured sixty-two *amot*. The *gemara* challenges: the *mizbe'ach* is thirty-two *amot* and the *kevesh* is thirty-two *amot* — that should total sixty-four, not sixty-two. The resolution is that the *yesod* and the *sovev* each consumed one *amah* of the *mizbe'ach's* base dimension, so the effective external length of the *mizbe'ach* was thirty *amot* rather than thirty-two, giving the correct total of sixty-two.

### Elevation Ratios

Rami bar Chama concludes the discussion with a general principle about ramp construction: *kol kivshei kvashim shalosh amot le-amah* — for all ramps generally, the standard elevation ratio is one *amah* of height for every three *amot* of horizontal distance. The *mizbe'ach* ramp, however, was constructed to a different ratio: *shalosh amot va-chatzi ve-etzba vi-shlish etzba be-zigufeta* — three and a half *amot* of horizontal distance, plus one *etzba* and a third, for every *amah* of elevation. How is this derived? The height of the *mizbe'ach* — excluding the *keranot* — was nine *amot*, and the length of the *kevesh* was thirty-two *amot*. Dividing thirty-two by nine yields three and a half with a remainder. The remaining half *amah* equals twelve *etzba'ot* (since one *amah* equals six *tefachim* and each *tefach* equals four *etzba'ot*, giving twenty-four *etzba'ot* per *amah*, and thus twelve *etzba'ot* per half-*amah*). Dividing those twelve *etzba'ot* among the nine *amot* of elevation gives one and one-third *etzba'ot* per *amah*, for a total ratio of three *amot* and one-third plus one *etzba* — consistent with the figure Rami bar Chama states. The *mizbe'ach* ramp was thus somewhat less steep than a standard ramp, reflecting the need for the *kohanim* to ascend comfortably and safely while performing the *avodah*.

---

---

# Zevachim 63

## Menachot Overview

### Opening & Context

Today's daf is 63, and we begin with the next *mishnah*. What makes this *mishnah* particularly interesting is that we are now moving into the subject of *menachot* — a topic that, of course, has an entire *masechet* devoted to it — but which appears here precisely to provide a contrast with what came before.

The previous *perek* was organized around the major distinctions governing *korbanot*: *kodshei kodashim* were slaughtered in the north of the *azarah*, while *kodshei kalim* were not; *kodshei kodashim* were eaten only within the *azarah*, *lifnim min hake'laim*, while the *shlamim*, as a representative *kodshei kalim*, could be eaten throughout all of *Yerushalayim*. That was the dominant framework of the previous *perek*. The opening of our *perek* then raised certain variations — what happens if one slaughters *kodshei kodashim* at the top of the *mizbe'ach* — essentially wrapping up residual questions from before. Now, with this *mishnah*, we turn to the *mincha*, which provides a revealing contrast.

### Mishnah: Kemitzah Anywhe…

The contrast is immediately striking. A *mincha* is, in every conventional sense, *kodshei kodashim*: it is eaten only by male *kohanim*, and only within the *azarah*. One might therefore have expected that the primary act of the *mincha* — the *kemitzah*, the taking of the handful of flour which is the analog to *shechitah* for animal offerings — would likewise be restricted to a specific location, presumably the north. But the *mishnah* opens by declaring otherwise:

> מְנָחוֹת הָיוּ נִקְמָצוֹת בְּכָל מָקוֹם בָּעֲזָרָה

*Menachot hayu nikmatzot bechol makom ba'azarah* — the *kemitzah* of *menachot* could be performed anywhere in the *azarah*; it was not restricted to the north.

The *mishnah* then continues with language that is virtually word-for-word identical to the rules governing *kodshei kodashim* in other respects: eaten by male *kohanim*, within the *azarah*, during the day and the following night until midnight, and so forth. The purpose of this *mishnah*, then, is specifically to highlight this one surprising divergence — that the location of the *kemitzah* carries no geographic restriction within the courtyard.

### Menachot vs. Kodshei Kod…

This sets up the central analytic tension of the *perek*: in what ways does the *mincha* follow the rules of *kodshei kodashim*, and in what ways does it deviate? The *mishnah* demonstrates that despite its status as *kodshei kodashim*, the *mincha* does not carry the northern requirement for its defining sacrificial act. The *Gemara* will now explore both the outer limits — can the *kemitzah* be performed even inside the *heichal*? — and the inner logic — why does the *mincha* not require the north at all?

---

## Mincha in Heichal

### R. Elazar: Heichal Kosher

Before the *Gemara* addresses the broad question of why the *mincha* is not restricted to the north, it first considers a more extreme possibility at the other end of the spectrum. Rabbi Elazar teaches:

> מִנְחָה שֶׁנִּקְמְצָה בַּהֵיכָל כְּשֵׁרָה

*Mincha shenikmetza baheichal kesheira* — a *mincha* whose *kemitzah* was performed inside the *heichal* itself is valid. This is already a *chiddush* of a different magnitude. We have established that the *kemitzah* is not restricted to the north; but does "anywhere in the *azarah*" encompass even the inner sanctum, the chamber housing the *shulchan* and the *menorah*?

### Lechem Hapanim Proof

Rabbi Elazar's source is the practice surrounding the *lechem hapanim*. The *lechem hapanim* is itself a form of *mincha*. Its *kemitzah*-equivalent — the act that permits the bread to be consumed — was not a taking of flour from the bread itself, but rather the removal of the two small bowls of frankincense resting atop the *shulchan*, which were then burned on the outer altar. That act of removal was performed inside the *heichal*, since that is where the *shulchan* stood. From this precedent, we learn that acts constituting the *kemitzah* of a *mincha* may legitimately be performed within the *heichal*.

### Heichal Permissibility

One might object — and the point is well-taken — that the case of the *lechem hapanim* was one of *ee efshar*, where there was no alternative: the frankincense was in the *heichal* and had to be taken from there. Perhaps where a choice exists, the *heichal* would be excluded. The *Gemara* will continue to engage this question, but for the moment, the ruling stands: the *heichal* is a permissible location for *kemitzah*, even if it is not the required one.

---

## R. Yirmiyah Challenge

### Kemitzah Restriction

Rabbi Yirmiyah challenges this ruling from a *baraita*. The verse describing the *kemitzah* reads:

> וְקָמַץ מִשָּׁם בִּמְלֹא קֻמְצוֹ מִסֹּלֶת הַמִּנְחָה וּמִשַּׁמְנָהּ עַל כָּל לְבֹנָתָהּ

*Vekamatz misham bimlo kumtzo misolet hamincha umishmanah ve'al kol levonasah* — and he shall take from *there* his handful of the fine flour of the *mincha* and of its oil. The *baraita* reads the word *misham* — "from there" — as delimiting the zone of valid *kemitzah*: only from the place where a *zar*, a non-*kohen*, may stand. A non-*kohen* may not enter the space between the *ulam* and the *mizbe'ach*, may not enter the *ulam*, and certainly may not enter the *heichal*. If the zone of valid *kemitzah* is wherever the *zar* may stand, then the *heichal* is explicitly excluded.

### Kemitzah Redo

Parenthetically, the *baraita* includes a ruling from Ben Beteira that illuminates how the word *misham* is being used. Ben Beteira asks: if the *kohen* performed the *kemitzah* with his left hand, what is the *din*? May he replace the flour and take the *kemitzah* again with his right hand? In this he differs from the rule governing *shechitah*, where a botched act cannot be redone. Ben Beteira derives the answer from the word *misham* — "from there": meaning, from the place where the *kemitzah* was already taken, one may take the *kemitzah* again. This reading of *misham* as licensing a redo is distinct from reading it as a geographic limit.

The implicit halakhic point here is significant: if the *kemitzah* performed with the left hand were an absolute nullity, there would be nothing "there" from which to redo it. The very possibility of a redo suggests that a *kemitzah* performed improperly has some degree of standing, even if it requires correction.

### Rabbi Yaakov Resolution

The *Gemara* then reports — some say Rabbi Yirmiyah himself resolved his own question, others attribute the resolution to Rabbi Yaakov responding to Rav Yirmiyah bar Tachlifa:

> לֹא נִצְרְכָה אֶלָּא לְהַכְשִׁיר כָּל הָעֲזָרָה כֻּלָּהּ

*Lo nitzrecha ela lehachshir kol ha'azarah kulah* — the clause "from where the *zar* stands" comes not to *restrict* the zone of valid *kemitzah*, but to *expand* it.

### Verse Expands Location

The resolution hinges on recognizing what the verse is actually teaching. One might have thought — returning now to the *mishnah*'s ruling — that since the *mincha* is *kodshei kodashim*, and since the Torah later specifies that the *kemitzah* follows the *hagashah* (the touching of the *mincha* to the altar) which must be done at the southwest corner, perhaps the *kemitzah* must also be performed specifically at the southwest corner. The verse *vekamatz misham* comes to counter this: wherever the *zar* brings the *mincha* — that is, anywhere in the *azarah* — the *kohen* takes the *kemitzah*. The phrase is thus an expansion, permitting *kemitzah* anywhere in the *azarah*. It does not function as a restriction excluding the *heichal*; that is simply not the verse's concern.

---

## No North Requirement

### North Requirement Questi…

With the geographic flexibility of *kemitzah* established, the *Gemara* now addresses the underlying question: why doesn't the *mincha* require the north at all? After all, it is *kodshei kodashim*, and the north is the defining feature of *kodshei kodashim* slaughter. The *Gemara* sets up what should have been a compelling *hava amina*:

> הוֹאִיל וְעוֹלָה קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים וּמִנְחָה קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים

*Ho'il ve'olah kodshei kodashim umincha kodshei kodashim* — since both the *olah* and the *mincha* are *kodshei kodashim*, perhaps just as the *olah* requires the north, so too the *mincha* requires the north. This would mean we *need* the verse *vekamatz misham* to override what would otherwise have been an obvious inference. But does this *hava amina* hold up under scrutiny?

### Failed Comparisons

The *Gemara* systematically dismantles each potential analogy. The *olah* requires the north — but the *olah* is *kalil*, entirely consumed on the altar. That is a distinctive feature the *mincha* does not share in its general form. Fine — compare instead to the *chatat*, which is also *kodshei kodashim* and also requires the north. But the *chatat* atones for sin; the *mincha* does not. Perhaps compare to the *asham* — but the *asham* involves *dam*, blood, and is a species of animal sacrifice. The *mincha*, with no blood and no slaughter, is simply not sufficiently similar to any animal *korban* to generate a compelling *hava amina* that it should require the north. And this logic extends to all the animal offerings together:

> וְכֵן לְכוּלְּהוּ מַה לְּכוּלְּהוּ שֶׁכֵּן מִין דָּמִים

*Vechein lekulhu mah lekulhu shekein min damim* — in every case, the animal offerings share the common feature of being blood offerings, which the *mincha* is not.

### Southwest Corner Logic

The *Gemara* therefore shifts its *hava amina* to an argument internal to *menachot* themselves. It is not that I would have compared the *mincha* to animal *korbanot* and required the north — that comparison was never strong enough. Rather, even within the internal logic of the *mincha*, I might have thought that the *kemitzah* must be done specifically at the southwest corner. Here is why: the Torah states *vehigisha el hamizbe'ach veheirim mimenu bikumtzo* — the *mincha* is first brought to the altar (*hagashah*) and then the *kemitzah* is performed. As we will establish shortly from two verses, the *hagashah* must be performed specifically at the southwest corner (*keren dromit maaravit*). Since the verse immediately thereafter commands the *kemitzah*, one might conclude that the *kemitzah* too must be performed at that same corner — *mah hagashah bekeren dromit maaravit, af kemitzah bekeren dromit maaravit*.

Therefore, the verse *vekamatz misham* is indeed necessary — not to dislodge a comparison to animal *korbanot*, but to clarify that despite the *kemitzah*'s proximity to the *hagashah* in the verse, it may be performed anywhere in the *azarah*.

---

## Shelamim in Heichal

### Shelamim Kosher

Having established that the *kemitzah* of a *mincha* is valid even inside the *heichal*, the *Gemara* turns to a parallel question regarding animal sacrifices. Rabbi Yochanan states:

> שְׁלָמִים שֶׁשְּׁחָטָן בַּהֵיכָל כְּשֵׁרִים

*Shlamim sheshchatam baheichal kesherim* — *shlamim* slaughtered inside the *heichal* are valid. This is a striking ruling, and it invites comparison to the *mincha* case. Why specifically *shlamim*? Because *shlamim* are the only animal *korban* that may be slaughtered anywhere in the *azarah* — *kodshei kodashim* require the north, and therefore the question of whether "anywhere" extends into the *heichal* arises only for *shlamim*.

### Kal v'Chomer Debate

The basis for Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is a *kal vachomer*. The verse states that *shlamim* are slaughtered *petach ohel moed*, at the entrance of the *ohel moed*. The *Gemara* has established that "entrance" is understood expansively to include the entire *azarah*. If so, argues Rabbi Yochanan, *velo yihyeh tafel chamur min haikar* — the secondary reference (proximity to the *ohel moed*) should not be more stringent than the primary location (inside the *ohel moed* itself). If slaughtering in reference to the *ohel moed* is valid, certainly slaughtering within it should be valid.

But this *kal vachomer* is immediately challenged.

### Kodshei Kodashim in Heic…

The challenge comes from a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira. He raises the case of a siege: if *ovdei kochavim* surrounded the entire *azarah*, what is the *din* for the *kohanim* who find themselves inside the *heichal*? May they eat their *kodshei kodashim* there? Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira derives permission from the verse *bakodesh hakodashim tochalennu* — "in the holy of holies you shall eat it" — which provides explicit textual authorization for eating *kodshei kodashim* within the *heichal*.

This *baraita* poses a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: if a *kal vachomer* sufficed to permit *shechitah* inside the *heichal*, why did the *Gemara* need a specific verse to permit *eating* inside the *heichal*? Should not the same *kal vachomer* — if something is permitted in proximity to the *ohel moed*, it is certainly permitted within it — apply equally to eating?

### Avoda vs. Achila

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between *avoda* and *achila*. When it comes to the *shechitah*, which is an *avoda* — an act of divine service — the *kal vachomer* is straightforward: if one may perform divine service at a certain remove from the sanctuary, one may certainly perform it in closer proximity. *Hatam avoda d'adam oved bimkom rabbo amrinan* — regarding service performed in the presence of one's master, we readily apply the logic that what is permitted further out is certainly permitted closer in.

But *achila* — eating — follows a different social logic entirely. *Ein adam ochel bimkom rabbo* — one does not eat in the presence of one's master. We would not instinctively assume that permission to eat in the *chatzer* extends to eating before the *heichal* itself. Therefore, a *kal vachomer* could not be applied to eating, and a specific verse was necessary.

The result is a somewhat counterintuitive hierarchy: the *kal vachomer* works to permit *shechitah* inside the *heichal* — which intuitively seems the most incongruous of all acts to perform in that sacred space — while eating requires an explicit verse. The logic is abstractly correct, but it does produce the odd conclusion that what is most visually incongruous is, from a *halakhic* standpoint, the most easily permitted.

---

## Chatat Ha'of & Mincha

### Chatat Ha'of Location

The *Gemara* now introduces the *chatat ha'of* — the bird sin-offering — as another point of comparison. Recall that with animal *korbanot*, the relationship between *chatat* and the other offerings is inverted when it comes to birds: whereas a mammal *chatat* requires the north (above the red line, *chut hasikra*), a bird *chatat* is performed below. The *mishnah* now tells us that the bird *chatat* was performed at the southwest corner (*keren dromit maaravit*) — the same location associated with the *mincha*'s *hagashah*.

### Three Things at Corner

The *mishnah* goes on to describe three acts performed at that corner below, and three above:

> בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים הָיְתָה עוֹשָׂה כְּמִין מְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת מִלְּמַטָּה וּבִשְׁלֹשָׁה מִלְמַעְלָה

*Uv'shlosha dvarim hayta osa kemin meshameshet milmata uv'shlosha milmala* — this corner served three functions below and three above.

Below (*milmata*): the *hagashah* of the *mincha* (touching the *mincha* to the altar), the *shechitah* of the *chatat ha'of*, and the *shiyurei hadam* — the spilling of the remnant blood at the base of the altar. Above (*milmala*), at the corner near the horn: *nisuch hayayin vehamayim* — the wine and water libations (which flowed down into the *hashitin* below), and the *olat ha'of* — the bird *olah*. The bird *olah* was normally performed at the southeast corner, but when that location became congested, it was moved to the southwest corner. Thus a single corner served as a multi-purpose focal point for multiple aspects of the *avodah*.

### Altar Traffic Rules

The *mishnah* then describes the general traffic pattern on the altar:

> כָּל הָעוֹלִים לַמִּזְבֵּחַ עוֹלִים דֶּרֶךְ יָמִין וּמַקִּיפִין וְיוֹרְדִים דֶּרֶךְ שְׂמֹאל

*Kol ha'olim lamizbe'ach olim derech yamin umakifin veyordim derech smol* — all who ascended the altar went up on the right and descended on the left, following a counterclockwise circuit. This is consistent with the broader principle that movements in *kedushah* contexts (carrying the *Aron*, processing with a *Sefer Torah*, and so forth) always bear to the right.

The exception to this rule was made for the three acts associated with the southwest corner — *nisuch hamayim veha'yayain*, and the *olat ha'of* when relocated there. For those, one ascended and made an immediate left, proceeding directly to the corner rather than completing the full circuit. Indeed, the *mishnah* adds that for those who performed these acts, *she'yihyu olim veyordim al ha'akev* — they would ascend and then retrace their steps downward, effectively reversing course rather than continuing along the normal circuit.

---

## Southwest Corner Derivat…

### Text Corruption

The *Gemara* now seeks the textual basis for requiring the southwest corner for the *chatat ha'of*. It cites a verse from the context of the *mincha brought as a chatat* in the *korban oleh veyored* — the sliding-scale offering where a penitent who cannot afford an animal may bring a bird, and one who cannot afford a bird may bring a *mincha*. That *mincha* is called a *minchat chotei*, and the verse about it states: *lo yasim aleha shemen velo yiten aleha levona ki chatat hi* — do not place oil or frankincense upon it, for it is a *chatat*. From this identification — *chatat karya mincha, mincha karya chatat*, the *mincha* is called a *chatat* and the *chatat* is called a *mincha* — the *Gemara* seeks to derive: just as the *chatat* requires the north, so too the *mincha* requires the north; and conversely, just as the *mincha* is associated with the southwest, so too the bird *chatat* is associated with the southwest.

However, the first half of this derivation — that the *mincha* requires the north — is immediately problematic. We have already established at length that the *mincha* does not require the north. And a bird *chatat* likewise does not require the north.

### Rashi's Position

Rashi addresses this directly and forcefully. On the phrase *mah chatat te'una tzafon af mincha te'una tzafon*, Rashi writes:

> יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁגִּרְסָא זוֹ שִׁבּוּשׁ

*Yode'a ani shegirsa zo shibush* — I know that this textual reading is corrupted. Neither the bird *chatat* nor the *mincha* requires the north, so the derivation as it stands cannot be correct. Rashi is unable to supply the correct reading, but he suggests a possible emendation: perhaps the comparison between *mincha* and *chatat* was intended to teach that just as a *chatat* performed *shelo lishmah* is invalid, so too a *mincha* performed *shelo lishmah* is invalid — a halachic point that belongs to the same context and makes sense as a derivation from the identification between these two offerings.

One could attempt to save the north-derivation by proposing that the verse specifically singles out the *minchat chotei* as requiring the north, in distinction from ordinary *menachot*. But Rashi rejects this as well: *ule'chatat behema makish lo, havei lei lemismaich matnissin* — if the *minchat chotei* required the north like a mammal *chatat*, our *mishnayot* — which are precisely organized around specifying the required locations for all these acts — would have said so somewhere. No *mishnah* anywhere indicates that the *minchat chotei* is performed in the north. The silence is conclusive.

Tosafot, by contrast, engage with the question of whether the text should simply be emended or whether the north requirement for *minchat chotei* should be taken seriously despite the silence of the other sources. This remains a major point of discussion.

### Two Verses Rule

Setting aside the north question, the *Gemara* proceeds to establish how we know the *mincha*'s *hagashah* is performed at the southwest corner. A *baraita* cites two verses. The first:

> הַקְרֵב אֹתָהּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן לִפְנֵי ה׳

*Hikreiv otah bnei Aharon lifnei Hashem* — bring it before God. *Lifnei Hashem* points to the west of the altar — the face directed toward the *ohel moed*, toward the *heichal*. This means the western side.

The second verse says: *el pnei hamizbe'ach* — toward the face of the altar. The "face" of the altar is understood to be where the ramp ascends, namely the south face.

These two requirements point in different directions. *Ha keitzad* — how are both satisfied? By performing the *hagashah* at the southwest corner, specifically at the very point of the corner (*kineged chudah shel keren*), one simultaneously faces west (toward the *heichal*, satisfying *lifnei Hashem*) and south (facing the ramp, satisfying *al pnei hamizbe'ach*). The *Gemara* adds *vedayo* — and this is sufficient. A separate *Gemara* elsewhere explains that *vedayo* indicates one need not actually touch the flour itself to the stone of the altar; touching the vessel suffices.

### R. Eliezer Alternative

Rabbi Eliezer offers a different analysis of how the two verses should be reconciled. Rather than requiring the exact corner point, he argues that one should identify *which single face* satisfies both verses simultaneously — and do the *hagashah* there, without necessarily standing at the precise corner.

His reasoning: whenever there are two verses, one of which (*A*) satisfies its own requirement and also satisfies the requirement of the other (*B*), while the other (*B*) satisfies only itself, we set aside *B* and follow *A*. *Tofsin et ze shemekayem atzmo umekayem chaveiro* — we adopt the reading that satisfies both.

Now, which face satisfies both? If one performs the *hagashah* at the western face (*maarav*), that satisfies *lifnei Hashem* but does not satisfy *al pnei hamizbe'ach*. The western face is not the face of the altar. So the west satisfies only one verse.

But if one performs the *hagashah* at the southern face (*darom*), that clearly satisfies *al pnei hamizbe'ach* — the south is the face of the altar. And, according to Rabbi Eliezer, it also satisfies *lifnei Hashem*. How? Because the south face is directly opposite the entrance to the *heichal*, making it *lifnei Hashem* as well. Therefore, one need not stand at the precise corner point; performing the *hagashah* anywhere along the southern face suffices.

### Rav Ashi's Explanation

The *Gemara* objects: how can the southern face be *lifnei Hashem* — in front of God, facing the *heichal* — if the *heichal* is to the west?

Rav Ashi explains: *hai tana savar kulei mizbe'ach batzafon kai* — this *tanna* holds that the entire altar stands within the northern half of the *azarah*. Given this positioning, the southern face of the altar is directly opposite the doorway of the *heichal*, because the *heichal*'s entrance spans the entire width of the building, and the southern face of the altar — though facing south rather than west — is in the direct line of sight from that entrance. Therefore, the southern face simultaneously constitutes *pnei hamizbe'ach* and *lifnei Hashem*, and the *hagashah* performed there satisfies both verses without requiring the precise corner point.

This is Rabbi Eliezer's position, distinct from the *tanna kamma* who requires the exact corner. Both positions, however, agree that the southwest region is the operative location.

---

## Melika & Hazaya

### Melika vs. Hazaya

Returning to the *mishnah*'s somewhat cryptic language about the bird *chatat* — it is performed at the southwest corner, yet could validly be done anywhere — Rav Ashi offers the proper reading:

> בְּכָל מָקוֹם הָיְתָה כְּשֵׁרָה לִמְלִיקָתָהּ אֶלָּא זֶהוּ מְקוֹמָהּ לְהַזָּיָתָהּ

*Bechol makom hayta kesheira limlikatah, ela zehu mekoma lehazatah* — anywhere in the *azarah* was valid for the *melika* (the severing of the bird's neck), but the southwest corner was the designated location for the *hazaya* — the squirting of the blood against the altar wall.

This creates a precise and elegant parallel with the *mincha*. The *kemitzah* (analogous to *shechitah*) may be done anywhere; the *hagashah* (the touching of the offering to the altar wall) must be at the southwest corner. In the bird *chatat*: the *melika* (severing) may be done anywhere; the *hazaya* (the blood that strikes the altar wall) must be at the southwest corner. In both cases, the act that makes contact with the altar wall requires the specific corner; the act of severance or taking is geographically unrestricted.

### Baraita Editing

The *Gemara* notes that this ruling is supported by a *baraita*, but the *baraita* as it stands requires careful reading — indeed, a degree of textual editing — to align with the *mishnah*'s ruling. The *baraita* states:

> מְלִיקָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם בַּמִּזְבֵּחַ כְּשֵׁרָה, הַזָּיַת דָּמָהּ בְּכָל מָקוֹם כְּשֵׁרָה

*Melika bechol makom bamizbe'ach kesheira, hazayat damah bechol makom kesheira* — the *melika* anywhere on the altar is valid, the squirting of its blood anywhere is valid. On a plain reading, this seems to permit the *hazaya* anywhere, contrary to what we have established.

The *Gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between *hazaya* — the initial squirting of blood — and *mitzuy* — the subsequent squeezing out of the remaining blood, analogous to the *shfichat shirayim* (pouring of the blood remnants) in animal sacrifices. The *baraita* should be read as stating: *mitzuy damah bechol makom kesheira* — the squeezing out of the blood may be done anywhere. The *hazaya* proper, the initial squirting, must be at the southwest corner.

### Dam Hanefesh

The *baraita* continues: *hazaya velo mitza kesheira* — if one performed only the *hazaya* and did not perform the subsequent *mitzuy*, it is still valid. This parallels the rule for animal *korbanot* where the *shfichat shirayim* is not *me'akev*. The *baraita* then adds the qualification *uvilvad sheyiten mikeneged hasovev ulemata* — as long as the blood was applied below the *chut hasikra*, the red line.

The *Gemara* parses this carefully: *dam hanefesh* — the soul blood, the initial burst of blood that issues at the moment of *melika* — that is what constitutes the valid *hazaya* and must be applied at the southwest corner below the *chut hasikra*. The subsequent *mitzuy*, the squeezing out of the remaining blood, is not *me'akev* and may be performed anywhere on the altar.

### Hazaya Southwest Only

The *Gemara*'s conclusion is thus consistent: both the *mishnah* and the *baraita*, properly read, establish that the *melika* may be performed anywhere, and the *mitzuy* (the squeezing out, analogous to *shfichat shirayim*) may likewise be performed anywhere since it is not *me'akev*. But the *hazaya* — the actual squirting of the *dam hanefesh* against the altar wall — must be performed specifically at the southwest corner. This is the precise parallel to the *mincha*: in both cases, it is the act of contact with the altar wall that is fixed to the southwest corner, while the act of severance or taking remains geographically flexible throughout the *azarah*.

---

---

# Zevachim 64

## Southwest Corner

### Locating SW Corner

The *daf* opens on the second line of 64a, continuing the *mishnah*'s discussion of bird sacrifices and their connection to the southwest corner of the *mizbeach*. The *mishnah* had established that three things were done at the bottom of that corner and three at the top. The three performed below are the *chatas ha-of* (the bird sin offering), the *mincha*, and the spilling of the remainder of the blood.

The *gemara* begins by asking: how do we know that the *chatas ha-of* is performed at the southwest corner? The answer was derived on the previous *daf* through a textual link between the *minchas chotei* and the *chatas ha-of*. The *pasuk* states *vehigisha el hamizbeach* — you shall bring it near to the altar — and specifies that this contact occurs *lifnei Hashem*. "The face of the *mizbeach*" refers to the south, from which one ascends the ramp, and *lifnei Hashem* refers to the west, which faces the *ulam* and the *heichal*. The intersection of south and west yields the southwest corner. It is from this derivation regarding the *mincha* — specifically the act of *hagashah*, the touching of the *mincha* to the *mizbeach* — that we also locate the *chatas ha-of*.

As for *shiurei hadam* — the remainder of the blood — the *gemara* derives its location from the *pasuk*: *ve'et kol dam hapar yishpoch el yesod mizbach hamizbeach*, "all the remnant of the blood you shall pour at the base of the altar." The *gemara* links the blood of a *chatas* performed atop the *mizbeach* to the procedure on *Yom Kippur* inside the *heichal*, where upon exiting one pours the remainder at the western base, which faces the *ulam* and the *heichal*. By analogy, when descending from the *mizbeach* after a *chatas*, one pours the remainder at the base immediately facing the descent — that is, the southern side — which places it precisely at the southwest corner.

### Why SW: No Base

Having established what is done at the southwest corner, the *gemara* asks why this corner specifically rather than the entire southern side. The answer lies in the structure of the *yesod*, the base of the altar. The *yesod* did not extend along the southern or eastern sides of the *mizbeach*. It began at the southwest corner, continued along the entire western side, then along the entire northern side, and concluded at the northeast corner. Since the *yesod* was required for the pouring of the blood remainder, only that corner — the point where the southern approach meets the beginning of the *yesod* — could serve this function.

### Three SW Practices

Turning now to the three practices performed at the *top* of the southwest corner, the *mishnah* identifies *nisuch hamayim veha-yayin* — the pouring of the water and the wine — as first among them. This was necessarily performed at the southwest corner because the *mizbeach* had been extended to the south and to the west so that this corner would sit directly above the *shittin*, the underground caverns, allowing the poured liquids to be absorbed into the ground beneath the altar.

The third practice at the top of the southwest corner is the *olat ha-of* when performed there — which requires explanation, since the *olat ha-of* is ordinarily performed at the southeast corner. The *mishnah* teaches that when there were too many bird *olot* being performed at the southeast corner, the service would be moved to the southwest corner. The *gemara* now turns to explain why the southeast corner is the standard location.

---

## SE Corner Default

### Proximity to Ashes

Rabbi Yochanan explains that the *olat ha-of* is ordinarily performed at the southeast corner because it is closest to the *beis hadeshen*, the place where the ashes are deposited. Two *pesukim* together establish the location of the *beis hadeshen*. The first, regarding the *terumas hadeshen*, states *vesamo etzel hamizbeach* — he shall place it beside the altar. The second, regarding the *olat ha-of*, states that the crop and innards shall be cast *etzel hamizbeach kedma* — beside the altar, to the east — *makom hadashen*, the place of the ashes. Combining these, the *beis hadeshen* is established as being to the east of the ramp. Since the *kohein* performing the *olat ha-of* at the southeast corner would be casting the crop and feathers toward this spot, proximity is maximized there. Rabbi Yochanan then adds: *bo re'e kama gadol kochan shel kohanim* — come and see how great was the physical strength of the *kohanim* — for there is nothing lighter among bird parts than the crop and surrounding feathers, yet there were times a *kohein* would have to throw them more than thirty *amos*.

### Throwing Distance Math

The *gemara* grounds this statement in a *mishnah* from *Tamid* describing the *terumas hadeshen* procedure. The *kohein* would take a silver shovel, ascend to the top of the *mizbeach*, scoop up the deeply burned ash, descend the ramp, and upon reaching the ground turn to face north — back toward the face of the altar. He would then walk to the east side of the ramp, proceeding *ke'eser amos* — approximately ten *amos* — inward toward the *mizbeach*, and pile the coals on the floor there, three *tefachim* away from the ramp. The same location served for depositing the crop and feathers of the *olat ha-of*, the ash of the inner *mizbeach* used for the *ketores*, and the ash of the *menorah*.

This establishes that the *beis hadeshen* lay on the east side of the ramp, twenty-two *amos* removed from the base of the *mizbeach*. When the *kohein* performed the *olat ha-of* at the southeast corner, the geometry of the throw can be modeled as a triangle: the ash pit is twenty-two *amos* from the wall of the *mizbeach*, and the southeast corner itself is approximately six *amos* up from the base (accounting for one *amah* for the *yesod* and one *amah* for the *sovev*). The diagonal distance from the southeast corner to the ash pit is therefore slightly more than twenty-two *amos* — well under thirty.

The more demanding case arises when the *kohein* is at the southwest corner. Now the triangle has two legs: twenty-two *amos* from the ash pit to the wall of the *mizbeach*, and twenty-two *amos* from that point along the base of the altar to the southwest corner (sixteen *amos* across the width of the ramp and another six *amos* to reach the corner). The diagonal is then 22 times the square root of 2. The *gemara* uses the approximation that the square root of 2 is 1.4 — a solid estimate — yielding 22 × 1.4 = 30.8, essentially thirty-one *amos*.

The *gemara* itself notes that the figure comes out to somewhat more than thirty-one *amos*. It then resolves the apparent discrepancy with the stated figure of thirty by noting: *mekom gavra lo kashiv* — the *kohein* does not count the space he himself occupies, that being approximately one *amah*, which brings the figure close enough to thirty *amos*. The force of Rabbi Yochanan's observation is thus clear: to throw something as light and insubstantial as a crop and feathers over thirty *amos* required extraordinary physical strength.

---

## Traffic Patterns

### Counterclockwise/SW Acce…

The *gemara* establishes that all who ascend the *mizbeach* normally proceed counterclockwise — all turns are to the right — and this applies to every standard service. However, for the three things performed at the southwest corner at the top of the *mizbeach*, rather than making the full counterclockwise rotation, the *kohein* would go directly to the southwest, turning left instead of right. The *gemara* asks: *mai taama* — what is the reason one is permitted to deviate from the normal directional pattern?

Rabbi Yochanan explains that for the *nesachim*, the wine and water, going the long way around risks their becoming smoky from all the burning on the *mizbeach*, rendering them *pasul*. For the *olat ha-of* similarly: *shema tamus ba-ashan* — the bird might die from the smoke as it is carried all the way around.

### Kohein Gadol Rotation

A challenge is raised from a *baraisa* discussing the *Kohein Gadol*, who was entitled to perform the *tamid* offering himself at any time, taking all its component services upon himself. After placing the dismembered pieces on the fire, he would rotate around the *mizbeach* before performing the pouring of the wine. The *baraisa* details his full counterclockwise rotation: from the southeast corner, to the northeast, to the northwest, and finally to the southwest — where *notnim lo yayin lenasech*, they would give him the wine to pour. This appears to contradict the principle that one carrying the *nesachim* may take the short route to avoid smoke.

The resolution offered by Rabbi Yochanan is elegant: *hakafa baregel* — the *Kohein Gadol* merely walked; he was not carrying the wine. Having ascended to perform the complete *tamid* service, including the burning of the meat, the wine was not in his hands during the circuit. He would complete the full rotation and receive the wine only upon reaching the southwest corner. Since he was not transporting the wine, there was no concern about it becoming smoky en route.

*Rava* adds a further textual confirmation — *deika nami de-katni* — that this reading is also supported by the precise language of the *baraisa*: it says *notnim lo yayin lenasech*, "they gave him wine to pour," not *omrim lo nasech*, "they told him to pour." The clear implication is that the wine was not yet in his possession until that moment. The *gemara* affirms: *shema mina* — this is indeed a valid inference.

### Ascent/Descent Rules

A *baraisa* is cited elaborating the traffic rules: *kol olim la-mizbeach olim derech yamin ve-yordim derech smol* — all who ascend the *mizbeach* go up on the right side and descend on the left. Equivalently, they go up on the east side of the ramp and descend on the west. The exception applies to those performing the three southwest-corner services: for these, one goes up on the west and descends on the west as well.

This detail is somewhat surprising. One might have assumed that even for these services, traffic would remain as normal as possible: go up on the east side, reach the top, then turn left. At the top, little traffic conflict would arise, since under normal counterclockwise flow no one traverses the space between the east and west sides of the ramp. But the *baraisa* states explicitly that for these three services one ascends on the left — the west — which would actually place one against the normal flow of descending traffic. The *baraisa* stands as stated.

### Directional Terminology

The concluding line of the *baraisa* refers to descending on the right — *derech yamin* — even though it is the west side, which has previously been called the left. The *gemara* raises the difficulty: *derech yamin? Derech smol hu!* — it is the left, not the right.

Two responses are offered. Ravina simply emends the text: *tani smol* — it should read "left." Rava, however, defends the text as written: *mai yamin yamin de-mizbeach* — "right" here refers to the right side of the *mizbeach* itself, as though the altar were a person whose face is the side from which one ascends. From the *mizbeach*'s perspective, the west is its right — even though from the perspective of a person facing the altar it is the left. This explains the inconsistency: the first part of the *baraisa* described the west as "left" from the observer's perspective (*smol de-gavra*), while the conclusion described it as "right" from the altar's perspective (*yamin de-mizbeach*). The *gemara* objects that the *baraisa* should have maintained a consistent perspective throughout — *kashya* — and so Ravina's emendation remains the more natural resolution.

---

## Bird Sin Offering

### Melikah Procedure

The *mishnah* now turns to a detailed account of the *chatas ha-of*. *Chatas ha-of keitzad hayeta na'asit?* — How was the bird *chatas* performed? The *kohein* would perform *melikah* — slaughtering by means of his thumbnail from the nape of the neck — but would *not* fully sever. "Not sever" carries a double meaning: first, the head would not be physically detached from the body, and second, only one of the two *simanim* — the trachea or the esophagus — would be cut, not both.

Following the *melikah*, the blood would squirt directly onto the wall of the *mizbeach* at the southwest corner, as established above. The remainder of the blood — *sheyarei hadam* — would *mitmatzeh el hayesod*, either dribbling naturally down to the *yesod* or being actively squeezed out against the wall until the remainder ran down to the base. Importantly, nothing of the bird would be burned on the altar; the blood alone was the *mizbeach*'s portion. The entire body of the bird was eaten by the *kohanim*.

The *gemara* cites a *baraisa* elaborating on the blood application: *vehizah midam hachattas miguf hachattas* — the blood is sprayed directly from the body of the *chatas* itself, not collected in a vessel and thrown from there. *Hakeitzad?* — how is this done? The *kohein* holds both the head and the body simultaneously, bending the head away so the blood can squirt directly outward onto the *mizbeach*. The *baraisa* specifies: the blood must hit the wall of the *mizbeach* itself — not the wall of the ramp, not the wall of the *heichal*, and not the wall of the *ulam*.

### Blood Below Midline

A careful question arises: is the blood of the bird *chatas* applied above or below the *chut hasikra*, the red line running around the middle of the *mizbeach*? The *baraisa* poses this as an internal question, noting that a logical argument could be made for above. By a mammal, the *olah* is applied below the line and the *chatas* above. Since the bird *olah* (to be discussed in the next *mishnah*) is applied at the top of the *mizbeach*, one might argue *kal va-chomer*: if even the bird *olah* is applied at the top, surely the bird *chatas* — which by mammals goes above — should also go above.

The *baraisa* rejects this inference from a *pasuk*: *vehanish'ar badam yimatzeh el yesod hamizbeach* — and the remainder of the blood shall be squeezed out to the base of the altar. The derivation is: *kir sheshirav mitmatzin liyesod* — the blood must be applied to a section of the wall from which the remainder will flow naturally to the *yesod*. Above the midline, there is an *amah*-wide protrusion — the *sovev*, the walk-around platform — that would intercept any blood running down the wall before it could reach the *yesod*. Only blood applied below the midline can flow directly and unimpeded to the base. This is therefore the proof that the blood of the bird *chatas* is applied to the lower portion of the wall.

One might then ask: why not apply the blood above the line for the primary *avoda* and then squeeze the remainder below? *Amar Rava*: the *pasuk* does not say *yimatzeh* in the *pa'al* form (active squeezing), but rather as a form that can be read as naturally flowing — *de-memaila mashma* — it dribbles down of its own accord. If the application itself will cause the blood to naturally flow down to the base, this means the blood must have been applied in a position from which it flows directly to the *yesod* — i.e., below the midline. There is no room, on this reading, for a separate act above the line followed by a separate squeezing below.

### Melikah Technique

*Amar Rav Zutra bar Tuvya amar Rav* — how exactly does one perform *melikah*? The *kohein* holds the bird in his right hand. He grips the wings with two fingers (Rashi identifies these as the index and middle fingers), the feet with two other fingers (the pinky and ring finger), and stretches the neck out along the breadth of his thumb — across the space between the thumb and index finger — with the right thumb. He then uses the thumbnail itself to slice through the neck.

A *baraisa* offers an alternative hold: *tzipra mi-levara* — the body of the bird is positioned at the back of the hand rather than in the palm, with the wings and feet held by the same fingers and the neck stretched out behind the fingers rather than in the crook of the thumb. In either description, the *melikah* is performed with the thumbnail against the stretched neck.

### Difficult Service

The *baraisa* concludes: *ve-zo hi avodah kashah she-be-mikdash* — this was the most difficult service in the *beis hamikdash*. The challenge is self-evident: the angle is inherently awkward, slaughtering with a fingernail while controlling the entire bird in one hand. The *gemara* challenges this superlative: is this truly the most difficult? Other *avodos* are also known to be exceptionally demanding — the *kemitzah*, taking a precise handful of *mincha* smoothed between thumb and pinky, and the *chafinah*, the double-fisted scooping of burning coals for the *Yom Kippur ketores* service. The *gemara* accordingly amends the claim: *zu avodah kashah me-avodos kashos she-ba-mikdash* — it is not uniquely the hardest, but *among* the most difficult services in the *beis hamikdash*.

---

## Bird Burnt Offering

### Complete Severance

The *mishnah* turns to the *olat ha-of*, which was performed at the top of the *mizbeach*. The *kohein* would ascend the ramp and proceed via the sub-ramp to the *sovev*, the walk-around platform, arriving at the southeast corner — or, in cases of overflow, at the southwest corner. Rashi notes that when performing the service at the southwest corner due to the large number of *olot*, the *kohein* would go all the way to the top of the *mizbeach* and turn left immediately, since there was no sub-ramp providing direct access to that corner from the walk-around.

The *melikah* of the *olat ha-of* contrasts sharply with that of the *chatas ha-of* in two respects. First, *u-mavdil* — the *kohein* does completely sever: he cuts through both the trachea and the esophagus, and fully detaches the head from the body. Second, the blood is applied in a single act of squeezing — *u-mitzah es damah al kir hamizbeach* — directly pressing the body against the wall, with no initial squirting as in the *chatas*.

Once the body's blood has been squeezed out, the *kohein* takes the now-severed head, turns the place of *melikah* against the *mizbeach* — *hikif beis melikaso la-mizbeach* — and squeezes out the remainder of the blood from the head as well. The head is then salted and cast onto the fire. The *mishnah* is precise in specifying these as two distinct acts of *mitzui*: the first from the body, the second from the head.

### Crop/Feathers Removal

After processing the blood of both body and head, the *kohein* removes the crop along with the surrounding feathers (*mor'ah venotzah*) and the innards that emerge along with them (*bnei me'ayim hayotzim imam*). These are cast to the *beis hadeshen* — thrown those twenty-two-or-more *amos* to the east of the ramp, as the geometric analysis above demonstrated.

### Salting & Burning

The salting of the body and its placement on the fire follow. However, the *mishnah* establishes a critical principle: *kol sheshina ba le-acharei mitzas hadam keshera* — any deviation that occurs after the blood-squeezing service has been properly completed does not invalidate the *korban*. Whether the *kohein* failed to remove the crop and innards, omitted the salting, or performed the burning incorrectly, the *korban* remains valid — just as with animal sacrifices, once the blood service is properly completed the *korban* is not undermined by subsequent procedural errors.

Conversely, errors in the blood service itself do invalidate the offering. *Hivdil b'chatas* — if the *kohein* fully severed for the *chatas* (either removing the head or cutting both *simanim*) — *pasul*. *Lo hivdil b'olah* — if he failed to fully sever for the *olah* — *pasul*. Similarly, if he squeezed the blood of the head but not of the body, it is *pasul*, since the primary blood service concerns the body. If he squeezed the blood of the body but not of the head, the *korban* remains *kosher*.

---

## Invalidations

### Improper Intent

The *mishnah* now addresses *shelo lishma* and *pigul* in the context of bird offerings. For the *chatas ha-of*, if the *melikah* was performed *shelo lishma*, or if the *mitzuy hadam* was performed *shelo lishma*, or if one of the two key *avodos* was *lishma* and the other *shelo lishma* — *pasul*. This mirrors the rule for the *chatas* of a *behemah*. Note that the bird *chatas* has only two *avodos* rather than the four of a mammal offering: the *melikah* (corresponding to *shechita*) and the squeezing of the blood (corresponding to the application of blood to the corners).

For the *olat ha-of*, performance *shelo lishma* renders the offering *kosher* — since *shelo lishma* by an *olah* is valid — provided that the owners do not thereby discharge their obligation.

### Pigul Requirements

The *mishnah* now addresses *pigul* for both bird offerings equally. If the *kohein* performed the *melikah* or the *mitzuy hadam* with intent to eat that which is normally eaten — the meat of the *chatas ha-of* — or to burn that which is normally burned — the meat of the *olat ha-of* — outside its proper location (*chutz limkomo*), the *korban* is *pasul* but does not carry *kares*. If the intent was to do so at the wrong time (*chutz lizimano*), the *korban* becomes *pigul* and eating it incurs *kares*.

However, this *pigul* status applies only when the *matir* — the permitting act — was performed *ke-mitzvaso*, in the proper manner. The *mishnah* specifies: if the *melikah* was performed without intent (*bi-shtikah*) and the *mitzuy hadam* with a *chutz lizimano* intent, or if the *melikah* was *chutz lizimano* and the *mitzuy* was *bi-shtikah*, or if both were performed with a *chutz lizimano* intent — in all these cases the *matir* is considered to have been performed *ke-mitzvaso* and *pigul* takes effect.

### Pigul Exceptions

The *mishnah* now delineates the cases in which *pigul* does not take effect, because the *matir* was *not* performed *ke-mitzvaso*. If the *melikah* was performed *chutz limkomo* and the *mitzuy hadam chutz lizimano*, or if the *melikah* was *chutz lizimano* and the *mitzuy chutz limkomo*, or if both were performed *chutz limkomo* — in all these instances the offering is invalid on account of *chutz limkomo*, but it does not attain the status of *pigul*. Where an additional invalidation (*chutz limkomo*) is present alongside the *pigul* intent (*chutz lizimano*), the *matir* is not considered to have been performed *ke-mitzvaso*, and the *pigul* mechanism does not activate.

The *daf* concludes here, with the remainder of this *mishnah* to be continued at the top of daf 65.

---

---

# Zevachim 65

## Melikah & Bird Offerings

### Melikah Overview

Daf 65 opens in the middle of a very long *mishnah* that began on the previous daf. After discussing where on the *mizbeach* the various bird sacrifices are performed, the *mishnah* turns to the mechanics of how one carries out those sacrifices — specifically, the process of *melikah*, the severing of the bird's head with the thumb. The *gemara* on the previous daf went into considerable detail about how the *kohein* actually holds the bird in order to perform this act.

### Olah vs. Chatas

The *mishnah* also distinguishes between the *olah* and the *chatas* in terms of where each is performed and how the blood is handled. The *olah* is performed at the top of the *mizbeach* and the *chatas* at the bottom — the reverse of the arrangement for mammal sacrifices. By the *olah*, the head is fully severed, both *simanim* (trachea and esophagus) are cut through, and the blood is squeezed out directly — there is no squirting. The head is salted and thrown onto the fire, and the body is salted and thrown onto the fire separately. By the *chatas*, the head is not fully severed; only one *siman* is cut, and the blood squirts out before the remainder is squeezed out. The *olah* involves burning the bird; the *chatas* does not.

### Lishmah & Pigul

The *mishnah* then reviews the familiar framework of *lishmah* and *pigul* as it applies to bird sacrifices — noting, as we have seen in prior discussions about mammal sacrifices, what the critical junctures are. Whereas by a mammal sacrifice there are four critical stages (slaughter, catching of the blood, transporting, and throwing), by a bird sacrifice there are effectively only two: the *melikah* itself, and either the squirting of the blood (for a *chatas*) or the squeezing out of the blood (for an *olah*).

---

## Chatas Shelo Lishmah

### Chatas Invalidation

The *gemara* at the top of 65a addresses the case of a bird *chatas* whose *melikah* was performed *shelo lishmah*. Just as with an animal *chatas*, performing the *melikah* *shelo lishmah* invalidates the bird *chatas* — though it does not create *pigul* and the owner receives no atonement. By contrast, a bird *olah* performed *shelo lishmah*, like its animal counterpart, is not invalidated outright; it simply does not count for the owner.

### Mixed Thoughts

The *gemara* then addresses the case in which a *shelo lishmah* thought is combined with a *pigul* thought — that is, where the *melikah* was performed *shelo lishmah* and the subsequent squeezing of the blood was intended *chutz lizmano* (outside its proper time). In such a case, by the *chatas*, the *shelo lishmah* thought derails the sacrifice from becoming *pigul*, since the *korban* was already invalidated through a different avenue. By the *olah*, however, this does not prevent *pigul* from taking effect.

### Separate Kezaysim

A further scenario is introduced: what if, rather than improper thoughts occurring at different stages of the *avodah*, the *kohein* had two different improper thoughts about two distinct *kezaysim* — intending, for example, to eat one *kezayit* *chutz limkomo* (outside its proper place) and another *kezayit* *chutz lizmano* (outside its proper time)? These are not thoughts about different stages of the *avodah* but rather thoughts about different portions of the animal. The *gemara* cycles through several permutations: one *kezayit* outside its location and one outside its time; the same in reverse order; half a *kezayit* outside its location and half outside its time; and again in reverse. In all these cases, the ruling is *pasul v'ein bo kares* — invalid, but without *kares* and without *pigul*.

In the last two cases, the absence of *pigul* follows clearly from the fact that the *chutz lizmano* thought encompassed only half a *kezayit*, which is insufficient to create *pigul* on its own. In the first two cases, the reasoning is that even though there was a full *kezayit* of *chutz lizmano* intent, the simultaneous intent to eat a *kezayit chutz limkomo* — a different type of invalidating thought — prevents the sacrifice from becoming *pigul*.

### Rav Yehuda's Order

Rav Yehuda disagrees with this blanket ruling. He holds that the order of the thoughts is determinative. If the *chutz lizmano* thought came first (*machsheves hazman kadma l'machsheves hamakom*), the sacrifice becomes *pigul* and one is *chayav kares*. In his view, once *pigul* has taken effect, a subsequent *chutz limkomo* thought about a different *kezayit* does not undo it. If, however, the *chutz limkomo* thought came first, the sacrifice has already been invalidated through that avenue, and a subsequent *pigul* thought cannot take hold — the ruling is *pasul v'ein bo kares*. This principle parallels what was established in prior discussions regarding *nesachim*.

### Chachamim Disagree

The *Chachamim* reject Rav Yehuda's distinction based on order. In their view, whichever thought came first, the combination of the two different invalidating thoughts prevents *pigul* from applying — in either sequence, the ruling is *pasul v'ein bo kares*.

### Eating & Burning

A final case is noted: if one had a thought to eat half a *kezayit* at the wrong time and to burn half a *kezayit* at the wrong time, this does not constitute *pigul*, because eating and burning do not combine to form a single *pigul* thought. The *gemara* observes that this review of the rules of *pigul* and *lishmah* as applied to bird sacrifices is not substantially new — all of it follows from what was established regarding larger animals. The *mishnah* could theoretically have stated simply that all the *pigul* laws applicable to animal sacrifices apply equally to bird sacrifices; it chose to record the *machlokes* explicitly.

---

## Pesukim Analysis

### Olah Pesukim

The *gemara* now turns to the *pesukim* in *Vayikra* that describe the procedures for bird sacrifices, since some of the laws discussed in the *mishnah* are derived from careful reading of these verses. The *pesukim* for the bird *olah* appear in the opening of *Vayikra* (1:14–17), where the Torah transitions from animal offerings to bird offerings. The relevant passage reads: *v'im min ha-of olah korbano la-Hashem v'hikriv min ha-torim o min bnei ha-yonah et korbano* — and if his offering is a bird *olah* to God, he shall bring from the turtle-doves or from the young pigeons. *V'hikrivo ha-kohein el ha-mizbeach* — the *kohein* shall bring it close to the altar. *U-malak et rosho v'hiktir ha-mizbei'ach* — he shall perform *melikah* on its head and burn it on the altar. *V'nimtza damo al kir ha-mizbeach* — and its blood shall be squeezed out on the wall of the altar.

The *gemara* notes immediately that this sequence is puzzling: it says first that the *kohein* burns it and then that he squeezes out the blood. Obviously, squeezing out the blood must precede burning the bird. The out-of-order presentation will prove significant for *derash*.

The passage continues: *v'hesir et murato b'notzatah v'hishlich otah etzel ha-mizbeach kedmah el mekom ha-deshen* — he removes the crop and throws it near the altar to the place of ashes. *V'shisa oto bichnafav lo yavdil* — he tears it open through its wings without fully separating it. *V'hiktir oto ha-kohein ha-mizbeicha al ha-eitzim asher al ha-eish* — and the *kohein* burns it on the fire on the altar. This is the second instance of *v'hiktir* in the passage, a duplication the *gemara* will exploit.

One further observation: the *olah* passage uses *v'nimtza* — the blood is squeezed out — and does not use the language of *v'hizah* (sprinkling). This stands in contrast to the *chatas* passage.

### Chatas Pesukim

The *pesukim* for the bird *chatas* appear at the end of *Parshas Vayikra* (5:8–9), in the section dealing with *korban oleh v'yored*. The passage describes a person bringing two birds — one as a *chatas* and one as an *olah*. For the *chatas*, it states: *v'hikriv et asher la-chatas rishona u-malak et rosho mimul orpo v'lo yavdil* — he shall bring forward first the one that is the *chatas*, perform *melikah* from opposite the nape of its neck, and not fully separate it. *V'hizah midam ha-chatas al kir ha-mizbeach* — he shall sprinkle (*hizah*) from the blood of the *chatas* on the wall of the altar. *V'ha-nishar ba-dam yimatzei el yesod ha-mizbeach* — and the remainder of the blood shall be squeezed out (*yimatzei*) at the base of the altar.

The key differences between these two passages thus emerge: the *chatas* specifies *mimul orpo* (from the nape), *v'lo yavdil* (without fully separating), *v'hizah* (sprinkling), and *yimatzei el yesod* (squeezing at the base). The *olah* specifies squeezing (*nimtza*) — no sprinkling — and its blood goes to the wall of the altar.

### Verb Comparison

Returning to the *olah* passage, the *gemara* examines the verbs with care. The sequence *u-malak* — *v'hiktir* — *v'nimtza* presents the burning before the squeezing of blood, which cannot reflect the actual order of operations. As the *gemara* will explain, this inversion is intentional and carries *halachic* weight: it serves to link the squeezing of blood (*nimtza*) to the burning (*hiktir*) and thereby derive that the squeezing must take place at the same location as the burning.

The *olah* passage also contains *v'hiktir* twice — once immediately after *melikah* and once at the end of the passage after the crop is removed and the body is torn open. This duplication, as the *gemara* will develop, teaches that the head and body of the *olah* are offered separately, and correspondingly that the *melikah* itself must completely separate the head from the body.

---

## Kohein & Melikah

### Kohein Required

The *gemara* now proceeds to a *baraita* that methodically derives the specific laws of *melikah* from the *pesukim*. The *baraita* begins: *v'hikrivo* — why does the verse need to say "he shall bring it"? The *baraita* first addresses the word *min ha-torim o min bnei ha-yonah*, which is in the plural. One might have thought that just as obligatory bird sacrifices typically involve two birds (one *chatas* and one *olah*), even a voluntary bird *olah* must consist of two birds. Therefore the verse says *v'hikrivo* in the singular — *afilu perida achat yavi*, even a single bird suffices.

The *baraita* then asks: why does the verse say *v'hikrivo ha-kohein el ha-mizbeach* — why is *ha-kohein* mentioned? After all, *shechita* of animal sacrifices does not require a *kohein*; a *zar* (non-*kohein*) may perform *shechita*. One might reason by *kal vachomer*: if a sheep, which is restricted to the north of the altar, does not require a *kohein* for slaughter, then a bird, which has no such geographic restriction, should certainly not require a *kohein*. Therefore, the verse must state *ha-kohein* explicitly — *likboa lo kohein*, to establish that *melikah* requires a *kohein*.

### No Knife Needed

The *baraita* proceeds to a second *kal vachomer*: *melikah* requires a *kohein* but no knife; *shechita* requires a knife but no *kohein*. One might therefore reason that since *shechita*, which does not require a *kohein*, nevertheless requires a knife — surely *melikah*, which requires a *kohein*, should also require a knife. The *gemara* answers from *talmud lomar kohein u-malak*: the *kohein* performs the *melikah* — implying with his own body, specifically with his thumbnail — and no knife is required.

### Akiva's Body Rule

Rabbi Akiva refines the *derash*. He asks: is it not already obvious that a *zar* cannot perform *melikah*? After all, *melikah* is performed directly at the *mizbeach* itself, in the immediate context of offering the blood — how could one imagine a non-*kohein* approaching the altar to perform such an act? Rabbi Akiva argues that the self-evident prohibition on a *zar* approaching the altar in the context of an *avodah* is understood without the verse needing to state it. The real teaching of *ha-kohein* must therefore be something else: *she-tehei melikah b'atzmo shel kohein* — that the *melikah* must be performed with the *kohein*'s own body, i.e., with his thumbnail, and not with any instrument.

### Why Kohein Matters

This raises a broader question: why is it that *shechita* of animal sacrifices does not require a *kohein* and is performed with a knife, while *melikah* of bird sacrifices requires a *kohein* and is performed with the finger? A conceptual explanation suggests itself. When a *kohein* is not required for *shechita*, the sanctifying element of the act is the instrument — the knife, which is a *kli shareit*, a sanctified temple vessel. The knife serves as the sacred object that effects the transformation of the animal's status. When, however, the act is performed with the finger — with no knife involved — there is no *kli shareit* present. The *kohein*'s own person substitutes: the finger of the *kohein* is, as it were, the sanctified instrument. This also connects to Rabbi Akiva's earlier point: the *melikah* occurs in the very context of the altar and the offering of the blood simultaneously, whereas by animal *shechita* the blood is caught, transported, and only then placed on the altar. That remove from the immediate altar context is what permits a non-*kohein* to perform *shechita*; the intimacy of *melikah* with the altar demands the *kohein* himself.

### Top of Altar

The *baraita* continues: perhaps *melikah* — and specifically the squeezing of the blood — may be performed either at the top half or the bottom half of the *mizbeach*. The verse teaches otherwise: *u-malak v'hiktir* — just as *haktara* (burning) takes place at the top of the altar where the fire is, so too *melikah* takes place at the top of the altar. The *chatas*, correspondingly, is at the bottom — the reverse of the arrangement for mammal sacrifices.

### Head Separation

The *baraita* then considers where on the bird's neck the *melikah* is performed. The verse says *mimul orpo* — from opposite the nape of the neck, i.e., the back of the neck rather than the throat. This is explicit in the *chatas* passage; the *baraita* links the *olah* passage to it by *gezeirah shavah* on the word *u-malak*.

However, the *chatas* passage also says *v'lo yavdil* — one does not fully sever the head. Should we derive from the *gezeirah shavah* that the *olah* also should not fully sever? No — here the other *derash* intervenes: *u-malak v'hiktir*, and since *haktara* involves head and body separately (*rosh l'atzmo v'guf l'atzmo*), so too *melikah* must fully separate head from body. How do we know *haktara* is separate? Because the verse says *v'hiktir* twice — once immediately after *melikah* and once at the end of the passage after the body is prepared. The first *v'hiktir* refers to burning of the head; the second *v'hiktir* refers to burning of the body. Therefore the two are offered separately, and correspondingly the *melikah* must achieve that separation. By the *chatas*, the *lo yavdil* means one need not — though need not is not the same as may not; we will return to that.

---

## Blood Location

### Top Half Required

Having established that both the *melikah* and the squeezing of blood must occur at the top half of the altar, the *baraita* explains how this is derived for the blood-squeezing specifically. The verse states *u-malak v'hiktir v'nimtza damo al kir ha-mizbeach* — but this sequence is impossible as a description of the actual procedure, for one cannot squeeze out blood after the bird has already been burned. The only purpose of placing *v'nimtza* after *v'hiktir* is therefore to teach that the squeezing of the blood must occur at the same place as the *haktara*: just as *haktara* takes place at the top of the altar (*b'rosh ha-mizbeach*), so too *mitzui* (squeezing) takes place at the top of the altar.

One might have thought otherwise: by mammal sacrifices, the *chatas* goes above and the *olah* below; by bird sacrifices, the *chatas* goes below — perhaps the *olah* should also go below? The *kal vachomer* would suggest this. But the verse, by juxtaposing *haktara* and *nimtza*, refutes it.

The *baraita* then describes the actual procedure: the *kohein* ascends the ramp (*kevesh*), turns to the *soveiv* (the walkway that encircles the altar at its midpoint), and arrives at the southeast corner. There he performs the *melikah* and squeezes out the blood against the wall of the altar.

### Altar Wall Only

The verse specifies *al kir ha-mizbeach* — on the wall of the altar. This means all the blood, and specifically the wall of the altar itself, not the wall of the *kevesh* (ramp) and not the wall of the *heichal*.

### Below Feet Allow

An allowance is noted: the *kohein* may squeeze out the blood up to one *amah* below his feet and it remains valid (*u-mamtzeh l'matta me-raglav afilu amah kesheira*). This is because the *soveiv* is at the six-*amah* mark of the altar's height, and the midpoint of the altar — the boundary between its upper and lower halves — is one *amah* below the *soveiv*. The *kohein* standing on the *soveiv* can squeeze the blood downward as far as that midpoint and still be within the upper half.

### Location Debate

Rabbi Nechemia and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagree: they hold that the entire act must be performed at the very top of the altar (*b'rosho shel mizbeach*), with no allowance for squeezing blood below the *kohein*'s feet.

### Fire & Placement

The *gemara* asks: *mai beinaihu* — what is the underlying point of this debate? Abaye and Rava both answer: the dispute hinges on whether one may place a fire (*maaracha*) on the *soveiv* itself. The reason the squeezing must relate to the burning — as derived from the juxtaposition of *v'hiktir* and *v'nimtza* — means that the squeezing must be in proximity to where the burning occurs. If a fire may be placed on the *soveiv*, then squeezing the blood below one's feet and placing it directly onto that fire is considered sufficiently proximate. If no fire may be placed on the *soveiv*, then the only genuine proximity to the fire is above the *soveiv*, and squeezing below the feet is too distant. This is not merely a question of which half of the altar one is in; it is a question of the functional juxtaposition between the squeezing of the blood and the burning.

---

## Crop Removal

### Crop Methods

The *gemara* turns to the removal of the crop (*murah* / *zefek*). The verse says *v'hesir et murato b'notzatah* — he removes the crop *b'notzatah*. One possibility is that one cuts around the crop with a knife and removes only the crop itself; the word *b'notzatah* would then be read as meaning "with its feathers." Abba Yosi ben Chanan holds that one takes it together with the *korkevan* (intestine).

### Surgical Cutting

The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads *b'notzatah* differently: one uses a knife to cut surgically around the spot on the outside of the bird's body directly opposite the crop, forming a circular incision (*k'min arubah*), so that when the crop is removed it comes out with only the skin and feathers directly adjacent to it — without taking excess body tissue.

### Tearing Open

The verse also says *v'shisa oto bichnafav lo yavdil* — he tears it open through its wings, not fully severing it. The *baraita* derives from the word *shisa* that this must be done by hand: *ein shisa ela b'yad*.
