A proof is brought from the verse in the context of Shimshon, *va-yishaseihu k'shesa ha-gedi* — "he tore it as one tears a young goat" — a tearing done with the hands. The *lo yavdil* here refers to not fully severing the body when tearing it open, which is distinct from the *lo yavdil* earlier in the *chatas* passage that refers to not fully severing the head.

### Post-Blood Acts

A further principle is established: if the *kohein* failed to remove the crop or to carry out these post-*melikah* procedures, the sacrifice remains *kasher*. The critical acts are those involving the blood; procedures performed after the blood stage do not invalidate the sacrifice if omitted.

---

## Both Simanim

### Mishnah Invalid

The *gemara* now notes that the *mishnah* is not in accordance with the position of Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon. The *mishnah* states — in the context of its earlier discussion — that if the *kohein* performed *melikah* on a bird *chatas* and severed both *simanim*, the *chatas* is invalid.

### R.E. Valid

A *baraita* records Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon's dissenting view: *shamati she-mavdilin b'chatat ha-of* — "I have heard that one may fully sever [both *simanim*] in the case of a bird *chatas*," and it remains valid.

### Squeezing Issue

Rav Chisda explains the underlying point of the debate. The *tanna kamma* holds that *mitzui chatat ha-of me'akev* — squeezing out the blood of a bird *chatas* is an indispensable requirement. Given this, if the *kohein* severs both *simanim* and then squeezes out the blood, he has performed both the distinctive acts of the *olah* procedure: fully severing the head and squeezing the blood.

### Like Olah

The operative assumption is that what renders the *chatas* invalid in this case is not the violation of the verse *v'lo yavdil* per se, but rather the fact that the *kohein* has treated the *chatas* exactly as he would treat an *olah* — *ma'aseh olah b'chatat ha-of*. This is what invalidates it. One might ask: by animal sacrifices, the same act of *shechita* is performed for both *chatas* and *asham*, yet this does not invalidate — why should it be different here? The *gemara* accepts the premise that here it does invalidate, and proceeds to analyze why.

### Flesh Cutting

Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon holds that *mitzui chatat ha-of lo me'akev* — squeezing out the blood is not an indispensable requirement. If so, even if the *kohein* severed both *simanim*, he has not replicated the procedure of the *olah* in a meaningful sense, because the *olah* procedure requires both the severing and the squeezing, and the squeezing here is not obligatory. Under this view, what the *kohein* has done is nothing more than cutting through flesh — *u-me-chattech basar b'alma hu* — which does not render the *chatas* invalid. Rashi notes that in practice, in such a case, the *kohein* should take care not to squeeze out the blood, so as not to replicate the *olah* procedure.

---

## Siman Status

### One Act vs. Two

Rava offers a different framework for understanding the debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon. He frames it as a conceptual question about the nature of the requirement to sever both *simanim* by the bird *olah*: is the second *siman* part of one continuous act of *melikah* (comparable to how both *simanim* of a mammal constitute a single act of *shechita*), or is it a separate, distinct requirement that follows after the primary *melikah* act is already complete?

This question has practical implications. In standard *hilchos shechita*, a pause (*shehiya*) in the middle of the *shechita* act invalidates it. If severing the second *siman* of a bird *olah* is part of a single unified act of *melikah*, then a pause between the first and second *siman* would invalidate the *olah*. If, however, the second *siman* is a distinct, subsequent requirement — not part of the *shechita* act itself — then a pause would not invalidate.

### Pause Relevance

This conceptual question is directly relevant to the *chatas*. By the *chatas*, there is a structural pause built into the process: after cutting the first *siman*, the *kohein* must complete cutting through the majority of the flesh of the neck (*rov basar*), and only then could he proceed to the second *siman*. This intervening step necessarily creates a pause between the two *simanim*. The question then becomes: does this pause make the *chatas* procedure look like a valid *olah* or an invalid one?

### Melikah Process

The physical mechanics of *melikah* illuminate why the pause is inherent. The *kohein* comes from the back of the neck with his thumbnail. He first cuts through a minority of the flesh of the neck, then cuts through the *siman*, then finishes cutting through the majority of the flesh of the neck. He cannot cut through most of the flesh first, because doing so before reaching the *siman* would effectively kill the bird before the *melikah* itself. Thus the sequence is: minority of flesh → first *siman* → majority of flesh → (optionally) second *siman*. The majority of flesh necessarily falls between the two *simanim*.

### Kamma Position

The *tanna kamma* holds that a pause between the two *simanim* does not invalidate the *olah*: *shehiya b'siman sheini b'olas ha-of lo me'akev*. Under this view, the second *siman* is a separate requirement, not part of the *shechita* act, so a pause is of no consequence. Given this, if a *kohein* performing a *chatas* cuts through both *simanim* — even with the intervening pause — he has replicated what is entirely valid by an *olah*. Therefore, the *chatas* is invalid because it has been treated just like an *olah*.

### R.E. Safe

Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon holds the opposite: *shehiya b'siman sheini b'olas ha-of me'akev* — a pause between the two *simanim* would invalidate the *olah*. Under this view, both *simanim* constitute a single unified act of *melikah*, and any interruption breaks that act. By the *chatas*, however, the *kohein* necessarily pauses between the two *simanim* in order to cut the majority of the flesh. At the moment that pause occurs, the *melikah* can no longer be considered a valid *olah*-type act. From that point on, cutting through the second *siman* is nothing more than cutting through flesh (*meichtichas basar b'alma*), and the *chatas* remains valid.

### Abaye's View

Abaye proposes a variation on this analysis. Rather than framing the debate around whether a pause invalidates the *olah*, Abaye frames it around whether cutting through the majority of the flesh (*rov basar*) is itself a required step in the process. Under Abaye's reading, everyone agrees that a pause would invalidate the *olah*. The debate is whether, when one cuts both *simanim* in a *chatas*, there is necessarily a pause at all. If one is required to cut the majority of the flesh between the two *simanim*, there is an inevitable pause and the *chatas* is safe. If, however, cutting the majority of the flesh is not required and one could proceed directly from the first to the second *siman* without stopping, then it would be possible to replicate the *olah* procedure exactly — and that would invalidate the *chatas*.

### Gemara Synthesis

The *gemara* notes that the debate between Rava and Abaye itself reflects a dispute between two *amora'im* — one of whom says that the core point of disagreement between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon is whether a pause between the two *simanim* invalidates the *olah*, and the other of whom says that all agree a pause would invalidate and the debate is instead about whether *rov basar* is a required intermediate step.

To summarize the final analysis: the reason cutting both *simanim* of a bird *chatas* would be invalid is not primarily a violation of *v'lo yavdil* but rather that doing so makes the *chatas* indistinguishable from an *olah*. The point of contention is how to define "indistinguishable." If an *olah* tolerates a pause between the two *simanim* (and the pause that necessarily occurs in a *chatas* does not differentiate it), the *chatas* is invalid. If an *olah* does not tolerate such a pause (and the *chatas* necessarily has one), then cutting both *simanim* in a *chatas* is not truly replicating the *olah* procedure, and the *chatas* remains valid. Alternatively, if the question is whether one must pause at all — that is, whether *rov basar* is required — then the debate shifts to whether the *chatas* can in principle be performed without any differentiating pause.

---

---

# Zevachim 66

## Chatas v. Olah Bird

### Core Differences

The daf opens by situating us within the broader contrast between the bird *chatas* and the bird *olah*. Both the location of the service and the handling of the blood differ fundamentally between the two. The *chatas* bird is performed below and the *olah* above — a reversal of the animal *korbanot*, where the *chatas* is the one performed at the top. More centrally for the discussion that follows, the *Torah* specifies distinct procedures for each. By the bird *chatas* the verse states *lo yavdil* — you do not sever the head — and this is understood to mean not only that you do not cut all the way through, but that you cut only one of the *simanim*, either the trachea or the esophagus. By the bird *olah*, the understanding is that you do fully sever, separating the head entirely. The blood procedures likewise differ: by the *chatas* the verse says *v'hizah* — the blood is first squirted, then the remainder is squeezed out (*venimtzah damo el yesod hamizbe'ach*); by the *olah* there is no *v'hizah*, only *venimtzah damo*, the squeezing alone.

### R. Eliezer bar R. Shimon

Against this backdrop, the *Gemara* had been engaged with the position of Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon, who ruled that if one performs the *chatas* bird in the manner of an *olah* — that is, severs both *simanim* — the offering nevertheless remains *kasher*. One might have thought that the very violation of *lo yavdil* should disqualify the offering by force of the negative command, but the *Gemara* does not focus on that line of argument. Instead, the question it pursues is whether severing both *simanim* constitutes performing the *chatas* in the manner of the *olah*, and it is that equivalence — doing it *like* an *olah* — that would be the operative basis for invalidation.

### Like an Olah?

The *Gemara* then raises the complicating consideration: even if you sever both *simanim* in a *chatas*, would that action actually be comparable to a valid *olah* procedure? This is where the requirement of *rov basar* — cutting the majority of the flesh of the neck — becomes critical. Once you have cut through to the first *siman* and severed it, you must complete the cutting of the majority of the flesh in that same act. By the time you would proceed to the second *siman*, there would necessarily have been a *shehiya*, a pause, between the two. The question then arises whether such a pause between *siman* one and *siman* two would have invalidated the service had this been an actual *olah*. If so, then what was done in the *chatas* would not have constituted a valid *olah*-style *melikah* in the first place, and on that basis Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon would say it does not invalidate the *chatas* — because you have not genuinely "done it like an *olah*."

---

## Rov Basar Rule

### Inference Rov Basar

The preceding discussion contains an implicit inference: the requirement to cut the majority of the flesh of the neck (*rov basar*) is a necessary component of the *melikah* of a *chatas* bird. The *Gemara* makes this explicit: *michlal de-ba'inan rov basar bit'chilah* — do we not conclude from all of this that it is indeed required to cut through the majority of the flesh, and that this must occur in coordination with the severing of the *siman*?

### Baraita Rules

The *Gemara* confirms this with a *baraita*: How does one perform the *melikah* of a bird *chatas*? One cuts through the spinal cord and the neckbone — but without cutting away the majority of the flesh (*belo rov basar*). The reason is straightforward: were you to sever the majority of the flesh before reaching the *siman*, the bird would in effect already be considered as having been killed before the valid ritual act was performed. The *baraita* therefore specifies that you continue cutting until you reach either the *veshet* or the *kaneh* — the esophagus or the trachea. Once you have reached one of them (*higia la-veshet o la-kaneh*), you sever that one *siman* or the majority of it — and in that same act you complete the cutting of the majority of the flesh (*v'rov basar imo*). The head remains attached, in fulfillment of *lo yavdil*.

### Chatas v. Olah Timing

By an *olah*, the *baraita* continues, you must sever both *simanim* or the majority of both. The structural difference is now clarified: for a *chatas*, you sever one *siman* and the *rov basar* is completed simultaneously in that act. For an *olah*, you must sever both *simanim* — and both must be severed before the *rov basar* is cut. The reason is the same as above: cutting through the majority of the flesh before completing the required *simanim* would constitute killing the bird prior to the valid ritual act.

### Shehiya Issue

This raises the *shehiya* question: if one pauses between the severing of the first and second *siman*, would that pause — after *rov basar* of the first stage has already been cut — constitute an invalidating interruption for the *olah*? Beyond the *shehiya* concern, there is a deeper conceptual question here. When the *Torah* requires two *simanim* by the *olah*, is it redefining the act of *melikah* such that no valid act has been performed until both are severed? Or does severing the first *siman* constitute a complete act of *melikah*, with the severing of the second being an additional requirement? This conceptual question bears directly on whether pausing between the two would be problematic — and indeed on whether proceeding from one *siman* to a second, after the *rov basar* has already been completed in the first act, is even possible within the structure of a valid *olah melikah*.

---

## R. Yirmiyah's Reading

### Tradition Intro

The entire preceding analysis — the debate over whether Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon's leniency is grounded in the claim that the dual *siman* procedure would not have been valid by an *olah* in any event — is now challenged by Rabbi Yirmiyah. He reports that this analysis has missed the actual reasoning of Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon entirely. The tradition he invokes runs through Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Das, who cited it in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Shamuah — a chain of two *Elazars*, ultimately transmitting the stated position of Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon.

### Lo Yavdil = Optional

Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon's actual reasoning, according to this tradition, is that *lo yavdil* does not mean *prohibited* — it means *not required*. The verse is not telling you that severing the head is forbidden; it is telling you that it is unnecessary. In his words: *shamati be-chattasot she-mavdilin* — I have received a tradition that severing is permissible for *chatas* birds. And the *lo yavdil* of the verse is to be read as *ein tzarich le-havdil* — there is no requirement to sever.

This is therefore an entirely different basis for his ruling than what the *Gemara* had previously been exploring. The earlier analysis assumed that *lo yavdil* carried a prohibitory force and sought to explain why the violation did not invalidate; Rabbi Yirmiyah's tradition says the premise was wrong — there is no prohibition in *lo yavdil* at all.

### Context Matters

Rav Achai the son of Rava raised a challenge to Rabbi Yirmiyah before Rav Ashi: does this reading not run into the same problem as reading *velo yechasenu* — "and he shall not cover it" — regarding the uncovered pit? Surely we would not read that verse to mean there is no *requirement* to cover a pit? The *Gemara* distinguishes the cases: there, the verse states explicitly that *ba'al ha-bor yeshalem* — the owner of the pit must pay — and it is precisely because he did not cover it that liability arises. The context makes unmistakably clear that the absence of covering generates a monetary obligation. Here, by contrast, the context supports a different reading, and the surrounding verses provide the interpretive framework.

### Olah First

The critical textual point is that the *olah* is mentioned first in the passage. And by the *olah*, the verse does not explicitly say *yavdil* — the requirement to sever is derived only by inference. Given that the *Torah* already distinguishes the *olah* procedure (*v'hikrivo* implies this one is different from that one), the *lo yavdil* by the *chatas* is best read as saying: severing is not required — not as a prohibition. Moreover, since the *olah*, which is discussed first, already carries an implicit inference that one *does* sever, the *lo yavdil* of the *chatas* can naturally be read as the contrasting permissive statement: you need not sever. Reading it as a prohibition, by contrast, would drive a more extreme contrast between the two, placing them at diametrically opposite poles — and since the *Torah* does not explicitly state what is done by the *olah*, the more modest interpretive move is to say that *lo yavdil* means it is optional, not forbidden. As the principle goes, *tafasta merubeh lo tafasta* — if you overreach, you lose the inference. We can move the distinction one degree; we are not entitled to flip the verses to complete opposites. The conclusion, then, is *shma mina ein tzarich lehavdil* — it is simply not required.

---

## Olah Blood Essence

### Body Blood Only

A *baraita* addresses a question about the blood procedure of the bird *olah*: even if the *kohen* squeezes out only the blood of the body (*dam ha-guf*) and does not squeeze out the blood of the head, the *olah* remains valid.

### Head or Body?

One might have reasoned the opposite — that the blood of the head should be the more critical component. The *baraita* addresses this by invoking the word *hu*: the verse says *olah hu* or *isheh reiach nichoach*, and the word *hu* indicates that only one of the two components is necessary. But the question remains: why is it specifically the body's blood that is indispensable, and not the head's?

### Ravina's Logic

Ravina provides a logical resolution: *mistavra de-rov damim be-guf shechichi* — it stands to reason that the majority of blood is found in the body, not in the head. Since most of the blood is in the body, it is self-evident that when the *Torah* speaks of squeezing out the blood of the *olah* as the essential act, it refers to the body's blood. The head's blood is a secondary quantity, and its omission does not invalidate.

---

## Chatas/Olah Swap

### Chatas Like Olah

With the *halacha* of *hadran* marking the conclusion of the previous chapter, the *Gemara* opens a new *perek* — though it is striking how seamlessly the new *mishnah* continues the very discussion that immediately preceded it. The *mishnah* takes up precisely the question we have been analyzing: what happens when one performs a *chatas* bird in the manner of an *olah*, or an *olah* bird in the manner of a *chatas*?

The *mishnah* first addresses the bird *chatas* done in a manner departing from its proper service. If it was performed below in the manner of a *chatas* but with *olah* intent (*leshem olah*), it is *pesulah*. If it was performed like an *olah* with *olah* intent (*kema'aseh olah leshem olah*), it is equally invalid — one might have thought that matching the method and intent to the *olah* would effectively redefine the offering, but that reasoning is rejected. The *chatas* cannot be redefined into an *olah* by intent or procedure.

### Olah Correct

If the *chatas* was performed *above* — in the domain of the *olah* — then regardless of whether one intended it as a *chatas* or as an *olah*, it is *pesulah*. The *mishnah* closes off both potential arguments: one might have said that doing everything precisely in the manner of a *chatas* with *chatas* intent should suffice despite the wrong location; or one might have said that performing it above with *olah* intent and *olah* procedure effectively transforms it into an *olah*. Both arguments are rejected. The correct procedure must be followed in the correct place.

Conversely, the bird *olah* done above (*lema'alah*), in the manner of an *olah* (*kema'aseh olah*), with *olah* intent (*leshem olah*) — when all three variables are correct — is *keshera*.

### Olah Like Chatas

Any deviation from those three variables, however, creates problems. If the *olah* was done in the manner of a *chatas*, the most obvious meaning of that is that only one *siman* was severed rather than two. That is clearly invalid — not because it is "like a *chatas*," but because the required *melikah* of the *olah* was simply not performed. Alternatively, "like a *chatas*" could refer to the blood procedure. If the *olah* was done with *chatas* intent (*leshem chatas*) but by an *olah* method — two *simanim* — it is similar to the case of *shelo lishmo*: the *olah* done with the wrong intent, which under ordinary rules would be *keshera* but not credited to the owner's obligation. The *mishnah* is nuanced on this point, and the *Gemara* will explore its details further.

### Wrong Location

The *mishnah* concludes: if the *olah* was performed below (*asah lematah kema'aseh kulan*), it is *pesulah* regardless of how it was done or what intent was held. One might have thought that doing it in the correct *olah* manner with correct *olah* intent would save it despite the wrong location. One might alternatively have thought that performing it below with *chatas* intent and *chatas* procedure effectively reconstitutes it as a *chatas*, which properly belongs below. Both arguments are rejected.

---

## Like What?

### Melikah or Blood?

The *Gemara* now analyzes what it means for the *mishnah* to say the *chatas* was done "like an *olah*." The two candidates are: (1) *melikah* — that both *simanim* were severed, as in an *olah*; or (2) *haza'ah* — that the blood was handled in the manner of an *olah*, meaning it was squeezed out without the prior squirting that the *chatas* requires.

If the *mishnah* means the *melikah* was changed — that both *simanim* were severed — then the *mishnah* takes a position in the very debate we analyzed earlier: against Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that severing both *simanim* does not invalidate the *chatas*. That is not necessarily a problem — the *Gemara* has already established that the *mishnah* does not follow Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon on this point. But the *Gemara* seeks a reading that is, if possible, not the subject of dispute.

### Haza'ah Focus

A cleaner reading is that the *mishnah* means the *haza'ah* was changed — that instead of squirting the blood as the *chatas* requires, the *kohen* only squeezed it. This is an obvious basis for invalidation: the required blood procedure of the *chatas* was not performed. On this reading, the invalidation is not because one "did it like an *olah*" in some abstract way, but because one failed to fulfill what the *Torah* positively requires of the *chatas* — the *v'hizah*.

### From Seifa Logic

The *Gemara* supports this reading by examining the *seifa* — the end of the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states that performing the *chatas* bird *above* (*lema'alah*) invalidates it, regardless of intent or method. When the *mishnah* says you did "it" above, the "it" refers to something that can be placed above or below. The *melikah*, however, can be performed anywhere on the *mizbe'ach* — as the principle states, *melikah be-khol makom bamizbe'ach kesherah*. Since the location of the *melikah* is irrelevant to validity, the invalidating factor of performing the service "above" must refer to the blood — specifically, where the blood was squirted. It was squirted against the upper portion of the *mizbe'ach* rather than the lower, and that is what disqualifies the *chatas*.

### Both Blood Focused

Since the *seifa*'s reference to performing "it" in the wrong location demonstrably refers to the blood, the *Gemara* argues that the *reisha*'s reference to performing "it" like an *olah* should similarly refer to the blood. Doing the *chatas* "like an *olah*" thus means treating the blood like an *olah* — squeezing rather than squirting. This reading is internally consistent and avoids embroiling the *mishnah* in an unresolved dispute.

The *Gemara* ultimately responds that this argument is not a formal proof — *ha-kedei'ita v'ha-kedei'ita*, each phrase means what it means in its own context. The *seifa* necessarily speaks about blood placement; that does not compel the *reisha* to do so as well. Both remain possible: if the *mishnah* speaks of *melikah*, the *chiddush* is that doing something formally extra — a second *siman* — invalidates because of the prohibition implied by *lo yavdil* or because of the principle of doing it "like the other *korban*," even though the *Gemara* never explicitly provides a textual basis for this conclusion. If the *mishnah* speaks of the blood, the invalidation is more transparent — the required act was simply not performed.

---

## Neveilah/Me'ilah

### Not Neveilah

A new *mishnah* addresses the status of the invalid bird offerings just discussed. Despite their invalidity, all of these bird offerings — whether a *chatas* done like an *olah* or an *olah* done like a *chatas* — do not convey *tum'ah* as *neveilah* would. This is a genuine *chiddush*: since *melikah* is performed from the back of the neck rather than through a proper *shechita*, one might have expected an invalid *melikah* to render the bird a *neveilah*, subject to the impurity of a carcass improperly slaughtered. The *mishnah* teaches otherwise. Even in the case of an *olah* performed like a *chatas* in which only one *siman* was severed — and thus the *melikah* was deficient — the bird is not treated as a *neveilah*. The reasoning is that since the act would have constituted a valid *melikah* for a *chatas*, it retains sufficient halakhic standing to preclude *neveilah* status.

Furthermore, the *mishnah* states that *me'ilah* applies to all of these invalid offerings. Since none of them ever became permissible — neither through valid consumption by *kohanim* in the case of the *chatas*, nor through a proper *olah* service — they remain in the domain of *hekdesh* and subject to the laws of misappropriation.

### Exception Debate

The *mishnah* records one exception: if the *chatas* bird was done below, in the manner of a *chatas*, with *chatas* intent — that is, in every respect as a proper *chatas* — then the offering is simply valid, and after the blood service the bird becomes accessible to the *kohanim*. In that case there is no *me'ilah* because the *hekdesh* has been properly discharged. This, however, is not the exceptional case; it is the standard valid scenario.

The genuine exception the *mishnah* introduces involves the bird *olah* done below, in the manner of a *chatas*, with *chatas* intent — where a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua applies.

### R. Eliezer: Me'ilah

Rabbi Eliezer holds that *me'ilah* does apply even in this case. The offering was and remains an *olah*; it was never properly discharged; and the fact that everything was done in the manner of a *chatas* does not transform it into a *chatas*. Since the *olah* is never permissible for human benefit even when performed correctly, it certainly retains *me'ilah* when performed invalidly.

### R. Yehoshua: No Me'ilah

Rabbi Yehoshua holds the striking position that *me'ilah* does *not* apply. When one performs the bird *olah* entirely in the manner of a *chatas* — below, with *chatas* intent, with *chatas melikah* — the offering is so thoroughly recategorized in practice that it steps out of the domain of *me'ilah*. It does not become *kasher* as a *chatas*; it remains *pasul*. But it is sufficiently reconstituted in character that *me'ilah* no longer attaches to it.

---

## Recategorization

### Chatas Le-Shem Olah

Rabbi Eliezer challenges Rabbi Yehoshua's position with a pointed argument. Consider the *chatas* bird itself: when a *chatas* is performed correctly, *me'ilah* does not apply after the blood is presented, because the offering is then consumed by the *kohanim*. That is precisely the one category that emerges from *me'ilah* through proper service. Now, if someone performs that *chatas* with *olah* intent (*leshem olah*) — attempting to recategorize it the other direction — the offering is invalid. And in that case, Rabbi Eliezer argues, *me'ilah* clearly applies, because the offering never became permissible. If you allow the logic of recategorization when an *olah* is treated as a *chatas* (Rabbi Yehoshua's position), you must accept the parallel: a *chatas* treated as an *olah* equally becomes *me'ilah*-liable because of its recategorization — now as an *olah*, which carries *me'ilah*. But that parallel only strengthens Rabbi Eliezer's case, not Rabbi Yehoshua's: the recategorization works against you either way.

### Reductio Case

Rabbi Eliezer presses further with a *reductio ad absurdum*. Suppose one takes *kodshei kodashim* — an *olah*, *asham*, or *chatas* — which are required to be slaughtered in the north, and slaughters them in the south (*badarom*) with the intent of *kodashim kalim*, specifically as a *shelamim*. This case attempts to recategorize an offering of the highest sanctity into an offering of lesser sanctity, one that — crucially — does not carry *me'ilah* for its meat. Should we say, following Rabbi Yehoshua's logic, that the recategorization succeeds, and *me'ilah* no longer applies? Surely not. *Me'ilah* applies in that case regardless. Yet here too, the intent and procedure were directed toward something without *me'ilah*. If recategorization does not help there, how can Rabbi Yehoshua maintain it helps by the bird *olah*?

### Reductio Refuted

Rabbi Yehoshua rejects the *reductio*. He concedes that in principle the logic of recategorization should apply to the animal case as well — were the *shelamim* an offering entirely exempt from *me'ilah*, he would indeed say that treating a *kodshei kodashim* entirely like a *shelamim* would remove it from *me'ilah*. But a *shelamim* is not completely exempt from *me'ilah*. The *emurim* — the fats and entrails — are burnt on the *mizbe'ach*, and *me'ilah* applies to them. Only the meat of the *shelamim* is accessible to human benefit; the *mizbe'ach* portions retain *me'ilah*. Therefore, recategorizing an *olah* as a *shelamim* does not place it into a category fully free of *me'ilah*, and the recategorization yields no benefit.

### Complete Exemption

The key distinction for Rabbi Yehoshua is the bird *chatas*. As the *mishnah* elsewhere states, *ein l'mizbe'ach bo klum* — the *mizbe'ach* has no portion in the bird *chatas*. After the blood service, the entire bird is consumed by the *kohanim*. There is no component that goes to the *mizbe'ach* and no portion that remains subject to *me'ilah*. The bird *chatas* is therefore the singular case of an offering *completely* exempt from *me'ilah* once its blood has been presented.

It is precisely this complete exemption that makes recategorization effective, in Rabbi Yehoshua's view. When one takes a bird *olah* and performs it in every respect as a bird *chatas*, one has recategorized it into the only category that is entirely free of *me'ilah*. This does not render the offering *kasher* — it remains *pasul*. But it is sufficient to remove the *me'ilah* that would otherwise apply. The discussion of this remarkable debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Zevachim 67

## Olah/Chatat Debate

### Mishnah Overview

The Mishnah that opens this section of the Gemara presents an extended debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerning the laws of *me'ilah* as they apply to bird sacrifices. The basic framework is as follows: when a bird *chatat* is performed correctly, the *kohanim* are permitted to eat it, and consequently it is not subject to *me'ilah* — the prohibition against deriving benefit from consecrated property. The *olah*, by contrast, is never eaten and therefore retains its *me'ilah* status throughout. If, however, either bird sacrifice is performed incorrectly such that even the *chatat* cannot be eaten, both birds remain under *me'ilah*, since no one is permitted to benefit from them.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Theory

Into this straightforward framework Rabbi Yehoshua introduces a striking and counterintuitive position. He maintains that if one performs a bird *olah* as though it were a *chatat* — bringing it below the altar rather than above, performing the *melikah* on only one *siman* rather than two, and directing the act toward the name of a *chatat* — this is sufficient to shift the bird out of the category of an *olah* and place it within the category of a *chatat*, such that *me'ilah* no longer applies to it.

The obvious objection is that the bird was sanctified as an *olah*. When a person consecrated it, days or weeks before presenting it at the Temple, they designated it as an *olah*. How can the *kohen*'s subsequent conduct at the altar redefine it as something else entirely? This is precisely Rabbi Eliezer's difficulty — and it is the tension that the Gemara now undertakes to resolve.

---

## Eliezer's Challenge

### Asham Counterexample

The Gemara introduces a *brayta* in which Rabbi Eliezer presses Rabbi Yehoshua with a series of counterexamples, each designed to show that performing an act differently does not suffice to recategorize a sacrifice. The first example: one slaughtered an *asham* in the north — the correct location for an *asham* — but with the intent of a *shelamim*. Rabbi Eliezer argues that this constitutes a *shinuy shem*, a change of name or designation, and yet *me'ilah* still applies. The implication is that if changing the designation alone does not strip a sacrifice of *me'ilah*, neither should it for the *olah* that Rabbi Yehoshua is discussing.

It is worth noting, as Rashi observes, that this is already an imperfect counterexample. By an *asham*, once the *zerikah* — the sprinkling of the blood — has been performed, *me'ilah* no longer applies to the meat in any case. So the presence of *me'ilah* in this scenario is only temporary, and the analogy to the *olah* is not precise. Nevertheless, the Gemara follows the argument through.

### Yehoshua's Response

Rabbi Yehoshua replies that the comparison is flawed. In Rabbi Eliezer's case of the *asham* slaughtered in the north for the sake of a *shelamim*, the location was not changed — it was still slaughtered in the north, which is the proper place for an *asham*, not a *shelamim*. By contrast, in Rabbi Yehoshua's own case, not only did he change the name, he changed the *makom*, performing the *olah* below in the place designated for a *chatat*. The question is therefore put back to Rabbi Eliezer: can you show me a case where both name and location were changed and there is still *me'ilah*?

### Second Counterexample

Rabbi Eliezer responds with a refined example: an *asham* slaughtered in the south — the place of a *shelamim* — with the intent of a *shelamim*. Now both the name and the location have been changed. Rabbi Eliezer argues that this constitutes a *shinuy shem* and a *shinuy makom* together, and yet *me'ilah* still applies. Therefore, even Rabbi Yehoshua's case of the *olah* done below in the manner of a *chatat* should retain its *me'ilah*.

### Ma'aseh Distinction

Rabbi Yehoshua responds once more, and here he introduces his sharpest distinction. In Rabbi Eliezer's new counterexample, he concedes, you have changed both name and location. But *v'lo shinah ma'asav* — you have not changed the actual *ma'aseh*, the act itself. The manner in which you slaughtered the *asham* is identical to the manner in which you would slaughter any large animal; the act of *shechitah* is the same regardless of intent or location. In Rabbi Yehoshua's case, however, the *ma'aseh* was also changed: the *melikah* was performed on only one *siman* rather than two, which is precisely the act of a *chatat*, not an *olah*. It is this complete recapitulation of the *chatat* act — name, location, and *ma'aseh* together — that accomplishes the recategorization.

---

## Rava's Analysis

### Me'ilah Distinction

Rava pauses to examine Rabbi Eliezer's counterexample more carefully and raises a conceptual difficulty. He observes that the comparison between an *asham* and a *shelamim* with respect to *me'ilah* is peculiar. Both an *asham* and a *shelamim* share a similar *me'ilah* structure: before *zerikah*, there is *me'ilah*, and after *zerikah*, there is not. So arguing that changing an *asham* into a *shelamim* fails to remove *me'ilah* is not a useful counterexample to Rabbi Yehoshua's position. Rabbi Yehoshua's position is specifically about removing *me'ilah* from an *olah* by redesignating it as a *chatat*; the *chatat* is a sacrifice from which *me'ilah* is absent entirely, which is what makes the redesignation meaningful.

### Zerikah Problem

The more fundamental problem with Rabbi Eliezer's counterexample, Rava notes, is that it asks about a stage before *zerikah* has occurred. Of course there is still *me'ilah* at that point — there is *me'ilah* at that point even in Rabbi Yehoshua's case, which concerns what happens after the *zerikah* or the equivalent completion of the *chatat* process. Rabbi Eliezer's example, in other words, is comparing apples to oranges. After *zerikah* of an *asham*, there is no *me'ilah* either — so the example proves nothing about whether redesignation can remove *me'ilah*.

One might then ask: why did the Gemara allow this exchange to proceed at all? The answer is that the conversation was serving a different purpose. What Rabbi Eliezer was groping toward was the broader question of whether any large-animal sacrifice could be fully redesignated through changed conduct — not merely whether the specific *me'ilah* comparison was apt.

### Concession Moment

Rava draws a striking conclusion from the fact that Rabbi Eliezer did not further press the counterexample by adding yet a third point of difference — for instance, specifying that the *asham* was done also with intention for a different owner. The Gemara notes: *mid'lo ka'amar leh hachi, shema mina nachit Rabbi Eliezer l'ta'ameh* — from the fact that he did not say so, we learn that Rabbi Eliezer came to understand Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning. The light went on, as it were. Rabbi Eliezer realized that Rabbi Yehoshua's claim was not simply "if you do enough strange things to a sacrifice, *me'ilah* disappears." Rather, Rabbi Yehoshua's claim was that the *olah* had been genuinely recategorized — and Rabbi Eliezer understood that with large-animal sacrifices, where the act of *shechitah* is always formally identical regardless of intent or location, no genuine recategorization is possible. The act itself never changes. Therefore, Rabbi Eliezer had no valid counterexample — not because he conceded Rabbi Yehoshua's point, but because he recognized that the two cases are structurally incomparable.

---

## Critical Moment Theory

### The Gap Concept

The Gemara now introduces a sharper formulation of Rabbi Yehoshua's position, attributed to Rav Adda bar Ahava. Until now, Rabbi Yehoshua's view had been understood as: if you perform enough acts consistent with a *chatat*, the *olah* gets redesignated as a *chatat*. But Rav Adda bar Ahava sharpens the reasoning considerably. The key is not the number of *chatat*-like acts performed, but a specific moment in time.

The *olah* of a bird requires that *both* simanim be cut in the *melikah*. The *chatat* of a bird requires that *only one siman* be cut. When a bird *olah* is being performed below, for the sake of a *chatat*, and the *kohen* cuts one *siman*, a specific and decisive moment has arrived. From the *chatat* perspective, the *melikah* is complete — this is exactly what a *chatat melikah* looks like. From the *olah* perspective, the *melikah* is not yet complete — you have only cut one *siman* and have yet to cut the second.

### Siman Echad Logic

This distinction is what generates the "gap." At the moment when one *siman* has been cut, the *chatat melikah* has already occurred, while the *olah melikah* has not yet occurred. The bird's identity as an *olah* has not yet been fully established through the act of *melikah*, because the defining act of an *olah melikah* — the cutting of both *simanim* — is still incomplete. The *chatat* definition, however, can already be said to have taken hold, because its defining act is already done.

### Two Lenses Framework

It is useful to think in terms of two analytical lenses applied to the identical moment. Through the *olah* lens: here is a bird being treated incorrectly — in the wrong place, with the wrong intent — and the *melikah* of an *olah* has not yet been performed. Through the *chatat* lens: here is a bird being processed in the correct place for a *chatat*, with the correct intent for a *chatat*, and the *melikah* of a *chatat* has just been completed. Both descriptions are simultaneously available at the moment after one *siman* is cut. The question is which identity takes hold.

### Identity Redefinition

The answer is that the *chatat* identity wins, because it is the one that has a completed act to its credit. The *olah* identity cannot fully assert itself because the defining act of an *olah* — the cutting of both *simanim* — has not yet taken place. In that gap between the completion of the *chatat melikah* and the still-incomplete *olah melikah*, the *chatat* definition jumps in and claims the bird. It is not magic, and it is not simply a matter of doing enough *chatat*-like things. It is a structural consequence of the asymmetry between the *chatat* and the *olah* with respect to how many *simanim* must be cut.

The *chatat* process finishes first. And finishing first, in a context where all the surrounding acts — location, intent — are oriented toward the *chatat*, is what allows the redesignation to take hold before the *olah* has had the opportunity to assert its identity.

---

## Reverse Case

### Challenge Posed

Having understood the logic of the redesignation, the Gemara immediately poses a symmetrical challenge. If the reasoning is that the *chatat* definition jumps into the gap before the *olah melikah* is complete, then why should the same logic not apply in reverse? Take a bird *chatat* and perform it above the altar in the place of an *olah*, for the sake of an *olah*, cutting both *simanim*. Should it not, by the same logic, become a valid *olah*?

The Mishnah treats such a bird as a *pasul chatat* — an invalid *chatat* — and requires that it be disposed of accordingly. But if Rabbi Yehoshua's principle really means that the sacrifice becomes the other *korban*, why is the reverse not equally true?

The Gemara initially considers whether the statement attributed to Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Benayah — that the specific framing of the Mishnah represents the precise contours of the dispute — might resolve the issue by confining Rabbi Yehoshua's rule to the one direction. The Gemara, however, does not accept this as a sufficient answer, since that statement could equally be read to mean that Rabbi Yehoshua's principle underlies the entire Mishnah.

### Rav Ashi's Answer

Rav Ashi resolves the question by demonstrating that the logic is inherently directional and cannot be reversed.

### Directional Asymmetry

The argument works as follows. When a bird *olah* is performed below like a *chatat*, the defining act of the *chatat* — cutting one *siman* — is completed before the defining act of the *olah* — cutting both *simanim* — can be completed. At the moment when one *siman* is cut, you have finished the *chatat melikah* but have not yet finished the *olah melikah*. Moreover, there is no valid *olah* process that takes place below at all — *olas ha'of lemata leisa*, there is no such thing as a bird *olah* offered below. So the *olah* identity has no foothold at that location. The *chatat* identity, having its *melikah* completed first and in the right place, seizes the definition.

Now consider the reverse: a bird *chatat* performed above like an *olah*. Here, the *kohen* cuts one *siman*. At this moment, the *chatat melikah* has already been completed — because a *chatat* requires only one *siman*. The *olah melikah* has not yet been completed. So the first identity to have a completed act is once again the *chatat* identity. And critically, performing the *melikah* above does not by itself identify the bird as an *olah*, because technically a *chatat melikah* may also be performed above; it is only the subsequent sprinkling of blood that must occur below. So the location alone does not establish an *olah* identity.

The result: even when you are attempting to treat a bird *chatat* as an *olah*, the moment you cut one *siman*, you have already reaffirmed — in its invalid, *shelo lishmo* form — the *chatat* identity. The *chatat pesulah* definition has already taken hold before the *olah* definition could jump in. There is no gap for the *olah* to occupy, because the *chatat* definition activates first and closes the window. The asymmetry is structural: cutting one *siman* always completes the *chatat melikah* first, and the *olah* never gets the opportunity to assert its identity before the *chatat* has already done so — in whichever direction the transformation is attempted.

---

## Kinnim Context

### Kinnim Overview

Having articulated Rabbi Yehoshua's position with precision, the Gemara turns to the tractate *Kinnim* to test it. *Kinnim* deals with the mathematically complex permutations that arise from bird sacrifices — particularly when birds belonging to different women are mixed together and the *kohen* no longer knows which bird belongs to whom or which is a *chatat* and which is an *olah*. Importantly, the *stam* of *Kinnim* — the anonymous, authoritative layer of its Mishnayos — is attributed to Rabbi Yehoshua. This authorial identification will become significant for the analysis.

### Women's Sacrifices

The primary context of *Kinnim* is women who bring their bird sacrifices following childbirth. A woman who gives birth is obligated to bring one bird as a *chatat* and one bird as an *olah*. The tractate's cases typically involve two or more women bringing their respective birds simultaneously, with confusion arising about which bird belongs to which woman and which serves as which offering.

### Designation Rules

An important principle governing these cases is that designations need not be made fully in advance. A woman may purchase two birds and leave the designation — which is the *chatat* and which is the *olah* — to be determined by the *kohen*'s actions at the altar: the bird sacrificed below becomes the *chatat*, and the bird sacrificed above becomes the *olah*. Similarly, when two women bring their birds together, the full designation of whose is whose can in some configurations also be deferred, with the *kohen*'s conduct at the altar resolving the question. This flexibility of designation is integral to the complexity that follows.

Additionally, a critical rule bears noting at the outset: if a person takes a *neder* — a vow — to bring bird sacrifices, those birds can only be *olos*. A *chatat* cannot be brought as a *neder*. This distinction between vow-birds and obligation-birds becomes important in the later cases.

---

## First Kinnim Case

### Uncertain Designation

The Gemara introduces the first relevant Mishnah from *Kinnim*. In this case, one woman still owes a *chatat* and another still owes an *olah* — each having previously brought one of her two post-childbirth birds. They now come together with their remaining birds. The *kohen* receives the two birds but does not know — or cannot remember — which belongs to which woman.

### Both-Above/Both-Below

If the *kohen* performs both birds above the altar, the result is *mechtza kasher, mechtza pasul* — half valid and half invalid. Whichever of the two birds was the *olah* is valid; the bird that was actually a *chatat* was done in the wrong place and that woman must bring another bird. Similarly, if the *kohen* performs both below, the *chatat* is valid and the *olah* is invalid — again half valid and half invalid, the woman obligated in an *olah* must return.

### Split Placement

The most problematic scenario is when the *kohen* performs one above and one below — one in each place. The Mishnah rules that both are invalid. The reasoning: we must assume the possibility that he got them backwards — performing the *chatat* above and the *olah* below, thereby invalidating both. Since this possibility cannot be excluded, neither woman can be considered to have fulfilled her obligation.

---

## Gemara Challenge

### Paradox Stated

The Gemara immediately raises a sharp question against this ruling. According to Rabbi Yehoshua's principle, when an *olah* is performed below in the manner of a *chatat*, it becomes redesignated as a *chatat*. If so, in the case where one bird was done above and one below, and we are concerned that the *olah* was the one done below — why not simply say that the *olah* done below has now become a *chatat*, and that woman should receive credit for her *chatat*? The ruling of total invalidity appears to contradict Rabbi Yehoshua's own principle.

### Person-Specific Limitati…

The Gemara offers a potential limitation: perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua's redesignation principle only applies when the woman bringing the *olah* is herself also obligated in a *chatat*. In that case, her own *olah*, done below, could be redesignated to fulfill her own *chatat* obligation. In the current scenario, however, the woman whose *olah* was done below is not the one who owes a *chatat* — it is the *other* woman who owes the *chatat*. An *olah* redesignated as a *chatat* cannot satisfy a third party's obligation. This could explain why the redesignation provides no benefit here.

### Testing Limitation

The Gemara, however, is not satisfied with this limitation, because it has not yet been proven. The question is whether Rabbi Yehoshua's principle can satisfy a *chatat* obligation in any case, or only in specifically configured ones. To test this properly, the Gemara needs a case where the woman whose *olah* was done below is herself obligated in a *chatat* — and yet we would still say she does not get credit. The Gemara therefore moves to a more complex Mishnah.

---

## Complex Kinnim Case

### Scenario Setup

The Gemara introduces a more intricate Mishnah from *Kinnim*. The scenario involves two women — call them Rachel and Leah — each of whom has had two childbirths. After the first childbirth, each brought one of the two required birds: Rachel brought her *olah* and Leah brought her *chatat*. This means that after birth one, Rachel still owes a *chatat* and Leah still owes an *olah*. After birth two, each now owes a full *chatat* and *olah*.

Tallying the outstanding obligations: Rachel owes a *chatat* (from birth one) plus a *chatat* and an *olah* (from birth two) — that is, two *chataos* and one *olah*. Leah owes an *olah* (from birth one) plus a *chatat* and an *olah* (from birth two) — that is, two *olos* and one *chatat*. Between them, they owe a total of three *chataos* and three *olos*, constituting three complete pairs of birds.

### Three Sets Types

They purchase three pairs of birds. Each pair is designated differently:

The first set — referred to simply as *chatat va'olah* — is fully designated. They specify explicitly: this bird is Leah's *chatat*, this bird is Rachel's *olah*.

The second set is *stumah* — unspecified. They hand both birds to the *kohen* without any designation, leaving it entirely to the *kohen* to determine which is the *chatat* and which is the *olah*, and to allocate credit between the two women. Whatever the *kohen* does establishes the identity of those birds.

The third set is *mefureshet*. Here, they have designated each bird by type — one is a *chatat* and one is an *olah* — but they have not specified *whose* is whose. The *chatat* is identified as a *chatat* and the *olah* as an *olah*, but which one belongs to Rachel and which to Leah is left for the *kohen* to resolve by his actions.

### All-Above Case

If the *kohen* performs all six birds above the altar, the outcome is straightforward. All three *olos* in the group are valid. Every obligation for an *olah* among the two women is thereby satisfied. All the *chataos*, however, were done in the wrong place and remain unfulfilled. The women will need to return with their *chatat* birds.

### All-Below Case

Symmetrically, if the *kohen* performs all six birds below, all the *chataos* are valid and all the *olos* are not. Every *chatat* obligation is satisfied; the *olah* obligations are not, and those birds must be brought again above.

### Split Case

The most complex situation arises when the *kohen* splits each set — performing one bird from each pair above and one below. For the explicitly designated set (*chatat va'olah*), this is potentially disastrous: the *kohen* knows which bird is which, but if he somehow reversed them, both are invalid. In the *mefureshet* set, the *kohen* knew which bird was the *chatat* and which was the *olah* but not whose was whose; if he reversed the locations of *chatat* and *olah*, both are invalid and no credit accrues to either woman. For the *stumah* set, however, the situation is actually favorable: since neither the identity of the birds nor whose is whose was designated in advance, the *kohen*'s actions themselves constitute the designation. Whatever he did above becomes the *olah* and whatever he did below becomes the *chatat*, and these count for one of the two women respectively. The Mishnah therefore rules: *eina kesheira ela stuma* — in the split scenario, only the *stumah* pair yields valid results; the *mefureshet* pair does not.

---

## Gemara Challenge

### Paradox Stated

The Gemara returns to its central difficulty. When the *mefureshet* set is split — one bird above and one below — why does the *olah* that was done below not simply become a *chatat* according to Rabbi Yehoshua's principle? In this pair, the birds were designated as a *chatat* and an *olah*, but not whose is whose. If the *olah* is redesignated as a *chatat* by virtue of being done below, then at least some woman should get credit for a *chatat* from that pair. Why does the Mishnah say both are invalid?

### Person-Specific Limitati…

The Gemara revisits the limitation it had proposed: perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua's rule only applies when the redesignation benefits the very person whose bird it was. But in the *mefureshet* case, the *olah* was not yet assigned to anyone — whose *olah* it was had not been determined. So it cannot be that the redesignation fails for lack of a matching personal obligation.

### Testing Limitation

The Gemara therefore presses the question: does Rabbi Yehoshua's principle lead to the conclusion that the woman whose *olah* was done below should receive credit for a *chatat* even in the *mefureshet* case? And if not, what precisely limits the scope of his ruling? To resolve this, the Gemara demonstrates that *Kinnim* is according to Rabbi Yehoshua — and then draws the decisive distinction about what his ruling actually means.

---

## Resolution

### Rabbi Yehoshua Authorship

The Gemara establishes that *Kinnim* was authored by Rabbi Yehoshua. The proof comes from the final Mishnah in *Kinnim*, on daf 68a, where after a complex ruling, Rabbi Yehoshua speaks in a distinctive narrator's voice: *zehu she'amru* — "this is what they meant when they said..." He is not merely being quoted as one opinion among others; he is wrapping up and interpreting the Mishnah's ruling as its author. This phrasing, the Gemara argues, marks Rabbi Yehoshua as the *stam* editor of the tractate. Since *Kinnim* is according to Rabbi Yehoshua, the question returns with full force: why, in the *mefureshet* split case, does the *olah* done below not count as a *chatat*?

### Me'ilah vs. Obligation

The Gemara provides its answer in the form of a precise limitation on Rabbi Yehoshua's principle. When did Rabbi Yehoshua say that an *olah* becomes a *chatat*? *L'apokei mi'yadei me'ilah* — to exempt it from *me'ilah*. His ruling was specifically and solely about the laws of *me'ilah*: by virtue of the redesignation, the bird is no longer subject to *me'ilah* liability. But *l'misak lei l'chova mi amar* — he never said that this redesignation fulfills a person's *chatat* obligation. The redesignation is real enough to remove *me'ilah*, but it does not constitute a genuine *chatat* that counts toward a person's outstanding sacrifice debt.

### Final Conclusion

The Gemara's resolution is therefore this: Rabbi Yehoshua's principle produces a partial and limited redesignation. The *olah* done below is, in a meaningful sense, no longer an *olah* — it has shed the *me'ilah* status that attaches to an *olah* and has taken on enough of a *chatat* identity to be exempt from it. In all likelihood, this also means the *kohanim* may eat the meat. But at the end of the day, the bird was sanctified as an *olah*, and its redesignation stops short of making it a fully valid *chatat* that satisfies a woman's post-childbirth obligation. The gap that the *chatat* jumped into was sufficient to resolve the question of *me'ilah*, but insufficient to transform the bird's fundamental status for purposes of obligation fulfillment.

---

## Neder Case

### Neder Setup

The Gemara now presents the final Mishnah of *Kinnim* under discussion, which involves a woman who took upon herself a *neder*, a vow, to bring two birds if she were to give birth to a male child. She subsequently does give birth to a male.

### Neder Constraint

The complication arises from the rule that a *neder* for bird sacrifices can only produce *olos*; a *chatat* cannot be brought as a *neder*. The two birds of her vow are therefore both *olos*. At the same time, her status as a woman who has given birth creates an independent obligation — one *chatat* and one *olah*. She thus owes two *olos* from the *neder* and one *chatat* plus one *olah* from the obligatory post-childbirth sacrifice: a total of three *olos* and one *chatat*.

### Kohen's Assumption

She brings two pairs of birds to the *kohen* — one pair for her *neder* and one pair for her obligatory post-childbirth sacrifice — but she does not specify clearly which set is which, or perhaps the *kohen* forgets. Seeing two pairs of birds presented by a woman who has given birth, the *kohen* reasonably assumes he is dealing with two post-childbirth pairs, each consisting of one *chatat* and one *olah*.

### Error Described

Operating under that assumption, the *kohen* does one above and one below from each pair. The correct procedure should have been: three birds above (the three *olos*) and one below (the *chatat*). Instead, he does two above and two below, incorrectly bringing one bird from the *neder* pair below as though it were a *chatat*.

### Obligation Shortfall

The consequence: from the *neder* pair, the bird brought below was an *olah* treated as a *chatat*. Since *neder* birds are always *olos*, this bird — one of her two vow-birds — was brought in the wrong place. She has therefore not fully satisfied her *neder*, and she must bring one additional bird above to complete it.

### Species Confusion

A further complication arises if the birds were not all of the same species — if one pair consisted of turtledoves and the other of pigeons. The *halacha* requires that a pair of birds within the same set be of the same species; a turtledove cannot be paired with a pigeon. The woman now needs to bring the mate to the *olah* she failed to fulfill, but she does not remember which set contained the turtledoves and which the pigeons. She therefore cannot know whether the remaining unfulfilled *olah* belongs to the turtledove pair or the pigeon pair, and consequently cannot identify which species she must bring.

### Mixed Species Solution

The resolution is that she must bring one bird of each species — one turtledove and one pigeon — to ensure that she covers the correct pairing for whichever set contained the unfulfilled *olah*. By bringing one of each, she guarantees that the required species is included. This is where the Mishnah leaves off for the day, with the more complex continuation of this case to be taken up in the following daf.

---

---

# Zevachim 68

## Kinnim & Olah/Chatas

### Kinnim Overview

Today's daf is 68, a relatively compact page whose complexity derives from its engagement with *kinnim* — the subject of an entire tractate at the end of Zevachim that consists exclusively of *mishnah* with no *gemara*, devoted entirely to the laws of mixed bird sacrifices. The classic case involves a *chatas* and an *olah* brought by a woman after childbirth, and the intricate questions that arise when those birds become mixed up and offered in the wrong manner. An additional layer of indeterminacy arises from the fact that the woman may hand the birds to the *kohen* without designating which is which, leaving the *kohen* to determine the assignment himself.

### Rabbi Yehoshua Position

The *gemara* brings this material into view because of a position stated by Rabbi Yehoshua: if a bird *olah* is performed below — in the manner of a *chatas* — it does not incur *me'ilah*. The *gemara* had initially assumed that this meant the *olah* actually transforms into a *chatas*. It then sought to bring evidence from *kinnim* that no such transformation occurs.

### Gemara Evidence

The evidence from *kinnim* establishes that an *olah* done in the manner of a *chatas* does not genuinely become a *chatas*. The *gemara* proceeds to demonstrate why that evidence is dispositive: because the author of the tractate *Kinnim* is none other than Rabbi Yehoshua himself.

### Authorial Voice

The *gemara*'s point is that if Rabbi Yehoshua authored *Kinnim*, and *Kinnim* demonstrates that performing an *olah* below does not convert it into a *chatas*, then Rabbi Yehoshua himself never intended to say that such a conversion occurs. His original statement was more limited: performing an *olah* in the manner of a *chatas* is sufficiently *chatas*-like that *me'ilah* no longer applies. Whether the *kohanim* would then be permitted to eat the meat is a separate question, but the fundamental claim was simply that *me'ilah* is removed — not that the bird's identity changes. The *kinnim* discussion will ultimately arrive at a closing statement whose authorial voice unmistakably sounds like Rabbi Yehoshua, and it is that closing statement which anchors the *gemara*'s identification. The purpose of citing this *mishnah* in full is not to analyze it in the manner of conventional *gemara* discussion, but to reach that punchline. What follows is an explanation of the *mishnah* itself, with the help of Rashi, so that the punchline can be appreciated in context.

---

## Kinnim Mishnah

### Woman's Vow

The *mishnah* opens: a woman declares, "I hereby take upon myself to bring two birds if I give birth to a male." She gives birth to a male and is now obligated to bring two pairs of birds — one pair for her *neder* (her personal vow, both birds of which are *olahs*) and one pair for her *chova* (her post-childbirth obligation, consisting of a *chatas* and an *olah*). She hands both pairs to the *kohen*.

### Same Type Birds

In the first case, all four birds are of the same species — either all *torim* (turtledoves) or all *bnei yonah* (young pigeons). What the *kohen* is required to do is perform three birds above (as *olahs*) and one below (as a *chatas*). An important rule, noted by Rashi, is that the first pair is always defined as the *chova* — the obligatory *chatas* and *olah* pair.

### Kohen's Error

The *kohen*, however, does not ask. He assumes that since a woman brought him two sets of birds, they must be for two separate childbirth obligations — one pair for each — and so he treats each pair symmetrically, offering one bird from each pair above and one from each pair below. He performs two above and two below rather than three and one. He does this without consulting the woman.

### Same Type Obligation

The first pair was handled correctly: one *chatas* and one *olah*, which is exactly what the *chova* required. But the second pair — which should have consisted of two *olahs* for the *neder* — was split, with only one offered above. What must now be done? She must bring one additional bird (*preidah achat*) and offer it above as an *olah*. This is straightforward when all the birds are of the same species: since we know the type, one more *tor* (or *ben yonah*, as the case may be) suffices to complete the missing *olah*.

### Two Types Birds

Now consider the case where the two pairs consisted of birds of two different species — one pair of *torim* and one pair of *bnei yonah* — and the *kohen* again split them two above and two below without consulting the woman. Rashi notes an additional complication: the *kohen* does not remember which pair he processed first. Since the first pair is always defined as the *chova*, and since the second pair that functions as the *neder* must be matched in species to the first pair of the *neder*, the uncertainty about ordering creates uncertainty about which species must be added.

### Two Types Obligation

If the *tor* was the first pair, then the *ben yonah* is the second (the *neder*), and one must add one *ben yonah* to complete the missing *olah* of the *neder*. If the *ben yonah* was first, then the *tor* is the *neder*, and one must add one *tor*. Since neither possibility can be ruled out, she must bring one *tor* and one *ben yonah* above — two birds total. That is the ruling for this case: *u-meshnei minim tavi shtayim* — when two species are involved, she brings two additional birds.

### Pirshah Nidrah

The third case is *pirshah nidrah* — the woman specified her vow. At the time she took the *neder*, she declared not only that she would bring two birds as an *olah*, but also that they would be a particular species — say, *bnei yonah*. However, by the time she comes to the *Beit HaMikdash*, she has forgotten which species she specified. Rashi's contribution here is essential; without it, the *mishnah* is nearly impossible to follow.

### Forgot Specification

Even before any *kohen* error enters the picture, her forgetting already creates an obligation. Her *chova* can be satisfied with any species — she was never required to specify that. But for the *neder*, she knows she promised a specific species and cannot recall which one. She must therefore bring enough birds to cover both possibilities. Even without the *kohen* mixing anything up, she arrives at the *Beit HaMikdash* with three pairs: one for the *chova* (whatever species she chooses) and two more for the *neder* (one of each species, since she does not know which she vowed). Had the *kohen* then acted correctly — performing the first pair as *chatas* and *olah*, and the next two pairs entirely above — everything would have been discharged. But the *kohen*, again acting without asking, assumed all the birds fell into the standard two-pair structure and split everything two above and two below.

### Pirshah Obligation

Now we must calculate what remains to be done. She was supposed to have three *olahs* for the *neder* (one of each species, and then a second of whichever species she specified — but she doesn't know which). She actually brought two pairs, and the *kohen* offered only one from each pair above. Compare what was needed with what was done: she is missing one additional *tor* and two additional *bnei yonah* (or vice versa, depending on which she specified) — a total of three additional *preidim* above. That is the ruling for *pirshah nidrah* when all birds are the same species: *tzricha she-tavi od gimmel peradim mimin echad*. When two species are involved, the uncertainty about ordering (which was first, which was second) compounds the uncertainty about her specification, and the total comes to four additional birds.

### Kava'ah Nidrah

The fourth and most complex case is *kava'ah nidrah* — the woman not only specified her vow in terms of species, but declared that she would bring her *neder* together with her *chova* as a single unified offering. The word *kava'ah* signals that she fixed them together as one integrated unit. Once again, Rashi is indispensable for understanding what this means in practice.

### Kava'ah Constraint

The key constraint introduced by *kava'ah* is that all the birds — the *neder* and the *chova* together — must be brought simultaneously as one combined *korban gadol*. They cannot be completed piecemeal. This creates a novel complication: if she brings some of the birds and not all of them at once, the *neder* portion is not satisfied, even if something was technically offered. However, the *chova* itself is not blocked — as soon as the *chatas* and *olah* of the *chova* are performed, she has fulfilled her post-childbirth obligation regardless. What the *kava'ah* means is that the *neder* cannot be discharged independently; it must come as part of one complete unit alongside the corresponding *olah* that corresponds to the *chova*.

This creates an unusual *halacha*: if she brought some birds and left others undone, the *neder* is entirely unresolved. To now satisfy the *neder*, she must bring all of the *neder*'s birds together — including an *olah* that corresponds in species to the *olah* of the *chova*, even though she has already technically fulfilled her *chova* obligation. That corresponding *olah* is not a second fulfillment of the *chova*; it is a requirement of the *neder* she bound to the *chova*. The effect is that one of the new *olahs* she brings will formally correspond to the *olah* of the obligatory pair, even though the obligation was already discharged when the original pair was offered.

### Kava'ah Obligation

She must now bring five additional *preidim* above. Why five? Because she was obligated to bring all of the *neder* birds simultaneously with the *chova*, and since she did not do so, none of the *neder* birds she brought previously receive credit. She must redo all of the *neder* — which consists of two possible *olahs* (for the two possible species she might have specified) plus additional coverage for not knowing which species she vowed — and she must include the *olah* corresponding to the *chova* pair. Since none of the previously offered *neder* birds count, she needs to bring all five from scratch.

When two species are involved, the uncertainty about which pair was first — and therefore which species must correspond to the *chova*'s *olah* — adds one more bird to the requirement, bringing the total to six.

### Woman Unclear

The final scenario in this *mishnah* is a state of complete compounded confusion. The woman handed the birds to the *kohen* without any clear indication of what she was giving him: she herself does not know whether she gave him all *torim*, all *bnei yonah*, or a mixture — *ve-eina yoda'as mah nasana*.

### Kohen Confused

The *kohen*, for his part, also has no idea what he did. He does not know whether he performed some above and some below, all above, or all below — *ve-eino yode'a mah asa*. Both parties are in a state of complete uncertainty.

### Both Unclear

What does she now owe? One might think she is obligated to cover every conceivable scenario from scratch, but there are limits. She must bring four *preidim* for the *neder* and two for the *chova*. The rationale for requiring two for the *chova* is that if the *kohen* brought everything above, then no *chatas* was performed for the *chova*, and we do not know what species the *olah* of the *chova* would need to correspond to, given that we do not know what the *chatas* was. She must therefore ensure coverage for both possibilities.

### One Chatas

The first opinion in the *mishnah* holds that she brings only one *chatas* in addition to the other birds. The reasoning is that the *chatas* determines the *olah* — not the reverse. If everything was brought above as *olahs*, she now brings a *chatas* of whichever species she chooses. That *chatas* then retroactively "selects" from among the *olahs* already brought which one corresponds to it as the matching pair. There is no need to bring two *chatatot* because the *chatas* is not determined by anything that was previously brought; she can choose freely, and whatever she chooses will align with one of the *olahs* above.

### Chatas vs Ola

The underlying question this debate turns on is directional: does the *chatas* determine which *olah* it pairs with, or does the first act performed determine what the second must be? If the *chatas* governs, it can be freely chosen and it will define the set. If the first act performed is always the *chova* and that first act defines the *matzav*, then the first *olah* brought above defines what species the *chatas* must be — and since we do not know what that first *olah* was, we do not know what species the *chatas* must be.

### Ben Azzai

Ben Azzai holds the latter view: *shtei chatatot* — two *chatatot* are required. For Ben Azzai, it is the first thing brought that determines the second. The first item offered is always defined as part of the *chova*, and therefore the first *olah* brought above defines the species of the *chatas*. Since we do not know what species was brought first, we cannot know what species the *chatas* must be, and we must bring one of each to be certain. For the *chachamim*, the *chatas* is open-ended and freely determined; for Ben Azzai, it is fixed by the first *olah* brought — and therefore, under conditions of total uncertainty, two *chatatot* are necessary.

---

## RY Connection

### Closing Statement

Having worked through the *mishnah*, the *gemara* returns to its original purpose. The closing statement of the *mishnah* — *amar Rabbi Yehoshua zehu she'amru* — is identified as the authorial voice of Rabbi Yehoshua. The phrase *zehu she'amru* carries the quality of a narrator stepping back and reflecting on what has just been discussed: not quoting a prior ruling so much as summarizing an insight. The *gemara* hears in that formulation the unmistakable voice of the *mishnah*'s author, and identifies that author as Rabbi Yehoshua.

---

## Ram Parable

### Ram Sound

What does Rabbi Yehoshua say in that closing statement? He offers a parable: when a ram is alive, it produces one sound — a single *beh*. When the ram dies and its parts are put to use, it produces seven sounds. The horns become musical instruments, the intestines become strings for a lyre, the hide becomes a drum. One living creature with one voice becomes seven different voices in its death.

### Expansion Theme

The application is clear from the *mishnah* just studied. Had the woman known exactly what she had vowed, remembered it clearly, and the *kohen* had acted correctly, she would have needed to bring four birds. She forgot her specification — the number grew to six. The *kohen* then compounded the confusion — the number grew to eight. Each additional error, each additional layer of forgetting or mishandling, does not simply add a fixed increment; it can trigger an expansion that multiplies the original obligation in ways that seem disproportionate to the initial mistake. This is the moral that Rabbi Yehoshua draws: things start one way and, through mishandling, expand beyond what anyone initially anticipated. As one student aptly noted, this is the spirit of *me'uvat lo yuchal litkon* — what has been made crooked cannot be straightened. You cannot simply start over; the errors already made shape what remains to be done, and sometimes the obligation to remedy the situation exceeds what would have been required had one acted correctly from the start.

---

## RY Connection (II)

### Clarification

Having now read the *mishnah* in full and identified its closing voice as Rabbi Yehoshua, the *gemara* delivers its conclusion. *Eima de-amar Rabbi Yehoshua la-apokei midei me'ilah* — when Rabbi Yehoshua said that an *olah* done below in the manner of a *chatas* is treated like a *chatas*, he meant only that it removes *me'ilah*. *Le-maskei lei le-chovah mi amar* — he never said it would actually fulfill the woman's *chova* obligation. The *kinnim* evidence confirms this: an *olah* performed in the manner of a *chatas* does not genuinely become a *chatas*, and Rabbi Yehoshua, as the author of *Kinnim*, could never have intended otherwise.

---

## Invalid Melikah

### Generic Opening

The *gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*. There is a question among the commentators whether its opening line belongs to the *mishnah* proper, though Rashi includes it. The line reads: *kol ha-psulim she-malku, melikatam psulah ve-einah metamei be-veit ha-beli'ah* — all the invalid ones who performed *melikah*, their *melikah* is invalid, and the bird does not convey *tum'ah* if swallowed.

### Baseline Halacha

To appreciate this, one must first understand the baseline *halacha*. Ordinarily, *melikah* performed on a non-consecrated bird — wringing the neck in the manner used for bird *korbanot* — renders the bird a *neveilah*. The marker of *neveilah* status that the *mishnah* employs is whether swallowing the bird conveys *tum'ah* to the one who swallows it. This formulation is used rather than simply saying the bird is forbidden to eat, because a bird *olah* is also forbidden to eat — for entirely different reasons — and we need a marker that specifically indicates *neveilah* status rather than mere *issur*. When *melikah* is performed properly in the context of a *korban*, however, it does not render the bird a *neveilah*, even though the same act on an ordinary bird would.

### Left Hand & Night

The *mishnah* then gives concrete examples of invalid *melikah* that nonetheless do not produce *neveilah* status. A *kohen* who performed *melikah* with his left hand — *malak b'smol* — has performed it invalidly, since *melikah* requires the right hand. A *kohen* who performed it at night — *o ba-lailah* — has also acted invalidly, since *korbanot* are offered during the day. Yet in both cases, the *melikah*, though *psulah*, does not render the bird a *neveilah*.

### Shechita Cases

Two additional cases involve *shechita* rather than *melikah*. If one performed *shechita* on an unconsecrated bird inside the *Beit HaMikdash* — *shachat chullin bifnim* — or on a consecrated bird outside the *Beit HaMikdash* — *ve-kodshim bachutz* — these are also not cases of *neveilah*. The *chiddush* here is that even though *shechita* is not the proper mode of slaughter for bird *korbanot* inside the *Beit HaMikdash*, and even though *shechita* of consecrated birds outside is a grave violation, since *shechita* was performed the bird retains the status of a properly slaughtered animal and is not a *neveilah*.

### Neveila Cases
