This is even simpler: *ze yikarev leshem mi shehu veze yikarev leshem mi shehu* — each is offered for whoever it belongs to. Since a *kohen* does not need to specify the owner at the time of offering, both can be brought without difficulty. In fact, the *chullin-kodshim* case resolves into this scenario once a buyer is found: the formerly *chullin* animal is sanctified, making both animals *kodshim* of the same type, and both can then be offered.

### Different Type Mix

*Kodshim bekodshim min beshe'eino mino* — a more complex problem arises when two *kodshim* of different types are mixed together, such as an *olah* and a *shelamim*. Here the problem is not about ownership but about procedure: an *olah* is fully burned on the altar, while a *shelamim* is eaten; the blood applications differ as well. If one cannot tell which animal is which, one cannot bring either correctly. The problem is compounded when the mixture involves, say, an *olah* and a *chatat*, where the ritual requirements diverge even more sharply.

### Two Piles Method

The solution begins, as before, with *yir'u ad she'yista'avu* — let them graze until each develops a *mum*, after which the *kedushah* can be moved to money. But here there are two distinct categories of *korban* to be replaced, requiring two piles of money. The procedure is as follows: one declares that whichever animal is the *olah* should have its *kedushah* transferred to this pile of money — and since the *olah* might be the more expensive animal, one must put an amount equal to the highest value of any animal in the group. Similarly, one declares that whichever animal is the *shelamim* should have its *kedushah* transferred to a second pile of money — again at the highest value. The first pile is used to purchase a replacement *olah*; the second to purchase a replacement *shelamim*. Both can then be offered properly.

The inevitable consequence is that the original owner must absorb a financial loss: *veyafsid hamutar mibeito* — the surplus must come out of his own pocket. Since one does not know which was more expensive, and since one must assign the maximum value to each animal for the purpose of the transfer, one ends up paying out more in total than the animals were actually worth. If one animal was worth one hundred dollars and the other ninety, one must place one hundred in each pile — a total of two hundred dollars — to buy replacements that together cost only one hundred and ninety. The extra ten dollars is lost; that is the price of the uncertainty.

## Olah-Bechor Mix

### Bechor Problem

The *mishna* now raises a more difficult scenario: *nitarvu bevochor uvima'aser* — an *olah* becomes mixed with a *bechor* (firstborn animal) or *ma'aser beheimah* (animal tithe). The problem is compounded here, because *bechor* and *ma'aser*, unlike ordinary *kodshim*, cannot be redeemed. They have an inherent *kedushah* that cannot be transferred to money. One cannot therefore apply the two-piles-of-money solution used above for *olah* and *shelamim*: one can redeem the *olah* side of the mixture, but there is no way to redeem the *bechor* or *ma'aser* side.

Nor can one simply bring them all: an *olah* is entirely burned, while a *bechor* and *ma'aser* are eaten; the blood of a *bechor* or *ma'aser* may be applied with one *matanah* at the base of the *mizbe'ach*, whereas an *olah* requires *matanah* on all sides. With no way to distinguish which animal is which, neither can be brought correctly.

### Eating as Bechor

The solution, once again, begins with *yir'u ad she'yista'avu* — let all the animals graze until they develop a *mum*. Once blemished, the *olah* can be redeemed: its *kedushah* transfers to money, which is used to purchase and bring a replacement *olah*. Now one is left with two blemished animals, one of which is *chullin* (the redeemed former *olah*) and one of which is *bechor* or *ma'aser* with a *mum*. A blemished *bechor* or *ma'aser* is permitted to be eaten without being brought to the *mizbe'ach*; and *chullin* may of course be eaten as well. So both animals can simply be eaten.

### Bechor Restrictions

But they must be eaten *kevochor ukhima'aser* — with the restrictions that apply to *bechor* and *ma'aser*. The *mishna* specifies: *yei'achel kevochor ukhima'aser*. What does this mean in practice? The *halacha* governing *bechor* with a blemish is that it may not be sold in a marketplace like ordinary meat, nor slaughtered and displayed in a butcher stall. In normal cases of *kodshim* that have been redeemed, the *kedushah* is entirely removed and the animal may be sold at full market price in any setting. But *bechor* and *ma'aser* are never fully redeemed — their *kedushah*, though diminished once a *mum* appears, is never entirely stripped away — and therefore the usual considerations of obtaining the best market price do not apply in the same way. They are to be treated with a degree of reverence even in their permissible state.

Since one of the two animals being eaten is in fact a *bechor* or *ma'aser*, and since one cannot know which is which, both must be treated as *bechor* and *ma'aser* and eaten under those restrictions.

## Exceptions & Summary

### Chatat-Asham Rule

The *mishna* concludes with a general principle: *hakol yecholim lehitaarev chutz min hachatat ve'asham* — all types of *korbanot* can in principle become mixed with one another and generate the types of problems described above, except for a *chatat* and an *asham*. The reason is simple: a *chatat* is always female, and an *asham* is always male. A mixture that requires one to ask "is this the *chatat* or the *asham*?" can never arise, since the two are externally distinguishable by sex. Accordingly, the *mishna* excludes this pairing from the entire framework of *ta'arovet* discussed in the *perek*.

## Gemara Clarification

### Mai Afilu

The *gemara* opens with a question on the language of the *mishna*: *mai afilu*? What is the force of the word "even" in the phrase *afilu achat beribo* — even one in ten thousand? The straightforward reading might suggest that ten thousand forbidden animals were mixed with one valid *korban*, which would obviously be problematic. The *gemara* corrects this: *hachi ka'amar* — this is what the *mishna* means. It is a flock of valid *korbanot* into which one *chatat hameitah* or one *shor haniskal* has fallen. *Afilu achat beribo* — even if the single forbidden animal is mixed into ten thousand otherwise valid *korbanot* — *yamutu kulam* — they all must die. The "even" modifies the number of valid animals, not the number of forbidden ones: even with odds of one in ten thousand, no *bitul* operates and the entire flock is condemned.

### Temurah Reference

The *gemara* then raises a broader observation: *tanina chada zimna* — have we not already been taught this principle elsewhere? The tractate Temurah contains a parallel *mishna*: *kol ha'asurin legabei mizbe'ach* — all animals that cannot be used for the *mizbe'ach* — for instance, a crossbreed, a Cesarean section, a *shor haniskal* attested by only one witness, and similar cases — *ve'asurin bechol shehu*, if they fall into a mixture with *chullin*, the entire mixture becomes forbidden for use on the *mizbe'ach*. The *gemara* quotes examples from that *mishna* including *harovea vehanirva* — animals involved in acts of bestiality — and others, making clear that the principle is essentially the same: one forbidden animal, mixed into a larger group, renders the entire group unusable for the *mizbe'ach*.

### Rav Ashi Query

Rav Ashi reports that he presented this apparent redundancy as a question: *amritih lishmateih kamei d'Rav Shimi* — I raised this discussion before Rav Shimi. And Rav Shimi responded that both cases are in fact necessary — *utzricha* — each one conveying something the other does not. The elaboration follows.

## Both Cases Needed

### Kodshim Strictness

Had the *gemara* only presented the case in Temurah — where animals disqualified from the *mizbe'ach* become mixed with *chullin* — one might have drawn a limited conclusion. *Hanei milei legavoah aval l'hedyot eima lo*: that case teaches that such a mixture may not be used for the *mizbe'ach*, since these disqualified animals have become mixed into ordinary *chullin* and the whole group is now forbidden for *hekdesh* use. One might reasonably say: the prohibition applies in the direction of *kodshim* use, since we want to guard against bringing a disqualified animal. But perhaps for a layperson, once the flock is redeemed, *bitul* might apply and the animals could be eaten or otherwise benefited from.

Our *mishna*, by contrast, concerns a *shor haniskal* — an animal that is *assur behana'ah* — mixed into a flock of *korbanot* that all must then die. The implication is clear: not only can the animals not be brought as *korbanot*, but even after the fact, they cannot be redeemed and benefited from by a layperson. The *shor haniskal*'s *issur hana'ah* infects the entire mixture such that there is no permissible avenue left — and this is something the Temurah case, which deals with animals that are merely *pasul* for the *mizbe'ach* but permissible in benefit, would not have taught us.

### C-Section Cases

One might then ask: is our *mishna* itself sufficient, and the Temurah case superfluous? The *gemara* argues no. Our *mishna* concerns *issurei hana'ah* — in the case of the *shor haniskal* and *chatat hameitah*, the forbidden animals are of the gravest halakhic weight. One could argue that specifically because of this severity — because the *issur* is so absolute — *bitul* fails to operate, and the result is that all must die. But perhaps if the disqualified animal mixed in were something lighter in *issur*, such as a *yotze dofen* — an animal that is merely *pasul* for the *mizbe'ach* but entirely permissible for layperson benefit — perhaps then *bitul* would apply and the mixture could be used for the *mizbe'ach* after all. *Aval hanei eima lo* — for those lesser cases, one might say, the mixture remains valid.

The Temurah case addresses precisely this: it involves animals like a *yotze dofen* — not *issurei hana'ah*, simply *pasul* for *korban* use — mixed into *chullin*, and even there, the entire mixture becomes forbidden for *mizbe'ach* use. The lesson is that even the lighter category of *pesul korban* without *issur hana'ah* is sufficient to contaminate a mixture and prevent its use on the *mizbe'ach*. *Tzrichi* — both cases are required.

### Takanata Solution

At this point the *gemara* raises a further challenge. The second half of our *mishna* — the part dealing with *yotze dofen* and similar cases mixed with *kodshim* — covers essentially the same ground as the Temurah *mishna* (disqualified-but-permissible animals mixed with other things, forbidding *mizbe'ach* use). So why state it twice? Why not rely entirely on the Temurah case for that lesson, and limit our *mishna* to the *issurei hana'ah* cases?

The *gemara* answers: *takanata itztricha lei* — our *mishna* is needed for its remedial content. The Temurah *mishna* simply declares that the mixture is forbidden; it does not tell you what to do about it. Our *mishna*, by contrast, provides a complete framework for how to address the problem: let the animals graze until a *mum* develops, redeem the *kedushah* onto money, use that money to purchase replacement *korbanot*, and so forth. This practical guidance — the *takana* — is what our *mishna* uniquely contributes in the case of *yotze dofen* mixed with *kodshim*. The Temurah *mishna*, dealing with a mixture of disqualified animals with *chullin*, naturally does not prescribe these remedies, since the situation there (disqualified animals mixed into non-sacred stock) does not require the same restorative procedure. Both *mishnayot* are therefore indispensable: Temurah for its principle (*afilu kol shehu*), our *mishna* for its practical remedy.

## Issurei Hana'ah

### Ve'eilo Asurin

The *gemara* now turns to a further question arising from the earlier discussion. It was said that our *mishna*'s case involving a *shor haniskal* — an *issur hana'ah* mixed into a flock of *korbanot* — implicitly teaches that *issurei hana'ah* are not *battel* even for a layperson, since there is no remedy available and all must die. But does our *mishna* need to be the source of this principle? Is it not already established elsewhere?

The *gemara* points to a *mishna* — *ve'eilu asurin ve'osrin bechol shehu* — "the following things are forbidden and render any mixture forbidden even in the smallest amount": *yein nesech* (wine of *avoda zara*) and an idol that was actually worshipped. These are paradigmatic *issurei hana'ah*, and the *mishna* there already establishes that *issurei hana'ah* are not subject to *bitul* even in infinitesimal proportions. The principle that *issurei hana'ah* cannot be nullified was thus already on the books.

### Preventing Bitul

The *gemara* therefore asks: if the principle that *issurei hana'ah* cannot be *battel* is already taught in the context of *avoda zara* and similar cases, why does our *mishna* need to teach it again through the *shor haniskal* case? Conversely, if our *mishna* teaches it, why does the case in the *avoda zara* context need to exist? The *gemara* answers: *tzrichi* — both are necessary, for the same structural reason that applied in the prior discussion. Each case operates in a distinct domain, and a ruling in one would not unambiguously extend to the other without being explicitly stated.

### Final Principle

The *gemara* works out the logic as follows. Had only the *avoda zara* case been stated — teaching that *issurei hana'ah* cannot be *battel* for a layperson — one might have reasoned that this applies specifically in the domain of ordinary use by laypeople, but not for *kodshim*. When it comes to *korbanot*, one might argue, the stakes are different: on one hand, we want to protect the sanctity of *kodshim* and surely should not allow a *shor haniskal* to potentially be offered — but on the other hand, perhaps we do not want to condemn an entire flock of valid *korbanot* to death when *bitul* might otherwise apply. So perhaps, in the domain of *kodshim*, *bitul* would operate even for *issurei hana'ah*. Our *mishna* therefore comes to teach: no, even there, *issurei hana'ah* are not *battel*, and all must die.

And had only our *mishna* been stated — teaching that *issurei hana'ah* are not *battel* in the context of *kodshim* — one might have attributed the ruling to the special stringency of *kodshim*: *kodshim dema'is*, sacred offerings that would be rendered repugnant by any possible admixture of something so deeply forbidden. But perhaps for a layperson, where no such concern about the integrity of sacred service applies, *bitul* might operate even for *issurei hana'ah*. *Aval chullin delo ma'is eima issurei hana'ah libatlu berov* — for ordinary use, where there is no comparable revulsion, perhaps the majority would suffice to nullify even an *issur hana'ah*. The *mishna* in the context of *avoda zara* is therefore also needed, to establish that *issurei hana'ah* are not *battel* in any context, whether for laypersons or for *kodshim*.

The combined teaching of both sources yields a comprehensive principle: *issurei hana'ah* cannot be nullified through *bitul* — not in the domain of *kodshim* (where the concern is the integrity of sacred offerings), and not in the domain of *chullin* (where the concern is the absolute prohibition on layperson benefit). Each case is logically necessary; neither alone would have been sufficient. With this, the *gemara* sets the stage for the next discussion, which will examine more directly the question of why *bitul* fails to operate for live animals — a question to which we will turn tomorrow.

# Zevachim 72

## Bitul & Forbidden Animals

### Daf Overview

The daf before us belongs to the eighth *perek* of Zevachim, a chapter that introduced the following principle: if one animal that is forbidden in *hana'ah* — such as a *shor haniskal*, an ox condemned to stoning, or a *chatat hameisos*, a sin-offering that must be left to die — becomes mixed with a group of sacrificial animals, none of those animals may be brought as offerings, and none may be used for any benefit. The forbidden animal is not *batel*, and therefore every animal in the mixture must be assumed to be the forbidden one; they are all left to die. Similarly, if an animal was disqualified as a sacrifice but not forbidden in *hana'ah* — for instance, a *treifah* or an animal born by Caesarean section — the animals need not be left to die, but none may be brought as an offering. The Mishnah describes how one waits for the animals to develop a blemish and then redeems their value.

The animating question of our daf, however, is more fundamental: the Mishnah states that the forbidden animal is not *batel* even if it falls into a mixture of ten thousand. Whatever happened to the laws of *bitul*?

### Why No Bitul

The Gemara poses the question directly: *venivtelu berova* — let the forbidden animal simply be nullified by the majority. The opening move of the sugya is to clarify what the phrase *berova* means in this context. Some *rishonim* note that when the Gemara asks "let it be *batel berov*," it does not necessarily mean precisely a majority; rather, it means let it be nullified by whatever standard number one might choose. The Gemara's immediate response is *vechi teima chashiv velo batil* — perhaps one would say that an animal, being a substantial and significant object, simply cannot be nullified. But this answer immediately runs into a difficulty, and the Gemara draws on a debate in the Mishnah about how to conceptualize which objects are significant enough to resist nullification.

### Kol vs. Et Shedarko

The Gemara introduces the distinction between two formulations: *kol shedarko limanot* and *et shedarko limanot*. The concept of significance that prevents *bitul* is framed in terms of whether an item is "normally counted." But the precise language matters enormously. *Kol shedarko limanot* — literally, "anything whose way it is to be counted" — encompasses things that are naturally sold or traded by the unit, even if they are sometimes sold by weight or volume as well. *Et shedarko limanot* — "that which [only] its way is to be counted" — is a narrower formulation, encompassing only those items that are exclusively sold by count and never by any other measure. The Gemara observes that the answer of *chashiv* — significance — works well according to one of these readings, but runs into difficulty according to the other, and the nature of that difficulty drives the entire subsequent discussion.

## Identity & Discreteness

### Watermelons vs. Cars

The difference between *kol shedarko limanot* and *et shedarko limanot* is best understood through practical examples. Watermelons or bananas are sometimes sold individually — four for a dollar on the street — and sometimes sold by the pound in a store. They are things that it is natural to count, and you would speak of having a hundred watermelons rather than a thousand pounds of watermelons, but they are not exclusively sold by count. That is *kol shedarko limanot*: things for which counting by unit is the natural mode, though not the only mode. Cars, on the other hand, are never sold by weight or volume. No one buys three tons of cars. Each car is always treated as a discrete unit. That is *et shedarko limanot*: things that are only and exclusively counted.

It should be noted that this distinction is not simply a function of cost. Rashi observes that eggs, for example, would not have qualified in earlier times as *et shedarko limanot* because one could buy a basket of eggs without specifying an exact count, or a farmer might add an extra egg as a bonus — so eggs were not sold with the strict individuation characteristic of *et shedarko limanot*.

### Logic of Bitul

Understanding the mechanism of *bitul* is essential for appreciating why this distinction matters. The consensus among most *rishonim* is that *bitul* of *yavesh beyavesh* — dry matter mixed with dry matter — works on principles analogous to *lach belach*, wet mixture. When a drop of blood falls into a pot of chicken soup, we say it loses its identity: there is no longer any distinct, concrete presence of blood — it fully disperses, and trace amounts are as if they do not exist. That is the logic of *bitul*.

Now consider a discrete object. If one has a problematic item mixed into a large collection of similar items — say, one tomato affected by *kilayim* among a hundred tomatoes — the argument is that because we cannot identify which tomato is problematic, the problematic one is, as it were, overwhelmed by the mass of the others and ceases to have an independent existence. We look at the collection as an undifferentiated whole, and within that whole the single problematic item is submerged and stops existing. This is the conceptual logic of *bitul*: a thing loses its identity in the mass.

But this logic depends on our actually looking at the collection as an undifferentiated whole, with no item possessing a distinct, individual identity. Once an item has genuine individual significance — once we always look at it as a discrete, independently weighty unit — the logic of *bitul* collapses. We cannot say this item has been submerged and lost its identity if we always regard it as a separate and independent entity. The question is therefore: what tells us that we regard each individual item as independently significant? The answer the Gemara proposes is the commercial mode of transaction. If items are sold by count — if you would say "I have a hundred such items" rather than "I have a hundred pounds of such material" — it means that in practice, each unit is always regarded separately and independently. And if each unit retains its distinct identity, it cannot be lost in the mass.

### People & Identity

There is a striking broader principle here that runs beneath the surface of this discussion. One never counts money and then counts people in the same way. Money can be summed: five dollars plus five dollars is ten dollars, and the individual coins or bills lose their separate identity in the aggregate. But a person cannot be summed in this way. Michael is always Michael; David is always David. One cannot amass them into a collective quantity where each individual ceases to have a distinct existence. No individual is interchangeable with another, and therefore the logic that works for amorphous collections — that the problematic element is swallowed by the larger mass — cannot work for persons.

This is precisely the principle underlying *et shedarko limanot* and *kol shedarko limanot*: when items always retain their distinct identity, when we cannot look at them as an undifferentiated mass without singling out each one individually, *bitul* does not apply. The threshold for that determination is whether these items are sold by count.

## Mishnah: Kilayim

### Fenugreek Bundles

The Gemara grounds this entire debate in a Mishnah from the laws of *kilayim*. The case: someone had bundles of fenugreek that were *kilayim* — grown in a vineyard in violation of the prohibition of *kil'ei hakerem* — and they must therefore be burned. If such a bundle becomes mixed with other, permitted bundles, the Mishnah discusses what happens. (There is also a textual variant involving the formula *b'acher b'acherim* — where one bundle gets mixed into a hundred, and then one of that hundred gets mixed into another hundred — raising the question of whether *sfek sfeika*, double doubt, applies here or whether that principle is limited to *avoda zara*. That is itself one of the major discussions among the *Tosafot* on this daf.)

### Rabbi Meir's Position

Rabbi Meir rules that even one forbidden bundle mixed into ten thousand forbids them all: *mekadesh* — it sanctifies everything, rendering it all forbidden. His reasoning: *kol shedarko limanot* (or, in the marginal variant, *et shedarko limanot*). Since fenugreek bundles are naturally sold by count, each bundle retains its individual significance and therefore cannot become *batel*, no matter how large the surrounding majority. Rabbi Meir thus holds that there is a general principle: any item that falls into the category of "normally counted" cannot be nullified.

### Sages & Rabbi Akiva

The Sages reject Rabbi Meir's broad principle entirely. They rule that fenugreek bundles are *batel* in 200 — the standard ratio for *kilayim*, which is double the 100 required for *terumah* (the elevated ratio reflecting the greater severity of *kilayim*, which is forbidden in *hana'ah*). According to the Sages, the principle of "normally counted" does not create a categorical exemption from *bitul*. Only six specific items are so significant that they resist *bitul* in any quantity. Rabbi Akiva adds a seventh: freshly baked home-baked loaves. The six (or seven) items enumerated are: the nuts of *Perach*; pomegranates of *Bedan* (*Rimonei Bedan*); sealed barrels of wine; bunches of beets; heads of cabbage; a Greek gourd; and, according to Rabbi Akiva, home-baked loaves. Some of these, being fruit, would fall under *orla*; others fall under *kilayim*.

The Sages and Rabbi Akiva thus have a fundamentally different structure: not a general principle governing any normally-counted item, but a closed (or nearly closed) list of items whose exceptional significance is recognized individually.

### Tosafot's Question

This is where Tosafot raises a pointed and arresting question. Tosafot observes that the entire debate between Rabbi Meir, the Sages, and Rabbi Akiva seems irrelevant to explaining why a head of cattle cannot be *batel*. Even if one accepts the narrower position of the Sages — that *bitul* fails only for the six or seven specified items — a head of cattle is surely at least as significant as a pomegranate from *Bedan*. Why should cattle's status depend on whether the operative principle is *kol shedarko limanot* or *et shedarko limanot*? If you have a box full of *Bedan* pomegranates alongside a herd of cattle, one would intuitively look at each individual cow as more independently weighty than each individual pomegranate. Tosafot does not arrive at a fully satisfying resolution, but the question itself is the natural and obvious one to ask.

## Yochanan vs. Lakish

### Rabbi Yochanan

The Gemara reports an *amoraic* dispute about the correct reading of Rabbi Meir's language in the Mishnah. Rabbi Yochanan says: the correct version in the Mishnah is *et darko limnot* — things that are *only* counted, the more restrictive formulation. That is what Rabbi Meir means when he says an item is not *batel*: it must be something exclusively sold by count.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish disagrees: the correct version is *kol darko limnot* — things that are *generally* counted, the more expansive formulation. Even something that is *sometimes* sold by count, though not exclusively so, falls within Rabbi Meir's principle and resists *bitul*.

### Problem for Yochanan

The Gemara immediately identifies the difficulty: this works out well according to Reish Lakish. Cattle are sometimes sold by the head — "how many head of cattle do you have?" — and that is enough to place them within the *kol shedarko limanot* category, explaining why they are not *batel*. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, who reads Rabbi Meir as requiring *et shedarko limanot* — exclusively counted — cattle would not qualify, since cattle are sometimes sold as part of a herd without individual counting. What can Rabbi Yochanan say?

As Tosafot notes, this is itself strange: intuitively, even according to Rabbi Yochanan, a head of cattle seems weighty enough to resist *bitul* on its own terms. But the Gemara apparently does not pursue that line of reasoning, and instead turns to a different answer.

Tosafot raises yet another question at this juncture: there is an independent principle that a *beriah* — a whole, discrete unit — is not *batel*. Should a cow not qualify as a *beriah*? Tosafot develops a precise definition of *beriah*: what makes something a *beriah* is not merely that it is large or intact, but that *it* is the specific thing the Torah has identified as forbidden. When the Torah says not to eat the *gid hanasheh*, the sciatic nerve is the *beriah* — it is the exact object the Torah named as the prohibition, and therefore even less than a *kezayit* incurs lashes and it is not *batel*. Similarly, any flying insect is a *beriah* because the Torah identified that specific creature as the forbidden thing.

A *shor haniskal*, however, is different. The Torah does not say "do not eat the ox"; it says "do not eat from the *meat* of" the condemned ox. The cow is not the unit the Torah has identified as forbidden — it is the meat that is forbidden, and the meat is simply an aggregate of material. Because the Torah never designated the cow itself as the forbidden unit, the cow does not achieve the status of *beriah*, regardless of its size, vitality, or individual importance. Therefore the *beriah* principle cannot rescue the ruling that the cow is not *batel*.

## Rav Papa & Pressed Figs

### Pressed Figs Case

Rav Papa offers a resolution. He says: the *tana* of our Mishnah — the one who rules that a cow is not *batel* even in ten thousand — is the *tana* of the case of *litra ketziot*, pressed figs. That *tana* holds: *kol davar she'yesh bo minyan afilu be-rabbanan lo batil* — anything that is sometimes sold by count is not *batel*, even when the prohibition involved is only rabbinic. This is the position of *kol shedarko limanot* — not restricted to items that are *exclusively* counted, but encompassing anything for which counting by unit is a natural mode of transaction. And since cattle are sometimes sold by the head, they fall within this principle.

Rav Papa's move is this: whatever precisely Rabbi Meir meant, there exists a *tana* who takes the broader position that *any* item which is *sometimes* counted resists *bitul* — and that *tana* applies the rule even to rabbinic prohibitions. *Kal vachomer*, all the more so does it apply to something biblically forbidden. Our Mishnah reflects the opinion of this *tana*, and on that basis the ruling that the cow is not *batel* is coherent.

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

The Gemara now identifies who this *tana* is by citing a *beraita* about pressed figs. The case: someone had a *litra* (a measure by weight or volume) of pressed figs, and stomped them into one of a series of barrel-tops — the method by which rounds of pressed figs, much like rounds of cheese, were produced. One would pack figs into a barrel, press them down so they formed a consolidated round on top, and repeat the process with successive barrels, eventually producing cylinders of pressed rounds. The *terumah* figs were stomped into one of these barrel-tops, and the person does not know which barrel. There are a hundred barrels in total.

Everyone agrees that *terumah* is nullified in a ratio of 100 to 1. The question is: what counts as the denominator? Do we look at all of the pressed figs across all the barrels — in which case even a handful of large barrels with many figs might suffice — or do we count the barrel-tops themselves?

Rabbi Meir reports the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Eliezer takes the lenient position: one looks at the top layer as if it were detached and free-floating throughout the combined mass. Since the doubt is which barrel-top contains the *terumah*, and if we treat the *terumah* round as separated and mixed throughout all the figs, we need only 100 times the quantity of the *terumah* figs — which might be achieved within relatively few barrels. The key distinction is whether the forbidden item has a *fixed location* in the barrel-top or is free-floating: if free-floating, the entire combined mass of all the figs becomes the denominator.

Rabbi Yehoshua, in Rabbi Meir's version, is more stringent: one focuses exclusively on the barrel-tops. Only if there are 100 other barrel-tops is the *terumah* top *batel*. If there are not 100 tops, the top of every barrel is treated as forbidden (or as a mixture that only a *kohen* may eat), while the contents below the top layer are permitted — since the doubt pertains only to the tops.

### Shedarko Limanot

Rabbi Yehuda presents a different version of the same debate. In Rabbi Yehuda's account, Rabbi Eliezer rules that one needs 100 barrel-tops — a moderately stringent position. Rabbi Yehoshua goes further still: even 300 barrel-tops are not sufficient to render the *terumah* round *batel*. The reason: this is a *davar shedarko limanot* — the rounds of pressed figs are sometimes sold and counted individually, and therefore each round retains its individual significance and cannot be nullified regardless of how many other rounds surround it. This is the *tana* Rav Papa had in mind: Rabbi Yehoshua (in Rabbi Yehuda's version) applies *kol shedarko limanot* — something sometimes counted — even to a rabbinic prohibition (*terumah* of fruit being rabbinic, or *terumah* in the present day being rabbinic), and rules that it is not *batel* in any quantity.

### No Fixed Location

The *beraita* concludes with an important limiting case. If one stomped the *terumah* figs into a barrel but does not know *where* within the barrel they were placed — whether to the north or south side, whether they are mixed throughout — then *divrei hakol ya'alu*: everyone agrees that the *terumah* is *batel*. The reasoning is clear: when the forbidden material has no fixed, distinct location and is simply dispersed throughout the barrel, it cannot be treated as a discrete, countable unit. The principle of *shedarko limanot* applies when the forbidden item occupies a specific, identifiable place — the top of a particular barrel — so that it retains the character of a discrete unit that one would count. When it is simply smeared throughout the whole barrel with no distinct location, it has lost that character entirely, and *bitul* applies normally.

## Living Things

### Rava's Solution

Rav Papa's answer, while resolving the Mishnah's ruling on its own terms, implicitly leaves it as the position of only some *tannaim* — those who hold *kol shedarko limanot*. The Sages and Rabbi Akiva, who reject that general principle and restrict non-*bitul* to their enumerated list, might still hold that a cow *is* subject to *bitul*. This would be troubling: give me a break, it is a cow.

Rava therefore provides the ultimate, definitive answer — and the one that is *halacha*. Rava says: *afilu teima rabbanan* — even according to the Sages, who reject the principle of *kol shedarko limanot* and limit non-*bitul* to their six (or seven) specific items, a cow is not *batel*. Why? Because *ba'alei chayyim chashuvin velo batlin* — living creatures are intrinsically significant and do not lose their identity through *bitul*.

The principle here returns to the fundamental logic discussed earlier. Objects — even important objects — can in principle be submerged into an undifferentiated mass, even if the threshold for that is high. But a living being is categorically different. A living creature always retains its distinct, independent identity. It cannot be summed or amassed into an aggregate the way objects can. Just as one counts money but cannot truly "count" people in the same reductive sense — because each person remains irreducibly and individually themselves — so too a living animal always stands before us as an independently significant entity that cannot be absorbed into the surrounding mass and nullified. This is not a matter of commercial practice or halachic categorization; it is an expression of the intrinsic nature of living things. And on this, Rava says, all opinions agree.

---

---

# Zevachim 73

## Davar Chashuv & Figs

### Intro & Rabbi Meir

The Gemara on daf 73 opens with a *beraita* invoked to identify a *tanna* who holds that even items belonging to the category of *kol she-darko limnot* — things that are normally or occasionally counted — are not *batel*. To situate this properly, recall the range of opinions concerning *davar chashuv*: Rabbi Meir's position addresses things that are exclusively or generally counted and holds they are not *batel*; the *Chachamim* and Rabbi Akiva restrict the category to a small enumerated list of six or seven items. Now the Gemara introduces a still more expansive definition — *kol davar she-yesh bo minyan*, any item that can be or is occasionally counted — which represents the broadest possible category of things that resist nullification.

### Pressed Figs Case

The *beraita* presents the following scenario: a *litra* of pressed figs of *terumah* — *litra ketsiot she-darsa al pi iggul* — were pressed into a round in a device used for making fig-rounds, but the owner no longer knows in which round he pressed them. The figs of *terumah* were pressed into one such round among many, but the question is which container it ended up in. The case is examined across three types of vessels: *al pi iggul*, pressed into one of these rounded devices; *al pi chavit*, placed into one of many barrels where each barrel contains multiple rounds stacked one upon another, and the *terumah* round is at the top — *al pi kaveret*, placed into a similar container of yet another type. In each case, *ve-eini yode'a be-eizeh darsah* — the owner does not know which container holds the *terumah*.

### R. Eliezer vs. R. Yehosh…

According to Rabbi Meir's version of the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, the positions are as follows. Rabbi Eliezer takes the lenient position: *ro'in et ha-elyonot ke-illu hen perudot ve-ha-tachtonot ma'alot et ha-elyonot* — we regard the top layer as though it were dispersed throughout the entire barrel, mixed together with all the rounds below it, and the lower contents effectively raise and mix with the upper. Even though we know that the *terumah* is at the top, Rabbi Eliezer allows us to treat the entire contents of all the containers as one aggregate. Since *terumah* is *batel* in a ratio of one in a hundred, and if the total rounds across all containers add up to a hundred, it is *batel*. This is a strikingly lenient position — and it is justified, in Rabbi Eliezer's view, by the fact that *terumah* nowadays is only *de-rabbanan*.

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees and adopts the more straightforward analysis: only the top layers are relevant, since we know the *terumah* is specifically among the top rounds. Therefore, *im yesh sham me'ah pumot ya'alu* — if there are a hundred top layers, a hundred barrels, then among those hundred top rounds the *terumah* is *batel*. But if not — *ve-im lav ha-pumot asurim ve-ha-shulayim muttarin* — then the top round of each barrel is forbidden while everything below is certainly permitted, since there is no question that the *terumah* is confined to the top layer.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Version

Rabbi Yehuda presents a different version of the same debate, with both positions shifted to a stricter register. In Rabbi Yehuda's version, Rabbi Eliezer already adopts what had been Rabbi Yehoshua's position in Rabbi Meir's version: Rabbi Eliezer says *im yesh sham kof pumot ya'alu* — one must find a hundred top layers for the *terumah* to be *batel*; if not, the tops are forbidden. This means that even the more lenient position in Rabbi Yehuda's version begins one level higher than Rabbi Meir's version. Accordingly, Rabbi Yehoshua's position in Rabbi Yehuda's version is stricter still: *afilu yesh sham shelosh me'ot pumot lo ya'alu* — even if there were three hundred top layers, the *terumah* is not *batel*.

### Not Batel Conclusion

Why would three hundred not suffice, when *terumah* is ordinarily *batel* at one in a hundred? The answer is precisely the principle under discussion: this *litra* of pressed figs belongs to the category of items that are *sometimes* counted. A round of pressed figs could be sold by weight, as part of a full barrel, or in various other ways — but it can also be sold as a round unto itself, and that occasional counting confers upon it the status of *davar chashuv*. Because it is occasionally counted, it is not *batel*, even by *terumah*, which is rabbinic. The *beraita* concludes with an additional case: *daras be-igul ve-eini yode'a be-eizeh makom be-igul darsah* — if the *terumah* was pressed somewhere within a single device but the owner cannot remember where — whether in the northern section or the southern, *o litzfonah o lidromah* — then *divrei hakol ya'alu*, everyone agrees that all the figs are combined together and the *terumah* is *batel*. In that case there is no identifiable layer and the mixture is genuinely uniform.

What emerges is a spectrum of positions on *davar chashuv*: from the six or seven items of Rabbi Akiva and the *Chachamim*, to things sold exclusively by count, to things sold usually by count, to things sold only occasionally by count. The Gemara's implication is that cows — which are certainly sometimes if not exclusively sold by number — would fall within at least the most expansive of these views, and therefore are not *batel* in the case of the *mishnah*. The argument from *davar chashuv* thus provides one basis for why the mixed herd cannot be nullified.

---

## Ba'alei Chayim Never Bat…

### Rav Ashi's Answer

Rav Ashi offers a more satisfying and broader answer. *Afillu teima Rabbanan* — even according to the *Rabbanan* or Rabbi Akiva, who do not accept the category of *darko limnot*, they would nonetheless maintain that there is no *bittul* in the *mishnah*'s case. The reason is independent of counting and significance in the marketplace: *ba'alei chayim chashivei ve-lo batli* — live animals are inherently significant and are never nullified. A living creature always retains its individual identity and can never be subsumed into an aggregate. This is why *bittul* simply does not apply to the herd in the *mishnah*, regardless of one's position on *davar chashuv*.

---

## Rov vs. Bittul

### Individual Cows & Rov

Having established that *bittul* does not operate here, the Gemara shifts to a fundamentally different mode of analysis. It is worth pausing to appreciate the conceptual move being made. There are two distinct ways in which a mixture of dry items — *yavesh be-yavesh* — can be resolved: one is collective nullification, where the minority loses its identity and is absorbed by the majority; the other is individual statistical determination, where we take each item separately and ask what the statistics say about its identity. The Gemara now abandons the first approach entirely, given that *ba'alei chayim* resist nullification, and instead proposes the second.

The Gemara asks: *ve-nimshach ve-nikrav echad minaihu* — why not simply take one cow out of the mixture and offer it? Not because the forbidden cow has been nullified, but because we can invoke *kol de-parish me-rubba parish* — anything that has separated, separated from the majority. Of a hundred cows, ninety-nine are permitted. If one wanders out, statistics dictate a 99-in-100 probability that it is a permitted animal. This is *azlinan batar rov* — following the majority — not as a tool of nullification but as a mechanism for determining the status of an individual item based on probability. Why not proceed this way, taking each cow one by one and offering it up on the *mizbe'ach*?

### Kol Kavua Principle

The Gemara rejects this proposal on the basis of the principle *kol kavua ke-mechtzah al mechtzah dami* — anything that is fixed is treated as though it were fifty-fifty. The cows in the mixture are *kavua*, fixed in place; they have not separated on their own. When we go to take one from the mixture, we are not looking at a separated item and asking where it came from; we are standing before the entire mixture, aware that the forbidden animal is somewhere among them, and selecting from that known aggregate. In that situation we cannot statistically discount the forbidden animal, because it is right there before us.

### Stores Example

The classic illustration clarifies the distinction. Suppose there are nine kosher butcher shops and one *treifah* shop on a street, and a piece of meat is found lying in the street with no indication of its origin. The *halacha* is that we apply *kol de-parish me-rubba parish*: the meat has separated from the group, and nine out of ten of those shops are kosher, so we assume it came from a kosher shop and it is permitted. But if a person went to one of the shops, purchased meat, and then could not remember which shop he had entered, the question has changed. He is no longer looking at a piece of meat and asking about its origin abstractly; he is looking at all the shops together, including the *treifah* shop, and asking which one was it. Each shop is *kavua*, fixed in its location, and the forbidden store is visibly part of the set. The principle of *kol kavua ke-mechtzah al mechtzah dami* applies, and the meat must be treated as though it is fifty-fifty.

This is the problem with taking a cow from the mixture. One is confronting the full group, which includes the forbidden animal, and selecting from it directly. The forbidden cow's presence cannot be statistically discounted in that moment. We are not looking at an individual cow and asking about its identity in isolation — we are looking at the herd and reaching in. That is *kavua*, and *kavua* is treated as fifty-fifty.

---

## Scattering & Priests

### Scatter Proposal

The Gemara then proposes a creative solution that would dissolve the *kavua* problem: *nichbishinhu de-naidi* — scatter them. If one throws a stone among the herd or startles them so that they disperse, each cow then wanders off on its own. At that point, no individual cow is any longer part of a fixed group; it has separated from the mixture. One could then approach each cow individually and say: here is a single animal, ninety-nine out of a hundred of these animals are permitted — *kol de-parish me-rubba parish* — and this one is permitted. This is not *kavua*; it is a separated item assessed on its own terms. So scatter the herd and then take each cow one at a time.

### Rava's Simultaneity Conc…

Rava responds with a concern. *Gezeirah shema yavo'u asarah kohanim be-vat achas ve-yakrivu* — there is a rabbinic decree based on the fear that ten *kohanim* might come simultaneously, each take a cow, and then bring them all to the *Beis Hamikdash* at the same time. If, say, the problematic animal is one of ten, and all ten *kohanim* arrive at the *mizbe'ach* together with their animals — or with their blood collected in basins — then collectively we know with certainty that one of the ten is invalid. At that point we can no longer look at each *kohen*'s offering in isolation; we are confronted with the aggregate again, and the statistics become unfavorable. Rashi's scenario involves a case of fifteen cows where the majority likelihood actually favors the problematic blood being present among what is brought.

### Basin Objection

One of the *rabanan* objects to this reasoning: *ela me-atah megisat asira* — does the collection basin then render it forbidden? The point of the objection is that once each *kohen* took his cow individually and its status was ruled upon at the moment of selection — *de-chezkinhu*, we assessed it as *kasher* — that ruling does not get revisited simply because the blood of multiple animals later appears together. The status of each animal was determined individually at the time of taking. Once individually assessed as *kasher*, the later aggregation of the blood should not reopen the question.

### Gemara's Reformulation

The Gemara therefore reformulates Rava's concern. The problem is not the simultaneous presentation of blood at the altar — it is the simultaneous *taking* of the animals. *Mishum shema yavo'u asarah kan be-vat achas ve-yikchu* — the concern is that ten *kohanim* will come simultaneously and each grab a cow from the scattered herd at the exact same moment. If they all take at the same time, then even though each one has before him an individual scattered cow, we are in effect looking at all ten together — and knowing that one of those ten is forbidden, we cannot tell each *kohen* that his animal is likely permitted. The analogy is to the case in *halacha* where two people walk two different roads, one of which has *tumah*, and ask separately about their status: each is ruled *tahor* individually. But if they come together simultaneously and ask, one of you must be *tamei*, and both are rendered *tamei*. The simultaneous confrontation prevents individual assessment.

### Likelihood Question

The Gemara then questions how realistic this concern is. *Asarah kohanim be-vat achas mi efshar* — is it truly plausible that ten *kohanim* would scatter the herd and each seize a different cow at the exact same instant? Even defining the moment of "taking" — is it when the hand touches the animal? When the question is posed to the decisor? — is itself unclear. This seems too unlikely a scenario to drive legal policy. And yet, this line of reasoning will lead to the Gemara's more definitive answer.

---

## Rava's Fear Answer

### Rava's Gezerah

Rava ultimately reformulates his answer more precisely: *mishum kavua*. The real concern is not that ten *kohanim* will literally act simultaneously — that is admittedly implausible. Rather, the rabbinic decree is that we do not permit one to scatter the herd and take individually, because if we were to allow that, people would reason: why bother scattering them? And they would then proceed to take directly from the undispersed mixture, where *kavua* genuinely applies and the taking is clearly forbidden. The *gezeirah* is therefore a fence: to prevent taking from the fixed mixture, the rabbis prohibit even the seemingly permissible act of scattering and then taking individually.

### Not Accepted

Rava then adds a further ruling: *hashta de-amri rabanan lo nakriv — ei nakriv lo martzi* — now that the *rabanan* have said one may not offer these animals, if one goes ahead and ignores the rabbinic ruling and offers one anyway, the *korban* will not be accepted. It is worth noting, as *Tosafos* points out, that the principle of *davar chashuv* not being *batel* is itself likely only *de-rabbanan*. So even if *de-orayta* the offering would be valid — since one could in principle follow the *rov* — once the rabbis have said it is forbidden, the violation of their ruling renders the *korban* invalid and not accepted. This sets up the debate about *nadchin* that the Gemara is about to address.

---

## Mixed Birds Challenge

### Mixed Birds Mishna

At this point, Rav Huna bar Yehuda challenges Rava from the *mishnah* in the tractate of *Kinnim*. The *mishnah* states: *chatas she-nit'arva be-olah ve-olah she-nit'arva be-chatas afilu achas be-ribbu yamus kulam* — if a *chatas* bird became mixed with an *olah* bird, or vice versa, even one forbidden bird among ten thousand causes them all to die. They are *ba'alei chayim* and are not *batel*; one cannot offer them all as *olot* lest one *chatas* be offered above, nor all as *chatat* lest one *olah* be offered below. The *halacha* is that they all must be left to die.

### Priest Consults

However, this ruling applies only in a specific circumstance: *be-kohein nimlach* — when the *kohen* consults the authority and asks what he should do. In that case, the ruling is clear: you may not offer any of them, and they must all die.

### Priest Acts Alone

But if the *kohen* does not consult — *be-kohein she-eino nimlach* — and simply proceeds on his own initiative, the *halacha* differentiates by what he does. If he performs *melika* on all of them above, which is the location for the *olah*: *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul* — one of them was legitimately offered as an *olah*, one was not, but he has at least validly offered whichever one was the *olah*. Similarly, if he does all of them below, the *chatas* is validly offered. If, however, he tries to resolve the mixture himself by doing one above and one below — *achas le-mata ve-achas le-ma'ala* — the ruling is *sheneihem pesulim*, both are invalid, because we say *she-ani omer chatas kerva le-ma'ala ve-olah kerva le-mata* — perhaps the *chatas* was done above and the *olah* below, and each was offered in the wrong location.

The challenge to Rava is clear: here is a case where the rabbis say you may not offer the mixed birds, but if the *kohen* ignores that ruling and goes ahead anyway, some of the offerings are valid. The rabbinic prohibition does not, after the fact, invalidate what was objectively a valid offering. This is a direct contradiction to Rava's ruling that *ei nakriv lo martzi* — if you violate the rabbinic decree and offer, it is not accepted.

---

## Nadchin Debate

### Two Nadchin Views

The Gemara resolves this contradiction by situating the two rulings within an existing *tannaic* dispute: *ha ke-man de-amar ba'alei chayim nidchin, ve-ha ke-man de-amar ba'alei chayim einam nidchin* — the case of the cows follows the opinion that *ba'alei chayim* are *nidchin*, while the case of the birds follows the opinion that *ba'alei chayim* are not *nidchin*.

### Nadcha V'Nir'ah

The concept of *nidchin* requires explanation. When an animal that has been consecrated as a *korban* enters a state in which it temporarily cannot be offered — it is described as *nidcha*, pushed away. When it subsequently becomes eligible again, the state is called *nidcha ve-nir'ah* — it was pushed away and then becomes fit once more. The question is whether the period of disqualification leaves a permanent mark. For inanimate objects — blood, for instance — there is broad consensus that once *nidcha*, the disqualification is permanent even when the original obstacle is removed. For *ba'alei chayim*, however, there is a debate: perhaps the living, dynamic nature of an animal means that labels do not adhere permanently, and when circumstances change and it becomes fit, that fitness is genuine and operative.

According to Rava, the rabbinic ruling that forbids offering the animals from the mixture renders them all *nidcha*. Once off the table, they remain off the table — even if one then scatters the herd and statistically the offering would be valid, the prior status of *nidcha* persists. This is the opinion that *ba'alei chayim nidchin*. The ruling in the *Kinnim mishnah*, where the *kohen* who acted without consulting finds some of his offerings valid, reflects the opposing view — *ba'alei chayim einam nidchin* — that a live animal does not permanently carry the label of *nidcha* and can recover its valid status.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Heads

### One Head Offered

The Gemara then introduces a further case — drawn from the *mishnah* at the top of daf 74a — to probe the application of *nidchin* to slaughtered items, where the debate about *ba'alei chayim* is no longer relevant, since *kol alma nidche* — everyone agrees that once something slaughtered becomes unusable, the disqualification is permanent for inanimate matter.

The *mishnah* involves the heads of *olot* that became mixed with one another when one of the animals was a *baal mum*. The *kohen* is told he may not offer any of the heads because of the unknown *pasul* one among them. Rabbi Eliezer rules: *im karev harosh shel echad meihem yikrevu kol haroshim* — if one head was in fact brought up on the *mizbe'ach*, then all the remaining heads may now be offered as well. The reasoning is that once one was brought up, we are entitled to assume — retroactively — that the problematic one was the one already offered, and the remaining heads are all presumed valid.

This ruling is striking for our discussion. The heads were initially forbidden by rabbinic ruling — *lo nakriv*. The *kohen* ignored this and brought one up anyway. Not only is that offering not invalidated retroactively, but the act of bringing one up *licenses* the remaining heads to be offered. According to Rava, who holds that ignoring the rabbinic prohibition renders the offering not accepted — *lo martzi* — this should not work. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Eliezer follows the view of *Chanan HaMitzri*.

---

## Chanan HaMitzri View

### Two Goats Case

Chanan HaMitzri holds a uniquely permissive position: he does not recognize the principle of *nidche* even for slaughtered items. The *beraita* states: *Chanan HaMitzri omer afilu dam be-kos meivi chaveiro u-mezaveg lo* — even if the blood is already collected in a cup, one may bring a new partner animal and pair it with that blood. The reference is to the two goats of Yom Kippur — the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* and the *sa'ir* whose blood is sprinkled inside the *Beis Hamikdash*. If the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* died and the blood of its slaughtered partner is sitting in the cup, one might think the blood is now *nidcha* — it cannot be used because it has no partner. Chanan HaMitzri says: simply bring a new live goat as the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach*, and that blood in the cup can still be used and the service can proceed. Even though there was a period during which that blood was unusable, it is not permanently *nidcha*.

### Rava vs. Others

Rava's ruling — that once the *rabanan* say *lo nakriv*, any offering made in violation is *lo martzi* — reflects the position that *nidche* applies even when the disqualification stems from a rabbinic restriction. Once rabbinically pushed off the table, the animal or its blood remains off the table, and acting in violation does not rehabilitate it. Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in the case of the mixed heads, by contrast, assumes that *nidche* does not apply — that a temporary rabbinic restriction does not permanently disqualify the offering — and this aligns with the view of Chanan HaMitzri, who rejects *nidche* across the board, even for slaughtered items.

The practical upshot is vivid: one who holds *ba'alei chayim nidchin* would say that ignoring the rabbis and offering from the forbidden mixture avails nothing — the *korban* is not accepted. One who holds *ba'alei chayim einam nidchin* would say that if it was done, the offering stands where it objectively was valid. The *sugya* leaves us with this dispute intact, mapping it onto the broader question of when rabbinically imposed disqualification becomes permanent and when the underlying fitness of an item can reassert itself.

---

---

# Zevachim 74

## Ring of Avoda Zara

### Ring Falls in Sea

Rav Nachman transmits a ruling in the name of Rabbah bar Bar Hana in the name of Rav: a *taba'at shel avoda zara* — a ring that had been used in idolatrous worship, or that served as an ornament beautifying an altar (*noy avoda zara*) — becomes mixed with a hundred similar-looking rings. Such a ring is not *batel*: whether because idolatry is categorically weighty and resists nullification, because the ring is a significant object in its own right, or some combination of the two, the entire mixture is forbidden. Then one of the rings falls into the Mediterranean Sea (*Yam HaGadol*). The ruling: *hutru kulan* — all the remaining rings are now permitted, for we say that the one which fell away was the problematic one. This reasoning — *hach denafal hainu de-issura*, the one that fell, that is the forbidden one — operates as a kind of legal fiction, attributing the loss to the prohibited item and thereby freeing the remainder.

One immediate question presents itself: may one throw the ring into the sea *lechatchila*, deliberately, in order to trigger this permission? Presumably not, as that would constitute *ein mevatlin issur lechatchila* — one may not intentionally bring about the nullification of a forbidden item.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

The ruling about the rings is attributed to the position of Rabbi Eliezer, as recorded in an earlier Mishnah: *Rabbi Eliezer omer im karev harosh shel echad mehen yikrevu kol haroshim kulam* — if the head of one of the mixed animals was already offered, all the remaining heads may be offered. The principle in both cases is the same: once something happens to one item — it was lost, destroyed, or used — we attribute the prohibition to that one and permit the rest. This is specifically Rabbi Eliezer's view, and as the Gemara will make clear, it is contested.

### Challenge to Rav Nachman

Rabbah challenges Rav Nachman directly from our Mishnah: *afilu achat be-ribo yamutu kulan* — even one forbidden animal mixed among ten thousand, they must all be left to die. Why, asks Rabbah, can we not apply the same logic? Inevitably one animal will die first — let us say *that* was the *shor haniskal*, the condemned ox, and permit the rest. Rav Nachman responds: Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Eliezer. Not everyone accepts the principle of blaming the loss on the prohibited item — it is a disputed position, and our Mishnah does not follow it. The debate is genuinely tannaitic.

### Two at a Time Requirement

The Gemara raises a further objection. Rabbi Elazar the Amora notes that Rabbi Eliezer — the Tanna whose principle underlies this ruling — did not give blanket permission when one item is lost or used. Rather, *lo hitar Rabbi Eliezer ela shenayim shenayim* — Rabbi Eliezer only permitted benefit when items are used two at a time. The reasoning is that when one takes two, at least one of them is certainly permitted, which creates a kind of doubled basis for permissibility: we assume the prohibited item was the one already lost, and of the two now being used, one is definitively acceptable. The response to this objection is: *ana nami tarti ka-amina* — the ruling about the rings was also stated with the understanding that they are used or sold two at a time. Rashi explains this in the context of sale: the rings are sold in pairs, so that the same two-at-a-time logic applies. One could similarly say they are worn two at a time — on a chain or together on a finger — though the precise mechanics matter less than the principle.

---

## Split Mixture Problem

### Forty/Sixty Split

Rav continues with a more complex case. A *taba'at shel avoda zara* was mixed into a hundred rings, and again the mixture is not *batel*. The pile of one hundred rings then splits: forty go off in one direction, sixty in another. Now, the ring of *avoda zara* is somewhere in one of these two groups, but we do not know which.

The question arising from this scenario is whether we can apply the principle of *kol de-parish me-rubba parish* — what separates from the majority is presumed to have come from the majority, and since the majority is permitted, the separated item is permitted. In theory, one might argue that each ring, wherever it ended up, came from the majority of the original hundred and is therefore acceptable. But the Gemara does not accept this reasoning here — just as it does not apply it to the case of a single animal that wanders away from a mixed herd. Once the items are part of an initial forbidden mixture, one cannot simply pick one up and say it came from the majority; this is the very same issue debated in the large *Tosafot* at the beginning of this sugya regarding when *kol de-parish me-rubba parish* does and does not apply. All forty rings remain forbidden, as do all sixty.

### One from Forty vs. Sixty

The ruling then turns to what happens when one ring from one of these sub-groups falls into a separate, new pile of rings. *Pirshah achat me-arba'im einah oseret* — if one ring from the group of forty falls into a new pile, it does not render that new pile forbidden. *Achat mi-shishim oseret* — if one ring from the group of sixty falls into a new pile, it does render it forbidden.

The logic is as follows. Even though both the forty and the sixty each contain the *ta'aroves* — the admixture of the forbidden ring — when a ring separates from the forty, we are prepared to say that the forbidden ring was more likely to have remained in the larger group of sixty. The sixty remain the "base" of the original forbidden mixture; the prohibited item is presumed to be there. By contrast, when something separates from the sixty, we assume it may well be the forbidden one, and the new pile into which it falls becomes forbidden.

This is acknowledged as a kind of fiction — but so is the original rabbinic ruling that even one in a hundred is not *batel*. The Rabbis created the stringency, and they also shaped the parameters of its application.

### Gemara's Question

The Gemara questions the asymmetry: *mai shna achat me-arba'im d'lo* — why is it that when one comes from the forty it does not render the new pile forbidden? *D'amrinan issura be-rubba isa* — we say the prohibited item remained with the majority. But then: *achat mi-shishim nami amrinan issura be-rubba isa* — when one comes from the sixty, we should equally say the forbidden item stayed with the majority (of the sixty that remains). The same reasoning should apply in both directions. If in each case we simply say the forbidden item stayed behind, then in neither case should a ring that separates render a new mixture forbidden.

### Entire Group Separation

The resolution: *ela im pirshu arba'im kulam le-makom echad ein oserot; shishim le-makom echad oserot* — the real operative distinction is not about a single ring separating, but about an entire sub-group moving as a whole into a new location. If all forty move together into a new pile, that pile is permitted. If all sixty move together into a new pile, the pile is forbidden. The reason is structural: when the entire larger group relocates together, it carries with it the probability that the forbidden ring is among them. When the smaller group relocates as a whole, the forbidden ring is presumed to have stayed with what was the majority.

This is, as the Gemara acknowledges, somewhat surprising. It seems to imply that even the single-ring case could be resolved by *kol de-parish me-rubba parish*, and the Gemara effectively concedes that point — though with the important caveat that specifically regarding *avoda zara*, Shmuel will shortly insist that these probabilistic moves are never permitted.

---

## Shmuel's Split Position

### Shmuel Never Batel

When Rav transmitted the ruling about the forty and sixty rings, he reports: *ki amrisa kamin d'Shmuel, amar li* — when I presented this analysis before Shmuel, Shmuel responded: *hanach le-avodat kochavim she-sfeika ve-sfek sfeika asurah ad sof ha-olam* — leave aside *avoda zara*, for by idolatry, even a doubt upon a doubt remains forbidden forever. By *avoda zara*, Shmuel holds, we never apply probabilistic reasoning across mixtures, no matter how many successive piles are involved. Not only does one ring from the minority group render a new mixture forbidden — even one ring from the majority group would render it forbidden. The chain of prohibition never breaks.

### Goblets Baraita

Against Shmuel's sweeping position, the Gemara raises a *Baraita*: *safek avodat kochavim asurah, ve-sfek sfeika muteret* — the first level of doubt by *avoda zara* is forbidden, but a *sfek sfeika* — a double doubt — is permissible. The illustrative case: a goblet (*kos*) of *avoda zara* fell into a warehouse (*otzar*) full of goblets — all are forbidden. One then fell from that mixture into a pile of ten thousand, and one from there into yet another pile of ten thousand: *mutarin* — at least by the third pile, they are permitted. That is at least a *sfek sfek sfeika*, and Tosafot notes that the lenient opinion might even permit the second pile. But the key point is that this *Baraita* explicitly applies *sfek sfeika* leniency to *avoda zara* — in direct tension with Shmuel's absolute position.

### Rabbi Yehuda/Shimon

The Gemara identifies the underlying tannaitic dispute by reference to a *Baraita* about *orlah* pomegranates from Badan — one of the categories not subject to standard *bittul*. Rabbi Yehuda says: *osrin bechol shehen* — even a single one in a large mixture is forbidden, and if one falls from the first mixture into a second mixture (*ribo*), and from there into a third, all remain forbidden. Rabbi Yehuda's position is maximally strict, and he does not limit it to *avoda zara* — this applies across the board to anything that lacks *bittul*.

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, citing Rabbi Shimon, takes a different view — and notably argues against his own father's position. Rabbi Shimon agrees that the first mixture (*leribo asurin*) and the second mixture also remain forbidden. But once we reach a third pile (*mi-shalosh le-makom acher*), even that is permitted. The Gemara initially questions why three are required: if the goal is a simple majority (*rubba*), two ought to suffice. The answer is that when the *Baraita* says "three," it means two were already there and the one item fell in to make three — so the majority of two out of three favors the permissible. An alternative reading is that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Eliezer's principle of using things two at a time, and therefore requires a total of four — meaning one must be able to take two, and then two more — which would require more than just three items.

### Shmuel vs. Tannaim

The Gemara now turns to the question of how Shmuel fits within this tannaitic debate. Shmuel says that by *avoda zara* specifically, even a *sfek sfeika* is forever forbidden. If Shmuel is following Rabbi Yehuda, then Rabbi Yehuda says this applies to *all* prohibitions, not just *avoda zara* — and that is too broad for Shmuel's formulation, which singles out *avoda zara*. If Shmuel is following Rabbi Shimon, then Rabbi Shimon says pile three is permitted even by *orlah* — and by extension, presumably by *avoda zara* as well, which directly contradicts Shmuel. Moreover, if Rabbi Shimon would say pile three is permitted even by *avoda zara*, then the *Baraita* about the goblets that permits the third pile by *avoda zara* is Rabbi Shimon — and Shmuel's position aligns with neither Tanna consistently.

The Gemara resolves this: *v'Shmuel savar lah ke-Rabbi Yehuda be-chada u-falig alei be-chada* — Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehuda in one respect and disagrees with him in another. Rabbi Yehuda says no prohibition — *avoda zara* or otherwise — ever undergoes *bittul* across successive mixtures. Shmuel agrees with that conclusion specifically regarding *avoda zara*, but disagrees for other prohibitions, where he follows Rabbi Shimon's view that by the third pile even a simple majority suffices. The *Baraita* about the goblets, permitting the third mixture by *avoda zara*, follows Rabbi Shimon in full — who makes no distinction between *avoda zara* and other categories. Shmuel effectively votes with Rabbi Yehuda on *avoda zara* and with Rabbi Shimon on everything else.

The bottom line is that Shmuel does not follow any single Tanna across the board. The tannaitic debate itself makes no categorical distinction between *avoda zara* and other prohibitions: either you follow Rabbi Yehuda and nothing is ever *batel* across successive mixtures, or you follow Rabbi Shimon and by the third pile it is *batel* even by *avoda zara*. Shmuel carves out a middle position that is his own.

---

## Barrel Falls in Sea

### Barrel Case Setup

Reish Lakish presents a parallel case: *chavit shel trumah she-nit'areva be-me'ah chavyot* — a sealed barrel of *terumah* wine mixed with a hundred other sealed barrels. As established earlier in the tractate, sealed barrels constitute one of the categories of items that do not undergo *bittul*, even where liquid *terumah* would ordinarily be nullified in a hundred. So the mixture is forbidden. Then one of the barrels falls into the Dead Sea (*Yam HaMelach*). The ruling: *hutru kulan* — all are now permitted, because *de-amrinan hai nafalah de-isura nafalah* — we say the one that fell was the forbidden one. This parallels both the logic of Rabbi Eliezer's principle regarding the animal heads and Rav's ruling about the ring of *avoda zara*.

### Ring and Barrel Needed

The Gemara notes that both teachings are independently necessary — Rav Nachman's ruling about the ring and Reish Lakish's ruling about the barrel — and neither can be inferred from the other. Had we only had Rav Nachman's ruling about the ring of *avoda zara*, one might have argued that the leniency is specific to *avoda zara* — *de-ein lahem matirin* — because idolatrous objects have no path to become permitted under any circumstances. Since the prohibition is absolute, perhaps the Rabbis were more willing to allow this fiction as the only available relief. But *terumah* is different: *trumah de-yesh lah matirin* — *terumah* does have a form of permissibility, since a *kohen* may use it. Because there is someone for whom *terumah* is accessible, perhaps the same leniency should not apply, and we would not permit blaming the loss on the fallen barrel.

Conversely, had we only Reish Lakish's ruling about the barrel, one might have thought that the leniency is limited to barrels precisely because *minchar nefilasah* — the falling of a barrel is conspicuous and its absence is noticed. Everyone looks at the row of barrels and perceives the gap. That perceptibility makes it psychologically coherent — and halachically supportable — to attribute the loss to the problematic item. But a ring — *lo minchara nefilasah* — its fall and its absence go unnoticed. Perhaps then we cannot apply the same fiction to the ring. Since each case teaches something the other cannot, both are required.

### Rava Limits to Barrels

Rava proceeds to formalize exactly this limitation. Reish Lakish, says Rava, only permitted the fiction of blaming the fallen item when the loss is perceptible — as with a barrel. *Aval te'ena lo* — but if the forbidden item was a fig mixed among other figs, and one fig fell away, we would not apply the same principle. The small size and imperceptibility of the fig's absence means the event of its falling into the sea does not carry the same halachic weight. Whether Rava would also restrict the ring case by *avoda zara* — or whether the distinctive severity of idolatry justifies greater leniency there regardless — is left somewhat open, but his explicit ruling concerns *terumah* and similar categories.

### Rav Yosef Permits Fig

Rav Yosef disagrees: *afilu te'ena kenefilatah kach aliyatah* — even a fig follows the same logic. Just as when the fig fell into the group of figs it made the entire group forbidden despite its small size and inconspicuousness, so too when it falls away, it should be sufficient to render the remainder permitted. The same measure that makes a small item capable of creating a prohibition should make it capable of dissolving one when it is lost. Rav Yosef thus extends the permission to small items as well.

---

## Open Barrel Solution

### Remove Proportion

Rav Elazar proposes an independent method for dealing with the case of a *chavit shel terumah she-nafla be-kuf chavyot* — one sealed barrel of *terumah* mixed among a hundred others. The standard situation is that none of the barrels are *batel*, since sealed barrels resist nullification. Rav Elazar's solution: *pote'ach achat mehen ve-notel heimena kedei dameha ve-shoteh* — open one of the barrels and remove from it a proportional amount, corresponding to the one-hundredth share that would represent the forbidden portion, and then drink the rest.

The mechanism is as follows. Once a barrel is opened, it is no longer a sealed barrel and therefore loses its status as a significant, non-*batel* item. At the moment of opening, if that barrel happens to be the *terumah* one, it immediately becomes *batel* within the rest of the mixture, because it is no longer distinct. Rav Elazar's instruction to remove a proportional quantity is not because the opened barrel is literally a blend — it is either entirely *terumah* or entirely permitted wine. Rather, removing one one-hundredth serves as a kind of acknowledgment that a *ta'aroves* existed and that there is something to account for. One thereby "pays" the symbolic price of the mixture before drinking, rather than simply opening the barrel and drinking freely as if nothing had occurred.

The elegance of the method is that if one proceeds through all the barrels this way, removing one one-hundredth from each, the total removed will equal the volume of a full barrel — which is, of course, the amount of *terumah* that was at stake. There is a certain integrity to the outcome even if the path to it is admittedly a legal construction.

### Nachman's Objection

Rav Nachman objects sharply: *gama ve-shasa* — what, you're just swallowing and drinking? How can one open a barrel *lechatchila* for this purpose? Doing so would constitute *mevatlin issur lechatchila* — actively engineering the conditions for *bittul* to take effect, which is forbidden. Opening the barrel is itself the act that removes the sealed-barrel status and enables *bittul*, and one may not perform that act with that goal in mind.

### Natural Opening Only

The correction: *nifchatzah achat mehen* — only if one of the barrels happened to open on its own, or broke, or was opened for some other reason, may one then remove the appropriate proportion and drink. In that case, the opening was not done for the purpose of achieving *bittul*, and there is no violation of *ein mevatlin issur lechatchila*. The parallel is the ring that fell into the sea on its own — one cannot throw the ring in deliberately, but if it fell, the consequences may be used. Similarly here, one cannot deliberately open the barrel to trigger *bittul*, but if it opened, Rav Elazar's method applies.

### Multiple Openings

Rabbi Oshaya extends the ruling to a more complex case: *chavit shel terumah she-nit'areva be-me'ah va-chamishim chavyot* — one *terumah* barrel mixed among 150 barrels. Then *niftachu me'ah mehen* — a hundred of them opened. The ruling: *notel mimena kedei dimu'a ve-shoteh* — one removes the appropriate proportion from each of the hundred opened barrels and may drink from all of them, while *ve-she'ar asurin ad she-yipatechu* — the remaining fifty sealed barrels stay forbidden until they too are opened, at which point the same process applies.

One might have thought to object: if a hundred barrels all open simultaneously, perhaps we should say *issur be-rubba isa* — the forbidden barrel must be among the majority of those that opened, and therefore those hundred collectively remain suspect. Rabbi Oshaya rejects this: *chidush hu* — this is not how the principle operates. The moment a barrel opens, *bittul* applies to it regardless of how many others open at the same time. There is no rule requiring that the forbidden item remain within the majority of opened barrels; each opened barrel simply joins the category of non-significant, *batel* items. The appropriate proportion is removed, and all the opened barrels become permitted.

---

---

# Zevachim 75

## Intro & Pasul Animals

### Opening

The daf under discussion is Zevachim 75, though we begin on 74b, roughly halfway down the page at the words *haroveiah v'hanirba*. The *mishna* has been discussing the case of animals becoming mixed up with one another, and it presents a long list of animals that are *pasul* to be brought as *korbanot* for a variety of reasons.

### Mishna Overview
