The *mishna* enumerates multiple categories of disqualified animals. *Roveiah* and *nirba* refer to an animal that played either the male or female role in an act of bestiality. *Muktza* is an animal that was set aside for *avodah zarah* but was not actually worshipped. *Ne'evad* is an animal that was itself worshipped. *Etnan* refers to the prohibition derived from the verse concerning payment given to a prostitute. *Mechir kelev* describes an animal whose value was used as purchasing power to acquire a dog — a prohibition explicit in the *Torah*. *Kilayim* refers to a crossbreed — for instance, sheep with wild sheep, or goats with wild goats. And *treifa* refers to an animal that has undergone a disqualifying injury, a topic that will be treated at great length in *Masechet Chullin*.

### Disqualifications

The *gemara*'s *sugia* here focuses primarily on the case of the *treifa*. *Bishlama kulhu* — for most of the animals on this list, one can readily understand how the problematic case arises: the animal has some non-physical disqualification, arising from a sin committed with it or from the manner in which it was used, so that *lo yadia* — it is not visually apparent — and if it becomes mixed into a larger flock, the problem of identification emerges naturally. But the *gemara* asks: *ela hai treifa heichi dami?* — what exactly is the case of a *treifa*? If an animal has sustained a serious enough injury to render it a *treifa*, that injury ought to be visible. How then could it become confused with other animals?

## Treifa Problem

### Treifa Mystery

This question is the pivot around which the *sugia* turns. Three *Amoraim* each offer their own answer, and the *gemara* provides no resolution among them — rather, each opinion stands on its own, connected to other *machlokot* elsewhere.

### Rabbi Yannai

*Amri de-vei Rabbi Yannai* — the school of Rabbi Yannai teaches: *hacha b'mai askinan, kegon de-irav nikuvat hakotz b'drusat haze'ev* — the case is where two different types of injured animals have become mixed with one another. One is *nikuvat hakotz*, an animal punctured by a thorn, which in all likelihood has not pierced any inner organ and therefore does not render the animal a *treifa*. The other is *drusat haze'ev*, an animal attacked by a wolf, where there is a far higher likelihood that internal organs were damaged and the animal has indeed become a *treifa*. According to Rabbi Yannai, both animals bear outward injuries that look similar enough to cause confusion, even though one is a *treifa* and one is not.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish offers a different scenario: *kegon de-it'arev bin'fulah* — the case involves an animal that fell, a *nefulah*. One might then ask: simply examine the animal to determine whether it is truly a *treifa*. The answer is that Reish Lakish holds the position that even if the animal stood up again after its fall (*amda*), it still requires *me'et le'et* — a twenty-four hour observation period — before one may conclude it was unharmed. And even if it was subsequently able to walk (*halcha*), it still requires *bedika* — a post-*shechita* examination. This is because, in Reish Lakish's view, once an animal has sustained an injury, its *chazakat kashrut* is disrupted. The animal is no longer presumed healthy; rather, the burden of proof has shifted, and one must now affirmatively demonstrate that it has recovered. Under this framework, an animal of uncertain status after a fall could easily become mixed with others before a definitive determination has been made.

### Rabbi Yirmiya

Rabbi Yirmiya offers a third approach: *kegon de-it'arev bivlad treifa* — the case involves not an animal that itself bears a visible injury, but rather a *vlad treifa*, an animal born from a mother who was herself a *treifa*. Such an animal carries a disqualification but has no physical mark by which it can be identified. This is precisely why the mixture is intractable. Rabbi Yirmiya's position is grounded in the view of Rabbi Eliezer: *de-amar vlad treifa lo yikarev legavei hamizbe'ach* — that the offspring of a *treifa* mother is disqualified from being brought as a *korban*.

To sharpen the point: all three *Amoraim* are answering the same underlying question — how can a *treifa* animal get confused among others? Rabbi Yannai's answer is that there *is* a visible injury on the *treifa*, but another animal in the flock also has a similar-looking injury that is not disqualifying, creating genuine confusion between the two. Reish Lakish's answer is that the animal's status is genuinely uncertain, having not yet been definitively resolved through the requisite observation and examination. And Rabbi Yirmiya's answer is that the *treifa* animal in question bears no injury at all — its disqualification is genealogical, and therefore invisible.

## Rejections

### Against Yannai

The *gemara* now explains why each *Amora* rejects the other positions. Why do Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yirmiya not accept Rabbi Yannai's answer? Because *bein nikuvat hakotz ledrusat haze'ev meda yadi'a* — the wound from a thorn and the wound from a wolf are actually distinguishable upon examination. *Hai mashich ve-hai agil* — the wolf's bite produces an elongated wound (the wolf tears at the flesh with multiple teeth, leaving a drawn-out mark), while the thorn produces a circular puncture. This distinction — *mashuch ve-agul* — appears elsewhere as well, for instance in discussions of *ketamim* in *Hilchot Niddah*, though in that context we are generally not strict about distinguishing between them. In the context of identifying a *treifa*, however, Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yirmiya maintain that the distinction is visually discernible and therefore Rabbi Yannai's case does not present a genuine problem of confusion.

### Against Lakish

Why do Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yirmiya not accept Reish Lakish's answer? *Kasvari amda einah tzerichah me'et le'et, halcha einah tzerichah bedikah* — they hold the more lenient position: if an animal stood up after its fall, no twenty-four hour waiting period is required, and if it was able to walk, no post-*shechita* examination is necessary. In their view, the animal's ability to stand and walk is itself sufficient demonstration that it did not sustain a serious injury. The *chazakah* is not disrupted by the fall once the animal has recovered its mobility, and therefore the scenario Reish Lakish describes — where an animal of uncertain status mingles with others before its condition is resolved — simply does not arise under their ruling.

### Against Yirmiya

Why do Rabbi Yannai and Reish Lakish not accept Rabbi Yirmiya's answer? Because *ke-Rabbi Eliezer lo mukmi* — they do not hold like Rabbi Eliezer that the *vlad treifa* is disqualified at all. If the offspring of a *treifa* mother is not itself considered a *treifa* in their view, then Rabbi Yirmiya's case is not a case of a *treifa* mixed with other animals. The elegance of the *sugia* lies precisely here: each *Amora* has a coherent position that generates both its own answer to the original question and principled grounds for rejecting every alternative.

## Korbanot Mix

### Kodashim Principle

The *mishna* continues with a new principle: *kodashim be-kodashim min be-mino, zeh yikarev leshem mi she-hu ve-zeh yikarev leshem mi she-hu* — when *korbanot* of the same type are mixed together and the owners cannot identify their individual animals, each animal is brought with the general intention that it be offered on behalf of whomever owns it. Rather than designating it for a specific person, the *kohen* employs a catch-all *machshavah* that covers whichever owner's animal this turns out to be.

### Semichah Problem

The *gemara* raises a challenge: *ve-ha ba'ei semichah* — does not a *korban* require *semichah*, the laying of hands by the owner? If the owners cannot identify which animal is theirs, how can *semichah* be performed *lechatchilah*? The *gemara* acknowledges that *semichah* is not *me'akev be-di'avad* — it does not invalidate the *korban* after the fact — but there remains a *chiyuv* to perform it, and deliberately bringing a *korban* without it seems less than ideal. The question, then, is how the *mishna* can endorse this procedure as a legitimate resolution.

### Rav Yosef

*Amar Rav Yosef*: the *mishna* must be speaking specifically about *korban nashim* — offerings brought by women — because women are not required to perform *semichah*. There is accordingly no problem of failing to fulfill the obligation of *semichah* when the owners cannot identify their animals.

## Abaye Challenge

### Baraita Cases

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef. He cites a *baraita*: *korban yachid she-nitarev be-korban yachid, u-ve-korban tzibbur she-nitarev be-korban tzibbur* — if one individual's *korban* was mixed with another individual's *korban*, or if one communal *korban* was mixed with another communal *korban*, or even if an individual's *korban* was mixed with a communal *korban* (*korban yachid ve-korban tzibbur she-nitarvu zeh ba-zeh*) — in all these cases, *noten arba matanot mikkol echad ve-echad*: the blood of each *korban* must be applied in four *matanot* on the four *karnot hamizbe'ach*, because one of the animals in the mixture might be a *korban chatat* for which this is required.

*Ve-im natan matanah mikkol echad yatza* — if, *be-di'avad*, only one *matanah* was given from each animal individually, that suffices, since even for a *chatat* a single *matanah* is valid after the fact. *Ve-im natan arba mikkullan yatza* — and even if the blood of all the animals was mixed together and only four *matanot* were given from the combined blood, that too is *yotzei*.

The *baraita* then distinguishes between two scenarios: *bemei devarim amurim keshe-nitarvu chayyim* — this applies when the animals were mixed while still alive; *aval nitarvu shechutim* — but if they were mixed after *shechita*, *noten arba matanot mikkullan* — one gives four *matanot* from each, and *ve-im natan matanah achat mikkullan yatza* — even one *matanah* from all the blood together suffices.

Abaye's challenge to Rav Yosef emerges from the *baraita*'s language: *katani yachid — dumya de-tzibbur* — the *baraita* discusses an individual's *korban* in terms that parallel the communal *korban*. Communal *korbanot* are funded by the *shekalim* donated by men (*gavrei*), and therefore the *tzibbur*'s *korbanot* are as if owned by men. By analogy, the *yachid* cases in the *baraita* should likewise refer to men's offerings — thereby undermining Rav Yosef's claim that the *mishna* speaks only of women's *korbanot*.

### Rava Interprets

*Amar Rava*: in fact this *baraita* supports Rav Yosef rather than contradicting him. Rava reads the *baraita*'s distinction more carefully. The contrast between animals mixed while alive and blood mixed after *shechita* is not really about the timing per se, but about the physical configuration. *She-nitarvu shechutim ke-ein chayyim* — "mixed after *shechita* in a manner similar to when alive" means that even after *shechita*, the blood was kept in separate containers (*be-kossot*), treating each animal's blood as distinct — analogous to the animals being separate while alive. *Aval be-vulul* — if, however, the blood was blended together into one vessel, then one gives four *matanot* from the combined blood, and a single *matanah* from the mixture suffices.

### Rabbi's Volume Test

*Rebbi omer*: *ro'in et ha-matanah im yesh bah kedei la-zeh ve-kedei la-zeh, keshera; ve-im lav, pesulah* — we examine whether the *matanah* placed on the *mizbe'ach* contains enough blood to account for a valid portion from each *korban*. If there is sufficient volume, it is *keshera*; if not, it is *pesulah*.

This raises a question: where does Rebbi derive the principle that the blood must be of sufficient quantity? For a *korban chatat*, only a minimal amount of blood would seem necessary. The *gemara* notes that a *Tosefta* in *Parah* records Rebbi as saying, in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: *hazaya kol she-hu metaheret* — even the tiniest drop of *mei chatat* suffices for purification, with no minimum measure required (*hazaya eina tzerichah shi'ur*). This appears to cut against Rebbi's position regarding the *matanah* of blood.

## Parah Rules

### Eliezer Minimum

The *Tosefta* in *Parah* records Rebbi stating, within the framework of Rabbi Eliezer's view: *hazaya kol she-hu metaheret* — that even the most minuscule quantity of *mei chatat* landing on the *tamei* person effects purification. There is no defined minimum measure of water required.

### Parah vs. Korban

The *gemara* raises the apparent difficulty: if Rebbi himself holds, following Rabbi Eliezer, that there is no minimum quantity for *hazaya*, how can he require a minimum volume for a *matanah* of blood? The resolution offered is *hazaya le-chud ve-netinah le-chud* — the act of sprinkling (*hazaya*) for *parah adumah* is categorically distinct from the act of placing blood (*netinah*) on the *mizbe'ach* for a *korban*. The very nature of sprinkling already implies atomized, minimal quantities. By contrast, the *matanah* of blood for a *korban chatat* — applied with the *kohen*'s finger to the *keren* — and certainly the *shtayim she-hen arba* applied with a vessel (*kos*) — involves a substantial, definite quantity of blood. The two acts are sufficiently different in kind that one may distinguish between them, and Rebbi's position on *parah* does not undermine his position on *korbanot*.

## Bechor Ma'aser

### Grazing Till Mum

The *mishna* addresses the case of *nitarvu bechor u-ma'aser* — when disqualified animals have been mixed with *bechor* animals or with *ma'aser* animals. *Yireu ad she-yistavu* — the entire group must graze until they develop a *mum*. Once a *mum* appears, *veyachlu ke-vechor u-ke-ma'aser* — they are eaten in the manner appropriate to a *bechor* or *ma'aser* that developed a blemish. The *mishna* then concludes: *ha-kol yecholim le-hitarev chutz min ha-chatat ve-ha-asham* — all categories of *korbanot* may potentially become mixed together and admit of resolution, except for *chatat* and *asham*, which have a unique and personal connection to the owner on account of the specific sin being atoned for.

### Bechor Restrictions

*Amar Rabbi bar Chama* — Rabbi bar Chama raises a series of questions about the practical implications of the *bechor*'s status. According to Beit Shammai, even a *bechor* that has developed a *mum* — and has therefore become, in a sense, ordinary — may not be fed to a woman in *niddah*. There is some residual *kedushat bechor* that persists. Rabbi bar Chama then asks a series of follow-on questions: *temuraso mahu* — what is the status of an animal exchanged for a *bechor* through *temurah*? Since *bechor eino nifdah* — a *bechor* cannot be redeemed — can one make a *temurah* with it at all? And separately: *bechor eino nishkal be-litra* — the *kohen* may not sell the *bechor*'s meat by weight in the marketplace; what then of its *temuraso* — does the same restriction apply to the animal received in exchange?

### Dual Kedusha

*Rami bar Chama* poses a related question to Rava: *hitpis bechor le-vedek ha-bayit mahu* — what if one attempted to donate a *bechor* to *bedek ha-bayit*, the Temple maintenance fund, thereby seeking to infuse it with *kedushat bedek ha-bayit*? *Mahu she-yishkol be-litra* — would this then permit the meat to be weighed out and sold retail after *shechita*? The reasoning: *ravcha de-hekdesh adif* — increasing the financial return for *hekdesh* by selling at retail prices might override the usual *bechor* restriction. On the other hand, *zilusa de-vechor adif* — perhaps one should instead give precedence to the dignity of the *bechor* and its associated laws, even at the cost of a lower yield for *hekdesh*.

*Rabbi Yosi bar Zavda* attempts to bring a proof from our *mishna*: the fact that animals mixed with *bechor* and *ma'aser* must graze until they develop a *mum* and are then eaten *ke-vechor u-ke-ma'aser* suggests that the *bechor* retains its distinctive restrictions even after developing a *mum* — including the prohibition against weighing the meat. This would seem to argue against any leniency flowing from the donation to *bedek ha-bayit*.

Rav Huna and Rabbi Chizkiya, students of Rabbi Yirmiya, respond: *mi dami? Hatam shtei kedushot u-shnei gufin* — in the *mishna*'s case, we have two distinct sanctities (*kedushat bechor* and the disqualified animal's status) in two separate bodies. *Hacha shtei kedushot ve-guf echad* — here, by contrast, we are discussing an attempt to impose two sanctities on one and the same animal: *kedushat bechor* and *kedushat bedek ha-bayit* simultaneously. That is a fundamentally different configuration and the *mishna* may not constitute a proof.

*Matkif lah Rabbi Yosi bar Avin*: if someone declared, "Redeem for me my *bechor* that I donated to *bedek ha-bayit*" — one would not heed him, since *bechor* cannot be redeemed (*eino nifdeh*). If the attempted donation to *bedek ha-bayit* cannot even be undone through *pidyon*, it suggests the donation itself may not have taken meaningful effect. *Amar Rabbi Ami*: *klum hikne zeh ela ma she-kanu lo* — the *bedek ha-bayit* does not genuinely acquire the *bechor*, because the *bechor* already bears its own *kedusha* as a *korban* and an animal destined for the altar cannot simply be redirected to *bedek ha-bayit* in this fashion. The attempted donation of a *tam* animal earmarked as a *korban* to *bedek ha-bayit* does not succeed in the ordinary way.

## Chatat Asham

### Gender Distinctions

The *gemara* returns to the *mishna*'s rule that *chatat* and *asham* cannot be mixed with other *korbanot*. The question is: why are these two specifically exceptional? One might suggest *de-hai zachar ve-hai nekeva* — that the *chatat* is typically a female animal and the *asham* is always male, and so distinguishing between them by gender seems straightforward. But the *gemara* immediately notes *chatat ve-ola nami* — the same logic would apply to *chatat* and *olah*, since *olah* must also be male. So why can a *chatat* not become mixed with an *olah*?

### Age & Type

The *gemara* responds: *ika se'ir nasi* — the *chatat* brought by the *nasi* must be a male *se'ir* (goat), which could in principle become confused with a male *olah*. Then: *hai se'ar ve-hai tzemar* — but a goat has hair (*se'ar*) and a sheep has wool (*tzemer*), so one can still distinguish between them visually.

The *gemara* then asks: *pesach ve-asham lama lo mitarev* — why then cannot a *korban Pesach* and a *korban asham* become mixed? Both can be sheep. The response is *hai ben shana ve-hai ben shtei shanim* — the *korban Pesach* must be in its first year and the *korban asham* must be in its second year, so their age serves as a distinguishing feature. The *gemara* counters: *ika asham nazir ve-asham metzora* — the *asham* of a *nazir* and the *asham* of a *metzora* need not be older animals and could fall within the same age range as a *korban Pesach*.

### Age Counting

*Ve-iba'it eima* — alternatively, one may say: *ika ben shana de-michzei ke-ven shtei shanim, ve-ika ben shtei shanim de-michzei ke-ven shana* — a one-year-old animal may look like a two-year-old, and vice versa. Moreover, the ages of animals are not counted from their individual birthdays. Since animals have a birthing season and are born around the same time of year, they are classified by seasonal cohort — from *Rosh Chodesh Elul* or *Rosh Chodesh Tishrei* — rather than by the precise date of birth. As a result, there is genuine ambiguity about whether a given animal falls into the one-year or two-year category, and this can generate real cases of confusion even when examining animals of nominally different age classes.

## Mixed Pieces

### Strictest Rule

The final *mishna* of the daf addresses a distinct case: *nitarvu chatichah be-chatichah* — when pieces of meat from different *korbanot* have already been cut and become mixed together, or *kodshei kodashim be-kodashim kalim* — when meat from those *korbanot* eaten only by *kohanim* (*kodshei kodashim*) is mixed with meat from those that may be eaten even by *Yisraelim* (*kodashim kalim*), or when meat from *korbanot* permitted for only one day becomes mixed with meat permitted for two days — *yochlum ke-chamur she-bahen* — in all such cases, they are eaten in accordance with the strictest applicable rule.

### Leftovers Concern

Rabbi Shimon's position, which is that one eats the mixture according to the most stringent category, is challenged: *ein mevivin kodashim le-beit ha-psul* — one should not bring *kodashim* into a situation of disqualification. If meat permissible to many people is now restricted to *kohanim* alone, the time window is shorter and the pool of permitted consumers is smaller, creating a significant risk that the meat will become *nosar* — leftover beyond the permitted time — and thereby be disqualified retroactively.

### Practical Override

The resolution is that for *chatichot* — pieces of meat that have already been slaughtered, over which the *zrikot* have already been performed, and which have already been cut up — the objection does not stand. One is no longer in a position to choose whether or not to bring the *korban*; the situation is already fixed. In such circumstances, the concern about *nosar* is outweighed by practical necessity. Rabbi Shimon's lenient approach — applying the strictest rule to the mixture and allowing the meat to be eaten under those constraints — is vindicated: of all the concerns one might weigh, the speculative future risk of *nosar* does not warrant preventing the valid consumption of what is already before us.

# Zevachim 76

## Mixed Asham/Shelamim

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* presents the following scenario: an *asham*, which is by nature a male sacrifice, becomes mixed up with a *shelamim*. The *asham* is male, a *chatas* is female, an *olah* is male, and a *shelamim* may be either male or female — which is precisely why the *shelamim* is the one sacrifice with which any other may become confused. The *Gemara* preceding today's daf had already worked through which combinations of sacrifices could realistically become intermixed, given that certain categories are exclusively male and others exclusively female. But anything can get mixed up with a *shelamim*.

### R. Shimon's Solution

Rabbi Shimon's proposed solution is elegantly practical: slaughter both animals in the north — the required location for an *asham* — and have male *kohanim* eat them. In doing so, whichever animal turns out to be the *asham* is handled correctly, and there is nothing halachically wrong with slaughtering a *shelamim* in the north or having male *kohanim* eat it. As for the blood, since only a *chatas* requires the blood to be applied above, both the *asham* and the *shelamim* have their blood applied in the same location, so no conflict arises there either.

### Rabbis' Objection

The *Chachamim* object that this approach is unacceptable because it invokes the principle of *ain mevi'im kodshim l'beit hapsul* — one does not place sacrifices into a context of invalidity. By treating both animals as an *asham*, the *shelamim* (whichever animal it turns out to be) is now subject to more restrictive conditions than it would otherwise face: it may only be eaten by male *kohanim*, and more significantly, it may only be eaten for one day rather than two. This dramatically increases the likelihood that some of the meat will become *nosar* and require burning. Restricting a *shelamim* in this manner constitutes bringing it into a house of invalidity.

### Redemption Solution

The *Chachamim* offer an alternative. One waits until the animals develop a blemish, at which point they can be redeemed. The owner then designates the proceeds: whichever animal is the *asham*, its value is directed toward this money, which is then used to purchase a proper *asham*; and whichever animal is the *shelamim*, its value is similarly directed to purchase a proper *shelamim*. This process restores clarity about which animal is which. Rabbi Shimon's implicit counter is: do you have a better solution? The *Chachamim* answer that they do — redemption upon the onset of a blemish — but it is understood that if no such solution existed, even the *Chachamim* might concede that Rabbi Shimon's approach would be preferable to simply allowing the animals to go to waste. The debate, then, is specifically about whether one may adopt Rabbi Shimon's approach when an alternative does in fact exist.

## Kodshim L'Beis Hapes (II)

### Shvi'is/Terumah Case

A *tanna* taught a *baraita* before Rav: produce money infused with the sanctity of the sabbatical year (*kdushas shvi'is*) may not be used to purchase *terumah* — *ain lokchim b'dameha trumah mipnei shemima'atin achilasah* — because doing so restricts the time in which the *terumah* may be eaten. The mechanism is this: *shvi'is* produce carries an obligation of *biyur* — when the relevant species of fruit is no longer available in the field, one must eliminate any such produce held at home. This sanctity transfers to money received in exchange for *shvi'is* produce and, in turn, to whatever is purchased with that money. If one buys *terumah* with such money, the *terumah* now acquires *kdushas shvi'is* and may be subject to the *biyur* deadline, thereby limiting the time available for its consumption. This, the *baraita* teaches, constitutes *ain mevi'im kodshim l'beit hapsul*.

It is worth pausing here to note that this principle, though formulated in the context of *kodshim* — sacrificial offerings — is being applied by the *Gemara* equally to non-sacrificial sanctified items such as *terumah* and *ma'aser sheni*. The principle of not placing something holy into a context that diminishes its sanctity is operative across the full range of halachic categories.

### Rava's Position

When the Rabbis heard this *baraita*, they observed to Rava that its author must not follow Rabbi Shimon — since Rabbi Shimon in the *mishnah* permits placing *kodshim* into a context of invalidity and would presumably also permit purchasing *terumah* with *shvi'is* money. Rava pushed back: even Rabbi Shimon, he insisted, would agree that one may not do so in this case. The key distinction is *d'i'avad* — after the fact. When did Rabbi Shimon permit treating a mixed *shelamim* as though it were an *asham*? Because the situation had already arisen — the animals were already mixed, the problem already existed, and Rabbi Shimon was proposing the best available solution to a pre-existing difficulty. That, however, is categorically different from taking perfectly ordinary *shvi'is* money and deliberately purchasing *terumah* with it. There is no pre-existing problem demanding a solution. Rabbi Shimon would never permit one to proactively place something in a diminished halachic state — *lechatchilah lo*. He permits it only when the circumstances already demand it.

## Tavlin Challenge

### Mishna Tavlin

Abaye challenges Rava's position. A later *mishnah* teaches that *kohanim* are permitted to eat sacrificial meat in any manner they choose — *l'ochlan tzloyim shelukim mevushalim* — roasted, double-boiled, or cooked — and they may season it with any spices, whether *tavlei chulin* (non-sacred spices) or even *tavlei terumah* (spices that are *terumah*). This is the ruling of Rabbi Shimon.

### Proof from Spices

Why is this a significant ruling? Because if a *kohen* takes a *terumah* onion and throws it into a pot of *chatas* stew, the *terumah* onion, now mixed with the *kodshim*, can only be eaten for a single day — the time restriction of the *chatas*. Ordinarily, *terumah* has its own eating window, but once combined with the *chatas*, it is constrained to the more restrictive *kodshim* timeline. This is a classic case of bringing *kodshim* into a house of invalidity — the *terumah* is the *kodshim* whose eating time is now being limited — and yet Rabbi Shimon permits it *lechatchilah*. This appears to be a strong proof against Rava's position.

## Tavlin Challenge (II)

### Rava Dismisses

Rava dismisses the challenge. *Tavlin* — vegetables such as onions and garlic used as spices — are only *terumah* on a rabbinic level; their *terumah* status is not biblical. Rava's position is therefore more nuanced than it initially appeared: Rabbi Shimon may well permit proactively limiting something whose sanctity is only *d'Rabbanan*, but he would still not allow it *lechatchilah* when the sanctity being restricted is *d'Oraisa*.

## Kodshim L'Beis Hapes (II)

### Rabbinic vs. Biblical

Rava's qualification, then, is twofold: Rabbi Shimon permits bringing *kodshim* into a context of invalidity only (1) when there is already a pre-existing problem — *bedi'eved* in the sense that the difficult situation has already arisen — or (2) when the sanctity being restricted is merely rabbinic. A proactive restriction of something possessing biblical sanctity Rabbi Shimon would not sanction. One might ask whether the *mishnah* of *ma'aser* supports this distinction. The *Gemara* cites another teaching: *ein lokchim terumah b'kesef ma'aser mipnei shemema'et b'achilasah* — one does not purchase *terumah* with *ma'aser sheni* money because it restricts the ability to eat it. *V'Rabbi Shimon mattir* — and Rabbi Shimon permits it.

Here a dispute between Rashi and Tosafot emerges regarding precisely what is being restricted. Rashi holds that the restriction falls on the *terumah* itself: *terumah* can normally be eaten anywhere, whereas *ma'aser sheni* can only be eaten in Jerusalem — so by purchasing *terumah* with *ma'aser sheni* money, one creates *terumah* that inherits the locational restriction of *ma'aser sheni*, limiting where it may be consumed. Tosafot reads the restriction in the opposite direction: the *ma'aser sheni* itself is being restricted, since *ma'aser sheni* is ordinarily available to anyone, but after it is used to purchase *terumah*, what remains can now only be eaten by *kohanim*. Either way, the restriction imposed is of a biblical character — *ma'aser sheni* and the prohibition against eating it outside Jerusalem are biblical — and yet Rabbi Shimon permits this *lechatchilah*. This appears to be a compelling proof that Rabbi Shimon allows *lechatchilah* limitation of even biblically sanctified items.

Having established that proof, the *Gemara* then pivots: though the point has been demonstrated, there are in fact other *mishnayos* that make the same point, and the subsequent discussion explores why Abaye chose this particular *mishnah* as his proof rather than those alternatives.

## Shvi'is/Terumah Oil

### Rav Yosef's Question

When Abaye later came before Rav Yosef and reported the exchange — how Rabbah had maintained that Rabbi Shimon does not allow it *lechatchilah*, and how Abaye had proven otherwise from the *mishnah* of *ma'aser sheni* — Rav Yosef asked: why did you not challenge Rabbah from this other *mishnah*? The reference is to a *mishnah* in *Shvi'is*: *ein m'vashlin yerek shel Shvi'is b'shemen shel terumah* — one does not cook a *shvi'is* vegetable in *terumah* oil — *shelo yavi'u kodshim l'veit hapsul*, so as not to bring *kodshim* into a house of invalidity. Notably, the very phrase *mevi'im kodshim l'veit hapsul* appears here explicitly, and it is applied to items that are not *korbanot* — demonstrating that the principle extends across all categories of sanctified items. *V'Rabbi Shimon mattir* — Rabbi Shimon permits it. In this case, it is the *terumah* oil whose eating window is being restricted by being cooked together with the *shvi'is* vegetable, and Rabbi Shimon allows this *lechatchilah*.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye explained why he had not raised this case. He had already challenged Rabbah from the *mishnah* of *tavlin* — the case of putting *terumah* onions into the *chatas* stew — and Rabbah had dismissed it by saying *hanach l'trumas tavlin d'Rabbanan*: vegetable-based *terumah* is only rabbinic, so Rabbi Shimon's leniency in that case tells us nothing about biblical sanctity. The same dismissal would have applied here, Abaye reasoned: the *shvi'is* vegetable is also only rabbinically restricted, so Rabbah would simply have said *hacha nami trumas yerek d'Rabbanan* and moved on.

### Rav Yosef's Rebuttal

Rav Yosef disagreed with this reasoning. The case of the *shvi'is* vegetable and *terumah* oil is not symmetrical in the way Abaye assumed. When you cook them together, what is being restricted? Not the vegetable. The *terumah* oil is what now has its eating window shortened by virtue of being cooked with the *shvi'is* vegetable. And *terumah* oil is explicitly biblical — the Torah itself specifies *dagan tirosh v'yitzhar* (grain, wine, and oil) as the three categories subject to *terumah* obligations. Rabbah's dismissal — "this is only rabbinic" — would have applied to cases where the sanctity being constricted is rabbinic. Here, the sanctity being constricted is that of the *terumah* oil, which is unquestionably biblical. Rabbi Shimon nonetheless permits it *lechatchilah*. If the *mishnah* had been written the other way — *yerek shel terumah b'shemen shel Shvi'is*, a *terumah* vegetable cooked in *shvi'is* oil — then one could indeed say that what is being restricted is only the rabbinic sanctity of the vegetable, and Rabbah's dismissal would hold. But as actually written, the case is a powerful proof that Rabbah could not have deflected.

### Bedi'eved Debate

Abaye then explains why he did not use this case: he had already challenged Rabbah from the *mishnah* of the mixed sacrificial animals — the *asham* and *shelamim* — and Rabbah had answered *d'i'avad*: once the animals are already mixed, Rabbi Shimon is simply finding the best available solution to a pre-existing problem. Abaye feared Rabbah would apply the same *d'i'avad* logic to the carrot-and-oil case: perhaps the carrot was already soaking in the oil before anyone made a decision, and Rabbi Shimon is only permitting it after the fact, not as an initial choice. Rav Yosef rejects this reading. If the scenario in that *mishnah* were one where the carrot and oil were already mixed, then the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon would have no leg to stand on — what else could one possibly do with a carrot already soaking in oil? The only reason the Rabbis could meaningfully prohibit it is if it is being addressed as an initial act, *lechatchilah*.

Abaye responds that even so, Rabbah would have said the Rabbis' objection makes sense because there is an alternative: squeeze the oil out of the carrot and salvage it. Rav Yosef counters — via Ravina — that this alternative is not really viable: if you squeeze thoroughly, *nischot tuva*, you destroy the carrot, which is *shvi'is* produce that must not be wasted; if you squeeze lightly, *nischot portza*, oil remains mixed in the carrot. There is no clean way to separate them. Therefore the case cannot be read as *bedi'eved*, and it does stand as proof that Rabbi Shimon allows it *lechatchilah* — and the proof from the *terumah* oil *mishnah* was a strong one that Abaye could indeed have deployed against Rabbah.

## Metzora Case

### Metzora Scenario

A new *mishnah* introduces another scenario that bears on the same question. The case involves a man who may or may not be a *metzora muchlat* — a fully declared *metzora* — who needs to bring the appropriate sacrifice on the eighth day to complete his purification process. The uncertainty might arise from questions about the original declaration by a *kohen*, and it creates a halachic quandary: how can one bring the mandatory sacrifice of a *metzora* when it is unclear whether the obligation even applies? Rabbi Shimon teaches: on the day following the man's seven-day process, he brings his *asham* and his *log* of oil, and makes stipulations.

### Stipulation Process

The stipulation is structured as follows: if this man is truly a *metzora*, then this animal is his *asham* and this is his *log* of oil for the *metzora* ritual. If he is not a *metzora*, then the *asham* is reconstituted as a *shelamim nedavah* — a freewill *shelamim*. One might ask: why not designate the animal as a freewill *olah* rather than a *shelamim*? Because an *olah* is entirely burned on the altar — there would be no meat for the *kohanim* to eat, which is wasteful. By making it a *shelamim*, the meat is consumed, and the *kohanim* benefit. A *chatas* is impossible both because it is female and because it requires a specific sin-obligation as its trigger.

### Ritual Procedure

The animal is slaughtered in the north, as required for an *asham* — and since a *shelamim* may also be slaughtered in the north without any violation, the location creates no conflict. Blood is applied to the man's ear (*matan bahonos*), as required for a *metzora asham*, and if it turns out to be a *shelamim*, no harm is done. *Semicha* is performed — Tosafot notes a discussion about whether *semicha* is required for an *asham* at the biblical level or only rabbinically. *Nesachim* — the wine, flour, and oil libations — are brought with the stipulation: if this is a *shelamim*, these are its *nesachim*; if it is an *asham*, they are brought as an independent voluntary *korban*. The *chazeh v'shok* (breast and thigh) are waved, and the meat is eaten for a day and a night — the time restriction of the *asham*.

### Abaye's Challenge

This *mishnah* is Abaye's next challenge to Rava. Rava had insisted that Rabbi Shimon permits limiting the sanctity of *kodshim* only *bedi'eved* — when a problem already exists. But here, Rabbi Shimon is proactively instructing the man to bring an animal that might be a *shelamim* while treating it with all the restrictions of an *asham*, thereby limiting the time it can be eaten *lechatchilah*. Rava's response is that this is not a *lechatchilah* case in the pure sense. True, the *korban* itself is not in a pre-existing problematic state — it is not mixed up or damaged. But the man himself is in a problematic state: he needs to achieve *taharah* and cannot do so without this procedure. *Tikunei gavra shani* — fixing a person's situation is different. Rava's position is that Rabbi Shimon allows the restriction of sanctity when circumstances — either the state of the *korban* or the state of the person — make it necessary. This does not prove that Rabbi Shimon would permit it as a pure *lechatchilah* where no such necessity exists.

## Oil Problem

### Oil Status Question

Having addressed the *asham*-or-*shelamim* question, the *Gemara* turns to the *log* of oil. The *metzora* ritual requires the *kohen* to pour the oil over his palm, sprinkle some toward the *kodesh*, and apply portions to the *metzora*'s ear, thumb, and big toe, before pouring the remainder on the man's head. If the man truly is a *metzora*, this works seamlessly. But if he is not a *metzora*, what becomes of the oil? One cannot simply leave it unsanctified, because bringing unsanctified oil (*chulin*) into the *azarah* and using it in a quasi-ritual context would violate the prohibition of *chulin ba'azarah*.

### Oil Stipulation

The solution, the *Gemara* proposes, is to sanctify the oil on a condition — *bitnai*. If the man is a *metzora*, the oil is sanctified as *metzora* oil. If he is not, it is sanctified as a voluntary offering — in the manner of a *mincha*-like donation of oil. The halacha permits one to bring oil as an independent voluntary *korban*: a *kmitzah* (handful) is taken and burned on the altar, and the remaining oil is eaten by the *kohanim*, much as with any *mincha*. The owner stipulates accordingly: if this man is a *metzora*, this oil serves his *metzora* ritual; if not, it is a voluntary oil offering to the altar. Either way the oil is sanctified, and the violation of *chulin ba'azarah* is avoided.

### Kmitzah/Refill

The *Gemara* then works out the procedural sequence. Since the oil may serve as a voluntary offering, the *kmitzah* must be performed — a handful is taken for the altar. But taking the *kmitzah* first depletes the *log*, and the *metzora* ritual requires a full *log* of oil. The solution is that one refills it, and the *Gemara* cites a *mishnah* in support: *hasar halog ad shelo yatzak* — if the *log* was diminished before the *kohen* poured it onto his palm, *yimalenu* — he refills it. So the procedure is: take the *kmitzah*, burn it on the altar, refill the *log*, and then proceed with the *metzora* ritual of sprinkling and application. The *Gemara* assumes this order — *kmitzah* and burning first, *metzora* ritual second — though the precise reason for this assumption will become significant in the discussion that follows.

## Remnant Oil Problem

### Remnant Rule

The *Gemara* now identifies a serious obstacle to this procedure. There is a general principle: *kol shemimenu l'ishim harei hu b'val taktiru* — anything of which a portion has been offered on the altar fire, the remainder may not itself be burned on the altar. The paradigm case is a *mincha*: once the *kmitzah* has been burned, the *shiyarayim* (remnant) cannot be returned to the altar fire. This is not merely a practical limitation but a formal prohibition.

### Order Dilemma

The *Gemara* traces out the dilemma. If you perform the *kmitzah*, then carry out the *metzora* sprinkling ritual, and only afterward burn the *kmitzah* on the fire — you have introduced the sprinkling between the *kmitzah* and the burning. This creates a different problem: *shiyarayim shechasru bein kmitzah l'haktarah v'ein maktirin et hakometz aleihem* — the remnant oil diminished between the taking of the *kmitzah* and its burning, and one may not burn the *kometz* when the *shiyarayim* have been compromised between those two steps. So burning the *kmitzah* after the sprinkling is impermissible. The alternative — burning the *kmitzah* first, then performing the *metzora* ritual — runs directly into the rule of *kol shemimenu l'ishim*: once part of the oil has gone to the fire, the remaining oil is the *shiyarayim*, and it cannot be used for another ritual act.

### Rashi's View

Rashi's interpretation of the prohibition here is striking. The verse says *lo saktiru mimenu isheh l'Hashem* — once a portion of a sacrificial item has been offered on the altar, the remainder may not be offered. Rashi reads *b'val taktiru* not merely as a prohibition against physically burning the remnant on the altar fire, but as a prohibition against using the remnant in any *mikdash* ritual act that is analogous to offering on the fire. Specifically, Rashi equates the sprinkling of the oil on the *metzora* and toward the *kodesh* with an act of *haktarah* — an act of bringing something before God in the Temple context. On this reading, the sprinkling is not merely a peripheral ritual act but a form of presentation analogous to burning a *korban* on the fire. Therefore, once the *kmitzah* has been burned, the remaining oil — now the *shiyarayim* — cannot be used for the *metzora* ritual any more than it could be burned again on the altar.

## Fuel/Water Loophole

### Fuel Principle

The solution is offered by Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon, drawing on a principle stated by Rabbi Eliezer: *l'reiach nichoach ee ata ma'aleh, aval ata ma'aleh l'shem eitzim* — there are things one may not burn on the altar as a *korban* offering, but which one may nonetheless place on the altar fire as fuel. When something cannot be offered in the conventional sacrificial sense, it may still be fed to the altar fire as mere wood — as a material that sustains the fire rather than as an act of sacrificial presentation.

### Our Application

Applied to the case of the *metzora* oil: if the man turns out not to be a *metzora*, and the oil has already had its *kmitzah* burned, then the remaining oil cannot be used for the *metzora* ritual in any formal sense — that would violate *kol shemimenu l'ishim*. However, according to Rashi, what one does is declare that if the man is not a *metzora*, the subsequent ritual actions — the sprinkling, the application to the ear and head — are not being performed as *korban* rituals at all. They are performed as if one is simply pouring water on the man. Just as burning something on the altar fire as mere fuel (*eitzim*) does not constitute a sacrificial act and therefore does not violate the relevant prohibitions, so too performing the sprinkling as a non-ritual act — as though it were simply water — circumvents the prohibition of using *shiyarayim* for a *mikdash* rite. The stipulation covers both possibilities: if the man is a *metzora*, the ritual is fully valid; if not, the physical acts are carried out but without sacrificial intent, and no prohibition is violated.

## Fuel/Water Loophole (II)

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

Rashi and Tosafot read the loophole differently, and the difference flows from their divergent understandings of what the underlying problem is.

## Remnant Oil Problem (II)

### Tosafot's View

According to Tosafot, the prohibition of *kol shemimenu l'ishim* is not about using the remnant oil for sprinkling — that is never what the *Gemara* was worried about. Rather, Tosafot understands the problem to be about burning on the altar itself. If the oil has been designated as *metzora* oil — sanctified for a particular ritual role — then burning it on the altar (as the *kmitzah*) is analogous to burning the *shiyarayim* of a *mincha* on the altar, which is forbidden. Just as the remnant of a *mincha* may not be burned because it has its own *korban* function (being eaten by the *kohanim*), so too oil designated for the *metzora* ritual may not be burned on the altar, because it has its own assigned ritual function. The loophole, on Tosafot's reading, is that the burning of the oil in the *kmitzah* is done not as a sacrificial act with respect to *metzora* oil, but as mere fuel — *l'shem eitzim* — thereby removing it from the category of the forbidden. According to Rashi, the loophole addresses the sprinkling: what would otherwise be a prohibited use of *shiyarayim* in a ritual act is reframed as mere water. According to Tosafot, the loophole addresses the burning: what would otherwise be a prohibited burning of ritually designated oil is reframed as mere fuel. Either way, the mechanism of treating a prohibited act as either fuel or water enables the entire dual procedure — *kmitzah* plus *metzora* ritual — to be carried out without violation.

---

---

# Zevachim 77

## Metzora Oil Procedures

### Metzora Stipulation

The daf opens by resuming a discussion that arose in passing from the broader theme of *mevi'in kodashim l'veit hapsul*. The case under examination involves a person uncertain whether he is a *metzora*. He brings an *asham* and stipulates that if he is not in fact a *metzora*, the animal shall serve as a *shelamim*. The animal is then treated with the stringencies of both categories simultaneously. The Gemara had been working through the practical consequences of this arrangement, particularly regarding the *log* of oil that accompanies the *metzora* purification rite. The conclusion reached was that one brings the *log* and treats it both as the oil used in the *metzora* purification and as a *nedavah* free-will offering — functioning similarly to a *minchah*, from which a *kometz* is taken and placed on the *mizbeach*.

### Kli Sharet Sanctification

The Gemara had to work out how both functions could be served by a single *log*. According to Tosafos, the difficulty is that *metzora* oil may not be burned on the altar as an *isheh*, since it was designated for a different sacrificial purpose — the prohibition of *kodesh mimenu l'ishin*. The resolution was that the oil is burned on the altar as fuel, not as an offering proper, to cover the scenario in which it turns out to be *metzora* oil. The *log* is then refilled, and that replenished oil is used in the sprinkling ceremony.

Rashi posed an independent difficulty: once some of the oil has already been offered on the altar, if this turns out to have been *nedavah* oil, how may the remnant on the altar be used in the subsequent ritual? To this the Gemara answered that in the scenario where the oil is not needed as *metzora* oil, one stipulates that it be treated as inconsequential — effectively like water — and it carries no further significance.

### Extra Oil Problem

The Gemara at the top of 77a now presses further: *v'ika shiyayim d'ba'i michlinehu — v'ika hach purta d'lo kamitzei lei*. After all the procedures are completed, what is done with the remnant of the oil? Normally it would be eaten. But recall that at the second stage, extra oil was poured in — oil needed in case the man is indeed a *metzora*. In the scenario where he turns out not to be a *metzora* and the oil functions as *nedavah* oil, the *kometz* was taken only from what was originally there. The additional oil that was poured in never had a *kometz* taken from it. How, then, may that extra oil be eaten together with the remainder? The *kohanim* would be eating what might be *chullin* mixed with *kodesh*.

### Redemption Solution

The Gemara's answer is *d'parik lei* — one redeems the added portion. In the scenario where the man is not a *metzora*, that extra oil was added after the *nedavah* process was complete. One stipulates at the time of adding it: if this man is a *metzora*, let this oil be fully sanctified through the *kli sharet* and used for the *metzora* ritual; if he is not a *metzora*, I do not intend for the *kli sharet* to sanctify it, and after the *metzora* procedure it will be redeemed on money, which money will go toward another *nedavah*.

Rashi notes an immediate difficulty with this redemption: once something has been sanctified in a *kli sharet*, it cannot simply be redeemed. But the Gemara clarifies that *kli sharet eino mekadesh ela l'daat* — a service vessel sanctifies only when one intends it to do so. The stipulation therefore controls whether the vessel sanctifies at all.

The Gemara then raises the problem of *chullin* in the *azarah*. Having redeemed the added portion, one now has a mixture of ninety percent *nedavah* oil that has had its *kometz* taken, and ten percent *chullin*. Does bringing *chullin* into the *azarah* constitute a violation? The Gemara considers two possibilities: if one redeems the oil while it is outside the *azarah*, *ipsulei b'yotzei* — the whole mixture becomes invalid by having left the sacred precincts. If one redeems it while inside the *azarah*, the oil was brought in while sanctified; it became *chullin* only subsequently, while already inside — *v'chullin mimeila havyan*. Since one did not carry *chullin* into the *azarah* but rather carried in sanctified oil that only later became *chullin*, the transgression is not triggered.

### Shimen Oil Nedavah

One final difficulty presents itself. The entire scheme depends on the stipulation that if the man is not a *metzora*, the oil will function as a *nedavah*. But Rabbi Shimon — whose ruling this mishna follows — himself holds that one may not *lechatchila* donate oil as a *nedavah*. How can this stipulation be part of the procedure at all? The Gemara answers: *tikunei gavra shani* — saving a person from uncertain *metzora* status is a special circumstance. Since *bedi'avad* an oil *nedavah* is certainly valid, and since we are constrained by the need to provide this person with a legitimate path forward, even Rabbi Shimon would permit it here.

---

## Asham Talui Question

### Talui Alternative

Rav Rechumi was sitting before Ravina and transmitted the following question in the name of Rav Huna bar Tachlifa. Setting aside the oil entirely and returning to the stipulation regarding the animal itself: the mishna has the person stipulate that if he is not a *metzora*, the *asham* shall be a *shelamim*. Rav Huna bar Tachlifa asks — why go all the way to a *shelamim*? Why not stipulate: if I am a *metzora*, this is my *asham metzora*, and if I am not a *metzora*, this shall be an *asham talui*? An *asham talui* is the guilt-offering brought for a doubtful transgression. Indeed, there is an opinion of Rabbi Eliezer that since one can never entirely exclude the possibility of having sinned unknowingly, one may bring an *asham talui* on any day without any concrete basis for concern. Why does the mishna not employ this option and remain entirely within the category of *asham*?

The inference drawn was: *shma mina man tanna d'palig alei d'Rabbi Eliezer Rabbi Shimon* — since the mishna (authored according to Rabbi Shimon's view) does not offer the *asham talui* option, we may deduce that Rabbi Shimon rejects Rabbi Eliezer's position and holds that an *asham talui* requires a concrete, identified basis for concern. That is why he had to resort to a *shelamim* instead.

### Shimon Rejects Talui

This inference seemed solid. The *asham talui* option would have been logically available; the fact that it was passed over implies a principled rejection of the view that one may bring an *asham talui* without a concrete cause.

### Sheep vs. Ram

Ravina responded sharply: *Torah Torah* — what happened to basic Torah knowledge? *Imi b'dachrei michalfei lach?* Did you confuse a sheep and a ram? An *asham metzora* is a one-year-old sheep. An *asham talui* is a two-year-old ram. One cannot stipulate that the same animal serve as either one, because they are entirely different animals. The only legitimate alternative use for a sheep is a *shelamim*, since a *shelamim* may also be a sheep. The option of *asham talui* was never available not because of any position regarding Rabbi Eliezer's ruling, but simply because the species and age requirements are incompatible. It is a striking reminder that even a great *amora*, absorbed in theoretical possibilities, can momentarily overlook the concrete specifics of *halacha*.

---

## Chatat Olah Mix

### Limbs Mixed

With the digression concluded, the Gemara moves to the next mishna, which shifts from animals mixed together to the cut limbs of sacrifices mixed together. The mishna states: *eivrei chatat shenitarvu b'eivrei olah* — the limbs of a *chatat*, which the *kohanim* would eat, become mixed with the limbs of an *olah*, which are to be burned on the altar. The problem is acute: the *kohanim* cannot eat the mixture, lest they eat *olah* meat; but they cannot simply burn it all on the altar, since that would mean burning *chatat* meat, which is designated for the *kohanim* to eat — a violation of the prohibition of *kodesh mimenu l'ishin*.

### Eliezer Firewood

Rabbi Eliezer says: *yitein l'ma'ala* — go ahead and place it all on the altar fire. *V'ro'eh ani et b'sar hachatat milma'ala k'ilu hen eitzim* — I regard any *chatat* meat placed on the fire not as an offering to God but as fuel. The *olah* meat is an offering; the *chatat* meat is merely combustible material feeding the fire. Rabbi Eliezer is not troubled by the destruction of *chatat* meat per se — the concern is only that one may appear to be offering something to God that is not designated as an offering, and that concern is resolved by declaring it to be fuel.

### Sages Notar

The Sages disagree. One cannot simply relabel *chatat* meat as firewood; meat placed on the altar fire is problematic if it has no sacrificial standing and was designated for eating. Instead they say: *te'avor tzuratan v'yeitzu l'veit hasreifah* — allow the mixture to remain until the following morning, by which point it will have the status of *notar* (sacrificial leftovers that have become time-invalid), and then burn it all outside the *Beit HaMikdash* — at the *beit hasreifah*.

The obvious question presents itself: is not allowing something to become *notar* itself a violation of *lo totiru mimenu*? The Gemara does not press this point, apparently assuming that since there is no permissible alternative course of action, one is in the position of an *onus* — coerced by circumstance — and the principle of *shev v'al ta'aseh* applies. One's hands are tied halachically, and the *notar* status arises without any affirmative act of transgression.

---

## Pasuk Exegesis

### Eliezer Derivation

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Eliezer?* What is his textual basis? The answer is the verse in Leviticus 2:11–12: *ki kol se'or v'chol dvash lo taktiru mimenu isheh l'Hashem; korban reishis takrivu osam l'Hashem v'el hamizbe'ach lo ya'alu l'rei'ach nicho'ach*. The verse forbids burning *chametz* and honey (*se'or v'chol dvash*) as an offering. They may be brought as *bikurim* — first-fruit offerings — but may not be put on the altar. Crucially, the verse says *lo ya'alu l'rei'ach nicho'ach* — they shall not ascend as a pleasing odor. Rabbi Eliezer derives from the qualification *l'rei'ach nicho'ach* that the prohibition applies only when something is being offered for its sacrificial purpose, as a pleasing odor to God. *L'rei'ach nicho'ach ee atah ma'aleh aval atah ma'aleh l'shem etzim* — for the purpose of a pleasing odor you may not place it, but for the purpose of firewood you may.

On this reading, the more general prohibition of *kodesh mimenu l'ishin* — which forbids burning the remnant of something from which a part was already offered — should similarly yield to the *l'rei'ach nicho'ach* qualification. If one burns the *chatat* meat not as an offering but as fuel, no prohibition is violated.

### Sages Counter

The Sages read the verse differently. They invoke the word *osam* — "those" — in the phrase *korban reishis takrivu osam l'Hashem*: *mi'eit Rachmana osam* — the Torah restricts the *l'rei'ach nicho'ach* leniency specifically to those items the verse is literally discussing — *se'or v'dvash*, chametz and honey (and by extension the *shtei halechem* of Shavuot and *bikurim*). These, if placed on the altar as firewood, are permitted. But the prohibition derived by inference from *mimenu isheh l'Hashem* — which forbids burning the remainder of something from which an *isheh* was offered — is not subject to the firewood leniency. The word *osam* delimits the leniency to the explicit subject of the verse.

The result is paradoxical: the items explicitly prohibited by the verse — chametz and honey — may be placed on the altar as firewood; the items prohibited only by inference — remnants of sacrifices — may not. It is counterintuitive, yet this is the Sages' position.

### Eliezer Reply

Rabbi Eliezer responds by redeploying the word *osam*, but in the opposite direction: *osam hu d'lo aleh l'rei'ach nicho'ach aval atah ma'aleh l'shem etzim — aval midi achrinei lo*. He reads *osam* as restricting the ramp prohibition (*el hamizbeach lo ya'alu*) rather than the firewood leniency. The chametz and honey — those items explicitly named — may not be placed even on the ramp of the altar, as the verse includes the ramp in *el hamizbe'ach*. But items prohibited only by inference, such as the remnants of a sacrifice, are forbidden only on the altar proper, not on the ramp.

The Sages, in turn, read *osam* as yielding two simultaneous teachings: first, that the ramp prohibition is stricter for chametz and honey than for inferred categories; and second, that the firewood leniency is available only for chametz and honey and not for sacrifice remnants. *Tarti shma mina* — both conclusions are derived from the same word.

Rabbi Eliezer's position, once one accepts that the verse teaches the firewood leniency at all, has its own internal logic: if firewood is permitted for chametz and honey, it should be equally permitted for sacrifice remnants. The Sages insist that the word *osam* confines the leniency exclusively to the explicit subjects of the verse.

---

## Explicit vs. Inferred

### Rashi Strictness

The distinction the Gemara draws is between the explicit prohibition in the verse and the prohibition derived by inference. For the explicit subject of the verse — chametz and honey — the prohibition of placing them on the altar is treated more severely: it extends even to the ramp. For items whose prohibition is derived from the verse by inference — such as the remnants of a sacrifice — the prohibition is confined to the altar proper and does not extend to the ramp.

### Sages Firewood

According to the Sages, the firewood leniency flows in the opposite direction. Because the verse says *l'rei'ach nicho'ach*, limiting the prohibition to a sacrificial-offering context, this leniency applies only to the explicit subject of the verse — chametz and honey. One who places chametz or honey on the altar as firewood does not violate the prohibition. But one who burns the remnants of a sacrifice as firewood does violate it, because the firewood leniency was never extended by the verse to inferred prohibitions. This produces the ironic structure: what is strictly forbidden by explicit text may nevertheless be placed as firewood; what is forbidden only by inference may not.

---

## Beraita Levels

### Three Severity

The Gemara notes: *matnisin d'lo k'hai tanna* — our mishna does not align with the following *tanna*, as preserved in a *beraita*. The *beraita* presents a three-tiered structure of cases rather than the two-tiered structure of our mishna. The three cases are: (1) limbs of a *chatat* mixed with limbs of an *olah*; (2) limbs of an unblemished *olah* mixed with limbs of a blemished one (*ba'alat mum*); (3) limbs of a kosher animal mixed with limbs of an animal used in bestiality (*rovea* or *nirba*). Each level represents an escalating degree of disqualification — respectively: a technical halachic incompatibility, a physical-aesthetic blemish, and a moral-sexual corruption.

### Agreement Extremes

On the two extremes, the *beraita* records no dispute. At the lenient end, where *chatat* and *olah* limbs are mixed, both Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages agree that one may proceed: the limbs from the inappropriate category are treated as firewood. At the strict end, where an animal involved in bestiality is part of the mixture, all agree that nothing may be placed on the altar — not even as firewood.

### Debate Locus

The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, according to this *beraita*, falls in the middle case: unblemished and blemished *olah* limbs mixed together. Here Rabbi Eliezer permits treating the blemished limbs as firewood and placing everything on the altar, while the Sages forbid it. Our mishna, by contrast, has Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages debating by the *chatat-olah* mixture and has Rabbi Eliezer himself conceding by the blemished case. The *beraita* thus represents a different tradition of where exactly the debate is located.

---

## Aesthetic vs. Moral

### Huna Minor Blemish

The Gemara now asks: according to the *beraita*'s version, what distinguishes the blemished animal from the one involved in bestiality, such that the firewood leniency applies in one case but not the other? Rav Huna offers an answer: *bedukin sheba-ayin va-aliba d'Rabbi Akiva* — the case involves minor ocular blemishes of the eye, and is ruled according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that such minor blemishes, once they have ascended the altar, need not be removed (*im alu lo yerdu*). Because this type of blemish is not a severe invalidity, the animal retains a degree of fitness for the altar, which distinguishes it from an animal involved in bestiality, which is absolutely disqualified.

### Firewood Challenge

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *eima d'amar Rabbi Akiva bedi'avad; lechatchila mi amar?* Rabbi Akiva's ruling that such an animal need not be removed applies only *bedi'avad* — after the fact. He does not permit placing it on the altar *lechatchila*. The only thing that would permit it *lechatchila* in this case is the firewood rationale. But if firewood is what permits it, then what functional difference is there between a blemished animal and one used in bestiality? Both are equally unfit *lechatchila*.

### Pappa Ramp

Rav Pappa proposes an alternative resolution: *hacha bemai askinan kegon she-alu agabei kevesh* — the case involves limbs that were already placed on the ramp. Once they are on the ramp, Rabbi Akiva's rule applies, and they need not be removed. This permits moving them to the fire — and this logic applies to the minor-blemish case but not to the bestiality case. Hence the distinction.

### Exegesis Mum

The Gemara rejects Rav Pappa's solution: *ei hachi afilu beinihu* — if that is the reasoning, it has nothing to do with the mixture at all. If a minor-blemished animal's limbs were already on the ramp, Rabbi Akiva would permit moving them to the fire even without any mixture being involved. The issue of *ta'arovet* — mixture — would be irrelevant.

The Gemara therefore turns to exegesis: *ella ta'ima d'Rabbi Eliezer mi'eit Rachmana mum bam*. The verse reads: *ki mashchatam bahem mum bam lo yeiratze lachem* — "for their corruption is in them; their blemish is in them (*mum bam*); they will not be accepted for you." The emphasis is on *bam* — in them, when the blemish is specifically and identifiably located in the animal being offered. The derivation is: *hu d'lo yeratzu ha yedei ta'arovet yeratzu* — when the blemish is specifically identified in a particular animal, it may not be offered; but when the pieces are mixed and the blemish cannot be pinpointed to any particular limb, the restriction does not apply and the mixture may be offered.

### Eliezer Acceptable

This is a striking turn in the Gemara's reasoning. The position attributed to Rabbi Eliezer is no longer that the blemished limbs are placed on the altar *as firewood* — it is that when the limbs are mixed, the blemished pieces are actually *acceptable as a legitimate offering*. *Mum bam* — the blemish is in them — is what disqualifies. When it is no longer possible to identify which piece bears the blemish, the disqualification lapses, and the mixed pieces may be offered as *korbanot mamash*.

### Sages Blemish

The Sages counter with their own reading of *mum bam*: the word *bam* does not mean "when specifically identified in them." Rather, it means "while the blemish is present in them." The verse is saying: as long as the blemish exists and has not passed, the animal is unacceptable. Once the blemish resolves on its own, the animal becomes acceptable. This is a ruling about the temporal persistence of the blemish, not about whether the blemish is individually identifiable. The mixture, in the Sages' view, changes nothing.

### Eliezer Bam

Rabbi Eliezer presses the linguistic argument further. The verse uses two words: *bam* (in them) and elsewhere *bahem* (in them, plural). *Mibam bahem* — one word addresses the case where the blemish is present and the animal is specifically identified (*bahem*), while the other addresses the case where the blemish is present but the pieces are mixed and no single piece is individually identified as the blemished one (*bam*). Each word carries a distinct teaching, and together they establish the distinction Rabbi Eliezer draws between an identified and an unidentified blemish.

The Sages do not accept this as two separate teachings: *bam bahem lo darshi* — they do not derive independent rulings from the two phrasings.

### Firewood Compromise

Having established Rabbi Eliezer's position that the mixed blemished pieces are actually *kosher* as an offering, the Gemara asks from the Sages' perspective: even if you reject Rabbi Eliezer's textual argument, why not at least permit the firewood rationale as a compromise? The Sages respond: *hacha meisi hatam lo meisi* — here it is disgusting (*ma'is*); there (by *chatat* and *olah*) it was not disgusting. The aesthetic repugnance of having pieces from a blemished animal on the altar prevents the Sages from applying even the firewood leniency in this case.

---

## Assumption Strategy

### Limbs Blemished

We now reach the next mishna, which addresses precisely the case that the *beraita*'s version of the debate — and our mishna's version as well — agrees is problematic: *eivrei olah temimah* mixed with *eivrei ba'alat mum*. Unblemished *olah* limbs are mixed with limbs from a blemished *olah*. Since the blemish renders those pieces *ma'is* and the firewood leniency is unavailable (according to the Sages) or unnecessary (according to Rabbi Eliezer, who considers the mixed pieces actually valid), the question is what practical course of action the *kohanim* should follow.

### Bad Already

Rabbi Eliezer says: *im kareiv rosh echad meihem yikrevu kol haroshim kulam* — if one head from the group has already been placed on the altar fire, the rest of the heads may be offered as well. Similarly, if the legs of one animal have been offered, all the legs may follow. The logic is an assumption strategy: since something was already placed on the altar without prior knowledge of which piece was blemished, we retroactively assume that the blemished piece was the one already offered. This removes the identification of the blemish from the remaining pieces, and they may now legitimately be brought up. Rabbi Eliezer requires some prior act to trigger this assumption — the act of having already offered one piece — because without it, the *ma'is* concern stands fully.

### Sages Burn

The Sages reject the assumption strategy entirely: *afilu karvu kulam chutz me'echad meihem yeitzei l'veit hasreifah* — even if all but one have already been offered, the remaining piece must be taken out and burned at the *beit hasreifah*. No matter how many have preceded it, one may never say regarding the last piece: the blemished one must have already been done. The Sages do not permit retroactive assumptions to override the concrete uncertainty that remains. So long as one piece remains unaccounted for, it might be the blemished one, and it may not be placed on the altar *lechatchila*.

---

## Assumption Strategy (II)

### Pairs Requirement

Rav Elazar clarifies Rabbi Eliezer's position: *lo hichshir Rabbi Eliezer ela shnayim shnayim* — Rabbi Eliezer permits proceeding only when the limbs are brought up two at a time. When one brings a pair, two considerations operate simultaneously: the general assumption that the blemished animal was already offered in an earlier round, and additionally, the knowledge that of any given pair, at least one is certainly from an unblemished animal, which lends support to treating the other as likely acceptable as well.

### One Pair

Rabbi Yirmiyah challenges this from the mishna itself: the Sages say that even if all but one have been offered, that one must go to the *beit hasreifah* — implying that Rabbi Eliezer would permit offering that final single piece. But if Rabbi Eliezer requires pairs, how can he permit offering a lone remaining piece? Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Tachlifa resolves this: *mai echad zug echad* — when the mishna says "one remains," it means one *pair* remains, not one individual limb. The mishna, read carefully, always envisions the pieces being brought in pairs, and Rabbi Eliezer's leniency applies exclusively in that configuration.

---

## Blood Mixtures

### Sight Principle

The Gemara now transitions to a new and far-reaching mishna dealing with blood mixed with other liquids. The fundamental conceptual principle established here is that when dealing with mixtures in a non-food context, the operative sense is sight rather than taste. In the laws of food, a prohibited substance mixed into a permitted one is evaluated by whether it imparts flavor — *ta'am*. In the sacrificial context, where the blood is not food, flavor is irrelevant. What determines whether the blood retains its identity — and may therefore be thrown on the altar — is whether it remains visually detectable: *mar'it dam*.

### Blood Water

The first case: *dam shenitarev bemayim* — sacrificial blood mixed with water. *Im yesh bo mar'it dam* — if the appearance of blood is still discernible, *kasher* — it is valid and may be thrown on the altar. This is the paradigm case establishing the *mar'it dam* principle.

### Blood Wine

The mishna then presents a significant *chidush*: *nitarev beyayin* — the blood is mixed with wine. Since wine is a dark red liquid, the blood may no longer be visually detectable even if substantial blood is present. Does the blood simply lose its identity? The mishna rules: *ro'in oto ke'ilu hu mayim* — we regard the wine *as if it were water*, and ask: had this been water, would the blood have been visible? If the answer is yes, the blood is deemed present even within the wine, and the mixture may be thrown on the altar.

This is a striking halachic fiction. In reality, the blood is not visible. Yet the mishna permits treating it as present by applying a counterfactual: *had it been water*. What authorizes this counterfactual reasoning as a basis for leniency is one of the distinctive features of this sugyah.

### Blood Blood

The same conditional visibility rule applies when blood is mixed with the blood of non-sacrificial animals — whether domesticated animals (*behema*) or deer (*chaya*). *Ro'in oto ke'ilu hu mayim* — again one asks whether the *korban* blood would be detectable had the other liquid been water. If yes, the blood is treated as present and the mixture is valid.

This has a parallel in the laws of *kashrut*: when a prohibited substance falls into a permitted substance of the same type — as when *treif* chicken falls into kosher chicken soup — taste cannot distinguish them. Nevertheless, the rule of *min b'mino* requires us to evaluate the mixture as if the two were different substances, which preserves the forbidden item's identity and prevents it from being nullified by the majority. Here the *mishna* applies the same logic in the lenient direction: evaluate as if the opaque liquid were transparent water, and if the blood would be visible under those conditions, treat it as present.

### Blood Blood

The same conditional visibility rule extends to blood mixed with the blood of non-sacrificial animals or deer: *ro'in oto ke'ilu hu mayim*, whether the *korban* blood would have been detectable had the other liquid been water. If yes, the blood is treated as present and the mixture may be offered.

### Yehuda Identity

Rabbi Yehuda goes further: *ein dam mevatel dam* — blood never nullifies blood. Even if the amount of *korban* blood is so small relative to the other blood that, had the mixture been with water, the *korban* blood would not have been visible, Rabbi Yehuda holds that when blood is mixed with blood, the *korban* blood retains its identity absolutely. Blood and blood can never effect mutual nullification.

### Spill Invalid

If the sacrificial blood becomes mixed with blood from invalid sacrifices — *dam pesulin* — even if the *korban* blood is still deemed present by the *mar'it dam* criterion, the mixture may not be thrown on the altar, because the blood of invalid sacrifices may not be offered. The ruling is *yishafech la'amah* — the mixture is spilled into the channel that carries it out of the *Beit HaMikdash*. Similarly, if the *korban* blood is mixed with *dam hatamtzit* — the residual blood that drains out after the life-force blood has been collected, which has no sacrificial standing — *yishafech la'amah* as well.

### Eliezer Permit

Rabbi Eliezer dissents regarding the mixture with *dam hatamtzit*: *Rabbi Eliezer machshir* — Rabbi Eliezer permits throwing this mixture on the altar. The precise grounds for his leniency in this case will require further analysis.

### Halakha Validity

The *halakha* as stated in the mishna is that *im lo nimlach venatan kasher* — if one did not pause to deliberate and simply threw the mixture on the altar, the offering is valid after the fact. Since the *korban* blood is still deemed present according to the *mar'it dam* criterion or its counterfactual extension, the act achieves its sacrificial purpose *bedi'avad*. The debate between the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer concerns whether one is permitted to proceed *lechatchila* with the mixture that includes *dam hatamtzit*.

The conceptual architecture of this mishna is of broad significance for the laws of mixtures throughout *halacha*. Two features distinguish it from the food-law model: first, validity is determined by sight rather than taste; and second — and more strikingly — the counterfactual visibility test is applied to create leniency rather than stringency. In food law, the analogous reasoning (*min b'mino*) preserves the identity of a forbidden substance in order to prohibit. Here, the same structural reasoning preserves the identity of a desired substance in order to permit. This sugya will be taken up further in the following session.

---

---

# Zevachim 78

## Blood Mixtures

### Mishnah Introduction

The *mishna* at the bottom of 77b introduces a discussion of what happens when the blood of a sacrifice becomes mixed with other liquids — a topic that connects directly to the broader *sugya* of *bitul*, the halachic nullification of forbidden or otherwise problematic substances that occurs when they are mixed into a larger quantity of a permissible substance. The classic analogy from the laws of *kashrut* is a drop of *chazir* soup that falls into one's chicken soup. But in the context of our *mishna*, the situation is reversed: rather than wanting the admixture to lose its identity, we want it to retain its identity, because the blood of a *korban* must be present and detectable in order to be placed on the *mizbeach*.

### Dam b'Mayim

The *mishna* rules: *dam shenitarev bemayim* — if blood of a sacrifice becomes mixed with water — *im yesh bo mareh dam kasher*, if the mixture still has the appearance of blood, the blood is considered present and may be placed on the altar. The precise meaning of "appearance of blood" is somewhat ambiguous: does it mean that the blood is detectable through the reddish hue it lends the water, or that the mixture as a whole must actually resemble blood? The former reading seems more plausible given the context, though the *mishna* leaves it incompletely defined.

What is particularly striking here is the criterion employed. When it comes to food, the operative standard is *ta'am* — taste. If a forbidden substance can still be tasted in the mixture, it is considered present; if it cannot be tasted, it is *batel*. The principle of *ta'am ke-ikar*, that the taste of a forbidden thing counts like the thing itself, is well established. Yet here, in the domain of blood placed on the altar, the *mishna* applies a different standard altogether: *mareh*, appearance. The reason for this distinction is rooted in the nature of the act. Sight is our primary mode of perceiving and categorizing the world. When the question is whether something is present before us to be offered or used — as with blood on the altar or water for a *mikvah* — we rely on how it looks, not how it tastes. Only when dealing with foodstuffs, where the act of eating is central, does the sense of taste become the relevant criterion. This is an important general principle: appearance governs presence in the domain of ritual use; taste governs presence in the domain of consumption.

### Dam b'Yayin

The *mishna* continues: *nitarev beyayin* — if the sacrificial blood becomes mixed with wine. Here the difficulty is immediate. Wine is red and dark, and the blood can no longer be detected by sight within it. Yet the *mishna* rules: *ro'in oto ke'ilu hu mayim*, you look at the wine as if it were water.
