The blood is then assessed hypothetically: had this been water, would the blood have been visible? If yes, the blood is considered still present and may be placed on the altar.

This ruling is striking in two respects. First, it employs the legal fiction of *ro'in* — treating one substance as though it were something else — in order to reach a *lenient* result. In the normal laws of *kashrut*, the analogous device is used to be strict. If a drop of *treif* chicken soup falls into kosher chicken soup, the rabbis say: had this been *chazir*, it could be tasted — and therefore even though it cannot be tasted now, it is still considered present, rendering the mixture forbidden. That is a rabbinic stringency, imposed because the principle of *min b'mino* — like-with-like mixtures — would ordinarily permit *bitul* by majority at the biblical level. Here the *mishna* applies the same logical structure — "had this been a different medium, it would be detectable" — but arrives at a leniency: the blood remains present and the *korban* is valid.

The deeper implication is significant. This suggests that the concept of treating *min b'mino* as *eino mino* — looking at identical substances as though they were different — may have a biblical foundation, not merely a rabbinic one. If we can use *ro'in* to be lenient at the level of *korbanot*, it implies that the technique is grounded in something more fundamental than a rabbinic decree of strictness.

### Dam b'Dam

The *mishna* extends the same logic to the case of blood mixed with blood: *nitarav bedam behemah bedam chulin* — if the sacrificial blood becomes mixed with the blood of a non-sanctified animal, or *bedam hachayah*, the blood of a wild animal. Here too, one cannot visually distinguish the two, and the *mishna* rules *ro'ehu ke'ilu hu mayim*: you regard the mixture as if it were water, and assess whether the sacrificial blood would have been detectable under those conditions. If yes, it may be placed on the altar.

Logically, if we permit this analysis for blood-and-wine mixtures, we must permit it for blood-and-blood mixtures as well. The principle of *ro'in* applies regardless of the medium.

### Rabbi Yehudah's Din

At the top of 78a, Rabbi Yehudah introduces a further ruling: *ein dam mevatel dam* — blood does not nullify blood. It is important to understand the direction of this ruling. The *chachamim* hold that even by *dam b'dam* mixtures, there is a point at which the sacrificial blood becomes *batel* — when the proportion of non-sacrificial blood is so great that, hypothetically viewing the mixture as water, the sacrificial blood would no longer be visible. Rabbi Yehudah disagrees. He holds that since both components are genuinely blood — not merely similar in appearance, but identical in substance — there can be no *bitul* at all. The logic is that *bitul* requires the predominance of one type of thing over another. When you have wine and blood, you can say there is so much wine that there is no longer any blood here. But when you have blood and blood, you cannot say there is so much blood that there is no longer any blood — it is all blood, and therefore the sacrificial blood remains perpetually present.

This ruling of Rabbi Yehudah is, paradoxically, a leniency in the laws of *korbanot*, even though Rabbi Yehudah is characteristically stringent in the laws of *kashrut*. The underlying principle is the same in both cases — *min b'mino lo batel*, that like-with-like cannot nullify — but the practical consequence differs by context. In *kashrut*, this prevents a forbidden substance from becoming *batel*; in *korbanot*, it ensures the sacrificial blood is never considered absent.

Two additional cases complete the *mishna*. If the blood becomes mixed with *dam psulim*, the blood of an invalid sacrifice such as a *ba'al mum*, the whole mixture must be poured into the drain, *yishafech la'amah*, even though Rabbi Yehudah would otherwise hold the sacrificial blood to be ever-present. The blood of invalid sacrifices may not go on the altar under any circumstances. Similarly, *bedam hatamtzit* — blood that drains from an animal after the initial spurting, which is not halachically considered life-blood even if from a *korban* — the ruling is likewise to drain it away. Rabbi Eliezer is lenient regarding the *hatamtzit* case, and both the *mishna* and the *Gemara* note that *im lo nimlach venatan kasher*: if one did not inquire and went ahead and placed the blood on the altar, the *korban* is valid after the fact, since the principle that the sacrificial blood is not *batel* was not violated. The rabbis' restriction on placing such blood on the altar is thus a purely procedural concern, not a statement about the blood's presence.

---

## Chozer ve'Ni'ur

### Water vs. Blood

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the ruling of the *mishna* — that blood mixed with water is valid if it still has the appearance of blood — applies specifically to the scenario *shenaflo mayim le-toch dam*: water falling into the blood. In that case, even if water is progressively added until the blood is barely visible, the blood is never *batel* so long as it retains some appearance of blood. But *aval nafal dam le-toch mayim* — if it was the blood that fell into the water, drop by drop — a different analysis applies. Each successive drop falls into a body of water so large that the drop is invisible and thus *batel*. When after many drops the accumulated blood finally renders the water visibly reddish, does the blood "come back"? Rabbi Yochanan holds that since each individual drop was *batel rishon rishon* as it fell in, those drops remain *batel*, and the eventual visible redness does not retroactively restore them.

It is important to note that this distinction does not conflict with the *mishna*, which is simply discussing what happens when a mixture of blood and water exists at a given moment, without specifying how the admixture came about. The *mishna*'s *pshat* is that all the liquid was mixed at once, in which case there is no question of sequence. Rabbi Yochanan is addressing a separate scenario of incremental addition.

### Reawakening Principle

This brings us to the principle of *chozer ve-ni'ur* — does nullification reverse when proportions shift? In general halacha, the answer is yes. If drops of *chazir* soup fall one by one into kosher chicken soup and are each initially *batel* due to the large proportion of kosher liquid, but accumulate until the *chazir* becomes detectable, the mixture becomes forbidden. The *chazir* "reawakens" once it reaches detectable proportions. This is the ordinary rule of *chozer ve-ni'ur*.

Why then does Rabbi Yochanan hold that by sacrificial blood, the *bitul* is not reversed when the mixture becomes reddish again? The answer lies in the principle of *dichuy*: once something in the domain of *korbanot* has been "pushed away" — rendered unfit — it cannot revert to fitness. The drops of blood that were *batel*, were in a state in which they could not be offered on the altar. They are *nidcha*. Even if the proportions later shift and the blood becomes visible again, the *dichuy* is irreversible in the context of sacrifices.

### Dichuy Exception

Rav Papa adds an important qualification: *ule-inyan kisui eino ken* — by the *mitzvah* of *kisui hadam*, covering the blood after slaughter, the same principle does not apply. If blood drips progressively into a puddle of water and the first drops are *batel* and invisible, but eventually enough blood accumulates to be visible, one may still perform *kisui hadam* on the mixture. Even though the first drops were temporarily *batel* and in a state where *kisui* could not have been performed on them, this does not constitute *dichuy* in the relevant sense. The reason is *she-ein dichuy be-mitzvos* — the concept of *dichuy* applies only to sacrifices, not to *mitzvot* generally. In the realm of *mitzvot*, there is no principle that once an object was temporarily unfit for a *mitzvah* it cannot later be used. Similarly, in the laws of *kashrut*, if drops of *chazir* soup accumulate until the *chazir* becomes detectable, the mixture becomes forbidden — the *chazir* has "reawakened" — because *dichuy* does not apply there either. The sole exception is *korbanot*, where *dichuy* is operative and once blood has been *batel* and *nidcha* it cannot be restored.

---

## Mixed Prohibitions

### Piggul/Notar/Tamei

Reish Lakish introduces a striking ruling: if one mixes together *piggul* (sacrificial meat rendered invalid through improper intention), *notar* (sacrificial meat left past its time), and *tamei* (ritually impure meat) — three distinct *issurim*, each carrying the penalty of *karet* — and then eats from the mixture, one is *patur*, exempt. The reason given is *ee efshar she-lo yarbeh min al chaveiro ve-yvatlenu*: it is impossible that one type of forbidden substance does not predominate over another and thereby nullify it. Since the three are roughly equal, whatever *issur* one focuses on, two-thirds of the mixture is not that particular *issur*, and two-thirds nullifies the one-third. The same logic applies to each of the three in turn, so none of them can be established as having been eaten in the requisite amount.

### Three Inferences

The *Gemara* derives three distinct principles — *shema mina telat* — from Reish Lakish's ruling.

The first and most fundamental: *issurin mevatlin zeh et zeh* — prohibitions can nullify one another. One does not need *heter*, permitted substance, to nullify *issur*. The standard paradigm of *bitul* imagines a large quantity of permitted material overwhelming a small amount of forbidden material. Reish Lakish tells us this is not a necessary condition. The analytical structure is simpler: we have *neveilah* and non-*neveilah*; since two-thirds of the mixture is non-*neveilah*, the *neveilah* is *batel*. The "non-*neveilah*" does not need to be kosher — it can itself be another *issur*. This is a significant *chiddush*.

The second inference: *noten ta'am berov lav de-oraita* — even if a substance imparts taste, as long as it is a minority it is nullified at the biblical level. This is the *Gemara*'s initial reading of the case. However, as we will see, the *Gemara* will walk this back: since *piggul*, *notar*, and *tamei* are all varieties of the same meat, they all taste identical, and the case is one of *min b'mino* where taste is irrelevant and majority alone governs. The real *chiddush* remains the first one.

The third inference: *hatra'at safek lo shemah hatra'ah* — a doubtful warning does not constitute a valid *hatra'ah* for purposes of lashes. This is where Rashi and Tosafot invest considerable effort in interpretation, because the case as described does not immediately present an obvious scenario of doubtful warning.

### Rashi's Approach

The way Rashi explains the *hatra'at safek* inference does not actually require three separate forbidden items — even two suffice. Imagine one places *piggul* and *notar* simultaneously into one's mouth and begins chewing. The question of which *issur* one is liable for depends on which occupies the majority of the chewed mass at any given moment. In the overlap — the region where the two are being masticated together — one of the two will be more prevalent and will nullify the other, meaning there is a full *kezayis* of the majority *issur* but not of the minority one. Since we do not know which is the majority in that overlap, we cannot specify for which *issur* a warning should have been issued. The warning is therefore inherently uncertain — a *hatra'at safek* — and does not count.

One might object, as Tosafot does, that here we know perfectly well the person is committing a punishable offense — we simply do not know which of the two *issurim* to pin on him. This is different from the classic case of *hatra'at safek* where there is genuine doubt about whether an *aveirah* is occurring at all. Tosafot therefore offers alternative explanations for the *Gemara*'s third inference. Leaving Tosafot's approach aside, the preferred reading is somewhat more metaphorical: just as one who commits an *aveirah* but cannot be warned for it escapes punishment because the *aveirah* cannot be definitively attributed to a specific act, here too the inability to attribute a specific *issur* to the person eating the mixture precludes liability.

---

## Taste vs. Majority

### Flour Mixture

Rava challenges the *Gemara*'s second inference — that majority alone suffices even when taste is imparted — from a *mishna* elsewhere. If one makes dough from a mixture of wheat flour and rice flour, *im yesh bah ta'am dagan chayeves be-challah*: if the wheat taste is still detectable, the dough is obligated in *challah* as though it were genuine bread, even if the majority of the mixture is rice flour. This demonstrates that taste, not majority, determines the presence of the wheat. How then can Reish Lakish imply that majority alone suffices?

The *Gemara* initially deflects: this rule requiring *challah* even from a rice-majority dough is only *miderabbanan* — a rabbinic stringency. Biblically, the wheat is *batel*. But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this from the *seifa* of that same *mishna*, which states that *adam yotzei bo yedei chovaso be-Pesach*: one may use this dough for *matzah* on Pesach. If the obligation of *matzah* is fulfilled, the wheat cannot be considered *batel* at the biblical level — the dough is genuinely considered wheat-based bread. This confirms that taste establishes biblical presence, and *ta'am ke-ikar de-oraita* is a genuine Torah principle.

### Min b'Mino Principle

The *Gemara* resolves the tension with a clean distinction: *min b'sheino mino beta'ama, min b'mino beruba* — when unlike substances are mixed, taste determines presence; when like substances are mixed, majority alone determines presence. Wheat flour and rice flour are unlike in taste; therefore the detectability of the wheat taste is the operative criterion. *Piggul*, *notar*, and *tamei* are all meat, identical in taste; therefore only majority governs, and taste adds nothing. There is, in truth, only a single underlying rule: a substance is present if it can be detected, where "detected" means tasted when the substances are unlike, and simply counted by proportion when they are alike. The apparent tension between Reish Lakish's case and the flour mixture dissolves entirely under this analysis.

This also retrospectively corrects the *Gemara*'s second inference. The ruling of Reish Lakish is not a *chiddush* that majority overrides taste even when taste is imparted. It is simply the ordinary rule for *min b'mino* mixtures, where taste is inherently irrelevant. The genuine *chiddush* remains the first inference: *issurim mevatlin zeh et zeh*.

---

## Ro'in Concept

### Ro'in Lenient Use

The *Gemara* now returns to examine the *ro'in* device employed by our *mishna* — the instruction to look at the wine mixed with blood as though it were water. This is a case where the *mishna* applies *ro'in* leniently: because the blood and wine look alike, one might expect *bitul* to operate, and yet the *mishna* says we treat the wine as water and assess whether the blood would still have been visible under those alternate conditions. If it would have been, the blood remains present and the *korban* is valid.

### Min b'Mino Tension

This raises an immediate difficulty. The *Gemara* has just established that for *min b'mino* mixtures, majority rules. But our *mishna* seems to say that even when two liquids look alike — blood in wine — we do not simply apply *bitul* by majority. Instead we apply *ro'in*, treating them as though they were unlike. Moreover, we do this to be *lenient*, not strict. If the *mishna* permits *ro'in* to be lenient — holding the blood present even when it cannot be seen — it would seem to imply that *ro'in* is a robust, generally applicable device. And if we use it to be lenient, surely we should use it to be strict as well — meaning that whenever two like substances are mixed, we should treat them as unlike and ask whether the forbidden substance would be detectable in a different medium.

The *Gemara* raises this challenge explicitly: *mai lav ro'in oto le-yayin k'ilu hu mayim* — does this not mean we look at the wine as if it were water, and treat the blood as still present? If so, the principle of *ro'in* works even to be lenient, and presumably also to be strict, which would seem to undermine the entire framework of *min b'mino* going by majority. The *Gemara* attempts to deflect by proposing the opposite reading — *lo*, we look at the blood as if it were water and it is immediately *batel* — but this reading is rejected as clearly contrary to the *mishna*'s *pshat*. The *Gemara* notes that if this were the *mishna*'s meaning, it would simply say the blood is *batel* without the language of *ro'in* at all. Furthermore, a *baraita* is cited in which Rabbi Yehudah explicitly uses *ro'in* in a way that preserves presence, confirming that *ro'in* is a device for holding something present, not for *bitul*.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *tannai hi* — this is a dispute between *Tannaim*. Whether *ro'in* is a valid operative principle — in any direction — is itself debated.

### White Wine Baraita

The *baraita* just referenced addresses the following case. A bucket contains white wine or milk. The bucket is immersed in a *mikvah* for purification. For the *tevilah* to be valid, the water of the *mikvah* must reach the interior of the vessel. But the vessel is filled with white wine or milk, which are indistinguishable in color from water. The question is whether the *mikvah* water that enters the vessel is considered the predominant substance.

The first opinion rules *holchin achar ha-rov* — we follow the majority. If the majority of the liquid inside the vessel is *mikvah* water, it is treated as ordinary water and the *tevilah* is valid. Since white wine and water look identical, there is no detectable difference, and majority alone governs — consistent with the *min b'mino* rule.

Rabbi Yehudah disagrees: *ro'in oto k'ilu yayin adom*, we look at the wine as though it were red wine. *Im dehah marehu kasher* — if the color of the mixture fades sufficiently (as if diluted red wine loses its color), the *tevilah* is valid; *ve-im lav pasul* — if not, it is invalid. Rabbi Yehudah here employs *ro'in* to be *strict*. Rather than accepting that the white wine is undetectable and simply applying majority, he asks: had the wine been red, would it still be detectable? If yes, we treat it as still present, and the *tevilah* has not been achieved.

This use of *ro'in* to be strict is familiar from the laws of *kashrut*: had this been a different (detectable) kind of forbidden substance, it would be present, and therefore we treat it as present now. The *chiddush* in our *mishna* was that *ro'in* is applied in the opposite direction, to be lenient. What the *Gemara* now says is that this is a dispute: Rabbi Yehudah holds of *ro'in* as a general operative principle — he applies it here to be strict. The *Gemara* accordingly proposes that our *mishna*, which applies *ro'in* to be lenient, also reflects Rabbi Yehudah's position, since *ro'in* for Rabbi Yehudah is a general tool, not limited to one direction. The *chachamim*, who reject *ro'in* in the *baraita* and simply follow majority, would presumably also reject *ro'in* as a leniency.

---

## Ro'in Debate

### Baraita Sources

A further *baraita* is cited to develop Rabbi Yehudah's position. Rabbi Yehudah says in the name of Rabban Gamliel: *ein dam mevatel dam* — blood does not nullify blood; *ein rok mevatel rok* — spit does not nullify spit (as in the case of the spit of a *zav* mixed with that of a *tahor* person); *ve-ein mei raglayim mevatlin mei raglayim* — urine does not nullify urine (as in the case of a *zav*'s urine mixed with a *tahor* person's urine). The principle articulated is *min b'mino lo batel* — like-with-like is never nullified. This is attributed to Rabbi Yehudah's rebbe, Rabban Gamliel.

### Abaye's Resolution

The *Gemara* observes that within the relevant *mishnah* about the immersion of vessels, there appears to be an internal tension. One clause seems to reflect the *ro'in* principle of Rabbi Yehudah, while another clause — regarding *mei chatat* mixed with *mikvah* water — rules that majority suffices. Abaye resolves this: *ha didei ha de-rabbei* — one ruling reflects Rabbi Yehudah's own position, and the other reflects the position of his rebbe, Rabban Gamliel. The *ro'in* device belongs to the rebbe's tradition; the ruling that majority suffices is Rabbi Yehudah's own view.

### Rashi's Explanation

Rashi explains the relationship between Rabbi Yehudah's *ro'in* and his rebbe's *min b'mino lo batel* as follows. When the *baraita* teaches that blood, spit, and urine do not nullify their like, that reflects the genuine case of *min b'mino* — identical substances — where there can be no *bitul* at all. When Rabbi Yehudah applies *ro'in* in the case of white wine and water, or in the case of blood mixed with wine, those are technically *eino mino* cases — the substances are genuinely different, and *bitul* would ordinarily be possible. But Rabbi Yehudah, coming from a tradition that fundamentally resists *bitul*, applies the same resistance even in cases that merely *look* like *min b'mino* — because the visual similarity makes them behave analogously. Since all these liquids appear uniform, Rabbi Yehudah imports the *min b'mino lo batel* logic of his rebbe's tradition and treats them accordingly — asking not "is the minority detectable now?" but "would it be detectable in a different medium?" And this resistance to *bitul* applies regardless of whether the result is a stringency or a leniency: Rabbi Yehudah resists *bitul* as a general posture, and the practical consequence depends on the context. In *kashrut*, resisting *bitul* means the forbidden substance remains present; in *korbanot*, resisting *bitul* means the sacrificial blood remains present and usable.

By contrast, where Rabbi Yehudah does allow majority to govern — the case of *mei chatat* — this represents his own position, independent of his rebbe's tradition, applicable to a case where the circumstances genuinely warrant it.

### Rava's Alternative

Rava offers a different resolution that does not require invoking the rebbe-versus-own-position framework. He says: *bidli she-tocho tahor ve-gabbo tamei askinan* — we are dealing with a bucket that is *tamei* only on the outside and *tahor* on the inside. This arises because *tum'at mashkin*, the *tum'ah* of liquids, is of rabbinic status and can in certain circumstances cause a vessel to become *tamei* only on its external surface, not internally. Since the *mikvah* water needs to reach only the exterior of the vessel to effect *tevilah*, technically no *mikvah* water need enter the interior at all. Why then does the *mishna* require a majority of *mikvah* water inside? Because the rabbis were concerned — *dilma chayis aleihu ve-lo matbil lei* — that one might be reluctant to fully submerge a vessel filled with precious *mei chatat* water, and might not immerse it completely. To counter this tendency, the rabbis imposed the requirement that *mikvah* water enter and predominate inside the bucket. But since this is only a rabbinic precaution, the *Gemara* concludes: *ve-keivan de-ika ribuya lo tzarich* — once the requirement to introduce *mikvah* water inside is operative, majority suffices. Since technically no *mikvah* water is needed inside at all, there is no reason to require more than a majority once the rabbis imposed the obligation.

According to Rava, then, Rabbi Yehudah's position throughout is consistently one of *ro'in*: he always views like substances through the lens of their differences in order to resist *bitul*. The reason *ro'in* is not applied to the *mei chatat* case has nothing to do with whose tradition is being invoked, but rather with the technical halachic fact that the inside of the vessel need not be immersed at all. Since the *mikvah* water's entry into the vessel is only a rabbinic safeguard rather than a genuine requirement, Rabbi Yehudah does not deploy *ro'in* to strengthen it further.

---

---

# Zevachim 79

## Bitul Principles

### Ein Dam Mevatel Dam

The daf begins in the middle of 79a, approximately halfway down the page, where the *gemara* presents Rava's summary statement. By way of context, the preceding discussion had been devoted to the principles of *bitul* — nullification — and specifically to the critical distinction between *min b'mino* (like nullifying like) and *min b'eino mino* (unlike nullifying unlike).

The most important position encountered in this context is that of Rabbi Yehuda: *ein dam mevatel dam* — blood does not nullify blood. This is an application of the broader principle that *min b'mino lo batel* — when a substance mixes with something identical to itself, it can never lose its identity, because there is no discernible difference between them. If *treif* chicken soup falls into kosher chicken soup, it is all the same substance; one cannot speak of the forbidden element dissolving into the permitted, since they are indistinguishable. Rashi's view is that we rule in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda — though, as will be noted, this is not the accepted *psak*.

### Rashi vs. Chachamim

The accepted ruling follows the *Chachamim*, who hold that *min b'mino* is fundamentally *batel* through *rov* — through majority. If the permitted substance constitutes the majority, the forbidden minority is nullified. This position is what the *halacha* follows in practice.

### Min Be'eino Mino

When the mixture involves *min b'eino mino* — unlike substances — the principle that governs food prohibitions is *notein ta'am*: if the forbidden substance can be tasted, it is discernible and therefore not *batel*; once it falls below the threshold of perceptibility to the palate, it is nullified. This is the standard framework for *issur* in the domain of forbidden foods.

### Bitul in Korbanot

In the context of *korbanot*, however, the relevant sense is not taste but appearance. When the question is not whether to refrain from eating something but whether blood may be applied to the *mizbeach*, the operative criterion is visual discernibility: if the presence of the blood can be detected by sight, it is not *batel*, and — crucially — in the context of *korbanot*, this works in a lenient direction. If the blood is not *batel*, it is still present and may therefore be used for the *zrika*.

### Lenient Eino Mino

A striking and somewhat surprising ruling emerges from the preceding discussion: even when *korban* blood becomes mixed with wine, water, or other blood — a case that is in reality *min b'mino* where one would normally expect the simpler majority-based rule — the *gemara* applies the *ro'in* principle leniently, imagining the case as though it were *eino mino*. In the domain of *issur*, one invokes the *eino mino* framework stringently — even when substances are alike, one imagines they were unlike, in order to disqualify. Here, the very same framework is applied in reverse, to permit: since had the blood been mixed with water it could have been visually discerned, the blood is deemed still present and may be placed on the *mizbeach*. That one can use this reasoning *leniently* is, as noted, quite unexpected.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot, in his commentary toward the end of 79a (the passage running in narrow columns alongside the *gemara* text), raises the difficulty directly. The question — beginning with the line *v'tzarich ledakdek* — is: what distinguishes the realm of *kodashim*, *tumah*, and *mikveh*, where the *ro'in* principle is applied, from the realm of *issur*, where *min b'mino* goes by *rov* and we do not invoke *ro'in*?

Tosafot's answer — *heicha d'itmar itmar, heicha d'lo itmar lo itmar* — is essentially that the rule was stated where it was stated, and was not stated where it was not stated. This is an acknowledgment that no overarching principle reconciles the two domains; the application is category-specific. The result remains striking: in the case of *korban* blood, *min b'mino* does not prevent the use of *ro'in* for a lenient outcome.

### Rava's Summary

Rava now presents a clean summary of the three approaches: *zimnin amri rabbanan b'ta'ama, v'zimnin amri rabbanan b'ruba, v'zimnin amri rabbanan b'chazuta* — sometimes the rabbis rule by taste, sometimes by majority, and sometimes by appearance.

*Min b'she'eino mino* — unlike mixed with unlike — goes by taste. A drop of *chazir* soup that falls into chicken soup is *batel* only if it cannot be tasted; otherwise it is still present. *Min b'mino* — like with like — goes by *rov*, by majority. A drop of non-kosher chicken soup (from an animal not properly *shachted*) that falls into kosher chicken soup is nullified by the majority. And where appearance is the operative criterion — *v'heicha d'ika chazuta b'mora* — one goes by visual discernibility.

### Rashi on Chazuta

Rashi explains the third category: *midi d'lo tali b'tama ella b'chazuta* — where the matter does not depend on taste but on appearance. Sight is the primary sense through which the world is experienced, and therefore in all domains outside of forbidden foods — such as the laws of *mikveh* — presence is determined by whether something is visible or visually detectable. When taste is the governing criterion (as in *issur* of food), one asks whether it can be tasted; when taste is irrelevant, one asks whether it can be seen.

### Notein Ta'am D'Oraita

Tosafot makes an important additional observation from this very *gemara*. Rashi holds that the principle of *ta'am k'ikar* — that a substance which imparts taste is treated as though still present — is only *d'rabbanan*, a rabbinic enactment. Tosafot disagrees, maintaining that it is *d'oraita*. Among his proofs is the present *sugya*: since Rava's summary identifies *min b'mino* going by *rov* as the *d'oraita* standard — and we know that in practice we always require *shishim* (one-in-sixty), a *d'rabbanan* stringency — the discussion here is clearly operating at the *d'oraita* level. And at that same *d'oraita* level, the *gemara* applies *notein ta'am* to the case of *min b'eino mino*. From here Tosafot derives that *ta'am k'ikar* is biblical in origin.

---

## Issurin Mevatlin

### Reish Lakish

The *gemara* now transitions: *u'pliga d'Rabbi Elazar* — and this disagrees with Rabbi Elazar. The reference is to the principle of Reish Lakish, introduced in the preceding daf, that *issurin mevatlin zeh et zeh* — forbidden substances can nullify one another. If, for example, one has three distinct *issurim* — *pigul*, *notar*, and *tamei* — mixed together, the majority of two *issurim* can nullify the third, even though the nullifying substances are themselves forbidden. The key point is that the *issurim* are different from one another; heterogeneous *issurim* can function as the *mevatel* against another *issur*.

### Rabbi Elazar

Rabbi Elazar disagrees. His principle: *k'shem she'ein mitzvot mevatlot zo et zo* — just as *mitzvot* do not nullify one another, so too *issurin* do not nullify one another. For *bitul* to operate, one needs *hetter* — permitted substance — against *issur*, or in the *korban* context, a neutral substance such as wine or water against *korban* blood. But when everything present is forbidden — even if under different prohibitions — no nullification can take place.

### Hillel's Korech

The source for the principle that *mitzvot* do not nullify one another is attributed to Hillel. The *gemara* cites the *baraita*: *amru alav al Hillel Hazaken shehayah korchan b'vat achat v'ochlan* — they said of Hillel the Elder that he would wrap them together and eat them, based on the verse *al matzot u'merorim yochluhu* — upon *matzot* and *maror* they shall eat it — which Hillel understood as requiring an actual sandwich. In this *korech*, all three components — *korban Pesach*, *matzah*, and *maror* — are chewed and swallowed together. Yet we do not say that the majority of *matzah* and *maror* nullifies the *korban Pesach*, leaving one without having eaten it. Each *mitzvah* retains its identity. From this principle, Rabbi Elazar extends the same logic to *issurim*: just as *mitzvot* are not *mevatel* one another, neither are *issurim*.

### Mitzvot Levels

Tosafot adds an important qualification. *Amru al Hillel shehaya korchan b'vat achat* — this practice of Hillel occurred *bizman habayit*, at the time of the Temple, when all three components — *matzah*, *maror*, and *korban Pesach* — were *d'oraita* obligations. Today, *matzah* is *d'oraita* while *maror* is *d'rabbanan* and *korech* is a *zecher* — a memorial practice. This distinction in levels matters: the reason we eat *maror* separately before *korech*, and the reason *korech* is performed as a separate act, is precisely because *matzah* and *maror* now operate at different levels. If a *d'oraita mitzvah* and a *d'rabbanan mitzvah* were to be conflated in a single act, the *d'rabbanan* one would not carry the same weight as a *mitzvah* in that context, and *bitul* could theoretically occur. The principle that *ein mitzvot mevatlot zo et zo* applies in full only when all the *mitzvot* involved are recognized as operating at the same halachic level. When they are at different levels, the lower-level *mitzvah* might indeed be subject to *bitul* by the higher-level one.

---

## Porous Vessels

### Zav Urine

At the top of 79b, the *gemara* opens a new *baraita*: *chosin shel zav v'zavah* — a chamber pot made of pottery that was used by a *zav* or *zavah* for urination. The urine of a *zav* or *zavah* is an *av hatumah*, a primary source of *tumah*. Because pottery is porous, the urine is absorbed into the walls of the vessel. Since the urine is no longer *b'ayin* — no longer visibly present — one might think the problem is resolved. It is not, because if the vessel were placed in an oven, or if liquids were placed inside it, the absorbed urine would seep back out through the pores and contaminate those liquids, rendering the vessel effectively *tamei*.

### Rinsing Requirements

*Pa'am rishonah u'shniyah tamei* — rinsing the vessel once or twice is insufficient; trace amounts of urine remain in the pores and will still emerge. *Shlishi tahor* — after three rinsings with water, the vessel is *tahor*, as by that point all remaining urine has been fully expelled. This is noteworthy in itself: ordinarily we say that vessels absorb only through heat, but pottery is sufficiently porous to absorb even cold liquids — a principle that also arises in *Avodah Zarah* in the context of wine absorbed in pottery vessels.

However, this three-rinse rule applies specifically *shenatan letocho mayim* — when one rinsed with water. If instead one used the vessel for ordinary urine — not from a *zav* or *zavah*, which is *tahor* — then even ten times (*afilu asiris tamei*) it remains *tamei*.

### Rashi on Urine

Rashi explains why: after three rinsings, there will still be trace amounts of urine seeping out of the pores. When rinsing with water, those trace amounts are *batel* — nullified by the majority of water. But when rinsing with ordinary urine, any trace of *zav* urine that emerges is *min b'mino* with the ordinary urine surrounding it, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, *min b'mino lo batel* — like substances do not nullify one another. Therefore the vessel remains *tamei* indefinitely, regardless of how many times ordinary urine is used.

### Rabbi Eliezer Ben Yaakov

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagrees: *shlishi af al pi shelo natan letocho mayim tahor* — three rinsings suffice even without water, because his position is that *min b'mino* is *batel*. In his view, even the trace amounts of *zav* urine that remain after three rinsings are nullified by the ordinary urine, and the vessel is *tahor*.

### Tanna Kamma = R. Yehuda

The *gemara* then identifies the *Tanna Kamma* — the first, anonymous opinion — with Rabbi Yehuda, since it is Rabbi Yehuda who maintains *min b'mino lo batel*, and it is precisely this principle that drives the stringent ruling that ordinary urine cannot effect *tahara* even after multiple uses.

---

## Flax & Nidda

### Dry vs. Wet Flax

An analogous *baraita* is now cited: *pishtan she-tavaso nidda* — flax spun by a woman who is a *nidda*. In the process of spinning flax, one would moisten the thread with saliva — *mashkeh pihah* — and the saliva of a *nidda* is an *av hatumah*. *Mesito tahor* — if the spun flax is now dry, moving it does not render one *tamei*, since the saliva has been absorbed into the fibers and is not presently accessible; there is nothing actively contaminating. *V'im haya lach mesito tamei* — but if it is still wet from her original saliva, then moving it conveys *tumah*, since the moisture is still present.

### R. Yehuda on Water

Rabbi Yehuda adds: *af harok b'mayim tamei mishum mashkeh piha* — even if the thread had dried out completely, if one subsequently wets it again with water, it is once again *tamei*. The introduction of water draws the absorbed saliva back out of the fibers and into the liquid medium, so that the saliva is no longer merely absorbed but is now effectively *b'ayin*, mixed with the water, and the *tumah* is reactivated. Moreover, the *gemara* specifies *v'afilu tuva* — even if one has rinsed the thread many times, according to Rabbi Yehuda it remains a problem.

### Apparent Contradiction

This creates an apparent tension in Rabbi Yehuda's positions. In the case of the chamber pot, the *gemara* identified the *Tanna Kamma* with Rabbi Yehuda, and that *Tanna Kamma* held that three rinsings with water suffice to render the pot *tahor*. But here, Rabbi Yehuda explicitly states that no matter how many times one wets the flax thread and allows it to dry, it remains *tamei*. How are these consistent?

### Rav Pappa's Answer

Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction: *shani rok d'karir* — saliva is different, for saliva is adhesive, almost viscous, and clings to the fibers of the thread far more tenaciously than urine clings to the pores of pottery. Urine, being more fluid and runny, is fully expelled from pottery after three rinsings. Saliva, being sticky, remains bound within the fibers of the thread no matter how many times one wets and dries it.

One might observe that there is a simpler answer available: in the thread case, the rinsing medium is water, which is not *min b'mino* with saliva, and so the trace amounts of saliva are not *batel* in it; whereas in the pottery case, after three rinsings with water, the trace amounts of urine are *batel* in the water since they are *eino mino*. This would explain the discrepancy without any appeal to the physical properties of saliva vs. urine. Indeed, the *acharonim* raise precisely this question, and note that the only way to deflect it is perhaps to say that Rabbi Yehuda does not consider saliva and water to be distinct substances — a strained position. The question stands, though Rav Pappa's physical distinction is what the *gemara* itself offers.

---

## Mixed Blood Issues

### Pasul Blood Mixture

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishnah* at the end of the chapter. *Nit'arev b'dam pasul yishafech l'amah* — if *korban* blood becomes mixed with *pasul* blood — whether the blood of an animal rendered *piggul*, or *ba'al mum*, or with *dam tamtzit* — the blood is spilled into the drainage channel of the *azarah*, rather than sprinkled. This ruling requires explanation, for we have already established that *korban* blood mixed with other substances is not *batel* and can still be used. Why then must it be discarded?

The *mishnah* presents two categories: blood mixed with *dam psulim* (invalid sacrificial blood) and blood mixed with *dam tamtzit*. *Dam tamtzit* is the blood that continues to drain from a slaughtered animal after the initial surge of *dam ha-nefesh* — the vital blood — has ceased. *Chazal* understood that it is only the initial spurting blood that is valid for the *zrika*; the residual blood that seeps out afterward, the *tamtzit*, may not be placed on the *mizbeach*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Lenient

Rabbi Eliezer takes a lenient position and permits the mixed blood to be used, consistent with his general principle of *ro'eh ani k'ilu hu mayim* — I regard the extraneous component as though it were water. The *Chachamim* disagree and require the blood to be spilled.

### Gezira in Mikdash

The *gemara* asks: what is the underlying dispute? Zvid explains: *b'gozin gezira b'mikdash kamiflagi* — they disagree about whether we enact preventive rabbinic decrees within the *Beit HaMikdash*. It is a well-known principle that certain *d'rabbanan* restrictions do not apply in the *mikdash* (for example, *shvut* of *Shabbat* does not apply to *kohanim* engaged in the *avodah*), because *kohanim* are presumed to be careful. The question here is whether we extend that principle to refrain from enacting *gezerot* in the *mikdash* generally, especially when the cost of a *gezera* is the waste of a *korban*.

What is the specific *gezera* at issue? Rashi explains: we are concerned that if we permit the use of mixed blood in cases where the *korban* blood is not yet *batel*, a *kohen* may come to use it in a case where the *korban* blood actually has been *batel* and the mixture is invalid. The earlier cases — blood mixed with wine, water, or the blood of non-sanctified animals — are rare occurrences in the *mikdash*, and we are not concerned that leniency there will lead to error. But *pasul* blood and *dam tamtzit* arise regularly in the *mikdash*, and so there is reason to be concerned.

### Rav Pappa on Frequency

Rav Pappa offers a different resolution: *d'chulei alma gozin* — everyone agrees that in principle we make *gezerot* even in the *mikdash* when a situation is common. The question is empirical: how common is it that *dam tamtzit* accumulates in such quantity that it would cause the valid *korban* blood to be *batel*? *Mar savar shchiach* — one opinion holds this is a realistic concern, occurring with sufficient frequency to warrant a decree. *Mar savar lo shchiach* — the other holds it is not common enough to be worried about. According to Rav Pappa, the *Chachamim* and Rabbi Eliezer agree that common cases require a *gezera*; they simply disagree about whether the case of *dam tamtzit* reaches the threshold of frequency to trigger that concern.

### Separate Cases

The *gemara* notes that according to Rav Pappa's reading, it makes perfect sense that the *mishnah* separates the two cases — *dam psulim* listed independently from *dam tamtzit* — because Rabbi Eliezer concedes the first case and debates only the second. Everyone agrees that *dam psulim* is a sufficiently common occurrence that we decree not to use the mixture; Rabbi Eliezer argues only that *dam tamtzit* causing *bitul* is not common enough to warrant a decree. The *mishnah*'s division of the cases thus neatly maps onto the scope of their dispute.

By contrast, according to Zvid's reading — where the dispute is about whether any *gezera* applies at all in the *mikdash* — Rabbi Eliezer should reject both categories equally, and the *mishnah* need not have separated them. The *gemara* concludes: *kashya* — this is a difficulty for Zvid's position.

### Tosafot on Gezira

Tosafot raises a further question: why does the *gemara* need to frame the dispute as being about a *gezera* at all? Why not simply say this is the longstanding dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim* — one holds that non-*korban* blood going onto the *mizbeach* is problematic, and the other says you regard it as water? If the *Chachamim* are categorically opposed to placing non-valid blood on the *mizbeach*, that would explain why they require the mixture to be spilled; and Rabbi Eliezer would permit it because he regards the problematic component as water.

Tosafot answers in two ways. First: if the dispute were framed as a fundamental objection to placing *pasul* blood on the *mizbeach*, Rabbi Eliezer should have explicitly stated his catchphrase — *ro'eh ani k'ilu hu mayim* — but the *mishnah* does not report him saying that here, suggesting the disagreement is based on something other than that principle. Second, and more substantively: the debate also encompasses *dam tamtzit*, and *dam tamtzit* has no more inherent connection to the *mizbeach* than wine or water — it is simply a byproduct of the slaughter process, no different in kind from any other non-sacred liquid. Therefore, placing it on the *mizbeach* is not a *fundamentally* problematic act in the same sense as offering genuinely *pasul* blood. The fact that they even debate the *tamtzit* case demonstrates that the argument cannot be about a fundamental prohibition against non-valid blood on the *mizbeach*; it must instead be grounded in the question of whether a rabbinic *gezera* applies.

---

## Temimim vs. Mumin

### Temimim & Mumin

The next *mishnah* addresses *dam tmimim b'dam ba'alei mumin* — the blood of unblemished animals (*tmimim*) mixed with the blood of blemished animals (*ba'alei mumin*). This parallels the category of *dam psulim* from the previous *mishnah*, insofar as the blood of a blemished animal may not be offered on the *mizbeach*.

### Unanimous Spilling

*Yishafech l'amah* — the mixture must be spilled, and this ruling is unanimous. Even Rabbi Eliezer, who permits use of mixed blood in the *dam tamtzit* case, does not debate this ruling. This observation connects back to Tosafot's point: the cases are not structured around a fundamental debate over whether *pasul* blood may go on the *mizbeach*, but around the more nuanced question of how common the relevant scenario is and whether a *gezera* is warranted. In the case of blemished animal blood — which is a meaningful and distinct category of *pasul* — perhaps everyone agrees that a *gezera* is appropriate, and Rabbi Eliezer's principle of *ro'eh k'ilu hu mayim* does not override the unanimous concern.

### Kos B'Kosot

A new case: *kos b'kosot* — one basin of *korban* blood among several basins, where one is the blood of a *ba'al mum* and one cannot identify which. This is structurally parallel to the case in other tractates of a prohibited limb mixed indistinguishably among permitted limbs.

### One Offered Logic

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *im kariv kos echad yikrevu kol hakosos* — if one basin was already offered, the rest may be offered as well. One may presume that the basin which was offered was the problematic one, and the remaining basins are all *kasher*. Underlying this position is Rabbi Eliezer's broader willingness to work with the fiction that the problematic element has been discharged — perhaps because he fundamentally accepts that in a case of *lach b'lach* (liquid mixed with liquid), *bitul* can operate or the problematic element is regarded as water, which gives conceptual coherence to his reliance on the presumption that the *pasul* basin was the one offered.

### Chachamim Strict

The *Chachamim* are far more stringent: *afilu karvu kulan chutz me'echad mehen yishafech l'amah* — even if all the basins save one have been offered, and it is nearly certain that the *pasul* blood has already been used, the final remaining basin must still be spilled. There remains a residual possibility that the last basin is the *pasul* one, and the *Chachamim* do not permit acting on the probability alone. This mirrors similar debates throughout the tractate about *vadai* and *safek* in the domain of *kodashim*.

---

## Above vs. Below

### Yabesh vs. Lach

The *mishnah* now turns to a qualitatively different type of mixture: *hanitannim lemata shenisarvu benitannim lemala* — blood that is applied *below* the *chut hasikra* (the red line midpoint of the *mizbeach*) that has become mixed with blood applied *above* the line. The paradigm case is the blood of a *chatat*, which is applied above the line, becoming mixed with the blood of an *olah* or *shelamim*, which is applied below.

This is also the appropriate point to introduce the conceptual framework that the *rishonim* employ: *yavesh b'yavesh* versus *lach b'lach*. *Yavesh b'yavesh* refers to distinct, individually identifiable items that have been commingled but not merged — one limb among other limbs, one basin among other basins. Each item retains its discrete identity even though one cannot determine which is which. *Lach b'lach* refers to liquids that have been poured together and have become fully intermingled; there is no longer any discrete particle that can be identified as belonging to one source or the other.

Rabbi Eliezer's principle of *ro'eh k'ilu hu mayim* — treating the extraneous blood as though it were water — operates specifically in cases of *lach b'lach*. In *yavesh b'yavesh* cases (distinct cups, distinct limbs), Rabbi Eliezer does not invoke this principle *lechatchila*; he requires that one basin actually be offered before permitting the rest. This distinction is significant: when the bloods have fully merged and every drop of what is sprinkled necessarily contains some of each, Rabbi Eliezer permits it because he treats the extraneous component as water and every act of sprinkling is necessarily an act of sprinkling the valid blood. But when the items remain discrete, one could theoretically sprinkle only the *pasul* one and never the *kasher* one, and so he requires the safeguard of one being done before proceeding.

### Rabbi Eliezer Lach

In the *lach b'lach* case before us, Rabbi Eliezer rules: *yiten lemala, v'roeh ani es hatachtonim milmala ke'ilu hem mayim* — one should first give the blood above, and the blood that belongs below (the *olah* blood) I regard as though it were water. Then proceed to give below as well.

### Two Applications

Rashi explains why this works both ways: when applying above the line, the *chatat* blood is valid for that application and the *olah* blood component is regarded as water. When then applying below the line, the *olah* blood is valid for the lower *zrika*, and the *chatat* blood that is included in the mixture constitutes *shfichat shirayim* — the pouring out of the blood remnants (*shirayim*) of the *chatat*, which is itself a required act that takes place at the base of the *mizbeach*. Thus both applications are legitimized, each in its appropriate way.

### Chachamim Oppose

The *Chachamim* disagree: *yishafech l'amah* — the mixed blood must be spilled entirely. They do not accept the principle of treating the extraneous blood as water, and they are not prepared to allow blood designated for one location on the *mizbeach* to be applied at a different location, even when commingled. They hold that the mixture is irremediably compromised and must be disposed of.

### B'Dieved Kosher

Nevertheless, the *mishnah* records an important *b'dieved* ruling: *v'im lo nimlach v'na'asah kasher* — if the *kohen* did not ask a *halachic* authority and simply went ahead and applied the mixed blood, it is *kasher* after the fact. Even according to the *Chachamim*, if *chatat* blood was applied above and *olah* blood below — all in one commingled application — the *korban* is not disqualified retroactively. The *Chachamim*'s position is *lechatchila*; *b'dieved*, the application stands.

---

## Matan Arba & Achat

### One Application

The *mishnah* now discusses a related question involving the number of blood applications (*matanot*) required for different *korbanot*. *Hanitannim b'matanah achat* — *korbanot* that require only one application (such as *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *pesach*): if their bloods become mixed together, *yinatnu b'matanah achat* — one application suffices and counts for all of them, since each requires only one, and every sprinkling contains some of each blood.

### Four Applications

*Matan arba b'matan arba* — two *korbanot* that each require four applications (understood as two diagonal corners): if, for example, the blood of an *olah* and the blood of *shelamim* become mixed, *yinatnu bematan arba* — one performs the two diagonal applications and both *korbanot* are discharged. Since both require the same structure, there is no difficulty.

### Four Mixed One

The complex case: *matan arba b'matan achat* — blood of a *korban* requiring four applications (such as an *olah*) becomes mixed with blood of a *korban* requiring only one (such as a *bechor*). Two options present themselves: perform all four applications — which gives the *olah* what it requires but subjects the *bechor* blood to three applications beyond its requirement — or perform only one application — which discharges the *bechor* but gives the *olah* only a fraction of what it requires, though this is valid *b'dieved*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Four

Rabbi Eliezer rules *yinatnu bematan arba* — perform all four applications. This follows consistently from his principle: the *bechor* blood that is mixed in is treated as water for the three applications beyond the first. He is doing the four applications for the sake of the *olah*, and the extraneous *bechor* blood is not a concern.

### Rabbi Yehoshua One

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees: *yinatnu b'matanah achat* — only one application should be performed. He is unwilling to adopt the fiction that the *bechor* blood is water; in his view, applying blood at three additional corners where it does not belong constitutes a prohibited act, and he would rather do the minimum — one application — which serves both *korbanot b'dieved*.

---

## Bal Tosif vs. Tigra

### Rabbi Eliezer Challenge

Rabbi Eliezer challenges Rabbi Yehoshua's position: *harei hu over al bal tigra* — by performing only one application when the *olah* requires four, Rabbi Yehoshua causes a transgression of the prohibition *lo tigre'u mimenu* — do not diminish from it. The verse *lo tosifu al hadavar asher anochi metzaveh etchem velo tigre'u mimenu* — do not add to the matter which I command you and do not subtract from it — is understood by *Chazal* not only as a prohibition against adding or subtracting from the corpus of *mitzvot*, but against altering the quantitative structure of an individual *mitzvah*.

### Bal Tigra Explained

*Bal tosif* in its most familiar form means: do not take five species for *lulav*, do not construct *tefillin* with five compartments. *Bal tigra* is a subtler category. One might ask: is there ever a way to be transgress *bal tigra*? If one simply does not do the *mitzvah*, one has merely failed to perform it — one has not actively subtracted from it. The answer is that *bal tigra* applies when one begins the *mitzvah* but performs it in a quantitatively lesser way — doing one corner instead of two, for example — while still technically fulfilling the *mitzvah*. The act was done, but a quantifiable dimension of it was diminished. This is a striking application of the principle, and notable precisely because the *mitzvah* is not entirely omitted but performed inadequately in a measurable respect.

### Counter to R. Eliezer

Rabbi Yehoshua responds in kind: *harei hu over al bal tosif* — according to Rabbi Eliezer's position, performing four applications when the *bechor* blood is present causes the *bechor* blood to be applied at three corners where it does not belong, constituting an addition to the *mitzvah* of *bechor* blood application — a transgression of *bal tosif*.

### Done for Olah

Rabbi Eliezer responds: *lo ne'emar bal tosif ela keshehu be'atzmo* — *bal tosif* is violated only when one takes the problematic element and performs a distinct act with it in its own right. Here, the blood of the *bechor* is not being applied for the sake of the *bechor*; it is fully intermingled with the *olah* blood, and every application is performed entirely for the sake of the *olah*. There is no independent act being done with the *bechor* blood. Rabbi Eliezer here may be extending his principle beyond the specific formulation of *ro'eh k'ilu hu mayim*: even setting aside that principle, he argues that there is no *ma'aseh* of adding to the *bechor*'s *mitzvah* because the intention and the act are directed entirely toward the *olah*. At the end of the day, one is not doing something extra with the *bechor* — one is doing what the *olah* requires.

### Passive vs. Active

Rabbi Yehoshua offers a final response: *lo ne'emar bal tigra k'sheu be'atzmo* — and similarly, one should not say I am transgressing *bal tigra* with the *olah* blood, because the reason I am performing only one application is not a desire to diminish the *olah*; it is because performing more applications would involve the *bechor* blood in a prohibited way. My abstention is forced by circumstances.

And beyond that structural argument, Rabbi Yehoshua articulates a broader principle: *keshenatata avarta al bal tosif asita ma'aseh beyadecha; keshelo natata avarta al bal tigra velo asita ma'aseh beyadecha* — if you perform four applications, you have transgressed *bal tosif* by a positive act; if you perform only one, you have transgressed *bal tigra* by omission. Given that one must choose between the two, it is preferable to commit a passive sin — failing to do what is required — than an active sin — doing what is prohibited. A sin of omission is less grave than a sin of commission, and therefore Rabbi Yehoshua holds that one should do only the one application and accept the passive shortcoming in the *olah*'s *avodah* rather than actively apply blood where it does not belong.

Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, appears to hold that this is not merely a forced choice between two bad options, but that his position avoids *bal tosif* entirely: since the extra applications are done for the sake of the *olah* and not as an independent act with the *bechor* blood, there is no transgression at all on that side, and therefore it is clearly preferable to do the full four applications and fulfill the *olah*'s *mitzvah* completely.

---

---

# Zevachim 80

## Blemished vs. Unblemished

### Limbs & Mixed Blood

The Gemara on Daf 80 opens by revisiting the debates that appeared in the Mishnah. The first component of the Mishnah recapitulated an earlier controversy: if a limb from a *baal mum* — a blemished animal — becomes mixed together with limbs of unblemished animals, what is the law? Rabbi Eliezer rules leniently: once one limb has already been brought up on the altar, one may bring the rest, attributing the *baal mum* limb to the one already offered. The *chachamim* disagree and prohibit this. Critically, this dispute operates even though each act of bringing a limb is a distinct act — the blood has not all been blended together. Yet Rabbi Eliezer permits it nonetheless.

The Mishnah then extends the same framework to a different case: bowls of blood from different sacrifices that have become intermingled. Here too Rabbi Eliezer rules that if one application was already performed, the rest may proceed; the *chachamim* counter that even if all applications were performed save one, the final bowl must be poured out, for we remain concerned that it contains *baal mum* blood.

### Pairs Only

The Gemara refines Rabbi Eliezer's position: *amar Rabbi Elazar lo hechshir Rabbi Eliezer ela lishnayim lishnayim* — Rabbi Eliezer's leniency applies only when one performs the applications in pairs, not individually. When proceeding two at a time, one can reason: first, the bowl already offered was the *baal mum*, and second, since two are being offered simultaneously and at least one of them must be valid, the other may be assumed valid as well. But if each bowl is offered individually, one cannot make that assumption.

### Rav Dimi's Challenge

Rav Dimi challenged this restriction. The Mishnah states that the *chachamim* say: *afilu karvu kulan chutz me'echad mehen yishapech la'amah* — even if all the bloods were applied except one, that last one must be poured out. This phrasing implies that for Rabbi Eliezer, even the single remaining bowl may be offered — suggesting his leniency extends even to individual applications, not merely to pairs. Rabbi Yaakov answered Rav Dimi by explaining: *mai echad — zug echad* — "one" here means one pair, not a single bowl. This is precisely the same resolution that was reached by the earlier case of the limbs.

### Two Cases Necessary

The Gemara then asks why both cases — limbs and blood — need to be stated at all. *Vetzricha* — both are necessary. Had the Mishnah taught only the case of the limbs, one might have thought Rabbi Eliezer permits it specifically because the main act of *kapparah* — atonement — was already performed through the *zerikat ha-dam*, and bringing up the remaining limbs is only a secondary completion. In that case, Rabbi Eliezer would allow one to fictively attribute the *baal mum* limb to the already-offered portion. But one might say that when it comes to the blood itself — the central act of offering — even Rabbi Eliezer would concede to the Rabbis and prohibit applying *baal mum* blood. Therefore the Mishnah must also state the blood case explicitly. Conversely, had only the blood case been stated, one might have thought the Rabbis' stringency is limited to that case, where the concern of applying *baal mum* blood is most acute, but that in the case of the limbs they would concede to Rabbi Eliezer. *Vetzricha* — both cases must be taught independently.

---

## Above & Below Blood

### Mixed Blood Cases

The Mishnah continues with a second distinct scenario: blood of sacrifices whose application belongs *above* the *chut ha-sikra* — the red line that divides the altar — becomes mixed with blood whose application belongs *below*. Rabbi Eliezer rules that one sprinkles above and also below, and the blood that does not belong in each location is to be viewed as water — *ro'in* — so that the appropriate blood in each location is what counts. The *chachamim* reject this principle entirely: one may not fictively "view" the inappropriate blood as water, and the entire mixture must be poured out.

The Gemara had also introduced the related concerns of *bal tosif* and *bal tigra* — the prohibitions against adding to or subtracting from the commanded rites — which arise in certain configurations of mixed blood. These concerns will be returned to later.

### Parah Adumah Case

To illuminate the underlying principles governing the mixed blood debate, the Gemara invokes a parallel case from *Masechet Parah*. The Mishnah there (*tnan hatam*) states: *tzluchit shenaflu l'tocha mayim kol shehu* — if a container holding the purification water of the *parah adumah* had ordinary tap water fall into it, what is the law? This water is used to sprinkle upon individuals who are *tamei* from *tumat met*, and the mixture raises the question of whether the purifying water remains valid. Rabbi Eliezer says: *yaze shtei hazayot* — one should sprinkle twice. The *chachamim* say: *psulin* — it is entirely invalid.

---

## Parah Adumah Analysis

### Chachamim Position

*Bishlama rabbanan* — the *chachamim*'s position is straightforward once their assumptions are identified. The *rabbanan* hold *yesh bilah* — that when two liquids of similar substance are combined, we assume perfectly equal distribution throughout the mixture. They further hold that *hazah tzrichah shiur* — a *haza'ah*, a sprinkling, requires a minimum amount of the *parah adumah* water to be valid. And they hold *ein mitztarfin lehaza'ot* — one cannot combine two partial amounts from two separate sprinklings to meet that minimum. Therefore, since any single sprinkling from the mixture will contain only a fraction of the required *parah adumah* water — the remainder being ordinary water, equally distributed — that sprinkling will never satisfy the minimum. The water is thus invalid regardless of how many times one sprinkles.

### Yesh Bilah Principle

At the heart of this analysis is the principle of *yesh bilah*, which requires some elaboration. The question is this: when a drop of ordinary water falls into *parah adumah* water, do we assume that the liquids fully and equally disperse throughout the mixture — *yesh bilah* — or do we assume that they remain non-uniformly concentrated — *ein bilah*? The Gemara treats this as a binary, without considering factors such as passage of time or stirring. *Yesh bilah* means that every spoonful of the mixture contains the same proportion of each liquid; *ein bilah* means that concentrations may be uneven and one cannot assume a given portion reflects the overall ratio.

This raises a related question: why is there no *bittul* — nullification — of the ordinary water when only a small amount falls into a large volume of *parah adumah* water? The answer lies in a fundamental distinction in how *bittul* functions. The classical operation of *bittul* removes a problematic status from a substance. But the question here is the inverse: can *bittul* confer a positive halachic status — can it make something that lacked validity now valid? This is a deeper question that the Gemara does not resolve here, and in any event the framework of the discussion proceeds without invoking *bittul* as a mechanism.

It should also be noted that the Gemara assumes a sprinkling is always performed in a fixed quantity of one unit. Why one cannot simply sprinkle a double amount is not fully explained, but the Gemara operates consistently on that assumption.

### Rabbi Eliezer Deduction

The more challenging question is Rabbi Eliezer's position. How does sprinkling twice help? The Gemara proceeds deductively. *Ei kasavar ein bilah* — if Rabbi Eliezer held there is no equal distribution, then even two sprinklings might both have come entirely from the ordinary water, and *ki maza shtei haza'ot mai hava, dilma tartaihu mayya kamazi* — perhaps both sprinklings were entirely ordinary water. It would therefore be impossible to rely on two sprinklings. Thus Rabbi Eliezer must hold *yesh bilah* — that the liquids are equally distributed.

Having established that Rabbi Eliezer holds *yesh bilah*, the Gemara continues: *ei kasavar ein hazah tzrichah shiur* — if Rabbi Eliezer held there is no minimum amount required for a valid *haza'ah*, then even one sprinkling should suffice, since even the tiniest amount of *parah adumah* water would validate it. But Rabbi Eliezer requires two sprinklings. This proves he holds *hazah tzrichah shiur* — there is a minimum amount. And by extension, since he allows the two sprinklings to work together, it follows that *mitztarfin lehaza'ot* — two partial amounts can combine to reach the minimum. This is a remarkably tight deductive argument: Rabbi Eliezer's three positions — *yesh bilah*, minimum amount required, and the ability to combine two sprinklings — are each proven from the internal logic of his ruling alone.

One further consequence follows: given *yesh bilah* and the requirement of a minimum amount, for two sprinklings to guarantee that the combined *parah adumah* water meets the minimum, the mixture must contain at least fifty percent *parah adumah* water. If it were less — say forty-nine percent — then each individual sprinkling would contain only forty-nine hundredths of a unit, and two such sprinklings would total only ninety-eight hundredths, falling short of the full unit required. This is the first answer proposed, and it sets the stage for the Amoraim who follow.

### Reish Lakish View

Reish Lakish states: *le'olam yesh bilah, vehazah tzrichah shiur* — the mixture is always equally distributed, and a minimum amount is required. The case under discussion is *kegon shenitarvu achat be'achat* — one where the two liquids are mixed in at least equal halves, so that two sprinklings will together yield a full unit of *parah adumah* water. This is precisely the framework laid out in the first answer above.

### Rava's Position

Rava offers a different reading: *le'olam yesh bilah*, the distribution is equal, but *hazah ein tzrichah shiur* — there is no minimum amount required at all. If so, even one sprinkling should be sufficient. Why then does Rabbi Eliezer require two? *Uknasa dekenasu rabbanan ki heichi delo lishtarshelu* — the rabbis imposed the requirement of two sprinklings as a penalty, so that one who is careless enough to allow foreign water to fall into the *parah adumah* water should not simply proceed as if nothing happened. The double sprinkling is a rabbinic deterrent against negligence, not a logical necessity.

### Rav Ashi's Approach

Rav Ashi takes a different approach entirely: *ein bilah* — the distribution is not equal. This immediately raises the difficulty already posed: if the liquids are not equally distributed, perhaps both sprinklings come entirely from the ordinary water. Rashi preserves a slightly different textual reading for Rav Ashi. On this reading, the reason the Mishnah specified that only a small amount — *kol shehu* — of ordinary water fell in is precisely because of this problem. If it is such a tiny quantity, then even under the assumption of unequal distribution, after one sprinkling that tiny amount is entirely used up. In the worst case, if the first sprinkling contained only ordinary water, that sprinkling exhausted the entire supply of ordinary water. The second sprinkling will then consist exclusively of *parah adumah* water. So Rav Ashi's reading turns on the specificity of the Mishnah's language: the case is deliberately limited to a minimal admixture.

### Braita on Small Amount

A *baraita* is then cited that addresses this directly. *Rebbi omer, ledivrei Rabbi Eliezer, hazah kol shehu metaheres* — according to Rabbi Eliezer, even the smallest amount of *parah adumah* water effects purification. The *baraita* states this in three formulations: first, that the smallest amount works; second, *hazah ein tzrichah shiur* — no minimum amount is required; and third, *hazah mechtzah kesherah umechtzah pesulah* — even a mixture that is half valid and half invalid suffices, as long as some small amount of the *parah adumah* water is present.

This *baraita* clearly supports Rava's and Rav Ashi's approaches — both of which deny a minimum requirement — and decisively rejects Reish Lakish's position. Reish Lakish had held that a minimum amount is required and that two half-units can combine to meet it. But the *baraita* teaches that for Rabbi Eliezer the tiniest amount suffices. Therefore, the reason two sprinklings are required must be either the rabbinic penalty described by Rava or the unequal-distribution concern described by Rav Ashi, not the combining of two partial units as Reish Lakish proposed.

---

## Bilah in Mixed Blood

### Braita Mixed Blood

A second *baraita* is then cited, explicitly connecting the *parah adumah* discussion back to the sacrificial blood scenario of our Mishnah: *hanitnin lema'alah shenitarvu banitnin lemata* — blood of sacrifices that belong above became mixed with blood of those that belong below. Rabbi Eliezer says: *yiten lema'alah vehatachtonim alu lo* — apply above, and the blood that belonged below will also have been discharged through that act.

At this stage, the discussion of *parah adumah* has served its purpose. The question now is focused specifically on our Mishnah and the case of mixed sacrificial bloods: does Rabbi Eliezer operate with *yesh bilah* — equal distribution — or *ein bilah*? The simple reading of the Mishnah and all the *baraitot* surrounding it clearly assumes *yesh bilah*: by putting blood above and blood below, both *korbanot* are satisfied, because the mixture is equally distributed and every sprinkling contains blood from both sacrifices. But the Gemara attempts to maintain the possibility that Rabbi Eliezer holds *ein bilah*, and it is worth tracking how it does so.

### Majority Blood Case

The Gemara says: *ve'i amrat ein bilah — amai alu lo?* If we assume unequal distribution, why would the below-blood discharge be considered accomplished? *Dilma ki yaheiv elyonim lemata vetachtonim lema'alah* — perhaps when he applied blood above, it was all the below-blood, and the above-blood went to the wrong location. The Gemara answers: *hacha bemai askinan kegon de'ika rubei elyonim* — the case involves a majority of above-blood. More specifically, six units of *chatat* blood (which belongs above) are mixed with four units of *olah* blood (which belongs below), and when applying above, one puts four and a bit more than four units. Given this configuration, even under *ein bilah*, one can guarantee that at least some *chatat* blood was applied above, and when the remainder is poured below, at least some *chatat* blood goes there as well.

Critically, however, this reading concedes that the *olah* is not necessarily completed. The claim *vehatachtonim alu lo katani* — that the blood for the below sacrifices was discharged — is interpreted not as meaning the *olah* was properly performed, but *leshem shirayim* — that the remainder was properly disposed of as *shirayim*, the remnant that is to be poured at the base of the altar. It is a forced reading, but it is the price of maintaining *ein bilah*.

This case also introduces a subtle wrinkle. When the Gemara describes a second *baraita* — *natan lemata velo nimlach, Rabbi Eliezer omer yachzor veyiten lema'ala vehatachtonim alu lo* — blood was placed below first without authorization; Rabbi Eliezer says go back and apply above, and the bottom application counts — the same forced answer is offered: the majority is above-blood, a precise quantity is applied above, and the bottom application counts only as *shirayim*, not as a valid application of the *olah* blood.

### Below Then Above

This second *baraita* — where the blood was first applied below, and then Rabbi Eliezer instructs it to be applied above — introduces a fascinating wrinkle noted by the *rishonim*. If what was done below counts only as *shirayim*, one must ask: can *shirayim* be poured out before the primary blood application has even been performed? Normally, *shirayim* refers to the remainder after the primary sprinkling. Rashi appears to read the Gemara as accepting precisely this: the application below is retroactively treated as *shirayim* once the primary application above is completed. Tosafot disagrees and reads the Gemara as requiring that after the above application is performed, the blood is brought below again. In Tosafot's reading, the first below-application does not itself serve as *shirayim*; rather, a new below-application is performed after completing the above. This is not merely a textual nuance — it reflects a substantive question about whether *shirayim* can precede the primary act it is the remnant of.

### Above First Agreement

A third *baraita* brings a further case: *natan lema'ala velo nimlach* — blood was applied above without authorization. *Eilu ve'eilu modim sheyachzor veyiten lemata* — both Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* agree that one should proceed and apply below. This is a striking point: the *chachamim*, who generally oppose Rabbi Eliezer's leniency, agree here. Why? Because once the blood has been applied above, the remaining blood must go somewhere. For the *chatat* blood, it should properly be poured *leshem shirayim* at the base below. For the *olah* blood mixed in, applying it below is the correct thing to do. Therefore the *chachamim* have no objection — regardless of whether *yesh bilah* or *ein bilah*, placing the remainder below is correct and necessary.

The *baraita* then says: *eilu ve'eilu alu lo* — both sacrifices were discharged. This phrase is what the Gemara seizes upon. If both sacrifices were properly completed, this seems to require *yesh bilah* — for without equal distribution, one could not know that both bloods reached their proper locations. The Gemara attempts the same answer as before: the case involves a majority of above-blood, applied in a precise quantity. But the *baraita*'s explicit language — *eilu ve'eilu alu lo* — both counted — is difficult to reconcile with *ein bilah* and only the *chatat* working.

The Gemara's resolution is elegant: *seifa atan lerabbanan de'amri yesh bilah* — the final clause, stating that both counted, reflects the *rabbanan*'s position, not Rabbi Eliezer's. The *rabbanan* hold *yesh bilah*, and for them, of course, both sacrifices were completed. The agreement that one proceeds below is shared by both Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim*, but the statement that "both counted" is the *chachamim*'s conclusion based on their holding of *yesh bilah*. For Rabbi Eliezer, we can still maintain *ein bilah*, with the forced answers given earlier — only the *chatat* necessarily worked, and the *olah* may not have.

Throughout all of this, the Gemara acknowledges that the plain and natural reading of every source is *yesh bilah* — equal distribution. The forced arguments are precisely that: the Gemara is stretching to preserve the possibility of *ein bilah* for Rabbi Eliezer, even as every case seems to point in the opposite direction.

---

## Single Application Proof

### Bechor & Maaser

The Gemara brings a further proof. The Mishnah discusses a case where *bechor* blood — the firstborn animal offering, which requires a single application — becomes mixed with *maaser* blood — tithe blood, which also requires a single application. In such a case, the Mishnah rules that one application is performed. The Gemara asks: if we assumed *ein bilah*, how would one application work? *Dilma mehai kahiv umehai lo kahiv* — perhaps the application consisted entirely of *bechor* blood and none of the *maaser*, leaving the *maaser* offering incomplete.

### One Application Question

The Gemara answers: *kegon shenitarvu achat be'achat* — the case is that equal amounts of each blood were mixed. But the Gemara presses further: even with equal amounts, if distribution is unequal, perhaps all the blood applied came from one and not the other. The answer cannot simply be that the amounts are equal; one still needs to explain how a single application can satisfy both.

### Rashi Four & Four

Rashi addresses this with a reading of the next case in the Mishnah as well: *matan arba b'matan arba* — blood requiring four applications becomes mixed with blood requiring four applications. The Mishnah rules that four applications are performed. Rashi explains that when the Mishnah says to perform four applications, it means to perform four for one sacrifice and then four for the other — in other words, use all of the blood, performing the prescribed applications for each. The mixture is used in full, and whatever the distribution, both bloods will reach the altar. While this is admittedly a strained reading of the Mishnah's simple language, it is the reading required to maintain consistency with *ein bilah*.

---

## Bal Tosif Debate

### Four & One Mixed

The most vexing case is *matan arba b'matanah achat* — blood requiring four applications becomes mixed with blood requiring only one application. Here the *bal tosif* and *bal tigra* debate emerges in full. Does one perform four applications? Then the blood requiring only one application may have been applied four times, violating *bal tosif*. Does one perform one application? Then the blood requiring four applications may not have received the full rite, violating *bal tigra*.
