The Mishnah indicates that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate this, and the very existence of the *bal tosif* concern demonstrates that the applications are in some way being performed with knowledge of what blood is going where — for otherwise, why would there be a *bal tosif* concern at all?

### Rashi Division

The Gemara asks: *ve'i amrat ein bilah* — if distribution is unequal — *amai alu lo?* How could any of it work? And the Gemara suggests the case is, once again, that exactly one unit of each blood was mixed. Rashi's reading of the Mishnah in this context is that when one performs four applications, each application contains one and a quarter units — the five total units divided across four applications. On this reading, the entire blood ends up on the altar and the *korban* requiring one application is discharged because all of its blood eventually reached the *mizbeach*. But the question then arises: why should there be any *bal tosif* concern? Rashi's understanding appears to be that placing more than the required quantity on the altar is the *bal tosif* issue. Yet the simpler understanding of *bal tosif* here — which the Gemara itself seems to favor — is that a blood type that was supposed to be applied only to one corner ends up being placed on four corners. The tension in Rashi's reading is acknowledged.

### Tosafot Minimum

Tosafot offers a different explanation. Tosafot assumes that there is a minimum visible amount required for each application to be halachically significant. With this in mind, Tosafot analyzes the *bal tosif* concern under *ein bilah* as follows. If the bloods are not equally distributed and we are dealing with precise amounts, the scenario where the single-application blood ends up spread across two or more corners with the minimum amount in each is extremely unlikely. In order for there to be a *bal tosif* problem — where the single-application blood has been applied to an additional corner with enough to count — one would need exactly equal distribution. Under *ein bilah*, any other distribution will result in the single-application blood failing to appear in a minimum amount in the extra corner, meaning there is no actual *bal tosif* violation. Therefore, says Tosafot, under *ein bilah* there is no realistic *bal tosif* concern in the constrained scenarios the Gemara has been working with. The *bal tosif* concern only makes genuine sense if one assumes *yesh bilah*, because it is only under equal distribution that one can be sure that the single-application blood appears in sufficient quantity in each of the multiple applications. This is, Tosafot argues, the Gemara's precise question: given the reading that limits the mixture to precise quantities and treats the distribution as unequal, why does the *bal tosif* concern arise at all?

---

## Vessels vs. Liquids

### Rava Distinction

After all the attempts to maintain *ein bilah* for Rabbi Eliezer, the Gemara proposes a clean resolution through Rava: *ella amar Rava, be-velulim lo peligi* — regarding liquids that have actually been blended together, there is no debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* about *bilah*. *Ki peligi — be-khosot* — their debate concerns separate vessels whose contents have become intermingled, not liquids that have been physically mixed together.

This is a decisive clarification. All the scenarios in the Mishnah and the *baraitot* — putting above, putting below, one counted, both counted — are not cases where the bloods were literally poured into one bowl and mixed. They are cases where the bowls themselves were confused, so that one does not know which bowl belongs to which sacrifice. When the Gemara says to apply the blood above from both and below from both, it means: take from each bowl and apply it to each location. In that framework, one need not worry about *bilah* at all — one is deliberately applying from each bowl to each location, and therefore the question of equal versus unequal distribution of liquids never arises.

The practical implications of *yesh bilah* and *ein bilah* for mixed liquids are not resolved here. If liquids were actually blended, then for Rabbi Eliezer — who by this reading takes no position on *bilah* — the various forced answers the Gemara offered earlier would be necessary. But the Mishnah itself does not concern mixed liquids. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* in the Mishnah is entirely about mixed vessels, and it turns not on *bilah* at all, but on *ro'in*: whether one may halachically "view" the inappropriate blood as if it were water. Rabbi Eliezer holds of *ro'in* and the *Rabbanim* do not.

### Rabbi Yehuda Braita

The Gemara challenges this reading by citing a *baraita*: *amar Rabbi Yehuda lo nechelku Rabbi Eliezer vachachamim al dam chatat shenitarev bedam olah sheyikarev* — Rabbi Yehuda says that Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* do not debate the case of *chatat* blood mixed with *olah* blood at all. Where there is no *baal mum* concern and both sacrifices are equally valid, everyone agrees the blood may be offered. Furthermore, everyone agrees that blood of an animal that was used in an act of bestiality (*rova venirva*) may not be offered. The actual debate, says Rabbi Yehuda, is limited to blood of an unblemished animal mixed with blood of a *baal mum*: *she-Rabbi Eliezer omer yikarev bein be-valla bein be-khosot* — Rabbi Eliezer says to offer it whether the liquids were blended or the vessels were mixed, and the *chachamim* say not to offer it in either case.

This *baraita* directly contradicts Rava's resolution. Rabbi Yehuda explicitly states that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling applies *bein be-valla bein be-khosot* — both to blended liquids and to mixed vessels. This would restore all the difficulties: if Rabbi Eliezer rules even for blended liquids, we are back to needing to determine his position on *yesh bilah*, and all the strained answers to the various *baraitot* are required.

### Rabbanim Vessels

The Gemara's response is that Rabbi Yehuda's formulation reflects his own understanding of Rabbi Eliezer's position — *Rabbi Yehuda aliba de-Rabbi Eliezer masik bein be-valla bein be-khosot* — Rabbi Yehuda attributes to Rabbi Eliezer a ruling that covers both scenarios. For Rabbi Yehuda, one must indeed work with the forced answers given earlier for the blended-liquid cases. But the *rabbanan* — the *chachamim* — understand their own dispute with Rabbi Eliezer as concerning only mixed vessels: *ve-rabbanan be-khosot peligi*. On this reading, the *chachamim* and Rabbi Eliezer agree about the case of blended liquids — perhaps because, without *ro'in*, blended blood can never be rendered valid regardless of *bilah* — and their actual disagreement is confined to the vessel-confusion scenario, where the question of *ro'in* is operative.

The upshot of the entire sugya is thus as follows. The simple and plain reading of the Mishnah and all the related *baraitot* assumes *yesh bilah* — equal distribution of mixed liquids. The Gemara labored to show that it is possible to read all the sources as consistent with *ein bilah* for Rabbi Eliezer, but those readings were uniformly forced and concede that results are partial at best. Rava's elegant resolution — that the debate concerns vessels, not blended liquids, and turns on *ro'in* rather than *bilah* — bypasses the *bilah* question entirely for the primary dispute in the Mishnah. And where Rabbi Yehuda's *baraita* insists that Rabbi Eliezer addresses blended liquids too, the Gemara confines that to Rabbi Yehuda's personal reading, while the *rabbanan* maintain that even their own controversy with Rabbi Eliezer never extended to that case.

---

---

# Zevachim 81

## Abaye: Initial Blood Only

### Abaye's Limitation

The daf opens in the middle of 81a, at the word *bekosot*, where Abaye introduces an important qualification to the preceding debate. The extended discussion that preceded this point concerned what happens when the blood of a *chatas* — which must be applied in the upper half of the altar — becomes mixed with the blood of an *olah* — which must be applied in the lower half. Since applying the mixture anywhere will necessarily place the wrong blood in the wrong location for one of the two sacrifices, the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* was about how to proceed. Rabbi Eliezer held that one may designate the mismatched blood as water and proceed *lechatchila*, while the *chachamim* refused to sanction the wrong placement *lechatchila*, even though they agreed *bediavad* that it would be valid. Running through all of that debate was the implicit assumption of *yesh bila* — that blood disperses equally throughout a mixture — so that whichever portion of the mixture one applies can be presumed to contain both bloods in proportion. The *gemara* had tried, in light of a statement by Rabbi Eliezer regarding the water of a *chatas* of the *parah adumah*, to argue that Rabbi Eliezer might actually hold *ein bila* — that equal distribution cannot be assumed — and then worked strenuously to fit his positions accordingly. Ultimately the *gemara* concluded that even under *ein bila*, one could explain the cases not as the bloods mixing together but as the various collection bowls becoming confused, so that one pours from each bowl and demonstrably includes both bloods in both applications. With that settled, the *gemara* now turns to a related point that emerged implicitly during the debate but is significant in its own right.

Abaye states: *lo shanu ella techilat hachatas v'olah*. The debate over what to do with a mixture applies only to the initial blood of the *chatas* and the initial blood of the *olah*, where there is genuine tension between the required locations of the two sacrifices. However, *aval sof hachatas v'olah, divrei hakol makom olah makom shirayim* — if one has the remnant blood (*shirayim*) of a *chatas* mixed together with *olah* blood, everyone agrees *lechatchila* that this may be placed in the lower half of the altar, at the wall, as if doing the *olah* application.

### Initial vs. Final Blood

The reasoning behind this distinction requires some unpacking. When the *kohen* first applies the *chatas* blood at the upper portion of the altar, that fulfills the essential application for the *chatas*. What remains is the *shirayim* — the remnant blood — whose proper place is the base of the altar. Now, the base is in the lower portion of the altar, and the *olah* blood is also thrown in the lower portion. So when the *shirayim* of a *chatas* is mixed with *olah* blood, there is no fundamental tension: the lower portion is the correct location for both. This is in fact implicit in a *braita* already cited earlier, which stated that even the *chachamim* agree with Rabbi Eliezer that one may *lechatchila* spill the remainder of the blood below — because the *chatas* blood is also properly placed below once the initial application at the top has already occurred.

The *chiddush* being made explicit here, however, is more subtle. When one performs the *olah* blood application, one throws the blood against the wall of the altar in the lower half — typically at a corner, striking two walls simultaneously — and from there the blood runs down toward the base. The *shirayim* of the *chatas*, on the other hand, is supposed to be spilled directly at the base, ideally onto a horizontal surface. Abaye's point is that throwing the mixture against the lower wall — as one would for the *olah* — also counts as an acceptable placement for the *chatas shirayim*, even though the blood reaches the base indirectly by running down rather than being poured directly onto it.

### Rav Yosef Disagrees

Rav Yosef, who was Abaye's teacher, challenges this. He cites a ruling in the name of Rav Yehuda: *shirayim tzrichim itztzaba* — the *shirayim* requires a horizontal platform. Pouring onto a vertical surface, even one from which the blood will naturally run down to the base, does not constitute a valid *shfichat shirayim*. The blood must be placed directly on the horizontal base, not on the wall. According to Rav Yosef, even if the blood runs to the base, the act of placing it on the wall is categorically insufficient.

### Rabbi Shimon Agrees

Rabbi Shimon is then cited as taking a position parallel to Abaye's: *lo shanu ella techilat hachatas v'olah* — the debate applies only to the initial blood. But when it comes to the *shirayim* of the *chatas* mixed with the *olah* blood, *divrei hakol makom olah makom shirayim* — all opinions agree that the wall in the lower portion of the altar is an acceptable place, and one may throw the mixture there *lechatchila*. This aligns with Abaye against Rav Yosef.

### Rabbi Yochanan Disputes

Rabbi Yochanan — with the alternative attribution of Rabbi Eliezer — disagrees, siding with Rav Yosef: *adayin hi machloket* — this question remains a matter of dispute even in the case of *shirayim*. The *chachamim* would still hold that this placement is insufficient, and it would be preferable to pour the remaining blood into the drain rather than treat the wall as an adequate location for the spilling of *shirayim*. So the debate between Abaye and Rabbi Yochanan turns on whether the lower wall of the altar constitutes an acceptable location for the discharge of *shirayim* — a question that will continue to generate analysis throughout the *sugya*.

---

## Ein Olin Mevatlin

### Kodesh Hem Proof

Rav Huna bar Yehuda now raises an objection to the preceding discussion — specifically to the assumption that this wall-versus-base question is the *chiddush* being taught by any relevant source. He cites the verse in Numbers 18:17, which discusses the *bechor*: *ach bechor shor o bechor kesev o bechor ez lo tifdeh kodesh hem, et damam tizrok al hamizbeach v'et chelvam taktira* — the firstborn of an ox, sheep, or goat may not be redeemed; they are holy. Throw their blood upon the altar and burn their fat. The word *kodesh hem* — "they are holy" — uses the plural, which is understood as carrying a *chiddush*: *she'im nitarav b'dam kodshim acheirim yikreivu* — even if the blood of a *bechor* becomes mixed with other sacrificial bloods, those bloods may still be brought on the altar. The plural *hem* signals that each blood retains its identity and does not disappear into the mixture.

Rav Huna bar Yehuda assumes that the specific *chiddush* of this verse is that the location where *olah* blood is applied — namely, the lower wall — counts as an acceptable place for the *shirayim* of the blood mixed with it. The case, as Rav Huna construes it, would be: you have already completed the primary *olah* application, and now you have the *shirayim* of the *olah* mixed with the blood of a *bechor*, and the verse tells you that you may throw this mixture against the wall as you would the *olah*. *U'shma mina makom olah makom shirayim* — one should learn from this verse that the location of the *olah* application counts as an acceptable place for the spilling of the *shirayim*.

### Source Debate

The *gemara* immediately deflects this inference. *Lo* — no. The case in the verse is not about *shirayim* but about the initial blood of the *olah* getting mixed with the initial blood of a *bechor*. Both involve initial applications, and neither has yet had any blood placed. But this raises the question: if it is the initial blood of an *olah* mixed with the initial blood of a *bechor*, what exactly is the *chiddush*? After all, *olah* blood requires four applications (two corners, each striking two walls, yielding four surfaces), while *bechor* blood requires only one application. When these two bloods become mixed together, one faces a dilemma between *bal tosif* — the prohibition against adding to the required service — and *bal tigra* — the prohibition against subtracting from it. If one does four applications to honor the *olah*, that is too many for the *bechor*; if one does only one application for the *bechor*, that is too few for the *olah*. This strikes Tosafot as the natural *chiddush* of the verse — the *pasuk* is telling you that you are still permitted to choose one or the other and proceed, rather than simply pouring the blood out.

The *gemara*, however, does not invoke this reasoning. Instead it says: *u'mai kamashma lan? De'ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh* — the *chiddush* is that things which are brought on the altar (*olin*) do not cause *bitul* for one another. This is the principle that when different sacrificial bloods become mixed, no blood is considered cancelled or nullified by the other, even if one blood vastly outnumbers the other. The minority blood does not disappear. In contrast to ordinary laws of *bitul* in *kashrut* — where Rabbi Yehuda holds that *min b'mino* (like substance with like substance) can never be *batel*, and the *chachamim* generally permit *bitul* in a majority — the *chachamim* agree that in the realm of sacrificial blood, *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh*: the blood of a *bechor* mixed with *olah* blood in any ratio is still considered present in its entirety.

This principle explains why all the preceding analysis about bloods getting mixed was never troubled by the question of whether one blood was simply too small to count: in the world of *kodshim*, there is no such thing. Now the *gemara* asks: if this is the *chiddush* of *kodesh hem*, why is there a need for an alternate derivation? The *gemara* answers: *tannai hi* — it is a dispute among *tannaim*. Some derive *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh* from *kodesh hem*, some from *u'lakach midam hapar u'midam hase'ir* — the verse about Yom Kippur — and some from the repetition of the word *dam dam* in the *parashah*. We will return shortly to analyze why each of these sources is preferred by different authorities and why no single verse commands universal agreement.

---

## Wall vs. Base Debate

### Tosafot's Questions

Before continuing the *gemara*'s own resolution of the source question, it is worth pausing on the serious questions raised by Tosafot regarding the premise of this whole discussion. Tosafot asks: what does it even mean to say that *makom olah* is *makom shirayim* — that the location of the *olah* application is an acceptable location for the spilling of *shirayim*? The question is not simply about the vertical-versus-horizontal problem that Rav Yosef raised. There is an additional geographic problem: the application of *olah* blood and the spilling of *shirayim* are not done at the same location on the altar. Visualizing the altar, with the ramp ascending on the southern side: when you descend the ramp, the designated place to spill the *shirayim* is at the southwestern corner of the base — the first base you encounter. But when you throw the *olah* blood, you throw it at the two corners — northeast and southwest, or whichever pair is designated. The corner where you throw the *olah* blood is not necessarily at the same location as the southwestern base where the *shirayim* would go. So even setting aside the wall-versus-base question, the two locations may not actually coincide.

Tosafot offers three responses. The first — that we may be discussing the second throwing of blood — is not the straightforward reading. The other two are more substantive. One is that perhaps since the *Torah* does not specify precisely which base is required, there may be some latitude: even if the *shirayim* is technically designated for one particular base, other bases might still be acceptable. The other answer turns on the direction the *kohen* faces when descending the ramp: the rule that one spills the *shirayim* at the southwest is based on the fact that if the *kohen* turns right upon descending, the southwest base is the first one he encounters. But if he turns left, the southeast is the first base he encounters — and that corner corresponds to the location of one of the *olah* blood-throwing positions. So Tosafot suggests that in this mixed-blood scenario, the *kohen* should simply turn left upon descending the ramp, and the location of the *olah* throwing would then coincide with the first base, making both applications valid at the same spot.

Tosafot raises the second question separately: if the *gemara* says the *chiddush* of *kodesh hem* is not about the wall counting for *shirayim* but rather about *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh*, is that truly a *chiddush* that requires a verse? Tosafot phrases this sharply: *teima tuva kamashma lan de'ikreivu, lemar kide'it lei matana shtayim shehen arba, u'lemar matana achat af al gav de'avar al bal tigra u'val tosif* — what a great *chiddush* the verse tells us, that when they are mixed you bring them — according to one view doing two applications that count as four, and according to another doing one application even though that involves *bal tigra* and *bal tosif*. This seems to be the genuinely counterintuitive ruling that a verse would be needed to convey: that you are permitted to proceed despite the *bal tosif/bal tigra* dilemma, rather than simply pouring the blood out. Tosafot answers that perhaps the logic of *bitul* — treating the extra blood as if it were water — would allow you to do the applications without technically violating *bal tosif* and *bal tigra*, or that the principle of *shev v'al ta'aseh* (passive inaction) neutralizes the concern. But Tosafot himself acknowledges that the question is stronger than the answer — if the natural concern when bloods are mixed is that one should pour them out rather than create a *bal tosif/bal tigra* situation, the verse that permits you to proceed is indeed a major *chiddush*, one the *gemara* seems to pass over without sufficient explanation.

### Baraita Proof

The *gemara* now introduces a *braita* that appears to provide direct evidence that the location of the *olah* application counts as valid for *shirayim*. The *braita* states: *natan lema'ala v'lo nimlach* — the mixture of *chatas* and *olah* blood was applied above without seeking guidance — *elu v'eilu modim sheyachzor v'yitein lematah* — both Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* agree that one should go ahead and now apply it below. Moreover, *eilu v'eilu olin lo* — both applications count; the lower application is valid both for the *chatas* and for the *olah*.

At first glance, this appears to be the clearest possible proof. The case as read is: the *chatas* and *olah* blood were mixed. The *kohen* applied some of the mixture at the top, fulfilling the primary *chatas* application. Now what remains is the *shirayim* of the *chatas* mixed with the *olah* blood. The *braita* says: go ahead and apply it at the bottom — and this is precisely the *olah* application method of throwing it against the lower wall. The *chachamim* agree that this is done *lechatchila* in this situation. And the conclusion is stated explicitly: both count. This seems to be direct proof that *makom olah makom shirayim* — the wall location used for the *olah* is also counted as valid for the discharge of *shirayim*.

The *gemara* says: *u'shma mina makom olah makom shirayim* — is this not a proof? And indeed, so it appears. But as the *gemara* is wont to do even after presenting a compelling proof, it proceeds to examine whether the *braita* can be read differently.

---

## Ein Olin Mevatlin (II)

### Yom Kippur Distinction

Returning to the question of the sources for *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh*, the *gemara* now explains why certain *tannaim* do not learn the principle from the Yom Kippur blood. The verse states: *u'lakach midam hapar u'midam hase'ir* — one takes from the blood of the ox and from the blood of the goat. The apparent *chiddush* is that even though the blood of the ox vastly outnumbers the blood of the goat, both are considered present in the mixture when applied on the *mizbeach hazahav*. However, some *tannaim* hold *ein me'arvin lekaranos* — that the two bloods are not actually mixed together but are applied separately, first the blood of the ox and then the blood of the goat. If the bloods were never combined, there is no scenario of mixture to generate a *chiddush* about *bitul*, and thus no proof for *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh* can be drawn from this verse.

### Three Sources Analyzed

This brings us to a full accounting of why each of the three candidate sources was not universally accepted. The three possible sources are: (1) *u'lakach midam hapar u'midam hase'ir* from Yom Kippur, (2) *kodesh hem* from the verse about the *bechor*, and (3) the repetition of *dam dam* in the *parashah*.

For *dam dam*: *dam dam lo mashma lehu* — the mere repetition of the word *dam* does not carry sufficient textual weight to generate this *halacha*. The *Torah* says to throw the blood on the altar, and it is unremarkable that the word *dam* appears more than once; it is not obviously an extra word carrying independent meaning.

The Yom Kippur source, as just explained, is rejected by those who hold that the two bloods are applied separately and never actually mixed.

### Kodesh Hem Limited

As for *kodesh hem* — why do some *tannaim* not derive *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh* from this verse? The *gemara* answers: *kasavri kodesh hem lo yalpi* — because they derive a different *halacha* from *kodesh hem*. *Hem krevim v'ein tmuratam kreva* — the verse "they are holy" teaches specifically about the *bechor*: the *bechorim* themselves are brought as sacrifices, but their *tmurah* — the animal substituted for them — cannot be brought as a sacrifice. A *bechor* is not sanctified through an owner's verbal declaration; it is sacred by virtue of birth. Therefore, when someone attempts to make a *tmurah* for a *bechor*, unlike with other sanctified animals whose *tmurah* can be brought, the *tmurah* of a *bechor* is sacred in the sense that it cannot be redeemed, but it cannot actually be offered. This is the *halacha* taught by *kodesh hem*, according to those *tannaim* — it has nothing to do with the mixing of bloods.

Those who do derive *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh* from *kodesh hem* must obtain the *tmurah* ruling from elsewhere: *nafka lei mishor im seh lashem hu* — "whether it is an ox or a sheep, it is for God" — from this phrase one learns that the *bechor* itself is brought (*hu karev*), while its *tmurah* is not (*v'ein tmuratam kreva*). With that *halacha* derived from a separate source, *kodesh hem* is freed to teach the law of blood mixture and *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh*. The unresolved question of whether the lower wall counts as a valid location for *shirayim* remains open, as the *braita* proofs examined thus far have not yielded a definitive ruling.

---

## Wall vs. Base Debate (II)

### Two Chatasim Theory

The *gemara* now provides the promised reinterpretation of the *braita*. When Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef arrived from Eretz Yisrael — and recall that Rabbi Yochanan, who disputes whether the wall counts for *shirayim*, was from Eretz Yisrael — he transmitted the following: *hachi amri b'ma'arava, hacha b'mai askinan, kegon de'eirev chatas chitzona b'shirayim* — here is what they say in the west about what the *braita* is actually discussing. The *braita* is not dealing with a mixture of *chatas* and *olah* blood. Rather, it concerns a mixture of two types of *chatas* blood: the blood of an outer *chatas* (*chatas chitzona*) and the *shirayim* of an inner *chatas* (*chatas pnimit*).

The inner *chatas* — such as the ox of Yom Kippur or the *par he'elem davar shel tzibur* — has its primary applications performed inside on the golden incense altar. The *shirayim* of the inner *chatas* is to be spilled at the base of the outer altar. Now, if the *shirayim* of the inner *chatas* becomes mixed with the blood of an outer *chatas*, one cannot put it at the top, since the *shirayim* does not belong there. If the *kohen* nonetheless applied some of the mixture at the top, then what remains in the mixture is *shirayim* and *shirayim* — the remnant of the outer *chatas* (now that its primary application was done above) and the *shirayim* of the inner *chatas*. In that case, the *braita* says: go ahead and spill the remainder at the base below, and both count. This is not about throwing it on the wall as one does for an *olah*; it is about spilling it directly at the base, which is exactly where *shirayim* belongs. There is no proof here at all that the wall counts for *shirayim*.

Abaye then presses: *v'neima mar kegon de'eirev b'shirayim d'shirayim* — why must the reinterpretation involve *shirayim* of an inner *chatas* mixed with an outer *chatas* blood? Why not simply say it is the *shirayim* of an outer *chatas* mixed with the initial blood of another outer *chatas*?

The *gemara* responds: *dilma ha kamashma lan afilu man d'amar shirayim me'akvin, chasrei ein me'akvin* — perhaps the *braita* is specifically designed to teach a *chiddush* regarding inner *chatasim*. There is a position that the spilling of the *shirayim* is *me'akev* — an indispensable step — for an inner *chatas*. For ordinary outer sacrifices, the *shirayim* is never *me'akev*; the sacrifice is fully valid whether or not the *shirayim* is properly discharged. The one possible exception is the inner *chatas*, where some hold the *shirayim* is required for full validity. By presenting the scenario of inner *chatas shirayim* mixed with outer *chatas* blood, the *braita* teaches a double *chiddush*: first, that even when the *shirayim* is *me'akev* (as it may be for the inner *chatas*), the arrangement of spilling it at the base of the outer altar satisfies that requirement; and second, that even if some of the *shirayim* was already diverted — applied mistakenly at the top — whatever remains can still validate the obligation. If the *braita* had simply described outer *chatas shirayim* mixed with outer *chatas* initial blood, none of these *chiddushim* would be in play, since outer *shirayim* is never *me'akev* and the question of sufficiency would not arise.

### Unresolved Status

The result of this analysis is that the *gemara* has successfully shown that the *braita* need not be read as dealing with *chatas* and *olah* blood at all, and therefore need not be read as affirming that the wall is a valid location for *shirayim*. The *braita* can be entirely reinterpreted as involving two categories of *chatas* blood — inner and outer — in which case the conclusion "spill it at the base" is simply about spilling it at the base, with no wall application implied. The question of whether the lower wall of the altar counts as an acceptable location for the discharge of *shirayim* thus remains unresolved.

---

## Baraita Reconciliation

### Limited Validation

Rav Tosfaa addresses Ravina with a point connecting the *braita* discussion back to the analysis of the previous daf. He notes: the attempted proof from the *braita* — that if the *kohen* already applied the mixture above, both should go ahead and apply it below — was being offered as evidence that the lower wall counts for *shirayim*. But Rav Tosfaa recalls that in the earlier analysis, they had established something more limited: when the mixture of *chatas* and *olah* blood is applied below, only the *chatas* component is validated, not the *olah*. The *olah* is not rendered valid by this placement. So even on the straightforward reading of the *braita* — that it concerns *chatas* and *olah* blood — there would be no proof about *makom olah* being *makom shirayim*, because the *olah* was not being validated by the wall application in the first place.

### Ein Bila Context

Rav Tosfaa clarifies that this earlier limitation — that only the *chatas* was being validated, not the *olah* — was itself contingent on the position of *ein bila*. It was when one entertained the hypothesis that equal distribution of blood through a mixture cannot be assumed, requiring a very forced reading of the *braita* with specific quantities (six units of *chatas*, four of *olah*, and so forth), that the conclusion was: only the *chatas* is being made valid, not the *olah*.

### Final Resolution

Ultimately, the *gemara* did not retain the *ein bila* explanation. The final resolution was *maskana bekosot pligi* — in the end, the debate is about the cups, not about whether the bloods disperse within a single vessel. Even those who hold *ein bila* explain these cases by saying the collection bowls became confused, so that when blood is thrown, it is thrown from each bowl — guaranteeing that both bloods are applied in both locations. Once the *braita* is read on this basis, both the *chatas* and the *olah* are validated by the application below. And if that is the case — if the *chachamim* permit throwing the mixture against the lower wall and thereby validate both the *olah* and the *chatas shirayim* — then it would seem to follow as a proof that the wall indeed counts for *shirayim*. The *gemara* ultimately retreats from this by reinterpreting the *braita* as concerning two *chatasim* rather than *chatas* and *olah*, and the question of whether the wall counts remains *lo pesika* — not definitively resolved.

---

## Inner and Outer

### Spill When Mixed

The *gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*, which introduces a different kind of blood mixture: *hanitnin bifnim shenisarvu benitnin bachutz yishpechu la'amah* — blood designated for the inner altar (inside the *heichal*) that became mixed with blood designated for the outer altar should be poured out into the drain. The two types of blood are so fundamentally different in their required locations that no application combining them is sanctioned. The *gemara* will subsequently ask why Rabbi Eliezer — who throughout the prior *mishnayos* was prepared to treat the wrong blood as water and permit *lechatchila* application — does not similarly assert here that one may simply proceed, viewing the mismatched blood as water.

### Outer Then Inner

The *mishnah* addresses the case where a *kohen* did not seek guidance and proceeded anyway. *Natan bachutz v'chazar v'natan bifnim* — if one first applied the mixture to the outer altar and then brought it to apply on the inner altar, the ruling is *kasher bediavad*. The sacrifice is valid after the fact. The outer sacrifices were validated when the blood was thrown on the outer altar; the subsequent inner application, while it involved bringing outer blood into the *heichal*, did not retroactively invalidate what had already been rendered valid.

### Inner First Debate

The reverse case — *bifnim v'chazar v'natan bachutz*, bringing the blood first to the inner altar and then to the outer — generates a dispute. *Rabbi Akiva posel v'chachamim machshirim* — Rabbi Akiva rules it invalid while the *chachamim* rule it valid. The question turns on what it means when the blood of an outer sacrifice is brought inside.

### Rabbi Akiva View

Rabbi Akiva's position derives from the verse: *v'chol chatat asher yuva midama el ohel mo'ed l'chaper bakodesh lo te'achel ba'esh tisaref* — any sin offering whose blood is brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the holy place shall not be eaten; it shall be burned with fire. This verse is understood on multiple levels. In its most basic sense, it refers to the category of *chatasim pnimiyos* — inner sin offerings like those of Yom Kippur — whose blood is designed to be brought inside, and whose meat is therefore burned rather than eaten. But Rabbi Akiva reads the verse more expansively: any blood whatsoever that is brought inside the *heichal* for the purpose of atonement, even the blood of an outer sacrifice, invalidates that sacrifice if its status had not yet been finalized. The critical factor is timing: if the outer sacrifice's blood had already been validly applied to the outer altar — as in the case of outer-first-then-inner — then when the blood is subsequently brought inside, the sacrifice is already *kasher* and cannot be retroactively invalidated. But if the blood is brought inside *first*, before any valid application has occurred, then the sacrifice is invalidated by the inner entry.

This logic applies not only to *chatas* blood but, according to Rabbi Akiva, to any sacrificial blood — even *olah* and *shelamim*. The verse does not limit the invalidation to *chatas*; the category of blood that matters is whether it was brought inside while the sacrifice's validity remained pending.

### Chachamim Limit

The *chachamim* disagree. *V'chachamim omrim chatat bilvad* — only *chatas* blood, when brought inside while still pending, causes the sacrifice to become invalid. Other bloods — *olah*, *shelamim*, and the like — are not governed by this rule. The verse is read as specifically addressing the *chatas* and its inner counterpart, not as a general principle applicable to all sacrificial blood.

### Rabbi Eliezer Adds

Rabbi Eliezer occupies an intermediate position: *af asham* — the *asham* (guilt offering) is added to the *chatas* as a type of blood whose inner entry invalidates. He derives this from the principle *kechatas ke'asham* — as the *chatas* so the *asham* — a parallel that he had also invoked earlier in the tractate regarding the laws of *shelo lishmah*. Accordingly, if *asham* blood is brought inside while the sacrifice's status is still unresolved, the *asham* too is invalidated. The spectrum of opinion is thus: Rabbi Akiva — all bloods; *chachamim* — only *chatas*; Rabbi Eliezer — *chatas* and *asham*.

---

## Inner/Outer Sequence

### Inner Before Outer

The *gemara* now asks: given Rabbi Eliezer's general position that one may proceed with a mixed blood offering by treating the wrong component as water, why does he not apply that reasoning here? Why does he not say that *lechatchila* one should go ahead and apply the mixture in both locations, treating the mismatched blood as water in each case? The *gemara* notes a structural constraint: *keshem shemitzvah lehaktim elyonim letachtonim kach mitzvah lehaktim pnim lechutz* — just as it is a *mitzvah* to perform the upper application before the lower one (i.e., the *chatas* before the *olah*, since the *chatas* provides atonement that prepares the person for the subsequent *olah*), so too it is a *mitzvah* to perform the inner application before the outer one. Inner sacrifices take precedence over outer ones in the order of service. This means that if one has a mixture of inner and outer blood, one must begin inside — and only then proceed outside.

### Invalidation Problem

This creates the difficulty for Rabbi Eliezer. In theory, one might suggest: bring the mixture inside first to honor the inner sacrifice, then bring it outside. But Rabbi Eliezer holds that *chatas* and *asham* blood, when brought inside while the outer sacrifice remains unvalidated, invalidates that outer sacrifice. If the mixture contains *chatas* or *asham* blood, the act of entering the *heichal* with it first — as required by the principle of inner before outer — would necessarily invalidate the outer sacrifice before it has had a chance to be validated. One cannot escape this by going outside first, because that would violate the required ordering. So Rabbi Eliezer finds himself in an inescapable bind.

### Uncertainty Rule

Why cannot Rabbi Eliezer simply permit the sequence for the cases where it would work — namely, when the outer sacrifice mixed in is an *olah* or *shelamim* rather than a *chatas* or *asham*? After all, Rabbi Eliezer does not hold, unlike Rabbi Akiva, that *all* blood brought inside invalidates. If it is *olah* blood mixed with inner *chatas* blood, one could bring it inside first (validating the inner *chatas*), then outside (validating the *olah*), and the *olah* would not be invalidated by the inner entry since Rabbi Eliezer only invalidates *chatas* and *asham*, not *olah*. The *gemara* answers: *lo pesika lei* — it is not categorical for Rabbi Eliezer. Since there exist scenarios — namely, *chatas* and *asham* mixtures — where going inside first would definitely invalidate the outer sacrifice, Rabbi Eliezer cannot issue a blanket ruling permitting the inner-then-outer sequence. He cannot say as a general rule that one may proceed *lechatchila*, because the validity of that instruction depends on the precise composition of the mixture, which is unknown. This uncertainty prevents him from offering categorical permission, and therefore the default ruling — spill it out — stands even for Rabbi Eliezer. The *gemara* leaves the sugya here, to continue the following day with the further analysis of Rabbi Akiva's position and the debate between the *chachamim* about which blood triggers invalidation when brought into the *heichal*.

---

---

# Zevachim 82

## Blood Inside Debate

### Mishnah Dispute

The daf opens three lines from the top of 82a, at the words *sheyehei Rabbi Akiva omer*. The *mishnah* records a dispute concerning the *pasuk* in *Tzav* that states: any *chatat* whose blood is brought inside — *el hakodesh pnima*, to atone in the sanctuary — shall not be eaten but shall be burned. At one level, the *pasuk* is simply describing the category of *chata'ot pnimiyot*, inner *chata'ot* — offerings such as the *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* and those brought on *Yom Kippur* — for which the *mitzvah* is to sprinkle the blood inside and burn the meat outside the *mikdash*.

However, the *pasuk* is also read to mean that a kosher, outer *chatat* whose blood was brought inside is thereby invalidated and must be burned. The question in the *mishnah* is whether this *din* is limited to a *chatat* alone. Rabbi Akiva maintains that it applies to all sacrifices: if one brings the blood of any *korban* inside, it is invalidated and must be burned. Rabbi Eliezer holds that it applies to a *chatat* — and, consistent with his position from the first *mishnah* of the *masechet*, to an *asham* as well, since an *asham* is treated like a *chatat*.

### Wine Mixing Analogy

The *gemara* now seeks to explain where Rabbi Akiva derives his position. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *mashal lema hadavar domeh* — to what is this comparable? To a student who had been mixing his master's wine with hot water. The master then asked him to pour more. The student asked: shall I mix it again with hot water? The master replied: need you ask? We have been dealing with hot water all along — you should have assumed hot water. But since you have gone to the trouble of asking me, fine: mix it however you like, with hot water or cold water.

The *nimshal*: the *Torah* was already speaking within the context of a *chatat* — *meichdi bechatat askinan*. Why then did it write *vechol chatat asher yuva midamah el ohel mo'ed el hakodesh pnima lo te'achel*? It should simply have written *vechol asher yuva midamah*, since the context already implied *chatat*. The fact that it went ahead and said *chatat* explicitly — just as the master, once pushed to speak, said whatever you like — signals that *chatat* here is not meant to limit but to expand. Thus *ela kol kodshim*: the *halacha* applies to all *kodshim*. The word *chatat*, rather than being purely restrictive, opens the door to a broader inclusion because of its very redundancy.

### Rav Huna Challenge

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua challenged this reasoning. He argued that the immediate context of the *pasuk* was not narrowly limited to a *chatat* in the first place, and therefore the word *chatat* in the *pasuk* cannot be read as redundant. The surrounding *pesukim* in *Tzav* open with the broad heading *zot torat hachatat* — this is the law of the *chatat* — and proceed through a series of *halachot*: the *chatat* is slaughtered where the *olah* is slaughtered; blood that spatters on a garment must be laundered in a holy place; a pottery vessel used to cook the *chatat* must be broken, while a copper vessel must be scoured and rinsed with water.

Crucially, this *halacha* of *merika ushfifa* — the scouring and rinsing of vessels — is established elsewhere in the *gemara* as applying not only to a *chatat* but to all *korbanot*. Therefore, the *pesukim* immediately preceding the clause about blood brought inside were already speaking in a context broader than *chatat* alone. Rav Huna therefore argues: *chatat dechativ Rachmana lamah li* — when the *Torah* says *chatat* in connection with blood brought inside, it cannot be dismissed as redundant, because the surrounding material was not narrowly about *chatat*. On the contrary, saying *chatat* here was necessary — and it limits the *din* to a *chatat* specifically.

In light of this objection, the *gemara* revises the *mashal*: it is more akin to a student who was mixing wine sometimes with hot water and sometimes with cold water, and the master explicitly said: please mix it with hot water. Hot water means hot water — it is not an expansion, it is a limitation. Accordingly, the *mashal* of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel no longer holds as originally formulated. The reason for Rabbi Akiva's position must be sought elsewhere.

### Expansive Language

The *gemara* concludes that the source for Rabbi Akiva is not the analogy of contextual redundancy but the expansive language of the *pasuk* itself — specifically the word *vechol*. It could have written simply *chatat asher yuva midamah*, but it wrote *vechol chatat* — and the word *vechol* carries an inclusive force. A *braita* makes this explicit: *chatat ein li ela chatat* — from the word *chatat* alone I know only a *chatat*. *Kodshei kodashim*, such as an *olah*, from where? *Talmud lomar vechol chatat*. *Asham* and *kodashim kalim*, such as *shelamim*, from where? *Talmud lomar vechol* — with the additional *vav* — *chatat*. These are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

### Rabbi Yose Response

Rabbi Yose HaGelili responds to Rabbi Akiva with a characteristic rejoinder: *afilu ata marbe kol hayom kulo eini shomea lach* — even if you try to include as much as you like all day long, I am not buying it. This is the classic tension between Rabbi Akiva, who derives extensive *halachot* from extra letters and words, and Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who resists reading small textual additions as radically expanding the scope of a *pasuk*.

To be clear, Rabbi Yose HaGelili does not reject the principle that *vechol* is inclusive. What he rejects is the forced reading that *vechol chatat* can mean something other than a *chatat*, when the *pasuk* explicitly says *chatat*. He accepts that *vechol* expands — but only within the category of *chatat* itself. Thus: *chatat ein li ela chatat yachid* — I know only an individual's *chatat*. *Chatat tzibur*, a communal *chatat*, from where? *Talmud lomar vechol chatat* — any *chatat*. And there is a further inclusion: *ein li ela chatat nekeva*, I know only a female *chatat* — the standard case. A male *chatat*, such as the *sa'ir* of a *nasi*, from where? *Talmud lomar vechol* — the additional *vav*. So *vechol* is inclusive, but its inclusion remains within the domain of *chatat*.

The *gemara* then asks: does Rabbi Yose HaGelili actually read the *pasuk* as being about an outer *chatat* at all? In fact, a *braita* records that Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds the entire passage is speaking only about *parim hanisrafim use'irim hanisrafim* — the inner *chata'ot* that are burned — and comes to teach two things: that if a *pesul* occurs in an inner *chatat*, its disqualified meat is burned within the *beit hamikdash* itself, in the *beit habirah*; and that there is a *lav* against eating the meat of such an offering. In his reading, the *pasuk* has nothing to do with invalidating an outer *chatat* whose blood was brought inside.

When asked where he then derives the *halacha* that an outer *chatat* is invalidated by having its blood brought inside, he answers: from the story of Moshe and Aharon, where Moshe says *hen lo huva et damah el hakodesh pnimah* — the blood was not brought inside — implying that had it been brought inside, the burning would have been understandable. It is from that narrative that he learns an outer *chatat* is invalidated. As the *gemara* concludes: *ledvarav de'Rabbi Akiva ka'amar* — when Rabbi Yose HaGelili was debating Rabbi Akiva, his point was: even according to your reading of the *pasuk* as concerning an outer *korban*, the word *vechol chatat* cannot be legitimately extended beyond the category of *chatat* itself.

---

## Outside vs. Inside

### Two Bowls Case

The *gemara* now transitions to explore various scenarios in which the invalidity arising from blood brought inside plays out. The *mishnah* presents the following case: a *chatat* whose blood was received in two bowls — *bishnei kossot* — and one of those bowls was taken outside the *beit hamikdash*. The blood in that bowl becomes invalid. But does the entire *korban* become invalid? The *mishnah* rules no: the outer blood is invalid, but the remaining inner bowl remains *kasher*, and if there is sufficient blood remaining, one proceeds to apply it on the *mizbe'ach*. The *korban* is valid. *Hapnimi kasher*.

The next case presents the mirror scenario: one of the two bowls was brought inside — *nichnas echad meihem lifnimah*, brought into the *heichal*. Here the dispute: Rabbi Yose HaGelili rules the outer blood remains *kasher* — *machshir bachitzon*. The *chachamim* rule that the entire *korban* is invalid — *poslin*.

### Partial Blood Inside

This asymmetry is striking, and Rashi articulates its textual basis clearly. The *chachamim* derive the *din* of blood brought inside from the *pasuk*: *vechol chatat asher yuva midamah el hakodesh pnimah* — the word *midamah*, "from its blood," signals that even some of the blood suffices to invalidate the *korban*. Rabbi Yose HaGelili, however, learns the *din* from the story of Moshe and Aharon, where the *pasuk* says *hen lo huva et damah* — all of its blood — not *midamah*. His source therefore implies that only bringing all of the blood inside would trigger the invalidity.

To clarify the practical scenario: the invalidity applies only when the blood has not yet been validly applied to the *mizbe'ach*. If one bowl was already properly applied and the second bowl was then brought inside, the *korban* is fine. It is only when no valid application has yet occurred that bringing blood inside — even a partial amount — creates the problem.

Rabbi Yose HaGelili now presses the *chachamim* with a *kal vachomer*. He notes the following asymmetry: the outside is a place where *machshava* — wrong intent — invalidates a *korban*. If a *kohen* has a thought of *chutz limkomo* during the service, directing his intent toward the outside, the *korban* is *pasul*. Yet despite the outside being such a powerfully invalidating domain that even thought invalidates there, the *halacha* is that some blood brought outside does not invalidate the remaining blood — *lo asa et hamishuyar kiyotze*. Inside the *heichal*, by contrast, thought directed inward does not invalidate — *makom she'ein hamachshava poselet*. If the outside, which is more severe by the measure of *machshava*, does not render the remaining blood invalid, then the inside, which is less severe by that measure, should certainly not invalidate the remaining blood.

This is a pointed challenge, and notably the *gemara* does not immediately provide an answer to it in the *mishnah* context.

### Intent & Atonement

The *mishnah* records further *machlokot* concerning blood brought inside. Rabbi Eliezer holds: *nichnas lechaper af al pi shelo chipar pasul* — if one brought the blood inside with the intent to apply it there for atonement, even if he never actually performed the application, the *korban* is invalid. The *pasuk* says *asher yuva midamah el hakodesh lechaper bakodesh* — and Rabbi Eliezer reads *lechaper* as describing intent alone, not requiring the act. Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *ad sheyichaper* — the blood must actually have been applied in some atonement ritual inside; mere entry without application does not invalidate. Rabbi Yehuda adds a further condition: *im hichnis shogeg kasher* — if one brought the blood inside inadvertently, the *korban* remains *kasher*, since the *pasuk* emphasizes purposive intent — *lechaper bakodesh*.

### Tzitz Validation

The *mishnah* then introduces a distinct and independent *halacha*: *kol hadamim pesulim shenitnu al gabei hamizbe'ach lo hurtzu* — invalid blood that was placed on the *mizbe'ach* does not become validated thereby. The *korban* is not rendered *kasher* simply because the blood made contact with the altar. Furthermore, *lo hirtza hatzitz* — the *tzitz*, the golden frontplate worn by the *kohen gadol*, does not validate such blood. The *tzitz* has the power to validate only in the case of *tumat hakodashim*: if blood that became *tamei* was applied to the *mizbe'ach*, the presence of the *tzitz* makes the offering valid. But blood that went outside — *hayotzei* — is not subject to the *tzitz*'s validating power. *Hatzitz mertze al hatamei ve'eino mertze al hayotzei*.

This is a completely separate *halacha* from the question of blood brought inside. It addresses what happens when already-invalid blood is placed on the outer *mizbe'ach*, and it distinguishes between two forms of invalidity: *tum'ah*, which the *tzitz* can overcome, and *yetziah*, blood that left its proper domain, which the *tzitz* cannot rectify.

---

## Logic of Inside

### Kal Vachomer

A *braita* records Rabbi Yose HaGelili's *kal vachomer* at greater length, and the exchange with the *chachamim* that follows illuminates the underlying conceptual structure. Rabbi Yose HaGelili states: *u'mah bemakom shemachshava poselet bachutz lo pasal dam shebachutz et shebifnim* — on the outside, where thought invalidates, some blood brought outside does not invalidate the remaining blood. *Makom she'ein machshava poselet* — on the inside, where thought does not invalidate — *eino din shelo yifsol dam shebifnim et shebachutz* — certainly blood brought inside should not invalidate the rest.

The *chachamim* respond: *harei omer asher yuva midamah* — the *pasuk* says *midamah*, even some of the blood. This is explicit: even partial blood brought inside invalidates.

Rabbi Yose HaGelili does not relent. He says: if you are going to accept that *midamah* means even partial blood invalidates on the inside, then by the same *kal vachomer*, partial blood brought outside should certainly invalidate — since the outside is the more powerfully invalidating place. *Kal vachomer leyotzei me'ata*: the outside, where even thought invalidates, should certainly be such that some blood brought outside invalidates the rest.

The *chachamim* respond: *harei omer asher yuva — hanichnas posel ve'ein hayotzei posel*. This is a special *halacha* grounded in the *pasuk*: *asher yuva*, specifically when brought inside. The *Torah* has established an asymmetry — inside invalidates even partially, outside does not — and yes, it is counterintuitive, but it is what the *pasuk* teaches. The logic does not dictate the *din*; the *din* is the *din*.

Stepping back to understand the conceptual logic: blood brought outside the *mikdash* becomes itself invalid — so the remaining blood is unaffected and can still be validly applied. Blood brought inside, however, does not simply become invalid blood. Rather, bringing the blood inside constitutes performing the ritual of an inner *chatat* — it is an act of *lechaper bakodesh*, of doing an atonement ritual in the inner sanctum. That act invalidates the *korban* as a whole. It is not that the inside is a "bad place" that contaminates whatever enters it; rather, performing the inner-*chatat* ritual upon an outer *korban* transforms its status and renders the entire *korban* invalid. That is why the *halacha* requires the element of *lechaper bakodesh* — purposive intent toward inner atonement — and why even a small quantity of blood suffices: it is not a threshold of volume but the performance of a ritual act.

The *gemara* then asks: now that we have established that the inside is more powerful than the outside when it comes to actual blood — should we extend this and say that *machshava* directed inward also invalidates? *Tehei machshava bifnim poselet mikal vachomer*: where the blood itself invalidates powerfully, should thought not do the same? The *gemara* answers: *harei hu omer — bayom hashlishi* — the verse that teaches the *din* of *chutz limkomo* uses the word *shlishi*, and that word requires that the place be *meshulash* — tripled, meaning that blood, meat, and *imurin* are all subject to invalidity there. The outside satisfies this: all three are invalidated when removed from the *mikdash*. The inside does not satisfy this criterion, because meat and *imurin* brought into the *heichal* are not thereby invalidated. Therefore thought about the inside does not invalidate.

### Meshulash Principle

The *gemara* then turns the *kal vachomer* in the opposite direction. Fine — thought about the inside does not invalidate because the inside is not *meshulash*. But now one might argue: since thought does not invalidate on the inside even though actual blood does, and since the outside is less powerful than the inside when it comes to blood — perhaps thought should not invalidate on the outside either? *Velo tehei machshava poselet bachutz mikal vachomer*: on the inside, where even a little blood invalidates the whole *korban*, thought still does not invalidate. On the outside, where a little blood does not invalidate the rest, certainly thought should not invalidate.

The answer: *talmud lomar shlishi* — we know from the word *shlishi* in the *pasuk* of *bayom hashlishi* that thought of the wrong time invalidates, and from the extra word *piggul* we learn thought of the wrong place. And *shlishi* establishes that this applies specifically to a place that is *meshulash* — where blood, meat, and *imurin* are all subject to invalidity. The outside satisfies this. Therefore, thought about the outside does indeed invalidate, and no *kal vachomer* can remove that. The *pasuk* has established it explicitly.

What is striking is the irony the *gemara* now makes explicit: thought about the inside does not invalidate even though the inside is more powerful than the outside when it comes to actual blood. Yet this is precisely what the *pesukim* teach. The criterion for *machshava* invalidation is not about which place is more "dangerous" in terms of actual blood, but about the quality of *meshulash* — whether all three components of a *korban* are at risk there.

### Meat Rules

The *gemara* presses the *kal vachomer* further into the domain of meat. *Bassar hayotzei lachutz pasul, hanichnas lifnim kasher*. Meat that goes outside the *mikdash* is invalid; meat brought inside the *heichal* is not. This is already counterintuitive given the pattern for blood. And the *gemara* asks: should we not say, by *kal vachomer*, that since the inside is more powerfully invalidating when it comes to blood, it should also invalidate meat? *Shehaya badin sheyifsol*: meat brought inside should be *pasul*.

The answer: *midamah* — the *pasuk* specifies "from its blood." *Damah velo bassar*. Only blood invalidates when brought inside; meat is explicitly excluded by the *pasuk*'s language. The unique *din* of *pnimah* applies only to blood.

Then the *kal vachomer* is reversed: since meat brought inside the *heichal* is not invalid, and the inside is such a powerful invalidator — certainly meat brought outside should also not be invalid? *Kal vachomer me'ata*: on the inside, where blood powerfully invalidates, meat does not. On the outside, which is less powerful in terms of blood, meat should certainly not be invalid.

The answer: *uvassar bassadeh tereifah lo socheilu* — we learn from the principle that meat in an uncontained place, in the *sadeh*, is rendered unfit. *Keivan sheyatza bassar chutz mimchitzato ne'essar* — once meat leaves its proper domain, it is forbidden. That is its own *din*, derived from its own source.

The conceptual resolution the *gemara* has arrived at is this: the inside is not simply a "bad place" that invalidates whatever enters it. The *heichal* is not off-limits in the way the outside is off-limits. The problem of blood brought inside is that it constitutes the performance of an inner-*chatat* ritual. Meat has no such ritual significance inside; it is never the instrument of atonement in the *heichal*. The outside, by contrast, truly is the wrong place — for blood, meat, and *imurin* — because those things are out of their proper *mechitzah* entirely. That is why the *din* of *bassar hayotzei* holds, and why meat brought inside does not trigger any analogous invalidity.

---

## Kodesh Scope

### Inner Chamber

The *gemara* cites a *braita*: *pnimah ein li ela pnimah* — from the word *pnimah* alone I would know only that blood brought into the innermost chamber, the *kodesh kodashim*, invalidates. *Heichal minayin* — how do I know that bringing blood into the *heichal* also invalidates? *Talmud lomar el hakodesh pnimah* — the extra word *kodesh* teaches that even *el hakodesh* — the *heichal* — suffices. So both words are required: *pnimah* for the *kodesh kodashim*, and *kodesh* for the *heichal*.

### Rava's Words

But Rava questions this: *viyomar kodesh ve'al yomar pnimah* — the *Torah* should have simply said *el hakodesh* referring to the *heichal*, and by *kal vachomer* I would have known that the more inner *kodesh kodashim* is certainly also included. Why was it necessary to say *pnimah* at all?

Rava answers: *bazeh velimmed al zeh* — this word teaches about the other. Had the *Torah* written only *kodesh*, I would have read *kodesh* to mean *kodesh kodashim* — the inner sanctum is the natural referent of *kodesh* in its most elevated sense. It is only because the *Torah* also writes *pnimah*, which clearly refers to the *kodesh kodashim*, that I know *kodesh* in this verse must mean the *heichal*. The two words thus work in tandem: *pnimah* establishes the outer reference of *kodesh* as the *heichal*, and *kodesh* in turn confirms that the *heichal* triggers the invalidity.

Rava supports this with an analogy: *midi dehava atoshav vesachir* — as we find with the terms *toshav* and *sachir* in the context of a *kohen*'s household. A *toshav* is a Hebrew slave owned until the *yovel*, and a *sachir* is a Hebrew slave for six years. The *Torah* says both cannot eat *terumah*. One might ask: just say *toshav* — the more permanent slave — and from a *kal vachomer* I would know the six-year slave certainly cannot eat *terumah* either. The answer: had it said only *toshav*, I might have read *toshav* to mean the six-year slave — the less settled one — and then concluded that the permanent slave, *kanui kinyan olam*, can indeed eat *terumah*. The word *sachir* establishes the lighter case, and thereby clarifies that *toshav* means the heavier, more permanent one. So too here: *pnimah* establishes what *kodesh* means.

### Abaye Objection

Abaye objects to this comparison. *Bishlama hatam trei gufei ninhu* — there it is justified because *toshav* and *sachir* are two different people. The *halacha* genuinely applies to both individuals, and even if one could have been derived from a *kal vachomer*, there is no harm in stating both explicitly — *milta de'ati bekal vachomer tarach vechatav lah kra*. The *Torah* sometimes states explicitly what could have been inferred.

But here, Abaye argues, the situation is fundamentally different. The *Torah* could have written *ohel mo'ed* explicitly — making clear it meant the *heichal* — rather than using the ambiguous term *kodesh*. And then there would be no need to address the *kodesh kodashim* at all. Why not? Because *keivan de'ifshal beheichal, lifnai velifnim mai ba'ei* — once the blood is invalidated in the *heichal*, it is already *pasul*. The *kodesh kodashim* adds no independent invalidity, since the invalidity occurred at the threshold of the *heichal*. So the *Torah* should have been explicit about *heichal* and said nothing about *kodesh kodashim*, since the latter contributes nothing. There is therefore no parallel to the *toshav-sachir* case, where both subjects are independently meaningful.

### Intent & Path

Abaye offers one possible resolution: *lo nitzrecha ela derech meshubash* — the *pasuk* concerning *kodesh kodashim* is needed for a case where one reaches the *kodesh kodashim* via a roundabout route, not through the *heichal*. In that case, the *heichal* threshold is bypassed and the invalidity of the *kodesh kodashim* is independently operative.

However, Rava is not satisfied with this answer: *vehuva ketiv asher yuva midamah* — the *pasuk* says *yuva*, brought in the natural way. An irregular route through the attic, for instance, does not qualify. Therefore Rava states his own resolution: *kol midi dechashiv alei lifnai velifnim lo mipasal beheichal* — any blood whose intent is directed specifically toward the *kodesh kodashim* is not invalidated when it passes through the *heichal*. The *pasuk* conditions the invalidity on *lechaper bakodesh* — purposive intent. If one's intent is to apply the blood on the *aron* in the *kodesh kodashim*, traversing the *heichal* does not trigger the invalidity; the invalidity occurs only when the blood reaches the place it was intended for. Thus the *kodesh kodashim* can serve as an independent source of invalidity for blood whose intent was directed there from the outset, and the *heichal* does not preempt it.

---

## Deeper Inner

### Par & Saʿir

Rava now raises a new question about a specific class of inner *chata'ot*. The *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* and the *sa'ir avodat kochavim* — the communal goat brought for unwitting idolatry — are inner *chata'ot* in the sense that their blood is applied inside, in the *heichal*. However, unlike the *Yom Kippur* offerings, their blood does not go into the *kodesh kodashim*. Entry into the *kodesh kodashim* is restricted by the verse *lo yavo bechol et el hakodesh*, and only on *Yom Kippur*, *bezot yavo Aharon el hakodesh*, does the *kohen gadol* bring blood into the *kodesh kodashim*.

### Yom Kippur Return

The question Rava poses: *shehichnis damam lifnai velifnim mahu* — what if the blood of the *par he'elam davar* or the *sa'ir avodat zarah* was brought all the way into the *kodesh kodashim*? Would that invalidate? Two possibilities are considered. On one hand: *mi amrinan el hakodesh pnimah — kol heicha dekarinan el hakodesh karinan lei pnimah* — perhaps the *din* of *pnimah* only applies where the *heichal* itself is already an invalidating threshold. These offerings are supposed to go into the *heichal* — so the *heichal* is not an off-limits place for their blood. Does taking it even further, into the *kodesh kodashim*, trigger invalidity? Or do we say: *she'lo bimkoman hu* — this is simply not their proper place, and bringing them where they do not belong invalidates them regardless?

The question is sharper still for the *Yom Kippur* offerings themselves. The blood of the *par* and *sa'ir* of *Yom Kippur* goes into the *kodesh kodashim* — that is precisely where it belongs. Once the application is made there, one exits and applies blood on the *parochet* and on the *mizbe'ach hazahav*, and then proceeds outward. If one then re-enters the *kodesh kodashim* with that same blood — *ve'hochnisan* — what is the rule? *Mi amrinan mekoman hu* — is the *kodesh kodashim* still simply its proper place? Or do we say *hovei nefik nefik* — once the blood has left, it has left, and re-entry constitutes bringing it to an inner place that it is no longer entitled to enter?

### Altar Zones

A final layer of the question concerns the *mizbe'ach hazahav* itself. On *Yom Kippur*, after applying blood on the *parochet*, one proceeds to the outer portion of the *mizbe'ach hazahav*. The *Torah* uses the word *ve'hotzi* — bringing it out — to describe this movement. One could interpret this as indicating that the outer portion of the *mizbe'ach* is halachically "outside" relative to the inner portion. If one then brings the blood back, not all the way to the *kodesh kodashim* but simply to the inner side of the *mizbe'ach* — *ve'hichnisan* — is that considered bringing it to an inner, off-limits place?

### Teiku

On this question the *gemara* asks: *hacha barei chad makom hu* — is the *mizbe'ach* one unified place, such that inner and outer are not halachically distinct zones? Or do we say *yatzinan karinan bei* — since the *Torah* describes the movement to the *mizbe'ach* as going out, then the outer zone of the *mizbe'ach* is defined as outer, and returning inward constitutes a transgression of place?

The *gemara* concludes: *teiku* — these questions remain unresolved. The boundaries of sacred space, the role of intent, the interaction between *heichal* and *kodesh kodashim*, and the question of whether blood that has already exited a zone may return — all of these remain as open questions with which we conclude the *daf*.

---

---

# Zevachim 83

## Nichnas Lifnim

### Intro: Blood Inside

Daf 83 opens by completing the discussion of the rule that when the blood of a *chatas* — and according to Rabbi Akiva, of other *korbanos* as well — is brought inside the *heichal* or the *kodesh hakodashim*, it renders the offering invalid. The *gemara* had closed the previous discussion with a related question: what if it was the *chatas* of *Yom Kippur*, whose blood was brought into the *kodesh hakodashim*, brought back out, and then brought in again? With those threads tied off, the discussion now turns to a specific question that arises from the relevant verse: *v'chol chatas asher yuva midamah l'chapper bakodesh el hakodesh penimah* — and any *chatas* whose blood is brought inside for the purpose of atonement. The operative phrase is *l'chapper bakodesh*: does this mean the *intent* with which the blood was brought, or does it mean the blood was actually *used* in a rite of atonement?

### L'Chapper: Intent vs. Use

A *braisa* records the debate between *tannaim* on precisely this question. The issue is how to interpret the phrase *l'chapper bakodesh* in the verse that invalidates an outer *chatas* whose blood was brought inside. Is it sufficient that the blood was brought in with the *intent* to effect atonement, or must the blood have actually been *used* in the atonement process?

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer argues for the first reading — intent alone is sufficient — by means of a *gezerah shavah*. The same phrase *l'chapper bakodesh* appears in the verse governing *Yom Kippur*: *v'chol adam lo yihyeh b'Ohel Moed b'vo'o l'chapper bakodesh*, that no person may be present in the *Ohel Moed* when the *Kohen Gadol* enters *l'chapper bakodesh*. There, Rabbi Eliezer observes, *l'chapper* clearly refers to prospective intent — people are required to clear out *before* any atonement is performed. The atonement has not yet happened; the *Kohen Gadol* is merely entering for that purpose. By linking the two uses of *l'chapper bakodesh*, Rabbi Eliezer concludes: just as in that case the phrase is forward-looking, so too by the outer *chatas*, it is the intent with which the blood is brought — not the actual performance of atonement — that is determinative.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon disagrees and reaches a different conclusion through a different link. He notes that *l'chapper bakodesh* also appears in a second *Yom Kippur* verse: *v'es par hachatas v'es se'ir hachatas asher huva es damam l'chapper bakodesh* — the ox of the *chatas* and the goat of the *chatas* whose blood was brought in to atone, *l'chapper bakodesh*. Unlike the verse cited by Rabbi Eliezer, this passage looks backward. It describes what was already done with the blood. Moreover, it is in this context that the subsequent burning of these animals is commanded — and that burning would only have been carried out if the blood had in fact been properly used in the atonement rite. Rabbi Shimon therefore concludes: *mah lehalan keshekipper af kan keshekipper* — just as in that verse the atonement was actually performed, so too in our case, the *l'chapper bakodesh* requires that the blood was actually used, not merely that it was brought with that intent.

### Gemara Resolution

The *gemara* then asks: *bemai kamiflagi* — what is the underlying principle that leads each opinion to its respective *Yom Kippur* verse? The answer is that each *tanna* follows a different rule of textual comparison.

Rabbi Eliezer holds *danim chutz michutz* — one compares an outer *chatas* to something that similarly belongs outside. The outer *chatas* blood steps over a boundary when it enters inside, just as the *Yom Kippur* verse about people leaving the *Ohel Moed* is also about a boundary: remaining outside while something proceeds within. Accordingly, both uses of *l'chapper bakodesh* share the feature of operating from the outside, and the verse there is clearly prospective — it is about intent, not completed action.

Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, holds *danim behemah mibehemah* — one compares the description of the blood to another description of blood, not to a description of a person's movement. In the verse about the outer *chatas*, it is the blood that is described as being brought *l'chapper bakodesh*; similarly, in the second *Yom Kippur* verse, it is the blood of the bull and the goat that is described as having been brought *l'chapper bakodesh*. The two instances share the same grammatical and conceptual structure — blood, not a person, is the subject — and in the latter verse the blood was unambiguously used in actual atonement. He further notes *v'ein danim behemah me'adam*: we do not derive the rule for blood from a verse about the *Kohen Gadol's* purpose in entering.

### Rabbi Yehudah: Intent

A third position in the *mishnah* belongs to Rabbi Yehudah, who reads *l'chapper* differently still: the blood must have been brought *b'meizid* — intentionally — not *b'shogeg*. The most plausible reading of his position is that it addresses a case where the one who brought the blood did not realize it was outer *chatas* blood, mistaking it for the blood of an inner *chatas*. This is a distinct dimension of the dispute, focusing on the actor's state of mind rather than on whether the ritual was completed. The *gemara* now wants to know how Rabbi Yehudah himself holds in the earlier debate: does he require that the blood was actually used in atonement, or is intent sufficient?

### Rabbi Yehudah Analysis

The *gemara* approaches this question through the words of Rabbi Yirmiyah, who directs attention to a *braisa*. By examining Rabbi Yehudah's use of a textual derivation in that *braisa*, the *gemara* will be able to determine which side of the intent-versus-use debate he occupies.

### Tumat Begadim

The *braisa* in question concerns the *halacha* of *tumat begadim*, the impurity contracted by garments. The verse describing the *Yom Kippur* offerings — *v'es par hachatas v'es se'ir hachatas asher huva es damam l'chapper bakodesh* — concludes by stating that the one who burns these animals must launder his garments. The *braisa* asks: from the phrase *asher huva es damam l'chapper bakodesh*, which characterizes the *Yom Kippur* offerings as those whose blood was brought in to atone, why does the verse use the words *par hachatas* and *se'ir hachatas* rather than simply *hapar* and *hase'ir*? One might have thought the *halacha* of *tumat begadim* applies only to the specific bull and goat of *Yom Kippur*. But we in fact know this *halacha* to apply to all inner *chatas* offerings — including the *par ha'elem davar* and the *se'ir avodah zarah*. The question is how we know.

Rabbi Yehudah in the *braisa* says: *talmud lomar chatas chatas* — from the repetition of the word *chatas* in *par hachatas* and *se'ir hachatas*. This extra word extends the *halacha* of *tumat begadim* to all inner *chatas* offerings.

Rabbi Meir disagrees: *eino tzarich* — no such extra derivation is needed. The verse itself already supplies the key: *asher huva es damam l'chapper bakodesh* — the defining characteristic is that their blood was brought inside to atone. Any inner *chatas* that falls into that category is subject to the same *halacha*. The words *par hachatas* and *se'ir hachatas* are therefore available for a different use entirely.

The *gemara* then presses: why doesn't Rabbi Yehudah himself use the phrase *l'chapper bakodesh* to establish the applicability to all inner *chatas* offerings, since that seems to be the more direct textual hook? The answer is *lav mishum d'mibai leh l'gzerah shavah* — it must be that Rabbi Yehudah is reserving *l'chapper bakodesh* for a different *halacha*, namely the *gezerah shavah* linking the outer *chatas* to the *Yom Kippur* usage. And since he uses the *l'chapper bakodesh* of the backward-looking verse — the one where the blood was actually used in atonement — this tells us that Rabbi Yehudah holds, in the main debate, that actual use of the blood is required, not merely intent. He therefore needs the extra *chatas chatas* to derive the *tumat begadim halacha* from a different source.

Rabbi Meir, by contrast, does not use *l'chapper bakodesh* for the *tumat begadim* derivation — he uses the explicit description of the verse — and must therefore be applying *l'chapper bakodesh* to the outer *chatas* question. Since the verse he would link to is the one describing blood actually used in atonement, Rabbi Meir similarly holds that actual use, not intent alone, is what renders the outer *chatas* invalid.

### Rabbi Yehudah Analysis 2

The *gemara* then explains why Rabbi Yehudah, having reserved *l'chapper bakodesh* for the *gezerah shavah*, cannot in turn derive the *tumat begadim* extension from the explicit description of the verse the way Rabbi Meir does. The reason is that Rabbi Yehudah needs the explicit description — *asher huva es damam l'chapper bakodesh* — specifically for the *gezerah shavah* that establishes the rule for the outer *chatas*. Since he has committed those words to that purpose, he must fall back on the extra word *chatas chatas* for the *tumat begadim* extension. Rabbi Meir, who does not need *l'chapper bakodesh* for the *gezerah shavah* (having derived it through a different route), is free to use it for *tumat begadim*, leaving *chatas chatas* available for nothing in particular.

The discussion closes with a brief exchange about the broader theological significance of the *kodesh* being cleansed — *l'chapper* as purifying the *mikdash* — but that is set aside for another occasion.

---

## Hamizbe'ach Mekadesh

### Intro: Altar Sanctifies

With the close of the previous *perek*, which encompassed extensive material on mixtures (*ta'arovot*) and related issues, the *gemara* now transitions to a new chapter. The central subject is the principle of *hamizbe'ach mekadesh et haraui lo* — the altar sanctifies things that are fit for it. This principle, encountered throughout the *masechet*, is now addressed directly: if something that is *pasul* is placed on the altar, under what conditions does it remain there rather than being removed? The phrase *haraui lo* — what is fit for it — is the crux of the debate.

### Rabbi Yehoshua: Fire

Rabbi Yehoshua states: *kol haraui l'ishim* — it applies to anything fit for the fire. If a *pasul* item belongs on the fire of the altar, once it is placed there it does not come down: *im ala lo yered*. The verse he derives this from is *hi ha'olah al mokdah* — it is the *olah* on the pyre.
