Just as an *olah* belongs on the fire, so too anything fit for the fire (*rauy l'ishim*) that ascends the altar does not descend, even if it is found to be *pasul*. What this excludes, on his view, are liquids like blood and wine — things placed on the altar but not designated for the fire. Those, if *pasul*, must be removed.

### Rabban Gamliel: Altar

Rabban Gamliel offers a broader criterion: *kol haraui lamizbeach im ala lo yered* — anything fit for the altar, once placed there, does not come down. His proof text is the same verse — *hi ha'olah al mokdah al hamizbeach* — but he reads the emphasis differently: not *al mokdah* (on the fire), but *al hamizbeach* (on the altar). Just as an *olah* belongs on the altar, so anything fit for the altar, including blood and wine, is sanctified by being placed there and does not come down even if *pasul*.

The *gemara* thus states: *ein bein divrei Rabban Gamliel l'divrei Rabbi Yehoshua ela hadam v'hanesachim* — the practical difference between them comes down to blood and wine offerings. According to Rabban Gamliel, if blood or wine that is *pasul* is placed on the altar, it stays. According to Rabbi Yehoshua, it must come down, since it does not belong on the fire.

### Debate: Blood & Wine

One might ask: according to Rabban Gamliel, who includes everything fit for the altar, what is ever *excluded* by the phrase *haraui lo*? That question will be developed in the *gemara* below. For now, the debate between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua is sharpened to its essential point: does *haraui lo* mean fit for the fire, or fit for the altar in any capacity?

### Textual Analysis

Before proceeding to the *gemara*, both Rashi and Tosafot make an important textual observation about the structure of this *mishnah*. The *mishnah* opens with an anonymous phrase — *hamizbe'ach mekadesh et haraui lo* — and then presents the debate between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua about what that phrase means. Tosafot notes that this pattern recurs elsewhere: for instance, in Tractate Pesachim, an early anonymous teaching that *shtei shurot b'martef* (two rows of the wine cellar) require checking is inherited by Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, who then debate what *shtei shurot* means. Similarly, the opening *mishnah* of Tractate Gittin states the rule that one who brings a *get* from overseas must declare it was written and signed in his presence, and later *tannaim* debate which locations count as "overseas." In all these cases, an early formulation was transmitted with undefined terms, and later *tannaim* debated the meaning of those terms. The opening phrase of the *mishnah* here — *hamizbe'ach mekadesh et haraui lo* — appears to be exactly such an early inherited teaching, and Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua are not simply expressing personal views but are interpreting a transmitted *mesorah* whose terms had become contested.

This is a significant structural feature to recognize throughout the *mishnayot*: what appears to be a simple three-part debate — anonymous opening statement, then two named opinions — is often better understood as an early formulation whose undefined terms are being clarified by later *tannaim*.

### Rabbi Shimon: Shikhlul

Rabbi Shimon presents a third criterion, structurally different from both of the previous ones. He holds that the key is not whether the item goes on the fire or merely on the altar, but whether the offering comes *biglal atzmah* — on its own account — or *biglal zevach* — by virtue of another offering. His derivation: *mah olah haba'ah biglal atzmah af kol haba'im biglal atzmah* — just as an *olah* comes entirely on its own account, so too anything that comes on its own account stays on the altar. *Yatzu nesachim habaim biglal zevach* — excluded are wine and flour offerings that come accompanying an animal sacrifice. If the *zevach* is valid but the *nesachim* are *pasul*, they come down; if the *nesachim* are valid but the *zevach* is *pasul*, the *nesachim* come down as well because they have nothing to accompany. Even if both are *pasul*, the *zevach* stays on the altar and the *nesachim* come down. For Rabbi Shimon, dependency (*shikhlul*) is the operative criterion, not the distinction between fire and altar.

---

## Harauy Lo Definition

### Komatim Pasul

The *gemara* now asks: *she'ein haraui lo lema'utei mai* — what does the phrase "not fit for it" actually exclude, especially according to the more expansive view of Rabban Gamliel, who includes even blood and wine? The answer will not be about the severity of the *psul* — that is a question for later *mishnayot* — but about how intrinsically connected an item is to the altar in the first place.

### Rav Pappa: Kometz

Rav Pappa answers: *lema'utei kmatzim shelo kidshu bikeli* — what is excluded is the *kometz* of a *mincha* that was not sanctified through placement in a *kli shares* (a service vessel). The normal procedure when taking a handful from a *mincha* is to place the *kometz* in a vessel, thereby sanctifying and designating it for the altar. If one bypassed this step and placed the *kometz* directly on the altar without first putting it in a vessel, it would have to be removed — even on Rabban Gamliel's expansive view.

The reasoning reflects a fundamental distinction between the *kometz* and other altar items. With animal offerings, one knows from the outset which parts are destined for the altar — the blood, the *emurim*, and in the case of an *olah*, the meat. These parts are effectively pre-labeled. With a *mincha*, however, the specific handful that will go to the altar is not designated until the *kometz* is taken and then placed in the vessel. The act of placing it in the vessel is what completes its designation as the altar's portion. Without that step, the item has not yet been fully connected to the altar, and therefore it is not *raui lo* — it is not fit for it in the relevant sense.

### Ravina Challenge

Ravina challenges this distinction by pointing to a case discussed by Ulla: *emurei kodshim kalim she-he'alam lifnei zrikas damam* — the *emurim* (designated limbs) of a *kodshim kalim* offering such as a *shlamim*, which were placed on the altar before the blood was sprinkled. Those too are not yet fully ready for the altar at the moment of their placement — the blood has not yet been thrown — and yet Ulla states that they remain on the altar and do not come down. If the *emurim* can remain despite not yet being fully designated in a *halachic* sense, why should the unsanctified *kometz* be different?

### Emurim Kodshim Kalim

The answer requires understanding a specific feature of *kodshim kalim*. A *shlamim* is characterized by the fact that the animal essentially remains in the owner's domain in a meaningful sense — that is why there is no *me'ila* (liability for misuse of consecrated property) with respect to a *shlamim* before the blood is thrown. The *emurim*, though physically identifiable as the altar's portion, are not yet fully under the altar's control — they have not yet become fully *God's portion*, as it were — until *zerikas dam* is performed. Before that moment, even the *emurim* are not subject to *me'ila*. In that sense, they resemble the unsanctified *kometz*: both lack full designation for the altar at the moment of placement.

### Missing Act vs. Designat…

Nevertheless, the *gemara* draws a key distinction between the two cases. By the *emurim* of *kodshim kalim*, nothing is *missing in the emurim themselves*. They are physically and substantively in the state they need to be. What is incomplete is an *external act* — the throwing of the blood — which is performed on a different object entirely. Because the *emurim* themselves lack nothing, they are considered sufficiently connected to the altar to remain there.

By the *kometz* that was not placed in a vessel, the situation is the reverse. The deficiency is *internal to the object itself*: the act that must be performed — placing the *kometz* in a *kli shares* — is an act that must be done to the *kometz* itself. The designation of the *kometz* as the altar's portion is simply not complete. This is therefore categorically different from the *emurim*, and the *kometz* must be removed.

---

## Four Positions

### Rabbi Yehoshua Fire

Returning now to the positions in the *mishnah*, the *gemara* examines the derivations underlying each view. Rabbi Yehoshua derives his principle from the verse *hi ha'olah al mokdah* — he emphasizes the word *mokdah*, the fire: just as an *olah* is fit for the fire, so only things fit for the fire (*rauy l'ishim*) remain on the altar once placed there. This excludes blood and wine, which are placed on or at the altar but are not consumed by fire.

It is worth noting — as Michael observed — that the *gemara* is explicit that the *mizbeach* itself is what sanctifies, not the fire. Accordingly, even Rabbi Yehoshua does not mean that an item must literally be on the fire to remain. The criterion is the *type* of object: if it is the kind of thing meant for the fire, it stays, wherever exactly on the altar it has been placed. What he excludes is an object that, by its very nature, is never burned.

### Two Mizbeach

Rabban Gamliel, by contrast, emphasizes the word *mizbeach* in the same verse: *hi ha'olah al mokdah al hamizbeach*. Rabbi Yehoshua acknowledges that *mizbeach* appears in the verse — so what does Rabban Gamliel do with the word *mokdah*, and what does Rabbi Yehoshua do with the word *mizbeach*? The *gemara* works through these questions carefully.

### Mizbeach Sanctifies

For Rabbi Yehoshua, *al hamizbeach* teaches not a criterion of eligibility but the mechanism of sanctification: it is the *mizbeach* that sanctifies upon contact, not the fire. An item placed on the *mizbeach* — even not yet on the fire — acquires the status of being sanctified by the altar. *Mokdah* is then the criterion: only items that are *the kind that go on the fire* are covered by this rule. For Rabban Gamliel, *mokdah* is not the eligibility criterion but rather conveys the separate *halacha* that logs that fly off the fire must be replaced — derived from *al mokdah* as a directive to maintain the fire — while *mizbeach* provides the broader criterion of fitness for the altar in any capacity.

### Two Pasul Types

The *gemara* introduces a further dimension: there are two *mezbeach* usages in the verse — *al mokdah al hamizbeach* — and the *gemara* suggests that one of them addresses an additional question: what kind of *psul* is covered by the rule? Specifically, *chad dehava lei shas hachosher v'chad dela hava lei shas hachosher* — one teaches about an item that had a *shas hachosher* (a moment when it was fit), and one teaches about an item that never had such a moment.

The distinction is significant. If blood was collected and was momentarily valid, then became *tamei*, it had a *shas hachosher* — a period of fitness. But if an animal was slaughtered with an intention of *pigul*, the blood and *emurim* were *pasul* from the very moment they became those objects — they never had a moment of fitness. One might have thought this latter type of *psul* is so fundamental that the altar could not sanctify it. One usage of *mizbeach* therefore teaches that even items that never had a *shas hachosher* are sanctified by the altar and remain there.

The opposing *tanna* holds that once the Torah has stated the novel principle that even *pasul* items remain on the altar, there is no reason to distinguish between the two types of *psul*: *lo shana dehava lei shas hachosher lo shana dela hava lei shas hachosher*. The inclusion is complete, and a separate derivation is unnecessary.

### Rabbi Yosi Kevasim

Rabbi Yosi HaGlili introduces yet another approach. The verse states *kol hanogeah bamizbe'ach yikdash* — whatever touches the altar is sanctified. One might have thought this applies universally, even to things with no connection to the altar whatsoever. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili therefore derives a limiting criterion from the adjacent verse, which mentions *kevasim bnei shanah* in the context of the *olat tamid*: *mah kevasim re'uyim af kol ra'uy* — just as lambs are fit (to be brought), so too only things that are fit (in the basic sense of being eligible as sacrifices) are sanctified by the altar. On his view, this excludes both birds — which are not included in *kevasim* — and *mincha* offerings.

### Rabbi Akiva Olah

Rabbi Akiva similarly derives from the verse *olah*: *mah olah re'uyah af kol ra'uy* — just as an *olah* is fit, so too only fit things are sanctified by the altar. Rabbi Akiva's term of reference (*olah*) includes birds, since bird *olos* exist; accordingly, he would include an invalid bird *olah*. But it excludes *mincha*, since *olah* refers to animal offerings. The word *kevasim* in the verse, for Rabbi Akiva, serves a different purpose: it rules out an animal that was a *ba'al mum* even when alive — one that was invalid even before entering the realm of *korbanot* entirely.

### Four Criteria

There are thus four distinct positions: Rabban Gamliel — anything fit for the altar, including blood and wine; Rabbi Yehoshua — only things fit for the fire; Rabbi Yosi HaGlili — things like *kevasim*, meaning animal offerings (excluding birds and *mincha*); and Rabbi Akiva — things like *olah*, meaning animal offerings including birds, but excluding *mincha*. Among these, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva are more restrictive than Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua in that they exclude *mincha* entirely, while differing from each other on the question of bird offerings.

---

## Test Cases

### Kometz in Vessel

Rav Pappa identifies the practical difference between the *tannaim* in the *mishnah* and the *tannaim* in the *braisa*: *kmatzim shekidshu bikeli ika beynaihu* — the case of a *kometz* that was properly sanctified in a vessel. Once the *kometz* has been placed in a *kli shares*, it is fully designated for the altar. For the *tanna* of the *mishnah* (Rabban Gamliel or Rabbi Yehoshua), once the *kometz* is in a *kli*, it is *raui* and remains on the altar. For the *tannaim* of the *braisa* (Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva), who require the item to be like an animal offering, a *kometz* — even properly sanctified — comes down, because it is a *mincha*.

### Independent Mincha

Reish Lakish then works through a series of cases to map out the implications of each position. First: a *mincha* that comes *bifnei atzmah* — on its own, independently. This would include a *minchas nesachim* brought on its own without an accompanying animal offering. For Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, such a *mincha*, if *pasul*, does not come down. For Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva, it comes down, since it is not an animal offering.

### Mincha with Zevach

Second: a *mincha* that comes *im hazevach* — accompanying an animal sacrifice. Now Rabbi Shimon's criterion of *shikhlul* (dependency) comes into play. For Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, it still does not come down — they do not distinguish between independent and accompanying offerings. But for everyone else — Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Shimon — it comes down, each for his own reason.

### Nesachim Alone

Third: *nesachim haba'im bifnei atzman* — wine offerings brought independently, not accompanying an animal. For Rabban Gamliel, they do not come down — anything fit for the altar remains. For Rabbi Shimon, they also do not come down — wine brought independently is coming *biglal atzmah*, on its own account. But for the other three — Rabbi Yehoshua (who requires fitness for the fire), Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, and Rabbi Akiva (both of whom require an animal-like offering) — the wine comes down.

### Nesachim w/ Zevach

Fourth: *nesachim haba'im im hazevach* — wine accompanying an animal sacrifice. Here, only Rabban Gamliel says the wine does not come down. Rabbi Yehoshua says it comes down because it is not fit for the fire. Rabbi Shimon says it comes down because it is not coming on its own account. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva say it comes down because it is not an animal offering. Rabban Gamliel alone includes it: he does not care whether the item goes on the fire, does not care whether it accompanies something else, and does not require it to be an animal offering. Any item fit for the altar in any capacity remains there.

### Positions Chart

The positions thus map cleanly: Rabban Gamliel is uniquely inclusive. Rabbi Yehoshua occupies an intermediate position — inclusive of *mincha* but exclusive of liquids. Rabbi Shimon cuts differently — inclusive of independent wine but exclusive of accompanying wine. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili and Rabbi Akiva share the most restrictive criterion (animal offerings only), differing only on whether bird *olos* are included.

### New Halacha

The *gemara* then presses: *pshita* — all of this could have been worked out without the case of the independently brought *minchas nesachim*. What *chiddush* does that case actually contribute? The answer is that the *chiddush* is the *halacha* itself — that one may bring a *minchas nesachim* independently.

### Rava Minchas

This is the ruling of Rava: *misnadeiv adam minchas nesachim b'chol yom* — a person may voluntarily bring a *minchas nesachim* on any day, independently, without bringing it as part of an animal offering. This is not self-evident, since a *minchas nesachim* is by its nature an accompanying offering; the *chiddush* is that it may nonetheless be brought independently as a voluntary contribution. The *gemara* asks: if that is the point, simply cite Rava's ruling directly rather than embed it in this more complex analysis. The *gemara* responds that the real *chiddush* lies elsewhere.

### Accompanying Nesachim

The genuine novelty is in the case of *nesachim haba'im im hazevach* — specifically what happens when the accompanying wine is brought not on the same day as the animal but on a subsequent day. The *halacha* is that if *nesachim* were not brought together with the animal, they may be brought the next day or even later. One might have thought that in such a case, since the wine arrives separately, it is effectively coming *bifnei atzman* — on its own — and Rabbi Shimon would concede that it does not come down. The *gemara* teaches: *kol mashma lan* — no. Even wine brought on a later day as a makeup offering for an animal sacrifice is still considered to be coming *biglal hazevach*, on account of the animal, not on its own account. Rabbi Shimon therefore maintains that it must come down even in this case. We will continue from here tomorrow.

---

---

# Zevachim 84

## Altar Sanctifies

### Principle Overview

The focus of this *perek* — as the name of the *perek* itself announces and as the first *mishna* introduced — is the principle that the altar sanctifies things placed upon it. Even if an offering is invalid, once it has been placed on the altar it may remain there and be consumed by the fire. The central question animating the chapter is not merely that such a rule exists, but which invalidity is so severe that the item must be removed despite having reached the altar.

### Types of Items

Before arriving at our *mishna*, the previous *mishna* addressed a prior question: what *types* of things are subject to this rule? The obvious cases are anything meant to be burned on the altar. But what of liquids — blood or wine? That was a matter of debate. What of items not yet fully designated, such as the *komets* of a *mincha* that had not yet been placed in the *kli*? One opinion held that only animals qualify; another perhaps excluded even birds. Having established the scope of objects to which the rule applies, the *mishna* now turns to the *nature* of the invalidity — which failures are tolerable and which are not.

---

## Elu Im Alu Lo Yardu

### Cases Staying Up

The *mishna* opens with the phrase *elu im alu lo yardu* — the following things, if they were placed on the altar, do not come down.

### Notar, Yotzei, Tamei

The first group encompasses items that once had a valid moment — a *sha'at hakosher* — but subsequently became *pasul*. *Halan*: something that slept overnight, i.e., *notar*, whether meat, *emurim*, or blood. If blood slept overnight, the sacrifice was never legitimately completed — yet it stays. *Ve'hayotzei*: the item was taken outside the *Beit HaMikdash* and became *pasul*, again whether meat, blood, or *emurim*. One might wonder: if it is already *yotzei*, how can one speak of putting it on the altar? The case is where an absent-minded *kohen*, still holding the bowl of blood or the *emurim* in hand, inadvertently stepped into the *Ezrat Nashim* and then returned and placed the item on the altar. Do not remove it. *Ve'hatamei*: something that became *tamei*.

### Improper Slaughter Cases

The *mishna* then turns to a different category: cases where the invalidity was present from the very instant of *shechita* — there was never a valid moment at all. *Ve'shenishchat chutz lizmano ve'chutz limekomo*: if a *chutz lizmano* thought — or the quasi-*piggul* variant of *chutz limekomo* — attended the *shechita*, the offering was *pasul* from that instant. Similarly, *ve'shekiblu psulim ve'zarku et damo*: a *pasul kohen* caught the blood or threw it on the altar. Even in a case where a *pasul kohen* threw the blood — meaning the blood never legitimately reached the altar — the remaining meat or *emurim* placed on the altar nonetheless stay there.

### Piggul Concept

The *piggul* case deserves brief mention: an item that is *piggul* is also included in this list and stays on the altar. It does not achieve atonement, but it is not removed.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Exceptions

*Rabbi Yehuda* agrees with the foregoing but carves out three additional exceptions. He holds that three cases must come down if they were placed up: *shenishchat balayla* — slaughtered at night; *venishpach damah* — the blood was spilled; and *veyatza damah chutz lakla'im* — the blood exited beyond the curtains, i.e., outside the *Azara*. In those three scenarios, *im alta tered* — if it went up, it must come down.

The distinction between these three and the other *psulim* requires explanation. One might ask: if the blood was spilled or the blood was taken outside, the blood is never going to legitimately reach the altar — but the same is true when a *pasul* person catches the blood. What makes these three worse? And *shenishchat balayla* is indeed different from *chutz lizmano*: in the case of *chutz lizmano*, at least the *shechita* was performed during the day and the problem entered only with a disqualifying thought. When the *shechita* itself was performed at night, the entire starting point is off. The question of why *nishpach damo* and *yatza damo chutz lakla'im* are worse than *kibel psulim* — given that the latter case also means the blood never legitimately arrived — is something the *gemara* and the *Rishonim* will need to address.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

*Rabbi Shimon* says: even those three cases do not come down. What then is his own limiting principle — where would he, and where would the *Tanna Kamma*, draw the line? That is the subject of the next section.

---

## Psuluto Bakodesh

### Kodesh Accepts

*Rabbi Shimon* formulates the principle as follows: *kol she-psulo ba-kodesh, ha-kodesh mekabelo* — anything whose invalidity occurred once it was already within the *kodesh* context, the *kodesh* receives it. The item got in the door, so to speak, and will not be ejected. Conversely, *lo hayah psulo ba-kodesh, ein ha-kodesh mekabelo* — if the invalidity preceded the *kodesh*, it is not accepted.

### Invalid Before Kodesh

The *mishna* then enumerates the items that fall under this latter category — *ve'eilu she-lo hayu psulan ba-kodesh*: *ha-rove'ah ve-ha-nirba*, an animal used in or subjected to an act of bestiality — its disqualification preceded its very sanctification. *Ve-ha-muktzeh ve-ha-ne'evad*, something designated for or actually worshipped as *avoda zara*. *Ve-ha-etnan ve-ha-mechir*, an animal given as payment to a prostitute or exchanged for a dog. *Ve-ha-kilayim*, a crossbreed — for instance, between a sheep and a goat. *Ve-ha-treifa*, an animal with an internal injury that would disqualify it even for non-*kodesh* use. *Ve-ha-yotze dofen*, an animal born by C-section, since only a vaginal birth satisfies the requirement of *ki yivaled*. And *u-va'alei mumin*, blemished animals.

### Ritual vs. Defect

A crucial conceptual point must be made here. While it is true that the *psul* of these items typically *precedes* the *kodesh*, the distinction is not merely chronological. The *gemara* learns elsewhere that all of these items must come down from the *mizbe'ach* even if their disqualification arose *after* the animal was sanctified — even if it occurred within the *Beit HaMikdash* itself. One might sanctify a perfect animal and then have it subjected to bestiality, or sanctify it and then watch it acquire a *mum*, or sanctify it in the *Beit HaMikdash* only for someone to accidentally make it a *treifa* with a misplaced knife.

What, then, is the meaning of *lo hayah psulo ba-kodesh*? The key is conceptual rather than temporal. All the *psulim* that are accepted — *notar*, *yotzei*, *tamei*, *chutz lizmano*, *chutz limekomo*, *kibel psulim* — are cases where what went wrong was a *mikdash ritual performed incorrectly*. The violation was embedded in the handling of the sanctified animal: it was kept too long, removed from the wrong area, rendered impure, or processed by an invalid officiant. These are failures *within* the ritual system of *korbanot*. By contrast, *treifa*, *yotzei dofen*, *rove'ah*, and their companions represent a different type of problem — not a ritual done wrong, but an intrinsic defect or an external circumstance that has nothing to do with *mikdash* ritual. Even if such a thing happened in the *Beit HaMikdash* after sanctification, it is conceptually unrelated to the *mikdash* process, and that is what is called *lo hayah psulo ba-kodesh*. 

There is also a simpler and practical way to draw this line: the *psulim* that are accepted as *psuluto ba-kodesh* all occur at the moment of *shechita* or afterwards — when the animal is already dead. Every single item in the *lo hayah psulo ba-kodesh* list is disqualified while the animal is still alive. That is an easy and accurate way to see where the line falls.

### Rabbi Akiva on Mumin

*Rabbi Akiva machshir be-va'alei mumin* — *Rabbi Akiva* rules that a blemished animal may remain on the altar. The question is immediately pressing: why should a *ba'al mum* be any better than, say, a *yotzei dofen* or a *treifa*? The *gemara* will limit *Rabbi Akiva*'s position to a very narrow case: a *mum* that has a comparable situation in which it would *not* be a *mum* — specifically in a bird, where the comparable type of blemish is not disqualifying. Because such a case exists in which it is not problematic, it has enough of a connection to the world of *kasher* to be treated more leniently. This limiting interpretation is not the simple reading of the *mishna*, but it is how the *gemara* constrains *Rabbi Akiva*'s ruling.

### Practice Testimony

*Rabbi Chanina sgan ha-kohanim* provides testimony from actual Temple practice that stands as a striking counterpoint to *Rabbi Akiva*. It is worth noting — something remarked upon in the discussion — that this is one of the very rare moments across nine chapters of *Zevachim* in which anyone introduces a firsthand memory of what was actually done in the *Beit HaMikdash*. *Rabbi Chanina* reports that his father — a *kohen* who served in the Temple — would physically push *ba'alei mumin* off the altar if they made it up there. He was insistent about it. This testimony directly contradicts *Rabbi Akiva*'s leniency and reflects a practice entirely consistent with the majority position that *ba'alei mumin* must come down.

### Reciprocity Principle

The *mishna* then states the reciprocity principle: *keshem she'alu lo yerdu, kach im yerdu lo ya'alu* — just as invalid things that went up do not come down, so too if they were brought down by accident, they may not go back up. This is in contrast to the ordinary rule for valid offerings, where *emurim* accidentally removed from the altar are replaced. Once these invalid items have been brought down, they remain down.

### Alive Animals

Finally, the *mishna* addresses a distinct case: *ve'kulan she'alu chayim le'rosh ha-mizbe'ach yerdu* — all of these, if they walked up alive to the top of the altar, must come down. The altar's sanctifying power does not extend to a living animal atop the altar — one cannot simply leave it there indefinitely. The cases to which this applies are largely those that could still be *ba'alei chayim* at the point of potential disqualification, such as *rove'a* and *nirba*. This observation reinforces the easier formulation of the *psuluto ba-kodesh* principle: things that are *pasul* while still alive fall in the *lo hayah psulo ba-kodesh* category. If, however, an inattentive *kohen* slaughtered an animal at the top of the altar — a question previously raised as to whether the top of the altar might constitute "the north" — the rule is *yafshit ve'yenatach bi'mkomah*: flay it and complete all the processing right there at the top, without bringing the carcass down.

---

## Textual Basis

### Zot Hi Ha'olah

A *braita* establishes the textual basis for the rule that things placed on the altar remain there. The *pasuk* cited is *zot torat ha'olah, hi ha'olah al mokdah al ha-mizbe'ach kol ha-layla ad ha-boker* — this is the *torah* of the *olah*, it is the *olah* upon its pyre on the altar all night until morning. The words *hi ha'olah* — that is the *olah* which is put up — teaches that things which ascend remain. There is also the *pasuk* of *kol hanogea ba-mizbe'ach yikdash*, which is more directly evoked by the language of *ha-mizbe'ach mekadesh* in the *mishna*, but the primary textual basis for the *im alu lo yerdu* rule is the verse just quoted.

### Three Limiting Words

*Rabbi Yehuda* derives his three exclusions from three limiting words in this *pasuk*. *Zot* — only this and not another. *Hi* — this and not another. *Ha'olah* — the *olah* and not something else. These are *gimel miyutim* — three exclusionary terms. They correspond to his three exceptional cases: *prat le-shenishchata ba-layla*, slaughtered at night; *ve-shenishpach dama*, the blood was spilled; *ve-sheyatza dama chutz lakla'im*, the blood was taken outside the curtains. Those three, if placed on the altar, must come down: *she'im alu yerdu*. Why these three correspond to those three limiting words is, at this stage, not yet fully explained.

### Torat as Inclusive

*Rabbi Shimon* takes a different approach. Rather than multiplying exclusions from the three limiting words, he focuses on the word *torat*. *Ein li ela olah kashira* — from the word *olah* alone I would know only a fully *kasher olah* stays up. The word *torat* functions as an inclusive umbrella: *torat* implies a general rule encompassing a broad category, bringing in all the cases about which both *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* agree — *halan*, *ha-yotzei*, *ha-tamei*, *chutz lizmano*, *chutz limekomo*, *kibel psulim ve-zarku et damo* — and even cases not mentioned explicitly in the *mishna*, such as blood applied to the wrong place or blood of an inner *korban* applied outside.

### Shimon's Expansion

*Rabbi Shimon* then asks: should I perhaps include also *rove'a*, *nirba*, *muktzeh*, *ne'evad*, *etnan*, *mechir*, *kilayim*, *treifa*, and *yotzei dofen*? The answer comes from the word *zot*: this and not those. But what determines the line between what *zot* excludes and what *torat* includes? Here the *gemara* presents *Rabbi Shimon*'s principle as a case of the *Torah* providing an inclusive and an exclusive term — *ribah* and *mi'et* — and then delegating to human wisdom the task of drawing the meaningful line. *Rabbi Shimon* draws it at *psuluto ba-kodesh*: items whose invalidity arose within the *kodesh* context are included; items whose invalidity was not the result of a *kodesh* ritual done wrong are excluded. The *Torah* tells us there is a line; the *Sages* determine where the line falls.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda Analogy

### Methodology Shift

Having explained *Rabbi Shimon*'s approach, the *gemara* now turns to *Rabbi Yehuda*'s methodology, which operates from a fundamentally different orientation. *Rabbi Shimon* begins with a presumption of inclusion — everything is in unless excluded — and then identifies a category to exclude. *Rabbi Yehuda* begins from the opposite direction: the text gives me exclusions, and I need to be persuaded why anything should be *included* in the category of *psulim* that stay on the altar. Do not tell me why something should come down; rather, convince me why it should be allowed to stay up. From this starting point, his list of three additional exclusions follows naturally: those are items for which he cannot find a persuasive justification for inclusion.

### Notar Analogy

The *braita* then presents *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning for each inclusion. *Mipnei mah amru lan be-dam kasher* — why is blood that slept overnight in the category that stays? *Mipnei she-harei lan kasher be-imurim* — because *emurim* that are *notar* and placed on the *mizbe'ach* get to stay. And why is *lan* tolerable for *emurim*? *She-harei lan kasher be-vasar* — because there is meat, namely *shlamim* meat, that is perfectly *kasher* the next day. Of course, the analog is imperfect: *shlamim* meat is *kasher* overnight because it is supposed to be, not because it has slept inappropriately. The *gemara* will raise this objection shortly.

### Yotzei Analogy

*Yotzei* — an item removed from the *Beit HaMikdash* — may stay because *she-ha-yotzei kasher be-vamah*: outside the *mikdash*, at a *bamah*, items brought outside are perfectly valid. This too presents difficulties: if we invoke the *bamah* precedent, it is not obvious why blood taken outside would not receive the same treatment, which would undercut *Rabbi Yehuda*'s own exclusion of *yatza dama chutz lakla'im*. *Rashi* is troubled by this, and the answer is not fully clear.

### Tamei Analogy

*Tamei* — an impure item — may stay *ho'il ve-hutar la'avodat tzibbur*, since a *korban tzibbur* that is *tamei* may be offered. This is actually the strongest of the analogies, because unlike the others it reflects a genuine and specific *halacha* that validates the *tamei* state in a comparable context.

### Chutz Lizmano Analogy

For *chutz lizmano*, the reasoning is *ho'il u-meratzeh le-piggulo* — the curious principle that in the context of *piggul*, the offering is viewed as *meratzeh*, as though it were properly received, precisely in order to render the act one of *piggul*. The *chutz lizmano* thought thereby participates in a suspended legal reality in which the offering is still treated as valid — and that suspended validity is enough to make it tolerable under *Rabbi Yehuda*'s framework.

### Chutz Limekomo Analogy

*Chutz limekomo* is carried along by *chutz lizmano*, the two being conceptually paired and in certain respects equated by the *halacha*. One might also have noted that *chutz limekomo* independently satisfies the *meratzeh* criterion, but the *braita* connects it to the *chutz lizmano* reasoning.

### Kibel Psulim Analogy

The case of *kibel psulim* — a *pasul kohen* receiving and throwing the blood — is the most difficult. When would a *pasul kohen*'s act ever be *kasher*? The *gemara* answers: *be-hanech psulei de-chazu la'avodat tzibbur* — the *mishna* is referring specifically to those *psulim* who are valid for a *korban tzibbur*, namely a *tamei* person. This, however, is emphatically not the plain reading of the *mishna*, which uses the word *psulim* broadly. If the *mishna* meant only a *tamei kohen*, it should have said *tamei*. So the explanation, while it resolves the logical problem, sits uneasily with the text.

### Gemara Critique

The *gemara* raises its formal objection to the entire methodology: *ve-chi danim davar she-lo be-hechshero mi-davar she-be-hechshero* — how can one draw an analogy from something valid to something invalid? The comparison between *notar* blood and overnight *shlamim* meat is not between two comparable cases of the same law; one is done correctly, the other is done incorrectly. You cannot bootstrap the validity of *shlamim* meat overnight into an argument that invalid blood which slept overnight should stay on the altar.

### Resolution via Torat

The *gemara*'s resolution is that *tanna azot torat ha'olah riba samich* — *Rabbi Yehuda* is not, in fact, making the analogical argument from a blank slate. He is not saying: because *shlamim* meat is valid overnight, *notar* blood or *emurim* should get to stay on the altar. That would indeed be a non-sequitur. Rather, he begins from *zot torat ha'olah* — the *Torah* has already told him that there is a category of *psulim* that get to stay on the altar. Given that this category exists, it is reasonable to identify its members as those *psulim* that bear some analogy to a world in which things can be *kasher*. The analogy does not provide the weight of the argument; the *Torah* does. The analogy merely helps identify *which* *psulim* belong to the category the *Torah* established. With this framing, even a weak analogy suffices — it need not be perfect, only meaningful enough to place the *psul* in the vicinity of a recognizable *kasher* context. Several of the analogies remain difficult even within this framework, particularly the *yotzei* case and the *shenishchat balayla* case when one considers the *bamah* precedent, and the *gemara* does not fully resolve every tension.

---

## Outside Mikdash

### Night Inside, Out

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: one who slaughters an animal — a *behema* — at night inside the *Beit HaMikdash* and then takes the meat and places it on a private altar outside, is *chayav* for *ha'alat chutz*. This is a statement about the laws of *shchutei chutz*, the prohibition against bringing offerings outside the *mikdash*. *Rabbi Yochanan* is speaking even according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, who holds that an animal slaughtered at night must come *down* from the altar if placed upon it. Even though from *Rabbi Yehuda*'s perspective this is so severe an invalidity that the offering would be removed from the altar, *Rabbi Yochanan* nonetheless says that one who brings the meat to a private altar outside is *chayav*.

### Comparative Logic

The reasoning: *lo tehei pechuta mi-shochet ba-chutz u-ma'aleh ba-chutz* — let it not be treated as less severe than one who slaughters outside the *Beit HaMikdash* and then places the meat on an external altar. In that classic case of *shchutei chutz*, both acts are fully prohibited and one is *chayav* for each. Now, critically, when someone slaughters outside the *Beit HaMikdash* and a second person then places the meat on an external altar, that second person is *chayav* — even though from the moment of the outside *shechita*, the meat could *never* have legitimately gone onto the altar inside. So too here: the night-*shechita* inside is certainly a *pasul shechita*, and the meat would have to come off the altar. Nevertheless, the act of *shechita* was a genuine act of *shechita*, and bringing the meat to an external altar makes one *chayav*, no less than in the paradigmatic outside case.

### Bird Exception

*Rabbi Chiya bar Avin* raised a *tiyufta* — a contradiction — against *Rabbi Yochanan* from a *mishna*: *ha-shochet of bifnim u-ma'aleh ba-chutz, patur* — one who slaughters a bird *inside* the *Beit HaMikdash* and then places it on an external altar is *exempt*. Whereas *shachat ba-chutz u-ma'aleh ba-chutz chayav* — one who both slaughters and offers outside is *chayav*. This is precisely the paradox *Rabbi Yochanan*'s principle would seem to produce for birds. If one is *chayav* when doing everything outside, one should by parity of reasoning be no less *chayav* when the *shechita* was done inside and the bringing-up was done outside. Yet the *mishna* rules *patur*. This appears to flatly contradict *Rabbi Yochanan*.

### Melikah Issue

The *gemara* does not simply accept the *tiyufta*. After stating it, the *gemara* offers a resolution: *shechitat of bifnim meta katla* — the *shechita* of a bird performed *inside* the *Beit HaMikdash* is categorically different from ordinary *shechita*. Inside the *Beit HaMikdash*, the proper act for a bird is *melikah* — pinching the back of the neck. *Shechita* as performed on a bird inside the *Beit HaMikdash* is not simply a *pasul* act of *shechita*; it is essentially no act of *shechita* at all. It is as though someone shot the bird in the head. There is no recognized *halachic* content to the act whatsoever — it does not even rise to the level of a *pasul shechita*, because *shechita* is simply not the applicable process for a bird in the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Mammal Distinction

This is why the *mishna*'s ruling of *patur* applies specifically to the bird case and does not contradict *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position regarding mammals. When a *behema* is slaughtered inside the *Beit HaMikdash* at night, the act is a genuine act of *shechita* — *pasul*, yes, but recognizable as *shechita*. The night invalidates the offering; it does not nullify the act. Therefore, when the meat is subsequently placed on an external altar, the person is *chayav*, because the original act was a meaningful *shechita* and the bringing-outside completes a prohibited sequence. By contrast, when a bird is slaughtered inside by *shechita* rather than *melikah*, the original act has no *halachic* standing as a legitimate killing of the bird for *korban* purposes, and the subsequent bringing-outside therefore produces no *chiyuv*. The *gemara* thus vindicates *Rabbi Yochanan*: his rule applies to mammals, and the *mishna*'s exception applies uniquely to birds by virtue of the *melikah* requirement.

---

---

# Zevachim 85

## Imurim Before Zrika

### Ulla's Statement

The daf opens in the midst of the broader discussion of *hamizbeach mekadeshan* — the principle that the altar consecrates whatever is placed upon it, such that even invalid offerings, once on the altar, need not be removed. The preceding material had explored the scope of this rule: what kinds of connection to the altar suffice, and how invalid must something be before the principle ceases to apply. The central dividing line that emerged was *psulo bakodesh* — whether the invalidating defect arose within the sacred context of the Temple service itself, as opposed to something that could have affected the animal while it was still alive.

The Gemara now continues on 85a, six lines from the top, with a statement of Ulla. *Imurei kodshim kalim she'he'elu lifnei zrikas hadam lo yerdu, na'asu lachmo shel mizbeach* — the *imurim* (the sacrificial portions, the fats and organs designated for the altar) of *kodshim kalim* that were placed on the altar before the blood-throwing (*zrikas hadam*) do not come down; they have become the bread of the altar. It is worth noting that Ulla chooses this distinctive phrase — *lachmo shel mizbeach*, the bread of the altar — rather than the standard formulation *hamizbeach mekadeshan*. This shift in language might have suggested that the fire must already have begun consuming them, but Ulla does not say that; that qualification will arise separately later.

### Chiddush: Partial Design…

The *chiddush* here is subtle but significant. One might have thought that just as the *kometz* of a *mincha* before it is placed in a *klei sharet* is not yet fully designated for the altar — and therefore falls outside the protective scope of *hamizbeach mekadeshan* — so too the *imurim* of *kodshim kalim* before *zrikas hadam* should be considered insufficiently designated. And indeed, the analogy is apt in a particular way: by *kodshim kalim*, there is not yet *me'ila* (the prohibition against misappropriating consecrated property) in the *imurim* prior to the blood-throwing, because *kodshim kalim* are fundamentally under the owner's control — the owner will be eating the meat, and the *imurim* only pass fully into God's domain, as it were, after the blood is thrown. Nevertheless, says Ulla, they are sufficiently connected to the altar that once placed upon it, they do not come down. The rule of *hamizbeach mekadeshan* applies even here.

---

## Rav Zeira's Kal Vachomer

### Rav Zeira's Parallel

Rav Zeira now seeks to find support for Ulla's ruling from an already-established Mishna. The Mishna records a case — according to Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Yehuda — where the blood was spilled or removed outside the Temple precincts and can therefore never be thrown. Even in that scenario, if the *imurim* were placed on the altar, they remain there. Rav Zeira constructs a *kal vachomer*: *uma hatam de'im ba lizrok ein lo lizrok* — in that case, if one wished to throw the blood, one could not do so at all, the animal is entirely beyond repair in this regard, and yet *amarta im alu lo yerdu* — we say that if they were placed on the altar they do not come down. Presumably this applies across all categories of offerings, not distinguishing *kodshei kodashim* from *kodshim kalim*. If so, *hacha de'im ba lizrok zorek* — in Ulla's case, where the blood has simply not yet been thrown but still can be, should the *imurim* not remain on the altar all the more certainly?

### Inference Objection

The Gemara rejects this inference. *Targema akodshei kodashim* — perhaps the Mishna is speaking exclusively of *kodshei kodashim*. This is important, because by *kodshei kodashim* the *imurim* are fully under divine dominion from the outset — there is *me'ila* immediately — and so the principle of the altar's hold over them is readily understood. By *kodshim kalim*, where the *imurim* are not yet fully God's until *zrikas hadam*, the question remains open. The Mishna cannot be used to prove Ulla's point.

### Pesach Example

The Gemara attempts to demonstrate that the Mishna does address *kodshim kalim*. After all, it explicitly mentions the *pesach* offered *shelo lishmo* as one of its cases, and a *pesach* is *kodshim kalim* — so the Mishna must be dealing with that category as well. The Gemara deflects this: *targema beshelo lishmo* — the *pesach* case refers only to *shelo lishmo*, a disqualification particular to that specific offering. The other cases in the Mishna regarding spilled blood remain limited to *kodshei kodashim*. One cannot fully prove from the Mishna that *kodshim kalim* are covered in the general rule, and Ulla's statement therefore retains its novelty.

---

## Living Creatures Rule

### All Living Animals Down

The Gemara attempts yet another angle. The Mishna concludes with a general statement: *vechulan she'alu legabei mizbeach yerdu* — all of these animals, if brought to the top of the altar while still alive, must be brought down and slaughtered below. The word *vechulan*, "all of them," appears after the mention of the *pesach*, suggesting that the Mishna is speaking broadly, encompassing *kodshim kalim* as well. If so, one might infer from this that if they were slaughtered at the top of the altar, they would stay — including *kodshim kalim* — even with various disqualifications.

### Living vs Slaughtered

The Gemara draws a careful distinction. The Mishna's rule about bringing living animals down applies to all animals — *kodshei kodashim* and *kodshim kalim* alike — but this says nothing about slaughtered animals. With slaughtered animals, the rule is not uniform: some would come down and some would not.

### No Inference

The Gemara is explicit: *lo, hashchutin mehem yerdu umehem lo yerdu* — do not read any inference about slaughtered animals into the Mishna's statement about living animals. The Mishna is speaking only about the scenario where the animal is still alive and must be brought down. When it says "all of them," it means all living animals must descend, regardless of whether they are *kodshei kodashim* or *kodshim kalim*. No conclusion about slaughtered animals of *kodshim kalim* with various defects follows from this.

---

## Minor Blemish Chiddush

### Why Down if Alive?

Once the Gemara has established that the Mishna's rule about living animals is not providing an inference about slaughtered animals, it raises the obvious question: *pshita* — is this not obvious? If a living animal is brought to the top of the altar, of course it must be brought down and slaughtered below. Why does the Mishna need to state this?

### Small Blemish Case

The Gemara answers: *le'olam achayin ubedukin sheba'ayin* — we are speaking of living animals, and the *chiddush* concerns animals bearing small blemishes of the eye, *dukin sheba'ayin*, according to Rabbi Akiva. The case must involve an invalidity that attaches while the animal is still alive but that, had the animal been slaughtered at the top of the altar, would have been tolerated there — meaning it would have been allowed to remain. The only such invalidity that fits this profile is the minor blemish addressed by Rabbi Akiva's position, which we will encounter explicitly later in the Mishna. A more serious disqualification — such as an animal used for a prohibited act — would require bringing the animal down even if it were already slaughtered, and so the contrast the Mishna draws between alive and slaughtered would be meaningless in such a case.

### Chiddush Explained

With this framing, the *chiddush* of the Mishna becomes clear. You have a living animal with a minor blemish. According to Rabbi Akiva, had this animal been slaughtered at the top of the altar, it would be permitted to remain there — the *hamizbeach mekadeshan* principle applies. One might therefore reason: leave it on the altar alive, because if it is slaughtered there, it can legitimately stay. The Mishna teaches otherwise: even so, while it is still alive, bring it down. And this carries a real consequence. Once the animal is brought down, if it is then slaughtered below — even though it was not supposed to be slaughtered, being a *ba'al mum* — there is no way to return it to the altar. An invalid offering not already on the altar cannot be placed there. So the act of bringing the animal down forecloses the possibility of the altar's protection entirely. The *chiddush* is that despite this loss, the Torah requires bringing it down.

To a student's question about whether leaving a sacrifice on the altar discharges the owner's obligation: the answer is no. The principle of *hamizbeach mekadeshan* allows the offering to burn on the altar, but it does not discharge the owner's obligation. Where the invalidity is in the blood itself, the obligation is never fulfilled regardless. Where the invalidity is in other aspects of the animal — as in this case of a minor blemish — it remains a question of what may remain on the altar, not whether the owner has fulfilled his *korban*.

---

## Olah Flaying Case

### Flaying at Top

The Mishna continues: *ve'chen olah she'altah chayah le'rosh hamizbeach tiered* — just as a living animal must come down, so too if an *olah* was brought alive to the top of the altar, it must descend. *Shachatah be'rosh hamizbeach yafshit viyenate'ach bimkomah* — but if it was slaughtered at the top of the altar, it should be flayed and dismembered right there.

### Flaying Invalid?

This immediately raises a difficulty. We have just established that the Mishna's *chiddush* about living animals concerns those bearing a minor blemish. If that is the backdrop of the Mishna, then when it proceeds to discuss an *olah* that was slaughtered at the top of the altar, it would seemingly refer to the same scenario — an animal with a minor blemish. But in that case, how can the Mishna say to flay and dismember it? The Torah explicitly states — *osah*, referring to a valid offering — that only a valid animal is subject to the procedure of *hefshet venituach*, flaying and dismemberment. An invalid animal is excluded.

The Gemara's first attempt to resolve this: *seifa atan leksherah* — the second half of the Mishna shifts to a different case entirely, a fully valid *olah* that was slaughtered at the top of the altar. There are thus two distinct teachings: the first, about living animals with a minor blemish that must come down; the second, about a valid *olah* slaughtered at the altar top, which should be flayed there. But the Gemara is dissatisfied: *u'mai ka mashma lan* — what is the novel teaching? If an animal is valid and was slaughtered at the top of the altar, it is obvious that one should flay it there. Tosafot addresses this directly, noting that everyone agrees to the plain meaning of the Mishna — that what is slaughtered at the top is flayed there. The debate the Gemara references concerns whether one may *lechatchilah* bring a carcass up to the altar top or slaughter there intentionally from the outset. If one holds that flaying at the altar top is always permitted, the Mishna teaches this as an extension. If one holds it is not always permitted, the Mishna's *chiddush* remains unclear. The Gemara is pressing: given the straightforwardness of the case, what exactly is being taught?

### Sha'at Hakesher

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: *hacha bemai askinan kegon shehayta lo sha'at hakesher venifsela* — we are dealing with a case where the animal had a moment of validity, *sha'at hakesher*, but subsequently became invalid. The living-animal portion of the Mishna discusses an animal with a minor blemish, whose *chiddush* is that it must come down even though slaughtering it at the top would have allowed it to remain. The flaying portion of the Mishna discusses a different invalidity — not a blemish, but something that arose after slaughter: for instance, the blood spilled after the slaughter, or the meat became *tamei* after the blood was thrown.

This is the position of Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon: *keivan shenizrak hadam vehurtzah basar sha'ah achat, yafshetenah* — once the blood was thrown and the meat became permissible for even a single moment, even if the meat subsequently became *tamei* or otherwise invalid, one may still proceed to flay the animal. The rationale is practical: the purpose of flaying an *olah* at the altar top is not the burning of the meat alone — it is also to allow the *kohanim* to receive the hide, which is valuable. Even if the meat can no longer be burned on the altar by reason of the invalidity, flaying it preserves the hide for the *kohanim*. The *chiddush* of the Mishna is thus that one proceeds with *hefshet venituach* even after the invalidity arose, because there was a *sha'at hakesher* — a valid moment.

---

## Braita Procedure

### Organs Down & Rinse

The Gemara now cites a *braita* that describes the procedure in detail. When an *olah* was slaughtered at the top of the altar: *morid et hakirbayim lemata umadichan* — one brings the inner organs down to the bottom and rinses them. The inner organs, primarily the small intestine, contain refuse and cannot be burned as they are.

### Why Rinse Invalid?

The Gemara presses: if we are dealing with a *pasul olah*, as we have established, what is the point of rinsing the organs? The rinsing is presumably preparatory to returning them to the altar. But once something invalid has been removed from the altar, it cannot be returned — the protection of *hamizbeach mekadeshan* applies only while it is already there. So why bother rinsing?

One might suggest: burn the organs as they are, with the refuse. To this the Gemara objects by quoting the verse in Malachi — *hakrivehu na lefachatecha hayirtzecha o hayisa fanecha* — "Bring it now to your governor; will he be pleased with you, or will he show you favor?" Something plainly disgusting cannot be offered. So burning refuse-filled intestines on the altar is ruled out. But the Gemara's actual question is not how to burn them — it is why rinse them at all if they cannot go back up? *Madichan lama li?*

The Gemara's first answer is somewhat surprising: the rinsing is done so that should an uninformed *kohen* come across the organs and not realize they are from an invalid offering, he might return them to the altar — and once on the altar, they would be allowed to remain. This answer itself triggers a further objection: *v'anan neiku v'na'avid lehu l'kohanim milta d'atu bah lidei takala* — are we to deliberately arrange a situation for the *kohanim* that could lead them into transgression? One may not set the stage so that an unwitting violation achieves a permitted result. This is reminiscent of debates in the laws of *kashrut* about whether one may passively arrange for an invalid item to become nullified through someone else's inadvertent act.

### Respect for Sacred

The Gemara concludes with a different rationale entirely: *afilu hachi adifa shelo yehei kodshei shamayim mutalim k'neveilah* — even granting all of the above, it is preferable that consecrated property not lie about like a carcass. The organs are rinsed out of respect for sanctified items, even if they can no longer be placed on the altar. Ultimately these materials will need to be burned — not on the altar, but in their designated place for *pasul* offerings — and one would not want the refuse to remain in them in the interim. This is the Gemara's operative reason for the rinsing: basic dignity for sanctified property, not any hope of returning it to the altar.

The *pshat* of the *braita*, however, clearly envisioned rinsing in preparation for returning the organs to the altar — which is why the Gemara had to work so hard to justify it under the assumption that the *olah* was invalid. The Gemara's conclusion is that the Mishna's final sections address various scenarios of *psulim*, and therefore the Mishna need not be read as addressing *kodshim kalim* in the way required to make Ulla's teaching obvious. Ulla's statement — and by implication Reish Lakish's related position — retains its character as a genuine *chiddush* not explicitly derivable from the Mishna.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan's Questio…

### Yerida Question

The Gemara now presents a related discussion attributed to Rabbi Yochanan — one that parallels and intersects with what Reish Lakish ruled. As reported by Rabbi Chiya bar Abba: *baei Rabbi Yochanan, eimurei kodshim kalim she'he'elum lifnei zrikat daman, yerdu o lo yerdu* — Rabbi Yochanan posed the question of whether the *imurim* of *kodshim kalim* placed on the altar before *zrikas hadam* must come down or may remain. This is precisely the question Reish Lakish had resolved decisively — they stay up — but Rabbi Yochanan apparently held it as an open question.

### Me'ila Alternative

Rabbi Ami responds: *v'tiba'i lach me'ilah* — why not ask the parallel question about *me'ila*? The underlying issue in both questions is the same. Since *kodshim kalim* are fundamentally under the owner's control until *zrikas hadam*, the *imurim* are not yet fully God's domain. This generates uncertainty both about whether they must descend from the altar and about whether the laws of *me'ila* apply to them at this stage.

### Stay Up, No Me'ila

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *me'ila lo kamiba'i li, d'zrika hu d'kava'ah lehu bime'ila* — the *me'ila* question does not trouble him, because it is clear that *zrika* is what establishes the *imurim* in the realm of *me'ila*. Until the blood is thrown, the *imurim* of *kodshim kalim* do not carry *me'ila*. What he does not know is *yerida* — the question of taking down — because *yerida* operates on a different logic. Many things remain on the altar even when they arguably should not. The question is whether this *imurim*, despite lacking *me'ila*, are sufficiently connected to the altar to stay there. The Gemara resolves this in accordance with Reish Lakish: *lo yerdu v'ein bahen me'ila* — they do not come down, and yet there is no *me'ila* in them. They are close enough to the altar to benefit from *hamizbeach mekadeshan*, even though they are not yet fully consecrated to the point of *me'ila*.

---

## Me'ila Version

### Me'ila Question

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak transmits an alternative version of this same exchange. Here, Rabbi Yochanan's original question was about *me'ila*: *eimurei kodshim kalim she'he'elum lifnei zrikat daman yesh bahen me'ila o lav* — do the *imurim* of *kodshim kalim* placed on the altar before *zrikas hadam* carry *me'ila* or not?

### Counter Question

Rabbi Ami pushes back in the opposite direction from the first version: *v'tiba'i lach yerida* — why not ask instead whether these *imurim* must come down from the altar? If the question is the extent to which these *imurim* are consecrated, the *yerida* question is equally pressing.

### Conclusion Both Versions

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *yerida lo kamiba'i li, d'nasu lehu lachmo shel mizbeach* — the *yerida* question does not trouble him. Using Reish Lakish's own terminology, he considers it obvious that once placed on the altar, the *imurim* become *lachmo shel mizbeach* — the bread of the altar — and the altar holds them firmly. What remains uncertain is whether they carry *me'ila*. The Gemara resolves both versions with the identical conclusion: *lo yerdu v'ein bahen me'ila* — they stay on the altar, and there is no *me'ila* in them prior to *zrikas hadam*. This is the ruling of Reish Lakish, now confirmed through the parallel tradition of Rabbi Yochanan.

---

## Psulo Lo Bakodesh

### Not in Kedusha

The Gemara moves to the final section of the Mishna: *v'eilu lo hayah psulan bakodesh* — and these are the cases whose invalidity is not *bakodesh*, listing various disqualifications that attached to the animal while it was still alive, prior to any sacred context. These fall outside the protective rule of *hamizbeach mekadeshan*.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva adds: even a *ba'al mum* — an animal with a physical blemish — if slaughtered at the top of the altar, remains there and is not brought down.

### Dukin Sheba'ayin Limit

The Gemara immediately qualifies this: *lo hechshir Rabbi Akiva ela b'dukin sheba'ayin* — Rabbi Akiva's lenient position applies only to *dukin sheba'ayin*, a minor cataract-like blemish of the eye. This is how Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Akiva, and it reflects a genuine exegetical problem: why should a *ba'al mum* be treated more favorably by the altar than other disqualifications that are less explicit in the Torah? Major blemishes are explicitly prohibited by the Torah, while other disqualifications — such as an animal used for bestiality — derive from more indirect sources. Yet those more obscure disqualifications seem to be handled more stringently. The absence of a clear logical basis for treating *baal mum* favorably forces the Gemara to restrict Rabbi Akiva's position to only the most marginal category of blemish.

---

## Eye Blemish Logic

### Birds Permit

The rationale offered for why *dukin sheba'ayin* would be valid at all — and thus within the scope of *hamizbeach mekadeshan* according to Rabbi Akiva — is: *ho'il veksherim b'ofot*, since such blemishes are valid in bird-offerings. Birds are only disqualified for missing a limb; all other physical irregularities are acceptable in a bird-offering. Since a minor eye blemish is *kasher* in a bird, there is some basis to treat it as less disqualifying in general, which provides the conceptual foothold for Rabbi Akiva's position.

### Rashi: Unseemly

A difficulty arises, however. If the rule for birds is that anything short of a missing limb is acceptable, why limit the comparison to the most minimal of blemishes? One could argue: as long as the animal is not missing a limb, it is analogous to what is valid in a bird. Why does Rabbi Akiva's position extend only to the tiniest eye blemishes rather than to any blemish less severe than a missing limb?

Rashi addresses this directly. Rashi notes that the verse — *tmimim zachar babakar bakshavim uva'izim* — requires both *tmimut* (being unblemished) and *zachrut* (being male) only by cattle and sheep; birds are exempt from both requirements. Accordingly, birds are broadly valid despite blemishes. However, Rashi continues, *mechusar eivar lo* — a bird missing a limb is disqualified — citing the very same verse from Malachi: *hakrivehu na lefachatecha* — bringing something to the governor in such a condition would not find favor. What disqualifies in this case is not simply the technical category of "missing limb" but the unseemly appearance it creates.

### Major Blemishes

Rashi's framing is deliberate and consequential. By grounding the limb-disqualification in the concept of *meguneh* — unseemly, repulsive appearance — rather than in a specific legal category, Rashi expands the principle: *vekol mum meguneh* — any major, conspicuous blemish falls within the same prohibition by birds. It is not limited to missing limbs per se; any blemish that is strikingly ugly or obviously disfiguring would be equally disqualifying. This is a significant *chiddush* in Rashi's reading. We are generally taught that birds are only disqualified for missing limbs, but Rashi is saying that in reality, birds are disqualified for missing limbs *because* they are unseemly — and therefore any sufficiently prominent, visible blemish would similarly disqualify. This explains why Rabbi Akiva's position is limited to the small eye-blemishes of *dukin sheba'ayin*: only those inconspicuous, barely noticeable blemishes avoid the category of *meguneh*. A major blemish, even if not a missing limb, would be *meguneh* even in a bird and therefore cannot serve as a basis for leniency. It is only the most minor, visually negligible blemishes that remain in a gray area and thus benefit from Rabbi Akiva's ruling.

---

---

# Zevachim 86

## Rabbi Akiva & Blemishes

### Akiva's Leniency

The daf opens with an explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position regarding the principle of *alu lo yerdu* — that items placed upon the *mizbeiach* need not be removed. The *gemara* on 85b had included animals with a *baal mum* among the cases where *im alu lo yerdu* applies, which is initially difficult. A *baal mum* is a classic example of *lo hayu psulan bakodesh* — the disqualification did not arise from a defect in a ritual performed within the context of sanctification. The question, then, is how Rabbi Akiva could extend *alu lo yerdu* to such a case at all.

### Yochanan's Limitation

The *gemara* resolves this by significantly narrowing Rabbi Akiva's position. Rabbi Yochanan states: *lo hichshir Rabbi Akiva ela bidukin sheba'ayin* — Rabbi Akiva only permitted the case of a minor blemish resembling a cataract of the eye. The reasoning is *ho'il vekasher be'ofos*: since this type of blemish has an analogue in the laws of bird offerings, where a bird is disqualified only if an entire limb is missing, there is a foothold for permitting the animal to remain on the *mizbeiach*. Without such an analogue, the animal would fall squarely into the category of *lo hayu psulan bakodesh* and would have to be removed.

One might note that many blemishes more severe than a cataract are equally inapplicable to birds, yet Rashi explains that more severe blemishes are *megunneh* — unseemly — and therefore inappropriate to present as an offering to God. The *gemara* thus limits Rabbi Akiva to something nearly invisible, even as the bird analogy might logically support a broader category. The tension is acknowledged but the *gemara* holds firm to the narrow reading.

### Blemish Before Kedushá

A further limitation is added: *vehu shekadam hekdeshan es mumam* — Rabbi Akiva's leniency applies only when the sanctification preceded the blemish, such that the *psul* arose after the animal was already consecrated. This brings the case closer to the category of *psulo bakodesh*, since the disqualification occurred within the context of sanctification. If, however, the blemish preceded the sanctification, then from the very outset the animal never acquired a genuine *kedushat mizbeiach*, and even according to Rabbi Akiva it would have to be removed if placed on the *mizbeiach*.

### Female Ola Case

On this basis, Rabbi Akiva would also concede the case of a female animal consecrated as an *olah*. Since an *olah* may only be male, a female animal designated as an *olah* is, at the moment of consecration, already unfit. The *gemara* analogizes this to a case where the *mum* preceded the *hekdesh*, since the disqualification was present from the moment the *kedushah* was conferred, and therefore no genuine *kedushat olah* was ever established. Even Rabbi Akiva would agree that such an animal, if placed on the *mizbeiach*, must be brought down. The *gemara* itself notes that being the wrong sex is not technically a *mum* — it acknowledges the category is being used loosely — but the operative principle is the same: when the problem antedated the consecration, *alu yerdu*.

---

## Nirva Be'ofot

### Yirmiyah's Question

The *gemara* transitions to a question posed by Rabbi Yirmiyah: *yesh nirva be'ofos o ein nirva be'ofos?* — does the disqualification of *nirva* (an animal that was the object of a sexual act by a human) apply to birds? The general rule, derived from the word *min habeheimah*, is that one may bring an offering from domesticated animals but not from all animals — and among the excluded categories are a *rovei'ah* (a male animal that penetrated a human) and a *nirva* (an animal that was penetrated by a human male). Rabbi Yirmiyah's question is whether these disqualifications extend to birds.

### Two Approaches

Two interpretive frameworks are proposed. The first holds that *nirva* and *rovei'ah* are a package deal: *kol heicha de'isa beroveia isa benireva, kol heicha delisa beroveia lisa benireva* — wherever the disqualification of *rovei'ah* applies, so does that of *nirva*, and wherever *rovei'ah* cannot apply, *nirva* does not apply either. Since it is anatomically impossible for a bird to perform an act of penetration upon a human, it cannot be a *rovei'ah*, and therefore the disqualification of *nirva* would not apply to it either.

The second framework rejects the package deal approach entirely and instead invokes an abstract category: *harei ne'evda ba aveira* — regardless of the specific mechanism, any animal used in an act of transgression is thereby disqualified. Under this reading, the inquiry into *rovei'ah* and *nirva* as paired concepts is beside the point; the mere fact of having been used in sin would suffice to disqualify the bird.

### Rava's Proof

Rava adduces a proof from Rabbi Akiva's position. The *mishnah* lists *rovei'ah* and *nirva* among the cases where *im alu yerdu* — where the animal must be removed from the *mizbeiach*. Rabbi Akiva disagrees only regarding *ba'alei mumim* and does not extend his leniency to *rovei'ah* and *nirva*. Rava reasons: *ve'im isa* — if birds were in fact permitted even in a case of *nirva*, Rabbi Akiva should have applied the same logic he used for the cataract blemish. Just as the cataract has an analogue in the laws of birds and thereby qualifies for *im alu lo yerdu* even in a large animal, so too, if birds were unaffected by *nirva*, Rabbi Akiva should have argued that the animal-*nirva* case has a bird analogue and warranted the same treatment. Since Rabbi Akiva says nothing of the kind, it must be that he concedes birds are also disqualified by *nirva*. The *gemara* accepts this: *shema minah*.

It should be noted, however, that the proof is not entirely airtight. Rabbi Akiva's position on the cataract has already been limited to an almost imperceptible blemish on the grounds that more severe blemishes are *megunneh*. One could argue that *nirva* falls into the same category of something unseemly and would not be permitted regardless of the bird analogy. The *gemara* acknowledges the logic but accepts Rava's inference nonetheless.

### Bechoros Evidence

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a stronger and more direct proof from the *mishnah* in Bechoros. That *mishnah* lists the categories of disqualified birds whose *melikah* renders them *neveilah* rather than a valid *korban* offering. *Melikah* — the incision made with the thumbnail at the back of the neck — is the proper mode of slaughter for bird offerings; if performed on an invalid bird, it does not constitute a valid act of slaughter, and the bird is classified as *neveilah*, which conveys *tum'ah* to one who swallows it. Among the invalid birds listed is *hanireva* — a bird that was penetrated. The *mishnah* thus explicitly places a bird-*nirva* in the category of disqualified offerings. *Shema minah* — this is a far clearer proof than the inference from Rabbi Akiva's silence.

---

## Chanina & Practice

### Temple Practice

The *mishnah* records that Rabbi Chanina Segan Hakohanim testified that his father, during the period of the *Beis Hamikdash*, would actually push *ba'alei mumim* off the *mizbeiach* — in direct disagreement with Rabbi Akiva. Since the *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah* had already ruled that such animals must be removed, the question is what additional information Rabbi Chanina is conveying. One possibility is that he is simply providing eyewitness confirmation: the halachic debate notwithstanding, this is how it was actually practiced, and such historical testimony carries significant weight.

### K'Achar Yad Method

A second possibility is that Rabbi Chanina is specifying *how* the animals were removed: *k'achar yad* — in a subtle, incidental manner. Rashi explains that this means it was done privately and unobtrusively, without making a conspicuous display of removing something from the *mizbeiach*. To ostentatiously remove an animal from the altar in full public view would constitute a denigration of it. The *k'achar yad* method thus reflects a sensitivity to the dignity of the *mizbeiach* even in the act of correcting an error.

---

## Yerdu Lo Ya'alu

### Non-Restoration

The *mishnah* continues with the reciprocal principle: *k'sheim she'im alu lo yerdu, kach im yardu lo ya'alu* — just as certain invalid items that were placed on the *mizbeiach* need not be removed, so too if those items were actually brought down, they may not be restored to the *mizbeiach*. The leniency of *im alu lo yerdu* does not confer upon those items a positive status that would entitle them to go back up once removed.

### Mashla Bahen Ha'ur

Ulla qualifies this principle. He states: *lo shanu ela shelo mashla bahen ha'ur* — the rule that removed items may not be restored applies only if the fire had not yet taken hold of them. Once the fire has seized the item — *mashla bahen ha'ur* — it is transformed in status. The item is now described as *na'asa lachmo shel mizbeiach*, having become as it were the bread of the *mizbeiach*, the *lechem isheh* consumed by the fire. At that point, even if the item falls off the *mizbeiach*, it may be restored — because it is no longer regarded as something *pasul* that happens to be on the altar, but rather as something that properly belongs to the consuming fire. This principle applies, at minimum, to items in the category of *im alu lo yerdu*; its extension to other cases will be developed further.

### Bones Dispute

There is a dispute between Rav Mari and Rav Chanina Misura regarding which portion of the *mishnah* Ulla's ruling addresses. Rav Mari applies it to the *reisha* — the earlier portion of the *mishnah* dealing with invalid *korbanos* — while Rav Chanina Misura applies it to the *seifa*, which concerns the bones, sinews, horns, and hooves of an animal.

The *seifa* of the *mishnah* states that these components, when still attached (*mechubarim*) to the animal, are offered on the *mizbeiach* together with the *olah*, but if they have become separated (*pirshu*), they are not offered. Ulla's principle, according to Rav Chanina Misura, means that even these separated items — which in their separated state should not be placed on the *mizbeiach* at all — if they were placed on the *mizbeiach* and the fire seized them and they then fell off, may be restored.

The *gemara* then draws out the logical relationship between the two applications. If one holds that Ulla's principle applies to the *seifa* (the bones and hooves), it certainly applies to the *reisha* (the invalid *korbanos*), since the latter are at least items that have some claim to being offered, having achieved the status of *im alu lo yerdu*. But if one holds that it applies only to the *reisha*, it does not necessarily follow that it applies to the *seifa*. The bones and hooves, being items that would never intrinsically belong on the *mizbeiach* by themselves — unlike the limbs of a *pasul olah*, which are classically the type of thing offered — represent a more fundamental inapplicability. The *gemara* notes that, counterintuitively, the *pasul* limb of an *olah* is in one sense less problematic than a hoof, because the limb at least represents the classical content of a *mizbeiach* offering, whereas the hoof standing alone is fundamentally alien to it.

### Fire Seizing Detail

The discussion of *mashla bahen ha'ur* also admits of two scenarios. In the first, the hoof was still attached when the leg was placed on the *mizbeiach*, and as the fire burned the leg the hoof separated and flew off. In that case Ulla's principle would clearly apply: the hoof was legitimately on the *mizbeiach* and was seized by the fire before it separated. In the second scenario, the hoof had already separated before being placed on the *mizbeiach*, was placed up improperly (with the status of *im alu lo yerdu*), and then, after the fire had seized it, fell off. In that case as well, Ulla's principle would permit restoration. The difficulty of tracking all the permutations is acknowledged; the bottom line is that once the fire has genuinely taken hold of an item, its relationship to the *mizbeiach* is qualitatively different, and a subsequent fall does not preclude restoration — at minimum in terms of *mutar*, even if the question of *chayav* remains to be developed on the following *daf*.

---

## Bones & Hooves

### Attached vs. Separated

The next *mishnah* enumerates items that, if placed on the *mizbeiach*, must be removed: meat of *kodshei kodashim* that is not an *olah* (such as a *chatas*), meat of *kodashim kalim* (such as a *shlamim*), the remainder of the *omer*, the *shtei halechem*, the *lechem hapanim*, the remainder of a *mincha*, and the *ketoret* — all of which are consumed by the *kohanim* or have their designated mode of offering on the inner *mizbeiach*, and therefore do not belong on the outer *mizbeiach*. If placed there, *im alu yerdu*.

The *mishnah* then introduces the case of the wool on the heads of sheep and the hair from the beards of goats, and then returns to the bones, sinews, horns, and hooves. The rule is: *bizman shehem mechubarim ya'alu* — when attached, they are offered, as the verse states *v'hiktir hakohen et hakol*, the *kohen* shall cause the entire thing to be burned. The basis is *v'asita olotecha habasar v'hadam* — the *olah* is defined by the meat and the blood. When the bones and hooves are still integrated into the limb, they are part of *et hakol* and go up. But *pirshu lo ya'alu* — if they have separated, they do not go up separately, for the verse has established that the essence of the *olah* is the meat and the blood.

### Baraita Position
