A *braita* takes the analysis further. Citing the same verse *v'hiktir hakohen et hakol*, the *braita* expands its scope to include the bones, sinews, horns, and hooves. The *braita* then considers whether perhaps even after separation they must be offered — *yachol afilu pirshu*. The tension with *v'asita olotecha habasar v'hadam* is resolved through the distinction: if attached, bring them up; if separated — but the *braita* then adds a further clause: *afilu hein berosh hamizbeach yerdu* — even if they are already atop the *mizbeiach*, they must be brought down. This goes beyond the *mishnah*, which had stated only *lo ya'alu* (they should not be brought up) without ruling that they must be removed if already placed. The *braita* also specifies that the obligation to restore pertains to the *basar v'dam* — the actual flesh — if it flies off the fire, but not to the bones and sinews, since those are not *basar v'dam*.

### Rabbi's View

The *gemara* identifies this ruling as that of Rabbi (Rebbi). A second *braita* is cited in which Rebbi reconciles the two verses: *et hakol* — when the parts are still joined — *ya'alu*; once they are *pirshu* — *afilu hein berosh hamizbeach yerdu* — even if they are already atop the *mizbeiach*, they are brought down.

This allows for up to three positions. The *mishnah*'s view: *lo ya'alu* if separated below, but if placed up, perhaps no obligation to remove. The *tanna kamma* of the *braita*: even if separated below, there is an obligation to bring them up (the separation does not eliminate the duty to offer), and the only distinction is that if they fly off the fire there is no obligation to restore them. Rebbi: *pirshu yerdu* — both that they should not be placed up and that if they were placed up they must be removed.

Rashi and Tosafot each consolidate these three into two positions but in opposite ways. Rashi holds that Rebbi is the *tanna* of our *mishnah* as well — the *mishnah*'s *lo ya'alu* implies *yerdu* if they were placed up, and the more radical position is the *tanna kamma* who says even separated below they are to be offered. Tosafot holds that Rebbi represents the most stringent position; the *braita*'s statement that *pirshu ya'alu* refers not to separation at the floor of the *Mikdash* but to separation that occurs atop the *mizbeiach* itself — in which case the fire may continue to consume them — and the *mishnah*'s *lo ya'alu* reflects the intermediate view that they should not be brought up but if they were, they need not be removed.

### Zeira's Direction

Rabbi Zeira adds a further refinement, addressing Rebbi's ruling that *pirshu yerdu*. He limits this to cases where the hoof separates *klapei mata* — in the direction away from the fire, moving downward. But if it separates *klapei ma'ala* — moving toward the fire — then *kruvei hu d'akrivei l'ochla*: it is still in the process of being offered and consumed, and is not considered truly separated. In that case it would not be subject to the requirement of removal even according to Rebbi.

### Zerikat Hadam

Rava then refines the entire framework. Setting aside the question of directional movement, Rava establishes: *lo shanu ela shepirshu l'achar zerika* — Rebbi's ruling that separated parts must be removed applies only when the separation occurs after *zerikat hadam*. Whether the separation occurred below at the floor of the *Mikdash* or at the top of the *mizbeiach*, if it happened after the blood-sprinkling, removal is required.

But *pirshu kodem zerika* — if the hoof was already separated before *zerikat hadam* — then the *zerikah* applied only to the attached portions of the *korban*. The hoof was never part of the *korban* to which the *zerikah* pertained, and therefore it is not sanctified in any binding sense. In such a case — *afilu l'mevad mineihu katatei d'sakina* — the *kohen* may even use the bone to fashion a knife handle. It has no *kedushas* that would preclude personal use.

This is a striking distinction: the status of the bones and hooves turns on whether they were physically integrated with the sacrificial animal at the moment of *zerikat hadam*. If they were, they become bound up in the *kedushah* of the *korban* and their separation creates a problem requiring proper disposal. If they were not, they never entered the sphere of *kodshim* at all.

---

## Bones Status

### Bones Permissible

The *gemara* now addresses the status of bones with respect to personal use, deriving from a *gezeirah shavah*. The verse by the *olah* states *lo yihiyeh* (regarding the skin going to the *kohen*), and the verse by the *asham* uses the same language regarding the meat of the *asham* going to the *kohen*. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael derives: just as by the *asham* the bones are permitted to the *kohen* for personal use (*mah asham atzmosav mutarin*), so too by an *olah* the bones are permitted (*af olah atzmos mutarin*). Despite the *olah* being entirely consumed, the *lo yihiyeh* applies analogously to items like the skin, bones, horns, and the like — permitting their use for any personal purpose, including fashioning a knife handle.

The *gemara* notes that these *lo yihiyeh* formulations are *mufni* — superfluous in their respective contexts and therefore available to form the basis of a *gezeirah shavah* that is impervious to logical challenge. If they were not *mufni*, one could *mifrach* — one could object: the *asham*'s bones are permitted because the *asham*'s meat is permitted; you cannot extrapolate from there to the *olah*, whose meat is not permitted. But since the words are superfluous to begin with, the *gezeirah shavah* stands even in the face of that logical distinction.

The framework underlying all of this, consistent with Rava's ruling above, is that these bones are permissible specifically when they were separated before *zerikat hadam* — when the *zerikah* never applied to them.

### Tosefta Challenge

Rav Adda bar Ahava raises a challenge from a *Tosefta*. The *Tosefta* teaches: *atzmos kodshim lifnei zerika mo'alin bahen* — bones of *kodshim* (other than an *olah*) are subject to *me'ilah* before *zerikat hadam*, since the *zerikah* is what releases the meat for permitted use; before the *zerikah*, everything remains in the domain of *me'ilah*. After *zerikah*, *ein mo'alin bahen* — the *zerikah* releases the bones as well, consistent with the *asham* ruling. But then the *Tosefta* states regarding an *olah*: *mo'alin bahen le'olam* — there is always *me'ilah* in the bones of an *olah*, both before and after *zerikah*, since the *olah* is entirely burned and nothing is ever released. This appears to directly contradict the ruling that bones separated before *zerikah* are entirely free of *kedushas* and may be used for any purpose.

### Before/After Zrika

The *gemara* resolves the challenge by reading a distinction into the *Tosefta*. The *Tosefta*'s statement *mol'alin bahen le'olam* is reread: *pirshu lifnei zerika — ein mo'alin bahen*, if the bones were separated before *zerikah*, there is no *me'ilah*, consistent with Rava. *Le'achar zerikah — mo'alin bahem*: if they separated after *zerikah*, they are subject to *me'ilah*, for they were part of the *korban* when the *zerikah* applied, and their subsequent separation leaves them as *kodshim psulim* — sanctified items that no longer have a valid mode of offering. They must be disposed of properly, and misappropriating them would constitute *me'ilah*.

### Rabbi Eleazar

Rabbi Eleazar takes the opposite view. According to Rabbi Eleazar, *pirshu lifnei zerikah — mo'alin bahem*: if the bones separated before *zerikah*, there is *me'ilah*. His reasoning, as explained by Rashi, is that in that case the bones were part of the *korban* but were never fit for offering — the *zerikah* never applied to them, so they had no *sh'at heter*, no moment of release. Something that is *kodesh* and never had a *sh'at heter* remains permanently in the domain of *me'ilah*. Conversely, *le'achar zerikah — lo nehenin v'lo mo'alin*: if they separated after the *zerikah*, the blood-sprinkling released them from *me'ilah* even though they never ascended the *mizbeiach*; on the other hand, one is still rabbinically prohibited from deriving benefit from them. This is the precise inverse of Rava's position.

---

## Falling Limbs

### Falling Items

The *mishnah* now states a general rule: *v'kulan she'paku me'al gabi hamizbe'ach lo yachzir* — all of the aforementioned items, meaning those in the category of *alu lo yerdu*, if they flew off the *mizbeiach*, are not returned. This is the correlative of *yerdu lo ya'alu*: the leniency of allowing them to remain does not translate into an obligation or even a right to restore them once they have left the *mizbeiach*. (The prior discussion of *mashla bahen ha'ur* qualifies this, as established by Ulla.) Similarly, a piece of charcoal (*gachelet*) that flies off the *mizbeiach* is not returned. Rashi reads *lo yachzir* regarding the *gachelet* as indicating no obligation to restore rather than a prohibition — the charcoal is not inherently problematic, and the *kohen* simply has no duty to retrieve it.

### Before Midnight

The *mishnah* then addresses the case of limbs of a genuine, valid *olah* burning on the *mizbeiach* that flew off. Here the *mishnah* draws a clear temporal distinction. *Kodem chatzot — yachzir*: before midnight, the limbs must be returned to the *mizbeiach*. In this case *yachzir* clearly means an obligation, since there remains a *mitzvah* of burning. Moreover, *u'mo'alin bahen* — there is still *me'ilah* in these limbs, since the *mitzvah* of *haktarah* has not been completed.

### After Midnight

*Le'achar chatzot — lo yachzir*: after midnight, there is no obligation to restore the limbs. Furthermore, *v'ein mo'alin bahen* — there is no *me'ilah*. The implications of *chatzot* are therefore twofold: it marks the point after which the limbs are considered halachically as though they have been consumed, eliminating both the *mitzvah* of restoration and the status of *me'ilah*. Why midnight should have this effect is not immediately obvious and will be explored in the *gemara*.

---

## Shariri & Night

### Meat Remains

The *gemara* opens with a direct question: *heichi dami* — what is the actual case in which *chatzot* makes a difference? *Im de'is behu mamash* — if there is still actual meat remaining that has not been burned, then *afilu achar chatzot nami*, even after midnight there remains a *mitzvah* to burn it and *me'ilah* should still apply. *Im de'las behu mamash* — if the meat has been entirely consumed and reduced to ash, then *afilu kodem chatzot nami lo*, even before midnight the *mitzvah* is done and there should be no *me'ilah*. How does midnight function as a determinative point in either scenario?

### Shariri Definition

The *gemara* answers at the top of 86b: *lo tzricha — b'shariri*. The ruling is needed for the case of *shariri* — meat that has been hardened by fire to the point where all moisture has been burned away, yet has not yet been fully reduced to charcoal and ash. Such material occupies an intermediate state: it is neither raw meat nor ash. For this ambiguous category, the *gemara* rules that *chatzot* is determinative.

### Two Phases

The *gemara* then asks: *minani mili* — from where is this derived? Rav answers by citing the relevant verses in the *parasha* of *tzav*. One verse states *kol halayla*, establishing that the *olah* burns on the *mizbeiach* the entire night. Another verse juxtaposes *kol halayla* with the act of *terumas hadeshen* — the removal of the ash — implying that the ash removal is also a nighttime activity. The apparent contradiction is resolved: *chalkeyu* — the night is divided. *Chetzyo l'haktara v'chetzyo l'harama* — the first half of the night is characterized by *haktarah* (burning), and the second half by *haramah* (ash removal). For *shariri*, the ambiguous case, this division is operative: during the first half, the emphasis is on burning, and *shariri* is treated as still requiring *haktarah*; during the second half, the emphasis is on ash and completion, and *shariri* is treated as already consumed. This ruling is clearly *d'oraisa*, since the question of *me'ilah* is at stake.

### Kahana Challenge

Rav Kahana challenges this framework from a *mishnah* in Yoma. The practice of *terumas hadeshen* varied according to circumstance: on a regular day it was performed from the cock-crowing (*mikrias hagever*); on Yom Kippur, from midnight (*mechatzot*), to accommodate the *kohen gadol*'s grueling schedule; and on the *regalim*, from the first watch of the night (*me'ashmores harishona*), because the volume of *korbanos* was so large that the *Mikdash* filled with worshippers before the cock crowed and the ashes needed to be cleared earlier. If the second half of the night is the designated time for *terumas hadeshen*, how could it be performed in the first third of the night on the *regalim*?

### Yochanan's Solution

Rabbi Yochanan addresses this by attending closely to the verse. The verse says *kol halayla* — the whole night — and also *ad haboker* — until the morning. Since *kol halayla* already implies *ad haboker*, the additional phrase is superfluous. Rabbi Yochanan applies the principle: *ten boker l'bokro* — give a morning to the morning of the first watch. The phrase *ad haboker* indicates that there is a "morning" earlier in the night, a point before dawn at which the transition to ash-removal emphasis may already take effect. This allows the practice of *terumas hadeshen* to be moved earlier when circumstances require it.

### Rashi's Reading

Rashi reads Rabbi Yochanan's ruling as a refinement rather than a replacement of the *chatzot* framework. The two phases of the night are not exclusive in their respective activities. The first half emphasizes *haktarah*, but *haktarah* continues throughout the night whenever there is meat that genuinely requires burning. The second half emphasizes *terumas hadeshen*, but the *ten boker l'bokro* principle allows *terumas hadeshen* to be moved earlier when the volume of offerings demands it. The practical rule, therefore, is: on a regular day, *terumas hadeshen* is performed from cock-crowing; on Yom Kippur, from midnight; on the *regalim*, from the first watch.

The *chatzot* division — first half for *haktarah*, second half for *haramah* — governs the intermediate case of *shariri* alone. For *shariri* in the first half of the night, the meat is treated as not yet consumed, *me'ilah* applies, and there is an obligation to restore it to the *mizbeiach* if it falls. For *shariri* in the second half of the night, it is treated as already consumed, there is no *me'ilah*, and there is no obligation to restore. But for fully unconsumed meat, the *mitzvah* of *haktarah* remains in force throughout the night regardless of *chatzot*, and for meat already fully reduced to ash, the *mitzvah* is complete regardless of when that occurred.

---

---

# Zevachim 87

## Hardened Meat & Timing

### Meat Falls Off Fire

The *daf* opens by resuming a discussion carried over from the bottom of 86b, where a *mishnah* established that if sacrificial matter falls off the altar fire before *chatzos*, there remains a *mitzvah* to return it, and the laws of *me'ilah* apply; after *chatzos*, the *mitzvah* has lapsed, *me'ilah* no longer applies, and one need not return it to the fire.

### Three States of Meat

The *Gemara* initially challenged this rule: what, after all, does *chatzos* change? Either the matter has already turned to ash, in which case one is finished with it even before *chatzos*, or it is still meat, in which case even after *chatzos* one returns it. The *Gemara*'s resolution is that *chatzos* is decisive only for an intermediate case — meat that has hardened to the consistency of stone but has not yet become ash. In that middle state, before *chatzos* it retains the status of burning matter with an associated *mitzvah* and *me'ilah*; after *chatzos* that status lapses and it is considered consumed.

### Chatzos on Mizbe'ach

The *Gemara* further assumes — and will shortly press this assumption — that what causes this hardened meat to be considered consumed is that it was atop the *mizbe'ach* at the moment of *chatzos*. The question then becomes: what if the meat was not on the *mizbe'ach* at *chatzos*?

### Off & Back Again

The *Gemara* therefore addresses a case in which the pieces of meat (*pirshu kodem chatzos vehichziran achar chatzos*) fell off the *mizbe'ach* before midnight and were returned after midnight. Assuming the meat was replaced at the top of the altar but was never actually consumed by fire — it remains hardened but not yet ash — will its status ever change given that it missed the first *chatzos* while it was on the *mizbe'ach*?

### Rabbah: Chatzos Sheni

Rabbah answers: *Chatzos sheni ochaltan* — the second midnight, Monday night, will confer the status of "consumed" upon this hardened meat. In Rabbah's view, every *chatzos* carries the power to reclassify hardened meat as consumed, so if the meat missed Sunday midnight, Monday midnight will suffice.

### Rav Chisda: Alot Hashach…

Rav Chisda disagrees: *Amud Hashachar ochaltan* — daybreak, rather than the following midnight, will change the status. For Rav Chisda, it is not necessary to wait until Monday midnight; the dawn of Monday morning renders the meat no longer fit for the *mizbe'ach*. This is not because it becomes classified as ash — rather, the meat becomes *notar*: with the arrival of the morning of the following day it is legally leftover and may not be returned to the altar.

### Rav Chisda's Logic

The reasoning attributed to Rav Chisda by the *Gemara* is a *kal vachomer*: midnight (*chatzos*) does not ordinarily produce *linah* — it does not render food that must be eaten or portions at the base of the *mizbe'ach* into *notar*. *Chatzos* has no operative significance for ordinary sacrificial matter in that respect. And yet midnight does have the power to reclassify hardened meat as consumed. How much more so, then, should *alot hashachar* — which does produce *linah*, causing all unconsumed matter to become *notar* — reclassify the hardened meat as consumed.

Stripped of the formal *kal vachomer*, Rav Chisda's point is straightforward: hardened meat sitting at the top of the *mizbe'ach* at daybreak should simply become *notar* along with everything else. One might suggest that *ha-mizbe'ach mekadesh* shields it even from *notar* status — but that complication is set aside for the moment. The underlying intuition is that it is incongruous to think this meat remains entirely unaffected by the arrival of daybreak.

### Scenario Two

The *Gemara* then introduces a second scenario: the meat came off before *chatzos* (say, at 11:50 PM Sunday night) and was not returned until after *alot hashachar* (say, at 5:10 AM Monday morning). In this case Rava holds that the meat's status still does not change, and one must wait until Monday midnight — *chatzos sheni* — to consider it consumed. Rav Chisda, consistently with his position, holds that since the meat missed both *chatzos* and *alot hashachar* while it was atop the *mizbe'ach*, its status never changes: *ein bein ichul le'olam* — it will never acquire the status of consumed.

### Location Matters?

Both Rava and Rav Chisda share a common assumption: the critical time periods confer the status of "consumed" only when the meat is actually atop the *mizbe'ach*. If the meat was elsewhere — whether at the foot of the altar or on the ground — neither midnight nor daybreak produces that reclassification while it is off the *mizbe'ach*.

Rav Chisda's consistent position is that only the time periods relevant to Sunday's sacrifices can affect Sunday's meat: Sunday midnight and Sunday *alot hashachar*. Monday's *chatzos* is relevant for Monday's meat; Monday's *alot hashachar* is relevant for Monday's *korbanot*. Once Sunday's windows have passed, no subsequent time has operative significance for Sunday's meat. Rava, by contrast, holds that each successive midnight retains the power to reclassify hardened meat, so there is always another opportunity.

On the question of why the meat does not simply become *notar* when it is lying at the foot of the *mizbe'ach* at daybreak: one possible answer is that it does in fact acquire *notar* status — but once it is placed atop the *mizbe'ach*, the principle of *mizbe'ach mekadesh* takes hold, and *notar* that has been brought to the top of the altar may remain there and be consigned to the fire. The sole thing that would definitively preclude returning it to the fire is if the meat were already classified as consumed. Whether an object that is wholly inedible but not yet ash would even acquire *notar* status is itself an interesting question, since *notar* presupposes the category of food — but in any event, once it is placed back atop the *mizbe'ach*, the *mekadesh* principle governs.

---

## Rav Yosef's Challenge

### Status Everywhere?

Rav Yosef presses on the shared assumption underlying the entire debate. Both Rava and Rav Chisda presuppose that *chatzos* changes the status of hardened meat only while it is atop the altar. But who says that is correct? *Man leima lan dechatzos beroash hamizbe'ach mashvei lei ikul?* — who told us that midnight reclassifies the meat only if it is at the top of the *mizbe'ach*? Perhaps — *deilma kol heicha d'mishtachach mashvei lei ikul* — wherever the meat happens to be, midnight confers the status of consumed upon it.

### Eretz Yisrael Rules

A ruling was then transmitted from Eretz Yisrael: *hilchesa keRav Yosef* — the *halacha* follows Rav Yosef. The status change occurs wherever the meat is located; the entire debate between Rava and Rav Chisda, which presupposed a location requirement, is built on a premise the *halacha* rejects.

### Tosafos Comment

Tosafos raises a pointed observation here. The *Gemara* records that "they sent from Eretz Yisrael" that the *halacha* follows Rav Yosef. One might have expected the *Gemara* to ask its standard question — why rule on matters relevant only at the time of the future Temple, since such rulings are purely theoretical? Tosafos explains: *perush yafeh amar* — the phrasing signifies that what Rav Yosef says is logically compelling, not that a formal practical ruling is being issued. Moreover, Tosafos notes, the *Gemara* will later reinterpret the positions in a way that shows they do not ultimately conflict with Rav Yosef's logic.

### Chiya & Bar Kappara

The *Gemara* cites corroborating *Tannaitic* and *Amoraic* testimony. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states: if the pieces fell off the *mizbe'ach* before midnight and were returned after midnight — *lo nehenin velo moalin* — midnight had the effect of removing *me'ilah* even though the meat was not on the *mizbe'ach* at the time. Bar Kappara teaches the same in a *baraita*: *pirshu kodem chatzos vehechzirun achar chatzos yotzin midei meilah* — if they came off before *chatzos* and were not returned until after, *me'ilah* no longer applies. Evidently, the status change effected by *chatzos* occurs wherever the meat is, consistent with Rav Yosef's position.

---

## Fatty Meat Exception

### Rav Papa Challenges

Rav Papa puts a sharp question to Abaye: if the ruling from Eretz Yisrael confirms Rav Yosef, and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and Bar Kappara both attest that *chatzos* changes status regardless of location, what exactly remains as the subject of dispute between Rava and Rav Chisda? Their entire debate, compelling as it is, appears to have no operative case.

### Fatty Meat Case

Abaye answers in a single word: *b'shmanim* — in fatty meat. Rashi explains that even after fatty meat has hardened on the outside, it is not yet considered consumed, because the fat retains some inner moisture that prevents it from reaching the status of ash. This creates a third intermediate category: harder than raw meat but not as fully desiccated as the standard hardened case.

### Clarified Scenario

The *Sfas Emes* and *Chazon Ish* offer a clarification that proves illuminating. The case is not simply one of fatty meat throughout; rather, the meat was still in a meaty, un-hardened state at the first midnight, and therefore midnight did not change its status at all — it was still too close to real meat. The meat was then returned to the altar and dried out further over the course of the night. By the time later critical hours arrive — the next *alot hashachar* or the following midnight — the meat has in fact reached the hardened state, and the question now is whether there is a subsequent time that will reclassify it as consumed. This resolves the conceptual difficulty: the first midnight was simply inapplicable because the meat had not yet hardened; the debate between Rava and Rav Chisda concerns what happens next.

### Debate Preserved

With this clarification, the positions of Rav Chisda and Rava remain live and meaningful. Rav Chisda holds that *alot hashachar* of the same night is the operative moment: if the meat was meaty throughout and had dried out only by dawn, that dawn renders it consumed — provided it is atop the *mizbe'ach* at that point. If it was not there at *alot hashachar*, no subsequent time applies. Rava, consistently, holds that the following midnight always retains the power to reclassify, and that one does not limit operative moments to those of the original night.

---

## Lina on Mizbe'ach

### Rabbah Asks

The *Gemara* opens a new inquiry: *ba'ei minei Rava mei'Rabbah* — Rava posed a question to Rabbah. *Lina mo'eles b'rosho shel mizbei'ach o einah mo'eles b'rosho shel mizbei'ach?* — does *linah* take effect at the top of the *mizbe'ach*, or does it not? The practical stakes are as follows. A *kohen* has meat that belongs to a *chatat* or an *olah*, sitting atop the *mizbe'ach* at daybreak. Does the arrival of daybreak render it *notar* even while it is physically on the *mizbe'ach*?

### Meat Falls Off

The *Gemara* immediately sharpens the question. If the meat is still atop the *mizbe'ach* after daybreak, the question is less pressing — *mizbe'ach mekadesh* allows it to remain and be consigned to the fire in any event. The genuinely difficult case is where the meat was atop the *mizbe'ach* when daybreak arrived, and subsequently fell off. The question is: since it was on the *mizbe'ach* at daybreak, did the *mizbe'ach* somehow insulate it from acquiring *notar* status? If so, even after it falls off it may be returned and burned. If not — if *linah* applies even at the top of the *mizbe'ach* — then once it falls off, the rule of *yardu lo ya'alu* (what has descended does not go back up) would apply, and it could not be returned.

The *Gemara* explores an analogy to the *lechem hapanim* on the *shulchan*. There, the *mishnah* rules *afilu hen al shulchan yamim rabim ein bekach klum* — even if the loaves remain on the table for many days, it is of no consequence; they do not become *notar*. Rashi explains the scenario: if the *kohanim* failed to set out the *lechem hapanim* on *Shabbos* and only placed it on Sunday, the proper time for the *bizichin* offering has not yet arrived — it is *mechusar zman*, the loaves must be on the *shulchan* for a full seven days. The next opportunity to offer the *bizichin* and eat the bread would be the following *Shabbos*, by which point the loaves would have been on the *shulchan* for thirteen days — yet they do not become *notar*.

### Kli vs. Ground

The question underlying the analogy is whether the *mizbe'ach* is to be regarded as a *kli* — a vessel — in which case its sanctifying power might extend to preventing *linah*, or whether it is to be regarded as the ground itself, in which case it would have no such effect. A *kli sharet* in principle insulates from *notar*; the ground does not. The *mizbe'ach* occupies an uncertain middle position.

### Rabbah's Answer

Rabbah answers: *ein linah b'rosh hamizbayach* — *linah* does not take effect at the top of the *mizbe'ach*. Accordingly, if meat was atop the *mizbe'ach* when daybreak arrived and then fell off, it has not become *notar* and may be returned to the fire and burned. It is worth noting that the *Gemara* formulates this in terms of *linah*, distinct from the earlier formulation of *mizbe'ach mekadesh*. Whether Rabbah's ruling would extend to meat that is meant to be eaten by *kohanim* rather than burned on the altar is a separate question the *Gemara* does not resolve here.

### Baraita Debate

A *baraita* addresses the case of *evarim she-lanu ba-azarah* — limbs of a *korban* that spent the night in the *azarah*. The *baraita* rules: if they remained at the top of the *mizbe'ach* — *lan b'rosh she-al mizbei'ach makater ve-holech le-olam* — they may be burned at any time, since *mizbe'ach mekadesh* applies continuously while they are atop the altar. If they descended — *yerdu* — this is precisely the case at issue: they were on the altar at daybreak and then came off.

### Rabbah vs. Rava

On this *baraita*, Rabbah says *ya'alu* — they may be returned and burned; Rava says *lo ya'alu* — they may not be returned. Rabbah holds that *linah* has no force at the top of the *mizbe'ach*, and so the meat never acquired *notar* status while it was there; having descended without becoming *notar*, it may go back up. Rava disagrees: *linah* does take effect even at the top of the *mizbe'ach*, and the meat is therefore *notar* upon descending, subject to the rule of *yardu lo ya'alu*. The *Gemara* notes that the *Rambam* rules in accordance with Rava on this question, against the intuitive reading.

The *Gemara* concludes: *shema mina lo kibla minei* — it is clear that Rava did not accept Rabbah's position, for they debate it openly.

---

## Mekadesh Concept

### Principle Extended

The *Gemara* now broadens the *mekadesh* principle beyond the *mizbe'ach* itself. Just as the altar sanctifies what comes upon it — enabling *pesulim* to remain and be burned — so too the *kevesh* (the ramp) and the *keilim sharet* (the service vessels) share in this sanctifying power. This extension is derived from explicit sources.

### Kevesh Derivation

The *baraita* states: *ha-nogea ba-mizbeach* — I know only that the *mizbe'ach* itself has this power. Whence do I derive the ramp? *Talmud lomar et ha-mizbeach* — the word *et* in the verse *umashachta et ha-mizbeach* ("and you shall anoint the *mizbe'ach*," which Rashi identifies as the verse in the passage concerning anointing, verse 37 of the relevant passage) serves as an expansive particle including the *kevesh*. There is a significant dispute among commentators as to precisely which verse is the source, but Rashi identifies it as the verse concerning the anointing that sanctifies.

### Keilim Sharet

For the *keilim sharet*, there is an explicit verse: *umashachta otam, kol ha-nogea ba-hem yikdash* — the verse that speaks about anointing the service vessels states explicitly that whatever touches them becomes sanctified. The same formulation — *kol ha-nogea yikdash* — that applies to the *mizbe'ach* applies to the *keilim sharet*, and so their sanctifying power is directly stated in the Torah.

### Reish Lakish Asks

Reish Lakish posed a question to Rabbi Yochanan: *kol klei shares mahu sheyekadesh es hapsulin* — what exactly is the nature of the sanctification conferred by a *kli sharet* upon invalid items placed within it? Rabbi Yochanan initially replied that this is taught in our *mishnah*, since the *mishnah* states explicitly that just as the *mizbe'ach* and the *kevesh* sanctify what is fit for them, so too the *kelim* sanctify. But Reish Lakish pressed further.

### Valid L'Chatchila?

Reish Lakish clarifies his question: *lechatchila likarev kamiba'ei li* — what he wants to know is whether the sanctification by a *kli sharet* is powerful enough to permit *lechatchila* offering of otherwise invalid items. Concretely: if blood was caught in a *kli sharet* by a *pasul* person, the blood is invalid. May one now proceed *lechatchila* to throw that blood on the *mizbe'ach*? Does the *kli sharet* render the blood sufficiently sanctified that one may go forward as if the *psul* did not exist?

The analogy to the *mizbe'ach* itself is instructive: when something *pasul* is on the *mizbe'ach*, the rule is that it remains there and may be moved to the fire. But that involves no dislocation — it stays in place and is burned where it is. For a *kli sharet*, the proposed act of *mekadesh* would require actively transferring the contents to the *mizbe'ach* — a materially different step. Whether *kli sharet mekadesh* extends that far is the question.

### Rashi's View

Rashi approaches the question of what *kli sharet mekadesh* means if it does not mean permission to offer *pasul* material *lechatchila*. He identifies the operative *nafka mina* not as *me'ilah* (as one might initially suppose) but as the question of *pidyon* — redemption. Before an item is placed in a *kli sharet*, it may in principle be redeemed; once it is placed in a *kli sharet*, it can no longer be redeemed. This is the sense in which the *kli sharet* literally sanctifies — it raises the object's sanctity to a level that precludes redemption, without necessarily permitting its use for the *korban* if it is otherwise *pasul*. On Rashi's reading, *kli sharet mekadesh* means that the item is elevated in sanctity, not that the *psul* is thereby overridden for purposes of *avodah*.

### Psul Catching Blood

The *Gemara* then cites a *baraita* case: *shekiblu psulim v'zarku es damo* — a *pasul* person caught the blood and threw the blood. The *mishnah* teaches that if this occurred, and the meat was subsequently placed on the *mizbe'ach*, the meat may remain, since *mizbe'ach mekadesh* applies.

### Both Actions Needed

Rabbi Yochanan reads the *vav* in the *baraita* as conjunctive — "and" rather than "or." A *pasul* person both caught the blood and threw it. This apparently redundant formulation has significance: if the *pasul* person only caught the blood, the blood is invalid — but since it is within a *kli sharet*, one might be permitted to proceed and throw it *lechatchila*. Only if the *pasul* person also threw it is the *avodah* definitively compromised. The implication of Rabbi Yochanan's reading is striking: catching invalid blood in a *kli sharet* might not disqualify the subsequent throwing; it is the invalid throwing itself that creates the *psul*.

### Unresolved Question

The *Gemara* pushes back on this reading. The word in the *baraita* is "or" — *shekiblu psulim ee nami shezarku psulim* — either catching or throwing suffices to render the meat *pasul* for this purpose. The attempt to derive from the *baraita* that blood caught by a *pasul* person in a *kli sharet* may be thrown *lechatchila* therefore fails as a textual proof. The larger question — whether *kli sharet mekadesh* is powerful enough to permit *lechatchila* offering of otherwise invalid matter, such that a *korban* would be entirely *kasher* — remains without a definitive *Gemara* resolution.

---

## Air Space of Altar

### Hovering Meat

The *Gemara* opens a new question: *avir mizbe'ach k'mizbe'ach dami o lo* — does the air space above the *mizbe'ach* have the same legal status as the *mizbe'ach* itself? If one has *pasul* or *tamei* matter hovering in the airspace directly above the altar — say, thrown up and caught there without actually touching the surface — does *mizbe'ach mekadesh* apply to it? Is the *kohen* permitted to place it on the fire, or must he remove it?

### Moving Meat Problem

The *Gemara* attempts to derive an answer from the established *halacha* that the *kevesh* too is *mekadesh*. Just as the altar sanctifies, so does the ramp. If the air space above the altar were not considered equivalent to the altar, then one would expect the same to be true of the ramp: the air space above the ramp would not be considered like the ramp. But this generates an immediate practical difficulty: *heichi masklei michevesh lemizbe'ach havei yerud?* — how could one physically transfer a piece of *pasul* meat from the ramp to the altar? The moment one lifts it up to carry it, it passes through the airspace. If the airspace is not considered part of the *mizbe'ach*, the act of lifting it constitutes removal from the *mizbe'ach* — and what has been removed may not be returned. The entire operation of bringing *pasul* matter from the ramp to the fire would be impossible.

### Dragging Solution

The *Gemara* proposes a solution: *denagdei* — one does not lift it at all, but rather drags it along the surface of the *kevesh* without ever lifting it, keeping it in continuous contact with the ramp's surface.

### Gap Problem

A new difficulty immediately presents itself: *veha avir yesh bein kevesh lemizbe'ach* — there is a small gap between where the *kevesh* ends and the *mizbe'ach* begins. When one drags the meat across this gap, part of it is suspended over empty space, not in direct contact with either the ramp or the altar surface. If the airspace is legally distinct from the altar, even this dragging would pass through a zone where the meat is, in some sense, off both surfaces simultaneously.

### Majority Rule

The *Gemara* resolves this: *rubo l'kevesh k'kevesh, rubo l'mizbe'ach k'mizbe'ach* — we apply the principle of majority. If the majority of the piece of meat is still on the ramp, the entire piece is considered to be on the ramp; if the majority is on the *mizbe'ach*, it is considered to be on the *mizbe'ach*. The small portion suspended over the gap is subsumed into the majority, and there is no problem. This resolution means the dragging scenario does not require the airspace to have the same status as the altar — the gap issue is resolved through *rubo*, not through *avir*.

### Chubur Question

The *Gemara* now notes a further implication: *tifshot meha d'ba'ei rami bar chama* — from this resolution one can perhaps answer the question Rami bar Chama raised elsewhere. Rami bar Chama asked: *yesh chibur l'olin o lo* — when bringing sacrificial matter up onto the *mizbe'ach*, do we treat it as a single connected unit, or do we evaluate each piece independently? The resolution through *rubo* presupposes that the piece of meat is treated as one unit — otherwise, the fragment suspended over the gap would need to be evaluated on its own, and the majority principle would be irrelevant. The implication, then, is that *yesh chibur l'olin* — matter being brought up is considered a single unit.

### Pigul Challenge

Ravva bar Rav Chanan challenges from the opposite direction. If one maintains that the airspace of the *mizbe'ach* is equivalent to the *mizbe'ach* itself, a problem arises regarding *olas ha'of*: *olas ha'of de-paslah bemachshavah heichi mashkachat lah* — how could one ever bring about *pigul* through an improper thought while performing the *melikah* of a bird offering?

### Pigul While Hovering

The *Gemara* explains the difficulty. The *melikah* of a bird is performed at the top of the *mizbe'ach*. The *kohen* performing it is standing over the altar — and therefore, whatever he holds is in the airspace of the *mizbe'ach*. Now, the underlying principle of *pigul* is that a *machshavah* (thought) cannot be more severe than the act itself. If one actually followed through on the thought — for example, burning the meat two days hence — that act would not be problematic, since the meat is in the airspace of the *mizbe'ach*, which we are assuming is equivalent to the *mizbe'ach* itself, and *mizbe'ach mekadesh* would apply for as long as it remains there. If the actual deed is permitted, how can the *thought* of that deed constitute *pigul*?

### Rav Shimi Answers

Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers: *alma lo* — the difficulty is misplaced. One can readily construct a scenario where a *pigul* thought would apply even to a bird offering performed in the airspace of the *mizbe'ach*. The scenario is: *hareini molek al menas lehoridah lemachar ulehaalosah lehaktarah* — the *kohen* performs the *melikah* with the explicit intention of removing the bird from the *mizbe'ach* after daybreak and then returning it to be burned thereafter. That act — bringing the bird down after daybreak and then returning it — would be *assur*, since it would have become *notar* in the interim. Since the thought envisions an actually impermissible act, it constitutes a valid *pigul* thought.

### Down & Up Solution

The *Gemara* notes that this solution works straightforwardly according to Rava, who holds that *linah* does take effect even at the top of the *mizbe'ach*: bring it down after daybreak, and it has become *notar*, so the thought of doing so later is a thought about something genuinely impermissible. According to Rabbah, who holds that *linah* does not take effect at the top of the *mizbe'ach*, the meat would not become *notar* if left there overnight — so the scenario requires refinement: *hareini molek al menas lehoridah kodem amud hashachar ulehaalosah le'achar amud hashachar* — the intention is to bring it down before daybreak (when it has not yet become *notar*) and return it after daybreak. That act too would be impermissible — since after *alot hashachar* it would then acquire *notar* status upon descent and could not be returned — and the thought of it therefore constitutes *pigul* even according to Rabbah.

### Birds as Proof

The *Gemara* pivots. Having introduced the bird case, it observes that the birds can actually serve as positive evidence that the airspace of the *mizbe'ach* is indeed equivalent to the *mizbe'ach* itself. Specifically, the *Gemara* raises the case of a *chatat ha'of* that was *pasul* — performed *shelo lishma*, for instance — and asks how the blood-sprinkling (*haza'ah*) of such a *chatat* could ever be performed if one maintains that the airspace is not equivalent to the altar. The discussion of how this plays out will continue at the top of the following *daf*.

---

---

# Zevachim 88

## Airspace = Mizbeach

### Kli Sharet Review

Today's *daf* is 88, and we pick up at the very bottom of 87b, in the middle of the discussion about whether the airspace over the *mizbeach* counts as the *mizbeach* itself — such that if a *korban* is in that airspace, it is treated as already on the *mizbeach*, and therefore, if it is *pasul*, it need not be taken down.

Before continuing, a brief clarification is in order regarding the previous session. The *mishnah* states that placing something in a *kli sharet* is also *mekadesh*. *Reish Lakish* asked *Rabbi Yochanan* whether this means one could even offer it up *lechatchila* even if it is *pasul* — for what else would the *mishnah* mean? *Rashi* explains that the alternative is one of the normal effects of a *kli sharet*: it elevates the *korban* to a higher level of sanctity, such that it can no longer be redeemed; it is no longer merely verbally designated but is fully consecrated.

### Meila & Kli Sharet Effec…

One point from yesterday requires explicit correction: it was mistakenly stated that entry into a *kli sharet* has an implication for *meila*. That is incorrect. *Meila* applies as soon as verbal sanctity takes place — this is a *meforash mishnah* in *Meila*. A *kli sharet* has two primary *nafkaminot*: first, the item placed within it can no longer be redeemed; second, it becomes *pasul* through *linah*, *yotzei*, lower levels of *tumah*, and removal from the *Beit Hamikdash*. If one sanctifies flour and oil at home verbally, the item does not become *pasul* by leaving the *Beit Hamikdash*; only after it enters a *kli sharet* does it acquire that susceptibility. *Meila*, however, begins at the moment of verbal consecration.

### Tosafot Alternative

*Tosafot* raises a lengthy discussion, troubled by the fact that across many *sugyot* in *Shas*, the evidence is consistent: placing something *pasul* in a *kli sharet* does not permit it to be offered *lechatchila* on the *mizbeach*. *Tosafot* never fully resolves the *hava amina* that would have allowed this, and ultimately concedes that all the evidence cuts against such a position, requiring one to reinterpret those many *gemarot*.

What *Tosafot* does offer, however, is an alternative explanation to *Rashi* of what the *mishnah* could mean when it says a *kli sharet* is *mekadesh*. Rather than reading it as relating to the laws of redemption or heightened susceptibility, *Tosafot* suggests the *mishnah*'s *chiddush* is as follows: if the item is in a *kli sharet* and is on the *mizbeach*, one does not have to remove it. One might think this is self-evident — it is on the *mizbeach* — but it is not, because the item is not physically touching the *mizbeach* itself. Even granting that the airspace of the *mizbeach* counts as the *mizbeach*, if the item is inside a *kli sharet*, there is a classical Talmudic question: if something is in my vessel but in your domain, in whose domain is it? So if an item is in a *kli sharet* sitting in the airspace of the *mizbeach*, one might have thought it is considered outside the *mizbeach* — in the separate domain of the vessel — and therefore should be removed. The *mishnah*'s *chiddush*, according to *Tosafot*, is that even in such a case the item is treated as fully on the *mizbeach* and need not be taken down.

*Reish Lakish*'s question to *Rabbi Yochanan*, then, was the further question: if the item was not yet placed on the *mizbeach*, can one place it there and thereby create a valid *korban*? And again, all the evidence across *Shas* is that one cannot — placing something *pasul* in a *kli sharet* does not permit it to be offered up.

### Bird Sacrifice Proof

Having clarified the previous discussion, the *gemara* now resumes at the bottom of 87b. The *gemara* asks: having spent so much time discussing the case of bird sacrifices and the question of *piggul* thought, let us use that discussion to actually prove the original question — *de'avir mizbeach kemizbeach dami*, that the airspace of the *mizbeach* counts as the *mizbeach* itself.

The proof proceeds as follows. If one performed *melikah* on a *chatat ha'of* that was *shelo lishma*, the bird is invalid. Yet the *halacha* — according to the position that birds are included in the rule that the *mizbeach* sanctifies — is that one may leave it on the *mizbeach* and may even sprinkle its blood. But consider the mechanics: when one holds the bird at the *mizbeach*, the blood is not on the *mizbeach* itself — it is only in the airspace. If the airspace does not count as the *mizbeach*, the blood should be considered *yerud*, having descended from the altar, and thus unusable. The fact that we permit sprinkling this blood demonstrates that the airspace counts as the *mizbeach*.

### Blood Airspace Problem

The *gemara* extends the same challenge to the case of other *pesulim*. Consider a case where an animal was *shechted* with a *pigul* thought or *shelo lishma*, the blood was collected while invalid, and it was then placed on the *mizbeach*. According to the opinion that the *mizbeach* sanctifies liquids — including blood — one may leave it there and presumably sprinkle it on the sides of the *mizbeach*. But how? The blood is sitting on the *mizbeach*, and the moment one lifts it and swings it at a distance to throw it, it leaves contact with the *mizbeach*. It is at best in the airspace. If the airspace is not equivalent to the *mizbeach*, this should be forbidden.

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this by suggesting *demagley lehu* — perhaps one holds the bird right up against the wall of the *mizbeach* and presses the blood directly against the surface without lifting it. But the *gemara* rejects this: *ha haza'ah hi? mitzuy hi* — is that sprinkling? That is squeezing. By a bird *olah* one squeezes; by a bird *chatat* one stands at a distance. And even setting aside the categorization, springing the act in such an unusual way — *derech haza'ah bekach, derech zerikah bekach* — is itself problematic; performing an act of blood service in a manner that departs from the normal form renders it invalid even if it does not technically fall into a different category. The inescapable conclusion is that once an item is on the *mizbeach*, the airspace plainly counts as the *mizbeach* itself.

### Rav Ashi Distinction

*Rav Ashi* steps in to clarify what the unresolved question about airspace actually was. *Amar Rav Ashi: ee dinakloo berosh mizbeach hachi nami* — if one is standing on the *mizbeach* and holding the bird or the blood in the airspace above, that is unquestionably considered on the *mizbeach*, for one's feet are anchored on the *mizbeach* and whatever one holds is treated as an extension of that position. There is no question about this case.

The residual question — left with *teyku* — concerns a different scenario: *kee kammar detaleenoo bekanya*, where one is not standing on the *mizbeach* at all, but is suspending the item in the airspace over the *mizbeach* or its ramp from outside, without one's feet touching the *mizbeach*. For example, one is standing off the ramp holding entrails in a basket, and those entrails hover over the airspace of the ramp without making contact. Does this count as having reached the *mizbeach*, such that they may now be brought up and burned? None of the cases discussed in the *gemara* addressed this precise configuration, and so it remains an open question.

---

## Kli Sharet Sanctification

### Liquid vs. Dry Vessels

The *gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*, which addresses the parameters of when *klei sharet* sanctify the items placed within them. The *mishnah* states: *klei lach mekadshin et halach* — the vessels used for liquids sanctify liquids placed in them. *Umidos yavesh mekadshin et hayavesh* — and dry measures sanctify dry things placed in them. The vessels for wine, blood, and related liquids sanctify liquids; the vessels used to measure out flour sanctify dry contents. A hybrid case — such as a *minchah* containing both flour and oil — will be addressed in the *gemara*.

The *mishnah* further states: *ein klei halach mekadshin et hayavesh velo hayavesh mekadshin et halach* — they do not sanctify cross-category: wine into a dry measure or flour into a liquid vessel does not produce sanctification.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

*Rashi* notices the terminological asymmetry in the *mishnah*: it calls the liquid category *kelim* — vessels — but calls the dry category *midot* — measures. Why not use the same word for both? *Rashi* explains that in the *Beit Hamikdash*, liquids were handled in both measuring vessels and non-measuring vessels (bowls for catching blood, dishes for holding a *minchah*), whereas for dry goods, the only dedicated vessels were measuring vessels — the *issaron* and the *chatzi issaron*. Therefore, the *mishnah* naturally calls the dry category *midot*, because that is all they were used for.

*Tosafot* disagrees. He argues that *Rashi*'s premise is false, and provides a list of counterexamples: the *biza* discussed in Perek Hakometz Rabbah, the *machta* used for the *ketoret* (which was used to scoop, not measure), the *kaf*, the *machteshet* mentioned in Shevuot, the *bazichin*, the *shulchan* — all of these were dry-purpose vessels in the *Mikdash* that were not measures. *Tosafot* therefore cannot accept *Rashi*'s reasoning.

### Liquid Measure Difficulty

*Rabbeinu Tam*, as cited in *Tosafot*, offers a different explanation of the terminological asymmetry: dry goods can be measured either level (*machuk*) or heaped (*gadush*), in any manner one chooses, which makes the concept of a "measure" apt and meaningful for dry goods. Liquid, by contrast, cannot be heaped — it cannot form a mound — and furthermore, *Tosafot* argues, liquid measurement is inherently less uniform: wine is thicker than water, and oil thicker than wine, meaning that volume measures of liquids do not translate consistently even across liquids, let alone as weight measures. Therefore, one cannot call a liquid vessel a *midah* in the same sense that one calls a dry vessel a *midah*.

This explanation is admittedly difficult. If these are purely volume measures, the issue of density or thickness should be irrelevant to volume. And if the concern is that dry goods can be measured both by volume and approximated by weight (because the same flour will always occupy roughly the same volume and weight), while liquids can only be volume measures — the point about inability to mound remains unclear as a distinguishing principle. The precise reasoning of *Tosafot* here remains elusive.

Returning to the *mishnah* itself: the *mishnah* concludes that if you use the wrong type of vessel for the contents — liquid in a dry measure, dry in a liquid measure — it does not sanctify. *Rashi* notes that for this reason, virtually all vessels except the two explicit dry measures (*issaron* and *chatzi issaron*) are categorized as *klei halach*. When a *minchah* of flour and oil is prepared, once measured it would be transferred to one of the generic bowls; according to *Rashi*, such bowls, even if they are "liquid vessels," sanctify the *minchah*.

### Broken Vessels

The *mishnah* continues: *klei hakodesh shenikvu* — if sacred vessels develop holes. *Im osim bahen me'ein melachtan* — if they can still perform a function similar to the function they performed when whole, *mekadshin* — they still sanctify. The standard is whether the vessel can still be used in substantially the same way it was used before the damage. If the hole is such that a vessel formerly used for blood can no longer hold blood but could still hold a *minchah*, that is not sufficient; it must be able to perform the same function as before. If, however, the hole is positioned so that it does not affect usability — say, a hole near the top that does not compromise capacity — then it remains valid. *V'im lav ein mekadshin* — if not, it loses its status as a *kli sharet*.

*Vichullan ein mekadshin ella bakodesh* — all of these vessels only produce sanctification when used within the sacred precinct, i.e., the *azarah*. This is internally coherent: one of the effects of a *kli sharet* is that the contents become *nifsal b'yotzei* — invalidated by removal from the *azarah*. Consequently, this effect can only be triggered in the *azarah* itself.

One might ask: if a vessel is taken outside the *azarah* and then brought back in, does it resume its sanctifying capacity when something is placed in it upon return? The answer would appear to be yes — it is the act of placing something within the vessel in the *azarah* that produces sanctification.

### Shmuel's 4 Conditions

*Amar Shmuel: klei sharet ein mekadshin ella sheleimim* — first, the vessels must be whole, unbroken. *Ein mekadshin ella mele'im* — second, they must be full. This does not mean literally filled to the brim, but that the full required measure has been placed within. If one was supposed to place an *issaron* worth of flour and placed only half, it has not been sanctified. *Ve'ein mekadshin ela mitokan* — third, only what is inside the vessel is sanctified, not anything mounded above the lip. *Ve'amrei lei*: some versions add that sanctification only operates *bipnim* — inside the *Beit Hamikdash*, i.e., the *azarah*, which is either a fourth independent condition (as *Rashi* reads *bipnim*) or simply a variant phrasing of *mitokan* (as *Tosafot* reads it).

The *gemara* asks *mai beinaihu* — what is the practical difference between saying *mitokan* versus *mibipnim*? The answer: *beirurei middot* — the mound that rises above the lip of the vessel. According to *mitokan*, only what is physically within the walls of the vessel is sanctified; anything mounded above the lip is excluded. According to *mibipnim*, the requirement is merely that the contents be on the inside rather than the outside — even mounded contents above the lip would count as *mibipnim*, while something placed in a hollow on the exterior of the vessel would not. So *mitokan* is a stricter standard than *mibipnim*, excluding the overflowing mound, whereas *mibipnim* would include it.

A *braita* teaches all four conditions together: *sheleimim, mele'im, mitokan, ubipnim* — where *bipnim*, in that formulation, clearly refers to inside the *Beit Hamikdash*, as *Rashi* maintains, making it a separate condition from *mitokan*.

*Amar Rav Ashi amar Rav Yochanan: lo shanu ela she'ein da'ato lehosif* — the rule that partial filling does not sanctify applies only when one is done — one deliberately placed only a half-measure and is finished. But if one is in the process of filling, *aval da'ato lehosif rishon rishon kodesh* — if one intends to continue adding until the full measure is reached, each increment becomes sanctified as it is placed in. This is somewhat counterintuitive — one might have argued that a mid-process state cannot produce sanctification — but the reasoning is that what matters is whether the contents are conceptually part of a complete measure. If the final measure will be complete, each portion is already part of that whole and is sanctified as it enters. *Rabbi Yossi* makes the identical ruling in the *braita*: *eimatai bizman she'ein da'ato lehosif* — the rule of non-sanctification applies when one does not intend to add more; *aval da'ato lehosif rishon rishon kodesh* — if one intends to continue, it is sanctified incrementally.

### Sanctify for Pasul

The *mishnah*'s rule that a liquid vessel does not sanctify dry contents and a dry measure does not sanctify liquid contents prompts *Amar Rav ve'iteima Rav Assi: ein mekadshin likarev aval mekadshin lipasel* — using the wrong category of vessel does not sanctify the contents so as to render them fit to be offered; but it does sanctify them in the negative sense, making them more susceptible to the invaliding consequences of *kli sharet* — they cannot be redeemed, they become *pasul* through *linah*, *yotzei*, and the like. The wrong vessel thus triggers the negative consequences of sanctification without conferring the positive effect of enabling the offering. This principle, as *Rav* notes, connects back to the opening discussion of the *daf*: placing something *pasul* in a *kli sharet* does not elevate it to be offered *lechatchila*.

### Forbidden Grain

A *braita* records: *ein mevi'in min hachosem umenachas behema uvikurim min hameduma* — one may not bring these *menachot* and associated offerings from *meduma* (a mixture of forbidden produce with permitted produce). *Rashi* understands *meduma* here in the context of the principle *mimashkeh Yisrael* — only what is permissible to all Israel may be offered on the altar — and extends this remarkably to say that even *terumah*, which is accessible only to *kohanim*, cannot be offered on the altar. *Tosafot* disagrees, understanding *meduma* to refer specifically to a mixture involving *orlah* or *kilayim* — genuinely forbidden produce. The *braita* confirms: certainly pure *orlah* and *kilay hakerem* cannot be offered.

*Ve'im heivi lo kidesh* — if one went ahead and placed such forbidden flour in a vessel, it was not sanctified. *Amar Rav ve'iteima Rav Assi: lo kidesh lekarev* — it has not been made fit to be offered. *Aval kidesh lefasul* — but the negative consequences of sanctification do apply: it cannot be redeemed. The question of what "becoming *pasul*" means for something already invalid resolves precisely here: the primary relevant consequence is that the vessel's sanctity has now made the item irredeemable. Just as using the wrong type of vessel sanctifies only for invalidity, so too forbidden grain is sanctified only in the negative sense — it acquires the irredeemability of consecrated property without becoming eligible for offering.

---

## Repair & Maintenance

### No Vessel Repair

The *gemara* continues with a *baraita* on the physical maintenance of sacred vessels and implements. *Klei kodesh shenikvu ein matichin osan* — if sacred vessels develop holes, one may not melt them down to fill the hole using their own material. *Ve'ein matichin l'sochan avar* — nor may one use lead (the ancient equivalent of soldering) to fill the gap. *Nifgemu* — if a vessel develops even a chip rather than a hole — *ein metaknin osan* — one does not repair it. The principle is that in the *Beit Hamikdash*, patching and repair have no place; once a vessel is compromised, it is retired. The *Mikdash* is a place of wealth, and nothing substandard remains in service.

### Knife Care

*Sakin shenifgam ein mashchizin es pgimasov* — a knife that develops a nick may not be sharpened. *Rashi* is somewhat troubled by the literalism of this: surely removing a nick through normal sharpening is not so severe an act? *Rashi* therefore clarifies that what is prohibited is sharpening in a manner that is visibly a repair — where the correction is apparent. If the sharpening were so thorough that no evidence of the prior damage remained, it would presumably not be prohibited. The simple reading of the *baraita*, however, forbids the repair.

*Nishmetah ein machzirin otah* — if the blade detaches from the handle, one does not reattach it. Again, the presumption is that once detached, a blade can never be perfectly restored — it will always be slightly loose or imprecise in its fit. And the broader principle is clear: the *Mikdash* maintains only pristine implements.

*Abba Shaul* relates an incident: *sakin metarefet haytah b'Mikdash* — there was once a knife in the *Mikdash* so delicate that in the very act of *shechitah*, the blade itself would nick, and the nick would render the animal a *treifah*. The *kohanim* took a vote and had it removed. If a knife is causing every animal to become a *treifah*, the conclusion is obvious.

### Priestly Garments

A similar standard applies to the priestly garments. *Bigdei kehunah ein osim ma'aseh machat* — the priestly garments may not be sewn; one does not take separate pieces of cut fabric and join them by needle and thread. *Ela ma'aseh oreg* — the entire garment must be woven as a single whole piece, just as the *menorah* was fashioned from a single block of gold. *She'ne'emar ma'aseh oreg* — as the Torah says, "the work of a weaver." The craftsmanship required to produce an entire garment — sleeves and all — as one continuous woven piece is extraordinary.

### Garment Soiling

*Nitga'alu* — if a garment becomes soiled. *Ein mechabsin* — one does not launder it. *Lo b'neter v'lo b'ohel* — neither with *neter* (a form of lye) nor with *ohel* (another type of cleanser). The *gemara* asks: does this mean one may clean it with plain water? Even plain water cleans less effectively than these agents, so why would water be permitted if the goal is to preserve the garment's integrity?

*Amar Abaye hachi ka'amar*: Abaye reframes the *baraita*. If the soiling is minor — the word *hugu* (*Rashi*: related to *gi'ul*, something repellent but mild, the sort of thing a little water could remove) — if plain water alone would suffice, then one is permitted to use *neter* and *ohel* to clean it and return it to service. That is, for a minor stain, proper cleaning and reuse is permitted. *Hugu l'neter v'ohel* — but if the soiling is severe enough that real cleansers are required — *af b'mayim ein mechabsin* — then one may not clean it at all, not even with water. It must be retired.

*V'yesh omrim ein mechabsin otam kol ikar* — and some say that one never launders the priestly garments at all, in any case. *She'ein aniyut b'makom ashirut* — there is no poverty in a place of wealth; one simply produces new garments. This raises the obvious question, noted by students: the *kohanim* were handling blood continuously. Blood spatters were unavoidable. Does one produce entirely new garments constantly? The sources indicate that worn-out garments were eventually repurposed — for instance, as wicks for the *Simchat Beit Hashoevah* — but the precise practice with blood-stained garments remains a genuinely puzzling question given the practical realities of the *avodah*.

---

## Meail Construction

### Meail Design

The *gemara* describes the construction of the *me'il* worn by the *Kohen Gadol*. *Me'il kulo shel techeiles haya* — the *me'il* was entirely of sky-blue (*techeiles*), as the verse states: *vaya'as es me'il ha'efod kelil techeiles* — he made the *me'il* of the *efod* entirely of *techeiles*.

The hem (*shulov*) consisted of alternating pomegranates and bells. The pomegranates were fashioned from three threads spun together: *techeiles*, *argaman* (purple), and *tola'as shani* (crimson). They were made in the form of pomegranates whose tops had not yet opened — complete, closed forms — and *Talmud* compares them further to the conical protrusions on helmets worn by children. The precise visual implication of this comparison is not entirely clear, but the general shape is that of a closed, rounded form.

### Bells Pomegranates

*U'mevi shivim u'shnayim zugim* — one brings 72 bells, with 72 clappers inside them. *Ve'toleh bahen shloshim ve'shishah mitzad zeh ve'shloshim ve'shishah mitzad zeh* — 36 bells are hung on one side and 36 on the other, alternating with pomegranates: 36 pomegranates and 36 bells on each of the two sides of the garment.

*Rabbi Dosa omer mishum Rabbi Yehudah*: the total was 36 bells and 36 pomegranates — 18 on each side. *Amar Rav Inini bar Sasson: kemachlokes kan kach machlokes be'tzara'as* — the same dispute of 72 versus 36 recurs in the context of the visible appearances of *nega'im*: *Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas* says 36, and *Akavya ben Mahalalel* says 72. The reason this parallel is drawn will become clearer momentarily.

---

## Garments Atone

### Sacrifices & Garments

Having quoted *Rav Inini bar Sasson*, the *gemara* continues with an *aggadic* teaching from the same *amora* that provides a fitting conclusion to the *masechet*. *Lama nismacha parashas korbanos le'parashas bigdei kehunah?* — why were the *parashah* of sacrifices and the *parashah* of priestly garments juxtaposed in *Tzav*? In *Shemot*, the construction of all the *Mikdash* furnishings and the garments are naturally grouped together. But in *Tzav*, the first half discusses the bringing of *korbanos*, and the second half discusses the dressing of *Aharon* and the *kohanim* in their *begadim*. The juxtaposition is deliberate. *Lomar lecha: mah korbanos mechaperim af bigdei kehunah mechaperim* — to tell you: just as sacrifices atone, so the priestly garments atone.

### Kesones Bloodshed

*Kesones mechaperes al shefichus damim* — the basic tunic worn by every *kohen* atones for the spilling of blood. The verse cited: *vayishchatu se'ir izim vayitbelu es hakesones badam* — they slaughtered a goat and dipped the *kesones* in blood, the episode of *Yosef*. Because the *kesones* was used to conceal something adjacent to bloodshed — the near-murder of *Yosef* and the slaughter of the animal — it correspondingly atones for bloodshed. The *Maharsha* explains the association structurally: the *kesones* is the garment closest to the body. The body is where blood resides; the *kesones* most intimately represents the human body. Therefore, the *kesones* atones for acts directed against the body — namely, murder.

An important qualification must be stated at the outset, and it will be elaborated further below: this does not mean that a murderer is forgiven because the *Kohen Gadol* wears a *kesones*. As *Tosafot* explains across this passage, these atonements address communal responsibility — the shared culpability of the community for having allowed such sins to occur, for failing to prevent them, to prosecute them, or to create a society in which they would not arise. Atonement for the individual sinner is a separate matter entirely.

### Breeches Miter Belt

*Michnasayim mechaper al giluy arayot* — the breeches (*michnasayim*) atone for sexual immorality. The connection is anatomical: the *michnasayim* covers *besar ervah*, the flesh of nakedness, as the verse states explicitly. Again, the *gemara*'s understanding, as clarified by *Tosafot*, is that this refers to communal responsibility for the prevalence of sexual sin.

*Mitznefet mechaper al gasei haruach* — the miter atones for arrogance. *Amar Rabi Chanina: yavo davar shebegovah veychaper al govah* — something placed at a height comes and atones for the one who exalts himself with haughtiness. The miter sits at the highest point of the body.

*Avnet mechaper al hirhur halev* — the belt atones for evil intentions of the heart. This is striking, since the tradition sometimes holds that improper thoughts alone are not reckoned by God as action. Yet the *gemara* here insists that thoughts of the heart do require atonement — perhaps the point being that while God does not treat evil thoughts as equivalent to acts, they are nonetheless not nothing. Notably, an *olah* is elsewhere said to atone for *hirhur halev* as well. The *avnet* is placed near the heart — not at the waist as one might assume, but higher, close to the chest and elbows, anatomically proximate to the seat of intention.

### High Priest Garments

The *Kohen Gadol* wears four additional garments, each with its own atoning function.

*Choshen mechaper al hadinim* — the *choshen* atones for a perversion of justice. The verse: *ve'asita choshen mishpat* — the *choshen* of justice.

*Efod mechaper al avodat kochavim* — the *efod* atones for idolatry. The verse: *ein efod utrafim* — there is no *efod* and no *trafim*. As the *Maharsha* notes, the *efod* was historically associated also with idolatrous practice — it was a garment worn by priests of other cults — and so the verse's pairing of *efod* and *trafim* links it to idolatry. Read as a consequence clause, the verse implies: because there is no *efod*, you will be punished for your idolatry.

*Me'il mechaper al lashon hara* — the *me'il* atones for evil speech. *Amar Rabi Chanina: yavo davar shebekol veyechaper al kol hara* — something that makes sound atones for the evil sound, the evil voice. The verse: *venishma kolo bevo'o el hakodesh* — his sound shall be heard when he enters the sanctuary; the bells produce sound with every movement. This is also why, *Maharsha* notes, the *gemara* earlier drew the parallel between the dispute about the number of bells and the dispute about the appearances of *tzara'at* — *tzara'at* too is traditionally the punishment for *lashon hara*, making the connection between the bells of the *me'il* and *tzara'at* thematically coherent.

*Tzitz mechaper al azut panim* — the *tzitz*, the golden plate worn on the forehead, atones for brazenness. Brazenness (*azut panim*) is distinct from arrogance (*gaavah*): one may be inwardly proud without acting with *chutzpah*, and one may be brazenly shameless without the internal haughtiness that the *mitznefet* addresses. The verse for the *tzitz*: *vehayah al metzach Aharon* — it shall be on *Aharon*'s forehead. The verse for brazenness: *umetzach ishah zonah hayah lach* — you had the forehead of a brazen woman. The forehead is the anatomical symbol of unrestrained boldness.

### Atone Challenge

The *gemara* raises an objection: is it really true that these garments atone for *shefichus damim* and *lashon hara*? *Ve'amar Rabi Yehoshua ben Levi: shenei devarim lo matzinu lahem kaparah bekorbanot umatzinu lo kaparah mimakom acher* — for two things we find no atonement in sacrifices, and we found atonement elsewhere: *shefichus damim* and *lashon hara*. *Shefichus damim* finds atonement through *egla arufa*; *lashon hara* finds atonement through the *ketoret*. This creates an apparent contradiction with our *baraita*, which assigns atonement for these sins to the *kesones* and the *me'il* respectively.

### Murderer Known/Unknown

*Lo kashia* — there is no contradiction. *Ha deyedia man katlei, ha delo yedia man katlei* — the *egla arufa* applies when the murderer is unknown; that is the classic case for which *egla arufa* was prescribed. When the murderer is known, the *kesones* atones — for the communal responsibility that accrued despite knowledge of the perpetrator's identity.

But here a further question arises: if the murderer is known, the community should simply prosecute him. Why does any atonement remain necessary? *Bemezid velo azhero bei* — he acted deliberately (*mezid*) but was not formally warned (*hatra'ah*) before committing the act. Without proper warning, he cannot be executed by the court even though he is known to be the murderer. The community knows who did it, cannot execute him, yet cannot claim complete innocence — they bear a residual communal responsibility for having created the conditions under which murder occurred and went unpunished. For this shared responsibility, the *kesones* atones.

### Speech Privacy

*Lashon hara lashon hara* — there is also an apparent contradiction regarding evil speech: does the *ketoret* atone for it, or the *me'il*? *Nami lo kashia* — this too is resolved. *Ha betzina, ha befarhesia* — the *ketoret* atones for *lashon hara* spoken in private; the *me'il* atones for *lashon hara* spoken publicly.

The derivation: *yavo davar shebachashai veyechaper al maaseh chashai* — something brought in secret atones for acts done in secret. The *ketoret* is brought in the *heichal*, and while it is being offered, no other *kohanim* are permitted to be present — not only on *Yom Kippur* but as a general rule. The *ketoret* is inherently a private act. *Lashon hara*, characteristically, is also spoken privately; people do not typically spread slander publicly. So the *ketoret*, brought in private, atones for speech that is spread in private. For *lashon hara* broadcast publicly, the *me'il* — which makes sound publicly, heard by all — provides atonement.

*Tosafot* again emphasizes that in all of these cases the atonement is for communal responsibility, not for the individual perpetrator.

### Communal Responsibility

It is striking to close *masechet Zevachim* here. The vast majority of the tractate is relentlessly technical: what makes a *korban* valid or invalid, what constitutes *pasul* and why, the precise mechanics of *shechitah*, *zerikah*, *melikah*, the parameters of *kli sharet*, and so on. The focus throughout is almost entirely on procedural correctness, not on the experiential or moral significance of what the *avodah* accomplishes.

Yet here, at the end, the *gemara* pivots entirely — to a discussion of what the *avodah* actually atones for, and to categories of sin that are not defined by technical halachic categories like *karet* and *chatas*, but by the texture of moral life: arrogance, evil thoughts, sexual misconduct, slander, brazenness, perversion of justice. These are the sins that ordinary people contend with, regardless of their familiarity with the laws of sacrifices.

And the mode of atonement described here is similarly accessible. *Korbanos* are remote from contemporary experience. But clothing — how one dresses, what one's garments represent, how one presents oneself to one's community — is not remote. The *gemara* elsewhere draws implicit comparisons between *tzitzit* and the *begadim* of the *Kohen Gadol*, and between *tefillin* and the *mitznefet*. The wearing of garments is itself an act of representing oneself, of signaling one's relationship to community and to moral aspiration. The placement of each atoning garment on a specific part of the body — the *mitznefet* on the head for arrogance, the *avnet* near the heart for hidden thoughts, the *michnasayim* over the loins for sexual sin — is not merely mnemonic. It suggests that the body itself is the site of moral responsibility, and that the priest who serves on behalf of the community is, in a sense, wearing the community's moral accounting on his person.

The *gemara* does not connect all the dots explicitly, and these observations should not be overstated. But the juxtaposition — ending a *masechet* of extraordinary technical detail with an *aggadic* passage about real, recognizable, human moral failures and the accessible language of clothing and comportment — feels deliberate and significant. *Hadran lach mizbeach mekadesh.*

---

---

# Zevachim 89

## Kol HaTadir

### Mishna Kol HaTadir

The tenth *perek* of Zevachim opens at the top of 89a with a general principle governing the order of sacrifices: *kol hatadir mechavero kodem et chavero* — whichever of the *korbanot* is more frequent precedes the other. The *mishna* then immediately applies this rule: *hatmidim kodmim lamusafim* — the *korban tamid*, the daily sacrifice brought every single day, takes priority over the *musafim*, the additional offerings. This ordering reflects the fundamental structure of the *avodah* in the *Beit HaMikdash*: the morning *tamid* is the first *korban* offered each day, and the afternoon *tamid* is always the last, with virtually every other *korban* sandwiched between them — the sole exception being the *korban Pesach*, which must be brought after the afternoon *tamid*.

### Rashi Examples

Rashi, at the very opening of this *perek*, offers the example of *Shabbat tadira meRosh Chodesh* — *Shabbat* occurs once a week while *Rosh Chodesh* occurs once a month, so *Shabbat* has priority. One might wonder why Rashi chooses *Shabbat* and *Rosh Chodesh* as his illustration, when the *mishna* itself provides what seems a more natural example. The *mishna*'s own case — the *tamid* preceding the *musafim* — is arguably a cleaner illustration of the principle, since the *tamid* is brought literally every single day.

### Tamid Over Musafim

The priority of the *tamid* over the *musafim* reflects the very logic embedded in the term *musaf* itself: the additional offering is, by definition, added on top of the *tamid*. The parallel in *tefillah* is familiar — *mussaf* is recited after *shacharit*, and when *Shabbat* and *Rosh Chodesh* coincide, *Shabbat* is mentioned first in the *mussaf* prayer, precisely because it is the more frequent of the two.

### Musafim Hierarchy

The *mishna* continues: *musfei Shabbat kodmin lemusfei Rosh Chodesh* — the *musaf* of *Shabbat* precedes the *musaf* of *Rosh Chodesh*, since *Shabbat* occurs weekly while *Rosh Chodesh* is monthly. And *musfei Rosh Chodesh kodmin lemusfei Rosh Hashanah* — *Rosh Chodesh* precedes *Rosh Hashanah*, since *Rosh Chodesh* recurs every month and *Rosh Hashanah* comes only once a year.

### Parshat Pinchas Source

The *mishna* cites a scriptural basis for this rule from *Parshat Pinchas*: *milvad olat haboker asher le'olat hatamid ta'asu et eleh* — "besides the morning *olah*, which is the continual *tamid*, you shall do these." The verse describing the *musaf* of *Chag HaMatzot* specifies that the *musaf* is brought in addition to the *tamid*, establishing the *tamid*'s precedence. The principle of *musaf* being supplementary to — and therefore secondary to — the *tamid* is thus embedded in the *Torah*'s own language.

### Menalan Derivation

The *gemara* then asks: *menalan?* — where do we derive the rule? The *mishna* already quoted a *pasuk*, so why must the question be asked again? The *gemara* explains: from the words *milvad olat haboker* alone, one might have thought the rule applies only to the relationship between the *tamid* and the *musafim* — that the daily sacrifice always precedes any additional offering simply because it occurs every day. But that would not yet tell us which *musaf* takes precedence when multiple *musafim* apply on the same day — such as on *Shabbat Rosh Chodesh*, *Shabbat Chol HaMoed*, or *Rosh Hashanah*.
