The *mishna* establishes a rule of taste determination: *im yesh bahen benosein ta'am* — if there is detectable taste in the second thing cooked that derives from what was absorbed in the walls of the pot from the first. When such taste is present, the *mishna* infers that the weightier item was cooked first and its absorbed taste transferred into the lighter item cooked afterward. The *mishna* relies on tasting rather than numerical computation, though in practice later authorities resolved the question through the framework of *bitul b'shishim*, nullification in sixty.

### Status Transfer

When taste transfer is confirmed — *harei hakalim ne'echalin k'chamurim shebahen* — the lighter item must be eaten with the restrictions applicable to the weightier one. *Chullin* that absorbed the taste of a *shelamim* must be eaten within Jerusalem and within the appropriate time frame, as if it were *shelamim*. A *shelamim* that absorbed the taste of a *chatas* may only be eaten by male *kohanim* within the *Beit Hamikdash*, in the manner of a *chatas*. The principle extends across all relevant dimensions: where it may be eaten, by whom, and within what timeframe.

A subtler question concerns *tumah*. If an ordinary piece of meat has absorbed *shelamim* taste, is it treated as *shelamim* with respect to *tumah* as well? That is, does contact with something *tamei* invalidate it as it would invalidate actual *shelamim*? This question is addressed shortly in the *gemara*.

### No Merika & No Touch

The *mishna* then states two apparently counterintuitive rules: *ve'einam te'unim merika u'shtifa* — no *merika u'shtifa* is required for the pot — and *ve'einam poslim bemaga* — the food does not become invalid through contact with something *tamei*. These statements invite scrutiny. Reading the *mishna* at face value, one might think it is saying that even when the lighter item takes on the status of the weightier one, the pot has been effectively kashered by the cooking and no further ritual is required, and that the *tumah* laws of *kodashim* do not extend to this derived status. But the *gemara* complicates this reading through a *chisorei mechasra* — a textual emendation explaining that the *mishna* is missing key words.

The full reading is: *if there is taste* — the lighter item is treated as the weightier, the pot requires *merika u'shtifa*, and touching something *tamei* to it *does* invalidate it. *If there is no taste* — the lighter item is not treated as the weightier, the pot does not require *merika u'shtifa* on account of the weightier item, and there is no *tumah* problem. The *gemara* thus smooths the rough edges of the *mishna* and resolves both apparent surprises: the *tumah* question is straightforwardly answered, and the absence of *merika u'shtifa* applies only when there is no taste.

### Abaye & Rava

The *gemara* then poses a further question. Even granting the full reading, if a *shelamim* is cooked in a *chatas* pot and there is no taste, one understands that the pot has been effectively kashered of the *chatas* taste and no *merika u'shtifa* is required on *chatas* grounds. But the *shelamim* itself was just cooked in the pot — shouldn't *merika u'shtifa* now be required on *shelamim* grounds? Two Amoraim respond differently.

Abaye says: the *mishna*'s statement that no *merika u'shtifa* is required refers specifically to the *chatas* dimension. As a *chatas* pot, no *merika u'shtifa* is needed, because the *chatas* taste was neutralized. The pot has now become simply a *shelamim* pot, and a fresh deadline begins — one will need to address *merika u'shtifa* after the *shelamim* eating window closes.

### Rava & Rabbi Shimon

Rava offers a more elegant answer: *ha manni Rabbi Shimon hi* — the *mishna* follows the position of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the specific ritual of *merika u'shtifa* only applies to a *chatas* and *kodshei kodashim*, not to *kodashim kalim*. Accordingly, once the cooking of the *shelamim* in the *chatas* pot has effectively constituted a *hagala* and removed the *chatas* taste, and since the *mishna* follows Rabbi Shimon, no *merika u'shtifa* is required for *shelamim* at all. The pot may still require the standard *hagala* at the appropriate time, but the distinctive ritual of *merika u'shtifa* does not apply.

### Two Scenarios

The *gemara* points out that Rava's reading explains why the *mishna* presented two distinct scenarios — *kodashim* cooked with *chullin*, and *kodshei kodashim* cooked with *kodashim kalim* — rather than just one. For Rava, the second scenario is necessary to convey the novel ruling that we follow Rabbi Shimon and that *shelamim* does not require *merika u'shtifa*.

For Abaye, however, both scenarios are also necessary — *tzericha*. Had the *mishna* only taught the *kodashim* and *chullin* case, one might have thought that it is specifically *chullin* that eradicates the *kodashim* absorption when there is no taste, because *chullin* is so categorically different — *delav minaiyhu* — that the contrast is stark enough to neutralize what came before. Conversely, had only the *kodshei kodashim* and *kodashim kalim* case been taught, one might have thought it is specifically *kodashim* that can neutralize other *kodashim*, because they share the same weighty category and can therefore absorb and override one another. Each scenario is needed to prevent a mistaken inference in the other direction.

---

## Absorption & Status

### Yikdash Principle

The *mishna* then introduces the broader principle of *yikdash*: *kol asher yiga* — anything that touches the flesh of a *chatas* becomes sanctified. The *gemara* notes that the Torah articulates this principle twice — once regarding the flesh of the *chatas* and once regarding the *mincha* — and from this repeated formulation a general rule is derived: when absorbed taste transfers from one *korban* to another item, the receiving item takes on the status of the source.

### Ta'am Ke'Ikkar

This is the principle of *ta'am ke'ikkar* — taste is equivalent to the thing itself. A drop of *neveilah* falling into a *cholent* renders the entire *cholent treif*. A drop of chicken broth falling into boiling milk creates *basar b'chalav*. In the domain of *kodashim*, the principle may operate even more stringently. In ordinary *kashrus* situations, the question is whether one has consumed the actual forbidden substance or merely its taste-equivalent — a question relevant to whether one has eaten a *kezayit* of *neveilah* or merely a tenth thereof. In *kodashim*, it is possible that the absorbed flavor confers the full identity of the source on the receiving item, not merely a proportional fraction.

### Absorption Required

The *gemara* is careful to limit the scope of *yikdash*: *yachol afilu shelo bala?* — perhaps mere touching, even without absorption, confers sanctified status? The answer is no. The verse specifies *bibsarah* — in its flesh — indicating that the transfer of status occurs only when there has been genuine absorption. The *chatas* must have penetrated into the *basar* of the receiving item. Reading *bibsarah* as referring to the flesh of the receiving item rather than the source, the *gemara* requires physical ingestion of the source material into the body of the recipient.

### Point of Contact

Once absorption is established as the operative mechanism, a further limitation follows: *yachol naga bemiktzas chatichah yiheye kulo pasul?* — if a *korban* touches only part of a piece of meat, does the entire piece become invalid? The verse emphasizes *yiga* — the point of contact — indicating that only the locus of absorption is affected. If one can cut away the area where absorption occurred, the remainder remains permissible: *chotech es makom shebalah* — cut away the place that absorbed, and the rest is fine. When the food is not being heated over a fire, absorption is localized; it does not spread through the entire piece. If it is being cooked over fire, the heat spreads the absorbed material throughout, but in the absence of fire, surgical removal of the affected area is sufficient.

### Flesh Only

The principle of *yikdash* applies only to the flesh of the *korban* — *bibsarah*, not *bigidin*, not *b'atzamot*, not *b'karnayim*, not *b'tlafin* — not sinews, bones, horns, or hooves. These parts carry no special halakhic status and are not capable of transferring taste in any practically relevant way. Only the flesh of the sacrificial animal is the vehicle for status transfer.

### Invalid Korban Transfer

The *gemara* now examines the flip side of *yikdash*: what happens when the source *korban* was itself invalid? The verse says *yikdash*, the receiving item becomes sanctified — *lihyot kamoah*, to take on the same status as the source. If the source was invalid, *im psulah hi tipaseil* — the receiving item also becomes invalid, because it now contains absorbed material from an invalid *korban*. If the source was valid but of a higher sanctity than the receiving item, *hi tocheil k'chamur shebah* — it must be eaten in the manner of the more stringent item.

Importantly, the mechanism here is physical, not the transitive transfer characteristic of *tumah*. In *tumah*, A makes B *tamei* and the *tumah* moves from A to B in diminished degree. Here the situation is different: little pieces of A have physically penetrated into B. If A was *pasul*, then B now contains fragments of *pasul* material within it, and that is why B cannot be eaten. B is not itself *tamei* in the *tumah* sense — it simply has embedded within it matter that may not be consumed.

### Positive Mitzvah Challenge

This framework generates a striking question. Suppose A is a *mincha* that became *tamei* through contact with something impure. It was absorbed into B, a valid *mincha*. Now 98% of B is entirely valid *kodesh* with a positive commandment to eat it. Why not invoke the principle of *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh* — a positive commandment overrides a negative prohibition? The positive *mitzvah* to eat the valid *mincha* is directly in tension with the prohibition against eating the *tamei* A-material embedded in B. Since there is no way to eat B without consuming the fragments of A within it, the conflict is irresolvable and direct. Should the *aseh* override the *lo ta'aseh*?

### Ein Aseh Docheh

Rava answers: *ein aseh docheh lo ta'aseh shebamikdash* — the principle that a positive commandment overrides a negative prohibition does not apply in the *Beit Hamikdash*. The proof is from the prohibition against breaking a bone of the *korban pesach*: *ve'etzem lo tishberu vo*. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rules that this prohibition applies whether or not the bone contains marrow. One might ask: if the bone has marrow in it and one needs to access it in order to eat the *korban*, why not say the positive commandment to eat the *korban pesach* overrides the prohibition of breaking the bone? From the fact that Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rules categorically that breaking the bone is forbidden in all circumstances, the *gemara* infers that *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh* does not operate in the *Beit Hamikdash*.

*Tosafot* notes that the *pesach* case is also somewhat different structurally — the *lo ta'aseh* of breaking the bone is violated before the *aseh* of eating is fulfilled, and furthermore there exist workarounds (e.g., placing the bone near a fire to let it open without breaking). Here, by contrast, the conflict is truly simultaneous and unavoidable. Nevertheless, Rava's answer holds: even under these optimal conditions for the *aseh* to override, it does not do so in the context of *mikdash* law.

### Yikdash as Aseh

Rav Ashi offers an alternative answer that is conceptually distinct. *Yikdash aseh hu* — the Torah's instruction that the receiving item takes on the status of the source is itself a positive commandment. Therefore, eating B as if it were ordinary *mincha* does not merely conflict with the prohibition against eating *tamei* matter; it also conflicts with the positive commandment to treat B as if it were A. *Ve'ein aseh docheh lo ta'aseh ve'aseh* — a positive commandment cannot override a negative prohibition *and* another positive commandment simultaneously. Even were one to accept that *aseh docheh lo ta'aseh* applies in the *Beit Hamikdash*, it would not help here because the positive commandment of *yikdash* stands in the way as well.

---

## Vezos HaTorah

### Umbrella Principle

The *gemara* now confronts a structural question: the Torah explicitly states *yikdash* only in the context of the *chatas* and the *mincha*. How do we know that the principle of status transfer through absorption applies to all other *korbanot* as well? Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Elazar finds the answer in the verse at the end of *Parshat Tzav*: *vezos hatorah la'olah v'la'mincha v'la'chatas v'la'asham v'la'milu'im u'lezevach ha'shelamim* — this is the law of the *olah*, the *mincha*, the *chatas*, the *asham*, the *miluim*, and the *zevach ha'shelamim*. This verse gathers all the *korbanot* under a single legislative umbrella, and the *gemara* proceeds to derive from it that legal principles established in connection with any one of these offerings can be extended to all the others.

### Olah & Kli

From the *olah*: *mah olah te'unah keli af kol te'unah keli* — just as the *olah* requires a *kli* (vessel) for *shechita*, so too all other *korbanot* require a *kli*. The *gemara* quickly establishes that this cannot refer to the bowl in which blood is caught — that is already known from the *shalmei tzibur* brought at Mount Sinai, where the verse states *vayasem ba'aganot*. The reference must therefore be to the *shechita* knife itself.

### Kli Sharet Debate

A significant dispute between Rashi and *Tosafot* concerns what kind of *kli* the knife must be. Rashi holds that we are deriving that the *shechita* knife must be a *kli sharet*, a sanctified Temple vessel. *Tosafot* disagrees: the requirement is that the knife be a fashioned implement — *kli* in the sense of something man-made — as opposed to using a naturally occurring sharp edge, such as a reed. On *Tosafot's* reading, the knife must be crafted, but it need not be a consecrated *kli sharet*. This is a striking debate given that *shechita* does not require a *kohen* and the *shochet* does not even need to stand within the *Beit Hamikdash* — only the animal must be inside. Whether the knife must therefore be consecrated as a *kli sharet* or merely be a fashioned implement is the point of contention.

### Akedat Yitzchak

The source within the *olah* context for the *kli* requirement is derived from the *Akeidat Yitzchak*. The verse states *vayikach es ha'machelet* — and he took the knife. The word *machelet* appears only here in the Torah to describe a knife used for *shechita*, and the emphasis placed on the taking of the knife — rather than simply on the act of slaughtering — teaches that a specific implement is required. *V'hasam ola hu* — and there it was an *olah*, as the verse states *vaya'alehu l'ola tachas bno*, referring to the ram offered in Yitzchak's place.

There is something deeply charged about this derivation. The *gemara* is locating the paradigm for the *shechita* knife used in the *Beit Hamikdash* in the scene of the *Akeidah*. The word *machelet* itself — related to *achila*, eating — evokes something of the horror of that moment. At the same time, the *gemara* subtly shifts its proof-text: rather than deriving from the command given to Avraham regarding Yitzchak (*v'ha'alehu sham l'ola*), it derives from the ram that was ultimately offered in his place (*vaya'alehu l'ola tachas bno*). This may reflect a purposeful choice: the model for sacrificial *shechita* is grounded in the animal that was brought as the substitute, not in the near-sacrifice of Yitzchak himself. The association nonetheless brings to the surface the deeper theological resonance of animal sacrifice as a replacement for something more primal — the idea that the *mizbe'ach* was consecrated by the *Akeidah*, and that every subsequent *shechita* in the *Beit Hamikdash* carries within it the shadow of that founding moment.

### Mincha & Male Kohanim

From the *mincha*: *mah mincha eina ne'echeles ela l'zichrei kehuna af kol einan ne'echalin ela l'zichrei kehuna* — just as a *mincha* may only be eaten by male *kohanim*, so too all other *korbanot* listed may only be eaten by male *kohanim*.

The *gemara* questions the novelty of this derivation. For a *chatas* and an *asham*, the rule that only male *kohanim* may eat it is stated explicitly: *kol zachar bakohanim yochlenah*. For *shalmei tzibur*, the rule derives from the verse in *Parshat Korach* (*b'kodesh hakodashim tochalnenu kol zachar yochal oso*), which the *gemara* reads as teaching that *shalmei tzibur* are eaten only by male *kohanim*. If each offering has its own source, what new information does the *mincha* verse contribute?

The *gemara* answers: *tanna'ei hi* — it is a dispute among *tanna'im* as to which verse serves as the source. Some derive the rule regarding *shalmei tzibur* from *Parshat Korach*; others derive it here from *Parshat Tzav* via the *mincha*. The substantive *halacha* is undisputed; only the exegetical source differs.

### Chatas & Absorption

From the *chatas*: *mah chatas miskadeshes b'valu'a af kol miskadeshes b'valu'a* — just as a *chatas* confers its status upon something that absorbs it, so too any *korban* that is absorbed into another item causes that item to take on the status of the *korban*. This is the very principle that has been under discussion throughout the *sugya*, and the verse *vezos hatorah* is the mechanism by which it is extended beyond the *chatas* and *mincha*, where the Torah states it explicitly, to all the *korbanot* listed in that verse.

### Asham & Fetuses

From the *asham*: *mah asham ein shapir v'shilya kadosh bo af kol ein shapir v'shilya kadosh bo* — just as an *asham* does not cause a fetus or placenta to become sanctified, so too with all other *korbanot*. The *asham* is male, so it obviously never has a fetus. But the *gemara* uses its absence as a halakhic model: since no fetus ever acquired sanctified status by virtue of an *asham*, we derive that fetuses of other *korbanot* — female animals that may be pregnant — do not become sanctified as a result of the mother's consecration.

This derivation relies on a hermeneutic principle: *efshar mi'she'ee efshar* — one may derive a rule about a possible case from an impossible one. Even though the situation of a fetus in an *asham* is impossible by definition, the Torah's implicit treatment of the *asham* as having no sanctified fetus allows us to project that principle onto cases where the scenario is actually possible. The underlying substantive position is *vladot kodashim b'havayasan hen kedoshim* — fetuses of *kodashim* are sanctified only at birth, not in the womb. Accordingly, whatever the mother's status, the fetus does not independently acquire the ritual status of the *korban* while still in utero.

### Miluim & Notar

From the *miluim*: *mah miluim mostroseihem bisreifah ve'ein baalei chayim bemostroseihem* — the meat left over from the *miluim* offerings is burned, and yet living animals are not treated as *notar* when associated with those offerings. The *gemara* is addressing a conceptual question: if one consecrated an additional animal as a supplement or backup to a *korban* — or consecrated a replacement after the original was lost, and the replacement was ultimately offered while the original was subsequently found — one might think the surviving animal should be treated as *notar*, analogous to leftover meat, and therefore burned.

The derivation from *miluim* teaches otherwise. In the *miluim* context, the Torah speaks of leftover meat being burned but never addresses the case of a living backup animal — because the scenario did not arise. The implicit message is that *notar* as a category does not apply to living animals. This is again an application of *efshar mi'she'ee efshar*: a case that never arose in the *miluim* context implicitly teaches a general principle, and *af kol mostroseihem bisreifah ve'ein baalei chayim bemostroseihem* — leftover meat is burned throughout, but living animal supplements do not become *notar*.

### Shelamim & Piggul

From the *zevach ha'shelamim*: *mah shelamim mapgilin u'mitpagrin af kol mapgilin u'mitpagrin* — just as *shelamim* is subject to the laws of *piggul* and can cause *piggul*, so too all other *korbanot* are governed by the laws of *piggul*. The Torah's explicit treatment of *piggul* is in the context of *shelamim*, where an improper intent during the sacrificial service — intending to eat the meat beyond its designated time — renders the offering *piggul*, carrying the severe penalty of *karet*. Through the umbrella verse of *vezos hatorah*, this principle is extended: the concept of *piggul* — both as a disqualifying intent that one may have during the service and as the resulting invalid status of the offering — applies across all the *korbanot* enumerated.

With this final derivation, the *gemara* completes its survey of the *vezos hatorah* principle. The verse at the conclusion of *Parshat Tzav* does not merely serve as a poetic coda summarizing the *korbanot*. It is a substantive legal instrument, extending specific *halachot* known from individual *korbanot* — the *kli* requirement from *olah*, the restriction to male *kohanim* from *mincha*, absorption and status transfer from *chatas*, non-sanctification of fetuses from *asham*, inapplicability of *notar* to living animals from *miluim*, and *piggul* from *shelamim* — to the full range of sacrificial offerings.

---

---

# Zevachim 98

## Absorption Source

### Absorption Principle

The daf opens by returning to a central *halacha* established in the preceding *perek*: when a *chatat* comes into contact with another substance and its taste is absorbed, that substance takes on the status of the *chatat*. This principle, originally stated by the Torah only in connection with a *chatat* and a *mincha*, is extended more broadly to all *korbanot* by means of the verse *zos hatorah la'olah ula'mincha v'lachatat v'la'asham v'lamiuim ule'zevach hashelamim* — "This is the Torah of the *olah*, the *mincha*, the *chatat*, the *asham*, the inaugural offerings, and the peace-offering." By invoking this principle of *zos hatorah*, the Gemara establishes that each *korban* in this verse teaches something that applies across the entire range of sacrificial offerings. From the *chatat*, the absorption rule had been derived. The previous discussion had also noted other remarkable *halachot* drawn from this verse, including details concerning the *olah* — the use of a *kli*, the connection to *Akeidat Yitzchak*, and whether the paradigm was Yitzchak or the ram.

### Rabbi Akiva Braita

The Gemara now introduces a *braita* taught *b'masnisa* in the name of Rabbi Akiva, which takes a different approach. Rather than deriving the rule of *beli'ah* — absorption — from the *chatat*, Rabbi Akiva's *braita* derives it from the *mincha*. The reasoning follows the structure of the verse: *ma mincha miskadeshes b'valu'a* — just as a *mincha* imparts its sanctity to something that absorbs it, so too does this principle apply to all *korbanot*. This leaves the *chatat* reference free to teach other *halachot*, and shifts the *mincha*'s role from teaching that it is eaten by male *kohanim* — a point the *braita* proposes to derive instead from the portion of *Korach* — to teaching the absorption rule.

### Both Sources Needed

The Gemara then asserts that in fact both are needed: *v'itztarech l'michtav mincha v'itztarech l'michtav chatat* — the Torah had to state the rule both by *mincha* and by *chatat*. Rather than choosing one at the expense of the other, the Gemara embraces both *braitot* simultaneously and asks why we cannot make do with just one source.

### Mincha Softness

The answer is that each source teaches something the other cannot. Had the Torah stated the absorption rule only by *mincha*, one might argue: *aydi d'rechicha mivla* — because the *mincha* is soft, it absorbs readily, and perhaps the rule applies only to soft substances. The softness of the *mincha* — whether referring to the *mincha* as the absorbing substance, or to whatever is placed in proximity to it — creates an especially strong fusion between the two materials. Perhaps such a deep, thorough absorption is required before the law is triggered; the lesser penetration characteristic of a *chatat* might not suffice. Hence *aval chatat eima lo* — one might have thought the rule does not apply to a *chatat*.

Conversely, had the Torah stated the rule only by *chatat*, one might reason *mishum d'karya* — because the *chatat* penetrates or adheres deeply — and conclude the rule applies only when absorption is that thoroughgoing. A *mincha*, by contrast, while soft and receptive, might not produce the same quality of fusion in every context. Hence *aval mincha eima lo*. The conclusion is *tzricha*: both are required. The principle of absorption applies regardless of whether the transference is easier or deeper in a particular case; as long as genuine absorption occurs, the *halacha* is triggered.

## Chatat Teachings

### Non-Sanctified Funds

Having established that the *mincha* teaches the absorption rule, the Gemara returns to the *braita* of Rabbi Akiva to ask what the *chatat* teaches in its place. The answer: *ma chatat eina ba'a ela min ha'chulin uvyom uvyado hayemanit* — just as a *chatat* may only be brought from non-sanctified funds, only during the day, and only using the right hand, so too these requirements apply to all *korbanot*.

The requirement of *chulin* funds means one may not satisfy a *korban* obligation using money or animals that already bear some sanctified status. The most vivid example is *ma'aser sheni* funds. The verse *vehikriv Aharon et par hachatas asher lo* — "and Aharon shall bring the bull of the *chatat* that is his" — is parsed by Rav Chisda as *me'asher lo*, from what is truly his own: *mishelo v'lo mishel tzibbur*, not from communal funds, *v'lo mishal ma'aser*, and not from *ma'aser sheni* money.

This *halacha* has a resonance beyond its immediate sacrificial context. The question of whether one may use *ma'aser* money — one's tithe set aside for charity or religious purposes — to fulfill other *mitzvah* obligations is a live discussion among the *Poskim*, and it turns in part on the precise model of *ma'aser* being applied: whether it is modeled on *ma'aser sheni* with its restrictions on designated use, or on *ma'aser ani*, or whether the function of monetary *ma'aser* is more akin to *tzedakah* in general. The Gemara's ruling here, that a *chatat* must come from funds entirely free of prior sanctification, feeds into those discussions.

### Day & Right Hand

The *braita* continues: *uvyom* — in the daytime — and *uvyado hayemanit* — with the right hand. These two requirements, once derived from *chatat*, are then applied universally: *af kol eino ba ela min ha'chulin uvyom uvyado hayemanit*.

### Alternative Sources

The Gemara, however, challenges whether both of these additional *halachot* truly require the *chatat* as their source. The requirement of daytime: *mibayom tzavoto nafka* — it already emerges from the general verse that God commanded Moshe to bring the *korbanot* *bayom tzavoto*, "on the day He commanded." Thus, citing daytime as something we learn from *chatat* is, the Gemara says, *kideina nasba* — an unnecessary addition, since the principle is derivable elsewhere.

Similarly, the right-hand requirement: *miderabba bar bar Chana nafka*, it already emerges from the teaching of Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Reish Lakish — *kol makom shene'emar etzba u'chehuna eina ela yamin* — wherever the Torah uses both the word *etzba* (finger) and *kehuna* (priesthood), it means specifically the right hand. The Gemara reads the connecting *vav* as "or" rather than "and," so that either *etzba* alone or *kehuna* alone suffices to imply right hand. Since *kehuna* appears throughout the laws of *korbanot*, the right-hand requirement needs no derivation from *chatat*. Again, the Gemara concludes *kideina nasba*.

The Gemara then offers an alternative: *v'ei ba'it eima*, or one may say that the *braita* here follows the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *etzba lo ba'ei kehuna* — the appearance of the word *etzba* does not by itself imply right hand unless it is accompanied by the word *kehuna*. If *kehuna* alone is also insufficient, then *chatat* — where both terms appear — becomes the necessary source for the right-hand requirement across all *korbanot*. In that case, the derivation from *chatat* is genuinely needed.

The upshot: according to the *braita* of Rabbi Akiva, the absorption rule is derived from *mincha*, and from *chatat* we learn the prohibition of using *ma'aser* funds — while the daytime and right-hand requirements may or may not require the *chatat* as their source, depending on one's position in the parallel dispute.

## Asham Bones

### Permitted Bones

The *braita* now turns to what is derived from the *asham*. In contrast to the derivation discussed previously — where the *asham* as a male *korban* lacking a fetus taught a broader rule about the offspring of sacrificial animals — this *braita* derives a different principle: *ma asham atzmotav mutarin* — just as the bones of an *asham* are permitted for ordinary use after the offering has been consumed, *af kol atzmotav mutarin*, so too for all *korbanot*.

Why is this not simply derived by logic? Rashi explains that it is indeed logical in most cases: *notar* applies only to meat, not to bones, and once the *kohen* has received his portion and consumed the meat, the bones are naturally free of any remaining sanctity that would restrict their use. One could reason this way for any *korban* where the meat is distributed to *kohanim*.

### Olah Bones

The one case where the logical argument breaks down is the *olah*. Since the *olah* is entirely consumed on the *mizbeach* — save for the hide, which goes to the *kohanim* — the bones of an *olah* are burned along with the rest. One might think that the bones of an *olah*, since they are part of an offering that is entirely dedicated to the *mizbeach*, remain permanently sanctified and may never be appropriated for personal use. It is therefore specifically for the *olah* that the derivation from *asham* is needed: even the bones of an *olah*, once separated from the animal, are permitted — a striking *halacha*. The *kohen* who handles an *olah* may take the separated bones and use them as he wishes.

Rashi raises a further question: if the derivation is ultimately logical, why derive it specifically from *asham* rather than from any other *korban* whose meat is eaten? One answer is that by the *asham* there is an additional verse — *lo yihyeh* — which might have been read as restricting the bones. By making the explicit statement that the bones of the *asham* are permitted despite this verse, the Torah gives us a firm anchor from which to generalize. This applies equally to bird sacrifices, where there is no reason to distinguish.

## Blood & Garments

### Blood Layering

Rava opens with what he calls *peshita li* — a conclusion he regards as self-evident — before posing a genuine difficulty. The *halacha* of laundering applies specifically to the blood of a *chatat*, not to the blood of other *korbanot*. Rava's scenario: a *kohen*'s garment is struck first by a splash of *olah* blood and then, at the exact same spot, by a splash of *chatat* blood. The assumption built into the scenario is that the *chatat* blood arrives on top of a spot already coated and crusted with dried *olah* blood, and therefore rests on the surface without being absorbed into the fabric itself.

*Dam chatat lemata vedam olah lemala taun kivisa* — if the *chatat* blood came first and the *olah* blood second, Rava says, the obligation to launder is obvious. The *chatat* blood was directly absorbed into the garment, and the subsequent *olah* blood is irrelevant.

### Absorption Requirement

The genuinely difficult case is the reverse: *dam olah lemata vedam chatat lemala* — first the *olah*, then the *chatat*. *Mahu*? Does the obligation to launder apply? Rava frames the question around two possible rationales for the laundering requirement: *mishum nogea hu*, because the blood is in contact with the garment — in which case even contact without absorption suffices — or *mishum baluah hu*, because the blood has been absorbed into the garment — in which case surface contact alone does not obligate.

Rava then concludes: *de-ein taun kivisa* — laundering is not required. His reasoning, though stated without explicit textual citation, is rooted in the nature of the ritual itself. If the requirement were merely about contact, one would expect a different response — perhaps wiping the garment rather than laundering it. The fact that the Torah prescribes *kivus*, laundering, implies that the concern is absorption into the fibers of the garment. This parallels the earlier discussion about a *cheres* vessel used for cooking *chatat*: the reason a clay pot must be broken rather than merely rinsed is that the absorbed taste cannot be extracted, demonstrating that the underlying concern is absorption into the walls of the vessel. By the same logic, laundering is the appropriate remedy precisely because it addresses material that has been absorbed into fabric. Mere surface contact, which can be wiped away, does not trigger the laundering obligation.

### Mixed Stains

Rava then raises a related question that at first glance appears to be an aside but in fact raises a structurally parallel problem. *Peshita li dam al bigdo chotzetz* — it is obvious to Rava that blood on a garment constitutes a *chatzitzah* when that garment is immersed in a *mikveh*. If the garment has become *tamei* and requires immersion, the dried blood interposes between the fabric and the water. However, if the owner is a butcher for whom bloodstains on clothing are entirely routine and unremarkable — *eino makpid* — the blood is not a *chatzitzah*, since what one does not mind does not interpose.

Similarly: *revav al bigdo chotzetz* — a grease stain on a garment is a *chatzitzah*. But if the owner is someone who regularly deals in greasy merchandise — a *mocher revav*, which one might render as a short-order cook or someone who handles fatty goods as part of his livelihood — then *eino chotzetz*, it does not interpose.

### Two Occupations

Rava's question: *dam verevav al bigdo mahu*? What is the *halacha* when the garment bears both a blood stain and a grease stain? The Gemara is initially puzzled: if he is a butcher, the grease is the problem; if he is a *mocher revav*, the blood is the problem. Either way there is a *chatzitzah* — so what exactly is being asked?

The Gemara resolves this: *lo tzricha de-avad ha ve-ha* — the question applies to a person who does both jobs. He is both a butcher and a short-order cook, and he has both types of stains on his garment. The question is whether each type of stain is neutralized individually — blood is fine for a butcher, grease is fine for a *mocher revav* — or whether the combination of both stains on a single garment signals a level of negligence that renders the owner *makpid* even if he would not care about either stain in isolation. *A'chada lo kapid, a'tarti kapid* — one type of stain, no problem; but two different types of stains together might make even this double-professional look slovenly. Or, alternatively, *a'tarti nami lo kapid* — people understand he holds two jobs, and he cares no more about the combination than about each one separately. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved: *teiku*.

It is worth noting that one might reframe Rava's question in a way that makes it parallel to his earlier question about blood layering. Suppose there is a blood stain on the garment — unremarkable to a butcher, hence not a *chatzitzah* — and now a grease stain rests on top of that blood stain without being absorbed into the fabric itself. The grease is not sitting on the garment; it is sitting on the blood. Does the grease constitute a *chatzitzah* on something that is not itself a *chatzitzah*? This parallels the question of a cast on a woman's arm going to the *mikveh*: since the cast is not a *chatzitzah*, we treat it as an extension of her body — but then, is dirt encrusted on top of the cast a problem? That very question is debated among the *Poskim*. While the Gemara itself does not frame the question this way, the structural similarity is striking.

## Tvul Yom Intro

### Daytime Impurity

With *Hadran alach Dam Chatat*, the daf transitions to the twelfth *perek*, whose header — *Tvul Yom* — somewhat obscures its primary subject. The *perek* is fundamentally about the division of *korbanot* among *kohanim*, and the distinction it draws is crucial: there is a difference between being permitted to eat from a *korban* and being entitled to an equal portion when the *korbanot* are distributed at the end of the day. A *kohen* who was *tamei* during the day may become *tahor* by nightfall and be perfectly permitted to eat; yet the *mishnah* will rule that he is not entitled to a portion.

The backdrop is a broader question about how the *korbanot* were allocated. Many verses in the Torah appear to indicate that the *kohen* who performed the *avodah* with a given animal was the one who received it: *hakohen hamchatei otah yochlenah* — the *kohen* who atoned with it shall eat from it. This would be analogous to a waiter keeping the tips from his own table. The *Chachamim*, however, understood the allocation in communal terms: all members of the *mishmar* — the priestly division serving that week — pooled their *korbanot* and divided them equally, much as some restaurants pool tips. The *perek* is dedicated to establishing precisely who is included in that communal pool and who is excluded.

The *mishnah* lists *tvul yom* and *mchusar kippurim* as examples of *kohanim* who, despite being *tahor* by nightfall, do not receive a portion. A *tvul yom* is one who became *tamei* during the day, immersed in a *mikveh*, but whose purification is not complete until nightfall. A *mchusar kippurim* — one who lacked atonement — is typically a *zav*, *metzora*, or similar individual who completed a seven-day waiting period and was required to bring a *korban* before becoming fully *tahor*. There is a significant discussion among *Tosafot* as to whether, even after bringing that final *korban*, a *mchusar kippurim* remains *tamei* until nightfall; the *mishnah* clearly implies that he does.

The logic of the *mishnah* is straightforward: since these individuals were not fit for *avodah* during the day, they do not receive a portion, even though by nightfall they will be fully *tahor* and permitted to eat whatever a fellow *kohen* may choose to share with them.

### Onen Status

An *onen* — a *kohen* who has lost a close relative but whose deceased has not yet been buried — presents a distinct case. An *onen* is not *tamei*; he may touch *korbanot* without disqualifying them. Nevertheless, he may not bring *korbanot* in his state of *aninut*. The *mishnah*'s formulation — *nogei'a v'eino makriv* — captures this precisely: he may touch but may not offer. Because he was not fit to perform the *avodah* on that day, he too does not receive a portion that evening.

### Blemished Kohanim

*Ba'alei mumim* — *kohanim* with bodily blemishes — occupy an exceptional position. Whether the blemish is transient (*ba'alei mumim ovrim*), such as a broken limb that will heal, or permanent (*ba'alei mumim kvu'im*), such as a congenital deformity, these *kohanim* cannot perform the *avodah*. And yet, the *mishnah* rules *cholkin v'ochlin* — they receive a full portion and eat. This is the exception to the general rule, and the *mishnah* notes it explicitly before stating the rule itself.

### Unfitness Rule

The rule is then stated directly: *kol she'eino ra'uy la'avodah eino cholek babasar* — anyone who is not fit for *avodah* does not receive a portion of the meat. And lest one think to claim at least a share of the hides: *v'kol she'ein lo babasar ein lo ba'orot* — entitlement to meat and entitlement to hides are coextensive. A *kohen* who has no share in the meat has no share in the leather.

### Blood Moment

The *mishnah* then adds a critical clarification: *afilu tamei b'sha'at zrikat damim v'tahor b'sha'at haktar chalavim* — even if the *kohen* was *tamei* at the moment of *zrikat damim* but *tahor* by the time of *haktar chalavim* — the burning of the fats, which in some cases did not occur until nighttime — he does not receive a portion. The determining moment is *sha'at zrikat damim*, the throwing of the blood. Everything hinges on fitness at that moment; later participation in the *avodah* of the *imurim* does not confer entitlement. The *mishnah* derives this from the verse *hamakriv et dam hashelamim* — he who brings the blood of the *shelamim* — *lo tihiyeh shok hayamin l'manah*, shall receive the right thigh as his portion. The word *chalavim* in the verse is bracketed by the *mishnah*, emphasizing that it is the blood, not the fats, that is the operative criterion.

## Fit vs. Performing

### Pasuk Reading

The Gemara opens its analysis with the question *mana hani milei* — what is the source for this rule? Reish Lakish cites the verse *hakohen hamchatei otah yochlenah*: the *kohen* who performs the *chituy* — the atoning service — shall eat from it. A straightforward reading suggests that only the *kohen* who actually performed the *avodah* eats from that *korban*.

### Fitness Principle

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *v'harei mishmar kullah de'einam mechatim v'ochlin* — the entire *mishmar*, the whole priestly division serving that week, eats from the *korbanot*, even those who did not personally perform the *chituy* with a given animal. The *halacha* of communal distribution is well-established. The Gemara therefore shifts its reading: *ra'uy l'chituy ka'amrinan* — we interpret *hamchatei* not as "the one who actually performed the *chituy*," but as "the one who is fit for performing the *chituy*." This is the first exegetical *chiddush*: the *kohen* need not have actually done the *avodah*, he must simply have been fit to do it.

### Minor Eats

The Gemara then presses further. A minor *kohen*, as will be established later in the tractate, is not fit for *avodah* — the verse *ish* indicates that only an adult male may serve — and yet a minor *kohen* is permitted to eat from the sacrificial meat. If *yochlenah* means merely "who is permitted to eat," then a minor would be included and the principle would not work as a limiting rule at all.

### Portion vs. Permitted

This leads to the second exegetical *chiddush*: *ela mai yochlenah yechalkenah* — *yochlenah* does not mean "shall eat" in the sense of permission; it means "shall receive a portion." The verse *hakohen hamchatei otah yochlenah* is to be read: the *kohen* who is fit for performing the *chituy* shall be entitled to a portion of it. The distinction between permission and entitlement is critical: a minor may be permitted to eat sacrificial meat, but he is not entitled to an allocated portion. The verse *kol zachar b'kohanim yochal otah* — "every male among the *kohanim* shall eat from it" — establishes who is permitted to eat. The verse *hakohen hamchatei* establishes who is entitled to a portion. Two distinct questions, two distinct texts.

## Blemish Exception

### Blemish Pasuk

The Gemara now addresses the exception of *ba'alei mumim* head-on. The *mishnah* ruled that despite being unfit for *avodah*, a *ba'al mum* is entitled to a portion. The Gemara explains: *ba'al mum rachmana rabyei* — the Torah explicitly included the *ba'al mum* in the category of those who eat from the *kodashim*. The verse states that a *kohen* with a blemish may not enter behind the curtain and may not approach the *mizbeach*, *umin hakodashim yochel* — but he eats from the holy offerings. Since we now read *yochlenah* as *yechalkenah* — entitled to a portion — this explicit inclusion of the *ba'al mum* establishes not merely his permission to eat but his entitlement to a portion.

### Inclusion Logic

But this raises a further question. The verse *kol zachar b'kohanim yochal otah* — "every male among the *kohanim* shall eat from it" — is a broad generalization. Why does this language include the *ba'al mum* rather than, say, the *tvul yom*? Both are categories of *kohanim* who are male and who are at some point in the day disqualified from full participation. Why not apply *kol zachar* to include the *tvul yom* in the entitlement to a portion?

The Gemara reasons: *mistavra ba'al mum havah lei lirbuyei* — it is more logical to include the *ba'al mum* than the *tvul yom*, *she-ken ochel* — because the *ba'al mum* was actually permitted to eat during the daytime when the *korban* was being brought. He was excluded from the *avodah*, but he was never excluded from the eating. Within the framework of who is connected to the eating of this *korban*, the *ba'al mum* was already participating — or at least eligible to participate — at the very moment the *korban* was brought. The *tvul yom*, by contrast, was *tamei* and could not eat during the day at all. The *ba'al mum* thus stands in a more fundamental relation to the *korban*, even on the day it was offered.

### Tvul Yom Objection

Rava objects: *adderaba tvul yom havah lei lirbuyei de-le-orsa michezi* — if anything, one might prefer to include the *tvul yom*, because by nightfall he will be fully *tahor* and fit to perform *avodah* in the future. His disqualification is entirely temporary and will expire that very evening, whereas the *ba'al mum*'s disqualification from *avodah* is potentially permanent.

### Critical Moment

The Gemara rejects this: *hashta miah lo chazi* — that is all well and good for tonight, but right now, at the critical moment, he is not fit. The operative question is: at *sha'at zrikat damim*, the moment the blood is thrown, who is more fundamentally connected to this *korban* — the *ba'al mum* or the *tvul yom*? The *ba'al mum*, even though permanently unfit for *avodah*, was nonetheless permitted to eat this *korban* at that very moment. The *tvul yom*, even though he will be fit for *avodah* in a matter of hours, was not permitted to eat this *korban* when it was brought. At the critical moment, the *ba'al mum* is more *b'farsha* — more fundamentally within the orbit of this *korban* — and therefore it is the *ba'al mum* who is included in the entitlement to a portion by *kol zachar*, not the *tvul yom*.

---

---

# Zevachim 99

## Fitness to Eat

### Rav Yosef's Drasha

The *mishnah* with which we have been engaged establishes a general rule: a *kohen* who was able to perform the *avodah* during the day is entitled to a portion of the sacrificial meat that night; one who was not able to do so receives no portion. The *ba'al mum* — a *kohen* with a permanent physical blemish — appears as an exception. The *mishnah* derives this from the verse *HaKohen HaMechattei Otah Yochalennah* ("the *kohen* who performs the sin-offering shall eat it"), reading *mechattei* not as the one who personally performed the offering but as the one who is *fit* to perform it, and reading *yochalennah* — "shall eat it" — as denoting entitlement, i.e., receipt of a portion. The *ba'al mum* is then included via an additional verse, *kol zachar bakohanim yochal otah*, on the grounds that, although he can never perform the *avodah*, at the time the *avodah* was being performed he at least possessed the capacity to eat from the meat.

Rav Yosef sharpens this analysis considerably. He asks: given that we have already determined that *yochalennah* means entitlement to a portion rather than merely permission to eat, why did the Torah not simply write *yechalkennah* — "shall receive a portion"? The deliberate use of the language of eating, Rav Yosef argues, is a *drasha*: *shema mina ra'uy l'achilah cholek she'eino ra'uy l'achilah eino cholek* — one who was fit to eat at the time of the *avodah* receives a portion; one who was not fit to eat does not. The operative criterion is not fitness to perform the *avodah* but fitness to eat at the time the *avodah* was performed. This reorients the entire framework. The *ba'al mum* is not an exception to a rule grounded in fitness for *avodah*; rather, he is a straightforward application of a rule grounded in fitness for eating. He can eat at all times, even though he can never perform the *avodah*, and so he receives a portion.

### Reish Lakish's Question

Building on this framework, Reish Lakish poses a pointed question: what is the status of a *ba'al mum* who becomes *tamei* during the day? He always carries his dispensation as a *ba'al mum* — the Torah itself includes him despite his inability to perform the *avodah*. Does this standing permission carry over even when he is also *tamei*? *Keivan d'lo chazi v'rachmana rabyei lo shena ma li tamei ma li ba'al mum* — since he was ineligible and the Torah included him anyway, perhaps it makes no difference whether the additional disqualification is his *mum* or his *tumah*. Or do we say *ra'uy l'achilah cholek she'eino ra'uy l'achilah eino cholek*: the decisive question at every moment is whether he was fit to eat?

The question itself maps directly onto the dispute between Rav Yosef's approach and the older reading. If the *ba'al mum* is truly an *exception* — the Torah acknowledging his ineligibility and granting him a special pass — then one might argue that his special permission remains intact even when he becomes *tamei*. But if Rav Yosef is correct and there is no exception at all, only a reformulation of the rule, then a *ba'al mum* who is *tamei* is simply someone who is not fit to eat, and the rule denies him a portion straightforwardly.

### Kohen Gadol Onen

Rabbah resolves both the question of Reish Lakish and the theoretical debate between the two approaches by citing a well-known *halakhah*: *kohen gadol makriv onen ve'eino ochel ve'eino cholek le'echol la'erev* — the *kohen gadol* who is an *onen* continues to perform the *avodah* (as the verse *u'min hamikdash lo yeitzei* requires him to remain and serve even in the face of bereavement) yet is forbidden to eat, and consequently does not receive a portion that night.

This is a decisive proof, and it is striking precisely because the *kohen gadol onen* is the mirror image of the *ba'al mum*. The *ba'al mum* can eat but cannot perform the *avodah*; the *kohen gadol onen* can perform the *avodah* but cannot eat. The ruling that the *kohen gadol onen* receives no portion at night — despite having performed the *avodah* that very day — demonstrates conclusively that fitness to perform the *avodah* is not what generates entitlement to a portion. Everything turns on fitness to eat. *Shema mina ra'uy le'achilah beinan shema mina* — we derive from this that fitness to eat is what we require, and from this we derive the answer.

Accordingly, there are no exceptions and no need for special passes. The rule applies uniformly: the *ba'al mum* receives a portion because he was fit to eat; the *kohen gadol onen* does not because he was not fit to eat; and a *ba'al mum* who becomes *tamei* does not, because a *tamei* person is not fit to eat.

### Tamei in Korbanos

Rav Oshaya poses a parallel question from a different angle: *tamei bekorbanos tzibur mahu sheyechalku lo* — what is the rule for a *tamei kohen* when it comes to communal sacrifices? A *korban tzibur* brought in a state of *tumah* — when the majority of *kohanim* or the community at large is *tamei* — may be brought in *tumah*, and in such a circumstance a *tamei kohen* is technically fit to participate in the *avodah*. However, even when a *korban tzibur* is brought *betumah*, it is not eaten *betumah*; the override applies only to the act of bringing, not to eating. So we have a case where the *tamei kohen* is eligible to perform the *avodah* but not to eat. Does he receive a portion that night?

The answer is provided by Ravina, who again cites the *kohen gadol onen*: *kohen gadol makriv onen ve'eino ochel ve'eino cholek le'echol la'erev*. The case is structurally identical. Ability to participate in the *avodah* without ability to eat generates no entitlement to a portion. *Shema mina ra'uy le'achilah beinan shema mina.* The principle is confirmed: there are no anomalies, no exceptions — every case is resolved by the single question of whether one was fit to eat at the time of the *avodah*.

---

## Onen Status

### Onen Touching

The *mishnah* now turns to the *onen* — one who has suffered the loss of an immediate relative — and states that an *onen* may touch *korbanos* but may not bring them or eat them, and therefore does not receive a portion. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah*, at least as it stands, is the opening clause: an *onen* is permitted to *touch* sacrificial offerings. He is not considered *tamei*.

But this is immediately challenged. A *mishnah* in *Chagigah* states that an *onen* and a *mechusar kippurim* require *tevilah* before touching *kodesh* — which implies that an *onen* has some degree of *tumah* that disqualifies him from contact with *korbanos*. How can our *mishnah* say he may touch?

Rav Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves the apparent contradiction: *kan shetaval kan shelo taval* — our *mishnah* speaks of an *onen* who has already immersed in a *mikvah*; the *mishnah* in *Chagigah* speaks of one who has not. This would be a sufficient answer — except that the *Gemara* immediately objects: even if the *onen* immerses, what good does it do? *Hadra lei aninus* — his *aninut* returns to him. As Rabbah bar bar Chana teaches, an *onen* who immerses: his *aninut* comes back upon him. *Tovel ve'aninus beyado* — he emerges from the *mikvah* still an *onen*, so the immersion changes nothing. The *mikvah* referred to in *Chagigah* must mean after the *aninut* is over — that night, once the *aninut* has passed, he immerses and is permitted. But during the day, immersion does not help. We are back to the original problem.

The *Gemara* then proposes: *ha de'asiach da'ateih, ha delo asiach da'ateih* — the two sources reflect two different scenarios. The *onen* who may touch is one who has not experienced *hesach hadaat*; the *onen* who may not touch is one who has.

### Hesach Hadaat

The concept of *hesach hadaat* — a lapse of attentiveness — is now developed in some detail. The concern is that an *onen*, preoccupied with the death of a relative and knowing he will not be entering the *Beis HaMikdash* that day, may have relaxed his vigilance against *tumah*. The *Gemara* distinguishes between different degrees of carelessness.

If the *onen* has experienced *hesach hadaat* entirely — he has stopped being careful about contracting *tumah* from a *meis* — then *shelishi ve'shevii bo*: he requires sprinkling on the third and seventh day, as Rav Yostai the son of Rabbi Mattun said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *hesach hadaat tzarich hazayah shelishi ve'shevii*. For such a person, a *mikvah* is wholly insufficient; he is treated as having become *tamei meis*.

But if the *hesach hadaat* was only partial — he was not careful about contact with a *sheretz* or other lower-grade impurity but was still careful about *tumat meis* — then the concern is only that he may have become a *sheni*, not a *rishon*. In that case, the *mikvah* is the appropriate remedy, but it only works after his *aninut* concludes. During the day, as noted, the *aninut* returns upon him even after immersion.

This yields a three-way distinction: the *onen* who was wholly careless (*hesach hadaat mi'meis*) requires three-and-seven sprinkling; the *onen* who was partially careless (*hesach hadaat mi'tumei sheretz*) is the default case — *tamei* for the day, with the *mikvah* not helping until the *aninut* is over; and the *onen* who was fully attentive is the case of our *mishnah* — he may touch *korbanos*.

The *Gemara*, however, challenges this intermediate category. If the concern regarding the partially careless *onen* is that he may have touched a *sheretz* and become a *sheni*, he should be prohibited from touching even *terumah*, not merely *korbanos*. Why does the source in *Chagigah* imply only a prohibition against *kodesh*?

Rabbi Yirmiyah offers a further refinement: *netiruta lepalga* — one can maintain a calibrated, partial level of vigilance. The *onen* can say: *nishmarti midevar hamatmeini velo nishmarti midevar haposleni* — I was careful enough to ensure I did not become a *sheni* (which would disqualify me from touching *terumah*), but I was not careful enough to prevent becoming a *shlishi* (which disqualifies me only from *kodashim*). This is admittedly a peculiar and fine-tuned form of self-monitoring, but the *Gemara* demonstrates its plausibility from a parallel case: a man tending a basket of figs with a shovel declares that he is watching the basket carefully but not the shovel. Rava explains: *be'omer shimartiha midavar metame'ah velo shimartiha midavar haposlah* — he watched the shovel carefully enough to prevent it from becoming a *rishon* (which would make the figs a *sheni*), but not carefully enough to prevent it from becoming a *sheni* (which would only make the figs a *shlishi*, thereby disqualifying *terumah* figs, but not *chullin*). This demonstrates that one can indeed maintain precisely calibrated levels of vigilance.

The analogy is then applied to the *onen*: the default *onen* maintained enough vigilance not to touch anything that would make him a *sheni* — protecting his capacity to touch *terumah* — but not enough to prevent himself from becoming a *shlishi*, which is why he is disqualified only from *kodashim*.

### Onen as Shlishi

Rabbi Abba bar Mamal then offers a far simpler resolution that makes the entire *hesach hadaat* discussion unnecessary. As Rav (cited by Rabbi Yochanan) taught regarding one who eats a *shlishi* of *terumah*: he becomes, through the act of eating, a rabbinic *shlishi* himself — *assur le'echol* but *mutar liga*, prohibited from eating *terumah* but permitted to touch it. The principle is that rabbinic *maalot* concerning *tumah* operate differently for eating than for touching: *b'achilah avdu rabbanan maalah, b'negiah lo avdu rabbanan maalah* — the Sages enacted their stringencies with respect to eating, not with respect to touching.

Applying this to the *onen*: the Sages conferred upon an *onen* a rabbinic *tumah* status akin to a *shlishi* or *revi'i* — enough to prohibit him from eating *kodashim*, but not enough to prohibit him from touching them. There is no need for any discussion of *hesach hadaat* at all. A normal *onen* — not particularly careless, not particularly vigilant — may touch *korbanos* freely, as our *mishnah* says. He simply may not eat them. This is a clean, unified rule: the Sages enacted a stringency regarding the *onen's* eating of *kodashim* by treating him as a rabbinic *shlishi* (or *revi'i*) for the purpose of eating, without extending that stringency to touch. And because immersion during the day does not resolve his *aninut*, this status persists throughout the day regardless of whether he visits the *mikvah*.

---

## Onen's Portion

### Eating at Night

Having established the *onen's* status during the day, the *Gemara* turns to the night. Our *mishnah* implies that while the *onen* receives no portion — since he could neither perform the *avodah* nor eat during the day — if others were to invite him to eat from their portions that night, he would be permitted to do so. Is this actually correct? Is an *onen* permitted to eat *korbanos* the night following the death?

The *Gemara* cites a *mishnah* in *Pesachim*: *onen tovel ve'ochel pischo la'erev, aval lo b'kodashim* — an *onen* immerses and eats his *korban Pesach* that night, but not other *kodashim*. This passage cuts two ways. On one hand, it confirms that the *onen's* prohibition against eating *kodashim* is rabbinic in nature, since we are willing to waive it for *korban Pesach*. On the other hand, it establishes that for all other *kodashim* the prohibition extends into the night — so why does our *mishnah* imply the *onen* may eat at night?

Rabbi Yirmiyah of Difti offers one resolution: our *mishnah* is speaking specifically of the night of *Pesach*, when the *onen* is given blanket permission regarding *korban Pesach* and is permitted to eat other *kodashim* as well, since *pesach ayidi d'achil pesach achil nami kodashim*. For all other nights of the year, the *onen* indeed may not eat *kodashim*. This is admittedly a narrow reading of our *mishnah* — who would have assumed it was addressing the *Seder* night? — and the *Gemara* treats it as such.

### Death & Burial

Rav Ashi provides a substantially cleaner resolution rooted in a distinction between biblical and rabbinic *onen* status.

### Night is Rabbinic

Rav Ashi's resolution turns on the question of when biblical *aninut* applies. The *mishnah* in *Pesachim* that allows the *onen* to eat his *korban Pesach* that night but not other *kodashim* must reflect the position of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that nighttime *aninut* — the extension of the *onen* status into the night — is only rabbinic: *ein onen midivrei Torah ela midivrei sofrim*. He proves this from the *mishnah* in *Pesachim* itself: if *aninut* at night were biblical, the permission to eat the *korban Pesach* would be inexplicable.

Rav Ashi adds a further structural refinement. Biblical *aninut* is created when the death and the burial occur on the same day — *yom mita* and *yom kvura* coincide. In that case, the *yom mita* generates biblical *aninut* during the day, and the rabbis extend a prohibition against eating *kodashim* into the night as well. But when the burial occurs on a day different from the day of death — the day of burial is a day of *aninut* only *miderabbanan* — then *yom kvura lo tafis leilo miderabbanan*: a day of burial that is itself only rabbinic does not generate a rabbinic nighttime extension. That night, the *onen* is free to eat *kodashim*.

The case of our *mishnah*, which implies that the *onen* may eat at night, is precisely this scenario: the death occurred on one day, the burial on the next. Since the burial day carried only rabbinic *aninut*, the following night carries no *aninut* at all — not even rabbinically — and the *onen* is fully permitted to eat *kodashim*. The narrow case in *Pesachim* where the *onen* eats only *korban Pesach* and not other *kodashim* refers to a night following a day of biblical *aninut* — death and burial on the same day — where the rabbis extended the prohibition into the night but waived it for *korban Pesach* alone.

---

## Shalem Requirement

### Shalem Drasha

The *Gemara* then asks: which *tanna* holds that nighttime *aninut* is rabbinic? *Mi-derabbi Shimon hi* — it is the position of Rabbi Shimon. A *baraita* is then cited in which Rabbi Shimon expounds the verse *v'im zevach shelamim korbano* ("and if his offering is a peace-offering"): *keshehu shalem mevi ve'eino mevi keshehu onen* — one brings offerings when he is *shalem*, complete, and does not bring them when he is an *onen*. This is a striking and novel *halakhah*. Rabbi Shimon derives that the *onen* is excluded not merely from performing the *avodah* within the *Beis HaMikdash* but from having any *korban* brought on his behalf at all — even by a *shaliach*, without his entering the sanctuary. The reasoning reflects a broader conception of *aninut*: one who has just suffered a devastating loss is, in a profound sense, not *shalem*, not whole. This is not the appropriate moment for the engagement of bringing a *korban* before the Almighty.

The *drasha* then extends this principle systematically. A *todah* is included — *sheken ne'echelet besimcha keshelamim* — because it is eaten in joy, like a *shelamim*, and joy is particularly incongruous with *aninut*. An *olah* is included — *sheken ba'ah beneder unedavah keshelamim* — because it is an act of generosity and dedication toward God, equally unsuitable for the *onen*. *Bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *Pesach* are included because *einam ba'im al chet* — they are not sin-offerings, and so their bringing reflects a positive relationship between the worshiper and God that presupposes a state of wholeness. A *chatas* and *asham* are included by the general derivation from *zevach*, every animal sacrifice requiring the offerer to be *shalem*. And finally, bird-offerings, *menachos*, wine, wood, and *levonah* are all included by the concluding term *shelamim korbano* — any *korban* whatsoever requires the one who brings it to be *shalem*. The formulation is sweeping: *kol ha-korbanot keshu mevi keshu shalem mevi ve'eino mevi keshu onen*.

### Pesach Exception

Having established that Rabbi Shimon excludes an *onen* from having any *korban* brought on his behalf — including, apparently, a *korban Pesach* — the *Gemara* returns to the *mishnah* in *Pesachim*, which states that an *onen* does eat his *korban Pesach* that night. This presupposes that the *korban Pesach* was in fact brought for him during the day. But if Rabbi Shimon excludes an *onen* from having any *korban* brought, how is the *korban Pesach* brought?

The *Gemara* asks: is the exclusion in the *baraita* perhaps meant to include even *Pesach*? *Lo levar miPesach* — no, Rabbi Shimon means only other offerings; he agrees that a *korban Pesach* may be brought for an *onen*. Rav Chisda confirms: *pesach kedi nasba* — the inclusion of *Pesach* in the *baraita's* list was incidental, a byproduct of working through the standard catalogue of *korbanos* (*bechor*, *ma'aser*, *Pesach*), and does not reflect Rabbi Shimon's actual *halakhah* with respect to *Pesach*.

### Tosafot on Pesach

This creates a conceptual tension: if Rabbi Shimon's principle of *shalem* is a genuine Torah-level requirement, what permits us to set it aside for *korban Pesach*?

Rashi resolves this by suggesting that the entire elaborate *drasha* of *shalem* is only an *asmachta* — a rabbinic ruling supported by scriptural allusion — and therefore flexible enough to be waived for *Pesach*.

Tosafot offer a more substantive and elegant resolution. All other *korbanos* have the bringing — the *zerikat ha-dam* and the sacrificial act — as their essential focus. For *korban Pesach*, however, the entire purpose is the eating. The *korban Pesach* is brought solely to enable the eating that night, which is why, unlike all other *korbanos* brought *betumah*, the *Pesach* itself is eaten even in a state of *tumah* when necessary. Because the *korban Pesach* is fundamentally defined by its eating, the requirement that the offerer be *shalem* at the time of bringing does not apply: the operative moment of *Pesach* is not the bringing during the day but the eating that night, and at night the *onen* is no longer in a state of *aninut*. He will be *shalem* when the *korban* is consumed — which is, for *Pesach*, the moment that matters.

This distinction carries through the entire sugyah. Rav Sheshet adds a final refinement: when the *baraita* says an *onen* may not send his *korban Pesach*, it means he may not bring the *shelamim* that accompany the *Pesach* — the *chagigah* offering — not the *korban Pesach* itself. The *Gemara* objects that this adds nothing to what was already said about *shelamim*, and resolves: the *baraita* teaches both *shelamim* brought independently and *shelamim* brought in the context of the *Pesach*, lest one think that since the *chagigah shelamim* comes as a package with the *Pesach* it is permitted — *ke-gufeih de-pesach dami* — as if it were part of the *Pesach* itself. The *baraita* therefore specifies that it is not. In all opinions, Rabbi Shimon holds that an *onen* may not have a *korban* brought on his behalf — with the sole exception of the *korban Pesach*, precisely because its essence lies not in the bringing but in the eating.

---

---

# Zevachim 100

## Onen at Night Setup

### Introduction

The daf begins at the bottom of 99b, with the words *rav mari amar* — Rav Mari's statement — serving as the springboard for the lengthy discussion that follows on 100a. The subject under examination is whether an *onen* (one who has lost a close relative and not yet buried them) may eat *korbanot* at night. The Gemara had inferred from the Mishnah that an *onen* is prohibited from eating *korbanot* only during the day, implying that on the night following the day of death, eating would be permitted. But the Gemara challenged this inference, noting that such leniency seemed to apply only to the *korban Pesach* and not to *korbanot* generally.

### Yom Misa/Kvura Distincti…

One of the central distinctions that emerged in the preceding discussion is the difference between *yom misa* — the day of death itself — and *yom kvura* — the day of burial, when that falls on a separate day. The Gemara established that whether the night following an *onen*'s day is forbidden depends on which of these two days is at issue. On the day of death, the following night is included in the prohibition; on the day of burial alone, when the death occurred on a prior day, the status may be different. This distinction will drive much of the analysis that follows.

### Shimon's Proof

The discussion also engaged with the position of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *aninus layla* — the mourning status at night — is not *de'oraisa*. His proof is that an *onen* may immerse in a *mikveh* and eat his *korban Pesach* at night, something that would be impossible if night-time *aninus* were biblical in force. This demonstrates, in Rabbi Shimon's view, that whatever prohibition applies at night is only rabbinic.

### Shimon's Contradiction

Yet Rabbi Shimon himself appears elsewhere to say the opposite — that one may not bring a *korban* on behalf of an *onen*, because only *keshe-hu shalem*, when a person is in a state of wholeness, may a *korban* be offered on their behalf. The word *shalem* alludes to *shelamim*, and Rabbi Shimon includes even the *korban Pesach* in this rule. So in one place he seems to say that a *Pesach* can be brought for an *onen* who will then eat it at night, and in another place he says it cannot be brought at all. The Gemara proceeds to work through several attempts to resolve this internal tension.

---

## Rav Mari's Answer

### Death/Burial Same Day

Rav Mari offers the first resolution at the top of 100a: *lo kashya* — the contradiction is not difficult. The key is precisely the distinction between *yom misa* and *yom kvura*. His answer turns on two different scenarios: one in which death and burial both occur on the fourteenth of Nisan, the day the *Pesach* is brought, and one in which only the burial takes place on the fourteenth while the death occurred on the thirteenth.

### Same Day Case

In the first case — *meis lo meiso be-yud daled ve-kivro be-yud daled* — the fourteenth is both the day of death and the day of burial. Because it is *yom misa*, the *aninus* is *de'oraisa*, and the Gemara states *yom misa tofes leilo mi-de'oraisa*: the day of death draws the following night into its prohibition on a biblical level. Since this *onen* will not be able to eat the *korban Pesach* that night, there is no point in bringing it on his behalf during the day. This, says Rav Mari, is where Rabbi Shimon rules that you do not bring the *Pesach* on behalf of the *onen*.

### Different Days Case

In the second case — *meis lo meiso be-yud gimmel ve-kivro be-yud daled* — the death occurred on the thirteenth and burial on the fourteenth, making the fourteenth only *yom kvura* and not *yom misa*. In this case, *aninus* is only *mi-derabbanan*, and *eino tofes leilo ela mi-derabbanan*: the night following is only rabbinically restricted. Since the night-time prohibition is merely rabbinic, we override it to permit eating the *korban Pesach*, and therefore we do permit bringing the *Pesach* on this person's behalf during the fourteenth. This is where Rabbi Shimon says the *Pesach* may be brought and eaten at night.

It should be noted that Rav Mari's answer focuses entirely on whether the *onen* will be able to eat the *korban Pesach* at night as the operative reason for permitting or forbidding its offering. This effectively sets aside the distinct concern raised by Rabbi Shimon in an earlier *baraita* — the idea of *shlemut*, that a *korban* cannot be brought for one who lacks wholeness — which has nothing inherently to do with nighttime eating. Tosafos raises this tension, and it may find its resolution in the answers that follow. For the moment, the discussion proceeds entirely on the question of whether eating at night is possible.

### Rav Ashi's Challenge

Rav Ashi challenges Rav Mari directly. The *baraita* quoted in support of Rabbi Shimon's position reads: *teda she-amru onen tovel ve-ochel es picho aval lo be-kodashim* — "know that they said an *onen* immerses and eats his *Pesach* but not other *kodashim*." This was Rabbi Shimon's proof to Rabbi Yehuda that *aninus layla* is not *de'oraisa*. But now Rav Mari has restricted Rabbi Shimon's proof to a case of *yom kvura* alone.

Rav Ashi presses: why couldn't Rabbi Yehuda simply respond that Rabbi Shimon's proof is irrelevant? The debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon about whether *aninus layla* is *de'oraisa* concerns *yom misa* — the day of death — as we know from the underlying derivation, which relates to the deaths of Nadav and Avihu, where the day of death and day of burial were one. When Rabbi Yehuda argues that the night is biblically forbidden, he is speaking of the night following *yom misa*. And when Rabbi Shimon brings his proof from the *onen* eating the *korban Pesach* at night, Rabbi Yehuda could simply retort: *kamina lach ana yom misa de'oraisa ve-amarta li at yom kvura derabbanan* — "I am speaking of *yom misa* and you are answering me with *yom kvura*!" The cases are not equivalent, and Rabbi Shimon's proof would fail to address Rabbi Yehuda's position. The Gemara concedes: *kashya* — this is indeed a difficulty. Rav Mari's answer does not fully resolve the contradiction.

---

## Abbaye's Answer

### Status Priority Principle

Abbaye offers the next resolution: *lo kashya* — it is not difficult. His answer accepts that we are indeed discussing *yom misa* throughout, directly engaging the scenario that Rav Ashi showed Rav Mari's answer could not handle. Abbaye's principle is this: when two competing statuses come into conflict, whichever took hold first takes precedence. The question of whether the *onen* status or the *korban Pesach* obligation governs this person depends on which one attached to him first.

### Death Before Chatzos

If the relative died before *chatzos* — before midday on the fourteenth of Nisan — then this person became an *onen* before any *Pesach* obligation existed for him. The obligation to bring the *korban Pesach* does not crystallize until midday on the fourteenth. In this case, *kodem chatzos she-lo echazi le-Pesach, chailei alei aninus* — before *chatzos* he was not yet fit for the *Pesach* obligation, and the *aninus* status took hold first. Consequently, the *Pesach* cannot be brought on his behalf; the *aninus* dominates, and Rabbi Shimon's rule applies: *keshe-hu shalem hu meivi*, only when he is in a state of wholeness.

### Death After Chatzos

If the relative died after *chatzos*, the situation reverses. By the time *chatzos* arrived, this person was already fit for and obligated in the *korban Pesach*. Then the relative died, and he became an *onen*. In this case, *lo chayla alei aninus* — the *aninus* does not take hold so as to push off the *Pesach* obligation that had already attached. The *korban Pesach* may still be brought on his behalf, and at night he eats it, since the night-time *aninus* is only *derabbanan* and yields to *achilas Pesach*.

This is Abbaye's elegant principle: it is not the intrinsic strength of *aninus* versus *Pesach* that determines the outcome, but rather the temporal sequence — which came first? Abbaye then proceeds to demonstrate this principle from *baraitot* dealing with *tumah* and the *Pesach* obligation, bringing proof that the same logic governs competing obligations generally.

### Yosef Story

The *baraita* opens with the general rule that a *kohen* has a *mitzvah* — indeed an obligation — to become *tamei* for his immediate relatives at death, even against his will. The *baraita* states *lo ratza, metamin oto al korcho*: if he refuses, his fellow *kohanim* force him. The story of Yosef the *kohen* illustrates this dramatically: his wife died on *erev Pesach*, and he did not wish to become *tamei*, both out of regard for the sanctity of his *kehuna* and because it would prevent him from bringing the *korban Pesach*. Nevertheless, his fellow *kohanim* voted and forcibly made him *tamei*, and he was therefore unable to bring the *Pesach*. This *baraita* implies that the obligation to become *tamei* for one's relative overrides even the obligation of *korban Pesach*.

### Nazir Baraita

Yet a second *baraita*, dealing with a *nazir*, seems to say the opposite. A *nazir* cannot become *tamei* even for immediate relatives. The *baraita* layers on additional statuses — a *kohen* and *nazir*, then a *kohen gadol* and *nazir* — teaching that even the combined weight of these stringent restrictions against *tumah* does not exempt one from the obligation of *meis mitzvah*, a body left without anyone to bury it. All of these layers were added precisely to show that *meis mitzvah* overrides everything, even the most severe prohibitions against *tumah*.

But crucially, the Gemara reads the mention of *korban Pesach* in this *baraita* — where the text describes someone on his way to *shecht* his *Pesach* and give *bris milah* to his son — as implying that the *Pesach* obligation by itself would prevent one from becoming *tamei* for a relative, even absent *nazir* and *kohen gadol* statuses. This is the reading the Gemara adopts, though Tosafos notes it is not straightforwardly the *pshat* of the *baraita*, since giving a *bris milah* to one's son does not generally override the obligation to bury a relative. The Gemara brackets that difficulty and focuses on the implication regarding *Pesach*.

So the contradiction stands: the story of Yosef the *kohen* says the obligation to become *tamei* for a relative overrides the *Pesach* obligation, while this *baraita* implies that the *Pesach* obligation prevents one from becoming *tamei* for a relative. Which is it?

The Gemara suggests perhaps the contradiction reflects the debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yishmael holds that becoming *tamei* for a relative is a *reshus* — a permission, not an obligation — while Rabbi Akiva holds it is a *chova*, a genuine obligation. Perhaps the *baraita* favoring *Pesach* is Rabbi Yishmael, and the story of Yosef is Rabbi Akiva. But the Gemara rejects this: the very *baraita* that seemed to favor *Pesach* — the one about the *nazir* going to *shecht* his *Pesach* — begins explicitly with Rabbi Akiva's view, stating there is an obligation to become *tamei* for a relative. So both *baraitot* represent Rabbi Akiva, and the contradiction remains.
