### Baraita Reconciliation

Abbaye resolves it as follows: *shema mina kan kodem chatzos, kan achar chatzos* — it must be that the two *baraitot* describe different temporal scenarios. The story of Yosef the *kohen*, where the obligation to become *tamei* for his wife overrode the *Pesach*, occurred in the morning of *erev Pesach*, before *chatzos*. At that point the *Pesach* obligation had not yet attached, and so the prior obligation of burial took precedence. The *baraita* about the *nazir* going to *shecht* his *Pesach*, where the *Pesach* overrides *tumah* for a relative, describes a situation after *chatzos*, when the *Pesach* obligation had already crystallized — and therefore the *Pesach* holds its ground.

### Inference to Onen

If this principle governs the relationship between the *Pesach* obligation and *tumah* — whichever comes first prevails — then by the same logic it governs the relationship between the *Pesach* obligation and *aninus* status. If one became an *onen* before *chatzos*, the *aninus* came first, and Rabbi Shimon rules that the *Pesach* is not brought on his behalf. If one became an *onen* after *chatzos*, the *Pesach* obligation came first, and the *aninus* does not push it off — the *Pesach* is brought, and at night, since *aninus layla* is only *derabbanan*, it is overridden and he eats. This is Abbaye's complete answer.

---

## Rava's Answer

### Bring vs. Eat

Rava offers a third and independently elegant resolution. *Idi ve'idi achar chatzos* — in both cases of Rabbi Shimon's seemingly contradictory statements, we are speaking of after *chatzos*. Even after *chatzos*, Rava holds, if one becomes an *onen*, the *aninus* would ordinarily override the *Pesach* obligation. The distinction Rava draws is not temporal but procedural: it is the difference between the stage before *shechita* and *zerika* and the stage after.

### Before Shechita

*Kodem she-shachtu ve-zarku alav* — before the *korban Pesach* has been slaughtered and its blood sprinkled, if one is an *onen*, the *Pesach* is not brought on his behalf. He is not *shalem*, and this is where Rabbi Shimon says one does not bring a *korban* on behalf of an *onen*. The *shechita* and *zerika* should not take place.

### After Shechita

*Le-achar she-shachtu ve-zarku alav* — after the *korban Pesach* has already been slaughtered and its blood sprinkled, the question shifts. Can this *onen* eat the *Pesach* that night? The answer, according to Rabbi Shimon, is yes. Where Rabbi Shimon says an *onen* immerses and eats his *Pesach* at night, he is speaking of a case where the *Pesach* was already brought — perhaps improperly, but the *korban* is *kasher* after the fact — and now the only remaining question is whether he may eat it that night. Since *aninus layla* is only *derabbanan* for Rabbi Shimon, and eating serves the fulfillment of the *mitzvah*, we allow it. This reading is quite beautiful in its precision: Rabbi Shimon's two statements address two entirely different questions, and there is no contradiction at all.

### Rav Adda's Challenge

Rav Adda bar Matna challenges Rava: once the *shechita* and *zerika* have already been performed, *mah de-hava hava* — what was done was done. The offering is complete. Why should we then permit this *onen* to continue down a problematic path by eating at night? Let him return to his *aninus* status and not eat, since the major acts of the *korban* have already been accomplished.

### Eating Me'akeiv

Ravina responds: *achilas pesachim me'akeiv* — eating the *korban Pesach* is essential and constitutive of fulfilling the *mitzvah*. One is not *yotzei* the obligation of *korban Pesach* merely by virtue of the blood being sprinkled. The eating itself is required for fulfillment of the *mitzvah*. This is based on the teaching of Rabba bar Rav Huna, which will be cited shortly. Rava affirms this response to Rav Adda bar Matna, telling him: *tzayis mah de-kamar lach rabach* — pay close attention to what your teacher Rav Huna is teaching in defense of this position.

### Pesach Eating Centrality

This focus on eating as *me'akeiv* reflects a fundamental feature of the *korban Pesach* that sets it apart from all other *korbanot*. In every other *korban*, the central act is *zrikas ha-dam*, the sprinkling of the blood; eating and burning of the fats are secondary. The *korban Pesach*, by contrast, is brought *for the purpose of being eaten*. This is why, for example, *tumah hutra be-tzibur* — when a communal *korban* is brought despite the community being *tamei* — the dispensation normally permits the offering but not the eating. The *korban Pesach* is unique: because it is fundamentally an offering brought in order to be eaten, the dispensation of *tumah hutra be-tzibur* for the *Pesach* extends even to permit the eating. Within this framework, there is a debate about whether, *be-di'eved*, failing to eat would nonetheless leave the *korban* as having been validly offered. The Gemara here, taken at face value, indicates the answer is no: eating is truly indispensable. Therefore, once the *Pesach* has been brought for this *onen*, we must permit him to eat it at night, overriding the rabbinic *aninus layla*, because the eating is essential to the fulfillment of the *mitzvah*.

---

## Yom Shmuah Baraita

### Baraita Text

The Gemara now introduces the *baraita* from which Rabba bar Rav Huna derives that *achilas pesachim me'akeiv*. The *baraita* states: *yom shmua ke-yom kvura le-mitzvas shiva u-shloshim* — the day on which one hears news of a relative's death (within the first thirty days) is treated like the day of burial for the purposes of *shiva* and *shloshim*. That is the day from which the seven and thirty days of mourning begin for someone who did not learn of the death at the time it occurred.

However, *ve-le-achilas pesachim ke-yom likut atzamot* — for the purpose of eating the *korban Pesach*, *yom shmua* is treated not like *yom kvura* but like *yom likut atzamot*, the day of the gathering of bones. The practice of *likut atzamot* refers to the secondary burial: after the body had decomposed, the bones would be collected and interred in a small niche within a burial cave. That day carried a secondary *yom kvura* status, though of lighter weight than the original burial. The *baraita* thus places *yom shmua* in this lighter category for purposes of eating the *korban Pesach*.

The implicit logic is revealing. On *yom kvura* proper, the *baraita* implies, one cannot eat the *korban Pesach* that night. On *yom shmua* and *yom likut atzamot*, which are of lesser *aninus* weight, one can. This teaches something important about the relative force of *aninus* and *Pesach* eating in different configurations. The Gemara then spells out the inference: *miklal de-yom kvura afilu erev nami lo achil* — from the fact that the *baraita* had to invoke the lighter category of *likut atzamot*, we learn that on *yom kvura* itself, even the night following, one cannot eat the *korban Pesach*. This is a departure from what had been suggested earlier — that *yom kvura* without *yom misa* would be only rabbinic and would yield to *Pesach* — but it reflects a different tannaitic position.

The *baraita* then continues: *echad ze ve-echad ze tovel ve-ochel be-kodashim la-erev* — whether it is the case of *yom shmua* or of *yom likut atzamot*, one may immerse in a *mikveh* and eat *kodashim* that night.

### Internal Contradiction

This creates a sharp internal tension. The first half of the *baraita* implied that on *yom kvura* one cannot even eat the *korban Pesach* at night; the second half, with its *echad ze ve-echad ze*, appears to say that whether you are speaking of *yom kvura* or *yom likut atzamot*, you may eat *kodashim* generally that night. But *kodashim* are subject to even stricter standards than *korban Pesach* — if you cannot eat the more leniently treated *Pesach*, you certainly cannot eat *kodashim* generally. So how can the second half permit *kodashim* at night in what seems to include *yom kvura*?

### Rav Chisda's Answer

Rav Chisda offers the first resolution: *tannai hi* — this is a dispute between *tannaim* that has been incorporated into a single *baraita*. The first half of the *baraita* and the second half represent two different tannaitic opinions regarding the night following *yom kvura*, and they were simply compiled together without marking the transition. One *tanna* holds that *yom kvura* extends into the night and forbids even the *Pesach*; the other holds it does not, and one may eat *kodashim* generally that night.

### Rabba Bar Rav Huna

Rabba bar Rav Huna offers a different resolution: *lo kashya* — there is no real contradiction. *Kan she-shama shmuah al meto samuch le-shkiat ha-chamma, ve-chen she-liktu lo atzamot samuch le-shkiat ha-chamma, ve-chen she-mes lo mes u-kvaro samuch le-shkiat ha-chamma* — the first half of the *baraita*, which restricts eating, addresses cases where the *shmuah*, *likut atzamot*, or *kvurah* occurred close to nightfall — that is, when these events happened at night, after the sun had already set on the fourteenth. The second half of the *baraita*, permitting *kodashim* that night, addresses the standard case: when the burial, *shmuah*, or *likut atzamot* happened during the day of the fourteenth. In that case, the night follows the day but does not carry the full force of the day's *aninus* into it, and one may eat *kodashim* that night.

To work through the cases: when the burial or *likut atzamot* or *shmuah* happened during the fourteenth — meaning it was still daytime — then at nightfall one may eat *kodashim*. When these events happened at night — meaning the night of the fourteenth itself was when the *aninus* first took effect — then the *aninus* is current and active during the very time of eating, which changes the analysis. On *yom kvura* occurring at night, one cannot eat even *korban Pesach*. On *yom shmuah* or *yom likut atzamot* occurring at night, the *Pesach* obligation overrides, and one may eat it, because these are lighter *aninus* statuses; but general *kodashim* one may not eat.

### Rav Ashi's Reading

Rav Ashi offers yet another reading of the *baraita*. He suggests that when the *baraita* says *echad ze ve-echad ze tovel ve-ochel be-kodashim la-erev*, the two cases of "this and that" refer not to *yom kvura* and *yom likut atzamot*, but only to *yom shmuah* and *yom likut atzamot*. On that reading, the *baraita* never claims *yom kvura* permits eating *kodashim* at night. The *baraita* first establishes that *yom shmuah* is like *yom likut atzamot* for *Pesach*, and then concludes that both *yom shmuah* and *yom likut atzamot* permit eating *kodashim* at night. *Yom kvura* is never included in the permissive ruling of the second clause.

### Rejection of Rav Ashi

The Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's reading. Since the *baraita* had already equated *yom shmuah* and *yom likut atzamot* in the first clause, if the second clause merely wanted to say that both of these allow eating *kodashim* at night, it should have said *zeh ve-zeh*, "both of them," which would simply be confirming a previously established equivalence. The language *echad ze ve-echad ze* — "whether this one or that one" — is inclusive and expansive, drawing in all the cases previously discussed, including *yom kvura*. The Gemara therefore concludes that Rav Ashi's reading is *bidusa* — untenable — and the resolution of Rabba bar Rav Huna, distinguishing between whether the *aninus*-triggering event occurred during the day or after nightfall, remains as the accepted answer. And from that resolution, the Gemara affirms: *shema mina achilas pesachim me'akeves* — eating the *korban Pesach* is constitutive and essential, for it is only on account of that that we allow the *onen* to eat when the *aninus* triggered at night but was of a lighter variety, such as *yom shmuah* or *yom likut atzamot*.

---

## Tanna Kamma/Rabbi Debate

### Duration of Onen

The Gemara now turns to a *baraita* that directly addresses the duration of *aninus* status: *ad masai misonen alav* — until when does one remain in the status of *onen* for a relative who has died?

### Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi

The *tanna kamma* says: *kol ha-yom* — the entire day. Rabbi says: *kol zman she-lo nikvar* — as long as the person has not been buried. On the surface, Rabbi's formulation seems to shorten the period: once burial takes place, even on the day of death itself, the *aninus* ends.

### Initial Problem

The Gemara raises an immediate difficulty. If both opinions are discussing *yom misa*, neither view makes sense in context. Everyone agrees that *aninus* extends into the night at least rabbinically — *mi ika de-leis lei de-yom misa tofes leila mi-derabbanan*? And furthermore, Rabbi's formulation — that *aninus* ends at burial — cannot mean that burial on the day of death itself would terminate *aninus* immediately, for the verse states that the day following a death is like a day of bitterness, implying the entire first day is included. So how can this *baraita* be understood?

### Rav Sheshes' Attempt

Rav Sheshes proposes that the *baraita* is not addressing *yom misa* at all, but rather *yom kvura* when it does not coincide with *yom misa*. The debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi is about how long *aninus* lasts on such a day: the *tanna kamma* says the day, Rabbi says only until the burial is complete.

### Rav Yosef's Challenge

Rav Yosef challenges this reading. The *baraita* discussed earlier — the one about *yom shmuah* and *likut atzamot* — implied, by limiting its permission to eat *kodashim* at night to those two lighter categories, that on *yom kvura* proper one cannot eat *kodashim* even at night. If that is so, then there must be a tannaitic position that *yom kvura* does extend into the night for the prohibition of *kodashim*. But Rav Sheshes' reading of this *baraita* would have both the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi agreeing that *yom kvura* does not extend into the night, since the *tanna kamma* says "the day" and Rabbi says "until burial," and neither explicitly includes the night. That would leave us without any tannaitic position that extends *yom kvura* into the night — contradicting the inference from the earlier *baraita*.

### Reinterpreted Debate

The Gemara therefore restructures the *baraita*. *Ela taritz hachi* — read it as follows: the *tanna kamma* says *kol oso ha-yom belo leilo* — the entire day, but without the night. The words *ve-leilo* are implicitly present in the *tanna kamma*'s position, even though not explicitly stated. The *tanna kamma* thus holds that *yom kvura*, when not coinciding with *yom misa*, carries *aninus* only for the day and not the night. Rabbi, by contrast, says *kol zman she-lo nikvar* — and extends this to: once buried, *tofes leilo*, it includes the following night. On this reading, Rabbi is the *machmir*: he holds that *yom kvura* draws the night into the *aninus* prohibition for *kodashim*.

This restructuring is necessitated because the Gemara also introduces a later *baraita* that shows Rabbi holding an even more expansive position: *kol zman she-eino nikvar, afilu mikan ve-ad asara yamim* — as long as the person has not been buried, even if that takes ten days, the *aninus* status continues, *divrei Rabbi*. The *chakhamim*, by contrast, say *aninus* applies only on the day of death. This second *baraita* reveals that Rabbi is consistently the *machmir* in extending *aninus*, which confirms that in the first *baraita* as well, Rabbi should be understood as the stringent position, not the lenient one. The Gemara therefore inverts the plain reading of the debate to make Rabbi the one extending *aninus* into the night of *yom kvura*.

### Final Position

The daf concludes with the following picture. Rabbi Shimon holds that *aninus layla* is *derabbanan*, that the night following the day of death is only rabbinically restricted. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and holds it is *de'oraisa*. Their debate concerns *yom misa*. As for *yom kvura* that is not *yom misa*, the Gemara has now established that there is itself a tannaitic dispute: the *tanna kamma* holds that *yom kvura* does not extend into the night for purposes of the prohibition of *kodashim*, while Rabbi holds that it does. When it comes to *likut atzamot* and *yom shmuah*, both are acknowledged to be of lighter *aninus* weight and do not extend into the night for *kodashim*, though for *korban Pesach* specifically, the eating — which is *me'akeiv* — can override even the *aninus* status of *yom kvura* at night, and certainly the lighter statuses.

---

---

# Zevachim 101

## Aninus: Yom Misa vs. Yom…

### Rabbi's Night Position

The *gemara* opens by presenting a debate between Rabbi and Rabbi Yose regarding the duration of *aninus*. As established in the preceding discussion at the bottom of 100b, Rabbi holds that *aninus* extends not merely through *yom misa* — the day of death — but through *yom kvura*, the day of burial, while Rabbi Yose maintains it is limited to the day of death. The *gemara* further unpacks this dispute: the real point of contention is whether *aninus* extends into the night. Rabbi Yose holds it applies only during the day, while Rabbi holds it applies even into the night following *yom kvura*.

The *gemara* then records that this position was reported before Rava: since Rabbi Yose holds that *yom kvura* "takes hold" of the night (*tofes layla*) — meaning the night following burial also carries *aninus* status — and this extension of *yom kvura* into the night is only rabbinic (*mi-drabbanan*), it must follow that *yom misa* itself extends into the night at the level of *doraisa* (*mi-doraisa*). After all, we would not extend a rabbinic category further than the Torah-level category on which it is modeled.

### Yom Kvura Night Inference

The *gemara* now challenges whether Rabbi truly maintains that *aninus layla* is a Torah-level obligation. The question is sharpened: if the rabbinically enacted *yom kvura* encompasses the night, this implies Rabbi holds the Torah-ordained *yom misa* likewise encompasses the night.

### Braisa: Hayom vs. Layla

To test this assumption, the *gemara* cites a *braisa* rooted in Aharon's words at the time of the deaths of Nadav and Avihu. Aharon's statement is read as: "*hayom* — today I was forbidden, and at night (*layla*) I would have been permitted." This becomes the basis for examining whether *aninus layla* carries Torah-level force or is merely rabbinic.

### Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Sh…

The *braisa* records a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that *aninus layla* is *doraisa* — even in future generations an *onein* may not eat a *korban* at night. Rabbi, by contrast, states explicitly: *aninus layla ein mi-divrei Torah ela mi-divrei sofrim* — the night dimension of *aninus* is only rabbinic in origin. This creates a tension with the earlier inference, which assumed Rabbi held *aninus layla* to be Torah-based.

### Yom Kvura Extension

The *gemara* resolves the tension. One might have thought that since *yom misa* is only a daytime prohibition at the Torah level, the rabbinic extension to *yom kvura* should likewise be limited to the daytime alone. The *gemara* answers: *le-olam drabbanan hi* — yes, *aninus layla* by *yom misa* is indeed only rabbinic. Even so, when the Sages extended *aninus* to encompass *yom kvura*, they went further than the Torah's own template. As the *gemara* states at the top of 101a: *ve-chachamim asu chizuk le-divreihem yoter mi-shel Torah* — the Sages reinforced their own enactments with even greater stringency than the Torah itself requires.

In summary: the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi (together with Rabbi Yose) concerns whether *aninus layla* by *yom misa* is *doraisa* or *drabbanan*. The separate question of *yom kvura* — universally acknowledged as rabbinic — is then extended into the night as well, representing a case where the rabbinic legislation exceeds the Torah's own standard.

---

## Nadav & Avihu Story

### Ki Chen Tzuveisi

The *gemara* now turns to the narrative surrounding the deaths of Nadav and Avihu and the burning of the *chatas*. The relevant *braisa* focuses on the phrase *ki chen tzuveisi* — "because I have been commanded" — which appears three times in the exchange between Moshe and Aharon. Each instance carries a distinct meaning.

The first occurrence, *ki chen tzuveisi ba-aninus yochluha*, indicates that Moshe told Aharon and his sons that they were commanded to eat the *korban* even though they were *onenim*. Moshe is saying: despite the deaths of Nadav and Avihu, God instructed me to tell you that you must eat the offering.

The second occurrence, *ka-asher tziveisi be-sha'at ma'aseh*, refers to the instruction Moshe conveyed at the time of the event itself. As Rashi explains — four lines from the top of his commentary — when the tragedy first occurred, Moshe told them that this day was singular, that God had revealed to him a distinction: *aninus hayom* in relation to *kodashim* differs from other days. He had been told explicitly that they could eat even as *onenim*. Subsequently, when Moshe discovered the *chatas* had been burned, he said: "You should have eaten it as I commanded you at the time — why did you not do so?"

The third occurrence, *ka-asher tziva Hashem*, represents Moshe's reaffirmation that this was not his own initiative but a Divine command — he was not speaking on his own authority.

Rashi's reading thus presents the following sequence: before the tragedy, Moshe conveys the license to eat as *onenim*; after discovering the burning, Moshe presses them by saying they should have followed what God had commanded through him at the time.

### Reconciling Sources

A contradiction now emerges. One source indicates that Moshe explicitly commanded them to eat even as *onenim* — meaning the license was given and the reason they did not eat must be something other than *aninus*. Yet another source states directly: *mipnei aninus nisrefah* — "it was burned on account of *aninus*." How can these two be reconciled?

### Shmuel's Resolution

Shmuel resolves the contradiction by identifying it as a dispute between Tannaim: the first source reflects the position of Rabbi Yehuda (and Rabbi Shimon), while the second reflects Rabbi Nechemia.

### Aninus vs. Tumah Debate

The *braisa* makes the division explicit. Rabbi Nechemia holds *mipnei aninus serafuha* — they burned it because they were *onenim*. According to Rabbi Nechemia, Moshe had not conveyed to them a license to eat as *onenim*, and therefore the reason for the burning was simply their *aninus* status.

Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, both hold *mipnei tumah nisrefah* — it was burned due to ritual impurity. In their reading, Moshe had indeed given them a license to eat as *onenim*, which is why the *ki chen tzuveisi* verses explicitly mention that license. The burning, therefore, must be attributed to some entirely separate cause — *tumah* — unconnected to the deaths of Aharon's sons.

### Three Challenges to Anin…

The *gemara* presents three arguments on behalf of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's position — three reasons why the burning cannot be attributed to *aninus*:

The first: *she-im atah omer mipnei aninus nisrefah hayu li-shloshan she-yisrefuha* — if the reason was *aninus*, all three *chatasot* should have been burned. As will be explained, there were three *chatas* offerings present: one associated with Nachshon, one from the eighth day of the *miluim*, and one for *Rosh Chodesh*. *Aninus* would have applied equally to all three, yet only one was burned. *Tumah*, by contrast, could have affected just one.

The second: *hayu ra'uy le-achlah la-erev* — if the problem was merely *aninus*, they could have waited and eaten the offering at night. Rashi notes this argument is more straightforwardly applicable according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds *aninus layla* is only rabbinic, in which case night would have been permitted. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *aninus layla* is *doraisa*, Rashi suggests there would have been a special exception in this particular case that would have permitted eating at night. Either way, *aninus* alone does not explain why they burned it outright rather than waiting.

The third: *v'lo Pinchas haya imahem* — Pinchas was present with them. Pinchas was not a close relative of Nadav and Avihu in the halakhically relevant sense — one is only an *onein* for seven relatives — and therefore he was not an *onein*. Had the sole obstacle been *aninus*, Pinchas could simply have eaten the *korban* himself. The fact that it was burned instead indicates the problem was something beyond *aninus* — namely, a *tumah* that rendered the offering unfit for anyone to eat.

---

## Kodshei Sha'ah vs. Dorot

### Rava's Explanation

Having established that Shmuel attributed the debate to Rabbi Nechemia on one side and Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the other, the *gemara* introduces Rava's alternative resolution. Rava proposes that *idei v'idei d'Rebbi Nechemia* — both *braisot* can in fact reflect the position of Rabbi Nechemia alone. There is no contradiction, because Rabbi Nechemia can maintain simultaneously that they had a license to eat as *onenim* and that the burning was due to *aninus*. The resolution lies in distinguishing between types of *korbanos*: *kodshei sha'ah* — offerings unique to that moment in history — and *kodshei dorot* — offerings that apply to all generations.

According to Rava's reading of Rabbi Nechemia, the license to eat as an *onein* applied exclusively to the *kodshei sha'ah*, the exceptional offerings brought only during that singular inaugural period. The *chatas* of *Rosh Chodesh*, however, was a standard offering applicable in all generations, and no special license extended to it. This immediately answers the first of the three challenges: only one *chatas* was burned — the *Rosh Chodesh* one — because only for that one did *aninus* remain operative. The other two were covered by the license.

### Three Chatasim Identified

The three *chatasot* referenced throughout this sugya are: the *seir* (goat) offering of Nachshon, the nasi of Yehuda, who brought the inaugural dedication offering on behalf of his tribe; the *chatas* of the eighth day of the *miluim*, the dedication of the Mishkan; and the *seir* of *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*. A *braisa* later in the discussion maps these onto the three words of the verse: *va-yidaresh darosh Moshe* — *va-yidaresh* refers to the *seir* of Nachshon, *chatat* refers to the *chatas* of the eighth day of the *miluim*, and *darosh* refers to the *seir* of *Rosh Chodesh*.

### Special vs. General Korb…

The conceptual divide is this: the *kodshei sha'ah* were offerings with no permanent counterpart in the ongoing sacrificial order. They existed as part of the singular, unrepeatable consecration of the Mishkan. For these, exceptional rules could be applied — including permitting an *onein* to partake. The *Rosh Chodesh* offering, however, was a paradigmatic *korban* of all generations, and no such special license could be extended to it.

---

## Moshe-Aharon Dialogue

### Nechemia's Reading

The *gemara* now asks how each school reads the actual *psukim* in Vayikra 10. Starting with Rabbi Nechemia's interpretation, the *gemara* reconstructs the implicit dialogue between Moshe and Aharon that underlies the verses. Moshe opens by asking Aharon: *madua lo achaltem* — why did you not eat the *chatas*?

### Blood & Kodesh Details

Moshe first probes whether there was a technical disqualification. He asks: *shema nichnas dama lifnai v'lifnim* — perhaps the blood of this *chatas* was brought into the inner sanctum, which would require the offering to be burned? Aharon answers: *hein lo huva dama* — no, the blood was not brought inside. Moshe then suggests the opposite: perhaps it was taken outside the boundaries of the Mishkan? Aharon answers: *ba-kodesh hayta* — it remained within the *kodesh*. Moshe then asks: *v'dilma ba-aninus hikravtem u-pesaltem otah* — perhaps you offered it while in a state of *aninus*, thereby disqualifying it? Aharon responds: *v'chi heim hikrivu* — did my sons bring it? *Ani hikravti* — I brought it. And a *kohen gadol* performs the *avodah* even as an *onein*.

This back-and-forth eliminates every possible ground for disqualification. The blood was not brought inside; it did not leave its proper area; it was not offered by an *onein* in a manner that would invalidate it. All the technical conditions were met.

### Aharon's Inference

Having cleared away all technical objections, Moshe then tells Aharon: *achol tochlu osah ka-asher tziveisi ba-aninus yochlu* — you should have eaten it as I commanded; eat it even in your state of *aninus*. Moshe is pressing: I gave you an explicit license to eat as *onenim*; why did you burn it?

At this point Aharon responds with his decisive argument: *hein hayom hikrivu et korbanam ve-et chatatam lifnei Hashem, va-tikrena oti ka-eleh, va-achalti chatat hayom ha-yitav be-einei Hashem?* — "Today my sons have died. Given that such a tragedy has befallen me, should I have eaten the *chatat hayom*? Would that have been good in God's eyes?"

Aharon's argument is substantive. He tells Moshe: perhaps your license was limited to *kodshei sha'ah*. I applied a *kal va-chomer*: if by *ma'aser*, which is a far less weighty matter than *korbanos*, the Torah states *lo achalti be-oni mimenu* — "I did not eat of it in my *aninus*" — then certainly with respect to *kodshei dorot*, offerings that apply for all generations, an *onein* should not eat. Therefore, even though you gave me a license, I understood that license to be restricted to the two exceptional *korbanos* of the *kodshei sha'ah*. For the *chatas* of *Rosh Chodesh*, which is a standard offering of all generations, I concluded that the license could not apply.

### Moshe's Concession

The *gemara* then states: *va-yishma Moshe va-yitav be-einav* — Moshe heard and it was good in his eyes. The *gemara* explains: *hoda v'lo bosh Moshe lomar lo shamati* — Moshe was not too proud to admit that he had not recalled this correctly. He acknowledged: *shamati v'shachachti* — I had heard this ruling and forgotten it. Aharon was right: the license applied only to the *kodshei sha'ah*, and the *Rosh Chodesh chatas* was correctly burned.

### Tumah Version

The *gemara* then presents how Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon read the same *psukim*. The initial exchange follows the same structure — Moshe asking whether the blood was brought inside, Aharon denying it, Moshe asking whether it left its boundary, Aharon denying that — but the final point of contention differs entirely.

In this version, once Moshe has eliminated the technical disqualifications, he presses a different challenge: *v'dilma agav meriraichu pashatem behu ve-itmu* — perhaps in your grief and bitterness you were negligent and the offering became *tamei*? Aharon responds with indignation: *kach ani be-einecha?* — Is that what you think of me? That I would show contempt for *kodshei shamayim*? *Va-tikrena oti ka-eleh, afilu ele ve-cha-eleh, eini mevaze kodshei shamayim* — even if tragedies far beyond this were to strike me, I would not fail in my protection of the *korbanos*. In other words, Aharon's defense here is not about *aninus* at all, but about rejecting any suggestion of negligence toward *tumah*. He is affirming that no matter the circumstances, he would not have permitted the offering to become *tamei* through carelessness.

There is a certain irony in this: Aharon ultimately defends himself against the accusation of negligence by saying he would never let *tumah* occur, and yet in the end *tumah* is precisely what happened. The resolution, as the *gemara* will clarify, is that the *tumah* came about through pure accident — *be-ones* — and was not the result of any failure on Aharon's part.

### Day vs. Night Alternative

The *gemara* then notes a parallel alternative reading within the Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon school. In this version, Aharon's pushback to Moshe's license is not about *kodshei sha'ah* versus *kodshei dorot*, but rather about day versus night. Aharon says to Moshe: *shema lo shamata ela ba-layla* — perhaps the license you received applied only to the night, not to the day. And during the day, he argues, a *kal va-chomer* from *ma'aser* applies: just as *ma'aser*, which is a lesser matter, is forbidden to an *onein*, how much more so *kodashim* during the day. Therefore, Aharon tells Moshe, I understood the license to mean: eat it at night, not during the day.

### Night Question & Tumah

The *gemara* immediately raises the obvious follow-up: *ibayalu li-shvuyei u-lemichlah be-orsah* — if that was Aharon's understanding, why didn't they simply wait and eat it at night? The answer is: *tumah be-ones basta* — an accidental *tumah* occurred to the offering, through no fault of anyone's, and therefore it had to be burned.

This version — the Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon approach — thus presents the following reconstruction: Moshe gave a license to eat as *onenim*; Aharon understood this license to apply only at night; they intended to eat it at night; but before they could do so, an accidental *tumah* rendered the one *chatas* unfit, and it was burned. The *aninus* remains part of the story, but it functions not as the cause of the burning but as the backdrop to the delay that led to the accidental *tumah*.

The *gemara* then shows how the words *hayom* and *hen hayom* are parsed differently by each school. According to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, Aharon's statement *va-achalti chatat hayom* means: "Had I eaten this *chatat* during the day" — the word *hayom* specifies the time, and Aharon is explaining he chose not to eat during the day. According to Rabbi Nechemia, *chatat hayom* does not mean "the *chatat* today" but rather "the *chatat* of the day" — that is, the *Rosh Chodesh chatat*, the ordinary daily-type offering. Similarly, the phrase *hen hayom hikrivu* — according to Rabbi Nechemia — means: did they bring this offering? Implying that Aharon was clarifying that it was he, not his sons, who brought it, and he did so as a *kohen gadol* who is an *oveid onein*.

---

## Which Chatas Burned

### Three Sources Identified

The *gemara* now focuses on the three *chatasot* in detail, drawing on the *braisa* that expounds the verse *va-yidaresh darosh Moshe et se'ir ha-chatat* (Vayikra 10:16). The three words — *se'ir*, *chatat*, and *darosh* — are each taken as a reference to one of the three offerings: *se'ir* refers to the *seir* of Nachshon; *chatat* refers to the *chatas* of the eighth day of the *miluim*; and *darosh* refers to the *seir* of *Rosh Chodesh*.

### Singular Burned

The *gemara* proves from the text that only one of the three was burned. The verse states *v'hinei soraf* — "and behold it was burned" — using the singular, indicating that only one, not all three, was burned.

### Two Questions

Moshe's investigation, signaled by the double language *darosh darash* — two acts of searching — corresponds to two distinct questions. The first: *mipnei mah chatat zu nisrefah* — why was this one *chatas* burned? The second: *v'eilu munachos* — why are the other two still sitting there uneaten? In other words, Moshe is pressing not only on the burning of one, but also on the delay in eating the other two.

### Rosh Chodesh Burned

The *gemara* then asks: which of the three was the one that was burned? The verse elsewhere identifies the *Rosh Chodesh* offering with the phrase *l'chatat la-Hashem* — "as a *chatat* for God" — and on this basis the *gemara* concludes: *hevei omer zeh se'ir shel Rosh Chodesh* — it was the *seir* of *Rosh Chodesh* that was burned.

### Nechemia's Answer

Rabbi Nechemia's answer is now fully coherent: *aninus* disqualified only the *Rosh Chodesh chatas*, because that was a *korban* of all generations for which no special license had been granted. The other two — Nachshon's *seir* and the *chatas* of the eighth day of the *miluim* — were *kodshei sha'ah*, and for those, the license to eat as *onenim* applied. That is why only one was burned and not all three.

---

## Pinchas's Kohen Status

### Pinchas Challenge

The *gemara* returns to the second and third challenges against Rabbi Nechemia. We already saw that the question of why they did not wait until night is resolved by Rabbi Nechemia's position that *aninus layla* is *doraisa* — even at night, the *Rosh Chodesh chatas* could not be eaten. But the third challenge remains: why couldn't Pinchas have eaten it? If the problem was *aninus* applying to Aharon and his sons, Pinchas was not a close enough relative to be an *onein*. He should have been available to eat the *chatas* and thereby avoid burning it.

### Pinchas Becomes Kohen

The *gemara* answers that Rabbi Nechemia holds in accordance with the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who said in the name of Rabbi Chanina: *lo niskahein Pinchas ad she-harag l'Zimri* — Pinchas did not attain the status of *kohen* until he killed Zimri. This is a striking ruling. Although Pinchas was the son of Elazar ben Aharon and thus a direct patrilineal descendant of Aharon, there is a technical reason why he would not automatically have inherited *kehunah* at birth. The *kehunah* was conferred specifically on Aharon, his sons Elazar and Itamar, and Nadav and Avihu. Any children born to those sons after the *kehunah* was conferred would be born into *kehunah*. But Pinchas had already been born before the *kehunah* was given, and his father becoming a *kohen* did not retroactively make Pinchas one. Therefore, at the time of the deaths of Nadav and Avihu, Pinchas was not yet a *kohen* and could not have eaten from the *korbanos*.

### Peace Mission

Rav Ashi disagrees and pushes Pinchas's attainment of *kehunah* even later. According to Rav Ashi, Pinchas did not become a *kohen* until he made peace between the tribes. This refers to the episode after the entry into the land, when the tribes of Gad and Reuven erected an altar and the other tribes feared a schism was imminent. Pinchas led a diplomatic delegation and averted what might have become a civil war. According to Rav Ashi, it was only at that point — the fulfillment of the *brit shalom* in its fullest sense — that Pinchas truly attained the status of *kohen*.

The *gemara* notes the beauty of this reading: the *brit kehunat olam* began with an act of violence at the Zimri incident, yet its realization came through an act of peace-making. The warrior becomes the diplomat.

### Verse Evidence

The textual basis for Rav Ashi's position is the verse *va-yishma Pinchas ha-kohen u-nesi'ei ha-eidah* — "And Pinchas the *kohen* and the princes of the congregation heard." This is the first time in the Torah that Pinchas himself is called *ha-kohen*, rather than merely *Pinchas ben Elazar ben Aharon ha-kohen*, where the title *kohen* refers to Aharon rather than to Pinchas. The opponent of Rav Ashi's view points out that the verse *ve-haysah lo u-le-zaro acharav brit kehunat olam* already conferred *kehunah* in the Zimri story. Rav Ashi replies: that verse is a *berachah*, a promise and blessing for the future, which was only actualized at the later episode of the peace mission.

And conversely, to the challenge that the verse *va-yishma Pinchas ha-kohen* is used merely to establish the *yichus* — the genealogical pedigree — of the *kohanim gedolim* who would descend from Pinchas, Rav Ashi responds that the direct attribution of *kehunah* to Pinchas in that verse goes beyond mere lineage and marks the moment of his own entry into *kehunah*.

---

## Moshe's Kohen Status

### Moshe Kohen Gadol

The discussion of Pinchas's *kehunah* naturally raises the broader question of who else was present and might have eaten the *korban*. Rav makes a sweeping statement: *Moshe Rabbeinu Kohen Gadol hayah* — Moshe our teacher was a *kohen gadol*. Having served during the period of the *miluim* and performed the *avodah*, Moshe retained a status of *kehunah*. Rav further states that Moshe *ve-choleik be-kodshei shamayim hayah* — he had a portion in all the heavenly offerings. This is derived from the verse *me-eil ha-miluim le-Moshe hayah le-manah* — from the ram of the *miluim*, Moshe had a portion.

### Moshe Eating Challenge

This creates an immediate difficulty for the claim that the *chatas* had to be burned because the *kohanim* were *onenim*. If Moshe was a *kohen gadol* and he was not an *onein*, why couldn't he simply have eaten the *korban*? Just as the challenge was raised about Pinchas — *v'lav Pinchas imahem hayah*, wasn't Pinchas there with them — so too one might ask: *v'lav Moshe Rabbeinu hayah imahem*, wasn't Moshe Rabbeinu there with them?

### Moshe Occupied

The *gemara* answers: *de-tarid ba-Shechinah* — Moshe was completely preoccupied with the Divine Presence. He was constantly in communication with God, ascending and descending from *Har Sinai* first thing in the morning and returning first thing in the morning, as the *gemara* records: *Moshe be-hashkamah alah, be-hashkamah yarad*. Although this specific detail relates to the period of *Har Sinai*, the principle holds here as well: Moshe was entirely absorbed in his prophetic and administrative engagement with the Shechinah. It was simply not possible for them to hold the meat and rely on Moshe to eat it. He was unavailable.

### Ba'al Mum Eating

The *gemara* then cites a verse regarding a *ba'al mum* — a physically blemished *kohen* who may not perform the *avodah* but retains the right to eat *korbanos*: *lechem Elohav mi-kodshei ha-kodashim u-min ha-kodashim yokhal* — "from the most holy offerings and from the lesser holy offerings shall he eat." This verse establishes that a *ba'al mum* may eat both *kodshei kodashim* and *kodashim kalim*.

### Why Both Mentioned

A *braisa* raises the question of why the verse had to specify both categories. One might think that mentioning *kodshei kodashim* suffices, since it is the weightier category — and the same *kal va-chomer* would include *kodashim kalim*. Conversely, mentioning *kodashim kalim* alone might seem sufficient. The *braisa* explains: had the verse stated only *kodshei kodashim*, one might conclude that *kodshei kodashim* are permitted to the *ba'al mum* because they were once permitted to a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — but *kodashim kalim* might not be, since they were never similarly opened to a *zar*. And had it stated only *kodashim kalim*, one might conclude the *ba'al mum* may eat the lighter offerings but not the heavier *kodshei kodashim*. Therefore both had to be stated explicitly.

### Zar Eating Analysis

The *braisa*'s argument rests on the premise that *kodshei kodashim* were once permitted to a *zar*. The question is: which *zar* ate *kodshei kodashim*? The obvious candidate would be Moshe Rabbeinu during the period of the *miluim*. If Moshe was a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — and nonetheless ate *kodshei kodashim*, this would explain why *kodshei kodashim* have a certain precedent of openness beyond the strictly *kohen*-exclusive framework.

But this reading would suggest that Moshe was a *zar*, not a *kohen* — in direct contradiction to Rav's statement that Moshe was a *kohen gadol*. This is the *gemara*'s challenge: *katani mi-hat she-harei hutar le-zar v'lahem, lav Moshe* — the *braisa* implies it was a *zar* who ate *kodshei kodashim*, which would indicate Moshe was a *zar*, not a *kohen*.

### Rav Sheshet Clarifies

Rav Sheshet resolves the difficulty. He explains: *lo, ba-bamah le-zar* — the reference is not to Moshe at all, but to a *zar* eating at a *bamah*, a private altar used before the centralization of worship. The principle being invoked is: according to the opinion that a *minchah* may be brought at a *bamah*, such a *minchah* — which is normally *kodshei kodashim* and eaten exclusively by male *kohanim* — would be eaten by a *zar* at a *bamah*, since the laws of *bamah* operate differently. That is the precedent for *kodshei kodashim* having been permitted to a *zar*: not Moshe's eating, but the *zar* who eats a *minchah* at a *bamah*.

The reason the *minchah* specifically is invoked is as follows: *kodshei kodashim* at a *bamah* — what might that look like? An *olah* is burned entirely; a *chatat* and *asham* are obligatory offerings not brought at a private *bamah*. The only *kodshei kodashim* that could practically be brought as a voluntary *nedavah* at a *bamah* and be eaten there by a non-*kohen* would be a *minchah*. That is the case the *braisa* envisions. And as for *kodashim kalim* — there is no *kohen*'s portion of *kodashim kalim* that a *zar* ever ate at a *bamah*, which is why the verse needed to explicitly extend the *ba'al mum*'s permission to that category as well.

The question of whether Moshe retained *kohen* status will continue in the subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Zevachim 102

## Moshe as Kohen

### Moshe Kohen Question

The daf opens in the middle of a rich discussion about whether Moshe was a *kohen* — or even a *kohen gadol*. The question emerged from an earlier analysis of *aninuth*: why was the *chatas* burned on the eighth day of the *miluim*? The most straightforward answer is *aninut*, which the *pesukim* themselves make apparent. But this raises a follow-up: why not simply have Pinchas perform the *avodah*? The answer given is that Pinchas was not yet a *kohen* at that point, despite being a descendant of Aharon. And why not give it to Moshe, if Moshe was a *kohen*? The answer is that Moshe was occupied with God. That exchange then opens up the broader question: was Moshe in fact a *kohen*?

### Kehunah Origins

What this question really does is reveal something conceptually important: *kehunah* is not, at its foundation, a status defined by descent from Aharon. The *pesukim* themselves attest to this. Malki Tzedek Melech Shalem is described as *vehu Kohen l'El Elyon* — he is a *kohen* to God Most High — and Yitro is called *Kohen Midian*. The original *kehunah* belonged to the *bechorim*, the firstborn. In each generation, certain individuals were designated to serve God — sometimes hereditary, sometimes recognized. The sons of Aharon represent one particular instantiation of this broader status, a hereditary channel. But *kehunah* conceptually precedes it and is not exhausted by it.

What the *gemara* is suggesting, then, is that Moshe may have been included within the class of *kohanim* during his time — a *kehunah* that simply did not pass to his descendants.

### Pinchas Non-Kohen

The other side of this coin is equally striking: Pinchas was a descendant of Aharon and yet, at least initially, was not a *kohen*. The *kehunah* status was granted to Aharon and his four sons — not to children already born to those sons. It is entirely conceivable that there were other grandchildren of Aharon who were alive at the time the *mishkan* was inaugurated, who never performed an act like Pinchas's killing of Zimri, and who therefore never received the *kehunah*. Indeed, there is a *midrash* that a descendant of Moshe himself became a *kohen* to idols — a reminder of how fluidly the Talmud can treat the boundaries of this status.

So we have two paradoxes running simultaneously: Moshe, who was not a descendant of Aharon, may have been a *kohen*; and Pinchas, who was a descendant of Aharon, was initially not one.

### Moshe Zar Proof

The *gemara* now challenges the proposition that Moshe was a *kohen*, citing a *baraisa* from the final line of 101b. The *meisivei* asks: *Miriam mi hisgira?* — who declared Miriam to be a *metzora* and formally placed her into her *tzara'at* status? The declaration requires a *kohen*. If you say Moshe did it — *Moshe zar hu* — Moshe was a *zar*, a non-*kohen*, and *ein zar ro'eh es hanega'im*, a non-*kohen* cannot examine *nega'im*. If you say Aharon did it — *Aharon karov hu* — Aharon was a relative, and *ein karov ro'eh es hanega'im*, a relative cannot rule on *nega'im*. This is, as Tosafot notes, actually a *machlokes* — the position that a relative cannot examine *nega'im* reflects Rabbi Meir's view, as stated in Masechet Negaim Perek 2, while the *tanna kamma* there holds that only one's own *nega'im* are excluded. The *baraisa* here follows Rabbi Meir.

But why not have Elazar do it? The question of how far the category of *karov* extends — whether it reaches nephews — is not fully resolved. It may be that having a nephew rule on his aunt would not be appropriate *kavod* for Miriam.

The *gemara*'s resolution is striking in its own right: *kvod gadol chalak haKadosh Baruch Hu leMiriam* — God Himself gave Miriam great honor in that moment. *Va'ani masguira va'ani potrah* — I will place her in her status as a *metzora*, and I will release her. There is something arresting about this formulation. God acting as a *kohen* to the extent of serving the people — teaching, ruling, imparting justice — is not as paradoxical as it might initially seem. The *kohanim* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* function as teachers of Torah, as members of the *beit din*, as examiners of *tzara'at*. In all of these capacities they represent God to the people. God can perform these same functions; what would be theologically incoherent is God serving in the *Beit HaMikdash* — serving Himself. But the outward-facing functions of *kehunah* have a natural divine analog.

What is halachically relevant for our discussion, the *gemara* says, is simply this: *Moshe zar*. The source explicitly calls Moshe a *zar*, and *ein zar ro'eh es hanega'im* — so you see that Moshe was not a *kohen*.

### Negaim Aharon

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak qualifies this proof: *shani mar'os nega'im de-Aharon u-vanav ketuvim be-parsha* — the examination of *nega'im* is a special case, because the *pasuk* does not merely say *ha-kohen*; it says *ve-huva el Aharon ha-kohen o el achad mi-banav ha-kohanim* — it is brought to Aharon the *kohen* or to one of his sons the *kohanim*. For *nega'im* specifically, it is not enough to be a *kohen*; one must also be a descendant of Aharon. So the fact that Moshe could not examine *nega'im* does not prove he was not a *kohen* — it only proves he was not a descendant of Aharon, which we already knew. (Of course, God also does not fall into this category of Aharon's descendants, but the *gemara* brackets that point.)

---

## Pinchas Kohen Status

### Elisheva Five Joys

The *gemara* continues testing whether Moshe was a *kohen*, now citing from *Seder Olam* a teaching about Elisheva, the daughter of Aminadav and sister of Nachshon — Aharon's wife. On the day the *mishkan* was dedicated, Elisheva had five sources of joy exceeding those of any other woman in Israel. Her *yavam* — her brother-in-law — Moshe, was a *melech*, a king; her husband Aharon was *kohen gadol*; her son Elazar was *sgan*, the deputy *kohen gadol*; her grandson Pinchas was *mashuach milchamah*, the one who would lead Israel into war; and her brother Nachshon was *nasi shevet*, the head of his tribe.

### Pinchas Future Status

The reference to Pinchas as *mashuach milchamah* is significant for our discussion. The *gemara* notes: *katani mihat* — what we can extract from this is that *yivamah melech*, her brother-in-law was a king, and the *baraisa* identifies him as simply a *melech* — not also as *kohen gadol*. If Moshe had been *kohen gadol*, would the *baraisa* not have listed that as a separate source of joy for Elisheva? The counter-response is *eima af melech* — we already credit *kohen gadol* status to her husband; that does not necessarily foreclose Moshe also having it. It is admittedly the weakest of the proofs accumulated thus far, but the overall weight of evidence is pointing toward Moshe not having been recognized as a *kohen*.

There is, however, an immediately striking implication in the reference to Pinchas as *mashuach milchamah*. This text is describing the day the *mishkan* was dedicated — long before the Zimri episode. If Pinchas was already designated as *mashuach milchamah* at that point, this presupposes that he already held *kohen* status, since the *mashuach milchamah* is a *kohen*. This is a direct challenge to the earlier discussion that Pinchas was not yet a *kohen*. The *gemara* has not yet fully resolved this tension, and it is a point a careful reader will notice.

---

## Moshe Kohen Tannaim

### God's Anger Result

The *gemara* now declares *katannai* — this question is in fact a *machlokes tannaim*. The entry point is the verse *vayichar af Hashem be-Moshe* — God's anger burned against Moshe when he persisted in refusing the mission, saying send someone else instead. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha states a general principle: *kol charon af she-ba-Torah ne'emar bo roshem* — every instance in the Torah in which anger burns against a person leaves a mark, some consequence. Rashi clarifies that this need not be a physical mark; it can be a public rebuke or some experienced consequence of that anger. The critical word is *be* — anger directed *at* someone, not merely burning within.

Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai applies this principle here: *af zeh ne'emar bo roshem* — this instance also left its mark. The proof is in the phrasing *halo Aharon achicha ha-Levi* — why call Aharon a *Levi*? He was going to be a *kohen*! Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai reads this as God saying: *ani amarti attah Kohen ve-hu Levi* — My original plan was that you, Moshe, would be the *kohen*, and Aharon would be the *Levi*. Now, because of all your resistance and complaints, it is reversed: Aharon is the *kohen*, and you, Moshe, will be the *Levi*. The phrase *Aharon achicha ha-Levi* is thus a pointed remark, emphasizing what was *supposed* to be Aharon's role — what he was going to be had Moshe not argued. The mark of God's anger was the removal of *kehunah* from Moshe.

### Chachamim Miluim

The *chachamim* disagree: *lo nitkahen Moshe ela shivat yemei hamiluim bilvad* — Moshe was *kohen* only during the seven days of *miluim*, and no more. As Rashi explains, the crucial distinction between the *chachamim* and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai is not about those seven days — both agree Moshe served as *kohen* during them — but about whether the *kehunah* had ever been intended for Moshe. According to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, the original divine plan had been for Moshe to be *kohen*, and God's anger stripped that from him. According to the *chachamim*, that was never the plan. Moshe simply served in a temporary capacity during the *miluim*, and there was nothing removed from him, because nothing had been designated for him beyond those seven days.

### Rav Kehunah

A third position is that of Rav — the *yesh omrim* of the *baraisa*. Rav holds: *lo paska kehuna ela mizaro shel Moshe* — the *kehunah* was not withheld from Moshe himself; he was indeed a *kohen*. It simply was not passed on to his children. The *kehunah* was granted to Aharon and his descendants, and to Moshe — but unlike Aharon's *kehunah*, Moshe's did not continue through his lineage. The *pasuk* in Divrei HaYamim supports this: *u-Moshe ish ha-elohim banav yikare'u al shevet ha-Levi* — his *children* are attributed to the tribe of Levi, but Moshe himself is described separately, implying his own status was distinct. The *gemara* also cites *Moshe ve-Aharon be-kohannav* — Moshe and Aharon among His *kohanim* — as further evidence that Moshe himself held *kohen* status. A textual question arises: *kohannav* might be read as singular (*kohano*), which would create a parsing difficulty, but the *gemara* proceeds with this reading nonetheless.

---

## Anger & Kingship

### Charon Af Principle

Having established the general principle of *charon af*, the *gemara* now examines it more carefully. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's claim is that *kol charon af she-ba-Torah ne'emar bo roshem* — every instance of burning anger recorded in the Torah leaves its mark on the target of that anger.

### Moshe Pharaoh Anger

The *gemara* challenges this with a counterexample: *vayetze me'im Paroh bechari af* — Moshe left Pharaoh's presence in fiery anger. Where is the mark here? *Velo amar leh velo midi* — he didn't even publicly rebuke him. One might respond that Pharaoh had all the power, and Moshe was in no position to lash out. But the *gemara*'s point is about the meaning of the word: if *charon af* always implies that the anger was directed outward and had an impact on the other person, where is that impact here?

Resh Lakish responds: *setaro* — he slapped Pharaoh in the face. The verse does not say this explicitly, but Resh Lakish reads the *charon af* as implying an acted-upon anger. This prompts the question: would Resh Lakish really say such a thing? After all, elsewhere Resh Lakish interprets the verse *v'nitzavta likraso al sfat hay'or* — you will stand to greet Pharaoh at the river — as meaning Moshe should show Pharaoh appropriate respect: *melech hu, v'hasber lo panim*, he is a king; present yourself respectfully. Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, reads *nitzavta* in an aggressive register, as in *Datan va-Aviram yatzu nitzavim* — a posture of confrontation, not deference. So the two positions need to be reversed: it is Rabbi Yochanan, not Resh Lakish, who holds the confrontational reading, and Resh Lakish who urges respect before Pharaoh.

### Fear of Kings

Rabbi Yannai draws a broader lesson: *l'olam t'he eimas malchus alecha* — the fear of the king should always be upon you, even when the king is wicked, even when God is clearly on your side. The proof is Moshe's own formulation to Pharaoh: *v'yerdu kol avadecha eleh elai* — all your servants will come down to me. Pharaoh himself was the one who would ultimately come to Moshe and plead for Israel to leave — yet Moshe did not say "you will come down to me." He showed deference in his phrasing even in a moment of triumph. This is the posture of one who maintains *eimas malchus* even while pronouncing the downfall of a tyrant. Fear and genuine respect are not the same thing, of course; the *gemara* does not conflate them. But here they express themselves in the same outward behavior.

Rabbi Yochanan adds another illustration: *v'yad Hashem hayta el Eliyahu v'yeshannes motnav va-yaratz lifnei Achav* — God's spirit was upon Elijah, and he girded his loins and ran before Achav. Despite Elijah's prophetic authority and his total opposition to Achav's ways, he placed himself in the position of a forerunner before the king — the secondary, attendant position. The respect shown to the office of kingship is maintained regardless of one's own standing.

### Moshe Kingship

Ulla introduces a striking teaching: *bikesh Moshe malchus ve-lo nitnu lo* — Moshe sought kingship and was not granted it. This requires clarification, since we have already referred to Moshe as a *melech*. What Ulla means by *malchus* is not mere political leadership but the full conception of hereditary kingship — a status that passes through the generations. The proof text is *al tikrav halom* — do not come close to *this place* — spoken to Moshe at the *sneh*. The word *halom* connotes royal status.

### Halom Hereditary

How do we know *halom* means kingship? By *gezeira shava* with the verse by David: *mi anochi Hashem Elokim ki heviatani ad halom* — who am I, Lord my God, that You have brought me to *this point*? David uses *halom* to describe his elevation to the throne. So *halom* at the *sneh* signals that kingship was being withheld from Moshe at the very moment he was being called.

Rava challenges: but the *baraisa* about Elisheva just called Moshe a *melech*! Rava resolves this: *lo l'zaro ka'amar* — what Moshe sought and did not receive was the hereditary dimension, the kingship that would continue through his descendants. The leadership he exercised was real, but it was not *malchus* in the dynastic sense.

The *gemara* then examines whether *halom* always implies hereditary kingship for all future generations. By Shaul, the word *halom* also appears: *havei od halom ish* — bring the man here. Yet Shaul's dynasty did not persist. Two responses are offered: first, Shaul's son Ish-Bosheth did in fact reign, even if briefly; second, and more fundamentally, *shani Shaul de-afilu begavei lo kayam* — what was granted to Shaul was indeed a hereditary kingship, but it was taken from him because of his failures. The grant was dynastic; the revocation was consequential.

This leads to a general principle stated by Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina: *besha'ah she-poskin gedulah le-adam poskin lo u-lezaro ad sof kol ha-dorot* — when a position of greatness is decreed for a person from above, it is decreed for that person and for all his descendants until the end of time. The verse is *lo yigra mi-tzaddik einav v'es melachim l'kise* — it is not withheld from a righteous person, and kings remain on their throne. But this is not unconditional: *ve-im higis da'ato Hakadosh Baruch Hu mashpilo* — if a person becomes arrogant, God will bring him low. The verse continues: *ve-im asurim ba-zikkim yilachdun be-chevlei oni* — if they are bound with chains they will be caught in ropes of poverty. Greatness granted by heaven is generational in principle, but forfeitable through pride.

---

## Ba'alei Mumim

### Mishnah Rule

The *gemara* now turns from *aggadata* to the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states the principle that *ba'alei mumim* — *kohanim* with blemishes, whether permanent or temporary — do not perform the *avodah* but do receive a portion in the *korbanos*.

### Kol Zachar

The *gemara* asks: *mina hanei milei* — where do we know this? The *rabbanan* taught: *kol zachar ba-kohanim yochal osah* — every male among the *kohanim* shall eat of it. This phrase appears three times in the Torah — by a *minchah*, by a *chatas*, and by a *shelamim* — and each occurrence serves to include a different category of *ba'al mum*.

The question in each case is *lemai* — for what purpose is the inclusion? If it is to permit eating, an explicit verse already states this: *lechem elohav mi-kodesh ha-kodashim u-min ha-kodashim yochel* — the *ba'al mum* may eat from the holiest and from the holy offerings. So the *kol zachar* cannot be coming to grant permission to eat — that is already established. Rather, it is coming to grant entitlement to a *portion*, meaning the *ba'al mum* actively receives his share.

The second *baraisa* addresses a second *kol zachar*: we have already used the first to establish that a *ba'al mum* receives a portion. But what if the *kohen* began without a blemish and developed one later? Perhaps the original *kol zachar* speaks only of someone who was whole and then became a *ba'al mum* — he had already established himself in the system, so perhaps he retains his entitlement. How do we know that someone born with a *mum* — a *ba'al mum me'ikara* — also receives a portion? The second *kol zachar* tells us so.

The third *baraisa* then asks: eating is established, receiving a portion is established, and inclusion of one born with a *mum* is established. What does the third *kol zachar* add? *Yachol ein li ela ba'al mum kavua, ba'al mum over minayin?* — I only know that a permanent blemish qualifies; how do I know a temporary blemish also receives a portion? *Talmud lomar kol zachar* — every male — even one with a temporary blemish.

### Avoda vs Achila

At this point the *gemara* raises an objection: *k'lapei laya* — which way is this going? It seems counterintuitive. Surely one would more naturally assume that a temporary blemish is included — since it will pass — and the *pasuk* should be needed to include the more surprising case of a permanent blemish. Rav Sheshes says: *eipoch* — reverse it. The verse is coming to include permanent blemishes, not temporary ones.

Rav Ashi disagrees: *l'olam lo teipoch* — do not reverse it. The verse is indeed needed for the temporary *ba'al mum*. Why might one have thought to exclude him? Because one might have analogized his status to that of a *tamei kohen*: just as a *tamei kohen* is only temporarily excluded and must wait until his *tumah* passes before eating, so too a temporary *ba'al mum* — perhaps wait until his blemish passes and then he will get his portion. The *pasuk* teaches that no — even now, while the blemish is present, he receives a portion.

### Rule Exceptions

This brings the *gemara* back to the larger question: is the operative rule in the *mishnah* about *avodah* or about *achilah*? The *mishnah* states that whoever is unfit for *avodah* does not receive a portion. The *gemara* notes that this cannot be an absolute rule in either direction. A *ba'al mum* is unfit for *avodah* yet does receive a portion — that is an exception to "unfit doesn't get." Conversely, a *tamei kohen* in the context of *korbanos tzibur* is fit for *avodah* yet does not receive a portion — that is an exception to "fit gets." So the rule as stated fails on both sides.

### Achila Reading

The *gemara* therefore concludes: *rauy l'achilah ka'amar* — read the *mishnah*'s rule as being about eating, not *avodah*. One who is unfit to eat does not receive a portion. This reading handles the cases of the *onen* and the *tamei* in *korbanos tzibur* cleanly: they cannot eat, so they do not receive portions. And the *ba'al mum* can eat, so he is entirely consistent with the rule — not an exception at all.

But a new counterexample emerges: *v'harei katan* — a minor can eat, yet does not receive a portion, because the verse *ish ke'achiv* teaches that only an adult (*ish*) shares. So the positive inference — anyone fit to eat does receive a portion — fails in the case of the *katan*. The *gemara*'s response is *ha lo katani* — the *mishnah* does not make that inference. Read only what the *mishnah* explicitly says: unfit to eat does not receive a portion. Do not infer its reverse. The *katan* who is fit to eat but still does not receive a portion is not a contradiction — it simply means the positive inference should not be drawn.

The *gemara* then considers whether one could return to the *avodah* reading and similarly say *ha lo katani* — just read it as the explicit statement and not the inference. If unfit for *avodah* does not receive a portion, one does not infer that fit for *avodah* always does. The cases of *kohen gadol onen* and *tamei bekorbanos tzibur* — who are fit for *avodah* yet do not receive a portion — would then be read as the non-inferred cases, not as contradictions. But the problem remains: if one reads the *mishnah* as being about *avodah*, then the *ba'al mum* — who is unfit for *avodah* yet does receive a portion — is a genuine exception to the explicit statement itself, not merely to its inference. *Rachmana rabyei* — the Torah specially included him. If one reads the *mishnah* as being about *achilah*, the *ba'al mum* is not an exception at all. This is why the *achilah* reading is preferable.

---

## Tumah Tahara

### Dam Status

The *mishnah* turns to the question of *tumah* and *tahara* and when a *kohen*'s status is assessed for purposes of portion entitlement. The *mishnah* states: even if a *kohen* was *tamei* at the time of *zerikat ha-dam* — the throwing of the blood — and became *tahor* by the time of *haktar ha-chalavim* — the burning of the fat — he does not receive a portion. The key moment is the *dam*. Conversely, a *kohen* who was *tahor* at the *dam* and *tamei* at the *haktar ha-chalavim* does receive a portion — the *mishnah* implies *cholek*, he shares.

### Abba Shaul

The *gemara* notes: *matnitin delo ke-Abba Shaul* — our *mishnah* does not follow the position of Abba Shaul. For Abba Shaul holds more stringently: *le'olam eino ochel ad she-yeheh tahor mi-she'at zrikah ve-ad she'at haktar ha-chalavim* — a *kohen* must be *tahor* at both the *dam* and the *chalavim* in order to receive a portion. The proof text is *ha-makriv et dam ha-shelamim ve-et ha-chelev* — the verse links blood and fat together, implying both must be performed by someone in a state of *tahara*. The verse then continues: *lo tihyeh shok ha-yamin le-manah* — the right thigh shall be his portion — meaning only if he has performed both.

### Rav Ashi Query

Rav Ashi raises an unresolved question within Abba Shaul's position: *nitma beintayim mahu?* — what if the *kohen* was *tahor* at the *dam*, became *tamei* in between, immersed in a *mikveh*, had *haarev shemesh*, and was again *tahor* by the time of *haktar ha-chalavim*, which is performed at night? Is Abba Shaul's requirement satisfied — *bishat zrikah uvishat haktara beinun*, you only need *tahara* at those two points, and both are present — or does Abba Shaul require an unbroken *tahara* throughout the entire interval from *zrikah* to *haktar ha-chalavim*? The *gemara* leaves this as *teiku* — unresolved.

---

## Tvul Yom Plea

### Mincha Request

Rava introduces a teaching: *hai dina de-Rabbi Eliezer berbi Shimon gmirna* — the following line of reasoning I learned from Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Shimon. He adds that Rabbi Eliezer told him he worked it out *be-veit ha-kisei* — in the bathroom, a detail the *gemara* will return to.

The discussion concerns the *tvul yom* — a *kohen* who has immersed in a *mikveh* that day but has not yet had *haarev shemesh* and is therefore still in a transitional state of *tumah*. Rather than presenting the rules abstractly, the *gemara* frames it as a drama: the *tvul yom* comes before his fellow *kohanim* and makes a series of requests for portions, each of which is refused via a *kal va-chomer*.

The *tvul yom* begins: *tenu li min ha-minchah ve-ochel* — give me a portion of the *minchah* and I will eat. His fellow *kohen* responds with a *kal va-chomer*: in the world of *chatas*, you — the *tvul yom* — have stronger entitlement. Why? Because when a *kohen* brings his own *chatas*, the meat belongs to him, rather than being divided among the *kohanim* of the *mishmar*. Despite that stronger position, we know that when a *tamei kohen* cannot participate in a *chatas* of a *yisrael*, he receives no portion. Now in the world of *minchah*, your position is even weaker — a *kohen*'s own *minchah* is entirely burned; no *kohen* eats from his own *minchah* at all. *Eino din she-adichacha mi-minchat Yisrael?* — how much more so should I be able to push you away from a *yisrael*'s *minchah*?

The *tvul yom* pushes back: perhaps you were able to exclude me from a *chatas* precisely because in that world your rights were stronger as well as mine. But by a *minchah*, where *my* rights are weaker, *your* rights are also weaker — so perhaps we are on more equal footing and you cannot exclude me. The *gemara* then says: this is why the verse *v'ha-kohen ha-makriv osah lo tihyeh* — the *kohen* who brings it, it shall be his — is needed specifically for the *minchah*. It teaches that even in the *minchah* context, the rule applies: *bo hakrev ve-echol* — come forward and perform the *avodah*, then you may eat. Since the *tvul yom* cannot perform the *avodah*, he receives no portion.

### Chatas Pivot

The *tvul yom*, denied a *minchah* portion, now pivots: *ten li mi-chatas Yisrael ve-ochel* — at least give me a portion of a *yisrael*'s *chatas*. His fellow *kohen* now turns the *kal va-chomer* around: if I was able to exclude you from a *minchah* even though my rights there are weak, in the world of *chatas* where my rights are strong — *makom she-yafeh kochi b'chatasi* — how much more so can I exclude you. The *tvul yom* again deflects: you could exclude me from the *minchah* precisely because your rights and mine were both weak. In the *chatas* world, yes, your rights are stronger — but so are mine. Perhaps the stronger rights on both sides means you cannot push me away. This is why a verse is needed for *chatas* as well: *ha-kohen ha-mechate osah yochlena* — the *kohen* who performs the *chatas avodah* shall eat it. *Bo chatei ve-echol* — come and perform the *avodah*, then you may eat.

### Shelamim Request

Denied again, the *tvul yom* makes a final request: *ten li me-chaze ve-shok ve-ochel* — give me the breast and the thigh of the *shelamim*. His fellow *kohen* responds: if I was able to push you away from a *chatas* where you have stronger rights, in the world of *shelamim* where your rights are weaker — *she-ein lecha bahen ela chaze ve-shok*, all you receive are the breast and the thigh — how much more so should I be able to exclude you? The *tvul yom* replies: perhaps you could exclude me from *chatas* because my rights and yours were both weaker with respect to *nashi ve-avadai* — in *chatas*, a *kohen* cannot give his portion to his wife and household servants. But in *shelamim*, even though I receive less meat, I have broader rights in what I do receive — I can share it with my wife and slaves. So perhaps the enhanced quality of my rights in *shelamim* means you cannot push me away. A third verse is therefore needed: *la-kohen ha-mazrek et dam ha-shelamim lo yihyeh* — it shall belong to the *kohen* who throws the blood of the *shelamim*. *Bo zerok ve-echol* — come and throw the blood, then you eat.

### Dejected Exit

*Yatza tvul yom* — the *tvul yom* walks out. The image is vivid: he leaves despondent, *kal va-chomer al rosho* — the weight of all the *kal va-chomer* arguments piled upon his head. Walking alongside him, *onein mi-yimino, mechusar kippurim mi-smolo* — the *onen* on his right, the *mechusar kippurim* on his left — all of them together, dejected, having tried every avenue and been turned away at each one.

---

## Rav Achai Bechor

### Bechor Question

Rav Achai poses a challenge: why did the *tvul yom* not also request a portion of a *bechor*? That would open yet another *kal va-chomer*. His fellow *kohen* could say: if I was able to exclude you from a *chatas* where your rights are weaker — you cannot share it with your wife and household — how much more so can I exclude you from a *bechor*, where my rights are at their strongest: *de-chulo dilei*, the entire *bechor* belongs to me alone. The *tvul yom* could retort: you could exclude me from *chatas* because your rights and mine were equally weaker there; in a *bechor*, just as your rights are stronger, so too mine are stronger — so perhaps you cannot exclude me. And then the verse would respond: *es damam tizrok al ha-mizbeach ve-es chelbam taktir u-vesaram yihyeh lach* — it belongs to you only when you perform the *dam* and the *chelev*. *Bo zerok ve-echol*.

The question is slightly odd, as Rashi notes: a *bechor* is not divided among the *kohanim* of the *mishmar* — it is given directly by the owner to whichever *kohen* he chooses. So the entire framing of the *tvul yom* requesting a share from the group does not quite fit the *bechor* case.

### Tosafot Achai

Tosafot raises a broader academic observation: *be-chol makom leshona meshuna* — in every instance where Rav Achai appears with a *perach* or a *pashit*, his language is somehow unusual or slightly off. Tosafot cites this pattern as it appears at the beginning of Kesuvot as well. Based on this pattern, Tosafot's teacher Rabbeinu Shmuel suggested that the Rav Achai in these passages is in fact Rav Achai Gaon — the same Rav Achai who authored the *She'iltos* — and that the *Rabbanan Savorai* recorded that his words appear *basar Ravina ve-Rav Ashi*, after the main redaction of the *gemara*. The implication is that Rav Achai Gaon's glosses were written into the margins and subsequently incorporated into the body of the text. Tosafot does note a complication: in Kesuvot, Rav Ashi appears to respond to Rav Achai's question, which would argue against Rav Achai being post-redactional there. The observation is recorded as an interesting textual and historical note without final resolution.

---

## Bathroom Torah

### Bathroom Question

The *gemara* closes with a question that arises from Rava's earlier attribution: he said the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Shimon was worked out *be-veit ha-kisei* — in the bathroom. But how could Rabbi Eliezer contemplate Torah there?

### Bathhouse Prohibition

The answer comes from a statement of Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *be-chol makom mutar le-harhir chutz mi-merchatz u-mi-beit ha-kisei* — contemplation of Torah is permitted in every place except the bathhouse and the bathroom. The *gemara*'s resolution: *le-onsho shani* — if one cannot control it, that is different. Sometimes the mind simply cannot be stopped. Torah enters unbidden.

### Torah vs Korbanot

This closing episode frames the entire discussion in a way that is worth dwelling upon. Throughout this *sugya*, the world of *korbanos* has been defined by rigid boundaries: who is included, who is excluded, who may approach and who must stand back. The *tvul yom*, the *onen*, the *mechusar kippurim* — each one is denied access. The *ba'al mum* gets a portion but cannot perform *avodah*. The sacred geography of *korbanos* is one of strict demarcation, of people being turned away, of entitlement carefully parceled out and withheld.

Torah, by contrast, transgresses every boundary. It enters even the bathroom — the place most removed from sanctity, the place from which Torah is explicitly supposed to be excluded. And not only does it enter, but the insight generated there is transmitted and becomes *halacha*. The contrast is stark: *korbanos* is a world of exclusion, of limited and bounded sacred space. Torah is a force that cannot be contained, that finds its way everywhere, that keeps no one out.

---

---

# Zevachim 103

## Skin & Meat Entitlement

### Zachah Principle

The daf opens at the top of 103a, where the *mishnah* pivots from the question of who is entitled to portions of the meat to the closely related question of entitlement to the skin — the hide of the animal, which clearly represented significant monetary value. The *mishnah* establishes a foundational principle: *kol she-lo zachah ha-mizbeiach bi-vesarah, lo zachu ha-kohanim be-orah* — whenever the altar does not merit the flesh, the *kohanim* do not merit the skin.

The underlying assumption, which the *gemara* will make explicit, is that the skin is distributed together with the meat: just as a *kohen* who was *tamei* or otherwise disqualified from receiving meat loses his share in the meat, so too does he lose his share in the skin. The *mishnah* is therefore addressing a more fundamental question — namely, when do the *kohanim* as a class forfeit their collective entitlement to the skin entirely? In such cases, the skin would presumably be sold, with the proceeds going to the *Beis HaMikdash*.

The vehicle through which the question is understood is the *olah*, where the flesh belongs to the *mizbeiach* rather than to the *kohanim*. If something occurred to invalidate the sacrifice, so that the meat may not be placed on the altar at all, then the *kohanim* have no claim to the skin either.

### Psul Before Zerikah

Rashi clarifies the operative principle with precision: *kegon she-ira bo pasul kodem zerikah* — for instance, if an invalidation occurred before the blood was thrown. The paradigm case is *shechita* performed with a *piggul* intention. The concept of *zachah* here does not mean that the flesh was actually placed on the fire; it means that the flesh merited being placed on the fire. That determination is made at the moment of *zerikah* — for it is the throwing of the blood that renders the flesh eligible to be burned on the *mizbeiach*.
