If at the moment the blood was thrown the sacrifice was valid, then the *mizbeiach* was *zocheh* in the flesh — even if the flesh was never actually burned, as in a case of *nosar* where the meat was left over past its time. Conversely, if the sacrifice was invalidated before the blood was thrown, there was never a moment at which the meat could have ascended to the altar, and the *kohanim* therefore have no claim to the skin.

### Tame & Neveilah Cases

One might ask about cases where the invalidity is not inherent to the *korban* as such but has affected it contingently. For example: what if the entire flesh became *tamei* before the blood was thrown? That is not a structural defect in the *korban* in the way that *piggul* is — one could have imagined that only part of the meat became *tamei*, leaving the remainder valid. The *gemara* does not resolve this question here, and it is left aside.

The clearer cases are those of all-or-nothing invalidity. If the animal died on its own before *shechita* and became a *neveilah*, the meat was never eligible for the *mizbeiach*, and the *kohanim* do not receive the skin. On the other hand, if the entire meat became *tamei* after *zerikah*, the *mizbeiach* had already merited the flesh at the moment the blood was thrown. Remarkably, in such a case the *kohanim* do receive the skin. The procedure would be to first flay the animal — giving the skin to the *kohanim* — and only then burn the invalid meat. Similarly, if the meat became *nosar* after *zerikah*, the *mizbeiach* had already been *zocheh* in the flesh, and the *kohanim* retain their entitlement to the skin.

### Olat Ish Concept

The *mishnah* then derives this from the verse (Vayikra 7:8): *vehakohen hamakriv et olat ish or ha-olah asher hikriv lakohein lo yihyeh* — the skin of the *olah* that the *kohen* brings shall be his. The phrase *olat ish* — a person's *olah* — implies that the offering must have *counted for someone* at the time of *zerikah*.

However, this *derashah* sits in some tension with the subsequent ruling: *af al pi shelo altah libe'alim,orah la-kohanim* — even if the sacrifice was not counted toward the owner's obligation, the *kohanim* still receive the skin. This means that an *olah* slaughtered *shelo lishmah* — not for its proper designation — which is *kasher* but does not fulfill the owner's duty, still grants the *kohanim* their claim to the skin. This appears to cut against the *derashah* that the *korban* must have "counted for someone." What the *derashah* is really targeting is whether the *korban* was valid — not whether it was attributed to a specific individual. The *gemara* will explain how this is all reconciled through the interplay of the phrase *olat ish* with the alternative formulation *or ha-olah*.

The *mishnah* continues: *echad olat ha-ish ve-echad olat ha-ishah, oram la-kohanim* — whether it is a man's *olah* or a woman's, the *kohanim* receive the skin. The word *ish* in the verse is not to be read restrictively. *Orot kodashim kalim li-ve'alim* — skins of *kodashim kalim* such as *shelamim* go to the owners, who receive the meat. *Orot kodshei kodashim la-kohanim* — and the skins of *kodshei kodashim* go to the *kohanim*.

---

## Korban Types & Skin

### Distribution by Type

Having established that the *kohanim* receive the skin of an *olah* — despite the fact that the flesh itself goes entirely to the *mizbeiach* — the *mishnah* proceeds to address the other categories of *korbanot*. The rule is crisp: *orot kodashim kalim li-ve'alim* and *orot kodshei kodashim la-kohanim*. The owners of *kodashim kalim*, such as *shelamim*, receive the skin together with their portion of the flesh. The *kohanim*, who receive the flesh of *kodshei kodashim* such as *chatat* and *asham*, likewise receive the skin.

### Lev 7:8 Citation

The source for the *kohanim*'s entitlement to the skin of the *olah* is the verse in Vayikra 7:8: *vehakohen hamakriv et olat ish, or ha-olah asher hikriv, lakohein lo yihyeh* — the *kohen* who offers a person's *olah*: the skin of the *olah* that he has brought shall be his. The verse specifies only the *olah*, yet the *mishnah* extends the ruling to *kodshei kodashim* as well. This extension requires justification, which the *mishnah* provides through a *kal vachomer*.

### Kal Vachomer Logic

The *kal vachomer* reasoning embedded in the *mishnah* is striking for appearing in this form in a *mishnah* itself: *umah im olah shelo zachah bi-vesarah zachah be-orah* — if even by an *olah*, where the *kohanim* do not receive the flesh (since it goes entirely to the *mizbeiach*), they nonetheless receive the skin, then *kodshei kodashim* — where the *kohanim* do receive the flesh of a *chatat* or *asham* — is it not all the more so clear that they should receive the skin?

### Mizbeiach Counterpoint

One might attempt to refute this *kal vachomer* by pointing to the *mizbeiach* itself: the altar receives the flesh of the *olah* but not the skin — does this not demonstrate that one can receive flesh without necessarily receiving the corresponding skin? The *mishnah* preempts this: *ain mizbeiach yokhiach* — the *mizbeiach* is no proof. The *mizbeiach* never receives the skin under any circumstances. There is no halachic category in which the skin of an animal is burned on the *mizbeiach*. Therefore, the *mizbeiach* can say nothing about the relationship between entitlement to flesh and entitlement to skin. When we ask whether someone entitled to the flesh is also entitled to the skin, we consider only entities that can in principle receive the skin — and there the *kal vachomer* holds: if the *kohanim* receive the skin even where they have no claim to the flesh, they certainly receive it where they do have a claim to the flesh.

---

## Olat Ish Exclusions

### Olat Hekdesh Exclusion

A *baraisa* introduces two cryptic exclusions from the rule that the *kohanim* receive the skin. Rabbi Yehuda derives from the phrase *olat ish* — a person's *olah* — that the *halacha* applies only to a private individual's *olah*, excluding *olat ha-hekdesh*, an *olah* belonging to the Temple itself. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda reads the phrase differently and excludes *olat geirim* — the *olah* of converts. Both readings appear puzzling at first glance, and the *gemara* will clarify them.

Regarding *olat ha-hekdesh*: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef explains that the case in question is an *olah* that comes from *motarot* — surplus funds originally designated for an *asham* or *chatat*. The scenario is familiar: someone sanctified an *asham*, it became lost or otherwise unavailable, and they brought another; when the original was found, it was allowed to develop a blemish, redeemed, and the proceeds used for an *olah*. Similarly, surplus *chatat* funds — where money designated for a *chatat* was not entirely used, or where replacement funds were used and the original funds were found — would be redirected into an *olah*. These *olahs* are communal, belonging to the *Beis HaMikdash* treasury rather than to any private individual, and therefore the *kohanim* do not receive the skin from them; instead, the *Beis HaMikdash* retains it.

### Motarot Funds Debate

The *gemara* immediately notes a complication: this explanation works well according to the opinion that *motarot* — surplus *asham* and *chatat* funds — go toward communal *nidvas tzibbur* offerings. But what of the opinion that such funds go toward a private *nidvas yachid* offering? In that case, the *olah* brought from these repurposed funds is the individual's own private *olah*, not a communal one. If so, what is there to exclude?

Rava resolves this: the exclusion can still function, but it is derived not from the word *ish* contrasted with *hekdesh* (private versus communal), but from the word *ha-olah* — with the definite article. A parallel *derashah* exists: *ha-olah — olah rishonah*, meaning only the primary designation as an *olah* qualifies, not something that has been converted into an *olah* from redirected funds. Just as there is a *derashah* that the definite article in *ha-olah* indicates the primacy of the *olat tamid*, so here it teaches that the *kohanim*'s entitlement to the skin applies only to an *olah* originally sanctified as such — not one that is an *olah* only because the designated funds were repurposed. Even if the repurposed *olah* is technically that person's private offering, since it derives from funds diverted from a different purpose, the *halacha* granting the *kohanim* the skin does not apply. In such a case, the *Beis HaMikdash* retains the skin.

The *gemara* also confirms: when the *baraisa* discusses six of the Temple's thirteen donation chests being used for such *motarot* funds, Rabbi Yehuda adds parenthetically that the *kohanim* do not receive the skin of those communal *olahs*. This is the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

However, Rabbi Nechemia — or, according to another version, Rabbi Shimon — challenges Rabbi Yehuda: if so, you have nullified the *midrash* of Yehoyada HaKohen, the ruling derived from the verse in the narrative of Yehoyada the *kohen* during the First Temple period. The verse reads: *kesef asham ve-chesef chatat lo yuva Beis Hashem, la-kohanim yihyu* — the money of the *asham* and the money of the *chatat* shall not be brought into the House of God; it shall belong to the *kohanim*. This implies that even when the funds of an *asham* or *chatat* are redirected, the *kohanim* still receive a portion.

The *gemara* provides the *midrash* of Yehoyada HaKohen: *asham hu asham asham la-Hashem* — the verse in the Torah speaks of the *asham* as both belonging to a person and as an *asham* to God. When the *asham* funds are repurposed into an *olah*, the flesh becomes God's (*asham la-Hashem*), but the skin — *orah la-kohanim*. The communal *olahs* funded by *motarot* are described as *basar la-Shem* and *or la-kohanim*, affirming that even communal *olah* offerings generated from repurposed *asham* or *chatat* funds grant the *kohanim* the skin.

In the face of this challenge, Rabbi Yehuda apparently fell silent and retracted his position. Rav Nachman accordingly needs a different reading of *olat ha-hekdesh*.

### Bedek Habayis Sanctifica…

Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yannai offers a distinct case. *Prat l'matfis olah l'vedek ha-bayis* — the exclusion applies to a case where someone sanctified an animal as an *olah* and then, on top of that, additionally sanctified it as a gift to the Temple treasury (*bedek ha-bayis*). This seems paradoxical: if the animal is already an *olah*, what remains to give to the temple treasury? Everything is going onto the *mizbeiach*. Is the second sanctification even meaningful? The *gemara* explains that the standard practice is to redeem the animal before it is slaughtered — the person would pay the animal's value to the *Beis HaMikdash*, and the animal would then proceed to be offered as an *olah*. But the question is whether, biblically, the second sanctification accomplished anything at all.

### Skin Ownership After Red…

The *gemara* now analyzes the skin's status with particular care. There are two positions regarding whether *kodshei vedek ha-bayis* — the sanctification for the Temple treasury — takes halachic effect when the animal was already an *olah*:

According to the view that *kedushas bedek ha-bayis* does take hold biblically (*tafsei mid'oraisa*), then the animal genuinely belongs to the Temple Treasury at some point, and this is sufficient to remove the skin from the *kohanim*'s entitlement.

But even according to the view that *kedushas bedek ha-bayis* does not take hold biblically in such a case, the *gemara* points out: *hani mili basar, aval or tafis* — that limitation applies only to the flesh, which was already consecrated as an *olah* and heading to the *mizbeiach*. The skin, however, is a different matter. When an animal is consecrated as an *olah*, it is the interior — the flesh — that is the *olah*. The skin surrounding it is not itself the *olah*; it is the skin of an *olah*, which will be given to the *kohanim* once the sacrifice is completed. Since the skin is not yet the *olah* at the time the animal is walking around before *shechita*, it can be sanctified to *bedek ha-bayis* even according to the more restrictive view. Therefore, when this person subsequently sanctified the animal to *bedek ha-bayis*, the skin — still part of the live animal — was validly acquired by the Temple Treasury.

The striking implication, as the *gemara* develops it, is that even after the animal has been redeemed, slaughtered, and offered — even after the act of redemption that preceded the *shechita* — since there was a moment at which the skin was owned by the Temple Treasury, the *kohanim* do not receive it. This is the *chiddush*: it is not only that one could slaughter the animal with the skin already designated for *bedek ha-bayis* (which would be obvious), but that even once the formal process of redemption and *shechita* has occurred, the prior ownership by *bedek ha-bayis* is sufficient to deny the *kohanim* their usual entitlement.

Rav Nachman accordingly locates *olat ha-hekdesh* — the *olah* whose skin goes to the Temple rather than the *kohanim* — in this second scenario: an animal sanctified as an *olah* with a subsequent *hekdesh* to *bedek ha-bayis*. The first scenario (communal *olahs* from *motarot*) is disqualified as a reading, since we have established that even communal *olahs* grant the *kohanim* the skin, per the *midrash* of Yehoyada HaKohen.

In fact, as the *gemara* makes clear, Rav Nachman concludes that the correct reading is altogether elsewhere: *mukmina lah b'makdish nechasav v'aliba d'Rabbi Yehoshua* — we locate the case in the scenario of one who sanctifies all his property (*hamakdish nechasav*), following Rabbi Yehoshua's position. That scenario is the subject of the next section.

---

## Property Sanctification

### Hamakdish Nechasav

The *mishnah* introduces the case of *hamakdish nechasav* — one who sanctifies all his property. If among his possessions were unblemished animals capable of serving as *korbanot*, what is their status? On the one hand, the general declaration of sanctification (*hakdashah*) is conventionally understood as dedicating property to *bedek ha-bayis* — the Temple treasury. On the other hand, these animals are fit for the *mizbeiach*, and one might interpret the sanctification differently with respect to them.

### R. Eliezer View

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *zecharim yimachru li-tzorchei olos* — the males shall be sold to those who need to bring *olahs*, and *nekevos yimachru li-tzorchei zivchei shelamim* — the females shall be sold to those who need to bring *shelamim*. The animals remain under the Temple's ownership, but because they are unblemished and consecrable, the *hekdesh* will not simply sell them for non-sacrificial use. Instead, the Temple will sell them at a discount to individuals already obligated to bring those respective *korbanot*, with the condition that the purchaser commits to using them for the appropriate offering. The Temple thus receives the sale proceeds into its treasury, and the animals still end up being offered on the *mizbeiach* as intended. *Ve-demeihem yiplu im she'ar nechasim le-vedek ha-bayis* — the proceeds of these sales join the rest of the dedicated funds in the Temple treasury.

### R. Yehoshua View

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees and reads the act of sanctification contextually. Although the same word — *makdish* — is used for all the property, its meaning is determined by the nature of the object being sanctified. For one's house, furniture, or other chattels, *makdish* means dedicating to the treasury. For unblemished male animals, Rabbi Yehoshua reads *makdish* as sanctifying them as an *olah* outright: *zecharim atzman yikrevu olos* — the males themselves shall be offered as *olahs*. This contextual interpretation tracks the principle that the word *makdish* always conveys dedication to the Temple in some sense; for an *olah*, however, the property goes entirely to the Temple through the *mizbeiach* rather than through the treasury.

The females present a difficulty. One might suggest they are sanctified as *shelamim*, but that would mean the owner retains much of the meat — which is insufficiently "Temple-oriented" to be consistent with the declared intent to sanctify everything. Rabbi Yehoshua therefore holds: *yimachru li-tzorchei shelamim*, they are sold to those needing to bring *shelamim*. But unlike Rabbi Eliezer, who deposits those proceeds in the treasury, Rabbi Yehoshua holds *ve-yavi bi-demeihem olos* — the proceeds are themselves used to bring *olahs*. The word *makdish*, even for the females, carries the sense of directing toward an *olah* in the fullest possible way: the females cannot be *olahs* themselves, but their proceeds become *olahs*. The rest of the property — the house, the car, the non-animal assets — *yiplu le-vedek ha-bayis*, falls to the Temple treasury.

### Skin as Bedek Habayis

Even according to Rabbi Yehoshua, who reads the sanctification of unblemished males as an *olah*, there is a significant qualification: *hani mili basar, aval or tafis* — that reading applies to the flesh, but the skin is still captured by *bedek ha-bayis*.

The logic is as follows. When the person said "I am sanctifying everything," every item defaulted to *bedek ha-bayis* unless contextual interpretation overrode it. For unblemished males, the contextual interpretation redirected the flesh to the *mizbeiach* as an *olah*. But as noted above in the context of Rabbi Yannai's ruling, the skin of a living animal designated as an *olah* is not itself the *olah* — it is the skin surrounding the *olah*. Therefore, the original force of the declaration — *bedek ha-bayis* — extends as far as it can, and it reaches the skin. Only when the contextual interpretation is at its strongest — with respect to the flesh heading to the *mizbeiach* — does it override the default. The skin, which was never explicitly covered by the contextual reinterpretation, remains dedicated to *bedek ha-bayis*.

This, then, is the case of *olat ha-hekdesh* that excludes the *kohanim* from receiving the skin: not a communal *olah* from *motarot* (which the *midrash* of Yehoyada HaKohen shows does grant the *kohanim* the skin), not merely an animal with a double sanctification (though that works too under Rabbi Yannai's ruling), but specifically the case of *hamakdish nechasav* according to Rabbi Yehoshua, where the default dedication to *bedek ha-bayis* applies to the skin even as the flesh is redirected toward the *mizbeiach*.

Summarizing the three possible accounts of *olat ha-hekdesh*: the simplest reading — that it refers to communal *olahs* from surplus *chatat* and *asham* funds — was rejected because Yehoyada HaKohen's *midrash* shows that even those *olahs* grant the *kohanim* the skin. The remaining two positions are variations on a single theme: an animal is an *olah* but the skin is *bedek ha-bayis*. This can arise either because an already-consecrated *olah* was subsequently dedicated to *bedek ha-bayis* (per Rabbi Yannai), or because a general sanctification of all property was contextually interpreted as an *olah* for the flesh but as *bedek ha-bayis* for the skin (per Rabbi Yehoshua's reading of *hamakdish nechasav*).

---

## Ish Filtering & Merit

### Ish Inclusivity

A *baraisa* now addresses the word *ish* in *olat ish* directly. The verse specifies an *olat ish* — a man's *olah*. Does this exclude women, slaves, and converts from granting the *kohanim* their skin entitlement? The *baraisa* states: *ein li ela olat ish* — I might have thought only a man's *olah* qualifies. How do I include women's and slaves' *olahs*? The verse adds *or ha-olah* — the skin of the *olah* — using the definite article and dropping the word *ish*, thereby broadening the scope: any *olah*, regardless of who brought it, grants the *kohanim* the skin. The word *ish* is thus not a restriction on who brings the *olah* in terms of the person's category — women, slaves, and converts are all included.

### Olah She'alah L'ish

If so, what work does the word *ish* do? The *baraisa* answers: *olah she-altah le-ish* — the *olah* must have counted as a valid offering for a person. The *ish* language introduces a qualitative criterion, not a categorical one. It must have been a legitimate, valid *korban* at the time of *zerikah*. *Prat she-nishchata chutz li-zmanah ve-chutz li-mkomah* — this excludes an *olah* slaughtered with an intention that renders it *piggul*. Such an offering, though it goes through the motions, never truly "counted" for anyone, and the *kohanim* do not receive the skin.

### Shelo Lishmah Challenge

This raises a further question: if *olah she-altah le-ish* is the operative criterion, then perhaps an *olah* slaughtered *shelo lishmah* — not for its designated name — should likewise be excluded? Such an *olah* is *kasher* and fulfills the technical requirements of the service, but it does not count toward the owner's obligation. One might argue that it too has not "counted" for the person in the relevant sense.

### Or Ha'olah Principle

The *baraisa* counters with the verse's second formulation: *or ha-olah* — the skin of the *olah*, without the limiting word *ish*. This phrase teaches that any valid *olah*, regardless of whether it was attributed to a specific person's obligation, grants the *kohanim* the skin. The interplay between *olat ish* and *or ha-olah* is thus precise: the former excludes genuinely invalid *korbanot* (like *piggul*); the latter restores entitlement for offerings that are valid but not credited to anyone. The real exclusion, in other words, is invalidity — not lack of attribution. As long as the *korban* was a legitimate *olah*, the *kohanim* receive the skin, even if it was offered *shelo lishmah*.

---

## Rabbi Yishmael Position

### Asher Hikriv Drasha

A further *baraisa* addresses the derivation of *kohanim*'s skin rights for *kodshei kodashim*. The *tanna kamma* derives this from the phrase *asher hikriv* — "that he brought" — which appears in the verse alongside *or ha-olah*. The force of *asher hikriv* broadens the rule beyond *olah* to any *korban* one brings. This is then balanced against the word *olah* to limit the extension to offerings that are *olah*-like in status — specifically, *kodshei kodashim*.

### Natural Unity Assumption

Rabbi Yishmael proposes instead a *kal vachomer*: if the *kohanim* receive the skin of an *olah* — where they have no entitlement to the flesh — then *kodshei kodashim*, where they do receive the flesh, certainly grant them the skin as well. This does not require *asher hikriv* as a textual source; logic alone suffices. Rabbi Yishmael then uses *asher hikriv* for a different purpose, which we will encounter shortly.

### Flesh-Skin Unity Examples

Rabbi (Rebbi) goes further still. For him, the premise that skin follows flesh is not derived at all — it is simply the natural baseline. The *Torah* treats the skin as part of the same unit as the flesh unless it explicitly separates them. This assumption is bolstered by the cases of *parim ha-nisrafim* — the inner *chata'ot* whose carcasses are burned outside the *Beis HaMikdash* — where the *Torah* explicitly states that they are burned along with their skins. For *chatat*, *asham*, and *zivchei shalmei tzibbur* — offerings where the *matanah* goes to the *kohen* — since the *Torah* never instructs flaying, the skin goes together with the flesh as a matter of course. The *kohanim* receive the entire carcass and may choose whether to flay it themselves or eat it as-is off the skin.

Similarly for *kodashim kalim* belonging to the owners: since the *Torah* never mandates flaying, the owners receive the full animal including its skin and may handle it as they see fit.

### Rabbi's Specification Vi…

According to Rabbi, the only case requiring explicit *Torah* specification is the *olah*, where the verse *ve-hifshit et ha-olah ve-nitteach otah li-netacheha* — flay the *olah* and cut it into its pieces — actively separates the skin from the flesh. Once separated, one might not have known what to do with the skin. Therefore the *Torah* states explicitly: *or ha-olah asher hikriv la-kohen ha-makriv otah lo yihyeh* — the skin of the *olah* that was brought belongs to the *kohen* who offered it. That verse was needed only for the *olah*. Everything else follows automatically from the baseline assumption that skin accompanies flesh.

---

## Service Fitness Requirem…

### Excluded Categories

The section of the *baraisa* that addresses who among the *kohanim* is entitled to the skin is anchored in the verse *ve-ha-kohen ha-makriv et olat ish* — the *kohen* who brings the *olah*. This phrase links the entitlement to the capacity to perform the service (*avodah*). A *tuvul yom* (one who immersed that day but whose purification is not yet complete), an *onen* (one in acute mourning before burial), and a *mechusar kipurim* (one who still lacks atonement) are excluded from receiving their portion.

### Consumption vs. Non-Cons…

One might have thought the exclusion applied only to the meat — since the disqualification of these *kohanim* from service is related to their inability to eat consecrated food — but that perhaps they retain a claim to the skin, which is not for consumption. The *baraisa* counters with the phrase *lo yihyeh*: it is the *kohen ha-makriv* — the one fit to perform the service — who receives the skin, just as he receives the meat. The fitness requirement for the skin tracks the fitness requirement for the *avodah*, not the fitness for *achilah*. A *kohen* unfit to perform the service receives neither meat nor skin.

### Bones & Skin Rights

Rabbi Yishmael, who uses *asher hikriv* to exclude *tuvul yom*, *mechusar kipurim*, and *onen* (rather than deriving this from *lo yihyeh*), has a use for *lo yihyeh* instead. Rabbi Yochanan reports in his name: *ne'emar be-olah lo yihyeh ve-ne'emar be-asham lo yihyeh* — the phrase *lo yihyeh* appears in the verse about the *olah* and also in the verse about the *asham*. This verbal parallel creates a *gezeirah shavah* linking the two. Just as with an *asham* the *kohen* receives the flesh and therefore obviously keeps the bones as well, so too with the *olah* — even though the flesh goes to the *mizbeiach* — *atzmotav mutarim*, the bones are permitted to the *kohen*. The *kohen* may take home the bones of the *olah* and make use of them.

The *lo yihyeh* in the *olah* verse is indeed superfluous (*mufni*), since the verse already establishes the *kohen*'s entitlement to the skin. Were it not superfluous, a logical challenge would block the *gezeirah shavah*: the *asham* entitles the *kohen* to eat the flesh, and naturally its bones too; the *olah*, where the *kohen* receives no flesh, should presumably not entitle him to the bones. But since *lo yihyeh* is an extra word, it forges the connection despite the logical asymmetry — teaching that not only does the *kohen* receive the skin of the *olah*, but the bones as well.

---

## Timing of Skin Entitleme…

### Psul Before/After Flaying

The subsequent *mishnah* introduces a different framework for determining when the *kohanim* lose their skin entitlement. Rather than focusing on whether the invalidity occurred before or after *zerikah* — which was the implicit standard of the earlier *mishnah* — this *mishnah* makes the pivotal moment the act of *hefshot*, the flaying itself. *Kol ha-kodashim she-ira bahem pasul kodem le-hefshetan* — all consecrated animals that became invalid before they were flayed: *einam la-kohanim*, the *kohanim* do not receive the skin. *Le-achar hefshatan* — if they became invalid after they were flayed: *hareiy hen shel kohanim*, the skin belongs to the *kohanim*.

The logic underlying this framework is that as long as the skin is still attached to the flesh, they form a single unit. If the *korban* becomes invalid while the skin is still on, the skin shares the fate of the flesh. Once the skin has been physically separated through flaying, it is an independent entity, and any subsequent invalidity of the flesh does not retroactively affect the skin's status.

### R. Chanina Sgan View

Rabbi Chanina Sgan Hakohanim — the deputy *kohen gadol* — testifies: *miyamai lo ra'iti or she-yetzei le-veis ha-sreifah* — in all my days in the Temple, I never saw a flayed skin taken out to be burned. This testimony is significant because it implies that the *mishnah*'s framework is correct: once a skin has been flayed, it always goes to the *kohanim*, never to the fire. The expected consequence of an invalid *korban* — burning the flesh — never extended to a separately flayed skin.

One might assume Rabbi Chanina Sgan Hakohanim is simply affirming the *mishnah*'s position. The *gemara*, however, identifies a deeper *chiddush* in his testimony. The *tanna kamma* of the *mishnah* holds that if an invalidity is discovered after flaying that was actually present from *before* the flaying — for instance, an animal was flayed and only then discovered to have been a *treifah* — the skin would be burned, since the invalidity predates the flaying. Rabbi Chanina Sgan Hakohanim disagrees: once a skin has been physically flayed and separated, the *kohanim* receive it regardless of when the invalidity occurred. Rabbi Akiva makes this explicit: *midvarav lamadnu she-ha-mafshit et ha-bechor ve-nimtza treifah, she-yoshu ha-kohanim ha-or* — from his words we derive that if one flays a *bechor* and it is then discovered to have been a *treifah*, the *kohanim* may still use the skin.

Thus the *mishnah* and Rabbi Chanina Sgan Hakohanim represent two distinct positions: the *mishnah* focuses on when the invalidity *existed* (before or after flaying), while Rabbi Chanina Sgan Hakohanim focuses on the physical act of separation — once separated, the skin is always the *kohanim*'s.

### Chachamim Counterpoint

The *chachamim* push back against Rabbi Chanina Sgan Hakohanim's proof from his personal experience: *ein lo ra'inu re'aya* — absence of evidence is not proof of absence. The fact that he never witnessed a separately flayed skin being burned does not establish that burning such a skin is halachically impossible or never occurred. Perhaps the scenario simply never arose during his tenure. The *chachamim* therefore maintain that if the invalidity was present before the flaying — even if discovered only after — the skin is burned along with the flesh: *yetzei le-veis ha-sreifah*.

### Zerikah vs. Flaying

This *mishnah*'s framework — invalidity before or after flaying — stands in apparent tension with the earlier *mishnah*'s framework, which made *zerikah* the operative moment. The earlier *mishnah* held: if the *korban* was invalid at the time the blood was thrown, the *kohanim* do not receive the skin; if valid at *zerikah*, they do. This suggests that even if the skin had already been flayed before *zerikah* — a theoretically possible though practically unlikely sequence — the skin's fate is still determined by the validity of the *korban* at *zerikah*. The later *mishnah*, however, makes flaying the operative moment: if flayed before invalidity, the *kohanim* receive it.

The *gemara* formulates the contradiction directly: according to the earlier *mishnah*, even if the skin was flayed before *zerikah*, an invalid *zerikah* (such as *piggul*) would deny the *kohanim* the skin — *af al gav d'afshateih le-or kodem zerikah*. This is consistent with the position that the blood-throwing's validity or invalidity determines the skin's status, irrespective of flaying. The later *mishnah*, by contrast, would grant the *kohanim* the skin once it is flayed, even if the *zerikah* is then performed invalidly. How are these two *mishnahs* to be reconciled?

---

## Mishna Reconciliation

### Abaye's Synthesis

Abaye resolves the contradiction by reading both *mishnahs* as following the opinion of Rabbi (Rebbi). The truly decisive moment, according to Rabbi, is the flaying — and specifically, whether the invalidity occurred before or after the skin was physically separated. This is the position of the later *mishnah* taken at face value.

The earlier *mishnah*'s formulation — focusing on the time of *zerikah* — does not contradict this. Rabbi concedes (*u-modeh Rebbi*) that flaying does not in practice precede *zerikah*. Flaying an animal is a time-consuming process; *zerikah* is essentially instantaneous. It would be entirely inappropriate to catch the blood and then wait for the animal to be flayed before throwing it. In the real world of Temple service, *zerikah* always comes first. Therefore, for all practical purposes, the time of *zerikah* and the question of whether the animal has been flayed are coextensive: if it was invalid at *zerikah*, it had not yet been flayed and the skin is not the *kohanim*'s; if it was valid at *zerikah*, flaying will follow and the skin is theirs.

But the *ikar* — the underlying halachic principle — is that the flaying is what truly matters. There exists a theoretical scenario where someone threw the blood only after the animal had been flayed; in such a case, if the *zerikah* was invalid, the *kohanim* would nevertheless receive the skin, since the invalidity occurred after flaying. That scenario, while virtually impossible in practice, is the logical implication of Rabbi's true position.

### Rav's Synthesis

Rav reads both *mishnahs* as following Rabbi Eliezer (Rabbi Eliezer ben Shimon), for whom the blood-throwing is the genuinely decisive moment. According to Rav, the language of the later *mishnah* — *kodem le-hefshetan* (before flaying) and *le-achar hefshetan* (after flaying) — is not to be taken literally. The phrases do not actually refer to the physical act of flaying. Rather, *kodem le-hefshetan* means before the *korban* reached the stage of readiness for flaying — that is, before *zerikah* — and *le-achar hefshetan* means after it reached that stage, i.e., after *zerikah*. The later *mishnah* is thus simply another way of expressing the same standard as the earlier one: validity at the time of *zerikah*.

The dispute therefore reduces to: does the truly operative moment track the physical separation of skin from flesh, or the legal moment of *zerikah* that renders the animal eligible for flaying? Abaye (following Rabbi) reads it as the former — with *zerikah* serving only as a practical proxy. Rav (following Rabbi Eliezer ben Shimon) reads it as the latter, with the language of flaying being metaphorical shorthand for *zerikah*-readiness. The *gemara* notes that this question will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Zevachim 104

## Skin & Meat Separation

### Intro: Physical Unity

The *mishnah* we are studying appears on 103b, and it shifts our focus from the question of which *kohanim* receive a portion of the meat to the question of who receives the *or* — the skin. The earlier *mishnah* had established that if the *mizbeach* is not *zocheh* in the *basar*, the *kohanim* do not receive the skin. The operative moment for the *mizbeach*'s entitlement to the meat of an *olah* is *zrikat hadam*: if the *korban* became invalid before the blood was sprinkled — as in the case of *pigul* — the *kohanim* do not receive the skin; if it became invalid afterward — for instance, the meat became *tamei* — they do, since the *mizbeach* had already acquired its entitlement to the meat.

Our *mishnah*, however, takes a strikingly different approach. It states: *kol hakodashim she'eira bahen pasul kodem lehefshetan ein oroteihem lakohanim* — all *kodashim* that became invalid before they were flayed, their skins do not go to the *kohanim*. The determining factor here is not *zrikat hadam* but physical unity: whether the skin and the meat still constitute a single, undivided entity. If the animal became invalid while still whole and unflayed, the skin follows the meat and is not given to the *kohanim*. If it became invalid after flaying — for example, the meat became *tamei* or was removed from the *Beit Hamikdash* — the skin and meat are already separate units, and *oroteihem lakohanim*: the *kohanim* do receive the skin. There is no mention of *zrikat hadam*; the sole criterion is whether the two are physically combined or apart.

This apparent contradiction with the earlier *mishnah* is what the *gemara* will now work to resolve.

### R. Chanina: No Separate…

The *mishnah* then cites a testimony from *Rebbe Chanina sgan hakohanim* — the deputy *kohen gadol*, a figure of considerable authority who was regularly present in the *Beit Hamikdash*. He states: *miyamai lo ra'iti or sheyotzei leveit hasreifa* — never in all my days did I see a skin taken out to the *beit hasreifa*. This is a remarkable testimony. It implies that in situations where the *korban* became invalid and the *kohanim* could not receive the skin, that skin would need to be ritually burned — yet he says he never witnessed this occurring with the skin alone, separately from the meat. As the *gemara* will emphasize, *zrikat hadam* is what permits the skin, and a skin belonging to an invalid *korban* retains its *kedusha* and must be burned rather than discarded or sold.

The *gemara* understands *Rebbe Chanina* as reaffirming the position of the *Tanna Kamma*: once the animal has been flayed, the skin will never thereafter become invalid on its own. He never saw the skin taken out separately to the *beit hasreifa* — though of course the skin was sometimes taken out still attached to the meat before flaying — because once flaying has occurred, the skin is already secure. This is a positive affirmation that the moment of flaying is the determining factor.

### R. Akiva's Inference

*Amar Rebbe Akiva*: from *Rebbe Chanina*'s words we can learn that if one flays a *bechor* and it is then discovered to be a *treifa*, *she'ye'outu hakohanim be'oro* — the *kohanim* are entitled to its skin. *Rebbe Akiva* takes one critical step further: what happens when the invalidity preceded the flaying, but was only discovered after the fact?

Consider the typical case: an animal is slaughtered, flayed, and then, while the *kohen* is eviscerating it and arranging the entrails for the *mizbeach*, he discovers a hole in the lung — a *treifa*. Most *treifot* are internal and invisible from the outside. The invalidity existed from before the animal was flayed. Yet since it was only discovered after flaying, does the skin still go to the *kohanim*?

*Rebbe Akiva* reasons from *Rebbe Chanina*'s statement: if *Rebbe Chanina* says the skin was never taken out separately to be burned, this must have encompassed even such cases. Because it is entirely possible — indeed, likely — that animals were slaughtered, blood was sprinkled, they were flayed, and then found to be *treifot*. Yet *Rebbe Chanina* says the skin was never taken out separately. The only coherent explanation is that the status of the skin is determined not by when the invalidity came into existence, but by when it was discovered. Since the *treifa* was discovered after flaying, the *kohanim* retain the skin. This is, as is frankly acknowledged, a counterintuitive *halacha*: since when does the moment of discovery govern? Nevertheless, this principle appears to apply specifically to the skin, which has an ambiguous status relative to the *korban* itself — the meat's invalidity does not automatically and retroactively divest the *kohanim* of what has already, in terms of timing, become theirs. One finds a partial analogue in the principle, discussed by the *Rosh*, that *bitul* in the laws of *kashrus* can in certain respects be conditioned on the moment of awareness.

Importantly, this discovery-based rule does not extend to the meat. If the blood was sprinkled and the animal was then found to be a *treifa*, one would not declare the *korban* valid on the grounds that the *treifa* was discovered only afterward. The rule applies solely to the skin, a further indication of the skin's unique, partly detached status vis-à-vis the *korban*.

### Sages Reject Proof

*Vachachamim omrim*: the *chachamim* respond with a pointed methodological objection — *lo reinu re'ayah*. The fact that *Rebbe Chanina* never witnessed a skin being burned separately proves nothing. Perhaps such cases were simply too infrequent, or occurred when he was not present. A man of great seniority and authority he may have been — the *sgan hakohanim* was unlike an ordinary *kohen* who served only two weeks a year, and so his testimony carries particular weight — yet the *chachamim* insist: absence of evidence is not evidence. One is reminded of the methodological dispute between the *Ba'al HaMaor* and the *Ramban*, where a similar argument was made that *lo ra'inu* proves nothing, to which the response was *kan ra'inu* — here, at least, we have seen it. The *chachamim* are not dismissing *mesora* as a category; they are simply refusing to draw halachic inferences from a negative observation. The skin, they maintain, goes to be burned whenever the invalidity existed before flaying — regardless of when it was discovered.

---

## Two Mishnayot Reconciled

### First Mishnah: Blood Sta…

The *gemara* now turns to the explicit tension between the two *mishnayot*. The earlier *mishnah* states: *kol shelo zachah mizbeach bvesarah lo zachu kohanim beorah* — wherever the *mizbeach* was not *zocheh* in the meat, the *kohanim* are not *zocheh* in the skin. And it adds: *ve-af al gav de'ifashtah le-or kodem zrikah* — even if the skin was flayed before *zrikah*, that is insufficient; the entitlement depends on *zrikat hadam*, not on flaying.

The *gemara* asks: whose opinion is that? It is *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* — and we will recall from earlier in the *masechet* that he is the one who said *ein adam meratzeh al ha-or bifnei atzmo*: one does not sprinkle the blood for the sake of the skin alone. By an *olah*, the purpose of the blood is to permit the meat to go on the *mizbeach*. If the meat became *tamei* and all that remains is the skin, one would not sprinkle the blood — and if one did, that sprinkling would not render the skin permissible. For *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*, the *mizbeach*'s entitlement and the *kohanim*'s entitlement are linked through *zrikat hadam*: *mishulchan gavoah zachu* — the *kohanim* receive only what derives from the *shulchan gavoah*'s own entitlement.

Now the *gemara* asks — *eima seifa* — let us look at the end of our *mishnah*. It states: *kol hakodashim she-hayu bahem p'sul kodem hefshetan eino osam lakohanim* — invalidity before flaying means no skin for the *kohanim*. And conversely, *le'achar hefshetan oram lakohanim* — after flaying, the *kohanim* are entitled to the skin. Importantly, this appears to apply even before the blood has been sprinkled: you flayed the animal, the meat became invalid, and even though *zrikat hadam* has not yet occurred — the *kohanim* are going to receive the skin. This is because, presumably, *zrikat hadam* will then be performed, and the skin's entitlement is secured. That sounds like *atya k'Rebbi* — it follows the view of *Rebbi*, who holds that *ha-dam meratzeh al ha-or bifnei atzmo*: the blood can work for the skin even when the meat is no longer present. So the *seifa* sounds like *Rebbi* and the *reisha* sounds like *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* — which creates a contradiction within the structure of the two *mishnayot*.

### Abaye's Reconciliation

*Amar Abaye*: since the *seifa* of the second *mishnah* follows *Rebbi*, the *reisha* — that is, the first *mishnah* — is also *Rebbi*. And *Rebbi* concedes: *she'ein hafshait kodem zrikah* — in normal practice, flaying does not precede *zrikah*. The procedure in the *Beit Hamikdash* was: slaughter, collect the blood, perform *zrikat hadam*, and only then process the meat, disembember the carcass, and flay the skin. In practice, the *kohanim* would never be entitled to the skin before *zrikat hadam* — not because *zrikat hadam* is the conceptual trigger, but because flaying always occurred after it. Thus when the first *mishnah* articulates the rule in terms of *zrikat hadam*, it is not establishing *zrikah* as the principled criterion; it is simply reflecting the practical reality that flaying always comes after *zrikat hadam*. The true principle is the moment of flaying, as stated in our *mishnah*, and the first *mishnah* is accurate only as a description of regular practice. Had someone flayed the animal before *zrikat hadam* — which never happened — our *mishnah*'s rule would govern, and the *kohanim* would receive the skin.

This reconciliation, it must be said, is somewhat counterintuitive. The first *mishnah* reads as though it is articulating a substantive principle about *zrikat hadam*, not merely describing a procedural sequence. But that is how *Abaye* reads it.

### Rava's Alternative

*Rava amar*: the opposite approach. Since the *reisha* of the two *mishnayot* reflects *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*, the *seifa* is also *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*. For him, *zrikat hadam* is the true criterion — and when our *mishnah* speaks of "before or after flaying," it does not mean the physical act of flaying literally. Rather, *kodem sheniru lehafshait, achar sheniru lehafshait* — "before or after it was appropriate to flay." And it is appropriate to flay only after *zrikat hadam*. Indeed, *Rava* goes further: according to *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*, one would never flay the skin prematurely precisely because the skin only acquires its independent status through the *basar* — it has no separate significance prior to *zrikat hadam*. Therefore, "before flaying" in our *mishnah* simply means before *zrikat hadam*, because that is the moment after which flaying becomes appropriate.

On this reading, both *mishnayot* articulate the same principle — *zrikat hadam* is determinative — and "before or after flaying" is merely an alternative formulation of the same idea. In the end, the two *mishnayot* appear to present genuinely different principles, and the *gemara* is working to read them in harmony with one opinion — though the most natural reading is that they represent different *tannaitic* positions: one that goes by *zrikat hadam* and one that goes by *hefshait*.

---

## Rebbi vs. R. Eliezer b.…

### Rebbi: Blood Works for S…

*De-tanya*: what exactly is the debate between *Rebbi* and *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*? *Rebbi omer*: *ha-dam meratzeh al ha-or bifnei atzmo* — the blood atones for, meaning renders permissible for the *kohanim*, the skin even when it stands alone. That is: after the skin has been flayed and is physically separate from the meat, if the meat became *tamei* or otherwise invalid, one may still sprinkle the blood and the *kohanim* receive the skin. Moreover — *u-k'shehu im habasar* — when the skin is still physically attached to the meat and not yet flayed, *nolad bo pasul bein kodem zrikah bein l'achar zrikah harei hu k'yotzei bo*: whether the invalidity arose before or after *zrikah*, as long as the skin was still joined to the meat, its status follows the meat's status entirely. This is a beautifully clear articulation of our *mishnah*'s principle: physical separation is everything. If the skin is a separate unit, the blood can work for it independently regardless of the meat's condition. If the skin is still part of the meat, it travels with the meat in every direction.

### R. E.b.S.: Blood Fails S…

*Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon omer*: *ein hadam meratzeh al ha-or bifnei atzmo* — the blood does not work for the skin by itself. Even when the skin has been physically separated through flaying, if the meat was already *tamei* or invalid at the time of *zrikat hadam*, the sprinkling does not help the skin. The reason is structural: by an *olah*, the function of *zrikat hadam* is to permit the meat to go on the *mizbeach*. If the meat is invalid, the blood is not being thrown for the sake of anything meaningful, and whatever status the sprinkling might confer on the skin is parasitic on the meat's validity. For *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*, the physical separation of skin from meat is irrelevant; what governs is the status of the meat at the moment of *zrikat hadam*. If the meat was valid when the blood was sprinkled — *hurtza basar sha'ah achat* — then even if the meat subsequently became invalid, *yafshitenu ve'oro lakohanim*: you flay it and the skin goes to the *kohanim*. If the meat was already invalid at the time of sprinkling, the skin does not go to the *kohanim* regardless of whether it has been flayed.

### Invalid Meat Application

In application, then: according to *Rebbi*, the question is whether the skin was physically separated from the meat at the point of invalidity. According to *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*, the question is whether the meat was valid at the moment of *zrikat hadam*. These are genuinely different principles, and each author, as the *gemara* notes, is the natural author of one of the two *mishnayot*. The most straightforward reading is that the two *mishnayot* simply represent these two positions, and the *gemara*'s attempts to read them as consistent — through *Abaye*'s and *Rava*'s reconciliations — are exercises in harmonization rather than reflections of the plain sense.

---

## R. Eliezer & R. Yeho (II)

### R. Yehoshua: Interdepend…

The *gemara* now asks whether the debate of *Rebbi* and *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* is rooted in an earlier dispute between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua*, which concerns the validity of the *korban* itself when the meat cannot be offered. The connecting *pasuk* is: *va'asita olotecha ha-basar veha-dam* — you shall perform your *olot*, the meat and the blood. *Rabbi Yehoshua* reads this as linking the two: *im ein dam ein basar, im ein basar ein dam*. Evidently if there is no blood there is no valid *korban*, since *zrikat hadam* is the essential act. But *Rabbi Yehoshua* goes further: if there is no meat, there is also no blood — that is, there is no point in sprinkling the blood of an *olah* if the meat cannot be placed on the *mizbeach*. Just as by a *pesach* the eating is so central that one would not bring it if unable to eat, so too by an *olah* there is a fundamental weight on the meat reaching the *mizbeach*, and if it cannot, one does not sprinkle the blood. The consequence, presumably, is that the *korban* is invalid, and the *kohanim* certainly do not receive the skin.

### R. Eliezer: Blood Indepe…

*Rabbi Eliezer omer*: *dam af al pi she'ein basar* — blood is independent of meat; you may and should sprinkle the blood even if the meat has become invalid. His source is *ve-dam zevachecha yishafech* — the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured — emphasizing the blood as an autonomous focus. The difficulty is that *zevachecha* normally does not refer to the *olah*, and the full verse continues *ve-habasar tochel*, which does connect the two — but *Rabbi Eliezer* reads the blood as having independent standing even for the *olah*. *Im kein ma talmud lomar va'asita olotecha ha-basar veha-dam*? That *pasuk* teaches something else: *mah dam bi-zrikah af basar bi-zrikah* — just as the blood is thrown upon the *mizbeach*, so too the meat is thrown. This teaches that there is a *revach* — a gap — between the *kevesh* and the *mizbeach*, from which the *kohen* would throw the pieces of meat.

---

## R. Eliezer & R. Yeho (II)

### Gemara Equations Debates

The *gemara* now proposes the equation: *leima*, let us say that *man d'amar hurtza* — the view that sprinkling the blood works for the skin even when the meat is invalid — follows *Rabbi Eliezer*, who holds the *korban* valid even without the meat; and *man d'amar lo hurtza* — the view that the *kohanim* do not receive the skin when the meat was invalid at the time of sprinkling — follows *Rabbi Yehoshua*, who says that without valid meat there is no valid blood. There is, however, an important caveat: the debate of *Rebbi* and *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* is not a debate about whether the *korban* is *kasher* — it simply assumes the *korban* is valid and asks who is entitled to the skin. The debate of *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* is about whether the *korban* itself is valid when the meat cannot be offered. These are different questions, and the *gemara* is really drawing a *kal vachomer* or a parallel rather than asserting strict identity: if the *korban* is invalid (*Rabbi Yehoshua*), then certainly the *kohanim* lose the skin; if it is valid (*Rabbi Eliezer*), then presumably the *kohanim* receive the skin — though the *gemara* acknowledges that even this is not ironclad, since there could be a technical rule relating skin entitlement to meat validity even within a *kasher korban*.

According to *Rabbi Eliezer*, the *gemara* says *kuli alma lo pligi* — all agree that the consequence of his position is that the *kohanim* receive the skin. The debate in the earlier *machlokes* only bears on what *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s position implies for the skin question.

---

## R. Yehoshua: L'chatchila…

### Rashi: L'chatchila/Bedia…

The *gemara* then addresses the crucial question: how could anyone hold that the *kohanim* receive the skin if *Rabbi Yehoshua* says the *korban* is invalid when there is no meat? The answer given is that *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s position must be understood as *lechatchila* rather than as an absolute invalidation. *Rashi* reads it this way: *lechatchila*, do not sprinkle the blood. Why would you? If the meat is already *tamei*, you cannot put it on the *mizbeach*. What would motivate the sprinkling? One might answer: to enable the *kohanim* to receive the skin. But *Rashi* reads the *gemara* as assuming that even if the blood is sprinkled *bediavad*, it works only to make the *korban kasher* in a technical sense, not to allow the owners to fulfill their *korban* obligation — a distinction introduced at the very opening of the *masechet*. Therefore, since there is nothing to be gained by the sprinkling — neither meat on the *mizbeach* nor fulfillment of the owner's obligation — *Rabbi Yehoshua* says *lechatchila* do not sprinkle.

### Meat Becomes Invalid Case

The *gemara* states that *Rabbi Yehoshua* says not to sprinkle the blood specifically *ela bevasar deleka pseda le-Kohanim* — in a case where the only thing at stake is the meat, and there is no prospective loss to the *kohanim*, since they have not yet acquired the skin. But *aval or de-ika pseda le-Kohanim* — when there is already a potential loss to the *kohanim* regarding the skin, meaning circumstances where if the blood is not sprinkled they will lose what might have been theirs — *afilu Rabbi Yehoshua modeh*, even *Rabbi Yehoshua* would concede. This is, frankly, a very strained reading of the *sugya*, and both *Rashi* and *Tosafot* acknowledge the difficulty. The plain sense of *ein basar ein dam* sounds like a categorical invalidation, not a *lechatchila* prohibition.

### R. Yehoshua Agrees Bedia…

That *Rabbi Yehoshua* does hold *bediavad* it works is established directly from a *mishnah*: *nitma basar o nifsul o sheyatza chutz lekla'im* — if the meat became *tamei*, or was otherwise invalidated, or left the *kla'im*: *Rabbi Eliezer omer yizrok* — *Rabbi Eliezer* says still sprinkle the blood. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer lo yizrok* — *Rabbi Yehoshua* says do not sprinkle. *U-modeh Rabbi Yehoshua she'im zarak hurtza* — but *Rabbi Yehoshua* concedes that if one did sprinkle, *bediavad* it worked. The language *hurtza* even suggests more than mere technical validity — it implies that the owners may even fulfill their obligation — which makes the earlier *gemara*'s reading even more complex. The *rishonim* resolve this by distinguishing between cases where the meat is present but invalid versus cases where it has been destroyed or lost entirely; *bediavad* validity applies only in the former category. The fundamental thrust, in any case, is that *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s position is a *lechatchila* prohibition, such that even his view can be reconciled with the position that the *kohanim* receive the skin when the blood was sprinkled under those circumstances.

---

## R. Chanina Reconsidered

### Burned Offerings Objecti…

The *gemara* returns to *Rebbe Chanina sgan hakohanim*'s statement that he never saw a skin taken out to be burned. An immediate objection is raised: *v'harei parim hanisrafim v'seirim hanisrafim* — what about the bulls and goats that are burned, like those of *Yom Kippur*, which are taken outside the *Beit Hamikdash* entirely and burned there? Surely their skins were burned as well.

### Separate Burning Clarifi…

*Mitzvatam lo kamina* — that is not what *Rebbe Chanina* was referring to. He was not speaking of *korbanot* where burning outside is itself the prescribed procedure and the fulfillment of the *mitzvah*. He was speaking specifically of skins that would need to be burned separately because the *korban* had become invalid — that is, cases where the skin would be taken out *because* it could not be given to the *kohanim*. Such a case he never witnessed.

A second objection is raised: *v'harei kodem hafshait v'kodem zrikah* — surely there were cases where the *korban* became *pasul* before it was flayed and before *zrikat hadam*, in which everyone would agree that the skin must be burned together with the meat? *Cholu kamina* — that is also not what he was addressing. He was specifically saying that he never saw a skin taken out *separately* and burned after it had already been flayed. The point is about the independent status of the flayed skin.

### Treifa Discovery Case

The *gemara* then raises the sharpest challenge: *v'haika nimtzas treifa bifnim b'me'ayim* — what about a case where a *treifa* is found in the internal organs, meaning the invalidity was not visible externally, and the animal had already been slaughtered, had its blood sprinkled, and been flayed? In that case, the *pasul* existed from the very beginning — before flaying, before *zrikat hadam* — and yet the *treifa* was only discovered after the fact. Should one not have to burn the skin in such a case?

The *gemara* answers: *kasavar nimtzas treifa bifnim b'me'ayim m'ratzeh* — the ruling is that discovery of a *treifa* in the internal organs after flaying does not retroactively invalidate the skin's status. This is the substantive *chiddush* in *Rebbe Chanina*'s testimony: the skin's status is governed by the moment of discovery relative to flaying, not by when the invalidity actually came into existence. This is precisely the point that *Rebbe Akiva* derived and that the *chachamim* contested.

Importantly, this is the case in which *Rebbi*'s view would permit the *kohanim* to receive the skin even here. Once flayed, if the problem is discovered only then, the *kohanim* retain the skin. Presumably one would also need to have sprinkled the blood — and indeed *Rebbi* does say *ha-dam meratzeh al ha-or bifnei atzmo* — meaning the blood may be sprinkled for the sake of the skin alone even when the meat is *pasul*. In the *treifa* case, of course, the *korban* was never a kosher *korban* at all, so in practice the blood would not have been sprinkled once the *treifa* is discovered; the point is that the skin, already separated at the time of discovery, is treated as belonging to the *kohanim*.

### Chanina = Rebbi Position

The conclusion is stated explicitly: *Rabbi Chanina k'Rebbi svira lei* — *Rebbe Chanina* holds like *Rebbi*. His testimony that the skin was never taken out separately to be burned reflects *Rebbi*'s position that once flayed, any problem with the meat does not affect the skin. Since *Rebbi* holds that flaying is the critical factor and that the skin is thereafter independent, there would indeed never be a case where a separately flayed skin needs to be burned. *K'Rebbi svira lei*.

The *gemara* adds: *v'ibait ayma afilu k'Rabbi Elazar BeRebbi Shimon* — alternatively, one could read *Rebbe Chanina*'s testimony as consistent even with *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon*, who holds that *zrikah* is the critical factor. The reason: *modeh Rebbi she'ein hafshait kodem zrikah* — in practice, flaying never preceded *zrikat hadam*. Therefore, if the *korban* became invalid before *zrikah*, it became invalid when the skin was still attached to the meat, and the skin was taken out together with the meat — not separately. And if it became invalid after *zrikah*, that means it also became invalid after flaying in normal practice, at which point even *Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon* agrees the skin goes to the *kohanim*. On this reading, *Rebbe Chanina*'s testimony is less halachically revelatory — it reflects the practical reality that the two critical moments, *zrikah* and *hefshait*, effectively coincide in practice — and the interesting *chiddush* is limited to the discovery rule in the case of an internal *treifa*.

---

## Bechor Application

### Why Bechor Example

This brings us directly to *Rebbe Akiva*'s use of the *bechor* example, which the *gemara* now explains. *Ve-lamai kamashmalan Rabbi Akiva* — what exactly is *Rebbe Akiva* teaching us with the case of a *bechor*? *Ha-kamashmalan afilu bigvulin* — he is teaching us that this rule applies even outside the *Beit Hamikdash*, in the provinces, in the case of *kodshim* that exist and are managed outside the Temple context. *Rebbe Akiva* lived after the *churban* and was addressing practical *halachot* relevant to his time.

### Bechor with Blemish Stat…

The *halacha* of a *bechor* with a permanent *mum* is as follows. A *bechor* must be given to a *kohen*, but in the absence of the *Beit Hamikdash* there is nothing the *kohen* can do with it as a *korban*. Once it acquires a permanent *mum*, the *kohen* is permitted to slaughter it and eat it outside the *Beit Hamikdash*. However, because it retains its *kedusha*, it is not a freely disposable animal — the *kedusha* limits what may be done with it to slaughter and consumption. It cannot be sold, it cannot be used as animal fodder, and the meat cannot be treated as *chulin*. Its *kedusha* functions more like an *issur* — a prohibition that circumscribes permitted use — than like a transferable sanctity. And because the entitlement is limited to eating, if the meat cannot be eaten, the *kedusha* has no vehicle for expression through the meat.

### Bechor Treifa Skin Quest…

The *halachic* question: the *kohen* slaughters his *bechor* with a *mum* outside the *Beit Hamikdash*, and in the course of processing the animal discovers that it is a *treifa*. He cannot eat the meat — it is *assur* as a *treifa* — and he cannot derive any other benefit from it because of its *kedusha*. What happens to the skin? Must the skin follow the meat and be subject to the same restrictions? Or does the moment of discovery, relative to flaying, determine that the skin is separate?

There is no *zrikat hadam* in this case — this is an animal slaughtered outside the *Beit Hamikdash* with no *mizbeach* and no *kohen* sprinkling blood on an altar. And yet *Rebbe Akiva* applies to it the same principle derived from *Rebbe Chanina*: the moment of discovery governs. If the *treifa* was discovered after flaying, the *kohanim* — or in this case, the *kohen* who owns the *bechor* — retain the skin. The principle of discovery-based determination of the skin's status, and the centrality of the moment of flaying, applies *bigvulin* just as it does within the *Beit Hamikdash*.

### Halacha: R. Akiva

*Amar Rebbe Chiya bar Abba amar Rebbe Yochanan*: *halacha ke-Rebbe Akiva* — the *halacha* follows *Rebbe Akiva*, at least with respect to the *bechor bigvulin*, that the skin's status is governed by the moment of flaying and discovery.

### Expert Verification Requ…

However, *ve'af Rebbe Akiva lo amar ela keshe-hutar mumcha aval lo hutar mumcha lo* — even *Rebbe Akiva* stated his ruling only where an expert has already examined and certified the *mum* as a permanent blemish. If no qualified expert has ruled on the blemish, the *kohen* may not rely on his own assessment even regarding the skin alone. One might have thought that since only the skin is at stake — a lesser *halachic* question — a lower standard of verification would suffice. The ruling is that it does not: expert certification of the *mum* is required regardless.

### Halacha: Sages on Korban

Finally, *ve-hilchesa ke-divrei chachamim* — the *halacha* also follows the *chachamim* with respect to a *korban* proper, meaning that for *kodshim* brought in the *Beit Hamikdash* context, the *halacha* does not follow the discovery rule but rather determines the skin's status based on when the invalidity actually existed. This appears to be in tension with the preceding ruling in favor of *Rebbe Akiva*, and *Rashi* resolves this by drawing a distinction: for a *bechor bigvulin*, we follow *Rebbe Akiva* and go by flaying and discovery; for a *korban* in the proper sense, we follow the *chachamim* and go by when the invalidity was present, not when it was discovered. We thus arrive at a divided ruling — *Rebbe Akiva* for the *bechor* outside the *Beit Hamikdash*, and the *chachamim* for *korbano* inside it.

---

---

# Zevachim 105

## Adayin Lo Higia Zmano

### Daf Location

We begin on 105a, on the second line, picking up from the sugya introduced at the end of 104a where the *mishna* opened the discussion. The broader context concerns the rules governing when a sacrifice becomes subject to *metamei begadim* — impurifying the clothing of those who handle it — and specifically the question of when the obligation to remove and burn certain offerings takes legal effect.

### Timing & Obligation

Rabbi Yirmiah bar Abba raises the following question: according to the opinion that holds *adayin lo higi'a zmano latzeit* — the sacrifice has not yet reached the time when it is obligated to be taken outside — does this rule apply specifically to meat that is not destined to be taken outside as a *chova*, a mandatory obligation? In that case, the restriction might reflect the absence of any future burning obligation. But what about offerings whose very nature requires that they ultimately be taken outside and burned? Is such an offering also subject to the limitation, or does its future *chova* status change the assessment even now?

The question is whether the threshold for *metamei begadim* tracks the current stage of processing or anticipates the ultimate obligation. Put differently: if an offering is destined to leave and be burned, does that future status already confer upon it some of the legal weight of having left?

### Psul & Incompleteness

Underlying this question is a general principle that runs through several areas of *hilchot kodashim*: incomplete processing prevents full legal consequences from taking effect. Just as a defect in the proper sequence of *avodah* can prevent *pigul* from attaching, so too, where a sacrifice has not yet completed the stage of *yetzia* — departure from the *azarah* — that incompleteness may insulate it from transmitting *tumah* to clothing. The rule is not merely formal; it reflects a substantive position that each stage of the sacrificial process must reach its threshold before subsequent legal effects can cascade from it.

---

## Levi Psul Beyetziato

### Baraita Source

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question from a *baraita*: *she'eira bo psul beyetziato* — a *Levi* in whom a *psul* occurred *beyetziato*, upon his leaving. The question is what exactly this phrasing indicates. Does it mean that the *psul* consists in the act of leaving itself — *psul yetzia* — implying that departure from the *Beit HaMikdash* is itself the disqualifying event?

### Psul Tuma not Yetzia

The Gemara answers: no. The *baraita* means rather that the *psul* occurred *while* the Levi was leaving, but the *psul* itself was not the act of leaving. Rather it was *psul tuma* — impurity — or *psul lina* — being left over — that happened to occur at the moment of departure. The phrasing *beyetziato* is circumstantial, not causal: the *psul* struck him as he was exiting, but the legal disqualification is grounded in *tumah* or *lina*, not in the act of *yetzia* per se. This reading defuses what initially appeared to be support for the view that departure itself triggers disqualification.

---

## Rov Behema vs. Rov Evarim

### Mixed Majority Query

Rabbi Elazar poses a question concerning the *parim hanisrafim* and *se'irim hanisrafim* — the bulls and goats that are burned outside the Temple precinct. The law holds that once the majority of the animal has exited the boundary, the departure is legally complete and the *metamei begadim* consequences attach. But what if the majority of the animal has exited only because of a minority of a single limb? The case is: *sheyatza rubo bemiut ever* — the majority of the animal's mass has crossed the boundary, but only because a minority portion of one particular limb pushed the total to more than half.

To visualize the problem: imagine the animal positioned precisely at the boundary, with exactly half its mass on each side. The only reason the outside portion counts as a *rov* is that the majority of a particular limb — say, the tail — lies outside, even though a minority of the overall animal is equally distributed. The question then is how we assess *rov* in this context: do we evaluate the animal as a single undivided mass, or do we subdivide it into its constituent *evarim* and assess the majority of each limb separately?

The underlying conceptual tension is something like the difference between a popular vote and an electoral college system. Does the animal's crossing threshold get measured holistically — fifty-one percent of total mass — or limb by limb, where the majority of each *ever* determines whether that limb counts as having exited?

### Half by Limb Majority

The Gemara initially suggests that the answer should be obvious: surely we assess the animal limb by limb, and thus we follow the majority of each *ever* rather than the majority of the whole animal. But on reflection, the harder case emerges. What if the animal is positioned such that it is *precisely* half on each side — neither side can claim a true majority of the overall mass — except that the majority of one particular limb happens to fall outside? In that scenario, the borderline between inside and outside cuts through the middle of a single limb, and the animal is otherwise exactly fifty-fifty. Does the majority of that one limb tip the legal balance and count the whole animal as having exited?

### Assessment Standard

The Gemara considers: do we say that the minority portion of that limb follows the majority of the limb it belongs to — *batar rov ever shadinan leh* — and therefore the animal is treated as having exited? Or do we assess the whole animal as a unit — *batar beheimah shadinan* — and since it is precisely fifty-fifty, we hold that it has not yet crossed the majority threshold?

### Teiku Case

This question is left unresolved — *teiku*. The case of exactly half the animal with the legal result turning on the majority of a single borderline limb has no conclusive answer within this sugya.

---

## Matni Lah Begavrei

### Workers Departure

Rabba bar Rav Huna offers a variant formulation of the majority question, but now applied not to the animal itself but to the people working on it. He teaches the rule *matni lah begavrei* — he frames it in terms of the workers. The case: five people are engaged in processing and transporting the sacrifice. Three of them depart from the *azarah*, while two remain inside.

### Workers vs. Animal

The question: do we follow the majority of the workers involved — *batar rov mit'askin azlinan* — so that since three of the five have exited, we treat the sacrifice as having legally departed? Or do we follow the status of the animal itself — *batar beheimah azlinan* — in which case, since the animal is still physically within the *azarah*, it has not yet achieved the status of *yotzei*? Rabba bar Rav Huna's framing implies a willingness to consider the sacrifice as *yotzei* even while the animal remains inside, based solely on the departure of a majority of those handling it — a striking and perhaps counterintuitive proposition.

### Teiku Dispute

This too is left unresolved — *teiku*. Whether the legal assessment of departure follows the workers or the animal's physical location receives no definitive answer.

---

## Yatzeu V'Chazaru

### Return Scenario

Rabbi Elazar poses another question: what happens in the case of *parim use'irim hanisrafim* that left the boundary and then returned — *sheyatzu vechazaru*? They exited, and then someone brought them back inside. What is their legal status at that point?

### Contamination Trigger

The question has two layers. First: does the act of leaving suffice to cause *metamei begadim* — that is, do the handlers who were involved in bringing the sacrifice outside now carry *tumah* that impurifies their clothing? And second: does the departure of the sacrifice itself give it the status of an *av hatumah* such that it becomes a source of *tumah* upon return? The fact that it was able to return — *de'i hadar hadar* — might indicate that the departure was not legally complete, or it might be entirely irrelevant once the threshold of departure was crossed. This question likewise does not receive an immediate answer within the sugya.

---

## Carrying on Poles

### Front Exit Scenario

Rabbi Abba bar Memel introduces a case intended to shed light on these questions. The sacrifice is being carried on wooden poles — *bemotot* — by four workers, two in front and two behind. As they carry the animal toward the exit of the *azarah*, the two front carriers cross the boundary of the *azarah* wall while the two rear carriers remain inside.

### Person vs. Animal

The ruling in this case is explicit: *harishonim sheyatzu chutz lechomat ha'azarah metamei begadim* — the front carriers who exited become *tamei* to the degree that they impurify their clothing. *Veha'acharonim ein metamei begadim ad sheyatzu* — the rear carriers who remain inside do not become *metamei begadim* until they themselves exit. The animal, meanwhile, is still in process — partially inside, partially outside — and yet the legal distinction applies entirely based on whether the individual person has crossed the boundary.

### Proof from Mishna

This ruling appears to support the position that the assessment follows the person, not the animal. If the legal consequence of *metamei begadim* depended on the animal having departed, then the rear carriers — who are also handling the same animal — should also become *tamei* once the front carriers cross the boundary with it. Yet they do not. The implication seems to be: we go by whether *the person* has exited, not by whether the animal has.

### Ravina's Answer

Ravina, however, pushes back on this inference. He argues that the reason the rear carriers are not yet *metamei begadim* is not because we assess by the person rather than the animal. Rather, it is because the *pasuk* explicitly requires *ve'achar yavo el hamachaneh* — afterward one shall enter the camp — meaning the *tumah* is triggered by the act of personally departing and then re-entering. If you have not yet left the *machaneh*, there is no applicable verse to make you *tamei*, regardless of what the animal has done. This is a textual criterion, not a statement about whether we track the animal or the workers.

One might then ask: does this resolve Rabba bar Rav Huna's *teiku* about the five workers? Ravina's answer addresses a different dimension — whether the person must personally exit — but Rabba bar Rav Huna's question was about whether a *majority* of workers having exited could legally stand in for the animal's departure. Those remain distinct questions, and Ravina's answer does not collapse them. The case of three workers out of five is not a question about whether those workers individually became *tamei* — obviously they did, having exited — but whether their majority departure confers *yotzei* status on the sacrifice for other legal purposes.

Ravina then clarifies the proper framing of Rabbi Elazar's original question about *yatzu vechazaru*. He suggests the case must be reconfigured: *kegon denakit leh bechulveta* — that the *kohanim* were positioned entirely outside the *azarah* and lifted the sacrifice out using a long implement, a kind of spear or hook. In this scenario, the handlers themselves were never inside, and therefore the verse's requirement of personally exiting and re-entering cannot apply to them. The question then becomes: is there any way in this configuration to ever achieve the status of *tamei*? It sounds as though, if done this way, the handlers might entirely avoid becoming *tamei* — a clever procedural workaround, even if somewhat impractical.

---

## Metamei Begadim Rules

### Types of Offerings

A new *baraita* is introduced: *parim ufarah useir hamishtaleach*. The *baraita* addresses three categories: the *parim hanisrafim* and *se'irim hanisrafim* — the bulls and goats burned outside; the *parah adumah* — the red heifer; and the *seir hamishtaleach* — the scapegoat sent to *Azazel* on *Yom Kippur*.

### Handler Impurity

The rule: *hamishale'ach vehasorfan vehamotzi'an metamei begadim* — the one who sends off the scapegoat, those who burn the offerings, and those who carry them out, all become *tamei* to the degree that they impurify their clothing. The act of processing these offerings confers upon the handler a high enough degree of *tumah* that even his garments become *tamei*.

### Animal Status Lower

A striking detail follows: *ve'hein atzman ein metamei'im begadim* — the animals themselves do not impurify clothing. That is, if a garment merely makes contact with the carcass of one of these animals, the garment does not become *tamei* to the degree of *metamei begadim*. The source of the *tumah* that rises to the level of *av hatumah* is the *person* involved in the process, not the animal itself. The animal occupies a lower rung in the *tumah* hierarchy.

### Food Impurity Only

*Aval metamei'im ochlin umashkin* — but the animals themselves can impurify foods and liquids. This places them at the level of *rishon l'tumah* in the food domain: they can make *ochlin* and *mashkin tamei* by contact, but they cannot impurify persons or vessels in the manner of an *av hatumah*. The person doing the work is the *av hatumah*; the animal is merely a *rishon*.

### Why Impurity Here

One might ask: why do these particular offerings convey *tumah* to the handlers at all? After all, these animals were properly slaughtered or processed — they are not *neveilah* in the ordinary sense. The *parim hanisrafim* and *se'irim hanisrafim* were slaughtered within the Temple; the *parah adumah* was slaughtered outside at *Har HaZeitim*; the *seir hamishtaleach* was pushed alive off a cliff and never slaughtered at all. None of them became *tamei* through the normal avenue of *neveilah*.

The answer lies in the nature of these *korbanot*. All of these offerings share the designation of *chatat*. The *chatat* is intrinsically bound up with the removal and absorption of *tumah* and sin.
