If one thinks in concrete terms about the mechanism of these rituals, these animals really are carrying a concentrated load of *tumah* — whether it is the *tumah* of *chet* borne by the *parim* and *se'irim* of *Yom Kippur*, the *tumah* of death that the *parah adumah* counteracts, or the sins explicitly loaded onto the head of the *seir hamishtaleach* before it is sent to *Azazel*. The Torah prescribes that involvement in transporting and processing this concentration of *tumah* makes the person himself *tamei* at the level of *metamei begadim*. This is not a consequence of touching a dead animal; it is a consequence of being the agent of this particular *avodah*.

---

## Derasha on Receptivity

### Meir's Rule

The Gemara now examines the doctrinal underpinning for this structure of *tumah* according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir relies on the *drasha* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, derived from the verse *al kol zera zarua* — concerning all planted seed. The *drasha* reads: just as seeds and foods cannot become *tamei* at the level of *tumah chamurah* — they can never become an *av hatumah* — and therefore they require *hechsher*, they must be wetted by liquid before they can become susceptible to *tumah* at all, so too anything else that can never become an *av hatumah* also requires *hechsher* before it can become *tamei* or transmit *tumah* to other things.

The logic of the *drasha* is a *mah matzinu*: since the paradigmatic case of *ochlin* that can only ever reach *rishon l'tumah* requires prior wetting to enter the *tumah* system, anything else similarly capped at below *av hatumah* also requires that prior wetting. This becomes a general hermeneutic rule: the *hechsher* requirement tracks the ceiling of *tumah* that something can reach.

### Kosher Bird Exception

The one case explicitly excluded from this rule is *neveilat of tahor* — the carcass of a kosher bird that was not properly slaughtered. Such a carcass is *metamei b'veit hablia'ah* — it conveys *tumah* specifically in the throat, when someone swallows a *kezayit* of it. This is one of the most sui generis cases in all of *hilchot tumah*. The person who swallows it becomes *tamei* to a degree that makes his clothing *tamei* — that is, he becomes an *av hatumah*.

The *neveilat of tahor* is therefore excluded from the *hechsher* requirement because *sofah litamei tumah chamurah* — ultimately it does produce *tumah chamurah*, it does yield an *av hatumah* (namely, the person who swallows it). Since that ceiling of *tumah chamura* is reachable, the *neveilat of tahor* does not need prior *hechsher* to enter the *tumah* system. The capacity for *tumah chamurah* is the criterion, and this carcass meets it.

---

## Rabbanan Position

### Consistency Challenge

The Gemara challenges the *Rabbanan* who reject Rabbi Meir's *drasha*. If they do not accept the hermeneutic of *tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael*, then they face a consistency problem. On one hand, they would seem obligated to say that even the *seir hamishtaleach* should require *hechsher* from an external source of *tumah* before it can transmit *tumah* — since it is a live goat that can never become an *av hatumah* in the normal sense. On the other hand, if they dispense with the *drasha* entirely, why should the *parah adumah* and *parim* be *metamei ochlin umashkin* at all, given that they also have not yet been contacted by an external *tumah* source?

### Rav Dimi's Answer

When Rav Dimi arrived from *Eretz Yisrael* to *Bavel*, he conveyed the teaching of the western academies: *tzrichin hechsher tumah mimakom acher* — these offerings require *tumah* from an outside source in order to then transmit *tumah* to other things. The *Rabbanan*'s position is that the *parim* and *parah*, in order to be *metamei ochlin umashkin*, must first have become *tamei* themselves from some external source — be it contact with a *sheretz*, a *neveilah*, or something similar. Their capacity to then make *ochlin* and *mashkin tamei* is derivative of their having first received *tumah* from outside.

### Meat Status Difference

Rashi explains the underlying distinction. The *parim* and *parah* are dead animals — they are meat. And meat, as a category of food (*ochlin*), is susceptible to *tumah* in principle once it has been contacted by a *tumah* source. So their capacity to be *metamei ochlin umashkin* is not intrinsic to their status as these specific *korbanot*; it is a consequence of their being beef — flesh in the category of food — that happens to have received *tumah* from an external source. They can then pass that *tumah* along to other foods and liquids in the normal way that foods do.

The *seir hamishtaleach*, by contrast, is a *ba'al chaim* — a living animal. A living animal does not belong to the *tumah* system in the same way as meat. It has no inherent susceptibility to *tumah* as an *ochel*, because it is not food. Therefore, the *seir hamishtaleach* itself cannot be *metamei* other things even if it contacts a *tumah* source — it simply is not in the relevant legal category. The *hamishale'ach*, the person who escorts it, does become *tamei*, but that is because of the *avodah* itself and the *pasuk* that prescribes it, not because the goat conveyed *tumah* to him.

---

## Neveilat Of Tahor

### Inside Impurity Status

Rabbi Elazar poses another question in this vein: do the *parim hanisrafim* and *se'irim hanisrafim* have the capacity to be *metamei ochlin umashkin bifnim* — even while they are still inside the *azarah*, before they have been taken outside? The operative question is whether the incomplete stage of processing — the fact that they have not yet been removed — prevents them from functioning as a *tumah* source even at the lower level of *metamei ochlin umashkin*.

### Incomplete = No Impurity

Rabbi Elazar then answers his own question: *mechusar yetzia kimechusar ma'aseh dami* — the fact that the offering has not yet completed the stage of departure is treated like the absence of a required act. Since the offering is still missing its essential processing stage — *yetzia* — it is as though the process is incomplete, and therefore it does not yet have the capacity to transmit *tumah* even to foods and liquids. The incompleteness of the *yetzia* is not merely technical; it forestalls the legal effect.

### Parallel Case

This resolution prompts an analogy. Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel asked Rabbi Chiya bar Abba: what is the rule for *neveilat of tahor* according to Rabbi Meir — at what minimum *shiur* does it convey *tumah*? The question is whether the *shiur* should be *kezayit*, as for regular *neveilah*, or *kabeitza*, as for *ochlin* that have become *tamei* secondarily. The parallel question: does the *neveilat of tahor*, since it only becomes *metamei* through swallowing (*beit hablia*), perhaps have rules that track the *ochlin* system rather than the *neveilah* system?

The question is then refined. If the bird is *demachta le'ara* — lying on the ground — there is no question, because there is no risk of *tumah* at all: the bird becomes *metamei* only through being swallowed, not through touch or carriage. Equally, if the bird is already *bepumei* — in the person's mouth — there is no question about the *shiur*, because at that point whatever other food is also in the mouth becomes *tamei* by contact, and those foods then make the person *tamei*, regardless of *shiur*. The hard case is *denakit leh bidei* — when the person has picked it up in his hand and is on the way to eating it.

---

## Bird Carcass Rules

### Timing of Impurity

The difficult question concerns the moment at which the *neveilat of tahor* becomes legally operative as a *tumah* source according to Rabbi Meir. When the bird is still on the ground — on the plate, so to speak — everyone agrees it conveys no *tumah*. When it is already being swallowed, everyone agrees it does. The question is the intermediate stage: what is the status of the bird when it has been picked up in hand and is about to be eaten?

### Stages of Impurity

If the bird is still on the ground, the question cannot even arise — there is not yet any *tumah* in play. If the bird is already in the mouth, the answer is clear in a different direction: the other food present in the mouth becomes *tamei* by contact, and that secondary *tumah* then makes the person *tamei*. The unresolved case is the hand: having picked up the bird with the clear intention to eat it, does any aspect of the *neveilat of tahor*'s *tumah* already apply?

### Incomplete Action

The question is framed as: *mechusar kreiva kimechusar ma'aseh dami o lo* — is the fact that the eating has not yet been completed analogous to an incomplete action (*mechusar ma'aseh*), such that it blocks the *tumah* from taking effect? Or is *mechusar kreiva* — the mere absence of the final approach to the mouth — not comparable to *mechusar ma'aseh*?

Abaaye resolves the question: *mechusar kreiva lav kimechusar ma'aseh dami* — the incompleteness of the *kreiva*, the final approach to swallowing, is *not* comparable to a missing act. This means, according to Rabbi Meir's position, that the bird in hand already has some operative *tumah* status. The reasoning connects to Rabbi Meir's general *drasha*: since the *neveilat of tahor* is *sofah litamei tumah chamurah* — its trajectory culminates in producing *tumah chamurah* — that capacity is not suspended merely because the final act of swallowing has not yet occurred. Rabbi Meir does not require the act to be complete before some aspects of the *tumah* scheme engage.

This is a striking and somewhat troubling position. The entire point of the *neveilat of tahor* rule is that *tumah* is conveyed only *beit hablia'ah* — specifically through swallowing. To then say that picking it up already activates some prior-stage *tumah* seems to undercut that premise. One might argue that since the person is in the process of doing something they are not supposed to do — eating *neveilah* — perhaps the *tumah* should only attach once the sin is actually committed, not in anticipation of it. But Rabbi Meir appears to hold that once the trajectory toward *tumah chamurah* is underway, the intermediate stage already falls within the orbit of that eventual *tumah* effect. It is also worth noting that this analysis concerns a rejected opinion being applied analogically to another case — an *amora* inferring what Rabbi Meir's rejected *shita* might say about a case where we also would not rule that way. There is no practical *halachic* difference on either side.

### Thirteen Rules Summary

A new *baraita* is introduced: *shelosha asar devarim ne'emru beneveilat of tahor* — thirteen *halachot* were stated about the carcass of the kosher bird, and this is one of them. The thirteen include, among others: *tzericha machshava* — it requires *machshava*, intent that the bird is being treated as food; *ve'einah tzericha hechsher* — it does not require *hechsher*, prior wetting with liquid; and *umetamei tumat ochlin bekabeitza* — it conveys *tumah* to other foods at the *shiur* of a *kabeitza*, the size of an egg.

The question arises: whose position does this *baraita* reflect? The middle clause — *metamei tumat ochlin bekabeitza* — which describes the bird as *metamei ochlin* even before swallowing, seems to align with Rabbi Meir's position. But it is claimed that it could equally be the position of the *Rabbanan*. The opening clause — *tzericha machshava ve'einah tzericha hechsher* — is however specifically the hermeneutic of Rabbi Meir, who holds that things which are *sofan litamei tumah chamurah* do not require *hechsher*. So the opening aligns with Rabbi Meir.

### Baraita Structure

This creates a structural puzzle: the *reisha* of the *baraita* reflects Rabbi Meir's position, the *seifa* also reflects Rabbi Meir (*shechita umelikatah metaheret terefatah mitumatah* — slaughter or *melika* removes the *neveilah* status from a *tereifa* — is specifically Rabbi Meir's view), and yet the middle clause appears to represent the *Rabbanan*. The Gemara is compelled to accept: *reisha veseifa Rabbi Meir umitziata Rabbanan* — the opening and closing of this *baraita* are Rabbi Meir's position, while the middle section represents the *Rabbanan*. This is an unusual and somewhat convoluted structure, and the Gemara arrives at it only because it has read each clause with strict fidelity to its attributed opinion.

---

## Rishon V'Sheni Rules

### Counting Levels

Rav Hamnuna addresses Rabbi Zeira directly and with some urgency: do not sit down until you explain this to me. The question: according to Rabbi Meir, do we count *rishon vesheni* — first and second degree *tumah* — for *neveilat of tahor*? That is, if the *neveilat of tahor* is an *av hatumah* that makes someone who swallows it into an *av hatumah*, does that person then transmit *tumah* to things he touches, creating a *rishon*, and does that *rishon* then create a *sheni*, in the ordinary cascading fashion?

### Contact Rule

Rabbi Zeira's answer establishes a general principle: *kol heicha demetamei adam bemaga, monin bo rishon vesheni* — wherever an *av hatumah* can make a person *tamei* by physical contact, we count outward from that *av* through the normal chain of *rishon vesheni*. The chain of *tumah* levels is grounded in and patterned after the *sheretz*, which is the paradigmatic *av hatumah* that conveys *tumah* by contact: you touch it, you become *tamei*; the vessel you then touch becomes *rishon*; the food that vessel touches becomes *sheni*.

### Sui Generis Status

*Neveilat of tahor*, however, does not impurify a person *bemaga* — by contact or carrying. It only conveys *tumah bevet hablia'ah* — through swallowing. Since the mechanism of *tumah* transmission is entirely different from the contact-based paradigm, the normal framework of counting *rishon vesheni* simply does not apply. The *neveilat of tahor* is genuinely *sui generis* in the *tumah* system, operating under its own rules, and the cascading *tumah* levels that flow from every other *av hatumah* do not cascade from it in the same way.

---

## Chibur Ochlin

### Connection Levels

Rabbi Zeira then poses a question to Rabbi Ami bar Chiyya — or, in another version, to Rabbi Avin bar Kahana — based on a *mishna* concerning *chiburei ochlin al yedei mashkin*. The case: two foods are connected by liquid — the same liquid touches both of them. The rule from the *mishna* is that this liquid connection counts as a *chibur* for *tumah kala*, light *tumah*, but does not count as a *chibur* for *tumah chamura*, severe *tumah*. That is: if a secondary source of *tumah* — a *vlad hatumah* — touches one food, the second food connected to it by liquid will also become *tamei*, because the connection is sufficient for purposes of this lesser *tumah*. But if an *av hatumah* touches one food, making it a *rishon*, the second food connected by liquid does not automatically become *tamei* at a *rishon* level — the liquid connection is insufficient for the purpose of the more severe degree of *tumah*.

This is somewhat counterintuitive. One would expect that the more powerful the *tumah* source, the more readily it would spread through any connection. Yet the opposite appears: for the lesser *tumah*, the liquid connection counts; for the more severe *tumah*, it does not. The resolution is that the lower levels of *tumah* in this domain are in many cases *derabbanan*, and the Sages were willing to extend *tumah* through the liquid connection for purposes of their own protective *gezeirot* without demanding the same stringency of physical connection that *tumah chamura* requires.

### Counting Question

The question Rabbi Zeira poses: in a case where the liquid connection counts only for *tumah kala* and not for *tumah chamura* — do we then count *rishon vesheni* from the connected food? That is, the second food became *tamei* through the connection, but only at the level of *tumah kala*. Can that food then go on to transmit *tumah* one further step down the chain — making something else *tamei* as a *sheni* — or does the unusual pathway by which it became *tamei* preclude the normal counting of *rishon vesheni*?

### General Principle

The answer again invokes Rav Hamnuna's principle: *kol heicha demetamei adam, monin bo rishon vesheni* — wherever the underlying *av hatumah* is of a type that can make a person *tamei* by contact, we count *rishon vesheni* from what that *av* touches. *Ein metamei'in adam* — if the *av* in question cannot make a person *tamei* by contact, then we do not count *rishon vesheni* from what it touches. The capacity of the originating *av hatumah* to impurify persons by contact is the threshold criterion. Where that capacity is present, the full cascade of *rishon vesheni* follows; where it is absent, the chain does not extend in the same manner.

---

# Zevachim 106

## Parim HaNisrafim

### Three Camps

The *daf* opens by returning to the *mishnah* treating the *parim hanisrafim* and *se'irim hanisrafim* — the *korbanot* burned outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. The Torah establishes that those who perform the burning, along with their garments, contract *tumah*. The *mishnah* taught that this *tumah* takes effect upon exiting the *azarah*: those carrying the front of the animal became *tamei* upon leaving, while those carrying the back became *tamei* only once they too had fully exited. Rabbi Shimon dissented, holding that *tumah* is generated not by the exit from the *Mikdash* but by actual participation in the burning itself.

The *Gemara* now asks: *mina hani mili* — what is the source for the ruling that *tumah* commences upon departure from the *azarah*? A *braita* provides the answer through a comparison: *lehalan*, in the earlier passages in *Vayikra* dealing with the *par kohen gadol* and the *par helam davar shel tzibur*, the Torah specifies that the burning takes place outside of three camps. Yet *kan*, in the passage treating the *par v'se'ir* of *Yom Kippur*, the Torah says only *el michutz lamachaneh* — outside of one camp. The purpose of this juxtaposition is to teach that while the actual burning must occur outside all three camps — *machaneh shechinah* (the *Beit HaMikdash*), *machaneh leviyah* (the *Har HaBayit*), and *machaneh yisrael* (Yerushalayim) — the *tumah* is incurred as soon as one exits even the first camp, the *azarah* itself.

### Redundant Language

This raises an immediate question: where is the source in the earlier *Vayikra* passages establishing that the burning is required outside all three camps? The *Gemara* addresses this through a careful analysis of redundant language. The *pasuk* reads: *v'hotzi et kol hapar el michutz lamachaneh el makom tahor el shefech hadeshen v'saraf oto al etzim ba'esh al shefech hadeshen yisaref.* One might have thought that *michutz lamachaneh* here refers to only one camp. But three separate instances of *michutz lamachaneh* appear in different contexts, each one adding an additional *machaneh*.

The first instance appears in the passage of the *par kohen gadol* — *el michutz lamachaneh* — indicating one camp. A second *michutz lamachaneh* appears in the passage of the *par helam davar shel tzibur*, which explicitly connects its burning to the *par kohen gadol* with the phrase *ka'asher saraf et hapar harishon*. Since the connection was already established, the repetition of *el michutz lamachaneh* is superfluous unless it is to add a second camp. A third *michutz lamachaneh* appears in the *tzav* section in the context of *terumat hadeshen* — the removal of ashes. Since the *parim* are already known to be burned *al shefech hadeshen*, the *pasuk* need not have repeated *michutz lamachaneh*; its repetition therefore adds a third camp. The combined three instances thus establish that the burning must occur outside all three camps. The single *michutz lamachaneh* of *Yom Kippur* cannot add a fourth camp — it therefore teaches instead that *tumah* attaches even upon exiting the first camp.

### Rabbi Eliezer

For Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *tumah* is created at the moment of burning rather than upon exit, the repeated *michutz lamachaneh* of *Yom Kippur* cannot serve the function the *chachamim* assign to it. So what does Rabbi Shimon do with this language? The *Gemara* answers by citing a *braita*: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the *michutz lamachaneh* by the *par v'se'ir* of *Yom Kippur* is meant to be linked via a *gezeirah shavah* to the *michutz lamachaneh* found in the passage of the *parah adumah* — *v'hotzi otah el michutz lamachaneh v'shachat otah lefanav*. The purpose of this linkage is to connect the place of burning of the *parim hanisrafim* to the place where the *parah adumah* ritual is performed. Just as the *parah adumah* is performed outside three camps, so too must the burning of the *parim hanisrafim* occur outside three camps.

### Location Debate

This linkage to the *parah adumah* has a further consequence: it establishes the geographic location of the burning. The *parah adumah* is performed to the *east* of Yerushalayim, because the *kohen* must sprinkle the blood toward *petach ohel moed*, and since that opening faces east, the *parah adumah* site must lie further to the east. Rabbi Eliezer's *gezeirah shavah* would therefore place the burning of the *parim hanisrafim* to the east of Yerushalayim as well, as stated explicitly at the top of 106a.

The *chachamim*, however, who use *michutz lamachaneh* to derive the timing of *tumah* and do not apply the *gezeirah shavah* to the *parah adumah*, maintain a different location. A *braita* teaches on their view: the burning takes place to the *north* of Yerushalayim, outside the three camps. Rashi explains — though the *Gemara* itself does not state it explicitly — that since these *korbanot* are *chataot*, and *chataot* are associated with the north side of the *mizbe'ach*, the natural location for their burning outside the city is also to the north.

### Ashes Requirement

Within this locational discussion, the *Gemara* considers the opinion of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, who states that the *parim hanisrafim* are burned *el beit hadeshen* — at the place where ashes are poured. This seems to merely restate the *pasuk*, which already says *al shefech hadeshen yisaref*. Rava therefore frames the question as: who disagrees with Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, and in doing so clarifies what the *chiddush* must be.

The answer is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. A *braita* cites two positions. The first holds that *al shefech hadeshen* means ashes must *literally* be present at the site — the ashes removed from the *mizbe'ach* must already be there when the *parim* are burned. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disagrees and holds that what is required is not actual ashes but an inclined terrain, such that ashes *could* be poured there. Abaye suggests a third possibility: perhaps the two opinions do not actually contradict each other, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov means that in *addition* to requiring ashes, the location must also feature a slope. The *Gemara* does not formally resolve the question, leaving open whether the opinions are mutually exclusive or complementary.

### Tumah at Burning

The *Gemara* now presents a *braita* that, in the manner of Rabbi Shimon, specifies when precisely *tumah* is generated for those involved in the burning. *Hasoref metamei begadim velo hamatzit et ha'or* — the one who burns contracts *tumah begadim*, but not the one who merely ignites the fire. And certainly not *hamasader hama'arachah* — the one who lays out the wood. Only active participation during the burning itself renders a person *tamei*: *hamisayei bish'at sreifah* — one who assists while the burning is in progress, whether by placing the animal on the fire or stoking the flames.

### Charcoal vs. Ash

The *braita* continues: one might think that even after the animal has fully turned to ash, there would still be *tumah begadim* for those involved. The Torah says *hasoref otam* — it is still *otam*, them, the original thing. Once the animal has become ash, it is no longer *otam*, no longer the same entity, and therefore *tumah begadim* no longer applies.

Rabbi Shimon adds a nuance: *otam metameim begadim nitach habasar ein metameim begadim* — once the flesh has congealed and hardened into a charred mass, it is no longer *metamei*. The *Gemara* asks: *mai beineihu* — what is the practical difference between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon? Rava answers: *ika beineihu deshavyei charucha* — the case of charcoal. If the flesh has become charcoal — no longer the original flesh, but not yet ash — the *tanna kamma*, who requires full reduction to ash before *tumah* ends, would still count this as *metamei begadim*, while Rabbi Shimon, who requires only that the flesh lose its character as *otam*, would already exempt the participants from *tumah begadim*.

The *hadran* of *Parim HaNisrafim* is recited at this point, marking the conclusion of the chapter.

---

## Shechutei Chutz

### Two Prohibitions

With the conclusion of *parim hanisrafim*, the *Gemara* opens an entirely new *halacha* — a new *perek* — addressing the *issurim* of bringing *korbanot* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. This *perek* is called *hashocheit v'hama'aleh bachutz*, and it deals with two distinct prohibitions: *shechutei chutz*, the act of slaughtering a sanctified animal outside the *Mikdash*, and *ha'alat chutz*, the act of burning or offering it up on an outside altar.

### Torah Sources

The *pesukim* underlying these laws come from *Vayikra* 17. Verse 3 reads: *ish ish m'beit Yisrael asher yishchat shor o chesev o ez bamachaneh o asher yishchat michutz lamachaneh v'el petach ohel mo'ed lo hevi'o l'hakriv korban la-Hashem lifnei mishkan Hashem dam yeichashev la'ish hahu dam shafach v'nichras ha'ish hahu mikerev amo.* The case described is one where an animal was sanctified as a *korban* but was slaughtered outside, without being brought to the *ohel mo'ed*. This constitutes *shechutei chutz* and carries the punishment of *kares*.

Verse 8 then addresses *ha'alat chutz*: *ish ish m'beit Yisrael u'min hager asher yagur b'socham asher ya'aleh olah o zavach v'el petach ohel mo'ed lo yavi'ennu la'asos oso la-Hashem v'nichras ha'ish hahu me'ammav.* Here, the operative word is *ya'aleh* — he who *offers up* outside — making clear that burning or placing the sacrifice on an outside altar, as distinct from the *shechita*, is also independently punishable with *kares*.

### Two Aveirot

The *mishnah* rules: *hashocheit v'hama'aleh bachutz chayav al hashechita v'chayav al haha'ala* — one who slaughters and offers outside is liable separately for each act. Since *shechita* and *ha'ala* are two independent prohibitions, even if both were performed within a single lapse of awareness (*b'shogeig*), two separate *korbanot* must be brought.

### Rabbi Yosi HaGlili

Rabbi Yosi HaGlili introduces a qualification: *shachat bifnim v'he'ela bachutz chayav* — one who slaughters *inside* the *Mikdash* and burns *outside* is liable for *ha'alat chutz*, because the meat was fit to be offered on the *mizbe'ach* at the time of *shechita*. However, *shachat bachutz v'he'ela bachutz patur* — if one slaughters *outside* and then burns *outside*, he is liable for *shechutei chutz* but *exempt* from *ha'alat chutz*. His reasoning: once the *shechita* took place outside, the meat was never fit to be placed on the *mizbe'ach* in the first instance. The prohibition of *ha'alat chutz* presupposes meat that *could have* been legitimately offered inside; meat from an outside *shechita* is *pasul* from the outset and therefore cannot generate liability for the *ha'ala*.

A logical consequence of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position is that one can never be liable for both *shechita* and *ha'ala* of the same animal: liability for the *shechita* precludes liability for the *ha'ala* of that same animal, and vice versa.

### Chachamim Refute

The *chachamim* respond: *af hashocheit bifnim u'ma'aleh bachutz* — even in your own favored scenario, where one slaughters inside and burns outside, there is a problem. *Keivan she'hotzi'o pasul* — the moment the meat was taken out of the *Mikdash*, it became *pasul*. So in *every* case of *ha'alat chutz*, the meat burned outside is already unfit for the *mizbe'ach*. Since even the case Rabbi Yosi HaGlili himself considers liable involves *pasul* meat, the distinction he draws between slaughtering inside versus outside becomes untenable. The liability for *ha'alat chutz* does not depend on the meat's current fitness; it depends on whether the animal began as a sanctified *korban*.

### Eating Korban

A parallel dispute illuminates the same underlying logic. The Torah states that a *tamei* person who eats *kodashim* is liable for *kares*. However, eating a *tamei korban* carries a *lav* but not *kares*. The *tanna kamma* rules: *ha-tamei she'achal bein kodesh tamei bein kodesh tahor chayav* — if the *person* is *tamei*, he is liable for *kares* regardless of whether the *korban* itself is *tahor* or *tamei*.

Rabbi Yosi HaGlili disagrees: *tamei she'achal tahor chayav, v'tamei she'achal tamei patur* — only if the person is *tamei* and eats a *tahor korban* is there *kares*; if the *korban* was also *tamei*, there is no *kares*, because *shelo achal ela davar tamei* — he ate something that was already defiled. The parallel to the *ha'ala* debate is clear: in both cases, Rabbi Yosi HaGlili holds that liability requires the object of the prohibited act to have been in its pristine, fit state.

The *chachamim* again respond: *af tamei she'achal et hatahor — keivan shenaga bo tim'o* — even in the classic case of a *tamei* person eating a *tahor* meat, the moment he touches it he renders it *tamei*. So in every scenario that generates *kares*, the person ends up eating something that has by that point become *tamei*. Since even the case generating liability necessarily involves *tamei* meat, the distinction Rabbi Yosi HaGlili draws cannot be sustained. All agree that *tahor she'achal tamei patur* — a *tahor* person who eats *tamei* meat is exempt from *kares*, since the liability is solely tied to *tumas haguf*, the impurity of the *person*.

### Kares Source

The *Gemara* now turns to the sourcing of both the punishment and the prohibition for each of the two *aveirot*. Regarding *ha'alat chutz*, both the *onesh* and the *azhara* are readily available. The *onesh* — the punishment of *kares* — is explicit in the *pesukim* of *Vayikra* 17 cited above. The *azhara* — the prohibitory warning — is found in *Devarim*: *hishamer lecha pen ta'aleh olotecha bechol makom asher tireh* — guard yourself lest you offer up your *olot* wherever you choose. In line with the principle stated by Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Elazar — *kol makom shene'emar hishamer pen v'al eino ela lo sa'aseh* — whenever the Torah uses the language of *hishamer*, *pen*, or *al*, it constitutes a negative prohibition. Thus for *ha'alat chutz*, both the *kares* and the *lo sa'aseh* are clearly established.

### Shechita Warning

For *shechutei chutz*, the *onesh* is similarly explicit — the same *pasuk* of *v'nichras ha'ish hahu* applies. However, the *azhara*, the prohibitory warning from which liability derives, is not obvious. The *Gemara* proposes: *amar kra v'lo yizbechu od et zivcheihem* — the *pasuk* states "and they shall no longer slaughter their sacrifices," which appears to function as the negative prohibition for *shechutei chutz*.

### Two Uses

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: that same phrase, *v'lo yizbechu od et zivcheihem*, is needed by Rabbi Elazar for a different teaching entirely — regarding *avodah zarah*. The question is how one becomes liable for *avodah zarah* when worshipping an idol in a manner that is *not* the standard form of worship for that deity. The *pasuk ikah ya'avdu hagoyim ha'eileh et eloheihem v'e'eseh chein gam ani* already prohibits performing the *classic* worship of foreign gods. The superfluous *v'lo yizbechu od et zivcheihem* is therefore applied *im eino inyan l'chedarkah* — since it is unnecessary for the standard mode of idol worship — *tenehu inyan l'shelo chedarkah* — to teach that even a *shechita* offered to an idol in a non-standard manner still generates *chiyuv* of *avodah zarah*.

If the entire phrase is thus consumed by the *avodah zarah* derivation, it cannot simultaneously serve as the *azhara* for *shechutei chutz*. Rabba resolves this by proposing a double reading: *krei beih v'lo yizbechu, u'krei beih v'lo od* — one should read the phrase in two stages. *V'lo yizbechu* — do not slaughter — serves as the *azhara* for *shechutei chutz*. *V'lo od et zivcheihem l'se'irim* — and no longer offer your sacrifices to the goat-gods — addresses the *avodah zarah* prohibition. The two *dinim* are derived from the same phrase read in two overlapping ways.

### Era 1: Mikdash

The *Gemara* then raises yet another challenge: that phrase is needed for a different *braita* altogether. The *braita* begins by noting: *ad kan hu m'daber b'kodashim she'hikdisham b'sha'at issur bamot v'hikrivam b'sha'at issur bamot* — the initial *pesukim* of *Vayikra* 17 address the paradigmatic case: animals sanctified and slaughtered *during the era of the Mikdash*, when *bamot* were already forbidden. The sin consists in not bringing them *el petach ohel mo'ed*. That case generates full *kares*, as stated explicitly: *v'nichras ha'ish hahu*.

### Era 2: Bamot

The *braita* then identifies a second scenario embedded in the subsequent *pesukim*: *v'lo yizbechu od et zivcheihem asher heim zovchim al pnei hasadeh* — and they shall no longer slaughter their sacrifices that they slaughter in the field. The phrase *asher heim zovchim al pnei hasadeh* — while they are currently slaughtering in the field — describes a different historical situation: animals that were sanctified *during the era when bamot were permitted*, when bringing *korbanot* outside the central *Mikdash* was acceptable. The *braita* reads the shift in *pesukim* as addressing a case where the *Mikdash* was subsequently built. Even though the animal was sanctified *b'sha'at heter bamot*, once the *Beit HaMikdash* was erected it could no longer be offered outside. One does not get "grandfathered in." The obligation is to bring it inside: *v'hevi'um la-Hashem* — and they shall bring them to God.

### Velo Yizbechu Od

The prohibition in this second scenario — that one may no longer slaughter such an animal on an outside *bamah* now that the *Mikdash* has been built — is derived from *v'lo yizbechu od*: they shall no longer continue doing so. The word *od* — "any longer" — fits this scenario with precision. There was a time when this was permitted; now that the *Mikdash* stands, it is forbidden. The *lo saaseh* of this second scenario is thus derived from *v'lo yizbechu od*, and this is the reading the *braita* requires.

### Punishment Limited

In this second scenario, if one violates the prohibition and slaughters outside or burns on an external *bamah*, what is the penalty? The *Gemara* establishes: there is a *mitzvas aseh* to bring the animal to God, and a *lo saaseh* against slaughtering it outside — derived from *v'lo yizbechu od*. But one might think *kares* applies here too. The *Gemara* rejects this: *talmud lomar chukas olam tihyeh zos lahem l'dorosam* — this shall be an eternal statute for all generations. *Zos lahem v'lo acheres lahem* — this, and not something else, applies to them. The *aseh* and the *lo saaseh* apply to this second scenario; *kares* does not.

The consequence is that *v'lo yizbechu od* is fully occupied by this second scenario — sanctified *b'sha'at heter bamot*, slaughtered *b'sha'at issur bamot* — and cannot simultaneously function as the *azhara* for the primary case of *shechutei chutz*. The *Gemara* thus leaves open the question of where the *lo saaseh* for the paradigmatic case of *shechutei chutz* — when the animal was sanctified and slaughtered entirely during the *sha'at issur bamot* — is actually derived from, carrying this question forward to the next *daf*.

---

---

# Zevachim 107

## Shechita Chutz

### Shechita—No Explicit Ver…

The daf under discussion opens mid-sugya, picking up from 106b, approximately ten lines down, with the words *ela amar Rav Avin* — though some versions read *ela amar Abaye*. The Gemara's driving question concerns the prohibition of *shechutei ve-ha'alot chutz*: the forbidding of slaughtering or burning an animal as a *korban* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* on a private altar. Performing either act renders one liable to *kares*, even when the offering is directed to God. The punishment is stated explicitly in the verses, but the difficulty is that while the Torah explicitly prohibits the act of *ha'ala'ah* — offering up — with the words *hishamer lecha pen ta'aleh olotecha*, "be careful lest you offer up your *olot*" — no parallel explicit prohibition is stated regarding *shechita* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*.

This creates a significant legal problem. The principle is that punishment presupposes a prior prohibition, and the implication of the Mishnah's language — "when are you *chayav*?" meaning when would you bring a *korban* for an unintentional transgression — requires both a negative prohibition and *kares* for the willful act. The Gemara has already attempted various approaches and found them inadequate. We now turn to what emerges as the operative solution.

### Rav Avin's Kal Vachomer

*Ela amar Rav Avin* — or *ela amar Abaye* — proposes deriving the prohibition from a *kal vachomer*. The reasoning proceeds as follows. An animal sanctified as a *korban* before the *Mishkan* was built and then slaughtered outside after the *Mishkan* was established is prohibited, even though the offender does not incur *kares* — since the animal was consecrated during a period when private altars were permitted. This is the *mah bimkom she-lo anash hizhir* case: even where there is no *kares*, there is still a prohibition. All the more so, then, *makom she-anash eino din she-yizhir*: in the case where we know *kares* applies — where the animal was sanctified after the *Beit HaMikdash* was built and is then slaughtered outside — surely there must also be a prohibition. The *kal vachomer* appears compelling.

### Ravina's Chelev Challenge

*Amar lei Ravina le-Rav Ashi*: Ravina immediately challenges this line of reasoning. If the Torah can communicate a prohibition through *kal vachomer*, why did it need to explicitly prohibit eating *chelev* — forbidden animal fat — which carries the punishment of *kares*? Let it simply state the *kares* and allow us to infer the prohibition by *kal vachomer* from *neveilah*, the improperly slaughtered animal, which is prohibited but carries no *kares*. Just as the lighter case of *neveilah* is prohibited, the weightier case of *chelev* should certainly be prohibited. *Teisi be-kal vachomer* — let it be derived logically. The fact that the Torah chose to state the prohibition of *chelev* explicitly suggests that *kal vachomer* is insufficient for establishing a prohibition.

### Rava's Chelev Analysis

*Amar lei* Rava: in fact, you cannot derive the prohibition of *chelev* from *neveilah* even if you tried, because the *kal vachomer* can be challenged. *Mah le-neveilah sheken mitama* — *neveilah* causes *tumah*, which is a weightier dimension not shared by *chelev*, so the *kal vachomer* does not hold. The Gemara then pursues a series of alternative bases for the *kal vachomer*: *shratzim temeim*, forbidden rodents that cause *tumah* — also disqualified because they cause *tumah*. *Shratzim tehorim*, forbidden creatures that do not cause *tumah* — disqualified because their prohibition applies even to a quantity smaller than a *ke-zayit*, making them in some respects weightier. *Orlah* and *kilayim* — disqualified because they are forbidden even in benefit. *Shevi'it* — disqualified because its sanctity transfers to money paid for it. *Teruma* — disqualified because there is never a circumstance in which *teruma* is permitted to a non-*kohen*.

And *chelev* itself, though it carries *kares*, is actually more lenient than all these other prohibitions in one respect: the *chelev* of a *chayah* — a deer, for example — is entirely permitted. So *chelev* has a dimension of leniency absent from every comparison case, and therefore *mah le-chelev she-lo hutra miklalo* — the prohibition was never fully universal — and no *kal vachomer* to *chelev* can succeed.

Rava then raises a broader concern: *ei kashya li ha kashya li*. What truly bothers him about using *kal vachomer* to establish a prohibition is the case of *Pesach* and *milah*, which carry *kares* but involve only a failure to perform a positive commandment, not a negative prohibition. With Rav Avin's logic, one might construct a *kal vachomer*: since *notar* — leaving over the *korban Pesach* — is prohibited without *kares*, then *Pesach* itself, which carries *kares*, should certainly generate a negative prohibition. But that is plainly not so. Rav Ashi reports that when he raised this with Rav Kahana, Rav Kahana responded that you cannot construct the *kal vachomer* from *motir* because it too can be challenged: *de-ika li-mifrach mah le-motir sheken ein lo takana* — once food has become *notar* it is ruined with no remedy, whereas the *Pesach* obligation has a remedy in the form of *Pesach sheni*. So again the *kal vachomer* fails on technical grounds.

### Ein Mazhirin Principle

The Gemara steps back from the local debates and states the overarching principle directly: *ve-chi mazhirin min ha-din?* Do we derive that something is prohibited from a *kal vachomer*? *Afilu le-man de-amar onshin min ha-din* — even according to the opinion that punishment may be derived from a *kal vachomer*, once you know something is prohibited you can perhaps determine the severity of the consequence logically. But the basic prohibition itself — *mazhirin min ha-din* — you cannot derive from logic alone.

There is something philosophically apt about this principle. A prohibition, in the framework of Torah law, is a divine command — it derives its force from God saying "do not do this." The use of *kal vachomer* is a human logical operation. While human reasoning has an authorized role in elaborating details and even in deriving consequences, the foundational commandedness of a prohibition cannot rest on human logical inference alone. It must proceed directly from the divine text. We are thus back to the beginning: how do we know *shechita* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* is negatively prohibited?

### Gezerah Shavah Solution

*Ela ke-Rabbi Yochanan*, the Gemara concludes: the prohibition is derived through *Rabbi Yochanan*'s principle of *atya havayah havayah* — a *gezerah shavah* linking the two *parshiyot* in Vayikra 17.

The first *parasha* (17:3–4) addresses *shechita*: *ish ish mi-beit Yisrael asher yishchat shor kesev o ez... v'el petach ohel moed lo hevi'o l'hakriv korban la-Shem... dam yechashev la-ish ha-hu dam shafach v'nichrat*. This passage states the *kares* for slaughtering outside but contains no explicit prohibition. The second *parasha* (17:8–9) addresses *ha'ala'ah*: *asher ya'aleh olah o zavach... v'el petach ohel moed lo yavi'enu v'nichrat ha-ish ha-hu me-amav*. This passage, by contrast, is preceded by the explicit prohibition *hishamer lecha pen ta'aleh olotecha*.

The link is forged through the shared language of *havi'ennu* and *hevi'o* — both expressing the act of bringing to the *ohel moed*. *Ma le-halan lo anash ela im ken hizhir af kan lo anash ela im ken hizhir*: just as by *ha'ala'ah* there is no punishment without a prior prohibition, so too by *shechita* there is no punishment without a prior prohibition — and the *gezerah shavah* transfers that prohibition to the case of *shechita*. Rava offers a parallel derivation *ke-Rabbi Yonah*, through a different *gezerah shavah* based on the word *olatecha*.

The conceptual distinction between this solution and the failed *kal vachomer* is significant. A *gezerah shavah* is understood as encoded within the text itself — it is God's own textual design that links these two passages. A *kal vachomer*, by contrast, is pure human logic applied externally to the text. The prohibition, derived through the *gezerah shavah*, therefore meets the requirement of originating in the divine word rather than in human inference.

---

## Burning Offerings

### Muktarei Pnim/Chutz

With the prohibition of *shechita* established, the Gemara now turns to a question arising from the debate in the Mishnah. We have established, the Gemara notes, *ashkechan muktarei pnim she-he'elah ba-chutz*: we understand the liability for burning outside things that were fit to be offered inside — i.e., an animal slaughtered within the *Beit HaMikdash* and then burned on an outside altar. In that case, the animal was *ra'uy li-fnim*, fit for the inside, and so the act of burning it outside is clearly a violation.

But the Mishnah's debate with Rabbi Shimon concerns the case of *muktarei chutz she-he'elah ba-chutz*: an animal slaughtered outside the *Beit HaMikdash* and subsequently burned outside. At the moment of the burning, this animal is no longer fit for the *Beit HaMikdash* — it was invalidated by being slaughtered outside. Rabbi Shimon accordingly rules *patur*. The Gemara asks: *minayin* — from where does the majority position derive that one is nonetheless *chayav*?

### V'Aleihem Tomar

*Amar Rav Kahana amar kra*: the verse says *v'aleihem tomar* (17:8). Reading *aleihem* as *aleihem* — "regarding those" rather than "to them" — Rav Kahana derives *al ha-semuchim tomar*: the prohibition of *ha'alah* stated in the second *parasha* applies also "regarding" the very things described in the preceding *parasha* — namely, animals slaughtered outside. The *vav* of *v'aleihem tomar* connects the two *parshiyot*, indicating that the prohibition of burning outside applies even to animals that were slaughtered outside and thus are not fit for inside.

### 37th Kareis Question

*Maskif lei Rava*: Rava challenges this. *Mi ksiv v'aleihem? V'aleihem ksiv* — the word is actually *va'aleihem*, "and to them," not *v'aleihem* in the sense of "regarding them," so the textual basis for Rav Kahana's reading is questionable. The Gemara therefore pivots to the formulation taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *v'aleihem tomar le-arev parshiyot* — the *vav* connecting the two sections links them, so that the prohibition of burning outside encompasses also the case of animals slaughtered outside.

Rabbi Yochanan offers an alternative derivation through a *gezerah shavah* on the word for "bringing": *lo yavi'enu* in the second *parasha* and *lo hevi'o* in the first. *Mah le-halan muktarei chutz* — just as the first *parasha* concerns animals slaughtered outside, so too the second *parasha*, through this link, includes animals slaughtered outside.

Rav Bibi then raises an objection. The Mishnah states that there are 36 categories in the Torah for which one incurs *kares*. If we now distinguish between burning something slaughtered inside the *Beit HaMikdash* (derived from the plain meaning of the verse) and burning something slaughtered outside (derived through a separate *derasha*), these should constitute two distinct prohibitions — and the count should reach 37. *D'ika ha-ma'aleh ve-ha-ma'aleh* — there is one *ma'aleh* for each sub-category, and treating them as separate derivations implies they are separate sins.

### One Prohibition Unity

The Gemara marks this difficulty with *kashya*, acknowledging the force of the objection. The underlying resolution implicit in the discussion is that although the two cases are derived from different textual sources, they constitute a single prohibition with two applications: the verse — read through the connecting *vav* or through the *gezerah shavah* — encompasses both within the scope of one prohibition. This is consistent with Rabbi Shimon's position as the background to the whole discussion: the Rabbanan hold that the *derasha* extends the prohibition to include *muktarei chutz*, but the extension belongs to the same prohibition, not a new one.

---

## Sprinkling Blood

### Zerika—New Category

The Gemara now introduces a new question. We have established *chiyuv* for *shechita* outside and *ha'alah* outside. But what about *zerika* — sprinkling the blood — performed outside the *Beit HaMikdash*? The next Mishnah will teach that one who sprinkles some of the blood outside is *chayav*. *Mina lan* — what is the source?

### Rabbi Yishmael—Dam

*Nafkha lei mi-de-is-tanya*: it is derived from a *baraita*. In the verse concerning *shechita* (17:4), it states *dam yechashev la-ish ha-hu dam shafach* — it is reckoned to him as the spilling of blood. Rabbi Yishmael focuses on this emphasis on *dam* — blood — and derives from it *le-rabbot ha-zorek*: to include the one who sprinkles the blood outside. The textual emphasis on blood in the context of *shechita* extends the prohibition to encompass the blood-ritual of *zerika* as well. This categorizes *zerika* together with *shechita*.

### Rabbi Akiva—Or

Rabbi Akiva derives *zerika* from a different verse entirely — the *parasha* of *ha'alah* (17:8–9): *asher ya'aleh olah o zavach*. The word *o* ("or") before *zavach* is read as an inclusion: *le-rabbot et ha-zorek* — to include the act of sprinkling blood. This derivation categorizes *zerika* together with *ha'alah*.

*Ve-Rabbi Yishmael hai o zavach mai avid lei?* What does Rabbi Yishmael do with the word *o zavach*? *Le-chalek* — it serves its normal grammatical function, indicating that one is *chayav* for either an *olah* or a *shelamim* independently, not only if both are offered together. Rabbi Yishmael has no need to derive *zerika* from this word because he already has *dam yechashev*.

### Zerika Grouping

*Ve-Rabbi Akiva le-chalek mena lei?* If Rabbi Akiva uses *o* for *zerika*, where does he derive that one is *chayav* for either offering independently? *Nafka lei mi-lo yavi'enu* — the verse says *lo yavi'enu* in the singular rather than *lo yevi'am* in the plural, teaching that even a single *korban* brought outside generates liability, without requiring two.

Rabbi Yishmael, in turn, uses *lo yavi'enu* for a different lesson: *al ha-shalem hu chayav ve-eino chayav al ha-chaser* — one is liable only if he burns a whole animal, not an incomplete one. And Rabbi Akiva derives the "wholeness" requirement from the phrase *la'asot oto* — "to make it" — which implies completeness.

This generates a further distinction between the two positions. Since Rabbi Yishmael uses both *lo yavi'enu* and *la'asot oto* to derive the "wholeness" requirement, he applies it in two distinct scenarios. *Ve-Rabbi Yishmael chad be-muktarei pnim she-chisru ve-he'elu ba-chutz ve-chad be-muktarei chutz she-chisru ve-he'elu ba-chutz* — one verse excludes the case of an animal fit for inside that was rendered incomplete and then burned outside; the other excludes the case of an animal fit only for outside that was rendered incomplete and then burned outside. In both scenarios, liability requires that the animal be whole.

### Shalem—Wholeness

A *baraita* elaborates Rabbi Yishmael's position. *Yachol muktarei pnim she-chisru ve-he'elu ba-chutz chayav* — one might have thought that for an animal slaughtered inside the *Beit HaMikdash*, even if it became incomplete before being burned outside, there would still be *chiyuv*. Rashi explains why: within the *Beit HaMikdash*, if a piece of an *olah* falls off the altar it is replaced; the norm for *muktarei pnim* is to continue burning even partial pieces. One might have thought this logic carries over to the case of burning outside. Therefore the Torah teaches: *talmud lomar la'asot oto* — liability applies only to burning the complete animal. Whether it was slaughtered inside or outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, one is exempt if only a partial animal is burned outside.

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. Having used *lo yavi'enu* to derive "one rather than two" and having only *la'asot oto* for the wholeness requirement, he has only one verse covering only one scenario. He would therefore rule that for *muktarei pnim* — an animal slaughtered inside — if it was incomplete and burned outside, one would still be *chayav*. The two Tannaim thus dispute both the derivation of *zerika* and the scope of the "wholeness" requirement.

The accounting of verses continues further. Rabbi Akiva uses *dam yechashev* to include *shechitat ha-of* — slaughtering a bird sacrifice outside — since one might have thought that since birds are normally processed by *melika* inside the *Beit HaMikdash*, *shechita* of a bird outside would generate no liability. Rabbi Yishmael derives this from the repetition of the verb *yishchat* in the verse (*asher yishchat ba-machaneh o asher yishchat mi-chutz la-machaneh*), the doubled usage being unnecessary and therefore coming to include bird *shechita*.

Both agree, however, that *melika* of a bird performed outside the *Beit HaMikdash* is exempt: Rabbi Yishmael derives this from *zeh ha-davar asher yishchat* — "this is the matter, of slaughtering" — the word *zeh* restricting the prohibition to *shechita* alone. Rabbi Akiva derives it from *lo yavi'enu* read as *al ha-shochet hu chayav ve-lo al ha-moleik*.

---

## Multiple Violations

### Shachat Vezarak

Rabbi Abbahu now draws out the practical implications of the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding the categorization of *zerika*. The question is: if someone, in a single state of forgetfulness that the prohibition existed, performed both *shechita* and *zerika* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, how many *chatat* offerings must he bring upon realizing his error?

*Shachat ve-zarak le-divrei Rabbi Yishmael chayav achat le-divrei Rabbi Akiva chayav shtayim.* Since Rabbi Yishmael derives *zerika* from the *parasha* of *shechita* — specifically from *dam yechashev* — he categorizes *zerika* together with *shechita* as a single prohibition. Performing both in one state of forgetfulness constitutes one sin committed twice, and only one *korban* is required. Rabbi Akiva, who derives *zerika* from the *parasha* of *ha'alah*, categorizes it together with burning — and therefore *shechita* and *zerika* constitute two distinct prohibitions, requiring two *korbanot*.

### Abaye's Unification

Abaye dissents from this framing of the Rabbi Akiva position. *Afilu le-divrei Rabbi Akiva eino chayav ela achat* — even according to Rabbi Akiva, one brings only one *korban* for *shechita* and *zerika* combined. Although Rabbi Akiva derives *zerika* from the verse of *ha'alah*, he nevertheless agrees on the conceptual categorization: *amar kra sham ta'aseh ve-sham ta'aleh* — the verse in Devarim states "there you shall perform your *korbanot*" and "there you shall offer up," distinguishing between a general category of ritual performance (*ta'aseh*) and the specific act of burning (*ta'aleh*). *Shechita* and *zerika*, being ritual acts other than burning, fall within the *ta'aseh* category and are thus grouped together as one type of prohibition, regardless of which verse derives *zerika*. *Kasav asiya le-khulhu avoda achat* — the Torah's formulation of *asiyah* makes all acts other than burning into a single *avoda* category.

### Zarak Veha'ela

The same reasoning applies in reverse. *Zarak ve-he'ela* — one who sprinkled blood and then burned the offering outside in a single state of forgetfulness: *le-divrei Rabbi Yishmael chayav shtayim* — for Rabbi Yishmael, since *zerika* is categorized with *shechita* and *ha'alah* is its own category, these are two distinct prohibitions and require two *korbanot*. *Le-divrei Rabbi Akiva eino chayav ela achat* — for Rabbi Akiva (on the non-Abaye reading), since *zerika* is derived from the *parasha* of *ha'alah*, the two are effectively one category, and only one *korban* is required.

Abaye again corrects: *afilu le-divrei Rabbi Akiva chayav shtayim* — even Rabbi Akiva holds that *zerika* and *ha'alah* are two distinct sins. The verse *sham ta'aleh ve-sham ta'aseh* separates *ha'alah* from all other ritual acts. However *zerika* is derived textually, it conceptually belongs to the *ta'aseh* category, not to *ta'aleh*, and therefore *zerika* and *ha'alah* remain two distinct prohibitions. *Ve-hachi pelaginhu kra* — this is how the verse itself divides them.

### All Three Violations

The final case: *ve-shachat ve-zarak ve-he'ela* — one who performed all three acts in a single state of forgetfulness. *Le-divrei ha-kol chayav shtayim* — according to all opinions, he brings two *korbanot*. Wherever *zerika* is categorized — whether with *shechita* (Rabbi Yishmael, or Rabbi Akiva per Abaye) or with *ha'alah* (Rabbi Akiva on the non-Abaye reading) — the three acts span both categories. In either case, one category is represented twice and the other once, yielding two distinct sins committed, and therefore two *korbanot*.

---

## Geographic Scope

### Three Camps Question

With the categories of prohibited acts now fully analyzed, the Gemara turns to the geographic question: where must the act take place for liability to arise? The relevant verse reads *asher yishchat ba-machaneh o asher yishchat mi-chutz la-machaneh* — "who slaughters in the camp or who slaughters outside the camp." The phrase *mi-chutz la-machaneh* normally denotes a location fully outside all three *machanos* — the *machaneh Shechinah*, *machaneh Leviyah*, and *machaneh Yisrael*, corresponding in the context of Jerusalem to the *azarah*, *Har HaBayis*, and Jerusalem itself. But the verse also includes *ba-machaneh* — in the camp — which implies that even slaughtering within the camp environs generates *chiyuv*, as long as it is not at the *petach ohel moed*.

### Shechita Ba'Darom

A *baraita* is introduced: *asher yishchat mi-chutz la-machaneh — yachol chutz li-shlosh machanos?* Perhaps *mi-chutz la-machaneh* means only fully outside all three camps, and one who slaughters within any of them is exempt? The verse therefore also says *ba-machaneh* — even within the camp — to establish that liability extends to locations within the camp perimeter. But this raises the converse question: *yachol ha-shochet olah ba-darom yei chayav?* Perhaps the inclusion of *ba-machaneh* means one is even *chayav* for slaughtering an *olah* in the southern section of the *azarah*?

This is not as strange as it sounds. The southern section of the *azarah* is not a valid location for the *shechita* of *kodshei kodshim*, including an *olah*, though it is valid for *kodshim kalim* like *shelamim*. One might have thought: since the verse says *ba-machaneh* to include locations within the camp, perhaps slaughtering an *olah* in the south — a place unfit for it — should generate liability for *shechutei chutz*. The *baraita* answers: *mi-chutz la-machaneh meyuchad she-ein ra'uy li-shchitat kodshim u-le-shchitat kol zevach* — the model for liability is a location unfit for the slaughter of *any* sacrifice whatsoever. The south, while unfit for *kodshei kodshim*, remains fit for *kodshim kalim*. Therefore it does not fall within the prohibition, and one who slaughters an *olah* there is not liable for *shechutei chutz* — though the *korban* is invalidated.

### Roof of Heichal

*Amar Ulla: ha-shochet al gago shel Heichal chayav.* Ulla proposes that if someone slaughters a *korban* on the roof of the *Heichal*, he is *chayav*. The roof of the *Heichal* is certainly not a valid location for any *shechita*, and therefore it would seem to fit the criterion of a place unfit for the slaughter of all sacrifices — thus generating liability for *shechutei chutz*. Ulla adds: *ho'il ve-ra'uy li-shchitat kol zevach* — since, had the act been performed inside, it would have been valid for any sacrifice.

### Petach Ohel Moed

*Matkif lah Rava*: Rava challenges Ulla. *Im ken nichtov kra mi-chutz la-machaneh ve-lo ba'ei petach ohel moed* — if geographic location outside any permitted zone were the sole criterion, the Torah should have simply stated "outside the camp" and had no need to add the phrase *v'el petach ohel moed lo hevi'o* — "he did not bring it to the entrance of the *ohel moed*." The fact that the verse specifies *petach ohel moed* indicates that the operative question is not merely where the act occurred but whether the animal was brought to the *ohel moed*. An animal on the roof of the *Heichal* is within the airspace and zone of the *ohel moed* — it was, in a meaningful sense, brought there. Therefore *petach ohel moed lamah li? Lav le-mi'utei gagot* — the reference to *petach ohel moed* is precisely to exclude the roof, teaching that one who slaughters on the roof is *patur*.

### Animal in/out Scope

*U-le-Rava im ken nichtov petach ohel moed ba-machaneh u-mi-chutz la-machaneh lamah li?* The Gemara presses back on Rava: if *petach ohel moed* does the work on its own, why does the verse need to specify both *ba-machaneh* and *mi-chutz la-machaneh*? What do those geographic qualifications add?

*Amar Rav Mari: la'atuyei kullah bifnim ve-tzavara ba-chutz* — they come to include the case where the body of the animal is standing inside the *azarah* while its neck protrudes outside, where the *shechita* occurs. In such a case, one might have argued that since the animal was brought into the *ohel moed*, there is no liability. The *ba-machaneh u-mi-chutz la-machaneh* teaches that one is nonetheless *chayav*.

The Gemara objects: *tzavara ba-chutz peshita* — that case is obvious. The act of *shechita* occurs at the neck, and the neck is outside. Even with the *petach ohel moed* verse alone, one would know that *shechita* occurring outside is the operative act. *Ela la-atuyei kullah ba-chutz ve-tzavara bifnim* — rather, the geographic qualifications come to include the reverse scenario: the body of the animal stands outside while its neck is inside the *azarah*. Without *ba-machaneh u-mi-chutz la-machaneh*, one might have argued that since the *shechita* itself occurs inside — at the neck, which is within the *ohel moed* — the offender should be exempt. The verse teaches that even here, since the bulk of the animal remains outside, one is *chayav*.

In summary, the geographic parameters work together: the references to *ba-machaneh* and *mi-chutz la-machaneh* clarify that *chiyuv* applies whether the location of the act is close to the *Beit HaMikdash* or far — even on *Har HaBayit* or in Jerusalem itself, the act is prohibited — and they further teach the edge cases involving an animal straddling the boundary of the *azarah*. The *petach ohel moed* language, for its part, excludes acts performed fully within the sanctified precinct, including, according to Rava, those performed on the roof of the *Heichal*, which falls within the zone of the *ohel moed*. Whether Ulla or Rava is correct on that final point remains the subject of the *itmar* that will be taken up in the next daf.

---

---

# Zevachim 108

## Shchutei Chutz Today

### Contemporary Altars

The daf opens at the bottom of 107b, where the Gemara turns to a thoroughly practical question: what is the law for someone who slaughters or offers up sacrifices outside the *Beis HaMikdash* in the present day? The entire discussion flows from the *issur* of *bamot* — not the mere possession of a private altar, but the act of using one. The Gemara introduces this with the word *itmar*, signaling an Amoraic dispute.

### Kedusha Rishona

*Rabbi Yochanan amar chayav* — Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who burns an offering on an altar today is *chayav*, subject to *kares*, for having offered a sacrifice outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. His reasoning: *kedusha rishona kidsah l'sha'atah v'kidsah l'atid lavo* — the first sanctification of the Temple site was effective for all future times. The *Makom HaMikdash* therefore retains its sanctity even after destruction, and that place alone remains the site at which sacrifices are acceptable. Since the location remains sanctified, any offering made elsewhere still violates the prohibition of *shchutei chutz* with full liability.

### Resh Lakish's View

*Resh Lakish amar patur* — Resh Lakish rules that one is exempt. His reasoning is the inverse: *kedusha rishona kidsah l'sha'atah v'lo kidsah l'atid lavo* — the first sanctification was only for its time and did not extend indefinitely into the future.

### First vs. Second Kedusha

It is worth pausing to clarify the precise contours of this dispute. The framing in terms of *kedusha rishona* should not mislead. The real question is not which *kedusha* — first or second — persists, but whether *any* sanctification of the *Makom HaMikdash* endures until the present day. The Rambam, for instance, holds by *Eretz Yisrael* that the *kedusha rishona* lapsed at the first exile, while the second *kedusha* persists even now. One could similarly argue that while the first *kedusha* of the Temple site may have dissipated, the second is stronger and more enduring. The essential question, regardless of which *kedusha* one invokes, is whether the sanctity of the *Makom HaMikdash* is operative today.

### Bamot & Transition

A further conceptual distinction is worth drawing here. The Gemara elsewhere cites the verse *ki lo batem ad atah el hamenucha v'el hanachala* — *hamenucha* refers to places like *Nov* and *Givon* and *Shiloh*, while *hanachala* refers to *Yerushalayim*. This verse implies that the era of private *bamot* was explicitly a transitional period in history, lasting only until a permanent central site was designated for the *Beis HaMikdash*. Once God designated that location as the permanent home of the *shchina*, the era of *bamot* closed — permanently. This point stands independent of whether the *kedusha* of the *Makom HaMikdash* itself persists.

It is thus possible to distinguish two separate questions: first, whether the *Makom HaMikdash* retains its *kedusha* such that sacrifices could theoretically be brought there today; and second, whether the *issur bamot* has been lifted now that the *Beis HaMikdash* lies in ruins. These need not stand or fall together. Even Resh Lakish, who rules *patur*, may well agree that the *issur bamot* remains in effect — that it is forbidden to bring sacrifices in one's backyard. His point may be more technical: the specific liability of *kares* for *shchutei chutz* requires that the act be *raui lepetach ohel moed*, fit in principle for the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. If the *Makom HaMikdash* no longer retains its *kedusha*, then nothing is *raui lepetach ohel moed*, and the trigger for *kares* is absent, even though a lesser prohibition remains.

### Raui Le'Petach

This is indeed the implication of the Gemara, which cites *v'el petach ohel moed lo heveio* — the verse that grounds the liability for *shchutei chutz* in the concept of *raui lepetach ohel moed*. Rabbi Yochanan holds that even today, in principle, a sacrifice could be brought to the *Makom HaMikdash* — it remains sanctified — and therefore the requirement of *raui lepetach ohel moed* is satisfied, and one is *chayav kares*. Resh Lakish denies this: without operative *kedusha*, there is nowhere that qualifies as *petach ohel moed*, and the *chiyuv kares* accordingly does not apply.

---

## Curtains in the Temple

### Rabbi Eliezer

The Gemara now asks whether this dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish is rooted in an earlier Tannaitic debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. The Gemara cites a *mishnah*: *amar Rabbi Eliezer*, when the builders were constructing the *heichal* during the Second Temple period, they would erect *kelayim* — curtains — both around the *heichal* and around the *azara*. There was a difference in practice between the two areas: for the *heichal*, the builders would work from outside the curtain, so as not to stand within the space where the *heichal* walls would be, whereas in the *azara* they would work from inside the curtain.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua responded: *shamati she'hayu makrivim af al pi she'ein bayis* — I have a tradition that offerings could be brought even without a standing Temple structure. Moreover, *kodshu kodoshim* could be eaten even without *kelayim* to demarcate the *azara*, *kodshim kalim* and *maaser sheini* could be consumed even without a wall encircling *Yerushalayim*. The reasoning is explicit: *mipnei shekedusha rishona kidsha l'sha'atah v'kidsah l'atid lavo* — because the first sanctification endured for all future times.

This is a striking *chiddush* within Rabbi Yehoshua's position. Even if one grants that *kedusha* persists, one might still argue that a physical structure — a *bayit*, walls, curtains — is required before sacrifices may be offered. Rabbi Yehoshua goes further: the *kedusha* is so deeply embedded in the place itself that even the complete absence of structure does not diminish it. The *makom ha'azara* remains defined as such without walls, *Yerushalayim* remains *kedushas Yerushalayim* without a surrounding wall.

### After Destruction

The Gemara then asks: does Rabbi Eliezer's position implicitly reject this? Since Rabbi Eliezer emphasizes that *kelayim* would be erected during construction, and Rabbi Yehoshua responds that *kelayim* are not halachically necessary, it seems as though Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *kedusha* did not persist — and that some form of renewed demarcation was required before sacrifices could resume.

### Ravina's Question

Ravina challenges this inference in a question posed to Rav Ashi: *dilma de'kulei alma kedusha rishona kidsha l'sha'atah v'kidsah l'atid lavo* — perhaps everyone agrees with the fundamental principle of Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua may simply be transmitting different traditions, each reporting what he had heard — *mar mai dishmei lei ka'amar u'mar mai dishmei lei ka'amar* — without any underlying disagreement about whether *kedusha* persists.

### Curtains for Modesty

This raises the obvious question: if Rabbi Eliezer also agrees that *kedusha* persists and that one may offer sacrifices without a structure, why does he emphasize the *kelayim*? The Gemara answers: *litzni'usa be'alma* — for modesty alone. Just as construction sites today are screened off from public view as a matter of propriety and respect, the *kelayim* around the emerging *Beis HaMikdash* served an aesthetic and decorous function, not a halachic one. They were not required to establish *kedusha* or to permit the offering of sacrifices.

---

## Bone & Salt

### Bird's Head Case

The Gemara now introduces another dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, this time concerning what counts toward the *kezayit* required for liability under *shchutei chutz*. The case: one places a bird's limb on the fire, but the meat alone does not constitute a *kezayit* — only together with its bone does the offering reach that measure. *Raui lepetach ohel moed* has been established as a condition; the question is what constitutes the required minimum.

### Chibbur Olin

*Rabbi Yochanan amar chayav* — Rabbi Yochanan rules that one is liable. His principle: *chibbur olin k'olin dami* — something connected to an item that is offered is treated as part of the offering itself. As Rashi notes, this is directly related to the earlier discussion that while a separated bone need not be placed on the altar, a bone still attached to the meat is burned along with it. Since it is connected, it counts as part of what is offered.

### Not Offered Per Se

*Resh Lakish amar patur* — Resh Lakish rules that one is exempt. His principle is the inverse: *chibbur olin lav k'olin dami*. It is true that the bone is burned when connected, but this does not mean the bone is itself *offered*. It is simply dragged along with the meat. It was never independently the object of the sacrificial act, and therefore it cannot contribute to the minimum measure that triggers liability.

### Salt Question

Rava then poses a question that builds on this debate: what if one places a bird's head on the fire where the meat alone does not constitute a *kezayit*, but the salt with which it is coated completes the measure? Salt is required to be brought with every sacrifice — *lo tashbit melach brit Elokecha me'al kol korbancha takriv melach* — so it is routinely offered together with the sacrifice. Rav Pappa bar Zeika suggests to Rav Ashi that this is simply the same dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. After all, salt is something placed on the *mizbeach* together with the sacrifice, just as a bone is.

### Organic vs. Supplementary

The Gemara rejects this, and the rejection is illuminating: *tiba'i l'Rabbi Yochanan tiba'i l'Resh Lakish* — the question applies independently to both positions, because the case of salt differs from the case of bone in ways that cut in opposite directions for each Amora.

Consider Rabbi Yochanan's position. He held that the bone counts because it is *mina d'bisra* — organically part of the meat itself, in addition to being physically connected. Salt, however, is clearly not an organic part of the bird. Even Rabbi Yochanan might therefore rule that salt does not contribute to the *kezayit*.

Consider Resh Lakish's position. He held that the bone does not count because if it were to separate, there would be no independent obligation to place it on the altar — it is only there because it happens to be attached. Salt, by contrast, if it were to fall off, there *would* be an obligation to reapply it, since salt is independently required on every sacrifice. Salt is thus not a mere passenger but an obligatory component of the offering. Even Resh Lakish might therefore rule that salt counts.

### Teiku

The question thus cannot be resolved by simple extension of the earlier dispute, since each side's reasoning points in an unexpected direction regarding salt. The Gemara concludes: *teiku* — the question stands unresolved.

---

## Rabbi Yosi HaGlili

### Fit for the Altar

The Gemara turns to a position of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, who holds that liability for *ma'aleh* — burning an offering outside — is limited to cases involving what the Gemara terms *mikudshai p'nim*, meat that was slaughtered inside the *Beis HaMikdash*. The requirement of *raui lepetach ohel moed* means, for Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, that the meat must have been fit for the altar. If one slaughtered outside and then burned the offering outside, the meat was never fit for the *mizbeach* — it was never *raui lepetach ohel moed* — and therefore there is no liability for *ma'aleh bachutz*.

### Rabbis' Challenge

The Rabbis challenge this position. Even if you slaughter inside the *Beis HaMikdash*, the moment you take the meat outside it becomes *pasul*. If liability still exists in that case — as Rabbi Yosi HaGlili presumably concedes — then you must accept that one can be liable even when the meat is no longer *raui*. What then is the meaningful distinction between slaughtering inside and slaughtering outside?

### Sha'as Kosher

*Heshiv Rebbe tachas Rabbi Yosi HaGlili* — Rebbe steps in to defend the position of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili. The distinction is *sha'as kosher*: when one slaughters inside the *Beis HaMikdash* and then takes the meat outside, there was at least one moment — at the time of slaughter — when the meat was fit for the altar, *raui lepetach ohel moed*. That moment of fitness is sufficient. *Tomar b'shochet bachutz u'ma'aleh bachutz shelo haysa lo sha'as kosher* — but when one slaughters outside and then burns it outside, the meat never had such a moment. It was disqualified from the outset, and the liability for *ma'aleh bachutz* is accordingly absent.

### Kodesh Mekablo

Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon also defends Rabbi Yosi HaGlili but frames the distinction differently. *She'chein kodesh mekablo* — when meat is slaughtered inside and then taken outside, even though it became *pasul* as *yotzei*, the *kodesh* still, in a sense, accepted it. One of the principles of the *mizbeach* is that if *pasul* meat that falls into the category of *psula bakodesh* is placed on the altar, it is not removed. Since meat slaughtered inside but taken outside would not be removed from the *mizbeach* if placed there, it remains *raui* in a meaningful sense. *Tomar b'shochet bachutz she'ein kodesh mekablo* — meat slaughtered outside, however, is not *psula bakodesh*, and if placed on the *mizbeach* it would be taken down. It is not *raui* in any sense.

### Night Slaughter

*Amar Zeiri* — what practical case distinguishes Rebbe from Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon? *Shechitas laila ika binaihu* — slaughter performed at night inside the *Beis HaMikdash*. Such slaughter is invalid, and therefore the meat never had a *sha'as kosher* according to Rebbe — the slaughter occurred inside, but it was never fit at any moment, so Rebbe would rule *patur*. Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, however, would hold that this is *psula bakodesh* — it is the kind of disqualification that occurs in the *kodesh* context — and if placed on the *mizbeach* the meat would be allowed to remain. Therefore Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon would hold one *chayav*.

### Non-Sacred Vessel

*Rabbah amar* — a parallel distinguishing case: if the blood was caught in a non-sacred vessel, *kli chol*, rather than a sacred vessel. Again, according to Rebbe, there is no *sha'as kosher* — the blood reception was invalid from the outset — and Rabbi Yosi HaGlili would therefore render one *patur*. According to Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, however, this is *psula bakodesh* and the meat remains on the *mizbeach*, generating liability.

---

## Tamei & Issur

### Double Tumah

The Gemara now moves to a parallel application of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's approach, this time in the context of *tumah*. The case: a person who is *tamei* eats meat of *kodashim* that is itself *tamei*. Two points of law are relevant: eating *kodashim* while personally *tamei* carries *kares*; eating *kodashim* that are *tamei* violates a *lav* but does not carry *kares*. What is the law when both obtain simultaneously?

### No Chiyuv

Rabbi Yosi HaGlili holds that one is *patur* from *kares* in this case. Since the meat was already *tamei* — already defiled — it was not *tahor* meat that the *tamei* person consumed, and the *chiyuv kares* cannot attach.

### Parallel Cases

The Rabbis challenge this position with a pointed observation. Rabbi Yosi HaGlili concedes that in the ordinary case — a *tamei* person eating *tahor kodashim* — there is a *chiyuv kares*. But by the very act of picking up the meat and eating it, a *tamei* person renders the meat *tamei* through contact. So even in the case that Rabbi Yosi HaGlili concedes generates *kares*, the meat ends up *tamei* by the time it is consumed. The Rabbis conclude: *shappir kamreiley rabbanan l'Rabbi Yosi HaGlili* — unlike the earlier debates where Rebbe and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon came to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's defense, here the challenge is judged a strong one, because at the end of the day the meat is *tamei* in both scenarios.

### Migu Principle

Rava resolves the apparent contradiction within Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position by drawing a crucial distinction. *Kol heicha d'nitma tumas haguf v'achar kach nitma basar d'chuley alma lo pligi d'chayav* — where one first became *tamei* as a person and only thereafter the meat became *tamei*, everyone agrees one is *chayav*. If I became *tamei* first, there was already a full *chiyuv kares* in place the moment that status obtained. The subsequent *tumah* of the meat does not dislodge that liability.
