The dispute concerns the reverse sequence: the meat became *tamei* first, and then the person became *tamei*. Here the question is one of *issur chal al issur* — whether the *issur kares* can take effect on top of a pre-existing lesser prohibition. The principle at stake is *migu*: when one becomes *tamei*, one does not merely become forbidden to eat this one piece of already-*tamei* meat. One becomes forbidden to eat all *kodashim*, including the many *tahor* pieces one might otherwise have consumed. This is an *issur kolel* — an inclusive prohibition, one that sweeps in things not previously forbidden. Since the *issur kares* takes hold on all those *tahor* pieces, it also takes hold — by virtue of *migu*, as a side effect of the broader prohibition — on this already-*tamei* piece. The *Rabbanan* accept this reasoning.

### No Migu

Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, however, *savar lo amrinan migu* — does not accept the principle that *issur chal al issur* operates by way of *migu* for an *issur kolel*. Even though the second prohibition has a broader scope, it does not take effect atop the pre-existing prohibition on this specific piece of meat.

### Which is Weightier

The Gemara presses Rabbi Yosi HaGlili: even without *migu*, is not *tumas haguf* weightier than *tumas habasar*? *Tumas haguf* carries *kares* and has a broader reach — it forbids the consumption of all *kodashim*. A weightier prohibition taking effect alongside a lesser one might be expected to override it. Rav Ashi responds: *mimai detumas haguf chamura?* — what makes *tumas haguf* unambiguously weightier? There is a sense in which *tumas habasar* is in fact weightier: *she'ein la tahara bemikvah* — the *tumah* of the meat cannot be removed through *immersion*. A person can immerse and become *tahor*; the meat, once *tamei*, cannot. From the perspective of the meat itself, its *tamei* status is more permanent, more deeply embedded. Since the question is whether the *issur kares* takes effect *on the meat*, the permanence of the meat's own *tumah* status may be precisely what blocks it.

---

## Stringencies (III)

### Shchita Stringent

The *mishnah* introduces a comparative analysis of *shchutei chutz* and *ha'alas chutz*: there are respects in which slaughtering outside is governed by stricter rules, and respects in which burning an offering outside is governed by stricter rules.

*Chomer beshchita* — the stringency of slaughter: *hashocheit lehediot chayav* — one who slaughters a sanctified animal outside the *Beis HaMikdash* for mundane purposes, simply to eat its meat, is nonetheless *chayav*. This is a considerable *chiddush*. Slaughter is not inherently a sacrificial act. If a person has an animal sanctified as a *shelamim* and decides to slaughter it for a barbecue, the act of slaughter carries no intrinsically sacrificial quality — it is simply preparation of meat. Yet because the animal was *kodshim* and was slaughtered outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, liability attaches regardless of the person's intent. By contrast, *ha'ma'aleh lehediot patur* — one who burns the meat outside as an act of homage to another person, or even as an offering to an idol, is *patur* from the specific prohibition of *ha'alas chutz*. Liability for burning outside requires that the act be performed as a sacrificial offering to God; slaughter outside generates liability regardless of purpose.

### Offering Stringent

*Chomer ba'aliyah* — the stringency of offering: *shnayim she'achazu besakin veshachtu peturin* — two people who jointly hold the knife and slaughter together are exempt. *Achzu b'eiver vehe'elu chayavin* — but two people who jointly place a piece of meat on the fire as a sacrificial act are both *chayav*. The rule that partnership in a *melachah* generates liability operates for burning outside but not for slaughtering outside. As the Gemara will explain, this differential treatment is anchored in the verse structure of the relevant *parshiyot*.

---

## Multiple Offerings

### Multiple Pieces

The *mishnah* then addresses the case where one places multiple limbs or pieces on the fire in succession, pausing between each. *He'ela v'chazar v'he'ela v'chazar v'he'ela chayav* — what is the law regarding repeated acts of placing on the fire? Are these counted as separate transgressions, each generating independent liability, or as one continuous act?

### Rabbi Shimon

*Chayav al kol aliyah divrei Rabbi Shimon* — Rabbi Shimon holds that if one places multiple limbs — say, the four legs of an animal — on the fire in succession, with an intervening moment of awareness between each act, each constitutes a separate transgression. The *nafka mina* for liability purposes is that if the acts were performed *b'shogeg*, each one would require a separate *korban*.

### Rabbi Yosi

*Rabbi Yose omer eino chayav ela achas* — Rabbi Yosi holds that if all the limbs belong to the same animal, there is only one *chiyuv*, regardless of how many times one placed pieces on the fire. The Gemara will debate the precise contours of this position in detail.

---

## Stringencies (III)

### Source: Ish Ish

The Gemara returns to ground the differential treatment of slaughter and offering in the text of the Torah. The prohibition of *shchutei chutz* employs the phrase *ish ish* — *ish ish mibit Yisrael asher yishchat shor o kesev o ez* — and concludes *v'nichrat ha'ish hahu*. The prohibition of *ha'alas chutz* similarly uses *ish ish* — *ish ish asher ya'aleh olah o zavach* — and concludes *el petach ohel mo'ed v'nichrat ha'ish hahu*. Both verses thus contain both *ish ish* and *ha'ish hahu*, but the Gemara derives different things from each phrase in each context.

---

## Stringencies (III)…

### Partnership & Divine

By *ha'alas chutz*, *ish ish* is read to mean that liability extends even to cases of partnership — two people together placing a limb on the fire are both *chayav*. This is in contrast to slaughter, where partnership exempts. The derivation of the rule for offering comes precisely from the *ish ish* of that *parasha*.

---

## Partnership Offering

### Kal VaChomer

The Gemara constructs a *kal vachomer* to challenge this derivation. If by *shchita* — where one who slaughters for a mundane person is nonetheless *chayav* — two people in partnership are *patur*, then by *ha'alah* — where one who offers for a mundane person is *patur* — surely two people in partnership should also be *patur*. The *kal vachomer* argues that *ha'alah* should be *more* lenient than *shchita* in every respect, and since slaughter does not generate liability for partnership, offering certainly should not.

### Ish Ish Split

The response is that *ish ish* in each *parasha* does different work. By *shchita*, *ish ish* teaches that one is *chayav* even if one slaughters the animal for another person — even for a mundane, non-sacrificial purpose. By *ha'alah*, *ish ish* teaches that one is *chayav* even in the context of partnership — two people together can both be liable. The two usages of *ish ish* are divided between the two contexts, each bearing a different *drasha*. The obvious question follows: why not apply *ish ish* by *shchita* to mean partnership as well? Because *ha'ish hahu* — the verse concludes with "that man" — which excludes the case of partnership. Only an individual is *chayav* by *shchita*.

### Hahu Exclusion

The Gemara asks: *ha'ish hahu* also appears by *ha'alah*, so it should likewise exclude partnership there. The response is that by *ha'alah*, *ha'ish hahu* is needed to exclude the case of *ones* — one who is compelled to perform the act — or one who acted under duress or error. The principle *ones rachmana patrei* is operative, and *hahu* here signals that one must have acted with independent volition to be *chayav*. Tosafot notes that this *drasha* of *hahu* might seem superfluous since *ones* is always exempt regardless, and suggests that the *hahu* more precisely excludes the case of one who acted in the mistaken belief that the act was permitted.

By *shchita*, a second *hahu* is available — *dam yeichasheiv la'ish hahu* appears earlier in that *parasha* — and this verse carries the burden of excluding *ones* and related cases. Thus the single *hahu* at the end of the *shchita* verse is freed to exclude partnership, while by *ha'alah* the only *hahu* must exclude *ones*, leaving *ish ish* to include partnership. This is the mechanism by which the Gemara justifies the asymmetric application.

Rabbi Yosi disagrees with the conclusion that *ish ish* by *ha'alah* includes partnership, maintaining that *hahu* there likewise excludes partnership. He derives the liability for slaughtering on behalf of another person not from *ish ish* but from *dam yeichasheiv la'ish hahu dam shafach* — even if the blood was shed for the sake of another person, liability attaches. Rabbi Shimon counters that without deriving partnership-liability from *ish ish* by *ha'alah*, that phrase becomes mere idiomatic expression — *dibrah Torah kilshon bnei adam* — with no independent halachic force, a position Rabbi Shimon is unwilling to accept.

The further question *v'ela l'Hashem lamah li* — why does the verse require that the act be directed toward God if one is *chayav* even for mundane slaughter — receives the answer: *l'hotzi sa'ir mishtale'ach* — to exclude the *sa'ir mishtale'ach*, the scapegoat of *Yom Kippur*, which was never designated as an offering *l'Hashem* in the usual sense. If one slaughters the *sa'ir mishtale'ach* outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, one is *patur*, since that animal was never in the category of being brought before God.

---

## Multiple Offerings (II)

### Resh Lakish

The Gemara returns to the debate of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosi regarding multiple offerings, now working through the precise interpretation of their positions. Resh Lakish reads the debate as concerning multiple whole limbs placed on the fire in succession — for instance, the individual legs of an animal offered one by one, with pauses between each.

### Whole Animal

On one reading, the underlying principle is *al hashalem hu chayav v'eino chayav al hachaser* — liability attaches only when one is offering from a whole animal. On this interpretation, one is *chayav* only when the entire animal was intact at the outset; once a portion has been offered, the remaining animal is *chaser* — incomplete — and subsequent acts of placing limbs on the fire generate no further liability. This would mean that liability obtains only for the first act of offering from the whole animal.

### Whole Limb

Tosafot reads the principle differently. *Al hashalem* refers not to the whole animal but to the whole limb — one is *chayav* when offering from a complete limb, and *patur* when the limb is already incomplete. On this reading, each whole limb offered in sequence could in principle generate its own *chiyuv* — since each limb is itself *shalem* at the moment it is placed on the fire. The debate between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosi then concerns whether the animal, once some of it has been offered, remains *shalem* enough that subsequent whole limbs from that animal still generate liability, or whether only one *chiyuv* is incurred for the entire animal.

### One Limb Split

Rabbi Yochanan reads the debate more narrowly: it concerns not multiple limbs but a single limb divided in two, where one half was placed on the fire and then the second half was placed subsequently. This is distinct from Resh Lakish's reading, which concerned multiple whole limbs.

### Inside vs. Outside

The context of slaughter matters here. If the animal was slaughtered *inside* the *Beis HaMikdash* and the limbs were then placed on a fire *outside*, even a partial limb would have been fit to go on the *mizbeach* inside. Since *muktarei p'nim* — pieces designated for the internal *mizbeach* — are placed there even when not whole, a partial limb qualifies as *raui*. If the animal was slaughtered *outside*, however, the standard is more demanding, and a whole limb is required.

### Ulla's Reading

Ulla states that on the matter of *muktarei p'nim* — animals slaughtered inside — everyone agrees one is *chayav* even for a partial limb placed outside, precisely because inside the *Beis HaMikdash* a partial limb goes on the *mizbeach*. The debate between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosi, according to Ulla, concerns only *muktarei bachutz* — animals slaughtered outside — where one opinion holds *patur* on a partial limb and the other holds *chayav*.

### Father of Shmuel

The father of Shmuel challenges Ulla's first position. He does so with a remarkable turn of phrase: *keman madlinan pekuin legabei mizbeach* — according to whose ruling do we restore to the *mizbeach* items that have fallen off? This question presupposes that there is a current practice of returning fallen pieces to the altar, and it asks which Tannaitic opinion such a practice reflects. The implication is that this practice reflects the view that even a partial limb goes back on the *mizbeach* — and that this view is not universally accepted. If Rabbi Yosi's position is understood as denying liability for a partial limb even in the case of *muktarei p'nim*, then the practice of replacing fallen pieces contradicts Rabbi Yosi and follows only Rabbi Shimon. The father of Shmuel thus understands the debate as concerning *muktarei p'nim* — the inside-slaughter case — rather than Ulla's reading, which placed the debate in the outside-slaughter context.

---

## Mizbeach Requirement

### Rabbi Yosi

The *mishnah* records a further debate: does the act of *ha'alas chutz* require that the offering be placed on a constructed altar, or does any elevated surface suffice? *V'eino chayav ad she'ya'aleh l'rosh hamizbeach* — Rabbi Yosi holds that one is not *chayav* unless one places the offering atop a *mizbeach*, a constructed altar.

Rav Huna identifies the source: *vayiven Noach mizbeach la'Hashem* — when Noach brought offerings outside any formal sanctuary, the Torah records that he *built* a *mizbeach*. The implication is that a constructed altar is required for an act of offering to be recognized as such. The further implication — and this is the conceptually fascinating move — is that one can infer from what was required when *bamot* were permissible what would generate *chiyuv* when *bamot* are forbidden. Whatever was always required for an acceptable offering to God — even in the era of permitted *bamot* — remains necessary for liability to attach in the era of forbidden *bamot*. If a rock was never acceptable when *bamot* were permitted, placing an offering on a rock is never considered a sacrificial act, and just as *ha'alah* to an idol does not generate liability for *ha'alas chutz*, neither does placing meat on a surface that was never recognized as an altar.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the source for Rabbi Shimon's opposing position: *vayikach Manoach et gdi ha-izim v'et haminchah vaya'al al hatzur la'Hashem* — Manoach placed his offering directly on a rock, and God accepted it. This demonstrates that a rock or stone surface can constitute an acceptable act of offering, without a constructed *mizbeach*.

Rabbi Yosi responds to this *rai'ya*: *hahu govha b'alma* — the word *vayiven* by Noach means he simply built up a height, a raised surface, not a formally constructed altar with halachic specifications. Rashi explains this as follows: Noach built it for convenience and as the common practice of the time, not because construction was ritually mandated. It is therefore no proof that a *mizbeach* is required.

Rabbi Shimon, in turn, responds to the case of Manoach: *hora'as sha'ah haysah* — that was a unique, exceptional dispensation not representative of the general rule.

### When Bamot Permitted

The Gemara then offers an alternative grounding for Rabbi Shimon's position based on a *drasha*: the verse *v'zarak ha-kohen et ha-dam al mizbeach Hashem petach ohel mo'ed* associates the requirement of a *mizbeach* specifically with *petach ohel mo'ed*, the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Only where there is an *ohel mo'ed* is a *mizbeach* mandated. When there is no *Mikdash*, and one is operating under the rules of a *bamah*, no *mizbeach* is required.

### Inference Logic

The logical structure of this argument is elegant: the conditions required for a valid *bamah* when *bamot* were permitted define what constitutes a meaningful sacrificial act. If no *mizbeach* was required for a private *bamah*, then offering on a rock was always a valid sacrificial act during that era.

### Two-Step Logic

The Gemara then addresses an apparent grammatical awkwardness in the *mishnah*'s formulation. The *mishnah* says *he'ela al ha-sela o al ha-even chayav* — "therefore one who places it on a rock or stone is *chayav*." But the preceding reasoning established what was *permitted* during the era of *bamot*, not what generates *chiyuv* when *bamot* are forbidden. The Gemara explains that the argument is two-step: since one fulfills one's obligation with a rock during the era of permitted *bamot*, therefore during the era of forbidden *bamot*, one is *chayav* for doing the same thing. The act on a rock was always a genuine sacrificial act — never a non-act — and therefore always falls within the prohibition of *ha'alas chutz*.

---

## Altar Components

### What Defines

Having established that Rabbi Shimon requires no *mizbeach* and Rabbi Yosi does require one, the Gemara raises a further question posed by Rabbi Yosef bar Chanina: if a *mizbeach* is indeed required, does it need to possess all the formal components of the Temple *mizbeach*? Must it have *keren* — horns at its corners — *kevesh* — a ramp — *yesod* — a base — and *ribu'a* — a square shape?

### Large vs. Private

The Gemara cites a *braisa* in response: *keren v'kevesh v'ribu'a v'yesod me'akvin b'vamah gedolah* — these components are required for a *bamah gedolah*, a large communal *bamah* such as those that functioned at Nov and Givon during periods when no *Beis HaMikdash* stood. *V'ein me'akvin b'vamah ketanah* — but they are not required for a private *bamah*, the kind maintained by individuals.

### Private Bamot

Since a private *bamah* does not require these components, it follows that one need not construct an altar with horns, ramp, base, and square dimensions in order to generate *chiyuv* under *shchutei chutz* and *ha'alas chutz*. The standard for liability tracks the standard for private *bamot*, and that standard requires only a basic elevated surface — not the full architectural specifications of the great communal altars.

---

---

# Zevachim 109

## Ra'ui Lepetach Ohel Moed

### Opening & Review

Daf 109 continues the discussion of when a person is liable for offering *korbanot* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. The previous daf addressed questions concerning which *avodot* trigger liability — *shechitah* and *ha'alah* are explicit in the verse, and the Gemara added *zrikat hadam* as well. There was also discussion about whether one who slaughters a *korban* for the sake of the meat, rather than as an act of divine offering, is nonetheless liable — a genuine *chidush*, given that the burning must be expressly for God. The present daf turns to the specifics of which types of *korbanot* fall within the scope of this prohibition.

### Ra'ui Principle

The Mishnah opens with the phrase *echad kodshim kesherim ve-echad kodshim pesulim* — liability applies whether the offering is valid or invalid. But not every category of *pasul* is included. The governing principle is *ra'ui lepetach ohel moed*: the offering must be of a type that is fit to be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. This is derived from the verse *el petach ohel moed lo hevi'o* — "he did not bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting" (Vayikra 17:4). If someone were to sanctify a duck or a deer — animals that are categorically ineligible as *korbanot* — and were to slaughter or burn them outside, he would not be liable, since these animals are not *ra'ui lepetach ohel moed*. The *chiyuv kares* for *shichutei chutz* or *ha'ala'as chutz* requires that the act be performed upon something that could, in principle, have been brought to the *Mikdash*.

### Psulan Bakodesh

The Mishnah then teaches *shehayah psulan bakodesh* — that the category of *pasul* offerings which does generate liability is specifically those whose disqualification arose within the sacred precincts, *psulan bakodesh*. The underlying principle is that if such an offering were placed on the *mizbeach*, it would remain there and would not be removed. This "stays-on-the-altar" standard is what qualifies them as sufficiently *ra'ui lepetach ohel moed* to generate liability when offered outside. The most intuitive understanding of the phrase is that the *psul* occurred after the animal entered the *Beit HaMikdash* — for instance, if the *shechitah* was performed *shelo lishmah*, if the blood was received by a *zar*, if the blood was taken outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, and so on.

### Baal Mum Exception

A *baal mum* — a blemished animal — does not qualify as *psulan bakodesh*, even if the blemish was acquired inside the *Beit HaMikdash* (say, if someone scratched the animal after it entered). The reason is that a blemish is not a *psul* generated by some deficiency in the ritual process within the *Mikdash*; it is entirely circumstantial, not arising from anything that went wrong in the performance of the *avodah*. Consequently, one who slaughters or burns a *baal mum* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* is not liable for *kares* for *shichutei chutz* or *ha'ala'as chutz*.

The case of *zarut* — a *zar* performing the *avodah* — is treated differently, because *zarut* was *hutrah b'bamah*: performing the *avodah* as a non-*kohen* was entirely permitted on a private *bamah*. So *zarut* does not generate a prior *psul* that would raise these questions.

---

## Ha'alah & Items

### Baraita Expansion

The Mishnah then states: *hamaleh kezayit min ha'olah umin ha'imurin bachutz chayav* — one who burns a *kezayit* from the *olah* or from the *imurim* outside is liable. The *baraita* begins by noting that the verse says *asher ya'aleh olah o zavach* — "who brings up an *olah* or a sacrifice" (Vayikra 17:8). One might think liability is limited to an *olah*. How do we know to include the *imurim* of an *asham*, the *imurim* of a *chatat*, the *imurim* of *kodshei kodashim*, and the *imurim* of *kodashim kalim*? The word *zavach* in the verse expands the prohibition. The implicit logic is that the *zavach* is read in parallel to the *olah*: just as an *olah* is paradigmatically the portion placed entirely on the *mizbeach*, so too with a *zevach* — only that portion which would normally ascend to the *mizbeach* is included. One is liable for the *imurim* of the other *korbanot*, but not for their meat.

### Non-Meat Items

The *baraita* then asks how we know to include non-animal items. *Minayin l'rabos hakometz vehalevonah* — how do we include the *kometz*, the handful of flour taken from the *mincha*, and the *levonah*, the frankincense that accompanies the *mincha*? Both of these are burnt on the *mizbeach*. The *baraita* continues: *vehaketores* — the daily *ketores* burnt on the golden inner *mizbeach* twice each day — and *minchas kohanim* and *minchas kohen mashiach*, the *minchah* offerings of *kohanim* that are burnt entirely. All of these are burnt on the altar, and the *baraita* establishes that they fall under the prohibition of *ha'alah* outside.

### Libations

The *baraita* then introduces something genuinely novel: *vehamenasech sheloshet lugin yayin vesheloshet lugin mayim* — one who pours a libation of three *lugin* of wine or three *lugin* of water. This is not a burning at all; it is a *nisuch*, a libation. Yet it falls within the scope of *ha'alah*. The three *lugin* of wine is the minimum quantity brought as a wine libation with a *korban*; the three *lugin* of water refers to the water libation performed during *Sukkos* as part of *nisuch hamayim b'chag*.

Rashi notes that for all of these items — wine, *mincha*, and water alike — it is not sufficient that one simply takes them from home and pours them. Just as one who slaughters an unsanctified animal outside is not liable, so too here the item must be sanctified. Rashi specifies regarding the water: *be-chag ka'amar umekudashim l'chag* — the law applies on *Sukkos*, and the water must have been sanctified for the *nisuch hamayim b'chag*. The principle of *ra'ui lepetach ohel moed* must be satisfied: only sanctified items, appropriate to their specific sacred context, are included.

The source for this expansion is the verse *v'el petach ohel moed lo yevienu* — "and he did not bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting" — from which we derive: *kol haba lepetach ohel moed chayavin alav bachutz* — anything that would be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, one is liable for performing outside. The scope of *ha'alah* extends beyond animals to any item that ascends to the *mizbeach*, whether by fire or by libation.

### Psulan Extension

Having established the scope of valid items, the *baraita* turns to the *pesulim*. *V'ein li ela kodashim kesherim minayin lerabos pesulim* — we have so far only established liability for valid offerings; how do we know to include certain *pesulim*? The *baraita* enumerates the qualifying categories of *psulan bakodesh*: *kegon halan* — meat or *imurim* that remained overnight (*nosar*); *vehayotzei* — portions that were taken outside the *Beit HaMikdash*; *vehatamai* — items that became ritually impure; those involving thoughts of *pigul*; cases where *pesulim* or a *zar* received or threw the blood; blood thrown in the wrong location — above or below the prescribed demarcation; blood of inner-altar offerings placed on the outer altar or vice versa; and a *pesach* or *chatat* slaughtered *shelo lishman* on the third day. All of these are *psulan bakodesh* — their *psul* arose from a defect in the ritual process itself.

How do we know these generate liability when burned outside? The verse says *lo yevienu la'asos* — "he shall not bring it to do." Rashi points out that *la'asos* implies an active role: these items, if found on the *mizbeach*, are not merely left in place — they are actively offered. One turns them on the fire, completes the burning. The word *la'asos* thus establishes that even these disqualified items retain a "doing" quality when on the *mizbeach*, and therefore if one performs this act outside, he is liable.

---

## Meat & Imurim

### Olah vs Shelamim

The Mishnah teaches: *hamaleh kezayit min ha'olah umin ha'imurin bachutz chayav* — if one burns a *kezayit* consisting of half a *kezayit* of the meat of an *olah* and half a *kezayit* of its *imurim*, he is liable, because both portions are burnt on the *mizbeach* and thus combine. This implicitly excludes the *shelamim*: a half *kezayit* of the meat of a *shelamim* and a half *kezayit* of its *imurim* do not combine, because one is not liable for burning the meat of a *shelamim* outside — the meat of a *shelamim* is not placed on the *mizbeach* in the *Beit HaMikdash*, so performing that act outside generates no liability.

The *baraita* then states: *olah ve'emureha mitztarfin lekezayit leha'alotan bachutz ulchayev aleihen mishum pigul notar vetamei* — an *olah* and its *imurim* combine to a *kezayit* for the purposes of *ha'ala'as chutz*, and also to generate liability for the prohibitions of *pigul*, *notar*, and *tamei*. The implication is that this combining applies to an *olah* and its *imurim* but not to a *shelamim* and its *imurim*.

### Pigul Question

The Gemara raises an objection. Granted that the meat of a *shelamim* does not combine with its *imurim* for *ha'alah* — the meat is never burnt on the *mizbeach*, so there is no act of *ha'alah* to speak of. But for *pigul*, *notar*, and *tamei*, which are prohibitions applicable to the entire *korban*, why shouldn't the meat and the *imurim* of a *shelamim* combine? Furthermore, there is an explicit Mishnah elsewhere stating *kol hapigulin mitztarfin v'chol hanos'arin mitztarfin* — all *pigul* items combine with one another and all *notar* items combine — which would seemingly permit even a half *kezayit* of *shelamim* meat and a half *kezayit* of *shelamim imurim* to combine for the prohibition of *pigul* or *notar*. This generates a direct contradiction: *kashya pigul apigul, kashya notar anotar*.

### Machshevet Pigul

The Gemara resolves the *pigul* contradiction with an elegant distinction. The *baraita* that implies no combining for a *shelamim* is referring to *machshevet pigul* — the disqualifying intention formed during the *shechitah* that the offering will be eaten or burnt outside its allotted time. In such a case, the entire animal is rendered *pigul*, and if one then eats a half *kezayit* of the meat and a half *kezayit* of the *imurim*, he is liable — he has consumed a full *kezayit* of *pigul* matter. That is the ruling of the Mishnah that says *kol hapigulin mitztarfin*.

What the *baraita* is addressing is a different scenario entirely: one formed the intention during *shechitah* to eat half a *kezayit* of the *shelamim* meat in three days and to burn half a *kezayit* of the *imurim* in three days. These two half-*kezayitim* do not combine to constitute a single *machshevet pigul*, because eating by a person (*achilas adam*) and burning on the *mizbeach* (*achilas mizbeach*) are categorically distinct acts, and a *machshevah* about one does not combine with a *machshevah* about the other. By contrast, if it were an *olah*, and one formed the intention to burn half a *kezayit* of the meat and half a *kezayit* of the *imurim* outside their time, these would combine — because both are acts of *achilas mizbeach*, burning on the altar. This elegantly parallels the rule of *ha'ala'as chutz*: in both cases, the *olah* and its *imurim* combine precisely because both are destined for the *mizbeach*, while for a *shelamim*, the meat and the *imurim* serve different functions and do not combine.

---

## Notar & Blood

### Notar Contradiction

The *pigul* question having been resolved, the *notar* contradiction remains. The Gemara's answer is as follows. The Mishnah that teaches *kol hanos'arin mitztarfin* — all *notar* items combine — refers to a case where the animal was already rendered *notar* and one ate half a *kezayit* of the meat and half a *kezayit* of the *imurim*. In that case they combine, since both are *notar* and the prohibition applies to the entire *korban*. What the *baraita* means when it implies that the meat and *imurim* of a *shelamim* do not combine for *notar* is a different scenario: *k'an bishenisosru ad shelo nizrak hadam* — where they became "left over" before the blood was thrown. That is: the animal was slaughtered, and somehow the bulk of the meat and *imurim* were lost or destroyed, leaving only half a *kezayit* of meat and half a *kezayit* of *imurim*, and the blood has not yet been thrown. The question now is whether the *kohen* may still throw the blood.

### Rabbi Yehoshua View

At this point the Gemara introduces the view of Rabbi Yehoshua: *kol hazevachim shebaTorahshenishta'yer bahen kezayit basar o kezayit chelev zorek es hadam* — for any sacrifice in the Torah, if at least a *kezayit* of meat or a *kezayit* of *chelev* (*imurim*) remains, one throws the blood. The basis is the principle, derived from various verses, that throwing the blood is only meaningful when it serves as a *matir* — permitting either the eating of the meat or the burning of the *imurim* on the *mizbeach*. If there is nothing left of substance — no *kezayit* of meat to eat and no *kezayit* of *chelev* to burn — the blood throwing serves no purpose and should not be done.

### Olah Blood Allowance

The Mishnah continues: *chatzi zayit basar v'chatzi zayit chelev eino zorek es hadam* — if only half a *kezayit* of meat and half a *kezayit* of *chelev* remain (in the context of a *shelamim*), one does not throw the blood. There is no full *kezayit* of anything that the blood throwing would permit. However, *be'olah chatzi zayit basar v'chatzi zayit chelev zorek es hadam mipnei shekulo kalil* — in the case of an *olah*, one does throw the blood even with only half a *kezayit* of each, because the entire animal is burnt. Both the meat and the *imurim* of an *olah* are destined for the *mizbeach* and belong to the same category — *achilas mizbeach* — so together they constitute a full *kezayit* of something the blood throwing renders permitted.

This is precisely parallel to everything discussed above. The three areas in which an *olah*'s meat and *imurim* combine — *ha'ala'as chutz*, *machshevet pigul*, and the question of throwing blood — are all rooted in the same principle: since both the meat and the *imurim* of an *olah* are burned on the *mizbeach*, they form a unified category. For a *shelamim*, they do not: the meat is for human consumption and the *imurim* are for the *mizbeach*, and therefore they never combine in any of these three contexts.

The *baraita* adds: *umincha afilu kula kayemes lo yizrok* — if only the *mincha* that accompanied the sacrifice remains (because all the meat and *imurim* were lost), one does not throw the blood even though there is something left to be done with. As Rav Papa explains, *mincha* refers here to the *minchas nesachim* that accompanies a *korban* — but this is not the sacrifice itself. Throwing the blood must function as a *matir* for the animal's own meat or *imurim*; the *mincha* that accompanies it is a separate item and does not fulfill that role.

### Rashi Resolution

The *baraita* stated that an *olah* and its *imurim* combine *lechayev aleihen mishum notar* — to generate liability for *notar*. On the analysis now developed, what this means is not simply that eating them generates *notar* liability. Rather, it means the following: if one had half a *kezayit* of *olah* meat and half a *kezayit* of *imurim* remaining, and went ahead and threw the blood, then the blood-throwing was *permitted* — since for an *olah* those half-*kezayitim* combine. Because the blood throwing was permitted and valid, it changes the halachic status of the remaining meat, elevating it so that it can subsequently become *notar* and generate liability. For a *shelamim*, by contrast, throwing the blood in such a circumstance was not legitimate — because a half *kezayit* of meat and a half *kezayit* of *imurim* do not combine. Even if the blood was thrown and one is perhaps *yotzei b'di'avad*, since the throwing was not properly connected to the meat, it does not change the meat's status. Therefore, if the meat subsequently became *notar* and was eaten, one is not liable — because the blood throwing never meaningfully "activated" the meat. This is Rashi's resolution: the license to throw the blood, when present, changes the meat's status in ways that have downstream consequences for *notar* and *tamei* liability.

---

## Non-Meat Shiur

### Burnt Items

The Mishnah then addresses non-meat items: *hakometz vehalevonah vehaketores uminchas kohanim uminchas kohen mashiach uminchas nesachim* — the *kometz*, the *levonah*, the *ketores*, the *minchah* of *kohanim*, the *minchah* of the *kohen mashiach*, and the *minchah* of libations. For all of these, if one burns a *kezayit* of any of them outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, he is liable, in accordance with the view of the *tanna kamma*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Full

Rabbi Eliezer dissents: *poter ad sheyakriv es kulan* — he exempts unless the entire amount is burned. The question naturally arises: why does Rabbi Eliezer agree that by the meat of an *olah* one is liable for a *kezayit* alone, yet by the *kometz* of a *mincha* he requires the full amount?

The answer lies in the concept of *matir*. The *kometz* is the *matir* for the remainder of the *mincha* — it is the act by which the *shirayim* are permitted to the *kohanim*. As a *matir*, it only functions when the full *kometz* is brought; a partial offering does not discharge the function. For the meat of an *olah*, by contrast, there is no separate *matir* — each *kezayit* of meat constitutes an independent meaningful act of placing it on the *mizbeach*. But for items that function as *matirim*, the entire amount must be brought to constitute a meaningful halachic act.

### Act vs Matir

Rabbi Eliezer therefore draws this distinction: where one is performing an act of *ha'alah* that functions as a *matir*, the only meaningful act is the complete one, and one is liable only for performing the complete act outside. Where one is performing *ha'alah* that is simply an act of burning — not tied to unlocking anything else — each *kezayit* is independently meaningful, and liability attaches to each *kezayit*.

However, Rabbi Eliezer agrees to the following: *vechulan shehikriv bifnim veshayar mehem kezayit vehikrivan bachutz chayav* — if one burned the bulk of the *kometz* or *ketores* inside and left over at least a *kezayit*, which he then burned outside, he is liable. Why? Because that remaining *kezayit* was, at that point, the last piece needed to complete the *matir* function. Had it been done inside, it would have been the culminating act that validated the *korban*. The remaining *kezayit* thus carried the full weight of the *matir* function, and performing it outside generates liability. Conversely, if even a minute quantity was missing from the offering — *vechulan shechosru kol shehu vehikrivan bachutz patur* — one is exempt, because such a diminished offering would not have been a valid *hakravah* inside the *Beit HaMikdash*, and what would not be valid inside does not generate liability when done outside.

---

## Ketores Debate

### Ketores Baraita

A *baraita* is now cited: *hamaktir kezayit bachutz chayav* — one who burns a *kezayit* of *ketores* outside is liable. *Chatzi pras bifnim patur* — if inside the *Beit HaMikdash* half the standard amount (i.e., less than the full *pras*) was burned, one is exempt. On first reading, this appears to generate a contradiction: if a *kezayit* outside makes one liable, why is a *zar* who brings less than the full amount inside exempt?

### Contradiction Noted

The apparent reading of *patur* would be *patur zar* — a non-*kohen* who burns less than the full amount inside is exempt from penalty. But this is strange: if the minimum for liability outside is a *kezayit*, why would a *zar* burning a *kezayit* inside be exempt? The *kezayit* is presumably meaningful enough to generate liability.

### Patur Tzibur

Rabbi Zeira, citing Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba citing Rav, resolves this by reinterpreting *patur*: *mai patur — patur tzibur* — "exempt" here does not mean the *zar* is exempt from punishment; it means the *tzibur* has discharged its obligation. In other words, *chatzi pras bifnim patur* means: if only half the prescribed amount was burned inside, the community has nonetheless fulfilled its *mitzvah*. Thus the *baraita* is saying that one is liable outside for a *kezayit*, and one is *yotzei* inside with a *kezayit* as well.

This is a striking reading, and it raises a further question addressed by Tosafot: what exactly is the position of the *tanna kamma* who disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer? There are two possible ways to understand the *tanna kamma*. The simpler reading would be that he agrees with Rabbi Eliezer that the full amount is needed to be *yotzei* inside — the *ketores* must be complete for the *mitzvah* to be fulfilled — yet he holds that a *kezayit* is sufficient to generate liability when burned outside, since it constitutes a meaningful act even without fulfilling the *matir* function. This is certainly how the *tanna kamma* operates with respect to the *kometz* of a *mincha*, where all agree the full *kometz* is required inside, yet a *kezayit* outside triggers liability. The Gemara, however, shifts in its understanding when it comes to *ketores*: it reads the *tanna kamma* as maintaining that a *kezayit* of *ketores* is sufficient to be *yotzei* inside as well, and therefore one is liable for a *kezayit* outside.

### Daily Ketores

Rava articulates the consensus underlying this reading: *behaktara deheichal de'chulei alma lo peligi* — regarding the daily *ketores* performed in the *Heichal*, everybody agrees that one is *yotzei* with a *kezayit*, and therefore everybody agrees one is liable for a *kezayit* outside. The reason is that the Torah does not specify a precise *shiur* for the daily *ketores*; the Rabbis established the amount of a *pras* in the morning and a *pras* in the afternoon, but *mid'oraisa* a *kezayit* suffices. The debate in the Mishnah, accordingly, does not concern the daily *ketores* at all — both Rabbi Eliezer and the *tanna kamma* agree that one is liable for a *kezayit* of the daily *ketores* burned outside. The disagreement, on this reading, concerns the *ketores* of Yom Kippur brought into the *Kodesh Kodashim*.

---

## Yom Kippur Ketores

### Abaye Resolution

Abaye, however, rejects this framing. The Torah states *v'hayesah zos lachem le'chukkas olam* specifically in the context of the Yom Kippur *avodah* in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, signaling that the *haktarah* inside there is defined by the Torah as a *chok* — a fixed requirement. And the Torah specifies *melo chofnav* — a full double handful — for the Yom Kippur *ketores*. There is no room to say that Yom Kippur *ketores* is *yotzei* with a *kezayit* inside; the requirement is incontrovertibly *melo chofnav*. Therefore the debate cannot be about Yom Kippur.

Abaye offers his own resolution: *behaktaras bifnim chulei alma lo peligi* — regarding the *ketores* of Yom Kippur burned in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, everybody agrees you need *melo chofnav* inside, and therefore everybody agrees that one is liable outside only for *melo chofnav*. *Ki peligi behaktaras chutz* — the debate is about what one is liable for when burning outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, specifically in connection with the daily *ketores*. Since everybody agrees one is *yotzei* with a *kezayit* for the daily *ketores* inside, everybody agrees one is liable for a *kezayit* of daily *ketores* burned outside. The debate is whether, given that the *tanna kamma* holds one is liable for a *kezayit* of daily *ketores* burned outside, he also says one is liable for a *kezayit* of Yom Kippur *ketores* burned outside — reasoning that the outside is linked to what makes one *yotzei* for the corresponding inside *avodah*. Rabbi Eliezer rejects this linkage: since the inside *avodah* on Yom Kippur requires *melo chofnav*, one is liable outside for Yom Kippur *ketores* only if the full *melo chofnav* is burned.

### Daily Debate

The structure of the debate can be mapped as follows. For the Yom Kippur *ketores*, everyone agrees: *melo chofnav* is required inside, and *melo chofnav* is required to generate liability outside. For the daily *ketores*, everyone agrees: a *kezayit* is sufficient inside, and a *kezayit* generates liability outside. The debate is about one specific case: Yom Kippur *ketores* burned outside. The *tanna kamma* argues that since the daily *ketores* generates liability for a *kezayit* outside, and the Yom Kippur *ketores* is still *ketores*, one is liable for a *kezayit* of Yom Kippur *ketores* burned outside as well, drawing a link between the two categories of *ketores*. Rabbi Eliezer refuses this link: since the inside Yom Kippur *avodah* requires *melo chofnav*, the outside requires *melo chofnav* as well.

### Rava Rejection

Rava, however, rejects Abaye's framework entirely. His objection is methodological: *hashta chutz m'chutz lo yalfei rabbanan pnim m'chutz miba'ei* — we do not apply *shiurim* from one category to another even within the category of *ha'ala'as chutz* itself; how much more so can we not apply the *shiur* of one type of *ketores* to another type? The proof is from the *baraita*: *yachol hama'aleh pachos mikezayit kometz... hayei chayav?* — perhaps one who burns less than a *kezayit* of *kometz* or less than three *lugin* of wine outside would be liable? The answer is no — *al hashalem hu chayav ve'eino chayav al hachaser* — one is liable only for the complete minimum amount relevant to that specific offering. Three *lugin* of wine is many times a *kezayit* in volume, yet we do not say that since one is liable for a *kezayit* of meat outside, one should therefore be liable for a *kezayit* of wine outside. Each category carries its own *shiur*. By the same logic, we cannot say that because one is liable for a *kezayit* of daily *ketores* outside, one is therefore liable for a *kezayit* of Yom Kippur *ketores* outside. The categories are distinct, and *shiurim* do not transfer across them.

---

## Kli Shares Solution

### Vessel Interpretation

Having rejected Abaye's framework, Rava proposes his own solution to the underlying difficulty. The question remains: Rabbi Eliezer agrees that one is *yotzei* with a *kezayit* of daily *ketores* inside, and therefore agrees one is liable for a *kezayit* outside. What then is the subject of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *tanna kamma*? Rava answers: *kegon dikav'inhu shenei chatzi pras bemana* — the case is where one placed two portions of *ketores*, each a half *pras*, into a single *kli shareis* together.

The scenario is as follows. A *kohen* prepares to offer the daily *ketores*. He places his material in the *kli shareis* — let us say two *kezayitim*, or two half-*prasim* — together in a single vessel. Had he only placed one *kezayit* in the vessel, everyone would agree he is *yotzei* if he burns it inside, and liable if he burns it outside. But because he placed more than a *kezayit* together in a single *kli shareis*, a question arises as to whether the vessel configuration changes the *shiur*.

### Chachamim View

The *chachamim* hold that placing multiple *kezayitim* together in a *kli shareis* is not halachically significant with respect to the minimum *shiur*. One is still *yotzei* if one burns only a *kezayit*, even when more was placed in the vessel together, and one is correspondingly liable for a *kezayit* burned outside.

### Rabbi Eliezer Vessel

Rabbi Eliezer holds that once two half-*prasim* are placed together in the *kli shareis*, the vessel configuration is significant — *keviusa demana milsa hi*. The act of placing them together in the vessel establishes the full combined amount as the operative minimum. Therefore, when the full amount has been placed in the vessel, one must burn all of it to be *yotzei*, and similarly, one is liable outside only for the full amount that was placed in the vessel together.

### Keviusa Demana

The dispute thus turns on the question of *keviusa demana* — whether the configuration of the *kli shareis* is halachically meaningful. The *tanna kamma* says it is not: *lav milsa hi*. The *shiur* remains a *kezayit* regardless of what else was placed in the vessel. Rabbi Eliezer says it is: *milsa hi*. Once the vessel was loaded with the combined amount, that becomes the operative *shiur*, and one is liable outside only for the full amount thus configured.

It is worth noting, as Tosafot observes, something unusual in the way this sugya has developed. Normally the *tanna kamma* holds that one is liable outside for a *kezayit* even when the full amount is required inside for the *mitzvah* to be fulfilled — as is clearly the case with the *kometz* of a *mincha*. Yet for *ketores*, the Gemara assumes throughout that the *tanna kamma* links the *shiur* of liability outside to the minimum *shiur* with which one is *yotzei* inside. Rava's final solution preserves this assumption — both Rabbi Eliezer and the *tanna kamma* agree that a *kezayit* is the *shiur* for the daily *ketores* inside when only a *kezayit* was placed in the *kli shareis*, and both agree this generates liability for a *kezayit* outside. The debate arises only when the *kli shareis* was filled with more, and turns entirely on the halachic significance of *keviusa demana*.

---

---

# Zevachim 110

## Kezayit Ketores & Kli

### Kezayit Ketores Debate

The *daf* opens in the midst of a *gemara* debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* concerning one who offers a *kezayit* of *ketores* outside the *Beis Hamikdash* when it does not constitute the full *shiur*. The *gemara* has been working through various formulations of this dispute, attempting to locate its precise parameters.

### Two Kezayisim in Vessel

The most recent explanation settled upon is a case involving two *kezaisim* placed together in a single *kli*. Under normal circumstances, Rabbi Eliezer would agree with the *chachamim* that a single *kezayit* is sufficient for *haktara* — for offering incense on the *Mizbeach Hazahav* — and that one would be *chayav* for performing that act outside. The one exception where Rabbi Eliezer requires more than a *kezayit* is *Yom Kippur*. The question, however, is whether placing two *kezaisim* together in a *kli* alters the *shiur*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *kli* now unifies them into a single unit, such that a *kezayit* is no longer sufficient if taken from this combined quantity; liability outside would require the full amount. The *chachamim*, by contrast, hold that the mere fact of being placed in a vessel together does not redefine the operative *shiur*.

### Kviusa Demana

The *gemara* encapsulates this dispute: *mar savar kviusa demana milta hi* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that fixing the material within the vessel is halakhically significant and establishes it as a new unit — *umar savar lav milta hi* — the *chachamim* hold that it is not significant, and a *kezayit* remains sufficient regardless.

## Wine Nesachim & Vessel

### Rava Six Log Wine

Rava proceeds to apply this framework to a parallel case involving wine libations. According to the *chachamim*, who hold that the placement in a *kli sharet* does not redefine the unit, consider the following: one filled a vessel with six *log* of wine for a cow — this being half of a *hin*, which equals twelve *log* — and then withdrew a portion and offered it outside. For the *chachamim*, since the vessel does not establish six as the new fixed *shiur*, one who takes four *log* from this vessel and offers them outside is still *chayav*, because four *log* is valid for a ram (*rauy l'ayil*), and the fact that it was drawn from a vessel containing six does not render anything less than six insufficient.

### Rams & Lambs Shiur

The same logic extends further: if one filled a vessel with four *log* for a ram and withdrew three *log* and offered them outside, one is likewise *chayav* — *reuyin lakeves* — because three *log* is the valid measure for a lamb. The point is consistent: in the view of the *chachamim*, placing a larger quantity in a vessel does not elevate the minimum threshold for liability.

### Chasar Minimum

There is, however, a limit. If the full minimum amount was lacking — *chasar kol shehu v'hikrivan bachutz* — meaning not merely that a portion was withdrawn but that the required minimum of three *log* was not present to begin with, then one would be *patur*. Rashi clarifies that this refers to falling short of the minimum three *log* threshold, not merely to falling short of the six; anything less than three renders one exempt. This sets the stage for the more complex discussion of *chasar* that follows.

## Ketores vs Wine

### Rav Ashi Ketores

Rav Ashi now addresses a point raised in yesterday's *gemara*. The *gemara* had proposed that one rationale for holding someone *chayav* for a *kezayit* of *ketores* of *Yom Kippur* offered outside is an analogy: since one is *chayav* for a *kezayit* of ordinary *ketores* offered outside, the same should apply to the *ketores* of *Yom Kippur*. This reasoning was challenged on the grounds that we do not generally apply *shiurim* across categories of outside offerings. We do not say that because a *kezayit* suffices for meat or *ketores*, the same *kezayit* suffices for wine — for wine the minimum is three *log*. Rav Ashi now makes this point explicit: *nisuch mehaketores lo yalpi rabbanan* — the *rabbanan* do not derive the *shiur* for *nisuch* from *haktara* of *ketores*. Even though both are assessed in the context of outside offerings, the categories differ too fundamentally for the *shiur* of one to govern the other.

### Ketores to Ketores

Nevertheless, and this is the resolution, *haketores mehaketores yalfei af al gav de-chutz mi-pnim* — one is prepared to derive the minimum *shiur* for *Yom Kippur* *ketores* from the *shiur* for ordinary *ketores*, even though one is offered in the *Heichal* and the other in the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. The distinction between the outer and inner categories is far less significant than the distinction between *ketores* and *nisuch*. Both are *ketores*, and therefore the cross-application is defensible. This confirms that the answer offered previously remains viable.

## Chasar Kometz

### Kometz Levona Lacking

The *gemara* now turns to a new *mishna*. The *mishna* states: *ve-chulan she-chasru* — in all cases where the *matir* was lacking. The context is the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* regarding outside offerings. Rabbi Eliezer holds that one is *chayav* only when offering the complete *matir* outside; the *chachamim* hold that a *kezayit* of the *kometz* or *levona* suffices for liability. The *mishna* then records that the *chachamim* agree that if any of the *matir* was lacking — if a portion of the *kometz* was missing — then even they concede that one is not *chayav* for offering a *kezayit* of what remains. This is because without the integrity of the full *kometz*, the *matir* is no longer meaningful; it no longer functions as a *matir* in any legitimate sense. Similarly, Rashi notes, if the *shirayim* of the *mincha* were lacking, one would not be *chayav* for offering the *kometz* outside.

One might find this initially puzzling. After all, *chasar* seems to fall within the category of *pesulo ba-Kodesh*, and we have established as a general principle that if *pesulo ba-Kodesh* — if a *korban*'s disqualification can occur within the *Beis Hamikdash* — then *im alu lo yerdu*, it cannot be removed from the altar, and one is *chayav* for offering it outside. Why should *chasar* be treated more severely than other *pesulim*? This question is precisely what the *gemara* will address.

### Chasar Chutz vs Pnim

The *gemara* raises the question: *chisaron de-chutz shme chisaron o lo shme chisaron?* What if the *kometz* was not lacking before it was taken outside, but became lacking only after it was removed from the *Beis Hamikdash*? Does that *chasar* disqualify it in the same way? Is one still *patur* for offering a *kezayit* of what remains?

### Yotzei & Pesul

The *gemara* presents two ways of framing the question. On one side: *mi amrinan keivan de-nafik ipsalu lehu* — once the *kometz* is taken outside, it is already disqualified by virtue of *yotzei*. And yet one is *chayav* for bringing it outside — that is the very nature of the *chiyuv* of *ha'alas chutz*. So if we do not disqualify it for the *pesul* of *yotzei*, why should we disqualify it for the *pesul* of *chasar*? *Mah li yotzei mah li chasar* — what is the operative distinction between one *pesul* and another, once we have already crossed that threshold?

On the other side, one might argue: *yotzei de-isaya be-einaya* — in the case of *yotzei*, the object is still intact and present; the *pesul* is a label attached to it, but the entity as a whole remains. *Chasar*, by contrast, does not merely label the *kometz* as defective — it changes the physical reality of what exists. Once something is missing, the entity is fundamentally altered, and perhaps that is why one cannot be *chayav* for bringing what remains.

### Abaye & Rav Proof

Abaye attempts to resolve the question from the *mishna*'s statement that Rabbi Eliezer exempts until the full *matir* is brought: *Rabbi Eliezer poter ad she-yakriv es kulan*. However, Rabbah bar bar Chana challenges Abaye: how can one derive anything from Rabbi Eliezer when the question pertains to the *chachamim*'s position? Abaye responds that he is not relying on a deduction from Rabbi Eliezer himself, but on an explicit tradition received from Rav: *b'feirush shmia li minei d'Rav* — the *chachamim* dispute Rabbi Eliezer only in a case where the *kometz* is intact, *de-isya b'inei*. If the *kometz* has a *chisaron*, however, *modei lei* — the *chachamim* agree with Rabbi Eliezer that one would not be *chayav*, because one no longer has a functional *matir*. Tosafot notes that this tradition from Rav is at least implicit in the *mishna* itself.

### When Lacking Occurred

Yet even this tradition does not settle the original question. The *gemara* asks: *lav d'chasar b'chutz?* — Is this tradition perhaps referring to a case where the *chasar* occurred outside the *Beis Hamikdash*? The *gemara* answers: *lo, d'chasar b'pnim* — no, we are speaking of a *chasar* that occurred inside, within the *Beis Hamikdash*. In that case the *kometz* was already compromised as a *matir* before being taken out. The question of *chasar b'chutz* — where the *kometz* was intact when removed and only became lacking outside — remains unresolved. The *gemara* attempts once more to press the language of the *mishna*, *ve-chulan she-chasru v'hikrivan bachutz patur*, asking whether this refers to *chasar b'chutz* — but again the response is that the *mishna* is clearly describing *chasar b'pnim*, and the case of *chasar* that occurs only after removal from the *Beis Hamikdash* remains an open question.

## Mincha & Kometz Mix

### Mincha Not Komtzed

The *gemara* transitions to the next *mishna*. *Mincha shelo nikmetza v'hikriva bachutz patur* — a *mincha* that was not *komtzed* and was brought outside in its entirety renders one exempt. The reason is that an uncomtzed *mincha* is not *rauy l'pesach ohel moed* — it is not fit for offering at the entrance of the *Ohel Moed* — and thus does not meet the threshold required for liability outside.

Before returning to the next clause, the *gemara* completes a loose end from the previous *mishna*. The case there involved one who wrapped the *imurin* in meat and offered them outside on the altar. The *mishna* held one *chayav*, and the *gemara* asked: *amai v'ha'ika chatzitza* — why should one be *chayav* if the meat interposes between the *imurin* and the fire? Three answers are given. Shmuel says: the case is where one turned them over, so the *imurin* came into direct contact with the fire. Rabbi Yochanan says: even if they were not turned over, the *mishna* follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that even placing something on a rock constitutes a valid act of offering on a *bama*, and therefore direct contact with fire is not required. Rava says: meat and meat do not constitute a *chatzitza* for one another — *min bemino eino chotetz* — and therefore the act is valid and one is *chayav*.

### Kometz Nullification

Returning to the *mishna*: *kimtza v'chozar kimtza l'tocha v'hikriva bachutz chayav* — if one took the *kometz* from the *mincha*, then dropped it back in and mixed it together, and subsequently offered the combined mixture outside, one is *chayav*. Why? Because although this mixed *mincha* would be irregular in the *Beis Hamikdash*, if it were placed on the *mizbeach* it would not be removed — and therefore it is considered as though the *kometz* had been placed there. One would be *yotzei* in the *Beis Hamikdash*, and correspondingly *chayav* for doing so outside.

The *gemara* raises an obvious challenge: *v'amai livatlu shirayim l'kometz?* — why should the *kometz* not be nullified by the majority of the *mincha* once it is dropped back in? If the *shirayim* constitute a majority, they should nullify the *kometz*, which would mean one has not effectively brought the *matir* at all and should be exempt.

Rabbi Zeira resolves this: *ne'emar haktara b'kometz v'ne'emar haktara b'shirayim* — the Torah uses the language of *haktara* both with respect to the *kometz* and with respect to the *shirayim*, the latter in the sense of a prohibition against burning them. This shared language creates a halakhic linkage between the two.

### Haktara Linked

Since the word *haktara* is applied to the *kometz* when it is placed on the *mizbeach*, and the same word is used regarding the *shirayim*, we derive that just as *kometz* and *kometz* do not nullify one another when mixed together on the *mizbeach*, so too the *shirayim* cannot nullify the *kometz* — despite being the majority.

### Ein Olin Mevatlin

The underlying principle is *ein olin mevatlin zeh es zeh* — things that go up on the altar do not nullify one another. When two *kometzos* from different *minchos* are mixed together and placed on the *mizbeach*, even if one is larger, neither is nullified, because both are designated for the altar. The same logic, extended by the linguistic link to *haktara* of *shirayim*, means that the *shirayim* cannot nullify the *kometz* either. The *kometz* therefore retains its identity within the mixture, and offering it outside — even in this mixed state — makes one *chayav*.

## Kometz & Levona

### One Matir Chayav

The next *mishna* states: *hakometz v'halevona shehikriv es echad mehen bachutz chayav* — if one offered outside either the *kometz* or the *levona*, which together serve as the two *matirin* for a *mincha*, one is *chayav*. This is the classic case of *chatzi matir*. The *chachamim* do not require the full *matir* and therefore hold one *chayav* for bringing even one of the two components outside.

### Full vs Partial Matir

Rabbi Eliezer, predictably and consistently, rules otherwise: *Rabbi Eliezer poter ad sheyakriv es hasheini* — Rabbi Eliezer exempts until the second *matir* is also brought. He requires the complete *matir* before liability attaches. The *mishna* then addresses the case of one *matir* inside and one outside: *echad bifnim v'echad bachutz chayav* — if one *matir* was already offered inside the *Beis Hamikdash*, leaving only the second, and one then brings that second one outside, even Rabbi Eliezer agrees one is *chayav*. At that point, what is brought outside constitutes the entirety of what remains of the *matir*, and thus the full *matir* has been engaged.

### Two Levona Spoons

The *mishna* applies the same debate to the *Lechem Hapanim*. The two spoons (*bezichin*) of *levona* that are burned on *Shabbos* serve as the *matir* permitting the *kohanim* to eat the showbread. If one burns one of the two spoons outside: the *chachamim* hold one *chayav*, while Rabbi Eliezer, consistent with his position, exempts until both are offered — *Rabbi Eliezer poter ad sheyakriv es hasheini*. Again, if one spoon was already burned inside the *Beis Hamikdash*, bringing the second one outside renders one *chayav* even according to Rabbi Eliezer. It is worth noting parenthetically that these *bezichin* may be less than a *kezayit* in quantity; however, the identity of each as a full spoon — a distinct, complete vessel — may itself confer sufficient halakhic significance to substitute for the *shiur* of *kezayit*.

## Matirin Status Question

### Rav Yitzchak Question

Rav Yitzchak bar Nafcha poses a penetrating conceptual question: *kometz mahu sheyatir k'negdo b'shirayim?* — when one of the two *matirin* of a *mincha* is offered on the *mizbeach*, what is the halakhic status of the *mincha* at that moment? Has it become half-permitted? Or does the first *matir* merely weaken the overall prohibition without actually permitting any portion?

One might frame the question this way, reading as Tosafot does: if the *kometz* is burned on the *mizbeach* and the *levona* has not yet been burned, is the *mincha* now in a state where half of it is permitted and half is not — though one cannot identify which half — such that eating two *kezaisim* might trigger liability of *malkos*? Or alternatively, does the first *matir* operate not by carving out half but by diminishing the overall prohibition, such that only when both are brought is the *mincha* fully permitted?

### Rabbi Meir Half Effect

The *gemara* asks: according to whom is this question being posed? If it is according to Rabbi Meir, who holds *mapiglin bechatzi matir* — that a *piggul* intention during one of the two *matirin* renders the *korban piggul* — then the very concept of *piggul* being operative through half a *matir* implies that the half-*matir* actually accomplishes something. It must effect some permissive change on at least part of the *mincha*, for otherwise the *piggul* thought at that *avoda* would be meaningless. Thus, for Rabbi Meir, it seems that bringing one *matir* does indeed make half the *mincha* permitted — *mishra shari*.

### Rabbanan No Effect

If the question is posed according to the *rabbanan*, who hold *ein mapiglin bechatzi matir* — that a *piggul* thought during only one of the two *matirin* does not make the *korban piggul* — then there is no evidence from *piggul* that the partial *matir* accomplishes anything at all. One cannot determine from their position whether the first *matir* permits half, weakens the prohibition, or has no effect whatsoever until both are brought — *lo mishra shari v'lo michlush kalish*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Tayku

The *gemara* suggests that the question might be posed according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one is not *chayav* for bringing outside until both *matirin* are offered — a position structurally parallel to the *rabbanan*'s view that *ein mapiglin bechatzi matir*. For Rabbi Eliezer, there is similarly no basis to conclude that either *matir* alone accomplishes anything prior to the completion of both. The *gemara* then concludes: the question is really meaningful only according to the *rabbanan* of the *mishna* — those who hold one is *chayav* for bringing a single *matir* outside. For them it seems clear that one *matir* does have some effect; the unresolved issue is the nature of that effect. And on that the *gemara* leaves the question standing: *tayku*.

## Dam & Shirayim

### Partial Dam Chayav

The final *mishna* of the page opens with a ruling that is intuitively straightforward: *hazorek miktzas dam bachutz chayav* — one who throws even part of the blood outside the *Beis Hamikdash* is *chayav*. This does not mean all the blood of the animal, but rather that even performing only some of the required blood applications — even just one corner of the altar — renders one liable.

### Rabbi Eliezer Dam

Notably, Rabbi Eliezer does not dispute this *mishna*, even though he generally requires the full *matir* before assigning liability. The explanation is that for blood, even in a *chatas* which has four required applications, we rule that any single application of blood is itself a *matir*. Since one application is *bediavad* sufficient as a *matir*, Rabbi Eliezer agrees that one is *chayav* for even a single application outside. Rava makes this point explicit — *u'modeh Rabbi Eliezer bedamim* — though it is largely implicit in the *mishna*'s silence on Rabbi Eliezer's dissent.

### Rava Chiddush Dam

However, Tosafot identifies Rava's true *chiddush* as the following: one might have thought that on *Yom Kippur*, where every individual blood application is *meakev* — where each and every application is indispensable to the atonement — Rabbi Eliezer would require all of the applications to have been done before assigning liability for a single one outside, since without all of them the *matir* is never complete. This would be a compelling argument. Rava's innovation is that even in that case, Rabbi Eliezer would hold one *chayav* for a single application offered outside.

### Where Spilling Begins

The source for this is a *braita*: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon say *mimakom shepasak hu matchil* — if some of the blood spilled during the service on *Yom Kippur*, one does not start over from the beginning; one resumes from where one left off. This demonstrates that even an incomplete set of applications accomplishes something — each application achieves its own portion of the *avoda* and need not be redone. This is why even one application is meaningful, even though the full *matir* has not yet been completed: it has permanently discharged that portion of the service. Accordingly, one would be *chayav* for bringing even a single application outside.

The *mishna* also records Rabbi Nechemiah's position: *sheyarei hadam shehikrivan bachutz chayav* — one who pours the *shirayim* hadam — the remnant blood poured at the base of the altar — outside the *Beis Hamikdash* is also *chayav*. Rabbi Nechemiah holds that the pouring of the *shirayim* is *meakev*, an indispensable component of the service. It is therefore still a form of *hakravah*, still falls within the category of *rauy l'pesach ohel moed*, and thus incurs liability when performed outside. This point will be developed further in the following *daf*.

## Nisuch Hamayim

### Water Libation Chayav

Rabbi Eliezer adds his own ruling in the *mishna*: *af hamenasech mehachag bachutz chayav* — one who pours the water of *Sukkos* outside the *Beis Hamikdash* is also *chayav*. The question immediately arises: what is the *chiddush*? If one is already *chayav* for *nisuch hayayin* — for the wine libation offered outside — why would water be any different? The *gemara* will explain.

### Rabbi Akiva Source

Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Menachem of Yudfaya, explains: *Rabbi Eliezer beshitas Rabbi Akiva rabbo amar* — Rabbi Eliezer is following the position of his teacher Rabbi Akiva. A *braita* records that Rabbi Akiva derives from the word *u'nesacheha* — written in the plural regarding the libations of the sixth day of *Sukkos* — that the Torah is speaking of two libations: one of wine and one of water. *Bishnei nesachim hakasuv medaber echad nisuch hamayim v'echad nisuch hayayin.* The *chiddush* of Rabbi Eliezer, then, is that *nisuch hamayim* is *d'oraysa* — a Torah obligation — and because it is *d'oraysa*, one is *chayav* for performing it outside the *Beis Hamikdash*.

This raises a striking point noted by Tosafot: the very framing of this derivation implies that there is an opinion holding *nisuch hamayim* to be merely Rabbinic. Tosafot finds this astonishing. Even setting aside the problem of *chullin ba'azarah* — the prohibition against bringing non-sacred items into the Temple precincts — the very idea that the Rabbis would institute a major and elaborate ritual within the *Beis Hamikdash*, *lechatchilah*, without any Torah warrant is deeply striking. A ritual that is not recognized by the Torah would render the water *chullin*, and yet it would be poured as though it were a sacred libation. Tosafot suggests that perhaps the centrality of water to the themes of *Sukkos* — it being a time of prayer for rain — was so compelling that the Rabbis felt it necessary to establish a ritual that would cause the Jewish people to be remembered before God in the days of rain. The theological implications of instituting an unsanctioned ritual in the *Mikdash* precisely to attract divine attention are, as Tosafot's language implies, not without difficulty.

### Reish Lakish Challenge

Reish Lakish presses Rabbi Yochanan with two challenges. The first: *im al hallan shloshah lugin af kan shloshah lugin* — if Rabbi Eliezer is basing himself on Rabbi Akiva, who derives *nisuch hamayim* from the analogy to wine, then the minimum *shiur* for the water should be three *log*, just as for wine. Yet Rabbi Eliezer implies one is *chayav* even for a minimal amount — *kol shehu* — which cannot be consistent with the analogy to wine.

### Sukkot Only Question

The second challenge: *v'im al hallan bish'ar yemot ha-shanah af kan bish'ar yemot ha-shanah* — if Rabbi Eliezer bases the obligation on Rabbi Akiva's derivation, which derives from the wine libation that applies throughout the year, then *nisuch hamayim* should likewise apply throughout the year, and one should be *chayav* for pouring water outside at any time. Yet Rabbi Eliezer says one is *chayav* only on *Sukkos*. Tosafot has an alternative textual reading here: the word *u'nesacheha* appears in the context of the sixth day of *Sukkos*, so according to Rabbi Akiva's derivation, the obligation would logically begin only on the sixth day, or perhaps only apply to the sixth and seventh days. The *gemara*'s challenge, in Tosafot's reading, is therefore *sh'ar yemot ha-hag* — why is Rabbi Eliezer *chayav* on all the days of *Sukkos* if Rabbi Akiva's derivation would limit it to day six and onwards? Either way, Rabbi Eliezer's position cannot be consistently explained by reference to Rabbi Akiva.

### Halakha Lemoshe

The *gemara* resolves both challenges with the word *ishtamitayh* — Rabbi Yochanan forgot. Specifically, he forgot another statement taught in his own name, as cited by Rabbi Assi: *ha d'amar Rabbi Assi amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Nehunia ish Bik'at Beis Hortan — esser nityos, aravah, v'nisuch hamayim halakhah l'Moshe mi-Sinai*. The water libation — together with the *aravah* ritual of *Sukkos* and a ruling regarding young plantings — is a *halakhah l'Moshe mi-Sinai*. It is not derived from *u'nesacheha* and is not dependent on Rabbi Akiva's analogy to wine. Rabbi Eliezer, according to this, holds that *nisuch hamayim* is *d'oraysa* because it is a *halakhah l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — an independent received tradition. Under this model, the minimum amount need not be three *log*, since the tradition itself may specify a smaller quantity; and the obligation applies throughout *Sukkos*, since that is how the tradition was received. Rabbi Yochanan, when he attributed Rabbi Eliezer to Rabbi Akiva, forgot that he himself had transmitted this alternative source.

## Water Minimum & Kli

### Three Log Water

A *braita* now states: *ha-menasekh shloshah lugin mayim be-hag ba-hutz hayyav* — one who pours three *log* of water on *Sukkos* outside the *Beis Hamikdash* is *chayav*. Rabbi Eliezer, in Tosafot's textual reading, concedes this: he says *im la'an l'sheim chag chayav* — if one filled the vessel with three *log* designated for the *chag*, then one would indeed be *chayav* for three *log*. His normal position is that even a *kol shehu* is sufficient, but he concedes the three *log* threshold when the vessel was filled with three *log* for the purpose of the *chag*.

### Kli Sharet Debate

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the underlying dispute: *b'yesher b'mayim kamiflegi* — they debate the minimum *shiur* of the water libation itself. The *chachamim* hold, perhaps following Rabbi Akiva's analogy to wine, that the minimum is three *log*, and therefore one is not *chayav* outside for less than three. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even a *kol shehu* suffices for *nisuch hamayim* inside the *Beis Hamikdash*, and therefore even the smallest amount incurs liability outside. However, Rabbi Eliezer's own principle of *kviusa demana* — that placing a quantity in a vessel establishes it as the halakhic unit — applies here as well. If one filled a vessel with three *log* intending that amount for *nisuch hamayim*, then three *log* is what is now established, and one would be *chayav* only for that full amount. The positions thus dovetail neatly: the *chachamim* maintain three *log* as an absolute minimum; Rabbi Eliezer says *kol shehu* in general, but agrees that three *log* becomes the binding *shiur* when the vessel was filled with that amount.

### Midbar Nesachim

Rav Pappa offers an alternative explanation, which is admittedly cryptic on its face: *b'kirbu nesachim bamidbar pligi* — the dispute concerns whether *nesachim* were brought in the *midbar*. Rashi bridges this to the practical question as follows. The Torah, in commanding the *nesachim* accompanying animal offerings, says *ki tavo'u el ha'aretz* — when you come to the land. The plain reading suggests that *nesachim* were not brought in the *midbar* and were reserved for *Eretz Yisrael*, implying that they belong to a centralized *Beis Hamikdash* context and were not offered on private *bamot*. If, however, one holds that *nesachim* were in fact brought in the *midbar*, then *ki tavo'u el ha'aretz* must mean something else: it instructs that upon entering the land, even when there is no central *Mishkan* and private *bamot* are permitted, *nesachim* should still be brought — even on those private altars.

This matters halakhically because offerings that are valid on a private *bama* do not require a *kli sharet* for sanctification. If *nesachim* were brought in the *midbar* — and hence on private *bamot* — then *nesachim* are valid without a *kli sharet*. Since what is valid on a *bama* during a time when *bamot* are prohibited generates *chiyuv* outside, one would be *chayav* for *nisuch* even without a *kli sharet*. Rabbi Eliezer holds that a *kli sharet* is required — the water must be filled in a sacred vessel, *mil'an l'sheim chag* — because without that sanctification it is not *rauy l'pesach ohel moed* and there is no liability. The *chachamim* hold that since *nesachim* were brought in the *midbar* and hence on private *bamot* without a *kli sharet*, a *kli sharet* is not required, and one is *chayav* even without it.

### Bamot Question

On this reading, the dispute is not primarily about three *log* versus *kol shehu* at all. Both sides might agree on the minimum amount; the disagreement concerns the role of the *kli sharet* as a prerequisite for liability. Whether *nesachim* were ever offered on private *bamot* thus becomes the axis of the entire debate.

### Ravina Water Wine

Ravina offers yet a third explanation of the dispute: *b'limadim nisuch hamayim mi-nisuch hayayin pligi* — the debate concerns whether *nisuch hamayim* can be derived from *nisuch hayayin* in the relevant respect. Everyone agrees that *nisuch hayayin* was practiced on private *bamot* without a *kli sharet*, and that it therefore generates *chiyuv* outside even without one. The question is whether *nisuch hamayim* follows the same rule. *Nisuch hamayim* was never offered on a private *bama* — it is a communal *Beis Hamikdash* ritual. One might therefore argue that it requires a *kli sharet*, since we cannot draw the parallel to wine. The *chachamim* hold that just as wine generates liability without a *kli sharet*, the same applies to water: one is *chayav* even without it. Rabbi Eliezer holds that water cannot be so derived from wine, and without a *kli sharet* there is no liability. Thus on Ravina's reading, both the question of *kli sharet* and the question of whether water follows wine stand at the heart of the disagreement, and the *daf* concludes here.

---

---

# Zevachim 111

## Water & Kli Sharet

### Three Logs Water

We pick up at the top of 111a, continuing a discussion of the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* regarding whether one who pours three *log* of water outside the Temple is liable. The dispute, as we have been exploring, turns on the precise conditions under which such liability attaches.

### Kli Sharet Definition

One way of defining the core of this debate is whether a *kli sharet* — a sacred service vessel — is required to sanctify the water in order to create liability. In the Temple itself, a *kli sharet* is certainly required. But the operative question is whether such a vessel was required on a private *bamah* during the period when private altars were permitted.
