The mechanism by which one becomes liable outside the Temple is not necessarily identical to the Temple rite; as we know, the standard for liability is *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed* — fitness for offering at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting — and that standard need not mirror every detail of the Temple service. The example is raised of placing an offering on a rock without fire, which would not be valid in the Temple but may have been valid on a *bamah*.

### Private Altars

This question — whether wine libations could be brought on a *bamah* without a *kli sharet*, and whether water libations could similarly be brought — frames the entire discussion. We will return to develop it further as the Gemara continues.

---

## Wine Libations

### Wine Rule

The Gemara introduces a closely parallel *baraita*: one who pours three *log* of wine outside the Temple — *hamenaseach shlosha lugin yayin bachutz*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon declares him liable. Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon then qualifies: *vehu shekidshen bikli* — only if he sanctified the wine in a vessel. This closely parallels the earlier formulation involving water, and the similarity is what led some authorities to emend the earlier text from "Rabbi Eliezer" to "Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon," or to read the earlier ruling as referring to a *kli sharet* rather than merely a vessel.

### Heaping Liquid

*Mai beinaihu* — what is the practical or conceptual crux of their disagreement? Rav Adda bar Abba explains: *beirutzei midos ika beinaihu* — they disagree about *beirutzei midos*, the heaping of liquid at the rim of a vessel. When a liquid is sanctified in a *kli sharet*, does the sanctification extend to the small overflow held in place at the rim by surface tension, or only to the liquid within the vessel walls? The *chachamim* hold that any measure of three *log* — however that quantity came together in the vessel — suffices for liability. Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon holds that sanctification in a vessel means precisely within the vessel walls; the overflow is not included. One might ask whether this same dispute applies to the *minchah* offering, and the answer is yes — it is not specific to wine or water libations.

### Libations Bamah

Rava bar Rabbah offers an alternative: *kirvu nesachim babamah ika beinaihu* — they disagree about whether libations were in fact brought on private altars when *bamot* were permitted. This is essentially equivalent to asking whether they were brought in the wilderness, as the Gemara treats these as related questions determined by the same sources. If libations were brought on a *bamah*, they were necessarily brought without a *kli sharet*, since *bamot* had no *kli sharet*. Thus the *Tanna Kamma* holds that three *log* of wine creates liability even without a *kli sharet*, because such a rite existed on a *bamah* and is therefore *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed* — or rather, fit for a *bamah* in the time when *bamot* were permissible. Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon holds that *bamot* never had libations, and therefore without a *kli sharet* the act is not sufficiently recognized as a sacrificial rite to generate liability.

---

## Private Altar Libations

### Rabbi's View

The Gemara notes that this debate connects to a dispute among *tannaim*, introduced with *detanya*. The *baraita* states: *bamas yachid einah tzericha nesachim* — a private altar does not require libations. This is the position of Rabbi. The question here is not merely whether libations were permitted on a *bamah*, but whether they were obligatory. However, the Gemara treats permissibility and obligation as two sides of the same coin in this context: if libations are not required, they are equally not practiced.

### Sages' View

The *chachamim* disagree: *te'unah nesachim* — a private altar does require libations. This is the opposing position. The debate is thus about whether the phenomenon of libations on a private *bamah* ever existed as a recognized institution.

### Debate Connection

The connection between these two *tannaitic* disputes is direct. Whether libations were brought on a private *bamah* — which, by definition, had no *kli sharet* — determines whether one can be liable for performing such a rite outside the Temple without a *kli sharet* today. If the *chachamim* hold that libations were practiced on private altars, then offering libations without a *kli sharet* is a form of worship that was once legitimate, and one who does so outside the Temple in a forbidden time becomes liable. If Rabbi holds that libations were never part of the private *bamah* rite, then performing them without a *kli sharet* has no template of legitimacy, and there is no liability.

---

## Scriptural Debate

### Yishmael Central

The Gemara now traces this dispute about libations on private altars back to a fundamental *tannaitic* disagreement about the meaning of the verse at the end of Parshas Shlach: *ki tavo el eretz moshvoseichem asher ani nosen lachem* — "when you come to the land of your dwellings that I give you" — followed by the requirement to bring wine, flour, and oil together with one's offering. Rabbi Yishmael reads the verse as follows: the default assumption is that the Torah is speaking of a *bamah gedolah*, a central altar. The phrase "when you come to the land" introduces the obligation of *nesachim* — libations — which applies only upon entry into the land and only at a central location. The phrase *moshvoseichem*, "your dwellings," is read collectively: the land given to you as a people, implying a single, communal place of worship. On this reading, libations were never obligatory — or practiced — in the wilderness, nor on private altars.

### Akiva Private

Rabbi Akiva reads the verse differently. His initial assumption is that the Torah is speaking of a *bamah ketanah*, a private altar. The word *moshvoseichem*, he argues, emphasizes the individual dwellings of each person: wherever you dwell, that is where you may bring your offering together with libations. This is consistent with the well-known practice of the period of the *bamot*, when, as the verse in Kings describes, the people sacrificed and offered incense on *bamot* everywhere — each person at his own private altar.

### Wilderness Inference

The Gemara draws a further inference: *keshtimtzai lomar* — one may say — that according to Rabbi Yishmael, libations were not brought in the wilderness at all, while according to Rabbi Akiva, they were. The connection runs as follows: if libations were already being brought in the *mishkan* in the wilderness, then the verse's instruction "when you come to the land" must be introducing something new — namely, the permission or obligation to bring libations on private altars throughout the land. If, however, libations were not yet brought in the wilderness, then "when you come" introduces the basic obligation for the first time, and it is directed toward the central location. The verse does not proceed to extend that obligation to private altars. This reasoning, while not immediately obvious from the verse alone, is elaborated by Rashi at length.

---

## Remaining Blood

### Nechemya Rule

The Gemara now turns to the end of the *mishnah*, where Rabbi Nechemya states: *shearei hadam shehikriv bachutz chayav* — one who sprinkles the remaining blood outside the Temple is liable. The *shirayim* — the remainder of the blood poured at the base of the altar — is not among the primary blood rites that effect atonement. Why, then, should sprinkling this remainder outside create liability?

### Yochanan Reading

Rabbi Yochanan explains: *tana d'Rabbi Nechemya k'divrei haomer shearayim me'akvim* — Rabbi Nechemya's teaching follows the position of those who hold that the pouring of the *shirayim* is essential, *me'akev*, for atonement. Only if the *shirayim* is indispensable to the *kapara* does it qualify as an act that is *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed*, and only then does performing it outside generate liability. This is a striking position when applied to an outer offering, since we are accustomed to hearing that the *shirayim* is *me'akev* only in the context of inner *chata'ot*, where every stage of the blood service is essential.

### Akiva Challenge

The Gemara challenges this interpretation by citing the *baraita* in which Rabbi Akiva engages Rabbi Nechemya directly. Rabbi Akiva asks: *v'halo shearei hadam shearei mitzvah hein* — surely the *shirayim* are merely the residual conclusion of the blood rite, not its essential core. Rabbi Nechemya responds: *evarim u'fedarim yochichu* — let the entrails and fats prove the point. One who offers the entrails and fats outside is liable, yet their offering does not effect atonement. Why should the blood *shirayim* be any different?

Rabbi Akiva replies: *im amarta b'evarim u'fedarim sheheim techilat avoda* — when you speak of the entrails and fats, you are speaking of an act that is the beginning and substance of its own distinct ritual. The offering of the *evarim* is not a coda to the blood service; it is itself an independent act with its own integrity. The blood *shirayim*, by contrast, is precisely that — a coda, a conclusion, a wrap-up of the primary blood rite. *Tomar b'shearei dam sheeinam techilat avoda* — can you say the same of the remaining blood, which is not the beginning of any act?

The discussion touches briefly on the view that *im basar ein dam* — that the validity of the blood may depend on the offering of the inner organs — which would give the *evarim* an additional significance in relation to the blood. But this position is itself disputed, and the Gemara does not pursue it further here.

The implication is clear: the straightforward reading of the *baraita* is that Rabbi Nechemya does not require the *shirayim* to be *me'akev* in order to establish liability outside. He holds simply that any blood rite, as long as it is still *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed*, generates liability. It is Rabbi Akiva who introduces the distinction between the *shirayim* and the *evarim* — a logical distinction, though perhaps not the only possible one. On this simple reading, Rabbi Nechemya's position does not depend on the claim that *shirayim* are *me'akev*.

The Gemara then presses Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation: *ve'im isa leima leh hani nami me'akvei* — if Rabbi Yochanan is correct that Rabbi Nechemya's position is premised on *shirayim* being *me'akev*, then when Rabbi Akiva challenged him, why did Rabbi Nechemya not simply respond that the *shirayim* are indeed *me'akev*? The failure to make that response is a *tiyuvta* — a clear refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's reading.

### Inner vs Outer

At this point the Gemara introduces the resolution of Rav Ada bar Ahava: *machlokes beshirayim pnimiyim aval beshirayim chitzoniyim divrei hakol lo me'akvei* — the debate about whether *shirayim* are *me'akev* applies only to the inner *chatas*, offered on the inner altar. By the outer *korbanot*, everyone agrees that the *shirayim* are not *me'akev*, which is entirely consistent with our understanding of the law. Once this is established, the Gemara can defend Rabbi Yochanan.

Rabbi Nechemya's original statement — that one is liable for sprinkling *shirayim* outside — was made in the context of an inner *chatas*, where he holds that *shirayim* are indeed *me'akev*. The debate between him and Rabbi Akiva, however, was conducted in the context of an outer *korban*. This explains why Rabbi Nechemya did not say to Rabbi Akiva "they are *me'akev*" — because by an outer *korban*, he agrees they are not. Of course, this raises a further question: why did Rabbi Nechemya not simply clarify to Rabbi Akiva that he was only speaking of an inner *chatas* and that the debate was therefore beside the point? The Gemara answers: *Rabbi Nechemya lidvarav de'Rabbi Akiva ka'amar* — Rabbi Nechemya was engaging Rabbi Akiva on his own terms. He was effectively saying: even if we speak about an outer *korban*, I will argue with you that a case could be made for liability. Rabbi Akiva then responds by drawing the distinction between the *evarim* and the *shirayim*, and that distinction stands for the outer *korban*.

The underlying question remains as to whether this is a *mesorah* — a received tradition — or whether Rav Ada bar Ahava and the other *amoraim* are simply applying logical reasoning to resolve the difficulties. Since no source is cited, it appears to be the latter.

---

## Bird Slaughter

### Melikah Pnimis

The Gemara turns to a new *mishnah*: *hamolek et ha-of bifnim ve-he'ela bachutz chayav* — one who performs *melikah* inside the Temple and then raises the bird outside is liable. *Melikah* — the pinching of the bird's neck — is the valid method of slaughter for bird offerings inside the Temple. Performing it there constitutes a valid act, and the subsequent *ha'ala'ah* outside therefore generates liability.

### Melikah Chutz

*Malak bachutz ve-he'ela bachutz* — if one performed *melikah* outside the Temple and then raised the bird outside, one is exempt on both counts. One is exempt on the *melikah* itself because the prohibition of *shechutei chutz* applies only through the framework of *halacha*, and *melikah* performed outside has no recognized standing. More significantly, the *melikah* performed outside invalidates the bird entirely, rendering the subsequent *ha'ala'ah* not *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed* — the bird is now disqualified, and lifting it outside does not constitute a meaningful sacrificial act.

### Shechitah Pnimis

*Hashochet et ha-of bifnim ve-he'ela bachutz* — if one slaughtered a bird inside the Temple and then raised it outside, one is exempt. Here the logic is reversed: *shechitah* — knife slaughter — is the valid method for animal offerings, but for birds inside the Temple, the proper method is *melikah*. Performing *shechitah* on a bird inside the Temple is therefore an invalid act, equivalent to striking the bird in the head. Since the initial act inside was meaningless, the bird is *pasul*, and the subsequent *ha'ala'ah* outside is also exempt.

### Shechitah Chutz

*Shachat bachutz ve-he'ela bachutz chayav* — if one slaughtered a bird outside and then raised it outside, one is liable. This is the counterintuitive case. *Shechitah* for a bird is entirely invalid inside the Temple, yet outside the Temple it is treated as the operative act that triggers liability for the *ha'ala'ah* that follows. The analogy to *piggul* is instructive: within the framework of what one is doing — performing a sacrificial rite outside the Temple — the fact that it takes place outside is bracketed, and the act is evaluated on its own terms. *Shechitah* of a bird outside fits the parameters of *shechitah* in a way that *melikah* outside does not. *Melikah* outside the Temple is not a recognizable ritual act at all; *shechitah* outside, while forbidden, is at least formally coherent as an act of slaughter.

### Location Context

The *mishnah* draws this together with the principle: *nimtza derech hechshero bifnim paturo bachutz* — the manner in which an act is valid inside is the manner in which performing it outside creates exemption, and vice versa. The Gemara will emend *hechshero* to *chiyuvo* for the second half of the formulation: *derech chiyuvo bifnim paturo bachutz*, *derech chiyuvo bachutz paturo bifnim*. Following Rashi's reading: the act that makes one liable when started inside — *melikah* — makes one exempt when started outside; the act that makes one liable when started outside — *shechitah* — makes one exempt when started inside. Everything is defined by its context.

---

## Shimon Principle

### Shimon Rule

Rabbi Shimon states: *kol shechayavin alav bachutz chayavin al kayotzei bo bifnim* — whatever one is liable for when performed outside the Temple, one is liable for the equivalent act performed inside, provided the sequence ends with *ha'ala'ah* outside. He then adds the exception: *chutz min hashochet et ha-of bifnim ve-he'ela bachutz* — except for the case of one who slaughtered a bird inside and raised it outside.

### Melikah Test

The Gemara asks: *ahi kai* — to which case in the *mishnah* is Rabbi Shimon responding? Could he be addressing the *melikah* case? If his principle is "what makes you liable outside makes you liable inside," and we apply it to *melikah*, it would mean: since *melikah* inside makes you liable (when followed by *ha'ala'ah* outside), therefore *melikah* outside should also make you liable. But Rabbi Shimon said the reverse — *if you're liable outside, you're liable inside* — which implies starting from the *chutz* case and deriving the *bifnim* case. That would mean he is trying to extend liability to something done inside based on what is liable outside. If he were discussing *melikah*, he should have said the opposite: *kol shechayavin alav bifnim chayavin al kayotzei bo bachutz* — what makes you liable inside makes you liable outside. The language of the *mishnah* does not fit *melikah*.

Alternatively, perhaps he is trying to *exempt* by analogy: since *melikah* outside does not make you liable, neither should *melikah* inside. But then he should have said *kol she'ein chayavin aleha bachutz* — what you are exempt for outside, you are exempt for inside. Again, the language does not fit.

### Bird Exception

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon must be addressing the *shechitah* case, and his principle reads as follows: *ki heichi d'bechutz mechayev bifnim nami mechayev* — just as *shechitah* of a bird outside makes one liable, so too *shechitah* of a bird inside should make one liable. The language fits perfectly: whatever you are liable for outside — *shechitah* — you are liable for the equivalent inside. But then he immediately carves out the exception: *chutz min hashochet ha-of bifnim ve-he'ela bachutz*, except for the case of one who slaughtered a bird inside and raised it outside. The very need to state this exception confirms that without it, his principle would have implied liability in that case. This is a striking move: the *mishnah* establishes a general rule — if liable outside, liable inside — and then immediately negates its most obvious application.

### Night & Vessel

Zeiri provides an example of where Rabbi Shimon's principle does apply: *shechitas behemah balaylah ika beinaihu* — the slaughter of an animal at night. The *Tanna Kamma* might implicitly apply the bird model, treating the *bifnim/bachutz* distinction as determinative even here. On that view: *hashochet behemah bifnim balaylah ve-he'ela bachutz patur* — if one slaughtered an animal inside the Temple at night, the *ha'ala'ah* outside generates no liability, since *shechitah* at night is *pasul* and does not withstand the test of *im alah teired* (whether an offering that ascended the altar must come back down — which Rashi understands as underlying the liability analysis throughout this section, though the Gemara does not address it explicitly). But *shachat bachutz balaylah ve-he'ela bachutz chayav* — if one slaughtered outside at night and raised it outside, one is liable, since we bracket the irregularity within the framework of the external act. Rabbi Shimon says: the general principle is that if you are liable outside — even in the *laylah* case — you are equally liable when you started the same act inside. The bird case alone is the exception.

Rava offers a parallel: *kabalah bikli chol ika beinaihu* — the reception of blood in a non-sacred vessel (*kli chol*) rather than a *kli sharet*. On the *Tanna Kamma*'s implicit model, reception in a *kli chol* inside the Temple would lead to exemption for any subsequent *ha'ala'ah* outside, but reception in a *kli chol* outside would generate liability. Rabbi Shimon again applies his principle: whatever generates liability outside — including reception in a *kli chol* — generates liability when the same act is performed inside, with the bird case alone excepted.

### Reversed Reading

The Gemara then introduces an alternative tradition: *avuha di-Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak* teaches a *baraita* in which Rabbi Shimon's principle is inverted. He teaches: *hamolek et ha-of bifnim ve-he'ela bachutz chayav* — we know this. *Malak bachutz ve-he'ela bachutz patur* — we know this. But then: *ve'Rabbi Shimon mechayev* — Rabbi Shimon declares him liable in the *melikah bachutz* case. On this reading, Rabbi Shimon's principle is not "what is liable outside is liable inside" but the reverse: "what is liable inside is liable outside." Since *melikah bifnim* makes one liable, *melikah bachutz* should also make one liable. The Gemara therefore reads Rabbi Shimon's words in the *mishnah* as follows: *kol shechayav alav bifnim ve-he'ela bachutz chayav alav bachutz* — whatever you are liable for when started inside, you are also liable for when started outside. This is a direct reversal of the earlier reading, and requires rereading the language of the *mishnah* as its mirror image.

---

## Blood Vessels

### One Vessel

The *mishnah* now presents a series of cases involving the blood of a *chatas* caught in one or two vessels. When the blood is received in a single vessel, it is entirely *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed* at the moment of reception. Therefore, regardless of the subsequent sequence — whether one pours some outside and then brings some inside, or brings some inside and then pours some outside — liability attaches in either case. The *mishnah*'s ruling of *chayav* in both directions, noted Rashi, follows Rabbi Nechemya's position: even the blood remaining after an initial *zerikah bifnim* retains the status of *shirayim* fit for their own rite, and pouring them outside thereafter generates liability.

### Two Vessels Inside

When the blood is received in two separate vessels and both are used inside the Temple, the ruling is *patur* — exempt. The first vessel effects *kapara*; the second vessel's blood, having been overtaken by the atonement already achieved, adds nothing and generates no liability.

### Two Vessels Outside

If both vessels are used outside the Temple, one is liable for each. The reason is that each vessel's contents were independently *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed* at the time of the act. Had one vessel's blood been used inside, the other vessel's blood could still have served that function. The mere fact that one vessel's blood was poured outside in a forbidden manner does not invalidate the other vessel's blood — it remains available for the proper rite. Therefore each act of *zerikah bachutz* generates its own liability.

### Mixed Inside First

If one vessel is used inside and one outside — in that order — one is exempt. The use of the first vessel's blood inside effects the *kapara*, rendering the second vessel's blood into a status of *dichuy* — rejected and no longer usable for any sacrificial purpose. When one then takes that second vessel's blood and pours it outside, it is no longer *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed*, and no liability attaches.

### Mixed Outside First

If, however, one vessel is used outside first and the second vessel inside — the ruling is *chayav* for the first act, and the second vessel *mechaper*. When the first vessel's blood was poured outside, it was fully *ra'uy le-pesach ohel mo'ed* at that moment, and liability attaches. The question is what happens to the second vessel. One might think that using the first vessel's blood in an act of *zerikah bachutz* — a forbidden act — should invalidate the remaining blood of the same *korban*. The Gemara demonstrates that it does not: the second vessel's blood remains valid and effects atonement when used properly inside.

### Two Animals

The *mishnah* provides an analogy to clarify this: one who designated a *chatas*, which was then lost, and designated a replacement. Both animals are then found standing together. If both are slaughtered inside, one is exempt — the first effects atonement, the second becomes *chatas hameisah* — a sin offering whose owners have already been atoned for, which must die. If both are slaughtered outside, one is liable for each — the first was fully *ra'uy le-korban*, and slaughtering the first outside does not render the second *chatas hameisah*; its owners could still retrieve it and bring it properly. If one is brought inside and one outside, the one brought inside effects atonement, the second becomes *chatas hameisah*, and one is exempt for the act outside. If one is slaughtered outside first and the second brought inside, one is liable for the first, and the second effects atonement — because slaughtering the first outside does not have the same invalidating effect as bringing one properly inside.

The parallel between the two-animal case and the two-vessel case is precise. The *chiddush* of the two-vessel case is that even though both vessels contain blood from the same *korban*, using one vessel's blood in an improper *zerikah bachutz* does not contaminate or invalidate the blood in the second vessel. There is no basis to say otherwise. The *mishnah* concludes with a cryptic remark — *keshem she-damah poteres basarah kach hi poteres et basar chavertah* — just as the blood of one animal releases its own flesh from the laws of *me'ilah*, so too does it release the flesh of the companion animal — which we will leave for further analysis in tomorrow's session.

---

---

# Zevachim 112

## Blood in Two Cups

### Chatat Blood Divided

The Gemara at the top of 112 wraps up the conclusion of the thirteenth chapter, *Hashochet Veha'aleh*, returning briefly to the preceding *mishnah*. The *mishnah* had presented the case of a *korban chatat* whose blood was collected in a single cup, with part of the blood sprinkled outside the Temple and the remainder sprinkled inside. The Gemara opens with the observation: *bishlama bachutz vehazar venatan bifnim* — it is perfectly understandable why one would be *chayav* if the blood was first applied outside and the remainder then brought inside, since the entire quantity had been suitable to be applied inside; by performing the *zerikah* outside, one violated the prohibition of *zerikah bachutz*. But the reverse case — *aval bifnim veha'alah bachutz* — where the blood was first applied inside and then the remainder taken outside, is more difficult. The remainder is merely *shi'arayim*, the leftover blood, and having already fulfilled the *zerikah* obligation, one might expect that taking the *shi'arayim* outside carries no prohibition of substance.

### Rabbi Nechemya Position

To account for this case, the Gemara proposes: *ha mani Rabbi Nechemya hi* — the *mishnah* follows the opinion of Rabbi Nechemya, who holds that *she'arey dam she'hikrivan bachutz chayav*, even the leftover blood that does not effect the *kaparah* falls within the prohibition of *hakravah bachutz*. Rabbi Nechemya thus adopts an expansive understanding of the prohibition, extending it even to the *shi'arey hadam*.

### Reisha vs Seifa

However, if one attributes the *mishnah* to Rabbi Nechemya, the *seifa* becomes problematic. The later clause of the *mishnah* addresses blood collected in two separate cups: if both cups are taken inside one is *patur*; if both are taken outside one is *chayav*; but if one is applied inside and one outside, one is *patur*. This sits uneasily with Rabbi Nechemya, who would presumably hold one *chayav* even for the second cup brought outside, since that blood — though now rendered *shi'arayim* after the first cup fulfilled the *zerikah* — was still brought beyond the Temple. The Gemara therefore concludes: *seifa ata l'Tana Kama d'Rabbi Elazar be'Rabbi Shimon* — while the *reisha* of the *mishnah* reflects Rabbi Nechemya's position, the *seifa* follows the opinion of Rabbi Elazar be'Rabbi Shimon, who articulates the principle *kos oseh dichei lechavero*: when blood is divided between two cups and one cup becomes disqualified, it renders the partner cup disqualified as well. The Rambam notes in his *Perush ha-Mishnayot* that this *sugya* makes clear that Rabbi Nechemya's position is rejected, and the Gemara is merely attempting to align parts of the *mishnah* with his view in order to account for the earlier clause.

### Two Animals Designated

The *mishnah* had then offered a *lema hadavar domeh* — an analogy comparing the case of blood divided between two cups to the following scenario: a person designated a *korban chatat*, it was lost, he designated a second animal as a replacement, and then the first animal was found. Now both animals stand as designated *korbanot chatat*. If both are slaughtered inside the *Beit HaMikdash* one is *patur*; if both are slaughtered outside one is *chayav*; if one is slaughtered inside and one outside one is *patur*. However, if the outside animal is slaughtered first and then the inside animal, one is *chayav* for the first, and the second still effects *kaparah*.

The Gemara asks: *lama li?* Why does the *mishnah* introduce this entire analogy at all? The answer is: *ha mani Rebbi hi* — this reflects the opinion of Rebbi, who holds *avudah beshas hafrasha meisah*: if the animal was lost at the time the replacement was designated, that first animal must die — it constitutes a sixth category of *chatas meisos* beyond the standard five. The purpose of the analogy is to explain why both animals are standing and must be addressed at all: the reason is precisely that the animal was lost in the interim, not that one tried to designate two *chatat* animals simultaneously from the outset. For if one had tried to designate two *korbanot* for the same liability at once, one of them would automatically revert to being a *korban olah*, as Rav Huna states in the name of Rav: an *asham* that was disqualified and sent to pasture, and then slaughtered *stam* without any particular intent, is valid as an *olah*.

### Rebbi's Limitations

However, the Gemara immediately challenges this: *mi dami? hatam asham zachar ve'olah zachar* — that case works because both the *asham* and the *olah* are male animals. But a *korban chatat* is a female animal, and a *korban olah* may only be brought from a male animal. Accordingly, one could not simply say that the second *chatat* animal reverts to an *olah*. Rabbi Chiyya of Vastinya therefore limits Rebbi's ruling to the very narrow case of *seir nasi* — the *chatat* of a ruler — which at the time of the *Beit Sheni* had perhaps highly limited application. Thus the *sugya* concludes that Rebbi's principle of *avudah beshas hafrasha meisah*, while compelling in theory, is confined by the *Amoraim* to a specific and uncommon case, since the general problem of the *chatat*'s being a female animal prevents it from reverting to any other category. With this, the Gemara closes the thirteenth chapter.

---

## Fourteenth Chapter Intro

### Parah & Seir

The fourteenth chapter, *Paras Chatas*, opens with the *mishnah* stating: *paras chatas she-serafah chutz mi-gitah* — if the *parah adumah* was burned outside its designated pit on Har ha-Zeitim, or if the *seir hamishtaleach* — which is supposed to be pushed off a cliff — was instead offered as a sacrifice outside the Temple, one is *patur* from the prohibition of *shechitat chutz*. The Scriptural basis is the verse *ve'el pesach ohel moed lo hevi'o*, from which the *mishnah* derives the principle: *kol she'ein ra'uy lavo el pesach ohel moed ein chayavin alav* — anything which has no obligation to be brought to the entrance of the *Ohel Moed* does not fall within the scope of the prohibition.

### Inherently Disqualified

The following *mishnah* catalogs a series of animals whose disqualification is inherent to their bodies — *begufan*: an animal involved in an act of bestiality (*rove'ah* or *nirba'at*), an animal designated or worshipped for *avodah zarah* (*muktzeh* or *ne'evad*), an animal given as *etnan zonah* or *mechir kelev*, a crossbred animal (*kilayim*), a *treifah*, or an animal born through the abdominal wall (*yotzei dofen*). If any of these animals were slaughtered outside the Temple one is *patur* from *shechitat chutz*. The Scriptural basis cited here is slightly different from the previous *mishnah*: *lifnei mishkan Hashem*, suggesting that these animals are abhorrent to God, and their exclusion thus derives from a different dimension of the verse than the quasi-sacrificial cases addressed earlier.

### Rabbi Shimon Lo Ta'aseh

The next *mishnah* addresses *ba'alei mumim* — animals with physical deformities, whether permanent (*kevu'im*) or temporary (*overim*). The *tanna kamma* holds that slaughtering any such animal outside the Temple renders one *patur*. Rabbi Shimon introduces an intermediate category. For permanent deformities he agrees: *patur*. But for temporary deformities he says *ba'alei mumim overim belo ta'aseh* — one violates the prohibition without incurring *karet*. This intermediate position — neither fully *chayav* nor fully *patur* — is the signature of Rabbi Shimon's approach throughout this chapter. The category of *lo ta'aseh* here does not mean one receives lashes; rather, it means one has transgressed the prohibition in a manner that, due to some deficiency, does not carry the penalty to its fullest extent.

### Age Disqualifications

The same structure applies to bird sacrifices. *Torim shelo higi'a zemanam* — turtledoves that have not yet reached their proper age — and *bnei yonah she-avar zemanam* — doves that have aged past their permissible stage — are invalid because turtledoves must be brought as older birds and doves must be brought as young birds. The *tanna kamma* holds that bringing either category outside the Temple renders one *patur*. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: *bnei yonah she-avar zemanam patur* — doves that are too old, *patur* — but *torim shelo higi'a zemanam belo ta'aseh* — turtledoves that are too young incur a violation of the prohibition without *karet*. Rabbi Shimon's reasoning reflects a consistent principle: a disqualification that lies in the past cannot be corrected, while a disqualification that has not yet arrived can still be resolved with time.

### Future Disqualifications

The *mishnah* extends Rabbi Shimon's principle to two further cases: *oto ve'et beno* — the prohibition against slaughtering a parent and its offspring on the same day — and *mechusar zeman* — an animal that has not yet reached its eighth day of life, as the Torah requires *shivat yamim yihyeh tachat imo*. Rabbi Shimon holds that both of these cases fall under *lo ta'aseh*: one violates the prohibition without incurring *karet*.

### Shimon's Principle

Rabbi Shimon's general principle is then articulated explicitly: *kol she-hu ra'uy lavo le-achar zeman harei zeh belo ta'aseh ve'ein bo karet* — anything which can be brought at a future time falls within the prohibition but without the punishment of *karet*. The logic is that because the time will eventually come when the offering may be brought legitimately, the transgression remains within the orbit of the prohibition even if full liability is not triggered.

### Chachamim Response

The *chachamim* reject this intermediate category entirely: *kol she'ein bo karet ein bo belo ta'aseh* — there is no such middle ground. Either one is liable with *karet* or one is wholly *patur*. This dispute represents a fundamental disagreement about the structure of the prohibition of *shechitat chutz*: whether it admits of gradations or whether it is binary in its application.

---

## Owner Deficiencies

### Mechussarei Kapparah

The *mishnah* now turns to *mechusar zeman bi-ve'alav* — a deficiency of time that pertains not to the animal itself but to its owners. The four cases of *mechussarei kapparah* are enumerated: a male *zav*, a female *zavah*, a *yoledet* — a woman who has given birth — and a *metzora*, whether male or female, who has recovered from *tzara'at*. All four must bring a *korban* as the final step of their purification before they may partake of other *korbanot*. Until that *korban* is brought, they are *mechussarei kapparah*. The *mishnah* will be addressed more fully in *Keritot*, but its application here is within the framework of *mechusar zeman* — it is not the animal that is not yet ready, but the owner who has not yet completed the process.

### Chatat/Asham Exempt

The *mishnah* states: *she-hikrivu chattatam ve-ashamam ba-chutz peturin* — if the owners of these four categories brought their *korban chatat* or *korban asham* outside the Temple, they are *patur* from the prohibition of *shechitat chutz*. The deficiency of the owner renders the *korban chatat* and *korban asham* in their hands analogous to disqualified sacrifices.

### Olah/Shelamim Liable

However, *oloteihen ve-shalmeihan ba-chutz chayavin* — if they brought their *korban olah* or *korban shelamim* outside the Temple, they are *chayav*. The *Gemara* will clarify the distinction, but the essential point is that the *olah* and *shelamim* are not inherently linked to the owner's deficiency in the same way that the *chatat* and *asham* are; those latter sacrifices are brought specifically to effect the *mechussarei kapparah*'s completion of *kaparah*, and in that capacity the owner's deficiency disqualifies them — whereas the *olah* and *shelamim* are not uniquely tied to the owner's incomplete status.

---

## Non-Central Avodot

### Burning Meat

The *mishnah* continues with a long list of actions performed outside the Temple for which one is nonetheless *patur*. The first and most obvious category is burning the meat of a *korban chatat* or other *kodshei kodashim* — that is, meat which is designated for consumption by *kohanim* rather than for the *mizbe'ach* — and similarly meat of *kodashim kalim* such as *shelamim*. Burning that meat outside the Temple does not constitute a violation of *ha'alah bachutz*, since it is the portions meant to be consumed, not the portions consigned to the fire of the *mizbe'ach*.

### Permitted Leftovers

Similarly *patur* are: *motar ha-omer* — the remainder of the barley brought on Pesach; *shtei ha-lechem* — the wheat loaves brought on Shavuot; *lechem ha-panim* — the showbreads prepared each Shabbat; and *shirei menachot* — the portion of the *korban minchah* left for the *kohanim* to eat. In all of these cases, what is being burned or consumed outside the Temple is not a sacrificial act directed at the *mizbe'ach* and therefore does not trigger the prohibition.

### Minor Avodot

Also *patur*: *ha-yotzek ve-ha-bolel* — one who sprinkles or mixes oil onto the flour of a *minchah*; *ha-potet* — one who crumbles the *minchah* breads into the required pieces before they are placed on the *mizbe'ach*; *ha-nimlach* — one who applies salt; *ha-menif* — one who performs the *tenufah*, the waving of various sacrifices; and *ha-magish* — the act of bringing the offering forward, which is part of the process of the *korban minchah* as will be discussed at length in the fifth chapter of *Menachot*.

### Priestly Acts

The *mishnah* adds: *ha-mesader et ha-shulchan* — one who arranges the *lechem ha-panim* on the *shulchan*; *ha-metiv et ha-nerot* — one who cleans and relights the lamps of the *menorah*; *ha-kometz* — one who performs the *kemitzah* of the *korban minchah*; and *ha-mekabel damim ba-chutz* — one who receives the blood in a receptacle outside the Temple. All of these are *patur*.

It is worth noting that *ha-metiv et ha-nerot* and *ha-mesader et ha-shulchan* are among the more striking examples on this list, since the *menorah* and *shulchan* are located in the *Heichal*, a space no *Yisrael* is permitted to enter. One suggestion that has been raised is that perhaps a *Yisrael* could technically light the *menorah* from a great distance through the doorway — though the practical difficulties are formidable. The deeper point may be that the *avodah* itself carries no inherent requirement of *kehunah*, even if circumstantially one must be a *kohen* to access the location.

### Lesser Avodot Rationale

Having enumerated all of these cases, the *mishnah* states: *ein chayavin alav lo mishum zarut ve-lo mishum tumah ve-lo mishum mechusar bgadim ve-lo mishum rechutz yadayim ve-raglayim* — none of the violations that ordinarily accompany improper performance of the Temple service apply here: neither *zarut* if a non-*kohen* performs them, nor *tumah* if a *tamei* person performs them, nor *mechusar bgadim* for lacking the *bigdei kehunah*, nor failure to wash hands and feet. The rationale is that all of these *avodot* are of a lesser rank — they are not among the most central and essential acts of the sacrificial service — and therefore they do not carry the full suite of prohibitions and penalties that attach to the primary *avodot*.

---

## Heter Bamot History

### Pre-Mishkan Period

The *mishnah* now pivots to an extended historical excursus on the periods of *heter bamot* and *issur bamot* — times when outside altars were permitted versus prohibited. This material is, in a certain sense, highly anachronistic: it has no future practical application, since the prohibition of *bamot* has been in effect since the building of the first *Beit HaMikdash*. Nonetheless, it constitutes a coherent and historically significant area of *halachah*.

The *mishnah* begins: *ad shelo hukam ha-mishkan, hayu ha-bamot mutarot, ve-avodah bi-vchorot* — before the *Mishkan* was ever built, outside altars were permitted and the sacrificial service was performed by the firstborn. This formulation is somewhat complex historically: the patriarchs brought *korbanot*, Moshe brought various *korbanot*, and not all of them were firstborns. The *mishnah* likely refers specifically to the *korban pesach* in Egypt and to the *korbanot* offered at Har Sinai in the period before the *Mishkan* was commanded or constructed, during which several months elapsed.

### Mishkan Established

*Mishehukam ha-mishkan ne'esru ha-bamot, ve-avodah b'kohanim* — once the *Mishkan* was erected, outside altars were prohibited and the service transferred to the *kohanim*. This is precisely why, at the beginning of *Sefer Bamidbar*, there are the elaborate arrangements for exchanging the tribe of Levi for all the firstborns among *Bnei Yisrael* — the right to perform the service was transferred from the *bechorim* to the *kohanim* and *Leviyim*, and the *bechorim* were thereby relieved of their original role. Some have suggested that this sheds light on why Yaakov was so eager to acquire the *bechorah* from Esav — to prevent Esav from serving in any sense in the future *Beit HaMikdash*.

The *mishnah* further describes that *kodshei kodashim* — like the *korban chatat*, *korban asham*, and the *zivchei shalmei tzibur* on Shavuot — were eaten *lifnim min ha-kela'im*, within the curtains of the *Mishkan*. Though this phrase appears anachronistically throughout *Zevachim* as an overlay on the *Beit HaMikdash*, here it is used literally, since we are speaking of the actual fabric curtains of the *Mishkan*. *Kodashim kalim* could be eaten throughout the entire *machaneh Yisrael*. The three concentric camps — *machaneh shekhinah* (the *Mishkan* itself), *machaneh leviyah* (surrounding the *Mishkan*), and *machaneh Yisrael* (the entire encampment of the Jewish people) — correspond respectively to the Temple precinct, the Temple Mount, and the halakhically designated city of Jerusalem. There is even a *sugya* in the Gemara elsewhere discussing whether the borders of Jerusalem might be greatly expanded in the future, as implied in *Sefer Yechezkel* toward its conclusion.

### Gilgal Period

*Ba'u le-Gilgal hutteru ha-bamot* — when the *Mishkan* was brought to Gilgal in the period of Yehoshua, outside altars were once again permitted. *Kodshei kodashim* could be eaten within the curtains of the *Mishkan*, and *kodashim kalim* could be eaten *bekhol makom* — anywhere at all. In Gilgal there was no designation of *machaneh Yisrael* as a bounded area, since the Jewish people were now spread across the Land of Israel and the *Mishkan* was in one location with no corresponding camp structure. Therefore, only the *machaneh shekhinah* — the curtained interior — defined what counted as the place for *kodshei kodashim*, while for *kodashim kalim* there was no geographic boundary, which is precisely the nature of the *heter bamot*: one could bring a *korban shelamim* on a local *bamah* and eat it there.

### Shiloh Period

*Ba'u le-Shilo ne'esru ha-bamot* — when the *Mishkan* was brought to Shiloh, outside altars were once again prohibited. At Shiloh a significant structural change occurred: rather than the wooden beams of the portable *Mishkan*, stone walls were built to support the structure, while the curtains and leather coverings were retained above. *Velo hayah sham tikrah, ella bayit shel avanim mil-mattan, yeri'ot mil-ma'alan* — there was no roof, just stone walls below and curtains on top. This more permanent physical structure gave Shiloh a more substantive and settled character.

The basis for the prohibition is the verse in Devarim 12:9: *ki lo vatem ad attah el ha-menuchah* — you have not yet come to the *menuchah*. Once the *Mishkan* reached Shiloh, which the Gemara identifies as the *menuchah*, the prohibition of *bamot* resumed. The structure at Shiloh was stable and designated as a central shrine, even if it was not yet the *Beit HaMikdash*, and that stability sufficed to reimpose *issur bamot*. *Kodashim kalim* and *ma'aser sheni* could be eaten *bekhol ha-ro'eh* — anywhere within sight of the *Mishkan* in Shiloh — not within the boundaries of a city, but within the visual lines of sight.

### Nov & Givon

*Ba'u le-Nov u-le-Giv'on hutteru ha-bamot* — when the *Mishkan* was brought to Nob and subsequently to Gibeon (with the *aron* absent from both locations), outside altars were once again permitted. *Kodshei kodashim* were eaten within the curtains, and *kodashim kalim bekhol arei Yisrael* — in any city of Israel. This is a more restricted formulation than the *bekhol makom* of the Gilgal period, where there was no geographic boundary at all; here the *mishnah* specifies *arei Yisrael*, restricting consumption to within city limits.

### Jerusalem Final

*Ba'u li-Yerushalayim ne'esru ha-bamot, velo hayah lahem od hetter* — once everything was brought to Jerusalem and the first *Beit HaMikdash* was built, the period of *bamot* ended permanently. There was no further *heter*. The Scriptural basis is the continuation of the verse from Devarim: *el ha-menuchah ve'el ha-nachalah* — the *menuchah* was Shiloh, and the *nachalah* is Jerusalem. Once the *nachalah* was established with the building of the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *heter bamot* was foreclosed entirely and irrevocably.

*Kodashim kalim* and *ma'aser sheni* could now be eaten only *lifnim min ha-chomah* — within the walls of Jerusalem. This provides a striking halachic context for the construction of Jerusalem's walls, as recounted in *Sefer Nechemiah*: beyond the obvious concerns of security and civic stature, there was a genuine halachic reason to define and maintain the city's walls.

---

## Sanctification Timing

### Both During Issur

The *mishnah* now addresses the question of sacrifices sanctified and offered during different periods of *issur bamot* and *heter bamot* — a scenario that could only have arisen historically during the transitions between these periods, and which has no future applicability, but which nonetheless defines the boundaries of the prohibition. The first case: *she-hikdishan bi-sha'at issur ha-bamot ve-hikrivan bi-sha'at issur ha-bamot bachutz* — if an animal was sanctified during a period when *bamot* were prohibited, and was then offered outside the Temple also during a period when *bamot* were prohibited, the full array of consequences applies: *harei elu b'aseh ve-lo ta'aseh ve-chayavin aleihem karet* — one has violated a *mitzvat aseh*, a *mitzvat lo ta'aseh*, and incurs *karet*.

### Sanctify Hetter Offer Is…

The second case: *hikdishan bi-sha'at hetter bamot ve-hikrivan bi-sha'at issur ha-bamot* — if the animal was sanctified during a period when *bamot* were permitted, and then offered outside the Temple during a period when *bamot* were prohibited. This could occur if, for example, the animal was sanctified while *bamot* were allowed, and then the *Beit HaMikdash* was built in Jerusalem before the sacrifice was offered, and the owner was still in the countryside when he brought it as a sacrifice. In such a case: *harei elu b'aseh ve-lo ta'aseh ve-ein chayavin aleihem karet* — one violates both an *aseh* and a *lo ta'aseh*, but does not receive *karet*. This represents exactly the intermediate category that Rabbi Shimon had articulated earlier in the chapter, and it may suggest that even the *chachamim* agree to Rabbi Shimon's framework in these historical cases, even if they dispute his principle for the categories addressed at the beginning of the *perek*.

### Sanctify Issur Offer Het…

The third case is the inverse: *hikdishan bi-sha'at issur ha-bamot ve-hikrivan bi-sha'at hetter bamot* — the animal was sanctified during a period of *issur bamot*, such as the time of Shiloh, but was then offered during a subsequent period of *heter bamot*, such as Nob. In this case: *harei elu b'aseh ve-ein bahem lo ta'aseh* — one violates a *mitzvat aseh* only, without any *lo ta'aseh*, since at the time of the offering one is in a period of *heter bamot*.

---

## Central vs Local

### Mishkan Required

The *mishnah* proceeds to clarify which sacrifices must be brought specifically at the *Mishkan* and which may be brought at a local *bamah* during periods when *bamot* were permitted. *Elu kodashim krevin ba-Mishkan — Kodashim she'hukdeshu le-Mishkan* — those sacrifices that were sanctified explicitly for the *Mishkan* must be brought there. Similarly, *korbanot ha-tzibur krevin ba-Mishkan* — communal sacrifices, offered on behalf of the *tzibur*, must be brought at the central shrine regardless.

### Individual Permitted

*Korbanot ha-yachid b'bamah* — individual sacrifices may be brought on a local *bamah* during the periods of *heter bamot*. However, *korbanot ha-yachid she-hukdeshu la-Mishkan, yikrevu ba-Mishkan* — if an individual specifically sanctified his animal with the intent of bringing it to the *Mishkan*, he is obligated to do so. *Ve'im hikrivan b'bamah patur* — but if he nonetheless brought it on a *bamah be-di'avad*, he is *patur*. He has not violated a prohibition, but he had a *le-chatchilah* obligation to bring it to the *Mishkan* as he had declared.

---

## Altar Differences

### Smicha & Direction

The *mishnah* enumerates the ways in which the *bamat ha-yachid* — an individual's private altar — differs from the *bamat ha-tzibur*, the central *Mishkan* which is itself called a *bamah gedolah* during periods of *heter bamot*. The following requirements apply only at the central shrine and not at a private *bamah*: *smicha* — the laying of hands on the animal before slaughter — does not apply at a *bamah*. Nor does *shechitat tzafon* — the requirement that *kodshei kodashim* such as *chatat*, *asham*, and *olah* be slaughtered on the north side of the *mizbe'ach*.

### Blood & Waving

*Matan saviv* — going around the four corners of the *mizbe'ach* to apply the blood — does not apply at a *bamah*. *Tenufah* — the waving of the various portions of the *korban shelamim* — also does not apply at a *bamah*. Nor does *hagashah* — the bringing-forward that is part of the *korban minchah* process.

### Rabbi Yehuda Mincha

Rabbi Yehuda goes further: *ein minchah ba-bamah* — there is no *minchah* offering at a *bamah* at all. Additionally, Rabbi Yehuda holds *ve-kehun* — there is actually no requirement for *kohanim* at a *bamah*; even a *zar* could bring *korbanot* on a private *bamah*.

### No Priestly Items

There is also no requirement for *bigdei sharet* — the priestly vestments are called *bigdei sharet* here rather than *bigdei kehunah* — and no requirement for *klei sharet*, sanctified vessels. There is no requirement to use formally designated containers for, for example, receiving the blood. And there is no *reiach nichoach* — the sacrifice does not achieve the same quality of spiritual acceptability as one brought at the central shrine. Rashi notes that *reiach nichoach* here refers to the principle established in the chapter of *Beit Shammai*: a sacrifice must be offered with the proper intent among the six purposes for which a sacrifice is brought (*leshem shishah devarim*), and there is no requirement for this mental awareness at a *bamah* because the offering does not achieve the same *reiach nichoach*.

### No Mizbe'ach Division

*Umechetza le-damim* — the *chut ha-sikra*, the red line that divides the *mizbe'ach* into its upper half (for blood applied above the line) and lower half (for blood applied below), does not apply at a *bamah*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, this is another element absent from the *bamah*. *Urechitzat yadayim ve-raglayim* — the washing of the hands and feet before performing the service is also not required at a *bamah*.

### Time & Notar Equal

Despite all of these differences, certain requirements apply equally at both the central shrine and the private *bamah*: *hazeman ve-ha-notar* — the laws of improper intention regarding time (*piggul*) and the laws of *notar*, sacrificial portions that have remained beyond their permitted time. And *ha-tamei* — if the sacrifice or its portions become *tamei*, they are disqualified. These laws are *shavim ba-zeh u-va-zeh* — identical in both contexts. With that, the *mishnayot* of *Masechet Zevachim* are complete.

---

---

# Zevachim 113

## Parah Adumah Location

### Gitta Definition

The daf opens in the final chapter of the tractate, whose *mishnah* — spanning all the *mishnayot* of this last *perek* — is now subject to Gemara analysis. The discussion continues within the framework of *shechutei chutz*. The *mishnah* stated that one who slaughters the *parah adumah* outside its *gitta* — literally, outside its vat or its proper location — is not liable for *shechutei chutz*, because the *parah adumah* is not *ra'uy le'ohel moed*: it is not fit to be brought into the *mikdash*.

The Gemara opens by asking: *mai chutz migitta* — what exactly is meant by "outside its location"? The *parah adumah* can presumably be brought anywhere outside *Yerushalayim*, so what constitutes the wrong place? Resh Lakish answers: *chutz mimakom habaduk lah* — outside a place that has been specifically checked and verified to be free of buried bones and graves, i.e., a place confirmed as definitely *tahor*. If one slaughters it in an area that has not been so verified and may be *tamei*, that is not the proper location for the *parah adumah* — and yet one is still exempt from *shechutei chutz* because the *parah adumah* is not the kind of offering brought in the *mikdash*.

### Eretz Yisrael Tahur

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Resh Lakish directly: *vechol Eretz Yisrael bedukah hi* — is not all of *Eretz Yisrael* presumed to be free of unknown dead bodies? The default assumption is that any area in *Eretz Yisrael* not officially designated as a cemetery requires no special checking. Cemeteries and suspected burial sites were carefully marked, and absent such marking, the land is presumed *tahor*. Therefore, the definition of an improper location for the *parah adumah* cannot hinge on the unchecked-versus-checked distinction, since *me'ikar hadin* all of *Eretz Yisrael* is presumed acceptable.

If so, Rabbi Yochanan must offer an alternative account of what constitutes the wrong place for the *parah adumah*. He does: *kegon sheshachtah lifnim mechomat Yerushalayim* — for example, if one slaughtered it inside the walls of *Yerushalayim*. Once Israel enters the land, *Yerushalayim* defines *machaneh Yisrael*, the camp, and the *parah adumah* must be slaughtered outside the camp. If slaughtered within the walls, it is not in its proper place — yet there is still no liability for *shechutei chutz* because the *parah adumah* does not belong in the *mikdash* to begin with.

### Facing Petach Ohel

One might ask: why not define the improper location more simply as anywhere outside *Yerushalayim* that does not face the entrance of the *beit hamikdash*? The *Torah* explicitly states regarding the *parah adumah* (Bamidbar 19): *unatatem otah el Elazar hakohen vehotzi otah el michutz lamachaneh* — take it outside the camp — *veshachat otah lefanav*, slaughter it before him, *velakach Elazar hakohen midamah be'etzba'o vehizah el nochach pnei Ohel Moed midamah sheva pe'amim* — and Elazar the kohen shall take some of the blood on his finger and sprinkle it toward the entrance of the Tent of Meeting seven times. The sprinkling must face *Ohel Moed*; should not the slaughter as well?

### Shechitah Keneged

This is precisely the subject of the next dispute. Rav Adda bar Ahava rules that if the *parah adumah* was slaughtered not facing the entrance of the *mikdash*, it is invalid — *shechtah shelo keneged hapetach psulah*. The derivation is from the juxtaposition in the verse: *veshachat vehizah* — just as the sprinkling must face the entrance, so too the *shechitah* must face the entrance. Rabbi Yochanan concurs with this *drasha*: *psulah*. Resh Lakish disagrees: *kesherah*. He reads the verse differently — *el michutz lamachaneh veshachat*, bring it outside the camp and slaughter. The requirement to face *Ohel Moed* applies only to the sprinkling of the blood, which is stage two. The *shechitah* itself need not be oriented toward the entrance.

Given this dispute, the Gemara could have argued that an improper location for the *parah adumah* is slaughter outside *Yerushalayim* but not facing the *mikdash*. Why, then, does Rabbi Yochanan choose the more dramatic example of slaughter inside the walls?

### Sreifa Dispute

The related dispute over the burning of the *parah adumah* is also recorded. If the *sreifa* — the burning — takes place not in the location facing the entrance of the *mikdash*, what is its status? Rabbi Yochanan rules *psulah*: invalid. He derives this from another juxtaposition — *vesharaf vehizah* — the burning is linked to the sprinkling, and just as the sprinkling must face *Ohel Moed*, so too the burning. Rabbi Oshaya rules *kesherah*: valid. He reads the relevant verse — *al pirsha yisrof* — as establishing an independent rule: the burning takes place where the animal has separated from life, i.e., where it actually died. One may slaughter it in one place, move with the blood to face the *mikdash* for the sprinkling, and then return to where the body lies — even a considerable distance away and not facing the *mikdash* — to perform the burning. The *sreifa* follows the location of death, not the location of the sprinkling.

### Lifnim Lechumah

Why does Rabbi Yochanan choose to illustrate the improper location with the case of *lifnim mechomat Yerushalayim* — inside the walls — rather than the seemingly more straightforward case of slaughter outside *Yerushalayim* in a direction not facing the *mikdash*? The Gemara explains with the principle of *lo mibaiya ka'amar*: it goes without saying. A location outside *Yerushalayim* that does not face the *mikdash* is obviously not the proper place for the *parah adumah*. That case involves an animal that is already a *parah adumah* — not brought inside the *mikdash* — combined with a location that is both further away and improperly oriented. Of course there is no liability for *shechutei chutz* there; no *hava amina* otherwise exists.

The genuine *chiddush* is the opposite case: slaughter inside *Yerushalayim*, closer to the *mikdash*. One might have supposed that proximity to the *mikdash* renders this a valid location — that only the remote, misdirected case is invalid, but the nearer case might actually qualify. The *mishnah* teaches that this is not so: even slaughter inside *Yerushalayim*, which brings the *parah adumah* closer to the *beit hamikdash*, is an improper location. And yet there remains no liability for *shechutei chutz*, since the *parah adumah* is not fit for the *mikdash* in the first place.

---

## Mabul Debate

### Yarad Lo Yarad

Having explored the halachic dimension of *Eretz Yisrael*'s presumed *tahara*, the Gemara pivots to an extended *aggadic* discussion of the underlying premise. The Gemara asks: *bemai kamifligi* — on what do Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan actually disagree? What is the source of their divergent assumptions about the status of unmarked land in *Eretz Yisrael*?

The Gemara answers: *mar savar yarad mabul l'Eretz Yisrael, u'mar savar lo yarad* — one holds that the flood reached *Eretz Yisrael* and one holds it did not. The relevance is straightforward: wherever the *mabul*'s waters reached, the population perished and their bodies were buried undetected in the mud — unmarked, unknown, and therefore a potential source of *tumah* for anyone passing overhead. If the *mabul* reached *Eretz Yisrael*, then even the land of Israel contains such buried bodies and cannot be presumed *tahor*. If the waters never reached *Eretz Yisrael*, no such mass burial occurred, and the land retains its presumption of *tahara*.

This is a striking Gemara. The Torah states *tachat kol hashamayim* — under all of the heavens — and it seems inconceivable that floodwaters covering the entire world would somehow not have reached *Eretz Yisrael*. *Tosafot* even notes a *Bereishit Rabbah* that appears to treat such a notion as absurd. Nonetheless, the Gemara here entertains it as a genuine halachic position.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds: *u'shneihem mikra echad darshu* — remarkably, both opinions derive from the same verse, reading it in opposite directions.

### Eretz Yisrael Lo Metoharah

The verse in question is from *Yechezkel* (22:24): *ben adam emor lah at eretz lo metoharah hi, lo gushmah beyom zaam* — Son of man, say to her: you are a land that is not pure; you have not been rained upon on the day of wrath. Rabbi Yochanan reads the verse as a rhetorical question addressed to *Eretz Yisrael*: *Eretz Yisrael mi lo metoharah at?* — Land of Israel, are you not a *tahor* land? Of course you are! *Lo gushmah beyom zaam* — the rains of the *mabul* did not fall upon you, and therefore the people of the *mabul* did not die and get buried in your soil. The verse is thus a declaration of *Eretz Yisrael*'s purity, grounded in the fact that the flood did not reach it.

Resh Lakish reads the verse simply, *kipshatei*: it is a plain statement — you are not a pure land. And the second clause is then the rhetorical element: *mi lo yardu alayich geshamim beyom zaam?* — Did the rains not fall upon you as they fell everywhere else on the day of wrath? They did, implying that the dead of the *mabul* are buried in *Eretz Yisrael* just as elsewhere.

One point that the Gemara does not directly address: the concern about bodies buried deep underground presupposes that *tumah* bursts upward through the earth. That principle — that a buried corpse conveys *tumah* to one passing overhead — applies, as *halacha* is generally ruled, only to Jewish bodies, not to non-Jews. Since the bodies in question are those of the generation of the flood, who were presumably not Jewish, this would be a complication. It is possible that this Gemara proceeds according to the minority opinion that non-Jewish bodies also convey *tumah* through the ground. In any case, this difficulty is not resolved here.

### Chatzerot Al Hasela

Resh Lakish now challenges Rabbi Yochanan from a *halachic* source. The Gemara cites: *chatzerot hayu biYerushalayim benuyot al ha-sela, ve-tachtehem chalul, mipnei kever ha-tehom* — there were courtyards in *Yerushalayim* built atop solid rock, with an airspace hollowed beneath the rock, because of concern for a *kever ha-tehom*: a grave of the deep, meaning an unknown and undetected burial somewhere below. The outcropping of rock, with its hollow air space beneath, served as a barrier: even if a body were buried many feet below in the earth, the *tumah* would rise, strike the underside of the rock, and be blocked from penetrating upward to those living or working above.

In these specially constructed courtyards, pregnant women would be brought and would give birth, and their children would be raised there from birth — never exposed to *tumat meit*. These children were then engaged to assist in aspects of the *parah adumah* process, specifically the sprinkling of the water mixed with the *parah*'s ashes upon the *kohen* who would perform the next *parah adumah* rite. When the time came to draw water from a spring for this purpose, the children were seated on broad wooden planks laid across the backs of oxen. As the oxen walked from the courtyard to the spring, any *tumah* rising from below would strike the underside of the plank, which served as an *ohel* — a roof — interposing between the ground and the child above. The children carried stone vessels, which cannot become *tamei*, filled them at the spring, and returned.

The existence of these elaborate precautions seems to contradict Rabbi Yochanan's position: if *Eretz Yisrael* is presumed *tahor* with no concern for buried bodies, why construct all this? The Gemara responds on Rabbi Yochanan's behalf: *ma'ala asu be-para* — these were extra-stringent measures adopted specifically for the *parah adumah*, due to the broader controversy involving the *Tzadokim*. They are not technically required *me'ikar hadin*. Resh Lakish, however, could counter that such extraordinary measures only make sense if there is some underlying concern — one does not go to such lengths if the worry is entirely without basis. The Gemara, however, resolves it as a simple *chumra* and moves on.

### Atzamot Bechazra

Rabbi Yochanan now challenges Resh Lakish from the opposite direction. A *Tosefta* records: *pa'am achat matzu atzamot be-lishkat deir ha-etzim* — on one occasion, human bones were found in the chamber of the wood storage in the *beit hamikdash*. In response, *bikshu ligzor tumah al Yerushalayim* — the authorities sought to declare all of *Yerushalayim tamei* rabbinically. The discovery of bones even within the precincts of the *beit hamikdash* — in a place one would have assumed most pure — seemed to warrant the gravest concern.

### Ayin Metei Mabul

Rabbi Yehoshua rose and objected: *lo busha vechalima lanu shenigzar tumah al ir avoteinu* — would it not be a shame and embarrassment to decree *tumah* upon the holy city of our ancestors? He then posed the rhetorical challenge: *ayei metei mabul, ayei metei Nevuchadnezzar?* — Where are the dead of the *mabul*? Where are the dead of Nevuchadnezzar? The implication being: people have died in *Yerushalayim* before — many people — and yet the city remains *tahor*. Whatever arrangements were necessary to ensure that *Yerushalayim* remain pure have always been made. We need not now suddenly declare it *tamei*.

### Havu U'Pinnu

Rabbi Yochanan reads this statement as a proof to his position: from the fact that Rabbi Yehoshua says "where are the dead of the *mabul*," is he not implying that they were never here — that the *mabul* never reached *Eretz Yisrael* and no one died here from it?

The Gemara immediately objects: *uleta'meich, harugei Nevuchadnezzar hacha nami delo havu?* — By that logic, you would have to say the victims of Nevuchadnezzar also never died in *Yerushalayim* — but Nevuchadnezzar unquestionably slaughtered Jews there. The Gemara therefore interprets Rabbi Yehoshua's statement differently: *ela havu upinnu, hacha nami havu upinnu* — both the dead of Nevuchadnezzar and the dead of the *mabul* died in *Yerushalayim*, but they were subsequently removed. The city was actively kept *tahor* through the removal of bodies.

This reading, however, seems to support Resh Lakish rather than Rabbi Yochanan — it concedes that people did die in *Yerushalayim* from the *mabul*. The Gemara presses: if, on Resh Lakish's view, bodies were cleaned out of *Yerushalayim*, why does Resh Lakish maintain a concern about *tumah* across *Eretz Yisrael*? The Gemara resolves this: *de'ihi de'ifni mi'Yerushalayim, mikol Eretz Yisrael lo ifni* — Rabbi Yehoshua was speaking only about *Yerushalayim* specifically, which was indeed cleared. But the rest of *Eretz Yisrael* was not subjected to the same comprehensive removal. *Yerushalayim* is *tahor*, but *Eretz Yisrael* outside *Yerushalayim* remains a concern on Resh Lakish's view. The Gemara then notes an alternative tradition (*ika de'amri*) in which the source is brought by Resh Lakish as a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan rather than the reverse — the logical reading of Rabbi Yehoshua's statement being that *Yerushalayim* was cleared but not all of Israel.

The Gemara ultimately deflects both readings, noting: *midei irya, ha kide'isa veha kide'isa* — perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua meant two different points simultaneously. The dead of the *mabul* never came to *Yerushalayim* at all (Rabbi Yochanan's position), and separately, the dead of Nevuchadnezzar died here but were removed (an independently valid point). This blended reading is admittedly strained, as the two clauses appear to be a single unified statement — but the Gemara records it. In any case, no decisive proof can be extracted from Rabbi Yehoshua's statement for either side of the dispute about whether the *mabul* reached *Eretz Yisrael*. And since the *parah adumah* must be taken outside *Yerushalayim* regardless, the question of the status of the rest of *Eretz Yisrael* is what remains practically at stake.

### Mikol Asher Bacharava

The Gemara now examines whether the *pesukim* of the *mabul* itself can resolve the dispute. The verse states: *mikol asher becharava meisu* — everything on dry land died. Resh Lakish observes: *bishlama ledidi* — according to me, who holds that the *mabul* reached *Eretz Yisrael*, this verse reads naturally. *Eretz Yisrael* is dry land; the waters came; everyone died. That is the straightforward reading of *pesukim*. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds the *mabul* did not reach *Eretz Yisrael* — *amai meisu?* — why does the verse say that everything on dry land died? If the people of *Eretz Yisrael* were not flooded, why did they perish?

### Hevla Killing

Rabbi Yochanan's answer is remarkable: *mishum hevla* — they died from the heat. Even though the waters of the *mabul* did not physically reach *Eretz Yisrael*, the catastrophic atmospheric conditions — the sulfurous heat and vapor generated by the worldwide flood — killed everyone in *Eretz Yisrael* as well. All who lived outside the ark perished, including those in *Eretz Yisrael*, but by heat rather than by water.

This answer creates an apparent difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan's entire thesis. His reason *Eretz Yisrael* is presumed *tahor* is that the *mabul* did not bury bodies in the mud there. But if everyone in *Eretz Yisrael* died nonetheless — from the *hevla* — then there are bodies buried in *Eretz Yisrael*. Why is it *tahor*? *Rashi* explains: those who died from the heat died on dry land, with their bodies remaining visible and accessible. *Noach* and his descendants could subsequently find them, bury them properly in marked graves, and the locations would be known. By contrast, those who perished in the flood itself were buried deep in the mud — covered by water, submerged, unmarked — making their graves permanently unknown. It is specifically those flood-buried bodies that create the *tumah* concern. Since *Eretz Yisrael* had no such flood, its bodies were properly buried and marked; hence the land remains *tahor*.

This approach to the verse — that *Eretz Yisrael* was spared the waters but not the heat — is a difficult reading, to say the least. The Gemara links Rabbi Yochanan's position to the teaching of Rav Chisda: *anshei dor hamabul beroschin kilkelu uveroschin nidonu* — the generation of the flood sinned through heated passion and were punished with boiling hot water. The word *vayashoku* (the waters abated) is read alongside *vachamas hamelech shachacha* (the king's wrath abated) to indicate that the waters of the *mabul* were boiling hot — and this intense heat would have killed even those not directly struck by the waters.

The Gemara also records the alternative formulation (*ika de'amri*) in which this same verse is cited by Rabbi Yochanan as a challenge to Resh Lakish. According to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds the *mabul* did not reach *Eretz Yisrael*, the verse *mikol asher becharava meisu* makes perfect sense: the people in *Eretz Yisrael* were on actual dry land — *mishum hachi havei charava* — and they died there. According to Resh Lakish, who holds the *mabul* did reach *Eretz Yisrael*, the Gemara asks: what does *charava* even mean? There was no dry land — it was all submerged. The Gemara answers simply: *charava shehaysa me'ikara* — it means what was formerly dry land before the flood began. The verse is then cited for its further implication: *lo nigzera gezeira al hadagim* — no decree of death was imposed on the fish. The sea creatures were exempt. The verse's emphasis on "dry land" demarcates who perished and who did not.

### Reima Survival

The Gemara now raises a different question rooted in the *mabul* debate: *bishlama leman de'amar lo yarad mabul le'Eretz Yisrael, hainu d'kam reima hasam* — according to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds the *mabul* did not reach *Eretz Yisrael*, one can explain how the *reima* survived: it walked to *Eretz Yisrael*, where the waters did not come, and the *hevla* perhaps did not kill it. But *ela l'man de'amar yarad mabul* — according to Resh Lakish, who holds that the flood did reach *Eretz Yisrael* — *reima heichi kam?* — where could the *reima* have gone, and how did it survive? The *reima* is an animal of such extraordinary size that it clearly could not have fit inside the ark.

Before exploring the answer, the Gemara pauses to establish just how large this creature was. Rabba bar bar Chana reported: *l'didi chazi li orzila d'reima bas yoma* — I personally saw a newborn *reima*, one day old, and *havi k'tur tavor* — it was the size of Mount Tabor. How large is Mount Tabor? *Arba'in parsi* — forty parsangs, approximately 160 kilometers. The neck alone was three parsangs (twelve kilometers) in length. The area where it would lay its head was a parsang and a half — six kilometers. And, the Gemara adds, when it defecated, its refuse blocked the Jordan River. This is manifestly a mythic creature, yet the Gemara treats its survival of the *mabul* as a genuine question.

Rabbi Yannai's answer for Resh Lakish's position: *guriot hichnisu b'teiva* — they brought baby *reimas* into the ark. To this Rabba bar bar Chana's description responds: even a one-day-old *reima* is the size of Mount Tabor — no baby *reima* could have fit in the ark either.

Rabbi Yochanan then offers: *rosho hichnisu l'teiva* — its head was inserted into the ark. The *reima* perhaps walked through the flood or was borne on the water's surface, and only its head was kept inside the ark so it could breathe. But the Gemara objects: the area where the *reima* rests its head is a parsang and a half across — how could its head fit in the ark? The Gemara revises: *ella rosh chotamo hichnisu l'teiva* — the tip of its nose was inserted into the ark, just enough to allow it to breathe, while its body floated in the water below.

A further difficulty: *v'ha kasagya teiva* — the ark was tossing up and down on the waters. The *reima*'s nose would have slipped out, and it would have drowned. Resh Lakish resolves this: *karnav kishru b'teiva* — its horns were tied to the ark, so the *reima* rose and fell with the ark and could maintain its connection to breathe.

The Gemara then returns to Rav Chisda's teaching that the waters of the *mabul* were boiling hot. If so, how could the *reima* have survived immersion in boiling water? The Gemara asks a pointed question: *u'l'ta'ameich* — if you worry about the boiling water, consider also that the ark itself would have been destroyed: the pitch sealing the ark's planks would have melted. And how did *Og Melech Habashan* survive — he reportedly clung to the outside of the ark? The resolution offered is *nes na'aseh lahem, shenitztanenu betzidei hateiva* — a miracle occurred: the water immediately surrounding the ark cooled. It was within this protected sphere that Og clung, the pitch held, and the *reima*'s head — or nose — was kept viable.

*Tosafot* makes a practically important observation in this context. Noting that *reima* is identified by some with the *re'em* of the *pesukim* (as in *karnei re'em karnav*), and that *Targum Onkelos* on *Devarim* renders *dishon* as *reima*, *Tosafot* emphasizes that the *reima* is unquestionably a *chaya* — a wild animal — and not a *beheima*, a domesticated animal. This matters halachically: the *cheilev* (forbidden fat) of a *chaya* is permitted, while that of a *beheima* is forbidden. *Tosafot* warns that one should not identify the *reima* with the buffalo (*bafalos*) found in the author's time. Buffaloes are a *beheima* — their *cheilev* is forbidden. Several proofs: buffaloes are small enough to have fit easily in the ark, and thus do not exhibit the extraordinary dimensions associated with the *reima*; furthermore, and decisively for purposes of the *chaya/beheima* distinction, buffaloes can be domesticated and used for labor — they can pull wagons and plow fields. The *re'em*, by contrast, is not domesticatable. A *chaya*, in the relevant halachic sense, is not merely an animal that happens to be wild but one that is in principle incapable of domestication.

### Metzan Babylonia

The Gemara concludes the *mabul* discussion with a question about Resh Lakish's own position. Since Resh Lakish holds the *mabul* reached *Eretz Yisrael*, why is he concerned about bodies buried there? The bodies of the flood's victims were not simply left in place: Resh Lakish himself taught that *Bavel* is called *Metzula* (swamp or depths) because *kol metei mabul nitztelelu l'sham* — all the dead of the *mabul* were swept there. *Bavel* was the lowest-lying land, and the bodies were carried there by the receding waters. Similarly, *Bavel* is called *Shinar* because *kol metei mabul ninaru l'sham* — all the dead were tumbled there. If the bodies were transported to *Bavel*, why should *Eretz Yisrael* remain suspect?

The Gemara responds: *ee efshar delo idbeku* — it is impossible that none were left behind. Even if the great mass of bodies was swept to *Bavel*, some surely remained stuck in the mud in *Eretz Yisrael*.

The Gemara appends further aggadic material on *Bavel*'s names. Rabbi Abbahu explains that *Shinar* alludes to *shemenaeret ashireha* — it empties its wealthy people, meaning sustained wealth does not endure there for more than three generations. And finally, Rabbi Ami states: *kol haochel me'afara shel Bavel, ke'ilu ochel besar avotav* — whoever eats of the soil of *Bavel* is as though eating the flesh of his ancestors, since all the bodies of the *mabul* decomposed there and mingled with the earth. Some say it is as though eating *shekatzim uremasim* — repugnant creatures — since those too perished and decomposed into the soil of *Bavel*. *Rashi* ties both formulations to the totality of death in the *mabul*.

---

## Se'ir Hamishtaleach

### Azazel Exclusion

With the aggadic discussion concluded, the Gemara returns to the *mishnah*. Another case in which one is exempt from *shechutei chutz* is the *se'ir hamishtaleach* — the scapegoat sent off to *Azazel* on *Yom Kippur* — because it is not brought as an offering to the *Ohel Moed*.

### Korban L'Hashem
