The Gemara raises a challenge from a *midrash halacha*. The verse underlying *shechutei chutz* speaks of one who slaughters outside the *beit hamikdash* and fails to bring it as *lehakriv korban l'Hashem* — a *korban* to God. The *midrash halacha* raises the question: perhaps the word *korban* is broad enough to include even *kodshei bedek habayit* — animals sanctified not as sacrifices on the altar but as contributions to the Temple treasury — since the word *korban* can refer to gifts generally, as evidenced by the verse *vanakreiv et korban Hashem* referring to the gold and valuables brought from the spoils of Midian.

The *midrash halacha* rejects this expansion: *ve'el petach Ohel Moed lo hevi'o* — the verse adds that the animal was not brought to the *Ohel Moed*. This limits liability to animals that are *ra'uy lavo be'Ohel Moed* — fit to be brought into the Tent of Meeting. *Kodshei bedek habayit* are therefore excluded: an animal sanctified to the Temple treasury is never brought into the *Ohel Moed* as a sacrifice, and thus falls outside the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*.

### Kodem Achar Goral

The *midrash halacha* then asks: having excluded *kodshei bedek habayit* on the ground that they are not fit for *Ohel Moed*, should one also exclude the *se'ir hamishtaleach*? The question is pointed: the *se'ir hamishtaleach* does begin its service in the *Ohel Moed* — both goats of *Yom Kippur* are brought to the entrance for the drawing of lots. So perhaps it is *ra'uy lavo b'Ohel Moed* and should be included in the prohibition.

The *midrash halacha* counters: *Talmud lomar l'Hashem* — the verse says the slaughter is to be a *korban l'Hashem*, a sacrifice to God. The *se'ir hamishtaleach* is not dedicated to God — it is sent *le'Azazel*. It is therefore excluded regardless of its connection to *Ohel Moed*.

This creates a tension with the *mishnah*, which says the *se'ir hamishtaleach* is excluded because it is not fit for *Ohel Moed*. But the *midrash halacha* implies the opposite — that it is fit for *Ohel Moed* (hence the need for the *l'Hashem* exclusion). The Gemara resolves this: *lo kashya, kan kodem hagoral, kan achar hagoral* — there is no contradiction. Before the lots are drawn, both goats are fit for *Ohel Moed* (and either could potentially be designated for any number of purposes), so the only basis for excluding the *se'ir hamishtaleach* from *shechutei chutz* liability is the *l'Hashem* verse. After the lots are drawn, the goat designated for *Azazel* is no longer fit for *Ohel Moed*, so it is excluded on that basis as well.

The Gemara refines this further: even after the lots, the *vidui* — the confession — over the *se'ir hamishtaleach* has not yet been performed, and the goat still has a connection to *Ohel Moed*. Rav Mani therefore corrects the dividing line: *kan kodem vidui, kan achar vidui* — it is the performance of the *vidui* that marks the transition. Until the *vidui*, the *se'ir hamishtaleach* retains a connection to *Ohel Moed*; only the *l'Hashem* exclusion applies. After the *vidui*, the goat is no longer fit for *Ohel Moed* either, and both exclusions apply simultaneously.

This connects to a discussion in *Yoma*: if one were to slaughter both goats outside the *beit hamikdash* before the lots are drawn, one would be liable for *shechutei chutz*. Before the lots, neither goat has been designated for *Azazel*, and both could theoretically be used for some other *korban*. Once the lots are drawn, the goat designated for God is *ra'uy l'ohel moed* and dedicated *l'Hashem*; the goat designated for *Azazel* is not *l'Hashem* and is thus exempt under the *midrash halacha*. After the *vidui*, the goat designated for *Azazel* is additionally no longer *ra'uy* for *Ohel Moed*.

### Rovei'a V'nirba

The *mishnah* also exempts an animal that engaged in or was subjected to bestiality (*rovei'a ve'nirba*) from *shechutei chutz* liability. Such an animal is disqualified from the altar — it is no longer *ra'uy* for *petach Ohel Moed* — and is thus excluded from liability. The Gemara's concern here is with the specific verse cited to exclude these animals: *lifnei mishkan Hashem*. Why is this additional phrase needed? Why not simply rely on the principle that they are not fit for *Ohel Moed*?

### Lifnei Mishkan

The Gemara explains: *bishlama rovei'a v'nirba maskachat lah de'akdishinhu me'ikara ve'hadar rav'o* — one can readily construct a scenario in which, at some earlier stage, such an animal was fit for *Ohel Moed*. One sanctified the animal as a *korban*, rendering it fit for *Ohel Moed*, and subsequently an act of bestiality occurred. At that earlier moment of sanctification, the animal was fit; one might therefore reason that the liability of *shechutei chutz* attaches at the point of sanctification and is not undone by the later disqualification. The verse *lifnei mishkan Hashem* is therefore needed to teach that what matters is the animal's current fitness, not its prior status: since it is now disqualified, there is no *shechutei chutz* liability, regardless of its history.

### Muktzeh V'ne'evad

The same question arises for *muktzeh* (set aside for idolatry) and *ne'evad* (worshipped as an idol). Here the Gemara notes a crucial limiting principle: *ein adam oser davar she'eino shelo* — one cannot impose a prohibition on something that is not his own. Once an animal has been sanctified as a *korban*, it is no longer the owner's property; he cannot then worship it and thereby impose the prohibition of *ne'evad* upon it. The only viable scenario of *muktzeh* or *ne'evad* that actually prohibits the animal is when the idolatry occurred before sanctification, meaning the animal was never *ra'uy* for *Ohel Moed* to begin with. If so, these cases seem to need no special verse — they are already excluded simply as not fit for *Ohel Moed*.

### Kodshim Kalim Mamon

The Gemara answers: the extra verse is required for the case of *kodshim kalim*, according to Rabbi Yosi HaGelili. Rabbi Yosi HaGelili holds that *kodshim kalim mamon be'alim hu* — *kodshim kalim* such as a *shelamim* remain, in a meaningful sense, the owner's property. Since the owner derives benefit from the meat and retains certain rights over the offering, Rabbi Yosi HaGelili considers the animal to still belong to him. Consequently, even after sanctification, if the owner worships the *shelamim* as an idol, he has the legal capacity to make it forbidden through that act of idolatry, since it remains "his." This creates a scenario where the animal was *ra'uy l'ohel moed* — it was a valid *korban shelamim* — and subsequently became disqualified through *ne'evad*. The verse *lifnei mishkan Hashem* is therefore needed to exclude such a case from *shechutei chutz* liability.

This is supported by the *baraita*: *u'maal maal b'Hashem* — regarding the violation of illicitly denying one's debt to a fellow Jew under oath — Rabbi Yosi HaGelili derives from the word *b'Hashem* that even *kodshim kalim* belong to the owner, such that stealing a friend's *shelamim* and denying it under oath constitutes theft and is actionable. The animal is sanctified, yet it is still considered the friend's property.

### Vladot Kodshim

The *mishnah* also lists *etnan* (a gift given to a prostitute), *mechir* (exchange for a dog), *kilayim* (a hybrid animal), and *yotzei dofen* (an animal born by Caesarean section) as cases exempt from *shechutei chutz*. The Gemara asks: how can any of these cases involve an animal that was previously fit for *Ohel Moed*? The disqualifications of *kilayim* and *yotzei dofen* are present from birth — an animal born as a hybrid or born through Caesarean section has those disqualifications from the moment of birth. When was such an animal ever *ra'uy l'ohel moed*?

The Gemara answers: *b'vladot kodshim, v'kasavar vladot kodshim behavayatan hein kedoshim* — the cases involve offspring of sanctified animals, according to the opinion that animals born from sanctified mothers acquire their own sanctity only at the moment of birth, not while still in the womb. Under this view, a fetus in the womb of a sanctified animal is not yet independently sanctified. It is, however, already *ra'uy l'ohel moed* in a meaningful sense — it will be brought along with its mother, participating in the mother's sacrifice — even though it has not yet acquired its own *kedusha*. Because it lacks independent *kedusha*, the owner retains sufficient legal standing to affect it: he can give it (by deed or transaction) as *etnan* to a prostitute, exchange it for a dog, and a hybrid fetus would carry that status from conception. The fetus is simultaneously *ra'uy l'ohel moed* (in potentia, through the mother) and subject to all these disqualifications — because the absence of independent *kedusha* means the owner can still impose these prohibitions.

### Yotzei Dofen Cases

When the animal is subsequently born, it acquires its own *kedusha* at the moment of birth. Now it is independently sanctified — but it is also now manifestly *etnan*, *mechir*, *kilayim*, or *yotzei dofen*, and thus disqualified for the altar. We thus have a case that was at one stage *ra'uy l'ohel moed* — when it was in the womb — and is now disqualified. The verse *lifnei mishkan Hashem* is required to teach that despite the earlier period of fitness, the current disqualification removes any liability for *shechutei chutz*.

The case of *yotzei dofen* follows naturally: the fetus is *ra'uy l'ohel moed* while in the womb, and it only becomes a *yotzei dofen* upon being born through Caesarean section. At the moment of birth, it acquires its own *kedusha* and simultaneously its disqualification. Thus the verse is needed to clarify that even this case — where the transition from *ra'uy* to *pasul* is instantaneous — nonetheless removes *shechutei chutz* liability.

---

---

# Zevachim 114

## Shechutei Chutz Overview

### Opening & Context

Daf 114 opens the final *perek* of the tractate, which continues the discussion of *shechutei chutz* — the prohibition of slaughtering outside the designated sacred space — while expanding into the question of *bamot*, the private altars that were permissible or forbidden at different stages of Jewish history. The immediate concern, however, is narrower: which categories of animal, when slaughtered outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, result in a transgression, and which do not.

### Parah & Seir Exceptions

The *perek* had already established that the *Parah Adumah* and the *Seir Hamishtaleach* are exceptions to the general rule of *shechutei chutz*. Since neither animal is designated for the *petach ohel moed* — their proper place is outside the *Beit HaMikdash* by design — slaughtering them elsewhere does not constitute *chutz*, and one is therefore *patur*. Tosafot notes, however, that if the *Seir Hamishtaleach* is slaughtered before the lottery has been drawn — before the lots determine which goat goes *la-Shem* and which goes to be sent away — one would in fact be *chayav*, because at that stage the animal has not yet been designated and could just as easily have become the goat offered inside.

### Mishna Invalidities

The *mishna* proceeds to discuss other categories of invalidity: animals used in the context of bestiality, animals used in idolatrous worship, and *baalei mumin* — animals with blemishes. In all these cases one is *patur* for slaughtering them outside. But Rabbi Shimon introduces a crucial distinction: if the animal is currently unfit but has the potential to become fit at a later time, one does not incur *karet* — the standard punishment for *shechutei chutz* — but one does transgress a negative prohibition. The *rabanan* disagree, maintaining that if the animal cannot be brought now, there is no transgression at all; for them, the absence of *karet* and the absence of any *lav* are linked.

---

## Rabbi Shimon & Mechusar…

### Shimon's Principle

Rabbi Shimon's position establishes a middle ground: something that cannot be offered today but will be capable of being offered in the future occupies an intermediate halachic space. It is close enough to the status of a valid *korban* to generate a *lav*, yet not sufficiently fit at the present moment to warrant *karet*.

### Mechusar Zman Examples

The *mishna* enumerates several examples of *mechusar zman* — offerings that lack the proper time. A passing blemish falls into this category: today the animal is *pasul*, but the blemish may heal. The prohibition of *oto v'et beno* provides another case: if the animal's mother or offspring was slaughtered today, this animal cannot be slaughtered today, though tomorrow it will be fully permitted. Similarly, a bird that is not yet old enough, or any animal that has not yet reached its eighth day, is *mechusar zman* — its time has simply not yet arrived.

A distinct subcategory arises when the problem lies not with the animal but with the owner: a *zav*, a *zavah*, or a *yoledet* who has not yet completed the days required before bringing their obligatory *korbanot* renders those sacrifices *mechusar zman be-baalim*, lacking the proper time because of the owner's status rather than the animal's.

### Three Cases Analysis

The *gemara* asks why the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *rabanan* must be stated explicitly in all three cases — *baalei mumin*, *oto v'et beno*, and the case of young birds. The answer is that each case carries a distinct reason why one might have thought the ruling would differ from the others.

Had the *mishna* stated only the case of *baalei mumin*, one might have reasoned that the *rabanan* rule *patur* specifically because the blemished animal is *me'isay* — repugnant — and therefore more thoroughly rejected from sacred service, even if the rejection is transitory. In that case, one might have assumed that for birds that are merely too young, with nothing repugnant about them, the *rabanan* would concede to Rabbi Shimon and at least acknowledge a *lav*.

Conversely, had the *mishna* stated only the case of young birds, one might have concluded that the *rabanan* rule *patur* because those birds were never fit in the first place and were thus entirely pushed away — *lo chazi ve-idchi*. But *baalei mumin*, which were once fit and only later became disqualified, might present a different picture. There is an argument that something *chazi ve-idchi* — fit and then rejected — is considered more thoroughly displaced than something that was never fit, which would be a reason for the *rabanan* to say *patur* even by Rabbi Shimon's logic. Or alternatively, one might reason in the opposite direction: since *baalei mumin* were once valid, they retain a stronger connection to *kedushah*, and Rabbi Shimon might agree to the *rabanan* that the repugnance of a blemish overrides that residual fitness.

Finally, had the *mishna* stated only these two cases, one might have concluded that the *rabanan* rule *patur* exclusively when the deficiency is intrinsic to the animal — whether due to its physical state or its developmental stage. But the case of *oto v'et beno* is different: the animal itself is entirely sound; the problem originates from something external, namely that its mother or offspring was slaughtered today. One might therefore have thought the *rabanan* concede to Rabbi Shimon in this case, since the animal's own fitness is unimpeachable. The *gemara* therefore concludes *tzrichi* — all three cases are necessary — because no matter the nature or degree of the disqualification, the *rabanan* hold that the inability to bring the offering today is decisive, while Rabbi Shimon maintains that future fitness generates a *lav* in every instance.

---

## Lo Ta'asun Verse Source

### Devarim 12:8 Citation

The *gemara* now turns to the question of Rabbi Shimon's textual basis. Rabbi Ilai citing Reish Lakish identifies the source in Devarim 12:8: *lo ta'asun ke-chol asher anachnu osim po ha-yom ish kol ha-yashar be-einav* — "Do not do as we are doing here today, each man whatever is right in his eyes."

### Lo Ta'asun Reading

The plain sense of the verse is that in the wilderness, *Bnei Yisrael* were offering *korbanot* in various locations, and Moshe warns them that upon entering the land there will be a central, designated place. The difficulty, of course, is that during the period of the *mishkan* in the desert there already was a single central location, and private offerings elsewhere were forbidden. How then does the verse imply that what they were doing at that time was bringing offerings *everywhere*?

The *gemara* resolves this by reading the verse as follows: Moshe tells the Jewish people that upon entering the land, during periods when private *bamot* are permitted (*heter bamot*), only *nedavot* — voluntary offerings such as *nedarim* and *nedavot* like *olot* and *shelamim* — may be brought on a *bamah*. *Chovot* — obligatory sacrifices like *chatas* and *asham* — may not. The phrase *ish kol ha-yashar be-einav* refers specifically to voluntary offerings brought according to one's own judgment and desire. The verse thus prohibits bringing obligatory sacrifices on a private *bamah*, even during periods when *bamot* are generally permissible.

### Nedavot vs Chovot

This reading gives rise to the foundational *halacha* that only *nedarim* and *nedavot* are *karev ba-bamah* — eligible to be brought on a *bamah* — while *chovot* are not. When there is a central *mishkan* or *Beit HaMikdash*, both *nedavot* and *chovot* are brought there. During *heter bamot*, one may bring *nedavot* on a private *bamah*, but *chovot* must wait until a central location is established.

### Gilgal & Shilo Analysis

How does this connect to Rabbi Shimon's principle of *mechusar zman*? The *gemara* draws the following analogy: Gilgal — the first settlement in the Land of Israel where a large communal *bamah* existed — is considered *mechusar zman* relative to Shilo. That is, during the period of Gilgal, obligatory *korbanot* such as *chatas* and *asham* could not yet be brought because the time of Shilo — the era of the central *mishkan* — had not yet arrived.

This is an admittedly unusual application of the concept of *mechusar zman*. One might more naturally describe the inability to bring *chovot* at Gilgal as a restriction arising from the laws of *heter bamot* rather than as a temporal deficiency in the *korban* itself. The *gemara* is effectively translating a restriction about the *categories* of sacrifice permissible during *heter bamot* into the language of *mechusar zman*: the *chatas* during the period of Gilgal is not yet the right time. From this, Rabbi Shimon derives that *mechusar zman* creates a *lav* even when the offering is not presently fit — since the verse *lo ta'asun* prohibits bringing obligatory *korbanot* even at Gilgal, where one might have thought the large communal *bamah* sufficed.

---

## Aseh vs Lo Ta'aseh Debate

### Yirmya's Objection

Rabbi Yirmya raises a pointed objection: if *lo ta'asun* constitutes a genuine *lo ta'aseh*, then anyone who violates it should receive *malkot* — lashes. This follows from the standard rule that transgressing a negative prohibition is punishable by lashes.

### Zeira's Resolution

Rabbi Zeira responds that the verse itself transforms the prohibition into an *aseh* only — *ha-katuv nitko la-asei*. It is not merely an *aseh nitak la-lo ta'aseh* in the conventional sense (where a negative prohibition is linked to a positive commandment that repairs the violation), but rather the verse converts the prohibition entirely into a positive commandment, removing the status of a *lo ta'aseh* altogether.

### Chullin Parallel

This principle has a parallel in *Chullin*. When one slaughters a *mechusar zman* animal inside the *Beit HaMikdash* — for example, offering an animal whose mother was slaughtered that same day — one might have thought that in addition to the prohibition of *oto v'et beno*, one also transgresses the prohibition of slaughtering a *pasul korban* in the *Beit HaMikdash* (*lo yiratzu*). The *gemara* in *Chullin* establishes, however, that the prohibition against slaughtering *mechusar zman* in the *Beit HaMikdash* is only an *aseh*, not a *lo ta'aseh*, and therefore one does not receive lashes for it. This is the principle that Rabbi Zeira invokes: *mechusar zman* is treated as an *aseh* violation, not a full *lo ta'aseh*.

### Shimon's Lashes

For Rabbi Shimon, who derives from *lo ta'asun* that there is a genuine *lo ta'aseh* associated with *mechusar zman*, the calculus is different. According to him, one who brings an obligatory *korban* at Gilgal — where bringing *chovot* is the equivalent of *mechusar zman* — would in fact receive *malkot*, since for Rabbi Shimon the prohibition retains its character as a *lo ta'aseh*.

### Gilgal as Outside

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a different resolution to the apparent contradiction. He proposes that the rule exempting *mechusar zman* from *malkot* — treating it only as an *aseh* — applies specifically when the *shechita* takes place *bifnim*, inside the *azarah* of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The inner sanctum of the *Mikdash* has a unique status that transforms the violation into a lesser *aseh* category. Gilgal, however, is not the inner sanctum. In relation to Shilo, Gilgal is considered *chutz* — outside. Therefore, bringing *mechusar zman* at Gilgal does not benefit from the rule that applies inside the *Mikdash*, and the violation retains its full character as a *lo ta'aseh* subject to *malkot*.

This leads to a broader conceptual picture, which the *gemara* works through with some difficulty. On one hand, there is the *halacha* from *Chullin* that *mechusar zman* inside the *Beit HaMikdash* is only an *aseh*. On the other hand, Rabbi Shimon's derivation from *lo ta'asun* treats bringing *chovot* at a *bamah* — or at Gilgal — as a *lo ta'aseh* with *malkot*. The resolution is either that Rabbi Shimon simply disagrees with the rule in *Chullin* and maintains it is a *lo ta'aseh* even inside the *Mikdash*, or — following Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak — that the *aseh*-only rule is limited to actions performed inside the *azarah*, and Gilgal, being treated as *chutz* relative to Shilo, falls outside that domain.

---

## Pesach Before Time Source

### Pesach Proof

Rava offers an alternative and more direct source for Rabbi Shimon's principle. A *baraita* records Rabbi Shimon himself deriving from the laws of *korban Pesach* that *mechusar zman* during a period of *issur bamot* generates a *lav*.

### Lo Tuchal Pesach

The verse in Devarim 16 states: *lo tuchal lizbo'ach et ha-Pesach be-achad she'arecha* — "You may not slaughter the Pesach offering in any of your gates." This is a centralization mandate: the *korban Pesach* must be brought at the designated national location. Rabbi Shimon asks: from where do we know that slaughtering a *korban Pesach* on a private *bamah* during a period of *issur bamot* constitutes a *lo ta'aseh*? The answer is from this verse.

### Pesach Timing Question

One might immediately object: why is a special verse necessary? At a time of *issur bamot*, anyone who slaughters a *korban* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* is already *chayav karet* for the standard violation of *shechutei chutz*. The prohibition of bringing a *korban Pesach* on a private *bamah* should be self-evident.

The *gemara* resolves this by clarifying the precise scenario. If we are speaking about slaughtering the *korban Pesach* after *chatzot* — after midday on the fourteenth of Nisan, when its time has properly arrived — then indeed one would be *chayav karet* for the classic *shechutei chutz*, and no special verse is needed. The special derivation must therefore address the case before *chatzot*, when the *korban Pesach* is still *mechusar zman* — its proper time has not yet arrived. In that scenario, the *rabanan* would say one is *patur* entirely, since the offering cannot yet be brought, while Rabbi Shimon argues that the verse *lo tuchal lizbo'ach et ha-Pesach* teaches that even then one transgresses a *lav*.

### Before Chatzot Scenario

The *gemara* entertains a counter-reading: perhaps the case is indeed after *chatzot*, but the verse operates in a context of *heter bamot* rather than *issur bamot*. Under this reading, *lo tuchal lizbo'ach et ha-Pesach* would be establishing that even during a period when *bamot* are generally permissible, a *korban Pesach* — being an obligatory sacrifice — may not be brought on a private *bamah*. This is then the verse from which one learns that bringing a *chovah* during *heter bamot* is prohibited.

### Pesach Always Forbidden

The *gemara* resolves the ambiguity in the *baraita* by noting that the two readings are not necessarily in conflict. The *korban Pesach* occupies a peculiar position: it has certain characteristics of a *korban yachid* yet is broadly obligatory. During a period of *heter bamot*, it remains forbidden to bring the *korban Pesach* on a private *bamah* precisely because it is a *chovah*. The verse *lo tuchal lizbo'ach et ha-Pesach be-achad she'arecha* functions as the textual anchor establishing this: the prohibition applies when *kol Yisrael nichnasim b'sha'ar echad* — when all of Israel enters through one gate, meaning when a central location exists — and in that context, the *Pesach* must be brought only at that center.

The first, simpler reading of the *baraita* — that it is addressing a case of *issur bamot* with the *korban Pesach* brought before *chatzot* — remains the most natural reading and provides Rabbi Shimon with the clearest and most direct textual basis for his principle. From this case, where there is no *karet* because the time has not fully arrived yet there remains a *lav*, Rabbi Shimon derives the general rule: during *issur bamot*, bringing something *mechusar zman* still carries a *lo ta'aseh*, even absent the full penalty of *karet*.

---

## Mechusar Zman Be'Bealim

### Owner Status Examples

The *mishna* now turns to cases where the *mechusar zman* arises not from a deficiency in the animal but from the status of the owner. A *zav*, a *zavah*, and a *yoledet* — individuals who have experienced a form of *tumah* requiring a process of purification and waiting — are obligated to bring specific *korbanot* once their period of purification is complete. Before that time, their *korbanot* are *mechusar zman be-baalim*: the animal may be entirely fit, but the owners have not yet reached the stage at which they may bring the offering.

### Yoledet's Sacrifices

An important distinction applies within this category. If a *yoledet*, before she has completed her post-partum period, slaughters her *olah* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, the one who did so is *chayav*: the *olah* is *ra'uy le-fesach ohel moed* because an *olah* is a category of offering that any person may bring at any time, and therefore this animal — even brought before the *yoledet's* own obligated time — could have been brought inside legitimately. Her *chatas*, however, is different. A *chatas* functions only within the parameters of its specific obligation: before the *yoledet* reaches the point of her obligation, this particular *chatas* has no path into the *Beit HaMikdash*, and it is therefore not *ra'uy le-fesach ohel moed*. Whoever slaughters it outside is *patur*.

### Metzora Inclusion

A difficulty arises in the *mishna*'s original formulation. The *mishna* refers to people who have an *asham* as part of their obligatory *korbanot*, but the individuals listed — *zav*, *zavah*, *yoledet* — do not bring an *asham*. Similarly, it refers to an *olah* and *shelamim*, yet not all of those listed bring a *shelamim*. Zeiri therefore instructs that *metzora* should be added to the list, since a *metzora* does indeed bring an *asham* as part of the *korbanot* required upon purification. This emendation was accepted and incorporated into the text of the *mishna*. Rav Sheshet additionally proposed adding *nazir* to address the *shelamim*, since a *nazir* brings a *shelamim* upon completing the *nezirut* period. However, *nazir* was not incorporated, as Tosafot explains: all the others on the list are *tamei*, whereas a *nazir* who has not yet completed the *nezirut* period does not share the same category of *tumah*-based disqualification. The *metzora* belongs organically among those who are *tamei* and awaiting purification; the *nazir* does not.

---

## Asham Shelo Lishmo

### Chilkiya's Rule

Rabbi Chilkiya be-Rabbi Tuvi introduces a striking ruling regarding the case of a *metzora's asham* slaughtered outside the *Beit HaMikdash* before its time. The *mishna* had established that slaughtering such an *asham* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* — since it is *mechusar zman* and not *ra'uy le-fesach ohel moed* — makes one *patur*. Rabbi Chilkiya limits this ruling: it applies only when the animal is slaughtered *lishmo* — with the correct intention, as an *asham*. If, however, it is slaughtered *shelo lishmo* — with a different intention, such as for the sake of an *olah* — one is *chayav*.

### Identity Change Logic

The reasoning is as follows: an *asham* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* inside the *Beit HaMikdash* would be *kasher*, albeit without fulfilling the owner's obligation. Since it would be *kasher bifnim* when slaughtered *shelo lishmo*, it is *ra'uy le-fesach ohel moed* in that modality. Therefore, when one slaughters this *mechusar zman asham shelo lishmo* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, one is *chayav*. The rationale is that the fitness of the offering — its *ra'uy* status — is evaluated by asking whether it *could* be brought inside the *Beit HaMikdash* in some valid capacity, and slaughtering it as an *olah* inside would have been valid.

### Initial Objection

The *gemara* immediately challenges this position. If slaughtering the *asham lishmo* outside is *patur* because it is *mechusar zman*, why should slaughtering it *shelo lishmo* be *chayav*? The argument for *chiyuv* is that had it been slaughtered *shelo lishmo* inside, it would have been *kasher*. But the same logic would seem to apply when it is slaughtered *lishmo* outside: even then, one could say that had it been slaughtered *shelo lishmo* inside, it would have been *kasher*, and therefore there exists a path by which this animal is *ra'uy le-fesach ohel moed*. Why, then, is the *lishmo* case *patur*?

### Identity Not Changed

The *gemara* answers: *ba'i akira* — identity change requires actual performance, not mere potential. Until the animal is in fact slaughtered *shelo lishmo*, its identity has not changed; it remains an *asham*. As an *asham*, it is *mechusar zman* and not *ra'uy le-fesach ohel moed*, and therefore slaughtering it *lishmo* outside yields *patur*. One cannot invoke a hypothetical reclassification: the animal's current identity as an *asham* is what determines its status. If, however, one actually proceeds to slaughter it *shelo lishmo* — thereby enacting the identity shift — then in that moment its status changes, and the *chiyuv* applies. As the *gemara* pointedly illustrates, one cannot say "if grandma had wheels she'd be a trolley car": the animal is what it is until the act of reclassification is actually performed.

### Rav Huna's Challenge

Rav Huna poses a fundamental challenge to the underlying assumption of Rabbi Chilkiya's ruling: is there any situation in which something is *not kasher lishmo* but *kasher shelo lishmo*? The challenge targets the claim that an *asham mechusar zman*, which is *pasul* when slaughtered as an *asham* (*lishmo*) due to *mechusar zman*, somehow becomes *kasher* when slaughtered as an *olah* (*shelo lishmo*). This seems paradoxical: slaughtering something with the wrong intention is generally a lesser form of validity, not a greater one. How can doing it *shelo lishmo* produce a more *kasher* result than doing it *lishmo*?

### Pesach Analogy

The *gemara* responds by pointing to the case of *korban Pesach* brought outside its season — on any day of the year other than the fourteenth of Nisan. In that case, a *Pesach* slaughtered *lishmo*, as a *Pesach*, is *pasul*, since it is not the time for a *Pesach*. But a *Pesach* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* — not with *Pesach* intent — is *kasher*, and it functions as a *shelamim*. Here, explicitly, *shelo lishmo* produces a *kasher* result while *lishmo* produces a *pasul* result.

The *gemara*, however, qualifies this answer: the reason this works is that a *Pesach* brought outside its season undergoes a full identity transformation — it *becomes* a *shelamim* by operation of *halacha*. Therefore, when it is slaughtered *shelo leshem Pesach*, it is not really *shelo lishmo* in the usual sense; it is simply being slaughtered for what it already is: a *shelamim*. This qualification sets up the difficulty that will be explored further: whether the *asham mechusar zman* undergoes a comparable identity transformation when slaughtered as an *olah*, or whether — unlike the *Pesach* outside its season, whose identity has already shifted — the *asham* retains its identity as an *asham* unless and until the act of *shelo lishmo shechita* is actually performed. The implications for the broader laws of *shelo lishmo* throughout the tractate will be taken up in the following session.

---

---

# Zevachim 115

## Rav Chilkiya Asham

### Chilkiya Thesis

The daf opens three lines down at *lameid mem mesayayei*, where the Gemara attempts to marshal support for what is, by any measure, a striking and radical position advanced by Rav Chilkiya. The scenario Rav Chilkiya addresses is this: a person *shachts* an *asham* on a *bama* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* before its time — meaning the individual who is obligated in the *asham*, say a *nazir* or a *metzora*, has not yet reached the point at which this *korban* is due. Were such a *korban* to be brought *lishmo* inside the *Beis HaMikdash*, it would not discharge the owner's obligation, and indeed it would be invalid. The question Rav Chilkiya raises is whether, when one *shachts* this *asham* outside and *shelo lishmo* — not for its designated name — one is liable for *shechutei chutz*.

### Identity Change

Rav Chilkiya's answer is yes, one is *chayav*. And this is where the genuine *chiddush* lies. Normally we assume that *shelo lishmo* invalidates a *korban* but does not do so completely — the owner is not *yotzei*, but the *korban* itself remains *kasher*. What Rav Chilkiya appears to be saying is something far more novel: *shelo lishmo* can, to some degree, change the very identity of the *korban*. An *asham* before its time is invalid. One would assume that an *asham shelo lishmo* before its time would be worse, or at the very least equally invalid. But Rav Chilkiya argues the opposite: slaughtering an *asham shelo lishmo* before its time — whether one is recasting it as an *olah*, a *shelamim*, or something else — renders it something other than a full *asham*, and therefore not subject to the invalidity that attaches to an *asham* brought prematurely. The result is that it is somehow more *kasher*, though Rav Chilkiya does not fully spell out what it then becomes or all the practical consequences that follow.

### Huna Challenge

Rav Huna challenged this position with an intuitive objection: how can performing a *korban shelo lishmo* make it *better*? That is the question the Gemara now takes up, as a series of *beraitot* is brought to bear on Rav Chilkiya's position.

---

## First Braita

### Olah vs Asham

The first *braita* begins by asking whether one might exempt from *shechutei chutz* an *olah* brought before the owner's time had arrived — for instance, a *yoledet* who brings her *olah* before her forty or eighty days have elapsed. The *braita* answers: no, one is still *chayav*. Even though the owner's obligation has not yet been triggered, an *olah* is intrinsically valid at any time, so there is no exemption. The *braita* continues: perhaps one should also exempt *asham nazir* and *asham metzora* whose time has not yet arrived. Again, the *braita* rules *chayav*, deriving this from the repetition of *shor* and *kesev* in the verse *asher yishchat shor o kesev bamachaneh* — the doubling of the terms is inclusive, coming to extend liability to these cases.

The *braita* then implies a distinction: while one would be *chayav* for an *asham*, one would be *patur* for a *chatat*. This immediately demands clarification. *Bemai askinan* — what exactly is the case? If the *korbanot* are being brought *bizmano*, when it is already the proper time for both, then of course one is *chayav* in either case, and there is nothing novel to say about an *asham*. The very fact that the *braita* needed a *pasuk* to teach the liability implies we are not in a simple *bizmano* case. *Ela shelo bizmano* — it must be that we are speaking of a case before the proper time. And since the *braita* implies *chayav* for the *asham* but *patur* for the *chatat*, this supports Rav Chilkiya's position precisely: *shelo lishmo* changes the identity of the *asham* in a way that makes it valid, while for a *chatat* no such transformation is available.

### Gemara Weak Read

The Gemara, however, resists this reading. It proposes instead: *le'olam bizmano v'shelo lishmo* — in fact, we are speaking of a case where it is the proper time, but the *korban* was offered *shelo lishmo*. On this reading, the *chiddush* is not that an *asham* before its time becomes valid through *shelo lishmo*, but rather that even *shelo lishmo* at the proper time does not exempt from *shechutei chutz* liability. One might have thought that since *shelo lishmo* would have invalidated the *korban* inside the *Beis HaMikdash*, it should also remove the liability outside. The *braita* teaches otherwise: at the moment of *shechita* the *korban* was *ra'uy l'pesach ohel moed*, and the fact that the intent at that moment would have invalidated it had it been inside does not remove the liability for *shechutei chutz*.

### Braita Chiddush

On this second reading, then, the *braita* is not distinguishing between *asham* and *chatat* at all. Rather, it is teaching about *asham* — and by extension *chatat*, since they are comparable — that *bizmano shelo lishmo* still generates *chiyuv*. According to this view, the reference to *asham* in the first *braita* is meant to include *chatat* as well, relying on the position of Rabbi Eliezer who equates *asham* to *chatat*. The *tanna* selected *asham* as its main example, but the same rule applies to *chatat*, and the *braita* is following Rabbi Eliezer who says *makshinan asham l'chatat* — the two are treated as a single category.

### Shelo Lishmo Limits

The Gemara then articulates the upshot of this reading: the first *braita* (which discusses *asham* and liability) and the subsequent *braita* (which discusses *chatat* and exemption) are actually talking about different scenarios — the first, *bizmano shelo lishmo*, where one is *chayav*; the second, *shelo bizmano* and *shelo lishmo* together, where one is *patur* because the *korban* is not *ra'uy l'pesach ohel moed*. Under this reading, there is no meaningful difference between *asham* and *chatat*, and no support for Rav Chilkiya.

This is, as the Gemara itself seems to acknowledge, a weak answer. The plain implication of juxtaposing the two *beraitot* — one singling out *asham* as *chayav* and the other singling out *chatat* as *patur* — is that there is a genuine distinction between the two *korbanot*. The Gemara's response essentially erases that distinction by saying one *braita* means *asham* and also *chatat*, and the other means *chatat* and also *asham*, just in different situations. That is a strained read, and the Gemara seems to strain against itself to avoid endorsing Rav Chilkiya through these first two sources.

---

## Second Braita

### Chatat Lacking Time

A second *braita* is introduced as a still more explicit source. It addresses an *olah* and a *chatat* that are *mechusar zman* — lacking the required time. By an *olah*, being *mechusar zman* in the *ba'alim* (the owner not yet obligated) does not matter, as an *olah* is always valid and one is *chayav* for *shechutei chutz*. But for a *chatat* where the owner's time of obligation has not yet arrived, the *braita* rules *patur*, deriving this from the verse *v'el pesach ohel moed lo hevi'o* — anything not fit to be brought to *petach ohel moed* does not incur liability. The implication is that for a *chatat* in this state, *shelo bizmano* renders it unfit, and consequently there is no *chiyuv* outside.

### Chayav vs Patur

The Gemara analyzes: *v'ilu asham shayrei* — the *braita* omitted *asham* from its list of exempt cases, implying that an *asham* in the same scenario — before the owner's time — would generate *chiyuv*. And again the question is pressed: *bemai askinan*? If the case is *lishmo*, then an *asham* before its time is clearly invalid, and one would also be *patur* — so why single out *chatat* as exempt if *asham* would equally be exempt? *Ela lav shelo lishmo* — it must be *shelo lishmo*. And if that is the case, then for a *chatat shelo bizmano shelo lishmo* one is *patur*, while for an *asham shelo bizmano shelo lishmo* one is *chayav* — which is precisely the proof to Rav Chilkiya's position.

### Gemara Pushback

Once again the Gemara deflects: *l'olam shelo lishmo* — yes, it is *shelo lishmo*, but the *braita* following Rabbi Eliezer treats *asham* and *chatat* identically, and one is *patur* for both. The *braita* mentions *chatat* as the primary example, but the same exemption applies to *asham* as well. As before, this is a demonstrably weak answer, eliminating the very distinction the *beraitot* appear to draw. The simple reading of these two *beraitot* side by side strongly supports Rav Chilkiya — that *asham shelo bizmano shelo lishmo* is *chayav* while *chatat* in the same situation is *patur* — and the Gemara's attempts to read around this are, by its own implicit admission, strained.

---

## Rav Dimi

### Rav Levi Braita

The Gemara now presents a more explicit and harder-to-deflect source. When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted the following from the house of Rav Levi: perhaps one might exempt from *shechutei chutz* an *olat mechusar zman b'va'alim* — an *olah* where the owner's time has not yet come. As established, an *olah* is always valid, so one is *chayav*. The *braita* then also includes *asham nazir* and *asham metzora* in the cases one might think to exempt, and concludes one is *chayav* for these as well — with the *pasuk* of *shor mikol makom kesev mikol makom* providing the derivation, as Ravina notes.

### Beit Status

Now the *braita* from Rav Levi's house turns to what happens inside the *Beis HaMikdash*. An *asham nazir* or *asham metzora* slaughtered *shelo lishmon* inside — *ksherim v'lo alu l'va'alim l'shum chova* — are valid, though they do not discharge the owner's obligation. However, if these *ashamot* were slaughtered *mechusar zman beva'alim* — before the owner's time had arrived — or if the animals were two years old rather than within the proper age range, they are *pasul*.

### Dimi Question

Rav Dimi noted an apparent contradiction. The first *braita* implies that an *asham shelo bizmano* is *kasher* — otherwise why would one be *chayav* for *shechutei chutz* outside? Yet the second *braita* from Rav Levi's house states explicitly that an *asham shelo bizmano* inside the *Beis HaMikdash* is *pasul*. How can the same scenario be *kasher* enough to generate *chiyuv* outside yet *pasul* when performed inside?

It is important to appreciate what Rav Dimi's question reveals. By framing it this way — asking why the *braita* implies *kasher* outside when the other *braita* says *pasul* inside — Rav Dimi implicitly demonstrates that his reading of the original *braita* was the straightforward one: that when it says one is *chayav* for an *asham* outside, it means *shelo bizmano shelo lishmo*. This shows that the Gemara's earlier deflections, however clever, do not represent the authentic understanding of those sources.

### Dimi Answer

Rav Dimi resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — kan lishmo, kan shelo lishmo*. The *braita* that says *shelo bizmano* is *pasul* inside is speaking of *lishmo* — when the *asham* is slaughtered in its own identity, before its time, it is invalid. The *braita* that implies *shelo bizmano* is *kasher* enough to create *chiyuv* outside is speaking of *shelo lishmo* — when one slaughters the *asham shelo lishmo*, the *shelo lishmo* changes its identity in such a way that it is no longer truly *shelo bizmano*, because it is no longer fully an *asham*. This is precisely Rav Chilkiya's position: *shelo lishmo* transforms the *korban's* identity, making it more *kasher*, not less. Rav Dimi's question and answer together serve as the clearest demonstration thus far that the strong reading of all these *beraitot* — contra the Gemara's earlier weak deflections — is indeed that there is a real distinction between *asham* and *chatat*, and the reason is the identity-transforming power of *shelo lishmo* by an *asham*.

---

## Rav Ashi

### Ashi Challenge

Rav Ashi then raised a parallel challenge of his own, *rami masnisin a-braita u'meshani kan lishmo v'kan shelo lishmo*. The *Mishnah* rules that one who slaughters an *asham* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* is *patur*, while the *braita* rules *chayav*. These appear to contradict one another directly.

### Ashi Answer

Rav Ashi resolves the tension with the same distinction: the *Mishnah* is speaking of *lishmo* — when the *asham* is slaughtered in its own name before its time, it is *pasul*, and one is *patur* outside. The *braita* is speaking of *shelo lishmo* — the *shelo lishmo* recasts the *korban's* identity, making it *kasher* enough that one is *chayav* for *shechutei chutz* outside. Rav Ashi's independent derivation of the same conclusion from a different contradiction confirms the force and necessity of Rav Chilkiya's position.

---

## Huna Concession

### Two Ashamot

All of this evidence, the Gemara observes, stands against Rav Huna, who had challenged Rav Chilkiya by asking how *shelo lishmo* could make something better. *Leima tehe tuvta d'Rav Huna* — should this all not constitute a definitive refutation of Rav Huna's position? The Gemara answers that Rav Huna can respond: *hacha bemai askinan* — here we are dealing with a specific scenario. Namely, one who separated *shtei ashamot le'achrayut* — from the very outset, two animals were set aside, one as the actual *asham* and the other as a backup in case the first is lost.

### Olah Identity

In this scenario, one of the two animals will inevitably become an *olah* — for if one of the *ashamot* is used to discharge the obligation and the other is no longer needed, the second, unlike a *chatat* (which would face *misah*), becomes an *olah*. Since from the moment of separation it is already determined that one of these animals will be an *olah*, when one slaughters it *shelo lishmo* — designating it as an *olah* — one is not mysteriously improving a *pasul asham* through *shelo lishmo*. Rather, one has simply identified which animal was already fated to be an *olah* and acted accordingly. That animal's identity as an *olah* was in place from the beginning, and therefore the *shelo lishmo* is consistent with a genuine *olah* designation, making it valid and generating *chiyuv* outside the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Grazing Asham

Rav Huna supports this with a precedent he himself stated in the name of Rav: an *asham shenitak lire'iya* — an *asham* set aside for grazing because the other animal was used to discharge the obligation — if slaughtered *stam*, without explicit intent, is *kasher l'olah*. In that case, once it is clear the animal will not be used as the *asham*, slaughtering it without specific intent is sufficient for it to be valid as an *olah*. By analogy, in the case of two *ashamot* separated from the outset, the animal that will become the *olah* is already on that trajectory, and intentionally designating it as an *olah* — the *shelo lishmo* — makes it valid. Rav Huna thus concedes that *shelo lishmo* can indeed make something more valid, but only because the animal was never fully a simple *asham* to begin with — one of the pair was inevitably an *olah* from the moment of separation.

---

## New Topic

### Burning Exemption

The Gemara now transitions to a new topic from the *Mishnah*: burning the meat of a *korban* or a *mincha* that is ordinarily meant to be eaten. If one burns such items on an external altar, one is *patur* from the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*, since burning is not the prescribed treatment for these items inside the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Enumeration

A *braita* enumerates the items that fall under this exemption: the meat of a *chatat*, the meat of an *asham*, the meat of *kodshei kodashim* — which would include something like *zivchei shalmei tzibur* — the meat of *kodashim kalim*, the leftover of the *omer*, *shtei halechem*, *lechem hapanim*, and *shiyarei mincha*. All of these are items meant to be eaten, and burning them on an outside altar does not generate liability.

---

## Burning Derivation

### Pasuk Logic

The derivation is sourced from the verse *asher ya'aleh olah o zavach v'el pesach ohel moed lo hevi'o*. The Gemara reasons: just as an *olah* is a *korban* whose prescribed completion inside the *Beis HaMikdash* is burning on the *mizbeach*, so too, only things whose designated completion is burning are included in the prohibition. Things that have an earlier prescribed finishing stage — namely, being eaten — are not included. The principle is that the prohibition attaches to activities or substances that mirror the *olah*, whose entire process culminates in fire.

### Prep Acts

The Gemara then extends this analysis to *avodos* — preparatory ritual acts. One might have thought that performing various *avodot* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* would also generate liability. The *braita* lists the following as *patur*: *hayotzek* (pouring oil on the *mincha*), *habolel* (mixing), *hapotes* (breaking up after baking), *hamole'ach* (salting), *hamenif* (waving), *hamagish* (touching the *mincha* to the altar), *hamesader hashulchan* (arranging the bread on the *shulchan*), *hametiv es hamenoros* (cleaning the *menorah*), *hakometz* (taking the *kometz*), and *hamekabel bachutz* (catching the blood). All of these, if performed outside, are *patur*.

### Process Principle

The underlying principle is the same: *mah ha'olah sheg'mar avodah* — the *olah*'s burning is the culmination of the entire process. Only acts that represent the *gemar avodah* — the definitive completion of the process — are included in the prohibition. Acts that are middle stages are exempt. This is why *zrikas hadam* does generate liability — it is not a middle stage but the end of the process. Similarly, *nisuch hayayin* — the wine libation poured on the altar — is the culmination of its own process and therefore also *chayav*. By contrast, everything listed in the *braita* constitutes a preparatory or intermediate stage, and therefore falls outside the scope of the prohibition. *Shechita*, while technically also a middle stage, is explicitly included in the verse. *Kmitza*, which is analogous to *shechita*, is not explicit in the *pesukim*, and therefore, since it is a middle stage, it is *patur* outside.

---

## Bechor Avoda

### Mishnah Claim

The Gemara now turns to what is one of the more historically fascinating topics in the *masechet*: who performed the *avoda* before the *Mishkan* was erected. The *Mishnah* states clearly: *ad shelo hukam haMishkan*, before the *Mishkan* was put up, it was the *bechor* — the firstborn — who performed the sacred service. The assumption is that the transition to *Kohanim* under Aharon and his sons occurred only on the first of Nissan of the second year in the desert, when the *Mishkan* was completed and dedicated. Until that point, the firstborn held the priestly role.

### Sinai Only

The Gemara now introduces a challenge to this picture. Rav Huna bar Rav Ketina was sitting before Rav Chisda and was reading the verse *vayishlach et na'arei bnei Yisrael vayizbechu zevachim shelamim l'Hashem parim* — the young men of Bnei Yisrael were sent and they slaughtered *shelamim* for God at Har Sinai. Rav Chisda said to him: thus did Rav Assi say — *u'pasku*, and they stopped after that. That is, the *bechorot* brought *korbanot* only at Har Sinai, and from that point forward, even before the *Mishkan* was erected, the *bechor* no longer performed the *avoda*. This contradicts the *Mishnah*'s claim that the *bechor* continued until the *Mishkan* was put up, since Har Sinai was approximately ten months before the *Mishkan* was completed.

### Kohanim Immediately

Rashi, however, reads the text differently. Rather than *u'pasku* — "they stopped" — Rashi's version has the sense that Rav Chisda interrupted the reading at *vayishlach et na'arei bnei Yisrael*, putting a full stop there. On this reading, the *na'arei bnei Yisrael* were sent merely to fetch the animals or assist in some logistical capacity. The actual *shechita* and *avoda* — *vayizbechu zevachim shelamim l'Hashem parim* — was performed by the *Kohanim* even then. Under Rashi's reading, the *Kohanim* had already assumed their role even at the moment of Har Sinai, and the *bechorot* were never officiating in the *avoda* at all.

---

## Braita Support

### Braita Main

A *braita* is introduced that supports the *Mishnah's* position that the *bechorot* performed the *avoda* until the *Mishkan* was erected. The *braita* states: *ad shelo hukam haMishkan*, before the *Mishkan* was erected, *bamot* were permitted and the *avoda* was performed by the *bechorot*. Furthermore, all kosher animals were acceptable for offering: *behema, chaya, v'of* — domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds alike.

### Animal Details

The *braita* elaborates: animals could be male or female, *temimim u-va'alei mumim* — unblemished or blemished. The sole requirement was that the animal be *tahor* — a kosher species — as non-kosher animals were excluded. And all of these offerings were brought as *olot*. This last point will be questioned in the Gemara, since the verse at Har Sinai mentions *shelamim* as well, but the *braita's* general assertion is that before the *Mishkan* the *olah* was the dominant form of offering.

### Flaying Detail

Remarkably, however, the *braita* states that one detail of the *olah* already applied even in this earlier period: *ve'ola she'hikrivuYisrael ba'midbar te'una hafshet v'nituach* — the *olah* that Yisrael brought in the *midbar*, before the *Mishkan*, required *hafshet v'nituach*, the flaying and chopping. This is striking because all the other details of sacrificial law — restriction to certain species, exclusion of blemished animals, designation of *Kohanim* — had not yet come into force. Yet this one technical detail of the *olah* already applied. The Gemara will grapple with this anomaly, noting also that non-Jews today, who are not subject to the prohibition of *bamot*, may still bring offerings on private altars.

---

## Kohanim Timing

### Bechor Version

The question of when the *Kohanim* assumed their role — at Har Sinai or only at the *Mishkan* — is resolved by identifying it as a debate among *Tannaim*. The *braita* asks: who are the *kohanim hanigashim el Hashem* of whom the Torah speaks at Har Sinai when God commands that the *kohanim* who draw near to God must sanctify themselves? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says: *zu prishus bechorot* — this directive was addressed to the *bechorot*, who had the priestly status at Har Sinai. Under his view, the transition did not occur until the *Mishkan*, consistent with the *Mishnah's* ruling.

### Kohanim Version

Rabbi Judah HaNasi (Rabbi) disagrees: *zu prishus Nadav v'Avihu* — the directive at Har Sinai was already addressed to Nadav and Avihu, who were already functioning as *Kohanim*. Under this view, the transition to *Kehuna* had already occurred at or before Har Sinai, and the *bechorot* never continued in that role past that point.

### Nadav Avihu

The Gemara then asks: according to Rabbi, who holds that it was Nadav and Avihu who were warned at Har Sinai, this supports the verse *hu asher diber Hashem* — that Moshe's statement to Aharon upon the death of his sons, namely *bikrovai ekadesh*, is understood as a fulfillment of what God had said even at Har Sinai. Those who draw close to God risk the very sanctification through death that fell upon Nadav and Avihu. The verse in the context of building the *Mishkan* — *v'noadeti shama livnei Yisrael v'nikdash bichvodi* — is read not as *bichvodi* but *bimchubadai*: I will be sanctified through those who honor Me, meaning that those who draw too close, even if they are the most honored, will face divine judgment, and that judgment itself sanctifies God before all of Israel.

---

## Nadav Avihu

### Sinai Warning

At Har Sinai, God had warned that those who draw near must maintain their distance — *pen yifrotz bam Hashem* — lest God burst out against them. This warning was directed, according to Rabbi, at Nadav and Avihu specifically, signaling their priestly status even at that moment.

### Moshe Consolation

When Nadav and Avihu died after the *Mishkan* was erected — killed for bringing a *eish zarah*, a strange fire — Moshe spoke to Aharon and said: this is precisely what God had told you, *bikrovai ekadesh* — I will be sanctified through those who are closest to Me. The death of Nadav and Avihu, as terrible as it was, communicated to all of Israel the awesome holiness that surrounds God's presence, and in that sense sanctified His name before the entire nation.

### Silence Reward

Aharon's response — *vaydome Aharon*, Aharon fell silent — is analyzed with care. The Gemara does not describe a man who was fully consoled or who intellectually accepted the explanation. It describes a man who, despite grief, despite the inadequacy of any explanation, permitted himself to receive God's judgment in silence. He did not protest. He did not demand an accounting. And for that silence — *v'kibel sachar* — he received reward.

### Silent Acceptance

The Gemara finds this principle of rewarded silence expressed elsewhere in *Tanach*. The verse in Psalms — *dome la'Hashem v'hitcholeil lo* — is rendered: be silent before God and long for Him, even when it seems as though corpses are falling around you, *af al pi shemapil lach chalalim chalalim*, still withhold protest. And Kohelet teaches: *eis lachashos v'eis l'dabber* — there is a time to be silent and a time to speak. Sometimes silence is the demanded response, and the reward is for that silence itself. Sometimes speech is demanded, and the reward is for that. The two are not opposed; the wisdom lies in recognizing which moment calls for which.

### Judgment Glory

The Gemara concludes with a teaching of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: what is meant by *nora elohim mimikdashecha* — God, You are awesome from Your holy place? Read not *mimikdashecha* but *mimikudashecha* — from those who sanctify You. When God executes judgment even against those who are close to Him, against the holy ones themselves, He is feared, glorified, and elevated. The very willingness to hold even the most beloved and dedicated to the strictest standard is what manifests God's true awesomeness before the world.

---

## Tannaitic Timing

### Ishmael Gradual

The Gemara now addresses the apparent anomaly regarding *hafshet v'nituach*. How is it that this one detail of the *olah* applied already before the *Mishkan*, while all other specifics — species restrictions, exclusion of blemishes, *Kohanim* performing the service — did not? The Gemara identifies this too as a *tannaitic* debate. Rabbi Yishmael holds: *klalos ne'emru b'Sinai, pratos b'Ohel Moed* — the general principles were communicated at Har Sinai, but the specific details were given only at *Ohel Moed*, meaning at the beginning of *Sefer Vayikra* once the *Mishkan* was standing. On this view, the detail of *hafshet v'nituach* did not apply before the *Mishkan*, because the detailed laws of *olah* were not yet in force.

### Akiva Complete

Rabbi Akiva holds the opposite: *klalos u'pratos ne'emru b'Sinai* — both the general principles and the specific details were already stated at Har Sinai. They were then repeated at *Ohel Moed*, and repeated again a third time at *Arvot Moav* before the entry into the Land. On this view, *hafshet v'nituach* did apply even before the *Mishkan*, because all details of the *olah* had already been communicated.

### Flaying Anomaly

This generates a genuine difficulty. If Rabbi Akiva holds that all details were already given at Har Sinai, then *hafshet v'nituach* correctly applies before the *Mishkan*. But what about all the other details — the restriction to certain species, the requirement of unblemished animals, the designation of *Kohanim*? Those evidently did not apply before the *Mishkan*. So even on Rabbi Akiva's view, it seems strange to single out *hafshet v'nituach* as already operative while treating all other *olah* specifics as not yet in force. The *braita's* picture — all kosher animals, male and female, blemished and unblemished, were brought before the *Mishkan* — implies that those laws were not yet applicable, yet *hafshet v'nituach* somehow was. The asymmetry is striking, and the Gemara does not fully resolve it here.

### Animal Acceptance

A related question is how we know that before the *Mishkan*, all types of animals — male and female, blemished and unblemished — were in fact acceptable. The source for this leniency, and how it interacts with the broader question of which rules applied and which did not in the period between Har Sinai and the erection of the *Mishkan*, remains to be worked out. The Gemara leaves this for continued discussion, and the shiur will resume tomorrow with these questions.

---

---

# Zevachim 116

## Noach & Animal Types

### Noach to Mishkan

The daf opens in the midst of a wide-ranging discussion of the pre-*Mishkan* period of sacrificial practice. In the earlier portion of the sugya, the Gemara addressed which functionaries performed the *avodah* before the erection of the *Mishkan* — whether it was the firstborn or the *kohanim* — and when precisely the *kohanim* assumed that role. A parallel question was raised about the details of the *olah*: one view holds that the procedural specifics of the *olah* were already in place at Har Sinai, while another view holds that those details waited until the giving of *Vayikra* at the *Mishkan*. The Gemara now turns to a related but distinct question: what categories of animals were eligible for sacrifice in that entire prior period, from the time of Noach through the *Mishkan*?

The working assumption is that whatever was true from the time of Noach remains in force until the laws change with the erection of the *Mishkan* and the giving of *Vayikra*. This raises an implicit and important question — when exactly did we cease being *Bnei Noach* and become *Bnei Yisrael*, with different rules beginning to apply? The most natural answer is that the transition occurs at *ma'amad Har Sinai*. Yet even granting that transition, the Gemara's position appears to be that many of the sacrificial rules remain unchanged until *Vayikra* introduces the full system, while some rules do shift at Har Sinai itself.

### Kosher Animals

A *baraisa* states that in this pre-*Mishkan* period, all types of animals were acceptable for sacrifice. The Gemara asks: *Mina'i milei* — what is the source? Rav Huna cites the verse describing Noach's sacrifice after leaving the ark: *Vayiven Noach mizbe'ach l'Hashem, vayikach mikol habeheima hatehora umikol ha'of hatehora* — he built an altar and took from every kosher animal and every kosher bird. The verse imposes no distinctions of male or female, blemished or unblemished. *Beheima kemashma'on* — the word *beheima* in its plain sense includes all domesticated animals; *chaya bichlal beheima* — wild animals such as deer are similarly included. So male and female, blemished and unblemished (*zachar u'nekeiva, temimim u'va'alei mumin*) — all were acceptable.

### Ark Source

One qualification, however, is that the animals must be *tehoros* — kosher species. This is derived directly from the verse's specification of *habeheima hatehora*.

### Exclusions

Two further exclusions are introduced: an animal missing a limb (*mechusar eiver*) and a *treifa*. How do we know these were disqualified even in the pre-*Mishkan* period, when the rules applied to *Bnei Noach*?

Rabbi Eliezer derives the disqualification of *mechusar eiver* from the verse describing the animals taken onto the ark: *umikol hachai mikol basar* — "from all that is alive, from all flesh." The word *hachai*, "alive," teaches that all of the animal's limbs must be intact; an animal missing a limb does not fully qualify.

The Gemara immediately challenges this: perhaps *umikol hachai* comes to exclude a *treifa*, since a *treifa* is presumed to be dying and thus not fully "alive"? The Gemara responds: the exclusion of *treifa* is derived instead from *lechayot zera* — the verse stating that animals were brought onto the ark to preserve seed, implying they must be capable of reproduction, and a *treifa* cannot give birth or sire offspring.

But the Gemara immediately raises a further objection: *hani nicha leman de'amar treifa eina yoledet* — this works well according to the opinion that a *treifa* cannot give birth. But according to the opinion that a *treifa* can give birth, the *lechayot zera* verse does not implicitly exclude a *treifa*, and we should need *umikol hachai* for that purpose, leaving us without a source for *mechusar eiver*.

The Gemara resolves this by citing the verse *itcha bedomim lach* — "with you, similar to you." God told Noach to bring animals onto the ark that are "like you." Just as Noach was not a *treifa*, so the animals could not be *treifos*. This frees up *umikol hachai* to address *mechusar eiver*.

The Gemara then asks: how do we know Noach himself was not a *treifa*? The verse says *tamim* — he was perfect — which presumably means physically sound. But perhaps *tamim* refers only to his moral character? The verse also says *tzaddik*, and the Gemara suggests that *tamim bedrachav* and *tzaddik bema'asav* are two distinct moral categories — one referring to character traits (the *mussar* dimension of humble, patient temperament), and the other to righteous actions (the *halachic* dimension of how one actually behaves). On this reading, both words describe his ethical standing, neither necessarily attesting to his physical health.

The Gemara's final resolution is elegant: *iy salka da'atach d'Noach gufei treifa havay, mi amar lei l'Noach d'chavaseich ayeil sheleimim lo tayeil* — if God knew Noach was himself a *treifa*, it would be incoherent for God to instruct him to bring animals "similar to you," as if God intended him to fill the ark with *treifos*. Clearly, the command *itcha* is only meaningful if Noach was healthy; the verse therefore implicitly establishes that Noach was not a *treifa*, and *umikol hachai* remains available to teach the exclusion of *mechusar eiver*.

The Gemara then asks what *lechayot zera* is adding if *itcha* already excludes *treifa* and *umikol hachai* excludes *mechusar eiver*. The answer is that without *lechayot zera*, one might have thought the animals were brought merely for companionship — *l'tzavta b'alma* — perhaps even old or sterile animals. *Lechayot zera* establishes that the purpose was to repopulate the world, and therefore old (*zaken*) or sterile (*saris*) animals would not have served.

To summarize the emerging picture: kosher animals of all species, male or female, blemished or unblemished, were acceptable in the pre-*Mishkan* period. However, an animal missing a limb or a *treifa* was excluded.

### Anachronism Issue

A striking question now surfaces. The entire derivation depends on the distinction between *beheima tehora* and *beheima teme'a* — kosher and non-kosher species. But the laws of *kashrut* were not yet given at the time of Noach. How can the verse assume Noach knew which animals were *tahor* and which were *tamei*? *Umi havei tamei vetahor beha'hi sha'ata* — since when did this distinction exist at that moment?

It should also be noted that the *girsa* in our text — the version of Rabbi Yishmael bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that reads *me'otan shelo na'avda bahen aveira* ("those not used in sinful acts") — appears to be a textual displacement from a different sugya. Elsewhere, the Gemara asks why the Torah says *ish ve'ishto* ("a man and his wife") regarding the animals boarding the ark, since animals do not observe the institution of marriage. The answer there is that *ish ve'ishto* means animals that had not been used in bestiality or inter-species breeding. That statement of Rabbi Yonatan properly belongs to that discussion, and it appears to have been imported here by association. The relevant *girsa* for our sugya is *me'otan ha'atidim lehitaher*.

### Future Kashrut

The correct resolution is *me'otan ha'atidim lehitaher* — the *tehoros* Noach brought were those animals that the Torah would eventually designate as kosher. It is not that the laws of *kashrut* applied to Noach; rather, those species that would later be classified as *tahor* are what the verse refers to.

But this prompts a secondary question: how did Noach know which species would eventually be so classified? The Gemara answers: *ki d'Rav Chisda* — as Rav Chisda teaches, the animals were passed before the ark, and those the ark admitted were *tahor* while those it did not admit were *tamei*. (This teaching is again borrowed by analogy from another sugya where the ark accepted only animals that had not engaged in sin; here it is adapted to explain the *tahor/tamei* distinction.) Rabbi Abbahu offers a different answer: *vehaba'im zachar u'nekeiva haba'im me'aleihem* — the animals came on their own, and those that came in groups of seven identified themselves as *tahor*, while those that came in pairs of two were *tamei*.

Rashi in his Torah commentary resolves the anachronism differently, stating that Noach had learned Torah — *melameid shelamad Noach Torah*. The Gemara does not give this answer here, a discrepancy that the *Maharsha* discusses at length. One could also note, as the *Ramban* points out in other contexts, that certain concepts antedated the formal commandments — just as the concept underlying *yibbum* appears in the story of Yehuda and Tamar before it was legislated. So too there may have been a way of categorizing animals that predated the formal prohibition on eating non-kosher species. The Gemara, however, does not pursue this line, resting instead on *ha'atidim lehitaher*.

---

## Olah vs. Shelamim

### Only Olot

The Gemara now addresses a further assertion from the *baraisa*: that throughout this period, all brought only *olot*. The Gemara asks: *olos in, shelamim lo* — are you truly saying they could not bring *shelamim*? The exclusion of *chatas* and *asham* is understandable, since the entire framework of atoning for specific transgressions had not yet been instituted. But why exclude *shelamim*?

The assertion is that the *olah* was universal — shared by *Bnei Yisrael* and *Bnei Noach* alike — while the *shelamim* was not available to *Bnei Noach*.

### Hevel's Fats

The Gemara immediately challenges this from the story of Hevel: *vehaktiv vayizbechu zevachim shelamim la'Hashem parim* — and it is written that they offered *shelamim* to God, cattle, right there at Har Sinai. This seems to contradict the assertion that only *olot* were brought until the *Mishkan*.

The Gemara resolves this by reinterpreting the statement: the *baraisa* should be read as saying that all people — both *Yisrael* and *Bnei Noach* — brought *olot*, meaning the *olah* was universal. The *shelamim*, however, was introduced specifically for *Bnei Yisrael* upon Har Sinai. So the foot of Har Sinai marks not only a transition in personal status from *Bnei Noach* to *Bnei Yisrael*, but also the moment at which *shelamim* became available. The laws governing which animals are eligible remain unchanged until *Vayikra*, but the category of *shelamim* is newly introduced here.

What is the basis for Hevel's *shelamim*? The verse says *umichelveihen* — and from their fats. The paradigm of a *shelamim* is precisely that the fats go on the altar while the meat is eaten: *eizehu davar shechelvoh karev legabei mizbeiach ve'ein kulo karev legabei mizbeiach hevei omer zeh shelamim* — that which has its fat offered on the altar but is not entirely consumed on the altar, that is a *shelamim*. If Hevel was offering only the fats to God while the rest was not burned, this looks exactly like a *shelamim*.

### Isaiah Verse

The opinion that *Bnei Noach* did not bring *shelamim* supports its position from the verse in Yeshayahu: *uri tzafon uvo'i teiman* — stir yourself from the north and come from the south. The Gemara interprets this as: may the nation that brings only from the north — i.e., only *olot*, which are brought at the northern side of the altar — be replaced by the nation that brings from both the north and the south, i.e., both *olot* and *shelamim*. The nation that brings only *olot* is *Bnei Noach*; the nation that brings both is *Bnei Yisrael*. One must acknowledge that this is a rather weak proof.

The Gemara then tests both sides. To the view that *Bnei Noach* did bring *shelamim*, how do you explain *umichelveihen* by Hevel? The answer: *mishmeneihen* — the verse means from the fat animals, not that only the fat was offered; perhaps the rest was simply discarded. To the view that *Bnei Noach* did not bring *shelamim*, how do you explain the verse in Yeshayahu? The answer: *hu bekibutz galuyot hu dechtiv* — that verse refers to the ingathering of the exiles at the time of *Mashiach*, not to the categories of sacrifice available to *Bnei Noach*.

Further verses are tested. The verse *vayomer Moshe gam atah titein beyadeinu zevachim ve'olot* — Moshe saying to Pharaoh that you will give us *zevachim* and *olot* — seems to show *shelamim* were brought before Har Sinai. The Gemara responds: *zevachim la'achilah ve'olot lehakravah* — the *zevachim* referred to meat for eating, not sacrificial *shelamim*, while the *olot* were the actual sacrifices.

### Yitro's Timing

The verse *vayikach Yitro chotein Moshe olah uzevachim l'Elohim* presents a starker challenge: Yitro brought both an *olah* and *zevachim* — apparently a *shelamim* — to God. And unlike the verse about Moshe and Pharaoh, here the *zevachim* is explicitly *l'Elohim*, offered to God, not for eating. The Gemara responds: *hahu le'achar matan Torah hu dechtiv* — that episode occurred after *matan Torah*.

This response presupposes two things simultaneously: that Yitro came after *matan Torah*, and that Yitro converted, such that as a member of *Bnei Yisrael* he was entitled to bring a *shelamim*. The *Maharsha* notes that the Gemara might have answered instead that *zevachim* here also refers to eating meat — and asks why it did not — since the verse says *l'Elohim*, making that answer unavailable.

### Three Triggers

This brings the Gemara to a formal *tannaitic* debate about when Yitro arrived. The sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi dispute: one holds that Yitro came before *matan Torah*, one holds he came after. The Gemara then cites a *baraisa* in which three *tannaim* each identify what Yitro heard that motivated him to come:

Rabbi Yehoshua says Yitro heard about the war with Amalek — which is narrated immediately before the account of Yitro's arrival in the Torah — and came. This places him before *matan Torah*.

Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i says Yitro heard about *matan Torah* and came, placing him after the events of Har Sinai. This reading, though against the plain chronological order of the *pesukim*, is supported by the observation that Yitro's advice to Moshe about delegating judgment makes more sense in the context of a fully constituted legal system after *matan Torah*.

Rabbi Elazar says Yitro heard about *kri'at Yam Suf* and came, which chronologically would place him before Har Sinai but after the Exodus. The verse in *Yehoshua* describing how all the kings of Canaan trembled when they heard about the splitting of the sea is adduced to show how far-reaching that event's impact was.

### Sinai Proclamation

The Gemara elaborates on the position that Yitro came because of *matan Torah*, developing a remarkable *aggadic* passage. When the Torah was given at Sinai, God's voice traveled from one end of the world to the other — *haya kolo holech misof ha'olam ve'ad sofo*. All the idolatrous kings trembled in their palaces. They sang praise, as the verse says *uveheichalo kulo omer kavod* — in His palace all declare His glory. They gathered before Bilam the wicked, their one prophetic access point to divine knowledge, and asked: what is this thunderous sound we have heard? Is it perhaps a flood?

Bilam answered: *Hashem lamabul yashav* — God already sat over the flood; He has already sworn not to bring another flood upon the world.

They pressed him: perhaps not a flood of water but a flood of fire, as the verse says *ki hinei Hashem ba'esh nishpat* — God will judge with fire? Bilam answered: He has already sworn not to destroy all flesh by any means.

Then they asked again: so what is this thunderous voice? Bilam answered: *chemda tova yesh lo beveit genazav* — there is a precious treasure in God's treasure houses, hidden away for 974 generations before the world was created, and God is now giving it to His children, as the verse says *Hashem oz le'amo yiten*. Immediately the kings opened and said: *Hashem yivarech et amo vashalom* — God should bless His people with peace.

The Gemara notes that the verse describing the Torah as *davar tziva le'elef dor* — the word commanded for a thousand generations — points to this same idea: God had been holding the Torah in reserve, not merely since creation but for a span of 974 generations prior, waiting for the moment to give it to *Bnei Yisrael*.

### Rachav Story

Rabbi Elazar's position that *kri'at Yam Suf* was the motivating event leads the Gemara into a digression about Rachav. The verse in *Yehoshua* describing the kings of Canaan — *velo kamah od ruach be'ish* — uses the phrase "spirit did not stand up in a man." Rachav herself says to the spies of Yehoshua that they heard how God dried up the waters of the *Yam Suf*. The Gemara compares an earlier verse about the kings of the *Emorim* — *velo hayah bam od ruach* — which says the spirit was not in them, to Rachav's formulation, which says the spirit did not *stand up*. What is the significance of "stand up" specifically in Rachav's context?

The Gemara answers bluntly: *de'afilu akshuyei nami lo akshu* — they were not even able to achieve an erection. The word *kamah* — to stand, to rise — is used deliberately in Rachav's formulation because she was a prostitute and knew from personal experience. *D'amar mar ein lecha kol sar venagid shelo ba al Rachav ha'Zonah* — there was not a single officer or dignitary who had not come to Rachav, and she thus had direct knowledge of this physiological effect of terror.
