The Gemara then records that Rachav was ten years old when *Bnei Yisrael* left Egypt, and she practiced her trade for the entire forty years they were in the wilderness, making her fifty when she converted upon the conquest of Yericho. She said: *yehei machul li bischar chevel chalon u'fishtim* — may I be forgiven in the merit of the rope, the window, and the flax with which she hid the spies. Rashi explains that these very objects had served as tools of her prostitution — the rope to let clients in through the window, the flax to conceal them — and now she was using them in the service of *Bnei Yisrael*, turning the instruments of sin into instruments of redemption.

### Final Position

The Gemara closes this section by establishing the final position. According to the *baraisa*, *Bnei Noach* could bring only an *olah*; the *shelamim* was limited to *Bnei Yisrael*. The position that *Bnei Noach* could also bring a *shelamim* is linked to the view that Yitro came before *matan Torah* — for if he arrived after *matan Torah* and converted, his *shelamim* poses no difficulty. Conversely, if one holds that *Bnei Noach* cannot bring a *shelamim*, one must hold that Yitro came after *matan Torah* and had converted by the time he offered that sacrifice.

One might ask what the conceptual basis is for this distinction between *olah* and *shelamim* with respect to *Bnei Noach*. The *olah* is the universal sacrifice — it is given entirely to God, nothing retained. The *shelamim*, by contrast, involves an act of extraordinary intimacy: the worshipper eats from the same animal, as the Gemara elsewhere puts it, *mishulchan gavoah kazkehu* — as one who partakes from the table on high. It is almost as if one is sharing a meal with God. Perhaps this greater degree of closeness is tied to the covenant of *Har Sinai* and the framework of *shemiras hamitzvos*, a level of relationship not available to those outside that covenant.

There is also something structurally striking in the contrast: *Bnei Noach* are permitted to build private altars anywhere and bring sacrifices without any central location — a dispensation that might seem, on its face, more permissive and perhaps more prone to the diffuse, localized character of paganism. Yet they are restricted to the *olah*, the more austere, entirely surrendered sacrifice. *Bnei Yisrael*, constrained to a single central location, are permitted the *shelamim*, the more intimate form. Perhaps the centralization of location makes the intimacy of the *shelamim* less theologically risky; distributed sacrifice everywhere, combined with the communal meal, might too easily shade into the patterns of ancient pagan feast religion.

---

## Non-Jewish Bamot

### Private Altars

Having established the *halacha* of *Bnei Noach* and sacrifices, the Gemara turns to a rule that operates in the present: *ve'ovdei kochavim bazman hazeh resha'im la'asot ken* — non-Jews today are permitted to do this. That is, they are permitted to build private altars (*bamot*) and offer sacrifices to God wherever they choose. There is no prohibition of *shechitat chutz* — the prohibition against slaughtering sacrifices outside the *Beit HaMikdash* — that applies to them.

### Source Verse

The source is derived from the verse introducing the prohibition of *shechitat chutz*: *daber el Bnei Yisrael* — speak to *Bnei Yisrael*. *Bnei Yisrael metzuvin al shechutei chutz* — *Bnei Yisrael* are commanded regarding slaughter outside the Temple — *ve'ein ovdei kochavim metzuvin al shechutei chutz* — but non-Jews are not so commanded. Therefore each individual non-Jew may build his own private *bamah* and offer upon it.

It should be noted that the term *ovdei kochavim* in our text is a later scribal substitution imposed by censorship; the original text used the generic terms *goyim* or *nochrim* — simply non-Jews. The irony of the current text is not lost: it uses the word "idolaters" while describing a permission predicated on offering sacrifices to the one God. The underlying legal framework, of course, assumes an idealized context in which the non-Jewish sacrifice is directed to God alone. Historically, the reality was quite different — pagans were offering to multiple gods and certainly not consulting *halachic* authorities about the propriety of their private altars. The rule thus operates within a theoretical framework that rarely matched lived reality.

### No Direct Help

Rabbi Yaakov bar Aha said in the name of Rav Assi: *asur lesayei'a vela'asot shlichutan* — it is forbidden for a Jew to actively assist or serve as agent in bringing a non-Jew's sacrifice. Even though the non-Jew is permitted to offer this sacrifice, and even though the sacrifice is not the Jew's own, a Jew may not be the one to physically place it on the altar or directly carry out the act of sacrifice. Whether this prohibition stems from the Jew's own transgression in performing an act that would be an *aveira* if it were his sacrifice, or whether it is a separate concern about being connected to a phenomenon that is off-limits for him, is a question *Tosafos* addresses. Either way, direct physical assistance is forbidden.

### Indirect Help OK

Rava rules: *ve'arunehu lehu sharei* — one may, however, give them instruction and advice. There is a meaningful distinction between actively performing the sacrifice and advising a non-Jew on how to do so properly. This question has broader analogues in *halachic* discourse. For instance, the question of whether a Jew may donate to the rebuilding of a church — a structure that for a Jew would implicate *avoda zara*, but for a non-Jew may be entirely permissible — touches on similar considerations. Directly building such a structure seems clearly problematic for a Jew; contributing money at a remove raises different questions. Here too, direct involvement is forbidden; indirect guidance is permitted.

### Ifra Hormiz Case

The Gemara illustrates this principle through a celebrated episode. Ifra Hormiz, the mother of Shapur the Persian king, sent a sacrifice to Rava with the message: *askeini ha lei l'Shem Shamayim* — offer this up for me to your God for the sake of heaven. This was evidently after the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*, so there was no question of bringing it to the Temple. Rava instructed his students, Rav Safra and Rav Acha bar Huna: go take two young non-Jewish men. Go find a place where the sea has recently deposited silt — newly exposed land that has never been used for mundane purposes. Take fresh wood that has not previously been used. Bring fire kindled from a new vessel. Have these young men offer the sacrifice on her behalf for the sake of heaven.

### Fresh Materials

Rava's meticulous insistence on fresh, previously unused materials in every dimension of the sacrifice — the land, the wood, the fire, and even the young men themselves — reflects a principle that everything connected to the divine service should be untouched by prior mundane use. The *Maharsha* notes that even the selection of young men who had not yet been associated with any particular trade may reflect this sensibility of freshness and prior non-use, however unusual it seems to apply such a concept to human beings.

---

## Fresh Materials Rule

### No Prior Use

Abaye asks Rava: according to whose opinion are you acting with such care that everything be fresh and unused? The answer is: *ke'Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua*. As taught in a *baraisa*, Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua derives from the altar itself a principle about the wood used upon it: just as the altar was never used by a commoner (*shelo nishtamesh bo hedyot*), so too the wood used on the altar must never have been put to mundane use. One may not take an old table or discarded furniture and use it as firewood on the altar.

### Bamah Question

The Gemara immediately raises an objection: but Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua himself apparently agrees that on a *bamah* — a private altar — used wood is permissible. If so, why did Rava apply the principle of fresh materials to this sacrifice for Ifra Hormiz, which was being offered on a private *bamah*, not on the central altar? Where is the evidence that Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua permits used wood on a *bamah*?

### David/Araunah

The evidence comes from a *baraisa* that grapples with an apparent contradiction between two verses concerning David's purchase of Araunah's threshing floor — the site of the future Temple. One verse says: *vayiten David l'Arnan bamakom shekalei zahav mishkal shesh meiot* — David gave 600 *shekel* of gold. Another verse says: *vayiken David et hagoren ve'et habakar bekesef shekalim chamishim* — David bought the threshing floor and the cattle for fifty *shekel* of silver. The discrepancy is twofold: 50 versus 600, and silver versus gold.

### Tribes' Gifts

The first resolution: *gava mikol shevet vashevet chamishim, shehen shesh meot* — David collected 50 from each tribe, and with twelve tribes, the total came to 600. This is an elegant harmonization.

### Price Distinctions

An alternative resolution is offered by Rabbi Yosei ben Dostai: the 50 referred to what David paid for the threshing floor itself and for the cattle; the 600 referred to the price of the entire site — *kol habayit kulo beshesh meot*. Each verse describes a different transaction covering a different scope of the purchase.

Elazar ben Shmuel offers a structurally identical resolution with the same breakdown: 50 for the floor and cattle, 600 for the entire site.

### Used Wood OK

What makes this *baraisa* relevant to the question about used wood on a *bamah* is the verse in which Araunah offers David: *re'eh habakar la'olah vehamorgim uklei habakar la'etzim* — behold the cattle for the *olah*, and the threshing sledge and the farm implements for wood. Araunah was offering his agricultural implements as firewood for the sacrifice. This appears to be an instance of repurposed, previously used items being offered as wood on an altar — and since David's altar at Araunah's threshing floor was a *bamah*, not the permanent central altar, it would seem that used wood is acceptable on a *bamah*.

### Implements New

Rava responds: *hatam b'chadati* — in that case, the implements were new. Just because Araunah possessed threshing sledges does not mean he had ever actually used them. They were brand new farm implements that happened to be in his possession, and therefore they qualified as unused wood even by Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua's standard.

This resolution is admittedly a bit surprising: farm implements are presumed to be functional tools, and yet the Gemara accepts that they could have been new and unused. Rava apparently holds that the requirement is that the wood not have been used — not that it be unworked or in its natural state — so fashioned but unused implements satisfy the requirement perfectly.

Accordingly, Rava's instructions to Ifra Hormiz's agents are fully consistent with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua: even on a private *bamah*, Rava required fresh, unused materials throughout.

The Gemara digresses briefly to identify the *morgim*: Ulla says it is a *mita shel Turbal*, and Abaye explains this as a flat plank fitted with spikes on the underside, upon which animals walk while trampling grain to thresh it — a threshing board. The verse in Yeshayahu — *hinei samtich lemorag charutz chadash ba'al pipiyot* — confirms this description: the *morag* is characterized by its sharp, new teeth or spikes.

### Silver/Gold Ratio

The Gemara concludes by returning to the contradiction between the two verses about David's payment, which Rava posed as a question to his son. The son resolved the 50-versus-600 discrepancy by noting that each of the twelve tribes contributed 50, yielding a total of 600. But the Gemara points out a remaining problem: the verse that says 50 specifies *silver*, while the verse that says 600 specifies *gold* — and these are fundamentally different in value. You cannot simply say each tribe gave 50 if one figure is silver and the other gold.

The final resolution: *goveh kesef bemishkal shesh meot zahav* — each tribe gave silver, but not merely 50 *shekel* of silver; rather, each gave silver equivalent in value to 50 *shekel* of gold. The contributions were made in silver, but the silver given by each tribe was worth the equivalent of 50 gold *shekel*, so that the total came to 600 gold *shekel* worth. Both verses are accurate: the currency was silver, the value expressed in gold terms was 600.

# Zevachim 117

## Three Camps Structure

### Ohel Moed Overview

The daf begins at the bottom of 116b, at the two dots, picking up the progression from before *ohel moed* to the period of *ohel moed* itself. The *ohel moed* represents the paradigmatic setup: *kodshei kodashim* are eaten within the space of the *chatzer* of the *ohel moed*, while *kodshei kalim* — essentially the *shelamim* — are eaten throughout all of *machaneh yisrael*. During this period, private *bamot* are prohibited.

### Kodshei Kalim Debate

The Gemara opens with the statement: *kodshim kalim ne'echalim bechol machaneh yisrael* — the lighter sacrifices may be eaten wherever the entire camp of Israel is situated, which in later generations translates to all of Jerusalem. Rav Huna then makes a striking remark: *bechol mekomos Yisrael* — in all places of Israel — and adds, *aval machaneh lo hava*, suggesting that there was no defined concept of *machaneh yisrael* even when the camp existed in the wilderness. This is a puzzling formulation.

Rav Nachman challenges Rav Huna: *u-machanos bamidbar lo hava?* — surely there were camps in the wilderness, and surely *machaneh yisrael* carried halakhic significance for *kodshei kalim*? He adduces a *braita*: the camps in the wilderness are the paradigm for the later structure of zones in Jerusalem. The *braita* then spells out the correspondence.

### Wilderness to Jerusalem

The *braita* establishes the three-camp parallel explicitly. From the beginning of Jerusalem until the Temple Mount (*Har ha-Bayis*) corresponds to *machaneh yisrael* — this is where *kodshei kalim* are eaten. From the Temple Mount until the Gate of Nikanor (*sha'ar nikanor*), the entrance into the *Azarah*, corresponds to *machaneh leviyah* — a buffer zone directly surrounding the Temple, even though the Levites did not literally inhabit it. From the Gate of Nikanor inward — where the *mizbei'ach* stands — corresponds to *machaneh shechinah*, paralleling the area within the curtains (*kla'im*) surrounding the *ohel moed* in the wilderness.

The Gemara then corrects Rav Huna's formulation: the point is not that *machaneh yisrael* was absent in the wilderness, but rather that it was not a fixed geographic location. Wherever the camp relocated, that place became *machaneh yisrael*. The Gemara asks: is this not obvious? The answer is that there is a genuine question about status in transit. When the cloud moved and the people began traveling, one who had begun eating *kodshei kalim* was now leaving the geographic coordinates of the original encampment — perhaps that constituted a violation of *yotzei*, taking the sacred food outside its permitted zone?

The *chiddush* is that even while in transit, if one remains within the camp, it retains the status of *machaneh yisrael*. The verse states: *v'nasa ohel moed* — even though the *ohel moed* is traveling, it remains *ohel moed*. Tosafos notes, however, that while *machaneh yisrael* retains its status in transit, *machaneh shechinah* does not, since once the structure is disassembled, the zone of the *ohel moed* itself is no longer operative — a person cannot meaningfully remain "within" *machaneh shechinah* as it moves. An interesting corollary question arises: could one bring a private *bamah* while in transit? The Gemara does not address this.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai adds that in the later Temple period there was an additional zone, the *cheil* — the wall surrounding *Ezrat Nashim* — which represents a level of sanctity higher than *Har ha-Bayis* but not yet *Ezrat Yisrael*. He notes that there was no specific punishment (*onesh*) for entering this zone while *tamei*, and it is generally understood that this higher level is of rabbinic status.

### Shilo Camps Question

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai then turns to the period of Shilo. Shilo was a precursor to Jerusalem — *bamot* were prohibited during that era, *kodshei kodashim* could only be consumed within the precincts of the *mishkan*, and *kodshim kalim* had defined zones. Yet Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that in Shilo there were only two camps, not three. The question immediately arises: which camp was absent?

The analysis suggests that *machaneh leviyah* is the most expendable from the perspective of *korbanot*. For sacrificial purposes, one needs *machaneh shechinah* to define where *kodshei kodashim* are consumed, and *machaneh yisrael* to define where *kodshim kalim* may be eaten. *Machaneh leviyah* might seem dispensable. Rabbah, however, argues the opposite: *mistavra de-machaneh leviyah havei* — it actually makes more sense that *machaneh leviyah* was present, and that *machaneh yisrael* was what was absent.

### Machaneh Leviyah Necessity

Rabbah's reasoning turns not on *korbanot* but on *tumah*. The Torah commands: *vayishalchu min ha-machaneh kol tzarua v'chol zav v'chol tamei lanefesh* — they shall be sent out of the camp. However, a *zav* and a *tamei meis* are permitted in *machaneh yisrael*; only a *metzora* is expelled from all three camps. The Torah further states *v'lo yetame'u et machanehem* — implying that each category of *tamei* person is sent out of a different number of camps: *ten machaneh lazeh u-machaneh lazeh* — give one camp to this one and a camp to that one. If there were no *machaneh leviyah*, then a *zav* and a *tamei meis* would only be expelled from *machaneh shechinah*, since they are permitted in *machaneh yisrael*. This would deprive them of a second camp to be sent out of, undermining the Torah's framework of graduated expulsion.

Rava presses back: if *machaneh yisrael* were absent instead, a *zav* and a *metzora* would both be expelled to the same zone — outside *machaneh leviyah* — which would violate the *metzora*'s status of *badad yeshev*, the principle that the *metzora* must dwell in a zone not designated for any other *tamei* person.

The Gemara's resolution: in Shilo, all three camps existed for *tumah* purposes, but only two of the three applied to the law of *miklat* — sanctuary. The statement that Shilo had only *shtei machanos* means it had only two camps for the purpose of providing refuge to an unintentional killer.

This gives rise to a larger observation: the primary halakhic significance of the camp structure, as the Torah presents it, may be the *tumah* framework — zones of permitted and prohibited entry for various categories of impurity — rather than the framework of where *korbanot* may be consumed. Indeed, immediately after establishing the camp structure in *Bamidbar*, the Torah commands the expulsion of *teme'im*, not the eating of sacrifices. The eating of *korbanot* within defined zones may operate on a distinct conceptual basis — perhaps connected to sight-lines or proximity to the *mikdash* rather than the formal camp designation.

## Cities of Refuge

### Miklat in Midbar

The Gemara now addresses a third dimension of *machaneh leviyah*: its function as a place of sanctuary (*miklat*) for an unintentional killer. The verse states: *va-samti lecha makom asher yanus shamah* — I will designate for you a place to which he shall flee. The word *lecha* — "for you" — addresses Moshe directly, and the *braita* explains: *mekoma* — your place, meaning where Moshe and the Levites dwelt, namely *machaneh leviyah*, would already function as a *miklat* during the wilderness period. Even before the establishment of the formal *arei miklat* across the Jordan, *machaneh leviyah* provided sanctuary. The verse's phrase *asher yanus shamah* — "that he shall flee there" — teaches that even in the wilderness this was operative.

This generates an important conceptual point: the Torah's institution of *arei miklat* may be built upon the paradigm of the space surrounding the *mikdash*. When *Chazal* teach that all forty-two cities of the Levites serve as *arei miklat* — not only the six designated cities — and that *machaneh leviyah* itself served as a *miklat*, this suggests that the *miklat* institution is fundamentally connected to sacred space, to the camp of the Levites surrounding the sanctuary.

### Ben Levi Refuge

A consequence follows: what happens when a *ben Levi* kills accidentally? Normally a killer flees to a different city of refuge. But the *ben Levi* already lives in a Levite city. The *baraita* teaches: *ben Levi she-harag goleh mi-pelekh le-felekh* — a Levite who kills goes into exile from one district to another. This reflects what happened in the wilderness, where there was only one *machaneh leviyah*: since there was nowhere else to go, the concept of exile within one's own territory must be valid. Hence: *ve-im galah le-pilko pilko kolto* — if he exiled himself within his own city, even that city absorbs him as a sanctuary.

### Internal Exile

This principle extends beyond the *ben Levi*. Anyone who already lives in an *ir miklat* and kills accidentally may go into exile within that same city, simply by relocating to a different neighborhood. One might assume this is only *bedi'avad* — a post-facto allowance when emigrating to another city is not feasible. Tosafos, however, raises the possibility that it could be *lechatchilah*, a legitimate primary option. The cost of this choice, though, is permanent: one who exiles within one's own city must forever remain barred from re-entering the neighborhood from which one fled. If one wished to retain freedom of movement throughout the city, one would need to uproot entirely and go to a different city. It is therefore an open question whether the two options — internal exile versus exile to another city — are halakhically equivalent alternatives, or whether external exile is preferred and internal exile is merely tolerated.

### Scriptural Source

Rav Acha son of Rav Ika provides the scriptural basis: *ki b'ir miklato yeshev* — he shall dwell in the city of his refuge. The phrase *ir shekaltato kvar* — the city that has already absorbed him — teaches that one who is already in the city can remain there even if it is his own city of origin. This is a remarkable *chiddush*: the verse anticipates and permits internal exile by specifying "the city that has [already] given you sanctuary."

The broader takeaway is that *machaneh leviyah* during the period of the *mishkan* served as the prototype for the *ir miklat* institution. The space around the Temple in Jerusalem presumably carried the same status, functioning as a sanctuary zone. In Shilo, however, this particular function was absent: even though *machaneh leviyah* existed for the purposes of *tumah*, it did not operate as a *miklat*. The standard *arei miklat* — the six designated cities and the other Levite cities — remained available; what was absent was the zone immediately surrounding the *mishkan* at Shilo serving as sanctuary space.

## Bamot Permitted

### Free-Will on Bamah

The Gemara now turns to the period of *heter bamot* — when private and central *bamot* were permitted — and asks what sacrifices could be offered in each setting. A *braita* states: *kol neder u-nedavah haya kareiv ba-bamah* — anything brought as a free-will offering, a *neder* or *nedavah*, could be offered on a *bamah*. Practically this means an *olah* and *shelamim*. A *chatat* or *asham* — obligatory sin offerings — could not be brought on a private *bamah*, since *she-ein neder u-nedavah ein kareiv ba-bamah*: if it is not a free-will offering it cannot be brought.

### Minchah & Nezirut

Two additional categories require separate analysis: *minchah* and *nezirut*. A *minchah* is entirely free-will in character, yet it is not a *zevach* — an animal sacrifice. Some of the relevant verses concerning *bamot* speak specifically of slaughtering (*vayizbechu et zivcheihem*), leading some to conclude that *minchot* were not permitted on a *bamah*. This exclusion has socioeconomic implications: the *minchah* and bird-offerings were the option for those who could not afford larger animals, so excluding them from the *bamah* effectively limited private *bamah* offerings to those of means.

Additionally, if one does permit *minchot* on a *bamah*, one encounters the question of *kodshei kodashim*: the remnants of a *minchah* may only be consumed within the zone of the *mikdash*, so permitting *minchah* on a private *bamah* generates difficult questions about where those remnants could be eaten.

Rabbi Meir holds that both *minchah* and *nezirut* could be brought on a *bamah*. The Nazirite vow begins as a free-will act; Rabbi Meir treats the resulting sacrifices accordingly. The Chachamim disagree, holding: *lo kareiv yachid ela olot u-shelamim bilvad* — an individual brings nothing but *olot* and *shelamim*.

### Rabbi Yehudah Gilgal

Rabbi Yehudah introduces a distinct category of analysis. He is not discussing the private *bamah* but the central *bamah* — the public sanctuary. He states: *kol she-tzibur v'yachid makrivin b'ohel moed she-bamidbar makrivin b'ohel moed she-bagilgal* — everything that both the community and the individual could bring at the *ohel moed* in the wilderness, they brought at the *ohel moed* at Gilgal. The central location at Gilgal functioned identically to the *mishkan* in the wilderness — every communal sacrifice, and every individual sacrifice, could be brought there. The sole difference between the wilderness period and the Gilgal period was the permissibility of private *bamot*; the central location itself was unrestricted. For his private *bamah*, Rabbi Yehudah agrees with the Chachamim: *lo hayah makriv aleha ella olah u-shelamim* — only *olah* and *shelamim*.

The implication of Rabbi Yehudah's position is that if an individual wished to bring a *korban chatat* or *asham*, he could simply go to Gilgal and bring it there.

### Chachamim Position

The Chachamim respond: *kol she-hatzibur makrivin b'ohel moed she-bamidbar makrivin b'ohel moed she-bagilgal* — whatever the community (*tzibur*) brought in the *ohel moed* in the wilderness, the community brings at Gilgal. But *kan u-kan lo karevu yachid ella olah u-shelamim bilvad* — in both settings, the private individual (*yachid*) is restricted to *olah* and *shelamim* alone. The Chachamim thus agree with Rabbi Yehudah regarding the *tzibur* — it brings everything at Gilgal — but they flatly disagree that the *yachid* at Gilgal may bring obligatory sacrifices. Even at the central location, an individual operates within the same restricted framework as he does on his private rooftop.

The practical consequences are acute. According to the Chachamim, a woman after childbirth (*yoledet*), a *zav*, or a *zava*, could never achieve *taharah* by bringing their required *korbanot* on a private *bamah*. They would be permanently barred from eating *korbanot*, including the *korban Pesach*, for the entire duration of their *tumah* — unless they made the journey to the central location. But according to the Chachamim, even if they arrived at Gilgal, they still could not bring their *chatat*, since individuals remain restricted even there. The result is that large categories of people could never achieve ritual purity during the entire period of *heter bamot* — an extraordinarily far-reaching consequence of this position.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon takes the most restrictive position of all, limiting even the *tzibur*: *af tzibur lo hikrivu ella pesachim ve-chovah ha-keva'ah lahem zman* — even the community brought only *pesachim* and sacrifices with a fixed time (*mussaf*, *tamid*, *Yom Kippur* offerings). Rashi mentions *par he'elam davar* as a potential communal exception, but Tosafos notes that Rabbi Shimon's ultimate position may be even broader, possibly excluding communal *chatot* as well. This fuller dimension of Rabbi Shimon's view will be examined further as the Gemara continues.

## Free-Will vs. Obligation

### Genre vs. Circumstance

With the debate about what could be brought on a private *bamah* established, the Gemara now probes the conceptual structure underlying it. The defining criterion for a private *bamah* is that the sacrifice must be a *neder* or *nedavah* — a free-will offering. The question is whether this criterion is defined by the *genre* of the sacrifice (*olah* and *shelamim* as opposed to *chatat* and *asham*) or by the *circumstances* of obligation (whether the person came to bring it voluntarily or under compulsion).

These two axes can diverge. An *olah* brought by a *yoledet* after childbirth is technically in the genre of *olah*, yet the circumstances are obligatory — she is required to bring it. Conversely, the *chatat* and *asham* of a *nazir* arise from circumstances that began as entirely free-will: no one compelled the person to accept *nezirut*. Yet the resulting *korbanot* are technically obligatory once *nezirut* is accepted. The question, then, is whether for the purposes of what is permissible on a *bamah*, we require: (a) the intersection — both the genre of *olah* and *shelamim* and free-will circumstances, (b) the union — either the right genre or free-will circumstances, or (c) only the genre, regardless of circumstances.

### Shmuel Chatat

Shmuel addresses the *nezirut* debate directly. He states: *machloket b'chatat v'asham* — the tannaitic dispute about *nezirut* concerns specifically the *chatat* and *asham* of the *nazir*. On this reading, the debate is whether free-will circumstances are sufficient to permit even a *chatat* and *asham* on a private *bamah*. Those who permit *nezirut* on a *bamah* would hold that since *nezirut* was accepted voluntarily, even the *chatat* and *asham* it generates may be brought — representing the "union" approach. Those who prohibit it hold that the *chatat* and *asham* are always barred regardless of circumstances. But according to Shmuel's initial formulation, all opinions would agree that the *olah* and *shelamim* of a *nazir* may be brought on a private *bamah*.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenges this reading from a *braita*. The *braita* discusses the *chazeh* and *shok* (breast and thigh) of a *shelamim* brought on a *bamah*: these priestly gifts apply at a central *bamah gedolah* but not at a private *bamah ketanah*. The *braita* also mentions the bread portions of a *todah* offering in this context. Rava notes, however, that the *braita* conspicuously fails to mention the cooked foreleg (*zroa b'sheilah*) of the *shelamim* of a *nazir* — the priestly gift given from the Nazirite's peace-offering. If, as Shmuel suggests, all opinions agree that the *nazir* brings his *olah* and *shelamim* on a private *bamah*, the *braita* should have stated that this foreleg gift does not apply there. The silence is inexplicable unless one assumes that no opinion permits the *shelamim* of a *nazir* on a private *bamah* at all — rendering there nothing to discuss.

### Resolution

Faced with this challenge, the Gemara concludes that Shmuel's statement must be reformulated. Rather than *machloket b'chatat v'asham*, Shmuel actually said: *machloket b'olah u-shelamim* — the debate concerns the *olah* and *shelamim* of a *nazir*, while regarding the *chatat* and *asham*, *divrei hakol chulin v'lo karvi* — all agree they are entirely off-limits on a private *bamah*, regardless of the circumstances of their origin.

The resolution thus establishes a two-part requirement for a private *bamah*: the sacrifice must belong to the genre of *olah* and *shelamim* (not *chatat* and *asham*), and it must arise from free-will circumstances. The *chatat* and *asham* of a *nazir* fail the first test and are universally excluded. The *olah* and *shelamim* of a *nazir* pass the first test but face ambiguity on the second: does one consider the circumstances free-will (since *nezirut* was voluntarily accepted) or obligatory (since once accepted, the *korbanot* are required)? That is the tannaitic debate.

According to the Chachamim who prohibit bringing any sacrifices of a *nazir* on a private *bamah*, the *olah* and *shelamim* of the *nazir* fail the second test: although the *nezirut* began freely, the resulting *korbanot* are obligatory and cannot be considered *neder u-nedavah*. This explains the *braita*'s silence about the *zroa b'sheilah*: the *braita* follows the Chachamim, according to whom no *korban nazir* whatsoever would be brought on a private *bamah* — hence there is nothing to say about what happens to its gifts.

The *olah* of a *yoledet* similarly fails under this framework: it falls in the right genre but arises from fully obligatory circumstances, and would not be brought on a private *bamah* according to any opinion.

The woman who gives birth, it should be noted, retains the option of bringing her obligatory offerings at the central location. During the period of *heter bamot*, Gilgal served as that central sanctuary, and Rabbi Yehudah would permit her to bring her *chatat* there. According to the Chachamim, however, even that avenue is unavailable for a *yachid*.

## Yachid in Gilgal

### Chachamim Reasoning

The Gemara now turns to the reasoning of the Chachamim regarding the central *bamah* at Gilgal. Even when a *yachid* comes to the central location, why should he be restricted to *olah* and *shelamim*? The Chachamim derive this from the verse *ish ha-yashar be-einav ya'aseh* — each man shall do what is right in his own eyes. They read *ish* as referring to the individual (*yachid*), who *vadai likrov* — who surely wants to bring — but *chovot lo yikrov* — may not bring obligatory sacrifices. The period of *heter bamot* is characterized by a kind of individuated religious expression: the individual operates in a mode of personal, voluntary engagement with the divine. He may not simultaneously participate in the system of collective obligation. The community (*tzibur*) retains its obligatory structure and brings everything in Gilgal, but the private individual, wherever he offers — on his rooftop or at Gilgal — remains in the voluntary mode. The *ish ha-yashar* phrase applies to him in all settings.

### Rabbi Yehudah Counter

Rabbi Yehudah disputes this. He holds that *ki ksiv ha-yashar be-einav* — the phrase "what is right in his own eyes" — applies specifically to the context of private *bamot*, not to the central location. When one is operating in one's own private space, governed by one's own eyes and one's own discretion, one is limited to voluntary sacrifices. When one enters the public, communal space of the central sanctuary, one exits the *be-einav* mode and participates in the full obligatory structure.

### Meaning of Ish

The Gemara raises a difficulty with Rabbi Yehudah's position: does not the word *ish* itself — "a man" — imply that any individual is always restricted? Rabbi Yehudah responds: *ki ksiv ish le-hachshir et ha-zar* — the word *ish* in this context teaches something else entirely. When serving on a private *bamah*, any person (*ish*) may perform the *avodah*, even a non-priest (*zar*). The verse is not restricting what the individual may bring; it is teaching that the private *bamah* service does not require a *kohen*.

One might have thought that on a private *bamah*, worship reverted to the pre-*mikdash* model and required a *bechor* — a firstborn. The verse's use of *ish* teaches that a *zar* may serve, without any requirement for sanctified lineage.

### Conclusion

The Gemara concludes by noting an apparent redundancy: the Chachamim who appear in the later discussion — who agree with Rabbi Yehudah that the *tzibur* brings everything at Gilgal while the *yachid* is restricted to *olah* and *shelamim* — seem identical to the initial *tanna kamma*. Rav Pappa resolves this: *kivvan de-nesachim bamidbar beineihu* — the sub-debate between these two positions concerns whether an *olah* and *shelamim* brought by a *yachid* on a private *bamah* are accompanied by *nesachim* — the wine, flour, and oil libations. All agree that the individual brings *olah* and *shelamim*, but the *tanna kamma* and the later Chachamim diverge on whether the *nesachim* accompany them, a question rooted in what was done during the wilderness period.

In summary: on the private rooftop *bamah*, the undisputed minimum is *olah* and *shelamim*, with a debate about *minchah* and the *nezirut* offerings (now clarified as concerning the *olah* and *shelamim* of a *nazir*), and a further debate about *nesachim*. At Gilgal, the *tzibur* brings everything according to all, and the debate between Rabbi Yehudah and the Chachamim concerns whether the *yachid* at the central location may bring obligatory sacrifices as well. Rabbi Shimon's more restrictive position, limiting even the *tzibur*, remains to be examined in the continuation of the *sugya*.

# Zevachim 118

## Prior Debate Summary

### R. Yehuda Position

The discussion on this *daf* — the third-to-last of the *masechet* — continues the running analysis of the various historical periods in which sacrifices could or could not be offered on *bamot*, and under what conditions. To orient the discussion, it is worth briefly recapping the debate that was worked through previously.

Rabbi Yehuda took a permissive stance regarding the *bamah ketanah*, the private altar. The question had been whether private *bamot* were limited to *olah* and *shelamim*, or whether they extended to a *minchah* or to obligatory sacrifices that arose from voluntary vows — such as the *olah* of a *nazir*. The conclusion was that fundamentally the private *bamah* was limited to *olah* and *shelamim*, and perhaps not even all of those, specifically excluding obligatory ones. Turning to the *bamah gedolah* in Gilgal, the public central *bamah*, the *tzibur* could bring everything, and the question became what an individual could bring there. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the individual could bring everything as well — the public *bamah gedolah* functioned very similarly to the *Beis Hamikdash* or to Shilo. The only meaningful distinction for Rabbi Yehuda between Gilgal and Shilo was whether private *bamot* were permissible at all. But within the public *bamah* at Gilgal, every individual could bring whatever he or she wished.

### R. Meir/Chachamim

Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* disagreed. Their view was that even when you come to the public central *bamah*, the individual remains limited to *olah* and *shelamim*, just as on the private *bamah*. The reasoning is conceptual: if one is operating as a free agent — as someone who worships privately wherever he chooses — then even when he comes to the central location, he cannot plug into the obligatory sacrificial structure. The freedom to worship privately is characterized as an expression of free will, not an entitlement to obligatory categories. The *tzibur*, by contrast, does bring all the normal communal sacrifices. This distinction between the *tzibur* and the *yachid* — restricted even at the public *bamah* — generates a troubling consequence: throughout the entire period of Gilgal, Nov, and Givon, no individual could bring a *chatas* to atone for sin. Moreover, anyone in a state of *tumah* — a *yoledes*, a *zav*, a *zava* — could not bring a *chatas* to achieve purification, and would therefore be unable to eat the *Korban Pesach* or any of the year's *korbanos*. Rabbi Yehuda's approach, being far more expansive, avoids this troubling situation.

### Aron & Bamah Status

One question that deserves explicit treatment is why Gilgal — which did have a single central public *bamah* — was not treated like Shilo. Why did the existence of that central location not trigger a prohibition on *bamot* elsewhere, the way Shilo did?

The answer lies in the *aron*. In places like Gilgal, Nov, and Givon, the *aron* was absent. At the time of Nov and Givon particularly, the *aron* had been taken captive by the *Plishtim* and was elsewhere entirely. Without the *aron*, there was no central locus of God's presence. The structure in Gilgal was not truly a *Mishkan* in the full sense — it was a *bamah gedolah*, a large communal *bamah*, but it was not the particular dwelling-place of the *Shechinah*. It was therefore conceptually not much different from a *bamah ketanah* — just a larger, communally shared one.

### Presence & Restriction

This brings into focus a powerful theological principle. If God is present in one particular place — if the *Shechinah* in some meaningful sense dwells more particularly there than anywhere else — then it makes sense that one cannot simply worship everywhere. The uniqueness of the location demands exclusivity. But if God is not more present in Gilgal than anywhere else, then there is no compelling reason to restrict worship to that one spot. God is equally accessible everywhere, and both the *bamah gedolah* and the *bamah ketanah* reflect that equal availability. It is precisely this principle — that restriction to one place follows from the concentration of divine presence in that place — that explains why the *issur bamot* applies in Shilo and the *Beis Hamikdash* but not in Gilgal.

---

## R. Shimon Model

### R. Shimon Position

Having laid out the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir with the *Chachamim*, the *Gemara* now turns to the position of Rabbi Shimon, who is even more restrictive than Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Shimon holds that even the *tzibur* in a place like Gilgal could only bring the *Korban Pesach* and sacrifices with fixed, scheduled obligations. Where Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* restricted the *yachid* at the *bamah gedolah*, Rabbi Shimon restricts the *tzibur* itself.

### Pesach Derivation

The textual basis for Rabbi Shimon's position is a verse from Yehoshua: *vaya'asu bnei Yisrael et haPesach beGilgal* — the children of Israel made the Passover offering in Gilgal. The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: isn't it obvious that they brought the *Korban Pesach*? The *pesukim* are telling a story — why would the text need to tell us this? The answer is that the verse is teaching something non-obvious: *dechovos ke'ein Pesach hu dekarav, hala ke'ein Pesach lo karav* — only obligatory sacrifices *like* the *Pesach* were offered; things that were not like the *Pesach* were not offered.

This, Rabbi Shimon's view holds, reflects the conceptual reality that even the *bamah gedolah* in Gilgal was not fundamentally different from a *bamah ketanah*. It was merely an expanded version of the private *bamah* — somewhat more capacious, but conceptually rooted in the same model. The *Korban Pesach* is permitted for several converging reasons: it is the central communal sacrifice reconnecting the people to their founding narrative; it also has a quasi-private character, since individuals bring it for themselves; and it functions somewhat like a *shelamim*. These features allow it to stand as an exception.

The *Gemara* at this point introduces an alternative understanding of the verse. The *Chachamim* who hold a permissive view — that the *tzibur* can bring everything at the *bamah gedolah* — need this verse for the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yose ben Nazir: that an *arel*, an uncircumcised man, can receive the *hazayah*, the sprinkling of the ashes of the *Parah Adumah*, for purification from *tumas meis*.

The reasoning is as follows. Before the first *Korban Pesach* in Gilgal, the people performed a mass *bris milah*. Based on the chronology in the *pesukim* — they crossed the Yarden on the 10th of Nisan, recovered for a day, and could not have performed *bris milah* before the 11th — there was a potential problem. Everyone who had been wandering in the wilderness for forty years was presumably *tamei meis*, since people had been dying throughout. Purification from *tumas meis* requires the sprinkling of *Parah Adumah* ashes on day three and day seven of a seven-day process. If one cannot receive this sprinkling while still an *arel*, then no sprinkling could have begun until after the *bris milah* on day 11. That would push the final sprinkling to day 17 at the earliest, which is the 17th of Nisan — well after the 14th when *Korban Pesach* is brought. The fact that they did eat the *Korban Pesach* proves they must have been *tahor* in time, which means the sprinkling must have been performed while they were still *arelim*. Hence Rabbi Yochanan derives from this narrative that an *arel* can indeed have the *Parah Adumah* ashes sprinkled upon him.

So the verse serves two functions: for Rabbi Shimon's school, it establishes the narrow range of what was permitted at the *bamah gedolah* in Gilgal; for the *Chachamim*, who already permit a broader range at the *bamah gedolah*, the verse teaches this *halacha* about the *arel* and *Parah Adumah*.

### Gemara Challenge

A *tanna* taught before Rav Ada bar Ahava: *ein bein bamah gedolah l'bamah ketanah ela Pesach v'chovos shekavua lahem zman* — the only difference between a *bamah gedolah* and a *bamah ketanah* is the *Korban Pesach* and fixed-time obligatory offerings. This is Rabbi Shimon's position — the *bamah gedolah* is essentially a *bamah ketanah* with a small increment.

The *Gemara* is troubled by this. The formulation assumes that the *bamah gedolah* is conceptually rooted in the *bamah ketanah* and merely extends it slightly. If that is the case, then whatever is permitted at the *bamah gedolah* must have a counterpart at the *bamah ketanah*. The *Korban Pesach* passes this test, for the reasons already noted. But if Rabbi Shimon means to include fixed-time *chovot* that encompass a *chatas* — such as the *chatas* brought every *regel* or on *Yom Kippur* — then that is categorically different from anything done on a private *bamah*, where no *chatas* is offered at all. The logic of the model breaks down: you cannot build off a *bamah ketanah* to arrive at something the *bamah ketanah* has no analogue for.

### Olot vs. Chatas

The *Gemara* resolves this by a narrow reading: Rabbi Shimon's reference to fixed obligatory offerings means only obligatory *olot*, not obligatory *chatat* offerings. The *olat tamid* — the twice-daily burnt offering — and the *olah* component of the *musafin* on *Shabbos* and the *regalim* all have a direct counterpart in the *bamah ketanah*, where a private individual may bring an *olah*. So obligatory *olot* can be brought at the *bamah gedolah* as an expansion of the private *bamah*'s *olah*, but the *chatas* of the *regel* or of *Yom Kippur* cannot, because there is no private *chatas* at the *bamah ketanah* to build upon.

The *Gemara* briefly raises the possibility of including the *minchat chovah* — for instance, the daily *minchah* of the *Kohen Gadol* — since an individual can bring a private *minchah* on his personal *bamah*, and therefore a communal obligatory *minchah* could serve as its parallel. The *Gemara* rejects this on the basis of the view that there is no *minchah* at a *bamah* at all.

The practical implications of Rabbi Shimon's model are significant, even if theoretically the *bamah gedolah* is grounded in the *bamah ketanah*. In practice it still meant that the *olat tamid* was brought daily, and the *musafin* on *Shabbos* and the *regalim* were brought — just without the accompanying *chatas*. The absence of the *Yom Kippur avodah* entirely is noted by the *Tosafot* as a striking consequence — though conceptually this makes a certain amount of sense, since the *Yom Kippur avodah* is fundamentally about cleansing the *Mikdash* and the place of the *Shechinah*, and in a location like Gilgal, which lacks that concentrated divine presence, such an *avodah* would be out of place.

---

## Move to Shilo

### Shilo Structure

The *Gemara* now moves on: *ba'u leShilo* — they came to Shilo. Shilo was the first location that functioned as a quasi-*Beis Hamikdash*: private *bamot* were forbidden during its entire period, and the laws of *bamot* only became permissible again after Shilo was destroyed. Once the *Mikdash* in Jerusalem was built, of course, the prohibition on *bamot* became permanent.

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for the particular structure of the Mishkan in Shilo? Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: there is an apparent contradiction between verses. One verse says *vatevi'ehu Beis Hashem Shilo* — "they brought him to the house of God in Shilo," using the word *beis*, which connotes a permanent stone structure. Another verse says *vayitosh Mishkan Shilo* — "God abandoned the *Mishkan* of Shilo," using the word *Mishkan*, which evokes the tent-like tabernacle of the wilderness. A third verse says *vayimas b'ohel Yosef uveshevet Ephraim lo vachar* — "He despised the tent of Yosef and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim" — using *ohel*, a tent. How are all three to be reconciled?

The answer is that the structure in Shilo was both: *lo haysa sham tikra ela avanim milmata viyeri'os milmala* — there was no permanent roof; instead, there were stone walls below and curtains above. The word *beis* refers to the stone walls; the word *ohel* refers to the curtain-like roofing, which functioned like the original *Mishkan*'s covering. This was the unique hybrid structure of the Mishkan in Shilo.

### Menucha Status

The *Gemara* notes that this structure made Shilo a *menucha* — a resting place — but not a *nachala*, a permanent inheritance. The term *menucha* indicates that it was a significant and settled dwelling of the *Shechinah*, but it was still temporary in character. After Shilo's destruction, private *bamot* became permissible again — something that did not happen after the destruction of Jerusalem. This impermanence is reflected in the physical structure itself: the temporary roofing over permanent walls captures the intermediate status of Shilo between the mobile *Mishkan* of the wilderness and the eternal *Beis Hamikdash* of Jerusalem. This hybrid character is echoed in the festival of *Sukkot*, where the *halachot* governing what makes a *sukkah* a temporary dwelling focus particularly on the roof — the *sechach* — while the walls may in principle be permanent. The temporary roof over stable walls is precisely the Shilo model.

### Kodashim Eating Rules

The discussion turns to the rules governing where one could eat *kodshei kodashim* and *kodashim kalim* at Shilo. *Kodshei kodashim* were eaten within the curtained enclosure in the usual manner. But *kodashim kalim* required a more extended zone — analogous to the walls of Jerusalem in the *Beis Hamikdash* period. The question is: what defined that zone in Shilo?

One might expect the answer to be the city of Shilo itself, serving as the equivalent of Jerusalem. But this was not the *halacha*. The city of Shilo had no special sanctified status comparable to Jerusalem's. Jerusalem carries a profound historical and theological weight; Shilo did not. Accordingly, the zone for eating *kodashim kalim* was not defined by the city limits of Shilo but by the line of sight to the *Mikdash* — from any place from which one could see the Mishkan, one could eat the *korbanos*. This could be miles away, provided there was no obstruction. It was not a geographical designation but a relational one: connection to the *Mikdash* through direct sight.

---

## Line of Sight

### Restriction Verse

The source for this principle is a verse cited by Rabbi Oshaya: *hishamer lecha pen ta'aleh olotecha bechol makom asher tireh* — "guard yourself lest you bring your *olot* in every place that you see." This verse, speaking of the prohibition of *bamot* when a central place exists, says you may not bring sacrifices wherever you see fit. The *Gemara* derives from this verse a positive analogue: *aval ata ochel bechol makom she'ata ro'eh* — but you may eat your sacrifices wherever you can see, meaning wherever you can see Shilo.

The *Gemara* anticipates an objection: perhaps the verse means that wherever you can see Shilo, you may slaughter (*zove'ach*) — not merely eat — your sacrifice? Rabbi Yannai resolves this from another verse: *sham ta'aleh, vesham ta'aseh* — "there you shall offer up, and there you shall perform." The offering and the *avodah* must occur in the single central place. The *avodah* is fully confined to the *Mikdash* in Shilo; only the *eating* extends to wherever sight permits.

### Yosef Midrash

Rav Dimi bar Rav Chisda brings another verse: *velo te'anach Shilo* — a verse describing the border of Yosef that goes eastward toward Shilo. Rashi candidly notes that he searched through all of *Tanach* and could not find this verse as quoted, but he did find a similar formulation: *venasav hagvul mizrachah Ta'anach Shilo* — the boundary turns eastward toward *Ta'anach Shilo*. The *Gemara* reads *Ta'anach Shilo* not as a place-name but midrashically: *makom shekol haroeh oso mit'ane'ach alav* — the place over which everyone who sees it sighs, remembering that *korbanos* were once eaten throughout the entire region within sight of that place.

Rabbi Abahu derives the same teaching from the verse about Yosef: *ben porat Yosef, ben porat alei ayin* — "a fruitful son is Yosef, a fruitful son by the fountain, whose branches run over the wall." The *Gemara* reads *alei ayin* as a reference to the eye: *ayin shelo ratztah lehannos midavar she'eino shelo* — the eye that refused to benefit from that which was not its own. Yosef refused to look upon what was not his — specifically, he refused to sin with the wife of Potiphar despite her persistence. Because Yosef guarded his eye and refused to take what was not his, his eye is rewarded: *tizkeh vesochalah kemlo eineha* — it merits to eat as far as the eye can see. The territory in which Yosef's descendants benefited from proximity to the Mishkan in Shilo extended as far as the eye could see.

Rabbi Yosi berabbi Chanina offers a parallel derivation from the verse in *Devarim*: *uretzon shocheni sneh* — the desire of the one who dwells in the thornbush, understood as God. Here again, the eye of Yosef that refused to benefit from what was not its own is rewarded: *tizkeh vesochalah bein hasnu'in* — it merits to eat even among those who hated him. The *Gemara* reads *sneh* not as thornbush but as *senu'in*, those who hated, referencing the brothers who despised Yosef — *vayisnu oso*. The reward is that even someone sitting in the territory of another tribe, one of those brothers' tribes, on a high place from which Shilo is visible, could eat the sacrifices by virtue of that connection to the Mishkan. That is how far Yosef's reward extended.

### Visibility Rules

A *Baraita* is cited that specifies the requirements: *roeh* — seeing. The question of exactly what "seeing" requires is then refined. The *Baraita* initially seems to imply *roeh kullo* — seeing all of it. But the essential qualification is *velo hamafsik beino leveino* — there must be no obstruction between the person and Shilo. This is the critical criterion: not distance, but unobstructed line of sight. One could be many miles away and still qualify; one could be quite close but disqualified by an intervening hill or structure.

Rabbi Shimon ben Yakam illustrates this for Elazar with a concrete example: the synagogue of *Ma'on* — a location presumably built on a high place where, despite the distance, Shilo was visible, and therefore it was a place where one could eat the *korbanos*.

### Partial Sight

Rav Pappa refines the ruling: *roeh she-amru lo roeh kullah* — when the *Sages* said "seeing," they did not require seeing the whole of Shilo. *Ela roeh miktzatah* — even seeing a portion of Shilo suffices. This clarifies the earlier formulation and may also explain why some versions of the *Baraita* text differ, with one version appearing to say *roeh kullo* ("seeing it all") while the *Gemara* now rules that partial sight is enough.

It is worth noting that throughout this discussion, "seeing Shilo" most naturally refers to seeing the *Mishkan* itself — seeing the actual location of the sacred structure. However, the plain meaning of the language could equally suggest that it was the town of Shilo that needed to be visible. This would be somewhat paradoxical, since it was established earlier that the city of Shilo has no independent sanctified status equivalent to Jerusalem. Nevertheless, if the relevant criterion is seeing the town rather than the *Mishkan* specifically, that does give the actual city some degree of legal significance.

### Edge Cases

Rav Pappa poses a further question: *omed v'roeh, yoshev v'eino roeh, mai* — if when standing one can see Shilo, but when sitting one cannot, what is the ruling? Does the ability to see while standing mean the location qualifies — so that one may even eat while seated — or does the inability to see while seated mean the location is disqualified entirely? The question cuts both ways and no resolution is given.

Rabbi Yirmiah, who characteristically enjoyed pressing such edge cases, posed an analogous question about a *nachal* — a wadi or ravine. If one stands at the edge of the wadi and can see Shilo, but descends into the wadi and can no longer see it, what is the ruling? Perhaps the wadi and its rim are considered one unified location and must be governed by a single rule; or perhaps the sight-line at each physical point determines the rule for that point. The *Gemara* leaves both questions unresolved: *teiku*.

---

## Divine Presence

### Rav Dimi Teaching

Rav Dimi, upon returning from *Eretz Yisrael*, cited a teaching in the name of Rabbi: *b'shlosha mekomot sharta Shechinah b'Yisrael* — the *Shechinah* dwelt in three locations among Israel: in Shilo, in Nov and Givon, and in the *Beis Olamim* — the eternal *Beis Hamikdash*. The larger claim is that all of these locations were exclusively within the portion of Binyamin: *u'v'chulan lo sharta ela b'chelko shel Binyamin*. This is derived from the verse *chofef alav kol hayom* — God hovers over Binyamin the entire day — which the teaching interprets to mean that every location of divine hovering was always within Binyamin's territory.

The mention of Nov and Givon as locations of the *Shechinah* is itself striking, since as was noted, it was precisely during the period of Nov and Givon that the *aron* was absent. Yet Rav Dimi calls them places of the dwelling of the divine presence. The *Gemara* does not fully unpack this tension.

### Shilo Location

When Abaye repeated this teaching before Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef reacted sharply — characterizing the transmission as muddled. His objection was textual: *vayitosh Mishkan Shilo, vayimas b'ohel Yosef uveshevet Ephraim lo vachar* — the verses explicitly say God abandoned Shilo in connection with Yosef and Ephraim, not Binyamin. Shilo is in the territory of Yosef, not Binyamin. These are different tribes — Binyamin is Yosef's brother, a fellow son of Rachel, but a distinct tribe with a distinct territorial allotment.

Rav Adda responds: *mai kakasheilei* — why is that a difficulty? Perhaps the same arrangement obtained at Shilo as is well-known from Jerusalem: the *Shechinah* — the location of the *aron* and the *mizbeach* — was in Binyamin's portion, while the *Sanhedrin* convened in Yosef's portion. Just as in Jerusalem the *Shechinah* was in Binyamin and the *Sanhedrin* was in Yehuda, so too in Shilo the *Shechinah* proper may have been in Binyamin while the *Sanhedrin* occupied the section that fell within Yosef's territory. The *Gemara* finds it fascinating to imagine that the *Sanhedrin* dwelt in the Mishkan complex in Shilo as well, paralleling its role in the *Beis Hamikdash*.

Rav Yosef challenges this analogy: *hachi hashta?* — Is the comparison valid? In Jerusalem, Yehuda and Binyamin are genuinely adjacent; their portions are contiguous, and a shared border makes the overlap at the *Mikdash* natural. But Ephraim and Binyamin — are their portions juxtaposed in the same way?

The *Gemara* responds: yes, they can be considered juxtaposed — *hachi nami mikravin*. Just as Rabbi Chama berabbi Chanina taught that a strip (*retzuah*) went out from Yehuda's portion into Binyamin's, giving Yehuda a share in the *mizbeach* — and over this strip Binyamin the righteous yearned, desiring to absorb it — so too here, a strip could go out from Yosef's portion into Binyamin's, situating the sacred core of Shilo in Binyamin even while a significant section of the complex fell within Ephraim. The verse *ta'anat Shiloh*, understood in this context as indicating an extension, would then reflect this strip of Yosef extending into the area of Shilo situated in Binyamin.

The *Gemara* is candid that if one places Shilo according to its known archaeological and geographical location, the neat parallel with Jerusalem's border between Yehuda and Binyamin does not work perfectly. But the conceptual point the *Gemara* wishes to establish is that the arrangement in Shilo could have mirrored that of Jerusalem: the *Shechinah* concentrated in Binyamin's portion, with Yosef/Ephraim contributing a strip that encompassed major aspects of the compound — just as in Jerusalem, Yehuda contributed the strip where the *mizbeach* stood.

The deeper background to all of this involves the recurring tension between the legacy of Yosef and the legacy of Yehuda — between *Bnei Rachel* and *Bnei Leah*, between the earlier focus of kingship and sacred space in Yosef's descendants (as exemplified by Shaul, who was from Binyamin, but more broadly in the centrality of Ephraim during the early period), and the eventual shift of both kingship and *Mikdash* to Yehuda. Binyamin functions throughout as the mediating presence, always adjacent to the center, captured by the phrase *chofef alav kol hayom* — God hovers over him always, making Binyamin the perpetual locus of divine nearness regardless of which surrounding tribe holds the larger territorial claim.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan offers a formulation that parallels Rav Dimi's teaching in its conclusion. His language — *Shechinah hovers over Binyamin perpetually in this world* — encompasses all periods of history, including Shilo.

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *Gemara* then reports that this question is in fact the subject of a *Tannaitic* dispute — *k'tannai*. The verse *chofef alav kol hayom, uvein kteifav shachen* is parsed by the first *Tannaim* to refer to discrete periods: *chofef alav* refers to the first *Beis Hamikdash*; *kol hayom* refers to the second *Beis Hamikdash*; and *uvein kteifav shachen* refers to the messianic period. On this reading, God's hovering presence in Binyamin was limited to the periods of the *Mikdash* — it did not encompass the period of Shilo. The implication is that Shilo was not within Binyamin, consistent with the plain reading of the verses about Yosef and Ephraim.

Rabbi, by contrast, reads the verse more expansively: *chofef alav* — *zeh olam hazeh* — in all of recorded history, God was always present in Binyamin. *Kol hayom* — *eilu yemot hamashiach* — refers to the messianic period. *Uvein kteifav shachen* — *zeh ha'olam habah* — refers to the world to come, which in the *Gemara*'s usage typically means not the afterlife of individual souls but the renewed world of the post-messianic era. According to Rabbi, even the period of Shilo falls within God's perpetual hovering over Binyamin, meaning Shilo was indeed considered to be within Binyamin's portion.

---

## Shilo Chronology

### 480-Year Framework

The *Gemara* now turns to a precise historical chronology, working out how long the Mishkan stood in Shilo. The framework is provided by the verse in *Melachim* stating that the *Beis Hamikdash* was built 480 years after the exodus from Egypt. The approach is essentially one of subtraction: identify all the other periods — the wilderness, Gilgal, Nov and Givon — subtract their totals from 480, and the remainder is the years Shilo stood.

### Final Subtraction

The known figures are as follows. The *Ohel Moed* in the wilderness stood for 39 years. The period in Gilgal was 14 years. The period in Nov and Givon was 57 years. Together these total 111 years (40 + 14 + 57, where the 40 accounts for the wilderness period in round terms). Subtracting 111 from 480 yields 369 years — *nishtayru le'Shilo gimel me'ot v'shiv'im chaser achas*, 370 minus 1 — for the period of Shilo. This is a remarkably long time. We tend to think of Shilo as a minor episode in the history of sacred space, but its 369 years compare closely with the 420 years of the first *Beis Hamikdash* — a difference of only about 50 years.

### Wilderness: 39 Years

How is the figure of 39 years derived for the wilderness period? As the tradition states: *shana rishona asa Moshe et haMishkan* — the first year was spent constructing the *Mishkan*; *shniya hukam haMishkan* — an explicit verse establishes that it was erected on *Rosh Chodesh Nisan* of the second year. Since the *Mishkan* was standing from year two through year forty, that is 39 years.

### Gilgal: 14 Years

The 14 years of Gilgal are derived from the testimony of Calev. He declares: *ben arba'im shana anochi b'shloach Moshe eved Hashem miKadesh Barnea l'ragel et ha'aretz* — I was 40 years old when Moshe sent the spies from Kadesh Barnea. The spies were sent in year two, so Calev was 40 in year two. They then entered *Eretz Yisrael* in year 40 of the wilderness, making Calev 78 at the crossing of the Yarden. He later declares *ve'ata hinei anochi hayom ben chamish v'shmonim shana* — I am 85 today. From 78 to 85 is 7 years — the seven years of conquest. The seven years of dividing the land are added to this. How do we know it took seven years to divide? One possibility offered is simply *sevara be'alma* — a hypothesis that since it took seven years to conquer, it took seven to divide. The *Gemara* offers a second derivation based on Yechezkel's statement that his prophecy came fourteen years after the destruction of Jerusalem, combined with calculations about the *Shemitta* and *Yovel* cycles: since the counting of *Yovel* begins only when every tribe is settled in its proper location, and various computations converge on the conclusion that this process could not have begun until the 14th year after entry, this confirms the 14-year total for the period in Gilgal.

### Nov/Givon: 57 Years

The 57-year figure for Nov and Givon requires a more complex derivation built up from several smaller units, and the overall structure is established through a key verse and several corroborating computations.

### Eli & Aron Capture

The *Gemara* anchors the transition from Shilo to Nov at the death of Eli. The verse records that when the *aron* of God was mentioned in his presence — that it had been taken captive by the *Plishtim* — Eli fell backwards and died. A *Tanna* teaches: *keshemet Eli HaKohen charav Shilo* — when Eli the priest died, Shilo was destroyed. This marks the end of the Shilo period and the beginning of what follows. The *Mishkan* operation moved to Nov, functioning without the *aron*. When Shmuel died, Nov in turn was destroyed (*charav Nov*), and the center moved to Givon.

### Aron Kiryat Ye'arim

A separate verse tracks the fate of the *aron* itself: *vayehi miyom shevet ha-aron beKiryat Ye'arim, vayirbu hayamim vayihyu esrim shana* — from the day the *aron* rested in Kiryat Ye'arim, the days multiplied and were twenty years. The *aron* had been returned by the *Plishtim* relatively quickly after its capture, and it then resided in Kiryat Ye'arim for twenty years before David brought it to Jerusalem. These twenty years are then broken down: ten years during which Shmuel ruled alone; one year during which Shmuel and Shaul overlapped; two additional years of Shaul's reign after Shmuel's death; and seven years of David's reign in Hevron before he moved to Jerusalem. Together these account for the twenty years during which the *aron* sat in Kiryat Ye'arim.

### David & Solomon

The remaining 37 years needed to reach the total of 57 are derived from the reigns of David and Solomon. The verse states that David reigned over Israel for forty years: seven in Hevron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. So after the *aron* arrived in Jerusalem, David reigned another 33 years. Adding these 33 years to the 20 years of Kiryat Ye'arim yields 53 years. Solomon then built the *Beis Hamikdash* not in year one of his reign but in year four: *vayachel livnot bishnat arba lemalchuto*. Adding those four years brings the total to 57 years — the full period from the destruction of Shilo through to the construction of the *Beis Hamikdash*.

Expressed differently: David's 40 years plus Shmuel and Shaul's combined 13 years plus Solomon's initial 4 years equals 57. This is the total period of Nov and Givon, and when subtracted along with the wilderness years and the Gilgal years from the 480-year framework, it leaves precisely 369 years for Shilo — a duration that commands reflection, reminding us that Shilo was not a brief transitional moment but a centuries-long center of Jewish sacred life.

---

---

# Zevachim 119

## Corrections & Intro

### Shaul Affiliation

Before proceeding into the body of the *daf*, two corrections from the previous lecture are in order. In the course of discussing the geography of the tribal territories — Binyamin, Yehuda, and Ephraim, and the way the *Beis Hamikdash* and Shilo were distributed among the children of Yosef — it may have been stated that Shaul was from Ephraim. That is incorrect: Shaul was from Binyamin. The broader observation remains interesting, namely how the *malchut* and the *Mikdash* were navigated among the children of Yosef and Yehuda — with Reuven cut out entirely, though he at least receives *Ever Hayardein*.

### Nob & Givon Status

The second correction concerns the status of Nob and Givon. We have been emphasizing that the reason Nob and Givon do not have the status of a *Mikdash* is because they lack *makom hashechina* — the locus of God's concentrated presence — and therefore there is no singular place of *avodah*. Since God's presence is not more concentrated there than anywhere else, there is a *heter bamot*, and one may offer sacrifices outside the central *bamah*. This is the logic that undergirds the *heter bamot* during the Nob and Givon period.

A student raised the question about the *aron* at Nob and Givon. When Shilo was destroyed, the *aron* was taken captive by the Philistines. After it was returned, it resided in Kiryat Yearim, and eventually David moved it — but the *aron* was never reunited with the central *mizbeach*. The central altar and the *aron* were simply not in the same place during the Nob and Givon period, and that is precisely the point.

### Gilgal Transition

The situation at Gilgal during the first fourteen years of the conquest is somewhat different. Gilgal did have the *aron*, yet it also had a *heter bamot*. The reason there is distinct: the *Bnei Yisrael* had just entered the land, had not yet conquered and settled it, and everything remained in a state of transition. One might note a certain irony: in the *midbar*, the nation was wandering with no fixed destination, yet they maintained a central *Mishkan* with an *issur bamot*. Here, at the threshold of settlement, the very goal was to establish permanence — and yet the situation was still too unsettled, too provisional, to anchor a singular place of *avodah*. It is like having just moved into a new home with all the furniture still unplaced. So while the *heter bamot* at Gilgal and the *heter bamot* at Nob and Givon are both real, they rest on different conceptual foundations.

---

## Heter Bamot Source

### Ki Lo Basem

Four lines into the *daf*, the *Gemara* asks: *minan hani mili* — from where do we derive the *heter bamot* during the interim periods? The source is the *pasuk* in Devarim: *ki lo basem ad ata el hamenucha v'el hanachala* — "for you have not yet come to the resting place and to the inheritance." During the period of entering the land, it is *ish hayashar b'einav*, each person acts as seems right in his own eyes, and one may offer on the *bamot*. The logic is that so long as the nation has not arrived at the *menucha* and the *nachala*, the state of transition renders *bamot* permissible.

### Menucha/Nachala

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *ki lo basem ad ata el hamenucha v'el hanachala — el hamenucha zo Shilo, nachala zu Yerushalayim*. The *menucha* is Shilo and the *nachala* is Yerushalayim. But how do we derive from this that *bamot* were permitted in the interim between Shilo and Yerushalayim? *Lama chilkan* — why were they divided? The answer: *kedai litten heter bein zeh lazeh* — to signal that there is a *heter* between the two. The *nachala* has a connotation of perpetuity: once the *Bnei Yisrael* inherit Yerushalayim, it remains their permanent inheritance; even when the *Beis Hamikdash* is destroyed, the sanctity does not migrate elsewhere.

### Et Repetition Gap

There is something noteworthy in the formulation of the *pasuk*. The phrase is *el hamenucha v'el hanachala* — with the prefix *el* repeated before each term. Had the *pasuk* said simply *el hamenucha v'hanachala*, we might read the two as a single unified concept. But the repeated *el* signals two distinct, separate referents with a space between them. This extra *vav-el* implies a gap — the very gap occupied by Nob and Givon — during which *bamot* become permissible once again. Rashi, by contrast, understands *lama chilkan* as asking why the *pasuk* needed to mention Yerushalayim at all: if the *issur bamot* had commenced at Shilo and continued from that point forward in Jewish history, the *pasuk* could simply have said *ki lo basem el hamenucha*. The additional mention of Yerushalayim tells us that there was a *heter* between the two. Both readings converge on the same conclusion, though the precise mechanism differs.

---

## Ma'aser Sheni

### Reish Lakish Q

The *Mishna* teaches that when the *Bnei Yisrael* came to Nob and Givon, *kodshim kalim* were eaten *bechol arei Yisrael* — throughout all the cities of Israel. Since one could bring *shelamim* anywhere during the *heter bamot* period, *kodshim kalim* were accordingly eaten wherever they were offered. *Kodshei kodashim*, by contrast — such as a *chatas* — were eaten only within the defined courtyard-like space of the central *bamah*, assuming they were brought there at all.

Reish Lakish posed a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan: *ma'aser sheni nami lisni* — why does the *Mishna* not mention *ma'aser sheni*? The significance of this question depends on the *girsa* of the *Mishna*. Our *girsa* does not mention *ma'aser sheni* at all, which implies that *ma'aser sheni* was simply not consumed during the Nob and Givon period — that there was no relevant context for it. Rashi's *girsa*, however, reads that *kodshim kalim* and *ma'aser sheni* were eaten everywhere, which raises the question from the other direction: why are we not instead bringing *ma'aser sheni* specifically to Nob and Givon?

The core issue is that the concept of *ma'aser sheni* is bound up with eating *lifnei Hashem*. If there is no *makom hashechina* — no place of concentrated divine presence — during the Nob and Givon period, then there is no place to which *ma'aser sheni* can be brought. Two consequences are possible: either one does not eat it at all, or, since there is no uniquely designated place, one may eat it anywhere. This symmetry parallels the logic for *korbanot*: the permissibility of *korbanot* everywhere during *heter bamot* follows from the principle *bechol makom asher azkir et shemi* — wherever I cause My name to be mentioned — since no central location has greater claim than any other. Whether the same logic applies to *ma'aser sheni* — yielding universal permissibility rather than total suspension — is precisely what is under discussion.

### Aron Link

The *Gemara* offers an initial answer: *ma'aser sham sham me-aron ka-yalfi* — the word *sham* ("there") appears in connection with *ma'aser sheni*, and the same word appears in connection with the *aron*. By *ma'aser* it says *ve-achaltem sham*, and by the *aron* it says *ve-nasata sham et ha-aron*. The *gezerah shavah* teaches that eating *ma'aser sheni* requires the same *lifnei Hashem* presence associated with the *aron*. Since the *aron* was not in Nob and Givon, *ma'aser sheni* has no operative context there. The *Gemara* then states: *keivan de-aron lo hava, ma'aser nami lo hava* — since the *aron* was absent, *ma'aser sheni* was likewise inapplicable.

### Pesach Question

The *Gemara* immediately presses further: *ei hachi, Pesach ve-kodashim nami* — if that is so, then by the same logic, the *Pesach* offering and all *korbanot* should also be excluded. After all, the *pasuk* says *ve-zavachta shelamim ve-achalta sham* — "you shall slaughter *shelamim* and eat there" — and the word *sham* appears there as well, linking all *korbanot* to the same *aron*-presence requirement. The *Gemara* presses to its conclusion: *de-keivan de-aron lo hava, inhu nami lo hava* — since the *aron* was absent, they too should be inapplicable.

One might ask: why should *ma'aser sheni* be more bound to *lifnei Hashem* than *korbanot* are? Conceptually the distinction is compelling — *korbanot* are inherently offerings wherever offered, but *ma'aser sheni* involves a pilgrimage, a carrying-up to a place of divine presence, analogous to *olat re'iah*, which similarly would not apply to Nob and Givon. Nevertheless, once one invokes the *sham-sham* derivation, the logic extends to everything — and the *Gemara* acknowledges as much.

### R. Shimon View

The *Gemara* resolves the challenge by identifying whose position this *Mishna* represents: *da-amar lach ha-mani Rabbi Shimon hi* — the *Mishna* follows Rabbi Shimon's approach. Rabbi Shimon holds that what was practiced in Nob and Givon was highly restricted: *af tzibbur lo hikrivu ela Pesach ve-chovot she-kavu'a la-hem zman* — even the community brought nothing there except the *Pesach* and communal obligations that are fixed to a specific time.

Tosafot is careful to note that the exclusion of *ma'aser sheni* is not so much because of the specific logic of Rabbi Shimon regarding communal fixed obligations, but rather because of the view of Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* who dispute Rabbi Yehuda. Their position is that even when an individual comes to the *bamah gedolah*, he brings only *nedavot* — voluntary offerings — and not obligatory ones. A private *bamah* is for an individual like his own rooftop. On this view, *ma'aser behemah*, which is an individual obligation but not a communal fixed obligation, would not be brought to the *bamah gedolah*. And since *ma'aser dagan* is linked to *ma'aser behemah* by *hekesh* — *ve-itkish ma'aser dagan le-ma'aser behemah* — *ma'aser sheni* is excluded as well.

The reason, then, that *ma'aser sheni* is absent from Nob and Givon has nothing to do with the *lifnei Hashem* framework introduced via the *aron* — that avenue was abandoned by the *Gemara* because it would have swept away all *korbanot* as well. Instead, the exclusion flows from a systemic principle: during the period of *bamot*, the framework of individual obligation simply does not operate. Just as there is no *chatas* for an individual at that *bamah*, no *ma'aser sheni*.
