The open question — what the individual actually does with *ma'aser sheni* he cannot bring — remains. By a *korban* without a valid venue, the *korban* simply is not brought. But *ma'aser sheni* is not a *korban*; it is produce. Does it therefore spoil unused, or may it be consumed in any location since there is no operative central site? This is the long discussion in Tosafot engaging Rashi's position, and it remains unresolved.

The *Gemara* then notes: *michlal de-Rabbi Yehuda kareiv* — by implication, according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an individual may bring obligatory *korbanot* at the *bamah gedolah*, one would indeed eat *ma'aser sheni* at Nob and Givon. This is stated explicitly: Rabba bar bar Chana teaches that *ma'aser sheni u-ma'aser behemah* were eaten at Nob and Givon according to Rabbi Yehuda. The *bechor* is implicit in this as well, and Tosafot addresses it directly.

---

## Heter Bamot Duratio (III)

### Birah Concept

The *Gemara* then raises a further challenge against Rabbi Yehuda's position: *ve-ha ba'ya birah* — does it not require a *birah*? The term *birah* functions as a way of expressing the concept of *lifnei Hashem* — a site worthy of bearing God's presence before which *ma'aser sheni* may be consumed. Rashi explains: *de-chtiv lifnei Hashem Elokeichem* — the *pasuk* says "before the Lord your God," which implies that *ma'aser sheni* requires a place of concentrated divine presence, not merely any *bamah*.

The *Gemara* resolves this by citing a teaching of Rav Yosef: there are three places that qualify as *birah* — Shilo, Nob and Givon (counted together as one), and *beit olamim*, the permanent *Beis Hamikdash*. Rav Yosef both taught and explained this *baraita*: the designation of *birah* is for the purpose of eating *ma'aser sheni*, and this is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda.

This is a striking conclusion. Throughout the discussion, the working premise has been that Nob and Givon lack *makom hashechina* — that the absence of the *aron* and the presence of a *heter bamot* combine to deprive them of any concentrated divine presence. Yet here, at least for the purpose of *ma'aser sheni*, Nob and Givon are designated as a *birah* and deemed to qualify as *lifnei Hashem*. The tension is real: in a matter of moments, the *Gemara* will enumerate a lengthy list of rituals — *semichah*, *tenufah*, *hagashah*, blood application, and more — that do not apply in Nob and Givon because the location is not considered *lifnei Hashem*. And yet for *ma'aser sheni* it counts. The *Gemara* offers no explicit resolution of this asymmetry; it simply states it as fact.

One clarification follows from this analysis: the *birah* designation of Nob and Givon works for Rabbi Yehuda because he holds that obligations may be brought to the *bamah gedolah*. Those who disagree with him regarding *chovot* would not necessarily contest the *birah* status of Nob and Givon itself — they would simply say that the prohibition on individual obligatory *korbanot* prevents bringing *ma'aser sheni* regardless.

---

## Pasuk Interpretation (II)

### R. Yehuda Order

Returning to the *pasuk ki lo basem ad ata el hamenucha v'el hanachala*, the *Gemara* now surveys four distinct ways in which *tannaim* understand the referents of *menucha* and *nachala*. The first, already introduced above, is that of Rabbi Yehuda: *menucha zo Shilo, nachala zu Yerushalayim* — the *menucha* is Shilo and the *nachala* is Yerushalayim. This reading is sequential and tracks the chronology. The verse mentions the two resting places in order, and the repeated *el* signals the gap between them during which *bamot* are permissible.

### R. Shimon Reverse

Rabbi Shimon reverses the identification: *menucha zo Yerushalayim, nachala zo Shilo*. This reversal is not chronological — Shilo preceded Yerushalayim — and the *Gemara* accordingly asks why the *pasuk* does not simply say *el hanachala v'el hamenucha*, which would at least match the inverted order. The *Gemara* answers: *hachi ka'amar* — this is what the verse is saying. *Lo mibei menucha d'lo matisu* — not only have you not yet reached the ultimate resting place, namely Yerushalayim; *ella afilu nachala nami lo basem* — you have not even reached the temporary resting place of Shilo. It is a *kal va-chomer* formulation embedded in the *pasuk*. The *pasuk* leads with the more exalted destination to underscore that the lesser one has not been reached either. The rationale for calling Yerushalayim *menucha* is drawn from the *pasuk* in Tehillim: *zot menuchati adei ad, po eshev ki ivisiha* — "this is My resting place forever; here I will dwell for I have desired it." The rationale for calling Shilo *nachala* is that it was the site where Yehoshua divided the land: *vayechalek lahem Yehoshua vayapel lahem goral be-Shilo al pi Hashem*.

As for the designation of *nachala* for Shilo: the *Gemara* notes that it is slightly ironic, given the principle that *Yerushalayim lo nitchalkah la-shvatim* — Yerushalayim was never apportioned among the tribes. It is indeed a national *nachala*, belonging to no single tribe individually, which is precisely why it is the permanent inheritance.

### R. Yishmael Both=Shilo

The school of Rabbi Yishmael (*tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael*) offers yet another reading: *zo v'zo Shilo* — both terms, *menucha* and *nachala*, refer to Shilo alone. The *pasuk* says nothing about Yerushalayim. On this reading, the *heter bamot* continues after Shilo's destruction, and there is no scriptural marker for the resumption of *issur bamot* when Nob and Givon functioned. Rashi is compelled to explain that this opinion would have to hold that there was a *heter bamot* even after Yerushalayim is destroyed — since Yerushalayim enjoys no greater status than Shilo on this reading, and the destruction of Shilo reinstated *heter bamot*, so too would the destruction of Yerushalayim. This is quite a radical implication.

---

## Heter Bamot Duratio (III)

### Shilo Alone Issue

The *Gemara* raises a pointed difficulty against the *zo v'zo Shilo* reading: in Sefer Shmuel there is clear evidence that people were offering *korbanot* on *bamot* throughout the land during the period of Nob and Givon, without any record of objection or censure. This evidence is precisely what compels Rashi to say that the *zo v'zo Shilo* position must be holding that *bamot* remained permissible even after the destruction of Shilo — otherwise there would be no way to account for the unquestioned practice attested in Shmuel. The *Gemara* does not resolve this cleanly and moves on.

---

## Heter Bamot Duratio (III)n…

### Yerushalayim Alone

The fourth position, that of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, is addressed in the following section.

---

## Pasuk Interpretation (II)

### R. Shimon bar Yochai

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states: *zo v'zo Yerushalayim* — both *menucha* and *nachala* refer to Yerushalayim alone. The *pasuk* does not speak of Shilo as a resting place. The consequence is the mirror image of the *zo v'zo Shilo* position: if the verse is pointing exclusively to Yerushalayim, then *bamot* were permissible throughout the entire 369-year period of Shilo. The *Gemara* states this explicitly — *aval Shilo havay shari b'bamot* — and cites as evidence the episode in Sefer Shoftim where Manoach slaughtered a kid and brought a *minchah* upon the rock, without being corrected. If *bamot* were forbidden during the Shilo period, how could Manoach have done this? The *Gemara* answers that for the positions that hold *bamot* to have been forbidden during Shilo, this episode constitutes a *hora'at sha'ah* — a one-time exceptional ruling. The *Gemara* adds: *tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael ke-Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai* — the school of Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position, and the mnemonic is *mashkei gavra l'gavri* — that one scholar drew an entire school to follow his view. The *Gemara* then consolidates: *bishlama le-man d'amar menucha zo Shilo nachala zu Yerushalayim*, or even the reverse, at least the *pasuk* is mentioning two distinct locations, which accounts for the repeated *el*. But for those who say *zo v'zo Shilo* or *zo v'zo Yerushalayim*, the verse should have simply said *menucha ve-nachala* without the repeated *el* — and the *Gemara* simply states *kashya*, it remains a difficulty.

---

## Shchutei Chutz

### Rav Kahana

The *Gemara* now returns to the topic of *shchutei chutz*. The *Mishna* teaches that if an animal was sanctified during the period of *heter bamot* and then slaughtered outside the proper location during the period of *issur bamot*, one is not liable for *karet*. One transgresses, but *karet* does not apply.

Rav Kahana qualifies this: *lo shanu ela bi-shchita* — this leniency applies only to *shchita*, the slaughter. But *ha'alah* — the actual offering up of the animal on the *mizbeach* — is different. Even if the animal was sanctified during *heter bamot*, if one performs *ha'alah* outside the proper place during *issur bamot*, *karet nami mechayev* — one is liable for *karet*. His reasoning is based on the *pasuk*: *va'aleihem tomar* — "tell them," which he reads as demarcating the earlier discussion of *shchita* as distinct from the subsequent discussion of *ha'alah*. The leniency derived from the timing of sanctification applies only *al hasmuchim*, the earlier section on *shchita*, and not to the laws of *ha'alah*.

### Rava 4 Categories

Rava challenges this position on two grounds. First, *mi ktiv va'aleihem tomar? aleihem ktiv* — the verse actually says *aleihem*, "to them," referring to the *Bnei Yisrael*, not *va'aleihem*; the word cannot be parsed so as to create the division Rav Kahana requires. Second, Rava cites a *baraita* in which Rabbi Shimon enumerates four categories concerning the timing of sanctification and the timing of slaughter or offering:

The first category: sanctified during *issur bamot*, slaughtered and offered outside during *issur bamot* — one violates a positive commandment and a negative commandment and is liable for *karet*. The second: sanctified during *heter bamot*, slaughtered and offered outside during *issur bamot* — one violates a positive and a negative commandment, but there is no *karet*. The third: sanctified during *issur bamot*, slaughtered and offered outside during *heter bamot* — one violates an *aseh*, the obligation of *ve-havaysem shammah* (since the animal was sanctified when a central place existed and was not brought there), but no negative commandment is violated. The fourth: sanctified during *heter bamot* and slaughtered and offered outside during *heter bamot* — *patur mi-klum*, entirely exempt.

### Ha'alah No Karet

The second category is decisive: it states explicitly that even when the animal was sanctified during *heter bamot* and subsequently offered (*ha'alah*) during *issur bamot*, there is no *karet* — directly contradicting Rav Kahana's position. *Tiyuvta de-Rav Kahana tiyuvta* — this is a definitive refutation of Rav Kahana.

### Issur to Heter

The third category also merits attention. If the animal was sanctified during *issur bamot* — for example, during the Shilo period when a central place existed — and then Shilo was destroyed and the owner offered it in his backyard during the now-reinstated *heter bamot*, the owner violates an *aseh*. The *aseh* is derived from the verse *ve-havaysem shammah*: since the animal was sanctified at a time when a central location was available, one was obligated to bring it there. That the destruction of Shilo was not the owner's fault is irrelevant; the *aseh* was activated at the moment of sanctification. Nevertheless, since *ha'alah* was performed during a time of *heter bamot*, no negative commandment is violated. One might note the curious use of the word *patur* for the fourth category — the *Gemara* could have said *muttar* — and this may reflect an open question about the theological valence of *sha'at heter bamot*: was offering on *bamot* then a positive religious act, or merely a concession?

---

## Lifnei Hashem Rituals

### Semicha/Tzafona

The *Mishna* enumerates the differences between a *bamas yachid*, a private altar, and a *bamas tzibur*, the public communal *bamah* at Nob and Givon. As noted above, this requires an important correction of what may have been stated in a previous session: all the rituals about to be listed did apply at Nob and Givon. The divide is not between Shilo/Yerushalayim on one side and Nob and Givon on the other, but between Nob and Givon (and Shilo and the *Beis Hamikdash*) on one side and the private *bamah* on the other. Nob and Givon, despite the absence of the *aron* and despite the *heter bamot*, are nonetheless considered *lifnei Hashem* for these ritual purposes — consistent with what was established above regarding *ma'aser sheni* and the *birah* concept.

*Semichah* — the laying of hands upon an offering — is derived from the phrase *lifnei Hashem v'samach*; it requires *lifnei Hashem* and therefore applied only at a central *bamah*. *Shechitas tzafona* — the requirement that an *olah* be slaughtered on the northern side of the altar — derives from *tzafona lifnei Hashem*; it likewise requires the context of *lifnei Hashem*. *Tenufah* — the waving of an offering — derives from *ve-henif ha-kohen lifnei Hashem* by the *minchah*; again, *lifnei Hashem* is explicit.

### Blood Application

*Matanos saviv* — the specific manner of blood application, whether around the altar or at two opposite corners — derives from *ve-zarak al ha-mizbeach saviv*. While *lifnei Hashem* does not appear directly in this verse, Rashi cites a proximate verse that does contain the phrase, and the word *ha-mizbeach* — with the definite article — implies the central communal *mizbeach* specifically. *Hagashah* — the bringing of the *minchah* to the altar — derives from *higishah el ha-mizbeach*, again pointing to the central *mizbeach*.

### Kohen Ritual

The requirement that the *avodah* be performed by a *kohen* is derived from *ve-zarak ha-kohen et ha-dam al mizbach Hashem* — *mizbach Hashem*, the altar of Hashem, which implies the context of the central *bamah*. *Bigdei sharet* — the priestly vestments — must be worn *le-shares bakodesh*, in the service of the holy precincts; and *klei sharet*, the service vessels, likewise must be used *ba-kodesh*. The concept of *bakodesh* thus constitutes a third operative category alongside *lifnei Hashem* and *ha-mizbeach* — and it applies to the central communal *bamah* but not the private one.

### Odor & Washing

*Reiach nichoach* — the concept that an offering rises as a pleasing aroma — is tied to the phrase *l'reiach nichoach l'Hashem*. This is a striking point: one would naturally assume that any offering to God, wherever made, constitutes a *reiach nichoach*. Yet the *Gemara* treats this as a function of the central *bamah* specifically, not merely of any *korban*. The *kodesh* designation, it seems, belongs to the place rather than solely to the offering. *Mechitza badamim* — the line marking the midpoint of the *mizbeach*, whereby some bloods are applied above and others below — derives from *ve-asah ha-reshes ad chatzi ha-mizbeach*, a law specific to the central *mizbeach*. *Richutz yadayim* — the washing of hands before the *avodah* — derives from *u-ve-korvam el ha-mizbeach yirchatzu*, once again specifying the central *mizbeach*.

A parenthetical dispute is interjected: Rabbi Yehuda holds that there was no *minchah* brought in a private *bamah* at all — only animal sacrifices qualify, based on the verse *ve-zavachta shelamim*, which speaks of *zevachim* and not *menachos*. Rav Sheshes links *menachos* and *ofor* offerings together: according to whoever holds that there was a *minchah* in a private *bamah*, there were also bird sacrifices; and according to whoever holds there was no *minchah*, there were no bird sacrifices either, since *melikah* is not a form of *shechita* and the verse speaks of *zevachim* specifically.

---

## Private vs. Public

### Rami: How Sanctified

Having enumerated the list of rituals that applied at the central *bamah* but not the private, the *Gemara* now turns to a nuanced question raised by Rami bar Chama. Are these distinctions determined by *where* the offering was brought, or by *how* it was sanctified — that is, for what type of *bamah* was it originally designated? Rami bar Chama's initial position (*ikka d'amri*) is that the distinctions follow the manner of sanctification. An animal sanctified for a *bamah gedolah* and brought there follows the full complement of rules; an animal sanctified for a *bamah ketanah* would not be subject to those rules even if it happened to be brought to the *bamah gedolah*.

### Chaza v'Shoke

Rami bar Chama brings a *baraita* in support: *chaze v'shoke* — the breast and thigh portions given to the *kohanim* — and *trumat lachmei todah* — the bread portions separated from a *todah* offering — apply to *kodshei bamah gedolah* and do not apply to *kodshei bamah ketanah*. The language of the *baraita* — *kodshei bamah gedolah* and *kodshei bamah ketanah*, "sanctifications of the great bamah" and "sanctifications of the small bamah" — appears to emphasize how the item was sanctified, not where it was ultimately offered. This would seem to support the view that status tracks sanctification rather than location.

The *Gemara*, however, deflects: *eima noheig b'vama gedolah v'eino noheig b'vama ketanah* — read the *baraita* as saying it applies *at* the great *bamah* and does not apply *at* the small *bamah*. The word *kodshei* may be imprecise, and the *baraita* may simply be specifying location. This reading neutralizes the proof.

---

## Private vs. Public (II)

### R. Elazar Absorption

Rava then cites the position of Rabbi Elazar, which bears directly on this question: *olat bamas yachid she-hichnisa bifnim kaltu ha-mechitzot* — if one had an *olah* that had been sanctified as a *bamas yachid* offering and brought it inside to Nob and Givon, the *mechitzot* — the enclosures of the central *bamah* — absorb it. The animal is now treated as belonging to the category of the central *bamah*, not the private one. This affirms that location, not sanctification, determines status — at least once the animal has been brought inside.

The second version of Rami bar Chama's position is in direct tension with Rabbi Elazar: Rami holds that even if a *kodshei bamah ketanah* is brought to the *bamah gedolah*, the rules pertaining to blood application — *mechitza badamim* — do not apply, because status tracks sanctification. Rabbi Elazar holds the opposite: once inside, it is fully absorbed. This remains a genuine dispute.

---

## Removal Reversion

### Zeira Question

Rabbi Zeira poses the final question of the *daf*, left unresolved: *olat bamas yachid she-hichnisa bifnim ve-hotzia la-chutz* — what if the animal sanctified as a *bamas yachid* offering was brought inside Nob and Givon and then removed? *Mai?* — what is the law? Two possibilities present themselves. *Mi amrinan keivan de-ayela kalta le-mechitzta* — do we say that the moment it was brought inside, the *mechitzot* absorbed and defined it, such that removing it constitutes an invalidation? Or perhaps — *keivan de-hadar, hadar* — once it is removed, it reverts to its prior status as a *bamas yachid* offering and the stricter rules no longer apply? The *daf* closes with this question unresolved, to be taken up in the final *daf* of the *masechet*.

---

---

# Zevachim 120

## Bamah Yachid into Bamah…

### Olah Transfer Question

The final daf of *Zevachim* opens with a question posed by Rav Zeira on the last line of 119b. The *masechta* has been concluding its discussion of the transition of the *mikdash* through its various historical stations — *Mishkan*, *Gilgal*, *Shilo*, *Nob*, *Gibeon*, and finally the *Beis Hamikdash* — and with it the laws governing sacrifices brought at a *bamah gedolah*, the central public altar, as opposed to a *bamah yachid*, a private altar in one's own domain. Among the distinctions noted in the *mishnah* is the requirement at a *bamah gedolah* to give the *chazeh* and *shok* to the *kohen* with *tenufah*, a requirement that does not apply at a *bamah yachid*.

Against this backdrop, Rav Zeira raises the following question: *olas bamas yachid she'hechnisa lifnim ve'hotzia lachutz mahu* — if one had an *olah* designated for a private *bamah*, brought it into the environs of the *bamah gedolah*, and then removed it, what is the law? The *gemara* frames the question as a binary: *mi amrinan keivan de'ayal katla mechitza* — do we say that once it entered, the *mechitza* of the *bamah gedolah* absorbed and redefined it, so that it now carries the status of a sacrifice brought at the *bamah gedolah*? Or do we say *keivan de'hadar hadar* — once removed, it simply reverts to its status as a *bamas yachid* offering?

### Rashi on Chazeh Shok

The *gemara* does not itself spell out the *nafka mina* of Rav Zeira's question, and Rashi and Tosafot understand the case quite differently. Rashi reads the case as one where the animal was slaughtered outside, then its parts were brought into the *bamah gedolah*'s environs, and then taken back out. On his reading, the practical question is *minhag bedin kodshei bama gedola lit'on terumas chazeh veshok* — whether the sacrifice has now acquired the status of a *bamah gedolah* offering and must have the *chazeh* and *shok* waved and given to the *kohen*. This interpretation does face an internal difficulty: the case involves an *olah*, which ordinarily has no *chazeh* and *shok* at all, since the entire animal is burnt. Rashi appears to be reading the case more naturally as a *shelamim* rather than an *olah*, even though the *gemara*'s language specifies *olah*.

### Tosafot Alternative Case

Tosafot offer an alternative reading that sidesteps this difficulty. On their reading, the animal was not yet slaughtered. It was sanctified for a *bamas yachid*, then brought alive into the environs of the *bamah gedolah*, and then slaughtered there. In that configuration, the *nafka minas* become numerous and sharper: does it now require a *kohen*, *bigdei kehunah*, *semicha*, slaughter in the north (*tzafon*), *kabbalas hadam* according to the stricter *bamah gedolah* standards? All of these requirements attach to *kodshei kodashim* and other *bamah gedolah* sacrifices, and the question is whether entry into the *bamah gedolah*'s precincts is sufficient to impose them.

### Rabba vs Rav Yosef

The *gemara* asks whether Rav Zeira's question is simply a replay of the dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef, as found in *Me'ila*. The *mishnah* there states that *kodshei kodashim* slaughtered in the south of the *azarah* — where they are not supposed to be slaughtered, since *kodshei kodashim* require the north — nonetheless remain subject to *me'ila*. The animal, despite having been slaughtered in the wrong place, has not lost its sanctified character to the degree that it would exit the framework of the *mikdash* entirely.

The *gemara* then records a dispute about what happens if such limbs were placed on the *mizbeach* and then removed — or, depending on the *girsa*, whether they may be placed on the *mizbeach* in the first place. There is significant uncertainty about the correct textual reading here, and the *gemara* acknowledges it. On Rashi's *girsa*, Rabba holds *yerdu* — the limbs must be brought down — while Rav Yosef holds the opposite. The *gemara* asks: is Rav Zeira's question simply this dispute restated?

### Mechitza Analysis

The *gemara* answers that no, Rav Zeira's question cannot be collapsed into the Rabba–Rav Yosef dispute. The question can in fact be posed from either direction: it remains open regardless of which position one holds in that debate.

On Rashi's *girsa*, Rabba says *yerdu* — the limbs must come down from the *mizbeach* — because the principle *mizbeach mekadesh* applies only when the object is fit for the *mizbeach*: *d'chazi leh mekadesh d'lo chazi leh lo mekadesh*. Something slaughtered in the south is not fully fit from the perspective of the *mizbeach*, and so the *mizbeach* does not redefine its status. But one could argue that the *mechitza* of the *bamah gedolah* operates differently — *aval mechitza af al gav d'lo chazi leh kalta*. The entry into the *bamah gedolah*'s precincts, even of something not originally designated for it, may suffice to redefine the sacrifice's status, because this is not a case of something fundamentally unfit. What was brought in from a *bamas yachid* was entirely valid — it was simply sanctified for a different context. That distinction may cause the *mechitza* to function differently from the *mizbeach*.

Conversely, even according to Rav Yosef, who says the limbs may stay on the *mizbeach*, the cases may diverge in the opposite direction. Rav Yosef's ruling applies where *chad makom hu* — it is all one place, all within the *beis hamikdash* environs. A limb slaughtered in the south but placed on the *mizbeach* has moved within a single sacred domain. But *hacha d'trei mekomot nin-hu* — here we are dealing with two fundamentally distinct places: the private *bamah* and the *bamah gedolah*. Perhaps in that case, even Rav Yosef would concede that crossing between two locations does not trigger a redefinition of status. *O dilma lo shena* — or perhaps it makes no difference, and either way the principle applies.

### Limbs Removed Question

The *gemara* then clarifies the relationship between its two discussions. What Rabba and Rav Yosef each knew clearly — their respective positions in the *me'ila* case — was actually the unresolved question that Rav Yannai had posed. It was Rav Yannai who originally asked the question that Rabba and Rav Yosef subsequently came down on different sides of.

Rav Yannai's question was: *evrei olat bamas yachid she'alu lamizbeach veyardu mahu* — if the limbs of an *olah* from a *bamas yachid* were placed on the *mizbeach* of the *bamah gedolah* and then removed, what is the law? May they be restored to the *mizbeach*, or not?

Rashi explains the analogy more fully. Something slaughtered at a private *bamah* is, from the perspective of the *bamah gedolah*, analogous to *chutz limkomo*: it was not slaughtered within the *bamah gedolah*'s precincts. The analogy to *kodshei kodashim* slaughtered in the south is that in both cases, the slaughter occurred in the wrong location from the *bamah gedolah*'s vantage point — even though in our case the slaughter at the *bamas yachid* was entirely permitted and *kasher* in its own right. Once the limbs are on the *mizbeach* of the *bamah gedolah*, has that location redefined them, such that they may remain or be restored? Or does the *bamah gedolah* view them as having originated in the wrong place, and require their removal?

### Fire Seizure Condition

The *gemara* introduces a conditional refinement. *Heicha delo mashla bahen haur lo tiba'ei lach* — where the fire has not yet seized the limbs, there is presumably no real question: they have not yet become *lachmo shel mizbeach*, the altar's own consumed matter, and should therefore either be brought down or not be restored. The genuine uncertainty arises specifically in the case where the fire has already taken hold: *ki tiba'ei lach heicha demashla bahen haur*. Once the fire has seized the limbs, does that irreversible physical act settle the question of their status? Or does it remain an open question even then?

### Teiku Resolution

The *gemara* leaves both questions unresolved: *teiku*. Whether the *mechitza* or environs of the *bamah gedolah* redefine the status of a *bamas yachid* sacrifice that enters its precincts, and whether fire's seizure of limbs on the *mizbeach* of the *bamah gedolah* creates a definitive redefinition — both stand without answer. It must be acknowledged that these analogies are difficult. The *gemara* is clearly pressing a connection between the *mizbeach mekadesh* discussions of an earlier *perek* and the present question about the *mechitza* of the *bamah gedolah*, but precisely why one set of principles should differ from the other is not spelled out with full clarity, and the comparison to the *me'ila* case of *kodshei kodashim* slaughtered in the south adds yet another layer of complexity to what was already a conceptually layered question.

---

## Nighttime Slaughter Deba…

### Elazar's Contradiction

The *gemara* turns to a cleaner question: is it permitted to perform *shechita* at night at a *bamas yachid*? Given how few rules seem to apply there, one might think night should pose no problem — yet the *gemara* records a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about exactly this point, and their debate turns on how to resolve a contradiction that Rabbi Elazar noted between two *psukim*.

Rabbi Elazar observed that the verses in Shmuel I tell a story with an apparent internal inconsistency. Shaul's people had pursued the Philistines in battle, and upon their victory the people took from the booty and slaughtered cattle, eating *al hadam* — before the blood had been properly dealt with. Shaul rebuked them: *begadetem* — you have transgressed. He commanded: *golu elai hayom even gedolah* — roll to me a great stone, apparently to serve as an altar. He then instructed the people, *higishu elai ish shoro ve'ish seyo ushchattem bazeh va'achaltem velo techte'u l'Hashem le'echol el hadam* — bring each person his ox and his sheep, slaughter here, and eat without sinning before God by eating over the blood. The verse then records that the people brought their cattle and slaughtered them *halailah* — that night.

The apparent contradiction is this: Shaul's initial command says *hayom* — today, during the day — which implies an emphasis that the slaughter must occur while it is still daytime. Yet the verse reports the actual slaughter occurring at night. How are we to reconcile these two verses?

### Chullin vs Kodshim

One resolution, attributed to one of the disputants (Rav or Shmuel), is to distinguish between *chullin* and *kodshim*. The daytime slaughter was the sanctified *korban* component — even at a *bamas yachid*, *shechita* of *kodshim* requires the day. The nighttime slaughter was simply of non-sanctified, profane meat, which has no such requirement. On this reading, even a *bamas yachid* requires that *kodshim* be slaughtered during the day.

### Central vs Private Alt

The other resolution distinguishes not between *chullin* and *kodshim*, but between sacrifices designated for the *bamah gedolah* and those designated for the *bamah ketanah*. Some of the people's offerings had been sanctified with the intent of bringing them to the central *bamah*; others were designated for a private *bamah*. The nighttime slaughter was for *kodshei bamas yachid*, while the daytime slaughter was for those designated for the *bamah gedolah* — and even if they were ultimately to be slaughtered at a private *bamah*, since they had been sanctified with the *bamah gedolah* in mind, the person was particular to perform the *shechita* during the day. This resolution thus concedes that a *bamas yachid* itself has no daytime requirement, while the other resolution insists that it does.

---

## Flaying Requirement

### Rav's Position

The *gemara* next records a dispute about another potential requirement at a *bamas yachid*: *hafsheit ve-nituach*, the flaying of the animal and its dismemberment into prescribed limbs before placing them on the altar. Rav rules *ein te'una hafshait ve-nituach* — an *olah* at a private *bamah* does not require flaying and dismembering. The whole animal may simply be placed on the fire, skin and all.

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. He rules *te'una hafshait ve-nituach* — even at a private *bamah*, the *olah* requires flaying and dismembering before being burnt.

### Yose HaGlili Source

Both positions root themselves in the *baraisa* of Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who states: *olah she'hikrivu Yisrael b'midbar ein te'una hafshait ve-nituach* — the *olot* that Israel brought in the wilderness, before the giving of the laws in *parshat Vayikra*, did not require flaying and dismembering. The technical requirement of *hafsheit ve-nituach* appears only in *Vayikra*, in the laws given at *Ohel Moed*: *she'ein hafsheit ve-nituach ela me-Ohel Moed va-eilech* — flaying and dismembering apply only from the time of *Ohel Moed* onward.

### Vayikra Application

This historical observation sets up the dispute. The question is whether, once the laws of *Vayikra* were given, they apply universally to all *korbanot* — including those of a *bamas yachid* — or whether they were directed specifically at the central sanctuary context. Rabbi Yochanan holds *lo shna bevama gedola ve-lo shna bevama ketana* — once *Vayikra* was given, the requirement applies regardless of whether one is offering at a *bamah gedolah* or a *bamah ketanah*. Rav holds the opposite: *bevama gedola in, bevama ketana lo* — the *Vayikra* legislation, situated as it is in the context of the *Mishkan*, applies to the central location but should not be assumed to extend to private *bamot*. One might also frame this by noting that the model for a *bamas yachid* predates *matan Torah* — it is rooted in the *Bnei Noach* mode of sacrifice — and so later Sinaitic specifications need not carry over.

### Baraita Support

The *gemara* records that the *baraisa* explicitly supports Rabbi Yochanan's position. Among the things it lists as *identical* between a *bamah gedolah* and a *bamah ketanah* is *hafsheit ve-nituach* — flaying and dismembering. The *baraisa*'s placement of *hafsheit ve-nituach* in the column of shared requirements, not the column of differences, is a direct proof for Rabbi Yochanan over Rav.

---

## Altar Distinctions

### Central Altar Only

The *baraisa* provides a structured accounting of the differences and similarities between the two types of altars. Those elements unique to the *bamah gedolah* include: *keren* (the horns of the altar), *kevesh* (the ramp), *yesod* (the base), *ribu'a* (the square shape), and *kiyyor ve-kanno* (the washbasin and its stand). None of these apply to a *bamah ketanah*. The common thread running through each of these requirements is that they are derived from contexts involving the phrase *lifnei Hashem* — before God. The presence of the Divine, the *Shechina*, is what generates these additional demands, and since a private *bamah* does not carry that same dimension of *lifnei Hashem*, these structural requirements fall away.

### Chazeh Ve-Shok

Similarly, *chazeh ve-shok* — the chest and foreleg given to the *kohen* — applies at the *bamah gedolah* and not at the *bamah ketanah*. Here too, Rashi emphasizes that the verse uses the language *lifnei Hashem*, tying this requirement to the divine presence associated with the central altar. This also clarifies the conceptual distinction: it is not merely a question of whether the *bamah* is public or private, but whether it carries the quality of being *lifnei Hashem*, of standing before God in a designated, consecrated space.

### Shared Requirements

The *baraisa* then enumerates what is the same at both: *shechita*, which must be performed in both contexts — the animal cannot be killed by other means; *hafsheit ve-nituach*, flaying and dismembering, as established by the preceding dispute; the role of *dam*, the blood, which at both types of *bamah* is the act that permits the limbs to be consumed (*dam matir*) and which also has the capacity to create *pigul* through improper intent (*dam mifagel*). The *baraisa* thus establishes *chutz lizmano* as operative even at a *bamah ketanah*, even though *chutz limkomo* is not. Blemishes (*mumim*) disqualify at both, and the time-frame for eating the meat operates at both as well.

---

## Time at Private Altars

### Initial Question

The *mishnah* states that *notar*, *hazman*, and *tum'ah* apply equally to both the *bamah gedolah* and the *bamah ketanah*. The *gemara* then asks: how do we actually know this? The question is not merely academic. The *baraisa* itself frames the challenge: *minalan la'asot zman bevama ketanah kevama gedolah* — from where do we derive that the time-based disqualifications that operate at a *bamah gedolah* also operate at a *bamah ketanah*?

### Space-Time Logic

The logical challenge to importing time restrictions into a *bamas yachid* is powerful. At a *bamah ketanah*, there is no concept of *chutz limkomo* — space is unrestricted. You can slaughter and eat the offering anywhere; there are no sacred precincts to exit. If the dimension of space carries no restrictions at a *bamas yachid*, why should the dimension of time be different? The argument runs: *mah yotze kasher bevama* — just as leaving the proper precincts creates no problem at a private *bamah*, so too *af lan kasher bevama* — sleeping over the meat should likewise create no problem. The parallel between spatial and temporal boundaries seems to argue for complete symmetry: if one falls away, so should the other.

### Bird Kal Vachomer

One might counter with a *kal vachomer* from birds. At the *Beis Hamikdash*, blemishes do not disqualify birds brought as offerings. And yet, time disqualifies birds just as it disqualifies other offerings. The inference is: *mah ofot she'ein mum posel bahen zman posel bahen* — birds, for whom blemishes are not a *pesul*, are nonetheless subject to the time restriction. So if at a *bamas yachid*, blemishes *are* a *pesul* — which the *baraisa* has already established — then by *kal vachomer*, *kodshei bamas yachid* should certainly be subject to the time restriction. If something more lenient (birds, where blemishes don't disqualify) still has time restrictions, then something stricter (a *bamas yachid* where blemishes do disqualify) should certainly have them.

### Objection to Comparison

The *gemara* rejects this *kal vachomer*. *Mah le'ofot sheken ein zar kasher bahen, tomar bamah ketanah shezar kasher bah* — birds in the *mikdash* have a stringency that *bamas yachid* does not share: bird offerings require a *kohen*. A *zar*, a non-priest, cannot perform the *melikah* of a bird offering. At a *bamas yachid*, by contrast, a *zar* is entirely valid. The greater demands placed on bird offerings in the *mikdash* context may well be why time remains so significant for them, and it does not necessarily follow that a *bamas yachid* — where even priesthood is irrelevant — shares the same framework. Once one concedes that the entire *kohen*-based structure does not apply, one cannot confidently draw any inference from the bird case to the *bamas yachid* case.

### Inclusive 'Torah'

The *gemara* resolves the question by appeal to the verse: *zos toras zevach hashelamim* — this is the *torah* of the *shelamim* offering. The word *Torah* is understood as an inclusive term, encompassing all of the laws that govern sacrifices and apply as a unified whole. When the Torah says *zos toras*, it signals that the disqualifying factors for *shelamim* — including the time-based ones — apply comprehensively, both at the *bamah gedolah* and at the *bamah ketanah*. This textual derivation bypasses the failed *kal vachomer* entirely and provides a direct source for *laasot zman bevama ketanah kezman bevama gedolah* — applying the same time restrictions at the minor private altar as at the central public one.

---

## Time Over Space

### Masechet Conclusion

With the derivation from *zos toras zevach hashelamim*, *masechet Zevachim* comes to a close. *Hadran alach perek chatas uslika lach masechet Zevachim.* The conclusion is, on its surface, a technical halakhic point: even where space does not bind — where an offering may be slaughtered and consumed anywhere without restriction — time still binds. *Notar* and the related time disqualifications remain operative even at a *bamas yachid*. Space and time are not symmetrical in the halakha of *bamot*; the liberalization of one does not entail the liberalization of the other.

### Shabbat Supremacy

There is something fitting, perhaps even intentional, about ending this great *masechta* on this note. The *kedushat hazman* — the sanctity of time — precedes and supersedes *kedushat hamakom*, the sanctity of space. *Shabbat* preceded the *mikdash* chronologically: the six days of creation culminate in the sanctity of the seventh day long before any *mikdash* is built. And the Torah consistently juxtaposes *Shabbat* and *mikdash* to make the same point: one does not violate *Shabbat* in order to build the *mikdash*. The *mikdash*, the supreme expression of spatial sanctity, yields to *Shabbat*, the supreme expression of temporal sanctity.

### Universal Accessibility

There is a further dimension. The *kedushah* of time is universally accessible. *Shabbat* comes to everyone equally — it cannot be entered or exited based on status, lineage, or geography. The *kedushah* of space, by contrast, is graduated and restricted: only *kohanim* enter the *azarah*, only the *Kohen Gadol* enters the *kodesh hakodashim*, and even ordinary Israelites had limited access. The fact that *masechet Zevachim* closes with a ruling that even where space has no hold, time still does, may be read as a statement about what is most fundamental in the structure of Jewish sanctity. Space can be opened up, as it was in the era of *heter bamot*. Time cannot. The *masechta* has been completed; tomorrow we begin *Menachot*.

---

---

# Menachot 2

## Opening & Overview

### Greeting & Masechet Intro

We begin a new *masechet*: Menachot, starting with *daf* 2. The first *mishna* is directly parallel to the first *mishna* in Zevachim, and the themes of the two tractates are deeply intertwined.

### Menachot Contents

Menachot deals with all of the grain sacrifices, and because it is quite a large *masechet* — comparable in scope to Zevachim — a range of additional topics manages to come up along the way. The *Omer*, for instance, is itself a type of grain sacrifice, and its attendant laws arise naturally. But through digression, there is also a fascinating section in the middle of the tractate devoted to *Tefillin*, *Mezuzah*, and *Tzitzit*. Other subjects will emerge as well.

---

## Mishna: Intent & Validity

### Shelo Lishman Principle

The *mishna* opens: *Kol ha-menachot she-nikmetzu shelo lishman kesherot ela shelo alu la-be'alim leshem chovah* — all *menachot* that were taken with the wrong intent are still valid, yet do not count toward the owner's obligation. If a *kohen* performed the *kemitzah* — the taking of the handful — with the wrong intent (and Rashi emphasizes here, as he did in Zevachim, that intent means articulated intent rather than a mere passing thought), the *mincha* as a *korban* remains fully valid: the *kohanim* may burn the *kometz* on the altar and eat the *shirayim*. However, if the owner had taken a vow to bring this *mincha*, that vow is not discharged.

### Exceptions: Chatat & Ken…

There are two exceptions: the *minchat chotei* and the *minchat kenaot*. Just as in Zevachim the *chatat* is exceptional — because a sin offering that becomes detached from its particular owner loses its entire purpose — so too here. The *minchat chotei* is a grain offering brought as an atonement. There are sacrifices that operate on a sliding scale (*oleh ve-yored*): certain oaths and certain cases of *tumah* allow a person of limited means to descend from the animal offering to a bird offering, and if they cannot afford even that, they bring a *mincha*. This *mincha* is a substitute for a *chatat*, and therefore carries the same *halacha*: if it is performed *shelo lishmo*, it is fully invalidated and must be destroyed rather than consumed. Similarly, the *minchat kenaot* — the *mincha* of the *sotah*, brought to determine whether she has committed adultery — is intrinsically linked to a specific individual and a specific determination. If it is not performed *lishmo*, it too is fully invalidated.

### Stamah & Explicit Intent

A further point carried over from Zevachim: *stamah* — unexplicated intent — is treated as valid. The problem arises only when there is explicitly wrong intent. As for what constitutes *shelo lishmo*, the most straightforward form is having in mind a different owner (*shinui be'alim*). But the more conceptually central form of *shelo lishmo* is having in mind a different *korban* — a different type of sacrifice. With animal sacrifices this is relatively easy to visualize: one might slaughter an *olah* while thinking it is a *shelamim* or a *chatat*. With a *mincha*, the question of what "wrong type" means will become a central issue in the *Gemara*.

---

## Four Services & Intent

### Parallel Services

The *mishna* is not limited to the *kemitzah* alone. The four *avodot* of a *mincha* are explicitly paralleled to the four *avodot* of an animal sacrifice. *Shechita* corresponds to *kemitzah*; catching the blood in a vessel corresponds to placing the *kometz* into a vessel; conveying the blood to the *mizbeach* corresponds to conveying the *kometz*; and sprinkling the blood corresponds to placing the *kometz* on the altar. The verse does not make this parallel explicit, but the Sages derived it. Therefore, just as we started with *shechita* in Zevachim, here we start with *kemitzah*, and just as all four acts in the animal sacrifice can be affected by wrong intent, so too *natan bi-kli* — placing in the vessel — *ve-halach* — the conveyance — and *ve-hiktir* — the burning — performed *shelo lishman* carry the same *halacha*: the *korban* is valid but the owners do not fulfill their obligation.

### Double Intent Cases

The *mishna* also addresses scenarios of double intent: *lishman ve-shelo lishman* or *shelo lishman ve-lishman* — where one's intent is partly correct and partly not. The ruling is *pesulah*: as long as the wrongful intent is present, whether it comes first or second, it invalidates the relevant aspect. The case of *lishman ve-shelo lishman* described in the *mishna* is: if one says this is a *minchat chotei* — which, as we have seen, requires *lishmo* — and simultaneously thinks it is also a *minchat nedava*, or vice versa, the wrong intent is operative and the result is invalidation.

### Oven/Fried Example

As a preview of where the *Gemara* will take us: the scenario of *shelo lishmo* for an ordinary *minchat nedava* is not about confusing a *mincha* with a *shelamim* or an *olah* — that would be almost nonsensical. Rather, it involves confusing one physical type of *mincha* with another. If, for example, a *ma'afeh tanur* — a baked oven *mincha* — is being offered and the *kohen* intends it as though it were a *marcheshes* — a deep-fried, bubbly *mincha* — that constitutes *shelo lishmo* for this purpose. The *Gemara* will explore whether such an intent can even be meaningful given the obvious physical reality in front of the *kohen*, but that is the scenario the *mishna* has in mind when it discusses double intent for an ordinary *minchat nedava*: *lishmo* as a *minchat chotei* and *shelo lishmo* as a *minchat nedava*, or the reverse. In such a case, what makes the intent "wrong" is not that anyone confuses a *mincha* with an animal sacrifice, but that the purpose — sin-expiation versus free-will — differs.

---

## Ela & Implications

### Use of Ela

The *Gemara* poses a stylistic question about the *mishna*: *l'mai li l'misnei ela* — why does the *mishna* use the word *ela* ("except") rather than simply saying *ve-lo* ("and not")? The *mishna* could have said the *menachot* are valid and did not count for the owners; instead it emphasizes that they are fully valid, *except* that the owners' obligation is unfulfilled. The force of *ela* is to underscore that the *mincha* as an object — as a *korban* — is entirely *kosher*. The unfulfilled obligation of the owner is a real and important point, but it is presented as a qualification of an otherwise complete and valid sacrifice, not as a general diminishment of status.

### No Multiple Invalidations

This emphasis has a practical implication: *ve-asur li-shunuyei* — one is forbidden to add further wrongful intent. One might reason: now that this *korban* has already been affected by one instance of *shelo lishmo*, what is the harm in yet another? The answer is that no: two acts of *shelo lishmo* do not combine to produce a *lishmo*. More fundamentally, once the *mishna* declares the *mincha* entirely and intrinsically *kosher*, the same standards apply to it as to any other *kosher* *mincha*. Its elevated status is not compromised; one is not released from the requirement to have proper intent for subsequent acts simply because one *shelo lishmo* thought has already occurred. This is analogous to a principle found elsewhere: if someone breaks their fast by eating inadvertently, the *Gemara* does not conclude they may now eat freely. Even when a status has been technically compromised, that does not license further violations — and certainly not here, where the *mishna* insists the *korban* itself remains fully intact.

### Rava's Proof

This principle is supported by Rava: *olah she-shachatah shelo lishmo asur lizrok damah shelo lishmo* — if an *olah* was slaughtered with wrong intent, it is still forbidden to sprinkle the blood with wrong intent. The fact that one act was performed *shelo lishmo* does not grant a license to continue doing so. The *Gemara* offers two grounds for this principle: *sevara* — pure logic (*mishum d'shani bah kol hani, lishnei bah pneisa?* — just because you made one mistake you would make another?) — and a verse: *motza sefasecha tishmor ve-asisa ka'asher nadarta la-Shem elokecha nedava*. This verse, whose analysis is developed further in the next section, teaches that even when a *neder* ends up functioning as a *nedava*, the full standards of proper service still apply.

---

## Neder vs. Nedava

### Neder Definition

The verse reads: *motza sefasecha tishmor ve-asita ka'asher nadarta la-Shem elokecha nedava* — what comes out of your lips you shall observe and do, as you vowed to God, a *nedava*. The *Gemara* is puzzled: if one took a *neder*, why does the verse call it a *nedava*? The two categories are halakhically distinct. A *neder* is a personal obligation — *harei alai*, "I accept upon myself an obligation to bring a *mincha*" — such that even if the designated *korban* is lost or destroyed, the person must bring another. A *nedava* is a designation of the object itself — *harei zo*, "this is hereby consecrated" — such that if it is lost, the obligation lapses along with it.

### Vow Fulfillment

The *Gemara* resolves the ambiguity: *ella im ke-moshe nadarta asita* — if you performed it as you originally vowed. If the *korban* was brought with the correct *lishma*, in accordance with the original *neder*, then *yehei neder* — it counts as a *neder* and the person receives full credit for the discharge of their obligation. This verse thus provides one of the textual anchors for the *mishna*'s foundational principle that a *korban* brought *shelo lishmo* remains valid but does not fulfill the owner's obligation.

### Nedava Status

*Ve-im lav* — but if it was performed with different intent — *tehei nedava*, it functions as a *nedava*. The *korban* is entirely *kosher* and the *shirayim* may be eaten and the *kometz* burned, but the owner receives no credit toward any personal obligation. This is because what was a *neder* has now been transformed, in its function, into a *nedava*. Importantly, this principle also makes clear that one may not say: since this *korban* no longer satisfies the owner's obligation, it now has the status of a mere *nedava*, and since a *nedava* never satisfies an obligation, there is no harm in another act of *shelo lishma*. That reasoning is flawed. Even an ordinary *nedava* — one that began as a free-will offering with no attendant personal obligation — must be performed with proper intent. The requirement of proper *kavanah* is not merely a consequence of the obligation; it is a function of the integrity of the *korban* itself. A *nedava* is a fully valid *korban* and must be treated as such. Thus, the *kohen* performing the service is never given license for wrong intent on the grounds that the owner's obligation is not at stake.

---

## Mishna Authorship

### Rabbi Shimon's View

The *Gemara* now turns to a striking question: *leima masnisatin de-lo ke-Rabbi Shimon* — perhaps our *mishna* does not reflect the position of Rabbi Shimon? A *baraisa* is cited in which Rabbi Shimon states: *kol ha-menachot she-nikmetzu shelo lishman kesherot ve-alu la-be'alim leshem chovah* — all *menachot* taken with wrong intent are valid and do indeed fulfill the owners' obligation. Rabbi Shimon does not dispute the general principle that *shelo lishma* is problematic; he holds that by *menachot* specifically, such a thought simply cannot be operative in any meaningful way.

### Physical Evidence Argument

The reason Rabbi Shimon gives is: *she-ein ha-menachot domot le-zevachim* — because *menachot* are not like animal sacrifices. By a *mincha*, the physical reality renders wrong intent self-evidently absurd. The act itself proclaims what it is.

### Examples of Self-Evidence

Rabbi Shimon provides illustrations. If you perform the *kemitzah* of a *machavat* — a flat, lightly-oiled fried *mincha* — while thinking it is a *marcheshes* — a deeper, bubbly, more heavily-oiled type — *ma'aseha mochiachin aleha she-hi machavat*: the act speaks for itself. The thing in your hands is plainly what it is; your contrary thought is simply contradicted by the observable reality. Similarly, if it is a *charevah* — a dry *mincha* such as a *minchat chotei* — and you are thinking it is a *belulah* — mixed with oil — the flour in your hand contains no oil and your thought is manifestly false. By contrast, *aval bi-zevachim eino kein* — with animal sacrifices this is not the case. *Shechitah achat le-kullan ve-zrikah achat le-kullan* — the act of slaughter looks the same regardless of what type of sacrifice is being offered, as does the act of sprinkling; there is nothing in the physical reality that reveals the intended category of the *korban*.

---

## Intent & Act Definition

### Intent Interpretation

This position of Rabbi Shimon admits of two possible interpretations. The first is that when *kavanah* is directly contradicted by physical reality, we simply discard it as silly — it is *batel da'ato*, nullified, because no reasonable person would credit it. The second, and arguably more precise, interpretation is that wrong *kavanah* does not invalidate merely because there is a thought in one's head; rather, it invalidates because *kavanah* defines the quality of an act. When one slaughters an *olah* with the intent of a *chatat*, one has performed a *shechitat chatat* on an *olah* — the *kavanah* has redefined what the act is. Similarly, a *zrikat shelamim* on an *olah* redefines the act. Intent is operative precisely because it gives the act its halakhic character.

### Physical Reality Priority

On this second interpretation, when physical reality is neutral — when nothing visible distinguishes one type of *shechita* from another — the *kavanah* can step in and define the act. But when physical reality speaks loudly and unambiguously, the *kavanah* that runs against it cannot succeed in redefining the act. It is not possible to say one performed a *kemitzat marcheshes* when the material in hand is plainly a *machavat* or a *ma'afeh tanur*. The act is defined far more powerfully by what is physically in front of the *kohen* than by a thought that contradicts it. This is the more persuasive formulation of Rabbi Shimon's position: wrong *kavanah* fails not because it is discarded as irrational, but because it cannot achieve the only thing that makes it halakhically significant — namely, redefining the act — when the act is already defined by incontrovertible physical evidence.

### Stamah Principle

This framework also elegantly explains why *stamah* — the absence of any expressed intent — is valid. One might ask: if there is a positive requirement for *kavanah*, why should the absence of *kavanah* suffice? The answer is that the requirement is not that one must affirmatively think the right thought; the requirement is that the act be, halakhically, a *shechitat olah* or a *zrikat olah*, as the case may be. In the absence of any problematic intent, the act is defined by the identity of the *korban* itself. If the animal is an *olah* and one slaughters it without expressing any contrary intent, one has performed a *shechitat olah* by default. The physical metaphysical reality — that the animal is an *olah* — is what defines the act when *kavanah* is neutral. *Kavanah* becomes operative only when it tries to redefine what would otherwise be correctly categorized. So *stamah* is perfectly valid, but an articulated wrong *kavanah* derails, because it attempts to — and under conditions of physical ambiguity, succeeds in — redefining the act away from its proper category. Rabbi Shimon's contribution is to say that when physical reality removes all ambiguity, the *kavanah* cannot succeed in this redefinition.

---

## Rav Ashi's Resolution

### Vessel vs. Category

The *Gemara* now considers the apparent contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Shimon: in one place he says wrong intent is meaningless by *menachot*, and yet shortly below (as the *Gemara* will show in full) he seems to say it does have effect. The *Gemara* introduces the resolution of Rav Ashi: *kan be-kometz machavat le-shem marcheshes, kan be-kometz minchat machavat le-shum minchat marcheshes* — the two cases differ in one critical word. In the first, one says "a *machavat* for the sake of a *marcheshes*" — referring to the physical vessel or form. In the second, one says "a *minchat machavat* for the sake of a *minchat marcheshes*" — referring to the halakhic category of *mincha*.

### Form vs. Halakha

When one's intent is articulated purely in terms of the physical vessel — *machavat* versus *marcheshes* — it is a thought about the concrete, observable thing, and since the physical reality directly contradicts it, it is meaningless and does not invalidate. But when one's intent is phrased in terms of halakhic category — *minchat machavat* versus *minchat marcheshes* — the situation is different. Halakhic categories do not always map cleanly onto observable physical reality. Just as halakhic adulthood (*bar da'as*) does not perfectly track visible maturity, so too the halakhic identity of a *mincha* as belonging to one category or another is not purely a matter of what one can observe in the hand. Therefore, a *kavanah* expressed in terms of halakhic category — "I am performing this as a *minchat marcheshes*" — is not obviously and absurdly contradicted by the physical reality, and retains the capacity to redefine the act halakhically. That *kavanah* therefore does invalidate.

### Reconciliation Attempt

According to Rav Ashi, there is thus no contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's positions. The *baraisa* where Rabbi Shimon says wrong intent is meaningless refers to intent expressed about the physical form of the vessel. The sources where Rabbi Shimon acknowledges that wrong intent has effect refer to intent expressed about the halakhic category of the *mincha*. And our *mishna* — which discusses *menachot* brought with wrong intent — is dealing with the case of *minchat machavat* versus *minchat marcheshes* in the halakhic-category sense, and therefore could in principle be consistent with Rabbi Shimon's view.

---

## Rabbah's Distinction

### Owner vs. Offering Type

The *Gemara* now turns to the resolution proposed by Rabbah: *lo kashya, kan be-shinuie kodesh kan be-shinuie ba'alim* — the distinction is not about the form of expression but about the content of the wrong intent. Rabbi Shimon concedes that an intent directed at a different *owner* — *shinui ba'alim* — does invalidate. The reason is that nothing in the physical act reveals who the owner is; the identity of the owner is not apparent from observing the *kemitzah*. Therefore, a *kavanah* about the wrong owner is not contradicted by observable reality and retains its halakhic force. By contrast, an intent directed at a different *type* of offering — *shinui kodesh* — is precisely what is revealed by the physical reality of the *mincha*, and therefore does not invalidate according to Rabbi Shimon.

### Mishna Fit

The *Gemara* then asks: but our *mishna*'s illustrative example of *shelo lishman* — the case of *lishm minchat chotei* and *lishm minchat nedava* — is a case of *shinui kodesh*, a change in the type of offering, not *shinui ba'alim*. And that is exactly the case where Rabbi Shimon says wrong intent does not invalidate. Therefore, according to Rabbah, our *mishna* cannot be reconciled with Rabbi Shimon — the scenario the *mishna* uses to illustrate invalidation is precisely the scenario Rabbi Shimon would permit.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Contradicti…

### Position 1: No Invalidat…

To this point, we have seen Rabbi Shimon in the *baraisa* saying that wrong intent by *menachot* is meaningless because the physical reality speaks for itself.

### Position 2: Intent Inval…

Yet in another *baraisa*, Rabbi Shimon says explicitly: *kodesh kodashim hi ke-chatat u-ke-asham* — this verse comparing the *mincha* to the *chatat* and the *asham* yields practical consequences. *Minchat chotei harei hi ke-chatat*: since the *minchat chotei* is like a *chatat*, performing it *shelo lishmah* renders it *pesulah* — fully invalid, just as a *chatat* done *shelo lishmo* is invalid. And *minchat nedava harei hi ke-asham*: an ordinary *minchat nedava* done *shelo lishmah* is *kesheirah* — valid — just as the *asham* is valid when done with wrong intent. But just as the *asham* in such a case is *kasher ve-eino meratzeh* — valid as a sacrifice but not credited to the owner — so too the *minchat nedava* done *shelo lishmah* is valid but does not fulfill the owner's obligation. So Rabbi Shimon does acknowledge that *shelo lishmo* can affect a *mincha* — either fully invalidating it (*minchat chotei*) or at minimum leaving the owner without credit (*minchat nedava*).

### Reconciliation Needed

These two positions appear to be in direct tension: Rabbi Shimon says wrong intent is meaningless by *menachot*, and yet Rabbi Shimon also says wrong intent by *menachot* can fully invalidate or at least deprive the owner of credit. The *Gemara* must determine which cases fall into which category.

---

## Abiyi's Challenge

### Broad Comparison Issue

Rabbah's resolution was that Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between *shinui ba'alim* (wrong owner — intent has effect) and *shinui kodesh* (wrong type — intent has no effect). Abaye challenges this: *michdi machshava de-fasla Rachmana heikesha hi* — the principle that *kavanah* can invalidate a *mincha* derives from the verse's comparison to *chatat* and *asham*. That verse draws a full and undifferentiated comparison. If the verse makes this comparison across the board, what justifies applying it only to *shinui ba'alim* and not to *shinui kodesh*? *Mai li shinui kodesh, mai li shinui ba'alim* — once the verse links the *mincha* to the *chatat* and *asham* in terms of *kavanah*, all forms of wrong intent should be equally operative.

### Sevara Limits Scope

Rabbah responds: *mah semuchin de-ka amar Rabbi Shimon, sevara hi* — the verse may appear categorical, but Rabbi Shimon applies his *sevara*, his logical reasoning, to determine the scope of the verse's application. This is the classic principle that Rabbi Shimon *doresh ta'ama de-kra* — he interprets the scope of a verse in light of its underlying reason. The most famous instance is the prohibition against taking as collateral the garment of a widow (*lo tachavol beged almana*): Rabbi Shimon holds that if a wealthy widow is involved, the reason for the prohibition does not apply, and therefore the prohibition does not apply. (His reasoning for the restriction itself is characteristically unexpected: he holds the concern is that constantly returning a poor person's collateral each evening requires repeated visits to the widow's home, which raises questions about propriety; a wealthy widow, whose collateral need not be returned daily, generates no such concern.) The broader principle is: Rabbi Shimon allows his understanding of the *ta'am* — the reason — to limit the scope of an otherwise categorical verse.

Here too, the verse compares *menachot* to *chatat* and *asham* in terms of *kavanah*, but Rabbi Shimon uses his *sevara* to limit that comparison. The principle is: *machshava de-lo minkara pasla Rachmana* — if a thought is not obviously contradicted by observable reality, the Torah does invalidate based on it. *Machshava de-minkara, lo pasla Rachmana* — if the thought is obviously contradicted by what is manifestly happening, it does not invalidate. The verse is thus not categorical; its application is modulated by Rabbi Shimon's logical principle that intent is only meaningful when it is not self-evidently absurd.

---

## Bird Sacrifices Analysis

### Location-Based Intent

The *Gemara* now probes Rabbi Shimon's principle by examining bird sacrifices. A bird *olah* (*olat ha-of*) is performed at the top of the *mizbeach*, while a bird *chatat* (*chatat ha-of*) is performed at the bottom. The *Gemara* asks: if one performed the *melika* — the pinching of the neck — of a bird *olah* at the top of the *mizbeach* with the intent that it is a bird *chatat*, should not the physical location make that intent self-evidently wrong and therefore meaningless according to Rabbi Shimon?

### Flexibility of Acts

The *Gemara* responds: *melika be-chol makom ba-mizbeach kesheirah* — the act of *melika* may be performed at any location on the altar. What determines above or below is where one squirts or squeezes out the blood, not where the *melika* itself occurs. Since a *melika* at the top is entirely consistent with a *chatat ha-of* — the *kohen* could perform *melika* at the top and then bring the bird's neck to the bottom for the *haza* — the act of *melika* at the top does not obviously betray that this is an *olah* rather than a *chatat*. The *kavanah* is therefore not obviously contradicted, and retains its force. The *Gemara* then moves to the blood act itself: if one squeezed out the blood (*mitzui dam*) of a bird *olah* at the top with intent for a *chatat ha-of*, that should be self-evidently wrong, since the blood of a *chatat ha-of* is squirted (*haza*) at the bottom, not squeezed at the top. Yet the *Gemara* responds here as well: *dilma mitzui de-vatar haza hu* — perhaps this squeezing is the squeezing of residual blood performed after the *haza* at the bottom, a procedure which may be done anywhere on the altar. *Mitzui dama be-chol makom ba-mizbeach kesheirah.* So even this act, performed at the top, is not obviously inconsistent with a *chatat ha-of*; such an act could exist as part of the procedure for a *chatat ha-of* after the primary *haza* has already been done at the bottom. The *kavanah* therefore retains its capacity to redefine the act.

### Bird vs. Grain

This is the key contrast with *menachot*: by bird sacrifices, even acts that appear to be inconsistent with the intended category turn out to be potentially consistent with it, because of the flexibility of where various steps may be performed. There is always some possibility that the act could belong to the intended category. That is sufficient to keep the *kavanah* operative.

### Reverse Case

The *Gemara* then takes the reverse case: a bird *chatat* whose blood was squirted (*haza*) at the bottom with the intent that it is a bird *olah*. Here the *Gemara* agrees: *hachi nami* — you are correct. In this case, the *kavanah* is self-evidently wrong. *Maaseh mochiah alav de-chatas hi* — the act speaks for itself as a *chatat*: the blood is being squirted at the bottom, and an *olah* is always done at the top with squeezing, not squirting. The wrong intent here is indeed obviously contradicted by the physical reality of the act, and therefore, consistent with Rabbi Shimon's principle, it would not invalidate.

### Tosafot's Cases

Tosafot raises a related challenge, noting that the *Gemara* itself could have asked about certain animal sacrifices where the act is also self-evident. The *Gemara* notes the general formulation that by Zevachim *shechitah achat le-kullan* — all slaughters look alike — but Tosafot points out that by *zerika* this is not always true. A *chatat* whose blood is applied at the upper corners with a finger (*lemala be-karnot u-ve-etzba*) while one has the intent for an *olah* — whose blood is applied below at the base (*lemata be-yesod u-vi-zerika min ha-keli*) — presents obvious physical differences that should make the wrong intent self-evidently absurd. Tosafot suggests that *ein hachi nami*: one could indeed apply Rabbi Shimon's principle there as well, and perhaps Rabbi Shimon would agree that in such cases the wrong intent does not invalidate for the animal sacrifice either. The *Gemara* may simply not have raised these cases because they are not the primary focus, but the logic of Rabbi Shimon's principle potentially extends there.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Synthesis

### Wrong Owner Matters

To summarize Rabbi Shimon's position as it emerges from the *sugya*: Rabbi Shimon agrees that wrong intent regarding a different *owner* — *shinui ba'alim* — has full halakhic effect. The identity of the owner is not revealed by any observable physical act; there is nothing in the *kemitzah* or the burning of the *kometz* that tells an observer whose *korban* this is. Therefore, a *kavanah* directed at the wrong owner is not contradicted by the physical reality and retains its capacity to redefine the act. It is a *machshava de-lo minkara* — a thought that is not self-evidently falsified — and therefore invalidates.

### Offering Type Variable

As for wrong intent regarding the *type* of offering — *shinui kodesh* — Rabbi Shimon's position depends on whether the wrong intent is self-evident. When the type of *mincha* is physically obvious from what is in the *kohen*'s hand, the wrong *kavanah* is meaningless and does not affect the validity or the owner's fulfillment of obligation. When the type is not self-evident — whether because the *kavanah* is expressed in terms of halakhic category rather than physical form (Rav Ashi's distinction), or because the act itself is physically ambiguous (as with certain acts of bird sacrifice) — the wrong *kavanah* does retain force and can invalidate or deprive the owner of credit.

### To Be Continued

The *sugya* has laid out the main positions and distinctions. The other proposed resolutions — Rava's distinction between a *kavanah* for a different *mincha* versus for a *zevach* entirely, and the further cases that flow from all of this — will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Menachot 3

## Rava's Approach

### Shelo Lishmah Intro

The third daf of Menachot continues to grapple with the position of Rabbi Shimon on the question of *shelo lishmah* — offering a sacrifice with intent for a different type of sacrifice. The parallel tractate, Zevachim, deals with this issue by *zevachim*, animal sacrifices, while Menachot addresses it in the context of flour offerings. Rabbi Shimon's distinctive position is that *shelo lishmah* does not invalidate a *mincha* when the false intent is self-evidently contradicted by physical reality. If a *kohen* performs the *kemitza* of a dry *mincha* while thinking of it as a wet one — or a fried one as a baked one — Rabbi Shimon holds that this *machshava* is meaningless, because the physical reality so plainly contradicts it that the intent cannot be taken seriously.

This logic is compelling on its face. Yet it must be reconciled with another statement of Rabbi Shimon, where he explicitly compares *mincha* to *chatas* and *asham* and affirms that a *shelo lishmah* intent does invalidate. How are these two positions to be reconciled?

### Rava's Clarification

Rava's answer takes Rabbi Shimon at his word. He affirms that ordinarily *shelo lishmah* is indeed meaningless when contradicted by reality, and that when Rabbi Shimon holds it *is* meaningful, that refers to intent involving a different owner — a case where the false premise is not self-evidently absurd. This is a straightforward reading of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: intent matters only when it reflects a coherent, even if incorrect, possibility.

### Gemara's Challenge

Having established this framework, the *gemara* presses further. If we accept that any intent plainly contradicted by reality is meaningless, there ought to be many such cases across the laws of *korbanos* — not just by *mincha*. Are there not similar cases involving birds? Are there not other scenarios where *shelo lishmah* intent is so obviously false that Rabbi Shimon would ignore it? The *gemara* proceeds through a series of examples, testing whether the principle truly extends as broadly as Rava's reading of Rabbi Shimon implies.

---

## Kodshei/Kalim Cases

### Kodshei Kodashim

The *gemara* opens with what might seem like a simple case. If *kodshei kodashim* — the most sacred offerings such as a *chatas* — are slaughtered in the north of the *azara* (as required) with intent that they are *kodashim kalim*, such as *shelamim*, should that intent be disregarded? The *maaseh mochiach aleihem* — the act itself proves their identity — because *kodashim kalim* are slaughtered in the south. The fact of the northern *shechita* makes the false intent self-evident.

However, the *gemara* immediately deflates this as a softball question. The *gemara* notes that *shelamim* are in fact permitted to be slaughtered anywhere in the *azara* — there is no restriction to the south. The Mishnah elsewhere states *shechitasan b'chol makom ba'azarah* — they may be slaughtered anywhere in the Temple courtyard. Slaughtering a *kodshei kodashim* in the north with intent for *shelamim* is therefore not patently absurd, since *shelamim* may legitimately be slaughtered in the north as well. So this case does not lend itself easily to the argument that the intent is self-evidently false.

### Kodashim Kalim

The *gemara* turns to the reverse: *kodashim kalim* slaughtered in the south with intent for *kodshei kodashim*, such as *chatas*. Here, one might argue, the *maaseh mochiach aleihem* — the southern *shechita* — shows it cannot be a *chatas*, which requires the north. The intent should therefore be disregarded as obviously wrong.

The *gemara* objects: although *chatas* must be slaughtered in the north, there is no rule that prevents an animal from being slaughtered in the south and thereby being treated *as if* it were a *chatas* done in the wrong location. That is, one cannot say with certainty that the scenario of a *chatas* slaughtered in the south is impossible — it can happen through error. An animal could have been consecrated as a *chatas* and accidentally slaughtered in the south. The intent that it is a *chatas* is therefore not categorically groundless, because the scenario, however mistaken, is conceivable.

### Mistake Scenarios

This raises a deeper problem. If we allow that mistakes occur — that a *chatas* can wind up being slaughtered in the south by accident, or a *marcheshes* brought incorrectly as a *machavat* — then virtually every *shelo lishmah* intent becomes potentially meaningful. After all, a person could always have vowed one thing and accidentally brought another. If the mere possibility of such a mistake renders an intent non-absurd, then the *gemara*'s entire theoretical framework for dismissing intent collapses.

The *gemara* illustrates this with the case of *machavas l'shem marcheshes*: if someone performs *kemitza* from a *machavat* — a flat pan — with intent that it is a *marcheshes* — a deep, heavily oiled pan — why not say this intent too is meaningful? Maybe this *mincha* was vowed as a *marcheshes* and accidentally brought as a *machavat*. If such mistakes can happen, the intent that it is a *marcheshes* is not absurd, and should therefore invalidate.

### Machavas/Marcheshes

The *gemara* provides a decisive resolution for this case, one that hinges on a principle specific to *minchas*: the physical vessel ultimately defines the identity of the offering, regardless of what was vowed. The *gemara* cites a *baraisa*: if one says *harei alai b'machavat* — I hereby undertake to bring a *machavat mincha* — and brings it in a *marcheshes*, or vice versa, whatever was actually brought is what was brought (*mah shehevi hevi*), though one has not fulfilled one's vow. The identity of the *korban* follows the physical reality of how it was prepared and offered, not the initial declaration.

This has a striking implication: once a *mincha* is brought in a *machavat*, it is, by definition, a *machavat* — whatever was said or vowed beforehand. This principle is stated explicitly in the Mishnah and is affirmed, crucially, by Rabbi Shimon himself. Rabbi Shimon holds that even if one directly sanctifies an object with the words *harei zo l'marcheshes* — I hereby designate this flour and oil as a *marcheshes* — and then brings it as a *machavat*, one has fulfilled one's vow, because the verbal sanctification is understood as a generic *harei zo l'mincha*, and the specific type is always determined by what is brought at the end. For Rabbi Shimon, the kind of *mincha* it is depends entirely on how it arrives, not on how it was sanctified verbally.

The consequence is definitive: there is no possible scenario in which an item brought in a *machavat* is actually a *marcheshes*. Even if one had originally sanctified the specific flour and oil as a *marcheshes*, once it is brought as a *machavat*, it is a *machavat*. This is not a matter of an error producing a mislabeled offering — the physical reality constitutes the identity absolutely. Therefore, intent that the *machavat* is a *marcheshes* is not merely unlikely or unusual; it is metaphysically impossible. There is no conceivable world in which this item being brought before us is a *marcheshes*. The intent is categorically groundless, and Rabbi Shimon therefore ignores it.

This contrasts sharply with the case of *shelamim* slaughtered in the south for the sake of *chatas*. There, one can conceive of a scenario — a *chatas* accidentally slaughtered in the south. The scenario is wrong, invalid, but it can occur. The intent, therefore, reflects a real if erroneous possibility, and is meaningful enough to invalidate. But for *machavas* and *marcheshes*, no such scenario exists. Whatever preceded the bringing, the brought reality is what it is, always and entirely.

The *gemara* briefly considers a complication: what if one said *harei zo l'marcheshes* — directly sanctifying the specific flour and oil — and then brought it in a *machavat*? Would not this be a case where the item was truly a *marcheshes* done incorrectly? The *gemara* answers: even then, one who has intent that this *machavat* is a *marcheshes* entertains an impossible premise. The *baraisa* teaches that even in the case of *zo l'marcheshes v'hevi b'machavat*, it is *pesulah* — invalid — meaning it does not validly serve as either, but its identity has nonetheless been resolved by the physical form in which it arrived. Rabbi Shimon's position that even *zo l'marcheshes* is fulfilled by a *machavat* removes this residual scenario entirely.
