This asymmetry — an animal perfectly acceptable to a layperson, yet rejected by the altar — seems to establish a *kal va-chomer* against *treifa* even more powerfully than *baal mum*.

The Gemara counters: *ma li yotzei dofen she-ken eino kadosh be-vichora* — a *yotzei dofen* has a more severe invalidity in another domain: it is not sanctified as a firstborn. The verse states *asher yivaled*, which *Chazal* interpret to mean a natural vaginal birth, excluding Caesarean delivery. A *treifa*, by contrast, is still sanctified as a firstborn if born naturally and then becomes *treifa* later, and a *kohen* who is *treifa* remains a valid *kohen*. So while a *yotzei dofen* animal has no *kedushat bechor* at all, a *treifa* animal has no such compounded invalidity.

The Gemara then cycles through the now-familiar *chazer ha-din* — the back-and-forth between *baal mum* and *yotzei dofen*, each illuminating what the other lacks, until the *tzad ha-shaveh* is reached: both are *mutar le-hedyot ve-assur le-gavoha*. If even things that a layperson may eat are forbidden on the *mizbe'ach*, then certainly a *treifa*, which a layperson cannot eat, should be forbidden as well.

At this point the Gemara raises a sharp counter: *mah le-ha-tzad ha-shaveh she-ba-hen she-ken lo hutru mi-khlalan* — the distinguishing feature common to *baal mum* and *yotzei dofen* is that they are never, under any circumstances, a valid *korban*. But *tomar be-treifa she-hutrah mi-khlalah* — a *treifa*, one might argue, does sometimes get an exception. The Gemara will now investigate what that exception could be.

Rav Acha son of Rava asks: what is this exception for *treifa*? Is it the *melika* of the bird *olah*? In that procedure, one first breaks the spinal cord — rendering the bird a *treifa* — before actually completing the killing by severing the trachea or esophagus. So a *treifa* state precedes the completed act, yet the *korban* is valid, and the *kohanim* may eat the *chatas ha-of*.

The Gemara objects to the *olat ha-of* example: birds are generally treated more leniently with respect to *korbanot*. The Torah's requirements of *tamut* and *zachrut* — unblemished and male — apply only to mammals. *Ein tamut ve-zachrut be-of* — for birds, these standards are not required. One cannot derive leniency for a mammal *korban* from leniences specific to birds.

But there is another dimension to the bird case: not only is the *olat ha-of* brought in a *treifa* state, but the *kohanim* eat the *chatas ha-of* even though it is a *treifa*. This would appear to represent an instance where the *treifa* prohibition is lifted for ordinary consumption — could that not justify bringing an animal *korban* from a *treifa*?

The Gemara responds: *kohanim mi-shulchan gavoha ka zachu* — when *kohanim* eat *kodashim*, they are eating from God's table. Their consumption is not lay eating; it is part of the sacred process of the *Mikdash*. Since birds are treated leniently as *korbanot* in general, the *kohanim*'s eating of the *treifa* bird is subsumed within that same leniency. No conclusion can be drawn from birds about mammals.

### Treifa Hidden Flaw

With the *treifa* exception deflated, the Gemara arrives at what will be the definitive answer. The final counter to the *tzad ha-shaveh* argument from *baal mum* and *yotzei dofen* is: *mah le-ha-tzad ha-shaveh she-ba-hen she-ken muman nikar* — both *baal mum* and *yotzei dofen* have one crucial feature in common: their disqualification is evident. The *mum* is visible; the *yotzei dofen* status, while not physiologically apparent, was known in the community — Tosafot notes that at the time such births were rare and well-documented.

*Tomar be-treifa she-ken ein mumo nikar* — but a *treifa* involves an internal injury that is entirely unknown and unknowable until after slaughter. No one can see it. No one knows about it. Perhaps what truly matters for the *mizbe'ach* is not the binary of *kosher* versus non-*kosher* in the abstract, but rather whether the disqualification is externally perceptible. In the world of the *Mikdash*, aesthetics and visible integrity carry real halachic weight — the entire institution of *baal mum* is oriented around what is discernible. So perhaps a *treifa*, whose flaw is hidden from all human eyes until the animal is slaughtered, should be accepted.

This, the Gemara concludes, is the genuine *hava amina* — and *mishum hachi itzterich kra*, this is precisely why we needed an explicit *pasuk* to exclude *treifa*. The logical arguments alone were insufficient to rule it out.

### Need for Pasuk

Having established why we need a *pasuk* to exclude *treifa*, the Gemara immediately raises a further question: *treifa me-hacha nafka?* — do we actually learn the exclusion of *treifa* from this *pasuk* in the Torah? Perhaps we learn it from the *pasuk* of *mimashkei Yisrael* in Yechezkel, which establishes that *korbanot* must be from what is permitted to Israel.

The Gemara acknowledges the point. As a matter of strict logic, one might wonder why we need any *pasuk* in the Torah at all, given the principle derived from Yechezkel. The answer, as the Gemara often treats such *pesukim* from *Nevi'im*, is that the verse in Yechezkel functions as a *giluy milta* — a disclosure or confirmation of a received tradition — rather than as an independent halakhic source. And as Tosafot explains, *mimashkei Yisrael* is the readily available shorthand reference for the entire body of reasoning establishing that non-*kosher* items are invalid as *korbanot*.

### Three Pesukim

The Gemara then explains why no single *pasuk* is sufficient and why three are needed. The first is *mimashkei Yisrael* — the principle that *korbanot* must come from what is permitted to Israel. The second is derived from *mikol asher ya'avor tachat ha-shevet* — the verse about *ma'aser behema*, which describes animals that "walk under the rod" as one counts them. A *treifa* is not considered an animal that walks under the rod, since *treifot* are sometimes sickly and may die prematurely; they lack the image of vigorous health. From this we extend the exclusion of *treifa* to all *korbanot*. The third is *min ha-bakar*, which will address a scenario the other two do not cover.

### Never vs. Later Treifa

Had we only the *pasuk* of *mimashkei Yisrael*, one might have thought it excludes only something that was *never* kosher — comparable to *orla* or *kilayei ha-kerem*, items forbidden from the very moment of their formation. *Aval hayta lah sha'at ha-kosher* — but if the animal had a period of permissibility before becoming a *treifa*, perhaps that earlier kosher status would allow it.

Had we only the *pasuk* of *mikol asher ya'avor tachat ha-shevet*, one might have thought it excludes only a case where the animal became *treifa* before being consecrated — *d'be'idna d'nitreifa, lo akdasha* — since at the moment it was made *treifa* it had no sanctity. But *hikdishah u-levasof nitreifa* — if one first sanctified the animal and it subsequently became *treifa* — then *d'be'idna d'akdeshah chazya hava*, at the moment of consecration it was fully fit. Perhaps the subsequent *treifa* status would not undermine its validity.

Therefore the Gemara concludes: *katav Rachmana min ha-bakar* — the third *pasuk* is needed to rule out even this last case. *Tzerichi* — all three are necessary. Together they establish, comprehensively, that whenever an animal reaches the *mizbe'ach* in a non-*kosher* state — whether it was always *treifa*, whether it became *treifa* before consecration, or whether it became *treifa* after consecration — it cannot serve as a valid *korban*. As Tosafot summarizes, *mimashkei Yisrael* serves as the encompassing rubric to which all of this reasoning is attributed.

---

## Mincha Invalidities

### Mincha Invalidities List

With the principle of *kosher* food for *korbanot* fully established, the Gemara moves to the next *Mishnah*, which addresses a different dimension of invalidity: not the nature of the food being offered, but the identity and status of the one performing the service. The *Mishnah* draws a parallel to a similar discussion in Zevachim, but with a tighter focus — whereas Zevachim opened at length with the issue of *shelo lishmah*, here we proceed directly to the various categories of individuals whose performance of *kamitza* invalidates the *mincha*.

### Zar & Kamitza

The *Mishnah* states that whether it is a *minchat chotei* or any other *mincha*, if any of the following individuals performed the *kamitza*, the *mincha* is invalid: a *zar* — a non-*kohen*. This warrants pause. We know from *shechita* that a *zar* may perform the slaughter of an animal *korban* — *shechita* is *kasher be-zar*. Yet *kamitza* — the handful-taking from the *mincha*, which is the functional analog of *shechita* — is not *kasher be-zar*.

Two explanations present themselves. The first is that *kamitza* and *melika*, unlike *shechita*, are performed with the *kohen*'s bare hands, which function in the manner of a *kli shares* — a sacred vessel. Since the hands of a non-*kohen* cannot serve in that capacity, the act is invalid. *Shechita*, by contrast, is done with a knife, and at least according to some *rishonim*, it is the knife — a *kli shares* — that is the operative instrument. The second explanation, following Tosafot, is that *shechita lav avodah hi* — *shechita* is not exclusively a *Mikdash* ritual, since one slaughters animals for lay purposes as well. *Kamitza* and *melika*, by contrast, exist only as specific *Mikdash* rites, and therefore require a *kohen*.

### Disqualified Kohanim

Beyond the *zar*, the *Mishnah* enumerates a series of *kohanim* who are themselves disqualified from performing *kamitza*. An *onen* — a *kohen* who has suffered the death of a close relative on that day — is disqualified. A *tvul yom* — one who has immersed in a *mikveh* but has not yet waited for nightfall to complete his purification — is similarly invalid, despite having already immersed. A *mechusar begadim* — a *kohen* not wearing the full and proper *bigdei kehuna* — renders the service invalid. A *mechusar kippurim* — one who has completed the purification process in every respect except for the final *korban*, such as a *zav* whose only remaining step is the offering — is likewise disqualified. The *Mishnah* also includes one who has not performed the required washing of hands and feet (*rechitzat yadayim ve-raglayim*), an *arel* — an uncircumcised *kohen*, even one who cannot be circumcised due to a medical condition — and one who is *tamei*.

Additionally, a *kohen* who performs *kamitza* while *yoshev* — seated — is disqualified, as the verse *la'amod le-shareit* requires the service to be performed standing. And one who stands elevated on a vessel, on an animal, or even on the foot of a fellow *kohen* — *al gabei raglei chaveiro* — is invalid. This last disqualification reflects the requirement that the *kohen*'s feet make direct contact with the floor of the *Mikdash*. The sanctity of the *Mikdash* is transmitted through that physical connection; any barrier between the *kohen*'s bare feet and the *Mikdash* floor severs that link and invalidates the service.

### Left Hand Kamitza

The *Mishnah* then states independently: *kamatz be-smol — pasul*. If the *kohen* took the *kamitza* with his left hand, it is invalid. Ben Beteira disagrees and says: *yachzir ve-yachzor ve-yikmotz be-yamin* — he should return the flour to the vessel and take the *kamitza* again with his right hand.

The simple reading is that Ben Beteira's dispute is limited specifically to the left-hand case, not to the entire preceding list. Two textual indicators support this: first, the left-hand case is presented as a separate and independent statement, after the list already concluded with *pasul*. Second, Ben Beteira does not say the act is *kasher* — he says one should redo it with the right hand. This distinction may carry conceptual weight. The cases on the list represent genuine *psul avodah* — a fundamentally flawed performance of the service that renders it *pasul* in the strong sense. Left-hand *kamitza*, by contrast, might be understood not as a *pasul* act but as a *non-act* — something so technically off that it does not rise to the level of a recognized service at all, and therefore can simply be disregarded and redone.

The Brisker analytical framework of distinguishing between something labeled *pasul* and something that simply is not *kasher* is relevant here. Ben Beteira may be holding that left-hand *kamitza* falls into a kind of neutral zone: not a positively disqualifying act, but not a valid act either — and therefore reversible. The Gemara, however, will generalize Ben Beteira's position to include the entire list, not only the left-hand case.

One might ask: if the argument is reversibility, several of the cases on the list — such as standing on a colleague's foot — are equally easy to reverse. Both that case and left-hand *kamitza* are minor technical failures. The response may be that the *halacha* draws a line differently than intuition might suggest: standing off the *Mikdash* floor may represent a disconnection from *kedusha* that makes the act substantively invalid, whereas using the wrong limb while otherwise fully qualified and properly standing may be a technical deficiency that does not rise to *psul*. These are interesting distinctions, though admittedly speculative.

### Pebbles in Kometz

The *Mishnah* turns to the practical mechanics of *kamitza* itself. If, while taking the *kometz*, a small pebble — *tzror* — or a grain of salt — *gargar melach* — or a small piece of the *levona* entered the hand, the *kamitza* is *pasul*. The reason is connected to the general rule: *ha-kometz ha-yater ve-ha-chaser pasul* — if the *kometz* contains too much or too little, it is invalid. A pebble or salt crystal displaces flour and makes the *kometz* deficient — *chaser* — in its content.

What constitutes *yater* — excess? *Shekematzto mevorat* — the *kometz* is overflowing, bursting beyond the hand, whether above, below, or through the fingers. What constitutes *chaser* — deficiency? *Shekematzto be-roshei etzbe'otav* — if the *kohen* merely used his fingertips, scooping only a small pinch rather than a full, properly measured handful.

### Mincha Sinner Phrase

The Gemara asks: why does the *Mishnah* need to say both *minchat chotei* and *kol ha-minchos*? One might simply have said "all *minchos*," and that alone would have included the *minchat chotei*. The Gemara answers: *le-Rabbi Shimon itzterich* — this formulation was necessary on account of Rabbi Shimon.

### Rabbi Shimon & Beauty

The *Mishnah*'s phrasing is required because of a position articulated by Rabbi Shimon in a *baraita*. Rabbi Shimon reasons as follows: *be-din hu she-tehei minchat chotei teu'na shemen u-levona* — strictly speaking, a *minchat chotei* should require oil and *levona*, just like other *minchos*, because *shelo yehei chotei niscar* — the sinner should not benefit by being allowed to bring a cheaper offering. Why then does the *minchat chotei* not require *shemen u-levona*? *Shelo yehei korbano mehudar* — so that the *korban* should not be beautiful and aesthetically impressive. The sin offering should be diminished in appearance, reflecting the gravity of the sin.

By the same token, Rabbi Shimon reasons that a *chatat chelev* should require *nesachim* — the accompanying libations of oil, flour, and wine that accompany *olos* and *shelamim* — so that the sinner does not get off easy. Again, the reason it does not is *shelo yehei korbano mehudar*.

Tosafot raises a difficulty: many *korbanot* have fixed costs, so it is not clear that omitting *shemen u-levona* actually saves the sinner money. Tosafot addresses this more specifically in the context of the *chatas* than the *mincha*, but the question remains open to discussion.

What matters for the *Mishnah*'s formulation is this: since Rabbi Shimon holds that the governing concern for the *minchat chotei* is *shelo yehei korbano mehudar*, one might have thought that even the various *psulim* listed in the *Mishnah* — performed by a *zar*, an *onen*, a *tamei* — should be tolerated or even welcomed in the case of a *minchat chotei*, since the worse and less presentable the performance, the more it aligns with the principle of *shelo yehei korbano mehudar*. The *Mishnah* therefore explicitly says *echad minchat chotei ve-echad kol ha-minchos* — even the *minchat chotei* is subject to the same invalidities.

### Zevachim Parallel

The Gemara presses: if that is the reason, why did the corresponding *Mishnah* in Zevachim not also specify *echad chatat chelev ve-echad kol ha-zevachim*? One could equally have argued that Rabbi Shimon would permit *psulim* in the *chatat* of sin!

The Gemara answers: in Zevachim, the *Mishnah* said *kol ha-zevachim* — "all animal offerings" — without exception. When a *Mishnah* says *kol* and lists no exclusions, *kol* is understood comprehensively, leaving no room to infer that any category is treated differently. Here in Menachot, the situation is different. The opening of this very chapter distinguished between a *minchat chotei* and other *minchos* with respect to *shelo lishmah*, creating the impression that the two categories might be treated differently throughout. Given that prior distinction, one might have read the list of invalidities as applying only to regular *minchos* and not to the *minchat chotei*, lest the sinner benefit from a *mehudar* offering. Therefore the *Mishnah* had to explicitly state that both categories are equally subject to these invalidities.

The Gemara then notes a further wrinkle. The first *Mishnah* of the chapter — which distinguished *minchat chotei* from other *minchos* in the context of *shelo lishmah* — was established as not following Rabbi Shimon. If so, one might conclude that this entire chapter does not represent Rabbi Shimon's view, and that the present *Mishnah* too is not Rabbi Shimon. In that case, the concern about *shelo yehei korbano mehudar* would not apply, and no special reason exists to allow *psulim* in the *minchat chotei*. Accordingly, saying *kol ha-minchos* alone should have been sufficient, without explicitly naming the *minchat chotei*.

The Gemara responds: *ka mashma lan* — nevertheless it was necessary to state it explicitly, lest one think the *seifa* of the *Mishnah* is also not like Rabbi Shimon and therefore does not address the concern that Rabbi Shimon would allow *psulim* by a *minchat chotei*. The explicit mention ensures clarity.

With this discussion concluded, the Gemara turns to the more central question of whether an invalid *kamitza* can be undone and repeated — the question of reversal that underlies Ben Beteira's position and opens the next sustained analysis.

---

---

# Menachot 7

## Rav & Ben Batera

### Rav's Zar Position

The *mishnah* at the opening of our sugya established that performing the *kmitzah* — the priestly handful — with the left hand renders the *minchah* invalid, and it recorded the dissenting view of Ben Batera, who ruled that if the *kmitzah* was taken with the left hand, it should be returned to the *kli* and the *kmitzah* taken again properly with the right. The *gemara* now extends this discussion by citing a statement of Rav: *zar shekamatz yachzir* — if a non-*kohen* performed the *kmitzah*, the handful should be returned and the act repeated. Rav thus takes the principle underlying Ben Batera's ruling and extends it even to the case of a *zar*.

### Gemara Questions Rav

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty. The *mishnah* itself declares such performances *pasul*, and we initially assume that Rav does not follow Ben Batera's position at all. So on the one hand, Rav appears to be expanding Ben Batera; on the other hand, he is following Ben Batera. The *gemara* therefore asks: *mai pasul pasul ad sheyachzir*? Perhaps the *mishnah*'s use of the word *pasul* does not mean the act is irremediably void but rather that it is invalid only until corrected — a temporary disqualification that permits a do-over.

### Psul Ad Sheyachzir

The *gemara* immediately objects to this reading: *ee hachi, haynu Ben Batera* — if that is what the *mishnah* means, then the *mishnah* is simply agreeing with Ben Batera, which cannot be right, since Ben Batera's view is presented as a minority dissent. The attempt to read the Rabbis as more lenient than Ben Batera — as permitting do-overs in a wider range of cases while Ben Batera merely adds one more — collapses under this pressure.

### Lacking Handful Debate

The *gemara* then proposes a different resolution: perhaps the Rabbis and Ben Batera do not argue at all when the original *kometz* is still intact and available. *Ee de'itay lekometz be'einay, lo pligi Rabbanan alei deBen Batera* — if the same handful can simply be returned as-is, perhaps everyone agrees that a do-over is permitted. The disagreement, on this reading, is limited to *dechasar kometz* — a case where the *kometz* is no longer available and must be replenished. There, the Rabbis hold *lo yavi mitoch beito vayamleinu* — one may not bring fresh flour from home to refill the handful — while Ben Batera holds *yavi mitoch beito vayamleinu*, that one may indeed do so.

### Refilling from Home

This reconstruction radically rewrites the *mishnah*, locating the entire dispute at the point where the original *kometz* has been lost and must be reconstituted from home. But the *gemara* finds this unacceptable. The language of the *mishnah* itself undermines the reading: Ben Batera says *yachzir veyachzor veyikmotz biyemino* — he should return it and take the handful again with his right hand. If the dispute were about refilling from home, Ben Batera should have said *yachzir veyavi mitoch beito vayamleinu veyachzor veyikmotz biyemino*. The plain language of the *mishnah* is clear: Ben Batera is speaking of returning the original *kometz*, and the Rabbis reject do-overs even in that case.

### Rav per Ben Batera

We are thus returned to the original question: what is the force of Rav's statement that a *zar* who performed the *kmitzah* may redo it? The *gemara* answers: *ki ka'amar Rav, leBen Batera* — Rav was speaking in accordance with Ben Batera's position, not the Rabbis'. The Rabbis clearly reject do-overs altogether. Rav's statement is situated within the framework of Ben Batera, extending it to a case beyond the left hand.

---

## Left Hand Analysis

### Left Hand Validity

Having established that Rav follows Ben Batera and extends the do-over principle beyond the left hand, the *gemara* now probes whether Rav's extension was necessary. The *gemara* reasons that one might well have thought Ben Batera's leniency was *specific* to the left hand, and therefore Rav had to tell us it applies more broadly. The question is: what is the logical basis for singling out the left hand as a distinctive case? The *gemara* answers: *mai shna smol, dashkechan lehachshara b'Yom Kippurim smol* — the left hand has a context in which it is entirely valid, namely on *Yom Kippurim*, when the *Kohen Gadol* carries the incense pan in his left hand as he enters the *Kodesh Kodashim*. Since the left hand is not categorically excluded from valid service, one might reason that it is less severely disqualified than other invalidities, and that Ben Batera's permission to redo applies specifically there.

### Zar in Shechita

The *gemara* then asks whether the same logic could apply to a *zar*: is there not a context in which a non-*kohen* performs a valid Temple act? *Ashkechan lehachshara b'shechitah* — *shechitah* can always be performed by a non-*kohen*, even in the *mikdash*. This might suggest that a *zar* is not categorically excluded from Temple service either.

### Shechita Not Avodah

The *gemara* rejects this parallel: *shechitah lav avodah hi* — *shechitah* is not an *avodah* in the technical sense. Therefore, the fact that a *zar* may perform *shechitah* does not demonstrate that we ever allow a *zar* to perform an actual priestly *avodah*. Rashi often explains this by saying that *shechitah* is permitted to a *zar* and therefore we know it is not an *avodah* — but Tosafot objects that this would make the *gemara*'s reasoning circular. Tosafot instead offers two independent grounds: first, that *shechitah* does not require the performer to stand within the *azarah* proper, whereas any genuine *avodah* requires standing within the *Beit HaMikdash*; and second, that *shechitah* is not a distinctively Temple act — it is performed for all animals whenever one wishes to eat meat — and therefore even when it occurs within the *mikdash*, it retains its generic character and does not become a Temple *avodah*.

### Parah Aduma

The *gemara* then raises a complication: did not Rabbi Zeira say in the name of Rav, *shechitat parah b'zar psulah* — that if a *zar* slaughters the *parah adumah*, it is invalid? And Rav himself explained: *Elazar v'chukah ktiv bah* — the Torah mentions Elazar and uses the word *chok*, indicating that a *kohen* is required. So we see that even for *shechitah* — which we just said is not an *avodah* — a *kohen* is necessary in this case, and a *zar* is excluded. This seems to undercut the argument that *shechitah* proves a *zar* is sometimes valid.

### Parah Kedushá

The *gemara* responds: *shani parah, d'kodshei bedek habayit hi* — the *parah adumah* is different, because its *kedushah* is not *kedushat mizbe'ach*. Since the *parah adumah* is slaughtered outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, it cannot be a *korban* in the full sense. The *gemara* describes it as having *kedushat bedek habayit*, which in this context means any sanctity that does not fall under *kedushat mizbe'ach*. This is a somewhat imprecise use of the term, since *bedek habayit* ordinarily refers to building materials and *klei sharet*, but the *gemara*'s intent is that the *parah adumah* represents a sui generis form of *kedushah* that cannot serve as a model for standard Temple *avodot*.

### Tzara'at Negai'm

But the *gemara* then proposes a *kal vachomer*: if something that is not a full *korban* requires a *kohen*, should not a *korban* itself require a *kohen* all the more? This would mean that when a *zar* performs *shechitah* on a *korban*, it is not a true exception but rather an anomaly — and therefore, just as with the left hand, one might argue that Ben Batera's do-over principle should apply here too. The *gemara* rejects this *kal vachomer* by citing Rav Sheshes son of Rav Idi: there are obligations that require *kohanim* even though they have nothing to do with Temple *avodot*, such as the declaration of *tamei* or *tahor* in cases of *tzara'at*. A *talmid chacham* may examine the blemish and instruct the *kohen*, but only the *kohen* may pronounce the words. Since *kohanim* can be required outside the context of *avodah*, the fact that *parah adumah* requires a *kohen* proves nothing about whether *shechitah* of *korbanot* in principle requires one.

### Shechita Logic

The conclusion is thus that *shechitat korbanot* in principle does not require a *kohen*, it is not an *avodah*, and the permission for a *zar* to perform it is not an exception at all. The *gemara* therefore maintains the original logical structure: the left hand has a genuine parallel where it is used in valid service (*Yom Kippurim*), giving a plausible reason to think Ben Batera's do-over was limited to that case. There is no comparable parallel for a *zar*. This establishes why Rav needed to teach that Ben Batera's principle extends beyond the left hand — there was a strong reason to have thought otherwise. It is worth noting an interesting textual curiosity along the way: the *gemara* reports that *Rabbi Zeira amar Rav* stated that the *shechitah* of the *parah* by a *zar* is invalid, and then records *v'amar Rav alah* — Rav commenting on his own statement as transmitted by Rabbi Zeira. The best explanation is that by the time the *gemara* was crystallized in its current form, Rabbi Zeira was the one who had originally published and circulated Rav's ruling; it was remembered as having come through his mouth, while Rav's subsequent clarification was recorded separately.

---

## Baraita & Ben Batera

### Baraita Witnesses

Having established that Rav had good reason to extend Ben Batera's principle beyond the left hand, the *gemara* raises a further challenge. It cites a *baraita*: *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda v'Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon omrim, machzir haya Ben Batera b'chol ha'psulim kulam* — these two *tanna'im* explicitly state that Ben Batera permitted a do-over for all invalidities, not just the left hand. If such a *baraita* exists and makes the extension explicit, who needs Rav? Rav's statement appears redundant.

One might respond that not everyone had access to this *baraita*, and Rav was teaching the same principle for those who did not know it. But the more precise analysis is that there is a genuine *machloket tanna'im* here. The *mishnah*, as incorporated by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, appears to reflect the view that Ben Batera spoke only of the left hand — for the logical reason we articulated, that the left hand has a valid application on *Yom Kippurim*. These two *tanna'im* in the *baraita* held that Ben Batera extended the principle to all invalidities. Rav, on this reading, was siding with the *baraita* against the implicit position of the *mishnah*. The *gemara*, however, does not frame it this way; instead, it treats the *baraita* as straightforwardly clarifying Ben Batera, and therefore presses: given the *baraita*, what remains for Rav to add?

### Komatz Misham

The *baraita* derives its ruling from a *pasuk*. The verse states *v'kamatz misham* — the *kohen* shall take the handful from there. The *tanna kamma* understands "from there" to mean from the place where the *zar* stands, establishing that the *kmitzah* may be taken anywhere in the *azarah*, including the area normally reserved for non-*kohanim*. Ben Batera, however, learns a different lesson: *minayin she'im kamatz b'smol she'yachazir v'yachzor v'yikmotz b'yamin? Talmud lomar v'kamatz misham* — the verse teaches that the *kmitzah* should be taken from the place from which it was already taken, i.e., it may be returned and taken again. This is the *pasuk*ic basis for Ben Batera's do-over principle.

### Stam Pasuk

Since the *pasuk* is written *stam* — without qualification — specifying neither the left hand nor any other particular invalidity, the *gemara* concludes that it gives no reason to limit Ben Batera's ruling to the left hand. *Mah li smol, mah li sha'ar psulim* — the same reasoning applies to any disqualification. Ben Batera's position, properly understood from its textual basis, extends to all invalidities.

### Rav Redundancy

This brings the *gemara* back to its pointed question: if the *baraita* makes all of this explicit, what is Rav's *chiddush*?

---

## Kamatz v'Afilu Kidesh

### Tannai'm on Timing

The *gemara* now answers by identifying a different dimension of Rav's teaching. The question is not simply whether Ben Batera's principle applies beyond the left hand, but rather: *until when* does the possibility of a do-over remain open? Is there a point in the process after which reversal is no longer permitted? The *gemara* presents the issue with the phrase *kamatz va'afilu kidesh* — Rav's teaching addresses the case where the *kohen* not only performed the *kmitzah* but also placed the *kometz* into the second *kli sharet*, thereby sanctifying it at the next stage. Rav holds that even at that point, the do-over remains available.

This is a meaningful *chiddush* because one might have assumed that placing the *kometz* into the second *kli sharet* completes the act and forecloses reversal — just as in chess, once you release the piece, you cannot take the move back. Once the *kometz* enters the vessel, the first act is done and the process has moved to its next stage.

### HaNachtom Limit

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* in which Rabbi Yosi ben Yosi ben Yassian and Rabbi Yehuda HaNachtom (the baker — the *gemara* notes this epithet with evident interest, suggesting his expertise in flour lent him particular authority in *menachot* discussions) rule: *bameh devarim amurim shekamatz v'lo kidesh* — Ben Batera's do-over applies only if the *kometz* was taken but not yet placed into the second vessel. *Aval kidesh, kidesh pasal* — once it has been placed in the second *kli sharet*, it is invalidated and no do-over is possible. There is also a version of the ruling that simply states *kamatz in, kidesh lo* — if only the *kmitzah* has been done, yes to a do-over; once it has been placed in the vessel, no.

On this reading, Rav's statement would not be extending Ben Batera but rather agreeing with the *tanna kamma* who opposes these two *tanna'im* — and rejecting the view of Rabbi Yehuda HaNachtom and his colleague. Rav's *chiddush* is to say that even *kamatz va'afilu kidesh*, even after the placement in the second *kli sharet*, a do-over remains available.

### Rav Nachman Analysis

Rav Nachman then poses a sharp analytical question: *mai kasvari hanei tanna'im* — what exactly are these *tanna'im* holding? There are two possible logical frameworks. If a *kmitzah* performed by an invalid person is itself considered a valid *avodah* — albeit a flawed one — then from the moment the *kmitzah* is taken it has the status of a *pasul avodah*, and even before the second vessel no do-over should be available. Conversely, if a *kmitzah* performed by an invalid person is so defective that it is considered as though no *avodah* occurred at all, then placing it in the second vessel should make no difference — there would never be any reason to foreclose the do-over.

Rav Nachman then resolves his own difficulty: *le'olam avodah hi* — it is indeed an *avodah*, but a flawed one, and here is the key: *dela gamrah avodatah ad de'avdieh lamatten kli* — the *avodah* is not complete until the act of placing in the second vessel. While the *avodah* remains in progress, correction is still possible. Once the *avodah* is fully executed and becomes past history, it can no longer be undone. This analysis is elegant and makes considerable sense: it is not that the *kmitzah* was nothing, but that it was an ongoing *avodah* that was still capable of being remedied until its completion. When it is complete, it is fixed — for better or worse.

One might ask what those who allow do-overs even after the second vessel would say. They may hold the alternative position Rav Nachman considered and then set aside — that an invalid *kmitzah* is not considered an *avodah* at all, and therefore the process can always be restarted, conceivably even after *holacha*.

---

## Kli Sharet Midaat

### Reish Lakish Query

The *gemara* now shifts its focus from Ben Batera's do-over principle to a related but distinct question: how does the *kli sharet* function in the *minchah* process? This becomes necessary because of a difficulty the *gemara* raises: if we grant that a do-over is possible, then when the *kohen* returns the *kometz* to the original *kli sharet* in order to perform the *kmitzah* again, why doesn't that act of returning itself count as the second stage? The original *kli sharet* would now be receiving the *kometz* for the second time, and nothing in principle requires it to be a *different* vessel. Tosafot notes that the presence of the remaining flour does not create a *chatzitzah* problem, since *min b'mino lo chotzetz*.

This question opens a broader inquiry into the mechanics of *kli sharet*. Unlike in *korbanot* involving animals, where the *kli sharet* appears primarily in the catching of the blood, the *minchah* involves numerous vessels at multiple stages — the flour is brought in a vessel, measured, mixed, the *kmitzah* is taken and placed in a vessel, and so forth. There is thus far more occasion in Menachot to examine precisely how *kli sharet* operates.

Against this backdrop, Reish Lakish poses a striking question to Rabbi Yochanan: *klei sharet ma sheyakdishu pasul l'chatchilah* — can a *kli sharet* take something that is invalid and render it fit to be offered? The question sounds radical, and it is. The underlying intuition is something like the principle of *hamizbe'ach mekadesh* — that the altar can sanctify objects placed upon it. Perhaps the *kedushah* of the *kli sharet*, when intentionally invoked, can similarly transform the status of a disqualified *kometz* and make it presentable on the *mizbe'ach*. Tosafot asks the obvious: if so, why could we not eliminate all *psulei zevachim* by placing the blood in a *kli sharet* with the intent to sanctify? Tosafot's response is that perhaps the *hava amina* was more limited — not that the *kli sharet* makes the *korban* fully valid and allows one to be *yotzei*, but rather that being in a *kli sharet* is analogous to being on the *mizbe'ach*, and therefore the physical material might at least be burned rather than destroyed. Even so, it is a remarkable question.

### Yochanan Answer

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *ein mekadesh* — the *kli sharet* cannot accomplish this. Even with full intent, it cannot take something invalid and make it fit to be offered. This answer is decisive and closes the *hava amina*.

### Midaat Requirement

But the *gemara* now refines the picture through a crucial distinction. Rabbi Yochanan's negative answer — *ein mekadesh* — does not mean the *kli sharet* has no effect at all. The *gemara* formulates it thus: *ein mekadesh l'kareiv, aval mekadesh l'pasel* — the *kli sharet* cannot render an invalid *kometz* fit to be offered, but it can designate it as having reached the second stage, which forecloses the do-over. This is not a full *kedushah* sufficient for the *mizbe'ach*, but it is enough to mark the process as having advanced. This distinction is coherent: the *kli sharet* draws the object into the next stage of the procedure even if it cannot repair its underlying defect.

This leads to a further principle, stated explicitly: *klei sharet ein mekadesh ela mida'as* — a *kli sharet* does not sanctify unless done with intent. When the *kohen* returns the invalid *kometz* to the original vessel as part of a do-over, he is not intending to advance the process to stage two — he is attempting to reverse it. Since the *kli sharet* requires *da'as*, and the *kohen*'s *da'as* here is directed toward reversal rather than sanctification, the vessel does not function to mark completion of the first stage. Therefore, the return of the *kometz* to the original vessel does not foreclose the do-over.

This principle — *klei sharet ein mekadesh ela mida'as* — is one of the important conceptual contributions of Menachot to the laws of *kli sharet*. It reveals that *kedushah* in this domain is not automatic and not mechanical; it depends on the intent of the one performing the act. Just as *piggul* and related concepts demonstrate the centrality of thought in *avodah*, here too the sanctifying power of the vessel is contingent on conscious direction. A student raises a sharp observation: the altar operates by the principle of *hamizbe'ach mekadesh*, which seems almost automatic — placing something on the *mizbe'ach* creates a connection that allows it to remain. Yet by *kli sharet* we do not apply that logic. The *gemara*'s implicit answer is that *kli sharet* and the *mizbe'ach* operate by different principles, and the centrality of *kavanah* is especially pronounced in the *kli sharet* domain.

---

## Vessel on Ground

### Overflowing Handful

The *gemara* now presents a related scenario via a statement of Rav Amram: *kegon shehechiziru l'visa gedushah* — the case where the do-over fails is one in which the *kometz* was returned to a vessel that was already overflowing. When the *minchah* fills the vessel to overflowing and the *kometz* is placed on top of the mound of flour rather than inside the vessel itself, the *kli sharet* cannot function, because only what is contained within the walls of the vessel is sanctified by it — not what spills above the rim.

### Same Vessel Return

The *gemara* asks: how was the *kmitzah* performed in the first place on such a *minchah*? A vessel overflowing with flour would itself seem to be problematic for the initial *kmitzah*. The *gemara* clarifies: *hacha shehechiziru l'visa tefufa* — here the *minchah* was returned to a vessel that was flattened down to the lip of the vessel, packed level.

### Lip vs. Inside

The problem, then, is whether placing the *kometz* on the flat, level surface at the rim counts as placing it inside the vessel. The *gemara* treats the rim and the interior as meaningfully distinct: only what is genuinely inside the walls of the vessel is subject to its *kedushah*.

### Monkey Act

But then the *gemara* raises a further subtlety: when the *kohen* made the original *kmitzah*, he created a hollow — an indentation — in the flour. When he returns the *kometz*, it goes back into that hollow and thereby falls into the vessel. Should this not count as returning it to the interior of the vessel? The *gemara* answers: *miki mahadar lei, manach lei adafna demana* — when he returns it, he places it at the wall of the vessel, and *venafal mimeila* — it falls in on its own. *Dena'aseh kemi shehechiziro ha'kof* — it is as though the monkey returned it. The image of the monkey is invoked in the *gemara* as a paradigm for an act that occurs without genuine human agency. The *kohen* did not actively place the *kometz* inside the vessel; his movement caused it to slide in passively. Since the *kli sharet* requires a conscious act of placement — even if it does not require specific *kavanah* to sanctify — the passive sliding does not count. There is no act, and therefore no sanctification.

This teaches a second important principle about *kli sharet*: even if we set aside the question of *da'as*, the vessel requires an act. A passive or inadvertent entry into the vessel is insufficient. The *kohen* must actively place the *kometz* within.

### Vessel Holding

With the analysis of the monkey act complete, Rabbi Yirmiya poses the question to Rabbi Zeira: *velokma kegon shehechezira likli hamunach al gabei karka* — why did you not simply say the reason the return fails is that the *kohen* placed the *kometz* into a *kli* that was resting on the ground, without a *kohen* holding it? This raises the question of whether the *kli sharet* must be held by a *kohen* in order to function. One might reason that just as the *kohen* must stand on the ground — grounded human agency creates the sacred context — so too the vessel must be held and connected to that human presence. Without it, the *kli sharet* is inert.

Rabbi Yirmiya notes: since Rabbi Zeira did not offer this explanation — a vessel on the ground — the implication is that such an explanation is not available. *Shema mina, komtzi mikli she'al gabei karka* — learn from this that one may indeed perform the *kmitzah* from a *kli* resting on the ground. Holding is not required.

### Rav Avimi Story

Rabbi Yirmiya adds that this was precisely the question being asked in the *beit midrash*. He relates an episode involving Rav Avimi, who had taught *menachot* in the academy of Rav Chisda. The *gemara* notes the apparent oddity: Rav Avimi was Rav Chisda's own *rebbe*, so why would he be learning *menachot* in Rav Chisda's house? The *gemara* explains: *masechta it'akra it'aker lei* — the *masechet* had been uprooted from him. Rav Avimi had lost his command of the text of *menachot* — the oral tradition he had memorized — and he needed to recover it. In a culture of oral transmission, mastery of the text was the essential prerequisite for all further analysis. Even a scholar of Rav Avimi's stature could find himself needing to relearn the words from a younger colleague who held them in memory. He chose to go to Rav Chisda himself rather than summon Rav Chisda to him — *savar hachi mistaya milta tfei* — reasoning that he would receive greater *siyata dishmaya*, divine assistance, by humbling himself and going as a student rather than demanding that his former student come to him.

The *gemara* mentions a related tradition about Rav Avimi's character: Rav Chisda once said he had received many *kufi tabi* — strikes — from Rav Avimi over the teaching that when a court auctions property for orphans and makes announcements daily, thirty days suffice, but when announcements are made only on Mondays and Thursdays (market days), sixty days are required, though spanning a longer calendar period. Rav Chisda praised this teaching and Rav Avimi apparently reprimanded him for circulating the praise — consistent with Rav Avimi's evident humility.

### Nachman Avimi

The story continues. Rav Nachman encountered Rav Avimi — presumably while Rav Avimi was at Rav Chisda's house — and asked him: *keitzad komtzin* — how does one perform the *kmitzah*? Rav Avimi pointed to a vessel near at hand, on the ground, and said: from a *kli* like this one. Rav Nachman challenged him: can you really perform *kmitzah* from a vessel that is on the ground? Rav Avimi immediately backed away: *d'magbah lei kohen* — I meant while a *kohen* is holding it. Rav Nachman then asked: *keitzad mekadshin et haminchos* — how does one sanctify the *menachot* into the next vessel? Again Rav Avimi pointed to a vessel and said: you place it into such a vessel. And again Rav Nachman challenged: can one sanctify into a vessel on the ground? Again Rav Avimi retreated: I meant that a *kohen* was holding it.

Rav Nachman then drew out the implication: *im kein, hutzrachta gimmel kohanim* — if a *kohen* must hold each vessel, you need three *kohanim* for the process: one to hold the original vessel, one to perform the *kmitzah* with his right hand, and one to hold the second vessel. Rav Avimi responded: *v'tei tlisha-sar k'tamid* — so what? We know the *tamid shel shachar* involved thirteen *kohanim* carrying limbs to the *mizbe'ach*. Having three *kohanim* is not inherently problematic.

### Sheshes Answer

Still, the question of whether a vessel must be held remained unresolved. The *gemara* then reports: *ba'u minei me'Rav Sheshes, mahoo likmotz mikli she'al gabei karka* — they asked Rav Sheshes the same question, whether *kmitzah* may be performed from a vessel resting on the ground. Rav Sheshes replied: *puk chazi mai avdin legav* — go look at what they did inside.

### Showbread Procedure

Rav Sheshes directs attention to the procedure for the *lechem hapanim* — the showbread — on *Shabbat*. The *mishnah* describes it thus: four *kohanim* enter the *heichal*, two holding the two new columns of bread and two holding the two *bezichin* — the small spoons of frankincense. And four *kohanim* precede them to remove the old bread: two to take the two columns of bread being removed, and two to take out the two spoons of incense. The incense was then burned and the *kohanim* would eat the bread — the spoons and frankincense serving the role of the *kometz*, and the bread serving the role of the remainder of the *minchah*.

### Table Not Held

The critical observation: *v'ilu magbi'ah et hashulchan lo katani* — the *mishnah* does not mention any *kohen* whose function was to hold up the *shulchan*, the table. The table rested on the ground. And the bread was taken off the table and the new bread placed on it — all without anyone holding the table.

The *gemara* anticipates an objection: perhaps the *mishnah* simply did not mention the one holding the table because it was only describing the *avodot* relevant for *piggul*, not all participants. This was the response given earlier when a similar question was raised from a different *mishnah*. But Rav Sheshes's proof is different in a crucial respect: *hacha nachit leminyana dechahanim* — this *mishnah* explicitly enumerates the number of *kohanim*. Four go in with the new items, four come out with the old. If anyone were holding the table, the *mishnah* would have counted him. The enumeration is precise and deliberate. The absence of a table-holder from the count demonstrates that no one held the table — and the service over the table was valid.

### Kometz Proof

The *gemara* draws the conclusion: *ela shema mina, kometz mikli al gabei karkah, shema mina* — learn from this that one may indeed perform the *kmitzah* from a *kli* resting on the ground. The vessel need not be held by a *kohen* for the *kli sharet* to function. The proof from the *shulchan*, while perhaps unexpected, is treated by the *gemara* as decisive. A table is of course naturally a floor-resting object, and one might have thought it different from a vessel that one would normally hold. But the *gemara* does not draw that distinction. Halachically, all *klei sharet* are treated uniformly, and if the *shulchan* — itself a *kli sharet* — functioned without being held, then any *kli sharet* may function without being held.

The practical implication is significant: only one *kohen* is required for the *kmitzah*, not three. The *ba'alim* — the owner — brings the *minchah*; the *kohen* takes the *kmitzah* and may either hand it to another *kohen* holding the second vessel or place it in a vessel resting on the ground.

This extended discussion of *kli sharet* yields three distinct principles. First, there is a debate regarding whether *kli sharet* requires *da'as* — explicit intent — to have its sanctifying effect; Rabbi Yochanan rules that it does. Second, even setting aside the question of intent, the *kli sharet* requires an actual conscious act of placement; passive entry — as in the monkey case — is insufficient. Third, the *kli sharet* can function effectively even when resting on the ground of the *mikdash*, without being held by a *kohen*.

---

---

# Menachot 8

## Kometz & Vessel Hold (II)

### Rava: Ground Vessel OK

The daf begins in the middle of 7b, approximately six lines from the top, where the Gemara has been exploring whether the *kli sharet* used in the *kometz* process must be held by a *kohein* or whether it may rest on the ground. Rava opens with a declaration: *peshita li* — it is obvious to me — that the *kometz* may be taken from a *kli sharet* that is resting on the ground. His proof is drawn from the *siluk bazeichin*: when the small spoons of incense are removed from the *shulchan*, those spoons function as the *kometz* of the *lechem hapanim*, insofar as the twelve loaves correspond to the *shirayim* of a *mincha* that are eaten, and the *bazikim* correspond to the portion that is burned. Even though there is no flour involved, the structural role they play mirrors that of the *kometz*. Since the *bazikim* are removed from a table that rests on the ground, we learn that the *kometz* may likewise be taken from a ground-based vessel.

Rava extends this logic further: one may also place the *mincha* into a *kli sharet* resting on the ground for the purpose of *kidush kli*, the initial sanctification. The proof again is from the *sidur bazeichin* — the original arrangement of the loaves and spoons on the *shulchan*, which is itself a ground-based vessel. So both the initial placing of the *mincha* into the *kli* and the subsequent taking of the *kometz* from it are established as valid even when the vessel is on the ground.

### Placing Kometz Stage

However, one stage of the process remains unaddressed: after the *kometz* has been taken, it must be placed into a second *kli sharet*. May that vessel also be on the ground? Here the logic shifts. From the moment the *kometz* is taken, the process of bringing it to the *mizbe'ach* has effectively begun — this is the stage at which *pigul* considerations become relevant, and the *kohein* is actively engaged in the *avoda*. When a vessel is left on the ground, the forward motion of the *avoda* is, in a sense, interrupted; the offering is no longer being actively brought. One might therefore argue that at this later stage, the vessel must be held by a *kohein*.

### Rava's Query

This is precisely Rava's question: *bai rava kidush kometz mai* — what is the law regarding the *kidush* of the *kometz* at this placement stage? Do we continue to learn from the earlier stages of the *mincha* itself, where the *kli* may be on the ground? Or do we now shift our analogy and learn from *dam* — from the blood of an animal *korban*? From the moment of *kmitza* onward, there is indeed a structural analog to *korbanot*: the *kometz* is caught in a *kli* and brought to the *mizbe'ach*, just as blood is caught in a vessel and brought to the *mizbe'ach*. If we draw that parallel, then the *kli* cannot be on the ground, since by blood the *avoda* of *kabbalas hadam* requires an active physical holding of the vessel — without that, there is no valid act of reception.

It is worth noting an important distinction: by blood, the *avoda* is defined as *kabbalah* — catching. Without holding the vessel, there is no act. By a *mincha*, however, the *avoda* is *netina* — placing. One can perform the act of placing even if the vessel rests on the ground. This difference could have justified treating the two cases differently. Nevertheless, Rava's question is whether, from this point on, we follow the analogy to blood.

### Learn from Dam

The Gemara records: *hadar pashat* — Rava ultimately resolved his question and concluded *midamya yalfinan*, that we do in fact learn from blood at this stage. The resolution is presented without detailed reasoning; it appears to rest on the logical observation that once the *kmitza* is taken and the *avoda* begins in earnest, the relevant model is that of animal *korbanot*, and accordingly the vessel must be held by a *kohein*. This means two *kohanim* are involved at that stage — one cannot hold the vessel in one's own other hand, given the requirement to use the right hand.

---

## Kometz Two Vessels

### Chalako B'Shnei Kelim

The Gemara immediately challenges whether Rava genuinely holds that we learn from *dam*, by citing a separate tradition: if one divided the *kometz* between two vessels — placing half into one *kli sharet* and half into another, rather than placing the entire *kometz* into a single vessel — what is the law? Rav Nachman says *eino kadosh*: it is not sanctified. Rava says *kadosh*: it is sanctified.

The relevance of this dispute to Rava's earlier position becomes clear when we trace the chain of reasoning that underlies it. The principle that the minimum required amount must all be caught in a single vessel derives from the law of *haza'ah* by *parah adumah*. From there it is extended to the *kabalah* of *dam* of a *korban* — the minimum amount necessary for sprinkling must all be caught in a single vessel. If Rava holds that the *kidush kometz* is learned from *dam*, one would expect him to require the entire *kometz* to be placed into a single vessel, just as the minimum amount of blood must be caught in a single vessel. Yet here Rava permits dividing the *kometz* between two vessels. The Gemara presses: if Rava truly learns from *dam*, why does he not apply the requirement of a single-vessel minimum to the *kometz* as well?

---

## Kometz Two Vessels (II)

### Rava Reverses

The Gemara records that *hadar beih Rava me-hahi* — Rava retracted from his position. Rashi explains that Rava reversed his ruling that the *kometz* placed in two vessels is *kadosh*, and ultimately agreed that one must place the entire *kometz* into a single vessel, consistent with learning from *dam*. This is the direction the Gemara has been building toward: the analogy to blood is the governing principle, and the requirement of a minimum amount in a single vessel applies equally to the *kometz*.

### Dam Minimum Amount

Having established that Rava reverses to align with the blood analogy, the Gemara turns to ask: where do we know in the first place that blood is not sanctified if less than the minimum amount is caught in each of two vessels? The source is a *braitah* taught by Rav Tachlipa bar Shmuel, which we will examine in the next section.

---

## Kometz & Vessel Hold (II)

### Learn or Not?

Before proceeding to that *braitah*, the Gemara raises a broader question: does Rabbi Eliezer in fact learn the laws of *mincha* from *dam*? This question is prompted by a teaching attributed to Rabbi Eliezer regarding the *chavitei Kohen Gadol*, which will be treated at greater length below. As the Gemara eventually establishes, Rabbi Eliezer does not learn *mincha* from *dam* at all — rather, he learns *mincha* from *mincha*, that is, from the *lechem hapanim*. This distinction is critical: it means that Rabbi Eliezer's rulings about the *mincha* cannot be challenged on the basis of what we know about blood, and conversely, what we know about blood cannot be straightforwardly imported into the *mincha* context according to his view.

---

## Dam One Vessel Rule

### Parah Minimum Teaching

The Gemara now presents the *braitah* of Rav Tachlipa bar Shmuel, which anchors the entire discussion. The *haza'ah* of *parah adumah* requires a minimum amount of liquid — enough to be absorbed by the hyssop and then sprinkled. If one sanctified less than that minimum amount in one vessel and less than that minimum amount in a second vessel, the water has not been sanctified, and one may not combine the two and use them for sprinkling. The entire minimum amount must have been present together at the moment of sanctification.

### Dam Same Law?

This rule is established for *parah adumah*, but the question is immediately raised: does the same law apply to the blood of a *korban*? One might argue that the *parah adumah* rule is a *halachah l'Moshe miSinai* — a technically arbitrary law transmitted from Sinai — and from such laws we do not extrapolate to other areas. Or perhaps the *parah adumah* rule derives from a *pasuk*, in which case the same *pasuk* or parallel reasoning would apply to *dam* as well.

### V'Taval B'Dam

The Gemara resolves this by examining the verse governing how the *kohein* dips his finger in the blood: *v'taval* — he shall dip — and *badam* — in the blood. The Gemara demonstrates that both terms are necessary and that each conveys a distinct requirement. Had the Torah written only *v'taval*, one would know that the act of dipping requires immersion in collected liquid rather than merely running the finger around the rim — what the Gemara calls *maspig*, a sponging motion — but one might have thought it permissible to collect a little blood in one vessel and a little in another, then combine them before dipping. Had the Torah written only *badam*, one would know that the minimum amount must be present from the outset, but one might have permitted the sponging motion. Both terms together establish: first, the act must be a genuine dipping in pooled liquid; and second, the minimum amount must have been present in the vessel from the beginning.

### Dam Original Amount

Rava confirms this reading with a supporting *braitah*: *v'taval* — not *maspig*; *badam* — *shete'hei badam shiur tvila m'ikaro*, that the minimum amount required for dipping must have been in the vessel originally, from the moment the blood was caught. This is now established as a *pasuk*-based rule applicable to the blood of *korbanot*, not merely to *parah adumah*, and it is on this basis that we apply the same requirement to the *kometz* — assuming one learns *kometz* from *dam*.

---

## Finger Remnants

### Fresh Dam Each Time

The Gemara then turns to the final phrase of the *braitah*: *min hadam shebe'inyan* — from the blood that is the subject of the matter. What does this phrase come to exclude? Rava explains: *l'mutei shirayim shebe'etzba* — it excludes the remnant blood left on the finger. If the *kohein* must perform multiple sprinklings — for example, the four corner applications of a *chatas*, or the seven sprinklings toward the *parochet* for an inner *chatas* — he may not use the blood remaining on his finger from the previous sprinkling. Rather, for each application he must return to the vessel and dip anew. The verse says *min hadam shebe'inyan* — from the blood that is in the vessel — meaning each sprinkling must draw from the original collected blood, not from whatever remains on the finger. This supports the ruling of Rabbi Elazar: *shirayim shebe'etzba psulin* — the remnant blood on the finger is invalid for further sprinklings.

### Splattered Blood

At this point, a student of Rava named Ravin bar Rav Adda raises a challenge. His fellow students cite a *braitah* in the name of Rav Amram that appears to contradict this conclusion. The *braitah* states: if one was sprinkling blood and some blood fell from his hand, the question is whether the garment on which it falls requires the special ritual laundering prescribed by the Torah for blood of a *chatas*. The answer given is: if the blood fell from the finger *before* the sprinkling, laundering is required; if it fell *after* the sprinkling, laundering is not required.

The *braitah* had been read as follows: *ad shelo gamar haza'ato* — before he finished the entire series of sprinklings, blood that drips on clothing requires laundering; *mishegamar haza'ato* — once he has finished the entire series, it does not. If this reading is correct, it implies that throughout the entire series the blood is still in its original pre-sprinkling state, which would mean the *kohein* was performing all the sprinklings from one dipping — using *shirayim shebe'etzba* — and not re-dipping between each application.

### Single Sprinkling Reading

The Gemara rejects this reading. There is no reason to interpret the *braitah* as describing a series of sprinklings at all. The far more natural reading is: before the finger releases the blood in a single sprinkling, any blood that splatters on clothes requires laundering; after the finger has discharged the blood in that single sprinkling, blood that splatters from the finger does not. The *braitah* is simply describing the before-and-after of one sprinkling, not the beginning and end of a multi-sprinkling series. The challenge therefore dissolves: there is no evidence that *shirayim shebe'etzba* are valid for continued use.

### Parah Hand/Finger

A related question is raised by Abaye from the procedure of *parah adumah*, where the *kohein* sprinkles blood seven times toward the *Mikdash*. The *braitah* states: *gamar milhazot mekanuach yado begufah shel parah* — when finished with the sprinkling, he wipes his hand on the body of the *parah* itself, since the verse requires all the blood to be burned together with the animal. But *lo gamar mekanuach etzba'o* — when he is not yet finished, he cleans only his finger.

Abaye reads this as evidence that the *kohein* performed all seven sprinklings in succession from one dipping, and only after finishing did he wipe his hand on the *parah*. The intermediate action — cleaning the finger — would then refer only to grooming between sprinklings, not to re-dipping.

The Gemara rejects this inference. The contrast is not between mid-series and end-of-series, but rather between two different cleaning actions: when *finished*, he wipes his entire hand on the *parah*, because the blood remaining on his whole hand must be burned; when *not yet finished*, he cleans only his finger — specifically, at the rim of the vessel (*b'sfat mizrak*), so that the finger is clean for the next dipping. The Gemara cites Abaye's own answer: the vessels used in this process are called *kipurei zahav*, golden *kipurim*, and *kipur* implies cleansing — accordingly, the rim of the vessel is precisely the place designed for cleaning the finger between dippings.

The implication is striking: even for the seven sprinklings of *parah adumah*, the *kohein* must re-dip between each sprinkling, cleaning his finger at the rim of the vessel before dipping anew. The *shirayim shebe'etzba* are invalid, consistent with Rabbi Elazar's ruling and Rava's derivation from *min hadam shebe'inyan*.

---

## Chavitei Split Sanctify

### Yochanan vs. Eliezer

The Gemara now turns to the substantive debate about the *chavitei Kohen Gadol* — the daily *mincha* offering of the *Kohen Gadol*, which was a minimum-size *mincha* of one *isaron* brought in two halves, half in the morning and half in the afternoon. The question is whether the *mincha* could be initially prepared and sanctified in two separate half-*isaron* portions, or whether it must first be combined as a whole and then divided.

Rabbi Yochanan says *enah kedushah l'chatza'in*: the *mincha* cannot be sanctified in halves; it must be sanctified as a whole. Rabbi Eliezer says *mitoch shekreva l'chatza'in kedushah l'chatza'in*: since the *mincha* is brought in halves, it may also be sanctified in halves. The *kli sharet* can function on each half separately.

### Mincha Min Mincha

This debate prompts the Gemara to ask whether Rabbi Eliezer can hold this position consistently with his ruling about blood — for if one learns the functioning of the *kli sharet* from *dam*, then just as the minimum amount of blood must all be caught in a single vessel, the *mincha* must all be placed in a single vessel. The Gemara resolves this by establishing that Rabbi Eliezer does not learn *mincha* from *dam* at all. Rather, he learns *mincha mimincha* — from one type of *mincha* to another. When Rabbi Eliezer validates *kmitza* performed in the *heichal* rather than the *azara*, his proof is *shekein matzinu b'sidur bazeichin*: the *bazikim* are placed on the *shulchan* inside the *heichal*, and this act corresponds to the *kmitza* of the *mincha*. He learns *mincha* from *lechem hapanim* — one type of *mincha* from another — but he does not cross the conceptual boundary from *mincha* to *dam*. Therefore, the rules that govern the functioning of the *kli sharet* in the context of blood cannot simply be transposed onto the *mincha* according to Rabbi Eliezer's view.

### Bread Breaking Cases

The Gemara proceeds to examine whether Rabbi Eliezer consistently learns *mincha* from *mincha* by testing it against a *braitah* about the *lechem hapanim*. The *braitah* states: if before the *bazikim* were removed from the *shulchan* a loaf of the *lechem hapanim* broke, the bread is invalid and the *bazikim* may not be burned. If after the *bazikim* were removed a loaf broke, the bread is invalid — the *kohanim* may not eat it — but the *bazikim* may still be burned; the *korban* retains its validity in that respect.

The parallel to a *mincha* is as follows: if part of the *mincha* was lost before the *kmitza*, the entire *korban* is invalid. If the *kometz* was taken and then part of the *shirayim* was lost, the *kometz* remains valid and may be burned on the *mizbe'ach*, but the *shirayim* may not be eaten and must be burned. This correspondence is clean and direct.

### Higia Zmanah Logic

Rabbi Elazar adds an important gloss to the *braitah*: the phrase "after the *bazikim* were removed" does not require that they were physically removed — it means only that the time to remove them has arrived. *Keivan shehigia zmana lefarek, af al pi shelo parka, kemi sheparka dami*: once the time to remove them came, it is as though they were already removed, even if the physical act had not yet occurred.

This principle — *higia zmanah* — cannot be applied to an ordinary *mincha*, and the Gemara explains why. In a *mincha*, the *kometz* has not yet been defined; it is a portion that must be taken from an undifferentiated mass of flour, and no one knows in advance which handful will be taken. One therefore cannot say "the time has come for the *kometz* to be taken" in a way that renders it already separated. With the *lechem hapanim*, by contrast, the *bazikim* are physically distinct objects sitting alongside the bread. They are clearly defined, identifiable, and separable. Once the time arrives to remove them, it is conceptually coherent to treat them as already removed.

A second difference, not raised by the Gemara but noted in the shiur: unlike a private individual's *mincha*, which may be brought at any time, the *lechem hapanim* has a fixed and precise time — Shabbat afternoon — at which the removal must occur. This fixed time makes it possible to invoke *higia zmanah* in a meaningful way.

### Machatzitah Pasuk

The Gemara now turns to the textual basis for Rabbi Yochanan's position. Rav Acha cites the verse: *mincha machatzitah baboker umachatzitah bein ha'arbayim* — the *mincha*, half of it in the morning and half of it in the afternoon. The word *machatzitah* — "half of it" — indicates that one begins with a whole *mincha* and then takes half. The verse thus presupposes the existence of a complete *mincha* at the outset, before the division occurs.

A *braitah* reinforces this reading: if the verse had said *mincha machatzit* — "a half-*mincha*" — one might have thought the *Kohen Gadol* brings half an *isaron* in the morning and makes it into a *mincha*, and another half an *isaron* in the afternoon and makes it into a separate *mincha*. But the verse says *machatzitah* — half of *it* — indicating that you start with one whole *mincha* and divide it. *Mechtza mishalem hu meivi*: he brings a half of a whole.

Against Rabbi Eliezer, the Gemara further notes that the Torah uses the language of *chok* — a fixed statutory requirement — in connection with the *chavitim*. Normally in the context of *korbanot*, the Torah's detailed specifications are not all *me'akeiv*, and failure to observe them does not necessarily invalidate the offering unless the Torah repeats or emphasizes the requirement, or uses the word *chok*. Since *chok* appears here, one might argue that the specific procedure of bringing a whole *mincha* and dividing it is indispensable.

Rabbi Eliezer responds: the *chok* requirement applies only to the stage of bringing a whole *isaron* from one's home before the *mincha* is sanctified. The obligation is that the flour, before it enters the *kli sharet*, must consist of a full *isaron*. Once that threshold is met, Rabbi Eliezer maintains that the *kli sharet* may sanctify each half independently. This is admittedly a striking answer, since one would ordinarily expect the whole-*mincha* requirement to govern the sanctification stage as well as the preparatory stage. But Rabbi Eliezer's underlying principle is that the question of *kedushah* — whether the *kli sharet* functions to sanctify — is analytically separate from the question of how the *avoda* must be performed. Even if the *avoda* ideally requires a whole *mincha* that is then divided, the *kli sharet* may still effect *kedushah* on portions presented to it separately.

---

## Partial Amounts

### Rav Half Invalid

The final section of the daf takes up a related question: what if a *kohein* places half an *isaron* into a *kli sharet* with the intention to add the remaining half subsequently? Is even this partial amount sanctified by the *kli*? Rav says *eino kadosh*: it is not sanctified, even with intent to add.

### Yochanan Half Valid

Rabbi Yochanan says *kadosh*: even a half-measure placed with the intent to complete the full amount is sanctified by the *kli sharet*.

### Yosi Intent Distinction

Rabbi Yosi refines the position with a crucial distinction: *bizman she'ein da'ato lehosif* — when one has no intention of adding more — the *kli* does not sanctify a partial amount. *Aval bizman sheda'ato lehosif, rishon rishon kadosh* — but when one intends to add more, each portion added becomes sanctified immediately as it is placed in the vessel. This is itself a *chiddush*: one might have thought that the full amount would become sanctified only at the end of the process, once the required measure is complete. Rabbi Yosi teaches that, since the entire process constitutes a single purposive act of filling the vessel, each increment is sanctified the moment it enters.

### Rav Learns Mincha

The Gemara demonstrates that Rav is willing to learn from one *mincha* context to another. Rav rules that a *mincha* may be sanctified in the *kli sharet* before the oil has been added, because the *lechem hapanim* — which has no oil — is nonetheless sanctified. Similarly, a *mincha* may be sanctified without the *levona* having been placed on it, because the *minchat nesachim* — the *mincha* accompanying animal offerings — has no *levona*. And a *mincha* may even be sanctified without either oil or *levona*, because we find such a case in the *minchat chotei*, for which the verse explicitly prohibits placing oil or *levona* on it. Since Rav is willing to draw these analogies across different *mincha* contexts, the Gemara presses: why does Rav not apply the case of *chavitim* — where Rabbi Eliezer would permit sanctification in halves — to permit sanctification of a half-*isaron* in other *mincha* contexts as well?

### Rav Like Yochanan

The Gemara's answer: *al korchacha Rav k'Rabbi Yochanan svira lei* — Rav must necessarily hold like Rabbi Yochanan, who rules that the *chavitim* must also be sanctified as a whole and may not be sanctified in halves. Since Rav applies the rule of the *chavitim* to other *mincha* offerings, and since Rav requires the full measure for those other offerings, Rav's position is only internally consistent if he agrees with Rabbi Yochanan that the *chavitim* themselves require the full measure at the time of sanctification.

The overarching theme that emerges across all these discussions is the functioning of *klei sharet* as the mechanism of *kedushah*. The questions of whether the vessel must be held, whether the minimum amount must be present, whether a half-measure can be sanctified, and whether *da'ato lehosif* makes a difference are all, at their root, questions about how *klei sharet* operate — not merely about the correct procedural form of the *avoda*. Rabbi Eliezer's position on the *chavitim* illustrates this cleanly: he agrees that the *avoda* should be performed by bringing a whole *mincha* and dividing it; his dispute is solely about whether, if that procedure was not followed, the *kli sharet* can nonetheless have effected *kedushah* on the portions presented to it. The *kedushah* of the *kli sharet* and the ritual correctness of the *avoda* are related but distinct categories, and much of the daf's analysis turns on keeping them carefully separate.

---

---

# Menachot 9

## Klei Shares & Mincha

### Rav: Sanctify Alone

The major theme of today's daf concerns the mechanics of *klei sharet* — the sacred Temple vessels — and specifically the question of whether they can sanctify a *mincha* even when not all of its required ingredients are simultaneously present in the vessel.

Rav states: *mincha kedusha belo shemen* — a *mincha* will be sanctified by the *kli sharet* even before the oil has been added. His proof is *shekein matzinu beLechem hapanim*: the *lechem hapanim* is a *mincha* that contains no oil, yet the *klei sharet* sanctify it. He extends this further: without *levona*, *shekein matzinu beminchat nesachim* — the *mincha* accompanying animal offerings contains no frankincense, yet the *klei sharet* function there. And even without both oil and frankincense, *shekein matzinu beminchat chotei* — the sinner's *mincha* contains neither, yet the *klei sharet* sanctify it nonetheless.

This line of reasoning is, on its face, surprising. One might object that in each of these proof-cases, the absence of the ingredient is entirely normative — that is simply how that particular *mincha* is meant to be brought. We are asking something different: whether the *klei sharet* sanctify the flour of a *mincha* that *does* require oil or *levona*, even before those ingredients have been added. The Gemara, however, frames this as *milta mimilta* — reasoning by analogy across cases even where the comparison is imperfect. Because the fundamental question is about the operative power of *klei sharet* and the nature of *kedushat klei sharet*, the analogies remain useful even if they are not perfectly parallel. If the *klei sharet* can function in those cases, it illuminates how *klei sharet* operate in general.

The practical implication of the flour being rendered *kadosh* at that early stage is primarily one of *chumra*: once the flour has intrinsic *kedusha* — *kedushat haguf* — it can no longer be redeemed. If it subsequently becomes *tamei* or otherwise *pasul*, it must be burned rather than redeemed.

Not only the flour but each of the other components individually: *veshemen ulevona kadshi hai belo hai vehai belo hai* — the oil and the frankincense can each be sanctified on their own in a *kli sharet*. For oil, the proof is *shekein matzinu belog shemen shel metzora* — the *log* of oil brought for a *metzora* is an independent offering placed in a *kli sharet*, demonstrating that *klei sharet* can sanctify oil alone. For frankincense, *shekein matzinu belevona habaa bevezikin* — the frankincense placed in the small spoons alongside the *lechem hapanim* is sanctified independently. The lesson is that since each of these ingredients can be sanctified alone when they *are* the entire offering, the *klei sharet* can similarly sanctify them even when they are merely components of a larger *mincha*.

### R. Chanina: All Together

Rabbi Chanina disagrees fundamentally: *lo zu kadesha belo zu velo zu kadesha belo zu* — one ingredient cannot be sanctified without the other; all ingredients of the *mincha* must be present together in the *kli* for sanctification to take effect. This is, it must be said, a very reasonable position on its own terms.

### Issaron Anointed

The Gemara now presses a question on Rabbi Chanina's position from an unexpected direction. Among the sacred vessels of the *Mikdash*, a vessel of the *issaron* measure — one-tenth of an *eifah*, approximately 2.49 liters, which is the minimum and standard flour measure for a *mincha* — was anointed with the *shemen hamishcha* and consecrated as a *kli sharet*. The Gemara asks: *verabbi Chanina issaron lama nimshach* — according to Rabbi Chanina, why was it necessary to anoint the *issaron* and make it a *kli sharet* at all?

The difficulty is as follows: if sanctification requires all ingredients to be present simultaneously, and a standard *mincha* consists of an *issaron* of flour together with a *log* of oil — approximately 0.6 liters — then the oil always exceeds the *issaron* measure. One would never place the flour alone into the *issaron* vessel expecting sanctification, because without the oil already present nothing is sanctified. The measuring vessel would function as an ordinary measuring cup, with no need for it to be a *kli sharet*.

The Gemara answers: *leminchat chotei* — the *minchat chotei* is brought without oil, and its measure is exactly an *issaron*. The sinner's *mincha* consists solely of flour in the amount of an *issaron*, and precisely for that case, the *issaron* vessel must be a *kli sharet* in order to sanctify it.

Similarly the Gemara asks: *halog lama nimshach* — why was the *log* measure itself consecrated as a *kli sharet*? Since oil is always mixed with flour, one might think a measuring vessel for oil alone would never be needed for sanctification. The Gemara answers: *lelog shel metzora* — the *log* of oil brought for the *metzora* is placed in a *kli sharet* and sanctified independently, and it is for this case that the *log* vessel required consecration.

### Shmuel: Vessels
