The *chutz lizmano* thought must be the necessary and sole reason for the invalidation. *Pigul* only applies when, were it not for the *pigul* thought, the *korban* would have been *kasher*. If it was going to be invalid regardless due to some other cause, it is *pasul* but not *pigul*.

### Pigul Success

The mishna illustrates through examples. *Keitzad karav hamatir k'mitzvato* — what does it look like when the *matir* was brought correctly? One scenario: you took the *kemitzah* in silence — the term *shtika* here, in contrast to explicit thought, is worth noting, though Rashi elsewhere in the tractate already explains that "thinking" in this context refers to articulated intent. Then you placed it in the vessel, carried it, and burned it *chutz lizmano* — or alternatively, you had the *pigul* thought during the *kemitzah* alone and completed the remaining *avodos* in silence. Both are simple cases of *pigul*.

The mishna adds: *she'kamat v'natan bakli v'holich v'hiktir chutz lizmano* — you harbored *pigul* thoughts throughout all four *avodos*. One might think this is problematic — since each individual *pigul* thought would have been "unnecessary" given the others. But this is not a concern. The logic of *karav hamatir k'mitzvato* is simply: bracket the *pigul* problem, and the *korban* would have been *kasher*. Multiple consistent *pigul* thoughts do not undermine one another.

### Pigul Fails

The mishna then asks: *keitzad lo karav hamatir k'mitzvato*? What does it look like when the *matir* was not brought correctly? The first example: you performed the *kemitzah* with a *chutz limkomo* thought, and then performed one or more of the remaining *avodos* with a *chutz lizmano* thought. Or you began with a *pigul* thought and introduced a *chutz limkomo* thought in a subsequent *avoda*. Or you had *chutz limkomo* throughout all four. In any of these combinations, where a *chutz limkomo* thought accompanies the *pigul* thought, the result is *pasul* but not *pigul* — the additional invalidating thought breaks the requirement that *pigul* be the sole operative problem.

The mishna then reminds us of another category of invalidating thought from the first mishna: *shelo lishma* by a *minchat chotei* or *minchat kanaot*. If the *kemitzah* of one of these was done *shelo lishma* — and then the remaining *avodos* had a *chutz lizmano* thought, or vice versa — this falls into the same category as *chutz limkomo*: there is an additional invalidating thought beyond *pigul*, and therefore it is *pasul* without *pigul*, as a case of *lo karav hamatir k'mitzvato*.

One might note that the debate between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar recorded in Zvachim 13a regarding *hiluch* — whether *holacha* in a non-direct path constitutes a valid *avoda* — does not reappear here in the mishna. This is presumably because we do not rule like those positions, and therefore the compilers saw no reason to replicate them here, though the question remains a fair one.

---

## Compound Thoughts

### Full-Portion Mix

The mishna turns now to compound thoughts — cases where during a single *avoda*, the *kohen* harbors two different types of invalidating intent regarding two different portions. The case: *le'echol k'zayis bachutz k'zayis lemachar* — planning to eat one *k'zayis* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* and one *k'zayis* the next day. Or the reverse order — first planning the *k'zayis lemachar* and then the *k'zayis bachutz*. In both orderings, the ruling is *pasul ve'ein bo kareit*. The logic appears to rely on the principle of *lo karav hamatir k'mitzvato*: even though this is not two separate *avodos* with different thoughts, the single act contains both a *chutz limkomo* element and a *chutz lizmano* element, and the *pigul* thought alone is not sufficient to invalidate.

### Half-Portion Mix

The case of half-portions is more straightforward: *kechatzayis bachutz kechatzayis lemachar* — half a *k'zayis* outside and half a *k'zayis* tomorrow, or the reverse. These are obviously *pasul ve'ein bo kareit*: there is not even a full *k'zayis* of *pigul* thought, and a thought cannot generate *pigul* unless it is directed at a *k'zayis*-equivalent portion.

---

## Hamatir K'mitzvato (II)

### R. Yehuda's Principle

Rabbi Yehuda now offers his own principle — *ze haklal* — which stands in disagreement with the mishna. He holds: *im machshavas hazman kadma lemachshavas hamakom* — if the *pigul* thought preceded the *chutz limkomo* thought, it locks in *pigul* status with *kareit*. The wrong-time thought arrived first and defined the *korban* as *pigul* before the wrong-place thought appeared. Conversely, *im machshavas hamakom kadma lemachshavas hazman* — if the wrong-place thought came first, it already defined the *korban* as *pasul* before the *pigul* thought could take hold, resulting in *pasul ve'ein bo kareit*.

### Sages' Position

The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda's sequential analysis entirely. Their position: *zeh vazeh pasul ve'ein bo kareit* — in every case where both thoughts are present, whether the *pigul* thought came first or the *chutz limkomo* thought came first, the result is *pasul* without *pigul*. *Pigul* can only function when it alone is responsible for the invalidation. The presence of any other invalidating thought, regardless of sequence, prevents *pigul* from taking hold. The *halacha* follows the Sages.

---

## Lost Shirayim

### Question Setup

The remainder of the *gemara* departs from the central *pigul* discussion of the mishna and takes up a theme established earlier: what happens when some *shirayim* are lost after the *kemitzah* but before the *haktarah*?

The question: *iba'ya lehu* — according to the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan, which we essentially rule like, that if some (not all) *shirayim* are lost between *kemitzah* and *haktarah* one may still burn the *kometz* — what would be the *pigul* implications?

We established earlier that Rabbi Yochanan's position carries an important qualification: *de'osin shirayim assurim be'achilah* — unlike an animal *korban* where if some of the meat is missing you simply eat the remainder, here if not all of the *shirayim* are present, you may not eat what remains. This is derived from a *pasuk*.

So the question is: if the *shirayim* are *assur be'achilah* anyway — due to this *chaser* situation — can one still make them *pigul* by harboring a *chutz lizmano* thought while burning the *kometz*? And correspondingly, does the *haktarat hakometz* in such a situation remove the *shirayim* from the category of *me'ilah*?

These are formally two separate questions — one about the parameters of *pigul*, one about the parameters of *me'ilah* — but they are united by a deeper conceptual issue: what is the nature of the prohibition against eating the *shirayim* when they are *chaser*? Is it that the *shirayim* as an object have become *pasul* — as in *yotzei* or *tamei* — or is it merely a restriction on the act of eating, without the object itself acquiring an intrinsic disqualification?

If the object is not *pasul* per se — if there is simply a halachic restriction on eating it, while the object itself retains its identity as a valid *korban* portion — then one might argue that a *pigul* thought remains relevant, and that the *haktarah* may still remove the *me'ilah* status. If, however, the *chaser* renders the object intrinsically invalid, then both the *pigul* thought and the removal of *me'ilah* status become irrelevant, because the *haktarah* cannot affect something that is fundamentally off the table.

To give this texture: ordinarily, *psulim* like *yotzei* and *tamei* render meat invalid, but they are in some sense external invalidations — the meat was taken somewhere wrong, or contracted a status from outside. *Chaser* — the very absence of part of the *mincha* — is arguably an intrinsic deficiency in the identity of the *korban* itself. The question is whether that intrinsic deficiency places it categorically beyond the reach of halachic acts like *haktarah*.

One should note that this *halacha* — that *chaser shirayim* renders the rest *assur be'achilah* — is itself unusual. Elsewhere in halacha, if some meat becomes *pasul*, the rest remains valid. Here we are told that the remainder cannot be eaten when some is missing. The *pasuk* for this is *v'hanoteret min hamincha yochlu aharon u'vanav* — "the remainder of the *mincha* shall be eaten by Aharon and his sons." The *drashah* is *v'hanoteret min hamincha*, not *v'hanoteret min hanoteret* — the remainder of the *mincha*, not the remainder of the remainder. This reads as a restriction on the circumstances under which eating is permitted, not as a pronouncement about the object's *pasul* status.

It also bears noting that if all the *shirayim* were lost — not just some — the question would not arise, because if one holds like the opinion that *zrikat hadam* cannot be performed when all the meat is gone, then the *haktarah* of the *kometz* itself could not be performed. And if no *haktarah* is performed, there is no act through which *pigul* could be generated with respect to the *shirayim*. The question is meaningful precisely in the case where some *shirayim* remain, the *haktarah* of the *kometz* can and should proceed, yet those *shirayim* which do remain cannot be eaten.

### Rav Huna

Rav Huna rules: *afilu l'Rabbi Akiva de'amar zrika mo'elet l'yotzei* — even according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *zrika* remains effective for meat that has become *yotzei*, in that case *yotzei* is an external invalidity — the meat is physically intact but located in the wrong place. It is *pasul* by reason of something extrinsic. *Hani milei yotzei de'ita b'einya u'pasul machmat davar acher* — that applies to *yotzei*, where the object is present and the invalidity is caused by something external.

*Aval chisaron d'psula d'gufeih hu* — but *chaser* is an intrinsic deficiency in the object itself. It is not merely in the wrong place; it is literally not fully there. *Lo mahani lei haktara* — the *haktarah* of the *kometz* cannot affect it. The *shirayim* are too fundamentally deficient to be reached by the *haktarah*. Rav Huna holds that *chaser* is a more severe invalidity than *yotzei*, and therefore even where Rabbi Akiva would apply *pigul* to *yotzei*, Rav Huna says *chaser* lies beyond even that.

### Rava's Position

Rava initially disagrees: *amar lei Rava, adra'ba* — on the contrary. He argues the opposite direction. Even according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds *ein zrika mo'elet l'yotzei* — that *zrika* has no effect when meat is *yotzei* — that is because *yotzei* means the meat is not in the *Beit HaMikdash*. *Hani milei yotzei de'leissa bifnim* — that is *yotzei*, where the meat is literally outside. *Aval chisaron de'ita bifnim* — but *chaser*, where the remaining *shirayim* are inside the *Beit HaMikdash*, since what is there is present and inside, the *haktarah* does apply to it. *Mahani lei haktara* — and therefore there would be *pigul*, and *me'ilah* status would be removed.

Rava's conceptual framing is that *chaser* is not a *psul* at all. The *shirayim* that are there are halachically intact; there is simply a restriction on eating them that arises from the absence of some of the others. Viewed that way, the object itself remains connected to the *korban* and can be affected by the *haktarah*.

---

## R. Chiya's Baraita

### Rava's Reading

Rava seeks to prove his position from Rabbi Chiya's *baraita*. Rava notes: *v'sani Rabbi Chiya* — Rabbi Chiya taught a *baraita* that parallels our mishna in all respects, except that he omitted the words *o k'zayis* — the case of intending to eat or burn merely a *k'zayis*.

Why did Rabbi Chiya omit *o k'zayis*? Rava argues as follows: *kegon* — the concern was that the phrase *o k'zayis* might be understood to indicate a case where all that remains of the *shirayim* is a *k'zayis* — i.e., the rest was lost, and only a *k'zayis* is left. This is precisely the case of *chasru shirayim*. Rabbi Chiya did not want to teach that case.

Now, *o k'zayis* by the *kometz* — meaning, a thought that one would burn a *k'zayis* of the *kometz* outside or at the wrong time — would also be problematic to state, because if all that remained of the *kometz* were a *k'zayis*, the entire process would be impossible: you cannot be *maktir* the *kometz* with less than the full amount. And since one cannot speak of *o k'zayis* in that context, Rabbi Chiya wanted to be consistent and removed the phrase from the *shirayim* context as well. Even though in the *shirayim* context, halachically a *pigul* thought on a *k'zayis* of remaining *shirayim* would in principle work, Rabbi Chiya edited the text minimally and uniformly, removing *o k'zayis* throughout. And since the *baraita* concludes with *pigul vichayavin alav kareit*, Rava infers that the *haktarah* is indeed effective — otherwise Rabbi Chiya would not have taught the *pigul* ruling at all in that context.

One must acknowledge the circularity here. Rava reads Rabbi Chiya's silence on *o k'zayis* as evidence that it would have worked in the *shirayim* case but was omitted only for consistency. But Rav Huna could equally read the silence as evidence that it would not work — that the case of *chaser* is so fundamentally invalid that *pigul* does not apply. The proof is not airtight. This is presumably why the *rishonim* struggle at length with what Rava's argument actually establishes.

### Abaye's Reading

Abaye offers a cleaner and less tortured reading. *Lo* — that is not why Rabbi Chiya omitted *o k'zayis*. *Ha mani Rabbi Eliezer hi* — it is because Rabbi Chiya follows Rabbi Eliezer.

### R. Eliezer Context

The basis: *detnan* — we were taught in a mishna: *hakometz v'halevonah v'haktores v'minchat kohanim v'minchat kohen mashiach v'minchat nesachim* — in all these cases where one is obligated for offering them outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *tanna kamma* holds one is liable from a *k'zayis*. *Rabbi Eliezer poter ad she'yakriv es kulo* — Rabbi Eliezer exempts unless one offers the complete unit. A *k'zayis* does not constitute an act of *haktarah* according to Rabbi Eliezer; only the full designated amount does.

This applies equally to the *machshava*: a thought of performing *haktarah* with a *k'zayis* is not an invalidating thought according to Rabbi Eliezer, because such an act would not be a real act of *haktarah*. Therefore, *o k'zayis* in the context of *haktarah* is simply not a valid case. Rabbi Chiya, following Rabbi Eliezer, removed it.

### Consistency Logic

One might ask: even granting that *o k'zayis* cannot be stated for *haktarah* according to Rabbi Eliezer, why should it be omitted for *achilah* — eating? For eating, everyone agrees that a *k'zayis* defines the act. The *shiur* for eating is universally a *k'zayis*. Why would Rabbi Chiya not say *o k'zayis* when the thought is about eating the *shirayim* at the wrong time or wrong place?

Abaye's answer: *v'kivan de'ba'aktaras kmitza lo masni lei k'zayis* — since he cannot state the *k'zayis* case for burning the *kometz*, he does not state it for eating the *shirayim* either, so that the parallel structure is preserved. *Bishirayim nami lo matni o k'zayis*. Even though in principle, a thought of eating a *k'zayis* of *shirayim* at the wrong time would generate *pigul* (because a *k'zayis* is indeed the *shiur* for eating), Rabbi Chiya edits the text with minimal change and removes *o k'zayis* uniformly.

This reading has nothing to do with the *chaser shirayim* question. Rabbi Chiya is not addressing the case of lost *shirayim* at all. He is simply operating with Rabbi Eliezer's definition of what constitutes an act of *haktarah*, which requires the full amount, and he streamlines the text accordingly. The case where only a *k'zayis* remains of the *shirayim* — which was Rava's reading of the omission — does not enter Rabbi Chiya's calculation at all.

Rabbi Eliezer carries a further implication regarding the *levonah*. The mishna we are working with assumes *mefaglin b'chatzi matir* — that a *pigul* thought during even one of the two permitting acts (the *kometz* or the *levonah*) suffices to make *pigul*, even though both together are what permit the *shirayim* for eating. Rabbi Eliezer, however, is consistent: *hakometz v'halevonah she'hikriv echad meihen bachutz chayav; Rabbi Eliezer poter ad she'yakriv es sheneihem* — to be liable for offering outside, you must offer both the *kometz* and the *levonah* outside. A *pigul* thought on only one would correspondingly be insufficient according to Rabbi Eliezer.

So then, how can Rabbi Chiya's *baraita* mention *pigul* for a thought during just the *kemitzah* of the *kometz*, without the *levonah*? The *gemara* answers: *lo nitzrecha ela lekometz deminchat chotei* — this applies to the *kometz* of a *minchat chotei*, which has no *levonah*. By a *minchat chotei*, there is only one permitting act, so a *pigul* thought on that one act suffices even according to Rabbi Eliezer. *Ven ki ata Rav Dimi amar Rabbi Eliezer kometz deminchat chotei hu Rabbi Eliezer hi* — and when Rav Dimi came, he confirmed: it is Rabbi Eliezer's position, and it concerns the *kometz* of a *minchat chotei*.

The *gemara* then raises an objection: is it not strange that the *tanna* restructured his entire *baraita* around the special case of *minchat chotei* without explicitly identifying it as such? The *gemara* answers: *ein* — yes, this is the case. The rationale is best understood as follows: Rabbi Chiya was working from an existing text and made the least intrusive edit possible. He crossed out the *o k'zayis* throughout. The resulting text still makes sense in the context of a *minchat chotei*, even if it no longer explicitly announces that context.

---

## Rava Retracts

### Lechem HaPanim

*Hadar amar Rava* — Rava then retracts his initial position. *Lav ma'alya hi de'amri* — what I said before is not correct. The proof comes from a *baraita* concerning *lechem hapanim*: *she-nifresa achat mehem kulam pesulot* — if one of the loaves broke, they are all *pasul*.

### Chaser Worse

This is the case of *chaser* for *lechem hapanim* — a loaf that is broken is *chaser*. And from this *baraita*, Rava infers: *hayatzata hani de-ika gavai ksherot* — the implication is that the loaves which are inside, i.e., intact, would be valid were it not for the breakage. And the further implication: if one was *yotzei* — taken outside — the remaining loaves would be *kasher*, because only *chaser* triggers universal *psul*. Thus *chaser* is worse than *yotzei*. And since *chaser* is worse than *yotzei*, even where Rabbi Akiva says *zrika* is effective for *yotzei*, he would not say so for *chaser*. Rava retracts his position and now holds: *chaser* is intrinsically more severe than *yotzei*, and therefore the *haktarah* does not render the *shirayim* subject to *pigul* or remove *me'ilah* status.

### Abaye Responds

Abaye responds: *mi katani hayatzata?* — does the *baraita* actually say that if one was *yotzei* it would be *kasher*? *Dilma hanitmas hanach ksherot* — perhaps what the *baraita* implies is only that if one loaf became *tamei*, the rest remain valid. *Mai ta'ama? Demartze tzitz* — because the *tzitz* atones for *tumah*, so *tamei* loaves do not invalidate the rest. *Aval yatzata lo* — but if one was *yotzei*, perhaps the rest would also be *pasul*. *Ve-Rabbi Eliezer hee, de-amar ein zrika mo'elet l'yotzei* — and the *baraita* would follow Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that *zrika* is not effective for *yotzei*, meaning that *yotzei* also completely invalidates. On that reading, the *baraita* gives the example of a broken loaf simply to teach us that even *chaser*, where the loaf is still inside the *Beit HaMikdash* and is not *yotzei*, is equally invalid. *De-afillu nifresa de-itah bifnim lo mahanya lah haktara* — even a loaf that broke but remained inside is just as bad as *yotzei*. The *baraita* is thus according to Rabbi Eliezer, and the implication about *yotzei* cannot be drawn from it.

### Conclusion

In the end, the *gemara* reaches the following conclusion: whether *chaser* is subject to *pigul* and removed from *me'ilah* through *haktarah* depends on the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer. According to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that *zrika* is effective even for *yotzei*, *haktarah* would be effective for *chaser* as well — the *pigul* thought would be relevant and *me'ilah* would be removed. According to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that *zrika* is not effective even for *yotzei*, *haktarah* would equally not be effective for *chaser* — *pigul* does not apply and *me'ilah* remains.

The original framing of the question allowed for the possibility that *chaser* might be worse than *yotzei* (Rav Huna's position), better than *yotzei* (Rava's original position), or equivalent to *yotzei*. The *gemara* concludes with them equivalent: the same *machlokes* between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer that governs *yotzei* governs *chaser* as well. Rava's retraction moves him away from his original position that *chaser* was more lenient, but Abaye successfully deflects his proof that *chaser* is more stringent. The matter remains dependent on the broader *machlokes tannaim*.

It is worth noting that Rava's original instinct — even setting aside his proof — is conceptually compelling. *Yotzei* is an externally imposed invalidity; *chaser* might not be a *psul* at all, but merely a contextual restriction on eating. If the *shirayim* that are present are halachically intact as objects, the *haktarah* could still interact with them. That conceptual position retains its appeal even if the ברייתא-based proof cannot bear the weight placed on it.

---

---

# Menachot 13

## Pigul & Half-Measures

### Intro & Half-Measures

Daf 13 opens not with entirely new material but rather as a continuation of the ongoing treatment of *pigul*, the disqualification arising from an improper intent during a sacrificial rite. We had just completed a digression concerning the effect of a *pigul* thought when the full measure of *shirayim* is no longer present — a digression that resolved nothing conclusively. We now return to the central mechanics of *pigul* as articulated in the *mishna* on 12b.

The *mishna* presents the following case: if a *kohen* performing the *kemitzah* — the scooping of the *kometz* from the *mincha* — intends to eat half a *kezayit* of the *shirayim* at the wrong time and to burn half a *kezayit* of the *kometz* at the wrong time, the offering is *kasher*. Not only is it not *pigul*, it is entirely valid, because neither intention, taken alone, constitutes a meaningful act — a half-*kezayit* of eating does not reach the requisite threshold, and a half-*kezayit* of burning similarly does not. Moreover, the *mishna* adds, *she'ein achilah ve-haktarah mitztarpin* — eating and burning do not combine with one another.

### Eating vs. Burning

The reasoning behind this ruling deserves careful unpacking. If instead of combining eating with burning, one were to combine two eating-thoughts — intending to eat half a *kezayit* of the *shirayim* on Tuesday and another half on Wednesday — that might well combine, though questions about *k'dei achilat pras* and how thought combines actions remain. The critical point is that we are dealing there with two acts of the same type, yielding a combined eating of a *kezayit*. But here we have an eating and a burning — two different categories of activity, each insufficient on its own, and the *mishna* rules they do not combine because they are separate and distinct acts.

### Tanna Identification

The *Gemara* proceeds to analyze the *mishna*'s implication. The reason eating and burning do not combine is, as the *mishna* says, that they are fundamentally different activities. But the *Gemara* notes that this framing carries an implicit inference: *ha le'echol u'le'echol davar she'ein darko le'echol* — if instead one combined two eating-thoughts, even eating something not normally eaten, namely the *kometz* itself, it sounds as though that would combine and create *pigul*. Yet this inference conflicts with an earlier *mishna*, which specified that one is only liable for *pigul* if one intends to eat *davar she'darko le'echol* — something normally consumed, i.e., the *shirayim* — not the *kometz*, which is destined for the altar. Why, then, does the present *mishna* appear to imply otherwise?

The *Gemara* answers: *man tanna* — who is the *tanna* of this *mishna* that would suggest eating of the *kometz* might combine with eating of the *shirayim*? Rabbi Yirmiyah identifies the *tanna* as Rabbi Eliezer, citing a *mishna* appearing several folios later: *hakometz et haminchah le'echol davar she'ein darko le'echol lehaktir davar she'ein darko lehaktir kasher* — if the *kometz* is taken with intent to eat the *kometz* (not normally eaten) or to burn the *shirayim* (not normally burned), it is *kasher* according to the first *tanna*, but Rabbi Eliezer rules it invalid. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even a thought directed at an unusual act with the object — eating the *kometz* or burning the *shirayim* — constitutes at minimum some form of *achilah* and thus renders the offering invalid, even if it does not rise to classic *pigul*. It is Rabbi Eliezer's view, then, that underlies the inference that eating and eating, even where one involves an improper object, would combine.

---

## Abaye's Reinterpretation

### Abaye Rejects Inference

Abaye rejects this inference entirely. *Afilu teima Rabbanan* — it is possible to attribute the *mishna* even to the Rabbis, without resorting to Rabbi Eliezer. Abaye argues that the *diyuk* — the inference drawn from the *mishna*'s phrasing — is unjustified. One should not read the *mishna* as implying that combining two eating-thoughts, even where one involves the *kometz*, would suffice. Rather, Abaye says, the correct implicit comparison would be: *achilah ve-achilah davar she'darko le'achilah* — eating and eating where both involve something normally eaten.

### Previous Mishna Cited

But if that is the *mishna*'s implication, what novel ruling does it teach? That two genuine eating-thoughts combine even when they represent different categories of invalidity — one a thought of wrong time and one a thought of wrong place — is already made explicit in the previous *mishna*: *kezayit bachutz u'kezayit lemachar, kezayit lemachar u'kezayit bachutz, kechatzi zayit bachutz ve'chatzi zayit lemachar, kechatzi zayit lemachar ve'chatzi zayit bachutz — pasul ve'ein bo karet*. Even half a *kezayit* of wrong-place intent combined with half a *kezayit* of wrong-time intent invalidates the offering, though without *karet*, because it does not constitute a full *kezayit* of a single type of *pigul*. This demonstrates that two eating-thoughts of different types combine to invalidate — and that is already stated explicitly. There is no need to infer it from our *mishna*.

### Simple Meaning Prevails

The *Gemara* on 13a then asks: *ha tu lama li* — why, then, do I need the present *mishna* at all? If the implication about combining eating-and-eating of the *shirayim* is already explicit, and the implication about combining eating of the *shirayim* with eating of the *kometz* is negated by the *reisha* of the earlier *mishna*, what is the present *mishna* teaching?

The *Gemara* resolves: *le'echol u'lehaktir itztricha* — it is necessary to state explicitly that eating and burning do not combine. One might have thought otherwise. It is true that eating the *kometz* does not combine with eating the *shirayim*, because eating the *kometz* is a wholly meaningless act — so the second eating contributes nothing. But the burning of the *kometz*? That is a perfectly meaningful and appropriate act. And eating the *shirayim* is equally meaningful. Perhaps when both acts are individually significant — each *ki orchiah*, each performed in its proper manner — they combine to form a composite act totaling a *kezayit*. Therefore the *mishna* must explicitly tell us: *le'echol u'lehaktir*, eating-intent and burning-intent do not combine, even when both are directed at the correct object.

The *Gemara*'s conclusion, then, is that there are no valid *diyukim* to be drawn from this *mishna* beyond its plain ruling. One is only liable for *pigul* if one intends to eat the *shirayim* or to burn the *kometz* at the wrong time. Directing one's intent at the wrong activity with the object — burning the *shirayim* or eating the *kometz* — counts for nothing. And even when the activity is correct, two separate categories of act — eating and burning — cannot be combined even when each is individually meaningful. That is the *pshat*, and the inferential readings do not stand.

---

## Rashbam's Note

### Rashbam Commentary

At this point — following the *Hadran alach kol haminachot* that concludes the *perek* — Daf 13 is strikingly short. The reason becomes apparent when one looks at what appears in the position of Rashi: a substantial explanatory note bearing the heading *dikduk sheperishu Harav Meir ve-Harav Shmuel beno*, the analytical commentary of Rav Meir and his son Rav Shmuel — that is, the Rashbam, Rabbi Shmuel ben Meir, grandson of Rashi, and the elder brother of Rabbeinu Tam. The colophon at the end confirms: *ad kan hadikduk sheperish Rav Shmuel ve'aviv Harav Meir*.

This piece is not Rashi's commentary; it is a standalone explanatory note by the Rashbam (with his father) on the *sugya* treated in the previous daf. The editors of the page included it alongside the Rashi text because it functions as running commentary on the *Gemara*, much as the Rashbam's commentary on Bava Batra does. In truth, the Rashbam does not introduce the kinds of probing cross-tractate questions characteristic of Tosafot; this is straight *perush*. What the Rashbam does here is re-explain the *sugya* analyzed in yesterday's shiur — the difficult passage where Rava derived from Rabbi Chiyya's omission of the word *kezayit* that he was speaking of the *shirayim*. The Rashbam's explanation adjusts one nuance in how that proof operates and thereby renders it somewhat more intelligible, though the difficulty was not entirely resolved even with this correction.

It is a fascinating editorial decision to include an independent piece by later *Rishonim* within the Rashi column on the page. In one sense it illustrates the broader phenomenon of textual difficulty in *Kodashim* — a tractate that was not widely studied and whose manuscripts were correspondingly less reliable. As Tosafot itself noted with respect to the text of this very *sugya*, whole stretches were corrupted beyond use, requiring scholars to copy in the parallel text from Zevachim where the same *sugya* appears. The Rashbam's inclusion here reflects a similar editorial impulse: to restore and clarify. In any case, it is the presence of this Rashbam note that accounts for the brevity of the actual *Gemara* on this daf.

---

## Levona & Matir Principle

### Levona Case

With the new *perek*, we remain firmly in the world of *pigul* — as we learned from Zevachim, once the *Gemara* enters the topic of *pigul*, it stays with it at length. The new *mishna* opens with a case that at first glance seems straightforward: *hakometz et haminchah le'echol shireha o lehaktir kumtza lemachar* — if the *kohen* performs the *kemitzah* with intent to eat the remainder tomorrow or to burn the *kometz* tomorrow, these are classic *pigul* thoughts, and *modeh Rabbi Yose b'zeh she'hu pigul* — Rabbi Yose agrees that this constitutes *pigul* and one is liable to *karet*. The *mishna* finds it necessary to state this agreement explicitly because Rabbi Yose is about to dispute a related case, and the editor wants to make clear from the outset that his dispute is limited and that he accepts the foundational principle of *pigul*.

The disputed case follows: *lehaktir levonah lemachar* — if one performs the *kemitzah* with intent to burn the *levona* tomorrow. Here the improper intent is directed not at the *kometz* or the *shirayim*, but at the *levona* that accompanies the *mincha*. Rabbi Yose rules: *pasul ve'ein bo karet* — the offering is invalidated, but there is no *karet*, because this does not constitute *pigul*. The Rabbis disagree: *pigul vechayavin alav karet* — it is full *pigul*, and one is liable to *karet*.

The Rabbis challenge Rabbi Yose: *mah shina zeh min hazevach* — how is this different from an animal sacrifice? In a *korban*, one can have a *pigul* thought not only about eating the meat but also about burning the *imurim* — the fats. Just as the *pigul* thought encompasses all elements whose improper disposition would be problematic, so too here, why should a thought about the *levona* not constitute *pigul*? Rabbi Yose replies: *hazevach damo u'vesaro ve'imurav echad* — in an animal sacrifice, the blood, the meat, and the entrails are all one unified entity. *Halevona eina min hamincha* — the *levona* is not part of the *mincha*. From his response, the plain reading of the *mishna* appears to be that Rabbi Yose's objection is grounded in the *levona* being conceptually a different object from the *mincha* itself. Though the *levona* is physically placed upon the *mincha* in the same vessel and must be brought along with it, the Torah defines it as something riding on top — a distinct object — and therefore a *pigul* thought cannot be generated by directing one's intent toward it.

This would have broader implications. Consider a *shlamim* offering brought together with loaves of bread: if one slaughters the *shlamim* with intent to eat the bread at the wrong time, would that constitute *pigul*? Or the *nesachim* — if one had a *pigul* thought about the libation? These cases would follow from Rabbi Yose's principle, and the *Gemara* will press on exactly what that principle is.

### Reish Lakish Explains

The *Gemara* turns to explain Rabbi Yose's position. *Amar Reish Lakish: omer haya Rabbi Yose* — Reish Lakish formulates what Rabbi Yose's reasoning was. The phrasing *omer haya*, as Rashi notes several lines later (*klomar hainu ta'ama de-Rabbi Yose*), does not indicate a direct tradition but rather Reish Lakish's interpretive reconstruction of the *ta'am*, the underlying rationale.

Reish Lakish proposes: *ein matir mefagel et hamatir* — one *matir* cannot create *pigul* in another *matir*. The principle of *pigul* operates when one performs an act with the *matir* — the element that renders the offering permissible — and directs improper intent toward what is permitted or toward the *matir* itself. The *kometz*, for example, is a *matir*: its burning renders the *shirayim* permissible for consumption. A *pigul* thought during the *kemitzah* can therefore be directed at eating the *shirayim* (the thing being permitted), or at the *kometz* itself (the *matir* performing the act). What it cannot do is extend to another *matir* that operates independently. The *levona* is also a *matir* for the *mincha* — it too must be burned as part of the process that validates the *mincha*. But because the *levona* and the *kometz* are two independent *matirim*, neither dependent on the other, one's thought during the *kemitzah* cannot generate *pigul* with respect to the *levona*.

The logic is elegant: the *pigul* thought during an act is relevant to what that act affects. The burning of the *kometz* affects the *shirayim* — the *shirayim* are dependent on the *kometz*, *dechama dela mitkatar kometz la mitchalu shirayim*, until the *kometz* is burned the *shirayim* cannot be eaten. My intent during the *kemitzah* is thus relevant to the *shirayim* and to the *kometz* itself. But it is not relevant to the *levona*, because the *levona* does not stand in a dependency relationship with the *kometz*. There is no chain of enabling: the *kometz* does not render the *levona* permissible or valid, and the *levona* does not render the *kometz* permissible or valid. They are two parallel paths, each contributing independently to the validity of the *mincha*.

### Two Bowls Case

Reish Lakish then applies this principle to a parallel case: *bi-shnei bezichei levona shel lechem hapanim* — the two bowls of *levona* accompanying the *lechem hapanim*, the showbread. There, two separate spoons of frankincense are burned, and their burning renders the bread permissible. Reish Lakish says that here too, *she'ein matir mefagel et hamatir* — if while burning one bowl one intends to burn the other bowl tomorrow, that does not create *pigul*. Even though the two bowls are the same physical substance — both *levona* — they function as two distinct *matirim*, neither dependent on the other. Burning one bowl does not affect the status of the other bowl; combining them makes the bread valid, but neither enables the other.

The *Gemara* notes, however, that one might have thought differently. Perhaps Rabbi Yose's ruling in the *mishna* is specific to the *levona* of the *mincha* because it is a conceptually distinct object — not the same *min* as the *mincha* flour — and *mishum delav mina demincha hi*, for that reason specifically it cannot generate *pigul*. In that case, the two bowls of *levona* for the *lechem hapanim*, being homogeneous with one another, might combine, and *pigul* thought from one might affect the other. The *Gemara* presses: *mahu deteima*... and then challenges the very premise of this reading.

---

## Dependency Analysis

### Rabbi Yose's Real Reason

The *Gemara* asks: *umi matzit amrat deta'ama de-Rabbi Yose belevonah lav mishum delav mina demincha hi* — how can you say Rabbi Yose's reason is simply that the *levona* is not the same type of object as the *mincha*? The *mishna* itself seems to say exactly that — Rabbi Yose's own reply to the Rabbis was *halevona eina min hamincha*, and the contrast he drew was between the unified blood-flesh-entrails complex of an animal sacrifice and the *levona* as an external element. Does the *mishna* not support reading his rationale as purely categorical — it's a different object?

The *Gemara* deflects: *mai einah mina demincha* — what does it mean that the *levona* is "not of the *mincha*"? It means *einah be'ikuv mincha* — it does not stand in the dependency relationship that characterizes the *mincha* itself.

### No Dependency Relation

This is the crucial reinterpretation. When Rabbi Yose says the *levona* is not of the *mincha*, he is not making a purely taxonomic observation about physical distinctness. He is saying it does not operate the way the *mincha* operates internally. The *mincha* is dependent on its own *kometz*: *dechama dela mitkatar kometz la mitchalu shirayim*, until the *kometz* is burned the *shirayim* cannot be eaten. The *kometz* holds back the *shirayim* — *ma'akev lahem*. The *levona*, by contrast, does not hold back the *kometz* and is not held back by it. *Halevona* is not *be'ikuv* the *mincha* in that sense. The dependency chain that runs from *kometz* to *shirayim* does not extend to the *levona*.

### Order Independence

The *Gemara* makes this concrete: *ela i bei hai maktar bereisha* — if one wishes, one may burn the *kometz* first; if one wishes, one may burn the *levona* first. The order is entirely interchangeable. Neither one is a *matir* for the other. Each stands independently in relation to the validity of the *mincha*, but they are not ordered or dependent with respect to each other. The *levona* is thus *lav mina demincha* not because it is a foreign object, but because it lacks the internal dependency relationship that characterizes the *mincha's* own components.

This understanding resolves what would otherwise be a tension in Rabbi Yose's position. If his rationale were purely about physical or categorical distinctness, one might challenge him with cases where objects of different types are nonetheless conceptually unified. But if his rationale is dependency — whether one *matir* enables or holds back another — then the principle becomes *ein matir mefagel et hamatir* in its precise form: because the *levona* and the *kometz* do not stand in a dependency relationship, a *pigul* thought during one act cannot generate *pigul* with respect to the other.

---

## Rabbis' Position

### Same Vessel Logic

The Rabbis agree with Rabbi Yose's underlying principle. *Ki amrinan ein matir mefagel et hamatir* — the *Gemara* concedes that the Rabbis accept the rule that one *matir* does not create *pigul* in another *matir*. They apply this rule themselves when analyzing the case of the two lambs of *Shavuot* that accompany the *shtei halechem*: those two lambs are equivalent *matirim* for the bread, neither dependent on the other, and therefore a *pigul* thought from one lamb cannot affect the other. On that case, the Rabbis and Rabbi Yose would agree.

But the Rabbis part ways with Rabbi Yose on the *levona* of the *mincha*. *Hani mili heicha dela ikvu behad mana* — the principle that one *matir* cannot generate *pigul* in another applies only when the two *matirim* are not placed together in one vessel. *Aval hacha de'ikvu behad mana, kechad dami* — here, where the *levona* is physically laid upon the *mincha* in the same vessel and sanctified together with it, they are treated as one. The Rabbis are saying: it is not that we disagree with the principle of dependency; we disagree about whether the *levona* qualifies as sufficiently integrated with the *mincha* to be treated as part of it. Because the *levona* is placed directly on the *mincha* in the same *kli*, it is conceptually unified with the *mincha* — and therefore a *pigul* thought during the *kemitzah* is relevant to the *levona* as well, yielding full *pigul* and *karet*. This is precisely what the *mishna* records: *vachachamim omrim pigul vechayavin alav karet*.

---

## Likut Levona Digression

### Rabbi Yanai's View

At this point the *Gemara* introduces a related digression that connects directly to the preceding analysis of the *levona*'s status. *Amar Rabbi Yanai: likut levona bezar pasul* — if a non-*kohen* gathers the *levona* off the surface of the *mincha* before handing it to the *kohen* for burning, this is invalid. The underlying question is whether *likut levona* — the physical act of gathering the *levona* from the *mincha* — constitutes an *avodah*, a formal sacrificial act, at all. The Torah does not describe this act explicitly; it simply states that the *levona* shall be burned. Yet before it can be burned it must be lifted from the *mincha*, and Rabbi Yanai rules that this act is invalid when performed by a *zar*.

### Rav Yirmiyah on Havicha

Rav Yirmiyah provides the conceptual basis for this ruling: *mishum holacha nag'u bah* — the gathering of the *levona* is governed by the category of *holacha*, conveying the offering toward the *mizbe'ach*. The act of picking up the *levona* from the *mincha* constitutes moving it — even a small displacement — in the direction of its ultimate destination on the *mizbe'ach*, and such conveyance is an *avodah*. *Kasavar holacha shelo beregel shemah holacha* — he holds that conveyance even without walking, a mere repositioning, qualifies as *holacha*. And since *holacha* is an *avodah* that requires a *kohen*, performing it as a *zar* renders the offering *pasul*.

---

## Four Avodot Analysis

### Four Avodot Listed

The *Gemara* now cites the *klal* from an earlier *mishna* as a springboard for deeper analysis. The *mishna* had stated: *kol hakometz ve-noten bikli ve-hamolich ve-hamaktir* — any of the four acts of the *mincha* — the *kemitzah*, placing in a vessel, conveying to the *mizbe'ach*, and burning — can serve as the moment at which a *pigul* thought takes effect. These four acts are the primary *avodot* of the *mincha*. The *Gemara* now examines why each one qualifies.

*Bishlama kometz* — it is clear why *kemitzah* is an *avodah*: *heinu shochet*, it parallels *shechitah* in a *korban behemah*, the act of separation that gains access to the element being offered. *Molich nami heinu molich* — conveying the *kometz* to the *mizbe'ach* parallels the *holacha* of the blood in an animal sacrifice. *Maktir — heinu zorek* — burning the *kometz* on the *mizbe'ach* parallels *zerikah*, the sprinkling of the blood, in that both are the culminating act of getting the offering onto the *mizbe'ach*, whether by throwing or by burning.

### Noten Bikli Debate

The difficulty is with *noten bikli* — placing the *kometz* into the vessel. *Ella noten bikli mai ka'avid* — why is this an *avodah*? The natural answer would be: *ilima mishum de'dami lekabbalah* — it parallels *kabbalah*, the receiving of the blood in a vessel. But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *mi dami* — are they really comparable? *Hatam mimmeila, hacha kashakul ve'ramei* — in *kabbalah*, the blood flows into the vessel on its own; here the *kohen* picks up the *kometz* and actively deposits it. The underlying activity is fundamentally different. *Kabbalah* is receiving; *noten bikli* is placing. These are not the same act.

### Necessity Principle

The *Gemara* then proposes an alternative rationale: *ella mishum de'keivan de'lo sagi lei de'lo avid lei* — since *noten bikli* is necessary, since the *kometz* requires *kedushat kli* (sanctification through placement in a vessel), the act is thereby significant. *Avodah chashuvah hi* — a necessary act is by definition an important act. *Al korchach meshavei lei ke'kabbalah* — its very necessity assimilates it to *kabbalah*, making it a pseudo-parallel even without a formal structural equivalence.

This raises a fundamental question in *lomdus*: what makes something an *avodah* in this context? Is an *avodah* defined by membership in the four formally established categories — the classical structure of *korban* procedure mapped onto the *mincha*? Or can any act that is necessary to accomplish the final result achieve the status of *avodah* by virtue of its necessity alone? The implications are significant. If necessity alone is sufficient, then *likut levona* — which is undeniably necessary — would also be an *avodah*, requiring a *kohen* and susceptible to *pigul* thought. If, on the other hand, an act must fit a defined category, then *noten bikli*'s status depends on whether it genuinely parallels *kabbalah*, and *likut levona* would require a separate analysis.

---

## Noten Bikli Resolution

### Noten Bikli = Kabbala

The *Gemara* now reverses course. *Le'olam de'dami lekabbalah* — in truth, *noten bikli* is like *kabbalah*, and that is the correct reason for its status as an *avodah*. Necessity alone does not elevate an act into the category of *avodah*. The *Gemara* therefore rejects the necessity-based rationale and returns to the structural parallel.

### Same Goal, Different Method

But what of the original objection — that *kabbalah* and *noten bikli* are mechanically different, one passive and one active? The *Gemara* dismisses it: *ravaihu kedushat kli hu* — both acts accomplish the same thing, namely getting the offering into the *kli* and thereby conferring *kedushat kli*. *Mah li mimila mah li kashakul ve'ramei* — what difference does it make whether it happens by itself or whether the *kohen* actively places it in? The end result — the *kometz* in a sanctified vessel — is identical. The means by which it gets there, whether the blood flows in or the *kometz* is placed, is not the defining criterion. What defines *kabbalah* as an *avodah* is that it is the act by which the relevant substance enters the vessel; *noten bikli* achieves precisely the same thing, and the difference in execution does not disqualify the parallel.

This resolution carries an important implication for *likut levona*. If an *avodah* requires a genuine structural parallel to the defined categories — not mere necessity — then the question is whether *likut levona* fits any such category. Rav Yirmiyah's answer was that it is a form of *holacha*. But a distinct possibility is that it parallels *kemitzah* more than *holacha*, since like *kemitzah* it is the act of separating the relevant element for its ultimate disposition on the *mizbe'ach*. The *Gemara*'s framing — *al korchach meshavei lei ke'holacha* — ultimately categorizes it under *holacha*, but the logical basis, as noted, seems more akin to a parallel with *kemitzah*. In any case, what emerges clearly is that the *Gemara* refuses to ground *avodah* status in necessity alone; what matters is whether the act fits within a recognized and structurally parallel category.

---

## Shtei Halechem Case

### Mishna Setup

The *Gemara* turns to a new *mishna* concerning the *shtei halechem* — the two loaves brought on *Shavuot* — and the two lambs that accompany them. *Shachat sheni kevasim le'echol achas min hachalos lemachar* — one slaughtered the two lambs with the intent to eat one of the loaves of the *shtei halechem* the next day. Alternatively, the same case arises with the *lechem hapanim*: one offered the two *bezichin* of *levona* intending to eat one column of the *lechem hapanim* tomorrow. In each scenario, the act was performed entirely — both lambs were slaughtered, or both bowls were offered — but the improper intent was directed only at one of the two loaves (or one column of the *lechem hapanim*), not both.

### Rabbi Yose's Position

*Rabbi Yose omer: oto hachalah ve'oto haseder shechishav alav — pigul, ve'chayavin alav karet; veha'sheni pasul ve'ein bo karet.* Rabbi Yose rules that the specific loaf or column about which one harbored the improper intent becomes *pigul*, and one who eats from it is liable to *karet*. But the second loaf, toward which no improper thought was directed, is merely *pasul* — invalid — without *karet*. Rabbi Yose's position is consistent with his general approach: *pigul* attaches specifically to the object of one's intent, not to the collective.

### Rabbis' Position

*Ve-chachamim omrim: zeh va-zeh pigul ve-chayavin alav karet* — the Rabbis rule that both loaves become *pigul* and carry *karet*. When one performs the act with an improper *pigul* intent regarding any part of the offering, the entire offering is infected. The dispute thus turns on whether *pigul* can be atomized to the specific object of one's thought, or whether it attaches to the whole when the foundational act — the *shechitah* of the lambs — is performed with improper intent.

---

## Specific Intent Principle

### Rav Huna Explains

*Amar Rav Huna: omer haya Rabbi Yose — pigul beyerech shel yamin lo nitpagel hayerech shel smol.* Rav Huna's formulation of Rabbi Yose's position is striking and goes well beyond what the *mishna* alone might suggest. Rabbi Yose holds that *pigul* applies only to the precise object of one's thought. It is not merely that distinct physical objects — two separate loaves — are unaffected by a *pigul* thought directed at only one. Even within a single animal, if one intends to eat the right thigh at the wrong time, the left thigh does not become *pigul* — it is merely *pasul*. The *pigul* is radically localized to the very thing one thought about.

### Thought = Action Logic

The *Gemara* provides a logical justification for this extreme position: *lo adifa machshava mimaaseh* — thought is no better than action. The principle underlying *pigul* is that the improper mental act is treated like the corresponding physical act. So one asks: what would happen if the corresponding physical act were performed only on the right thigh? If, for example, one left the right thigh beyond the allotted time, would it make the left thigh into *notar*? It would not. The *notar* status would attach to the right thigh, not the left. If the physical act is limited in its effect to the object on which it was performed, the thought should likewise be limited to the object toward which it was directed. Thought cannot be more powerful in its reach than action.

### Textual Source

The *Gemara* also cites a textual basis: *vehanefesh ha'ochelet mimenu avona tisa* — the soul that eats *from it* bears its sin. The word *mimenu* — from it, from that specific object — implies that liability attaches only when one eats from the very thing one thought about, not from the associated items that were not the object of the improper intent.

---

## Baraita Challenge

### Baraita Cited

Rav Nachman challenges Rav Huna from a *baraita*: *le'olam ein bo karet ad she'yefagel bi-shteihen bi-kezayit* — one is never liable to *karet* unless one had a *pigul* thought regarding both of the loaves together, with a combined *kezayit*. This appears to say that one must have harbored the improper intent concerning both loaves — and furthermore that a half-*kezayit* from this loaf and a half-*kezayit* from that loaf can combine to constitute the *kezayit* of *pigul*. If so, the two loaves are being treated as a single unit for this purpose, and thought directed at one does extend to the other.

### Tanna Identified

The *Gemara* identifies whose view this *baraita* reflects. *Bishteihen in — be'achat mehen lo*: one is liable only when both loaves were the object of the improper thought; if one thought only about one of them, no *karet* applies when eating from the other. This cannot be the Rabbis' position — the Rabbis hold that both loaves become *pigul* even if one thought only about one, and one would certainly be liable for eating from either. The *baraita* must therefore reflect Rabbi Yose's position.

---

## One Unit vs. Distinct

### One Unit Theory

The *Gemara* now offers an elegant resolution to the apparent tension. *I amarta bi-shlama chad gufa hu, mishum hachi mitztaref* — if you say Rabbi Yose's position is that *pigul* thought directed at one part of a unified entity affects the whole, and that his dispute with the Rabbis in the *mishna* concerns whether the two loaves of the *shtei halechem* constitute one unit or two distinct units — then the following follows naturally. When one intends to eat half a *kezayit* from this loaf and half a *kezayit* from that loaf, one is in one's own mind treating them as a single collection. One is thinking about a combined consumption of a *kezayit* that spans both. On Rabbi Yose's theory, this mental unification can indeed work: because one conceived of them as one unit in one's improper intent, the two half-*kezayit* measures combine, and that combined *kezayit* generates *pigul* across both loaves. This is how the *baraita* makes sense — it is Rabbi Yose's view, and it is consistent with his underlying principle.

### Distinct Objects Theory

But if instead one adopts the more extreme reading of Rabbi Yose's position — *ela i amarta trei gufei ninhu* — that Rabbi Yose holds everything to be fundamentally and irreducibly distinct, such that even physically connected parts of one animal are treated as separate objects, then it becomes very difficult to explain how the two half-*kezayit* measures could combine at all. *Mi mitztarfei* — how would they join? If the right thigh and the left thigh of a single animal are distinct objects for *pigul* purposes, then certainly a half-*kezayit* from one loaf and a half-*kezayit* from another loaf — which are unquestionably separate physical entities — cannot combine into a single *kezayit* of improper intent. On this reading, the *baraita*'s allowance for combination becomes difficult to account for. This tension is left for continuation in the following session.

---

---

# Menachot 14

## Rabbi Yosi vs. Chachamim

### Pigul Overview

The daf begins well into the discussion of *pigul*, a topic that occupied much of Masechet Zevachim and that in Menachot affords even richer opportunities for analysis — not only regarding *pigul* in its own right, but using *pigul* as a lens through which to examine the relationships between the various components of a *korban*. How do the *kometz* and the *levonah*, for instance, operate jointly or independently? These structural questions animate the sugya at every turn.

### Shavuot Lambs & Loaves

The Mishnah addressed the case of the two lambs brought on Shavuot — *shenei kevasim* — whose slaughter renders the two loaves of bread, the *shetei halechem*, permitted for consumption. Similarly, the two bowls of frankincense on the *shulchan* (*bazikhin*) permit the *lechem hapanim* to be eaten. These cases raise the question of *mefaglin be-chatzi matir* — whether a *pigul* thought entertained during only one of the two lambs, or one of the two bowls, suffices. But the primary debate introduced by the Mishnah is a different one: if the *kohen* performing the service intends to eat one of the two loaves at the wrong time, does *pigul* attach to both loaves or only to the one he was thinking about?

The general principle is that if one thinks during the service of a *korban* about eating even a minimal amount at the wrong time, the *pigul* status applies to the entire *korban*. The question here is how to define the "object" — what counts as a single unit for this purpose. *Rabbi Yosi* holds that the *pigul* status attaches only to the loaf one was thinking about; the *Chachamim* hold that it attaches to everything, treating both loaves as a single unit.

### Rabbi Yosi's Narrow View

The Gemara initially attempts to read Rabbi Yosi's position in an even more radical direction. On this reading, Rabbi Yosi would not merely distinguish between separate loaves as distinct objects; he would maintain that *pigul* is so localized that even within a single *korban*, only the precise portion one was thinking about becomes *pigul*. So if one intended to eat specifically from the right thigh, the left thigh would remain unaffected. The Gemara pursues this interpretation, though — as the lecturer makes clear from the outset — it will ultimately be rejected. The conclusion toward which the entire discussion moves is this: everyone agrees that *pigul* applies to the whole defined object; the debate is exclusively about how that object is defined.

### Half-Kezayit Proof

The Gemara advances a *baraita* as evidence that even Rabbi Yosi would agree that *pigul* applies to the whole unit when properly defined. The *baraita* states that if one thinks about eating a *kezayit* drawn jointly from both loaves — half a *kezayit* from each — both loaves become *pigul*. The Gemara reasons: this case cannot reflect the position of the *Chachamim*, because according to the *Chachamim*, a *pigul* thought about one loaf alone would already render both loaves *pigul* — there would be no need to combine the two loaves into a shared *kezayit*. Therefore, the *baraita* must reflect the position of Rabbi Yosi, who normally treats the loaves as distinct. And yet Rabbi Yosi allows that if one conceptually joins them — by thinking about a *kezayit* spanning both — they become a single unit, and *pigul* attaches to the whole. This would demonstrate that Rabbi Yosi agrees in principle that *pigul* applies to the entire unit; his dispute is only about unit definition.

### Attribution Question

The Gemara, however, deflects this proof. It suggests that the *baraita* may not reflect Rabbi Yosi's position at all, but rather that of *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi). A *baraita* is cited: one who slaughters the first lamb with the intent to eat a half-*kezayit* from one loaf, and then slaughters the second lamb with the intent to eat a half-*kezayit* from the other loaf, is told by Rebbi: *omer ani shezeh kasher* — I say this is entirely valid, no *pigul* has been created.

### Chatzi Matir Concept

The reason Rebbi gives is instructive. It is not merely that the two half-*kezayit* thoughts fail to combine; it is that the thought during each lamb was entertained during only a *chatzi matir* — half of the operative act. Since both lambs together constitute the *matir* that permits the loaves, each lamb individually is only half of that enabling act. A *pigul* thought during half of a *matir* does not create *pigul*, in accordance with the principle of *ein mefaglin be-chatzi matir*.

### Same Thought Requirement

The Gemara then clarifies what *would* create *pigul* according to Rebbi: if during the slaughter of each lamb one had the very same thought — "I intend to eat a *kezayit* taken jointly from both loaves" — then both lambs carried the identical *pigul* intention throughout the complete act. This resolves the *chatzi matir* problem, since the same intent persisted through both halves of the *matir*, and *pigul* would result. The Gemara thus distinguishes sharply between two scenarios: thinking a half-*kezayit* from each loaf separately during each respective lamb (no *pigul*, due to *chatzi matir*), versus thinking the same combined *kezayit* from both loaves during each lamb (genuine *pigul*).

This means the *baraita* that seemed to prove Rabbi Yosi's position was actually about Rebbi's position and the principle of *ein mefaglin be-chatzi matir* — the requirement that one have the *pigul* thought during the full *matir*, not merely during one half of it. The word *bishneihem* (masculine, referring to the lambs) rather than *bishteihen* (feminine, referring to the loaves) is the key: Rebbi requires the thought during both lambs, not necessarily about both loaves. This, the Gemara concludes, reflects the view against Rabbi Meir, who holds that *mefaglin be-chatzi matir*. Once this is understood, the *lamed-vav* — the word *l'olam* ("never") — in the formulation makes sense: it flags that two separate requirements must both be met, against two opposing positions: against Rabbi Meir who holds one lamb suffices, and against the *Rabbanan* who hold one loaf suffices.

The reinterpretation of the *baraita* as belonging to the *Rabbanan* (not Rabbi Yosi), and as addressing the lamb requirement (not the loaf combination), means the proof for Rabbi Yosi's agreement with the whole-unit principle has dissolved. *Hadra kusha l'duchta* — the question returns to its place.

### Rashi on Lebona

At this juncture, Rashi raises a point that demands attention. If we accept the principle of *ein mefaglin be-chatzi matir*, a question arises about our paradigm case of *pigul*: how can taking the *kometz* of a *mincha* create *pigul*, given that there is a second *matir* — the *levonah* — which has not yet been burned? Would not the *kemitza* alone constitute only a *chatzi matir*?

Rashi answers that the concern about *chatzi matir* applies only at the stage of *haktara* — the burning. At that stage, both the *kometz* and the *levonah* must be burned, and having a *pigul* thought during the burning of one without the other raises the *chatzi matir* issue. But at the *kemitza* stage, no parallel act exists for the *levonah*: the Torah does not describe any *avoda* of gathering the *levonah* prior to burning it. The only *avoda* prescribed for the *levonah* is the burning itself. Therefore, during *kemitza*, *holecha*, or *nesinat kelli*, there is only one thing happening — the acts associated with the *kometz* — and the *chatzi matir* concern simply does not apply at that stage. The *levonah* enters the picture only at the *haktara* stage, when both must be burned together.

This explanation, while elegant, leaves open the question of why the gathering of the *levonah* — which some authorities consider a valid *avoda* — would not also count as a parallel *matir* act alongside *kemitza*. Rashi's position is noted here without full resolution.

---

## Proofs for Whole Unit

### Inner Chatat Proof

The Gemara now turns to positive proof that Rabbi Yosi agrees *pigul* applies to the whole unit — that his dispute with the *Chachamim* is exclusively about unit definition, not about whether *pigul* spreads through a single defined unit. The first proof is introduced with the formula *de-ha amar Rav Ashi ta shma* — "did not Rav Ashi say, come and hear." This framing is slightly unusual: ordinarily one who says *ta shma* is the one answering a question. The suggestion is that at an earlier editorial stage, Rav Ashi responded to the question about Rabbi Yosi's view by citing this *baraita*, and the later editorial framing has embedded that citation into its current context.

The *baraita* cited by Rav Ashi is from the *Sifra* (Torat Kohanim) and concerns *pigul* by the inner *chatat* — *chatat ha-pnimiot*. The inner *chatat* involves sprinkling blood inside the *Heichal* (toward the *parochet*) and burning the meat outside the *Mikdash*. Examples include the Yom Kippur bull and the *par he'elam davar* brought when the *Beit Din* rules incorrectly and the entire community acts upon that erroneous ruling.

The paradigm for *pigul* in the Torah is *shelamim*, where both the slaughter and the blood service occur outside the *Heichal*, on the outer *mizbe'ach*. Rabbi Yosi (as quoted by Rebbi) derives from this that *pigul* by the inner *chatat* requires a precise structural parallel: the *pigul* thought must occur during an *avoda* performed outside the *Heichal*, and that thought must concern an act that is likewise performed outside the *Heichal*.

The *baraita* enumerates the cases: if one stands outside the *Heichal* and says "I am slaughtering this with the intent to sprinkle its blood tomorrow" — no *pigul*, because although the thought occurred outside, the intended act (the sprinkling) is performed inside the *Heichal*. If one stands inside the *Heichal* and says during the sprinkling "I will burn the *imurin* tomorrow" or "I will pour the *shirayim* tomorrow" — acts done on the outer *mizbe'ach* — again no *pigul*, because although the intended act is outside, the thought occurred inside. Only when one stands outside during *shechita* and intends to pour the *shirayim* on the outer *mizbe'ach* tomorrow, or to burn the *imurin* tomorrow, does *pigul* result: thought outside, intended act outside.

### Blood Spilling Problem

A sharp question now emerges. When one slaughters with the intent to pour the *shirayim* at the wrong time, what exactly becomes *pigul*? The *shirayim* themselves? The *dam* (blood)? The Gemara considers each possibility methodically. Could it be the *dam* that becomes *pigul*? No — *dam lo mifagal*. Blood does not become *pigul*. This is established by a *mishna* that lists the items that cannot become *pigul* even when one has had a *pigul* thought during their service: the *kometz*, the *levonah*, the *ketores*, the *minchat kohen*, the *minchat nesachim*, the *minchat kohen mashiach*, and the blood. The reason: all these items are themselves *matirs* — they are the enabling acts that permit the *korban* to proceed to its next stage. *Pigul* operates by rendering *pigul* what the *matir* is working upon, not the *matir* itself. Thus the blood, which is the *matir* enabling the meat to be eaten and the fats to be burned, cannot itself become *pigul*.

### Meat Becomes Pigul

If the blood cannot become *pigul*, what can? The *basar* — the meat. And here lies the proof. One was thinking about the *shirayim* (blood), yet what becomes *pigul* is the meat. The *pigul* thought was about one component of the *korban*, and the *pigul* status attached to a completely different component. The Gemara draws the inference explicitly: *hashta u'mah hasam d'lo chashiv beih basar gufei amar Rabbi Yose mesagel* — "now, if even there, where one did not think about the meat at all but only about spilling the blood at the wrong time, Rabbi Yosi says *pigul* applies — then here, where one is thinking about the *zevach* itself, specifically about one thigh, how much more so should *pigul* spread to the other thigh." The *a fortiori* argument is powerful: if a *pigul* thought about the blood — a distinct component from the meat — renders the meat *pigul*, certainly a *pigul* thought about one part of the meat renders the other part *pigul* as well.

One might respond, as was noted during discussion, that the blood has a unique relationship to the whole *korban* as its *matir* — so naturally a *pigul* thought about the *matir* affects everything dependent upon it. But when one thinks about a specific piece of the edible meat, perhaps the effect is limited to that piece. The Gemara acknowledges this implicitly by adducing a second proof.

### Kometz Proof

Ravina adds another demonstration, introduced again with the formula *amar Ravina ta shma*. The case: one takes the *kometz* of a *mincha* with intent to eat the *shirayim* tomorrow, or to burn the *kometz* tomorrow. Rabbi Yosi agrees — *modu Rabbi Yose b'zo shepigel vechayavin alav karet* — that *pigul* results and one is liable to *karet* for eating it. This is not in doubt. The Gemara then probes: what becomes *pigul*? Can it be the *kometz*? No — the *kometz* is a *matir* and, as established, *matirs* themselves do not become *pigul*. Therefore, the *shirayim* — the remainder of the *mincha* — become *pigul*. And the inference follows: *hashta u'ma hatam d'lo chashivei be'shirayim gufei mifagli* — even though one was thinking only about the *kometz*, the *shirayim* become *pigul*. If that is so when the thought concerned the *matir* itself, certainly when one thinks about one part of the edible matter the *pigul* status should spread to the whole *korban*.

### Unit Definition

Both proofs carry the same structural limitation noted in discussion: one could argue that in both cases — blood and *kometz* — the *pigul* thought concerns the *matir*, and it is natural for a *pigul* thought about the *matir* to affect everything the *matir* enables. This is a less compelling proof of what happens when the thought concerns part of the edible portion itself. Nonetheless, the Gemara treats the two proofs as decisive.

The conclusion, attributed to Rabbi Yochanan, is unambiguous: *hainu ta'ama de'Rabbi Yose* — this is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosi. He agrees entirely in principle that *pigul* applies to the whole unit. *Ha-katuiv asan guf echad ve-ha-katuiv asan shnei gufim* — the Torah itself treats the *shetei halechem* both as one unit and as two units. The debate between Rabbi Yosi and the *Chachamim* is therefore not a fundamental dispute about whether *pigul* spreads through a unit, but a specific dispute about the unit definition of the *shetei halechem* and *lechem hapanim*.

---

## One and Two Units

### Torah's Dual Language

Rabbi Yochanan's resolution is built on a close reading of the Torah's language regarding the *shetei halechem*. The Torah employs both singular and plural designations for these two loaves. One verse uses the singular *lechem* — "you shall bring *lechem* of waving" — treating the two loaves as a single entity. Another verse specifies *shtayim* and *shnei esronim* — two loaves, two tenth-*ephah* portions — treating them as distinct objects. The same principle is then extended by *seder* to the *lechem hapanim*, which the Gemara notes is derived (*yalfinan*) from the *shetei halechem*.

### Interdependence

The Torah's treatment of the loaves as one unit is evidenced by their mutual interdependence: *de-ma'akvi ahadadi* — they prevent one another from being valid. If only one loaf is present, the *korban* is not fulfilled. The *korban* requires both; neither is complete without the other. This functional unity justifies viewing them as a single *guf* in one respect.

### Separate Creation

At the same time, the Torah treats them as two separate units — *shnei gufim* — because, as the Gemara notes, *de-amar Rachmana hai lachudei avidah ve-hai lachudei avidah*: the Torah indicates that each loaf is made independently. One does not prepare a single large dough and divide it; each loaf requires its own separate dough, kneaded and formed individually. This physical and procedural distinctness is what makes each loaf its own *guf* in another respect.

### Conceptual Combination

The practical rule that emerges from Rabbi Yosi's position is as follows. *Ervinhu mitarvin* — if one conceptually combines the loaves, by framing one's *pigul* intention in terms of a *kezayit* drawn from both together, one has invoked the Torah's recognition of them as a single unit. Since the Torah does treat them as one *guf* in the sense that each requires the other, this conceptual joining is legitimate, and *pigul* attaches to both. *Pilginhu mefalgi* — if one separates them conceptually, thinking only of a *kezayit* from one loaf without reference to the other, then the Torah's alternative recognition of them as two separate *gufim* governs, and *pigul* attaches only to the loaf one was thinking about.

This is the precise scope and logic of Rabbi Yosi's position. He does not limit *pigul* to a fragment of a unit; he limits it to the unit as defined. The dispute with the *Chachamim* is therefore about which model — the Torah's single-unit reading or its two-unit reading — is the operative default when one has not explicitly combined or separated the loaves in one's intention.

### Generalized Principle

Rabbi Yochanan then poses the question of how far Rabbi Yosi's principle extends. *Ba'ei Rabbi Yochanan: pigul be-lachmei toda mahu? Be-minchat ma'aseh mahu?* Does the same logic apply to the forty loaves of *lachmei toda*, or to the *minchat ma'aseh tanur* whose breads come in two distinct forms — loaves and wafers? Are those collections each internally one unit, or are they multiple distinct units?

The question was answered when Rav Tachlifa from the west — from Eretz Yisrael — presented a *baraita* that explicitly extended Rabbi Yosi's ruling to these other cases: *vechen ata omer be-lachmei toda, vechen ata omer be-minchat ma'aseh*. Rabbi Yosi consistently applies his framework across all breads brought as *korbanot*: where the Torah provides grounds for categorizing collections of breads as distinct, a *pigul* thought about one collection does not affect another. So the two columns of *lechem hapanim*, the four varieties of *lachmei toda*, the two forms of *minchat ma'aseh tanur* — each collection is treated as its own unit, and *pigul* on one does not spread to another unless one has conceptually combined them.

---

## Combining Avodot

### Shechita & Zrika

The Gemara now shifts to a related but distinct question: can *pigul* thoughts entertained during two separate *avodot* — not during two halves of the same *matir*, but during two complete and distinct *avodot* — combine to constitute a single *pigul* intention? A *baraita* addresses this directly: *beshe'at shechita chishav le'echol chatzi zayit, u-veshe'at zerika chishav le'echol chatzi zayit* — during *shechita* one intended to eat a half-*kezayit*, and during *zerika* one again intended a half-*kezayit*. The ruling is *pigul*, because *shechita* and *zerika* combine: *mipnei she-shechita u-zerika mitztarfin*.

It is worth pausing to distinguish this case from the earlier discussion of *chatzi matir*. There, the concern was that the *avoda* being performed constituted only half the enabling act — one lamb out of two required, one bowl of frankincense out of two. Here, each *avoda* is complete in itself — the *shechita* is the full *shechita*, the *zerika* is the full *zerika* — but the *pigul* intention at each stage covered only half a *kezayit*. The question is whether these two half-intentions, spread across two separate complete *avodot*, combine to form a full *pigul* intention.

### Which Avodot Combine

The *baraita* establishes that *shechita* and *zerika* combine, but it leaves open whether other pairs of *avodot* do as well.

### Matirin Opinion

One opinion limits the combination to *shechita* and *zerika* specifically, because both belong to the same category: both are *matirs*. *Shechita* enables the blood to proceed to the *mizbe'ach*; *zerika* enables the meat to be eaten and the fats to be burned. Since they share this enabling function, their respective *pigul* intentions may combine. *Kabala* and *holecha*, by contrast, are necessary *avodot* but are not themselves *matirs* in the same sense, and therefore cannot combine.

### Distant Avodot View

A second opinion inverts the logic. If even *shechita* and *zerika* — the most distant of the four *avodot*, the first and the fourth — combine, then *kabala* and *holecha*, which stand between them and are adjacent in sequence, certainly combine as well. On this view, proximity in the chain of *avoda* is a stronger basis for combination than functional category.

### Levi's Position

The Gemara presents a challenge from a *baraita* taught by Levi: *arba avodot ein mitztarfin le-pigul* — the four *avodot* do not combine at all for *pigul*. This directly contradicts the first *baraita*, which permitted the combination of *shechita* and *zerika*.

### Rabbi vs. Rabbis

Rava resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — ha Rabbi, ha Rabbanan* — these are not conflicting rulings but represent two sides of an ongoing debate between Rebbi and the *Rabbanan*. The *baraita* that permits combination reflects one position; Levi's *baraita* reflects the other.

### Rabbi's View Clarified

Abaye, however, objects to how Rava has characterized Rebbi's position. The *baraita* used to identify Rebbi's view — the case of slaughtering one lamb with intent to eat half a *kezayit* of one loaf and the second lamb with intent to eat half a *kezayit* of the other — is not a case of two separate complete *avodot* with a half-*kezayit* thought during each. That case involves *chatzi matir* and *chatzi achila* simultaneously: not only was the *pigul* intention only half a *kezayit* each time, but each *shechita* was itself only half the *matir*. Abaye insists the case Rava is trying to address is fundamentally different: *kulo matir ve-chatzi achila* — a complete *avoda*, with a half-*kezayit* intention during each. That is the genuine question of whether half-*kezayit* thoughts during two separate complete *avodot* combine, and Rebbi's ruling in the lamb case sheds no light on it.

Rava bar Rav Chanan then presses further, noting that if Rebbi's position on the complete-*matir* case could be inferred from the absence of a rabbinic decree (*gezeira*), one might be able to establish indirectly what Rebbi holds — though this argument is introduced at the very close of the daf and its full development extends beyond the present passage.

---

---

# Menachot 15

## Piggul & Rabbinic

### Chatzi Matir

The daf opens four lines before the *mishnah* on 14b, completing the previous *sugya*. The discussion had been focused on the principle of *chatzi matir* — the case where one plans, during the *shechitah* of one of the two lambs of *Shavuos*, to have a *piggul* thought involving only a *kezayis* of that one lamb in the wrong location, but not extending the thought to the other lamb. The *gemara* now turns not to *chatzi matir* as such, but to what it calls *chatzi achila* or *chatzi zayis*: a case in which, during one complete *avodah* — the *shechitah* — one thinks about half a *kezayis*, and during another complete *avodah* — the *zrikah* — one thinks about the other half *kezayis*. A *braisa* had established that this mechanism does work; the question was whether it extends to intermediate *avodos*. A second *braisa* suggested it does not, and the *gemara* attempted to identify whether this constitutes a *tannaim* dispute.

The *gemara* had cited *Rebbe* to the effect that if one performs a *chatzi kezayis* thought by one lamb and a *chatzi kezayis* thought by another lamb, they do not combine — but that case is dismissed because each lamb represents only half of the work, making it also a *chatzi matir*.
