The *gemara* then notes that if *Rebbe* truly held that a *chatzi zayis* from two separate *avodos* combine to create *piggul*, he should have issued a *gzeira* in that case as well. This observation lays the groundwork for an important principle: in many *mishnayos* where the ruling is not *piggul* but *passul*, that *passul* is in fact *passul d'rabbanan*, a rabbinic prohibition arising from proximity to genuine *piggul*.

### Passul D'Rabbanan

The *gemara* states, five lines above the word *matnisin* on 14b: *hachi nami mistavra* — it makes sense — *d'taama d'rabbanan mishum hachi hu*, that the reason the Rabbis in certain cases declare something *passul* rather than fully *mutar* is precisely this concern about where leniency might lead — a form of *gzeira*.

### Minchat Chotei

The end of the *braisa* addressing *chatzi matir* reads: *modim chachamim l'Rebbe Meir b'minchas chotei u'minchas kenaos* — the Rabbis concede to *Rebbe Meir* regarding the *minchas chotei* and the *minchas kenaos*, the *mincha* of a sinner and the *mincha* of the *sotah*, neither of which contains *levonah*. In these cases, the *gemara* says, if one had a *piggul* thought during the *kometz*, *piggul* is achieved and one is *chayav kares*, because there the *kometz* alone is the *matir* — *she'hakometz hu hamatir*. One might ask why this needs to be stated at all, since it is obvious that where there is only one *avodah*, a *piggul* thought during that *avodah* completes the violation. The *gemara* answers: *lav hacha ka'mashma lan*. Rather, it is teaching us why the Rabbis say *passul* even when there is a *levonah* and the thought is expressed only at the *kmitzoh* — the *chatzi matir* scenario. Why not leave such a case entirely *mutar*? Because there exists an analogous scenario in which the *kometz* alone genuinely creates *piggul* — namely, the *minchas chotei*. Since that parallel case exists, the Rabbis impose a *passul* even in the incomplete case, lest the slippery slope lead to treating the genuine *piggul* case with insufficient stringency. The *gemara* accepts this proof.

The takeaway of this closing section of the prior *sugya* is thus the consistent refrain throughout many *mishnayos* — "not *piggul* but *passul*" — reflects a rabbinic prohibition grounded in proximity to genuine *piggul*, because there exists an analogous case where the act truly is *piggul*.

---

## Tumah & Krban

### Nitoshah Mishnah

The *mishnah* reads: *nitla achas min hachalos o echad min hasedarim* — if one of the loaves became *tamei*, or one of the columns of the *lechem hapanim* became *tamei*.

This *mishnah* concerns *tumah*, not *piggul*, and its setting is the *menachos* associated with a *korban* — offerings that are of particular interest in this tractate because their *matir* lies in another element, such as the *bazichin* or the lambs. The *mishnah* thus provides a natural complement to the prior *piggul* discussions: in those discussions, the *gemara* explored how a thought affecting one part of a *korban* can spread to the whole; here it explores how *tumah* affecting one part operates.

### Yehuda Debate

*Rabbi Yehuda* rules: *shneihem yeitziu l'veis hasreifah* — both go out to be burned. His reasoning: *she'ein korban tzibbur chaluk* — one does not divide a *korban tzibbur*. It is conceived as a unified whole, and if one part becomes *tamei*, the entire *korban* is treated as if it were *tamei*. *Chachamim* disagree: *hatamei b'tumaso v'hatahor yeiacheil* — the *tamei* portion remains *tamei* and the *tahor* portion is eaten.

This is a notable contrast to the prior *mishnah*, where *Rabbi Yosi* held that a *piggul* thought affecting one loaf does not affect the remaining loaves — an unusual position, since the dominant principle is that *piggul* applied to part of a *korban* spreads to the whole. In that *piggul* context, the *chachamim* hold the more expansive view. By *tumah*, the positions are different: *tumah* ordinarily affects only what it touches, and the *tahor* portions remain *tahor* — except according to *Rabbi Yehuda*, who applies the *ein korban tzibbur chaluk* principle here as well.

### Lifnei Zrikah

*Rabbi Elazar* establishes: *machlokes lifnei zrikah* — the dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *chachamim* applies only when the *tumah* occurred before *zrikas hadam* in the case of the lambs and bread, or before the burning of the *levonah* in the case of the *lechem hapanim*. But *l'achar zrikah* — after the *zrikah* — everyone agrees: *hatamei b'tumaso v'hatahor yeiacheil*. The question then becomes: what specifically is at issue before the *zrikah* that changes matters?

### Tzitz & Eating

*Rav Pappa* answers: *b'tzitz meratzeh al ha'achilos kamiflagi* — the debate turns on whether the *tzitz* is effective with respect to the eating dimension of *tumah*. This requires some background. The *tzitz*, the golden headplate worn by the *Kohen Gadol*, operates on the principle of *meratzeh al avon hakodashim asher yakdishu Bnei Yisrael* — it papers over problems of *tumah* regarding the *korbanos* themselves. The verse specifies *avon hakodashim*, not *avon hamakdishim* — it concerns the *korbanos* being *tamei*, not the people being *tamei*. A person who is *tamei* and eats a *korban* remains *chayav kares* regardless; the *tzitz* does not extend to permit eating.

### Tzitz Achilos

The *gemara* now applies this to the case before us. If part of this *mincha* is *tamei*, can the *shechitah* of the lambs or the offering of the *bazichin* proceed? In an animal *korban*, missing meat does not prevent the *zrikah*; but if a *mincha* is *chaser* — deficient — one cannot bring the *ketores* or burn the *bazichin*. The concern here is that the *tamei* portion renders the *mincha* deficient, blocking the next stage. The *tzitz* does not permit eating from the *tamei* portion, but the question is whether it sufficiently papers over the problem to allow the *hakravah* to proceed — making the *korban* effective even if eating is still prohibited.

*Rabbanan* hold that the *tzitz meratzeh al ha'achilos*: even though what is being placed on the *mizbeach* is not the *tamei* object itself — it is the *kvashim* or the *bazichin* — the *tzitz* brackets the *tumah* problem enough that the *hakravah* is valid. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *ein ha'tzitz meratzeh al ha'achilos*: the *tzitz* does not help here, and therefore it is as if the *mincha* is *chaser*, disabling the *hakravah*. On *Rabbi Yehuda*'s view, the reason everything must be burned is not that the *tumah* spreads conceptually to the whole *korban*, but rather that the *tumah* creates a deficiency that prevents the *zrikah* from being performed at all — and since the *zrikah* never occurred, the entire *korban* is lost.

### Tzitz Philosophy

A student raised the question: the *tzitz* is worn only by the *Kohen Gadol*, and there is a question whether it is effective only when he is wearing it or whether the very availability of the *tzitz* suffices. More fundamentally, what is the religious meaning of the *tzitz*'s atoning power?

The *gemara* connects this to the phrase *Kodesh LaHashem* engraved on the *tzitz*, and to the function of the *Kohen Gadol* on *Yom Kippur* — whose entire *avodah* is to be *metaher* the *Beis HaMikdash* from *tumos Bnei Yisrael*. The *tzitz* serves as a focus on the Divine, allowing God's presence to remain in the *Mikdash* by somehow absorbing the *tumah*. The deeper point, as articulated in the discussion, is the verse *hashochein itam besoch tumosam* — God declares His intention to dwell among Israel even within their *tumah*. Other conditions of disqualification, such as *arla*, are not *hutrah b'tzibbur*; only *tumah* is overridden in the public sphere. This is because the entire existence of the *Mikdash* is a divine acknowledgment that God's desire to dwell *besoch Bnei Yisrael* will override *tumah* problems — an acknowledgment of human frailty and a divine declaration of presence nonetheless.

As one student aptly noted, the *tzitz* does not cancel *tumah*, it does not achieve *tahara*, but it is *meratzeh* — it lets things proceed. This distinction parallels what Rav Soloveitchik describes as the difference between *kapara* and *tahara*: *kapara* forestalls consequences without fully resolving the underlying condition. The *tzitz* is precisely *meratzeh* in this sense — not atonement in the sense of full repair, but a going-forward in the face of acknowledged imperfection.

### Tumah Hutra

*Rav Huna the son of Rav Nachman* challenged *Rav Pappa*: if the debate is really about the *tzitz*, then even in the case of *olin* — objects actually placed on the *mizbeach* — where everyone concedes the *tzitz* is effective, we should find agreement. Yet a *braisa* shows the same dispute applies even there: *nitma echad min habazichin* — one of the *bazichin* becomes *tamei*. *Rabbi Yehuda* says: *shneihem ya'asu b'tumah*, you might as well perform both in a state of *tumah*. Since it is a *korban tzibbur* and *tumah hutrah b'tzibbur*, you may proceed even with the *tamei bazich*. But *Rabbi Yehuda* goes further: since we already conceive of the entire *korban tzibbur* as if it is *tamei* once any part of it is *tamei*, there is no fault in making the other *bazich tamei* as well. *Chachamim* say: *hatamei b'tumato v'hatahor b'taharato* — the *tamei* is *tamei* and the *tahor* remains *tahor*; you do not spread *tumah* gratuitously.

This makes clear that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position has nothing to do with the effectiveness of the *tzitz* — since he is actually permitting the intentional extension of *tumah*, the *tzitz* cannot be the operative mechanism. His position is entirely about how a *korban tzibbur* is conceptually conceived as an indivisible unit: when any part becomes *tamei*, the whole is treated as *tamei*, and consequences flow from that across the board.

*Rav Ashi* adduces a further proof. A *braisa* states: if an entire *shevet* becomes *tamei* while the rest of Israel is *tahor*, *Rabbi Yehuda* says they all bring the *korban Pesach b'tumah*. The reasoning: a *shevet* constitutes its own *kahal*, its own mini-*tzibbur*. Once a defined *tzibbur* is *tamei*, *tumah hutrah b'tzibbur* applies — and since *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that *tumah* affecting any part of the communal body is treated as affecting the whole, everyone may bring their *korban Pesach b'tumah*. Here the *tzitz* is entirely irrelevant — it operates only on the *korban* itself, not on the *tumah* of people — and yet the same principle of *ein korban tzibbur chaluk* produces the same outcome.

### Bazichin Tamei

*Ravina* then cites the *mishnah* itself: *nitma achas min hachalos o achas min hasedarim* — if one of the loaves or one of the columns becomes *tamei* — *Rabbi Yehuda omer shneihem yetzu l'veis hasreifa*, and *chachamim* say the *tahor* portion is eaten. The point *Ravina* raises: if *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position truly rests on the *tzitz* not being *meratzeh* for *achilos*, one would expect the *mishnah* to state the reason that way. Instead, *Rabbi Yehuda* gives his standard reason: *she'ein korban tzibbur chaluk*. From this *Ravina* concludes that the *tzitz* explanation is not *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning at all.

### Ein Krban Chaluk

The *gemara* accepts this: *ela amar Rabbi Yochanan* — *Rabbi Yochanan* says — *limud aruch hu b'fiv shel Rabbi Yehuda* — it is a set, arranged teaching in the mouth of *Rabbi Yehuda* that *ein korban tzibbur chaluk*, that a *korban tzibbur* is not divided. *Rashi* notes that when *Rabbi Yochanan* uses the phrase *limud aruch*, he means that *Rabbi Yehuda* received this as a tradition from his teachers, since there is no compelling scriptural derivation or logical necessity that would independently generate this rule. It was transmitted to him as a *halakha*.

*Rabbi Yehuda*'s position thus rests entirely on this principle: wherever you are dealing with a *korban tzibbur*, if part becomes *tamei*, it is as if all of it is *tamei*. The practical consequence of this depends on context. Where *tumah* means you cannot eat — as with the remnant of *shtei halechem* or *lechem hapanim* — then if one part is *tamei*, do not eat any of it. Where *tumah* means you are permitted to bring the *korban* because *tumah hutrah b'tzibbur* — as when a *shevet* is *tamei* or when one of the *bazichin* becomes *tamei* — then the logic cuts the other way: once *tumah* is acknowledged in any part of the *korban tzibbur*, it applies to everything, and therefore one might as well bring all of it in *tumah*. The impact of the principle *ein korban tzibbur chaluk* thus depends entirely on what the *tumah* permits or forbids in the specific case.

---

## Toda & Bread

### Toda Mefagelet

The *mishnah* states: *HaToda mefageles es halechem v'halechem eino mefagel es haToda* — the *toda* sacrifice renders its accompanying bread *piggul*, but the bread does not render the *toda piggul*. Similarly: *hakvashim mefaglin es halechem v'halechem eino mefagel es hakvashim* — the two lambs of *Shavuos* render the bread *piggul*, but the bread does not render the lambs *piggul*.

The *mishnah* then works through the cases. If one slaughters the *toda* intending to eat its meat the next day, *hi vehalechem mefugalim* — both the animal and the bread are *piggul*, because once the animal is *piggul* the principle applies to everything dependent on it. But if one intends to eat only the bread the next day, *halechem mefugal v'hatoda einah mefugeles* — the bread is *piggul* but the *toda* itself is not affected, because the thought was directed at the secondary, dependent element and cannot retroactively affect the primary *korban*.

The same structure governs the two lambs of *Shavuos*. If the lambs are made *piggul*, the bread of *shtei halechem* is also *piggul*; but if only the bread is targeted by the *piggul* thought, the lambs remain valid. The *mishnah* and *gemara* here explore the structure of dependency as expressed through *piggul*, making *Shavuos* — with its two lambs, each a *chatzi machshir*, and the *shtei halechem* dependent upon them — a particularly rich model for these discussions.

### Lachmei Toda

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for these laws? Perhaps it follows from what *Rav Kahana* said: *minayin le'lachmei todah she'nikru todah* — how do we know that the breads accompanying the *toda* are themselves called by the name *todah*? He derives it from the verse *v'hikriv al zevach hatodah challos* — the word *todah* is juxtaposed with *challos*, implying that the bread shares the identity of the *toda*. If so, one might expect the relationship to run symmetrically — if the bread is called *toda*, then a thought directed at the bread should also affect the *toda*.

The *gemara* answers: *lechem ikrei todah, todah lo ikrei lechem* — the bread is called *todah*, but *todah* is not called bread. If I am thinking about the *toda*, that encompasses everything named *toda*, including the bread. But if I am thinking about bread, bread means bread — it does not carry with it the animal *korban* upon which it depends.

### Glal Todah

The *gemara* then raises the case of the lambs of *Shavuos*: *heicha ashchan de'ikrei kvasim lechem* — we have no verse calling the *shtei halechem* by the name *kvashim*, and yet the *mishnah* states that the lambs render the bread *piggul*. This shows that the ruling cannot be based on the biblical juxtaposition alone. The *gemara* therefore rejects *Rav Kahana*'s derivation as the operative reason and instead identifies the underlying logic: *lechem glal todah* — the bread comes by reason of, or in the wake of, the *toda*; *v'ein hatodah glal de'lechem* — the *toda* does not come because of the bread. Similarly, *lechem glal de'kvasim* — the *shtei halechem* is drawn along in the wake of the lambs — *v'ein kvasim glal de'lechem* — and the lambs are not drawn along by the bread.

The word *glal*, related to *galgal* — to roll — means something like "rolled along with" or "drawn in the wake of." It is not a question of what motivates one to bring the *korban* in the first place; one might well say that the focus of *Shavuos* is the *shtei halechem*, and the lambs are brought for the purpose of enabling that unique bread *korban*. But *glal* here describes operational dependency, not motivational priority: the bread's validity flows from and depends upon the lambs, while the lambs stand independently. The *toda* does not depend on its bread; it is the bread that depends on the *toda*.

### Tenufah Union

The *gemara* continues: *u'tzrichi* — both cases, the *toda* and the *Shavuos* lambs, needed to be stated. Had the *mishnah* only taught the case of *toda*, one might have reasoned that there the bread does not affect the *toda* because they are clearly distinct objects — *d'lo huskeku ze la'ze b'tnufah*, because the *toda* and its bread are not waved together in the *tenufah* ritual. Since they undergo no shared ritual, they are more conceptually distinct, and it makes sense that the bread cannot affect the *toda*. One might then suppose that by the lambs of *Shavuos*, where *d'huskeku ze la'ze b'tnufah* — the two lambs and the two loaves are waved together in a single act — perhaps that act of unification is so binding that the bread does affect the lambs. The *mishnah* therefore needed to teach both cases, establishing that in both instances the same principle applies: the bread is dependent on the animal *korban*, and that relationship is asymmetric regardless of whether there is a shared waving ritual.

It is worth noting that although the *gemara* earlier cited a verse connecting the breads of *toda* to the *toda* itself, by this point the *pesuk* ceases to function as the operative reason. The ruling is entirely derived from the logical structure of dependency. What defines something as a unified halakhic unit is whether the *avodah* is performed together — not what a verse calls the object by name.

---

## Chatzi Kezayis Mix

### Rav's Answer

*Rav Eliezer* posed a question to *Rav*: *hashocheit es hatodah v'leechol kezayis mimenah u'milachmah l'machar* — if one slaughters the *toda* intending to eat tomorrow a *kezayis* composed of half from the *toda* meat and half from the bread, what is the law?

The question regarding the *toda* itself becoming *piggul* does not arise, as *Rav Eliezer* notes: *hashta kula milachma lo mifagla* — since even a full *kezayis* directed entirely at the bread does not cause the animal *korban* to become *piggul*, certainly a hybrid thought incorporating half a *kezayis* of bread will not do so. The question is specifically whether the bread becomes *piggul*: since the bread is dependent on the *toda*, and a *piggul* thought about a full *kezayis* of the *toda* meat renders the bread *piggul*, can half a *kezayis* of meat combine with half a *kezayis* of bread to render the bread *piggul*?

*Rav* answered: *af zo* — yes, even in this case, the bread is *piggul* while the *toda* is not. From the bread's perspective, it is all one: the thought encompasses a full *kezayis* of what is connected to the bread's status, and the bread is therefore *piggul*.

### Kal VaChomer

The *gemara* challenges this ruling with a *kal vachomer*. The argument runs as follows: the meat — in this hybrid scenario — is the *mefagel*, the element that is participating in making the bread *piggul*. Yet the meat itself does not become *piggul*; it is not *mitpageil*. The bread, on the other hand, has been *haba lefagel velo figeil* — it has been attempting to render the meat *piggul* but cannot do so. If the very thing that makes the bread *piggul* is itself exempt from becoming *piggul*, is it not all the more so that the bread — which could not even make the meat *piggul* — should certainly be protected from becoming *piggul* itself?

### Kilayim Case

The *gemara* then asks: do we in fact apply a *kal vachomer* of this kind? A *braisa* records a case: someone planted his neighbor's vineyard when the grapes were still at the *semadar* stage — not yet fully formed, meaning the vines could still acquire the prohibition of *kilayim*. The principle of *ein adam oser davar she'eino shelo* — one cannot render forbidden something that does not belong to oneself — generally protects the owner's property from prohibitions incurred through another's act. However, since this person physically planted seeds in the vineyard, a physical *kilayim* reality was created. The case was brought before the Sages, who ruled: the seeds are forbidden, but the vine is permitted, based on *ein adam oser davar she'eino shelo*.

Now, could one not apply a *kal vachomer* here as well? The vine — the *oser*, the thing that renders the seeds forbidden — is itself not rendered forbidden. The seeds — *haba leesor velo asar*, coming to make the vine forbidden but failing to do so — should certainly not themselves become forbidden. The *gemara* notes that this *kal vachomer* was not applied, which would seem to undermine the *kal vachomer* in the *piggul* case as well.

### Kanbus Luf

The *gemara* rejects the comparison: *hatam kanvus v'luf asrah Torah* — there, the Torah only specifically prohibited *kanvus* (hemp) and *luf* (identified as *arum palaestinum*) as non-grain plants that create *kilayim* in a vineyard; *shar zerai midrabbanan hu d'asiri* — all other seeds and plants are only rabbinically forbidden in this context. Since the prohibition on these seeds in the vineyard is rabbinic, the mechanism is not a natural spreading prohibition but a *kenas* — a fine imposed by the Rabbis. *Hai d'avid issura kansua rabbanan* — the one who committed the wrong act is penalized; *d'lo avid issura lo kansua rabbanan* — the one who did no wrong is not penalized. The structure of the *kilayim* ruling is therefore not about how the prohibition mechanically operates but about whom the Rabbis chose to punish. You cannot derive a *kal vachomer* from a fine, because fines are imposed selectively on wrongdoers, not based on abstract logical principles about the mechanism of *issur* and *ne'esar*.

By contrast, by *piggul* — *aval hacha leima kal vachomer* — the prohibition is not a fine but the natural operation of halakhic status. Therefore, a *kal vachomer* about the mechanism of *mefagel* and *mitpageil* is in principle applicable here, and the *gemara* does not definitively dismiss it.

### Kvashim Parallel

The *gemara* then states: *v'ika d'matni lah a'kvasim* — there is a parallel version of this entire discussion formulated with respect to the lambs of *Shavuos* rather than the *toda*. *Rav Eliezer* asks *Rav*: if one slaughters the lambs intending to eat a hybrid *kezayis* — half from the lambs and half from the *shtei halechem* — what is the law? The question about whether the lambs become *piggul* is again dismissed immediately: even a full *kezayis* directed at the bread does not make the lambs *piggul*, so certainly a hybrid does not. The question is whether the half *kezayis* of lamb meat combines with the half *kezayis* of bread to make the bread *piggul*. *Rav* gives the same answer — *af bezo halechem mifgal v'hakvasim einam mefugalim* — and the *gemara* raises the same *kal vachomer* and the same *kilayim* reductio. The two versions of the question are substantively identical; the reason both versions were transmitted is discussed below.

### Chaveiro Term

The *gemara* cites a further question attributed to *Rabbi Abba Zuti*, reporting on behalf of *Rabbi Elazar* who asked *Rav*: *hashochet es hakeves leechol kezayis mechaveiro l'machar* — if one slaughters one of the two lambs of *Shavuos* intending to eat tomorrow a *kezayis* from its *chaveiro*, what is the law? The word *chaveiro* is ambiguous. Does it mean the fellow lamb — the other one of the two *kvashim* — or does it mean the bread, which is also associated with and in some sense the "companion" of the lamb?

If *chaveiro* means the other lamb, the answer is straightforward: there is no *piggul* at all, because of the principle *ein matir mefagel matir* — one *matir* does not render another *matir piggul*. The two lambs each function as *matir* for the *shtei halechem*, but they do not function as *matir* for each other; a thought during the *shechitah* of one lamb about eating the other lamb is simply irrelevant to the validity of either.

### Ayin Matir

The *gemara* answers by pointing to a later *mishnah*: *shachat echad min hakvasim leechol mimenu l'machar hu piggul v'chaveiro kasher* — one slaughters one of the lambs intending to eat from it the next day; it is *piggul* and its *chaveiro* is valid. There, the *mishnah* uses *chaveiro* to mean the fellow lamb. Thus *leechol mechaveiro l'machar* — slaughtering with intent to eat the fellow lamb tomorrow — produces a ruling of *shneihem kesherim*, both are valid, because *ein matir mefagel matir*.

This established that *chaveiro* in the *mishnah* refers to the other lamb. The *gemara* deflects: perhaps the *mishnah* only means the other lamb because the context makes it explicit — *d'parish v'amar chaveiro keves* — but absent that context, the word *chaveiro* is not a fixed technical term and could refer to the bread. The *gemara* does not fully resolve which interpretation *Rav Eliezer* intended.

What the discussion illuminates, however, is the full structure of the *Shavuos* model of dependencies: two lambs, each a *chatzi matir* for the *shtei halechem*, dependent upon both; a thought during one lamb's *shechitah* affects the lamb itself and the bread dependent on it, but it does not affect the other lamb, because the two lambs are not dependent on each other.

As for why both versions of *Rav Eliezer*'s question — the *toda* version and the *kvashim* version — needed to be transmitted: *maan d'matki lah l'toda kol she'ken kvashim* — the one who formulated the question about the *toda* would certainly apply the same reasoning to the lambs of *Shavuos*. But *maan d'matki l'kvasim* — the one who specifically formulated it about the lambs might not have applied it to the *toda*, because the lambs and the *shtei halechem* are *huskeku ze la'ze b'tnufah* — they are bound together in the shared waving ritual — making them more of a unified entity, whereas the *toda* and its bread are not, making them more distinct. It was therefore necessary to teach both cases explicitly.

---

## Nesachim

### Zevach Mefagel

A new *mishnah* extends these principles to *nesachim* — the wine libation and the flour-and-oil mixture accompanying a *korban*. *Hazevach mefagel es hanesachim* — the *zevach* renders the *nesachim piggul*; *hanesachim einam mefaglim es hazevach* — but the *nesachim* do not render the *zevach piggul*. This is a direct application of the dependency logic established for the *toda* and the *Shavuos* lambs: the *nesachim* depend on the *zevach*, and not the reverse.

The *mishnah* works through the case: *hashocheit es hazevach le'echol mimenu l'machar* — if one slaughters the sacrifice intending to eat from it tomorrow, *hu u'nesachav mefugalim* — it and the *nesachim* are *piggul*. *L'hakriv nesachav l'machar* — if one intends only to bring the *nesachim* tomorrow, *hanesachim mefugalim hazevach eino mefugal* — the *nesachim* are *piggul* but the *zevach* is unaffected.

### Rabbi Meir

The *chiddush* of this *mishnah* lies not in the general principle — which follows directly from the *toda* and *kvashim* cases — but in the question of when the *nesachim* become identified with the *korban* such that the *korban*'s status can affect them. *Misheyikdeshu bichli divrei Rabbi Meir* — once the *nesachim* have been placed into a vessel, according to *Rabbi Meir*, they are identified with this *korban* and the *zevach*'s *piggul* status applies to them.

### Unified Unit

The *gemara* cites the Rabbis' objection: *halo adam meivi zivcho hayom u'nesachav ad asara yamim* — a person may bring his animal sacrifice today and his *nesachim* as late as ten days later. This demonstrates that the *nesachim* are not inherently one unit with the *zevach*. Moreover — and this point bears on the very nature of *piggul*, which is defined by time — the *korban* must be eaten within its designated time, while the *nesachim* retain their own separate time parameters. If they are not tied together in time, why should a *piggul* thought about the *zevach* define the temporal status of the *nesachim*?

### Separate Days

This is what distinguishes the *nesachim* from the *lachmei toda* and the *shtei halechem*. The breads of the *toda* are brought with the *toda* and have no other purpose; the *shtei halechem* are brought with the lambs of *Shavuos* and wave together with them. Those things are identified. But the *nesachim* may be brought on an entirely different day — and that very permissibility indicates that the Torah has declared them a distinct entity, not bound to the *zevach* in the same way.

### Rava's View

*Rava* articulates *Rabbi Meir*'s position: *kasavar Rabbi Meir hukvu bishchitah ke'lachmei toda* — *Rabbi Meir* holds that the *nesachim* become fixed as one unit with the *zevach* at the moment of *shechitah*, just as the breads of the *toda* become identified at *shechitah*. The rationale: until *shechitah*, yes, the *nesachim* happen to be present with the owner in the *Mikdash*, but they have not yet been formally linked to this *korban*. At the moment of *shechitah*, when the owner stands before the *Mikdash* with both the animal and the *nesachim*, that act binds them together as one. The *Chachamim* disagree: since the Torah permitted the *nesachim* to be brought separately, they always retain their independent status, and no act of the owner can permanently bind them to a specific *korban*.

### Log Shemen

The *gemara* then brings a parallel case involving the *matzora*: *log shemen shel matzora chayavin alav mishum piggul* — the *log* of oil brought by the *metzora* can become *piggul*, because *dam asham matiro le'ihana* — the sprinkling of the blood of the *asham* permits the use of the oil. *Rabbi Meir* says so; the Rabbis object with the same argument — *adam meivi ashamo hayom ve'logo mikan ad asara yamim* — one may bring the *asham* today and the oil up to ten days later, demonstrating they are not one unit. *Rabbi Meir* answers that he only said this when they are brought together. The Rabbis counter that even when brought together, the oil can always be redirected to another *asham* — *efshar leshnoso le'asham acher* — and therefore it never becomes irrevocably identified with this *korban*. *Rava* again states *Rabbi Meir*'s response: *kasavar Rabbi Meir hukvu bishchitah ke'lachmei toda* — the oil is fixed as one unit with the *asham* at the moment of *shechitah*, just as the bread of *toda* is.

The fundamental dispute between *Rabbi Meir* and the *Chachamim* thus comes into focus: *Rabbi Meir* holds that once the owner brings the *nesachim* or the *log* to the *Mikdash* and performs the *shechitah*, that moment of conjunction creates a halakhic unity equivalent to the unity of the *toda* and its bread. The *Chachamim* hold that because the Torah explicitly permitted bringing them on separate days, they can never be fully identified as a single unit — their independent status is not overcome by the accident of being present together, since the owner always retains the option of separating them.

---

---

# Menachot 16

## Pigul & Chatzi Matir

### Kometz/Levonah Case

We begin today's daf at the very top of 16a, where a new *mishnah* opens. We remain in the extended discussion of *pigul*, and we now arrive at the *mishnah* that directly addresses the principle of *mephaglin b'chatzi matir* — whether one can render a *korban pigul* through an intent expressed during only half of the *matir*.

The *mishnah* states: *Pigel b'kometz v'lo bi'levonah* — if someone had a *pigul* thought while offering up the *kometz* on the *mizbeach* but not during the *levonah*, or conversely, had the thought during the *levonah* but not the *kometz* — *Rabbi Meir omer pigul v'chayavin alav karet*: Rabbi Meir holds it is *pigul* and one incurs *karet* for eating the *shirayim*. *V'chachamim omrim ein bo karet ad she'yefagel b'chol ha'matir*: the Sages hold there is no *karet* until the *pigul* intent encompasses the entire *matir*. The terminology implicit in the *mishnah* itself — *chatzi matir* versus *kol ha'matir* — captures the heart of the dispute. It should also be noted that even according to the Sages, who deny *karet*, the *korban* is presumably *pasul* at the rabbinic level, a point the *Gemara* addressed two *dapim* earlier, where it established certain *de'rabbanan* rulings of *pasul* precisely because of the proximity to a genuine *de'oraita* violation.

### Rabbi Meir's View

Rabbi Meir's position is that a *pigul* thought during only half of the *matir* — here, either the *kometz* or the *levonah* alone — is sufficient to render the *korban pigul* and to obligate one who eats the *shirayim* in *karet*. He employs the principle of *mephaglin b'chatzi matir*: even partial *pigul* intent, applied to one of two necessary acts, is halakhically operative.

### Chakhamim's View

The Sages disagree. Their position is that *pigul* takes effect only when the intent to consume the *korban* outside its proper time encompasses the entire *matir*. In the case of the *minchah*, both the *kometz* and the *levonah* must be offered upon the *mizbeach* before the *shirayim* become permissible for eating. Each of these acts is therefore only half of what is required. If one had the *pigul* intent for only one and not the other, the Sages hold that the *pigul* is incomplete and *karet* does not apply.

### Chakhamim's Exceptions

The *mishnah* then records: *u'modim Chachamim l'Rabbi Meir b'Minchat Choteh u'vi'Minchat Kenaot* — the Sages concede to Rabbi Meir's ruling in the case of the *minchah* of a sinner (*Minchat Choteh*) and the *minchah* of jealousy (*Minchat Kenaot*, brought by the *sotah*). In these offerings there is no *levonah*; the *kometz* alone is the *matir*. Accordingly, if one had a *pigul* thought during the *kometz*, the *korban* is *pigul* and *karet* applies, *she'ha'kometz hu ha'matir* — because the *kometz* is the sole *matir* and thus constitutes the entire *matir* on its own. The Sages have no objection to the *kometz* in isolation; their dispute is only where a second act is also required and the intent did not extend to it. The *Gemara* had noted earlier that this clarification, though seemingly obvious, was stated in order to explain why even at the stage of half a *matir* the Sages impose a *de'rabbanan* disqualification — because in cases such as *Minchat Kenaot* the same act would be a fully operative *de'oraita pigul*.

### Shtei Hakvashim

The *mishnah* then introduces what becomes one of its most instructive case studies: the *shtei ha'kevasim*, the two lambs brought together with the *shtei ha'lechem* on *Shavuot*. The lambs of *Shavuot* function as the *matir* of the two loaves — the *shtei ha'lechem* can only be eaten once the lambs have been sacrificed. The bread may be conceptually primary (it is what the *Shavuot* offering is fundamentally about, since one does not bring leavened bread on the *mizbeach*), but in terms of what actually effects its elevated status as a *korban* to enable its consumption, it is the *hakravah* of the two lambs that achieves this. The relationship is analogous to the *korban Pesach*: from the beginning of *Zevachim* we learn that the *achilas* (eating) is primary, yet the *korban* only attains its status as *korban Pesach* through the *zerikas ha'dam*. The question of what is most significant is not the same as the question of what constitutes the *matir*.

The *mishnah* presents the case: *Shachat echad min ha'kevasim l'echol shtei chalot le'machar* — he slaughtered one of the two lambs with the intent to eat the two *challot* of the *shtei ha'lechem* the following day, which is a *pigul* thought. Similarly: *hiktir echad min ha'bazichim l'echol shtei sedarim le'machar* — he burned one of the two *bazichim* of *levonah* for the *lechem ha'panim* with intent to eat the bread the next day. In both cases, Rabbi Meir holds it is *pigul* and *karet* applies; the Sages hold *ein bo karet ad she'yefagel b'chol ha'matir* — you need the intent to encompass both lambs, or both *bazichim*, for the *pigul* to be complete.

### Three Perspectives

What makes the *shtei ha'kevasim* case so rich analytically is that the two lambs and the loaves illuminate *chatzi matir* from three distinct angles simultaneously.

First, relative to the bread: together the two lambs function as the *matir* of the *shtei ha'lechem*, so each lamb individually is only a *chatzi matir* for the bread. This is the case under debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

Second, relative to the lamb itself: the *mishnah* states *shachat echad min ha'kevasim l'echol heimenu le'machar* — he slaughtered one lamb with intent to eat from that same lamb the next day. Here the *avodah* performed with respect to that lamb — slaughtering and then sprinkling its blood — is the complete *matir* for the lamb's own meat. This is not a *chatzi matir* at all; it is a full *pigul* intent, rendering that lamb *pigul* while the other remains *kasher*: *hu pigul v'chaveiro kasher*.

Third, relative to the other lamb: *le'echol me'chaveiro le'machar* — if one slaughtered a lamb with intent to eat from the *other* lamb tomorrow, *shneihem kesheirim* — both are *kasher*. This is because of the principle *ein matir mefagel matir*: one lamb has no halakhic dependency on the other. The bread depends on both lambs; the lambs have no dependency on one another. Hence one lamb's *avodah* cannot affect the status of the other.

The *mishnah* thus offers three clean perspectives from a single pair of lambs: each lamb is a *chatzi matir* for the bread; each lamb is a full *matir* for its own meat; and the lambs have no relationship to each other as potential *matirim*.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav's Position

The *Gemara* now records the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding how to delimit the case under debate. Rav says: *machlokes she'natan et ha'kometz b'shtika v'et ha'levonah b'machshava* — the debate of Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies specifically when the *kometz* was performed in silence, without any *pigul* thought, and the *levonah* was performed with the *pigul* thought. We assume the *kometz* was done first, though as noted earlier this is not strictly required. That is the case where we debate *mephaglin b'chatzi matir*.

However, says Rav: *aval natan ha'kometz b'machshava v'et ha'levonah b'shtika* — if the *kometz* was performed first with the *pigul* thought, and then the *levonah* was performed in silence, *divrei hakol pigul* — everyone agrees it is *pigul*. The reason: *she'kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona hu oseh* — one who performs subsequent acts does so under the framing of the initial intent. Once the *pigul* intent has been articulated at the first stage, the subsequent act of silence is interpreted as proceeding under that same mindset, and accordingly the entire *matir* is encompassed by the *pigul* intent. It is therefore not a case of *chatzi matir* at all.

### Shmuel's Rebuttal

Shmuel disagrees: *u'Shmuel omer adayin hi machlokes* — it is still a dispute. Unless a fresh *pigul* intent is expressed or held at the second stage, one cannot assume the second act is defined by the first. Shmuel thus holds that even when the *pigul* thought preceded, subsequent silence does not carry the first thought forward. The case remains one of *chatzi matir* and the debate of Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies.

### Mindset vs. Speech

This dispute reveals something philosophically important about the nature of *pigul* intent. Both Rashi and Tosafot hold that *pigul* thought must be articulated — it is not sufficient to merely think it internally. Yet even granting this, there is a crucial distinction between articulation as an expression of thought and a pure speech act in the manner of *hakdashah* or *kri'as ha'Torah*. If *pigul* were purely a speech act — like a legal declaration — it could not be said that silence following such a declaration constitutes a repetition of it. One simply did not speak. The most one could say is that having articulated what one was thinking at the first stage, it is clear one continues to hold that thought, or that the second act is framed by the prior statement. This is precisely what Rav claims: *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona hu oseh* is a claim about mindset, not about repeated utterance. The first articulation reveals and frames the operative *da'as*; subsequent silence is governed by it. Shmuel denies this framing: without an explicit expression of intent at each stage, there is no basis to carry it forward.

The very structure of this debate — Rav appealing to *da'as rishona* and Shmuel rejecting its reach — demonstrates that *pigul*, even for those who require articulation, is fundamentally about *da'as*, about mental orientation, not about a performative speech act. The articulation is a vehicle for revealing and concretizing the intent, but the halakhic substance is the intent itself.

### Tosefta Evidence

A *Tosefta* is now cited that bears directly on this debate. The *Tosefta* first supplies important framing for a question implicit in the earlier *mishnah*: if we have always discussed *pigul* arising at the stage of *kemitzah*, why was the *levonah* never considered? The *Tosefta* clarifies: *bameh devarim amurim* — when is the *kometz* alone sufficient and the *levonah* not a concern? During *kemitzah*, *matan kli*, and *hiluch*. But *aval bau l'haktarah* — when it comes time to burn: there the *levonah* matters, because at the stage of *haktarah* the *levonah* is an *avodah* and a *matir*. It is only then that *natan et ha'kometz b'shtika v'et ha'levonah b'machshava* — performing the *kometz* in silence and the *levonah* with the *pigul* thought, or *et ha'kometz b'machshava v'et ha'levonah b'shtika* — performing the *kometz* with the *pigul* thought and the *levonah* in silence, generates the debate of Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

Two reasons explain why earlier stages do not implicate *chatzi matir*. First, there is no *avodah* of the *levonah* at the stage of *kemitzah* or *hiluch* — the Torah's discussion of the *levonah* concerns only its burning. Second, and more conceptually: the *matir* in the phrase *chatzi matir* refers not merely to a necessary *avodah* in the process, but to an act that *effects a change of status*. The *kometz* and *levonah*, when burned, change the status of the *shirayim* — they render the remainder permissible. Nothing that precedes the *haktarah* effects such a change. A necessary *avodah* is not the same as a *matir* in the operative sense. The principle at stake is not *mephaglin b'chatzi avodah* but *mephaglin b'chatzi matir*.

Now, the *Tosefta*'s relevance to the Rav-Shmuel debate: the *Tosefta* presents the two scenarios — *kometz* with thought then *levonah* in silence, and *kometz* in silence then *levonah* with thought — as equally subject to the debate of Rabbi Meir and the Sages. Even where the *pigul* thought came first, the Sages do not declare it *pigul* by virtue of *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona hu oseh*. They still treat it as *chatzi matir*. This is direct evidence against Rav and in favor of Shmuel.

The *Gemara* presses: *ktani mihat* — let us focus on this one point — that the debate applies even in the case of *natan et ha'kometz b'machshava v'et ha'levonah b'shtika*, the *pigul* thought having come first, yet the Sages still debate and do not rule it unambiguously *pigul*. This refutes Rav's contention that *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona* resolves the question.

An attempt is made to reread the *Tosefta*: perhaps *natan et ha'kometz b'machshava* means that the *kometz* was described first but actually performed second — i.e., the *levonah* had already been done in silence before the *kometz* with the thought. The *Gemara* raises two objections — *shtei teshuvot ba'davar*. First, this would be redundant with the preceding case. Second, other *baraitot* explicitly use the language *v'achar kach*, "and afterwards," referring to the *levonah* in silence, confirming that the *levonah* followed rather than preceded. So the reread fails.

Rav Chanina defends Rav differently: *targema be'vei de'ot* — interpret the *Tosefta* as describing two *kohanim*, two separate individuals. *Kohen* A performed the *kometz* with the *pigul* thought, and *Kohen* B performed the *levonah* in silence. In that case, *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona* would not apply because one *kohen*'s intent does not define another's. The scenario remains a genuine *chatzi matir* not because of anything about the sequence of intent, but because we cannot project one person's *da'as* onto another's acts. The *Gemara* allows this but proceeds to further challenge Rav from other evidence.

---

## Evidence Against Rav

### Yom Kippur Case

The *Gemara* introduces a strong *ta shema* from a *baraita* concerning the blood sprinklings of *Yom Kippur*. A preliminary clarification: while for blood placed on the outer *mizbeach* the first application is generally determinative and subsequent applications do not affect *pigul* status, the inner blood applications — those of the *par* and *se'ir* on *Yom Kippur* — are different. Every single application of the inner blood is *me'akev*, indispensable. A *pigul* thought at any one of these applications is thus potentially operative.

The *baraita* identifies the inner blood of *Yom Kippur*: *mem gimel shel Yom HaKippurim* — the 43 applications of *Yom Kippur*, as well as the 11 of the *par kohen mashiach* from *Horayot* and the 11 of the *par helam davar* from *Horayot*. Working through the count for *Yom Kippur*: inside the *Kodesh Hakodashim*, eight applications (one up, seven down) are made for the *par* and the *se'ir* separately, yielding 16. Then, against the *paroches*, again separately for each, yielding 32. After the bloods are mixed, the four corners and seven on top of the *mizbeach ha'zahav* yield another 11, for a total of 43.

Regarding the 11 for the regular cases: seven applications toward the *paroches* and four on the four corners of the *mizbeach ha'zahav*, totaling 11.

The *baraita* then states: *pigel bein b'rishona bein b'shniya bein b'shlishis* — whether the *pigul* thought occurred at the first set (inside the *Kodesh Hakodashim*), the second set (against the *paroches*), or the third set (on the *mizbeach ha'zahav*) — Rabbi Meir says it is *pigul* and *karet* applies; the Sages say *ein bo karet ad she'yefagel b'chol ha'matir*. And *u'pligi* — they debate.

The critical observation: even when the *pigul* thought occurred at the first set — *rishona* — the Sages still debate. The *baraita* makes no distinction based on whether the thought came first. This is clear evidence against Rav: we do not say *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona hu oseh*.

The attempt is made to rescue Rav by appealing to the scenario of *shtei de'ayos* — two *kohanim*, two intellects — suggesting that perhaps the *Kohen Gadol* performed the first set with a *pigul* thought and then died or was replaced, and a second *Kohen Gadol* performed the subsequent sets. In that case, *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona* would not apply since they are different individuals. However, the *Gemara* notes that this depends on a disputed point: *hani'a l'man de'amar b'par va'afilu b'dam moshe par* — this works according to the opinion that a successor *Kohen Gadol* may continue the *Yom Kippur* service mid-process even with the blood of the original animal. But according to the opinion that holds *b'par v'lo b'dam moshe par* — that a new *Kohen Gadol* must begin again with a new living animal — the scenario of two *kohanim* completing the same blood sequence cannot arise. Yet the *baraita* presents the case without qualification, apparently applying the debate even where a single *Kohen Gadol* carried through all three sets. *Mah ika l'meimar* — what can one say?

### Rava's Defense

Rava attempts to save Rav's position with an interpretive move: *kegon she'pigel b'rishona v'shatak b'shniya u'pigel b'shlishis* — the case described is one where the *Kohen Gadol* had a *pigul* thought at the first set, was silent at the second, and then had a *pigul* thought again at the third. In this configuration, Rav could concede that the second act of silence is not governed by the first thought, since the *Kohen Gadol* himself went on to articulate the *pigul* thought explicitly at the third stage — thereby demonstrating retroactively that his silence at the second stage was not mere continuation of the first intent. *De'amrinan ei salka da'atach kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona hu oseh, mehadar pigulei b'shlishis lamah li* — if subsequent acts were automatically governed by the initial *da'as*, why would he have bothered to repeat the *pigul* thought explicitly at the third stage? The fact that he did so reveals that he understood his silence at the second stage to signify something different, not a continuation of his original intent. Thus, this is a legitimate case of *chatzi matir* even where the *pigul* thought preceded.

### Rav Ashi's Challenge

Rav Ashi objects: *midi shatak tani?* — does the *baraita* say anything about silence? The *baraita* says *bein b'rishona bein b'shniya bein b'shlishis* — whether at the first, second, or third. This formulation does not describe the complex scenario of thought–silence–thought; it simply states that the *pigul* thought occurring at any one of these stages — the first, or the second, or the third — triggers the debate. Rava's reading is not what the *baraita* says.

Rav Ashi therefore proposes his own reading: *kegon she'pigel b'rishona u'v'shniya* — the case is where the *pigul* thought was present at the first and second sets but not at the third. Some textual versions add *v'shatak b'shlishis* explicitly. This fits the *baraita*'s language better: *bein b'rishona bein b'shniya bein b'shlishis* means: whether the thought was present in the first and second (but not the third), or whether it was present only in the third. The same principle then applies: *ei salka da'atach kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona hu oseh, mehadar pigulei b'shniya lamah li* — if the first thought governed everything, why articulate the *pigul* thought again at the second stage? The repetition at the second stage demonstrates that silence genuinely means a different mindset, not a continuation.

### Conclusion

The *Gemara* concludes: *v'ha bein bein ktani* — the *baraita* simply says "whether at the first, whether at the second, whether at the third," indicating that any single one of these stages, alone, suffices to create the case under debate. Neither Rava's reading nor Rav Ashi's reading actually fits the plain text. *Kashya* — it remains a difficulty.

The conclusion is clear: all the evidence aligns with Shmuel against Rav. The debate of Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding *mephaglin b'chatzi matir* applies regardless of whether the *pigul* thought came first or later. The principle of *kol ha'oseh al da'as rishona hu oseh* — that subsequent acts are governed by an initial articulated intent — does not operate in this domain. Silence after an expressed *pigul* thought does not carry that thought forward. This has significance beyond *pigul*: the extent to which prior articulated intent frames subsequent silence is a live question in other halakhic contexts as well. Here, the *Gemara* firmly rules it does not apply.

---

## Technical Clarifications

### Completion Principle

Returning to the earlier-cited *baraita* about the *Yom Kippur* blood, the *Gemara* examines an important foundational principle: *karet lo mechayev ad she'yakrivu kol ha'matirim* — one does not become obligated in *karet* for eating *pigul* unless all the acts that would normally permit the *korban* have been properly completed. This is not a point of dispute but a precondition shared by all opinions. The verse *pigul hu lo yeiratzeh* — "it is *pigul*, it will not find favor" — is read to require that the *korban* must have been in a position to "find favor," i.e., it must have been performed correctly in all other respects. *Hartza'as kasher kach hartza'as pasul*: just as a *kasher korban* requires completion of all the *matirim*, so too *pigul* requires that all those same acts be completed — save for the *pigul* thought itself, which is the sole defect.

### Blood Mid-Process

This principle generates a sharp question regarding the *Yom Kippur* case. Suppose the *Kohen Gadol* had a *pigul* thought while sprinkling blood inside the *Kodesh Hakodashim*. *Keivan de'chashav bah bifnim, paslah* — that thought at the inner stage has invalidated the blood. When he then exits and approaches the *heichal* to sprinkle toward the *paroches*, *maya be'alma deka mati* — it is as though he is sprinkling water: the blood is no longer *kasher* and the subsequent *avodah* is not being performed with a valid *korban*. How then can the *pigul* be considered completed when the very blood used for subsequent stages has been rendered invalid by the initial *pigul* thought?

Rashi raises the obvious counter-question: if this reasoning were applied universally, *pigul* could never take effect. If a *kohen* slaughters the animal with a *pigul* thought, the blood thereby becomes blood of a *pigul* animal — so when he proceeds to the *zrikah*, he is sprinkling the blood of something invalid. Yet we know *pigul* does apply! Rashi explains that the principle must be that we bracket *pigul* and set it aside: we evaluate the subsequent *avodot* as though the *pigul* defect did not occur, and ask whether they were otherwise properly performed.

The question then is whether this bracketing applies within a single, continuous process involving the same blood. Perhaps we can bracket *pigul* only when the *avodah* in question is a distinct subsequent *avodah*, but when the very same blood is being applied in multiple stages, we cannot set aside the defect that arose mid-process.

### Bracketing Solution

Rava resolves this: *diskomi meratzi* — for the purpose of assessing *pigul*, the defect is bracketed. When we ask whether *hartza'as kasher k'hartza'as pasul* — whether the *korban* was performed in a manner that could have found favor — we mean: setting aside the *pigul* problem itself, was everything else done correctly? This bracketing applies even in the midst of a single extended process. The answer to the question is therefore straightforward: yes, even when the *pigul* thought arose during the inner blood applications, we evaluate the subsequent applications as if they were being performed with valid blood, and the *pigul* is complete once all applications are done. Rava had also briefly noted another theoretical resolution — that one might have used multiple animals (*arba'ah parim v'arba'ah se'irim*), refreshing the blood at each stage — but the operative answer is the bracketing principle.

### Blood Counts

The *Gemara* addresses a discrepancy in the count of blood applications on *Yom Kippur*. We cited the number 43. But a *baraita* counts 47. *Lo kashya*: the debate hinges on whether the bloods of the *par* and *se'ir* are mixed before or after the four corner-applications of the *mizbeach ha'zahav*. All agree they are mixed before the seven applications on top of the *mizbeach*. But if the mixing occurs only after the four corners, then those four applications are performed separately for the *par* and the *se'ir*, adding four more applications and yielding 47.

A further *baraita* counts 48. *Lo kashya*: this reflects the dispute whether the *shirayim* — the pouring of the remaining blood on the base of the outer *mizbeach* — is *me'akev* in the inner *chatat*. Normally, *shirayim* are not considered indispensable. But there is an opinion that because these are *chatat penimiyot*, the *shirayim* retain their *me'akev* status even when poured on the outer *mizbeach*. According to that view, there is one additional application that is halakhically significant, bringing the count to 48.

---

## Nature of Matir

### Pigul in Holachah

The *Gemara* now addresses the question that the earlier discussion made acute. We established from the *Tosefta* that the *levonah* is not a concern during the earlier stages of *kometz* processing — *kemitzah*, *matan kli*, and *hiluch*. The *Tosefta* explained that the debate of *chatzi matir* arises only at *haktarah*. But we also noted from an earlier *Gemara* that the collecting of the *levonah* from atop the *minchah* — the *likkut* of the *levonah* — may itself constitute an *avodah*, classified as a kind of *holachah* that brings the *levonah* to its place. If there is indeed a *holachah* of *levonah*, then at the stage of *holachah* of the *kometz*, there is a parallel *avodah* of *levonah* taking place. Does this generate a *chatzi matir* issue?

*Ibbaya lehu: pigul b'holachah mahu?* — the question is formally posed: if one had a *pigul* thought during the *holachah* of the *kometz*, what is the law?

### Rabbi Yochanan's Theory

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *holachah ke'kemitzah* — *holachah* is like *kemitzah*. The *levonah* is irrelevant; the *pigul* thought during *holachah* of the *kometz* is a full *pigul*, without any issue of *chatzi matir*. Even granting that there is a *holachah* of *levonah*, this does not create a *chatzi matir* problem at the stage of *holachah*.

### Reish Lakish's Theory

Reish Lakish disagrees: *holachah ke'haktarah* — *holachah* is like *haktarah*. Since there is a *holachah* of *levonah*, the *holachah* of the *kometz* is only one of two parallel *avodot* being performed at this stage, and is therefore a *chatzi matir*. *Bishlama l'Reish Lakish ika nami holachah de'levonah* — Reish Lakish's position is internally coherent: the *holachah* of the *levonah* exists, and the *kometz*'s *holachah* is thus only half.

Rava explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: *kasavar Rabbi Yochanan, kol avodah she'einah materes, avodah chashuvah hi le'fagel aleha bifnei atzmah* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that any *avodah* that does not itself effect a *matir*, does not produce a change of status, is to be considered a self-sufficient *avodah* in its own right for purposes of *pigul*. It is not half of anything; it is the entirety of what that *avodah* is. The concept of *chatzi matir* — doing only half of what is needed — only applies when the *avodah* in question is functioning as something that effects a change of status. When the *avodah* is producing an end result, when it is a *matir* in the operative sense, then we can say it has done only half of what is needed, because the entire point of the act is to effect a certain outcome and that outcome requires a complementary act. But when the *avodah* is simply a necessary step — a *hiluch* that is not yet producing any change — it is entirely itself. The existence of a parallel *avodah* is simply irrelevant.

Conceptually, Rabbi Yochanan's position distinguishes sharply between the logic of process and the logic of result. When an act is understood primarily as a necessary process step, its identity is defined by what it does, not by what else must happen. When an act is understood primarily as producing a result — effecting a change of status — then its adequacy is measured by whether it has fully achieved that result, and if it needs a complementary act to do so, it is only half adequate.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rabbi Yochanan: *harei shechitat echad min ha'kevasim, de'avodah she'einah matirathah* — consider the slaughter of one of the two Shavuot lambs relative to the *shtei ha'lechem*. The *shechitah* of the lamb does not render the bread edible; the bread becomes permissible only through the *zerikas ha'dam*. Yet the *mishnah* records the debate of Rabbi Meir and the Sages even for this case — *shachat echad min ha'kevasim v'al shtei ha'chalot le'machar*, with the Sages requiring the intent to encompass both lambs. How can Rabbi Yochanan say *chatzi matir* only applies when effecting a change of status, if the *shechitah* does not yet change the status of the bread?

### Rabbi Yochanan's Response

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *mi savrat lechem ba'tanur kadosh?* — do you assume the bread is already fully sanctified from when it was baked in the *Mikdash*? *Shechitat kvasim mikadsha lei* — the slaughter of the lambs effects a status change in the bread itself. It may be that the bread has *kedushas damim* before the lambs are slaughtered, and *kedushas ha'guf* — full sanctification as a *korban* — only after. The point is that the *shechitah* of the lambs actively elevates the bread's sanctified status. *De'ha ba l'kadesh k'ba l'hatir dami* — coming to sanctify is halakhically equivalent to coming to render permissible. *Matir* in this analysis is not limited to making something edible; it means effecting a status change. Any act that effects such a change is a *matir* in the relevant sense, and if two such acts are jointly required to produce the full change, each is a *chatzi matir*.

### Korban Pesach Case

Rav Shimi bar Ashi raises a further challenge from a *baraita* in the name of *Acheirim* concerning *korban Pesach*: *hikdim moolim l'areilim kasher, hikdim areilim l'moolim pasul* — if one slaughtered the *korban Pesach* first with intent for those who are circumcised and then for the uncircumcised, it is *kasher*; if the uncircumcised came first in one's intent, it is *pasul*. The *Gemara* in Pesachim establishes that this debate turns on the issue of *chatzi matir*: specifically, the two *simanim* — the trachea and the esophagus — of the *shechitah* of the *korban Pesach*. A *pigul* intent during one sign but not the other constitutes a *chatzi matir* case.

But the *shechitah* of the *korban Pesach* is not yet a *matir*: the *pesach* becomes *mutar* only through the *zerikas ha'dam*, not the *shechitah*. How then does Rabbi Yochanan's principle apply?

The response parallels what was said about the Shavuot lambs: *amar lei mi savras dam b'tzavar beheimah kadosh?* — do you assume the blood in the animal's neck is already sanctified at the appropriate level? *Dam sakin mikadsha lei* — the knife, the act of *shechitah*, sanctifies the blood. The blood goes from being an ordinary fluid in the animal's neck to being blood with *kedushas damim* — eligible to be offered on the *mizbeach*. This is an active status change. *De'ha ba l'kadesh k'ba l'hatir dami* — coming to sanctify is like coming to render permissible. The two *simanim* of the *shechitah* jointly effect this status change on the blood, and thus each is a *chatzi matir* for it. This reasoning also lends support to the view among the *Rishonim* that the knife used for *shechitah* must be a *kli sharet*.

### Tannaitic Support

A *baraita* is cited that appears to strongly support Rabbi Yochanan: *bameh devarim amurim b'kemitzah u'vmatan kli u'vehiluch* — the clause limiting the debate to stages prior to *haktarah*, and stating that only at *haktarah* does the *levonah* matter, seems to indicate that even at the stage of *holachah* — where Reish Lakish posits a *holachah* of *levonah* — there is no *chatzi matir* issue. *Mai lav hiluch de'haktarah* — does this not refer to the *holachah* that leads to the *haktarah*, the real *avodah*? If so, the *baraita* directly contradicts Reish Lakish, who would say that at this stage the *holachah* of *levonah* creates a *chatzi matir*.

### Reish Lakish Reinterprets

Reish Lakish attempts to reread the *baraita*: *lo, hiluch de'matan kli* — the *hiluch* mentioned is not the *holachah* that is the real *avodah*, but rather the movement involved in transferring the *kometz* from the *minchah* into the *kli sharet*. This would be a preparatory step, not the *avodah* of *holachah* itself, and so the *baraita* would not be speaking about the stage where the *levonah*'s *holachah* matters.

The *Gemara* objects on two grounds. First: *ei hachi, b'matan kli u'vehiluch*, the *baraita* lists *matan kli* first and *hiluch* second — which implies that the *hiluch* comes after the *matan kli*, i.e., it is the real *avodah* of *holachah* that follows the placing of the *kometz* in the vessel. If it were the *hiluch* of placing it into the vessel, the order would be reversed: first the *hiluch*, then the *matan kli*. Second: the *baraita* then says *ba lo l'haktarah* — it came to *haktarah* — implying the stage it just described is prior to *haktarah*, i.e., the *holachah* to the *mizbeach* for burning. According to Reish Lakish, the *baraita* should have said *ba lo l'holachah* as the pivot point where *chatzi matir* begins, since that is where the *holachah* of *levonah* becomes relevant. *Kashya* — this remains difficult for Reish Lakish.

Furthermore: *ela natan et ha'kometz b'shtika* — the *baraita* phrases the debate in terms of *natan et ha'kometz*, the placing of the *kometz*, in silence. According to Reish Lakish, it should have said *holich*, in the *holachah*, in silence. The *baraita*'s language does not support Reish Lakish's reading. The strong evidence of the *baraita* thus aligns with Rabbi Yochanan: the only stage at which the *levonah*'s presence creates a *chatzi matir* issue is the *haktarah*.

---

## Conceptual Conclusion

### Rabbi Yochanan Prevails

Rabbi Yochanan's principle prevails. The concept of *chatzi matir* — doing only half of what is required — applies exclusively to acts that effect a change of status. An *avodah* that is merely a necessary step in the process, without itself producing a change of status in any object or substance, is a self-sufficient *avodah* for *pigul* purposes. The fact that a parallel *avodah* exists at the same stage is immaterial unless both of those parallel acts are effecting a change of status jointly.

Reish Lakish's position — that any parallel *avodah* generates a *chatzi matir* problem — cannot be reconciled with the *baraita*'s explicit ruling that only *haktarah* triggers the debate.

### Minchah Application

Applied to the *minchah*: the only stage at which the burning of the *kometz* and the *levonah* function as a *chatzi matir* — effecting the change of status of the *shirayim* to render them permissible for eating — is the *haktarah*, the burning. No earlier stage changes the status of the *shirayim*. The *kemitzah*, the *matan kli*, and the *holachah* are all necessary *avodot*, but they do not themselves effect a change of status in conjunction with anything else. Accordingly, the debate of Rabbi Meir and the Sages over *mephaglin b'chatzi matir* applies, in the case of the *minchah*, only at the stage of *haktarah*.

---

---

# Menachot 17

## Piggul & Shiyarim

### Sesame-Grain Offering

The daf opens in the midst of the broader discussion of *mefaglin b'chatzi matir* — whether a *pigul* thought expressed during the performance of only one of two required acts (*chatzi matir*) is effective. The case under examination involves the *kometz* of the *minchah* and the *levona*: each is a half of the combined *matir* that permits the *shiyarim*, the remainder of the flour-offering, to the priests. The familiar debate between Rebbi Meir and the Rabbanan over *mefaglin b'chatzi matir* provides the theoretical backdrop.

The Gemara now introduces a far more intricate case. Rather than simply placing the *kometz* on the *mizbe'ach* with a *pigul* intent to eat a *kezayis* of *shiyarim* tomorrow — which would be a straightforward application of *pigul* — the scenario involves offering the *kometz* one sesame-grain (*shumshum*) at a time. With each individual grain placed upon the *mizbe'ach*, the *kohen* declares an intent to eat a correspondingly tiny amount of the *shiyarim* tomorrow. This continues grain by grain until the entirety of the *kometz* has been offered. In the aggregate, the accumulated intentions cover a *kezayis* or more of *shiyarim*, but no single act of *haktara* was accompanied by an intent involving a full *kezayis*, or indeed any halachically significant quantity, of *shiyarim*. The question is whether this incremental process generates *pigul*, renders the offering *pasul* without *pigul*, or leaves it entirely *kasher*.

### Chisda/Hamnuna/Sheshes

Three Amoraim — Rav Chisda, Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Sheshes — dispute the outcome. One holds the offering is *pigul*, subjecting one who eats the *shiyarim* to *kares*. A second holds it is *pasul* but not *pigul*. A third holds the *shiyarim* remain entirely *kasher*.

### Rebbi Meir Position

The Gemara attempts to align these three views with known Tannaitic positions. The opinion that the offering is *pigul* maps most naturally onto Rebbi Meir, who holds *mefaglin b'chatzi matir* — that even a *chatzi matir* suffices to generate *pigul*. In this reading, each individual grain of the *kometz* constitutes a *chatzi matir*, and the *pigul* intent accompanying each grain combines to create effective *pigul* over all the small portions of *shiyarim* envisioned.

It should be noted, however, that this is a somewhat unusual application of the concept of *chatzi matir*. The canonical cases of *chatzi matir* involve qualitatively discrete acts — the *kometz* and the *levona* as separate components, the two lambs of *shtei halechem*, perhaps the *kaneh* and *veshet* of animal slaughter. Each is a defined, independent act that together with another forms the complete *matir*. Here, by contrast, the division is purely quantitative: one has simply performed successive portions of the same act until the full *kometz* is consumed. Whether treating each such increment as a *chatzi matir* is conceptually apt is a question the Gemara will press. Nevertheless, this is how the Gemara frames the position at this stage.

### Rabbanan Position

The opinion that the offering is *pasul* — but not *pigul* — maps onto the Rabbanan, who reject *mefaglin b'chatzi matir*. Even so, the Rabbanan hold that an attempt to create *pigul* through a *chatzi matir* renders the *korban* at minimum *pasul* on a Rabbinic level. Thus, while the incremental *haktara* of the *kometz* with fragmented intent cannot achieve full *pigul*, it is sufficient to disqualify the offering.

### Rebbi Position

The opinion that the offering is entirely *kasher* maps onto Rebbi, who ruled earlier (on daf 14) that slaughtering one lamb with intent to eat a half-*kezayis* of one loaf, and then slaughtering the other lamb with intent to eat a half-*kezayis* of the other loaf, is entirely *muttar*. Rebbi holds that separate half-*kezayis* quantities directed at distinct acts do not combine. By analogy, each tiny grain of *kometz* offered with intent toward a tiny increment of *shiyarim* cannot aggregate into a disqualifying *machshava*, and the offering remains *kasher*.

### Conditional Analysis

The Gemara immediately challenges this neat alignment. In each case, one can construct a reading under which the Amora's position could equally well reflect a different Tannaitic view.

Consider Rebbi Meir first. His principle of *mefaglin b'chatzi matir* may apply specifically when the *machshava* accompanying the *chatzi matir* involves a full *kezayis* of *shiyarim* — that is, where the only deficiency is that the *matir* was only half performed, but the intended object was of full halachic significance. Here, however, each grain of *kometz* was paired with an intent concerning only a vanishingly small amount of *shiyarim*. Rebbi Meir might not extend his principle to a case where no single act of *haktara* was accompanied by an intent of sufficient magnitude.

Similarly for the Rabbanan: their rejection of *mefaglin b'chatzi matir* applies where only one of the two *matirim* was performed with *pigul* intent — say, the *kometz* but not the *levona*, or vice versa. Here, however, the *machshava* accompanied every single grain of the *kometz*, meaning the intent encompassed the entire *matir*. This is not a case of *chatzi matir* at all — the *matir* was performed in full, grain by grain. The Rabbanan's concern with *chatzi matir* is therefore irrelevant, and the question becomes a different one entirely: whether the atomized intent, fragmentary in its object rather than its subject, constitutes valid *pigul* intent.

And as for Rebbi: his ruling of *kasher* concerned two separate lambs, each associated with a half-*kezayis* from a *different* loaf. The crucial feature there is that the two half-*kezayis* amounts derived from distinct acts of *shechita* on distinct offerings, with distinct objects. Here, by contrast, it was the same *kometz* throughout, and all the fragmented intentions toward tiny amounts of *shiyarim* arose within a single act of *haktara*. Rebbi might hold that when all the intentions arise from one unified *avodah*, they aggregate, and the offering would be *pasul*.

### All Three Valid

Given that none of the three Amora positions can be pinned definitively to a single Tannaitic source, the Gemara concludes that each of the three outcomes — *pigul*, *pasul*, and *kasher* — could in principle be maintained according to all Tannaitic positions. Rav Adda bar Ahava's framework makes this explicit: whether the result is *pigul*, *pasul*, or *kasher* depends not on which Tanna one follows, but on which empirical and halachic premises one accepts about the nature of this particular act.

### Piggul Analysis

The position that the outcome is *pigul* — *divrei hakol* — rests on two combined premises: first, that performing the *haktara* a tiny drop at a time constitutes a *derech haktara*, a valid manner of offering; and second, that intending to eat in corresponding tiny increments constitutes a *derech achila*, a cognizable manner of eating. If both premises hold, then one has performed a valid *haktara* accompanied by a genuine intent to eat the *shiyarim* at the wrong time — the classic formula for *pigul*. The further assumption, which the Gemara leaves implicit, is that all those tiny intentions toward tiny amounts of *shiyarim*, occurring within a single act of *haktara*, coalesce into a single intent of a *kezayis*, the threshold for *pigul*.

### Passul Analysis

The position that the outcome is *pasul* rests on accepting the first premise while rejecting the second: eating in tiny successive increments — a grain here, a grain there — does not constitute a *derech haktara* in the first place. If offering the *kometz* one sesame-grain at a time is not a valid *haktara* at all, the *korban* is *pasul* because it never underwent proper *haktara*, and no *pigul* can attach. The Gemara notes that such a *minchah* is comparable to one whose *haktara* was never performed. Interestingly, whether the *derech achila* criterion is met becomes irrelevant: once *haktara* fails, there is no valid *pigul* process to speak of.

### Kasher Analysis

The position that the outcome is *kasher* — again applicable according to all opinions — rests on accepting that doing the *haktara* incrementally is a valid *derech haktara*, while rejecting that incremental eating constitutes a *derech achila*. The *haktara* succeeds and the *korban* is properly offered. But the accompanying intent — to eat a grain here and a grain there in tiny successive amounts — does not meet the definition of *achila* required for *machsheves pigul*. Since the intent does not rise to the level of cognizable *achila*, no *pigul* thought has been formed, and the offering is entirely *kasher*. The question of *chatzi matir* is not germane here at all: the full *matir* was performed, and the thought simply did not constitute a valid *machshava* to eat.

---

## Haktara Debate

### Pumbedita Opinion

The daf turns to a distinct but related question. The *charifei d'Pumbedita* — identified by Rashi in Sanhedrin as Eifa and Avimi, the sons of Rechava — maintain that *haktara mefagelet haktara*: that performing the *haktara* of the *kometz* with the intent to offer the *levona* tomorrow constitutes *pigul*.

This claim must contend with two distinct obstacles. The first is *mefaglin b'chatzi matir*: the *kometz* alone is only a *chatzi matir*, and even Rebbi Meir's position applies to *chatzi matir* situations; the Rabbanan reject the very possibility. The second, left implicit at this stage but surfacing shortly, is *ein matir mefagel matir* — a *matir* cannot generate *pigul* in relation to another *matir* — since both the *kometz* and the *levona* are themselves *matirim* for the *shiyarim*.

The *charifei d'Pumbedita* address the first obstacle as follows. The Rabbanan's principle of *ein mefaglin b'chatzi matir* applies when one's intent during the *kometz* concerns the *shiyarim* while the *levona* remains unaddressed — that is, when only half of the *matir* structure is engaged by the *machshava*, and the *levona* stands entirely apart. In that standard case, the intent is genuine only as to the *kometz*, and since the *kometz* is but half the *matir*, it is insufficient. Here, however, the intent accompanying the *haktara* of the *kometz* directly involves the *levona* — the very other half of the *matir*. True, the *levona* appears as the object of the thought rather than its subject. But because the *machshava* encompasses the *levona*, it is as though the entire *matir* has been drawn into the intent. The Gemara acknowledges that this is a *chiddush* — one would ordinarily require that the *machshava* bear upon the full act as its subject — but the *charifei* maintain that since the thought relates to the *haktara* of the *levona*, it implicates the complete *matir* structure and thereby achieves *pigul*.

### Meshna Challenge

Rava — or perhaps Abaye — adduces support from an earlier Mishnah. That Mishnah formulates the general principle governing *pigul*: anyone who performs *kmitza*, *netina b'kli*, *holacha*, or *haktara* with intent to eat something *she'darko le'echol* (normally eaten) at the wrong time, or to offer something *she'darko lehaktir* (normally offered) at the wrong time, generates *pigul* — *chutz lizmano pigul v'chayavin alav kares*. Rava argues that when the Mishnah lists *haktara* alongside the earlier three *avodot*, it implies that the intent of *haktara* during the *haktara* stage can encompass the same range as the other stages — including *lehaktir davar she'darko lehaktir*, that is, offering the *levona* at the wrong time. This would vindicate the *charifei d'Pumbedita* that an intent during the *haktara* of the *kometz* to offer the *levona* tomorrow creates *pigul*.

### Gemara Response

The Gemara demurs. The Mishnah does not necessarily equate the *haktara* stage with the earlier stages regarding the range of valid *pigul* intentions. In the earlier stages — *kmitza*, *netina b'kli*, *holacha* — the thought could be either to eat the *shiyarim* at the wrong time or to offer the *kometz* at the wrong time, *bein le'echol bein lehaktir*. At the stage of actual *haktara*, however, one might distinguish: the intent to eat the *shiyarim* at the wrong time (*le'echol*), yes, can generate *pigul*; but the intent to offer the *levona* at the wrong time (*lehaktir*) may not, whether because of *ein mefaglin b'chatzi matir* or because of *ein matir mefagel matir*. The Mishnah's inclusion of *haktara* in the general formula does not, of itself, establish that the *haktara* stage can produce *pigul* through an intent directed at the other *matir*.

### Chisda's Position

The opposing view is then stated explicitly.
