Rav Menashya bar Gadda, seated before Abaye, transmits in the name of Rav Chisda — and this transmission is subsequently confirmed as going back to Rav himself — the categorical ruling: *ein haktara mefagelet haktara*. The *haktara* of the *kometz* cannot generate *pigul* when the accompanying intent is to offer the *levona* tomorrow.

### Non-Relation Logic

The reasoning is compelling. Rav Chisda distinguishes between two types of intent during the *kometz's* *haktara*. When one intends to eat the *shiyarim* at the wrong time, the *pigul* thought is effective — even according to the Rabbanan — precisely because the *kometz* is a *matir* for the *shiyarim*. It stands in a constitutive relationship to the *shiyarim*: the *kometz* is what permits the *shiyarim*, even if only as half the combined *matir*. The *machshava* regarding the *shiyarim* thus flows directly from and attaches to the act of *haktara* of the *kometz*.

But the *kometz* is not a *matir* for the *levona*. Both the *kometz* and the *levona* are jointly *matirim* for the *shiyarim*, but they do not bear any constitutive relationship to one another. The *levona* can be offered before the *kometz*; the *kometz*'s *haktara* does not alter the *levona's* halachic state in any way. They operate in parallel, not in sequence. Since the *kometz* has no bearing on the *levona*, an intent formed during the *haktara* of the *kometz* concerning the *levona* is simply disconnected — the thought has no purchase on the *levona*, and therefore cannot generate *pigul* in relation to it.

### Two Lambs Proof

Abaye finds support for Rav Chisda's position in a Mishnah. If one slaughters one of the two lambs of *shtei halechem* with intent to eat from that lamb tomorrow, that lamb is *pigul* while its companion remains *kasher*. But if one slaughters lamb one with intent to eat from lamb two tomorrow — the thought directed not at the lamb being slaughtered but at the companion — *shneihem kesherim*, both are entirely *kasher*. The reasoning, as Abaye understands it, is precisely Rav Chisda's logic: since lamb one is not a *matir* for lamb two, a *pigul* thought during the slaughter of lamb one that is directed at lamb two is entirely without effect. The two lambs, like the *kometz* and the *levona*, each serve as *matir* for the bread, but they have no constitutive relationship to one another.

### Vessel Unity Issue

The Gemara, however, resists drawing this conclusion. The cases are distinguishable: the two lambs are never combined into a single vessel. They remain separate entities. In the case of the *minchah*, by contrast, the *kometz* and the *levona* are both placed together in the same *kli* — the vessel that holds the *minchah*. By virtue of this shared vessel, they may be regarded as *kechad damu*, constituting a unified whole. One could therefore argue that the *kometz* does bear a relationship to the *levona* mediated by their joint presence in the *kli*, even if that relationship is not one of *matir* to *matir*. If so, the *lambs* case does not successfully demonstrate that the *kometz* cannot implicate the *levona* through *pigul* intent. The proof from that Mishnah, while suggestive, is not conclusive.

### Hamnuna Synthesis

Rav Hamnuna now introduces a teaching he received from Rabbi Chanina, which he treasures so deeply that he likens it to the weight of the entire Talmud. The formulation is this: *hiktir kometz lehaktir levona leechol shirayim lemachar* — one who offers up the *kometz* with the combined intent to offer the *levona* tomorrow and to eat the *shiyarim* tomorrow — the result is *pigul*.

Taken at face value, this ruling incorporates two distinct elements: the intent regarding the *levona* (*haktara mefagelet haktara*) and the intent regarding the *shiyarim* (*mefaglin b'chatzi matir*). Each element can be understood as a separate *chiddush*. The absence of the conjunctive *vav* before *leechol shirayim* suggests that these two intents are being bundled as a single, unified *machshava* rather than presented as two independent propositions.

### Text Structure

The Gemara presses the textual structure. If Rabbi Chanina meant to teach the *chiddush* of *haktara mefagelet haktara*, he should simply have stated: *hiktir kometz lehaktir levona lemachar* — the *kometz* was offered with intent to offer the *levona* tomorrow, and that is *pigul*. Why add the *leechol shirayim*? Conversely, if the *chiddush* is *mefaglin b'chatzi matir*, simply state *hiktir kometz leechol shirayim lemachar* — offering the *kometz* with intent to eat the *shiyarim* tomorrow generates *pigul* even though it is only a *chatzi matir*. Why bundle them? And if both *chiddushim* were intended, use the *vav* and state them as two separate principles: doing the *kometz* to be *maktir* the *levona* tomorrow is *pigul* (because of *haktara mefagelet haktara*), and doing the *kometz* for the *shiyarim* tomorrow is *pigul* (because of *mefaglin b'chatzi matir*). The unusual combined formulation, lacking the *vav*, demands explanation.

### Combined Principles

Rav Adda bar Ahava provides the key. He reads Rabbi Chanina's teaching as making precisely the opposite point from what the *charifei d'Pumbedita* assumed. In truth, *ein haktara mefagelet haktara* — the intent during the *kometz* to offer the *levona* tomorrow does not, by itself, generate *pigul*. And *ein mefaglin b'chatzi matir* — the intent during the *kometz* to eat the *shiyarim* tomorrow does not, by itself, generate *pigul* either. Each principle, standing alone, fails to achieve *pigul*: the first because the *kometz* and *levona* do not stand in a *matir* relationship to one another; the second because one has performed only a *chatzi matir*.

The *chiddush* of Rabbi Chanina's formulation is that when both intents are present simultaneously — the intent to offer the *levona* tomorrow and the intent to eat the *shiyarim* tomorrow — they combine in a way that neither could achieve alone, and the result is *pigul*. The Gemara expresses this by saying that the *machshava* spreads throughout (*pashta lei machshava bekulei mincha*). The most coherent reading of this principle is that the combined intent effectively draws together both halves of the *matir*. The intent regarding the *shiyarim* overcomes the *chatzi matir* problem by being supplemented through the intent regarding the *levona* — since that intent brings the *levona* into view, the act of *haktara* of the *kometz* now relates, at least in the sphere of *machshava*, to the full *matir* structure, both halves. With the full *matir* thus engaged, the intent toward the *shiyarim* at the wrong time achieves *pigul*.

The discussion concludes with a brief textual difficulty. A *tanna* recited before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba that offering the *kometz* with intent to eat the *shiyarim* tomorrow is *pigul divrei hakol*. The Gemara objects: this is precisely the debate of Rebbi Meir and the Chachamim. The formulation must be corrected to *pasul divrei hakol* — universally invalid — since all agree it is at minimum disqualified, even as the Rabbanan would stop short of full *pigul*. The Gemara further notes that one cannot simply substitute the phrase *harei zeh pigul* for *divrei hakol pigul*, preserving the term *pigul* while attributing it to one opinion. The textual corruption is intelligible in only one direction: a *tanna* who was originally taught *divrei hakol pasul* might plausibly have substituted the similar-sounding *pigul* for *pasul*, but one taught *harei zeh pigul* would not have garbled that phrase into *divrei hakol*. With that, the tractate's first chapter, *Ha-Kometz et ha-Mincha*, concludes.

---

## Wrong Category

### Rebbi: Kasher

The new chapter opens with its own *Ha-Kometz et ha-Mincha*, presenting the following law: if one performs the *kmitza* of the *minchah* with the intent to eat something *she'ein darko le'echol* — something not normally eaten by a person in the context of this *korban* — or to offer something *she'ein darko lehaktir* — something not normally placed on the *mizbe'ach* — the offering is *kasher*.

The two examples are immediately apparent from the structure of the *minchah*. The *levona* is placed on the *mizbe'ach* but not eaten; the *shiyarim* are eaten by the priests but not offered on the altar. If one performs the *kmitza* intending to eat the *levona* tomorrow — a substance that the *korban* assigns to the *mizbe'ach*, not to human consumption — this intent, though misdirected, does not generate *pigul* and the *minchah* is *kasher*. Likewise, if one intends to offer the *shiyarim* on the *mizbe'ach* tomorrow — an act directly contrary to the *shiyarim*'s assigned role — that too does not constitute *machsheves pigul*, and the *minchah* is *kasher*. The operative principle is that *machsheves pigul* requires an intent to do at the wrong time precisely what is normally done: eat what is normally eaten, or offer what is normally offered. Crossing the categories — intending to eat what belongs on the *mizbe'ach*, or to offer what belongs to the priest — removes the thought from the domain of *pigul* entirely.

### Eliezer: Passul

Rebbi Eliezer disagrees. He holds that such category-crossing intent, while not generating *pigul* in the full sense, nonetheless renders the offering *pasul*.

### Sub-Kezayis Exception

Immediately, however, the Mishnah qualifies Rebbi Eliezer's ruling. If one intended to eat something *she'darko le'echol* or to offer something *she'darko lehaktir* — the normal categories, no crossing — but the quantity envisioned was less than a *kezayis*, the offering is *kasher* even according to Rebbi Eliezer. The *kezayis* threshold is sine qua non for disqualification.

### Non-Combination Rule

Moreover, and distinct from the category-crossing cases: if one intended to eat a half-*kezayis* and to offer a half-*kezayis* — that is, combining an *achila* intent with a *haktara* intent, each below the threshold on its own — these two do not combine (*ein achila v'haktara mitztarfin*). The *achila* component and the *haktara* component are categorically distinct forms of consumption and cannot be aggregated to reach the *kezayis* required for disqualification.

Rebbi Eliezer's ruling thus applies to category-crossing with a full *kezayis*: intending to eat the *levona* — a *kezayis* of something that belongs on the *mizbe'ach* — or to offer a *kezayis* of the *shiyarim* — something normally eaten. Below a *kezayis*, and in cases of mixed-category combinations that fall short, Rebbi Eliezer agrees the offering is *kasher*.

### Pasuk Basis

Rabbi Assi, transmitting in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, addresses the exegetical foundation of Rebbi Eliezer's position. The *pasuk* that serves as the primary source for the laws of *pigul* reads: *v'im he'achol ye'achel mibesar zevach shelamav* — "and if it will surely be eaten from the flesh of his *shelamim*." The doubled expression — *he'achol ye'achel*, the infinitive absolute followed by the main verb — is the source from which the Gemara elsewhere derives the principle that intention (*machshava*) operates like action. The verse speaks of eating, but the Sages read it as applying to intent to eat at the wrong time.

The further question is what the doubled language teaches. The Gemara establishes that *bishtei achilot hakatuv medaber* — the verse speaks of two types of consumption: *achilat adam*, human eating, and *achilat mizbe'ach*, the altar's "consumption" through burning. The basic derivation is that just as *pigul* applies when one intends for a human to eat at the wrong time (*achilat adam*), so too *pigul* applies when one intends for the *mizbe'ach* to "eat" — i.e., to burn the *korban's* designated portions — at the wrong time (*achilat mizbe'ach*). This is uncontroversial; all agree to this derivation.

### Eliezer's Reading

Rebbi Eliezer goes further. He derives from the doubled language that the two categories of *achila* — *achilat adam* and *achilat mizbe'ach* — work across one another. Just as *pigul* applies to intra-category crossing (*me-achilat adam le-achilat adam*, *me-achilat mizbe'ach le-achilat mizbe'ach*), so too, Rebbi Eliezer reads, *pigul* — or at least some form of invalidity — applies to inter-category crossing: *me-achilat adam le-mizbe'ach* (intending to offer on the altar something normally eaten by a person) and *me-achilat mizbe'ach le-adam* (intending to feed to a person something normally burned on the altar). The doubled but slightly varied language (*he'achol ye'achel*) is, in Rebbi Eliezer's reading, the Torah's signal that a *chiddush* is embedded: the two types of *achila* can be crossed.

It must be noted that this exegetical move is counterintuitive. One might expect that a change in language signals distinction rather than equivalence — that had the verse used identical language (*he'achol he'achol*), one might conclude the categories are the same, whereas the variation implies they are separate domains. Yet this is a recognized Talmudic interpretive technique: the change of language is read as pointing to an additional *chiddush*, namely the cross-category application, rather than as marking a categorical boundary.

### Pasuk Limits

The Rabbanan read the same doubled language differently. For them, *dafkei rachmana lehaktara belashon achila* — the reason the Torah expresses *haktara* in the language of eating — is not to enable cross-category *pigul*, but to convey that the principles governing *achilat adam* apply equally to *achilat mizbe'ach*. Specifically: just as *achilat adam* requires a *kezayis* to generate *pigul*, so too *achilat mizbe'ach* requires a *kezayis*. Alternatively, the equivalence teaches that whether your intent is *I will have it eaten* or *I will have it burned* — both construed as forms of *achila* — either intent in the wrong time generates *pigul*. But the categories themselves remain distinct: *achilat adam* refers to what a human normally eats (*shiyarim*), and *achilat mizbe'ach* to what the *mizbe'ach* normally "eats" (*kometz*, *levona*). The doubled language does not sanction the import of one type of intent into the domain properly assigned to the other.

Rebbi Eliezer's counterargument is that if all the Torah wished to convey was that *achilat mizbe'ach* follows the rules of *achilat adam*, it could have written *im ye'achel ye'achel* or some equivalent uniform expression. The specific variation *he'achol ye'achel* must be generating an additional *chiddush*, which is the cross-category application.

The *machloket* between Rebbi Eliezer and the Rabbanan thus reflects a fundamental dispute over whether the verse's doubled language opens the categories to cross-application, or merely equates the operational rules governing each category when applied within its proper domain.

---

## Animal Sacrifice Cases

### D'Oraita vs Rabbanan

Having established Rebbi Eliezer's position and its *pasuk* basis, the Gemara notes — through a dialogue between Rabbi Zeira and Rav Assi — that there is a *machloket* among the *Tannaim* themselves regarding the nature of Rebbi Eliezer's ruling. Rabbi Yochanan had stated that Rebbi Eliezer concedes there is no *kares*. Yet the exegetical derivation from *he'achol ye'achel* implies a *d'Oraita* prohibition that would seem to yield *pigul* and hence *kares*. Rav Assi acknowledges the tension and resolves it: this very question — whether Rebbi Eliezer holds his ruling is *d'Oraita* (amounting to *pigul* with *kares*) or merely *d'Rabbanan* (a Rabbinic *pasul*) — is itself disputed among the *Tannaim*. The *braita* that follows is brought to illustrate this Tannaitic disagreement.

### Drink/Burn Cases

The *braita* examines analogous category-crossing cases in animal sacrifices. If one slaughtered a *korban* with intent to drink from its blood tomorrow — blood is placed on the *mizbe'ach*, so this is intending for a human to "eat" what belongs to the altar — or with intent to burn the flesh on the *mizbe'ach* tomorrow — flesh of a *shelamim* is eaten by people, so this is intending for the *mizbe'ach* to "eat" what belongs to humans — in both cases, the Chachamim hold the *korban kasher*. Category-crossing intent of this type has no *halachic* consequence in their view, consistent with the Mishnah's ruling.

### Eliezer Invalidates

Rebbi Eliezer disagrees and renders both cases *pasul*, consistent with his position in the *minchah* context. Whether this *pasul* is *d'Oraita* or *d'Rabbanan* is precisely what is in dispute.

### Lehaniach Case

The *braita* then introduces an additional case: intent to leave the blood over — *lehaniach midamo l'machar* — neither drinking it nor placing it on the *mizbe'ach*, but simply allowing it to remain and become *notar*. This is categorically distinct from the previous cases. *Pigul* is defined entirely in terms of eating or *haktara*, whether by a human or the altar. Intending to leave something over belongs to the domain of *notar*, not *pigul*. No Amora or Tanna would describe *lehaniach* as an instance of *machsheves pigul* in the classical sense.

### Yehuda's Distinction

Rabbi Yehuda holds that in the *lehaniach* case, the offering is *pasul*. Critically, however, he does not frame this as part of the debate between Rebbi Eliezer and the Chachamim. For Rabbi Yehuda, the Rebbi Eliezer / Chachamim debate concerns category-crossing *achila* — intent to eat what belongs to the altar, or to burn what belongs to the priest. That debate, Rabbi Yehuda implies, involves *pigul* or something very close to it; it is about the *d'Oraita* structure of *machsheves pigul* and whether category-crossing falls within it. The *lehaniach* case, by contrast, is a separate matter: it is simply a Rabbinic *pasul*, grounded not in the logic of *pigul* at all, but in the impropriety of forming any intent to mishandle the *korban's* components.

### Elazar's Position

Rabbi Elazar disagrees. He states that the *lehaniach* case is equally governed by the dispute between Rebbi Eliezer and the Chachamim — *af b'zo Rabbi Eliezer posel v'Chachamim machshirin*. By assimilating *lehaniach* into the Rebbi Eliezer / Chachamim debate, Rabbi Elazar implies something significant about how he reads that debate. Since *lehaniach* is self-evidently not *pigul* in any traditional sense, and since Rabbi Elazar is saying it is governed by the same dispute, his reading must be that the entire dispute of Rebbi Eliezer and the Chachamim — including the category-crossing cases — is not about *d'Oraita* *pigul*, but about a Rabbinic *pasul*. If even *lehaniach* falls under the same debate, and *lehaniach* is at most a Rabbinic disqualification, then all of Rebbi Eliezer's rulings in this area must be Rabbinic in nature.

### Unresolved Status

The Gemara identifies the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar as reflecting precisely this underlying question. Rabbi Yehuda reads the Rebbi Eliezer / Chachamim debate as concerning *d'Oraita pigul* (or something approaching it) in category-crossing cases, with the *lehaniach* case being a separate, lesser Rabbinic disqualification. Rabbi Elazar reads the entire cluster — category-crossing and *lehaniach* alike — as involving nothing more than a Rabbinic *pasul*, and so the debate of Rebbi Eliezer and the Chachamim applies uniformly to all.

The Gemara signals that this reading of the *braita* is not the only possible one, and that the daf will continue to examine whether Rabbi Elazar's assimilation of *lehaniach* into the core debate necessarily implies a Rabbinic character for all of Rebbi Eliezer's rulings. That analysis will carry over into the following daf.

---

---

# Menachot 18

## Levona & Kometz Order

### Levona Placement

We begin at the bottom of 17b, but before turning to the text, it is worth resolving a disagreement that had emerged in the course of the previous sessions. The question concerned the mechanics of how the *levona* was brought in the preparation of the *mincha*. One understanding — based on a book that had been consulted — was that the *levona* was placed together with the *kometz* into the *kli* and then everything was brought to the *mizbeach* together. The other understanding, consistent with the way the *gemara* has been reading throughout the preceding dapim, is that the *kometz* is first taken into the *kli*, and only afterwards is the *levona* gathered — that the two are performed as separate acts. This is borne out by the *gemara*'s extended discussion of *pigul*, which throughout assumes that the *kometz* and *levona* are handled separately, and even considers cases where one might be done before the other, or where the order is reversed.

### Rambam vs Rashi

Upon investigation, it becomes clear that the first understanding reflects the position of the Rambam. The Rambam does hold that the *levona* and *kometz* are placed together in the *kli*, and he bases this on a line found in the *gemara* in Sotah. However, the *Griz*, the *Keren Orah*, and other *Acharonim* point out that this stands directly against Rashi, who throughout our *gemara* has consistently maintained the other position — namely, that they are separate. These authorities argue that even the Rambam would have to concede that *b'dieved*, if the *levona* was placed in a separate *kli* and burned separately, the *korban* would be valid, for otherwise the many *sugyot* we have been learning cannot be reconciled with his view. His position, they conclude, is a reading of a single passage in Sotah that is in tension with the dominant thrust of our *sugya*.

There is a further distinction between the two positions. According to Rashi — and according to the simple reading of all these *gemarot* — there is no *avoda* associated with the *levona* until the moment it is burned. There is no *nesinas kli* for the *levona*, no *hilluch*; the *avoda* is the burning itself. This explains why the discussion of *mafgil b'chatzi matir* only arises at the point of the actual *haktara* — until then, the *levona* is not performing any halachic function. The Rambam, by contrast, who holds that the *levona* has a *nesinas kli* and a *hilluch* of its own, accordingly extends the concept of *chatzi matir* to those earlier stages as well — an approach that is very much against the *gemara* as we have learned it, which at most considered it at the point of *hilluch*.

### Separate vs Together

This also illuminates a practical question: according to Rashi, how does one physically manage the two separate acts? The *kometz* is taken in hand, then one walks to the *mizbeach* and burns it — but one is already holding it, so the two must necessarily be done sequentially. One could, of course, bring the *mincha* to the top of the *mizbeach* and perform the acts one after the other there. The Rambam's reading simplifies the physical process considerably, but it does so on the basis of that single line in Sotah rather than on the *sugyot* we have before us. A further point: according to Rashi, since the acts must be done separately, either two *kohanim* are involved or it requires a degree of juggling — a practical consideration that underscores the different implications of the two approaches.

---

## Lehanniach Status

### Tanna Kamma

The *gemara* at the bottom of 17b now sets out a three-way debate regarding the status of *lehanniach* — the case where one performs the *avoda* of the *mincha* while intending to leave over some of it. The debate that has been discussed until now concerned the cases of *achilas adam* and *achilas mizbeach* — that is, intending to eat the *shirayim* or to burn the *kometz* or *levona* outside its proper time. The *braisa* did not specify what the *halacha* would be if one intended merely to leave something over. The *gemara* now clarifies that there are three distinct positions on precisely this question.

The *tanna kamma* holds that the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* applies only to *achilas adam* and *achilas mizbeach*. As for *lehanniach* — the thought of leaving it over — this is *divrei hakol kasher*, everyone would agree that the *korban* is valid. Even Rabbi Eliezer, who rules *pasul* in those other cases on a *derabanan* level, would not be troubled by *lehanniach*, because *lehanniach* falls entirely outside the category of *pigul*. The category of *pigul* is narrowly defined: it concerns thoughts of eating or burning or *zerikat hadam*. The thought of leaving something over is a qualitatively different kind of thought, and therefore, even according to the *derabanan* position of Rabbi Eliezer, it would not generate a problem.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda takes the opposite position. He holds that the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* applies to *achilas adam* and *achilas mizbeach*, but that *lehanniach* is *divrei hakol pasul* — everyone would agree it is *pasul*, even the *rabbanan* who otherwise are more lenient. The *gemara* immediately explains the reasoning.

### Kol Damo Gezeira

The *gemara* offers a *gezeira*: *maktzas damo atu kol damo* — we apply a *gezeira* from the case of leaving over part of the blood to the case of leaving over all of the blood. The *gemara* asserts that even those *rabbanan* who maintain that a *machshava* to leave over the blood does not constitute a *d'oraisa* problem would agree that if one intended to leave over *all* of the blood, it would be *pasul d'oraisa*. The reason is that were one to actually do so — to leave over all the blood rather than performing *zerikat hadam* — the *korban* would never have had its blood duly sprinkled, and it would consequently be *pasul*.

This connects to a *mishna* in Zevachim — recorded at 36 — which discusses the case of one who slaughters a *zevach* intending to leave over its blood or *eimurim* until the next day, or to take them outside their proper boundary. There, Rabbi Yehuda rules *pasul* and the *chachamim* rule *kasher*. The logic of the *gezeira* here is that since *lehanniach kulo* — leaving over all the blood — would be *pasul d'oraisa* if actually done, the *rabbanan* who are lenient about the *machshava* in the ordinary cases would still acknowledge that a thought to leave over even *part* of the blood constitutes a *psul derabanan*, by *gezeira* from the more severe case. It is not a fully airtight proof, but this is the structure of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: *lehanniach*, precisely because of its potential to shade into the gravely disqualifying *lehanniach kulo*, is treated more severely than *achilas adam* or *achilas mizbeach*.

One might ask: what exactly is *lehanniach miktzas*? If one performs *zerika* in the ordinary way, there is always some blood left over that gets poured out — so what meaningful thought of *lehanniach miktzas* can one have? The answer is that *lehanniach miktzas* here means something like: one catches the blood in the *kli* and intends not to do anything with it — not to perform the *zerika* at all, or to leave some portion that should have been *nizrak* sitting untouched. Once this is clarified, it becomes clear why Rabbi Yehuda's position is internally coherent: the thought that one would not properly perform *zerika* on part of the blood is a thought that strikes at the validity of the *korban* in a way that thoughts about *achilas adam* do not.

### Rav Elazar

The third position belongs to Rav Elazar. He says that *lehanniach* falls within the same debate as all the other cases: Rabbi Eliezer rules it *pasul* and the *chachamim* rule it *kasher*. According to Rav Elazar, there are two separate questions: first, whether the debate of *dam mizbeach* — intending to sprinkle blood at the wrong altar — applies, and there the *gemara* had offered a fairly convincing argument that it could constitute real *pigul*, but since Rabbi Eliezer says only *pasul*, it must be purely *derabanan*; and second, what is the status of *lehanniach*? The *tanna kamma* says it is better — entirely outside the *derabanan* category. Rabbi Yehuda says it is worse — everyone agrees it is *pasul*. Rav Elazar places it in the same category as all the contested cases: Rabbi Eliezer renders it *pasul derabanan*, and the *chachamim* say it is *kasher*.

---

## Yosef HaBavli Story

### Repeated Kasher Answers

The *gemara* now introduces a *braisa* that serves a halachic purpose, but does so through a remarkably moving narrative. The *braisa* opens: *keshenachti limtzos midosav* — when I came to clarify my learning, or, in the alternate reading, to distill the essence of the teaching of Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. Rashi explains *limtzos midosav* as *leida mitzui talmudo* — to know the distillation or essence of what he had learned, to get things clear. So the speaker — identified shortly as Rabbi, Rebbi — went to Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua for precisely this purpose.

There, he found Yosef HaBavli seated before Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, described as exceedingly dear to him — *chaviv lo beyoter ad leachat*. Rashi notes two possible readings: either Yosef was an exceptionally prized student of Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, or Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua was himself exceedingly dear to Yosef. The word *leachat* may simply mean "to an extreme," and indeed the *Megillat Setarim* of Rabbeinu Nissim understands *ad leachat* as *ad meod* — to an extraordinary degree. Rashi also offers that it could mean that their relationship held together *until* the following particular *halacha* — which is about to be described.

Yosef HaBavli asked Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua: if one slaughters a *zevach* and intends to leave over its blood until the next day, what is the *halacha*? Note that this is not a *menachot* case but the *mishna* from Zevachim — though it is being cited here by way of reference in the Tosefta of Zevachim, chapter 2, as noted in the margin of the page. Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua answered: *kasher*. That evening, Yosef asked again, and was told *kasher*. The following morning, *kasher*. At midday, *kasher*. The impression is either that they were reviewing the teaching in the manner of an oral culture, or that Yosef kept pressing — kept returning to the question.

### Rabbi Eliezer Dispute

Finally, by *mincha* time, Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua added a qualification: the ruling is *kasher*, but *ella sheRabbi Eliezer posel* — it is true that there is an opinion of Rabbi Eliezer that this is *pasul*. That caveat had been withheld through an entire day of questioning, and only now, by the afternoon, did it emerge.

At that moment, *tzahavu panav shel Yosef HaBavli* — Yosef HaBavli's face lit up. Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, seeing this, said to him: Yosef, *kimdumani shelo kivanu shemuateinu ad ata* — it seems to me that our learning has not been aligned until now. The implication is pointed: here he had been teaching this student the *halacha*, and the student was not satisfied with the ruling he gave — instead, the student lit up at the mention of the dissenting opinion. For a rabbi trying to raise his prize student to *pasken halacha* according to the accepted view, this was troubling.

### Yosef's Explanation

Yosef responded: Rabbi, I accept entirely what you rule as *halacha*. I am not trying to *pasken* otherwise. But *Rabbi Yehuda pasul shana li* — when I learned from Rabbi Yehuda, he taught me that it was *pasul*. I do not follow that ruling over yours, but I was seeking the source for Rabbi Yehuda's position. *Dechazarti al kol talmidav uvikashti mechaveirai velo matzati* — I consulted all of Rabbi Yehuda's students, I sought corroboration from my colleagues, and no one could confirm it. Rashi explains that Yosef was therefore worried that he had misremembered — that perhaps what he recalled in Rabbi Yehuda's name was inaccurate. *Achshav sheshanita li pasul, hechzarta li avedati* — now that you have told me that Rabbi Eliezer says it is *pasul*, you have returned to me my lost object. Now I know that what I remembered from Rabbi Yehuda is in fact authentic — there is indeed an opinion out there that supports what I heard.

It bears noting that Yosef HaBavli is explicitly identified in the Tannaitic literature as coming from Bavel, just as Hillel before him was called *habavli* — because the dominant *tannaim* were in Eretz Yisrael, and those who came from Bavel were labeled accordingly.

### Emotional Response

What followed was extraordinary. *Zalgu einav dimaot shel Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua* — Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua's eyes poured with tears. He said: *ashreichem talmidei chachamim* — praised are the students of the *chachamim*. Here *talmidei chachamim* is used in its narrowest sense: Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua is the *chacham*, and Yosef was his *talmid*. He said: *divrei Torah chavivin aleichem beyoter* — the words of Torah are excessively dear to you. He then recited the verse *mah ahavti Toratecha kol hayom hi sichati* — how much I love Your Torah, all day long it is my speech. The tears came because he saw that this student was not merely after the *halacha* for practical purposes; he cared about every opinion, every tradition, and was so distressed at the thought of having misremembered even a minority position that he spent tremendous effort seeking corroboration. That, Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua said with tears, is what it means to love Torah.

### Transmission Resolved

The *gemara* then resolves the chain of transmission. Rabbi Yehuda was the son of Rabbi Ilai. Rabbi Ilai was a student of Rabbi Eliezer. Therefore, Rabbi Eliezer's teaching that *lehanniach* is *pasul* was transmitted through Rabbi Ilai to his son Rabbi Yehuda, and that is precisely what Yosef had heard from Rabbi Yehuda. *Lefichach shanah lecha mishnat Rabbi Eliezer* — that is why Rabbi Yehuda transmitted to you the position of Rabbi Eliezer. This does not mean it is the ruling *halacha*, but it does confirm that what Yosef had remembered was a legitimate and traceable opinion. The question of why none of Rabbi Yehuda's other students could corroborate it remains intriguing, but the *gemara* leaves it unaddressed.

The *gemara* brought this entire story to resolve a precise halachic point — and it is remarkable how it uses such a deeply human and emotionally resonant narrative to resolve what is ultimately a narrow question of whose opinion Rabbi Yehuda was transmitting.

---

## Divrei HaKol Analysis

### Lost Object Problem

The *gemara* now turns to analyze Rabbi Yehuda's claim that *lehanniach* is *divrei hakol pasul*. The *gemara* challenges: if Rabbi Yehuda was indeed claiming that everyone agrees it is *pasul* — both Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* — then when Yosef HaBavli said *hechzarta li avedati*, you have returned to me my lost object, what sense does that make? What was returned to him?

The problem is this: Yosef had heard from Rabbi Yehuda that *lehanniach* is *pasul*, and he was concerned he had misremembered. He came to Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, who told him that the *halacha* is *kasher* but that Rabbi Eliezer says *pasul*. Now, if Rabbi Yehuda was claiming *divrei hakol pasul*, then Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua's statement actually tells the opposite story — Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua is saying it is a *machlokes* between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim*, not that everyone agrees it is *pasul*. In that case, Yosef should not have felt his lost object was returned; the teaching he received from Rabbi Yehuda — that it is *divrei hakol pasul* — has not been corroborated at all. What has been corroborated at most is that there exists some opinion of *pasul*, but Rabbi Yehuda's stronger claim — that it is *divrei hakol* — has actually been *contradicted*.

The *gemara* sharpens this: *ihu plugta ka'amar lei* — perhaps Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua was presenting a *machlokes*, telling Yosef that it is debated. If so, what Yosef heard from Rabbi Yehuda and what Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua said would be two different things: Rabbi Yehuda apparently transmitted it as though everyone says *pasul*, while Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua says it is a dispute. The lost object, such as it is, would only be the bare fact that there exists a *pasul* opinion — but Rabbi Yehuda's specific claim of *divrei hakol* has not been vindicated.

Furthermore, the *gemara* notes, when the narrative explains why Rabbi Yehuda taught this — *ha mipnei sheRabbi Yehuda beno shel Rabbi Ilai, Rabbi Ilai talmido shel Rabbi Eliezer* — that framing sounds like Rabbi Yehuda was presenting the view of Rabbi Eliezer and his tradition, not claiming universal agreement. The very explanation given for why Rabbi Yehuda said *pasul* — that he was following his father's *rebbe* — implies that he was presenting one side of a dispute, not asserting consensus.

### Explicit Divrei HaKol

The *gemara* pushes toward the conclusion that Rabbi Yehuda explicitly claimed *divrei hakol pasul* — that in his formulation, it was not presented as a *machlokes* at all. The problem this creates for the story is then answered: *dehadar leh mishum paslus d'alma* — what was returned to Yosef was, at minimum, the corroboration that there is an opinion of *pasul* out there. Even if what Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua told him does not fully vindicate the specific framing of *divrei hakol*, it at least establishes that the underlying tradition of *pasul* is real — that Yosef had not confabulated it. The *avedah* that was returned was not the precise wording of Rabbi Yehuda's claim, but the kernel of truth within it.

A cleaner way to read the story, it might seem, would be to say that Rabbi Yehuda was not being precise about whether his position was *divrei hakol* or merely his own ruling; he simply stated *pasul* because he was following the tradition of Rabbi Eliezer, without explicitly asserting it was unanimous. But the *gemara* concludes that from the way Rabbi Yehuda stated it — simply *pasul*, without qualification — it does sound as though he was claiming consensus. The *gemara* thus lands on the position that Rabbi Yehuda did claim *divrei hakol*, and the story works because the return of the *avedah* is understood in the more modest sense of confirming that the *psul* tradition is authentic, even if not that it is universally held.

---

## Mincha Defects List

### Lo Yatzak

The *gemara* now turns from the question of invalid intentions to the actual process of preparing the *mincha* — though characteristically, it approaches the process through the lens of which defects are or are not *me'akev*. The *mishna* presents a list of procedural omissions or errors that do not invalidate the *mincha*. The first is *lo yatzak* — the pouring of oil was not performed. By way of background: the basic preparation of a *mincha belula b'shemen* involves placing oil in the vessel, then the flour, mixing the two, and finally performing *yetzika* — an additional pouring of oil on top. The full *log* of oil must be used, and that is *me'akev*; but many of the ways in which the oil is applied and mixed are not. *Lo yatzak* refers to the case where the *yetzika* was not done — though as the *gemara* will immediately clarify, the precise meaning of this phrase requires examination.

### Lo Balal

*Lo balal* — the flour and oil were not mixed together; the flour was left sitting atop the oil without being kneaded into dough. The *mishna*'s inclusion of this case implicitly teaches that *belila* is not *me'akev*, at least not as an absolute requirement.

### Other Defects

The *mishna* continues with a series of additional defects, each of which nevertheless leaves the *mincha kasher*. *Lo pitet* — the priest did not break the baked *mincha* into pieces. Certain *minchot* are baked, and the Torah states *patot otah pitim* — one must break them after baking, folding and breaking into pieces so that the *kometz* can be taken. Rashi clarifies that one had to break a small part to enable the taking of the *kometz*, but the requirement to break the whole thing into pieces was not fulfilled. *Lo malach* — salt was not applied, despite the Torah's requirement *al kol korbancha takriv melach*. One has violated a *lav*, but the *korban* as a *cheftza* remains *kasher*. *Lo henif* — the waving was not performed; only certain *minchot* require *hanafa*, namely *minchat chotei*, *minchat kanaot*, and the *omer*, and even for those, failure to wave does not invalidate. *Lo higish* — the *mincha* was not brought to touch the corner of the *mizbeach*, as the Torah requires before the *kometz* is taken. *O shepitetan pitim merubot* — or one performed *ptita* but produced large chunks rather than the properly sized pieces. *Lo mashchan* — the *meshicha*, the anointing-style application of oil to certain *minchot* such as the *rkikei matzot*, was not performed. In all of these cases: *kasheira* — the *mincha* is valid.

---

## Yetzika Me'akev

### Yetzika Required

The *gemara* immediately interrogates the opening case. *Mai lo yatzak* — what does *lo yatzak* mean? *Ilima lo yatzak klal* — if it means that no *yetzika* was performed at all, there is an immediate difficulty: the Torah indicates that *yetzika* is *me'akev*. Rashi explains the source: the verse *veyatzakta aleha shemen, mincha hi* — the word *hi* signals that it is essential, that without the pouring it is not a *mincha*. The *gemara* takes this as given and does not even bother to spell out the derivation at length; it simply assumes that *yetzika* is *me'akev* and asks how the *mishna* could say *lo yatzak* is *kasher*.

### Non-Kohen Yetzika

The *gemara* therefore answers: *lo yatzak kohen ela zar* — *lo yatzak* does not mean that no *yetzika* was performed, but that a non-*kohen* performed it. The principle governing the *mincha* is *mikmitza va'eilach mitzvas kehuna* — from the taking of the *kometz* onward is the domain of *kehuna*. Everything prior to the *kometz* — including the *yetzika* and the *belila* — can be done by a non-*kohen*, a *zar*. The *mishna* is therefore teaching that even when a *zar* performed the *yetzika*, the *mincha* is *kasher b'dieved*.

One might ask: is the *mishna* teaching what is *b'dieved* permissible, or merely stating what is the case *lechatchila*? The question is apt, as reading *lo yatzak* to refer to a *zar* is clearly departing from the plain meaning — the *pshat* would suggest it means the *yetzika* was not done at all.

### Tosefta Support

The *gemara* then asks: by the same logic, should not *lo balal* also be read as referring to a *zar*? And if so, the implication would be that if *belila* was not done at all, it would be *pasul* — only the case of a *zar* performing it would be *kasher*. But this is demonstrably not so: the *mishna* elsewhere teaches *shishim nivlalim, shishim ve'echad ein nivlalim* — sixty *isronot* of flour can be mixed together with their *log* of oil, but sixty-one cannot, because at that quantity a proper *belila* is physically impossible. And the *gemara* there had asked: *ki ein nivlalim mah havi* — if they cannot be mixed, why does it matter? Does not our *mishna* say *lo balal kasheira* — even if you didn't mix it at all, it is *kasher*? That question, and the answer of Rav Zeira to be discussed shortly, treats *lo balal* entirely literally — as meaning it was not mixed at all. The *gemara* therefore accepts that *lo balal* is taken at its plain meaning, and resolves the tension between *lo yatzak* and *lo balal* simply: *ha ke-isa ve-ha ke-isa* — each phrase means what fits its context. *Lo yatzak* means a *zar* performed it; *lo balal* means it was not done at all. This is not an entirely satisfying answer given the symmetry of the two phrases, but the *gemara* is compelled to it by the established principle that *yetzika* is *me'akev* while *belila* is not.

---

## Mincha Defects List (II)

### Fitness for Mixing

The *gemara* now returns to the principle articulated by Rav Zeira in the context of the sixty-*isronot* discussion: *kol haraui l'blila ein blila me'akevet bo, v'chol she'eino raui l'blila blila me'akevet bo* — anything fit for mixing is not invalidated by the absence of actual mixing, but anything that is not fit for mixing is invalidated. The principle sounds paradoxical: if something cannot be mixed, it is *pasul*, but if it can be mixed and simply was not, it is *kasher*. The point is that *b'dieved* one does not have to perform the *belila*, but the *mincha* must have been capable of being mixed. Hence, sixty *isronot* in one *kli* — which could, with considerable effort, be mixed — are *kasher* even without actual mixing. Sixty-one *isronot* — which physically cannot be properly mixed — are *pasul* and must be brought in two separate *keilim*.

This principle, *kol haraui l'blila*, has a reach that extends far beyond the laws of *menachot*. Anyone who has learned any significant portion of *Shas* will have encountered Rav Zeira's principle deployed across a wide range of contexts, where the *gemara* invokes the idea that something does not need to be actually done, only to be capable of being done. Tosafot addresses the question of when this principle applies and when it does not, and offers an answer that goes to the heart of the matter: it depends on whether the Torah is describing a quality or character of the object, or mandating an action. When the Torah says *mincha belula ba'shemen* — a *mincha* that is mixed with oil — the word *belula* is an adjective describing the character of the *mincha*, not a verb commanding an act of mixing. One can therefore say: is this a *mincha belula*? It has the potential to be *belula* — that is sufficient to regard it as having that quality. But when the Torah mandates that one must perform an act, the mere capacity to have performed it does not substitute for the act itself.

This same logic underlies similar principles elsewhere in *halacha*. *Kol ha'omed liktzira kekatzur dami*, *kol ha'omed ligiza kigzuz dami* — produce ready for harvest is treated as already harvested, wool ready for shearing is treated as already shorn. In all of these, what is at stake is the characterization of an object at a certain stage of readiness, not the completion of an act. The principle does not apply where an action is itself the requirement, because if the act has not been done, it has simply not been done. This is also why attempts to extend the principle humorously — as if potential for prayer counted as prayer — are not taken seriously; acts are acts, and fitness to perform them is not their performance.

An interesting related application occurs in the laws of *tevila*: one need not have water actually enter the mouth or other orifices, but there must be no *chatzitza* — the orifice must be *ra'ui l'viat mayim*, capable of water entering, even if water does not actually enter. Whether this is a genuine application of the same principle is a more complex question, given that the *tevila* itself is an act — but at minimum, the *gemara* invokes the underlying logic of fitness versus actuality in that context as well.

### Ptitim Merubot

The *gemara* now jumps to the last case in the *mishna*: *o she'pitetan pitim merubot, kasher* — or one performed the *ptita* but produced *ptitim merubot*, and it is *kasher*. The *gemara* initially asks: if *lo patat klal* — not performing *ptita* at all — is *kasher*, is there any question that making large pieces would be *kasher*? Surely if doing nothing is fine, doing something imperfectly is certainly fine. Rashi clarifies that in the case of *lo patat klal*, one had done a minimum breaking in order to enable the taking of the *kometz*, but had not broken the rest.

The *gemara* therefore resolves that *ptitim merubot* does not mean large pieces; it means the opposite — that one over-broke the *mincha*, producing too many small pieces. The word *merubot* here means numerous, not large. The question then becomes: why would I think that breaking it into too many pieces might be *pasul*? The reasoning would be: perhaps, having gone past the point of no return — having reduced the *mincha* to pieces too small — one has entered a qualitatively different and invalidating state. From *lo patat klal* I might invoke something like *kol haraui*, since the *mincha* could still be broken into proper pieces; but once it has been excessively broken and cannot be reconstituted, perhaps that crosses a line.

The *gemara* then offers an alternate answer: perhaps *ptitim merubot* does mean large pieces, and the *chiddush* is the following — *hava amina* that one might invalidate large pieces because they occupy an intermediate state: they are no longer *chalot*, whole loaves (*torat chalot*), and they are not *ptitim*, properly sized small pieces (*torat ptitim*). The Torah associates the *mincha* with recognized forms — *chalot matzot belulot ba'shemen*. If one has broken them but not into the appropriate small pieces, perhaps this middle state, recognizable as neither one form nor the other, has no halachic standing. *Kama'shmalan* — the *mishna* teaches that even this is not *me'akev*; the *mincha* is *kasher b'dieved* regardless.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Position

### Rabbi Shimon's View

The *gemara* now observes: *leima matnitin d'lo k'Rabbi Shimon* — let us say that our *mishna* does not accord with the view of Rabbi Shimon. This brings us back to the earlier point about *lo yatzak* being performed by a *zar*, which the *mishna* treats as *kasher*. The *gemara* cites a *braisa*: Rabbi Shimon says, *kol kohen she'eino modeh ba'avoda ein lo chelek bakehuna* — any *kohen* who does not agree to the *avoda* has no portion in *kehuna*. The meaning is that a *kohen* must be prepared to perform all of the *avodot* and must affirm their value. There are *gemarot* elsewhere that discuss *kohanim* who disparage certain parts of the *avoda*, and this raises questions about their legitimacy. Rabbi Shimon appears to go further: one who does not affirm the *avoda* — whether by refusing to perform it or by failing to accept it as meaningful — has no portion in *kehuna* and may not perform the *avoda* at all, even those parts he would prefer to do. The verse cited is *hamakriv et dam hashlamim v'et hachelev mibnei Aharon, lo tihiye shok hayamin lemana* — the one who offers the blood and the *chelev* from among the sons of Aharon, to him shall be the right thigh as a portion. The *gemara* reads this as: only *hamakriv* — one who participates fully — receives a portion.

### Fifteen Avodot

From this verse, one might have thought the principle applies only to the *shlamin*. The *braisa* therefore asks: *minayin l'rabot tet-vav avodot* — how do we know to extend it to all fifteen *avodot* of the *kohen*? The list that follows is striking for what it includes. *Hayetzikot* — the pouring of oil — appears at the head, indicating that Rabbi Shimon regards *yetzika* as an act requiring a *kohen*. *V'hablilot* — the mixing. *V'haptitot* — the breaking into pieces. These three are precisely the acts that our *mishna* treats as performable by a *zar*, and Rabbi Shimon places them in the category of *avodot* requiring a *kohen*. The list continues: *v'hamilchot* (salting), *v'hatnufot* (waving), *v'hahagashot* (the bringing to the *mizbeach*), *v'hakmizot* (the taking of the *kometz*), *v'hahaktarot* (the burning), *v'hamlikot* (the *mlika* of bird offerings), *v'hakabalot* (receiving the blood), *v'haza'ot* (sprinkling the blood). Notably absent is *holacha*, the carrying of the blood, which, as Tosafot notes, Rav Shimi holds may be done by a *zar*. The list then extends beyond the *Mikdash* entirely: *v'hashkat sota* (making the *sota* drink), *v'arifat egla arufa* (breaking the neck of the *egla arufa*, which is not performed in the *Mikdash* at all), and *taharat metzora* (the purification of the *metzora*, which includes *marot nega'im* as well — a *kohen*'s function but not limited to the *Mikdash*). Finally, *u'nesiat kapayim bein mibifnim bein mibachutz* — the *birkat kohanim*, whether performed inside the *Mikdash* or outside. The inclusion of these last items is fascinating: Rabbi Shimon's principle of *modeh ba'avoda* extends to any act that is defined as an *avoda* of the *kohen*, regardless of whether it is specific to the *Mikdash*.

The source for extending beyond the *shlamin* to all fifteen *avodot*: *talmud lomar mibnei Aharon* — any *avoda hamesura livnei Aharon*, any act entrusted to the sons of Aharon — a *kohen* who does not affirm it has no portion in *kehuna*.

### Rav Nachman's Resolution

Rav Nachman says it is not difficult: *kan b'minchat Kohanim, kan b'minchat Yisrael* — the distinction is between a *minchat Yisrael* and a *minchat Kohanim*. A *minchat Yisrael* is one that has a *kmitza* — only the *kometz* is burned, and the *shirayim* are consumed by the *kohanim*. For such a *mincha*, the principle *mikmitza va'eilach mitzvas kehuna* applies: everything prior to the *kometz*, including *yetzika* and *blila*, can be performed by a *zar*. The verse *limed al yetzika u'blila sheksheira b'zar* — teaches that a non-*kohen* may perform these preparatory acts. Rabbi Shimon, Rav Nachman suggests, would agree with this. Where Rabbi Shimon says the full process requires a *kohen* is in the case of *minchat Kohanim*, where there is no *kmitza* — the entire *mincha* is burned. Since there is no act of *kmitza* to mark the transition to *kehuna* work, the requirement of *kehuna* applies *me'ikara*, from the very outset.

### Rava's Objection

Rava challenges this resolution. *Michdi minchat Kohanim meheicha itrabbi l'yetzika?* — from where does the *Torah* derive that *yetzika* is required in a *minchat Kohanim* at all? It is derived *miminchat Yisrael* — from the *mincha* of a *Yisrael*. If so, *mah hatam kesheira b'zar, af hacha nami kesheira b'zar* — just as a *zar* is *kasher* in that case, so too a *zar* should be *kasher* in the case of *minchat Kohanim*. The same argument is then repeated in the parallel version of the discussion: *minayin she'ein nekmatzot* — how do we know that the acts for *minchot* without a *kmitza* are required? We learn from *minchot* that do have a *kmitza*. Therefore they should follow the same rule: if a *zar* is valid there, a *zar* should be valid here too. Rava concludes: *ela michvarta, matnitin d'lo k'Rabbi Shimon* — it is better to simply say that our *mishna* does not accord with Rabbi Shimon's view. Rabbi Shimon holds that the entire process of a *mincha* requires a *kohen* from the beginning, while the *tanna* of our *mishna* holds that only from the *kmitza* onward is it *mitzvas kehuna*.

### Kedusha Analysis

A beautiful observation of Rav Soloveitchik on Rabbi Shimon's principle of *kol kohen she'eino modeh ba'avoda*: Rav Soloveitchik notes a fundamental difference between the structure of *kehuna* and the structure of *leviya*. *Leviim* are defined by their *tafkid* — their specific job. A *levi* is a gatekeeper or a singer; his role is defined by the particular function he performs. *Kohanim*, by contrast, are not primarily defined by any specific task they perform. Rather, as we have just seen, a *kohen* who is not prepared to perform all the *avodot* — who picks and chooses — has no portion in *kehuna*. This is because *kohanim* are defined not by their function but by an intrinsic *kedusha*. *V'kidashto ki lechem Elokecha* — you shall sanctify him, because he brings the bread of God. The *kedusha* of a *kohen* is not derived from the acts he performs; rather, it is an intrinsic sanctity that demands total dedication and readiness for any act of *avoda*. A *kohen* who would claim a portion in *kehuna* while refusing certain *avodot* has fundamentally misunderstood the nature of *kehuna*: the *kedusha* does not come from the specific role, but from the total commitment to service in the *Mikdash* — and that commitment must be wholehearted and without reservation.

---

---

# Menachot 19

## Yetzika & Kohen

### Yetzika Dispute

The daf begins on the last three lines of 18b, with the Gemara asking *mai ta'ama d'rabbanan* — what is the reasoning of the Sages? Recall the background: a *machlokes* was introduced between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon concerning whether *yetzika*, the pouring of oil onto the *mincha*, must be performed by a *kohen*. The *mishna* itself had stated that *yetzika* is not *me'akev*, but the Gemara immediately reinterpreted this: *yetzika* is indeed required — what the *mishna* means is that it is not *me'akev* with respect to requiring a *kohen*. Yet Rabbi Shimon's position, as cited previously, is that a *kohen* who does not accept all of the *mitzvot* of the *kehuna* has no portion in it — and among the acts he enumerated were *yetzika* and *belila*, acts that precede the *kemitza*. The working understanding, then, is that Rabbi Shimon requires a *kohen* for these pre-*kemitza* acts, while the *chachamim* do not.

A parenthetical note: the relevant *pasuk* quoted there, *lo yihye shok hayamin limana*, uses the language of *chelek* — a portion — and the Rambam reads this as relating to a *kohen*'s entitlement to a share in the *korbanot*, not as a restriction on his performing the *avoda* itself. The *Tosefta*, however, implies an actual restriction on performing the *avoda*, and extends this to a *levi* as well. The Rambam *paskens* this restriction for a *levi* but not for a *kohen* — a tension that Rav Soloveitchik addresses and that merits separate treatment.

### Yetzika Not Me'akev Kohen

The Gemara explains the reasoning of the *rabbanan* from the *pasuk*: *veyatzak aleha shemen u'natan aleha levona*, and then, *vehevia el bnei Aharon hakohanim*, and then *vekamatz misham*. The structure is telling. The owner pours on the oil, places the *levona*, and brings it to the *bnei Aharon hakohanim* — and then they take the *kemitza*. Since the *kohanim* are introduced into the *pasuk* only at the moment of *kemitza*, the straightforward reading is that *kemitza va'eilach mitzvat kehuna* — from the *kemitza* onward is the *mitzvat kehuna*. What precedes it — the *yetzika* and *belila* — may be performed by a non-*kohen* and is *kasher bezar*.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

How does Rabbi Shimon dispute this? The Gemara states that Rabbi Shimon employs the hermeneutic principle of *mikra nidrash lefanav ul'acharav* — a phrase in a *pasuk* can be read not only forward to what follows it, but also backward to what precedes it. The phrase *bnei Aharon hakohanim*, though it appears in the middle of the *pasuk*, extends, on his reading, back to the *yetzika* and *belila* that came before. The *pasuk* thus reads as though the *bnei Aharon hakohanim* performed the pouring and mixing as well. Admittedly, this is a difficult *pshat* — the text says *vehevia*, "and he brought it," which sounds as though the object was not yet in the *kohanim*'s possession — but Rabbi Shimon maintains that the entire passage centers on the *bnei Aharon hakohanim*.

### Rabbi Shimon's Reading

The Gemara, however, will ultimately reject this reading — not merely on grounds of *pshat*, but on account of another position that Rabbi Shimon himself holds.

### Challenge to Hermeneutic

The challenge begins at the last word of the first line of 19a: *vesavar Rabbi Shimon mikra nidrash lefanav ul'acharav* — does Rabbi Shimon truly subscribe to this hermeneutic of reading a phrase both forward and backward? The Gemara is asking whether Rabbi Shimon is genuinely prepared to interpret a *pasuk* based on a middle phrase even when that phrase clearly refers only to the latter portion of the verse, not the opening. The Gemara will now demonstrate from a separate case that Rabbi Shimon does not, in fact, accept this principle.

---

## Chattat Blood Case

### Blood Placement Debate

The Gemara introduces a *baraita* concerning the *chatat* blood placement: *velakach hakohen midam hachatat be'etzba'o, venatan al kornot hamizbeach* — the *kohen* shall take from the blood of the *chatat* with his finger and place it on the corners of the altar. The *baraita* derives from *etzba'o* that the right hand is required — since *etzba* was previously learned from the *metzora* to signify the right hand — and reads the *pasuk* in both directions. Reading *be'etzba'o* back onto *velakach*, the *baraita* derives that the *kabala*, the catching of the blood, must also be performed with the right hand: *melamed shelo tehe kabala ela biyamin*. Reading *be'etzba'o* forward onto *venatan*, it likewise derives that the placing must be with the right hand: *melamed shelo tehe netina ela biyamin*.

It should be noted that the plain sense of the *pasuk* is that *etzba* modifies both verbs quite naturally — one dips one's finger and then places it on the corners. What the *baraita* is doing is reading *velakach* not as "dip" but as the catching of the blood itself, and treating *etzba* not as literally "finger" but as a signal for "right hand." This is an interpretive move, not a *pshat* reading.

### Abaye's Framework

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with this *baraita*. He asks: *v'chi ne'emar yad b'kabala* — does the *pasuk* actually say "hand" by the act of catching the blood? Since it does not, *kibel bismol kasher* — the *kabala* may even be performed with the left hand. One might read this as Rabbi Shimon simply questioning whether the verb *velakach* can plausibly be taken to refer to catching blood. But Abaye explains that the fundamental dispute is precisely about *mikra nidrash lefanav ul'acharav*. The *chachamim* hold that *be'etzba'o* can be read backward to apply to *velakach* — the catching. Rabbi Shimon holds that *be'etzba'o* refers only forward, to *venatan* — the placing. He does not apply the word backward to the earlier verb.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

This is quite striking. In the case of the blood, the *pshat* of the *pasuk* actually supports reading *etzba* as applying to both verbs — one dips one's finger and places it. Yet even there, Rabbi Shimon refuses to apply the middle word backward. The Gemara concludes from this that Rabbi Shimon simply does not employ the principle of *mikra nidrash lefanav ul'acharav*. If that is so, then his position regarding the *mincha* — that *bnei Aharon hakohanim* applies backward to the *yetzika* and *belila* — cannot rest on this hermeneutic.

The Gemara then resolves the apparent contradiction: *ela hacha haynu ta'ama d'Rabbi Shimon* — here, in the *mincha* case, Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is different. The *pasuk* says *vehevia*, "and he brought it," with a *vav*. The *vav mosif al inyan rishon* — the conjunctive *vav* links the bringing to the *bnei Aharon hakohanim* with what came before it, drawing the *kohanim* into the earlier acts of pouring and mixing. It is not a case of reading the middle word backward; it is the *vav* itself that binds the earlier actions to the *bnei Aharon hakohanim*. Normally Rabbi Shimon would not apply the reference to *kohanim* backward — but here the linking *vav* provides the textual basis for doing so.

The Gemara, however, immediately challenges this: *v'savar Rabbi Shimon vav mosif al inyan rishon* — does Rabbi Shimon truly hold that a *vav* pulls the *kohanim* into earlier acts? If so, consider the *pasuk* concerning animal sacrifice: *veshachat et ben habakar vehikrivu bnei Aharon hakohanim et hadam vezarku et hadam al hamizbe'ach saviv* — one slaughters the animal, and then the *bnei Aharon* take the blood and sprinkle it. Since *bnei Aharon* are introduced only after the *shechita*, we learn *mi'kabala ve'eilach mitzvat kehuna* — from the receiving of the blood onward is the *kohen*'s domain — and accordingly the *shechita* is *keshera bezar*, valid when performed by a non-*kohen*. But there too the *pasuk* has a *vav* — *vehikrivu* — introducing the *bnei Aharon*. If Rabbi Shimon's principle is that the *vav* draws the *kohanim* backward, should he not then say that the *shechita* also requires a *kohen*?

---

## Animal vs Mincha

### Two Verses

This challenge forms the transition into a broader comparison of the two *psukim* — the one governing animal sacrifice and the one governing the *mincha*. The structure of both is parallel: an action precedes the introduction of *bnei Aharon hakohanim*, and in both cases there is a *vav* connecting the *kohanim* to what follows. The Gemara's question is pointed: if the *vav* is enough to draw the *kohanim* backward in the *mincha* case, why would it not do so in the animal sacrifice case as well?

### Gemara Objection

The Gemara makes the parallel explicit. By the animal sacrifice: *veshachat et ben habakar vehikrivu bnei Aharon*. By the *mincha*: *vayatzak aleha shemen venatan aleha levonah ve'hevi bnei Aharon hakohanim*. In both *psukim*, the *bnei Aharon* are introduced only after a prior act. In both, there is a *vav*. If everyone agrees that *shechita* can be done by a non-*kohen* because the *kohanim* only appear in the *pasuk* after the *shechita*, why should anyone dispute this by the *mincha*? The *vav* is present in both.

### Semicha Distinction

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam de'amar kra vesamach veshachat* — there it is different, because the *pasuk* on animal sacrifice begins with *vesamach yado al rosh korbano* — the owner leans his hand upon his *korban* — and then says *veshachat*. The beginning of the *pasuk* is unambiguously about the owner. When it says *veshachat*, we read it as the owner slaughtering. The *pasuk* thus makes explicit, through the juxtaposition with *semicha*, that the subject performing the *shechita* is the owner, not the *kohen*. This clarity means we do not need to extend the *bnei Aharon* backward.

### Ambiguity Argument

By contrast, in the *mincha pasuk*, the subject of the earlier actions is not so explicitly defined. It begins: *nefesh ki takriv korban mincha l'Hashem solet yihiyeh korbano* — a person who brings a *mincha*, it shall be his offering — *vayatzak aleha shemen venatan aleha levonah*. The *pshat* is undeniably that the person is performing these acts. But Rabbi Shimon's point is that at the moment of the *yetzika* and *belila*, the text does not juxtapose an act uniquely tied to the owner — as *semicha* is — that would anchor the subject as the owner. The *pasuk* could, at least implicitly, be read as shifting to a *kohen* performing those acts. The *mincha pasuk* is thus sufficiently ambiguous that Rabbi Shimon reads the *kohanim* into the earlier acts via the *vav*; the animal sacrifice *pasuk* is not ambiguous in the same way, because *semicha* pins the subject as the owner.

One might press further: could we then say that not only does the *shechita* not require a *kohen*, but it must be done specifically by the owner — since *semicha* is by the owner, and the juxtaposition with *veshachat* would imply the owner must slaughter too? The Gemara addresses this: *im smichah b'be'alim af shechitah b'be'alim* — if you push the argument from the connection of *shechita* to *semicha*, you would reach the conclusion that the owner himself must perform the *shechita*, which no one has ever said. This *reductio ad absurdum* undermines the argument.

### Ambiguity Argument (continued)

The Gemara, however, responds that this conclusion could not stand regardless, because of a *kal vachomer*: if *zerika*, which is the core act of atonement (*ikar kaparah*), does not require the owners to perform it — it is done by the *kohen* — then *shechita*, which is not the primary act of atonement, certainly does not require the owners. Therefore, we would never arrive at the conclusion that the owners must perform the *shechita*, and the argument from *semicha* cannot be weaponized to that extent.

The Gemara further considers the counter-argument — *ein danin efshar mi'she'ee efshar*, one cannot draw a proof from a case that has no alternative to a case that does have an alternative. By *zerika*, only a *kohen* may perform it, so the owners have no choice; perhaps when an act can be done by the owner, we require the owner. But this reasoning is also dismissed.

### Yom Kippur Exception

The Gemara's final resolution comes from a *gilui* of the *Torah* on Yom Kippur: *v'shachat et par hachatat asher lo* — Aaron slaughters the bull of the *chatat* which is his own. The Torah specifically emphasizes that he slaughters his own animal. *Michlal d'shechitah d'alma lo ba'inan be'alim* — from the fact that Yom Kippur requires a special emphasis on the owner performing the *shechita*, we learn that ordinarily *shechita* does not require the owners. Yom Kippur is the exception that proves the rule.

This is the foundation of Rabbi Shimon's complete position: the *mincha pasuk* is sufficiently ambiguous at the stage of *yetzika* and *belila* that the *vav* draws the *kohanim* into those acts; the animal sacrifice *pasuk* is not ambiguous, because *semicha* clearly identifies the owner as the subject up through and including *shechita*, and we independently know that *shechita* does not require the owner.

---

## Me'akev Principle

### Torah & Chok

Having concluded the analysis of Rabbi Shimon and the *chachamim*, the Gemara now turns to a related but distinct theme: the general principle by which any act in a *korban* is deemed *me'akev*, such that its omission invalidates the offering. This is the deeper question underlying the *mishna*, which lists a series of acts in the *mincha* that are not *me'akev*. Why not? If the Torah prescribes them, one might assume they are all indispensable.

The Gemara establishes that the principle of *shana alav hakatuv l'akeiv* — the Torah must repeat an act to render it *me'akev* — governs *korbanot*. This is counterintuitive: in no other area of *halacha* do we assume that an act is dispensable simply because it is mentioned only once. But the *rishonim* understood that the Torah's extraordinary level of detail regarding *korbanot*, and the fact that so much of that detail appears to be repeated, led the *chachamim* to the conclusion that not everything mentioned is indispensable — rather, indispensability is signaled by repetition.

Rav states the principle more precisely: *kol makom shene'emar Torah vehukah, eino ela l'akeiv* — wherever the Torah uses both the language of *torah* and *chok* (or *chukah*), that signals that what follows is *me'akev*. The paradigmatic case is *Parshat Parah*, which says *zot chukat hatorah* — employing both words together.

### Both Required?

The Gemara initially assumes that Rav requires both *torah* and *chukah* to appear together. It raises a series of challenges to test whether this dual requirement is truly necessary.

### Nazir Tenufah

The first case: by the *nazir*, the concluding *pasuk* says only *zot torat hanazir* — only *torah*, not *chukah*. Yet Rav himself says that *tenufah* by the *nazir* is *me'akev*, even though *tenufah* is ordinarily a prime example of an act that is not *me'akev*. The *pasuk* describes the ceremony: *ve'asah es zevach shelamim vegillach hanazir pesach ohel mo'ed velakach es se'ar rosh nizro venasan al ha'eish, velakach hakohen es hazroa beshela min ha'ayil, vechallat matzah achat min hasal urekik matzah echad, nasan al kapei hanazir vehinif osam hakohen* — one takes the cooked foreleg, breads from the basket, places them on the hands of the *nazir*, and the *kohen* waves them. The Gemara asks: how can the *tenufah* be *me'akev* if only *torah* appears, not *chukah*?

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam, keivan dichtsiv kein ye'aseh al torat nizro* — the *pasuk* adds the phrase "so shall he do," underscoring the obligation in a way that is *keman dichtsiva bei chukah dami* — equivalent to the text having written *chukah* as well. The double emphasis provides the necessary reinforcement.

### Todah Connection

The second case: the *todah*. By the *todah*, only *torah* appears — *vezot torat zevach hashelamim asher yakriv l'Hashem im al todah yakrivenu*. Yet the *mishna* teaches that the four types of loaves brought with the *todah* are *me'akvin zeh es zeh* — each type is indispensable, and the absence of any one invalidates the others. How is this *me'akev* without *chukah*?

The Gemara answers: *shani todah de'itkaish lenazir*. The *todah* is connected to the *nazir* because it is a type of *shelamim*, and the *pasuk* by the *todah* says *al zevach todat shelamav*, which a master teaching elsewhere derives to include the *shalmei nazir* for a particular *halakha*. Once the *todah* and the *shalmei nazir* are linked through that verse, the *me'akev* status that applies to the *nazir* extends to the *todah* as well.

### Metzora Case

The third case: the *metzora*. There too only *torah* appears — *zot tihye torat hametzora beyom taharato vehuva el hakohen* — and we have no *chukah*. Yet the *mishna* teaches that the four elements of the *metzora* ritual — the cedar wood, the hyssop, the red string, and the bird's blood — are all *me'akev*. The Gemara answers: *keivan dechtiv bei zot tihye* — the word *tihye* ("it shall be") re-emphasizes the obligation in a manner that is *keman dechtiv bei chok dami* — equivalent to *chok* having been written. Once again, a form of double emphasis substitutes for the explicit use of *chukah*.

### Yom Kippur

The fourth and most striking case: Yom Kippur. By Yom Kippur, the *pasuk* says only *chok* — *chukat olam ledoroteichem* — and does not say *torah*. The *mishna* teaches that the two goats of Yom Kippur are *me'akvin zeh es zeh* — they are mutually indispensable. The difficulty is that until now the Gemara had been assuming you need *torah* (or an equivalent) alongside *chok*. Here there is only *chok*. Rashi quotes: *vehayeta zot lachem lechukat olam lachaper al bnei yisrael mikol chatatam achat bashana* — and earlier, *vehayeta lachem lechukat olam bachodesh hashevi'i be'asor lachodesh ta'anu et nafshoteichem* — though that second instance concerns *inuy*, fasting, rather than the *avoda* itself, raising a question about which verse precisely the Gemara has in mind. Regardless, the *pasuk* concerning the Yom Kippur *avoda* speaks only of *chok*, not *torah*.

This presents a genuine difficulty for the position that both are required.

### Either Suffices

The Gemara's resolution is elegant: *o torah o chukah* — either is sufficient. One does not need both. The word *torah* alone — when properly emphasized or underscored — is enough to render something *me'akev*, and *chukah* alone is likewise sufficient. This explains the Yom Kippur case, where only *chok* appears.

But the Gemara immediately presses a counterpoint: if *torah* alone is enough, why is it not *me'akev* by all *korbanot*? The Torah states *zot hatorah la'olah lamincha velachatat vela'asham velamilu'im* — it says *torah* for all the major offerings — yet we do not say that every detail of every *korban* is *me'akev*. The Gemara therefore refines the conclusion: *torah* by itself, standing alone without additional emphasis, is not sufficient. What is required is either *chukah*, or *torah* that is reinforced by some form of re-emphasis — repetition, the word *tihye*, the phrase *kein ye'aseh*, or the like. *Chukah* on its own, by contrast, does carry sufficient weight without further reinforcement — as in the Yom Kippur case.

---

## Mincha & Repetition

### Rav's Rule

With the general principle now established, the Gemara turns to its application to the *mincha* specifically. Rav states: *kol makom shehechezir lecha hakatuv betorat minchah vetzav, eino ela l'akeiv* — wherever the Torah repeats something about the *mincha* in *Parashat Tzav* (having already mentioned it in *Vayikra*), that repetition signals that the act is *me'akev*. What is not repeated in *Tzav* is not *me'akev*, and omitting it is therefore not a problem *bedi'avad*.

### Problem Stated

The Gemara, however, immediately raises a difficulty. By the *mincha*, the Torah does use the language of *chok*: *kol zachar bivnei Aharon yochalena chok olam* — every male among the sons of Aaron shall eat it, it is an eternal *chok*. If *chukah* is sufficient on its own to render everything *me'akev*, why does Rav need the additional criterion of repetition in *Tzav*? The *chok* alone should make all aspects of the *mincha* *me'akev*.

### Shmuel's View

Shmuel offers a strikingly different position: *geres veshemen me'akvei, ve'ein davar acher me'akev* — only the flour (*geres*) and the oil (*shemen*) are *me'akev*; nothing else about the *mincha* is *me'akev*. This is a sweeping claim that cuts against the apparent logic of the *me'akev* principle. The Gemara immediately registers surprise at Shmuel's methodology: would Shmuel say that even when the Torah explicitly repeats an act in *Tzav*, it is still not *me'akev*? That would be a rejection of a fundamental *halachic* principle as it applies to *korbanot*.

The Gemara resolves this by reconstructing Shmuel's position more carefully. He does not actually reject the rule that repetition implies *me'akev*; rather, the dispute between Rav and Shmuel concerns one specific act: the *kemitza* itself, and whether it must be performed with the hand or may be done with a vessel.

### Challenge to Shmuel

The *pasuk* in one place says *melo kumtzo*, "the fullness of his hand," and in another says *bekumtzo*, "with his hand." The tension between these formulations raises a question: does *melo kumtzo* merely define a quantity — a volume equivalent to a full handful — such that one could use a vessel of appropriate size? Or does *bekumtzo* require literally using the hand itself? The Gemara explains that this is what Rav and Shmuel actually disagree about, not the general principle.

### Hand vs Vessel

A *baraita* rules explicitly: *melo kumtzo bekumtzo — shelo yaaseh middah lakometz* — one may not fashion a measuring vessel for the *kemitza*; the hand itself must be used. Rav accepts this and treats the matter as *me'akev*, while Shmuel disagrees.

### Rav on Aaron

Rav maintains that the *pasuk* in *Shemini* constitutes a repetition that renders using the hand *me'akev*: *va'yikriv et hamincha va'yimale chapo mimena* — Aaron brought the *mincha* and filled his palm from it. Since the narrative describes Aaron using his literal hand (*chapo*), and this narrative appears alongside the regular description of *kemitza*, Rav counts it as a textual repetition sufficient to establish *me'akev* status.

### Shmuel: One-Time

Shmuel rejects this: *dorosh mi'sha'ah lo yafinan* — one does not derive permanent *halachic* principles from a one-time event. The offering in *Shemini* was part of the *miluim*, the inauguration — a singular, unrepeated ceremony. The fact that Aaron used his hand on that occasion cannot be the basis for a permanent rule. Shmuel is not rejecting the principle that a narrative can serve as a textual repetition; he is rejecting this particular narrative because the underlying event was a *sha'ah*, a one-time occurrence, and therefore not instructive for ongoing practice.

This explains Shmuel's statement about *geres veshemen* more precisely: where the Torah has genuinely repeated something in the context of the regular *mincha* practice, Shmuel agrees it is *me'akev*. His dispute with Rav is limited to whether the *Shemini* narrative counts as such a repetition, given that it records a one-time event.

### Nesi'im Offering

The Gemara challenges Shmuel: does he truly hold that one may never learn from a one-time event? The Gemara cites Shmuel's own ruling elsewhere: *lei lach mekadesh es halach, umidas yavesh mekadesh es hayavesh* — liquid measuring vessels sanctify liquids and dry measuring vessels sanctify dry goods, but they do not work cross-purposes.
