Shmuel himself teaches an exception: *aval mizrakos*, the bowls used for blood, can sanctify even dry contents — *shneihem mele'im soles*, as the *pasuk* records that the *nesi'im* brought their *mizrakot* filled with flour. Yet that too was a one-time event. How can Shmuel learn from it?

### Repeated Events

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam detana bei kra treisar zimnei* — there it is different, because although it was a one-time event, it was repeated twelve times, once for each of the twelve *nesi'im* who each brought the identical offering. By repeating the same act twelve times in succession, the Torah has transformed what would otherwise be a singular *sha'ah* into something that carries the force of a general principle. *Tosafot* notes briefly that one might ask whether twelve repetitions of the same one-time event should instead be treated as *shnei ketuvim haba'im k'echad* — two (or more) texts coming to teach the same thing, which ordinarily signals that the lesson should *not* be generalized — but presumably twelve times constitutes too clear an affirmation of the principle to be dismissed.

The upshot is that Shmuel can indeed learn from a *sha'ah* when it is sufficiently repeated; he cannot learn from Aaron's single act of *kemitza* in *Shemini* precisely because it occurred once and only once.

---

## Acts Not Me'akev

### Hagasha

With the general framework in place, the Gemara turns to examine specific acts from the *mishna*'s list of things that are not *me'akev* by a *mincha*. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi raise the first challenge to Rav's rule: *veharei hagasha* — what about the act of *hagasha*, bringing the *mincha* vessel into contact with the *mizbe'ach* before the *kemitza*? The *pasuk* says *el pnei hamizbe'ach*, and this act is indeed repeated in *Tzav*. According to Rav's principle, repetition in *Tzav* implies *me'akev*. Yet the *mishna* teaches that *hagasha* is not *me'akev*.

### Location Purpose

The Gemara responds: *hahu likvo'a lo makom hu de'ata* — that repetition in *Tzav* does not serve to establish *me'akev* status. It serves an entirely different purpose: to specify the precise location where the *hagasha* must be performed. The act was already known and required; the *Tzav* repetition adds topographical information.

### Location Details

The relevant *pasuk* in *Tzav* reads: *zot torat hamincha, hakreiv otah bnei Aharon lifnei Hashem el pnei hamizbe'ach* — bring it before God, to the face of the altar. But these two phrases do not obviously point to the same spot. *Lifnei Hashem* — before God — means facing the *heichal*, which lies to the west; this would place the *hagasha* at the western wall of the *mizbe'ach*. *El pnei hamizbe'ach* — the face of the altar — means its front, the side facing the ramp, which is the south. One phrase implies west; the other implies south. A *baraita* resolves the tension: *hagisha bekheren dromit ma'aravit* — one performs the *hagasha* at the southwest corner, thereby satisfying both *lifnei Hashem* and *el pnei hamizbe'ach* simultaneously, *keneged chudah shel keren*, opposite the tip of the horn at that corner.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer disagrees with the corner solution. He holds that one need not synthesize the two phrases by choosing a corner; rather, one may read them as offering a choice — either the west or the south. He then applies a hermeneutic rule: *kol makom she'ata motze shnei mikra'ot, echad mekayem atzmo umekayem chaveiro, ve'echad mekayem atzmo umevatel chaveiro* — when two *psukim* each imply a different option, and one option satisfies both *psukim* while the other satisfies only itself at the expense of the other, one chooses the option that satisfies both. The question is: which of the two options — west or south — can satisfy both? Rabbi Eliezer reasons that choosing the west (*lifnei Hashem*) would negate *el pnei hamizbe'ach*, since the west side is not the face of the altar at all. But choosing the south (*el pnei hamizbe'ach*) — *kiyamta lifnei Hashem* — also satisfies being before God. Therefore, the south is the correct location.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi offers a different explanation of how the south satisfies *lifnei Hashem*: *kasvar hai tana kulo mizbe'ach batzafon ka'i* — this *tanna* holds that the entire *mizbe'ach* stands in the northern portion of the *azara*. If the *mizbe'ach* is situated entirely to the north, then its southern face — *pnei hamizbe'ach* — stands precisely at the opening of the *heichal*, directly facing it. In that case, performing *hagasha* at the south of the *mizbe'ach* simultaneously fulfills *el pnei hamizbe'ach* and *lifnei Hashem*, since that position is directly in front of the entrance to the sanctuary.

### Conclusion

The Gemara's answer to Rav Kahana and Rav Assi's challenge is thus complete: *hagasha* is indeed repeated in *Tzav*, but the repetition is not there to signal *me'akev* — it is there to specify location. Whether that location is the southwest corner (per the *baraita*) or the south alone (per Rabbi Eliezer and Rav Ashi), the repetition has a clear explanatory purpose that is independent of *me'akev* status. This establishes the critical methodological point: not every repetition in *Tzav* signals *me'akev*. When the repetition can be explained as serving a different purpose — here, specifying where an act must be done — it does not invoke Rav's principle. The *daf* concludes at this point, with the Gemara set to continue examining the *mishna*'s remaining acts one by one to determine whether each repetition is *me'akev* or serves some other function.

---

---

# Menachot 20

## Rav's Principle

### Intro to Rav

The sugya under discussion concerns whether a *pasuk* is repeated in *Tzav*, given that it first appears in *Vayikra*. Rav's general principle is that if a law is repeated, it is *me'akev* — essential and disqualifying if omitted — and if it is not repeated, it is not *me'akev*. Today's daf, daf 20, picks up from 19b, two lines from the bottom, and we now examine whether this principle truly holds.

The previous session addressed *hagashah*, which is not *me'akev* despite being repeated — with the resolution that the repetition serves to specify precisely where the *hagashah* is performed.

### RavHuna's Challenge

The Gemara presents a challenge from Rav Huna: *harei melach* — what about salt? When the Mishnah taught that salt is not *me'akev*, this came as a shock, given that the Torah states *lo tashbit melach berit elokecha me'al minchatecha* — do not allow the salt of your God's covenant to be absent from your *mincha*. The Gemara now interrogates this specifically in light of Rav's principle.

### Salt's Absence in Tzav

The law of salt appears in *Vayikra* but not in *Tzav*, which runs against the general pattern underlying Rav's principle. The standard framework is that *Tzav*, which opens with *Tzav et Aharon*, represents a repetition of *Vayikra* from the perspective of the *kohanim*, while *Vayikra*, which opens with *Daber el bnei yisrael lemor*, addresses the one who brings the *korban*. Yet the entire requirement to salt all *korbanot* appears in *Vayikra* and not in *Tzav*, which does not fit neatly into that pattern.

Be that as it may, the Gemara's question stands: *delo tana bei kra* — the Torah did not repeat the salt law — and yet salt is *me'akev*. This is already a striking point: the Gemara is operating against the plain reading of the Mishnah, which says salt is not *me'akev*.

### Assumption vs Rav

The Gemara begins by assuming that salt is *me'akev*, citing a *baraita*, and it is apparent that the Gemara is intuitively persuaded by this position — presumably because the Torah calls salt a *brit olam*, an eternal covenant. The Gemara then turns this around and presses Rav: you said that a law must be repeated to be *me'akev*, yet salt is not repeated. How does Rav account for this?

Tosafot already flags the underlying assumption here. When Rav articulated his principle that repetition signals *me'akev* status within the laws of *menachot*, the Gemara initially understood him to mean that repetition is the *only* means by which something becomes *me'akev* in this domain. Yet we know from elsewhere that *me'akev* status can derive from other formulations — *chok*, *Torah*, *brit*, and similar expressions. Tosafot explains that the Gemara understood Rav's statement narrowly and specifically in the context of *mincha*, such that within that domain repetition was thought to be the exclusive criterion. The Gemara is about to revise that assumption.

---

## Defending Rav

### First Defense

Rav Yosef offers the first defense: *Rav ketanna didan sevira lei* — Rav holds in accordance with our Mishnah. The Mishnah itself states *lo malach kesheira* — if one did not perform *melicha*, the offering is valid. If so, Rav need not be troubled: even though the Torah calls salt a *brit olam*, it is simply not *me'akev*, consistent with the plain meaning of the Mishnah.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye pushes back sharply. He argues that one cannot read the Mishnah so straightforwardly. Consider the Mishnah's parallel statement about *yetzika* — if one did not pour the oil, the offering is valid. The Gemara has already established, even without extensive proof texts, that *yetzika* is in fact *me'akev*. To reconcile this, the Gemara reinterpreted *lo yetzak* not to mean that *yetzika* was omitted entirely, but that the pouring was performed by a *zar* — a non-*kohen* — rather than a *kohen*. That is: the Mishnah permits the offering when a non-*kohen* performed the pouring, not when the pouring was skipped altogether.

If that is how we read *lo yetzak* in the Mishnah, Abaye argues, then we should read *lo malach* the same way: not that the *melicha* was omitted, but that a non-*kohen* performed it. The Mishnah would then teach that if a non-*kohen* salted the *kometz*, the offering is still valid — while *melicha* itself remains *me'akev*. This preserves the *brit olam* language without contradicting the Mishnah, and simultaneously undermines Rav Yosef's defense of Rav.

### Non-Kohen Problem

The Gemara objects to this reinterpretation: *ve-chi ta'aleh al da'atcha she-zar kareiv l-gabei mizbeach?* Can one really entertain the notion that a non-*kohen* could approach the *mizbeach*? The *melicha* is performed on the *kometz* immediately before it is burned, meaning one would have to be at the top of the altar. The very idea seems untenable.

The *Shita Mekubetzet* raises the obvious difficulty: even granting that it would be highly improper for a non-*kohen* to ascend the *mizbeach*, that impropriety does not by itself determine whether the offering is valid after the fact. He resolves the difficulty by pointing to the principle established earlier: *mi-kmitza ve-eilach mitzvat kehuna* — from the *kemitza* onward, the service belongs exclusively to the *kohanim*. The Gemara's objection is therefore not merely about decorum or the affront of physical proximity to the *mizbeach*, but about the halakhic impossibility of a post-*kemitza* action being performed by a non-*kohen*. That category has never been opened, even theoretically. While this may not be the most straightforward reading of the Gemara's language, the broader point — that a non-*kohen* performing the *melicha* at this stage is genuinely inconceivable within the halakhic framework — is what forces the Gemara's hand.

### Accept Pshat

The Gemara is compelled to accept the *pshat* of the Mishnah: if one did not perform *melicha*, the offering is valid. This squares with Rav's principle. Yet the Gemara is equally compelled to account for the phrase *brit olam*. It therefore concludes: *ve-iba'it eima keivan di-chtiva beih brit k-man di-tna beih kra dami* — since the *pasuk* uses the word *brit*, it is as though the law were explicitly repeated. The word *brit*, like the words *chok* or *yihiye*, carries the same force as an explicit repetition.

What is striking about this Gemara is the trajectory it traces. It begins by virtually taking for granted that *melicha* is *me'akev* — presumably because of the *brit olam* language — and is reluctant to read the Mishnah according to its plain meaning. Only after the various attempts to reinterpret the Mishnah fail does the Gemara accept the *pshat*. And then it concludes that either salt is not *me'akev* at all, consistent with the Mishnah, or, alternatively, even Rav would acknowledge that *brit* functions as a form of repetition. The Gemara's strong intuition that salt should be *me'akev*, driven by the *pasuk*, is ultimately what shapes the resolution.

What the Gemara has clarified along the way is important: when Rav said that a law must be repeated to be *me'akev*, he did not mean that repetition is the only pathway. *Brit*, *chok*, and similar formulations serve the same function. The Gemara had initially — and incorrectly — read Rav's principle as exhaustive within the domain of *menachot*.

---

## Salt Repetition

### Where's Repetition?

The Gemara now reconsiders the factual premise of the earlier challenge. The question was: *v'lo tana bei kra* — did the Torah not repeat itself regarding salt? But in fact, is that true? The *pasuk* states *v'chol korban minchatcha b'melach timlach* — every offering of your *mincha* you shall salt with salt. Has salt not been stated more than once?

Until now, repetition has been understood to mean a law stated once in *Vayikra* and again in *Tzav*. Here, however, the text does not appear in *Tzav*. So one might instead argue that the repetition is internal to the *Vayikra* passage itself: the verse *v'chol korban minchatcha b'melach timlach* and the verse *brit melach olam* mentioned at the end of *Korach* could together constitute a repetition.

However, this presents its own difficulty. The phrase *brit melach olam* in *Korach* appears at the conclusion of the discussion of priestly gifts in Bamidbar, where the Torah uses the covenant of salt as a symbol for the eternal promise to the *kohanim*. It states: *kol trumas hakodashim asher yarimu bnei yisrael l'Hashem nasati lcha u'lvanecha u'lvnotecha itcha l'chok olam, bris melach olam hi lifnei Hashem lcha u'lzarcha itcha.* The passage lists everything the *kohen* receives and characterizes it as a *brit melach olam* before God. The *brit* of salt here is invoked as the paradigm for an enduring covenant, applied to the *kehuna*; it is not directly legislating the need for salt on *korbanot*.

It is an interesting inversion. The *baraita* earlier compared salt to *kehuna* — just as *kehuna* is always required, so too is salt always required, since the same *pasuk* applies the *brit melach olam* to both. But the Gemara we just read reversed the analogy: *k'sheim she'efshar l'korbano blo kehuna, kach efshar l'korbano blo melach* — just as a *korban* can, in certain circumstances, be valid without a *kohen*, so too can it be valid without salt. The *kehuna* is taken as the more axiomatic baseline, and salt is the unexpected case. There is something almost playful about this reversal.

### Rabbeinu Tam

Given the difficulty in using the *Korach* verse as the repetition of salt, Rabbeinu Tam emended the *girsa* of the earlier Gemara. He argues that the cited *pasuk* was never meant to be *brit melach olam* from *Korach* at all. Within *Vayikra* itself, the salt requirement is actually stated twice in adjacent verses: first, *v'chol korban minchatcha b'melach timlach*, and second, *v'lo tashbis melach bris elokeicha me'al minchatecha — al kol korbancha takriv melach*. The word *bris* appears in this second verse within *Vayikra* itself — *melach bris elokeicha* — and that is what the Gemara meant when it said the *pasuk* uses *brit*. There was no need to invoke the verse from *Korach* at all.

Whether or not Rabbeinu Tam's emendation is accepted, the more natural understanding of *tana bei kra* is that the very same section in *Vayikra* repeats the salt requirement more than once in its own right. The idea that you must salt the *korbanot* is stated, then restated — that is what constitutes the repetition.

### Baraita's Logic

The Gemara responds to the apparent redundancy by explaining: *ha-hu miba-ye lei l'ched-tanya* — that verse is needed for what is taught in the *baraita*. The verse *v'chol korban minchatcha b'melach timlach* is not simply a reiteration; it is the source for the *baraita*'s detailed derivation of precisely which offerings require salt and which do not. The verse's emphasis on *minchatcha* — your *mincha* — is doing specific halakhic work, and that work cannot be reduced to mere repetition.

This also provides the structural logic of what the Gemara is accomplishing in this section. Under the framework of Rav's principle — explaining what is and is not *me'akev* in the Mishnah — the Gemara is, in the course of asking whether a law was repeated, simultaneously teaching the substantive details of how these laws are performed. Just as the discussion of *hagashah* yielded an explanation of how *hagashah* works, the discussion of salt now yields the full scope of the salt requirement.

---

## Baraita's Drasha

### Only Mincha?

The *baraita* proceeds as follows. *Ilu ne'emar korban ba-melach* — had the Torah simply said "your *korban* with salt," without mentioning *mincha*, I might have thought that even wood brought to the *mizbeach* and blood itself require salt, since both can be called a *korban*. *Talmud lomar mincha* — therefore the Torah specifically uses *mincha* as the paradigm. Just as *mincha* is distinct in that other things come with it as an obligation — *ma mincha meyuchedet she-acherim ba'im chova lah* — so too, everything else that requires something else to come with it as an obligation requires salt.

What does it mean that other things come with the *mincha* as an obligation? The Gemara explains: it means wood — *etzim*. In order to burn the *kometz* on the altar, one must have wood. The *mincha* paradigm therefore teaches that anything which is placed on the fire and burned on wood requires salt. Blood is sprinkled, not burned; wood is itself the fuel, not something burned on other wood. Both are therefore excluded.

The Gemara, however, immediately presses: why should the relevant characteristic of *mincha* be that things come with it (i.e., that it is burned on wood) rather than that it is a *matir* — the agent that permits the remainder to be consumed? The *kometz* is the *matir* of the *mincha*; the blood is the *matir* of the animal *korban*. If we focus on the *matir* characteristic, we would include blood and exclude most of the things we want to include: the *evarim* of an *olah*, the *imurim* of a *chatat* and *asham*, and so on. So which characteristic of *mincha* is the operative one?

The *baraita* then addresses a further question within its own logic. Having established that we include everything burnt on wood, the *baraita* asks: *ve'ein li ela kometz* — I only know this from the *kometz*; *minayin lerabot et halevona* — how do I know to include the *levona*? The answer given is *sheken ba'ah imah bikli echad* — because the *levona* comes together with the *kometz* in the same vessel and was sanctified along with it. But this immediately prompts a further question: if the *levona* that accompanies the *mincha* is included on the basis of sharing a vessel, how do I know about *levona* that comes by itself — as an independent donation — or the *levona* that sits in the bowls alongside the *lechem hapanim*, or the *ketoret* that is burned on the inner altar? The *baraita* eventually teaches: *talmud lomar al kol korbancha takriv melach* — from the general phrase "on all your *korbanot*," we include all of these.

The Gemara then notes the structural difficulty: the *baraita* appeared to have already settled the matter by establishing the general principle — everything burned on wood requires salt — yet it then doubled back to ask specifically about *levona* as if the earlier derivation had not resolved it. The Gemara explains: *hachi ka'amar* — the *baraita* anticipated a challenge based on *klal u'prat*. One might have argued that *korban* is a *klal*, *mincha* is a *prat*, and by the rule of *klal u'prat*, the *prat* limits the *klal* so that only a *mincha* itself — and nothing else — requires salt. The final clause, *al kol korbancha takriv melach*, then restates a general term, creating a *klal u'prat u'klal* structure: we include everything similar to the *prat*, i.e., everything that shares the relevant characteristic of *mincha*.

This interpretive move actually fits well with the structure of the *pesukim*. The passage emphasizes *mincha*, *mincha*, *mincha* in successive verses — *kol korban minchatcha bamelach timlach*, *velo tashbit melach bris elokeicha me'al minchatecha* — and then concludes with the broad phrase *al kol korbancha takriv melach*. The natural reading of this progression is that *mincha* is exemplary and the final clause extends the requirement broadly to everything relevantly similar. The limitation implied by the *klal u'prat u'klal* structure is not that something must be identical to a *mincha*, but that it must share the characteristic that makes *mincha* the paradigm — namely, that it is burned on wood.

The *baraita* then clarifies the scope of what is included: the *kometz*, the *levona* of the *mincha* together with it in the same vessel, *levona* brought independently, *levona* in the bowls of the *lechem hapanim*, the *ketoret*, the *minchat kohanim* and *minchat kohen mashiach* — both of which are fully burned without *kemitza*, the *minchat nesachim*, the *imurei chatat* and *imurei asham*, the *imurei kodshei kodashim* (which includes the communal *shalmei tzibur* of *Shavuot*), the *imurim* of *kodashim kalim*, the *eivrei olah*, and the *olat ha'of*. All of these require salt, derived from the verse *al kol korbancha takriv melach*. The principle unifying them is that they are offered on the fire.

### Expand to All

The Gemara quotes the *baraita*'s conclusion: *ma mincha meyuchedet she-acherim ba'im chova lah, af kol she-acherim ba'im chova lo* — just as *mincha* is distinct in that other things must come with it as an obligation, so too with everything for which other things must come as an obligation. The Gemara then asks what this phrase means in practice. The answer is: *etzim* — wood. The characteristic that other things must come with it as an obligation is the characteristic of being burned on wood, since wood must be brought to enable the burning. This is the defining feature that connects all salted offerings.

### What's Similar?

The Gemara then raises a sharper challenge to the identification of this characteristic. *Ei ma mincha meyuchedet she-materet af kol she-matir* — one might equally have said that the defining characteristic of *mincha* is that its *kometz* is a *matir*, the agent that permits the remainder to be consumed. By this logic, one would require salt on everything that functions as a *matir* — which means the blood, not the *imurim*. So how do we know which characteristic of *mincha* to select?

The Gemara's resolution is that *minchatecha* appears twice in the relevant verses. The doubling signals: not everything similar to *mincha* in any respect, but only things similar in one specific respect. The question then becomes: which specific characteristic?

One might further suggest that two characteristics must be shared — both that the offering is burned on wood and that it is a *matir* — which would narrow the required salt to the *levona* of the *lechem hapanim* (which is both a *matir* for the *lechem hapanim* and is burned). The Gemara dismisses this: *midei itztarich me'al minchatecha velo me'al damecha* — the very fact that the *pasuk* needed explicitly to exclude blood (*me'al minchatecha velo me'al damecha*) tells us that the category was assumed to be large, requiring narrowing. Had we been limiting inclusion to those things sharing two characteristics, the category would never have been broad enough to include blood in the first place, and no explicit exclusion would have been needed. The explicit exclusion of blood therefore confirms that the category was indeed broad — based on a single characteristic — and requires narrowing by one specific characteristic rather than by adding a second requirement.

The operative characteristic is not the *matir* quality but the quality of being burned. Anything burned on the altar requires salt; blood and wine, which are respectively sprinkled and poured rather than burned, do not.

---

## Blood Question

### Blood as Matir

The Gemara has established that the principle of *she-acherim ba'im chova lah* — other things come with it as an obligation — is to be understood as referring to wood, meaning that what requires salt is what is burned on wood. The Gemara now asks whether there is any way blood could have entered the category. After all, the initial framing of the *baraita* says: *shome'a ani afilu etzim ve-dam* — I might have thought that even wood and blood require salt, since both can be called a *korban*. The Gemara here probes whether blood could qualify on the basis of being analogous to the *kometz* in its function as a *matir*.

The *kometz* is the *matir* of the *mincha*. Blood is the *matir* of the animal *korban*. If the relevant characteristic of *mincha* that generates the salt requirement were its role as a *matir*, blood would be the natural counterpart in animal *korbanot* and would require salt. The question therefore becomes: is there any grounds on which to read the characteristic of *mincha* as its *matir* function rather than its being burned?

### Nisachim Group

The Gemara introduces a conceptual distinction to rebuff the suggestion that blood is linked to the *nisachim*: *nesachim bahadi imurin hu de'atu* — the *nisachim* are conceptually associated with the *imurim*, not with the blood. The argument is geographic and functional: the *nisachim* are brought to the top of the *mizbeach* and are offered there alongside the *imurim*, which are also burned on the *mizbeach*. The blood, by contrast, is sprinkled at the base or the sides of the altar. If one were to ask where things "come with" the *korban*, the *nisachim* conceptually accompany the *imurim*, not the blood.

### Food & Drink

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason to group *nisachim* with *imurim* rather than with blood? The answer is *achila u-shtiya* — eating and drinking. The *mizbeach* "eats" the *imurim* and "drinks" the wine. This anthropomorphic framing is more honest with the *pesukim* than it may initially seem: the Torah repeatedly refers to the *korbanot* as *lechem isheh* — bread consumed by fire — and the concept of *shulchan gavoah*, the table of the Most High, is well-attested. Within this framework, the wine of the *nisachim* is the drink of the *mizbeach*, and the *imurim* are its food. The blood, by contrast, is not in this category of *achila u-shtiya*; it is sprinkled, not consumed as food or drink.

### Kaparah Link

The Gemara considers a counterargument: *aderaba — kapara v-simcha* — on the contrary, one could link blood and wine through *kapara* and *simcha*. Blood effects atonement; wine brings joy; and atonement is accompanied by joy. Therefore, the wine of the *nisachim* might conceptually belong together with the blood rather than with the *imurim*, since they share the context of atonement and its ensuing joy.

This is a striking argument. We do not usually associate joy with the atonement process itself, but the Gemara draws on the idea that once atonement has been achieved, joy is its natural companion — a concept that surfaces also in the dictum *lo hayu yamim tovim b'Yisrael k'Tu B'Av u-k'Yom HaKippurim*. Rashi explains the connection as the joy of one whose sin has been atoned: *d'mi she-nitkaper chato sameach*.

There is, however, a conceptual weakness in this linkage: the *minchat nesachim* and its accompanying wine are brought specifically with free-will *korbanot* — an *olah* or *shlamim* — and not with a *chatat* or *asham*, which are the paradigmatic *korbanot* of atonement. If the connection between wine and blood were really about the joy of *kapara*, we would expect wine to accompany the *chatat*, which it does not. Furthermore, the argument then pivots: even if we were to say *nisachim* accompany the blood conceptually, the mechanism by which *nisachim* are said to "come with" the *korban* is not the same tight connection that *levona* has to the *kometz*. *Levona* is sanctified together with the *kometz* in the same vessel; *nisachim* have no such intimate structural connection to the blood.

The Gemara makes this explicit: *ella levona ba'ah imah b'kli echad nesachim ein ba'in b'kli echad* — the *levona* comes with the *kometz* in the same vessel; *nisachim* do not come in the same vessel as the blood. Even if we had tried to include blood by arguing that things come with it — namely the *nisachim* — there is no way to get blood included through the back door of the *kometz*-*levona* relationship, because that relationship is structurally unique in its closeness.

The Gemara adds a further point: *aval etzim ki heichi d'mitkashra behu mincha hachi mitkashra b'chulhu korbanot* — when "comes with" is understood as referring to wood, then *mincha* has no closer connection to wood than any other *korban* that is burned. All burned offerings require wood equally, and therefore the characteristic of being burned on wood is genuinely universal among the burned offerings. This allows the category to expand properly outward to everything that is burned, which is exactly what the verses' final clause — *al kol korbancha takriv melach* — seems to require.

It is notable that throughout this discussion, the Gemara never suggested including the *mincha* component of the *minchat nesachim* together with the blood. It focused exclusively on the wine component. This is presumably because the *mincha* component of the *minchat nesachim* — the flour and oil — is naturally grouped with the *imurim* as a burned offering, not with the blood. The Gemara only explored whether the wine could be linked to the blood through either the *achila u-shtiya* or the *kapara v-simcha* framework.

### One Characteristic

The Gemara resolves: *mide'itztarich me'al minchatecha velo me'al damecha — michlal dehanach kulehu atu bechad tzad* — since the *pasuk* explicitly needed to exclude blood, it follows that the entire category is built on a single point of similarity rather than two. Had two points of similarity been required — being burned *and* being a *matir* — blood would never have entered the category to begin with, and no exclusion would have been necessary. The fact that an explicit exclusion of blood was required confirms that the category was constructed on one characteristic, and the *pasuk* is telling us: do not assume any characteristic of *mincha* will suffice; the specific characteristic that generates the salt requirement is being burned, not being a *matir*.

---

## Ashbanat Tamei

### Six Points

The Gemara now asks: given that both blood and the *evarim* (and *imurim*) have some similarity to the *kometz*, why do we choose to include the *evarim* and *imurim* rather than the blood? The answer is: *shekein Ashnavat Tamei siman* — there is a mnemonic encapsulating the multiple ways in which the *kometz* resembles the *evarim* and *imurim* as opposed to the blood.

The mnemonic — *alef, shin, beit, nun, tet, mem* — stands for six characteristics:

*Alef* — *acherim ba'im chova lah*: the *kometz* and *evarim* are burned on wood, while blood is not.

*Shin* — *ishim kamosa*: both the *kometz* and the *evarim* are offered directly to the fire, the *ishim*, while blood is not.

*Beit* — *bachutz kamosa*: the *kometz* and the *evarim* are offered on the outer *mizbeach*, while blood is sometimes offered on the inner *mizbeach* and thus does not share this characteristic uniformly.

*Nun* — *notar kamosa*: one who leaves over the *kometz* or the *evarim* overnight transgresses *notar* and is liable to *kares*. The laws of *notar* do not apply to blood; although blood that has become old may not be sprinkled, one is not liable for *notar* in connection with blood.

*Tet* — *tuma kamosa*: eating the *kometz* or the *evarim* in a state of *tuma* renders one liable for the transgression of *tum'as ochel kodesh*, carrying a penalty of *kares*. This liability does not apply to blood in the same way.

*Mem* — *me'ila kamosa*: *me'ila* — the prohibition against misusing consecrated property — applies to the *kometz* and to the *evarim*, but blood is excluded from *me'ila*. The fact that blood is excluded from so many of these categories is itself striking; the Gemara has not yet explored these exclusions in depth, but the pattern is consistent.

### Tosafot: Ochel

Tosafot raises the question of the *alef* in the mnemonic. If the mnemonic is *shin, beit, nun, tet, mem* — *Ashnavat* without the *alef* — the *alef* would be superfluous. Tosafot therefore argues that the *alef* is not merely a mnemonic convenience but carries substantive content: *ochel kamosa* — food. The *kometz* and *evarim* are types of food, in the broad sense that they are things one normally salts. This is the point raised earlier: we salt meat and bread; we do not normally salt blood. This practical, almost prosaic observation supports the intuition that salt belongs on the *kometz* and the *evarim*, not on the blood. And since we eat meat to remove the blood from it, the very act of salting in ordinary practice reinforces the halakhic conclusion that blood is not in the category of what is salted.

### More Similarities

The Gemara acknowledges the counterargument: *aderaba dam havi lei leribuyei shekein matir kamosa* — one could equally argue in favor of blood, which resembles the *kometz* in being a *matir*, and also shares the characteristic of *nifsal bishki'as hachama kamosa* — both the blood and the *kometz* become invalid after sunset (*sheki'at ha-chama*). Once the *matir* has been performed — the blood sprinkled, the *kometz* burned — the remaining portions of the *korban* may be burned throughout the night. But the *matir* itself must be performed during the day; blood that has not been sprinkled by nightfall can no longer be used, just as the *kometz* cannot be burned after sunset. Tosafot notes that one could add that both blood and the *kometz*, as *matirim*, are also exempt from *piggul* — improper intent does not disqualify the *matir* itself, only what the *matir* permits.

Nonetheless, the Gemara concludes: *hanach nefishan* — the list of similarities between the *kometz* and the burned offerings is simply much longer than the list of similarities between the *kometz* and the blood. The six (or seven, counting *ochel*) characteristics in the *Ashnavat Tamei* mnemonic all point toward including the burned offerings rather than the blood. The shorter list of *matir*-related similarities to blood is outweighed.

The significance of the phrase *nifsal bishki'as hachama* is not lost on Tosafot, who takes the occasion here to elaborate at length on the position of Rabbeinu Tam regarding the definition of nightfall. The Gemara in Shabbat teaches that *bein hashmashos* — twilight — begins approximately three-quarters of a *mil* after visible sunset, roughly thirteen to fifteen minutes. Rabbeinu Tam, however, based on a Gemara in Pesachim, maintained that nightfall (*layla*) does not truly begin until four *mil* — seventy-two minutes — after visible sunset.

The astronomical model underlying the Gemara's discussion is that the sun, after setting in the west, travels through the thickness of the *rakia*, and some light escapes during this transit, which accounts for the visible light after sunset. The thickness of the *rakia* corresponds to a travel time of four *mil*. Rabbeinu Tam argued that *bein hashmashos* does not begin at the start of this transit but only near its end, when the sun is about to emerge on the other side. Therefore, true nightfall is only at the second sunset — the point at which the sun has fully passed through the *rakia*.

Rabbeinu Tam deployed this view not only stringently — to delay the end of Shabbat — but also leniently, since he held that true *bein hashmashos* does not even begin until close to an hour after visible sunset. In practice, however, virtually no one today rules leniently based on Rabbeinu Tam; the stringency of a late Shabbat conclusion is observed in some communities, but the leniency of ignoring what happens after visible sunset is not.

Rabbeinu Tam's position is influenced partly by geographic realities: in the high latitudes of France, it remains light for a very long time after visible sunset, and the transition to darkness is gradual. In lower latitudes, such as Eretz Yisrael, nightfall comes much more rapidly after sunset — a phenomenon familiar to anyone who has experienced a Jerusalem evening versus a New York one. This latitude effect shaped Rabbeinu Tam's intuition about when true darkness begins.

The reason Tosafot elaborates on all of this here is that the statement *nifsal bishki'as hachama* prompted questions about exactly what *shki'as hachama* means and when it occurs. By *korbanot*, Tosafot in the name of Rabbeinu Tam argues, the invalidation occurs at the first visible sunset, not the second. This required reconciling two *pesukim* about performing the service while it is still day, and Rabbeinu Tam used the distinction between the two sunsets to explain why two separate verses were needed. The detailed treatment of this issue is the substance of the large Tosafot that accounts for much of the material in this section of the daf.

---

## Baraita's Drasha

### Only Mincha?

Returning to the *baraita*, the Gemara presents the derivation more formally. *Ilu ne'emar korban ba-melach* — had the Torah said only "your *korban* with salt" without specifying *mincha*, I would have included even wood (*etzim*) and blood (*dam*), since both can be called a *korban*. *Talmud lomar mincha* — the Torah therefore specifies *mincha* to provide the paradigm. The *mincha* is distinct in that other things must come with it as an obligation (*she-acherim ba'im chova lah*), meaning it is burned on wood. Everything else for which other things must come as an obligation — i.e., everything burned on wood — likewise requires salt.

The *baraita* then continues with the expansion: *talmud lomar al kol korbancha takriv melach* — the general clause at the end broadens the category back out to include all burned offerings. And then: *talmud lomar me'al minchatcha velo me'al damecha* — the *pasuk* excludes blood, teaching that not every characteristic of *mincha* generates inclusion in the salt requirement.

---

## Blood Question

*(continued from the Baraita's analysis above)*

---

## Ashbanat Tamei

*(continued from the Baraita's analysis above)*

---

## Wood as Korban

### Wood Offering

The *baraita* has referred to wood as a *korban*, citing the verse from Nechemiah: *ve-ha-goralot hipallnu al korban ha-etzim* — we cast lots for the *korban* of the wood. This establishes the premise that individuals can voluntarily donate wood to the *mizbeach* as a type of offering. The *baraita* teaches: *melamed she-mitnadvim etzim* — this teaches that one may donate wood as a voluntary offering, the minimum quantity being two logs (*shenei gezerim*).

### Rebbi: Wood Mincha

Rebbi goes further: *etzim korban mincha hen* — wood is not merely a *korban* in the broad sense; it is actually a type of *mincha*. This is an expansive reading of the *mincha* category, but it is consistent with the general tendency of *chazal* to extend the concept of *mincha* to include a range of basic foodstuffs and materials that a person might offer — flour, oil, wine, and, according to Rebbi, even wood. The analogy is apt: the *mincha* exists as an offering accessible to someone who cannot afford an animal, and the willingness to treat even wood as a form of *mincha* reflects the principle that whatever a person is able to give, they may bring before God in a formal way.

### Rebbi's Rules

Because Rebbi categorizes *etzim* as a *mincha*, he derives several halakhic consequences. *Ve'te'unim melach* — wood requires salt, since it is a *mincha*. *Ve'te'unim hagasha* — it requires *hagasha*, the presentation of the offering to the *mizbeach*, just as a *mincha* requires *hagasha*. Rava adds: *etzim te'unim kmitza* — according to Rebbi, wood also requires *kemitza*, the taking of a handful. This last point initially seems strange: *kemitza* is normally the act that separates the part burned on the altar from the remainder that is eaten. If the wood is simply going to be burned entirely, what sense does *kemitza* make? Tosafot explains that there are other cases where *kemitza* is performed even when the remainder is also eventually burned, and Rebbi's position on *etzim* would fit into that pattern. Rav Pappa adds a further consequence: *etzim tzrichim etzim* — wood itself needs to be burned on other wood, since it is treated as a full offering placed on the fire in the regular manner.

### Remove Etzim

Given that Rebbi's position — that *etzim* are a *mincha* — is a minority view against the *Chachamim*, the Gemara says: *sami mikan etzim* — remove wood from the list. The *baraita*'s original suggestion that wood might require salt because it is called a *korban* was premised on Rebbi's classification. Since the *Chachamim* do not treat *etzim* as a *mincha*, and since the *baraita* that calls *etzim* a *korban* is most naturally read in line with Rebbi's view, the broader consensus holds that wood does not require salt. Tosafot clarifies: the emphasis on *etzim* being a *korban* in the *baraita* is the language of Rebbi, who gives it full *korban* status; the *Chachamim* acknowledge that one may donate *etzim*, but they do not give it the halakhic character of a *mincha* and therefore do not require salt on it.

---

## Final Exclusions

### Me'al Question

Having worked through the full scope of what requires salt, the Gemara returns to the verse *me'al minchatecha velo me'al damecha* — from your *mincha* and not from your blood — which served throughout as the proof text excluding blood from the salt requirement. The question now is: *ela kra leme'utei mai* — at the end of the day, what is this verse excluding? If blood is excluded by *velo me'al damecha*, what else needed to be said? Is blood the only thing explicitly excluded?

### Blood & Wine

The Gemara answers: *afik etzim ve'ayal nesachim* — remove *etzim* from the included list and add *nisachim* to the excluded list. The two things that are not salted, beyond the excluded category of wood (which was never truly in the category under the view of the *Chachamim*), are blood and the wine of the *nisachim*. The *minchat nesachim* — the flour and oil that accompany a free-will *korban* — is salted, since it is burned. But the wine that is poured down the side of the *mizbeach* is not burned; it is poured. Like blood, which is sprinkled rather than burned, wine is not subject to the salt requirement.

Thus the final picture is clean: blood is sprinkled, wine is poured, and neither is burned. Everything that is burned on the *mizbeach* — the *kometz*, the *levona*, the *imurim*, the *evarim*, the *ketoret*, and all the varieties of *mincha* that are wholly burned — requires salt. These two exclusions, blood and wine, represent the offerings that come to the *mizbeach* by means other than fire. With this, the Gemara's analysis of the salt requirement concludes, and the discussion continues in the following session.

---

---

# Menachot 21

## Salt Requirements

### What Gets Salted

The daf opens with a discussion of which offerings require salting on the *mizbe'ach*. The basic conclusion already established is that one salts things that are burnt on the *mizbe'ach*, but not blood, and there is a question regarding wood — specifically, whether wood is offered as a *mincha* in its own right, or simply used as fuel that is burnt directly. The *gemara* opens with the words *appik eitzei d'ayalu l'nesachim* — "take out wood" (which is debatable, since according to Rebbi wood would be salted as a proper *mincha*) "and put in *nesachim*," the wine libations, which are not burnt but poured down a conduit along one of the *karnot* of the *mizbe'ach*, and therefore do not require salting.

### Four Exceptions

A *braita* is then cited listing four things that do not require salting: *aval hayayin vehadam veha'eitzim vehaktoret ein te'unim melach* — "but the wine, the blood, the wood, and the *ketoreth* do not require salt." Wine and blood are readily understood as things that are not burnt. Wood is back on the list — if one follows the position that it is not a *korban* in its own right but simply serves as fuel, it is excluded. And then there is *ketoreth*, the incense, which is strange, because *ketoreth* is indeed burnt — yet it is burnt on the *mizbe'ach hazahav*, the inner golden altar.

The *gemara* asks: whose opinion does this *braita* reflect? If it is Rebbi's view, then the inclusion of wood is difficult, since Rebbi holds wood requires salting. If it is the *chachamim*, then the inclusion of *ketoreth* is difficult, since *ketoreth* is something that is burnt.

### Ishmael's Criteria

The *gemara* resolves this by attributing the *braita* to a specific *tanna*: *Rabbi Yishmael b'no shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka omer*. He derives the rule from an explicit verse and establishes three criteria for what requires salting: (1) it must be *mekabel tumah* — capable of becoming ritually impure; (2) it must be *oleh l'ishim* — burnt on the altar fire; and (3) it must be placed on the outer *mizbe'ach*. Each criterion excludes one of the problematic items on the list.

### Blood & Wine

The criterion of *oleh l'ishim* — that the item be burnt — excludes blood and wine. Blood is not burnt; nor is wine. Everyone, regardless of position on wood, would agree that since neither blood nor wine is burnt, neither requires salting. (It is worth noting that there is an opinion in the *gemara* that one would sprinkle the wine toward the fire and allow it to be partially burnt; according to that view, salting the *nesachim* might indeed be required.)

### Incense Exception

The criterion of the outer *mizbe'ach* excludes *ketoreth*. The incense is burnt every morning and afternoon, but on the *mizbe'ach hazahav*, the inner golden altar, not on the outer *mizbe'ach*. Hence, despite the fact that *ketoreth* is burnt, it does not meet this third criterion and does not require salting.

### Wood Status

The criterion of *mekabel tumah* — susceptibility to ritual impurity — excludes wood, which is neither food nor a vessel and therefore does not ordinarily become *tamei*. The *gemara* acknowledges a complication: there is a principle of *chibas hakodesh*, by which items dedicated to the *Mikdash* and placed on the *mizbe'ach* attain a heightened significance that renders them susceptible to *tumah*. The *gemara* explicitly includes wood in that category elsewhere. How then can the *mishnah* say wood is not *mekabel tumah*?

Rashi resolves this by saying that *chibas hakodesh* is only a *derabanan* concept; *de'oraisa*, wood is simply not *mekabel tumah*. Tosafot disagrees and considers *chibas hakodesh* to be *de'oraisa*, and therefore offers two alternative explanations. First, Tosafot suggests that whether wood qualifies under *chibas hakodesh* may depend on the very dispute between Rebbi and the *chachamim*: if, like Rebbi, one treats wood as a genuine *korban mincha* — food for the *mizbe'ach*, as it were — then it functions similarly to other offerings and is *mekabel tumah*. If, like the *chachamim*, wood is merely used as fuel and not as an offering in its own right, it does not qualify for *chibas hakodesh* and remains not *mekabel tumah*. Second, Tosafot suggests that *ein mekabel tumah* in this context may simply mean that in ordinary, non-*Mikdash* contexts, wood is not *mekabel tumah*, and that is enough to exclude it from the salting requirement, even if within the *Mikdash* it might technically qualify.

---

## Cooked Blood

### Blood Exclusion

The *gemara* now draws on the exclusion of blood from the *pasuk* itself: *minchascha velo damecha* — "your *mincha*," but not your blood. Were blood not explicitly excluded by the verse, one might have thought it should be salted. This prompts a deeper question: even granting the theoretical possibility of salting blood, once you salt blood it is no longer considered blood in the halakhic sense, and therefore cannot be used for *kaparah*. How could there ever have been a *hava amina* to salt it?

### Cooked Blood

The *gemara* cites the teaching of Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina: *dam shebishlo eino over alav* — if you cooked blood and then ate it, you do not transgress the prohibition of blood. There is no *kares*, and possibly no *de'oraisa* violation at all. The reason appears to be rooted in the connection the *Torah* draws between the prohibition of eating blood and its use on the *mizbe'ach*: it is the *dam shehaneshama yotzeis bo* — the lifeblood that exits at the moment of death — which both carries the prohibition and which is valid for *zerikah*. Once the blood is no longer in its natural state, it is no longer in that category.

### Salt Like Heat

Building on this, Rav Yehuda says in the name of Ze'iri: *dam shemalcho eino over alav* — not only cooked blood, but even salted blood exempts one from the prohibition. This is presumably based on the principle of *maliach harei hu ke-rosei'ach* — salting is equivalent to roasting. This principle is most familiar from the laws of *kashrus*, where the same logic explains how salt draws out blood from meat (as heat would draw it out on a spit), and how a heavily salted food can transfer flavor to other foods, creating concerns about *basar bechalav* or *treifus*. Here, the *gemara* applies the same logic in the other direction: just as cooking transforms blood such that one is no longer *chayav* for eating it, salting also transforms it and removes the prohibition.

### Salted Blood Problem

This creates a genuine difficulty. If salted blood is no longer considered halakhic blood, it would follow that it cannot be used for *zerikah* either. The assumption underlying both rules — the prohibition against eating blood and its use on the *mizbe'ach* — is that they apply to the same substance. If one is exempt from the prohibition of eating, one also cannot use that blood for the *korban*. So how could the *gemara* have entertained any *hava amina* that one should salt the blood at all, given that the act of salting would itself disqualify it for its essential temple use?

The connection is further illuminated by considering *yayin mevushal*: cooked wine cannot be used on the *mizbe'ach*, and significantly, it is also excluded from many of the restrictions of *stam yeinam*, because cooked wine was not relevant to the world of idolatrous worship. The theme is consistent: substances that exist in their natural state — wine, blood — are subject to both their respective prohibitions and their *korban* uses. Cooking or transformation removes them from both categories simultaneously. There is, of course, the entire tractate of Menachot devoted to the *mincha*, which is baked — but the *mincha* is by nature something processed. For blood, wine, and similar items, *bishul* removes them from their fundamental category.

### Salt Quantity

The *gemara*'s resolution is elegant: *mishtaba b'mashehu l'mitzvah d'alma* — the theoretical *hava amina* was that one might have applied just the tiniest amount of salt, a *mashehu*, not enough to constitute a full act of *melicha*, not enough to invoke *maliach ke-rosei'ach*, and thereby perform the *mitzvah* of salting while leaving the blood legally intact. The verse comes to exclude even this minimal approach, because blood — as something not burnt on the *mizbe'ach* — is excluded from the salting requirement entirely.

---

## Congealed Blood

### Congealed Challenge

The *gemara* now turns to the broader teaching of Ze'iri. Rava was sitting and reviewing this teaching when Abaye challenged him from a *braita*: *hikfeh et hadam ve'achalo* — if one congealed the blood and ate it; *o shehimchehu et hachelev u'gma'o* — or if one liquified forbidden fat and drank it. In both cases, the normal mode of consumption has been altered — blood was eaten rather than drunk, *chelev* was drunk rather than eaten. The *braita* rules that one is nevertheless *chayav*. This seems to contradict Ze'iri's position, since congealing blood would appear to be a form of transformation analogous to cooking.

### Fire vs Sun

The *gemara* answers: *lo kashya: kan shehikfeh be'ur, kan shehikfeh bechama* — there is no contradiction, because the two cases involve different mechanisms of congealing. If the blood was congealed by fire, one is exempt; if it was congealed by the sun, one is *chayav*. The *gemara* states the principle explicitly: *be'ur lo hadar, bechamah hadar* — what is done by fire does not revert to its original state; what is done by the sun does revert.

The underlying logic here is worth examining carefully. Ordinarily, the distinction between fire and the sun is invoked in contexts where the nature of the *act* matters — as on *Shabbat*, where one is *chayav* for cooking with fire, the standard human method, but not for leaving something in the sun, which is considered an unusual method. Here, however, the focus is not on the act but on the state of the object. Why should it matter whether it was fire or sunlight?

Rashi explains that the critical variable is irreversibility. Fire produces a genuine, irreversible transformation — the blood changes permanently and is no longer the same substance. The sun, being natural, does not produce that kind of transformation. The blood hardens temporarily, but it can revert to its prior liquid state. It has not truly changed; it is merely in a practically altered condition. The distinction may also reflect whether the process is human-made and thus "manufactured" or natural — what is produced by a natural process remains, in a sense, part of the natural order and can be restored to it.

### Mani's Question

The *gemara* now introduces a related question. Rabbi Mani asked Rabbi Yochanan: *dam shekarash ve'achalo mahu* — if blood congealed and one ate it in its hardened state, is one *chayav*? This appears equivalent to the earlier case of *hikpah et hadam ve'achalo*. Rabbi Yochanan's answer: *ho'il venidchah yidacheh* — since it was already pushed off from eligibility for the *mizbe'ach* in its congealed state, it remains pushed off. One would therefore not be *chayav* for eating it.

### Dichuy Principle

This invokes the principle of *dichuy* — once an item is disqualified from its sacred purpose, it remains disqualified even if it later returns to a fit state. In the context of blood, the argument runs as follows: while the blood is congealed, it cannot be used for *zerikah* and is therefore *dachuy* — pushed off — from the *mizbe'ach*. The assumption underlying the prohibition against eating blood is that it is precisely the blood used on the *mizbe'ach*. If the blood was in a state where it could never have been used on the *mizbe'ach*, perhaps one should not be *chayav* for eating it. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling adopts this reasoning.

This *dichuy* framework also resonates with the broader question of *nosar*: blood that is left over does not lose its physical character as blood, yet it cannot be used for *zerikah*. In that case, however, the blood was never disqualified by a change of state — it simply became *nosar*. The comparison is instructive precisely because it highlights what is distinctive about a state-change disqualification.

### Inner vs Outer

Abaye, challenged by Rabbi Yochanan's silence in the face of the contradicting *braita*, offers a distinction: perhaps the difference lies between blood of the outer *chataot* — *chataos hachitzoniyos* — and the inner *chataos* — *chataos hapnimiyos*. Rav Chisda is then cited for the following rule: congealed blood of an outer *chatas*, if eaten, makes one *chayav*, because the outer *chatas* requires *lekicha vinesinah* — taking the blood and placing it on the *mizbe'ach* — and even congealed blood can be smeared onto the altar. You can take a piece of hardened blood and press it onto the *mizbe'ach*; therefore the blood remains in the halakhic category of valid *korban* blood, and one who eats it is *chayav*. However, blood of an inner *chatas*, if congealed, makes one *patur* if eaten, because the inner *chatas* requires *tevila vahaza'ah* — dipping and sprinkling — and congealed blood cannot be dipped or sprinkled. In that case, the blood is practically disqualified from its required purpose, and therefore eating it does not incur liability.

### Heat Transforms

Rashi and Tosafot are in essential agreement on the underlying structure, though Tosafot's version of Rashi differs from the text of Rashi before us, leading Tosafot to think he is arguing with Rashi when in fact they may agree. The position of our Rashi is as follows: anything transformed by fire — whether cooking or salting — is a complete and permanent transformation. The blood is categorically different, it is *patur* everywhere and for anyone, whether the blood of an inner *chatas*, an outer *chatas*, or ordinary blood from an animal slaughtered in a private context. Sunlight, by contrast, does not transform at all — it merely creates a temporary practical obstacle. The blood is not really different; it is just currently hard and cannot be sprinkled. Given this, the distinction between inner and outer *chatas* applies only to sun-congealed blood: only for the inner *chatas*, where the temporary hardening creates a complete practical disqualification for its specific mode of application, does the *dichuy* argument apply. For sun-hardened blood of the outer *chatas*, and for all ordinary blood (whether from a *korban* or not), the blood remains in its halakhic category and one is *chayav* for eating it.

This reading is critically important: it confines Ze'iri's teaching about cooked blood — and by extension salted blood — to fire-based transformation. The entire exemption of *dam shebishlo* and *dam shemalcho* applies only where fire or salt produces an irreversible state-change. The separate discussion of sun-congealed blood and the inner versus outer *chatas* is a distinct analysis with no bearing on the cooking or salting question.

---

## Halachic Application

### Tosafot Leniency

Tosafot seizes on Ze'iri's teaching and extends it into a broad practical principle: whenever meat is cooked without having been properly salted — as when a piece of meat went directly into the pot — the violation is at most *issur d'rabbanan*. The phrase *eino over alav* could technically mean only that there is no *kares*, while a *lav de'oraisa* might still apply. But Tosafot reads the *gemara* as eliminating even the *de'oraisa* prohibition entirely, leaving only a rabbinic prohibition. This has significant *halakhic* implications in cases of *safek* and in assessing the status of a pot in which unsalted meat was cooked.

### Rambam View

The Rambam never ruled this way. Reading the Rambam in *hilchos* *shechita*, the approach is striking. He rules that if one cooked a heart without first slitting it open to release the blood, one is not *chayav kares* for a bird's heart — because there is not a *kezayis* of blood in the heart of a bird. But for the heart of a large animal: *chayav kares sheharei yesh bo kezayis midam shebetoch halev shechayavim alav kares* — one is *chayav kares*, because there is a *kezayis* of blood that carries the *kares* liability. The Rambam thus essentially ignores the *gemara* of *dam shebishlo* entirely. Perhaps the Rambam held this *sugya* is not *le'halacha*, or perhaps he understood *eino over alav* as referring only to the absence of *kares* while a *de'oraisa lav* still applies. Either way, the Rambam treats cooked blood as carrying a full *de'oraisa* violation, and the extensive practice of generations of women carefully salting meat reflected exactly this understanding.

### Practical Case

The practical stakes of this dispute are real. A common scenario: one purchases a chicken and places it in the oven, only to discover afterward that the giblets — liver and other organs that require special salting or broiling — were left inside in their bag, unsalted, and cooked along with the chicken. The question then becomes whether the chicken and the pot are prohibited, how much leniency can be applied, whether *bitul* or *shishim* is relevant. If one holds that *dam shebishlo* is only *d'rabbanan*, that opens more latitude than if one treats it as a full *de'oraisa* with potential *kares*. As a practical matter, the experience of those who kept meticulous *hilchos dam* treated the prohibition as entirely *de'oraisa*, and the work of properly salting meat was taken with complete seriousness even if, reading this *gemara* carefully, Tosafot would characterize any residual blood after cooking as only *d'rabbanan*.

---

## Congealed Blood (II)

### Rava's View

The *gemara* now records Rava's independent position: *afillu b'chatas hapnimiyos ve'achalo chayav* — even if one ate blood of an inner *chatas* in its congealed state, one is *chayav*. Rava's reasoning: *ho'il u'k'negdo ra'uy b'chatas hachitzoniyos* — since this same type of blood, if it were blood of an outer *chatas*, could be used even in its congealed state (by smearing), it remains within the category of valid *korban* blood. Even the blood of an inner *chatas*, where congealed blood cannot be dipped and sprinkled, is not pushed out of the category of *korban* blood because the outer *chatas* validates congealed blood as a halakhically viable form of *korban* blood. One may not be *yotzei* the *korban* obligation by using it this way, but the person who ate it is nonetheless *chayav*.

### Donkey Blood

Rav Papa draws the logical conclusion: *hilkach, dam chamor shekarash ve'achalo chayav* — therefore, even donkey blood that congealed, if eaten, makes one *chayav*. Donkey blood cannot be used on the *mizbe'ach* at all, and it is congealed. Yet one is still *chayav* for eating it. The reasoning follows from Rava's principle: since blood of the same type — were it *kosher* animal blood — could be used on the outer *chatas* even in congealed form, it remains within the category of blood that carries the prohibition. Non-*kosher* animal blood, and even congealed blood, does not fall out of this category.

The implication for the overall discussion is significant. If the *gemara*'s discussion of congealed blood is understood as applying even to fire-congealed blood (and not only sun-congealed blood), then the entire discussion becomes moot — Rava and Rav Papa push back all congealed blood into the *chayav* category, and the only way to maintain Ze'iri's teaching as practically operative is to confine it exclusively to blood transformed by cooking or salting, which represents a complete and irreversible transformation in a way that mere congealing does not.

---

## Blood Chatzitza

### Blood Chatzitza

The *gemara* transitions to a related topic. Rav Gidel says in the name of Rav Iri: *dam bein lach bein yavesh chotzetz* — blood, whether dry or wet, creates a *chatzitza* for immersion in a *mikvah*. This would apply both to a person immersing and to a *kohen* performing *avoda* who has blood on his body.

### Dried vs Wet

A *mishnah* in Mikvaot is then cited which appears to contradict this: *hadam vehadio veha'dvash veha'chalav — yaveshim chotzetzim, lachim einam chotzetzim* — blood, ink, honey, and milk — when dry, they are a *chatzitza*; when wet, they are not, because in their wet state they are permeable to water and do not block it from reaching the skin.

### Adhesiveness

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — ha d'sarich, ha d'la sarich* — it depends on whether the substance is adhesive. Blood that is wet but sticky is a *chatzitza* because it blocks the water; blood that is wet but flows freely allows water through and is not a *chatzitza*. The principle is that adhesiveness, not mere wetness or dryness, determines whether a substance interposes between the body and the water of the *mikvah*. Honey presents a similar case — loose honey flows off, but thick or adhesive honey would remain and block the water.

---

## Salt Mitzvah

### Timlach Usage

The *gemara* now turns to the *mitzvah* of salting offerings and examines the precise language of the verse: *korban mincha b'melach timlach* — "every offering of your *mincha* you shall salt with salt." The word *melach* already indicates salt; what does *timlach* — the verbal form "you shall salt" — add?

### Sodomite Salt

A *braita* is cited: *b'melach* — with salt — *yachol tedunehu* — perhaps you should saturate it with salt — *talmud lomar timlach* — therefore the verse says "you shall salt it," meaning in the normal manner that people salt things. Continuing: *ei timlach* — if salted — *yachol b'mei melach* — perhaps even salt water would suffice — *talmud lomar b'melach* — no, only actual salt. Then: *v'lo tashbit melach* — "do not let salt rest from your *korban*" — *havei melach she'eina shovetet* — bring salt that does not rest. This means *melach Sedomit*, the salt of Sodom. This is sea salt — Sodom sits at the Dead Sea — and the sea is always producing salt, even on *Shabbat*, which is the reason it is called *she'eina shovetet*: it does not rest. The Aruch explains the phrase precisely this way: sea salt continues to wash up on shores even on *Shabbat*, unlike mineral salt, which requires human labor and therefore would not be mined on *Shabbat*.

### Salt Types

If *melach Sedomit* — sea salt — is the ideal, the *gemara* asks: how do we know that if sea salt is unavailable, one may substitute mineral salt — *melach istrokanit*? From the word *takriv* in the verse, which the *gemara* interprets as *takriv mikol makom* — bring it from wherever available — and *takriv kol shehu* — any type of salt will do. The word *takriv* also teaches: *va'afilu beShabbat* — even on *Shabbat*, the salting of offerings is required; *va'afilu betumah* — even in a state of *tumah*, as is true for any *korban tzibbur* brought in conditions of communal *tumah*, the salting requirement applies equally. Rashi adds that *takriv mikol makom* further means the salt need not come from *Eretz Yisrael* specifically.

### Tavunuhu Debate

The *braita* also states: *yachol tedunehu*, which the *gemara* now attempts to parse. What does *tedunehu* mean? Rabbah bar bar Chana suggests it comes from the word *teven* — straw — meaning one might have thought you should pack the offering in salt the way one packs straw into plaster, an enormous quantity. The verse then comes to teach the normal mode of salting. Abaye objects that the grammar would require *yitbonenu* if the root were *teven*, not *tedunehu*. Abaye himself suggests *tedunehu* means to build up salt layer upon layer, like a structure — *kevinyan*. Rava in turn objects that the grammar for that meaning should be *yivnenahu*. 

### Binah Metaphor

Rav Ashi offers a different reading: *yachol yitein bo ta'am kevinah* — perhaps one should add just a small amount of salt, enough to give a hint of flavor, like *binah* — wisdom — which takes what is dull and gives it depth and refinement, just as a small amount of wisdom elevates a person without overwhelming them. On this reading, the *hava amina* was to use only a tiny, symbolic amount of salt. The verse teaches that the normal manner of salting is required — neither too little nor excessively much.

The Aruch, cited in the margin of the *gemara*, offers yet another interpretation of *tedunehu*: even a small amount, enough to taste the salt — *ad kedei lehavin sheyesh bo ta'am melach*. The verse then teaches that the required amount is the normal way people salt things, which is more substantial.

### Salting Method

The *gemara* clarifies the practical method: *meivi ha'eiver venoten alav melach, vechozer vehofcho, venoten alav melach, umaleihu* — one brings the limb, places salt on it, flips it, places salt on the other side, and then places it on the *mizbe'ach*. One full layer of salt on each side, nothing perfunctory but nothing excessively heavy.

### Pot Comparison

Abaye then adds: *v'chen lakdeira* — and so too for the pot. These two words are of great halakhic significance, and there is a disputed *girsa*: some texts read *v'chen litzli* — and so too for roasting. The difference is substantial. For roasting on an open fire, the blood flows out easily and one does not strictly need salt. If the *girsa* is *v'chen litzli*, then the method described — one layer on each side — is a minimal, essentially perfunctory application, and the same light touch would apply to *korbanot* on the *mizbe'ach*. If the *girsa* is *v'chen lakdeira*, salting for the pot, then the method is more meaningful: the salt must have real force to extract blood without the assistance of heat. On this reading, the method of salting for *korbanot* requires genuine salting, not merely a token gesture — but the verse equally teaches that it should not be excessive, since the *braita* describes a defined and moderate method. The same moderate, effective salt application then informs the halakha of *melicha* for *kashrut*. Sefer Rabbeinu Gershom preserves the *girsa* of *v'chen litzli*, which Tosafot notes creates a certain tension with what precedes.

---

## Salt & Me'ilah

### Me'ilah Status

A *braita* rules: *melach she'al gabei ha'eiver mo'alin bo* — salt that has been placed on the offering itself is subject to *me'ilah*. But salt *she'al gabei hakeves v'sheberosh hamizbe'ach* — salt on the ramp or at the top of the *mizbe'ach*, before it has been placed on the actual *korban* — is not subject to *me'ilah*. Once the salt is applied to the *korban*, it becomes like the *korban* itself and carries the full sanctity. Before that moment, it is available for use and has not yet achieved the status of *me'ilah*.

### Pesuk Source

Rav Papa asks: what is the *pasuk* source? *Hikravtem lifnei Hashem ve'hishlichu hakohanim aleihem melach, vehe'alu otam olah laHashem* — "you shall bring them before God, and the *kohanim* shall cast salt upon them, and bring them up as an offering to God." The *gemara* reads *vehe'alu* — "bring them up" — in the plural, encompassing the salt together with the offering, indicating that once the salt is placed, it is drawn into the sanctity of the *korban* and subject to *me'ilah*.

### Shekalim Source

The *gemara* cites a *braita* from the Talmud Yerushalmi of Shekalim: one of the stipulations of the *Beit Din* was that the *kohanim* were permitted to make use of the wood and salt in the *Mikdash* — *al hamelach v'al ha'eitzim she'hayu hakohanim ne'eisim bahem*. This means that *kohanim* could benefit from these materials without incurring *me'ilah*. For example, a *kohen* working at the top of the *mizbe'ach* on a cold day could warm himself by the fire without concern for *me'ilah*. The *gemara* will now apply this principle specifically to salt.

---

## Salt Locations

### Chamber Salt

A *braita* identifies three locations in the *Mikdash* where salt was stored, each serving a distinct purpose. The first is *lishkat hamelach*, the chamber of salt. Salt from this room was used to salt the hides — *oros kodshim* — of the offerings. Processing the leather of an *olah* or a *chatas* was necessary to make it useful, and the salt from the chamber served this function.

### Ramp Salt

The second location is the ramp, the *keves*. Salt kept there was used to salt the *eivarim* — the limbs of the animals — and the internal organs, all the meat that would be placed on the *mizbe'ach*. This salting was done on the ramp, as the *kohanim* carried the limbs upward toward the altar.

### Top Salt

The third location is the top of the *mizbe'ach*, *rosh hamizbe'ach*. Salt there was used for the non-meat items: *hakometz vehalevona* — the *kometz* and the *levonah*; *haktoret* — the *ketoreth*; *minchas kohanim* and *minchas kohen mashiach* — the *mincha* of the *kohanim* and of the *kohen mashuach*, which are wholly burnt; *minchas nesachim* — the *mincha* accompanying the wine libations; and *olas ha'of* — the bird *olah*. The appearance of *ketoreth* on this list requires comment: *ketoreth* is burnt on the *mizbe'ach hazahav*, the inner golden altar, not on the outer *mizbe'ach*. Why is it salted at the top of the outer *mizbe'ach*?

### Cleanliness Reason

Tosafot explains that the separation between locations reflects a concern for cleanliness. The area where animal limbs are salted is bloody; the area where non-meat items are salted should be kept free of that. Therefore, items like *ketoreth* — even though they will ultimately be burnt on the inner *mizbe'ach* — are salted in the clean space at the top of the outer *mizbe'ach*, rather than in the bloodied salting area on the ramp. The *kohen* would salt the *ketoreth* at the top of the outer *mizbe'ach*, then descend and carry it to the *mizbe'ach hazahav* inside the *heichal*. This is admittedly an indirect route, but it reflects the deliberate organizational logic of the three distinct salting zones.

---

## Salt Usage Rules

### Shmuel View

The *gemara* now addresses what use *kohanim* may make of the *Mikdash* salt under the *Beit Din*'s stipulation. Shmuel rules: *lo shanu ela l'korbanan* — the permission applies only *l'korbanan*, for use in connection with their *korban*. But *achal lo* — for eating, they may not use the *Mikdash* salt. This requires clarification: what does it mean to use the salt "for their *korban*"? And what does "for eating" mean?

### Permitted Uses

The initial reading of Shmuel's statement is that *kohanim* may use the salt to salt the *korban* for burning on the *mizbe'ach*, but not to salt the meat of the *korban* for their own eating. However, this creates an immediate problem.

### Prohibited Uses

The *gemara* objects: if *kohanim* are permitted to use *Mikdash* salt to salt the *oros kodshim* — the hides of the *korbanot* — for their personal use and benefit, surely they should be permitted to use it to salt the *korban* meat they are eating, which is itself a *mitzvah*. Eating *kodashim* is a halakhically mandated act; it can hardly be less permitted than tanning leather. How then can Shmuel restrict the salt?

### Use Distinction

The *gemara* therefore reinterprets Shmuel. *Mai l'korbanan* — what does "for their *korban*" mean? It means *l'achilat korbanan* — for eating the meat of their *korban*. And *mai l'achila* — what does "eating" that is prohibited mean? *Achila d'chulin* — eating non-*korban* food. *Kohanim* were instructed to eat a quantity of ordinary food, or *terumah*, before eating the *korban* itself, so that they would come to the *korban* in a state of *sova* — fullness — and eat it with dignity rather than hunger. One might have thought that since this ordinary eating serves the purpose of *korban* consumption, the *Mikdash* salt could be used for it too. Shmuel teaches: no. Even though that eating serves a *korban* purpose, the salt from the *Mikdash* may not be used for food that is not itself *kodashim*. The distinction is between direct use on *kodashim* — permitted — and serving a *korban* purpose only indirectly — prohibited. Using the salt to preserve the leather of a *korban*, to salt the meat of a *korban*, or to salt any item directly categorized as *kodashim* is permitted. Using it for *chulin*, even *chulin* consumed as part of the process of eating a *korban*, is not.

---

---

# Menachot 22

## Salt & Priests

### Intro & Salting

Today's daf properly begins at the bottom — or perhaps middle — of 21b, treating the practice of salting everything that would be burned in the *Beit HaMikdash*. The salt applied to *korbanot* was provided by the Temple, and this raises a series of related questions about who is entitled to use it and on what basis.

The established position is that *kohanim* are given salt both for the purpose of salting the portions they burn on the *mizbeach* and, by a special stipulation, for salting the *korban* meat they eat. Crucially, this privilege does not extend to salting non-*korban* food they happen to eat alongside their *korban* meal.

### Ravina's Q

Ravina poses a question to Rav Ashi: *pshita* — is it not obvious what the stipulation must have been referring to? If one were to suppose that *Beit Din*'s stipulation was needed to permit *kohanim* to use the salt for burning their *korbanot* on the *mizbeach*, that would be strange. The logic Ravina presses is: *hashta l'Yisrael yahvina le-Kohanim lo yahvina* — if we give salt to an ordinary Israelite who brings a *korban*, why would we imagine that a *kohen* would require a special dispensation to do the same? It follows that the stipulation must have addressed something less obvious: the use of communal salt for eating *korban* meat. But to establish this, the *Gemara* must first confirm that the *Beit HaMikdash* indeed provides salt to everyone who brings a *korban*.

### Baraita Proof

The *Gemara* cites a *Baraita* to address who bears responsibility for providing the salt. One might have thought: *yakhol ha-omer harei alai mincha yavi melach mi-toch beito kederech she-mevi levona mi-toch beito* — perhaps one who vows to bring a *mincha* must also supply the salt from his own home, just as he must provide the *levona* (frankincense). The parallel is apt: when a person vows to bring a *mincha*, the Torah independently mandates that *levona* accompany it; he never explicitly committed to the frankincense, yet it is required of him. So perhaps the salt, equally mandated by the Torah alongside any *mincha*, should similarly be the donor's responsibility.

The *Baraita* frames this as a formal *binyan av*: it says bring a *mincha* and bring salt, and it also says bring a *mincha* and bring *levona*. Perhaps just as *levona* must come from one's own home, so too must salt. On the other hand, one could construct a parallel comparison: it says bring a *mincha* and bring salt, and it also says bring a *mincha* and burn it on wood. If wood is provided by the *Beit HaMikdash*, perhaps salt should be as well.

### Salt Communal

The *Gemara* now weighs these two analogies against each other. Which comparison is more apt — salt to *levona*, or salt to wood?

The argument for comparing salt to wood runs as follows: *danin davar ha-noheg be-khol ha-zevachim mi-davar ha-noheg be-khol ha-zevachim* — we derive the rule for something that applies across all *korbanot* from another thing that applies across all *korbanot*. Salt, like wood, is required for every *korban* that meets certain conditions. *Levona*, by contrast, does not apply universally — it accompanies a *mincha* but not animal sacrifices. So the more natural comparison is salt to wood, and since wood is provided communally, so too salt.

The counterargument is: *danin davar ha-ba imo bi-khli echad mi-davar ha-ba imo bi-khli echad* — we derive the rule for something placed in the same vessel from another thing placed in the same vessel.
