Both the salt and the *levona* are placed together with the *korban* in its vessel before the *kemitza*, making them more integral to the *korban* itself. Wood, by contrast, is never placed in the same vessel; it sits on the fire beneath. Perhaps this vessel-based integration means the salt, like *levona*, is the owner's responsibility.

The *Baraita* resolves this by citing a verse: *berit melach olam hi* — an eternal covenant of salt — which the Torah links to the phrase *me-et benei Yisrael berit olam*, appearing in connection with the *lechem ha-panim*. Just as *lechem ha-panim* is provided from communal funds, so too the salt. The salt is provided *mishel tzibur*, from the public treasury, not by the individual who brings the *korban*.

### Salt Approaches

This raises the question of what conceptual difference exists between the two approaches. On one reading, salt is analogous to the *kometz* — something physically integrated with the *korban* and placed in the same vessel — which might suggest it is the donor's obligation. On another reading, salt is like wood: a universal operating expense of the *Beit HaMikdash* applicable to every *korban*, and therefore logically a communal expense. The *Baraita*'s resolution via the *berit melach olam* verse settles the matter in favor of communal provision, but the underlying conceptual tension between these two ways of understanding salt's status remains instructive.

### Ben Buchri

This brings the *Gemara* back to the original question: given that the *Beit HaMikdash* provides salt for everyone who brings a *korban*, why would *kohanim* need any special stipulation to use it for burning their own *korbanot*? Every Israelite gets that salt automatically — why would *kohanim* be different?

Rav Mordechai explains in the name of Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi: *lo nitzrecha ela le-Ben Buchri* — the stipulation is only necessary according to the position of Ben Buchri. To understand this requires a detour into a famous *Talmudic* dispute.

### Ben Buchri Testify

The *Gemara* cites a *Mishna*: Rabbi Yehuda reports that Ben Buchri testified at Yavneh — *kol Kohen she-shokel eino chotei* — any *kohen* who contributes the *shekel* does not sin. The implication is that *kohanim* were not obligated to contribute to the communal *shekalim* fund; contributing was optional and praiseworthy, but the obligation did not apply to them.

### RYbZ Counter

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai disagreed sharply: *lo ki — ela kol Kohen she-eino shokel chotei* — on the contrary, any *kohen* who does not give the *shekel* sins. According to him, *kohanim* are fully obligated to contribute to communal funds just like any other Israelite.

### Priests' Drasha

The *Gemara* then explains the *kohanim*'s own rationale. They interpreted a verse to their advantage: *ve-khol minchat Kohen kalil tihiyeh lo techachel* — every *mincha* of a *kohen* must be completely burned; it shall not be eaten. Their reasoning: if *kohanim* were to contribute to communal funds, they would thereby acquire a partial ownership stake in all communal *korbanot* — the *shtei ha-lechem*, the *lechem ha-panim*, the *omer*. But a *mincha* that is partly owned by *kohanim* must be entirely burned. Since these communal offerings are not, in fact, burned entirely, the *kohanim* concluded they must have no share in them — meaning they should not contribute to communal funds in the first place. Indeed, they went further: it is not merely that they are exempt; they are positively prohibited from contributing, lest they acquire an ownership interest that would render those offerings invalid.

Returning now to the *Gemara*'s point: according to Ben Buchri, *kohanim* have no stake in communal funds and therefore no inherent right to the communal salt. The salt belongs to those who contributed to the *lishkah*. One might therefore have thought — *salka daitach amina ki zachu lehu rachmana be-Yisrael de-it lehu lishkah* — the Torah granted rights to the salt only to those Israelites who contributed to the treasury. *Ha-Kohanim de-leit lehu lishkah* — the *kohanim*, who have no share in the communal fund, might not be entitled to the salt even for burning their own *korbanot*. Hence, a stipulation was necessary. The *Gemara* does note that even according to Ben Buchri, when *kohanim* do choose to contribute voluntarily, those funds are genuinely transferred to the *tzibur* — *demayiti u-masar lehu la-tzibur* — and so there is no concern about *chulin* entering the *azarah*. But absent that contribution, their claim on communal resources required explicit authorization.

### RYbZ Counter

*(See above — Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's position is treated in context of the Ben Buchri discussion.)*

### Entitlement

This dispute is, on reflection, quite striking. A *Tosafot* notes that since the *kohanim* interpreted this verse *le-atzmanam* — for their own benefit — it implies Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was not himself a *kohen*. A citation in the *Sifrei* regarding the *Parah Adumah* where Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai refers to what "my hands served" is addressed by *Tosafot* as well: this language does not mean he personally performed the service, but rather that it was carried out under his rulings and teaching, and he had forgotten the precise details.

Beyond the textual point, there is something worth dwelling on in the psychology of the *kohanim*'s position. The instinct to say "I work for this institution; I should not have to pay into it" has an obvious surface logic. A *kohen* devotes himself to the *avodah*; why should he also be required to fund it? But Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response — insisting on the obligation to give even a half-*shekel* — captures something important. Being served by an institution and working for it are not mutually exclusive. To exempt oneself from contribution on the grounds of one's role is to establish a posture of pure entitlement, positioning oneself as only a provider and never a recipient. What Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai insists upon is that even those who labor at the center of the institution are also served by it and must participate in sustaining it. This dynamic feels all the more pointed coming from the figure who would lead the transition from a Temple-centered Judaism to a *Torah*-centered one. The critique of *kohen* exemption is, in a subtle way, a critique of a certain priestly self-understanding that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai spent his life pushing against.

There is also a deeper question lurking here: according to the *kohanim*'s position, does that mean all *korbanot tzibur* were brought exclusively on behalf of *Klal Yisrael* excluding *kohanim*? Or is it that the *kohanim* assumed they would of course receive the credit — simply by virtue of being the ones who performed the service — without needing to formally contribute? That kind of assumed entitlement, where one expects the benefits of collective endeavor without formal participation, is precisely what the insistence on giving the *shekel* is designed to correct.

---

## Wood & Fire

### Wood Baraita

The *Gemara* now addresses the question of wood, which had been assumed in the earlier discussion to be provided by communal funds. The basis for this assumption requires its own derivation. A *Baraita* asks: might someone who declares "I hereby take upon myself an *olah*" be required to bring the wood from his own home, just as he must bring *nesachim* from his own home? After all, the *nesachim* — the wine, flour, and water that accompany an animal *korban* — are not something he separately vowed; the Torah simply requires them as an accompaniment. Yet he must provide them. Perhaps the wood is analogous.

The *Baraita* rejects this by citing the verse: *al ha-etzim asher al ha-eish asher ha-mizbeach* — the *kohen* is to arrange the *olah* on the wood that is on the fire that is on the *mizbeach*. The inference: *ma mizbeach mishel tzibur* — just as the altar itself is provided by communal funds as part of the institutional infrastructure of the *Beit HaMikdash*, so too *af etzim va-eish mishel tzibur* — even the wood and fire are communally provided.

### Elazar Fresh

Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua offers a different formulation: *ma mizbeach shelo nishtamesh bo hedyot* — just as the altar was never used by a layperson, *af etzim va-eish shelo nishtamesh bahen hedyot* — so too the wood and fire must not be items that a layperson has used. The concern here is not merely the source of funding but the status of the materials themselves: the wood and fire for the *mizbeach* must be fresh, unused by any private individual.

This raises a practical question about fire, since in an era without matches, fire required active effort to produce. The principle would mean one cannot take a burning log from a private barbecue and use it to light the *mizbeach*; one would need to kindle a genuinely new fire for the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Fresh vs Source

The *Gemara* notes: *mai beinayhu* — what is the practical difference between these two positions? *Ika beinayhu chadta* — the difference lies in new wood. According to the first opinion (wood must come from communal funds), the *Beit HaMikdash* could theoretically purchase secondhand wood — previously used by others — so long as it is now owned and provided by the *mikdash*. The key criterion is the source of provision, not the physical history of the material. According to Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, what matters is whether the wood itself is new, regardless of who provides it.

Conversely, one could imagine wood that is brand new yet donated directly by a private individual. These two positions — communal provision versus newness of material — are therefore genuinely distinct, and both criteria could, in principle, apply or fail independently.

The *Gemara* then asks: does Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua mean that old, used wood simply cannot be brought at all? Does not the verse in connection with David and Aravnah indicate that Aravnah offered the threshing implements — *ha-morigim* — and the cattle implements as wood for the altar? This appears to be a case of used items serving as wood for the *mizbeach*.

### Morag

The *Gemara* resolves this: *hacha nami be-chadatin* — in that case, the implements were brand new; they had been fashioned but not yet actually used for threshing. Despite having been manufactured into instruments, since they had never been put to use, they retained the status of new materials.

This prompts the *Gemara* to clarify the meaning of *morigim*. Ulla explains: *mita shel tarbal* — a spiked board. Rav Yehuda elaborates: *iza de-korkasa* — a thick plank fitted with spikes. Rashi explains that *korkasa* denotes a thick plank and that the device consisted of a heavy spiked board drawn by cattle across the harvested grain, functioning as a threshing implement to separate the kernel from its husk. Rav Yosef adduces the verse: *hinei samticha le-morag charutz chadash ba'al pipiyot tadush harim* — "Behold I have made you like a new sharp threshing sledge with many teeth; you shall thresh mountains." The word *morag* in that verse clearly refers to a threshing instrument, confirming Ulla's identification.

---

## Kometz Mixing

### Kometz Mixed

The *Mishna* now addresses what happens when *korban* portions become mixed together — a topic familiar from parallel discussions in Zevachim concerning blood and animals. The *Mishna* states: *nitarv kometz be-kometz chaveiro* — if a *kometz* becomes mixed with another *kometz* of a different *mincha*, or with the *minchat kohanim*, or with the *minchat kohen mashiach*, or with a *minchat nesachim* — all of these are *korbanot* whose portions are entirely burned — the mixture is *kasher*. Since everything in the mixture must in any case be burned on the *mizbeach*, one simply burns the entire mixture, and every component has received its proper treatment. No portion is lost and no invalid material has been introduced.

The scenario is a practical one: two *kohanim* each take their *kometz*, they collide, the two portions mix in the same vessel. The solution is straightforward: burn everything.

### RY Thick/Thin

Rabbi Yehuda, however, rules differently in two specific cases: if a *kometz* becomes mixed with a *minchat kohen mashiach* or with a *minchat nesachim*, the mixture is *pesulah*. His reasoning: *she-zo bililatah avah ve-zo bililatah rakkah ve-hen bole'ot zo mi-zo* — one has a thick consistency and the other a thin consistency, and they absorb from one another.

The proportions are as follows. A standard *mincha* uses one *issaron* of flour — approximately two and a half liters — combined with one *log* of oil, roughly half a liter: a one-to-five ratio, producing a dough-like consistency. The *minchat nesachim*, by contrast, uses the same quantity of flour but three *log* of oil — a *revi'it* of a *hin*, which is a quarter of twelve *log* — producing a much looser, batter-like consistency. The same higher oil ratio applies to the *minchat kohen mashiach*. When a dense dough-*kometz* and a thin batter-*mincha* come into contact, each absorbs something of the other. The dough becomes somewhat thinner; the batter becomes somewhat thicker. The result is that you no longer have a proper *kometz* of the standard proportions, nor a proper *minchat nesachim* of its proper proportions. Rabbi Yehuda holds that this physical alteration invalidates the mixture.

---

## Nullification

### Blood Water

The *Gemara* now turns to a *Mishna* from Zevachim dealing with mixtures and the principle of *bitul*. If blood of a *korban* falls into water, the rule is: *im yesh bo marit dam kasher* — if the mixture still has the appearance of blood, it is *kasher* and may be sprinkled on the *mizbeach*.

This standard is notably different from the *kashrut* context. In food law, the key criterion for nullification is taste — even a trace detectable amount of a forbidden substance is enough to render something *treif*. Here, however, we are not dealing with food, and the dominant criterion shifts to visual appearance. *Tosafot* clarifies that "the appearance of blood" means something precise: *lo be-admumit me'at makhshir* — a slight reddish tinge is not sufficient. *Ela mar'it dam gamur ka-amar* — it must genuinely look like blood itself, not merely like a pinkish liquid. *Li-mi'utei heikha de-deiha mar'iso* — a pale, watered-down appearance does not qualify.

There is an interesting asymmetry here. In *kashrut*, even a trace amount of the forbidden substance — sufficient to impart flavor — renders the mixture *treif*; a tiny contaminant disqualifies. But here, to establish that the blood remains *kasher* and usable, it is not enough that there be a little blood present; it must truly look like blood. For disqualification, a little goes a long way; for qualification, a strong positive presence is required.

### Blood Wine

If blood becomes mixed with wine, the rule is: *ro'in oto ke-ilu hu mayim* — we treat the wine as though it were water, and then assess whether the mixture would still look like blood in water. If yes, it is *kasher*. *Tosafot* finds this surprising: this is actually a *leniency*, since one would have thought to simply say the red wine overwhelms the blood's appearance and renders it invalid. Instead, we imaginatively substitute water for the wine, which is a less visually dominant medium, and assess the blood's visibility in that hypothetical. *Tosafot* acknowledges some difficulty in identifying the source for this principle, since treating a present substance as something else is not a standard rule of *bitul*.

### Blood Blood

Similarly, if *korban* blood becomes mixed with non-*korban* blood — blood of an animal that was not a sacrifice — the rule is again: *ro'in oto ke-ilu hu mayim* — we treat the non-*korban* blood as if it were water. If the *korban* blood would still appear as blood in that quantity of water, the mixture is *kasher*.

### RY No Null

Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *ein dam mevatel dam* — blood does not nullify blood. According to him, when blood of a *korban* mixes with non-*korban* blood, no *bitul* occurs regardless of proportions, and one can always proceed to *zerikat ha-dam*. The mixture is never invalidated through quantity, because like-substances do not nullify one another.

### YK Blood

Rabbi Yochanan states that both the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda derive their respective positions from the same verse. On Yom Kippur, the *Kohen Gadol* took blood from the bull and blood from the goat — *ve-lakach mi-dam ha-par u-mi-dam ha-sa'ir* — and it is understood that he mixed these two bloods together before applying them to the *karnot* of the *mizbeach*. Yet the Torah still refers to them as both present: the blood of the bull and the blood of the goat remain distinct. This is the shared proof-text. The question is what principle each derives from it. *Ha-davar yadua* — it is well known that the blood of an ox is considerably greater in volume than that of a goat, yet the mixture is still described as containing both. Why?

### Olim

The Rabbis derive: *mikan le-olin she-ein mevatlin zeh et zeh* — from here we learn that things which go up on the *mizbeach* — *korbanot* — do not effect *bitul* upon one another. The reason the mixture is described as still containing both bloods is not because of any inherent property of blood, but because both are *korban* bloods destined for the *mizbeach*. This principle resolves a recurring puzzle from Zevachim, where *mishna* after *mishna* treated cases of mixed *korbanot* — a *chatat* mixed with other animals, various blood mixtures — without invoking *bitul*. The operative rule underlying all those cases is *ein olin mevatlin zeh et zeh*: when the mixed substances are both *korbanot*, they do not nullify each other. Non-*korban* blood, however, can effect *bitul* on *korban* blood.

### Min Bemin

Rabbi Yehuda derives something entirely different from the same verse: *mikan le-min be-mino she-eino batel* — from here we learn that like nullifies not like. According to him, the reason both bloods remain present after mixing is not their *korban* status but the simple fact that they are both blood. The principle is general and has nothing to do with *korbanot* at all. In the realm of *kashrut*, according to Rabbi Yehuda, a drop of *treif* chicken soup falling into kosher chicken soup — however large the quantity of kosher soup — would not be nullified, because the substances are identical: *min be-mino lo batel*. This is a sweeping and practically consequential position. Indeed, *Rashi* rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda on this point, though the accepted *halakha* does not follow *Rashi*.

### Feature Debate

The *Gemara* now probes why each side learns its respective principle rather than the other. The Yom Kippur verse has two features simultaneously: the bloods are *olin* (offered on the *mizbeach*), and they are *min be-mino* (like and like — both blood). Each feature could independently explain why *bitul* is absent. What drives the Rabbis to emphasize the *olin* feature, and what drives Rabbi Yehuda to emphasize the *min be-mino* feature?

The *Gemara* argues: had the Torah provided an example of *olin* with substances that are not *min be-mino* — say, blood and wine — the Rabbis would have a clean proof for the *olin* principle without ambiguity. Since the example happens to also be *min be-mino*, one might counter that it is the *min be-mino* feature that matters. The *Gemara* replies: *hashta de-ashmi'inan olin* — since the Torah chose an example within the world of *olin*, we assume it is the *olin* feature that is determinative. But then: *ve-dilma ad de-ika min be-mino ve-olin* — perhaps you need both features simultaneously: only when substances are both *olin* and *min be-mino* is there no *bitul*? *Kashya* — this remains difficult.

The symmetrical challenge applies to Rabbi Yehuda: had the Torah given an example of *olin* of different types — not blood and blood but two distinct substances — we would have a clean proof for the *olin* principle. *Hashta de-ashmi'inan min be-mino* — since the Torah's example happens to be blood and blood, Rabbi Yehuda concludes that the *min be-mino* feature is salient. But again: perhaps both features are required together? *Kashya*.

The *Gemara* acknowledges that it cannot resolve which single feature — or whether the combination of features — is the true determinant. In the end, the Rabbis intuitively read the verse as establishing a *korban* exception, while Rabbi Yehuda intuitively reads it as establishing the logical principle that like does not nullify like. There is a certain coherent rationale available for each position: *bitul* depends on loss of identity through difference, which is why identical substances retain their identity and resist nullification (Rabbi Yehuda's logic); and there is equally good reason to see this as one of many special rules that govern the world of *korbanot* specifically (the Rabbis' logic). The *Gemara* is candid that neither derivation can be fully grounded from the text alone.

### Liquid Solid

*Tosafot* addresses a problem: throughout Zevachim and elsewhere in *Shas*, there appear to be cases where Rabbi Yehuda seems to admit *bitul* even in cases of *min be-mino*, which would contradict his principle. *Tosafot* works through these cases and arrives at what it considers its most satisfying resolution: a distinction between *lach be-lach* and *yavesh be-yavesh*. Rabbi Yehuda's principle that *min be-mino lo batel* applies specifically to liquid mixtures. When two liquids of the same type combine, they form a single homogeneous mass with no distinguishable identity for the minority component — and Rabbi Yehuda holds that a substance that retains the same identity as the majority cannot be said to lose itself in it. In the case of solids — *yavesh be-yavesh* — the situation is different. Each discrete item retains its separate physical identity, and one can pick up each piece individually and ask: is this the *kasher* one or the *treif* one? The determination is then made by statistical majority (*rov*) rather than by the logic of identity-loss. Rabbi Yehuda may well admit *bitul* in that context. *Tosafot* acknowledges that this distinction does not perfectly resolve every case but regards it as the clearest available answer.

---

## Mencha Mixture

### Similar Mix Q

The *Gemara* now returns to our *Mishna*'s case: the *kometz* mixed with a *minchat nesachim* or *minchat kohen mashiach*, which Rabbi Yehuda holds is *pesulah* because one has a thick consistency and the other thin, and they absorb from one another. The *Gemara* asks a sharp question: *ve-chi balu ze mi-ze mai havei* — so they absorbed from each other; why does that matter? *Min be-mino hu* — it is all *min be-mino*! The oil from the batter-*mincha* that seeps into the dough-*kometz* is mixing with oil that is already there. Both are oil. The flour is mixing with flour. According to Rabbi Yehuda himself, *min be-mino lo batel* — like does not nullify like. So the oil from the *minchat nesachim* that enters the *kometz* should not be *batel* at all, and vice versa. What is the *pesul*?

*Tosafot* is candid that he finds the *Gemara*'s framing puzzling from the outset. The problem with the mixture seems straightforwardly physical: by absorbing from each other, the two *menachot* change their actual oil-to-flour ratios. You no longer have a proper dough-*kometz* and a proper batter-*minchat nesachim*; you have a dough that has become somewhat looser and a batter that has become somewhat denser. Neither one conforms any longer to its required specification. This has nothing to do with *bitul* — it is simply a question of physical alteration of the *korban*. Yet the *Gemara* insists on framing the issue as one of *bitul*, which is what necessitates the answer that follows.

### Flour Nulls

Rava answers: *kasavar Rabbi Yehuda kol she-hu min be-mino ve-davar acher* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that when you have a mixture of *min be-mino* but also *davar acher* — a third, different substance — the rule changes. *Salek et mino ke-mi she-eino* — remove the like-substance from the equation; treat it as if it were not there. *Ve-she-eino mino raba alav u-mevatlo* — the unlike substance then predominates over and nullifies the minority component.

Applied to our case: the oil from the *minchat nesachim* seeps into the *kometz*. Now, there is already oil in the *kometz* — that oil is *min be-mino* and will not create *bitul*. But there is also flour in the *kometz* that is a *davar acher* relative to the absorbed oil. So: ignore the oil-to-oil aspect (it does nothing either way), and what you are left with is: absorbed oil surrounded by flour. The flour is a *davar acher*, and it will *mevatel* the absorbed oil. The absorbed oil loses its identity, meaning the *kometz* is now missing whatever oil was nullified out of it — and the receiving *mincha* is correspondingly deficient. Hence *pesulah*.

### Sages View

This resolution, while addressing Rabbi Yehuda's position, creates a difficulty for the Sages, who rule that such a mixture is *kasher*. If Rava's analysis is correct and there is a genuine *bitul* problem — the flour nullifying the absorbed oil — why do the Sages not agree? The Sages certainly accept the principle of *bitul* in general. If the oil is truly being nullified by the flour, the Sages should also see a problem here. The answer must be that the Sages do not see the physical mixing of these *korbanot* as generating a *bitul* issue at all — perhaps because, as *Tosafot* initially suggested, the problem is one of changed physical proportions rather than *bitul*, and the Sages are not concerned with that degree of incidental absorption. The tension between these positions — and between the *Gemara*'s *bitul*-framing and *Tosafot*'s alternative physical account — is left without full resolution.

---

---

# Menachot 23

## Oil & Minchat Chotei

### Intro: Mixed Menachot

The *gemara* on 23a opens against the backdrop of the *mishnah* that deals with different *menachot* becoming mixed with one another — a dry, doughy *mincha* getting mixed up with a more liquid, batter-like one. The *mishnah* presents two principal positions. The *chachamim* hold that *olim ein mevatlin zeh et zeh* — things that go up on the *mizbeach* do not perform *bittul* on one another. Rabbi Yehuda holds that *min b'mino lo batel* — if it is the same type of thing, *bittul* does not operate. Both positions were introduced on the previous daf and are now brought to bear on a new set of questions that the *gemara* pursues.

### Kometz + Oil: Pasul

The *gemara* opens with an *itmar*: *kometz mi-minchas choteh she-shimno* — what is the law if one takes the *kometz* of a *minchat chotei*, the sinner's meal offering described at the end of Parshat Vayikra, and adds oil to it? This is not immediately obvious as a case of *bittul* at all, but rather a strange scenario in its own right. Rabbi Yochanan rules *pasul*. His reasoning is clear: the *minchat chotei* is required to be *charev* — dry, without oil. By introducing oil, one has transformed it into a different category of *mincha* entirely, and the *kometz* is therefore invalid.

### Resh Lakish: Oil OK

Resh Lakish disagrees. His position is that not only is this permissible, but it is the correct procedure: *hu atzmo meshachshacho bi-sheyarei ha-log u-malo'ehu* — one rubs this *kometz* against the residue of the *log* of oil and thereby gives it a slight coating of oil before placing it on the *mizbeach*. The idea behind Resh Lakish's view appears to be that it is not proper to place anything on the *mizbeach* without some oil. The source of this oil is the film of residue remaining in the measuring vessel after a full *log* of oil has been poured out for a normal, oil-and-flour *mincha* — not the *minchat chotei* itself, which takes no oil.

### Tosafot: Practical Impos…

*Tosafot* immediately raises a question: if there is still a residual film of oil left in the measuring vessel, how was the original *mincha* for which that oil was measured *kasher*? It would have been *chasar shemanav* — lacking its full required oil content. *Tosafot* resolves this with the important principle of *lo nitnah Torah l'malachei ha-shareis* — the Torah was not given to ministering angels. It is practically impossible to extract every last trace of oil from a vessel, and therefore the tiny residual film does not constitute a deficiency. The oil is considered to have been fully dispensed. This principle has broad application in *halacha* — for instance, in the requirement that *tefillin* be perfectly square, the standard of precision demanded must be one achievable by human beings, not angels.

### Pasuk Challenge

A more direct challenge to Resh Lakish emerges from the *gemara* itself. The *pasuk* explicitly states, in the context of the *minchat chotei*, *lo yasim aleha shemen v'lo yiten aleha levonah* — one shall not place oil upon it and shall not place frankincense upon it. This is a direct Scriptural prohibition. How can Resh Lakish permit even a minimal application of oil?

### Resolution: Lo Yikba

The *gemara* resolves this by reading the *pasuk* narrowly: *hahu she-lo yikba la shemen k'chavertah* — the prohibition means only that one should not *establish* for it a mixture of oil like one does for a normal *mincha*. A full oil-and-flour mixture is forbidden. But a slight residual shmear of oil does not rise to the level of *lo yikba*, and is therefore permitted according to Resh Lakish. This is a striking reading, given how absolute the *pasuk* appears on its face, but the *gemara* accepts it as the operative resolution of Resh Lakish's position.

### Challenge: Charev & Balul

Rabbi Yochanan then challenges Resh Lakish from a *braita*: *charev she-nitarev b'valul yakriv* — if a dry *mincha* became mixed with an oil-and-flour *mincha*, one may offer it up. This is the position of the *chachamim*, whose rationale is *ein olim mevatlin zeh et zeh*. Rabbi Yehuda says *lo yakriv* — one may not offer it up. Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Resh Lakish is that this *braita* seems to be discussing precisely his case: the *kometz* of a *minchat chotei* — the dry *mincha* — that became mixed with the *kometz* of a *minchat nedavah* — the normal oil-bearing *mincha*. And the *braita* implies that even according to the *chachamim*, who permit the offering, the only reason they do so is because of *ein olim mevatlin zeh et zeh* — the oil is attributed to the other *mincha*, not to the *minchat chotei*. This would confirm that oil on the *minchat chotei* is indeed a fundamental problem, as Rabbi Yochanan holds, and contradict Resh Lakish's permissive approach.

### Minchat Parim vs. Kvasim

The *gemara* deflects Rabbi Yochanan's challenge on behalf of Resh Lakish: *lo, minchas parim v'eilim b'minchas k'vasim* — the *braita* is not speaking of a *minchat chotei* at all. Rather, it is speaking of two types of *minchat nesachim* — the meal offering that accompanies animal sacrifices — that differ in their oil-to-flour ratios. When a lamb is brought, the *nesachim* call for one *issaron* of flour and a *revi'is ha-hin* of oil, which equals three *log*, giving a three-to-one oil-to-flour ratio. For rams and bulls, the proportions are different: a ram requires two *isronos* of flour and a *shlishis ha-hin*, which is four *log* of oil — a ratio of two-to-one. A bull requires three *isronos* of flour and a *chatzi ha-hin*, which is six *log* of oil — also two-to-one. The *minchat k'vasim* therefore has a proportionally higher oil content than the *minchat parim* and *eilim*, making the latter relatively "dry" by comparison. The *braita*'s reference to *charev* and *balul* describes this contrast, not a *minchat chotei* with no oil at all. Accordingly, Resh Lakish's position regarding the *minchat chotei* remains intact and untouched by the *braita*.

The *gemara* does note that the *braita* explicitly mentions both the case of *minchat parim v'eilim b'minchas k'vasim* and a separate case of *charev she-nitarev b'valul*. The answer is that the latter phrase is simply explaining the former — the *braita* is clarifying why there is a *bittul* problem between these *minchat nesachim*: because the *minchat k'vasim* is oilier relative to the others, making it a case of a relatively dry *mincha* mixed with a relatively oily one. It is a difficult reading, but the *gemara* accepts it in order to protect Resh Lakish's position.

### Squeezed Oil Question

The *gemara* now introduces a question from Rava: *kometz she-mitzah shamno al gabei eitzim mahu* — if one took a *kometz* of flour and oil and squeezed some of the oil out onto wood, what is the law? The operative question is: *chiburei olin k'olin damu o lav k'olin damu* — is something attached to something that goes up on the *mizbeach* treated like the thing that goes up, or not?

Rashi offers two distinct approaches to the case. The first reading understands the wood to be the wood already on the top of the *mizbeach*. The oil is squeezed onto that wood first, and then the *kometz* — now with somewhat less oil — is placed on top. The question is whether we consider the oil that already sits on the wood and the *kometz* placed atop it as one unified offering, such that one has in effect offered a complete *kometz*. This would depend on the principle of *chiburei olin k'olin damu*.

Rashi's second reading understands the wood to be ordinary firewood, unrelated to the *mizbeach*. The oil has been squeezed into this firewood and absorbed. The question then becomes whether the oil absorbed into that wood must itself be placed on the *mizbeach*, since it is connected to — *chiburei* — the flour of the *kometz*, which does go up. This second reading is conceptually rich: it requires us to think of the oil as something added to the *mincha* rather than intrinsic to it — analogous to *levonah*, which is also described in the *pasuk* about the *minchat chotei* as something placed upon the base offering. Just as the *pasuk* says *lo yiten aleha shemen v'lo yiten aleha levonah*, one might understand the oil as an addendum to the fundamental *mincha*, which is flour. If that is correct, then when one takes a *kometz*, the essential component is the flour, and the oil is something attached to it. This raises the startling possibility that perhaps not all of the oil must be offered on the *mizbeach*, since the oil may not be considered as intrinsic as the flour itself. *Tosafot* offers a third approach, though the shiur leaves it aside.

### Chiburei Olin Debate

Ravina raises this question to Rav Ashi: *lav hainu d'Rabbi Yochanan v'Reish Lakish* — is this not already the subject of an existing dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish? That dispute, previously cited in another context, concerns someone who is *ma'aleh* — who offers up — a limb outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, creating a question of liability for *ha'alas chutz*. The rule is that one is liable only if one offers up a *kezayit* of meat. If the limb contains less than a *kezayit* of meat but has a bone that brings the total to a *kezayit*, is that sufficient? Rabbi Yochanan rules *chayav* — liable — because *chiburei olin k'olin damu*, what is attached to something that goes up is treated as if it goes up. Resh Lakish rules *patur* — exempt — because *chiburei olin lav k'olin damu*, attachment does not render something equivalent to the thing going up.

### Oil as Intrinsic vs. Add…

The *gemara* responds that the question about the squeezed oil cannot simply be resolved by reference to the Rabbi Yochanan–Resh Lakish dispute, because the question remains open under either position. One could ask according to Rabbi Yochanan: perhaps Rabbi Yochanan said *chiburei olin k'olin damu* only in the case of bone attached to meat, because a bone is a natural part of the animal — it grows together with the flesh in its natural formation, and one is offering the limb in its natural state. But oil is not a natural part of the *kometz*. Flour and oil do not grow together. The Torah prescribes mixing them together, but the oil is introduced from outside. Perhaps even Rabbi Yochanan would not extend the principle of *chiburei olin k'olin damu* to an externally added substance like oil.

Conversely, one could ask according to Resh Lakish: perhaps Resh Lakish ruled *patur* in the case of bone not because attachment is irrelevant, but because even though bone is natural to the limb, there is no direct *chiyuv* to offer the bone on the *mizbeach*. A bone that falls off the *mizbeach* need not be replaced — this was established in Zevachim. Since there is no direct *mitzvah* to offer the bone, it is not one with the *kezayit* of meat for purposes of liability, despite their natural attachment. But oil is different: oil is never supposed to be separated from the *kometz*. If the oil is absorbed into the wood, it has been improperly separated from what it belongs to. By that logic, perhaps even Resh Lakish would say the oil must go up along with the *kometz*.

### Teiku: Unresolved

The *gemara* reaches no resolution and concludes with *teiku* — the question is left unresolved. The underlying conceptual tension, particularly striking in light of Rashi's second reading, is the possibility of treating oil as something additive rather than intrinsic to a *mincha* — a perspective one would not have arrived at naturally, yet which the *gemara* takes seriously enough to leave open.

---

## Two Unmeasured Mixed

### Separate Measurement Wor…

The *gemara* turns to the next *mishnah*, which presents a series of cases involving *menachot* that have become partially mixed before the *kometz* is taken. The image is that of two circles overlapping: *mincha* A and *mincha* B each retain distinct sections, but there is an AB overlap zone where the flour and oil of both have blended into a single homogeneous mass. The *mishnah* rules: *im yakhol likmotz mi-zo bifnei atzmah u-mi-zo bifnei atzmah, kesherot* — if one can take a full *kometz* from the A section alone, and a full *kometz* from the B section alone, without relying on the AB overlap, both *menachot* are *kesherot*. One simply takes the *kometz* from each distinct section, and the overlapping zone does not compromise either offering.

### Cannot Separate: Pasul

However, if one cannot take a full *kometz* from A alone or from B alone — if a complete *kometz* can only be formed by drawing from the AB overlap — then both *menachot* are *pasul*. In that case, any *kometz* taken for A will inevitably include flour and oil from B, and vice versa, rendering neither *kometz* a valid one from its own *mincha*.

### Kometz + Unmeasured

The second case: a *kometz* that has already been taken from *mincha* A falls and becomes mixed with *mincha* B, which has not yet had its *kometz* taken. Here the *mishnah* rules *lo yaktir* — one should not offer this mixture on the *mizbeach*. The reason is that B has not yet had its *kometz* separated, and offering the entire mixture would mean placing B on the *mizbeach* — something only the *kometz*, not the *shirayim* and certainly not an un-*kamtzed mincha*, may be placed on the *mizbeach*.

### If Offered: One Kosher

Nevertheless, if one went ahead and offered the mixture in violation of this ruling, the *mishnah* states: *zo she-nikmetza alta liba'alim, vezo she-lo nikmetza lo alta liba'alim* — A, whose *kometz* was properly taken, counts and fulfills the owner's obligation, since the valid *kometz* was offered up. B does not count, because no *kometz* was ever properly taken from B; the entire mass of B was burned without the prior step of *kemitza* having been performed.

### Kometz Back to Shirayim

The third case: a *kometz* is taken from A and then accidentally dropped back into A's own remainder (*shirayim*), or the *kometz* of A is dropped into the *shirayim* of B. In either situation, the *mishnah* again rules *lo yaktir* — one should not offer this. The prohibition here derives from a *derasha*: the verse *kometz mimenu leishim* teaches that once a portion of a *mincha* has gone up to the *mizbeach*, the remainder may not be offered up. Offering the *kometz* together with the *shirayim* would place the *shirayim* on the *mizbeach*, which is a *lav*.

### Offered: Kometz Works

Yet if one violated this and offered the mixture anyway — *v'im hiktir, alu liba'alim* — it counts and the owner's obligation is fulfilled. The reason is that one has nonetheless performed a valid *kemitza* and that *kometz* was offered on the *mizbeach*, even if it was mixed together with *shirayim* at the time of the offering. The *kemitza* remains valid, and therefore the *mincha* is *kasher*.

---

## Rav Chisda: Bittul Rules

### Neveilah Batel to Schechu…

The *gemara* introduces a new principle from Rav Chisda. If one has three pieces of meat — one piece of *neveilah* (an animal not properly slaughtered) and two pieces of *shechutah* (properly slaughtered meat) — and one needs to determine whether *bittul* operates, Rav Chisda rules: *neveilah betelah bishchutah* — the *neveilah* is *batel* to the *shechutah*. The reason is *she'ei efshar lishchutah she-te'aseh neveilah* — because it is impossible for the *shechutah* to become a *neveilah*. Once an animal has been properly slaughtered, that piece of meat can never revert to *neveilah* status. This matters for the larger framework Rav Chisda is developing, as will become clear.

### Shechutah Not Batel

The reverse case does not work. If one has two pieces of *neveilah* and one piece of *shechutah*, the two pieces of *neveilah* do not perform *bittul* on the *shechutah* — they do not cause it to be treated as *neveilah* for purposes of *tumah*. The reason is *she'efshar le-neveilah she-te'aseh shechutah* — because it is possible for the *neveilah* to become like the *shechutah*. How? *Delichi masracha, parchah tumatah* — if the *neveilah* were to spoil and decompose, its *tumah* would depart. A spoiled *neveilah* no longer carries the status of *neveilah* and is no longer *tamei*. In that sense, the *neveilah* could theoretically arrive at a status similar to that of the *shechutah* — not *tamei* — and therefore *bittul* does not apply.

### Min B'Mino Framework

The *gemara* now establishes the conceptual framework underlying Rav Chisda's principle. The cases of *neveilah* and *shechutah* involve meat and meat — physically the same substance. Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina are operating within the model of *min b'mino lo batel*, which is the position of Rabbi Yehuda. The standard understanding of Rabbi Yehuda is that *min b'mino* means the same physical object: blood with blood, *mincha* with *mincha*. What Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina are doing is *narrowing* Rabbi Yehuda's rule. It is not enough, they are saying, that objects be physically identical. For Rabbi Yehuda's *min b'mino lo batel* to apply, the objects must also have a sufficiently close relationship in terms of their *halakhic* status.

### Rav Chisda: Look at Meva…

Rav Chisda's formulation is that one looks at the *mevatel* — the majority, the thing performing the *bittul*. If the *mevatel* can never achieve the same status as the minority, then despite being the same physical substance, it is considered *min b'eino mino* with respect to status, and *bittul* does occur. In the case of the *shechutah* majority trying to perform *bittul* on the *neveilah*: the *shechutah* can never become a *neveilah*, and therefore it is treated as *min b'eino mino*, *bittul* operates, and the *neveilah* is nullified. But in the reverse case — where the *neveilah* majority tries to perform *bittul* on the *shechutah* — the *neveilah* could spoil and lose its *tumah*, thereby arriving at a status comparable to the *shechutah*. That makes it *min b'mino*, and no *bittul* occurs.

### Rabbi Chanina: Look at B…

Rabbi Chanina articulates the same principle but measures it differently: *kol she-efshar lo lihyot kamohu eino batel* — whatever is capable of becoming like the thing doing the *bittul* is not *batel*. Rabbi Chanina looks at the *batel* — the minority, the thing at risk of being nullified — rather than the *mevatel*. If the minority could potentially achieve a status similar to the majority, it is *min b'mino* and does not undergo *bittul*. If it cannot, it is *min b'eino mino* and *bittul* applies. Applied to the *neveilah*/*shechutah* cases: when there are two *shechutah* pieces and one *neveilah*, the *neveilah* (the *batel*) could spoil and lose its *tumah*, thereby becoming like the *shechutah* — so it is *min b'mino* and is not *batel*. When there are two *neveilah* pieces and one *shechutah*, the *shechutah* (the *batel*) can never become *neveilah* — it is *min b'eino mino*, and the *shechutah* is therefore *batel* to the *neveilah* majority.

### Whose Position?

The *gemara* asks whose position Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina are interpreting. If they are working within the framework of the *rabanan*, this makes little sense: the *rabanan* hold that only *olim* are not *mevatel* one another, but *min b'mino* is *batel* according to the *rabanan*. And if they are working within Rabbi Yehuda's framework, there is a difficulty: the established understanding of Rabbi Yehuda is that *min b'mino* means physically identical objects — *batar chazuta azil* — he goes by appearance. He has never been understood to condition his rule on the alignment of *halakhic* statuses.

### Narrowing Rabbi Yehuda

The *gemara* resolves this by identifying the text being interpreted: it is a *braita* of Rabbi Chiya, who teaches that *neveilah* and *shechutah* perform *bittul* on one another. Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina are both interpreting this teaching of Rabbi Chiya, each restricting it in a different directional sense. And they are doing so within the framework of Rabbi Yehuda's *min b'mino lo batel*. The *gemara* confirms that this is indeed a narrowing of Rabbi Yehuda: when Rabbi Yehuda says *min b'mino lo batel*, this is true only where the objects are physically identical *and* where their *halakhic* statuses are sufficiently close — only then is there no *bittul*. Where the objects are physically the same but their statuses have no realistic overlap, even Rabbi Yehuda would agree it is *min b'eino mino* and *bittul* applies. The debate between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina is purely over *which* party's status one examines to make this determination.

---

## Apply to Menachot

### Why No Bittul to Overlap?

Having established the principle, the *gemara* now attempts to apply it to the *mishnah*'s cases of mixed *menachot*, and in so doing tries to determine whether the *mishna* supports Rav Chisda's view or Rabbi Chanina's. The opening case is the scenario of the two *menachot* that overlap — A, B, and the AB zone. The *gemara* notes that once one takes the *kometz* from A, the remaining flour of A together with the AB overlap becomes *shirayim*. One might then ask: why don't those *shirayim* perform *bittul* on B's section of the AB overlap, thereby ruining B's *kometz*? After all, once A's *kometz* is taken, the *shirayim* are no longer *olim* — they do not go on the *mizbeach* — so the principle of *ein olim mevatlin zeh et zeh* no longer applies to them. And if it is not *olim* performing the *bittul*, the *mishnah* should be a question of *min b'mino* between the *shirayim* and B.

One must figure out which position this *mishnah* reflects. If it goes according to the *rabanan*, the *rabanan* hold that only *olim* do not perform *bittul* on one another — and *min b'mino* is still *batel* according to the *rabanan*. The *shirayim* are no longer *olim*, so *bittul* should apply and B should be compromised. But the *mishnah* does not say that — it says B remains *kasher*. So the *mishnah* must be going like Rabbi Yehuda. Fine — but then comes Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina's refinement of Rabbi Yehuda. If one goes by the *mevatel* (Rav Chisda's approach): the *mevatel* here is the *shirayim* of A, endangering B. Can the *shirayim* become like B — i.e., like an un-*kamtzed mincha*, a *tevel*? The *shirayim* can never retroactively become like an untaken *mincha*. So according to Rav Chisda, the *shirayim* and B would be *min b'eino mino*, *bittul* should operate, and the *mishnah*'s ruling that B remains *kasher* is difficult. If one goes by the *batel* (Rabbi Chanina's approach): the thing at risk of *bittul* is the AB overlap belonging to B. Could that portion of B become like the *shirayim* of A? Yes — once the *kometz* is taken from B, its remainder will also become *shirayim*. So from Rabbi Chanina's perspective, B is *min b'mino* with A's *shirayim*, and no *bittul* occurs. The *mishnah* would thus support Rabbi Chanina's view.

However, before this can be treated as a proof, the *gemara* considers whether the entire framing is necessary.

### Rabbi Zeira: No Bittul

The *gemara* answers that in the context of a *mincha*, a special rule applies regardless: *hatam k'Rabbi Zeira* — there it goes according to Rabbi Zeira.

### Derasha Source

Rabbi Zeira stated: *ne'emar haktara b'kometz v'ne'emar haktara b'shirayim* — the verb *haktara* (burning/offering) appears both in connection with the *kometz* and in connection with the *shirayim*. Regarding the *kometz*, the *pasuk* commands its offering. Regarding the *shirayim*, the *pasuk* says *ki chol se'or v'chol devash lo taktiru mimenu isheh la-Hashem* — one may not offer up on the *mizbeach* something from which a portion has already gone up to the *aish*, the altar fire. The same verb *taktiru* is used, one as a *chiyuv* and one as an *issur*, indicating that the *kometz* and the *shirayim* occupy a parallel and linked halakhic category. The consequence of this linkage is that just as one *kometz* does not perform *bittul* on another *kometz* — which is obvious, since they are identical and *min b'mino lo batel* — so too the *shirayim* do not perform *bittul* on the *kometz*, and by extension, no *bittul* operates among the components of a *mincha* at all.

### Rabbi Zeira Applies Here

This same principle of Rabbi Zeira is then applied to the second case of the *mishnah*: the *kometz* of A that falls into the un-*kamtzed* B. Here the *gemara* was troubled by why the *tevel* of B — which is a *mincha* not yet *kamtzed* — should not perform *bittul* on the *kometz* of A. According to the *rabanan*, they are not *olim* in the relevant sense that would trigger *ein olim mevatlin zeh et zeh*, and they are physically both *mincha* material. Rabbi Yehuda would normally say *min b'mino lo batel*, but that requires the statuses to be aligned (per Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina). Since a *kometz* can never become like an un-*kamtzed mincha*, and an un-*kamtzed mincha* cannot become a *kometz* without a proper act of *kemitza*, the statuses are not close — and *bittul* should apply. Yet the *mishnah* says A's *kometz* remains valid. Rabbi Zeira's principle resolves this: when it comes to the components of a *mincha*, there is no *bittul* between *kometz* and *shirayim*, or between *kometz* and *tevel*, as an independent *halakhic* rule derived from the *pasuk*.

### Testing Frameworks

The *gemara* then tests whether this case — apart from Rabbi Zeira — could be resolved by the frameworks of Rav Chisda or Rabbi Chanina on their own terms. Going by the *mevatel* (Rav Chisda): the *mevatel* here is B, the un-*kamtzed mincha*. Can B become like A, the *kometz*? Yes — *d'chol purtza chazi l'mikmatz*, any part of B is eligible to be the *kometz*. So by Rav Chisda's reading, B is sufficiently close in status to A, making it *min b'mino*, and no *bittul* would apply. This supports the *mishnah*'s ruling. Going by the *batel* (Rabbi Chanina): the thing at risk of *bittul* is the *kometz* of A. Can the *kometz* of A ever become like B — like an un-*kamtzed mincha*? No. The *kometz* has already been separated; it cannot revert to the status of an untaken *mincha*. So by Rabbi Chanina's reading, it is *min b'eino mino*, and *bittul* should apply — which contradicts the *mishnah*. This would seem to refute Rabbi Chanina's position — but the *gemara* again deflects: *ha nami k'Rabbi Zeira* — this case too is governed by Rabbi Zeira's special principle, not by the general *bittul* framework. No proof can be drawn.

### Kometz & Shirayim

The *gemara* extends Rabbi Zeira's principle to the third case: the *kometz* of A that falls back into A's own *shirayim*, or into B's *shirayim*. The *gemara* now tests this case as well. Here, the *shirayim* and the *kometz* are clearly different things — neither can become like the other. The *kometz* cannot become *shirayim*, and the *shirayim* cannot become a *kometz*. Whichever direction one looks — whether by the *mevatel* (Rav Chisda) or by the *batel* (Rabbi Chanina) — these are *min b'eino mino*, and *bittul* should apply. Yet the *mishnah* says that if offered, the *kometz* counts. Why no *bittul*? This is precisely where Rabbi Zeira made his original statement: *amar Rabbi Zeira — ne'emar haktara b'kometz v'ne'emar haktara b'shirayim* — the *pasuk* establishes that *kometz* and *shirayim* are in a linked halakhic category and do not perform *bittul* on one another. That is the core of Rabbi Zeira's teaching. The earlier references to his principle were applications of this rule to adjacent cases; here is the original source.

The *gemara* thus concludes that the entire series of *mishnah* cases cannot be used to adjudicate between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina, because the *mincha* domain is governed by Rabbi Zeira's independent principle — one that may apply even according to the *rabanan*, not only according to Rabbi Yehuda.

---

## Spiced Matza Test

### Spiced Matza Kosher

The *gemara* makes one final attempt to resolve the debate between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina from a *braita* regarding *matzah*. The *braita* teaches: *tibelah b'ketzach* — if one spiced one's *matzah* with black cumin, *b'shumshemin* — with sesame, or with any other type of spice, *kesherah* — it is still *kasher* as *matzah*. *Matzah hi* — it retains the status of *matzah* — *ela she-nikret matzah metubellet* — but it is called "spiced *matzah*."

### Challenge: Bittul?

The *gemara* frames this as a potential challenge by assuming — in the limiting case — that the volume of spices actually exceeds the volume of *matzah* in a given section. Why then do the spices not perform *bittul* on the *matzah*, rendering it no longer *matzah* for the *mitzvah* of the *seder* night?

### Rav Chisda's View

Testing Rav Chisda's framework: one looks at the *mevatel* — the spices, which are in the majority. Can the spices ever become *matzah*? No — spices can never become *kasher matzah* for the *seder*. So they are *min b'eino mino*, and *bittul* should apply. But the *braita* says the *matzah* is still *kasher* — a challenge to Rav Chisda's framework.

### Rabbi Chanina's View

Testing Rabbi Chanina's framework: one looks at the *batel* — the *matzah*, which is in the minority. Can the *matzah* become like the spices? *Delakhi me'akhsha havei lei k'tavlin* — if the *matzah* spoils, it becomes like spices in the sense that it is no longer usable for the *mitzvah* of *matzah*. So the *matzah* could arrive at a status similar to that of the spices, making it *min b'mino*, and no *bittul* would occur. This supports the *mishnah*'s ruling. It would thus seem to be a proof for Rabbi Chanina over Rav Chisda.

### Resolution: Matza Majori…

The *gemara* dismisses the challenge: *hacha b'mai askinan — de-lo afshi lei tavlin* — the case in the *braita* does not involve a majority of spices at all. *De-ruba matzah hi* — the *matzah* is the majority. That is why there is no *bittul*. The *braita* never contemplated a scenario where spices dominate; it describes spiced *matzah* in which the *matzah* predominates.

### Inconclusive Proof

The *gemara* confirms this reading from the *braita*'s own language: it says *matzah hi* — it *is matzah* — which implies that the *matzah* constitutes the essential and majority substance. *Shema mina* — that reading of the text is confirmed. But as the *gemara* acknowledges, once this is the correct reading of the *braita*, it says nothing about a case where spices outnumber *matzah*, and therefore it contributes nothing to the debate between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina. The attempted proof collapses.

It is worth noting an additional subtlety here. The case of spiced *matzah* involves *min b'eino mino* — *matzah* and spices are fundamentally different substances. Up to this point, the entire discussion of Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina has been framed as a refinement *within* Rabbi Yehuda's principle of *min b'mino lo batel* — an extra requirement of halakhic-status proximity, layered on top of physical identity. The spiced *matzah* case tried to use the status framework alone, setting aside the physical dimension entirely. But the *gemara* rejected the proof entirely on other grounds, leaving the debate between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Chanina — as well as whether their narrowing of Rabbi Yehuda's position is operative *halakha* — without definitive resolution.

---

---

# Menachot 24

## Kli Metzaref

### Rav Kahana's Teaching

The daf opens at the end of 23b, picking up from a lengthy discussion concerning the mixing of *menachot* and questions of *bittul* and *min b'mino* according to Rabbi Yehuda. We now turn to a distinct topic introduced by the phrase *ki salik Rav Kahana* — when Rav Kahana went up to Eretz Yisrael, he found the sons of Rabbi Chiya (*bnei Rabbi Chiya*) sitting and discussing the following *halacha*.

### Two Piles Combining

The case: an *isaron* — the flour designated for a *mincha* — has been divided into two separate piles, not touching one another, and placed together in a single vessel. A *tvul yom* then touches one of the piles. The *tvul yom* is someone who has immersed in a *mikvah* that day and will be fully *tahor* that evening, but for now retains the status of a *sheni l'tumah*, sufficient to render *terumah* or *kodesh* items *tamei*. This serves as an example of someone with a minimal level of *tumah* who can still effect contamination of sacred items. The question — *mahu?* — is whether his touching one pile renders the other pile *tamei* as well.

The basis for thinking it might is a well-known *mishna* in Chagiga: *kli metzaref mah sheb'tocho l'kodesh* — a vessel combines whatever is inside it when dealing with *kodesh* items for the purposes of *tumah v'tahara*. But perhaps that principle only applies when the items inside the vessel are actually touching one another. Maybe when the two piles are entirely separate, the *kli* cannot bridge the gap between them. Or perhaps, as the other possibility runs, it makes no difference — even completely separate piles within the same vessel are considered one unit. One might further ask: if they are touching one another, why would the *kli* need to do any combining at all? Even if each pile retains its distinct shape — perhaps because oil has already been mixed into each — two piles merely touching are not yet a single unit, and without the *kli*, a *tvul yom* touching pile A would need pile A to independently transfer *tumah* to pile B, which it might not be able to do in the ordinary workings of *hilchot tumah*.

### Metzaref vs Mechaber

Rav Kahana responded to the *bnei Rabbi Chiya* with a careful linguistic observation: *mi tnan kli mechaber?* — the *mishna* does not say the vessel *joins* the contents. It says *kli metzaref* — it *combines* them. The word *mechaber* would imply the vessel fuses them into a single physical unit, which would presuppose actual contact. *Metzaref*, by contrast, denotes a less tight form of connection — the items remain distinct, yet the vessel draws them together. This language itself signals that even in the absence of direct contact, the vessel connects all its contents. Therefore, even across an air space, if one pile is touched it renders the other *tamei*.

### Extraneous Flour

The discussion continues: *hoshit echad beineihen mahu?* — what if one places an additional half-*isaron* between the two proper halves? This third pile does not belong to the *mincha*; it is extraneous. Rav Kahana replied: *tzarich l'kli kli metzarfo, ein tzarich l'kli ein kli metzarfo* — something that requires the *kli shares* to constitute a *mincha* is combined by the vessel; something that does not require it, that has no proper claim on the vessel, is not combined by it. The extraneous flour is therefore not drawn into the *tziruf* and does not participate in the connection.

### Air Space Transfer

A further question: *hoshit tvul yom et etzba'o beineihem mahu?* — what if the *tvul yom* did not touch either pile directly but inserted his finger into the air space between pile A and pile B? If the two piles are considered a single combined unit, perhaps the air space between them is also suffused with the status of *mincha*, and touching that air space should be enough to transfer *tumah* to everything. Rav Kahana rejected this: *ein lecha davar shemitamei me'avir ela kli cheres bilvad* — nothing transmits *tumah* through air space except a *kli cheres*. The principle of *kli metzaref* combines the discrete physical items that need the vessel and are appropriate to it; it does not convert the air inside the vessel into an extension of those items. *Tumah* still travels by direct contact. The *kli* simply treats all such items as one, so that touching any one of them affects all — but only if an item is actually touched.

### Kli Cheres Exception

This ruling clarifies the scope of *kli metzaref*: it is a principle of combination for *kodesh* items that belong within the vessel, not a principle that fills the vessel's interior with a continuous field of *tumah*. The transmission of *tumah* through air — *tumah me'avir* — is a separate and exceptional concept, confined to *kli cheres* by explicit *halacha*. The two principles must not be conflated.

---

## Tziruf Kli & Kometz

### De'Oraita Question

Having taught the *bnei Rabbi Chiya*, Rav Kahana now turned the tables and posed his own question to them: *mahu likmotz mizeh al zeh, tziruf de'oraita o derabbanan?* Can one take a *kemitza* from one of the two separate piles in the *kli shares* and have it count as a valid *kemitza* for the entire *mincha*? The deeper question is whether *tziruf kli* — the combining effected by the vessel — operates at the *de'oraita* level or only *derabbanan*. The potential *de'oraita* basis would be the verse *kaf achat asara zahav*, from which one might derive that everything in a *kaf* is considered a single unit. If *tziruf kli* is *de'oraita*, then the two piles genuinely constitute one *mincha* and a *kemitza* taken from one serves the whole. If it is only *derabbanan*, the combining may be no more than a stringency for *tumah*, and *de'oraita* the piles remain distinct — so that even in the same vessel they would not constitute a valid *mincha* and the *kemitza* would not be properly taken.

### Two Menachot Proof

The *bnei Rabbi Chiya* acknowledged they had no direct answer — *zu lo shamanu* — but they had heard something in a related context from which they believed a proof could be drawn. The *mishna* teaches: *shtei menachot shelo nikmetzu venitarvu* — two *menachot* that have not yet had the *kemitza* taken from them became mixed together. In such a case, if one can take the *kemitza* from the A-section alone and from the B-section alone — meaning each *mincha* still has a portion that remains unmixed with the other — both are valid, because a pure A *kemitza* and a pure B *kemitza* were each taken. But if the mixing is so thorough that the overlap area is required for either *kemitza*, both are invalid. The Gemara reads this *mishna* as implying that the A-section, the AB-overlap, and the B-section are three separate piles, not touching. Yet the *kemitza* from A can combine with the flour in the mixed AB pile, which only makes sense if they are all in the same *kli shares* and *tziruf kli* is working to make them one — even for purposes of validating the *kemitza*. This would suggest *tziruf kli* operates at the *de'oraita* level.

### Comb Analogy

Rava challenged this proof: *dilma b'gushim hamachulakim asuyim k'masreik* — perhaps the *mishna* is not describing three separate non-touching piles at all. Rather, the configuration resembles a comb (*masreik*): the base of the comb is the mixed AB section, and the separate teeth of the comb are the pure A portion and the pure B portion. Everything is in fact touching; there are simply sub-regions that are purely A and purely B emerging from a shared base that contains both. On this reading the *mishna* requires no appeal to *tziruf kli* bridging a gap, and the question of whether *tziruf kli* is *de'oraita* remains unanswered.

### Mimenu Braita

Rava himself then offered a different source: *ta shma, detanya, v'herim mimenu — mimenu min hamachubar*. The *pasuk* governing the *kometz* requires that the taking of the handful be from a single connected unit. The *braita* derives from *mimenu* that one may not divide the *isaron* into two separate vessels and take the *kemitza* from one of them. The implicit inference is: *ha b'kli echad dumya d'shnei kelim* — but if it were in one vessel, even if it resembled two vessels in being two separate piles, it sounds as though the *kometz* would be valid. This seems to be a solid proof that *tziruf kli* works at the *de'oraita* level to make a *kemitza* valid.

### Compartmented Vessels

Abaye qualified the proof: *dilma shnei kelim heichi dami k'gon kviza b'kava* — perhaps what the *braita* is ruling out when it disqualifies "two vessels" is a specific configuration, namely a measuring vessel (*kfiza*) carved within a larger vessel (*kava*), where the dividing wall between the compartments runs the full height of the vessel. In that case, even if the flour in the two compartments happens to touch above the rim, the division below makes it as though there are two separate vessels — and that is what the *braita* rejects. The scenario the *braita* considers valid, on this reading, is one in which the dividing wall ends before the top of the vessel — like a trough for chickens (*arivata shel tarnegolim*), as Rashi explains — so that the contents of the two compartments touch one another within the walls of the vessel itself. That is what the *braita* means by "one vessel similar to two." But fully separate, non-touching piles without even that upper connection are not addressed by the *braita* at all. The question — *heicha dela nagei klal tiba'ei lach* — therefore remains open.

---

## External Connections

### Water Connection

Rami bar Yirmiyah posed a sequence of thought experiments pushing the logic of *tziruf kli* further. The first: *tziruf kli v'chibur mayim mahu* — what happens when the principle of *kli metzaref* intersects with a connection by water? As Rashi explains the scenario: pile A and pile B are inside the vessel, and pile C is outside the vessel, connected to pile B through a flowing liquid — perhaps the oil from B is running outward and making contact with C. Normally a connection through liquid between two separate food items might be sufficient to treat them as joined. The question is whether, when A touches B via *tziruf kli* inside the vessel, the *tumah* then continues outward to C via the liquid connection. Do we say *kli metzaref mah sheb'tocho l'kodesh* applies only to items on the inside of the vessel — *hanei milei d'gavai, aval d'barai lo* — or do we say that since there is a connection, the connection simply continues — *keivan d'mchaber, mchaber* — and C is pulled along as well? It should be noted that Tosafot struggles with this Gemara, since it is not at all obvious why a liquid connection between B and C would ordinarily combine them for purposes of *tumah*; the Gemara seems to take it as a given that liquid does connect them and confines the question to whether *tziruf kli* extends across that connection.

### Extending Tumah

The next step is the reverse direction: *chibur mayim v'tziruf kli, v'naga tvul yom mi'bachutz mahu* — what if a *tvul yom* touched C, which is outside the vessel? Because C and B are connected by liquid, B becomes *tamei*. Now, since B and A are inside the same vessel, would *tziruf kli* transfer the *tumah* from B to A? The argument against it: when does the principle of *kli metzaref* operate? Perhaps only when the *tumah* originates within the vessel — *ki tnan kli metzaref hanei milei d'naga mi'gavai* — so that if one touches A inside the vessel, the *tumah* jumps to B, and vice versa. But if the original touch occurred outside the vessel on C, and C contaminated B, the initial *tumah* event occurred outside the vessel. Perhaps in that case *tziruf kli* does not carry it further to A. Or perhaps it makes no difference — *o dilma lo shna*.

### Tumah Origin (Teiku)

The Gemara leaves both questions unresolved — *teiku*. The underlying difficulty, as noted, is the very premise that liquid connection ordinarily would combine B and C; but leaving that aside, whether *tziruf kli* can extend *tumah* outward to an externally connected item, and whether the *origin* of the *tumah* — inside or outside the vessel — affects the principle's operation, remain open questions.

---

## Sava Lei Tumah

### Tvul Yom on Zav

Rava raised a new question: *isaron shechilko, v'nitma echad mehen, v'hiniach b'visa, v'chazar tvul yom v'naga b'oso tamei mahu*. You have an *isaron* divided into two piles, A and B, not yet in a vessel. Pile A is touched by a *zav* and becomes a *rishon l'tumah*. Then both A and B are placed together in the same vessel. Since A was already *tamei* before being placed in the vessel, it does not transfer its existing *tumah* to B through *tziruf kli* — the combining principle only operates when *tumah* occurs within the vessel, not when something already *tamei* is introduced into it. So B remains entirely *tahor*. A *tvul yom* then comes and touches A while it is in the vessel. The *tumah* event now occurs within the vessel: the *tvul yom* touches A, and this should cause A's *tumah* to transfer to B via *tziruf kli*. The complication is that the *tvul yom* is himself a *sheni l'tumah*, and touching him would make A a *shlishi* — a far weaker level of *tumah* than the *rishon* A already is. Does the act of touching A matter at all? *Mi amrinan sava lei tumah* — do we say A is already "sated" with *tumah* at a high level and cannot receive an additional weaker level? Or do we not say this — *o lo* — and A does indeed become a *shlishi* as well, and that *tumah* event within the vessel then activates *tziruf kli* to make B *tamei*?

### Sheet & Midras

Abaye challenged the premise that we would ever say *sava lei tumah*. He cited a *mishna* in Kelim: *sadin tamei midras* — a sheet has contracted *tumah* as a *midras*. The concept of *tumah* through *midras* derives from the explicit verses — *kol hamishkav asher yishkav alav hazav yitma, v'chol hamerkav asher yirkav alav hazav yitma* — that anything serving as a sitting or lying surface for a *zav* or *zava* becomes an *av hatumah*, even without direct physical contact. So the sheet used as bedding by a *zav* is an *av hatumah*. Now the owner declares he is no longer using it as a sheet and hangs it as a curtain (*vilon*) dividing two rooms. Since it no longer functions as a surface for lying or sitting, it can no longer carry *tumah* as a *midras*; the *tumah* of *midras* requires that the object continue to function as something upon which one sits or lies. Yet the *mishna* rules *aval tamei maga midras* — it retains the *tumah* of having touched a *midras*. This is a striking ruling: the sheet touched no external *midras*; it *was* a *midras*. The answer is that while it was a *midras* it was also simultaneously touching itself, and so when the *midras* status departs, the status of having touched a *midras* remains, leaving it as a *rishon l'tumah*. The sheet held two levels simultaneously — *av* and *rishon* — and the departure of the higher level leaves the lower one behind, which implies that something can indeed hold a weaker level of *tumah* alongside a stronger one.

### Rabbi Yosi Dispute

Rabbi Yosi in the *mishna* disputed this reasoning: *v'chi b'eizeh midras naga zeh?* — this sheet never touched a *midras*; it *was* a *midras* and that is a different matter entirely. Merely being a *midras* does not confer the status of having *touched* a *midras*. However, Rabbi Yosi conceded: *ela ela shennaga bo hazav, tamei maga hazav* — if a *zav* actually touched the sheet directly, then when the *midras* status departs, the sheet retains the *tumah* of having been touched by a *zav*, leaving it as a *rishon*. And if the sheet was a *midras* by virtue of the *zav* sitting on something above it — so that the *zav* never touched the sheet directly — then when it becomes a curtain it is entirely *tahor* according to Rabbi Yosi.

The Gemara now draws an inference from Rabbi Yosi's position: when a *zav* did touch the sheet, *ki naga bo hazav mi itamei* — it is indeed *tamei*. And presumably, Rava argues, this includes a case where the *zav* touched the sheet *after* it was already a *midras* — meaning the sheet was already an *av hatumah*, and a *zav's* touch can ordinarily only make something a *rishon*, yet Rabbi Yosi would accept that it acquired that *rishon* status in addition. If so, this would prove that an object that already has a high level of *tumah* can still acquire a weaker level on top of it — *sava lei tumah* does not apply.

### Rabbi Yosi Dispute

Rava replied: *u'mi mayiti d'hai shennaga bo hazav l'vatar midras?* — what grounds are there to assume that Rabbi Yosi was describing the *zav* touching the sheet after it was already a *midras*? Perhaps the reverse sequence is meant: first the *zav* touched the sheet, making it a *rishon*, and then the *zav* sat on it, making it a *midras* and an *av*. In that case, the lighter *tumah* came first and then the heavier *tumah* was added — *tumah chamurah al tumah kalah* — and of course something can accumulate levels when they arrive in ascending order. That is entirely unremarkable. But in our case — *aval hacha d'eidi v'eidi tumah kalah* — whether both levels of *tumah* are similarly light, or a lighter one comes after a heavier one, there may well be a reason to say that the earlier, stronger *tumah* prevents the later, weaker one from registering. So the argument from Rabbi Yosi's case remains inconclusive, because we do not know the sequence Rabbi Yosi had in mind.

### Multiple Tumah Levels

The Gemara then tries to prove from the *seifa* of that same *mishna*: *modeh Rabbi Yosi* — Rabbi Yosi concedes the following. If two blankets are folded one atop the other, and a *zav* sits on the top one, both blankets are *tamei midras* — both are cushions of the *zav* — but the *zav's* body only physically contacts the upper one. Now the upper blanket (A) is a *midras* directly by the *zav*, and the lower blanket (B) is also a *midras* because it too is a surface the *zav* makes use of, but additionally, B was touched by A, which is a *midras*, giving B also the status of *maga midras*. The *mishna* rules that the upper blanket is *tamei midras* and the lower is *tamei midras* and *maga midras*. But B was already an *av* by virtue of being a *midras* — why does it also receive the lighter status of *maga midras*? Does Rabbi Yosi not say *sava lei tumah*?

### Simultaneous Levels

The Gemara resolves this: *hatam b'vat achat, hacha b'zeh achar zeh* — there it happened simultaneously; here it is sequential. At the very moment B became a *midras*, it also became a *maga midras*, because both events occurred in the same instant. There is no objection to something holding multiple levels of *tumah* if they arise at the same time — it is only the question of adding a weaker level *after* the fact of a higher level that is in dispute. The case of the two blankets therefore does not resolve whether *sava lei tumah* applies when a lighter *tumah* arrives subsequent to a heavier one already present. The question accordingly remains open.

---

## Lost & Replaced

### Three Halves Setup

Rava raised another question, one that the lecturer aptly characterizes as a "Schrödinger's *mincha*." An *isaron* is divided into two halves, A and B. B is then lost. A replacement half is set aside to take B's place — call it B-prime — so the *mincha* is now to consist of A and B-prime. Then B, the original lost half, is found. All three — A, B, and B-prime — are now sitting together in the same vessel.

### Connection Logic

The crux of the problem is that the *kli* is *metzaref*, it combines — but which piles does it combine? Either B or B-prime is the true second half of the *mincha* together with A, but both are in the vessel. The *tziruf* accordingly operates in ambiguous directions.

### Lost Tamei Transfer

*Nitma avud* — if B, the originally lost half, becomes *tamei*: then *avud v'rishon mitztarfin* — B and A are connected, because B's only legitimate partner is A, not B-prime. *Mufrash ein mitztaref* — B-prime does not become *tamei* through B, since there is no connection between B and B-prime; they are both competing, as it were, for A's position, but they have no relationship to one another directly.

### Replacement Tamei

*Nitma mufrash* — if B-prime becomes *tamei*: then *mufrash v'rishon mitztarfin* — B-prime and A are connected. *Avud ein mitztaref* — B does not become *tamei* through B-prime, for the same reason: B and B-prime have no point of connection to one another.

### Original Tamei

*Nitma rishon* — if A becomes *tamei*: then *shneihem mitztarfin* — both B and B-prime become *tamei*, because A is potentially connected to either of them, so *tziruf kli* carries the *tumah* in both directions.

### Household Unity

Abaye went further: *afilu nitma echad mehen nami shneihem mitztarfin* — even if any one of the three becomes *tamei*, all three become *tamei*. His reasoning: *kulhu bnei bikta dehadadi ninhu* — they are all members of the same household. Even though B and B-prime have no direct connection to each other, they are both connected through A, and all three share the same vessel. Abaye uses the analogy of a household with three siblings: A and B are half-brothers through their mother, A and B-prime are half-brothers through their father. B and B-prime share no direct relation — yet they all live under one roof, and what affects one affects all. Abaye's rule is a stringency (*lechumra*): even *tumah* originating in B or B-prime flows to all three.

### Kometz Consumed

The same logic governs the *kemitza*. *Kamatz min ha'avud* — if the *kometz* was taken from B: then *shirayu v'rishon ne'echalin, mufrash eino ne'echal* — what remains of B after the *kemitza*, together with A, may be eaten; the *mincha* has been defined by the act of taking from B as consisting of B and A. B-prime may not be eaten, since B-prime is not the same *mincha* as the one defined by B and A.

### Indeterminate Kometz

*Kamatz min hamufrash* — if the *kometz* was taken from B-prime: then what remains of B-prime and A may be eaten; B may not. *Kamatz min harishon* — if the *kometz* was taken from A: then *shneihem einam ne'echalim* — neither B nor B-prime may be eaten.
