The reason is that a *mincha* consists of precisely one *isaron*, and when the *kometz* is taken from A, it is entirely indeterminate whether B or B-prime is the second half of this *mincha*. Since the one that is *not* part of the *mincha* cannot be eaten — it is *kodesh* but not designated for this offering — and since it cannot be determined which is which, neither B nor B-prime may be consumed. Abaye added his characteristic stringency here as well: *afilu kamatz me'echad meihem shneihem einam ne'echalim* — even when the *kometz* is taken from B or from B-prime, neither B nor B-prime may be eaten, because *kulhu bnei bikta dehadadi ninhu* — all three are members of one household, and B-prime retains its indeterminate status regardless of whether the *kometz* was taken from B.

### Deficient Kometz

Rav Papa raised a difficulty: if A and B-prime and B are all treated as part of the same *mincha* due to their household unity — with B and B-prime in an indeterminate relationship to the *mincha* — then the *kometz* taken from A effectively represents three piles. The *kometz* ought to work for A and whichever of B or B-prime is the true second half, but it cannot simultaneously represent three halves when the *mincha* only consists of two. One could think of it as follows: one-third of the *kometz* is working for A, one-third for B, and one-third for B-prime — but only two of those thirds are legitimate, since only two halves constitute the actual *mincha*. That means a third of the *kometz* is not legitimately accounted for, which represents a *kometz* that is effectively only two-thirds of what it should be. Expressed differently: a sixth of B and a sixth of B-prime are not properly covered by this *kometz*, so there is a portion of the offering — approximately a sixth — that cannot validly be offered up. Rav Papa son of Rav Masharshiya sharpened the question further: it is not merely the *shirayim* that are problematic — *kometz gufeh heichi karev?* — how can the *kometz* itself be offered at all? *Ha'ika tilta d'chulin* — one-third of it is *chulin*, representing whichever of B or B-prime is not actually part of the *mincha*.

### Kohen's Intent

Rav Ashi resolved both difficulties: *kometz b'da'atei d'kahana talya milta* — the *kometz* is determined by the intent of the *kohen*, and *ki kamatz isaron ka kamatz* — when the *kohen* takes the handful, he is taking it as a *kometz* from a single *isaron*. It is true that the identity of the second half of the *isaron* cannot be objectively determined — is it B or B-prime? — but the *kohen* is not taking a *kometz* from an *isaron* and a half. His intent is to serve whichever *isaron* this actually is, however indeterminate that may appear from the outside. We do not say the *kometz* is working for three piles, thereby invalidating a third of itself. Rather, because the *kohen's* intent governs the *kometz*, and his intent is squarely for one *isaron*, the *kometz* is valid — and the question of which half is B and which is B-prime does not fractionate the *kometz* or render part of it *chulin*.

---

---

# Menachot 25

## Tzitz Meratzeh

### Mishnah: Tamei/Yotzei

The Mishnah that opens our discussion introduces a fundamental rule governing the *tzitz*, the golden headplate worn by the *Kohen Gadol*. The Mishnah presents two contrasting cases. In the first, the *kometz* — the handful of flour taken from a *mincha* offering, which serves as the operative element validating the sacrifice — became *tamei* and was nevertheless offered on the *mizbeach*. The ruling is *hatzitz meratzeh*: the *tzitz* renders it acceptable. Despite the *tumah*, the *korban* is valid *b'dieved*.

In the second case, the *kometz* was taken outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, thereby acquiring the status of *yotzei*, and was then offered on the *mizbeach*. Here the ruling reverses: *ein hatzitz meratzeh*. The *tzitz* does not render the *korban* acceptable.

### Tzitz Mechanism

The Mishnah thus establishes a clear asymmetry: the *tzitz* forgives the problem of *tumah* — or more precisely, it alleviates the *tumah* status in a way that preserves the *korban*'s validity — but it does not do so for the disqualification of *yotzei*. It is important to note from the outset what *meratzeh* does and does not mean. The *tzitz* does not in any moral sense absolve the sin; rather, it wipes away the invalidating consequence of the *tumah* with respect to the *korban*'s status. The *korban* becomes *leratzon*, acceptable before God, despite the *tumah* that affected the *kometz* or, in an analogous case, the blood of an animal sacrifice.

---

## Braita: Tzitz Power

### V'nasa Aharon

The Gemara opens with a *braita* deriving the scope of the *tzitz*'s power from the verse *v'nasa Aharon es avon hakodashim* — "and Aaron shall bear the sin of the sacred offerings" (Shemos 28:38). The *tzitz* is the instrument through which Aaron carries, and thereby removes, that sin. But this immediately raises the question: which sin, precisely, does the *tzitz* carry?

### Not Pigul

The *braita* methodically tests each candidate. Could the *tzitz* cover the sin of *pigul* — a sacrifice rendered invalid through the improper intention to offer or eat it outside its designated time? No. The Torah in that context explicitly states *lo yeichashev* — it shall not be reckoned, categorically invalidated. Where the Torah has spoken an absolute negation, the *tzitz* cannot override it.

### Not Nosar

Could the *tzitz* cover *nosar*, the sin of meat left over beyond its permitted time? Again, no. There the Torah states *lo yeiraize* — it shall not be acceptable. *Tosafos* helpfully notes that the *braita* cannot literally mean the disqualification of *nosar* itself, since the *tzitz* functions to validate the *korban* at the time of the *avodah*, and *nosar* is a problem that arises only afterward. Rather, *Tosafos* understands the *braita* as addressing the intent to eat at the wrong time, analogous to *pigul*. In any case, any form of wrong thought — wrong time, wrong place, or other disqualifying intent — is explicitly excluded by the Torah's own language.

### Tumah Hutra

What remains? *Ha eino nosei ela avon tumah shehutra miklala b'tzibbur* — the *tzitz* carries only the sin of *tumah*, which is itself in certain circumstances overridden or permitted. The principle is *tumah hutra b'tzibbur*: when a communal sacrifice must be brought and the *kohanim* or the offering are *tamei*, the Torah itself permits proceeding. Rabbeinu Tam adds a further dimension: the end of the verse reads *l'ratzon lahem lifnei Hashem* — it shall be *leratzon*, acceptable, before God. This phrasing implies that the *tzitz* can only confer *ratzon* on something that in other circumstances already admits of *ratzon*. Since *tumah* is sometimes overridden and the offering proceeds acceptably, *tumah* is the category that the *tzitz* addresses. This is also why the operative term throughout is *meratzeh* — making it *leratzon*.

---

## Rav Zeira Challenge

### Yotzei Proposal

Rav Zeira challenges the *braita*'s conclusion. Perhaps the *tzitz* covers not *tumah* but *yotzei* — the very disqualification the Mishnah contrasted with *tumah*. His reasoning: *shehutar miklalo b'vamos* — during the era when *bamot*, private altars, were permitted, there was no category of *yotzei* at all. When there is no *Beis Hamikdash*, offering outside its boundaries is not only not prohibited but is precisely how sacrifices are brought. Since the Torah in that historical context permits what we otherwise call *yotzei*, one might argue that *yotzei* too "admits of *ratzon*" in other circumstances, and therefore qualifies as the sin the *tzitz* covers.

The question is admittedly a subtle one. During the era of *bamot*, there is no *halacha* of *yotzei* — nothing is taken "out," because there is no defined sacred space from which one can exit. Still, the underlying logic of the question is that since the Torah has not always treated offerings outside a central sanctuary as categorically impermissible, the *psul* of *yotzei* might be considered lighter and thus subject to the *tzitz*'s power.

### Abaye: Lifnei Hashem

Abaye rejects this proposal by returning to the verse's phrasing. *L'ratzon lahem lifnei Hashem* — the *ratzon* must be achieved *lifnei Hashem*, before God, in the *Beis Hamikdash*. The sin that the *tzitz* addresses must be one that arises *lifnei Hashem*, within the sacred precincts. The disqualification of *yotzei*, by contrast, is defined precisely by the fact that the offering left that space — the problematic act occurred outside, not inside. Accordingly, the verse cannot be read as empowering the *tzitz* to address it.

---

## Rabbi Ila Challenge

### Smol Proposal

Rabbi Ila proposes another candidate. Perhaps the *tzitz* covers the *avon* of *smol* — the disqualification that arises when a *kohen* performs the *avodah* with his left hand rather than his right. Such an *avodah* is invalid. And yet, Rabbi Ila notes, this too admits of an override: *shehutar miklalo b'Yom HaKippurim*. On Yom Kippur, when the *kohen gadol* carries the fire pan in his right hand and the incense pan in his left, the *avodah* with the left hand is not only permitted but required. Since the left hand has been accepted in that context, perhaps *smol* too qualifies as an *avon* that the *tzitz* can address.

### Yom Kippur Exception

Abaye again provides the decisive rebuttal. *Avon avon shehaya bo vedachtay* — the *tzitz* addresses something that is inherently problematic but is being overridden or pushed aside in other circumstances. *Tumah hutra b'tzibbur* exemplifies this: *tumah* is always an *avon*, always a problem, but under communal necessity the Torah overrides it. The left hand on Yom Kippur is categorically different. On that day, performing the *avodah* with the left hand is not a problem being overridden; it is precisely how the Torah prescribes that the *avodah* must be done. It is not an *avon* at all in that context. There is therefore no parallel with *tumah*, and the *tzitz* cannot address *smol*.

---

## Avon Hakodashim

### Kodshim vs. Makdishim

Rav Ashi offers a different and, as he reads it, more straightforward derivation from the verse itself. The verse says *v'nasa es avon hakodashim* — the sin of *hakodashim*, of the sacred objects themselves. This is a remarkable precision. The *tzitz* addresses only *avon hakodashim* — a defect inherent in the sacrificial object — not *avon hamakdishim* — a defect introduced by the action of those who offer it.

This immediately eliminates the case of *smol* without requiring Abaye's argument. If a *kohen* performs the *avodah* with his left hand, the problem lies entirely with his action, not with the sacrifice itself. The *kodashim* — the animal, the blood — bear no intrinsic defect. The problem is entirely in the *makdishim*, the officiating *kohen*. The verse's plain language therefore excludes any *psul avodah* from the *tzitz*'s scope. The *tzitz* addresses only something wrong with the *korban* itself, such as *tumah* affecting the blood or the *kometz*.

Rav Simi son of Rav Idi (and some say, Rav Simi son of Rav Ashi) then pressed Rav Ashi: perhaps the *tzitz* covers the case of a *baal mum* — a blemished animal — which is also a defect of the *kodashim* themselves. And where do we find that *baal mum* "admits of *ratzon*" in some circumstances? With birds. The Torah requires *tamim* (unblemished) and *zachar* (male) only for animal offerings — *tamus vezachros bivehema* — but for bird offerings, the Torah does not require either. So there is a sense in which *mum* is not universally an *avon* of the sacrifice.

Rav Ashi responds: the Torah itself preempts this argument. In the context of *baal mum*, the verse states *lo yeratzeh* and *ki lo leratzon yihiyeh lachem* — it shall not be acceptable, the precise opposite of *leratzon*. Just as *pigul* and *nosar* were eliminated by explicit Torah negations, *baal mum* is eliminated the same way. What remains, definitively, is *tumah* — and only *tumah* — as the *avon* the *tzitz* is empowered to address.

---

## Shogeg/Mezid Distinction

### Dam Tamei

A second *braita* introduces an important qualification. *Dam shenitma v'zarko beshogeg hurtzah, b'meizid lo hurtzah* — blood that became *tamei* and was then sprinkled: if done *b'shogeg*, unintentionally — either because the *kohen* was unaware of the *tumah* or did not realize it was prohibited to proceed — the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* and the *korban* is valid. If done *b'meizid*, intentionally, the *tzitz* is not *meratzeh*.

This requires clarification. The Gemara will make clear that the *shogeg/meizid* distinction here is not a matter of *d'oraita* law — the *tzitz* in principle operates regardless of intent. Rather, the exclusion of the *meizid* case is a Rabbinic *knas*, a fine: we do not wish the sinner to benefit from his violation (*choteh niskar*), so the Rabbis imposed the penalty of invalidating the *korban* when the *tumah* was knowingly disregarded. The *korban* must then be brought again.

### Yachid vs. Tzibbur

The *braita* then qualifies the qualification: *bameh devarim amurim, b'yachid* — when is the *shogeg/meizid* distinction applied? Only for an individual's *korban*. *Aval b'tzibbur, bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid hurtzah* — for a communal sacrifice, the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* whether the violation was intentional or not. Indeed, the concept of *meizid* is somewhat difficult to apply in the communal context given the principle of *tumah hutra b'tzibbur*, and in any case the Rabbis did not extend the *knas* to communal sacrifices.

### Oved Kochavim

A non-Jew (*oved kochavim*) may bring a *korban*, and the *braita* addresses that case as well. *Bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid bein b'ones bein b'ratzon, lo hurtzah* — whether unintentional or intentional, whether under compulsion or willfully, the *tzitz* does not render a non-Jew's *korban* acceptable when there is a problem of *tumah*. This is understood as a *d'oraita* limitation: the verse says *l'ratzon lahem*, "for them" — specifically for *Bnei Yisrael*.

One might wonder: why does it matter whether a non-Jew's *korban* is *hurtzah*? Two practical implications present themselves. First, a non-Jew may have taken a vow and depends on the *korban* to fulfill it; whether the *korban* is valid bears on whether that obligation is discharged. Second, and more tangibly, the *kohanim* may not eat the meat unless the *korban* was valid. Since a non-Jew can sanctify a *korban*, the question of validity determines whether the meat is permitted.

---

## Braitot Conflict

### Meat/Chelev

The Gemara now introduces a further *braita* that complicates the picture. *Al mah tzitz meratzeh? Al hadam, v'al habasar, v'al hachelev shenitma* — what does the *tzitz* make acceptable? Blood, meat, and fat that became *tamei*. This is a significant expansion. The validity of a *korban* hinges on the blood (*dam*) or, in the case of a *mincha*, the *kometz* — not on the meat or the fat (*chelev*). The *chelev* is burnt on the *mizbeach* and the meat is consumed by the owners, but neither is what makes the *korban* valid. To say that the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* for meat and *chelev* suggests that its operation extends beyond validating the *korban* itself to somehow alleviating the *avon* associated with those elements. This is a conceptually new dimension of the *tzitz*'s power, to which we will return.

Moreover, this *braita* says the *tzitz* works *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid bein b'ones bein b'ratzon, bein b'yachid bein b'tzibbur* — in all cases, with no distinction for individuals between *shogeg* and *meizid*.

### Contradiction Emerges

The contradiction is stark. The first *braita* restricts the *tzitz*'s effectiveness to *shogeg* for individuals, while this second *braita* applies it in all cases without distinction.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef proposes the straightforward resolution: the two *braitot* reflect a *machloket*. One represents the position of *Rabbanan* who impose a *knas* for *meizid*; the other represents Rabbi Yosi, who does not. The analogy for this debate is the *terumah* case.

---

## Terumah Parallel

### Terumah Min Tamei

The *braita* used to establish this pattern: one may not separate *terumah* from *tamei* grain to cover *tahor* grain — that is, one should not take *terumah* from the *tamei* pile when the *tahor* pile is available, thereby giving the *kohen* *terumah teme'ah* when *terumah tehorah* was possible. *V'im taram beshogeg terumato terumah, b'meizid ein terumato terumah* — if one did so *b'shogeg*, the *terumah* takes effect; if *b'meizid*, Rabbinically it does not. This is the *knas* for intentional violation.

### Rabbi Yosi: Mezid OK

Rabbi Yosi dissents: *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid terumato terumah* — even if done intentionally, the *terumah* takes retroactive effect. Rabbi Yosi does not impose the *knas*. The structural parallel is clear: a case involving *kodesh* in some sense (*terumah*), a problem of *tumah*, and a debate over whether *meizid* is penalized. Rav Yosef therefore identifies the *braita* that permits *meizid* with Rabbi Yosi, and the *braita* that restricts to *shogeg* with the *Rabbanan*.

---

## Attribution Debate

### Rabbi Yosi/Meat

The Gemara scrutinizes this attribution carefully. Even granting that Rabbi Yosi's *terumah* position aligns with not penalizing *meizid*, the second *braita* says two things: it works even *b'meizid*, and it works for meat and *chelev*. Attributing the *braita* to Rabbi Yosi would therefore require Rabbi Yosi to hold both positions. Does Rabbi Yosi indeed say that the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* for *achilos*, for the things being consumed?

### Braita: RE vs. RY

A named *braita* speaks directly to this question. *Rabbi Eliezer omer: hatzitz meratzeh al ha'achilos* — Rabbi Eliezer says the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* for *achilos*. *Rabbi Yosi omer: ein hatzitz meratzeh al ha'achilos* — Rabbi Yosi says it is not. The explicit attribution is thus exactly the reverse of what Rav Yosef's attribution would require: it is Rabbi Eliezer who extends the *tzitz* to meat, and Rabbi Yosi who restricts it.

---

## Ipoch: Reverse Names

### Proposed Reversal

The Gemara suggests: *ipoch* — reverse the names. Given that this is an oral tradition and names can become transposed, perhaps it was Rabbi Yosi who said the *tzitz* works for *achilos* and Rabbi Eliezer who said it does not.

### Harmony via Reversal

If reversed, the second *braita* — which says the *tzitz* works for blood, meat, and fat without regard to intent — could consistently be attributed to Rabbi Yosi: he neither penalizes *meizid* nor restricts the *tzitz* to the *korban*-validating elements.

---

## Rav Sheshet Refutes

### Cannot Reverse

Rav Sheshet objects that the reversal is impossible. An independent source establishes that it is indeed Rabbi Yosi who holds that the *tzitz* does not work for *achilos* — so the original attribution cannot be reversed. The names as transmitted are accurate: Rabbi Eliezer extends the *tzitz* to meat; Rabbi Yosi does not.

---

## Tamei Eats Meat

### Yachol Basar

At this point the Gemara introduces a *braita* on what might appear to be a different topic, but which will prove essential to identifying the authorship of the disputed *braitot*. The *braita* addresses when a *tamei* person incurs *kares* for eating *basar kodshim*. One might have thought: if a *tamei* person ate meat of a *korban* before *zerikas damim* — before the blood was sprinkled on the *mizbeach* — he would be liable for *tumah*. Perhaps the verse's prohibition applies even in that case.

### Nitur Letahorim

The *braita* rejects this. The verse says *kol tahor yochal basar* — only one who is *tahor* may eat the meat — and then describes the *tamei* person who eats from *zevach hashelamim* as incurring *kares*. The *braita* derives: the operative category is *hanitir l'tehorim* — meat that has been made permissible for *tahorim*. Only meat that has reached that state of permissibility is subject to the *kares* prohibition for a *tamei* person eating it. Before *zerikas damim*, the meat is not yet permitted even to *tahorim*; it therefore does not fall within the verse's prohibition, and a *tamei* person who eats it does not incur *kares* for *tumah* (though it remains *assur* and may implicate *me'ilah*).

### Sha'at Kosher Test

The *braita* then refines the principle. One might ask: does "permitted to *tahorim*" mean currently permitted, or does it mean that the meat once had a moment of permissibility — a *sha'at kosher*? This distinction matters for cases like *lan* (meat left overnight, becoming *nosar*) and *yotzei* (meat taken outside the *Beis Hamikdash*). In those cases, the blood was sprinkled and the meat had a moment when *tahorim* could eat it, but subsequently became forbidden. A *tamei* person who eats such meat at that later stage: is he liable?

The *braita* includes an expansive term — *asher la'Hashem riba* — to extend liability to such cases. Even though the meat is currently not permitted to *tahorim* (because it is *lan* or *yotzei*), since it once had a *sha'at kosher* when the blood was thrown, a *tamei* person who eats it incurs *kares*. The *braita* simultaneously limits: *mizevach hashelamim* serves as a narrowing term. The Gemara then frames the rule: include cases that had a *sha'at kosher* (*lan* and *yotzei*); exclude cases that never had one (*pigul*, which was disqualified from the very moment of the *machshava*).

### Tamei at Zrika

A further question arises within the *braita*. What if the meat became *tamei* before *zerikas damim* and was then eaten after *zerikas damim*? At the moment of *zerikas damim*, the meat was *tamei* — it was never *nitir l'tahorim* in the straightforward sense, because *tahorim* could not eat it at that moment. Yet the *braita* implies that a *tamei* person who eats such meat is nonetheless liable. How?

### Tzitz Meratzeh Meat

*Mipnei shehatzitz meratzeh* — because the *tzitz* is *meratzeh*. This is the pivotal statement. The *tzitz*'s *meratzeh* on the meat means that we treat the meat as though the *tumah* has been alleviated at the level of status. Even though no *tahor* person could literally eat the meat at the moment of *zerikas damim* (since it was *tamei*), the *tzitz* retroactively alleviates that *tumah* status, and we regard the meat as having had a *sha'at kosher*. Consequently, it falls within the category of *nitir l'tehorim*, and a *tamei* person who eats it is liable.

---

## Meratzeh Meaning

### Braita Implies Meat

The Gemara draws the immediate implication: this *braita*, by invoking *tzitz meratzeh* in the context of meat, demonstrates that the *tzitz* indeed operates on *achilos* — the consumable elements — not only on the *dam* or *kometz* that validates the *korban*.

### Only Tumah Here

At the same time, the *braita*'s discussion is framed exclusively around *tumah*. It does not extend the *tzitz*'s *meratzeh* to *yotzei*. The case of meat that was taken outside the *Beis Hamikdash* and had its *sha'at kosher* is handled without invoking the *tzitz* — liability derives from the *sha'at kosher* analysis alone. The *tzitz meratzeh* is invoked only for the *tumah* scenario. This is fully consistent with the Mishnah's ruling and with the *braita*'s derivation limiting the *tzitz* to *avon tumah*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Auth

The Gemara now observes that this *braita* — which says the *tzitz* works for *achilos* and simultaneously limits it to *tumah* (not *yotzei*) — must be attributed to Rabbi Eliezer. The reasoning: a position that the *tzitz* does not apply to *yotzei* is explicitly associated with Rabbi Eliezer in the context of *me'ilah* (*ein zerika mo'eles l'yotzei — Rabbi Eliezer*). The *braita* before us adopts precisely this view: *chad mishum tumah v'chad mishum yotzei lo* — the *tzitz* addresses *tumah*, not *yotzei*. And the *braita* also says the *tzitz* works on *achilos*. Therefore, this *braita* is Rabbi Eliezer, and it confirms that Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* on meat.

This makes the reversal (*ipoch*) proposed earlier impossible. The *braita* naming Rabbi Eliezer as holding *tzitz meratzeh al ha'achilos* is confirmed by this independent source.

---

## Rav Chisda: RE

### First Braita RE

Rav Chisda now proposes a full resolution. The *braita* at the top of the *amud* — which says the *tzitz* works for blood, meat, and fat without distinction between *shogeg* and *meizid* — is Rabbi Eliezer. This is consistent with the demonstration that Rabbi Eliezer holds *tzitz meratzeh al ha'achilos*.

### RE: Terumah Mezid

Furthermore, Rav Chisda points out, there is a *braita* in which Rabbi Eliezer says exactly what Rabbi Yosi said regarding *terumah*: *Rabbi Eliezer omer bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid terumato terumah* — even if done intentionally, the *terumah* takes effect. Rabbi Eliezer too does not impose the *knas* for *meizid* in the *terumah* case.

### Infer: Korban Mezid

Therefore, Rav Chisda concludes, Rabbi Eliezer consistently holds: *b'meizid* is not penalized. The *braita* that says the *tzitz* works even *b'meizid* is Rabbi Eliezer — he holds both that the *tzitz* extends to *achilos* and that *meizid* does not disqualify. The *braita* that restricts to *shogeg* is *Rabbanan*, who impose the *knas*.

---

## Challenge Rav Chisda

### Kalah/Chamimah

The Gemara presses: when Rabbi Eliezer says *b'meizid* does not forfeit the *terumah*, that is by *terumah*, which is halachically lighter (*terumah dekalah*). How can we automatically extend this to *korbanot*, which are weightier (*kadashim dechamimei*)? Perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would be stricter in the *korban* context and would agree with the *Rabbanan* that *meizid* forfeits the *tzitz*'s benefit.

### Braita Proof

Rav Chisda's answer is characteristically practical: we have a *braita* before us that explicitly says the *tzitz* works even *b'meizid* in the context of *korbanot*. We need to find its author. The attribution to Rabbi Eliezer is the most coherent, given his explicit position that the *tzitz* works on *achilos* (confirmed by the independent *braita*) and his established *terumah* ruling. One can theoretically distinguish *terumah* from *korbanot*, but one must still account for the *braita* — and Rabbi Eliezer fits it best.

---

## Ravina: Occur vs. Act

### Tumah Occurred

Ravina proposes an elegant alternative that dissolves the contradiction between the two *braitot* without requiring a *machloket* at all. His key is a close reading of each *braita*'s precise language. The second *braita* — the one at the top of the *amud* — says *shenitma bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid*, "that became *tamei*, whether *b'shogeg* or *b'meizid*." The subject of the *shogeg/meizid* qualification is the *tumah* occurring — how the *tumah* came about. On this dimension, says Ravina, the *tzitz* works regardless of intent: whether the object became *tamei* accidentally or deliberately, the *tzitz* is still *meratzeh*.

### Zrika Shogeg

The first *braita*, by contrast, says *dam shenitma v'zarko beshogeg hurtzah, b'meizid lo hurtzah* — "blood that became *tamei* and was sprinkled; *b'shogeg*, it works; *b'meizid*, it does not." Ravina reads the *shogeg/meizid* qualification here as attaching to the *zerika* — the act of sprinkling. The *zerika* must be *b'shogeg*; if the *kohen* knowingly and intentionally performed the *zerika* with *tamei* blood, the *tzitz* does not work.

### Harmony: Ravina

The two *braitot* thus address different variables and are entirely consistent. The *tumah* may occur *b'meizid* without consequence for the *tzitz* — but the *zerika* must be *b'shogeg*. No *machloket* is required.

---

## Rav Sheila: Reverse

### Zrika Lenient

Rav Sheila presents the precise inverse of Ravina's reading. The *zerika*, says Rav Sheila, may be *b'meizid* without disqualifying the *tzitz* — the act of sprinkling is where leniency applies. It is the *tumah*'s occurrence that must be *b'shogeg*: if the object became *tamei* intentionally, the *tzitz* does not work. Thus the first *braita*'s *shogeg/meizid* distinction applies to how the *tumah* occurred, and the second *braita*'s permissiveness applies to the *zerika*.

---

## Test Rav Sheila

### Language Check

The Gemara now tests Rav Sheila's reading against the actual language of the *braitot*. The second *braita* — the one that applies *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid* without restriction — uses the word *shenitma*: "that became *tamei*, whether *b'shogeg* or *b'meizid*." This language speaks directly to how the *tumah* occurred. That is precisely what Ravina says: the *tumah* occurring can be *b'meizid* and the *tzitz* still works. This supports Ravina and undermines Rav Sheila, for whom that *braita* should be about the *zerika*, not the *tumah*.

### Strained Read

Rav Sheila is forced to read the *braita* very differently: *shenitma* ("became *tamei*") together with *v'zarko* ("and sprinkled") must be parsed as a single compound unit — the entire event, *tumah* plus *zerika*, is the subject of *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid*. Rav Sheila would then read: "(if it) became *tamei* and was sprinkled (*shenitma beshogeg*) — whether *b'shogeg* or *b'meizid*" — meaning the *v'zarko* can be *b'meizid* so long as the *nitma* was *b'shogeg*. This is a forced and strained parsing.

### Natural Read

Ravina's reading, by contrast, follows the natural structure of the *braita* straightforwardly: *shenitma* (became *tamei*) is qualified by *bein b'shogeg bein b'meizid* — the *tumah*'s occurrence may be either. The *zerika* is addressed in the first *braita*, where *beshogeg hurtzah, b'meizid lo hurtzah* attaches naturally to the act of sprinkling.

---

## Conclusion & Recap

### Ravina Wins

Ravina's reading is the most linguistically consistent with both *braitot*. The language of each *braita* maps cleanly onto the variable Ravina identifies: the second *braita* speaks to how *tumah* occurred, the first to how the *zerika* was performed. No debate between *Tannaim* is required; both *braitot* represent a single coherent position.

### Meratzeh: Status

A deeper point emerges from the discussion as a whole. *Tzitz meratzeh* does not mean moral forgiveness, nor does it mean that the problematic act becomes retroactively permitted. It means the alleviation of a *halachic status*. When the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* for *tumah*, it removes the disqualifying *tumah* status that would otherwise invalidate the *korban* or the offering's subsequent consequences. Similarly, when the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* for the meat, it treats the meat's *tumah* status as though alleviated — not permitting anyone to eat it, but affecting how the law regards its status for other *halachic* purposes.

### Implications

This understanding has concrete *halachic* implications. As we saw from the *braita* about a *tamei* person eating *basar kodshim*: the *tzitz*'s alleviation of the meat's *tumah* status is what allows us to regard the meat as having had a *sha'at kosher*, thereby making a *tamei* person who eats it liable for *kares*. Far from benefiting the offender, the *tzitz meratzeh* on the meat can increase liability. Similarly, the question of whether the *tzitz* is *meratzeh* affects the *me'ilah* status of the meat — if the *tzitz* alleviates the *tumah* and the meat is treated as valid *kodesh*, the laws of *me'ilah* may apply differently than if the *tumah* remains fully in force. The *tzitz* thus operates as a mechanism that adjusts *halachic* status, with consequences that ripple through multiple areas of the laws of *kodashim*.

---

---

# Menachot 26

## Remnants & Kometz (III)

### Mishna Overview

The *mishna* opens with a case involving the *shirayim* — the remnant of the *mincha* left over after the *kometz* has been taken. Three scenarios are presented in which the *shirayim* are lost to the *kohein*: *nitme'u shi'areiha*, the remnant became *tamei*; *nisrefu shi'areiha*, it was burned; *avdu shi'areiha*, it was lost. The question is whether, in any of these circumstances, the *kometz* may still be brought and the *mincha* remain valid. The *mishna* records a dispute: *k'midat Rabbi Eliezer k'sheira* — according to Rabbi Eliezer's view, it is valid — while *u'k'midat Rabbi Yehoshua psulah* — according to Rabbi Yehoshua's view, it is invalid.

### R. Eliezer vs. R. Yehosh…

This dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua is known from elsewhere in *Shas*. Their debate concerns whether one may perform *zerikat hadam* — the sprinkling of the blood — if nothing remains of the *korban* aside from the blood itself. Does there need to be some fat to burn on the *mizbe'ach*, or some meat either to burn (in the case of an *olah*) or to eat (in the case of other *korbanot*)? Rabbi Eliezer holds that even if all one has is the blood, the *zerikat hadam* may be performed and the *korban* is valid. Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the blood functions as a *matir* — it enables the next stage, whether eating or burning — and if there is nothing left for it to permit, it cannot serve that function. The same logic applies to the *kometz* of a *mincha*: does the *kometz* require *shirayim* to exist in order to be valid?

### Rav's Position

The *gemara* opens with a statement of Rav: *v'hu shenitme'u kol shi'areiha* — when the *mishna* identifies *tum'ah* as a problem according to Rabbi Yehoshua, it refers specifically to a case where *all* of the *shirayim* became *tamei*. If only a minority of the *shirayim* became *tamei*, Rabbi Yehoshua would concede that the *kometz* may be brought, since something remains.

### Tumah & Tzitz

The *gemara*, however, focuses on Rav's specific invocation of the case of *tum'ah* and asks: *mai kasavar* — what precisely is his reasoning? *Ka salka daitach* — one might have thought — that Rav singled out *tum'ah* because it enjoys a special status by virtue of the *tzitz*. The *tzitz*, the golden frontplate worn by the *Kohen Gadol*, has the power of *ritzui*, rendering certain otherwise-problematic *korbanot* acceptable. A question debated in the previous *mishna* was whether the *tzitz* is *meratzeh al ha'ochlin* — whether its acceptance extends not only to things burned on the *mizbe'ach* but also to the edible portions of a *korban*. Crucially, this does not mean the *tzitz* permits eating *tamei* meat; rather, the question is whether, *vis-à-vis* establishing the validity of the *korban*, the *tzitz* can bracket the problem posed by the *tum'ah* of the edible portions. If it can, then even when all the *shirayim* are *tamei*, the *tzitz* would treat them as if they were present and valid, and Rabbi Yehoshua would concede.

With this in mind, the *gemara* presses: *mai kasavar* — what does Rav actually hold? If he holds *shiura milta hi* — that even a small remnant is sufficient — then why does he single out *tum'ah*? Even if most of the *shirayim* were lost or burned, as long as a little remains it should suffice. If, on the other hand, he holds *shiura lav milta hi* — that a small remnant is not significant and all of the *shirayim* must remain — then why does *tum'ah* not constitute a problem? Is it because the *tzitz* renders it as if the *shirayim* still exist?

The *gemara* resolves the tension: *le'olam kasavar shiura milta hi* — Rav's actual position is simply that a small remnant suffices. His reference to *tum'ah* carries no special significance; he mentioned *tum'ah* only because the *mishna* itself opens with the case of *tum'ah* (*reisha hu nakat*), not because *tum'ah* enjoys any distinct legal status in this context.

## Tzitz Validation

### Tzitz Scope

The *gemara*'s discussion of the *tzitz* bears clarification. When it asks whether the *tzitz* works *al ha'ochlin*, it does not mean that *tum'ah* is lifted such that the *tamei* meat could be eaten. The *tzitz* operates exclusively in the domain of making the *korban* valid — it does not override prohibitions of eating in a state of *tum'ah*. The question is purely functional: can the *tzitz*'s power of *ritzui* stand in, *vis-à-vis* the validity of the *korban*, for edible portions that have become *tamei*? If yes, Rabbi Yehoshua could agree that the *korban* is valid even when the only remaining *shirayim* are *tamei*, because the *tzitz* treats those portions as though they are halachically present.

A related question, noted but not yet fully resolved in the tractate, is whether the *ritzui* of the *tzitz* requires the *Kohen Gadol* to actually be wearing it at the moment, or whether the mere existence of the *tzitz* — so long as it has not been broken or lost — is sufficient. That debate remains open.

## Remnants & Kometz (III)

### Shiura Requirement

The *gemara* brings a *baraita* to support the conclusion that Rabbi Yehoshua does not require all the *shirayim* to be present, but only some meaningful portion: *Rabbi Yehoshua omer kol hazvachim shebatorah shenishtayer mehen kezayit basar o kezayit chelev* — Rabbi Yehoshua says that for all animal *korbanot* in the Torah, as long as a *kezayit* of meat or a *kezayit* of fat remains, *zorek et hadam* — one may perform the *zerikat hadam*. If only half a *kezayit* of meat and half a *kezayit* of fat remain, *eino zorek et hadam* — one may not.

There is, however, an exception for the *olah*. Since the entire *olah* is burned — both the meat and the fat — a half *kezayit* of meat combined with a half *kezayit* of fat yields a full *kezayit* of something that will be burned on the *mizbe'ach*, and that suffices. By contrast, when the *korban* is not an *olah*, the fact that one has half a *kezayit* to eat and half a *kezayit* to burn does not constitute a meaningful *kezayit* of either function; one needs a full *kezayit* of one or the other. The principle applies equally to the *mincha*: Rabbi Yehoshua does not require all the *shirayim* to remain, only that some significant amount — a *kezayit* — be present.

## Tzitz Validation (II)

### Tzitz Wearing

The question of whether the *tzitz* requires active wearing by the *Kohen Gadol* or whether its mere presence suffices is a debate that surfaces in the *gemara*, though it has not yet been explicitly encountered in the course of this tractate's discussion. Under normal circumstances, the *Kohen Gadol* wore the *tzitz* as part of his standard priestly vestments whenever he performed the *avodah*. The practical upshot of the *tzitz*'s *ritzui* is not to permit eating *tamei* portions *lechatchilah*, but rather that *bedi'avad*, if a *korban* was offered under such circumstances, it is considered accepted. This is the framework within which Rabbi Eliezer's position operates as well — he holds that even if the entire *shirayim* are gone, the *korban* is valid — though the *gemara*'s analysis of *tum'ah* and the *tzitz* was directed primarily at clarifying Rabbi Yehoshua's more limited concession.

## Remnants & Kometz (III)…

### Kezayit Standard

A *baraita* confirms that for Rabbi Yehoshua, what is needed is that a *kezayit* of the animal itself — either of the parts to be burned or the parts to be eaten — be present at the time of *zerikat hadam*. The *baraita* also introduces the question of the *minchat nesachim* — the *mincha* that accompanies the wine libation brought together with an animal sacrifice.

## Minchat Nesachim

### Blood with Mincha

The *gemara* raises the following question: if none of the meat of the animal remains but the *minchat nesachim* — the accompanying *mincha* — is entirely intact, may one perform *zerikat hadam*? The reasoning one might advance in favor of permitting it is *ho'il uvahadei zevach ka'atya* — since the *minchat nesachim* comes together with the animal sacrifice, one might think it has the status of the animal's body itself (*kegufei dizevach dami*), and thus constitutes the requisite remnant.

### Rav Papa's View

Rav Papa rules that this reasoning is rejected. The *minchat nesachim* is not considered part of the body of the sacrifice itself. When the *baraita* teaches that Rabbi Yehoshua requires something of the *korban* to remain — specifying *chelev* — it establishes that the remnant must be an intrinsic part of the animal, not something attendant to it. The *minchat nesachim* does not meet that standard, and therefore even if it remains intact, one may not perform *zerikat hadam* if no portion of the animal itself survives.

## Remnant Amount

### Kezayit Source

The *gemara* then asks: *minayin* — what is the source? Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yishmael (and some versions attribute it to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya), derives the answer from the *pasuk*: *vehiktir hachelev lerei'ach nichoach l'Hashem* — "and he shall burn the fat as a pleasing scent to God." The surrounding verse reads: *ve-zarak hakohein et hadam al mizbe'ach Hashem* — "the *kohein* shall sprinkle the blood" — followed immediately by the burning of the fat. The *gemara* reads this as establishing a connection: the *zerikat hadam* is linked to the subsequent burning of the *chelev*. From this we learn that *chelev af al pi she-ein basar* — even if all that remains is the fat (and no meat), one may perform the *zerikat hadam*. And once we accept that not everything must remain — that even a single component suffices — the broader principle follows: one needs a meaningful amount, a *kezayit*, of something that will be burned or eaten, but not the entirety of the *korban*.

This is precisely the point of disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *zerikat hadam* is itself the essential act of the *korban*, and it stands on its own. Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the blood functions as a *matir* — it must be enabling something at the next stage — and if there is nothing left to enable, the *dam* cannot serve its proper function. The *matir* must have something to permit. Crucially, what it permits must be something of the animal itself, not something that merely accompanies it.

### Organs Suffice

The *gemara* then asks: *ve'ashkechan chelev* — we have established the rule from the *pasuk* for the case of fat. But what of the *yoteret u-shtei klayot* — the lobe of the liver and the two kidneys? These too are placed on the *mizbe'ach* together with the *chelev*, but they are organs, not fat in the strict sense. Does their presence suffice to permit *zerikat hadam* even if no *chelev* remains?

The answer is derived from the *baraita* itself: since Rabbi Yehoshua rules that even when the entire *mincha* of the accompanying libation is intact, *lo yizrok* — one may not sprinkle the blood — the *baraita* contrasts this with a case where what remains is the *yoteret ushtei klayot*, and rules *yizrok* — one may sprinkle. This establishes that Rabbi Yehoshua accepts any part of the animal's body that is designated for the *mizbe'ach* as the requisite remnant, not only the *chelev* in the narrow sense.

### Torah Redundancy

Rabbi Yochanan in his own name then explains the *pasuk*-level derivation. The *pasuk* says *lerei'ach nichoach* — a pleasing scent — which is a broad category encompassing anything burned as part of the *korban*. *Kol she'ata ma'aleh lerei'ach nichoach* — anything that you burn as a pleasing scent — would suffice to permit *zerikat hadam*. This would seem to include even the *minchat nesachim*.

Why, then, does the Torah write *chelev* — fat — at all? *De'i ktav chelev hava amina chelev in yoteret ushtei klayot lo* — had the Torah written only *chelev*, one might have thought that only the fat counts, and that the lobe and kidneys do not. Therefore the Torah writes *lerei'ach nichoach* to broaden the category to include those as well. Conversely, *ve'i ktav rachmana lerei'ach nichoach* alone, one might have thought even the *minchat nesachim* suffices — since it too is burned with the *korban*. Therefore the Torah writes *chelev* to establish that the remnant must be part of the animal's body itself.

The logic is elegant: the two expressions are each necessary. *Chelev* excludes the *minchat nesachim*; *lerei'ach nichoach* includes the *yoteret* and *shtei klayot*. Neither term alone would achieve both results.

## Kli Sharet Debate

### R. Yehuda's Logic

The *mishna* states: *shelo bekli sharet* — if the second stage of the *mincha* service, after taking the *kometz*, was performed without a *kli sharet*, it is *pasul*. The *kometz* must be received into a sanctified vessel, parallel in some ways to the reception of blood in a *kli sharet* during animal sacrifices. Yet Rabbi Shimon declares it valid.

Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Chiyya explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from a *pasuk*: *kodesh kodashim hi ka-chatat ve-ka-asham* — the *mincha* is compared both to a *chatat* and to an *asham*. The comparison carries halachic weight. Rabbi Shimon holds, based on positions expressed elsewhere, that by an *asham*, where the blood is thrown from a vessel rather than applied with a finger, the requirement of right hand does not apply — even a left hand is valid. From this he constructs a two-track approach for the *mincha*: *ba le-ovdah beyad ovdah biyamin ka-chatat* — if you wish to perform the burning by hand, use your right hand, as with a *chatat*. *Bikli ovdah besmol ka-asham* — if you wish to use a vessel, you may use your left hand, as with an *asham*. There is therefore no absolute requirement of a *kli sharet* as such; rather, there are two valid modes: hand to *mizbe'ach* using the right hand, or vessel using the left.

Two different framings of Rabbi Shimon's position are possible. One is that there is simply no requirement of a *kli sharet* after taking the *kometz* — just a requirement of getting the *kometz* onto the *mizbe'ach*, either by right hand or by vessel. The other framing is that the right hand of a *kohein* itself counts as a *kli sharet*, and if one instead uses a physical vessel, the left hand becomes permissible as well. Both framings, however, agree that there is no absolute mandate of a physical *kli sharet* when using the right hand.

### R. Yannai Extreme

Rabbi Yannai goes considerably further. He states: *keivan she-kamtzo mi-kli sharet, ma'alehu u-maktira afilu be-hemyano ve-afilu be-makida shel cheres* — once you have taken the *kometz* from the *kli sharet*, you may place it on the *mizbe'ach* even if you are carrying it in the *kohein*'s belt or in a pottery bowl. There is no requirement whatsoever of a *kli sharet* after the initial taking, nor even of the right hand.

According to Rabbi Yannai's reading of Rabbi Shimon, the essential act of the *mincha* service is the taking of the *kometz*. From that point onward, the process of getting the *kometz* onto the fire is not formally defined in the way that the sprinkling of blood is formally defined. It does not matter how you carry it or in what vessel. What matters is that it reaches the *mizbe'ach* and burns.

This position invites a deeper reflection on the nature of the *kometz* as a sacrificial act. The *kometz* occupies an unusual space: on the one hand, it is burned as an offering to God, paralleling the burning of *chelev* and the limbs of an *olah*; on the other hand, it functions as a *matir*, enabling the eating of the *shirayim*, paralleling the role of the blood. If one emphasizes its *matir* function — its resemblance to the *dam* — then the formal process of how it is carried to the *mizbe'ach* becomes significant, just as the catching and sprinkling of blood is formally defined. If, however, one emphasizes its nature as something burned, then what is significant is its presence on the fire — not the act of placing it. Rabbi Yannai reads Rabbi Shimon as emphasizing the latter: the *kometz* is ultimately about *lerei'ach nichoach*, about being on the *mizbe'ach* and burning, and not about a carefully delineated sequence of acts.

This is reinforced by the observation that even Rabbi Yannai concedes that a *piggul* thought is meaningful when the *kometz* is burned on the *mizbe'ach*, even if not when it is merely being carried. The act of placing it on the fire has at least the status of an *avodah*; what Rabbi Shimon downplays is the procedural formality surrounding how one arrives at that moment.

### R. Nachman Middle

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak takes the most restrictive position among those who read Rabbi Shimon leniently. He argues: *hakol modim bekometz she-ta'un kiddush* — everyone agrees, even Rabbi Shimon, that the *kometz* must be placed into a *kli sharet* after it is taken. What Rabbi Shimon permits is only the transfer from the *kli sharet* to the fire — the *kohein* need not upturn the *kli sharet* directly onto the altar but may remove the *kometz* with his hand and then place it on the fire. The debate between Rabbi Shimon and the *chachamim* is therefore narrower than it appears: it concerns only the final step, whether one must burn the *kometz* directly from the *kli sharet* or may take it out first.

As the *gemara* works through this position, it consistently finds that the evidence does not support it. The *baraitot* cited indicate clearly that Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer do not require a *kli sharet* even at the stage of placing the *kometz* into a vessel after it is taken. The *gemara* ultimately concedes: *tyufta d'Rav Nachman tyufta* — this is a conclusive refutation of Rav Nachman's position.

### Tosefta Support

A *tosefta* from Zevachim provides striking support for Rabbi Yannai's reading. It states that the burning of fats (*chalavim*), limbs (*eivarim*), and wood — *bein beyad bein bikli, bein biyamin bein bismol* — whether by hand or vessel, right or left, are all valid. The *tosefta* then adds: so too the *kometz*, the *levona*, the *ketoret*, and the *minchat nesachim*, burned *bein beyad bein bikli bein biyamin bein bismol* — are all valid regardless of how they are placed on the *mizbe'ach*.

This *tosefta* is the conceptual foundation for Rabbi Yannai's position. The first category — fat, limbs, wood — are clearly not the sacrifice in the primary sense; they are what is burned, but the blood is the *ikar*. The second category — the *kometz*, *levona*, and *ketoret* — are the primary elements of their respective services, analogous to blood in animal sacrifices. Yet the *tosefta* treats them identically: in both cases, what matters is that they are on the *mizbe'ach* and burning, not the act by which they arrived there. The *tosefta* therefore implicitly argues that the *kometz* is more like burning than like blood.

## Hand & Vessel

### Hand Options

The *gemara* returns to the position of Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Chiyya and asks how it reconciles with the *baraita* that permits the use of the left hand. He explains: *lastudim ktani* — the *baraita* does not permit any combination freely but rather presents two valid tracks that must be read in parallel. "By hand" means by the *right* hand; "by vessel" means by vessel, and in that case either right or left is permitted. The *baraita* does not sanction left hand without a vessel, nor does it sanction any arbitrary mix.

This reading is admittedly strained — the plain sense of the *baraita* seems to allow all combinations — but it is the interpretation Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya must adopt to preserve his position.

### Three Stages

A second *baraita* elaborates the position of the *chachamim* with precision: the *kometz* must be taken from a *kli sharet*, placed into a *kli sharet*, and burned from a *kli sharet*. This is a three-stage requirement, each stage requiring a sanctified vessel. *Rabbi Eliezer v'Rabbi Shimon makhshirim mimatan kli* — Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon, however, declare it valid in a case where the intermediate stage — the placing into a *kli sharet* — was omitted.

The *gemara* initially considers whether the *baraita* might be reread — *eima mimatan kli* — to say that Rabbi Shimon only waives the requirement of burning *from* the *kli sharet*, not the requirement of *placing into* it. But as with all such attempts, the plain sense of the text resists this reading, and the *gemara* finds it necessary to revise the text artificially.

### Shimon vs. Sages

The essential dispute, stated plainly, is this: the *chachamim* hold that every stage of the *kometz*'s journey from the initial taking through to its burning requires a *kli sharet*. Rabbi Shimon holds that once the *kometz* has been taken, the subsequent stages are not formally constrained in the same way.

### Supporting Text

A further *baraita* states the positions clearly: the *chachamim* require that the *kometz* be taken from a *kli sharet*, placed in a *kli sharet*, and burned from a *kli sharet*; *Rabbi Shimon omer keivan she-kamat* — Rabbi Shimon says: once it has been taken from the *kli sharet*, it may be placed directly on the fire. The *gemara* again attempts to reframe this as referring only to the final step (*mimatan kli va-eilach*), but the straightforward reading continues to support the more expansive position attributed to Rabbi Yannai.

### Left Hand Invalid

A *baraita* now poses a direct challenge: *kometz beyamino ve-natan bismalo* — one took the *kometz* in his right hand and then transferred it to his left, *yachzir leyamino* — he must return it to his right. If while the *kometz* was in his left hand he had a thought of *piggul* — *bein chutz limkomo bein chutz lizmano* — whether about the wrong place or wrong time — the *korban* is *pasul* but there is no *karet*, because the left hand alone is not a valid position for such a thought to be halachically significant. The *baraita* concludes: *divrei Rabbi Eliezer v'Rabbi Shimon* — this is the view of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon. The *chachamim*, by contrast, say: *keivan shenatno lishmalo psalto matnato* — once it was transferred to the left hand, it is invalidated, and one cannot return it to the right.

### Left Hand Status

The *gemara* analyzes the *chachamim*'s position: *mishum d'ba'ei kedusha bikli* — they hold that the *kometz* must immediately go into a vessel upon being taken. If instead it goes into the left hand, it is treated like *dam she-nishpach mitzvar behemah al haritzpah* — blood that spilled from the animal's neck onto the ground rather than being caught in a vessel. Just as such blood cannot be gathered and then sprinkled, so too the *kometz* in the left hand cannot be retrieved and corrected.

Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, do not require immediate placement into a *kli sharet*. Accordingly, the left hand is not a fatal deviation — it is simply not a valid resting position. It is not good enough for a *piggul* thought to take effect (since it is not a position of valid *avodah*), yet it does not irrevocably invalidate the *kometz* either, because the left hand is not inherently disqualifying — it is one of two potential valid modes if a vessel accompanies it.

This analysis supports Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya's framing most naturally: the left hand without a vessel is a kind of liminal state, neither valid nor invalid, and therefore must be corrected by returning to the right hand or placing in a vessel. The *gemara* acknowledges that this *baraita* provides support for his position (*mesaye'a lei*), while noting that it poses a difficulty for Rabbi Yannai's more expansive reading. Rabbi Yannai responds that this *baraita* simply does not reflect his view — he reads Rabbi Shimon according to the other *baraita*, the *tosefta*, which explicitly permits left hand, right hand, vessel, and no vessel without distinction, and he maintains that the two *tannaitic* sources represent differing opinions.

## Multiple Stages

### Halves & Quarters

The *mishna* states: *hiktir komtza pa'amayim k'sheira* — if the *kometz* was burned in two stages, it is valid. The *gemara* now turns to this second clause.

### R. Y. ben Levi

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi qualifies the ruling: *pa'amayim v'lo pa'amei pa'amayim* — the *mishna* permits burning in two halves, but not in halves of halves — that is, not in quarters. This is not an arbitrary distinction; it rests on two premises. First, *ein kometz pachot mishnei zeisim* — every person's handful is at minimum the size of two *zeisim*, so each half is at least one *zayit*. Second, *ein haktara pechuta mi-kezayit* — there is no valid act of *haktara* with less than a *kezayit*. If every half is at least a *kezayit*, then burning in halves is valid. But dividing into quarters would result in each part being less than a *kezayit*, which would not constitute a valid *haktara*.

### R. Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan permits even quarters: *pa'amayim ve'afilu pa'amei pa'amayim*. He holds *yesh kometz pachot mishnei zeisim* — there are individuals whose handfuls are smaller than two *zeisim*. If the *mishna* permits burning in halves and the *mishna*'s ruling must be universally applicable, it must be that a *haktara* less than a *kezayit* can be valid when it is part of a larger process. Once that principle is established, there is no distinction between halves and quarters.

### Per-Stage Size

As Rabbi Zeira frames it: *yesh kometz pachot mishnei zeisim v'yesh haktara pechuta mi-kezayit ika beinayhu* — the practical debate between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan comes down to whether a *haktara* of less than a *kezayit* at each individual stage is a valid act, when the cumulative total constitutes a full *kometz*. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says no: each act must independently be a *kezayit*, and the *mishna*'s permission of halves implicitly guarantees that. Rabbi Yochanan says yes: the *mishna* permits halves precisely because it accepts the principle that individual acts in a staged *haktara* need not each be a *kezayit*, and once that door is open, quarters are equally permissible.

This debate carries a practical implication worth noting: if a normal *kometz* is at least two *zeisim*, that provides useful perspective on the size of a *kezayit* more generally.

## Kometz Validity

### Shirayim Permission

The *gemara* now addresses a question that connects directly to the nature of the *kometz* as a *matir*: *kometz mei'emaisai matir shirayim ba'achilah* — from what point does the burning of the *kometz* render the *shirayim* permissible for eating? This question underscores how the *kometz* is unlike the *dam* of an animal sacrifice. By *zerikat hadam*, the moment the blood touches the wall of the *mizbe'ach*, the meat becomes permitted. But the *kometz* is burned — it does not simply make contact; it must undergo a process. So at what stage of that process has the *kometz* discharged its function?

### R. Chanina

Rabbi Chanina says: *mi-she-timshila bo ha'or* — from the moment the fire takes hold of it. The *shirayim* are permitted as soon as the fire begins to burn the *kometz*.

### R. Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *mi-she-tatzis bo ha'or be-rubo* — only when the fire seizes the *majority* of the *kometz*. The word *berubo* — the majority — is what Rabbi Yochanan's formulation adds, and Rashi identifies this as the critical distinction between the two positions, rather than the difference in the verbs (*timshila* versus *tatzis*).

### Oven Source

Rav Yehuda explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning to Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak. The *pasuk* describing the destruction of Sodom uses the phrase *ve-hineh ala kitor ha'aretz ke-kitor ha-kivshan* — the smoke rose from the earth like the smoke of an oven. The word *kitor* — pillar of smoke — is related to the root of *lehaktir*. The *gemara* reasons: *ein kivshan ma'aleh kitor ad she-tatzis ha'or be-rubo* — an oven does not produce a pillar of smoke until the fire seizes the majority of its contents. Since *lehaktir* means to cause the *kitor* to rise, the act of *haktara* is not complete until the majority of the object has been seized by fire.

This is a powerful conceptual point. *Lehaktir* is not simply "to place on fire" — it means to cause the thing to rise up as smoke, as incense. That process does not begin the moment the object touches the flame; it is only underway when the fire has taken hold of most of it. Until then, the *kometz* has been placed on the fire but has not yet been *muktir*.

### Day vs. Night

Rav Amram cites a *baraita* that introduces a complication. The *baraita* distinguishes between things normally offered at night — such as the *eivarim* and *padarim*, the limbs and fats of an *olah*, which are placed on the fire after sunset and continue burning through the night — and things normally offered during the day: the *kometz*, the *levona*, the *ketoret*, the *minchat kohanim*, the *minchat kohen mashiach*, and the *minchat nesachim*. For the latter category, the *baraita* asks: *minayin* — how do I know that even these may be placed on the fire before sunset and continue burning into the night?

The question appears paradoxical: if these are things that must be offered during the day, how can any part of the *haktara* extend into the night?

### Sunset Resolution

The *gemara* resolves this: *kan liklot kan lehaktir* — there is a distinction between *klitatah* — the moment the fire takes hold of it and it is considered attached to the *mizbe'ach* — and *haktara* — the completion of the burning process. The act that constitutes the *avodah*, the placing on the fire, must occur during the day. But the completion of the burning — the majority of the *kometz* being seized by fire — may extend into the night. The *baraita* teaches that *zot torat ha-olah* — the law of the *olah* — comes to include that these items, placed on the fire before sunset, remain valid even as they continue to burn afterward.

This is not a contradiction of Rabbi Yochanan's position. Rather, it refines it: the *kometz* does not become fully *muktir* — and thus does not fully permit the *shirayim* — until the majority of it has been seized by fire. But what must happen before sunset is the placing on the fire, not the completion of the burning. The completion can occur afterward, and the *kometz* is still valid.

### Act vs. Completion

This resolution reflects a broader principle about acts that are initiated by a human being and then completed by an autonomous process. The *gemara* draws a parallel to the laws of *Shabbos*: if one plants seeds on *Shabbos*, one is liable even though the seeds do not take root until weeks later. The act of planting is defined by the human initiation of the process, not the biological completion. Similarly, the act of *haktara* is initiated by placing the *kometz* on the fire before sunset; the completion — the fire seizing the majority — may occur afterward, and the *korban* is nonetheless valid.

This insight dovetails elegantly with the positions discussed earlier regarding the process of placing the *kometz* on the *mizbe'ach*. Rabbi Shimon, and most fully Rabbi Yannai, argued that the formal procedural requirements of *how* one gets the *kometz* onto the fire are not the primary concern — what matters is that it burns. The present discussion reinforces that perspective from a different angle: the moment of validity is not the act of placing but the completion of burning. The human act initiates the process; the *haktara* is the result. And in that sense, the *kometz* is indeed more like the burning of fat and limbs than like the sprinkling of blood — it is not a discrete instantaneous act but a process, one that begins with the *kohein* and concludes on its own, by fire.

# Menachot 27

## Kometz Sunset

### Kometz Before Sunset

The sugya opens at the bottom of 26b, where the *gemara* resolves a tension regarding the validity of the *mincha* offering. The question is whether the *kometz* must be substantially consumed by fire — that is, whether the fire must seize the majority of it — in order for the *mincha* to be considered valid. How, then, can we infer from an earlier *beraita* that it suffices to place the *kometz* on the fire immediately before sunset, allowing it to continue burning into the night?

The *gemara*'s answer is that this arrangement is entirely valid: the *mincha* does not achieve its valid status until the fire has seized the majority of the *kometz*, yet so long as the human act of the *avodah* — the placement on the fire — was performed during the day, the burning may continue and complete itself after nightfall. The point at which the fire seizes the majority, even if that moment occurs at night, is when the *mincha* becomes valid.

### Action & Process

This resolution reflects a broader principle found elsewhere in *halacha*: where a human act must be performed at a specific time, the subsequent process of completion — which unfolds on its own — may extend beyond that window. A parallel example is placing an item on a flame before *Shabbat* begins: since the act of placement was performed before *Shabbat*, the cooking that continues over *Shabbat* is attributed to that initial act. The *gemara* understands the *kometz* similarly: the act of the *avodah* defines the legal moment; the process of combustion carries forward from there.

### Rabbi Elazar Pikuin

Rabbi Elazar offers an alternative reading of the *beraita*. He does not require us to invoke the principle of the ongoing process at all. Instead, he reads the *beraita* as referring to *pikuin* — items that popped off the *mizbe'ach*. In such a case, the *kometz* had originally been placed on the altar during the day; it subsequently fell off; and it may then be restored even after nightfall. According to this reading, we are not permitting a nighttime *avodah* in any primary sense, but merely allowing restoration of something that was properly placed during the day and accidentally dislodged.

This principle is corroborated by Rav Dimi, who reported in the name of Rabbi Yanai: the *beraita* indeed concerns *pikuin*.

### Inner vs Outer Altar

A question immediately arises, however: does Rabbi Yanai himself actually hold that items which fell off the *mizbe'ach* may be restored after nightfall? For Rabbi Yanai himself taught that *ketoret* which flew off the *mizbe'ach* — even the tiniest fragment — may not be restored. This appears to contradict the principle of *pikuin* entirely.

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between the inner and outer *mizbe'ach*. Rabbi Chanina bar Minyumi teaches in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: the source for restoring fallen items is the verse *asher tochal ha'esh et ha'olah al hamizbe'ach* — the fire consumes the *olah* on the altar. The verse specifies things burned like the *olah*, and on the *mizbe'ach* in question: that is, on the outer *mizbe'ach*. From this we derive that items which fall off the outer *mizbe'ach* may be restored — but items belonging to the inner *mizbe'ach*, such as the *ketoret* burned on the golden altar, are not subject to this principle at all. The *gemara* therefore concludes: remove *ketoret* from this discussion. The *kometz* and the *levonah* — which belong to the outer *mizbe'ach* — may be restored after nightfall if they fell off. The *ketoret* of the inner *mizbe'ach* may not.

The logic here is precise: we are speaking of items that must *lechatchila* be placed during the day — not items like the limbs and fats of the *olah*, which may be placed *lechatchila* at night as well. If such daytime-required items were placed properly and then fell off, the question is whether they may be restored at night. The answer is yes for the outer *mizbe'ach*, no for the inner.

---

## Kometz Burning Method

### Kometz Under Wood

Having resolved the temporal questions surrounding the *kometz*, the *gemara* turns to a different set of concerns: the precise manner in which the *kometz* must be burned on the *mizbe'ach*. These are distinct from the earlier questions and involve the physical arrangement of the offering relative to the firewood.

Rav Assi reports that when Rabbi Elazar was studying Menachot, he posed the following question: if one arranged the *kometz* on the *mizbe'ach* and then placed the firewood on top of it — rather than placing the *kometz* on the wood — what is the *halacha*? Is this considered *derech haktara*, the normal manner of burning an offering? Or is it not *derech haktara*, and therefore invalid?

The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

One might understand this question as bearing on the formal act of placing the *kometz* on the *mizbe'ach* — whether there is a required manner of deposition, as there is with blood. Alternatively, the concern may be more functional: when the *kometz* is beneath the wood rather than atop it, the smoke may not rise as effectively. The question thus may implicate not only the legal act but the physical result of the burning.

### Olah Under Wood

Chizkiya posed a closely parallel question regarding the limbs of an *olah*: if one arranged the limbs on the *mizbe'ach* and then placed the firewood on top of them, what is the *halacha*? Here the question carries an additional dimension, because the Torah explicitly states *al ha'etzim* — on the wood — implying that the limbs must rest upon the firewood. Does *al ha'etzim* mean specifically that, and only that arrangement? Or does the verse *asher tochal ha'esh et ha'olah al hamizbe'ach* — that the fire consumes the *olah* on the altar — suggest that any configuration which results in burning on the altar suffices, and either arrangement is acceptable?

The *gemara* again answers: *teiku*.

What is significant here is the nature of the comparison. The *kometz*, in this discussion, is being treated not as something analogous to blood — which requires a formal act of application — but as something analogous to the fats and limbs of an animal, which are simply placed on the *mizbe'ach* to burn. Unlike those items, the *kometz* is a *matir*, the component that renders the *korban* valid. Yet the *gemara*'s framing suggests that the legal concern is less about a formal act of placement and more about the factual result: is it burning in a legitimate configuration?

### Limbs Beside Wood

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha posed a third question: what if one arranged the limbs of an *olah* not on top of the firewood, but alongside it — adjacent to the *ma'aracha* rather than upon it? The fire will still reach the limbs; they will still burn. So what is the *halacha*?

The *gemara* frames this question around a linguistic debate about the word *al*. If *al* means literally "on," then placing the limbs beside the wood rather than on it clearly fails the requirement of *al ha'etzim*. But if *al* can sometimes mean "near" — as in *al yerech hamizbe'ach tzafona*, which means near the side of the *mizbe'ach* rather than literally on its flank — then perhaps *al ha'etzim* could be satisfied even when the limbs are merely adjacent. Against this, one could argue that the phrase *al ha'etzim* parallels *al hamizbe'ach*, and just as the latter means literally on the altar and not merely near it, so too the former must mean literally on the wood.

The *gemara* again concludes: *teiku*.

The cumulative effect of these three unresolved questions reinforces the earlier observation: the *gemara* is treating the burning of the *kometz* as more akin to the burning of animal parts than to the act of applying blood. The concern is less the formal legal act and more the physical manner and arrangement of combustion.

---

## Me'akev Components

### Individual Requirements

With the beginning of daf 27a, the *gemara* enters a major new *mishna*, one that will generate extended discussion spanning numerous topics across all of *halacha*. The *mishna* introduces the principle of components that are *me'akev* — that is, that hold one another back, such that if one is missing the entire offering is invalid.

The *mishna* opens with individual quantitative requirements: even the smallest portion of the *kometz*, if lacking, invalidates the rest — *mi'uto me'akev et rubo*, the minority holds back the majority. Similarly, the *isaron* of flour that constitutes the *mincha* must be complete; even the smallest deficiency invalidates the *isaron* as a whole. The same applies to wine and to oil: whatever amount the Torah prescribes for a given *korban*, the full amount is required, and any shortfall renders the remainder invalid.

### Flour & Oil

The *mishna* then moves beyond individual measurements to address the interdependence of distinct components. This is a more significant step: it is no longer merely a question of how much of a single ingredient is required, but of whether entirely different components of a *korban* are bound up with one another.

*Hasolet v'hashemen me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the flour and the oil of a *mincha* are mutually interdependent. A *mincha* without the proper amount of flour is not valid, but equally, a *mincha* without the proper amount of oil is not valid. The relationship is not one-directional; each requires the presence of the other.

### Kometz & Levona

Similarly, the *kometz* and the *levona* — the handful of the *mincha* and the frankincense placed upon it — are mutually interdependent. Both must be present for the *mincha* to be valid. The absence of either one prevents the other from functioning.

### Textual Sources

The *gemara* then methodically traces the textual basis for each of these requirements.

For the *kometz*: the Torah uses the phrase *melo kumzo* — the fill of his handful — twice, which the *gemara* reads as emphatic: the full *kometz* is required, and any deficiency invalidates.

For the *isaron* of flour: the verse uses the possessive form *misolta* — its *solet* — conveying that it must be exactly its proper amount. Any deficiency renders it invalid.

For the wine accompanying offerings: the verse states *kacha ye'aseh lashor ha'echad o la'ayil ha'echad* — "so shall you do for each ox or each ram" — using the word *kacha*, meaning "thusly" or "exactly so." This formulation implies that any deviation from the prescribed amount invalidates.

For the oil: by *minchat nesachim*, the verse likewise uses *kacha*; by the free-will *mincha*, the verse says *u'mishamnah* — "from its oil" — the possessive again conveying that the exact amount is required.

Here a general principle of *korbanot* deserves notice. Unlike most areas of *halacha*, where a single statement in the Torah is presumed to carry the full weight of a requirement, by *korbanot* the principle is *shana alav hakatuv le'akev*: the Torah must repeat or reinforce a detail in order for us to conclude that its absence invalidates. This seems counterintuitive — one might think that the dense and elaborate ritual of the *avodah* would be precisely the domain where every detail is indispensable. Yet *Chazal* reasoned in the opposite direction: the sheer profusion of details in the sacrificial laws makes it implausible that every one is strictly *me'akev*. A repetition or emphasis in the verse is therefore needed to establish that a particular requirement is truly indispensable.

For the interdependence of flour and oil: the Torah says *misolta u'mishamnah* — "from its flour and from its oil" — linking them together. A second verse then repeats *migrasah u'mishamnah* — "from its meal and from its oil" — and the repetition establishes the interdependence.

For the *kometz* and *levona*: one verse says *al kol levonatah* — "upon all of its frankincense" — and another says *ve'et kol halevona* — "and all of the frankincense" — specifically in the context of offering it *asher al hamincha*. The repetition establishes that neither can be offered validly without the other.

---

## Multi-Component Systems

### Yom Kippur Goats

The *mishna* now proceeds through an extended catalog of cases organized on a numerical principle, moving from two-component systems to three, four, and seven.

*Shnei se'irei Yom Hakippurim me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the two goats of Yom Kippur hold one another back. One goat is sent to *Azazel*; the other is slaughtered and its blood is sprinkled inside the *heichal*. Their processes are quite distinct from one another, yet both must be present and both must be valid for either to be meaningful. This is worth pausing over: unlike the *kometz* and *levona*, which are offered together in a unified act, the two Yom Kippur goats are processed very differently. And yet the *mishna* teaches that they are interdependent — if something happens to one before the other is completed, neither may proceed. The extensive treatment of this problem in the *mishnayot* of Yoma reflects just how live and consequential this interdependence is.

The textual basis: the verse at the conclusion of the Yom Kippur *avodah* in *Acharei Mot* states *v'hayta zot lachem l'chukat olam* — this shall be a perpetual statute for you. The word *chukkah* is understood to require that the *avodah* be performed exactly as specified; and that *chukkah* encompasses the interdependence of the components within it.

### Shavuot Lambs Bread

*Shnei kivsei Atzeret me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the two lambs of Shavuot hold one another back. The textual basis is *solet tihyena* — "fine flour they shall be" — and the word *tihyena* conveys "it shall be exactly thus." Though this verse speaks directly of the *shtei halechem*, the *gemara* applies the force of *havayah* — the word "shall be" — to the lambs as well.

*Shtei chalot me'akvot zu et zu* — the two loaves of the *shtei halechem* hold one another back. Likewise from *havayah*.

*Shnei sedarim me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the two columns of *lechem hapanim* hold one another back. The verse states *me'ishei Hashem chok olam* — an everlasting statute of God's fire-offerings — and the word *chok* requires exactness.

*Shnei bezichin me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the two cups of frankincense that accompany the *shulchan* hold one another back. The same verse containing *chok* applies.

*Hasedarim vehabezichin me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the columns of bread and the cups of frankincense are mutually interdependent as well. You cannot burn the frankincense without the bread being present, and you cannot eat the bread without having burned the frankincense.

It is worth noting that while the word *chukkah* appears repeatedly and carries the work of establishing these interdependencies, it does not by itself define the scope of what is grouped together. For the *shulchan* and its components, the *gemara* identifies everything as required. For Yom Kippur, we group certain elements together but do not say, for instance, that the inability to bring the *par* of the *kohen gadol* prevents the *se'ir* from being offered. The application of *chok* to establish *me'akev* relationships therefore always involves a measure of conceptual grouping that the *gemara* takes as understood.

### Nazir Parah Todah

*Shnei minim shebanazir me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the two types of bread that accompany the *shlamim* of a *nazir* hold one another back. The textual basis is *ken ya'aseh al torat nizro* — "so shall be done according to his *nazirite* law" — the word *ken*, meaning "thus," conveying exactness.

*Gimel shebeparah me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the three components of the *parah adumah* purification, the *agudat ezov*, the *eitz erez*, and the *shni tola'at*, all hold one another back. The textual basis is *zot chukat hatorah* — this is the statute of the Torah — where both *zot* (this, exactly this) and *chukkah* reinforce the requirement.

*Arba shebetodah me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the four types of bread of the *todah* offering hold one another back.
