All forty loaves — ten of each type — must be present; if any type is missing, none of the loaves is valid, and none may be eaten. The textual basis is a linkage: the verse by the *todah* says *al zevach todah shlamav* — upon the slaughtering of his *todah* of his *shelamim* — and there is a teaching that the word *shlamav* serves to link the *shalmei nazir* to the *todah*. Since the interdependence of the bread types of the *nazir* is established by *ken ya'aseh*, and the *todah* is linked to the *nazir*, the same rule applies to the *todah*.

### Lulav Metzora

*Arba shebalulav me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the four species of the *lulav* hold one another back. The textual basis is the drasha of *lekicha tama*: the verse says *u'lekachtem*, and the *gemara* reads this as *lekicha* that is *tama* — a whole, complete taking — meaning all components must be present.

*Arba shebemetzora me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the four components of the *metzora* purification hold one another back. These are the *agudat ezov*, the *shni tola'at*, the *eitz erez*, and the birds — whose blood is used for the sprinkling. The textual basis is *zot tihyeh torat hametzora* — this shall be the law of the *metzora* — where *tihyeh* conveys that it must be exactly this way.

The organizational principle of this section of the *mishna* is explicitly numerical: it proceeds through two, three, four, and will continue to seven. This explains what might otherwise appear to be arbitrary jumps between topics — from bread offerings to the *parah adumah* to the *lulav* — as the *mishna* is simply following the count.

### Seven Sprinklings

*Sheva hazayot shebeparah me'akvot zu et zu* — the seven sprinklings of the *parah adumah* toward the *beit hamikdash* hold one another back. If any one of the seven is missing, the purification process is invalid. The textual basis is *chukkah*.

*Sheva hazayot shebein habadim ve'al parochet ve'al mizbe'ach hazahav me'akvot zu et zu* — the seven sprinklings of the inner *chata'ot*, whether performed between the staves of the *aron* on Yom Kippur, or upon the *parochet*, or upon the golden altar, all hold one another back. This applies to Yom Kippur, to the *par kohen hamashiach*, to the *par he'elam davar*, and to the goats brought for communal *avodah zarah*, all of which are inner *chata'ot*.

The textual basis for the inner *chata'ot*: the verse by *par he'elam davar* states *v'asa lapar ka'asher asa lapar harishon* — he shall do for the *par* as he did for the first *par* — meaning the procedure of the *kohen gadol*'s *par* is the template. But why does the Torah need to state this? It is to double and reinforce the *haza'ot*, teaching that every individual sprinkling is required, such that if even one is missing, nothing was accomplished: *she'im chisar achat m'kol hamatanot lo asa klum*.

---

## Lulav Unity Lesson

### Fruit Bearers

Having enumerated the four species in the context of *me'akev*, the *gemara* now elaborates on the *lulav* specifically, introducing a *beraita* that contains both a legal and a moral dimension.

Rav Chana bar Rava teaches: the rule that the four species are mutually interdependent (*me'akvin zeh et zeh*) applies only when one does not possess all four. If one has all four species available, *ein me'akvin* — they do not hold one another back. What this means will be developed shortly, but the basic point is that the *me'akev* relationship is triggered by actual absence, not by the choice to take them separately when one owns all of them.

The *gemara* then raises a challenge from a *beraita*: the four species of the *lulav* — two of which bear fruit (the *lulav*, which yields dates, and the *etrog*) and two of which do not (the *hadas* and *arava*) — are mutually dependent in both directions. The fruit-bearers need the non-fruit-bearers, and the non-fruit-bearers need the fruit-bearers. And the *beraita* states: *ein adam yotzei yedei chovato bahen ad she'kulam b'agudah achat* — a person does not fulfill his obligation unless all of them are in a single bundle.

### Divine Bundle

The *beraita* then draws its moral: *v'chen Yisrael b'hartza'ah* — so too with Israel when they come seeking divine favor. They must all be gathered together as one. The proof-text is *haboneh bashamayim ma'alotav va'agudato al eretz yesadah* — He who builds His chambers in the heavens, His bundle is established upon the earth. When the Jewish people are unified — forming God's *agudah* on earth — the divine presence is properly established above and God responds to their prayers.

The moral deserves attention. The *beraita* is careful to make the dependency mutual: it is not only that those who do not bear fruit depend upon those who do, but equally that the fruit-bearers depend upon the non-fruit-bearers. One reading is that we need the non-fruit-bearers for the sake of unity — that we must not exclude any Jew. But the language suggests something more: that those who do not practice *mitzvot* in the conventional sense nonetheless contribute qualities and strengths to the Jewish people that those who do are not providing. The building of *Eretz Yisrael*, for instance, was carried forward by those who were not engaged in *Torah* study, and that contribution is, in its own way, indispensable.

### Bundle Debate

The *beraita*'s statement that all four species must be *b'agudah achat* — in one bundle — points toward a debate among the *tanna'im* that the *gemara* now introduces: must the *lulav* be physically bound? According to the *rabbanan*, it is valid whether bound or not. According to Rabbi Yehuda, if it is bound it is valid; if not bound it is invalid. Rabbi Yehuda derives this from a *gezeirah shavah* of *kicha kicha*: the Torah says *u'lekachtem lachem* using the root *lekicha*, and elsewhere it says *agudat ezov* — a bundle of hyssop — also in the context of *kicha*. Just as there a bundle is required, so too here. The *rabbanan* do not accept this *gezeirah shavah*.

A further *beraita* teaches: it is a *mitzvah* to bind the *lulav*, but if one did not bind it, it is still valid. The *gemara* asks: whose position is this? If it is Rabbi Yehuda's, why is it valid when not bound? And if it is the *rabbanan*'s, why would binding be a *mitzvah* at all? The *gemara* resolves: it follows the *rabbanan*, and the *mitzvah* of binding is derived from *zeh keili v'anveihu* — the principle of enhancing a *mitzvah* through beauty. Binding makes the *lulav* look more beautiful, and so it is praiseworthy though not required for validity.

However, this explanation may be incomplete. If the *rabbanan* agree at the conceptual level that the four species constitute a single act of taking — which the *gemara* elsewhere implies — then the *mitzvah* of binding may not be merely aesthetic. Binding them together physically expresses and reinforces their unity as a single *mitzvah*. On this reading, the *mitzvah l'ogdo* is about making the act more fully what it is meant to be — a single, unified taking — not merely about appearance.

It is also worth noting that even Rabbi Yehuda does not require the *etrog* to be literally bundled together with the others; the verse *u'lekachtem lachem bayom harishon pri etz hadar kapot temarim* does not link the *etrog* to the *lulav* with a *vav*, leaving the *etrog* somewhat apart even according to his view. This suggests that even Rabbi Yehuda's requirement of *agud* is more conceptual than physical at the level of the *etrog*, though one holds them together in practice.

### Lekicha Tama

Returning to Rav Chana bar Rava's ruling — that if one possesses all four species they are not *me'akev* — the *gemara* specifies what this means practically. It does not mean one can take three and omit one. Rather, it means they need not be bound in a single *agudah*. The taking of each one separately, when all are present and owned, is not disqualified by the absence of a bundle.

*Tosafot* cites *Halachot Gedolot* and notes that the *Rambam* goes even further: if all four species are available (*yesh lo*), one may take them in four separate sequential acts rather than simultaneously, and still be *yotzei*. The *Rambam* apparently reasons that since one could have taken them all at once, taking them sequentially is viewed as if they were taken together.

The logical question this raises is profound: the verse says *u'lekachtem* — a single verb, a single act. By *tefillin*, the Torah uses two verbs — *ukshartem l'os al yadecha* and *v'hayu l'totafot bein einecha* — and it is easier to understand why they might constitute two distinct *mitzvot* that happen to be interdependent. For the *lulav*, there is one verb and one act; how can we permit four separate acts? The answer given by *Halachot Gedolot* and the *Rambam* seems to be that since one owned all four and could have performed a single act, any sequential performance is retrospectively viewed as equivalent to the single act one could have performed.

The *Rambam*'s ruling goes still further: he holds that if one does take them separately, separate *brachot* are recited over each — one for the *etrog*, one for the *lulav*, one for each of the other species. This is a striking ruling, suggesting that at some level they are conceived of as distinct *mitzvot*. Yet this sits in tension with the single verb of *u'lekachtem*. This tension — between whether interdependent components constitute a single unified *mitzvah* or distinct *mitzvot* that are merely bound together — is precisely the conceptual question that will occupy the *gemara* for many dafim to come.

---

## Sprinklings Intent

### Parah Adumah

The *gemara* now takes up a *baraita* addressing the seven sprinklings of the *parah adumah* toward the *ohel mo'ed*, and two conditions under which they may be invalidated.

The first condition is *shelo lishmo* — performing the *haza'ot* without the proper intent. The Torah refers to the *parah adumah* as a *chata't*, and the general rule established in the first *mishna* of Zevachim is that a *chata't* performed *shelo lishmo* is *pasul*. Accordingly, if the sprinklings of the *parah adumah* are performed without the proper intent, they are invalid.

The second condition is *shelo m'chuvanot* — performing the sprinklings without proper direction. The verse specifies *el nochach pnei ohel mo'ed* — directly facing the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. If the *kohen* sprinkled in the wrong direction, entirely missing the orientation toward the *beit hamikdash*, this too is *pasul*.

### Inner Chata'ot

The same *baraita* addresses the sprinklings of the inner *chata'ot* — those performed inside the *heichal*, between the staves of the *aron*, upon the *parochet*, and upon the golden altar — as well as the sprinklings associated with the purification of a *metzora*.

For both the inner *chata'ot* and the *metzora*, performing the sprinklings *shelo lishman* — without proper intent — renders them *pasul*. For the inner *chata'ot*, this follows from the rule that a *chata't shelo lishmo* is invalid. For the *metzora*, it requires additional discussion, since the sprinkling in that context is part of an *asham* rather than a *chata't*; the *gemara* will need to explain what *shelo lishmo* means in that context.

### Direction Contradiction

Here a striking contradiction emerges. The *baraita* stated that for the *parah adumah*, sprinklings that are *shelo m'chuvanot* — not directed correctly — are *pasul*. Yet the same *baraita* then says that for the inner *chata'ot* and the *metzora*, sprinklings that are *shelo m'chuvanot* are *kasherot* — valid even if not precisely directed. How can the same condition (improper direction) invalidate one set of sprinklings but leave another set valid?

This is a genuine contradiction within the *baraita*, and the *gemara* treats it as such.

### Facing Debate

Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. One ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda and the other follows the *rabbanan*. The two positions are rooted in a larger debate about the meaning of the Torah's description of the *avodah* on Yom Kippur. The verse in *Acharei Mot* states *v'al yavo b'chol et el hakodesh mibeit laparochet el pnei hakaporet* — no one may enter the inner sanctum, from within the *parochet* facing the *kaporet*. The phrase *el pnei hakaporet* — toward the face of the *kaporet* — triggers a debate: are one's obligations (and prohibitions) defined by being in the *kodesh kodashim* at all (*mibeit laparochet*), or only when one is directly facing the *aron* (*el pnei hakaporet*)?

This debate about the meaning of "facing" in the context of Yom Kippur entry carries over into the laws of sprinkling. Whether the requirement to sprinkle toward the *kodesh kodashim* means precisely facing it, or merely facing its general direction, depends on the same underlying dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *rabbanan*. The *parah adumah* ruling reflects one position on this, and the inner *chata'ot* ruling reflects the other.

The full elaboration of this debate — with its nuances and halachic implications — will occupy the beginning of the next shiur.

---

---

# Menachot 28

## Blood Sprinkling Debate

### Intro & Contradiction

The present discussion begins as a continuation of 27b, where the Gemara had set up a contradiction between two *braitot*. One *braita* holds that the sprinkling of blood toward the *heichal* — even if not precisely directed — is valid (*kasher*); the other holds that while this imprecision is generally acceptable, by the *parah adumah* it renders the sprinkling invalid (*pasul*). The question the Gemara investigates is what this debate is actually about, and it unfolds in the larger framework of *me'akev* — the principle that certain component parts are indispensable to the validity of a ritual act.

### Kodesh Hakodashim Entry

To explain the debate over directional precision, the Gemara anchors the discussion in a *braita* about entry into the *kodesh hakodashim*. The *braita* opens with the laws of *mechuserai kaparah* — those whose *tahara* process is complete except for the final bringing of a *korban*, representing the lowest level of residual *tumah*. If such a person enters the *azarah* unintentionally (*bishogeg*), he is liable to bring a *chatat*; if willfully (*b'meizid*), he is liable to *kares*. This applies *kal vachomer* to those with more substantial *tumah*, including the *tvu'el yom* and certainly those who have not yet gone to the *mikveh* at all.

The *braita* then turns to those who are ritually pure (*tahorim*) but go beyond their permitted boundaries. One who enters the *heichal* — the roofed inner sanctum housing the *shulchan* and the golden *mizbeach* — is punishable by lashes, since the verse *v'lo yavo bechol et el hakodesh* constitutes a negative prohibition, applying even to a *kohen* who enters without a legitimate purpose (*bi'ah reikanit*). If, however, one enters *mibeis laparoches* — into the *kodesh hakodashim* behind the curtain — and stands *el pnei hakaporet*, directly in front of the *aron*, the punishment is divine death (*mita biyedei shamayim*). That is the first opinion.

*Rabbi Yehuda* disputes this. In his view, the entire *heichal* and the *kodesh hakodashim* alike are subject only to lashes. Divine death applies exclusively when one stands *el pnei hakaporet* — directly in front of the *aron*.

### Verse Parsing

The Gemara asks: *b'mai kamifligi* — what precisely are they debating? The answer is that they disagree over how to parse the verse in *Vayikra*: *daber el Aharon achicha v'al yavo bechol et el hakodesh mibeis laparoches al pnei hakaporet asher al ha'aron v'lo yamus* — "Speak to Aharon your brother, and he shall not come at any time into the sanctuary, behind the curtain, in front of the *kaporet* that is upon the *aron*, lest he die." Three locational phrases appear: *el hakodesh* (into the sanctuary), *mibeis laparoches* (behind the curtain), and *al pnei hakaporet* (in front of the *kaporet*). The outer phrases are not contested: *el hakodesh* is clearly the negative prohibition of entering, and *al pnei hakaporet* — when combined with *v'lo yamus* — is clearly a case of divine death. The dispute is about the middle phrase, *mibeis laparoches*: does it attach to the first half of the verse (the prohibition of entry), or to the second half (the death penalty)?

### Rabbanan Position

The *rabbanan* hold that *el hakodesh* — the prohibition of entry — refers to the *heichal*, and that both *mibeis laparoches* and *al pnei hakaporet* together trigger the death penalty. Their reasoning is textual: if *Rabbi Yehuda* were correct that one incurs *mita* only when standing directly in front of the *aron*, then the phrase *mibeis laparoches* would be entirely superfluous. The Torah could simply have written *el hakodesh* (negative prohibition) and *al pnei hakaporet* (death), and one would naturally have known that the *heichal* prohibits entry and that standing before the *aron* triggers death. Since the *heichal* is already prohibited, there is no need to separately prohibit the *kodesh hakodashim* — it is obviously included. The only reason to write *mibeis laparoches* is to teach that even entering the *kodesh hakodashim* alone, without confronting the *aron*, is sufficient to incur divine death. Furthermore, *d'heichal kulei ikrei kodesh* — the *heichal* is already called *kodesh*, as the verse states that the *paroches* separates *bein hakodesh u'vein kodesh hakodashim*, making clear that *kodesh* is the *heichal*. There is therefore no possibility of confusion requiring clarification.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

*Rabbi Yehuda* defends his reading by turning the same argument around. If we had only written *el hakodesh*, one might have thought this referred to the *kodesh hakodashim* — interpreting *kodesh* as the holiest place — and thereby excluded the *heichal* from any prohibition entirely. The Torah therefore had to include *mibeis laparoches* explicitly as a clarification that *kodesh* means the *heichal*, and that the *heichal* is prohibited. Once the *heichal* and *kodesh hakodashim* are both under a negative prohibition through this reading, the separate phrase *al pnei hakaporet* followed by *v'lo yamus* is unnecessary unless it is coming to tell us something new: only when one stands directly in front of the *aron* is the penalty death — otherwise it is merely a negative prohibition.

The Gemara then asks how the *rabbanan* account for the phrase *al pnei hakaporet* if they already derive *mita* from *mibeis laparoches*. The answer is *l'mivti derech meshupash* — the phrase is not superfluous but teaches that divine death applies only when entry is made facing the *aron* directly, not indirectly. A *braita* of *Beis Rav Eliezer ben Yaakov* is cited: *al pnei hakaporet keidma* — facing the *kaporet* toward the east — establishes a paradigm (*binyan av*) that wherever the Torah says "facing" (*pnei*), it means the eastern face.

---

## Directional Precision

### Eastern Facing

This paradigm is grounded in a broader structural observation about biblical orientation. The Torah consistently assumes that a person stands facing east: hence the word for south (*teimana*) derives from *yamin* — right — because if one faces east, the south is to the right. West is described as *acharei derech mivo hashemesh*, "behind toward the setting sun," since *achor* is opposite *kadim* (east). Avraham's offer to Lot — *im hasmol v'eimina v'im hayamin v'asme'ila* — is understood as referring to south and north respectively, since he assumes an eastward orientation.

### Rashi's Forward Entry

*Rashi* draws from this the precise implication for the *kodesh hakodashim*: the phrase *pnei hakaporet* teaches that one incurs *chiyuv mita* only if one enters facing the *aron* — through the front, as it were. If one digs a tunnel and enters from the side or from below, or enters walking backwards, or enters at an angle, one would not be liable, because one is not entering *facing* the *aron*. Without the phrase *pnei hakaporet*, we would have derived liability from simply entering the *kodesh hakodashim*; the phrase comes to qualify that: one must enter in a forward-facing manner. The question is purely physical — how one is oriented upon entry — not a matter of intent.

### El Means Exact

*Rabbi Yehuda* then pushes further. If all the Torah wished to convey was the requirement of forward-facing entry, it could have simply written *pnei*. Why does it write *el pnei*? *Shma mina: el davka* — the word *el* (toward, in front of) means precisely and directly in front, not merely in that general direction. This is the crux of *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position, and it carries implications that extend far beyond the *kodesh hakodashim*.

### Parah Adumah Link

The connection to the opening debate now becomes clear. *Rabbi Yehuda*, who holds that *el pnei hakaporet* means exactly in front, reads similarly the verse concerning the *parah adumah* — *v'hizah el nochach pnei ohel moed*, he shall sprinkle toward the face of the *ohel moed* — as meaning the sprinkling must be directed precisely in that direction. The *rabbanan*, by contrast, hold that *el* does not require exact precision, only general orientation, and so by the *parah adumah* as well, approximate direction suffices.

---

## Sprinkling Exceptions

### General Non-Precision

The Gemara now faces a secondary question: even granting the debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *rabbanan* over the *parah adumah*, why do all opinions agree that by other *korbanot* — including the Yom Kippur inner service — imprecise direction is valid?

### Yom Kippur Challenge

*Rav Yosef* presses *Rav Yehuda*: if *el davka* means precise direction, consider the verse *al pnei hakaporet* used in the context of the Yom Kippur sprinkling. Would *Rabbi Yehuda* say the blood must literally strike the cover of the *aron*? And further — in the *beis hamikdash sheni*, where there was no *aron* and no *kaporet*, would *Rabbi Yehuda* say there could be no sprinkling at all?

### Ark Exception

*Rava bar Ulla* resolves this: the verse *v'chiper et mikdash hakodesh* — "he shall sanctify the sanctuary of the holy place" — teaches that atonement is achieved through the *makom hamekudash lakodesh*, the location sanctified for holiness, even when all the vessels are not present. So *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position accommodates the Yom Kippur service in the *beis hamikdash sheni* by means of this special verse. The general principle stands: *Rabbi Yehuda* reads *el* and *al* as precise, but the particular circumstance of the *beis hamikdash sheni* is addressed separately.

*Rava* then offers an alternative resolution to the whole contradiction between the *braitot* on sprinkling direction. He holds that both *braitot* represent the *rabbanan*'s position — that is, directional precision is generally not required. The distinction between them is not about who is right or wrong in principle, but about what angle of deviation is being discussed. When the celebrant is oriented east-west — generally facing toward the *mikdash* — slight imprecision is acceptable, and the *braita* says it is *kasher*. When oriented north-south — entirely off-axis — one is not sprinkling toward the *mikdash* at all, and the *braita* says it is *pasul*. The two *braitot* address different physical situations, not different legal opinions.

### Metzora Oil

The *braita* then addresses a related case: *v'she-bifnim v'she-bi-metzora she-lo lishmah psulot* — the inner *korbanot* and the sprinkling done in connection with the *metzora* are invalid if performed *shelo lishmah* (not for their designated purpose), but *shelo mechuvanos kesheros* — if not precisely directed, they remain valid. This is immediately challenged: does a contradicting *braita* not say that even *shelo lishmah* is valid by the *metzora*?

To understand the contradiction, the nature of the *metzora*'s ritual must be clarified. The verse from this week's *parasha* (Vayikra 14) describes how the *kohen* takes the blood of the *asham*, applies it to the *metzora*'s ear, and then dips his finger in the *log* of oil and sprinkles it seven times *lifnei Hashem* — toward the *heichal*. The question of *shelo lishmah* applies to this sprinkling of oil, whose status is linked to the *asham* that accompanies it.

### Asham Status

*Rav Yosef* identifies the contradiction as a dispute between *Rabbi Eliezer* and the *rabbanan*. *Rabbi Eliezer*, as established at the beginning of Zevachim, holds that an *asham* is analogous to a *chatat* — both come to atone for sin — and therefore an *asham* performed *shelo lishmah*, like a *chatat* performed *shelo lishmah*, is invalid. Since *Rabbi Eliezer* links the *asham* to the *chatat*, he likewise links the *log* of oil to the *asham*: just as the *asham shelo lishmah* is invalid, so is the sprinkling of the oil *shelo lishmah*. The *rabbanan*, by contrast, do not equate *asham* with *chatat*, and so both the *asham* and its associated oil remain valid even *shelo lishmah*.

The Gemara then raises a further difficulty: can *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling about the oil rest on this reasoning? The rule that an *asham* is like a *chatat* is itself derived through a *hekesh* (analogy), and there is a general principle that a *davar halamad b'hekesh* cannot in turn serve as the basis of another *hekesh*. If the *asham's* invalidity *shelo lishmah* is itself only known through *hekesh*, it cannot be used to derive that the oil is also invalid.

### Rava's Resolution

*Rava* therefore resolves the contradiction differently: *ha v'ha rabbanan* — both *braitot* represent the position of the *rabbanan*, who agree that the *asham* and oil are valid even *shelo lishmah*. The key is the first *mishna* of Zevachim: a *korban* performed *shelo lishmah* is valid, but it does not *alah l'baalim l'shem chova* — it does not count toward the owner's obligation. Applying this to the *metzora*: the *braita* that says the sprinkling is valid means the *korban* retains its sanctity — the meat may be eaten, the remainder of the oil may be consumed — but the *metzora* does not thereby become *tahor*, since the ritual did not fulfill its designated purpose. The *braita* that says it is invalid means it does not achieve its goal of *tahara* for the *metzora*. One *braita* speaks to the validity of the object (*hechsher*), the other to whether it accomplishes what it set out to do (*hartzah*).

With this resolution, the Gemara concludes the extended digression into sprinkling direction — prompted by the *mishna*'s discussion of the number of sprinklings being *me'akev* — and pivots to the *mishna*'s next major theme: the interdependency of component parts in the *menorah*, *mezuzah*, *tefillin*, and *tzitzit*.

---

## Interdependent Parts

### Shift to Vessels

Having addressed the world of *korbanot* and their internal requirements, the Gemara now turns toward *klei hamikdash* and the practical *mitzvot* of everyday Jewish life. The structural framework of the earlier *baraita* had organized its cases numerically: two loaves, three elements of *parah adumah*, four *minim* of *lulav*, and seven sprinklings. The *mishna* now returns to a similar numerical ascent — two, four, four — but now speaks of objects rather than sacrificial acts, and specifically of objects with which Jews engage daily: the *menorah*, the *mezuzah*, the *tefillin*, and the *tzitzit*.

### Menorah Components

*Sheva kanei menorah me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the seven branches of the *menorah* prevent one another from being valid. A *menorah* with fewer than seven branches is not a valid *menorah*; one cannot simply light what is present and fulfill the *mitzvah* on the remaining branches. Similarly, *sheva neroteha me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the seven lamps. The *kaneh* (branch) is the structural arm itself; the *ner* is the small vessel placed at the top of each branch to hold the oil and wick, which actually produces the flame. Both the branches and their lamps are mutually indispensable.

The verse undergirding this mutual indispensability is *kaftorehah u'kenotehah mimena yihyu* — "its spheres and its branches shall be from it" — and more broadly, the Gemara learns from *havaya*, "shall be," that the *menorah* must exist in precisely this form.

It is worth noting in this context the well-known dispute regarding the *menorah*'s physical shape. The familiar image of arching, curved branches is consistent with contemporary archaeological evidence — the depiction on Titus's arch, and the engravings found in the Burnt House near the *kotel*, which clearly show arched branches. The *Rambam*, however, drawing on the silence of the *Torah*'s descriptions regarding curves, understood the branches as extending at straight diagonal angles from the central shaft, and drew this accordingly in his own hand. While his diagram was reproduced and debated, the physical evidence clearly supports the arched form.

### Daily Mitzvot

*Shtei parshiot shebamezuzah me'akvin zu et zu* — the two *parshiot* of *Shema* and *V'hayah im shamo'a* are mutually indispensable in the *mezuzah*. Not only that, but *afilu ktav echad me'akev* — even a single defective letter invalidates the entire *mezuzah*.

*Arba parshiot shebatefillin me'akvin zu et zu* — the four *parshiot* of *tefillin* (*Shema*, *V'hayah im shamo'a*, *Kadesh li*, and *V'hayah ki yevi'acha*) are all required, and again *afilu ktav echad me'akvan* — a single letter in any of them invalidates all.

*Arba tzitzit me'akvot zu et zu* — all four *tzitziyot* at the four corners of the *beged* are interdependent. One cannot claim to have fulfilled three-quarters of the *mitzvah* by attaching *tzitzit* to three corners. This is because *she-hen mitzvah achat* — they constitute a single *mitzvah* of a garment with *tzitzit*. *Rabbi Yishmael*, however, says *arba'tan arba mitzvot* — they are four separate *mitzvot*. The Gemara will explore the implications of that position in due course.

---

## Menorah Material

### One Beaten Unit

The Gemara now addresses the *menorah*'s material requirements in detail. A *braita* states: *Menorah hayetah ba'ah min ha-ashet u'min ha-zahav* — the *menorah* was made from a single lump of ore, fashioned from gold. *As'ah min ha-gruta'ot, psulah* — if one assembled it from individual pieces, even if melded together, it is invalid. *Mishar minei matachot, kesherah* — if made from other metals besides gold, it is valid.

### Chashmonaim Evidence

The historical evidence confirms this ruling. When the *Chashmonaim* rededicated the *mikdash*, they initially constructed a *menorah* that was not of gold, and yet it was used for the service — demonstrating that gold is not *me'akev*, but the requirement of being fashioned from one beaten piece is.

### Mikshah Havaya

The Gemara derives this from the *psukim*. Why is assembling from pieces invalid? *D'chtiv mikshah* — the verse writes *mikshah* (beaten), *d'havaya* — and "it shall be," *yihyu*, meaning it must be exactly this way. But if the verse says both "gold" and "shall be," why not require gold precisely as well? The Gemara answers: *amar kra ta'aseh* — "shall be made" implies a certain latitude in how it is made. The word *ta'aseh* comes to include other metals. Moreover, *mikshah* is written twice in the *parashah* — once in *mikshah ta'aseh et ha-menorah* and again at the end, *kula mikshah achat zahav tahor* — indicating that the requirement of being beaten in one piece is uncompromisable.

### Reconciling Repetition

The Gemara then addresses the apparent redundancy of both *mikshah* and *zahav* each appearing twice. The question raised is: could the doubling of *zahav* similarly indicate that gold is required precisely and cannot be substituted? The Gemara's response is structural: *ha'inhu zahav zahav mikshah mikshah lidrasha* — the repetitions are there to generate a *drasha* that clarifies what is and is not essential. The position that other metals are valid but assembled pieces are not is the only reading that gives meaningful content to all the doubled terms.

The Gemara then identifies how this works. The verse *kikar zahav tahor ya'aseh otah et kol hakeilim ha'eileh* — "one *kikar* of pure gold shall he make it, all these vessels" — establishes a list of requirements that apply when gold is used. *Ba'ah zahav ba'ah kikar* — when gold is used, the *kikar* weight applies; *eina ba'ah zahav eina ba'ah kikar* — when other metals are used, the precise weight requirement does not apply. Similarly: *ba'ah zahav ba'ah gevi'im kaftorim u'ferachim* — when gold is used, all the ornamental cups, spheres, and flowers are required; *eina ba'ah zahav eina ba'ah gevi'im kaftorim u'ferachim* — if not gold, these ornaments are not mandatory.

The Gemara asks whether one might further extend this: perhaps when not gold, one need not even have seven branches? The answer is *hu pumit mikrei* — a single-branched lamp is simply not called a *menorah* at all; it is called a lamp. The seven-branch structure is definitional, not merely a gold-dependent enhancement.

*Ba'ah zahav ba'ah mikshah* — when gold is used, it must be one beaten piece; *eina ba'ah zahav eina ba'ah mikshah* — when other metals are used, this requirement does not apply. This confirms the overall framework: gold triggers a maximally demanding set of requirements, while other metals require only the seven-branched form itself. The doubled words of *mikshah* and *zahav* are therefore not redundant but structurally necessary, each pair working together to define a linked system of conditional requirements.

### Trumpets Inverse

The Gemara derives the second instance of *mikshah* — *mikshah ta'aseh* — as serving to exclude the *chatzotzrot* (trumpets) that Moshe fashioned. The *chatzotzrot* represent the precise inverse of the *menorah*: they must be silver, but they do not need to be fashioned from a single beaten piece. A *braita* states: *chatzotzrot hayu ba'ot min ha-ashet u'min ha-kesef* — the trumpets could come from a single piece or from silver; *asan min ha-gruta'ot, kesheirah* — if made from melted-together pieces, valid; *mishar minei matachot, psulim* — other metals, invalid. Why must they be silver? *D'chtiv kesef v'havaya* — the verse writes silver and "shall be" together, establishing silver as precise and non-negotiable. Why does the *Torah* not similarly insist on a single piece? Because the verse *hi v'lo chatzotzrot* — "it [the *menorah*] is one beaten piece, and not the *chatzotzrot*" — specifies the *menorah* as the single item requiring a unitary beaten form.

The Gemara then records a *braita* on the vessels of Moshe generally: *kol ha-keilim she'asah Moshe kesheirim lo u'kesheirim l'dorot* — all the vessels Moshe made were valid for his time and for all subsequent generations. The *chatzotzrot* are an exception: *kesheirot lo u'psulot l'dorot* — they were used in his generation but not in future ones, since their primary function was moving the camp. The verse *aseh lecha* — "make for yourself" — is read as *lecha v'lo l'dorot*, for your generation and not for future ones, precisely because both the context (mobilizing a moving camp) and the double use of *lecha* in the verse (*aseh lecha* and *v'hayu lach*) signal temporal limitation. By contrast, similar language by the *aron* (*v'asita lach aron etz*) does not limit it to Moshe's generation, since there the *lach* is read either as indicating Moshe's personal contribution of funds or as God expressing that ideally the *aron* would be Moshe's own — both readings that preclude the limiting interpretation.

---

## Permitted Materials

### Rav Pappa List

*Rav Pappa brei de-Rabbi Chanin* taught a *braita* before *Rav Yosef*: the *menorah* comes from a single beaten lump and from gold. If made of silver — valid. Of tin (*bedi'il*), lead (*oferet*), or *gisteron* (a metallic alloy) — *Rabbi* invalidates, *Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda* validates. If made of wood, bone, or glass — non-metallic materials — *divrei ha-kol psulah*, everyone agrees it is invalid.

### Rav Yosef Alt

*Rav Yosef* responded by presenting an alternative *braita*, which he considered more accurate: *klei sharet she-asahan shel eitz* — service vessels fashioned of wood — *Rabbi* invalidates, *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* validates. This formulation places the debate not over cheap metals, but over non-metals entirely: wood versus metal.

### Hermeneutics

*Rav Yosef* then asks *Rav Pappa*: according to your version, what interpretive method are both opinions using? *Rav Pappa* responds that both employ *klal u'prat u'klal*: *v'asita menorah* is the *klal* (general); *zahav tahor* is the *prat* (specific); *v'kikar et ha-menorah* is the return to *klal*. By the rules of *klal u'prat u'klal*, one includes anything like the specific — like gold. *Rav Yosef* finds this unsatisfying, since by his reading the debate is governed instead by *ribuy u'mi'ut*: *v'asita menorah* is the *ribuy* (broad inclusion); *zahav tahor* is the *mi'ut* (restriction); *v'kikar et ha-menorah* is the renewed *ribuy*. The rule of *ribuy mi'ut v'ribuy* is that one excludes only what is most dissimilar to the specific term.

### Material Positions

Under *klal u'prat u'klal*, as both sides agree in *Rav Pappa*'s version, the debate is about what "like gold" means. *Rebbi* holds: *mah prat meforash shel matechet, af kol shel matechet* — just as the specific (gold) is a metal, anything that is a metal qualifies. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* holds: *mah prat meforash davar chashuv, af kol davar chashuv* — just as gold is a distinguished material, anything distinguished qualifies, implying precious materials beyond metals might also be included, while inexpensive metals might be excluded.

Under *ribuy mi'ut v'ribuy*, as *Rav Yosef*'s version has it, almost everything is included by default; only the thing most dissimilar to gold is excluded. *Mi'et shel cheres* — pottery alone is excluded. Everything else — metals, wood, bone, glass short of pottery — would be included according to *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Evidence Consolidation

*Rav Pappa* pushes back: why should I abandon my *braita* in favor of yours? *Rav Yosef* replies that multiple *braitot* converge on the position that the debate concerns non-metals, not distinctions within metals. One *braita* states: *ein lo zahav mevi af shel kesef, shel nechoshet, shel barzel, shel bedil, shel oferet* — if one does not have gold, one may bring the *menorah* from any other metal: silver, copper, iron, tin, lead. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda machshir af be-shel etz* — *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* further validates even wood. This pattern repeats across several *braitot*, all of which show that *Rabbi* and *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* are not debating the rank of metals among themselves, but whether non-metallic materials such as wood are included at all.

---

---

# Menachot 28b

## Menorah Materials

### Temple Replicas

The Gemara at the bottom and middle of 28b continues its discussion of the *menorah*, turning from the question of what materials may be used for it to the broader prohibition against fashioning replicas of Temple vessels. A *braita* states: *lo yaaseh adam bayit tavnit heichal, achsadrah keneged ulam* — a person may not construct his house according to the dimensions of the *heichal*, nor may he build his *achsadrah* corresponding to the *ulam*. The *achsadrah*, a Roman-era portico with three walls open on the fourth side, functions like the *ulam* in that it serves as an entry-hall; the *ulam*'s opening was twenty *ammot* wide and thirty *ammot* high, effectively giving it the character of such a space. Similarly, one may not make his courtyard according to the dimensions of the Temple *azarah*, nor a table according to the dimensions of the Temple *shulchan*, nor a *menorah* corresponding to the Temple *menorah*.

Several practical questions arise from this prohibition. If one fashions a *menorah* not of gold, there is an irony at work: a non-gold *menorah*, if used in the *Mikdash*, would require far fewer of the ornamental features mandated for the golden *menorah*. This actually makes the prohibition more stringent in a subtle way — a non-gold *menorah* is a closer functional analog to a valid *Mikdash menorah* because it needs so few conditions to be acceptable. One might therefore need to be more careful that it not be considered something fit for Temple use. The exact threshold of the prohibition — whether proportions must match precisely, or whether a change in size suffices to avoid the prohibition — is a question the *poskim* address at length.

The *braita* then draws an important distinction: one may make a candelabra with five, six, or eight arms — but not seven. Furthermore, the prohibition applies even to a *menorah* made of other metals, *vaafilu shel sh'ar minei matachot*, since the *menorah* in the *Mikdash* itself would be *kasher* if made from other metals.

An intriguing tradition connects this passage to *Chanukah*. The prohibition against fashioning a seven-branched candelabra is derived not from the *braita* alone but from the *pasuk* in *Rosh Hashanah*: *lo ta'asu iti*, read as "do not make things that are associated with Me." This is understood to prohibit replicating objects of the *Mishkan* for lay use. One opinion cited in the literature holds that precisely this is why *Chanukah* was established for eight days rather than seven: had it been seven, people would have fashioned small *chanukiot* that would amount to *menorot*, thereby violating this prohibition. That is a striking derivation.

Regarding the *menorah* constructed by *Machon HaMikdash* and displayed near the *Kotel*, the position of the institution is that the prohibition applies only when the object is intended for ordinary use — since they intend theirs for use in the future *Beit HaMikdash*, no prohibition applies.

### Metals Debate

The Gemara's focus in this passage is on the debate among the *Tannaim* about what materials are acceptable for the *menorah*. Rav Yosef maintains that the dispute is not between precious metals and all metals, but rather between all metals on one side and non-metallic materials on the other — and that no one requires specifically precious metals. The *braita* cited supports this framing: the debate is about whether wood and similar materials would suffice.

### Historical Evidence

Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda argues that even wood is a valid material for the *menorah*, and cites historical evidence: *kederekh she'asu malkhei beit Hashmonai* — as the Hasmonean kings did when, upon rededicating the *Beit HaMikdash* without the resources for a proper *menorah*, they fashioned one from wood. Since a wooden *menorah* would therefore be valid, one may not make a wooden seven-branched candelabra even at home.

The Sages respond: *misham ra'aya?* — can you really bring proof from there? Those were not wood at all, they say. *Shappudin shel barzel hayu* — they were iron rods, covered with tin, *bavatz*. When the Hasmoneans grew wealthier, they replaced the iron-and-tin *menorah* with one of silver, and eventually with one of gold.

What is striking about this exchange is that throughout the tractates of *Zevachim* and *Menachot* — pages of rigorous *halakhic* analysis — it is almost unheard of to see the *Tannaim* debating not a *pasuk* or a logical argument but a piece of collective historical memory. Yet here, both sides are appealing to what people remembered of the Hasmonean *menorah*. Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda remembered it as wood; the Sages maintained it was iron coated with tin. It is also worth noting that iron coated with tin would look more lustrous than bare iron — tin gives a more polished appearance. One could perhaps understand how a rusted iron object might be mistaken for wood, but how a tin-coated object would look like wood is less clear.

---

## Menorah Dimensions

### Height Debate

The Gemara now turns to the dimensions of the *menorah*. Shmuel, in the name of an elder (*mishmei desaba*) whose identity is not preserved, states: *gova shel menorah shemonah asar tefachim* — the height of the *menorah* was eighteen *tefachim*. Since a *tefach* is approximately three inches, eighteen *tefachim* comes to roughly 54 inches — about four and a half feet. This is considerably shorter than most people envision the *menorah*. The relief on Titus's Arch shows the *menorah* being carried, and a rough scaling against the human figures depicted suggests it was closer to the height of a person — perhaps somewhat taller. Yet the Gemara's figure, taken literally, gives a much more modest object.

### Structure Breakdown

The Gemara proceeds to give a *tefach*-by-*tefach* breakdown of the *menorah*'s structure from base to top. Beginning at the bottom: the base and the flower (*ha-raglayim ve-ha-parach*) occupy three *tefachim*. Then two *tefachim* of smooth, unornamented shaft. Then one *tefach* containing a cup (*gavia*), a sphere (*kaftor*), and a flower (*perach*). Then two more *tefachim* of smooth shaft, followed by a *tefach* that is a sphere — a *kaftor* — from which two arms branch outward (*shenei kanim yotzim mimenu, echad eilech ve-echad eilech*), reaching the full height of the *menorah*. The pattern continues: one *tefach* of smooth shaft, a sphere from which two more arms branch, one smooth *tefach*, and a third sphere from which the final two arms branch. At the top of the structure, two more *tefachim* of smooth shaft bring one to the topmost section, where three *tefachim* are reserved for the uppermost ornaments of each arm: *she-bahem gimmel gvi'im ve-kaftor va-perach* — three cups, a sphere, and a flower.

As for the appearance of these ornaments: the cups (*gvi'im*) are described as Alexandrian goblets (*kousot Alexandriyim*); the spheres (*kaftorim*) resemble Cretan apples — apparently a variety of olive-shaped or apple-shaped fruit, described in some sources as what might be called Ceracean apples; and the flowers (*prachim*) resemble the floral capitals of columns.

The *mishnah*'s language is notably terse, simply stating that the arms "go out" and "reach the height of the *menorah*" without specifying whether they arch. A number of *Rishonim* consequently assume they were angular — extending outward at an angle and then rising straight up — but this conflicts with the visual evidence from Titus's Arch, coins, and mosaics, all of which consistently depict arched arms in the form we typically envision.

### Contemporary Evidence

The pictures that survive from antiquity — Titus's Arch, coins, mosaics — are broadly consistent with one another in the appearance of the arms and the general shape of the *menorah*, though they diverge considerably in their depictions of the base. Some show a triangular base, some a pyramidal form, some a rectangular one. It may be that most artisans simply did not have access to a clear view of the base, or that the base was partially obscured, and so they reconstructed it from imagination. This divergence is itself historically interesting.

One might also note that virtually all the contemporary images appear to show ornamentation distributed along the full length of the arms, not merely concentrated at the junction points and the top, as the Talmudic description implies. While the *Torah* is explicit that there are *shelosha gvi'im* on each arm, the number of *kaftorim* and *prachim* on those arms is not stated with equal clarity — the *pasuk* says *kaftor u-farach*, and the *Rabbis* derive a minimum of two of each. The surviving artistic depictions may reflect a tradition that there were additional ornaments along the shaft, or they may simply reflect artistic elaboration.

### Cups & Flowers Count

The Gemara now enumerates the total number of cups, spheres, and flowers. There are twenty-two cups, eleven spheres, and nine flowers. The Gemara derives each figure from *pesukim*.

For the cups: the *pasuk* states *u-va-menorah arba'ah gvi'im meshukadim, kaftoreiha u-feracheiha* — on the *menorah* (meaning the central shaft) there are four cups. These four consist of three at the top and one in the lower section. Each of the six side arms has three cups, for *shisha* times three equals eighteen. Adding the four of the central shaft gives twenty-two.

For the spheres: the central shaft has *kaftoreiha* — the plural indicating two — one at the lower-middle juncture and one at the top. Each of the six arms has one *kaftor*, giving six more, for a total of eight. Adding the three junction-point spheres (*kaftor, kaftor, kaftor*) gives eleven.

For the flowers: the central shaft has *feracheiha* — two — and the six arms contribute one each, for eight. The ninth flower is derived from the *pasuk*, *ad yerechah ad pirchah mikshah hi* — meaning that from its very base to its very flower it is one beaten piece — which implies there is a flower at the very base, yielding the ninth.

All of these components are *me'akvei zeh et zeh* — each holds the others back. If any of the twenty-two cups is missing, the *menorah* is not valid for the *Mikdash* when made of gold. The same applies to the spheres and flowers taken individually, and furthermore all three categories are interdependent: the full complement of all three is required. This holds, however, only for a gold *menorah*; for a *menorah* of other materials, these ornamental requirements do not apply.

The Gemara then turns to a dispute about the height. Rav says *govhah shel menorah tisha tefachim* — the height was only nine *tefachim*. Rav Shimi bar Chiya challenges this: does the *mishnah* not teach that there was a stone before the *menorah* with three steps, upon which the *kohen* would stand to tend the lamps? If the *menorah* were only nine *tefachim*, why would anyone need to ascend a pedestal to reach it? Rav responds somewhat sharply — *Shimi at?* — saying that his nine *tefachim* was measured only from where the branches begin, not from the ground.

### Pedestal & Steps

The mention of the pedestal raises a question in its own right. Even at eighteen *tefachim* — four and a half feet — it is not immediately obvious why a *kohen* would need to stand on a raised platform to tend the lamps. The top of the *menorah* at that height would be within easy reach of an adult standing at floor level. Several possible explanations arise: people in antiquity were, on average, meaningfully shorter than today, perhaps six inches to a foot shorter; and the *kohen* may have needed to be at a certain height not to reach the top, but to pour oil without spilling. The Gemara itself states that the base and flower are three *tefachim* — it is not entirely clear whether the stone pedestal is included within the eighteen *tefachim* or is additional.

The *tefach* measurement itself is independently attested by archaeological evidence. The *mikvaot* found at Masada, for example, allow one to calculate the size of a *se'ah* and thereby derive the size of a *tefach*, consistently yielding approximately 3.2 inches. This figure is independent of the height of the people who built them.

---

## Gold Purity

### Solomon's Menorot

The Gemara now cites a *pasuk* from the account of *Shlomo*'s construction of the *Beit HaMikdash*: *ve-ha-perach ve-ha-nerot ve-ha-melkachayim zahav, michalot zahav* — the flower, lamps, and tongs were of gold, *michalot zahav*. What does the phrase *michalot zahav* mean? Rav Ami explains: *she-kilato le-chol zahav sagur shel Shlomo* — making the *menorah* used up all of the *zahav sagur*, the purest and most precious form of gold, belonging to Shlomo. Rashi explains that *zahav sagur* is a gold so precious that it would "close the markets" — its mere appearance would cause the gold market to shut down, as no other gold could compare.

But how could making one *menorah* — which requires only one *kikar* — exhaust all of Shlomo's store of *zahav sagur*? The answer lies in the process. The Gemara teaches that Shlomo made not one *menorah* but ten, and for each one *ve-le-chol achat ve-achat heivi elef kikar zahav* — he began with one thousand *kikar* of gold, *ve-hichnisuha elef pe'amim la-kur* — and smelted it one thousand times in the furnace to remove all impurities — *ve-he'imiduha al kikar* — until only one *kikar* remained. Starting with ten thousand *kikar* total and reducing each to one *kikar* would exhaust a vast store of gold.

One must note the difficulty with this literally. Gold as an element does not comprise only one part in a thousand of raw ore — the ratio imagined here would represent an almost inconceivably low grade of material. The Gemara itself appears aware that this is hyperbolic or metaphorical, emphasizing through exaggeration just how utterly pure the gold of the *menorah* was. There is an additional technical puzzle: pure gold is extremely malleable, and it is not clear that an object of pure gold without any alloy would have the structural integrity needed to stand unsupported. Nonetheless, this is the picture the Gemara paints.

A further challenge arises: another *pasuk* states that all of Shlomo's drinking vessels and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were *zahav sagur*, and that silver was considered worthless in Shlomo's time — implying that *zahav sagur* was abundant. How then could the *menorot* have exhausted all of it? The Gemara resolves this: the statement that all the gold was used up refers specifically to the *zahav sagur*, not to all forms of gold. Shlomo had abundant ordinary gold; it was this singular, supremely pure grade that was entirely consumed in the making of the *menorot*.

### 80 Smeltings

The Gemara then questions whether the figures given — one thousand smeltings reducing a thousand *kikar* to one — are plausible at all. A *braita* is cited: Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda reports that once a *menorah* in the *Beit HaMikdash* was found to be slightly heavier than Moshe's *menorah* by the weight of one *dinar* — specifically, a Gordian *dinar* (*kordaikini*). Since the *menorah* must weigh exactly one *kikar*, no more and no less, something had to be done. The solution: *ve-hichnisuha peh pe'amim la-kur* — they smelted it eighty times — *ve-he'imiduha al kikar* — until it was reduced to exactly one *kikar*.

This raises an immediate practical question: the smelting presumably involved heat and refashioning the metal. But if the *menorah* had already been formed, why would one smelt it rather than simply remove a small amount directly? And why eighty smeltings to remove the weight of a single *dinar*? The Gemara's answer is that after the initial thousand-fold purification process, the gold was already nearly perfectly pure — *keivan de-kai kai* — there was almost no remaining impurity. At that stage, even tiny residual impurities required many passes through the furnace to extract. The eighty smeltings were thus not inefficiency but a consequence of starting from an already-purified state, in which even the smallest remaining dross is exceedingly difficult to remove.

### Meaning of Pure

All of this elaborate discussion of smelting and purity is, in the end, a *drasha* on a single word: *zahav tahor*, pure gold. The *menorah* is uniquely described in the *Mikdash* as *zahav tahor*, and the Gemara elaborates the full weight of that term.

The Gemara now shifts to consider the word *tahor* as applied not only to the gold but to the *menorah* as a whole. Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan asks: what does it mean when the *pasuk* in *Vayikra* refers to the *menorah ha-tehorah*, the pure *menorah*, in the context of Aharon lighting the lamps? Everything in the *Mikdash* is meant to be *tahor* — so what is this word singling out?

The Gemara first proposes: *she-yardu ma'aseha mi-makom tahara* — its form descended from a place of purity, meaning the vision of it came from heaven. The *menorah*'s design was divinely revealed. The Gemara then asks: but the *pasuk* also refers to the *shulchan ha-tahor*, the pure table — does the same apply there? Should we say that the design of the *shulchan* also descended from heaven?

The Gemara responds: by the *shulchan*, *tahor* means something quite different and quite practical — *miklal she-hu tamei*, it implies that the *shulchan* can become *tamei*. This is a matter of real *halakhic* significance. The *shulchan* was a wooden vessel plated with gold. Ordinarily, a wooden vessel made to remain permanently in place — *kli etz ha'asuy le-nachat* — does not contract *tumah*, because such a vessel is treated as a fixture rather than a chattel. The *shulchan* would seem to fall into that category, and one might therefore think it cannot become *tamei*. The *pasuk* therefore teaches that it can — because, as Resh Lakish explains, the *shulchan* was not actually left permanently in place: it was lifted and shown to the pilgrims on the *shalosh regalim*.

---

## Divine Image

### Heavenly Vision

The Gemara now turns to why *tahor* applied to the *menorah* is treated differently from *tahor* applied to the *shulchan*. By the *shulchan*, as established, *tahor* conveys a *halachic* ruling about *tumah*. By the *menorah*, however, the same rationale does not apply — the *menorah* is a metal vessel, and metal vessels contract *tumah* regardless of whether they are permanently positioned. One does not need a *pasuk* to tell us that the *menorah* can become *tamei*. Therefore, *tehorah* as applied to the *menorah* must be teaching something else entirely. The conclusion: *she-yardu ma'aseha mi-makom tahara* — its form came down from a place of purity, from heaven.

The Gemara then brings an extended discussion of what it means that things "came down from heaven." A *tanna* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches: *aron shel esh ve-shulchan shel esh u-menorah shel esh yardu min ha-shamayim* — an *aron* of fire, a *shulchan* of fire, and a *menorah* of fire descended from heaven, *ve-ra'ah Moshe ve-asah kemotam* — and Moshe saw and made like them. The word *tahor* applied to the *menorah* thus points to this fiery heavenly vision.

But the Gemara challenges this: surely the same applies to other Temple vessels and to the *Mishkan* structure itself? Another *pasuk* states *ve-ha-kemota et ha-Mishkan ke-mishpato asher horeita ba-har* — you shall erect the *Mishkan* according to its law, as you were shown on the mountain. Does this not suggest that Moshe was also shown a heavenly vision of the entire *Mishkan*?

The Gemara answers with a careful textual distinction: by the *Mishkan* the language is *ke-mishpato* — "according to its law" — indicating primarily verbal instruction, even if some visual element was present. By the *menorah*, the language is *kazeh* — "like this," pointing to a specific image. And similarly in the *pasuk u-re'eh ve-aseh be-tavnitam asher atah mor'eh ba-har* — look and make, according to the image which you are shown on the mountain. The language of seeing and of *tavnit*, image, makes clear that Moshe was shown not merely a verbal description but an actual visual form. The *menorah* in particular thus carries the quality of being *tehorah* in the deepest sense — its design is of heavenly origin.

Regarding the *shulchan* and the pilgrims: when the *shulchan* was displayed during the *regalim*, it was carried into the *azarah* and the people were shown the *lechem ha-panim* with the words *re'u chibatkhem lifnei ha-makom* — see how beloved you are before God. The miracle associated with this, as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches, was that *siluko ke-siduro* — when the bread was removed, it was as warm and fresh as the day it was placed on the table. Because the *shulchan* was moved during the *regalim*, it was not a permanent fixture, it was not *asuy le-nachat*, and it therefore could contract *tumah* — and the *pasuk* saying *tahor* comes precisely to teach this.

### Gabriel & Three Hard Thi…

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *Gavriel*, the angel of fire, appeared *chagur ke-min pesikya* — wearing what appears to be a smelter's or craftsman's apron — and showed Moshe the construction of the *menorah*, *ve-her'ah lo le-Moshe ma'aseh menorah*. The proof-text is *ve-zeh ma'aseh ha-menorah* — "and this is the construction of the *menorah*" — where the word *zeh*, "this," implies a pointed, demonstrative act of showing: here, look at this.

A *tanna* of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that there were three things Moshe found difficult — *kashin lo* — that required God, as it were, to show him directly with His finger: the *menorah*, *rosh chodesh*, and *sheratzim* (the categories of impure insects). The *menorah*, as established, was shown through *ve-zeh ma'aseh ha-menorah*. *Rosh chodesh* was shown through *ha-chodesh ha-zeh lachem* — this month — where *zeh* points to the precise sliver of the new moon that constitutes the beginning of the month and must be recognized by witnesses. *Sheratzim* are identified through *ve-zeh lachem ha-tamei* — these are the impure creatures — pointing to the precise identification of each category. Some add a fourth: *shechita*, based on *ve-zeh asher ta'aseh al ha-mizbe'ach* — this is what you shall do on the altar — since the details of the act of slaughter are intricate and demanding enough that a direct visual demonstration was necessary.

The common thread in this list is worth noting: these are cases where verbal description alone was insufficient, where the complexity or subtlety of the matter required a direct, demonstrative showing. The word *zeh* in each case marks that moment of pointing. A related tradition in the *Gemara* mentions the *machatzit ha-shekel* as another thing Moshe found hard to grasp, but *Tosafot* distinguishes the two: by the *machatzit ha-shekel*, Moshe's difficulty was philosophical — what is the significance of half a shekel? — whereas in the cases listed here, the difficulty was purely practical — what does this actually look like?

There is a play on words underlying this entire discussion: the *menorah* was made *mikshah* — beaten from a single piece of gold — and Moshe was *mitkasheh*, found himself struggling (*kasheh*) to understand it. The difficulty of grasping the *menorah* was such that, according to some *midrashim* (not in this *Gemara* itself), Moshe ultimately gave up and God told him simply to throw the gold into the fire, whereupon the *menorah* emerged formed on its own. This *Gemara* does not go that far, but it does insist that the image itself had to descend from heaven, shown by Gavriel in the visual form of fire.

---

## Mezuzah Portions

### Kotzo Shel Yud

The *Gemara* now transitions to the laws of *mezuzah*, beginning with the principle that *shtei parshiyot she-ba-mezuzah me'akvot zu et zu* — the two portions of the *mezuzah*, *Shema* and *Ve-haya Im Shamoa*, prevent one another from being valid. Even one letter that is defective or missing invalidates the *mezuzah*. The *Gemara* initially treats this as self-evident — *peshita* — though, notably, in the case of the *Megillah* a much higher degree of incompleteness is tolerated. Here the *Gemara* takes it for granted.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds a striking specification: *lo nitzrecha ela le-kotzah shel Yud* — the ruling that even one defective element invalidates the *mezuzah* is needed particularly for the *kotzah shel Yud*, the tiny tapered point of the letter *Yud*. Rashi explains that this refers to the small left leg of the *Yud* that gives the letter its distinctive shape; without it, the letter might resemble a square and could be unrecognizable as a *Yud*. *Tosafot* disputes this, arguing that without a left leg the letter would indeed be unrecognizable and obviously invalid — and identifies the *kotzah shel Yud* instead as the tiny point on the upper right of the letter, which a reader would still intuitively read as a *Yud* even without it, yet which *halakha* requires for validity. The precise identification is debated, but the phrase *kotzah shel Yud* has become a lasting idiom in rabbinic discourse for the smallest, most easily overlooked detail — in the same spirit as Rabbi Akiva's *drasha* on the *kitrei otiyot*, the crowns atop letters.

The *Gemara* again asks *peshita* — is this not also obvious? — and the answer points to a deeper principle: *kol ot she-ein gevil mukaf lah me-arba ruchoteha pesulah* — any letter that does not have parchment surrounding it on all four sides is invalid.

### Parchment Around Letters

This principle, *mukaf gevil*, requires that every letter be fully surrounded by blank parchment — it may not be attached to or touching an adjacent letter on any side. Even a letter that is perfectly formed but rests against another letter without a clear break is invalid. The ruling about the *kotzah shel Yud* now becomes contextually richer: we are not simply saying that a missing stroke invalidates the letter. We are establishing that even the most apparently minor element of a letter's form — even a tiny point that any reader would still recognize as a *Yud* — carries the full weight of the *halakha*, and its absence disqualifies the *mezuzah*.

### He Letter Rules

The *Gemara* concludes with a ruling transmitted by Rav Zeira in the name of Rav Huna, and corroborated by Rav Yaakov in the name of Rav Yehuda: *nikev tocho shel He kasher, yerekho pasul* — if a hole forms in the interior of the letter *He*, it is valid; if the defect is in the leg of the *He*, it may be invalid.

The *He* has a distinctive feature: a small freestanding leg (*yerekh*) that hangs from the upper portion of the letter but does not reach the base. If a hole forms within the enclosed body of the letter, the *mukaf gevil* concern does not apply to interior space — the letter's surrounding parchment is unaffected by an interior hole. But if the hole is in the leg itself, two problems arise: first, the *mukaf gevil* question — the remnant of ink on the leg may not be fully surrounded by blank parchment — and second, and perhaps more fundamentally, the structural integrity of the letter itself is compromised.

The ruling is: *im nishtayer bo ke-shi'ur ot ketanah kasher* — if what remains of the leg is at least the size of a small letter (that is, the size of a *Yud*, the smallest letter), the *He* is still valid. *Ve-im lav, pasul* — if less remains, it is invalid.

A practical case is recorded: Iggra, the father-in-law of Rabbi Abba, found that the leg of a *He* in a *Sefer Torah* — or, according to Rashi, in *Tefillin* — had been compromised by a hole in the word *ha-hem*. The question was brought before Rabbi Abba, who applied exactly this standard: if enough of the leg remains to constitute the size of a small letter, the text is *kasher*; if not, it is *pasul*. The discussion of the precise standards for the *He* and other letters will continue in the following *shiur*.

---

---

# Menachot 29

## Letter Recognition

### Mezuzah & Mukaf Gvil

Today's daf is 30, though we are picking up at the very top of 29b, on the *mishnah* that speaks about *parshiyot* of the *mezuzah* as indispensable — that even a single letter can invalidate it. The *mishnah*'s statement that "even one letter" matters prompts the *gemara* to specify what that means in practice, since it is taken for granted that a missing letter renders the *mezuzah* invalid. The discussion turns to particular requirements: for instance, the rule of *mukaf gvil*, that each letter must be surrounded by parchment and cannot be touching neighboring letters.

On the question of a hole in the middle of the *heh*: the *gemara* rules that this is *kasher*, because *mukaf gvil* concerns the outer perimeter of the letter, not a void within its body. The inner legs of the *heh* may be adjacent to a hole without that rendering the letter invalid.

### Hole in Hei, Kotzo

A separate question arises when part of a letter is broken — not merely adjacent to a hole, but where the ink itself does not form a complete line. The *gemara* rules that the leg of the letter must be at least the size of the smallest letter, which is the *yud*. There is debate among the *rishonim* about how this applies to the *heh* specifically: the Rosh holds that the requirement of appearing like a *yud* applies to the large outer leg, while the inner leg need only be as small as a tiny dot. Many other *rishonim*, however, require that even the inner leg meet the minimum size of a *yud* — calibrated, presumably, to the same font as the rest of the writing.

The *gemara* in general does not lay out detailed specifications for what each letter must look like; rather, the standard is that it must resemble the familiar form of the letter, as we shall see shortly with the test of a child. Nevertheless, there are other formal criteria beyond mere appearance — such as *mukaf gvil* and minimum stroke length — and these are independent of whether the letter looks recognizable. If one consults the *Mishnah Berurah* in the *Hilchot Tefillin* section — *siman* 36 — one finds a letter-by-letter guide to what each letter must look like; any trained *sofer* will elaborate even further. But the *gemara* itself provides relatively few of these specifics.

### Testing Broken Letters

At four lines from the top of 29b, we encounter the following case. Rami bar Chamri — who is the father-in-law of Rami bar Dikuli — found that the leg of the *vav* in the word *va-yeharog* (within one of the four *parshiyot* of *tefillin*) had been broken, forming a hole. He brought the question before Rabbi Zeira, who said: go and bring a child who is neither too clever nor too simple — average intelligence. The reasoning is precise: one does not want a child so intelligent that he deduces what the word must be from context rather than from the letter's appearance, but one also does not want a child so limited that he cannot recognize letters at all. If the child reads it as *va-yeharog*, it is *kasher*; if instead he reads it as two *yuds* — treating the *vav* as having shortened into a *yud* — then it is *pasul*, because the *vav* has lost its distinctive length.

This test applies specifically to questions of ambiguity in a letter's shape: is this long enough to be a *vav*, or is it so short as to be a *yud*? There are other categories of defect, however, that constitute clear formal invalidities regardless of appearance. If a letter violates *mukaf gvil* by touching a neighboring letter, no child's reading can cure that — the disqualification is structural, not visual. The child-test is reserved for cases where the formal structure is intact but the proportions are uncertain.

### Formal vs. Appearance

This distinction — between formal invalidities and appearance-based issues — is a central organizing principle of the entire discussion. Some defects are categorical: touching a neighboring letter, or a letter that was never properly surrounded by parchment. Others are a matter of degree: is the stroke long enough? Does the shape still read as the intended letter? For the latter category, the child's reading provides an objective standard.

### Shulchan Aruch Rules

The *Shulchan Aruch* codifies this precisely. If one of the letters is broken — and the *Rama* specifies this refers to letters with simple straight strokes, such as a *vav* or *zayin*, where the ink has snapped rather than formed a clean line — then one brings a child who is neither too clever nor too simple and who knows how to read. If he reads it correctly, it is *kasher*; if not, it is *pasul*. The *Shulchan Aruch* adds that one need not cover the surrounding letters to prevent the child from using context, though that is the common practice.

The *Rama* then introduces an important caveat: even if the child reads the letter correctly, if we ourselves can see that the letter's form does not meet the standard — that it is objectively not recognizable as the proper letter — it is *pasul* regardless of the child's reading. This creates an instructive tension: on one hand, we use the child as an objective observer of appearance; on the other hand, expert judgment can override that reading when we know the form has categorically failed. A child might guess correctly from proximity or elimination without actually recognizing the letter, and in such a case, his reading carries no weight.

### Hole Conditions

The *Shulchan Aruch* adds one more crucial qualification: the leniency regarding a hole or broken ink applies only when the letter was originally written *kasher* and the defect occurred afterward. If, however, there was a hole in the parchment at the moment of writing, the letter was never *mukaf gvil* to begin with — the end of the ink was always touching void rather than *klaf*. The same applies if the leg of the *kuf* was bent toward the edge of the parchment from the outset. In such cases, the letter is *pasul* from the moment it was written, and no subsequent reading by a child can repair that original deficiency. One must therefore verify not only the present state of the letter but also that it was properly formed at the moment of writing.

---

## God & Crowns, Rabbi Akiva

### Moshe's Vision

Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: when Moshe ascended to the heavens to receive the Torah, he found the Holy One, blessed be He, sitting and tying crowns to the letters. Before proceeding, it is worth identifying what these crowns are. As we shall see later in Rava's teaching, the letters *shin*, *ayin*, *tet*, *nun*, *zayin*, *gimmel*, and *tzadi* — the *shatnez get* — each receive three-pointed crowns. These are not the simple *tagin* that appear on many letters, but distinctive triple-pronged ornaments. The *Tosafot* provides an illustration: the three points spread over the top of the letter, with one rising higher at the center and the two flanking ones coming close by, though not quite as spread as one might imagine. Various styles of *ksav* handle these slightly differently, but all converge on the essential three-pronged form — referred to as *karnin*.

Moshe, seeing God occupied with this labor, asked: *Ribbono shel Olam*, who is holding back Your hand? The phrase is a curious one, since God's hand is not being held back; He is actively at work. The sense of the question is evidently: why are You still here adding these crowns? Give the Torah already! What is keeping You?

God answered: there is one person who will exist at the end of many generations, Akiva ben Yosef by name, who will in the future interpret on every single *kotz* — every little jot and tittle — *tilei tillin shel halachot*, mountains upon mountains of laws. That, God says, is what is keeping Me: I must put on these little crowns so that he will have the material to interpret.

### Crowns & Creativity

This is striking on reflection, and it raises an honest difficulty. Do we actually find Rabbi Akiva interpreting the *tagin* anywhere in the literature? In fact, we do not — he is far more associated with deriving laws from extra *alephs*, *yuds*, and the word *et*, not from the crowns themselves. One might even ask: if the crowns appear on a fixed and predictable set of letters — every *shin*, every *nun*, every *gimmel* — what room is there for creative interpretation? The placement is not arbitrary; it can be predicted entirely. And this is precisely why we do not find Rabbi Akiva explicitly doing it.

The deeper meaning of this *aggadata* seems to be about the nature of *Torah she-ba'al peh* and the power of human creativity within the tradition. To some degree, the crowns function as a metaphor: God builds into the Torah a kind of excess, an invitation, and human beings — Rabbi Akiva above all — accept that invitation and generate from it *tilei tillin shel halachot*, even when those derivations are not strictly *peshat*, even when they go beyond what was originally intended in the simple sense. That is the meaning of the partnership: we are not merely recipients of a fixed text but active participants in an ongoing interpretive process. The crowns represent the space that God leaves open for human creativity.

Rav Moshe Feinstein, in the introduction to his *Igros Moshe*, focuses on precisely this *gemara* in articulating the authority of a *posek*. If a *posek* approaches his responsibility with integrity — examining all the sources, reasoning carefully, seeking truth — then his ruling is by definition correct. This is the implication of *Torah she-ba'al peh*: what Rabbi Akiva says ultimately becomes God's Torah. Its authority derives from the fact that it is a genuine, honest development from what God communicated to Moshe. That is the relationship between the written Torah and its oral interpretation.

### Moshe in Class

God told Moshe: turn around. Moshe went and sat at the back of the eighth row in Rabbi Akiva's classroom. And he did not know what they were talking about. The material seemed entirely foreign to him; the *halacha* being discussed bore no resemblance to what he had received. *Tashash kocho* — he felt weak, despondent, as if his own Torah had become unrecognizable.

### Halacha L'Moshe

Then, when they arrived at one particular ruling, Rabbi Akiva's students asked him: *Rebbi*, where do you derive this from? And Rabbi Akiva answered: *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — it is a tradition going all the way back to Moshe at Sinai. At that moment, *nityashevah da'ato* — Moshe's mind settled, his composure was restored. He was satisfied, because even this unfamiliar development was ultimately attributed back to him.

One might press the question: why was it specifically Rabbi Akiva who received this capacity and not Moshe himself? One answer from the *Meshech Chochma* frames the difference in terms of what each figure represents within the tradition — Moshe as the embodiment of the direct divine command, Rabbi Akiva as the great architect of *gezeirot* and *takanot*, the rabbinic safeguards that protect against transgression. Whether or not that reading is entirely convincing, the larger point of the *aggadata* seems clear: if Moshe Rabbeinu himself were to sit in a *daf yomi shiur* and listen to the *gemara* being discussed, he might not recognize what was being said — because that is what *Torah she-ba'al peh* is. It grows, it develops, it generates from itself *kotzei kotzim shel halachos* that were not in the original. And yet in the end, it all traces itself back to the Torah that Moshe gave. The source is his; the development is ours. And that is the relationship. *Nityashevah da'ato* — he made his peace with it, and perhaps more.

The image of Moshe being told to *chazor le'achorecha* — turn around, go to the back — carries a resonance beyond the simple narrative. It echoes the moment in *Parashat Ki Tissa* when Moshe asked to see God's face and was told *ve-achorai tir'ah* — you will see My back, not My face. There too, the full picture is withheld; one gets only a glimpse of how God acts in history. Here, similarly, Moshe gets to see the future without fully inhabiting it. He steps, as it were, out of human history — and when God tells him to look behind, he must reintegrate himself into the flow of time to witness what will become of what he began.

### Martyrdom & Justice

Moshe then returned before God and said: *Ribbono shel Olam*, You have a person of such quality — why are You giving the Torah through me? God replied: *shtok* — silence. *Kach ala be-machshava lefanai* — this is what arose in My thought. This was My plan.

Moshe then asked: show me his Torah — and show me his reward. Again God said: turn around.
