# Menachot 30

## Last 8 Verses

### 8 Verses Dispute

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion about how a *sefer Torah* must be written, building on the preceding *gemara* about Moshe's ascent to receive the Torah. The discussion now turns to a theologically and halachically rich topic: the status of the last eight *pesukim* of the Torah.

The chain of tradition runs as follows: *Amar Rav Yehoshua bar Abba amar Rav Giddel amar Rav* — Rav taught that the final eight *pesukim* of the Torah, an individual reads them in the *beit knesset* (*yachid korei otan beveit haknesset*). The precise meaning of *yachid korei otan* will be unpacked shortly, but the *gemara* first asks: *ke-man* — like whom does this ruling go? The answer it proposes: *de-lo ke-Rabbi Shimon* — apparently not like Rabbi Shimon.

The *gemara* then introduces the underlying dispute by way of a *baraita*. The verse in question is *vayamot sham Moshe eved Hashem* — "And Moshe the servant of God died there in Arvot Moav." This verse opens the final eight *pesukim* of Devarim. The *baraita* poses the obvious difficulty: *efshar Moshe chai ve-katav vayamot sham Moshe* — is it really possible that Moshe was alive and wrote the words "and Moshe died there"? That would have been, at the time of writing, not merely emotionally devastating but factually false.

### Rabbi Yehudah View

Rabbi Yehudah resolves the problem directly: *ella ad kan katav Moshe, mikan ve-eilakh katav Yehoshua bin Nun* — up until this point Moshe wrote the Torah; from here onward, Yehoshua bin Nun wrote the final eight *pesukim*. Some attribute this position to Rabbi Nechemia rather than Rabbi Yehudah, or to both. By contemporary standards, attributing any portion of the Torah's authorship to Yehoshua might sound like the height of *kefira*, and yet here Rabbi Yehudah advances exactly that position.

### Rabbi Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon responds sharply: *efshar sefer Torah chaser oti echat* — is it conceivable that the *sefer Torah* should be missing even a single letter? He marshals a verse in support: *lakoach et sefer ha-Torah ha-zeh ve-samtem oto* — "take this Torah scroll and place it near the Ark." These were Moshe's own words to the Levites. If Moshe called it a *sefer Torah* — a complete Torah scroll — he clearly had written the entire thing before handing it over. The final eight *pesukim* must therefore have been written by Moshe as well.

This argument carries both a practical dimension — Moshe's use of the phrase *sefer Torah* implies a complete text — and a deeper theological resonance. Is it even conceivable that the Torah received through Moshe was not fully given by God through him? The entire *sefer Torah* must have come from Moshe.

### Writing with Tears

But this immediately raises the difficulty of how Moshe could write something untrue. The *gemara* answers that up until these final eight *pesukim*, the process of transmission was: *Hakadosh Barukh Hu omer u-Moshe kotev ve-omer* — God would dictate, Moshe would repeat the word aloud and then write it. This practice of vocalizing before writing is in fact what scribes do today when writing a *sefer Torah*, *mezuzot*, or *tefillin*, in order to guard against error.

When it came to the final eight *pesukim*, however, the formulation changes: *Hakadosh Barukh Hu omer u-Moshe kotev be-dema* — God dictated and Moshe wrote with tears (*be-dema*). The *gemara* draws support from a verse in Yirmiyahu describing Barukh, Yirmiyahu's scribe: *mi-piv yikra elai et kol ha-devarim ha-eleh va-ani kotev al ha-sefer be-diyo* — "From his mouth he would read to me all these words and I would write them in the scroll with ink." The contrast, as Rashi reads it, is that Barukh says he wrote — but does not say he repeated the words back aloud first. The passage concerned tragedy and lamentation, and so the process of verbalization gave way to silent, tearful writing.

### Rashi & Maharsha

According to Rashi, the plain meaning of *be-dema* is that Moshe was weeping as he wrote. It was so painful to write the words "and Moshe died there" that he could not bring himself to vocalize them. The transmission was still entirely from God to Moshe; Moshe wrote every word — but instead of repeating them aloud, he wept as he wrote. The picture is deeply poignant. Rashi's reading, however, does not fully address the underlying theological difficulty: how could Moshe write something that was, at the moment of writing, not yet true?

The Maharsha, not in this *gemara* but in Bava Batra where the same passage appears, offers a brilliant reading that addresses this directly. He argues that Rabbi Shimon is making two distinct points that differentiate the final eight *pesukim* from everything that preceded them.

The first distinction concerns the process of vocalization. Throughout the Torah, the formulation is *Moshe omer ve-kotev* — Moshe would say and then write. For the final eight *pesukim*, it becomes simply *kotev* — he wrote, without saying. This departure from the established mode of transmission was itself a signal — a kind of flag embedded in the very process of writing — that these *pesukim* were different in nature, that they described events that had not yet occurred.

The second and even more striking distinction is the Maharsha's reading of *be-dema* in contrast to *be-diyo*. The *gemara* in Yirmiyahu uses the phrase *kotev be-diyo* — writing with ink. Here, the Torah says *kotev be-dema* — writing with tears. The Maharsha understands this not merely as a description of emotional state but as a description of the medium: Moshe actually wrote the final eight *pesukim* in tears, not in ink. It was, in effect, invisible ink. The *sefer Torah* was complete — Moshe had written every word — but the final eight *pesukim* were written in tears, and Yehoshua subsequently filled them in with ink. This reading beautifully holds the tension between two truths: the *sefer Torah* was entirely written by Moshe, and yet Moshe could not have written those words in the normal sense while they remained unfulfilled.

The Vilna Gaon is reported to hold a similar position. He understands *be-dema* as referring to a teardrop that had not yet fully formed into the precise shape of letters, and Yehoshua subsequently shaped those drops into the proper letters of the text. However one reads the specific mechanism, both approaches resolve the same tension: the entire Torah came through Moshe, but the final eight *pesukim* were written in a qualitatively different mode that acknowledged their as-yet-unrealized character.

### Yachid Kore Otan

The *gemara* then returns to the question with which it opened: the principle of *yachid korei otan* seems to reflect the position of Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that those *pesukim* were written by Yehoshua and therefore carry a different status. But the *gemara* says *afilu teima Rabbi Shimon* — even according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that Moshe wrote everything, one could still affirm the special status of *yachid korei otan*. The reason: *ho-il ve-ishtani ishtani* — since they were changed, they are different. Whether through the absence of vocalization, through the medium of tears, or through whatever the *gemara* understood to distinguish those eight *pesukim*, their altered mode of transmission confers upon them a distinct status — and that distinction expresses itself in the rule of *yachid korei otan*.

What does *yachid korei otan* mean in practice? Rashi explains that it means only a single individual may receive all eight *pesukim* as a single *aliyah*. They cannot be divided between two *aliyot*. Because they constitute a distinct and singular unit, they must be treated as one block, and this reflects their unique status. This reading is apparently also that of the Yerushalmi.

Tosafot records an alternative interpretation in the name of Rav Meshullam, suggested by Rabbeinu Tam: *yachid korei otan* means that the *ba'al korei* would not read alongside the *oleh* — the person called up to the Torah would have to read it himself, without the assistance of the reader. There is something almost poignant in that reading — a certain aloneness in those final *pesukim*, as though the reader stands alone before the words of Moshe's death. Tosafot itself, however, objects that in the time of the *gemara* there was no *ba'al korei* at all — each *oleh* read for himself — so the distinction the *gemara* draws cannot have been contrasting those two modes. Tosafot ultimately agrees with Rashi: the rule is that one *oleh* receives all eight *pesukim* together.

### Rambam Ruling

The Rambam rules on this in Hilchos Tefilla, Perek 13, Halacha 6. He writes: *shmoneh pesukim she-besof ha-Torah mutar likros osam be-veit ha-knesset be-pachot me-asarah* — the final eight *pesukim* of the Torah may be read in the synagogue with fewer than ten. We *pasken* like Rabbi Shimon, the Rambam affirms — *af al pi she-kol ha-Torah hayu Moshe mi-pi ha-Gevurah amram* — even though the entire Torah was spoken by God through Moshe, including these final eight *pesukim* — nevertheless, *ho-il u-mashmaam she-heim achar misat Moshe, harei nishtanu* — since they convey the sense of events that took place after Moshe's death, they are different. And because they are different, *mutar le-yachid likros otan* — they may be read without a *tzibur*.

This is a striking ruling. The Rambam locates the distinctive status of the final eight *pesukim* not in the mode of their writing — not in tears versus ink, not in the absence of vocalization — but simply in the jarring dissonance of their content: they sound as though they were written after Moshe died. And from this difference in character, the Rambam derives a practical leniency — that they can be read without a full *minyan*.

### Raavad Critique

The Raavad is sharply dismissive. He writes: *lo shamanu davar zeh me-olam* — we have never heard of such a thing. His reading of *yachid korei otan* is simply that of Rashi: you do not interrupt it; one *oleh* receives all eight together. He then adds, in the spirit of Tosafot's observation, that the local practice is indeed that the *oleh* reads it himself without a *chazzan* reading alongside him — not as the explanation of the *gemara*, but as an additional layer of the *minhag* — again evoking that sense of solitude and weight in those final *pesukim*.

Raavad closes with a pointed rejoinder to the Rambam: *u-mah she-katav hu inyan zarus hu me-od* — what the Rambam wrote is particularly bizarre, *ve-tzibur heichan halchu* — and where did the *tzibur* go? If you have just been reading the Torah with a full *minyan* for the preceding *aliyot*, why would you suddenly be reading the final eight *pesukim* without one? While it is theoretically possible — a small *minyan* in which one person departs — it seems strange to formulate a special halachic status around such a marginal case.

## Buying vs Writing

### Purchasing Merit

The *gemara* now turns to a different aspect of the *mitzvah* of *sefer Torah*, introducing a chain of teaching: *Rami bar Abba amar Rav Giddel amar Rav* — Rav taught that one who purchases a *sefer Torah* from the marketplace is like one who snatches a *mitzvah* from the marketplace (*ke-chotef mitzvah min ha-shuk*). The image is telling. Purchasing an existing *sefer Torah* involves no creative effort; the Torah scroll simply changes hands. You have acquired a *mitzvah* — presumably there is a *mitzvah* in owning a *sefer Torah* — but you have contributed nothing to the world of Torah. The word *chotef*, "snatches," even carries a slightly unflattering connotation: someone else may have lost it while you gained it.

### Writing Merit

By contrast, one who actually writes a *sefer Torah* — *kasvo* — *ma'aleh alav ha-katuv ke-ilu kiblo me-Har Sinai* — Scripture considers it as though he received it from Har Sinai. The act of writing creates a profound personal connection to the words themselves. One does not merely acquire the physical object; one participates in the very transmission of Torah. That intimate engagement is what the *gemara* expresses with the phrase *ke-ilu kiblo me-Har Sinai* — as though he himself stood at Sinai and received it. This is even more than commissioning a *sefer Torah*, where at least a new scroll is brought into the world through one's investment — writing it oneself establishes a degree of ownership over the words that cannot be replicated by a transfer of funds.

### Correcting Letter

Rav Sheshet adds a further nuance: *im higiah afilu ot achat, ma'aleh alav ha-katuv ke-ilu ketavo* — if one corrected even a single letter in a *sefer Torah*, Scripture considers it as though he wrote the entire scroll. This is a one-degree upgrade, not two: correcting a letter is treated as equivalent to writing the scroll, but not as equivalent to receiving it at Sinai — that higher level is reserved for one who writes the whole thing from start to finish. The logic is that correcting an error transforms the scroll from unusable to usable; one has performed a genuine act of writing, not merely a transfer. People who participate in a *sefer Torah* dedication by "buying a letter" and guiding the *sofer*'s hand in writing it participate in something of this spirit — a personal connection through direct involvement in even a single letter.

## Scroll Specs

### Column Rules

The *gemara* now proceeds to the physical specifications of a *sefer Torah*. A *baraita* states: *oseh adam yeriah mi-bat shalosh dapim* — one may make a single *klaf* (parchment panel) with a minimum of three columns, *ve-ad bat shemonah dapim* — and a maximum of eight. The *sefer Torah* is composed of individual *klafim* sewn together, and each *klaf* must have a reasonable number of columns — not so few that the columns become excessively wide, and not so many that they become excessively narrow.

*Pachot mi-kan ve-yeter mi-kan lo ya'aseh* — more than eight or fewer than three columns in a single *klaf* one should not do. It should be noted that most of these instructions have the character of *le-chatchila* guidance — aesthetic and practical standards for proper Torah writing — rather than absolute rules whose violation would render the scroll *pasul*.

Rashi's explanation of *ve-lo yarbeh ba-dapim* — do not have more columns than is appropriate for the *klaf* — is that even within the range of up to eight columns, a small *klaf* should not be forced to accommodate six, seven, or eight narrow columns, because then it will resemble a letter (*iggeret*), which was apparently written in narrow columns. Conversely, *ve-lo yama'it ba-dapim* — do not have fewer columns than is appropriate — because overly wide columns cause the eyes to wander (*einav meshottetot*): reading to the far end of a very long line, the reader must then return all the way to the beginning of the next line and risks losing his place.

### Column Width

The ideal column width is specified by reference to the word *le-mishpachoteichem*: the column should be wide enough to fit three iterations of this ten-letter word — *le-mishpachoteichem le-mishpachoteichem le-mishpachoteichem* — giving an optimal column width of thirty letters. Tosafot, in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, qualifies this: the thirty-letter standard applies only when writing in a particularly narrow script. When the letters are large and thick, as is common in beautiful *sifrei Torah*, the eye does not wander as much, and the column may be correspondingly wider.

### Dividing Klaf

If one happens to obtain a piece of *klaf* that could accommodate nine columns, one does not want to use it as a single panel with nine columns. It must be cut. But how should it be divided? *Lo yachlok shalosh le-kan ve-shesh le-kan* — do not divide it into a three-column piece and a six-column piece. Rather, *ela arba le-kan ve-chamesh le-kan* — four and five, or five and four. The *klafim* should be of roughly similar sizes, and a four-five division is visually more balanced than a three-six division.

### End Exception

An important exception applies at the conclusion of the *sefer Torah*. *Ba-meh devarim amurim bi-tchilat ha-sefer* — the rule that *klafim* must have between three and eight columns applies throughout the *sefer* until its very end. But *aval be-sof ha-sefer* — at the end, *afilu pasuk echad ve-afilu daf echad* — even a single *pasuk* in a single column is permissible.

The *gemara* itself challenges this: *pasuk echad salka da'at?* — can one really have just one *pasuk* in a column? The question, as some *meforshim* understand it, arises from the earlier teaching that the text must reach the bottom of the column. If you have only one *pasuk* left on your final *klaf*, how do you reconcile placing a single *pasuk* in a column while also filling the column to the bottom? The *gemara* clarifies: *ela eima pasuk echad be-daf echad* — one *pasuk* filling one column. That is, if the final *klaf* has only one *pasuk* remaining, the scribe writes it in very large letters, one word per line if necessary, stretching that single *pasuk* to fill the entire column from top to bottom. Some *rishonim* specify that this is done with notably large letters.

### Margin Sizes

The *gemara* now specifies the margin dimensions. *Shiur gilyon* — the minimum margins: the bottom margin is a *tefach* (four finger-breadths); the top margin is three finger-breadths (*shalosh etzba'ot*), slightly smaller. The reason the bottom margin is larger is presumably that the scroll is more likely to be handled, rested upon, or rolled up from below, warranting greater protection. *U-vein daf le-daf ki-melo ruchav shtei etzba'ot* — the space between adjacent columns is two finger-breadths in width.

For *chumashim* — bound codices rather than scrolls — the margins are somewhat smaller: the bottom margin is three finger-breadths, the top is two, and the inter-column space is the width of a thumb. These proportional reductions reflect the different physical handling of a codex. As with the column rules, these margin specifications have the character of proper conduct and aesthetic standard — considerations of *kavod* and ease of reading — rather than absolute conditions of validity, though this is not explicitly stated.

### Letter Spacing

*U-vein shita le-shita ki-melo shita* — between each line of text, the space should equal the height of one line of text; this is what we would call double-spacing. *U-vein teiva le-teiva ki-melo ot ketana* — between each word, the space must be at least the width of a small letter, such as a *yud*, so that words are clearly distinguishable from one another. A *sefer Torah* in which the words are not clearly separated is not *kosher*. *U-vein ot le-ot ki-melo chut ha-sa'arah* — between each letter within a word, even a hairbreadth of space suffices, but they must be distinct. Letters that touch and are not clearly separate render the scroll *pasul*.

### Letter Size Rule

*Al yima'et adam et ha-ktav lo mi-pnei revach shel mata ve-lo mi-pnei revach shel ma'alah* — a scribe must not make his letters smaller than the norm of the column's script in order to achieve the required bottom or top margin. If the scoring of the *klaf* was done slightly too close to the edge, and the scribe realizes he will not achieve the full required margin, he must nonetheless maintain consistent letter size throughout. *Ve-lo mi-pnei revach she-bein shita le-shita* — nor should he shrink the letters to achieve proper double-spacing between lines. *Ve-lo mi-pnei revach she-bein parsha le-parsha* — nor to create proper white space between one *parsha* and the next. The letter size established at the outset of a column must be maintained uniformly, regardless of the resulting margin or spacing dimensions.

## Word Overflow

### 5-Letter Word

The *gemara* now addresses what happens when a word does not fit within the column boundary. In the absence of hyphens and without electronic typesetting, the scribe must manage overflow manually.

The rule for a five-letter word that reaches the end of a column: *lo yichtov shtayim betoch ha-daf ve-shalosh chutz la-daf* — do not write two letters inside the column and three outside. Rather, *ela shalosh betoch ha-daf ve-shtayim chutz la-daf* — three letters must fall within the column and two may extend beyond it. The principle is that the majority of the word must remain within the column itself. While ideally the text should be both right and left justified, when that cannot be achieved, the overflow is acceptable provided that the majority of the overflowing word sits within the column boundary. This is the transition from the end of 30a to the top of 30b.

### 2-Letter Word

A two-letter word presents a different problem. *Lo yizrakena levein ha-dapin* — do not think that because two letters may overhang the column, you may place an entire two-letter word entirely in the inter-column space. That is prohibited. *Ela chozer ve-kotev bi-tchilat ha-shita* — instead, go back and begin writing the word at the start of the next line.

This ruling may seem obvious — if a five-letter word must have its majority inside the column, certainly a two-letter word cannot be placed entirely outside — but the *gemara* states it explicitly, presumably to forestall the mistaken inference that since two letters are allowable outside, two-letter words may be placed there in their entirety.

## Name Corrections

### Erasing Name

The *gemara* now turns to the specific problem of an error involving the divine name. The scenario is this: the scribe was meant to write *vayedaber Hashem el Moshe leimor* but accidentally wrote *vayedaber el Moshe leimor*, omitting the divine name. The name must somehow be inserted. What are the options?

### Rabbi Yehudah

Rabbi Yehudah's position: *gorer ma she-katav* — scrape away (with a dry scraping instrument) what has been written. Since one cannot practically erase back to *vayedaber* and redo everything from that point if many lines have been written since, the procedure is more targeted. The scribe scrapes away *el Moshe leimor*, writes the divine name on the line in its place, and then *toleh et ma she-garar* — suspends the scraped text (*el Moshe*) between the lines, in the inter-column double-spacing, in a position that indicates clearly that those words follow the divine name on the line. The result on the line reads *vayedaber Hashem*, while between the lines the words *el Moshe* are written in a way that marks them as the continuation, followed by *leimor* back on the line itself. This is analogous to the caret insertion mark in written correction. Rabbi Yehudah's view is that the divine name must be on the line itself in its proper position, and the displaced words are accommodated between the lines.

### Rabbi Yitzchak

Rabbi Yitzchak takes a different approach: *af mochek ve-khotev* — one may simply erase (*mechikah*, as opposed to scraping) the displaced text and rewrite the name directly on the line. The precise distinction between *gorer* and *mochek* is not entirely clear — *gorer* refers to scraping after the ink has dried, while *mochek* may leave more of a stain — but the practical import of Rabbi Yitzchak's ruling is that one may correct the line straightforwardly by erasing the displaced text and writing the name cleanly in its place.

### R. Shimon Shezuri

Rabbi Shimon Shezuri articulates a qualification to the *toleh* approach: *kol ha-shem kulo tolin, miktzato ein tolin* — one may suspend the entire divine name between the lines, but one may not suspend part of it. The divine name may not be split, with part between the lines and part on the line itself. It is a refinement of the position that allows *tiluy* — suspension — of the name, insisting that if one uses this method the name must appear as a complete, intact unit wherever it is placed.

### Rabbi Meir

Rabbi Shimon Elazar rules in the name of Rabbi Meir with the most stringent position of all: *ein kotsvin et ha-shem lo bi-mekom ha-garar ve-lo bi-mekom ha-machak* — one may not write the divine name either where it has been scraped or where it has been erased. *Ve-ein tolin oso* — and one may not suspend it between the lines either. If none of these corrective methods are available, *keitzad oseh* — what does one do? *Mesalek et ha-yeriah kulah u-gonzah* — one must remove the entire *klaf* and put it in *genizah*. There is no permissible repair; the *klaf* must be replaced entirely. The concern underlying Rabbi Meir's position is that any erasing or scraping in the vicinity of the divine name — or any suspension that leaves the name in an improper position — is impermissible, and since there is no way to correct the error without one of these prohibited acts, the entire *klaf* must go.

### Amoraic Rulings

The *gemara* then records two *amoraic* rulings. Rav Chananel in the name of Rav rules: *halacha tolin et ha-shem* — the law follows the position that suspends the divine name between the lines. Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel rules: *halacha mochek ve-khotev* — the law is to erase and rewrite on the line.

The *gemara* asks why each *amora* stated his position as a *halacha* ruling rather than simply saying "the law follows Rabbi Yehudah" or "the law follows Rabbi Yitzchak." The answer: *mishum de-ichalfei* — because there was confusion about which *tanna* held which position. To avoid ambiguity arising from a misattributed *tannaic* name, each *amora* stated the ruling itself rather than identifying the *tanna* whose position he endorsed.

### Shimon Shezuri Ruling

A final ruling is then recorded: *Amar Ravin bar Chinana amar Ulla amar Rabbi Chanina, halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon Shezuri* — Ulla ruled in the name of Rabbi Chanina that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's position — that the entire divine name may be suspended between the lines but not part of it — is thus the adopted *halacha*. And Ulla adds a sweeping general principle: *ve-lo od, ela kol makom she-shana Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, halacha kimoto* — and not only here, but wherever Rabbi Shimon Shezuri states an opinion — in a *Mishna* or a *baraita* — the law follows him.

## Shimon Shezuri Analysis

### Anchoring Challenge

The *gemara* now asks: *ahai* — on what case was Ulla's sweeping statement anchored? Ulla said two things: the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri in the matter at hand, and in general the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri wherever he appears. But what was the specific ruling that prompted the general declaration? Where did Ulla actually *anchor* his blanket statement?

The *gemara* then attempts to identify that anchor case by examining each case where Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds an opinion, and testing whether Ulla's statement could have been made in reference to it. The methodology is elegant: if Ulla's statement was about a given case, one would expect Ulla to have been in conversation with other *Amoraim* who discussed that same case. But Ulla's statement appears to have been made independently of any other *amora's* ruling. Therefore, any case where another *amora* already ruled like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri cannot be the anchor of Ulla's statement.

### Get Case

The *gemara* first suggests that Ulla's statement was anchored in the following *Mishna*. Originally it was taught that someone being led out in chains to be executed (*ha-yotzei be-kolar*) who said "write a *get* for my wife" — his statement is treated as authorization not only to write and sign the *get* but also to deliver it, even though he did not explicitly say "deliver it." The reason for this leniency is contextual: one does not speak of writing a *get* when about to be executed unless one intends it to be delivered; he simply did not articulate the full instruction because he was understandably distracted.

Subsequently, the sages extended this ruling: *af ha-mifaresh ve-ha-yotzei be-shayara* — even someone embarking on a sea voyage or joining a caravan may rely on the same principle. Here too, the urgency of departure and the risk of not returning provide sufficient context to interpret his words as full authorization to write, sign, and deliver the *get*.

Rabbi Shimon Shezuri extends the principle further: *af ha-mesukan* — even someone who is ill or in danger, though not with the same degree of immediate urgency as someone being led to execution or racing to catch a departing ship, is nonetheless in a situation of sufficient contextual pressure that his words are interpreted as full authorization. Perhaps this is where Ulla's general endorsement of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri was anchored?

The *gemara* rejects this: *ha itmar alah* — this case already had a ruling issued upon it. *Zeiri amar Rabbi Chanina, halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon Shezuri* — Zeiri in the name of Rabbi Chanina ruled that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri in the case of the *mesukan*. If Ulla's blanket statement was anchored in this case, he should have said it together with Zeiri's ruling. Since Ulla's statement stands independently, it cannot be referring to this case.

### Terumah Case

The *gemara* proposes another candidate: *terumat ma'aser shel demai she-chazra li-mkomah* — the case of *terumat ma'aser* of *demai* that fell back into the produce.

The background: *demai* is produce purchased from an *am ha-aretz* — an ordinary farmer not part of the rabbinic community — regarding whom we are uncertain whether he separated *ma'aser* and *terumat ma'aser*. We assume he separated *terumah* but not necessarily the tithe and its priestly portion. If the buyer purchased such produce and *Shabbat* arrived before he had separated *ma'aser* and *terumat ma'aser*, the rabbis were lenient and allowed him to ask the seller whether he had already separated them; if the seller said yes, the buyer could rely on him. Tosafot adds a reference from the Yerushalmi that *eimat Shabbat al amei ha-aretz* — the awe of *Shabbat* makes an *am ha-aretz* more likely to tell the truth; and Rashi adds that this leniency also assumes there is nothing else to eat.

Now: what if the buyer did separate *terumat ma'aser* before *Shabbat*, but then the *terumah* fell back into the produce and mixed in? The entire mixture is now forbidden, since *terumah* may not be eaten by a non-*kohen* and it is mixed throughout. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rules: *af be-chol sho'alo ve-ochlo al piv* — in this situation, even on a weekday one may ask the *am ha-aretz* seller and rely on his statement that he had already separated *ma'aser* previously, thereby retroactively rendering the buyer's own separation of *terumat ma'aser* unnecessary, and the entire produce is permitted. The leniency is extended beyond *Shabbat* need to weekday cases involving significant loss.

This could be the anchor case for Ulla's ruling. But again the *gemara* rejects it: *amar Rabbi Yochanan, halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon Shezuri be-mesukan u-ve-terumat ma'aser shel demai* — Rabbi Yochanan already ruled like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri in both the *mesukan* case and this *terumat ma'aser* case. If Ulla's statement referred to either of these, he should have been in conversation with Rabbi Yochanan. Since he was not, neither can be the anchor.

### Legume Case

The *gemara* now proposes yet another candidate. Rabbi Yosei ben Kipar says in the name of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri: the case of the *pul ha-mitzri* — the Egyptian legume — that was planted for its seeds. When a crop is planted for its seeds, the obligation of *terumot u-ma'asrot* attaches when the plant takes root, not when it is picked. If some of the plants in a given row took root before Rosh Hashanah and others took root after, the produce belongs to two different titheing years — some to year two and some to year three — and one may not tithe from one year's produce on behalf of another year's.

The problem is that all the plants grow together in a mixed row, and it is impossible to know which plants belong to which year. *Ein tormin mi-zeh al zeh le-fi she-ein tormin u-ma'asrin lo min ha-chadash al ha-yashan ve-lo min ha-yashan al ha-chadash* — one may not take *terumah* from the new on behalf of the old or from the old on behalf of the new.

Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's ruling: *tzovro gorno le-tocho* — harvest everything together into the same threshing floor, then take *terumah* and *ma'aser* from the combined pile. One assumes that the mixture is proportionally distributed — if, say, sixty percent of the plants belong to the prior year and forty percent to the new year, then the portion of *ma'aser* taken from the combined pile will be proportionally sixty percent from the old year and forty percent from the new, and each portion will count for its appropriate year.

### Multiple Discussions

The *gemara* immediately raises the same objection it has raised to each prior candidate: *amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yochanan, halacha Rabbi Shimon Shezuri* — Rabbi Yochanan already ruled like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri in the Egyptian legume case as well. *Ve-im ita, hu nami leima* — if Ulla's statement was anchored in this case, he too should have been part of that discussion. Since he was not, this cannot be the anchor case either.

The pattern is now fully exposed. Ulla made a sweeping declaration that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri — both in the case at hand and wherever he appears. Yet every case in which Rabbi Shimon Shezuri expresses a view has *already* been the subject of an *amoraic* ruling by another *amora*. If Ulla had been referring to any one of those cases, one would have expected his ruling to appear in conversation with those other *amoraim*. But Ulla's statement stands alone, disconnected from all prior *amoraic* discussions. The challenge, therefore, is to identify a case where Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds an opinion but no other *amora* has ruled upon it — that would be the true anchor of Ulla's blanket principle. The *gemara* leaves this as the question at the close of the daf.

# Menachot 31

## Rabbi Shimon Shezuri

### Ulla's Independence

The daf begins at the bottom of 30b with a recapitulation of why the ruling of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Chanina cannot be anchored in the case of the grain mixture discussed previously. The principle at stake is straightforward: Ulla's statement that "the *halachah* is like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri — and not only here, but everywhere Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rules, the *halachah* follows him" must be grounded in some specific case of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri about which no other *amora* had already weighed in. The reason is simple: if an *amora* had already ruled on that very case, then Ulla, by voicing his own ruling, would have been entering into dialogue with that *amora*, and the statement would have been formulated differently.

This is precisely the problem with the grain mixture case. The Gemara notes: *ha itmar alah amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yochanan, halachah k'Rabbi Shimon Shezuri* — Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the *halachah* follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri. Since Rabbi Yochanan had already ruled on that case, if Ulla's anchor had been this case, he would have framed his statement in relation to Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, not independently. The fact that Ulla speaks without reference to any other *amora* means we must still identify a case of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri on which no *amora* had commented. Two candidates are proposed: Rav Papa says the anchor is the case of the *shida* (a large box), while Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is the case of wine.

### Shida Measurement

The *Mishnah* in Keilim teaches that a very large vessel — one capable of holding two *kor* of dry measure — is classified more like furniture than like a vessel and therefore does not become *tamei*. The *shida*, a large storage chest, is the paradigm case. The question is: how do you measure whether this vessel meets the two-*kor* threshold?

Beis Shammai rules *nimdedes mibifnim* — you measure the interior volume. This is eminently logical: the whole point is whether the vessel is large enough to contain two *kor*, so you measure what it actually contains. Beis Hillel rules *mibachutz* — you measure from the outside. The thickness of the walls is treated as if it too constitutes contained volume. This is a *kula*, a leniency: the more volume we can attribute to the vessel, the more readily we can say it has crossed the threshold and therefore does not become *tamei*.

Both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree, however, that the thickness of the legs and the thickness of the decorative metalwork or grating around the top are not measured toward the volume — these structural elements do not define any enclosed space.

Rabbi Yosi introduces a surprising position. He says both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree that the thickness of the legs *and* the metalwork *is* measured, but the space *between* the legs is not. The Shita Mekubetzet notes a different textual reading of this *mishnah*. That the space between the legs is not measured makes obvious sense — they enclose nothing. But that the thickness of the legs themselves should be counted toward the volume, while the walls are not, is quite strange. This is nevertheless Rabbi Yosi's position.

### Legs & Space

Rabbi Shimon Shezuri goes further still with an even more lenient position: *im hayu raglayim gevohot tefach, ein beinehem nimdad; ve-im lav, beinehem nimdad* — if the legs raise the box a full *tefach* or more off the ground, the space between the legs is not counted; but if the legs are less than a *tefach* high, the space between them *is* counted toward the volume. The reasoning is that short legs, being insignificant in their own right, are treated as mere extensions of the walls of the box — the walls are understood to continue downward through them, and the enclosed space between them is therefore attributed to the vessel itself. This is a substantial leniency, and it presumably operates according to Beis Hillel's approach.

Here, then, is a ruling of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri on which no *amora* on record voiced an opinion — making it a plausible candidate for the anchor case of Ulla's general statement.

### Solidified Wine

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes the case of wine instead. The *Mishnah* in Taharot deals with a principle from Rabbinic law: whenever *tumah* touches a liquid — regardless of whether the *tumah* is an *av*, a *rishon*, or a *sheni* — that liquid always becomes a *rishon le-tumah*. Normally, *tumah* is transmitted in degrees: an *av* makes something a *rishon*, a *rishon* makes something a *sheni*, and so on. But liquids are always elevated immediately to *rishon* status. The question taken up in the *Mishnah* is what happens when the classic liquids — oil, honey, and wine — solidify. Are they still considered liquids for the purposes of these *tumah* laws?

Tosafot clarifies that nobody disputes that oil, honey, and wine constitute liquids in their natural state; the dispute concerns only their solidified forms. Rabbi Meir rules that oil (*shemen*), even when solidified, retains its status as a liquid and therefore still becomes *rishon le-tumah* regardless of what degree of *tumah* touches it. The Sages add that honey (*dvash*) in solidified form likewise retains liquid status, which is somewhat surprising since people eat solid honey and might expect it to be classified as food rather than liquid. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds: *af hayayin* — even wine, when solidified, is still considered a liquid.

This raises a difficulty: if the *tanna kamma* (the earlier opinion) holds that solidified oil and honey are still liquids, how could solidified wine be any less so? Wine is the paradigmatic liquid; surely it would be classified as a liquid even more readily than oil or honey. The Gemara therefore reinterprets Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's statement. Rather than *adding* wine to the list, he is *restricting* it: oil and honey, when solidified, lose their liquid status and become solids for purposes of *tumah*. Only wine, as the quintessential liquid, retains its liquid status even after solidifying. This is thus a ruling of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri that no *amora* had addressed — the second plausible anchor for Ulla's statement.

### Mixed Tevel

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita* featuring yet another case involving Rabbi Shimon Shezuri: *amar Rabbi Shimon Shezuri: paam achat nisarev li tevel b'chulin u'vati v'shaalti et Rabbi Tarfon* — "One time *tevel* became mixed with *chulin* and I came and asked Rabbi Tarfon." Rashi clarifies that this is *tevel de'oraita* — grain from which *terumos u'maasros* had not been separated, with a full Biblical obligation — which had become mixed with *chulin*, grain already properly tithed. The challenge is that *tevel* is a *davar she'yesh lo mattirin* (something that has a permitted state awaiting it), and for such things *bittul* does not apply even Rabbinically. How, then, can one separate *terumos u'maasros* for *tevel* buried in a mixture?

Rabbi Tarfon's solution: go to the marketplace and buy grain of the same type. Marketplace grain purchased from an *am ha'aretz* has the status of *demai* — doubly tithed produce that is Rabbinically obligated but Biblically exempt. Then separate *terumos u'maasros* from the purchased *demai* in proportions that also cover the *tevel* mixed into the *chulin*.

The elegance of this solution lies in the symmetry of obligations. The *tevel* in the mixture is, *de'oraita*, rendered *batel* by the majority of *chulin* — Rabbi Tarfon holds that *bittul* operates Biblically even for *tevel*. It thus carries only a Rabbinic obligation. The *demai*, meanwhile, is Biblically exempt because Rabbi Tarfon holds that the majority of *amei ha'aretz* do tithe (*rov amei ha'aretz me'asrim*), so one may rely on that majority Biblically, yet Rabbinically the obligation remains. Both are therefore Biblically exempt and Rabbinically obligated, and separating from one works for the other: *havei lei k'torem min ha'patur al ha'patur*, it is like separating from the exempt for the exempt.

One might ask why Rabbi Tarfon did not simply separate *terumos u'maasros* from within the mixture itself — taking, say, ten percent of the combined mixture as the portion for the *tevel* mixed within it. Rashi addresses this: since the *chulin* component is entirely exempt, it is not meaningful to designate a separation that is predominantly *chulin* as serving the *tevel*. We cannot take *terumos u'maasros* from within the mixture; an external, equivalently-obligated source must be used instead.

The Gemara then asks: why specifically *demai*? Why not buy grain from a non-Jew? Grain owned by a non-Jew in Eretz Yisrael is also, according to some opinions, Rabbinically obligated but Biblically exempt. The answer is that Rabbi Tarfon holds *ein kinyan l'oveid kochavim b'eretz Yisrael l'hafkiya miyad maaser* — a non-Jew's ownership in Eretz Yisrael does not suffice to exempt his produce Biblically. Grain from a non-Jew thus carries a full Biblical obligation, making it incompatible with the Rabbinically-obligated mixture.

An alternative version of the discussion reverses the scenario: Rabbi Tarfon actually told Rabbi Shimon Shezuri to buy from a non-Jew, because Rabbi Tarfon holds *yesh kinyan l'oveid kochavim* — non-Jewish ownership *does* suffice to create Biblical exemption — so the non-Jew's grain parallels the *tevel*-in-*chulin* mixture perfectly. In that version the Gemara asks: why not use *demai* instead of grain from a non-Jew? The answer: Rabbi Tarfon holds *ein rov amei ha'aretz me'asrim* — he does not rely on the majority of *amei ha'aretz* tithing — and therefore *demai* is not Biblically exempt at all but rather a *safek de'oraita*, a Biblical doubt, which would make it incompatible with the mixture that is fully exempt Biblically.

## Universal Application

### Mixed Case Query

Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Shmuel sent a question to Rav Pappa: Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Chanina that the *halachah* follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri — and moreover, *v'lo od ela kol makom sheshana Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, halachah k'moaso* — not only in that case but everywhere Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rules, the *halachah* follows him. Does this sweeping statement extend even to the case just discussed, where *tevel* became mixed with *chulin* and the solution involved separating from *demai* or from grain of a non-Jew?

### Mishnah & Baraita

Rav Pappa replied: yes, *amar lei in* — it applies there as well. Rav Ashi then reported that Mar Zutra told him that Rabbi Chanina of Sura was in fact bothered that the question was even raised. *Pshita* — it is obvious! When Ulla said "everywhere Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rules," he did not say "everywhere Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rules in the *Mishnah*." The formulation *kol makom sheshana* means everywhere he teaches — whether in a *Mishnah* or in a *baraita*. The grain mixture case, which appears in a *baraita*, is therefore included without any question.

With that, the extended discussion of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's rulings — spanning *tumah*, vessel measurement, solidified wine, and *terumos u'maasros* — reaches its conclusion. The anchor case for Ulla's general ruling is identified as either the *shida* measurement or the solidified wine, both being rulings of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri on which no *amora* had previously commented.

## Tears & Sewing

### Two-Line Tears

The Gemara turns to a new topic: tears in the *klaf* of a *Sefer Torah*. Rav Zeira said in the name of Rav Chananel in the name of Rav: *kera haba bishtei shitin yitpor* — a vertical tear that passes through two lines of text may be sewn. Even if a letter in one of those lines is broken by the tear, the *klaf* may be sewn and the letter then rewritten, since one cannot form a letter through the act of sewing — the letter must be written on the *klaf* directly. Subject to that condition, however, the *Sefer Torah* remains *kosher* with a repaired two-line tear.

### Three-Line Limit

*Bishalosh lo yitpor* — if the tear passes through three lines, it may not be sewn. A tear of that magnitude, if patched together with thread, makes the *Sefer Torah* look like patchwork, which is unseemly. In such a case, the entire *klaf* must effectively be replaced, which is a significant requirement. Rav Zutra reported to Rav Ashi that Rav Yirmeyah of Difti said in the name of Rava: the ruling that a three-line tear may not be sewn applies only to an old *Sefer Torah* (*atikta*). An old scroll that is patched in multiple places reaches a point of genuine unsightliness. But a new *Sefer Torah* (*chadta*) — *leit lan bah* — we have no objection to sewing even a three-line tear.

### Gall Nut Treatment

"Old" and "new" in this context are not literal chronological designations. *Lo atikta atikta mamash, velo chadta chadta mamash* — old does not literally mean old, and new does not literally mean new. Rather, *ela ha de-afitzan ha de-lo afitzan*: "old" means a *klaf* that has been treated with gall nut, and "new" means one that has not. Gall nut treatment was applied to *klaf* to darken its surface, giving it the appearance of age and making any scraping of the ink visible. The practical effect is that a *klaf* treated with gall nut has a distinctive dark, aged appearance — and it is *that* appearance which triggers the concern for unsightliness when multiple sections are sewn together. A *klaf* without such treatment, regardless of its actual age, is considered "new" for purposes of this *halachah* and may be sewn even where three lines are torn.

### Catgut Requirement

*Mahani mili be-gidin* — all of the above, regarding when sewing is permitted, applies only when catgut is used: thread made from animal intestine. *Aval be-gardin* — but with regular thread, sewing is not permissible. There are two ways to understand this restriction. Some hold that there is a *halachah le-Moshe mi-Sinai* requiring catgut for the sewing of *klafim*, and this extends to repairs as well. Others maintain that the *halachah le-Moshe mi-Sinai* applies only to the sewing of *klafim* to one another (joining columns), not to repairing a tear; the objection to regular thread is purely aesthetic — regular thread stands out too prominently against the *klaf* and makes the repair visually conspicuous.

### Between Lines

Rav Yehuda bar Abba posed an unresolved question: what if the tear runs three lines vertically but falls entirely *bein daf le-daf* — in the blank space between columns — without cutting into any text? Or *bein shita le-shita* — what if it is a horizontal tear running between two lines of text, cutting only the blank space between them? In these cases the tear does not visually disrupt the written text in the same way a tear through lines of writing would. Does the three-line restriction still apply, or may such tears be sewn regardless of their extent? The Gemara leaves this as an unresolved question.

## Mezuza Format

### Two Per Line

A *mezuza* written with only two words per line — a very long, narrow text — is *keshera*, valid. This is Rashi's reading of the formulation *shtayim shtayim*.

### 2-3-1 Pattern

*Iba'ya lehu: shtayim ve-shalosh ve-achat mahu?* — the question was posed: what if the *mezuza* is written with two words on one line, three on the next, and one on the following, in a repeating pattern? For a visual illustration, the Shita Mekubetzet provides examples: *vehayu hadevarim* on the first line, *ha'eileh asher anochi* on the second, *metzavecha* on the third, and so on. Is such a format *kosher*?

One might have assumed that a *mezuza*, like a *Sefer Torah*, requires uniform columns with consistent line lengths. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer is striking: *kol shekein she'as'ah keshira* — not only is it valid, it is particularly fine. The staggered 2-3-1 pattern resembles the formatting of *shira* in the Torah — specifically the format described by the Gemara as *ariach al gabei leveinah*, "a brick over a space," like the song *Az Yashir*, in which text and space alternate in a staggered pattern across lines. This type of arrangement is treated as an especially appropriate form for the *mezuza* text, though Rashi and Tosafot do not offer an explanation of *why* this should be so.

The Gemara then raises an apparent difficulty from a *baraita*: if one wrote a section that should be formatted as normal columns in the style of *shira*, or wrote a *shira* section (such as *Shirat Hayam* or *Ha'azinu*) in the format of normal columns, it is *pesulah* — invalid. Does this not contradict the ruling that a *shira*-like format is acceptable?

The Gemara resolves this immediately: *ki tanya hahi b'Sefer Torah* — that teaching refers to a *Sefer Torah*. In a *Sefer Torah*, the *shira* sections (*Az Yashir*, *Ha'azinu*) must be written in their distinctive staggered format, and the regular text must be written as standard columns. Mixing the formats in a *Sefer Torah* is *pesulah*. A *mezuza*, however, does not operate under the same constraints, and its text may be written in a *shira*-like pattern without invalidation.

This is further confirmed by a parallel tradition: *amar Rabbah bar bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan, mezuza she'as'ah shtayim ve-shalosh ve-achat kesheira* — a *mezuza* written in the 2-3-1 pattern is valid.

### Avoid Tent/Tail

Two conditions attach to this leniency. *Shelo ya'asennah ke-kuvah* — one must not write it in the shape of a tent, meaning a progressively widening pattern of one word, then two, then three (1-2-3). And *shelo ya'asennah ke-zanav* — one must not write it like a tail, meaning a progressively narrowing pattern of three, two, one (3-2-1). The Gemara's reasoning, implicit in the discussion, is that the staggered 2-3-1 pattern is recognized as echoing the structure of *shira* — short, long, short, long — a pattern that repeats with balance and symmetry. A simple triangle (tent) or inverted triangle (tail) has no analog in any recognized Torah text format and is therefore seen as visually incoherent or aesthetically disqualifying.

### Al Ha'aretz

Rav Chisda rules: *al ha'aretz be-shita acharona* — the words *al ha'aretz* should appear on the final line of the *mezuza*. This is indeed the practice.

### Positioning

Two opinions are cited regarding exactly where on that final line *al ha'aretz* should appear. *Ika de'amrei besof shita* — some say it is left-justified, appearing at the end of the line with blank space before it. *Ve-ika de'amrei be-tichlas shita* — others say it is right-justified, appearing at the beginning of the line. The Shita Mekubetzet provides visual depictions of both options.

Each position carries a visual rationale. The one who says *besof shita* — left-justified — draws on the phrase *kegova shamayim al ha'aretz*: the heavens are positioned directly above the earth, visually, with *shamayim* in the line above *aretz*, and *aretz* below it. The one who says *be-tichlas shita* — right-justified — points to the verse *ki heichi d'merachka shamayim mei-aretz*: the point is that heaven is *distant* from earth, and placing *aretz* as far as possible from where *shamayim* appears makes that separation visually manifest.

In current practice, *al ha'aretz* does appear on the last line of the *mezuza*, right-justified. The *mezuza* itself is written in standard justified columns rather than in a *shira* pattern. The question of how to format the break between the two paragraphs — *Shema* and *Ve-haya im shamo'a* — will be addressed in the next shiur.

# Menachot 32

## Parshiyot Setumot

### Rav Huna's Practice

The Gemara on 36b records the following teaching: Rabbi Chelbo reports that he observed Rav Huna rolling his *mezuzah* from *Echad* towards *Shema* — that is, scrolling it up from left to right so that when one opens it, one begins at the beginning. Rabbi Chelbo further notes that Rav Huna made its *parshiyot setumot* — he arranged the two sections, *Shema* and *Ve-hayah im shamoa*, with only a closed, partial break between them.

### Petuchot/Setumot

To appreciate the significance of this practice, one must understand the distinction between *petuchot* and *setumot*. In a traditional *Chumash* — such as the classic *Chumash Vistretz* — this is indicated visually by the letters *peh* and *samech*, which Artscroll renders graphically. *Peh* stands for *patuach* and *samech* for *setum*. Despite the *samech* being rarer, *setum* actually represents the smaller break. *Setum* means closed: a line of text ends mid-line, a span of white space follows, and then the next section begins on the same line toward the end — a paragraph-level break but not a full section break. *Patuach*, by contrast, means open: the text stops mid-line, white space fills the remainder of that line, and the next section begins on the following line — a larger, section-level break.

*Tosafot* cites the *Yerushalmi* and other opinions suggesting an even larger variant of *patuach*: the text ends mid-line, the rest of the line is left blank, and then an entire additional blank line follows before the next section begins — equivalent to a double line-feed. There is no established *mesorah* for this form in the Torah, though apparently some Dead Sea Scroll texts do employ it where a conceptually larger section break is warranted. The fundamental distinction, then, is that *patuach* is the larger break and *setum* is the smaller one.

### Shema in Torah

The question of how the *mezuzah* sections relate to one another depends on how they actually appear in the Torah text itself. When one examines the Torah, one finds that the *Shema* — *Devarim* 6:4–9 — concludes with *u-visharecha*, after which there is only a *setum*, a minor break, before *Ve-hayah ki yeviacha*. Similarly, *Ve-hayah im shamoa* (*Devarim* 11:13–21) is also *setum* with respect to the parasha that precedes it. The implication is that the *Shema* flows into what follows it with a measure of continuity, and *Ve-hayah im shamoa* is similarly continuous with what precedes it. If one were placing these two *parshiyot* side by side in a *mezuzah* and wished to reflect their character as they appear in the Torah, the natural choice would be *setumot* — indicating a measure of continuity or modest separation — rather than *petuchot*. That is precisely what Rav Huna did.

## Rabbi Meir/Shimon

### Rabbi Meir Method

The Gemara then introduces a challenge from the following *beraita*. Rabbi Shimon Elazar reports that Rabbi Meir — one of the most celebrated scribes in the Talmud, who actually practiced this craft professionally — would write the *mezuzah* on *duchsostos*. We will address precisely what *duchsostos* is below, but it is a specific type of parchment derived from a particular layer of the animal hide. Rabbi Shimon Elazar further records that Rabbi Meir would write it *k'min daf* — in the format of a page, meaning, as Rashi notes, *arucha u-ketzara*, a narrow column rather than a wide format. Rabbi Meir would also make a *revach* — a margin — above and below. And crucially: *ve-oseh parshiyoteha petuchot* — he made the *parshiyot petuchot*, with a full, open break between the two sections.

### Shimon's Question

Rabbi Shimon Elazar then describes his own exchange with Rabbi Meir. He says: *Rebbi, mah ta'am* — why do you write the *parshiyot petuchot*, given that they appear *setumot* in the Torah? The implicit argument is that the natural presentation, as the sections appear in the Torah itself, would suggest making the break *setum* rather than *patuach*.

### Not Juxtaposed

Rabbi Meir answered: *ho'il ve-ein smuchot min ha-Torah* — since in the Torah the two *parshiyot* are not actually juxtaposed with one another. The *Shema* and *Ve-hayah im shamoa* appear in entirely different places in the Torah, separated by intervening text. The quality of *setum* reflects a sense of visual and textual continuity between adjacent sections of a single text. Since these two *parshiyot* do not actually appear next to one another in the Torah, the *setumot* designation is inapplicable — there is no actual continuity to reflect. Therefore, Rabbi Meir chose to write them *petuchot*.

One might ask whether Rabbi Meir means that *petuchot* is the only valid option, or merely that *petuchot* is permissible given the absence of actual juxtaposition in the Torah. The Gemara will address this question shortly.

## Margins/Rav Ruling

### Ruling: Margins

The Gemara records: *Amar Rabbi Chananel amar Rav, halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon Elazar* — we rule like Rabbi Shimon Elazar. This is notable, since the discussion was structured as a story about Rabbi Meir's scribal practice, yet the Gemara understands it as a halachic dispute and issues a ruling accordingly. The implication would seem to be that we rule in favor of *petuchot* over *setumot*, in apparent contradiction to Rav Huna's practice of *setumot* described at the outset.

### Clarification

The Gemara immediately asks: *mai lav a-petuchot* — does this ruling not refer to the *petuchot* question? And it answers: *lo, a-revach* — no, perhaps the ruling refers specifically to the matter of margins, not to *petuchot* versus *setumot*. Since Rabbi Meir is recorded as making margins above and below the text, and this practice is not self-evidently required, the ruling *like Rabbi Shimon Elazar* who cited Rabbi Meir may simply mean that margins are halachically necessary — not that we are endorsing *petuchot* over *setumot*.

## Resolution

### Scrolls Evidence

This is a genuine *chiddush*, because the historical evidence suggests that margins were not standard practice. The Dead Sea Scroll *tefillin* fragments — a transcription and near-visual reproduction of which was distributed for examination — show that when scribes of that period wrote *tefillin*, they left no margins whatsoever. Because *tefillin* and *mezuzah* parchments were typically byproducts of the larger sheets prepared for *Sifrei Torah* — the scraps and off-cuts from the edges of those larger sheets — they were small pieces of parchment onto which text was squeezed as efficiently as possible. Given that neither *tefillin* nor *mezuzah* are generally opened and read, aesthetic concerns of *hiddur* were less pressing. The ruling that one *does* require a margin for a *mezuzah* is therefore a meaningful halachic statement. And it is this requirement — the *revach* — that constitutes the content of the ruling like Rabbi Shimon Elazar, not the *patuach*/*setum* question.

## Margins/Rav Ruling (II)

### Margin Width

The Gemara then asks: *ve-kamah revach* — how wide must the margin be? Rav Menashya bar Yaakov, and some say Rav Shmuel bar Yaakov, answers: *ke-melo itba de-safrei* — like the width of an *itba de-safrei*. Rashi explains that an *itba de-safrei* was a thin implement — something like a paperclip or narrow holder used to clip pages together and prevent them from folding. The margin required for a *mezuzah* is therefore minimal — nothing like the three or four fingers required for a *Sefer Torah*. Since the *mezuzah* is typically not viewed once installed, the aesthetic requirements are calibrated accordingly, and only a narrow, thin margin is mandated.

## Practice/Minhag

### Abaye Questions

At this point Abaye raises a question to Rav Yosef: *ha lav tishparta* — do you not hold that when Rav said we rule like Rabbi Shimon Elazar, we must be speaking about the margins and not the *patuach*/*setum* question? For how could Rav be ruling in favor of *petuchot* when established practice clearly runs in the other direction? *Ve-ha Rav it lei minhaga* — Rav, after all, holds that *minhag* governs.

### Minhag Principle

This phrase — *Rav it lei minhaga*, that Rav follows *minhag* — requires careful unpacking, because it involves a central question in the theory of *psak halacha*: how much weight does established communal practice carry relative to canonical textual sources?

One must distinguish between two related but distinct concepts. The Hebrew word *minhag* can refer either to a custom — a non-mandated activity that communities have adopted over time — or to a *practice*, meaning what the people have actually been doing. The critical halachic question is whether *psak halacha* is determined primarily by what the canonical sources say, or significantly by what established practice has been.

Haym Soloveitchik, in his essay "Rupture and Reconstruction," explores this tension at length. We have become, in modernity, a thoroughly text-based tradition — and we are therefore sometimes startled to encounter the idea that accepted practice might override or reframe what a *gemara* seems to say. But this was not always the dominant orientation. In traditional societies, the living tradition — what was actually handed down and practiced — was primary. Indeed, Jacob Katz, the pioneering historian of *halacha*, observes that when *Tosafot* sought to refine or adjust halachic norms based on the written *Gemara*, they were perceived by contemporaries as the innovators, even the reformers. "Our practice has always been thus — you want to change it because of something written in a book somewhere?" In this light, what we read as *Tosafot*'s accommodation of practice to text was actually, from the traditional perspective, a revolutionary move toward textualism. *Tosafot* does maintain a dialectic — they are prepared at times to bring practice under the scrutiny of the text — but the older model gave practice primary weight.

This dynamic is visible in the contrast between the *Mishnah Berurah* and the *Arukh HaShulchan*. The *Mishnah Berurah* proceeds from the *Rishonim* and *Acharonim* and issues rulings accordingly, at times explicitly correcting what the community is doing. The *Arukh HaShulchan*, by contrast, frequently invokes *minhag Yisrael Torah hi* or *minhag Yisrael kedoshim*, and sees it as a *mitzvah* to find ways of sustaining established communal practice — reinterpreting sources to align with what communities have been doing, and sometimes simply stating that despite the *machloket* in the literature, the *minhag* in *Lita* has always been such-and-such, and therefore that is what we do. Part of this difference in orientation reflects not only differing intellectual approaches but differing institutional positions: *halacha* has traditionally been *paskened* by rabbis embedded in communities, not by those operating within the *yeshiva* context — a distinction with significant implications for how *psak* functions today.

With this in mind, returning to our Gemara: the practice at the time was that *mezuzot* were written with *setumot* — the smaller, closed break — rather than *petuchot*. Given that Rav follows the weight of established practice, how could one suppose that Rav issued a ruling in favor of *petuchot*? The answer is that he did not. When Rav said we rule like Rabbi Shimon Elazar, he must have been speaking about the *revach* — the margin — not about overriding the established practice of writing *setumot*.

### Eliyahu/Chalitzah

The Gemara now brings the source that establishes Rav's principle regarding *minhag*. Rabbah said in the name of Rav Kahana, who said in the name of Rav: *Im yavo Eliyahu veyomar, choltzin be-min'al, shomein lo* — if Eliyahu HaNavi were to come and declare that *chalitzah* may be performed with a *min'al* (a closed shoe, as opposed to an open sandal), we would listen to him. But *ein choltzin be-sandal, ein shomein lo* — if Eliyahu were to say that a *sandal* is invalid for *chalitzah*, we would not listen to him. Why? *She-kvar nahagu ha-am be-sandal* — because the people have long established the practice of using a *sandal* for *chalitzah*, and that practice cannot be overridden.

This is a striking *gemara*. One should note, however, that the principle is stated with respect to Eliyahu HaNavi, whose halachic authority is itself not straightforward. The principle that *ein navi rasha'i lechadesh davar* — a prophet has no standing to introduce new halachic rulings — applies to Eliyahu as to any prophet. His weight in halachic discourse may be no greater than that of any rabbi, and perhaps less. Invoking Eliyahu, therefore, does not necessarily imply that established practice would override a weighty, unambiguous canonical source. What the Gemara does establish is that Rav assigns meaningful halachic weight to well-established communal practice — enough to resist even prophetic instruction. There is also a parallel formulation in the *Yerushalmi* — *minhag mevattel halacha* — that goes even further, and was occasionally cited by the *Geonim*, though how far that principle extends remains its own question.

### Ambiguous/Established

The Gemara then records a second version of the teaching from Rav Yosef: Rav Kahana said in the name of Rav — if Eliyahu were to declare that a *min'al* is *invalid* for *chalitzah*, we would listen to him; but if he declared that a *sandal* is invalid, we would not, again because of established practice.

The two versions differ: the first says we would listen to Eliyahu *permitting* the *min'al*; the second says we would listen to Eliyahu *prohibiting* the *min'al*. The Gemara asks: *mai beinayhu* — what is the practical difference between these two versions? The answer is: *min'al le-chatchila ika beinayhu* — the question of whether the *min'al* is currently acceptable in the first place. The version that says we would follow Eliyahu in permitting the *min'al* assumes the *min'al* is currently in a state of limited or ambiguous use — not established practice, not clearly prohibited, but not commonly employed. We would accept prophetic guidance to normalize it. The version that says we would follow Eliyahu in prohibiting the *min'al* assumes the *min'al* is currently somewhat acceptable, at least in practice, but since it is not firmly established, we would accept guidance that it should be discontinued. In either case, what both versions share — and what is the operative point for our discussion — is that neither version would follow Eliyahu if he sought to invalidate the *sandal*, because the use of the *sandal* is thoroughly established. The distinction, then, is between an ambiguous practice with some currency but no consensus, which remains susceptible to authoritative guidance, and a well-established practice, which does not.

### Ashkenazi/Sephardi

Chaim Soloveitchik has observed that this tension between text and practice played out historically along geographic and communal lines. *Ashkenazi* communities tended to assign greater weight to established practice, and for understandable reasons: these were cloistered, insular communities that had maintained their traditions through enormous sacrifice, including the martyrdom of the Crusades. For such communities, one looks at the practices of one's community and presumes they are correct — the *frumkeit* of the people is not in question. *Sefardi* communities, by contrast, were more integrated into the surrounding culture, more socially variegated, and in moments of extremity — such as forced conversion — more prone to internal deviation. When *Sefardi Rishonim* looked at their communities' practices, they were less confident that every deviation from the canonical text reflected a legitimate tradition rather than laxity. This difference in communal self-perception directly shaped the methodology of *psak*: whether one approaches an established practice with deference, seeking to validate it from the sources, or with scrutiny, evaluating it against the text.

## Resolution (II)

### Proof Source

Returning to the main thread: the Gemara says *ela lav, shema mina* — this must be a proof that when Rav ruled like Rabbi Meir, it was specifically about the *revach* (the margin), not about *petuchot*, since the established practice is *setumot* and Rav would not issue a ruling against established practice. *Shema mina* — this is accepted.

The Gemara then seeks to support the view that even Rabbi Meir would concede the validity of *setumot*. It cites a *beraita*: *Sefer Torah she-bala u-tefillin she-balu* — if a *Sefer Torah* has worn out and *tefillin* have worn out with age, can one reuse the parchment? The *beraita* rules: *ein osim mehem mezuza* — one may not use such parchment to make a *mezuzah* — whether by writing new text upon it or by cutting out the *Shema* and *Ve-hayah im shamoa* and placing them in a *mezuzah*. The reason is *lefi she-ein moridin mi-kedusha chamura li-kedusha kala* — because one may not lower an object from a higher *kedusha* to a lower one. A *Sefer Torah* and *tefillin* possess a higher *kedusha* than a *mezuzah*, and therefore one may not repurpose their parchment for a *mezuzah*.

### Rav Natan Ruling

The Gemara then offers a direct resolution of the *patuach*/*setum* question. Rav Natan bar Yitzchak states: *mitzvah la-asotan setumot* — the proper practice, *lechatchila*, is to write the *parshiyot* of the *mezuzah setumot*, reflecting how each *parsha* appears individually in the Torah. *Ve-im avdinan petuchot, shapir dami* — but if one wrote them *petuchot*, as Rabbi Meir chose to do, this is also acceptable. Since the two *parshiyot* are not actually juxtaposed in the Torah, there is latitude in either direction. *Setumot* is preferable because it reflects the independent character of each *parsha* as it appears in its own context in the Torah; *petuchot* is valid because, in the *mezuzah*, these sections do not appear next to one another in the way that would demand *setum* continuity.

### Support

The Gemara then clarifies the meaning of Rabbi Shimon Elazar's quotation of Rabbi Meir: *u-mai petuchot di-kamar Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar? De-kamar af petuchot* — when Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar cited Rabbi Meir's practice of *petuchot*, he meant that Rabbi Meir holds that even *petuchot* is acceptable. This is not quite the same as Rabbi Meir's own *lechatchila* preference for *petuchot*, since we now establish *setumot* as the *lechatchila* and *petuchot* as the *bediavad*. But the practical conclusion holds: the two positions are not in fundamental contradiction. The halacha is that *lechatchila* one writes *setumot*, but *bediavad* *petuchot* is valid.

The Gemara attempts to further support the view that even Rabbi Meir accepts *setumot* from the *beraita* regarding recycled *Sefer Torah* parchment. The argument is as follows: if not for the problem of *moridin* — lowering from higher to lower *kedusha* — one could in principle use *Sefer Torah* parchment for a *mezuzah*. Yet in the *Sefer Torah* the relevant sections appear *setumot*, while in the *mezuzah* Rabbi Meir writes them *petuchot*. If this transfer were permissible, it would presumably be in the *setum* format in which they appear in the Torah. This implies that even Rabbi Meir would agree that *setumot* is a valid way to write the *mezuzah*. The Gemara, however, deflects this proof: *lo, dilma le-hashlim* — perhaps the *beraita* is speaking only of a case where one is supplementing an incomplete *mezuzah* — adding, say, the *Shema* from a *Sefer Torah* to a *mezuzah* that already has the *Ve-hayah im shamoa*, or vice versa. In that case, since only one *parsha* is being added rather than both being juxtaposed, no inference about the *setumot*/*petuchot* question can be drawn. The proof remains inconclusive, but the ruling stands as stated.

### Tosafot Variants

*Tosafot* at the top of the page offers an illuminating discussion of what *petuchot* and *setumot* actually look like in practice, reflecting the range of opinions and the lack of universal standardization. *Tosafot* cites Rashi's view and then adds: *ve-anu nohagim lehani'ach chalak me'at bi-tchilat shita ve-achar kach matchil Ve-hayah im shamoa ve-shema gam ze karui stuma* — our practice is to leave a small blank at the beginning of the line and then begin *Ve-hayah im shamoa*, and perhaps this too is called *setuma*. This is, in effect, what we would call indenting — beginning the new *parsha* not at the very start of the line but a few spaces in — which creates a visible but modest break.

*Rabbeinu Tam*, by contrast, explains *patucha* as the case where a *parsha* ends in the middle of a line and the remainder of the line is left blank — the measure being approximately the space of the word *le-mishpechoteihem*. If that space is not left, the result is something different, and he goes on to distinguish multiple variants depending on the size of the gap and where it falls. One variant that particularly stands out is leaving not just the remainder of the line blank but an entire additional blank line — a double line-feed — which apparently appears in some Dead Sea Scroll texts at points of major conceptual transition. The Gemara does not spell out these visual formats with precision, and *Tosafot*'s discussion makes clear that the exact visual rendering of *setum* and *patuach* was not universally standardized, even among the *Rishonim*.

## Klaf/Duchsostos

### Halacha Moshe

The Gemara now turns to a related question: on what type of parchment must *tefillin* and *mezuzah* be written? The discussion is grounded in a *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*: *tefillin al ha-klaf u-mezuzah al duchsostos* — *tefillin* are written on *klaf* and *mezuzah* on *duchsostos*.

### Leather Parts

What are *klaf* and *duchsostos*? The Gemara explains: *klaf be-makom basar, duchsostos be-makom se'ar* — *klaf* is the surface of the skin that faced the flesh of the animal, and *duchsostos* is the surface that faced the hair.

To understand this practically: the leather taken from an animal has a certain thickness. That thickness is split into two layers. One layer is the inner layer — the side that was in contact with the animal's flesh; the other is the outer layer — the side that was in contact with the hair. *Klaf*, used for *tefillin*, is the inner layer, and one writes on the surface of the *klaf* that faced the flesh — the *makom basar*. *Duchsostos*, used for *mezuzah*, is the outer layer, and one writes on the surface that faced the hair — the *makom se'ar*. The terminology *duchsostos* is Greek in origin.

### Recycling

This specification raises the question of recycling parchment. The *beraita* already cited establishes: *ein osim mehem mezuza* — one may not use worn *Sefer Torah* or *tefillin* parchment to make a *mezuzah*. On what basis?

Two distinct grounds are relevant. The first is the rule of *moridin*: one may not lower an object from higher *kedusha* to lower *kedusha*. The second is the parchment specification just stated: *tefillin* require *klaf* and *mezuzah* requires *duchsostos*, and one cannot repurpose parchment designated for one across the *klaf*/*duchsostos* divide.

### Moridin

One would like to cut out the *Shema* from a worn *Sefer Torah* and place it in a *mezuzah*, or take the *Shema* from *tefillin* parchment and reuse it. This is prohibited by *lefi she-ein moridin mi-kedusha chamura li-kedusha kala* — one does not lower from a higher *kedusha* to a lower one. A *Sefer Torah* and *tefillin* possess a higher *kedusha* than a *mezuzah*. By contrast, the reverse direction — taking parchment from a *mezuzah* and using it for *tefillin* or a *Sefer Torah* — would be an elevation in *kedusha* and is in principle permissible, following the principle of *ma'alin ba-kodesh ve-lo moridin*.

### Flexibility

The Gemara then discusses the degree of flexibility available by *mezuzah* relative to *tefillin* with respect to parchment type. A *beraita* states that *shina*, changing the parchment specification, renders the object *pasul*. The Gemara clarifies that this stringency applies specifically to *tefillin*: the *klaf* for *tefillin* must be precisely the designated type, and any variation — whether using *klaf be-makom se'ar* instead of *klaf be-makom basar*, or using *duchsostos be-makom basar* instead of the correct side — invalidates the *tefillin*. By *mezuzah*, however, there is greater latitude: the range of parchments that may be used is broader. Were it not for the *moridin* prohibition, one could theoretically use *tefillin* parchment for a *mezuzah*, since the *mezuzah* tolerates a wider range of parchment types. The *tefillin* parchment specification, by contrast, admits no flexibility — any deviation from the precise *klaf be-makom basar* is *pasul*.

The upshot is that while the *mezuzah* has a specified parchment in its *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, it is somewhat more flexible in what it accepts than the highly precise *klaf* requirement of *tefillin*. This asymmetry is itself notable: in certain formal requirements, such as *ke-sidran* and the parchment specification, the *mezuzah* and *tefillin* differ in degree of stringency, and not always in the direction one might expect.

---

---

# Menachot 33

## Sefer Torah Status

### Bed & Sefer Torah

The daf opens with a brief but striking account reported by Rabbi Chelbo. He relates that he observed Rav Huna sitting on a bed upon which a *Sefer Torah* was resting. Rather than simply remaining on the bed, Rav Huna upturned a jug on the ground, placed the *Sefer Torah* upon it, and only then was willing to continue sitting on the bed. The operative principle, the Gemara explains, is that Rav Huna held it to be forbidden to sit on a bed upon which a *Sefer Torah* is resting — *asur leishev agabei mita sheSefer Torah munach aleha*. This ruling reflects a distinct dimension of the *Sefer Torah*'s sanctity, one that does not appear to extend to other sacred books.

### Rabba bar bar Chana
