This position, however, conflicts with a ruling transmitted by Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, who permits sitting on such a bed — *mutar leishev agabei mita sheSefer Torah munach aleha*. A seemingly powerful counter-proof is raised: there is a well-known story of Rabbi Eliezer who, while sitting on a bed, suddenly remembered that a *Sefer Torah* was lying on it, and slipped off immediately as though he had been bitten by a snake. Surely this demonstrates that one may not sit on a bed together with a *Sefer Torah*?

### Gemara's Correction

The Gemara does not accept this challenge. It corrects the story: the *Sefer Torah* was not on the bed at all. Rabbi Eliezer was sitting on the bed and realized that someone had left the *Sefer Torah* on the ground — *agabei karka* — and it was in response to that indignity that he leapt off the bed and sat on the ground himself. The story, then, does not speak to the question of sitting on the same bed as a *Sefer Torah*; it speaks rather to the impropriety of leaving a *Sefer Torah* on the ground while one sits elevated above it.

### Kissei Hakodesh

This exchange introduces, without elaborating, the broader framework of *kissei hakodesh* — the elevated status of sacred writings. The Gemara here is not placing this ruling in a wider comparative context, and it does not explore how the ruling would apply to *tefillin*, *mezuzot*, or other *sfarim*. Those questions are discussed elsewhere in the Gemara and among the *rishonim* and *poskim*, but not here. What the Gemara does establish is that the ruling pertains specifically to the unique sanctity of a *Sefer Torah* — *kedushas Sefer Torah* — and not to sacred writings generically. Whether the *Sefer Torah* in question was housed in a protective covering, whether a *chumash* printed today would carry an equivalent status, and how all of this maps onto a broader taxonomy of *kedushat sfarim*, are questions left open by this sugya.

---

## Mezuzah Writing

### Igeret vs. Sefer

The Gemara now shifts its focus toward the laws of *mezuzah* in particular. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: if one wrote the *mezuzah* like a letter — *katva igeret* — it is invalid, *pesulah*. Rashi understands this to refer specifically to the *mezuzah*. The general question being raised is what kind of document the *mezuzah* must resemble: a *sefer*, a formal sacred book, rather than an *igeret*, an informal letter.

### Precision & Spelling

What exactly does *igeret* mean, and why would that form render the *mezuzah* invalid? The Gemara does not spell this out in detail, but Rashi and Tosafot offer explanations. One possibility is that *igeret* refers to writing without *sirtut* — the scored lines that are required in the writing of a *mezuzah*, as discussed earlier in the Gemara. Another possibility is that it refers to a lack of precision in spelling. When one writes an informal letter, one does not necessarily attend to the exact orthographic form of every word, particularly where variant spellings are customary or unnoticed. If the *mezuzah* was written with acceptable spelling variants that nonetheless deviate from the precise form in which those words appear in the Torah, the *mezuzah* would be invalid. The point is not about the width of the columns — indeed, the Gemara has already established that even two words to a line is acceptable in a *mezuzah* — but about the exacting standard of spelling required.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The Gemara invokes a *gezeirah shavah* to derive that the *mezuzah* must be written as a *sefer* and not as an *igeret*. The reasoning would be that while *mezuzah* is not explicitly described in the Torah with the word *sefer*, a verse elsewhere — such as *vekasav lah sefer kerisut* in the context of a *get*, or a verse concerning the writing of *sefer* by *Amalek* or by *Yehoshua* — contains that language, and by linking the verbal context of *uchtavtem al mezuzot beitecha* to a verse that uses the word *sefer*, one derives that the *mezuzah* must have the character of a *sefer*. The Gemara itself is notably vague here: it does not specify which word the *gezeirah shavah* is built upon, and the argument raises its own difficulty — why do we know the source any better than we know the *mezuzah* verse itself? Tosafot, for his part, rejects the suggestion that this is derived from a *get*, since there is no independent source that a *get* requires *sirtut*, which would make the derivation circular.

---

## Mezuzah Placement

### On Stick Invalid

The Gemara turns to the question of where the *mezuzah* must be physically affixed. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: if one suspended the *mezuzah* on a stick — *telaah bemakel* — it is invalid. The apparent practice being addressed is that of travelers who would carry a portable *mezuzah* mounted on a stick, which they would prop near a doorway when staying somewhere that lacked a *mezuzah*. Such an arrangement, the Gemara rules, is invalid. The reason is grounded in the verse: *bisharecha* — in your gates. The *mezuzah* must be affixed within the doorpost itself, not merely positioned near it.

A *baraita* corroborates this ruling. If one suspended the *mezuzah* on a stick, or placed it behind the door — *achar hadelet* — it is described as involving danger with no *mitzvah* fulfilled. The term *sakanah*, danger, here admits of two readings. Rashi understands the danger to be that once the *mezuzah* is not fulfilling its *mitzvah*, it no longer serves to protect the house — a reading that reflects the assumption that the *mezuzah* has a kind of protective function. Tosafot offers a more straightforward explanation: the danger is purely physical. A *mezuzah* improperly placed — say, sticking out awkwardly in a spot where one might walk — poses the risk of injury. This reading is strongly preferable. The question of the *mezuzah*'s protective role is one the Gemara handles with considerable subtlety, as we will see further on.

The question of *churei hadelet* — placing the *mezuzah* behind the door — refers to a situation where the door, when open, swings back to conceal the doorpost. In such a case, the *mezuzah* would be hidden and thus not properly affixed in the meaningful sense. The *sakanah* of Tosafot's reading in such a case would apply if the *mezuzah* were somehow protruding in a way that could cause someone turning a corner to strike their head against it, though admittedly the danger in that specific case is less obvious.

### Munbaz's Inns

A passage regarding the household of King Munbaz illustrates one form of *mezuzah* practice observed beyond the strict letter of the obligation. The members of his royal retinue would affix *mezuzot* in the inns where they lodged — *fundekaoteihen* — even though they were not technically obligated, as they did not own or rent the premises long-term. They did so as a *zecher lemezuzah*, a remembrance of the obligation, so as not to dwell in a place without any *mezuzah* at all.

This is a significant detail. The Gemara does not say they did this because of *sakanah* or for protection. It says they did it as a *zecher*, firmly grounding the practice in a *halacha mitzvah* framework rather than in a superstitious or apotropaic one. The parallel to *batei kenesiot* and *batei midrash*, which are also not technically obligated but for which the custom is to affix a *mezuzah* nonetheless, is instructive in the same direction.

### Door Thickness

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: the *mitzvah* is to place the *mezuzah* within the actual interior space of the doorframe — *betoch chalalo shel petach* — not on the front or the back face of the doorpost. The Gemara initially responds that this is obvious from the verse *bisharecha*, but then explains why one might have thought otherwise. Since Rava had ruled that the *mitzvah* is to place the *mezuzah* in the *tefach* of the doorframe's thickness closest to the *reshut harabim* — the public domain — one might have supposed that even farther outward would be better, and thus placing it on the exterior face of the doorpost entirely would be optimal. The Gemara rejects this: the requirement remains that the *mezuzah* be *besharecha*, inside the gate, within the thickness of the frame itself, not on its outer surface facing the street.

### One Parchment

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: if one wrote the *mezuzah* on two parchments — *al shenei dapin* — it is invalid. A question arises as to what *dapin* means here. Earlier in the tractate, *daf* referred to a column within a *Sefer Torah*; here it most naturally means two separate pieces of parchment. The Gemara works through a *baraita* that addresses the case of writing on two columns and placing them in two separate doorposts — *bishnei sipim* — and rules it invalid, while permitting placement in a single doorpost. The Gemara resolves the apparent tension by clarifying that when the *baraita* says "two doorposts" it means parchment *fit* to be placed in two doorposts — i.e., two separate pieces of parchment — not literally two separate doorposts with a single piece of parchment cut across two columns. The upshot is that the *Shema* and *Vehaya Im Shamoa* must both appear on a single, continuous piece of parchment. A *mezuzah* composed of two physically separate pieces of *klaf* sewn or otherwise joined together is invalid.

### Door Hinge

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: with respect to *mezuzah*, one should follow the *heker tzir* — the location of the door hinge. The Gemara asks what *heker tzir* means. Rav Adda explains it refers to the *afta*, the socket or hole in which the door's pivot sits.

Rashi's explanation clarifies the practical application. The rule that a *mezuzah* is affixed on the right-hand side as one enters a doorway is well known, but in certain cases the question of which direction constitutes "entering" is ambiguous. For a doorway leading from the street into a house, the direction of entry is obvious. But for an interior door between two rooms, the question may be genuinely unclear. The Gemara specifies that such a door should arise between, for example, the men's section and the women's section of a house — *bei gavrei* and *bei nashei* — and the direction of primary travel is determined by where the hinge is located.

The key point is not whether the hinge is on the left or the right of the door, but rather which *side* of the door it faces. A door hinge is placed on the interior side to prevent anyone outside from being able to remove the door by lifting the hinge pin. The side of the door that does *not* show the hinge is considered the exterior — the side from which one approaches. The assumed direction of travel is therefore from the side where the hinge is hidden toward the side where the hinge is visible. Whatever is the right-hand side when moving in that direction is where the *mezuzah* is affixed.

The Gemara observes, almost in passing, that by framing this rule as it does, it presupposes the principle of affixing the *mezuzah* on the right-hand side of entry — a rule the Gemara has not formally introduced, but simply treats as background.

The Gemara also acknowledges a broader question lurking here. In the time of the Gemara, it was common for a *bayis* to refer to a single room, and entire families often lived in one such room. Whether the modern practice of requiring a *mezuzah* on every interior room reflects the Gemara's own assumed context is not entirely clear. One *rishon* held that individual interior rooms within a house did not require *mezuzot* separately. The *halacha* as universally practiced today does require *mezuzot* on all rooms, and there are *gemarot* in this sugya that speak of individual rooms — but the degree to which the Gemara's cases map directly onto our contemporary multi-room dwellings is worth noting as an academic observation.

### Resh Galuta

When the *Resh Galuta* — the secular head of the Jewish community in Babylonian exile — built a new home, he sent to Rav Nachman asking him to arrange for the *mezuzot* to be affixed. Rav Nachman's response was: first hang the doors, then place the *mezuzot* — *tali dashei bereisha*.

Rashi explains that Rav Nachman needed there to be a physical doorframe in place before the *mezuzah* could be affixed; placing the *mezuzah* in the carved-out space first, before the frame was erected, would raise questions about the requirement for a physical doorframe. Tosafot offers a different explanation: Rav Nachman needed to see where the hinges were placed in order to determine the direction of primary passage between the rooms, and thereby to know on which side the *mezuzah* should be affixed. Until the doors were actually hung with their hinges, that determination could not be made.

---

## Angle Debate

### Nagar Invalid

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: if one made the *mezuzah* like a *nagar* — a peg or nail — it is invalid. According to Rashi's illustration, this refers to placing the *mezuzah* horizontally into the doorframe rather than vertically; one has, as it were, driven it in like a nail, and this is *pesulah*.

### Rabbi's House

The Gemara immediately challenges this ruling. When Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported that all of the *mezuzot* in Rebbe's house were made like a *nagar* — *kemin nagar havei avidun* — and were evidently considered valid. Parenthetically, the Gemara notes at this point that the small door Rebbe used to pass from his private quarters into his *beis medrash* did not have a *mezuzah* — a point that will be addressed in the next section.

### Horizontal vs Vertical

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: the two cases are not comparable. In one case the *mezuzah* was placed like a *sichta* — a peg driven horizontally — which is invalid. In the other case it was placed like an *istavira*, which the Gemara identifies as the joint connecting the hip to the thigh. The question is what *istavira* means in terms of actual placement.

### Rashi vs Tosafot

Rashi offers two explanations. On the first reading, the *istavira* — the hip-thigh joint — is vertical when one is standing, and therefore placing the *mezuzah* like an *istavira* simply means placing it vertically. The invalid placement is horizontal, and the valid placement is vertical. On Rashi's second reading, the joint creates a right angle when one is seated, suggesting a bent or angled form — one that, practically speaking, would require carving a strangely shaped recess in the doorframe.

Tosafot offers a third reading: *istavira* refers to a diagonal placement. This is neither horizontal nor fully vertical but at an angle, which is geometrically natural and could correspond to a diagonal cut in the doorframe.

More significantly, Tosafot argues with the very premise of Rashi's ruling about what is *lechatchila*. Rashi holds that the *nagar* which is invalid is horizontal, and the proper placement is vertical. Tosafot reads the Gemara in precisely the opposite direction: the *nagar* that is invalid is vertical, and the proper placement is horizontal. Tosafot grounds this in the practice of how *klafim* are stored. While we are accustomed to *Sifrei Torah* being stored upright in the *aron*, there are traditions in which *Sifrei Torah* were stored lying flat, and that was considered the more dignified position — the parchment is settled and at rest rather than held awkwardly upright. Tosafot extends this logic to the *klaf* in *tefillin* as well, asking whether the *klaf* should be placed standing or lying flat. Tosafot then cites Rabbeinu Tam, who notes that when the *Sefer Torah* stands on the *bima* everyone rises, but when the *shaliach tzibbur* lays it down, everyone sits — suggesting that the lying-down position is the natural resting state, and thus the more respectful one for storage.

Given this direct contradiction between Rashi and Tosafot, Tosafot himself proposes a resolution: perhaps what Rebbe's house exemplified was the diagonal placement — the *istavira* understood as an angle. If so, both Rashi (who requires vertical) and Rabbeinu Tam (who requires horizontal) might agree that a true compromise at the diagonal satisfies both opinions. This is the origin of the *minhag* to place the *mezuzah* at an angle. Nevertheless, there were those who followed Rashi outright — the Vilna Gaon among them — and in Yerushalayim it is common to see *mezuzot* placed completely straight vertically, following the *minhagei haGra*. In practice, even those who follow the diagonal do not place it at a full 45-degree angle; rather, the *mezuzah* is placed primarily vertically with a modest tilt of perhaps 20 to 30 degrees.

### Doorbolt Analysis

Daniel Sperber, in the first volume of his *Minhagei Yisrael*, brings archaeological evidence that illuminates this entire discussion. Before turning to *minhagim* broadly, Sperber's primary scholarly focus was on the physical realia of the Talmudic period, using archaeological findings to reconstruct what Talmudic-era objects and structures actually looked like. He argues that the *nagar* referred to in the Gemara was not simply a generic nail or peg but specifically the doorbolt — the horizontal bar that secured the door from the inside.

Sperber shows, with diagrams of ancient Israelite homes from archaeological excavations, that doorframes were constructed with a deliberate asymmetry: one side was a single continuous column of stone, while the other side was composed of two stones with a deliberate gap between them. This gap served as the slot into which the doorbolt could be inserted to lock the door from the inside. Crucially, he notes that in many of these structures, the bolt-hole was positioned approximately one-third from the top of the doorframe — precisely the region where a *mezuzah* would be placed. The Gemara's ruling, then, makes immediate physical sense: do not place your *mezuzah* in the hole you carved for your doorbolt. Sperber also reports that angled bolt-holes have been found archaeologically, corresponding to Tosafot's reading of the house of Rebbe, but no purely horizontal placements are attested. Sperber's analysis supports Rashi's basic understanding that what is invalid is horizontal placement, and that the diagonal configuration attributed to Rebbe's house reflects a real architectural feature.

### Ashkenazi Angle

The practice of placing the *mezuzah* at an angle is specifically an *Ashkenazic* custom. In *Sefard* the practice of placing the *mezuzah* straight vertically was apparently unproblematic. There is a folk tradition — for which no clear documentary evidence has been cited — that the angled placement developed during the period of the Crusades. According to this account, Crusaders who entered Jewish spaces would take a piece of wood and strike the vertically placed *mezuzah* sideways, turning it into the shape of a cross. In response, Jews began placing the *mezuzah* at an angle to prevent this from being easily done. This may be legend, and it deserves further investigation, but it is worth noting as a proposed historical explanation for the specifically *Ashkenazic* emphasis on the diagonal.

---

## Secondary Doors

### Rabbi's Door

Returning to the parenthetical point raised earlier: the small door that Rebbe used to pass from his private quarters directly into his *beis medrash* did not have a *mezuzah*. The Gemara implies that not every doorway requires a *mezuzah* — the opening must constitute a meaningful and significant passageway. Rebbe's private entrance to his *beis medrash* was not the primary access point; it was a small, personal door used exclusively by Rebbe himself to move between his rooms. The main entrance to the *beis medrash* was used by all the students. Since this small door represented only Rebbe's private passage rather than a genuine communal entryway, it did not require a *mezuzah*.

### Rav Huna's Door

The Gemara challenges this with a counter-example: there was a door that Rav Huna used to enter his *beis medrash*, and that door did have a *mezuzah*. How can this be reconciled with the case of Rebbe's door? The Gemara answers: Rav Huna's door was *ragil* — commonly used, either by Rav Huna himself on a frequent basis or by others as well. It thus constituted a genuine passageway rather than a private, minor opening. The precise quantitative threshold between a *ragil* door and one that is not is not spelled out.

### Tosafot's Reading

Tosafot reads the passage somewhat differently. Examining the language of the Gemara carefully — *petach habayit she'hayu yotzim mimenu l'Beis Medrash* — Tosafot argues that the reason Rav Huna's door required a *mezuzah* was not simply because it was a *beis medrash* door, but because it was a *house* door. It was the door through which one exited a private residence on the way to the *beis medrash*. Tosafot adds explicitly: a door to a *beis medrash* itself — *petach Beis haMidrash atzmo* — does not require a *mezuzah*, because a *beis medrash* is not a place where people live. This is, in fact, the answer to the famous question attributed to Korach against Moshe: does a house full of *sefarim* require a *mezuzah*? The answer, *al pi din*, is no — a *beis midrash* or *beis knesses* where no one actually lives and sleeps does not require a *mezuzah*. The universal *minhag* is to affix one anyway, on the basis of custom alone.

### Common Usage

The principle articulated by the Gemara at this point — *halach achar haragil*, go by what is commonly used — serves as the general rule for *mezuzah* in cases involving multiple doorways. Rashi explains: if a single room has two doorways leading into the same adjacent space, and one of those doorways is the primary one used while the other is secondary, only the primary doorway requires a *mezuzah*. The underlying logic is that the *mezuzah* obligation attaches to a meaningful passageway between two spaces, not merely to any physical opening. If the primary passage from room A to room B already has a *mezuzah*, a secondary, less-used door between those same two spaces does not independently require one. The parameters of what qualifies as primary versus secondary remain somewhat fluid, but the governing principle is clear: follow the common usage.

---

## Height Placement

### Top Third

Rav Zeira said in the name of Rav, and Rav Matna said in the name of Shmuel: the *mitzvah* is to place the *mezuzah* at the beginning of the upper third of the doorframe — *bit'chilat shelish ha'elyon*. This means the *mezuzah* should be positioned so that its lower edge begins at the point two-thirds of the way up the doorframe, with the *mezuzah* itself occupying part of the upper third.

### Rav Huna's Range

Rav Huna disagrees, or at least broadens the acceptable range significantly. He states: the *mezuzah* should be raised at least one *tefach* from the ground and kept at least one *tefach* below the top of the doorframe, and within that range the entire doorway is valid for placing the *mezuzah* — *kol hapetach kulo kasher limezuzah*. These two positions are not necessarily in direct conflict; the statement about the top third was phrased as *mitzvah lehaniach* — the ideal placement — suggesting that even according to the view requiring the top third, placement elsewhere within Rav Huna's range may be acceptable *bedieved*.

### Rabbi Yose's Top

A *baraita* presents the ruling of Rabbi Yehuda — essentially identical to Rav Huna's formulation: one *tefach* from the ground, one *tefach* from the ceiling, and anywhere in between is valid. Rabbi Yose, however, derives a more stringent rule from a *gezeirah shavah* between *ukshartem* — the binding of *tefillin* — and *uchtavtem* — the writing of *mezuzah*. Just as *tefillin* are bound on the upper part of the body, whether the head or the upper arm, so too the *mezuzah* must be placed at the top. This suggests not merely the upper third but placement as high as possible within the doorframe, short of the top *tefach*.

### Floor vs Ceiling

The Gemara asks: given Rav Huna's ruling that the entire range is valid, he is clearly going like Rabbi Yehuda. But according to whom does Shmuel — who specifies the top third — rule? Not like Rabbi Yehuda, since Rabbi Yehuda allows the entire range; and not like Rabbi Yose, since Rabbi Yose would require placement at the very top. Rav Huna the son of Rav Natan resolves this: Shmuel does in fact rule like Rabbi Yose, and when Shmuel says *bit'chilat shelish ha'elyon*, he does not mean the top third is the ideal target — he means it is the lowest permissible point. One should not go below the top third, but within the top third, placement higher is better. The practical implication is that the *mezuzah* should be placed as high as possible, at least no lower than where the upper third begins.

### High Arches

Tosafot notes a passage in the Yerushalmi that addresses the case of a very high doorway. When the doorframe is so tall that the top third is far above reach, the *mezuzah* should be placed at shoulder height — *k'neged ktefav*. Tosafot observes that this position diverges from our own Talmud's conclusion. The practical *halacha* as we rule it follows the top third as the operative zone, without explicitly endorsing the view that higher within the top third is always better. In cases of very high arches, such as those found in ancient structures in Yerushalayim, the practice of placing the *mezuzah* at shoulder height reflects the Yerushalmi's approach.

---

## Protection Purpose

### Closest to Outside

Rava — the same ruling cited earlier in the context of the door's thickness — states: the *mitzvah* is to place the *mezuzah* in the *tefach* of the doorframe's thickness closest to the *reshut harabim* — *b'tefach hasamuch lereshut harabim* — i.e., the outermost portion of the frame's depth. Two reasons are offered for this preference.

### Immediate Encounter

The Rabbis explain: *kedei she'yifga b'mezuzah miyad* — so that a person immediately encounters the *mezuzah* upon entering the house. This rationale is grounded in the psychological and religious dimension of the *mezuzah*: the moment one crosses the threshold, the first thing one meets is the *mezuzah*, reinforcing awareness of God and the obligations it embodies.

### House Protection

Rav Chanina of Sura offers a different reason: *ki heichi d'tinaterei* — so that the *mezuzah* protects the house. The idea here is that if the *mezuzah*'s protective function is to guard the household, it should be positioned at the outermost boundary of the home, so that the protection begins as far outward as possible. This reasoning has a quasi-mechanical character: the precise location of the *mezuzah* within the doorframe's depth determines the boundary of the zone it protects.

One might ask: why not place the *mezuzah* entirely on the exterior wall if maximal outward protection is the goal? The answer, as the Gemara has already established, is that *bisharecha* requires the *mezuzah* to be within the doorframe, inside the gate — not on the external face of the wall. Given that constraint, the outermost viable position is the *tefach* closest to the public domain.

### God's Protection

The Gemara then shifts registers entirely with a statement by Rabbi Chanina: *bo ure'e shelo kemidat Hakadosh Baruch Hu midat basar vadam*. Come and see that the way of the Holy One Blessed be He is not like the way of flesh and blood. When a human king sits in his inner chamber, his guards stand on the outside protecting him from external threat. God's way is the reverse: *avadav yoshvim mibifnim vehu meshamer mibachutz* — His servants dwell inside, and He protects them from the outside. The proof-text is from Tehillim: *Hashem shomrecha, Hashem tzilcha al yad yeminecha*.

### Superstition Downplay

This shift is not incidental. The Gemara has presented two competing explanations for why the *mezuzah* should be placed at the outermost *tefach*: one psychological and one protective. The protective explanation — that the *mezuzah* itself guards the house from the outside — carries with it the potential to slide into a view of the *mezuzah* as a charm or amulet. The Gemara does not follow that path. Instead, it almost immediately pivots to a theological statement in which the protection comes not from the *mezuzah* as a magical object but from God, who stands watch over His servants from the outside.

This appears to be a deliberate strategy. There is ample archaeological evidence that *kameot* and magical amulets were widespread in Jewish practice throughout the *bayis sheni* period and beyond, and it is evident that many people associated the *mezuzah* with apotropaic power. The Gemara, however, consistently handles *mezuzah* through a *halachic* lens. Even Rashi's reading of the *baraita* — that a *mezuzah* placed behind the door creates *sakanah* because it no longer protects the house — reflects the protective view. But the Gemara does not elaborate on that view, and by concluding with *Hashem shomrecha*, it redirects: any protection associated with the *mezuzah* is ultimately God's protection of those who are mindful of His presence, not the operation of a physical charm. The Rambam, characteristically, makes this explicit: the protection comes from the heightened religious awareness generated by encountering the *mezuzah* each time one enters and exits, which orients the person toward God — not from any power inherent in the object itself.

---

## Depth & Multiple Doors

### Burial Depth

Rav Yosef the son of Rava taught in the name of Rava: if one embedded the *mezuzah* more than a *tefach* deep into the doorframe — *he'emikah tefach pesulah* — it is invalid. Once the *mezuzah* is buried beyond a *tefach* into the thickness or substance of the frame, it is no longer considered properly affixed as part of the doorframe itself.

### Adding Stone

A *baraita* is brought as a potential support. The *baraita* addresses two related cases: placing the *mezuzah* in the *patzin* — the doorframe — or subsequently attaching a stone or block — *malben* — over the area where the *mezuzah* was placed, effectively burying it deeper. The *baraita* states that if under these circumstances there is a *tefach* of doorframe below the *mezuzah*, a separate *mezuzah* is required; if not, no separate *mezuzah* is needed.

### Doors Behind Doors

The Gemara, however, declines to accept this as a direct proof for the rule about depth of embedding. It reinterprets the *baraita*: the case being discussed there is not a standard doorframe in which a *mezuzah* has been buried too deep, but rather a case of *petach she'be'churei hadelet* — a door situated behind another door. This refers specifically to a configuration in which two doors meet at a perpendicular angle, so that the opening of one door gives directly onto the space of the other. The question in such a case is whether these count as one doorway or two, and consequently whether one or two *mezuzot* are required.

### Tefach Separation

The determining criterion, the Gemara explains, is whether the two perpendicular doorways are separated from one another by a *tefach*. If the space between them is at least a *tefach*, they are counted as two distinct doorways, each requiring its own *mezuzah*. If the separation is less than a *tefach*, they are treated as a single continuous doorway and only one *mezuzah* is required. The Gemara confirms that the end of the *baraita* states this explicitly: *petach she'achorei hadelet* — the opening behind the door — requires a separate *mezuzah* if there is a *tefach* separating it from the primary door, and does not require one if there is not. This rule is entirely independent of the preceding question about how deeply the *mezuzah* is embedded into the doorframe.

---

## Tasseh Principle

### Reed Case

A *baraita* presents a final case concerning the construction of the doorframe itself and the manner in which the *mezuzah* is inserted into it. If the doorframe is made of reeds — *malben shel kanim* — the procedure is as follows: one cuts open a single reed and inserts the *mezuzah* into it — *chotech shefoferet umenichah*. Whether the reeds run horizontally or vertically determines which reed is to be cut, but assuming the standard vertical orientation, the *mezuzah* is placed inside one of the vertical reeds, which now serves as the *mezuzah*'s housing within the frame. This in itself is unremarkable.

### Frame First

Rav Acha the son of Rava adds a critical qualification: the ruling applies only when the doorframe was first erected and *subsequently* the reed was cut open and the *mezuzah* inserted — *she'he'emido uvasof chatcho*. In that sequence, the act of cutting and placing is an active, deliberate deed performed upon an already-existing doorframe, and the *mezuzah* is properly made in its place.

### Tasseh v'Lo

If, however, one first cut the reed and placed the *mezuzah* inside it, and *then* erected the doorframe — *chatach v'heniach uvasof he'emido* — the *mezuzah* is invalid. The principle invoked is *ta'aseh v'lo min he'asui*: you must actively make or do, not simply allow something to come into being automatically. This principle is most familiar from the laws of *sukkot*, where the verse *chag hasukkot ta'aseh lecha* teaches that one must actively construct the *sukkah* — a *sukkah* that forms itself automatically, such as by digging a hollow in a haystack, is invalid because no act of making was performed. Here, if the doorframe is erected with the *mezuzah* already inside the reed, the *mezuzah* has not been actively affixed to an existing doorframe; instead, the doorframe and *mezuzah* came into their combined state simultaneously, without any discrete act of placing the *mezuzah* upon an already-standing frame.

Notably, the Torah does not use the word *ta'aseh* in the context of *mezuzah* — the relevant verse reads *uchtavtem al mezuzot beitecha*. Nevertheless, the Gemara applies the principle of *ta'aseh v'lo min he'asui* here, understanding it as a general *halachic* requirement: the *mezuzah* must be written upon an existing doorpost and then actively placed, not come to be in place as a byproduct of the doorframe's construction.

---

---

# Menachot 34

## Doorframe Structure

### Desolate Doors

The *sugya* opens by completing a passage from the bottom of 33b. Rava teaches: *hanei pitchai shamai* — those doors that are desolate or abandoned — are exempt from *mezuzah*. The Gemara asks: what exactly are these desolate doors? Rav Rechumi and Abaye Yosei debate the matter. One says the door lacks a *tikra* — a ceiling or roof element — and the other says it lacks *shikufi*.

Rashi reads these terms fairly literally. The first opinion concerns a room without a ceiling; the second concerns the absence of a lintel — the horizontal structural element at the top of the door — and the absence of doorposts. The alternative reading of Rashi assumes that a missing ceiling is not itself disqualifying, and therefore interprets the first term as well to mean missing lintel, and the second as referring to missing doorposts. However one resolves the internal ambiguity within Rashi, the underlying principle is clear: it is not sufficient that a space merely happens to take the *form* of a doorway. There must be an actual architectural structure functioning as a frame.

### Frame vs. Shape

This brings us to a foundational debate between Rashi and Tosafot with significant practical ramifications. In many homes, the passageway between a living room and a dining room is shaped like a doorway — formed by the way the walls terminate — but has no actual inset wooden or metal frame. We affix a *mezuzah* to such openings. Is that halachically justified?

Rashi, read strictly, would seem to require an actual physical structure — a true doorframe — not merely the incidental shape of a doorway. Tosafot, however, reads the Gemara differently. Tosafot to *d'leisu lei tikra* explains: *peirush makom shehapetach shokef sham milmala eino shaveh* — the issue is that the top of the opening is not flat or straight. The stones coming from the arch above are jutting in and out — *even nichneset ve'even yotzet* — making it jagged rather than even. According to Tosafot, the disqualification is not about the absence of a physical frame but about the absence of the correct *shape*. So long as the lines are straight — even if the opening is simply the natural termination of two walls — a *mezuzah* is required. The practice to affix *mezuzot* on frameless interior openings follows the position of Tosafot.

This distinction — physical frame versus shape alone — recurs throughout the *sugya* and will resurface in the discussion of the *akarna* corner door.

## Achsadra & Entrances

### Achsadra Structure

Rabbah bar Shila said in the name of Rav Chisda: an *achsadra* — a portico, open on one end, with walls or columns on three sides — is exempt from *mezuzah*, because *ein lah pitzimin*: it does not have doorposts. Since the entire side is open, there is no frame, no doorway, and no defined entrance at all.

The Gemara immediately presses: does this imply that if the *achsadra* did have columns, it would be *chayav*? The Gemara rejects this inference: *le-chizuk tikrah hu de-avidi* — even those columns are there only to support the ceiling, not to structure a doorway. They do not functionally constitute a *pitzimin*. The Gemara therefore corrects the formulation: even if an *achsadra* had such columns, it would still be exempt, since those columns do not serve the function of doorposts. Abaye then reports that he saw the *ispalidi* — some manner of portico or esplanade — of the master's house, which had columns and yet had no *mezuzah*, consistent with the ruling that such columns, being there only to support the roof, do not transform the structure into a proper doorway.

## Doorframe Structure (II)

### Doorway Function

The Gemara raises a deeper principle here that extends beyond the physical structure: even if a space happens to have the shape of a doorway, that shape must be the result of deliberate architectural function. It cannot be accidental. This applies equally to the debate between Rashi and Tosafot — whether one requires a physical structure or merely the correct shape — because in either case, the shape must be intentional, not merely incidental. A space that happens to look like a doorway because of how stone walls happen to fall is not the same as one designed to serve as a doorway.

The word *mezuzah* in the verse *al mezuzot beitecha u'visharecha* does not refer to the parchment scroll but to the doorframe itself. The obligation attaches to that doorframe, and the frame must be recognizable as such — not only structurally but functionally.

Beyond structure, there is a second requirement: *beit dirah*. A *mezuzah* is obligated only on a dwelling or on something directly appended to a dwelling. This is why a *beit midrash* or *beit kenesset* does not require a *mezuzah* *mid'oraita* — these are not places of living. The *achsadra* or portico, though not itself a *beit dirah*, does have a connection to one, and the Tosafot at the bottom of the page addresses this directly. The Tosafot cites a *baraita* from Yoma which might have excluded a *beit shaar*, *achsadra*, and *mirpeset* from the obligation. The resolution offered by Mar bar Rav Ashi is that *mid'oraita* such structures are indeed exempt — since one does not live in them — but *miderabbanan* they do require a *mezuzah* because they serve or connect to a *beit dirah*. The principle is therefore layered: architectural form, intentional function, and relationship to a dwelling all determine the obligation.

## Achsadra & Entrances (II)

### Rav's Achsadra

The Gemara raises an apparent contradiction. A *baraita* states that a *beit shaar*, an *achsadra*, and a *mirpeset* are all *chayavin bemezuzah*. But we just established that an *achsadra* is exempt because it has no doorframe. The Gemara resolves this: the *achsadra* referred to in the *baraita* is the *achsadra debei Rav* — the portico of Rav's house. Rashi glosses *indrona* — the term the Gemara uses to characterize it — with *chambra*, i.e., chamber. The Gemara is saying that whatever Rav's *achsadra* was, it was in reality a true enclosed chamber with four walls and a doorway, not an open portico at all. It thus tells us nothing new that such a structure requires a *mezuzah*.

### Roman Achsadra

The Gemara then offers the real answer: the *baraita* refers to an *achsadra rumisa* — a Roman-style *achsadra*. Rashi describes this as a structure with many windows, something resembling a gazebo in feel — very open — but nonetheless possessing a defined entranceway. Unlike a standard *achsadra* whose entire side is open, this structure has a proper doorway. It therefore requires a *mezuzah*. The principle emerging is that what matters is not the name or general character of the structure, but whether it has a functioning doorway — and, of course, its connection to a *beit dirah*.

## Bei Chaziki

### Two Mezuzot

Rechava said in the name of Rav Yehuda: *bei haziki chayav bishtei mezuzot* — the *bei haziki* requires two *mezuzot*. The Gemara asks: what is a *bei haziki*? Rav Papa said in the name of Rav: it is a *beit shaar* — a gatehouse — that opens into a *chatzer*, a shared courtyard, with houses that open off that *beit shaar*. The structure thus has two doors: one connecting the *chatzer* to the *beit shaar*, and one connecting the *beit shaar* to the residential area.

The *chiddush* is that both doors require a *mezuzah*. The inner door, from the *beit shaar* to the houses, is straightforwardly connected to the dwelling. But the outer door, from the *chatzer* into the *beit shaar*, is not yet at the threshold of any individual home. Nevertheless, since the *beit shaar* has become an extension — an appendage — of the residential quarters, even the outer door is drawn into the obligation. The connectedness to a *beit dirah* is sufficient.

### Beit Shaar

The Gemara then introduces a *baraita* addressing a smaller-scale version of the same question. A *beit shaar* that opens both into a garden (*gina*) and into a small private house (*kaitonit*) has two doors — one facing the garden, one facing the house. Which of them, if any, requires a *mezuzah*?

Rabbi Yosi says the *beit shaar* is treated as an extension of the *kaitonit* — the small house — and therefore requires a *mezuzah*. The rabbis say it is treated as a *beit shaar*, which in Rashi's reading means it is associated with the garden and is therefore exempt.

The Gemara's underlying question is whether the *beit shaar* is judged by its connection to the garden or to the house, and whether that judgment changes depending on which door one considers. The function and association of the space — not just its physical structure — governs the analysis.

### Rav vs. Raba

Rav and Shmuel both rule: *mi-gina l'bayis* — when going from the garden toward the house — everyone agrees it is *chayav*. This refers to the door connecting the *beit shaar* to the *kaitonit*: that door is plainly an entry into the dwelling. The debate applies only to the door connecting the *beit shaar* to the garden. One opinion holds *kaitonit ikar* — even that door is seen as an appendage of the house and is *chayav*. The other holds *gina ikar* — that door is associated with the garden and is *patur*.

Raba and Rav Yosef take the opposite and more lenient position: *mi-bayis l'gina* — everyone agrees the garden-facing door is *patur*, as it is plainly an opening into the garden. The debate applies only to the door connecting the *beit shaar* to the house — one opinion says it is *bei d'bayis hu* and is *chayav*; the other says even that door should be seen as an exit from the garden, not an entrance into the house, and is *patur*.

Abaye and Rava ruled like Raba and Rav Yosef, who were their teachers. Rav Ashi ruled like Rav and Shmuel, the more stringent position. The *halacha* follows Rav and Shmuel *l'chumra*, which means both doors — the one toward the house and the one toward the garden — require a *mezuzah*. The takeaway is clear: the obligation of *mezuzah* depends not only on architectural form but on function and connectedness to a *beit dirah*, and even individual doors within the same structure may be judged differently based on what each one is seen as serving.

## Internal Doors

### Lul to Attic

The Gemara discusses a *lul* — a passage connecting a ground-floor house to an upper-floor *aliya*, an attic or upper dwelling rented to a separate family. Since the upper-floor tenants had no independent street exit, they would descend through the main house. To preserve the privacy of both households, a small enclosed stairwell would be constructed with doors at both the upper and lower landings — somewhat like a private lobby. When someone from the *aliya* descended, they would arrive on a landing and knock on the door to enter the main house; similarly, entering from the main house into the *aliya* required passing through the landing door.

Rav Huna rules: if the *lul* has one door, one *mezuzah* is required; if it has two doors, two *mezuzot* are required. However many doors, that is how many *mezuzot*. The door connecting the stairwell to the main house is, by any measure, not the primary door of that house. It is not how the homeowner enters or exits. Yet it is still *chayav in mezuzah*.

### Four Doors

Rav Papa derives from Rav Huna's ruling a broader principle: a chamber — *androna* — that has four doors leading in four different directions is *chayav* in four *mezuzot*. This is striking, because one might have thought that only the primary entrance requires a *mezuzah*, or that secondary doors are exempt. The Gemara says *pshita* — obviously — and then clarifies: *lo tzricha af al gav d'ragil b'chad* — the novelty is that even though one door is used most frequently, the others still require *mezuzot*.

This raises the question of how to reconcile this with a story elsewhere in the Gemara about Rebbe, who had a small private door to the *beit midrash* that did not require a *mezuzah*. Perhaps Rebbe's door was exempt because it was a private door for personal use, as opposed to a door available for general use. Alternatively, perhaps that case involved multiple doors all leading into the same room — where only the primary door matters — whereas here we are speaking of doors leading into different spaces. The practical implication is clear: one should affix *mezuzot* to every doorway, and this is indeed the common practice.

### Akarna Corner

Meimar rules that a *pitcha d'akarna* — a corner door — is *chayav bemezuzah*. Rav Ashi challenges him: does it not lack *pitzimin*? A door cut into a corner of a house does not present a naturally shaped doorframe; two walls simply converge without forming a classic rectangular opening.

Meimar responds: *adai ptzimi* — there are indeed *pitzimin*. Rashi explains: *eilu rashei ha'ktalim hen hen ptzimin* — the ends of the walls themselves serve as the doorframe. The point where one wall terminates on each side constitutes the two doorposts of the opening. This is significant on two levels. First, it confirms that a separate physical structure is not required — the walls themselves suffice. Second, even an unconventionally shaped opening — two walls meeting at an angle rather than framing a standard rectangular doorway — can constitute a valid doorframe by using the wall terminations as its posts.

This is somewhat in tension with the stricter reading of Rashi from the earlier discussion, where Rashi seemed to require a physical doorframe structure. It is possible that the earlier Rashi was not absolute, and that in principle Rashi also agrees with Tosafot that the shape suffices, even if described differently. What Rashi here clearly demonstrates is both that a physical separate structure is not required, and that an unusual configuration can still qualify.

The Gemara continues. Rav Papa visited the house of Mar Shmuel and observed a door that had only one *ptzima*, a doorpost structure on the left side, and nevertheless a *mezuzah* had been placed. Rav Papa challenged this: like whom? Like Rabbi Meir? But Rabbi Meir only permits a *mezuzah* on a one-sided doorframe when the *single* post is on the *right* — where the *mezuzah* is placed. If the only post is on the left, even Rabbi Meir would not permit it.

The Gemara then explains Rabbi Meir's position. The *baraita* teaches: a house that has only one doorpost — *bayit she'eino ella ptzim echad* — Rabbi Meir says it is *chayav bemezuzah*; the sages say it is *patur*. Rabbi Meir's reasoning is derived from a *kal vachomer* on the word *mezuzot*: the Torah uses both the form *mezuzat* (singular or defective) and *mezuzot* (plural or full), which in rabbinic hermeneutics signals a *ribui achar ribui* — a doubling of inclusion — which by the rule *ein ribui achar ribui ella lema'eit* actually narrows the requirement. The conclusion is that even one doorpost suffices.

Rabbi Yishmael explains Rabbi Meir's position through this analysis. Rabbi Akiva does not need this derivation, since he learns it from the use of *shtei hamezuzot* — the two doorposts — in the context of *Pesach Mitzrayim*, which by being explicit there (*al hamashkof v'al shtei hamezuzot*) teaches that ordinarily *mezuzot* does not presuppose two. Until the Torah specifies "two," a single post suffices.

A related *drasha* establishes that the *mezuzah* is placed on the right side of the entryway. From *bi'atcha min hayamin* — you enter leading with your right — and supported by a verse in Melachim where Yehoyada the Kohen placed the charity box *miyamin* at the entrance to the *beit Hashem*, we learn that entry is associated with the right side, and the *mezuzah* follows accordingly. The question of what defines the doorpost — whether it requires a physical structure or merely the shape — thus runs through this entire section and remains live.

## Writing Mezuzah

### Parchment Writing

The Gemara now concludes the laws of *mezuzah* with the requirement that the text be written on parchment. *Uchtavtam* — "and you shall write them" — one might think means to write directly on the stones of the doorpost, which is what the plain reading of *al mezuzot beitecha* seems to suggest. The Gemara therefore introduces a *gezerah shavah*.

### Gezerah Shavah

The word *ktivah* — writing — appears both in the context of *mezuzah* and in the context of a *get* (where the Torah says *vechatav lah sefer keritut*) or, according to Tosafot, in the context of *sotah*. The *gezerah shavah* teaches: just as writing there refers to writing on a *sefer* — a parchment document — so too here, writing on *mezuzah* must be on parchment. Alternatively, one might propose a *gezerah shavah* from the writing on the stones at Gilgal, where the Torah says *al ha'avanim* — suggesting the *mezuzah* text should be inscribed directly on the stone doorpost. The Gemara resolves this by ruling that one applies a *gezerah shavah* from writing that is practiced for all generations (*ktivah hanohaget ledorot*) to another obligation that spans all generations, not from a one-time commandment like the writing on the stones, which was fulfilled at a specific historical moment.

Rav Acha the son of Rava raises a striking challenge to Rav Ashi: but the Torah says explicitly *al mezuzot* — on your doorposts! How can you override the plain meaning with a *gezerah shavah*? Rav Ashi responds that the derivation is not solely from the *gezerah shavah*. The word *uchtavtam* itself implies *ktivah tamah* — a complete, perfect writing. One cannot write perfectly on stone. Therefore the *pasuk* itself instructs: write it properly — which means on *klaf*, parchment — and *then* place it on the *mezuzah*. The *gezerah shavah* adds the further point that writing nicely on a flat stone and then affixing the stone to the doorpost would not suffice either.

It is somewhat striking that of all the *mitzvot* in this section, this is the one that draws the challenge "but the Torah says it explicitly." After all, *ukeshtartam* — "and you shall bind them" — in the context of *tefillin* is also not taken literally as tying the text to one's body, and yet no such objection is raised there. The Gemara here, in any case, offers the resolution and moves forward.

### Four Parshiyot

The Gemara then states: the four *parshiyot* of *tefillin* are interdependent — each is indispensable to the others, and even a single letter invalidates the whole. The Gemara says this is *pshita* — obvious. The novelty is established more precisely: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that even the *kotzo shel yud* — the tiny tagin or serifs of the letter *yud* — is indispensable. This was already discussed in the context of *mezuzah*, and the Gemara pushes further: even that the letters must be *mukaf gevil* — surrounded by parchment on all four sides, with no letter touching another — is required, as established earlier.

## Tefillin Intro

### Totafot Etymology

The Gemara now turns to *tefillin* and derives the requirement for four *parshiyot* and four compartments from the word *totafot*. The word appears three times in the Torah: twice in a defective spelling (without a *vav*) and once in the full spelling. The Gemara counts: *l'totafot l'totafot l'totafot* — here are four. Rabbi Yishmael derives four from the numerical value suggested by these three appearances. Rabbi Akiva does not rely on this: *kat d'kafti shtayim, pat b'afriki shtayim* — in a certain language the element *tat* or *kat* means two, and in African the element *pat* means two, yielding four together. The Torah uses a word whose linguistic roots in two foreign languages each contribute the number two.

Tosafot notes a difficulty with Rabbi Yishmael's count — the one time *totafot* is written "fully," the additional *vav* appears between the two *tets*, not as a standard plural marker, and does not obviously imply plurality. But regardless of the technical derivation, the tradition was clearly that four *parshiyot* and four compartments are required; the *drasha* serves to anchor that tradition in the text.

### Meaning of Terms

Tosafot to *l'totafot* offers a fascinating observation. The word *totafot* may refer to the location on the head where *tefillin* are placed — above the forehead, between the eyes. Tosafot also raises the possibility that in Aramaic the word relates to seeing or being seen — from a root meaning *l'hatzit*, to gaze. In that reading, *totafot* parallels the *tzitz* of the Kohen Gadol, which bore God's name on the forehead. The *tefillin* too bear God's name on the head, and both are associated with being visibly marked as God's.

Tosafot concludes by favoring the reading that *totafot* refers to what others see: *v'ra'u kol amei ha'aretz ki shem Hashem nikra alecha* — all the nations of the earth will see that God's name is called upon you. The *tefillin* are testimony, worn visibly on the body as evidence of Israel's relationship with God.

The word *tefillin* itself — a rabbinic term not found in the Torah — is the singular of *tefilla*, prayer. Though in Talmudic times *tefillin* were worn all day and not specifically limited to the time of prayer, Tosafot offers a deeper explanation for the name. About two-thirds down the relevant Tosafot, the word *tefillin* is connected to the root of *plilim* — argumentation or justification before a court. *Tefillin* are *eidut v'hochacha* — testimony and proof — that God's name is called upon us, that we are His people, and that this inspires *yir'ah* among the nations. Wearing *tefillin* is an act of bearing witness to the covenant, and the term reflects that quality.

### Shel Rosh Structure

The Gemara now specifies the construction of the *shel rosh*. A *baraita* teaches: one might think the four *parshiyot* should be written on four separate parchments and placed in four completely separate compartments — four independent *batim* in no way connected. The Torah therefore says *ul'zikaron bein einecha* — it must be a single *zikaron*, one unified object, not several separate ones. How then is this achieved? One writes the four *parshiyot* on four separate parchments (*arba orot*) and places them in four compartments (*arba batim*) constructed out of a single piece of leather (*b'or echad*). Four compartments, but one object.

## Shel Rosh Build

### Spaced Parchments

The Gemara raises a further possibility: what if one wrote all four *parshiyot* on a single parchment and inserted it into the four *batim*? Rabbi — Rebbe — says this is valid (*yatza*), provided one leaves sufficient space between the columns of text (*revach beineihem*) so that the parchment can be separated into four portions, each fitting into its respective compartment. The way Rashi understands this: one writes the four *parshiyot* in four vertical columns on one parchment, then folds or inserts each column into its corresponding compartment. The parchment, remaining connected at its base, spans all four. Since the *bayit* itself is one unit made from one hide, a single parchment similarly unified should be acceptable.

The rabbis disagree and say no space is required. This is somewhat puzzling — it is not entirely clear how the rabbis envision the parchment fitting into four separate compartments without some division. Nevertheless, all agree on the next point.

### Visible Grooves

Both Rabbi and the rabbis agree that one must place a cord or demarcation between each compartment (*chut o meshicha bein kol achat v'achat*), and crucially: *im ein charitzah nikeret, pesulot* — if the groove or incision between compartments is not visible from the outside, the *tefillin* are invalid. The division between the four compartments must be discernible externally. Looking at a *shel rosh* one should see the four sections clearly delineated. An interior division that is invisible from without does not suffice.

## Shel Yad Build

### Gluing Parchments

The Gemara now addresses the *shel yad*. A *baraita* teaches: the *shel yad* is written on one parchment (*or echad*). If one wrote it on four parchments and placed them in the single *bayit* of the *shel yad*, one is *yotzei* — but one must glue them together (*tzarich ledabek*). The reason: *vehayah lecha le'ot al yadecha* — it must be a single *ot* on your hand. Just as the outside presents one unified appearance, the inside must be one unified object. This is the position of Rabbi Yehudah.

### Separate Parchments

Rabbi Yosi disagrees: *eino tzarich* — gluing is not required. Four separate parchments placed inside the *shel yad* without being glued are entirely valid. This is a remarkably lenient ruling — one that runs counter to what most would intuitively expect.

### Converting Structures

Rabbi Yosi then adds that Rabbi Yehudah would agree with him in the following case: if one lacks a *shel yad* but has two *shel rosh tefillin*, one may take one of the *shel rosh* units, stretch a piece of leather (*or*) over it so that on the outside it appears as a single compartment, and wear it as a *shel yad*. Rabbi Yosi argues that Rabbi Yehudah, having retracted his position on gluing, would accept this as valid. The Gemara objects: but this appears to be precisely the point of their dispute. Rava resolves this: from the very fact that Rabbi Yosi said Rabbi Yehudah would agree, we infer that Rabbi Yehudah in the end retracted his position and agreed that separate parchments in the *shel yad* are acceptable.

This yields a remarkable picture. The *shel rosh*, which is four compartments constructed from one hide, presents four visible divisions on the outside — the *charitzim* are essential. The *shel yad*, which is one compartment, can in practice contain four separate parchments on the inside, as long as the exterior presents the appearance of a single unit. The outside appearance of the *shel rosh* matters greatly; the interior reality of the *shel yad* allows significant flexibility.

### Kedushah Hierarchy

The Gemara now raises a difficulty. Rabbi Chanina transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a *shel yad* may be converted into a *shel rosh*, but a *shel rosh* may not be converted into a *shel yad*. The reason is *ein moridin mikedushah chamurah likedushah kalah* — one does not descend from a higher *kedushah* to a lower one. The *shel rosh* is considered holier: it sits higher on the body, and — more concretely — it bears two-thirds of God's name on the *bayit* itself. The *shin* appears on the box; the *dalet* is formed by the knot; only the *yud* is formed by the knot of the *shel yad*. The *shel rosh* thus carries greater intrinsic sanctity.

But if that is so, how did we just permit converting a *shel rosh* into a *shel yad* by stretching leather over it? The Gemara answers: *lo kashya — ha b'atikta ha b'chadta* — the ruling about conversion applies to old, used *tefillin*, while the permission to stretch leather applies to new *tefillin* that have never yet been used as a *shel rosh*. An unused *shel rosh* has not yet acquired the formal status of *shel rosh*, and so descending from it presents no problem.

### Designation Exception

A further answer applies to those who hold *hazmana milta* — that designation alone, without actual use, confers halachic status. According to that opinion, even unused *tefillin* designated as a *shel rosh* would already carry its status and could not be downgraded. The resolution is that if one stipulated from the very outset (*atin ala me'ikara*) — at the time of making the *tefillin* — that they might be converted or used differently, then the designation was conditional from the start and the *kedushah* of *shel rosh* was never fully conferred.

The *sugya* thus ends with a picture of far greater flexibility in *tefillin* construction than one might have assumed, combined with a strict hierarchy of sanctity once objects have been properly designated and used. We stop here, as the next two lines open the famous debate of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam regarding the order of the *parshiyot* in the *tefillin* — which will be the subject of the next shiur.

---

---

# Menachot 35

## Rashi vs. Rabbeinu Tam

### Kesidran Dispute

One final issue in the *machloket* between Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam concerns the *halacha* of *kesidran* — the requirement that the *parshiyot* be written in sequential order, such that if they are written out of order they cannot be used. The question is: what defines "sequential" according to Rabbeinu Tam? Is it the order in which the *parshiyot* are placed in the *tefillin*, or the order in which they appear in the *Torah*?

### Rabbeinu Tam's Logic

Tosafot cannot imagine that there should be one order for the way you write the *parshiyot* and a different order for the way you place them. Nevertheless — and despite quoting various *gemarot* bearing on the debate — that is precisely how we *pasken* within the position of Rabbeinu Tam.

### Shel Yad Writing

For the *shel rosh*, this presents no great difficulty: you simply write the *parshiyot* in the order in which they appear in the *Torah*, and then place them in their compartments in a different order. The challenge arises with the *shel yad*, where all four *parshiyot* are written on a single *klaf*. Numbered in the order they appear in the *Torah*, they are: *Kadesh* (1), *VeHaya Ki Yeviacha* (2), *Shema* (3), and *VeHaya Im Shamoa* (4). The order in which they are placed in the *tefillin* according to Rabbeinu Tam is 1, 2, 4, 3. Yet *kesidran* requires that they be written 1, 2, 3, 4 — the *Torah* sequence. The practical consequence is striking: when writing *tefillin shel yad* according to Rabbeinu Tam, one must leave a blank space, write the fourth *parsha*, and then go back and fill in the third in the space left open, so that the writing proceeds in *Torah* order even though the placement order differs.

### Tosafot & Pasken

Tosafot finds this deeply unsatisfying and objects to the notion of divergent writing and placement orders. Yet, unusual as it is, this is indeed how we *pasken* within the position of Rabbeinu Tam. The underlying logic of Rabbeinu Tam's entire position — expressed memorably in the *She'eilot u-Teshuvot Min HaShamayim*, which frames the dispute as a debate between God and the angels — seems to be that *Shema* should appear on the outside of the *tefillin*. You do not want to bury *Shema* in the middle; it belongs at the outer position. Nevertheless, the accepted ruling follows Rashi, who holds that the order is simply the order in which the *parshiyot* are written in the *Torah*.

One might ask whether the concept of *kesidran* in the Gemara — described as *hakorei*, "the one who reads" — perhaps refers specifically to the *shel yad*, since the *shel rosh* consists of four separate compartments. For Rashi, reading them out in order would naturally correspond to how they are arranged, whereas for Rabbeinu Tam the tension between writing order and placement order makes the phrase *hakorei* a curious one indeed.

---

## Invalid Reversals

### Hichlif Parshiyot

The Gemara on the last two lines of 34b states: *Amar Yochanan amar Rav: hichlif parshiyoteiha pesulah* — if one reverses the order of the *parshiyot*, the *tefillin* are invalid. The order is not merely a preference; it is *me'akev*. This is also why one cannot fulfill both Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam with a single pair of *tefillin* — wearing the *parshiyot* in one order renders them invalid for the other.

### Gavayeta & Briyata

Abaye then refines this ruling. The invalidity does not apply to every possible reversal: *lo amaran ela gevayata l'vrayta u'vrayta l'gevayata* — the problem arises specifically when an inner compartment (compartment 2 or 3) is placed in an outer position (box 1 or 4), or an outer compartment is placed in an inner position. The concern is the inversion of a compartment's inner or outer designation. But *gevayata l'gevayata u'vrayta l'vrayta* — reversing two inner compartments with each other (2 and 3), or two outer compartments with each other (1 and 4) — *leit lan bah*, that is not a concern. This is, incidentally, what Yigael Yadin found at Qumran: *tefillin* structured according to the Rashi order but with the two inner compartments reversed.

### Rava's Objection

Rava challenges Abaye's position. He argues: *mai shna d'yativ l'vrayta vrayta d'yativ* — why is outer-to-inner problematic? Because *d'hach d'ba'ei l'mechzi avira lo kachzi* — the compartment that needs to be exposed to the air is not being exposed, *v'hai d'lo kaba'ei l'mechzi avira kachzia* — and the one that is not supposed to be exposed is being exposed. Each compartment has a proper orientation. But if that logic holds, Rava continues, then reversing outer-for-outer and inner-for-inner should equally be a problem: *braisa l'vrayta gavizta l'gavizta nami* — these too should be invalid.

### Directional Exposure

The reason, Rava explains, is that *hach d'ba'ei l'mechzi avira d'yamin kachzi avira d'smol* — the compartment that should face the right-hand air is now facing the left-hand air, and the one meant for the left is facing the right. One cannot generalize and say "outer" and "inner" are generic categories. Every position is specific: leftmost outer, rightmost outer, leftmost inner, rightmost inner. Any change from the proper position is a change, and any change is invalid. The conclusion — *ela lo shna*, it makes no difference — is that any reversal, of any kind, renders the *tefillin* invalid.

### Historical Variations

Beyond the theoretical legal framework, this passage likely reflects a reality of actual variation in *tefillin* practice. Abaye is presumably not speaking purely in the abstract; there was evidently a degree of divergence in how *tefillin* were constructed, which also helps explain how Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam could each be pointing to different inherited traditions. Whether some of this variation may also reflect sectarian practices — given how much of the *halachot* of *tefillin* rest on *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* rather than explicit *pesukim* — remains an open and suggestive question.

---

## Titura & Ma'abarta

### Structure Basics

The Gemara states: *d'amar Rav Chananel amar Rav: titura d'tefillin halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* — the *titura* of *tefillin* is a *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*. The *titura* is the square base on which the *bayit* — the cube containing the *parshiyot* — sits. The *ma'abarta* is the extension projecting beyond the *titura* through which the strap passes, functioning like a bridge. Together these two elements form the distinctive bottom structure of the *tefillin*.

### Notching Requirement

The Gemara specifies that the *ma'abarta* must be notched in order to preserve the visual squareness of the *titura*. Without such a notch, the entire bottom would appear rectangular, and one could not simply draw an imaginary line in the mind to distinguish the two sections. A physical separation is required so that the *titura* retains its square identity as a distinct structural element, *nikar* — recognizable as such.

### One Piece Debate

Rashi and Tosafot debate whether the *titura* must be one continuous piece of leather with the *bayit*. The *bayit* is ideally not made from four separate compartments glued together but rather from a single piece of leather with four protrusions. The further question is whether that structure must be continuous with, or separately attached to, the base. Rashi holds that the *titura* must be one piece together with the *bayit*. Tosafot acknowledges that the accepted *minhag* is indeed to make everything from *or echad* — a single piece of leather — including the *ma'abarta*, achieved by cutting and shaping rather than by assembling separate pieces. In different eras, when the technology or materials did not always permit this, practices varied.

### Halacha L'Moshe Mi'Sinai

This point in the Gemara marks the first explicit introduction of the category of *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* in the discussion of *tefillin*. It is striking in retrospect that all the earlier discussion — the order of the *parshiyot*, the logic of inner and outer, the reasoning through *sevara* — did not invoke this designation. Yet now a string of physical structural features are declared *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* in rapid succession. Abaye adds: *ma'abarta d'tefillin halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*. And further: *shin shel tefillin halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* — the *shin* embossed on the outside of the *shel rosh* is likewise *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*.

This raises a broader question about the nature of the designation itself. For people who have studied the laws of *tefillin*, *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* appears constantly — it seems to cover virtually everything. But there is an important distinction at work. Some details are derived from *pesukim*, even if *sevara* is needed to work out the specifics. The four *parshiyot*, for instance, can be anchored in the fact that the *Torah* commands *tefillin* four times and in the *drasha* on the word *totafot* — *tat* (two in one language) plus *pat* (two in another) equals four — yielding four compartments. For items of this kind, we do not say *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* because there is at least a *pasuk* to hang the ruling on, however much *sevara* fills in the gaps. But for elements like the *titura*, the *ma'abarta*, the *shin*, and the squareness — where there is no *pasuk* that can even serve as a starting point — the ruling is simply declared *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*.

There is also something intuitively compelling about why *tefillin* in particular should accumulate so many *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* designations. Unlike an abstract *halacha* such as the definition of *melacha* on *Shabbat*, where *Torah she-ba-al Peh* develops interpretive categories through a creative process, *tefillin* describes a specific physical object. If the *Torah* commands you to bind something as a sign on your arm and between your eyes, it almost certainly had a specific physical referent in mind. The Rambam makes a similar point regarding the *arbaah minim*: the *pesukim* that discuss *peri etz hadar* were always accompanied by a *mesorah* identifying exactly which fruit was meant, and the derivations were at most *ex post facto* confirmation of an already-transmitted tradition. The same intuition applies to *tefillin*: the physical object the *Torah* described was always known, transmitted from father to son through the actual craft of making *tefillin*, and the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* label captures that the specific physical details were never up for interpretive debate.

---

## Compartment Furrow

### Furrow to Base

The Gemara continues with the requirement: *v'tzarikh sheyagiya kharitz limkom hatefer* — the *charitz*, the furrow between the compartments of the *shel rosh*, must reach the place of sewing. There are two ways to understand this. One reading is that the tip of the *shin* must reach down to the actual base, to the place where the *bayit* contacts the *titura* and is sewn or threaded. The other reading — and likely the more straightforward one — takes *charitz* literally as the furrow running between each compartment. The *shel rosh* is made from a single piece of leather shaped into four distinct protrusions, separated by these furrows. The requirement is that those furrows extend all the way down to the base of the *titura*, ensuring that the compartments are truly and fully separated — not merely indicated at the top but continuous as genuine individual chambers all the way to the foundation.

This must be understood in context of how *tefillin* are actually constructed. The *bayit* is essentially formed like a glove from within, with the compartments pushed up and the furrows pressed down between them. The resulting structure, viewed from the outside, shows only slight visible lines between compartments; the depth of those furrows is an internal structural matter. Nevertheless, Abaye rules that genuine separation must be achieved all the way to the *titura* itself. The compartments must also have some visible separation at the top — they must be visibly distinct — but full structural separation reaching to the base is required.

### Visual Separation

Rav Dimi of Nardea disagrees: *keivan de-minchar lo tzarich* — once it is evident that they are separate compartments, nothing further is required. Even if the furrow does not penetrate all the way to the base, as long as the compartments appear sufficiently separate at the top, the *tefillin* are valid. On this view, the practical construction of *tefillin* — in which the furrows are pressed down but may not fully reach the very bottom — is adequate, provided the separateness of the compartments is visually recognizable.

---

## Klaf Inspection

### Pre-writing Check

Abaye states: *hai klapha de-tefillin tzarich le-mivdakei de-dilma is bei re'usa* — the *klaf* for *tefillin* must be checked before writing, lest there be a tiny flaw. If a scribe writes a letter and a small hole happens to fall adjacent to it, the letter will not be *mukaf gvil* — fully surrounded by parchment on all sides — and the writing will be invalid.

The stakes here are particularly high because of the requirement of *kesidran*. If one *parsha* is found to be *pasul*, all four *parshiyot* must effectively be redone. Each *parsha* must be written *kasidran* relative to those before and after it in sequence. If, say, *parsha* number 3 of the *shel rosh* is defective, a replacement can only be used if it was written after *parsha* 2 and before *parsha* 4 of that same *tefillin* — a condition that is practically almost impossible to satisfy after the fact. For this reason the Gemara requires: *u-be'inan ketivah tama* — we need a perfect, complete writing — *mukaf gvil*, and a pre-inspection of the *klaf* is the means to secure that.

The point extends to the broader question of why the order of writing matters as opposed to merely the order of placement. Just as one would not regard *tefillin* written in reverse sequence as valid simply because the physical end product looks correct, so too the integrity of the *klaf* itself must be confirmed in advance, because any flaw discovered later triggers the *kesidran* problem in full.

### Quill Detection

Rav Dimi of Nardea offers an alternative: *lo tzarich; kulmosa badik leh* — no prior inspection is needed, because the quill itself will detect any imperfection. As the scribe writes, if the quill encounters a bump or inconsistency in the surface of the *klaf*, he will feel it and know to stop. Pre-inspection is therefore unnecessary according to this view, as the writing process itself provides a built-in form of detection.

---

## Black Straps Halacha

### Black = HLM

Rav Yitzchak states: *retzu'os shechoros halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* — black *retzuot* are a *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*. This is immediately challenged.

### Color Permissibility

A *baraisa* is cited: *tefillin ein koshrin oso ela be-mino* — the *keshira* of *tefillin* may only be done with something of their own kind, meaning the straps must be leather. But as to color — *bein yerokos bein shechoros bein levanos* — whether green, black, or white, any color is acceptable, as long as the material is leather. One exception is stated explicitly: *adumos lo ya'aseh* — do not make red straps. Two reasons are given: *mipnei gnai ve-davar acher* — because it is unseemly and because of something else left unspoken. Rashi explains the *gnai*: red straps might lead observers to think the *tefillin* rubbed against scabs and became bloodied, which is repulsive in appearance. As for the *davar acher*, Rashi suggests — admittedly fancifully — that people might assume the red came from contact with a *niddah* during a prohibited intimacy. These are the explanations Rashi offers, however far-fetched they may seem.

### Blue Strings Story

Rabbi Yehuda continues with a story: *maaseh b'talmido shel Rabbi Akiva she'haya kosher tefillav b'lashon shel techeiles* — there was an incident involving a student of Rabbi Akiva who would tie his *tefillin* not with leather straps but with blue strings. This is remarkable: we take the leather strap as so foundational to *tefillin* that it barely seems worth mentioning, yet here is a student of one of the greatest *Tannaim* using something else entirely.

*V'lo amar lo davar* — and Rabbi Akiva said nothing. An anonymous voice in the *baraisa* challenges this: *efshar oso tzaddik ra'ah talmido v'lo micha bo?* — is it possible that such a *tzaddik* saw his student doing this and did not protest? Rabbi Yehuda — or perhaps Rabbi Yehuda responding to that challenge — replies: *hein, lo ra'ahu* — yes, you are right, he did not actually see him doing it. *V'im ra'ahu, lo haya manicho* — had he seen it, he would not have permitted it.

### Red Strings Story

A parallel case follows: *maaseh b'Hurkenos beno shel Rabbi Eliezer ben Hurkenos she'haya kosher tefillav b'lashon shel argaman* — Hurkenos the son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hurkenos would tie his *tefillin* with *argaman*, purple-red strings. Again, *v'lo amar lo davar* — his father said nothing. Again the challenge: *efshar oso tzaddik ra'ah beno v'lo micha bo?* — could such a righteous man see his own son doing this and not object?
