And again the reply: *lo ra'ahu* — he did not see it; *v'im ra'ahu, lo haya manicho* — had he seen it, he would not have permitted it.

What is striking about these two stories is not the legal resolution — which is clear, that leather is required — but what they imply about historical practice. The Gemara is not denying that these things actually happened. The only question is whether the great *Tannaim* in question were aware. Presumably they were not, or they would have intervened. But the stories suggest that divergent practices regarding *tefillin* straps were genuinely occurring. One possible explanation for why the fathers did not notice: if blue and purple could plausibly be mistaken for leather straps in certain light, perhaps they saw the *tefillin* from a distance and assumed the straps were simply dark-colored leather.

One might further ask whether some of this variation reflects sectarian practices — particularly given how much of *tefillin* law rests on *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* rather than explicit *pesukim*. Karaites and others who diverged from rabbinic *tefillin* traditions come to mind. The phrase *efshar oso tzaddik ra'ah v'lo micha bo* carries an urgency that seems to go beyond a simple halachic slip, as though something of greater religious consequence is at stake. This remains speculative, but the *gemara* is suggestive in this regard.

### Inner/Outer Color

Having established that the *baraisa* permits multiple colors, the Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction with Rav Yitzchak's statement: *lo kashya; kan mibifnim kan mibachutz* — there is no difficulty. The requirement of black applies to the outer surface of the strap — the side facing away from the body. The inner surface, which rests against the skin, may be any color. This resolution also provides context for why red is specifically prohibited: although one might think that the *gnai* applies only to the inner side (since only there could blood from scabs accumulate), the Gemara notes that *zimnin d'mithapchan leh* — sometimes the strap turns around. Anyone who has worn a *shel rosh* knows that this happens. Therefore red is prohibited even on the inner side, because it may become exposed.

### Black Box Mitzva

The question naturally arises: if black *retzuot* are *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*, surely the *bayit* itself must equally require black? In fact, the *Shulchan Aruch* treats these two requirements differently. Regarding the *retzuot*, it states explicitly that they must be black on the outside as a *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*. But regarding the *batim* themselves, the *Shulchan Aruch* formulates it differently: *or habatim mitzvah la'asoto shachor* — it is a *mitzvah* to make the *bayit* black. Not *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*, but *mitzvah*. And the *Mishnah Berurah* notes: *mashma d'bedi'eved eino me'akev* — this implies that after the fact, black *batim* are not strictly indispensable. For those who wear *tefillin* daily and assume every detail is equally *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*, this is a genuinely surprising ruling.

### White Boxes

Tosafot drives the point home explicitly: *yesh she'osim batim shel tefillin miklaf lavan velo ba'ei shachrut ela retzuot* — there were those who made the *batim* of *tefillin* from white *klaf* and required black only for the *retzuot*. This was not a fringe or uninformed position; it reflects the halachic logic that only the *retzuot* are subject to the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* of black coloring.

The practical consequence is worth noting: because the black of the *retzuot* is *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*, if the outer surface of a strap becomes worn and loses its black color, it must be corrected immediately. The *bayit*, being only a *mitzvah* rather than *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*, affords somewhat more latitude. As a practical matter, the blackening of *tefillin* can be accomplished with ordinary black paint available at any *tefillin* store — or even, in a pinch, with a permanent marker, though one should be mindful that any substance used ideally have *hazmana* for the *mitzvah*, and there is the additional question of whether the dye or ink must be made from kosher materials.

---

## Squareness Requirement

### Square HLM

The Gemara cites a *baraisa*: *tefillin meruba'ot halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* — the squareness of *tefillin* is a *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*. This applies to the *bayit*, the cube itself.

### Diagonal Measurement

Rav Papa refines this: *bitfuran u'be'alchsonan* — squareness is required both in their sewing and in their diagonal. These are two distinct requirements. The sewing requirement means that when the *tefillin* is stitched shut — and we have seen from the pictures that both the compartments and the base involve substantial threading and stitching — the process of sewing must not stretch or distort the shape away from the square. The stitches must be worked carefully so that the tension they create does not pull the *bayit* out of square.

The second requirement — *alchsonan*, the diagonal — refers to how squareness is measured and verified. Rather than simply measuring two adjacent sides and confirming they are equal, squareness is determined by checking the diagonal.

### Math of Diagonal

The Gemara employs the well-known approximation that the diagonal of a unit square is 1.4 — a rough rounding of the square root of 2 (which is 1.414...). This approximation appears in various places in the Talmud and is considerably more accurate than the Talmudic approximation of *pi*. The significance of measuring by diagonal is that it provides a practical standard for what counts as "square enough." Rather than requiring a geometrically perfect square — which would demand measuring side lengths to an impossibly fine degree of precision — the standard is that if the diagonal of the *tefillin* measures approximately 1.4 times the side, it satisfies the requirement. This becomes an important model for understanding *halachic* tolerance more broadly: *lo nitna torah lemalachei hasharet*, and squareness in this context means "square within a defined margin of error," with the diagonal serving as the operational test for that margin.

### Circular Danger

The Gemara attempts to bring a proof that squareness is required: *ha'oseh tefillato agula sakana ve'ein bah mitzvah* — one who makes his *tefillin* circular (or more precisely, spherical) faces a danger and has performed no *mitzvah*. The danger is geometrical: a sphere rests on a point. Whereas a flat-bottomed *bayit* distributes pressure across its surface, a spherical *tefillin* placed on the head creates a concentrated point of contact. If one were to walk into a wall or a doorframe — and this is not entirely hypothetical for anyone who has worn a *shel rosh* while navigating tight spaces — a spherical *tefillin* would drive that point into the skull rather than distributing the impact. Hence the *sakana*. The absence of *mitzvah* follows from the lack of squareness. The *gemara* therefore appears to demonstrate that squareness is a genuine requirement.

### Papa's Objection

Rav Papa objects: *matnitin de'avida ke'egoz* — the *baraisa* is speaking of a nut-shaped *tefillin*, i.e., something ellipsoidal or ovoid that truly comes to a sharp point. That shape creates an acute danger precisely because of its pointed geometry. But one cannot conclude from this that *any* non-square shape is unacceptable. There might be other shapes — not square, but also not nut-shaped — that pose no danger and might still satisfy some form of the requirement. The proof from circular *tefillin* therefore does not conclusively establish that squareness is strictly required beyond the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* declaration.

This exchange is characteristic of a broader pattern in this section of the Gemara: things that seem intuitively obvious and beyond dispute — the squareness of *tefillin*, the blackness of the *batim* — turn out upon examination to be more nuanced, and the Gemara itself questions whether proofs establish what they appear to establish. One might also note that the requirement as stated — *meruba'ot* — could refer to being square in cross-section, but whether this entails that the *tefillin* must also be a perfect cube (height equal to width equal to depth) is a separate question not fully resolved here.

---

## Wall Integrity

### Outer Face Test

The Gemara turns to the internal structural integrity of the *shel rosh*. Rav Huna rules: *tefillin kol zman she'pnei tavla kayemes kesheira* — *tefillin* are valid as long as the outer face remains intact. Even if the inner partition walls between the compartments develop holes or breaks, as long as the exterior surface of the *bayit* is undamaged, the *tefillin* remain *kasher*.

### Three Walls Rule

Rav Chisda qualifies this. The *shel rosh* has four compartments separated by three internal walls. Rav Chisda rules that if up to two of those inner walls are broken, the *tefillin* remain valid. But if all three inner walls are broken — *shalosh pesulah* — it is invalid. The logic is straightforward: if all three walls are gone, there are no longer four compartments. The whole structure collapses into a single *bayit*, and the fundamental requirement of four distinct compartments is lost.

### Opposite Holes

Rava further refines Rav Chisda's ruling. Even where only two walls are broken and the *tefillin* would otherwise be *kasher*, this leniency applies only when the breaks are *zeh shelo keneged zeh* — not directly opposite one another. Imagine the four compartments arranged in a row with three walls between them. If wall 1 (between compartments 1 and 2) has a hole, and wall 2 (between compartments 2 and 3) has a hole, but those holes are at different heights — one high, one low — then compartment 2 is not fully compromised, because neither hole alone traverses it completely. But if the hole in wall 1 and the hole in wall 2 are directly opposite one another — *zeh keneged zeh* — then effectively compartment 2 has no wall on either side at that point, and the structural separation is lost. In that case, *pesulah*. Rashi offers an alternative reading of *zeh keneged zeh*: if the holes are at the same location within their respective walls — both near the bottom, or both near the top — as opposed to one at the top and one at the bottom. Either way, the principle is that the position of the holes matters, not just their number.

One might also ask: does the size of the hole matter? A pinhole and a gaping break are presumably not equivalent. This too is an open question bearing on when a hole is sufficient to be considered a structural breach.

### New vs. Old

The Gemara adds a further qualification: *ela be'chadta* — this entire discussion of opposite holes causing *pesul* applies specifically to new *tefillin*. For old *tefillin* — *be'atika leit lan bah* — we do not apply these concerns.

The analogy offered is that of a new car: the smallest scratch on a brand-new vehicle is conspicuous and significant, whereas the same scratch on a car owned for years barely registers. But the Gemara's point here has an additional dimension: with new *tefillin*, holes that appear in the leather signal poor quality material. If *tefillin* are newly made and the leather is already cracking or perforating, this is an indictment of the quality of the leather itself — comparable to discovering a serious defect in a product shortly after purchase — and that in turn calls into question the validity of the entire item. With old *tefillin*, wear and minor damage are expected, and isolated holes do not carry the same implications.

### Elasticity Test

Abaye asks Rav Yosef: *heichi dami chadta ve'heichi dami atika?* — what exactly defines "new" and "old" in this context? Rav Yosef replies: *kol heicha de'ki matu lei be'shicha ve'hadar chalim atika* — if you stretch the leather and it recovers, pulling back to its original shape, it is classified as old. *Ve'idach chadta* — and the other kind is new. The logic is that leather which has been worn and used over time has already been stretched and conformed to shape; it has reached a stable equilibrium. If you pull it, it does not take a new shape but returns to what it was. Fresh, new leather, by contrast, has not yet been worked in; stretching it will deform it and it will not simply spring back. This elasticity — or lack thereof — serves as the practical diagnostic for determining whether *tefillin* are to be treated as new or old for purposes of the wall-integrity *halacha*.

A variant formulation is also cited: *kol heicha de'ki matu lei be'masna asya basra chadta* — if when you pull the leather it stretches along with you, following the pull and taking a new shape, that is new leather. *Ve'idach atika* — and the other, which does not follow the stretch but returns, is old. Rashi's several readings of this passage converge on the same underlying principle: new leather is deformable under stress, while old leather has settled and resists deformation.

---

---

# Menachot 35b

## Broken Strap & Tashmishe…

### Knot vs. Sewing

The daf opens with a scene involving Abaye and Rav Yosef. Abaye was seated before Rav Yosef when his *retzuah* broke. He asked Rav Yosef: may he repair it by knotting the two broken halves together? Rav Yosef replied with a verse: *ukshartem* — "you shall bind" — which carries the implication of *she-tehei keshira tama*, that the binding must be whole and unbroken. A strap repaired with an additional knot does not meet that standard, and therefore one may not fix a broken *retzuah* by knotting the broken halves.

### Interior Stitching

Rav Acha, son of Rav Yosef, then posed a related question to Rav Ashi: rather than knotting, what if one were to sew the break, placing the stitches on the inside of the strap so that they would be invisible from the outside? This would constitute a far more complete repair aesthetically and structurally.

### Puk Chazi Principle

Rav Ashi replied with the principle *puk chazi mai ama devar* — go out and see what the people do. Rashi understands this to mean that since people do not do this, it must be forbidden. Tosafot, by contrast, reads this principle as operating in the direction of leniency, since it is typically invoked to permit something based on widespread practice. Tosafot therefore concludes that since people do sew straps in this manner, it is permitted.

Tosafot's reading reflects his general assumption that *puk chazi mai ama devar* is a *kula* formulation. One might ask, however, whether the principle is even applicable in a situation that rarely arises in practice — if it never occurs, there is no observable custom to invoke in either direction. Rashi's position is similarly complicated: if the reason nobody does it is simply that the situation never arises, the absence of practice cannot serve as evidence of prohibition. It is worth noting as well that these discussions apply most acutely to thin straps that might tear easily; the thick leather used today makes such breaks far less common.

### Two Categories

The *gemara* now introduces a structural principle that has broad halakhic significance. Rav Papa states that *gardumei retzuot kesherot* — remnants of tefillin straps remain valid. The concept of *gardumim* assumes that there is a requisite minimum length to begin with, but if the strap started at the right length and subsequently broke or tore, leaving a shorter remnant, it is still acceptable — analogous to the rule regarding *tzitzit*, where a string that began at the proper length and later tore may still be used.

However, the *gemara* rejects Rav Papa's position. It invokes the teaching of the sons of Rabbi Chiyya that *gardumei techelet* and *gardumei ezov* are valid — the remnant of a *tzitzit* string or a hyssop bundle used for *Parah Adumah* or the purification of a *metzora* remains acceptable even if it has been reduced. But the *gemara* draws a distinction: *hatam hu detashmishei mitzvah ninhu* — those cases involve objects that are categorized as *tashmishei mitzvah*, things that serve a *mitzvah*, whereas *aval hacha detashmishei kedusha ninhu lo* — here, where tefillin straps are categorized as *tashmishei kedusha*, the lenient rule of *gardumim* does not apply.

This introduces a fundamental distinction between two categories of *mitzvah*-related objects. *Tashmishei mitzvah* are what we might call *mitzvah* objects — a *lulav*, a *shofar*, *tzitzit* strings — items that serve the performance of a *mitzvah* but do not possess intrinsic *kedusha*. Their significance derives from their use in the *mitzvah*, and once that use is complete, they are no longer governed by strict rules of sanctity. One may not discard them disrespectfully, and ideally one repurposes them for another *mitzvah* — using a *lulav* for fuel when burning *chametz*, for example — but there is no ongoing, inherent sanctity.

*Tashmishei kedusha*, by contrast, are objects associated with *kisei hakodesh* or, more specifically, with *shem Hashem*. Their sanctity is not contingent on their current use; it is intrinsic. That is why they require *sheimes* — storage in a geniza — once they can no longer be used, whereas one would never place a *lulav* in *sheimes*. Tefillin straps are *tashmishei kedusha* because they serve the *klafim*, the parchments inside the batim. And since they are *tashmishei kedusha*, a higher standard of completeness is demanded — the full length of the *retzuah* is required, and a mere *gardum* is not sufficient.

### Tefillin Status

The *gemara*'s application of this distinction here is, admittedly, not entirely intuitive. The question of whether *gardumim* suffice is, at its core, a question about *yetziat yedei mitzvah* — whether one fulfills the *mitzvah* of tefillin — which would seem to address tefillin in their dimension as *tashmishei mitzvah*, not as *tashmishei kedusha*. Why should the category of *tashmishei kedusha* determine whether a broken strap is still *kasher* for the *mitzvah*?

One way to understand the *gemara*'s reasoning is that the concept of *tashmishei kedusha* creates a heightened sense of belonging: the strap belongs to the tefillin in a stronger way than a *lulav* leaf belongs to the *lulav*. When something breaks off a *tashmishei mitzvah* object, it simply ceases to be part of it. But for a *tashmishei kedusha* object, the severed piece retains a stronger conceptual attachment, and the loss of that portion is correspondingly more significant. Under this reading, *gardumim* are problematic not because of a formal rule about length, but because the strap's sanctity demands wholeness. The *gemara*'s conclusion, in any case, is clear: for tefillin, *gardumim* are not acceptable, and the full minimum length of the *retzuah* is required.

It should be noted that tefillin are in fact both *tashmishei mitzvah* and *tashmishei kedusha* simultaneously — they are *mitzvah* objects in their own right, and they also serve the sacred *klafim* inside. This dual status will be relevant to subsequent discussions, including the question raised by Tosafot regarding the *bayit* of the *shel rosh* and its *shin*, which may occupy yet a third, higher level — closer to *kedusha* itself.

---

## Strap Length Requirements

### Minimum Shiur

The *gemara* draws an inference from the discussion of *gardumim*: since the entire topic presupposes that the strap began at a required length, it follows that there is indeed a minimum *shiur* — a minimum length — for the *retzuah*. The *gemara* then asks: what is that minimum?

### Finger Length Measure

Rabbi Bar Chama in the name of Resh Lakish answers: *ad etzba tzerada* — until the snapping finger. Rashi identifies *etzba tzerada* as the forefinger, while Tosafot objects that one does not snap with the forefinger and identifies it instead as the middle finger.

### Bent vs. Straight

Two Amoraim demonstrate different configurations. Rav Kahana demonstrated the measurement in a *kaphuf* position — bent — while Rav Ashi demonstrated it in a *pashut* position — straightened out.

### Two Interpretations

There are two distinct ways of understanding this measurement. The first explanation, accepted by both Rashi and Tosafot (though they debate which finger is intended), is that *ad etzba tzerada* refers simply to a unit of length — the span between the thumb and the forefinger according to Rashi, or the thumb and the middle finger according to Tosafot. On this reading, *kaphuf* means the finger is fully spread, yielding a longer measurement, while *pashut* means not fully spread, yielding roughly half that length. The *gemara* on this reading is discussing how long the strap must extend below the knot of the *shel rosh* or past the fastening on the arm.

The second explanation — which is how we rule in practice — is that the *gemara* is discussing the *shel yad*, and the requirement is that the strap reach from the fastening point all the way to the middle finger. On this reading, the debate between *kaphuf* and *pashut* concerns whether the finger is bent downward, so that reaching the palm suffices, or extended, so that the strap must reach out to the fingertip. Our practice follows the extended reading: the strap must be long enough to wrap and ultimately reach the middle finger. The familiar custom of making seven wraps on the arm is not a formal *halacha* requirement in itself, but the length of strap needed for that is a practical expression of the *shiur*.

### Shel Rosh Length

If the *gemara* is indeed discussing the *shel yad*, it leaves open the question of how long the *shel rosh* straps must be. The *Shulchan Aruch* is not particularly explicit on this point. Tosafot, in the discussion beginning with *puk chazi*, cites the *Shimusha Rabba* — a Geonic work frequently cited in *hilchos tefillin* that appears to have been an authoritative handbook on the subject — which provides the following: one strap of the *shel rosh* must reach down to the point of *mila*, i.e., below the waist, on the right side, and the other must reach to the heart on the left. Tosafot elsewhere also cites an opinion that the right strap need only reach approximately to the navel.

### Directional Requirements

The directional requirements — right side toward *mila*, left side toward the heart — derive from the *Shimusha Rabba* and reflect the practical concern about strap length when tefillin is actually worn. This distinction becomes practically significant in situations where the *retzuah* breaks or where the black coloring wears off, since only the portion of the strap within the minimum *shiur* must meet these standards. Beyond the *shiur*, the strap is not subject to the same requirements.

### Strap Width

Tosafot also records a tradition regarding the width of the straps: ideally they should be wider than a grain of wheat but narrower than a grain of barley — *yoser mi-chita u-fachos mi-se'ora*. If the strap is wider, it remains acceptable. Our straps are considerably wider than this, which the sources indicate is not a problem.

A notable feature of this entire discussion is that the *gemara* itself is not explicit about whether it is addressing the *shel yad* or the *shel rosh*, and much of what governs our practice in this area derives not from the *gemara* directly but from works like the *Shimusha Rabba*. This also illuminates the broader question — discussed at length in the context of Rashi's and Rabbeinu Tam's tefillin — of how halakhic practice in areas where the *gemara* is sparse was shaped by these written handbooks. The Rambam in a famous *teshuva* describes having worn tefillin according to the order of *havayot b'emtza* — the Rabbeinu Tam arrangement — while living in Spain, influenced by a work on tefillin laws by a Rav Moshe of Cordoba. He writes: *oso chibur hu shehatani v'heta kol anshei hamaarav milfanai* — it was that work that misled me and led astray all the people of the West. He was ultimately moved to abandon that position by consulting older manuscripts, finding that Rav Hai Gaon's own tefillin followed the arrangement he now maintained, and by a version of the *gemara* that explicitly listed the *parshiyos* in their Torah order: *Kadesh Li*, *V'haya Ki Yeviacha*, *Shema*, *V'haya Im Shamoa*. He notes that this version of the *gemara* was not found in the manuscripts in Spain, but that he found it in all the older manuscripts he subsequently consulted — and that the tradition of *Eretz Yisrael*, where people were more exacting about tefillin, supported the same arrangement. The power of a written code to shape practice — and the role of manuscript evidence in reshaping it — is vividly illustrated by this episode.

---

## Strap Placement Customs

### Raba's Method

The *gemara* records several practices regarding what one does with the hanging straps of the *shel rosh* after tying. Raba would tie his tefillin and then fling the straps behind his back.

### Rav Acha's Method

Rav Acha bar Yaakov, by contrast, would hang the straps in front of him after tying.

### Current Practice

Mar brei deRavina followed the practice common in his time, which Rashi identifies as hanging the straps in front. What is notable about this *sugya* is that what one might assume to be a settled and straightforward halakhic requirement — that the straps hang in front — is here presented simply as varying practice among Amoraim, without any of these options being characterized as definitively wrong. That the straps should fall in front has a certain naturalness to it as a requirement, but equally, there is something natural about a headdress flowing behind. The *gemara* leaves the matter as one of custom.

---

## The Kesher Knot

### Halacha LeMoshe

Rav Yehuda son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav states that the *kesher shel tefillin* — the knot of tefillin — is *halacha leMoshe miSinai*. The form of the knot is thus rooted in the oldest and most authoritative source in *halacha*.

### Rashi's View

Rashi explains that what was transmitted as *halacha leMoshe miSinai* is specifically this: the knot of the *shel rosh* is shaped like a *dalet*, and the knot of the *shel yad* is shaped like a *yud*, and together with the *shin* on the *bayit* of the *shel rosh*, they spell the divine name *Shakai*. This shaping of the knots to form letters of *shem Hashem* is, in Rashi's view, the substance of what was transmitted from Sinai.

### Tosafot's Objection

Tosafot questions this. The concern is whether the *retzuot* shaped into a *dalet* and a *yud* actually constitute letters of *shem Hashem* in any meaningful halakhic sense. This is not merely an aesthetic objection; it has structural implications. Tosafot points out that if the knots truly formed *shem Hashem*, then the tefillin would not merely be *tashmishei kedusha* — objects serving the sacred *klafim* — they would themselves be in the category of *kedusha atzmo*, actual sanctity comparable to *kisei hakodesh*, objects upon which *shem Hashem* is literally written. Since the halakhic classification of tefillin is *tashmishei kedusha* rather than that higher category, Tosafot is reluctant to affirm that these formed letters constitute a genuine *shem Hashem*. Whatever the substance of the *halacha leMoshe miSinai* is, it establishes that there must be a *kesher* and governs certain features of how it appears — but Tosafot does not concede that it rises to the level of *shem Hashem* inscribed on the tefillin itself.

There is also a significant *machlokes* regarding the form of the *dalet* on the back of the head — whether the standard form suffices or whether one uses what is called a double *dalet*, a square shape formed by two *dalet*s joined together. The double *dalet* has limited basis in *halacha* and is more characteristic of certain Chassidic custom. The underlying question — which precise features of the *kesher* are the substance of the *halacha leMoshe miSinai* and which are later elaboration — remains unresolved.

---

## Black Exterior

### Black Outward

Rav Nachman rules that the attractive side of the strap — which means the black side — must face outward. This is a formal requirement, not merely aesthetic guidance.

### Inverted Strap

Rav Ashi was seated before Mar Zutra when his *retzuah* flipped, exposing the inside. Mar Zutra pointed out to him: do you not hold that the attractive side must face outward? Rav Ashi replied that he had simply not been paying attention. The incident illustrates how easily the strap can become inverted, particularly on the *shel rosh* where the straps are more exposed to movement.

### Bathroom Concerns

Tosafot raises a question attributed to the Rebbe Yaakov of Orleans regarding entry into the bathroom: is it necessary to remove the *shel yad* before entering *beit hakisei*? His reasoning in favor of possibly permitting it is that the parchment — which is the true object of concern — is covered by the leather of the *bayit*, and it is the parchment that one may not bring into the bathroom. *Tashmishei mitzvah* objects such as *tzitzit* may be brought into the bathroom without restriction; one does so routinely every time one enters while wearing a *tallit katan*. The question is whether the same latitude applies to the *shel yad* whose *klafim* are covered.

The reason the *shel rosh* poses a different problem is, Tosafot suggests, *shekashur shin ba-or* — the *shin* is bound into the leather of the *bayit* itself. The *shin* on the *shel rosh* may give the *bayit* a status approaching *kedusha* in its own right — not merely *tashmishei kedusha* as a vessel serving the *klafim*, but something closer to an object bearing *shem Hashem* directly. Even Tosafot, who elsewhere is cautious about calling the formed knots genuine letters of *shem Hashem*, acknowledges here that at minimum the *shin* lends a degree of sacred weight to the *shel rosh* that the *shel yad* does not possess in the same way.

This analysis reveals the layered structure of tefillin's sanctity. The *klafim* inside are *kisei hakodesh* in the fullest sense. The tefillin themselves — *shel yad* and *shel rosh* — are *tashmishei kedusha* because they house those *klafim*, and simultaneously *tashmishei mitzvah* because the *mitzvah* is performed through them. The *shel rosh* may occupy an intermediate zone above ordinary *tashmishei kedusha* by virtue of its *shin*. The case or cover of the tefillin — analogous to the mantle of a *Sefer Torah* — would be *tashmish detashmish*, serving the tefillin that serve the *klafim*, and thus further removed.

---

## The Kesher Knot (II)

### God's Tefillin

The *gemara* cites a *baraisa*: Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol interprets the verse in which God says to Moshe *va-hasirosai et kapi ve-ra'ita et achorai* — "I will remove my hand and you shall see my back" — as referring to what Moshe was shown. Rav Hana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida teaches: this means that the Holy One showed Moshe the *kesher shel tefillin* — God's own tefillin knot — because God, as the *gemara* in Berakhot establishes, wears tefillin. The back of God's head is where one sees the *kesher*. The *gemara* is not incidentally noting the geography of the scene; there is clearly something significant about the *kesher shel tefillin* specifically being what Moshe is granted to see, though the full depth of that meaning is not elaborated here.

### Kesher Position

Rav Yehuda rules that the *kesher shel tefillin* must be *lemala* — above — meaning positioned high at the back of the head, not low toward the neck or below the hairline. In practice, the *kesher* is placed where one can feel the base of the skull before the slight depression at the nape — high, not low.

### Symbolic Meaning

The reason given is *kedei she-yisrael yehei lemala ve-lo lemata* — so that Israel should be above and not below. This is a striking *drash*: the positioning of a physical knot is made to carry a statement about the standing of the Jewish people. Whether this is a purely symbolic teaching or a formal halakhic requirement with consequences for the validity of the tefillin is left unclear. 

The statement connects meaningfully, however, to the content of God's own tefillin as described in Berakhot: *mi ke-amcha Yisrael goy echad ba-aretz* — who is like Your people Israel, a unique nation on earth. Just as our tefillin express the elevation of God in our consciousness, God's tefillin express His relationship with Israel. The *kesher* positioned *lemala* — with Israel above — is thus in direct dialogue with the theme of God's own *tefillin* and with the vision Moshe was granted: the very back of God's head, where the *kesher shel tefillin* sits, was what he was privileged to see. As Rambam explains regarding this passage, seeing God's "back" means perceiving God's ways in the world — the echo of the divine presence as it operates in history — rather than God's essence directly. If God's tefillin proclaim *mi ke-amcha Yisrael*, then perhaps the *kesher shel tefillin* that Moshe saw was a vision of how God's relationship with Israel is, so to speak, bound into creation.

### Shin Design

Regarding the *shin* on the *shel rosh*: the *gemara* itself mentions only the *shin* without specifying its form. Tosafot, citing the *Shimusha Rabba*, records the practice of placing a three-armed *shin* on one side of the *bayit* and a four-armed *shin* on the other — a practice we follow today, even though it is not found in the *gemara* itself but in this Geonic work. Some have suggested that the four-armed *shin* alludes to the four *parshiyos* within the tefillin. Others note that the negative space within a four-armed *shin* contains the mirror image of a three-armed *shin*, and that this inversion has significance: the white space and the black, the letters formed by absence and by presence, reflect a deeper visual theology of *esh shechora al gabei esh levana* — black fire upon white fire — which is how the Torah is described in its primordial form.

The placement of the *shin* facing outward is also connected to the broader requirement that the straps face properly. The verse cited is *ve-tzarich she-yisyimu ke-lapei panim* — they must face forward — so that Israel should be *lifnim* and not *le-achor*. Rashi understands this to mean that the black must face outward and the white remain inward, and that this orientation must be maintained.

---

## When to Bless

### Time of Placement

The *gemara* asks: when does one make the *beracha* on tefillin? The initial answer is *mi-sha'as hanachasam* — from the moment one places them on.

### Placement to Tightening

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: the rule of *kol ha-mitzvos kulam mevarech aleihen over la-asiyasan* requires that a *beracha* be recited before the act, not after it has been completed. *Mi-sha'as hanachasam* sounds as though the tefillin have already been placed, making the *beracha* retrospective. Abaye and Rava resolve this: the *beracha* is recited from the moment of placing, meaning between the initial placement of the tefillin on one's body and the final *keshira* — the tightening that completes the act. One places the *shel yad*, recites the *beracha*, and then tightens; then places the *shel rosh*, recites the *beracha*, and then tightens. The *beracha* is thus made *over la-asiya* — preceding the completion of the act.

### Literal Knot Making

Tosafot finds a remarkable implication in the phrase *ad she'as keshira*. Citing Rabbeinu Eliyahu, Tosafot suggests that *keshira* here should be taken literally: one must actually make the knot each day — not merely tighten an existing one, but insert the strap, form the loop, and complete the full act of knotting. Tosafot notes that this probably applies to the *shel yad* rather than the *shel rosh*, whose knot is more elaborate. The supporting verse is *uk'shartam le-os al yadecha* — you shall bind — which Tosafot reads as mandating an active, daily act of binding, not merely the static wearing of tefillin already knotted.

Tosafot himself then hedges, acknowledging that *keshira* in this context may simply mean tightening — *lav davka keshira* — and that the plain sense of *uk'shartam* is the act of attaching the tefillin to one's arm, which one does by tightening, not necessarily by constructing the knot from scratch. Yet the interest of the position lies in how it foregrounds the active verbal dimension of the *mitzvah* — *uk'shartam*, you shall bind — as against the static dimension of *ve-hayu*, they shall be. One might observe that if Rabbeinu Eliyahu's position were correct, the natural *nusach* of the *beracha* would be *le-kashair tefillin* rather than *le-haniach tefillin*, a consideration that presents a real challenge to that reading.

---

## One or Two Blessings

### Speech Requires New Bles…

Rav Chisda rules: *sach bein tefillah le-tefillah chozer mevarech* — if one spoke between the *shel yad* and the *shel rosh*, one must return and make another *beracha* on the *shel rosh*. Implicitly, if one did not speak, a second *beracha* is not necessary.

### Yochanan's Nusach

A letter sent in the name of Rabbi Yochanan from *Eretz Yisrael* reports a different *nusach* for the two *berachos*: on the *shel yad* one says *baruch asher kideshanu be-mitzvosav ve-tzivanu le-haniach tefillin*, and on the *shel rosh* one says *baruch asher kideshanu be-mitzvosav ve-tzivanu al mitzvas tefillin*. The two formulations differ meaningfully.

### Rashi's Logic

Rashi explains the difference in grammatical terms: *le-haniach* is an infinitive expressing an action in progress — you are still in the act of putting on tefillin, since the *shel rosh* has not yet been placed — while *al mitzvas tefillin* is a phrase denoting completion, used once the full *mitzvah* has been accomplished.

### Pesuk-Based Logic

A more structurally grounded explanation observes that the two formulations directly mirror the *pesukim*. The verse governing the *shel yad* — *uk'shartam le-os al yadecha* — uses an active verb of binding and doing, which is reflected in the active infinitive *le-haniach*. The verse governing the *shel rosh* — *ve-hayu le-totafos bein einecha* — uses a static verb of being, a state rather than an action, which is reflected in *al mitzvas tefillin*, denoting the status of wearing rather than the act of placing.

### Abaye & Rava Rule

Abaye and Rava formalize the rule: *lo sach mevarech achas, sach mevarech shtayim* — if one did not speak between the two, one makes one *beracha*; if one spoke, one makes two.

### Sefardi Custom

The straightforward reading of Abaye and Rava — and the position adopted by Rashi — is that without a *hefsek*, a single *beracha* covers both. This is *minhag Sefarad*: Sefardim recite only one *beracha* on tefillin — *le-haniach tefillin* — unless a *hefsek* occurred between the *shel yad* and the *shel rosh*, in which case a second *beracha* is added.

### Ashkenazi Custom

*Minhag Ashkenaz* is to always recite two separate *berachos* — *le-haniach tefillin* on the *shel yad* and *al mitzvas tefillin* on the *shel rosh* — regardless of whether any speech intervened. The additional *beracha* is always made on the *shel rosh*. If, however, a *hefsek* also occurred, the Ashkenazi practice is to add yet another *beracha* on the *shel rosh*, meaning two *berachos* are recited on the *shel rosh* alone in that case: first *le-haniach* and then *al mitzvas tefillin*. If one cannot put on the *shel yad* at all — due to injury, a cast, or any other reason — both *berachos* are recited on the *shel rosh* alone, since each represents an independent *mitzvah* dimension.

Tosafot raises the analogy of other *mitzvos* involving extended processes: *bedikas chametz*, which is clearly a unified process on which one *beracha* covers the entire search regardless of how long it takes; *shechitah* of many animals, where one *beracha* covers all the individual acts of *shechitah* performed sequentially. Tefillin occupies a different position: *shel yad* and *shel rosh* are in some sense independent (*ein me'akvin zeh et zeh* — one does not prevent the other, as the *gemara* will establish), yet when performed together they form a larger, unified *mitzvah*. What constitutes a *hefsek* significant enough to disrupt that unity may be different in each of these three models.

### Process vs. Separate

The deeper issue underlying the Ashkenazi–Sefardi dispute is how to conceptualize the relationship between the two *mitzvos*. For Sefardim, the dominant framework is unity: when no *hefsek* occurs, the *beracha* of *le-haniach* covers both, treating the donning of both *shel yad* and *shel rosh* as one continuous process. The *shel rosh* is acknowledged as distinct only when something has interrupted the process.

For Ashkenazim, each of the two retains its distinct identity even within the unified process. The *shel yad* involves the act of placing — *le-haniach* — and the *shel rosh* involves the state of having tefillin on — *al mitzvas tefillin* — and both dimensions deserve their own *beracha* regardless of continuity. This may reflect the view that there are two genuinely distinct aspects of the *mitzvah*: the act of binding (*uk'shartam*) and the state of bearing (*ve-hayu*), and that each demands its own acknowledgment.

A difficulty with the Ashkenazi position deserves mention: it seems to involve making two *birchos ha-mitzvah* — both of the *asher kideshanu* form — on what is arguably one *ma'aseh mitzvah*. This is not a familiar category; typically a complex *mitzvah* receives a single *birkas ha-mitzvah*. The Sefardi reluctance to adopt the Ashkenazi approach may reflect precisely this unease. Yet the Ashkenazi position may be understood as asserting that the act-dimension and the state-dimension of tefillin are genuinely distinct enough to each carry their own *beracha* — a claim that has textual grounding in the two different verbs used by the *pesukim* governing each.

---

## Talking Between Them

### Aveira & Remedy

A *baraisa* teaches: *sach bein tefillah le-tefillah aveira hi be-yado* — one who speaks between the two tefillin has committed a transgression. The *baraisa* then connects this to the verse about returning from battle — *mi ha-ish ha-yarei ve-rach ha-leivav* — suggesting that even one who has spoken between his tefillin and thereby committed this *aveira* may return from the front on that account. Whether this is meant to impress upon us the severity of the transgression, or whether it reflects the more modest point that even the smallest sin provides grounds for the returning soldier provision, is not entirely clear from the context — though the former reading seems more natural.

### Nature of Problem

Rashi understands the problem of speaking between the two tefillin specifically in terms of the *beracha*: one spoke and thereby failed to make the proper *beracha* at the right moment. This frames the *aveira* as rooted in the *beracha* violation. Tosafot, however, probes further and notes that on this reading, one encounters the problem of *bracha she-eina tzricha* — by now needing to make another *beracha*, one has caused an unnecessary *beracha* to be required, which is itself a transgression. The *aveira* thus ramifies in both directions.

There is, however, a deeper question about the nature of the problem that goes beyond the *beracha* entirely. Given that the *beracha* of *le-haniach* on the *shel yad* normally extends to and covers the *shel rosh* as well — treating the process as unified — the act of speaking between them may constitute an *aveira* not merely because of the *beracha* consequences, but because it breaks apart what is meant to be a unified act. The goal is a single, uninterrupted process of donning both tefillin together as one larger *mitzvah*. Even if one were somehow to solve the *beracha* problem, the separation itself — treating the *shel yad* and *shel rosh* as two independent acts rather than parts of one whole — may remain problematic. The *gemara* does not entirely resolve whether the *aveira* is solely about the *beracha* or also about the fragmentation of the *mitzvah* process.

---

## Donning & Doffing Order

### Putting On Order

A *baraisa* establishes: *k'shehu meniach meniach shel yad ve-achar kach meniach shel rosh* — when one puts on tefillin, one places the *shel yad* first and then the *shel rosh*.

### Pesuk Order

The source is straightforward: *uk'shartam le-os al yadecha*, the verse about the *shel yad*, precedes *ve-hayu le-totafos bein einecha*, the verse about the *shel rosh*. The order of the *pesukim* governs the order of the acts. Notably, this framing treats the donning of both as a single process unfolding in a defined sequence — not as two independent acts each with their own order, but as a unified *mitzvah* with a beginning and a progression.

### Taking Off Order

The *baraisa* continues: *uk'shehu choletz choletz shel rosh ve-achar kach choletz shel yad* — when removing, one first takes off the *shel rosh* and then the *shel yad*. This is the reverse order.

### Rabba's Logic

The source for reversing the order upon removal is explained by Rabba bar Rav Huna: the verse *ve-hayu le-totafos bein einecha* uses the word *ve-hayu*, which is plural and refers to both tefillin together. This teaches that *kol zman she-bein einecha yehu shtayim* — for as long as the *shel rosh* is between your eyes, both tefillin must be on you simultaneously. The *shel rosh* presupposes the presence of the *shel yad*; it builds upon it as its foundation. Therefore, one may not remove the *shel yad* while the *shel rosh* is still in place, for that would eliminate the foundation before the structure above it. The *shel rosh* must come off first.

### Action vs. State

This distinction illuminates a recurring theme throughout the *sugya*. The order of putting on derives from the *pesukim*' sequential verbs — *uk'shartam* (bind) and then *ve-hayu* (they shall be) — which govern the *action* of placing. The order of removal, however, derives from *ve-hayu* as expressing a required *state*: as long as the *shel rosh* is present, the *shel yad* must also be present, because *ve-hayu* demands that both exist simultaneously on the wearer.

Thus the donning order reflects the logic of action — you perform the acts in the order the *pesukim* prescribe. The doffing order reflects the logic of state — you must preserve the required state of simultaneous wearing for as long as either item remains on you. The two orders are governed by different halakhic principles derived from the same verse, depending on which dimension of the *mitzvah* is in view.

---

## Timing of Wearing

### Before Dawn

The *gemara* asks: from what point may one recite the *beracha* on tefillin, and how does that interact with wearing them before daybreak? A case is presented: one woke early before dawn and wished to travel, fearing that tefillin carried in a bag might be lost. So one placed them on even before the proper time.

### Blessing After Dawn

The ruling: *u'ch'she-yagia zman memashmesh bahen u-mevarech aleihen* — when the proper time arrives, one feels the tefillin on one's body and then recites the *beracha*. The act of touching and feeling the tefillin functions as a kind of renewed placement, sufficient to serve as the basis for the *beracha* even though the physical act of putting them on occurred earlier. This is consistent with the ruling for *tzitzit* worn before the proper time: when dawn arrives, one touches the *tzitzit* and recites the *beracha*.

What is theologically and halakhically significant here is the implication that the *beracha* is not exclusively tied to the moment of the initial physical act. The state of wearing tefillin is itself a continuous reality, and *kol zman she-manichan* — for as long as one is wearing them — the *beracha* has a basis. This reframes the principle of *mi-sha'as hanachasam*: it refers not merely to the moment of placement but to the ongoing condition of having tefillin on one's body. The act of feeling them at daybreak is a moment of re-recognition of that state, and it is in that moment that the *beracha* is most naturally made. This parallels the tension throughout the *sugya* between the action-dimension and the state-dimension of the *mitzvah*.

### Sunset Limit

*Ve-ad masai menichan? Ad she-tishka ha-chama* — how long may one wear tefillin? Until sunset.

### Two Rationales

Two distinct reasons are given for not wearing tefillin at night. The first is *layla lav zman tefillin* — night is formally not the time for tefillin, derived from the *pesukim* in a manner analogous to other *mitzvos* that apply only by day. This is a categorical halakhic statement about the scope of the *mitzvah* itself. The second reason is practical concern: one may fall asleep while wearing tefillin and, in that state, pass gas, which is incompatible with the *kedusha* of tefillin.

### Yaakov's Extension

Rabbi Yaakov holds that one may continue wearing tefillin beyond sunset until *ad she-tichleh regel min ha-shuk* — until the foot traffic in the marketplace has ceased and people have gone home. This is analogous to the time limit for *ner Chanukah*. On this view, the operative concern is the practical one of falling asleep; as long as people are still active in the street, there is no realistic concern that one will fall asleep inadvertently, and so wearing tefillin remains permissible.

### Bedtime Limit

The *Chachamim* extend this further: one may continue wearing tefillin until *zman sheina* — until it is normally bedtime, whenever that is for the individual or community. Like Rabbi Yaakov, the *Chachamim* are evidently operating from the concern about sleep rather than a categorical exclusion of nighttime, but they set the limit at the point when sleep actually becomes likely.

### Bathroom Exception

The *Chachamim* agree with Rabbi Yaakov on one point: if one removed tefillin after sunset — for example, to enter a bathroom or a bathhouse — and sunset then fully passed during the interim, one does not put them back on. The *Chachamim*'s permission to wear tefillin into the evening is a concession to continuity; it applies when one has kept them on continuously, but it does not sanction *lechatchila* putting them back on once nightfall has arrived.

### Rav Nachman Rules

Rav Nachman rules *halacha ke-Rabbi Yaakov* — we follow Rabbi Yaakov's position, which means that the governing concern is falling asleep, and one may continue wearing tefillin after sunset until the streets empty of traffic. This implies that *layla lav zman tefillin* is not a categorical exclusion — it is a concern of bodily propriety that becomes pressing only when sleep is a realistic prospect.

### Night Prayer Dispute

The *gemara* records that Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna would pray — presumably *Maariv* — while wearing tefillin at night. One version understands this as a corroboration of Rabbi Yaakov's position, since they clearly continued wearing tefillin into the evening. But the *gemara* then introduces a contrary view: *ein halacha ke-Rabbi Yaakov* — we do not rule like Rabbi Yaakov — which would mean that tefillin must be removed at sunset. This creates an apparent difficulty: what then were Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna doing wearing tefillin at night? The *gemara* answers that they were among those who disputed this and held that night-time wearing is in fact permissible. The question of whether *layla lav zman tefillin* constitutes a formal halakhic exclusion demanding removal, or only a practical concern that governs when one *lechatchila* puts tefillin on, will be the subject of continued discussion on the next daf.

---

---

# Menachot 36

## Broken Strap Repair

### Knotting Broken Straps

The daf opens with a scene: *Abaye hava yativ kamei d'Rav Yosef* — Abaye was sitting before Rav Yosef when his *retzuah* of *tefillin* broke. He posed the question: *mahu lemiktarei* — may he repair the strap by knotting the broken halves together?

### Perfect Binding Required

Rav Yosef's response was crisp and textually grounded: *u'kshartem ksiv* — the Torah says "you shall bind," and this implies *shetihyeh kshirah tamah*, that the binding must be whole and unbroken. Accordingly, a broken strap that is merely knotted together does not constitute a valid, perfect binding.

### Sewing Alternative

A related question was then posed by Rav Acha, son of Rav Yosef, to Rav Ashi: *mahu lemitfrei d'ayiley l'tifey legav* — rather than knotting the break, what if one sews the strap and places the stitching on the inside, so that from the outside the repair is invisible? This would appear far more like a genuine restoration of the strap's integrity.

### Puk Chazi Dispute

Rav Ashi's response was the classic *puk chazi mai ama devar* — go out and see what the people are doing. This deceptively simple directive is the subject of a well-known interpretive dispute. Rashi reads it to mean that since people do not do this, it is *assur*. Tosafot, by contrast, understands *puk chazi* as typically deployed in a *kula* context, and therefore reads the passage to mean that since people do it, it is *mutar*.

One might observe that in practice this question rarely arises, given that Ashkenazi tradition employs *or behemah gassah* — thick hide — for the straps, making tearing far less common. Moreover, if the sewing is truly invisible from the outside, the evidentiary value of common practice is limited: one simply cannot tell by observation how others have handled the rare case.

---

## Mitzvah vs. Kedusha Stat…

### Tzitzit vs. Tefillin

The discussion of the *retzuah* leads naturally into a broader taxonomic question about the objects of *mitzvot*. The Gemara introduces the principle via the concept of *gardumim*. Rav Pappa had stated that *gardumei retzuot kesherot* — remnant straps are valid. The reasoning by analogy was to *tzitzit*: the sons of Rebbi Chiyya taught that *gardumei techelet v'gardumei ezov kesherim* — remnant strings of the blue *tzitzit* thread, and remnant *ezov* (hyssop) used in the purification rites of *parah adumah* or the *metzorah*, remain valid so long as they began at the requisite length. If a string tore and only a small piece remains, one is still *yotzei*.

The Gemara, however, rejects Rav Pappa's extension to *tefillin* straps: *hatam hu de'tashmishei mitzvah ninhu* — there it is valid because those objects are *tashmishei mitzvah*. *Aval hacha de'tashmishei kedusha ninhu lo* — but here, where the straps are *tashmishei kedusha*, the more lenient rule does not apply, and remnant length is insufficient.

### Definitions and Examples

The distinction being drawn here is foundational. *Tashmishei mitzvah* — literally "service objects of a *mitzvah*" — refers to objects such as *tzitzit*, *lulav*, and *shofar*: things with which one performs a *mitzvah*, but which do not possess intrinsic *kedusha*. *Tashmishei kedusha*, by contrast, are objects associated with *kitvei hakodesh* and, more specifically, with *shem Hashem*, which endows them with an intrinsic, ongoing sanctity.

### Intrinsic Holiness

The practical difference is significant. *Tashmishei mitzvah* objects are governed primarily by considerations of respect *during* the performance of the *mitzvah*. After the *mitzvah* has been fulfilled, one may dispose of them — albeit with some care, such as wrapping a *lulav* before discarding it, or ideally repurposing it for another *mitzvah* (such as using the *lulav* as kindling for burning *chametz*). There is no requirement of *sheimos*, and no ongoing sanctity.

*Tashmishei kedusha*, however, carry an intrinsic, status-based *kedusha* that persists independent of whether a *mitzvah* is actively being performed. This is why one does not simply discard a *mezuzah* case: it directly serves *kitvei kodesh*. And this ongoing sanctity is precisely why one would never place a *lulav* in *sheimos*, whereas a *tefillin* strap would require such treatment.

The connection to *shem Hashem* and *kitvei hakodesh* is the operative criterion. A *sefer Torah* that contained too many errors from the outset and was never valid retains its *kedusha* not because it was used but because of the presence of *shem Hashem* within it. The intrinsic sanctity is thus not contingent on functional use.

### Tefillin Status Question

This raises a genuine conceptual puzzle. When the Gemara invokes the category of *tashmishei kedusha* in order to disqualify *gardumim* for *tefillin* straps, it is reasoning about whether one can fulfill the *mitzvah* — a question that seems naturally to fall under the rubric of *tashmishei mitzvah*. Why should the higher standard of *tashmishei kedusha* determine the shiur for a mitzvah performance question? 

One possible resolution is that the very categorization of *tefillin* as *tashmishei kedusha* — given that the straps serve the *klafim* within, which contain *shem Hashem* — elevates the standard of completeness required of all their components. When something breaks off from an object in the category of *tashmishei mitzvah*, the broken piece simply ceases to serve a mitzvah purpose and may be treated as ordinary. But when something breaks off from an object of *tashmishei kedusha*, the sense that it belongs to and has been severed from a sacred whole is weightier. This may be what informs the Gemara's conclusion, even if the precise logic is not stated explicitly.

### Shel Rosh and Shin

Tosafot raises a further question that pushes the analysis deeper. *Tefillin* occupy two statuses simultaneously: they are *tashmishei mitzvah* — objects through which the *mitzvah* of *tefillin* is performed — and *tashmishei kedusha* — serving the *klafim* inside, which contain *shem Hashem*. The *klafim* themselves, of course, are not *tashmishei kedusha* but *kitvei hakodesh* proper.

But what of the *bayit* of the *shel rosh*, with its embossed *shin*? Tosafot suggests that because the *shin* is part of *shem Hashem* — specifically forming part of the divine name *Shin-Dalet-Yud* — the *shel rosh* may not merely be *tashmishei kedusha*. It may carry something closer to *kedusha atzma*, akin to *kitvei hakodesh* themselves, given that an element of *shem Hashem* is literally inscribed on its exterior. We will return to this point at greater length in the discussion of the *kesher*.

---

## Strap Length Requirements

### Gardumim Rejected

From the Gemara's rejection of *gardumim* for *tefillin* straps, the Gemara draws an inference: *v'lav milta hi* — the position of Rav Pappa is incorrect. And more: *mi'da'amru bnei Rebbi Chiyya*, since the Gemara demonstrated a valid parallel of *gardumim* by *tzitzit* but rejected that parallel for *tefillin*, it follows that *de-is lehu shiura* — there must be a minimum length requirement for *tefillin* straps. The question then becomes: what is that *shiur*?

### One Finger Measure

Rami bar Chama in the name of Resh Lakish gives the answer: *ad etzba tzerada* — until the *etzba tzerada*. Rashi identifies this as the forefinger; Tosafot disagrees, arguing that the term refers to the snapping or middle finger.

### Kafuf vs. Pashut

The Gemara records that Rav Kahana demonstrated the length *kafuf* — with the finger bent — while Rav Ashi demonstrated it *pashut* — with the finger extended straight out.

### Two Interpretations

Two explanations of this dispute are offered. The first, advanced by both Rashi and Tosafot (though they disagree about which finger is meant), understands the *shiur* as simply a finger's length — the span between the thumb and the relevant finger, with *kafuf* being the wider spread and *pashut* roughly half that. The second explanation — and this is the operative *psak* — understands the passage as speaking of the *shel yad*: after making the initial knot, the strap must be long enough to reach all the way to the middle finger.

### Practical Application

On this second reading, *kafuf* means the strap reaches the finger when the finger is bent downward toward the palm, and *pashut* means it reaches the finger when fully extended — the latter being the operative ruling. The *halacha* thus requires that after one loop and knot on the arm, the remaining strap must extend all the way to the finger. The custom of making seven wraps around the arm, while widespread, is not strictly required; one wrap and the extension to the finger constitutes the minimum.

### Shel Rosh Length

If the Gemara's *shiur* applies to the *shel yad*, one might ask: what is the required length for the straps of the *shel rosh*? The Gemara does not say, and the *Shulchan Aruch* is notably imprecise on this point. Tosafot, however, at the conclusion of his discussion, cites the *Shimusha Rabba* — an early Geonic work that is frequently cited in the laws of *tefillin* and which appears to have codified much of what was transmitted by tradition. The *Shimusha Rabba* states that one strap of the *shel rosh* must reach *k'neged mila* — below the waist — on the right side, while the other must reach *k'neged halev* — to the heart — on the left. Tosafot elsewhere cites an opinion that the right-side strap need only reach the navel rather than below the waist.

### Strap Width

The *Shimusha Rabba* also addresses the required width of the straps: the width should be more than a wheat grain (*shiora*) but less than a barley grain (*k'shora b'atzmala*). If it is wider, one is still *kasher* — and in fact, straps in common use are considerably wider. The source of these width specifications is not a Talmudic passage but transmitted tradition, as preserved in the *Shimusha Rabba*.

### Practical Relevance

These measures have practical implications in two categories of situations: when the black paint wears off a portion of the strap, or when the strap tears. If the defect occurs in a portion of the strap beyond the minimum *shiur*, it is not a problem. If it occurs within the *shiur*, it becomes an issue of *kashrus*. One who has a strap with worn black paint might cut off the affected segment — though even without cutting, if the affected area is beyond the *shiur*, it may not constitute a problem, though this would require further verification.

---

## Rashi-Rabbeinu Tam Histo…

### Rambam's Evolution

The fact that Tosafot relies so heavily on the *Shimusha Rabba* — a written handbook — for so many of the laws of *tefillin* naturally prompts reflection on how much the transmission of these laws depended on such texts. This is dramatically illustrated by a famous *teshuvah* of the Rambam. The questioners noted that his rulings in the *Mishneh Torah* followed what we would call the Rashi *tefillin* position, while their own community had a tradition of *havayos ba'emtza* — the order associated with Rabbeinu Tam. The Rambam's response contains a remarkable personal confession.

He writes: *kach haya dati mikodem kachem* — I myself used to hold like you, like the *havayos ba'emtza* position. He continues: *ve-tefillin hayu li be-Eretz Ma'arav* — when I lived in the West, in Spain, those were my *tefillin*. And why? *Ve-kasav kaze asher chibbar ha-tefillin u-shemo Rav Moshe mi-Cordova* — because of a handbook about the laws of *tefillin* composed by a certain Rav Moshe of Cordova. (In some manuscript versions of the *teshuvah*, this figure is called *Rav Moshe bar Maimon mi-Cordova*, which is clearly erroneous; he was a different scholar.)

The Rambam states with striking candor: *ve-oto ha-chibbur hu she-hitani ve-hita kol anshei ha-Ma'arav milfanai* — that handbook is what led me astray and what led astray all the people of the West who had come before me. This is a vivid illustration of the power of a written code, and of how a single authoritative-seeming handbook could redirect the practice of an entire community across generations.

### Cordova's Handbook

The influence of Rav Moshe of Cordova's handbook extended not only to the Rambam's personal practice during his years in Spain but, as the Rambam implies, to the entirety of Western Jewry — Spain and possibly Provence — who followed it uniformly. The Ri, in one *teshuvah*, also reflects the *havayos ba'emtza* position. This was not, in other words, a marginal opinion: it was the standard practice across a vast geographic and cultural region, attributable to a single textual source.

### Rabbeinu Hai Evidence

The Rambam then explains what ultimately moved him to adopt the other position. He writes that *chachamim ne'emanim* — reliable scholars — told him that after the death of Rabbeinu Hai Gaon, his *tefillin* were opened and examined, and *matzu she-ketuvin al ha-seder she-amarti be-chibbur* — they were found to be written in the order the Rambam himself had described in his legal code — that is, the Rashi order, not *havayos ba'emtza*. This was significant because Rabbeinu Hai had been cited in support of the *havayos ba'emtza* position; the physical examination of his own *tefillin* overturned that assumption.

### Manuscript Variants

The Rambam also points to the textual dimension of the question: the Gemara's passage concluding *ha-koreh koreh al ha-seder* — the reader reads in order — had been read cryptically, without specifying which order. The Rambam found a *girsa* of the Gemara that explicitly enumerated the parshiyot in sequence: *Kadesh Li, ve-Haya ki Yevi'acha, Shema, ve-Haya im Shamo'a* — the sequential order that corresponds to the Rashi arrangement. He notes that *ve-nusach ze lo haya be-sifreinu be-Eretz Ma'arav* — this reading was not found in the manuscripts available in Spain. But upon examination of older manuscripts, he found it there: *kol ha-nusachot ha-yeshanot ve-kach katuv ba-hen*.

### Geographic Traditions

The Rambam also appeals to the traditions of *Eretz Yisrael* and the Eastern communities, who had stronger and more careful traditions regarding *tefillin*. He notes that many of the *Geonim* and the people of the East — *anshei Mizrach* and the *anshei Eretz Tzvi* — stood opposed to the *havayos ba'emtza* position. Taken together — the physical evidence of Rabbeinu Hai's own *tefillin*, the manuscript tradition, and the authority of Eastern practice — these factors moved the Rambam to change his position.

Scholars have speculated that it was this *teshuvah*, perhaps more than any other single factor, that turned the tide and established the Rashi arrangement as normative. Without it, one might ask whether the widespread Spanish practice of *havayos ba'emtza*, rooted in a popular handbook, might have prevailed. The episode illustrates how dependent so much of *hilchos tefillin* is on handbooks, manuscript traditions, and the testimony of scholars — and how much a single authoritative written response can reshape collective practice.

---

## Physical Placement

### Strap Placement Methods

Turning now to the physical placement of the *tefillin* straps, the Gemara records different practices among the Amoraim. Rava would tie his *tefillin* and fling the straps behind his back — *pashit v'shadi lehu*, as Rashi explains it. Rav Acha bar Yaakov, by contrast, after tying would place the straps in front. Mar brei d'Ravina, the Gemara reports, did as *we* do — which Rashi understands as placing the straps in front.

The striking feature of this passage is its casual tone. One might have expected the placement of the straps to be a firm and settled *halacha*; instead, the Gemara presents it as simply what different scholars happened to do, with no clear resolution. In some respects it might seem more natural for the straps to flow behind — one thinks of a headrest from which straps naturally fall backward.

### Black Faces Out

Rav Yehuda transmits a ruling: *v'noyeihen l'var* — the attractive side, meaning the black side, must face outward.

### Flipped Strap Case

This ruling is immediately illustrated by an incident. Rav Ashi was sitting before Mar Zutra when his *retzuah* flipped — the inner side turned outward. Mar Zutra pointed out to him: *lo savar leh mar v'noyeihen l'var* — does the master not hold that the attractive side must face out? Rav Ashi replied: *lav ada'atai* — I had not noticed. The correction was promptly made.

---

## Kesher as Halacha L'Moshe

### Kesher Status

The Gemara now states: *kesher shel tefillin halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* — the knot of the *tefillin* is a transmitted law going back to Moses at Sinai. This was transmitted by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav.

### Rashi's Shem Hashem

Rashi explains the content of this *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* as follows: the knot of the *shel rosh* is shaped to resemble the letter *dalet*, and the knot of the *shel yad* is shaped to resemble the letter *yud*, and together with the *shin* embossed on the *bayit* of the *shel rosh* they spell the divine name *Shin-Dalet-Yud*. This formation, according to Rashi, is what is transmitted as *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*.

### Tosafot Challenge

Tosafot challenges this. Do the knots, as actually formed, truly resemble the letters *dalet* and *yud* closely enough to constitute a genuine rendering of *shem Hashem*? Tosafot is skeptical, and the basis of his skepticism is not merely aesthetic but halachic: the *tefillin* are categorized as *tashmishei kedusha* — they serve the *klafim* inside — and not as *kedusha atzma*. If the knots genuinely formed *shem Hashem*, they would not merely be serving the *klafim*; they would themselves be objects of *kedusha atzma*, equivalent in status to *kitvei hakodesh*. Since we do not treat the *tefillin* that way, Tosafot argues, the knots cannot truly constitute *shem Hashem*.

### Kedusha vs. Atzma

This brings into sharp focus the distinction introduced earlier. *Tashmishei kedusha* serves *kitvei hakodesh* or *shem Hashem* but is not itself sacred in the same intrinsic way. The *tefillin* straps and boxes serve the *klafim*, which are *kitvei hakodesh*. If the knots themselves were *shem Hashem*, they would be on the level of the *klafim* — *kedusha atzma* — rather than *tashmishei kedusha*. Since they are treated as the latter, Tosafot concludes they cannot be *shem Hashem* in any operative halachic sense. Tosafot does not deny that the knots are made in a particular prescribed form — the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* of their shape is not disputed — but he denies that this confers on them the sanctity of *shem Hashem*.

For comparison: the *tefillin* are more holy than the mantle of a *sefer Torah*, which is *tashmishei d'tashmishei* — serving the *tefillin*, which serve the *klafim*. The *tefillin* themselves directly serve the *klafim* and are *tashmishei kedusha*. Yet even they fall short of *kedusha atzma*.

### Shin Status

The *shin* on the *shel rosh*, however, may be a different matter. When the Gemara says *v'ra'u kol amei ha'aretz ki shem Hashem nikra alecha* and the *Tanna* identifies this with the *tefillin shel rosh*, Rashi explains that the *shin* and the *dalet* together constitute two-thirds of *Shin-Dalet-Yud*. Tosafot pushes back again: the *shin* is present on the leather, but the *dalet* is questionable and the *yud* is questionable; do not call this *shem Hashem*.

Nevertheless, even within Tosafot's framework there is an important concession. The *shin* is exposed on the exterior of the *shel rosh* — it is literally inscribed on the leather box itself. And it is at least *representative* of *shem Hashem*, even if one does not wish to ascribe to it full *kedusha atzma*.

### Bathroom Entry Question

Tosafot records a fascinating position attributed to Rabbi Yaakov d'Orleans, who raised the question of whether one must remove the *shel yad* before entering a *beit hakisei* — a bathroom. The consideration: the *klafim* inside the *bayit* are covered by leather, and it is the *klafim* that are actually prohibited from being brought into the bathroom. Since the *klafim* are covered, perhaps the *shel yad*, with its leather covering, is permissible.

One can enter a bathroom wearing *tashmishei mitzvah* — one does so every time one enters wearing *tzitzit* — but one may not enter carrying the parchment. So if the *klafim* are fully covered, perhaps the *shel yad* poses no problem.

But the *shel rosh* is different, Rabbi Yaakov d'Orleans suggests: *d'lo asru ela tefillin shel rosh she'kasuv shin ba'or* — what is prohibited is the *shel rosh*, because the *shin* is written on the leather itself. The *shin*, being exposed and associated with *shem Hashem*, may give the *shel rosh* a quasi-status approaching *kedusha atzma* — not merely *tashmishei kedusha* serving the *klafim* inside, but itself bearing something of the sanctity of *shem Hashem*.

This line in Tosafot is striking. It creates a layered taxonomy: the *shel yad* is *tashmishei mitzvah* and *tashmishei kedusha*; the *shel rosh* may carry an additional dimension approaching *kedusha atzma* by virtue of the exposed *shin*. Whether the voice here is fully consistent with Tosafot's earlier skepticism about the letters forming *shem Hashem* is a reasonable question — but at minimum, Tosafot concedes that even if one does not grant the full weight of *shem Hashem* to the *dalet* and *yud* of the knots, the *shin* on the *shel rosh* carries independent force.

---

## Biblical Source

### God's Back Kesher

A *Tanna* teaches: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol interprets the verse *v'hasiroti et kapi v'raita et achorai* — "I will remove My hand and you shall see My back" — as referring to the *kesher shel tefillin*. Rav Kahana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida elaborates: *melamed she-her'ah lo HaKadosh Baruch Hu l'Moshe kesher shel tefillin* — this teaches that the Holy One Blessed Be He showed Moses the knot of the *tefillin*. The Gemara in Berachot famously teaches that God wears *tefillin*; what Moses saw at the back of God's head, so to speak, was the *kesher shel tefillin*.

Why, of all the things Moses might have perceived in that singular moment of partial revelation, is the *kesher shel tefillin* what he saw? The Gemara does not spell out the significance explicitly, but there is evidently something weighty being communicated — not merely a descriptive observation about the back of God's head, but a theological point about what the *kesher shel tefillin* represents or signifies.

---

## Biblical Source (II)

### Israel Above

The Gemara continues: Rav Yehuda states that *kesher shel tefillin tzarich she'yehei l'ma'alah* — the knot must be positioned above — *kedei she'Yisrael yihiyu l'ma'alah v'lo l'mata* — so that Israel should be above and not below. The knot is placed at the nape of the neck, above the hairline, not low on the neck or near the shoulder.

Whether this is a formal *halacha* or an evocative *drash* is not entirely clear. It may be that both are intended: there is a real positional requirement for the *kesher*, and the symbolic resonance gives expression to its meaning.

### God's Tefillin

The symbolic resonance becomes clearer when one recalls the Gemara in Berachot: God's *tefillin* contain the words *mi k'amcha Yisrael goy echad ba'aretz* — "Who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the earth?" Just as Israel's *tefillin* express the elevation of God — affirming His singularity and sovereignty — so God's *tefillin*, in a sense, express God's elevation of Israel. The requirement that *Yisrael yihiyu l'ma'alah v'lo l'mata* is thus not merely a positional rule but a reflection of the reciprocal relationship expressed through the *kesher*.

When Moses saw the back of God — the *kesher shel tefillin* — he was seeing, in the Rambam's terms, not the essence of God (which cannot be apprehended) but God's ways: specifically, God's relationship to and elevation of *Bnei Yisrael*. The *kesher shel tefillin* becomes, on this reading, the emblem of that relationship visible in the world — how God acts in history in connection with Israel.

---

## Kesher Position

### Kesher Above

Rav Yehuda's requirement that the *kesher* be *l'ma'alah* — above — means it is placed at the nape of the neck at the base of the skull, in that slight indentation where the bone ends. It is not to be positioned low on the neck. Whether *pasul* if placed incorrectly is not stated explicitly, leaving open the question of whether this is a formal *din* or an aspirational *drash*.

---

## Shin Variants

### Shin Variants

The *Shimusha Rabba*, cited by Tosafot on the preceding *daf*, addresses the *shin* on the *shel rosh*. It specifies that one side of the *shel rosh* bears a three-armed *shin* and the other bears a four-armed *shin* — and this is indeed the practice today, though, notably, the source is the *Shimusha Rabba* rather than the *Gemara* itself.

### Geometric Relationship

The *Shimusha Rabba*'s distinction is further elaborated in a geometric observation: the white space — the negative space between the arms — of an upside-down three-armed *shin* fits within a four-armed *shin*. Tosafot makes this point explicitly. There is thus a kind of geometric complementarity between the two forms.

### Symbolic Meanings

Tosafot connects the four-armed *shin* to the four *parshiyot* of *tefillin*. There is also a conceptual link to the *luchot*: the letters of the *luchot* were formed by cutting through the stone, leaving the form defined as much by the space as by the solid material. Something of that dialectic — what is seen versus what is defined by the absence — may be evoked by the relationship between the three- and four-armed forms. The four-armed *shin*, in any case, is not found in standard Hebrew script and is distinctive to the *shel rosh*.

---

## Proper Orientation

### Klapei Panim

The Gemara states: *v'tzarich she'yehei klapei panim* — the *kesher* must face toward the front. What exactly "facing front" means in this context is somewhat ambiguous. Rashi explains it to mean that the black must be on the outside and the white on the inside — that the *retzuah* must be properly oriented. The *kesher* itself must be oriented correctly and face forward.

### Israel in Front

The reason given is parallel to the earlier principle: *kedei she'yehei Yisrael lifnim v'lo l'achor* — so that Israel should be in front, not behind. The directional symbolism — above rather than below, in front rather than behind — consistently expresses the covenantal dignity of the Jewish people.

---

## Blessing Timing

### Timing Window

When does one make the *beracha* on *tefillin*? The answer, transmitted through a chain of Amoraim, is *mishat hanachatan* — from the time of placing them on. The Gemara immediately questions this: but the general rule is that one makes a *beracha* before performing a *mitzvah* — *over la'asiyatan* — not after one has already placed the *tefillin* on!

### Abaye and Rava

Abaye and Rava resolve this together: *mishat hanacha v'ad she'at keshira* — from the moment of placement until the tightening of the *kesher*. In other words, one places the *tefillin* on the hand or head, makes the *beracha*, and then performs the *keshira* — the tightening. The *beracha* thus occurs after the initial placing but before the finalizing act, satisfying the requirement of *over la'asiyatan*.

Tosafot takes the word *keshira* quite literally and, building on this phrase, cites the position of Rabbeinu Eliyahu: *she'tzarich adam likshor tefillin bechol yom* — one must actually *make* the knot of the *tefillin* each day, not merely tighten a pre-existing loop.
