Under this view, one would arrive each morning, pass the strap through the *tefillin*, form the loop, and execute the *keshira* from scratch — at least for the *shel yad*, where the *pasuk* reads *u'kshartem l'os al yadecha* with an active verbal construction.

Tosafot himself, however, notes the obvious rejoinder: the *pasuk* for *mezuzah* says *u'chtavtam al mezuzot beitecha*, yet we do not take out a quill and write the *mezuzah* each day. The *pasuk*'s active verb does not necessarily require the action to be repeated; having the object in place may itself constitute the ongoing fulfillment. Tosafot allows that *keshira* in the Gemara's phrase may mean *lav davka keshira* — not literally knotting but simply tightening. Nonetheless, Tosafot is drawn to the possibility that the *pasuk*'s active language has some operative significance, particularly in contrast to the static verb *vehayu* used for the *shel rosh*.

---

## Two Blessings

### Sach Rule

Rav Chisda rules: *sach bein tefillah l'tefillah chozer u'mevarech* — one who talks between the *shel yad* and the *shel rosh* must return and make another *beracha*. The Gemara asks: this implies that talking requires an additional *beracha*, but not talking does not — yet we know from an authoritative letter of Rabbi Yochanan that there are two distinct *nusachot* for the *tefillin* blessings, one for each of the two *tefillin*. If there are always two blessings, why should talking matter?

### Yochanan Letter

Rabbi Chiyya son of Rav Huna transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: on the *shel yad* one says *asher kideshanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu lehaniach tefillin*, and on the *shel rosh* one says *asher kideshanu b'mitzvotav v'tzivanu al mitzvat tefillin*. The two formulations are different, and they appear to be two independent blessings.

### Nusach Difference

The difference in *nusach* is significant. The verb *lehaniach* — "to place" — is an infinitive expressing an active, ongoing action: one is still in the process of placing, still *meniach*, when one recites this blessing. The phrase *al mitzvat tefillin* — "on the *mitzvah* of *tefillin*" — is a static formulation: one is now in the status of bearing *tefillin*; the act is complete and one speaks of being in the state of the *mitzvah*.

This difference maps neatly onto the *pessukim* themselves. The verse for the *shel yad* uses the active verb *u'kshartem* — "you shall bind"; the verse for the *shel rosh* uses the static verb *vehayu l'totafot* — "and they shall be frontlets." The *beracha* formulations mirror these verbal dimensions: active doing versus static being.

### One or Two Blessings

Abaye and Rava jointly resolve the tension: *lo sach mevarech achat, sach mevarech shtayim* — if one did not talk between the two, one makes one *beracha* total; if one talked, one makes two. The correct reading of Rav Chisda's statement, then, is not that one always makes two blessings, with talking merely requiring an *additional* one. Rather, the default is one *beracha* — the *lehaniach* on the *shel yad* covers the *shel rosh* as well — and talking between the two necessitates a second, separate *beracha* on the *shel rosh*.

When is the *nusach* of *al mitzvat tefillin* used? When there has been a *hefsek* between the two, and the *shel rosh* requires its own *beracha* as an independent act. This also becomes practically relevant beyond the case of talking: if a person cannot wear the *shel yad* — due to a cast, an injury, or some other *chatzitza* — and puts on only the *shel rosh*, that *shel rosh* would receive both *berachot*, since it now stands alone as a separate *mitzvah*.

### Ashkenazi Position

The Ashkenazi practice is to always recite a separate *beracha* on the *shel rosh* — *al mitzvat tefillin* — regardless of whether one talked between the two. The reasoning, understood within this framework, is that the *shel rosh* retains its distinct identity even within the unified process: each *tefillin* has its own dimension, and the *shel rosh*'s separate status as a *mitzvah* of *vehayu l'totafot* — of being, of static presence — is acknowledged through an independent *beracha*. The two dimensions of *tefillin* — the active *u'kshartem* of the *shel yad* and the static *vehayu* of the *shel rosh* — are each given explicit expression.

### Sefardi Position

The Sefardi position holds that one *beracha* — *lehaniach tefillin* — suffices for both, unless there was a *hefsek* between the two. The *lehaniach* blessing covers both, reflecting the unified process: when performed without interruption, placing the *shel yad* and then the *shel rosh* constitutes a single, larger *mitzvah* act, and one *beracha* governs the whole.

When a Sefardi who talked between the two must make a separate *beracha* on the *shel rosh*, it is *al mitzvat tefillin* — not a second *lehaniach*. The active, placement-oriented formulation remains associated with the *shel yad* alone, and the *shel rosh* is addressed in its static dimension. A Sefardi who has only the *shel rosh* would recite *al mitzvat tefillin* on it.

### Action Dimension

This leads to a broader question: does the *shel rosh* carry any dimension of active placement — *keshira*, *hanacha* — at all? For Ashkenazim, evidently yes: even on the *shel rosh* alone, one would say *lehaniach*, meaning the concept of placing applies to it as well. For Sefardim, the active dimension of the blessing is identified primarily with the *shel yad*, and the *shel rosh* is addressed in terms of its status.

This in turn connects back to the debate about Rabbeinu Eliyahu's position on actually making the *kesher* each day. The question of how much active *keshira* is intrinsic to the *mitzvah* of the *shel rosh* — as opposed to the *shel yad*, where the *pasuk* reads *u'kshartem* — runs through multiple dimensions of this sugya: the *nusach ha'beracha*, the distinction between *lehaniach* and *al mitzvat*, and the Ashkenazi versus Sefardi approaches to the number of *berachot*.

---

## Talking Prohibition

### Speaking Aveirah

A *baraita* is cited: *sach bein tefillah l'tefillah aveirah hi b'yado* — one who talks between the *shel yad* and the *shel rosh* commits a transgression.

### War Exception

The Gemara adds a striking corollary: *v'chozer aleha m'orchei milchama* — this person may return from the battle lines on account of this transgression. The verse *mi ha'ish ha'yarei v'rach ha'leivav* — "who is the man who is fearful and faint-hearted" — is interpreted by the Gemara as *rach ha'leivav min ha'aveirah she'b'yado*, referring to the faint-heartedness induced by the *aveirah* in one's hand. Even the relatively minor transgression of talking between the two *tefillin* qualifies as a reason to return from war.

The intent of this reference is ambiguous: it may be meant to impress upon us the gravity of the *aveirah*, or conversely, it may be read as pointing out that even this small infraction — which falls at the minor end of the spectrum of sins — still allows one to return, emphasizing the breadth of the exemption rather than the severity of the act.

### Problem Analysis

Rashi understands the *aveirah* as the failure to make the correct *beracha* subsequently — having talked, one now requires an additional *beracha*, and perhaps one failed to recite it, resulting in a *beracha* made in vain (*bracha she'eina tzricha*). Tosafot explores at length how serious a problem *bracha she'eina tzricha* actually is.

But there is a deeper dimension to consider. If, as argued above, the *shel yad* and *shel rosh* are not merely two independent *mitzvot* but together constitute a larger unified *mitzvah* process — evidenced by the fact that the *beracha* on the *shel yad* normally covers the *shel rosh* as well — then talking between them does not merely create a *beracha* problem. It ruptures the unity of the process. Even if one subsequently recites the correct *beracha* on the *shel rosh*, the *aveirah* of separating what should be a unified process may persist independently of the blessing question. The Gemara does not make this explicit, but the language of *aveirah hi b'yado* — framed as a categorical transgression, not specifically a *beracha*-related infraction — is consistent with this reading.

---

## Order of Putting On (III)

### Putting On Order

A *baraita* teaches: *k'she'hu meniach, meniach shel yad v'achar kach meniach shel rosh* — when one puts on *tefillin*, one puts on the *shel yad* first, then the *shel rosh*. The source is straightforward: *dichviv ukshartem l'os al yadecha v'hadar v'hayu l'totafot bein einecha* — the *pasuk* first mentions binding on the hand and then mentions the *totafot* between the eyes. The Torah itself prescribes the order.

### Taking Off Order

When removing, however, the order reverses: *choleitz shel rosh v'achar kach choleitz shel yad* — one removes the *shel rosh* first, then the *shel yad*. The question the Gemara asks is: the putting-on order is mandated explicitly by the *pessukim*, but where does the taking-off order come from?

Rabba cites Rav Huna's explanation: *amar kra v'hayu l'totafot bein einecha* — the verse uses the word *v'hayu*, which is plural. This plural encompasses both the *shel yad* and the *shel rosh* together, meaning: *kol zman she'bein einecha yehu shtayim* — for as long as the *shel rosh* is between your eyes, both *tefillin* must be on you. The *shel rosh* is in a sense built upon the foundation of the *shel yad*: it presupposes the *shel yad*'s presence. Therefore, when removing, one must first remove the *shel rosh* — which depends on the *shel yad* — before removing the *shel yad* itself. To remove the *shel yad* while the *shel rosh* is still on would be to tear away the foundation from what rests upon it.

This dependency is not a strict halachic prohibition in the sense that one cannot wear the *shel yad* or *shel rosh* independently — the Gemara acknowledges *ein me'akvin zeh et zeh*. But it expresses an ideal structure: the two together constitute a unified *mitzvah*, with the *shel rosh* presupposing and building upon the *shel yad*.

---

## Time Restrictions

### Placement Timing

The Gemara asks: *mei'ematai nevarech aleihen?* — from when does one make the *beracha* on *tefillin*? The answer is *mishat hanachatan* — from the time of placing them on.

---

## Order of Putting On (III)

### Veyayu Plural

Rav Kahana, in explaining the dependency of the *shel rosh* on the *shel yad*, grounds it in the same verse: *v'hayu l'totafot bein einecha* — the plural *v'hayu* signifies that both must be present simultaneously whenever the *shel rosh* is being worn. This provides the basis for the rule that one removes the *shel rosh* before the *shel yad*.

---

## Order of Putting On (III)…

### Building Dependency

The underlying principle is a distinction between *state* and *action*. The *shel rosh* is dependent on the *shel yad* in terms of the state of wearing: the proper state is one in which both are present, with the *shel rosh*'s presence presupposing the *shel yad*'s. This is a dependency of *havayah* — of being — rather than of the initial act of placement. As such, while one can put on either independently, the ongoing state of wearing the *shel rosh* is halachically conditioned on also wearing the *shel yad*.

---

## Time Restrictions (II)

### Early Placement

The question of timing the *beracha* connects to a further scenario. What if someone wakes up early, before daybreak, and wants to wear their *tefillin* so as not to risk losing them on a journey? The Gemara addresses this: *haya mashkim latzet laderech umityarei shema yovedu* — if one rises early to travel and fears the *tefillin* might be lost if left behind, *menichan* — one may put them on even before daybreak.

### Touching When Light

When the time for *tefillin* arrives — at daybreak — one touches and feels them: *u'kshe'yagia zman memashmesh bahen u'mevarech aleihen*. The act of touching them at the proper time constitutes a renewed placing-on, and one then makes the *beracha*.

This halakha illuminates the interplay between *keshira* and *hanacha* discussed earlier. The initial act of putting the *tefillin* on — the *keshira*, the tightening, the binding — was performed before the proper time. What activates the *beracha* is not merely the initial physical act but the *state* of wearing at the right time. The touching reframes the situation: one is now *meniach* — bearing the *tefillin* — during the valid period, and the *beracha* applies to that state. This reinforces the idea that the *mitzvah* of *tefillin* has a dimension of *havayah* — of being in the state of wearing — and not only of the initial act of placing.

### Sunset Removal

How long may one wear *tefillin*? *Ad shetishka ha'chama* — until sunset.

### Night Prohibition

Two distinct rationales are offered for not wearing *tefillin* at night. The first is *laila lav zman tefillin* — night is simply not the halachic time for *tefillin*, derived from the *pessukim* in a manner paralleling other *mitzvot* that are time-bound to the day. This is a formal *din* defining the temporal scope of the *mitzvah*. The second concern is entirely different in character: a fear that one will fall asleep while wearing *tefillin* and pass gas, which would be a violation of the *kedusha* of the *tefillin*. This is a rabbinic concern rooted in bodily propriety, not in a definitional exclusion of nighttime.

The two rationales lead to different practical consequences, as the subsequent opinions make clear.

### Market Clearing

Rav Nachman rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Yaakov* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yaakov, who said one may continue wearing *tefillin ad shetichleh regel min hashuk* — until the foot clears the market, meaning until people have finished their business and the streets have emptied, sometime after sunset. This standard is not based on the formal *din* of *laila lav zman tefillin* but on the practical concern of sleep: as long as people are still active in the market, the risk of falling asleep is not yet acute.

### Evening Prayer Dispute

The Gemara reports that Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna *matzlu behu b'orta* — they prayed the evening prayer while wearing *tefillin* at night. This is recorded as support for wearing *tefillin* after nightfall, at least for *Ma'ariv*.

However, an alternative reading of this tradition is offered: *ein halacha k'Rabbi Yaakov* — we do not rule like Rabbi Yaakov — meaning one must remove *tefillin* at sunset, not later. Under this view, if the formal *din* is *laila lav zman tefillin*, then wearing *tefillin* after sunset would be impermissible, and the practice of Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna constitutes a position that some hold and others dispute. The *machloket* is thus whether one may keep *tefillin* on into the evening, particularly for *Ma'ariv* — a question that remains open and will be taken up in the continuation of the *sugya*.

---

---

# Menachot 36b

## Night & Tefillin

### Night: Time for Tefillin?

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion about whether night constitutes a proper time for wearing *tefillin*. The *Gemara* had already introduced several opinions about when one must remove *tefillin*: at the moment of halachic nightfall, at *bein hashmashos* (twilight), when people have finished commuting home (*tichleh regel min hashuk*), or when it is time to sleep. The latter two criteria are not, strictly speaking, halachic definitions of night and day. Rather, they reflect a rabbinic concern that if one is still wearing *tefillin* at the hour when people typically go to sleep, one risks falling asleep while wearing them.

### Sleep & Impurity

The concern about falling asleep with *tefillin* is not simply one of discomfort or negligence — it is specifically a concern that one might pass gas while unconscious. This is the driving rabbinic worry. One might reasonably ask: why is this concern limited to nighttime? Throughout the day, a person is awake and can exercise control; if one is about to pass gas, one removes the *tefillin*. The answer, of course, is that nighttime brings the risk of falling asleep unawares, which removes that conscious self-regulation.

### Mitzvah vs. Prohibition

This raises a deeper conceptual question. Even granting that *laila lav zman tefillin* — night is not a time for *tefillin* — why should that fact generate an active prohibition against continuing to wear them? There are many *mitzvos* that do not apply at night: one is not obligated to take *lulav* at night, yet no one suggests it is *assur* to hold a *lulav* after nightfall. *Tzitzis* presents an analogous case — there is debate about whether wearing a four-cornered garment at night creates any obligation, yet we do not routinely tear off our *tzitzis* at nightfall.

Part of the answer may involve *bal tosef* — adding to the commandment in a prohibited manner — if one is intentionally wearing *tefillin* at night as an act of the *mitzvah*. But beyond that, there is a deeper structural point. *Tefillin* involves two distinct dimensions: there is the active dimension of *ukshartam*, the act of binding, and there is the dimension of *vehayu*, a state of being. The *Gemara* will shortly compare *tefillin* to the *tzitz* worn by the *Kohen Gadol*, and the comparison illuminates this point. A state of being that is "always on," without temporal boundaries, loses its character as a meaningful state. For something to function as an *ot* — a sign — it requires limits. If it is perpetually present, it is no longer a sign; it is simply background.

### Rav Huna's Case

The *Gemara* raises a difficulty from an earlier ruling of Rabbah bar Rav Huna. The *Gemara* asks: did Rabbah bar Rav Huna really say one may continue wearing *tefillin* into the night? Yet Rabbah bar Rav Huna himself ruled that during *bein hashmashos* — the ambiguous twilight period — one neither removes the *tefillin* already on nor puts on new ones. The implication of that ruling is that once it is definitely night (*vaddai chashecha*), one must remove them (*choletz*). How, then, could Rabbah bar Rav Huna have kept his *tefillin* on when it came time to *daven Maariv*, as was described at the end of the previous *daf*?

### Shabbat Exception

The *Gemara* resolves this by specifying: *hatam b'erev Shabbos itmar* — the ruling about removing *tefillin* at definite nightfall was stated specifically in reference to Friday night. On a Friday night, one is not merely confronting the question of whether night is a time for *tefillin*; one is confronting *Shabbos*, which everyone agrees is *lav zman tefillin*. Rabbah bar Rav Huna may have taken a more lenient position regarding ordinary weeknights — where the concern is only about sleeping and passing gas, such that he held one need not remove *tefillin* already in place — but on Friday night, the onset of *Shabbos* itself, which is unambiguously *lav zman tefillin*, would require removal.

The *Gemara* then sharpens the question. What does Rabbah bar Rav Huna actually hold? If he holds that *laila lav zman tefillin* — that night is not a time for *tefillin* — then *Shabbos* should follow the same logic, since *Shabbos* is excluded by the same verse. If he holds that night *is* a time for *tefillin*, then *Shabbos* requires a separate exclusion. The *Gemara* answers: it is indeed from a separate source that we exclude *Shabbos*, and this is where the *Gemara* turns to the *derashos*.

---

## Sources for Exclusions

### V'shamarta Source

A *braisa* is cited: the verse *v'shamarta es hachuka hazos l'moadah miyamim yamima* — "You shall observe this statute at its appointed time, from year to year" — appears in the context of *Pesach*, but also in proximity to the verse *v'haya l'os al yadecha ul'totafos bein einecha* regarding *tefillin*. The question is whether *v'shamarta* applies only to the *korban Pesach* or also to *tefillin*. The phrase *miyamim yamima* — "from days to days" — is read as: *yamim*, days and not nights; and *miyamim*, some days and not all days, excluding *Shabbosos* and *yamim tovim*. This is the view of Rabbi Yosi ha-Glili.

### Yosi vs. Akiva

Rabbi Akiva disputes this reading. He says *lo ne'emar chuka zu ela l'Pesach bilvad* — this statute refers to *Pesach* alone, not to *tefillin*. According to Rabbi Akiva, the verse excluding night and *Shabbos* simply does not apply to *tefillin*. Yet Rabbi Akiva still holds that one does not wear *tefillin* on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*. How does he know this?

### Akiva's 'Ot' Logic

The *Gemara* cites another *braisa* where Rabbi Akiva states: one might think a person should put on *tefillin* on *Shabbosos* and *yamim tovim*. Therefore the verse teaches: *v'haya l'os al yadecha ul'totafos bein einecha* — the sign on your hand and the *totafos* between your eyes. The *tefillin* are worn only when they are needed to serve as an *ot*, a sign. Therefore: *yatzu Shabbosos v'yamim tovim she-gufam os* — *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* are excluded because they themselves are an *ot*. And it is on this basis that Rabbah bar Rav Huna — who follows Rabbi Akiva — held that one may wear *tefillin* on an ordinary night but must remove them on Friday night at the onset of *Shabbos*.

### 'Ot' as Sign

The conceptual significance of the *ot* framework deserves attention. For something to function as a sign, it must have limits. If it is constant, it ceases to be a sign — it is simply the ambient condition. The implication is not merely that one is exempt from wearing *tefillin* on *Shabbos*, but that one is actively prohibited from doing so. Wearing *tefillin* on *Shabbos* would in some sense undermine the *kedushas Shabbos*, treating *Shabbos* as insufficient to serve as its own sign. The result is that both *tefillin* and *Shabbos* are diminished: neither is fully expressing its own unique character as an *ot*.

A striking parallel emerges with the *Kohen Gadol* and the *tzitz*. The *Kohen Gadol* wears the *tzitz* to maintain God-consciousness. But on *Yom Kippur*, when he performs the *Avodas Yom HaKippurim* and enters the *Kodesh Kodashim* in *bigdei lavan*, he does not wear the *tzitz*. Why? Because the *tzitz* exists to remind one of God. If one is directly encountering God in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the *tzitz* is not only unnecessary — wearing it would in some sense be an incongruity, even a *p'gia*. The same logic applies here: who needs the *ot* of *tefillin* when one is having the encounter of *Shabbos* itself?

### Tosafot: Ot Extension

This leads directly to the question of *Chol HaMoed*, which is not discussed in the *Gemara* at all but is a major *machlokes Rishonim* that remains unresolved until today. The relevant *Tosafos* is found a few wide lines into the *daf*. *Tosafos* says: *yatzu Shabbosos v'yamim tovim she-ein atem keruyin os*. The *ot* of *Yom Tov* is not — *Tosafos* emphasizes — a function of *issur melachah*. He writes explicitly: *de-afilu Chol HaMoed de-shari ba-asiyas melachah ika os* — even on *Chol HaMoed*, where *melachah* is permitted, there is nonetheless an *ot*. What constitutes the *ot* of *Yom Tov*? *Tosafos* answers: it is the *mitzvos ha-yom* — *Pesach* through the prohibition of *chametz*, *Sukkos* through the obligation to dwell in the *sukkah*. These *mitzvos aseh* constitute the experiential memory and distinctive character of the *Yom Tov*. Since *Chol HaMoed* participates in those *mitzvos*, it too is an *ot*, and therefore one does not wear *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed* according to *Tosafos*.

Other *Rishonim* strongly disagree and ground the *ot* exclusively in *issur melachah*. On this view, *Chol HaMoed* does not fully qualify, and *tefillin* should be worn. Different communities have different *minhagim* reflecting this *machlokes*. Some who were careful to perform *melachah* on *Chol HaMoed* would wear *tefillin* there, and when they reached a stage of life where they no longer worked on *Chol HaMoed*, they stopped. A reasonable middle position is to wear *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed* without a *berachah*, thereby fulfilling the *mitzvah* in case it is obligatory while acknowledging the *safek* — though the practical difficulty is that one tends to recite the *berachah* by force of habit.

One further dimension: the *Gemara* states that the *ot* of the *shel yad* is *lecha le-os* — for you, not for others. *V'lo le-acherim le-os*. The *ot* of the *shel yad* is internal; the *ot* that is visible to others is the *shel rosh*, about which it says *ve-ra'u kol amei ha-aretz*. This distinction is relevant because the question of whether *tefillin* functions as a *lecha le-os* or a public sign shapes how we think about who must be "seeing" the *ot*, and therefore what days or times qualify as already possessing an *ot* sufficient to render *tefillin* superfluous.

*Tosafos* also cites the famous practice of the *benei ma'arava* — the Jews of *Eretz Yisrael* — who would make a *berachah* upon removing their *tefillin*, based on the verse *v'shamarta es hachuka hazos*: *Baruch Atah Hashem... asher kidshanu be-mitzvosav ve-tzivanu lishmor chukkav*. This is a *berachah acharonah* upon removal. *Tosafos* suggests this practice would make sense specifically when one is removing *tefillin* close to nightfall — taking them off because the time of *tefillin*-wearing is ending. This reinforces the conceptual point that *tefillin* is not merely an act (*ukshartam*) but a defined state (*vehayu*), analogous to *Kiddush* and *Havdalah* that bracket *Shabbos*: one enters the state and then formally exits it. The *berachah* at removal reflects this framing of *tefillin* as a period, a bounded state of being, rather than simply a discrete act.

---

## Active Prohibition

### Elazar's Prohibition

The *Gemara* now states explicitly: *amar Rabbi Elazar: kol hamaniach tefillin achar shekias hachamah over b'aseh* — one who leaves *tefillin* on after sunset violates a positive commandment. The prohibition is derived from the verse *v'shamarta es hachuka hazos*, which the *Gemara* reads as a command to actively observe the proper time-bound parameters of *tefillin*.

### Elazar vs. Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan goes further: *over belav* — one violates a negative prohibition. The dispute turns on the rule articulated by Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ila: whenever the Torah uses the formulation *hishamer*, *pen*, or *al*, it always denotes a *lo sa'aseh*, a negative prohibition. The *Gemara* initially suggests that Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan may simply disagree about whether to accept this rule. The *Gemara* rejects this: *kulei alma is lehu de-Rabbi Avin* — everyone accepts the rule of Rabbi Avin. The dispute is more nuanced. Rabbi Elazar holds that *hishamer de-aseh* — a *shimur* formulation attached to a positive obligation — produces a positive commandment, not a negative one. Rabbi Yochanan holds that *hishamer de-aseh nami lav* — the *shimur* language always generates a *lo sa'aseh* regardless of whether it is commanding action or restraint.

### Protection Exception

The *Gemara* qualifies the prohibition: *amar Rabbi Elazar: de-im leshomram mutar* — if one's intention in keeping *tefillin* on at night is to protect them, it is permissible. *Rashi* extends this further: it is even permissible to put *tefillin* on at night for the purpose of protecting them — for example, if one is traveling and fears that removing the *tefillin* would result in damage or loss. The classic *Gemara* discussion about *Shabbos* offers a similar context: if one finds *tefillin* in a public domain on *Shabbos* and has no *eiruv*, is one permitted to wear them in order to carry them to safety? This scenario interweaves both the question of *Shabbos lav zman tefillin* and the question of whether wearing them constitutes carrying. The rationale for permitting such wearing for protection is that *tefillin* worn purely for protective purposes are not being worn as an *ot* — and if they are not functioning as an *ot*, the concern that generates the prohibition does not apply.

### Rav Ashi's Case

Ravina reports a striking anecdote: *havina yasivna kamei de-Rav Ashi* — I was sitting before Rav Ashi. It grew dark, and Rav Ashi put on *tefillin*. The others asked him: *lishmor ka bei lehu mar?* — Are you doing this to protect them? He said yes. But Ravina records: *vachaziteih bedateih de-lav lishmor bei* — I could see from his manner that protecting them was not actually his intention. A textual note: the *Tzeidah LaDerech* emends the reading, suggesting Rav Ashi had not put them on but merely left them on, which would better conform to the earlier *Gemara* holding that at minimum everyone agrees one does not *put on* *tefillin* at night. But the core point stands regardless of the version.

### Halacha V'Ein Morin

Why the ruse? *Kasavar: halacha v'ein morin kein.* Rav Ashi held the *ikar halacha* to be that night is indeed a time for *tefillin*, but he held equally that this *halacha* should not be publicly taught — *halacha v'ein morin kein*. The reason is evident: if people knew that wearing *tefillin* at night was permitted, it would inevitably lead to sleeping with them on and passing gas, which the Rabbis were specifically concerned to prevent. Even though *me'ikar hadin* one could leave them on well into the night, this was not something to publicize.

This raises interesting broader questions about the doctrine of *halacha v'ein morin kein*. Does a rabbi in such a situation say the *halacha* is otherwise? Does he simply decline to answer? Does he permit some degree of obfuscation? A famous *Gemara* in *Beitzah* illustrates the tension: someone asked an *Amora* whether it was permitted to extinguish a light on *Yom Tov* for a couple wishing privacy. The *Amora* kept suggesting alternatives — go to another room, put up a partition — and finally expressed exasperation. Several *Rishonim* conclude that the *Amora* held *halacha v'ein morin kein* and therefore refused to state the *halacha* directly, but the questioner was not taking the hint. The broader tension — between accurately representing *halacha* and managing what information flows to the general public — is something the *Gemara* takes seriously as a genuine category of rabbinic authority.

---

## Constant Awareness

### Touching Tefillin

Rabbah bar Rav Huna teaches: *chayav adam lemashmesh bitefillin bechol sha'ah* — a person is obligated to constantly be touching and aware of his *tefillin* at every moment. The term *lemashmesh* is instructive: while it might suggest literal touching, the underlying intention is to remain continuously conscious of the fact that one is wearing *tefillin*, not to allow one's attention to drift entirely elsewhere.

### Kal Vachomer

This obligation is derived through a *kal vachomer* from the *tzitz*. The *tzitz* bears only a single mention of God's name — *Kodesh l'Hashem*. Yet the Torah says *ve-hayah al mitzcho tamid* — it shall be on his forehead *always*. From the word *tamid*, the *Gemara* derives *she-lo yasiach da'ato heimenu* — he must never allow his awareness of it to lapse. *Tefillin*, by contrast, contain many mentions of God's name. *Al achas kama v'chama* — how much more so must one maintain constant awareness of *tefillin*.

### Purpose: Awareness

The conceptual significance is profound. The purpose of carrying *Shem Hashem* on one's body — whether in the *tzitz* or in *tefillin* — is to sustain God-consciousness. If one's awareness lapses entirely, the purpose of the *mitzvah* is defeated even while one remains technically in compliance with wearing it. The *Gemara*'s comparison to the *tzitz* returns us to the earlier theme: just as the *Kohen Gadol*'s *tzitz* and the *tefillin* of every Jew both function to direct consciousness toward God, both require that consciousness to be maintained to fulfill their purpose. And just as the *tzitz* is not worn in the *Kodesh Kodashim* because that encounter supersedes the need for a symbolic reminder, so too does *Shabbos*, as an encounter with holiness, render the symbolic *ot* of *tefillin* unnecessary — indeed, inappropriate.

---

## Shel Yad Placement

### 'Yadcha' = Left

A *braisa* is cited: *yadcha zu smol* — *yadcha*, "your hand," refers to your left hand. The question is raised: perhaps it refers to the right? Two proofs are offered from *Tanach*. First: *af yadi yasdah eretz vi-ymini tipchah shamayim* — "My hand founded the earth and My right hand stretched out the heavens." Here *yad* is distinguished from *yamin*, which denotes the right, so *yad* by itself would refer to the left. A second proof, from the story of Yael: *yadah la-yased tishlachnah vi-yminah la-halmus amelim* — "Her hand she stretched toward the tent peg, and her right hand toward the workers' hammer." Since Yael needs one hand on the tent peg and the other to wield the hammer, the two hands must be distinct. The *yad* holding the peg is her left hand; the *yamin* wielding the hammer is her right. This proof is stronger because it involves a two-handed action that clearly differentiates the two.

### HaCharum Challenge

Rabbi Yosi HaCharum — about whom *Tosafos* notes that *Rashi*'s reading of his name as a reference to a physical feature (*chotmo meshuka*, a pressed-in nose) is difficult, since calling a *Tanna* by a derogatory nickname is problematic; *Tosafos* suggests *Chorem* was the name of a place — objects that *yad* can in fact refer to the right hand. His proof: *vayar Yosef ki yashis aviv yad yemino* — "And Joseph saw that his father placed his right hand." Here *yad* is used with the modifier *yemino*, the right. The *Gemara* responds: *yad yemino ikrei* — with an explicit modifier specifying the right, *yad* may indeed refer to the right. But *yad stama* — *yad* without any modifier — *lo ikrei*, it would not naturally refer to the right. Unmodified *yad* denotes the left.

### Natan: Bind Right

Rabbi Natan offers an independent derivation. He says: *eino tzarich* — there is no need for those proofs. The verse says *ukeshartem ukhtavtam* — "you shall bind and you shall write." Just as writing (*ktivah*) is done with the right hand, so too binding (*kshirah*) is done with the right hand. And since the *kshirah* must be performed by the right hand, the *tefillin* must be placed on the left — for one binds upon the arm that bears the *tefillin* using the opposite, stronger hand.

This derivation reframes the *mitzvah* in a significant way. Rather than saying "the *halacha* is that *tefillin* is worn on the weak hand," Rabbi Natan says: "the *halacha* is that *tefillin* must be bound with the right hand; the consequence is that they are placed on the left." This shifts the conceptual center of gravity. The *ikkar* of the *mitzvah*, on this reading, is the act of *ukshartam* — the binding — and the placement on the left arm is a derivative of that primary obligation. This bears on the broader question of whether *tefillin* is primarily a *mitzvah* of *ukshartam*, an active binding, or a *mitzvah* of wearing and the resultant state of *vehayu*.

### Weak vs. Left

The *Gemara* also introduces a third derivation: from the word *yadechah* written with a *kaf-hei* (as opposed to a *kaf sofit*), read as *yad kehah* — your weak arm. Rava challenges: perhaps the *kaf-hei* stands for *koach*, indicating the strong arm. Rav Ashi responds: it is not written with a *ches* but with a *hei*; therefore it means *kehah*, weak, not *koach*, strong.

The *nafka mina* between the objective criterion (left hand) and the subjective criterion (weak hand) is the case of a lefty. According to the objective reading, every person — righty or lefty — wears *tefillin* on their anatomical left hand. According to the *yad kehah* reading, a lefty wears *tefillin* on their right hand, because that is their weak hand. A *braisa* states: *iter maniach tefillin bi-yemino* — a lefty puts his *tefillin* on his right hand, meaning his weak hand, which is anatomically his right. Another *braisa* appears to say even a lefty puts it on his anatomical left. Abaye resolves the contradiction: the second *braisa* refers to *shotef shtei yadav* — an ambidextrous person, who has no dominant hand. For such a person, we follow the majority of people and treat the person as right-handed, placing *tefillin* on the anatomical left.

### Tosafot Refinement

*Tosafos* raises a more nuanced case: what about someone who writes with their right hand but performs most other tasks with their left — or vice versa? *Tosafos* poses the question explicitly: *yeish l'histapeik d'eizeh meihen maniach tefillin* — which hand does such a person use? If we emphasize *ukeshartam ukhtavtam*, the hand of writing is determinative, and such a person is treated as a righty. If we emphasize *yad kehah*, then the question of which is truly the "weak" hand becomes complex, and the answer may depend on which activities we weight more heavily.

*Tosafos* concludes: *v'shema yeish l'dimoto k'shotef shtei yadav* — perhaps such a person is treated like an ambidextrous person, defaulting to the majority rule and placing *tefillin* on the left. The consideration here is that on the *ukeshartam ukhtavtam* reading, writing clearly tips in favor of treating this person as right-handed. And even on the *yad kehah* reading, writing is a highly significant activity, so the *kehah* of the non-writing hand remains arguable. The two considerations compound: *ukeshartam* clearly points to treating the person as a righty, and *yad kehah* is at best indeterminate, so together they favor the anatomical left.

The case becomes more complicated in the mirror image: a person who writes with the left but does everything else with the right. Here *ukeshartam ukhtavtam* points to treating this person as a lefty — placing *tefillin* on the right hand — while *yad kehah* arguably points the other way, or at minimum is unclear. The halachic literature on people who were trained to write right-handed in Europe despite being naturally left-handed engages exactly this question and reflects the genuine conceptual tension between these two derivations.

---

## Physical Requirements

### Gidam Debate

The *Gemara* addresses the case of a *gidam* — a person with an amputated arm. One *braisa* states: *ein lo zeroa patur min ha-tefillin* — if a person does not have an arm, he is exempt from *tefillin*. Another *braisa* cites *Acheirim*: the word *yadechah* — with the *kaf-hei* of *yad kehah* — comes to include even the *gidam*, indicating that even a person with an amputation is obligated. The presumption is that the amputation is not complete — that enough of the muscle of the upper arm remains to constitute a viable *mekom hanachah*.

### Shulchan Aruch Ruling

The *Rema* in *Siman* 27 rules: a *gidam* who has lost the hand but retains the *zeroa* — the upper arm — puts on *tefillin belo berachah*, without a blessing, splitting the difference between the two *beraisos* given the halachic *safek*. The *Mishnah Berurah* adds: if there is no left arm at all, and there is no place to put the *tefillin shel yad*, then the person does not wear the *shel yad*. One might ask whether such a person wears the *shel rosh* alone. The answer is yes — and with both *berachos*, since the *shel rosh* requires two *berachos* of its own when worn without the *shel yad*.

### Missing Right Arm

If, however, it is the right arm that is missing — meaning the person has no arm with which to perform the binding — the *Mishnah Berurah* rules that someone else performs the *kshirah* on his behalf. He still wears *tefillin* on his left arm; he simply cannot do the binding himself. This ruling is highly revealing for the conceptual question. If the primary *mitzvah* were the act of *ukshartam* — binding — one might say that a person who cannot bind is an *onnes* who is entirely exempt. Instead, the *halacha* assumes that the *mitzvah* of wearing *tefillin* remains fully in force, and the physical binding is merely a means to that end. The person still has a left arm on which to *wear* *tefillin*, and someone assists in placing them there.

### Feinstein: Paralysis

Rav Moshe Feinstein was asked about a person who suffers paralysis in his left arm. Is this person in a situation analogous to not having an arm — and therefore exempt or required to wear without a *berachah* — or is the arm halachically present since it is physically there? Rav Moshe distinguishes carefully. If the arm is shriveled and has no blood flowing through it — even if it remains physically attached — he holds it is not considered a halachically viable arm, and the person would not make a *berachah*. However, if the paralysis stems from a neurological cause — a problem in the brain or spinal cord — and the arm itself is physically healthy with normal blood flow and no atrophy, then the arm is fully present. The inability to move it does not render it halachically absent. Such a person wears *tefillin* on the paralyzed arm with a full *berachah*.

Rav Moshe adds a poignant personal note at the close of the *teshuvah*: *z'chorni she-abba mari hagaon zatzal she-hayah lo alaynu choleh shiva chodashim ha'acharonim machamat machalas haparalysis mitzido hasmoli* — "I recall that my father, the *gaon*, spent the last seven months of his life ill from paralysis of his left side, and he put on *tefillin* on his left paralyzed arm" — in accordance with this ruling.

---

## Shel Rosh Location

### Anatomy Definition

*Tanna d'vei Menashe* provides the anatomical definitions: *al yadecha* — "on your hand" — refers to *kibores*, the muscle of the upper arm. *Bein einecha* — "between your eyes" — refers to *kadkod*, the skull or cranium, not the forehead. These definitions resolve a natural reading: the verse seems to say the *tefillin* of the head should go literally between the eyebrows. *Tanna d'vei Menashe* establishes that *bein einecha* means the top of the skull.

### Infant's Soft Spot

The school of Rabbi Yannai pinpoints the location more precisely: *makom she-mocho shel tinok rofes* — the place where the soft spot on an infant's skull is located. This is the fontanelle, situated not near the forehead but higher up on the crown. The *Gemara* also establishes that *tefillin* must be placed *bemakom se'ar*, where hair grows, and notes that there is a sufficient span of space on the head to accommodate *tefillin* — indeed, the *Gemara* says *makom yesh ba-rosh lehaniach shenei tefillin*, there is room on the head for two sets of *tefillin*, alluding to the dispute between *Rashi* and *Rabbeinu Tam*. In practice, one places the bottom edge of the *tefillin* at the hairline and the *tefillin* sits upward from there.

### Two Heads Case

The *Gemara* introduces one of its most striking narratives. Plimo — a name that may itself be significant, since *peli* in Aramaic means to mock or jest — asked Rabbi: if someone had two heads, on which one does he put *tefillin*? Rabbi was outraged and told him: either go into exile (*kum gali*) or accept *shamta* upon yourself — some form of communal sanction — as punishment for asking such a disrespectful, absurd question.

At that very moment, a man walked into the *beis medrash* and said: a baby was just born to me with two heads — *ittalid li yenuka d'is lei srei rashi* — and since it is a *bechor*, how much do I owe the *kohen*? The verse says one gives five *shekalim per gulgoles* — per head. One *bechor*, two heads: does he give five *shekalim* or ten?

A certain elder arrived and taught a *braisa*: *chayav lisein lo yud sla'im* — he must give ten *sela'im*. So the absurd case not only actually occurred, but had been codified in halachic literature. Rabbi had grown furious at what he took to be a frivolous question, only to discover that the question was entirely legitimate, had a precedent in a real case, and had been formally addressed *lehalacha*.

The *Gemara* then notes that a *braisa* of Rami bar Chama raises another complication: the verse *pado tifdeh bechor ha-adam* might imply an obligation of *pidyon* even if the infant is a *treifah* — that is, cannot survive. The *Gemara* cites *ach* to exclude this. The *Gemara* then asks: but the case of two heads may itself suggest non-viability — would such an infant be considered a *treifah*? The *Gemara* responds: *shani hacha de-begulgoleth tala Rachmana* — the Torah's formulation "per head" makes the *pidyon* contingent on heads, and once the questions of viability and *treifah* status are addressed, the question of five or ten *shekalim* is entirely legitimate.

The *Gemara* ends without telling us which head the *tefillin* goes on.

### Height Derivation

The *Gemara* now returns to the derivation. It asks: *minalan* — from where do we know that the *shel rosh* goes on the height of the head rather than literally between the eyes? A *braisa* derives it through *gezerah shavah*: the same phrase *bein einecha* appears in the context of *tefillin* and in the prohibition against making a bald spot: *lo tasimu karcha bein eineichem lamet* — do not make a bald spot between your eyes for the dead. The latter passage refers unambiguously to the area where hair grows, and the *gematria* of bodies confirms this is the height of the head. *Mah lehallan b'gova sheba-rosh makom she-oseh karchah* — just as there it is the height of the head where a bald spot is made, so too here.

### Yehuda Alternative

Rabbi Yehuda offers an independent derivation from the laws of *negaim*, skin lesions. The Torah places *tefillin* on the hand and on the head: *hanach tefillin beyad hanach tefillin barosh*. Just as the *tefillin* of the hand is placed where only a single category of *nega* applies — skin lesions — so too the *tefillin* of the head must be placed where only a single category of *nega* applies. If the *tefillin* were placed literally between the eyes — on the forehead just above the eyebrows — there would be two categories of *negaim* present: the skin of the forehead and the hair of the eyebrows. There would be the *nega* of white hair (*seiar lavan*) and the *nega* of yellow hair (*seiar tzahov*), each applicable to a different substrate. The only place on the head where only a single category of *nega* applies is the scalp covered by hair — *bemakom se'ar* alone — and that is where *tefillin* goes.

With this derivation, the *Gemara*'s treatment of *tefillin* concludes, and the *masechta* turns to the laws of *tzitzis*, which will occupy the next chapter entirely.

---

---

# Menachot 37

## Night & Tefillin

### Night as Zman

The discussion on 36b continuing into 37 concerns the question of whether night constitutes a designated time for wearing *tefillin*. The *gemara* had introduced a range of opinions regarding precisely when one must remove *tefillin*: some hold that removal is required as soon as the sun sets — which is the *halachik* definition of night — while others point to *tichleh regel min hashuk*, the time when people finish returning from work, or the onset of the time for sleeping. These latter two criteria are not *halachik* definitions of night at all. Rather, they reflect a rabbinic concern that a person may fall asleep while wearing *tefillin*, which could lead to a violation involving bodily awareness — *pacha gas*. The question of whether night is in principle *layla lav zman tefillin*, not a time for *tefillin*, thus hinges on whether the prohibition is rooted in Torah law or in this rabbinic concern about losing bodily control during sleep.

### Chasheicha Levels

A distinction must be carefully maintained here. The two later criteria — *tichleh regel min hashuk* and the time for sleeping — are not statements about when night halakhically begins. They are expressions of a rabbinic concern that one might doze off. The first criterion, sunset, is a genuine *halachik* definition. Understanding which category a given opinion belongs to determines whether we are dealing with a Torah-level question about *zman tefillin* or a rabbinic precaution against inadvertent sleep.

### Torah vs. Rabbinic

A natural question arises: even granting that night is not the designated time for *tefillin*, why does that fact generate an active prohibition to continue wearing them? After all, many *mitzvot* are not operative at night without any suggestion that one is forbidden to perform them nocturnally. It is not a *mitzvah* to take *lulav* at night — but is it prohibited to hold one's *lulav* at night? There may be a concern of *bal tosif* if one holds it as part of an act of performing the *mitzvah*, but it is not self-evidently *assur* merely because the daytime obligation has passed.

### Lulav & Tzitzit

*Tzitzit* presents an even more instructive comparison. We are not scrupulous about removing *tzitzit* at nightfall — and indeed there is debate whether one might in fact be *chayav* to wear them at night as *mitzvot beged yom*, an obligation that attaches to the garment by day. Part of the answer for *tefillin* may indeed involve a form of *bal tosif*, but part of it may be something deeper — that even the Torah's definition of *tefillin* as a *mitzvah* only during the day, and not at night, is connected to the concept of awareness and consciousness that the *mitzvah* requires.

### Action vs State

There is a deeper conceptual dimension here that connects to a fundamental question about the nature of the *mitzvah* of *tefillin*: is the *mitzvah* one of *ukshartem* — an act of binding — or of *vehayu* — a state of being? The language of the *pesukim* invokes both. If the *mitzvah* is primarily a *state*, then the Torah is effectively defining a bounded period during which that state must be maintained. A state without temporal limits is almost a contradiction in terms — it collapses the structure that gives it meaning.

### Kedusha Boundaries

This connects to a broader principle about *kedusha*. For something to possess sacred status, it requires definition — beginning and end, inside and outside. If a *mitzvah* could be performed at all times without limit, it would paradoxically lose the very character that makes it significant. Boundaries are not merely restrictions; they are constitutive of the *kedusha* itself. The limitation of *tefillin* to daytime is thus not simply a technical exclusion but part of what makes the wearing of *tefillin* meaningful as an *ot*, a sign.

---

## Rabba bar R. Huna

### Contradiction Setup

The *gemara* now presses a pointed question: the *gemara* reports that Rabba bar Rav Huna held that one who was already wearing *tefillin* during the day could continue wearing them into the night — suggesting that night is in some sense a permissible time. Yet the *gemara* cites another ruling by the very same Rabba bar Rav Huna: *safek chasheicha safek lo chasheicha — lo choleitz velo mani'ach*. If it is *bein hashemashot*, the twilight period, one neither removes the *tefillin* nor puts on new ones. The implication of this ruling is *ha vadai chasheicha choleitz* — if it is definitively night, he must remove them. This appears to contradict his apparent leniency in a prior story where he wore his *tefillin* when it came time to daven *Ma'ariv*.

### Erev Shabbat Context

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction: *hatam be'Erev Shabbat itamar* — that ruling about definitive nightfall requiring removal was stated specifically in the context of *Erev Shabbat*. What Rabba bar Rav Huna requires one to remove on Friday night is not rooted in the principle that night is *lav zman tefillin*. Rather, it is because *Shabbat* itself — which everyone agrees is *lav zman tefillin* — has arrived. If night were simply another period governed by the same rule as *Shabbat*, the distinction would collapse. Instead, the *gemara* treats the two as categorically different: *Shabbat* definitively excludes *tefillin*, while ordinary nighttime does not carry that same absolute exclusion.

### Safek Chasheicha

The *gemara* then asks directly: *mai kasavar?* — what did Rabba bar Rav Huna actually hold? If he held *layla lav zman tefillin*, then *Shabbat*, which is derived from the same *pasuk*, should also be excluded. If he held *Shabbat lav zman tefillin*, then by the same logic night should be excluded as well, since *demeheicha d'memaatet Shabbas me-hasam memaatet layla* — the same source that excludes *Shabbat* excludes night. His leniency in leaving *tefillin* on into the evening demonstrates that he held *layla* to be a permitted time; and his stringency on *Erev Shabbat* demonstrates that *Shabbat* itself is a separate and independent category of exclusion.

---

## Parashat Kadesh

### Source Text

The *gemara* now turns to the underlying scriptural derivation. It cites a *braita* built on the *pasuk* in *Parashat Kadesh*: *ve-shamarta et ha-chuka ha-zot l'moada mi-yamim yamima*. This verse appears in the context of *Pesach* and also in proximity to the *parshiyot* of *tefillin*. The phrase *m'yamim yamima* is parsed as follows: *yamim* — days and not nights; *mi-yamim* — some days and not all days, to exclude *Shabbatot* and *yamim tovim*. This exclusion is understood to apply to *tefillin*.

### R. Yosi vs. R. Akiva

This reading is the position of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, who understands the *pasuk* as addressing *tefillin*. Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *lo ne'emar chuka zu ela le-Pesach bilvad* — this *chuka* refers exclusively to the *korban Pesach*, not to *tefillin*. However, Rabbi Akiva nonetheless holds that *tefillin* are not worn on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* — he derives this from a different source entirely.

### Reconciling Views

The *gemara* therefore notes: *nafka lei me-heicha d'nafka lei l'Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva's exclusion of *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* from the time for *tefillin* comes from elsewhere. A second *braita* records Rabbi Akiva's own derivation: *yachol yani'ach adam tefillin be-Shabbatot u-ve-yamim tovim?* — perhaps one should wear *tefillin* on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*? The Torah says *ve-haya l'ot al yadecha u-le-totafot bein einecha* — they shall be a sign. The principle follows: *mi she-tzrichin ot* — only when a sign is needed. *Yatze'u Shabbatot ve-yamim tovim she-hen gufan ot* — excluded are *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, which are themselves signs, and therefore do not require this additional marking.

---

## Ot Framework

### R. Akiva Ot

Rabbi Akiva's derivation rests on a compelling conceptual logic: *tefillin* serve as an *ot*, a sign. The function of a sign is to mark and remind. When days already carry their own inherent significance as signs — as *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* do — the wearing of an additional *ot* does not supplement that significance; it undermines it. For something to function as a sign, it must stand out. If everything is always a sign, nothing is. Thus the very nature of the *ot* limits when it is appropriate.

The comparison to the *tzitz* of the *Kohen Gadol* is illuminating. The *Kohen Gadol* wears the *tzitz* — engraved *Kodesh l'Hashem* — on his forehead at all times as a reminder of God's presence and as an instrument of atonement. Yet on *Yom HaKippurim*, during the *avodat Yom HaKippurim*, he does not wear the *tzitz*; he wears *bigdei lavan* and enters the *Kodesh Kodashim*. The reason is precisely analogous: when you are in the immediate presence of the Divine, you do not need a reminder of that presence. The *tzitz* is for ordinary moments of service; the encounter in the *Kodesh Kodashim* transcends it. Similarly, *Shabbat* itself is an encounter of such depth that the *ot* of *tefillin* would be not merely superfluous but somewhat incongruous.

### Sign Function

There is a further dimension to this. The prohibition is not merely that one *need not* wear *tefillin* on *Shabbat* — one is *not allowed* to. This follows from the *pasuk*: if *tefillin* are excluded by Torah law from *Shabbat*, then wearing them would constitute a violation. The idea of the *ot* reinforces this: wearing *tefillin* on *Shabbat* would imply that *Shabbat* is insufficient as a sign on its own — a kind of *pgiya* in the *kedushat Shabbat*. Neither sign functions properly when the other is present simultaneously, because the presence of one appears to compensate for a deficiency in the other, and no such deficiency exists.

### Tosafot Ot

*Tosafot* on this *sugya* grapple with how to extend the *ot* logic to *Yom Tov*. The *Torah* does not explicitly call *Yom Tov* an *ot* in the same way *Shabbat* is called *os hi beini u-veineichem*. *Tosafot* therefore articulate that the *ot* of *Yom Tov* is not constituted by the prohibition of *melacha* — because even *Chol HaMoed*, on which *melacha* is permitted in various forms, can still be considered to carry an *ot*. Rather, *Tosafot* ground the *ot* of *Yom Tov* in the *mitzvot asei* that characterize those days — on *Pesach*, the prohibition of eating *chametz*; on *Sukkot*, the obligation to dwell in the *sukkah*. These *mitzvot* function as inherent commemorations of what the *yamim tovim* represent historically, and they constitute the *ot* that makes wearing *tefillin* unnecessary.

### Chol HaMoed

This analysis bears directly on *Chol HaMoed*, which is one of the major *machloket Rishonim* — a debate that runs through the medieval authorities and remains unresolved in the *gemara* itself. The *gemara* simply does not address *Chol HaMoed* explicitly; the entire discussion belongs to the *Rishonim*, particularly the *Hagahot Mordechai*. According to *Tosafot*, since *Chol HaMoed* carries its own *ot* — through the *mitzvas hayom*, the special and unique character of those days — one does not wear *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed*. Other *Rishonim* strongly disagree, tying the exclusion more directly to the *issur melacha*, which is less operative on *Chol HaMoed*. The dispute is serious on both sides: on one hand, *mitzvas tefillin* is a *mitzvas asei d'Oraita*; on the other, the *gemara*'s logic about the *ot* suggests that there are days when this *ot* must be withheld.

---

## Practices & Minhag

### Gemara Position

The *gemara*'s clear position is that *tefillin* are not worn on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. The question of *Chol HaMoed* is left unresolved within the *gemara* itself and belongs entirely to the realm of *Rishonim* and later *poskim*.

### Ashkenazi Minhag

The Ashkenazic *minhag* is to refrain from wearing *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed*. Sephardic communities have different practices, with variations regarding whether a *bracha* is recited if *tefillin* are worn. One approach among those who do wear *tefillin* on *Chol HaMoed* is to do so without a *bracha*, on the grounds that the *halacha* is genuinely unresolved and one should not risk a *bracha l'vatala*.

### No-Bracha Option

The logic of wearing *tefillin* without a *bracha* on *Chol HaMoed* is that one thereby fulfills the *mitzvah* while acknowledging the *safek* — the unresolved question — and thus avoids either neglecting the *mitzvas asei* entirely or desecrating the day through an unauthorized *bracha*. In practice, however, the challenge with this approach is the risk of reverting to *autopilot*: as soon as the *tefillin* goes on, the *bracha* can come out automatically, creating the further complication of what to do when one reaches the *shel rosh*.

---

## Awareness Obligation

### R. Elazar's Rule

The *gemara* states: *kol ha-meniach tefillin achar shki'at ha-chama over b'asei* — anyone who puts on *tefillin* after sunset has transgressed a positive commandment. This is Rabbi Elazar's position, grounded in the *pasuk* of *ve-shamarta*. Rabbi Yochanan goes further: *over b'lav* — one transgresses a negative prohibition, based on the use of *shimur* in the sense of *lo ta'aseh*, comparable to *shamarta et yom ha-Shabbat*. The *gemara* then considers whether Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan are in fact disputing the principle of *Rabbi Avin* citing *Rabbi Ila'a* — namely, that wherever the Torah uses the language of *hishamer*, *pen*, or *al*, it signifies a negative prohibition. The *gemara* concludes that this is not the crux of their dispute; rather, they differ on whether *hishamer d'asei* — a *shimur* that introduces a positive obligation — also carries the force of a *lav*.

### Lishmoran

There is an important exception: *d'im lishomram mutar* — if one keeps *tefillin* on after nightfall in order to protect them, it is permitted. If one is traveling at night and fears that removing the *tefillin* will result in their loss or damage — that they cannot be safely kept except by remaining on the body — then wearing them into the night is permitted under these circumstances.

### Halacha Without Moring

*Ravina* recounts that he once sat before Rav Ashi when it grew dark, and Rav Ashi put on his *tefillin*. When asked whether he was doing so *lishmuran* — to protect them — Rav Ashi confirmed that he was. But Ravina could discern from his manner — *ve-chazinan be-da'atei d'lav lishmuran hu ba'ei* — that protecting the *tefillin* was not in fact his intent. The explanation offered is that Rav Ashi held *halacha v'ein morin kein* — this is the *halacha*, but we do not teach it publicly. He genuinely held that *layla zman tefillin*, that night is a permitted time for *tefillin*, but he did not wish to broadcast this ruling lest it lead people to sleep while wearing them and thereby come to *pacha gas*. There is a textual variant — the *Tzeidah Laderech* switches the *girsa* to indicate that Rav Ashi simply did not remove *tefillin* he was already wearing, rather than actively putting on new ones — which would bring the story into conformity with earlier statements that everyone agrees one does not actively put on *tefillin* anew at night, even according to those who are lenient about keeping them on.

The category of *halacha v'ein morin kein* raises profound questions about the rabbinic communication of *halacha*. The approach is not to misrepresent the *halacha*, but to decline to publicize it — a kind of deliberate reticence — when the concern is that broader knowledge of the lenient ruling will lead to laxity and violation. A parallel case appears in *Beitzah*, where an *Amora* asked about turning off a light on *Yom Tov* for a couple seeking privacy, and kept deflecting with alternative suggestions until cornered into declaring the act *assur* — which some *Rishonim* understand as a case of *halacha v'ein morin kein* in which he held a lenient view but could not bring himself to state it openly.

### Mashmesh Concept

The *gemara* records: *chayav adam le-mashmesh be-tefillin be-chol sha'ah* — a person is obligated to constantly be in awareness of his *tefillin* at every moment. The proof comes from a *kal va-chomer* from the *tzitz*: the *tzitz* contains only one mention of God's name, *Kodesh l'Hashem*, yet the Torah says *ve-haya al mitzcho tamid* — it shall be on his forehead constantly. From the word *tamid* we learn *she-lo tassiach da'atenu mimenu* — he must not let his awareness wander from it. *Tefillin*, which contain many mentions of God's name, must certainly require this constant consciousness. The term *mashmesh* — touching or feeling — is a technique, a physical gesture that reinforces mental awareness; the underlying obligation is to remain consciously present to the fact that one is wearing *tefillin* and to what that wearing signifies. This connects back to the *ot* framework: the *tzitz* is not worn when entering the *Kodesh Kodashim* because at that moment one is in the direct presence of what the *tzitz* is meant to remind one of. Similarly, on *Shabbat*, the day itself accomplishes what *tefillin* are designed to accomplish.

---

## Which Hand

### Yad Definition

The *gemara* turns to the specific *halachot* of how *tefillin* are worn. The first question is which hand. A *braita* establishes: *yadcha — zo smol* — "your hand" means the left. The *gemara* offers scriptural support: *af yadi yis'dah aretz vi-ymini tipchah shamayim* — my "hand" founded the earth, while my "right" formed the heavens — demonstrating that *yad* and *yamin* are distinct terms, with *yad* denoting the left. A second proof comes from the account of *Yael* killing *Sisra*: *yadah layated tishlachnah vi-yminah le-halmut amelim* — her *yad* reached for the tent-peg while her right hand held the hammer. Since both hands are occupied simultaneously, they must be different hands, and since one is specified as *yemin* (right), the *yad* must be the left.

Rabbi Yose HaChareim objects: we find *yamin* itself called *yad*, as in *vayar Yosef ki yashit aviv yad yemino* — Joseph saw that his father placed his right *yad* on Ephraim. The *gemara* responds: *yad yemino ikrei* — with the modifier "right," *yad* can mean the right hand. But *yad stam* — the unmodified word *yad* — would not on its own denote the right hand.

### R. Natan Logic

Rabbi Natan takes a different approach: *eino tzarich* — one need not derive it from those verses at all. The *pasuk* itself says *u-keshartem u-chesavtem* — you shall bind and you shall write. Just as writing (*kesiva*) is done with the right hand — since most people are right-handed — so too the binding (*keshira*) is done with the right hand. If binding is performed with the right hand, then *hanacha bi-smol* — the placement must be on the left, because you are binding it *onto* your left arm with your right hand. This derivation is strikingly different from the others because it shifts the emphasis: the point is not primarily which body part *receives* the *tefillin*, but rather which hand *performs* the act of binding. The *mitzvah* is framed as an act of *kesharim* — tying — performed with one's dominant hand.

### R. Akiva Spelling

Rabbi Akiva derives the placement from the spelling of *yadcha*: *mi-yadcha*. The word is written *kaf hey* — with a *heh* — rather than *kaf* alone. Reading the *heh* as indicating *kehah* — weakness — the verse implies *yad kehah*, the weak hand. Since most people are right-handed, their weak hand is the left, and that is where *tefillin* are placed.

The *gemara* records a challenge from Rava to Rav Ashi: perhaps the *kaf hey* should be read as if written *kaf chet* — implying *koach*, strength — your strong hand? Rav Ashi responds: *mi ksiv be-chet?* — it is not written with a *chet*; the spelling with a *heh* is deliberate and indicates weakness.

### Lefty Rule

A *tanna'itic* dispute follows. One *braita* rules that a left-handed person (*itter*) places *tefillin* on his right hand — which is *his* weak hand — while another *braita* appears to say that even a left-handed person places *tefillin* on the left hand, as is the norm for everyone. Abaye resolves the contradiction: *ki tanya hi bi-ktu'ei bishtei yadav* — the latter *braita* speaks of an ambidextrous person. Since such a person has no genuinely weak hand, we default to the conventional norm — the objective left hand — rather than attempting to identify a subjectively weak one. For a true left-handed person, the ruling of the first *braita* applies: *tefillin* go on the right, because that is his *yad kehah*.

### Tosafot Balance

*Tosafot* raise a nuanced complication. The *gemara* has two partially overlapping derivations — *u-keshartem* (bind with the right hand, place on the left) and *yad kehah* (the weak hand). For a pure lefty, both lead to the same result: he writes with the left, so his binding hand is the left, and his weak hand is the right, meaning *tefillin* go on the right. But what about a person who writes with his right hand but performs most other tasks with his left? *Tosafot* note the uncertainty: from the perspective of *u-keshartem*, such a person would be treated as right-handed and would place *tefillin* on the left. From the perspective of *yad kehah*, the question of which is actually his weaker hand is less clear. *Tosafot* suggest that since the determination based on *u-keshartem* is unambiguous — writing is the primary indicator of handedness — and since even from the perspective of *yad kehah* the answer is debatable, one tips toward the conventional ruling and treats this person as right-handed, placing *tefillin* on the left. The harder case is the reverse: someone who writes with the left but does most other activities with the right, since there *u-keshartem* would point toward the left hand as dominant.

### Action vs Wearing

This entire discussion crystallizes a fundamental conceptual question: is *tefillin* primarily a *mitzvah* of *kesharim* — binding — or a *mitzvah* of *levisha* — wearing? Framing it as a *mitzvah* of *u-keshartem* shifts the focus: the real *ma'aseh mitzvah* is the act of tying, performed with the dominant hand, and the placement on the opposite arm is a consequence of that act. Framing it as *yad kehah* places the emphasis on the wearing — on which body part the *tefillin* must be worn. Most of the time these two framings converge on the same practical result. The divergence emerges precisely in the edge cases — the ambidextrous person, the person who writes with one hand but functions dominantly with the other — and in those cases the conceptual orientation becomes *halachically* determinative.

---

## Missing Limbs

### Gidem Status

The *gemara* turns to the *gidem* — one who lacks a hand but retains the upper arm. Two *beraitot* are cited with apparently conflicting rulings: one holds *ein lo zeroa patur min ha-tefillin* — if one lacks an arm, one is exempt from *tefillin*; another position (cited as *acherim omerim*) derives from the spelling of *yadcha* with a *kaf heh* that even a *gidem* remains *chayav* — since the verse expressly includes those lacking a hand, the obligation persists wherever there is still a viable *makom hanachah*.

### Rema Ruling

The *Rema* in *Siman* 27 rules: *gidem she-ein lo yad rak zeroa — yani'ach be-lo berachah* — a person who lacks the hand but retains the upper arm places *tefillin* without a *bracha*. The *Mishnah Berurah* clarifies the limits of this ruling: if the person does not have even the part of the upper arm muscle (*kiboret*) where *tefillin* are normally placed, then placing *tefillin* on the remaining stump is not meaningful, and the person does not wear *shel yad* at all. The underlying logic is that without a viable *makom hanachah*, there is no obligation to place, and placing without such a location serves no purpose.

### Shel Rosh Pivot

If the weak arm is entirely absent, the *halacha* pivots to *shel rosh*. Since *shel yad* and *shel rosh* are *einan me'akvin zeh et zeh* — they are not interdependent — the person still has a full *mitzvah* of *shel rosh*, and wears it with both *brachot*. This itself is a significant ruling: the loss of the weak arm creates an *ones* with respect to *shel yad* — the person is exempt from what they cannot perform — but does not diminish the obligation regarding the head *tefillin*.

### Rav Moshe Detail

Rav Moshe Feinstein was asked about a person with paralysis in the weak arm. The question is whether paralysis renders the arm legally absent — equivalent to the *gidem* case — or whether it is treated as an arm that is fully present despite its dysfunction. Rav Moshe reasons that paralysis in the arm is typically not caused by a pathology *in the arm itself* — *ela mitsad machala she-ba-moach* — but rather in the brain or spinal cord. The arm retains its blood supply — *barur she-motzi dam harbeh* — and is therefore not comparable to a shriveled limb that has lost circulation. Where a limb has truly atrophied to the point of having no blood flow, Rav Moshe holds that even physical presence does not constitute a *zeroa* for purposes of this *mitzvah*; one would not make a *bracha*. But paralysis — where the arm is present, healthy in terms of circulation, and simply cannot be moved — does not reduce the arm to the status of *chasar* (absent). Such a person remains *chayav* in *tefillin shel yad* and wears them with a *bracha*.

### Father's Testament

In the final lines of this responsum, Rav Moshe adds a deeply personal note: *zecharono zecharuni* — his memory came back to him. His father, *hagaon zatzal*, was paralyzed on his left side during the last seven months of his life — *machalat ha-paraliz* — and nonetheless wore *tefillin* on his paralyzed left arm throughout that period. This personal testimony undergirds and authenticates the ruling: the principle that presence with loss of function still obligates was not merely a theoretical position for Rav Moshe, but one that his own father embodied in the most intimate circumstances.

---

## Body Placement

### Hand Placement

The *gemara* establishes where precisely on the arm *tefillin* are placed. *Al yadecha — zu govah she-ba-yad* — "your hand" in the context of *tefillin* refers to the elevated part of the hand, namely the upper arm muscle, the *kiboret*. The *gemara* raises the possibility that *al yadecha mamash* might mean literally the palm, but rejects this through a *hekkesh*: the same way the placement on the head is at its height — a point to be established from the *pasuk* on head *tefillin* — so too placement on the hand is at its height, which is the upper arm. Rabbi Yitzchak offers a corroborating derivation: *ve-samtem et devarai eileh al levavchem — u-keshartem* — it should be placed *kineged ha-lev*, adjacent to the heart. This is another convergent reason why *tefillin* go on the upper arm, on the left side, closest to the heart.

### Two Heads

The *gemara* presents one of its more striking exchanges in a discussion of where *tefillin* are placed on the head. *Pleimo* — whose name may itself derive from the Aramaic root *plai*, meaning to jest or mock — asked Rebbi: *mi she-yesh lo shenei rashim, be-eizeh meihem meniach tefillin?* If someone had two heads, on which does one place *tefillin*? Rebbi was deeply offended by the question, offering *Pleimo* the choice of either going into exile (*goleh*) or accepting *niddui*, and declaring it a disgraceful question unworthy of serious treatment.

The irony is that almost immediately a man arrived and reported to Rebbi: *islyid li yenuka de-is lei terei reishi* — he had just had a newborn with two heads. He wished to know how much to give the *kohen* for *pidyon ha-ben*, since the *pasuk* specifies payment *la-gulgolet* — per head — and a *bechor* with two heads might seem to require ten *shekalim* rather than five. An elder appeared and taught a *braita*: such a person is *chayav litten asara zuz*. Rebbi was left without a response: the case he had dismissed as absurd had both occurred in practice and been codified.

The *gemara* then notes a *braita* of Rami bar Chama raising whether a multiply-anomalous infant might be considered a *treifa* and thus exempt from *pidyon*, citing the verse *padot tifdeh et bechor ha-adam* with the limitation *ach* — implying not in all cases. The *gemara*'s response is *shani hacha de-vegulgolet tela Rachmana* — the Torah tied the obligation to the *gulgolet*, the head, and if there are two viable heads, one pays per head. The fate of the original question — which of two heads receives *tefillin* — remains technically unresolved.

### Head Placement

The *gemara* establishes where on the head *tefillin* are placed. *Bein einecha — zu govah she-ba-rosh* — "between your eyes" means the height of the head, not literally the space between the eyes. The derivation proceeds through *gezeirah shavah*: the same phrase *bein einecha* appears in the prohibition of making a *korcha* (*lo tasimu korcha bein eineichem la-met*). Since the *korcha* prohibition refers to making a bald spot where hair grows from — which is on the top of the skull, not at eye level — so too the placement of *tefillin bein einecha* is at the height of the head, at the place where hair grows. *Mah le-halan be-govah she-be-rosh, mekom she-oseh korcha, af kan be-govah she-be-rosh, mekom she-oseh korcha.*

The *gemara* further grounds this in the observation attributed to the academy of Rabbi Yannai: the location is *makom she-moach shel tinok rofes* — where the fontanelle of an infant pulsates, which is higher up on the skull. The common practice is to place the bottom edge of the *tefillin shel rosh* at the hairline, with the body of the *tefillin* resting above it.

---

## Privacy & Visibility

### R. Eliezer Ot

The *gemara* cites Rabbi Eliezer's view in the context of establishing the placement of *tefillin shel yad* on the upper arm. *Ve-haya lecha le-ot — lecha le-ot ve-lo le-acherim le-ot* — it shall be a sign for *you*, not a sign for others. This principle militates against the palm as a placement location: the palm, being naturally visible to others, would make the *ot* public, whereas the Torah frames it as a personal sign. The upper arm, by contrast, is positioned against the body and is less inherently visible, making it the appropriate location for a sign intended primarily for the wearer's own consciousness.

### Covering Custom

This principle of *lecha le-ot* generates the widespread *minhag* to cover *shel yad* when wearing it. In practice, one typically either pulls the sleeve down over the *tefillin* or places a small protective cover — a plastic casing — over the *shel yad*. The reason for the casing is pragmatic: pulling a sleeve repeatedly over the *tefillin* can rub away the sharp edges and compromise the required *ribuah* (squareness). The casing preserves the *tefillin* while still keeping them from being prominently visible. Strictly speaking, based on the continuation of the *sugya*, covering the *tefillin* is not a formal *halachic* obligation — it reflects the location principle of *lecha le-ot* — but it is the recognized and accepted *minhag*.

### Wound Story

The *gemara* records that Rav Ashi was once sitting before *Ameimar* and had a wound on his arm, causing him to tear his sleeve to relieve pressure on the injury. As a result, his *tefillin* became visible. *Ameimar* asked: does the Rav not hold by *lachem le-ot ve-lo le-acherim le-ot*? Rav Ashi responded: *be-makom "lachem le-ot" itmar* — the principle refers to the *place* where *tefillin* are worn, not to an independent obligation to cover them at all times. The requirement is that the *tefillin* be located in a spot that is inherently private — the upper arm — not that they be covered at every moment regardless of circumstance. When visibility occurs incidentally, as through a torn sleeve necessitated by a wound, no violation has occurred.

---

## Body Placement (II)

### R. Yehuda Negaim

Rabbi Yehuda offers an alternative derivation for the placement on the head, distinct from the *korcha* analogy. He reasons through an implicit *hekkesh* between the arm and the head: just as *tefillin* on the arm are placed where skin is subject to a single category of *negaim* — *or ha-basar*, the skin alone — so too *tefillin* on the head must be placed where only one category of *negaim* applies. If *tefillin* were placed literally between the eyes, the site would encompass both skin (*or ha-basar*) and the hair of the eyebrows, generating two distinct categories of *negaim*. The proper location on the head — where only *negei se'ar* apply — is the place where hair grows on the skull, which is the upper part of the head, not the forehead between the eyes. Rabbi Yehuda thus arrives at the same halakhic conclusion through a different *limud*, using the laws of *Negaim* as the terminological framework for defining which anatomical zones are in play.

---

## Conclusion & Next

### Tefillin Summary

With this we conclude the discussion of *tefillin* in Menachot.
