The *sugya* has traversed a remarkable range of questions: when in the day *tefillin* may be worn and when they must be removed; whether the operative prohibition at night is *de-Oraita* or rabbinic; how *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* are excluded through the *ot* principle; the precise placement on the body — arm and head — derived through comparison to *negaim*, *korcha*, and the heart; which hand bears the obligation, and how handedness affects the ruling for the lefty and the ambidextrous; the status of the *gidem*; the requirement of continuous *mashmesh* — mental awareness — while wearing *tefillin*; and the principle of *lecha le-ot*, a sign for the self rather than for public display. Running through all these discussions is the recurring tension between *tefillin* as a *mitzvah* of *kesharim* — an act of binding — and *tefillin* as a *mitzvah* of *levisha* — a state of wearing.

### Tzitzit Intro

With the conclusion of *tefillin*, the *masechet* moves into *Perek* 4, though it is incorporated here. The opening *Mishnah* of that *perek* reads:

> *Ha-techelet eina me'akevet et ha-lavan, ve-ha-lavan eino me'akev et ha-techelet. Tefilla shel yad eina me'akevet shel rosh, ve-shel rosh eina me'akevet shel yad.*

The *techelet* does not prevent the *lavan*, and the *lavan* does not prevent the *techelet*. *Tefillin shel yad* does not prevent *shel rosh*, and *shel rosh* does not prevent *shel yad*.

This *Mishnah* introduces the concept of *me'akev* — interdependence. Normally, when a *mitzvah* consists of multiple components, the absence of one component might invalidate the others. Here the *Mishnah* teaches that the pairs listed are *einan me'akvin zeh et zeh* — each can stand independently. The first pair, *techelet* and *lavan*, are the two threads of *tzitzit*: the blue-dyed thread and the white. Since the identity of the *chilazon* — the creature from which *techelet* was produced — has been lost, the ruling that *techelet* is not *me'akev lavan* is of profound practical importance, enabling the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* to be fully observed today with white threads alone. The second pair reaffirms what the *sugya* has just established about *tefillin*: *shel yad* and *shel rosh* are independent obligations, and if one is unavailable for any reason — whether through absence of a limb or any other circumstance — the other retains its full obligatory force.

---

---

# Menachot 38

## Tzitzit & Four Corners

### Opening & Transition

The daf opens with a transition from the previous *perek*'s focus on *sefarim*, *tefillin*, and *mezuzot* to the subject of *tzitzit*. This topic is introduced at the close of the third *perek* and becomes the central concern of the fourth. We pick up from the final lines of 37b, where the *mishna* is quoted.

### Four Corners Requirement

*Arba tzitziot me'akvot zu et zu she'arba'tan mitzvah achat* — the four *tzitziot* on the four corners of the garment prevent one another, meaning they are all mutually required, and all four together constitute a single *mitzvah*. The practical implication is stark: if one of the four *tzitziot* is missing, one does not fulfill three-quarters of a *mitzvah*, or even three *mitzvot* — one fulfills zero *mitzvot*.

### Tanna Kamma vs. R. Ishma…

The *mishna* records a dissenting view. Rabbi Ishmael holds: *arba'tan arba mitzvot* — the four *tzitziot* are four separate *mitzvot*. The *gemara* seeks to understand the precise nature of this dispute and articulate its practical ramifications.

### Mai Beinihu

The *gemara* asks: *mai beinihu* — what is the practical difference between these two positions? The most fundamental *nafka mina* is already apparent: if you have only three corners with *tzitzit*, according to the *tanna kamma*, who holds that all four combine into a single *mitzvah* and according to whom we *paskin*, you have fulfilled no *mitzvah* at all. According to Rabbi Ishmael, you have fulfilled three *mitzvot*, having simply failed to fulfill a fourth.

### Linen & Wool Case

Rav Yosef identifies a secondary *nafka mina*: *sadin be-tzitzit* — a linen garment with *tzitzit*. Since *techeiles* is necessarily wool, attaching *techeiles* strings to a linen garment creates a mixture of linen and wool, i.e., *shatnez*. This mixture is ordinarily forbidden but is permitted when one is fulfilling a *mitzvah*. According to the *tanna kamma*, however, if one lacks even a single *tzitzit*, no *mitzvah* is being performed at all, and one would therefore be violating the prohibition of *shatnez* without justification. According to Rabbi Ishmael, who holds that each corner is an independent *mitzvah*, the wool *techeiles* on a linen garment is permissible because a *mitzvah* is indeed being fulfilled. This represents a second-degree *nafka mina* — it follows from, rather than directly expresses, the underlying dispute.

### Five-Cornered Garment

Rava Bar Ahina identifies yet another *nafka mina*: *talis ba'alat chamesh* — a garment with five corners. A *pasuk* teaches that even a five-cornered garment is obligated in *tzitzit*. According to the *tanna kamma*, who holds that there is one *mitzvah* requiring four *tzitziot*, a five-cornered garment must have *tzitzit* on four of its five corners — the *mitzvah* is defined by four corners, not by covering every corner. But according to Rabbi Ishmael, since each corner is an independent *mitzvah*, a garment with five obligated corners would require five *tzitziot*. Again, we *paskin* like the *tanna kamma*.

### Shabbat Carrying Issue

Ravina identifies a further *nafka mina* based on a teaching of Rav Huna: one who goes out on *Shabbat* wearing a garment with *tzitzit* that are not fulfilling the *mitzvah* as required — *she'eina metuyezet ke-hilchata* — is liable for *chatat*, because the strings hanging from the garment are not serving as a proper part of the garment. When *tzitzit* fulfill the *mitzvah*, they are considered integral to the garment and carrying them is no different from wearing a garment. But when they fail to fulfill the *mitzvah*, they are merely objects hanging from the garment, and wearing it constitutes carrying on *Shabbat*. The *nafka mina* is therefore: does a garment with *tzitzit* on only three of its four corners count as fulfilling the *mitzvah*? According to the *tanna kamma*, it does not, and the wearer is liable. According to Rabbi Ishmael, three *mitzvot* are still being fulfilled, and the wearer is not in violation. All of these *nafka minas* flow from the single foundational question of whether the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* can be fulfilled with fewer than four corners.

---

## Shape Modification & Loo…

### Shortening Garment

Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi rules: *hai man de-vatzrei le-glimei lo avad ve-lo klum* — one who rends or cuts a garment so as to divide a corner, turning a four-cornered garment into something he hopes will be differently shaped, has accomplished nothing. As the *gemara* notes, he has merely created a five-cornered garment — *shavyei talis bat chamesh* — and as we have just established, a five-cornered garment is fully obligated in *tzitzit*. The attempt to escape the obligation fails.

### Knotting Garment

Rav Mesharshiya rules similarly: *hai man de-tzayeirei leh le-glimei lo avid ve-lo klum* — one who ties up his garment has also accomplished nothing with respect to *tzitzit*. Rashi explains the case as one where the garment was too long; the person bunched it up and knotted it to create a new hem at a higher point, then affixed *tzitzit* at what is now the new corner. The reason this fails is stated in the *gemara*'s own terms: *di-kheman de-sharya dami* — it is as though the knot is undone. Since the garment has not been permanently altered — it has only been knotted, not sewn — its *halachic* shape is assessed in its unknotted state. The *tzitzit* placed at the new knotted hem do not count.

### Knotted Vessels

The *gemara* draws a parallel from the laws of *tumah*: *kol ha-chamatot ha-tzrurot tehorot chutz mi-shel Arviyim* — all types of leather flasks that have been knotted shut at one end are not *mekabel tumah*, because knotting does not fundamentally transform the object. The flask, knotted at one end but not sewn, is still assessed in terms of its natural, unknotted shape, and since in that shape it is open at both ends and cannot truly contain liquid, it does not qualify as a vessel susceptible to *tumah*. The exception is the flask of the Arabs, for whom this type of knotting was the standard method of closure and thus constituted the actual shape of their vessels. The *gemara* invokes this to demonstrate that merely knotting something does not change its fundamental *halachic* character.

### Sewing Garment

Rav Dimi of Nehardea extends the principle further: *hai man de-chaytei le-glimei lo avid ve-lo klum* — even sewing up a garment does not achieve the intended result. Why not? *Ei ita de-lo miba'ei leh li-fsok u-lishadyeih* — if this person truly did not want this portion of the garment, why did he not simply cut it off and discard it? The *gemara* is saying that folding and sewing, rather than cutting, reveals that the person did not genuinely intend to alter the garment's shape, and therefore the shape is not changed *halachically*.

### Rashi's Reinterpretation

This ruling is conceptually difficult, and Rashi himself recognizes this. There are any number of legitimate reasons one might fold and sew rather than cut: the extra material could allow the garment to be lengthened later for another wearer, or a folded hem may be more durable. Furthermore, as Rashi acknowledges, a *gemara* elsewhere explicitly states that sewing a garment at a new position does change its recognized shape. These considerations lead Rashi to reinterpret the entire sugya — the knotting case and the sewing case alike — as dealing not with shortening the hem but with attempting to eliminate corners. The person is not trying to make the garment shorter; he is trying to curve or tuck in a corner so that the garment no longer has four distinct corners and he can evade the obligation of *tzitzit*. In that context, doing so by knotting is clearly insufficient because the knot can be undone and the corner remains present in the garment's fundamental shape. And even sewing it shut does not help, because the *gemara* can see that this person is transparently trying to circumvent the *mitzvah* rather than making a genuine structural alteration — for if it were genuine, he would simply cut off the corner. Were someone genuinely and sincerely altering the shape of the garment, the sewing would indeed be *halachically* effective. The special rule here applies only because the intent is transparently evasive.

---

## Torn Tzitzit Incident

### Following Chachamim

At this point the *gemara* cites the ruling: *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel, halacha ke-Rabbi Yishmael* — Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules in accordance with Rabbi Ishmael, that the four *tzitziot* constitute four independent *mitzvot*. The *gemara* immediately overrides this: *ve-leis hilkheta ka-vasei* — we do not rule in accordance with Rav Yehuda's ruling in the name of Shmuel. The *halacha* follows the *chachamim*, not Rabbi Ishmael: all four *tzitziot* combine to form a single *mitzvah*, and without all four, no *mitzvah* is fulfilled.

### Witness Story

The *gemara* then recounts an incident. Ravina was walking behind Mar bar Rav Ashi on a *Shabbat* when the latter's community was preparing to study the *halachot* of the *regel*. While they walked, *ifsik karna de-chusei* — the corner of Mar bar Rav Ashi's garment tore, causing one of his *tzitziot* to come off. Mar bar Rav Ashi was unaware of this. Ravina, walking behind him, saw what had happened but said nothing — *ve-lo amar lei ve-lo midi*. At that point Mar bar Rav Ashi was walking on *Shabbat* wearing a garment with *tzitzit* on only three corners, which according to the *chachamim* means he was not fulfilling the *mitzvah* and was effectively carrying in the public domain. When they reached Mar bar Rav Ashi's home, Ravina informed him: *me-hasam ifsik* — your *tzitzit* tore off some time ago. Ravina had kept silent because had he informed Mar bar Rav Ashi at the moment it occurred, the latter would have been compelled to remove his *tallit* in the street and walk home without it — an undignified situation. Ravina chose to allow him to remain ignorant so he could return home without embarrassment. Mar bar Rav Ashi responded that Ravina had erred: *ei amrat lei me-hasam, shadyisei* — had you told me then, I would have removed my *tallit* immediately. You should have told me so I would not have unknowingly continued to carry.

### Two Story Versions

The *gemara* then challenges the first version of the story. Surely Ravina was right to say nothing? After all, we are taught — *gadol kevod ha-briyot she-docheh lo ta'aseh she-ba-Torah* — human dignity is so great that it overrides a negative prohibition in the Torah. If so, the consideration of Mar bar Rav Ashi's dignity should have permitted Ravina to remain silent, and Mar bar Rav Ashi's criticism was unwarranted. The *gemara* responds by citing the qualification offered by Mar bar Rav Shila in the name of Rav Kahana — a qualification that the *gemara* in Berakhot (top of 38a) makes as well: when we say *kevod ha-briyot* overrides a *lo ta'aseh she-ba-Torah*, we do not mean a literal Torah-level negative prohibition. We mean it overrides the *de-Rabbanan* prohibition of *lo tasur*, the obligation to follow rabbinic enactment. *Kevod ha-briyot* does not override a *de-oraita* prohibition. Therefore, if one sees another person inadvertently violating a Torah-level negative prohibition, one must inform him, even if it causes embarrassment, because human dignity cannot override a biblical transgression. This is why Mar bar Rav Ashi insisted he should have been told — carrying on *Shabbat* in a *reshut ha-rabim* would have been a *de-oraita* violation, and *kevod ha-briyot* does not override that.

The *gemara* then presents a second version of the story: *ve-ika de-amri* — some say that in fact Ravina did inform Mar bar Rav Ashi at the moment the *tzitzit* tore. Mar bar Rav Ashi responded: *mai dei'tach* — why are you telling me this? You expect me to remove my *tallit*? And he invoked the principle of *gadol kevod ha-briyot she-docheh lo ta'aseh she-ba-Torah* — my dignity overrides the obligation, and I will not remove my *tallit*. The *gemara* again raises the objection: but *kevod ha-briyot* only overrides a *de-Rabbanan* prohibition, not a *de-oraita* one! And answers: *hacha nami carmelit havah* — in this case they were walking through a *karmelit*, a domain that carries only a *de-Rabbanan* prohibition of carrying on *Shabbat*. In that circumstance, *kevod ha-briyot* does override, and Mar bar Rav Ashi's position is defensible.

### Kevod Habriyot Principle

In both versions of the story, the underlying *halacha* is identical and undisputed. *Kevod ha-briyot* overrides a *de-Rabbanan* prohibition but does not override a *de-oraita* one. The practical consequences differ by domain: in a *reshut ha-rabim*, carrying constitutes a *de-oraita* violation, and one must be informed immediately so as not to continue transgressing, even if it is embarrassing. In a *karmelit*, the violation is only *de-Rabbanan*, and *kevod ha-briyot* applies — but even then, as the first version of the story shows, it may be preferable to allow the person to remain unknowing rather than inform them and thereby convert an inadvertent violation into a deliberate one.

---

## White & Blue Strings

### Mishna Statement

The *gemara* now enters the fourth *perek* with a new *mishna*: *ha-techeiles eino me'akev et ha-lavan ve-ha-lavan eino me'akev et ha-techeiles* — the blue strings of *tzitzit* do not hold back the white, and the white do not hold back the blue. This means one is *yotzei* the *mitzvah* even with only white or only blue strings.

### Four Strands Assumption

This *mishna* calls for careful analysis of what exactly is being described. As is well known, *tzitzit* consists of four strands inserted through a hole in the corner and folded over, producing eight loose strings — though the *mitzvah* is structured around four strands. The question of how many of those four strands should be *techeiles* is a matter of dispute among contemporary *poskim* who reintroduce *techeiles*, with some holding that two of the four are *techeiles* and others holding differently. For purposes of the *gemara's* discussion, we assume two of the four strands are *techeiles* and two are white — *lavan*.

What does *eino me'akev* mean in its plain sense? If taken simply, it would suggest that having only two white strands without the two blue, or only two blue without the two white, is sufficient to fulfill the *mitzvah*. This would mean *tzitzit* can be performed with only two strands rather than four. A major *Tosafot* here grapples with this reading and ultimately leans toward understanding the *mishna* differently — that four strands are always required and the question of what *eino me'akev* addresses is whether all four must be white or all four must be *techeiles*, not whether one can reduce to fewer than four. The *mitzvah* can be fulfilled with four all-white or four all-*techeiles* strands, and indeed this is the basis for the universal practice of wearing four white strings when *techeiles* is unavailable.

### Tefillin Parallel

The *mishna* offers a parallel: *tefilla shel yad eino me'akevet et shel rosh ve-shel rosh eino me'akevet et shel yad* — the *tefilla* of the hand does not hold back the *tefilla* of the head and vice versa. Each *tefilla* constitutes its own independent *mitzvah*, so that even if one has only one of the two, the *mitzvah* of that one is fulfilled. This stands in deliberate contrast to *tzitzit*, where — according to the *tanna kamma* — having only three corners with *tzitzit* fulfills no *mitzvah* at all.

### Braisa Dispute

The *gemara* raises a challenge: *leima masnisin de-lo ke-Rabbi* — perhaps our *mishna* does not follow the view of Rabbi (Rebbi, i.e., Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi). A *Braisa* is cited: *ur'isem oto, melamed she-me'akvin zeh et zeh, divrei Rabbi* — the verse says "and you shall see it" (in the singular), teaching that the components — white and *techeiles* — hold each other back and are required together, in the words of Rabbi. *Ve-chachamim omrim: ein me'akvin* — and the sages say they do not hold each other back. Our *mishna*, which says they do not hold each other back, would thus seem to follow the *chachamim* against Rabbi.

### Rabbi's Reasoning

Before attempting to reconcile the *mishna* with Rabbi's view, the *gemara* first elaborates on Rabbi's reasoning. The Torah states: *al tzitzit ha-kanaf pesil techeiles* — on the *tzitzit* of the corner, a thread of blue. The phrase *ha-kanaf min kanaf* — from the [material of the] corner — indicates that the base *tzitzit* are of the same type as the garment. Since a standard garment is white, the base *tzitzit* are white. The Torah then adds the blue to the white. It then states *ur'isem oto* — you shall see it, in the singular — teaching that both the white and the blue combine into a single unified object. *Ad de-ika tarvaihu be-chad* — only when both are present together is the *mitzvah* fulfilled. Without both, one is not *yotzei*. On this reading, of course, none of us who wear only white *tzitzit* would be fulfilling the *mitzvah* at all.

### Chachamim's Reasoning

The *chachamim* read *ur'isem oto* differently. *Kol chad le-chudei mashma* — "you shall see it" refers to each one individually. The word "it" can denote each component separately — you see the white, you see the blue — and the presence of one does not require the other. The *peshat* of the verse, as Rashi notes, is arguably that the singular "it" refers specifically to the *techeiles*, which is the most proximate antecedent and which, with its color evoking the heavens and the divine, serves as the memory-trigger for all the *mitzvot*. Either way, for the *chachamim*, white and blue are independent of one another, and each can stand alone.

---

## Reconciling Mishna

### Rav's Interpretation

The *gemara* now attempts to reconcile our *mishna* with Rabbi's position, which holds that white and *techeiles* are mutually required. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav proposes: *afilu teima Rabbi* — even Rabbi can be made consistent with our *mishna*, by reinterpreting what *eino me'akev* refers to. *Lo nitzrecha ela le-akdeim* — the *mishna* is not discussing whether both colors are required; it is discussing the *order* in which they are placed. Both white and *techeiles* are indeed necessary for the *mitzvah* according to Rabbi, but the *mishna* is teaching that the *order* is not *me'akev*.

### Order of White & Blue

A *Braisa* is cited to establish what the correct order is: *mitzvah le-hakdim lavan le-techeiles* — it is a *mitzvah* to put the white first and the blue second. The basis for this is the verse *al tzitzit ha-kanaf pesil techeiles*: first the *tzitzit* of the corner (the white, matching the garment), and then the *pesil techeiles* (the blue thread) is added to it. White precedes blue.

### Blue First Result

If, however, one reverses the order — *im hikdim techeiles le-lavan* — one is still *yotzei*, but *ela she-chisar mitzvah* — something is lacking. This is what the *mishna* means when it says the blue does not hold back the white: having placed the blue first does not invalidate the white that follows. The order failure does not prevent fulfillment of the *mitzvah* itself.

### Missing Ideal

The *gemara* then asks: *mai chisar mitzvah* — what exactly is lacking? One reading would be that you fulfilled the *mitzvah* of blue but lost the *mitzvah* of white, since white was supposed to come first. But this cannot be correct according to Rabbi — *ikvuvei me'akevei ahadadi* — Rabbi holds that without both white and blue you cannot fulfill any *mitzvah* at all, so "losing the *mitzvah* of white" is not a coherent category within Rabbi's framework. Rather, Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains: *she-chisar mitzvah ve-asah mitzvah* — you are lacking a *mitzvah* but you are also doing the *mitzvah*. That is, you have fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* itself, but you have failed to perform it in the ideal manner — *de-lo avid mitzvah min ha-muvchar* — you did not fulfill the *mitzvah* of doing it in the correct order. The *mitzvah* stands; what is lost is the ideal performance.

### Two-Direction Problem

The *gemara* now presses: *ha teinach* — this works well for one phrase in the *mishna*, but not both. The phrase "white does not hold back *techeiles*" can be read as: having not placed the white first does not prevent the *techeiles* from counting — that is, if you put blue first, the blue is still valid. That fits the ordering interpretation. But *techeiles de-eino me'akev et ha-lavan mai hi* — what does the other phrase mean, that blue does not hold back white? If in a standard white garment white always comes first, then doing white first is simply doing it correctly. There is no scenario in which the prior presence of blue would threaten to invalidate subsequently placed white strings. The order interpretation can only work in one direction; it does not explain both phrases of the *mishna*.

### Blue Garment Case

Rami Bar Chama resolves this: *lo nitzrecha ela le-talis she-kula techeiles* — the second phrase addresses the case of a garment that is entirely blue. In this case, based on the principle of *kanaf min kanaf* — that the *tzitzit* match the type of the corner — the *tzitzit* matching the blue garment would be *techeiles*, and *techeiles* would therefore properly come first. If the white strings were then placed second, that would be the correct order for a blue garment. But if someone doing a blue garment placed white first anyway, the question is whether white jumping the line prevents the blue from counting. The answer: *leis lan bah* — no it does not, the order is still not *me'akev*. And that is what the *mishna* means when it says *techeiles eino me'akev et ha-lavan* — having placed white first when blue should have gone first does not prevent the white from counting. In the standard garment, white comes first; in a blue garment, *techeiles* comes first; in both cases, violating the order does not invalidate the *mitzvah*.

This interpretation is further corroborated by an exchange between Levi and Shmuel. Levi pressed Shmuel — *Aryoch*, he called him, like a lion, refusing to let him rest until he explained the *mishna* — asking how to understand the two directions of *eino me'akev* given that Rabbi requires both components. Shmuel's initial response focuses on the linen garment case, where the garment-matching color comes first; Rami Bar Chama then provides the blue garment as the solution to the second phrase, as described above.

---

## Rava's Objection

### Color Irrelevance

Rava objects to this entire framework: *midi tzivah ka garim* — what does color have to do with it? The principle of *min kanaf* should not be understood as requiring us to assess each garment's particular color and adjust the order of *tzitzit* accordingly. As Rashi reads it, *min kanaf* establishes the standard color for a standard garment, and since the standard garment was white, white always comes first — regardless of the actual color of the garment before us.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* sharpens this point with a textual argument. The verse says *al tzitzit ha-kanaf pesil techeiles* — add the *techeiles* to the *tzitzit* of the corner. The verse's very formulation places *techeiles* as the addition to an already-present base *tzitzit*. This means *techeiles* always comes second, and the white always comes first — not because we assess the color of each garment, but because the verse itself establishes this fixed sequence. Even if the garment happens to be blue, you do not put the *techeiles* first. White precedes blue, always.

### Unresolved Color Issue

With Rava's objection accepted, the case of the blue garment no longer serves as the explanation for the second phrase of the *mishna*. This reopens the question of how to read our *mishna* according to Rabbi. It also leaves unresolved an underlying question: is the principle of *min kanaf* understood to mean that the *lavan* strings are always white specifically, or does it mean that the strings should match the color of the garment — so that a red garment would have red *tzitzit* and blue, a blue garment blue and blue, and so on? Whether color-matching to the garment is actually required by *min kanaf* is a question the *gemara* has raised but not fully resolved at this point.

### Unresolved Material

A parallel unresolved question concerns material rather than color. The principle of *min kanaf* — that the *tzitzit* match the type of the corner — might extend beyond color to the material of which the garment is made. If the garment is linen, should the base *tzitzit* strings be linen? This is significant because *techeiles* is always wool; if a linen garment requires linen *tzitzit* as the base component matching *min kanaf*, then on such a garment the *techeiles* will always be the non-matching element and will always come second — not on account of the verse's word order alone, but because linen is what the garment dictates for the first component. These questions — whether color-matching matters and whether material-matching matters — are left open for further consideration.

---

## Remnant Requirement

### Rava Alternative

Having rejected the ordering interpretation as a way of reconciling the *mishna* with Rabbi's position, Rava now offers an entirely different reading: *lo nitzrecha ela le-gardumei* — the *mishna* is not discussing the initial configuration of *tzitzit* at all. It is discussing remnants — *gardumin* — what remains after some of the strings have snapped.

### Blue Snaps Scenario

*De-igdem techeiles ve-ka lavan* — if the *techeiles* strings got torn and one is left only with the white strings. After tying the knots and wraps, if the *techeiles* snaps below the last knot there is still a small remnant of the *techeiles* wrapped up within the structure. In such a case, one is still *yotzei* the *mitzvah*. The *mishna*'s statement that *techeiles* does not hold back *lavan* means: if the *techeiles* is mostly gone and only its remnant remains, that does not prevent the white from counting.

### White Snaps Scenario

*Ve-igdem lavan ve-ka techeiles* — symmetrically, if the white strings snapped and one is left with only the *techeiles*, *leis lan bah* — one is still *yotzei*. The absence of intact white strings does not invalidate the *mitzvah* when they began intact and later broke. This is what *lavan eino me'akev et ha-techeiles* means: the remnant situation does not disqualify the *mitzvah*.

Under this reading, the *mishna* is fully compatible with Rabbi's position. Rabbi holds that both white and *techeiles* are required components — and indeed they are: you must begin with both. But if one of them subsequently snaps and only a remnant remains, the *mitzvah* is not retroactively voided. You started correctly; the breakage after the fact does not undo what was already in place.

### Bnei R. Chiyya

This is supported by a teaching of the sons of Rabbi Chiyya: *gardumei techeiles kesherim* — remnants of the *techeiles* strings are still *kosher*, still valid. And similarly, *gardumei eizov kesherim* — even remnants of the hyssop used in the sprinkling of the ashes of the *parah adumah* remain valid. In each case, what started as a complete and proper component retains its *halachic* validity even when reduced to a remnant.

---

## Remnant Measurement

### Loop Standard

The *gemara* asks: *ve-khamah shiur gardumin* — how large must the remnant be in order to still be considered valid? Rav Hamduri in the name of Shmuel rules: *ke-dei le-onvan* — enough that one can make a loop from it. That is, the remnant must be of sufficient length that it can be looped around itself.

### Together vs. Individually

A question arises immediately: *ke-dei le-onvan kulhu be-hadadi, o dilma ke-chad ve-chad le-chudei* — does the standard mean that the remnants collectively must be long enough to loop all of them around each other together, or does each individual remnant need to be long enough to loop around itself? The difference is significant, since looping several strings together requires more length per string than looping a single string onto itself. The *gemara* leaves this question unresolved: *teiku*.

### Thickness Problem

Rav Ashi poses a further question: *alimei de-lo ma'anvei va-havu ketinei ma'anvei mai* — what if the remnant strings are thick, so thick that they cannot be looped around themselves, whereas if they were thinner they would have sufficient length to loop? Is such a thick remnant still considered *ke-dei le-onvan* and thus valid?

### Thickness Resolution

Rav Acha son of Rava responds to Rav Ashi: *kol she-kein de-minchar mitzvata* — there is no question; thick strings are even more valid. Rav Ashi's concern was that a thick string which cannot loop might fall below the threshold, but Rav Acha points out that thickness means the string is more present, more visible, more substantial. If the string has the requisite length — that is, the length that would be sufficient to loop were it thin — then its thickness only enhances it. Greater visibility of the *mitzvah* object is an advantage, not a disqualification. The *daf* concludes here.

---

---

# Menachot 39

## Techelet vs. Lavan

### Both Colors Required?

The *daf* opens by returning to a question left unresolved at the end of 38b: who is the *tanna* whose position underlies the *mishnah*'s ruling that *techelet* and *lavan* do not impede one another? The *mishnah* states that if one lacks the blue string, one may fulfill the *mitzvah* with white alone, and vice versa. The *gemara* had attempted to read the *mishnah* in accordance with Rabbi's stricter position — that one is not *yotzei* without both — by interpreting the case as one in which the strings snapped after the fact or were applied in the wrong order. But the plain sense of the *mishnah* resists that reading. The *gemara* now identifies the view that supports the *mishnah* at face value.

### R. Yochanan ben Nuri

The *tanna* in question is Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, as transmitted through a *braita*: Rabbi Yitzchak said in the name of Rabbi Natan, transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yose HaGlili, transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri — *ein lo techelet matil lavan*: if one lacks *techelet*, one may attach white strings and fulfill the obligation. This establishes the lineage of the position that *techelet* and *lavan* are not mutually indispensable, tracing it back to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri himself.

### Tosafot's Structure

A major *Tosafot* at the beginning of this *perek* explores a structural question that this ruling raises: when Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says one may use white in place of blue, does that mean all four strings may be white, or does it mean only the two white strings remain (since the standard arrangement consists of two blue and two white, as understood by both Rashi and Tosafot)? The language *ein lo techelet matil lavan* — "if one lacks *techelet*, one inserts white" — could suggest that one replaces the absent blue strings with white ones, implying all four strings are in play. But Tosafot concludes this particular formulation is not decisive proof either way, and the question remains a subject of broader discussion.

---

## Knots & Wrappings

### Multiple Wrappings

The *gemara* now shifts, somewhat abruptly, back to the position of the sons of Rabbi Chiya, which had been cited at the close of the previous discussion: if a *tzitzit* string snaps, as long as a *gardum* — a small remnant — remains, the *tzitzit* is still *kasher*. The remnant, it was established, must be sufficient to form a small knot on its own.

Rava draws an inference from this ruling. He says: *shema mina tzarich likshor al kol chulya v'chulya* — we may deduce that one is obligated to tie a knot after each wrapping section, not merely a single knot at the outset. The reasoning is as follows: if all one had were a single top knot with strings hanging freely below, and one of those strings snapped right at the point where it meets the knot, the knot itself would come undone. With so little string remaining on the loose side to hold the tension, the knot unravels. In such a scenario, one cannot even claim to have a valid knot — because a knot that will not hold is arguably not a knot at all. The only way the doctrine of *gardumim* makes sense, Rava argues, is if there are additional knots below the top knot: then even if a string snaps close to one of the lower knots, the structure above it remains intact, and the *gardum* doctrine applies.

### Knot Undoing

The *gemara* pushes back: *dilma de-iktar* — perhaps one simply happened to have made multiple knots, but this does not prove such knots are *required*. The ruling about *gardumim* being valid could be describing a case where extra knots were made by chance, without establishing any *halachic* necessity for them. So while the discussion introduces the concepts of strings, knots, and *chulyot* (wrapping sections), the inference that multiple knots are obligatory remains unproven at this stage.

### Tosafot Extreme

Tosafot, commenting on this passage at the bottom of 38b, takes the analysis a striking step further. Where the *gemara* considers the possibility that a single knot might come undone if a string snaps near it, Tosafot pushes to an even more extreme conclusion: *keivan de-ishtarei chad ishtarei kulhu* — once one element unravels, the whole structure unravels. In such a case, Tosafot says, *ve-ein kan gedil* — there is no knot at all. And even according to the view that *tzitzit* requires only *either* a knot *or* a free-flowing string (a position we will encounter shortly), Tosafot argues that in this situation *afilu p'til leika* — there is not even a string present, because *de-sofo lipol* — the string will ultimately fall off entirely. Without the knot holding it in place, the string has no structural integrity and cannot be counted even as a dangling strand. This is Tosafot's own extension of the *gemara's* logic, not the *gemara's* own conclusion.

---

## Top Knot Biblical

### Kilayim Proof

Rava makes a second inference, this one regarding the *kesher elyon* — the top knot. He states: *shema mina kesher elyon de-oraita* — we may deduce that the top knot is a biblical requirement. The proof runs as follows: if the top knot were only rabbinic, then the knot binding the *tzitzit* strings to the garment would impose no biblical obligation. In that case, *mai itztrich lemishrei sadin be-tzitzit* — why would the Torah need to permit the use of *kilayim* in *tzitzit*? The juxtaposition in the Torah that allows *kilayim* in the context of *tzitzit* would have been entirely unnecessary.

### Shatnez Juxtaposition

The *gemara* understands the juxtaposition of two adjacent verses as the source for this permission: *lo tilbash shatnez tzemer u-fishtim yachdav* — do not wear *shatnez*, wool and linen together — followed immediately by *gedilim ta'aseh lach* — make for yourself *gedilim* (knots, braids, *tzitzit* effectively) *al arba kanfot kesutcha asher techaseh bah* — on the four corners of the garment with which you cover yourself. The Talmudic tradition reads this adjacency as the Torah's authorization for *tzitzit* to override the prohibition of *kilayim*. The classic case is the *techelet* string: the blue dye must be applied to a wool string, so if one's garment is linen, attaching a wool *techelet* string creates *shatnez* — and the juxtaposition tells us this is permitted. It is worth noting, as the *gemara* anticipates, that we will discuss later whether the Torah is granting permission only where *kilayim* is unavoidable, or whether *tzitzit* is entirely exempt from *kilayim* restrictions even when they could be avoided.

### Binding Requirement

Rava's argument is that the permission for *kilayim* in *tzitzit* would only have been necessary if the strings were actually bound to the garment in a halachically significant way. *Kilayim*, after all, requires that wool and linen be genuinely joined — merely passing a string through a hole and letting it dangle is not considered *chibur*, a proper connection. The *gemara* states explicitly: *tokef tifa achas eino chibur* — simply threading through a single hole is not considered a joining. Therefore, the Torah's need to permit *kilayim* in *tzitzit* presupposes that the strings are knotted. And if knotting is what triggers the *kilayim* concern, then knotting must be a Torah-level requirement — *shema mina de-oraita*. Rava is working backwards from the established tradition that the juxtaposition of the *shatnez* verse and the *gedilim* verse was intended to permit *kilayim* in *tzitzit*, treating that as a fixed datum and deriving from it the biblical status of the top knot.

It is worth pausing here to appreciate what Rava is doing across both inferences. He is looking at a practice with clear ancestral tradition — knots, wrappings, a top knot, intermediate knots — and attempting to determine which elements carry biblical authority and which are rabbinic. Unlike the laws of *tefillin*, where the *gemara* frequently invokes *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* to ground the details, the laws of *tzitzit* offer fewer such explicit anchors. Rava is thus engaged in a form of legal archaeology: working from the juxtaposition of *pesukim*, from inferences about *kilayim*, from the structure of *gardum* doctrine, to establish which features of the observed practice have biblical grounding.

---

## Snapped Strings

### Complete Severance

A new ruling is cited: Rava bar Rav Adda said in the name of Rav — *im nifsaka ha-chut me-ikaro pesula* — if an entire string is cut off at its root, the *tzitzit* is invalid. This is to be distinguished from the *gardum* case: if a string snaps partway down, leaving a small remnant, the *tzitzit* remains *kasher*. But if a string is severed at the very base — at the point where it loops through the hole in the garment, leaving nothing attached — the *tzitzit* is disqualified. This holds even though the other three strings (or in the doubled configuration, the other portions) remain intact. One completely missing string invalidates the whole.

### Initial vs. Final

Rav Nachman was sitting and transmitting this ruling when Rava challenged him from a *braita*: *bameh devarim amurim be-techilato* — when does the requirement for a minimum length apply? Only at the outset, when the *tzitzit* is first attached. But *aval sofo* — at the end, when something has happened to the *tzitzit* after it was properly made — *shiyerav ve-gardumav kol shehu*, even the smallest remnant of the string suffices. Rava reads this *braita* as potentially encompassing even the case of complete severance (*nifsaka me-ikaro*): perhaps *shiyerav* refers to strings that were entirely cut away, while the remaining strings constitute the *shirayim* — what survives. If so, the *braita* would permit the *tzitzit* even when a full string has been severed.

### Remnants Defined

The *gemara* presses on the precise meaning of *shiyerav ve-gardumav*. *Mai shiyerav u-mai gardumav* — what does each term mean? One reading: *shiyerav* refers to strings that were cut entirely (*de-ifsak mineihu*) while others remained — i.e., some strings were completely severed while some survived. *Gardumav* refers to strings that were partially snapped and partially remained. Under this reading, *shiyerav ve-gardumav kol shehu* means: even if some strings are entirely gone and others have only a tiny remnant, the *tzitzit* is *kasher*. The *gemara* pushes back: if that were the meaning, why use both terms? The word *gardumav* alone communicates that part of the string broke and part remained. The word *shiyurei* is added to teach something additional: *dibe'inan shiyura le-gardumav* — even the remnant that remains must itself have a meaningful amount. That is, the *gardum* is not valid with an arbitrarily microscopic fragment; there must be a sufficient remnant.

### Minimum Knot Amount

How much must remain? *Kedei le-onvam* — enough to tie a knot. This standard was introduced earlier: the string that broke near the knot must still have enough length protruding beyond the knot to allow it to be tied around the other strings or itself to form a small loop. This is the *shiur* for *gardumim* to be valid.

A practical note: when making *tzitzit*, one ensures that the two halves of each folded string fall on opposite sides of the initial knot. This way, even if one side of the string is cut entirely at the root, the other half remains as a *gardum* from the other side — and the two cannot be confused as a single string lost entirely. The *gemara* itself rarely makes explicit the standard practice of folding four strings through the hole to produce eight, and Tosafot notes that Rabbeinu Tam had a distinct approach: he simply passed four strings straight through without folding, and tied a knot at the top. That version of *tzitzit* looks much more like a simple tassel than the elaborate knotted structure we know, which is itself a point worth noting when considering how highly ritualized these technical requirements have become.

---

## Wrapping String Count

### String Counts

The next ruling: Rava sat and said in the name of Rav — *chut shel kerach oleh min ha-minyan* — the wrapping string counts as one of the four required strings. This might seem obvious, but there is conceptual space to question it. If one imagines the four strings hanging freely and a fifth string used exclusively for the wrapping and knotting, the wrapping string might seem like a separate functional element rather than one of the four constitutive *tzitzit* strings. Rava rules that this is not the case: the string used for wrapping is itself counted as one of the four. There is no need for a separate fifth string.

### Attribution Correction

Rav Yosef immediately corrects the attribution: *Shmuel amrah ve-lo Rav* — it was Shmuel who said this, not Rav. This is corroborated by an independent tradition: Rabbah bar bar Chana reported that Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha told him — *chut shel kerach oleh lo min ha-minyan* — the wrapping string counts toward the four. The ruling is thus confirmed, with its attribution properly placed with Shmuel.

---

## Kerach & Pil Ratios

### Majority Wrapped OK

The *gemara* now turns to the proportional requirements — how much of the *tzitzit* should consist of knots and wrappings versus free-flowing strings. Rava sat and said in the name of Shmuel: *techelet she-karach rubah kesherah* — even if the majority of the *tzitzit* was knotted and wrapped, it remains *kasher*. A note on terminology: the word *techelet* here functions as a general term for the *tzitzit* as a whole, not specifically the blue string — an irony given that *techelet* is not in use today.

Rav Yosef again corrects an attribution, this time in the opposite direction: *Rav amrah ve-lo Shmuel* — it was Rav who said this, not Shmuel. This is then confirmed by a full chain of transmission: Rav Huna bar Yehuda said in the name of Rav Sheshet, who said in the name of Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba, who said in the name of Rav — *techelet she-karach rubah kesherah* — even if the majority was knotted and wrapped rather than left as free strands, the *tzitzit* is *kasher*. This is a *bedi'avad* ruling: if one deviated from the ideal proportion, the *tzitzit* is not disqualified.

### Single Wrapping OK

The *gemara* extends this in the opposite direction as well. A variant formulation adds: *ve-afilu lo karach bah ela chulya achat kesherah* — even if one performed only a single wrapping section (*chulya*) and no more, the *tzitzit* is *kasher*. This is striking given that earlier the *gemara* assumed *al kol chulya ve-chulya* — that there are multiple wrapping sections. The reconciliation is that while multiple *chulyot* are the standard expectation, a single *chulya* with a knot is sufficient *bedi'avad*. The standard practice — as reported by the Rosh and Tosafot — involves three *chulyot*, while our own practice consists of four sections with wrappings of seven, eight, eleven, and thirteen winds, bounded by five knots.

One should also note that the source of the requirement for *chulyot* at all is not entirely clear from the *gemara*. The biblical obligation derives from the word *petil* (free-flowing string) and *gedil* (knot), but the specific concept of a *chulya* — a section of wrapping — is not explicitly derived. The *gemara* here nonetheless treats at least one *chulya* as necessary.

### 1/3 Knots 2/3 Fringe

The ideal proportion is then stated: *noi techelet* — the beauty of *tzitzit*, the aesthetically ideal configuration — is *shlish gedil u-shnei shlishei anaf*: one-third knots and wrappings, two-thirds free-flowing fringe (*anaf*). The *gemara* does not here specify which string is used for the wrapping, but Tosafot assumes it is the *techelet* string, and further suggests that the aesthetic ideal of *noi techelet* is precisely that having multiple wrapping sections and knots allows the blue to stand out more distinctly. The one-third to two-thirds proportion appears to be an aesthetic judgment — what a beautiful fringe looks like — rather than a strict *halachic* derivation.

---

## 7-13 Wrappings

### Range 7-13

A *braita* is cited defining the limits of each wrapping section: *ha-pochet lo yifchos mi-sheva ve-ha-mosif lo yosif al shalosh esrei* — one who makes fewer should not make fewer than seven wraps per section, and one who adds more should not exceed thirteen. This establishes the range within which each *chulya* must fall. Rabbi's independent ruling — that a minimum of three wraps is required (*kedei she-yichroch ve-yishneh ve-yishalesh*, wrap, repeat, triple) — appears to set a lower technical floor, distinct from the symbolic range.

### Heavens Symbolism

The numbers seven and thirteen are grounded in cosmological symbolism. The minimum of seven corresponds to the *shiva rekiyim* — the seven heavens — reflecting the connection between *techelet* and the sky. The maximum of thirteen corresponds to *shiva rekiyim ve-shisha avirim she-beineihem* — the seven heavens and the six air spaces between them — totaling thirteen. The entire range, in other words, is mapped onto a picture of the heavens, reinforcing the thematic resonance of *techelet* as a reminder of the divine realm.

### Gematria Significance

Within this range, our practice — wrapping seven, then eight, then eleven, then thirteen — carries its own numerical significance, noted already in the *Shulchan Aruch*. Seven and eight together sum to fifteen, which is the *gematria* of *Yud-Heh*, one of the divine names. Adding eleven brings the total to twenty-six, the *gematria* of the four-letter divine name *Yud-Heh-Vav-Heh*. The final thirteen — the *gematria* of *echad* ("one") — completes the sequence: the accumulated sum of the last two sections (26 + 13) encodes *Hashem Echad*. The *Mishnah Berurah* records the significance of the total thirty-nine, though the precise connection warrants checking.

Tosafot raises a question about whether the seven-to-thirteen range refers to the number of wraps within each *chulya* or to the number of *chulyot* themselves. He reports that the practice of Tosafot's circle was to have five knots and three sections — an initial knot, then one section, knot, one section, knot, one section, knot — all double knots. Our practice of four sections (with the top knot and four additional double knots for a total of five knots) is close but not identical.

The *gemara* also records a well-known *gematria*: the numerical value of the word *tzitzit* (*tzadi-yud-tzadi-yud-taf*) is 600. Adding eight strings (assuming the standard folding-over of four strings to produce eight) and five knots yields 613, corresponding to the traditional count of the *mitzvot*. Tosafot notes a difficulty: whenever *tzitzit* is written in the Torah, it is spelled with only one *yud*, yielding 590. His resolution is that one of the appearances is prefaced with the letter *lamed* (*le-tzitzit*), whose value is 30; dividing those 30 points equally among the other three occurrences adds 10 to each, restoring the value to 600. The use of numeric symbolism here — in contrast to *tefillin*, where the strings and boxes carry the actual divine names in written form — represents a different strategy for making the physical object a vehicle for consciousness of God. With *tefillin*, the Names are literally present; with *tzitzit*, the connection to God and to the 613 *mitzvot* is encoded structurally in the count of winds, strings, and knots.

---

## Wrap Order

### White First Last

A *tanna* taught: *keshe-hu maschil hu maschil be-lavan* — when one begins the wrapping, one begins with the white. The rationale offered is *ha-kanaf min kanaf* — the corner should match the corner, meaning the wrapping that is closest to the garment should reflect the primary material. Since most garments are white, and since the white string is understood as the primary constituent of *tzitzit* (as we will see, one is *yotzei* even without *techelet*), the wrapping begins with white so that white is adjacent to the garment.

This raises the question of how the wrapping works when there are both blue and white strings available: the practice implied by the *gemara* is that the two strings alternate in performing the wrapping — sometimes the white string does the winding, sometimes the *techelet* string. The *gemara* is thus discussing which of the two starts the winding. White begins.

The question of what people who actually have *techelet* today do with these wrapping rules is genuinely open. The detailed *halachot* of *techelet* — which string wraps, how many times, in which sections — were never developed into an established *psak* during the centuries when *techelet* was unavailable. Now that some communities have reintroduced it, those questions arise afresh, and the answers are drawn from varying interpretations of the *rishonim* on the *gemara* rather than from a developed halachic tradition. Whatever practice one adopts, however, the *bedi'avad* position is clear: if one has only white strings, one is *yotzei* regardless.

### Ascending Holiness

*U-mesayem mesayem be-lavan* — and one ends with white as well. The *techelet* wrappings occupy the middle sections, flanked by white on both sides. The reason one ends with white: *maalin ba-kodesh ve-lo moridin* — we ascend in holiness and do not descend. This is a striking application of the principle. One would naturally assume that *techelet* — the string connected to the sky, the heavens, and the reminder of divine presence — occupies the higher level of *kedushah*, and ending with white would represent a descent. Yet the *gemara* inverts this: because white is primary and *techelet* is supplementary (after all, one is *yotzei* without *techelet* altogether), white is considered the higher level here, and the wrapping must conclude with it. One may not end on a lower note.

---

## All Knotted Debate

### Full Knot Garment

The *gemara* presents an illustrative case. Rava and Rabbah bar bar Chana were sitting when a man passed by wearing a garment — *michsei glima* — that was entirely blue, and whose *tzitzit* was entirely knotted — *gidelei migdal* — with no free-flowing strand at all. The entire length of the *tzitzit* had been wound into knots with nothing hanging loose.

### Rabbah: Or Requirement

Rabbah bar bar Chana assessed the situation positively: *ya'ei glima ve-ya'ei tzitzis* — a beautiful garment and beautiful *tzitzit*. He holds the man is *yotzei*. His reasoning: the Torah uses two distinct terms — *gedilim*, which the *gemara* reads as indicating knots or braids, and *petil*, a strand of *techelet*. Rabbah bar bar Chana reads these as alternatives: *o gedil o p'til* — either knots or free strands suffice. *Tzitzit* may be constituted by either element alone; there is no requirement for both simultaneously. A garment that is entirely knotted, with no free strand, would be *kasher* on this view.

### Rav: Both Needed

Rav, however, disagreed: *ya'ei glima ve-lo ya'ei techeilta* — a beautiful garment, but not beautiful *tzitzit*. He holds that the man is not *yotzei*. Rav requires *l'olam psil ba'inan* — one always needs free-flowing strands in addition to the knots. The word *gedilim* in the Torah is not teaching that knots alone suffice; rather, it serves a different purpose.

### Four Strings & Emergence

What then is the role of the word *gedilim* according to Rav? *Le-minyano hu de'ata* — it comes to teach the number. *Gedil* implies two (like a braid of two), *gedilim* implies four. This is the source for the requirement of four strings (which, once doubled over, become eight). The word *gedilim* establishes that there must be four strings, while the requirement for free-flowing strands (*petil*) remains independently in force. Both are required.

The *gemara* then adds: *aseh gedil u-ftulehu mi-tocha* — make the knot and let the free strands emerge from within it. Rashi explains: this teaches that the string used for the wrapping counts among the four strings (*chut shel kerach oleh min ha-minyan*, as established earlier) — it is *mi-tocha*, from within the knot structure itself, not a separate fifth string. Tosafot offers a different reading: *ptulehu* could mean "double over," teaching that the strings must be folded — though this reading is less smooth given the context, which is clearly focused on the relationship between *gedil* (knot) and *petil* (strand). Rashi's reading fits the flow of the *gemara* more naturally.

---

## String Materials

### Wool & Linen Mix

Shmuel said in the name of Levi: *chutei tzemer potrin be-shel pishtan* — wool strings fulfill the obligation when attached to a linen garment. This opening statement establishes the baseline: wool strings are universally acceptable regardless of the garment material. The question that immediately follows is the more challenging one.

It is useful to first orient the broader discussion. The *gemara* has already established that *techelet* must be a wool string, since the blue dye adheres properly only to wool. This means that for any non-wool garment — linen, silk, or otherwise — attaching a *techelet* string automatically creates *kilayim* (wool in a non-wool garment). The Torah's juxtaposition of the *shatnez* prohibition and the *gedilim* command permits this. But the question now is whether the same tolerance extends beyond the unavoidable case.

### Linen on Wool?

*Shel pishtan mahu she-yiftru be-shel tzemer* — what about linen strings on a wool garment? Here the logic divides. For a linen garment, wool strings are understandable: since the *techelet* must be wool anyway, introducing additional wool strings creates no further problem. But for a wool garment, there is no inherent necessity to introduce linen. One could fulfill the entire *mitzvah* with wool strings alone. So does introducing linen strings — thereby creating *shatnez* — remain permitted even when avoidable?

### Juxtaposition Permits

The *gemara* raises the possibility that the juxtaposition — *lo tilbash shatnez tzemer u-fishtim yachdav* followed by *gedilim ta'aseh lach* — is making a sweeping statement: not only where *kilayim* is unavoidable, but across the board, *tzitzit* strings may be a combination of wool and linen. *Lo shna tzemer be-fishtim ve-lo shna pishtim be-tzemer* — it makes no difference whether it is wool strings in a linen garment or linen strings in a wool garment. The *tzitzit* context simply permits the combination.

### Universal Exemption

This is then confirmed by a *braita* cited by Rechava in the name of Rav Yehuda: *chutei tzemer potrin be-shel pishtan, ve-shel pishtan potrin be-shel tzemer* — wool strings fulfill in a linen garment and linen strings fulfill in a wool garment. And then the cumulative statement: *chutei tzemer u-fishtim potrin be-chol makom* — wool and linen strings fulfill the obligation everywhere. This can be read as saying that either wool or linen strings work for any garment, or that a combination of both wool and linen strings together works universally. The explicit conclusion for our purposes is that linen strings on a wool garment are *kasher* — the creation of *kilayim* in the *tzitzit* is permitted even when it was entirely avoidable. *Tzitzit* is not merely an override where *kilayim* is forced upon you; it is an outright exemption from the *kilayim* prohibition within the context of *tzitzit* strings.

---

## Silk & Other Materials

### Rav Nachman Exempt

The *braita* just cited adds: *ve-afilu bi-shirayim* — wool and linen strings work even on silk garments. But this immediately conflicts with the position of Rav Nachman, who states: *ha-shirayim peturim min ha-tzitzit* — silk garments are exempt from the obligation of *tzitzit* entirely. Rav Nachman's position reflects a more restrictive definition of what counts as a *beged* — a garment — for purposes of the biblical *mitzvah*. On his view, the Torah's obligation applies only to wool and linen garments; other materials do not qualify.

This reflects a broader question about what counts as a *beged* for purposes of *tzitzit*. Wool and linen are clearly within the Torah's definition. Silk (*shirayim*, *kalach*, *serikin* — all apparently variants of silk or fine material) is the *gemara's* test case. Cotton and synthetic fibers, such as polyester, represent further extensions: many *poskim* hold that polyester does not even qualify for a rabbinic obligation and that no *bracha* may be recited over it. Cotton, by contrast, is generally understood to carry at least a rabbinic obligation, though whether it is biblical is debated — which is why a *bracha* may be recited on cotton *tzitzit*.

### Braita Obligates

Rava challenged Rav Nachman from a *braita*: *ha-shirayim ve-ha-kalach ve-ha-serikin kulan chayavin be-tzitzit* — all three types of silk are obligated in *tzitzit*. Rav Nachman responds: the obligation referenced by the *braita* is rabbinic, not biblical. The importance of this distinction: even a rabbinic obligation means the person must attach *tzitzit* and may recite the *bracha*.

### Level Determines Rules

The *gemara* presses: *ei hachi eima seifa* — if the *braita* means only rabbinic obligation, consider its concluding clause: *ve-kulan be-tzemer u-fishtim potrin ba-hen* — all these garments are fulfilled with wool and linen strings. If this means wool *and* linen strings combined, then for a silk garment (which has only a rabbinic obligation) one would be introducing *kilayim* into a garment without any biblical need to do so. The earlier discussion established that *kilayim* in *tzitzit* is permitted for biblically obligated garments because the Torah's own juxtaposition authorizes it. But if the silk garment carries only a rabbinic obligation, that Torah-level authorization cannot apply, and creating *kilayim* would remain prohibited.

The *gemara* resolves this: *o tzemer o fishtim* — read the *braita* as "either wool or linen," not "wool and linen combined." When the *braita* says wool and linen strings work for silk garments, it means either type works individually — not that a combined wool-and-linen string is authorized. This reading dissolves the *kilayim* problem, since using a pure wool string or a pure linen string on a silk garment creates no *kilayim* at all.

### Kanaf Min Kanaf

This resolution is supported by the *sifa* of the *braita* itself: *hen be-minam potrin, u-she-lo be-minam ein potrin* — these garments (silk and other non-wool-or-linen materials) are fulfilled by strings of their own kind, but strings of a foreign material (other than wool or linen) do not fulfill the obligation. This clause is derived from the verse *ha-kanaf min kanaf* — the corner (*kanaf*) from the same type as the corner. Just as the garment defines what is "the corner," the strings should be *min kanaf* — from the same type as the garment. A silk garment can thus be fitted with silk strings; a cotton garment with cotton strings. But these same-material strings only work for their own kind of garment, unlike wool and linen, which are universal.

### Two Pesukim Resolved

This leads to the resolution offered by Rava of an apparent conflict between two *pesukim*. One verse implies *ha-kanaf* — from the same material as the garment. Another verse implies *tzemer u-fishtim* — the material is specifically wool or linen (derived from the juxtaposition of the *shatnez* verse and the *gedilim* command). How are these reconciled?

*Tzemer u-fishtim potrin bein be-minam bein she-lo be-minam* — wool and linen strings fulfill the obligation universally, whether the garment is of their own kind or of a different kind. They are the universal standard, like a universal blood type. *Shear minim be-minam potrin, she-lo be-minam ein potrin* — other materials fulfill only when matched to a garment of the same material; they cannot cross over to fulfill the obligation for a different kind of garment. Wool and linen are thus established as inherently valid *tzitzit* materials for any garment whatsoever, while all other materials are valid only on matching garments.

The upshot is clear: for garments that carry only a rabbinic *tzitzit* obligation — like silk, and quite possibly cotton — the strings must either be wool, linen, or the same material as the garment itself. Creating *kilayim* in the strings is not authorized for rabbinic-level garments. For garments that carry a biblical obligation — wool and linen — *kilayim* in the *tzitzit* strings is permitted by the Torah's juxtaposition, even when avoidable. This is the full architecture of the *gemara's* resolution.

---

---

# Menachot 40

## Tzitzit Obligation

### Wool & Linen Only

The *daf* properly begins a few lines before the top of 40, picking up from the bottom of 39b. There, Rav Nachman cites the *Tana Debei Rabbi Yishmael* on the question of which garments are obligated in *tzitzit*. The position of the school of Rabbi Yishmael runs as follows: wherever the Torah speaks of a *beged* without further specification, and then specifies wool or linen in one particular instance — as it does by *shatnez* ("*lo tilbash shatnez tzemer u'pishtim yachdav*") and by *nega'im* ("*beged tzemer o beged pishtim*") — we derive that whenever the Torah says *beged*, it means specifically a wool or linen garment. The conclusion is *af kol tzemer u'pishtim*: whenever the Torah mentions a garment in the context of a *mitzvah*, it intends only wool or linen. Accordingly, garments made of cotton, silk, or other materials would carry only a rabbinic obligation in *tzitzit*, not a biblical one.

### Contradictory Teachings

Abaye immediately raises a difficulty: *ve'hai Tana Debei Rabbi Yishmael mehapech me'idach Tana Debei Rabbi Yishmael* — this teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael appears to contradict another teaching from the very same school. That second teaching begins by acknowledging that when the Torah mentions *beged* in the context of *tum'ah* — whether in the laws of *nega'im* (as Rashi holds) or in the laws of what becomes *tamei* through contact with a *sheretz* (as Tosafot prefers) — one might think only a standard woolen garment is included. Yet the verse then says "*o beged*," and the inclusive word *o* is taken to broaden the category to include garments of camel hair, rabbit wool, goat hair, and various forms of silk. The very same school of Rabbi Yishmael that restricts *beged* to wool and linen in one context appears to expand it dramatically in another.

Tosafot presses further: by *tzitzit*, the Torah uses the phrase *al ha-kanaf*, from which the *Gemara* derives *min kanaf* — seemingly including all types of garments. By *tum'ah*, the broadening comes from the word *o beged*. It is therefore difficult to determine which ruling is the general principle and which is a particular exception. Tosafot acknowledges that the *Gemara*'s comparison across these contexts is puzzling, and offers no fully satisfying resolution. The underlying question — whether non-wool-and-linen garments are obligated in *tzitzit* at a biblical or merely rabbinic level — thus remains genuinely contested.

### Practical Stringency

The practical stakes of this debate are significant. If one simply happens to be wearing a four-cornered garment, the question of whether the obligation is biblical or rabbinic matters little in practice; either way one is obligated in *tzitzit* and recites a *beracha*. The question becomes acute because of the widespread *minhag* to go out of one's way to wear a four-cornered garment specifically in order to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit*. If one is deliberately seeking to fulfill the *mitzvah*, one would naturally prefer to fulfill it at the biblical level. This is the reasoning behind the practice of wearing wool *tzitzit* even on a *tallit katan* — since a wool garment is definitively obligated *de'oraita* according to all opinions.

That said, this *chumra* can paradoxically produce a *kula*. In warm weather, wool *tzitzit* on an undershirt can become sufficiently uncomfortable that a person abandons wearing *tzitzit* altogether. The *Mishnah Berurah* recommends the stringency of wool, but a person who finds it genuinely unmanageable is far better served by wearing cotton *tzitzit* — on which all agree there is at least a *derabbanan* obligation — than by resolving to wear wool and then wearing nothing at all.

### Ashkenazi/Sephardi

The *Shulchan Aruch* rules in accordance with the *Tana Debei Rabbi Yishmael* as cited by Rav Nachman — that only wool and linen garments are biblically obligated in *tzitzit*, and all other materials carry only a rabbinic obligation. The *Rama* rules the other way, holding that all garments are obligated at a biblical level. The question of synthetic materials — fabrics that are neither wool, linen, nor any traditional fiber — raises its own distinct set of considerations that extend beyond what the *Gemara* here directly addresses.

---

## Sadin Bitzitzit

### Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

Turning now to the top of 40a, the *Gemara* presents a *baraita*: *sadin bitzitzit* — the case of a linen garment in which one seeks to attach *tzitzit*. *Beit Shammai potrin u'Veit Hillel mechayvin*: Beit Shammai exempts such a garment from *tzitzit*, while Beit Hillel obligates it. The tension, as Rashi notes, is that if one is exempt from *tzitzit* in a linen garment and nevertheless attaches wool strings — and *techelet* must be wool — one will be wearing *shatnez*. So Beit Shammai's ruling amounts not merely to an exemption but to a prohibition against attaching wool *tzitzit* to a linen garment at all.

One might initially think the problem is narrower: if the non-blue strings need not be wool, why not simply attach white linen strings and omit the blue? The answer appears to be that Beit Shammai follows the position — consistent with the view of Rebbi, against the *Mishnah* — that *techelet* is *me'akev* the white: the blue is so integral to the *mitzvah* that without it, the white strings cannot stand alone. Since one cannot attach valid *techelet* in a linen garment without incurring *shatnez*, and since without valid *techelet* the white is also invalid, Beit Shammai concludes that a linen garment is entirely exempt. To put wool strings on it anyway would constitute a transgression of *shatnez*.

### Techelet Requirement

The deeper question is: given that the Torah itself juxtaposes *shatnez* and *tzitzit* — a juxtaposition understood to permit *shatnez* in the context of *tzitzit* — why does Beit Shammai not simply permit it? And whatever happened to *asei docheh lo ta'aseh*, the principle that a positive commandment overrides a negative prohibition?

### Rashi's Explanations

Rashi offers two distinct readings of Beit Shammai's position. The first is that Beit Shammai simply does not accept the *drasha* that the Torah's juxtaposition of *shatnez* and *tzitzit* constitutes a blanket permission to wear *shatnez* in *tzitzit*. On this reading, Beit Shammai holds that *shatnez* remains prohibited even in this context, leaving the linen garment fully exempt — and any wool strings added to it a violation.

The second explanation, which fits more naturally with the continuation of the *Gemara*, is that Beit Shammai is speaking at a rabbinic level only. Biblically, Beit Shammai would agree that a linen garment is obligated in *tzitzit* and that *shatnez* is permitted in that context. But Beit Shammai is concerned: if one becomes accustomed to wearing *shatnez* strings in one's *tzitzit*, one may come to wear *shatnez* in situations where it is not permitted — for instance, when the blue strings are invalid. Better, therefore, to prohibit it rabbinically across the board. This second reading resolves a further difficulty: on the first reading, Beit Shammai's language says one is "exempt" rather than that one "transgresses," which is odd if wool strings in a linen garment are an outright biblical violation. On the second reading, there is no actual transgression — only a rabbinic exemption designed as a safeguard.

### Rabbinic Authority

Rashi himself raises the obvious objection: if Beit Shammai prohibits attaching *tzitzit* to a linen garment entirely, then one is left walking around with a four-cornered linen garment bearing no *tzitzit* at all. Does the rabbinic authority to protect against potential transgression extend to directing a person to passively fail to fulfill a biblical positive commandment? Rashi answers that yes, this is precisely a power the rabbis possess — to instruct one to *shev ve'al ta'aseh*, to passively refrain from a *mitzvah*, when they deem it necessary. The precedents are familiar: the rabbis prohibited sounding the *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah* that falls on *Shabbat*, and taking the *lulav* on *Sukkot* that falls on *Shabbat*. Even in cases that might seem to involve a *bitul asei*, not merely passive restraint, as long as the person's own action is passive, the rabbinic authority extends that far.

This reading of Beit Shammai is, in a sense, its own philosophical statement: so concerned is Beit Shammai about the possibility that permitting *shatnez* in *tzitzit* will eventually lead to an actual *shatnez* violation, that they are willing to tell a person not to perform a biblical *mitzvah* entirely. Beit Hillel, by contrast, says: the Torah permits it, you are obligated, do it — and do not manufacture concerns about what might go wrong. *Ve'halacha k'divrei Beit Hillel*, and the ruling follows Beit Hillel.

---

## Shatnez & Ignorance

### Jerusalem Practice

The *baraita* itself records that the *halacha* follows Beit Hillel. Yet immediately afterward, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok observes: *v'lo kol hamatilah techelet b'sadin b'Yerushalayim eino ela min hamitmitemin* — anyone who placed *techelet* in a linen garment in Jerusalem was regarded with shock and astonishment. Even according to Beit Hillel, the practice in Jerusalem was simply not done. The *Shita Mekubetzet* adds the words *techelet b'sadin*, making the linen garment explicit. Whatever the technical *halacha*, the pious circles of Jerusalem — where there appears to have been a norm of heightened stringency in such matters — maintained that one did not wear blue strings in a linen garment.

### Ignorance Problem

Rabbi then asks: *im ken lama asruha* — if it is technically permitted, indeed if it is a *mitzvah*, why was it treated as forbidden? The *Gemara* answers: *mipnei she'ein beki'in* — because people are not knowledgeable. Rashi explains: the general population does not know that *shatnez* is permitted in *tzitzit*. If they see someone wearing wool strings in a linen garment, they will not think "ah, here is someone fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* according to Beit Hillel." They will think: here is someone wearing *shatnez* — and they will conclude that *shatnez* must be generally permissible, and begin wearing *shatnez* themselves even where it is not a *mitzvah* context at all. This is a concern closely related to *maris ayin* — but with a crucial nuance: the ignorance here is ignorance of *halacha*, not ignorance of fact.

This distinction matters enormously. The classic case of *maris ayin* involves ignorance of fact: I melt soy cheese on a hamburger and the observer, not knowing that my cheese is pareve, thinks I am eating a genuine cheeseburger. There, the observer's error is about what is happening, not about what the law permits. In our *Gemara*, however, everyone can plainly see what is happening — wool strings in a linen garment — and the error is that they do not know this is permitted by law. Rav Moshe Feinstein rules that *maris ayin* does not apply when the ignorance is of the law rather than of the facts: we cannot be held hostage to people's lack of halakhic knowledge; the appropriate response is to educate them.

### Public Demonstration

Rava bar Rav Chana proposes to Rava: *v'lirmu beia asarah* — why not gather ten upstanding people, have them go out into the marketplace wearing linen garments with proper *techelet*, and *u'mefarsem l'milsa* — publicize the matter? Rather than accommodating the public's ignorance by restricting the practice, challenge that ignorance directly. Make it visible and widespread, and eventually people's assumptions will shift.

### Demonstration Fails

The *Gemara* rejects this: *kol shekein d'metamhei alayhu* — on the contrary, this would only increase the astonishment and censure directed at those individuals. Ignorance, when deeply ingrained, does not yield to counter-examples. Rather than reconsidering their assumptions, people will simply condemn those doing it — or, as a student perceptively noted, in an era of greater sectarianism, people might regard the practice as the mark of an aberrant group rather than as legitimate *halachic* behavior. The *Gemara* is making an astute psychological observation: deeply ingrained assumptions tend to reinterpret disconfirming evidence rather than revise themselves.

### Teaching Solution

The *Gemara* then proposes what seems like the correct solution: *v'lidrosh b'pirka* — why not address the ignorance directly through public teaching? Gather people at the communal learning sessions and expound clearly that *shatnez* is permitted in *tzitzit*, that this is a special dispensation carved out by the Torah, and then people will understand what they see and draw the right conclusions.

This is a striking moment in the *Gemara*. It insists that one should not give in to ignorance of the law. Public teaching — *limmud* — is the right instrument to address it, and it is a more appropriate response than either suppressing a legitimate practice or staging a public demonstration that will only backfire. The ultimate answer the *Gemara* offers, however, is that a different concern entirely prevents us from allowing this practice even if we were to teach about it: the problem of *kala ilan*.

---

## False Techelet

### Kala Ilan Concern

The *Gemara* now pivots to what it identifies as the real reason behind the restriction: *gezeirah mishum kala ilan* — a rabbinic decree on account of the artificial dye *kala ilan*. *Kala ilan* was a plant-based indigo dye that was visually indistinguishable from genuine *techelet* but was far cheaper to produce. As a result, a significant market developed in which merchants sold *kala ilan* at a discounted price for *techelet*, often deceiving buyers who believed they were purchasing the authentic dye. The concern is therefore not primarily about public perception or ignorance of *halacha* — it is about the real possibility that the wool strings a person attaches to a linen garment will not be genuine *techelet* at all, but *kala ilan*.

If the strings are *kala ilan* and not true *techelet*, the person is not fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *techelet*. And if they are not fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *techelet*, there is no *mitzvah* basis for the *shatnez* — meaning the wool strings in the linen garment constitute a prohibited mixture without any corresponding *mitzvah* to justify it.

### No Techelet = Shatnez

The *Gemara* then asks: even if the *techelet* turns out to be *kala ilan*, why not treat the strings as equivalent to white strings — *v'lo yehei ella lavan* — and still permit the practice on the basis of the *mitzvah* of white *tzitzit*? The *Gemara* rejects this by invoking the principle of Reish Lakish: *kol makom she'atah motzei asei v'lo ta'asei*, whenever a positive commandment conflicts with a negative prohibition, if one can fulfill the positive commandment without triggering the negative — *im ata yachol lekayeim et shneihem mutav* — one must find that alternative. Only where no alternative exists does *asei docheh lo ta'asei* apply. Here, since it is entirely possible to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* using linen strings in a linen garment — *keivan d'efshar b'minah lo* — there is no justification for using wool strings and thereby creating *shatnez*.
