The tests of Rav Yitzchak and Rav Adda are useful precisely for someone who is buying from a *mumche*. Why? Because the danger of *kala ilan* can be detected by these tests. You test your sample, confirm it is genuine *techelet* and not counterfeit, and then you know you have the real article.

But a separate problem remains: even if the dye is genuine *techelet*, perhaps the craftsman who prepared it invalidated the entire vat by performing *te'ima* improperly during production — that is, by testing the dye in a way that caused *pesul*. If the craftsman did not know the *halachos* governing *te'ima*, he might have unknowingly ruined everything he produced, even if the raw material was authentic. This is what *ein lah bedika* means for Tosafot: not that you cannot test whether the color is genuine, but that you have no way of knowing after the fact whether the producer invalidated the vat through improper *te'ima*. The *mumche* requirement addresses this second concern — you need a seller who knows the *halachos* well enough not to have made that mistake.

The *Rambam*'s formulation runs parallel: *Ha'techeiles einan nilkachas ella min hamumche choshesh shema lo nitpal lishma* — one acquires *techelet* only from a *mumche* out of concern that it was not processed *lishma*. The *lishma* concern in the Rambam functions analogously to Tosafot's *te'ima* concern: the *mumche* is necessary because some form of invalidation — either improper intent or improper testing — cannot be detected by the consumer's inspection alone, even if the tests confirm the dye is genuine.

---

## Purchase Standards

### From Non-Jews

From Eretz Yisrael came the ruling that confirmed the sequential reading of the two tests — *shmu'ah ahadadi itmar*, they were stated together. Alongside this, it is reported that Rav Mani was careful to purchase *tzitzit* only as the *braisa* requires, exclusively from a *mumche*, and a certain elder confirmed that his predecessors had followed the same practice to great success.

The *gemara* then introduces a *braisa* governing the purchase of a *tallis metzuyetzes* — a garment already fitted with *tzitzit* — from different sources. If purchased from a Jew in the marketplace, it is presumed *keshera*; the Jew is assumed to have attended to the requirements properly. If purchased from a non-Jew, the ruling is more nuanced: from a merchant (*tagar*) it is *keshera*, but from a layperson (*hediyot*) it is *pesulah*.

The distinction rests on the nature of the transaction. The non-Jewish merchant is in the business of reselling goods; the garment he is selling was almost certainly acquired second-hand from a Jewish owner who had already outfitted it with proper *tzitzit*. His role is that of a reseller, not a manufacturer, and so the *tzitzit* on the garment can be presumed to have been attached correctly by the original Jewish owner. By contrast, the non-Jewish layperson who has a single garment to sell might be attempting to enhance its appeal to Jewish buyers by attaching *tzitzit* himself — a suspect motive — and so no presumption of validity attaches.

### From Jews

The purchase of a *tallis metzuyetzes* from a Jew in the marketplace carries a presumption of *keshera* by virtue of the general assumption that Jews attend to their *mitzvot* properly. The seller is presumed to have used the garment for his own observance, and the *tzitzit* on it are therefore assumed to have been placed there correctly.

### Selling Restrictions

The *braisa* notes an apparent tension: it is forbidden to sell a *tallis metzuyetzes* to a non-Jew without first removing the *tzitzit*, yet the above ruling presupposes that such garments do sometimes pass into non-Jewish hands. The *gemara* resolves this by saying that although the sale is prohibited, it does nonetheless occur on occasion, and the *tagar*'s stock is therefore plausibly composed of such garments.

The *gemara* gives two reasons for the prohibition on selling a *tzitzit* garment to a non-Jew. The first (*mishum zona*) is that the non-Jew might give the garment to a prostitute, who would then appear to her Jewish customers to be associating with a Jew — evoking the famous aggadic narrative that will appear later in the *daf* about a man saved from sin by his *tzitzit*. The second reason, attributed to Rav Yehuda, is the danger of murder: a non-Jew wearing a garment with *tzitzit* could pass as Jewish and thereby gain the trust of Jews who would otherwise not travel with him into dangerous circumstances.

Both concerns reflect a broader theme of the *daf*: that clothing is a fundamental marker of identity. A garment with *tzitzit* identifies its wearer as Jewish in a palpable, visible way. The *gemara* notes the parallel to *tefillin*, about which it is written *u'rau kol amei ha'aretz ki shem Hashem nikra alecha* — all the nations of the earth shall see that God's name is called upon you. *Tzitzit* operates somewhat differently — *v'zachartem*, it is addressed to the wearer's internal remembering — but in practice, anyone wearing *tzitzit* visibly is no less clearly marked as Jewish.

---

## Rav Yehuda's Practice

### Women & Tzitzit

The *gemara* reports that Rav Yehuda would affix *techelet* to the *parzuma* — a type of cloak — belonging to the women of his household. From this practice, the *gemara* infers that Rav Yehuda held *tzitzit* to be *mitzvas asei she-lo hazman grama* — a positive commandment not limited by time — since if it were time-bound, women would be exempt. The question of whether *tzitzit* is time-bound turns on whether nighttime is excluded from the obligation: if night garments are exempt, then time limits the *mitzvah*, and women are accordingly exempt by the general rule that women are *peturot* from positive time-bound commandments.

### Daily Blessing Puzzle

The *gemara* then notes a second practice of Rav Yehuda: *mevarech kol tzafra lihit'atef betzitzit* — every morning he recited the blessing *lihit'atef betzitzit*. This creates a puzzle. If Rav Yehuda holds that *tzitzit* is *she-lo hazman grama* — that the obligation is continuous and unrestricted by time — why does he make a new *beracha* each morning? He is presumably always under the same unbroken obligation. One might push the question further: should he not have made a single *beracha* his entire life, since the obligation never lapses?

### Blessing Resolution

The *gemara* answers by appeal to the ruling of *Rebbi*: *kol zman shemenichan mevarech aleihem divrei Rebbi* — every time one puts on *tefillin* one recites the *beracha*, according to Rebbi. The point is that making a new *beracha* upon each donning is not contingent on a lapse in obligation. Even within an unbroken period of *chiyuv*, the act of removing and replacing the garment is sufficient to generate a new *beracha*.

The *gemara* then asks: if every re-donning triggers a new *beracha*, Rav Yehuda should have been reciting blessings throughout the day every time he put his garment back on, not merely in the morning. The *gemara* responds: *Rav Yehuda inish tznia hu* — Rav Yehuda was a man of exceptional modesty who never removed his garment throughout the day. He dressed once in the morning and kept his garment on until nightfall. Consequently, for him, *kol tzafra* — every morning — was the only time he put on his garment anew, and that is when he recited the blessing. When the *gemara* says he blessed each morning, this does not reflect a principle unique to mornings; it reflects a principle about every fresh donning, which for Rav Yehuda happened to occur only once daily.

One might raise a further question: if Rav Yehuda held *laila zman tzitzit*, he should also be making a *beracha* when putting on his night garments. The *gemara* notes *ina hachi nami* — indeed that would follow. The discussion that flows from this bears on the broader question of whether *tzitzit* is *chovat gavra* — a personal obligation that activates upon wearing — or *chovat mana* — an obligation that inheres in the garment itself. If the latter, the *mitzvah* is in some sense accomplished when the *tzitzit* are tied to the garment, and each morning's *beracha* might be understood not strictly as a *birkas hamitzvah* triggered by performance, but more as a *birkas hashevach* — a blessing of praise upon encountering the *mitzvah* — analogous in certain respects to *birchas haTorah*, which is recited once daily and is understood by some authorities to carry a dimension of praise beyond the strictly obligatory.

---

## Women's Obligation

### Universal Obligation

The *gemara* now turns to a *braisa* that states *hakol chayavin betzitzit* — everyone is obligated in *tzitzit*: *kohanim, leviyim, v'yisraelim*, as well as converts, women, and slaves. The inclusion of converts is notable since converts are almost never singled out as a distinct category in this kind of context. Women and slaves are mentioned because this *braisa* follows the view that *tzitzit* is *she-lo hazman grama*, so women are fully obligated alongside men. Rabbi Shimon is then cited as dissenting: *poter benashim mipnei shemitzvas asei shehazman grama hi* — he exempts women on the grounds that *tzitzit* is a time-bound positive commandment.

### Kohanim Exclusion

The *gemara* asks an obvious question: *peshita* — it is self-evident that *kohanim, leviyim,* and *yisraelim* are obligated. Who else would be? Why does the *braisa* need to state this? The *gemara* answers that the inclusion of *kohanim* is in fact a genuine *chiddush*, because one might have thought to exclude them. The reasoning runs as follows: the juxtaposition in the *parasha* places the prohibition of *shaatnez* (*lo silbash shaatnez, tzemer u'fishtim yachdav*) immediately before the commandment to make *gedilim* (*tzitzit*). One might infer that the obligation of *tzitzit* applies only to those who are fully governed by the prohibition of *kilayim* — that is, to ordinary Israelites. *Kohanim*, however, are permitted to wear *kilayim* in the context of *bigdei kehunah*. Since *kilayim* is effectively waived for them in their priestly garments, one might have thought they are not in the category addressed by the *parasha* and therefore not obligated in *tzitzit*.

The *gemara* rejects this: *kohanim* are only permitted *kilayim* during *idan avodah*, when they are actively performing the Temple service. *B'lo idan avodah* — when not engaged in the *avodah* — they are no more permitted *kilayim* than anyone else. Since the exemption from *kilayim* is not categorical but situational, they cannot be considered outside the ambit of the *parasha*, and the *braisa* must therefore tell us explicitly that they are included in the obligation of *tzitzit*.

This reasoning contains a striking subtext worth noting. The *gemara* frames the *hava amina* for exempting *kohanim* by associating them with *kilayim*-bearing garments — that is, with *bigdei kehunah*. The implicit logic is that *tzitzit* and *bigdei kehunah* occupy analogous conceptual space: one who already wears *bigdei kehunah* might not need *tzitzit*, and conversely, *tzitzit* functions for the *yisrael* as a kind of substitute for *bigdei kehunah*. This parallel is reinforced by Tosafot's observation, noted in connection with an earlier discussion, that the *shaatnez* present in *tzitzit* — wool strings tied to a linen garment or vice versa — is explicitly modeled on *bigdei kehunah*, and the garment bearing such *tzitzit* is categorically excluded from the laws of *kilayim* in the same way *bigdei kehunah* is. The two central priestly garments — the *kesones* (a linen garment, the *sadin*) and the *me'il* (which is entirely blue, *kulah techeles*) — correspond suggestively to the two garments that the *gemara* elsewhere treats as paradigmatic for *tzitzit*: the *sadin betzitzit* and the *tallis shekulah techeles*.

The implication — that *tzitzit* democratizes the sanctity of *bigdei kehunah*, extending to all of Israel a form of priestly identity that was formerly restricted to one group in one place — is one of the *daf*'s deepest themes. We no longer have a *Mikdash* and no longer have *kohanim* in active service; what we do have is *tefillin* (corresponding to the *tzitz*, as noted elsewhere in the *gemara*) and *tzitzit*, which serve as our *bigdei kehunah* and our form of sanctity extended throughout the world.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

Rabbi Shimon's exemption of women is grounded in a careful exegesis. The *pasuk* says *u're'isem oso* — you shall see it. Rabbi Shimon reads this as excluding garments that are not fit to be seen or are not normally seen by others, which he identifies as night garments (*khasuso layla*). A competing derivation might have suggested that the exclusion targets garments of a blind person, who cannot see the *tzitzit* at all. The *gemara* resolves this through a *ribui*: the phrase *asher t'khasse bah* — the garment you cover yourself with — is an expansion that includes even the garment of a blind person, since *others* can see it. The limiting principle is therefore not about the wearer's capacity to see but about whether the garment is the kind worn during daytime — when others see it — or nighttime — when it is not normally visible. *U'motzi ani khasuso layla she'einah b're'iyah etzel acherim* — I exclude night garments because they are not seen by others.

The Rabbis, who do not accept this exclusion, require a different reading of *asher t'khasse bah*. They use it instead to include five-cornered garments within the obligation of *tzitzit*: since a five-cornered garment contains four corners within it, *arba v'lo shalosh* — the Torah's specification of four corners excludes only three-cornered garments, while five-cornered garments are included. For the Rabbis, *u're'isem oso* does not exclude anything based on visibility; it generates the *mitzvah* of seeing and remembering generally. Rabbi Shimon, who derives the inclusion of five-cornered garments from the word *asher* alone, is free to use *asher t'khasse bah* for the exclusion of night garments.

The practical *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon that nighttime creates some form of exemption, though the *rishonim* debate whether the exemption applies to the time of night itself or to garments designated for nighttime use. This question has significant practical implications: it determines whether one makes a *beracha* upon donning *tzitzit* at night, and whether four-cornered pajamas would require *tzitzit* at all.

---

## Seeing & Remembering

### Shema Connection

The *gemara* now shifts into more explicitly *aggadic* territory. Having disposed of the technical question of night-garment exemption, it asks what the Rabbis do with the phrase *u're'isem oso uzachartem* — you shall see it and remember — if they do not use it to exclude night garments or blind persons. The answer is that they use it for an entirely different *drasha*, preserved in a *braisa*: *re'eh mitzvah zo u'zchor mitzvah acheres hatluyah bah* — see this *mitzvah* and remember another *mitzvah* that is connected to it. And which *mitzvah* is that? *Krias Shema*.

The connection to *Shema* is explained by the *mishnah* in Berachot: *me'eimasai korin es Shema b'shacharis* — when does one begin reciting *Shema* in the morning? When one can distinguish between the blue and the white of the *tzitzit* strings. *Tzitzit* thus supplies the measure for when *Shema* becomes obligatory; the two *mitzvot* are functionally intertwined. Tosafot goes further and notes that *Shema* itself, according to some opinions, is rabbinic in origin — and yet the *gemara* draws the connection back to a *pasuk* in the *tzitzit* portion. The deeper point is not about the *shiur* for *Shema*, but about the *parshiyot* of *Shema* — which contain *kol mitzvos Hashem* — being evoked each time one looks at one's *tzitzit*. The same *parshiyot* appear in *tefillin* and are inscribed in *mezuzot*: they are the distillation of all the *Torah*'s obligations, the *zecher l'yetzias mitzrayim*, the reason we observe every *mitzvah*.

### Kilayim Connection

A second *braisa* identifies a different *mitzvah* connected to *tzitzit*: *mitzvas kilayim*. The textual basis is the juxtaposition in the *parasha* — *shaatnez, tzemer u'fishtim yachdav* is immediately followed by *gedilim ta'aseh lach* — and the implication is that one should see the *tzitzit* and be reminded to guard against *kilayim* in other contexts. One reading of this is cautionary: be careful not to let the permitted *kilayim* of *tzitzit* lead you into a slippery slope toward *shaatnez* elsewhere. Another reading sees a broader message: the *tzitzit* reminds you of both the positive and the negative dimensions of obligation — the *asei* of doing and the *lo ta'aseh* of refraining. The juxtaposition of *kilayim* and *tzitzit* thus encapsulates the full structure of Jewish religious obligation.

This also illuminates a tension in how *tzitzit* is understood. Is its function to strengthen one's sense of positive Jewish identity and draw one into engaged, joyful observance? Or is it primarily a protective device, a reminder to guard against transgression when going out into the world? The *shema* connection leans toward the former; the *kilayim* connection leans toward the latter.

### Causation Chain

A further *braisa* makes the sequence explicit: *u're'isem oso uzachartem va'asitem* — you shall see, you shall remember, and you shall do. This is a chain of causation. *Re'iyah mevi'ah lidei zechirah, uzechirah mevi'ah lidei asiyah* — seeing leads to remembering, and remembering leads to doing. The sequence has a striking counterpart in the verse that closes the *parasha* of *tzitzit*: *velo taturu acharei levavchem ve'acharei eineichem asher atem zonim achareihem* — do not stray after your hearts and after your eyes. *Chazal* teach that the eyes and the heart are *sirsurei aveirah*, middlemen to sin: one sees something desirable, one comes to desire it, and desire leads to action. *Tzitzit* inverts this chain. Instead of the eye drawing the person toward transgression, the eye is directed toward the *tzitzit*, which draws the person toward remembering and doing. The same mechanism — seeing, desiring, acting — is redirected from the pull of *aveira* toward the pull of *mitzvah*.

### Divine Presence

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai closes this section with the teaching: *kol hazahir bemitzvah zo zocheh umekabel pnei Shechinah* — whoever is careful with this *mitzvah* merits receiving the Divine Presence. The exegetical basis is a *gezerah shavah* between *u're'isem oto* — you shall see it — and *et Hashem Elokecha tira ve'oto ta'avod* — the *oto* of seeing God. What one ultimately sees, through the chain of *tzitzit* → remembrance → observance, is God Himself.

---

## Israel's Identity

### Seven Mitzvot

The *gemara* presents a teaching of the Rabbis: *chavivin Yisrael shesivvan Hakadosh Baruch Hu bemitzvot* — how beloved is Israel, that God surrounded them with *mitzvot*. *Tefillin* on the head and on the arm, *tzitzit* on their garments, and a *mezuzah* on their doorpost. David expressed this in the verse *sheva bayom hillalticha al mishpetei tzidkecha* — seven times each day I praise You for Your just laws. The seven correspond to: four corners of *tzitzit*, two *tefillin*, and one *mezuzah*.

What is most striking about this teaching is not the enumeration of *mitzvot* but its framing: these are not merely obligations, they are a surrounding, an envelopment of the person in sacred markers. The *mezuzah* on the doorpost is not a personal adornment but it too marks the Jewish space, the Jewish home. The theme is identity — being recognizably, constitutively Jewish in one's person and in one's dwelling.

### David's Comfort

This theme is illustrated immediately by the account of David entering the bathhouse. Upon seeing himself naked — *arom*, unadorned — he cried out: *oy li she'e'emod arum belo mitzvah* — woe is me that I stand naked without *mitzvot*. The very absence of the physical markers of Jewish identity caused him distress. Then he remembered the *brit milah* inscribed in his flesh, and *nityashvah da'ato* — his mind was settled. He was not, after all, without a *mitzvah*. The *brit milah* is indelible in a way that *tefillin* and *tzitzit* are not: one can remove a garment, one cannot remove the mark of the covenant.

After leaving the bathhouse, where Torah speech would have been inappropriate, David sang — and the psalm he sang is *lamenatze'ach al hashminit mizmor ledavid*, understood as referring to the eighth, the *brit milah* given on the eighth day. The *Maharsha* adds that *milah* was also the eighth *mitzvah* given to the world, after the seven *mitzvot* of the children of Noah.

This narrative raises a question — implicit in the *gemara*, though the lecturer notes it explicitly — about what this framework says about women, who are not obligated in the full complement of these surrounding *mitzvot* and for whom no mark is inscribed in the flesh. The question is left open, an important one to sit with.

### Three-Cord String

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds: *kol sheyeish lo tefillin berosho utefillin bizro'o vetzitzit bevigdo umezuzah befitcho* — one who has *tefillin* on his head and arm, *tzitzit* on his garment, and a *mezuzah* on his doorpost — *hakol bechizuk shelo yecheta*, it is with certainty he will not sin. The proof text is *vehachut hameshulash lo bimehera yinatek* — a three-cord string is not easily broken. The three cords are *tzitzit*, *tefillin*, and *mezuzah*. Together they form a reinforcing structure that protects a person from sin.

The *gemara* appends: *omer choneh malach Hashem saviv liyre'av vayechaltzem* — God's angel encamps around those who fear Him and delivers them. This is the point the Rambam makes in his discussion of *mezuzah*: the protective force is not magical. It is the function of these *mitzvot* as reminders — constant, embodied reminders of obligation — that keeps a person from sin. The concern is always that the *mezuzah* in particular may come to be treated as an amulet, a talisman, rather than as a reminder, and the *gemara* here is insisting on the latter understanding.

---

## Cosmic Blue

### Rabbi Meir Derivation

The *daf* closes with a teaching of Rabbi Meir: *mah nishtanah techeilet mikol minei tzeva'onim* — what distinguishes *techelet* from all other colors? *Mipnei shehatecheilet domeh layam veyam domeh larakia, verakia lekise hakavod* — because *techelet* resembles the sea, and the sea resembles the sky, and the sky resembles the *Kisse Hakavod*, the Throne of Glory. The derivation is supported by two *pesukim*: *vetahat raglav kema'aseh livnat hasappir uke'etzem hashamayim latohar* — under God's feet was like a sapphire pavement, like the essence of the heavens in its purity — and *kemareh even sappir demut kisei* — like the appearance of sapphire stone was the likeness of the throne.

The connection is not direct. *Techelet* is not literally the color of the *Kisse Hakavod*. It is blue like the sea, the sea is blue like the sky, the sky is blue like the *sapir* of the divine pavement, and that *sapir* is the blue of the Throne of Glory. Each link in the chain is one of resemblance, not identity.

### Keren Ora Insight

The *Keren Ora* offers an insight that deepens the significance of this chain. The point, he argues, is not merely that *techelet* eventually, through many derivations, evokes the divine. The chain works in both directions. If *techelet* leads upward — from ocean to sky to throne — then the throne leads downward: the sky, the ocean, the world of nature, all relate to God. Seeing the *techelet* on one's *tzitzit* does not merely prompt a thought of God as an abstract terminal point; it links everything in the natural world to God. The ocean reflects God; the sky reflects God; the entire visible world is a manifestation of the divine presence.

This returns us to the tension the *daf* has traced throughout. Is *tzitzit* primarily about protection — a reminder to guard against *kilayim*, a cord that binds one against sin? Or is it about identity and engagement — a garment that marks the wearer as Jewish, that connects every aspect of the natural world to God, that turns the act of going out into the world into an encounter with the divine? The *daf* holds both possibilities in view without resolving them. To wear *tzitzit* is to be protected, and to be marked, and to see God in the sea, the sky, and the world through which one moves.

---

---

# Menachot 44

## Lavan vs. Techelet

### White String Punishment

The daf opens with a *tanya*: *hayah Rabbi Meir omer gadol onsho shel lavan yoter me'onsho shel techelet* — the punishment for neglecting the white strings of *tzitzit* is greater than the punishment for neglecting the blue strings. The reasoning is straightforward: the white strings are far easier to obtain and affix than the *techelet*, and therefore one's blameworthiness for neglecting them is correspondingly greater. When transgression requires no effort at all to avoid, negligence is all the more culpable.

### King's Seal Parable

To what can this be compared? *L'melech basar v'dam* — to a human king who instructs two of his servants to bring him a seal. To one he says: bring me a seal of plaster. To the other: bring me a seal of gold. Both are negligent and fail to deliver. Who deserves the greater punishment? Clearly the one who was asked for the plaster seal, since his task was so much simpler. The *mashal* may not be strictly necessary to grasp the underlying logic — that *techelet* is harder and thus its neglect is more understandable — but it contributes something beyond mere illustration.

### Identity & Belonging

These seals, as the parable makes vivid, were worn by animals or slaves to indicate to whom they belonged. The *tzitzit*, the Gemara thus implies, function similarly: they are markers of identity, signs of belonging to God. The slave bears the king's seal; the Jew wears *tzitzit*. This transforms *tzitzit* from a ritual garment detail into a statement of identity and allegiance.

---

## Hundred Blessings

### Hundred Blessings Obliga…

The Gemara continues with another *tanya hayah Rabbi Meir omer*, a second teaching of Rabbi Meir in a series: *chayav adam l'varech me'ah berachos bechol yom* — a person is obligated to recite one hundred *berachos* every day.

### Me'ah Reinterpretation

The source is a *pasuk* in Devarim: *ve'ata Yisrael mah Hashem Elokecha sho'el me'imach* — "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you?" Rashi explains, and this is the most widely accepted reading, that one should not read *mah* — "what" — but *me'ah* — "one hundred." God asks of you one hundred *berachos*.

What justifies such a reinterpretation of the *pasuk*? The Maharsha offers a beautiful explanation. The Gemara elsewhere struggles with the apparent triviality implied by *mah* — "what does God ask of you?" — as if it were a small thing, when the continuation of the verse lists a demanding program: *ki im l'yirah et Hashem Elokecha*, to fear God, to walk in His ways, to love Him, to observe all His commandments. That is an enormous ask, not a modest one.

### Maharsha's Teaching

This tension pushes Rabbi Meir to read the verse differently. And the Maharsha adds a second, equally beautiful dimension: by reading *me'ah* — one hundred *berachos* — the verse itself supplies the answer to how one achieves *ki im l'yirah et Hashem Elokecha*. It is through reciting *berachos* throughout the day — in the *Shemoneh Esrei* petitioning God for our needs, over food, over the performance of *mitzvos* — that we bring God into our consciousness at every turn. The hundred *berachos* are not an arbitrary number but the very mechanism by which *yirat Shamayim* is cultivated. *Tosafos* adds a further observation: the word *sho'el* spelled with a *vav* yields exactly one hundred letters in the *pasuk* — a striking textual corroboration.

### Blessings on Yom Tov

On a regular weekday, reaching one hundred *berachos* is not difficult. Three *Shemoneh Esreis* of nineteen *berachos* each yields fifty-seven; add *Birchas HaTorah*, *berachos hashachar*, *birchas krias shema*, *bentching*, and the number is readily reached. The challenge arises on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, when the *Shemoneh Esrei* has only seven *berachos* rather than nineteen. The Gemara records that Rabbi Chiya the son of Rav Avya, on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* — *b'Shabso u'vyomei Tovei* — would go to the effort of filling up the hundred *berachos* with fragrances and delicacies: eating many different fruits, smelling various *besamim*, each generating its own *bracha*. This practice of smelling snuff on *Shabbos* to accumulate *berachos* was well known in later generations, and *Yom Kippur* presents a similar challenge since one cannot even rely on food *berachos*.

---

## Three Identity Blessings

### Identity Blessings List

A third *tanya hayah Rabbi Meir omer* follows — though it should be noted that in the *Tosefta* the text reads *Rabbi Yehuda omer*; it is cited here in the sequence of Rabbi Meir's teachings: *chayav adam l'varech shalosh berachos bechol yom* — a person is obligated to recite three *berachos* of identity each day. The Gemara then enumerates them.

### Censorship & Phrasing

The first blessing, as the footnote to our text makes clear, was originally *shelo asani goy* — "who did not make me a non-Jew." The formulation *she'asani Yisrael* — "who made me a Jew" — is a product of censorship, adopted in times when communities engaged in self-censorship of the Talmud to avoid provoking Christian authorities who might take offense at an explicit negative formulation about non-Jews.

This raises a natural question: why not simply say it in the positive permanently? There are two difficulties. First, the three *berachos* form a descending gradation — *shelo asani goy*, *shelo asani eved*, *shelo asani isha* — and the negative formulation allows each to remain meaningful in relation to the preceding one. A *goy* is not a slave, but one can still be grateful not to be a slave even after being grateful not to be a *goy*. If one says *she'asani Yisrael*, it renders the next *bracha* — *she'asani ben chorin* — superfluous, since being Jewish already implies freedom; the order would need to be reversed. Second, and more substantively, there is a reason the *shelo asani* formulation was chosen in the first place. We often come to appreciate the gifts we have by reflecting on what it would mean not to possess them. The negative phrasing focuses attention on what one might have lacked and thereby deepens the gratitude.

It is also worth noting that these *berachos* closely parallel a sentiment attributed to Thales, the Greek philosopher, who expressed gratitude to Fortune for three things: that he was born human and not animal, man and not woman, and Greek and not barbarian. It is notable that a similar triad of identity-gratitude already existed in pagan Hellenic culture.

### Women & Mitzvot

The second *bracha* is *shelo asani isha* — "who did not make me a woman." This reflects the general rabbinic assumption — which need not come as a surprise to anyone — that men bear a greater obligation in *mitzvos* than women, and that this difference in obligation was understood in the *Gemara* as constituting a kind of hierarchy of religious status. Rav Moshe Feinstein addresses this directly in a well-known *teshuvah*, making clear that this difference in function carries no implication of a different level of *kedushah* — *chas v'shalom* — and that the *kedushah* of every Jew is equal. Nevertheless, the *pshat* assumption of the *Gemara* that men have a higher degree of obligation is plainly present in the text.

### Modern Interpretations

There is a great deal of contemporary literature on the *bracha* of *shelo asani isha* and how communities relate to it today. Some *shuls* have shifted to a positive formulation, though as noted this creates its own structural difficulties with the sequence of blessings. Others have chosen not to recite these *berachos* aloud in communal prayer, out of sensitivity to the pain they can cause. One interpretive approach that has been offered is to read the *bracha* not as an expression of gratitude for social advantage, but as a form of social critique: a recognition that even today men generally navigate society with fewer obstacles than women, and that rather than simply feeling grateful for those advantages, the *bracha* ought to sensitize us to the unfairness that persists and call upon us to address it. A parallel reading might apply to *shelo asani eved* — a recognition that slavery still exists in various forms in the world, and that the *bracha* should mobilize us to eradicate it. There is, needless to say, an extensive literature on all of this.

### Ignoramus Blessing Debate

The third *bracha*, as it appears in the original *baraita*, is *shelo asani bor* — "who did not make me an ignoramus." The Gemara then records: Rav Acha bar Yaakov heard his son reciting this *bracha* and challenged him: *kulei hai nami?* — you're going that far? Rashi offers one reading of the challenge: who says you're not a *bor*? Don't be so certain of your own learning. But a more incisive explanation is also possible. The *shelo asani* framework is predicated on circumstances of birth — conditions into which one is born and which are entirely outside one's control. Being a non-Jew, a woman, or a slave are statuses one is born into. But whether one becomes a *talmid chacham* or remains an ignoramus is, to a significant degree, within one's own control. One cannot appropriately thank God for the result of one's own choices — or failures — in the same way one thanks God for the natural circumstances of one's birth.

### Slave Blessing

Rav Acha bar Yaakov's son then asks: so what *bracha* should I say instead? The answer given is *shelo asani eved* — "who did not make me a slave." A person may be born into slavery or captured and enslaved against their will; either way, it is not a condition they chose. The Gemara then anticipates an objection: *hainu isha* — is that not already covered by *shelo asani isha*, since the reason we recite that *bracha* is the lesser degree of *mitzvah* obligation, and a slave's obligations are similarly limited? The Gemara responds: *eved zil tefei* — a slave's social condition is nonetheless lower than that of a woman. The obligations may overlap, but the statuses are distinct, and the *bracha* over being free from slavery speaks to a different dimension of existence than the *bracha* over being a man rather than a woman.

---

## Chilazon Identification

### Chilazon Properties

At the top of 44a, the Gemara turns to the source of the *techelet* dye. *Tanu Rabbanan*: the *chilazon* — *chilazon zehu* — *gufo domeh layam*: its body resembles the sea. The *chilazon* is understood today to be a type of snail, though the animal itself is not blue. The description *gufo domeh layam* is therefore understood to refer to the color of the dye extracted from it, which resembles the color of the ocean. *U'vriato domeh ledag* — it is created similarly to a fish, a description that led the Radziner Rebbe to conclude it was a type of fish rather than a snail; the phrase may refer to the creature living inside the shell. *V'oleh achas leshivim shanah* — it surfaces or washes ashore only once every seventy years.

### Techelet Expense

*U'vidamo tzovin techelet* — its blood is used to produce the *techelet* dye. *Lefichach damav yekarim* — and therefore, because of its extreme rarity and the difficulty of obtaining it, it is extraordinarily expensive. This contextualizes the earlier ruling of Rabbi Meir: the inaccessibility of *techelet* diminishes, though does not eliminate, culpability for its neglect; the ready availability of the white strings makes neglecting them far less excusable.

---

## Reward for Mitzvot

### Rabbi Natan's Principle

*Tanya amar Rabbi Natan*: Rabbi Natan teaches the governing principle that frames what follows. *Ein lecha kol mitzvah kalah shebatorah she'ein matan secharah ba'olam hazeh ule'olam haba* — there is no *mitzvah* in the Torah, even the most trivial and easiest to perform, that does not carry reward both in this world and in the world to come. The precise formulation varies across manuscript traditions: one reading emphasizes that there is both *olam hazeh* reward and *olam haba* reward, while another reading — which appears to be the more correct one — emphasizes that we know there is reward in this world, *kamah*, some quantity, but as for the world to come, *eini yodea kamah*, the reward is so vast it cannot even be estimated.

### Tzitzit Story Intro

*Tze ulemad mimitzvas tzitzit* — go and learn from the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit*. There follows one of the most famous *aggadic* passages in the Talmud. *Ma'aseh be'adam echad shehayah zahir bemitzvas tzitzit* — there was a man who was scrupulous in the performance of *tzitzit*, though he was not without other weaknesses. He heard that there was a certain prostitute in the distant isles of the sea who charged four hundred gold coins for her services.

### Seven Beds Scene

He sent her the four hundred *zuzim* and arranged an appointment. When the appointed day arrived, he went and waited at her door. Her maidservant entered and informed her that the man who had sent the four hundred *zuzim* had arrived. The prostitute said: let him enter. He entered. She had prepared for him seven beds — *shesh shel kesef ve'achas shel zahav* — six of silver and one of gold, arranged in ascending order with silver ladders between each level and a golden ladder leading to the uppermost bed, building anticipation and effort step by step. It is hard to avoid noticing that the seven beds and the six spaces between them echo, in an inverted fashion, the seven heavenly *rekiyos* and the six spaces between them — the same numbers that inform the thirteen wrappings of the *tzitzit*. The parallel seems intentional, a dark reflection of the sacred structure in a context of transgression.

### Tzitziot Slap Him

She ascended to the topmost golden bed and waited for him, unclothed. He too began to climb and was in the process of disrobing when — *bau arba tzitziosav vetapchu lo al panav* — his four *tzitziyos* came and struck him in the face. Whether this occurred as the *tzitzit* swung free as he was climbing, or as he removed the garment, the effect was the same. He was overcome: the spell of his desire was broken, his more rational and responsible self reasserted itself. *Nishmat veyashav lo al gabi karka* — he slipped down and sat on the floor. She, seeing he was not ascending, descended as well and sat beside him on the ground.

### Man Explains Tzitzit

She said to him: *gapah shel Romi* — by the god of Rome (as Rashi understands *gapah*) — I will not release you until you tell me what blemish you found in me that caused you to reject me. He said to her: *ha'avodah* — in truth, I have never seen a woman as beautiful as you. But God has commanded us in one *mitzvah*, and it is called *tzitzit*, and it says twice in that *mitzvah*, *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* — in the final verse, *Ani Hashem Elokeichem asher hotzeiti etchem me'eretz Mitzrayim lihyot lachem l'Elokim Ani Hashem Elokeichem*. The repeated invocation of God's name underscores that *tzitzit* is meant to keep us cognizant of God and our obligations to Him.

It is worth noting — though the man himself does not quote it — that the very *parasha* of *tzitzit* contains the phrase *v'lo taturu acharei levavchem v'acharei eineichem asher atem zonim achareihem* — you shall not stray after your hearts and after your eyes after which you go astray. The words *zonim*, desire, fornication, vision, longing — are woven directly into the text of *tzitzit*. The *mitzvah* is explicitly designed to prevent precisely the situation this man found himself in.

He continued: the words *Ani Hashem Elokeichem* serve as a reminder. *Ani hu she'atid l'hipara* — I am the One who will exact punishment from transgressors. *Ani hu she'atid l'shalem sachar* — and I am the One who will reward those who fulfill the commandments. And now, he said, these four *tzitziyos* appeared to me as four witnesses — two to testify regarding punishment for transgression, two to testify regarding reward for fulfillment.

### Woman Converts

She was so overwhelmed by this encounter, by the moral clarity and religious conviction it revealed, that she said: I will not leave you until you tell me your name, the name of your city, the name of your teacher, and the name of your *beit midrash* where you study Torah. He wrote out all of this information and placed it in her hand.

### Bedspreads Redeemed

She then arose and distributed her property: a third to the government — Rashi explains this was necessary to secure permission to convert — a third to the poor, and a third she retained for herself. The one additional thing she did not distribute was those very bedspreads, *matza'ot*, that she had laid out for him. She came to the *beit midrash* of Rabbi Chiya and said: *Rebbi, tzavei alai v'ya'asuni giyoret* — appoint students to instruct me and make me a convert. Rabbi Chiya asked whether perhaps her eyes were set on one of the students and she was seeking conversion for the sake of marriage — a disqualifying motivation. She produced the note that the student had written and gave it to him, explaining everything that had occurred. Rabbi Chiya said to her: *lechi zechi b'mikchech* — go and take possession of your acquisition. Yes, he would convert her, and she could also marry the very man whose righteousness had so moved her.

### Bedspreads Redeemed

*Otan matza'ot she-hetzi'ah lo b'issur hetzi'ah lo b'heter* — those very same bedspreads that she had spread out for him in a context of prohibition, she now spread out for him in a context of permissibility and sanctity, within the bounds of marriage. There is something resonant here in the image of the cloth itself transformed — the same bedspreads, the same physical objects, now sanctified by the changed relationship between the two people.

### Reward Fulfillment

*Zeh matan sachar ba'olam hazeh* — this is the reward in this world. The man who restrained himself from transgression was granted that same opportunity, with the same woman, in a manner fully permitted and sanctified. And *ule'olam haba eini yodea* — as for the reward in the world to come, it is simply beyond reckoning.

---

## Thirty Days Rule

### Borrowed Tallit

Rav Yehuda teaches: *talit she-ulah kol shloshim yom patur min ha-tzitzit* — a borrowed *talit* is exempt from the obligation of *tzitzit* for the first thirty days. *Mi-kan ve-eilech chayav bah* — beyond thirty days, it is obligated. *Tosafos* explains that in truth a borrowed garment is always exempt *de-Oraita*, since the verse *al arba kanfot kesutcha* — upon the four corners of your garment — implies that you must own the garment; a borrowed one does not belong to you and thus falls outside the Torah obligation. Nevertheless, after thirty days of continuous use, people will assume the garment is yours, and for that reason the Rabbis obligated you to affix *tzitzit* at that point. Alternatively, after thirty days one develops a degree of relationship to the garment that approximates ownership, and the obligation attaches for that reason — even though *de-Oraita* one is still technically exempt.

### Rented House Mezuzah

A parallel rule applies to *mezuzah*: *ha-dar be-pundak be-Eretz Yisrael ve-hasocher bayit be-chutz la-aretz kol shloshim yom patur min ha-mezuzah* — one staying at an inn in Israel or renting a house outside the land of Israel is exempt from *mezuzah* for the first thirty days; *mi-kan ve-eilech chayav*, beyond that one is obligated.

The underlying principle parallels the borrowed *talit* discussion. One view holds that renting, like borrowing, creates no *de-Oraita* obligation, since the verse says *mezuzot beitecha* — the doorposts of your house — implying ownership. After thirty days the obligation is rabbinic, based either on the appearance of ownership or on the relationship that develops to the dwelling. A second view holds that renting does in fact create a *de-Oraita* obligation, but that a rented dwelling does not become a *beit dirah* — a genuine domicile, a home — until one has settled into it, and that process of settling takes thirty days. On this view, the obligation is biblical in principle but only activates once the threshold of genuine habitation is reached. An interesting question that flows from this: if one signs a lease from the outset for more than thirty days, is one obligated immediately, or must one wait the full thirty days regardless? May one affix a *mezuzah* with a *bracha* from the first day? These questions are debated, but the simple language of the Gemara implies no obligation — and no *bracha* — until thirty days have elapsed, whatever the length of the original lease.

### Eretz Yisrael Exception

*Aval hasocher bayit be-Eretz Yisrael oseh mezuzah la-altar mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael* — but one who rents a house in the land of Israel must affix a *mezuzah* immediately, on account of settling the land of Israel. Rashi explains this as an incentive structure: requiring immediate *mezuzah* makes a person more likely to remain in the house, since one is reluctant to leave behind a *mezuzah*, and the presence of a *mezuzah* may encourage others to move in. Alternatively, *mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael* is not merely a practical incentive but a substantive halachic principle: because of the obligation to settle and inhabit the land, even a brief stay there constitutes "coming home," and the full status of dwelling attaches immediately, without any thirty-day threshold. The phrase *mishum yishuv Eretz Yisrael* more naturally reads as an incentive rationale, but the substantive reading is also present in the *rishonim*.

---

## Tefillin Interdependence

### Hand & Head Tefillin

The Gemara moves to a brief but analytically significant discussion of *tefillin*. The *Mishna* states: *tefillah shel yad einah me'akevet* — the *tefillin shel yad* does not prevent the *tefillin shel rosh*, and vice versa. They are two separate *mitzvos*, and the absence of one does not negate the other.

### Chisda's Restriction

Rav Chisda qualifies this: *lo shanu ela she-yesh lo* — this rule that each *tefillin* stands independently applies only when one possesses both but is currently wearing only one (for whatever reason). *Aval ein lo me'akevet* — but if one does not own both, then failing to have one does prevent one from fulfilling the *mitzvah* of the other. This is a striking position. If *tefillin shel yad* and *tefillin shel rosh* are two separate *mitzvos*, why should the fact that one does not own one of them affect whether one has fulfilled the other?

### Chisda Reverses

The Gemara records that when challenged — *amru lo, amarta?* — Rav Chisda reversed himself: *lo*, he denied having said it. The Gemara understands this not as a denial of having uttered the words, but as a reversal of his position. *Ela man d'leit lei trei mitzvos chada mitzvah nami lo le'avid?* — what, if someone does not have both, should he not perform even one *mitzvah*? Of course, even if one lacks the other, one is *yotzei* the *mitzvah* of whichever one does possess and wear.

### Gezerah Incentive

The Gemara then asks: *ume'ikara mai savar* — what was Rav Chisda's original reasoning? The answer is *gezeirah shema yifsha* — he initially held that position as a rabbinic *gezeirah*: if one tells people that owning only one *tefillin* suffices to fulfill at least that one *mitzvah*, there is no incentive for people to acquire the other. By telling them that without both they fulfill neither, one creates a strong incentive for full acquisition. In the end, however, the Gemara rejects this reasoning: the goal of incentivizing complete observance is not sufficient justification for telling a person not to perform the *mitzvah* available to him. The *mitzvah* at hand must be performed even without the other.

---

## Transgression Counts

### Eight Tefillin Violations

Rav Sheshet teaches: *kol she'eino mani'ach tefillin over bi-shmonah asei* — whoever does not put on *tefillin* transgresses eight positive commandments. The four *parshiyos* of *tefillin* each contain verses commanding their donning — *u'kshartem l'ot*, *v'hayu l'totafot*, *v'hayu l'zikaron*, *u'kshartem*, and *v'shamarta et ha-chukah ha-zot* — and when tallied, there are eight imperative verbs, four directed primarily at the *shel yad* and four at the *shel rosh*, yielding eight distinct positive commandments violated by a failure to wear *tefillin*.

### Five Tzitzit Violations

*V'chol she'ein lo tzitzit b'vigdo over b'chamisha asei* — one who has a garment that is obligated in *tzitzit* but fails to affix them transgresses five positive commandments. Rashi, in the final comment on the page, lists them: *v'asu* — they shall make *tzitzit*; *v'natnu* — they shall place the *techelet*; *v'haya lachem l'tzitzit* — it shall be *tzitzit* for you; *u're'item* — you shall see them; and *u'gdilim ta'aseh lach* — you shall make twisted cords. Five *aseis* violated by the failure to attach *tzitzit* to an obligated garment.

### Two Mezuzah Violations

*Kol she'ein lo mezuzah b'fitcho over b'shnei asei* — one who lacks a *mezuzah* on his doorpost transgresses two positive commandments: *u'chtavtam* from the *parasha* of *Shema*, and *u'chtavtam* again from the *parasha* of *v'haya im shamo'a*, each commanding the writing of a *mezuzah*.

### Priestly Blessing Violat…

*V'chol kohen she'eino oleh la-duchan over b'gimmel asei* — any *kohen* who fails to ascend to the *duchan* to bless the congregation transgresses three positive commandments: *amor lahem* — say to them; *koh tevarachu* — thus shall you bless; and *v'samu et shmi* — and they shall place My name upon them. This *halacha* regarding the priestly blessing does not fit neatly into the surrounding discussion of *tefillin*, *mezuzah*, and *tzitzit*, but it is included here as a related enumeration of positive commandments that are violated by inaction.

---

## Tefillin & Long Life

### Extended Days Promise

Reish Lakish offers a teaching on the reward for *tefillin*: *kol hamani'ach tefillin ma'arich yamim* — whoever puts on *tefillin* will have extended days.

### Head & Heart Verse

The source is the verse at the top of 44b: *Hashem aleihem yichyu* — "God upon them they shall live." The Maharsha explains the *derashah*: *Hashem aleihem* refers to the *tefillin shel rosh*, placed upon the head; and *u'lechol bahen chiyei ruchi* — "and all those in whom is the spirit of my life" — refers to the *tefillin shel yad*, placed opposite the heart, speaking to the *ruach*, the life-spirit within us. *V'tachlimeni v'hachayeni* — and it healed me and gave me life. The one who wears *tefillin* thus brings divine vitality to bear on both head and heart, and is promised extended days as a result.

---

## Mincha vs. Nesachim

### Mincha First Order

With this the extended discussion of *tefillin*, *mezuzah*, and *tzitzit* concludes, and the Gemara returns to matters directly relevant to *Menachos*. The *Mishna* had noted that the *solet* and the *shemen* do not prevent the wine, and the wine does not prevent them; they are brought together with the *korban* but are not mutually interdependent. The Gemara now takes up the question of order: when bringing the *mincha* and the *nesachim* — the flour-and-oil offering and the wine libation — that accompany a *korban*, which is offered first?

A *baraita* addresses this: *u'minchasam v'niskeihem* — the Torah phrases it: their *mincha* and then their *nesachim*. *Havei mincha v'achar kach nisachim* — the *mincha* comes first, then the libations.

### Rebbi's Order

Rebbi disagrees, citing a different verse: *zevach u'nisachim* — the sacrifice and the libations. *Havei zevach v'achar kach nisachim* — after the sacrifice comes the libation, and the *mincha* comes only afterward. So there is a dispute: the *Rabbanan* hold that *mincha* precedes the *nesachim*, while Rebbi holds that after the animal *korban* come the *nesachim* and only then the *mincha*.

### Verse Attribution

The Gemara now asks: if Rebbi bases himself on *zevach u'nisachim* to argue that libations come after the sacrifice, what does Rebbi do with the verse *u'minchasam v'niskeihem* that the *Rabbanan* used? And conversely, if the *Rabbanan* base themselves on *u'minchasam v'niskeihem* for the order of *mincha* before *nesachim*, what do they do with *zevach u'nisachim*?

The Gemara resolves this by pointing out that these verses are already needed for entirely different *drashos*. The verse *u'minchasam v'niskeihem* — appearing multiple times in the *psukim* in various forms — is needed to teach that the *mincha* and *nesachim* may be brought separately from the *korban*: they can be brought at night, or even on a different day, when the *korban* itself was offered during the day. The verse is thus teaching not order but separability: the *mincha* and *nesachim* need not be offered simultaneously with the *korban*, though when brought together they must be.

### Zeira's Principle

The verse *zevach u'nisachim*, meanwhile, is needed for a completely different principle, that of Zeira: *ein nisachim miskadshim ela bishchitas ha-zevach* — the *nesachim* are not consecrated except through the *shechitah* of the *korban* they accompany. The verse *zevach u'nisachim* conveys that they come as a package: the wine and flour that accompany a *korban* become linked to and sanctified by that specific *korban* only at the moment of its slaughter. Until *shechitah* they can be reassigned to a different *korban*; after *shechitah* they are bound to this one.

There is a dispute among the *rishonim* as to the precise meaning of this consecration. One view holds that it refers to *kedushah* in the sense of *kedushas ha-guf*: after *shechitah* the *nesachim* become fully sacred such that removing them from the *Beis HaMikdash* renders them *pasul*. Another view holds that the consecration refers specifically to their attachment to a particular *korban*: before *shechitah* they remain fungible; after, they are dedicated to this offering alone.

### Separate Order Logic

Since neither *u'minchasam v'niskeihem* nor *zevach u'nisachim* can serve as the basis of the dispute — both verses are required for other *drashos* — the Gemara establishes the actual source of agreement and dispute. When the *mincha* and *nesachim* are brought together with the *korban* at the same time, the Gemara concludes that everyone agrees: after the *korban*, one first brings the *mincha* and only then the *nesachim*. This is derived from the phrase *olah u'mincha* — after the *olah* comes the *mincha*, and the wine follows. That much is uncontested.

The dispute pertains only to the case where the *mincha* and *nesachim* are brought separately, on a different occasion from the *korban* itself. In that case, what is the correct order?

The *Rabbanan* argue: since when they are brought together with the *korban* the order is *mincha* then *nesachim*, the same order should apply when they are brought separately. Order established in one context carries over to the other.

### Wine & Levite Song

Rebbi's reasoning runs differently. When the *mincha* and *nesachim* come together with the *korban*, there is an internal logic: one has begun with the animal, which is food, and therefore continues with the *mincha*, which is also food — something that is eaten — before proceeding to the wine. *Hatchil be'achilah gemar lah lechulah miltah de'achilah* — having started with the food, complete all the food-related offerings before moving to the drink. But when they are brought separately, that logic does not apply. In that independent context, *nesachim adifi* — the wine takes priority. Why? *Hu demis'amra shirah aleihu* — because the *shirah* of the *Levi'im* is sung at the pouring of the wine. The *nesachim* are the occasion for *Levitical* song, and *ein omrim shirah ela al ha-yayin* — song is said only over wine. The importance of the wine as the vehicle for *shirah* elevates it, and therefore when brought independently, the *nesachim* come first.

---

## Altar Placements

### Single Placement Works

The Gemara returns to the *Mishna's* ruling: *ha-matanot she'al ha-mizbeach ha-chitzon ein me'akvot zu et zu* — the placements of blood on the outer altar do not prevent one another. Whether one is speaking of the four applications of the blood of a *chatat* or the two *zerikos* of other *korbanos*, all the placements on the outer altar are non-indispensable: even if only one placement is performed, *be-di'eved* atonement is achieved. This principle was established earlier in Zevachim.

### Scriptural Basis

The Gemara asks: from where is this derived? *Tanu Rabbanan: minayin le-chol ha-nisanim al ha-mizbeach ha-chitzon she-nisnu matanah achas she-kiper?* — how do we know that for all blood applications on the outer altar, a single placement suffices? *She-ne'emar: ve-dam zevacheicha yishapech al mizbeach Hashem Elokecha* — as the verse says, the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured upon the altar of the Lord your God. The verse speaks of a single pouring — *yishapech*, in the singular — indicating that one placement, one act of applying the blood to the altar, is sufficient to achieve atonement *be-di'eved*, even where multiple placements would ideally be performed.

---

---

# Menachot 45

## Me'akvin Overview

### Topic Transition

Today's daf, Menachot 45, picks up with the *mishna* at the bottom of 44b. Having concluded the extended discussion of *tefillin*, *sefer torah*, *mezuzah*, and *tzitzis*, the tractate returns to the world of *korbanot* — though *menachos* will continue to figure prominently. We are now in a section organized around the principle of *me'akvin zeh et zeh* or *ein me'akvin zeh et zeh*: when two components of a *mitzvah* or *korban* are brought together, does the absence of one invalidate or prevent the other?

### Me'akvin Principle

This framework was already present in the previous *mishna*, which addressed *minchas nesachim* — the flour, oil, and wine that accompany animal *korbanot*. The present *mishna* extends the analysis to the various animals of the *musafim*, the additional festival sacrifices, though *menachos* will continue to surface throughout the discussion.

---

## Hapirim V'Ha'eilim

### Mishna Text

The *mishna* states: *hapirim veha'eilim vehakevasim ein me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the bulls, the rams, and the sheep do not prevent one another. The context is a *musaf* offering that includes a combination of all three types of animals. If some animals are unavailable, those that are on hand are still brought. As the *gemara* will clarify, this applies not only across species — that missing rams does not prevent bringing bulls — but even within a species: if the full complement of a given animal cannot be obtained, whatever is available is still offered.

### Rabbi Shimon

*Rabbi Shimon* offers a divergent position. If the congregation had enough funds to purchase the full number of bulls — say, fourteen for *Sukkot* — but doing so would leave nothing for the *minchas nesachim*, the flour, oil, and wine that accompany each animal, he rules: *yavvi par echad venesachav velo yakrivu kulam belo nesachim* — it is better to bring one bull together with its *nesachim* than to bring all of them without any *nesachim* at all. In *Rabbi Shimon*'s view, the animal together with its *nesachim* constitutes a complete, unified offering. An animal brought without its *nesachim* is, as it were, a second-rate offering. Therefore, it is preferable to offer one complete unit than to offer many incomplete ones.

---

## Which Korban?

### Sukkot Exception

The *gemara* opens by asking: *hanei parim uchevasim deheicha* — which *korbanot* does the *mishna* have in mind? Since the context is a *musaf* with multiple bulls, rams, and sheep, the *gemara* must identify a *musaf* with plurals of all three. *Sukkot* is immediately excluded: the Torah uses the phrase *kemishpat* or *kemishpatam* in connection with the *Sukkot musaf*, which the *gemara* understands to mandate the full complement of every animal. *Sukkot* is thus an exception to the *ein me'akvin* rule, even though the *mishna* does not state this explicitly.

### Rosh Chodesh & Shavuot

The *gemara* therefore identifies the relevant *korbanot* as those of *rosh chodesh* and *shavuot* as recorded in *Bamidbar* — referred to by the *gemara* as *Chumash HaPikudim*, the Book of Numbers. Other holidays are not mentioned because, as *Tosafot* notes, the *gemara* is looking for a *musaf* that features genuine plurals of all three animal types simultaneously. *Pesach*, *Rosh Hashanah*, *Yom Kippur*, and *Shemini Atzeret* each have only a single ram and a single bull, so they do not fit the *mishna*'s language of *parim*, *eilim*, and *kevasim* in the plural.

### Multiple Animals

Even *rosh chodesh* and *shavuot* do not fully satisfy this requirement. The *gemara* examines the relevant verses: for *rosh chodesh* the Torah states *parim b'nei vakar shnayim ve'ayil echad kevasim b'nei shana shiva temimim* — two bulls, one ram, seven sheep. For *shavuot* in *Bamidbar* (*Pinchas*), the formulation is identical: two bulls, one ram, seven sheep. In neither case does one find multiple rams. Where, then, does a *musaf*-like offering with multiple rams appear?

### Emor Passage

The *gemara* directs attention to *parashat Emor* in *Vayikra*, where the Torah presents a special *olah* brought together with the *shtei halechem* on *Shavuot*: *shiv'at kevasim temimim b'nei shana u'far ben bakar echad ve'eilim shnayim yihyu olah la'Hashem* — seven lambs, one bull, and two rams. Here, finally, is a context with multiple rams.

### Korban Comparison

This passage, however, reveals a key discrepancy. The *musaf* of *Shavuot* in *Pinchas* reads: two bulls, one ram, seven sheep. The special *olah* of *Emor* reads: one bull, two rams, seven sheep. The counts of bulls and rams are inverted. The *gemara* concludes that these cannot be the same *korban*. The offering in *Emor* is a distinct *korban* — specifically the *olah* connected to the *shtei halechem* — and is separate from the standard *musaf* listed in *Pinchas*.

### Eilim Resolution

With this clarification in hand, the *gemara* explains the *mishna*'s statement regarding rams. *Lo eilim d'Toras Kohanim me'akvei lei l'ayil d'Chumash HaPikudim v'lo ayil d'Chumash HaPikudim me'akvei lehu l'eilim d'Toras Kohanim* — the two rams of the special *olah* in *Vayikra* do not prevent the single ram of the *musaf* in *Bamidbar*, and conversely. These belong to two distinct *korbanot* that operate independently of one another. It is important to note, however, that internally to the *olah* of *Emor* — which uses the language *yihyu*, "shall be" — all the animals are required and are indeed *me'akev* one another; the *mishna*'s *ein me'akvin* applies only to the relationship between the two separate *korbanot*.

### Different Scenarios

This produces a somewhat jarring reading of the *mishna*, and the *gemara* acknowledges it directly: *tani mili mili katani* — the *mishna* is speaking to different scenarios in different clauses. When it says the bulls and the sheep are *ein me'akvin zeh et zeh*, it refers to the *musaf* itself — even within the *musaf*, if not all the animals of a given species are available, whatever can be brought is brought, and the missing animals do not invalidate the rest. When it speaks of the rams, however, it refers to something entirely different: the relationship between the ram of the *musaf* in *Bamidbar* and the rams of the *korban* associated with the *shtei halechem* in *Vayikra*. The *mishna* thus addresses two distinct halakhic scenarios under a single heading. This is admittedly a complex reading, but it is the *gemara*'s resolution of what would otherwise be an intractable textual problem.

---

## Yechezkel Difficult Texts

### Yechezkel 46:6

Having established the basic rules of *me'akvin*, the *gemara* turns to derive and reinforce these *halachos* from the prophecies of *Yechezkel*, while simultaneously resolving passages in *Yechezkel* that appear to contradict the Torah. The first such passage is *Yechezkel* 46:6, which describes the *rosh chodesh* sacrifice of the future *Beis Hamikdash*: *par ben bakar temimim ve'sheses kevasim ve'ayil tamim yihyu* — one bull, six sheep, and one ram. This stands in direct tension with the Torah's prescription of two bulls and seven sheep for *rosh chodesh*.

### Fewer Animals

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by reading *Yechezkel*'s reduced numbers as halakhic instruction. The verse says *par* — a single bull — even though the Torah mandates two. This teaches: *u'minayin she'im lo matza shnayim mevi echad talmud lomar par* — how do we know that if two bulls cannot be obtained, one may be brought? *Yechezkel* tells us so. Similarly, the verse says *sheses kevasim* — six sheep, rather than the seven mandated by the Torah. This teaches that if seven cannot be obtained, six are brought. And the next verse continues: *ve'lakvasim ka'asher tasig yado* — for the sheep, whatever one can afford. This extends the principle down: if six cannot be had, bring five; if five cannot be had, four; and so on, down to even a single sheep. One brings whatever is available.

### Me'akvin Nuance

This raises an immediate question: if the principle is that one brings whatever one can, why did *Yechezkel* specify six sheep in particular? The *gemara* answers: *kama de'efshar le'haduyei mahadrinan* — to the extent possible, one strives to bring as many as possible. The fact that fewer animals remain valid does not license indifference. One may not reason that since the full seven cannot be had, one animal is just as good as six. Rather, one maximizes the offering within whatever constraints apply.

Yet the very next verse uses the word *yihyu* — "shall be" — by the ram: *ve'ayil tamim yihyu*. Does this not reintroduce the requirement? The *gemara* asks: *u'minayin she'me'akvin zeh et zeh* — how do we know they are *me'akev* one another? And the answer from *yihyu* is somewhat surprising, given everything just said. *Tosafot* offers two readings of what this *me'akev* means in context. First, citing *Rashi*: if the full complement is available and one deliberately brings less, one has not fulfilled the obligation. Second, reflecting the position of the sages who implicitly disagree with *Rabbi Shimon*: having the full number of animals together constitutes a qualitatively distinct *kiyum*, and one must work to achieve that complete unit even if it means forgoing *nesachim*, rather than bringing fewer animals with their *nesachim* as *Rabbi Shimon* would prefer. A third reading offered by *Tosafot*: if one has exactly the right number of sheep, one may not redirect one of them to the afternoon *tamid* sacrifice in order to have a *musaf* sheep with *nesachim* — the full unit of seven for the *musaf* takes priority. In all these readings, *me'akvin zeh et zeh* does not mean that a partial offering is entirely invalidated, but rather that the full complement constitutes an integrated unit that commands halakhic priority.

### Yechezkel 45:18

The *gemara* now turns to an earlier chapter, *Yechezkel* 45:18, which presents a different set of difficulties. That verse reads: *koh amar Hashem Elokim ba-rishon be-echad la-chodesh tikach par ben bakar tamim ve-chiteita et ha-mikdash* — so says the Lord God, on the first day of the first month you shall take a bull and you shall perform *chittuy* — a purification — of the *Mikdash*. The first of the first month is *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*, and the sacrifice on that day is the *musaf* of *rosh chodesh*, which is an *olah*. Why, then, does *Yechezkel* describe the bull as being used for a *chitta'ut*, a purification associated with a *chatat*?

### Miluim Process

*Rabbi Yochanan* declares: *parsha zu Eliyahu atid l'darsha* — this passage *Eliyahu* will expound in the future. The verse remains unexplained for now. *Rav Ashi*, however, offers a resolution: *miluim hikrivu bimei Ezra k'derech shehikrivu bimei Moshe* — this passage was prophesying that at the time of the dedication of the Second *Beis Hamikdash*, a *miluim* process would be performed, analogous to the initiation rites performed during the time of *Moshe* for the *Mishkan*. In the original *miluim*, an ox was used and its blood was applied to the altar as a form of purification. The dedication of the Second *Beis Hamikdash* would similarly occur on *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*, and *Yechezkel* was prophesying that corresponding sanctification rites would be performed then. *Tosafot* acknowledges that the parallels are not exact, but maintains that it is nonetheless a form of *miluim*-style initiation.

### Rabbi Yehuda & Rabbi Yose

A *baraita* confirms that this was already a matter of dispute among *Tannaim*. *Rabbi Yehuda* had taken the same position as *Rabbi Yochanan* — *parsha zu Eliyahu atid l'darsha* — I have no satisfactory explanation, and the matter awaits *Eliyahu*. *Rabbi Yose* responded with the *miluim* explanation: this prophesied the initiation rites of the Second *Beis Hamikdash* in the days of *Ezra*, modeled on those performed in the days of *Moshe*. *Rabbi Yehuda* replied: *tanuach datcha shehinachta es daati* — may your mind be at ease, for you have put my mind at ease. His acknowledgment is elegant: by conceding that he had been troubled and that *Rabbi Yose* had resolved his difficulty, he affirms the correctness of the explanation.

### Yechezkel 44

Another difficult passage appears in *Yechezkel* 44: *ve-chol neveila u'treifa min ha'of u'min habeheima lo yochlu hakohanim* — *kohanim* shall not eat any *neveila* or *treifa*, whether from birds or from animals. The obvious difficulty: does this imply that ordinary *Yisraelim* may eat *neveila* and *treifa*? The prohibition against *neveila* and *treifa* applies universally; restricting the verse to *kohanim* makes no sense as a general prohibition. *Rabbi Yochanan* once again resorts to *Eliyahu atid l'darsha*. *Ravina*, however, offers a resolution: the verse is specifically needed to address *kohanim*, because one might have thought they have special license. Since *kohanim* perform *melikah* — severing a bird's neck from the back — in the *Mikdash*, and that act would render a non-sacrificial bird a *neveila*, one might infer that *kohanim* are permitted to eat *neveila* and *treifa* more broadly. The verse teaches otherwise: even *kohanim* may not eat *neveila* or *treifa* outside the permitted sacrificial context. The mention of both *of* and *beheima* is apt precisely because *melikah* applies to birds — yet even for birds, outside the sacrificial framework, the prohibition remains fully in force.

### Par Helem Davar

The *gemara* addresses yet another passage from *Yechezkel* 45: *ve-chein taaseh beshivah bachodesh me'ish shogeh u'mipeti ve-chipertem es habayis* — and so shall you do on the seventh of the month, from an erring and foolish person, and you shall atone for the House. Following the passage about the *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* purification, this verse mentions an act of atonement to be performed on the seventh of *Nissan*. What does "seventh of the month" mean in this context? *Rabbi Yochanan* explains that this is not a reference to the seventh of the month at all, but to the *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* — the communal bull brought when the *Beis Din* rules incorrectly and the majority of the nation follows that ruling in error, the subject of the entire tractate of Horayot.

The reading is ingenious: *shiva* refers not to the seventh day but to seven tribes — if seven of the tribes sin, even if they do not constitute a numerical majority of the entire people, that counts as the nation having followed the ruling. The word *chodesh*, rather than meaning "month," is read as *chidush* — innovation — referring to the *Beis Din*'s innovative but erroneous ruling. And then *me'ish shogeh u'mipeti* — from an erring and foolish person — teaches: *melamed she'ein chayavim ela al he'elam davar im shigegat ma'aseh* — the communal *korban* is not triggered by an incorrect ruling alone; there must also be a corresponding act of error among the people who followed that ruling. Both elements — the ruling and the people's erroneous compliance — are required.

### Par Helem Requirements

This double requirement — an innovative erroneous ruling by the *Beis Din* and subsequent erroneous action by the people following it — is derived elegantly from the combination of terms in *Yechezkel*'s verse. The *he'elam*, the concealment, refers to the ruling; the *shegagah*, the error, refers to the people's action. Both must be present for the *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* to be obligated.

### Chanina ben Chizkiya

The *gemara* concludes this sequence with a remarkable statement. *Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav*: *zachor oto ha'ish letov ve-Chanina ben Chizkiya shemo* — that man should be remembered for good, and his name is *Chanina ben Chizkiya*. The reason: *she'ilmala hu nignaz sefer Yechezkel* — were it not for him, the book of *Yechezkel* would have been suppressed and excluded from the canon. Why? *Shehayu devarav sotrim divrei Torah* — because on their face, many of its passages contradict the Torah, as we have seen throughout this *sugya*: the animal counts differ from the Torah, the *chitta'ut* on *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* seems anomalous, and the passage about *neveila* and *treifa* appears to grant *kohanim* what it forbids to others. What did *Chanina ben Chizkiya* do? He brought three hundred flasks of oil — fuel to keep the lamps burning through many long nights — sat in his upper chamber, and worked through all the difficult passages until he found ways to interpret them that brought them into harmony with the Torah. This was the scholarly labor that preserved *Yechezkel* as part of *Tanach*.

---

## Rabbi Shimon & Nesachim

### Eifa Measurements

The *gemara* now returns to *Rabbi Shimon*'s position stated in the opening *mishna*, and demonstrates that he derives it from a verse in *Yechezkel*. A *baraita* cites *Yechezkel* 45:24: *ve'eifa la'par ve'eifa la'ayil ya'aseh mincha ve'lakvasim ka'asher tasig yado ve'shemen hin la'eifa* — an *eifa* for the bull and an *eifa* for the ram shall he prepare as a *mincha*, and for the sheep as he is able to afford, and oil, a *hin* per *eifa*. *Rabbi Shimon* notes a textual difficulty: is the measure for a bull and a ram truly the same *eifa*? In fact, they do not have the same measure. Moreover, the measure specified here does not match the standard Torah prescription. So what is the verse conveying?

### Animal Priority

*Rabbi Shimon* reads the verse as follows: since the Torah's prescribed measure is not being stated here literally, the verse must be conveying a halakhic principle. *She'im hayu lahem parim merubim velo hayu lahem nesachim yaviu par echad venesachav ve'ayil echad venesachav velo yakrivu kulam belo nesachim* — if they had the funds for many bulls but not enough for their *nesachim*, they should bring one bull with its *nesachim* and not sacrifice all of them without any *nesachim*. The verse teaches that the measure — the *mincha* and *nesachim* — must be paired with its animal, and that a paired offering is qualitatively superior to an unpaired one. The unit of animal-plus-*nesachim* is the ideal, and it is better to realize that ideal for one animal than to sacrifice many animals in a diminished form.

### Ram Priority

The same principle extends to rams: if there are funds for many rams but insufficient funds to provide each with its *nesachim*, one should bring a single ram with its proper *nesachim* rather than many rams without. *Rabbi Shimon*'s position, rooted in his reading of *Yechezkel*, is that completeness of the individual offering takes precedence over multiplicity of incomplete offerings.

---

## Ha-Par v'Ha-Eilim

### Mishna Text

The second *mishna* addresses the relationship between the various animals and the *shtei halechem* on *Shavuot*. It states: *ha-par veha'eilim veha'kevasim veha'se'ir ein me'akvin es ha-lechem* — the bull, the rams, the sheep, and the goat do not prevent the *shtei halechem*. The *korban* in question is the special *olah* brought together with the two loaves of *Shavuot*, comprising seven sheep, two rams, and one bull, plus a *se'ir* as a *chatat*. The *mishna* rules that the absence of any of these animals does not prevent bringing the *shtei halechem*, and the reverse is equally true: *velo halechem me'akvan* — if the *shtei halechem* is unavailable, the animals may still be offered. Each of the two *korbanot* can stand independently of the other.

### Rabbi Akiva

This independence between the *olah* and the bread does not, however, resolve the question of the relationship between the *shtei halechem* and the two lambs of *shelamim* that are waved together with it. These are distinct from the *olah*: the Torah states *u'shenei kevasim b'nei shana le'zevach shelamim*, two yearling lambs as a peace offering, and these are waved *al shenei kevasim* — specifically on the two lambs, together with the bread. This is a far tighter halakhic connection than the one between the *olah* and the bread.

Regarding these two lambs, *Rabbi Akiva* rules: *halechem me'akev es ha-kevasim ve'ein ha-kevasim me'akvin es ha-lechem* — the bread prevents the lambs, but the lambs do not prevent the bread. The bread is primary. Without bread, the lambs serve no purpose and should not be brought. But if the lambs are unavailable, the bread may still be brought on its own.

### Ben Nanos

*Ben Nanos* disagrees and reverses the ruling: *ha-kevasim me'akvin es ha-lechem ve'ha-lechem eino me'akev es ha-kevasim* — the lambs prevent the bread, but not the reverse. The lambs can stand without the bread; the bread cannot stand without the lambs. His proof: when *Bnei Yisrael* were in the wilderness for forty years, they brought the *korbanot* prescribed in *Emor* — including these lambs — but did not bring *shtei halechem*, since the Torah conditions the *shtei halechem* on entry into *Eretz Yisrael*. Thus we have historical precedent: the lambs were offered without the bread. The reverse was never done. Therefore, the lambs are the foundation, and the bread depends on them, not the other way around.

### Rabbi Shimon's Ruling

*Rabbi Shimon* rules: *halachah kedivrei Ben Nanos* — the law follows *Ben Nanos*. The lambs may be brought without the bread, but not vice versa. However, he explicitly rejects *Ben Nanos*'s reasoning.

### Wilderness Offering

*Rabbi Shimon* does not accept the claim that the lambs were actually offered without the bread during the wilderness period. His own reasoning is based on a different principle: *shekol ha'amur b'Chumash HaPikudim karav ba-midbar ve-chol ha'amur b'Toras Kohanim lo karav ba-midbar* — everything prescribed in *Bamidbar* (*Pinchas*) was offered in the wilderness, but what is prescribed in *Toras Kohanim* — specifically the *Shavuot* passage in *Emor* — was not offered in the wilderness at all.
