Since the special *olah* and the two lambs of *shelamim* are described in *Emor* in connection with the *shtei halechem*, and the *shtei halechem* only applies upon entry into *Eretz Yisrael*, the entire complex of *korbanot* described in that passage — the *olah*, the lambs, and the bread together — did not come into force until they entered the land. *Ben Nanos* is therefore wrong to say the lambs were offered without the bread in the wilderness; none of it was offered at all.

### Matir Concept

If the entire *Emor* complex only began in *Eretz Yisrael*, why does *Rabbi Shimon* still rule that the lambs may be brought without the bread? Because the determining factor is not conceptual primacy but the halakhic *matir* — the mechanism that renders a *korban* permitted for consumption after it has been consecrated. A sanctified offering cannot simply be eaten; something must first be placed on the *mizbeach*, and that act serves as the *matir* that releases the rest for consumption. For the two lambs of *shelamim*, the *matir* is their own blood, which is sprinkled on the *mizbeach*. They function as a complete, self-contained *korban* and may be offered independently. For the *shtei halechem*, however, there is no intrinsic *matir*: nothing from the bread itself goes on the *mizbeach*. The only act that serves as a *matir* for the bread is the slaughter of the lambs and the sprinkling of their blood. *Mipnei shehakvasim matirim et atzmam ve'lo halechem matir et atzmam* — the lambs have a *matir* and the bread does not. Consequently, the lambs can be brought without the bread; the bread cannot be brought without the lambs. This is *Rabbi Shimon*'s reasoning — entirely distinct from *Ben Nanos*'s historical argument, though they arrive at the same practical ruling.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Obligation

A *baraita* opens: *ve'hikravtem al halechem chova* — "and you shall bring upon the bread" (from the *Emor* passage describing the special *olah*) — this is an obligation incumbent upon you. The text then states *shiv'at kevasim temimim* — seven lambs — and from this formulation the *baraita* derives that this *olah* may be brought even without the bread: *af al pi she'ein lechem*. The *olah* is independently obligatory, not merely incidental to the bread.

### Independence

This creates an apparent tension: the verse says *al halechem*, "upon the bread," linking the *olah* to the bread, yet the *baraita* derives that the *olah* may be brought without the bread. If so, what work does the phrase *al halechem* do? The *gemara* resolves this below.

### Rabbi Tarfon

*Rabbi Tarfon* explains: *melamed shelo nitchayvu bikvasim kodem shenitchayvu belechem* — the phrase *al halechem* teaches that the obligation to bring these *korbanot* did not take effect until the obligation of the bread took effect. In other words, the entire package — the *olah*, the lambs of *shelamim*, and the bread — was conditioned on entry into *Eretz Yisrael*, since the *shtei halechem* only applied there. The phrase *al halechem* signals that conceptually, all of this is "because of the bread," and therefore none of it began until the bread became obligatory. But in practice, once they entered *Eretz Yisrael*, the *olah* and the bread are not *me'akev* one another — each may be brought independently of the other.

### Rabbi Akiva

*Rabbi Akiva* builds on this and makes a further argument. One might have thought that the seven lambs described in *Emor* are the same as the seven lambs described in the *musaf* of *Shavuot* in *Pinchas*. If so, the *olah* in *Emor* would simply be the standard *musaf*, and the phrase *al halechem* would link the *musaf* itself to the bread. *Rabbi Akiva* refutes this: when one looks at the bulls and rams, the numbers are reversed. *Pinchas* prescribes two bulls and one ram; *Emor* prescribes one bull and two rams. This proves they are distinct *korbanot*. The *olah* in *Emor* is specific to the *shtei halechem*, while the *musaf* in *Pinchas* is the standard *Shavuot musaf* that has nothing to do with the bread. *Halalu ba'in biglal atzmam ve'halalu ba'in biglal lechem* — the former come on their own account and the latter come on account of the bread. Consequently, the *musaf* of *Bamidbar* was offered in the wilderness; the *olah* of *Emor* was not, consistent with what *Rabbi Shimon* stated in the *mishna*.

### Order Proof

The *gemara* raises a further challenge: perhaps both passages describe the same *musaf* and the Torah is simply offering a choice — two bulls and one ram, or one bull and two rams? The *gemara* rejects this by noting that not only are the numbers different, but the order of presentation is also different. In *Emor*: *shiv'at kevasim temimim u'far ben bakar echad ve'eilim shnayim* — seven sheep first, then one bull, then two rams. In *Pinchas*: *parim b'nei vakar shnayim* — it opens with the bulls. The Torah goes out of its way to present the animals in a different sequence, signaling unambiguously that these are fundamentally different *korbanot*.

### Conclusion

The *gemara* concludes: the *olah* in *Emor* is intrinsically connected to the *shtei halechem* — *al halechem* teaches that its time did not begin until they entered *Eretz Yisrael* — but once it came into force, the two *korbanot* do not prevent one another. The *olah* may be brought without the *shtei halechem* and the *shtei halechem* without the *olah*. Both *Rabbi Tarfon* and *Rabbi Akiva* affirm this principle, differing only in the specific derivations they emphasize. The *mishna*'s ruling — *ein me'akvin* between the animals and the bread — thus holds for this entire complex of offerings. The discussion of the two lambs of *shelamim* and their relationship to the bread, which turns on the *matir* principle analyzed above, will continue in the next *mishna*.

---

---

# Menachot 46

## Shtei Halechem Debate

### Kivsei Atzeret Intro

The daf begins at the bottom of 45b, with the statement *halechem ma'akevet hakevasim* — the bread prevents the lambs. This brings us into the *shtei halechem* discussion that closes the perek. While the broader theme of this section concerns which components of a *korban* are *not* mutually *me'akev*, the Gemara pauses on a notable exception: the relationship between the *shtei halechem* and the two lambs that accompany them on Shavuot. These lambs — the *kivsei atzeret* — are *shalmei tzibur*, communal peace offerings brought together with the bread. The Torah states that they are waved together with the bread and that they stand in a relationship of mutual dependency, but the precise direction of that dependency is the subject of a famous debate.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva holds that the bread is *me'akev* the lambs: without the bread, you do not bring the lambs. The lambs exist only for the sake of the bread. The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Akiva* — what is the reasoning behind this position?

The answer is that Rabbi Akiva derives it through a *gezeirah shavah* — *gamar "yihyu" mi-"tihiyena"*. In the passage in Emor, the Torah uses the word *yihyu* when speaking of both the bread and the two lambs together: *kodesh yihyu l'Hashem lakohen*. The underlying assumption is that this *yihyu* refers to only one of the two components, singling out whichever element is truly *me'akev*. Earlier in the same passage, when speaking of the bread alone, the Torah uses the word *tihiyena*: *solet tihiyena, chametz te'afena*. Rabbi Akiva therefore draws the connection: just as *tihiyena* there referred to bread, *yihyu* here refers to bread — *mah lahalan lechem, af kan lechem*. It is the bread that is the essential element.

### Ben Nannas Position

Ben Nannas reaches the opposite conclusion: the lambs are *me'akev*, not the bread. If you have the lambs alone, bring them; if you have the bread alone, do not bring it. His reasoning is also a *gezeirah shavah* — but he learns *yihyu mi-yihyu*. Earlier in the same *parsha*, the Torah uses *yihyu* in connection with the large group of animals that accompany the *shtei halechem*: *shivat kevasim temimim... par ben bakar... ve-eylim shnayim yihyu ola l'Hashem*. This *yihyu* refers to the animal component. Ben Nannas therefore reads the *yihyu* of *kodesh yihyu* as pointing back to the animal — specifically to the lambs — *mah lahalan kevasim, af kan kevasim*.

### Gezeirah Shavah Analysis

The Gemara immediately raises a question: why doesn't Ben Nannas simply learn from *tihiyena*, the same word used for the bread, as Rabbi Akiva does? Tosafot notes that while the words are not identical, the connection is direct — *tihiyena* appeared earlier in the very same passage describing the *shtei halechem*. Why not draw the obvious link?

The Gemara answers: *danin yihyu mi-yihyu, ve-ein danin yihyu mi-tihiyena*. We prefer a *gezeirah shavah* built from identical words. The principle invoked here — drawn from the *tanna de-vei Rabbi Yishmael* regarding *tzara'at*, where even words with merely similar meanings sufficed — is clarified: that leniency applies only when there is no identical word available. When an identical match exists, we must use it. Ben Nannas therefore correctly prefers the *yihyu-yihyu* connection over the *yihyu-tihiyena* one.

The Gemara then turns the question around on Rabbi Akiva: why does he not also use *yihyu mi-yihyu*, connecting to the earlier *yihyu* that referred to the animals? The answer is: *danin davar she-matanah la-kohen mi-davar she-matanah la-kohen*. The verse *kodesh yihyu l'Hashem lakohen* speaks of something that goes to the *kohen*. Both the bread and the lambs go to the *kohen* — the *kohen* eats the bread and eats the *shelamim*. But the other animals — the one bull, two rams, and seven lambs — are *olot*, which go entirely to God and not to the *kohen*. It is therefore more appropriate to link this *yihyu* to an earlier *yihyu* also associated with something given to the *kohen*, rather than to the *yihyu* of *olot* that go exclusively to God.

### Kodesh Yihyu Pasuk

The Gemara adds a second approach to the debate: *ve-iba'it eima bi-kra gufei kamifligi* — perhaps they are debating the *pasuk* itself. The verse *kodesh yihyu l'Hashem lakohen* is written at the conclusion of the section describing both the bread and the two lambs, and both Rabbi Akiva and Ben Nannas read the same word *yihyu* as pointing to only one of the two components.

Rabbi Akiva asks: *eizehu davar she-kulo la-kohen?* — which of these two components goes entirely to the *kohen*? It must be the bread. The lambs are *shelamim*, and the *eimurim* — the fats and certain innards — go to the altar. So the lambs do not go fully to the *kohen*. Therefore *yihyu l'Hashem lakohen* refers to the bread, which passes entirely to the *kohen*.

Ben Nannas counters: *mi ksiv kodesh yihyu la-kohen?* The verse does not say simply *la-kohen*. It says *l'Hashem lakohen* — to God, and to the *kohen*. *Eizehu davar she-miktzaso la-Shem u-miktzaso la-kohen?* Which component is partly to God and partly to the *kohen*? That is the lambs, which are *shelamim* — the *eimurim* go to God and the meat goes to the *kohen*.

Rabbi Akiva's rejoinder: *mi ksiv kodesh yihyu l'Hashem ve-la-kohen?* The conjunction *ve-* is not there. The verse says *l'Hashem lakohen*, not *l'Hashem ve-la-kohen*. The formulation follows the principle articulated by Rav Huna: *kana'ah Hashem u-netanah la-kohen* — God acquired it and gave it to the *kohen*. This is the general principle that *kohanim mishulchan gavoah zachu* — the *kohanim* eat from God's table, as it were. When a *korban* is consumed by the *kohanim*, it is not simply given to them; rather, it passes through God to them. The *kohen*'s eating is conceptually similar to the altar's consumption and is part of the *kapara* process. Accordingly, *l'Hashem lakohen* means it goes to God, and from God passes fully to the *kohen* — which describes the bread, not the lambs.

Whether the debate turns on the *gezeirah shavah* from *yihyu* and *tihiyena*, or on the internal reading of *kodesh yihyu l'Hashem lakohen*, the Gemara frames the dispute as a technical question about which component the *yihyu* is pointing to — not, as the *mishnah* might have suggested, a purely conceptual argument about which offering is the *ikar*.

---

## Zikah & One Unit

### Rabbi Yochanan Zikah

Rabbi Yochanan articulates a foundational principle: *hakol modim she-im huzkequ zeh la-zeh she-me'akvin zeh et zeh* — everyone agrees that once the bread and the lambs have become connected to one another, they are mutually *me'akev*. Even Rabbi Akiva, who holds that the bread can be brought without the lambs, concedes that when they come together and that connection is established, they function as a single unit. If any component is then missing, the whole is invalid.

The question is: what act creates this connection — this *zikah*? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *shechita*. When the lambs are slaughtered, that act of *shechita* is *mekadesh* the bread, conferring upon it *kedushat haguf*. Prior to *shechita*, the bread possesses only *kedushat damim* — it is owned by the *beis hamikdash* but not yet sanctified in body. Removing it from the *Mikdash* would not invalidate it, since *kedushat haguf* has not yet been conferred. Once the lambs are slaughtered, the bread acquires *kedushat haguf*, and at that moment the entire offering becomes one coherent unit.

This is conceptually parallel to what was said earlier regarding the *musaf* offerings: once you have the full set of components, that defines the whole as a package, and the loss of any one piece renders the whole invalid. Here too, once the *shechita* of the lambs establishes the *zikah*, the bread and lambs are that package.

It is worth noting the word *zikah* itself, familiar to anyone who has learned Yevamos. There, *zikah* describes the quasi-marital connection created between a surviving brother and his sister-in-law by virtue of the deceased brother — a connection that can manifest fully as *yibum* or be severed through *chalitza*. Here the same word appears in an entirely different context, describing the bond that links the bread and lambs into a single sacrificial unit. The word in both contexts captures the same essential concept: a legally meaningful linkage between two entities.

Regarding Rabbi Akiva's position within this framework: one might have thought that since Rabbi Akiva permits bringing the bread without the lambs, he would view the two components as always operating somewhat independently, even when brought together. The Gemara does not accept this. Even Rabbi Akiva agrees that the normative mode of bringing the bread is through the lambs — the *shechita* of the lambs and the sprinkling of their blood constitutes the act of *hakravah* that validates the offering. When they come together, they work as a unit through the lambs. Rabbi Akiva's leniency — allowing the bread to function independently — applies only in exceptional circumstances, not to the normal bringing of the offering.

### Tenufah vs Shechita

The Gemara cites a question that arose in Eretz Yisrael: *tnufa osa zikah o eina osa zikah?* Before the lambs are slaughtered, the *kohen* waves both the lambs and the bread together in the act of *tenufah*. Perhaps this waving — which is performed jointly with both components present — is itself sufficient to define them as a unit?

The Gemara initially proposes to resolve this from Rabbi Yochanan's statement: since Rabbi Yochanan says *shechita* creates *zikah*, one might infer that *tenufah*, which precedes *shechita*, does not. The Gemara rejects this inference, noting that Rabbi Yochanan's statement may itself be the subject of the question. Perhaps Rabbi Yochanan merely meant to establish with certainty that *shechita* creates *zikah*, without ruling out the possibility that *tenufah* creates it earlier.

### Shechita Makes Zikah

An attempt is made to resolve the question from a textual argument: the verse *kodesh yihyu l'Hashem lakohen* is written after the *tenufah* in the *parasha*, yet Rabbi Akiva and Ben Nannas still debate based on it — implying that even after the waving, only one component is *me'akev* the other, not both. If *tenufah* had created *zikah*, they would both be mutually *me'akev* and the debate would be moot. This would seem to prove that *tenufah* does not create *zikah*.

The Gemara deflects this: the verse appears at the end of the entire section, after *tenufah*, after *shechita*, and after the entire offering is brought. It cannot be read as speaking to any particular stage in the process. *Ela meiikara ka'ei* — the verse refers back to an earlier status, describing what the offering was at a prior point, before either waving or slaughtering. *Davar she-sofo la-kohen* — it describes something that would ultimately reach the *kohen*, not necessarily something already at that stage.

The Gemara then returns to the direct question of whether *shechita* truly creates *zikah*, and introduces a *baraita* about the *todah* offering as a challenge.

---

## Todah Case Study

### Bread Break Before

The *baraita* is elegantly structured, examining three types of invalidity that can befall the bread of a *todah* — a bread breaking, the bread going *yotzei* outside its proper boundary, and the bread becoming *tamei* — each considered at three points in time: before *shechita*, after *shechita*, and after *zerikah* (the sprinkling of the blood). The *todah* comes with forty loaves: ten of *chametz* and thirty of *matzah*, spread across four types, and the bread is eaten within Yerushalayim.

The underlying assumption is that if even one loaf is incomplete — a piece has broken off — the entire collection of bread is invalid. Rashi acknowledges uncertainty about the precise derivation of this rule, suggesting a possible analogy to the *lechem hapanim*.

If a piece of bread broke before *shechita*: there is no problem. Anything that occurs before *shechita* can be corrected. The broken loaf is replaced — *yavi lechem acher ve-shofre* — and the *korban* proceeds normally.

### Bread Break After

If the bread broke after *shechita*: the situation cannot be repaired. The *shechita* has already conferred *kedushat haguf* upon the bread and defined the offering as a unit; no substitution is possible at this stage. The *baraita* rules: *hadam yizarek ve-habasar ye'achel, ve-yidei nidro lo yatza* — sprinkle the blood and eat the meat, but the owner has not fulfilled his obligation of *todah*. Why? Because the offering was effectively brought without its bread. The entire collection of bread is invalid; the single broken piece invalidates all forty loaves, and since it cannot be replaced after *shechita*, the animal is brought as a *korban* without bread. A *todah* without bread is a *shelamim*. Rashi understands that one must have *kavanah* at the time of *zerikah* to bring it as *shelamim*; alternatively, it may revert automatically, analogous to the laws of *pesach* brought at other times of the year. Either way, the owner has brought a *shelamim*, not a *todah*, and his obligation remains unfulfilled. The bread, now invalid, is burned.

### Yotzei Before Shechita

If the bread went outside Yerushalayim before *shechita*: no problem. At this stage the bread has only *kedushat damim*, not *kedushat haguf*. Removing property of the *beis hamikdash* from Yerushalayim does not invalidate it, since the prohibition of *yotzei* that renders a *korban* invalid applies only once *kedushat haguf* is present. The solution is simply *machziro* — bring the bread back in — and proceed to *shechita*.

### Yotzei After Shechita

If the bread went outside Yerushalayim after *shechita*: now the bread has acquired *kedushat haguf* through the act of *shechita*, and removing it from Yerushalayim invalidates it. The blood has not yet been sprinkled. The *baraita* rules identically to the case of bread breaking after *shechita*: *hadam yizarek ve-habasar ye'achel ve-yidei nidro lo yatza* — proceed with the *korban*, but you have not fulfilled your obligation of *todah*. The animal reverts to *shelamim*. The bread that went outside is invalid, *ve-halechem pasul*.

If the blood was sprinkled before the bread went outside — *nizrak hadam* — then the *korban* was already valid at the moment of *zerikah*, and the owner has fulfilled his *todah* obligation. The loaves that subsequently went outside cannot be eaten, but the remaining bread inside Yerushalayim is valid. The *kohen* is given his portion — four whole loaves — from the bread that remained inside: *torem mimah shebifnim al shebichutz*.

### Tumah Before Shechita

If the bread became *tamei* before *shechita*: it can be corrected. Bring new bread and proceed to *shechita* — *meivi lechem acher ve-shochet*.

### Tumah After Shechita

If the bread became *tamei* after *shechita*: the situation is different from the other cases of post-*shechita* invalidity. Here the *baraita* rules: *hadam yizarek ve-habasar ye'achel, u-videi nidro yatza* — the owner *does* fulfill his obligation. Why? *She-ha-tzitz meratzeh al ha-tamei* — the *tzitz*, the golden forehead-plate of the High Priest, atones for and overrides problems of *tumah* in *korbanos*. This requires some analysis. It is not the *korban* itself that is *tamei* — the lambs are *tahor* — it is the bread. The *zerikah* therefore proceeds without any *tzitz* needed to permit it. The question is only whether a *todah* was validly brought, i.e., whether the *dam* was sprinkled in the context of a *todah* that had its bread present. The *tzitz* effectively renders the *tumah* of the bread transparent for purposes of the *korban*'s validity: it is treated as though the bread were present and valid, and the offering counts as a *todah*. The owner is therefore *yotzei*. The bread itself remains *pasul* — the *tzitz* does not permit eating *tamei* bread — but vis-à-vis the validity of the *korban*, it is counted as a *todah*.

After *zerikah* — if the blood was sprinkled while the bread was *tahor* and only then a loaf became *tamei*: the *korban* is fully valid, the obligation fully fulfilled. The *kohen* receives his four loaves from the *tahor* bread — *torem min ha-tahor al ha-tamei* — the *tamei* loaf is disposed of, and the owner eats the remaining *tahor* bread.

### Post-Shechita Irreversib…

The *baraita* establishes a clear structural principle: the moment of *shechita* is decisive. Everything that goes wrong before *shechita* can be remedied; everything that goes wrong after *shechita* — whether breaking, *yotzei*, or *tumah* — cannot be corrected by substitution, and the offering either reverts to *shelamim* (in the cases of breaking and *yotzei*) or is validated by the *tzitz* (in the case of *tumah*). The bread cannot be replaced once the *shechita* has occurred.

This now generates a sharp question. We have said that *shechita* creates *zikah* — it binds the bread and the animal into one unit. If that is so, then when a problem arises after *shechita* that invalidates the bread, the *zikah* should make the whole offering invalid. The animal cannot be brought as a *shelamim* if it has been fused into one unit with the bread. Why, then, is the animal salvageable?

---

## Todah vs Shtei Halechem

### Torah Names Todah

The Gemara answers: *shani toda de-Rachmana karyei shelamim* — the *todah* is different because the Torah itself calls it *shelamim*. The verse states *al zevach todat shelamav*, referring to the *todah* as a type of *shelamim*. From this the Gemara derives: *mah shelamim kereivim belo lechem af todah kereivah belo lechem* — just as *shelamim* is brought without bread, so too a *todah* can exist without its bread. The *todah* therefore always retains an independent *shelamim* identity to revert to, even after the *zikah* of *shechita* has been established. The bread can conceptually be separated off and the animal can continue to exist as a valid *korban*.

### Shtei Halechem Unique

The *shtei halechem* would seem to face the same problem. The lambs too are called *shelamim* — the verse refers to them as *shnei kevasim... lezeva'ch shelamim*. Why can they not similarly revert to an independent *shelamim* status when the bread is invalid after *shechita*?

Rashi and Tosafot note the distinction. The *todah* exists as a category of *korban* entirely independent of its bread. There is a concept of a *todah* animal; the bread is an additional component that elevates it to *todah* status, and without bread it is simply a *shelamim* of the ordinary kind. By contrast, there is no such thing as *shalmei tzibur* in the Torah apart from the *kivsei atzeret*. The entire category of *shalmei tzibur* is defined by and inseparable from the *shtei halechem*. There is no pre-existing *shelamim* identity for the lambs to revert to once they have been defined as part of the *shtei halechem* unit. Alternatively, one might frame it this way: the *todah* is fundamentally a *korban* to which bread is added as an accessory that confers *todah* status; the bread can be stripped away and the core *korban* remains. The *shtei halechem*, however, is fundamentally about the bread — the loaves are the *ikar*, and the lambs are what enable the bread to be brought. Once they form a unit, there is nothing independent for the lambs to revert to.

The discussion that follows elaborates on this distinction. If the answer to Abaye's later question about why only the lambs — and not the large *olah* complement — create *zikah* with the bread is to be "because only *shelamim* are linked to bread," then that principle must also explain why the *todah*'s link to its bread persists even after *shechita*. The *todah* is called *shelamim* by the Torah, and the association of bread with *shelamim* — not with *olah* — is the mechanism by which the link is created and sustained.

---

## Abaye's Question

### Why Only Lambs?

Abaye poses his question to Rava: *mai shna shnei kevasim d'makdeshei lechem u-me'akvi?* — what distinguishes the two lambs, such that their *shechita* sanctifies the bread and makes them mutually *me'akev*? And *mai shna shiva kevasim u-far ve-eilim* — what distinguishes the seven lambs, the bull, and the two rams (written in that order in the Torah) such that their *shechita* does *not* sanctify the bread and creates no *zikah* at all? All of these animals come with the *shtei halechem*. Why should the two lambs alone be linked to the bread?

### Rava Answer

### Tenufah Qualifier

Rava answers: *hov ve-huzkequ zeh la-zeh bi-tenufah* — the Torah specified that only the bread and the two lambs are waved together in *tenufah*. This act of joint waving defines them as a single unit and explains why the *shechita* of the lambs subsequently sanctifies the bread and why they are mutually *me'akev*. The large *olah* component — the bull, rams, and seven lambs — is never waved together with the bread and therefore stands in no such relationship to it.

### Todah Counterargument

The Gemara challenges this: *ve-harei todah de-lo huzkequ zeh la-zeh bi-tenufah* — the *todah* animal is never waved together with its bread, and yet the *shechita* of the *todah* sanctifies its bread and they are mutually *me'akev* in the sense that without the bread the offering does not count as a *todah*, and without a *todah* animal there is no reason to bring the bread. *Tenufah* cannot be the explanation for the link between the *todah* and its bread.

### Bread-Shelamim Link

The Gemara therefore reframes the answer: *ela ke-todah* — the principle is like the *todah*. *Mah toda shelamim, af hacha nami shelamim* — just as by the *todah* it is the *shelamim* component that is linked to the bread, so too here it is the *shelamim* component — the two lambs — that is linked to the bread, and not the *olah* component. This is not merely a formal rule but reflects a substantive principle: whenever the Torah links bread to a *korban*, that link is always to a *shelamim*, never to an *olah*. The association of bread with *shelamim* is built into the structure of *korbanos*.

The Gemara anticipates an objection: if that is so for the *todah*, why does the large *olah* component not also create a link? After all, there are multiple *zevachim* present, and perhaps they should all share equally in the connection to the bread. The Gemara answers: *hatam leika zevachim achrini bahadei* — by the *todah* there are no other *korbanos* present, so it is clear that the *shelamim* alone carries the link. Here, where multiple *korbanos* are present, one might have thought the link should be distributed among all of them. The Gemara will resolve this through the proof from the *nazir*.

### Nazir Ram Proof

The proof is brought from the ram of the *nazir*. When a *nazir* completes his term, he brings a set of *korbanos*: a lamb as an *olah*, a ewe-lamb as a *chatat*, and a ram as a *shelamim*, accompanied by a basket of *matzah* — *challot belulot bashamen* and *rekikei matzot meshuchim bashamen*. The Torah then says explicitly: *ve-et ha-ayil ya'aseh zevach shelamim l'Hashem al sal ha-matzot* — the ram shall be made a *shelamim* offering together with the basket of *matzah*. Even though an *olah* and a *chatat* are also being brought simultaneously, the Torah makes clear that the bread is associated exclusively with the *shelamim* ram, not with the other *korbanos*.

The *baraita* derives from this: *melamed she-ha-sal ba chavah la-ayil* — the basket comes as an obligation associated specifically with the ram. *Lefikach, shachto shelo lishmo, lo kidshu ha-lechem* — therefore, if the ram was slaughtered *shelo lishmo* (not for its designated purpose), the bread is not sanctified. The link between the bread and the *nazir*'s offering runs exclusively through the *shelamim* component, even in the presence of other *korbanos*.

This proves the principle definitively: bread is always associated with *shelamim*, not with *olah*. The large *olah* component of the *shtei halechem* offering — the bull, the two rams, the seven lambs — therefore creates no *zikah* with the bread. The *zikah* belongs solely to the two lambs that are *shalmei tzibur*. That is why their *shechita* sanctifies the bread, and that is why they alone are mutually *me'akev* with the bread once the *shechita* has occurred.

---

---

# Menachot 47

## Shtei HaLechem Alone

### Tanu Rabbanan

The daf opens in the middle of *amud bet* of daf 46 with a *baraisa*: *shtei halechem haba'os bifnei atzman* — if the *shtei halechem* are brought by themselves, without the *shnei kevasim*. This proceeds within the position of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that the *shtei halechem* may be brought without the two lambs. But the question immediately arises: where is the *matir*, the permitting element that is offered on the *mizbeach* to render the bread permitted? The *baraisa* prescribes a peculiar middle course: *yunfu* — let them be waved — *v'tu'avar tzurasan* — let their form be degraded, meaning let them remain overnight so that they become invalid through *lina* — *v'yeitz'u l'veis hasereifa* — and then, now that they are *nosar*, they are burned.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this with a *manafshach* — make up your mind. *Ee l'achila asyan* — if according to Rabbi Akiva the *shtei halechem* brought alone can be eaten, since they require no *matir*, then *lichlu* — eat them. *Ee l'sereifa asyan* — if Rabbi Akiva holds they cannot be eaten because they have no *matir*, then *lishrifinu l'alter* — burn them immediately. What is this intermediate position of waiting overnight? *Lamma lahu ibbur tzurah* — why the delay until the next morning?

### Rav Rav Ava Dispute

The *Gemara* presses the contradiction sharply. The *baraisa* seems to treat the *shtei halechem* as neither simply edible nor simply subject to immediate burning. Both positions have internal logic, but this middle path demands explanation.

### Rabbah's Gezeirah

Rabbah resolves the difficulty: *l'olam l'achila asyan* — fundamentally, according to Rabbi Akiva, the *shtei halechem* when brought alone may in principle be eaten, even without a *matir* placed on the *mizbeach*. Why then do we not eat them? *Gezeirah shema yizdamnu lahen kevasim l'shana haba'ah* — it is a rabbinic enactment (*gezeirah*) lest in a future year lambs be available. If this year people eat the bread alone, what will they say next year when lambs are present? *V'yomru* — they will say: last year we ate the bread without lambs; let us do so again. *V'innu lo yadi d'ishtakad lo hava kevasim* — they will not realize that last year there were no lambs and the bread was its own *matir*, whereas this year, *kivan d'ika kevasim, kevasim hu d'sharei lei* — when lambs are present, even Rabbi Akiva agrees that the *zrikas hadam* of the lambs is required to permit the bread for eating.

Therefore we do not eat the bread, but we also cannot simply burn it immediately, since it is *kodesh kodashim* and is in principle edible. We must wait until it becomes invalid through *lina* — overnight — at which point it is *nosar* and may be burned.

Rabbah further asks: *m'na amina la* — how do I know that according to Rabbi Akiva the *shtei halechem* brought alone may in principle be eaten? From the *Mishna* regarding Ben Buchri's testimony in *Yavneh*. The *Mishna* records a dispute about whether *kohanim* are obligated to contribute their half-*shekel* to the communal funds. Rabbi Yehudah cites the testimony of Ben Buchri that a *kohen* who contributes does not sin; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai counters that one who does not contribute does sin. The *kohanim* sought to exempt themselves by invoking the verse *v'chol minchat kohen kalil tihiyeh lo tei'achel* — every *mincha* of a *kohen* must be entirely burned and may not be eaten — arguing: since the *shtei halechem* and the *lechem hapanim* would partly belong to us, they would have to be burned rather than eaten, and therefore we should not be required to contribute.

The *Gemara* asks: which *shtei halechem* are they discussing? If it is the *shtei halechem* that comes with the *shnei kevasim*, their argument collapses — after all, *toda* bread is not burned even when a *kohen* brings a *toda*, because the Torah does not call that bread a *mincha*. The *kohanim* could not use the *shtei halechem* that comes with the lambs as an argument for burning, since everyone already knows that such bread is eaten. Therefore they must be discussing *b'vo'ot bifnei atzman* — the *shtei halechem* brought alone, according to Rabbi Akiva. And the *baraisa* asks: *heich ne'echelu* — how would they be eaten? The implicit assumption is that even when brought alone, they are eaten. Thus Rabbah has a proof that according to Rabbi Akiva the *shtei halechem* brought alone are fundamentally *l'achila*. Abaye, however, pushes back: even if the *kohanim* were arguing about the *shtei halechem* that comes with the lambs, their argument still holds, because the bread of *toda* is not called a *mincha*, whereas the *shtei halechem* is explicitly called *mincha* in the verse *b'hakrivchem mincha chadasha l'Hashem*. Thus the proof is deflected.

### Rav Yosef Opinion

Rav Yosef offers an entirely different account. *L'olam l'sereifa asyan* — according to Rabbi Akiva, the *shtei halechem* when brought alone must be burned. So why not burn them immediately? *Lefi she-ein sorfin kodashim beyom tov* — because the *shtei halechem* is brought on *Shavuos*, and one may not burn *kodashim* on *Yom Tov*. The waiting, then, is not a matter of wanting to allow for *lina* and *nosar*, but simply a consequence of the prohibition against burning *kodashim* on *Yom Tov*.

### Abaye Challenges

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef directly. *Mi dami?* — You cannot compare the two cases. The general rule against burning *kodashim* on *Yom Tov* applies when the burning is incidental — when the *halacha* is that the item should be eaten but something went wrong (e.g., it became *tamei*) and therefore it must be burned after *Yom Tov*. But here, if Rabbi Akiva's position is that the *mitzvah* of the day is precisely to burn these loaves, then that burning is itself the *mitzvah* and we would perform it on *Yom Tov*, just as we burn the *par v'sa'ir* of *Yom Kippur* even when it falls on *Shabbos*.

Rav Yosef therefore reformulates his *gezeirah*: the reason we do not burn them immediately is not the prohibition of burning *kodashim* on *Yom Tov*, but rather *gezeirah shema yizdamnu lahem kevasim le-achar mikan* — lest lambs be found later that same day. If one burns the *shtei halechem* immediately and then lambs are located before the end of the day, the bread will have been destroyed needlessly.

Abaye presses further: *teinach zman hakrava* — granted, during the time when the lambs could still be brought one should not burn the bread. But *le-vasar hakhi lisreifinhu* — after nightfall, when lambs can no longer be brought, why not burn them then? Why wait until morning? The *Gemara* resolves this by reinterpreting the phrase *tu'avar tzurasan*. Rather than meaning the form of the loaves degrades overnight, it means *tu'avar tzuras hakravasan* — the period during which they could be offered passes, i.e., nightfall. Once night falls and the lambs can no longer be brought, burn them. So the waiting is not until the next morning but only until the end of the day.

### Rava's Proof

Rava agrees with Rabbah that the *shtei halechem* brought alone are fundamentally *l'achila* and that we do not eat them only because of the same *gezeirah* Rabbah articulated — lest people confuse the practice with the case when lambs are present and think they can eat the bread without *zrikas hadam*. *U-velav mi-tamei* — but Rava does not accept Rabbah's proof. He has a stronger scriptural basis.

### Bikurim Comparison

Rava's proof is from the verse itself: *moshvoseichem tavi'u lechem tenufa shtayim shnei esronim... bikurim l'Hashem* — you shall bring a *lechem tenufa* as *bikurim* to God. Because the *shtei halechem* is called *bikurim*, Rava derives: just as *bikurim* come by themselves without any animal sacrifice, so too the bread may come by itself. And just as *bikurim* are eaten, so too the *shtei halechem* is fundamentally designated for eating. This is a clean and compelling proof. The reason we do not eat it in practice remains the *gezeirah* — so that no one will confuse the practice of eating bread alone with eating bread when lambs are present without the requisite *zrikas hadam*.

---

## Shechita and Zerika

### Rabbi vs. Rabbi Elazar

The *Gemara* now turns to a related but distinct question: when exactly does the *shtei halechem* acquire its *kedushah*? We noted in passing when discussing the *toda* that the *shechita* of the accompanying animal sanctifies the bread — not merely connecting it to the animal through *hukkeku ze la-ze*, but elevating it from ordinary Temple ownership (*kedushas damim*) to the higher sanctity of a *korban* proper (*kedushas haguf*), with all attendant consequences: it cannot be redeemed, it becomes invalid if taken outside *Yerushalayim*, and so on. The *Gemara* now focuses this question on the *shtei halechem* of *Shavuos*.

A *baraisa* is cited: *kivsei atzeres ein mekadeshim es halechem ela bishchita* — the lambs of *Atzeres* sanctify the bread only through *shechita*. The *baraisa* then spells out the cases. If the lambs were slaughtered *lishmo* — with proper intention — and the blood was sprinkled *lishmo*, the bread is sanctified. If both were done *shelo lishmo*, the bread is not sanctified. The mixed cases remain open. In the case of *shachatan lishmo ve-zarak daman shelo lishmo* — where the *shechita* was proper but the *zerika* was not — the ruling is *kadosh v'eino kadosh* — it is sanctified yet not sanctified. This is the position of Rabbi. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *le-olam eino kadosh ad sheyishchot lishmo ve-yizrok daman lishmo* — there is no *kedushah* at all until both a valid *shechita* and a valid *zerika* have occurred.

### Rabbi's Proof

What is the source for Rabbi's position? The verse regarding the *Nazir* states: *ve-es ha-ayil ya'aseh zevach shelamim l'Hashem al sal hamatzot* — he shall make the ram a *zevach shelamim* to God, together with the basket of *matzos*. Rabbi reads *ya'aseh zevach* as: it becomes *l'Hashem* through the act of *zevicha* — slaughter — and at that same moment the *matzos* are drawn along with it. Thus the *shechita* alone sanctifies the bread.

### R. Elazar Opinion

Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon agrees the verse is the source but reads it differently: *ya'aseh* means you must do *kol asiyato* — all the acts associated with making it a *shelamim*, including both *shechita* and *zerika*. Only then is the bread sanctified.

And how does Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon handle the word *zevach* that Rabbi uses to emphasize *shechita*? He holds that word is needed for a separate *halacha*: the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan that *hakol modim shetzarich sheyei lechem b'sha'at shechita* — everyone agrees that the bread must be present at the time of *shechita*. Even though for Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon the operative moment of sanctification is the *zerika*, the *shechita* is still a critical juncture at which the bread must be in existence. The word *zevach* in the verse teaches this requirement.

### Kadosh V'Eino

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai kadosh v'eino kadosh* — what exactly is this intermediate state according to Rabbi? Abaye says: *kadosh v'eino gamur* — it is sanctified but not fully so. Rava says: *kadosh v'eino nitar* — it is fully sanctified but not yet permitted for eating. Rava's reading is conceptually clean: the *shechita* confers complete *kedushas haguf* upon the bread. You cannot redeem it, and it becomes invalid if taken outside. What the *zerika* adds is purely the *matir* — the permitting element that allows it to be eaten. Until the *zerika*, the bread has full *kedushas haguf* but cannot yet be eaten. Abaye's reading places the bread at an earlier, incomplete stage of *kedushah* — not yet fully *kedushas haguf* even after *shechita*.

### Nafka Mina

What is the practical difference between Abaye and Rava? *Ika beinaihu l'mitpas pidyono* — whether the bread can be redeemed. Note that Rashi ultimately rejects the reading of this *sugya* as it appears in our text and establishes the correct reading as the inverse: according to Abaye, since the *kedushah* is not yet complete after *shechita* alone, *pidyon* — redemption — remains possible. According to Rava, since the *shechita* confers complete *kedushas haguf*, redemption is no longer possible after *shechita*.

A further practical difference is identified: *l'ipsulei b'yotzei* — whether the bread becomes invalid if taken outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. According to Abaye, the *shechita* confers enough of a *kedushah* that taking the bread outside invalidates it, even though it does not yet reach the level that bars redemption. According to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, the bread has no *kedushas haguf* whatsoever until *zerika* — it can be redeemed and is not rendered invalid by *yotzei*.

### Abaye-Rava Debate

To summarize the three-way positions: according to Rava's reading of Rabbi, *shechita* alone creates complete *kedushas haguf* — no *pidyon* and *pasul* by *yotzei*; according to Abaye's reading of Rabbi, *shechita* creates partial *kedushah* — not enough to bar *pidyon* but enough that *yotzei* invalidates it; according to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, there is no *kedushas haguf* whatsoever until both *shechita* and *zerika* — *pidyon* is possible and *yotzei* does not invalidate. The *Gemara* then asks: given that for Abaye the bread after *shechita* can still be redeemed, in what way does Rabbi actually differ from Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon? The answer: *l'ipsulei b'yotzei* — by *yotzei*. For Rabbi, even on Abaye's reading, *shechita* confers enough of a *kedushah* that taking the bread outside the *Beis Hamikdash* does invalidate it, which is not the case according to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon.

---

## Mixed Shechita-Zerika

### Shechita Zerika Mix

The *Gemara* now turns to the mixed cases — specifically, the scenario of *shachatan lishmo ve-zarak daman shelo lishmo*: *shechita* performed with proper intention and *zerika* performed without proper intention. Can the bread be eaten?

### R. Elazar Rule

According to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, the answer is straightforward. Since for him the *zerika* is entirely responsible for sanctifying the bread — *hagmar zerika hi d'makadsha* — and this *zerika* was *shelo lishmo* and thus invalid, the bread never attained *kedushah*. It can be redeemed and eaten only after *pidyon*; it certainly cannot be eaten directly as a *korban*.

### Rabbi's Rule

According to Rabbi, the *shechita* was valid and therefore conferred *kedushas haguf* upon the bread. The *zerika*, however — even though it was *shelo lishmo* — remains the *matir*, the permitting element. Between Abaye and Rava both agree: *kadosh v'eino nitar* — it is sanctified but not permitted for eating. The *shechita* having been valid, the bread has its *kedushah*, but since the *zerika* was not valid, there is no *matir* and the bread cannot be eaten.

---

## Piggul Status

### Bread Yotzei

The *Gemara* introduces a more complex scenario. A *tanna* — the father of Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba — teaches: *shtei halechem sheyatzu bein shechita l'zerika* — the bread of the *shtei halechem* was taken out of the *Beis Hamikdash* between *shechita* and *zerika*. Assuming we follow Rabbi, the *shechita* already conferred *kedushas haguf*, and so taking the bread outside rendered it *pasul* through *yotzei*. Then *zerika* of the blood of the lambs was performed with the intention of eating the offering *chutz l'zmano* — beyond its proper time — making it a *zerika* of *piggul*. Does the *piggul* status attach also to the bread, which is already invalid by virtue of *yotzei*?

### R. Eliezer Position

Rabbi Eliezer holds: *ein balechem mishum piggul* — the bread does not receive *piggul* status. An already-invalid item cannot be further defined by a *zerika* of *piggul*.

### R. Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva holds: *yesh balechem mishum piggul* — the bread does receive *piggul* status, even though it was already *pasul* through *yotzei*.

### Rav Sheshet Explain

Rav Sheshet explains that both these *tanna'im* hold like Rabbi — that *shechita* sanctifies the bread. Their debate is the well-known dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva about whether *zerika* has any effect on something already *pasul*: *Rabbi Eliezer l'ta'ameih d'amar ein zerika mo'eles l'yotzei* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that *zerika* does not operate on something that is *yotzei*. *Rabbi Akiva l'ta'ameih d'amar zerika mo'eles l'yotzei* — Rabbi Akiva holds that *zerika* does operate on *yotzei*, and therefore a *zerika* of *piggul* can impose *piggul* status even on bread that has already been invalidated by *yotzei*.

### Imurim Meila

The *Gemara* brings a parallel from a *mishna* at the top of 47b. The *imurim* — the innards designated for the *mizbeach* — of *kodashim kalim*: there is no *meila* by *kodashim kalim* in general, since they are considered to belong to the owners and are eaten outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. The only exception is the *imurim*, which go on the *mizbeach* and become fully God's — but only once the *zerika* has rendered them fit for the *mizbeach*. If the *imurim* were taken outside the *Beis Hamikdash* before *zerika*, becoming *pasul* through *yotzei*, and then *zerika* was performed — does the *zerika* raise them to the status where *meila* applies? And similarly, if that *zerika* was a *zerika* of *piggul*, do the *imurim* receive *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* status?

Rabbi Eliezer says: *ein mo'alin bahen* — no *meila* applies, and they are not subject to *piggul*, *nosar*, or *tamei*, because they are already *pasul*. Rabbi Akiva says: *mo'alin bahen* — *meila* does apply, and they are subject to *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei*. This is the same structural debate.

### Rav Papa Qestion

Rav Papa challenges whether the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva in our context necessarily concerns the case of bread that is *yotzei* outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. Perhaps, he suggests, when it comes to *yotzei* bread everyone would agree that the *zerika* of *piggul* does not apply — the *imurim* and the bread are simply different. Perhaps their debate concerns a different configuration entirely: *de'ailu pligi* — when the bread went out and then came back in. In that case, the question is whether the bread ever became *pasul* at all, which depends on the underlying dispute of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Eliezer in the *piggul* debate holds like Rabbi — the *shechita* creates *kedushas haguf*, and therefore taking it outside creates *yotzei*, and bringing it back in does not undo the invalidation. So the bread is *pasul* and the *zerika* of *piggul* cannot reach it. Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon — the *shechita* does not create *kedushas haguf*, so taking it outside before *zerika* does not invalidate it, and the bread is perfectly valid when it returns; the *zerika* of *piggul* therefore can define it as *piggul*.

### Gemara Rejects

The *Gemara* rejects this reinterpretation. If Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon that the *shechita* does not sanctify the bread, then for the *zerika* of *piggul* to make the bread *piggul*, the *zerika* would have to do two things simultaneously: first confer *kedushas haguf* upon the bread (since there is none yet), and then impose *piggul* status. But this cannot work. The principle established by Rav Gidel in the name of Rav is: *zerikas piggul einah mevia lidei meila ve-einah motzia midei meila* — a *zerika* of *piggul* does not change an item's *meila* status. It cannot elevate something to *meila* status, nor can it remove something from *meila* status, precisely because it is an invalid *zerika* and cannot alter levels of *kedushah*. If so, a *zerika* of *piggul* certainly cannot confer initial *kedushas haguf* on the bread. Rabbi Akiva's position, then, must be that the bread already had *kedushas haguf* — which means he holds like Rabbi, not like Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon. And the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva is indeed the classic dispute of whether *zerika mo'eles l'yotzei*.

The *Gemara* notes that the proof from Rav Gidel may itself be subject to challenge elsewhere, but that complication does not unsettle the main analysis here. The initial question posed — whether a *zerika shelo lishmo* could somehow render the bread of *shtei halechem* permissible by analogy to *piggul* affecting an already-*pasul* item — is clearly inapt: the cases are fundamentally different in kind. The *piggul* debate concerns imposing an additional negative status on something already *pasul*; one cannot reason from that to a *zerika shelo lishmo* positively permitting something to be eaten.

---

## Lost Bread Case

### Lost Bread Query

A new question is posed: *kivsei Atzeres sheshachtan lishmon ve'avad halechem* — the lambs of *Atzeres* were slaughtered *lishmo* and then the bread was lost. Since the bread and the lambs are *me'akev zeh es zeh* — indispensable to one another — the *korban* cannot proceed as the *shnei kevasim* of *Shavuos*. But can one perform *zerika* of the blood *shelo lishmo* in order to reclassify the lambs as ordinary *shelamim* and thereby permit the meat to be eaten? This is reminiscent of the earlier discussion about the *toda* where doing *zerika shelo lishmo* after the bread was lost was shown to be valid.

### Kasher Argument

The question carries a hidden conceptual difficulty: *yesh lach davar she'eino kasher lishmo vekasher shelo lishmo?* — do you ever have something that is invalid if done for its designated purpose yet valid if done for a different purpose? The *zerika lishmo* here would be invalid because the bread is gone and the *korban* is defective as *kivsei Atzeres*. But the *zerika shelo lishmo* — doing it as an ordinary *shelamim* — might make it valid.

### Pesach Example

One might answer from the case of the *korban Pesach*: before *chatzos* on the fourteenth of Nisan, a *shechita* performed *lishmo* as a *Pesach* is invalid (since the *Pesach* is only slaughtered in the afternoon), yet a *shechita shelo lishmo* as a *shelamim* would be perfectly valid. So there is indeed a precedent for something invalid *lishmo* yet valid *shelo lishmo*.

The *Gemara* then refines the question: the real concern is *yesh lach davar shenira lishmo venishchat lishmo venidcha milishmo* — something that was fit for its purpose, was slaughtered for its purpose, got onto the track of its proper identity, and was then pushed off that track (because the bread was lost) — *ve'eino kasher lishmo vekasher shelo lishmo?* Can such a thing be saved by doing it *shelo lishmo*? The *Pesach before chatzos* case does not fully answer this, since there the animal was not yet slaughtered *lishmo* before the change.

### Gemara Rejects

And yet the *Gemara* notes that the *toda* case does seem to fit: the *toda* was slaughtered *lishmo* and then the bread was lost, yet we have established that doing the *zerika shelo lishmo* is valid. So the question becomes: why not do the same here with the *shtei halechem*?

### Toda Unique

The *Gemara* answers with the same principle introduced earlier: *shani Toda derachmana karya shelamim* — the *toda* is categorically different because the Torah itself calls the *toda* a type of *shelamim*. Therefore if the *toda* cannot function as a *toda* (because the bread is lost), it can revert to functioning as a *shelamim*, which is its Toraitic identity. The *shnei kevasim* of *Shavuos*, however, even though they too are a form of *shelamim* (*shalmei tzibur*), derive their entire identity from their relationship with the bread. Without the bread, one cannot actively reassign their identity by performing a *zerika shelo lishmo*, and it appears that even *bedi'eved* such a *zerika* would not be valid.

---

## Four Loaves Case

### Four Loaves Setup

The *Gemara* presents a new scenario in a *baraisa*: *shechat shnei kevasim al arba chalos* — someone slaughtered the two lambs over four loaves of bread rather than two. What is the status?

### Rabbi Unknown Two

According to Rabbi, the *shechita* confers *kedushas haguf* on two of the four loaves. But which two? In the abstract, two out of four have *kedushas haguf* and two do not — but their identities are indeterminate. The *baraisa* says: take two, perform *tnufa* (waving), and the remaining two may be eaten after *pidyon* (redemption), since the *shechita* connected only to two loaves, and the other two carry only *kedushas damim* and can be redeemed.

### Chulin Ba'Azarah

The *rabbanim* before Rav Chisda object: this cannot go according to Rabbi. According to Rabbi, the *shechita* already created *kedushas haguf* in two of the four loaves. When you attempt to redeem the two loaves that lack *kedushas haguf*, you face an insoluble problem. If you take them outside the *Beis Hamikdash* to redeem them there, the two that *do* have *kedushas haguf* will become *pasul* through *yotzei* — since you don't know which two they are, you must take all four outside, and two of them are *kedushat haguf* and will be invalidated. If you attempt the redemption inside the *Beis Hamikdash*, you will wind up with two non-sanctified loaves (*chulin*) inside the *azarah*, which is a separate prohibition of *chulin ba'azarah*. Moreover, since you cannot identify which two are which, the *kohanim* will end up eating all four as if they were *kodshim*, which means they are eating *chulin* as *kodshim*.

### Rav Chisda Fix

Rav Chisda attempts to save the case: *le-olam k'Rabbi* — it can still work according to Rabbi — *ufarak lehu gavai* — do the redemption inside the *Beis Hamikdash*. And as for the problem of *chulin ba'azarah*: *vechulin m'meila k'havian* — they do not actively bring *chulin* into the *azarah*; the loaves were all *kodesh* and then one happened to become *chulin* through the redemption. The situation arises by itself, not through any deliberate act of bringing *chulin* in.

### Ravina Challenge

Ravina challenges Rav Chisda before Rav Ashi from a *baraisa*: *k'shehu podan ein podan ela bachutz* — when one redeems the loaves, the redemption must be performed outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. This directly contradicts Rav Chisda's solution of redeeming inside.

### Concede R.Elazar

Faced with this *baraisa*, the *Gemara* concedes: *ha vadai Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon hi* — the *baraisa* describing the case of four loaves must be following Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon and not Rabbi. This also explains why the *baraisa* only requires waving two, not all four: according to Rabbi, if two out of four have unknown *kedushas haguf*, one would logically have to wave all four, since it is unknown which two are the ones of *kedushas haguf*.

### R.Elazar Works

According to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, the solution is elegant. Since *shechita* alone does not create *kedushas haguf* — the bread requires both *shechita* and *zerika* before it has *kedushas haguf* — all four loaves after *shechita* have no *kedushas haguf* whatsoever. They have only *kedushas damim*. One may therefore freely choose which two to redeem, take them outside the *Beis Hamikdash* (where there is no problem of *yotzei* since they have no *kedushas haguf*), redeem them there, and then proceed to wave the remaining two and do the *zerika* — which will then confer *kedushas haguf* on those two. The case works perfectly within Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's framework.

### Toda Challenge

Rav Acha the son of Rav raises a further question to Rav Ashi: does this analysis not create a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan? For Rabbi Yochanan taught, regarding a *toda* slaughtered over eighty loaves instead of forty: *lo kidshu arbaim mitoch shmonim* — forty loaves do not become sanctified out of eighty; if the wrong quantity of bread is brought, none of it becomes *kodesh*. In our case everyone is assuming that when you bring four loaves over two lambs, two of the four do become *kodesh*. Is that not in tension with Rabbi Yochanan?

### Resolution Two Four

The *Gemara* resolves this. Rabbi Zeira taught: *hakol modim heicha d'amar likdeshu arbaim mitoch shmonim d'kadshu* — everyone agrees, even Rabbi Yochanan, that if one explicitly designates forty out of eighty to be sanctified, they are sanctified. Rabbi Yochanan only said that when one attempts to sanctify all eighty (an incorrect quantity), none of them become *kodesh*. *Hacha nami* — here too, the four-loaves case is understood as one in which the person designated two out of the four to be sanctified: *d'amar likdeshu tarti mitoch arba* — two out of four. In that case, even Rabbi Yochanan would agree that those two become *kodesh*, even if their precise identities are unknown. The remaining question — how you navigate which two, how you perform *tnufa*, how you redeem — is resolved differently according to Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, as outlined above.

---

---

# Menachot 48

## Four Lambs, Two Loaves

### Braita Setup

The daf opens with a *braita* taught by Rabbi Chanina Tirsa in the presence of Rabbi Yochanan. The case presented is the inverse of what the Gemara had been discussing previously: whereas the earlier discussion concerned two *kivsei atzeret* paired with four *challot*, here we have four *kevasim* paired with only two *challot*. The *braita* thus begins: *shachat arba kevasim al shtei challot* — he slaughtered four lambs alongside two loaves.

### Two Valid, Two Invalid

The structural problem is immediately apparent. Only two of the four lambs can function as *kivsei atzeret*, since there are only two loaves to pair with them. The other two lambs, however many they may be, cannot achieve the status of *kivsei atzeret* without their accompanying bread. If one were to perform *zrikas hadam* on all four *lishmo* — with the intent of *kivsei atzeret* — the latter two would become *kivsei atzeret* without *lechem*, which renders them *pasul*. On the other hand, if the two surplus lambs are instead treated as *shlamim*, they are entirely valid.

### Making Two Invalid

The *braita*'s solution is *mash'neh shnayim mehem be-zorek hadam she-lo lishmo*: deliberately perform *zrikas hadam* of two of the lambs *she-lo lishmo*, thereby converting them into *shlamim*. This we have already seen: a *korban* from *kivsei atzeret* upon which *zrikas hadam* is performed *she-lo lishmo* loses its status as *kivsei atzeret* but is valid as a *shlamim*. With two thus converted, the remaining two are proper *kivsei atzeret* paired with their bread, and those two become valid as *shalmei Yisrael*. The *braita* adds: *ve-im ee ata omer kach* — if you do not proceed this way, and instead you perform *zrikas hadam lishmo* on all four, then two of them will necessarily be *pasul* as *kivsei atzeret* without *lechem*.

### Alternative Problem

A natural question arises: why not simply perform *zrikas hadam lishmo* on the first two and *she-lo lishmo* on the last two, rather than pre-selecting which ones to designate *she-lo lishmo*? The answer depends on an important technical distinction. The *shechita* was already performed, and the question is now about *zrikas hadam*. If one were to throw the blood of the first two *lishmo*, those become the valid *kivsei atzeret*, and the remaining two are then potentially left without *lechem*.

### Rashi's Dichuy

Rashi raises the concern of *dichuy*. Once the first two have been designated as the valid *kivsei atzeret* via *zorek hadam lishmo*, the last two — which had also been candidates (*ra'uy*) — may now be considered *nidcheh*, rejected. A *korban* in the state of *ra'uy ve-nidcheh* is *pasul*, and if that is the case, performing *zrikas hadam she-lo lishmo* on them afterward would not help. Rashi acknowledges some ambiguity here, since the earlier Gemara was not entirely clear that *dichuy* would in fact apply in this manner. Nevertheless, the preferred approach is to select two lambs proactively to be rendered *she-lo lishmo* from the outset, before any others have been validated, so that the situation is clear.

### Simultaneity & Zika

This raises a further question. Is not the *shechita* itself already significant? Does the act of *shechita lishmo* of the first two not already establish a *zika* — a legal bond — between those lambs and the *lechem*, thereby automatically leaving the remaining two without any connection to the bread? The answer is that the *shechita* does not definitively establish which lambs are paired with the bread; it is the *zrikas hadam* that *koveia* the final relationship. Nonetheless, if the *shechitot* were performed sequentially rather than simultaneously, one might argue that even the *shechita* of the first lambs creates a *zika* that preemptively excludes the others. This is a cogent point, and it may well be that the *braita* presupposes a scenario of simultaneous *shechita* — two *kohanim* slaughtering at the same time — so that all four remain equal candidates throughout, and the pre-selection of two *she-lo lishmo* effectively resolves the situation cleanly.

---

## Chata Kedei Shetizkeh

### Omer Lo Leadam

Rabbi Yochanan's response to the *braita* is sharp: *vechi omer lo leadam amod vachata bishvil shetizkeh?* — do we instruct a person to go and sin in order that there be a benefit? This is a variation on the familiar principle of *chata kedei sheyizkeh chavercha*, though here it is not exactly a case of sinning for the sake of another person. The question is more precise: do we allow a violation of the *mikdash*'s procedural norms — performing *zrikas hadam she-lo lishmo* — in order to achieve a net gain?

### Bread Analogy

A classic illustration of this type of question involves bread being baked in an oven on *Shabbat*. If the bread has not yet finished baking, one has not yet violated *chillul Shabbat d'oraitta*. A bystander who wishes to prevent the violation might remove the bread before it finishes baking, but this itself constitutes an *issur d'rabbanan* — removing baking bread from an oven on *Shabbat* is a *chochma ve'eina melacha*, rabbinically prohibited. May one commit an *issur d'rabbanan* to prevent another's *chillul Shabbat d'oraitta*? The *chata kedei sheyizkeh chavercha* question encompasses a complex set of variables: the magnitude of each party's violation, whether the original actor is acting *bemezid* or *beshogeg*, and whether rescuing a *mezid* is even warranted.

### Sin vs. Procedure

The present case, however, is not quite the same as that scenario. As Tosafot essentially makes the same point: when one performs *zrikas hadam she-lo lishmo*, it is not obviously a personal sin in the conventional sense. The *Rambam* speaks of a positive obligation to perform every act of a *chattat* or *shelamim* according to its proper procedure, but whether violating that procedure constitutes a personal transgression in the ordinary sense is not entirely clear. The better framing, then, is not "do we permit sinning to benefit a neighbor," but rather: do we permit a violation of the *mikdash*'s procedural norms — departing from the established way the *mikdash* operates — for the sake of a net gain? If one performs *zrikas hadam she-lo lishmo*, two *korbanot* are salvaged as *kivsei atzeret* and the remaining two continue as *shlamim*. If one does nothing wrong and proceeds entirely *lishmo*, or if one is simply passive and allows events to unfold, two *korbanot* are lost. Is that trade-off warranted?

### Mixed Limbs Debate

A parallel case from the *mishna* sharpens the question considerably. The case is *eivarei chattat shenitarvu be'eivarei olah*: the limbs of a *chattat* became mixed with the limbs of an *olah*. Both *korbanot* were validly slaughtered and the blood properly thrown. The problem arises in completing the service: the limbs of the *olah* must be burned on the *mizbeiach*, while the limbs of the *chattat* must be eaten by the *kohanim*. Since they are now mixed and indistinguishable, eating everything is out of the question — one may not eat the meat of an *olah*, which would constitute *me'ila* or equivalent violation. Simply doing nothing means waiting for everything to become *pasul belinah* overnight and then burning it all. The third option is to burn everything on the *mizbeiach*, treating the *chattat* limbs as firewood. This is what Rabbi Eliezer permits: *yitnu lemalah* — place it all on the *mizbeiach* — and consider the *chattat* limbs as wood, not as an *haktarah* of the *chattat* itself. Still, this involves actively disposing of *chattat* limbs incorrectly in order to salvage the *olah*. The *chachamim* disagree. They rule *te'aver tzuratan* — let their form deteriorate overnight, let everything become *pasul belinah*, and burn it all. Better to be entirely passive and lose everything than to actively do something procedurally wrong, even in service of a net gain. This debate maps precisely onto Rabbi Yochanan's objection: the *chachamim* reject the very logic of doing one thing wrong to salvage another.

---

## Same Category Principle

### Same Category Allowed

The Gemara presses further. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the *braita*'s proposed solution — performing *zrikas hadam she-lo lishmo* on two lambs to salvage the others — involves instructing someone to violate procedure for a net gain. The Gemara asks: does Rabbi Yochanan's principle apply equally to cases within a single category? The answer is: *amod vechatei bechatas bishvil shetiskei bechatas amrinan* — if the violation and the benefit both fall within the category of *chattat*, we might indeed permit such a trade-off.

### Cross-Category Forbidden

However, *amod vechatei bechatas bishvil shetiskei be'olah lo amrinan* — to sin with a *chattat* in order to benefit an *olah* is a different matter entirely. We do not permit cross-category violations. When the violation occurs in one ledger column and the gain appears in another, we cannot simply take a step back and declare a net gain. The violation in the *chattat* column cannot be bracketed by pointing to a gain in the *olah* column. They remain separate, and the loss on each side is real.

### Shlamim Category

What then is the *tanna*'s case in the *braita*? All four lambs are intended as *kivsei atzeret*; when two are converted *she-lo lishmo* they become *shlamim*; the remaining two are valid *kivsei atzeret* which themselves ultimately function as a species of *shalmei Yisrael*. The entire operation takes place within the *shlamim* column. There is a procedural violation — *zovcham shelo lishmam* — but within that same category there is a net gain: two *korbanot* that would otherwise have been *pasul* or burned are instead eaten, their *emurim* offered, the *avodah* completed. When the calculation is performed entirely within a single category, perhaps one may bracket the violation and recognize the overall gain. That is the logic the Gemara entertains for the *tanna*'s position, and it is a logic Rabbi Yochanan contests.

### Shabbat Zrikas

The Gemara now tests the same-category principle against a new case involving *Shabbat*. The scenario: *kivsei atzeret* were slaughtered on what was thought to be *Shavuot*, but it emerged that *Shavuot* had actually fallen the day before. The lambs were slaughtered — already a *chillul Shabbat* — but what should be done about the blood? If nothing is done, the blood will become *pasul belinah* by nightfall. If *zrikas hadam* is performed, the blood of what is now merely a *shlamim* is thrown on *Shabbat* — but there is no *melacha* involved in throwing blood on a *mizbeiach*. The prohibition is not one of *melacha* but of the *mikdash*'s own rule against bringing on *Shabbat* a *korban* that is not designated for *Shabbat*. Should one violate that *mikdash* rule — throw the blood on *Shabbat* to salvage the *korban* — so that by *Motzei Shabbat* one may burn the *emurim* and eat the meat? The *braita* rules: *lo yizrok* — do not throw the blood. And if one did throw it, *hurtza* — it is accepted, and one may burn the *emurim* that evening. The Gemara asks why one should not act, given that the violation and the benefit appear to fall within the same sphere. The Gemara answers: the violation occurs on *Shabbat*, while the benefit — eating the meat and burning the *emurim* — accrues only *Motzei Shabbat*, in *chol*. That is already a cross-category situation: *amod vechatei biShabbat kidei shetizke bechol lo amrinan*. The benefit does not accrue on *Shabbat* itself; it accrues afterward. We will not countenance a *Shabbat* violation for a gain that materializes in a different time-domain.

### Passive Approach

Having established the same-category principle, the Gemara raises one final challenge from the laws of *terumah*. A barrel of *terumah* wine breaks in the upper vat of a wine press while the lower vat contains *chulin tamei* wine. As the *terumah* pours downward, it will become *terumah teme'ah* upon contact with the *tamei chulin* below, rendering the entire contents forbidden. One might wish to intercept the *terumah* by catching it in available *tamei* vessels — actively rendering it *tamei* in one's hands — thereby preventing it from mixing with the *chulin* and preserving the *chulin*. Is one permitted to actively be *metamei* the *terumah* in order to salvage the *chulin*?

The *mishna* records that both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that if one can salvage a *revi'it* of the *terumah* in a pure state, one is obligated to do so and may not deliberately render it *tamei*. If no *terumah* can be salvaged — the *terumah* is lost regardless — Rabbi Eliezer rules *tered vetitame ve'al yetame'enah beyad*: let it descend and become *tamei* on its own; do not actively render it *tamei* with your own hands. Rabbi Yehoshua rules *af yetame'enah beyad*: actively catch it in *tamei* vessels to save the *chulin*. The Gemara considers whether Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling represents the cross-category trade-off that the Gemara has been debating — rendering *terumah tamei* to salvage *chulin* — and whether this contradicts the principle that we do not permit cross-category violations. The Gemara answers: *shani hatam delivei tumah ka'azla* — that case is different because the *terumah* was already heading toward *tumah* regardless. Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency is not a paradigmatic case of introducing a new violation to achieve a gain; the *terumah* was going to become *tamei* no matter what. The marginal harm of catching it in one's hands is minimal. In contrast, the blood of the *chattat* or the blood of the *shlamim* on *Shabbat* was not fated to become invalid — those are cases where one introduces a novel procedural violation, and for those we do not apply the trade-off logic across categories.

The Gemara leaves the matter without a definitive resolution regarding the same-category case. Its conclusion is that cross-category trade-offs are clearly impermissible, but whether the same-category argument — which the *tanna* of the *braita* apparently accepted — is ultimately valid remains open.

---

## Wrong-Age Lambs

### Shelo K'Mitzvatan

The Gemara now transitions to a new topic: the *halachot* of *kivsei atzeret* themselves, setting aside for the moment the relationship between the lambs and the loaves. When Rav Yitzchak came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he taught a *braita*: *hakevasim sheshachtan shelo k'mitzvatan psulin* — if the lambs of *atzeret* were slaughtered not in accordance with their commandment, they are *pasul*. Furthermore, they require *ibbur tzura* — one does not burn them immediately; one waits until they become *pasul belinah* overnight — and then *veyatze l'veit hasreifa*, they are burned. The question turns on the phrase *shelo k'mitzvatan*. What precisely was done incorrectly?

Rashi's first reading is that it refers to *shelo lishmo* — an incorrect *kavana* at the moment of *shechita*. However, this reading creates an immediate tension, since the entire earlier Gemara proceeds on the assumption that *shelo lishmo* still produces a valid *korban* as a *shlamim*. This is, after all, one of the foundational rules from the opening of *Zevachim*: *shechita shelo lishmo* renders a *korban* valid for every species except a *chattat* and a *pesach*, though it does not fulfill the owner's obligation. If this *braita* declares such a *korban pasul*, it would be arguing against the most basic premises of the entire tractate.

Rashi therefore offers a second explanation, which Tosafot also strongly endorses and which fits far better with the continuation of the Gemara: *shelo k'mitzvatan* means the lambs were the wrong age. *Kivsei atzeret* are required to be one year old — *bnei shana* — and the *braita* addresses a case where two-year-old animals were brought. The phrase *sheshachtan*, Rashi acknowledges, is slightly awkward for this reading since the problem with the animal's age arises at *hakdasha*, before *shechita*. Nevertheless, this second reading governs the subsequent discussion.

The underlying question is stark: if an animal that was meant to be *kivsei atzeret* is too old to qualify, does it remain *pasul* entirely — or can we salvage it as a generic *shlamim*, since a two-year-old animal is perfectly valid for an ordinary *shlamim*? Rav Yitzchak's *braita* declares it *pasul*. The question is whether that ruling can be sustained.

### Rav Yitzchak Link

Rav Nachman explains Rav Yitzchak's reasoning. The *pasuk* dealing with *kivsei atzeret* juxtaposes them with a *chattat*: *se'ir izim echad l'chattat ushnei kvasim bnei shana l'zevach shlamim* — one goat for a *chattat*, and two yearling lambs as a *zevach shlamim*. This juxtaposition — *makish lehu l'chattat* — invites us to apply to *kivsei atzeret* the same stringencies that govern a *chattat*. Just as any variation in a *chattat* renders it *pasul* — and a *chattat* that has passed its year (*chattat she'avra shnata*) is among the *chataot hameitot*, the category of *chataot* that must die — so too any variation in *kivsei atzeret* renders them *pasul*, with no possibility of salvaging them as *shlamim*.

### Tana D'Bei Levi

Against this position stands the *tana d'bei Levi*, who draws an entirely different inference from the same *pasuk*. Since the *kivsei atzeret* are explicitly called *shlamim* in the *parsha*, the *tana d'bei Levi* reasons that we should evaluate them in the context of general *shlamim*. The principle is *degamar shalmei chova mishalmei nedava*: we understand an obligatory *shlamim* in light of a voluntary *shlamim*. The result is that even if the lambs were too old, the *korban* remains *kasher*, since a two-year-old animal is valid for a free-will *shlamim*. The *tana d'bei Levi* can thus rule: *tani ksheirin* — even a wrong-age animal is valid.

This position finds explicit support in a *tosefta* in *Nazir*. The *korban* of a *nazir* involves an analogous structure — *shalmei nazir* are accompanied by bread, just as *kivsei atzeret* are, and the same juxtaposition with *chattat* appears in the *parsha* of *nazir* as well. The *tosefta* states: *v'shear shalmei Nazir sheshachtan shelo k'mitzvatan... vene'echalim leyom valayla ve'ein te'unim lo lechem velo zeroa* — if the *shalmei nazir* were slaughtered not in accordance with their commandment, they remain valid and are eaten for a day and a night, but they do not require the accompanying bread, the *zeroa*, or the other special elements of *shalmei nazir*. They are no longer *shalmei nazir*; they are ordinary *shlamim*. The *korban* is salvaged. That the *tana d'bei Levi* would apply the same logic to *kivsei atzeret* follows naturally.

Rashi notes a further dimension to this leniency. Even if someone made a *neder* to bring a one-year-old *shlamim* and instead brought a two-year-old, the *korban* would still be valid as a *shlamim*, even though the owner's obligation is unfulfilled. This establishes that the *halacha* can tolerate an age discrepancy in *shlamim* — the *korban* stands even when it does not match the owner's obligation — which supports the *tana d'bei Levi*'s position that the wrong-age *kivsei atzeret* can be salvaged similarly.

### Asham Age Problem

The Gemara now introduces a *braita* that appears to challenge Rav Yitzchak directly. The *braita* states: *asham ben shana vehevi ben shtayim* — if one owed a one-year-old *asham* and brought a two-year-old, or owed a two-year-old *asham* and brought a one-year-old, they are *psulim* and must undergo *ibbur tzura* before being burned. This applies specifically to *asham*. But the *braita* continues: if one brought a wrong-age animal as an obligatory *olah* — *olat nazir*, *olat yoledet*, or *olat metzora* — and the animals were two years old when they should have been one year old, they are *kasher*. The ruling is then generalized: *kol hakasher be'olat nedava kasher be'olat chova* — anything valid for a free-will *olah* is valid for an obligatory *olah*.

This *braita* seems to directly disprove Rav Yitzchak. It demonstrates that a wrong-age obligatory *korban* can still be valid — so why should wrong-age *kivsei atzeret* be entirely *pasul*?
