The Gemara dispenses with the challenge efficiently: *hai tanna tanna devei Levi hu* — this is simply a *baraita* from the school of Levi, representing one side of an already-established *tannaitic* dispute. The *braita* proves nothing new; it merely confirms that the *tana d'bei Levi* and Rav Yitzchak are in disagreement.

### Olat Principle

The *braita*'s principle — that anything valid for a free-will *olah* is valid for an obligatory *olah* — rests on a conceptual foundation that runs through this entire discussion. When an obligatory *korban* of a given type is brought with the wrong specifications, the question is whether the *korban* can be reconfigured as the free-will version of the same type. For *olah* and *shlamim*, such free-will versions exist and permit a range of ages. This makes it possible to say: even though you did not fulfill your obligation by bringing a two-year-old animal when a one-year-old was required, the *korban* itself is still valid as a *korban* — it functions as a *nedavah* of that type even if it fails to satisfy the *chovah*.

### Asham Unique

The case of *asham* is categorically different. An *asham* has no *nedavah* form — there is no such thing as a free-will *asham*. One brings an *asham* only when obligated to do so. Therefore, if the wrong-age animal is brought for an *asham*, there is no conceptual "floor" to fall back on — no free-will version of the *asham* into which the *korban* could be reconfigured. One cannot say "treat it as a *stam* voluntary *asham*," because no such animal exists. The *korban* is therefore entirely *pasul*. This is also why a *chattat she'avra shnata* is among the *chataot hameitot*: the *chattat* similarly has no *nedavah* form, and therefore no wrong-age variation can be salvaged.

The *braita* cited earlier makes this explicit: *chutz mishelo lishmo* — the only exception is *shelo lishmo*. If an *asham* is slaughtered *shelo lishmo*, the *korban* remains valid even for *asham*, unlike the analogous rule for *chattat*. But if the animal is the wrong age, there is no path to validity, because no free-will *asham* exists. This asymmetry between *asham* and *olah* or *shlamim* is the linchpin of the distinction.

### Shimi's Rule

The Gemara then asks: why not learn from an *asham* to an *asham*? We have two-year-old *ashamos* — *asham gezelot* and *asham me'ilot* — and we have one-year-old *ashamos* — *asham nazir* and *asham metzora*. Why not say that since both one-year and two-year *ashamos* exist, one can salvage a wrong-age *asham* by analogy with the correctly-aged version of the other category? Shimi bar Ashi formulates the answer as a general rule: *donin davar she-lo be-hachshero mi-davar she-lo be-hachshero ve'ein donin davar she-lo be-hachshero mi-davar she-be-hachshero* — we may learn an incorrect case from another incorrect case, but we may not learn an incorrect case from a case that is fundamentally proper.

The rule operates as follows. When we permit a wrong-age *olah* to function as a valid free-will *olah*, we are drawing an analogy to the case of *nedavah* where someone vowed to bring a one-year-old *olah* and instead brought a two-year-old — even that case, where the person did something incorrect relative to their *neder*, produces a valid *korban*. That is a case of *shelo be-hachshero* — incorrectly executed — that still generates a valid outcome. We can therefore learn from it that our obligatory wrong-age *olah* is also valid. But for *asham*, the only analogous cases are *ashamos* brought in their correct form — *asham gezelot* as a two-year-old is *be-hachshero*, that is precisely how it is supposed to be. We cannot learn from a correctly brought two-year-old *asham* to validate an incorrectly brought two-year-old *asham* for a *chovah* that requires one year. There is no parallel case of an incorrect *asham* that was nevertheless accepted. The analogy simply does not hold.

---

## Shelo Lishmo Meaning

### Kavashim Eilim

The Gemara now opens what is, in many respects, the most fundamental question of the entire laws of *shelo lishmo* — one that arguably should have been raised at the very beginning of *Zevachim*, in the first *daf* where *shelo lishmo* was discussed. What precisely does *shelo lishmo* mean? Does it mean that the *kohen* knew the *korban*'s identity but deliberately attempted to redefine it — slaughtering a *shlamim* consciously intending it as an *olah*? Or does it also encompass an honest mistake — the *kohen* genuinely believed the animal was something other than what it was? The Gemara poses this question through a specific case: *Kivsei Atzeret sheshachtan lishum Eilim kesherim* — if one slaughtered the lambs of *atzeret* thinking they were rams (*eilim*), Rabbah bar bar Chana taught before Rav that such *korbanot* are valid, though the owners do not fulfill their obligation.

This is a striking formulation. We have never previously encountered a *pesul* based on thinking the animal is the wrong species, as distinct from thinking the *korban* is the wrong type of *offering*. The familiar cases of *shelo lishmo* concern *kavana* about the *zevach* — intending an *olah* when one is slaughtering a *shlamim*, or intending the wrong *ba'al*. Here the *kavana* concerns the animal's physical identity — the *kohen* believes these are rams, not lambs. Rabbah bar bar Chana rules this creates a *pesul* equivalent to *shelo lishmo*, such that the owners do not fulfill their obligation. Rav responds with a dismissive *alu va'alu* — this is simply not a problem.

### Rava's Position

Rava enters the discussion with a general principle: *akira b'ta'us lo havei akira* — an unintentional uprooting of an object's definition, an honest mistake about its identity, does not constitute a genuine redefinition. The implication for all of *Zevachim* is vast. If a *kohen* genuinely believed the animal was an *olah* and slaughtered it with that *kavana*, but in fact it was a *shlamim*, the *korban* according to Rava would be entirely *kasher*, not merely valid in the diminished sense of *lo alu l'be'alim l'shem chova*. The mistake simply does not register as a redefining *machshava*. A truly honest mistake leaves the *korban*'s status entirely unaffected.

### Rav's Response

Rav's *alu va'alu* is now understood against this backdrop. The animals are lambs; the *korban* is being offered correctly. Whatever is going on in the *kohen*'s head about rams is irrelevant, because the *kohen* is not consciously attempting to change anything. The animals are what they are; the *avodah* proceeds on that basis.

### Honest Mistake

Rav Chisda moves to clarify — and significantly limit — what Rav's ruling covers. *Mistavra milta d'Rav bechasavur Eilim v'shachtan lishum Kevashim* — Rav's ruling that it is *kasher* applies specifically to the case where the *kohen* thought the animals were rams but then slaughtered them as lambs. That is: the *kohen* is told these are *kivsei atzeret* but thinks someone made an error and brought rams by mistake. When the *kohen* then performs *shechita*, he says to himself: "These should have been lambs — I will slaughter them as lambs, treating them as the lambs they ought to have been." In this case, the animal is a lamb, the *kohen*'s intent at the moment of *shechita* is to treat it as a lamb, and the only "mistake" is a mistaken belief about the animal's species that has already been corrected in the *kohen*'s own *kavana*. There is no effective *shelo lishmo* at all.

### Akira B'Taos

However, *aval kasavur Eilim v'shachtan lishum Eilim* — if the *kohen* thought they were rams and slaughtered them as rams, this is *lo kasher*. Why? *Akira b'taut havi akira* — even an honest mistake that redefines the animal's status is still a redefining act. If the *kohen* genuinely thought these were rams and his *shechita* was performed with the intent of slaughtering rams, he has effectively declared: "These are rams, and I am slaughtering rams." Even though he is wrong, even though it was an honest error, the act of mentally categorizing them as rams — and performing *shechita* with that identification — constitutes an *akira*, a displacement of their true status. This position — that *akira b'taut havei akira* — stands in tension with Rava's view that *akira b'ta'us lo havei akira*.

### Pigul Analysis

The Gemara now presses the question further through the lens of *pigul*. A *mishna* in *Gittin* records: if *kohanim* rendered *korbanot* invalid through *pigul*, those who acted *mezidin* must compensate the owner, while *shogegin* are exempt from payment. Yet a *baraita* adds: *pigulam pigul* — even the *shogeg* has made *pigul*. How can one create *pigul* unintentionally? The Gemara considers the case where a *kohen* thought the *korban* was a *shlamim* — valid for two days — when in fact it was a *chattat*, valid only for one day. Thinking it was a *shlamim*, the *kohen* entertained the intent to eat it the next day, which is the classic *machshava* of *pigul*. But this intent arose from an honest mistake about the *korban*'s identity. If *akira b'ta'us lo havei akira*, how can this honest mistake generate *pigul*? The Gemara thus appears to demonstrate that an honest mistake does still have halachic effect — which would support the position that *akira b'ta'us havei akira*.

### Rabbi Shimon

Abaye responds: the case of the *shogeg* who does not pay is not one of mistaken identity at all. Rather, the *kohen* knew exactly what the *korban* was — he knew it was a *chattat* — but did not realize that his intent to eat it the next day would constitute *pigul* and invalidate the *korban*. His *shogeggut* was in the *violation*, not in the *korban*'s identity. This preserves Rava's position: *akira b'ta'us lo havei akira* means that a genuine mistake about the *korban*'s identity has no effect. A mistake about whether one's thought constitutes a violation is an entirely different matter. A *kohen* who consciously entertains an out-of-time eating intent — even while mistakenly believing this is harmless — has still performed a real *pigul machshava*. But a *kohen* who simply misidentifies the animal has not performed any real mental act of redefinition.

### Machshava Rules

Rav Zeira then challenges from a *mishna* involving Rabbi Shimon's ruling about *menachot*. Rabbi Shimon holds that for *menachot*, the physical reality of the *korban* overrides *machshava*: *kol menachos shenikmetzu shelo lishmon kshairos* — all *menachot* whose *kometz* was taken with incorrect intent are valid and the owners fulfill their obligation. The reason, Rabbi Shimon explains, is that *menachot* are not like animal *korbanot*: *shechita achas l'kulan, kabala achas l'kulan, zrika achas l'kulan* — with animal sacrifices, every animal undergoes the same external acts, making *machshava* the only distinguishing factor. But with *menachot*, the physical reality is self-evident: if the vessel contains the quantity of oil appropriate for a *machvas*, the physical reality declares it a *machvas* — *ma'aseha mochiachin aleha*; if the *mincha* is a *chariva*, dry without oil, physical reality declares it so. Therefore *machshava* cannot override what is physically manifest.

How does this intersect with the debate about *akira b'ta'us*? Rav Zeira argues that Rabbi Shimon's ruling must concern an honest mistake. If the *kohen* knew it was a *machvas* and deliberately tried to redefine it as a *marcheshes*, why would Rabbi Shimon excuse the *machshava*? Even Rabbi Shimon would agree that willful redefinition matters. The only reading that makes sense for Rabbi Shimon's leniency is that the *kohen* made an honest mistake and thought the *korban* was a *marcheshes*. And Rabbi Shimon says: even that honest mistake is overridden by the physical reality. This implies that absent such physical evidence, *akira b'ta'us* would be a genuine *akira* — an honest mistake would still constitute a redefinition. That would contradict Rava.

Abaye responds to preserve Rava's position: *le'olam d'yada d'machvas hi v'ka kametz lah l'shum marcheshes* — Rabbi Shimon's case actually involves a *kohen* who knows it is a *machvas* and deliberately attempts to treat it as a *marcheshes*. The *kohen*'s *machshava* is willful, not mistaken. And even so, Rabbi Shimon rules the *korban* is valid. Why? Because the physical reality is so demonstrably clear — *ma'aseha mochiachin aleha* — that even a willful attempt to redefine it cannot take effect. The vessel, the oil, the form of the *mincha* — all of these shout what it actually is. Rava then articulates this as a general principle: *machshava d'lo minkara pasal Rachmana, machshava d'minkara lo pasal Rachmana* — a *machshava* that is not externally evident, where nothing about the physical reality contradicts the intent, the Torah treats as operative and potentially invalidating. A *machshava* that is obviously contradicted by the physical reality — where the *machshava* does not register as credible against the evidence of the world — the Torah does not treat as operative. Applied to *menachot*, the *machshava* is always contradicted by the physical form of the *korban*, and therefore never invalidates. Applied to animal *korbanot*, the *machshava* is never independently visible, and therefore always carries weight — whether the intent is willful or mistaken.

This leaves the Gemara at its closing point — and it is a genuinely open one. Throughout the many chapters of *Zevachim* in which *shelo lishmo* was discussed, the assumption was that a *kohen* who performs *zrikas hadam* of a *shlamim* with the intent of an *olah* has done something that invalidates the *korban* for the owner's *chovah*. But the Gemara has now surfaced the question of whether that assumed rule applies only when the *kohen* knew what the *korban* was and willfully redefined it, or whether it applies equally when the *kohen* was genuinely mistaken. The debate between Rav Chisda and Rava — *akira b'ta'us havei akira* versus *akira b'ta'us lo havei akira* — runs through the entirety of *Zevachim* without resolution, and the Gemara leaves us here, at the end of these pages, with a question that reaches all the way back to the very beginning.

---

# Menachot 49

## Ein Me'akvin Overview

### Theme & Context

The overarching theme of this section of Masechet Menachot is *ein me'akvin* — the principle that the absence of one element does not necessarily prevent or invalidate another. Having worked through the intricate relationship between the *kivsei atzeret* and the *shtei halechem*, the Mishnah now turns to a broader set of *korbanot* and examines the interrelationships among them.

### Mishnah Text

The Mishnah opens with two symmetrical rulings: *hatmidim ein me'akvin et hamusafim* — the *tamidim* do not hold back the *musafim* — and *velo hamusafim me'akvin et hatamid* — the *musafim* do not hold back the *tamid*. Concretely: if one has lambs sufficient only for the *tamidim* but not for the *musaf* of Shabbos, one may still go ahead and bring the *tamid*. Conversely, if one has *korbanot* for the *musaf* but lacks what is needed for the *tamid*, one may still bring the *musaf* even knowing the *tamid* cannot be brought.

### Musafim Interrelation

The Mishnah continues: *velo hamusafim me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the *musafim* do not hold each other back. The *musafim* are typically a large group: two cows, a ram, seven sheep, and so on. If one cannot bring the entire complement, one may still bring whatever portion is available. Moreover, on a day such as Shabbos Rosh Chodesh, when two separate *musaf* obligations apply, one does not render the other indispensable — each stands independently.

### Two Tamidim

The Mishnah adds: *lo hikrivu keves baboker yakrivu bein ha'arbayim* — if the morning lamb was not brought, the afternoon lamb may still be brought. The two *tamidim* are thus not *me'akev* one another. This is somewhat striking — one might have expected them, as a matched pair, to operate on an all-or-nothing basis. But the Mishnah treats them similarly to the *musafim*: bring what you can.

### R. Shimon: Tamidim

Rabbi Shimon qualifies this ruling sharply: *eimatai? bizman shehayu anusim o shogegin* — when is this true? Only when the failure to bring the morning *tamid* was beyond one's control, whether due to compulsion (*ones*) or inadvertence (*shogeg*). But *im hayu mezidin* — if it was a willful choice — *lo yakrivu bein ha'arbayim*: they may not bring it in the afternoon.

This position of Rabbi Shimon connects to a stance he takes elsewhere in Masechet Menachot: if one must choose between bringing some of the *musafim* with their *nesachim* or bringing all of them without, Rabbi Shimon holds it is better to do fewer correctly than to do all of them improperly. A consistent thread runs through both rulings: do not make a deliberate choice to perform something in a half-measure. If the choice is willful, either do it properly — both *tamidim* — or do not do it at all. The relationship between the two *tamidim* is, in Rabbi Shimon's view, no less binding than the relationship between each animal and its *minchat nesachim*. If the failure was not a willful choice, *ones* or *shogeg*, the matter stands differently.

### R. Shimon: Musafim

Rabbi Shimon does not, however, apply this same restriction to the *musafim* generally. Nor does he quarrel with the Mishnah's ruling about the *musafim* holding each other back.

### Incense: Morning

The Mishnah continues with a parallel ruling regarding the *ketoret*: *lo hiktiru ketoret baboker yiktiru bein ha'arbayim* — if the morning *ketoret* was not burned, it may be burned in the afternoon. The *ketoret* was divided into two equal portions, half offered in the morning and half in the afternoon.

### R. Shimon: Incense

Here Rabbi Shimon appears to accept the principle that the afternoon *ketoret* may stand alone. But he adds a significant qualification: *vekulaso hayata kreva bein ha'arbayim* — when bringing only the afternoon *ketoret*, one brings the full measure, not merely the half-portion that would ordinarily be offered in the afternoon. The reasoning will be developed in the Gemara. The difference between the *ketoret* and the *tamidim* in Rabbi Shimon's system — why he accepts the afternoon *ketoret* alone but not the afternoon *tamid* alone — will require analysis. Notably, whereas by the two *tamidim* the Mishnah emphasizes that they form a pair, by the *ketoret* Rabbi Shimon concedes that the afternoon can stand independently, even while insisting on the full measure.

### Altar Inauguration

The Mishnah then shifts to a related set of rulings about *chinuch* — the inauguration of the Sanctuary's vessels and altars. The golden altar (*mizbeach hazahav*) is inaugurated only through the burning of the *ketoret hasamim*. The outer altar (*mizbeach ha'olah*) is inaugurated only through the *tamid shel shachar*. The *shulchan* is inaugurated only through the *lechem hapanim* on Shabbos. The *menorah* is inaugurated only through the lighting of all seven lamps in the afternoon. Each vessel is inaugurated through the performance of its characteristic *avoda*.

The ruling connecting the outer altar specifically to the *tamid shel shachar* is not incidental to the earlier discussion. It provides implicit support for Rabbi Shimon's position: since the morning *tamid* is the *avoda* that gives the outer altar its foundational identity — it is through the morning *tamid* that the altar is inaugurated and that is why the altar is always called *mizbeach ha'olah* — one should not make a willful choice to skip it and rely on the afternoon alone. The Gemara will elaborate on all of this.

---

## Priority Question

### R. Chiya's Question

Rav Chiya bar Avin posed a question to Rav Chisda: *tzibur she-ein lahem temidim u-musafim eizeh me-hem kodem?* — if a community lacks sufficient animals for both the *tamidim* and the *musafim*, which takes precedence?

### Same Day Case

The Gemara immediately asks: what exactly is the case? If we are discussing a choice between the *tamidim* and the *musafim* of the same day — say, Shabbos, where one has only two lambs and must choose between using them for the two *tamidim* or for the *musaf* of Shabbos — the answer is straightforward.

### Tadir Principle

*Peshita temidim adifei* — obviously the *tamidim* take precedence. The principle at work is *tadir u-mekudash*. The *tamid* is more *tadir* — more frequent, brought every day — than the *musaf*, which is only brought on Shabbos. Furthermore, the *tamid* of Shabbos is no less *kadosh* than the *musaf* of Shabbos, so there is no counterweight on the side of sanctity. There is in fact an entire hierarchy in a chapter of Zevachim establishing that *kol hatadir me-chavero kodem et chavero* — whatever is more frequent takes precedence — and similarly *kol hamekudash me-chavero kodem et chavero* — whatever is of greater sanctity takes precedence. For the same-day case, the *tamid* wins on both counts.

### Tamidim Tomorrow

The genuinely difficult case is: *temidim de-machar u-musafim de-ha-idna* — tomorrow's *tamidim* versus today's *musafim*. Suppose the *Beis Hamikdash* has four lambs and knows with certainty that no additional animals can be obtained before tomorrow, given the requirement to check animals four days in advance. Even if someone arrived at the door with lambs tonight, they could not be used tomorrow. The question is: do you use two lambs for today's *musaf* and forgo tomorrow's *tamid*, or do you set aside two for tomorrow and forgo today's *musaf*?

### Planning Ahead

The Gemara frames two possible answers. *Temidim adifei she-ken tadir* — perhaps tomorrow's *tamidim* take priority because the *tamid* is the *tadir* par excellence; nothing better exemplifies frequency of obligation than the *tamid*. Or: *musafim adifei d'hava lei mekudash* — perhaps today's *musafim* take priority because they carry the quality of *mekudash*. Rashi offers two readings of *mekudash* here. The first is that a *korban* of a sacred day — Shabbos — carries implicitly greater *kedusha* than a *korban* of an ordinary weekday, so today's Shabbos *musaf* is of a higher order than tomorrow's weekday *tamid*. The second reading is more intriguing: *mekudash* here does not mean inherently holier, but rather that the *kedusha* is presenting itself now, today, and one should address what is before oneself rather than plan for tomorrow. In this reading, the question is not about the comparative sanctity of the two offerings but about a philosophy of obligation: does one prioritize the present moment or plan ahead?

This case is in certain respects unique, because the Gemara stipulates that tomorrow is genuinely foreclosed — one cannot rely on providence to resolve things. If there were any possibility of obtaining more animals in the interim, one might simply focus on today's obligations and see what the morning brings.

It is also worth noting that the principle of *kodem* — priority — as it appears in the chapter in Zevachim typically governs sequencing when all the offerings are present, not necessarily the choice to bring one at the expense of another. The Gemara here is indeed using *kodem* in the stronger sense: which offering has enough priority that one actively forfeits the other on its behalf.

### Mishnah Evidence

Rav Chisda responds: *tanituha* — we have already taught the answer in our Mishnah. The Mishnah states that the *tamidim* do not hold back the *musafim* and the *musafim* do not hold back the *tamidim*. What can this prove?

The Gemara asks: what is the case that the Mishnah is addressing? If it means that you have all the animals and the ruling concerns order — that if one performed them in reverse order it remains valid — that cannot be right, because a *baraita* teaches: *menayin shelo yehei davar kodem letamid shel shachar* — from where do we know that nothing may precede the morning *tamid*? The verse states *v'arach aleha ha'ola* — "arrange upon it the burnt offering" — and Rava derives from this that the *ola* goes first, meaning the *tamid*, and nothing precedes it. So if the Mishnah were speaking about order, it would be saying something already known to be impermissible.

Therefore, the Gemara concludes, the Mishnah must be speaking about a case where one does not have all the animals and must choose which to bring. And if it is the same-day choice, why does the Mishnah treat the *musafim* as equivalent — saying that the *tamidim* do not hold back the *musafim*? On the same day, it would obviously be wrong to choose the *musaf* over the *tamid*. The fact that the Mishnah treats them symmetrically — neither holds back the other — implies that the Mishnah is speaking about a choice between today's *musafim* and tomorrow's *tamidim*. And since the Mishnah says neither holds back the other, both choices are equally valid, implying that there is no mandatory precedence of tomorrow's *tamidim* over today's *musafim* or vice versa.

### Abaye's Counter

Abaye rejects this reading. *Le'olam de-it lehu* — in truth, the Mishnah is speaking about a case where one has all the animals, and the ruling concerns what happens if they were brought out of order. The fact that *lechatchila* one must not bring anything before the *tamid* is, as Abaye explains, merely a *mitzva* — an ideal — and the Mishnah is ruling that *bedi'avad*, after the fact, it is valid even if the order was reversed. Therefore, Abaye concludes, the Mishnah says nothing at all about the *lechatchila* choice between today's *musafim* and tomorrow's *tamidim*. The Mishnah is a *bedi'avad* ruling, not a *lechatchila* directive, and cannot serve as proof for the priority question.

---

## Six Sheep Reserve

### Baraita Text

The Gemara now introduces a new potential source: *ein pochtin me-shisha tela'im ha-mevukarim be-lishkat ha-tela'im* — there were never fewer than six inspected sheep in the chamber of lambs. The *Beis Hamikdash* maintained a reserve of sheep in a dedicated room, the *lishkat ha-tela'im*, that had been checked (*mevukarim*) four days in advance.

### Shabbos/RH Case

The Baraita specifies: *kedei le-Shabbos u-le-shnei yamim tovim shel Rosh Hashanah* — enough for Shabbos and the two days of Rosh Hashanah, the only two-day *Yom Tov* observed in Eretz Yisrael. The reasoning seems intuitive: when a run of days prevents one from going out to obtain animals on short notice, one must draw on reserves. Two lambs are needed for the *tamidim* of Shabbos and another two for each day of Rosh Hashanah — hence six. The striking implication is that the reserve is stocked for the *tamidim* alone, not for the *musafim*, which on Rosh Hashanah alone require seven lambs, two cows, and a ram. Why is the reserve focused exclusively on the *tamidim*?

### Challenge to Six

The Gemara, however, challenges whether six is even sufficient for the described scenario. *Heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If the reserve is meant to supply both *tamidim* and *musafim* for Shabbos and Rosh Hashanah, *tuva havu* — that would require far more than six animals. The *musafim* of Rosh Hashanah alone run to many animals. So the reserve must be only for the *tamidim*, not for the full complement. *Ela lav de-leis lei* — it must be that one does not have enough animals for everything, and the reserve is designed so that when forced to choose, one ensures the *tamidim* are covered. This appears to prove that *tamidim adifei* — the *tamidim* take precedence.

Rashi sharpens the implication further. Suppose Shabbos falls immediately before the two days of Rosh Hashanah. On Shabbos itself one has six animals in reserve. If the intent were to cover both Shabbos and Rosh Hashanah fully, one would bring the *tamid* and *musaf* of Shabbos — using four animals — and have only two left for both days of Rosh Hashanah, which is insufficient. But if one deliberately brings only the two *tamidim* on Shabbos, forgoing the *musaf*, one preserves four for Rosh Hashanah's *tamidim*. So one is explicitly choosing tomorrow's (and the day after's) *tamidim* over today's *musaf*.

However, the Gemara pulls back: *lo le'olam de-islei* — in truth, one does have enough animals for everything. The reserve is not about choosing *tamidim* over *musafim* when resources run short.

### Ben Bag Bag

The Gemara asks: whose view underlies this Baraita? The answer is Ben Bag Bag. *Ben Bag Bag omer: minayin letamid she-ta'un bikur arba'ah yamim kodem shechitah* — from where do we derive that the *tamid* requires inspection four days before slaughter?

### Why Check Tamidim

Ben Bag Bag derives it through a *gezerah shavah* from the *Korban Pesach*. The Torah states regarding the *tamid*: *tishmru lehakriv li bemo'ado* — "you shall guard to bring it in its appointed time." Elsewhere, regarding the Pesach, it says: *vehayah lachem lemishmeres ad arba'ah asar yom* — "it shall be kept by you until the fourteenth day." The Pesach was set aside on the tenth, giving four days of inspection before slaughter on the fourteenth. Just as the Pesach requires four days of prior inspection, so too the *tamid* requires four days of prior inspection. Crucially, Ben Bag Bag limits this requirement to the *tamid* specifically — not to every *korban*. The *musafim* require no such advance checking.

There is something genuinely striking about this pairing: the two offerings singled out for the rigorous requirement of four-day advance inspection are, at opposite extremes, the *Korban Pesach* — the singular event of the year, brought once — and the *tamid* — brought every single day. Nothing stands between these two poles. The common thread seems to be a message about degrees of care: the once-a-year event demands intensive preparation as a matter of course, but so does the daily offering, precisely because its very regularity invites negligence. The opening of Parashat Tzav and Rashi's comment there — *ziruz miyad uledorot*, that special urgency is required precisely for the daily tasks that Kohanim might take for granted — resonates with this theme.

### Mnemonic Only

The Gemara now resolves the earlier challenge. The reference to Shabbos and Rosh Hashanah as the case that motivates the reserve of six is not a literal specification of the scenario but a *simana be'alma* — a mnemonic device. The number six corresponds to the *tamidim* for those three days, and that serves as a convenient way to remember it, but the actual operative rule is simply that the *Beis Hamikdash* always maintained a standing reserve of six inspected lambs in the *lishkat ha-tela'im*, ready to be drawn upon at any time. The reserve was not specifically calibrated for a Shabbos-Rosh Hashanah emergency. The evidence for this reading is linguistic: the Baraita says *kedei le-Shabbos* — "the equivalent of Shabbos" — not *le-Shabbos*, "for Shabbos." The phrasing suggests a numerical mnemonic rather than a literal purpose.

This resolution also addresses a structural problem: if the reserve were literally calibrated for Shabbos followed by two days of Rosh Hashanah, one would need not six but seven lambs, because the morning *tamid* of the day following Rosh Hashanah would also need to be available, and by then no opportunity to replenish and inspect new animals would yet have arisen. The Gemara acknowledges this — *mikkol makom shiva havu* — and it is this unresolvable arithmetic that ultimately confirms that the Baraita was never literally speaking about that scenario in the first place.

### Rotation System

What, then, is the logic of the reserve? Rashi and the *Shittah Mekubetzet* explain that the six sheep represent a rotating queue. Every day, two new sheep are introduced into the *lishka* and two are drawn out for use. Since each sheep must be inspected four days before it can be used, the reserve maintains enough inspected animals to bridge the four-day gap between intake and availability. The system is continuous: animals enter at one end of the queue, are inspected over the course of four days, and are drawn from the other end when ready.

The *Shittah Mekubetzet* works through the logic in detail. If one begins bringing *korbanot* on a Wednesday, one starts inspecting animals the preceding Shabbos, giving Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday — four days. Two animals begin inspection on Shabbos (for Wednesday), two more on Sunday (for Thursday), and two more on Monday (for Friday), yielding eight animals in the *lishka* before the first day of *hakravah* begins. As the process continues, one draws two from the bottom of the queue each morning and adds two to the top each afternoon, maintaining the cycle.

The question of checking or procuring animals on Shabbos itself is worth noting. The *Tosafot* suggest that the *Beis Hamikdash* need not have performed the checking itself; suppliers were in the business of preparing and inspecting lambs for sale to the *Beis Hamikdash*, and the *Beis Hamikdash* could purchase from such suppliers who certified that the animals had been checked for four days. The limitation was not commercial activity per se but the practical impossibility of reaching suppliers in the middle of the night when the morning *tamid* had to be offered at first light.

### Six Explained

Why, given all this, does the number six appear — rather than eight, which would seem to be the logically required minimum? The *Shittah Mekubetzet* offers an explanation: at one particular point in the rotation, after two animals have been drawn out for the day's *tamid* but before the two replacement animals have been introduced that same day, the *lishka* holds exactly six. The ruling that there be "no fewer than six" refers to this interim count — six after the day's draw and before replenishment. Strictly speaking, eight would be needed to maintain a fully continuous supply, but the rule captures the count at the momentary low point in the cycle. It is a somewhat compressed formulation, though the *Shittah Mekubetzet* demonstrates that the logic holds.

The ultimate conclusion of all this is that the Baraita about the six sheep cannot answer the original question of whether *tamidim* take precedence over *musafim*. The reserve exists because the *tamid* requires an advance preparation that the *musafim* do not — not because the *tamid* is prioritized when resources are scarce. The two concerns are distinct, and the question posed by Rav Chiya bar Avin remains unresolved.

---

## Tamidim Debate

### Afternoon Option

The Gemara now turns to a closer analysis of the Mishnah's ruling that if the morning lamb was not brought, it may be brought in the afternoon. Taken at face value, this is what the Mishnah permits. But the Gemara, working through the positions of the *chachamim* and Rabbi Shimon, introduces important qualifications that were not visible in the Mishnah alone.

### Chachamim: Inauguration

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the Mishnah's permissive ruling and the end of the Mishnah's statement about inauguration through a reading it introduces as *chisorei michsra* — the Mishnah is missing contextual material. Even the *chachamim*, who generally permit the afternoon *tamid* when the morning was not brought, agree that this applies only *aval nitchanech hamizbe'ach* — once the altar has already been inaugurated. Before inauguration, one may not start with the afternoon lamb; the inauguration of the outer altar requires specifically the *tamid shel shachar*. The end of the Mishnah — *ein mechanchen et hamizbe'ach hachitzon ela be-tamid shel shachar* — reflects this shared premise. The *chachamim* concede that the morning *tamid* carries foundational weight. Their disagreement with Rabbi Shimon is only about how far that weight extends.

### R. Shimon Restricts

Rabbi Shimon, as noted in the Mishnah, goes further. Even after inauguration, if the failure to bring the morning *tamid* was willful, the afternoon *tamid* may not be brought — *lo hikrivu keves baboker, lo yakrivu bein ha'arbayim*. Only in cases of *ones* or *shogeg* does he permit the afternoon alone.

### Second Only

The Gemara now brings a *baraita* that grounds this entire discussion in the scriptural text. The verse states: *et hakeves ha'echad ta'aseh baboker ve'et hakeves hasheni ta'aseh bein ha'arbayim* — "the first lamb you shall do in the morning and the second lamb you shall do in the afternoon." The *baraita* derives: *sheni bein ha'arbayim velo rishon bein ha'arbayim* — the second is in the afternoon, not the first. The afternoon lamb must be the *second*, meaning it must follow a morning lamb that was already brought. If the afternoon lamb would be the first offering brought, it is inappropriate.

This, however, applies with the qualification already noted: *bameh devarim amurim shelo nitchanech hamizbe'ach* — when is this restriction operative? When the altar has not yet been inaugurated. There the verse's pairing is mandatory. But *aval nitchanech hamizbe'ach, afilu rishon bein ha'arbayim* — once inaugurated, even if the afternoon lamb is the first and only offering of the day, it is acceptable.

This ruling has roots in the way the *Torah* introduces the *tamid* in Parashat Tetzaveh (Shemos 29:38–46), which reads: *vezeh asher ta'aseh al hamizbe'ach, kevasim bnei shanah shnayim layom tamid... et hakeves ha'echad ta'aseh baboker ve'et hakeves hasheni ta'aseh bein ha'arbayim*. The passage is both an instruction for regular daily practice and an account of how the altar first begins to function. The *chachamim* read the pairing requirement as pertaining to the inauguration context, not to every subsequent day. The identification of the altar as *mizbeach ha'olah* — the altar of the burnt offering — and the description of the *tamid* as *ha'asuya behar sinai lere'ach nicho'ach* (as found in the *tamid* passage in Pinchas 28:6) reinforces the sense that the morning *tamid* is the foundational act through which the altar achieves its identity. The *chachamim* locate that requirement in the act of inauguration; Rabbi Shimon holds it extends to every willful choice thereafter.

### Post-Inauguration

Once the altar has been inaugurated, the *chachamim* hold that the afternoon *tamid* may be brought even without the morning one. The morning *tamid* retains its primacy as the anchor of the altar's identity, but that primacy expresses itself through the inauguration, not through a perpetual requirement of pairing on every subsequent day.

### Kohanim Negligence

One might ask: if Rabbi Shimon's restriction on willful omission of the morning *tamid* is meant to protect the integrity of the service, does it not punish the *mizbe'ach* for the negligence of the *kohanim*? If the *kohanim* were derelict in the morning, why should the *mizbe'ach* go without a *tamid* altogether for that day?

### Rabbah's Answer

Rabbah resolves this: *lo hikrivu heim aval acherim yakrivu* — the ruling does not mean that no *tamid* is brought at all. It means that *those* negligent *kohanim* are not entitled to bring it in the afternoon. Other *kohanim* may step in and bring it. The system of the *tamid* continues; what is forfeited is the right of the derelict *kohanim* to perform the afternoon service. The *mizbe'ach* does not suffer; the negligent parties do.

---

## Incense Debate

### Afternoon Incense

The Mishnah rules that if the morning *ketoret* was not burned, it may be burned in the afternoon. This is a permissive ruling without restriction — at least from the *chachamim's* perspective, and apparently from Rabbi Shimon's as well, with the caveat about the full measure. The question is: why is the *ketoret* treated more leniently than the *tamid*? Rabbi Shimon disallows the afternoon *tamid* in a case of *mezid* but seems to permit the afternoon *ketoret*. What distinguishes them?

### Rarity Factor

The Gemara explains: *decheivan delo shechichi u-me'atra* — since the *ketoret* is not a common opportunity and it makes one wealthy. The *ketoret* was brought by a single *kohen*, chosen by lot, and the opportunity was offered only once in a lifetime — a *kohen* who had already performed the *ketoret* was excluded from future lots. This rarity made the service extraordinarily precious to those who served. Thirteen *kohanim* might be involved in bringing the *tamid* up to the *mizbe'ach*; the *ketoret* belonged to one.

### Incense Reward

*U-me'atra* — and it made one rich. There was a tradition that burning the *ketoret* brought material prosperity. This confluence of rarity and reward meant that *kohanim* who were privileged to perform it took extraordinary care. The motivation to be present and diligent was essentially self-reinforcing.

### Rabbinic Concern

The Gemara's treatment of this distinction also subtly reframes Rabbi Shimon's position. Throughout the Mishnah, Rabbi Shimon speaks in terms of *shogeg* versus *mezid*. But once the Gemara understands his restriction as rabbinic in character — a *gezeirah* meant to guard against carelessness — rather than a principled ruling that the *tamid* intrinsically cannot be valid without the morning component, the analysis shifts. The Gemara now speaks not of *mezid* but of *poshe'a* — negligent. The restriction is a rabbinic protection against *peshi'ah*, dereliction. Where *peshi'ah* is structurally implausible — as with the *ketoret*, where the rarity and reward make negligence virtually inconceivable — the protection is simply unnecessary and therefore not imposed.

*Chaviva lehu velo pash'i* — it is beloved to them and they will not be negligent. This is the Gemara's explanation for why no parallel *gezeirah* was enacted for the *ketoret*: the motivation structure itself serves as the protection.

### R. Shimon: Full

Rabbi Shimon rules that when the afternoon *ketoret* is brought alone, the full measure is brought — not merely the half-portion that would ordinarily constitute the afternoon offering. Why this should be so is taken up in the following discussion.

---

## Incense Debate (II)

### Full Amount Why

Rabbi Shimon's ruling that the full measure of *ketoret* is brought in the afternoon connects, as the Gemara will now show, to his view about the *chinuch* of the *mizbeach hazahav*.

---

## Golden Altar

### Afternoon Inauguration

Rabbi Shimon adds: *she'ein mechanchen et mizbeach hazahav ela biketoret samim shel bein ha'arbayim* — the golden altar is inaugurated only through the *ketoret* of the afternoon, not the morning. This phrase, *shel bein ha'arbayim*, does not appear in the Mishnah as we have it; the Gemara reads it as part of Rabbi Shimon's position. If the afternoon *ketoret* is the more fundamental act for the golden altar — the one through which the altar achieves its inaugural status — then it makes sense both that the afternoon alone is acceptable to Rabbi Shimon and that the full measure should be brought when only the afternoon offering can be made.

### Tanaic Debate

The Gemara immediately notes a *baraita* that contradicts Rabbi Shimon: *vehatanya biketoret samim shel shachar* — the *chinuch* of the golden altar is through the morning *ketoret*, not the afternoon. So there is a *tanaic* dispute about which *ketoret* — morning or afternoon — is the more foundational, and correspondingly which one effects the *chinuch* of the golden altar.

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye rules in accordance with the view that the afternoon *ketoret* is the more primary: *mistabra keman de'amar biketoret samim shebein ha'arbayim* — it is more reasonable to say that the *chinuch* is through the afternoon *ketoret*.

### Menorah Link

Abaye's reasoning is as follows. The verse states: *baboker baboker beheitivo et haneirot yaktirenna* — every morning, when one tends the lamps of the *menorah*, one burns the *ketoret*. The *ketoret* and the *menorah* are thus paired: the morning *ketoret* accompanies the morning cleaning of the *menorah*, and the afternoon *ketoret* accompanies the afternoon lighting of the *menorah*. Now, the morning cleaning of the *menorah* — *heitiv* — can only take place because the *menorah* was lit the previous evening. The lighting of the *menorah* is the starting point of the *menorah*'s cycle; the cleaning is the secondary act. If the *ketoret* is linked to the *menorah*, then the starting point of the *ketoret*'s cycle is the afternoon/evening, when the *menorah* is first lit. The morning *ketoret*, by this logic, is the secondary act. Therefore, the afternoon *ketoret* — paired with the initial lighting of the *menorah* — is the more primary, and it is through this more primary act that the *chinuch* of the golden altar is effected.

The argument, as presented, is suggestive rather than fully compelling, and the Gemara does not press it further. But the underlying intuition is clear: the *ketoret* derives its primary orientation from the *menorah*, and the *menorah*'s primary moment is the evening lighting, making the afternoon/evening *ketoret* the anchor of the cycle.

### Parallel View

The opposing view — that the morning *ketoret* effects the *chinuch* — draws by analogy from the outer altar. Just as the outer altar is inaugurated through the morning *tamid*, so the golden altar is inaugurated through the morning *ketoret*. Both are altars; both follow a morning-afternoon cycle; the morning is the starting point for the outer altar and should be the starting point for the golden altar as well. *Mah lahalan betamid shel shachar af kan biketoret samim shel shachar*.

### Altar Placement

The deeper question underlying this dispute concerns how the golden altar is to be categorized. Is it essentially a parallel to the outer altar — both are altars, both operate on a morning-afternoon cycle, and the morning is therefore primary for both? Or does the golden altar belong to a different conceptual category, aligned with the other vessels of the *heichal* — the *menorah* and the *shulchan* — whose primary cycle runs from evening to morning? If the golden altar is fundamentally aligned with the *menorah*, then its primary moment is the afternoon and evening; if it is fundamentally aligned with the outer altar, its primary moment is the morning.

Rabbi Shimon holds that the afternoon is primary for the golden altar, and from this flows his ruling that the afternoon *ketoret* alone can stand independently, that the full measure is brought when only the afternoon is offered, and that the *chinuch* of the golden altar is effected through the afternoon *ketoret* specifically. The *chachamim* who hold the morning *ketoret* effects the *chinuch* implicitly align the golden altar with the outer altar, where the morning is the foundational moment.

---

---

# Menachot 49b

## Ein Me'akvin Korbanot

### Ein Me'akvin Intro

The overarching theme of this section of Menachot concerns the principle of *ein me'akvin* — that the absence of one korban does not prevent or invalidate another. Having dealt previously with the tight relationship between the *kivsei atzeret* and the *shtei halechem*, the Mishnah now turns to other groupings of *korbanot*.

### Tamidim Musafim

The Mishnah opens with the rule that *hatamidim ein me'akvin et hamusafim velo hamusafim me'akvin et hatamid*: the *tamidim* do not hold back the *musafim*, nor do the *musafim* hold back the *tamid*. That is, if on Shabbat one has lambs sufficient only for the *tamidim* but not for the *musaf*, one may still bring the *tamidim*; conversely, if one has animals for the *musafim* but not for the *tamid*, the *musaf* may still be offered without the *tamid*.

### Musafim Mutual

The principle extends further: *velo hamusafim me'akvin ze et ze* — the *musafim* do not hold one another back. If one lacks the full complement of animals required for a given day's *musafim* — which can be a substantial group, a bull, rams, and seven sheep — one may bring whatever is available. This is true even when two sets of *musafim* coincide, as on Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, when the *musafim* of Shabbat and those of Rosh Chodesh do not impede one another.

### Two Tamidim Case

The Mishnah then states: *lo hikrivu keves baboker yakrivu bein ha'arbayim* — if the morning lamb was not brought, the afternoon one may still be offered. This is noteworthy: one might have assumed that the two *tamidim* form a matched pair such that one cannot stand without the other, much as we saw with the *musafim*. The Mishnah establishes that each may be brought independently.

### Rabbi Shimon Tamidim

*Rabbi Shimon* qualifies this ruling. *Eimatai?* — when does the above apply? *Bizman shehayu anusim o shogegim* — only when the failure to bring the morning *tamid* was due to circumstances beyond one's control, whether compulsion (*ones*) or inadvertence (*shogeg*). But *aval im hayu mezidin* — if the failure was a willful choice — *lo yakrivu bein ha'arbayim*: they may not bring the afternoon *tamid* at all.

This position reflects a broader tendency in Rabbi Shimon's thinking. Elsewhere in an earlier Mishnah, Rabbi Shimon held that if one must choose between bringing some of the *musafim* with their *nesachim* or bringing all of them without *nesachim*, it is preferable to bring fewer offerings done properly. The same logic applies here: he regards there as a meaningful relationship between the two *tamidim*, and he would rather that no *tamid* be brought at all than have the afternoon offered as if it stands entirely on its own — at least when the omission of the morning one was a deliberate choice.

### Nesachim Priority

The connecting thread is that Rabbi Shimon, in both contexts, insists that *korbanot* be performed correctly and completely. Just as he maintained the bond between each animal and its *minchat nesachim*, here he maintains the bond between the morning and afternoon *tamid*. Either bring both, or — if the omission of the morning was *meizid* — bring neither. If there was no choice, the *anusim* or *shogeg* case, the afternoon offering remains valid.

### Ketoret Morning Night

The Mishnah continues: *lo hiktiru ketoret baboker yaktiru bein ha'arbayim* — if the *ketoret* was not offered in the morning, it may be offered in the afternoon. Recall that the full daily measure of *ketoret* — one *maneh* — was divided: half in the morning and half in the afternoon. Rabbi Shimon's position here is striking. He does not contest the legitimacy of the afternoon *ketoret* on its own, as he did with the *tamid*. However, he does add: *amar Rabbi Shimon vechulah hayeta krevah bein ha'arbayim* — if the morning *ketoret* was not offered and only the afternoon offering remains, the entire full measure should be brought in the afternoon, not merely the half that was originally designated for that time.

The Mishnah then turns to the laws of *chinuch*, the inauguration of the vessels and altars of the Mikdash. The *mizbeach hazahav*, the golden altar, is inaugurated specifically by the burning of *ketoret*; the outer *mizbeach ha'olah* is inaugurated by the *tamid shel shachar*; the *shulchan* by the *lechem hapanim* on Shabbat; and the *menorah* by the lighting of its seven lamps in the afternoon. Each vessel is inaugurated through the performance of its characteristic *avodah*. The mention of the *tamid shel shachar* as the vehicle for inaugurating the outer altar is, as the *gemara* will develop, the key to understanding Rabbi Shimon's position regarding the primacy of the morning *tamid*.

---

## Precedence Tamidim

### Precedence Question

The Gemara opens this section with a question posed by *Rabbi Chiya bar Avin* to *Rav Chisda*: if the community lacks sufficient animals for both *tamidim* and *musafim*, which takes precedence? This is not a question about the order in which they are offered when all are available, but rather — when a genuine choice must be made and only one set of offerings can be brought — which one is to be given priority?

### Same vs. Different Day

The Gemara immediately draws a distinction. If the question is about choosing between the *tamidim* of today and the *musafim* of today — say, on Shabbat, when two lambs are needed for the *tamidim* and two for the *musaf* — that case is straightforward.

### Tadir Principle

*Pshita tmidim adifei* — obviously the *tamidim* take precedence. The reason is *tadir*: the *tamidim* are more frequent, brought every single day, and the principle *kol hatadir mechaveiro kodem et chaveiro* — the more regular precedes the less regular — is well established. Moreover, the *musaf* of Shabbat is no more *kadosh* than the *tamid* of Shabbat. When frequency and sanctity both point in the same direction, the answer is obvious.

### Tadir Mikudash

Rashi and Tosafot both note that *mikudash* here does not mean that the *tamid* is holier than the *musaf* in any absolute sense, but that it is at least as holy. Since the *tamid* of Shabbat is no less *mikudash* than the *musaf* of Shabbat, and is additionally *tadir*, it clearly prevails. The genuinely difficult case is when *tadir* and *mikudash* do not align — when one offering is more frequent but the other is more sanctified — but the same-day case presents no such tension.

### Tomorrow Tamid Today

The hard case is the one the Gemara actually presses: *tmidim delmachar umusafim de'idna* — must one choose between tomorrow's *tamidim* and today's *musafim*? Suppose the Mikdash has four lambs and no prospect of obtaining more before the next day — since animals must be inspected four days in advance, even a last-minute delivery could not be used. The question becomes: does one seize today's opportunity, bringing today's *musaf*, or does one plan ahead and preserve the animals for tomorrow's *tamidim*?

This framing itself generates a subsidiary question. On one side, *tmidim adifei sheken tadir* — the *tamidim* warrant priority as the more frequent offering, and there is no better example of *tadir* than the daily *tamid*. On the other side, *musafim adif dehavei lemikudash* — perhaps the *musafim* are weightier, since today's offerings, whatever their character, belong to a sanctified context. Rashi offers two readings of *mikudash* here. One reading is straightforward: today is Shabbat, a sacred day, and a *korban* tied to a *kadosh* day implicitly carries greater association with sanctity than a *korban* of an ordinary weekday. The other reading is more provocative: *mikudash* does not denote greater inherent holiness at all, but rather the pressing reality of the present moment — today's obligation presents itself now and demands to be addressed now, whereas tomorrow's concern is not yet here. This second reading casts the question in terms of present urgency versus future planning, which is itself a fascinating dimension of the problem.

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question from the opening Mishnah — *hatamidim ein me'akvin et hamusafim* — arguing that it can only be making sense if it addresses the case of choosing between today's *musafim* and tomorrow's *tamidim*, and that in such a case neither prevails over the other, meaning the choice is equivalent. However, *Abaye* rejects this reading. He maintains that the Mishnah is speaking *bediavad* — about what happens after the fact when one offering was performed without the other — and not about *lechatchila* choices at all. The rule *shelo yehei davar kodem letamid shel shachar*, derived from the verse *ve'arach aleha ha'olah*, establishes that nothing may precede the *tamid lechatchila*; Rashi cites Rava's statement *ha'olah olah rishona* in support. Abaye acknowledges that this applies only *lechatchila*, and that *bediavad* the offering remains valid if done out of order. But the consequence is that the Mishnah cannot be pressed as a proof for how to choose between today's *musafim* and tomorrow's *tamidim*. The question, therefore, remains unresolved at this point in the Gemara.

---

## Reserve Sheep Checking

### Six Sheep Reserve

The Gemara introduces a *baraita*: *ein pochtin me'shisha tela'im hamevukarin belishkat hatela'im ledei Shabbat uleshnei yamim tovim shel Rosh Hashanah* — there must be no fewer than six inspected sheep in the chamber of sheep (*lishkat hatela'im*), sufficient for Shabbat and the two days of Rosh Hashanah. The straightforward reading suggests that this reserve was maintained to ensure that if Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah — the only two-day *yom tov* observed in Eretz Yisrael — arrived without opportunity to acquire new animals, the *tamidim* would still be available. Six sheep would cover two *tamidim* for Shabbat and two *tamidim* for each day of Rosh Hashanah, with the *musafim* conspicuously absent from this accounting.

The Gemara challenges this reading: if the purpose were to ensure the full complement of *korbanot* for those days, six is grossly insufficient — *tuva havu*, far more would be needed, since the *musafim* of Rosh Hashanah alone include seven lambs, two bulls, and a ram. The Gemara therefore concludes that *ela lav deleis lei* — the scenario is one where the community lacks sufficient animals and must choose, and the reserve is exclusively for the *tamidim*. This would suggest *shema minah temidin adifei* — the *tamidim* take priority even over today's *musafim*, including tomorrow's *tamidim* over today's *musafim*.

Rashi sharpens the inference: if Shabbat precedes Rosh Hashanah, the community would bring only two animals on Shabbat — the *tamidim* — deliberately foregoing the Shabbat *musaf*, in order to preserve the remaining four for the two days of Rosh Hashanah's *tamidim*. That is a direct prioritization of tomorrow's *tamid* over today's *musaf*.

### Ben Bag Bag Source

The Gemara then explains why the reserve addresses only *tamidim* and not *musafim*. *Ben Bag Bag* derives from a *gezerah shavah* — comparing the phrase *tishmeru lehakriv li bemo'ado* regarding the *tamid* to *vehayah lachem lemishmeret* regarding the *korban Pesach* — that the *tamid* specifically requires four days of prior inspection before *shechitah*, just as the *korban Pesach* was set aside on the tenth of Nisan and slaughtered on the fourteenth. No such requirement applies to other *korbanot*, including *musafim*. The reserve in the *lishkat hatela'im* exists precisely because of this four-day requirement: animals cannot simply be acquired at the last moment and used for a *tamid*. The *musafim*, by contrast, need no such advance preparation and are therefore not part of this reserve system.

The pairing of the *korban Pesach* and the *tamid* in this *gezerah shavah* is itself notable. The *korban Pesach* is the most singular annual event — brought once a year with enormous national significance. The *tamid*, by contrast, is brought every single day, and it is precisely the dailiness of the *tamid* that risks making it feel routine or taken for granted. That these two extremes — the once-yearly pinnacle and the daily constant — are the only two *korbanot* requiring the same four-day degree of preparation and vigilance is a meaningful statement: the care one invests in the extraordinary must equally be invested in the ordinary.

### Six vs Seven

*Ravina* raises a difficulty to *Rav Ashi*: given the purpose of the reserve, six sheep are actually insufficient — there should be seven, or perhaps even eight. If, for example, Shabbat precedes Rosh Hashanah, the six sheep in reserve will be drawn upon during Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah, but by the morning after Rosh Hashanah, all six will have been used, and no inspected sheep will remain for the *tamid* the following morning. *Ha'ika tzafra detilsa beshabbta* — there is the morning of the third day of the week, by which point the reserve is exhausted. How will the *tamid* be brought then? Conversely, Rav Ashi might respond that according to Ravina's logic one should need eight, since even the *erev Shabbat* afternoon *tamid* — *kamei detamid shel bein ha'arbayim* — requires a checked animal, and by that point there would similarly be no time to replenish.

### Mnemonic Explanation

The Gemara resolves both objections by concluding that the *baraita* is not literally about preparing for Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah specifically. *Simana be'alma* — the mention of Shabbat and two days of Rosh Hashanah is simply a mnemonic for the number six, not a prescription for those days exactly. The actual rule is that the *lishkat hatela'im* should maintain a standing reserve of six inspected sheep as a general operational standard. Naturally, if Shabbat or Rosh Hashanah were approaching, the reserve would be augmented. The Gemara notes this can also be inferred from the *baraita*'s language: it says *kedei Shabbat*, meaning "equivalent to" or "in the amount of," rather than *leShabbat*, "for Shabbat" — a subtle linguistic indicator that Shabbat and Rosh Hashanah serve as a mnemonic frame rather than the operative purpose.

### Rotation System

The *Shittah Mekubbetzet* elaborates on the underlying operational logic. The *lishkat hatela'im* operated as a rotating reserve: two new animals were introduced into the chamber each day, each set requiring four days of inspection before use. If one traces through the rotation — animals placed on Sunday drawn for use on Thursday, and so forth — the system actually requires eight sheep to be present at any given moment, not six. The *Shittah Mekubbetzet* resolves this by noting that six is the number that remains in the chamber at the precise moment after that day's pair has been withdrawn for *shechitah* but before the day's two new animals have been added. It is admittedly a somewhat strained accounting — logically, one would have said the minimum is eight — but it explains how the figure of six emerges from the mechanics of the rotation. The central point is clear: this is a management system designed to ensure a constant supply of *tamidim* with the required four-day lead time, and it has nothing to do with choosing between *tamidim* and *musafim*.

The Gemara's attempted proof from this *baraita* — that the preference for *tamidim* in the reserve demonstrates that tomorrow's *tamid* takes precedence over today's *musaf* — therefore fails. The reserve focuses on *tamidim* not because of any comparative ranking between *tamidim* and *musafim*, but because only *tamidim* require the four-day advance inspection. The original question of which takes precedence thus remains without a definitive answer.

---

## Afternoon Tamid Only

### Mezid Restriction

The Gemara now engages directly with Rabbi Shimon's position in the Mishnah. The baseline rule — that if the morning *tamid* was not brought, the afternoon one may still be offered — is read in light of the Mishnah's closing lines about *chinuch hamizbeach*. The Gemara frames it as follows: the Mishnah states *lo hikrivu keves baboker lo yakrivu bein ha'arbayim* (Rabbi Shimon's formulation for the *meizid* case). This apparently raises an acute problem: is the *mizbeach* to suffer on account of the *kohanim*'s failure?

### Chinuch Mizbeach

The Gemara introduces the device of *chisorei mechasra* — the Mishnah is missing context — and supplies it. The rule that one may not bring the afternoon *tamid* alone applies specifically *shelo nitchanech hamizbeach*, when the outer altar has not yet been inaugurated. As the Mishnah itself establishes, the *mizbeach ha'olah* is inaugurated by none other than the *tamid shel shachar*. Therefore, before inauguration, the morning offering is indispensable — one cannot begin with the afternoon. *Aval nitchanech hamizbeach yakriv bein ha'arbayim*: once the altar has been inaugurated, one may offer the afternoon *tamid* even without the morning one, provided there was no willful neglect.

This also clarifies the position of the *chachamim*. They do not dispute the primacy of the *tamid shel shachar* — the Mishnah's statement about inauguration itself acknowledges it. Their disagreement with Rabbi Shimon is more limited: they accept that the morning *tamid* is foundational and that one must begin with it, but they do not extend this to a rule barring the afternoon *tamid* when the morning was not brought through *meizid*. For the *chachamim*, the weight given to the morning *tamid* is expressed through the *chinuch* requirement, not through a general restriction on the afternoon offering.

The verse cited — *vezeh asher ta'aseh al hamizbeach, kevasim benei shanah shenayim layom tamid* (Shemot 29:38) and following — is read not only as describing ongoing procedure but also as prescribing how the *avodah* of the *mizbeach* begins. The Torah's strong identification of the *mizbeach* as the *mizbeach ha'olah*, and the *tamid* as the foundational *korban* offered there *asuyah beHar Sinai*, both reinforce the primacy of the morning *tamid* at the moment of inauguration.

### Ketoret Afternoon OK

The Mishnah's treatment of the *ketoret* proceeds differently. *Lo hiktiru ketoret baboker yaktiru bein ha'arbayim* — if the morning *ketoret* was not offered, the afternoon one may be brought — and here Rabbi Shimon does not interpose the same *meizid* restriction that he applies to the *tamid*. The implication is that for the *ketoret*, the afternoon offering is legitimate even when the omission of the morning was willful. Rabbi Shimon adds that in such a case, the full measure of *ketoret* — the entire *maneh*, not merely the half ordinarily designated for the afternoon — should be offered then.

The source for restricting the afternoon *tamid* is derived from the verse: *et hakeves ha'echad ta'aseh baboker ve'et hakeves hasheni ta'aseh bein ha'arbayim* — *sheni bein ha'arbayim velo rishon bein ha'arbayim*. The afternoon offering must be the second, not the first. If nothing was offered in the morning, the afternoon offering would be the first, which is impermissible. The *baraita* then qualifies this: *bameh devarim amurim shelo nitchanech hamizbeach* — this restriction on doing the afternoon offering as a "first" applies only when the altar has not yet been inaugurated. *Aval nitchanech hamizbeach afilu rishon bein ha'arbayim* — once inaugurated, even the afternoon can serve as the first in the day, at least where the omission was beyond one's control. Rabbi Shimon then limits even the post-inauguration leniency to *anusim o shogegim*.

### Kohanim Replacement

The question stands: if Rabbi Shimon's concern is rabbinic in character — a protective measure against negligence — then why should the *mizbeach* suffer because of what the *kohanim* did or failed to do? *Amar Rava hachi ka'amar*: Rabbi Shimon does not mean that no *tamid* will be offered at all. Rather, *lo hikrivu hen aval acherim yakrivu* — those particular *kohanim* who were negligent in the morning are not permitted to perform the afternoon *tamid*, but other *kohanim* may do so. The system continues; it is only the negligent *kohanim* themselves who are barred. This reframing positions Rabbi Shimon's ruling as a disciplinary measure directed at individuals, not as a withholding of *avodah* from the *mizbeach* itself.

---

## Tamid vs Ketoret

### Ketoret Rarity

The Gemara now directly addresses why Rabbi Shimon treats the *ketoret* differently from the *tamid* and does not apply the same protective restriction to it. The explanation offered is: *dechivan delo shechichi um'atrah* — since the *ketoret* is rare and enriches those who perform it. This requires clarification: the *ketoret* is offered daily, so in what sense is it rare? The answer lies in the structure of its performance. While the *tamid* involved many *kohanim* — the Mishnah in Tamid describes thirteen *kohanim* engaged in various aspects of the offering — only a single *kohen* burned the *ketoret*, and the privilege was awarded by lottery. No *kohen* who had previously won the *ketoret* lottery could participate again until every other eligible *kohen* had had his turn. In practical terms, a given *kohen* might wait his entire career in the Mikdash before the opportunity came around. Furthermore, the tradition held that offering the *ketoret* brought wealth to the one who performed it. Given both its rarity and its desirability, *chaviva lehu velo pash'ei* — the *kohanim* held it dear and would not be negligent about it. A *gezeirah* protecting against morning negligence is therefore unnecessary.

The Gemara's language here also shifts subtly: whereas Rabbi Shimon spoke of *mezidin*, the Gemara frames his concern in terms of *peshi'ah*, negligence. This shift is deliberate. It signals that Rabbi Shimon's position in the *tamid* case is not a principled ruling grounded in the inherent pairing of morning and afternoon offerings, but rather a rabbinic protective measure against laxity — and where laxity is not a realistic concern, as with the *ketoret*, no such protection is needed.

### Full Ketoret Amount

Rabbi Shimon's statement that when the *ketoret* is offered only in the afternoon, the full measure — the entire *maneh* — should be offered, follows from the same logic. If the afternoon *ketoret* is legitimate on its own, it should not be treated as merely half an offering, a truncated substitute for what was missed. It stands in its own right, and it should therefore be offered in full.

### Zahav Olah Chinuch

The Mishnah's statement about *chinuch* — that the *mizbeach hazahav* is inaugurated by the *ketoret* and the *mizbeach ha'olah* by the *tamid shel shachar* — is now read as part of Rabbi Shimon's continuing statement in the Gemara. Specifically, the phrase *she'ein mechanchin et hamizbeach hazahav ela biktoret samim shel bein ha'arbayim* — the golden altar is inaugurated specifically by the *afternoon ketoret* — appears in Rabbi Shimon's view with the addition *shel bein ha'arbayim*, a phrase absent from the straightforward reading of the Mishnah. This addition is significant: Rabbi Shimon holds that it is the *afternoon ketoret* that serves as the vehicle for the inaugural act on the golden altar, not the morning one.

This stands in direct contrast to the outer altar, where the inaugural act is the *tamid shel shachar*, the morning offering. The two altars thus operate on different founding orientations: the outer altar's *chinuch* belongs to the morning; the golden altar's *chinuch* belongs to the afternoon. This asymmetry may itself explain why Rabbi Shimon is more permissive about an afternoon-only *ketoret* than about an afternoon-only *tamid*: for the *mizbeach hazahav*, the afternoon is not a fallback position but the more fundamental expression of the *avodah*.

### Tannai Debate

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *vehatanya biktores samim shel shachar?* — another *baraita* states that the *mizbeach hazahav* is inaugurated with the morning *ketoret*, not the afternoon. The Gemara acknowledges the contradiction and concludes: *tannai hi* — this is a dispute among *tannaim*. There is thus a genuine disagreement about whether the morning or the afternoon *ketoret* is the more fundamental expression that grounds the *chinuch* of the golden altar.

### Menorah Connection

*Abaye* offers a proof that the opinion favoring the afternoon *ketoret* is more compelling. The verse states *baboker baboker behitivo et hanerot yaktirena* — every morning when the *kohen* cleans the lamps of the *menorah*, he burns the *ketoret* (Shemot 30:7). Abaye reasons: *ee lav de'avid hadlaka me'ourta hatava betzafra meheicha* — the only reason the *kohen* can clean out the *menorah* in the morning is because it was lit the evening before. The *ketoret* and the *menorah* are linked in the Torah's presentation: *ketoret* accompanies the lighting of the *menorah* in the evening and the cleaning of the *menorah* in the morning. Since the *menorah*'s cycle begins with the evening lighting — not the morning cleaning — the *ketoret* cycle similarly has its origin in the evening. By extension, the afternoon *ketoret* (which precedes the evening lighting) is the more fundamental of the two. This is, as Abaye's own formulation suggests, an indirect argument, and it may not fully convince on its own terms.

### Olah Pattern

The alternative derivation — supporting the view that the morning *ketoret* grounds the *chinuch* — reasons from an analogy to the outer altar: *gamar mimizbach ha'olah*. Just as the outer altar's system of morning and afternoon is anchored in the morning *tamid shel shachar*, so too the golden altar's system of morning and afternoon *ketoret* should be anchored in the morning. The two altars are structurally parallel: both involve a morning and afternoon *avodah*, both are *mezbeichot* of the Mikdash, and the governing logic of one should map onto the other.

The underlying dispute, then, is about how to categorize the *mizbeach hazahav*. Is it most naturally grouped with the *mizbeach ha'olah* — in which case the morning is primary for both — or is it grouped with the other furnishings of the *heichal*, the *menorah* and *shulchan*, which operate on a cycle that begins in the afternoon or evening? If the *mizbeach hazahav* is seen as the incense-counterpart of the *mizbeach ha'olah*, the morning is primary. If it is seen as part of the inner *heichal* complex, the afternoon is primary. Rabbi Shimon's broader permissiveness toward the afternoon-only *ketoret* — and his insistence that the full measure be offered — may itself reflect his implicit alignment of the *mizbeach hazahav* with the *heichal* complex rather than with the outer altar, making the afternoon *ketoret* not merely acceptable but foundational.

# Menachot 50

## Tamidim & Musafim

### Ein Me'akvin Concept

The overarching theme of this section of Menachot concerns the principle of *ein me'akvin* — that certain ritual components do not hold one another back — now applied to the world of *korbanot*. Having already examined the tight relationship between the *kivsei atzeret* and the *shtei halechem* within a single *korban*, the Mishna turns to broader groupings of communal offerings.

The Mishna states: *hatmidim ein me'akvin et hamussafim* — the *tamidim* do not prevent the *musafim*, and conversely, *velo hamussafim me'akvin et hatmidim* — if one has animals for *musafim* but not *tamidim*, the *musaf* may be brought even without the *tamid*, and vice versa.

### Musafim Independence

The principle extends further: *velo hamussafim me'akvin zeh et zeh* — even among the *musafim* themselves, they do not hold one another back. On a day such as *Shabbos Rosh Chodesh*, when there are two separate *musaf* obligations, if one cannot bring both, one may bring whichever is available. Even a partial complement of the *musaf* animals — which typically comprises a large group of bulls, a ram, and seven lambs — may be brought without the remainder.

### Two Tamidim Debate

The Mishna continues: *lo hikrivu keves baboker yakrivu bein ha'arbayim* — if the morning lamb was not brought, the afternoon lamb may still be brought. The two *tamidim* are thus not mutually dependent, just as the individual animals of the *musaf* are not mutually dependent. One might have assumed that since they come as a natural pair, it should be all or nothing — but the Mishna rules otherwise.

Rabbi Shimon, however, qualifies this: *eimatai? bizman shehayu anusim o shogegim* — when is this permitted? Only when the failure to bring the morning *tamid* was beyond one's control (*onus*) or inadvertent (*shogeg*). But *aval im hayu mezidim* — if it was a willful choice — *lo yakrivu bein ha'arbayim* — they may not bring it in the afternoon.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon's position here reflects a broader principle visible elsewhere in his rulings. Recall his earlier ruling that if one must choose between bringing some of the *musafim* with their *nesachim* or all of them without their *nesachim*, it is better to bring fewer but bring them properly. There is a consistent theme: do it right, or do not do it at all. Here too, Rabbi Shimon holds that one should not volitionally choose to do only one of the *tamidim*. If forced by circumstance, perhaps; but as a free choice, one may not elect the afternoon *tamid* while foregoing the morning one. The relationship between the two *tamidim*, in his view, is too significant to allow a deliberate half-measure.

This also connects to what the Mishna implies through its phrasing *ve'et hakeves hasheni* — the emphasis on "the second" presupposes a "first." Rabbi Shimon reads this language as establishing an interdependence, while the *chachamim* are not persuaded.

## Mizbeach Inauguration

### Altar Inauguration Ways

The Mishna then introduces a series of rules about how the various sacred vessels are inaugurated: *she'ein mitchaneket mizbach hazahav ela biktoret hasamim* — the golden altar is inaugurated through the burning of the *ktoret*; *v'lo mizbeach ha'olah ela b'tamid shel shachar* — the outer altar is inaugurated only with the morning *tamid*. The *shulchan* is inaugurated with the *lechem hapanim* on *Shabbat*, and the *menorah* is inaugurated by lighting its seven candles in the afternoon. The principle is that each vessel is inaugurated by performing its characteristic *avodah* upon it for the first time.

As the Gemara will later add, the *mizbach hazahav* is specifically inaugurated with the *ktoret hasamim shel bein ha'arbayim* — the afternoon incense — a point whose significance will be discussed.

### Outer Altar & Tamid

The Mishna's statement that the outer *mizbeach* is inaugurated specifically with the *tamid shel shachar* is not incidental. It underscores the foundational status of the morning *tamid* in relation to the outer altar. This provides at least a contextual basis for Rabbi Shimon's position: since the *tamid shel shachar* serves as the anchor and beginning of the altar's service — indeed, as its very act of inauguration — one should not make a deliberate choice to skip it and perform only the *tamid shel bein ha'arbayim*.

## Today vs Tomorrow

### Limited Resources

The Gemara opens its analysis with a question posed by Rav Chiya bar Avin to Rav Chisda: *tzibur she'ein lahem tmidim u-musafim eizeh me-hem kodem* — if a community does not have animals for both *tamidim* and *musafim*, which takes priority?

The question requires careful framing. *Kodem* here does not mean which is performed first in sequence, but rather which is preferred when only one can be brought. The easy case is clear: if one must choose between today's *tamid* and today's *musaf* — say, on *Shabbos*, with only two lambs — *pshita tmidim adifei*, the *tamidim* take precedence, because of the principle *tadir v'she-eino tadir tadir kodem*: the more frequent offering precedes the less frequent one. Moreover, the *tamid* of *Shabbat* is no less *mikudash* than the *musaf* of *Shabbat*, so there is no competing consideration of greater sanctity.

The genuinely difficult question is: *tmidim d'limachar u-musafim d'ha-idna* — what if one must choose between today's *musaf* and tomorrow's *tamidim*? This could arise, for instance, on *Shabbos* with four lambs and no prospect of acquiring more before the next morning — given that animals must be inspected four days in advance, even a supplier arriving that evening could not provide valid animals for tomorrow's *tamid*. Do you address today's needs and bring the *musaf*, or do you plan ahead and preserve animals for tomorrow's *tamid*?
