The Gemara frames the tension as: *tmidim adifei she-ken tadir* — perhaps the *tamidim* are preferred because they are more frequent — versus *musafim adif de-havu le-mikudash* — perhaps the *musafim* take precedence because they are of greater sanctity, or because, in one reading of Rashi, *mikudash* does not refer to greater intrinsic holiness but rather to the immediacy of today's obligation. Rashi offers two approaches: one in which a *korban* brought on a sacred day like *Shabbat* is considered to carry a heightened quality by virtue of its association with that day's *kedusha*; and one in which *mikudash* simply means "the pressing matter of today" — the question being whether one's obligation is to address the present moment or to plan for the future.

### Mishna Proof Attempt

To resolve the question, the Gemara cites the Mishna itself: *hatmidim ein me'akvin et hamussafim velo hamussafim me'akvin et hatmidim velo hamussafim me'akvin zeh et zeh* — the *tamidim* and *musafim* do not prevent one another, and the *musafim* do not prevent each other.

The Gemara asks: what precisely does this Mishna mean? If it means that one has all the animals available and the Mishna is speaking about order — i.e., if one performed them out of sequence it is still valid — that cannot be its meaning, because we know from a *braita* that nothing may precede the *tamid shel shachar*: *minayin shelo yehe davar kodem letamid shel shachar — talmud lomar ve-arach aleha ha-olah*, and Rava states explicitly that *ha-olah olah rishona* — the *tamid* must be the first offering on the fire, with nothing preceding it.

The Gemara therefore concludes that the Mishna must be discussing a case of *leis lei* — where one does not have all the animals and must choose which to bring. And since the Mishna seems to permit either choice — bringing the *tamidim* without the *musafim*, or bringing the *musafim* without the *tamidim* — as a volitional *le'chatchila* decision (since later in the Mishna Rabbi Shimon is discussing deliberate choices), it appears to treat both options as equivalent. Choosing today's *musaf* over tomorrow's *tamid* would be fine; choosing tomorrow's *tamid* over today's *musaf* would also be fine. This would suggest that neither is categorically preferred.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye objects: *le-olam de-is lehu* — the Mishna is in fact discussing a case where one has all the animals available. *U-lekadem* — the point of the Mishna is indeed about performing them out of sequence. The *braita* that says nothing may precede the *tamid shel shachar* is only a *le'chatchila* requirement; *be-di'avad*, if one reversed the order, it is still valid. Abaye thus reads the Mishna as a *be-di'avad* statement, not a *le'chatchila* prescription about which to choose. The Mishna is not offering guidance on priority; it is simply stating what happens when things have gone differently than planned. No proof can therefore be drawn from it regarding today's *musaf* versus tomorrow's *tamid*.

## Reserve Sheep Supply

### Six Sheep Rule

The Gemara continues its search for a resolution and cites a Mishna: *ein pochsin mi-shisha t'layim ha-mevukarim be-lishkas ha-t'layim kedei le-shabbat u-lishnei yamim tovim shel Rosh Hashana* — there may be no fewer than six inspected lambs kept in the chamber of the lambs (*lishkat ha-telayim*), enough to supply *Shabbat* and the two days of *Rosh Hashana* — the only two-day *yom tov* observed in Eretz Yisrael.

The idea of a reserve makes practical sense: during *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana*, there is no opportunity to go out and acquire new animals. The reserve ensures that the *tamidim* can be brought even under those constrained circumstances.

### Reserve Interpretation

The Gemara initially assumes this Mishna is discussing a case where one does not have animals for both *tamidim* and *musafim*, and notes that the reserve is calibrated specifically for the *tamidim* — two lambs for *Shabbat* and two lambs for each of the two days of *Rosh Hashana*, for a total of six. The *musafim* are not provided for in this reserve. This would indicate that when planning in advance, the community's primary concern is for the *tamidim*, not the *musafim* — suggesting that *tamidim* are prioritized even over a *Shabbat* or *Rosh Hashana* *musaf*.

Rashi sharpens this further: if *Shabbat* falls immediately before *Rosh Hashana*, then on *Shabbat* itself, one would bring only two of the six lambs — for the *tamid* — deliberately preserving the remaining four for the *tamidim* of the two days of *Rosh Hashana*, even though one could theoretically bring the *musaf shel Shabbat* today. This would represent an active, live choice of tomorrow's *tamid* over today's *musaf*.

The Gemara, however, rejects this reading: *le-olam de-is lei* — in truth, the reserve is not premised on a shortage of animals. If it were talking about providing the full complement for *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana*, including *musafim*, the number would be far greater than six. *Rosh Hashana* alone requires seven lambs for its *musaf*, in addition to bulls and a ram. The number six therefore cannot be about fully provisioning all *korbanot* for these days.

### Ben Bag Bag Requirement

The Gemara therefore reinterprets the Mishna entirely: *ein pochtin me-shishah telayim ha-mevukarin be-lishkas ha-telayim arba'ah yamim kodem shechitah* — there must be no fewer than six lambs that have been inspected for four days prior to their slaughter. The mention of *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana* was not the reason for the reserve; it was merely a mnemonic for the number six.

The actual rule is grounded in a *braita* attributed to Ben Bag Bag: *minayin le-tamid she-ta'un bikkur arba'ah yamim kodem shechitah?* — whence do we know that the *tamid* requires four days of prior inspection before it is slaughtered? He derives it through a *gezerah shavah*: the Torah says *tishmeru le-hakriv li be-mo'ado* regarding the *tamid*, and separately states regarding the *korban Pesach* that it must be kept *ad arba'ah asar yom* — the *korban Pesach* was designated on the tenth of Nisan and slaughtered on the fourteenth, a four-day period of inspection. Just as the *Pesach* requires four days of checking, so too does the *tamid*.

Critically, Ben Bag Bag specifies that this requirement applies specifically to the *tamid*. Not every *korban* requires four days of advance inspection — only the *tamid*. The *musafim*, by contrast, have no such requirement. This explains why the reserve chamber holds specifically *tamid* animals: they require extended advance preparation that *musafim* do not. The existence of a dedicated reserve for *tamid* lambs thus reflects a technical *halachic* demand, not a normative judgment that *tamidim* take priority over *musafim*.

This point also carries a striking conceptual resonance. The two offerings that require four days of advance preparation are the *korban Pesach* — the singular once-a-year event — and the *tamid* — the most daily and routine of all *korbanot*. These two extremes, the most exceptional and the most regular, require equal degrees of preparation and care. The *tamid*, which is brought every single day without exception, demands the same level of attention as the most celebrated offering of the year. This parallels the theme articulated by Rashi at the beginning of *Parshat Tzav*, where the instruction to the *kohanim* concerning the daily removal of ashes — *zeiruz miyad kan u-ledoros* — comes precisely because daily repetition breeds complacency. The things most in need of safeguarding are often those done every day.

### Ravina Challenge

Ravina raises a challenge to Rav Ashi: if the six lambs are indeed intended to cover the *tamidim* for *Shabbat* and two days of *Rosh Hashana*, the number is actually insufficient. Consider the scenario where *Shabbat* comes first and is immediately followed by two days of *Rosh Hashana*. Six lambs would cover the three days — two for *Shabbat* and four for the two days of *Rosh Hashana*. But the morning after *Rosh Hashana* ends, the *tamid* must be brought, and there will be no inspected animals available. Since four days of prior checking are required, there is no way to have a valid animal ready first thing the next morning without some reserve remaining. So why is six sufficient?

Ravina further objects: one could equally argue the reserve should be eight, because the afternoon *tamid* on *erev Shabbat* — just before *Shabbat* begins — also depletes the supply, and one has no opportunity to replenish it before *Shabbat* enters. The Gemara deflects this second challenge: the count of six refers to what remains *after* the day's *korbanot* have been brought, not before. But the challenge about the morning after *Rosh Hashana* still stands.

### Mnemonic Resolution

The Gemara's response is decisive: *ela tanna b'alma ka'ei* — the reference to *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana* is simply a mnemonic (*simna b'alma*), not a literal prescription for those specific days. The Mishna is not saying that six lambs are designed to cover exactly *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana*. Rather, six is the standing minimum reserve that must be maintained at all times. When *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana* are actually approaching, one would increase the reserve accordingly. *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana* are invoked only as a memorable reference point for the number six, not as the operational purpose of the reserve.

This is also inferred from the Mishna's precise language: it says *kedei le-Shabbat* — "enough as for *Shabbat*" — using *kedei* rather than *le-Shabbat*, which would mean explicitly "for *Shabbat*." The phrasing suggests the number is calibrated by analogy to the *Shabbat* and *Rosh Hashana* scenario, not that it is literally meant to serve those days.

### Rotation System

The Shittah Mekubetzet attempts to explain the logic of six more precisely by describing the rotation system. If a new *mizbeach* is being inaugurated on a Wednesday, one would begin designating and checking lambs on the *Shabbat* before — two lambs checked on *Shabbat* for use on Wednesday, two checked on Sunday for use on Thursday, and two checked on Monday for use on Friday. That gives six animals in the chamber, all in various stages of their four-day inspection cycle. On Tuesday, two more lambs would be added for the following *Shabbat*.

This continuous rotation — two animals added each day, two drawn upon each day — keeps the *lishka* in constant operation. Technically, the system requires eight animals to maintain perfectly, since at any given moment there must be a full four-day queue. But the Shittah Mekubetzet explains that when the two oldest animals are drawn out for today's use and before new ones have been introduced, there are exactly six remaining. The number six thus represents the minimum point in the rotation cycle, the moment between drawing on the reserve and replenishing it.

This also raises the question of who performs the inspection. From a comment in Tosafot on 50a, it emerges that the *Beit Hamikdash* could acquire animals from external suppliers who had themselves conducted the four-day inspection and could certify that the animals were *mevukarim*. The problem Ravina identifies — that there would be no inspected animals available first thing the morning after *Rosh Hashana* — is resolved in practice because suppliers could be contacted in advance. The one scenario that cannot be resolved this way is if one needs an animal in the very first hours of the morning without any opportunity to have arranged it the night before.

In any case, the conclusion of the Gemara is that no proof can be derived from this Mishna for the original question of priority between today's *musaf* and tomorrow's *tamid*. The reserve system has nothing to do with choosing between *tamidim* and *musafim*; it exists solely to meet the unique technical requirement that the *tamid* must be inspected four days in advance.

## Afternoon Service

### Afternoon Tamid Question

The Gemara now turns to a direct examination of the Mishna's ruling regarding the afternoon *tamid*: *lo hikrivu keves baboker lo yakrivu bein ha'arbayim* — if they did not bring the morning lamb, they may not bring it in the afternoon. The question is how to properly contextualize this ruling.

### Shimon Mezid Distinction

Rabbi Shimon's position, as stated, is that if the failure to bring the morning *tamid* was due to *onus* or *shogeg*, the afternoon *tamid* may be brought; but if it was *mezid* — willful — they may not bring the afternoon one. When it comes to the *ktoret*, however, Rabbi Shimon permits bringing only the afternoon *ktoret* even when it is *mezid*. This asymmetry demands explanation.

The difficulty with Rabbi Shimon's position, as the Gemara notes, is that if his reasoning were purely principled — that the two *tamidim* form a necessary pair and one cannot stand without the other — then the distinction between *shogeg* and *mezid* would be irrelevant. A principled pairing requirement would apply regardless of intent. The fact that Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between inadvertent and willful failure suggests that his concern is not about the intrinsic necessity of the pair but rather about something else entirely.

### Distinction Basis

The Gemara develops this by reading the Mishna in context. The end of the Mishna states that the outer *mizbeach* is inaugurated only with the *tamid shel shachar*, which implies that the morning *tamid* carries foundational significance. The Gemara suggests reading the Mishna's ruling as follows: *bameh devarim amurim she-lo nitchanech hamizbe'ach* — the rule that you cannot bring the afternoon *tamid* without the morning one applies when the *mizbeach* has not yet been inaugurated. The *chachamim* agree that when establishing the service of the *mizbeach* for the first time, you must begin with the morning *tamid* — you cannot inaugurate it beginning in the afternoon. But *aval nitchanech hamizbe'ach* — once the altar has been inaugurated — *afilu rishon bein ha'arbayim* — even if the afternoon *tamid* is the first offering of the day, it is acceptable, because the foundational act of inauguration has already been performed.

To this, Rabbi Shimon adds: *eimatai?* — when is this permission to bring only the afternoon *tamid* granted? *Bizman shehayu anusim o shogegim* — only when the failure to bring the morning one was not the *kohanim*'s fault. *Aval im hayu mezidim* — if they willfully skipped the morning *tamid* — *lo hikrivu baboker lo yakrivu bein ha'arbayim* — they forfeit their right to bring the afternoon one.

This reading integrates the inauguration discussion naturally into the Mishna. The *chachamim* acknowledge the primacy of the morning *tamid* as the inaugurating act, but hold that once the *mizbeach* is inaugurated, the afternoon one stands independently. Rabbi Shimon agrees with the premise but adds a rabbinic safeguard for the case of willful neglect.

### Ketores Different

The Gemara then addresses the *ktoret*. The Mishna states: *lo hiktiru ketoret baboker yaktiru bein ha'arbayim* — if the *ktoret* was not burned in the morning, it may be burned in the afternoon. Unlike the *tamid*, Rabbi Shimon does not restrict this to cases of *onus* or *shogeg*. Why is the *ktoret* treated differently?

The Gemara seeks the source for the basic rule. A *braita* cites the verse: *et hakeves ha'echad ta'aseh baboker ve'et hakeves hasheni ta'aseh bein ha'arbayim* — the second lamb is specifically designated for the afternoon, and not the first. This teaches: *sheni bein ha'arbayim velo rishon bein ha'arbayim* — what may stand in the afternoon is only "the second," only what was paired with a first. If there was no morning offering, then the afternoon offering cannot be the "second" — it would be the first, which is not its proper designation for the afternoon. This is what prevents doing only the afternoon *tamid* — it cannot be called *hasheni* if there was no *ha'echad*.

However, this restriction applies only to inaugurating the *mizbeach* for the first time, as explained above. Once the *mizbeach* is inaugurated, the *pessukim* in *Pinchas* — which govern the ongoing *tamid* — are read as not imposing the same pairing requirement as a mandatory matter, and the afternoon *tamid* may be brought independently in cases of *onus* or *shogeg*.

The association of the *tamid* with the *mizbeach ha'olah* runs deep throughout the Torah's language. The outer *mizbeach* is consistently called the *mizbach ha'olah*, and the *tamid* is described as *olat tamid hasuya behar sinai* — linked to the very inauguration of the service at Sinai. These *pessukim* establish the morning *tamid* as the defining act of the *mizbeach*'s identity and its service.

## Shimon Rabbinic

### Rava Interpretation

Rava clarifies the fundamental nature of Rabbi Shimon's ruling: *lo hikrivu heim aval acherim yakrivu* — when Rabbi Shimon says that if the morning *tamid* was not brought, the afternoon one may not be brought by those same *kohanim*, he does not mean that no afternoon *tamid* is brought at all. Rather, the *kohanim* who were negligent in the morning are disqualified from performing the afternoon service; other *kohanim* may step in and bring it. The altar does not suffer for the priests' misconduct. This framing confirms that Rabbi Shimon's restriction is not a principled ruling about the necessary pairing of the two *tamidim*, but a disciplinary measure directed at the *kohanim* who were at fault.

This also accounts for why it is described in terms of *mezid* — willful conduct — rather than as a categorical requirement. If the pairing were essential to the *korban* itself, it would be irrelevant whether the failure was deliberate or inadvertent; the *korban* would be invalid either way. Since Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between *shogeg* and *mezid*, the ruling is necessarily about accountability, not about the intrinsic structure of the service.

### Ketores Exemption

With this framework in place, the Gemara explains why the *ktoret* is treated differently from the *tamid*. The reason is captured in the phrase *de-lo shechichi u-ma'ashra* — the *ktoret* is both rare and enriching. In contrast to the *tamid*, where a large team of *kohanim* was involved each morning, the *ktoret* was performed by a single *kohen*, and was so rare an opportunity that most *kohanim* never had the chance to perform it even once. Moreover, there was a tradition that performing the *ktoret* brought the *kohen* wealth. Given how prized and infrequent the opportunity was, *chaviva lehu velo pashei* — they cherish it and will not be negligent. There is simply no need to establish a rabbinic safeguard against negligence in a domain where negligence is almost inconceivable.

### Tamid Needs Protection

The *tamid*, by contrast, is brought every single day. Its very regularity creates the risk of complacency. The *kohanim* assigned to bring it might begin to treat it as routine and allow it to slip. It is precisely because it is performed daily — *tadir* in every sense — that it requires the protection of a rabbinic deterrent. If *kohanim* know that deliberate neglect in the morning forfeits their right to bring the afternoon *tamid*, they will be more careful to attend to the morning service properly.

This connects directly to the theme of Ben Bag Bag's four-day inspection requirement: the *tamid* is the *korban* most in need of structural safeguards and careful preparation, not because it is more sacred than others, but precisely because its regularity makes it vulnerable to neglect. The things that are done every day are the things that need *chizuk* — reinforcement and vigilance — most of all.

## Afternoon Ketores Full

### Full Ketores Amount

The Mishna records a further ruling of Rabbi Shimon: *vekula hayata kreva bein ha'arbayim* — if the afternoon *ktoret* is brought without a morning *ktoret* having been offered, the full measure is brought in the afternoon, not merely the half. The standard practice divided the *maneh* of *ktoret* between morning and afternoon, half at each time. If one missed the morning, Rabbi Shimon's ruling is not that one brings only the afternoon's half; rather, the full measure is brought in the afternoon.

The Gemara introduces this by noting that the version of the Mishna connected to Rabbi Shimon includes the phrase *she'ein mitchanchin et mizbach hazahav ela biktoret hasamim shel bein ha'arbayim* — you only inaugurate the *mizbach hazahav* with the afternoon *ktoret*, not the morning one. This is the Gemara's version of Rabbi Shimon, which differs from the plain text of the Mishna, and leads into the next set of discussions.

### Ketores-Menorah Link

The Gemara raises an immediate challenge from a *braita*: *biktoret hasamim shel shachar* — another source indicates that the *mizbach hazahav* is inaugurated with the morning *ktoret*, not the afternoon one. The Gemara resolves this as a *tannaitic* dispute: it is a debate among the *tannaim* as to which *ktoret* service — morning or afternoon — is more fundamental, and accordingly which one inaugurates the *mizbach hazahav*.

The significance of this question for Rabbi Shimon's ruling about the full measure is as follows: he permits bringing only the afternoon *ktoret* without the morning, and mandates that the full amount be brought in that case. If the afternoon *ktoret* is the more fundamental service — as demonstrated by its role in the inauguration of the *mizbach hazahav* — then it is coherent to say that one may bring only the afternoon, and moreover, that one should bring the full measure when doing so alone.

Abaye is cited as supporting the view that the afternoon *ktoret* is indeed the more fundamental: *mistabra k'man d'amar biktoret hasamim shel bein ha'arbayim*. His reasoning is drawn from the verse *baboker baboker betivo et hanerot yaktirena* — every morning, when the *kohen* cleans out (*heitiv*) the lamps of the *menorah*, he also burns the *ktoret*. But for there to be a morning cleaning of the *menorah*, there must have been a nighttime lighting. The *menorah* is lit at night and cleaned in the morning; the *ktoret* accompanies both. This means the *ktoret* is organically linked to the *menorah*'s cycle, and the *menorah*'s cycle begins at night — with the afternoon/evening lighting — not in the morning. Therefore the primary orientation of the *ktoret* also begins in the afternoon, making the afternoon *ktoret* the more foundational of the two.

### Parallel to Tamid

Abaye's position is contested by those who hold that the morning *ktoret* is the inaugurating act. Their reasoning: *gmar mi-mizbach ha'olah* — just as the outer *mizbeach* follows the model of morning as foundational (the *mizbeach ha'olah* is inaugurated with the *tamid shel shachar*), so too the *mizbach hazahav* should be understood as following the same morning-first model. Just as the outer *mizbeach* is characterized by the morning *tamid*, the inner *mizbeach* should be characterized by the morning *ktoret*.

In both cases — whether one emphasizes the morning or the afternoon — the underlying principle is to identify which service is most fundamental to the altar's identity and function.

### Mizbeach Identity

This debate crystallizes a deeper question about the nature of the *mizbach hazahav* itself: is it best understood as a parallel structure to the *mizbeach ha'olah*, with a morning-first orientation, or is it more properly categorized with the other vessels of the *heichal* — particularly the *menorah* — which operate on a night-morning-night cycle? 

The *mizbeach ha'olah* and its *tamid* operate on a morning-to-afternoon rhythm, with the morning as the inaugurating and fundamental moment. The *menorah*, by contrast, begins its cycle at night: *Shabbat* evening, morning, the following evening, and so on. Since the *ktoret* accompanies the *menorah* at both its moments, the question of whether the *mizbach hazahav* belongs to the *mizbeach ha'olah* family or the *menorah* family determines whether its foundational service is in the morning or the afternoon.

What remains implicit in Rabbi Shimon's position — though the Gemara does not spell it out fully — is that by identifying the afternoon as the fundamental *avodah* of the *mizbach hazahav*, Rabbi Shimon can coherently (a) permit bringing only the afternoon *ktoret* without the morning, and (b) require that when it is brought alone, the full measure be used. If the afternoon is primary, then bringing it alone is not a deficient substitute for the morning; it is the essential act, now performed in its fullness.

---

---

# Menachot 50b

## Chinuch & Kiddush

### Three Inaugurations

The mishnah catalogues several distinct inaugurations of the Tabernacle vessels. The golden inner altar — the *mizbe'ach hazahav*, synonymous with the *mizbe'ach haketoret* — is inaugurated through the *ketoret hasamim*. The outer altar, the *mizbe'ach ha'olah*, is inaugurated through the *tamid shel shachar*. And now the mishnah turns to the third item: *velo et hashulchan ela belechem hapanim beshabbat* — the *shulchan* is inaugurated specifically through the *lechem hapanim*, and specifically on *Shabbat*.

### Chinuch vs Kiddush

The Gemara asks whether the mishnah's insistence on *Shabbat* carries an implicit permissive inference: since it says you cannot *be-mechanech* the *shulchan* except through the *lechem hapanim* on *Shabbat*, perhaps the *chinuch* (inauguration) requires *Shabbat*, but mere *kiddush* (sanctification) could be accomplished on a weekday?

The Gemara rejects this reading entirely. The mishnah is not trying to separate *chinuch* from *kiddush* — it is coming to tell us precisely the opposite: *chinuch ve'kiddush shulchan beshabbat hu* — the inauguration and the sanctification occur together, at one and the same moment. Do not infer from the word *chinuch* that the two can be disentangled.

### Menora Lighting

The point becomes clearer from the fourth item in the mishnah's list: *velo et hamenora ela beshiva neroteiha bein ha'arbayim* — the *menora* is inaugurated only through the lighting of its seven lamps in the evening. This is simply stating what the Torah already prescribes: the lamps are lit at night, not during the day. There is no daytime lighting. The *kiddush* comes precisely when the proper time arrives, and the *chinuch* follows as a matter of course. Since both arrive simultaneously, you must wait for the designated moment. For the *shulchan*, that moment is *Shabbat*, as the Torah specifies for the *lechem hapanim*.

---

## Ketoret of Nesi'im

### Individual Ketoret

The Gemara now introduces a *baraita*: *zehu ketoret she'alta leyachid hamizbe'ach hachitzon hora'at sha'ah hayta* — this refers to an *ketoret* offering brought by an individual on the outer altar, and it was a one-time dispensation. The reference is to the *nesi'im*, the tribal princes, each of whom brought among his offerings a *kaf* filled with *ketoret*. This offering was placed on the outer *mizbe'ach* — which is the striking anomaly, since the *ketoret* is ordinarily brought on the inner *mizbe'ach hazahav* — and it was a *hora'at sha'ah*, an exceptional temporary instruction, not a permanent norm.

### Voluntary Ketoret

The Gemara proceeds to parse the implications from multiple angles. The *baraita* noted that an individual brought *ketoret* on the outer altar. Does this mean that, as a rule, an individual may not bring *ketoret* on the outer altar — but could bring it on the inner? And conversely, does it mean only an individual is excluded from the outer altar, while the community (*tzibbur*) could bring *ketoret* there?

Taking this further: might an individual bring *ketoret* as a voluntary offering (*nedavah*)? After all, the Torah says *kol aniyah motze picha tishmor ve'asita* — one may fulfill a vow of *nedavah* — and we know that voluntary offerings are routinely brought. Could *ketoret* function similarly?

The answer is drawn from the *pasuk* in *parashat Tetzaveh* which commands: *lo ta'alu alav ketoret zarah* — you shall not offer *ketoret zarah*, alien incense, upon the inner altar. This prohibition encompasses any *ketoret* that is not the prescribed communal *ketoret*. A *yachid* bringing a voluntary *ketoret* would constitute *ketoret zarah* — and that is categorically forbidden on the inner altar.

### Ketoret Zarah

The Gemara then asks whether, while an individual is barred from the inner altar, maybe the *tzibbur* could bring a voluntary *ketoret* there. After all, the community does bring *ketoret* regularly. But *lo ta'alu* is a plural formulation — Rashi notes this explicitly — and it excludes the community as well from bringing anything other than the prescribed communal obligation on the inner altar.

Having disposed of the inner altar, the question shifts: perhaps *ketoret* — whether brought by an individual or by the community — could be offered on the outer *mizbe'ach hachitzon*? After all, the inner altar's prohibition has been established, but nothing yet seems to address the outer one.

### Klal Ufrat Analysis

The answer to this final question comes from the end of *parashat Ki Tisa*, where God speaks to Moshe regarding Betzalel's charge. The passage lists the vessels: the *Ohel Moed*, the *shulchan*, the *mizbe'ach haketoret*, the *shemen hamishchah*, and the *ketoret hasamim* — and it is bookended by the general phrase *ve'asu et kol asher tzivitcha ya'asu*, "they shall do all that I have commanded you," appearing at both the opening and close.

This structure is a *klal uferat uklal* — a general statement, specific details, and another general statement — from which the rule is *ein lecha ela mah she'amur be'inyan*: you cannot derive any permission beyond what the specific content of the passage itself specifies. And what does it specify? The *mizbe'ach haketoret* — the inner golden altar — as the designated site. The outer altar is implicitly excluded. *Mah she'amur bebinyan* refers exclusively to the inner *mizbe'ach*: that is where the *ketoret* belongs, brought as an obligation by the community.

The logic, when a question is raised about it, runs as follows. The passage describing the construction of the *mishkan* and its vessels was not crafted to permit an individual to bring a personal *nedavah*. Its frame of reference is the *chovah* — the communal obligation — and the inner altar. Once the *klal uferat uklal* deduction is applied, neither community nor individual may bring *ketoret* on the outer altar, and neither may do so as a voluntary offering on the inner one.

### Final Ketoret Rule

The conclusion is stated with the logic of *lo mibaya*. It goes without saying that the *tzibbur* cannot bring *ketoret* on the outer *mizbe'ach*, since there is no precedent (*lo ashkachan*) for that ever occurring. It likewise goes without saying that an individual cannot bring it on the inner *mizbe'ach*, since again there is no precedent. But one might have thought that even an individual could bring a voluntary *ketoret* on the outer *mizbe'ach* — after all, we do find a precedent in the *nesi'im*. The answer is: that was a *hora'at sha'ah*, a unique one-time dispensation, which by definition implies that nothing like it may be replicated going forward.

The upshot: the *ketoret* may be brought only by the *tzibbur*, only as an obligation, and only on the inner *mizbe'ach hazahav*. Every other configuration is excluded.

---

## Chavitin Structure

### Chavitin Intro

The Gemara now introduces a new mishnah concerning the *chavitin* of the *Kohen Gadol*. The relevant *pesukim* are in *parashat Tzav* (Vayikra 6). The passage begins: *zeh korban Aharon uvanav asher yakrivu l'Hashem b'yom himashach oto* — this is the offering of Aharon and his sons which they shall bring to God on the day he is anointed. It is an *asirit ha'ephah* of *solet*, brought as a *tamid*, with half in the morning and half in the evening: *machatzitah baboker umachatzitah ba'erev*.

The key point is that while the offering is ultimately divided and offered in two halves, it does not begin as two halves. The *chavitin* — so named because, as the continuation of the passage specifies, it is made *al machavat*, on a frying pan — is prepared as a unified whole. The mishnah states: *chavitei Kohen Gadol lo hayu ba'in chatzayan* — they do not come in halves. Rather, *mevi isaron shalem ve-chotzehu* — one brings a full *isaron* and then divides it — *makriv mechtzah baboker umechtzah bein ha'arbayim*.

### Whole Unit

The conceptual significance of this rule is established by the *baraita*: had the Torah simply written *minchah machatzit* (a half-portion offering), one might have concluded that a *Kohen* brings half an *isaron* in the morning from his own funds and another half in the evening, each half independent of the other. But the Torah writes *machatzitah* — half *of it*, with the possessive suffix indicating half of a previously constituted whole. The Gemara derives: *me-chatzi meshalem hu makriv* — he offers half that comes from a whole. The procedure is therefore: bring a complete *isaron*, halve it, offer one half in the morning, the other half in the evening.

### Priest Death

What happens if the half designated for the evening becomes *tamei* or is lost? Here again the principle applies: the *Kohen* may not simply bring a new half-*isaron* from his own funds. He must bring another complete *isaron*, divide it, offer one half, and let the other half be disposed of. Consequently, on such a day: *nimtzu shenei chatza'in krevim ve-shenei chatza'in ovdin* — two halves are offered and two halves are lost, drawn from two separate *isronot*.

The same analysis applies when the *Kohen Gadol* dies between the morning and evening offerings. A new *Kohen Gadol* is appointed to serve at *minchah*, and the question is posed: may the new *Kohen Gadol* bring just his half from his own funds, or use the remaining half from the deceased's *isaron*? The *baraita* answers from the same word: *machatzitah ba'erev* — *machetza mishalem hu mevi umakriv*, he must bring half that derives from a full unit. He therefore brings a new complete *isaron*, divides it, offers one half in the evening, and the remaining half is lost. Combined with the morning half that the first *Kohen Gadol* already offered (the second half of which can no longer be brought since the *Kohen* died), the day ends with two halves offered and two halves disposed of — each pair coming from a different *isaron*.

### Two Halves Lost

A *baraita* formalizes this: *mechetza rishon umechetza sheni te'ubar tzuratan veyeitz'u l'beit ha-sreifa* — both the first half and the second half that are not offered must have their form changed (*te'ubar tzuratan*), meaning they must be left overnight, and only then taken to the *beit ha-sreifa* for burning.

---

## Spoilage & Burning

### Overnight Spoilage

The term *te'ubar tzuratan* — literally "their form is altered" — is borrowed language, more naturally applied to meat (which would visibly change overnight without refrigeration), but applied here by analogy to a flour offering. Practically, it means leaving the remaining halves overnight, after which they are taken to the *beit ha-sreifa* and burned.

### Second Half Question

This requirement prompts a pointed question from Rav Nachman. He understands why the first half — the half belonging to the deceased *Kohen Gadol* that cannot be offered — must undergo *ibur tzurah* before burning. It was originally intended for the *mizbe'ach*, so it requires a process of invalidation before it can be burned. But why does the second half of the new *Kohen Gadol*'s *isaron* need to stay overnight? That half was never going to be offered from the outset. The new *Kohen* brings a full *isaron*, divides it, offers one half in the evening, and the other half was — from the moment of division — destined not to go on the *mizbe'ach*. Why does something that was never valid require overnight invalidation?

### Pigul Comparison

The response invokes *pigul*: even an offering rendered invalid through improper intent (*pigul*) — which by definition can no longer be placed on the *mizbe'ach* — still requires *ibur tzurah* before burning. The source is the school of Rabbah bar Avuha: *afilu pigul ta'un ibur tzurah*. By the same principle, anything designated for the *mizbe'ach* that cannot ultimately be offered must go through this overnight process before burning. That is simply the rule — anything headed for the *beit ha-sreifa* must first be left overnight.

### Rashi's View

Rashi offers an additional rationale, one that applies even according to the *rabbanan* who hold that *pigul* does not require overnight spoilage before burning. Rashi's reasoning focuses on the nature of the division itself. When the new *Kohen Gadol* brings his full *isaron* and divides it in two, it is not as if one specific half was always designated for the *mizbe'ach* and the other was always destined to be discarded. Either half could have been the one offered; either half could have been the one set aside. Since both halves were potentially candidates for the *mizbe'ach* — *i ba'ei hai makriv ve'i ba'ei hai makriv*, he could have offered this one or that one — both halves are, in a sense, attached to the *mizbe'ach*. The altar lays claim to both, as it were. Therefore, even the half that is ultimately not offered requires overnight treatment before it may be burned.

---

## Three Methods

### Order Challenge

The *pasuk* in Vayikra 6 describes the preparation of the *chavitin* with a sequence that is, on its face, puzzling: *al machavat bashemen te'aseh murbechet tevi'ena tufinei minchat pitim takriv* — on a pan, with oil it shall be made, scalded (*murbechet*), you shall bring it baked (*tufinei*), a broken offering you shall bring. Three distinct processes appear: frying (on the *machavat*), scalding (*murbechet*, where water is poured on it), and baking (*tufinei*). The Torah lists them in that order: fried, scalded, baked. Yet the question of which process actually precedes which — specifically whether baking comes before frying or after — is where the debate will focus.

### Visual Demo

To appreciate the practical stakes, it helps to see the three states. The first is the fried state: the dough placed on the *machavat*, the frying pan, cooked in oil. The second is the scalded state (*murbechet*): water is poured over or applied to the dough. The third is the baked state (*tufinei*): placed in an oven and baked.

The question of sequence is not merely academic. If one fries the dough and then pours water over it, the result may turn to mush — a concern that is at least intuitive even if not technically disqualifying, since the *chavitin* is not eaten (*vekhol minchat Kohen Gadol tihiyeh chalil lo tei'achel*). Yet the offering must still be aesthetically presentable. One might argue that the water step logically comes first — before anything is done to the dough — or perhaps last. What the *baraita* will address, however, is not the position of the scalding step per se, but the relative order of baking and frying.

Note also that a misprint in Rashi seems to suggest he is addressing the scalding step in the debate, but this does not appear to be correct. The debate is specifically about whether baking precedes frying or frying precedes baking; the scalding step's placement, while curious given the Torah's stated order, is not the subject of the *machloketh*.

### Frying vs Baking

The *amora'im* disagree directly on this question. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ofeyhan ve-achar kach metagnah* — one bakes first and then fries. Rabbi Assi says in the name of Rabbi Chanina: *metagnah ve-achar kach ofeyah* — one fries first and then bakes.

Each position is supported by a reading of the word *tufinei*. Rabbi Chiyya, following Rabbi Yochanan, reads *tufinei na'eh* — a beautiful, attractive baking. Since frying tends to char or otherwise mark the surface, baking should come first while the dough is still pristine, so that the baked result is *na'eh*, aesthetically fine. Rabbi Assi reads *tufinei na* — baked in a state of *na*, meaning partially done, referring to something not yet fully cooked through its own process. This implies that the baking comes after the frying has already partially prepared it.

This dispute maps directly onto a *tannaitic* debate. The *Tanna Kamma* reads *tufinei na* (frying first, supporting Rabbi Assi). Rabbi, however, reads *tufinei na'eh* (baking first, supporting Rabbi Yochanan). A third opinion, that of Rabbi Yose, reads *tufinei rabbah* — a great or abundant baking — and Rashi offers three explanations for this position. One understanding is that both *na* and *na'eh* apply, which would yield the sequence: bake, fry, bake — the dough is baked once, then fried, then baked again. A second explanation of *tufinei rabbah* is that it means making the dough large: by spreading it on the *machavat* one can move the pan to extend the dough, which points to frying first so as to expand it, then baking. A third explanation reads not *rabbah* but *rakah* — soft — meaning a great deal of oil is used in frying so that the dough becomes tender, and then it is baked. Thus under the first reading of Rabbi Yose the order is bake-fry-bake; under the second and third readings it is fry-then-bake.

---

## Location & Sabbath

### Inside Requirement

A mishnah cited from elsewhere states: *chavitei Kohen Gadol lishatan va'afiyatan bifnim dochot et hashabbat* — the kneading and baking of the *Kohen Gadol*'s *chavitin* must be performed inside the Temple precincts, and this work overrides the Sabbath. These preparations may not be done at home and brought in; they must be carried out within the *azarah* itself.

### Freshness Rule

From where do we derive this? Rav Huna says it follows from *tufinei na'eh* — it must be baked beautifully — and *afilu me'etmol ipshah*, even the day before it would become stale. Since the preparation must be done fresh each day to ensure the offering looks its best, and since the *chavitin* is brought daily, this necessarily requires work on the Sabbath as well. Abaye derives it differently, from the word *tamid* in the *pasuk* — just as the *temidin* are offered on every day including *Shabbat*, so too must this offering be prepared on every day. Rava derives it from the technical rule that any item that must be prepared in a *keli* (vessel) is invalidated by *lina* (staying overnight), so preparation must occur that very day — and this applies on *Shabbat* as well.

### Preservation Method

Rav Yosef raises a challenge: why is Sabbath violation necessary? Perhaps the *chavitin* could be prepared the day before and then wrapped in vegetable leaves to preserve its freshness, avoiding the need to cook on the Sabbath. The implicit question is pointed: this offering is neither eaten nor tasted — it is ultimately burned in its entirety — so why must one violate the Sabbath simply so it should appear fresh? The Gemara responds: *de-vairabbi Yishmael tanna te'aseh afilu be-shabbat, te'aseh afilu be-tumah* — the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the word *te'aseh* in the *pasuk* that the preparation is required even on *Shabbat* and even in a state of communal *tumah*. Rava's derivation via *al machavat* and *lina* similarly compels same-day preparation with no room for a workaround.

---

## Oil Quantity

### Comparison Setup

Having established that the *chavitin* must be prepared on a *machavat* with oil (*bashemen te'aseh*), the question turns to quantity: how much oil is required? The *baraita* acknowledges it does not know and proceeds to examine two possible analogs. The first is the *tamid* offering — which the *chavitin* resembles in several respects, given that both are brought constantly, both override *Shabbat*, and both override *tumah*. The second analog is a voluntary *minchah* offering (*minchat nedavah*), brought by an individual. These two comparisons yield starkly different answers: the *tamid* requires three *lugin* of oil per *isaron*, while the voluntary *minchah* requires only one *log*.

### Tamid Approach

Rabbi Shimon beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka resolves the question by appeal to the *pasuk* itself. The verse describing the *chavitin* uses the word *tamid* — *solet minchah tamid*. Since it says *tamid*, just as the *minchat temidin* uses three *lugin* of oil per *isaron*, so too should the *chavitin*: *ma minchat temidin sheloshah lugin isaron, af zu sheloshah lugin isaron*.

### Proportionality

Rabbi Shimon independently approaches the question through the word *bashemen* — "with oil" — which implies adding a substantial quantity of oil. But how much? He considers two possible comparisons. On one hand, the *minchat kevasim* (the flour offering accompanying a lamb) uses three *lugin* per *isaron*. On the other hand, the *minchat parim ve-eilim* (accompanying rams and bulls) uses two *lugin* per *isaron*. Which is the correct analog?

The resolution comes from a principle of proportionality: *denin minchah ha-ba'ah be-isaron mi-minchah ha-ba'ah be-isaron* — we compare a *minchah* that comes in a single *isaron* to another *minchah* that comes in a single *isaron*. We do not compare it to offerings that come in two or three *isronot*, since those proportions are structurally different. The lamb offering comes with one *isaron*, just like the *chavitin*, and its oil ratio is three *lugin* per *isaron*. That ratio fits proportionately for the *chavitin*; the ram-and-bull ratio does not match when scaled to a single *isaron*. Therefore: three *lugin*.

### Contradiction

A difficulty now emerges from within the *baraita* itself. It opened by saying *bashemen lehosif lo shemen* — *bashemen* teaches that one must add a generous quantity of oil, implying a large amount. Yet it then proposed comparing the *chavitin* to the *minchat nedavah* — which requires only one *log*. These two positions appear contradictory: if *bashemen* means to add a lot, one *log* hardly qualifies; and if the comparison to the *nedavah* is valid, there is nothing especially large about one *log*.

### Bahsemen Logic

The resolution is attributed to the school of Rabbah bar Avuha, and its logic is clarified by Abaye: the one who said *bashemen lehosif shemen* is Rabbi Shimon. The reasoning is as follows. Since the *pasuk* already says *al machavat* — on the frying pan — it is obvious that oil must be used, because you do not fry on a *machavat* without oil. If *bashemen* merely meant "use oil," it would be superfluous given *al machavat*. Therefore *bashemen* must mean something additional: add more oil than the *machavat* itself implies. It signals a generous, additional quantity of oil.

But then, why propose comparing it to the *nedavah* at all? Because Rabbi Shimon entertained the possibility that *bashemen* might not be teaching a quantity but merely emphasizing the type — confirming that oil must be used, lest one think the *chavitin* is like a *charvot* (a dry flour offering, not fried), since some *menachot* are indeed brought without oil. *Bashemen* would then rule out the dry alternative, without specifying a large quantity. It is only after this possibility is considered and the comparison to the *nedavah* (one *log*) explored that Rabbi Shimon concludes the logical comparisons are inconclusive, making the explicit *bashemen* indispensable as a directive to use more oil — and then the deductive work of proportionality brings him to three *lugin*.

### Rava Reconciles

Abaye and Rava both hold that the entire passage reflects Rabbi Shimon's reasoning, but they organize the internal steps somewhat differently. Rava's version: *bashemen* signals additional oil; if there were no explicit *bashemen*, Rabbi Shimon would have tried to derive the amount by analogy — comparing it to the *tamid* (three *lugin*) or to the *nedavah* (one *log*) — but these logical comparisons prove inconclusive because valid arguments point in both directions. Therefore the explicit word *bashemen* is indispensable, and Rabbi Shimon then establishes three *lugin* through the proportionality argument comparing *isaron*-to-*isaron* offerings. In both Abaye's and Rava's accounts, all the positions in the passage belong to Rabbi Shimon beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, with the internal sequence reflecting his own working-through of the question before arriving at the final ruling of three *lugin* per *isaron*.

---

---

# Menachot 51

## Death Between Portions

### Chavitai Overview

The daf begins with a *mishna* concerning the *chavitai kohen gadol* — the *mincha* offering that the *kohen gadol* brings each day, half an *issaron* in the morning and half in the afternoon. The preceding *mishna* had addressed the case where the *kohen gadol* dies between the two portions and a new *kohen gadol* is immediately appointed in his stead; it detailed how that successor brings his half. The present *mishna* takes up the same basic scenario but with a different conclusion.

### No Replacement

Here, the *kohen gadol* dies between the morning and afternoon portions, but no new *kohen gadol* is appointed right away — it simply takes time. The *mishna* therefore asks: *mishel mi haysah kreiva?* — from whose funds does the offering continue to be brought, whether for that very afternoon or during the interim period more generally? The assumption of the *mishna* is that it does continue to be brought; the question is one of funding and not of obligation.

### Shimon vs. Yehuda

On this question, *Rebbi Shimon* and *Rebbi Yehuda* disagree. *Rebbi Shimon omer mishel tzibur* — it is brought from communal funds. His underlying logic seems to be that the *chavitai* is fundamentally a daily obligation assigned to the office of *kohen gadol*, and when there is no *kohen gadol*, the *tzibur* assumes responsibility for it. *Rebbi Yehuda omer mishel yorshim* — it is brought from the heirs of the deceased *kohen gadol*. According to this view, the *chavitai* is more properly understood as the *kohen gadol*'s own *korban*, funded from his personal wealth; since it ordinarily comes from his money, it remains, even in his death, the obligation of his estate rather than a communal sacrifice.

### Full Portion Agreement

Despite their disagreement on funding, both *Rebbi Shimon* and *Rebbi Yehuda* agree on one critical point: when the offering is being brought in the absence of a living *kohen gadol* — whether by the *tzibur* or by the heirs — it is not split into two half-portions but is brought as a full *issaron*. The *mishna* states explicitly: *ushleimah haysah kreiva*, it was brought whole.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda's Source

### General Continuation

The *Gemara* opens with a *Tannu Rabbanan* that frames the question in broader terms. The *kohen gadol* died and no replacement was immediately appointed: *minayin shetehai minchato kreiva?* — how do we know the offering continues to be brought at all? One might have assumed that since the *chavitai* belongs specifically to the *kohen gadol*, with no *kohen gadol* there is simply no obligation. The *baraita* insists otherwise, and proceeds to derive — consistent with *Rebbi Yehuda*'s position — both the fact of continuation and the identity of the payer.

### Mibnav Ya'aseh

The source for *Rebbi Yehuda* is a creative reading of the *pasuk*: *v'ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav mi-banav ya'aseh otah* — the *kohen* who is anointed in his stead, of his sons, shall make it. At the plain level, *mi-banav* indicates that one looks first to the sons of the deceased *kohen gadol* when selecting a successor. The *baraita*, however, reads *mi-banav ya'aseh otah* as a legislative statement: when the deceased *kohen gadol* is no longer present to bring the offering himself, it is *mi-banav* — from his sons, his heirs — who are responsible for funding it.

### Otah = Complete

The same *pasuk* also supplies *Rebbi Yehuda*'s source for the *mishna*'s second ruling, that the offering is brought whole. *Yachol yakrivennah chatzyim* — one might have supposed that when brought by heirs, it is still divided into two half-portions, morning and afternoon. The *pasuk* says *ya'aseh otah*: he shall make *it* — *otah*, *kullah v'lo chetzyah*, the entire offering and not half of it. These are the words of *Rebbi Yehuda*: from *mi-banav* he derives that heirs are the payers, and from *otah* he derives that they bring a complete unit.

---

## Rabbi Shimon's Chok

### Chok Olam

*Rebbi Shimon* derives his position from a different part of the same *pasuk*. The conclusion of the verse reads *chok olam l'Hashem kalil toktar* — an eternal edict for Hashem, it shall be burnt completely. *Rebbi Shimon* reads *chok olam* as *mishel olam*: the offering belongs to the world at large, to the community. This phrase simultaneously teaches that the obligation is perpetual — even without a living *kohen gadol* — and that it falls upon communal funds.

### Kalil Toktar

*Rebbi Shimon* derives from *kalil toktar* — it shall be burnt completely — that when the *tzibur* brings the offering, it must be brought as a single complete unit. *Shetehai kullah behaktarah*: all of it goes up in fire. The *tzibur* does not divide it into two halves of an *issaron*, morning and afternoon, but presents it as one whole. In this way *Rebbi Shimon* extracts from the concluding phrase of the *pasuk* both the identity of the funder (*chok olam* — the community) and the requirement of wholeness (*kalil toktar* — brought complete).

---

## Hedyot vs. Gadol

### Challenge to Yehuda

The *Gemara* now presses *Rebbi Yehuda*: how can he use *mi-banav ya'aseh otah* to derive that the heirs are responsible for funding the *korban*? We need that *pasuk* for something else entirely — namely, for what is derived in a *baraita*. The *pasuk* reads: *zeh korban Aharon u-vanav asher yakrivu l'Hashem b'yom himashach oto asirit ha-eifah solet minchah tamid machatzitah ba-boker u-machatzitah ba-erev* — this is the offering of Aharon and his sons that they shall bring before Hashem on the day he is anointed, a tenth of an *eifah* of fine flour as a perpetual *mincha*, half in the morning and half in the afternoon. The verse then continues: *v'ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav mi-banav ya'aseh otah, chok olam l'Hashem kalil toktar, v'chol minchat kohen kalil tihyeh lo teiachel* — the *kohen* anointed in his stead, of his sons, shall make it; an eternal edict for Hashem, it shall be burnt completely; and every *mincha* of a *kohen* shall be complete, it shall not be eaten.

The question is whether *Aharon u-vanav* in the opening section refers to *Aharon* and all future *kohanim* generally, or more narrowly to *Aharon* and his successors as *kohen gadol*. One might reasonably read the opening and closing sections as a single unit all describing the *kohen gadol*'s offering, since the end of the *pasuk* speaks of the anointed successor.

### Section Division

The *Gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between two sections of the *parsha*. The phrase *Aharon u-vanav* in the opening section is meant to teach something distinct from the phrase *mi-banav* in the closing section. Perhaps they are bringing the same *korban*, one could say — *yachlu yihiyu Aharon u-vanav makrivim korban echad*, maybe they together bring a single unified *korban*. No: *asher yakrivu l'Hashem* reads them in the plural, as distinct categories — *Aharon bifnei atzmo u-vanav bifnei atzmam*, Aharon in his own right and his sons in their own right, teaching that they represent different halachic categories.

The *Gemara* then raises the question: *banav eilu kohanim hedyotot* — does *banav* in the opening refer to ordinary *kohanim*, or perhaps *kohanim gedolim*? After all, the closing section explicitly describes the *kohen gadol* who succeeds Aharon; perhaps the *banav* at the beginning of the section refers only to those sons who themselves become *kohen gadol* after him. To this the *Gemara* answers: *keshehu omer v'ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav mi-banav* — since the closing section already explicitly speaks of the successor *kohen gadol*, *ha-mah ani mekayem banav eilu kohanim hedyotot* — the *banav* in the opening section must be referring to ordinary *kohanim*. The two sections are thus parsed as addressing two separate categories: the opening section (*zeh korban Aharon u-vanav*) covers a *kohen hedyot* bringing a *mincha* at the outset of his *avodah*; the closing section (*v'ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav mi-banav ya'aseh otah*) addresses the *kohen gadol*'s perpetual daily offering.

### Hedyot's First Day

Once this division is established, the *halacha* of the *kohen hedyot* comes into focus. Before a *kohen hedyot* begins his Temple service for the first time, he brings a *mincha* — a full *issaron* of *solet* — as his inaugural offering. This is the meaning of *zeh korban Aharon u-vanav asher yakrivu l'Hashem b'yom himashach oto*: on the day they are initiated into their *avodah*, each *kohen* brings this offering. Note that even the *kohen gadol* himself, when he first assumes his role, brings such a *minchat solet*. The transition to *machatzitah ba-boker u-machatzitah ba-erev* — half in the morning and half in the afternoon — then shifts attention to the *kohen gadol*'s ongoing daily obligation, the *chavitai* that continues every day, split between morning and afternoon.

### Mibnav Reconciled

This analysis, however, creates a problem for *Rebbi Yehuda*: if *mi-banav ya'aseh otah* is already needed to divide the opening and closing sections of the *parsha* — establishing that the opening *banav* speaks of *kohanim hedyotim* while the closing refers to the successor *kohen gadol* — how can *Rebbi Yehuda* simultaneously derive from *mi-banav ya'aseh otah* that the heirs fund the offering when the *kohen gadol* is deceased?

The *Gemara* resolves this: *im ken likhtov kra ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav mi-banav ya'aseh* — if the *pasuk* were only coming to tell us that the heirs bring the offering, it would have sufficed to write *v'ha-kohen ha-mashiach tachtav banav ya'aseh otah*, with *banav* alone. Why does it add the prefix *mem* and say *mi-banav*? The *mem* signals the *peshat* reading: the *kohen* who takes his place *from among* his sons — referring to the properly anointed successor. *Shma mina tarti* — we learn two things simultaneously. At the *peshat* level, *mi-banav* identifies the anointed heir who assumes the *kehunah gedolah* and thereby preserves the section division. At the *drash* level, *banav ya'aseh otah* teaches that when the *kohen gadol* is deceased, it is his sons — his heirs — who fund the bringing of the offering.

---

## Shimon's Otah

### Succession Otah

The *Gemara* now turns to the other side and asks: *Rabbi Shimon, hai otah mai avid lei?* What does *Rebbi Shimon* do with the word *otah*? For *Rebbi Yehuda*, *otah* teaches that when the heirs bring the offering, they bring it as a complete unit rather than divided into halves. But *Rebbi Shimon* does not read *mi-banav ya'aseh otah* as referring to the heirs at all — he reads it as the standard succession scenario. So what does *otah* teach *Rebbi Shimon*?

### New Kohen Full Unit

*Rebbi Shimon* applies *ya'aseh otah* to the very case the *pasuk* describes at face value: the new *kohen gadol* who is appointed after his predecessor dies. The teaching is *she-lo yavi chetzi issaron mi-beito v'lo chetzi issaron shel rishon* — the incoming *kohen gadol* should not bring merely half an *issaron* from his own home, nor should he use the remaining half-portion of the *issaron* that belonged to the first *kohen gadol*. Rather, *ya'aseh otah* — he must begin with a full *issaron*, bring it whole, and divide it himself. This is precisely what was taught the previous day: even if he is appointed only in the afternoon, the new *kohen gadol* must start with a complete *issaron* and offer his half from that whole. He cannot pick up where his predecessor left off.

### No Vav Derivation

One might ask: why does *Rebbi Shimon* need *otah* to teach this ruling? Yesterday's discussion derived the same point from the extra *vav* in *u-machatzitah* — the *vav* adding emphasis that even for a successor, the afternoon half must come from a whole. The *Gemara* answers simply: *vav lo darish* — *Rebbi Shimon* does not make *drashot* from an extra *vav*. Since he does not employ that device, he needs *otah* explicitly to convey the requirement that the new *kohen gadol* bring a full unit.

---

## Yehuda's Chok Olam

### Chok = Perpetual

The *Gemara* now asks the parallel question about *Rebbi Yehuda*: *hai chok olam mai avid lei?* What does *Rebbi Yehuda* do with *chok olam*? He does not need it to derive communal funding — he derives that from *mi-banav* — so what purpose does *chok olam* serve for him? The answer is *chukah l'olam tehei*: at its most straightforward level, *chok olam* teaches that this offering is always in force, not merely a one-time inauguration for the generation of Aharon. This is simply *peshat*: the *chavitai* is a permanent, perpetual daily obligation.

### Kalil Gzerah Shavah

That still leaves *kalil toktar* — it shall be burnt completely. For *Rebbi Shimon*, this teaches that when the *tzibur* brings the offering, it must be presented as a whole unit. But *Rebbi Yehuda* already derives the requirement of wholeness from *otah*. What then does he do with *kalil toktar*? The *Gemara* answers: *mi-baei lei l'chid'tanya* — he needs it for what is taught in a *baraita*. The *baraita* states: *ein li ella elyonah minchat kohen gadol b'kalil toktar v'tachtonah minchat kohen hedyot b'lo teiachel* — I know only that the upper offering, the *mincha* of the *kohen gadol*, must be burnt completely (*kalil toktar*), and the lower offering, the *mincha* of the *kohen hedyot*, must not be eaten (*lo teiachel*). But how do we know that the *kohen hedyot*'s *mincha* must also be fully burnt? And how do we know that there is a *lav* against eating the *kohen gadol*'s *mincha*?

### Eating Issurim

The answer is a *gzerah shavah*: *kalil kalil ligzeirah shavah* — the word *kalil* appears in the verse concerning the *kohen gadol* and also in the verse concerning the *kohen hedyot*. *Ne'emar kan kalil v'ne'emar lehallan kalil*: just as *kalil toktar* by the *kohen gadol* mandates complete burning, so too *kalil tihyeh* by the *kohen hedyot* mandates complete burning. And just as *lo teiachel* by the *kohen hedyot* creates a *lav* against eating his *mincha*, so too a *lav* applies to eating the *kohen gadol*'s *mincha* — *af kan litein lo ta'aseh al achilato*. One might wonder why *kalil* cannot simply be taken at face value to mandate burning, without requiring a *gzerah shavah*. The answer is that since the surrounding verses already state *machatzitah ba-boker u-machatzitah ba-erev*, it is already evident that the entire offering goes onto the *mizbeach*; once that is clear, the additional *kalil toktar* must be carrying out another function — and that function is to establish the *gzerah shavah* that binds the two categories of *minchat kohen* together.

---

## Seven Takkanot

### Funding Source Q

Having established how each *tanna* derives his position, the *Gemara* raises a striking challenge against *Rebbi Shimon*. His position is that the *chavitai* during the interim period is brought *mishel tzibur* from communal funds. But is this really a *d'oraita* ruling? The *Gemara* quotes *Rebbi Shimon* himself in another *mishna*: *amar Rebbi Shimon shiv'ah devarim hitkinu beit din v'zeh echad mehem* — there were seven things that *beit din* enacted, and the communal funding of the *kohen gadol*'s *mincha* is one of them. If it is a rabbinic *takkanah*, how can the *Gemara* have been treating it as Torah-derived?

### Takkanot List

*Rebbi Shimon* presents a cluster of *takkanot* of a similar genre, all involving the use of communal funds to cover the *minchat nesachim* or the *mincha* itself in cases where the individual responsible cannot or does not provide them. These are not arbitrary extensions of communal obligation but responses to specific practical gaps that arose in the operation of Temple service.

### Found Animals

The first case mentioned just before our passage involves animals found near Yerushalayim within certain designated areas. Such animals are presumptively *shlamim*, and whoever discovers them is obligated to bring them to the *Beis HaMikdash* along with funding for the *minchat nesachim* that accompanies the offering. When people began declining to bother with this obligation — simply not returning the animals — the *takkanah* was instituted that the animal should be brought and the communal funds would cover the *nesachim*, removing the burden from the finder.

### Non-Jew Olah

A second case: a non-Jew who sends an *olah* offering from overseas. Non-Jews may send *korbanot* to be brought in the *Beis HaMikdash*. If he sent along sufficient funds for the *minchat nesachim* that accompanies the offering — *shalach imah nesachim* — those funds are used. *V'im lav kreivin mishel tzibur*: if he did not, the community provides. It is not feasible to send word back overseas demanding the additional funds; communal resources fill the gap.

### Ger's Sacrifices

A third case: a *ger* who dies leaving behind *korbanot* but no heirs. This can happen when a convert has no blood relatives remaining after conversion. If he left funds designated for *nesachim*, those are used; if not — *v'im lav kreivin mishel tzibur*. The *Gemara* adds: *v'tena'i beis din hu* — this is a condition of the court. When communal funds are collected annually, the court has standing discretion over their application, and covering *nesachim* in such cases is one of the purposes to which those funds may legitimately be directed.

### Kohen Gadol Death

The fourth case is our own: *Kohen Gadol shemeis v'lo minu Kohen acher tachtav* — the *kohen gadol* dies and no replacement is immediately appointed. *Shtei minchosav kreivos mishel tzibur* — both of his *minchos* are brought from communal funds. This parallels the previous cases structurally: a *mincha* must be brought, the individual responsible is absent, and communal funds fill the obligation. The language of *takkanah* here seems to imply a rabbinic enactment, which sits in tension with the *Gemara*'s earlier analysis treating communal funding as Torah-derived.

---

## Two-Stage Theory

### De'oraita Source

*Rabbi Abbahu* resolves the tension: *shtei takkanos havo* — there were not one but two stages to this arrangement. The starting point is *de'oraisa mishel tzibur*: the Torah itself establishes that in the absence of a *kohen gadol*, the *chavitai* is brought from communal funds. This is what the *Gemara* derived earlier from *chok olam* and the surrounding *psukim*. The rabbinic *takkanah* comes later, responding to a practical problem.

### Burden Relief

The difficulty was that during the period of the second *Beis HaMikdash*, *kohanim gedolim* were being replaced with troubling frequency — sometimes annually — which meant that extended periods without an appointed *kohen gadol* were recurrent. The communal fund was being drained: *keivan d'chazu d'ka midchaka lishka*, they saw that the *lishka*, the communal treasury, was being pressed hard.

### Heirs Pay

In response, the first *takkanah* was enacted: *tiknu d'ligavei miyorshin* — they established that the heirs of the deceased *kohen gadol* would bear the cost. The heirs would transfer funds to the *tzibur*, but the financial burden shifted away from communal resources onto the estate of the deceased. This is the ruling of *Rebbi Yehuda*: the heirs pay.

### Heirs Default

The arrangement did not hold. *Keivan d'chazu d'ka pash'ei bah* — they saw that the heirs were being negligent in fulfilling this obligation. *Ukma ade'oraisa* — they restored the original Torah rule. What *Rebbi Shimon* calls a *takkanah*, then, is in fact a *takkanah* to revert to the *de'oraita*: the second rabbinic enactment undid the first and reinstated communal funding as the Torah had originally mandated. The word *takkanah* in *Rebbi Shimon*'s list thus refers to this second-stage restoration, not a novel rabbinic creation.

---

## Red Heifer Parallel

### Ashes No Me'ilah

The *mishna* of *Rebbi Shimon*'s seven *takkanot* includes another item of this same structure: *v'al parah shelo yehei mo'alin be'afrah* — the ashes of the *parah adumah* are not subject to *me'ilah*. If someone uses those ashes for personal benefit, there is no transgression of *me'ilah*. This, says the *mishna*, is also among the seven things enacted by *beit din*.

### Chatas Derivation

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this framing: *de'oraisa hi* — this is a Torah law, not a rabbinic enactment. The proof is from a *baraita*: *chatas hi* — the *parah adumah* is called a *chatas*, and this teaches *shemo'alin bah*, that there is *me'ilah* while the *parah* is still intact as an offering. But the verse specifies: *bah mo'alin, be'afrah ein mo'alin* — the *me'ilah* applies to *it*, the *parah* itself; it does not apply to *its ashes*. The exemption of the ashes from *me'ilah* is thus a Torah ruling. How then does *Rebbi Shimon* describe it as a *takkanah*?

### Ashes Misused

*Rav Ashi* applies the same two-stage analysis: *shtei takkanos havo* — there were two stages here as well. The Torah baseline is clear: *de'oraisa bah mo'alin be'afrah ein mo'alin* — by Torah law, one is liable for *me'ilah* on the *parah* itself but not on its ashes. The problem arose when *keivan d'chazu d'ka mezalzeli bah* — they saw that people were treating the ashes disrespectfully. Specifically, *veka'avdi minah lemachtan* — they were using the ashes to apply to their wounds, as ashes were considered medicinally beneficial. This is a striking detail: the ashes of the *parah adumah* were extraordinarily precious and presumably guarded carefully, yet somehow the ruling that ashes carry no *me'ilah* led to their being treated as ordinary material.

### Rabbinic Me'ilah

In response, *gazru bah me'ilah* — the Sages decreed rabbinic *me'ilah* on the ashes. Using them for personal benefit would now constitute a rabbinic transgression, even though Torah law exempts the ashes. This was the first *takkanah*.

### Purification Reluctance

The decree, however, created an unintended consequence. *Keivan d'chazu d'ka parshi misafek haza'os* — they saw that people were avoiding the sprinkling of the *parah adumah* ashes even when it was genuinely needed for purification. The reasoning was: if I am uncertain whether I incurred *tumas meis* — corpse impurity — and I am not entirely sure I need the purification, then being sprinkled would mean benefiting from the ashes under doubtful circumstances, risking a *me'ilah* violation. This fear caused people to forgo the *taharah* process when they should have undergone it.

### Back to Torah

*Ukma ade'oraisa* — they reverted to the Torah rule: no *me'ilah* on the ashes. The second *takkanah* undid the first, restoring the original *de'oraita* position. As with the *kohen gadol*'s *mincha*, the *takkanah* listed by *Rebbi Shimon* refers to this second-stage restoration. Both cases follow an identical three-part pattern: the Torah establishes the base rule; a rabbinic *takkanah* modifies it in response to misuse; a second *takkanah* reverts to the Torah rule when the modification produces worse results than the original problem. The *mishna*'s designation of both as *takkanot* refers to the final enactment — the restoration — rather than an original rabbinic innovation.

---

---

# Menachot 52

## Par He'elam Davar

### Funding Debate

Today's daf is Menachot 52, and with it we complete the *perek*. We pick up five lines from the top, beginning with a *tanu rabbanan*. The preceding discussion has centered on the debate between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the *minchat chavitin* of the *kohen gadol* when no *kohen gadol* exists — specifically, whether the *mincha* is funded by the heirs or by communal funds. The Gemara now extends this general question to a related set of communal sacrifices.

*Tanu rabbanan*: the *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* and the *seirei avodah zarah*. The *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* is the communal *chatas* brought when the *Beis Din HaGadol* ruled incorrectly and the majority of *Am Yisrael* followed that ruling — the subject of Masechet Horayos. The *seirei avodah zarah* refers to the case where the community collectively sinned in the realm of *avodah zarah*. The question is: from where does the funding for these communal sacrifices come?

Rabbi Yehuda says *b'techilah magbin lahen* — one conducts a special collection for them. The reasoning is intuitive: the entire *tzibur* sinned, and there is a certain appropriateness in having each member consciously contribute, so that the community is not entirely oblivious to the *korban* being brought on their behalf. Rabbi Shimon says *mitrumas halishkah hein ba'in* — they come from the regular communal funds drawn upon each year.

### Conflicting Braitot

The Gemara immediately raises a complication: *ha'tanya ipcha* — there is a *braisa* that records Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon holding the reverse positions. Rather than simply declaring one *braisa* erroneous, the Gemara attempts to determine which version reflects the later, authoritative ruling. *Hai mineihu achrita?* — which one is the reliable final position?

### Rav Ashi's Resolution

The rabbis before Rav Ashi suggested that the first version we cited — where Rabbi Shimon says the sacrifices come from communal funds — should be regarded as the authoritative latter position. Their reasoning: *d'shameinan lei l'Rabbi Shimon d'chayish l'pshia* — we know that Rabbi Shimon is concerned about negligence. As discussed on the preceding daf, Rabbi Shimon observed that the heirs were neglecting the *kohen gadol*'s *mincha* and therefore moved it back to the *de'oraisa* arrangement of communal funding. That demonstrated concern for negligence aligns well with his position here, where he insists on drawing from existing communal funds rather than relying on a new ad hoc collection that people might fail to contribute to adequately.

Rav Ashi, however, responds that one can even say the second *braisa* is the authoritative one — meaning that in the context of the *par he'elam davar shel tzibur*, Rabbi Shimon would actually be comfortable with a special collection. Why the distinction? *Ki kachayish Rabbi Shimon l'pshia b'milsa d'leisa beh kapara b'gavah* — Rabbi Shimon is concerned about negligence only in a case where there is no personal atonement at stake for the parties responsible for funding. The heirs of a deceased *kohen gadol* bear an obligation but derive no personal atonement from fulfilling it; left to their own devices, they may shirk it. But *b'milsa d'is beh kapara b'gavah* — in a case like the *par he'elam davar* or *seirei avodah zarah*, where the entire community that sinned must contribute toward their own atonement, the personal stake involved means Rabbi Shimon is not concerned they will be negligent. This distinction also has the character of a one-time event rather than a recurring obligation, which further reduces the concern.

### Textual Proof

The Gemara then asks *mai havah alah* — what is the conclusion? Rav Zuta said to Rav Ashi: come and hear. The verse concerning the *tamid* reads: *es korbani lachmi l'ishai rei'ach nichochi tishmeru l'hakriv li b'mo'ado* — "My offering, My bread for My fire-offering, a pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to bring to Me in its appointed time." The extra language *es lachmi l'ishai* comes to include the *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* and the *seirei avodah zarah*, indicating that just as the *tamid* comes from *trumas halishkah*, so too do these sacrifices — and this is the position of Rabbi Shimon.

This establishes consistency: Rabbi Shimon in our *Mishnah* rules that the *minchat chavitin* of the *kohen gadol* comes from communal funds when no *kohen gadol* has been appointed, and here too, Rabbi Shimon derives from a *pasuk* that the *par he'elam davar* and *seirei avodah zarah* come from the same communal funds. It may be that this ruling has nothing to do with the concern for negligence at all and is simply *pasuk*-based — which would explain why the *braisa* presenting this as Rabbi Shimon's authoritative position should be preferred. The conclusion is thus that it is Rabbi Yehuda who requires a special collection for these sacrifices, while Rabbi Shimon holds they are funded from the regular *trumas halishkah*.

---

## Mincha When No Kohen Gad…

### Two Halves or Whole

Returning to our *Mishnah*, which established that when there is no *kohen gadol* the *mincha* is brought as a complete, undivided unit (*ushlema tikrav*), Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that this raises an obvious question: *shlema shacharis ushlema bein ha'arbaim o dilma shlema shacharis u-vetela bein ha'arbaim* — are you bringing a full *issaron* in the morning and a full *issaron* in the afternoon, or are you bringing one full *issaron* only in the morning and nothing in the afternoon? Under normal circumstances, one *issaron* is divided into two halves, one offered each time. The question is whether, when the circumstance changes and the offering must be complete and undivided, you bring two complete offerings — one at each of the two daily intervals — or consolidate into a single complete offering in the morning alone.

### Rava's Proof

Rava proposed a proof. The *Mishnah* describing the division of labor among the *kohanim* in the daily *avodah* states that the eighth *kohen* brings the afternoon *chavitin* of the *kohen gadol*. This *chavitin* was brought between the components of the afternoon *tamid*. Now, Rava reasons: *v'i issa de-vatela bein ha'arbaim* — if it were ever the case that there is no afternoon *chavitin* to bring, such as when there is no *kohen gadol* and the morning offering is the only one, then *hazimnin d'lo mashkachas la shmini b'chavitin* — sometimes the *Mishnah*'s designation of "the eighth brings the *chavitin*" would be inapplicable. The *Mishnah* assumes there will always be afternoon *chavitin*, which implies that even without a *kohen gadol*, a full *issaron* is brought in the morning and a full *issaron* in the afternoon.

### Standard vs. Aberration

The rabbis reported Rava's argument to Rabbi Yirmiyah in Eretz Yisrael. His reaction was sharp: *Bavla'ei tipshai* — "Those foolish Babylonians, because they dwell in a dark land they say dark ideas." The proof, he insisted, proves nothing. The *Mishnah* lists that the seventh *kohen* brings the *mincha* of the afternoon *tamid*, the eighth brings the *chavitin* of the *kohen gadol*, and the ninth brings the wine of the afternoon *tamid*. Does that mean those offerings can never fail to appear? We know explicitly that *minchasam v'niskaihem balaila minchasam v'niskaihem afilu l'machar* — the *menachos* and *nesachim* of a *korban* remain valid if brought that night or even the following day, meaning that on some days the afternoon *tamid* might not have its *mincha* and wine accompanying it in real time. The fact that the *Mishnah* assigns these tasks to specific *kohanim* does not mean it is impossible for them not to occur. *Ela de'i lo katani* — the *Mishnah* is teaching standard operating procedure.
