It does not trouble itself with exceptional, aberrant scenarios. Therefore, the fact that the *Mishnah* assumes afternoon *chavitin* tells us nothing about what happens in the anomalous case where there is no *kohen gadol*.

The rabbis returned to Rava and relayed Rabbi Yirmiyah's objection, including his caustic remark. Rava responded with characteristic sharpness: *mibishutan amri kamaihu mitivutan lo amri kamaihu* — "They report my weak ideas before him but do not report my good ones." The bad news travels; the brilliant teachings of Bavel go unreported, leaving Rabbi Yirmiyah with a distorted impression. But Rava then said *hanei nami tivutan havu* — "You know what? Even this position is one of my good teachings." The conclusion he drew, he maintains, is correct. He simply acknowledges that the proof from the *Mishnah* was not valid — and Rabbi Yirmiyah was right to dismiss it.

### Tamid Proof

Rava now offered a different proof entirely. The verse concerning the *chavitin* reads *solet mincha tamid* — "flour, a *mincha*, *tamid*." This tells us the *chavitin* is to be treated like the *minchat tmidim*, the *mincha* brought with the daily *tamid*. Just as the *tamid* is always brought once in the morning and once in the afternoon, so too the *chavitin* must always have a morning component and an afternoon component. Consequently, when there is no *kohen gadol* and the offering must be brought whole, you bring a full *issaron* in the morning and a full *issaron* in the afternoon, mirroring the structure of the *tamid* — half-and-half when a *kohen gadol* is present, full-and-full when none exists.

### Baraita Resolution

The Gemara asks *mai havya alah* — what is the final ruling? Rav Natan bar Yitzchak says: come and hear — there is a *braisa*: *shlema shacharis u'shlema bein ha'arbayim*, a full *issaron* in the morning and a full *issaron* in the afternoon. This resolves the question in accordance with Rava's position.

---

## Levonah Debate

### Two Full Handfuls

Having established that when there is no *kohen gadol* a full *issaron* is brought morning and afternoon, the Gemara steps back to examine certain details of the *minchat chavitin* as it is normally brought when a *kohen gadol* is present. Rabbi Yochanan states that a dispute between Abba Yossi ben Dostai and the rabbis addresses the following question. The standard *minchat chavitin* consists of one *issaron* divided into two halves, offered morning and afternoon. Each portion of a *mincha* normally requires *levonah* — frankincense — in the amount of a *kometz* (a handful), with the exception of the *minchat chote*. How much *levonah* is brought for the *chavitin*?

Abba Yossi ben Dostai says *mafrish lah shnei kmatzim* — two full handfuls of *levonah*, one in the morning and one in the afternoon: *kometz shacharis v'kometz bein ha'arbayim*. Even though the morning and afternoon portions each represent only half an *issaron*, each receives a complete *kometz* of *levonah*.

### One Handful Divided

The rabbis disagree: *mafrish lah kometz echad* — only one *kometz* of *levonah* in total, divided in half: *chatzi kometz shacharis v'chatzi kometz bein ha'arbayim*. Just as the single *issaron* is split into two offerings, so too the single *kometz* of *levonah* is split between morning and afternoon.

### Never a Half-Handful

What is the root of this disagreement? Abba Yossi ben Dostai reasons: *lo ashkechan chatzi kometz d'kariv* — we have never found a precedent for offering a half-handful of *levonah* on the *mizbeach*. Yes, it is already a *chiddush* to offer half an *issaron* of flour as a distinct *mincha*. But we should not extend one *chiddush* further than necessary. If *levonah* is to be offered at all, it must be brought in the normal minimum unit — a full *kometz*. Accordingly, each half-offering receives a full *kometz*.

The rabbis counter: *lo ashkechan issaron d'va'ei shnei kmatzin* — we have never found that a single *issaron* of a *mincha* requires two *kmatzim* of *levonah*. The natural proportion is one *kometz* per *issaron*. Since the offering is one *issaron* divided into two, the *levonah* follows the same division. That reasoning strikes most as more internally consistent — but the debate stands.

---

## Doubling Proportions

### Doubling Levonah?

Rabbi Yochanan now asks a derivative question that flows from the positions just articulated. In the scenario where the *kohen gadol* has died and no substitute has been appointed, we have established that a full *issaron* is brought in the morning and a full *issaron* in the afternoon. The question is posed specifically for the rabbis, whose position in the normal case is a *chatzi kometz* of *levonah* morning and afternoon. Now that the flour has doubled, does the *levonah* double as well?

The question can be framed two ways. On one hand: *mitoch shehuchpela solto huchpela levonato* — since the flour has been doubled, the *levonah* should be doubled proportionally, which would bring us to a full *kometz* per offering. This is appealing both because it maintains consistent proportions and because a full *kometz* is the natural, standard quantity. On the other hand: *mai degali gali mai delo gali lo gali* — the Torah introduced a *chiddush* specifically regarding the flour, doubling it in this circumstance. That *chiddush* is confined to what was explicitly stated. The *levonah* was not mentioned; it therefore remains as it was, a *chatzi kometz* each time, even though the flour has now doubled.

The question is not asked regarding Abba Yossi ben Dostai, for whom the *levonah* is already a full *kometz* in the normal case. If the flour doubles, one might think to also double the *levonah* and produce two *kmatzim* per session, but that would yield the highly unusual quantity of two full handfuls of *levonah* per offering — a sufficiently strange outcome that we might simply say for Abba Yossi ben Dostai the *levonah* remains stable at one *kometz* per half. But the question for the rabbis is genuine.

### Doubling Oil?

A second question follows. Regardless of which position one holds regarding *levonah*, there is a separate question about the oil. When the *kohen gadol* was present, the offering consisted of one *issaron* of flour with three *lugin* of oil, divided in half: one and a half *lugin* with the morning half and one and a half *lugin* with the afternoon half. This preserves a ratio of one *issaron* to three *lugin*. Now that there is no *kohen gadol* and a full *issaron* is offered each session, does the oil also double to three *lugin* per session — maintaining the ratio — or does it remain at one and a half *lugin* per session even though the flour has doubled?

This question applies to both Abba Yossi ben Dostai and the rabbis alike. Their debate concerned the *levonah*; neither of them addressed the oil in their dispute. Yet the same structural tension applies: do we maintain proportionality and double the oil, or do we treat the doubling of flour as a discrete *chiddush* that does not extend to the accompanying amounts?

### Five Handfuls Proof

Rava attempts a proof. A *Mishnah* later in the tractate teaches that there are five instances of a *kometz* in the *Beis Hamikdash* — the *kometz* of *levonah* from a *mincha*, the *kometz* of a *mincha* itself, and so on. Notably absent from that enumeration is the *kometz* of *levonah* accompanying the *chavitin* of the *kohen gadol*. In a standard situation, the *levonah* of the *chavitin* comes in halves — *chatzi kometz* each time — and the *Mishnah* speaks only of whole *kmatzim*, so the normal *chavitin* is naturally excluded. But, Rava argues, *v'i isa* — if it were true that when there is no *kohen gadol* you bring a full *kometz* of *levonah* in the morning and a full *kometz* in the afternoon according to the rabbis, then *zimnin d'mashkachat lei shiva* — sometimes you would have seven *kmatzim* (the standard five, plus two for the *chavitin* morning and afternoon). The fact that the *Mishnah* never mentions seven *kmatzim* indicates that even when there is no *kohen gadol* and the flour is doubled, the *levonah* is not doubled — it remains at *chatzi kometz* morning and afternoon in accordance with the rabbis' position.

### Aberration Counter

Rav Pappa sat and contemplated this argument. Rav Yosef bar Shmaya raised an objection: *veha ma'aleh kometz bachutz* — the *Mishnah* listing five *kmatzim* also includes the case of one who takes a *kometz* of a *mincha* and offers it *outside* the *Beis Hamikdash*, making him liable for *ha'alas chutz*. That is manifestly not standard operating procedure — it is an aberrant, prohibited act. Yet the *Mishnah* includes it in its enumeration. This would suggest that the *Mishnah* is not limited to normal cases; it catalogues all instances of a *kometz*, including anomalous ones. If so, the fact that seven *kmatzim* are never mentioned cannot be used to prove that the doubled *chavitin* does not yield two additional full *kmatzim* — the *Mishnah* would have included even that aberrant case if it were applicable.

This objection is compelling, and the Gemara does not reject it outright. The matter therefore remains unresolved through that proof alone.

---

## Oil/Levonah Stability

### Baraita Teaching

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the entire cluster of questions by citing a *braisa*. The *braisa* states regarding a *kohen gadol* who died without a successor: *sheleima shacharis v'sheleima bein ha'arbayim* — a full measure of flour in the morning and a full measure in the afternoon, as already established. *U-mafrisha bei kmatzim* — two *kmatzim* of *levonah*, a *kometz* in the morning and a *kometz* in the afternoon. *U-mafrisha shlosha lugin* — and three *lugin* of oil in total, *log vachetzi shacharis v'log vachetzi bein ha'arbayim* — one and a half in the morning and one and a half in the afternoon.

The picture is now clear: the flour doubles (a full *issaron* each session), two *kmatzim* of *levonah* are brought (one per session), and the oil remains at one and a half *lugin* per session rather than doubling to three.

### Abba Yossi Ben Dostai

The Gemara asks: *mani* — whose position does this *braisa* follow? If we say it reflects the opinion of the rabbis, a problem immediately arises. The rabbis hold that in a normal case the *levonah* is *chatzi kometz* each time. But this *braisa* says two full *kmatzim* are brought when there is no *kohen gadol*. That would mean the *levonah* doubled while the oil did not — *mai shna levonah d'huchpela mai shna shemen d'lo huchpela*. Why would we double the *levonah* to restore it to a full *kometz*, when we would not double the oil to restore it to three *lugin*? A log and a half is not a standard meaningful measurement in the same way a full *kometz* is. There is no coherent basis for treating *levonah* and oil differently in this respect. Therefore the *braisa* cannot reflect the rabbis' position.

Rather, the *braisa* must follow Abba Yossi ben Dostai, who holds that even in a normal situation the *chavitin* requires a full *kometz* of *levonah* morning and afternoon. For Abba Yossi ben Dostai, the two *kmatzim* of *levonah* in this *braisa* are not a doubling — they are exactly what would have been brought even when the *kohen gadol* was alive. The *levonah* is stable, not doubled. And similarly, the oil is stable at one and a half *lugin* per session.

### Parallel Inference

This analysis yields an important inference for the rabbis as well. *Hash'ta d'amar Abba Yossi ben Dostai v'levonah lo huchpala v'shemen lo huchpal* — since we see that for Abba Yossi ben Dostai, when the flour doubles, both the *levonah* and the oil remain stable, we can conclude that the same principle applies for the rabbis: *levonah v'shmanah l'rabbanan nami lo huchpalu* — both the *levonah* and the oil do not increase. The only question between Abba Yossi ben Dostai and the rabbis is the baseline amount of *levonah* brought in a normal situation with a living *kohen gadol*. But the structural rule — that doubling the flour does not lead to doubling the *levonah* or the oil — is common ground. For the rabbis, therefore, when there is no *kohen gadol*, the *levonah* remains *chatzi kometz* each session and the oil remains one and a half *lugin* each session.

### Final Ruling

Rabbi Yochanan rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Yosi ben Dustai* — the *halacha* follows Abba Yossi ben Dostai that a full *kometz* of *levonah* is brought each session. Tosafot notes the obvious question: *teima hilchata lemashiach?* — are we rendering a practical *halachic* ruling for the era of *Mashiach*, when the Temple will be restored? The question of the *chavitin* is an entirely theoretical exercise in our current reality. Yet the Gemara states the ruling, and Tosafot flags the peculiarity of doing so.

### Objection/Resolution

A further difficulty is raised: *u'mi amar Rabbi Yochanan hachi?* — did Rabbi Yochanan really rule this way? Rabbi Yochanan himself is known for the principle that *halacha k'stam Mishna* — we rule in accordance with an unattributed *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* listing five *kmatzim* — which, as discussed, must reflect the position of the rabbis rather than Abba Yossi ben Dostai, since for him the *chavitin* would generate more than five — is an unattributed *Mishnah*. How then can Rabbi Yochanan rule against it?

The Gemara resolves this with the observation that *Amoraim ninhu aliba d'Rabbi Yochanan* — there is in fact a dispute among *Amoraim* as to what Rabbi Yochanan himself held. One *Amora* attributes to Rabbi Yochanan the principle that we always follow the *stam Mishna*, which would point to the rabbis' position. The other *Amora*, who attributes to Rabbi Yochanan the ruling like Abba Yossi ben Dostai, must hold that Rabbi Yochanan did not apply the *stam Mishna* principle universally or without exception. Both attributions exist, and the Gemara records them without definitively adjudicating between them.

With this, we conclude the *perek*. *Hadran alach hatchelet*.

---

---

# Menachot 53

## All Menachot - Matzah

### Chapter Overview

We begin at the bottom of 52b with a new *perek* called *Hamenachot*. The previous two *prakim*, though we spent a wonderful time dealing with *tallis*, *tzitzis*, and *tefillin*, were structured around the theme of *ma'akvin zeh et zeh* — things that prevent one another from being *yotzei*. The preceding *perek* concluded with discussions about the *chavitei Kohen Gadol*, the daily *korban* that the *Kohen Gadol* would bring — half in the morning, half in the afternoon — and also discussions about which *korbanot* are *ma'akev zeh et zeh*.

Now there is a major shift. We are no longer discussing *ma'akvin zeh et zeh*. In a manner similar to Zevachim, where after working through five or six *prakim* one finally arrives at the beginning of the conversation about how to actually bring a *korban*, so too here we now begin discussing the rules governing how a *mincha* is actually made. Having worked through all the things that can invalidate and all the *ma'akvin*, we arrive at what might have been the beginning of the entire *masechta*.

### Matzah Rule & Exceptions

The *Mishnah* opens: *kol hamenachot ba'ot matzah* — all *menachot* must come as *matzah*. The *Torah* explicitly states *lo te'afeh chametz*, you may not make them *chametz*; you must bring them *matzah*, and this is stated openly in the *pesukim*. The only exceptions are the forty loaves accompanying a *todah* — ten of which are *chametz* — and the *shtei halechem*, the two loaves brought with the lambs of *Atzeret* on *Shavuot*, about which the *Torah* states that they come *chametz*.

Notably, the bread accompanying the *Nazir*'s sacrifice — some of which is also *chametz* — is not mentioned here, though it arose in the previous *perek*.

### Exceptions - Not Burned

Despite being *chametz*, those loaves that come as exceptions are never placed on the *mizbe'ach*. The *Torah* states clearly: *ki kol se'or vechol devash lo taktiru mimenu isheh l'Hashem* — any leaven or honey shall not be offered as a fire-offering to God — and thus *al hamizbe'ach lo ya'alu l'rei'ach nichoach*. In the case of the *todah*, one slaughters it and sprinkles its blood; in the case of the *shtei halechem*, the two lambs are slaughtered and their blood is sprinkled. No *kmitzah* is ever performed on the loaves themselves to place anything on the *mizbe'ach*. In this way these loaves differ from a standard *mincha*, where either the *kometz* — for a normal *mincha* — or the entire offering — for a *minchat kohanim* — is burned.

*Tosafot* is bothered by the inclusion of the *lachmei todah* in this *Mishnah*, since the *Torah* does not itself call those loaves a *mincha*. The *Torah* does apply the term *mincha* to the *shtei halechem* and to the *minchat nesachim*, so the mere fact of accompanying another offering would not alone be a reason to exclude it from the *mincha* category. Yet the *lachmei todah* are not directly called *mincha*. *Tosafot* is left somewhat troubled by this, and there is no straightforward resolution offered as to why the loaves of the *Nazir* similarly go unmentioned.

---

## Making Chametz - R. Meir

Having established that certain loaves must come *chametz*, the *Mishnah* now discusses how one actually produces *chametz* for those loaves. It is worth pausing to appreciate the novelty: we spend an entire holiday figuring out how to prevent things from becoming *chametz*, and here we discuss how to deliberately make *chametz*. Notably, no opinion suggests simply waiting for the dough to rise on its own; all assume that some form of *se'or* — sourdough — is required to produce the fermentation.

*Rebbe Meir* says: *hase'or boded lahem mitochen* — you take *se'or* from the middle of what you are making. One has the flour, adds water to make the *isah*, takes a piece of it from the middle, allows it to ferment and become sourdough in a damp environment, and then returns it to the mixture. Since this process takes time, one would naturally not do this in *klei shares*, which would render the offering *pasul* due to *linah*.

*Rabbi Yehuda* objects: *af hi einah min hamuvchar* — that method is not ideal. Good sourdough is sourdough that has been fermenting for a long time, handed down and continuously maintained, not quickly produced from the middle of one's own dough. *Rabbi Yehuda* therefore says: *meivi es hase'or* — bring sourdough from home, *venosno lesoch hamidah* — place it in the measuring vessel, and then *umemale es hamidah* — fill the remainder of the vessel with flour to the required measure.

---

## Measuring Issues

The *Chachamim* respond to *Rabbi Yehuda*: *af hi haysah chaseirah o yeseirah* — even this method will result in an inaccurate measure of flour; it will either be too much or too little.

The reason, as Rashi explains, is that sourdough is denser than flour. Sourdough is flour plus water, and when flour is mixed with water and fermented, it can become either more or less dense than plain flour. Consider the case where the sourdough is denser than flour: the quantity of flour that went into producing that sourdough would, had it remained flour, occupy more volume. When the dense sourdough is placed in the measuring vessel and the rest is filled with plain flour, one ends up with more flour than intended, because the flour that went into making the sourdough is taking up less space than it would have occupied as loose flour. Conversely, if the sourdough is less dense than flour, the result would be too little flour.

---

## Flour Measurement Basis

All of this rests on an important principle that the *Gemara* states explicitly: the measurement of flour for a *mincha* is determined by the amount of flour that went into it, not by the current volume of whatever one has in front of one. When the *Torah* says *issaron soles*, it means the quantity of flour that went into the preparation, not the current measure once it has been combined with water and made into dough.

This leads to broader and interesting discussions about how *shiurim* are determined generally — especially in the context of *chametz* on *Pesach* and *matzah*. The question of how to measure a *kezayis* of something like a cookie or *challah* is well known: does one measure the item as it is, with all its air pockets, or does one determine the flour that went into it? Or does one compress it to remove the air pockets?

---

## Tosafot - Measuring

Before turning to the *Gemara*, attention should be directed to *Tosafot* on the words *chaseirah o yeseirah*, the third *Tosafot* in the section. *Tosafot* cites *Rabbeinu Chaim*, who derives from here a rule about how flour is measured when there is a need to determine *shiurim* on *Pesach* — either for the purpose of *challah*, that is, determining whether one has sufficient dough to be obligated in the separation of *challah*, or for the purpose of *matzah*. *Tosafot* rules: *ein lehachbid al hasolet* — one does not compress the flour.

The reasoning follows directly from the logic of the *Mishnah*: if sourdough can be denser than flour, it must be the case that flour is measured as it naturally settles, without compression. For if flour were compressed when measured — eliminating all air pockets — it would be impossible for sourdough to be denser than the flour, since sourdough contains additional ingredients beyond plain flour. The fact that the *Gemara* entertains the possibility that sourdough is denser than flour proves that flour must be measured in its natural, uncompressed state.

*Rabbeinu Chaim* applies this to *challah* — that is, determining the *shiur* obligating one to separate *challah* — and to *matzah*. With respect to *matzah*, he appears to be referring to the *minhag* of using a measure equivalent to an *issaron* or similar *korban*-based measure to bake the three *matzos* used for the *mitzvah* at the Seder, which would directly parallel what was done for a *mincha*. In any case, already in these early sources we encounter the question of whether *shiurim* are measured by volume of flour, by current volume, or by compressed volume — a question with profound practical implications for how much *matzah* one must eat and for *beracha* obligations.

---

## Source for Matzah

The *Gemara* now opens with a question from *Rav Preida* to *Rav Ami*: *minalan de'chol menachot ba'ot matzah* — from where do we know that all *menachot* must come as *matzah*?

*Rav Ami* responds that the answer seems simple: for some *menachot*, the *Torah* explicitly states that they must be *matzah*. For those where the *Torah* does not explicitly state this, the *Torah* states at the opening of *Tzav* — *Zot torat hamincha* — this is the law of the *mincha*, followed by the verse that the remainder *matzot te'achel*, shall be eaten as *matzah*. Since it cannot be eaten as *matzah* if it was not baked as *matzah*, and since this is the stated law of the *mincha*, we derive that all *menachot* must be *matzah*.

*Rav Preida* replies: *mitzvah lo ka'mivaya li* — that it is a *mitzvah* to do it is not my question; I know those *pesukim* too. *Ki ka'mivaya li l'akev* — what I want to know is how we derive that if a *mincha* is not made as *matzah*, it is invalid. The general principle by *kodashim* is that the *Torah* must repeat something to indicate that failure to observe it invalidates the offering. One might have thought this principle should not apply here — after all, a *mincha* is a manufactured object. When the *Torah* specifies that it must be *matzah*, it seems to be defining the object itself, not merely prescribing a ritual detail. Just as the requirement that an *olah* be male defines what kind of animal we are speaking about, so too the *matzah* requirement might be understood as defining the type of object that constitutes a valid *mincha*, such that a *chametz* version simply is not the object. Yet the *Gemara* treats it as requiring a repeated source, as it does for other requirements.

*Rav Ami* responds: *va-akev nami ketiv* — you also have a *pasuk* that tells you failure renders it invalid. The *Torah* says *lo te'afeh chametz* — do not bake it as *chametz*. Paired with *matzot te'achel*, you have both a positive and a negative commandment repeating the same requirement, which suffices to establish *ikuv*.

---

## Chametz Nuksheh

*Rav Chisda* challenges this answer: *ve'eima lo te'afeh chametz ella se'or* — the conclusion does not follow. The *Torah* says do not make it *chametz*, but *chametz* and *matzah* are not exhaustive opposites. There is a middle space between them.

*Se'or* — which in this context the *Gemara* identifies with what is called *chametz nuksheh* elsewhere — is a substance that has begun to ferment but has not fully fermented. It is neither *chametz* nor *matzah*. How do we know that bringing a *mincha* in this quasi-fermented state is invalid? I may be violating the requirement to bring it as *matzah*, but that was stated only once. And I am not violating the prohibition against bringing *chametz*, because this is not real *chametz*. Therefore, since neither *pasuk* addresses this middle category twice, perhaps *bedi'avad* such a *mincha* is valid.

---

## R. Meir vs. R. Yehuda

The *Gemara* then asks: whose *se'or* are we discussing — *Rabbi Meir*'s or *Rabbi Yehuda*'s? This refers to a well-known dispute in *Pesachim* regarding when dough reaches the problematic intermediate stage during *Pesach*.

When dough is left alone, fermentation begins. The external surface first develops a hardened crust — *hichsifu paneha*. At a later stage, cracks begin appearing in that crust, described by the *Gemara* as resembling a spider's web or the horns of a locust.

*Rabbi Meir* is strict: once the crust forms, the dough has already entered the intermediate category and is *chametz nuksheh*. There is a special *pasuk* — *kol machmetzet lo tochelu* — that includes this quasi-*chametz*, and one who eats it on *Pesach* would receive *malkut*. Once the cracks appear, it is full *chametz* and one would receive *karet*. *Rabbi Meir* thus holds that the middle category of *chametz nuksheh* exists and begins at the crusting stage.

*Rabbi Yehuda* is lenient in both directions. He holds that the only relevant stage is the cracking, not the crusting. Moreover, even at that stage, he is not certain there is a *Torah* problem — one would not even receive *malkut*. *Rabbi Yehuda* may thus effectively deny the existence of any *Torah*-level middle category.

The *Gemara* works through the permutations: if the *se'or* in question is *Rabbi Meir*'s stage — the crusting — then from *Rabbi Yehuda*'s perspective it is *matzah me'alya*, perfectly good *matzah*, so there is no middle category to worry about. If it is *Rabbi Yehuda*'s stage — the cracking — then from *Rabbi Meir*'s perspective it is *chametz me'alya*, full *chametz*, and similarly presents no middle category. The only scenario in which a genuine middle ground exists is *Rabbi Yehuda*'s stage from *Rabbi Yehuda*'s perspective: the cracks have appeared, it is *assur*, yet one does not receive *malkut*. The *Gemara* assumes this means it is neither *chametz* nor *matzah* at the *Torah* level — a genuine intermediate state.

*Tosafot* notes a potential difficulty: if *Rabbi Meir* says one receives *malkut* for eating the crusted dough on *Pesach*, that might actually indicate it is full *chametz* — after all, for full *chametz* one receives *karet*, while *malkut* without *karet* suggests it is treated as a lesser category. The *Gemara* initially assumes that lashes indicate full *chametz*, but *Tosafot* points out this is not obvious, and indeed the *Gemara* itself will later clarify this.

---

## Boiled Dough

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* raises yet another challenge: *ve'eima lo te'afeh chametz ella chalut* — what if the *mincha* is not baked as *chametz*, but is instead boiled? Throwing the dough into boiling water before it has a chance to ferment stops the fermentation process, yet it also does not produce *matzah*, since *matzah* is unfermented bread — and boiled dough, though unfermented, is not bread in the conventional sense.

The underlying assumption of the *Gemara* is that *matzah* and *chametz* are not merely categories defined by the presence or absence of fermentation in any cooked product. They must also qualify as *lechem*, as bread. Dough cooked by boiling would seem to lack this quality: it is flour and water that has been cooked, but in a manner that does not produce bread. One might argue that if *matzah* simply means flour and water that has not fermented, then boiled dough qualifies. But the *Gemara* appears to understand that *matzah* means unfermented bread specifically, and boiling produces something categorically different.

This parallels a broader principle that the *Rambam* seems to articulate: for something to be *chametz* in the full *Torah* sense requiring *karet*, and for something to be *matzah* in the *mitzvah* sense, it must also be describable as *lechem*. There are cases in the *Rambam* where even fermented items do not carry the full punishment of *karet* seemingly because they fall short of qualifying as *lechem*.

So *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* asks: perhaps boiled dough occupies the same middle ground as *chametz nuksheh* — neither *chametz* nor *matzah* — and perhaps a *mincha* brought in this form is valid *bedi'avad*, since it violates neither the prohibition on *chametz* nor the requirement for *matzah* in a fully repeated way?

---

## Mincha Revucha

The *Gemara* responds to this challenge: *chalut mai nihu — revucha* — what is this boiling? It is *revucha* — a *mincha* that is boiled in oil. That is an established category of *mincha*. If one is actually bringing the *mincha revucha* that is supposed to be brought that way, then there is no question — one has done precisely what was required.

But the *Gemara* presses further: *ve'ha lo ketiv bah revucha* — what about a *mincha* for which the *Torah* does not say *revucha*? Can one bring it as *revucha bedi'avad* and still be valid? The *Gemara* entertains the thought that where the *Torah* specifies *revucha*, the *mitzvah* is to do it that way, but perhaps where it does not, one has the option to bring it either as *revucha* or as *matzah*. In other words, maybe the specification of *matzah* for those *menachot* is not *me'akev*, and one could have validly brought them boiled. If so, the *Torah*'s description of a *mincha* as a *machavat* or some other type is simply describing one permitted mode, not an exclusive requirement, and *bedi'avad* bringing it boiled would be acceptable.

---

## Prohibition vs. Validity

*Ravina* raises a third challenge to the original proof. The *Gemara* had argued that *lo te'afeh chametz* — do not bake it as *chametz* — combined with *matzot te'achel* constitutes a double statement establishing both the positive obligation and the *ikuv*. But *Ravina* objects: *ve'eima lo te'afeh chametz lameikam gavra belav b'alma* — perhaps the *Torah* is not establishing *ikuv* at all. Perhaps it is telling you that you, the person, will have transgressed a *lav*, but *ufesulei lo mifsal* — the actual *korban* will not be rendered invalid.

This is a striking point. Most of the procedural details of the *beit hamikdash* are stated descriptively: here is how you perform *shechitah*, here is where you sprinkle the blood. The *Torah* does not typically say "you may not do it wrong" as a prohibition — it simply describes the correct process, and violation invalidates. Here, by contrast, the *Torah* frames the matter as a personal prohibition: *lo te'afeh chametz*. *Ravina* argues that this framing suggests something different: the *Torah* is imposing a personal obligation not to do it, much as the *Rambam* suggests this prohibition may be rooted in the need to distance the *mikdash* from associations with spring fertility rites involving fermented grain. The *Torah* emphasizes: *you* may not do this. But perhaps the *korban* itself remains *kasher* if one did.

This gives us three separate challenges to the simple proof: first, there is the middle category of *chametz nuksheh* not addressed by either *pasuk*; second, there is boiled dough, similarly a middle category; and third, even for real *chametz*, perhaps the prohibition addresses personal culpability without invalidating the *korban*.

---

## Baraita Resolution

After all these challenges, the *Gemara* concludes: *ella minalan — k'detanya* — from where do we derive the rule? From a *baraita*. The *baraita* cites the *pasuk* by the *mincha al hamachavat* (Vayikra 2:5): *u'mincha al hamachavat korbancha soles belulah bashemen matzah tihyeh* — your meal offering on the flat pan shall be of fine flour with oil; *matzah tihyeh*. The *baraita* asks: *yachol mitzvah* — perhaps this is only a *mitzvah*, not obligatory? *Talmud lomar tihyeh* — the word *tihyeh* teaches that it shall be. *Hakasuv keva'ah chovah* — the *Torah* makes it an absolute obligation.

What is the mechanism? Had the *Torah* wished only to establish *ikuv*, it would have written *matzah hi* — it is *matzah*. The use of *tihyeh* — it shall be — implies something more: the *Torah* makes it an ongoing, obligatory state. Now of course this *pasuk* is by one specific *mincha*, the *machavat*. How does one generalize to all *menachot*? *Tosafot* explains that the detail was already known for this *mincha*, and therefore the *Torah*'s act of repeating it is itself the generalization — teaching a rule applicable to all *menachot*. The derivation is somewhat anti-climactic: after all the sophisticated arguments about middle categories, personal prohibitions, and the structure of *pasuk* pairs, the answer rests on the word *tihyeh* in one specific context being generalized to the whole.

---

## Lukewarm Water & Vigilan…

*Rav Preida* now poses a further question to *Rav Ami*: *minayin l'chol hamenachot sheniloshos befoshrin umishmartan shelo yachmitzu* — from where do we know that all *menachot* must be kneaded with lukewarm water, and that one must be vigilant to ensure they do not become *chametz*? A later *Mishnah* establishes that lukewarm water is used when making a *mincha* — hot water accelerates fermentation — and that one must be constantly vigilant, working the dough and taking care throughout the process. But where is the source for a positive obligation to be vigilant?

One might suggest: *nilmadenah miPesach* — let us learn it from *Pesach*, where the *Torah* says *u'shmartem es hamatzos* — you shall watch over the *matzot*. Perhaps the same concept of watchfulness applies to *menachot*.

*Rav Ami* responds: there is no need to derive it from *Pesach*, for *begufah ksiv* — it is written in the *mincha* itself. The same *pasuk* — *matzah tihyeh* — teaches this. 

---

## Matzah Tihiyeh Derash

The *Gemara* now explains the derivation. If the *Torah* wished only to establish *ikuv*, it would have sufficed to write *matzah hi*. The use of *tihyeh* yields an additional teaching: *shema mina tarti* — derive from it two things. First, failure to make it *matzah* renders the *mincha* invalid. Second, the word *tihyeh* carries a sense of *techayeh* — give it life, bring it to life as *matzah* — communicating an obligation of active vigilance to ensure it remains *matzah* and does not become *chametz*.

The connection to *Pesach* is telling: the idea of vigilance — *shmirah* — is central to *Pesach*, where the prohibition of *chametz* is framed as much as a mental and attitudinal stance as a physical one. Here, too, the *Torah* is not merely prohibiting the wrong product; it is mandating a posture of active watchfulness throughout the preparation. There is an interesting parallel to how the *Gemara* at the beginning of this *masechta* assumed the use of water — a detail never explicitly mentioned in the *Torah* — yet the whole framework of making a *mincha* without fermenting it presupposes water used carefully and deliberately.

There is also an interesting interplay between the *hei* and the *chet* in this *derash* — reading *tihyeh* as containing a sense of *techayeh*. This same linguistic dynamic will arise again later in the *sugya*.

---

## Rav Preida & Rabbi Ezra

The *Gemara* now transitions to an aggadic passage. The *rabanan* — the students in the *beit medrash* — said to *Rav Preida*: *Rabbi Ezra bar bereih d'Rabbi Avtulas* — Rabbi Ezra, grandson of Rabbi Avtulas, *de'hu asiri l'Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah* — who is a tenth-generation descendant of *Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah*, *de'hu asiri l'Ezra* — who was himself a tenth-generation descendant of *Ezra Hasofer* — *kai abava* — is standing at the door, wishing to enter the *beit medrash*.

*Rav Preida* responded: *mai kulei hai* — what is all this introduction about his lineage? *Ei bar oryan ihu, ya'ei* — if he is a *ben Torah*, that is nice. *Ei bar oryan u'var avohan, ya'ei v'ya'ei* — if he is a *ben Torah* and also has fine *yichus*, that is doubly nice. But *ei bar avohan velo bar oryan* — if he has *yichus* but is not a *ben Torah* — *esh techeilneih* — let fire consume him. I am unimpressed with *yichus* alone; this is a *yeshiva*.

The students confirmed: *bar oryan hu* — he is indeed a *ben Torah*. *Rav Preida* immediately said: *leiyel, v'leisei* — let him come in. So *Rabbi Ezra* entered the *beit medrash*, and the *Gemara* reports that *Rav Preida* observed that he was in a foul or darkened mood — perhaps, one may reasonably infer, because his proud *yichus* had just been pointedly dismissed as insufficient grounds for entry on its own.

---

## God's Gratitude

*Rav Preida* decided to open with an *aggadeta* to address the mood in the room. The *pasuk* he chose was from Tehillim: *amarta l'Hashem Adonai atah, tovasi bal alecha* — you said to God, "You are my God; my goodness is not upon You." This is a striking *pasuk*: why would the Congregation of Israel say that their goodness is not upon God?

The *Gemara* explains: *Knesses Yisrael* said to God — *Ribbono Shel Olam, hachzeik li tova*, grant me credit. Why? *De-hodia'ticha ba-olam* — I have made Your fame known in the world; I have spread recognition of Your existence and Godhood. Give me credit for that.

God responds — *amarta, tovasi bal alecha*: my gratitude is not for you, *ein ani machzik tova* — I have no debt of gratitude toward you. My gratitude is *ela l'Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov*, for it was they who first made My name known in the world — *she-hodia'uni techilla ba-olam*. The next *pasuk* continues: *likdoshim asher ba-aretz heimah, v'adirei kol cheftzi bam* — to the holy ones in the land, the mighty ones in whom all My desire resides. The *adirim* — the mighty ones — are associated here with the *Avot*.

One of the *mefarshim* suggested that *Rav Preida* was indirectly saying to *Rabbi Ezra*: it is your grandparents to whom credit belongs, not to you yourself. Another *mefaresh* suggested *Rav Preida* was saying that the students deserved credit for vouching for him and spreading his name. But the more compelling reading is that *Rav Preida* was explaining his own position: do not take offense. *Knesses Yisrael* says "look at all we have accomplished," and God says the credit belongs to the ancestors. Children do not inherit the merit of what their ancestors did. You don't get credit for your *yichus*. Whether this was meant to console *Rabbi Ezra* or further explain *Rav Preida*'s position is not entirely clear — it might not have been immediately comforting to someone proud of his lineage.

---

## Drashot on Affinity

Upon hearing the word *adir* in *Rav Preida*'s exposition, *Rabbi Ezra* recalled a *drasha* on that same concept, and opened with a series of closely related *drashot* on the theme of affinity between similar things.

*Yavo adir veyipara la'adirim me'adirim be'adirim* — let the *adir* come and pay back the *adirim* from the *adirim* in the *adirim*. Who is each? *Yavo adir* — the mighty one — *zeh Hakadosh Baruch Hu*, God, who is *adir bamarom*. *Veyipara la'adirim* — and let Him pay back the *adirim* — *elu Yisrael* — this is Israel — *de'ketiv v'adirei kol cheftzi bam*. Crucially, *Rabbi Ezra* reads this *pasuk* differently from *Rav Preida*: where *Rav Preida* applied *adirei kol cheftzi bam* to the *Avot*, *Rabbi Ezra* reads it as referring to Israel itself. *Me'adirim* — from the mighty ones — *elu haMitzrim*, the Egyptians — *de'ketiv tzalelu ka'oferet bemayim adirim*, they sank like lead in the mighty waters. *Be'adirim* — in the mighty ones — *elu hamayim* — the water — *de'ketiv mikolot mayim rabim adirim mishberei yam*. Thus: God, the mighty one, paid back Israel from and through the Egyptians in the sea.

The second *drasha*: *yavo yedid ben yedid, veyivneh yedid l'yedid bechelko shel yedid, veyitkapru bo yedidim* — let the beloved son of the beloved come and build the beloved thing for the beloved one in the portion of the beloved one, and let the beloved people be atoned through it. *Yavo yedid* — *zeh Shlomo HaMelech*, who was called *Yedidyah* — *ba'avur ki Hashem aheivo*. *Ben yedid* — the son of the beloved — *zeh Avraham*, not David, interestingly — *de'ketiv mah liyedidi beveisi*, a *pasuk* from *Yirmiyah* which will be expounded shortly. *Veyivneh yedid* — and let the beloved build — *zeh Beis HaMikdash* — *de'ketiv mah yedidos mishkenosecha*. *Leyedid* — for the beloved — *zeh Hakadosh Baruch Hu*. *Bechelko shel yedid* — in the portion of the beloved — *zeh Binyamin*, for the *Beis HaMikdash* was located in the portion of *Binyamin* — *de'ketiv l'Vinyamin amar yedid Hashem yishkon lavetach alav*. *Veyitkapru bo yedidim* — and let the beloved ones be atoned through it — *elu Yisrael* — *de'ketiv nasati es yedidus nafshi bechaph oyveha*.

The third *drasha*: *yavo tov veyekabel tov mitov l'tovim* — let the good come and receive the good from the good one for the good. *Yavo tov* — *zeh Moshe* — *de'ketiv vateira oso ki tov hu*. *Veyekabel tov* — and receive the good — *zu Torah* — *de'ketiv ki lekach tov nasati lachem*. *Mitov* — from the good one — *zeh Hakadosh Baruch Hu*, for God is good to all. *Letovim* — for the good — *elu Yisrael* — *de'ketiv heitivah Hashem letovim*.

The fourth *drasha* strikes one as the most abstract: *yavo zeh veyekabel zot mizeh le'am zu* — let this one come and receive this from this one for this people. *Yavo zeh* — *zeh Moshe* — *de'ketiv ki zeh Moshe ha'ish*. *Veyekabel zot* — *zot Torah* — *de'ketiv vezot haTorah*. *Mizeh* — from this — *zeh Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — *de'ketiv zeh Keli va'anvehu*. *Le'am zu* — *elu Yisrael* — *de'ketiv am zu kanita*.

---

## Lineage & Torah

What is the point of this series of *drashot*? The theme running through all of them is affinity: *adir* connects to *adirim*, *yedid* builds for *yedid*, *tov* gives to *tovim*, *zeh* gives *zot* to *am zu*. When entities share the same essential character, they naturally work together and belong together.

*Rabbi Ezra* is implicitly making a response to *Rav Preida*. He is not saying that *yichus* alone entitles one to anything. He heard *Rav Preida*'s point. But he is saying something more nuanced: when *yichus* and *Torah* combine, there is a special power in that combination. He is himself the bearer of both — he is a *ben Torah*, as the students confirmed, and he descends from *Ezra Hasofer*. The poetry of *yavo yedid ben yedid* speaks precisely to this: let Ezra come for Ezra, for Ezra — there is something poetically and substantively real about a family of *Torah* carrying *Torah* forward. The affinity is not merely decorative.

It is worth noting that *Rav Preida*'s own *girsa* says simply *ya'ei v'ya'ei* — it is good and it is good — when someone has both *Torah* and *yichus*. *Rabbi Ezra* seems to be pressing that the combination is not merely additive but constitutes something of its own. The historical record bears this out: one need only observe that the vast bulk of the marginal commentary on the *Gemara* — *Rashi* on one side, *Tosafot* on the other — was produced by a single family. *Rashi*'s grandsons were *Rabbeinu Tam* and the *Rashbam*, and the *Ri* was a nephew. One family, across generations, produced the foundational *rishonim* on virtually the entire *Shas*. When *Torah* and *yichus* align, they can reinforce each other in ways that are historically consequential.

The *Gemara* also invokes the principle of *machzik ma'asei avotav beyado* — when one follows in the ways of one's ancestors, the reward or consequence of those ancestors is reinforced and renewed in the current generation. That dynamic, for good or for ill, is what *Rabbi Ezra* is gesturing toward. He is not asking for unearned credit. He is pointing to the way in which *yichus*, when paired with genuine *Torah* learning, carries a particular resonance — and the poetry of *adir* paying back *adirim*, of *yedid* building for *yedid*, captures something real about how the world of *Torah* works across generations.

The *aggadeta* is brought here in the context of *Rav Preida*, who was the *Amora* featured in the previous legal discussion. The *drashot* at the end of this section touch on *pesukim* that in their fuller context relate to the *Churban Habayis*, giving the passage a broader resonance with the general themes of *Kodshim* that will be taken up in the shiur to follow.

---

---

# Menachot 54

## Abraham & Churban

### Opening Dialogue

The *aggadata* under discussion was introduced somewhat earlier in the tractate in connection with a different sage, but it is brought here to connect with the *kodshim* context, touching on the destruction of the *Beit Hamikdash* and linking to a *pasuk* cited the previous day. The passage reads: *be-sha'ah shecharav Beit Hamikdash*, when the Temple was destroyed, God found Abraham standing within it. God said to him, *ma liydidi b'veisi* — "What is my beloved doing in my house?" This invokes the *pasuk* we had encountered in which Abraham is called *yedidi*, "my beloved." Abraham replied: *al iskei banai bati* — "I have come on account of my children; their Temple has been destroyed and they have been exiled." God responded bluntly: *banecha chatu v'galu* — they sinned and they were punished with exile.

### Abraham's Arguments

Abraham did not relent. He pressed forward with a series of increasingly focused arguments, each met by a divine rejoinder. First he proposed: *shema bishogeg chatu* — perhaps they sinned unintentionally and did not deserve so severe a punishment. God replied with a *pasuk* from Yirmiyahu indicating that their deeds were willful and premeditated — *mezimah*, a calculated act.

Abraham then shifted to a quantitative argument: *shema mi'utam chatu* — perhaps it was only a minority who sinned, not the whole people. God replied: *harabim* — it was the majority. Abraham then invoked the covenant: *haya lecha lizkor brit milah* — You should have remembered the *brit milah* they observed; surely that merit should have counted in their favor. God responded with a *pasuk* suggesting that the holy flesh — the *brit milah* — had effectively been abandoned, whether through the Hellenistic practice of surgically reversing the circumcision, or simply through non-observance. In either reading, the argument from *brit milah* is deflected.

There is something striking about this entire interchange. Abraham is arriving, as it were, after the fact — the Temple is already destroyed, the people already in exile. What precisely is he trying to accomplish? He is not interceding to prevent a punishment; he is contesting the justice of one already executed. This is very much the posture Abraham adopted at Sodom and Gomorrah: standing for justice, demanding an accounting, refusing to simply accept the outcome.

Even more remarkable is the implicit bracketing of *zekhut avot*. At no point does Abraham say: remember what Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did — *haya lecha lizkor l'Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov*. Even when Abraham mentions *brit milah*, the context is not his own keeping of the covenant but whether *they*, his descendants, kept it. The entire appeal is on their own terms. This connects to a theme noted elsewhere — Rav Preada's position that what matters is not your ancestors' accomplishments but your own, and that even lineage from *talmidei chakhamim* does not protect one who has not lived up to their example. The *gemara* here seems to give powerful expression to that view: even with Abraham himself as the advocate, the argument is entirely about judging Israel by their own deeds, not by ancestral merit. The *brit* of the patriarchs — *v'izkarti et briti Yaakov v'af et briti Yitzchak v'af et briti Avraham ezkor* — is conspicuously absent from the exchange.

### Heavenly Voice & Olive

Abraham then offered one final plea: *shema himtanta lahem hayu chozrim b'teshuvah* — perhaps had You waited, they would have repented; the punishment came too swiftly. God replied with a *pasuk* indicating that they rejoiced in their evil — Rashi understands this to mean their wickedness was entrenched and return was not forthcoming. At this point, *miyad haniach yado al rosho vehayah tzo'ek uvoche* — Abraham placed his hands on his head and broke into weeping, crying out: perhaps, *chas v'shalom*, there is no remedy for them at all, and they will never return.

It is worth pausing to note how unusual this imagery is. In the vast landscape of poetry, prayer, and *midrash* surrounding the destruction of the Temple, one typically encounters Rachel weeping for her children, the prophets lamenting — but not Abraham cast in this role of anguished intercessor crying over the *churban*. Yet here he is.

What follows is equally striking: *yatzta bat kol v'amra lo* — a heavenly voice emerged and spoke to him. Notably, it is no longer God who responds directly; it is the *bat kol*. This shift in voice might reflect the tension in the narrative between *middat hadin* and something softer — just as at the *akeidah* it was God who commanded and the angel who saved the day, here the heavenly voice steps in at the moment of crisis.

The *bat kol* quoted: *zayit ra'anan yafeh pri to'ar kara Hashem shmecha* — "A flourishing olive tree, beautiful of fruit, God has called your name." The interpretation given: *mah zayit zeh achrito b'sofo* — just as an olive tree yields its benefit at the end, after a long period of waiting (whether because the fruit ripens all at once or because the harvest must wait until the season arrives), so too *af Yisrael achritan b'sofan* — for Israel, the ultimate good will come at the end. The present moment is one of terrible difficulty, but the comparison to the olive tree promises eventual flourishing.

### Spies & Merglim

The *gemara* continues with the earlier part of the *pasuk*, which describes a *hamulah gedolah*, a great tumult, with fire set upon it and its young shoots shaken. Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa reads *hamulah* as an allusion to the words of the *meraglim* — the spies — and *nitra'u daliyoseihen shel Yisrael*, the foundational shoots of Israel were shaken to their roots and the future of the nation endangered. Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa elaborates: *davar gadol dibru meraglim b'otah sha'ah* — the spies said a terrible, weighty thing. The verse they uttered was *ki chazak hu mimennu* — "they are stronger than we." Reading *mimennu* not as "from us" but "from Him," the *gemara* invokes the principle of *al tikri* and understands the spies to have been saying, implicitly, that even God cannot drive them out — *kivyachol she'afilu ba'al habayit eino yachol l'hotzi eilav misham* — as though even the owner of the house cannot remove the squatters from within it. This blasphemy was so profound it placed the entire future of Israel in jeopardy.

Rabbi Chiya bar Chanina objects: if the allusion were to the words of the spies, the text should have used *milah* (word) rather than *hamulah* (tumult), so the reading is linguistically strained. The *gemara* therefore returns to the primary narrative and reads *hamulah* differently: the *bat kol* told Abraham that God said *kolcha shamati*, "I have heard your voice," and *chamulah*, playing on the letters, *vachimalti aleihem* — "I have had great compassion upon them." The shift between *heh* and *chet* underlies this reading; the *gemara* notes that in manuscripts of this period the two letters were sometimes written in ways difficult to distinguish, which facilitated such plays on the text.

### Four Kingdoms

What then was the fire set upon the olive tree? The *gemara* understands God to be telling Abraham: *ani amarti sheyishta'adu b'arba malchuyot* — I decreed that they would be subjected to the four kingdoms, each for a full measure of servitude, on the model of the exile in Egypt, which lasted its full span. The four kingdoms understood by *chazal* are Egypt, Babylonia — corresponding to the destruction of the First Temple — Persia and Media, Greece, and Rome, which in *chazal*'s framework extends through Christianity to the present. Not all these kingdoms lasted equal durations: Media was brief, lasting only a few years, which illustrates the divine concession that follows. God says: *hashta kol chad v'chad mai d'pasik lei* — each kingdom will receive only its allotted portion, not the full weight originally intended for each.

There is also a second version: *ani amarti b'zeh v'zeh* — I originally meant for them to serve these kingdoms sequentially, one after another; *achshav b'vat achas* — now I am allowing them to serve concurrently, so that some Jews are under Greece while others are under Persia, the exiles overlapping, and the total duration thereby shortened. This is the meaning of God's compassion in response to Abraham's plea.

### Eternal Survival

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks: why is Israel compared to an olive tree? To teach that *mah zayit ein alav noshrim lo b'yamot hachamah v'lo b'yamot hageshamim* — just as an olive tree's leaves do not fall whether in summer or in the rainy winter season, it is a perennial that retains its foliage year-round — *af Yisrael ein lahem beteilah olamit* — so too the Jewish people will never be destroyed, *lo b'olam hazeh v'lo b'olam haba*, neither in this world nor in the world to come. There will be suffering, oppression, and catastrophic tragedy, but ultimate survival is assured.

### Suffering & Teshuvah

Rabbi Yochanan then offers a parallel reading of the same comparison. Why is Israel likened to an olive tree? Because *mah zayit eino motzi shemano ela al yedei ketisha* — an olive yields its oil only through pounding — *af Yisrael ein chozrim l'mutav ela al yedei yissurim* — so too, Israel returns to the right path only through suffering.

This is a jarring note on which to conclude what had seemed to be building toward consolation. The *gemara* invokes a well-known *midrash* from Tractate Megillah: all the admonitions of the prophets across centuries could not accomplish what the single handing of Achashveirosh's ring to Haman accomplished. The threat of catastrophe — the crisis hanging over the people — moves them to *teshuvah* in a way that words alone cannot. Rabbi Yochanan's point is realistic rather than comforting: yes, Israel survives, but the mechanism of return is often suffering itself. The concluding image is not a gentle one. This *aggadata* ends not with the softness of the heavenly voice and the olive tree parable but with Rabbi Yochanan pulling the reader back into a sober reckoning with how the world actually works.

---

## Making Chametz

### R. Meir vs. R. Yehuda

It is something of a relief to turn from the *aggadata* to the *halakhic* discussion, and, notably, to a discussion not of how to prevent *chametz* but of how to create it. Most *menachot* must be *matzah*; even those that are brought as *chametz* — most prominently the *shtei halechem* on *Shavuot* and certain loaves of the *todah* — may not be offered on the *mizbe'ach* in that state. But they must be made as *chametz*. How is this done?

Rabbi Meir says: you take some of the flour from within the measure, fashion it into sourdough (*se'or*), and reintroduce it to leaven the rest. Rabbi Yehuda objects that this will produce weak sourdough and prefers instead to take already-prepared sourdough from elsewhere, introducing it into the flour and then filling up the measure with the remaining flour.

### Density & Measure

The problem Rabbi Yehuda faces is one of accurate measurement. Sourdough differs in density from plain flour — it may be more compact or more airy. If you place sourdough into the measuring vessel and then fill the rest with flour, the total amount of flour will not accurately reflect one *issaron*, because the sourdough occupies volume differently than flour would. Rav Chisda articulates this precisely: if the sourdough is dense, it compresses into less space, leaving more room for flour than normal, resulting in more flour than the *issaron* calls for; if it is loose and airy, it takes up more space, resulting in less flour than required.

### Original vs. Current

One might ask: why not simply fill the measure to the top and accept whatever we have? Rabba and Rav Yosef both say: *likemot shehein hayu mesharinan* — you measure not according to what you now have in front of you but according to what it should have been originally. The Torah specifies an *issaron solet* — an *issaron* of flour, not of dough. The measuring standard is the original ingredient, the flour, not the current mixture.

One proposed solution is to take a portion of flour outside the *Beit Hamikdash*, prepare it as sourdough there, and then bring it back in — either following Rabbi Meir's approach over a longer period to produce stronger sourdough, or using the outside preparation as a test run to determine how much flour would fill the *issaron* at the relevant density, thereby enabling accurate approximation.

### Gezeira & Appearance

The *gemara* rejects this approach on account of a *gezeira*: *dilma ati l'ashvuyei me'alma* — people will see sourdough being brought in from outside and placed into the measure after the initial measuring, and they will conclude that one may add sourdough to the flour after measuring, as though the sourdough need not constitute part of the measured quantity. This misleading appearance is unacceptable. The result is that one must measure everything together at once. According to Rabbi Meir, the sourdough is fashioned quickly from part of the flour itself; according to Rabbi Yehuda, the outside sourdough is placed in first and the remaining flour is used to fill the measure, without ever removing and reintroducing material.

---

## Fruit Juices & Water

### Mei Peirot Principle

The *gemara* now addresses a further dimension of *chametz* in the context of *menachot*: the principle that *mei peirot* — fruit juices — do not create *chametz*. Water is the agent required for leavening; other liquids, including fruit juices and, as the *gemara* will discuss, egg, do not cause real *chametz*. This principle has significant implications both for the question of how certain *menachot* become *chametz* and for the well-known discussions about egg *matzah* on *Pesach*.

### R. Chanina vs. Rabbanan

The *mishnah* rules that one may not use apple juice to make the *chametz* required for a *minchah*. However, in the name of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, the view is stated that apple juice (*tapuchim*) does create *chametz* — so that, according to this view, apple juice could in principle be used for a *minchah* requiring *chametz*. Rav Kahana transmits this ruling in the name of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon rather than Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel. There is an additional question lurking here: even if apple juice could create *chametz*, on what basis would one be permitted to introduce an ingredient not specified by the Torah? The flour and oil are given; water is not mentioned at all. The implicit understanding is that since the Torah requires these *menachot* to be *chametz*, the process of leavening — whatever it entails — is part of fulfilling the Torah's requirement, granting some latitude in the choice of leavening agent. Still, the question is notable, particularly since, as will emerge, water itself is similarly unmentioned in the Torah's text.

### Trumos Evidence

The *gemara* attempts to determine which position — Rabbi Chanina's or the *rabbanan*'s — is supported by a *mishnah* in Tractate Trumos (perek 3, mishnah 2). The case: an apple that is *terumah* is crushed and placed into dough. The general rule is that *terumah* becomes *battel* — nullified — when mixed with a much larger quantity of non-*terumah* material. However, one exception is when the *terumah* causes the dough to ferment: in that case its effect is felt throughout and it cannot be considered nullified. The *mishnah* rules that the dough is *asur* — forbidden — meaning the apple is considered still present, because it caused fermentation. This seems to prove that apple juice is *machmitz* — it creates leavening — which would support Rabbi Chanina's position.

The *gemara* responds that this proof can be deflected even by the *rabbanan*. The *rabbanan* who prohibit apple juice for a *minchah* may acknowledge that apple juice creates *chametz nuksha* — a quasi-*chametz*, the intermediate state between full leavening and true *matzah* that was discussed previously. This quasi-*chametz* would be sufficient to prevent *bittul* in the *trumos* context, since the apple's fermenting effect is still operative, even if it does not rise to the level of *chametz gamur* required for the *minchah*.

This raises a further question about the definition of *chametz* and *matzah* in the context of *menachot*. When the Torah requires a *minchah* to be *matzah*, we established previously that it must be genuine *matzah* — *chametz nuksha* will not satisfy the requirement. By the same logic, when the Torah requires *chametz*, presumably one needs *chametz gamur*, real leavening — not this intermediate quasi-*chametz* produced by fruit juices, at least according to the *rabbanan*.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot engages at length with the broader question of *mei peirot* and *chametz*, both in this tractate and in Tractate Pesachim. The difficulty is that different *gemarot* seem to point in different directions: some suggest that *mei peirot* can produce real *chametz* — *chametz gamur* for which one would be liable to *karet* on *Pesach* — which would represent the position of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel; others seem to indicate that fruit juices pose no problem at all, not even *rabbinically*, and that one could leave flour kneaded with fruit juices unattended without concern that it would become *chametz*.

Tosafot's general resolution — though he works through it with considerable back-and-forth — is that without water, fruit juices will never produce real *chametz*. At most, one might arrive at *chametz nuksha*, and only in certain circumstances. Real *chametz*, or *chametz* that arises faster than normal, occurs when fruit juices are combined *with* water. A separate *gemara* states that *mei peirot* can cause *chametz* to develop faster than water alone; Tosafot understands this to refer to the combination of fruit juices and water together. Without water, fruit juices alone never create real *chametz* according to this analysis.

This position underpins the entire discussion about egg *matzah* on *Pesach*. The *minhag* not to eat egg *matzah* on *Pesach* — except for the elderly or ill who cannot eat ordinary *matzah* — arises precisely because it is possible to read the *gemara* that says fruit juices accelerate leavening as referring to fruit juices without water. If fruit juices alone can produce *chametz* faster than water does, one would have very little confidence in the *chametz*-free status of egg *matzah*. But according to Tosafot, that concern only applies when water is also present.

### Mishnah & Rambam

This brings the discussion to the question of water in the *menachot* generally. The Torah specifies flour and oil; it does not mention water. Yet a later *mishnah* — which will be reached in approximately two days — states that *kol haminchot niloshot b'poshrim*, all *menachot* are kneaded with lukewarm water. The *gemara* there raises an objection: what about the *minchat nesachim* — the flour offerings that accompanied animal *korbanot* — where the *gemara* seems to assume no water was used? This then opens a renewed discussion of *mei peirot* and *chametz*.

Tosafot addresses the apparent inconsistency. If all *menachot* had water, why does the *gemara* assume the *minchat nesachim* did not? Tosafot explains that the *minchat nesachim* was distinguished by having a much larger proportion of oil mixed into the flour. Because of this, Tosafot reasons, it is assumed that the oil functioned in place of water in the kneading process, and therefore the *minchat nesachim* may not have required water and may have had no capacity to become *chametz*. According to this reading, all other *menachot* did include water — hence the relevance of the *chametz* prohibition — with the *minchat nesachim* as the lone exception due to its oil-heavy composition.

The Rambam reads the same *mishnah* differently. Rather than *kol haminchot niloshot b'poshrim*, the Rambam's version is *kol haminchot hane'afot niloshot b'poshrim* — only those *menachot* that are *baked* are kneaded with lukewarm water. Certain *menachot* are not baked but are rather fried in oil — essentially flour cooked in oil — and for those, no water is involved and no issue of *chametz* arises. According to the Rambam, water enters the picture only for *menachot* that take the form of bread: either unleavened bread (*matzah*) or leavened bread (*chametz*). The *shtei halechem* and similar *chametz* loaves are baked and thus require water; the question of whether they must be *matzah* or *chametz* is then precisely a question about what is done with that water — whether one allows leavening or prevents it. The Rambam's approach neatly contains the relevance of water to the baking context, explaining why the Torah does not treat it as a primary ingredient: it is a means to an end in bread-making, not an offering in its own right.

The practical upshot is that, according to Tosafot, *mei peirot* alone are insufficient for *chametz* — water is essential. This in turn explains the entire halakhic framework of *chametz* versus *matzah* in the *menachot*: the *chametz*-or-*matzah* question only arises where water is present, whether in all *menachot* (Tosafot) or only in the baked ones (Rambam).

---

## Minchat Chotei

### Kemitzah Problem

The *gemara* turns now to the *minchat chotei* — the sinner's meal offering. Rav Ila states: *ein lecha kasheh likmitzah yoter miminchat chote* — there is nothing more difficult to perform *kemitzah* on than the *minchat chotei*. The *kemitzah* — the taking of a precisely measured handful — is the central act of the *minchah* service, and it must be done from the flour of the offering. The problem with the *minchat chotei* is that it contains nothing but plain flour: *lo yasim aleha shemen velo yiten aleha levonah* — no oil and no *levonah* are added, because it is a *chatat*-type offering and must be treated accordingly. Without oil to bind the flour together, taking a precise *kemitzah* from loose dry flour is extraordinarily difficult — particles spill, it is nearly impossible to hold an exact quantity in one's hand.

### Adding Water Solution

Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi proposes a solution: *minchat chote megablah bemayim uksheirah* — one may knead the *minchat chotei* with water, and it remains *kasher*. Adding water binds the flour together sufficiently that *kemitzah* becomes practicable. This is a striking ruling, since water is not an ingredient prescribed by the Torah for this offering. Here, as with the earlier discussion of apple juice for leavening, the *gemara* seems unconcerned about the introduction of an unlisted ingredient. One might ask further: even if the addition does not invalidate the *minchah*, does placing this water-and-flour mixture on the *mizbe'ach* not constitute *chullin ba'azara* — a non-sacred substance being brought into the Temple precincts? The *gemara* appears to set this concern aside, perhaps because the water is wholly incidental and functional rather than something presented as part of the offering itself. The *gemara* elsewhere seems to operate on the implicit assumption that a *minchah*, as a constructed offering, allows for a measure of tolerance regarding ancillary ingredients.

This also clarifies an important point raised in connection with the earlier discussion. According to Tosafot, all *menachot* except the *minchat chotei* included water. The *minchat chotei* and the *minchat sotah* — which similarly consists of plain dry flour — would be the exceptions that never had water. The present passage reveals that even here, water can be added *post facto* to enable the *kemitzah* procedure.

### Chareivah Definition

The *gemara* then frames the underlying dispute. The position of Rav Ila — who did not hold that water may be added — is explained as follows: the Torah uses the term *chareivah* to describe this *minchah*, meaning dry. The question is what *chareivah* excludes. One view is *chareivah mishemen* — dry means without oil; since the Torah says dry, it excludes oil, but water would be permissible. The other view is *chareivah mikol davar* — dry means without any liquid whatsoever, and therefore water is equally forbidden. This is the actual debate, and it is a straightforward question of how to read the Torah's descriptive term. If *chareivah* only excludes oil — the liquid specifically associated with *menachot* — water remains available as a practical tool. If it excludes all liquids, the *minchat chotei* must remain entirely dry, leaving the difficulty of *kemitzah* unresolved.

---

## Measurement Principle

### Uktzin Mishnah

The *gemara* now transitions to a more general question about measurement that extends beyond the context of *menachot* entirely. The broader *halakhic* issue is: when an object changes in size, do we assess its status based on its current size or its original size? A *mishnah* in Tractate Uktzin provides the launching point. The case involves *basar ha'eigel* — flesh of a calf — which, when left around, tends to expand and bloat, and *basar zekeinah* — flesh of an old animal — which tends to shrivel and contract. The minimum quantity required to transfer *tumah* is generally a *kebeitzah* — the size of an egg. So: if calf meat started below a *kebeitzah* and bloated to a *kebeitzah*, or if aged meat started at a *kebeitzah* and shriveled to below a *kebeitzah*, does one measure based on the current state or the original state?

The *mishnah* states *mishta'arin kemot shehen* — we measure according to the way they are. The difficulty is whether this phrase means *as they are now* or *as they were then*, and two groups of *amora'im* read it differently.

Tosafot notes, parenthetically, that whatever conclusion is reached in this *tumah*-related discussion need not apply mechanically to the *minchah* context. There, the Torah explicitly says *issaron solet* — an *issaron* of flour. The logic of measuring by the original ingredient is independently compelling from the wording of the verse itself, regardless of how we resolve the general principle for *tumah*.

### Amoraim Dispute

Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan read the *mishnah* as *mishta'arin kemot shehen* — we measure according to the way they are *right now*. Shmuel, Rabbi Shimon b'Rabbi, and Reish Lakish read it as *l'kemot shehayu* — we measure according to the way they *were* originally. The textual difference hinges on whether one reads *kemot shehen* (as they are) or *l'kemot shehen* / *l'kemot shehayu* (toward what they were), with the addition of a *lamed* directing the phrase backward in time. The *gemara* notes that the distinction between *kemot shehen* and *l'kemot shehen* is subtle enough that the clearer formulation *l'kemot shehayu* was perhaps the original reading, or alternatively that some manuscripts already carried this more explicit version.

### Calf Meat Braitah

A *braitah* is then cited that appears quite explicit: *basar ha'eigel shelo haya bo kishiur v'tapach* — calf meat that did not have the requisite measure and then expanded. The *braitah* rules: *tahor l'she'avar v'tamei mikan ul'hava* — it was *tahor* until now and is *tamei* from this point forward. The ruling is unambiguous: once the meat has reached the size of a *kebeitzah*, it now communicates *tumah*, regardless of having started below that threshold. This appears to straightforwardly support the view that current size governs.

Those who hold that original size governs respond that this *braitah* reflects only a Rabbinic stringency — *mi'derabbanan*. Biblically, they would insist, you go by what the object's size was originally, and since it started too small, it never attained the proper status; but *rabbinically* the ruling is that if it now reaches the threshold, it will communicate *tumah* going forward.

The *gemara* presses: if this is only Rabbinic, how does the *braitah* proceed to apply the same logic to *pigul* and *notar*? One does not become *chayav* — subject to *karet* — for a Rabbinic prohibition. If eating a re-expanded piece of *pigul* or *notar* makes one *chayav*, that liability must be biblical. The *gemara* resolves this by reinterpreting the *braitah*'s reference to *pigul* and *notar*: it does not mean one who *eats* them is *chayav*, but rather that *pigul* and *notar* can themselves *communicate tumah*, since these categories of invalidated sacrificial meat carry a Rabbinic *tumah*. The *braitah* is saying that once calf meat reaches the required size, even if it is *pigul* or *notar* — and thus a source of Rabbinic *tumah* — it will communicate that *tumah*. The concern was that piling a Rabbinic *tumah* status onto a Rabbinic rule about measurement would be excessive; *kol hai b'derabbanan lo avid rabbanan* — the Rabbis would not compound Rabbinic ruling upon Rabbinic ruling to that degree. The *braitah* teaches that they did.

### Old Meat Shrinkage

The *gemara* then examines the reverse case from the same *braitah*: *basar zekeinah shehaya bo kishiur v'tzamak* — aged meat that had the requisite measure and then shriveled. The ruling: *tamei l'she'avar v'tahor mikan ul'hava* — it was *tamei* before and is *tahor* from this point forward. This case cuts in the opposite direction from the calf meat. Here, the ruling is explicitly lenient: the meat started at the right size, shriveled below it, and is now treated as *tahor* based on its current state. One cannot argue this is merely a Rabbinic leniency; no Rabbinic principle makes things *tahor* that are biblically *tamei*. This appears to be a clear, binding ruling that current size governs, and that the original size cannot sustain *tumah* status once the meat has shriveled below the threshold.

---

## Rava's Framework

### Three Scenarios

Rava steps in to reconcile the various positions and minimize the scope of the dispute. His analysis proceeds through three logical scenarios. First: an object that originally had the required size — there is no question that it had the status corresponding to that size. Second: an object that currently retains the required size — there is similarly no question that whatever consequences flow from that size apply now. Third: an object that both originally had and currently has the required size — again, unambiguous.

### The Real Dispute

The case where opinions diverge is far narrower: an object that *originally* had the required size (*deikara havei keshiur*), then *shriveled* below it (*v'tzamak*), and subsequently *re-expanded* back to its original size (*v'chazar v'tipach*). It started at the threshold, temporarily fell below it, and is now back at the threshold. Rava emphasizes that both camps — those who say you measure by current state and those who say you measure by original state — would agree on the easy cases. Nobody would say that something currently below the threshold communicates *tumah* because it once was large enough; that position would be indefensible. And conversely, nobody would deny that something currently at the proper size has the requisite status if it *also* originally had that status. The genuinely contested case is only when there has been an intermediate period of loss.

### Dichuiy Debate

Rava frames the dispute in terms of *dichuiy* — the concept of an object being "pushed off" or losing a status it once had. The term appears most prominently in the laws of *korbanot*, where an animal that became invalid at some point can in certain cases be considered permanently disqualified even if the condition that invalidated it later resolves. Rava applies this concept more broadly to *issurin* — forbidden items and their associated statuses. *Yesh dichuiy b'issura*: once the object temporarily lost the minimum size and with it the capacity to communicate *tumah* or the status of a forbidden food, that status was permanently expelled; re-expansion cannot restore what was once lost. *Ein dichuiy b'issura*: the intermediate shrinkage is inconsequential; since the object began at the required size and has returned to it, its original status governs.

---

## Forbidden Foods Proof

### Eggs in Sun

The *gemara* now challenges the view that *yesh dichuiy b'issura* — that temporary loss of size permanently negates status — by citing a *mishnah*. The case: *kebeitzah ochlin shehinicha bachamah v'nitmaatu* — an egg's worth of food was left in the sun and shriveled to less than a *kebeitzah*. The food can only receive or transmit *tumah* if it is of the requisite size. Similarly, *kezayit min hamet* — an olive's worth from a human corpse; *kezayit min haneveilah* — an olive's worth from the carcass of an animal that was not properly slaughtered; *ka'adasha min hasheretz* — the size of a lentil from certain creeping things; and *kezayit pigul, kezayit notar, kezayit chelev* — an olive's worth of *pigul*, *notar*, or forbidden fat (*chelev*), which are forbidden foods that Rabbinically also communicate *tumah*. If any of these shriveled below the required measure, the ruling is *tehorin* — they are *tahor*, meaning they no longer communicate *tumah*. And one would not be *chayav* for eating the *pigul*, *notar*, or *chelev* if they have shriveled below a *kezayit*.

### Pigul & Notar

The *mishnah*'s next clause is decisive: *henicham b'geshamim v'taphachu* — if one then left these items out in the rain and they re-expanded. *Teme'in* — they become *tamei* again. *V'chayavin aleihem mishum pigul v'notar v'tamei* — and one is *chayav* for eating them under the categories of *pigul*, *notar*, and *chelev*.

### Re-expansion Logic

What makes this case remarkable is that we understand precisely how the re-expansion occurred: the items absorbed water from the rain. This is not an internal biological or chemical process restoring the food to its prior state — it is external liquid being absorbed, causing the items to return to their original volume. And yet the *mishnah* rules unambiguously that they are once again *tamei* and one is *chayav* for eating them. The intermediate state of shrinkage is treated as inconsequential.
