Rabbi Yose HaGelili corrects this assumption: one may add water, the offering remains valid, and therefore the prohibition of *chametz* is applicable if one does so.

---

## Lechem Hapanim

### Kedusha Timing

The question regarding *lechem hapanim* is of a different character entirely. *Lechem hapanim midas yavesh* — the *lechem hapanim* is prepared using only dry measures, since it contains no oil and no specified liquid measure of water. And *midas yavesh lo nitkadshu* — Rabbi Akiva holds (in a *sugya* later in the tractate, at 94) that dry measuring vessels were not sanctified. This is the heart of the problem.

The prohibition of *chametz* in a *mincha* requires that the offering possess *kedushas haguf* — intrinsic sanctity. For animals, this sanctity attaches at the moment of *hakdasha*. For *minchos*, however, the established principle is that *kedushas haguf* is conferred by contact with a *kli shares* — a sanctified Temple vessel. Once flour comes into contact with a sanctified vessel, it acquires intrinsic *kedusha* and the prohibition of *chametz* becomes applicable.

But if the dry measuring vessels were not sanctified, then measuring the flour for the *lechem hapanim* does not confer *kedusha*. The water has no specified measure and requires no measuring vessel. The kneading — as will be established shortly — is done on a flat surface, not in a sanctified bowl. The baking oven may or may not be a *kli shares*. If the first moment of contact with a *kli shares* is when the baked loaves are placed on the *shulchan* — the table in the Sanctuary — then *kedushas haguf* is acquired only after baking is complete. At that point, the bread is already fully baked and the possibility of *chametz* is foreclosed. There would therefore be no moment at which the *lechem hapanim* simultaneously possesses *kedushas haguf* and is capable of leavening, making the prohibition of *chametz* inapplicable.

This is why the *baraisa* requires a special derivation — *asher takrivu* — to include the *lechem hapanim*: without it, one might conclude that no transgression is possible given the absence of sanctified contact before baking. And it is this problem that forces the reattribution of positions: whoever rules that *chametz* applies to *lechem hapanim* must hold that dry measures *were* sanctified, since otherwise the prohibition has nothing to attach to at any stage when leavening is still possible.

### Name Reversal

The message transmitted from *Eretz Yisrael* — introduced by *shlach* — confirms the structure but corrects the names. The attribution in the *baraisa* as originally read is reversed: *asher takrivu* is invoked by Rabbi Yose HaGelili to include *lechem hapanim* (meaning he holds dry measures were sanctified), while Rabbi Akiva invokes it to include *minchas nesachim* (meaning he, not Rabbi Yose HaGelili, holds that dry measures were *not* sanctified, and therefore the *chametz* prohibition for *lechem hapanim* does not apply). Rabbi Yochanan explicitly states this reversal is necessary to align the *baraisa* with the known positions of each *tanna*.

### Sanctified Dry

Rabbi Yochanan proceeds to note that Rabbi Yose HaGelili and one of the students of Rabbi Yishmael stated essentially the same position, and identifies that student as Rabbi Yoshiya. In a *baraisa*, the verse *vayimshachem vayikadesh osam* — describing Moshe's anointing and sanctification of the Temple vessels — is parsed carefully. The word *osam* is a limiting term. Rabbi Yoshiya interprets it as limiting, not eliminating: *midas halach nimshachu bein mibifnim bein mibachutz* — liquid measures were anointed both inside and outside; *midas yavesh nimshachu mibifnim ve'ein nimshachu mibachutz* — dry measures were anointed on the inside only, not on the outside. They were therefore sanctified — on the inside — and can confer *kedusha* on what is measured within them. The *kedusha* of the dry measures is thus partial rather than absent. This position aligns with Rabbi Yose HaGelili's ruling that the prohibition of *chametz* applies to *lechem hapanim*.

### Inside Only

Rabbi Yoshiya's position thus reflects a middle path. He does not dispute that there is some difference between the treatment of dry and liquid measures — the verse's limiting force is acknowledged. But the limitation is spatial, not categorical: dry measures lacked the outer anointing but retained the inner anointing that is functionally relevant for sanctifying contents. In this view, *kedushas haguf* would be conferred on the *lechem hapanim* flour when measured in the dry measuring cups of the Sanctuary, making it possible to transgress the *chametz* prohibition during the preparation process.

### Proof Text

Rabbi Yonatan takes the opposing position: *midas yavesh lo nimshechu kol ikar* — dry measures were not sanctified at all. He offers a proof from the verse concerning the *shtei halechem* on Shavuot: *mimoshvoseichem taviu lechem tenufah shtayim shnei esronim solet tihyena chametz teiafena bikurim l'Hashem* — you shall bring from your homes the two loaves, two *esronim* of *solet*, they shall be baked as *chametz*, *bikurim l'Hashem*.

Rabbi Yonatan reads the verse as follows: *eimasi heim l'Hashem l'achar shenaafu* — they are designated *l'Hashem* only after they have been baked. The word *bikurim l'Hashem* does not apply to the loaves before baking, only after. This is because before baking they have not yet acquired intrinsic sanctity — *kedushas haguf* — since no sanctified vessel has been used in their preparation. The *shtei halechem*, like the *lechem hapanim*, contains no oil and thus requires no liquid measuring vessel; the flour would be measured in dry vessels; and since those vessels were not sanctified, no *kedusha* is conferred until the loaves enter the baking oven (which does possess *kedusha*) or are subsequently placed on the *shulchan*.

This proves, in Rabbi Yonatan's view, that the dry measuring vessels do not sanctify their contents, because otherwise the *shtei halechem* would have acquired *kedushas haguf* when measured, long before baking. The fact that the verse locates their status as *l'Hashem* at the point after baking demonstrates that no earlier sanctification occurred.

### Debate Summary

The debate on the sanctification of dry measures thus emerges with three positions. Rabbi Yonatan (aligning with Rabbi Akiva) holds that dry measures were not sanctified at all; the limiting word *osam* excludes the outer anointing of liquid measures but operates against a background assumption that dry measures are simply secular — *midas yavesh chol hu*. Therefore the verse needs no work to exclude them, and *osam* is used instead to limit the liquid measures: even they are anointed on the inside only, not outside. Rabbi Yoshiya (aligning with Rabbi Yose HaGelili) holds that dry measures were sanctified, though only on the inside; *osam* limits their anointing spatially. Rabbi Yochanan notes that Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Yoshiya "said the same thing" — both maintain that dry measures do confer *kedusha*, making it possible to transgress the *chametz* prohibition in preparing the *lechem hapanim*. The question of whether one can align Rabbi Akiva with Rabbi Yonatan is answered negatively, because while their practical positions regarding *lechem hapanim chametz* liability are equivalent, they diverge on the status of liquid measures: Rabbi Akiva holds liquid measures were sanctified inside and outside, while Rabbi Yonatan holds inside only.

---

## Kneading Bowl

### Bisah Question

Rav Pappa poses a further challenge to Abaye: *ve-ha ika bisa de-lachma* — there is the *bisa*, the kneading trough. The *bisa* is a vessel used for kneading dough, and unlike the dry measuring cup, it handles a wetter, more liquidy mixture. Should it not be classified as a liquid vessel, and therefore sanctified? If the *bisa* was a *kli shares* that was sanctified, then the *lechem hapanim* dough would come into contact with a sanctified vessel during kneading — before baking — and would thereby acquire *kedushas haguf* at that earlier stage. If so, the argument that *lechem hapanim* has no opportunity for *chametz* liability would collapse even according to those who hold dry measures were not sanctified.

### Standard Practice

The Gemara responds: *kegon de-lasha al gabei katbalya* — the case is where one kneaded the dough on a flat surface, a butcher block or table, rather than in a kneading bowl. The Torah cannot legislate based on the assumption that the *bisa* will always be used, because there is no requirement to knead in a bowl. Normal bread-making — *lechatchila* — can perfectly well be done on a table. The Torah's prohibitions are addressed to standard, normative practice, and standard practice for kneading bread does not presuppose the use of a *bisa*. Therefore, the possibility of kneading on a table renders the *bisah* argument moot: one cannot assume the sanctified kneading vessel will necessarily be used.

### Measure Vs Knead

The Gemara then raises a follow-up: if this reasoning is accepted, why could Rabbi Yonatan not have responded similarly to the proof from *shtei halechem*? When Rabbi Yonatan argued that *shtei halechem* acquires *kedusha* only after baking because dry measures are not sanctified, one might have countered: perhaps that case involved using an unsanctified household dry measure (*bisa de-chol*) while the sanctified dry measures in the *Mikdash* were in fact sanctified and would have conferred *kedusha*. Why doesn't the "just use a different vessel" argument work there too?

The Gemara's answer establishes a fundamental distinction. When it comes to the *bisa*, the Torah never prescribed its use. Since there is no obligation to knead in a bowl, one cannot assume the Torah's baseline involves a sanctified kneading vessel. *Lo katav rachmana de-leivad be-bisa* — the Torah never said to use a *bisa*. Kneading on a table is entirely normative.

But when it comes to measuring, the Torah explicitly requires *isaron* — a specific measure. *Keivan de-amar rachmana avid isaron* — since the Torah mandates using an *isaron* measure, the Torah's baseline assumption is that one uses the *isaron* of the *Mikdash*, not one brought from home. *Shavik isaron de-kodesh ve-chayal be-isaron de-chol?* — would the Torah simply assume one bypasses the sanctified measuring vessel of the Sanctuary and uses a secular one from home? That assumption is untenable. Since the Torah requires a measured *isaron*, it assumes the standard Sanctuary measuring vessel — and therefore, if that vessel confers no *kedusha*, we learn that the dry measuring vessels are in fact not sanctified.

The lesson is one of asymmetry between prescription and possibility. Where the Torah prescribes a particular act — measuring by *isaron* — we read the Torah as assuming the standard Sanctuary implementation of that act, which makes the sanctity-status of those vessels directly relevant. Where the Torah prescribes no particular implement — kneading — no assumption about which vessel is used can be imposed, and the Torah cannot be read to predicate a prohibition on the contingent use of a *bisa*. This asymmetry resolves the apparent parallel and closes the discussion.

---

---

# Menachot 58

## Chametz in Lechem HaPanim

### Lechem HaPanim Review

The daf begins at 58a, picking up in the middle of 57b with a *tanu rabbanan*. Before turning to new material, it is worth summarizing the preceding discussion, which concerned the prohibition of *chametz* in the context of the *lechem hapanim* and the *minchas nesachim*.

Regarding the *minchas nesachim*, the *gemara*'s central concern was the presence of water. Since *chametz* cannot form without water, the question arose whether water was even a component of the other *menachos* — and the *gemara*'s general assumption is that it was. The same assumption applied to the *minchas nesachim*. Regarding the *lechem hapanim*, a distinct and important question arose: if the dough was rendered *chametz*, why not simply say that it no longer qualifies as a *mincha*? The *gemara* answers that one can only transgress the prohibition of *chametz* in a *mincha* once the dough has been designated with *kedushas haguf* — intrinsic *kedusha* as a *mincha* — which normally occurs when the dough is placed into the designated measuring or kneading vessels. This became complicated by the question of whether the dry measures in the *beis hamikdash* were sanctified as *klei shareis*. If the dough contained no oil — only flour and water — there would be no vessel specifically designated for measuring the water, and the dry measure was used only for flour. Without sanctification through a *kli shareis*, the dough may never have achieved *kedushas haguf* until baking, by which point *chametz* is no longer a risk. That was the crux of the *lechem hapanim* discussion.

### New Derasha Introduction

Having reviewed those conclusions, the *gemara* now pivots to a completely different *derasha* drawn from the same *pasuk* concerning *chametz* — one that yields a fundamentally different prohibition. The transition is marked by a new *tanu rabbanan*, and the focus shifts from what the *pasuk* prohibits in the literal sense to what it implies about other categories of prohibited *haktara* on the *mizbeach*.

---

## Kol Shemimenu L'Ishi (II)

### Tanu Rabbanan Teaching

The *tanu rabbanan* asks: from where do we know that one who takes the meat of a *chatat*, the meat of an *asham*, the meat of any of the other *kodshei kodashim*, or the meat of *kodashim kalim* — items that are ordinarily designated to be eaten — and burns them on the *mizbeach* instead, has transgressed a negative prohibition? The *gemara* clarifies what *kodshei kodashim* apart from *chatat* and *asham* could have edible meat: it is the meat of the *zivchei shalmei tzibur* whose flesh, together with the *shoke v'chazeh*, was eaten on *Shavuos*. The prohibition likewise applies to *mosar ha'omer* — the remainder of the *omer mincha* that the *kohanim* eat after the *kometz* is taken — *mosar shnei halachem*, the entirety of the *shtei halachem* themselves (since no part of the *shtei halachem* itself is ever placed on the *mizbeach*), *lechem hapanim*, and indeed the remnant of any *mincha*.

The source for this prohibition is the *pasuk*: *ki kol se'or v'chol devash lo saktiru mimenu isheh laShem* — you shall not offer up from it a fire-offering to God. How does this *pasuk* yield the prohibition under discussion? The *gemara* reads the phrase *mimenu isheh* — "from it a fire-offering" — as *mimenu l'ishim*: anything from which a portion goes to the fire. The rule derived is *kol shemimenu l'ishim*, *harei hu b'val saktiru*: anything whose designation includes a portion going to the fire, such that another portion is meant to be eaten, is covered by the prohibition of *lo saktiru*. In other words, the *pasuk* about *se'or u'dvash* is being read not merely as a prohibition against bringing leaven or honey to the altar, but as a broader prohibition: if a *korban* has a portion that goes on the *mizbeach*, one may not take the remaining portion — which is meant to be eaten — and burn it on the *mizbeach* as well.

This is conceptually striking. The normal understanding of the prohibition against *chametz* on the *mizbeach* concerns the nature of the physical object — leaven simply does not belong there. Here, however, the physical object in question is entirely appropriate for the *mizbeach*; the issue is purely one of designation. A *kometz* of the same *mincha* dough goes on the *mizbeach* lawfully; it is the remaining portion, designated for eating, that one is forbidden to offer up. The principle is, as it were, that everything must go to its proper place: what is meant to be eaten must be eaten, and what is meant for the *mizbeach* goes on the *mizbeach*.

### Hagasha Requirements

The *gemara* immediately raises a question about the *shtei halachem* and *lechem hapanim*: are these truly considered *shemimenu l'ishim* — that from them goes to the fire? After all, the *shtei halachem* themselves are never placed on the *mizbeach*; it is the *imurin* of the accompanying *kevasim* that are burned. Similarly, by the *lechem hapanim*, it is the *levonah* in the golden dishes on the *shulchan* that is burned, not the bread itself. Can it be said that from these offerings something goes to the fire?

This question is sharpened by a *braisa* discussing *hagasha*. *Hagasha* — the act of touching the *mincha* to the corner of the *mizbeach* before offering — is required for *menachos* whose substance goes on the *mizbeach*. The *braisa* states explicitly that *shtei halachem* and *lechem hapanim* are excluded from *hagasha*, precisely because nothing of the *mincha* itself goes on the fire. Does this mean the *kol shemimenu l'ishim* prohibition likewise does not apply to them?

Rav Sheshet resolves the tension by distinguishing the parameters of these two *halachos*. For *hagasha*, the relevant criterion is narrow: something of the *mincha* itself — not merely something associated with it — must go on the *mizbeach*. Since the *shtei halachem* and *lechem hapanim* do not themselves go on the fire, *hagasha* is inapplicable. There is a clear conceptual logic to this: the act of touching the *mincha* to the *mizbeach* is meaningfully connected only to cases where the *mincha* itself will subsequently ascend there. For the prohibition of *kol shemimenu l'ishim*, however, the operative category is broader: even if the offering itself does not go on the fire but something connected with the package does — the *imurin* of the *kevasim* that accompany the *shtei halachem*, or the *levonah* associated with the *lechem hapanim* — that suffices to trigger the prohibition. Accordingly, the prohibition applies even to the *shtei halachem* and *lechem hapanim*, while the *hagasha* requirement does not. The difference is conceptually sensible: the prohibition is about protecting the appropriate use of each portion of the *korban*, and for that purpose, a broader definition of the "package" is appropriate.

---

## Kibesh Dispute

### Ramp Case Dispute

The *gemara* introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar concerning a case where someone places *chametz* or honey on the *kibesh* — the ramp leading up to the *mizbeach* — rather than on the *mizbeach* proper. Rabbi Yochanan rules the person is *chayav*, while Rabbi Elazar rules the person is *patur*.

The dispute must be understood against the backdrop of a general question, familiar from *Zevachim*, about the status of the *kibesh*: to what degree is the ramp treated as an extension of the *mizbeach* itself? Note that the scenario involves actually burning the item on the ramp — it is not merely a question of placing it there — and so the act does constitute *haktara*. The question is whether doing so on the ramp rather than on the *mizbeach* proper triggers the prohibition.

### Elazar Rationale

Rabbi Elazar's position is grounded in a close reading of the *pasuk*. The verse reads: *ki kol se'or v'chol devash lo saktiru mimenu isheh laShem korban reishit takrivu otam laShem v'el hamizbeach lo ya'alu l'rei'ach nicho'ach*. The phrase *v'el hamizbeach lo ya'alu* — "they shall not ascend toward the *mizbeach*" — uses the word *el*, meaning "toward," which, Rabbi Elazar acknowledges, can extend the prohibition to the ramp. However, he argues that this extension applies only to *se'or u'dvash* themselves, as the *pasuk* reads: *korban reishit takrivu otam* — you shall bring *them* as a *korban reishit*. The word *otam* — "them" — links the clause about ascending toward the *mizbeach* specifically back to *se'or u'dvash*.

The *peshat* of the *pasuk* is instructive: *shtei halachem* are made of *chametz* but are brought as a *korban reishit*; *bikurim* contain *dvash* in the sense of date honey and are also called *reishit* — yet neither goes on the *mizbeach*. Both are kept off the *mizbeach* (*v'el hamizbeach lo ya'alu*) even while being part of the sacrificial package. According to Rabbi Elazar, the ramp prohibition therefore applies specifically to *se'or u'dvash*, since the *pasuk* is talking about them. The new, broader category — items designated to be eaten that are wrongly burned — is a less severe violation, and Rabbi Elazar maintains that transgressing on the ramp applies only to the more stringent case of *se'or u'dvash* proper. There is a certain logic here: *se'or u'dvash* represents an inherent problem with the object itself, whereas the *kol shemimenu l'ishim* category concerns an object that is perfectly legitimate but has been misused. The Torah's focus on keeping *se'or u'dvash* away from the *mizbeach* is accordingly more intense, extending even to the ramp.

### Yochanan on Otam

Rabbi Yochanan, who rules one is *chayav* even on the ramp for all categories, must then account for the word *otam* differently. His answer is that *otam* is needed for an entirely different *derasha* — namely, the teaching that *shtei halachem* cannot be brought as a *nedavah*. That *derasha* is taken up in the following section.

---

## Shtei HaLechem Nedavah

### Nedavah Hypothetical

The *gemara* now addresses the question of whether an individual or the *tzibur* could bring *shtei halachem* as a free-will offering. The *braisa* raises the hypothetical: might one think an individual could voluntarily bring *shtei halachem* as a *nedavah*? The reasoning that would support such a *hava amina* is that one could invoke *motza sefatecha tishmor v'asita* — once one has made a *neder*, one is obligated to fulfill it — and perhaps the *beis din* would permit such an offering. One might further ask: even if an individual cannot bring *shtei halachem* as a *nedavah* since he never brings them as an obligatory *korban*, perhaps the *tzibur* — which does bring *shtei halachem* as a *chovah* on *Shavuos* — could bring them as a *nedavah* on some other occasion?

It should be noted, parenthetically, that there are other *korbanos* of which *chametz* bread is a component — notably the *korban toda*, which includes ten loaves of *chametz* — so the *hava amina* here is not that no *korban* can ever incorporate *chametz* bread. As Rashi notes later on the daf, the bread of the *toda* may even be brought at a somewhat later time than the animal, making it less tightly integrated into the package; the *shtei halachem* by contrast are a more integral part of their *korban*. Regardless, the *gemara* here is focused on whether the *shtei halachem* specifically can come as a *nedavah*.

### Korban Reishit Derasha

The prohibition is derived from the *pasuk*: *korban reishit takrivu* — "you shall bring a *korban reishit*" — the plural "you" referring to the *tzibur*, not an individual. *Korban reishit* encompasses both the *shtei halachem*, which are the first offering of the new wheat crop and are considered a form of *bikurim* and *reishit* before the *mizbeach*, and the *bikurim* themselves, which are called *reishit* as the first fruits. This establishes that the *tzibur* — not the individual — is the one who brings *shtei halachem*.

The *braisa* then asks: perhaps the individual cannot bring *shtei halachem* simply because he never has an obligatory *shtei halachem* offering, and therefore lacks the option of a parallel *nedavah*. But the *tzibur*, which does bring *shtei halachem* as a *chovah* on *Shavuos*, might be permitted to bring them as a *nedavah* at other times. Here is where Rabbi Yochanan deploys the word *otam*: *korban reishit takrivu otam laShem* — "them" you shall bring. The word *otam* restricts the permissible occasions for bringing offerings involving *chametz* or *dvash* to precisely those cases the Torah has prescribed. There is no latitude to bring *shtei halachem* as a *nedavah* — neither by an individual, nor by the *tzibur* on some day other than *Shavuos*. The prescribed cases are: *shtei halachem* from *chametz* on *Shavuos*, and *bikurim* which include *dvash* from dates. Both are *reishit*, both come as part of a package — *v'el hamizbeach lo ya'alu l'rei'ach nicho'ach* — and neither may be offered up on the *mizbeach*. Those are the only permissible contexts; a *nedavah* of *shtei halachem* is thus foreclosed entirely.

### Se'or Hutar Miklalo

Having established that *shtei halachem* cannot come as a *nedavah*, the *gemara* returns to an earlier observation embedded in the *braisa*: the statement that *se'or hutar miklalo bamikdash* — leaven has been permitted as part of a broader package in the *mikdash* — while *devash lo hutar miklalo bamikdash* — honey has never been so permitted. What does this mean?

The *gemara* considers whether *se'or hutar miklalo* refers to the *hava amina* that *shtei halachem* might be brought as a *nedavah*, implying that *se'or* could lawfully enter the *mikdash* in that fashion. Rashi explains that the *hava amina* imagined bringing *shtei halachem* as a *nedavah* without the accompanying *kevasim*, in which case one would be taking a *kometz* and placing it on the *mizbeach* — which would mean actually burning *chametz* on the *mizbeach*. This is of course a striking *hava amina* given all the *pesukim* forbidding *se'or* on the *mizbeach*, but the *gemara* is exploring whether the voluntary context might somehow have permitted it.

Rav Amram resolves the question. *Se'or hutar miklalo bamikdash* does not mean that *se'or* is actually brought on the *mizbeach*; rather, it means that *se'or* is permitted as part of a package in which another component goes on the *mizbeach*. The *shtei halachem* are brought together with the *shtei kevasim*, whose blood and *imurin* are offered on the *mizbeach*. The *shtei halachem* themselves never go on the *mizbeach* — that is the whole point of *v'el hamizbeach lo ya'alu* — but they are *hutar miklalo*: permitted as part of a broader sacrificial package. This, and not any direct offering of *se'or* on the *mizbeach*, is the leniency by *se'or* that distinguishes it from *devash*.

The *gemara* then asks: but does not *devash* also come to the *mikdash* as part of a package, since *bikurim* — which include date honey — are brought there? Could one not say that *dvash* too is *hutar miklalo*? The answer is that with *bikurim*, nothing connected to the *bikurim* themselves goes on the *mizbeach* at all. While the *mishna* records that those bringing *bikurim* would bring turtle doves placed on top of the baskets, which would be offered as *olos*, the *gemara* explains that those birds came merely *le'ater bikurim* — to beautify or accompany the *bikurim* — and have no *halachic* connection to the *bikurim* as such. They are not part of the *bikurim* package in any *halachic* sense; they are simply a nice accompaniment. Therefore *devash* is truly never permitted in the context where any part of the associated package goes on the *mizbeach*, whereas *se'or* is, through the *shtei kevasim* that accompany the *shtei halachem*.

This, then, is the *peshat* of the *pasuk*: *korban reishit takrivu otam v'el hamizbeach lo ya'alu* — bring it as a package together with the *shtei kevasim*, but do not put the *shtei halachem* on the *mizbeach*. To that degree, *se'or* is *hutar miklalo*, even though it never ascends to the *mizbeach* itself.

---

## Kol Shemimenu L'Ishi (II)

### Chatat HaOf Analysis

The *gemara* returns to the *kol shemimenu l'ishim* discussion. Rami bar Chama poses a question to Rav Chisda: does the prohibition against burning the edible portions of a *korban* on the *mizbeach* depend strictly and literally on the criterion of *mimenu l'ishim* — that some part of the same *korban* goes to the fire — or is it actually a broader principle that any *korban* whose edible portions are wrongly burned on the *mizbeach* constitutes a violation?

The test case is the *chatat ha'of*, the bird *chatat*. In a *chatat ha'of*, the blood goes on the *mizbeach*, the *kohanim* eat the flesh, and crucially, no part of the bird is burned on the *mizbeach*. Unlike every other *korban* — where the *kometz* of a *mincha* is burned, or the *imurin* of an animal are burned, or in the case of *shtei halachem* the *imurin* of the accompanying *kevasim* are burned, or in the case of *lechem hapanim* the *levonah* is burned — the *chatat ha'of* has absolutely nothing that goes on the *mizbeach* as a fire-offering. If someone were to take the meat of a *chatat ha'of* and place it on the *mizbeach* rather than eating it, would that constitute a transgression? Or, since no part of it is *mimenu l'ishim*, is there no prohibition?

Rav Chisda answers: it is not the *mimenu l'ishim* that is the operative category, but rather *kol sheshmo korban* — anything that is called a *korban* by the Torah. As long as the Torah designates something as a *korban*, one may not burn the portion designated for eating. The *mimenu l'ishim* was the linguistic hook in the *pasuk* that generated the *derasha*, but the underlying principle, once derived, is broader: any *korban* — even one where nothing is burned on the *mizbeach* — carries the prohibition against burning its edible portions.

### Eliezer vs. Akiva Debate

The *gemara* identifies this dispute as one between *tannaim*. Rabbi Eliezer holds *kol shemimenu l'ishim*: the prohibition applies only when a part of the *korban* goes to the fire, which more starkly designates the remaining portion as the part that is not burned and is to be eaten. Rabbi Akiva holds *kol sheshmo korban*: any *korban* is subject to the prohibition, regardless of whether any of it is burned.

The *nafkah minah* between these positions is precisely the *chatat ha'of*. Rav Chisda identifies the meat of the *chatat ha'of* as the case that divides them. Rava offers an additional case: the *log shemen* of the *metzora*. The *metzora* brings a *log* of oil together with his *korbanos*; no part of the *log* is offered on the *mizbeach*, and the remnant is to be eaten by the *kohanim*. Whether burning that oil on the *mizbeach* would be prohibited depends on whether it is classified as a *korban*. Rava cites a teaching of Levi: *kol korbanam* — "all of their *korbanos*" — *l'rabos log shemen shel metzora*, that this phrase comes to include the *log* of oil of the *metzora*, establishing that it bears the name *korban*. Therefore, under Rabbi Akiva's view, the prohibition applies.

One might ask whether the *log shemen* of the *metzora* is not itself considered *mimenu l'ishim* on the grounds that the *shelamim* of the *metzora* goes on the *mizbeach*, just as the *kevasim* accompanying the *shtei halachem* are considered to make the *shtei halachem mimenu l'ishim*. Rashi addresses this: the *kevasim* and the *shtei halachem* are a tightly integrated package — one cannot bring the *shtei halachem* without the *kevasim*, and the two are halachically inseparable. The *log shemen* of the *metzora*, by contrast, is more separable from the *shelamim* and therefore is not considered *mimenu l'ishim* in the same sense.

Tosafot notes one further implication: although the prohibition against burning edible portions exists, there are circumstances in which it might be necessary to do so — for example, if the limbs of an *olah* become intermingled with the limbs of a *chatat*, there is a dispute among *tannaim* about whether to leave everything at the base of the *mizbeach* until it becomes *pasul* or to place everything on the top of the *mizbeach*. According to the opinion that one places them on top, what of the prohibition against burning the edible portions of the *chatat*? Tosafot explains that in such a case, those pieces are treated as firewood rather than as an offering. They are placed on the *mizbeach* as fuel, not as a sacrificial act, and this framing falls outside the prohibition — which is defined as burning the portions as an *isheh*, not as wood.

In the end, the *gemara* adopts the broader definition: the prohibition against burning edible portions of a *korban* on the *mizbeach* applies to any offering that the Torah designates as a *korban*, not only to those where a separate portion is burned on the *mizbeach*.

---

## Shiur Debate

### Kol as Indicator

The *gemara* now focuses on the word *kol* — "any" — in the *pasuk*'s prohibition: *kol se'or v'chol devash lo saktiru*. A *tanu rabbanan* is cited that derives from this word *kol* that the prohibition applies even to less than a full measure. The question is: why did the Torah need to say *kol* separately by both *se'or* and *dvash*? Could it not have stated it by one and let us infer it applies equally to the other?

The answer is that there are characteristics of *se'or* not shared by *dvash*, and characteristics of *dvash* not shared by *se'or*. Since each has its own *kulos* and *chumros*, one cannot learn the rule of "even a small amount" from one to the other. The differences: *se'or hutar miklalo bamikdash* — as discussed above, *se'or* is permitted as part of a broader package involving the *mizbeach*, which *devash* is not — while *dvash hutar b'shirei mincha* — the remnant of the *mincha* that the *kohanim* eat may have honey added to it, an allowance that does not exist for *chametz*, since *lo te'afeh chametz chelkam* prohibits even letting the remnant become *chametz*. Since each substance has a relevant leniency that the other lacks, neither can serve as a model for the other with respect to the *kol*, and therefore both must state it explicitly.

### Abaye Position

Abaye reads the *tanu rabbanan* as follows. When the Torah says *se'or bal taktiru*, one might have thought one only transgresses with a *kezayit* — the normal minimum measure we associate with acts of eating and the like. The word *kol* teaches that one transgresses even with half of a *kezayit*. And once the threshold is below a full *kezayit*, there is no further minimum — any amount whatsoever is sufficient. For Abaye, then, the practical outcome is that the prohibition is violated by even an infinitesimal amount. The same reasoning is then applied to *devash* via the phrase *ki chol*, understood as an intensifier indicating that even in any form — including mixed into a *taarovet* — one transgresses.

### Rava Position

Rava reads the *tanu rabbanan* differently. The baseline measure for *haktara*, he argues, is a *kometz* — not a *kezayit* — since that is the normative amount offered on the *mizbeach* in the context of a *mincha*. When the Torah says one transgresses even a lesser amount and uses the word *kol*, it means even half of a *kometz*. For Rava, one transgresses even without a full *kometz*, but one must still have at least a *kezayit*, since half of a *kometz* is still at least a *kezayit*.

### Kometz Baseline

The *gemara* clarifies that both Abaye and Rava agree that the point of departure is a *kometz*, not a *kezayit*. Abaye also begins from the *kometz*, but holds that a *kometz* may exist that is less than two *zeitim* in volume. When the Torah says to transgress even with half the normal amount, half of a sub-two-*zayit kometz* yields less than a *kezayit*, and therefore *yesh haktara pechutas mikezayit* — an act of *haktara* less than a *kezayit* is halachically cognizable. Once one is below a *kezayit*, there is effectively no lower limit.

Rava, by contrast, holds *ein kometz pachot mishnei zeitim* — a *kometz* is always at least two *zeitim*. Halving a *kometz* therefore still yields at least one *kezayit*, and *ein haktara pechutas mikezayit* — an act of *haktara* requires at minimum a *kezayit*. Tosafot notes that this question — whether *haktara* requires a *kezayit* — has implications in other areas as well, such as the debate regarding *machshevet pigul* (where a *kezayit* is the relevant measure, possibly because of its connection to *achila*) versus *ma'aleh bechutz* (where the relevant measure for *chiyuv* is a *kometz*).

---

## Ta'aroves Lashes

### Rava: Four Lashes

The *gemara* now addresses the question of *malkos* for someone who places *se'or* and *dvash* together on the *mizbeach*, including separate quantities and a *taarovet* — a mixture of the two. Rava's position is that such a person receives four sets of *malkos*: one for the *se'or* alone, one for the *dvash* alone, one for the *taarovet* of *se'or* (which violates *kol se'or*), and one for the *taarovet* of *dvash* (which violates *kol dvash*). Tosafot understands the physical case as follows: there is a discrete quantity of *se'or* on one side, a discrete quantity of *dvash* on the other, and a mixture of the two in the middle. The pure *se'or* yields one *lav*; the pure *dvash* yields another; in the middle the mixture violates both *kol se'or* and *kol dvash*, thus generating two additional sets of *malkos*.

### Abaye: Generic Lav

Abaye, citing Rav Chisda, holds *ein lokin alav shebiklalos* — one does not receive *malkos* for a *lav shebiklalos*, a prohibition that is expressed in generic or broadly inclusive terms. The prohibition *kol se'or v'chol dvash* — especially via the expansive word *kol* and the further extension *ki chol* — encompasses *se'or* alone, *dvash* alone, *taarovet se'or*, *taarovet dvash*, and countless other combinations and forms. Because the prohibition's *taarovet* aspect sweeps in an indefinite range of possibilities, it constitutes a *lav shebiklalos* for which *malkos* are not administered. Abaye therefore does not give *malkos* for the mixed portions.

### Tosafot Interpretation

The *gemara* records two versions of Abaye's position. According to one version, *chada miha laki* — one receives at least one set of *malkos* for any form of *taarovet*, regardless of its composition. According to the other, *chada nami lo laki* — one does not even receive one set, because the *lav* is not sufficiently singled out in the manner of the paradigmatic prohibition of *chasimah* — *lo sachsom shor b'disho* — which the Torah juxtaposes with the laws of *malkos* and which is therefore the model of the specific, well-defined prohibition that warrants lashes.

Tosafot considers the more radical reading — that the *lav shebiklalos* disqualifies the entire *pasuk* from generating *malkos* for any of its elements, including even straight *se'or* or straight *dvash* — and rejects it as too extreme, pointing to numerous cases where one clearly does receive *malkos* for prohibitions stated in inclusive language. The simpler reading, endorsed by Rashi as well, is that one still receives *malkos* for the *se'or* and *dvash* taken separately; the debate between Abaye and Rava concerns only the middle portion, the mixture. Rava says the mixture generates two sets of *malkos* — one for *taarovet se'or* and one for *taarovet dvash*. Abaye says either zero — because the generic category of *taarovet* is too broad a *lav shebiklalos* to warrant any *malkos* — or, at most, one, because while a single generic *lav* may still yield a single set of *malkos*, the same act of mixing cannot generate separate *malkos* for the *se'or*-mixture dimension and the *dvash*-mixture dimension, since both fall under the same undifferentiated *lav*. With this discussion, the *gemara* concludes the relevant sugya and turns to a new *mishna*.

---

---

# Menachot 59

## Oil & Frankincense

### Four Categories

The *mishnah* at the top of 59a opens in the middle of the *perek*'s broader discussion of the physical constitution of *menachot*. The previous *mishnah* had established that all *menachot* are kneaded with lukewarm water and that one must take great care to prevent them from becoming *chametz*. Our *mishnah* now turns to features that distinguish one *mincha* from another, beginning with the requirements of oil and frankincense. Four categories are enumerated: *menachot* requiring both oil and frankincense, those requiring oil but not frankincense, those requiring frankincense but not oil, and those requiring neither.

### Require Both

The *mishnah* identifies the following as requiring both oil and frankincense: *minchat hasolet*, *hamachavat*, *hamarcheshet*, *hachalot*, and *harikikin* — that is, all the standard voluntary *menachot* described at the opening of Vayikra, whether of plain flour, a pan, a deep pan, loaves, or wafers. To these the *mishnah* adds *minchat kohanim* — a *mincha* brought by a *kohen*, which shares the same physical composition as a standard *mincha* even though the entire offering is burnt on the *mizbeach* rather than having a *komets* separated. Similarly included are *minchat kohen mashiach*, the *chavitin* brought by the anointed *kohen* in two halves daily; *minchat ovdei kochavim*, since non-Jews may bring *korbanot*; *minchat nashim*, since nothing in the *pesukim* suggests any difference between a *korban* brought by a man or a woman; and *minchat ha'omer*, the *mincha* of the *omer*, which likewise requires both oil and frankincense.

### Nesachim Category

By contrast, *minchat nesachim* — the flour-and-oil *mincha* accompanying an animal *korban*, together with the wine libation — requires oil but not frankincense. The reasoning, as the *Gemara* will develop, is that the *minchat nesachim* is not an independent offering but rather an accompaniment to the animal *korban*, and the *pesukim* describing it mention only flour and oil, never frankincense.

### Lechem Hapanim

The *lechem hapanim*, the showbread arranged on the *shulchan* in the *Heichal*, falls into the inverse category: it requires frankincense but not oil. The bread itself is made of plain flour and water. The frankincense, placed in two small vessels on the *shulchan*, is what is offered on the *mizbeach*, while the bread itself is eaten by the *kohanim*. That this most prominent of Temple fixtures contains no oil is striking, and the *Gemara* will address it directly.

### Neither Oil/Frankinc.

The final category — neither oil nor frankincense — comprises *shtei halechem*, *minchat chotei*, and *minchat kenaot*. The *shtei halechem* of Shavuot is made of flour and water and, unlike the *lechem hapanim*, has no frankincense offered alongside it; the *kivsei atzeret* are offered separately, and since the *shtei halechem* itself is *chametz*, nothing directly attached to it is burnt on the *mizbeach*. The *minchat chotei*, the *mincha* variant within the *korban oleh ve'yored* for certain sins, explicitly lacks both oil and frankincense, since these beautifying and fragrant additions would be incongruous with an offering of atonement. And the *minchat kenaot*, brought on behalf of a woman suspected of adultery, is likewise explicitly stripped of both, as the Torah states: *lo yiten aleha shemen v'lo yasim aleha levonah ki minchat kenaot hi minchat zikaron mazkeres avon* — "he shall place on it neither oil nor frankincense, for it is a *minchat kenaot*, a *mincha* of remembrance, recalling sin."

---

## Rav Papa's Ruling

### Rav Papa Intro

The *Gemara* opens this section with a statement of Rav Papa: *kol heicha d'tnan esser tnan* — "whenever we state [a type of *mincha*] in the *mishnah*, we mean ten [*chalos*]." The point is that each type of *mincha* mentioned in the *mishnah* is brought in units of ten.

### Two Explanations

Rashi offers two distinct explanations of this remark. The first is straightforward: when the *mishnah* enumerates types of *menachot* — *machavas*, *marcheshes*, *chalos*, *rekikin* — it means that each type is brought as ten units. The second explanation is more ingenious: count the *menachot* listed in the *mishnah* as requiring both oil and frankincense, and you arrive at exactly ten. *Solet* is one; *machavas*, *marcheshes*, *chalos*, *rekikin* bring the total to five; *minchat kohanim* is six, *minchat kohen mashiach* seven, *minchat ovdei kochavim* eight, *minchat nashim* nine, and *minchat ha'omer* ten.

### Vs. Rabbi Shimon

Either way, Rav Papa's statement is directed against the position of Rabbi Shimon. A later *mishnah* records a dispute about the *minchat ma'afeh tanur*, the oven-baked *mincha*. The Torah there mentions both *chalos matzos belulos bashemen* and *rekikei matzos meshuchim bashemen*, presenting both loaves and wafers. Rabbi Shimon reads this as permitting a mixture: one could bring half *chalos* and half *rekikin*, or any proportional combination including an equal split of five and five. The *Hachamim* disagree, holding that the Torah presents two discrete options — either all ten are *chalos* or all ten are *rekikin* — with no mixing permitted. According to Rabbi Shimon, there would be an eleventh valid category: a *mincha* comprising five *chalos* and five *rekikin*. Rav Papa's ruling — whether understood as "ten of each type" or "ten types total" — thus establishes that our *mishnah* does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

---

## Oil Derivation

### Pasuk ונתת שמן

The *Gemara* now turns to the Talmudic derivation underlying the categories established by the *mishnah*, beginning with the requirement of oil. The *baraita* cites the *pasuk* in Vayikra 2:14-15, which describes the *minchat ha'omer*: *v'nasata aleha shemen v'samta aleha levonah mincha hi* — "you shall place on it oil and put on it frankincense, it is a *mincha*." From the word *aleha* — "on it" — the *Gemara* derives: oil on *this* and not on the *lechem hapanim*. The *lechem hapanim* is nowhere explicitly told to receive oil, and the word *aleha* functions as a limiting term, confining the oil requirement to the *menachot* under immediate discussion.

### Kal Vachomer Logic

One might, however, have reasoned otherwise. The *Gemara* voices a *kal vachomer*: if the *minchat nesachim*, which does not require frankincense, nevertheless requires oil, then the *lechem hapanim*, which does require frankincense and is therefore in some sense "weightier," should certainly require oil as well. If requirements are assumed to stack linearly — that a *mincha* possessing one element should possess the other as well — then the *lechem hapanim*, which already has the frankincense the *minchat nesachim* lacks, ought also to have oil.

### Talmud Lomar

The *Talmud lomar* rejects this inference: *aleha shemen* — on *it*, oil, and not on the *lechem hapanim*. The word *aleha* forecloses the *kal vachomer* by insisting that the requirement remains where it is stated and does not travel to contexts where it is not. The *lechem hapanim* does not mention oil; it does not receive oil.

---

## Frankincense Derivation

### Pasuk לבונה

The same *pasuk* then yields the parallel derivation for frankincense: *v'nasata aleha levonah* — "you shall place on it frankincense." Here *aleha* likewise functions as a limiting term: frankincense goes on *this* — the *omer* and the *menachot* explicitly mentioned — and not on the *minchat nesachim*, which nowhere mentions frankincense. The *Gemara* states: *aleha levonah v'lo le-minchat nesachim levonah* — the frankincense requirement stays with the *menachot* where it is spoken, and may not be extended to those where it is silent.

### Kal Vachomer (Frankinc.)

Again, a *kal vachomer* might have suggested otherwise. We have just learned from a *pasuk* that the *lechem hapanim* receives no oil and yet receives frankincense. If the *lechem hapanim*, which lacks oil, still gets frankincense, then the *minchat nesachim*, which does have oil and is therefore in some sense more substantial, should certainly receive frankincense as well. The logic is the same as before: if the lesser has the feature, the greater should too.

### Limit Frankincense

The *Talmud lomar* again closes this off: *aleha levonah v'lo le-minchat nesachim levonah*. Keep the frankincense requirement where the Torah placed it; do not extend it through inference to the *minchat nesachim*. The *Gemara* then turns to the final word of the *pasuk*, *mincha hi* — "it is a *mincha*." The word *mincha* functions inclusively, extending the oil and frankincense requirement to the *mincha* brought on the eighth day of the *miluim*, which was not otherwise mentioned. The word *hi* ("it") then functions as a limitation, excluding the *shtei halechem*, for which neither oil nor frankincense was mentioned. The principle throughout is consistent: read the *pesukim* as they stand. Where oil is not mentioned — as by the *lechem hapanim* — do not add it. Where frankincense is not mentioned — as by the *minchat nesachim* — do not add it. Where neither is mentioned — as by the *shtei halechem* — add neither.

---

## Minchat Kohanim

### Question Posed

Having established these derivations, the *Gemara* begins to interrogate them. If *aleha shemen* is a limiting term that excludes the *lechem hapanim* from receiving oil, why should it not equally exclude the *minchat kohanim*? After all, the Torah does not explicitly say oil by the *minchat kohanim* either. If the *pasuk* is being read as an exclusion, perhaps it is the *minchat kohanim* that should be on the outside.

### Include Position

The *Gemara* answers: *mistabra minchat kohanim hava lei le-ribuy* — it is more reasonable to assume that the *minchat kohanim* falls within the included group of standard *menachot* and that the *lechem hapanim* is what stands apart. The question is which side of the line each offering belongs on, and the *Gemara* now marshals the evidence.

### Shared Features

A series of similarities between *minchat kohanim* and the standard *menachot* is adduced. First, *isaron*: both a standard *mincha* and a *minchat kohen* use an *isaron* of *solet*, whereas the *lechem hapanim* uses a substantially larger measure. Second, *kli*: both are prepared using a *kli sharet*, a sacred vessel, whereas the *lechem hapanim* is sanctified in the oven or on the *shulchan*. Third, *chutz*: both the standard *menachot* and the *minchat kohen* are performed in the *azarah*, outside the *Heichal* proper, whereas the *lechem hapanim* is placed inside the *Heichal* itself. Fourth, *tzura*: both become invalid (*pasul*) by the following morning, losing their valid form overnight — the *lechem hapanim* by contrast remains on the *shulchan* throughout the entire week. Fifth, *hagasha*: both a standard *mincha* and a *minchat kohen* undergo *hagasha*, the touching of the *mincha* to the *mizbeach*, which is not done for the *lechem hapanim*. Sixth, *ishim*: some part of both goes onto the *mizbeach* fire — the *komets* of a standard *mincha* and the entire *minchat kohen* — whereas of the *lechem hapanim* itself nothing is placed on the *mizbeach*; only the *levona* from its accompanying vessels is burnt.

### Counter Position

The *Gemara* pushes back: *adaraba*, the opposite. Perhaps it is the *lechem hapanim* that should be included with the standard *menachot*, and the *minchat kohanim* that should stand apart. On a different set of criteria, the *lechem hapanim* resembles the *minchat ha'omer* — the very *mincha* whose *pasuk* is under discussion — more closely than the *minchat kohanim* does.

### LH Similarities

Several points of comparison are enumerated. First, *tzibur*: the *lechem hapanim* is a *korban tzibur*, a communal offering, as is the *minchat ha'omer*, whereas the *minchat kohanim* is always a *korban yachid*, an individual's offering. Second, *chova*: the *lechem hapanim* is obligatory, as are the *omer* and other fixed *menachot*, whereas the *minchat kohanim* is always a voluntary, free-will offering. Third, *tumah*: the *lechem hapanim* and the communal *menachot* are subject to the principle of *tumah hutrah b'tzibur* — communal obligations override impurity and may be offered even in a state of *tumah* — whereas the *minchat kohanim*, being a *yachid* offering and always voluntary, would never override *tumah*. Fourth, *achilah*: the *lechem hapanim* is eaten by the *kohanim*, as are the portions of standard *menachot* not burnt on the *mizbeach*, whereas the *minchat kohanim* is entirely burnt. Fifth, *pigul*: the *lechem hapanim* and standard *menachot* can become *pigul*, since they have a *matir* — the *komets* in the case of a standard *mincha*, and the *levona* in the case of the *lechem hapanim* — whereas the *minchat kohanim*, being entirely burnt with no remaining portion, has no *matir* and therefore cannot become *pigul*. Sixth, *Shabbat*: the *omer* and other obligatory communal *menachot* override *Shabbat*, whereas the *minchat kohanim* does not.

### Nefesh Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the impasse by identifying *nefesh* as the decisive criterion. The opening *pasuk* of the *mincha* laws in Vayikra 2:1 reads: *v'nefesh ki takriv korban mincha l'Hashem solet yihiyeh korbano v'yatzak aleha shemen v'natan aleha levona* — "when a soul brings a *mincha* offering to Hashem, it shall be of *solet*, and he shall pour oil on it and place frankincense on it." The word *nefesh* — "soul," denoting an individual — frames the entire discussion of oil and frankincense as applying to personal, individual offerings. Since the *minchat kohanim* is always the *korban* of a private individual, it falls naturally within this framework. The *lechem hapanim*, a communal offering brought by the *tzibur*, stands outside this framework, and that is why it does not receive oil. Rashi further notes that even beyond the *pasuk* of the *omer*, which has been the textual focus, the very first *pasuk* of the *mincha* laws leads with *nefesh* and immediately prescribes oil and frankincense, making clear that oil and frankincense are the hallmarks of the individual *mincha*. The *minchat kohanim* is included; the *lechem hapanim* is excluded.

---

## Minchat Nesachim

### Question Posed

The *Gemara* now applies the same structure to the frankincense derivation. If *aleha levonah* is limiting and excludes the *minchat nesachim* from receiving frankincense, why should it not instead exclude the *minchat kohanim*? The *minchat kohanim* also does not have frankincense explicitly mentioned in its own *parasha*. Perhaps it is the *minchat kohanim* that should be on the outside.

### Exclude Position

The *Gemara* responds: *mistabra minchat kohanim hava lei le-ribuy* — it is more reasonable to keep the *minchat kohanim* inside the standard group, and to read the *pasuk* as excluding the *minchat nesachim*. The evidence is again marshaled comparatively.

### MK Differences

A series of ways in which the *minchat kohanim* resembles standard *menachot* — and the *minchat nesachim* does not — is presented. *Isaron*: the *minchat kohanim* uses one *isaron* of flour, as does a standard *mincha*, whereas the *minchat nesachim* varies in quantity depending on the animal it accompanies. *Balul*: the *minchat kohanim* is described as mixed with oil (*belulah bashemen*), the same language used for standard *menachot*, whereas the *minchat nesachim* mentions oil but not this mixing formulation. *B'log*: the *minchat kohanim* uses only a *log* of oil, as do standard *menachot*, whereas the *minchat nesachim* requires multiple *logim* depending on the animal. *Mugash*: the *minchat kohanim* undergoes *hagasha*, the presentation to the *mizbeach*, as do standard *menachot*, whereas *hagasha* is not performed for the *minchat nesachim*. *Biglal atzmo*: the *minchat kohanim* is brought in its own right as an independent offering, whereas the *minchat nesachim* is brought only as an accompaniment to a primary animal *korban*.

### MN Similarities

The *Gemara* counters: *adaraba*, one could argue that the *minchat nesachim* should be on the inside, and it is the *minchat kohanim* that should be excluded.

### MN Characteristics

*Tzibur*: the *minchat nesachim* accompanies communal *korbanot* such as the *korban tamid* and *musaf*, just as the *omer* is a communal *korban*, whereas the *minchat kohanim* is always a private offering. *Chova*: the *minchat nesachim* accompanying obligatory *korbanot* is itself obligatory, just as the *omer* is obligatory, whereas the *minchat kohanim* is always voluntary. *Tumah*: since the *minchat nesachim* accompanies *korbanot* that can be brought in a state of *tumah* when the community is impure, the *nesachim* themselves can be brought in that state — something never applicable to the *minchat kohanim*. *Shabbat*: the *minchat nesachim* is brought on *Shabbat* when it accompanies the *korban tamid* or *musaf*; the *minchat kohanim* is never brought on *Shabbat*.

### Nefesh Resolution

The resolution is the same as before: *mistabra nefesh*. The opening *pesukim* of the *mincha* laws frame oil and frankincense as characteristics of the personal, individual *nefesh* offering. Any *korban* that is personal — including the *minchat kohanim* — is thus naturally included in the requirement of oil and frankincense. What is excluded are offerings that fall outside that personal framework: the *minchat nesachim*, which is not an independent *nefesh* offering but an accompaniment, and the communal *shtei halechem*, *lechem hapanim*, and similar offerings. The various *pasuk* words — *aleha*, *aleha*, *hi* — simply reinforce: do not extend what is not written, and read each *mincha* according to its own *pesukim*.

---

## Shtei Halechem

### Question Posed

The *Gemara* applies the identical framework a third time, now regarding *shtei halechem*. If *hi* is coming to exclude *shtei halechem* from receiving oil and frankincense, why should it not instead exclude the *minchat kohanim*? Once again, the *minchat kohanim* does not have oil and frankincense explicitly stated in its own *parasha*.

### Exclude Position

The *Gemara* answers: *mistabra minchat kohanim hava lei le-ribuy* — it is more reasonable to include the *minchat kohanim* with the standard *menachot* and to read the exclusion as applying to the *shtei halechem*. The *minchat kohanim* bears numerous characteristics that align it with standard *menachot* rather than with *shtei halechem*.

### MK Differences

*Isaron*: the *minchat kohanim* and standard *menachot* are each brought as an *isaron* of flour, whereas the *shtei halechem* is not measured in *esronim* in the same way. *Kli*: standard *menachot* and *minchat kohanim* are kneaded or prepared in a *kli sharet*, whereas the *shtei halechem* — like the *lechem hapanim* — is sanctified in the *tanur*, and indeed it is *pasul* if kneaded in a *kli sharet*. *Matza*: all standard *menachot* are *matza*, and the *minchat kohanim* is likewise *matza*, whereas the *shtei halechem* is explicitly *chametz*. *Ve'etzem*: the *minchat kohanim* and standard *menachot* are each brought independently, *biglal atzmo*, on their own account, whereas the *shtei halechem* comes together with the *kivsei atzeret*. *Hagasha*: standard *menachot* and *minchat kohanim* undergo *hagasha*, whereas this is not performed for the *shtei halechem*. *Ishim*: some part of both a standard *mincha* and a *minchat kohanim* — whether the *komets* or the entire offering — is placed on the *mizbeach* fire, whereas nothing of the *shtei halechem* itself goes on the *mizbeach*.

### SH Similarities

The *Gemara* again counters: *adaraba*, one could argue that the *shtei halechem* is in fact the offering most similar to the *omer* — the very *mincha* whose *pasuk* anchors this entire derivation — and should therefore be included.

### SH Characteristics

A lengthy and detailed enumeration follows. *Tzibur*: the *shtei halechem* is a *korban tzibur*, as is the *omer*. *Chova*: both are obligatory. *Docheh tumah* and *docheh Shabbat*: both override impurity and *Shabbat* by virtue of being obligatory communal offerings. *Achilah*: both the *omer* and the *shtei halechem* are eaten — standard *menachot* have a portion eaten by the *kohanim* — whereas the *minchat kohanim* is entirely burnt. *Pigul*: both the *omer* and the *shtei halechem* have a *matir* and can therefore become *pigul*; the *minchat kohanim*, being entirely burnt, cannot. *Tnufa*: both the *omer* and the *shtei halechem* are waved (*tenufa*), whereas ordinary *menachot* are not waved, and the *minchat kohanim* is not waved. *Ba'aretz*: both must come from grain grown in *Eretz Yisrael*. *Bizman*: both come at a fixed, specific time — the *omer* on Pesach, the *shtei halechem* on Shavuot. *Chadash*: both come from the new grain. Indeed, the *shtei halechem* and the *minchat ha'omer* are genuinely parallel offerings: one from barley, one from wheat; one permitting the new grain to the populace outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, the other permitting the new grain to be brought as an offering within it. The *Gemara* notes that the list of similarities here is actually more numerous (*v'hani nefishin*) than in the previous cases.

### Nefesh Final

Nevertheless, the conclusion is the same: *mistabra nefesh*. Despite the remarkable convergence between *shtei halechem* and *minchat ha'omer*, *nefesh* is the decisive factor. Oil and frankincense are the markers of the individual, personal *mincha* — the offering of a *nefesh*. The *shtei halechem* is not a *nefesh* offering; it is communal, and frankincense and oil are not mentioned in its *parasha*. Therefore it does not receive them.

The governing principle of this entire sugya is thus made fully explicit: the various words *aleha*, *aleha*, and *hi* throughout the *pasuk* are each saying the same thing — do not go beyond what the Torah states. Where oil is not mentioned, do not add it; where frankincense is not mentioned, do not add it; where neither is mentioned, add neither. The only reason the *Gemara* raises the question of *minchat kohanim* at all — in each of the three iterations — is that the *minchat kohanim* also lacks explicit mention of oil and frankincense in its own *parasha*, and one might therefore have thought it should be excluded along with *lechem hapanim*, *minchat nesachim*, and *shtei halechem*. The answer in every case is *nefesh*: the *minchat kohanim* is the offering of an individual *nefesh* and is therefore naturally drawn into the group of personal *menachot* that receive oil and frankincense, while the non-*nefesh* offerings remain outside.

---

---

# Menachot 59b

## Shemen v'Levonah

### Intro: Menachot Types

The *mishnah* on 59b continues the discussion of the different types of *menachos* and their constituent ingredients. The *mishnah* on 59a had established that some *menachos* receive both oil and *levonah* (frankincense), some receive one or the other, and some receive neither. The two offerings that receive neither are the *minchas chotei* — the sin-offering *minchah* brought in the context of a *korban oleh v'yored*, whose form varies according to the donor's economic means — and the *minchas kena'os*, the *minchah* of a *sotah*. In both of these cases the *Torah* states explicitly: *lo yasim aleha shemen v'lo yiten aleha levonah* — one may not place oil on it nor give frankincense upon it. This constitutes a negative prohibition, and it is the subject of the present *mishnah*.

### Oil/Frankincense Transgr…

The *mishnah* establishes that one transgresses the prohibition for placing oil alone and for placing *levonah* alone; even a single violation is sufficient. Furthermore, if one places oil on the *minchah*, the *mishnah* states *nasan aleha shemen pasalah* — one has not only transgressed but has invalidated the *minchah*, rendering it unfit for use. The *levonah*, by contrast, is different: *yelaktenah*, one simply picks it off, and the *minchah* remains *kasher*. This is because *levonah* — as has been noted previously — is not like salt or other loose substances but resembles crystals or pebble-like granules, and it can therefore be physically removed from the surface of the flour. One transgresses even though the violation is correctable.

The *mishnah* then adds: *nasan shemen al sheyareha eino over b'lo sa'aseh* — if one places oil upon the *shirayim*, the remnants of the *minchah* after the *kemitzah* has been taken, one does not transgress the negative prohibition. This is in contrast to the prohibition of *lo sei'aseh chametz mechlekam*, which applies even to remnants. The implication is that the prohibition of oil applies specifically before the *minchah* has been fully processed, not to the remnants afterward.

### Oil vs. Frankincense

A *baraita* is introduced that makes the distinction explicit. The verse states *lo yasim aleha shemen* — do not place oil on it — and *if* one places it, one has invalidated. One might think the same is true of *levonah*: place it and it is invalidated. The *baraita* explains the asymmetry: *posolni bashemen she'ee efshar lekato* — oil invalidates because it is impossible to gather it back up once absorbed — *u'machshirni be'levonah she'efshar lilketa* — but *levonah* leaves the *minchah kasher* because it can be picked off and removed. The physical reality of absorption versus removability is the operative distinction.

### Vessel Upon Vessel

The *mishnah* also clarifies that *nasan kli al gabei kli lo pasalah* — if one placed a vessel containing oil on top of the *minchah*, the *minchah* is not invalidated. The prohibition of *lo yasim aleha shemen* is understood to mean direct application; placing oil in a vessel that rests on the *minchah* does not constitute the prohibited act. By the same logic, such an act would presumably not constitute a transgression either.

One might raise the question — drawn from the laws of *lav hanitak la'aseh* — of why one transgresses when the *levonah* can be removed. The answer is that the concept of *lav hanitak la'aseh* requires a specific *mitzvat aseh* linked to the prohibition; the mere fact that a violation is physically reversible does not prevent transgression. One can, for example, turn on a light on *Shabbos* and extinguish it afterward, and the transgression has occurred regardless.

### Baraita: Oil/Frankincense

The *baraita* thus presents the rule cleanly: oil, once applied, is absorbed and cannot be recovered, so it invalidates; *levonah*, being crystalline and unabsorbed, can be picked off and the *minchah* restored. The word *ki chatas* — "for it is a *chatas*" — in the relevant verse signals that even after a foreign substance has been placed, the *minchah* retains its status as a *chatas*, provided it can be corrected.

A question arises regarding who may actually transgress this prohibition. It need not be the *kohen* alone. Since some stages of the *minchah*'s preparation — in particular *kiddush kli*, the sanctification in a vessel — can occur before the *kohen* takes over at the stage of *kemitzah*, the owner of the *minchah* could theoretically apply oil or *levonah* and thereby transgress.

### Ground Frankincense

*Rava bar bar Chanah* posed a question to *Rabbi Yochanan*: *natan lah levonah shechukah mahu* — what is the rule if one took *levonah* and ground it to a powder, reducing the crystals to something resembling fine salt? Such ground *levonah* would embed itself within the flour of the *minchah*, becoming so thoroughly mixed that it could not be gathered up and removed. Does this constitute an invalidation?

The question has two possible framings. The *baraita* said that *levonah* does not invalidate because *efshar lilketa* — it can be picked off. If that is the operative criterion, then ground *levonah*, which cannot be picked off, would invalidate the *minchah*. But perhaps the real criterion is simply *d'lo mivla* — that it is not absorbed into the substance of the flour itself. Ground *levonah* mixed with flour is, after all, analogous to *yavesh beyavesh* — discrete particles sitting adjacent to one another — even if the mixture is inseparable in practice. If non-absorption is the standard, then even ground *levonah* would not invalidate, since each granule merely rests beside each kernel without chemically infusing into it.

There is an additional practical complication: if ground *levonah* is mixed throughout the flour, how could one perform *kemitzah*? A *kemitzah* taken from such a mixture would be a *kemitzah chaserah* — deficient — since it would not consist entirely of the correct ingredient. The *gemara* does not directly address this concern at this stage, proceeding instead with the theoretical question of invalidation.

### Absorption vs. Removal

*Rav Huna* asks the same question of *Rabbi Yochanan* and frames it as follows: is the *kashrut* of *levonah* on a *minchah* predicated on the fact that *efshar lilketa* — it can physically be gathered up — or is it sufficient that *lo mivla* — it is not absorbed? The *mishnah* itself says *yelaktenah*, pick it off. The *baraita* likewise says it is *kasher* because it can be picked off. The *gemara* attempts to argue that these sources perhaps state *chada v'od* — one condition and an additional stronger one — meaning: first, it is not absorbed (*d'lo mivla*), and second, as a further advantage, it can actually be removed. On this reading, non-absorption alone might be sufficient.

However, when pressed, *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* cites a *baraita* that settles the matter. The *baraita* rules that if *levonah* was placed on a *minchas chotei* or *minchas kena'os*, one removes it and the *minchah* is *kesheirah*. Crucially, the *baraita* then specifies: if before the *levonah* was removed a *kohen* entertained a *machshavah* — a disqualifying intention — of *chutz lizmano* (the wrong time, yielding *pigul*) or *chutz limkomo* (the wrong place), the *minchah* is *pasul* but carries no *karet*. After the *levonah* is removed, a subsequent thought of *chutz lizmano* does create *pigul* with *karet*.

The proof is decisive: if the *minchah* were *kasher* even while the *levonah* remained (provided only that the *levonah* is not absorbed), one would expect a *pigul* thought at that stage to take full effect. But the *baraita* shows that while the *levonah* is present, the thought does not achieve the status of *pigul* — it produces *psul* without *karet* — because the *minchah* is in a *pasul* state. Only once the *levonah* is actually removed does the *minchah* return to full *kashrut*, and only then can a subsequent thought create *pigul* with *karet*. The conclusion is therefore that physical removal is required, not merely non-absorption. If the *levonah* cannot be removed — as in the case of ground *levonah* — the *minchah* remains *pasul*.

---

## Reversibility & Dachuy

### Baraita: Removal & Pigul

The *baraita* cited by *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* presents the following scenario in full: if *levonah* was placed on a *minchas chotei* or *minchas kena'os*, one picks off the *levonah* and it becomes *kesheirah*. If, however, before the *levonah* was removed a *kohen* had a thought of *chutz lizmano* or *chutz limkomo*, the *minchah* is *pasul* and there is no *karet*. The reason a *chutz lizmano* thought does not generate *pigul* at this stage is that the *minchah* is currently *pasul* due to the presence of the *levonah*, and one cannot render a *pasul* offering into *pigul*. After the *levonah* is removed, the *minchah* is restored to *kashrut*, and a subsequent *chutz lizmano* thought would create full *pigul* with *karet*.

*Rashi* and *Tosafot* interpret the *baraita* somewhat differently. According to *Tosafot*, the *pasul* mentioned in the *baraita* — the result of the *machshavah* before the *levonah* is removed — simply describes the existing state: the *minchah* is *pasul* because the *levonah* is on it, not because the thought itself created any new *psul*. On *Tosafot*'s reading, once the *levonah* is removed the *minchah* is fully restored. According to *Rashi*, the wrong thought itself, even though insufficient to constitute *pigul*, carries enough force to create an independent disqualification; and therefore even after removing the *levonah*, the *minchah* remains *pasul* by dint of the thought.

### Reversible Invalidity

This *baraita* raises a profound conceptual difficulty. The *minchah* was *kasher*, then became *pasul* (upon the addition of *levonah*), and then returns to being *kasher* (upon removal of the *levonah*). This is a striking *gemara*: we have an instance of reversible *psul*. The principle of *dichuy* — that once a *korban* has been rejected or pushed aside, it cannot be restored to its original status — would seem to apply here. How can something be *pasul* as a *korban* and then become *kasher* again?

This question is especially sharp because *dichuy* is not a concern limited to animals or living things; it applies to inanimate objects and certainly to offerings. The principle is: *mi she'nirah v'nidche* — something that was once valid, became invalid, and was pushed aside cannot simply re-enter the circle of eligibility.

The *gemara* as we have it reads *v'tehave pach* — why is the presence of *levonah* not treated like a vessel of oil overturned on the *minchah*, which would fully invalidate it? And further, why does any *machshavah* at all have effect if the *minchah* is already *pasul* and therefore *dachuy*?

### Tosafot Textual Criticism

*Tosafot* offers a remarkable analysis of the textual tradition here. *Tosafot* maintains that the original *girsa* of the *gemara* was simply *v'tehave dichuy* — let it be *dichuy*; how does the *minchah* escape the fate of being permanently pushed aside? At some point, a commentator wrote in the margin a *peirush* — an explanation — asking, *u'mai pasla b'machshava*, why does any thought have effect? The word *peirush*, written in an abbreviated form (*peh-yud* with a slash), was subsequently misread by a later copyist as the word *pach*, and the entire phrase was incorporated into the body of the text, generating the version we now have. *Tosafot* thus reconstructs how the current *girsa* came to be, and argues that the core question is simply the *dichuy* problem — the subsequent question about *machshavah* is a secondary gloss that became embedded in the text.

### Abaye's Answer

*Abaye* answers the *dichuy* question as follows: *chatas karya rachmana* — the *Torah* itself calls it a *chatas*, and by insisting on this designation even when the *levonah* has been placed upon it, the *Torah* is signaling that the *minchah* retains its fundamental status. It does not become fully *nidche* — fully cast aside — because the *Torah* is asserting its continued identity as a valid *chatas* that merely requires correction.

### Rava & Rav Ada

*Rava* offers an alternative answer: this entire passage follows the opinion of *Chanina Hamitzri*, who fundamentally does not subscribe to the principle of *dichuyin*. A *baraita* records that *Chanina Hamitzri* rules that on *Yom Kippur*, even if the *sa'ir hamishtale'ach* (the scapegoat) died and the blood of the other goat is already in the vessel, one brings a replacement goat *shelo b'hagralah* — without a new lottery — and partners it with the existing blood. In that scenario, the blood was technically *nidche* while no paired goat existed, yet it is reused once the problem is fixed. *Chanina Hamitzri* is thus the authority who does not recognize *dichuy* as a categorical bar, and the present *baraita* would be following his view.

### Rav Ashi: B'Yado

*Rav Ashi* advances yet another answer, one that operates without relying on either a special *pasuk* or *Chanina Hamitzri*'s dissenting position. He states the principle: *kol she'b'yado lo havei dichuya* — anything that lies within one's power to correct is never considered *dichuy* in the first place. The very concept of *dichuy* implies that the object has been cast away beyond recovery. Something that can be fixed immediately and easily — like scooping *levonah* off the surface of flour — was never truly rejected. It occupied a temporarily impaired state, but the impairment was always understood to be correctable, and so the *korban* never left its central standing.

### Rabbi Yehuda & Dachuy

*Rav Ada* adds that the reasoning of *Rav Ashi* is in fact the most compelling, and supports it from the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*, who is normally the authority who maintains the stringency of *dichuyin*. A *mishnah* records that *Rabbi Yehuda* rules: if the blood of the *Yom Kippur* service was spilled, the *sa'ir hamishtale'ach* must be left to die, and if the *sa'ir hamishtale'ach* died, the blood must be spilled — because in each case, the remaining element was *nidche* during the interval it had no valid partner. So *Rabbi Yehuda* takes *dichuy* seriously.

Yet a *baraita* also records that *Rabbi Yehuda* says that at the end of *Pesach*, one would fill a vessel with the mixed blood that had pooled on the floor of the *Beis Hamikdash* — blood from the various *korban Pesach* offerings — and throw it in a single casting against the base of the *mizbe'ach*, in case any individual's blood had accidentally spilled and never been properly applied. Here, blood that was at some point not in a *klei shareis* and therefore technically unusable is nevertheless employed once collected. The reason *Rabbi Yehuda* permits this is precisely *b'yado* — it was always within the ability of the *kohanim* to collect and reapply the blood. When the means of correction are readily at hand, even *Rabbi Yehuda* does not classify the situation as *dichuy*.

This demonstrates that *b'yado* is the operative distinction even for the strictest authority on *dichuy*. Not every situation where something is temporarily invalid constitutes true *dichuy*; only where the impairment lies beyond one's ability to rectify does the status of *dichuy* attach. The case of *levonah* placed on a *minchah*, where one can simply pick the *levonah* off, is therefore never *dichuy* — it is merely a correctable impairment that leaves the *minchah*'s fundamental status intact.

---

## Shiurim: Oil & Levonah

### Oil Shiur

Having established the nature of the prohibitions and the conceptual framework of *dichuy*, the *gemara* turns to the question of *shiurim* — the minimum quantities required for a transgression. *Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef* cites *Rabbi Yochanan* on the measure required for oil.

### Oil: Kol Shehu

*Rabbi Yochanan* rules: *natan mashehu shemen al gabei kezayit minchah pasal* — even the smallest amount of oil placed upon a *kezayit*'s worth of *minchah* invalidates. The reasoning proceeds from the verse *lo yasim* — the word *simah*, "placing," carries no inherent minimum; it can refer to depositing even the tiniest quantity. There is no implied *shiur* in the act of placing. However, there must be a meaningful quantity of *minchah* upon which the oil is placed, and we derive this from the word *aleha* — upon it — which implies that the *minchah* itself must be of some significance. The minimum measure of significance for an edible substance is a *kezayit*, since that is the smallest *shiur* recognized for eating. The requirement is therefore any amount of oil on at least a *kezayit* of *minchah*.

### Frankincense: Kezayit

The rule is reversed for *levonah*. *Rabbi Yochanan* rules: *natan kezayit levonah al gabei mashehu minchah pasal* — one must place a *kezayit*'s worth of *levonah* to transgress, but even on the smallest amount of *minchah*. The reasoning turns on the word *lo yiten* — "do not give." *Netinah*, giving, implies conveying something of substance; to give something suggests there was a thing of significance being transferred. Accordingly, the *levonah* must amount to a *kezayit*. As for the *minchah* itself, the word *aleha* now operates differently: because the *Torah* has already used *aleha* once (by oil), and invokes it again (by *levonah*), we apply the principle of *ein ribui achar ribui ela lema'et* — a doubled expression of inclusion actually serves to restrict — and therefore the *minchah* need only be the smallest amount.

### Double Language Rule
