Beyond that, the substance of the ruling raises an obvious question: if the entire point of *tenufah* is the owner's presentation of the offering to God — as the *torah* itself emphasizes with the phrase *yadav taviena l'hanifo oso*, "his hands shall bring it to wave it" — how can the *kohen* perform it on the woman's behalf?

---

## Women Excluded

### Braita Text

A *braita* is cited: *bnei yisrael menifim v'ein ovdei kochavim menifim, bnei yisrael menifim v'ein hanashim menifot* — Jews perform *tenufah*, not non-Jews; Jews perform *tenufah*, not women.

### Rav Yoshiya Q

Rav Yoshiya immediately raises what is the natural challenge to this ruling. We have a precedent, he notes, in *semicha*: the *torah* distinguished between the *korban* of a male Jew, that of a non-Jew, and that of a woman in the context of *semicha*, such that women's *korbanot* and non-Jews' *korbanot* do not require *semicha*. Should we not similarly conclude that a woman's *korban* requires no *tenufah* at all — meaning not that someone else does it, but that the obligation is altogether absent, just as *semicha* is absent?

---

## Women Excluded (II)

### Gemara Response

The *gemara* rejects this line of reasoning by drawing a fundamental distinction between *semicha* and *tenufah*. When it comes to *semicha*, the act is performed exclusively by the owners — there is no other participant. If women cannot perform *semicha*, then for women's *korbanot* there is simply no *semicha* at all. The logic of exclusion in *semicha* reflects the nature of *semicha* itself: it is an act of ownership designation, and if the owner cannot do it, nobody can. *Tenufah*, by contrast, is an act in which the *kohanim* participate alongside the owners. Since *tenufah* involves the *kohanim* as well, it remains possible to exclude women from the act while still requiring *tenufah* for their *korbanot* — the *kohen* can perform it on the woman's behalf.

This distinction maps onto a deeper conceptual difference between the two acts. *Semicha* is fundamentally about symbolizing ownership — the owner leans on the animal, identifying it as his. If the owner cannot perform it, the act loses its entire meaning, and there is nothing left to do. *Tenufah*, however, is a ritual that belongs to the broader process of *hakrava*, of bringing the offering before God. While the *torah* emphasizes the owner's role, *tenufah* is not exclusively an ownership act in the same way *semicha* is. Many of the core acts of *hakrava* are performed by *kohanim*, and so it is conceptually coherent to say the waving is done by the *kohanim* without violating the nature of the rite.

A word should be said here about Jacob Milgrom's analysis, which is directly relevant. On *semicha* specifically, Milgrom argues — consistent with what the *gemara* itself says — that *semicha* is fundamentally an act of asserting ownership. He supports this from the pattern of which sacrifices do *not* require *semicha*: a *mincha*, a bird-offering, and a *korban tzibbur*. A *mincha* or bird-offering can be held entirely in one's hand — the ownership is manifest in the very act of holding it, so no additional symbolic gesture is needed. An animal walked into the *beit hamikdash* is no longer obviously "yours" in the same tactile sense, and so *semicha* serves to assert: this is my *korban*. A *korban tzibbur*, by definition, involves no single private owner to assert ownership, so *semicha* is simply irrelevant. Milgrom does not cite the *gemara*, but his approach aligns closely with how it frames the question here.

### Gender Patterns

It is worth pausing to note a recurring pattern: whenever one encounters a direct, tactile contact between a person and the *korban* in a ritual act, that is precisely where women are being excluded. The same dynamic appears in both *semicha* and *tenufah*. There is clearly a common denominator at work, a structural limitation on women's direct ritual engagement with the *korban*. The question of whether women are *permitted* — even if not *obligated* — to perform *semicha* is itself a *tannaitic* dispute, and the matter is similarly debated in the *braita* regarding *tenufah*.

### Women in Temple

What seems to be reflected here is a broader sociological reality of the *beit hamikdash*: women had access to the Temple precincts, but their designated space — the *ezrat nashim* — was explicitly distinct from the *ezrat yisrael*, the space of primary ritual activity. The very contrast in terminology between *yisrael* and *nashim* in the Temple's architecture mirrors the contrast one finds in these legal texts. Women could bring *korbanot*, but they were not regarded as primary participants in the *azara*'s ritual activity. This is an uncomfortable reality to sit with, and it has obvious implications: the model of *mechitza* based on the *ezrat nashim* is, as a result, a deeply problematic model — it encodes not merely separation but a hierarchy of access to the sacred space. The *gemara*'s language here reflects that hierarchy directly.

---

## Owners & Kohanim (II)

### Semicha vs Tenufah

The *gemara*, having established this conceptual divide, now proceeds to describe how the *tenufah* is physically performed. The *kohen* places his hands beneath the hands of the owners — *kohen mani'ach yado tachat yad habe'alim u'menif* — and both wave together. Whether the *kohanim* are positioned directly beneath or slightly adjacent, the combined act constitutes a valid *tenufah*.

The key asymmetry remains: because *semicha* is exclusively an act of the owners, excluding a category of people from *semicha* eliminates *semicha* for their *korban* entirely. Because *tenufah* involves the *kohanim* as co-participants, excluding a category of people from *performing* *tenufah* does not eliminate *tenufah* from their *korban* — the *kohen* steps in as the performing agent.

### Milgrom Analysis

Milgrom's treatment of *tenufah* itself is illuminating. He notes that the *torah* at times interchanges *tenufah* and *terumah*, as in the phrase *chazeh hatnufa veshok hatruma*. His reading is that *terumah* is essentially a verbal or conceptual designation of something as given to God — it is the act of separating and declaring, which can be accomplished without a physical gesture. *Tenufah* functions similarly, but is always *lifnei Hashem* — performed within the sacred precincts — and is therefore expressed through a physical act of elevation and waving rather than verbal designation. The reason *tenufah* is required, he argues, is because these items — particularly the *kodashim kalim* — are not fully designated to God from the outset. With a *shelamim*, for example, the *gemara* elsewhere teaches that there is no *me'ila* on *kodashim kalim* until after *shechita* and until the *eimurim* are placed on the *mizbe'ach*, because until that point the offering remains substantially under the owner's domain. *Tenufah* serves as the symbolic act of taking something that was the owner's and formally presenting it to God.

This reading aligns well with the *torah*'s insistence on *yadav taviena* — the owner's hands bring it — and explains why *tenufah* is demanded precisely for those items that are not yet fully removed from private ownership. Milgrom does acknowledge that the *menachot* associated with the *omer* and the *shtei halechem* are *kodshei kodashim* and seem to present a more complex case, but his general thesis is that the essence of *tenufah* is this act of transfer — from the human owner to God — carried out through physical gesture in the sacred space. That being said, the *gemara* here does two things simultaneously: it reads the *mishna* as limiting women's participation in *tenufah* (a reading that is, as noted, at least debatable as *pshat* in the *mishna* itself, though supported by the *braitot*), and then justifies that reading by contrasting *tenufah* with *semicha* in a way that, arguably, sits in tension with Milgrom's emphasis on *tenufah* as ownership-transfer.

---

## Converts & Slaves

### Derivation

A second *braita* is introduced: *bnei yisrael* — is this the only category included? What about converts and freed slaves, who are now fully Jewish? The *braita* derives their inclusion from the word *hamakriv* — "the one who brings" — which appears in the relevant *pasuk* and is understood as broadening the category beyond *bnei yisrael* in its narrowest reading. Yet one might counter that *hamakriv* refers to the *kohen* who offers the sacrifice on the *mizbe'ach*, not to the owner at all. The *braita* resolves this by noting that the *pasuk* also says *yadav taviena* — "his hands shall bring it" — which clearly refers to the owner, not the *kohen*. Therefore *hamakriv* must be extending the category of owners to include converts and freed slaves.

### Tosafot Q

Tosafot raises a sharp question here: ordinarily, we assume that converts and freed slaves are included in any obligation that applies to Jews. Why would we need a special derivation to include them? Tosafot's answer is that the *gemara* is operating from a maximally narrow baseline assumption — that by default, only a naturally born Jewish male is included, requiring explicit derivations to extend the obligation to converts, freed slaves, or anyone else. The inclusivity of converts and freed slaves here is thus not taken for granted but affirmatively derived.

---

## Physical Tenufah

### Parts Arrange

The *gemara* now describes the physical mechanics of the *tenufah* when performed on the actual sacrificial components of a *shelamim* — the *eimurim* (fats), *chazeh*, and *shok*. The *eimurim* are placed on the owner's palm — directly on the hand, since this is not done with a *kli sharet* — and the *chazeh* and *shok* are placed on top of the *eimurim*. One naturally wonders both about the practical challenges of this arrangement and why the *eimurim* go below rather than above.

### Bread Role

Whenever bread accompanies the *chazeh* and *shok* in the *tenufah* — as occurred at the *miluim*, the inaugural offerings — the bread is placed on top of everything else, above the meat. The *gemara* attributes this observation to Rav Pappa, who identifies the *miluim* as the one instance in which a *shelamim* is waved together with bread, making it the model case for this arrangement.

### Pesuk Conflict

The rationale for placing the *eimurim* below is drawn from a *pasuk*: *shok haterumah v'chazeh hatnufah al ishei hachalavim yavi'u* — the thigh and breast shall be brought *on* the fire-offerings of the fats, indicating that the meat goes above and the fats below. But a second *pasuk* states *et hachalavim al hachazeh yevi'enu* — bring the fats *on* the breast — which would seem to reverse the arrangement. The two *pesukim* directly contradict each other on which element is on top.

### Abaye Flip

Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two stages of the process. When the *kohen* first brings the pieces from the slaughterhouse to the owner, the meat is on the bottom and the fats are on top — this satisfies the second *pasuk*. When it is then placed in the owner's hands for *tenufah*, the arrangement is flipped: fats below, meat above — satisfying the first *pasuk*. A third *pasuk* — *vayashimu et hachalavim al hachazot*, the fats were placed on the breasts — describes yet a further stage: after *tenufah*, the pieces are handed to another *kohen* to bring to the *mizbe'ach*, and at that point they are again inverted so that the fats end up on top, as befits their being placed on the *mizbe'ach*'s fire. The practical logic is clear: the fats, which are destined for the *mizbe'ach*, should be on top when approaching it so that they can be placed on the fire without needing to extract them from under the meat.

### Three Kohanim

The *gemara* notes an implication of Abaye's three-stage solution: the process involves three separate *kohanim*, one for each stage of handling. The *gemara* endorses this not merely as a technical consequence but as a value in itself, grounded in the principle of *berov am hadrat melech* — "in the multitude of people is the king's glory." It is preferable to involve more participants in a sacred act, as it increases the honor rendered.

---

## Shtei Halechem

### Source Context

The *mishna* had stated that the two loaves of *shavuot* — the *shtei halechem* — together with the two lambs are waved by the *kohen*. The *torah* describes this as *v'henif hakohen otam al lechem habikkurim*, waving them together with the bread of the first fruits.

### Pesuk Ambig

A *braita* is introduced that surfaces a contradiction in the relevant *pesukim* parallel to the one we just saw regarding the *eimurim* and meat. One *pasuk* seems to indicate that the lambs are placed on the bread — *yachol yanich kevasim al gabei halechem*. Another *pasuk* states *al shnei kevasim* — which would imply the bread is placed on the lambs. The text is thus, in the *braita*'s words, *nishtakel hakatuv* — the *pasuk* is evenly weighted, pointing in both directions simultaneously, and it is impossible to determine from the *pasuk* itself which element goes on top.

The *braita* therefore turns to a normative principle: wherever else we find bread waved together with other sacrificial items, the bread goes on top. Following Rav Pappa's earlier identification, the model case is again the *miluim*, where the *torah* places the bread last in the sequence before saying *v'hanafta otam tenufah lifnei Hashem* — and the *chachamim* understood from this that the bread is on top. So here too, the default should be bread on top.

This resolves which arrangement is standard, but it does not explain why the *torah* uses contradictory language. The three *tannaim* who follow take different approaches precisely to address this.

### Rabbi Yosei

Rabbi Yosei ben Hamishulam maintains that the lambs go on top. He preserves this position by reading *al shnei kevasim* — "on the two lambs" — not as a physical description of placement but as a relational statement: the bread is designated as coming *together with*, or *connected to*, the two lambs specifically, as distinct from the other seven lambs brought as part of the *musaf* offerings on *shavuot*. The *torah* is establishing a unique pairing — the *shtei halechem* are linked specifically to the *shnei kevasim* and not to the larger collection of animals. The word *al* here means "in relation to" or "connected to," not "on top of." This reading reconciles the contradictory *pesukim* while preserving the lambs-on-top arrangement.

### Chanani Sandwich

Chanani ben Chakinai proposes a more creative solution. The *shtei halechem* are placed between the thighs of the lambs — *bein yarchoteihem shel kevasim*. This arrangement physically satisfies both *pesukim* simultaneously: the bread is *on* the lambs because it rests between a thigh above, and the lambs are *on* the bread because the other thigh lies above the other loaf. Both statements are true simultaneously because the bread is sandwiched.

### Decorum Obj

Rabbi rejects Chanani's solution firmly. *Lifnei melech basar vadam ein osim ken* — one would never present a gift to a human king by stuffing the bread between the legs of the animals. Certainly, *lifnei melech malchei hamelachim Hakadosh Baruch Hu al achat kama v'khamah* — before the King of kings this is all the more inappropriate. Decorum before God demands a more dignified arrangement.

### Rabbi Side

Rabbi's own position is that the bread and lambs are placed side by side — *mani'ach zeh betzad zeh u'menif* — and waved together in that configuration. The word *al* in both *pesukim* does not mean "on top of" but rather "adjacent to" or "beside." Both *pesukim* can therefore be read as saying that each is placed beside the other, without physical layering. This removes the contradiction entirely.

### Al Meaning

The *gemara* then cites Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna (with the standard note that it is uncertain which one said it to the other) to the effect that Rabbi is consistent with his broader linguistic position: *Rebbi letamei*, Rabbi goes according to his own reasoning, for Rabbi elsewhere interprets *al* as meaning *besamuch* — nearby, not literally on top.

The proof-text is drawn from the *lechem hapanim*: the *pasuk* says *v'natata al hamareches levona zakha*, "you shall place *on* the arrangement *levona*." But the *levona* is not placed on top of the stacked loaves — it is placed on the table next to them. There, *al* clearly means adjacent. Rabbi adds another proof: *v'sakota al ha'aron et haparochet* — "the curtain shall provide shade *on* the *aron*." The *parochet* does not lie literally on top of the *aron*; it stands beside it and casts its shade upon it. Here too *al* means proximity rather than direct contact. This confirms that Rabbi's reading of *al* as *besamuch* has consistent textual grounding.

---

## Tenufah Motions

### Cosmic Offering

The *gemara* turns to the physical motions of *tenufah*: *moli'ach u'mevi ma'aleh u'morid* — forward and back, up and down. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the forward-and-back motion is directed toward *lemi she-haruchot shelo* — the One who controls the winds; the up-and-down motion toward *lemi she-hashamayim ve-ha'aretz shelo* — the One who controls heaven and earth. This framing aligns naturally with Milgrom's understanding: *tenufah* is fundamentally an act of giving something over to God, and the waving in all directions — toward every wind, toward heaven and earth — is a physical enactment of that total dedication. The directions of the motion are a kind of cosmic presentation.

### Bad Weather

The *gemara* then introduces an alternative formulation from the West, *Eretz Yisrael*, attributed to Rabbi Chama bar Ukva in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina. In this version, the forward-and-back motion is performed *kedei latzor ruchot ra'ot* — in order to restrain the bad winds; the up-and-down motion *kedei latzor tlalim ra'im* — to restrain the bad rains (*tlalim* here carrying the sense of adverse precipitation generally). This is a notably different emphasis: rather than a theological statement about giving to God, the waving is here understood as having an apotropaic, protective function — warding off destructive natural forces.

This framing is striking, even somewhat surprising. One might have expected the formulation to be positive — praying for good winds, for beneficent rains. Why is it cast in the negative, as a protection against harm? This question deserves serious attention. One possible answer: the *shtei halechem* and the *omer* are agricultural sacrifices, which naturally carry a double valence — gratitude for the present harvest together with an implicit petition for the future. And *tenufah* in this context may encode both. Yet the *gemara* frames it specifically as preventative.

### Remnant Value

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Avin draws a striking practical lesson from this: *zot omeret she'arei mitzvah me'akvin et hapuranuyot* — from here we learn that even the "remnants" of a *mitzvah*, the supplementary elements of an obligation rather than its core, are sufficient to forestall punishment and hold back destructive forces. *Tenufah* is not required for one to have fulfilled the sacrificial obligation — it is, in some sense, an addendum to the *korban*. Yet even this element, precisely because it functions as a *mitzvah*, carries protective power. The lesson extends far beyond the *beit hamikdash*: even partial or secondary observances carry weight and matter.

### Lulav Model

Rava extends the principle: *v'chen lulav* — the same holds for the lulav waving on *sukkot*. The same motions, in the same directions, carry the same meaning and the same preventative effect against bad winds and rains. This connection is natural: *sukkot* is the other great agricultural festival, the time when the liturgy shifts to *mashiv haru'ach u'morid hagashem* and when the communal *bakashah* for rain begins. The *tenufah* of the *shtei halechem* and the *omer* serves as the template — the halachic and conceptual model — for the waving of the *lulav*.

The emphasis on averting the negative rather than soliciting the positive may also be better understood in the *sukkot* context: at that season the concern is precisely about timing and excess — one does not want rain during *sukkot* itself, as it would be a sign of divine displeasure, even as one prays for it to come in its proper season thereafter. Perhaps that is why the tradition articulates the gesture as warding off harm rather than inviting blessing.

### Rav Acha

Rav Acha bar Yaakov would wave his *lulav* with an aggressive stabbing or thrusting motion — *mamti lei u'mayti lei* — and would declare: *giri be'einei d'sitna* — "an arrow in the eyes of the *satan*." The image is vivid: he is wielding the *lulav* as a weapon against the evil force, not merely performing a liturgical gesture. The *gemara*, however, rejects this approach: *v'lav milta hi* — this is not the right way to do it, because *mishum d'ati l'igruyei bei* — it is liable to provoke and incite the *satan* rather than neutralize him. One does not pick a direct fight with demonic forces; caution and indirection are the appropriate posture. The mention of *ruach ra'ah* — the bad wind or evil spirit — in this context connects to the same vocabulary used in discussions of *netilat yadayim* and similar protective rituals, where *ruach ra'ah* denotes a demonic presence rather than merely a natural force.

---

## Communal Tenufah

### Communal Rule

A *braita* teaches that the *zivchei shalmei tzibbur* — the communal *shelamim*, which refers exclusively to the *shnei kevasim* brought with the *shtei halechem* on *shavuot* — require *tenufah* both before and after *shechita*. The pre-*shechita* waving is explicit in the *pesukim* — it is the waving of the live lambs together with the bread that we have been discussing. The post-*shechita* waving is the subject of the *braita*: *te'unin tenufah l'achar shechitah*, and it is done *kemot shehen* — with the animal as it is, meaning the full carcass. This is the position of Rabbi. The *chachamim* disagree, holding that after *shechita* one waves only the *chazeh* and *shok*, as with a private *shelamim*.

The disagreement is immediately puzzling on its face. With a standard private *shelamim*, the *kohen* receives the *chazeh* and *shok* while the *mizbe'ach* receives the *chelev*. The *chazeh* and *shok* are thus distinct and distinctive — they are the portion that goes to the *kohen*, and waving them enacts the transfer. But with the *shnei kevasim*, the *kohanim* eat the entire animal. There is nothing halachically distinctive about the *chazeh* and *shok* here. So the *chachamim*'s position of limiting the post-*shechita* waving to *chazeh* and *shok* seems difficult to justify.

### Hermeneutic Q

Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna (again with uncertainty as to which one addressed which) identify the debate as turning on a general hermeneutic question: *don minah u'minah* versus *don minah v'okei b'asrah*. When one derives a law for case A from case B, does one also import the details and context of case B (*don minah u'minah* — learn from it and from it), or does one derive only the general principle from B and then apply that principle within the natural context of A (*don minah v'okei b'asrah* — learn from it and establish it in its place)?

### Rabbi vs Sages

This framing sets up the two positions. The source from which the post-*shechita* waving of the *shnei kevasim* is derived is the private *shelamim*, which also requires *tenufah* after *shechita*. The question is: when we apply that principle to the *shnei kevasim*, do we take along the full context of the private *shelamim* (including the limitation to *chazeh* and *shok*), or do we merely carry over the principle (post-*shechita* waving is required) and then determine its parameters according to the internal logic of the *shnei kevasim*?

### Sages Logic

The *chachamim* hold *don minah u'minah*: learn the law from the private *shelamim* and take the full context along. Just as there the waving is limited to *chazeh* and *shok*, so too here. The original context follows the rule into its new setting.

### Rabbi Logic

Rabbi holds *don minah v'okei b'asrah*: derive the principle — post-*shechita* waving — from the private *shelamim*, but then establish its application within the natural logic of the *shnei kevasim*. What is the underlying principle that determines *which parts* get waved in a private *shelamim*? It is not an arbitrary selection: one waves the portion being given to the *kohen*. That is the internal logic of the private *shelamim*'s *tenufah*. Apply that logic in the context of the *shnei kevasim*, where everything goes to the *kohanim*, and you wave the entire animal. Rabbi's position thus has the advantage of coherence — it makes the same principle operative in both cases, applying it to the facts on the ground in each context.

### Rav Papa

Rav Pappa offers a different reading of the dispute. He argues that in fact everyone holds *don minah u'minah* — everyone agrees one derives the law together with its original context. The question is: what exactly is the "context" of the private *shelamim's tenufah*? If one reads the context narrowly — the specific parts waved are *chazeh* and *shok* — then one limits the *shnei kevasim* post-*shechita* waving to *chazeh* and *shok*. But if one reads the context more deeply — the underlying principle is that one waves whatever goes to the *kohen* — then applying *that* context to the *shnei kevasim* yields waving of the entire animal, since the entire animal goes to the *kohanim*. According to Rav Pappa, this is what Rabbi is doing: he applies *don minah u'minah* but reads the contextual principle at a deeper level of abstraction, and at that level the principle leads to waving the whole animal.

### Ravina

Ravina proposes the opposite resolution. According to Ravina, everyone actually holds *don minah v'okei b'asrah* — everyone derives the principle from the private *shelamim* and then applies it in the new context of the *shnei kevasim*. Placing the law in the context of the *shnei kevasim*, where the entire animal goes to the *kohanim*, should by rights lead everyone to wave the whole animal. So why do the *chachamim* limit it to *chazeh* and *shok*? Because there is an explicit *pasuk* that narrows it: *et chazeh hatnufah v'et shok haterumah lakachti mei'et bnei yisrael mizivchei shalmeihem* — "from their *shelamim*" — the use of the plural *shalmeihem* is understood to include *shalmei tzibbur* within the *pasuk*'s scope, explicitly restricting the post-*shechita* waving of all *shelamim* — private and communal alike — to *chazeh* and *shok*. Rabbi, who disagrees, does not accept this derivation. Of the two positions, Rabbi's is conceptually the more coherent: it is strange to limit the *shnei kevasim*'s post-*shechita* waving to *chazeh* and *shok* when those parts have no distinctive status here.

---

## Three Types

### Framework

Rabbi Shimon introduces a systematic framework. There are three categories of sacrifices, each possessing two of three possible ritual characteristics — *semicha*, *tenufah chaim* (waving while alive), and *tenufah shechutim* (waving after *shechita*) — but lacking the third. No single category has all three.

### Private

The private *shelamim* requires *semicha*, which is performed while the animal is alive, and *tenufah* after *shechita* — the waving of the *chazeh* and *shok*. It does not require *tenufah* while alive.

### Communal

The *shnei kevasim* of *shavuot* require *tenufah* both while alive — as explicitly stated in the *torah* — and after *shechita*, as derived from the private *shelamim*. They do not require *semicha*, since *semicha* is categorically inapplicable to communal sacrifices.

### Asham

The *asham* of the *metzora* requires *semicha* — because it is a private *korban* — and *tenufah* while alive — as stated in the *torah*. It does not require *tenufah* after *shechita*: it is an *asham*, not a *shelamim*, and so the derivation that extends post-*shechita* waving from the private *shelamim* to the communal *shnei kevasim* does not reach it.

### Kal Vachomer

The *gemara* attempts to derive each missing characteristic by *kal vachomer*. Take the private *shelamim*: it has *semicha* but no *tenufah chaim*. The communal *shnei kevasim* have *tenufah chaim* but no *semicha*. A *kal vachomer* suggests: if the communal sacrifice, which lacks the "weight" of *semicha*, nevertheless requires *tenufah chaim*, surely the private *shelamim*, which has the additional stringency of *semicha*, should also require *tenufah chaim*. Similarly, one can attempt the reverse: if the private *shelamim*, lacking *tenufah chaim*, still has *semicha*, surely the communal *shnei kevasim*, which have *tenufah chaim*, should also have *semicha*.

### Pesuk Limits

Both *kal vachomer* arguments are rejected by explicit *pesukim*. In the case of *tenufah chaim* for the private *shelamim*: the *pasuk* describing the waving of the live *shnei kevasim* uses the word *otam* — "them" — which is interpreted as an exclusion: only they are waved alive, not the analogous private *shelamim*. In the case of *semicha* for the communal sacrifice: the *gemara* cites the tradition — *gimiri* — that there are only two instances of *semicha* on communal sacrifices, and the *shnei kevasim* on *shavuot* is not among them. The general rule is that *semicha* does not apply to communal sacrifices, with the notable exceptions of the *par he'elem davar shel tzibbur* — the bull brought when the *sanhedrin* rules incorrectly — and the *sa'ir hamishtale'ach*, the scapegoat of *yom kippur*. Rashi identifies these two exceptions. What they share is not ownership per se but a dimension of collective *sin* and *responsibility*: the *zikney ha'edah* perform *semicha* on the communal bull as an expression of their accountability for having misled the public, and the *sa'ir hamishtale'ach* involves a direct transfer of sin. These are structurally different from ordinary communal *musaf* offerings, where there is no ownership to assert and no sin to transfer. The system is therefore not arbitrary: *semicha* tracks meaning, and where the relevant meaning is absent, *semicha* is absent.

---

## Partnership

### Partners

A *braita* concludes: if five people brought a single *korban* as partners — something possible with a *shelamim*, which may be brought in joint ownership — one person may perform the *tenufah* on behalf of all. The notion that one representative can wave for the group introduces the principle of representation in *tenufah*.

### Women's Rep

From this principle, the *braita* draws a direct implication for women's *korbanot*: *veha'isha, kohen menif al yadeiha* — when a woman brings a *korban*, the *kohen* performs the *tenufah* on her behalf. The parallel to the partnership case is deployed here to justify the *kohen*'s representative role. One should note, however, that the parallel is not perfect: in the partnership case, the person performing *tenufah* is himself one of the owners. The *kohen* performing *tenufah* for the woman is not an owner at all. This is a meaningful leap, though the *gemara* treats it as a natural extension.

### Remote Owner

The principle is extended further still: *v'chein hashole'ach korbanotav mimedinat hayam, kohen menif al yado* — if someone sends a *korban* from overseas, unable to be present, the *kohen* performs *tenufah* on his behalf. This introduces the concept of *shlichut* — representation or agency — in *tenufah*. The logic is consistent: since *tenufah* is not understood as purely an act of ownership-assertion (unlike *semicha*), it can be performed by an agent. The owner's presence, while normally integrated into the act, is not so essential that *tenufah* cannot proceed in his absence. No analogous accommodation exists for *semicha*: if the owner of such a *korban* were overseas and could not perform *semicha*, there would simply be no *semicha*. The contrast once again underscores the different nature of the two acts.

### Tosafot Concern

Tosafot raises a serious concern about the case of the *korban* sent from overseas. *Semicha* is a real obligation for a male owner of an appropriate *korban*. If someone sends his *korban* from *medinat hayam* and the *kohen* performs *tenufah* in his absence, that is unproblematic — *tenufah* can be delegated. But how is it permissible to bring a *korban* that requires *semicha without semicha* having been performed? With women, the answer is that they cannot perform *semicha* and so the obligation is structurally inapplicable to them. But a male owner of a private *shelamim* is obligated in *semicha*. Can he simply send his animal to Yerushalayim without having performed *semicha* on it? Tosafot finds this troubling, noting that other *gemara* passages reflect a real reluctance to bring a *korban* without the owner being physically present to perform *semicha*. He ultimately acknowledges that the practice of sending *korbanot* from abroad is attested, but the tension he identifies is genuine and instructive.

---

## Milgrom Appendix

### Hagashah Symbol

A final observation, offered as a postscript to the preceding day's material: Milgrom provides a compelling reading of *hagashah* — the presentation of the *mincha* to the *mizbe'ach* — that illuminates Rabbi Shimon's position discussed there. He begins from the literary context in which *mincha* appears in *Vayikra*: the *torah* presents the *mincha* as an offering parallel to the *olah*, essentially a grain substitute when one cannot afford an animal. The *olah* is burned entirely; the *mincha*, by contrast, is only partially burned on the *mizbe'ach* while the remainder is eaten by the *kohanim*. The *hagashah* — the act of pressing the entire *mincha* against the *mizbe'ach* — serves to symbolically place the whole *mincha* on the *mizbe'ach*, demonstrating that conceptually the entire offering is dedicated to God and is as if being consumed by the *mizbe'ach*. The *kohanim*'s subsequent eating of the remainder is, on this reading, analogous to the *mizbe'ach*'s consumption — both partake of what has been fully dedicated.

### No Hagashah

This framework elegantly accounts for Rabbi Shimon's ruling that a *minchat kohanim* — a *mincha* brought by a *kohen*, which is burned entirely with no portion remaining for eating — does not require *hagashah*. The symbolic function of *hagashah* is to demonstrate, through the gesture of placing the whole *mincha* against the *mizbe'ach*, that it is all being given over even though in practice only part will be burned. When the entire *mincha* is in fact being burned, there is nothing to demonstrate — the reality speaks for itself, and the symbolic gesture is unnecessary. The *hagashah* requirement is thus precisely calibrated to cases where the outward act of offering requires this additional declarative moment to clarify what is actually happening.

---

---

# Menachot 63

## Intro & Vessels

### Opening Remarks

Daf 63 of Menachot marks the final daf of this perek — a perek that was among the first to focus directly and systematically on describing the various types of *menachot*, how they are made, and the constituent steps of their preparation. The full step-by-step process of kneading, baking, and so forth has not yet been exhaustively covered, but we are drawing close, and the relevant stages are coming into view one by one.

### Hagasha & Tenufa

The preceding material addressed which *menachot* require *hagasha* and which require *tenufa*. Now the discussion narrows further to focus on the specific types of *mincha* described distinctly in Vayikra. The Torah's baseline assumes a *mincha* that is unbaked — flour mixed with oil: *ki takriv korban mincha la-Hashem, solet yihiyeh korbano, v'yatzak aleha shemen v'natan aleha levonah*. But the Torah then describes several baked variations: *v'chi takriv mincha ma'afeh tanur* — if you bring one baked in an oven; *v'im mincha al ha-machavat korbanecha* — if it is in a flat pan; *v'im mincha marcheshet korbanecha* — if it is in a deep pan. The *mishnah*'s organizing question, then, is: given that a person may take a personal *neder* to bring a *korban*, and the nature of that *neder* determines what must be brought, what are the legal consequences of specifying one vessel type over another?

---

## Machavat/Marcheshet

### Mishna Text

The *mishnah* opens: *ha-omer harei alai ba-machavat* — one who declares "behold, I take upon myself to bring a *mincha* in a *machavat*." The ruling is *lo yavi ba-marcheshet* — he may not bring it in the *marcheshet*. Conversely, if he specified a *marcheshet*, he may not bring it in the *machavat*. These are two distinct obligations that cannot be interchanged.

### Vessel Distinction

The *mishnah* then asks: *mah bein machavat le-marcheshet?* — what is the difference between them? The *marcheshet yesh lah kisui* — the *marcheshet* has a cover, *u-machavat ein lah kisui* — while the *machavat* does not. In practical terms, the *machavat* functions like a flat frying pan, and the *marcheshet* more like a saucepan or deep pan. These are the words of Rabbi Yose HaGelili.

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel adds a complementary distinction: *marcheshet amuka* — the *marcheshet* is deep — *u-ma'aseh rochashin* — and what is prepared in it moves, bubbles, and churns. When flour and oil are cooked in a deeper vessel with more liquid, the result is something softer and more fluid in texture. The *machavat*, by contrast, is flat — *tzafah* — the contents rest on the surface without being immersed in oil, and *ma'aseh kashin* — what emerges is harder and more solid, like something fried rather than simmered.

### Rabbi Yose HaGelili

The *gemara* probes the reasoning behind Rabbi Yose HaGelili's distinction. Why would it matter to a person vowing to bring a *mincha* whether it is made in a covered or uncovered vessel, especially if the baking is done in the *mikdash* by the *kohanim*? The *gemara*'s answer reveals how distant we are from that world: the two vessel types carried distinct symbolic associations that, while no longer intuitively obvious to us, would have been meaningful to those bringing these offerings.

The *gemara* proposes that the word *marcheshet* is connected to *rachush* — the movements or stirrings of the heart. Rashi explains this as *hirhur aveira*, sinful thought. The textual support is the verse *rachash libi davar tov* — "my heart stirred with a good thing" — where *rachash* connotes inner emotional movement. Since the heart is internal and concealed within the body, the vessel that represents it would naturally be a covered one, with contents that move and bubble unseen beneath the lid. On this reading, one who brings a *marcheshet* is atoning for the hidden movements of the heart — for sinful thoughts.

The *machavat*, the open and flat vessel, would then correspond to speech. The word *machavat* is linked to *mach'bu'ei*, meaning utterances or spoken words. As people say, *minvach nivuchei* — he barked or voiced aloud — suggesting speech. Speech is by nature uncovered and externally expressed, just as the *machavat* is open. Rashi associates this with *rechilut* and *lashon ha-ra*, which, while technically speech rather than action, can be far more destructive than many physical transgressions. The *mincha* offered in an open *machavat* would thus symbolize an atonement connected to what one has spoken.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* immediately challenges this symbolic association: *eima ipcha* — perhaps it is precisely the reverse. Perhaps *machavat* connects to *mach'vo* — concealment — the *hidden* thoughts of the heart. The supporting verse is Lavan's complaint to Yaakov, *lama nachbeita livro'ach* — "why did you hide your intention to flee?" — where the same root conveys concealment. On this reading, the covered *machavat* represents the hidden inner life of the heart, and the *marcheshet* — whose root *rachash* means to move — refers to the movement of the lips, i.e., speech: *hava merachshan sifvosei*, his lips were moving and muttering.

The symbolic reasoning could plausibly run in either direction. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ella gemara gemiri lah* — the distinction is not derived through symbolic inference at all, but is received as a tradition. Rabbi Yose HaGelili knew that the *machavat* is uncovered and the *marcheshet* is covered through received knowledge, not through the kind of symbolic analysis the *gemara* had been attempting. What the attempted analysis reveals, however, is precisely how removed we are from this world: associations that once felt natural and obvious to those bringing these offerings are no longer self-evident to us.

It should also be noted that Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel need not be seen as arguing. One describes the distinction in terms of covered versus uncovered; the other in terms of deep versus flat. Both characteristics may simultaneously be true of the same vessels.

### Rabbi Chanina

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's distinction — that the *marcheshet* is deep — is supported more directly from the *pesuk* itself. The verse says *ve-chol na'aseh ba-marcheshet* — "all that is made *in* the *marcheshet*" — using the preposition *be-*, indicating genuine interior depth. By contrast, the verse says *ve-al machavat* — "on the *machavat*" — using *al*, "upon," just as one speaks of grilling *on* a grill or frying on a completely flat skillet. The prepositions themselves, *be-* versus *al*, encode the distinction between a vessel with real inner depth and one that is essentially a flat surface.

---

## Beit Shammai vs Hillel

### Beit Shammai

A *baraita* records a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai says: one who declares *harei alai marcheshet* — "behold, upon me is a *marcheshet*" — the matter *yehei munach ad she-yavo Eliyahu* — should be set aside until Eliyahu comes. This formulation, familiar from monetary disputes, places the matter in permanent escrow when no determination can be made. In the classic monetary case, two people each deposited funds — one two hundred, one one hundred — and the custodian forgot which depositor gave which amount. Since each claimant insists on the larger sum, the custodian returns a hundred to each and the disputed remainder is left *ad she-yavo Eliyahu*. Here too, Beit Shammai rules that the vow is indeterminate and cannot be resolved.

It is worth noting that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel lived during the time of the *mikdash*, or at least spoke in terms of what the *halacha* would be in that setting, imagining it as fully operative. Without the explicit qualifier *ba-zman ha-zeh*, we do not read their rulings as addressed to a post-*mikdash* reality.

### Ambiguity

Why is the vow indeterminate? The *gemara* explains: *mesapka lehu ei al shum kli nikre'u o al shum ma'aseihem* — they are uncertain whether the word *marcheshet* is the name of the vessel — a specific type of cooking pan — or whether it functions as a descriptive adjective characterizing a type of *mincha*, i.e., a bubbling or moving one.

The distinction matters practically. If *marcheshet* is the name of a vessel and one declares *harei alai marcheshet*, one is donating the vessel itself to the *beit ha-mikdash*, not undertaking to bring a *korban*. If, however, *marcheshet* is an adjective describing the character of a *mincha*, then *harei alai marcheshet* is understood as a vow to bring a *minchat marcheshet*. Without knowing which usage applies, we cannot determine what the person has obligated himself to bring — or whether he has obligated himself to bring a *korban* at all.

### Tosafot

Tosafot raises a pointed question: why not simply ask the person what he meant? The tension here runs deeper than mere inquiry. In legal contexts, our general principle is *devarim she-ba-lev einam devarim* — unexpressed intention has no legal standing. This principle applies most strictly to bilateral transactions such as commerce and contracts, where the only accessible reality is what was actually said. But for one-sided transactions — gifts, and especially ritual vows — there is far more room to factor in what the person actually intended. In the domain of *nedarim*, we additionally invoke *piv ve-libo shavin* — the alignment of heart and speech — as a condition for a valid vow, which gives inner intention significant purchase.

Tosafot considers a scenario in which the person has already designated money or flour *le-marcheshet*, leaving it ambiguous whether the funds are destined for the vessel or for the *korban*. He asks: why not instruct the person to purchase a *marcheshet* vessel with separate non-sacred funds, and then declare that if he originally meant the vessel, the *kedushah* transfers to this newly purchased one, and if he meant the *korban*, then the original funds go toward the *mincha* and the new vessel goes to the *beit ha-mikdash*? This covering-of-bases approach is normally what we would demand of someone who created an ambiguous situation.

Tosafot's answer is that the case involves someone who declared that the funds should go *le-marcheshet* in whatever sense the linguists determine the word to mean — *l'mah she-yidreshu chachmei ha-lashon*. The person deliberately abdicated the determination of meaning to an external authority. In that case, the resolution does not depend on what the person meant but on what the word objectively means — and that remains undetermined, hence *yehei munach ad she-yavo Eliyahu*.

This connects to a broader principle running through the Beit Shammai–Beit Hillel debates on *hekdesh*: Beit Shammai generally holds that *hekdesh bi-ta'ut* — a mistaken dedication — remains *hekdesh*, whereas Beit Hillel holds it does not. Beit Shammai thus attends more rigorously to the speech act itself, giving it binding force independent of the speaker's actual intention. Beit Hillel, by contrast, gives more weight to what the speaker genuinely had in mind. The ruling of *yehei munach* is thus consistent with Beit Shammai's characteristic posture: the words were said, we cannot determine their objective meaning, and the speaker's private intent does not resolve the impasse.

### Beit Hillel

Beit Hillel rules otherwise: *kli hayah ba-mikdash u-marcheshet shemah* — there was a vessel in the *mikdash* and *marcheshet* was its name. For Beit Hillel, the term *marcheshet* unambiguously denotes a specific vessel. Accordingly, one who says *harei alai marcheshet* is straightforwardly donating that vessel to the *beit ha-mikdash*. No uncertainty remains, because the meaning of the word is settled: it refers to the *kli*, not to a type of *mincha*. Beit Hillel does not need to inquire into the speaker's intent, because the language itself is clear.

### Marcheshet Description

Beit Hillel then describes this vessel: *v'domeh ke-min kalvos amuk* — it resembles a deep *kalvos*, a specific type of container. Rashi's description, reflected also in the diagram in the *Shita Mekubetzes*, depicts a vessel with indented interior compartments — something like a muffin pan — though another rendering shows a single central deep space. The common feature is that the vessel has distinct interior recesses. *U-khe-sheha-batzeik nach be-tocho* — when the dough settles into these indentations — *domeh ke-min tapuchei ha-bartin* — it resembles tree growths or knots, and *ke-min blutei ha-yevanim* — like the acorns of the Greek oak. That is, the baked dough would protrude from the vessel's compartments in rounded forms. The *gemara* concludes by citing the verse *ve-chol ha-na'aseh ba-marcheshet u-va-machavat* — using *be-* for the *marcheshet* (in) and *al* for the *machavat* (on) — confirming that these names belong to the vessels themselves, *al shem ha-keilim nikre'u ve-lo al shem ha-ma'asim*.

---

## Baked Mincha

### Mincha Be-Tanur

The *mishnah* turns to the *ma'afeh tanur*, the oven-baked *mincha*. If one declares *harei alai ba-tanur* — behold, I undertake to bring the *mincha* made in an oven — the *mishnah* specifies what does and does not fulfill that vow.

### Prohibited Vessels

The *mishnah* rules: *lo yavi ma'aseh kupach* — one may not bring something baked in a *kupach*, a small individual oven. The *kupach* was a compact, teepee-like structure in which fire burned at the base and heat concentrated near the top — an oven for a single person's use, as opposed to the larger communal *kira*. Nor may one bring *ma'aseh re'afim* — something baked on tiles, a flat surface rather than an enclosed oven. Nor *ma'aseh yorot ha-arviyim* — something baked in Arab pots, a method in which the pot itself serves as the baking chamber rather than an oven. Each of these is disqualified because the vow specified a *tanur*, and these alternatives do not constitute a genuine *tanur*.

### Home Preparation

One detail that emerges clearly from the *mishnah*'s framing is that the person is understood to be preparing the *mincha* at home and then bringing it. The formulation *lo yavi* — do not bring — and the specification of various household baking vessels all suggest that the vower is engaged in the baking process personally, outside the *mikdash*, before presenting the finished product. This is a significant assumption that will continue to require attention as the discussion develops.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda reads the double mention of *tanur* in the *pesuk* — *ma'afeh tanur* appearing twice in the relevant passages — through the principle that a doubled term expands the law's scope: *ein ribuy achar ribuy ella lerabot*. Since the Torah says *tanur* twice, Rabbi Yehuda infers that the law need not be limited to a full-sized oven; even a *kupach*, a smaller oven-like structure, is included and valid.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon reads the doubled *tanur* differently. The two mentions do not expand which vessels qualify; rather, they teach two distinct requirements: *echad she-tehei afiyatam ba-tanur* — the baking must take place in an oven — *ve-echad she-tehei hekdesham ba-tanur* — and the *mincha* must also become sanctified in the oven. The *tanur* in the *mikdash* itself functioned as a *kli sharet*, a sacred vessel, and it is through placement in that oven that the *mincha* acquires its *kedushah*. This sets the stage for the *gemara*'s subsequent probing of this position.

---

## Kedusha Timing

### Yotzei Problem

The *gemara* challenges Rabbi Shimon's position sharply. If the oven sanctifies the *mincha*, then any *mincha* removed from the *mikdash* after baking would be *pasul be-yotzei* — invalidated by having left the Temple precincts in a state of *kedushah*. Yet we know from a later *mishnah* that Rabbi Shimon himself says the *shtei ha-lechem* and *lechem ha-panim* are valid even when prepared in *Beit Pagi* — an area just outside the wall of the *azarah*. If these offerings had already acquired *kedushat ha-guf* in the oven, how could they be brought outside without becoming *pasul*?

### Mincha Kedusha

This question highlights a striking and fundamental difference between a *mincha* and an animal *korban*. When one designates an animal as an *olah* — *harei zu le-olah* — it immediately acquires *kedushat ha-guf*; *me'ilah* applies from that moment, and no *kli sharet* is required to achieve this sanctity. A *mincha*, by contrast, progresses through stages. The initial declaration is more like *kedushat damim*, and full *kedushat ha-guf* requires additional steps — the *kli sharet*, and in many cases further ritual acts — before it reaches its full sanctity.

### Tosafot on Kedusha

Tosafot raises the question in a still sharper form. The *gemara* elsewhere establishes that a *mincha* accompanying an animal offering — such as the *shtei ha-lechem* — does not achieve full *kedushat ha-guf* until the *zerikat ha-dam* of the accompanying animals. This means it can be taken outside the *mikdash* before that point without being rendered *pasul*. But is this a special rule limited to *menachot* that accompany animals, or does it apply to all *menachot*? Tosafot entertains the possibility that even after *kedushat kli* — sanctification through a sacred vessel — a *mincha* that stands alone may still be removed from the *mikdash* without being invalidated. This would distinguish *menachot* fundamentally from animal *korbanot*, where *kedushat ha-guf* renders removal immediately problematic.

### Rava's Reinterpretation

To resolve the difficulty, Rava offers a radical reinterpretation of Rabbi Shimon's ruling. *Eima she-yehei hekdesham le-shum tanur* — what Rabbi Shimon means is not that the oven itself confers *kedushah*, but that at the time of sanctification, one must explicitly designate the *mincha* as a *minchat ma'afeh tanur* — specifying the type of *mincha* it is to become. The requirement is not about the oven as a sanctifying instrument, but about the precision of the owner's declaration at the moment of dedication.

This is admittedly a significant re-reading of the plain meaning. But bracketing the hermeneutic move, what the discussion illuminates is that the *kedushah* of a *mincha* does not crystallize at the moment of baking, even when baked in the *mikdash's* own *kli sharet*. The *mincha* retains a degree of legal fluidity well past the point of its physical preparation — which, as noted, further supports the possibility that baking and preparation may take place outside the *mikdash* entirely. The level of sanctity that would lock the *mincha* within the Temple precincts comes later in the process, not at the point of cooking.

---

## Chalos/Rekikin Mix

### Vow Text

The *mishnah* addresses the case of one who vows *harei alai minchat ma'afeh* — to bring a baked *mincha*. The Torah describes this offering in Vayikra: *solet chalos matzot belulot ba-shemen u-rekikei matzot meshuchim ba-shemen* — fine flour loaves unleavened mixed with oil, and wafers unleavened anointed with oil. The question is whether one who vowed to bring a *minchat ma'afeh* may bring a mixture of both types, or must choose one.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda holds that one who vowed to bring a *minchat ma'afeh* may not bring half *chalos* and half *rekikin*. The *korban* must be of a single type. His source: *talmud lomar korban mincha* — the Torah uses the singular *korban mincha*, implying *korban echad amarti lecha ve-lo shenayim u-sheloshah korbanos* — I told you one *korban*, not two or three. Bringing half of one type and half of another would constitute, in effect, partial fulfillment of two separate categories rather than a single cohesive *korban*.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon permits bringing half *chalos* and half *rekikin*, arguing that both fall under a single *korban*. His textual argument is elegant: the word *korban* appears only once in the relevant verse, covering both *chalos* and *rekikin* together. Had the Torah intended two distinct *korbanot*, it would have repeated the word *korban* — one for each type. Since it uses *korban* once and then specifies both variations under that single header, the two forms are not separate *korbanot* but rather two options within a single category. One may therefore choose all loaves, all wafers, or a mixture of both.

### Mixing Method

A practical question arises: if bringing both types, how is the *kemitzah* performed? The *mincha* must have a *kometz* — a handful — taken from it. Rabbi Shimon's answer is that one bakes both the *chalos* and the *rekikin*, then breaks them into pieces, mixes the pieces together — *ubolelan* — and takes the *kometz* from the mixture — *v'komaitz mi-sheneihem* — so that the handful represents both types. Moreover, *im kamatz ve-alah be-yado me-echad al sheneihem* — if the handful happened to contain only pieces of one type, one is nonetheless *yotzei*. Since the two types are fundamentally one *korban*, the *kemitzah* of any portion of it is representative of the whole.

---

## Rabbi Yose's Drasha

### Different Pasuk

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda reaches the same practical conclusion as his father — that one may not bring half *chalos* and half *rekikin* — but derives it from a different verse. Rather than citing the verse about the *minchat ma'afeh tanur* itself, he turns to a passage in *Tzav*.

### Kol Mincha Drasha

The verse in *Tzav* reads: *ve-chol mincha asher te'afeh ba-tanur ve-chol na'aseh ba-marcheshet ve-al machavas* — listing the three baked types of *mincha* — *le-chohen ha-makriv otah lo tihyeh*. Then the verse continues: *ve-chol mincha belulah ba-shemen va-charevah* — and every *mincha* mixed with oil, and every dry one — *le-chol bnei Aharon tihyeh*. The two unbaked categories are *belulah ba-shemen* — the standard flour offering — and *charevah* — the dry one, used for the *minchat chote* or *sotah*, which contains no oil. These are completely distinct from one another in character, purpose, and legal status.

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda reasons: *mah ve-chol ha-amor le-mata shnei minin chalukin, af ve-chol ha-amor le-mala shnei minin chalukin*. Just as the *ve-chol* mentioned below — covering the two unbaked *menachot* — refers to two wholly separate categories, so too the *ve-chol* mentioned above — *ve-chol mincha asher te'afeh ba-tanur* — implies that the *ma'afeh tanur* encompasses two wholly separate categories: *chalos* and *rekikin*. And since they are categorically separate, they cannot be combined.

### Shemen Shemen

The *gemara* now returns to evaluate Rabbi Yehuda's position in light of Rabbi Shimon's response. The key is the verse's repetition of the word *shemen*: *chalos matzot belulot ba-shemen u-rekikei matzot meshuchim ba-shemen*. The word *shemen* appears twice. The *gemara* argues that this double mention functions *ke-man de-khtiv korban korban* — as if the Torah had written *korban* twice — marking the two sub-types as genuinely distinct options. This is what prevents Rabbi Shimon from reading *chalos* and *rekikin* as interchangeable components of a single undifferentiated offering.

### Rabbi Shimon Response

Rabbi Shimon, however, accounts for the doubled *shemen* differently. Had the Torah not written *ba-shemen* twice — *ee lo ketiv ba-shemen ba-shemen* — Rabbi Shimon says he would have thought the *only* valid option was half and half: *davka mechtza chalos u-mechtza rekikin*, which one might argue is actually the plain reading of the verse. *Aval chalos le-chudaihu ve-rekikin le-chudaihu — eima lo*: one might have thought that all-loaves or all-wafers alone would not fulfill the vow. The double *shemen* comes to teach that one may bring entirely one type or entirely the other. But the single *korban* header still permits bringing of both — so the full range of options remains: all *chalos*, all *rekikin*, or a mixture of both.

### B'Diavad Distinction

The *gemara* notes that Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda and his father Rabbi Yehuda arrive at the same *lechatchilah* ruling — do not bring half and half — but differ in a crucial *be-diavad* implication. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the prohibition on mixing is a formal requirement, but if one nevertheless brought half *chalos* and half *rekikin*, one would still be *yotzei*: the mixture still constitutes a valid *minchat ma'afeh tanur*, just not the preferred way to bring it. For Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, however, since he analogizes *chalos* and *rekikin* to the completely distinct unbaked categories — which are as different from each other as, say, a *minchat machavat* is from a *minchat marcheshet* — the categories are genuinely separate. Bringing a mixture would be like bringing part of one type of *mincha* for another, and one would not be *yotzei* even *be-diavad*.

With this, the *gemara* closes the perek: *hadran alach kol ha-menachot*. This was a perek devoted to the practical reality of what a *mincha* is.

---

## Perek Rabbi Ishmael

### Omer Introduction

The new perek begins with the words *Rabbi Yishmael omer* — and appropriately so, as the entire perek is devoted to the *omer*, the sheaf offering brought on the sixteenth of Nisan, together with the laws of *sefirat ha-omer* that follow from it.

### Starting Amounts

The *mishnah* opens with a dispute about how much grain one must begin with in order to produce the required *issaron* — one tenth of an *eifah* of fine flour — for the *omer*. Rabbi Ishmael rules: if the sixteenth of Nisan falls on *Shabbat*, one begins with three *se'im* of grain; on a weekday, one begins with five *se'im*. The *chachamim* disagree and hold there is no distinction: whether *Shabbat* or weekday, the *omer* was always produced from three *se'im*. On their view, three *se'im* is both sufficient and the consistent standard.

---

## Chananya's Cutting Rules

### Shabbat Procedure

Rabbi Chananya Segan HaKohanim describes how the *omer* grain was cut, and his account distinguishes sharply between *Shabbat* and weekday. On *Shabbat*, *be-yachid u-ve-magal echad u-ve-kupah achat* — a single person was sent out, using one scythe and one basket. The procedure was deliberately minimized and conducted without public display.

### Weekday Procedure

On a weekday, the cutting was done *be-sheloshah u-vi-shalosh kupot u-vi-shalosh magalot* — by three people, with three scythes and three baskets. The procedure was carried out openly and with conspicuous communal participation.

### Chachamim

The *chachamim* disagree with Rabbi Chananya's differentiation. In their view, the procedure was the same on *Shabbat* and weekday alike: three people, three scythes, three baskets, regardless of when the sixteenth fell.

### Sadducee Refutation

An important motivating factor underlies this dispute. The cutting of the *omer* overrides *Shabbat* — if the sixteenth falls on *Shabbat*, the grain must still be cut that night. This position was contested by the Sadducees, who disputed both when the *omer* was to be brought and whether it could override *Shabbat*. The public, conspicuous procedure — three people, three scythes, three baskets — served *le-hotzi mi-liban shel Tzadukim*, to refute the Sadducee position and demonstrate that the *omer* indeed overrides *Shabbat*, openly and without apology. Rabbi Chananya Segan HaKohanim's differentiation suggests a different balance: minimize the incursion into *Shabbat* on *Shabbat* itself, while maximizing public display on a weekday. As *Segan HaKohanim* — deputy to the *Kohen Gadol* — Rabbi Chananya was presumably speaking from direct experience of the Temple's procedures.

---

## Grain Amount Analysis

### Isaron Quality

The *gemara* questions Rabbi Ishmael's position directly. If on a weekday one uses five *se'im* and on *Shabbat* only three, the implication is that the quality or ease of producing the *issaron* differs based on starting quantity. But what exactly does Rabbi Ishmael hold? If a choice *issaron* can only be obtained from five *se'im*, then *Shabbat* should pose no obstacle — the *omer* overrides *Shabbat*, so use five *se'im* even then. And if three *se'im* suffices for a choice *issaron*, then why use five on a weekday?

### Rava's Explanation

Rava resolves this: Rabbi Ishmael holds that a choice *issaron* can indeed be obtained from three *se'im*, but it requires significantly more labor. From five *se'im*, the same quality is achieved more easily — *belo tircha ati me-chamesh, be-tircha ati mi-shalosh*. The reason is straightforward: when starting with a larger quantity, one can pass the grain through a coarser sieve and still obtain a sufficient yield of fine flour from the first pass, without repeated sifting. With only three *se'im*, achieving the same fineness demands more intensive sifting effort. 

### Shabbat Minimization

On a weekday, one uses five *se'im* for two reasons: it is more praiseworthy — one can say that five full *se'im* were processed to yield this single *issaron* — and it requires less effort, making the process smoother. On *Shabbat*, by contrast, one uses only three *se'im* — despite the extra labor involved — because the guiding principle is to minimize *Shabbat* violation.

### One vs. Many Melachot

The specific form of minimization is instructive. *Mutav she-yarbeh be-melacha achat be-harkadah ve-al yarbeh be-melachot harbeh* — it is better to perform one *melacha* many times over than to perform many distinct *melachot*. Performing repeated acts of a single category of labor — even many times — is preferable to involving multiple different categories of labor. While the *halachic* difference may not be fully expressed in terms of formal violations, there is an experiential and perhaps deeper sense in which performing many *melachot* of different kinds constitutes a greater rupture of *Shabbat* than repeating a single *melacha* many times. This principle has resonance in other *Shabbat* contexts as well — for instance, the rules governing how multiple unintentional violations are counted and what *korbanot* they require.

### Five Melachot

Rashi specifies the *melachot* involved in producing flour from grain: *she-yiktzor* — cutting; *ve-yizreh* — winnowing; *ve-yivror* — sorting (*borer*); *ve-yitchan* — grinding; *ve-yirkod* — sifting. These are five distinct *melachot*. Each additional *se'ah* of grain that must be harvested and processed requires engaging all five. By contrast, additional rounds of sifting alone — which is what the smaller quantity requires — involves only the single *melacha* of *harkadah* (sifting), performed repeatedly. On *Shabbat*, therefore, the calculus favors fewer categories of *melacha*, even at the cost of greater physical effort within that single category.

---

## Minimizing Violation

### Same Principle

Rava observes that Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka expressed essentially the same principle. Both are concerned with limiting *Shabbat* violation — or at least the scope of incursion into *Shabbat* — even in contexts where such violation is halachically permitted.

### Effort or Deeper

The question is whether their shared concern is merely about effort and convenience, or whether it reflects something more substantive — a principled view that even permitted *Shabbat* violations should be kept as narrow and contained as possible, not just for practical reasons but as an expression of the sanctity of *Shabbat* itself.

### Korban Pesach

The case of Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka illustrates this. A *baraita* teaches: when the fourteenth of Nisan falls on *Shabbat* and the *korban Pesach* must be brought, the animal is flayed — *mapshit es ha-Pesach ad ha-chazeh* — up to the chest. The chest area is the anatomical threshold: once that point is reached, the belly is sufficiently exposed to remove the *eimurim*, which must be burned on the altar even on *Shabbat*. Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka rules that one flays only to that point — no further. The *chachamim* disagree and hold that one flays the entire animal.

The logic of Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka is that once the religious purpose has been achieved — the *eimurim* can be removed — there is no warrant for continuing to flay. Additional flaying serves no sacred function and represents an unnecessary extension of *Shabbat* violation. *Kol heicha de-efshar lo tarchinan* — wherever possible, we do not exert effort beyond what is required.

### Religious Purpose

The *gemara* raises a subtle challenge, however, to the equation of Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka. Perhaps their reasoning differs in a critical way. Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka may limit the flaying not merely because it involves extra *melacha*, but specifically because of *bizayon kodshim* — the degradation of a sacred object. A partially flayed animal, left in that state, does not present a respectful appearance for a *korban*. This specific concern — that the sanctified object should not be treated disrespectfully — may be what limits him, not a general principle of minimizing *Shabbat* incursion. In a case without *bizayon kodshim*, he might hold like the *chachamim* and permit doing the full task.

### Omer Warranted

Conversely, Rabbi Ishmael's ruling about the *omer* may not be fully analogous to Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka either. When Rabbi Ishmael says to use three *se'im* rather than five on *Shabbat*, the two extra *se'im* are not merely gratuitous — they genuinely improve the process and make it easier to achieve a fine *issaron*. There is a legitimate religious benefit to using more grain. Perhaps in such a case, where the extra effort actually serves the *mincha* itself, Rabbi Shimon b'R. Yochanan ben Beroka would agree with the *chachamim* — permitting or even mandating the fuller procedure — because the additional *melacha* is genuinely warranted for the *mitzvah*. The *gemara* leaves open whether the two positions truly cohere or whether the relevant circumstances differ enough to keep them distinct.

---

---

# Menachot 64

## Minimizing Chilul Shabbos

### Rabbi Yishmael's Approach

The daf opens in the middle of a sustained discussion about *chilul Shabbos* in the context of Temple service. The *mishnah* had presented Rabbi Yishmael's position regarding the *omer* offering: when the *omer* falls on Shabbos, one should minimize the degree of Shabbos violation involved in its preparation. The *gemara* now attempts to identify other *tanna'im* who share an analogous approach — that even when Shabbos may legitimately be violated for certain *mitzvos* or Temple needs, one ought to do so in the way that minimizes the violation. The *gemara* frames this as a series of comparisons, each one an opportunity to examine not merely whether the positions are substantively identical, but what different types of calculations might govern the question of how much violation is warranted.

### Rava's Comparison

Rava proposes that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Chanina *segan ha-kohanim* said *davar echad* — the same thing. To establish this, the *gemara* invokes a *mishnah* that records Rabbi Chanina's position.

### Mishnah: Cutting & Proce…

Rabbi Chanina *segan ha-kohanim* rules: when the *omer* is cut on Shabbos, it is cut by one person alone, using one scythe and one basket. On a weekday, three people cut it, using three scythes and three baskets. The Rabbis, by contrast, hold that even on Shabbos one uses three people with three scythes and three baskets.

### Rabbi Chanina's Method

The *gemara* identifies the underlying principle: *keivan de'efshar lo trachinan* — since it is possible to accomplish the task with fewer people, we do not engage in the additional effort. Notably, the *gemara* uses the phrase *lo trachinan*, "we do not exert ourselves," even though the issue is not really about exertion but about the degree of *chilul Shabbos*. In fact, it might actually be less laborious to use more people — the point is simply that additional manpower means additional violation, and we minimize that wherever possible.

The parallel to Rabbi Yishmael is drawn: just as Rabbi Chanina minimizes the violation at the stage of cutting by using fewer personnel, Rabbi Yishmael minimizes violation at the stage of processing by cutting only three *se'ah* of grain rather than five, even though five *se'ah* yields finer flour for the *omer*. Each authority addresses a different stage — Rabbi Yishmael the quantity of wheat harvested, Rabbi Chanina the number of individuals involved — but both reflect the same underlying impulse to reduce *chilul Shabbos* even when it is technically permitted.

One might note that in terms of formal culpability, whether one cuts three *se'ah* or five in a single *shogeg* act would still produce only one *chatas* obligation, since the *shiur* has been met regardless of quantity. This question of whether continuous performance of a forbidden act constitutes one violation or many — depending on *hasra'ah* and other formal factors — is important and will resurface later in the *gemara*.

### Distinguishing Positions

The *gemara* immediately objects: *mima'i* — how do we know these two positions are truly equivalent? Perhaps they should be distinguished.

### Pirsumei Milsa Factor

The *gemara* raises the possibility that Rabbi Yishmael's call to minimize *chilul Shabbos* applies specifically in contexts where there is no countervailing benefit to doing more. By the *omer*, however, there is a significant consideration on the other side: *pirsumei milsa* — publicizing the deed. The more people involved in the cutting, the more the act becomes a public event, which matters particularly in the context of the *omer* because of the *Tzedukim*. The *Tzedukim* disputed the rabbinic reckoning of when the *omer* is to be brought, and the elaborate public ceremony of the cutting was designed in part to assert the correct *halacha* openly. If so, perhaps Rabbi Yishmael would actually *endorse* using more people for the cutting — for the sake of *pirsumei milsa* — and only minimize at the sifting stage where no such benefit applies.

There is a deeper point here as well. The *mitzvah* of the *omer* inaugurates the count toward *Shavuos*, and the *Torah* itself frames this with the phrase *u'sefartem lachem mi'macharas ha-Shabbos* — you shall count from the day after the Shabbos. The very day on which the counting begins is contested, and thus publicly declaring and marking that day is not merely a polemical gesture against the *Tzedukim* but is organically connected to the *mitzvah* of *sefirah* itself. The *pirsumei milsa* of the *omer* cutting may therefore be understood as intrinsic to the *mitzvah*, not merely incidental politics.

It is admittedly somewhat striking that a value like *pirsumei milsa* — or even the goal of countering the *Tzedukim* — could tip the scales and justify *more* rather than less *chilul Shabbos*, particularly if one understands the obligation to minimize as a *de'oraisa* concern, stemming from the position that Shabbos violation for Temple needs is *dechuyah* rather than *hutrah*. Yet one can argue that when the publicizing of the act is itself religiously significant and connected to the content of the *mitzvah*, it enters into the calculation of what is halachically warranted.

### Tzorech Gavoa Discussion

A second distinction is then raised: Rabbi Chanina *segan ha-kohanim* may have said to use only one person precisely because using one person versus three does not affect the end result. Whether one person cuts or three, the same quantity of grain is eventually harvested — it simply takes the one person three times as long. The *tzorech gavoah*, the Temple's religious interest, is served equally well either way. Here, however, the case of Rabbi Yishmael may be different: if one processes only three *se'ah* rather than five, the quality of the flour may be compromised. Fine flour is easier to obtain when you begin with a larger quantity; with only three *se'ah*, achieving the required fineness requires considerably more effort and may yield a less refined product. If so, the *tzorech gavoah* is better served by the five-*se'ah* approach, and Rabbi Chanina might concede this point — he would limit *chilul Shabbos* only when the end result is not thereby diminished, but not when the Temple's interest is materially affected.

The *gemara* thus leaves us with a rich and unresolved picture: we cannot simply say Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Chanina hold the same position in all cases. They share a general disposition toward minimizing *chilul Shabbos* where possible, but the specific calculations — whether *pirsumei milsa* is at stake, whether *tzorech gavoah* is affected — may yield very different conclusions in particular applications. As one student observed, we know what each authority said about his own case but cannot necessarily extrapolate to the other's. When we say they said *davar echad*, we mean they share the same underlying principle, not that they would necessarily rule identically in every scenario.

---

## Rabbi Yishmael & Rabbi Y…

### Rav Ashi's Proposal

Having found the comparison between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Chanina insufficient, the *gemara* tries again. Rav Ashi proposes: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yosi said *davar echad*. A *mishnah* is cited: whether the new moon was seen *ba'aliyah* — clearly, on a cloudless night — or *shelo nira ba'aliyah* — obscurely, under cloudy conditions — one violates Shabbos if necessary to travel to Jerusalem and testify before the *beis din*, thereby establishing *Rosh Chodesh* for that day. The urgency is real: if testimony is not delivered on the day the moon was sighted, that day cannot be sanctified as *Rosh Chodesh*. Riding a horse or being carried on a bed — whatever it takes — is warranted to arrive in time.

### Rabbi Yosi's Position

Rabbi Yosi dissents from the *tanna kamma* on one point: if the moon was seen *ba'aliyah* — clearly visible to all, on a bright night — then one need not violate Shabbos to come and testify. One can assume that many witnesses saw it, and this particular individual's testimony is not necessary. Rabbi Yosi's reasoning maps neatly onto *keivan de'efshar lo trachinan*: since the result can be achieved without this person's violation, we do not require that person to commit the violation.

### Keivan De'Efshar Princip…

The *gemara* draws the parallel to Rabbi Yishmael: just as Rabbi Yosi says that when testimony can be delivered without your Shabbos violation, you should not violate Shabbos, Rabbi Yishmael says that when the *omer* flour can be produced adequately with three *se'ah*, one should not harvest five. The underlying principle — *keivan de'efshar lo trachinan* — is the same in both cases.

### Case Distinctions

The *gemara* again probes whether this parallelism holds. Perhaps Rabbi Yishmael's position is limited to contexts where there is no further concern about what happens if we tell the witness not to come. Here, by *Rosh Chodesh*, there is precisely such a concern: if we discourage witnesses from coming on Shabbos when the moon was seen clearly, those witnesses may internalize the lesson incorrectly. The next time the moon is seen under partly cloudy conditions, a would-be witness might think, "They probably don't need me — surely others have seen it more clearly," and stay home. But if that person was in fact the only viable witness, *Rosh Chodesh* cannot be established. The policy concern is: *nimtze'as ata machshilo le'asid lavo* — you will end up tripping people up in the future. Rabbi Yishmael might therefore tell all witnesses to come, regardless of how clearly the moon was seen, in order to instill in them the habit of always coming forward.

A second distinction is introduced from the other direction: perhaps Rabbi Yosi's position is limited to cases where there is no *tzorech gavoah* at stake. When the moon is clearly visible and many witnesses are available, this individual's testimony contributes nothing to the Temple's interests — the day will be sanctified without him. Since no religious need is being served, *lo nitna Shabbos lidechos* — there is no basis to push aside Shabbos. But by the *omer*, the one already engaged in cutting three *se'ah* is already in the midst of a Shabbos violation.
