The person standing in the field cutting wheat is not analogous to the witness who has not yet taken a single step toward Jerusalem. For the one already involved, the question is only whether to do more or less of the very act already underway, and the *tzorech gavoah* consideration — that more grain yields finer flour — may be sufficient to justify doing more.

### Unified Principle

This distinction is striking. The witness who has not yet begun any violation is in an entirely different position from the Kohen already mid-harvest. For the witness, Rabbi Yosi says: you haven't started, others will do it, stay home. For the one already cutting, the question is only one of degree, and *tzorech gavoah* may tip that calculation toward doing more. The same principle — *keivan de'efshar lo trachinan* — generates different conclusions depending on whether one is already embedded in the act or is considering whether to begin it.

What emerges is that the *gemara*'s project of finding a *davar echad* is not about establishing doctrinal uniformity. Rather, it uses the exercise of comparing authorities to illuminate the different factors — *pirsumei milsa*, discouraging future witnesses, *tzorech gavoah*, and whether one is already mid-act — that enter into the question of how much *chilul Shabbos* is warranted when Shabbos is legitimately overridden. Whether one understands this as a *de'oraisa* regime of *dechuyah* — where only the minimum necessary violation is permitted — or as something more complex, the *gemara* makes clear that the calculations are subtle and highly context-dependent.

---

## Two Chataos Problem

### Case Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a distinct but related case: one slaughtered two *chataos* offerings belonging to the *tzibur* on Shabbos, when only one was required. According to Rashi's reading, one of the animals was the *korban* of the day — a *se'ir* for the *mussaf* — while the other was a different communal *chatat* that had not yet become obligatory to bring that day. The person accidentally slaughtered both.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava — or as the *gemara* notes, some attribute this to Rabbi Ami — rules: *chayav al ha-shniyah, patur al ha-rishonah*. One is liable for the second slaughter, which constituted an unjustified *chilul Shabbos*, but the first was entirely proper and one has in fact fulfilled the obligation of the day with it.

### No Retroactive Justifica…

The *gemara* then adds a striking corollary: even if the blood of the first animal spilled after the second was slaughtered, and the community therefore ended up using the second animal as its *korban*, this does not retroactively justify having slaughtered the second one. The determination is made as of the moment of the act. If the first animal's blood had spilled *before* the second was slaughtered, one would have been told to go ahead and slaughter a second — at that point it was necessary. But when both animals were slaughtered in sequence and only afterward the blood of the first spilled, the violation had already been committed when the second was slaughtered. Hindsight does not exonerate.

Similarly, the *gemara* adds: even if after slaughtering the first animal it was discovered to be *kachusha* — scrawny and inferior — one is still not retroactively justified for having slaughtered the second. The first animal, whatever its quality, was available and usable; the second slaughter was therefore unnecessary at the time it occurred.

### Nicer Korban Principle

The *gemara* then raises a pointed internal contradiction: did Rava really say this? For did Rava himself not also rule elsewhere that if one had two *chataos* before him — one fat and healthy, the other scrawny — and slaughtered the scrawny one first, one may not only go ahead and slaughter the fat one afterward without liability, but is in fact *instructed* to do so? *Havei shmena l'chatchila u'shchos* — bring a fat one and slaughter it. This is an astonishing ruling. Rava holds that even after the first animal has already been slaughtered and could technically satisfy the *chatat* obligation, if it is inferior, one is *permitted* — indeed encouraged — to violate Shabbos again by slaughtering a superior animal in its place.

This means that the license to violate Shabbos for Temple service extends not merely to fulfilling the bare minimum requirement, but encompasses bringing the *korban* in an ideal manner. The *mitzvah* of offering the *korban* properly — what we might call *hidur mitzvah* in the context of *korbanos* — is itself sufficient grounds for the additional Shabbos violation.

This is a genuinely large *chiddush*, and its moral and halachic implications are considerable. Not only does one violate Shabbos to bring a nicer *korban*, but the practical consequence is that the first animal — a *chatat* that has already been slaughtered — must now be set aside and destroyed, since a *chatat* shelamim cannot simply be reassigned. For the sake of a more aesthetically or halachically ideal offering, a validly slaughtered sacrificial animal is effectively wasted. One might ask whether any notion of *hidur mitzvah* can justify what is simultaneously a violation of the sanctity of *kodshim* and an obvious waste of animal life. These are not easy questions, and the *gemara* does not resolve them — it simply reports Rava's position as a *chiddush* of considerable scope.

### Attribution Question

The contradiction between Rava's two apparent positions is resolved in two ways. First, the earlier ruling that includes the *kachusha* case may simply need to be corrected: excise the clause about the scrawny animal from the first ruling, since Rava himself permits slaughtering a second animal in that scenario. Second, the *gemara* suggests: perhaps the stricter ruling was never Rava's to begin with. The original statement was attributed either to Rava or to Rabbi Ami — *ve'iseima Rabbi Ami*. Once it becomes clear that Rava permits slaughtering a superior animal even after a valid one has already been slaughtered, the stricter ruling must be attributed to Rabbi Ami alone.

### Moral Concerns

The moral dimension of Rava's position — permitting and even encouraging the discard of one *korban* in favor of a better one — was noted above. One might frame it as a concern purely internal to *kodshim*: does the value of bringing a nicer *korban* justify rendering a previously slaughtered *chatat* *pasul* in effect? And from a broader moral perspective: is the notion that "God deserves better" a sufficient justification for what is, by any ordinary reckoning, a significant waste of resources and of life?

The response one might offer is that *hidur mitzvah* is not merely about satisfying a divine preference in an anthropomorphic sense. Just as one spends money on a finer *esrog* rather than donating that sum to *tzedakah*, the religious value of beautifying the performance of a commandment is recognized as independently significant, even when it comes at a tangible cost. But the force of the question remains: choosing the finest available *esrog* before the fact is one thing; discarding what one has already consecrated and slaughtered because something better appeared is quite another. Rava's position is undeniably a *chiddush* of the highest order, and the discomfort it generates is not without basis.

---

## Intent vs. Reality Debate

### Ravina's Question

Ravina poses a further question to Rav Ashi, pressing the *kachusha* case in a more nuanced direction. The previous ruling had addressed a case where the first animal was openly scrawny — visible to the eye before slaughter. What if the animal appeared fine at the time of slaughter but was only discovered to be scrawny *b'vnei me'ayim* — in its innards, upon being opened up? Rashi understands this either as a discovery made when examining the carcass closely, or more literally as a finding about the quality of the internal organs and fats — a small liver, insufficient fatty portions to place on the *mizbe'ach* — which are precisely the parts of the *olah* and *chatat* that go on the altar. These defects are only detectable after the slaughter is complete.

The question then is: one slaughtered the first animal, which appeared healthy; then slaughtered a second; then discovered that the first was actually of inferior quality internally. Is one liable for the second slaughter or not?

### Machshava vs. Ma'aseh

This is where the *gemara* introduces its central conceptual question: *batar machshava azlinan* or *batar ma'aseh azlinan* — do we follow the person's intention at the time of the act, or do we follow the objective reality of the act itself?

If we follow *machshava* — subjective intent — then one is liable, because at the moment of the second slaughter, the person had no awareness that the first animal was deficient. In his mind, he was committing an unjustified violation: he thought the first animal was adequate, and he slaughtered a second anyway. *De-gavra issura ka-michavein* — subjectively, the person was oriented toward performing a prohibited act, even if not with malicious intent. Rashi notes that the person was not actually trying to do something wrong — he was sincerely trying to bring a *korban* — but the point is that he did not have, in his subjective awareness, any justification for the second slaughter.

If we follow *ma'aseh* — the objective reality of the act — then one might be exempt, because at the time of the second slaughter, the fact that justified it was already present in the world, even if unknown to the slaughterer. The first animal *was* scrawny; the scrawniness existed; and therefore the act of slaughtering the second was objectively warranted, even if the person did not know it.

This distinguishes the *kachusha* case sharply from the spilled-blood case discussed earlier. When the blood spilled *after* the second slaughter, the fact that would have justified it did not exist at the time — it came into being only later. That is pure retrospect and cannot exonerate. Here, however, the inferior quality of the first animal was already a fact at the moment of the second slaughter. The only missing element was *awareness* of that fact. The question is therefore: does the objective presence of a justifying reality suffice, or must the actor be subjectively aware of it?

### Drowning Infant Case

The *gemara* responds that this is precisely the debate between Rabbah and Rava, and introduces the famous case: one heard that an infant was drowning in the sea, but instead of trying to save the infant, one cast out a net to catch fish. As a result, both fish and the infant were hauled up. Is one liable for *chilul Shabbos* or exempt?

Casting a net on Shabbos is a *melachah*. If one cast the net purely to catch fish — which one clearly intended — one has performed a prohibited act with prohibited intent. But the very same act also saved a life, which is not only permitted but obligatory on Shabbos. The act is objectively an act of *hatzalas nefesh* and simultaneously an act of *chilul Shabbos* motivated by prohibited intent. How do we characterize it?

### Rabbah vs. Rava

Rabbah says: *patur* — exempt. *Zil batar ma'aseh* — follow the objective reality of the act. The act saved a life; it cannot be characterized as a prohibited *chilul Shabbos*. Rava says: *chayav* — liable. *Zil batar machshava* — follow the subjective intent. The person intended only to catch fish; that intent defines the nature of the act, which is therefore a *ma'aseh chilul Shabbos* rather than a *ma'aseh hatzalas nefesh*.

### Reconciling Rabbah

The *gemara* then offers a refinement of Rabbah's position. It suggests that Rabbah does not hold a purely objectivist view — he does not say the act is defined solely by what it accomplishes regardless of what the actor was thinking. Rather, Rabbah holds that even the most callous fisherman, if he *heard* that an infant was drowning, has some degree of concern for the infant in his heart — *amina nami da'tei a'tinok* — his mind is also on the infant. If so, even subjectively there is a dimension of *mitzvah* motivation. This is why Rabbah exempts: not because he ignores intent entirely, but because he believes that hearing of the drowning infant necessarily creates some minimal intention to help, even if the person refuses to admit it.

Consequently, if the person *did not hear* about the infant — if he cast his net in complete ignorance that anyone was drowning — then even Rabbah would hold him liable, because in that case there is no conceivable element of *mitzvah* motivation, and the act is purely a forbidden one that happened, by happenstance, to produce a beneficial result.

### Application to Animal

Applying this to Ravina's question: the person who slaughtered the second animal had no knowledge that the first was scrawny. He was entirely unaware of the fact that would have justified the act. Under the first reading of the *gemara*'s discussion, this means both Rabbah and Rava would hold him liable — Rava because subjective intent is what matters and the person had no awareness of any justification, and Rabbah because even on his more objective approach, some awareness is required for one's intent to be directed toward the *mitzvah*. Without any knowledge of the first animal's deficiency, neither the subjective nor the objective approach can exonerate him.

Under the alternative reading — *ve'ika d'amri* — the case of the scrawny animal discovered in the innards is itself the very debate between Rabbah and Rava. Rabbah, on his purely objectivist reading, would exempt the slaughterer because the objective fact of the first animal's inferiority existed at the time of the second slaughter, regardless of whether the person knew it. Rava, who follows *machshava*, would hold him liable, since the person had no subjective awareness of any justification.

---

## Pikuach Nefesh Priority

### Multiple Helpers Case

The *gemara* now turns to the case of *pikuach nefesh* directly, a subject that had been raised earlier in discussion and that now receives formal treatment. Rabbah — or on some textual variants, Rava — states the following: an ill person (*choleh*) was assessed to need one unit of dried figs (*grogaros*) to save his life on Shabbos. Ten people ran to bring figs, each performing a *melachah* — perhaps *hotza'ah* without an *eruv* — and each brought one, so that ten were brought in total when only one was needed.

### All Exempt Rule

All ten are exempt. Even those whose figs were completely unnecessary — because others had already brought more than enough — are not liable for *chilul Shabbos*. The *gemara* goes further: even if they did not arrive simultaneously but sequentially, *beze achar ze*, each one is still exempt.

### Recovered Patient

And further still: even if the first person's fig was so quickly administered that the patient recovered *before* the second person even arrived — so that by the time the second person walked in with his fig there was no longer any sick person present — even that person is exempt.

### Intent Principle

The governing principle is clear: what defines the act is the actor's intention at the time of performing it. Each of the ten people, at the moment they performed their act of *melachah*, was doing so in order to save a life. That intention — sincere, reasonable, and directed toward a genuine *pikuach nefesh* — is sufficient to characterize the act as a permitted one, regardless of whether it turned out to be necessary.

This directly addresses the earlier question about the *machshava*-versus-*ma'aseh* debate. For *pikuach nefesh*, the subjective dimension — *intending* to save a life — is what matters. Even if objectively no life was at risk by the time the act was completed, the intention to save renders the act permissible.

### Permissive Standard

This case stands in stark contrast to the Temple-service cases discussed earlier, where the *gemara* was carefully calibrating exactly how much *chilul Shabbos* was warranted and asking whether minimization was required. By *pikuach nefesh*, the standard is dramatically more permissive: one does not minimize, one does not hold back because others are already handling it, and one does not reassess based on whether the effort turned out to be needed. Anyone who reasonably believed they were contributing to saving a life is fully exempt.

The question of whether the *gemara*'s ruling is *Rabbah* or *Rava* matters, because the two have just been presented as holding opposite positions on the objectivist-subjectivist spectrum. If the ruling is Rava's, it is straightforward: Rava holds that *machshava* governs, and since all ten people subjectively intended to save a life, all ten are exempt, even though objectively most or all were unnecessary. If it is Rabbah's ruling, it is particularly striking: Rabbah, who was shown to take the more objective view, here embraces a purely intentionalist standard. One way to reconcile this is to say that Rabbah applies his principle of leniency in both directions — wherever the act can be characterized as non-violative, whether because it objectively saves a life (the fish case) or because the person sincerely intended to save a life (this case), Rabbah will not call it *chilul Shabbos*. The practical upshot is that for *pikuach nefesh*, even Rabbah would say: if in your mind you are still engaged in saving this person, you act — you do not hesitate, you do not calculate whether others have already done enough, and you are not held responsible if it turns out to have been unnecessary.

This has direct practical significance. The *gemara*'s ruling that ten people running simultaneously are all exempt — each one performing a separate *melachah* — establishes that when it comes to saving a life, we do not want people holding back out of an excess of scruple. The danger of over-calculation in a *pikuach nefesh* situation is that someone who could have helped does not act, on the assumption that others will. The *gemara* forestalls that reasoning entirely.

---

## Multiple Fruit Locations

### Fruit Distribution Case

The *gemara* closes with Rabbah's final question, which returns to the theme of minimizing *melachah* acts and directly engages the issue of *shiurim* raised earlier. A sick person on Shabbos requires two units of fruit — two figs — to save his life. On the tree before us, there are two figs growing on two separate stems (*uktzim*), and a separate stem bearing three figs.

### Picking Strategy Question

The question: which do we pick? Do we pluck two figs from two separate stems — two acts of *ketzira*, harvesting — bringing exactly what is needed? Or do we pluck the three figs from the single stem — one act of *ketzira* — bringing one more than is strictly required?

### Minimize Acts

The *gemara* answers without hesitation: *peshita d'shalosh maitinan* — it is obvious that we bring three from the single stem. The goal is to minimize the number of acts of *melachah*, and a single act that brings three is preferable to two separate acts that bring only two.

### Distinguished from Omer

The *gemara* then carefully distinguishes this from Rabbi Yishmael's ruling about the *omer*. There, Rabbi Yishmael says to harvest *less* grain — three *se'ah* rather than five — even though that means more effort in sifting. Why? Because in that case, reducing the quantity of grain harvested also reduces the act of *ketzira* — less cutting corresponds to less grain. The reduction in quantity and the reduction in the number or extent of the prohibited act go hand in hand.

### Unified Principle

Here, by contrast, the relationship is inverted: bringing *less* quantity — two figs instead of three — would actually require *more* acts of *melachah*, since the two figs are on separate stems. When minimizing quantity and minimizing the number of prohibited acts pull in opposite directions, the correct calculation is to minimize the number of acts, even if that means bringing a slightly larger quantity than strictly necessary.

The principle that emerges is clean and important: a single act of *melachah*, even if it yields more than the minimum required quantity, is always preferable to multiple acts of *melachah* that together yield only the minimum. One violation, however substantial, is categorically less than two violations, however small. This also clarifies the question about *shiurim* that arose earlier: when the *gemara* discusses continuous acts — continuous sifting, continuous drinking by a *nazir* — the question of whether that constitutes one violation or many depends on how the act is divided and whether formal warnings intervene. But when we have clearly discrete, separate acts — two pluckings from two stems — those are unambiguously two violations, and one act producing more quantity is unambiguously preferable. Rabbi Yishmael's preference for more sifting over more cutting is perfectly consistent with this: more sifting is one extended act, while more cutting means engaging separately with more grain — conceptually closer to multiple acts. The distinction between quantity within a single act and multiplicity of acts is the key to resolving what might otherwise appear to be contradictory positions.

---

---

# Menachot 64b

## Omer Source & Karmel

### Intro: Omer from Karov

The *mishnah* opens with a fundamental principle governing the *omer* offering: *mitzvat ha-omer lehavi min ha-karov* — the obligation is to bring the barley for the *omer* from grain that grows near Yerushalayim. If the grain nearby has not yet ripened — *lo biker ha-karov bi-Yerushalayim* — then one brings it from anywhere in Israel, though the *mishnah* elsewhere makes clear that the grain must come from within the Land of Israel. The *beit din* did not maintain its own dedicated fields; rather, they drew from privately owned grain in the surrounding area. The *mishnah* then records two historical exceptions: *ma'aseh she-ba ha-omer mi-gagot srifin* — there was once an occasion when the *omer* had to be brought from a distant place called *Gagot Tsrifin*, meaning "the rooftops of the tent-structures," and the *shtei halechem* of Shavuot had to come from a valley known as *Ein Socher*.

### Karmel & Ma'avirin

The *Gemara* asks: what is the reason that one must ideally bring the *omer* from nearby grain? Two rationales are offered. The first is *mishum karmel* — because the Torah describes the *omer* offering using the word *karmel*, which the *Gemara* reads as a composite of *rach u-malei*, meaning soft and full. Grain brought from nearby Yerushalayim will be fresher, not yet hardened, and thus better satisfies the *karmel* quality requirement. The second rationale is *mishum de-ein ma'avirin al ha-mitzvot* — one does not pass over an available opportunity to perform a *mitzvah* in favor of a more distant or elaborate alternative.

### Ein Ma'avirin Principle

The principle of *ein ma'avirin al ha-mitzvot* has its own extensive *sugyot*. A classic example discussed earlier in Menachot concerns *tefillin*: one puts on the *tefillin shel yad* before the *tefillin shel rosh*. If one reaches into the bag and accidentally withdraws the *tefillin shel rosh* first, does *ein ma'avirin* require placing it on immediately, setting aside the proper order? In practice, one does set aside the *tefillin shel rosh* in order to first don the *tefillin shel yad*, because the importance of maintaining the correct sequence overrides the principle in that case — illustrating where these two considerations come into tension.

The application here is somewhat unusual. Normally, *ein ma'avirin* describes a scenario where one has physically encountered a *mitzvah* opportunity and must not pass it by. Here, however, the case may be that grain to the east of Yerushalayim is ripe and closer, while grain to the west is also ripe but farther away and perhaps of better quality. One has not yet physically encountered the eastern grain, yet the principle seems to require going toward the nearer source rather than passing it over for a more distant alternative. It is, in any event, a matter of *mitzvah* in the optimal sense — *be-geder mitzvah* — and not a question of *eikuva*, of whether the *omer* brought from a distant field would be disqualified after the fact. The *mishnah* presupposes that it would be valid; the obligation to bring from nearby is an ideal, not an invalidating condition.

---

## Hashmonean Siege Story

### Siege Context

Having established that the *omer* ordinarily must come from nearby grain, the *Gemara* now brings the *baraita* that explains the exceptional cases of *Gagot Tsrifin* and *Ein Socher*. *Tanu rabbanan*: when the kings of the *beit Chashmonai* were laying siege one against the other — *keshesharu malkhei beit Chashmonai ze al ze* — Horkanous was outside Yerushalayim conducting the siege, while Aristobolus was within the city walls. These were descendants of the Hasmoneans, two brothers contending over kingship, at various points enlisting outside alliances to gain the upper hand. The *Gemara*'s phrasing that they were *tzarim ze al ze* — besieging one another — is notably accurate: as Josephus records in the *Antiquities*, the situation reversed itself over time; at an earlier stage Aristobolus had been on the outside and had captured Yerushalayim, but at this point in the conflict Aristobolus held the city from within while Horkanous pressed from without.

Each day, those inside would lower a basket with coins down the wall — *meshalshelim lahen dinarei be-kupah* — and the troops outside, despite conducting a siege, would send up lambs for use as *temidim*. Whatever their political differences, both sides apparently recognized the sanctity of the *Beit Hamikdash* and continued to facilitate its worship.

### Traitor & Greek Wisdom

At this point, *hayah sham zaken echad she-hayah makir be-chokhmat Yevanit* — there was a certain elder who was versed in *chokhmat Yevanit*, Greek wisdom. From the context it is clear this refers to some mode of communication that could be used without detection — whether it meant the Greek language itself, or some system of signals akin to a code. *Tosafot* raises the possibility that it involved a form of visual signals. Whatever the precise meaning, this elder was a traitor operating from within, and he communicated to the besieging forces outside using this method: *kol zman she-asukim ba-avodah ein nimisarin be-yadkhem* — as long as those within are engaged in the Temple service, they will not be delivered into your hands. This is perhaps best understood not as a metaphysical secret but as a morale observation — the people inside drew their confidence and resilience from their ongoing worship, and so long as that continued, the siege would not succeed.

The very next day, those outside lowered the coins as usual, but instead of sending up a lamb, they sent up a pig. When the pig reached the midpoint of the wall, *naatz tzipornav ba-homah* — it dug its nails into the wall — and the entire Land of Israel shook four hundred *parsah* by four hundred *parsah*, that being the *Gemara*'s conventional measure for the dimensions of Eretz Yisrael.

### Consequences & Curses

At that moment, they declared: *arur she-yigadel hazir* — cursed be one who raises pigs — *ve-arur she-yelameid beno chokhmat Yevanit* — and cursed be one who teaches his son Greek wisdom.

### Burned Fields Context

*Rashi* explains the connection to our *mishnah*: a standard tactic in siege warfare was to burn the surrounding fields so that the besieged city could not draw sustenance from the area. Accordingly, all the nearby fields of barley and wheat were scorched, making it impossible to source the *omer* and *shtei halechem* from the usual nearby locations. The tradition recorded in the *mishnah* — that the *omer* once came from *Gagot Tsrifin* and the *shtei halechem* from *Ein Socher* — dates to this period. It is also possible that the distant sourcing occurred after the siege was resolved and the city was taken, at which point the besieging forces had already burned the nearby fields; this would better explain how those who brought the *omer* and *shtei halechem* could do so without depending on the cooperation of troops still outside the walls.

### Deaf-Mute & Gagot Tserif…

When it came time to bring the *omer*, no one knew where to find suitable barley — *lo havu yad'i meheika aytuyei omer* — as all the nearby grain was gone. An announcement was made: if anyone knows of a place where barley is available, please come forward. A mute person appeared — *ata hahu charesha*; the word *cheresh* can mean deaf-mute, but here the emphasis is on his inability to speak, though presumably he heard the announcement or was informed of it. He placed one hand on the roof of a nearby building — *oteiv chada yadei a-igra* — and his other hand on a *tsrifa*, a tent-like structure — *ve-chada yadei a-tsrifa*.

*Mordechai* — identified by *Rashi* as the original Mordechai of the Purim story, though *Tosafot* finds this chronologically difficult — interpreted the gesture and said to those around him: is there perhaps a place called *Gagot Tsrifin* or *Tsrifin Gagot*? For the gesture placed one hand on a roof (*gag*) and one on a tent-structure (*tsrif*). *Badku ve-ashkechu* — they investigated and found that indeed such a place existed — and that is where they brought the *omer* from.

### Ein Socher Discovery

When the time came for the *shtei halechem* and once again no one knew where to find ripe wheat, the same procedure repeated itself. Another announcement was made, and another mute person came forward. This one placed one hand over his eyes — *oteiv yadei a-einei* — and his other hand on a *sikhra*, which *Rashi* explains is the hole through which a door bolt passes, the mechanism known as a *socher*. Mordechai again interpreted: is there a place called *Ein Socher* — *ayin* meaning eye, *socher* meaning the bolt — or perhaps *Socher Ayin*? They checked and found such a place, and the *shtei halechem* was brought from there.

### Traitor vs. Mordechai

The structure of this passage is striking. Earlier in the narrative, a traitorous elder used *chokhmat Yevanit* — a covert mode of communication — to pass information to the enemy, which ultimately led to the pig being sent up and the desecration of the Temple service. Here, Mordechai uses gestural interpretation — a different but analogous form of unconventional communication — in order to restore and enable the sacred service. The methods of communication are in themselves neutral; the question is entirely how they are deployed. The traitor used such techniques to subvert and corrupt, while Mordechai used a comparable creative interpretive capacity to serve and repair.

There is also a symbolic resonance in the pig itself. *Chazal* famously note that the pig is the only non-kosher animal that possesses split hooves without chewing its cud — it displays the outward sign of *kashrut* while lacking the inward reality. The image of the pig digging its nails into the wall of Yerushalayim, pressing in as though to enter, evokes something of this deceptive quality. The Hasmonean brothers, descendants of the very heroes who fought against Antiochus's decrees, were now reenacting the central violation of those decrees: the sacrifice of swine. As the Book of Maccabees records, among the edicts of Antiochus was the command to sacrifice swine and other unclean animals. This context makes the episode all the more devastating — it is not merely a military stratagem but an embrace of the very desecration the Hasmoneans had once died to prevent.

The parallel with the Josephus account in *Antiquities* 14:2 is also notable. Josephus does not mention a pig; he describes the arrangement of exchanging coins for sacrificial animals during the Passover season, the betrayal when the animals were not delivered, and God's punishment through a destructive storm that destroyed the crops across the entire country — which accounts for the unavailability of nearby grain. The *Gemara*'s inclusion of the pig may reflect an interpretive layer that consciously connects the episode to the Antiochian decrees, placing the Hasmonean civil conflict within the same moral framework as the earlier persecution.

Regarding *chokhmat Yevanit* and the curse against it: the scholar Saul Lieberman, in his works *Greek in Jewish Palestine* and *Hellenism in Jewish Palestine*, argues that what the sources actually forbid is specifically teaching *chokhmat Yevanit* to one's son — to a young and impressionable child — because of the concern that it would open the gateway to Hellenistic culture and influence. For an adult, there was no prohibition beyond the question of *bittul Torah*. *Tosafot* notes the tension between this curse and the tradition permitting the study of *chokhmat Yevanit* to one who has already mastered all of Torah, and suggests that the curse may not have constituted a formal prohibition but rather an expression of strong disapproval, which only later developed into a more formal restriction.

---

## Mordechai & Bird Offerin…

### Three Women's Birds

The *Gemara* continues with another episode in which Mordechai's interpretive genius is on display. Three women arrived at the *Beit Hamikdash*, each bearing a pair of birds — *kinin* — as an offering. The first said she was bringing it *le-zivati*, for her flow; the second said *le-yamati*, for her ocean; and the third said *le-onati*, for her period. On the surface, all three seemed to be indicating conditions related to uterine bleeding and thus presenting their birds as the *korban* of a *zavah* — a woman who experiences a non-menstrual uterine flow and who, after seven clean days, brings one bird as a *chatat* and one as an *olah*.

### Mordechai's Interpretati…

Those present assumed that *zivati* meant she was literally a *zavah*, that *yamati* meant a heavy flow, and that *onati* referred to her menstrual period — all variants of the same *tum'ah*-based obligation, each requiring one *chatat* and one *olah*. Mordechai intervened. He suggested: *shema be-zov sakanah*, *shema be-yam sakanah*, *shema be-oness sakanah* — perhaps what each woman meant was not that she had suffered from a *tum'ah*-related flow, but that her flow had posed a health danger. She had been in peril and recovered, and was now bringing her birds not as an obligatory *korban* for *tum'ah*, but as a voluntary *olah* — a thanksgiving for her recovery. Under this reading, all six birds are *olot*, not one *chatat* and one *olah* per pair. *Badku ve-ashkechu* — they investigated and found that Mordechai's interpretation was correct.

### Petachiah/Balshan Identi…

This connects directly to the *mishnah* at the opening of 65a: *Petachyah al ha-kinin* — one of the officers of the *Beit Hamikdash* who oversaw the funds designated for bird offerings was named Petachyah. The *Gemara* identifies this Petachyah as Mordechai. Why was Mordechai called Petachyah? *She-poteach devarim ve-dorshanam* — because he would open up words and interpret them, as demonstrated in both the gestural communication stories and the women's bird offerings. Additionally, *veyodeia be-shivim lashon* — he knew all seventy languages — which presumably enabled this capacity for creative interpretation across linguistic registers.

### Seventy Languages

But the *Gemara* immediately raises an objection: the entire *Sanhedrin* knows all seventy languages. As Rabbi Yochanan teaches, one may only be seated on the *Sanhedrin* if one possesses wisdom, fine appearance, proper stature, seniority, and knowledge of *kshafim* — witchcraft — the last requirement understood by *Rashi* as enabling judges to counter the use of witchcraft by those being tried, and by *Tosafot* more practically as familiarity with such matters so as to properly evaluate testimony involving them. Critically, members of the *Sanhedrin* must also know all seventy languages, *shelo tehei Sanhedrin shoma'at mi-pi ha-torgeman* — so that the court need not rely on a translator, whose rendering might, whether deliberately or inadvertently, distort what was actually said. *Tosafot* acknowledges the difficulty of this requirement literally and suggests that perhaps only a portion of the members needed this knowledge, and one or two trusted members who knew the language could reliably relay the testimony to the rest.

If Mordechai was himself a member of the *Sanhedrin*, his knowledge of seventy languages was unremarkable. The *Gemara* therefore qualifies: *de-havei bala lishnei ve-darish* — what made Mordechai unique was that he could blend languages and interpret from them creatively. This is the meaning of the name *Balshan* by which Mordechai is also known in Nehemia — *bolel lashon*, one who mixes language. The capacity to think across linguistic boundaries, to hear in one language and understand what is being expressed through the conventions of another, was his distinctive gift. The *Gemara* thus identifies Mordechai of the Purim story with Balshan of Nehemia, and this identification becomes the interpretive key to his role in the *Beit Hamikdash* narratives above.

The larger thematic thread tying these stories together is the use and misuse of communicative skill. The traitorous elder deployed *chokhmat Yevanit* — whatever covert communication system it entailed — to pass damaging information to the enemy. Mordechai, by contrast, deployed his linguistic and interpretive gifts to locate grain for the *omer*, to identify a source of wheat for the *shtei halechem*, and to correctly identify the status of women's bird offerings. The methods of unusual communication are not inherently wrong; their moral valence depends entirely on the purpose to which they are put.

---

## Omer Harvesting Procedure

### Marking & Gathering

The following *mishnah* describes the actual harvesting of the *omer* in detail. *Shluchei beit din yotzim me-erev yom tov* — agents of *beit din* would go out on the eve of *yom tov*, the day before the *omer* is to be cut, *ve-osim otan kerichot mechubar la-karka* — and they would tie bands around stalks of barley while the grain was still attached to the ground. This was preparatory work: they identified the precise stalks they intended to cut, bound them together so they could be cut efficiently, and thereby eliminated any unnecessary delay once the actual cutting began that night. This is reminiscent of the custom of making a small incision in the *challah* before reciting *ha-motzi*, so that after the blessing one can begin cutting immediately without pausing to find the right spot — though in practice, as noted, one often forgets where the mark was made.

*Kol ha-ayarot ha-smuchot l'sham mitkansot l'sham* — all the villages near that field would gather there, *kedei she-yeikatzar be-esek gadol* — so that the harvesting would take place amid great public ceremony and tumult. The reason for this public gathering was to make unmistakably clear which day the *omer* was being cut and the counting begun, and consequently which day, fifty days hence, would be *Shavuot* — matters that were actively disputed by the *Baitusin* sectarians.

### Triple Affirmation

Once nightfall arrived — for the cutting had to take place at night, so that the *omer* could be brought as an offering the following morning, both the night and the following day being halachically the same calendar date — the procedure was conducted with elaborate public affirmation. The one designated to cut would ask the assembled crowd, *ba ha-shemesh?* — has the sun set? — and they would answer *hen*, yes. He would ask again, *ba ha-shemesh?* — and again they would answer *hen*. He would then hold up the scythe and ask *magal zu?* — shall I cut with this scythe? — *hen*. And again, *magal zu?* — *hen*. Then *kuppa zu?* — shall I use this basket? — *hen*, and again *kuppa zu?* — *hen*. If the harvesting fell on *Shabbat*, he would ask *Shabbat zu?* — shall I do this even though it is *Shabbat*? — *hen*, *Shabbat zu?* — *hen*. Finally, *ektzor?* — shall I now cut? — and the crowd would call back *katzor*, cut! *Ektzor?* — *katzor!* Each element of the procedure was affirmed three times by the assembled crowd: *ve-hem omrim lo hen hen hen*.

### Anti-Baytusin Framing

The *Gemara* explains this elaborate procedure: *kol kach lama? mipnei ha-Baitusin* — why all this? Because of the *Baitusin*, who maintained that the *omer* harvest should not take place on *motzaei yom tov* — the night following the first day of Pesach — but rather on *mimocharat ha-Shabbat*, on a Sunday. By assembling the entire surrounding population and conducting the harvesting with this repeated, unanimous public affirmation, the rabbinic authorities were not merely announcing their practice; they were framing the rabbinic position as universal consensus, with any alternative view rendered marginal and eccentric. The theatrical structure of the questioning and the crowd's affirmation was designed to convey: every normal person understands that this is how it is done.

---

## Tamid Individual/Communal

### Megillat Taanit Source

The *Gemara* now cites *Megillat Ta'anit*, an ancient text from the Second Temple period that records minor holidays — days on which fasting and, for the more significant ones, even eulogizing was prohibited. It is from *Megillat Ta'anit* that the eight days of Chanukah derive their status. The relevant passage reads: from *Rosh Chodesh Nisan* until the eighth of Nisan — *me-reish yarcha de-Nisan ad tamanya bei* — *itokam tamida d'lo l'mispad*: the proper practice of the *tamid* offering was established, and therefore one may not eulogize on those days. From the eighth of Nisan until the end of *Pesach* — *itosaf chaga de-shavuaya* — the holiday of *Shavuot* was established in its proper form, and one does not fast or eulogize during that period.

### Tzedukim Position

What was the dispute about the *tamid*? *She-hayu ha-Tzedukim omrim: yachid mitnadeiv u-meivi tamid* — the Sadducees held that an individual could personally donate and bring the *tamid*. Their textual basis was the verse: *et ha-keves ha-echad ta'aseh va-boker ve-et ha-keves ha-sheni ta'aseh bein ha-arbayim* — "you," in the singular, shall make the one lamb in the morning and the one lamb in the afternoon. The singular form of *ta'aseh* implies, in their reading, that an individual could sponsor and thereby "own" a given day's *tamid* offering — in effect, having today's *tamid* brought in his name.

### Pharisaic Counter

The Pharisaic response drew on another verse: *et korbani lachmi le-ishai tishm'ru* — "you," in the plural, shall observe my offerings. The plural *tishm'ru* indicates that the *tamid* is inherently a communal obligation, funded by communal *shekalim*, not by individual donation. This answer was considered decisive, though as a matter of textual argument one might equally note that singular language in the Torah can refer to the collective — "you" the nation — without implying individual sponsorship.

### Subtext: Individual vs.…

Beyond the textual argument, there is a notable subtext: it is consistently the *Tzedukim* who seek to break from the communal framework. Whether in the case of the *tamid* or, as we will see, in the calendar debates, their positions allow for individual assertion — a single donor imposing his identity on a communal sacrifice — at the expense of the shared, consensual reality. *Chazal*, writing as the victors in these debates, frame themselves as the mainstream and the *Tzedukim* and *Baitusin* as sectarians. One should bear in mind that each party considered itself the authentic carrier of tradition. The rhetorical framing — the overwhelming consensus, the dismissal of opposing positions as self-evidently absurd — is a polemical strategy, not necessarily a reflection of how evenly or unevenly matched the underlying arguments were. The debate over the *tamid*, whatever its substance, lasted eight days before resolution, which itself suggests it was not a foregone conclusion.

---

## Shavuot Day Debate

### Baytusin: Sunday Only

The second dispute recorded in *Megillat Ta'anit* concerns the date of *Shavuot*. The *Baitusin* held *atzeret achar ha-Shabbat* — that *Shavuot* falls on a Sunday, because the counting of the *omer* begins on *mimocharat ha-Shabbat* — the day after *Shabbat* — which they read as referring to the weekly *Shabbat*, not to *yom tov*. Under their reading, the *omer* is always cut on a Saturday night and *Shavuot* always falls on a Sunday, fifty days later.

### Ben Zakkai Dismissal

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was assigned to engage them — *nitpal lahem Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* — though the verb *nitpal*, from *tafel*, connotes something secondary or ancillary, already signaling that the engagement is not being taken entirely seriously. His opening was blunt: *shotim* — idiots — where do you derive this idea? The text reports that no one was willing to answer him: *ve-lo hayah adam echad she-hayah meshivo*. This is unsurprising given the rhetorical framing; when the presiding authority opens by calling the opposing position idiotic, few will volunteer to defend it.

### Elder's Defense

One elder did engage — *chutz mi-zaken echad she-hayah mitatpeit kenegdo* — though the verb *mitatpeit* is itself dismissive, suggesting sputtering or chattering rather than coherent argument. His position was this: *Moshe Rabbeinu ohev Yisrael hayah* — Moshe Rabbeinu loved the Jewish people — *ve-yodeia she-atzeret yom echad hu* — and he knew that *Shavuot* was only a single day. Therefore, *amad ve-tiknah achar Shabbat* — he arranged that *Shavuot* would always fall on a Sunday, *kedei she-yisrael mitangrin shnei yamim* — so that Jews would enjoy two consecutive days of celebration, the Sunday of *Shavuot* following immediately on *Shabbat*.

### Ben Zakkai Rebuttal

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response was to quote the verse *achad asar yom me-Chorev derech har Se'ir* — it is eleven days from Sinai to Eretz Yisrael. If Moshe Rabbeinu truly loved Israel and was willing to arrange the calendar for their pleasure, *lama ikevam ba-midbar arbaim shanah?* — why did he make them wander in the desert for forty years, when the journey was only eleven days? The argument from Moshe's love for Israel is therefore an absurd foundation for a calendrical claim. The elder's response was: *rabbi be-chach ata potrani?* — is that really how you dismiss me? — implying that the rebuttal was rhetorically clever but substantively inadequate. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's final word: *shoteh* — again, idiot — *ve-lo tehei Torah shleimah shelanu ke-sichah beteilah shelachem*: our complete Torah cannot be equated with your frivolous speech.

### Debate Assessment

The debate is troubling to read on its own terms. The *Baitusin* position is not obviously absurd: the plain meaning — *peshat* — of *mimocharat ha-Shabbat* does appear to refer to the day after the weekly *Shabbat*, and that reading is not unreasonable. The Pharisaic interpretation, that *Shabbat* here means *yom tov*, depends on a tradition that runs against the surface reading of the text. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's refusal to engage substantively — his reliance instead on the rhetoric of contempt — may reflect an awareness that the argument on purely textual grounds is not easily won. As was observed, this is a situation where one might say: argument weak, speak harshly. The deck is not simply loaded by superior logic; it is loaded by the exercise of institutional authority. The *Gemara* will spend the remainder of the *daf* attempting to supply the textual proofs that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai treated as self-evident — which in itself suggests they required more work than his dismissive posture implied.

---

## Textual Proofs: 50 Days

### 50 Days & 7 Weeks

The *Gemara* now turns to the textual arguments. One verse says *tisperu chamishim yom* — count fifty days; another says *sheva shabbatot temimot tihyena* — there shall be seven complete weeks. How are both fulfilled?

### Full Weeks Conditional

The resolution offered is: *kan be-yom tov she-chal lihyot be-Shabbat, kan be-yom tov she-chal lihyot be-emtza Shabbat* — one verse speaks to the case where *yom tov* falls on *Shabbat*, and the other to when *yom tov* falls on a weekday. *Sheva shabbatot temimot* — full weeks — means weeks that begin on Sunday. This is achievable only when *yom tov* itself falls on *Shabbat*, so that the *omer* counting begins on Sunday, producing seven complete weeks. When *yom tov* falls on any other day of the week, the counting begins on a day other than Sunday, and the weeks are not complete in that sense; in that case, only the day-count of fifty applies. This reconciliation makes clear that the counting is anchored to *yom tov* — to Pesach — and not to the weekly *Shabbat*. If it were always anchored to *Shabbat*, it would always start on Sunday and always produce full weeks, making the two verses redundant with each other rather than complementary.

### 50 vs. 49 Days

A further problem is that the *omer* is actually counted for forty-nine days, not fifty. Why does the verse say *chamishim yom*? This question is not addressed in the *Gemara* itself but is treated by the *Rishonim*. *Tosafot* offers two approaches: first, that the counting is *until* the fiftieth day — *ad ve-lo ad bi-khlal* — meaning the fiftieth day marks the endpoint but is not itself counted; second, reading the full verse — *ad mimocharat ha-Shabbat ha-shvi'it tisperu chamishim yom ve-hikravtem mincha chadasha la-Hashem* — the fiftieth day is *Shavuot* itself, the day of the new offering, but the counting of fifty terminates at that day rather than including it. The *Rosh* offers a third answer: the Torah engages in a form of rounding — just as the Torah prescribes forty lashes and *Chazal* derive that only thirty-nine are actually administered, so too fifty days is a rounded figure meaning forty-nine. It is notable that this question about the fifty versus forty-nine is addressed by the *Rishonim* but not explicitly by the *Gemara* here.

---

## R. Eliezer & Beit Din

### Singular vs. Plural Count

Rabbi Eliezer disagrees with the foregoing analysis, saying *eino tzarich* — this proof is unnecessary — and derives the same conclusion from a different verse. The verse *tispar lach* uses the singular form of the verb — count, for yourself in the singular — whereas elsewhere the verse uses *usfartem lachem*, the plural, which *Chazal* understand to mean that each individual Jew counts the *omer*. The plural implies individual, personal counting. The singular *tispar lach* points to something different: a counting that is the act of the collective as a single entity.

### Exclude Shabbat Rule

How does this counting function as a collective act? *Sefira tluya be-veit din* — the counting is dependent on *beit din*, specifically on *beit din*'s determination of when the new month begins. *She-hein yodein le-chadesh mimocharat ha-Shabbat mimocharat yom tov* — they know when *mimocharat ha-Shabbat* is, because it is *mimocharat yom tov*, the day after *yom tov*, and *yom tov* is determined by *beit din*'s establishment of the new month. This excludes the weekly *Shabbat bereishit* from playing any role — *yatzta Shabbat bereishit* — because *she-sefira be-chol adam*, the weekly *Shabbat* is not established by any act of *beit din*; it comes automatically, cycle after cycle, regardless of *beit din*.

### Pesach Dependency

The conclusion is that the counting is dependent on Pesach — on when *beit din* establishes Nisan — and not on the weekly *Shabbat* cycle. This is the point that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai treated as so obvious as to require no argument: *Shabbat* in *mimocharat ha-Shabbat* means *yom tov*, and *yom tov* is set by *beit din*, and the counting of the *omer* is therefore anchored to the determination of the Jewish calendar by rabbinic authority. The *Gemara* will continue on the following *daf* with additional proofs of this fundamental position.

---

---

# Menachot 65

## Omer from Nearby

### Omer Mitzvah

The *mishnah* opens with the rule that the *mitzvah* of the *omer* is to bring it from grain that is near Jerusalem — *mitzvas ha'omer lehavi min hakarov*. If the grain nearest to Jerusalem had not yet ripened, one may bring it from anywhere else in the land of Israel. The *gemara* had already established in an explicit *mishnah* that the *omer* may only come from grain grown in Israel, but the ideal is grain grown as close to Jerusalem as possible.

### Karmel & Avir

The *gemara* offers two explanations for this preference. The first derives from a *drasha* on the word *karmel*, which appears in the context of the *omer*: read as *rach u'malei*, meaning soft and full, it implies that the grain must be plump and fresh. The closer the grain is to Jerusalem, the more recently it was harvested and the fresher it remains — it has not yet hardened with age.

The second explanation invokes the principle of *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvos* — one does not pass over a *mitzvah* that lies at hand in favor of another opportunity further away. If suitable grain is available nearby, bypassing it in search of superior grain elsewhere constitutes a violation of this principle.

*Tosafos* dedicates considerable discussion to delineating what exactly constitutes *ma'avir al hamitzvos*. The classic illustration from elsewhere in Menachot involves *tefillin*: the *tefillin shel yad* is put on before the *tefillin shel rosh*, but if one reaches into one's bag and inadvertently grasps the *tefillin shel rosh* first, the principle of *ein ma'avirin* would seem to require placing it on immediately. Yet in practice one does set it aside to first don the *tefillin shel yad*, because the correct order itself is a competing *halachic* priority — so the two principles come into tension.

The application here, however, is somewhat unusual. The ordinary understanding of *ein ma'avirin* involves literally passing over a *mitzvah* object that one has already encountered. Here, one need not have encountered the nearby grain at all — the principle seems to extend even to a case where one is simply choosing a direction: going east toward closer grain rather than west toward more distant grain. This broader application — choosing the more proximate opportunity even before physically encountering it — appears to be included within the rubric of *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvos*, though it is somewhat surprising that it reaches that far. One might note, as was suggested, that the *mishnah* likely means this only when the nearby grain satisfies all the required criteria equally; if all conditions are equal, naturally one goes closer. Whether the principle applies even when the more distant grain is of appreciably better quality is a genuine question.

### Hashmonean Exception

The *mishnah* then notes a historical anomaly: *maaseh sheba omer migagot tzerifin* — there was an occasion when the *omer* had to be brought from a place called *Gagot Tzerifin*, the rooftops of *Tzerifin* (referring to a village whose name evokes teepee-like structures), and when the *shtei ha'lechem* had to come from a valley called *Ein Socher*. The *gemara* will now explain why this was so, and the explanation involves one of the most striking and historically resonant narratives in this entire *sugya*.

---

## Siege Narrative

### Greek Wisdom

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *keshe'tzaru malkhei beit Hashmonai zeh al zeh* — when the kings of the Hasmonean dynasty were laying siege to one another. Specifically, Hurkanus was outside Jerusalem besieging the city, while Aristobulus was within. This description is historically precise: as Josephus records, the conflict between these two brothers oscillated — first Aristobulus was outside and eventually conquered Jerusalem, becoming king; then the situation reversed, and Hurkanus regrouped, gathered allies, and besieged the city from without. The *gemara*'s phrasing, *tzarin zeh al zeh*, captures exactly this oscillating quality.

In this moment, with Hurkanus outside and Aristobulus inside, a remarkable arrangement existed: every day those inside the walls would lower a basket with *dinarim*, and in return those outside — despite being enemy troops prosecuting a siege — would send up lambs to be used as *temidim*. Whatever their quarrel over kingship, the Temple service was treated as a separate matter entirely: at least for the moment, both sides acknowledged the sanctity of the *avodah* and cooperated to maintain it.

There was at this time a certain elder inside Jerusalem who was *makkir be'chochmat Yevanit* — he was conversant in what the *gemara* calls Greek wisdom. From context it is clear this refers to some form of communication that could not be easily detected by others — perhaps a kind of code, perhaps the Greek language itself, perhaps a system of signals analogous to Morse code. *Tosafos* suggests it may have been a system of signs or signals rather than language per se. Whatever its precise nature, *chochmat Yevanit* here functions as a covert means of communication.

### Betrayal Message

This elder was in fact a traitor. He used *chochmat Yevanit* to communicate from inside Jerusalem to Hurkanus's troops on the outside: *kol zeman she'asukim ba'avodah ein nimsarim be'yedekhem* — as long as those inside are engaged in the *avodah*, they will not be delivered into your hands. The oddity of this intelligence is worth noting: this is hardly a military secret. The idea that the protection of the Temple service conferred divine protection upon the besieged would have been known to all. One compelling reading of this passage is that the message was about morale rather than theology — that the *avodah* sustained the resolve and morale of the defenders, and that disrupting it would collapse their will to resist.

### Pig Sent

The next day, those outside lowered the *dinarim* as usual — but instead of sending up a lamb, they sent up a pig. When the pig reached halfway up the wall, *na'atz tzipornav ba'chomah* — it dug its claws into the stonework. At that moment, the entire land of Israel shook, four hundred *parsa* by four hundred *parsa* — the dimensions the *gemara* uses to measure the expanse of the land of Israel.

### Curse & Wisdom

*Be'otah sha'ah amru* — at that moment they declared: *arur she'yegadel chazirim* — cursed is the one who raises pigs; *ve'arur she'yelamed beno chochmat Yevanit* — and cursed is the one who teaches his son Greek wisdom. These dual curses, emerging from a single catastrophic moment, will each require further analysis.

The connection to the *mishnah* is now explained: *rashi* notes that when an army lays siege to a city, it employs a scorched-earth strategy, burning the surrounding fields to cut off the besieged from any source of sustenance. As a result, all the grain fields near Jerusalem were destroyed. Even if the troops outside may have continued to assist with *korbanot* for a time, there was simply no nearby grain available for the *omer* or the *shtei ha'lechem*. It was during this period that the *omer* was brought from the distant *Gagot Tzerifin*, and the *shtei ha'lechem* from the valley of *Ein Socher*. Alternatively, it is possible that this occurred after the city was conquered — once the siege ended, those who had just won would have needed to bring these offerings, but found that the surrounding fields had already been destroyed.

---

## Mute's Signal

### Gagot Tzerifin

*Ki mata omer* — when it was time to bring the *omer*, *lo havu yadei me'heicha le'ityei* — they did not know where to obtain barley. An announcement was made: does anyone know of a suitable field? *Ata hahu charasha* — a certain *cheresh* arrived. While *cheresh* typically denotes a deaf-mute, the emphasis in this context is on his muteness; presumably he heard the announcement through some other means or was informed by others. This mute person placed one hand on a roof of a building — *igra* — and the other hand on a teepee-like structure — *tzerifa*. He gestured simultaneously toward a rooftop and something resembling a pointed hut.

*Amar lehu Mordechai* — Mordechai, who was present, addressed those around him: *mi ika duchta de'shama Gagot Tzerifin o Tzerifin Gagot?* — is there a place called Gagot Tzerifin, or Tzerifin Gagot? For the mute had placed one hand on the *gagot* (roofs) and one on the *tzerifin* (the huts). They investigated and found that indeed such a place existed, *Gagot Tzerifin*, and from there they brought the barley for the *omer*.

*Rashi* identifies this Mordechai as the original Mordechai of the Purim story; *Tosafos* demurs, noting the chronological difficulty this creates, and suggests it was a different person who bore the same name and was similarly distinguished for wisdom and leadership. The *gemara* itself will ultimately weigh in on this identification.

### Ein Socher

When it came time for the *shtei ha'lechem*, they again did not know from where to bring wheat. Another announcement was made. Again a mute arrived — *ata hahu charasha*. This time, he placed one hand over his eye and the other on a *sichra*, a bolt-hole, the aperture through which a door-bolt passes, which in Hebrew is called a *socher*. Mordechai again interpreted: *mi ika duchta de'shama Ein Socher o Socher Ein?* — is there a place called Ein Socher, or Socher Ein? For the mute had placed his hand over his *ein* (eye) and on the *socher* (bolt-hole). They investigated and found the place called *Ein Socher*, and from there they brought the wheat for the *shtei ha'lechem*.

There is a striking structural parallel running through this whole passage: an elder uses covert signaling — *chochmat Yevanit* — to communicate the means by which the city's defenders could be undermined, leading to the abomination of the pig being sent as a *korban*. Now, a mute uses non-verbal physical gestures to communicate the means by which the proper *korbanot* can be restored. The misuse of cryptic communication brought catastrophe; the correct use of cryptic communication brings renewal. The theme of coded and interpreted messages — their use and misuse — runs through the entire narrative.

---

## Siege Narrative (II)

### Pig Symbolism

Returning to the episode of the pig: there is something deeply ironic and theologically charged about its appearance in this context. *Chazal* frequently note that the pig is unique among non-*kosher* animals in that it possesses one of the two signs of *kashrut* — split hooves — while lacking the other, for it does not chew its cud. The pig, as it were, presents its hooves and appears to declare itself *kosher*, while concealing the disqualifying truth. When the pig in this story *na'atz tzipornav ba'chomah* — dug its claws or hooves into the wall — one might read in this act a symbolic resonance: something that presents itself as legitimate, even *kosher*, attempting to penetrate the walls of Jerusalem. The entire episode of the Hasmonean civil war has this quality — descendants of the Maccabees, presenting themselves as rightful Jewish kings, engaged in a struggle that is anything but holy.

More pointed still is the connection to the decrees of Antiochus. The Book of Maccabees records the explicit content of those decrees: to forbid burnt offerings and sacrifices in the sanctuary, to profane Sabbaths and festivals, to defile the priests, and — crucially — *to sacrifice swine and other unclean animals*. The pig was the signature abomination of Antiochus's campaign against the Temple. These are the very Hasmoneans who fought and died to reverse those decrees, who risked everything to restore the Temple service and remove the pig from its walls. And now, in their internecine struggle for power, their own agents are sending a pig up the same walls. The symbolism could not be more devastating.

Josephus, in Antiquities 14:2, records a version of this story as well, and the parallels are instructive. He describes how those besieged with Aristobulus needed sacrifices for Passover, how money was lowered over the walls, and how those outside accepted the money but treacherously withheld the animals. God's punishment, in Josephus's account, came in the form of a violent storm that destroyed the crops of the entire country — which is why wheat became extraordinarily expensive, a *modius* selling for eleven drachmas. There is no pig in Josephus's account. Whether the pig entered through a separate historical tradition preserved by *Chazal*, or whether it represents a thematic crystallization of the Antiochene associations into this narrative, it seems almost certain that the pig is present in the Talmudic account precisely because of its evocative power as the symbol of Antiochus's persecutions — the very horror the Hasmoneans had ostensibly conquered.

### Greek Wisdom Ban

The second curse pronounced at that moment — *arur she'yelamed beno chochmat Yevanit* — requires careful analysis. *Tosafos* already raises the obvious difficulty: elsewhere we find that *chochmat Yevanit* was simply used by sages and was not universally forbidden. Saul Lieberman, in his essay "The Alleged Ban on Greek Wisdom" at the opening of *Hellenism in Jewish Palestine*, addresses this directly. His conclusion, supported by a survey of all the relevant sources, is that the prohibition was entirely limited to *melamed et beno chochmat Yevanit* — teaching it to one's son, meaning to the young. The concern was that exposure to Greek wisdom — whether the Greek language itself, or the broader cultural world of Hellenism that it opened — posed a genuine threat of assimilation when absorbed in youth, when a person is impressionable and still forming. For an adult already rooted in Torah, no such prohibition applied; the only concern there was *bitul Torah*. The specific phrase *beno* — his son — was not incidental. It was the entire basis of the restriction.

---

## Mute's Signal (II)

### Three Women

The *gemara* now presents another episode involving Mordechai, this one connected to the *mishnah* in Menachot 62a. Three women arrived at the *Beit Hamikdash*, each carrying *kinin* — pairs of birds brought as sacrifices. The first said she was bringing them *le'zivasi* — for her flow. The second said she was bringing them *le'yamasi* — for her ocean, understood as a reference to a heavy flow. The third said she was bringing them *le'onasi* — for her period.

The natural reading of all three statements was that each woman was a *zava* — a woman who had experienced abnormal uterine bleeding outside the normal menstrual cycle — and was now bringing the required *korban* upon completion of her clean days: one bird as a *chatat* and one as an *olah*.

Mordechai, however, intervened. He suggested an alternative reading of each statement: *shema be'zov sachna* — perhaps she means that because of her flow she had been in mortal danger, not that her flow rendered her *tamei* in the sense of *zivah*; and similarly for the others. If so, none of the three were bringing *korbanot* as *zavot* at all; rather, each had survived a health crisis connected to her flow and was now bringing a *korban toda*-style *olah* in gratitude. In that case, *kulhu olot ninhu* — all the birds are *olot*, not the combination of *chatat* and *olah* required for a *zava*. They investigated and found that Mordechai was correct.

### Mordechai ID

This episode is the basis for identifying Mordechai with the figure named *Ptachya* in the *mishnah* (Menachot 62a): *Ptachya al ha-kinin* — Ptachya oversaw the *kinin* sacrifices. *Zeh Mordechai* — this was Mordechai. *Ve'lamah nikra shemo Ptachya?* — why would Mordechai be called Ptachya? *She'poteach devarim ve'doresham* — because he was able to open up words and interpret them, to discern what people meant and to articulate what others could not. The name *Ptachya* — *poteach*, opener — captures precisely the interpretive gift we have just seen demonstrated three times over.

The *gemara* adds that Mordechai *yodea be'shivim lashon* — he knew all seventy languages. This prompts an immediate objection: the entire *Sanhedrin* was required to know all seventy languages, as *Rabbi Yochanan* taught — *ein moshivin be'Sanhedrin ela ba'alei chochma, ba'alei mareh, ba'alei komah, ba'alei ziknah, ba'alei keshafim* — only those possessing wisdom, fine appearance, stature, seniority, and knowledge of witchcraft may sit on the *Sanhedrin*. *Rashi* explains the requirement of witchcraft knowledge as enabling the judges to neutralize any attempt by an accused sorcerer to escape judgment through mystical means; *Tosafos* takes a more prosaic view, that judges must simply be conversant enough to evaluate testimony in such cases. And crucially, *she'lo tihei Sanhedrin shoma'at mipi ha'meturgeman* — so that the *Sanhedrin* need not rely on a translator, whose rendering might distort, whether intentionally or otherwise, what was actually said. *Tosafos* notes, realistically, that the requirement may have been satisfied if even one or two members possessed this knowledge and could be trusted to relay accurately what was said to the others.

But given that the entire *Sanhedrin* knew seventy languages, what was distinctive about Mordechai? The *gemara* responds: *de'hava bala lishnei ve'dorash* — he would blend languages together and interpret the mixture. That is, he possessed not merely passive competence in multiple languages but the active capacity to draw meaning from across linguistic boundaries, to hear something expressed obliquely in one language mixed with another and still extract its intent. *De'hainu de'ketiv: Mordechai Bilshan* — this is why Mordechai is called *Bilshan* in the Book of Nechemia. *Bilshan* is *bolela lashon* — one who blends or mixes language. The identification with the original Mordechai of the Purim narrative becomes more plausible, since the figure of *Bilshan* in Nechemia belongs to a period that could chronologically accommodate that identification.

The larger theme drawing together all of these episodes — the traitor using *chochmat Yevanit*, the mute using physical gestures, and Mordechai interpreting the ambiguous words of three women — is the question of communication itself: how meaning is encoded, how it is decoded, and whether the capacity to work across the boundaries of ordinary language is put to use in service of *kedusha* or in its subversion. Mordechai's gift, his ability to *bolel lashon*, to penetrate the surface of speech and find what lies beneath, is the constructive counterpart to the elder's treachery. There is nothing inherently wrong with mastery of indirect communication — everything depends on whether it is directed toward bringing the right *korbanot* or toward introducing the pig.

---

## Omer Harvest

### Pre-Yom Tov Mark

The next *mishnah* turns to the practical procedure for harvesting the barley of the *omer*: *keitzad hein osim?* — how was it actually done? *Shluchei Beit Din yotzin me'erev Yom Tov* — emissaries of the *Beit Din* would go out on *erev Yom Tov*, the fourteenth of Nissan, and *ve'osim otan krichot* — they would bind bands around stalks of standing grain, wrapping together the barley they intended to harvest the following night. This was done while the grain was still attached to the ground.

The reason is this: the *halacha* requires that the actual cutting of the *omer* take place on the day of the bringing itself, derived from the relevant *pasuk*. But one need not squander time searching and selecting grain in the darkness. So the *shluchei Beit Din* would invest that preparatory effort on *erev Yom Tov*, marking and binding the grain they had chosen, so that when the time came — immediately after nightfall on the night of the sixteenth — they could proceed directly to cutting without delay. The analogy sometimes drawn is to the practice of scoring the *challah* before making *hamotzi* so that the blessing is not interrupted by searching for where to cut, though in practice the mark is often forgotten by the time the blessing concludes.

### Public Ceremony

*Kol ha'ayaros ha'smuchos l'sham miskansos l'sham* — all the villages in proximity to that field would gather there. This was done *k'dei she'yehei niktzar be'esek gadol* — so that the harvesting would take place amid great public commotion, a large visible gathering. The reason, as the *mishnah* will shortly make explicit, was to publicize the correct day of the *omer* harvest and thereby the day from which the *sefirah* begins and, by extension, the day on which *Shavuot* would fall fifty days hence. This question was bitterly contested, and the public gathering was a deliberate act of declaration — not merely announcing the date, but staging the consensus, presenting the normative practice as the obvious, universally shared position, and marginalizing the opposing view as the eccentric aberration.

### Question Procedure

*Keivan she'chashecha* — when nightfall came on the night of the sixteenth, the one in charge would address the assembled crowd in a carefully choreographed series of questions. Has the sun set? — *hen*, yes. Has the sun set? — *hen*, yes. Should I use this scythe? — *hen*, yes. Should I use this scythe? — *hen*, yes. Should I use this basket? — *hen*, yes. Should I use this basket? — *hen*, yes. If the night happened to fall on *Shabbat*, he would add: should I do this even on this *Shabbat*? — *hen*, yes. Should I cut? — *ketzor*, cut. Should I cut? — *ketzor*, cut. Each element was repeated, and the procedure was performed three times over, with the crowd affirming each step with *hen, hen, hen*.

### Anti-Baitusim

*Kol kach lamah? Mipnei ha'Baitusin* — why all of this? Because of the *Baitusin*, who maintained that the *omer* was not cut on *motzei Yom Tov* — the evening after the first day of Pesach — but on *motzei Shabbat*, *mimacharas ha'Shabbat*, on a Saturday night, so that the *omer* would always begin on a Sunday. By staging this elaborate, publicly confirmed, consensual ceremony, the *Beit Din* was making a pointed statement: not merely *this* is what we do, but *everyone here knows* this is what we do, and agreement is total and universal. The form of the questioning — calling for affirmation at every step — shapes the practice as common knowledge rather than contested position.

---

## Tamid Debate

### Tamid Victory

The *gemara* quotes from *Megillat Ta'anit* — the ancient register composed during the Second Temple period listing the days on which fasting, and in some cases even eulogizing, is forbidden, in commemoration of various historical victories. *Megillat Ta'anit* is also the source from which we learn of the eight days of Chanukah as days on which fasting and eulogizing are prohibited. Among its entries: from *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* until the eighth of Nissan, *it'ukom tamida d'lo le'mispid* — the *tamid* offering was established, and therefore one may not eulogize on those days.

### Tzadok Position

The underlying debate: *she'hayu Tzedukim omrim, yachid mitnadev u'mevi tamid* — the Sadducees held that an individual could privately sponsor and donate the daily *tamid* offering. Their *drasha* derived from the *pasuk* — *et ha'keves ha'echad ta'ase ba'boker ve'et ha'keves ha'sheni ta'ase bein ha'arbayim* — which addresses the reader in the second person singular, implying that an individual, rather than the community as a whole, could be the donor. In practical terms, this would mean that any given day's *tamid* could be underwritten by a private individual's pledge.

### Pharisaic Refutation

The response: the *pasuk* says *et korbani lachmi le'ishai tishmeru* — you (plural) shall observe my offerings — which indicates that the *korbanot* are communal obligations, and the verse *she'kulam ba'im mi'trumat ha'lishka* — they must all come from the communal *lishka* funds collected through the half-*shekel* levy. Beyond the textual argument, there is a broader subtext here: the Sadducees were framing the *tamid* as something an individual could claim and control, wresting the most central act of Temple worship from its communal foundation. *Chazal*, from their perspective, were defending not merely a *halakhic* ruling but the very communal nature of the *avodah*. That this debate lasted eight days before being resolved likely reflects the reality that such disputes are rarely settled by the force of textual argument alone.

---

## Shavuot Debate

### Baitusim Shavuot

The next entry in *Megillat Ta'anit*: from the eighth of Nissan until the end of *Pesach*, *itotav chaga de'shavuaya* — the festival of *Shavuot* was established as it should be. *She'hayu Baitusin omrim, Atzeret achar ha'Shabbat* — the *Baitusin* maintained that *Shavuot* always falls on a Sunday because the *omer* begins on a Sunday — specifically, on the first Sunday following the beginning of *Pesach*, reading *mimacharas ha'Shabbat* to mean literally the day after the weekly *Shabbat*.

### Yochanan Response

*Nitpal lahem Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* — Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was dispatched to engage them. The verb *nitpal* is pointed: it derives from *tafel*, something secondary or trivial, signaling from the outset that he was not treating this as a serious intellectual confrontation requiring genuine engagement. He opened: *shotim* — idiots. *Minayin lachem* — where do you get this idea from? No one initially stepped forward to respond. The rhetorical framing had already loaded the debate heavily against the *Baitusin* before a single substantive argument was made.

### Elder's Argument

*Chutz mi'zaken echad she'haya mepatpet knegdo* — except for one elder who began to sputter, or chatter, against him. The verb *mepatpet* is deliberately deprecating — it conveys not reasoned argument but babbling or sputtering. And indeed, the elder's argument is striking precisely for what it does *not* do: he makes no textual argument whatsoever. Instead: *amar, Moshe Rabbeinu ohev Yisrael haya* — he declared that Moses loved the Jewish people; *ve'yodea she'Shavuot yom echad hu* — and knowing that *Shavuot* is only a one-day holiday, he arranged it to fall on a Sunday, so that Israel could enjoy two consecutive days of celebration — the Sunday *Shavuot* combined with whatever immediately preceded or followed. The pastoral concern for Israel's enjoyment of a two-day celebration is the entirety of the argument.

### Yochanan Refute

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai replied with the *pasuk*: *achad asar yom me'Chorev derech Har Seir* — the journey from Sinai to the Land of Israel was eleven days. *Im Moshe Rabbeinu ohev Yisrael haya, lama icharam ba'midbar arbaim shana?* — if Moses loved Israel so much as to arrange the calendar for their pleasure, why did he keep them wandering in the desert for forty years when they were eleven days from the Land? The argument is not so much a refutation as a reductio: if you invoke Moses's love for Israel to explain any particular arrangement, you must contend with the forty years of wandering, which sits poorly with the premise.

### Debate End

The elder responded: *bakifach ata potrani* — is this really how you dismiss me, with that kind of response? Give me a serious answer. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai replied: *bakhshum shoteh* — idiot. *She'lo tehei Torah shelemah shelanu ke'sicha batela shelachem* — our complete Torah cannot be equated with your idle chatter.
