The first is from Rabbi Eliezer, based on a *gezeirah shavah*: *ne'emar aviv beMitzrayim vene'emar aviv ledorot* — the word *aviv* appears both in the context of Egypt and in the context of the *omer* for all generations. Regarding Egypt, the Torah states *ki hase'orah aviv* — the barley was ripe — which is why it was destroyed by the hail while the wheat survived. Just as *aviv* in Egypt refers to barley, so too does *aviv* as it pertains to the *omer* for all generations refer to barley.

The second source is from Rabbi Akiva: *matzinu yachid shemeivi chovato min hachittin vechovato min hase'orin* — we find that an individual brings his obligatory sacrifice both from wheat and from barley. The obligatory individual *korban* from wheat is the *minchat chotei* (the *chatat* offering of a poor person, brought as flour — which, though it lacks oil and frankincense, does consist of wheat); the obligatory individual *korban* from barley is the *minchat sotah*. Similarly, *ve'tzibur shemevi'im chovatam min hachittin* — the community brings its obligatory sacrifice from wheat in the form of the *shtei halechem*. By parallel reasoning, the community must also have an obligatory sacrifice from barley, and that is the *omer*. If you were to say the *omer* comes from wheat, *lo matzinu tzibur shemeivi chovato min hase'orin* — we would never have a barley sacrifice of the community at all, which would disrupt the symmetry.

The third argument — *davar acher* — is directly relevant to our question: *im atah omer Omer ba min hachittin* — if the *omer* came from wheat, *ein Shtei Halechem bikkurim* — the *shtei halechem* cannot be *bikkurim*, the first of the new grain in the *Beis Hamikdash*. If the *omer* were also from wheat, a wheat offering would already have been brought before the *shtei halechem*, and the *shtei halechem* could not claim the status of *bikkurim*. This is considerably stronger than the first problem the *omer* poses for *bikkurim* status, since at minimum one can argue that the *omer* (being barley) is in a different grain category; if both were wheat, no such bracketing is possible.

### Different crops

The *Gemara* now applies this *braita* to Rami bar Chama's question. The argument runs as follows: if the *shtei halechem* can operate *shelo kesidran* — permitting grain that encountered the *shtei halechem* before the *omer* — then one could in theory bring the *omer* from wheat without violating the *bikkurim* status of the *shtei halechem*. Here is how: one takes grain that took root between the *omer* and the *shtei halechem* of the previous year — grain that first encountered the *shtei halechem* and then the *omer*, in reverse order — and uses it for the *omer* as wheat. For the *shtei halechem* itself, one uses grain that grew in the normal sequence — taking root after the previous year's *shtei halechem* and before the current *omer*. The *shtei halechem* could then claim to be *bikkurim* of the new wheat in the *Mikdash*, since the wheat used for the *omer* would be defined as "old" grain (having already passed through both the *omer* and *shtei halechem*) while the wheat used for the *shtei halechem* would be "new." This argument would explain how a wheat *omer* need not compromise the *bikkurim* status of the *shtei halechem* — and thus the third proof that the *omer* must come from barley would be unnecessary. Since that proof is in fact cited, it must be that we cannot bring the *omer* from wheat through this device, which in turn implies that the *shelo kesidran* mechanism does not work.

### Refutation

The *Gemara* rejects this attempted proof: *mi savrat bikkurim le'pirka amrinan?* — do you think that when we say the *shtei halechem* must be *bikkurim*, we mean merely the first of the new fruit in terms of crop cycle? No, *le'mizbe'ach amrinan* — it means the first new grain to make its way upon the *mizbe'ach*. And on that criterion, *ve'ha achlei le'mizbe'ach mi'peira de'hai shata* — the *mizbe'ach* would still have consumed wheat from this year's crop, since whether or not we define the grain that grew in the middle period as "old," the *mizbe'ach* at that stage still received wheat. Rashi attempts to finesse this difficulty by arguing that the wheat in question should still be called new because of how it relates to last year's *shtei halechem*, but that is essentially the very issue the question was exploring. Accordingly, the *Gemara* concludes that this *braita* cannot serve as a proof one way or the other regarding whether the *omer* and *shtei halechem* work *shelo kesidran*. That question remains open. What the *braita* does yield, however, is an illuminating threefold exploration of why the *omer* must come from barley.

---

## Stage of growth

### Rami: growth stage

The *Gemara* presents a further question of Rami bar Chama (found on 68b). The question is: *shtei halechem hanatza sharya o chanata sharya?* — what stage must a fruit reach for the *shtei halechem* to be said to have "passed over" it, such that the new fruit cannot be brought to the *Mikdash* before that point? We know that for the *omer*, grain must have taken root (*hashrasha*) before the *omer* is brought in order for the *omer* to render it permissible. What is the analogous stage for the *shtei halechem* in relation to fruit? Is it the *hanatza* — the flowering — or the *chanata* — the budding of the fruit?

### Taking root vs leaves

The *Gemara* immediately clarifies what is meant: *ilima hanatza de'peira ve'chanata de'peira* — if the question concerns the flowering or budding of the actual fruit itself, the answer is straightforward: *hashta hashrasha sharya hanatza ve'chanata mibaya?* — if even taking root is sufficient for grain, surely the far more advanced stage of the fruit flowering or budding is sufficient as well. That cannot be the question.

Rather, says the *Gemara*: *ella hanatza de'ala ve'chanata de'ala* — the question concerns the flowering or budding of the leaves that surround the fruit on the tree. Just as *hashrasha* is the relevant threshold for grain — the point at which the seed has entered a new mode of existence and is considered to "exist" in relation to the *omer* — so too there must be some analogous threshold for tree fruit in relation to the *shtei halechem*. The blossom of the encasing leaves precedes the emergence of the fruit itself, much as cherry blossoms appear before the fruit forms. Does the *shtei halechem* apply when those leaves flower, or when they bud? *Mi havei ke'hashrasha o lo* — is either of these stages analogous to taking root for purposes of the *shtei halechem*?

### Teiku

*Teiku* — the question is left unresolved.

This *sugya* makes explicit what is only implicit in the *mishnah*: the prohibition of bringing new produce before the *shtei halechem* extends beyond wheat and grain. It applies to new fruit as well, because the *shtei halechem* must be *bikkurim*, and no new fruit of any kind may be brought before it. The *Gemara* earlier raised this point in connection with wine made from new grapes. It is worth noting, however, that the general prohibition of *chadash* never applied to fruit — only to grain. The prohibition on new fruit before the *shtei halechem* operates on a distinct basis entirely, which is why the *Gemara* earlier concluded that *b'di'avad* such fruit would be *kasher* — because it bears no relation to the prohibition of *chadash* in any way.

---

## Planted seeds status

### Rabbah: seeds in ground

The *Gemara* presents a question posed by Rabbah bar bar Channah: *chittin she'zaran bekarka* — if one planted wheat seeds in the ground, *Omer matiran o ein Omer matiran* — does the *omer* render them permissible or not? At first glance this seems a completely absurd question. The *Gemara* responds: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? *Ee ashrush, tanina* — if they have taken root, we already learned the answer in a *mishnah*. *Ee lo ashrush, tanina* — and if they have not taken root, we also learned the answer. The *mishnah* states explicitly: *im hishrishu kodem la'Omer Omer matiran ve'im lav asurin ad she'yavo Omer haba* — if seeds took root before the *omer*, the *omer* renders them permissible; if they took root only after the *omer* was brought, they remain forbidden until the following year's *omer*. Both cases appear to be covered.

The *Gemara* therefore reframes the question: *lo tzericha* — the case that requires resolution is as follows: *de'chatzdinhu ve'zarinhu kodem la'Omer* — you harvested seeds from the previous year's grain and planted them before the *omer*, *ve'ata Omer ve'chalaf laihu* — and then the *omer* came and passed. The seeds have not yet taken root. Can you extract them from the ground and eat them?

The scenario requires careful framing. These seeds came from grain that had not yet been permitted by an *omer*. Had the person left them in his pocket, the *omer* would have arrived, and they would have become permissible — he could have eaten them directly. Instead, he put them in the ground. Now the *omer* has come and gone. The question is how the law treats these planted, unrooted seeds.

### Vessel analogy

*Ke'man de'shadi bekada damya* — are they like seeds sitting in a vessel? If so, the *omer*'s arrival made them permissible just as it would have had they been in a jar. *O dilma, batlu legabei ara* — or have they been absorbed into the ground such that they are no longer treated as food waiting for the *omer*, but rather as planted material on a different legal track — one requiring actual *hashrasha* before the *omer* can relate to them at all?

The ground makes things worse, not better. A jar simply holds the seeds as food; the ground transforms their status. If they are now framed as planted seeds rather than as food, then the rule is that the *omer* only operates on grain that has taken root, and since these have not, they are not yet within the *omer*'s reach. The question is precisely how quickly that transformation occurs upon planting.

### Three questions

This uncertainty ramifies into three subsidiary questions about the legal status of planted but unrooted seeds, each of which maps onto the same underlying axis: are they still independent *metaltelin*, or have they already been subsumed into the *karka*?

### Ona'ah

The first subsidiary question: *yesh lahem onaah o ein lahem onaah?* — do the laws of *onaah* (overcharging) apply to planted seeds or not? The laws of *onaah* do not apply to *karka* — real estate. This is derived from a *klal prat ukhlal* and supported by the logic that real estate is inherently difficult to value with precision, and that any given parcel may be worth far more to a particular buyer than its nominal market rate. By contrast, *onaah* does apply to *metaltelin*.

A preliminary point must be established: we are not discussing a case where a precise quantity was misrepresented. Rava rules that anything sold by an exact measure, weight, or number — *kol davar shebemidah veshebemishkal veshebeminyan* — is subject to reversal even for a discrepancy smaller than the standard *onaah* threshold (normally one-sixth), because when an exact quantity is specified, any deviation from it is simply not what was agreed. This applies regardless of whether the item is *karka* or not: if I sell you a plot of land and tell you it is exactly one acre, and it proves to be less, the defense of "no *onaah* by *karka*" does not apply, because I simply gave you a different quantity than I said.

The relevant case is therefore where no exact number was stated: *ella d'amar leh shadi bat kora hi* — the seller said, "This land has been sown with the appropriate amount of seed," without specifying a number. Witnesses then testify that in fact it was insufficiently seeded. Here, because no precise quantity was named, the standard *onaah* framework applies — and the question becomes whether the seeds are chattel (subject to *onaah*) or already part of the *karka* (not subject to *onaah*). Did I cheat you on the seeds, or did I cheat you on the land? *Keman d'shadi bekadya dami, v'yesh lahen onaah* — if the seeds are like those in a vessel, they are *metaltelin* and subject to *onaah*; *od dilma battalu legabei ara* — or if they are already part of the land, it is the land that was misrepresented, and *onaah* does not apply.

### Shevu'ah

The second question: *nishba'in aleihen o ein nishba'in aleihen?* — can an oath (*shevuah*) be administered regarding planted seeds? Oaths in civil disputes are only applicable to claims involving *metaltelin*; they cannot be administered over disputes about *karka*. If, for example, there is a *modeh bemiktzat* situation — partial admission — regarding these seeds, is the resulting *shevuah* possible? *Keman d'shadi bekadya dami u'kemetalteli damu, v'nishba'in aleihen* — if they are like seeds in a vessel and are treated as chattel, an oath is possible; *od dilma battalu agav ara u'kekarka damu, v'ein nishba'in aleihen* — or if they have been subsumed into the land, no oath can be administered.

### All Teiku

On all three questions — whether the *omer* renders them permissible, whether *onaah* applies, and whether a *shevuah* can be administered — the *Gemara* answers *teiku*. The legal status of seeds planted in the ground before they have taken root remains unresolved across all three dimensions.

---

## Dung & kernels

### Rami: kernels status

Rami bar Chama next poses a question that, while no longer directly about *chadash* or *omer*, flows from the broader focus on wheat: *chitim shebegilalei bakar use'orin shebegilalei behemah mahu?* — what is the status of wheat kernels found in cattle dung, or barley kernels found in the dung of other animals? Rashi notes that the *Gemara* mentions wheat specifically for cattle, since cattle tend to eat wheat, while other animals eat barley. The question is: what is the *halachic* status of these intact, undigested kernels visible in the dung?

### Extracting matters

The *Gemara* cites a *braita* (apparently from the *Tosefta*): *chitim shebirei bakar use'orin shebegilalei behemah* — wheat kernels in cattle dung and barley kernels in other animals' dung — *chishev aleihen l'achilah, ein mitammei tum'at ochlin* — if one merely intends to eat them, without doing anything, that intention alone does not confer upon them the status of food, and they cannot become *tamei* with *tum'at ochlin*. However, *liktan l'achilah, mitammei tum'at ochlin* — if one actually extracts them from the dung with the intention of eating them, the act of extraction transforms them into food, and they can then become *tamei*.

### Dung-grown grain

The question then shifts from the kernels themselves to grain grown from them. If one extracts these kernels from the dung and plants them, and from them grows new wheat — may that new grain be used for a *mincha*? The *Gemara* immediately cites the verse *hakrivehu na l'pachatecha hayirtzecha o hayisa panecha* — bring it to your governor; would he be pleased? Would he show you favor? The point is obvious: something inherently disreputable is not suitable as a *korban*. One would not bring such a thing to an important person, and certainly not to the Almighty.

### Two theories

This leads to the follow-up question about grain grown from such planted kernels: *lo tzericha d'naktinhu ve'zarinhu* — you extracted these kernels and planted them, and grew new wheat from them. *Mahu l'asuyei Menachos minei* — can you use this new grain for a *mincha*? Two theories are presented. *Mishum d'meisusa hu, ve'cheivan d'zarinhu, azlah lah meisusayih* — perhaps the disqualification was only because of *me'isus*, disgustingness, and once planted and grown anew, the disgustingness is entirely gone. After all, one fertilizes grain with dung regardless; one cannot be overly fastidious about this. The new grain is a completely fresh product with no remaining connection to its origins. Alternatively, *mishum k'chishusa hu, v'hacha nami k'chushen* — perhaps the problem runs deeper: the kernels that passed through an animal, even undigested, may have lost some of their potency or vitality, and the grain grown from them may therefore be of a weakened, substandard quality — making it unsuitable for the *Mikdash* regardless of its appearance. *Teiku* — this too remains unresolved.

---

## Digestion & status

### Elephant & palm

Rami bar Chama then asks a question that continues the theme of things passing through animals: *pil she'bala kfifah mitzris v'hiki'ah derech beis ha're'i* — an elephant that swallowed an Egyptian basket woven from palm leaves, and it came out the other end. What is the status of this basket?

### Dung vs palm

The *Gemara* clarifies the question: *l'mai halacha?* For what legal purpose? If the question is *l'mivtal tumas'ah* — whether the basket loses its prior *tumah* by having passed through the elephant — the answer is already established. The *mishnah* teaches: *kol hakeilim yordin lidei tumasan b'machshava* — all vessels attain susceptibility to *tumah* through intention (when the craftsman designates the completed object as a vessel). *V'ein olin mi'tumasan ella b'shinui ma'aseh* — but they do not lose their *tumah* except through a physical act of change. Since passing through an elephant presumably does not physically alter the basket, it would remain *tamei*. That question is therefore no question.

The real question is a different one: the elephant swallowed not a finished basket but raw palm leaves (*utzam*) — strips of palm used for weaving — and then excreted them. Someone took these excreted palm leaves and fashioned them into an Egyptian basket. *Mi havei ikul* — are they considered digested, *havei lehu k'chlei glalim* — and must the resulting basket be classified as a vessel made from dung? If so, *ein mikablin tumah* — it cannot become *tamei*, since dung vessels, along with stone and unbaked earthen vessels, do not become *tamei*, neither biblically nor rabbinically (*lo midivrei Torah v'lo midivrei Sofrim*). Or *lo havi ikul* — are they not considered digested, and is the material therefore still legally palm, making the basket susceptible to *tumah* as a normal woven vessel?

### Wolves story

The *Gemara* suggests an answer from a ruling cited by Ulla in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: *ma'aseh u'bau ze'evim shenei tinokot ever ha'Yarden* — there was a tragic case in which wolves swallowed two infants across the Jordan river and subsequently excreted them. The question came before the sages: does the excreted material convey *tumas meis*? *V'tiharu es ha'basar* — the sages ruled that the flesh was *tahor*, no longer considered human flesh. It had changed status through digestion. *V'timu es ha'atzamos* — but the bones were ruled *tamei*, retaining their original status as human bones capable of conveying *tumas meis*.

### Intermediate status

Why can't we derive our answer from this *braita*? The *Gemara* draws the distinction: *shani basar d'rachikh* — flesh is different because it is soft; it is genuinely transformed by digestion, and the sages therefore ruled that it changed status. *Shani atzamos d'kashi tfei* — bones are at the other extreme; they are very hard, and passing through an animal does not alter them at all. Palm leaves fall somewhere in between. They are neither as soft as flesh nor as hard as bone. Perhaps their status changes upon digestion; perhaps it does not. *Teiku* — the question is left unresolved.

### Tosafot's principle

*Tosafos* engages this question extensively, bringing parallel *sugyos* that involve items found inside animals — for example, a kosher fish with non-kosher crustaceans in its stomach (which have not yet been digested, having only been swallowed), and the case of a chicken slaughtered on Pesach with undigested wheat kernels found in its stomach: is that *chametz*? *Tosafos* notes that there are apparent contradictions across different *gemarot* on these questions. *Tosafos* articulates what the *Gemara* leaves implicit in its soft/hard framework: if the form of the object has not changed, one should presume its status remains the same. As long as the item still looks like what it originally was, we should be strict and treat it as retaining its original *halachic* identity.

---

## Grain from clouds

### Zeira: rain question

The *Gemara* concludes with a question posed by Rabbi Zeira: *chittim she-yardu be-avim* — if wheat fell from the clouds, what is the law? Rashi understands the scenario as one in which a whirlwind or similar phenomenon carried wheat aloft and it then fell back down; *Tosafos* frames it as a straightforward miraculous occurrence, *derech nes*. The question is whether such wheat may be used for the *shtei halechem*.

### Two interpretations

The question turns on the interpretation of the phrase *mi-moshvoseichem* — "from your dwellings" — which conditions the *shtei halechem*'s wheat. One might read this phrase to mean anywhere that is not *chutz la'aretz*: the wheat need not come from outside the Land of Israel, but it does not strictly have to grow from Israeli soil. Under this reading, Israeli clouds would be sufficient. *Aval avim shapir dami* — the clouds are, after all, Israeli clouds; they are not *chutz la'aretz*. Alternatively, *mi-moshvoseichem davka* — perhaps the verse requires that it grow specifically from where you dwell, from the land itself, and *ve-afilu de-avim nami lo* — even clouds do not suffice; the wheat must actually grow from the ground of Israel.

### It can happen

Before leaving the question unresolved, the *Gemara* asks: *u-mi ika ki hai gavna?* — can such a thing actually occur? The answer is yes: *ki de-addi taya nechisa lei rum kizba chitti bi-tlasa parsei* — there was an Arab nomad for whom it rained wheat: it fell to the height of approximately one or two *tefachim* deep, spread across three *parsa'ot* of land. Because this event actually occurred, Rabbi Zeira's question is not merely theoretical — it is a genuine *halachic* inquiry about a known phenomenon.

---

---

# Menachot 70

## Stalk Uprooted & Replant…

### R. Shimon ben Pazi's Case

The sugya opens with a question posed by Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, found seven lines above where the lines widen on the page — twelve lines from the bottom. The case runs as follows: *shibbolet she-hevi'ah shlish kodem ha-Omer ve-akrah u-sh'talah le-achar ha-Omer* — a stalk of grain that had reached one-third ripeness before the *Omer* was brought, was then uprooted, and was replanted after the *Omer*.

Why does one-third ripeness matter? Because reaching *shlish* — a third of full development — is the threshold at which grain acquires the status of *peri*, actual fruit or produce, and becomes subject to the obligations of *terumot* and *ma'asrot*. Before that point the grain is merely fodder, lacking full halachic grain-status. Once it crosses that threshold, it is considered grain in the halachic sense.

The scenario, then, is this: a stalk reached one-third ripeness while still in the ground. At that stage it has the full status of grain — and therefore the *Omer* offering, when it arrives, renders it permitted. The grain is then uprooted and, after the *Omer* has come and gone, replanted as a stalk. Now it continues to grow. Had this stalk simply remained in the ground throughout, everything about it would be permitted by virtue of the *Omer*. And had someone planted entirely new seeds after the *Omer*, what grew from those seeds would be *chadash* — new grain forbidden until the following year's *Omer*. This case sits precisely between those two poles. The stalk itself is not new seed; it is the very thing that had been in the ground before the *Omer*. Yet it was removed and replanted. To what degree is the subsequent growth a continuation of what was already permitted, and to what degree is it a new planting — making the growth *chadash*?

The *Gemara* assumes as its starting point that the new growth is indeed considered a new planting, so that what grows afresh is, at least in principle, *chadash*. The question is then framed precisely: *batar ikar azlinan* — do we go by the *ikar*, the foundation? The base stalk was already rendered permissible by the *Omer*; perhaps the new growth is subordinate to that foundation and inherits its permitted status. Or do we instead go *batar tosefet* — after the addition that grows subsequently — treating the new growth as possessing its own distinct status, such that the stalk is a mixture of the permitted original grain and forbidden new growth, requiring one to wait until *ha-Omer ha-ba*, the following year's *Omer*?

### Orlah & Grafting

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve the question by invoking a ruling cited by Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *yaldah she-sivchah bi-zekeinah* — a young tree intertwined with an old one. This refers to the laws of *orlah*: fruit growing from a tree in its first three years is *orlah* and forbidden, while an old, established tree bears permitted fruit. The *Gemara* here understands "intertwined" to mean grafted — a branch from a young tree (whose fruit would be *orlah*) has been grafted onto an old tree, and some fruit was already growing on the branch at the time of grafting. That initial fruit is *orlah*. After grafting, the branch continues to grow while connected to the old tree, so the additional growth derives from the old, permitted tree. Yet the ruling is: *afilu hosif be-matayim assur* — even if the new growth is two hundred times the original forbidden amount, the entire thing is forbidden.

This is striking. Normally, *orlah* that falls into a mixture of non-*orlah* is *batel* — nullified — in a ratio of one to two hundred. Yet here, even when the permitted growth dwarfs the original *orlah* by a factor of two hundred, it is not nullified. The reason, apparently, is that since the *ikar* — the foundation upon which all subsequent growth rests — was forbidden, the later growth is treated as an extension of that forbidden base rather than as something independent that could nullify it.

Tosafot note that this understanding of the case derives from the Yerushalmi, which envisages the branches becoming intertwined before the young tree takes root, such that it is regarded as a mere extension of the old tree. Our *Gemara*, however, understands the case as a graft, even though the standard term for grafting (*hirkiv*) is not used here.

The inference the *Gemara* draws is the following: if the *ikar* principle is applied stringently in the *orlah* case — so that a forbidden foundation contaminates even a two-hundredfold permitted addition — perhaps the same principle should apply leniently in the case of the replanted stalk. There, the foundation is permitted grain (already sanctioned by the *Omer*), and the new growth is the forbidden addition. Perhaps the new growth should be considered subordinate to the permitted base.

### Kilayim & Onion Case

A parallel ruling, cited by Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, reinforces the point. *Batzal she-shatalo be-kerem* — an onion that was planted in a vineyard creates a problem of *kilayim*, specifically *kilei ha-kerem*, the forbidden mixture of vegetables with a vineyard. If the vineyard was then completely removed, the onion remains but its initial growth occurred under *kilayim* conditions. Now, with the vineyard gone, the onion continues to grow. The ruling: *afilu hosif be-matayim assur* — even if the onion now grows to two hundred times its original size, the entire mass is forbidden. Normally *kilayim*, like *orlah*, is nullified at one in two hundred; yet here no nullification occurs, because the subsequent growth of *heter* built upon a foundation of *issur* takes on the status of the *issur* and cannot create *bittul*.

The *Gemara* proposes drawing the inverse inference for the replanted stalk: just as a forbidden *ikar* renders forbidden even a massive addition of *heter*, so too a permitted *ikar* should render permitted even a significant addition of *chadash*.

### Foundation Principle Lim…

The *Gemara* deflects this reasoning. *Hi gufah ka-miba'ya lei* — that very case was precisely the question Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi was asking. He wanted to know whether one could learn from the *orlah* and *kilayim* rulings. The *Gemara* then articulates two possible readings of those earlier rulings: either it is perfectly clear to the Rabbis that one always goes *batar ikar* regardless of whether that yields stringency or leniency — *lo shenah le-kula ve-lo shenah le-chumra* — and the inference to our case is straightforward; or perhaps the Rabbis actually had a doubt about the *ikar* principle and adopted it only in cases where it produced a stringency, *le-chumra*, but would not apply it to produce a leniency, *le-kula*. The question remains unresolved — *teiku*.

This is a genuinely interesting result. One might instinctively feel that the *ikar* principle and the rules of *bittul* are simply different conceptual frameworks: the question of whether something growing in the ground is defined by its origin or by its current state seems categorically distinct from the question of whether a small forbidden quantity is nullified in a larger permitted mixture. The *Gemara* is asking whether these cases are governed by a single unified principle or whether the *ikar* concept operates only directionally — only to be stringent. The answer, for now, is that we do not know.

---

## Ma'aser & Replanting

### Rabbah's Ma'aser Q

A related series of questions follows. Rabbah (the *girsa* here is debated) asks: what would be the analogous case in the domain of *ma'aser* rather than *chadash*? The scenario: you harvested your grain, took *ma'aser* — giving a tenth to the Levite — so that the remaining ninety percent is now exempt and permitted. Instead of replanting seeds (which would give rise to a straightforwardly new crop, fully obligated in *terumot u-ma'asrot*), you replanted the stalks themselves. More grain grew. The question operates on a premise: assume, following the unresolved question above, that we do not go leniently *batar ikar* — the new growth is not subsumed into the status of the old base and instead has its own independent status, rendering it obligated in *ma'aser*. Fine. But then the opposite extreme presents itself: if we take the new growth's status seriously as something genuinely new and independent, does the status of newness redefine even the old base? Must one now take *ma'aser* off of one hundred percent of what is harvested — including the original stalks from which *ma'aser* was already taken — or only off the fifty percent (or whatever proportion) that is truly new?

The structure of the question, then, involves three possibilities: the new growth is absorbed into the old base and requires nothing; the new growth is obligated on its own but the old base retains its exempt status; or the new growth, if it triggers the stricter ruling, redefines even the old base, making everything obligated again.

### Abaye's Distinction

Abaye responds to Rabbah's question by asking: *mai shana mi-kol chitei u-sa'arei de'alma?* — how is this different from any wheat or barley in the world? When you replant seeds and harvest a crop, you take *terumot u-ma'asrot* over the entire yield. Rabbah replies that the case is categorically different: *davar she-zaro kaleh lo miba'ya li* — when the seed disintegrates underground, giving rise to something entirely new, there is no question that everything harvested is fresh and fully obligated. The question arises only *davar she-ein zaro kaleh* — when what you replanted does not disintegrate. You replanted the stalks; when you come to harvest, the original stalks are still physically present, identifiable as the old base that had already been tithed. Does the continued growth redefine them, or not?

The *Gemara* then attempts to resolve this from a ruling of Rav Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *litra batzal* — a liter's worth of onions from which *terumot u-ma'asrot* had been taken was then replanted to produce more. The ruling: *mit'aser lefi kulo* — when you harvest, you take *ma'aser* from the total quantity, not from the total minus the original liter. The old base, even though it had already been tithed, is swept into the new tithing obligation once new growth occurs on top of it.

This seems to answer Rabbah's question squarely — the new growth redefines even the old base. But the *Gemara* rejects the comparison: *hatam hainu zri'atah* — there, that is the normal method by which onions are planted. Onions are grown by planting bulbs, and when one plants bulbs and harvests a larger yield, everything harvested is treated as new produce and fully obligated, regardless of whether the original bulb remains intact. This is simply how onion cultivation works, and halachically it is treated the same as planting seeds: the entire harvest is new. *Hacha lav hainu zri'atah* — here, however, replanting a grain stalk is not the standard method of growing grain. Because it is an unusual mode of planting, one cannot assume that the old base is simply redefined as new. The question of what happens to the original base in such an unusual case remains open.

### Flower Pot Analogy

Rabbi Chanina bar Minyumi poses a related question to Abaye: *atiz she-eino nakuv mahu?* — what is the law regarding a flowerpot without a hole? The *Gemara* is well-acquainted with the distinction between *atiz nakuv* — a flowerpot with a hole, which is halachically connected to the ground and subject to biblical obligations of *terumot u-ma'asrot* — and *atiz she-eino nakuv* — a flowerpot without a hole, which lacks direct physical connection to the ground and is exempt from those obligations at the biblical level, though rabbinically it retains some status of planting.

The *Gemara* first dismisses the question as trivially obvious — if there is no hole, there is no hole — but then recognizes what the real question must be: *chazar ve-nakvo ka-amart* — the case is one where it started without a hole and then someone drilled a hole in it. Some growth occurred while there was no hole, during which the plant was not biblically obligated; then a hole was made, connecting it to the ground, so that subsequent growth is fully obligated. The question mirrors the one about replanted stalks: does making the hole redefine the status of the growth that had already occurred while there was no hole?

The *Gemara* distinguishes this case from Rabbah's question on a different axis: *hacha chada zri'ah hi* — here it is one single planting throughout, and the question is merely whether a change in the pot's connectivity to the ground (the hole being made) redefines the existing growth. *Hatam shtei zri'ot ninhu* — there, in the case of the replanted stalk, there are two distinct plantings: the original planting before the *Omer* and the replanting afterward. These may be governed by different considerations.

Rashi's understanding of the distinction is that in the one-planting case, where nothing was physically uprooted and replanted, the old growth stands separate from the new and is not redefined by the subsequent change. The *Shitta Mekubetzes* reads it in the opposite direction: once the hole is made and the plant is now drawing from the ground, even the earlier growth is considered as though it were growing from the ground all along. The upshot, in either reading, is that the two cases — flowerpot and replanted stalk — may yield different halachic conclusions, and neither question is resolved by the other.

---

## Terumah on Growing Stalks

### R. Abahu's Terumah Q

Rabbi Abahu raises yet another variation on these themes. *Shibbolet she-marcha ba-keri u-shatalah* — a stalk of grain that had been smoothed on the pile (*mericha ba-keri*) and was then replanted. The *mericha* — smoothing of the grain heap — is the act that renders grain fully obligated in *terumot u-ma'asrot* and makes it *tevel*: forbidden to eat until the appropriate portions have been set aside. So this stalk, at the time of replanting, was already at the stage of full *chiyuv*. It was *tevel* in the fullest sense — forbidden to eat, but possessing the latent capacity to become *terumah* once designated. Now the stalk is replanted and it grows. Can it still become *terumah* while it is growing?

Normally, the only route to *terumah* is through harvested, processed, pile-ready grain. Growing grain cannot become *terumah*. But this grain has already passed through that entire process. The question is whether the act of replanting strips away the prior status — reverting the stalk to the condition of something *mechubar*, attached to the ground and therefore outside the category of things that can be *terumah* — or whether the prior status persists through the replanting, leaving open the theoretical possibility that it could be designated *terumah* even while growing.

### Abaye's Terumah Answer

Abaye's initial inclination is toward the latter option: since the grain was fully smoothed and rendered *tevel* before replanting, and since *tevel* is precisely the status from which *terumah* emerges through designation, perhaps even now — while growing — one could designate it as *terumah*. The replanting, on this view, does not sever the prior status.

### Objection to Terumah

The Rabbis immediately challenge Abaye: *im ken matzinu terumah be-mechubar le-karka* — if what you are saying is correct, then you have created the phenomenon of *terumah* on something attached to the ground. But the established principle is *lo matzinu terumah be-mechubar le-karka* — there is no *terumah* on something attached to the ground. How can you allow this replanted grain to become *terumah* while it is still growing?

### Eating Off the Stalk

Abaye clarifies his position. The statement that there is no *terumah be-mechubar* does not mean that the grain literally cannot have the status of *terumah* while growing. What it means is that there can be no *chiyuv* — no liability — for eating it while it is still attached. The laws of *terumah* impose on a non-*kohen* who eats *terumah* either *mitah bi-ydei Shamayim* if done deliberately, or repayment plus a *chomesh* if done inadvertently — but these penalties attach only to an act of *achilah*, an act of eating. Why would eating growing *terumah* not constitute such an act?

Two sub-cases: *de-ei talash ve-achal* — if you plucked the grain from the stalk and then ate it, then at the moment of eating it is no longer *mechubar*, it is *talush*, detached, so the scenario of eating it while attached never arose. *Ve-ei gachin ve-achal* — if you bent over and ate it directly from the stalk without first plucking it, then *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* — your manner of eating is so deviant from normal human behavior that it cannot be counted as a proper act of eating at all. No reasonable person eats grain by lowering their mouth to the stalk; such behavior is not recognized by halacha as *achilah*.

This is a genuinely notable point. Usually when the *Gemara* determines that something does not count as normal eating, the reason involves the character of the food itself — it is disgusting, or unfit, or was consumed in a grossly excessive quantity. Here, the food itself is perfectly fit to eat; it is only the manner of consumption that is bizarre. The *Gemara* is saying that the *mode* of eating, not just the *object* of eating, can be abnormal enough to disqualify the act from the category of *achilah*. That said, one might wonder: if a person stood on their head and ate grain, we would presumably still call it *achilah* even though that too is not normal. The distinguishing factor, as the *Gemara* will make clearer, is that when the object itself is *mechubar* — still attached — that feature of attachment is what makes the act categorically abnormal, not merely quirky.

Importantly, a search of the *Masoret ha-Shas* — that remarkable cross-reference apparatus that covers the entire *Gemara* — reveals a striking admission. On the statement that "there is no *terumah be-mechubar le-karka*," the *Masoret ha-Shas* notes: *likotzer da'ati lo yadati letzayen mekomo be-mishnah o ve-braita she-ein meforash davar zeh* — because of my limited knowledge, I cannot locate this statement in any *mishnah* or *baraita*. This is a remarkable concession from the person who cross-referenced the entire *Gemara*. What it really means is that there is no such explicit *mishnah* or *baraita*. Perhaps the *Gemara* is not saying that a *mishnah* explicitly states this principle, but rather that the phenomenon simply never occurs — *lo matzinu* in the sense of "we have never encountered it," implying it would be anomalous for Abaye to be inventing it now.

### Egg in Bird Analogy

The *Gemara* now introduces a parallel case, described as written in the notebook of *Ilfa* — *pinkusa de-Ilfa*. The case involves *beitzai nivlas of tahora* — eggs found in a kosher bird that was not slaughtered properly (*neveilah*). The halachic category of *nivlas of tahora* — a kosher species improperly slaughtered — conveys *tum'ah* specifically through the act of swallowing: one who swallows it becomes *tamei*, together with the garments being worn at that moment (*metamei begadim be-veit ha-beli'ah*). This is a consumption-triggered *tum'ah*, making it critical to define what counts as an act of eating or swallowing.

The case: an egg that was partially laid at the moment the bird died — *miktzatam bachutz u-miktzatam bifnim* — half outside the bird's body, half still inside. The ruling: the half that is inside (*mibifnim*) causes *tum'ah* through swallowing, while the half outside (*mibachutz*) does not. The inside portion is treated as part of the bird; eating it is like eating the *neveilah* itself. The outside portion has left the bird and is no longer considered meat.

The *Gemara* understands this to mean not merely where the egg was at the moment of death, but where it is at the moment of consumption: if you eat the egg while it is still inside the bird, the act of consumption counts as eating *neveilah*; if you removed the egg and then ate it, it does not.

A question naturally arises — one that students raise: how does one eat half of an egg while it is inside a bird? One answer suggested by the *Gemara*'s framing is that you ate the whole egg, but halachically we only attribute to you the eating of the half that was inside at the relevant moment. The *shiur* for *tum'ah* purposes counts only that portion. The *Gemara* then asks why eating the inside portion while it is still within the bird is considered a normal act of eating at all. Who eats an egg while it is still inside a chicken? Should that not also be classified as *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* — an act so bizarre as to be disqualified from the category of *achilah*?

### Attached Objects Not Eat…

The *Gemara* draws the distinction: when an object is *talush* — fully detached, like an egg that has come out of the bird — *avid inish de-achli hachi*, people can and do eat such things in various ways, even unconventional ones. The egg is a normal food object in a normal state, and how you choose to consume it does not redefine the act. But *mechubar la-karka* — or here, something still physically connected to and enclosed within a living body — *lav avid inish de-achli* — no person normally eats things in that manner. The attachment itself redefines the act, not merely the quirky posture of the eater. This is the conceptual key: it is the state of the *object* — being attached — that renders the act of eating categorically abnormal, whereas eccentricities in the manner of eating a detached, normal object do not undermine the act's status as *achilah*.

This distinction clarifies Abaye's earlier ruling as well. When growing *terumah* is eaten directly off the stalk, it is the *mechubar* status of the grain — not merely the unusual posture of the consumer — that prevents it from being considered a proper act of eating. Hence no *chiyuv* for *mitah* or *chomesh* arises, even if in theory the grain has the status of *terumah*.

The *Gemara* closes this sequence with a ruling of Rav Tiviumi bar Kisna in the name of Shmuel: *ha-zore'a kilayim be-atiz she-eino nakuv assur* — one who plants *kilayim* in a flowerpot without a hole transgresses a prohibition. Abaye responds: if you were telling us that such a person receives *makat mardut* — rabbinic lashes — that would be a significant ruling, since it would affirm that a flowerpot without a hole has rabbinic status equivalent to actual ground, strong enough to trigger rabbinic punishment. But if all you are telling me is that it is merely forbidden, what are you adding? We already know from an established teaching that an *atiz she-eino nakuv* has at least rabbinic status as planting: for if one takes *terumah* from produce grown in an unholed pot to cover produce grown in a holed pot, the *terumah* taken is technically valid *terumah* (because the unholed pot has rabbinic status), yet it does not cover the obligation of the holed-pot produce (because the difference in biblical status makes them incompatible), and so one must return and take *terumah* again. The fact that the first designation had any status at all proves the rabbinic standing of the unholed pot. Shmuel's statement adds nothing to that already known principle.

---

## Five Grains Identified

### Five Grains Mishnah

The sugya now turns to the *mishnah* that defines the five halachic grains and their shared legal properties. The *mishnah* lists: wheat (*chitim*) and barley (*se'orim*), which are familiar, and then three others — *kusmin*, *shibolet shual*, and *shifon*. These five together constitute the *chameshet ha-minim*, the five species of grain that are the foundation of a broad range of halachic categories.

The *mishnah* states: *harei elu chayavin be-challah* — these are obligated in *challah*, the dough-portion separated when making bread. Moreover, *u-mitztarfim zeh im zeh* — they combine with one another. Even if one's dough is made from a mixture of wheat flour, barley flour, and spelt flour, all the components combine toward the *shiur* — the minimum quantity — that obligates one in *challah*. You do not need a full qualifying quantity of each individual grain.

The *mishnah* then states: *ve-asurin be-chadash mi-lifnei ha-Pesach* — all five grains are forbidden as *chadash*, new grain, before the *Omer* is brought on the sixteenth of Nisan. This is precisely why the topic is relevant in Menachot: the *Omer* is an offering of barley, but its effect — and the prohibition of *chadash* — extends to all five grain species, not to barley alone. Rice, fruit, and other produce are entirely unaffected; only these five grains are subject to the *chadash* prohibition.

The *mishnah* further specifies: *u-miktzar mi-lifnei ha-Omer* — not only is it forbidden to *eat* the new grain, it is forbidden to *cut* or harvest any of these grains until after the *Omer* has been harvested. One may pick fruit, harvest rice, but one may not cut any of the five grain species until the *Omer* itself is cut.

The mechanism by which the *Omer* permits the grain is also articulated: *hishrishu kodem la-Omer, ha-Omer matiran* — if the grain has taken root by the time the *Omer* is brought, then the *Omer* renders it permitted, even if it continues to grow thereafter. *Ve-im lav, asurin ad she-yavo ha-Omer ha-ba* — if the grain had not yet taken root when the *Omer* was brought, then this year's *Omer* has no effect on it, and it must wait for the following year's *Omer*. This resolves a practical question: in a field of wheat, how does one determine whether a given planting had taken root by the time of the *Omer*? The answer lies not in physically examining the roots, but in calculating from the time of planting: if the grain was planted two weeks before the *Omer* (with a competing view of one month), it is considered to have taken root. The determination is thus chronological, not observational — which is the only practical way to make such an assessment across an entire field.

### Grain Categorization

A *baraita* is cited that categorizes the three lesser-known grains: *kusmin* is *min chitin* — a type of wheat — while *shibolet shual* and *shifon* are *min seorin* — types of barley. This taxonomic classification matters practically, because a *mishnah* in tractate Challah specifies that only grains of the same type combine toward the *shiur* of *challah*. Wheat-type grains combine with one another; barley-type grains combine with one another; but wheat-type and barley-type flours mixed together do not combine toward a single *shiur* of *challah*. Knowing whether *kusmin* belongs in the wheat column or the barley column (and it seems to straddle both) thus determines when a mixed-flour dough achieves the requisite *shiur*.

### Rashi's Identifications

The *Gemara* presents the Aramaic identifications of the three grains. *Kusmin* is identified as *gulba*; *shifon* as *dishra*; and *shibolet shual* is rendered literally — *shiboleta de-tala*, the stalk of the fox (*shual*), which is simply an Aramaic translation of the Hebrew name.

Rashi provides more interpretively useful identifications. For *kusmin*, Rashi says *aspilta* — spelt. For *shifon*, Rashi says *sigla* — the precise word is obscure, but it is standardly identified as rye. For *shibolet shual*, Rashi says *avina*, and *avina* is actually the scientific term used for oats. On the basis of these identifications by Rashi — and the Soncino translation that followed them — the standard received understanding became that the three lesser-known grains are spelt, oats, and rye. This identification has the force of *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* in the popular consciousness.

### Feliks's Challenge

Professor Yehuda Feliks, the great scholar of flora and fauna in the *Mishnah* and *Tanakh*, author of *HaChai VeHaTzomeach BaMishnah* and *HaChai VeHaTzomeach BaMikra*, raised a pointed challenge specifically to the identification of *shibolet shual* with oats. Professor Feliks argued that *shibolet shual* was in fact a particular variety of barley — a species consistent with the *Gemara*'s own classification of it as *min seorin*, a type of barley. He found it impossible that *shibolet shual* could be oats, for two reasons: first, oats lack gluten, and he understood the capacity to ferment and become *chametz* — which the *Gemara* treats as a defining property of the five grains — to be bound up with the presence of gluten; second, oats were not known in the regions where *Chazal* lived during the period of the *Mishnah* and *Gemara*.

Professor Feliks relates that his identification had practical halachic consequences. After he published his conclusions, Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach — the preeminent *posek* of his generation — began reciting *she-hakol* over his morning oatmeal rather than *borei minei mezonot*, on the grounds that if oats is not one of the five grain species, oatmeal does not merit the *mezonot* blessing. This practice came to the attention of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, who reportedly reproved Rav Shlomo Zalman sharply: one cannot overturn hundreds of years of Jewish practice and the consensus of the *Rishonim*, who all identified *shibolet shual* with oats, on the basis of a single academic scholar's opinion.

### Canonical Interpretation

This exchange crystallizes a fundamental question about the nature of *Torah she-ba'al peh*. As one interlocutor observes, virtually all the *Rishonim* who provided identifications did translate *shibolet shual* as *avina*. All the *Rishonim* who weighed in on the matter agreed. Whatever the grain may have been in some original historical-botanical sense — and Professor Feliks may well be right that oats were unknown in Eretz Yisrael during the *talmudic* period — the *Rishonim*'s canonized interpretation becomes *halacha*. The nature of *Torah she-ba'al peh* is not solely about what was originally meant by a source; it is about what becomes the authoritative, canonized interpretation. When all the *Rishonim* say *avina*, that designation becomes the halacha, regardless of whether it accurately reflects what *Chazal* originally had in mind.

There is also a practical dimension worth noting: precisely because oats lacks gluten, it provides a grain option for those who suffer from celiac disease. Oat *matzah* and oat products fulfilling the obligation of the five grains become available to populations who cannot tolerate wheat, barley, spelt, or rye. Whatever the botanical history, the halachic identification of oats as one of the five grains serves an important practical function.

A similar question applies to *kusmin* — spelt. Professor Feliks argued it was more likely *emmer wheat* or *farro* rather than what we call spelt today. But again, the received tradition identifies it as spelt, and that is what it remains in practice.

---

## Rice & Millet Excluded

### Gezeirah Shavah

Having established which grains are included among the five, the *Gemara* asks why rice and millet are excluded. Reish Lakish answers: *atya lechem lechem mi-matzah* — a *gezeirah shavah* is drawn from the word *lechem* appearing both in the obligation of *challah* (*ve-haya be-achalchem mi-lechem ha-aretz*) and in the context of *matzah* (*lechem oni*, bread of affliction). Just as the *lechem* of *matzah* refers to something that can ferment and become *chametz*, so too the *lechem* of *challah* — and by extension *chadash* — refers only to grains that can undergo genuine fermentation.

### Fermentation vs. Rot

The defining characteristic of the five grains, then, is not merely that they grow in the ground or that they can be ground into flour, but that they ferment — *baim lidei chimutz*. Rice and millet do not ferment in the sense that wheat and barley do; instead, *she-ein bahen lidei chimutz ela lidei sirchon* — rather than fermenting, they rot. Fermentation is a specific biological process distinct from simple spoilage, and the *Gemara* treats the capacity for genuine fermentation as the criterion that places a grain within the five halachic species. Rice and millet lack this capacity and are therefore excluded.

This distinction is not arbitrary: rice has no gluten, millet has no gluten, and neither will rise when moistened with water. They will spoil and smell, but they will not produce the characteristic rise and sour that defines *chametz*. Wheat, barley, spelt, oats, and rye share this capacity, which is why they alone constitute the halachic five.

### Fermentation Principle

The operative principle, then, is: *devarim ha-baim lidei chimutz, adam yotzei bahen yedei chovato ba-Pesach* — things that can ferment can be used for the *mitzvah* of *matzah* and fall within the prohibition of *chametz*. *Devarim she-ein bahen lidei chimutz, yatzu elu* — things that cannot ferment are excluded from *chametz*, *matzah*, and *lechem* in the halachic sense. Rice and millet are explicitly in this excluded category. This is the *Gemara*'s formal grounding for why the five grains are five and not seven or more.

---

## Grain Combinations

### Baraisa: Combine Together

A *baraisa* teaches that *ha-teru'ah ve-ha-kemachim ve-ha-batzekot mitztarfim zeh im zeh* — the whole grain kernels, the flour, and the dough, even when representing different stages of processing and different grain species among the five, all combine with one another for various halachic purposes. The *Gemara* then asks: for what *halacha* exactly? It cannot be *challah*, since *challah* is taken only from dough, not from whole grain kernels or loose flour. What then is the purpose of stating that kernels and flour and dough all combine?

### Rav Kahana: Chadash

Rav Kahana answers: *le-inyan chadash* — for the prohibition of *chadash*. If one ate a *kezayit* composed of a mixture of new grain in various states — some whole kernels, some flour, some dough — from different grain species, all of it combines toward the *kezayit* that makes one liable for transgressing the *chadash* prohibition and subject to lashes.

### Rav Yosef: Chametz

Rav Yosef answers: *le-inyan chametz be-Pesach* — for the prohibition of *chametz* on Pesach. Different grains and different states of processing combine to make a *kezayit* of *chametz* for which one is liable. Rashi notes that even whole grain can ferment: if water is added to kernels and they crack, fermentation can occur. Therefore the combination of whole grains, flour, and dough is entirely relevant to the *chametz* prohibition.

### Rava: Tumah of Food

Rav Pappa suggests the combination applies to *ma'aser sheni* — but this answer is recognized as weak, since *ma'aser sheni* applies to all produce, not specifically to grain, and there is no reason grain in different states would need a special rule about combining. Rava offers the correct answer: *le-inyan tum'at ochlin* — they combine for the purposes of *tum'at ochlin*, the *tum'ah* of food.

### Food & Beitzah

*Tum'at ochlin* requires that the object be considered food and that it reach the minimum quantity of a *kebeitzah* — an egg's volume. Foods of different types and states can combine toward this measure. What Rava's answer teaches is that whole kernels, flour, and dough — even from different grain species among the five — all combine toward the *kebeitzah* required for *tum'at ochlin* to apply. They are all food, and food combines.

The *Gemara* explains more precisely: *sikyaya de-tvu'ah ve-kamchim dumya de-batzakot* — grain and flour are analogous to dough in that they are all genuine food. Just as dough is *ochla be-einiah* — real, recognizable food in its own right — so too are whole grain and flour. And since they are food, they combine for *tum'ah* purposes.

### Barley Hulls Issue

But a complication arises. If grain and flour combine for *tum'ah*, one might think that means barley in any state — including with its hulls — combines. The *Gemara* draws a distinction: wheat, even with its hull or outer covering intact, combines — because the hull of wheat is edible, and therefore the whole thing counts as food. But barley with its hull (*she-einah klufah*) does not combine, because the hull of barley is inedible. Moreover, Rashi goes further: the presence of inedible hulls does not merely render the hull itself irrelevant — the hulls create a *chatzitzah*, a separation, between one food item and another, so that even the edible grain inside cannot be counted together with other food items toward the *kebeitzah*.

### Seeds With Hulls

The *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael, however, seems to contradict this: the verse says *al kol zera zerua asher yizarei* — regarding any seed that is sown — implying that seeds are susceptible to *tum'ah* in the state in which they are sown. And *chitah be-klipatah u-se'orah be-klipatah* — wheat with its hull and barley with its hull — that is how one takes them out to plant. So even barley with its hull should be considered food and susceptible to *tum'ah*.

### Moist vs. Dry Hulls

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *ha be-lachot, ha be-yaveshot* — one case refers to moist hulls, the other to dry hulls. When the hulls are moist, they are edible; edible hulls are part of the food, and the entire grain including hull combines for *tum'ah* purposes. When the hulls are dry, they are inedible; inedible hulls do not count as food and, as Rashi explains, they prevent even the inner grain from combining with other food toward the *kebeitzah*. The *baraita* that permits barley-with-hull to combine refers to moist conditions; the ruling that barley-with-hull does not combine refers to dry, hardened hulls that no one would eat.

---

## Chadash All Five Grains

### Lechem Prohibition

The final point of the sugya brings together the threads concerning *chadash* and the five grains. The *mishnah* stated that all five grains are forbidden as *chadash* before the *Omer*. The *Gemara* asks: *mi-nayin mili* — what is the source for extending the *chadash* prohibition to all five grains and not only to barley, from which the *Omer* itself is brought?

Reish Lakish answers: *atya lechem lechem mi-matzah* — the same *gezeirah shavah* of *lechem lechem* from *matzah* that was used earlier to define the five grains for *challah* purposes applies here as well. The Torah states: *lo tochal alav chametz, shivat yamim tochal alav matzot lechem oni* — you shall not eat *chametz* on it, for seven days you shall eat *matzot*, bread of affliction. From this the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives: *devarim ha-baim lidei chimutz, adam yotzei bahen yedei chovato ba-Pesach* — things that can ferment into *chametz* are the things from which one can fulfill the obligation of *matzah*, and those same things are subject to the prohibition of *chadash*. Since the word *lechem* in the verse about not eating *chadash* refers to things that can become bread — and bread is defined as things that ferment — the prohibition of *chadash* extends to all five grains and none other. Rice and millet, which do not ferment, are excluded from *chadash* for the same reason they are excluded from *challah* and from *chametz* and *matzah*: they simply cannot become bread in the halachic sense of that word.

---

---

# Menachot 71

## Five Grains & Omer

### Five Grains Overview

We pick up on *daf* 71a, having introduced at the two-dot mark — approximately twelve lines from the bottom of the preceding *amud* — the foundational principle that the identity of the five grains carries profound halachic implications. The question of which grains fall into this category bears directly on the laws of *chametz*, *matzah*, the prohibition of *chadash*, *Hamotzi*, *Mezonos*, and related matters. The particular question of oats, though traditionally assumed to be among the five, continues to be debated in later authorities. With that background established, the *Mishnah* moves forward to address the next set of restrictions: until the *Omer* is brought, one may neither harvest nor eat any of the new grain. This prohibition is not limited to barley — it applies to all five grains.

### Cutting Before Omer

The *Mishnah* states that one may not *liktzor* — cut — the new grain before the *Omer*, and may not eat *chadash* before the *Omer* is brought. This raises the central question of when, precisely, the restriction on cutting lapses.

### Cut vs. Brought

Does the prohibition on cutting end when the *Omer* is cut, or only when the *Omer* is brought? This is the primary issue the *Gemara* now takes up, and there is a significant dispute between Rashi and Tosafot as to how to read the *Gemara*'s text. We proceed here according to Tosafot's reading.

---

## Reishit & Gezeira Shava

### Gezeira Shava Source

The *Gemara* opens with the question *mina hanei mili* — where is the prohibition on cutting derived? Rabbi Yochanan answers: from a *gezeira shava* of *reishit-reishit* linking the *Omer* to *challah*. The *Omer* is described as *reishit ktzirchem* — the first of your cuttings — which establishes that nothing may be cut before it, lest it compromise the *Omer*'s status as *reishit*. But this would seem to apply only to barley. The extension to all five grains comes through the *gezeira shava*: the *Omer* is called *reishit*, and *challah* is also called *reishit*; *challah* in turn is defined in terms of *lechem*, which connects to *chametz* and *matzah*, and from there we derive the full list of five grains. Consequently, the prohibition on cutting applies not to barley alone but to any of the five grains. In practice, of course, only barley would typically be ripe at that time of year — the chance of having ripe wheat or ripe oats at *Omer* time is remote — but in principle, if any of the five grains happened to be ripe, one could not cut it.

### Omer as Reishit

The *Gemara* then turns to the precise meaning of *kodem la'Omer* — before the *Omer*. The question is whether the *Omer*'s status as *reishit ktzirchem* means it must be the first thing cut when it is cut, or whether it need only represent the first bringing. Both readings are plausible from the *pesukim*: if the *Omer* is *reishit*, perhaps the critical moment is the cutting, since that is when the act of harvesting takes place; or perhaps it suffices that when it is brought it still represents a kind of firstness.

### Kodem Cutting vs Bringing

The *Gemara* records the dispute explicitly. Rabbi Yochanan says *kodem ketzirat ha'Omer* — the prohibition on cutting new grain extends only until the *Omer* is cut; once the *Omer* has been cut, others may begin to cut. Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Zavda says *kodem hava'at ha'Omer* — the restriction remains in place until the *Omer* is actually brought.

The *Gemara* then attempts to resolve this from the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* states: *asurin b'chadash lifnei ha'Pesach v'liktzor lifnei ha'Omer* — the new grain is forbidden before *Pesach* and one may not cut before the *Omer*. This formulation is puzzling, since one cannot eat *chadash* until the second day of *Pesach*, not before *Pesach* itself. Tosafot's *girsa* reverses the two terms: *asurin b'chadash lifnei ha'Omer v'liktzor lifnei ha'Pesach* — one may not eat *chadash* until the *Omer*, and one may not cut until *Pesach*.

---

## Tosafot Text Emendation

### Tosafot's Girsa

Tosafot's reversal of the text is an emendation, but it produces a significantly cleaner reading of the *Gemara*, and we proceed accordingly. The eating prohibition is naturally stated as lasting until the *Omer* is brought, which is beyond dispute. The cutting prohibition is stated as lasting until *Pesach*.

### Eating vs Cutting

Why does the *Mishnah* say two things — don't eat until the *Omer*, don't cut until *Pesach* — rather than simply saying don't do anything until the *Omer* is brought? The answer depends directly on the dispute. If the prohibition on cutting ends when the *Omer* is cut rather than when it is brought, then the two prohibitions terminate at different moments: eating ends when the *Omer* is brought, cutting ends when the *Omer* is cut. It therefore makes perfect sense that the *Mishnah* states them separately. But if the prohibition on cutting likewise extends until the *Omer* is brought, then both restrictions share the same endpoint and the *Mishnah* should have combined them into a single statement: don't eat *chadash* or cut before the *Omer* is brought. The fact that the *Mishnah* distinguishes them is strong evidence that cutting and eating are governed by different thresholds.

### Yom Tov Restrictions

Why is the cutting restriction phrased as "until *Pesach*" rather than "until the *Omer* is cut"? The answer is that since *Pesach* itself is *Yom Tov*, no one would imagine that one may go out and harvest on the first day of *Pesach*. The *Yom Tov* prohibition on field labor — the principle that one may only perform *melachos* related to food preparation in the home domain, from the stage of *lisha* onwards, and not the *melachos* of the field — itself prevents any cutting on *Yom Tov*. Stating the prohibition as "until *Pesach*" is therefore entirely safe: one will not interpret it as permission to cut on *Pesach* itself.

### Motzei Yom Tov Cutting

The earliest practical moment to cut would therefore be *motzei Yom Tov*. By that time, the *Omer* would already have been cut — the Temple would have cut it the previous night, at the outset of the sixteenth. So by the time an individual could actually go out to his field after *Yom Tov*, the *Omer* would already have been cut. This dovetails precisely with the position of Rabbi Yochanan: that cutting is permitted from the moment the *Omer* is cut, not from when it is brought. The *Gemara* therefore concludes: the question of whether *kodem la'Omer* refers to cutting or bringing is resolved from the *seifa* — the final clause of the *Mishnah* — not from this earlier passage.

---

## Hashrashah Question

### Final Mishna Clause

The final clause of the *Mishnah* states: *im hishrishu kodem la'Omer, ha'Omer matiran* — if the grain took root before the *Omer*, the *Omer* permits it. The *Omer* does not permit grain that came into existence after it was brought; it only applies to grain that already existed — meaning grain whose seeds had already taken root — at the relevant time. The question now is: what is the relevant time?

### Unresolved Debate

*Mai kodem la'Omer* — when do we evaluate whether the grain has taken root? Rabbi Yochanan says *kodem hava'at ha'Omer*: the *Omer* permits all grain that had taken root before it was brought. Rabbi Yossi bar Zavda says *kodem ketzirat ha'Omer*: the operative moment is before the *Omer* was cut, since the process of the *Omer* begins with the cutting. The *Gemara* leaves this unresolved. In practice, the general assumption adopted in other contexts is that we judge by the grain that had taken root at the time the *Omer* was brought, not when it was cut.

The overall picture, according to Tosafot's reading, is therefore as follows: cutting new grain becomes permissible from the moment the *Omer* is cut; eating new grain is permitted only from the moment the *Omer* is brought; and the *Omer* renders permissible all grain that had taken root by the time it was brought.

---

## Sprouting Source Question

### Elazar's Challenge

We now arrive at the top of *amud alef*. Rav Elazar said to Rav Yoshia — his contemporary, not the earlier Tanna of the same name — *lo taysiv akara*, do not sit down until you explain this *Mishnah* to me: *menayin la'Omer she-matir b'hashrashah* — from where do we know that the *Omer* permits grain at the stage of having taken root? Perhaps the *Omer* only permits grain that is already standing and fully grown, and grain that sprouted later would simply have to wait until the following year's *Omer*. What is the source for the rule that mere *hashrashah* — taking root — is sufficient?

### Aviv Source

The answer begins with the word *Aviv*. The *Omer* is described as *Aviv* — ripened grain. The inference is: *lav mikhlal d'ika d'lav Aviv* — the very fact that the *Omer* must be brought from ripened grain implies that there is other grain in the field that is not yet ripe, and the *Omer* presumably relates to that grain as well — otherwise why would the *Torah* need to specify that the *Omer* itself must be ripened? So we see that the *Omer* applies to grain that has not yet fully ripened.

### Narrowing Scope

The *Gemara* pushes back at each stage. Very well — the *Omer* applies to grain that is not yet ripe. But perhaps at minimum it must have reached one-third ripeness (*shlish*), which is the critical threshold at which grain acquires a recognized status as a food product. The *Gemara* then adduces a second verse: *me-hachel chermesh ba-kamah tachel lispor* — from when the sickle is put to the standing grain you shall begin to count. This implies there is other grain that is not yet ready for the sickle, and the *Omer* relates to it. But perhaps that grain is still at the stage of *shachas* — stalks without ripened heads, fit for fodder but not for harvesting. Still, we have not reached the mere seedling in the ground. Rabbi Yitzchak adds: *kamah* — standing grain — implies there is grain not yet at the standing stage. But perhaps it is still above the ground, emerging as shoots. Each successive inference narrows the scope further without yet reaching the point of bare roots in the soil.

---

## Chametz to Planted

### Shtei HaLechem Proof

Rava offers the decisive proof. He turns not to the *Omer* itself but to the *Shtei HaLechem* — the Two Loaves brought on *Shavuot*. The verse states: *v'chag ha-katzir bikkurei maasecha asher tizra ba-sadeh* — the festival of harvest, the first of your deeds, that which you plant in the field. Rava understands this verse as referring back to grain that had already passed through the *heter* of the *Omer*: the *Shtei HaLechem* is brought only from grain that the *Omer* already permitted. Yet this grain is described as *asher tizra* — that which you plant. This means the *Omer* was *matir* the grain even when it was at the stage of *asher tizra* — when it had merely been planted.

### Asher Tizrah Stage

The implication is that the *Omer* renders permissible grain even from the earliest stage of having been planted — *mishaat zriah*, from the time of planting. This gets us far closer to mere *hashrashah*.

### Rav Pappa Objection

Rav Pappa challenges Rava: if the criterion is merely *asher tizra* — having been planted — then even a seed that was placed in the ground but has not yet taken root should be permitted by the *Omer*. Rava responds with a single word: *Sudani* — a term of address that Rashi understands as connoting a Torah scholar, though it may alternatively be a reference to Rav Pappa's trade as a brewer, either as praise or gentle rebuke. The response: *ba-sadeh k'siv* — the verse says *asher tizra ba-sadeh*, in the field. For something to be truly *in the field* — to have become part of the field — it must have taken root. A seed that was merely placed in the ground has not yet become part of the field.

### Conclusion Sprouting

The conclusion is thus established: the *Omer* permits all grain that has taken root — *hishrishu* — before the *Omer* was cut, and as noted earlier, the *Gemara* generally holds that the moment of evaluation is when the *Omer* was brought. This is a *drasha* that the *Gemara* takes seriously, and it must be correct in substance: if the *Omer* were limited to grain already standing and ready for harvest, then all the wheat and later-ripening grains that sprout after the *Omer* would never be permitted — which is plainly not the intent of the law.

---

## Permitted Pre-Omer Harve…

### Reishit Problem

Having established that cutting the new grain is permitted from the moment the *Omer* is cut, and that eating it is permitted from when the *Omer* is brought, the *Mishnah* turns to a further question: are there circumstances in which grain may be harvested even before the *Omer* is cut? The difficulty is that the *Omer* must be *reishit ktzirchem* — the first cutting — and any prior harvesting would appear to compromise that status.

### Non-Omer Fields

The *Mishnah* states: *kotzrin beis ha-shlachin she-ba'amakim* — one may cut irrigated fields in the valleys. But one may not *godesh* — make sheaves — from them. The principle is that from fields where the *Omer* cannot be brought, the *Omer*'s status as *reishit* is not impinged upon by an earlier harvesting. There are two reasons underlying the practical permission. First, there is a technical halachic basis: since the *Omer* is ideally not brought from these fields — either because their grain is considered lower quality, or possibly because irrigated fields are not sufficiently tied to the natural seasonal cycle of rain and therefore cannot serve as the *reishit* of the natural harvest — cutting from them does not compromise the *Omer*. Second, there was a practical concern of *hefsed* — financial loss — if the grain in these fields was not cut when ready. The combination of technical permissibility and practical necessity justified the allowance. The restriction against *godesh* — making sheaves — was maintained to prevent it from looking like a full-scale harvest operation prior to the *Omer*.

### Jericho Case

The *Mishnah* continues: *anshei Yericho kotzrin b'ratzon chachamim* — the people of Jericho would harvest with the approval of the Sages, since they apparently had these irrigated valley fields. However, *v'godshin shelo b'ratzon chachamim* — they would bundle the grain without the Sages' approval. *V'lo michu biyadam* — yet the Sages did not actually protest or attempt to stop them. There is an important distinction here between disapproval and active protest. The Sages were not happy with the bundling, but they tolerated it rather than making a formal objection. The reason for not bringing the *Omer* from the irrigated valley fields is not fully explicated in the *Gemara*, but it is treated as self-evident, and Tosafot and other *Rishonim* note that the qualifier *ba-amakim* — in the valleys — is disputed as to whether it is essential to the ruling.

---

## Fodder Harvesting

### Fodder Not Harvesting

The *Mishnah* next addresses a different category of permissible pre-*Omer* cutting: *kotzer le-shachas u-ma'achil li-vheima* — harvesting for animal fodder. In this case, the field in question might otherwise be a valid source for the *Omer*, but the manner of harvesting removes it from the category of prohibited cutting altogether. The rationale is that the halachic prohibition applies specifically to harvesting grain for human food consumption. A cutting done for animal fodder — *shachas* — is not classified as the type of *ketzira* the *Torah* restricts, and therefore it is entirely permissible before the *Omer*.

### Yehuda's Position

Rabbi Yehuda introduces a qualification: *eimasai* — when does this apply? Only *bizman she-hitchil ad she-lo hevi shlish* — when one began the fodder cutting before the grain had reached one-third ripeness. At that stage, the grain is objectively not fit for human consumption, and the entire cutting is therefore unambiguously for the sake of animal fodder. Even if the harvesting continues after the grain reaches a greater degree of ripeness, the character of the operation was defined at its outset. If, however, one began cutting only after the grain had already reached one-third ripeness, it is forbidden — since at that point the grain has already acquired the status of a food product.

### Shimon's Position

Rabbi Shimon takes a more expansive position: *yiktzor vi-ya'achil af mi-she-hevi shlish* — one may cut and feed to the animals even once the grain has reached one-third ripeness. For Rabbi Shimon, the determinative factor is not the degree of ripeness but the intention and nature of the cutting. If one's purpose is to provide animal fodder, then regardless of how ripe the grain is, it is not considered a halachic act of harvesting. The underlying principle shared by both opinions is that only a harvesting oriented toward human food consumption falls under the restriction; the dispute is whether intention alone suffices or whether objective ripeness also plays a role.

---

## Mitzvah Harvesting

### Kilayim Clearing

The *Mishnah* continues with additional categories of pre-*Omer* cutting that are permissible on account of *mitzvah* purposes. *Ha-kotzetz mipnei netiot* — cutting on account of plantings. Rashi offers two readings. The first is similar to the *beis ha-shlachin* case: the grain grows among tree saplings and there is concern of *hefsed*, of mutual destruction, if one does not cut early, and additionally the *Omer* cannot be brought from a field that contains trees. The second reading, which Rashi himself prefers as it coheres with the thematic thrust of what follows, is that the situation involves *kilayim*: grain is growing in a field where a tree has unexpectedly taken root — perhaps an acorn that had lain dormant in the ground — creating a prohibited mixture. One may cut the grain to resolve the *kilayim* concern. Cutting for the sake of a *mitzvah* constitutes a permissible *ketzira* before the *Omer*, and this is the interpretive frame for the cases that follow.

### Mourning Space
