*Mipnei beis ha-avel* — cutting to create space for mourners. After a burial, it was customary to conduct *nichum avelim* in an outdoor courtyard near the burial site. If that space was occupied by grain, one could cut it to make room for the mourners to sit. This is a *ketzira* done for the sake of a *mitzvah* — the *mitzvah* of comforting mourners — and it is therefore permissible before the *Omer*.

### Study Hall Space

*U-mipnei bitul beis ha-midrash* — cutting to create space for Torah study. In an agricultural society, outdoor study spaces were common, and if a wheat field occupied a space needed for additional students or for the study hall to expand, one could cut the grain to make room. The cutting is for the sake of the *mitzvah* of Torah study, and is likewise permissible.

### Bundle Restriction

In all of these *mitzvah*-based cases, the *Mishnah* imposes a restriction parallel to the one imposed in the *beis ha-shlachin* case: *lo ya'asem kerichot* — do not form them into bundles. *Aval menichim tzvatim* — one may leave them in small piles. The distinction between *kerichot* and *tzvatim* — formal bound bundles versus informal loose piles — serves to ensure that the cutting does not take on the appearance of a full-scale harvest operation prior to the *Omer*.

---

## Omer Details

### Standing vs Sheaves

The *Mishnah* now describes the preferred and acceptable manners of bringing the *Omer* itself. *Mitzvas ha'Omer lavo min ha-kamah* — the *mitzvah* is ideally to cut the *Omer* from standing grain, grain that has not previously been cut. If standing grain was unavailable, *yavi min ha'amarim* — one may bring it from sheaves, even grain that had been cut previously and perhaps for other purposes. *Bedi'avad*, this is acceptable.

### Fresh vs Dry

*Mitzvasah lavo min ha-lach* — the *mitzvah* is to bring the *Omer* from fresh grain, as derived from the word *karmel*, which indicates softness and freshness. If fresh grain was unavailable, *yavi min ha-yavesh* — one may bring it from dry grain, as long as it is from the current year's crop.

### Night vs Day

*Mitzvasah liktzor ba-layla* — the *mitzvah* is to cut the *Omer* at night, on account of *temimut*, the requirement that the seven-week count be complete, which begins properly only when the cutting is done at the start of the sixteenth. *Niktza ba-yom kasher* — if the *Omer* was cut during the day, it is valid after the fact.

### Overrides Shabbat

Finally: *docheh et ha-Shabbat* — the cutting of the *Omer* overrides *Shabbat*. Since the *Omer* must be brought on the sixteenth of *Nissan*, it is the *mitzvah* of that specific day, and like other *korbanot* that have a fixed time, it overrides *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* when necessary. One does not say "in principle I could have cut it earlier"; the nature of *korbanot* is that the day's *mitzvah* is performed on that day. In the Temple period, since *Pesach* was set *al pi ha-re'iya* — according to the appearance of the moon — the sixteenth could fall on *Shabbat*.

---

## Rabbi Benjamin's Source

### Two Verses

A *baraisa* is cited: Rabbi Benjamin observes an apparent tension between two verses. One verse states *u-ktzartem et ktzira* — you shall cut its cutting — referring to the general act of harvesting. Another verse, appearing in the same context, states *reishit ktzirchem* — the first of your cuttings. The first verse, speaking of cutting without the qualifier *reishit*, seems to imply that other cuttings are occurring alongside or before the *Omer* cutting. The second verse insists that the *Omer* be the first. How are they reconciled?

### Geographic Resolution

*Mi-makom she-ata meivi, ee ata kotzer* — from a place from which you may bring the *Omer*, you may not cut before the *Omer*, because to do so would compromise its *reishit* status. *Mi-makom she-ee ata meivi, ata kotzer* — from a place from which you cannot bring the *Omer*, you may cut, since cutting there does not impinge on the *Omer*'s standing as the first cutting.

### Species vs Field

The *Gemara* considers an alternative reading of the same textual tension: perhaps the permission has nothing to do with which field but rather with which species. Perhaps one is prohibited from cutting barley — the grain of the *Omer* — but is free to cut wheat or oats before the *Omer*. This reading is rejected because of Rabbi Yochanan's *gezeira shava* established earlier: the prohibition on cutting before the *Omer* applies to all five grains, not barley alone. Since that *drasha* extends the prohibition across all five species, the permission must be geographic — based on the type of field — rather than species-based.

---

## Jericho & Pesachim

### Six Things

The *Gemara* now turns to a *baraisa* found in Pesachim that provides important context for understanding the status of the people of Jericho's practices. The *baraisa* states: *shisha devarim asu anshei Yericho* — the people of Jericho did six things. *Shelosha b'ratzon chachamim* — three with the approval of the Sages, and *shelosha shelo b'ratzon chachamim* — three without their approval.

### Three Approved

The three approved practices were: *markivin d'kalim kol ha-yom* — grafting palm trees all day on *Erev Pesach*. Normally, one is expected to refrain from significant labor on *Erev Pesach*, particularly from *chatzos* onwards, in order to prepare for bringing the *Korban Pesach*. However, Jericho was *ir ha-temarim* — the city of palm trees — and the particular type of grafting involved was considered relatively simple and was simultaneously at risk of severe *hefsed* if delayed. For these reasons the Sages approved. *Korchin et Shma* — they would recite the *Shema* in a wrapped or connected manner, without pausing between sections or between certain words. This was not considered exemplary practice but was sufficiently innocuous that the Sages did not disapprove. *V'kotzrin lifnei ha'Omer* — and they would harvest before the *Omer*, which, as established, fell under the approved category due to the combination of their *beis ha-shlachin* fields and concerns of *hefsed*.

### Three Tolerated

The three practices done without Rabbinic approval were: *godshin lifnei ha'Omer* — bundling before the *Omer*, which the Sages disapproved of but did not protest. *U-matirin gamziyot shel hekdesh shel charuv v'shel shikmah* — they would make use of the secondary growths (*gamziyot*) of carob trees and sycamore trees that had previously been consecrated as *hekdesh*. The reasoning of the people of Jericho was that since these growths appeared after the *hekdesh* designation, they were not themselves *hekdesh*. The Sages disagreed: *gidulei hekdesh* — growths from consecrated property — remain *hekdesh* and belong to the *Beis Ha-Mikdash*. *U-portzin pratzot b'ganoteihem u-fardeisethem k'dei l'ha'achil la-aniyim nesher b'Shabbatot u-v'yamim tovim* — and they made holes in the roofs and walls of their orchards and gardens, especially in years of famine, so that fruit falling from the trees would collect in accessible places and the poor could eat from it on *Shabbat*. While the humanitarian intention was praiseworthy, the Sages were concerned about the *muktzah* status of fruit that fell on *Shabbat* and the broader concern that eating fallen fruit on *Shabbat* might lead to actually picking fruit from a tree on *Shabbat*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Critique

Rabbi Meir is identified as the author of the *baraisa* as quoted above. Rabbi Yehuda responds: *im birtzon chachamim hayu osim, hayu kol adam osim kein* — if these practices had truly been approved by the Sages, why did everyone not do them? The fact that it was only the people of Jericho implies that these were not normatively approved practices. Rabbi Yehuda's counter-position is therefore: *eilu v'eilu shelo birtzon chachamim* — all six practices were done without the Sages' approval. The distinction, in his view, is not between approved and unapproved but between tolerated and actively protested: *shelosha michu biyadam v'shelosha lo michu biyadam* — three they protested and three they did not. The three they did not protest were: the grafting of palm trees, the wrapping of the *Shema*, and the cutting and bundling before the *Omer* — both the *kotzrin* and the *godshin* together. The three they did actively protest were: the *gamziyot shel hekdesh*, the holes in the rooftops for the poor on *Shabbat*, and — an additional item Rabbi Yehuda introduces — *v'notnin pe'ah la-yarak*, their practice of giving *pe'ah* from vegetables. Since vegetables are not subject to *pe'ah*, what they designated as *pe'ah* was not halachically valid *matanot aniyim*, and the poor who ate from it had therefore not exempted it from *terumot u-ma'asrot*, making the consumption problematic.

### Gemara Resolution

Rabbi Yehuda's position now creates an arithmetical difficulty: if all six original practices were wrong, but he added a seventh (*pe'ah* from vegetables), he would have seven total, not six, and the *baraisa*'s structure of six things breaks down. The *Gemara* resolves this by emending Rabbi Yehuda's list: *sami mikan k'tzira* — remove the cutting from Rabbi Yehuda's list of unapproved practices. According to Rabbi Yehuda's corrected position, cutting irrigated fields before the *Omer* is entirely and universally permissible — not a Jericho-specific anomaly but a practice open to anyone with such fields. The *Mishnah*'s formulation that cutting was done *b'ratzon chachamim* is therefore consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's position, because Rabbi Yehuda's point is precisely that if the Sages genuinely approved something, it should have been universally adopted — and indeed, the cutting of irrigated fields *was* universally available to anyone in that situation. What was specific to Jericho and what Rabbi Yehuda includes among the unapproved-but-tolerated practices is the *godesh* — the bundling — not the cutting. This resolves the consistency between our *Mishnah* and the *baraisa* from Pesachim.

---

## Field Division Pe'ah

### Pe'ah Introduction

The *Gemara* now introduces a *Mishnah* from tractate Pe'ah that will illuminate the question of whether fodder harvesting constitutes real harvesting. The background: *pe'ah* — the corner of the field left for the poor — must be given from each field separately. If a single large field is divided by some barrier or intervening feature, each section counts as a separate field requiring its own *pe'ah*. The question is: what divides a field for this purpose?

### Natural Barriers

The *Mishnah* in Pe'ah lists the dividers. *Ha-nachal* — a *nachal*, a riverbed or wadi, even if dry, divides the field, as the *Yerushalmi* clarifies. *Ha-shlulit* — a running stream. The distinction between *nachal* and *shlulit* is one of size and permanence: a *nachal* is a significant riverbed that divides even when dry; a *shlulit* is a smaller running stream that divides only when water flows through it. *Derech ha-yachid v'derech ha-rabim* — a private path or public road. *Shvil ha-rabim v'shvil ha-yachid* — a public or private pathway, provided it is *ha-kavu'a bi-ymot ha-chamah u-vi-ymot ha-geshamim*, established and usable in both summer and rainy seasons. *Ve-ha-bur ve-ha-nir* — an unplanted section (*bur*) or a fallow-but-plowed section (*nir*). The distinction between these two is that *nir* is a field left fallow but worked — the soil is turned over — while *bur* is simply abandoned and unworked. Either one, if running through the middle of a field, divides it. *Ve-zera acher* — a strip of a different crop in the middle likewise creates a division.

### Fodder Divides Field

*Ve-kotzer li-shachas mafsik, divrei Rabbi Meir* — and harvesting for fodder divides the field, so says Rabbi Meir. If one cuts a strip in the middle of one's field for animal fodder — which takes place earlier in the season before the grain is fully ripe — that harvested strip separates the two sides of the field for *pe'ah* purposes. *Va-chachamim omrim: ein mafsik ela im ken charash* — but the Sages say: it does not divide the field unless that section was subsequently plowed over. Merely cutting for fodder is not enough; only if one then turned the soil would the section become analogous to a *nir* and thereby divide the field.

---

## Pe'ah-Omer Connectio (II)

### Meir as Shimon

*Amar Rabba bar bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Meir k'shittas Rabbi Shimon amra* — Rabbi Meir's position in the *Mishnah* in Pe'ah was stated in the same framework as Rabbi Shimon's position in our *Mishnah* about the *Omer*. Recall that Rabbi Shimon held that cutting grain for animal fodder is not considered a real act of harvesting even if the grain has already reached one-third ripeness — intention alone determines whether it is *shachas* or genuine *ketzira*. Rabbi Meir likewise treats cutting for fodder as not a real harvesting regardless of ripeness, which is why it suffices to divide the field: it constituted a genuine transformation of that section — not a harvesting but a fodder-cutting — without any need for plowing.

### Fodder Not Real

Both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon are therefore understood as operating on the same principle: a cutting done for the sake of fodder, regardless of the grain's state of ripeness, is categorically not a *ketzira* in the halachic sense. By the *Omer*, this means one has not compromised the *Omer*'s *reishit* status. By *pe'ah*, this means the fodder-cutting effectively redefines that strip as a different kind of section, dividing the field.

---

## Pe'ah-Omer Connectio (II)

### Locusts Test

The *Gemara* then tests this equation with a challenge from a *Tosefta* in Pe'ah. *Achlah chagav* — if locusts consumed a strip in the middle of one's field; *karsimuha nemalim* — or ants gnawed it down; *shivsah ha-ruach* — or the wind destroyed a section — *ha-kol modim* — everyone agrees that this alone does not divide the field. *Charash mafsik, lo charash eino mafsik* — only if one subsequently plowed it over does it divide the field; if not, it does not.

Now the *Gemara* asks: *ha-kol modim, man* — when the *Tosefta* says "everyone agrees," who has shifted position? The one who would normally not require plowing is Rabbi Meir — he said a fodder-cutting by itself divides the field. Yet here Rabbi Meir agrees that natural destruction requires plowing. Why the difference?

The *Gemara* proposes a resolution based on the degree of ripeness. One might reconcile Rabbi Meir's two positions as follows: when the *Mishnah* in Pe'ah says fodder-cutting divides the field without plowing, that is specifically where the cutting was done before the grain reached *shlish* — when it was objectively unripe and the cutting was unambiguously fodder-cutting with no resemblance to grain harvesting. In that case, the cutting suffices to redefine the section. When insects destroyed the grain, however, the *Tosefta* evidently deals with grain that was already one-third ripe — at which point its grain status is more firmly established, and therefore even natural destruction requires subsequent plowing to redefine the section.

### Meir as Yehuda

If this is correct, Rabbi Meir's position on fodder turns out to parallel not Rabbi Shimon but Rabbi Yehuda: it is only cutting before one-third ripeness that qualifies as true *shachas* and escapes the category of real harvesting. Rabbi Yehuda in our *Mishnah* similarly held that the fodder exemption applies only when cutting began before *shlish*.

However, a further difficulty arises. Our *Mishnah* specifies cutting for fodder *le-vheima* — to feed to animals — and the question of whether cutting for human consumption of fodder-like food also falls under this leniency is not addressed in our *Mishnah*. If Rabbi Meir's position corresponds to Rabbi Yehuda's and both only care about the grain being less than one-third ripe without any qualification about animals versus humans, then Rabbi Meir would be saying something different from the first opinion in our *Mishnah*, creating a three-way dispute among the *Tanna kamma*, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon.

### Meir as Akiva

The final resolution is brought by Rav Dimi — or in some versions Ravin — upon his return from *Eretz Yisrael*: *Rabbi Meir k'shittas Rabbi Akiva rabo amra* — Rabbi Meir's position follows the framework of his teacher Rabbi Akiva, and should not be compared directly to any of the opinions in our *Mishnah* at all. Rabbi Akiva held that even cutting for human use, when the grain is less than one-third ripe, is not considered real harvesting — *af le'adam nami lo hevei k'tzira*. Rabbi Meir, following Rabbi Akiva, does not draw a distinction between cutting for animals and cutting for humans, and does not engage with the animal-versus-human axis that structures the debate in our *Mishnah* between the *Tanna kamma*, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon. His criterion is simply the stage of ripeness: below one-third, it is *shachas* and not *ketzira* regardless of for whom it is intended. This disentangles Rabbi Meir from our *Mishnah* entirely and resolves the difficulties that arose from trying to identify him with either Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yehuda.

---

## Field Division Pe'ah (II)

### Natural Destruction

The *Tosefta*'s ruling about natural destruction — whether by locusts, ants, or wind — establishes that acts of nature alone do not redefine a section of a field for *pe'ah* purposes, even if they leave that section bare. Unlike a deliberate human act, whether harvesting or plowing, a natural event does not carry the intentional, definitional weight needed to divide a field. Only when such natural destruction is followed by deliberate plowing — which transforms the cleared section into something analogous to a *nir* — does the division take halachic effect. This ruling is accepted unanimously, as the *Tosefta* states *ha-kol modim*, and serves as the background against which the various positions on fodder-harvesting are ultimately measured.

---

---

# Menachot 72

## Fodder Cutting Rules

### Fodder Cutting

We pick up on the bottom of 72a, completing a brief carry-over from the previous session. The discussion had centered on what types of cutting are permitted before the *omer*, and specifically on the case of cutting grain as *shachat* — fodder for animals. The *Mishnah* debated whether such cutting must be performed when the grain is less than one-third ripe (clearly animal food) or even when it has reached one-third ripeness. This question was then connected to a parallel ruling of Rabbi Meir regarding *pe'ah*.

### Rabbi Meir & Pe'ah

Rabbi Meir holds that if one cuts for fodder in the middle of a field in a spotted pattern — the practice called *menamér* — it divides the field into separate sections for purposes of *pe'ah*, since it is not considered the beginning of a harvest but rather a different type of cutting. The *Gemara* is attempting to identify precisely what Rabbi Meir holds, because our *Mishnah* emphasized that the cutting must be done explicitly for animal consumption, whereas Rabbi Meir did not specify this. Since there was apparently a category of fodder that could also serve human purposes — where one is interested not in the grain itself but in the straw or the like — Rabbi Meir's position appears to diverge from the *Mishnah*'s framing.

### Rav Dimi Report

The *Gemara* now moves to identify the source of Rabbi Meir's view. The relevant passage begins with the word *tani*, nine lines from the bottom of the page. *Ela ki ata Rav Dimi* — when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported: *Rebbi Meir beshitat Rebbi Akiva rabbo amrah* — Rabbi Meir followed the position of Rabbi Akiva, his teacher. It should be noted that Rabbi Akiva was in fact the *rebbi* of all the major *Tannaim* of the *Mishnah* — Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon — they were all *talmidei Rebbi Akiva*.

What is Rabbi Akiva's position? *De'afilu adam nami la havei ketzirah* — even if one cuts *shachat* for human consumption, it is not considered a harvesting. The source is the *Mishnah* dealing with *hamenamer sadeh* — one who "leopards" a field, cutting it in spots. If *kelachim* — stalks that are not yet ready for harvest — are left standing, the implication is that what was harvested was also not fully ripe, and therefore this was effectively a fodder cutting. Rabbi Akiva rules: *pe'ah lechol echad ve'echad* — each remaining section is treated as a separate field for *pe'ah*, meaning the cutting is not considered an act of harvesting that unifies the field. The *chachamim* disagree: *me'echad al hakol* — it is still one field and a single *pe'ah* suffices.

This ruling was qualified, however, by a statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *lo chiyev Rebbi Akiva ela bemenamer lekaliyot* — Rabbi Akiva's ruling applies only when the spotting was done for *kaliyot*, roasted grain, which according to Rashi means the grain had not yet reached one-third ripeness. *Aval bemenamer le'otzar lo* — but when one is cutting for *otzar*, storage, which implies the grain is already ripe, Rabbi Akiva would agree that it constitutes the beginning of harvest and the field remains unified.

### Ravin's Report

The *Gemara* challenges this: is it truly the case that everyone agrees that cutting for storage does not divide the field? *Ve-ha ki ata Ravin amar Rabbi Yochanan* — when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mechayev hayah Rabbi Meir af be-mana le-otzar* — Rabbi Meir maintained his position even when cutting for storage, even when the grain is ripe. The *Gemara* resolves this: *savar lah kavateih be-chada u-falig aleih be-chada* — Rabbi Meir agrees with Rabbi Akiva in one respect but disagrees in another. Rabbi Akiva went so far as to say that any fodder cutting, regardless of the grain's state of ripeness, is a non-harvesting act. Rabbi Meir agrees when the grain is less than one-third ripe, but does not go as far as Rabbi Akiva when the grain is already ripe.

The practical upshot, to wrap up this thread, is that cutting for fodder is not considered a harvesting and may therefore be done before the *omer* is cut. The question of how precisely to define "for fodder" — whether by the cutter's intention, by the objective ripeness of the grain, or by whether it is destined for animals or humans — is exactly what these various positions have been working out.

---

## Mitzvah Harvesting

### Cutting Purposes

We now continue with a new but related topic, at the top of 72b. The *Mishnah* states: *ha-kotzer mipnei ha-netiot u-mipnei beit ha-avel u-mipnei beit ha-midrash* — one who harvests on account of saplings, on account of a mourning house, or on account of a study hall. These are types of harvesting that are permitted before the *omer*.

What do these cases mean? *Mipnei ha-netiot* refers to a situation where grain is growing together with tree shoots, creating a *kilayim* problem, and one cuts the grain down so that the prohibited mixture should not persist. *Beit ha-avel u-beit ha-midrash* — one wishes to clear space in a wheat field so that mourners may gather there after a funeral, sitting in an open *chatzer*, or so that a group may convene for study. In these cases, the person is not interested in the grain as grain; the goal is to clear the space. Since this is not a harvesting for eating purposes but for a *mitzvah* purpose, it is permitted before the *omer*.

### Talmud Rationale

*Mai ta'ama* — what is the reason? The *Gemara* answers with elegant brevity: *ketzirchem amar Rachmana ve-lo ketzir mitzvah* — the verse says "the first of *your* cuttings" (*reshit ketzirchem*), implying that the prohibition on cutting before the *omer* applies to cuttings that serve one's own mundane purposes, but not to cuttings performed for the sake of a *mitzvah*, for a divine purpose.

This type of *derashah* is familiar from elsewhere. A parallel principle appears on *Erev Shabbat*: *cheftzecha asur cheftzei shamayim muttarim* — your own affairs are restricted on Shabbat, but affairs of Heaven are permitted. This is why a *shul* may make announcements about events scheduled for after Shabbat. Another parallel is *osek be-mitzvah patur min ha-mitzvah*, derived from the verse by *Keri'at Shema* — *u-ve-lechtecha va-derech*, when you go about your own purposes, implying that when you are engaged in *mitzvah* purposes, the exemption applies.

That said, one could argue that the *mitzvah* framing is not even strictly necessary in our case. Since the person has no interest in obtaining the grain — the goal is simply to clear the space or eliminate *kilayim* — one might argue that it does not qualify as a "cutting" in the relevant sense at all, regardless of whether it is a *mitzvah*. The exemption may follow simply from the fact that this is not a grain-harvesting act. Both rationales are at work here.

One might also raise the question — and it is a genuinely interesting one — of whether it would matter if someone cut grain entirely for eating but then donated the entire yield to the poor. Would that transform it into a *mitzvah* cutting? The answer likely depends on which of the two rationales one emphasizes. Similarly, if the field were owned by *hekdesh* — by the *Beit HaMikdash* — the grain would not be "yours" in the relevant sense, and there might be grounds to permit cutting on an entirely different basis. These questions are not addressed by the *Gemara* here.

As for whether the prohibition on *katzirah* applies *b'zman ha-zeh* — today when there is no *omer* — one would presume there is no *issur katzirah* at all, since the entire prohibition of cutting is defined by the *omer's* status as *reshit ketzirchem*. The *issur chadash* on eating new grain does apply today — the sixteenth of Nisan is the time that permits it even without an actual *omer* being brought — but the cutting prohibition, which is entirely a function of defining the *omer* as the first cutting, presumably has no application *b'zman ha-zeh*.

### No Bundles

The *Gemara* adds one qualification: *v'lo ya'aseh krichot ela manicham tzvatim* — even when these various pre-*omer* cuttings are permitted, one should not make formal bundles out of the cut grain; rather, one should leave them in small informal piles. *D'chama d'efshar lo tarchinan* — as much as possible, we do not invest effort in the full harvesting process before the *omer*. Some things are necessary and we permit them, but we do not want the full harvesting apparatus to be set in motion before the *omer* is brought.

---

## Omer Source Rules

### Standing Grain

*Mitzvat haOmer l'havi min hakama* — the *mitzvah* of the *omer* ideally requires that it be brought from standing grain: one harvests grain that is still in the field, specifically for the sake of the *omer*. This is the optimal fulfillment. However, the *Mishnah* goes on to rule that if standing grain was not cut for the *omer* — whether permissibly or not — and one has already-cut grain on hand, that grain may be used.

### Alternatives

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *v'im takriv minchat bikurim* — the verse "if you bring a *minchah* of the first fruit," understood here as referring to the *omer* (and not to the *Shtei HaLechem*). The verse teaches that the ideal *mitzvah* is to bring it from standing grain. How do we know that if standing grain cannot be found one may bring from sheaves, from already-cut grain? *Talmud lomar takriv* — the repetition of the word *takriv* at the end of the verse ("you shall bring") teaches: just bring it, regardless of how you obtained it.

*Davar acher* — another application of the same verse: the *omer* ideally should be fresh. How do we know that if fresh grain cannot be found, dry grain may be used? *Talmud lomar takriv* — just bring it. Another *davar acher*: since the *mitzvah* is to cut the *omer* at night — as this creates *temimot*, ensuring the count of seven full weeks begins from the night — how do we know it is valid if cut during the day? *Talmud lomar takriv*.

Before arriving at that last point, the *baraita* also teaches that the *omer* overrides Shabbat: *talmud lomar takriv*, bring it under any circumstances. *Takriv kol shehu* — bring whatever you can find, even grain still in sheaves. *Takriv mikol makom* — Rashi understands this phrase literally: from any location in Eretz Yisrael, not only from the fields near Yerushalayim. *Takriv afilu b'Shabbat* — bring it even if it is Shabbat; and by extension, *takriv afilu b'tumah* — bring it even if there is a *tumah* problem, since this is a fixed-time communal sacrifice and such sacrifices override Shabbat.

---

## Day Cutting Debate

### Megilla Mishna

The *baraita* has stated that if the *omer* was cut during the day it is *kasher*. This is challenged from a *Mishnah* in Megilla that lists *mitzvot* categorized by when they may be performed. The *Mishnah* there states: *kol halaila kasher l'ktzirat ha'omer* — the entire night is valid for cutting the *omer* — and *u'lehaktir chalavin ve'evarim* — and for burning the fats and limbs of a *korban*. The *Mishnah* there then articulates a general principle: *davar shemitzva'to bayom kasher kol hayom* — anything whose *mitzvah* is by day may be done the entire day; *davar shemitzva'to balaila kasher kol halaila* — anything whose *mitzvah* is by night may be done the entire night.

The *Gemara* draws an inference: *katani laila dumya d'yom* — the night category is presented as parallel to the day category. Just as day *mitzvot* may not be performed at night — one cannot take a *lulav* at night — so too night *mitzvot* may not be performed during the day: *af laila bayom nami lo*. If the cutting of the *omer* is a night *mitzvah*, it follows that it cannot be done during the day. How then can our *Mishnah* rule that it is *kasher* if cut during the day?

A subtle but important question arises: does the mention of "day" in our *Mishnah* refer to the day before, or to the day after the night of cutting? Tosafot clarifies that since the night of cutting is the earliest valid time — the day before is clearly too early — the question must concern the day after. The *Mishnah* in Megilla, with its *diyuk* that night *mitzvot* are restricted to the night, would then exclude the following day as well.

The *Gemara* is aware that one might argue that night *mitzvot* are rare and perhaps begin at night but continue into the day. The *Gemara* declines to read the *Mishnah* in Megilla that way. The question then is how we rule (*pasken*) — and the answer, as the *Gemara* will show, is that this is a dispute between *Tannaim*.

As for the practical rationale for cutting the *omer* at night: while it may not have been logistically simple, the *Gemara* derives it from *temimot* — the requirement for seven complete weeks — which demands that the count begin from the night. Tosafot, notably, connects this entire question to *Sefirat HaOmer* itself: if the ruling of the *Mishnah* in Megilla is normative — meaning the *omer* is exclusively a night *mitzvah* and invalid if done during the day — then *bedi'avad* one cannot fulfill *Sefirat HaOmer* during the day either. Tosafot acknowledges that missing a day does not disqualify one from continuing to count, but the principle that the count is a night *mitzvah* is what he derives from here.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya, ha Rebbi v'ha Rebbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon* — there is no difficulty; one source reflects the position of Rebbi and the other reflects the position of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon. The *Gemara* then cites a *baraita* that makes their dispute explicit.

### Tumah Case

The *baraita* presents a case: a *kohen* was in the process of offering the *Minchat HaOmer* when it became *tamei* just before being placed on the *mizbe'ach*. What is to be done? *Im yesh acheres* — if other grain is available, *omer lo havei acheres tachte'ha* — he is told to go and bring another *omer*; do not use the *tamei* one. *Ve'im lav* — but if it is not possible to obtain replacement grain in time, *omer lo havei pike'ach ushtok* — he is told to be prudent and keep it to himself — that is, proceed with the *tamei* grain without drawing attention to the fact.

This is the position of Rebbi. Rashi explains the instruction to remain quiet as a concern about misleading people: if it becomes known that a *tamei* *minchah* was offered, observers might conclude that *minchos* in general may be brought in a state of *tumah*, without realizing that this applies specifically to the *Minchat HaOmer* as a fixed-time communal *korban*. It is somewhat unclear why this concern is more acute here than in other cases of *tumah* in communal sacrifices — the *omer* ceremony is quite distinct from a private *minchah* — but that is Rashi's reasoning.

The position of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon differs sharply: *bein kach uvein kach, omer lo havei pike'ach ushtok* — regardless of whether replacement grain is available or not, he is told to proceed quietly with the current grain. The reason: *shekol haomer sheniktzar shelo kemitzvaso pasul* — any *omer* that was cut not in accordance with its proper manner is invalid. Going back to the field during the day would produce grain cut *shelo kemitzvasah* — and since the cutting was done at the wrong time, the grain would be *pasul*. According to Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, the *mitzvah* requires cutting specifically at night, and grain cut during the day cannot serve as an *omer* at all.

This is the crux of the dispute: according to Rebbi, grain cut during the day is *kasher bedi'avad*, so one should attempt to obtain valid grain; according to Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, daytime cutting is *pasul*, so there is no point in trying.

One might ask whether the *Mishnah* in Megilla — which treats cutting the *omer* as a night *mitzvah* exclusively — could still be distinguished from the question of whether the grain is *kasher bedi'avad* for the *korban*. One could theoretically hold that the *mitzvah* of cutting was not fulfilled and yet the grain remains usable for the offering. The *Gemara's* framing, however, places the question squarely in terms of *shelo kemitzvaso*: the debate is not merely about whether the *mitzvah* was properly performed but about whether the grain cut outside the designated time is *pasul* for the *korban* itself.

A further question the *Gemara* leaves open: according to Rebbi, who holds that *bedi'avad* daytime cutting is valid, how should one prioritize among the various *bedi'avad* alternatives the *baraita* listed — from sheaves rather than standing grain, dry rather than fresh, day rather than night? The degrees of *bedi'avad* are not ranked.

---

## Day Cutting Debate *(continued)*

The *Gemara* then traces the intellectual genealogy of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's position. *Rabbah bar bar Chanah* said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon b'shitat Rabbi Akiva rabo shel aviv amrah* — Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon stated his position following the approach of Rabbi Akiva, who was the teacher of his father. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai — whose yahrtzeit falls around this time of year, at Lag BaOmer — was a student of Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Elazar is his son.

---

## Shabbat Override

### Akiva Principle

The *Gemara* now transitions to the question of whether the *omer* overrides Shabbat. We established from the *baraita* that it does, but the precise reasoning requires careful analysis. The *Gemara* invokes a principle of Rabbi Akiva: *kol melachah she'efshar lah l'asot m'erev Shabbos einah docha es haShabbos* — any *melachah* that could have been performed before Shabbat does not override Shabbat. Rabbi Akiva articulated this in the context of *milah* and its *machshirim* — preparatory acts like sharpening the scalpel or transporting the knife, which could have been done before Shabbat and therefore should not be done on Shabbat itself.

The *Gemara* now applies this principle to the *omer*. If the 16th of Nisan falls on Shabbat, why do we cut the *omer* on Shabbat? If it would be *kasher bedi'avad* if cut earlier, why not cut it before Shabbat? The obvious answer would seem to be that the *mitzvah* is specifically to cut it on *mimacharat haShabbat* — the sixteenth — and therefore even if an earlier cutting would be *kasher bedi'avad*, the *mitzvah* demands it be done on Shabbat, just as the *mitzvah* of *milah* on the eighth day overrides Shabbat precisely because the *mitzvah* is tied to that day.

### Elazar's Argument

Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon provides what the *Gemara* treats as a compelling proof for his position. *Ve-i salka da'atach niktzar she-lo ke-mitzvato kasher* — if one were to say that grain cut at the wrong time (*shelo kemitzvaso*) is still *kasher*, then *amai dachi Shabbat*? Why would the cutting of the *omer* override Shabbat at all? One could simply cut it before Shabbat — not on *erev Shabbat* itself which is *Yom Tov*, but two days before — and it would be valid. *Ella mi-de-dachi Shabbat* — since we know the cutting does override Shabbat, the implication is that cutting it at any other time would be invalid. And if it is invalid when done too early, it must equally be invalid when done too late — specifically, when cut during the day rather than at night.

This argument has real force, but it is not without counterarguments. One might distinguish between "too early" and "too late" — the daytime of the same *halachic* day is not obviously comparable to a completely different day. Nevertheless, this is Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's position, and the *Gemara* treats it as a serious argument.

### Shimon Counterargument

The *Gemara* then notes that Rebbi was also a student of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, establishing this through a *baraita* in which Rebbi himself describes how they would carry oil and towels from courtyard to roof to *karfif* on Shabbat in order to reach the spring where Rabbi Shimon would bathe. (This incidentally demonstrates that rooftops, courtyards, and enclosed yards were considered a unified domain for purposes of carrying — a matter that will be treated extensively in Eruvin.) The point here is simply to confirm that Rebbi was a direct student of Rabbi Shimon, and therefore the same chain of tradition — Rabbi Akiva → Rabbi Shimon → Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon — also reaches Rebbi.

Why then does Rebbi not adopt the same conclusion? The *Gemara* answers: *savar lah ke-idach de-Rabbi Shimon* — Rebbi follows a different ruling of Rabbi Shimon himself. *Dé-tanya*, in a *baraita*: Rabbi Shimon says, come and see how dear is a *mitzvah* in its proper time — *bо u-re'eh kama chaviva mitzvah be-sha'atah*. For example, one is permitted to burn the innards and fats of *korbanot* the entire night, and yet we do not wait until night; when a *korban* is brought on Shabbat, the burning of the *imurim* is done on Shabbat itself even though it could technically be deferred to the night. Why? Because it is important to perform the *mitzvah* at its proper time rather than postpone it. And this is exactly the logic that applies to cutting the *omer*: even if it would be *kasher bedi'avad* if cut earlier or later, the right time is the night of the sixteenth, and therefore it overrides Shabbat.

This is also precisely what distinguishes the *omer* from the preparatory acts of *milah* — sharpening the scalpel, transporting the knife. Those have no *mitzvah* component that designates Shabbat as the correct time to perform them. There is no reason to do them on Shabbat. Here, by contrast, the *mitzvah* is to cut the *omer* at night on the sixteenth, and that designation is reason enough to override Shabbat.

### Rebbi Position

Given such a compelling argument, why does Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon not accept it? *Lo shmiah lei* — the *Gemara* says he had not heard of this principle of his father regarding performing *mitzvot* at their proper time.

But Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon has a rejoinder of his own: *dachsah shechitah es hashabbos* — the case of burning the *imurim* on Shabbat is not comparable. In that case, one began with a license to violate Shabbat: the slaughter and sprinkling of blood of the *korban* were already performed on Shabbat — and once the initial *avodah* is underway, it follows naturally that one completes the *korban* on the same day. The burning of the fats overrides Shabbat only because the process was already set in motion by acts that themselves legitimately overrode Shabbat. From there, one cannot derive that one may *initiate* a violation of Shabbat for a *mitzvah* that could alternatively have been performed without any Shabbat violation at all.

### Evidence Review

Given the force of this counterargument, the *Gemara* turns to an even more striking conclusion: *kasavar Rebbi lo dachya shabbos* — the *Gemara* posits that Rebbi holds the cutting of the *omer* does *not* override Shabbat. This requires explaining away an array of evidence. Our *Mishnah* states that whether on Shabbat or the weekday the *omer* is cut — *d'lo k'Rebbe*, this is not Rebbi's view. Another *Mishnah* (involving the three-person procedure with three baskets and three sickles, performed whether on Shabbat or the weekday) — also *d'lo k'Rebbe*. Another *Mishnah* depicting the public ceremony in which the cutter asks "shall I cut on Shabbat?" and the gathered crowd responds affirmatively — *d'lo k'Rebbe*.

This is a striking turn. The *Gemara* is creating an entirely new position — that Rebbi holds the *omer* does not override Shabbat — which is not stated anywhere explicitly, but follows logically from the intersection of his rulings: that *bedi'avad* daytime cutting is *kasher*, and that anything which can be performed without violating Shabbat must be performed without violating Shabbat.

### Rebbi Teaching

Adding to the complexity, the *Gemara* cites a *baraita* in the name of Rebbi himself: *Rebbi* derives from the verse *vayidaber Moshe et mo'adei Hashem* — "Moses spoke the appointed times of God to Israel" — that the *omer* and the *Shtei HaLechem* with their associated *korbanot* override Shabbat and *tumah*. The source for communal fixed-time *korbanot* generally overriding Shabbat comes from the verse *eleh ta'asu la-Hashem b'mo'adeichem* in *Parashat Pinchas*, which establishes *mo'ed* as a fixed-time designation analogous to the *Tamid* and the *Pesach* — both of which are explicitly stated to override Shabbat and *tumah* via the word *b'mo'ado*, "in its appointed time, even on Shabbat, even in *tumah*." The *omer* and *Shtei HaLechem*, however, appear in *Parashat Emor* and are not included in the *Pinchas* passage; the concluding verse of *Emor* — *vayidaber Moshe et mo'adei Hashem* — thus extends the override to these as well.

### Baking Logic

The *Gemara* now presses: *l'mai* — to what *melachah* does Rebbi's ruling refer? If overriding Shabbat means bringing the *omer* or *Shtei HaLechem* as a *korban* on the *mizbe'ach*, the *Shtei HaLechem* cannot be burned on the *mizbe'ach* since it is *chametz*. So the Shabbat override must refer to preparation. But what preparation of the *Shtei HaLechem* cannot be done before Shabbat?

The *Gemara* answers: *le-afiyah* — the baking. Everything else — grinding, sifting — could be done beforehand. Only the baking cannot, because — *ve-savar Rebbi tanur mekadesh* — Rebbi holds that the *tanur*, the oven, sanctifies the bread. Once baked, the bread is *kadosh*, and if it were to remain overnight it would become *pasul bi-linah*. Therefore, baking on the day before would produce bread that was already invalid by the time it was needed. Since there is literally no alternative but to bake on the day itself, the baking overrides Shabbat.

By analogy, this clarifies Rebbi's position on the *omer* as well: only that which cannot be done in advance may override Shabbat. Since according to Rebbi the grain is *kasher bedi'avad* even if cut at other times, the cutting can in principle be performed in advance, and therefore it does not override Shabbat. This is entirely consistent with Rabbi Akiva's principle that anything which can be done before Shabbat must be done before Shabbat.

### Sanctification

The *Gemara* then challenges the premise that Rebbi holds the *tanur* sanctifies: *ve-hatanya, kivshei atzeret ein makdishin et halechem ela bishchita* — a *baraita* teaches that the lambs of *Shavuot* sanctify the *Shtei HaLechem* through their slaughter. The *baraita* details the various combinations: if both the *shechita* and the *zerikah* were performed *l'shman* — for the proper purpose — the bread is sanctified. If both were done *shelo l'shman*, it is not sanctified. If the *shechita* was *l'shman* but the *zerikah shelo l'shman*, Rebbi says it is in an intermediate state — *kadosh ve'eino kadosh* — partly sanctified. Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon holds there is no sanctification at all until both stages are performed correctly: *le'olam eino kadosh ad sheyishchat l'shman v'yizrok daman l'shman*.

This seems to contradict the claim that the *tanur* sanctifies — if slaughter sanctifies, how can baking also sanctify?

Rav Nachman resolves this: *hukva v'lo hukva ka'amar* — the language "sanctifies" as applied to the slaughter was imprecise. What the slaughter of the lambs does is *hukva* — it establishes and binds the lambs and the bread as a unified entity. The actual sanctity — from which the bread cannot be redeemed, and after which it becomes *pasul* if left overnight — was conferred already at the moment of baking in the oven. The sprinkling of the blood then renders the bread permissible for consumption. The three stages — baking, slaughter, and *zerikah* — are thus distinguished: the *tanur* confers *kedushah*, the *shechita* establishes the link between the lambs and the loaves, and the *zerikah* permits eating.

The deeper point that the *Gemara* has been building toward throughout this entire discussion is a precise and remarkable principle: in the *Mikdash*, even for a *mitzvah* that is designated for a specific day, even when the full context of *Beit HaMikdash* *avodah* is operative, one may not initiate a Shabbat violation at the start of a process if that process could have been commenced without violating Shabbat. Only where there is truly no alternative — as with baking the *Shtei HaLechem*, which would be invalidated if done the day before — may one begin the process on Shabbat. Once a process has been legitimately initiated through an act that overrides Shabbat — such as the *shechita* of a *korban* — the entire completion of that *korban* may follow on Shabbat. But to start fresh on Shabbat when an alternative existed: that the *Gemara*, at least in Rebbi's view, does not permit.

It remains worth noting that this conclusion could have been avoided more simply: one might have argued that grain cut before the sixteenth is by definition not *omer* grain at all — just as *milah* before the eighth day is entirely invalid regardless of whether it would be valid later — and therefore there was never any alternative to cutting on the sixteenth itself. The *Gemara* does not take this path, and its insistence on deriving Rebbi's position through the logic of Shabbat-avoidance, with all of its attendant complexity, is what makes this a particularly striking *sugya*.

*Hadran alach Rabbi Yishmael* — with this we conclude the chapter, and we will begin a new *perek* on Shabbat.

---

---

# Menachot 73

## Menachot with Kemitzah

### Ten Menachot Categories

The new perek opens with a classification of which menachos require kmitzah, identifying those whose remainder is eaten by the kohanim: *ve-elu menachos nikmatzos u-shiyureihen la-kohanim*. The list includes minchas hasoles, the machavas, the marcheshes, the chalos, and the rekikhin — the five standard menachos enumerated at the beginning of Vayikra, representing flour, frying pan, saucepan, loaves, and wafers (the two variations of ma'afeh tanur). The mishna adds minchas ovdei kokhavim (brought by non-Jews), minchas nashim (brought by women — not a separate halakhic category in the Torah, yet grouped here for completeness), minchas ha-omer, minchas chotei, and minchas kena'os. The final three are all brought from barley: the omer offering, the korban of the oleh ve-yored at the end of Parshas Vayikra, and the minchas kena'os of the sotah. Notably, the last two lack oil and levonah.

### Rabbi Shimon: Minchat Ko…

Rabbi Shimon introduces a position regarding a category conspicuously absent from the list: the minchas kohen. Since a minchas kohen is burned entirely, one might assume that no kmitzah is performed — the kmitzah's function is to designate what goes on the fire while the remainder is eaten, and if everything is burned, the distinction collapses. According to the Chachamim, the entire minchas kohen is treated as the korban, analogous to a single undifferentiated offering to God.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *minchas chotei shel kohanim nikmetzes ve-hakometz karev le-atsmo ve-hashiyurayim krevim le-atsman* — even for a minchas kohen one performs kmitzah, and the kometz is offered as a distinct ritual act, after which the remainder is also burned separately. The conceptual point appears to be that even in the case of a minchas kohen, the kmitzah retains its intrinsic halakhic significance as the formal act of dedication to God. The remainder would ordinarily be eaten by a kohen other than the owner, but since here the owner is himself the mekareiv, it cannot be eaten; it is therefore consumed on the fire — yet as a categorically separate act from the offering of the kometz itself.

### Rav Papa's Ten Menachot

*Amar Rav Papa: kol heikha de-tenan eser, tenan* — wherever the mishna enumerates menachos, it counts exactly ten. The Gemara asks: what is this intended to teach? *le-apukei rabbi shimon de-amar mechtza chalos mechtza rekikhin yavi* — to exclude Rabbi Shimon's view that a minchas ma'afeh tanur could consist of five chalos and five rekikhin (rather than ten of one type), which would produce an eleventh category. Rav Papa teaches that the mishna implicitly rejects this position.

Rashi offers two readings of the "ten" principle. The first, and preferable, reading counts the ten menachos as follows: solet, machavas, marcheshes, chalos, and rekikhin (five), plus ovdei kokhavim, nashim, omer, chotei, and kena'os (five more). Since there are exactly ten, Rabbi Shimon's mixed category of half-chalos and half-rekikhin would constitute an eleventh — and the mishna's insistence on ten implicitly refutes him. The second reading holds that the point is simply that each category comprises ten full loaves, such that Rabbi Shimon's case of chalos and rekikhin would yield only five of each.

The mishna further states *ve-shiyureihen la-kohanim* — the remainder of all these menachos is eaten by the kohanim. The Gemara asks: from where is this derived? *de-chtiva chtiva* — for those menachos where the Torah explicitly prescribes kmitzah, the halacha is written directly; *u-delo chtiva, chtiva bi* — for those where it is not explicit, the general pasuk in Tzav applies: *ve-zos tihye toras hamincha* — this is the law of the mincha — *ve-hanoseres mimena yokhlu Aharon u-vanav* — what remains is eaten by Aaron and his sons. The rule is thus universally established: where there is kmitzah, the remainder belongs to the kohanim.

---

## Remainder Eaten by Kohan…

### Sources for Eating

The Gemara refines the question. There is no difficulty regarding wheat-flour menachos: *behai lo kamibaya lan* — we are not asking about the standard case. *ki kamibaya lan d'seorim* — our question concerns the menachos brought from barley flour. Does *ve-zos toras hamincha* extend to those as well? As Tosafos notes, this is not merely a formal question. Wheat flour is standard human food; barley was conventionally fodder for animals. It might therefore be argued that the concept of remainder-eaten-by-kohanim does not apply to the barley menachos.

### Barley Menachot Question

One might respond: the very fact that kmitzah is performed on the barley menachos implies that the remainder is eaten — for what else would the kmitzah be designating? *ki d'seorim nami, m'na yad'inan d'shayeraya l'kohanim* — surely the act of kmitzah itself signals that the remainder serves a distinct purpose, namely being consumed.

### Kemitzah Implies Eating

The Gemara rejects this inference: *aliba d'Rabbanan lo kamibaya lan* — according to the Chachamim, this argument is indeed valid, since they hold that wherever kmitzah is performed the remainder is always eaten. Their position entails a strict equivalence between kmitzah and subsequent consumption. But *ki kamibaya lan aliba d'Rabbi Shimon* — the question is acute according to Rabbi Shimon, *d'amar ika minchah d'mikamtza v'lo misachla* — who holds that there can be a mincha where kmitzah is performed yet the remainder is not eaten, namely the minchas kohanim. According to Rabbi Shimon, then, the performance of kmitzah on the barley menachos does not by itself prove that their remainder is eaten. A separate source is required.

### Rabbi Shimon: Kemitzah A…

Chizkiyah supplies the derivation from a pasuk in Tzav: *ve-chol mincha belulah vashamen va-charevah le-chol benei Aharon tihyeh ish ke-achiv* — any mincha mixed with oil or that is dry shall belong to all of the sons of Aaron, each equally as his brother. This pasuk mentions two types: one mixed with oil (belulah) and one dry (charevah). Since the cases of belulah she-shel chitim (wheat mixed with oil) and charevah she-shel chitim (dry wheat mincha) are already established elsewhere, the pasuk cannot be coming to teach them. The principle of im eino inyan therefore redirects: *tenahu inyan li-velulah shel se'orim* — the reference to belulah teaches that the minchas ha-omer (a barley mincha mixed with oil) is eaten by the kohanim; *tenahu inyan le-charevah shel se'orim* — the reference to charevah teaches the same for the minchas sotah (a dry barley mincha). The remainder of both barley menachos is thus established as eaten by benei Aharon.

---

## Equal Division Among Koh…

### Chizkiyah's Derivation

The Gemara immediately challenges Chizkiyah's derivation: *ve-hai le-hachi hu de-asa?* Is this pasuk really coming to teach that the barley menachos are consumed by the kohanim? Perhaps it is needed for a much more elaborate teaching about the mechanics of distribution, as developed in a lengthy braita. The braita addresses the question of how the kohanim divide sacrificial portions among themselves. *minayin she-ein cholkin menachos keneged zevachim* — how do we know that one cannot offset menachos against animal sacrifices, giving some kohanim the flour portions while others receive the meat portions? *talmud lomar: ve-chol mincha asher te-afeh ba-tanur le-chol benei aharon tihyeh ish ke-achiv* — the Torah insists on equal division of the menachos to all benei Aharon, from which we learn that menachos must be divided within their own category.

### Ravina: Korach Portion

The braita proceeds through a series of progressively more refined exclusions, each taught by an additional word or phrase in the pesukim. Perhaps menachos cannot be divided against zevachim because they are categorically unrelated, but they could be divided against bird sacrifices, since birds can substitute for a mincha in the case of a korban oleh ve-yored? *talmud lomar ve-chol na'aseh ba-marcheshet* — the mention of the marcheshes insists that even this division is prohibited. Perhaps bird sacrifices and animal sacrifices, both being blood offerings, could be apportioned against one another? *talmud lomar ve-al machavat* — yet another item in the pasuk insists otherwise. Perhaps different types of menachos could be traded off against each other within the category of flour offerings? *talmud lomar ve-chol mincha belulah ba-shemen* — no, each sub-category must be divided within itself. Perhaps at least two identical menachos — one machavat against another machavat — could be pooled together and divided? *talmud lomar ve-charevah* — even this is excluded. The final conclusion is that each individual sacrifice must be divided separately among the kohanim. 

The magnitude of this requirement is striking: in the Beis HaMikdash on a busy day, every single sacrifice — of every type, brought by every individual — would need to be individually subdivided among all the eligible kohanim. Tosafos suggests an alternative reading of *lo yachloku*: rather than requiring active individual division of each korban, the principle may mean that no formal apportionment takes place at all — the portions are simply made available for any and all kohanim to partake, without a structured allocation. Tosafos wavers between this reading and the more demanding literal one.

The braita proceeds to apply the same principle to kodshim kalim. *yachol lo yachloku be-kodshei kodashim aval yachloku be-kodshim kalim* — perhaps the restrictions apply only to kodshei kodashim (consumed only within the Beis HaMikdash), but the breast and thigh of the shelamim, which may be eaten anywhere in Yerushalayim and might seem more like personal property, could be divided differently? *talmud lomar ish ke-achiv ve-im al todah* — the pasuk continues with the todah and shelamim, extending the principle: *ke-shem she-ein cholkin be-kodshei kodashim, kach ein cholkin be-kodshim kalim*.

### Inclusive Language in Ko…

The braita concludes with one further teaching derived from the word *ish*: *ish cholek va-afilu ba'al mum, ve-ein katan cholek va-afilu tam* — an adult kohen receives his portion even if he is a ba'al mum (physically blemished), while a minor kohen does not receive a portion even if he is unblemished. The right to the sacrificial portions belongs to adult kohanim, not to minors.

### Rav Huna: Non-Jews Limit…

The Gemara now asks: given all this, how can Chizkiyah's derivation stand? If the pasuk *ve-chol mincha belulah vashamen va-charevah le-chol benei Aharon* is entirely consumed by the braita's teachings about division, it cannot simultaneously teach that the barley menachos are eaten by the kohanim. *hahu mikol nafka* — the Gemara responds that the additional teachings about division are derived from the word *kol* (in *ve-chol*), while the fundamental teaching that the barley menachos are consumed — *belulah... va-charevah... le-chol benei Aharon* — remains intact as the plain meaning of the pasuk. And the earlier teaching cited in connection with a different perek (*le-Rabbi Yosi be-Rabbi Yehuda*) is derived from the extra *vav* of *ve-chol*. Thus the same pasuk yields three distinct layers of derivation: the *vav* for the prior teaching, the *kol* for the rules of division, and the plain meaning for the entitlement of the kohanim to the barley menachos.

---

## Non-Jews Bringing Sacrif…

### Rav Shizbi's Challenge

*Ravina amar: asya mi-detani Levi* — Ravina offers a cleaner derivation, from what Levi teaches, based on the pasuk in Bamidbar 18 following the episode of Korach, where the Torah reaffirms the priestly entitlements in sweeping terms: *le-chol korbanam, le-chol minchasam, le-chol chatasam, u-le-chol ashamam* — all their korbanos, all their menachos, all their sin offerings, all their asham offerings — which they return to Me, holy of holies, it is for you and your sons. The broad framing of *le-chol minchasam* straightforwardly includes the barley menachos among the priestly portions, without the complex series of redirections required by Chizkiyah's approach.

### Rabbi Yochanan: Debate R…

The Gemara then examines what each phrase in this pasuk comes to include beyond what would otherwise have been known. *kol korbanam* — this includes the log of oil of the metzora in the purification process. Since the preceding words speak of *min ha-esh* (portions derived from the fire, i.e., from the mizbeach), one might have thought only offerings involving the mizbeach confer rights to the kohanim. *kol korbanam* extends the principle to the metzora's oil, which is used ritually but not burned on the mizbeach.

### 'Ish' Verse Analysis

*Le-chol minchasam* — all their menachos. *le-rabbos minchas omer u-minchas kena'os* — this explicitly includes the minchas ha-omer and the minchas kena'os of the sotah. The hava amina would have been that only offerings connected to atonement (*asher kupar bahem*) are eaten by the kohanim; the omer is not brought for kapara but to render the new grain permissible (*le-hatir ka'asya*), and the minchas sotah is brought not as a definitive atonement but as a clarificatory test (*levarer ka'asya*). *minchasam* teaches that even these are eaten by the kohanim — and since both happen to be barley menachos, this is a much cleaner source for the very question we have been addressing, as Tosafos acknowledges. *le-chol chatasam* includes the bird chatas: one might have thought that since the bird is not slaughtered through normal shechita but rather by the kohen's fingernail at the back of the neck, it would be considered a neveilah and forbidden; *chatasam* teaches that the kohanim eat it nonetheless. *le-chol ashamam* includes the asham of the nazir and the asham of the metzora. Since *ki ke-chatas ha-asham hu la-kohen* is written explicitly regarding the metzora's asham, the derivation from *ashamam* must come to include the nazir's asham. The hava amina for excluding the nazir's asham is that it comes *le-hachshir* — to reconstitute the nezirus after tumah — rather than as a straightforward atonement offering.

The pasuk concludes *asher yashivu* — that which they return. This is interpreted as referring to *gezel ha-ger*: if one swore falsely to a ger that he had not stolen from him, he must return the stolen property with an added fifth and bring an asham. If the ger dies without heirs, the restitution money goes to the kohen. Finally, *lecha hu u-le-vanecha* — it is yours and your sons' — teaches the degree of ownership the kohen has in his portion: *afilu le-kadesh bo et isha*, it is sufficiently his property that he could use it to effect kiddushin, a point elaborated upon in Maseches Kiddushin.

---

## Non-Jews Sending Offerin…

### Rabbi Shimon's Ordinance

The Gemara transitions to a new topic, introduced because it will shortly engage our mishna directly. *amar rav huna: shlamei ovdei kochavim olot* — if a non-Jew dedicates an animal as a shelamim, it is treated as an olah. Rav Huna offers two justifications. The first is a sevara: *ovdei kochavim libehu la-shamayim* — a non-Jew, when dedicating something to God, intends to give it over entirely to heaven. The notion of eating from a sacrifice in God's presence may seem, from a non-Jewish perspective, insufficiently absolute — he therefore effectively means olah even when he says shelamim.

The second justification is from the pasuk itself. The Gemara cites Vayikra 22, which begins: *ish ish mi-beis Yisrael u-min ha-ger be-Yisrael asher yakriv korbano le-chol nidreihem u-le-chol nidvotam asher yakrivu l'Hashem le-olah* — any man from the house of Israel or from the sojourner among Israel who brings his offering, for all their vows and all their freewill offerings that they bring to Hashem, as an olah. It is striking that although the pasuk heavily emphasizes benei Yisrael, Chazal derive from *ish ish* that even non-Jews may bring offerings. And the end of the pasuk — *asher yakrivu l'Hashem le-olah* — teaches that whatever a non-Jew brings is treated as an olah: *kol de-mikrevi olah lehavei*.

### Nesachim Status

Rav Chama bar Guria challenges from a Tosefta: *oved kokhavim she-hitnadev le-havi shelamim* — if a non-Jew took a vow to bring a shelamim, *netanam le-Yisrael, Yisrael okhlam; netanam le-kohen, kohen okhlam* — if he gives it to a Yisrael, a Yisrael eats it; if to a kohen, a kohen eats it. This teaching seems to confirm that a non-Jew can bring a shelamim, directly contradicting Rav Huna.

### Reconciling Sources

Rava resolves the Tosefta: *al menat she-yitkapru bahen Yisrael, Yisrael okhlam; al menat she-yitkapru bahen kohen, kohen okhlam* — the non-Jew is not bringing his own shelamim. Rather, he is dedicating his animal to serve as the shelamim of a specific Yisrael or a specific kohen. The animal originates with the non-Jew but is consecrated as the korban of the named recipient. The non-Jew is thus not the owner of the shelamim in any halachic sense; he merely provides the animal. This resolves the contradiction: Rav Huna's ruling addresses a non-Jew's own sacrifice, whereas the Tosefta addresses a case of vicarious dedication.

### Rav Shizbi challenges via Mishna

Rav Shizbi then challenges from our own mishna: *elu menachos nikmatzos ve-shiyureihen la-kohanim — minchas ovdei kokhavim* — the mishna explicitly includes the mincha of a non-Jew among those subject to kmitzah, whose remainder is eaten by the kohanim. This indicates that a non-Jew can bring a mincha — a sacrifice other than an olah — and this challenges Rav Huna's position.

---

## Rabbi Yosi vs. Rabbi Aki…

### Rabbi Yochanan resolves dispute

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the difficulty: *lo kashya — ha Rabbi Yosi HaGlili ve-ha Rabbi Akiva* — there is no contradiction. Rav Huna's statement reflects the position of Rabbi Akiva, while our mishna (which permits a non-Jew to bring a mincha) follows Rabbi Yosi HaGlili. The two Amoraim are simply aligned with opposing tannaitic positions.

### Derasha from Ish Ish pasuk

The underlying dispute is developed from a braita on the pasuk already cited. *ish ish mi-beis yisrael u-min ha-ger... asher yakrivu l'hashem le-olah* — the braita first establishes, from *ish ish*, that non-Jews may make vows and freewill offerings as Jews do. It then proceeds to expand the scope of permitted offerings through successive derivations: *nidreihem* teaches that vows include shelamim; *nidvotam* extends it to todah; *le-chol nidreihem* and *le-chol nidvotam* include bird offerings, wine, frankincense, and wood — anything a Jew may consecrate and offer, a non-Jew may likewise consecrate. The question then is: why does the pasuk conclude *le-olah*, specifying olah?

### Rabbi Yosi HaGlili position

According to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili: *olah perat le-nezirut* — the word *le-olah* excludes only the olah of a nazir. Since a non-Jew cannot become a nazir, he cannot bring the nazir's olah. This is the only restriction Rabbi Yosi HaGlili derives; in all other respects, a non-Jew may bring the full range of offerings.

### Rabbi Akiva position

Rabbi Akiva reads the pasuk differently: *asher yakrivu l'Hashem le-olah — ein li ela olah bilvad* — only an olah. The concluding phrase is definitive and restrictive: a non-Jew may bring only an olah. Rabbi Akiva does not explain how he accounts for the expansive language earlier in the pasuk, but the debate is clear: our mishna permitting a non-Jew's mincha follows Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, while Rav Huna's ruling follows Rabbi Akiva.

---

## Non-Jews and Nedirut

### Nezirut exclusion source

The Gemara asks: does Rabbi Yosi HaGlili really need our pasuk to exclude a non-Jew from the nazir's olah? A separate source already establishes that non-Jews cannot become nezirim: *dabber el benei Yisrael ve-amarta alehem ish ki yafli lindor neder nazir le-hazzir — benei Yisrael nodrim ve-ein ovdei kochavim nodrim*. The Gemara answers: if we had only the pasuk in Nezirus, one might have concluded that the restrictions apply to the korban alone — a non-Jew cannot bring the korban of a nazir — but that nezirus itself might take effect upon him. The pasuk in our context teaches that the nezirus cannot take effect at all; the pasuk in Nezirus teaches that he cannot bring the korban. Both teachings are therefore necessary, though the Gemara leaves somewhat open why the exclusion from the korban cannot simply follow from the impossibility of becoming a nazir.

### Rabbi Shimon's seven enactments

The Gemara asks: *ke-man azla ha de-tenan* — which tannaitic opinion underlies the teaching of Rabbi Shimon that *beis din* enacted seven enactments, one of which is: if a non-Jew sent an olah from overseas and sent with it the accompanying nesachim, they are offered from his own funds; if he did not send the nesachim, they are covered from public funds. This teaching implicitly presupposes that a non-Jew can send an olah — the question is only whether his nesachim must accompany it or may be funded communally. The Gemara initially suggests this follows Rabbi Yosi HaGlili rather than Rabbi Akiva, since Rabbi Akiva would seem to prohibit even the accompanying nesachim. But the Gemara replies: *afilu teima Rabbi Akiva — olah ve-chol chavratah* — even Rabbi Akiva would permit the nesachim that accompany an olah, since they are integral to the olah offering itself.

### Nesachim requirements

A further braita raises a related question: *ezrach mevi nesachim ve-ein ovdei kochavim mevi nesachim* — a citizen brings nesachim but a non-Jew does not. One might then conclude that even the olah of a non-Jew cannot come with nesachim. *talmud lomar kachah* — the Torah insists on the proper procedure, establishing that the olah of a non-Jew does require nesachim; but a non-Jew cannot independently dedicate nesachim on their own.

### Competing interpretations resolved

The Gemara asks: *mani* — whose view does this braita reflect? Apparently neither Rabbi Yosi HaGlili nor Rabbi Akiva straightforwardly: if it is Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, he explicitly permits a non-Jew to bring wine independently, yet this braita excludes wine; if it is Rabbi Akiva, he permits only olah, yet this braita permits olah with its nesachim. The Gemara resolves the apparent incompatibility in both directions. *ei ba'it eima rabbi yosi haGlili — sami mikan yayin*: the braita may follow Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, with wine alone excluded (derived from the word *ezrach*), though this exclusion of wine is admittedly difficult given his own earlier formulation. The preferable resolution is *ei ba'it eima Rabbi Akiva — olah ve-chol chavratah*: the braita follows Rabbi Akiva, who permits an olah together with everything integral to it, but prohibits any other korban or independent dedication of nesachim. This accounts for the braita's position cleanly: a non-Jew brings an olah with its accompanying nesachim, but he may not dedicate nesachim independently, nor any sacrifice other than an olah.

---

---

# Menachot 74

## Minchas Chotei

### Kohen's Sin Mincha

The daf opens by picking up at the very bottom of Ayin Gimel Amud Beis. The underlying question is one that runs through the entire opening sugya: the Torah establishes that when a Kohen brings a Mincha, the entire offering is burned — there is no Kmitza and no eating of the remainder. But that rule was formulated with a standard Mincha in mind, one that functions somewhat like an Olah. What happens when the Mincha is a Minchas Chotei — a sin-offering — where there is no logical parallel to burning the whole thing, since it is functioning as a type of Chatas? The Tanna Kamma rules that you burn the whole thing regardless. Rabbi Shimon disagrees: you perform a Kmitza, burn the Kmitza separately, and burn the remainder separately. Both agree, then, that everything is ultimately burned — the Minchas Chotei Shel Kohanim is not excluded from the general category of Minchas Kohen. The dispute is whether it retains the structure of a Minchas Chotei by requiring a Kmitza.

### Scriptural Analysis

The Gemara asks: Mena Hanei Mili? Where is this derived from? Detanu Rabbanan — our Rabbis taught from the pasuk in Vayikra Hei: V'hayisaho Lakohen Kamincha — "and it shall be for the Kohen like a Mincha." This pasuk appears at the conclusion of the Olah V'Yored passage, which describes the situation of one who cannot afford birds and brings instead an Asiris Ha'eifah Soles — a tenth of an ephah of fine flour — as a Chatas. The passage ends: V'chiper Alav Hakohen Al Chata'aso Asher Chata Me'achas Me'eleh V'nislach Lo V'hayisaho Lakohen Kamincha. Even though this Mincha functions as a Chatas, the Torah concludes that it is "like a Mincha." What does that phrase come to teach?

The Beraisa offers two possible readings. The first is Shetei Avodah Kashera Bo — that the word Lakohen teaches that even if this is the Kohen's own Chatas, he may still perform the Avodah for it himself, a previously unestablished principle. The second possibility: O Eino Ela L'hatir Minchas Chotei Shel Kohanim — perhaps the pasuk comes to permit the Kohen to eat the remainder of his own Minchas Chotei, treating it like an ordinary Minchas Yisrael where the Kohen eats the Shirayim. If that reading were correct, how would one reconcile it with the general pasuk V'chol Minchas Kohen Kalil Tihyeh Lo Seiachel — every Mincha of a Kohen shall be fully burned and not eaten? That general prohibition, one might argue, applies only to B'minchas Nedavaso — his free-will Mincha — whereas by his Chovaso, his obligatory Mincha brought for a sin, perhaps it may be eaten.

### Kamincha Interpretation

To resolve this, the Beraisa invokes the word Kamincha. The argument runs as follows: had the Torah said only Lakohen — that it belongs to the Kohen — one might have read it as granting him the right to eat the remainder. But the addition of Kamincha, "like a Mincha," forces a comparison. The question is: like which Mincha? Like the Kohen's own standard Mincha — that is, his Minchas Nedava, which is fully burned. The derivation is Makish Chovaso L'nedavaso — his obligatory Mincha is compared to his free-will Mincha. Mah Nedavaso Einah Ne'echeles, just as a free-will Mincha of a Kohen is not eaten but fully burned, Af Chovaso Einah Ne'echeles, so too his obligatory Mincha is not eaten. The reading is thus: Kamincha points to the Kohen's own standard Mincha, meaning it is fully burned, while Lakohen teaches that he retains the right to perform the Avodah himself.

### Separate Burning

Rabbi Shimon pushes back. Vechi Ne'emar Vehaya Lakohen Kaminchaso — does the Torah say "like his Mincha," in the possessive, which would force the comparison to the Kohen's own Minchas Nedava? V'hallo Lo Ne'emar Ella Kamincha — it says only "like a Mincha," without the possessive. Therefore, Rabbi Shimon reads Kamincha differently: Lehakish Minchas Chotei Shel Kohanim Kaminchas Chotei Shel Yisrael — to connect the Minchas Chotei of a Kohen to the Minchas Chotei of a Yisrael. Not to a Minchas Nedava, but to the parallel Minchas Chotei that a Yisrael would bring.

Rabbi Shimon does not go so far as to say the Kohen may eat the remainder — the general pasuk prohibiting any Kohen from eating his Mincha is still operative. But at minimum, the comparison to the Minchas Chotei of a Yisrael teaches that a Kmitza is performed and the Kometz is separated from the remainder. Mah Minchas Chotei Shel Yisrael Nikmetzes, just as the Minchas Chotei of a Yisrael requires a Kmitza, Af Minchas Chotei Shel Kohanim Nikmetzes, so too the Minchas Chotei of a Kohen requires a Kmitza.

One might then ask: should we draw the equation all the way? Ei Mah Minchas Chotei Shel Yisrael Nikmetzes V'shireiha Ne'echalin — just as a Minchas Chotei of a Yisrael has Kmitza and the remainder is eaten, perhaps Af Minchas Chotei Shel Kohanim Nikmetzes V'shireiha Ne'echalin, so too the Minchas Chotei of a Kohen has Kmitza and the remainder is eaten. The Beraisa rejects this: Talmud Lomar V'hayisaho Lakohen Kamincha. The word Lakohen teaches that the Kohen treats it in the manner of a Mincha — meaning, from the Kohen's perspective, he performs the Avodah as he would for any Minchas Chotei, with a Kmitza. But Velo Le'ishim Kamincha — with respect to the fire, it is not like a standard Minchas Chotei. The fire takes everything. The formulation is striking: for the Kohen, Kamincha — it is like a Mincha; for the Ishim, it is not like that Mincha.

The upshot is that both the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon agree that the Kamincha of this pasuk is the decisive word, but they dispute whether it refers to the Kohen's own Minchas Nedava (Chachamim) or to the Minchas Chotei of a Yisrael (Rabbi Shimon). The Tanna Kamma reads it as one unified unit to be burned in full; Rabbi Shimon reads it as having the structural form of a Minchas Chotei — with a Kmitza — while still burning everything.

### Kohen's Rights

The Gemara then turns to the other element derived from the pasuk — the right of a Kohen to perform the Avodah for his own korban. Hashata Avoda Ksheira Bo — now that we know a Kohen may perform the Avodah of his own Minchas Chotei, do we learn this principle from here, from the word Lakohen? Mei'hacha Nafka? The Gemara objects: we already know from another source. A Beraisa asks, Minayin L'kohen She'ba U'makriv Korbonosav B'chol Eis U'v'chol Sha'ah She'yirtzeh — how do we know a Kohen always has the option of bringing his own personal Korbanos and performing their Avodah himself? This relates to the system of rotating mishmaros — each family of Kohanim served in a fixed weekly rotation, and within each week the sub-families had their days. Nevertheless, for one's own Korbanos, a Kohen always retains the right to serve. This is derived from the pasuk in Devarim: U'ba B'chol Avas Nafsho V'sheireis — and he shall come whenever his soul desires and serve.

If we learn this principle from there, why is it also needed here, from the Minchas Chotei? Im Mei'hasam Hava Amina Hanei Mili Davar She'ein Ba Al Cheit — from that pasuk alone, one might have thought the rule applies only to a Korban that is not sin-related. A free-will Korban, which a Kohen brings by choice, seems more naturally one over which he retains personal control. Aval Davar Sheba Al Cheit, Eima Lo — but for a sin-related Korban, one might have thought the Kohen may not serve for himself. The intuition is significant on two levels. First, there is something fitting about autonomy in voluntary giving; you are acting from choice and so can also choose how to present it. Second, and more compellingly, there is a structural logic to the Beis HaMikdash where someone else performs atonement on your behalf. If anywhere that logic should apply, it is precisely when the Kohen himself is the sinner — that he would need another to bring his Korban before God. Therefore, the pasuk of Kamincha is needed to teach that even for a sin-related Mincha, the Kohen may perform his own Avodah.

### Devarim Source

The Gemara presses further. Ela Ma'ata Avoda She-bachutz, Aima Lo? Even granting the above, what about Avodah performed outside the Mikdash — does the Kohen have the right to bring his own Korban even there? The Gemara notes: Ha Nami Mehacha Nafka — we learn even that from a different pasuk, namely V'chiper Hakohen Al Hanefesh Hashogeges B'chet Bishgaga, from the passage in Bamidbar Tet-Vav about a certain Chatas. This pasuk is read as Melamed She-hakohen Mitkaper Al Yedei Atzmo — teaching that the Kohen may bring his own Chatas and achieve atonement through his own act.

But then: I Me-hahu, if the principle came only from that pasuk, Hava Amina Hani Mili B'shogeg — one might have thought it applies only when the sin was committed B'shogeg, in error. The pasuk explicitly says Bishgaga — in error — and there is a certain logic to saying: if the sin was accidental, the Kohen is less morally compromised and so may present himself before God. Aval B'meizid, Lo — but if the sin was intentional, perhaps he has no right to bring his own Korban.
