The Minchas Chotei is therefore needed as an additional source because it is part of the Olah V'Yored framework, which includes certain cases of B'meizid — notably Zadon Shvua, a deliberate false oath in the context of Shvuas Eidus. In those cases as well, the Kohen may bring his own Korban. The word B'meizid in the printed text carries a dalet marking it as a later gloss — Rashi did not have those words — and it appears to have been a marginal note by a later editor identifying the relevant case, subsequently incorporated into the text.

---

## Kohen's Own Korban

### Sin Limitation

The Gemara now presents a second Beraisa. Rabbi Shimon holds that the Kometz of the Minchas Chotei Shel Kohanim is brought on its own and the Shirayim are burned on their own. His son, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, goes further: Hakometz Kareiv Be-atzmo V'hashirayim Mitpazrim Al Beit Hadeshen — the Kometz is brought by itself, but the remainder is scattered on the Beit Hadeshen. The reasoning: you cannot eat the Shirayim because it is a Minchas Kohen; you cannot burn them on the Mizbeach as an act of Hakrava because you have already performed the Kmitza and only the Kometz is offered. So what do you do with the Shirayim? You scatter them on the Beit Hadeshen.

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yochanan raised a question about this: Beit Hadeshen De-heicha — which Beit Hadeshen is meant? I De-le-ma'ala — if it means the ash pile on top of the Mizbeach where things are burned and ashes collect, then Hainu Avuha — this is the same position as Rabbi Shimon his father. You are effectively saying the Shirayim are burned on the Mizbeach. I De-le-mata — if it means the lower Beit Hadeshen, the place at ground level in the Azarah: Rashi understands this as the area beside the ramp where ashes were deposited after Trumat Hadeshen in the morning, while Tosafot understands it as the place in the Azarah where Parim Hanisrafim V'se'irim Hanisrafim are burned. Either way, the act is not one of Hakrava — it is disposal.

Rabbi Abba responds: Dilma Le-ibbud — perhaps it simply means you destroy it. The Shirayim cannot be eaten, cannot be offered, so you destroy them. The Gemara mocks this answer — Achichu Alei — asking: Ve-chi Yesh Lecha Davar She-karev Le-ibbud? Is there any case where something is Lechatchila brought specifically to be destroyed? Yet this objection is itself puzzling, because the parallel to Parim Hanisrafim — where the blood is offered inside, portions burned on the Mizbeach, and the remaining meat destroyed — seems a reasonable comparison. Nevertheless, the Gemara treats it as an anomalous category.

### Bagegel/Bameizid

The position of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon thus creates a genuinely unusual structure: the Kometz is offered on the Mizbeach as normal, while the Shirayim occupy a kind of limbo — they may not be eaten, they may not be offered, and the only resolution is destruction. This is, as noted, the core tension his position occupies.

### Philosophy

The Gemara then cites a Beraisa attributed to the father of Rabbi Avin: Kol Minchas Kohen Kalil Tihyeh Lo Se'achel — every Mincha of a Kohen shall be Kalil, shall be complete, it shall not be eaten. This pasuk in Tzav comes immediately after the Torah makes explicit what is done with the Minchas Chavitin of the Kohen Gadol — half brought in the morning, half in the afternoon — and the Torah states there Chok Olam L'Hashem Kalil Tuktar, burn it all. Then follows the general statement: V'chol Minchas Kohen Kalil Tihyeh Lo Se'achel.

The key observation is that the general pasuk does not use the language Kalil Tuktar — fully burn it — but only Kalil Tihyeh Lo Se'achel: it shall be Kalil, it shall not be eaten. The Beraisa notes: L'achila Hikishtih V'lo L'davar Acher — the pasuk equates it to eating, and nothing else. It says do not eat it, but it does not explicitly command burning it fully. This is the textual basis from which Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon derives his middle position. He holds that a Kmitza is taken based on the earlier pasuk; the Shirayim cannot be eaten because of Lo Se'achel; they need not be burned as a full offering because the pasuk does not say Kalil Tuktar; and therefore they are destroyed. The prohibition is against eating — and nothing more can be derived from the text.

### Position Statement

Mai Ka'amar — what exactly is Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon saying through this pasuk? Amar Abaye Hachi Ka'amar — Abaye explains the reading as follows: the pasuk Kol Minchas Kohen Lo Se'achel addresses the Chovato, the obligatory Mincha — do not eat it — while Kalil Tihyeh addresses the Nedavaso, the free-will Mincha — burn it fully. The free-will Mincha, like an Olah, is fully burned; the obligatory Minchas Chotei is not eaten but also not burned as a full offering — its Shirayim are destroyed on the floor.

Rashi and Tosafot both note the derivation's internal logic: if the Torah wanted only to say "burn it fully," it would have been sufficient to say so without adding Lo Se'achel — of course you are not eating something that is fully burned. The redundancy teaches that there are two distinct categories: one that is burned fully (the Minchas Nedava) and one that is neither eaten nor burned fully (the Minchas Chotei), with the remainder destroyed.

Rava objects: Sakina Charifa Mafska Krai — a sharp knife that divides the pasuk? You are taking half the pasuk as addressing the Minchas Chova and the other half as addressing the Minchas Nedava. Yet the objection is immediately puzzling, because Rava himself proceeds to do the exact same thing. Ela Amar Rava — rather, says Rava: Kol Minchas Kohen Kalil Tihyeh addresses the Nedavaso, burn it fully; Lo Se'achel addresses the Chovaso, do not eat it — but also do not burn it. As Rashi and Tosafot observe, the only difference between Abaye and Rava is the order in which the pasuk is read: Abaye reads it in reverse (Chovah then Nedava), while Rava reads it in the natural forward sequence. The substantive halakhic positions are identical.

V'eipoich Ana — the Gemara raises the possibility of reversing the assignments: perhaps it is the Minchas Chotei that is burned fully and the Minchas Nedava whose Shirayim are destroyed. The Gemara responds that it is more sensible to say the Nedava is compared to the Minchas Chavitin: Mistavra Nedavaso Hvei L'ribuyei, the free-will Mincha should be equated with the Chavitin because Shekein Tadira — both are recurring (the Nedava can come at any time), Lo Choti — neither comes for a cheit, and Basim Reichei — both have a pleasing odor because both contain oil, whereas the Minchas Chotei has no oil, and the phrase Reiach Nichoach is never applied to the Minchas Chotei, reflecting not only the absence of oil but the fact that it is not framed as a positive offering.

### Beit Hashen Debate

The Gemara raises the counter-argument: Aderaba — perhaps the obligatory Minchas Chotei should be the one compared to the Chavitin, since Shekein Isaron — both are limited to one Isaron of flour, unlike the Minchas Nedava which may be larger, and Chovah — both are obligatory. The Gemara responds: Hanei Nefishan — the points of similarity with the Nedava are more numerous (three versus two), and therefore we conclude that it is the free-will Mincha that is burned fully while the Minchas Chotei's Shirayim are handled differently.

It is worth noting that this entire analysis belongs to Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon. The Chachamim hold there is simply no difference — both the Minchas Chotei and the Minchas Nedava of a Kohen are fully burned in the same manner. The more nuanced and arguably more persuasive positions are those of Rabbi Shimon and his son, who recognize that a Minchas Chotei, which is structurally parallel to a Chatas, should at least preserve the Kmitza structure that defines that category.

---

## R. Elazar Position

### Leibbud Defense

The Gemara then asks: V'rabbanan Hai Kol Minchas Kohen Kalil Tihyeh Lo Se'achel — if the Chachamim do not split this pasuk to address two different types of Mincha, what do they do with it? Miba'u Lei Lachada Tanya — they use it for a different teaching entirely. The Beraisa states: Ain Li Ela Elyonah B'kalil Taktir V'tachtonah B'lo Se'achel — from the earlier texts alone, I know only two separate things: the Minchas Chavitin has a positive commandment to be fully burned (Kalil Taktir), while the general Minchas Kohen has a negative prohibition against eating (Lo Se'achel). But I do not yet know whether each prohibition extends to the other case: does the Minchas Chavitin also carry a Lav against eating, and does the general Minchas Kohen also carry a positive Mitzvah to fully burn it?

Minayin Liten Es Ha'amur Shel Zeh Be-zeh V'es Ha'amur Shel Zeh Be-zeh — how do I know to apply the content of each pasuk to the other?

### Kalil Tihyeh

Talmud Lomar Kalil Kalil Le-gezeirah Shavah — the word Kalil appears in both places, in the context of the Minchas Chavitin (Kalil Tuktar) and in the context of the general Minchas Kohen (Kalil Tihyeh). Through this Gezeirah Shavah: Mah Lalan B'kalil Taktir Af Kan B'kalil Taktir — just as by the Minchas Chavitin there is a positive Mitzvah to fully burn it, so too for every Minchas Kohen there is a positive Mitzvah to fully burn it. U'mah Kan Liten Lo Sa'aseh Achilaso Af Lalan Liten Lo Sa'aseh Achilaso — and just as by a general Minchas Kohen there is a negative prohibition against eating it, so too by the Minchas Chavitin. Rather than using the pasuk to distinguish between two categories of Mincha — as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon does — the Chachamim use it to unify all Minchos of a Kohen, establishing both a positive obligation to fully burn and a negative prohibition to eat, for every case.

---

## Chachamim Position

### Gezeirah Shavah

Ba'ei Ravina — Ravina raises a question: Kohen She-achal Min Ha-imurin Mahu? A Kohen who eats from the Imurin — the portions burned on the Mizbeach — what is the law? The question is not about the Lav of Zarut, which applies to a non-Kohen who eats Kodshim; Ravina is asking something different. Regarding the Lav de-Zarut — Lo Kamibaya Li — that is obvious, because even though he is a Kohen, vis-à-vis things that are burned on the Mizbeach he is considered a Zar, a foreigner with no right to eat them. Ki Kamibaya Li Lav D'chalil Tihyeh — the question is whether there is a separate, generalized Lav derived from Kalil Tihyeh Lo Se'achel. Does that prohibition extend beyond the context of a Minchas Kohen to anything that is designated to be fully burned on the Mizbeach? Tosafot notes that the question brackets the issue of Me'ilah entirely, focusing specifically on this additional Lav.

### Positive/Negative

Rav Aron responds to Ravina: Ta Shema D'tanya — come hear, for a Beraisa teaches: Rabbi Eliezer Omer Kol Shehu B'chalil Tihyeh Liten Lo Ta'aseh Al Achilato — Rabbi Eliezer says that anything governed by the rule of Kalil Tihyeh carries a negative prohibition against eating it. Therefore, if a Kohen eats from things that are to be fully burned on the Mizbeach, he transgresses this Lav, beyond the transgression of Zarut. What emerges from Rabbi Eliezer's position is that the prohibition of Lo Se'achel is not confined to the Minchas Kohen specifically but extends to any item governed by the principle of Kalil — anything that shall be wholly burned. Tosafot has a broader discussion reconciling this with other Gemaras that seem to limit the transgression of Zarut to items that a Kohen is himself permitted to eat; but in any case, what Rabbi Eliezer's ruling establishes here is the existence of this generalized Lav.

---

## Imurim Question

### Ravina's Query

The Mishnah presents two contrasting categories. Minchas Kohanim U'minchas Kohen Mashiach U'minchas Nesachim L'mizbeach — the Mincha of an ordinary Kohen, the Minchas Chavitin of the Kohen Gadol, and the Minchas Nesachim that accompanies a free-will animal Korban — all of these go entirely to the Mizbeach. V'ein Bahem L'kohanim — the Kohanim receive nothing from them. U'vaze Yafe Ko'ach Mizbeach Mikoach Kohanim — in this category, the Mizbeach has the greater portion over the Kohanim.

The Gemara immediately asks: V'tu Leika? Are there no other things that go entirely to the Mizbeach? V'ha'ika Olah — what about an Olah? The answer: Ika Or L'kohanim — the Olah is not fully to the Mizbeach; the Kohanim receive the hide. V'ha'ika Olat Ha'of — what about a bird Olah, which goes entirely on the Mizbeach with no hide to distribute? The answer: Ika Mor'ah V'notzah — the crop and feathers are cut out and thrown beside the Mizbeach, so it does not all go on the fire. V'ha'ika Nesachim — what about the wine of Nesachim, which goes entirely to the Mizbeach? L'shitin Azli — the wine goes into the caverns or underground channels; it does not burn on the Mizbeach itself.

### R. Eliezer Rule

U'mai Baze — why then does the Mishnah emphasize that these are the unique cases? L'afukei Mi'd'Shmuel — to exclude the opinion of Shmuel. D'amar Shmuel Ha-minadev Yayin Meivi U-mezalfo Gavye Ishim — Shmuel holds that if one donates wine to the Mizbeach, he sprinkles it directly on the fire. If Shmuel were correct, donated wine would constitute another category of something burned fully on the Mizbeach. The Mishnah, read as covering all cases in the world of Korbanos rather than being limited to the context of Minchos alone, excludes this position. Kamashma Lan D'le-shitin Azlei — only the items enumerated in the Mishnah go fully on the Mizbeach; donated wine is not one of them. It goes into the Shitin, like all wine of Nesachim.

### Abaye/Rava

Having excluded one position of Shmuel, the Gemara notes that the Mishnah also supports a different position of his. Misayei Lei L'Shmuel D'amar Shmuel Ha-minadev Shemen Komtzo Ve-shiyaro Ne'echalin — Shmuel holds that if one donates oil to the Mizbeach, one performs a Kmitza on the oil and the remainder is eaten by the Kohanim, treating donated oil like a Mincha. If the halakha were that donated oil is burned entirely on the Mizbeach, then it would constitute an additional case of something fully going to the Mizbeach, and the Mishnah's enumeration would be incomplete. Since the Mishnah presents its list as exhaustive — at least within the domain of edible Kodshim — and donated oil is not on the list, this supports Shmuel's position that donated oil undergoes a Kmitza-like process and the remainder goes to the Kohanim.

The entire phenomenon is remarkable: the Torah lists specific Korbanos one may bring, and the intuition is that one cannot simply ad-lib an offering of shemen. Yet the sugya establishes not only that one can donate oil, but that such a donation is treated as a quasi-Mincha, with a Kmitza performed on oil — a striking and unusual procedure.

### All to Altar

The Mishnah then presents the contrasting category: Shtei Halechem V'lechem Hapanim Ne'echalin L'kohanim V'ein Bahem L'mizbeach — the two loaves of Shavuot and the Lechem Hapanim of every Shabbos are eaten entirely by the Kohanim, and nothing from them goes to the Mizbeach. For the Shtei Halechem, the Mizbeach receives the blood of the Shenei Kivshei Atzeret — the two lambs — but none of the bread itself, since it is Chametz and Chametz cannot be placed on the Mizbeach. For the Lechem Hapanim, the Mizbeach receives the Levona on the Shulchan, but none of the bread itself. U'vaze Yafe Ko'ach Hakohanim Mikoach Hamizbeach — in this case the Kohanim have the greater portion over the Mizbeach.

The Gemara asks: V'tu Leika? Are these the only cases where the Kohanim receive everything? V'ha'ika Chatas Ha'of — a bird Chatas is eaten entirely by the Kohanim, with no Eimurim going to the Mizbeach. The answer: Amar Ika Dama — the blood is placed on the Mizbeach, even if in a trivial amount. V'ha'ika Log Shemen Shel Metzora — the log of oil of the Metzora is largely consumed by the Kohanim, yet Ika Matnosav — there are sprinklings from that oil directed toward the Kodesh Kodashim, and additional applications to the ear, thumb, and toe of the Metzora, so the full amount does not go to the Kohen.

U'mai Bazu — why then does the Mishnah enumerate these as special cases? L'afukei Mi-man D'amar Shtei Halechem Haba'os Bifnei Atzman Li-sreifa Azlan — there is an opinion that if the Shenei Kivshei Atzeret, the lambs that accompany the Shtei Halechem, cannot be brought, the loaves themselves are burned, since without the lambs there is no mechanism to offer the loaves and they cannot go on the Mizbeach as Chametz. The Mishnah excludes this view: Kamashma Lan D'bazu Yafeh Ko'ach Kohanim L'olam — in this category, the Kohanim always receive the Shtei Halechem fully, even in the absence of the lambs. What exactly constitutes the act of Hakrava in that case is not fully resolved, but the Mishnah's ruling is read to cover even that unusual circumstance, somewhat reminiscent of Bikkurim, where there is no burning on the Mizbeach — only a waving and declaration — and yet it is considered a valid act of Hakrava.

---

## R. Elazar Position (II)

### All to Kohanim

The next Mishnah introduces a new topic: Kol Haminchot Hana'asot B'kli Te'unot Shalosh Matanot Shemen — every Mincha made in a vessel requires three applications of oil. The Mishnah lists them in reverse order: Yetzika, pouring or anointing; U'velila, mixing; and U'matan Shemen Bakli Kodem La'asiyatan, placing oil in the vessel before making it. Logically the sequence is: first you put oil in the vessel, then you mix the flour with the oil, then you drizzle oil on top — a sequence analogous to preparing a recipe, with the pan oiled first, the dough mixed, and the finished product dressed.

### Exhaustive List

The Mishnah then addresses a distinction in how oil is applied to two types of baked offerings. Hachallos Te'unot Belila — the Challos, referring here to the Challos of the Ma'afeh Tanur, the oven-baked Mincha described in the Torah as Challos Matzot Belulot Bashemen, require mixing with oil. V'harkikin Meshicha — the Rekikin, the wafers, described in the Torah as Rkikei Matzot Meshuchim Bashemen, require anointing with oil. Keitzad Moshchan — how does one anoint them? K'min Kai — in the shape of a Greek chi, that is, an X-shaped mark across the wafer.

The Mishnah adds: Bolelan — you mix them with oil. This is the position of Rabbi, who understands, as Rashi explains, that after the Challos are baked and hardened, you break them up and mix them again with oil. Vachachamim Omrim Solet — the Chachamim hold you mix with oil at the flour stage, before baking. This dispute concerns whether the second application of oil to the Challos occurs before or after baking — a question whose full elaboration is reserved for subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Menachot 75

## Four Types Menachot

### Overview & Categories

The Mishna on Daf Ayin-Daled Amud Bet describes the process by which Minchos are prepared. It states that all Minchos are first made by placing oil in the vessel, then adding flour and mixing it with oil, and finally performing Yetzikah — pouring oil on afterwards. The Gemara opens by noting that this applies specifically to Minchos that are made in a vessel, and proceeds to ask: what does that qualifier exclude?

### Minchat Soles

Rav Pappa answers that it excludes the Minchat Ma'afeh Tanur — the oven-baked Mincha. This is, on its face, a puzzling answer, and the Meforshim struggle with it. One might object on two grounds: first, the Minchat Ma'afeh Tanur does include oil according to the Torah, so it is not obviously different from the other Minchos in this respect; second, an oven is itself a vessel, so the criterion of "made in a vessel" would seem to apply equally to it. Tosafot addresses this by suggesting that perhaps according to this opinion the oven was not considered a Kli Shareis — but even so, that does not readily explain how the Mishna's language of "made in a vessel" succeeds in excluding it.

One of the Meforshim of the Rambam offers a different approach: when the Mishna states that "all Minchos made in a vessel" follow these three stages, the implication is that some things do not follow this rule — even if they technically are made in a vessel. The difficulty with this reading is obvious: if the thing we are excluding meets the stated criterion, the exclusion is logically strained. Rather than forcing this interpretation, the more productive approach is simply to understand what the Mishna is telling us affirmatively: these three oil stages — oil first in the vessel, then flour mixed with oil, then oil poured on afterwards — apply to the Minchat Marcheshes, Minchat Machvas, and Minchat Soles, but not to the Minchat Ma'afeh Tanur. The specific stage that does not apply to the oven-baked Mincha is, as we shall see, the final pouring of oil.

### Machvas & Marcheshes

Before turning to the Gemara's derivation, it is worth clarifying the four types of Minchos presented in Vayikra. The first is the Minchat Soles — simply flour and oil, not baked. The Rambam, notably, does not include water in the Minchat Soles, which makes sense: if one does not bake it, there is no mechanism by which it could become Chametz, and so no need for water to be present. The resulting product is essentially a raw dough of flour and oil; the Kohanim would eat the remainder after the Kometz is taken. The second and third types are the Machvas and Marcheshes — shallow and deep frying pans respectively. These do include water, because they do have the halakhic possibility of becoming Chametz, and the flour and oil and water mixture is then fried in one of the two pans. The fourth type is the Ma'afeh Tanur — flour, oil, and water are combined into a dough and baked in an oven. It is this last type that does not follow the same three oil stages as the others.

### Ma'afeh Tanur Offering

The Gemara cites a Tanna DeVei: the Braita opens by quoting the verse regarding the Marcheshes — "Soles bashamen te'aseh" — and derives from the phrase "bashamen" that oil is first placed in the vessel before the flour. Then, via a Gezeira Shava on the word "Korbanacha" — which appears both by the Machvas (Pasuk Hey) and by the Marcheshes (Pasuk Zayin) — the Gemara links the two: just as the Marcheshes requires oil to be placed in the vessel first, so too the Machvas; and just as the Machvas requires Yetzikah and Belilah — pouring and mixing — so too the Marcheshes.

To understand where the Yetzikah and Belilah come from by the Machvas, one must read Pesukim Hey and Vav together. Pasuk Hey says "Solet blulah bashamen" — the flour is mixed with oil. Pasuk Vav then says "Patot otah pitim, v'yatzakta aleihem shemen" — break it into pieces and pour oil over them. So by the Machvas: you mix the flour with oil (and water, since Chametz and Matzah are relevant), fry the dough, break it into pieces afterwards, and then pour oil on the broken pieces. From the Marcheshes: oil is already in the vessel before the flour goes in. Combining the two descriptions, one derives all three stages: (1) oil in the vessel first, (2) flour added and mixed with oil, and (3) oil poured on afterwards.

The Gemara will proceed to extend these three stages to the Minchat Soles as well — even though there is no frying or baking involved — and to exclude the oven-baked Mincha from the third stage. The precise reasoning for that exclusion will become clear as the discussion of the Minchat Ma'afeh unfolds.

---

## Three Oil Stages

### Pesukim Analysis

The Mishna and the subsequent Gemara discussion center on a Machloket between Rabbi (Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi) and the Chachamim concerning when the Belilah — the primary mixing of oil — takes place by the oven-baked Mincha.

The Braita states: "Solet belulah — melamed shenivelelet solet." The Chachamim understand this to mean that the flour itself is mixed with oil: at the flour stage, before any baking, one adds oil to the flour, mixes it together thoroughly (along with water, to enable the possibility of Chametz), kneads it, bakes it, breaks the baked product into pieces, and then performs the final pouring of oil. Rabbi, however, disputes this. He reads the operative phrase not from the Machvas but from the Ma'afeh Tanur, where the Torah says "chalot matzot belulot bashamen" — baked loaves mixed with oil. From this Rabbi derives that the Belilah, the serious mixing with oil, is performed on the baked product, not the flour. His view of the process is therefore: first place oil in the vessel, then add flour with water only (no additional oil at the flour stage), knead it, bake it, break it into pieces, and only then — once the loaves are broken — mix them thoroughly with a large quantity of oil, and subsequently pour the remaining oil on top before performing the Kemitza.

It is noted that this is a striking position, since the plain reading of the verse by the Machvas — "solet blulah bashamen," flour mixed with oil — seems to describe the flour stage, not the baked stage. Rabbi is reading the paradigm of the oven-baked Mincha back into the general description. The Tosefta adds that in the end Rabbi retracted his position and agreed with the Chachamim.

### Oil Stages Explained

The Chachamim respond to Rabbi with a counter-example from the Todah offering: "Vehalo lachmei Todah nemar bahen chalot" — by the bread of the Todah the Torah also uses the language of "chalot" mixed with oil, "ve'i efshar levololan keshehen chalot" — yet it is impossible to mix them after they are already baked.

The Gemara clarifies why: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak explains that the Todah brings forty loaves total, and twenty of those loaves receive only a Revi'is of oil — approximately three and a half ounces — split among them. Once loaves are baked they are highly absorbent, and three and a half ounces of oil distributed across twenty loaves cannot create any meaningful or coherent mixing. "Heich mislachlachas" — there is simply no way it would work. The oil must therefore have been added at the flour stage. This dismantles Rabbi's argument: you cannot use the language of "chalot belulot" to prove that mixing occurs after baking, because the very case that uses that language — the Todah — demonstrates that post-baking mixing is practically impossible.

### Combining Sources

Following the Chachamim's position, the Gemara sets out the proper procedure for the Machvas and Marcheshes: as described by the Braita cited earlier, the כיצד עושה is as follows. One first places oil in the vessel, adds flour, then adds more oil to the flour. Water is also added — though not mentioned explicitly in the Torah, it is required to create the possibility of Chametz versus Matzah. The dough is kneaded, then fried (on the flat pan or deep pan respectively). After frying, the product is broken into pieces using the Pesisa, and finally oil is poured on top. It is from this complete procedure that the three stages are drawn and applied to the Minchat Soles as well — with the modification that for the Soles there is no baking or frying stage, so the Rambam's view that water was not added there (and thus no possibility of Chametz arose) fits naturally.

The standard amount is one Issaron of flour — roughly equivalent to a five-pound bag — and one Log of oil, which is approximately fourteen ounces (four times a Revi'is, which is roughly three and a half ounces, the standard measure for a Kiddush cup on Shabbat). According to the Chachamim, that oil goes into the flour stage, not into a post-baking mixing, making Rabbi's position the more difficult one practically as well as textually.

---

## Rabbi vs. Chachamim

### Rabbi's Position

Returning to the Ma'afeh Tanur, the oven-baked Mincha, the Gemara clarifies the difference between its two forms. The Torah says: "Solet challos matzot belulot bashamen, u'rekikei matzot meshuchim bashamen" — either loaves mixed with oil, or wafers anointed with oil. The Gemara understands this as establishing two fundamentally different treatments of oil. The Challos — the loaves — have oil incorporated into the dough at the flour stage, just as by the Machvas and Marcheshes, and they are then baked. The Rekikin — the wafers — are baked simply from a dough of flour and water, with no oil added beforehand, and only after they come out of the oven is oil applied to them. The difference in terminology is precise: Belilah, mixing, applies to the Challos; Meshichah, anointing, applies to the Rekikin.

This is precisely why the Ma'afeh Tanur does not follow the three-stage model of the other Minchos. For the other Minchos, oil appears at all three stages — first in the vessel, then mixed with the flour, then poured on after frying or baking. For the Ma'afeh Tanur, the Torah specifies two distinct and mutually exclusive treatments: the Challos get their oil during mixing, the Rekikin get their oil afterwards. The Gemara therefore concludes: "Challos te'unos belilah, ve'rekikin meshichah" — Challos require the mixing, Rekikin require the anointing.

### Todah Problem

The Braita then raises what might seem like a logical argument: since the Challos require Belilah, and the Rekikin require Meshichah, could one not argue by Kal VaChomer that the Rekikin — which already get anointed with oil at the end — should also receive oil at the mixing stage? After all, if the Challos, which do not get anointed, nevertheless receive mixed oil, surely the Rekikin, which do get anointed, should also receive oil at mixing? The Torah answers by specifying "Challos belulos velo rekikin belulin" — only the Challos are mixed. Similarly, the reverse Kal VaChomer: perhaps the Challos, which already get mixed, should also get the post-baking anointing? The Torah answers: "Rekikin meshuchim velo challos meshuchos" — only the Rekikin are anointed.

Rava then provides the justification for why we do not simply learn them from one another — as we do with the Machvas and Marcheshes — and require both treatments for both. He employs a "lo lishtamit kra" argument: the verse never, in any context, refers to "Challos meshuchos" or "Rekikin belulin." It only ever specifies Challos with Belilah and Rekikin with Meshichah. Since the Torah consistently maintains this distinction and never inverts it, we should understand the exclusive assignment as intentional.

This is, however, a notably weak form of argument from silence. The strength of a lo lishtamit argument depends on whether one would have expected the alternative to have been stated somewhere had it been true. In this case, the Torah discusses the Ma'afeh Tanur only once, and by analogy we do apply Machvas to Marcheshes even though neither verse states the other's rule explicitly. The argument from silence here thus carries considerably less logical force than it might in other contexts — a point the Gemara implicitly acknowledges by framing it as Rava's response, rather than a direct textual derivation.

### Process Explained

Having established that the Rekikin receive Meshichah rather than Belilah, the Gemara asks: "Keitzad moshchan?" — how exactly does one anoint them? The answer is "k'min ki" — in the shape of a Chi. Rav Kahana explains this means k'min ki Yevani — the Greek letter Chi, which is an X. After this anointing, whatever oil remains from the Log is eaten as Shirayim.

It is worth noting that Rashi and Tosafot display some uncertainty about the exact shape. Tosafot records that in one version of Rashi's commentary on Chumash the shape is described as a Tet, and in another as a Gimmel — though Tosafot correctly notes neither is quite right, while acknowledging that a Gimmel, with its diagonal stroke and attached line, comes closest among Hebrew letters to approximating an X. The Rambam, however, clearly identifies the pattern as an X.

---

## Challos vs. Rekikin

### Measurements

The Gemara now turns to a case, formulated under Rabbi Shimon's assumption that a Ma'afeh Tanur offering may be brought as half Challos and half Rekikin. A Braita states: if one brings a Mincha that is half Challos and half Rekikin, one brings a Log of oil and divides it in two. Half — approximately seven ounces — goes toward the Challos, where it is mixed into the dough at the flour stage. The other half goes toward the Rekikin, which are baked first as plain dough and then anointed afterwards.

However, the Braita adds a further detail: "U'mosheach es ha'rekik pnei kulo" — when anointing the Rekikin, one anoints the full outer surface of the loaf. After performing this anointing, the remaining oil — and there will be a significant amount remaining if one has seven ounces and is merely coating the surface — is returned to the Challos. This means the Rekikin must be processed first, so that whatever oil is left over can be folded back into the Challos dough before baking.

### Two Baked Types

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon disagrees. He holds that the anointing is done "k'min ki" — in the X-pattern only — and the remaining oil is not returned to the Challos but rather eaten by the Kohanim. This is a striking position: normally everything in the Mincha is understood to be incorporated into the final product. Rabbi Shimon apparently holds that where the modality of oil application is defined as anointing — Meshichah — rather than mixing, the oil that is not absorbed into the wafer itself does not need to be incorporated into the Mincha as a whole. It is analogous, he suggests, to the Log shemen of the Metzora, which is brought separately and partially eaten rather than fully absorbed. The majority view, by contrast, requires the full Log to be consumed within the Mincha offering, whether by repeated anointing until the oil is exhausted, or by return to the Challos.

A subsequent Braita addresses the case of bringing Rekikin alone, without any Challos. Here one has a full Log of oil — fourteen ounces — and one is applying it only through anointing. The first opinion holds that one anoints and anoints again repeatedly until the entire Log is absorbed: "Umoshchan v'chozer umoshchan ad she'yichleh kol hashemen she'be'log." Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon repeats his position: make a single X, and the remainder is eaten by the Kohanim.

---

## Ptita Requirement

### Anointing Method

The next Mishna states: "Kol haMinchos hana'asos b'kli te'unos Pesisa" — all Minchos made in a vessel require breaking into pieces. This rule applies broadly: the Machvas, Marcheshes, and oven-baked Minchos all require Pesisa, though not the Minchat Soles in the usual sense, since it is a raw dough and the verse "patot otah pitim" does not apply to flour.

### Half-and-Half Mix

The Gemara asks "l'ma'utei mai" — what does this qualifier exclude? Rav Pappa answers: it excludes the Shtei HaLechem and Lechem HaPanim. Neither of these communal offerings requires Pesisa.

The Braita derives the requirement from the verse by the Machvas: "Patot otah pitim — Mincha hi" — it is a Mincha, which might suggest the rule extends to all Minchos, including the Shtei HaLechem and Lechem HaPanim. The word "otah" — "it," in the singular and limiting — restricts the application and excludes certain categories. Similarly, "v'yatzakta aleha shemen — Mincha hi" might have suggested extending the final oil-pouring to the Ma'afeh Tanur; "aleha," "on it," limits it, and "hi" introduces a second restriction.

Two reasons are given for why Pesisa does not apply to the Shtei HaLechem and Lechem HaPanim. First, the primary function of Pesisa is to enable Kemitza — once the Mincha is broken into small pieces, the Kohen can take his three-finger handful. The Shtei HaLechem and Lechem HaPanim do not require Kemitza at all: the Lechem HaPanim has its Levonah burned, and the Shtei HaLechem is accompanied by the Kivsei Atzeres. Second, these are communal offerings and are thus outside the framework of the individual Mincha described in Parshat Vayikra. It is the combination of both factors — no Kemitza and communal status — that removes them from the Pesisa requirement. The Omer, by contrast, is also a communal offering but does require Pesisa, because it does require Kemitza.

### Full Rekikin

Rava then addresses the question of why the two rules — Pesisa and the final oil pouring — have different scopes. Pesisa extends to the Ma'afeh Tanur; the final oil-pouring does not. Why does the single word "otah" exclude only the Shtei HaLechem and Lechem HaPanim from Pesisa, while the oil rule requires two exclusionary terms ("aleha" and "hi") to exclude the Ma'afeh Tanur?

Rava's answer is that the Ma'afeh Tanur has two components — Challos and Rekikin — and thus it needs two limiting words to exclude both of them from the general rule of post-baking oil pouring. The Shtei HaLechem and Lechem HaPanim, being single categories, need only one limiting word to exclude them from Pesisa. Since the Torah itself describes the oil of the Ma'afeh Tanur differently for Challos and Rekikin, we do not derive the oil stages of the Ma'afeh Tanur from the Machvas and Marcheshes — we accept the Torah's own account of how oil is applied there.

---

## Bracha on Menachot

### Ptita Derivation

The next Mishna describes the method of Pesisa — the breaking into pieces — for different categories of Mincha. For a Minchat Yisrael — brought by a non-Kohen — the procedure is: "Kofel echad l'shnayim v'shnayim l'arba" — fold it once in half, then fold that in half again, producing four sections, and then "mavdil" — separate the pieces. The baked or fried product, whether it resembles something like a flat bread or a pita, is folded into quarters and then the quarters are pulled apart.

### Folding Process

For a Minchat Kohanim, one folds it in the same manner — one fold then another, making four — but one does not actually separate the pieces. Since a Minchat Kohanim is burned entirely on the Mizbe'ach and no Kemitza is taken, there is no practical need to achieve discrete pieces. Yet the Chachamim hold that one still performs the folding, without the final separation.

### Kohanim Offerings

The Mishna states that for the Minchat Kohen Gadol — the Chavitin brought half in the morning and half in the afternoon — "lo haya mekapla," he would not fold it at all, according to the first position. The Gemara, however, reconciles this with a Braita that says you do fold the Minchat Kohen Gadol, by attributing different meanings to each source. Rava explains: "Eino mekapel l'arba, aval mekapel l'shnayim" — the Mishna means he does not fold it into four, but he does fold it once into two. This is consistent with the Torah's description of the Kohen Gadol's Mincha as "tufinei minchat pitim" — the word "pitim" appears once, not the fuller phrase "patot otah pitim" which implies a double fold. One instance of "pitim" yields one fold.

### Rabbi Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with the Chachamim on two counts. First, he holds that the Minchat Kohanim and Minchat Kohen Gadol require no Pesisa whatsoever: "Ein bahem ptita, mipnei she'ein bahem kmitza" — because there is no Kemitza, there is no Pesisa. "V'chol she'ein ba kmitza ein bahem ptita." Second, he holds that for those Minchos that do require Pesisa, the pieces should be broken down to the size of a Kezayit — olive-sized — rather than merely folded into quarters. At olive-size, one can readily perform Kemitza from the pieces.

Rabbi Shimon's two positions are internally consistent: the entire logic of Pesisa is to enable Kemitza. Therefore, if Kemitza is absent, Pesisa is absent entirely; and where Kemitza is performed, the pieces must be small enough to actually allow it. The Chachamim, by contrast, hold that Pesisa carries independent significance beyond merely enabling Kemitza — otherwise, why require it for the Minchat Kohanim with only folding and no separation?

---

## Deriving Pesisa Requirem…

### Hamotzi Source

The Gemara derives the proper method of Pesisa from the verse "patot otah pitim." The word "pitim" might have implied breaking each piece again — pieces of pieces. The word "otah" — "it," referring to the original — limits this: you break the original once into pieces, but you do not then take those pieces and break them again. "V'lo ptiteha l'pitim" — do not break the pieces into further pieces.

At the same time, "pitim" — the plural — implies more than just two pieces. So the derivation runs: "Yachol l'shnayim" — maybe just two? No, "pitim" implies more. "Yachol ya'asenah perurin" — maybe crumbs, tiny fragments? No, "otah" requires that the original integrity be maintained. The result is the procedure described in the Mishna: the Minchat Yisrael is folded into halves and then quarters — two folds, producing four sections.

### Abaye Challenge

The Braita then states that the Minchat Kohanim and Minchat Kohen Gadol were folded. The Mishna appears to say the Kohen Gadol did not fold at all. As Rava resolves: the Mishna means not folded into four; the Braita means he did fold into two. Both sources are compatible once we understand that the Mishna denies only the full four-fold process, not all folding.

This reconciliation highlights the underlying principle: the Chachamim see folding as possessing value independent of Kemitza — since even the Minchat Kohanim, where there is no Kemitza and no separation, involves folding. Rabbi Shimon, who sees Pesisa as exclusively instrumental to Kemitza, would have no use for any folding in a Minchat Kohanim.

---

## Bread Crumbs & Blessings…

### Crumb Status

Rav Yosef now introduces a ruling that connects directly to contemporary Halacha. He states: "Hai chavitza d'it beh perurin kezayit, mivarchinan aleha hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz" — a Chavitza that contains crumbs each of which is a Kezayit, one recites Hamotzi over it. If the crumbs are smaller than a Kezayit, one recites Borei minei mezonot.

The Chavitza requires clarification. Rashi understands it as a cooked or baked product containing bread crumbs. Tosafot, however, argues from the subsequent Gemara that the Chavitza was not rebaked or recooked — because rebaking could independently transform the Bracha — and that the later Gemara comparison to the broken Mincha pieces mixed with oil makes clear that the Chavitza is bread crumbs combined with honey or oil without further cooking. We proceed with Tosafot's understanding: it is crumbs embedded in a honey or oil mixture, not rebaked.

The practical analog is familiar: croutons or bread crumbs mixed into other ingredients. What Bracha does one recite? Rav Yosef's answer is that it depends on the size of the crumbs: Kezayit-sized crumbs yield Hamotzi; smaller crumbs yield Mezonot.

### Final Bracha Rule

Rav Yosef derives this principle from a Braita. The Braita describes someone bringing Minchos in Yerushalayim: upon beginning the offering, he says "Baruch shehecheyanu v'kiyemanu v'higi'anu lazman hazeh." The mere fact that a Shehecheyanu is recited over the bringing of a Korban is itself arresting — it is almost never discussed in this context. Whether it is the Yisrael who owns the Korban or the Kohen who performs the service is a matter of debate. Rashi offers two possibilities. Tosafot argues for the Kohen, noting that an individual Kohen, serving on rotation, would typically serve only twice a year, making each occasion genuinely significant in a seasonal, cyclical way — precisely the type of event over which Shehecheyanu is appropriate.

The Braita continues: when he then takes the Mincha pieces to eat them — "natlan v'achlan" — he recites Hamotzi. This clearly refers to the Kohen eating his portion, since only the Kohen eats the Minchos. And what do we know about those Minchos? From the earlier Mishna: "V'chulan potasim kezayis" — following the view that pieces can be as small as a Kezayit. So we have little pieces of baked bread, each at least a Kezayit, mixed with oil — and over these the Kohen makes Hamotzi. From this Rav Yosef infers the general rule about the Chavitza.

---

## Mincha Crumbs & Motzi Br…

### Braita on Blessed Offering

Abaye, however, challenges Rav Yosef's derivation. He argues that the source cannot be relied upon because of the opinion of the Tanna of the School of Rabbi Yishmael, not mentioned in our Mishna, who holds that the Pesisa process goes far further — pieces are broken down until they return essentially to flour: "Mefarchan ad shemachziran lesoltan." If we follow that view, the resulting material would no longer be recognizable bread, and one might then ask whether the Kohen would recite Hamotzi on it at all. If the answer were no, then Rav Yosef cannot cite the Kohen's Hamotzi as a reliable source for the minimum crumb-size principle.

### Abaye's Crumb-Size Question

Abaye then suggests: perhaps according to the Tanna of the School of Rabbi Yishmael, the Kohen indeed would not recite Hamotzi on such thoroughly pulverized material. The Gemara entertains this possibility in order to sharpen the question.

### Combined Crumbs Retain Motzi

To rebut the suggestion that Hamotzi cannot be recited on very small crumbs, the Gemara cites a Braita: "Liket mikulan kezayit v'achalo" — if one gathered from all the crumbs a Kezayit and ate it, then if it was Chametz on Pesach, one incurs Karet; and if it was Matzah on Pesach, one fulfills one's obligation. Tosafot understands this Braita as referring to the five grain species generally — crumbs from Chametz that are gathered to a Kezayit-total retain their identity as Chametz, and similarly Matzah crumbs gathered to a Kezayit fulfill the Mitzvah. The implication is that even small individual crumbs, when combined, are still considered bread for halakhic purposes.

### Braita on Chametz & Matzah Crumbs

The Gemara, however, pushes back against this citation. One might say: "Hacha b'mai askinan — b'she'ersan" — perhaps the Braita refers only to the case where the crumbs were re-moistened with water and kneaded back into a single dough — "aisa shleima." In that case, of course they would retain their identity as bread; it would be one unified mass. The Gemara, however, disproves this: the Braita concludes "vehu she'achlan bichdei achilas pras" — the condition is that one ate them within the time-frame of eating a half-loaf. If the crumbs had been reassembled into a single dough, the text would have said "she'achalah" — it, singular — not "she'achlan" — them, plural. The plural form indicates they remained separate crumbs. Therefore, even as separate crumbs, gathering them to a Kezayit retains Hamotzi and fulfills the Matzah obligation.

### Pesika Standard: Shape of Bread

The Gemara then resolves the apparent conflict between Rav Yosef's condition (crumbs must be Kezayit-sized) and the Braita showing that even sub-Kezayit crumbs can retain Hamotzi. Rav Sheshes rules: "Afilu perurin she'ein bahen kezayis" — even crumbs smaller than a Kezayit, one makes Hamotzi over them. Rava then qualifies: "Vehu d'ika toresa denahama alaihu" — only if they still bear the form, the recognizable shape, of bread.

The Gemara harmonizes all the sources: the requirement for a Kezayit applies when the bread crumbs never came from a large loaf to begin with — they were always small units. In such a case, they require Kezayit-size to warrant Hamotzi. But if they came from "lekhem gadol" — a large loaf — they retain Hamotzi even as small crumbs, so long as they still bear the form of bread. The Mincha of the Kohen clearly originated from a larger baked product; therefore, even once broken into tiny pieces with oil mixed in, Hamotzi is recited.

Rava's formulation — "toresa denahama" — is the most practically difficult criterion in the laws of Brachot. The principle is clear in the abstract: it is not enough that a food is made from flour and water; it must look like bread. Crackers and pretzels, made from identical ingredients, do not receive Hamotzi precisely because they fail this criterion. What exactly "looks like bread" means in practice is a major and ongoing question, but the rule itself is anchored here: Hamotzi requires both the correct composition and the recognizable form of bread.

---

---

# Menachot 76

## Rubbings & Poundings

### 300 & 500 Requirement

The daf opens with the Mishnah's statement: *kol hamenachot te'unot shalosh me'ot shifa vachamesh me'ot be'ita* — all of the menachot require 300 rubbings and 500 poundings. These are striking numbers. The rubbings are presumably performed on the wheat kernels in order to loosen the shells and bran, while the poundings — Rashi understands the term *be'ita* as striking with the fist — are performed as part of the physical preparation of the offering. The word *be'ita* is related to the word for kicking with a leg, but Rashi, based on context, applies it to pounding with the fist.

### Tanna Kamma vs. R. Yosi

The Mishnah continues: *shifa u've'ita bechitim* — the rubbing and the pounding were both performed with the wheat. It is not entirely clear how pounding the wheat kernels differs from grinding them; one might have expected the process to involve a millstone rather than a mortar-and-pestle style pounding. The suggestion is that the pounding loosens the grain and prepares it for subsequent processing. Whatever the precise physical mechanics, the Tanna Kamma locates both actions at the stage of the wheat.

### Ten vs. Twelve Loaves

Rabbi Yosi disagrees: *babatze'ik* — it was with the dough. For Rabbi Yosi, the pounding in particular makes considerably more sense as an action performed on dough, since one rolls and pounds dough as a natural part of its preparation. The rubbing of dough is less intuitive but still plausible.

### Alternating Pattern

What is especially striking about this dispute is its epistemological character. Neither the Tanna Kamma nor Rabbi Yosi appears to be basing himself on a *pasuk* or on a first-hand memory of how the procedure was actually performed. They had inherited a tradition — the earlier, apodictic Mishnah statement that all menachot require 300 rubbings and 500 poundings — and they are attempting to reconstruct its context. Was that tradition speaking about the wheat or the dough? That is the question they are debating.

This reflects a broader phenomenon well attested in Mishnaic literature. Scholars have observed that the later Tannaim were frequently the inheritors of earlier, terse Mishnah traditions and that what appears in a Mishnah as a tannaitic dispute is often, in reality, commentary and interpretation of an older, undisputed statement. A clear parallel is the first Mishnah in Gittin, where the global statement about bringing a *get* from *chutz la'aretz* to *eretz yisrael* is followed by several Tannaim each explaining what *chutz* means — each interpreting the original line rather than independently framing a new debate. The same structure is present here: the apodictic statement — 300 rubbings and 500 poundings — was the tradition, and the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosi are each explaining what context that tradition referred to.

### Back & Forth Count

A Braita then explains how one practically maintains the three-to-five ratio of rubbings to poundings. Rather than performing all 300 rubbings followed by all 500 poundings, the practitioner alternates: *shaf achat bo'et shtayim* — one rubbing followed by two poundings; then *shaf shtayim bo'et shalosh* — two rubbings followed by three poundings. In this way, the ratio of three to five is preserved throughout the process. According to the Tanna Kamma, this alternating sequence is how one would loosen the shell and bran from the wheat kernels.

### R. Yosi on Dough

Rabbi Yirmiya raises a question about how to count the rubbings. When one performs a rubbing, the natural motion is back and forth. Does that back-and-forth movement count as one rubbing or as two? — *amtuyei ve'atuyei chad*, back and forth is one, *o dilma amtuyei ve'atuyei trei*, back and forth is two? The Gemara leaves this unresolved: *teiku*. This question recurs in other contexts in the Gemara where actions performed back and forth must be counted a fixed number of times.

### Mixed Approach

The Gemara also raises the question of whether Rabbi Yosi intends to say that the rubbing and pounding were performed *only* with the dough and not at all with the wheat, or whether he agrees that they were also performed with the wheat and is merely adding that they were performed with the dough as well. A Braita resolves this: Rabbi Yosi's repetition of the verbs *shifa u've'ita* in his statement — rather than simply saying "also with the dough" — implies that the rubbing and pounding belonged to the dough alone, not to the wheat.

However, the left-hand column of the standard printed edition notes a different *girsa*: *shifa bechitim u've'ita babatze'ik* — the rubbing is with the wheat, and the pounding is with the dough. A note indicates *vechein mashma baRambam* — this is also the implication of the Rambam. This third reading is arguably the most logically intuitive of all: rubbing is a natural action to perform on wheat kernels to separate the shell, while pounding is a natural action to perform on dough during its preparation. Yet notably, no one derives their position from a *pasuk* or from any remembered practice; all positions are reconstructions of a shared older tradition.

---

## Model Selection Debate

### Paradigm Question

The Mishnah continues: *kol hamenachot ba'ot eser eser chutz milechem hapanim* — all of the menachot come in ten loaves, except for the lechem hapanim, which explicitly comprised twelve loaves arranged in two columns of six on the shulchan, and the chavitei Kohen Gadol — the daily minchat chavitin that the Kohen Gadol brought half in the morning and half in the afternoon — which also come in twelve. This is the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

### R. Yehuda: Ten

Rabbi Meir takes the opposite position: *kulam ba'ot shtem esrei* — all of the menachot come in twelve loaves, except for the chalot Toda and the breads accompanying the Nazir offering, which come in ten. The dispute is, in essence, about which is the general rule and which is the exception: is the paradigm ten loaves with twelve as the anomaly, or is the paradigm twelve with ten as the anomaly?

### Mincha & Toda Comparison

The Gemara establishes first the basis for the chavitei Kohen Gadol being twelve. By the lechem hapanim the Torah uses the word *chok*: *kodesh kodashim hu lo me'ishei Hashem chok olam*. By the chavitei Kohen Gadol it says: *chok olam la-Hashem kalil tuktir*. The shared term *chok* constitutes a gezeirah shavah — *atya chukah chukah millechem hapanim* — from which we derive that just as the lechem hapanim came in twelve, so too the chavitei Kohen Gadol come in twelve.

### Lechem Hapanim Model

Having established twelve for the lechem hapanim and, through the gezeirah shavah, for the chavitei Kohen Gadol, the Gemara asks: *kol hamenachot de'ba'ot eser eser minalan* — what is the source for the general rule of ten? *gamar milachmei todah* — we derive it from the breads of the Todah offering. *mah le'halan eser af kan eser* — just as each type of bread there came in ten loaves, so too here each type of bread comes in ten.

The source that lachmei Toda themselves came in ten is derived from the Torah's language. The Torah describes four types of bread accompanying the Todah — three types of matzah and one type of chametz — and says that one of each type is to be given to the Kohen as a *terumah*, a gift. The term *terumah* appears elsewhere in the context of *terumas ma'aser*, where the Levites give a tenth of their tithe to the Kohen, and there the Torah explicitly calls that tenth a *terumah*. From this, Chazal understood that the *terumah* separated from the Todah breads likewise represents one-tenth — meaning each type must have comprised ten loaves in order for one of them to constitute a *terumah*. Once the lachmei Toda are established as coming in ten, that number serves as the paradigm for all other menachot.

### Mincha & Lechem Comparis…

The Gemara raises an obvious question: we have two available models — the lachmei Toda at ten and the lechem hapanim at twelve. Why does Rabbi Yehuda choose the lachmei Toda as the paradigm and treat twelve as the exception, rather than making the lechem hapanim the rule and treating ten as the exception? *mah le'halan shteim esrei af kan shteim esrei* — why not derive that everything comes in twelve?

### Kohen Gadol Model

The Gemara answers: *mistavra milachmei Todah havei leih lemilaf* — it is more logical to derive from the lachmei Toda. The points of comparison between a normal mincha and the lachmei Toda, and the ways in which they differ from the lechem hapanim, are as follows. *sheken yachid* — both a normal mincha and lachmei Toda come as an individual's korban, whereas the lechem hapanim is a communal offering of the tzibbur. *hamitnadeiv* — both come through a voluntary vow, whereas the lechem hapanim is an obligatory offering. *shemen* — both have oil, whereas the lechem hapanim is baked without oil and is plain bread. *shelo b'shabbat* — neither overrides Shabbat, whereas the lechem hapanim, being a communal and fixed-time offering, does. *shelo b'tumah* — neither is brought in a state of tumah, again reflecting that both are personal and not fixed-time offerings, in contrast to the lechem hapanim.

### Kohen Gadol Similarities

The Gemara counters: *adrabah*, on the contrary — *milechem hapanim havei lei lemilaf* — one should derive from the lechem hapanim instead. Here are the ways in which a normal mincha resembles the lechem hapanim and differs from the lachmei Toda. *sheken hekdesh* — both a normal mincha and the lechem hapanim are kodesh kodashim, eaten by the Kohanim within the Beit HaMikdash. The lachmei Toda, by contrast, accompanies a Todah animal which is a shelamim — kodashim kalim — and is therefore itself eaten as kodashim kalim, outside the Mikdash in Yerushalayim. This is the one case in which a bread brought to the Beit HaMikdash has the status of kodashim kalim. *levonah* — both a normal mincha and the lechem hapanim have levonah, whereas the lachmei Toda, accompanying the animal offering, has none. *matzah* — both are entirely matzah, whereas ten of the forty Todah loaves are chametz. *ve'etzem* — both come as independent offerings in their own right, whereas the lachmei Toda is merely an accompaniment to the animal; the animal is the primary korban.

### Chosen Model Rationale

The Gemara resolves the tension: *hanehu nefishin* — the first list has more points of comparison. The lachmei Toda model is supported by five points while the lechem hapanim model has four, and therefore the lachmei Toda serves as the paradigm.

### R. Meir Counters

The Gemara now raises a more sophisticated challenge. The chavitei Kohen Gadol were learned from the lechem hapanim via the gezeirah shavah of *chukah-chukah*. The question is whether *davar halamed bigezeirah shavah chozer umelamed bibinyan av* — can something that was itself derived through a gezeirah shavah then be used as a paradigm to teach other cases through binyan av? If yes, then one need not use the lechem hapanim directly; one can use the chavitei Kohen Gadol — which is an individual's offering rather than a communal one — as the model, and its many points of comparison with a normal mincha would seem to make it a superior paradigm.

### R. Meir's Exceptions

The Gemara spells out why the chavitei Kohen Gadol might be a better model than the lachmei Toda. *sheken issaron* — both the chavitei Kohen Gadol and a normal mincha consist of a single issaron of flour, whereas a Todah brings a much larger quantity. *kli* — both attain their full kedushah through a kli sharet, a sacred vessel, whereas the lachmei Toda attain their full kedushah only through the slaughtering of the accompanying animal, since the Todah is a shelamim and the slaughter of the animal functions as the act of haktrava for the bread. *hekdesh* — both are kodesh kodashim, whereas the lachmei Toda is kodashim kalim. *levonah* — both have levonah, as they are brought as independent offerings. *matzah* — both are entirely matzah. *ve'atzmam* — both come as independent offerings on their own account. *hagasha* — both require the act of hagasha, touching the mincha to the mizbeach, a requirement that does not apply to lachmei Toda which merely accompanies an animal. *ve'ishim* — portions of both are actually burned on the altar's fire, again unlike the lachmei Toda. This is a considerably longer list than what the lachmei Toda model offered, and the Gemara acknowledges: *vehanach nefishen* — these points are more numerous.

A separate dimension of comparison introduced here concerns *pigul*. Both a normal mincha and lachmei Toda are susceptible to pigul — the mincha through an improper thought during the taking of the kometz, and the lachmei Toda through an improper thought during the sprinkling of the blood of the accompanying animal, which serves as the *matir* for the bread. The chavitei Kohen Gadol, however, is entirely burned on the altar — it has no *matir* in the sense of one act permitting a separate item — and therefore the mechanism of pigul does not apply to it. Similarly, both a normal mincha and lachmei Toda are personal, non-fixed-time offerings and therefore do not override Shabbat or tumah, while the chavitei Kohen Gadol does.

### Shmuel's Leniency

Despite the longer list of comparisons favoring the chavitei Kohen Gadol as the paradigm, the Gemara concludes: *hedyot mehedyot adif leh* — the fact that both the lachmei Toda and a normal mincha are lay offerings, brought by ordinary Israelites rather than by the Kohen Gadol, is a more fundamental and persuasive point of comparison. Even a longer list of technical similarities cannot outweigh the categorical difference between a korban of a *hedyot* and a korban of the Kohen Gadol. It is preferable to derive the rule for a lay offering from another lay offering. This is Rabbi Yehuda's position.

### Teruma Problem

The Gemara now turns to Rabbi Meir, who holds that the general rule is twelve. *mai kasavar* — what does he maintain? Two possibilities are presented. If Rabbi Meir holds *davar halamed bigezeirah shavah chozer umelamed bibinyan av* — that something derived via gezeirah shavah can subsequently be used as a binyan av — then he would derive his rule of twelve from the chavitei Kohen Gadol, using that as his paradigm and relying on the longer list of points of comparison established above. If, however, he holds that something derived via gezeirah shavah cannot be used as a binyan av, then he cannot use the chavitei Kohen Gadol as his model, since it was itself derived from the lechem hapanim through the *chukah-chukah* gezeirah shavah. In that case, Rabbi Meir would derive his rule of twelve directly from the lechem hapanim. His rationale: *hekdesh mehekdesh adif lei* — just as Rabbi Yehuda argues that it is preferable to derive the rule for a lay offering from another lay offering (*hedyot mehedyot*), Rabbi Meir argues the mirror principle: it is preferable to derive the rule for a korban that is kodesh kodashim from another korban that is kodesh kodashim. A normal mincha is kodesh kodashim; the lechem hapanim is kodesh kodashim; this categorical kinship outweighs the advantage the lachmei Toda model offers through the *hedyot* comparison, since the lachmei Toda are kodashim kalim.

### Separation Solution

Having established twelve as the general rule, Rabbi Meir acknowledges the two explicit exceptions. *chutz milachmei toda u'nezirut de'atyan eser eser* — the breads of the Todah and of the Nazir come in ten. For the lachmei Toda, *be'hedya ketiv bei* — it is as if written explicitly, through the derivation from the word *terumah* that we have already seen. The Gemara notes with characteristic irony that calling it *be'hedya* ("explicitly written") is somewhat generous, given that the number ten is derived from the word *terumah* by way of comparison to *terumas ma'aser* — but since this is an established *drasha*, it is treated as though it were explicit. As for nezirut, the Gemara explains: we learn the laws of the Nazir's breads from the lachmei Toda because the Torah uses the superfluous phrase *al zevach todat shelamav* when describing the Todah. The word *shelamim* is redundant — it could have simply said *al zevach hatodah* — and so *lerabot shlamei nazir*, the word *shelamim* is there to include the shelamim of a Nazir. From this inclusion we derive that many of the laws of the Todah apply to the Nazir's offering, including the number of loaves: ten.

---

## Number Not Meakev

### Baraitot on Meakev

Having established the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir regarding the required number of loaves, the Gemara turns to the question of *bedi'avad* — what is the status after the fact when the prescribed number was not achieved? Rav Tuvi bar Kisna said in the name of Shmuel: *lachmei Toda she'afan arba chalot yatza* — if one baked the breads of the Todah as four loaves — one of each of the four types — rather than the required ten of each type, one has fulfilled the obligation after the fact. The full quantity of flour is used but shaped into one enormous loaf of each variety rather than ten. The number ten is *le'chat'chila*; *bedi'avad* it is not indispensable.

### Toda Number Meakev

A difficulty arises immediately. The Torah requires that one complete loaf from each of the four types be given to the Kohen as *terumah*. If one has only one loaf of each type, how can one give the Kohen a complete loaf while still retaining the remaining loaves for oneself? One cannot give him a broken-off piece, because the Torah's use of the word *echad* — one — is understood to require a complete, unbroken loaf: *shelo yitol paros*. And one cannot give the Kohen the entire loaf of that type, because that would eliminate the character of *terumah*, which by definition involves separating one portion from the rest.

### R. Huna on One Loaf

The resolution offered is: *d'afrishinhu b'lisha* — one separates the Kohen's portion during the kneading of the dough, before baking. When preparing each type, one sets aside a portion of the dough at the kneading stage and bakes it separately. This separate piece then constitutes the complete loaf given to the Kohen, while the main mass of dough is baked as the owner's portion. The result is that one does not in fact end up with exactly four loaves, since one has baked the Kohen's portions separately; one ends up with eight distinct pieces. But the essential point — that the Kohen receives an intact, complete portion — is preserved.

### R. Papa Counters

The Gemara now cites a Braita with a broader ruling: *kol haminachot sheriba bemidat challatan o shemi'eit bemidat challatan kesherot* — any of the menachot for which one made more than the prescribed number of loaves, or fewer, is still valid. The prescribed number is a *mitzvah* — it is the *le'chat'chila* ideal — but it is not *me'akev* for most menachot. The exceptions are the lechem hapanim and the chavitei Kohen Gadol, for which twelve is indispensable. This is presumably because the *chukah* language of the gezeirah shavah implies a strict requirement, and in the case of the lechem hapanim in particular, the physical arrangement of twelve loaves on the shulchan cannot be achieved with any other number.

### Omer Ratio

The Braita adds two further exceptions: *ve'yesh omrim af lachmei Toda u'nezirus* — some say that even the breads of the Todah and the Nazir must be ten, and this too is *me'akev*. The basis for treating the ten as *me'akev* in these cases — given that the number is derived from *terumah* rather than from an explicit *chukah* formulation — is a matter of some difficulty. It may be that since the number is derived from an explicit textual comparison rather than purely by analogy, it is treated as though the Torah stated it directly.

### Shtei Halechem Ratio

The Gemara explains Shmuel's ruling — that one is *yotzei* with only four loaves of lachmei Toda — by noting that Shmuel follows a Tanna who does not include the lachmei Toda and nezirut among the *me'akev* exceptions. The Braita in question reads: *kol haminachot sheriba bemidat challatan o shemi'eit bemidat challatan kesherot — chutz milechem hapanim vachavitei Kohen Gadol* — excluding only the lechem hapanim and the chavitei Kohen Gadol, but not the lachmei Toda. Shmuel aligns with this Tanna and therefore rules that four loaves of lachmei Toda are valid after the fact.

### Lechem Hapanim Ratio

Rav Huna offers a more restricted ruling: *mincha ma'afeh she'afah challah achat yatza* — if one baked the oven-baked mincha as a single loaf rather than the prescribed ten, one has nonetheless fulfilled the obligation. His basis is a textual observation: the word in the Torah is *matzat* — spelled without the letter *vav* — which can be read as a singular form, indicating that *bedi'avad* even one *matzah* suffices. Rav Huna limits this ruling to the *mincha ma'afeh* specifically, based on this *pasuk*, and is not prepared to extend it to all menachot on the basis of the broader Braita.

### Ratio Explanation

Rav Pappa challenges this line of reasoning. If the logic is that *matzat* without a *vav* permits a reduced number, then by the breads of the Todah the Torah writes *matzot* — with a *vav* — and yet Shmuel rules that even four loaves are valid there. The presence of the full plural spelling *matzot* would, on Rav Huna's reasoning, imply that the full number is required, not that a reduced number is acceptable. This constitutes a challenge to Shmuel's ruling from Rav Huna's logic: if spelling matters in one direction, it ought to matter in the other. Tosafot reconciles this by suggesting that once Rav Huna derives *bedi'avad* validity from the defective spelling in *mincha ma'afeh*, one may extrapolate that principle broadly to all menachot — and from that extrapolation one could support Shmuel's position as well.

---

## Wheat-to-Flour Ratios

### Quality Clarification

The Mishnah now addresses the quantities of wheat required for the three major communal flour-based offerings. The Omer requires one issaron of flour — approximately a five-pound bag of flour by rough modern equivalence — and the starting wheat for this is three *se'in*. Three *se'in* constitute one *eifah*, and one *eifah* equals ten *issaronim* (the issaron being one-tenth of an eifah, as the Torah states: *asirit ha'eifah*). The ratio of starting wheat to finished flour is therefore ten to one.

### Sieve Numbers

The shtei halechem requires two *esronim* of flour — one issaron per loaf — also from three *se'in* of wheat. Since three *se'in* yield two *esronim*, the ratio here is five to one, exactly half that of the Omer.

### R. Shimon Opinion

The lechem hapanim requires 24 *esronim* — two *esronim* per loaf for each of the twelve loaves, as the Torah states explicitly: *shtei esronim yihyeh hachalah ha'achat* — from 24 *se'in* of wheat. Since 24 *se'in* is eight *eifot*, which is 80 *issaronim*, the ratio of starting wheat to finished flour is approximately 80 to 24, or roughly three and one-third to one. The ratio thus decreases progressively: ten to one for the Omer, five to one for the shtei halechem, and approximately three and one-third to one for the lechem hapanim.

### Alternating Sieves

The Gemara explains why the ratios differ. For the Omer: *keivan d'michadsha ati* — it comes from newly harvested grain, *u'mise'orin ati* — and from barley. Two factors combine to require a high ratio. First, newly harvested grain that has not yet dried out retains considerably more bran and chaff, requiring proportionally more starting material to produce a given quantity of fine flour. Second, barley itself has substantially more *psolet* — dross, hulls, and waste — than wheat. For these two reasons, *issaron muvchar lo ati ela mishalosh se'in* — a fine, high-quality issaron of solet cannot be obtained from less than three *se'in*, yielding the ten-to-one ratio.

### Sieve Purposes

The shtei halechem comes from newly harvested grain as well — these are the two loaves of the new wheat crop brought on Shavuot — but it is wheat rather than barley. The two factors therefore partially cancel: newly harvested grain increases the ratio, but wheat rather than barley cuts it in half. *af al gav d'michadsha atyan* — although they come from new grain, *keivan d'michitin atyan* — since they come from wheat, the ratio is halved, and two *esronim* can be obtained from three *se'in*.

### Progressive Method

The lechem hapanim benefits from two favorable factors simultaneously. *keivan d'michitin atu* — it comes from wheat, and *umiyashan atu* — it comes from aged, dried grain. The lechem hapanim, unlike the Omer or shtei halechem, need not come from the newly harvested crop; it can be brought from whatever wheat is available at any time of year, and older grain that has dried out yields a much higher proportion of fine flour. With both favorable factors in play, *issaron muvchar ati mise'ah* — a fine issaron can be obtained from a single *se'ah*, yielding the lowest ratio of approximately three and one-third to one.

An important clarification follows: one should not infer from the higher starting ratio of the Omer that the standard of flour quality required for the Omer is higher. The end product — a fine issaron of solet — is the same in all cases. The higher ratio simply reflects the inferior starting material: more wheat must be processed to produce the same quality of finished flour. The quality of the result is identical; what differs is how much raw material is needed to achieve it.

### Buy Flour

A Braita makes this distinction explicit and gives it halachic force: *kol hamenachot sheriba bemidat isronam o shemi'eit bemidat isronam pesulot* — any mincha for which the quantity of finished flour was more or less than the prescribed issaron is invalid. The issaron is *me'akev*. However, *riba bemidat se'im shelahen o shemi'eit bemidat se'im shelahen kesherot* — if one started with more or less wheat than the prescribed three *se'in* but still arrived at the correct issaron of fine flour, the mincha is valid. The ratios of starting wheat to flour are provided as practical guidance for achieving the correct quantity of solet, not as independent requirements. What must be precise is the finished product; the process of arriving there carries latitude.

---

## Sifting Process

### Buy Wheat

The final Mishnah of the daf addresses the sifting process. The Omer was sifted through thirteen sieves. The shtei halechem was sifted through twelve. The lechem hapanim through eleven. The numbers decrease as the ratio of starting material to finished flour decreases — which is intuitive, since the inferior starting material of the Omer (new barley) requires more processing to achieve the same quality of solet. What is somewhat striking is that the differences between the three offerings are each only one sieve, even as the differences in the starting wheat ratios are quite dramatic. The Gemara does not offer an explicit explanation of this; the numbers appear to carry a degree of symbolic or conventional character.

One may also note that the Mishnah specifies numbers for these three communal offerings but does not prescribe a fixed number of sieves for an ordinary personal mincha. This reflects a broader pattern: the communal offerings were subject to precise, standardized procedures, whereas the personal mincha was held to a standard of *solet* — fine flour — without the same degree of procedural specification.

### Lechem Exception

Rabbi Shimon disagrees with the fixed numbers entirely: *lo haya lahen kitzva ela solet menufa kol tzorcha haya mevi* — there was no fixed number of sieves; rather, one would bring finely sifted flour sifted as much as necessary. His source is the verse *ve'lakachta solet ve'afita otah* — you shall take solet and you shall bake it. Rabbi Shimon reads a play on *ve'afita* — connecting it to the concept of being well-sifted (*menufa*) — to indicate that what matters is achieving sufficiently fine flour, not the specific number of sieves used. This is arguably the more logically coherent position: if the goal is *solet*, then one sieves until *solet* is achieved, whatever number of passes that requires.

### Expense Principle

A Braita describes the order of sifting: *b'daka b'gasa b'daka b'gasa* — one alternates between a fine-holed sieve and a coarse-holed sieve. The two types of sieves serve opposite purposes. The fine-holed sieve is designed to allow small particles — sand, dust, and fine debris — to pass through while retaining the grain; in this way, the fine *psolet* falls out below. The coarse-holed sieve is designed to allow the grain to pass through while retaining large particles such as bran above. By alternating the two types and progressively adjusting the sizes of the holes — the fine holes becoming progressively finer and the coarse holes becoming progressively coarser — more and more of the waste material is removed at each stage until only pure solet remains.

### Shimon b Elazar Sieves

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar — a distinct figure from Rabbi Shimon of the Mishnah — describes a different arrangement: *shlosha asar nefot hayu bamikdash, zu lemala mizu vezu lemala mizu* — there were thirteen sieves in the Temple, each one arranged above the other, *elyona koletet subin vetachtona koletet solet* — the topmost sieve catches the bran, and the bottommost catches the solet. On Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reading, rather than alternating fine and coarse sieves, the thirteen sieves are arranged in a descending series from largest holes to smallest, so that the grain passes progressively through ever-finer sieving, with the bran caught at the top and the finest solet collected at the bottom. This is a single hierarchical system rather than an alternating back-and-forth process.

### Torah Saves Money

A Braita addresses the question of how the flour was obtained. The verse *ve'lakachta solet ve'afita otah* — you shall take solet and bake it — teaches that *solet* may be purchased directly from the marketplace. One need not produce the flour oneself from scratch; purchasing pre-sifted flour from a vendor is permitted. Furthermore, *u'minayin she'afilu chitin* — how do we know one may even purchase raw wheat rather than flour? *talmud lomar ve'lakachta* — the word *ve'lakachta*, "you shall take," indicates that one may acquire the grain in whatever form it comes, even as unprocessed wheat.

However, *yachol af bish'ar menachot ken* — one might have thought that this latitude to purchase raw wheat applies to all menachot. The Braita implies that for other menachot it does not apply — for them one must purchase flour rather than unprocessed wheat — and the reason offered is *mipnei hachisachon*, because of the financial saving. The Gemara asks: *mai mipnei hachisachon* — what does this mean?

### Torah: Mammon Yisrael

Rabbi Elazar explains: *haTorah chasah al mamonam shel Yisrael* — the Torah is concerned about the financial expenditure of Israel. Specially sifted and processed flour, of the quality required for the Mikdash, carries a significant premium — particularly for the lechem hapanim, which required 24 *esronim* of solet and was brought every week. Purchasing that quantity of premium flour from the marketplace week after week would be enormously expensive. Therefore, the Torah permits purchasing raw wheat for the lechem hapanim so that the processing can be done in-house, reducing the cost.
