# Menachot 78

## Teruma & Michubar

### Michubar Concept

We pick up at the bottom of ayin-zayin amud bet, having just quoted an extremely long braita, and now turn to unpacking it. The braita begins with amar mar: *ve-hikriv mimenu* — you shall bring from it. This concerns the breads of the toda and the principle that the separation must be made *min hamichubar*, from what is connected — meaning, as Rashi explains, that all the loaves remain together in the same location when the separation is performed, so that the gift represents a lifting-up from a unified whole.

### One-in-Ten Ratio

The Gemara immediately raises a challenge: the word *mimenu* also appears elsewhere in the Torah — *et kol chelbo yarim mimenu*, you should lift up all the fat from the sacrifice. There too it says *mimenu*, yet what is the novelty? Of course the fat is *mechubar* — it is literally inside the animal. Tosafot answers that this is precisely the point: the fact that it is so obviously connected is why the Torah need not innovate there. What we learn from that verse, as Rav Chisda said in the name of Avimi, is a procedural instruction: *she-lo yenateach basar kodem she-yitol emurav* — do not first chop up the meat and then remove the fat. Rather, the fat should be removed while still forming one whole with the korban.

### Excluding Midyan/Challah

This is not merely a technicality. The concept of *mimenu* and *mechubar* captures the very essence of terumah: a gift that represents the whole from which it is separated — and specifically the finest of that whole. The *chelev* represents the choicest part of the korban; presenting it while still unified with the animal conveys that this is the gift of the entire korban to God. The same logic applies to terumah from grain and to the loaves of the toda: one does not simply hand over some bread to the kohen — one lifts a gift from the entirety of the forty loaves.

### Mimenu Exclusion

The Gemara continues: *nemar kan terumah ve-nemar be-terumat ma'aser terumah* — the word *terumah* appears here by the toda-loaves, and the same word appears by terumat ma'aser. It is through this verbal analogy that we derive the proportion: one loaf out of ten. One might then ask: why not derive the proportion from *trumat Midyan*? There the Torah also uses the word *terumah*, and the proportion there is one in five hundred — a very different ratio.

### Mita v'Chomesh

The Gemara answers: *danim terumah hanohaget ladorot mi-terumah hanohaget ladorot* — we derive a terumah that applies for all generations from another terumah that applies for all generations, namely terumat ma'aser. The gift from the booty of Midyan, *trumat Midyan*, was a one-time event, *she-eina nohaget ladorot*, and therefore cannot serve as a halachic model.

### Dimua Question

The Gemara then asks: let us instead derive the proportion from *trumat challah*, which also uses the word *terumah*. There the Sages indicate the amount is one in twenty-four — why not apply that proportion here? The school of Rabbi Yishmael responds by focusing on a more precise verbal parallel. The verse by the toda uses the phrase *mimenu terumah l'Hashem*, and the verse by terumat ma'aser uses the analogous phrase *mimenu trumat Hashem*. Both share not only the word *terumah* but also the word *mimenu*. The case of *trumat challah*, by contrast, does not use the word *mimenu* — and this additional word therefore serves *l'afukei trumat challah*, to exclude the challah proportion from the comparison. We thus confirm that the proportion is one in ten, as derived from terumat ma'aser.

---

## Rava's Questions

### Double Yud Derivation

Having established that the toda-loaves are called *terumah*, Rava raises a fascinating question: *trumat lachmei todah — chayavin aleha mita v'chomesh o ein chayavin aleha mita v'chomesh?* If a non-kohen eats this bread, does he incur *mita b'yadei shamayim* for intentional consumption? And does he add a fifth when paying back for inadvertent consumption — the classic laws that apply to terumah?

### Assara Esronot

The question is whether the word *terumah* here is technical or merely generic, meaning simply a gift or separation. The classic agricultural terumah — grain, challah, bikurim, terumat ma'aser — all share the character of being standard, obligatory gifts from the produce of the land, given to the kohen as God's representative. The toda-loaves operate in an entirely different conceptual universe: the toda offering is optional, and the loaves accompany it not as a gift from agricultural bounty but as an appurtenance of the korban itself. The *terumah* here is lifted not from the grain of one's field but from the forty loaves one has prepared. This raises the genuine question of whether the technical halachic consequences of terumah-status follow.

Rava formulates the question precisely: since the toda-bread is *itkash*, linked, to terumat ma'aser through the gezeira shava, perhaps it is *k'terumat ma'aser dami* — similar to terumat ma'aser in all its laws. Or perhaps the verse *bo v'chamishito* and *u-metu vo* — the death penalty and the added fifth — specifically exclude this case, as the "it" (*bo*) limits these consequences to classic terumah.

### Matza Piggyback

The question of mita and chomesh is left unresolved. Similarly, the Gemara asks whether the toda-bread creates *dimua* — the status that results when terumah becomes mixed with non-sanctified produce, rendering the mixture forbidden to non-kohanim. This too is left as *teiku*. It is worth noting that the laws of dimua are in large part rabbinic in origin, which makes the question somewhat unusual, yet the Gemara raises it nonetheless.

### Gezeira Shava Chain

The Gemara now returns to the braita. The next point concerns the measure of flour per loaf. The question is whether we should understand the model of *shtei halechem* to mean one *issaron* per loaf — which would give ten *esronot* for the ten *chametz* loaves — or merely two *esronot* total divided across all the loaves. The braita says: *talmud lomar tihyena* — the verse says *tihyena*.

### Tavyu Inclusion

The Gemara asks: *mai talmuda* — what exactly do we derive from this? Rav Yosef bar Avdimi explains: *tihyena ksiv* — it is written *tihyena*, with a double *yud*. Both Rashi and Tosafot explain that the double *yud* signals that the measure applies to ten loaves. Since *shtei halechem* is two loaves each of one *issaron*, the verse signals by means of *tihyena* that this unit of one *issaron* per loaf applies equally to the ten *chametz* loaves of the toda — yielding *asara esronot* for those ten loaves.

One might then ask: perhaps the *yud* teaches ten, but perhaps ten of a different measure — ten *kafizi* rather than ten *esronot*? Rava answers: *be-esronot diber ha-kasuv* — the Torah speaks in units of *esronot*. The verse explicitly calls the *shtei halechem* by the measure of *shtei esronot*, and therefore when the word teaches ten, it must mean *asara esronot*.

### Miluim Three Types

We have thus established that the ten *chametz* loaves of the toda require *asara esronot* — one *issaron* per loaf.

### Revucha Identification

The Gemara now asks: *asara l'matzah minayin* — how do we know that the thirty *matzah* loaves are also prepared from *asara esronot*? The verse says *al chalos lechem chametz* — alongside the *chametz* loaves bring these *matzah* loaves. This teaches *keneged chametz havei matzah* — the *matzah* is equivalent in total flour to the *chametz*. While the *chametz* consists of ten loaves and the *matzah* of thirty, the total quantity of flour is the same: *asara esronot*. Each *matzah* loaf is therefore one-third the size of each *chametz* loaf.

### Kohen Gadol Initiation

Tosafot raises a significant methodological objection. We learned the *issaron*-per-loaf principle from *shtei halechem* (source A), and applied it to the *chametz* loaves of the toda (B). Now we are deriving the *matzah* measure (C) from the *chametz* (B). This is a daisy-chained derivation: A to B, then B to C. The Gemara's principle is *v'chi davar ha-lamad be-hekkesh chozer u-melamed be-hekkesh?* — can something learned through a *hekkesh* turn around and teach through another *hekkesh*?

### Nazir Proportions

The Gemara answers: *himenu ve-davar akher hu* — it is "from it and another thing." The principle is that when you are already learning something locally from B to C — in this case, the equivalence of *chametz* and *matzah* flour directly from the verse — then you may *schlepp* along what you additionally learned from A. This is the distinction between a pure daisy-chain, which is prohibited, and a piggyback, which is permitted: since the connection from the *chametz* to the *matzah* is established on its own terms, one may bring along the measure of *asara esronot* as well.

The Gemara then asks: what of the opinion that even *himenu ve-davar akher* is still considered a *hekkesh* and is therefore forbidden? *mai ika le-meimar?*

### Matzos Klal Prat

The answer is *tavi'u ribuya hi*. The derivation of the *chametz* measure from *shtei halechem* was based on the verse *mimoshvoteichem tavi'u lechem tenufah shtayim esronim*. The word *tavi'u* — "you shall bring" — is understood as an inclusive term, encompassing many different cases of bringing. Just as it was used to extend the *issaron* measure to the *chametz* loaves, the same word *tavi'u* can be read to include a teaching about the *matzah* loaves as well — and this operates not as a *hekkesh* but as a *ribbui*, an amplification. This sidesteps the problem of chaining *hekkesh* derivations entirely.

To summarize what we have established: we know there are ten loaves per type because of the *terumah* gezeira shava with terumat ma'aser, and the Gemara has explained why we do not learn from *trumat Midyan* or *trumat challah*. One loaf of each type goes to the kohen, yielding forty loaves total with one loaf from each set of ten going to the kohen. Rava raised the open question of the halachic status of that gift. And we have established that the ten *chametz* loaves require *asara esronot* — one *issaron* per loaf — which means each chametz loaf is enormous, approximately the size of a loaf baked from a full five-pound bag of flour. The thirty *matzah* loaves share the same total quantity of flour, so each *matzah* loaf is one-third the size. In total, a person bringing a toda presents forty loaves made from the equivalent of twenty such five-pound bags — a staggering quantity of bread.

---

## Ten Loaves & Flour

### Inside-Outside Rule

The Mishnah now transitions to a historical note: *ha-miluim haya ba'im ke-matzah she-ba-toda* — when they inaugurated the kohanim into the avodah, they brought loaves similar to the *matzah* of the toda. There was no *chametz* component in the miluim, but there were three types of *matzah* loaves. The Mishnah identifies these as *challos, rekikin, u-revichah*.

### Location Debate

By a nazir, who brings certain loaves with his *shlamim* upon completing his nazirite vow, the Mishnah states: *hayta ba'ah shtei yadot ke-matzah* — he brings two-thirds of the *matzah* types brought by the toda. Specifically, *challos* and *rekikin* — but not *revuchah*, the heavily oil-soaked type.

The calculation follows directly. The toda's thirty *matzah* loaves use *asara esronot*, which equals fifteen *kavim* in the wilderness measure. Since the nazir brings only two of the three types, proportionally he uses two-thirds of that flour. Two-thirds of ten *esronot* is six and two-thirds *esronot*, which in the Jerusalem measure equals *asara kabin Yerushalmiyot* — ten Jerusalem *kavim*, as the Mishnah states.

### Pesach Chametz Parallel

The Gemara asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for saying the miluim included these three types of *matzah*? Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Chama bar Guria: the verse describing the miluim states *u-misal ha-matzot asher lifnei Hashem lakach challat matzah achat ve-challat lechem shemen achat ve-rakik echad* — from the basket of matzot before God he took one *challat matzah*, one *challat lechem shemen*, and one *rakik*.

### Yerushalayim Requirement

Two of the three are readily identified by the Gemara: *bishlama challos challos* — when the verse says *challat matzah* by the miluim, that parallels the *chalos matzos* of the toda; and *rakik* is simply *rakik*, matching the *rekikin* of the toda. Two out of three are straightforward.

### Crust Requirement

The third type mentioned by the miluim is *challat lechem shemen* — a loaf of oily bread. The Gemara naturally assumes this corresponds to the *revuchah* of the toda. But Rav Chavya bar Rav Avia challenges this: *eima anta de-mishcha* — perhaps *challat lechem shemen* means simply some kind of oil-drenched cake, *uga shel shemen*, something entirely different from the *revuchah* mentioned by the toda. The identification of *lechem shemen* with *revuchah* is attractive but not logically compelled. The pseudo-Rashi goes even further, entertaining the possibility that *challah* might not refer to bread at all here, though he acknowledges the difficulty given that the verse says *challat lechem*.

### All Loaves Must Be Bread

The Gemara resolves the question through a teaching of Nachman bar Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Tavla. The verse states: *zeh korban Aharon u-vanav asher yakrivu la-Hashem beyom himashach oto* — this is the korban of Aharon and his sons that they shall bring on the day of their anointing. This verse serves multiple functions: it records what was brought at the historical miluim, and it also establishes a principle for all future kohanim, *makkish chinucho le-himashcho* — it equates the *chinuch*, the initiation, of a kohen into the avodah with the anointing of the Kohen Gadol. The daily *minchah* that the Kohen Gadol brings — his *chavitin* — is the expression of *himashcho*, his anointed status. The verse in Vayikra describing the Kohen Gadol's daily offering uses the word *murbeches*, which is precisely the *revuchah* form.

### Lishmah Requirement

From this equation, the Gemara derives: *mah himashcho bi-revuchah af chinucho bi-revuchah* — just as the Kohen Gadol's daily *chavitin* is *revuchah*, so too the initiation offering of any kohen entering the avodah for the first time is *revuchah*. This identifies the third type of the miluim loaves. Rav Chisda applies this to a practical halacha: a Kohen Gadol entering service for the first time must bring two *minchot* — one for his daily *chavitin* obligation (*l'himashcho*) and one for his initiation into the avodah (*l'chinucho*). Mar bar Rav Ashi adds that if this Kohen Gadol has never previously served even as a regular kohen, he requires three *minchot*: one to initiate him into the priesthood generally, one to initiate him as Kohen Gadol specifically, and one for his daily *chavitin*. The two opinions are not in dispute — *v'lo pligi* — they address different cases: where the individual had previously served as a regular kohen before assuming the high priesthood, and where he had never served at all.

### Non-Stringy Standard

Having established the three types of miluim loaves and their connection to the toda, the Gemara turns to why the nazir's offering excludes the *revuchah*.

### Forty Sanctified

A braita is cited connecting the toda and the nazir through the shared term *shlamav* — the toda is called *zevach todas shlamav*, a sacrifice of thanks among his *shlamim*, which serves to include the *shlamei nazir* within the framework of the toda. This connection establishes the amount of flour (ten *kavim*) and the proportional amount of oil for the nazir's offering.

### All-or-Nothing

One might think the nazir should bring all three *matzah* types including the *revuchah*. Rav Pappa answers through a verbal analogy: the verse by the nazir says *sal matzos*, a basket of *matzos*, and then specifies *challos* and *rekikin*. The word *matzos* appears explicitly when describing both *challos* and *rekikin* in the toda verse — but the *revuchah* is called *solet murbechet* without the word *matzah*. Since the nazir verse specifies *matzos*, it connects the nazir only to those types described as *matzah*, thereby excluding the *revuchah*.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a more elegant resolution: the verse by the nazir employs *klal u-prat* — a general statement (*matzos*) followed by a specification (*challos ve-rekikin*). By the rule of *klal u-prat ein ba-klal ela mah she-ba-prat*, one applies only what is explicitly enumerated and nothing more. There is thus no need to derive the exclusion of *revuchah* from the toda at all — the Pasuk explicitly limits the nazir's loaves to just these two types. Tosafot notes that the purpose of stating a general term before specifying is precisely to signal exclusivity: had the Torah enumerated only the two types without a preceding general term, one might have thought other similar types are also included. The *klal* followed by *prat* signals: only these, and nothing else.

What then is derived from the connection to the toda? The amount of flour and the proportional amount of oil — information not stated explicitly in the nazir's passage.

---

## Miluim Bread Types

### Explicit Intent

The Mishnah on ayin-chet amud bet presents a foundational principle about how the toda loaves acquire sanctity: *ha-shochet et ha-toda lifnim ve-lachmah chutz la-chomah — lo kideish ha-lechem*. If one slaughtered the toda offering inside while the bread was outside the wall, the bread is not sanctified. The slaughtering of the toda, rather than any vessel or oven, is what creates the *kedushah* of its accompanying loaves. This is structurally different from a regular *minchah*, whose sanctity is established through its placement in a *kli sharet* without any associated korban. By the toda-bread, full kedushah is achieved only at the moment of shechitah.

### Knife Power Debate

The Mishnah further rules that if the loaves had not yet developed a crust in the oven — *ad shelo karmu paneha ba-tanur* — they are not yet considered *lechem* and thus cannot be sanctified by the shechitah. Furthermore, even if all the loaves but one had formed a crust, *lo kideish ha-lechem* — none of them are sanctified. The Mishnah thus establishes three requirements: the slaughtering must be done as a toda; the bread must be within the appropriate boundary; and all loaves must qualify as *lechem* by having formed a crust.

### Rabbi Yochanan vs Reish Lakish

The Gemara asks: *mai chutz la-chomah* — which wall are we speaking of? Reish Lakish says: *chutz le-chomat ha-azarah* — outside the wall of the Azarah itself. The word *al* in *al chalos lechem chametz*, he argues, means the bread must be literally alongside the korban — *be'inan al be-samoch*. If the korban is slaughtered inside the Azarah, the bread must be there with it. Rabbi Yochanan says: *chutz le-chomat Beit Pagi* — only if the bread is outside the outer wall of Jerusalem is it a problem. Within Jerusalem anywhere is sufficient; *lo be'inan al be-samoch*, the word *al* does not require physical proximity. Rabbi Yochanan's position is conceptually grounded in the status of the toda as *kodashim kalim*: since these breads may be eaten throughout Jerusalem, their sanctification can occur throughout Jerusalem, and need not be confined to the Azarah proper.

### Pesach chametz parallel

The Gemara notes that this dispute parallels an earlier argument between the same Amoraim regarding *la tishchat al chametz dam zivchi* — do not slaughter my Pesach sacrifice while *chametz* exists. The question there is likewise what *al* means: does the *chametz* have to be physically present in the Azarah with the one performing the slaughter, or does it suffice that the person owns *chametz* somewhere, even at home? Reish Lakish holds the former; Rabbi Yochanan holds the latter.

### Need both cases explained

The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: *tzricha*. Had Rabbi Yochanan stated his lenient position only by *chametz* and Pesach, one might have conceded that in a context of prohibition, the Torah cares wherever the chametz is — but by sanctification of bread, perhaps Rabbi Yochanan would agree with Reish Lakish that physical proximity is required. Conversely, had Reish Lakish stated his strict position only regarding the toda-bread, one might have thought that in the context of a positive act of sanctification, closeness is logically required, but regarding *chametz* he might agree with Rabbi Yochanan that ownership anywhere constitutes a problem. Since both scholars maintain their positions in both cases, both rulings are necessary.

### Braita like Rabbi Yochanan

A braita is cited in support of Rabbi Yochanan: *ha-shochet et ha-toda bifnim ve-lachmah chutz le-chomat Beit Pagi — lo kideish ha-lechem*. If the bread is outside of Beit Pagi — outside Jerusalem — it is not sanctified. This implies that bread anywhere within Jerusalem, even outside the Azarah, is sanctified by the shechitah, consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's position. The braita is noted as surprising given that the logic of the Gemara would seem to favor Reish Lakish, yet the braita sides with Rabbi Yochanan.

---

## Nazir Bread Types

### Crust requirement definition

Having established the wall-boundary requirement, the Gemara turns to the crust requirement. The source is a braita: *al chalas lechem chametz yakriv korbano al zevach* — he shall bring on the loaves of chametz bread alongside the slaughtering. The word *lechem* teaches that the bread must qualify as *lechem*: *she-lo kideish ha-lechem ela im kein karmu paneha ba-tanur* — it does not become sanctified unless its surface has crusted in the oven. The verse also teaches two further principles: the slaughtering of the korban is what sanctifies the bread (*she-ein ha-lechem kadosh ela bi-shechitat ha-zevach*); and if the korban was slaughtered *shelo lishmah* — not with the intent of offering it as a toda — the bread is not sanctified. A shechitah lacking proper *kavanah* cannot impart full toda-status to the animal, and therefore cannot activate the accompanying bread.

### Pesach matzah cooking standards

The Gemara connects the *lechem* requirement to the analogous question of what constitutes adequate baking for *matzah* on Pesach. A braita taught: *yotzin be-matzah na* — one can fulfill the mitzvah of matzah even with under-baked matzah, and even with matzah baked in a pot rather than an oven. The Gemara asks: *mai matzah na* — what precisely is under-baked matzah, and what is the minimum threshold?

### Strands test for bread

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *kol she-porsa ve-ein chutin nimshachin heimena* — any loaf that when broken does not produce doughy strands pulling from the interior has sufficiently baked. If breaking it still reveals stretching strands of raw dough, it has not achieved the status of bread.

### Lechem definition parallel

Rava then applies this standard explicitly to toda-bread: *ve-chen le-inyan lachmei toda* — the same measure applies to the loaves of the toda. The Gemara asks: *peshita* — is this not obvious? Both cases use the word *lechem*, and therefore the same definition must apply: *hacha lechem ketiv ve-hacha lechem ketiv*. Rava's contribution, the Gemara clarifies, is to forestall a possible objection: since one loaf of ten must be given intact to the kohen, *echad amar Rachmana she-lo yitpares*, one might worry that a barely-baked loaf, while meeting the definition of bread, might crumble too easily and thus effectively be a *paris* — a broken piece, which would not be valid. Rava therefore teaches *ka mashma lan* that once the bread meets the threshold of *lechem*, it is fully valid regardless of its structural fragility.

---

## Bread Sanctification

### Eighty loaves scenario

The Gemara now addresses a vivid practical case: *toda she-shachata al shemonim chalot* — someone brought eighty loaves with the toda instead of the required forty and then slaughtered the korban. What is the result?

### Chizkiya forty sanctified

Chizkiya holds: *kidshu arbaim mitoch shemonim* — forty of the eighty loaves become sanctified. The shechitah operates on those forty for which it is halachically effective. One does not know which forty, and therefore all eighty must be treated stringently — eaten within Jerusalem, within the allotted time — but the person has fulfilled his toda obligation.

### Rabbi Yochanan all or nothing

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *lo kidshu arbaim mitoch shemonim* — none of the loaves are sanctified. Since the person brought eighty and the toda only accommodates forty, the shechitah cannot partially operate. All or nothing: since it cannot sanctify all eighty, it sanctifies none, and the toda is therefore brought without its accompanying bread.

### Rabbi Zeira intent resolution

Rabbi Zeira clarifies the limits of the dispute. All agree that if the person explicitly stated his intent — *likdeshu arbaim mitoch shemonim*, "let forty of the eighty be sanctified" — then forty are sanctified. All also agree that if the person said explicitly that forty should be sanctified only if all eighty are sanctified — making it conditional — then nothing is sanctified, because the Torah does not recognize eighty. The dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan concerns only *stama* — when no explicit intent was stated. Chizkiya holds we presume the extra loaves were *le-achrayut*, a backup in case some were lost. Rabbi Yochanan holds we presume the person intended a *korban gadol*, a grander offering with all eighty, and since that cannot work, nothing works.

### Abaye kli sharet debate

Abaye reframes the dispute. He holds that everyone agrees the person intended all eighty — *le-korban gadol kamichaven*. The disagreement is about a different question: *be-kli sharet mekadeshin shelo mida-at kamifligei* — does a *kli sharet* sanctify independently of the owner's intention? Here, the *kli sharet* at issue is not a bowl or vessel but the *sakin*, the slaughtering knife, since it is the act of shechitah that conveys sanctity to the bread. Chizkiya holds that a *kli sharet* sanctifies regardless of intent, and therefore the knife's action sanctifies forty even though the person wanted eighty. Rabbi Yochanan holds that a *kli sharet* only sanctifies in accordance with intent, and since the intent was for eighty — which cannot be sanctified — nothing is sanctified.

### Rav Papa knife power

Rav Papa offers yet another framing. He holds that everyone agrees a *kli sharet* requires *da'at* — intent — to operate. The debate, rather, concerns whether the *sakin* is more powerful than a standard *kli sharet*: *ve-hacha be-sakin kamifligei*. Chizkiya holds *sakin alimah mi-kli sharet* — the knife is more potent than an ordinary sacred vessel. Precisely because a knife has no *toch*, no containing space, and yet the Torah empowers it to impart sanctity to the bread, this shows that it operates in a uniquely powerful manner, overriding even the owner's contrary intention and sanctifying forty. Rabbi Yochanan holds *sakin lo alimah mi-kol sha'ar kli sharet* — the knife is not more potent. Since it lacks a container, it functions no differently from a standard *kli sharet*, which requires *da'at*. The owner's intent for eighty controls, and since eighty cannot be sanctified, nothing is sanctified.

This final sugya weaves together several deep questions simultaneously: the all-or-nothing logic of partial fulfillment, the independent sanctifying power of sacred vessels, and the unique status of the shechitah-knife as a mechanism of *kiddush lechem* — a rich conclusion to a daf devoted to every dimension of the toda's bread.

---

---

# Menachot 79

## Shechita Sanctifies Bread

### Toda & Bread Intro

We begin on the bottom of 79b. The Torah presents a fascinating hybrid in the Toda: it has a korban element and a bread element — though it is worth noting that the bread is not quite a standard Mincha. The Toda is Kodshim Kalim rather than Kodshei Kodshim, it is not brought independently, and so its bread component occupies a somewhat ambiguous category. Nevertheless, the Gemara treats it in relationship to Mincha law, and what we are focused on is how the Toda relates to its bread. As we saw previously, the slaughtering of the korban — the shechita — is what confers Kedusha upon the bread. The discussion that follows examines the conditions and limitations of that principle.

### Chutz Lizmano/Limkomo

The Mishna presents several cases. If the Toda was slaughtered with a thought of Chutz Lizmano or Chutz Limkomo — and here we should recall from Masechet Zevachim that these terms do not literally mean the wrong time or the wrong place, but rather a thought directed toward the wrong time or the wrong place — the result is Kadesh Venifsal. The bread does become Kadosh, but since the korban is Pasul, the bread is Pasul as well. This is the worst of all scenarios: the bread is sanctified and therefore linked to the korban, but since the korban is invalid, the bread cannot be used for anything else.

### Treifa vs. Mum

By contrast, if the korban was slaughtered and was subsequently found to be a Treifa — meaning it had an internal injury that renders it non-viable — the ruling is Lo Kadesh Halechem: the bread is not sanctified. The distinction is fairly clear at the outset. A Treifa is a problem that predated the shechita; the animal was already a Treifa before the knife came down, and therefore the act of shechita was meaningless from the beginning. Since the shechita was not a valid act of sanctification, it could not confer Kedusha upon the bread. And that outcome, counterintuitively, is the better one — because if the bread was not sanctified, it remains free to be used for another korban.

A further case illuminates the underlying principle from a different angle. If the shechita itself was technically defective as a physical act — for instance, if pressure was applied in a way that would render the animal a Treifa under normal Kashrut law, or if the cut was performed improperly — then Lo Kadesh Halechem as well, because there was no valid Ma'aseh Shechita at all.

The more interesting case is that of a Ba'al Mum, where the act of shechita was technically Kasher — it would have been valid outside the Mikdash — but the korban had a blemish, which is a korban-level disqualification rather than a general Kashrut problem. The shechita as an act of shechita was fine; the problem was the animal's status as a korban. One way to frame the debate that follows is precisely this distinction: was there a valid Ma'aseh Shechita or not? A Treifa means the shechita accomplished nothing. A Mum means the shechita was technically valid but the korban was compromised.

### Rabbi Eliezer/Yehoshua

The Gemara now provides a Braisa that identifies the underlying rule — attributed to Rabbi Meir — and presents it as a general principle: Kol she-pisulo kodem shechita, Lo Kidesh Halechem. Any invalidity that predated the shechita means the bread is not sanctified, because by the time one reaches the shechita the animal was already Pasul and the shechita cannot be meaningful. Conversely, if the Psul did not predate the shechita — if the shechita was approached with the animal in a valid state — then Kidesh Halechem. The Braisa then runs through the cases in reverse order: shechita with a thought of Chutz Lizmano or Chutz Limkomo results in Kidesh Halechem, because the Psul was introduced at the moment of shechita but did not predate it; whereas shechita of a Treifa results in Lo Kidesh Halechem, because the Psul predated it.

### Shelo Lishma

This brings us to the top of 79a and the case of Ba'al Mum. The Braisa records: Shachat ve-nimtza ba'alat mum — Rabbi Eliezer says Kidesh, Rabbi Yehoshua says Lo Kidesh. According to the framework of predating or not predating, it is initially difficult to understand Rabbi Eliezer's position, since a Mum surely predated the shechita. We will return to that difficulty. The Braisa identifies this as the position of Rabbi Meir — meaning Rabbi Meir understood the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua to be specifically about the case of Ba'al Mum.

### Ze Haklal Principle

Rabbi Yehuda, however, presents an entirely different account of what Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua were debating. He says: Lo necheleku Rabbi Eliezer ve-Rabbi Yehoshua al she-shachat ve-nimtza Treifa — nobody disputed that case, everyone agrees Lo Kidesh Halechem, because it was not a good shechita. And regarding Chutz Lizmano — a Piggul thought — everyone also agrees Kidesh Halechem, because the Psul did not predate. And furthermore, even regarding Ba'al Mum, everyone agrees Lo Kidesh Halechem, because a Mum predated the shechita just as a Treifa does.

What, then, was the actual debate? Al Chutz Limkomo. This is striking. Throughout the entirety of Masechet Zevachim, Chutz Lizmano and Chutz Limkomo functioned as virtual twins — one was Piggul with Karet, the other was not Karet, but in terms of how they invalidated a korban, they were treated identically. Here, for the first time, we encounter a serious suggestion that Chutz Limkomo might have a different scope than Chutz Lizmano in at least one context. According to Rabbi Yehuda's version, Rabbi Eliezer holds that Chutz Limkomo also results in Kidesh Halechem, just like Chutz Lizmano, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds that Chutz Limkomo is categorically different and Lo Kidesh Halechem.

### Treifa Examples

Rabbi Yehuda preserves not only the two positions but a full account of the back-and-forth between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Eliezer opens with a straightforward analogy: Hol ve-Chutz Lizmano Pasul, ve-Chutz Limkomo Pasul — both are invalidities born of improper thought. Ma Chutz Lizmano Kidesh, af Chutz Limkomo Kidesh. Since both are thought-based disqualifications, the bread should be sanctified in both cases. The weight of this argument seems clear.

Rabbi Yehoshua counters by proposing a different comparandum: Hol ve-Chutz Limkomo Pasul, u-va'alat Mum Pasul — both are invalidities. Ma Ba'alat Mum Lo Kidesh, af Chutz Limkomo Lo Kidesh. This comparison is immediately problematic: one is a thought-based Psul that does not predate the shechita, while the other is a physical defect that does. They are not analogous in any obvious way.

Rabbi Eliezer responds to this directly: I compared Chutz Limkomo to Chutz Lizmano; you compared it to Ba'al Mum. Let us determine which comparison is more apt. He then articulates the principle: Donin Psul Machshava mi-Psul Machshava, ve-ein Donin Psul Machshava mi-Psul ha-Guf. One derives a thought-based invalidity from another thought-based invalidity, not from a physical defect. This is a reasonable and compelling argument.

Rabbi Yehoshua then offers an improved argument. He accepts the framework of comparing thought to thought, but invokes a different example: Donin Psul she-ein bo Karet mi-Psul she-ein bo Karet. Chutz Limkomo has no Karet; therefore derive it from Ba'al Mum, which also never carries Karet — and not from Chutz Lizmano, which does. This argument is weaker on its face, since the severity of the punishment does not necessarily speak to the substantive character of the Psul. But Rabbi Yehoshua then adds a stronger point: V'od Nidunenu mi-Shelo Lishma. Let us derive Chutz Limkomo from the case of Shelo Lishma. That too is a Psul Machshava — a thought-based invalidity — and it also has no Karet, and in that case everyone agrees Lo Kidesh Halechem. So why learn Chutz Limkomo from Chutz Lizmano? There is an equally valid thought-based model where the bread is not sanctified.

At this point, the arguments seem fairly evenly matched. If anything, our intuition would remain with Rabbi Eliezer: Chutz Lizmano and Chutz Limkomo are paired throughout the Torah and throughout Shas. And yet: Ve-shatak Rabbi Eliezer — Rabbi Eliezer fell silent. The Gemara interprets this silence not as a draw but as concession: Rabbi Eliezer ultimately admitted that Rabbi Yehoshua was correct, and that Chutz Limkomo does not sanctify the bread.

This outcome requires explanation, since from a purely logical standpoint the argument seemed to favor Rabbi Eliezer. The Gemara's presentation remains perplexing without further elaboration, and Tosafot grapples with it at length.

### Chutz Limkomo Debate

Tosafot raises the deeper question: even granting that there are two competing models, why should Chutz Lizmano — which is a greater Psul, carrying Karet — retain the power to sanctify the bread, while Chutz Limkomo — in our ordinary understanding a weaker version of Piggul — would not? The apparent irony is that the more severe disqualification results in Kidesh Halechem, while the less severe does not.

The answer Tosafot proposes — and which the shiur identifies as the most compelling explanation — turns on the concept of Meratzeh L'Piggulo. The Torah states Lo Yeiratzeh with respect to Piggul, which implies that for something to be Piggul it must be Meratzeh in all other respects — it must be otherwise fit for acceptance. The halachic mechanism of Piggul involves a kind of bracketing: we set aside the Piggul thought and ask whether, but for that thought, the korban would have been Meratzeh. If yes, then the Piggul takes effect. What this means is that when evaluating a korban affected by Chutz Lizmano, we are able, within the framework of Piggul, to suspend the disqualifying element and view the shechita as having been a valid one — Meratzeh L'Piggulo. That retrospective validity is what allows the shechita to sanctify the bread.

Chutz Limkomo, however, does not operate within the Piggul framework. There is no mechanism for looking at a Chutz Limkomo shechita and saying, "bracket the Psul — was it otherwise Meratzeh?" That lens simply does not apply. And therefore, without that capacity to retroactively view the shechita as valid, there is no basis to say Kidesh Halechem. The same logic applies to Shelo Lishma and to Ba'al Mum: in none of those cases do we invoke the concept of Meratzeh, and therefore the Psul prevents the shechita from sanctifying the bread.

Tosafot adds a further observation: the reason we have not encountered this distinction anywhere in Zevachim or in other Gemaras is that this is a subtle difference that only manifests when the shechita is called upon to affect something external to itself — namely, the bread. With respect to the korban itself, the shechita is equally Kadosh regardless of which Psul is present. It is only when asking whether the shechita has the power to extend Kedusha to the bread — a derivative Kedusha — that this slight distinction between Chutz Lizmano and Chutz Limkomo becomes operative.

The Gemara then presents an additional discussion. Ismar: a Chatat that was slaughtered with a thought of Chutz Lizmano — if it was placed on the Mizbe'ach, it is not taken down, since im alu lo yeired applies to Piggul. But if it was slaughtered with a thought of Chutz Limkomo — Rava says Tered, take it down; Rabbah says Lo Tered. The Gemara notes that explicit Beraitot elsewhere in Shas state that im alu lo tered applies equally to Chutz Lizmano and Chutz Limkomo, which makes this debate startling. Tosafot is deeply troubled by it and considers various resolutions, including emending the text from Chatat to Todah, in order to confine this entire discussion to the limited context of Kidesh Halechem.

The Gemara connects Rava's position to Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbah's to Rabbi Eliezer. It then notes that V'hadar beih Rabbah le-gabei de-Rava — Rabbah ultimately reversed his position and agreed with Rava, just as Rabbi Eliezer had fallen silent before Rabbi Yehoshua. The Gemara then presents a counter-tradition: even if Rabbi Eliezer ultimately conceded to Rabbi Yehoshua on Kidesh Halechem, Rabbah did not necessarily follow suit on the question of the Mizbe'ach. The reason Rabbi Eliezer conceded was that there existed a competing model — Shelo Lishma — which provided an equally valid basis for saying Lo Kidesh. But regarding im alu lo tered, there is no competing model, because all psulei machshava — including Shelo Lishma — are subject to im alu lo tered. There is therefore no reason to treat Chutz Limkomo differently from Chutz Lizmano on that question. The difference, if it exists at all, applies only to Kidesh Halechem, precisely because in that domain there are competing models pointing in different directions.

The Gemara concludes this remarkable discussion by noting that in any case, according to Rabbi Meir's version, the world returns to its normal equilibrium: Chutz Lizmano and Chutz Limkomo are identical, both result in Kidesh Halechem, and the only debate concerns Ba'al Mum. The Gemara returns to explain Rabbi Eliezer's position on Ba'al Mum in light of the framework of psulo kodem shechita.

According to the Gemara, Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that Ba'al Mum results in Kidesh Halechem is limited to Dukin she-ba'ayin — a cataract of the eye, a barely noticeable blemish — and is specifically in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that for such a minor, unnoticeable Mum, im alu lo yeired: if the animal were placed on the Mizbe'ach, it would not be taken down. Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning, then, is that although this Mum predated the shechita, it is not so devastating a Psul that it renders the shechita entirely meaningless. Since this animal could theoretically remain on the Mizbe'ach, it retains sufficient sanctity that the shechita is still powerful enough to be Mekadesh Halechem. By contrast, a major Mum that would require the animal to be removed from the Mizbe'ach would prevent the shechita from sanctifying the bread, because there the Psul is too central.

Rabbi Yehoshua responds that this distinction may apply to the animal itself, but not to the bread. When it comes to the derivative Kedusha of the bread, even a minor Psul that predates the shechita is sufficient to interrupt the capacity to sanctify. Only a thought-based Psul that operates within the Piggul framework — where meratzeh l'piggulo applies — can coexist with Kidesh Halechem.

One might object that if the debate turns on the nuance of Dukin she-ba'ayin, the Mishna ought to have stated that explicitly. The shiur acknowledges this difficulty and notes that the simpler reading of the debate may be the one offered earlier: Rabbi Eliezer holds that a korban-level Psul — a Mum, a wrong thought — does not prevent a technically valid shechita from being Mekadesh, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds that any Psul predating the shechita prevents it. But that is not how the Gemara frames it; the Gemara's own resolution is the one based on Dukin she-ba'ayin and im alu lo yeired.

### Eliezer: Same as Pigul

The Mishna adds: Shelo Lishma — if the Toda was slaughtered without the proper intention of being a Toda — then Lo Kidesh Halechem, the bread is not sanctified. This is not because the korban is Pasul; in fact, Shelo Lishma ordinarily leaves the korban Kasher, only it is lo alu l'ba'alim l'shem chova. The reason the bread is not sanctified in this case was derived in a previous discussion from the pasuk al zevach todah shlamav — the korban must be slaughtered as a Toda for its bread to become Kadosh.

The conceptual reason is that what links the bread to the animal in the first place — what makes the shechita of the korban relevant to the bread — is the animal's identity as a Toda. If one is not slaughtering it as a Toda, there is no basis for the connection between the korban and the bread, and so the bread cannot be sanctified. One might ask whether Shelo l'shem ba'alim — slaughtering with intent for the wrong owner — would similarly prevent Kidesh Halechem. The pasuk reads al zevach todah shlamav, with the emphasis on its identity as a Toda, and so the intent to slaughter it for the wrong person, while it may affect who is yotzei chova, arguably does not sever the animal's identity as a Toda. The question is an interesting one that warrants further research.

The Mishna includes parallel cases: the Eil Miluim and the Shnei Kavsei Atzeret — both instances of Shelamim accompanied by bread — and states that if they too were slaughtered Shelo Lishma, Lo Kidesh Halechem.

## Psulo Kodem Shechita

### Yehoshua: Learn Shelo

Rav Papa notes a curiosity: why does the Mishna mention the Eil Miluim, which is a purely historical case — it occurred only at the time of the inauguration of the Mishkan — rather than the Eil Nazir, which is the practically relevant example of a Shlamim accompanied by bread? The Eil Nazir is more common and, to the extent any of this is practically relevant, more useful to discuss. The Gemara answers: Ikar milsa nokat — the Tanna preferred to refer back to the first instance. The first time the Torah linked bread to a Shlamim was at the Miluim, and so the Tanna anchored his discussion there, even at the cost of citing a case of only historical interest.

## Eliezer/Yehoshua Debate

### Silence Indicates Conces…

The Mishna now turns from the bread to the Nesachim — the wine libations — and their relationship to the korban. Any Olah or Shlamim requires an accompanying Mincha of flour and oil and a certain amount of wine; as the Musaf liturgy reflects: Minchasam ve-Niskeihem ke-mishpat, shlosha esronim la-par, shnei esronim la-ayil. Unlike the bread of the Toda, which must be brought on the same day as the korban and is tightly bound to it, the Nesachim have an important independence: Niskeihem afilu mi-kan ve-ad asara yamim — the Nesachim may be brought up to ten days after the korban itself. This fundamental difference in the structure of the relationship between the korban and the Nesachim is what makes the following discussion so significant.

### Meratzeh L'Piggulo

The Mishna states: Ha-Nesachim she-Kiddshu bi-kli — Nesachim that were already sanctified through placement in a Kli Sharet — ve-nimtza Zevach Pasul — and the korban was found to be Pasul — im yesh Zevach acher, Yakrivu imo: if there is another korban available, bring the Nesachim with that one. Ve-im lav, Yipslu be-Lina: if there is no other korban, the Nesachim will become Pasul through Lina — by remaining overnight.

The simple reading of this Mishna is straightforward: the shechita of the Zevach has nothing to do with the Kedusha of the Nesachim. They were sanctified through the Kli Sharet independently. The Mishna is drawing a direct contrast with the bread of the Toda: whereas the bread's Kedusha derives from the shechita, the Nesachim's Kedusha derives from the Kli alone. If the korban is Pasul, the Nesachim are unaffected — go find another korban and use them there. If no other korban is available and the Nesachim have already been sanctified in the Kli, then they will eventually become Pasul through Lina. The whole Gemara that follows, as we will see, ultimately struggles mightily against this simple reading — and the simple reading will prevail.

### Mum vs. Treifa Gap

Ze'iri, however, makes a bold and surprising claim: Ein ha-Nesachim mitkadshim ela bi-shchitat ha-Zevach. The Nesachim are also only sanctified through the slaughtering of the korban, just as the bread of the Toda is. His source is the pasuk Zevach u-Nesachim, davar yom be-yomo — the korban and its Nesachim are linked by the Torah. This places Ze'iri in direct tension with the plain reading of the Mishna.

### Rabbi Akiva Minor Mumim

The Gemara now asks: if Ze'iri is correct that the shechita sanctifies the Nesachim, how can our Mishna say that if the Zevach was Pasul the Nesachim may be used for another korban? If the shechita sanctified the Nesachim and the shechita was Pasul, surely the Nesachim would be bound up with that invalid korban. The Gemara resolves this by reinterpreting the phrase ve-nimtza Zevach Pasul: it does not mean the Psul occurred at the shechita; rather, lo d'ipsal bi-Zrika — the Psul occurred only at the Zrika. The shechita was valid and therefore did sanctify the Nesachim; the problem arose later, at the stage of Zrika.

This resolution is already forced, since the Mishna's language of nimtza Zevach Pasul most naturally suggests the shechita itself was Pasul. More fundamentally, even if we accept this reinterpretation, a deeper problem remains: if the shechita links the Nesachim to the korban, how can the Nesachim be reassigned to an entirely different korban?

### Eliezer Minor Mum Logic

The Gemara addresses this by invoking the earlier discussion — recalled from approximately two months earlier in the course of learning — about the Shtei Halechem and the Kivsei Atzeret. There, Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon held that two independent stages of the avodah — shechita and Zrika — each operate as Matir, and that without both working correctly, the bread is not sanctified. Rabbi, by contrast, held that the shechita alone, as one stage, was sufficient to sanctify the bread even if the Zrika was subsequently performed incorrectly.

The Gemara asks: is Ze'iri's position compatible only with Rabbi, who holds that one stage of the two-stage process is sufficient? The Gemara answers no — even Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon would agree here, in the specific case at hand. What is that case? Kegon she-kibel daman be-kos ve-nishpach — the blood was received properly in a vessel but then spilled before Zrika could be performed. In this circumstance, Rabbi Shimon's principle of Kol ha-omed lizrok ke-zaruak dami applies: anything that was ready to be thrown is considered as if it had been thrown. Since all that remained was the Zrika and the blood was fit for it, the situation is treated as if the Zrika had already occurred — at least for the purpose of establishing Kedusha — even though the act of Zrika was never performed.

The critical distinction is between spilling the blood — where the Zrika was never done but never invalidated — and performing the Zrika Shelo Lishma — where one actively ruined that stage. If the second stage is never invalidated but simply left undone, ke-zaruak dami gives us credit for having reached the point where it could have been done, and the Kedusha is established. If, however, the second stage was actively performed incorrectly, it cannot be retroactively treated as valid.

### Yehoshua: All Mumim Block

Even granting all of the above, a major difficulty remains: if the shechita of Korban A sanctified the Nesachim and linked them to it, how can those Nesachim be brought with an entirely different Korban B — one whose shechita had no relationship to these Nesachim whatsoever? The Gemara notes the analogy to Rav Chisda's ruling: Shemen she-hifrishu le-shmo Mincha zo Pasul le-shmo Mincha acheres — oil designated for one Mincha cannot be used for another Mincha. If mere designation creates that restriction, all the more so when the shechita itself was the act of sanctification.

### Chatas Chutz Limkomo

Rav Yannai answers: Lev Beis Din Masneh Aleihem. Beis Din stipulates at the outset that if the Nesachim turn out to be needed for another korban, they shall be considered as never having been designated exclusively for the original one. This stipulation preserves the freedom to use them wherever needed. One might immediately ask: is this principle applicable to a private korban, or only to communal offerings — where Beis Din has clear authority? Indeed, this question is precisely what someone in the shiur raises, and it is noted that the principle of Lev Beis Din Masneh is very often invoked specifically in the context of communal korbanos. The question of whether it extends to private korbanos remains to be examined.

### Rava: Remove It

The Gemara then raises another objection. If we can make such stipulations, why not do the same for the Shemen that Rav Chisda says cannot be reassigned? The Gemara answers: Shemen gufa de-Mincha hu — the oil is not merely assigned to the Mincha, it is a direct constituent of it. One cannot restipulate that an ingredient will become an ingredient of a different offering.

A further challenge: if Beis Din can stipulate that the item was never formally consecrated to the original korban, why not simply say that it reverts to Chulin entirely? The Gemara answers: Gezeira shema yomru motzin mi-Kli Sharet le-Chulin. People will observe that an item that was in a Kli Sharet has now become ordinary property, and they will draw the erroneous conclusion that sanctified items can revert to Chulin — which they cannot. Similarly, there is a concern that people will observe Nesachim being transferred from one korban to another and mistakenly conclude that this is ordinarily permissible, not understanding that a special stipulation was in place.

### Rabbah Reverses

The Gemara introduces the baraita of Matya ben Yehuda, which specifies: Kegon she-haya Zevach zavuach be-osa sha'a — the case where another korban had already been slaughtered at that very moment. The reason this addresses the Gezeira shema concern is that there is no opportunity for observers to be confused: the Nesachim are immediately assigned to a korban that was already slaughtered and waiting. There is no visible transfer, no prolonged period of ambiguity.

### Gemara Contra

The Gemara then asks: what if there is no such already-slaughtered korban available? Aval ein Zevach zavuach be-osa sha'a — what then? The Mishna itself says: Yipslu be-Lina. And the Gemara notes that the Mishna should therefore have stated explicitly: Be-mah devarim amurim — in what circumstances may the Nesachim be used for another korban? Only when another korban was already slaughtered at that moment. But if there was no such korban, then Na'ase ke-mi she-Yipslu be-Lina — it is as if the Nesachim have already become Pasul through Lina. The Gemara confirms: hacha nami ka-ma — that is indeed the intended meaning of the Mishna.

All of this amounts to an extraordinarily forced reading. The Mishna's plain language does not suggest any of these qualifications. And a fundamental conceptual tension remains: if the shechita of Korban A is what created the Kedusha of the Nesachim, then Beis Din's stipulation effectively decouples that Kedusha from Korban A and transfers it to Korban B — whose shechita never had any relationship to these Nesachim at all. This is a very strange result if one insists that shechita is the operative mechanism.

### Timing Difference

The Gemara now asks whether Rabbi Shimon — whose principle of ke-zaruak dami was invoked to support Ze'iri's position — actually accepts the concept of Lev Beis Din Masneh. The Gemara cites a tradition: Ve-amar Rav Idi bar Avin amar Rav Amram amar Rabbi Yitzchak amar Rabbi Yochanan: Temidim shelo hutzrechu la-tzibur — communal Temidim purchased with public funds that turn out to be surplus (for instance, because the animal that was lost was subsequently found) — Rabbi Shimon holds Ein nifdin Temimim, they cannot be redeemed because they have no Mum. The Chachamim, however, hold Nifdin Temimim — they may be redeemed, invoking the principle of Lev Beis Din Masneh Aleihem. Rabbi Shimon explicitly does not accept this principle.

Since the entire analysis supporting Ze'iri was built on Rabbi Shimon's framework — both ke-zaruak dami and the two independent stages — and Rabbi Shimon does not accept Lev Beis Din Masneh, the structure begins to collapse. How can we invoke Lev Beis Din Masneh within a discussion premised on Rabbi Shimon's rulings?

### Rav Chisda Objection

The Gemara answers: Shani hasam de-is lehu takanta bi-re'iya — the case of the extra Tamid is different because there is a practical solution available. The surplus animal can be allowed to develop a Mum naturally, at which point it can be redeemed. There is no need to invoke Lev Beis Din Masneh because the problem has another resolution. Tosafot in Menachot adds that the animal could also be brought as an Olah, functioning as Kayitz ha-Mizbe'ach. When a solution exists, we do not need to say Lev Beis Din. In the case of the Nesachim, if we cannot transfer them, there is no solution — they will simply become Pasul through Lina. It is precisely because there is no alternative that Lev Beis Din Masneh is invoked.

### Beis Din Stipulation

The accumulated weight of all these difficulties — the forced reading of the Mishna's language, the conceptual strangeness of decoupling the Nesachim from the shechita that supposedly sanctified them, the tension with Rabbi Shimon's rejection of Lev Beis Din, the requirement to limit the permissible transfer to a case where another korban was already slaughtered at that exact moment — all of this argues powerfully for the simple reading of the Mishna. The simple reading distinguishes the Nesachim from the bread of the Toda precisely because the Nesachim may be brought on a different day and are not closely bound to the korban. Their Kedusha derives from the Kli Sharet, not from the shechita. The Mishna is making exactly this contrast. It is Ze'iri's contrary position, insisting that shechita sanctifies the Nesachim just as it sanctifies the bread, that creates all of the difficulties that the Gemara then labors so strenuously to resolve.

And indeed, the Gemara notes that Ze'iri's position may itself be limited to the circumstance where the korban and the Nesachim were brought together on the same occasion. Where they were brought on different days, Ze'iri would concede that the shechita could not have sanctified the Nesachim. But again, that very concession further undermines Ze'iri's position — if the shechita's capacity to sanctify the Nesachim depends on their being brought together, that suggests the operative principle is not really the shechita at all.

The conclusion stands: the simple sense of the Mishna, and the more defensible halachic position, is that Nesachim are sanctified by the Kli, not by the shechita of the Zevach. And with that, we complete the daf.

# Menachot 80

## Todah & Derivatives

### Mishnah Overview

Daf 80 of Menachot continues the tractate's engagement with the todah offering, a korban that carries a distinctive bread requirement: forty loaves accompanying the sacrifice, comprising thirty matzah and ten chametz. Because the todah is thus intimately bound up with a minchah-type obligation, it finds its natural place in Menachot. The sugya opens by examining which animals, though possessing the kedushah of a todah, are nonetheless exempt from that bread requirement — and it proceeds to develop a series of increasingly nuanced principles about the relationship between the todah and its accompanying lechem.

### Baraita Derivation

The Mishnah at the bottom of 79b presents three cases in which an animal bearing the kedushah of a todah does not require bread. The first is the vlad todah: since a female animal may serve as a todah, its offspring inherits a todah kedushah — yet it is not the todah itself. The second is the temurah: the Torah prohibits exchanging a sanctified animal, but if one attempts to do so, the second animal acquires kedushah even as the first retains it. The third case is הפריש תודה ואבדה והפריש אחרת תחתיה — one designated a todah, it was lost, and so a second was sanctified in its stead; the first was then found, leaving both animals standing. One of them will serve as the todah proper; the other bears only a derived kedushah.

In all these cases, the Mishnah rules einah te'unah lechem, as the verse states, וְהִקְרִיב עַל זֶבַח הַתּוֹדָה — the todah requires bread, but not its child, not its substitute, and not its temurah. Only the todah itself carries the bread obligation.

### Textual Analysis

A baraita elaborates the derivation. The verse reads: זֹאת תּוֹרַת זֶבַח הַשְּׁלָמִים אִם עַל תּוֹדָה יַקְרִיבֶנּוּ וְהִקְרִיב עַל זֶבַח הַתּוֹדָה חַלּוֹת מַצּוֹת בְּלוּלֹת בַּשֶּׁמֶן רְקִיקֵי מַצּוֹת מְשׁוּחִים בַּשֶּׁמֶן. The baraita asks: if one separated a todah, it was lost, a second was sanctified in its stead, and then the first was found — leaving both animals present — how do we know that either one may be brought to fulfill the obligation, and that whichever is brought may be accompanied by its bread? The answer is derived from the phrase אִם עַל תּוֹדָה יַקְרִיבֶנּוּ — whichever is the todah, either may be brought.

One might then suppose that the second animal — the one not brought — also requires bread. The baraita therefore derives from יַקְרִיבֶנּוּ, "he shall bring it" — one, not two. Only one todah receives the bread; the other does not.

### Kapara Condition

The baraita now turns to a sharper reading of the pasuk. The phrase אִם עַל תּוֹדָה יַקְרִיבֶנּוּ contains the word al, which had initially been read together with toda as a unified phrase. Parsed separately, however, im al toda — "if upon a toda," that is, something that stands over or derives from a toda — the word al signals that even derivative animals, those not directly sanctified to serve as the toda itself, are included in the category of animals that may be brought as an offering.

### Obligatory vs. Free-will

Having established through im al toda that derivative animals — the vlad and the temurah — may nonetheless be brought as offerings, the baraita considers whether they should also require bread. One might argue that since they have not been displaced by another animal competing for the same obligation, perhaps they should carry the full bread requirement. The verse responds with the phrase וְהִקְרִיב עַל זֶבַח הַתּוֹדָה חַלּוֹת מַצּוֹת, where al zevach hatodah limits the bread obligation to the animal actually serving as the todah itself. Derivative animals may be offered but do not require bread. The principle is thus: im al toda expands the category of animals eligible to be brought; al zevach hatodah limits the bread requirement to the todah proper. The baraita concludes: תּוֹדָה טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם וְלֹא וְלָדָהּ וְלֹא חֲלִיפָתָהּ וְלֹא תְמוּרָתָהּ טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם.

---

## Bread & Kapara

### Todah Nedava

Three lines from the bottom of 79b, the Gemara introduces a statement transmitted by Rav Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא לְאַחַר כַּפָּרָה אֲבָל לִפְנֵי כַּפָּרָה טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם. The ruling that bread is not required applies only after kapara has been achieved — that is, after the sacrifice has been legitimately offered and the obligation fulfilled. Before kapara, the animal would require bread. The Gemara then devotes considerable effort to unpacking what case this distinction is meant to address.

### Vlad Nedava

Rabbi Abin challenges Rabbi Yochanan's formulation by asking on which case the before/after kapara distinction actually applies — a necessary question, since different cases yield different results.

### Vlad Chova

The first candidate is chalufei todah chova: one who had a personal obligation — either through a vow (harei alai) or through the circumstances that Chazal identified as giving rise to a todah obligation, such as crossing a desert or a sea — designated an animal as a todah, it was lost, and a substitute was sanctified. This is precisely the case analyzed in the baraita at the daf's opening. But as Rabbi Abin notes, the distinction between lifnei kapara and le'achar kapara is already explicit there: before either animal has been brought, both are lifnei kapara and whichever is offered gets the bread; once one has been offered and the obligation is satisfied, the other is le'achar kapara and receives no bread. Since the baraita already teaches this, Rabbi Yochanan's statement would be adding nothing. אִי לִפְנֵי כַּפָּרָה תְּנִינָא, אִי לְאַחַר כַּפָּרָה תְּנִינָא — both sides of the distinction were already taught.

### Shevach Hekdesh

The Gemara then proposes that Rabbi Yochanan may be speaking of chalufei todah nedava — a free-will todah with no underlying personal obligation. In this case, if the todah is lost and a substitute is sanctified, the person has incurred no obligation; the first animal was sanctified as a voluntary offering. The Gemara concludes, however, that this cannot be Rabbi Yochanan's case either, because here בֵּין לִפְנֵי כַּפָּרָה בֵּין לְאַחַר כַּפָּרָה טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם — both before and after the first todah has been offered, the second also requires bread. Since there is no obligation being discharged, each animal is simply another todah in its own right. מַרְבֶּה בְּתוֹדוֹת הוּא — one is simply bringing additional todot.

### Abaye's Analysis

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan must be speaking of vlad todah chova — the offspring of an obligatory todah. In this case, there is a personal obligation, the todah gives birth, and the question is whether the offspring may be used to discharge the obligation and whether it requires bread.

The ruling: לִפְנֵי כַּפָּרָה טָעוּן לֶחֶם, לְאַחַר כַּפָּרָה אֵין טָעוּן לֶחֶם. Before the mother has been offered — lifnei kapara — the vlad requires bread. After the mother has been offered — le'achar kapara — the vlad does not. The Gemara notes that one might have assumed the opposite: since the vlad is always a derivative animal, it should never require bread, regardless of whether the mother has been offered. The question then is why it would ever require bread at all.

### Chilufei Cases

The answer lies in Rabbi Yochanan's foundational principle: דְּקָסָבַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָדָם מִתְכַּפֵּר בְּשֶׁבַח הֶקְדֵּשׁ — a person can achieve atonement through the increase of hekdesh. When a sanctified animal gives birth, the offspring represents a natural increase, a shevach hekdesh. Rabbi Yochanan holds that in the case of an obligatory offering, this natural increase has the power to satisfy the owner's obligation — the offspring can serve, in effect, as the obligatory sacrifice itself. It is, in Rabbi Yochanan's view, akin to the principle of ubar yerech imo, the fetus as an extension of the mother: whether the animal became pregnant before or after it was sanctified (as Tosafot clarifies), the offspring carries sufficient connection to the original sanctity to discharge the obligation.

Consequently, if one brings the vlad of an obligatory todah before the mother has been offered, that vlad is functioning as the todah itself — it is satisfying the personal obligation — and it therefore requires bread. However, once the mother has been brought and the obligation discharged, the vlad is no more than a derivative animal with todah kedushah; it is le'achar kapara and receives no bread. This is the precise distinction Rabbi Yochanan is drawing.

### Chatas vs. Todah

Abaye independently investigated which case Rabbi Yochanan's statement was addressing and arrived at the same conclusion: the reference is to vlad todah chova. This is confirmed by a parallel citation — אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן — which explicitly states the relevant case. Chalufei todah nedava, the substitute for a free-will todah, requires bread both before and after — מַרְבֶּה בְּתוֹדוֹת הוּא, each is simply an additional todah. But vlad todah chova: לִפְנֵי כַּפָּרָה טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם, לְאַחַר כַּפָּרָה אֵינָהּ טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם.

---

## Shmuel's Principle

### Five Chatot

The Gemara introduces a parallel principle from Shmuel: חָמֵשׁ בְּחַטָּאת מֵתָה בְּתוֹדָה אֵין טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם, חָמֵשׁ בְּחַטָּאת רוֹעָה בְּתוֹדָה טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם. Shmuel draws a direct correspondence between the laws of the chatas and the todah: any scenario in which a chatas animal must be left to die has its parallel in a todah scenario where the animal does not require bread; and any scenario in which a chatas animal is left to graze until it develops a blemish and is then redeemed has its parallel in a todah scenario where the animal does require bread.

### Rav Amram's Q

The five types of chatas that must die are encoded in the acronym ViTiMNA. Vav stands for vlad chatas — the offspring of a chatas, which cannot be brought for the sin and must be left to die. Tet stands for temuras chatas — the temurah of a chatas, which likewise cannot be used for the sin and must die. Mem stands for mesu ba'aleha — cases where the owners have died, rendering the offering purposeless with respect to the sin. Nun stands for nevda — the animal became lost, a substitute was sanctified and used, and the original was then found; one was brought and the other must die. Ayin stands for avar shnato — the animal has passed its first year and is therefore no longer eligible as a chatas.

Of these five, the ayin — avar shnato — is simply not relevant to the todah, since a todah has no such age requirement. The remaining four categories — vlad, temurah, nevda (the niskaper ba'acher case), and mesu ba'aleha — in principle map onto todah scenarios where bread would not be required.

### Rebbe vs. Chachamim

Rav Amram raises an objection against Shmuel by citing the baraita with which the daf opens: the case of הִפְרִישׁ תּוֹדָתוֹ וְאָבְדָה וְהִפְרִישׁ אַחֶרֶת תַּחְתֶּיהָ וְנִמְצֵאת הָרִאשׁוֹנָה, where one brings whichever animal he wishes and the second receives no bread. The baraita appears to confirm Shmuel's correspondence: the second todah gets no bread, just as by the parallel chatas the second would die.

The objection, however, rests on a closer examination. By a chatas in that same scenario, there is actually a dispute. The baraita regarding chatas — הִפְרִישׁ חַטָּאתוֹ וְאָבְדָה וְהִפְרִישׁ אַחֵר תַּחְתָּיו וְנִמְצְאָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה וַהֲרֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם עוֹמְדִין — records a dispute. Rebbe says: you bring whichever you wish and the second must die. But the case in question is where both animals are found simultaneously, before either has been offered.

### Shmuel & R. Shimon

The Chachamim disagree with Rebbe. The Chachamim hold that a chatas dies only when it was found after the owners were already atoned through the second animal — אֵין חַטָּאת מֵתָה אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּמְצֵאת לְאַחַר שֶׁנִּתְכַּפְּרוּ הַבְּעָלִים. If the first was found before either was offered — kodem sheniskapru — then since both were still potentially usable, the unused one does not die; rather, it grazes. According to the Chachamim, then, the case of niskaper ba'acher where both animals are simultaneously present is a case of ro'eh, not mesa. Yet by a todah the second animal does not get bread. This would violate Shmuel's principle: a case of ro'eh by chatas should correspond to bread by todah, yet here by todah there is no bread.

### Shmuel's Chiddush

The Gemara resolves that שְׁמוּאֵל כְּרַבִּי סְבִירָא לֵיהּ — Shmuel holds like Rebbe. Shmuel does not distinguish between whether the first animal was found before or after the second was offered; in any scenario where niskaper ba'acher occurs, the unused chatas dies. This aligns perfectly with our case: whether both todot are standing before you simultaneously or one is found afterward, the one not used for the obligation does not get bread, and the corresponding chatas would die.

### Mesu Ba'aleha Gap

If Shmuel holds like Rebbe, a new question arises: what scenario would Rebbe recognize as a case of ro'eh, where the unused chatas grazes rather than dies? If Rebbe says that any case of niskaper ba'acher — in any configuration — results in the unused animal dying, it is difficult to find a chatas case that he would classify as ro'eh at all.

The Gemara answers with the scenario of Rav Oshaya: הִפְרִישׁ שְׁתֵּי חַטָּאוֹת לְאַחְרָיוּת מִתְכַּפֵּר בְּאֵיזוֹ מֵהֶן שֶׁיִּרְצֶה וְהַשְּׁנִיָּה תִּרְעֶה. Here, from the very outset, one separates two animals explicitly as backups for each other, with the intention that either may fulfill the obligation. Neither was lost; neither was designated as a replacement for a lost animal. Both were sanctified simultaneously as joint candidates for the obligation. In this case, the unused animal grazes, not dies — because, unlike the niskaper ba'acher scenario where one animal was temporarily unavailable, here both were always fully present and designated from the start.

However, the Gemara notes that in the todah parallel to this scenario — where two todot were separated together from the outset — the second still does not receive bread. The verse הַתּוֹדָה teaches that whatever the configuration, if two animals are competing to fill the same obligatory slot, only one receives bread. Shmuel's principle breaks down here: this is a case where the chatas grazes, yet the todah still does not get bread.

### Rabbi Abba

The Gemara therefore concludes that שְׁמוּאֵל כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן סְבִירָא לֵיהּ — Shmuel holds like Rabbi Shimon, who maintains that in all five chatas cases, without exception, the animal dies. Rabbi Shimon would apply the ruling of mesa to any scenario of niskaper ba'acher, including Rav Oshaya's case. Under this approach, there is no case of ro'eh for Shmuel, and his first principle — that wherever a chatas dies, the todah does not get bread — maps cleanly onto the Mishnah and baraita without contradiction.

But this raises a different problem: if Rabbi Shimon recognizes no ro'eh case at all, why did Shmuel state the second half of his principle — that wherever a chatas grazes, the todah does get bread? The Gemara answers: שְׁמוּאֵל נַמִּי חֲדָא קָאָמַר — Shmuel was in fact only stating the first part of his statement. He said only כָּל שֶׁבְּחַטָּאת מֵתָה בְּתוֹדָה אֵינָהּ טְעוּנָה לֶחֶם. Yet even this formulation seems to be teaching nothing new, since the Mishnah and baraita already cover the relevant cases. The Gemara therefore explains: לְאַפּוּקֵי מִדְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן — the purpose of Shmuel's statement is to reject Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yochanan holds that a person can achieve kapara through shevach hekdesh and therefore that the vlad of an obligatory todah, brought before the mother, requires bread. The vav of ViTiMNA stands for vlad chatas — since the vlad of a chatas must die, its counterpart in a todah does not get bread. Shmuel thereby rejects Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: דְּקָא מַשְׁמַע לָן דְּלָא — the vlad todah does not get bread even lifnei kapara.

### Owner-Possessed

Strikingly, the Gemara does not explore the case of mesu ba'aleha as it applies to the todah — that is, where the owners have died, a scenario in which a chatas must die. On the face of it, this presents a potential challenge to Shmuel's principle: why should the death of the owners prevent a todah from requiring bread? A todah is not inherently tied to an act of sin; there exists such a thing as a todas nedavah, a free-will todah entirely uncoupled from personal circumstance. It would seem logical that even if the owners died, the todah should still carry its bread requirement.

The Yerushalmi, in fact, takes exactly this position — that a todah whose owners died does require bread — which would constitute a direct contradiction to Shmuel's parallel. This question is not addressed anywhere in the Bavli, and it is notable that no Rishonim appear to have raised it explicitly. One commentator on the Yerushalmi does ask the question, but the silence in the Bavli remains striking.

---

## Todah & Bread

### Rava's Extension

Rabbi Abba introduces a principle that clarifies the nature of the relationship between the todah and its bread: זוֹ תּוֹדָה וְזוֹ לַחְמָהּ — if one separates out an animal and declares it a todah, then separately designates bread or flour for the accompanying lechem. אָבַד הַלֶּחֶם מֵבִיא לֶחֶם אַחֵר — if the bread is lost, one may bring substitute bread for the todah. But אָבְדָה תוֹדָה אֵינוֹ מֵבִיא תוֹדָה אַחֶרֶת — if the todah itself is lost, one may not bring another todah for the purpose of using this bread. The originally designated bread cannot simply be transferred to a new todah.

### Rav Kahana

The reasoning is: לֶחֶם לְגַבֵּי תוֹדָה וְאֵין תוֹדָה לְגַבֵּי לֶחֶם. The bread is an appurtenance of the todah; the todah is the possessor and the bread is the possessed. Substitute bread may be brought to serve the todah, because it is the todah that stands as the primary entity and may receive new bread. But if the todah is lost, the designated bread has lost its anchor; it is linked specifically to that todah and cannot be redirected to serve a different one.

### Asymmetry

Rava applies the same principle to money. If one sets aside funds for his todah and there is leftover money — מֵבִיא בָּהֶן לֶחֶם — the surplus may be used to purchase the accompanying bread, since the bread is encompassed within the todah designation. If, however, one sets aside funds specifically for the bread of his todah and there is leftover money — אֵין מֵבִיא בָּהֶן תּוֹדָה — that surplus may not be used to purchase the todah animal. Money designated for bread cannot be redirected to the todah itself.

### Setup

Rav Kahana grounds this asymmetry in a verse: וְהִקְרִיב עַל זֶבַח הַתּוֹדָה חַלּוֹת מַצּוֹת. Reading הַתּוֹדָה חַלּוֹת מַצּוֹת — the challot matzot are themselves part of the todah — Rav Kahana derives that the bread is subsumed under the name and category of the todah. Hence, money designated for the todah includes money for the bread, since the bread is a component of the todah.

### Rava's Analysis

But this derivation would seem to be symmetrical, raising a difficulty: if the bread is called a todah, then money designated for bread should equally be available for the todah animal. The Gemara resolves this with a precise formulation: לֶחֶם אִיקְרֵי תוֹדָה, תּוֹדָה לָא אִיקְרֵי לֶחֶם. The bread may be called todah — it is part of the todah — but the todah is not called bread. Money designated for the todah encompasses everything that goes by the name todah, including the bread. But money designated for bread encompasses only what goes by the name lechem, and the animal does not fall within that category. The bread is an extension of the animal, not the reverse.

---

## Triple Todot

### First Offered

Rava now presents an elaborate scenario. A person has an obligatory todah. The first animal is designated and then lost; a second animal is designated in its stead. The second is then also lost; a third animal is designated in the stead of the second. At this point, the first and second animals are both found, and all three stand together: number one, number two (which had been a substitute for number one), and number three (which had been a substitute for number two). The question is: whichever of the three is used to fulfill the obligation, how do the remaining two fare regarding the bread requirement?

### Third Offered

If one uses number one to fulfill the obligation, number two does not receive bread. Number two had been designated as a substitute for number one; they were both competing for the same obligatory slot. Since number one was brought and filled that slot, number two is not the actual todah, and does not get bread. Number three, however, does get bread. Number three had been designated as a substitute for number two. But with the benefit of hindsight, number two was never going to be the obligatory todah — its place was taken by number one. Number three, as a substitute for a non-obligatory animal, is therefore simply an additional todah being brought — מַרְבֶּה בְּתוֹדוֹת הוּא — and as such it receives bread. Notably, this means a derivative animal receives bread while the animal for which it was substituting does not — a striking result.

### Middle Offered

Conversely, if one uses number three to fulfill the obligation, number two again does not receive bread — this time because number two and number three were both competing for the same slot, and number three won out. Number one, however, does receive bread. Number one was the original todah, standing entirely on its own, not competing with any other animal for the obligation at the time it was designated. It receives bread in its own right.
