### Abaye's View

If one uses number two — the middle animal — then שְׁתֵּיהֶן אֵינָן טְעוּנוֹת לֶחֶם, neither number one nor number three receives bread. Number two was competing with number one for the first obligatory slot, and it was also the animal for which number three was designated as a substitute, placing two and three in competition for the second slot. Since number two fills the obligation, both number one (the other competitor for the obligation) and number three (whose principal, number two, turned out to be the actual todah) are left without bread.

### Abaye Simpler

Abaye offers a simpler and more sweeping analysis. אֲפִלּוּ נִתְכַּפֵּר בְּאַחַת מֵהֶן שְׁתֵּיהֶן אֵינָן טְעוּנוֹת לֶחֶם — regardless of which of the three animals is used, the remaining two never receive bread. כּוּלְּהוּ חֲלִיפֵי דַּהֲדָדֵי נִינְהוּ — all three are, in effect, substitutes for one another. Even though number three was designated as a substitute for number two and not directly for number one, the entire chain of substitution was directed toward satisfying the same single obligation. All three were competing, at some level, for the same box. Whichever animal enters that box, the other two are not the actual todah per se and therefore receive no bread.

---

---

# Menachot 81

## Three Animals Analysis

### Three Substitutes Setup

The daf opens in the middle of a broader discussion about the relationship of lachmei todah to the todah itself, particularly regarding what happens when a substitute is created. The Gemara introduces a parallel case involving a chatas. The text reads: *ve-chein le-inyan chataot* — the same halacha applies to a chatas.

The case unfolds as follows. You separated a chatas — *hifrish chatato* — and it was lost. You then designated a second animal in its place, and then the second was also lost, so you designated a third. Then the first one was found. Now all three stand before you. The relevant background halacha is that by a todah, a substitute that is not ultimately used does not receive bread; by a chatas, the unused substitute must die — *meisa*.

### Rava Pairwise

Rava's position is that you analyze the animals in sequential pairs. If you use the first animal for your chatas — *nitkaper berishona* — then the second dies, since it was the substitute chatas that went unused. But looking at the two-three pair: since the second never actually functioned as a chatas, the third was never truly a substitute chatas, and therefore need not die — it may graze until it develops a mum and is then redeemed — *tire*. Conversely, if you use the third animal, the second dies due to the three-two pairing, and the first is permitted to graze, again because the second never functioned as a chatas. If, however, you use the middle animal — *nitkaper bamtza'is* — then in the one-two pairing the first was the substitute for the second, and in the two-three pairing the third was the substitute for the second; both therefore have the status of an unused substitute chatas, and *shteihan yamusu* — both must die.

Abaye disagrees entirely. His position is *kulu chalifin de-hadadi ninhu* — they are not simply pairs; everything was created to replace the original lost animal, and they are all constant replacements of one another. Therefore, regardless of which animal you use, the other two are unused substitute chatot and must both die.

### Abaye All Die

The Gemara asks: *mai ve-chein* — why was it necessary to state this whole second case about a chatas? The parallel to the todah is obvious. The answer is that one might have thought Rava's logic applies only to a todah, because by a todah there always exists the possibility of simply being makreiv a new todah — if you designate another animal without a standing obligation it may be considered a brand-new todah rather than a substitute. That is what allows Rava to say that certain animals, not being paired with an ultimately used todah, are treated as independent todot and therefore do bring bread. But by a chatas, *de-leika le-meimar marbe be-chataot* — you cannot simply multiply chatot — so perhaps Rava would have conceded to Abaye's position. The Gemara therefore teaches us — *ka mashma lan* — that Rava maintains his pairing logic even by a chatas: if the animal something is paired with never functioned as a chatas, then that animal never acquired the status of a substitute chatas and need not die; it is simply allowed to graze.

---

## Rabbi Chiya Mixed

### Why Repeat Chatas

With that clarification behind us, Rabbi Chiya introduces an entirely new and considerably more vexing case — one that will consume the remainder of this daf and the first amud of the next before the Mishna resumes. *tani rabbi chiya*: you have a todah and its tmura. One brings bread and one does not — a tmura retains only a derivative kedusha and never receives bread — but they have become mixed up, so you no longer know which is which. Then one of them dies. Now you are left with one animal of uncertain identity.

*Chavratah ein lah takanah* — the remaining animal has no solution. You cannot bring it with bread, because if it is the tmura, the bread would constitute chulin b'azarah. You cannot bring it without bread, because if it is the todah, a todah brought without bread does not fulfill the obligation.

### Chiya Case Intro

The Gemara asks: *heichi na'avid* — what should be done? Should you bring bread with it? Perhaps it is the tmura, in which case the bread is chulin, and the problem of chulin b'azarah arises. Should you not bring bread? Then if it is the todah, *dilma toda hi*, you fail to fulfill the obligation.

This is an opportunity for Tosafot to analyze when exactly something becomes chulin b'azarah. Tosafot explains that the prohibition is not triggered simply by carrying non-sanctified items into the azarah. Rather, chulin b'azarah applies when the item is being presented as part of a korban. What makes these loaves fall into that category? The answer leads directly to the next point.

### Chullin Ba'azarah

At this juncture the Gemara makes explicit something that had not been stated until now: four of the loaves that are given to the kohen — out of the forty total — are waved together with the todah, just as the breast and thigh of a shelamim are waved. Since those four loaves are involved in the tenufah ritual, they are being actively presented as part of the korban. Tosafot further assumes that even before the formal ritual of tenufah, the very act of bringing the loaves into the Mikdash and associating them with the korban frames them as being presented in a korban context. This is what makes bringing them conditionally — knowing that they might not be required — a chulin b'azarah problem.

One might ask: why not bring the animal and then say conditionally that if this is the todah these loaves are its bread, and if not, then this bread is merely stam — ordinary food — and no chulin b'azarah results? The problem is precisely that. If you did not sanctify the loaves, they are chulin, and you are presenting chulin as part of a korban. If you did sanctify them conditionally — saying if I need them they are lachmei todah, and if I do not they are not — then in the case where they are not needed, you have brought sanctified-conditionally-unsanctified bread into the azarah in the context of a korban, which is still a chulin b'azarah concern.

The Gemara is quite interested in this puzzle. The amoraim seem to have treated it almost as an engaging riddle — how can one possibly solve this problem?

---

## Rabbi Chiya Mixed (II)

### Chullin Defined

The Gemara now systematically considers a series of attempted solutions and rejects each one. It opens: *heichi na'avid* — what shall we do?

First: why not simply bring bread and state conditionally, *ei hach d'kayma toda hi* — if the surviving animal is the todah, this is its bread; *v'ei lo*, and if not, let the bread revert to being chulin? The response is immediate: *v'chi machnisin chulin l'azarah* — you may not bring chulin into the azarah! Presenting the bread as part of the korban while it might not be sanctified is exactly the chulin b'azarah problem.

The Gemara then introduces a more sophisticated solution through the phrase *amru lemadim lifnei Rebbi* — students said before Rebbi. They proposed: bring a new behemah along with bread, and stipulate as follows. If the surviving animal is the tmura, the new animal is the todah and the bread is its bread. If the surviving animal is the todah, the bread belongs to that original todah and the new animal — *tehei achrayus* — should be a backup korban. The logic is elegant: a backup, like a chalifei todah, does not require bread. So regardless of which way the uncertainty resolves, exactly one animal needs bread, and the bread is present.

Rebbi responds: *lo tzericha de'amar harei zo* — the case here is precisely one where the person only said *harei zo*, designating a specific animal, rather than *harei alai*, accepting a personal obligation. The concept of achrayus — of designating a backup animal — operates only within the framework of a personal obligation. If I have no personal obligation, there is nothing for the backup to back up. Since he said harei zo, not harei alai, the concept of achrayus is inapplicable and the solution collapses.

One might ask: why not then simply say harei alai, create a personal obligation, and use the achrayus structure? The Gemara will address this at the very end of today's discussion.

### Initial Solutions

The Gemara now considers another proposal. Bring a new behemah with bread and stipulate: if the surviving animal is the tmura, *harei zu todah v'ha lachmah* — the new animal is the todah with its bread. If the surviving animal is the todah, the bread goes to it, and *v'ha tehei shelamim* — let the new animal be a shelamim.

This has real appeal. Either the new animal is a todah with bread, or it is a shelamim, and either way everything is kadosh and the bread is associated with an appropriate korban. No chulin b'azarah problem arises. However, Rebbi rejects this as well: *mishum d'ka memayet b'achilah d'shelamim* — because you would be limiting the eating time of the shelamim. A todah is eaten only for one day; a shelamim for two. If you designate the new animal as a shelamim but must treat it as a possible todah to be safe, you will restrict its eating to one day, thereby reducing the allotted eating time and potentially creating notar. The principle is *ein mevi'in kodashim l'veit hapesul* — you do not bring a korban into a situation in which less than its full eating time is available.

A third proposal is then put forward, this time by Levi directly to Rebbi. Bring a behemah with bread, and stipulate: if the surviving animal is the tmura, the new one is the todah with its bread. If the surviving one is the todah, the bread goes to it, and *v'ha tehei motar d'todah* — let the new animal be the motar of the todah, its leftover, which per our Mishna does not receive bread.

### Conditional Bread

Rebbi's response to Levi is famous for its sharpness: *k'midumeh ani she-ein lo moach b'kadkado* — it appears to me that whoever would suggest such a thing has no brain in his skull. The rebuke is softened somewhat by the distancing formulation — Rebbi says "he," not "you" — but the point is clear. *v'chi mafrishin techilah l'mosarot* — you cannot designate something ab initio as a motar. Motar is a result, not a category of kedusha one can impose in advance. You cannot sanctify an animal with the kedusha of notar todah from the outset. And as noted, the concept of achrayus is also unavailable here because the vow was harei zo, not harei alai.

### Backup Rejected

The discussion now shifts to the amoraic period. Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta was sitting before Rav Nachman and proposed yet another solution: bring a behemah with bread and stipulate as follows. If the surviving animal is the tmura, the new one is the todah and the bread is its bread. If the surviving animal is the todah, the bread goes to that todah, and *v'ha tehei tmura* — let the new animal be a tmura of the original todah, which would not require bread.

Rav Nachman's reply is even sharper than Rebbi's: *ani mari, arba'im b'katfeih v'chasher* — my master, forty lashes on his back and he thinks this is permitted? The Torah explicitly prohibits making a tmura: *lo yachalifenu v'lo yamir oto*. The proposal is to solve a halachic problem by having the person violate a lav and incur lashes. That is no solution at all.

---

## Bread Conditional (II)

### Rejection Chullin

The discussion continues among the amoraim. Rav Ila fell ill and Abaye and the rabanan came to pay a bikur cholim visit. As was customary, they sat and discussed Torah. One of them raised the following: *im ita l'de'Rabbi Yochanan* — if we rule like Rabbi Yochanan, who said *chutz l'chomat ha'azarah kadosh* — that the lachmei todah may be situated outside the wall of the azarah and still be considered kadosh — then the whole chulin b'azarah problem disappears. Earlier in the perek there had been a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on exactly this point: does the bread that accompanies the todah need to be inside the Mikdash at the time of the offering, or may it be anywhere within Yerushalayim? Rabbi Yochanan held that it may be anywhere within Yerushalayim.

The proposed solution: bring the bread and leave it outside the azarah wall. Stipulate: if the surviving animal is the todah, this bread is its bread — sitting validly outside the azarah per Rabbi Yochanan. If the animal is not the todah and the bread is not needed, then *lo lichol aleih kedusha* — the kedusha simply does not take effect, and there is no chulin b'azarah problem because the bread was never inside the azarah. If the kedusha did take effect, one eats the bread within the day as befits lachmei todah, and all is well.

### Backup Suggested

The Gemara immediately identifies the flaw: *mishum d'ika arba'ah l'hanif* — because there are the four loaves that must be given to the kohen and waved as a tenufah together with the animal. This is what makes their status as part of the korban so acute. Those four loaves must be inside the Mikdash for the tenufah. If you do the tenufah outside — *linfinhu avrai* — this is invalid, because whenever tenufah is required it must be performed *lifnei Hashem*, before God, meaning inside. If you bring them inside — *l'gavai* — *ka mayti chulin l'azarah* — you are back to the chulin b'azarah problem, since those loaves might not be sanctified. *hilkach lo efshar* — therefore this solution cannot work either.

### Split Conditional

Rav Sheshet brei d'Rav Idi raises yet another approach. He invokes an earlier discussion in the perek about Chizkiyah, who held that *kidshu arba'im mitoch shmonim* — if you bring eighty loaves and explicitly designate forty of them as kadosh, that designation takes effect on forty out of the eighty. Tosafot notes that this is not disputed when stated explicitly; the earlier debate concerned only ambiguous cases.

The proposed solution: bring a new behemah and eighty loaves, and stipulate as follows. If the surviving animal is the todah, *ha nami tehvei todah* — let this new animal also be a todah, and these eighty loaves serve both of them, forty each. If the surviving animal is the tmura, the new animal is the todah, and again the eighty loaves accompany it with forty being kadosh. The other forty are *achrayus* — backup loaves — and are not chulin b'azarah, because bringing items that serve a functional purpose for the korban, as backups or supports, is analogous to the famous account of Hillel, who would bring his animal into the Mikdash before being makdish it — since it was brought as part of the korban process, it was not considered chulin b'azarah.

The Gemara's objection concerns the four loaves that must be given to the kohen. If there are potentially two todot, eight loaves must be given to the kohen. But if some of those loaves were not actually required — because only one todah was ultimately present — then you have limited whose hands they can be eaten in, restricting them to kohanim rather than allowing them to be eaten by any Israelite. The Gemara treats this, to some degree, as the concern about *ein mevi'in kodashim l'veit hapesul* in relation to the four loaves, though the precise formulation is debated in the grisaot — some versions read *d'arba'ah*, of the four, and some read differently. Either way the Gemara does not find this satisfactory.

It is worth noting that the Gemara seems less troubled by the concern of performing unnecessary rituals — the tenufah — with items that do not require it, than it is by chulin b'azarah. As long as everything is kadosh, performing a ritual with something that technically did not require that ritual is not treated as a comparable problem. The chulin b'azarah issue is what drives the analysis throughout.

### Time Limit Problem

Rav Ashi said to Rav Kahana: consider another earlier ruling. Rabbi Yochanan said: *hifrish chatas me'uberes veyalda, ratza bah mitkaper ratza bivladah mitkaper* — if someone designated a pregnant animal as his chatas and it gave birth, he may choose to use either the mother or the offspring for atonement. The kedusha attaches equally to both, since the animal was sanctified while pregnant. This is not a case of creating a substitute — no human act of temurah was performed — but the child naturally inherits the full kedusha of the mother.

By analogy, one might solve the todah problem as follows. The whole difficulty arose because the vow was harei zo rather than harei alai, so the concept of achrayus was unavailable. But you do not need achrayus here. Get a pregnant behemah, sanctify it as a todah, wait for it to give birth, bring eighty loaves, and stipulate as follows. If the surviving original animal is the tmura, then both the mother and the child are todot, and the eighty loaves serve both. If the surviving animal is the todah, the mother is also a todah, the eighty loaves go to the two todot, and the child is motar todah — the leftover of a todah — which does not bring bread.

The key insight is that unlike Levi's rejected proposal, you are not designating anything ab initio as motar todah. Rather, you are creating motar todah naturally through the birth process. And unlike the standard halacha where motar todah does not receive bread, Rabbi Yochanan's principle — *ratza bah mitkaper ratza bivladah mitkaper* — grants the owner the choice to treat the child as a full todah in its own right or to treat it as motar todah. That flexibility is precisely what makes the conditional stipulation viable.

### Levi Motar Proposed

A sharp question arises from the audience: what about oto v'es beno — the prohibition against slaughtering a mother and its offspring on the same day? If you are bringing the mother and the child together, you cannot sacrifice both on the same day.

The answer is clear: bring the mother on one day and bring the child together with the uncertain original animal on the next day. The bread functions properly throughout: the mother definitively requires forty loaves; on the second day, either the leftover is the todah and the child is the motar todah, with the forty loaves going to the todah, or the leftover is the tmura and the child is a full todah, with the loaves going to it. The two days separate the two slaughterings and the atonement vow for the chatas requires the animal to be within a year, whereas a todah has no upper age limit, so the mother's eligibility is not a concern.

However, the Gemara ultimately rejects even this solution. *man leima lan* — who told us that Rabbi Yochanan means *im shiyuro meshuyar*, that the owner has a genuine choice to designate both mother and child as full independent todot? Perhaps Rabbi Yochanan's intent is only that the child can be used to fulfill the obligation — functioning through *adam mitkaper b'shvach hekdesh*, being atoned through the enhanced value of the hekdesh — but if the child is used, the mother automatically becomes motar todah, rather than both being simultaneously equal. If so, Rabbi Yochanan's ruling simply means that one of them serves as the todah and the other is its motar, without the owner having a free choice to configure them as two distinct todot. That limited reading of Rabbi Yochanan's opinion destroys the solution, because we cannot then say that in either branch of the stipulation both animals could simultaneously carry the full kedusha of a todah.

### Rabbi Rejects

The sugya reaches its final proposed solution in the amoraic period. Ravina came to Mahuza, where Rav Dimi bereih de-Rav Huna of Mahuza posed the following to him. The entire problem, he noted, stems from the fact that the vow was harei zo rather than harei alai — because without a personal obligation, the concept of achrayus is unavailable. So why not simply create a personal obligation? Say harei alai, take a new neder for a todah, bring two new animals and eighty loaves, and stipulate as follows. If the surviving original animal is the tmura, these two new animals are both todot, and the eighty loaves serve them. If the surviving original animal is the todah, then the first new animal — sanctified by harei alai — is also a todah, with the forty loaves going to the original and forty to the new one; and the third animal, designated conditionally, is an achrayus — a backup — which does not require bread.

This is structurally clean: three animals, but regardless of how the uncertainty resolves, exactly two require bread and one does not, and the eighty loaves cover the two that need them.

Ravina's response invokes the verse from Koheles: *tov asher lo sidor mi-she-tidor ve-lo teshalem* — better that you not make a vow than that you make one and fail to fulfill it. The Torah discourages making unnecessary nedarim. And you are proposing that this person should stand up and take an additional neder simply to solve a technical halachic impasse?

Tosafot acknowledges that in some circumstances — for example, where failing to solve the problem would permanently prevent a nezir from completing his nazirite term and bringing his korbanos — we might permit and even encourage a creative neder to resolve the situation. But here, the consequence of leaving the problem unsolved is merely that one animal remains in an uncertain state: it cannot be brought, and so it grazes until it develops a mum, is redeemed, and the money goes to הדיוט purposes. That outcome is not so severe as to justify encouraging a neder. And so the Gemara leaves Rabbi Chiya's case without a clean resolution.

It is striking that of all the proposed solutions, this last one is in some ways the most natural — and the Gemara's objection to it is somewhat unusual, given that the Gemara throughout the entire Talmud routinely assumes that people take nedarim and never once protests the practice the way it does here. But perhaps, as the discussion suggests, the Gemara was reluctant to allow what had been an engaging halachic puzzle to be resolved by so simple a measure as an ad hoc neder.

---

## Backup Without Oblig (II)

### Temura Proposed

With the extended discussion of Rabbi Chiya's case complete, the Gemara now turns to the next Mishna. The Mishna states: *ha'omer harei alai todah* — one who takes an obligation to bring a todah — *yavi hi ve-lachmah min ha-chullin* — must bring both the animal and its bread from non-sanctified money. This stands in contrast to ma'aser sheni. One might think that since ma'aser sheni funds are designated to buy food and eat it in Yerushalayim — which is precisely what a todah and its bread are — one could use ma'aser sheni money to fund the todah. The Mishna rules otherwise: the principle is *ein mevi'im davar min ha-chovah mima'os ma'aser sheni* — you cannot discharge a personal obligation using ma'aser sheni funds. You may only use such funds for non-obligatory korbanot.

This principle carries significant weight for certain poskim when addressing the contemporary question of ma'aser kesafim — whether one may use money set aside as ma'aser to pay for obligations such as children's tuition or shul membership. The extent to which ma'aser kesafim is modeled on ma'aser sheni — and specifically on the prohibition of using it to discharge pre-existing obligations — varies among poskim, but the present principle is a key source in that discussion.

### Temura Violation

The Mishna continues with variations. If one says *todah alai min ha-chullin ve-lachmah min ha-ma'aser* — I obligate myself to bring the todah from chullin but the bread from ma'aser — the stipulation is ineffective and both must come from chullin: *yavi hi ve-lachmah min ha-chullin*. The reason is that the todah is the ikar and the bread follows its status, as we established yesterday. Since the todah must come from chullin, the bread must as well, regardless of what the owner specified about the bread.

Conversely, if one says *todah min ha-ma'aser ve-lachmah min ha-chullin* — the todah from ma'aser and the bread from chullin — this works. But this formulation is best understood as one where the person never took a personal obligation in the first place. He is not saying *harei alai*, creating a chiyuv; he is saying, in effect, "Let this ma'aser money be used for a todah," investing it with the kedusha of a todah without a standing personal obligation. Since there is no personal obligation being discharged, the prohibition of using ma'aser funds for chovah does not apply.

If one says *hi ve-lachmah min ha-ma'aser* — both the animal and the bread from ma'aser — then one brings exactly as stated, since that is fully permitted in the scenario where there is no personal obligation.

Furthermore, the Mishna notes that even when use of ma'aser sheni funds for the bread is permitted, *lo yavi mechittei ma'aser sheni* — one should not use actual wheat of ma'aser sheni to bake the loaves; rather, one uses money of ma'aser sheni — *mimot ma'aser sheni* — to purchase the bread. The reason for this distinction will be explained in the Gemara.

### Outside Bread Idea

Rav Huna opens the Gemara on this Mishna with a related ruling: *ha'omer harei alai lachmei todah* — one who says I obligate myself to bring bread of a todah. What is the effect of such a declaration? The Gemara answers: *mevi todah ve-lachmah* — he must bring the todah with its bread. He cannot bring the bread alone, because everyone knows that lachmei todah without a todah is not a coherent entity. Therefore, when he said "lachmei todah," he must have meant the todah with its bread. The Gemara adds: *vehai todah ve-lachmah ka'amar* — by saying "bread of a todah," he was in effect articulating the complete obligation, since speaking of the end product — the bread — encompasses the primary item upon which it depends. *sof milta nakat* — he described the terminal component, but the whole package is implied.

### Four Loaves Inside

The Gemara then examines the internal logic of the Mishna's various stipulations. The Mishna taught that if one says *todah min ha-ma'aser ve-lachem min ha-chullin*, one brings as stipulated. One might ask: since the word "bread" can sometimes implicitly encompass "bread together with the todah" — as Rav Huna taught — why when someone says the bread is from chullin does that not extend to mean both the bread and the todah must come from chullin?

The Gemara resolves this: *shani hasam* — that case is different. Once he already said "the todah is from ma'aser," by the time he reaches the clause about the bread, the todah obligation has already been separately articulated. The subsequent mention of bread is therefore understood as referring only to the bread component, in the manner of someone who says "I will bring bread to discharge the todah obligation of so-and-so" — *harei alai lachem liftor todato shel ploni* — meaning the bread alone, not the whole package.

The Gemara then asks: by the same logic, when one says *todah min ha-chullin ve-lachem min ha-ma'aser*, why should the todah clause contaminate the bread clause? He already said the todah comes from chullin — could we not treat the todah clause as referring only to the animal, allowing the bread to remain from ma'aser as stipulated? The Gemara dismisses this: *bishlama lachem le-miftar todah ati* — bread is naturally secondary and functions to fulfill an obligation created by a standing todah. But *todah le-miftar lachem mi ati* — you would never frame the todah as secondary and the bread as primary. The todah is structurally the ikar, and you cannot read the declaration as if the todah were a subordinate element accompanying independently committed bread.

### Eighty Proposed

A baraita is cited: *ha'omer harei alai todah belo lachem ve-zevach belo nesachim, kofin oto mevi todah ve-lachmah, zevach u-nesacheiha* — if someone declares he will bring a todah without bread or a zevach without nesachim, we compel him to bring the complete package. No korban can be brought with its attendant obligations stripped away by stipulation; this is matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah.

One might infer from this baraita that the obligation to bring bread exists only because the person said the word "todah" — and that therefore if one had said only "bread" without mentioning "todah," one would not be obligated to bring the todah. The Gemara rejects this inference: *hu ha-din af al gav de-lo amar todah* — even if one had said only "bread," one would be obligated to bring the todah with it. The reason the baraita mentions the todah formulation is structural. The baraita needed to pair the todah-without-bread case with the zevach-without-nesachim case. It could not formulate the latter as "nesachim without a zevach," because nesachim may in certain contexts be brought independently, and therefore a declaration of nesachim alone would not imply a zevach. The parallel construction required mentioning the todah explicitly, but this does not mean that saying only "bread" would be legally different. The Gemara's conclusion on both sides is the same: the todah and its bread are a unified whole, and neither can be taken without the other.

The Gemara will continue tomorrow with the substantive analysis of the ma'aser sheni provisions that form the heart of this Mishna.

---

---

# Menachot 82

## Stipulated Conditions

### Intro: Todah & Ma'aser

The daf picks up in the middle of Menachot 81b, where the discussion concerns a case introduced in the previous Baraita: when somebody declares that he will bring a Todah on the condition that he not be required to bring the accompanying bread, the ruling is that we force him to bring the bread. The Gemara raises an immediate challenge to this ruling — why not say that this is a case of *neder u'pitcho imo*, a vow with its own opening? The reasoning would be as follows: since the person explicitly declared that he wanted to bring a Todah *without* the bread, we ought to look at the statement in its totality. He never truly intended to obligate himself in the complete package, so his vow should not be binding at all — he should bring nothing. Why do we sever the first half of his declaration ("I want to bring a Todah") from the second half ("without the bread") and hold him to the first part alone?

### Forcing Full Obligation

Chizkiyah answers that the ruling follows Beit Shammai, who hold *tfos lashon rishon* — we seize the first part of the statement. Beit Shammai, in general, take a more objective view of declarations in the domains of nedarim and hekdesh, giving primacy to what was actually said rather than to what the speaker had in mind. The Gemara cites a Mishnah in support: if someone says *hareini nazir min ha-grogrot u'min ha-dveilah* — "I am going to be a nazir so as to avoid eating figs or dates" — Beit Shammai rule that he is a nazir, a genuine nazir bound by the restrictions concerning wine, because he uttered the word *nazir*. Beit Hillel rule that he is not a nazir, because we assess the totality of the statement and it is clear he had no intent to become a nazir in any recognized sense. So too in the case of the Todah: Beit Shammai hold that the person said the word *todah*, and that alone is binding, regardless of the larger context in which the declaration was made.

### Beit Shammai's View

Rabbi Yochanan argues that the original ruling can be maintained even according to Beit Hillel. In his reading, the case involves someone who says explicitly: *ilu hayiti yodea she-ein nodvin kach lo hayiti noder kach ela kach* — "Had I known that one cannot bring a Todah without its bread, I would of course have obligated myself to bring the Todah with the bread." That is, he is clarifying that his preference for a Todah without bread stemmed from his mistaken belief that such a thing was possible. Had he known that the choice was all or nothing, he would have chosen the full Todah.

The question this raises is whether the person literally said those words or whether we simply assume that this is what any reasonable person would have meant. The two cases are quite different. Someone who declares himself a *nazir* from dates clearly has in mind that he does not want to eat dates — it is not at all reasonable to infer that he would have wanted to become a nazir from wine had he known there was no such thing as a nazir from dates. Those are completely different intentions. But someone who says "Todah without bread" may plausibly be understood as preferring the partial arrangement only insofar as it is available, and as being prepared to bring the full Todah if it is not.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Position

A further Baraita clarifies the situation. It reads: one who says *harei alai Todah belo lechem ve-zevach belo nesachim* — "I obligate myself to bring a Todah without its bread, or a sacrifice without its libations" — is told by the court: bring the Todah with its bread and the sacrifice with its libations. He then responds: *ilu hayiti yodea sheken lo hayiti noder* — had I known you would force me to bring the whole package, I would never have taken the vow at all. I wanted to do it partially, and if that is not permitted, I want to do nothing. The ruling is *kofin oto* — he is compelled to bring the full Todah, and we say to him *shemor ve-shama'ta*, observe and listen.

The Gemara then notes that this Baraita sits comfortably with Chizkiyah, who assigns the ruling to Beit Shammai. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, who sought to reconcile even such a case with Beit Hillel, the difficulty is acute: here the person explicitly states he would prefer to do nothing at all, so why should Beit Hillel hold him to his original declaration? Rabbi Yochanan's resolution is that this second Baraita is indeed Beit Shammai. He was attempting to explain a *different* Baraita according to Beit Hillel. In the end, Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan do not fundamentally disagree about the Beit Shammai–Beit Hillel debate itself; the dispute between them concerns only which Baraita is attributed to which school. All agree that Beit Shammai binds a person by the words he uttered, without regard to the broader context, while Beit Hillel looks at the whole statement.

### Baraita Example

The Gemara turns to explain the phrase *shemor ve-shama'ta* that is cited at the conclusion of the Baraita. Abaye says: *shemor* — observe what you said, namely the Todah, and bring it; *ve-shama'ta* — and hear what the Torah demands, namely the bread that accompanies it. Rava says: *shemor* — observe and bring the Todah with its bread, as the Torah requires; *ve-shama'ta* — and take heed, so that you do not put yourself in these situations in the future, so that you understand the laws before making stipulations that cannot be satisfied.

---

## Ma'aser & Todah

### Shamor Veshamata

The Gemara now returns to the Mishnah. The Mishnah teaches: *hi ve-lachmah min ha-ma'aser* — if someone says he obligates himself to bring a Todah, stipulating from the very outset that he may bring it from Ma'aser Sheni funds, he may do so. Although as a general rule — a rule the next Mishnah will articulate explicitly as *davar shebechova eino ba min hachulin* — an obligatory sacrifice cannot be brought from sanctified Ma'aser Sheni funds, when a person stipulates this condition from the outset, it is permitted. The underlying logic is that one may in any case use Ma'aser Sheni money to purchase voluntary offerings such as Shelamim or a Todah brought not as a personal obligation. When someone stipulates from the beginning that his Todah obligation is conditioned on the ability to fund it from Ma'aser Sheni, he is in effect structuring his vow in a manner that the halacha recognizes.

### Stipulation Permitted

The Gemara asks: *yavi* — must he bring it from Ma'aser Sheni money? Does his stipulation create a requirement to use those funds? Rav Papa and Rav Chisda answer: no. *ratzah meivi* — if he wishes, he may bring it from Ma'aser Sheni money, because he stipulated that this should be permitted. *lo ratzah lo meivi* — if he prefers to use Chulin funds instead, he may do so. The stipulation creates a permission, not an obligation.

One might ask why we read his declaration as creating an option rather than a binding commitment to use Ma'aser Sheni funds. Part of the answer lies in the mechanics of nedarim: a neder creates a status, not a personal obligation to perform a specific action with specific funds. If one truly wished to obligate himself to use Ma'aser Sheni funds and no others, the appropriate vehicle would be a shevua, which governs actions. A neder, by contrast, creates the status of being obligated in a Todah; it cannot itself restrict which funds satisfy that obligation. The Gemara therefore reads the declaration charitably — as allowing the use of Ma'aser Sheni funds, rather than requiring it — consistent both with the technical workings of nedarim and with the most natural understanding of what the person was trying to accomplish. He wanted to ensure that his Ma'aser Sheni funds could be used; he was not trying to preclude himself from using Chulin funds.

### Yavi Interpretation

The Mishnah adds: *ve-lo yavi me-chitei ma'aser sheni ela mi-me'os ma'aser sheni* — but one should not bring the Todah bread from the actual wheat grain that was set aside as Ma'aser Sheni. Rather, one should redeem the Ma'aser Sheni produce into money, and use that money to purchase the Todah and its bread.

Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda both explain: the prohibition is specifically against using the actual Ma'aser Sheni grain itself. But if one used Ma'aser Sheni money to purchase grain or flour, that purchased grain may be used to make the bread of the Todah — which seems straightforward, since this is precisely how one would use Ma'aser Sheni money for bread-baking in this context.

### Permission Not Obligation

Rabbi Yirmeyah was sitting before Rabbi Zeira and stated the same position as Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda: only the original Ma'aser Sheni grain is forbidden; wheat purchased with Ma'aser Sheni money may be used. Rabbi Zeira challenged him sharply: do you really say this? I say that even wheat purchased with Ma'aser Sheni money may not be used to make the Todah bread.

Rabbi Zeira then explains both positions. He begins with Rabbi Yirmeyah's reasoning: where do we know that Ma'aser Sheni money may be used for a Todah at all? We derive it from Shelamim — *sham sham mi-ma'aser*, a gezeira shava linking the word *sham* in the verse concerning Shelamim to the word *sham* in the verse concerning Ma'aser Sheni. Since Shelamim may be purchased with Ma'aser Sheni money, so too may a Todah. Just as the Shelamim offering itself is never Ma'aser Sheni grain — cattle and sheep are never tithe produce — so too when funding a Todah from Ma'aser Sheni, the Todah itself cannot be the Ma'aser Sheni grain directly. But if one uses Ma'aser Sheni money to buy wheat, that wheat is not itself Ma'aser Sheni grain, so it is permitted. That is Rabbi Yirmeyah's reasoning.

Rabbi Zeira then presents his own position: the inference from Shelamim to Todah tells us not merely that the actual Ma'aser Sheni grain cannot become Todah bread, but that anything used for the Todah bread must be entirely of a type that *could never be Ma'aser Sheni*. Shelamim meat, by its nature, is never a category of produce that can be Ma'aser Sheni — meat is never tithed. Therefore, when one uses Ma'aser Sheni funds for a Todah, one must use them to purchase items that are likewise not of a kind that could ever be Ma'aser Sheni. Wheat is precisely a kind of produce that can be Ma'aser Sheni. Therefore one may not use Ma'aser Sheni money to purchase wheat for Todah bread. The implication — and Rashi understands it this way — is that the Ma'aser Sheni money should be used to buy the bread itself, already baked, rather than wheat or flour. This is admittedly a striking position, since it requires that the bread be produced by a third party, but Rabbi Zeira's reasoning about the category-type of the purchased item leads inescapably there.

---

## Wheat vs. Bread

### Grain vs. Money

Rabbi Ammi's statement now introduces the broader conceptual question about doubling sanctity. Before reaching that, the Gemara establishes that the basis for using Ma'aser Sheni funds for Shelamim or Todah is the gezeira shava of *sham sham*, linking the verse about Shelamim — *ve-achalta sham* — to the verse about Ma'aser Sheni — *ve-natata ba-kesef be-yadecha ve-achalta sham lifnei Hashem Elokecha*. Both contexts speak of eating before God in Yerushalayim.

This connection is not arbitrary. The entire institution of Ma'aser Sheni is designed to bring the person into the center of kedusha, to eat before God in Yerushalayim. The Torah frames it as *lifnei Hashem Elokecha*, even though one is not required to enter the Beit HaMikdash itself. The Shelamim offering shares precisely this character: the eating is in the presence of God, evoking the *simcha* and wholeness of being in communion with the Divine. In fact, the Mishnah in Ma'aser Sheni makes clear that if one wished to eat meat with Ma'aser Sheni funds, one was expected to bring a Shelamim rather than purchasing *basar ta'avah* — ordinary unsanctified meat — because the goals of Ma'aser Sheni and the goals of eating Shelamim in Yerushalayim are deeply aligned. Since Todah is a form of Shelamim, Ma'aser Sheni funds may equally be directed toward it.

### Rav Nachman's Position

It is from this same conceptual framework that the Mishnah's restriction about using the actual Ma'aser Sheni grain for Todah bread emerges. To take the Ma'aser Sheni grain itself — the produce that grew and was separated as Ma'aser Sheni — and transform it into bread of a Todah, represents a kind of compromise of its original identity. When one uses Ma'aser Sheni *money* to purchase an item that then assumes its own sanctity as a Shelamim or Todah, the money has been appropriately deployed toward the ends of Ma'aser Sheni without any confusion of identity. But to take the grain itself, which *is* the Ma'aser Sheni, and overlay upon it the identity of *lachmei Todah*, is to try to make it two things at once in a way that undermines the clarity of each.

### Rabbi Zeira's Stricture

Rabbi Ammi states: *ha-matpis ma'os ma'aser sheni le-shelamim lo kanu shelamim* — if one attempts to impose the sanctity of Shelamim upon Ma'aser Sheni money itself — to declare that the money has the status of Shelamim funds — it does not work. The Shelamim sanctity does not take hold. This is a striking ruling. After all, one is permitted to use Ma'aser Sheni money to purchase an animal and bring it as a Shelamim. So what is the difference between using the money to buy an animal that becomes a Shelamim versus imposing Shelamim sanctity on the money itself?

Rabbi Ammi's reasoning is: *de-lo alima kedushas ha-shelamim le-meichel kedushas ma'aser sheni* — the sanctity of Shelamim is not powerful enough to take effect on top of the existing sanctity of Ma'aser Sheni. The analogy to the grain case is illuminating. Just as it is problematic to take the Ma'aser Sheni grain itself and turn it into Todah bread — because that forces the same object to carry two competing identities — so too it is problematic to impose Shelamim sanctity directly upon money that already carries the identity of Ma'aser Sheni funds. Ma'aser Sheni money has a very defined character: it is to be used *be-chol asher te'aveh nafshecha* — for whatever food one desires, within the framework of eating before God in Yerushalayim. When one purchases an animal with that money, the money fulfills its function and the animal now stands separately as a Shelamim. That is not a conflict. But to declare the money itself to be simultaneously Ma'aser Sheni money and Shelamim money is to redefine its character and limit what it can be used for — something the sanctity of Shelamim cannot accomplish over and above the pre-existing sanctity of Ma'aser Sheni.

### Rabbi Zeira Explains

The Gemara challenges Rabbi Ammi's ruling from a Mishnah in Ma'aser Sheni. The Mishnah teaches that one who purchases a *chayah* — a deer or other non-domesticated animal — intending to bring it as a Shelamim, or who purchases livestock intending to eat it as ordinary meat (*basar ta'avah*), is doing something irregular. The normal expectation is the reverse: if you want ordinary meat, buy a deer, which cannot be brought as a Shelamim; if you want to bring a Shelamim, buy livestock. The Mishnah rules that *lo yatza ha-or le-chulin* — in these irregular cases, the leather does not go out to non-sanctified status.

Under ordinary circumstances, when one makes a standard, approved purchase with Ma'aser Sheni money — such as buying wine, where part of the cost goes to the bottle — the container or accessory element is considered as freed from Ma'aser Sheni sanctity, in the same way that the leather of an animal properly purchased for Shelamim is freed from Ma'aser Sheni status once the transaction is legitimate. The principle of *yatza or le-chulin* reflects the general rule that a normal, appropriate purchase with Ma'aser Sheni money frees the non-food components from further Ma'aser Sheni obligations. But in these reversed, irregular cases, the purchase is considered abnormal, and so the leather does not gain this benefit.

The Gemara assumes that when the Mishnah says the leather *lo yatza le-chulin* in the case of one who bought livestock for ordinary meat, it may be implying that the leather has both Ma'aser Sheni sanctity *and* Shelamim sanctity — since Shelamim sanctity apparently attached despite the irregular purchase. If so, this would contradict Rabbi Ammi's ruling that Shelamim sanctity cannot take hold on Ma'aser Sheni money or property.

Rav responds: *lo kani Shelamim* — in fact, no Shelamim sanctity attaches at all. When the Mishnah says the leather *lo yatza le-chulin*, it means only that the leather retains its Ma'aser Sheni sanctity. *lo yatza le-chulin* describes the failure of the leather to be freed from Ma'aser Sheni, nothing more. Why does it retain this sanctity and not benefit from *yatza le-chulin*? Rava explains: *na'aseh ke-kone'ach shor la-charishoh* — this purchase is like using Ma'aser Sheni funds to buy an ox for plowing, a complete misappropriation. In such a complete misuse, the normal rules of *yatza le-chulin* do not apply at all; the entire transaction retains its Ma'aser Sheni character, and the skin is simply not freed. There is no doubling of sanctity, and Rabbi Ammi's position stands.

The Gemara then presents a fresh formulation of the original debate as a direct Tannaitic dispute. *ha-matpis ma'os ma'aser sheni le-shelamim* — one who imposes Shelamim sanctity upon Ma'aser Sheni money: Rabbi Yochanan says it takes effect; Rabbi Elazar says it does not.

---

## Doubled Sanctities

### Analogy to Shelamim

The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar concerning whether one can impose Shelamim sanctity on Ma'aser Sheni money is now framed in terms of the classic dispute about the underlying nature of Ma'aser Sheni.

### Avoiding Double Identity

The Gemara explains: *ve-aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda de-amar ma'aser mamon hedyot hu de-kuli alma lo pligi de-kani* — according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that Ma'aser Sheni is *mamon hedyot*, lay property that essentially belongs to the owner, all agree that Shelamim sanctity can take effect upon it. If it is your property, you have the ability to impose an additional sanctity upon it.

### Practical Difficulty

The classic dispute in the Gemara between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir concerns whether Ma'aser Sheni is *mamon hedyot* or *mamon gavoah* — whether it is fundamentally the owner's property or temple property. The kedusha of Ma'aser Sheni defines restrictions on its use and the way in which it is consumed, but unlike hekdesh in the sense of a donation to the Beit HaMikdash, Ma'aser Sheni is ultimately eaten by the owner. So the question is whether the concept of kedusha here is one of ownership — like hekdesh, where the temple owns the item — or one of status, where the owner retains the item but it has a defined sacred character. Rabbi Yehuda holds it is the owner's property; Rabbi Meir holds that because its use is so constrained, it is in effect temple property. One of the classic tests for this question in the Gemara is whether one may use Ma'aser Sheni produce to betroth a woman — *harei at mekudeshet li* — since that requires giving her something of value that is one's own.

The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar, the Gemara explains, is relevant only according to Rabbi Meir, who holds it is *mamon gavoah*. *ki pligi aliba de-rabbi meir*: the one who says the Shelamim sanctity does *not* take hold follows Rabbi Meir straightforwardly — if it is not your property, you have no authority to impose a new sanctity upon it. But the one who says it *does* take hold — *keivan de-ma'aser karev Shelamim ki matpis lei nami tapis* — argues that since Ma'aser Sheni is naturally and characteristically brought as a Shelamim, imposing Shelamim sanctity upon it is not really a reorientation of its character but rather a directing of it toward its most natural use, and therefore even if it is not fully your property, imposing this sanctity does not constitute a contradiction.

One might ask: why frame this entire debate within Rabbi Meir's position? Even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says it is *mamon hedyot*, there could still be a question of whether the competing kedushos conflict. The answer implicit in the Gemara seems to be that once you have resolved the problem of the competing sanctities — which the reasoning about Ma'aser naturally being brought as Shelamim addresses — and once you have established that the person has the property rights to impose a new sanctity, both conditions are satisfied. The Gemara places the debate within Rabbi Meir because that is where the more interesting question lies: can one address the conflict-of-sanctities problem even when the prerequisite of ownership is itself in doubt?

### Rabbi Ammi's Rule

A Baraita is cited that directly assumes one can impose Shelamim sanctity upon Ma'aser Sheni money: *ha-matpis ma'os ma'aser sheni le-shelamim, kshe-podan mosif aleihem shnei chumashim — echad le-kodesh ve-echad le-ma'aser* — one who subsequently redeems this doubly-sanctified money adds two fifths: one for the Shelamim sanctity and one for the Ma'aser Sheni sanctity.

This is itself a notable ruling, since we do not normally find the requirement to add a fifth when redeeming Shelamim sanctity — the fifth is a feature of redeeming Ma'aser Sheni and of redeeming certain forms of hekdesh, but it is not routinely applied to Korban sanctity. Tosafot notes the difficulty, citing a passage in Perek HaZahav which implies there is no fifth for redeeming Shelamim. In any case, the Baraita clearly assumes that both sanctities are present and that the matpis indeed takes effect.

The Gemara responds: *mi savas de-be'al korcho* — who said this Baraita represents a unanimous position? *ha mani* — this is Rabbi Yehuda. We already established that according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds Ma'aser Sheni is mamon hedyot, all agree the matpis takes effect. A Baraita consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's position does not resolve the dispute as it stands according to Rabbi Meir.

---

## Sanctifying Ma'aser

### Sanctity Hierarchy

The Gemara now turns to the main rule of the Mishnah that follows: *minayin le-omer harei alai Todah shelo yavi ela min ha-chulin* — from where do we know that if someone says *harei alai Todah*, I undertake to bring a Todah, he may only bring it from Chulin funds, not from Ma'aser Sheni money? The source is the verse: *ve-zavachta Pesach la-Hashem Elokecha tzon u-vakar* — you shall slaughter the Pesach offering to Hashem your God, sheep and cattle. This verse presents a well-known halachic difficulty: the Pesach comes only from sheep and goats, not from cattle. What then does the verse mean by *tzon u-vakar*?

The answer is: the verse creates a *hekesh*, linking all offerings brought from sheep and cattle to the Pesach. *mah pesach davar shebechova ve-ein ba ela min ha-chulin* — just as the Pesach is an obligatory offering and comes only from Chulin funds, so too *kol davar shebechova ein ba ela min ha-chulin* — all obligatory offerings may only come from Chulin funds. Therefore, if someone says *harei alai Todah* or *harei alai Shelamim* — once he has made it an obligation — he may only bring it from Chulin funds.

The best available reconciliation of *tzon u-vakar* with the plain sense of the text is that the cattle (*bakar*) refer to the Shelamim offerings that accompanied the Pesach, not to the Pesach animal itself. That reading at least makes the verse internally coherent, even if it is not the most obvious pshat.

The Mishnah adds that Nesachim — libation offerings — may *never* be brought from Ma'aser Sheni funds, even without an explicit obligation, because Nesachim are never consumed by the owner. The entire rationale for permitting Ma'aser Sheni funds for voluntary Shelamim or Todah is tied to the eating — the *ve-achalta sham* framework, the consumption before God that is the common thread between Ma'aser Sheni and these offerings. Nesachim are poured on the Mizbeach and nobody eats them. Using Ma'aser Sheni money for something that will never be eaten at all is a fundamental contradiction of the purpose of Ma'aser Sheni funds.

### Ownership vs. Sanctity

The same principle extends to other offerings that are not eaten by the owner. An Olah, for example, is entirely consumed on the Mizbeach, and there would be no basis for using Ma'aser Sheni funds toward it, since the rationale of *ve-achalta sham* does not apply. The Mishnah chose Nesachim as its example, perhaps because they represent a somewhat lower-profile case than Olah, but the logic applies equally. The permissibility of Ma'aser Sheni funds for Shelamim and Todah is rooted specifically in the shared character of eating before God in Yerushalayim; remove that element and the permission falls away.

### Improper Uses

The Gemara now asks: we have used the Pesach as the paradigm case for the rule that obligatory offerings come only from Chulin — but how do we know that the Pesach itself may not be brought from Ma'aser Sheni money? A Baraita records the dispute. Rabbi Eliezer argues by a gezerah shavah of sorts, comparing the *pesach mitzrayim* to the *pesach le-dorot*: just as the Pesach in Egypt did not come from Ma'aser Sheni money — because Ma'aser Sheni had not yet been commanded, and in any case Ma'aser Sheni applies only to produce grown in the Land of Israel — so too the Pesach for all future generations comes only from Chulin.

### Yatza Or L'Chullin

Rabbi Akiva challenges Rabbi Eliezer: *ve-chi danin efshar mi-she'ee efshar* — can one learn from a case where something was possible to a case where it was impossible? In Egypt, using Ma'aser Sheni money was not merely impermissible — it was categorically unavailable. One cannot derive a prohibition for later generations from a situation where there was simply no option.

Rabbi Eliezer responds: *af al pi she'ee efshar, raya gedolah hi* — even though it was impossible, it is still a significant proof. The fact that the Pesach could only come from Chulin funds, even in a situation where Ma'aser Sheni did not exist and never could have applied, establishes the essential character of the Pesach as a Chulin obligation.

Rabbi Akiva presses again with a different challenge: even setting aside the *efshar/ee efshar* problem, the Pesach Mitzrayim was fundamentally different from the Pesach le-dorot — it did not involve the placing of blood and the *eimurim* on the Mizbeach (*matan damim ve-eimurim le-gabei mizbeach*). How can one derive rules for the Pesach le-dorot, which requires this altar service, from a Pesach that had none of it?

Rabbi Eliezer responds with a verse: *ve-avadta et ha-avoda ha-zot ba-chodesh ha-zeh* — "and you shall perform this service in this month." This verse, given during the Pesach Mitzrayim, explicitly states that all future observances of the Pesach will follow the model of the first. Thereby all future Pesachim are linked to the Pesach Mitzrayim, and the rules of the latter apply to the former.

### Direct Sanctification

The Gemara then notes an apparent difficulty in the flow of the argument: why did Rabbi Eliezer, when faced with Rabbi Akiva's second challenge about the absence of Mizbeach service in the Pesach Mitzrayim, not simply shift to the *pesach midbar* — the Pesach brought in the desert, which did involve blood and eimurim on the Mizbeach, and equally could not have involved Ma'aser Sheni money since there was no Ma'aser Sheni produce growing in the desert? Why did Rabbi Eliezer need the *ve-avadta* verse at all?

The Gemara resolves this by explaining that Rabbi Eliezer was addressing Rabbi Akiva on his own terms. Rabbi Akiva holds that one cannot derive rulings from *ee efshar* situations. Both the Pesach Mitzrayim and the Pesach Midbar were equally impossible cases for Ma'aser Sheni, so according to Rabbi Akiva's principle, neither can serve as a source. Therefore Rabbi Eliezer shifts strategies: instead of offering another *ee efshar* example, he produces the *ve-avadta* verse, which explicitly links the Pesach Mitzrayim to all future Pesachim. Once there is an explicit textual link, the objection that one cannot derive from the possible from the impossible becomes irrelevant.

### Mamon Hedyot vs. Gavoah

This leads to Rav Sheshet's conclusion: *zot omeret ein meshivin al ha-heikesh* — this tells us the famous principle that one does not refute a hekesh. Once the Torah explicitly links two cases, as *ve-avadta* links the Pesach Mitzrayim to the Pesach le-dorot, the ordinary categories of objection that might be raised against a logical inference — such as the *efshar/ee efshar* distinction or the difference in Mizbeach service — no longer apply. The textual equation overrides them. This principle, noted by Rav Sheshet here, is cited frequently throughout the Gemara and reflects the qualitatively different and conclusive force of an explicit Scriptural equation compared to an inferential one.

---

---

# Menachot 83

## Pesach & Non-Sanctified

### Intro: Pesach Debate

The daf opens in the middle of a sustained debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva concerning the source for the principle that a korban Pesach may only be purchased from non-sanctified, non-ma'aser sheini funds. Rabbi Eliezer derives this rule from the Pesach Mitzrayim, while Rabbi Akiva rejects that inference on the grounds that one cannot apply a principle derived from a ma'aseh she-ee efshar — a situation that was impossible under normal circumstances — to a ma'aseh efshar, a situation that is entirely possible. The Gemara had already established that Rabbi Eliezer's derivation rests on an explicit hekesh linking the two cases, and invokes the famous principle ein meshivin al ha-hekesh: once a biblical linkage is explicit, objections based on logical inconsistency no longer apply.

### Chozer u'Melamed

The Gemara now wraps up this discussion with a question posed u've-tarbitza — in the academy, among the students, in the sense of harbatzat Torah. The question is: ve-chi davar ha-lamed be-hekesh chozer u-melamed be-hekesh? We learned Pesach Dorot from Pesach Mitzrayim through a hekesh; can we then take Pesach Dorot and apply its principles to all other korbanot through another hekesh? The Gemara answers: be-khulala it-mar — it was stated as a general category. Kula chada milta hi: all instances of korban Pesach constitute a single unified category. Even though a hekesh was required to extend the law from Pesach Mitzrayim to Pesach Dorot — because the one applied only once in history while the other is a general ongoing obligation — the derivation does not constitute daisy-chaining from A to B to C. Rather, it is a single category being made whole, and from that unified Pesach category one may legitimately extend principles to all other korbanot.

### Rabbi Akiva's Source

Rabbi Akiva does not dispute the ruling itself — that a Pesach, and by extension all obligatory korbanot, must come from non-ma'aser sheini funds. His disagreement is solely with the source. He cannot learn it from Pesach Mitzrayim, which is a she-ee efshar case. Instead, the Gemara explains, nafka lei me-ha d'amar Shmuel mishum Rabbi Elazar — he derives it from a statement of Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Elazar. That statement will emerge from a general pasuk that simultaneously teaches numerous laws shared across all korbanot: Zot ha-Torah la-olah ve-la-minchah ve-la-chatat ve-la-asham ve-la-miluim u-le-zeivach ha-shelamim. The Gemara will mine each entry in that list for a law that is explicit in one korban and then, by virtue of the pasuk's linkage, applied to all others. Notably, an almost identical exposition of this same pasuk appears near the end of Masechet Zevachim — the same literary phenomenon by which a summing-up verse generates a comprehensive set of shared halakhot toward the close of the tractate.

---

## Zot HaTorah Pasuk

### Zot HaTorah Intro

The Gemara begins with olah: mah olah te'unah keli — just as an olah requires a vessel, so too every korban requires a vessel. The Gemara first considers whether the vessel in question is a mizrak, a bowl for catching the blood. After Har Sinai, it says, the Torah records that they slaughtered olot and shelamim and placed the blood ba-aganot — in bowls — and from there one might derive that blood-catching requires a vessel. The Gemara objects: but that is written by shelamim as well, not uniquely by the olah. The vessel we are focused on, then, is something specific to the olah: the sakin, the slaughter knife.

### Olah: Knife

The Gemara then asks: ulo'ah gufah minalan — how do we know the olah itself required a knife-vessel? The source is va-yishlach Avraham et yado va-yikach et ha-machelet lishchot et bno: Abraham reached out his hand and took the machelet — a notably graphic term for a knife, one that evokes the act of cutting into flesh — to slaughter his son. The Gemara establishes that Yitzchak was being treated as an olah: after the akeida, the Torah says regarding the ram va-ya'alehu le-olah tachat bno, he offered it as an olah in place of his son, which confirms that the son had been intended as an olah. Since Abraham used a knife for what was being treated as an olah offering, we derive that an olah requires a knife.

This source is striking — and more than a little disturbing. The derivation of korban law from the akeida is unavoidable: olah tachat bno makes the substitutionary logic explicit. The Gemara does not shy away from this, even as we might prefer to bracket it.

A closer look reveals that this passage also bears on the question from Masechet Chulin of whether the slaughter knife must be detached — mechubar le-karka — and we learn from Abraham that it must be. But our Gemara is adding something beyond mere detachment. The word kli suggests that for a korban, the knife must meet the standard of a vessel — something fashioned to function as a knife — as opposed to, say, a sharpened rock. Tosafos raises a further question: does the korban requirement extend to a kli sharet, a sanctified vessel? The Gemara here says only kli, not kli sharet, and it is not obvious from the akeida passage that the machelet was sanctified. Tosafos attempts to derive it from an extra word but acknowledges the difficulty. In practice, there are three distinct levels: the general shechitah requirement that the knife be detached; the korban requirement that it be a proper fashioned vessel; and the debated requirement among Rishonim that it also be a kli sharet.

### Abraham & Isaac

The Gemara proceeds to minchah: mah minchah einah ne'echelet ela le-zichrei kehunah — just as a minchah is eaten only by male kohanim, so too af kol eino ne'echal ela le-zichrei kehunah — anything from among the korbanot that goes to the kohanim is restricted to the male kohanim. This differs from terumah, which the kohen may feed to his entire household including women and children; the portions of the korbanot allocated to kohanim are reserved for the males exclusively.

The Gemara then asks: by which korban is this actually needed? If we are speaking of a chatat or asham, the law is stated explicitly in the relevant pesukim. The one case where this is not explicit is zivchei shalmei tzibbur — the communal shelamim, a category whose only real member in practice is the kivsei atzeret, the lambs of Shavuot, since these go to the kohanim rather than to the owners. The Gemara responds that me-ribuyah de-kra atya — we actually derive this from an extra expression in the pasuk in Parshat Korach, where in reiterating all the priestly entitlements the Torah says kol zachar yochal oto after already having said tochelen — the repetition of "eat it" comes to include shalmei tzibbur among those eaten only by male kohanim. The Gemara therefore concludes tannai hi: it is a tannaic dispute as to which pasuk one learns this from — some derive it from the minchah entry in Zot HaTorah, others from the extra formulation in Parshat Korach.

### Mincha: Male Kohanim

Ve-la-chatat: mah chatat mekadesh be-valua af kol mekadesh be-valua. Just as a chatat sanctifies by absorption, so too any korban sanctifies through absorption. The Torah states by the chatat: kol asher yiga be-visarah yikdash — anything that touches the flesh of the chatat becomes holy. The Gemara interprets this as yikdash lihyot kamoha: it becomes holy in the same mode as the chatat itself. If the chatat was valid, an item that absorbed some of its juices adopts its restrictions — for instance, if the chatat was a one-day sacrifice, the item that absorbed from it may only be eaten for one day. Ve-im pasul, if the chatat was itself invalid, then tipasel — the other item also becomes invalid. This is the principle of mekadesh be-valua: sanctification through being absorbed.

One might ask why this is a special korban principle at all, since the general laws of mixtures already mandate that when something is not batel it conveys the more stringent status. The answer is that by korbanot this applies even in cases where under ordinary mixture principles the forbidden substance would have been batel — the Torah overrides the normal threshold. That expanded stringency is the chiddush of mekadesh be-valua, and af kol mekadesh be-valua extends it to all korbanot.

### Chatat: Sanctifies

Ve-la-asham: mah asham ein shapir ve-shilya kadosh bo — just as by an asham the placenta and embryo carry no sanctity, af kol ein shapir ve-shilya kadosh bo — by no korban do the placenta and embryo carry sanctity. The logic is that an asham must be male, so a placenta and embryo could never exist in an asham in the first place. Applying this to a female korban like a chatat, we learn that even there, if one finds an embryo or placenta inside the animal, it possesses no kedushah: it need not be offered on the mizbeach, and it has none of the attendant restrictions of korban meat. As Rashi notes in Zevachim, the question of whether one must even remove the kidneys and fat of the embryo is itself resolved — the answer is no, since the embryo has no sanctity whatsoever.

The Gemara specifies the two assumptions underlying this derivation: first, that veladot kodashim be-havayatan hen kedoshin — the offspring of a consecrated animal acquires its kedushah only upon birth, not while still in the womb. Second, ve-danin efshar mi-she-ee efshar — one may derive a law applicable in a possible case from a situation that is impossible. This second assumption, notably, is the very principle Rabbi Akiva rejects in the earlier debate. The Gemara is careful to note that the entire braita here is amar Shmuel mishum Rabbi Elazar, i.e., it proceeds from the school of Rabbi Eliezer, who does accept danin efshar mi-she-ee efshar. Rabbi Akiva's own derivations will be addressed separately.

### Asham: No Embryo

Ve-la-miluim: mah miluim mosreihen bi-sreifa — just as by the miluim sacrifices, the leftover meat is burned, ve-ein ba'alei chayim mosreihen bi-sreifa — but live animals are not burned as notar. The Torah says explicitly to Aaron and his sons by the miluim: if anything is left over from the meat, burn it in the fire. While the law of notar applies broadly, the explicit command to burn notar appears not by every case but specifically here by the miluim. By virtue of Zot HaTorah, this applies to all korbanot: af kol mosreihen bi-sreifa — notar meat of any korban is burned.

The second half of the rule — that live animals are not treated as notar subject to burning — arises from the case of a korban that becomes "leftover" not as meat but as a live animal. The classic instance is when one designates a replacement for a lost korban, then recovers the original: one of the two is a kind of leftover. Rashi notes that the Torah never actually addresses the case of burning a live animal by the miluim; shelo matzinu sreifa ba-miluim ela be-vasar le-achar shechitah. The Torah speaks only of burning the remaining meat after shechitah, not of any living animal. So this too is in the category of she-ee efshar — the case simply does not arise. The rule is therefore: notar meat is burned across all korbanot; this does not extend to a live animal that has been rendered "leftover."

### Miluim: Burning

The final term in the pasuk is ul-zeivach ha-shelamim: mah shelamim mifaglim u-mitfaglim — just as shelamim both creates piggul and becomes piggul itself, so too af kol mifaglim u-mitfaglim. The paradigm case of piggul in the Torah is the shelamim, and from there the principle extends to all korbanot.

Tosafos explains the formulation mifaglim u-mitfaglim in light of the fundamental structure of piggul: for piggul to apply, there must be two distinct components — an act being performed (such as zerikah, the sprinkling of the blood) that is matir, i.e., permits, something else (such as the basar, the meat). If a kohen sprinkles the blood with intent to eat the meat outside its proper time, that invalid intent is mefagel the basar. This is why a minchat kohen, which is entirely burned and has no portion to be "permitted" by the burning of the kometz, cannot have piggul — there is no two-part structure. The expression mifaglim u-mitfaglim therefore means: it creates piggul in the remaining portion, and correspondingly that portion itself becomes piggul. This applies to all korbanot that share the two-part structure.

---

## Rabbi Akiva's Chatat

### Shelamim: Pigul

The Gemara now introduces a parallel braita: be-matnitin tana mishmeih de-Rabbi Akiva — taught in the name of Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva proceeds through the same pasuk of Zot HaTorah but draws different lessons from each term. The olah entry is apparently skipped, perhaps because the knife-vessel law is the same; we proceed directly to minchah.

Rabbi Akiva learns mekadesh be-valua — sanctification through absorption — not from the chatat (as Rabbi Eliezer's tradition did) but from the minchah, where it is equally written: kol asher yiga bahem yikdash. The Gemara then asks why the Torah found it necessary to write the rule both by the chatat and by the minchah. The answer is that each case carries a unique rationale that would not have been extended to the other: had the Torah written it only by the minchah, one might have thought the principle applies because the minchah is soft and readily absorbs — mishum de-rachicha balah — but that a chatat, being meat, would not. Had the Torah written it only by the chatat, one might have thought the principle applies because meat is fatty and penetrates — mishum de-vasar agav de-shamein kadir — but that a minchah, being soft and flour-like, would not. Tzricha: both were required.

One difficulty remains in this reasoning. The rationale offered for the minchah is that "it absorbs" — but the direction of transfer in mekadesh be-valua is that the minchah's juices penetrate something else, not that the minchah takes on substance from something else. A minchah's softness would make it more susceptible to absorbing from other things, which is actually the lesser chiddush. The chiddush is precisely that when a drop of minchah gets absorbed into something else, the minchah's kedushahstatus follows it. The Gemara's formulation here — de-rachicha balah — does not map cleanly onto that direction, and the precise logic remains difficult.

### Akiva's Chatat Use

This is the derivation the entire discussion was building toward. Rabbi Akiva reads the chatat entry of Zot HaTorah as follows: machatat einah ba'ah ela min ha-chulin — a chatat comes only from non-sanctified funds. And from the pasuk's linkage, af kol einah ba'ah ela min ha-chulin — so too all obligatory korbanot must come from non-ma'aser sheini funds.

How do we know this specifically of the chatat? Rabbi Chisda teaches: the pasuk in the Yom Kippur passage says ve-hikriv Aharon et par ha-chatat asher lo — "that is his" — lo mishelo, from his own personal funds, ve-lo mishel ma'aser, and not from any other source including ma'aser funds. From the word lo we derive that the chatat must come from the kohen's own non-designated funds. By virtue of Zot HaTorah, this extends to all korbanot.

The Gemara notes that two additional laws were mentioned in conjunction with the chatat: that it must be brought in the daytime, and that the kohen must use his right hand. Both, however, are ultimately superfluous as derivations from this context: the daytime requirement is already learned from the pasuk mi-yom tzavoto — "on the day God commanded" — a general rule for all korbanot; and the right-hand requirement is derived from the principle of Rabba Bar Bar Channah quoting Reish Lakish that wherever the Torah mentions etzba and kehunah together it refers to the right hand. The Gemara concludes regarding both: kidi nasba — they were included gratuitously. The essential and purposeful derivation from the chatat entry is solely the requirement of chulin funds.

### Akiva: Mincha

Ve-la-asham: mah asham atzmotav mutarin — just as by an asham the bones are permitted for personal use, af kol atzmotav mutarin — so too by all korbanot the bones are permitted. This means that the bones, like the hide, are given to the kohanim without any of the restrictions that apply to the korban's meat — no time limit, no geographic restriction, and no obligation to treat them with kedushah. They may be used for whatever purpose one wishes.

This rule is effectively self-evident for most korbanot, since the pesukim speak of the kohanim eating the meat and implicitly exclude non-meat components from the same restrictions. The significant case is the olah, which is entirely burned on the mizbeach. One might have thought that since the entire olah must go up in flames, even the bones are included. This derivation teaches otherwise: even by the olah, the bones are excluded from the korban's sanctity and need not be placed on the mizbeach. The kohen may take the bones home and use them freely.

---

## Pesach: Shelamim

### Akiva: Chatat Only

The Gemara now turns to Rabbi Akiva's reading of the pasuk in Devarim: u-zavachta Pesach la-Hashem Elokecha tzon u-vakar. Rabbi Eliezer had used the word bakar — cattle — to extend the principles of Pesach to all other korbanot, since a Pesach cannot come from cattle. Rabbi Akiva, who cannot accept that usage (it would constitute learning from a she-ee efshar case), instead applies the pasuk mi-bayei lei le-chide-Rav Nachman — to teach the ruling of Rav Nachman.

Rav Nachman, quoting Rabbah bar Avuha, asks: minayin le-motar Pesach she-karev shelamim — how do we know that what is left over from a korban Pesach is brought as a shelamim? Motar Pesach refers to the classic case of a Pesach that was lost, replaced by a substitute, and then recovered — one of the two animals must now be dealt with, and it has the status of "leftover." The answer: she-ne'emar u-zavachta Pesach la-Hashem Elokecha tzon u-vakar. Since a Pesach cannot come from bakar, the word bakar must be teaching something else: that the motar Pesach — which can no longer be a Pesach — becomes a korban of the type that comes from both tzon and bakar, namely a shelamim. The Pesach is similar to a shelamim in that it is eaten by its owners, and when it can no longer function as a Pesach it becomes precisely that.

The Gemara then challenges: but do we not already derive this from the pasuk cited by the father of Shmuel? For it is written by the shelamim: im min ha-tzon korbano le-zevach shelamim. The father of Shmuel asks why the Torah says im min ha-tzon rather than im min ha-kevasim — why the broad "flock" rather than the specific "sheep"? Because davar ha-ba min ha-tzon — something that comes only from the flock. What comes only from flock animals? The Pesach — it comes only from sheep or goats. Yehei le-zevach shelamim: if it can no longer be brought as a Pesach, it becomes a shelamim.

A third pasuk is then cited from a braita: the Torah says by the shelamim, im keshev hu makriv — if it is a sheep he brings. Le-rabbot et ha-Pesach la-alyah — this comes to include the Pesach in the requirement of burning the fat tail. And subsequently: ke-she-hu omer im keshev — when it says if it is a sheep — le-havi Pesach she-avrah shenato — this includes a Pesach whose year has passed, and shelamim ha-ba'im machmat Pesach — shelamim that arise on account of the Pesach. Le-khol mitzvot shelamim — they are subject to all the rules of shelamim: semichah, nesachim, tenufat chazeh ve-shok. These are things one does not do with a Pesach itself but does with a Pesach that has transformed into a shelamim. The pasuk then says ve-im ez — if it is a goat — and this interruption, hifsik ha-inyan, teaches she-einah te'unah alyah — a goat's small tail is not burned, unlike a sheep's fat tail.

### Akiva: Asham Bones

The Gemara asks: tlata kra'ei ktivu — there are three pesukim, each apparently teaching that a Pesach becomes a shelamim. Why are all three needed? Chad le-avar zmano ve-avrah shnato — one addresses the case where Pesach has already passed and the animal is also more than a year old, rendering it entirely disqualified from ever serving as a Pesach. Mishum de-idchei lei le-gamrei — since it has been completely rejected from the category of Pesach, its transformation into shelamim seems obvious.
