Ve-chad le-avar zmano ve-lo avrah shnato — a second is needed for when Pesach has passed but the animal is still within its first year. Here, d'chazi le-Pesach sheni — it could in theory be used for Pesach Sheni, the makeup Pesach of the fourteenth of Iyyar. Since it has not been fully rejected from potential Pesach use, one might have thought it does not become a shelamim if slaughtered in the interim. The second pasuk teaches that it does.

Ve-chad de-lo avar zmano ve-lo avrah shnato — the third is needed for when it is the right age and Pesach has not yet arrived — it is, say, Purim. The animal is fully eligible to serve as a Pesach in a few weeks. One might have thought that if slaughtered now it carries the status of a Pesach. The third pasuk teaches that even here, if brought before Pesach, it has the status of a shelamim and is not treated as a Pesach. Tzricha: all three cases required their own derivation.

### Pesach Pasuk Issue

The summary of this extended discussion is as follows. The entire debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva ultimately yields the same ruling through different sources: an obligatory korban cannot come from ma'aser sheini funds. Rabbi Eliezer derives it from Pesach Mitzrayim; Rabbi Akiva derives it from the chatat entry of Zot HaTorah. As for the difficult pasuk u-zavachta Pesach la-Hashem Elokecha tzon u-vakar, Rabbi Eliezer reads bakar as extending Pesach principles to all other korbanot; Rabbi Akiva reads it as establishing that a motar Pesach — in any of its three forms — takes on the status of a shelamim.

---

## Minchot: Sources

### Motar Pesach

A new perek begins, redirecting the discussion back to the laws of menachot. Kol korbanot ha-tzibbur ve-ze ha-yachid — all communal and individual korbanot, by which the mishna means all communal and individual menachot in context — ba'im min ha-aretz u-mi-chutz la-aretz: the grain used for them may come from Israel or from outside Israel. Min ha-chadash u-min ha-yashan: they may come from new grain or old, recently harvested or stored.

### Three Pesukim

Chutz min ha-omer u-shtei ha-lechem — with the exception of the Omer and the Shtei HaLechem brought on Pesach and Shavuot respectively. She-einam ba'im ela min ha-chadash: these two must come from new grain, since their entire purpose is to represent the new barley and wheat harvest. U-min ha-aretz: they must also come from grain grown in Eretz Yisrael, since they are the first harvest of the Land. These are the only two menachot so restricted.

### Pesach Cases

Ve-khulam einam ba'im ela min ha-muvchar — and for all menachot, one must use choice flour. Ve-eizeh u muvchar shelahem? — what counts as the choicest? Machnis ve-Zatcha, two locations in Eretz Yisrael famed for superior grain — some manuscripts read Michmas u-Meyunicha or Machmas ve-Zanocha. Whatever the precise identification, the Mishnah describes them as alfa le-solet — grade A flour, the alpha of fine flour. Shniyah lahem, second to them in quality, is Aforayim ba-bika, from the valley region called Aforayim. Kol ha-aratzot hayu kesherot — all lands were technically valid, ela mi-kan hayu mevi'im — but this is where they would actually bring from, as these produced the best grain. Whether this final specification refers to all menachot or specifically to the Omer and Shtei HaLechem is not entirely clear from the mishna. Rashi reads kol artzot shel Eretz Yisrael kesherot, limiting himself to Eretz Yisrael, which suggests he is speaking of the Omer and Shtei HaLechem specifically, the only menachot required to come from Israeli grain.

---

## Omer & Shtei HaL

### Grain Sources

The Gemara now challenges the mishna: matnitin de-lo ke-hai tanna — our mishna does not accord with the following tanna. For a braita teaches: Omer ha-ba min ha-yashan kasher — if the Omer is brought from last year's grain, it is valid. Shtei ha-lechem ha-ba'ah min ha-yashan kesherah — and likewise the Shtei HaLechem brought from old grain is valid. Ela she-chisar mitzvah — one has merely failed to fulfill the mitzvah optimally. This stands in clear tension with our mishna, which states that these two must come from new grain.

How does the braita permit this? By the Omer the Torah says takriv et minchat bikurecha — you shall bring your first-fruits offering — and from the additional verb takriv the braita derives that one may bring it even afilu min ha-aliyah, even from stored grain in the attic. Similarly by the Shtei HaLechem, the Torah says mi-moshvoteichem tavi'u — from your dwelling places you shall bring — and from the inclusive word tavi'u (you shall bring) the braita derives that one may bring it from anywhere, even stored grain, though mi-moshvoteichem simultaneously excludes grain from chutz la-aretz.

### Choice Flour

The Gemara presses: ve-ha-kativ reishit — the Torah explicitly says it must be the first of the cutting! And: ha-kativ chadashah — it must be a minchat chadashah, a new grain offering! How can the braita permit old grain in the face of these explicit terms?

The Gemara answers: hai mi-bayei lei li-khe-de-tanya — the word chadashah is needed for what the following tanna teaches.

### Old Grain Braita

Rabbi Natan ve-Rabbi Akiva amru: Shtei ha-lechem ha-ba'ot min ha-yashan kesherot — Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Akiva both hold that Shtei HaLechem brought from old grain is nonetheless valid. U-mani mekayem chadashah — how then do they understand the requirement that it be chadashah? She-tehei chadashah le-khol ha-menachot: it must be new relative to all other menachot — meaning that until the Shtei HaLechem is brought, no other minchahmay be offered from the new grain's harvest. The word chadashah does not mandate that the Shtei HaLechem itself come from new grain; it mandates that it inaugurate the new grain season for all other menachot. Paradoxically, on this view the Shtei HaLechem need not itself consist of new grain, yet once it is brought, all other menachot may now use the new grain. The requirement of chadashah is thus relational — it defines the Shtei HaLechem's role as the gateway to the new grain season — rather than intrinsic to the composition of the offering itself.

A final note on the mishna's opening statement: although it says kol korbanot ha-tzibbur ve-ha-yachid, the context makes clear that menachot are the subject. Tosafos raises the question of analogous rules for animal korbanot — whether there are limitations regarding where the animals come from or distinctions between new and old. He concludes from the Tosefta that kol korbanot ha-tzibbur ve-ha-yachid ba'in me-eretz u-mi-chutz la-aretz afilu mi-ben ovdei kochavim: all animal korbanot may come from Israel, from outside Israel, and even from non-Jews. The notable exceptions are the bechor and ma'aser behemah, where there may be restrictions, a topic that will be addressed more fully in Masechet Bechorot.

---

---

# Menachot 84

## Omer from Chutz La'aretz

### Mishnah Review: Eretz Yi…

The daf begins on the very last line of 83b. The Mishnah taught that all Menachot may come from old grain or new grain, and from grain grown in Eretz Yisrael or Chutz La'aretz — with one significant exception: the Omer and the Shtei HaLechem, whose entire purpose is to represent the new grain. Those must come from Eretz Yisrael and from the new crop.

In the preceding sugya, however, the Gemara introduced a striking irony: a number of Tannaim hold that the very Korbonot whose function is to permit the new grain may themselves come from old grain. Now the Gemara turns to the second axis of the question — must these Korbonot come from grain grown in Israel?

The last line of 83b frames the transition: עד כאן לא פליגי אלא בחדש — the only debate among the Tannaim so far has concerned whether the Omer and Shtei HaLechem require new grain. But regarding the requirement that they come from Eretz Yisrael — לא פליגי — there is no dispute, at least not among those Tannaim previously cited. The Gemara then signals that the ruling of the Mishnah holds only according to those Tannaim, but not like the following:

### R' Yose: Omer from Diasp…

דתניא — there is a Braita: Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda says, עומר בא מחוץ לארץ — the Omer may come from outside of Israel. How then does he interpret the verse "ki tavou el ha'aretz," which frames the entire obligation in terms of entering the land? He explains: שלא נתחייבו בעומר קודם שנכנסו לארץ — the verse is teaching that the obligation of the Omer did not begin until Israel entered the land. But once that obligation took effect, it applies universally and the Omer itself may come from anywhere.

The Gemara thus identifies our Mishnah as departing from this position. It is worth noting that the manner in which the Gemara introduces this — כמאן? דלא כהאי תנא — is somewhat unusual, though perhaps understandable given the structure of the discussion.

### Chadash De'oraita Link

The Gemara feels compelled to explain the internal logic of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda's position, because it is not self-evident. One might readily understand why the Omer need not come from new grain — textual derivations can be marshaled for that. But to say that it may come from grain grown outside Israel is another matter entirely, especially given that the agricultural Korbonot of the Yamim Tovim seem so organically rooted in the land.

The Gemara's explanation: דקסבר חדש בחוץ לארץ דאורייתא — Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda holds that the prohibition of Chadash outside of Israel is biblical. How does he know this? דכתיב ממושבותיכם — it says "from all your dwelling places." כל מקום שאתם יושבין — wherever you live, even outside Israel. The phrase "ki tavou el ha'aretz," then, establishes the starting point of the prohibition — once you have entered the land, the prohibition of Chadash applies everywhere you dwell.

The logical consequence follows: וכיון דאורייתא היא — since the prohibition of Chadash is de'oraita and applies everywhere — אקרובי נמי מקריבין — so too the Omer, which is מתיר for that grain, can be brought from that grain. The Omer does not merely permit barley grown in Israel; it permits grain wherever the prohibition extends. And if the prohibition extends to Chutz La'aretz, the Omer can logically be brought from Chutz La'aretz.

This is indeed a compelling line of reasoning, even if it gives one pause.

### Diaspora Grain Ideology

The more conventional understanding of the relationship between Eretz Yisrael and Chutz La'aretz in this context is hierarchical: the Torah's fundamental frame of reference is the Jewish people in their land, and the grain of the land of Israel is primary. The prohibition of Chadash outside Israel is derivative — it follows because Israel's prohibition extends outward, in the same way that the unnatural state of the Galut is understood as a dependent extension of a reality whose center is Israel. On this view, the Omer, which resolves the prohibition, naturally comes from its source — Eretz Yisrael — even while the prohibition itself radiates outward.

What Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda appears to be saying is something different: that the Torah does not treat the diaspora as merely derivative, but rather as a legitimate domain of agricultural life in its own right. The prohibition of Chadash applies there not as a secondary consequence but as an independent reality — and therefore, grain grown there is appropriate material for the Omer. This is, on Yom Yerushalayim, ideologically striking. It seems to undercut the sense that Galut is an unnatural state, and implies that the Torah itself regards the diaspora harvest as something it takes seriously on its own terms.

### Chadash Leniency Argument

It is worth noting that several Poskim who seek to explain the widespread leniency regarding Chadash in Chutz La'aretz have pointed to this Gemara on two grounds. First, the Gemara uses the language קסבר — "he is of the opinion" — which implies that it is the singular view of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda and is not necessarily the accepted position. Second, this Gemara explicitly links the two principles: if Chadash is prohibited in Chutz La'aretz then the Omer may come from Chutz La'aretz, and conversely, since we rule like our Mishnah that the Omer comes only from Eretz Yisrael, we may infer that we likewise rule that the biblical prohibition of Chadash applies only in Eretz Yisrael.

This argument has its limitations — the Gemara is presenting the positions as linked in Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda's view, and others may disagree that the concepts are necessarily linked — but it is nonetheless a Gemara that enters the discussion among the Poskim on this question.

### New Grain vs. Land Debate

A further speculation is worth raising. Even granting that Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda permits the Omer to come from Chutz La'aretz, it does not necessarily follow that he permits old grain. If one had to identify the primary conceptual core of the Omer and Shtei HaLechem — what they are fundamentally about — it would be the new harvest. ראשית קצירכם, the first of your cutting, is the essential idea. Being from Eretz Yisrael, while certainly important, may be secondary.

It is therefore quite plausible that Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, who permits Chutz La'aretz grain, would nonetheless insist on new grain — just as the Tannaim who permitted old grain likely insisted on Eretz Yisrael grain. Each position relaxes one of the two requirements while preserving the other. Our Mishnah, by contrast, insists on both.

---

## Omer on Shemittah

### Shomrei Sefichin

The Gemara now turns to a Mishnah in Shekalim — the tractate concerned with the annual collection of funds for the Trumat HaLishka, the communal treasury used for public Korbonot, principally the daily Tamid and other communal sacrifices. The Mishnah states: שומרי ספיחין בשביעית נוטלין שכרן מתרומת הלשכה — the guardians of the Sefichin during Shemittah are paid from the communal treasury.

Sefichin are plants that grow on their own without being planted — since planting is forbidden in Shemittah, the only grain available is that which has grown spontaneously from seeds that fell naturally, wild grain that was never cultivated. The context of this Mishnah is the guarding of such grain for use in bringing the Omer. Since the Omer is a communal Korban, the wages of those who protect this grain are paid from the communal funds.

### Burning Shmita Grain Pro…

Rami bar Chama posed a pointed question to Rav Chisda. On the one hand, the Mishnah in Shekalim assumes that the Omer is indeed brought from Shemittah grain. On the other hand, the Torah says regarding Shemittah produce: והיתה שבת הארץ לכם לאכלה — it shall be for you to eat. From this the Rabbis derive ולא לשריפה — you may not burn Shemittah produce. Yet the Omer requires taking a Kemitza and burning it. How, then, can one burn Shemittah grain in the service of the Omer without violating le'ochla?

Rav Chisda's initial response is almost rhetorical: רחמנא אמר לכו לדורותיכם — the Torah commanded the bringing of the Omer for all generations. Would you nullify it? Rami bar Chama pushes back: he was not suggesting nullifying the Omer. His proposal was more specific.

### Karmel: Must Be Fresh

Rami bar Chama suggests: ליתי מדישתקד — let the Omer be brought from last year's crop. This, he notes, is precisely what certain Tannaim allow, and here would be a practical rationale: on a Shemittah year one might prove that old grain must be permitted, for there is no other way to bring the Omer without violating le'ochla.

The response, however, is: בעינא כרמל וליכא — we require karmel and it is not present. This introduces a different biblical basis for requiring new grain — not the word ראשית, reishit, as was emphasized in the previous discussion, but the word כרמל, which denotes grain that is fresh and moist.

A natural follow-up: could one bring something that was once fresh — grain ground into flour the previous year when it was still fresh? The flour, having been processed when the grain was new, might still bear some character of freshness. But the Gemara rejects this as well. אמר קרא כרמל תקריב — the pasuk says, next to the word karmel, takriv — you shall offer it. The verse places the requirement of karmel at the moment of the offering: בעינא כרמל בשעת הקרבה וליכא — you need it to be karmel at the time of the offering, and that cannot be satisfied by grain that was processed the previous year.

### Yochanan vs. Elazar: Sou…

The Gemara now records a tannaitic dispute — or rather a dispute among Amoraim — about the textual source for the requirement of new grain. Rabbi Yochanan derives it from the word כרמל: the grain must be fresh at the time it is brought, and therefore last year's grain is invalid. Rabbi Elazar derives it instead from the phrase ראשית קצירכם: ראשית קצירך ולא סוף קצירך — the first of your harvest, not the end of a previous harvest. If one were to bring grain from last year's crop, that grain would now represent the conclusion of last year's harvest season, not the beginning of this year's — and therefore it fails the requirement of ראשית.

Both Amoraim agree on the halacha; they differ only on which pasuk provides the derivation.

### Rabba: Bikkurim Source

Rabba then poses a question, not about the halacha but about the source. A Braita derives the requirement of new grain from neither כרמל nor ראשית קצירכם, but rather from the term ביכורים — "first fruits." The Gemara records this as a potential tiyuvta, a contradiction, because this represents a third, independent pasuk as the basis for the very same halacha.

This is a striking feature of the sugya: the Gemara treats a disagreement about which pasuk teaches an undisputed halacha with the same gravity it would apply to a substantive legal dispute, even invoking the strong language of תיובתא. One would expect the Gemara's concern to be reserved for contradictions in the halacha itself; here, everyone agrees that the Omer must come from new grain. The implication may be that the precise textual basis shapes some dimension of how the requirement is defined, even if that dimension is not fully spelled out.

### Omer from Barley: Proofs

The Braita opens with a question that, on reflection, is more surprising than it first appears: from what type of grain does the Omer come? The answer — barley — is entirely familiar. Yet the Torah never states explicitly that the Omer is of barley. The verse speaks of ראשית קצירכם, אביב קלוי באש גרש כרמל — but nowhere does it specify שעורים.

Rabbi Eliezer derives it through a gezera shava on the word אביב. In Egypt, the verse describes the plague of barad: כי השעורה אביב — for the barley was in its aviv stage, ripe and standing. The ripe barley was destroyed; the flax and spelt, still immature, were not. Rabbi Eliezer argues: מה אביב האמור במצרים שעורים — since aviv in Egypt refers to barley, the word אביב in the Omer passage — אביב קלוי באש — likewise refers to barley. This is also consistent with the calendar: barley ripens around Nissan, the time of the exodus, which is why it was the crop struck by the final plague before the departure.

Rabbi Akiva takes a different approach, reasoning from symmetry between the individual and the community. An individual may be obligated to bring a barley Mincha — the Minchat Sotah — and an obligatory wheat Mincha — a Minchat Choteh in the context of a Korban Oleh v'Yored. By analogy, the community should have both an obligatory wheat Mincha and an obligatory barley Mincha. The wheat Mincha of the community is the Shtei HaLechem — already established. Therefore the communal barley Mincha must be the Omer. If the Omer were of wheat, there would be no communal barley Mincha at all.

A third consideration: אם אתה אומר עומר בא מן החיטים — if the Omer were from wheat, then אין שתי הלחם בכורים — the Shtei HaLechem could not qualify as ביכורים, as the first of the new wheat, because a wheat Korban would already have been brought as the Omer. The Shtei HaLechem must be the first communal Korban from the new wheat. For this to hold, the Omer must be of barley.

This last point contains a subtle irony. The Shtei HaLechem is called ביכורים — first — yet strictly speaking, the Omer precedes it. The Omer is brought from new grain before the Shtei HaLechem. The resolution is that the Shtei HaLechem is ביכורים of the wheat. The Omer, being barley, does not preempt its status as the first wheat Korban. Yet there is something paradoxical: even after the Shtei HaLechem is brought, it does not mean something has been placed on the mizbeach before it from the new wheat — but the Omer was brought from new barley, which is still grain. Nevertheless, the Braita is insisting that we cannot further erode the ביכורים status of the Shtei HaLechem by having it precede an Omer of wheat.

### Tiyuvta: Conflicting Pes…

The Gemara records this as a tiyuvta. The substance of the contradiction is not in the halacha — all agree the Omer requires new grain — but in the derivation. Rabbi Yochanan cited כרמל; Rabbi Elazar cited ראשית קצירכם; the Braita about barley relies on ביכורים. Three distinct pesukim, each independently generating the same requirement. The Gemara treats this multiplicity as a genuine problem, even in the absence of a substantive disagreement on the law.

### Omer Overrides Shemittah

Returning to the Shemittah question, there are in fact several distinct problems involved in bringing the Omer during a Shemittah year — not merely the le'ochla issue raised by Rami bar Chama.

First: harvesting. The Torah prohibits שדך לא תקצור — you may not harvest your field in Shemittah. Yet the Omer requires קצירכם — harvesting. Tosafot offers two responses. The simpler is that the obligation to bring the Omer overrides Shemittah restrictions, as it overrides Shabbat. The more conceptually interesting response is that the prohibition of harvesting in Shemittah targets private ownership — the exertion of proprietary control over one's field. The Torah does not require produce to die on the vine; the poor may eat it, and one may pick and eat freely. What is forbidden is asserting dominion over the land as in an ordinary year. When the Beit HaMikdash harvests a portion of grain for the Omer — a communal act in service of a communal Korban — it is not private ownership being asserted. The nature of the act is categorically different, and therefore may not constitute a violation of Shemittah's harvesting prohibition at all.

Second: guarding the grain. The Mishnah in Shekalim speaks of paid guards watching the Sefichin, but guarding one's field in Shemittah can itself constitute an improper assertion of ownership. Tosafot addresses this similarly. One answer is that the guardians would not forcibly bar anyone from entering; they would simply inform passersby that the grain was intended for the Omer, and people would refrain voluntarily. A second and more principled answer follows the same logic as before: prohibiting the guarding of one's field in Shemittah is targeted at private property interests. Protecting grain for the communal Korban of the Beit HaMikdash is a categorically different act — communal stewardship rather than private ownership — and therefore may not fall under the same prohibition.

In both cases, Tosafot's deeper answer is not a technical override but a substantive argument: much of what Shemittah prohibits is the exertion of private ownership, and actions taken on behalf of the Beit HaMikdash for communal Korbonot simply do not share that character.

---

## Bikkurim: Choice Produce

### Bikkurim: Seven Species

The Gemara shifts to a Mishnah in Maseches Bikkurim: אין מביאין בכורים חוץ משבעת המינים — Bikkurim may only be brought from the seven species for which Eretz Yisrael is praised: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates (where the honey of dates — devash temarim — is the agricultural product intended by the Torah). But even within those seven species, there are further limitations. ולא מתמרים שבהרים — not from dates that grow on the mountain tops, where the quality is inferior. ולא מפירות שבעמקים — and not from other fruit that grows in the valleys, where similarly the conditions produce less choice produce.

The principle underlying both exclusions, though not stated explicitly in the Mishnah, is that Bikkurim must come from grade A produce — the best of its kind from the most favorable growing conditions.

### Muvchar: L'chatchila/B'd…

Our Mishnah in Menachot likewise states that all Menachot — and especially the Omer and Shtei HaLechem — must come from המובחר, the choice grain. It specifies which regions produce the finest grain for each type of Mincha. The language אין באים אלא מן המובחר — they may only come from the choice — is strong. Yet the natural intuition is that this is a lechatchilah requirement; bedi'avad, if inferior grain was used, the Mincha would remain valid.

The analogous question arises for Bikkurim: if one brought Bikkurim from non-choice fruit — fruit from the mountaintops or from non-ideal growing locations — do the Bikkurim become sanctified? This is more complex. On the one hand, one might argue that the notion of "first" admits no quality restriction — first is first, regardless of quality. On the other hand, ביכורים carries a conceptual dimension of "best" alongside "first," and if the produce is not from an ideal growing environment, perhaps the very status of Bikkurim is undermined even after the fact.

### Ulla: Non-Choice Not Val…

Ulla rules decisively: אם הביא לא קידש — if one brought Bikkurim from non-choice fruit, they are not sanctified. The Bikkurim are invalid even bedi'avad. This is a stringent position: not only is one obligated to bring from choice produce lechatchilah, but bringing from inferior produce fails to achieve the status of Bikkurim altogether.

### Shtei HaLechem: First of…

Rabbah was recounting Ulla's ruling when Rav Acha bar Abba challenged him from a Braita. The Braita discusses the status of the Shtei HaLechem as a קרבן ראשית — a korban of firsts — that must precede all other Menachot and Bikkurim. The challenge is embedded in the details of what exactly the Shtei HaLechem must precede, which the Braita proceeds to elaborate at length.

### Shtei HaLechem Precedence

The Braita opens by establishing that the Shtei HaLechem is the Korban Reshit — the first — that must precede all Menachot. It derives this from the verse בהקריבכם מנחה חדשה לה' בשבועותיכם, which refers to the Shtei HaLechem brought on Shavuot. The Shtei HaLechem is the first new-grain Mincha of the year.

The word חדשה appears twice in the relevant pesukim. From the first חדשה the Braita learns that the Shtei HaLechem must precede all Menachot of new wheat. The second חדשה, rendered superfluous by the first, extends the requirement: אם אינו עניין לחדשה של חיטים — if it is not needed for what we already know about wheat — תנהו עניין לחדשה של שעורים — apply it to the new barley. Thus the Shtei HaLechem must also precede any Mincha brought from new barley. The exception, of course, is the Omer itself, which necessarily precedes the Shtei HaLechem.

This clarifies the scope of what each Korban accomplishes. The Omer permits new grain — of all varieties — for eating outside the Beit HaMikdash. The Shtei HaLechem permits new grain — again of all varieties — for use on the mizbeach in the Beit HaMikdash. Although the Omer is barley and the Shtei HaLechem is wheat, neither is restricted to its own species in what it permits. Nothing of the new grain, whether barley or wheat, may be placed on the mizbeach until the Shtei HaLechem is brought.

The Braita then turns to Bikkurim: how do we know that the Shtei HaLechem must precede Bikkurim as well? תלמוד לומר וחג שבועות תעשה לך ביכורי קציר חטים — the Torah describes Shavuot as the holiday of the first of the wheat harvest. The use of ביכורי — first — signals that the Shtei HaLechem, brought on Shavuot, must be the absolute first, even before Bikkurim of wheat.

But must it also precede Bikkurim of barley? The phrase ביכורי קציר חטים specifies wheat. For barley Bikkurim the Braita derives from וחג הקציר ביכורי מעשיך אשר תזרע בשדה — the holiday of harvesting, the first of all your labors that you sow in the field. Here Shavuot is called the festival of the first of all one's agricultural labors, not limited to wheat. Therefore the Shtei HaLechem must precede Bikkurim of barley as well.

The Braita continues to expand the scope. The phrase אשר תזרע — which you sow — refers to planted crops. But what of things that grow on their own without planting, שעלו מאליהן? The word בשדה, in the field, is broad enough to include spontaneous growth in a field, and so the Shtei HaLechem must precede Bikkurim even of such produce. Then: ואין לי אלא בשדה — I know only things that come from a field. What of things that grew on a rooftop, in a vacant lot, in a flowerpot, or on a boat — שבגג ושבחורבה ושבעציץ ושבספינה? From the verse בכורי כל אשר בארצם — the first of all that is in their land, said in the context of what goes to the Kohanim — the Braita derives that ביכורים applies broadly to everything that grows, not only to field crops.

Finally, the Braita asks: how do we know the Shtei HaLechem must also precede Nesachim — wine libations — and fruit? From the verse regarding Sukkot, באספך מעשיך מן השדה, which describes the harvest festival in terms encompassing all agricultural produce: grain, fruit, and wine. A gezera shava on the word מעשיך links Shavuot's "first of your labors" to Sukkot's encompassing harvest, establishing that the Shtei HaLechem is first relative to all of these.

The halachic bottom line of this entire Braita is one ruling: nothing of the new produce — whether brought as a Mincha, whether wheat or barley, whether grown in a field or a flowerpot or a boat, and whether grain, fruit, or wine — may be brought to the Beit HaMikdash until the Shtei HaLechem has been offered.

### Shavuot: Chag HaBikkurim

This Braita affords a rare opportunity to reflect on the agricultural significance of Shavuot — חג הביכורים — in its most direct biblical sense. The Shtei HaLechem represents the first expression of the year's agricultural bounty: the gratitude and the recognition of God's hand in the harvest. Everything that follows — the Bikkurim brought over the summer months, the libations, the fruit — waits upon this first act. In transposing Shavuot's meaning primarily onto Matan Torah, something of this dimension is inevitably lost. The sugya presents an occasion to recover it.

### Boat/Roof: Mincha Not Bi…

The relevance of this Braita to Ulla's ruling now becomes clear. The Braita states that the Shtei HaLechem must precede even produce that grew on a rooftop or in a boat. Since the Shtei HaLechem must precede it, one might infer that such produce can legitimately be brought as Bikkurim — for why mention that the Shtei HaLechem takes precedence if there were no possibility of bringing Bikkurim from such produce? This would contradict Ulla's ruling that non-choice produce cannot be sanctified as Bikkurim even bedi'avad.

The Gemara resolves: סיפא אף מן המנחות — the latter clause of that Braita applies to Menachot, not to Bikkurim. The Shtei HaLechem must precede not only Bikkurim but also Menachot from the new grain. When the Braita says the Shtei HaLechem must precede produce grown on a rooftop or a boat, it is saying that such produce may be used in a Mincha — and the Mincha must wait for the Shtei HaLechem. The implication for Bikkurim is the reverse: such produce is not eligible for Bikkurim at all. This is consistent with the assumption, implicit throughout this discussion, that the requirement of muvchar for Menachot operates at most at the level of lechatchilah, while bedi'avad a Mincha from non-choice grain is valid. The debate about Bikkurim is categorically different.

### Kol Tahor: Bikkurim or M…

Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges this resolution. The Gemara was reading the verse בהקריבכם מנחה חדשה as referring to the requirement that the Shtei HaLechem precede Menachot. But the same passage in Parashat Korach continues: כל טהור בביתך יאכל אותה — every pure person in your house shall eat it. This phrase, however, cannot apply to a Mincha, which is Kodshei Kodashim and may only be eaten by male Kohanim. The phrase "every pure person in your house" is inclusive of women and children — a description that fits Bikkurim, not Menachot. If so, the pasuk must be referring to Bikkurim, and the inference that it also speaks about rooftop and boat produce being valid for Menachot unravels.

### Two Pesukim Resolution

Rav Mesharshia resolves the difficulty: תרי קראי כתיבי — there are two pesukim. The Braita in Korach states: בכורי כל אשר בארצם אשר יביאו לה' לך יהיה — the first of all in their land that they bring to God shall be yours — כל טהור בביתך יאכלנו. Where it says לך יהיה, to you, the reference is to the Kohanim specifically, and this speaks of Menachot, eaten only by male Kohanim. Where it says כל טהור בביתך, every pure person in your house, that speaks of Bikkurim, which may be eaten by all members of the Kohen's household. Thus two distinct pesukim are at play, one for each category, and the Braita's reference to rooftop and boat produce need not imply that Bikkurim can come from such locations — it refers to Menachot.

Rav Papa proposes a different resolution: כולה במנחות — the entire section refers to Menachot. What then is meant by כל טהור בביתך? וסיפא דקרא אתיא ללחמי תודה — the end of the verse refers to the bread of the Todah offering. Lachmei Todah, while technically a form of Mincha, occupies a unique position: it is Kodashim Kalim rather than Kodshei Kodashim, and the four loaves given to the Kohanim from a Todah are treated like Terumah — eaten by members of the Kohen's household, not only by male Kohanim. Thus "every pure person in your house" fits Lachmei Todah, and the entire passage can be understood as referring to Menachot in their various forms, without any reference to Bikkurim.

---

## Yochanan-Reish Lakish: B…

### Lo Kidesh vs. Kidesh

The Gemara now restates the underlying dispute in its proper form. Rabbi Yochanan rules: אם הביא לא קידש — if one brought Bikkurim from produce grown on a rooftop, in a flowerpot, or on a boat, the Bikkurim are not sanctified, even bedi'avad. Reish Lakish rules: אם הביא קידש — if one brought such Bikkurim, they are sanctified. His reasoning is drawn from an analogy: נעשה ככחוש בקדשים — it is like a scrawny animal in the domain of Korbonot. An animal that is thin and not ideal is still valid as a Korban bedi'avad. Similarly, Bikkurim from non-ideal conditions, while far from the ideal, are still valid after the fact.

This analogy also speaks implicitly to the question of the muvchar requirement for Menachot and Korbonot of animals: bedi'avad, inferior quality does not invalidate. The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is therefore specifically and exclusively about Bikkurim.

### Dream Defense: Mei-reish…

The Gemara seeks to explain Rabbi Yochanan's position. Rabbi Elazar states that he saw Rabbi Yochanan in a dream — which Rashi understands not as receiving a direct communication from Rabbi Yochanan in the dream, but as the dream inspiring him with the intellectual confidence and divine assistance to articulate a defense of Rabbi Yochanan's view. He then offers:

אמר קרא מראשית כל פרי האדמה תביא מארצך — the verse says, "from the first of all the fruit of the land you shall bring from your land." The derasha proceeds on two levels. מראשית — ולא כל ראשית — from the first, but not from all firsts, which might limit Bikkurim to the Shivat HaMinim rather than all fruit. More importantly: מארצך — ולא כל ארצך — from your land, but not from every part of your land. This excludes produce that did not grow in optimal conditions — on rooftops, in boats, in non-grounded flowerpots. The requirement is not merely that the individual fruit be of high quality, but that it grew in conditions representative of the best of what the land of Israel produces. Produce from a rooftop or a boat is not growing in conditions that represent the choicest of the land, and therefore falls outside the biblical definition of Bikkurim.

### Reish Lakish: Aretz Shiv…

Reish Lakish, who holds that such Bikkurim are valid bedi'avad, must account for the word מארצך and explain what he does with the limitation ולא כל ארצך. He does not use it to exclude non-ideal growing locations. Instead he uses it differently: מבעי ליה לכדתניא — he requires the word ארץ for a different drasha, as the Braita of Beniyei bar Rebbi teaches.

The Braita applies a binyan av: נאמר כאן ארץ ונאמר להלן ארץ — it says ארץ here by Bikkurim, and it says ארץ there in the verse ארץ חטה ושעורה וגפן ותאנה ורמון — the land of wheat and barley and grapes and figs and pomegranates. מה להלן שבח הארץ — just as that verse refers to the special praise of the land, i.e., the Shivat HaMinim — אף כאן שבח הארץ — so too here, Bikkurim must come from the Shivat HaMinim. For Reish Lakish, then, the word ארץ limits Bikkurim to the seven species, not to ideal growing locations. Produce from non-ideal locations remains valid bedi'avad as long as it is from one of the Shivat HaMinim.

As for the implication of מארצך that Rabbi Yochanan uses to exclude non-ideal locations, Reish Lakish is simply not persuaded by that reading: ואידך ארץ מארצך לא משמע ליה — he does not read ולא כל ארצך from the formulation מארצך.

### Mevi v'Kore vs. Eino Kore

The Gemara notes that there are two contradictory Braitot regarding Bikkurim from the locations in question. One Braita rules מביא וקורא — one brings and recites the declaration, which indicates that the obligation is fully biblical and the Bikkurim fully valid. The other Braita rules מביא ואינו קורא — one brings but does not recite the declaration, indicating a lower level of obligation, presumably rabbinic rather than biblical.

At first glance these two Braitot seem to correspond to the positions of Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan respectively. But the question is whether each position can accommodate both Braitot. The Gemara proceeds to show how Reish Lakish — who holds that Bikkurim from non-ideal locations are valid — can reconcile both.

### Cave Roof vs. Building R…

The Gemara resolves the rooftop cases: גג אגג לא קשיא — one Braita and the other are not contradictory. הא בגג דמערה הא בגג דבית — the distinction is between the roof of a cave and the roof of a building. The roof of a cave is earth — actual ground. Although it may not be the most nutrient-rich environment, since the soil depth is limited, it is nonetheless earth connected to the land of Israel. Produce growing there is considered to grow from ארץ ישראל, and therefore if it is brought as Bikkurim, one brings and recites the declaration — it is fully biblical. The roof of a building, by contrast, is not earth; it is a built surface elevated above the land. Produce growing there does not grow from ארץ ישראל in any meaningful sense, and so if brought, one brings but does not recite the declaration — it does not rise to the level of a full biblical obligation.

### Nakuv vs. Not Nakuv Pot

The flowerpot cases are resolved on a familiar principle: כאן בנקוב כאן בשאינו נקוב — one Braita speaks of a flowerpot with a hole in its bottom, the other of a flowerpot without a hole. A perforated flowerpot — atzitz nakuv — placed on the ground is treated as though the plant is growing directly from the earth; the hole provides the critical connection. There, one brings and recites the declaration. A sealed flowerpot — she-eino nakuv — contains dirt but is not connected to the actual land, and therefore produce from it is at most rabbinic; one brings but does not recite.

### Pottery Boat: Grounded H…

The boat cases are similarly resolved: כאן בספינה של עץ כאן בספינה של חרס — one Braita speaks of a wooden boat, the other of a pottery boat. This distinction is elaborated by a significant discussion in Tosafot.

The matter involves three criteria for a boat to be treated as though it is connected to the land. First, the hull must be pottery, which is porous, rather than wood, which creates a complete barrier between the growing medium and the earth below. Second — a point the Gemara here does not state explicitly but which emerges from another Gemara — the hull must be grounded: its bottom must rest in the actual soil of the riverbed or seabed, not floating above it. Third, Tosafot argues — in line with the principle of atzitz nakuv — that the pottery hull must have a hole in it. Rashi holds that pottery in the ground is sufficient without a hole, since pottery is inherently porous. Tosafot, however, maintains consistency with the flowerpot principle and requires an actual perforation. A boat satisfying all three conditions — pottery, grounded hull, perforated — is treated as though the produce grows from the land of Israel, and one brings and recites the declaration. A wooden boat, or one that is not grounded, or one without a hole, does not achieve that connection, and at most one brings without the declaration.

How the Tanna'im who hold מביא וקורא understood a grounded pottery boat with a hole is indeed a striking image, but the legal logic follows the same principles that govern every other case in this sugya: connection to the actual earth of ארץ ישראל is what determines whether growth is of the land in the biblical sense required for Bikkurim.

# Menachot 85

## Bikkurim Debate Resolved

### RY vs RL: Bikkurim

The daf opens at its very first word with the continuation of a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerning the validity of bikkurim that come from less than ideal growing conditions. The question was whether such bikkurim are patur bedi'avad — that is, whether they fail to discharge the obligation even after the fact. Reish Lakish maintained that they are valid bedi'avad, drawing an analogy to a scrawny animal. Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, held that they are not valid, invoking a special pasuk and arguing that the nature of bikkurim demands something more — that the fruit represent the genuine choice of one's produce, grown under fitting conditions.

The dispute was complicated by two conflicting baraitot. One braita ruled that bikkurim brought from rooftops and boats are valid and require the korei, the formal declaration — which is to say the bringer is biblically obligated. The other braita ruled that one brings but does not make the korei, implying only a rabbinic obligation at most. Reish Lakish could resolve this readily: the case where one brings and makes the korei reflects his position that bikkurim from non-ideal conditions are valid, while the case where one does not make the korei refers to produce grown on an ordinary rooftop — not a cave roof — meaning it is not considered to be rooted in the ground of Eretz Yisrael at all, and thus falls below even the threshold of bedi'avad validity.

### Tannai Hi Resolution

The difficulty, as the Gemara opens on 85a, is for Rabbi Yochanan: ela le'Rabbi Yochanan kashia. How does he account for the braita that says one brings from a rooftop and makes the full declaration? The Gemara's answer is tannai hi — it is a Tannaitic dispute. Rabbi Yochanan cannot escape the braita, but he aligns with those tannaim who invalidate bikkurim from non-ideal conditions. The braita that validates them reflects a dissenting tannaitic view.

### Rooftop Bikkurim Cases

The Gemara then cites a braita that refines the picture further. Shebegag shebachur vemevi vekorei — from a cave roof and from an open area, one brings and makes the declaration, even though these are non-ideal growing conditions. However, shebakis shebesfina eino mevi kol ikkar — when it comes from a flowerpot on a boat, one cannot bring bikkurim at all. The reason is either that such pots have no holes and the produce is not considered to be growing from the land of Eretz Yisrael, or that these growing conditions are so profoundly substandard that even bedi'avad the bikkurim would not be acceptable in any sense.

### Bikkurim vs. Menachot

The upshot is as follows. Reish Lakish holds that bikkurim are valid bedi'avad even from non-ideal conditions. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. The baraitot that appear to support Reish Lakish reflect a dissenting tannaitic opinion, and even those tannaim who permit bikkurim from non-ideal conditions would distinguish between varying degrees of inadequacy.

This stands in striking contrast to what the previous Mishnah had established regarding flour for menachot. Throughout the entire discussion of grain quality, there was never a suggestion that the offering is invalid bedi'avad. The only debate about bedi'avad invalidity arose in the context of bikkurim — and this is understandable, since bikkurim by their very concept must represent the choicest of one's produce. As was noted, this does not necessarily mean the fruit itself must be at its physical peak — the very first fruits of the season are sometimes somewhat scrawny — but it does mean the produce must represent the best of what one's land can offer, grown under proper conditions. The Mishnah concludes accordingly: vekulan ein ba'in ela min hamuvchar — all of these offerings come only from the finest sources. Yet the implication — and the next Mishnah will make it explicit — is that if they are not ideal, they are still valid bedi'avad.

---

## Straw to Ofrayim Aggada

### Afurayim Introduction

Among the places named in the Mishnah as premier sources of solet, Michmas and Zanoach are listed as the top-grade sources, with Afurayim ranked just beneath them — the second-finest wheat. This mention of Afurayim gives the Gemara occasion for an aggadic digression.

### Yochna & Mamre Taunt

Amru lei Yochna u-Mamre le-Moshe — two figures named Yochna and Mamre, identified from context as chartumei Mitzrayim, Egyptian sorcerers whom Moshe had to contend with, said to him: teven ata machnis l'Ofrayim — you are bringing straw to Ofrayim. Rashi, it should be noted, cites the phrase as l'Mitzrayim in his version, though the substance is the same. The taunt is the equivalent of "coals to Newcastle." Since Afurayim was renowned as a source of abundant grain and wheat, it was naturally a place overflowing with straw as well. The sorcerers were mocking Moshe: who needs your tricks and wonders here? You are bringing what we already have in abundance.

### Moshe's Comeback

Moshe replied: amar lehu — amri inshi, l'mata yarka yarka shakil — people say, in the city of vegetables, that is precisely where you bring your vegetables. There is a market for the finest goods precisely where people know quality. As one of the commentators explains, in a place where everyone is buying vegetables, the best vegetables rise to the top. Moshe's point, then, is: precisely here, where Egypt is full of sorcery, is where it will become clear whose power is genuine. If what I do surpasses what you are doing in your own domain, that will prove beyond doubt that what I perform is not sorcery at all, but the hand of God.

---

## Grain Quality & Crop Rot…

### Non-Ideal Fields Mishna

The Gemara now turns to the next Mishnah, which makes explicit what had only been implied before: bedi'avad, if one has not brought ideal flour, the offering is still valid. Ein mevi'im lo mibeit hazevalim — one may not bring flour from grain grown in a manured field. Rashi offers two explanations for why manure disqualifies the grain. His first explanation is that the field requires external fertilization and thus did not grow sufficiently on its own — suggesting the grain is of lesser quality. His second explanation is that shezevela mav'isha umekalkel ta'am haperot — heavy dung affects the taste and quality of what grows in it.

V'lo mibeit hashlachim — and not from a field that is heavily irrigated. The underlying principle is that if the grain cannot flourish on natural rainfall alone, it is not considered of the highest quality. Velo midei ilan — and not from a grain field that had trees growing within it, since the competition between grain and trees means neither is receiving the full nourishment it needs. It is worth noting that trees interspersed with grain need not constitute kilayim if they are spaced appropriately or otherwise configured to avoid the prohibition; the concern here is purely one of grain quality.

Ve'im hevi kasher — but if one brought from any of these, it is valid bedi'avad. This is the clear contrast with the bikkurim debate: for menachot, even grain from these non-ideal conditions will discharge the obligation after the fact.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot Scope

A significant disagreement between Rashi and Tosafot concerns the scope of this Mishnah's requirements. Rashi reads the Mishnah — possibly influenced by its plural language and its placement at the end of the previous perek — as referring specifically to the communal menachot, namely the Omer and the Shtei HaLechem. These offerings are akin to bikkurim in character: they represent the choice of the crops on behalf of the entire community, and therefore the higher standards apply to them in particular. Tosafot, by contrast, understands the Mishnah to be speaking of grain for all menachot without exception, not limiting the requirements to the Omer and Shtei HaLechem.

This ambiguity persists throughout the subsequent discussion and is not fully resolved. Every source that might seem to settle the question carries some element that reintroduces uncertainty.

### Nira & 70-Day Planting

The Mishnah then describes the ideal method for producing the finest grain. Nira hashana — the first year, one overturns the soil but leaves the field fallow. The word nir does not mean merely leaving the field unplanted; it means actively turning over the soil. Uvashana shniya — in the second year, zar'ah kodem lePesach shiv'im yom — one plants the grain seventy days before Pesach. The timing is deliberate: the grain grows during the period when the sun is strengthening into the spring, which produces the finest yield. Vehu oseh solet meruba — and this produces an abundance of fine flour, with each stalk yielding a high quantity of grain.

Here again the question of scope is genuinely ambiguous. The reference to seventy days before Pesach need not be specifically about the Omer; it may simply reflect the agronomic principle that early spring planting produces the best grain. So the Mishnah may well be speaking about grain for all menachot, and Rashi and Tosafot are in dispute about precisely this question.

### Gizbar Flour Inspection

Keitzad bodek et hakemach — how does one check that the flour has been properly sifted? Hagizbar machnis yado letocha — the gizbar, the Temple treasurer, inserts his hand into the flour. Ala be'avak psula — if dust or fine dirt clings to his hand when he withdraws it, the flour is invalid ad sheyinafe — until it has been properly resifted. Once sifted to the requisite standard it becomes kasher. Ve'im hitli'a, psula — but if the flour has become wormy, it is invalid outright; one cannot simply remove the worms and use the rest.

This raises a question about the context. If the Mishnah is speaking about the Omer, the involvement of the gizbar is readily understood, since the Omer is produced within the Beit Hamikdash itself. But if we are speaking of private menachot — which may in some cases have been prepared at home — how would the gizbar have the opportunity to inspect the flour? This question reinforces the ambiguity about whether the discussion is limited to the Omer or extends to all menachot.

What is particularly striking about the flour inspection is the severity of the standard. Even dust — avak — is treated as a disqualifying impurity. The language used is psula, invalid, even though the flour can be resifted and thereby validated. This is noteworthy precisely because the same Mishnah says that grain from a manured or irrigated field is valid bedi'avad — yet flour that has not been perfectly sifted is psula until remedied. The threshold for physical purity of the final flour is remarkably high.

### Once or Twice Plowing?

The Gemara now focuses its attention on the crop rotation method described in the Mishnah. Keitzad oseh — nira shana rishona — one overturns the soil the first year. The question the Gemara raises is: how precisely should the phrase be parsed? Ibayah lehu, heichi ka'amar — does it mean: nira shana rishona u'shniya nira u'zra — you overturn the soil in year one, and in year two you overturn the soil again and then plant? Or does it mean: nira shana rishona, u'shniya zra belo nira — you overturn the soil in year one, and in year two you simply plant without any additional overturning?

The second reading is what the Mishnah appears on its surface to say. But the Gemara wonders whether the first year's overturning suffices, or whether the second year requires its own overturning before planting. Rashi notes an important clarification: one should not conflate overturning the soil with the routine plowing done at the time of planting. When one plants, one always makes furrows — that is inherent in the word zra. The question here is whether, prior to the planting season in year two, there would be a separate and substantial overturning of the soil, analogous to what was done in year one. The agricultural logic of overturning is that it aerates the soil and allows the seed to penetrate more effectively — so there is a compelling reason to do it even in year two, in addition to the furrows made at the time of planting.

### Southern Fields Braita

Ta shema — the Gemara brings a braita to address this question. Amar Rabbi Yose: af chitei karzayim u'kfar achim — even the places called Chitei Karzayim and the village of Achim — ilmalei smuchos l'Yerushalayim, hayu mevi'im mehem — had they been closer to Yerushalayim, they would have brought the Omer and the Shtei HaLechem from them. The principle established here is that ideally the Omer is brought from the closest available source to Yerushalayim. These places were close enough to be ideal in terms of grain quality but were passed over because of distance.

The braita then states: lefi she'ein mevi'im et ha'omer ela min hasados hamidromos — the Omer is brought only from the southern fields, ve'hamenunarot — and from fields where the soil has been overturned. Rashi interprets "southern" as meaning south of Yerushalayim. Tosafot, however, argues that what matters is not geographic direction relative to Yerushalayim but rather southern exposure — that is, the field faces south and therefore receives the full force of the sun throughout the day, particularly in the spring and early summer when the sun travels along a more southerly arc. The sun shines on these fields from the moment it rises and departs from them only at sunset, meaning they receive the maximum possible daily sunlight. Tosafot's reading is strengthened by the Gemara's own subsequent elaboration: shebehen chama zorachat, umehem chama shoka'at — the sun rises on them and sets from them.

The braita then describes the full process for these southern fields: nirash shana rishona — the soil is overturned in year one. Uvashana shniya — in year two, choresh, veshoneh — one plows and then plows again, vezara — and then plants, kodem lePesach shiv'im yom — seventy days before Pesach, kedei shetehei smucha lechama — so that the growing grain is close in time to the onset of the warm season.

This braita is explicit: in the second year, there is both a choresh — a plowing — and a shoneh — a second plowing — before the planting. The soil is turned twice in the year of planting, in addition to the overturning done in year one.

Tosafot raises a difficulty with this braita's attribution of the entire process to the Omer. In the braita's description of the production process, it mentions desh — threshing. Yet in earlier discussions of the Omer, the grain was not threshed in the conventional sense; the stalks were beaten rather than threshed in the standard manner. Tosafot therefore concludes that this discussion is not limited to the Omer — it encompasses grain for menachot more broadly. This is the ongoing ambiguity: the Omer is mentioned explicitly, yet certain details do not fit exclusively an Omer context. One of the places is even named Chitei Karzayim, "the wheat of Karzayim" — and of course the Omer is brought from barley, not wheat, though Tosafot notes that this may simply be the name of the locality rather than a description of what is brought from it.

Regarding the southern field requirement — the Gemara later records Rabbi Yochanan stating this as an Amoraic ruling as well: ein mevi'in et ha'Omer ela min hasadot hamudramot shebe'Eretz Yisrael, shebehen chama zorachat umehem chama shoka'at. It is not uncommon for Amoraic statements and baraitot to duplicate one another in this fashion.

Abba Shaul is also cited: Omer haya ba mibik'at Beit Makle — the Omer would come from the Valley of Beit Makle. Kevat gimmel se'in — this place was three se'in in size, with se'ah here being used as an area measurement rather than a volume measurement. It is perhaps worth noting that the Omer offering requires beginning with what amounts to three se'in of barley (in volume), which is then processed down to one-tenth of that quantity in flour. That the Omer field is itself measured in three se'in of land may reflect the assumption that one se'ah of land yields roughly one se'ah of grain. Sadeh mudramot haita — it was a southern exposure field. Uva chama zorachat umimena chama shoka'at — the sun rose upon it and set from it. Nir chetzya vezoreia chetzya — they would alternate: one half of the field would be overturned in a given year while the other half was planted, and in the following year they would reverse.

### Zeret & Shibbolet Yield

The result of following this entire regimen — the southern exposure, the overturning of soil, the precise timing — is grain of exceptional quality and yield. Ve'oseh kaneh zeret veshibolet zartayim — the stalk is one zeret in height while the ear is two zeretayim. A zeret is the span from thumb to pinky when the hand is spread open, approximately two tefachim. The ear — the part of the stalk bearing the actual grain — is twice the height of the stalk itself. This two-to-one ratio of ear to stalk represents an extraordinary yield, almost certainly expressed as an idealized description of abundance rather than a precise agronomic measurement. The point is clear: this regimen produces grain of an unmatched quality and quantity.

### Full Production Steps

The braita then enumerates the complete production sequence. Vekotzer — one harvests it. Ume'amer — one gathers it into sheaves. Vedash — one threshes it. Vezoreh — one winnows it, separating the grain from the chaff. Uborer — one sorts out the pebbles and other impurities that winnowing alone does not remove. Vethochen — one grinds it. Umeraked — one sifts it. Umevi etzel gizbar — one then brings the flour to the gizbar. Vegizbar machnis yado letocha — the gizbar inserts his hand into the flour. Im alah bah avak hasemadak — if dust rises when he withdraws his hand, he tells the bringer: chazor unifola sheniya — go back and sift it a second time.

Rabbi Natan describes an alternative method for the gizbar's inspection: gizbar sach yado shemen — he coats his hand with oil, then inserts it into the flour, so that all fine dust and impurities adhere to his oiled hand when he withdraws it. He is not merely an inspector but an active participant in ensuring the quality of the flour.

Tosafot notes a difficulty: in the context of the Omer, the Gemara elsewhere refers to shluchei Beit Din rather than to the gizbar as the responsible party. This is yet another indication that the discussion here may not be limited to the Omer, but extends to the broader production of flour for menachot.

### Avoda vs. Lo Avoda

Having established from the braita that in year two one plows and plows again — choresh veshoneh — the Gemara confronts the apparent discrepancy with our Mishnah, which mentions only an overturning in year one and planting in year two without mentioning a second overturning. Tani hatam choresh veshoneh — the braita indeed says you plow twice. But matnitin lo tani shona — our Mishnah does not say shoneh. So at best one might say this is a debate between the braita and the Mishnah, but the braita does not help determine what the Mishnah itself intended.

The Gemara resolves this: ha lo kashya — there is no difficulty. Kan ba-avoda, kan beshe-eina avoda — here we are speaking of a field that was already worked, there of a field that was not previously worked. Rashi explains: if the field had already been plowed in earlier years — avoda — then when I begin the rotation, there is already one overturning in its history. Therefore in year one I turn it over once more, and in year two I plow and plant, achieving a total of two overturnings. But if the field had not been previously worked — she-eina avoda — then I need to count two overturnings myself: once in year one and once in year two before planting. The goal in either case is to achieve two substantial overturnings of the soil before planting. The Mishnah describes the former scenario; the braita, the latter.

The Gemara then cites an additional source that discusses rotating the field: nir chatziya vezoreia chatziya — one overturns half the field while planting the other half, then in the following year reverses. This passage describes an ongoing alternation without any mention of a double overturning. The Gemara acknowledges that this adds little beyond the Mishnah's own description, and the question of double plowing remains resolved through the distinction of avoda versus she-eina avoda.

### Shmitta & Plowing

The question naturally arises: can one plow a field without planting in a Shmitta year? This was addressed in the previous session. The answer offered was that there are two possible grounds for permitting it. The first is that the Beit Hamikdash can simply override the prohibition of Shmitta, as it can override Shabbat. The second — and arguably more intellectually interesting — explanation is that some of the prohibitions of Shmitta are rooted in the idea of asserting private ownership over the land. When the labor is carried out not for private benefit but for communal purposes, and not as an exercise of personal ownership — especially when shluchei Beit Din are the ones who go out to protect the field and plow it — the prohibition may not apply in the same way. The great theme of Shmitta is precisely that one does not exert private ownership; when Beit Din has, in effect, taken the field over, that condition is satisfied even if the field is technically in private hands.

### RY: Southern Field Omer

The Gemara records Rabbi Yochanan stating as an Amoraic ruling: ein mevi'in et ha'Omer ela min hasadot hamudramot — one brings the Omer only from the southern fields of Eretz Yisrael, shebehen chama zorachat umehem chama shoka'at — on which the sun shines from rising to setting. Tanya nami hachi — a braita teaches similarly, giving this a dual support from both Amoraic and Tannaitic tradition. As noted, such duplication between an Amoraic statement and a baraita does occur.

### Abba Shaul: Beit Makle

Abba Shaul omer — Abba Shaul says the Omer would come from Bik'at Beit Makle, a valley of that name. Kevat gimmel se'in — it was three se'in in area. Sadeh mudramot haita — it was a southern exposure field. Uva chama zorachat umimena chama shoka'at — the sun rose and set upon it. Nir chetzya vezoreia chetzya — one half was overturned while the other half was planted, and the years alternated, as described above.

### Rav Hilkiya's Field

Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi hava lei karna de'ar'a — Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi had a small corner of a field. He applied this alternating regimen — nir chetzya vezoreia chetzya, nir chetzya vezoreia chetzya — and ve'avda chad terei — it produced double the normal yield, precisely as the Gemara described: an ear twice the size of the stalk. Umazbin lehu lechitei desmida — he would sell this wheat for smida, which Rashi explains means for use in menachot.

This story introduces a final layer of ambiguity. The entire preceding discussion appears to be about the Omer, yet here a private individual practices the rotation and sells the resulting grain for menachot generally. This may simply mean that any extraordinarily high-quality grain, whatever its original purpose, would naturally be sought for use in menachot broadly — or it may be another indication that the entire discussion of ideal grain production was never exclusively about the Omer to begin with. The ambiguity is not resolved; it is simply the nature of this sugya.

---

## Wormy Flour & Ba'al Mum

### Majority Wormy = Pasul

The Gemara had already established in the Mishnah that wormy flour is pasul outright and cannot be remedied simply by removing the worms. The Gemara now clarifies the standard. Tanu Rabbanan: solet she-hitlia ruba psula — if the majority of the flour is wormy, it is invalid. Ve-chittin she-hitliau rubam psula — similarly, if the majority of the wheat itself has become wormy before grinding, it too is invalid. The critical qualifier is ruba — the majority. If only a minority of the flour or wheat is wormy, one discards the affected portion and uses the rest.

### Rov Chitin or Rov Se'ah?

Having established that majority-wormy flour is pasul, Rabbi Yirmiya raises a precise question: baya Rebbi Yirmiya: be-rov chittin o be-rov se'ah? How does one measure the "majority"? Does it mean that each individual grain must itself be majority wormy — that is, more than half of each kernel has been eaten through — or does it mean that a majority of the grains in the se'ah are wormy, even if each wormy grain is not fully consumed?

The practical difference is significant. If the standard is the former — each grain majority wormy — then one could in principle remove the fully wormy grains and preserve any grain that is less than majority affected. If the standard is the latter — a majority of grains in the batch are wormy at all — then even if each individual grain is only slightly wormy, once the majority of grains are touched, the entire batch is invalid and the remaining minority of unaffected grains cannot be preserved separately. The Gemara answers: teiku — the question stands unresolved.

### Rava: Lashes for Worm?

Baya Rava: hiktishan mahu she-yilke aleihen mishum Ba'al Mum? — if one sanctifies this wormy grain, does he receive lashes as one would for consecrating a blemished animal? The relevance of the question turns on the conceptual underpinning of the grain's disqualification. The Torah does not explicitly enumerate standards for grain quality; the invalidity of substandard grain appears to derive by analogy from the prohibition of ba'al mum — the prohibition against offering or even consecrating an animal with a physical blemish. If the analogy to ba'al mum is what drives the invalidation, the question is how far that analogy extends: does it reach all the way to the prohibition's penal consequence, namely lashes for the act of consecration?

Keivan de-pasul ke-Ba'al Mum dami — one could argue that since wormy grain is pasul, it must be that we are comparing it to a ba'al mum. O dilma — or perhaps ein Ba'al Mum ela be-behemah — the formal category of mum applies only to animals. On this view, the analogy tells us the grain cannot be used, but it does not make the grain a mum in the legal sense, and therefore one does not incur lashes for consecrating it. The act is disrespectful and improper, but not a punishable transgression. The Gemara answers: teiku.

### Wormy Wood for Mizbe'ach

The Gemara now applies the same analysis to a different type of offering. Tnan hatam: kol etz she-nimtza vo tola'at, pasul legabei Mizbeach — any piece of wood found to contain a worm is disqualified for use on the Mizbeach. Amar Shmuel: lo shanu ela lach — this applies only to moist wood, because in moist wood the worm infestation spreads and cannot be fully removed. Aval beyavesh — but if the wood is dry, gorero vechasher — one can scrape out the wormy portion and the rest remains valid. For use as firewood, then, the standard may be somewhat more lenient than for a mincha — a practical distinction reflecting the different nature of the offering.

### Wood Ba'al Mum Teiku

Ba'i Rava: hikdisho, mahu sheyilke alav mishum ba'al mum? — the same question is asked of wormy wood: does sanctifying it incur lashes for ba'al mum? Keivan depasul kiba'al mum dami — since it is pasul, perhaps we compare it to a mum. O dilma ein ba'al mum ela bebehema — or perhaps the concept of mum is categorically limited to animals. Teiku — here too the question is left unresolved.

Tosafot explains why Rava asks the question separately for wood rather than simply extending the answer from solet. Even if one were to conclude that wormy solet carries some analogy to ba'al mum, solet is clearly a type of korban — its relationship to the Mizbeach is through consecration as an offering. Wood is a more ambiguous case: some hold that donated wood functions as a korban in its own right, requiring other wood beneath it; others see it as simply the fuel. If wood is not considered a true korban, the analogy to ba'al mum may not apply even where it would for solet. Hence the question must be posed independently. Teiku — it remains unresolved.

---

## Oil: Tekoa & Aggadot

### Tekoa Premier Oil Source

The Mishnah now turns from grain to oil. Tekoa — spelled with a kuf-vav-ayin — is designated as the premier source of olive oil: Tekoa alfa leshemen, A-grade oil. Abba Shaul omer sheniya lah — second to it is Regev in Ever HaYarden. Kol ha'aratzot hayu kesherot ela mikan hayu mevi'im — all lands were technically valid but they would bring from these preferred locations.

### Oil from Ever HaYarden?

The mention of Regev in Ever HaYarden immediately raises a question. We know that the Omer must come from grain grown in Eretz Yisrael — it represents the reishit ktzirchem, the first of the harvest. The Mishnah in Kelim enumerates ten levels of kedushah in Eretz Yisrael, stating: shemevi'im mimenah ha'omer vehabikkurim veshtei halechem mah she'ein mevi'im mikol ha'aratzot — it is from Eretz Yisrael that one brings the Omer, the bikkurim, and the Shtei HaLechem, which cannot be brought from other lands. Similarly, we know one cannot bring bikkurim from Ever HaYarden. The question, which deserves further examination, is whether the same restriction applies to the Omer.

But this Mishnah concerns the oil of the menachot, not the grain. Even if the Omer grain must come from Eretz Yisrael, the question of whether the oil for the Omer is subject to the same requirement is a separate and less obvious one. This gives rise to two distinct questions: first, whether the oil for the Omer must come from Eretz Yisrael at all; and second, assuming it must, whether Ever HaYarden qualifies as Eretz Yisrael for this purpose, given that bikkurim cannot be brought from there. The broader question also remains — whether this Mishnah is speaking specifically about the Omer or about menachot in general — and that ambiguity has continued throughout the daf. These questions are noted but not resolved here.

### Disqualified Oil Sources

The Mishnah then enumerates the disqualified sources of oil, in direct parallel to the disqualified sources of grain discussed earlier. Ein mevi'in lo mibeit hazvalim velo mibeit hashlehin — one may not bring oil from olive trees that were heavily fertilized or that required irrigation. Velo mima shenizra beinehem — and not from groves where grain was planted among the olive trees. Just as grain quality suffers when trees compete with it for nutrients, so olive quality suffers when grain is planted among the olive trees. The competition works both ways.

Ve'im hevi kasher — but if one brought from any of these, the oil is valid bedi'avad. So far the parallel to grain is exact.

The Mishnah then adds prohibitions with no exact parallel in the grain discussion. Ein mevi'in anpakton — one may not bring oil pressed from unripe olives. Ve'im hevi kasher — bedi'avad it is valid.

Ein mevi'in min hagargerin shenishru bamayim — one may not use olives that were soaked in water before having their oil extracted, since the soaking dilutes the oil. Velo min hakvashim — and not from olives that were pickled before extraction. Velo min hashlikim — and not from olives that were boiled. Ve'im hevi pasul — if one brought oil from any of these last three categories, it is invalid, with no bedi'avad leniency. This is a notable departure from the earlier pattern. The first set of disqualified sources — manured groves, irrigated groves, grain-interspersed groves, and unripe olives — are valid bedi'avad. The latter set — soaked, pickled, and boiled olives — render the oil pasul outright. The practical distinction likely reflects the degree to which the oil itself is physically compromised or adulterated.

The question of how we know these standards — since the Torah does not enumerate them explicitly for oil any more than it does for grain — is similar to the issues that arose regarding the grain. The prohibition by the Menorah is shemen zayit zach katit lama'or, but the standards for other uses of oil in the Beit Hamikdash are derived by extension and tradition.

### Yoav to Tekoa: Oil=Wisdom

The Gemara departs from halacha for an aggadic observation prompted by the Mishnah's mention of Tekoa. Vayishlach Yoav Tekoa vayikach misham isha chachama — and Yoav sent to Tekoa and took a wise woman from there. This episode, in which Yoav arranged for a woman from Tekoa to approach David with a fabricated story of mourning in order to persuade David to reconcile with Avshalom, raises the question: mai shna Tekoa — why specifically Tekoa?

Amar Rabbi Yochanan: mitoch sheragilim beshemen zayit, chochma metzuya bahen — because the people of Tekoa were accustomed to olive oil, wisdom was found among them. Rashi cites other passages in the Gemara that speak of olive oil sharpening the mind: deshemen zayit mefake'ach et haleiv. Olive oil, in the Gemara's view, was a kind of brain food — and since Tekoa was the premier source of the finest olive oil, its inhabitants partook of it in abundance and were accordingly blessed with exceptional wisdom.

### Asher's Oil Blessing

Tanu rabanan: vetovel bashemen raglo — and he dipped his foot in oil. Ze chelko shel Asher — this is the portion of Asher, shemoshech shemen kema'ayan — where oil flows like a wellspring. The territory of Asher, identified as being in the north of the land (in the vicinity of Gush Chalav and Meron), was extraordinarily abundant in olive oil.

### Ludkaya Oil Story

Amru pa'am achat nitzrechu lahem anshei Ludkaya — one time the people of Ludkaya, a non-Jewish city, had a pressing need for oil. Minu lahen pulmostos echad — they appointed an officer, the word being a Greek loanword for a military or administrative official. Amru lo: lech ve-havi lanu shemen be-me'ah ribbo — they instructed him to go and procure oil worth a million maneh, a sum of staggering proportions, sufficient to acquire either an enormous quantity or the finest quality of oil available — or both.

Halach li-Yerushalayim — he went to Yerushalayim, the natural first destination for anyone seeking goods from the Jews. They directed him: lech le-Tzor — go to Tzor. Tosafot notes that this cannot be Tyre, since that is outside Israel; it refers to a different place of that name. From there he was directed to Gush Chalav, and from there he was sent to a particular individual — lech etzel ploni, la-sadeh ha-laz — go to so-and-so, in that field over there.

He went and found the man working under his olive trees — u-matza'o she-hayah ozek tachat zeito. The precise meaning of the word ozek is debated: he was either removing stones, collecting fallen olives, building fences around his trees, or engaged in some other form of ordinary fieldwork. The officer asked him: yesh lecha shemen be-me'ah ribbo she-ani tzarich — do you have a million maneh's worth of oil for me? The man replied: hamten li ad she-asayem melachti — wait for me to finish what I am doing.

Himtin ad she-siyem melachto — the officer waited. When the man finished his fieldwork, he put his implements in his knapsack and, as he walked home, continued removing stones from the path — vehayah mesakel u-va ba-derech. This small detail is telling: even after completing the day's labor, the man was cleaning up the road, a picture of simple, humble industry. The officer, seeing all this, began to doubt. He said to himself — or perhaps aloud — ki medumanni she-sechok se-chaknu bi ha-Yehudim: I think the Jews are mocking me. They send me from place to place and finally direct me to this field hand, who is supposed to have a million maneh's worth of oil?

### Mitroshesh VeHon Rav

Keivan shehigi'a le'iro — when they arrived at the man's home, his maidservant brought out a large urn of hot water — kumkum shel chamin — and he washed his hands and feet from the dust of the journey and the day's labor. Then hotzi'ah lo safal shel zahav malei shemen — she brought out a gold bowl filled with oil, vetaval bo yadav veraglav — and he dipped his hands and his feet in it, lekayeim mah shene'emar — to fulfill the verse: vetovel bashemen raglo — and he dipped his foot in oil. This was the portion of Asher made manifest in one man's household.

They ate and drank, and then madad lo shemen beme'ah ribo — he measured out a million maneh's worth of oil for him. And then: klum atah tzarich leyoter — is that all you need? Do you want more? The officer said he did want more — ela she'ein li damim, I simply have no money left. The man replied: im atah rotzeh likach kach, take as much more as you need, va'ani imcha ve'etol damav — and I will accompany you home and collect the balance there.

Madad lo shemen bishmonah asar ribo — he measured out another 180,000 in oil beyond the million. And lo heniach oto ish lo sus velo fered velo gamal velo chamor be'eretz yisrael shelo secharo — the officer was forced to hire every horse, mule, camel, and donkey in Eretz Yisrael to transport all of this oil back to Ludkaya.

Keivan shehigi'a le'iro, yatz'u anshei iro lekalso — when the officer finally arrived home, the people of his city came out to praise him for having procured the vast quantity of oil they needed. He told them: lo li kalsuni — do not praise me. Ela zeh sheba imi shemadad li shemen beme'ah ribo, veharei nosheh bi bishmonah asar ribo — praise this man who came with me, who gave me a million maneh's worth of oil, and to whom I now owe another 180,000 — so much oil did he have.

Lekayeim mah shene'emar: yesh mitasher ve'ein kol, mitroshesh vehon rav — to fulfill the verse: there is one who acts rich but has nothing, and one who appears poor yet possesses great wealth. The man worked in his field like a simple laborer, cleaned stones from the path as he walked home, lived without ostentation — and yet possessed more oil than an entire city could purchase for any price. The wealth of Asher in olive oil, and the humble greatness of those who held it, was thus fulfilled to the letter.

---

# Menachot 86

## Previous Review

### Omer & Shtei HaLechem

Our daf opens with a brief review of issues raised in the previous shiur. Upon reflection, it becomes clear that no authority — not even a hint — suggests that the oil for the Omer must come specifically from Eretz Yisrael.
