The assumption throughout is that the geographic restriction applies to the grain of the Omer, which makes contextual sense. The Rambam, like Tosafot, understands that all the discussions about the source and grade of flour and oil are not limited to the Omer and Shtei HaLechem but apply to all menachot generally. This framing is important to keep in mind as we move through the sugyot ahead.

### Bikkurim Sourcing

There is, however, a significant Sifrei regarding bikkurim that merits mention. The Sifrei explicitly states that bikkurim must come from Eretz Yisrael proper and not from Ever HaYarden. Two distinct drashot underlie this ruling. The first derives from the phrase *eretz zavat chalav u'devash*, with the Sifrei arguing that Ever HaYarden does not meet this description. The second drasha is even more striking: it is based on the phrase *ha'adama asher natata li* — the land that You gave me — and the Sifrei reads into this *velo shenatalta me'atzmechem*, meaning land that you did not simply take for yourselves. This is an interesting theological point embedded in the halakhic derivation. Notably, there is no parallel discussion regarding the Omer or Shtei HaLechem on this question, though the Acharonim debate it extensively. No earlier authority addresses it in that context.

---

## Oil Sourcing

### Anpaktan Debate

The Gemara opens the main discussion of our daf at the very last line of 85b, establishing that just as grain from a manured field or a field requiring heavy fertilization is invalid for offerings, so too is oil derived from olives grown under those conditions. The Mishnah then states that one may not bring *anpaktan* — or *anpaknon* in some readings — which, as will become clear, refers to oil pressed from unripe olives. However, the Mishnah continues, *v'im hevi kasher* — if one did bring it, it is valid after the fact.

Here a textual difficulty arises immediately. Rashi's girsa of the Mishnah reads *v'im hevi pasul* — that even b'di'avad it is invalid — rather than kasher. Meanwhile, a Braita explicitly states: do not bring anpaktan, and if you did bring it, it is pasul, adding the reason *mipnei shehu seraf* — because it is not really oil at all but rather a kind of sap or raw juice. According to Rashi's reading, both the Mishnah and the Braita agree that it is invalid b'di'avad, and the question between them is whether it constitutes invalid oil or no oil at all. According to the girsa of Tosafot and most other Rishonim, the Mishnah says it is kasher b'di'avad while the Braita says it is pasul, and the question is simply whether this substance qualifies as oil for the purposes of menachot.

### Rabbi Chiya vs Rabbi Shi…

Rav Yosef resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya* — it is not difficult. The Mishnah reflects the view of Rabbi Chiya, and the Braita reflects the view of Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi. Both were contemporaries in the household of Rebbi: Rabbi Chiya was Rebbi's nephew, and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi was Rebbi's son. Their disagreement concerns whether unripe olive oil is treated as something functional — edible oil of a lower grade — or essentially discarded as unfit substance.

The Gemara provides a mnemonic: *ashirin mekamtzin* — the wealthy are stingy. Rabbi Shimon, son of the Nasi Rebbi, who came from a wealthy household, would not waste the oil pressed from unripe olives and would actually use it — *matpil bah*, he would dip his food into it. Rabbi Chiya, by contrast, would throw it away — *zarik lah* — regarding it as not genuinely usable. The point of the mnemonic is that the wealthy, paradoxically, do not like to waste even lower-quality materials. The disagreement thus determines whether such oil constitutes a legitimate, if inferior, oil that would be kasher b'di'avad for menachot, or whether it is so fundamentally not-oil that it fails even b'di'avad.

### Shemen Hamor

Since the discussion concerns oil from unripe olives, the Gemara takes an aggadic detour in connection with the verse in Esther describing the six months of purification using *shemen hamor*. The Gemara asks: *mai shemen hamor* — what exactly is this myrrh oil? Rav Huna bar Chiya identifies it with *satkesta*. Rav Yosef suggests it might be cinnamon. Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba offers the identification that connects this passage to our sugya: *shemen zayit shelo hevi shlish* — oil from olives that have not reached one-third of their ripening. In other words, shemen hamor is understood by Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba to be none other than what our Mishnah calls anpaktan.

A Braita confirms this identification. Rabbi Yehuda states explicitly: *anpaknon* — oil from olives that have not yet reached shlish — *lama sakhin oso?* Why would one anoint oneself with it? Because *meshir et hase'ar* — it acts as a depilatory, causing body hair to fall away — *um'aden et habasar* — and it beautifies and moisturizes the skin. This explains why it was used in the purification regimen for women. It also illuminates why one might not be able to use it for a mincha: it is not primarily a food substance but rather a cosmetic agent, and its status as genuine oil for ritual consumption is accordingly uncertain.

### Bad Oils & Ba'al Mum

The end of the Mishnah lists additional prohibited sources, and the Gemara cites a Braita expanding on them: *shemen zayit kavush, shaluk, sharui, veshel shemarim, veshel reach ra* — olive oil derived from pickled olives, boiled olives, olives soaked in water, oil that came from the lees of olives, or oil with a bad smell. Regarding all of these, *lo yavi — v'im hevi pasul* — one should not bring them, and if one did, the offering is invalid. The Gemara notes the remarkable absence of any explicit pesukim here; this is entirely a determination of Chazal that these substances either do not constitute oil at all or certainly do not constitute the kind of fit oil required for the mikdash. The Gemara does indicate that by the Menorah there is at least a pasuk — *shemen zayit zach* — that provides some textual criterion, but no such pasuk exists for menachot.

Rava then poses a question that parallels exactly what he asked earlier regarding wormy wood and wormy wheat: *hikdisho mahu sheyilkeh alav mishum ba'al mum?* If someone consecrated such oil — oil from soaked, boiled, or pickled olives — do we consider it formally analogous to a *ba'al mum*, such that one would transgress by consecrating something with a mum? The question is: *keivan depasul k'ba'al mum dami* — since it is invalid, should we treat it literally as a ba'al mum to the point of incurring a transgression for consecrating it? Or does *ein ba'al mum ela b'behema* — the concept of ba'al mum applies only to animals, and while this oil is invalid and we may draw analogies from ba'al mum, we would not impose the actual transgression? The Gemara leaves this *teiku* — unresolved. Tosafot notes, interestingly, that this exact question with the exact same language is asked in three places — by flour, by wood, and now by oil. It is possible that Rava asked it only once and the Gemara applies it to all three contexts.

---

## Harvests & Pressings

### First Harvest Process

The Mishnah now teaches: *shlosha zeisim hem* — there are three olive harvests — *uvahen shlosha shlosha shemanim* — and within each harvest, three grades of oil. The first harvest involves picking the individual ripe olives — *gargara* referring to the individual olive — from the top of the tree, where they receive the most sunlight and ripen first. After collecting these olives, one performs *kotesh* — grinds them — and places them *letoch hasal*, into a wicker basket. The basket functions as a sieve: the actual olive paste remains above while the oil flows through. This yields the first extraction. Then *chazar veta'an bekora* — one places the heavy beam upon it — pressing out additional oil. This is the second extraction. One then grinds again and presses again under the beam, yielding the third extraction.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Method

Rabbi Yehuda offers a series of refinements throughout, consistently oriented toward maximizing the purity and clarity of the oil. Rather than grinding with a *reichayim* — a millstone — Rabbi Yehuda says one should use a *machteshet*, a mortar and pestle, which pounds the olives without grinding them as intensively and therefore keeps the oil cleaner. Instead of pressing with the beam, Rabbi Yehuda says *ba'avanim* — one should use stones. Rashi explains that stones, depending on their size relative to the beam, would apply pressure more slowly, requiring more patience but ultimately pressing out pure oil without the same degree of forcing impurities through. And rather than placing the ground olive paste at the base of the basket, Rabbi Yehuda says *svivot hasal* — one should place it at the inner upper lip of the basket, so that the olive paste adheres to the top and the oil runs cleanly down and is then filtered through the sieve, rather than having the paste potentially pass through the sieve from the bottom.

One might ask whether these debates reflect genuine uncertainty about actual practice or whether they concern what should have been done in the Beit HaMikdash specifically. Since the Tannaim lived in Eretz Yisrael and were still producing olive oil themselves, all of these phenomena were in use. Some practitioners used the millstone; others used the mortar and pestle. Some placed the paste at the base of the basket; others at the lip. The Tannaim are debating which practice should be considered standard and paradigmatic. Rabbi Yehuda's position is consistently that one should take whatever steps produce the clearest, most refined oil for the mikdash.

The Gemara then raises an internal tension in our Mishnah. The Mishnah says *kotesh* — it uses mortar-and-pestle grinding — which the Braita identifies as the position of Rabbi Yehuda. Yet the Mishnah then says the olive paste goes into the *sal*, the basket, at the base — which the Braita identifies as the position of the Chachamim. Our Mishnah thus appears to be a hybrid, agreeing with Rabbi Yehuda on one point and with the Chachamim on another. The Gemara confirms this: *ha tanna savar lah k'vateih b'chada u'palig aleih b'chada* — the tanna of our Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda in one respect and disagrees in another.

The Braita also addresses the word *mizito* — from the verse *shemen zayit zach* — which Rashi understands to require that the olives ripen on the tree itself rather than after being picked. This raises a subtle tension with what the Mishnah says about the third harvest, which apparently ripens after it is brought to the pressing house. That Braita may reflect a debate with the Mishnah, since it does not mention using the third harvest for the Menorah, unlike the Mishnah which does permit it.

The Gemara also raises an ambiguity in the Mishnah's language: does it say *migargrot* — picking the individual ripe olives one by one — or *migalgolot* — a word that implies waiting for the olives to reach ripeness? The difference is subtle: *migargro* emphasizes identifying and selecting the ripe individual olives, while *migalgolo* might emphasize allowing not-yet-ripe olives to ripen before using them. A Braita uses the reading *migalgolo*, though this does not definitively resolve what the Mishnah itself says.

### Later Harvests

For the second harvest, one collects the individual olives not from the very top of the tree but from a mid-level — described as the rooftop level, since one would climb to the rooftop or ladder to reach that height — and then proceeds through the same three-stage process of initial extraction, beam pressing, re-grinding, and pressing again. *harishon limnora* — the first extraction may be used for the Menorah — *vehashar limnachot* — the remainder may be used for menachot.

The third harvest presents a different scenario. These are olives that never fully ripened on the tree due to lack of sunlight, so one brings them to the *beit habad* — the olive pressing house — and waits *ad sheyilkeh* — until they soften, until they become ripe after picking. One then brings them up to the rooftop and spreads them out — *ke'min tamara*, Rashi says, in a pyramid shape — *ad sheyazuvu meimav*, until the water content flows off. This is significant: freshly pressed olives have a high water content, and the water must be separated from the oil. After the water drains off, one brings the olives to the pressing house, grinds them, places them in the basket, and proceeds through the same three-stage extraction process. Surprisingly, the ruling is the same: *harishon limnora* — even the first pressing of the third harvest is fit for the Menorah — *vehashar limenachot* — the rest for menachot.

The principle that emerges is that for the Menorah, it does not matter which harvest the oil comes from; what matters is that it is the first pressing, which produces clear, pure oil regardless of the harvest's overall quality. For menachot, any pressing from any harvest is acceptable as long as it constitutes genuine oil.

### Oil Grading System

The next Mishnah introduces a grading system for oil quality. The scheme is elegant: add the harvest number to the pressing number, and the lower the sum, the higher the grade. *haRishon shebarishon* — the first pressing of the first harvest (1+1=2) — *ein lema'ala himenu* — there is nothing superior to it. *haSheni shebarishon* and *harishon shebasheini* — the second pressing of the first harvest and the first pressing of the second harvest (both summing to 3) — *shavin*, are of equal grade. *haShlishi shebarishon*, *hasheni shebasheini*, and *harishon shebashlishi* (all summing to 4) are equal grades. And so on up through *hashlishi shebashlishi* (3+3=6) — *ein lemata himenu* — the lowest grade of all.

The Gemara immediately raises a difficulty: when the Mishnah says these pairs are *shavin* — equal — is that true? Surely the first pressing of the third harvest differs from the third pressing of the first harvest, because the first pressing of any harvest is fit for the Menorah, while the third pressing is not! Rav Pappa bar Yitzchak resolves this: *mai shavin — shavin limenachot* — the Mishnah means they are equal specifically for the purpose of menachot. When ranking oil for menachot, where the criterion is taste and quality, these pairs are indeed equivalent in grade. But when the question is Menorah eligibility, the first pressing of any harvest is in a separate category precisely because what matters for the Menorah is not taste but clarity and clean burning.

---

## Menorah vs Menachot Oil

### Kal VaChomer Logic

The Mishnah reflects explicitly and in a notably self-aware way on the derivation of the purity standard. It opens: *af kol hamenachos hayu vadin* — in principle, all menachot should be required to use pure olive oil. The kal vachomer would run as follows: *mah menorah she'einah le'achila te'una shemen zayit zach* — the Menorah, which is not for eating, requires pure beaten olive oil — *menachos shehen le'achila, eino din sheyit'anu shemen zayit zach?* — menachot, which are eaten by the Kohanim, should certainly require pure beaten oil all the more so. This is a striking formulation in the Mishnah itself, offering not merely a ruling but a reflection on why the kal vachomer might have applied.

### Zach Katit LaMe'or

Yet the Mishnah immediately states: *talmud lomar zach katit lame'or* — the Torah says pure, beaten oil *for the light* — *ve'ein zach katit limenachos* — and not for menachot. The verse limits the requirement to the Menorah. A Braita elaborates on the meaning of the terms. *ein zach ela naki* — zach means free of impurities, clean. Rabbi Yehuda says *ein katit ela katush* — katit means specifically pounded with a mortar and pestle rather than ground with a millstone. Together, *zach katit* describes oil that is both uncontaminated and produced through the more careful pounding method.

The Braita then entertains the possibility that this high-grade oil — *zach katit* — might actually be forbidden for menachot, since the verse assigns it specifically to the Menorah. This possibility is resolved by a *gezera shava*: the Torah uses the word *katit* both by the Menorah (*shemen zayit zach katit lame'or*) and by a mincha (*belula beshemen katit revit hahin*). The shared term teaches that the same quality of oil used for the Menorah is also permissible for menachot. The direction of the inference thus runs the other way from the initial concern: we use the gezera shava not to exclude the oil from menachot but to confirm it may be used for both.

### Chisachon Principle

If the same oil is permissible for both, *im kein ma talmud lomar lame'or?* — why does the Torah specify that it is *for the light*? The answer: *mipnei hachisachon* — because of fiscal burden. Rabbi Elazar explains: *haTorah chasa al mamonam shel Yisrael* — the Torah is solicitous of the financial resources of Israel. This principle appeared earlier at 76b and is applied here in a specific way. The first pressing is the most expensive oil to produce. For the Menorah, which was funded from communal resources and required a relatively fixed, limited quantity of oil, the Torah mandates the highest standard. But for menachot, which were brought far more frequently and primarily by private individuals — and notably, it was the poor who most commonly brought menachot — the Torah allows the full range of acceptable oils rather than demanding the most expensive first-pressing oil exclusively.

---

## Menorah Theology

### Purpose of Menorah

The Gemara now pivots to the theological significance of the Menorah, taking up the verse *veyikchu eilecha shemen zayit zach* — they shall take for you pure olive oil. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani focuses on the word *eilecha* — for you — and reads it as addressed to Israel: the Menorah is for your sake, not for Mine. *veliora ani tzarich?* — does God need the light? Of course not. Tosafot notes that this should not be read as God speaking about His own needs in the abstract but, in light of another Gemara, as referring even to the Kohen who entered: the Kohen who worked in the Beit HaMikdash also did not need the Menorah's light in any ordinary functional sense. The point of the Menorah is symbolic — it represents the presence of God — not to illuminate a room for practical purposes.

### Arrangement Symbolism

Rav Zutra in the name of Rabbi Elazar expands the theme: *lo le'achila ani tzarich ve'lo le'ora ani tzarich* — I do not need food and I do not need light. The Shulchan was in the north and the Menorah in the south — placed on opposite sides of the sanctuary. Rashi and Tosafot observe that in a normal domestic setting, one would place the lamp near the table. The fact that they are on opposite sides signals that neither is for God's benefit. God provides food and light to Israel; Israel is not providing these things to God. The table and the lamp are there for Israel, as symbols of divine provision, not divine need.

### Windows & Divine Light

The verse in Kings describing the windows of Shlomo's Beit HaMikdash states they were *shakufim atumim* — transparent and sealed, seemingly contradictory terms. A Tanna resolves: *shakufim mibifnim ve'atumim mibachutz* — wide on the inside, narrowed to a point on the outside. Tosafot reads this as the windows being the exact reverse of ordinary windows. Normal windows are wider on the outside to channel sunlight in, narrowing as they approach the interior. The windows of the Beit HaMikdash were the opposite: narrow on the outside, widening on the inside. The purpose was not to bring external light into the sanctuary but to channel the inner light of the Beit HaMikdash — the light of the Shechinah — outward to the world. This is entirely consistent with *lo le'ora ani tzarich*: God does not receive light from outside, God sends light outward.

### Ner Ma'aravi Miracle

The Gemara cites the verse: *michutz laparochet ha'edut be'ohel moed* — this is where the Menorah is to be lit — *edut hi lechol ba'ei olam shehashechina shora b'Yisrael* — it is a testimony to all people of the world that the Divine Presence dwells among Israel. The Menorah is not merely a lamp but a proclamation. *ve'im tomar le'ora ani tzarich* — and lest one argue that we light it for God's benefit — *vahalo kol arbaim shana shehalchu Yisrael bamidbar lo halchu ela le'oro* — for forty years in the desert, Israel walked by God's light, the pillar of fire. God is the source of light, not the recipient.

Rava identifies the specific proof of this testimony: *zeh ner ma'aravi* — it is the western light of the Menorah. One lights all the lamps of the Menorah with equal amounts of oil at nightfall, giving each enough to burn through the night. Yet the ner ma'aravi would remain burning in the morning when all the others had gone out, and — miraculously — it would continue burning through the entire following day even though it had been given only enough oil for the night. The Kohen would clean the other lamps first thing in the morning but would not extinguish and clean the ner ma'aravi until the following nightfall, because it was still burning. One then lit the other lamps from the ner ma'aravi before extinguishing it, putting in new oil and new wicks and relighting it — so that there was essentially an unbroken continuity of fire, never a moment when all lights were fully extinguished and a new fire started from scratch. This practice subsequently becomes relevant in the Gemara in Shabbat in discussions of *madlikin miner lener* — lighting one lamp from another.

There are other Gemarot that indicate this miracle operated specifically *be'itim she'hayu Yisrael osim ratzono shel Makom* — in periods when Israel was faithful, as in the time of Shimon HaTzaddik. During periods when the leadership of the Beit HaMikdash was less ideal, the ner ma'aravi would also extinguish in the morning. In order to sustain the visible continuity of the practice, oil would be added in the morning to ensure the ner ma'aravi burned until nightfall, even though it was no longer miraculous. The concept of *ner tamid* is understood in this context — and may be related as well to *eish tamid*, which is stated explicitly by the mizbeiach. This testimony — the continuous western light — was thus the ongoing visible sign that the Shechinah dwelt among Israel.

---

## Wine Sourcing

### Wine Regions

The Mishnah now turns to wine. It is worth noting at this point — and it becomes obvious here — that the earlier Mishnayot about flour and oil were not limited to the Omer: the discussion has become entirely general, covering all offerings, because wine was not a mincha at all, yet it is discussed in the same sequence and with the same structure.

*Me'ayin hayu mevi'in et hayayin?* — from where was the wine brought? Keduchim and Atulin are identified as *alfa leyayin* — the alpha, the finest wine regions. Second to them are Beit Rima and Beit Lavan in the mountains, and Kfar Signa in the valley. Nevertheless, *kol ha'aratzot hayu kesherot* — all lands were fit, even outside of Eretz Yisrael — but the ideal was to bring from these superior regions.

### Bad Wine Sources

The Mishnah then lists disqualifying conditions that mirror those for grain and oil. *ein mevi'in lo mibeit hazivalim* — one does not bring wine from vineyards grown in manured fields — *velo mibeit hashlachim* — nor from irrigated fields — *velo mima shenizra beineihem* — nor from vines between which other crops were planted, which produces inferior-quality grapes regardless of any kilayim concerns. In all these cases, *ve'im hevi kasher* — if one brought it after the fact, it is valid. One also may not bring *helistion* — grapes that became overly ripe, producing an excessively sweet wine — though if one did, it is kasher b'di'avad. Similarly, one may not bring wine that is excessively sweet, *matok*, which appears to refer to wine that is sweetened differently from helistion — perhaps artificially sweetened or sweetened after extraction.

### Old Wine Debate

The Mishnah states: *ein mevi'in yashan* — one may not bring old wine. This is a surprising ruling. One would expect that aged wine is superior, and in fact elsewhere old flour was permitted. Yet *divrei Rabbi* — this is Rebbi's position — and *chachamim machshirin* — the Sages validate old wine. The Gemara will address why Rebbi has a concern with old wine, and if the Sages consider it superior, one might expect them to go further and say *mutav sheyehei* — it is preferable. These questions will be taken up in the Gemara.

### Cooked Wine

The Mishnah then states that one may not bring *me'ushan* — smoked wine — nor *mevushal* — cooked wine — *ve'im hevi pasul* — and if one brought either of these, it is invalid even b'di'avad. This is a significantly stricter standard than the categories above. The halakhic significance of yayin mevushal extends into contemporary practice: the Rambam holds that wine used for Kiddush must be wine that could have been brought al gabei hamizbe'ach. Since our Mishnah rules yayin mevushal as pasul even b'di'avad for the altar, Sefardim accordingly do not use yayin mevushal for Kiddush.

### Vine Growing Method

*Ve'ein mevi'in min hadaliyyot* — one may not bring wine from vines that grew on trellises — *ella min haregaliyyot* — but only from vines that grow along the ground — *umin hakeramim ha'avudim* — and from worked, cultivated vineyards. The Gemara will explain what *keramim ha'avudim* means precisely. The reasoning appears to be that trellis-grown vines do not produce the same quality grapes as ground-growing vines.

### Wine Processing

The Mishnah specifies that one should not gather the grapes in *chatzavim gedolim* — large vats — but rather in *chaviyot ketanot* — smaller barrels. One should not fill the barrel all the way to its lip; leaving a gap preserves the aroma, since *ke'dei shereiccho nodef* — so that the fragrance is captured within rather than escaping. When extracting the wine, one does not take it from the very top of the barrel, *mipnei hakemachim* — because of the impurities that float to the surface — nor from the very bottom, *mipnei hashemarim* — because of the lees. Rather, *mevi mi-shlisha*, *me'emtza'ah* — one draws from a point a third of the way up from the bottom, or from the middle — installing a faucet in the middle of the barrel and drawing from that point.

### Quality Inspection

The Mishnah describes how the gizbar — the Temple treasurer — would conduct quality inspection. He would sit with a stick in hand and open the faucet. First he would discard *hage'ir* — the initial cloudy discharge that flows out when a faucet is first opened, much as one lets a tap run to clear the cloudy initial flow. After discarding that, he would bang the stick — *hikish bakane* — to signal silence. The Gemara indicates there was a belief that human speech adversely affects the quality of wine as it is drawn, so the bang of the stick was not merely procedural but was a call for everyone to be quiet as the wine was extracted.

### Impurity & Ba'al Mum

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda takes a stricter position: *she-yesh bo kemachim pasul* — wine that has any of these floating impurities is entirely invalid, not merely requiring that the impurities be removed. He derives this from the verse *temimim yiheyu lachem u-minchatam... temimim yiheyu lachem ve-niskeichem* — the offerings must be *temimim*, perfect. Although the term *ba'al mum* is not used explicitly, the requirement of *tamim* implies that any imperfection — including floating impurities in the wine — renders the entire offering invalid.

---

## Ba'al Mum Analysis

### Abaye: Choleh Case

Abaye challenges this reasoning. Even granting that inferior quality can invalidate an offering without a formal ba'al mum, this should cut both ways for flour and oil as well. He adduces the case of *choleh* — a sick animal — which the Mishnah rules is pasul even though it has no technical physical mum. The source is the verse *vechi tagishu pise'ach vecholeh* — and when you bring the lame and the sick, it is invalid. This shows that inferior physical condition is sufficient to render an offering pasul, independent of any formal enumerated blemish. By analogy, inferior-quality flour or oil should also be pasul by virtue of their deficiency alone, without needing to characterize them as ba'al mum.

### Rava: Gezeirat HaKatuv

Rava responds: the case of choleh is different. There is a *gezeirat hakatuv* — an explicit scriptural decree — that addresses the sick animal and declares it pasul. That pasuk provides the basis for invalidating the choleh despite the absence of a formal mum. But we have no comparable pasuk addressing the invalidation of inferior-quality flour or oil on their own terms. Without such a textual source, one cannot automatically transfer the logic from choleh to oil and flour.

---

---

# Menachot 87

## Sweet Wine Validity

### Prohibitions

The *gemara* opens by citing the *mishnah*'s ruling: *ein mevi'in lo matok velo mevushal velo me'ushan* — one may not bring wine that is sweet, cooked, or smoky for the *nesachim*, and if one does bring such wine, it is invalid. This ruling is worth noting for a practical aside: there are those who hold that *yayin mevushal* may not be used for *kiddush* on the grounds that it is not *ra'uy agabei mizbe'ach* — not fit for use on the *mizbe'ach*. That position is not the widespread practice, but it reflects the real halachic weight of these Temple-based categories.

### Heliston Contradiction

A tension immediately presents itself. The earlier clause of the *mishnah* stated: *ein mevi'in et ha-Heliston* — one does not bring *heliston*, which is understood to be a particularly sweet type of wine — *ve'im hevi kasher*, yet if one did bring it, it is valid *b'di'avad*. How does this square with the subsequent ruling that sweet wine is invalid even *b'di'avad*?

Ravina resolves the contradiction with the principle of *karch u-teni* — read the two clauses together, weaving them into a unified ruling. *rashi* understands this to mean that the word *kasher* is effectively removed from the earlier clause, and sweet wine is invalid in all cases. *tosafot*, however, reads it in the opposite direction: the ruling on sweet wine is reinterpreted so that *b'di'avad* it is in fact valid. Either way, the contradiction is resolved by harmonizing the text — the direction of the harmonization is what remains debated.

### Rav Ashi Analysis

Rav Ashi offers an independent resolution that turns not on textual harmonization but on a substantive distinction in the nature of the sweetness itself. *chuya deshimshe lo ma'is* — sweetness that results from overexposure to the sun is not considered disgusting or wholly inappropriate. *chuya de-pere ma'is* — sweetness that is intrinsic to the grape variety itself is regarded as an inappropriate quality in sacrificial wine. The underlying principle, though no explicit *pesukim* are cited here, appears to be the broader concept of *hakrivehu na le-pechatecha* — would you offer this to a person of high standing? Wine whose character is fundamentally unsuited to refined consumption falls outside the acceptable range for the *mizbe'ach*, regardless of how it got that way. If, however, the sweetness is merely an artifact of sun conditions and not native to the grape, the wine does not cross that threshold.

---

## Old Wine Debate

### Rabbi vs. Rabbis

The *mishnah* rules: *ein mevi'in yashan divrei Rebbi* — one does not bring old wine; this is the position of *rebbi*. The *chakhamim*, by contrast, are *makhshirin* — they permit it outright. The instinct here might be to wonder why older wine would be problematic at all, given that wine often improves with age. The question is not one of quality in the conventional sense, but whether there is a specific requirement that the wine be of the current year.

### Lamb-Wine Analogy

*Chizkiya* offers the rationale behind *rebbi*'s position. The *pasuk* juxtaposes the wine offering with the lamb — *lakeves yayin* — and since a *keves* must be *ben shnato*, one year old, for the same linguistic juxtaposition teaches that the wine too must be *ben shnato*, of that year. The *gemara* immediately presses this analogy: just as a lamb that is two years old is invalid as a *keves* (having become an *ayil*), should we not say that wine more than one year old is also invalid *b'di'avad*? *rebbi* never went that far. Moreover, a *braita* states explicitly: *yayin ben shtei shanim lo yavi* — one should not bring two-year-old wine, *v'im heivi kasher* — but if one did, it is valid. Since *rebbi* is the only authority who holds *l'chat'chila* that old wine is problematic, this *kasher b'di'avad* must reflect even his own position. The lamb-wine analogy therefore cannot be the real basis for *rebbi*'s view, since that analogy, taken seriously, would generate a *b'di'avad* concern that the sources plainly reject.

### Rava's Redness Basis

*Rava* therefore offers an alternative foundation for *rebbi*'s position. The *pasuk* states: *al tere yayin ki yitadam* — do not be drawn to wine because it is red — which implies that redness is what makes wine most attractive and desirable. The preference for red wine is well established, and finds expression in the practice of *leil ha-seder* as well. Apparently, wine in its first year retains its redness most vividly, and *rebbi* therefore holds that *l'chat'chila* one should bring wine of the current year. This raises a genuinely interesting conceptual question: when presenting something on the *mizbe'ach*, is the relevant standard one of taste or of appearance? The *torah* describes the *mizbe'ach* as consuming *lechem isheh* — food of fire — which might suggest taste is paramount. Yet since we certainly do not imagine that God consumes the offering in any literal sense, perhaps the symbolic and visual dimension is what matters most, and the standard would then be one of appearance. *rava*'s derivation seems to favor that latter position — *rebbi* grounds his *l'chat'chila* preference in the visual quality of wine's redness, not in its taste.

---

## Wine Source & Cultivation

### Trellis vs. Ground

The *mishnah* further specifies that one does not bring wine from *daliyot* — grapevines grown on trellises — but rather from *ragliyot*, vines that grow along the ground. Beyond that, the wine should come specifically from *kramim ha-avudim* — worked, cultivated vineyards, not wild or neglected ones, where the ground has been dug and tended.

### Rav Yosef Example

A *baraita* teaches that *kramim avudim* are those that are worked twice a year. The *gemara* illustrates this with a striking practical example: Rav Yosef had a corner of a vineyard, *karna d'pardisa*, in which he performed an extra digging — more than what was standard. The result was a wine, *chamra d'dari maya chad b'trei*, so potent that it could be diluted at twice the normal ratio. Typically wine was mixed with water at a three-to-one ratio; this wine was strong enough to be diluted six-to-one. The story concretely demonstrates how extra cultivation of the soil produces grapes of superior quality and concentration.

### Wine Storage

The *mishnah* further rules that the wine would not be stored in large barrels but in medium-sized jars — *chaviyot*, *kadiyot*, *ludiyot* — with the *baraita* specifying jars of the *lod* variety. Additionally, *ein manichin oto shnayim shnayim* — the jars would not be stored two together in the same place. *ela echad echad* — each jar was kept separately, so that if one were to go bad it would not contaminate its neighbor and compromise the quality of the wine.

---

## Wine Quality Control

### Gizbar Inspection

Returning to the *mishnah*: *keitzad bodek ha-gizbar* — how does the *gizbar* inspect the wine to ensure its quality? He would sit holding a testing rod — *yoshev v'kaneh b'yado*. According to *rashi*'s reading, when the spigot was opened and white dross emerged near the top, the *gizbar* would bang the rod to signal that the spigot should be closed. A *tana* elaborates: *zarak ha-gir shel shemarim* — if the lees and white dross came spurting out, the *gizbar* would bang his rod to signal rejection.

### Silent Rejection

One might ask: why does the *gizbar* not simply say aloud that the wine is unacceptable? Why does he reject it wordlessly? The *gemara* answers that this practice supports the teaching of *rabbi yochanan*.

### Speech Effect

*Rabbi Yochanan* taught: *keshem shehadibur yafeh labsamin* — just as speech is beneficial when working with spices (in the preparation of the *ketoret*, speaking certain words enhances the quality of the beating and blending), *kach dibur ra l'yayin* — so too speech is harmful to wine. When wine is in a sensitive state, speaking near it negatively affects its quality. The *gizbar* therefore communicates by gesture rather than voice, so as not to damage the very wine he is inspecting.

---

## Flour Impurities

### Impurity Ruling

The *mishnah* concludes with the ruling of *rabbi yossi bar rabbi yehuda*: if the wine contains *kemachim* — flour-like impurities and similar adulterants — it is invalid. His source is the *pasuk*: *temimim yihyu lachem uminchatam veniskeihem kamishpat* — the sacrifices must be *temimim*, unblemished, and the *mincha* and the *nesachim* are included in that requirement of wholeness.

### Mum Query

*Rabbi Yochanan* raises a question that he poses in several analogous contexts throughout the *gemara*: does the concept of *mum* — blemish — extend beyond animals to non-animal offerings? The question is specifically: if one sanctifies this wine — wine containing these flour-like impurities — does one incur lashes for having sanctified a *ba'al mum*? The prohibition of sanctifying a blemished animal carries *malkot*; does that *lav* extend to non-animal sacrificial items?

The argument for extending the prohibition is straightforward: *keivan d'pasul, ba'al mum dami* — since it is invalid, it is treated like a *ba'al mum*. And in this specific case there is particular force to the argument, since the *pasuk* of *temimim* is explicitly applied. The counterargument is: *ein ba'al mum ela b'beheimah* — the concept of *mum* and the accompanying *lav* apply only to animals. The *gemara* here, as in the parallel discussions, concludes with *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

---

## Animal Quality

### Geographic Sources

Having completed the *mishnah* and its *gemara*, a *baraita* now rounds out the picture of where the best sacrificial materials were sourced. The Sages taught: *eilim miMoav* — the finest rams came from Moav; *kevasim miHevron* — the best lambs from Chevron; *agalim miSharon* — the finest calves from the Sharon; *gozalot meHar hamelech* — the best birds from Har Hamelech.

### Wide-Backed Lambs

*Rabbi Yehuda* adds a qualitative specification: *mevi'im kevasim shegavham kerachbam* — one should bring lambs whose backs are as wide as they are high, or in the variant reading, *shegavan rechovim*, lambs with notably wide backs — large, broad-backed animals.

### Scripture Basis

*Rava bar Rav Shila* identifies the scriptural source for *rabbi yehuda*'s preference. The *pasuk* states: *yireh miknecha bayom hahu kar nirchav* — your cattle shall graze on that day in a wide pasture. The word *kar* can denote both a lamb and something wide and expansive — *kar nirchav* can also mean a broad cushion or wide support. *rabbi yehuda* thus reads into the term *kar* a preference for lambs that are themselves *nirchav*, wide and broad.

This discussion reinforces the earlier question about whether sacrificial standards are governed by taste or by appearance. The emphasis here is clearly on appearance — on the visual impressiveness and aesthetic appeal of the animal — rather than on any quality that would bear on taste. The focus on appearances in this context seems to be the animating principle across these rulings.

---

## Watchers Coda

### Watchers' Plea

The *perek* of *kol korbanot tzibur* closes not with a strictly halachic passage but with a moving *aggadeta*, introduced by a quotation from *rava bar rav shila* and naturally arising from the broader lens the *gemara* has adopted — looking not just at individual *korbanot* in their technical details but at the entire living reality of the *beit haMikdash*: where the wine came from, where the flour came from, where the oil came from, how these materials were cultivated and prepared. From that broader perspective the *gemara* brings a verse from *yeshayahu*: *al chomosayich Yerushalayim hifkadeti shomrim kol hayom v'chol halayla tamid lo yecheshu hamazkirim et Hashem al dami lachem* — on your walls, O Jerusalem, I have appointed watchers; all day and all night they shall never be silent; those who call upon God, do not be silent. These are the watchmen stationed around the ruins of Jerusalem after the *churban*, constantly speaking, evoking the memory of the *mikdash*. What would these watchers say? *rava bar rav shila* teaches: *ata takum terachem tziyon* — may You, God, arise and have compassion upon Zion, rebuild the *beit haMikdash*. *rav nachman bar yitzchak* adds: *bonei yerushalayim hashem* — God will rebuild Jerusalem.

### Original Statement

And what did these same watchers say originally, when the *beit haMikdash* still stood? *rava bar rav shila* teaches again: *ki bachar hashem b'tziyon ivah l'moshav lo* — for God has chosen Zion; He desired it to be His dwelling place.

With that, the *gemara* declares *hadran alach kol korbanot tzibur* — the conclusion of the *perek*.

---

## Dry Measures

### Two Measures

The new *perek* opens with the *mishnah*: *shtei midot shel yavesh hayu b'mikdash* — there were two dry measures in the *beit haMikdash*. These were used for measuring flour and are thus directly relevant to *menachot*: an *isaron* and a *chatzi isaron* — a tenth-measure and a half-tenth-measure. The *isaron* is the standard unit for a *mincha*. Larger *menachot* exist — the *minchat nesachim* for a lamb requires one *isaron*, for a ram two, for an ox (*par*) three — but all measurement was done in individual *isaron* increments. Crucially, the Temple did not maintain a two-*isaron* or three-*isaron* vessel; one would simply use the single *isaron* measuring cup multiple times. The *chatzi isaron*, as the *gemara* will explain, was used specifically for the *chavitay Kohen Gadol* — the daily *mincha* of the *kohen gadol*, which consisted of one *isaron* divided equally between morning and afternoon.

### Meir vs. Sages

*Rabbi Meir* holds: *isaron isaron v'chatzi isaron* — there were in fact two types of *isaron* vessels plus the *chatzi isaron*, making three measuring vessels in total. Since the two *isaron* vessels must have served distinct purposes, they cannot have been identical in size; they were presumably of slightly different measurement. *the sages* maintain that there was only one type of *isaron* vessel, plus the *chatzi isaron*, making two in total.

---

## Heaped vs. Leveled

### Double Language

A *baraita* cites *rabbi meir*'s derivation. The *torah* in *parshat pinchas*, listing the festival *korbanot*, uses the doubled formulation *isaron isaron lakeves ha'echad* — one *isaron*, one *isaron* — for each of the seven lambs. Why the repetition? *melamed sheshtei isronot hayu bamikdash* — it teaches that there were two *isaron* vessels in the *beit haMikdash*: *echad gadush ve'echad machuk* — one was heaped (*gadush*) and one was leveled (*machuk*). The distinction is familiar from everyday usage: a heaping measure versus a level measure. The *gadush* vessel was slightly smaller in physical capacity, such that when flour was allowed to mound above the rim, the total quantity equaled one *isaron*. The *machuk* vessel was precisely one *isaron* when leveled flat to the rim — and therefore physically larger as a container.

### Usage by Type

*Rabbi Meir* teaches that the *gadush* vessel — the heaping measure — was used *shebo hayu modedin lechol haminchos*, for measuring all the standard *menachot*. The implication may be that for those offerings a small degree of imprecision was tolerable; the mound atop the rim could conceivably add a slight extra amount, but that was acceptable. The *machuk* vessel — the precisely leveled measure — *shebo hayu modedin lechavitei Kohen Gadol*, was used specifically for the *kohen gadol*'s *mincha*. *rashi* explains the reasoning: when you level off the top of the vessel, you can pour and divide the contents into two equal halves without any spillage from a mound. Precision in division demands a level starting point. One might add that the very fact of dividing into exact halves calls for a more exacting standard of measurement throughout.

---

## Sages' Position

### Single Type Argument

The Sages counter *rabbi meir*'s position by citing a different verse: *ve'isaron echad lakeves ha'echad* — one *isaron* for one lamb. The phrase *isaron echad*, "one *isaron*," teaches that there was only one type of *isaron* vessel in the *beit haMikdash*, not two.

### Half-Isaron Derivation

If so, what does the Sages' position do with the doubled language of *isaron isaron* from which *rabbi meir* derived two types of *isaron*? *lirbot chatzi isaron* — the repetition comes to include the *chatzi isaron*, teaching that there is a variant on the *isaron* in the form of the half-measure, but not that there are two distinct full-*isaron* vessels. And *rabbi meir* — where does he derive the *chatzi isaron*? From the *vav* of *ve'isaron echad lakeves ha'echad* — the conjunctive *vav* indicates something additional to the standard *isaron*, which he reads as the *chatzi isaron*. The Sages, however, do not derive anything from that *vav*, and so they take the *chatzi isaron* from the doubled *isaron isaron* instead.

A *baraita* cited by *rabbi yossi* further illuminates this: the *torah* places a scribal dot — a *nekuda* — over the *vav* of the first *isaron* in the *succot* readings, on the first day of *yom tov*. The purpose is to teach *she'lo yimdod lo beshel gimel lapar v'lo beshel shnayim la'ayil* — that even for an ox, which requires three *isronot*, and for a ram, which requires two, one must never use a larger vessel but must use only the single *isaron* measure repeatedly. The dotted *vav*, in effect, emphasizes: only the *isaron*, singular.

### No Large Measures

For *rabbi meir*, the *nekuda* teaches nothing — he does not derive *halacha* from scribal dots — and he learns the prohibition against multi-*isaron* vessels from the verse *isaron echad lakeves ha'echad*, which the Sages instead read as teaching a single type of *isaron*.

---

## HP Mincha Division

### Measure Clarified

An apparent tension arises from the *mishnah*'s statement that one would *moded* — measure — with the *chatzi isaron* for the *chavitei Kohen Gadol*: half in the morning, half in the afternoon. Yet a separate *braita* rules explicitly: *chavitei Kohen Gadol lo hayu ba'im chatzaim* — one does not bring the *kohen gadol*'s *mincha* in separate halves. Rather, *ela meivi isaron shalem v'chotzeihu* — one brings a full *isaron* and then divides it in two. This means the primary measurement was done with a full *isaron*, not a *chatzi isaron*. In what sense, then, was the *chatzi isaron* used for *measuring*?

*Rav Sheshet* resolves this: *mai moded nami de'katani mechaleik* — when the *mishnah* says the *chatzi isaron* was used for *moding*, it means it was used for *dividing* — specifically, for dividing the already-measured full *isaron* into its two equal halves. The *chatzi isaron* was not the primary measuring instrument but the tool by which the full *isaron* was apportioned correctly.

---

## Heaping Logic

### Rami's Question

*Rami bar Chama* posed a question to *rav chisda*: for *rabbi meir*, who holds that there were two types of *isaron* vessels — one *gadush* and one *machuk* — what was the *chatzi isaron*? Was it a heaped measure or a leveled measure?

The *gemara* immediately broadens the question: and why ask only about *rabbi meir*? For the *rabbanan*, too, we want to know what their single *isaron* vessel was — heaped or leveled?

### All Measures Leveled

*Rav Chisda* responds that from *rabbi meir*'s position one can derive the answer for *rabbi meir* regarding his *chatzi isaron*, and from *rabbi meir* one can also derive the answer for the *rabbanan*. Here is the logical chain: since *rabbi meir* explicitly states that the *machuk* — leveled — *isaron* was used for the *chavitei Kohen Gadol*, and since the *chatzi isaron* was also used for the *chavitei Kohen Gadol*, it follows that the *chatzi isaron* for *rabbi meir* was likewise *machuk*. The logic is reinforced by the practical consideration: if you need to divide an *isaron* into two precise halves, working with a leveled measurement affords far greater precision than working with a mound.

From this one can derive the *rabbanan*'s position as well. The *rabbanan* never disagreed with *rabbi meir* about the *chatzi isaron* — their dispute was only about whether there were two types of full *isaron* vessels. Since both agree the *chatzi isaron* was *machuk*, and since the *rabbanan* use their single *isaron* for everything including the *chavitei Kohen Gadol*, and since that *isaron* must accommodate precise halving just as the *chatzi isaron* must, one can conclude that the *rabbanan*'s single *isaron* was also *machuk*. The result is that across all opinions, all Temple dry measures were leveled — a conclusion that makes sense on its own terms, since greater precision is served by a level measure, and the requirement of exact halving makes imprecision particularly problematic.

---

## Dough Division

### By Hand Method

*Rami bar Chama* asked *rav chisda* a further question: when dividing the dough for the *chavitei Kohen Gadol* — taking each half-*isaron* of flour and forming six individual *challot* from it — *bameh mechalkan lachallot*? How does one divide the dough into sixths? *beyad*, by hand and approximation? Or *bichli*, using some kind of precise measuring vessel? *rashi* understands the question as arising after the flour has been mixed and one is working with actual dough; *tosafot* understands it as a question about dividing the dry flour into sixths before mixing.

### Against Scales

*Rav Chisda* responds: it is obvious that the division is done *beyad*, by hand. The reason is captured in the phrase *torat aniyah tachnis* — do you want to bring in the *torah* of poverty, the symbolism of scarcity? To measure out flour or dough in such small increments as a twelfth of an *isaron*, one would need a precision scale. That kind of weighing is associated with *dochak* — deprivation and shortage. The *pasuk* in the curses of *vayikra* warns: *veheishivu lachmechem bemishkal* — they will weigh out your bread — meaning bread rationed by weight in times of famine. To measure dough on a scale is to evoke that curse. *rashi* applies this directly to the dough context. *tosafot* extends it even to the flour: using a precision scale in the *mikdash* to measure tiny amounts is itself inappropriate, since the *mikdash* should project abundance rather than scarcity.

---

## Shulchan Sanctity

### Sanctification Q

*Rami bar Chama* posed yet another question to *rav chisda*: *shulchan mahu sheyekadesh kematzim begodesh shelo* — can the *shulchan* in the *beit haMikdash* sanctify things placed upon it other than the *lechem hapanim*, specifically in the mound (*godesh*) above its surface? *rashi* understands *kematzim* as referring to the *levonah* — the frankincense offered as part of the *lechem hapanim* service — which, if placed directly on the *shulchan* surface rather than in the *bezychin* (the small spoons designated for it), would raise the question of whether the *shulchan* sanctifies it. *tosafot* understands the question as referring to a *kometz* of a *mincha*: ordinarily one places a *kometz* in a *kli sharet* to sanctify it before bringing it to the *mizbe'ach*; what if instead it were placed on the *shulchan*?

Either way, the question has two dimensions. First, does the *shulchan* function as a *kli sharet* capable of sanctifying things that are not the *lechem hapanim* it was designed for? Second — and this is where the *godesh* language becomes critical — even if the *shulchan* sanctifies what rests on its surface, does that sanctity extend to a mound of material rising above the surface, which has no enclosing walls around it? The conceptual parallel to the *gadush/machuk* debate about dry measures is precise: just as one asked whether the measuring vessel sanctifies the mounded flour that rises above its rim, so too one asks whether the *shulchan* sanctifies whatever rises above its flat surface.

### Mound Sanctification

The *gemara* frames the alternatives: *midei demakadesh lechem kematzim nami makadesh* — since the *shulchan* sanctifies the *lechem hapanim*, perhaps it sanctifies these other items as well, since the bread itself sat directly on the flat surface with no enclosing walls around it. Or: *dechazi lei makadesh dela chazi lei lo makadesh* — perhaps the *shulchan* sanctifies only what it was designated for; frankincense placed directly on the surface, or a *kometz* placed there, is simply not what the *shulchan* was made to sanctify, and therefore no sanctification occurs.

*Rav Chisda* answers: *eino makadesh* — it does not sanctify them, presumably because the *shulchan*'s sanctifying power is limited to what it was designated for.

### Airspace Height

The *gemara* challenges this from a teaching of *rabbi yochanan*. *rabbi yochanan* said — and this connects to a later discussion about the dimensions of the *lechem hapanim* — that the *shulchan* sanctifies a vertical airspace above its surface. If the walls of each loaf of *lechem hapanim* were folded up two and a half *tefachim*, then with six loaves stacked in each column, the *shulchan* sanctifies up to fifteen *tefachim* above its surface. If the walls were two *tefachim*, it sanctifies up to twelve *tefachim* above its surface. The point is that *rabbi yochanan* is teaching something beyond the obvious — we all know the *shulchan* sanctifies the *lechem hapanim* itself. The teaching about height must be coming to tell us that something placed within that airspace — something other than the *lechem hapanim* — becomes sanctified. This seems to directly contradict *rav chisda*'s ruling that the *shulchan* does not sanctify items other than those it was designated for.

### Partial Sanctity

The *gemara* resolves the tension: *eino makadesh lehikarev aval makadesh lehipasel*. The *shulchan* does not sanctify such items with the full sanctity that would make them fit to be offered on the *mizbe'ach*. It does not transform the *levonah* into something ready for the altar, nor does it complete the sanctification of a *kometz* for burning. However, it does impart a partial sanctity — enough that the item is now susceptible to the categories of *pesul* that apply to *kodashim*: it can become invalid through *tumah*, or through being taken outside its proper domain. This is the concept of *makadesh lehipasel* — sanctified to the extent that it can become disqualified — without being *makadesh lehikarev* — fully sanctified to the point of fitness for the *mizbe'ach*. This nuanced category of partial sanctification, in which an object acquires enough *kedusha* to be vulnerable to invalidation but not enough to be offered, is a concept the *gemara* has visited before and will return to again.

---

---

# Menachot 88

## Seven Liquid Measures

### Seven Measures Intro

The Mishnah with which we open Daf 88 takes up the subject of liquid measures used in the Beit HaMikdash. Having dealt with dry measures previously, the Mishnah now turns to the lach: שבע מדות של לח היו במקדש — there were seven liquid measures in the Mikdash.

### Log & Revi'it Units

The foundational unit of liquid measure is the log, approximately fourteen ounces. A hin is twelve log. The revi'it — literally "a quarter" — is a quarter of a log, roughly 3.2 to 3.4 ounces, the familiar minimum measure for kiddush. These two units — the log and the revi'it — form the baseline from which the other measures are derived.

### Hin to Quarter-Log

The Mishnah lists the seven measures as follows: a hin, a half-hin (six log), a third of a hin (four log — the portion accompanying a par, as the Torah specifies: שלישית ההין לפר), a quarter of a hin (three log, for an ayil), a log, a half-log, and a quarter-log. Notably, the list moves from the largest measure down to the smallest, and the Torah's language — שלישית ההין לפר ורביעית ההין לכבש — grounds the larger measures in explicit scriptural usage.

### One Hin w/ Lines

Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok offers an alternative to the picture of seven distinct vessels. He holds that שנתות היו בהין — there were graduated markings, or notches, on a single hin vessel, indicating the fill lines for the various sacrifices: עד כאן לפר, עד כאן לאיל, ועד כאן לכבש. Rather than maintaining multiple separate measuring vessels, one vessel served all purposes by means of these calibrated lines. This approach is at least conceptually less precise than having dedicated vessels, though Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok clearly finds it acceptable.

### Rabbi Shimon: No Hin

Rabbi Shimon takes a more radical stance: לא היו שם הין — there was no hin at all in the Beit HaMikdash. His reasoning is functional: וכי מה היה הין משמש? What was the hin ever used for? The largest quantity actually required for any sacrifice was a half-hin (for the par), so a full hin vessel was never actually needed. In its place, Rabbi Shimon says, there was a special measure of a log-and-a-half: מדה יתירה של לוג ומחצה היתה שם, used to divide the oil for the minchat chavitin of the Kohen Gadol — a log-and-a-half in the morning and a log-and-a-half in the afternoon.

The Rabbis push back: but you already have a half-log measure; simply use it three times and you have a log-and-a-half. Why fabricate an entirely new vessel? Rabbi Shimon replies in kind: that argument proves too much. By the same logic, why have a half-log at all — just use the revi'it twice? Why have a full log — just use the half-log twice? The answer is the standing principle of the Mikdash: כלי שמשמש מידה זו אינו משמש מידה אחרת — a vessel designated for one measure is not pressed into service as a substitute for another. If a particular measure is regularly needed, a dedicated vessel is created for it rather than improvising with multiples of a smaller one.

Tosafot notes the Rabbis' implied response: the log-and-a-half measure is needed only twice daily and only for the Kohen Gadol's chavitin, whereas the commonly used measures — a half-log, a log — serve many different purposes throughout the Temple service and therefore clearly warrant dedicated vessels of their own.

---

## Meir vs. Yehudah Debate

### Baraita Recitation

The Gemara now presents a Baraita that records the same list of seven measures but in ascending order — from smallest to largest: רביעית, לוג, חצי לוג, רביעית ההין, שלישית ההין, חצי ההין, והין. This, the Baraita states, is דברי רבי יהודה — the position of Rabbi Yehudah. Rabbi Meir then gives the exact same list in descending order — hin first, down to the quarter-log. The Baraita also records Rabbi Shimon's position (no hin; the log-and-a-half substitute), which we have already encountered in the Mishnah. The question that immediately presents itself: since Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah appear to list the identical seven vessels in merely different orders, what substantive disagreement underlies the difference in direction?

### Dedicated Vessels

Before reaching that question, the Gemara completes the Baraita's discussion of Rabbi Shimon's position. The Rabbis respond to him: הוי הין דעבד משה לשמן המשחה — the hin that Moshe used when he prepared the shemen hamishcha was preserved. The Torah explicitly states שמן זית הין in that context, so Moshe clearly had a hin vessel. One opinion holds: since it was not needed for later generations, Moshe used it at the time and then it was put away, genzu. The other opinion holds: since it existed, it was retained — כיון דהוה הוה. Furthermore, the Gemara notes that we have a received tradition — גמירי דשבע מדות הלח היו במקדש — that there were precisely seven liquid measures, analogous to the tradition (cited by Ravina in another context) that semicha was performed on precisely two communal sacrifices. If Rabbi Shimon eliminates the hin, he must replace it with something, and he does so with the log-and-a-half.

### Overflow & Tension

Returning to the central question of Rabbi Meir versus Rabbi Yehudah: אמר רבי יוחנן, בירותי מדות איכא בינייהו — Rabbi Yochanan says their dispute concerns the beirutei middot, the overflow that rides atop the surface of a filled measuring vessel due to surface tension. The disagreement is over whether this extra amount — the liquid held above the rim of the vessel — is sanctified by the vessel along with the rest of its contents.

### Transfer Direction

Rashi explains the connection between the ordering of measures and this question of overflow as follows. Rabbi Yehudah, who lists measures from small to large, holds that the beirutei middot are sanctified. According to this view, God gave Moshe the small revi'it as the standard — ורביעית יהב ליה רחמנא למשה — and told him to measure with it, accumulating small measures into larger ones. When pouring from a small vessel into a larger vessel, the overflow on top of the smaller one can be captured: if you tip the small vessel quickly into the larger one, even the tiny amount held by surface tension goes along. Rabbi Meir, who lists measures from large to small, holds that the beirutei middot are not sanctified. According to his view, God gave Moshe the hin — the large measure — and instructed him to divide downward into halves, thirds, and quarters. When transferring from a large vessel into smaller ones, that extra surface liquid simply spills away; it cannot be preserved in the transfer.

The analogy is intuitive: anyone who has filled a kiddush cup to the brim and then tried to pour it into small cups knows that the overflow spills rather than transfers cleanly. By contrast, when pouring from a small vessel into a large one, the extra amount on top rides along into the larger vessel.

One might note a tension here: Rabbi Meir earlier appeared to endorse a גדוש, a heaping measure, for the dry measures — which would suggest he favors counting overflow as part of the sanctified quantity. The relationship between his position on dry measures and his position here on liquid overflow remains to be worked through.

### Sanctification Question

Abaye offers a different analysis entirely. He says that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah is not about whether the beirutei middot are sanctified at all — both could hold either position on that question. Rather, their dispute concerns the meaning of מלאים in the verse (שניהם מלאים סלת): what does it mean to fill the measure?

According to Rabbi Meir, who enumerates from large to small, מלאים שלא יחסר ושלא יותיר: the measure must be filled exactly — no less and no more. There is a strict maximum as well as a minimum. According to Rabbi Yehudah, who enumerates from small to large, מלאים means שלא יחסר — do not leave it short — but if you overfill it, אבל יותיר, מלאים קרינא ביה: that too counts as "filled." The direction of enumeration is a kind of סימן — a signal — for this underlying orientation: counting upward suggests that "more" is the direction of acceptability, while counting downward signals that maximums are as binding as minimums.

Tosafot notes that the directional ordering is more of a mnemonic signal for the underlying positions than a logical derivation from them.

This raises the question: is this not identical to the first dispute about beirutei middot? The Acharonim clarify that these are genuinely two distinct questions. One question is whether the liquid that overflows and sits atop the vessel by surface tension is itself sanctified by that vessel. A separate question is whether one is permitted, at the outset, to bring slightly more than the prescribed measure — whether the Torah's requirement functions as a strict maximum or merely as a minimum. One could maintain, for instance, that overfill is halachically permissible to bring, but that the overfill itself does not become sanctified through the measuring vessel; rather, it would only become sanctified when poured into a separate kli sharet. Or one could hold the converse: the overfill is sanctified, but one is nonetheless required to remove it and bring only the exact amount. These are logically independent questions.

---

## Shimon's Challenge

### Hin Never Used

Having presented the Baraita's full treatment of the debate, the Gemara turns back to examine Rabbi Shimon's position more closely. Rabbi Shimon maintains that the hin was simply never functionally required: לא היו שם הין — no offering demanded a full hin's measure of wine or oil, so why maintain such a vessel?

### Moshe's Hin Preserved

The Rabbis respond that the hin Moshe used for the shemen hamishcha — for which the Torah explicitly writes שמן זית הין — was preserved in the Mikdash. The question then is whether it was preserved permanently or only used for that original occasion. Rabbi Shimon holds: כיון דלדורות לא הוי צריך, לפי שעה הוא דעבד וגנזו — since it was not needed for future generations, Moshe made it for the moment and it was secreted away. The Rabbis hold: כיון דהוה הוה — once it existed, it remained part of the Temple's complement of vessels.

### Seven Measures Tradition

The Gemara then addresses why Rabbi Shimon cannot simply eliminate the hin and leave only six measures. The answer is drawn from a parallel: just as Ravina states elsewhere that גמירי שתי סמיכות בציבור — there is a received tradition that communal semicha was performed on exactly two specific korbanot — so too here, גמירי דשבע מדות הלח היו במקדש: there is a received tradition that the liquid measures in the Mikdash numbered precisely seven. Rabbi Shimon, who accepts this tradition, is therefore compelled to substitute the log-and-a-half measure in place of the hin in order to preserve the count of seven.

### Measures vs. Vessels

The Gemara then addresses Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok, who holds that there was only one hin vessel with graduated lines rather than multiple distinct vessels. Does he reject the tradition of seven measures altogether? The Gemara answers: ואיבעית אימא, מאי שבע מדות? שבע מדידות — he need not reject it. One can distinguish between seven distinct vessels and seven distinct measures. Even if some or all of the measures were marked on a single vessel, the tradition of seven different measures used in the Mikdash remains intact. Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok accepts the seven measures; he simply holds that they were incorporated into a single physical vessel rather than expressed through seven separate keilim.

---

## Applications of Measures

### Revi'it Uses

The Mishnah now catalogues the specific uses of each liquid measure. The revi'it — approximately 3.2 ounces, the familiar minimum for kiddush — was used for two purposes: רביעית מים למצורע, the water used in the purification process of the metzora (where the bird is slaughtered over mayim chayyim held in a vessel, and the Gemara elsewhere establishes the minimum as a revi'it), and רביעית שמן לנזיר, the revi'it of oil incorporated into the lechem of the nazir when he brings his korban. It is worth noting that this is a standard revi'it — a quarter of a log — and not a revi'it ha-hin, which is three log, a very different quantity.

### Half-Log Uses

The chatzi log served two functions: חצי לוג מים לסוטה — the half-log of water used for the sotah, into which the megillah was scraped and which she then drank — and וחצי לוג שמן לתודה, the half-log of oil incorporated into the bread of the todah offering. The derivations of these specific quantities come from other sugyot; some are learned from pesukim, others rest on tradition alone.

### Log for Menachot

The log was the standard measure for all menachot: ובלוג היה מודד לכל המנחות. Just as the standard unit of flour for a minchah was an isaron — roughly a five-pound measure — the standard amount of oil was one log, approximately fourteen ounces. This is analogous to the rule regarding dry measures: even for a large minchah requiring many isronot, one uses the single isaron measure repeatedly rather than a larger vessel. The same principle applies to oil: אפילו מנחה של שישים עישרון נותנים לה שישים לוג — even a sixty-isaron minchah would receive sixty log of oil, measured out with the log vessel sixty times.

### Large Menachot Debate

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov dissents: אפילו מנחה של שישים עישרון, אין לה אלא לוגה — even a sixty-isaron minchah receives only a single log of oil, no more. In other words, when a donor vows to bring a larger-than-standard minchah, he may increase the flour but not the oil. The oil remains fixed at one log regardless of the quantity of flour. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives this from the phrase לַמִּנְחָה וְלֹג שָׁמֶן — the minchah receives a log of oil, full stop.

The reason the Mishnah specifies sixty isronot as the example is deliberate: as a later Mishnah will teach, sixty isronot is the maximum that can be effectively blilah'd — effectively kneaded and mixed. A minchah exceeding sixty isronot must be split into two separate offerings. The familiar rule כל הראוי לבילה אין בילה מעכבת בו — that which is capable of being mixed, failure to mix does not invalidate — applies precisely to a minchah of sixty isronot or fewer. Thus sixty isronot is the largest single minchah possible, and the Mishnah uses it to stake out the dispute's outer limit.

### Sacrifices & Menorah

The Mishnah then assigns specific measures to the libations accompanying animal sacrifices: six log for the par (a half-hin), four log for the ayil (a third-hin), and three log for the keves (a quarter-hin). Although the Mishnah here expresses these in log, the actual measuring vessels used in practice would have been the chatzi ha-hin, shlishit ha-hin, and revi'it ha-hin respectively; the Mishnah is simply clarifying the log equivalencies for completeness.

For the menorah: שלושה ומחצה למנורה — three and a half log in total, with חצי לוג לכל נר — a half-log per lamp. The assumption is that a half-log of oil is sufficient to sustain a lamp through the longest winter night; this standard amount was maintained year-round. Seven lamps at a half-log each yields three and a half log. As for the summer months when nights are shorter, any oil still burning in the morning would be extinguished at the time of the morning service — except for the ner maaravi — and the surplus oil would be poured out.

---

## Sanctity of Vessels

### Revi'it Sanctity

The Gemara now records a series of questions and answers between Rebbe (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) and his colleagues concerning the status of the liquid measures as כלי שרת — sanctified Temple vessels. Rebbe's starting assumption is that the liquid measures were indeed keilei sharet, as distinct from the dry measures, about which there had been an earlier debate. The question is then: for what purpose would each measure require this sanctified status?

יתיב רבי וקא קשיא ליה — Rebbe sat and was troubled: רביעית למה נשנית? Why was the revi'it designated as a kli sharet? The Mishnah says the revi'it was used for the metzora's water and the nazir's oil. But the metzora's purification took place outside the Mikdash — חוצה הוא — so no kli sharet was needed there. And the nazir's oil accompanies his shlamim, and לחם נזיר בשחיטת איל הוא דקדיש — the lechem of the nazir is sanctified through the slaughtering of his ayil, not through a measuring vessel. So what sanctification role does the revi'it vessel serve?

### Kohen Gadol Oil

Rabbi Chiya resolved Rebbe's question: שבה היה מודד לחביתי כהן גדול — it was used to portion out the oil for each individual challah of the Kohen Gadol's minchat chavitin. The total oil for each half of the minchat chavitin was a log and a half; there were six challot per half; and a log and a half divided among six challot yields a revi'it per challah. In order to apportion the oil individually to each challah — and in that context, one would want the oil itself sanctified before it was applied — the revi'it served as the kli sharet for that purpose.

Rebbe was delighted, and he applied to Rabbi Chiya the verse מארץ מרחק איש עצתי — "from a distant land comes my counselor" — alluding to Rabbi Chiya's origins in Bavel.

### Half-Log Sanctity

The Gemara records the parallel inquiry: יתיב רבי וקא קשיא ליה — Rebbe again sat troubled, this time over the chatzi log. חצי לוג למה נמשח? Why did the half-log require sanctification? The Mishnah says it was used for the sotah's water and the todah's oil. But the water for the sotah was drawn from the kiyor — the laver — and the Torah itself calls it מים קדושים: it was already sanctified through the kiyor, not through a measuring vessel. And the oil for the todah's lechem, like the nazir's, is sanctified through the slaughtering of the todah offering: לחמי תודה בשחיטת תודה הוא דקדשי. So again: why would the chatzi log need to be a kli sharet?

### Menorah Oil Portions

This time it was Rebbe's own son, Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbe, who provided the resolution: שבה היה מחלק חצי לוג שמן לכל נר ונר — the half-log was used to measure and distribute the oil to each individual lamp of the menorah. As the Mishnah stated, each of the seven lamps received a half-log of oil, and that oil needed to be sanctified as it was dispensed. The chatzi log kli sharet was the instrument through which this sanctification was effected.

Rebbe responded: נר ישראל כך היה — "Light of Israel, so it was" — commending his son with this epithet particularly fitting to the subject of the menorah's lamps. Tosafot notes that the phrase נר ישראל appears in another Gemara context as well, not limited to this passage.

---

## Menorah Lighting

### Lamp Extinction

The discussion of the chatzi log and the menorah's oil naturally leads into a broader treatment of how the menorah was actually maintained. The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rebbe: נר שכבתה — if one of the lamps of the menorah went out — נדשן השמן ונדשנה הפתילה — and the oil or the wick had become charred and ashy, כיצד עושה? What is the procedure? מטיבה — you clean it out, ונותן בה שמן — you refill it with oil, ומדליקה — and you relight it.

The printed Rashi reads this as a halachic characterization rather than a physical description: once the lamp is extinguished, the oil and wick are treated as rendered inert — like ashes, halachically spent — and must be discarded and replaced regardless of their physical condition. The kesav yad Rashi (the manuscript version), however, takes it literally: the text is discussing a case where the oil and wick have actually become charred and dirty, making reuse inappropriate. Either way, the underlying assumption of this sugya — at least according to the straightforward reading — is that if a lamp goes out during the night, there is an obligation to relight it so that the menorah burns through the night. The Rashba disputes this reading entirely and argues, based on other sugyot, that there is no requirement to relight an extinguished lamp; he therefore construes the Gemara differently. The peshat reading, however, is that the menorah is expected to burn through the night and relighting is required.

### Refill Amount

Once it is established that one must relight an extinguished lamp, a further question presents itself — one posed by Rabbi Zeira: כשהוא נותן בה שמן, כמדת ראשונה או כמה שחסרה? When refilling the oil, does one put in the full original measure — a half-log — or only enough to replace what was actually consumed?

The logic of the second option is not unreasonable: if the lamp went out midway through the night, it only needs to burn through the remaining hours, so perhaps only half a half-log, or some partial amount, is needed rather than the full measure.

### Full Measure Standard

Rabbi Yirmiyah disposes of the question decisively: פשיטא דכמדת ראשונה — obviously you put in the full measure. His reasoning: if you were to put in only the amount consumed, how would you know precisely how much that was? מנא ידעינן מה חסר? And if you say you would measure the remnant oil after removing it, and then replace exactly that amount — אם כן, שבע מידות נפשו להו מידות טובא — you would need measures far beyond the seven established measures, since you would need smaller sub-units to gauge the remnant. Since the Mikdash operated with exactly seven standard liquid measures and no others, there is no mechanism for measuring out a partial amount. The only workable answer is: always put in the full standard half-log.

On this resolution Rebbe applied the verse רכב על דבר אמת וענוה צדק — riding on the matter of truth and righteous humility. The statement is also transmitted in a parallel tradition: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, and in another version Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Chanina in the name of Rebbe himself — indicating this ruling was attributed to Rebbe directly in some traditions.

### Rambam Twice Daily

The Rambam takes a position on the menorah that stands entirely alone among the Rishonim. The near-universal understanding is that the menorah was lit at night and cleaned in the morning — the oil measure of a half-log per lamp being calibrated to last through the longest winter nights — and that the morning service of הטבת הנרות (cleaning the lamps) was distinct from the evening הדלקה (lighting). This is grounded in the verse בבוקר בבוקר בהטיבו את הנרות יקטירנה, which speaks of the morning cleaning in conjunction with the morning incense offering.

The Rambam, however, understands the menorah as burning continuously — through both night and day, tamid in the literal sense. According to him, the procedure of הטבה and הדלקה was performed twice daily, morning and evening, but in each case the process was the same: one checked the lamps, and if a lamp was burning cleanly, one added oil; if a lamp had gone out or needed attention, one cleaned it, refilled it with a half-log, and relit it. Thus for the Rambam, this Gemara's scenario — a lamp that has gone out and must be cleaned and relit — describes not a rare nighttime occurrence but the routine morning procedure.

Under the Rambam's reading, the half-log per lamp need not be calibrated to last a full night; the measure is added at each of the two daily servicings and is sufficient to last until the next one. All other Rishonim disagree and understand the menorah as lit at night and cleaned by day.

---

## Menorah Construction

### Jointed Lamps

The discussion of how lamps are cleaned leads naturally to a question about how the lamps were physically constructed. Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav Sheshet: נר שבמקדש, פרקים הוו — the lamps of the menorah were jointed. That is, they were not rigidly fixed but had flexible joints that allowed them to be bent, making it possible to clean them out effectively while they remained attached to the menorah.
