This is significant because it is an obligatory *olah*, yet it still attracts the *nesachim* requirement.

The same phrase also teaches the case of the eleventh animal in the *ma'aser behemah* count. If one mistakenly called the eleventh animal the tenth, it too becomes consecrated and is brought as a *shelamim*. Remarkably, this derivative *shelamim* requires *nesachim*, even though the *ma'aser behemah* itself does not. The Gemara notes the paradox: normally we do not find a subsidiary more stringent than its source. But this case joins a broader class of such derivatives — an *asham* that became an *olah*, a *pesach shelo b'zimano* that becomes a *shelamim* — all of which carry the *nesachim* requirement even though their source-categories do not.

---

## Obligatory Olos

### Olas Yoledet

Building on the above, the Gemara confirms that obligatory *olot* in general require *nesachim*. The *olat yoledet* is the paradigm: although brought under obligation, it is not tied to a fixed calendar time, and it retains sufficient similarity to a voluntary *olah* to attract the *nesachim* requirement.

### Ail Aharon

The Gemara next addresses the ram that *aharon* brings on *yom kippur* — *ayil echad l'olah* — and asks whether the extra phrase *o la'ayil ta'aseh mincha* is needed to include this. The answer initially seems unnecessary, since the *moadim* verse (*b'moadeichem*) already covers obligatory festival offerings. But the Gemara distinguishes: *b'moadeichem* covers communal (*tzibur*) offerings at the appointed times; one might have thought that an individual's (*yachid*) obligatory offering tied to a specific time is different. Furthermore, even the precedent of the *olat yoledet* does not resolve this, because the *olat yoledet* has no fixed time — it may be brought whenever the obligation arises — whereas *aharon*'s ram is fixed to a specific date. An offering fixed to a particular day might fall into a distinct category that neither *b'moadeichem* nor *olas yoledet* covers. Hence the extra *pasuk* is required to include it.

### Palgas Animal

The same phrase *o la'ayil* is also cited by Rabbi Yochanan as the source for the *halacha* of the *palgas* — an animal in its thirteenth month, beyond the *keves* stage (one year old) but not yet fully an *ayil* (a two-year-old male). The *palgas* occupies an intermediate status, and the question is whether it brings the *nesachim* quantities of a *keves* or those of an *ayil*.

### Palgas Debate

Rabbi Yochanan holds that the *palgas* is its own distinct category (*birya hi*) — neither *keves* nor *ayil* — but that the *halacha* is that it brings the *nesachim* of an *ayil*. This is derived from the *o la'ayil*, which extends the *ayil* standard to something that falls within the *ayil*'s ambit without being a full *ayil*. The *mishna* is cited in support: if someone offered a *palgas*, the ruling is that one brings with it *nischei ayil* — the *nesachim* quantities of a ram — yet the offering does not discharge a *neder* to bring a *keves* or an *ayil*, since the *palgas* is neither.

Bar Parda disagrees with this conceptual framework. In his view, the *palgas* is not a third category; it is simply a case of doubt — the animal is either a *keves* or an *ayil* and we do not know which. Accordingly, one brings the larger quantity (that of the *ayil*) and makes a stipulation: if this animal is indeed an *ayil*, the full quantity of *nesachim* is applied to it; if it turns out to be a *keves*, only the *keves* quantity applies and the remainder of the flour and wine is donated as a *nedavah*. On Bar Parda's reading, no extra *pasuk* is needed — and indeed no *pasuk* can include a doubtful case by extension. The Gemara acknowledges this difficulty: the extra *o* is genuinely difficult (*kashya*) for Bar Parda to account for.

---

## Summary Distinctions

### Ox Uniformity

The closing passage of the *nesachim* parsha — *kacha ya'aseh lashor ha'echad o la'ayil ha'echad o laseh bakvasim o baizim* — is now read as a series of limiting statements, each preventing an unwarranted analogy. The phrase *lashor ha'echad* is noted: since the Torah distinguishes between the *nesachim* of a *keves* and those of an *ayil* (sheep versus ram), one might have thought to draw a parallel distinction between a calf and a full-grown cow. The phrase *lashor ha'echad* teaches that for the ox, there is no such distinction — a calf and a cow are treated uniformly for purposes of *nesachim*.

### Ram Uniformity

Similarly, *o la'ayil ha'echad*: since the Torah distinguishes between a one-year-old sheep (*keves*) and a two-year-old ram (*ayil*), one might extend the logic and distinguish between a two-year-old ram and a three-year-old ram. The phrase *o la'ayil ha'echad* teaches that within the ram category there is no distinction — two years old and three years old are treated the same.

### Sheep Uniformity

The phrase *o laseh bakvasim*: since the Torah distinguishes between a *keves* and an *ayil*, one might further distinguish between a one-year-old female sheep (*kivsah*) and a two-year-old female sheep (*rechelah*). While a two-year-old male crosses into the *ayil* category, a two-year-old female has no such elevation, and one might have thought to impose an analogous distinction. The phrase *o laseh bakvasim* teaches that all sheep, regardless of age or sex, are uniform — no distinction between a *kivsah* and a *rechelah*.

### Goat Uniformity

Finally, *o ba'izim*: since the Torah distinguishes male sheep by age, one might analogously distinguish between a *gedi* (kid goat) and a *sa'ir* (older male goat). The phrase *o ba'izim* teaches that goats are uniform — no distinction is made within the goat family.

The principle is clear: do not extend the single existing distinction (between *keves* and *ayil*) by analogy to create distinctions that the Torah did not explicitly mandate.

### Mishna Proof

The Gemara concludes with a practical proof from the *mishna*. Rav Pappa reports that Rava once tested his students with the question: *niskei rechelah bekama* — how much *nesachim* does an older female sheep require? The answer is proven from the *mishna*, which states that a *gedi* — a receipt for *nesachim* — served (*meshamesh*) as the standard ticket for the *nesachim* of *tzon* generally: of large and small, male and female, with the sole exception of *eilim* (rams). Since everything other than the male ram shares the same *nesachim* standard — including older female sheep — the *rechelah* follows the standard *keves* measure and does not receive the elevated *ayil* quantity. This is precisely what the phrase *o laseh bakvasim* established, and the *mishna* bears it out directly.

---

---

# Menachot 92

## Semicha Rules Overview

### Mishna Context

The mishna that opens Menachot 92a begins: *kol korbanos hatzibur ein bahem semicha* — all communal sacrifices do not require *semicha*, the laying of hands upon the animal's head, with two exceptions: the *par he'elem davar shel tzibbur* and the *se'ir hamishtalach*. At first glance, this mishna seems out of place in Masechet Menachot, which is primarily concerned with flour offerings and their associated laws. The explanation lies in the structure of the surrounding mishnayot. The previous mishna addressed *kol korbanos hatzibur ve'yachid teunim nesachim* — which sacrifices require *nesachim*, the accompanying wine libation and flour-and-oil offering — and it drew a line between communal and individual offerings. Before that, another mishna discussed the measuring vessels used in the *mikdash*, which were also relevant to the flour and oil. This mishna, then, continues in the same *kol*-formulation style, even though it concerns animal sacrifices rather than *menachos* proper.

### Tzibbur vs. Yachid

The structural logic of the mishna divides along the axis of *korban tzibbur* versus *korban yachid*. The communal sacrifices, as a rule, do not receive *semicha*. One can appreciate why: *semicha* signifies ownership and personal connection between the offerer and the sacrifice. By definition, a *korban tzibbur* belongs to the entire community, and it is simply not feasible to have all of *am yisrael* lay their hands upon it. Even if some representative body were to do so, this raises the question of whether that adequately captures the ownership relationship that *semicha* is meant to express. The *maamados* described in Masechet Taanis offer a partial model of communal representation, but the sense of individual ownership is attenuated in any communal sacrifice.

### Par He'elem Davar

The first exception is the *par he'elem davar shel tzibbur*, the special ox brought when the *beis din* issues an erroneous ruling and the community acts upon it in error. This is the subject of Masechet Horayos and is described in Parshat Vayikra. The relevant text reads:

> וְסָמְכוּ זִקְנֵי הָעֵדָה אֶת יְדֵיהֶם עַל רֹאשׁ הַפָּר לִפְנֵי ה' וְשָׁחַט אֶת הַפָּר לִפְנֵי ה'

The elders of the congregation lay their hands upon the ox before God, and the ox is slaughtered. The explicit mention of *semicha* in this *pasuk* is what mandates it here. This exception is understandable: although the offering is technically communal, it is closely tied to the *beis din* — a small, defined body of individuals whose ruling caused the sin. The *sanhedrin* acts as the identifiable owners in a much tighter sense than the diffuse public behind ordinary communal offerings.

The mishna also records that Rabbi Shimon extends this framework: *af se'ir avodas kochavim* — even the special goat brought when the community commits *avodah zarah* following a mistaken ruling of the *beis din* requires *semicha*. This is rooted in Parshat Shelach, where the Torah describes a scenario in which the entire community errs regarding one of all the commandments — understood by *chazal* as a reference to *avodah zarah*, the sin that is *keneged* all the *mitzvos*. The verse prescribes both an ox and a goat as a *chatat*, yet does not mention *semicha* explicitly. Rabbi Shimon argues that this offering too should carry *semicha*.

### Yachid Exceptions

The second portion of the mishna addresses individual sacrifices: *kol korbanos hayachid teunim semicha* — all individual offerings require *semicha* — with three exceptions: *bechor*, *ma'aser*, and *pesach*. These three are categorically different from ordinary individual offerings. The *pesach* is fundamentally oriented toward the experience of eating and the celebration of *yetzias mitzrayim*; the act of *hakrava* is in service of the eating rather than standing as an independent act of connection to God. Similarly, *bechor* and *ma'aser* function more as gifts transferred to the *kohen* via the sacrificial process than as direct expressions of the individual's personal devotion. If *semicha* is an expression of ownership and personal identification with the offering as a vehicle of connection to God — whether in atonement or in gift — then these three occupy a fundamentally different category. Just as they are treated differently with respect to *nesachim* based on their distinct character, so too they are excluded from the requirement of *semicha*.

### Yoresh Inherit

The mishna then raises the case of the *yoresh*, the heir. If a father consecrated an animal and died before bringing it, and his son inherited it, is the son considered the *ba'al* — the owner — such that he may perform *semicha*? The mishna answers affirmatively: *hayoresh somech umevi nesachim umeimir*. The heir performs *semicha*, brings the required *nesachim*, and is even capable of effecting *temurah* — the legally prohibited yet halachically operative exchange of a consecrated animal, which transfers sanctity to the substitute. All three of these — *semicha*, *nesachim*, and *temurah* — share a grounding in ownership. The mishna's ruling that the heir may do all three reflects a consistent principle: inheritance creates full legal ownership, sufficient for all halachic purposes tied to the status of *ba'alim*.

### Se'ir Hamishtalach

The second exception in the communal category is the *se'ir hamishtalach*, the goat sent off to *azazel* on Yom Kippur. Here the Torah is explicit — Aharon lays both hands upon the head of the living goat, confesses the sins of all Israel, and sends it to the wilderness. This case is qualitatively different from ordinary *semicha*. The *se'ir hamishtalach* is not brought as an offering to God and is not about a *ba'al* expressing ownership. Rather, the act is one of transferring sin — placing the transgressions of the community symbolically onto the goat's head. The *semicha* here is not an act of ownership; it is an act of confession and transfer. That explains why it functions as an exception to the general rule: it is exceptional not merely in being permitted despite being a communal sacrifice, but because its *semicha* is of an entirely different nature.

---

## Baraita & Debate

### Baraita Text

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* that refines the positions recorded in the mishna. The *baraita* states: *kol korbanos hatzibur ein bahem semicha chutz mipar haba al kol hamitzvos ushirei avoda kochavim divrei Rabbi Shimon* — all communal sacrifices do not receive *semicha* except for the ox brought for all the commandments and the goats for *avodah zarah*, in the words of Rabbi Shimon. Two features of this *baraita* are immediately striking compared to the mishna. First, Rabbi Shimon here does not include the *se'ir hamishtalach* in his list of exceptions, even though the Torah explicitly mandates *semicha* there. Second, he instead includes the *se'irei avodas kochavim* as his second exception alongside the *par he'elem davar*.

### R. Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *se'irei avodas kochavim ein bahem semicha* — the goats for *avodah zarah* do not receive *semicha*. The *baraita* then records a curious move on Rabbi Yehuda's part: since he rejects the *se'irei avodas kochavim* as an exception, he requires a substitute for the second slot. Ravina explains this by citing a tradition — *gemiri shtei semichot batzibbur* — that there are exactly two cases in which the *tzibbur* performs *semicha*. Since the tradition fixes the number at two, and Rabbi Yehuda does not accept the *se'irei avodas kochavim*, he must find an alternative. That alternative, in his view, is the *se'ir hamishtalach* itself.

---

## Baraita & Debate (II)

### R. Shimon Rejoins

Rabbi Shimon responds to Rabbi Yehuda's inclusion of the *se'ir hamishtalach*: *vahalo ein semicha ella be'ba'alim, v'zeh Aharon uvanav somchim bo* — but surely *semicha* is only valid when performed by the owners themselves, and in this case it is Aharon and his sons who perform the *semicha*! Rabbi Shimon is not denying that Aharon lays his hands on the goat; he is arguing that that act is not *semicha be'ba'alim* — not the *semicha* of ownership. The entire discussion of who counts as a *ba'al* for purposes of *semicha*, including the ruling about the *yoresh*, presupposes that *semicha* must be performed by those who stand in an ownership relationship to the offering. The *se'ir hamishtalach* belongs to *am yisrael* — as the verse says, *ume'es adas bnei Yisrael yikach shnei se'irei izzim l'chatat* — two goats, for the community. Aharon performing *semicha* is therefore not the *semicha* of an owner; it is an act of placing sins on the goat's head. That is a fundamentally different category.

---

## Aharon Semicha Type

### Semicha Be'ba'alim

The conceptual crux of Rabbi Shimon's objection is the distinction between *semicha be'ba'alim* and other forms of hand-laying. Ordinary *semicha* is an act of ownership and identification: the *ba'al* presses both hands on the head of his offering, expressing that this animal represents him and goes in his stead. The prohibition against designating a *shaliach* to perform one's *semicha* flows directly from this: *semicha* is inherently personal and cannot be delegated. The act that Aharon performs on the *se'ir hamishtalach*, by contrast, is one of confession and transference of sin — *vehitvada alav et kol avonot bnei Yisrael*. That the physical gesture resembles ordinary *semicha* does not make it halakhically equivalent.

### Aharon Representative

Rabbi Yehuda counters with a pointed response: *af zeh Aharon uvanav miskapprim bo* — Aharon and his sons are themselves among those atoned for by the *se'ir hamishtalach*. Thus, even if the goat formally belongs to all of Israel, Aharon is not acting as a mere functionary or *shaliach*. He is among the *ba'alim* — one of the owners in the sense that he is one of those whose sins are being atoned for. He represents the community not merely as its agent but as one of its members, and that membership gives his act the character of *semicha be'ba'alim*.

### Yirmiya Synthesis

Rabbi Yirmiya observes that this dispute is not isolated: *v'azdu l'ta'amayhu* — both Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda are following their respective positions as known from elsewhere. The disagreement about whether Aharon's act on the *se'ir hamishtalach* constitutes *semicha be'ba'alim* is a downstream consequence of a deeper disagreement about the structure of atonement on Yom Kippur, which each *tanna* applies consistently across multiple contexts.

### Shevuot Baraita

A *baraita* from Masechet Shevuot is then cited to illuminate this deeper disagreement. The *baraita* interprets the sequence of verses at the end of the Yom Kippur service:

> וְכִפֶּר אֶת מִקְדַּשׁ הַקֹּדֶשׁ וְאֶת אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד וְאֶת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ יְכַפֵּר וְעַל הַכֹּהֲנִים וְעַל כָּל עַם הַקָּהָל יְכַפֵּר

The *baraita* parses each phrase: *mikdash hakodesh* — this is the *lifnai v'lifnim*, the inner sanctum; *ohel moed* — this is the *heichal*, where the blood was sprinkled on the *paroches*; *hamizbe'ach* — this is straightforwardly the golden altar. The initial phrase *vekipper* thus covers the atonement of the *mikdash* itself through the blood sprinklings. Then the verse continues: *yechapper al hakohanim v'al kol am hakahal yechapper*. This final *yechapper* refers to the *azaros* — the Temple courtyards, even where no blood sprinkling took place, which are also purified through the service. And then: *kohanim kemashma'an* — the *kohanim* are the *kohanim*; *kol am hakahal* — these are *yisrael*; and the additional *yechapper* explicitly includes the *levi'im*, who might otherwise have been subsumed within *yisrael*. The conclusion of this *baraita* according to Rabbi Yehuda is: *hushvu kulam l'kappara achat shemiskapprim b'se'ir hamishtalach* — all of them — *kohanim*, *yisrael*, and *levi'im* — are equated in receiving one atonement, namely the *se'ir hamishtalach*.

---

## R. Shimon Parallel

### Par-Se'ir Parallel

Rabbi Shimon's position is structured around a precise and elegant parallelism between the ox and the goat of Yom Kippur. His formulation is: *keshem shedam se'ir hane'aseh bifnim mechapper al Yisrael al tumat mikdash v'kodashav, kach dam hapar mechapper al hakohanim al tumat mikdash v'kodashav* — just as the blood of the goat done on the inside atones for Israel for *tumat mikdash v'kodashav*, so the blood of the ox atones for the *kohanim* for *tumat mikdash v'kodashav*. The ox — the *par* on which Aharon performs *semicha* and recites *viduy* — is the exclusive property of the priestly atonement process, not a communal offering in the usual sense. The Torah's statement that Aharon brings atonement for himself and his household and all the congregation of Israel is understood as describing two separate tracks operating in parallel, not a single unified atonement.

### Viduy Division

The parallelism extends to *viduy* and the atonement for all other sins. Rabbi Shimon continues: *keshem sheviduy shel se'ir hamishtalach mechapper al Yisrael b'she'ar aveiros, kach viduy shel par mechapper al hakohanim b'she'ar aveiros* — just as the *viduy* recited over the *se'ir hamishtalach* atones for Israel for sins other than *tumat mikdash*, so the *viduy* recited over the *par* atones for the *kohanim* for their other sins. The logic maps neatly: the two goats together form a single *korban* for Israel — one goat's blood goes *bifnim* for *tumat mikdash*, the other is sent to *azazel* with the *viduy* for *she'ar aveiros*. The *par* serves the same dual function for the *kohanim*: its blood goes *bifnim* for their *tumat mikdash*, and the *viduy* accompanying it covers their other transgressions. There is no separate *korban* carrying the *kohanim's* sins in the *she'ar aveiros* category; their *par* does double duty.

This is not merely a technical claim about how atonement is allocated. It reflects a principled reading of the Torah's structure: *ume'es adas bnei Yisrael yikach shnei se'irei izzim l'chatat* — the two goats are taken from the community and are for the community, while the *par* is explicitly Aharon's. The *viduy* on the *se'ir hamishtalach* is therefore not Aharon's *viduy* as one of the atoned; it is the *kohen's* functional act performed on behalf of *yisrael's* offering. From Rabbi Shimon's standpoint, this disqualifies it as *semicha be'ba'alim*.

One might ask why Rabbi Shimon would insist on separating the *kohanim* from the rest of Israel even for *she'ar aveiros* — general sins seemingly unrelated to their priestly function. A possible way of understanding this is that in the Torah's conception, all human sin generates a kind of metaphysical *tumah* that penetrates the *mikdash* — *lo titam'u bahem* applies even to sins like *ma'achalos assuros* or *arayos*. The verse at the end of the Yom Kippur section says *hashochen itam betoch tum'osam* — God manages to dwell among Israel even amidst the *tumah* they generate, and the Yom Kippur service makes this possible. If that is so, then the *kohanim*, who are more centrally embedded in the *mikdash*, may generate a qualitatively more penetrating *tumah* through their sins. Their atonement therefore requires a more interior track — one that parallels the interior sprinkling of blood — even for general sins.

### Equality Question

Having articulated this parallel structure, the *gemara* presses Rabbi Shimon: does the *pasuk* not explicitly equate *kohanim*, *yisrael*, and *levi'im* in a single atonement — *v'al hakohanim v'al kol am hakahal yechapper*? If the verse places them all in one category, how can Rabbi Shimon insist that their atonements come through different vehicles?

### Each Group Atoned

The resolution is concise and precise: *hushvu — dibnei kappara ninhu. Mihu, kol chad vechad mechapper bidnafshei* — yes, they are equated in the sense that all of them are atoned for. But the atonement of each comes through its own channel. The verse affirms that everyone receives *kappara*; it does not demand that the *kappara* come through a single mechanism. Rabbi Shimon reads the verse as guaranteeing the outcome — everyone is atoned — while leaving the structure of how each group achieves that atonement to be derived from elsewhere.

---

## Tumaa Comparison

### R. Yehuda Tumaa

The *gemara* now sharpens the contrast between the two positions. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the differentiation between *kohanim* and *yisrael* applies only in the domain of *tumat mikdash v'kodashav*. There, *yisrael* is atoned for through the blood of the goat done on the inside, while the *kohanim* are atoned for through the blood of the ox. In this one domain their paths diverge. But for *she'ar aveiros* — all other sins — *elu va'elu miskapprim beviduy se'ir hamishtalach*: both groups are equally atoned for through the *viduy* of the *se'ir hamishtalach*, with no differentiation.

This view has an internal attractiveness. When it comes to *tumat mikdash*, one can understand why the *kohanim* would require a distinct atonement: they are the ones who work in the *mikdash*, they are more deeply implicated in its *tumah*, and perhaps their culpability in this particular domain is categorically different. But for general sins, the egalitarian position seems more intuitive — we are all sinners before God, *kohen* and *yisrael* alike, and the communal atonement of the *se'ir hamishtalach* reaches everyone.

### R. Shimon All Cases

Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, maintains the separation across all categories. Even for *she'ar aveiros*, the *kohanim's* atonement comes through the *viduy* of the *par*, not through the *se'ir hamishtalach*. The two goats are entirely for Israel; the ox is entirely for the *kohanim*. This parallel structure is complete and admits of no exceptions.

### Source Confirmation

The *gemara* confirms this disagreement from the *baraita* in Shevuot: *echad Yisrael v'echad kohanim v'echad kohen mashiach* — all receive atonement for *tumat mikdash v'kodashav*. The *baraita* then asks what distinguishes them: *ella she'dam hapar mechapper al hakohanim al tumat mikdash v'kodashav divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — the only distinction, according to Rabbi Yehuda, is that the blood of the ox atones for the *kohanim* for *tumat mikdash*, while the blood of the goat does so for *yisrael*. Beyond that, they share equally in the atonement of the *se'ir hamishtalach*. Rabbi Shimon's position, as the *baraita* in Shevuot continues, extends the parallel to *she'ar aveiros* as well: *keshem shedam se'ir hane'aseh bifnim mechapper al Yisrael... kach dam hapar mechapper al hakohanim... keshem sheviduyo shel se'ir hamishtalach mechapper al Yisrael, kach viduyo shel par mechapper al hakohanim*.

This disagreement now clarifies why Rabbi Shimon cannot include the *se'ir hamishtalach* in his list of communal sacrifices that require *semicha be'ba'alim*. For Rabbi Shimon, Aharon's act on the *se'ir hamishtalach* is the act of a *kohen* performing a ritual function for Israel's offering — not the act of a *ba'al* connecting to his own sacrifice. Since the *se'ir hamishtalach* belongs entirely to *yisrael* and Aharon's atonement comes through the *par*, Aharon is not among the *ba'alim* of the *se'ir hamishtalach* for Rabbi Shimon's purposes, and his *semicha* on it cannot qualify as *semicha be'ba'alim*.

---

## Avodas Kochavim

### Yehuda Excludes

The *gemara* now turns to the question of why Rabbi Yehuda excludes the *se'irei avodas kochavim* from *semicha*. A *baraita* is cited: *v'samchu ziknei ha'edah et yedeihem al rosh hapar* — this verse from Parshat Vayikra, describing the *semicha* on the ox of the standard *par he'elem davar shel tzibbur*, is read by Rabbi Yehuda as establishing that the ox specifically requires *semicha*: *par ta'un semiha v'ein se'irei avodas kochavim te'unim semicha divrei Rabbi Yehuda*. The explicit mention of *semicha* by the *par* implicitly excludes the goat that accompanies the sin-offering for communal *avodah zarah*, even though that goat is part of the same general category of *par he'elem davar*. When *beis din* errs on the matter of *avodah zarah*, the offering includes both an ox and a goat, but only the ox carries *semicha*.

### Shimon Chai

Rabbi Shimon's source for excluding the *se'irei avodas kochavim* from the *semicha* performed by Aharon — while simultaneously including them in a different kind of *semicha* — comes from a different *pasuk* entirely. The verse describing Aharon's act on Yom Kippur reads:

> וְסָמַךְ אַהֲרֹן אֶת שְׁתֵּי יָדָיו עַל רֹאשׁ הַשָּׂעִיר הַחַי וְהִתְוַדָּה עָלָיו אֶת כָּל עֲוֹנוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל

The phrase *al rosh hase'ir hachai* — on the head of the *living* goat — teaches, according to Rabbi Shimon, that it is specifically this living goat that receives this particular form of *semicha*: *chai ta'un semiha b'Aharon v'ein se'irei avodas kochavim te'unim semicha b'Aharon*. The *se'irei avodas kochavim* receive *semicha*, but not the *semicha* performed by Aharon — rather, they receive the *semicha* of the *zekeinim*, *semicha be'ba'alim*. This is the second exception Rabbi Shimon lists alongside the *par he'elem davar*.

### Sheshes Challenge

At this point the *gemara* encounters an apparent contradiction. When responding to the *pasuk* of the *par he'elem davar*, Rabbi Shimon had said that the *se'irei avodas kochavim* receive *semicha* with the *kohanim*. But now, responding to the *pasuk* of the *se'ir hachai*, he says they receive it with the *zekeinim*. These two statements cannot both be correct. Rav Sheshes, before even addressing the contradiction, questions whether the first *baraita* is reliable at all: *v'tisbara deha kammaita metaretzta hi?* — Is the first *baraita* even internally coherent? Given that Rabbi Shimon consistently emphasizes *semicha be'ba'alim* and is skeptical of any *semicha* not performed by genuine owners, it would be strange for him to say that the *kohanim* perform *semicha* on the goat for *avodah zarah*. The *kohanim* are not the *ba'alim* of that offering in any obvious sense. The first *baraita* is therefore suspect on its own terms.

### Corrected Reading

The corrected reading of the two *baraisos* proceeds as follows. The first *baraita* records only Rabbi Yehuda's position: *par ta'un semicha v'ein se'irei avodas kochavim te'unim semicha divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — the ox requires *semicha*, and the goats of *avodas kochavim* do not. Rabbi Shimon does not respond to the *par* at all in this context. Instead, in the second *baraita*, Rabbi Shimon responds from his own *pasuk* — *chai ta'un semicha b'Aharon v'ein se'irei avodas kochavim te'unim semicha b'Aharon ella b'zekenim* — the living goat gets *semicha* through Aharon, and the goats of *avodas kochavim* do not get the *semicha* of Aharon; they get the *semicha* of the elders. The *gemara* then articulates precisely what Rabbi Shimon is saying to Rabbi Yehuda: *se'irei avodas kochavim ba'u semicha* — the goats for *avodah zarah* do require *semicha*. If you have a tradition that they do not, that tradition is about the specific *semicha* of Aharon; it does not mean they receive no *semicha* at all. The *miyut* — the limiting teaching — derives from *hachai*, and what it limits is the *semicha* of Aharon, not the institution of *semicha* altogether. The goats of *avodas kochavim* receive *semicha be'ba'alim* performed by the *zekenim*, and that is precisely their *semicha* — a genuine *semicha* of owners, not a priestly act of transference.

---

## Nasi Offering Source

### Yehuda Nasi

The *gemara* now asks: from where does Rabbi Shimon derive that the *se'irei avodas kochavim* require *semicha* in the first place? The derivation is traced to a *baraita* interpreting a *pasuk* from the section in Parshat Vayikra dealing with the *nasi* who sins:

> וְסָמַךְ אֶת יָדוֹ עַל רֹאשׁ הַשָּׂעִיר

The *nasi* who unintentionally violates one of God's commandments brings a male goat as a *chatat*, and he performs *semicha* on its head. The *baraita* presents the debate over what the phrase *al rosh hase'ir* — rather than the simpler *al rosho* — comes to include. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the additional specification of *hase'ir* serves to include the goat of *nachshon* — that is, the goats brought by the *nesi'im* at the *chanukas hamishkan*, the dedication of the Tabernacle. Each *nasi* brought, among other offerings, *se'ir izim echad l'chatat* — a goat as a *chatat*. The need for a *pasuk* here is non-trivial: the *chatat* brought by the *nesi'im* was *hora'as sha'ah*, a temporary exceptional ruling, since one ordinarily cannot voluntarily bring a *chatat*; a *chatat* is brought only for an inadvertent sin. Since this *chatat* was exceptional in its origin, one might have thought that *semicha* would not apply to it. The *pasuk* by the *nasi* comes to include even this exceptional case within the requirement of *semicha*.

### Shimon HaSe'ir

Rabbi Shimon reads the same phrase differently. He does not apply it to the *nesi'im's* offering at the *chanukas hamishkan*. Rather, he reads *al rosh hase'ir* as including the goats for *avodah zarah* — *lerabot se'irei avodas kochavim lismicha*. The definite article, signaling that *this* goat's head (not simply *its* head) is specified, points toward an additional goat in a different context that also requires *semicha*. For Rabbi Shimon, that additional goat is the *se'ir* of communal *avodah zarah*.

### Blood Inside Rule

Rabbi Shimon is recorded as having a general principle: *kol chatat shenichnas damah lifnim te'una semicha* — any *chatat* whose blood is brought inside the sanctuary requires *semicha*. This functions as a *siman*, a mnemonic, helping identify which offerings carry the requirement. The offerings whose blood enters the inner sanctuary include the *par he'elem davar shel tzibbur*, the *par* and *se'ir* of Yom Kippur, and the *se'irei avodas kochavim*. However, this rule is not a precise halakhic derivation; it is explicitly acknowledged to be *simana be'alma* — a memory device rather than the source of the law.

---

## Why Not Se'ir

### Why Avodas Kochavim

The *gemara* immediately presses the obvious question: if Rabbi Shimon is learning from the *pasuk* of the *nasi* that a certain additional goat requires *semicha*, why does he apply this to the *se'irei avodas kochavim* rather than to the *se'ir hane'aseh bifnim* — the goat whose blood is brought inside on Yom Kippur? That goat is a *korban tzibbur* with no *semicha*, and it too involves blood brought inside. Why not extend the derivation there?

### Specific Known Sin

The answer lies in the character of the *nasi's* offering. The *se'ir* of the *nasi* atones for a specific, known *aveirah* — the *nasi* sinned intentionally enough to recognize he did something wrong and now brings his *chatat* for it. The *se'irei avodas kochavim* similarly atone for a specific, identified sin — the community committed *avodah zarah* knowingly in the sense that the *beis din's* ruling was acted upon, and the nature of that sin is defined. The *se'ir* brought on Yom Kippur for *tumat mikdash*, by contrast, atones for a type of *tumah* that was committed unknowingly — the person was unaware that *tumah* had occurred. This puts it in a categorically different position from the *nasi's* offering, and the analogy therefore does not extend to it.

### Two Semichos Limit

The *gemara* then returns to Ravina's statement that there is a tradition of *shtei semichot b'tzibbur* — exactly two cases where the community performs *semicha*. Given this tradition, once Rabbi Shimon has the *par he'elem davar* as the first exception, he needs exactly one more. But without the limiting function of the *pasuk*, one might have argued for additional exceptions: the *se'ir hane'aseh bifnim* of Yom Kippur, or perhaps *zivchei shalmei tzibbur* — communal peace offerings — via a *kal vachomer* from individual *shelamim*. The tradition that there are only two cases therefore does real limiting work by capping the number. At the same time, the tradition alone would not tell us which goat fills the second slot.

### Pasuk Tradition

The *pasuk* and the tradition thus function together. The tradition tells us there are exactly two, preventing the inclusion of additional candidates. The *pasuk* from the *nasi's* offering — read through the lens of *dumya d'se'ir nasi d'mechapper al aveiras mitzva yedu'a* — tells us which specific goat fills the second slot: the *se'ir* for communal *avodah zarah*, not the *se'ir hane'aseh bifnim* of Yom Kippur and not *shalmei tzibbur*. The *gemara* concludes: without the tradition, we would know one more case is required but not which one; without the *pasuk*, we would know the number but have no basis for identifying the specific case. Together, they produce Rabbi Shimon's complete position.

---

## Conclusion Principles

### Semicha Nature

The *sugya* of Menachot 92a revolves around two interlocking conceptual questions. The first is the nature of *semicha* itself: what is it expressing, and who is qualified to perform it? The *sugya* consistently treats *semicha* as fundamentally an act of ownership and personal identification — the *ba'al* connects himself to his offering, declaring that this animal represents him. This is why the heir (*yoresh*) can perform *semicha*: he has genuinely inherited ownership. It is why a *shaliach* cannot: ownership cannot be delegated. And it is why ordinary *korbanot tzibbur* are exempt: the diffuse collective ownership of the community does not crystallize into the kind of identifiable personal ownership that *semicha* requires. The exceptional cases — the *par he'elem davar*, the *se'irei avodas kochavim* according to Rabbi Shimon — are exceptions precisely because the *beis din* or *zekenim* stand in a sufficiently defined ownership relationship to those specific offerings.

### Division Atonement

The second conceptual question is whether the atonement of *yom kippur* treats *kohanim* and *yisrael* as a single undifferentiated community or as two distinct groups each requiring its own track of atonement. Rabbi Yehuda takes the more egalitarian position: for *tumat mikdash*, their atonements diverge by necessity, but for general sins they converge in the *se'ir hamishtalach*. Aharon performing *semicha* on the *se'ir hamishtalach* is therefore *semicha be'ba'alim*, because he too is atoned through it. Rabbi Shimon draws a complete parallel: the two goats of Israel and the one ox of the *kohanim* each operate as fully independent atonement systems, covering both *tumat mikdash* and *she'ar aveiros* for their respective constituencies. Aharon's act on the *se'ir hamishtalach* is therefore a priestly function, not an owner's act. These two disagreements — the conceptual nature of *semicha* and the structure of Yom Kippur atonement — are thus not independent. As Rabbi Yirmiya observes, each *tanna* applies his position consistently, and the dispute about *semicha* on the *se'ir hamishtalach* is the direct and necessary consequence of their deeper disagreement about how the Yom Kippur service is structured.

---

---

# Menachot 93

## Semichah on Korbanot

### Communal & Individual

The daf begins at the bottom of 92b, where the Mishnah turns from the various questions of measure to the laws of semichah — the act of laying hands upon the korban. The Mishnah states: *kol korbanos hayachid te'unin semichah* — all individual korbanot require semichah. We had already learned that communal korbanot are essentially two: the par for helam davar, when the beis din rules incorrectly, and then there is a debate as to whether the second is the goat brought for avodah zarah when beis din rules incorrectly, or the goat for azazel on Yom Kippur. The act of semichah on the se'ir hamishtale'ach is something we recall every Yom Kippur in the Mussaf avodah, though the question of whether it constitutes classic semichah turns on whether the kohanim themselves are considered part-owners of that korban.

The Mishnah now turns to individual korbanot, stating that all require semichah — the chatas, the asham, the olah, the shelamim — with the exception of the bechor, ma'aser, and pesach. This is a striking exception. The excluded three are obligatory korbanot, yet they fall into a kind of intermediate category: they are obligatory, but they are kodshim kalim. The chatas and asham, also obligatory, do require semichah. The free-will korbanot — olah and shelamim — also require it. Only these three fall between the cracks.

### Mishnah Overview

The Gemara proceeds through a baraita: *korbano* — the possessive form, "his korban" — is written three times in the context of semichah by shelamim, and each instance is understood as an exclusionary term. The Torah says *v'samach yado al rosh korbano* — he shall place his hand on the head of his korban — and the possessive ו signals that it refers to some offerings but not all.

From the first *korbano*: not the bechor. From the second: not ma'aser. From the third: not the pesach.

### Textual Exclusions

Before accepting the exclusions, the baraita presents kal vachomer arguments that would have argued for including each of these three. Regarding the bechor: since shelamim — which do not possess intrinsic sanctity from the womb — require semichah, the bechor, whose sanctity begins from the moment of birth without any act of designation, all the more so should require semichah. The Torah therefore writes *korbano* to exclude it.

Regarding ma'aser: shelamim do not sanctify the animals before and after them in the counting, yet require semichah. The ma'aser, however, does sanctify the animals on either side of it — if the counter errs and designates number nine or number eleven as the tenth, those animals also acquire the sanctity of ma'aser. Given this greater sanctifying power, one might have thought ma'aser should certainly require semichah. The Torah therefore writes *korbano* again to exclude it.

Regarding the pesach: shelamim, which are a free-will offering, require semichah. The pesach, which is obligatory — *b'amud v'haya* — all the more so should require semichah. Yet the Torah writes *korbano* a third time to exclude it.

### Kal Vachomer

The logic of the exclusions calls for explanation. It is not simply a matter of obligatory versus free-will korbanot, because semichah is performed on the chatas and asham, which are obligatory. Indeed, the entire act of semichah on Yom Kippur — where the kohen lays his hands on the korban and recites the viduy — is the paradigmatic example of semichah on an obligatory offering. So what is the principle?

Rashi, in a very compressed comment near the bottom of the page, explains: *korbano* — written three times in the context of semichah by shelamim — teaches that semichah applies to a korban *she'ba l'shum ritzui v'doron*, one that comes as an expression of appeasement or as a gift to God. The bechor, ma'aser, and pesach are excluded because *she'einam ba'im l'ritzui* — they are not coming as voluntary expressions of relationship — *ela chova heim alav* — they are pure obligations — and furthermore *v'lo l'kapara* — they do not serve an atoning function.

This points toward the deeper meaning of semichah. One might initially have thought that semichah is simply a formal act of identification — placing one's hands on the animal to establish that this is one's korban. But if that were its entire purpose, there would be no reason ever to exempt anything, since one always wishes to identify the korban as one's own. The fact that there are exemptions suggests that semichah is conceptualized differently.

What accompanies semichah by a chatas? Viduy — verbal confession. The act of laying hands while reciting the viduy is an act of designating the purpose of the korban: this animal is connected to my sins, it is being brought to atone for what I have done. That is the personal, specific dimension of semichah. By the shelamim and the olah, even when one is not atoning, there is something personal being expressed — one is choosing to give this offering, and the semichah moment is an opportunity to articulate what one wishes to express through the giving.

The bechor, ma'aser, and pesach fall into neither category. They are not atoning offerings where one could confess specific sins. Nor are they chosen gifts where one expresses something personal. Every Jew is obligated to give these. One does what the Torah commands, but there is no specific personal dimension to it. This, it seems, is the logic underlying Rashi's formulation.

### Ma'aser Logic

Although this understanding does not appear explicitly in the Gemara, the Rambam develops a strikingly parallel idea. He writes *yeira'eh li* — it would seem to me — that when bringing a shelamim one should also recite a verbal declaration. This is remarkable: the Rambam is introducing, without direct Talmudic backing, the principle that every korban requires some form of verbal declaration at the moment of semichah to designate its function.

What precisely does one say? For a chatas or asham, the Rambam specifies: *chatasi, avisi, pashati, v'asisi kach v'kach, v'chazarti b'teshuvah lefanecha, v'zu kaparasi* — I have sinned, transgressed, committed iniquity, done such-and-such, I have returned in teshuvah before You, and this is my atonement. Notably, the Rambam incorporates teshuvah into the formula of the korban, which is theologically significant. For the shelamim, he says *yeira'eh li* — it appears to me — that one does not recite viduy but does recite *divrei shevach*, words of praise and thanksgiving.

The Rambam's formulation strongly supports the understanding that semichah is fundamentally about designating the personal meaning and function of the korban. This is precisely what is lacking — and therefore not required — by bechor, ma'aser, and pesach. There is nothing personal to declare.

## Logic of Exclusions

### Pesach Exclusion

The Gemara now raises a challenge to the entire structure of the kal vachomer exclusions. One could ask: why was there ever a basis to apply semichah to the bechor, ma'aser, and pesach in the first place? These korbanot cannot simply be extended from shelamim, since shelamim is distinctively different — it requires nesachim, the wine libation and mincha, and the waving of the chazeh and shok. Perhaps semichah was always unique to shelamim and those korbanot explicitly included alongside it, and there was never a basis for extending it to the others.

The Gemara accepts this point: *kra asmachto be'alma* — the verses excluding bechor, ma'aser, and pesach are merely asmachta; one would never have thought to apply semichah to them from a kal vachomer in the first place. If so, what work is the word *korbano* actually doing?

### Rashi's View

The Gemara answers: *korbano velo korban chaveiro* — his korban and not the korban of another. One may not perform semichah on someone else's korban; the act must be performed by the owner on his own offering. Additionally, *korbano velo korban oved kochavim* — a non-Jew's korban does not require semichah. As is noted, this is not entirely distinct from the exclusion of *korban chaveiro*, since the assumption that a non-Jew does not enter the Azara — though this is only a rabbinic restriction — would mean that any non-Jew's korban would necessarily be brought by someone else, making the problem of performing semichah on another's korban automatic. The separate derivation is nevertheless needed according to the logic of the Gemara.

### Viduy & Declaration

A third use of *korbano* is the phrase *korbano lerabot kol ba'alei korban lisemichah* — if a korban is owned in partnership, the question of semichah becomes complex. When two people jointly bring an olah or shelamim — though one cannot bring a chatas in partnership — how does semichah work? This phrase is ambiguous. It could mean that any one partner may perform semichah on behalf of the group, analogous to what we saw with the kohen gadol performing semichah on behalf of all of Klal Yisrael by the se'ir hamishtale'ach. Or it could mean the opposite: no individual can represent the group, and all partners must perform semichah themselves. The Gemara will clarify this on 93b.

## Korbano Exclusions

### Question Raised

The Mishnah continues: *hayoresh somech* — an heir who inherits a korban may perform semichah on it. The scenario is one where, for example, a person's father died and left him a sanctified animal. By a chatas this question does not arise, since if the owner dies the chatas is left to die. But by an asham, if the owner dies and the animal had been set aside to graze until it develops a blemish, and it was then inadvertently slaughtered, it functions as an olah — and on an olah semichah is performed. The Mishnah rules that in such cases the heir performs semichah.

### Asmachta Only

Rabbi Chanina taught a version of this teaching before Rava with the opposite ruling: *yoresh eino somech, yoresh eino meimir* — an heir does not perform semichah, and an heir cannot make temurah. Rava challenged him: but our Mishnah explicitly says *hayoresh somech*! Rabbi Chanina asked: should I reverse my version? Rava replied: no — do not reverse it. Your version represents the position of Rabbi Yehudah, and the two texts represent a genuine dispute between tanna'im.

The baraita itself is explicit: the first opinion holds that an heir performs semichah and makes temurah; Rabbi Yehudah says the heir does neither.

### Korbano Teachings

What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehudah? He learns from the same word *korbano* — his korban, not his father's korban. The heir has inherited the animal as property, but the korban does not fully belong to him in the relevant sense. It is not the korban he sanctified; it is not connected to any personal obligation of his own. He therefore lacks sufficient connection to perform semichah, which is fundamentally about personal relationship to the offering.

Rabbi Yehudah then adds a structural argument: *u'tchilat hekdesh misof hekdesh* — we learn the beginning of the process of kedushah from its end. The end of the process is semichah, and we have established that an heir cannot perform semichah. Therefore, at the beginning of the process — the act of transferring kedushah through temurah — the heir likewise cannot do so. The heir's inability to perform semichah reflects his insufficient connection to the kedushah of the korban, and that same insufficiency means his attempt to make temurah is ineffective.

### Heir Dispute

Tosafot raises an objection: there are many ways in which the beginning and end of the process of kedushah differ, so how can we simply derive one from the other? Tosafot answers that this is not an arbitrary structural parallel. The point is not merely that what applies at the end applies at the beginning or vice versa. Rather, the question being asked in both cases is identical: are you considered the owner of this korban in the relevant sense?

This is the heart of the matter. The heir has inherited a piece of property. In monetary terms, he is the owner. But the kedushah of this animal — its sanctity as a korban, its identity as a designated offering — is something he did not create and to which he has no intrinsic link. The question of whether the heir can perform semichah and the question of whether his temurah is effective are both expressions of the same underlying question: does the heir's proprietorship over the animal extend to its status as a korban? Rabbi Yehudah says no; the chachamim say yes.

### R. Yehudah View

The chachamim derive their position differently. The Torah uses the double language *hemir yamir* — if he shall make temurah — and this amplified formulation is understood as inclusive, extending to include even the heir: *lerabot et hayoresh*. If the heir can make temurah, we reverse the direction of the learning: *v'yalif sof hekdesh mi'tchilat hekdesh* — we learn the end of the process from the beginning. Since at the beginning of the process the heir counts as an owner sufficient to make temurah, so too at the end of the process — at semichah — the heir performs semichah.

For Rabbi Yehudah's part, the double language of *hemir yamir* is needed for a different purpose entirely. Since Rabbi Yehudah does not learn from it that the heir can make temurah, he must use that language to teach the inclusion of women in the laws of temurah — as the Gemara will now explain.

## Heir Debate

### Tchilat from Sof

The entire parshah of temurah is written in the masculine. One might therefore have thought that women are excluded from the prohibition and its effects — that if a woman attempts to make temurah, it would neither be prohibited nor effective.

### Ownership Concept

The Gemara brings a baraita that asks directly: since the entire subject is discussed in masculine language, how do we include women? The answer is the double language *hemir yamir* — according to Rabbi Yehudah, it is this amplified formulation that includes women. The chachamim, however, derive the inclusion of women from *ve'im*, the word "if" that introduces the verse — the additional letter ו serving as a ribui to include women.

### Rabbis Counter

This raises an obvious question: the Torah almost universally uses masculine language, and we routinely assume women are included unless explicitly excluded. Why would we need a special derivation here to include women in temurah?

Tosafot addresses this by citing the Gemara in Temurah: the reason is that temurah is not universally applicable. There is no temurah by communal korbanot, and there is no temurah by korbanot owned in partnership. Since the prohibition and its effects are not applied universally across all cases, one might have been inclined to read the masculine language more restrictively — perhaps this too is a case where it does not apply, and women are excluded. The double language or the word *ve'im* therefore comes to explicitly include women, establishing that even though temurah is not universal, when a woman attempts it, she is prohibited and the act takes effect.

## Who Does Semichah

### Verse Resolution

The Mishnah turns from which korbanot require semichah to who may perform it. The list of those excluded is: the cheresh, shoteh, and katan; the blind person; the non-Jew; the slave; the agent; and the woman. The Mishnah then adds several important qualifications: semichah is *she'yarei mitzvah* — the remnant of the mitzvah, meaning that its omission does not disqualify the korban. It must be performed *al harosh*, on the head of the animal; with both hands; in the place where the shechita will occur; and the shechita must immediately follow.

### Women & Temurah

The Gemara identifies the underlying principle uniting the exclusions: *korbano velo korban chaveiro* — it must be his own korban, not another's. The entire list — slave, agent, woman — is read by the Gemara as referring not to these individuals performing semichah on their own korbanot, but to whether any of them may serve as a substitute for the owner, performing semichah on the owner's behalf. The answer in every case is no. The personal connection between the owner and the korban is what semichah expresses, and that cannot be delegated.

### Mishnah List

The Gemara begins with the cheresh, shoteh, and katan: *bilshama Cheresh Shoteh ve'Katan de'lav bnei de'ah ninhu* — these are not people of intellect, and therefore their exclusion is self-evident. This, however, raises a deeper question. If semichah were merely a formal ritual act — analogous to, say, placing an object — there would be no obvious reason to disqualify those lacking mental capacity, provided the physical act was performed. The fact that they are excluded points precisely to semichah being something more. The connection being forged between the person and the korban requires mental engagement; it is not a bare physical gesture.

This is illustrated by considering the scenario where someone sanctifies a korban and then loses mental capacity. Even if the korban could theoretically be brought in that state, semichah would not be appropriate — not because the person is exempt from mitzvot in that state, but because semichah is about an active, conscious connection to the korban. The question of whether a korban brought on behalf of a mentally incapacitated person achieves kapparah in some technical sense is a separate and interesting one, but semichah in any case requires the person to be *bnei de'ah*. The Gemara takes this for granted.

### Shiyrei Mitzvah

The non-Jew's exclusion from semichah is derived from the verse at the opening of Vayikra — *daber el bnei yisrael* — which restricts the obligation of semichah to the children of Israel: *bnei yisrael somchin ve'ein ovdei kochavim somchin*.

### Mental Capacity

The exclusion of the blind person requires derivation, and two amoraim dispute its source. One holds: *atya semicha semicha mi'Ziknei ha'Edah* — we derive the law of semichah by a gezeirah shavah from the elders who perform semichah by the par helam davar. Since members of the Sanhedrin cannot be blind, and those elders perform semichah, we apply that restriction to semichah performed by individuals.

The other holds: *atya semicha semicha mi'Olat Re'iyah* — we derive it from the korban of the olat re'iyah, the obligatory olah brought on the three regalim. The Gemara there makes the famous drasha: *yireh yira'eh* — just as it says you shall appear before God, so too you must be able to see. *keshem sheba'im leira'ot kach ba'im lirot* — just as they come to be seen, so they come to see. One who is blind, even in one eye, is exempt from olat re'iyah, and therefore exempt from the semichah associated with it. By extension, this restriction on semichah applies universally.

It is worth noting that the simple reading of the pasuk is actually *yireh et pnei Hashem Elokecha*, where *et* marks the object of the verb — meaning the person does the seeing of God's presence. The more anthropomorphic implication prompted the traditional reading as *yira'eh* — he shall appear. The drasha in a sense restores the plain meaning: the verse really does speak of the person seeing, and that requires sight.

The Gemara then explains the reasoning of each position. The one who learns from the olat re'iyah prefers it because *danin yachid miyachid* — we prefer to derive laws governing individual korbanot from other individual korbanot rather than from the communal par helam davar. The one who learns from the elders of the Sanhedrin prefers it because the par helam davar explicitly mentions semichah in the text itself, whereas the olat re'iyah never explicitly mentions semichah — it must first be derived that semichah applies to olat re'iyah at all (from the verse *va'ya'aseh ka'mishpat* — he did it according to the law of the free-will olah), making it an indirect source for a law about semichah. The elders source, by contrast, speaks of semichah directly.

Tosafot notes a difficulty: in neither the case of the Sanhedrin nor the case of olat re'iyah do we derive any other legal criteria from these contexts. We do not require that those performing semichah be eligible for Sanhedrin membership in other respects, nor do we extend all the criteria of olat re'iyah to all semichah. Only this one criterion — vision — is derived. Tosafot does not offer a fully satisfying resolution.

## Agent & Wife

### Blind Exclusion

The Gemara introduces a baraita that derives the exclusion of the slave, the agent, and the wife from the word *yado* — his hand. Three repetitions of *yado* in the context of semichah exclude each of these three candidates for substitution, and each exclusion requires its own derivation because each presents a distinct argument for why it might have been permitted.

### Non-Jew & Slave

*Yado* — his hand, and not the hand of his slave. A Canaanite slave is not obligated in positive time-bound commandments and is therefore not fully a bar mitzvah in the relevant sense. One who is not personally obligated in a mitzvah cannot discharge another's obligation through it. The slave therefore cannot stand in for his master.

### Shaliach Principle

*Yado* — his hand, and not the hand of his agent. Here the argument for inclusion is far stronger: the agent is a fully obligated Jew, and we have the general principle *shlucho shel adam kemoto* — a person's agent is like the person himself. One might have thought that precisely here, where we need a personal connection to the korban, the agent — who is legally the alter ego of the principal — could serve that function. The Torah therefore requires an explicit exclusion: even an agent cannot perform semichah in place of the owner.

### Wife Excluded

*Yado* — his hand, and not the hand of his wife. The argument for including the wife is even stronger than that for the agent. We sometimes speak of the wife as *kegufo damya* — as though she is his very body. If anyone might be considered an extension of the person himself for purposes of performing a deeply personal act like semichah, it would be his wife. The Torah nonetheless excludes her as well.

### Woman's Own Korban

The Gemara concludes that all three exclusions are necessary: each presents an independent argument for inclusion that the others do not. The underlying principle is absolute: *ani velo hashaliach* — I, and not my agent. Semichah must be performed by the owner himself, directly and without intermediary. No matter how close the relationship — slave, agent, or wife — the connection must be the owner's own, unmediated connection to his korban.

## Semichah & Kaparah

### Verse Analysis

The Mishnah describes semichah as *she'yarei mitzvah* — the remnant of the mitzvah. This phrase, which the Gemara also uses in connection with tenufah and similar acts, conveys that while semichah is a genuine and important mitzvah, its omission does not disqualify the korban. *be'dieved*, the korban still achieves its purpose.

### Blood & Semichah

The baraita in the Gemara probes the verse *v'samach v'nirtzah* — he shall perform semichah and it shall be accepted for him. Does semichah itself achieve the atonement? The Gemara answers: *v'halo ein kaparah ela b'dam* — atonement is achieved only through the blood, as it is written *ki hadam hu banefesh yechaper*. Semichah alone is not the vehicle of kapparah. Rather, as the Gemara explains, *ela lomar lecha* — the verse teaches that if one treated the semichah as a mere remnant of the mitzvah — that is, if one omitted it — the Torah regards it as though no atonement occurred.

### Hollow Atonement

This is a subtle but important distinction. The formal statement is that omitting semichah is treated *k'ilu lo kiper* — as if atonement was not achieved. Yet the Gemara also says *v'chiper* — technically, the bare atonement does occur. The korban is not invalidated. There are thus two levels: the full and intended atonement, which is bound up with the entire experience of semichah and its accompanying viduy; and the bare technical atonement, which is achieved by the blood even when semichah was not performed.

### Tenufah Parallel

The Gemara notes an identical formulation in the laws of tenufah, the waving of the chazeh and shok. The verse says *u'tenufah l'chaper* — the waving achieves atonement — and the same analysis applies: obviously only blood achieves atonement, so the verse must mean that if tenufah was treated as a mere remnant and omitted, it is as if no atonement occurred, though technically the korban still achieves bare atonement.

It is worth pausing to note that this parallel is somewhat surprising. Semichah, understood as the moment of personal identification and purpose-designation for the korban, carries enormous weight in the experience of offering. The tenufah — the presenting of the chazeh and shok — is important but does not carry the same central symbolic weight; it is not the defining act of the korban but rather a secondary element connected to the priestly portions. Yet the Gemara gives them precisely equal weight in terms of their status as *she'yarei mitzvah*. This sheds light on how seriously the tenufah is regarded as part of the full korban experience, even if it is not the korban's essential act.

## Semichah Details

### On Head

The Mishnah states *al harosh* — semichah must be performed on the head of the animal. The Gemara elaborates through a baraita that excludes several alternative locations.

### Sides Query

The baraita specifies: *yado al harosh v'lo yado al hatzavar* — on the head and not on the neck; *v'lo al hagabayim* — not on the back; *v'lo yado al hachazeh* — not on the chest. The Gemara asks why all three need to be excluded separately. Each exclusion addresses a different argument that might have permitted the alternative location.

Had the Torah said only *al harosh*, one might have thought it excludes the neck because the neck is not at the same plane as the head. The back, however — particularly the upper back of the neck — might have been thought to be an extension of the head and at the same plane, and therefore acceptable. A second exclusion is therefore needed for the back. And had only those two been excluded, one might have thought the chest — which is waved during the tenufah of certain korbanot — has a special elevated status and might therefore be a valid location for semichah as well. The third exclusion addresses this possibility.

### Both Hands

A further question is raised: *yado al hatzdadim mahu* — what about the sides of the head, meaning the cheeks? Do they qualify as part of the head for purposes of semichah? The Gemara resolves this from a baraita in which Abba Bira in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov states: *yado al harosh v'lo yado al hatzdadim* — on the head and not on the sides. The cheeks are excluded.

### R. Elazar Story

Rabbi Yirmiyah raises a further question: if a cloth or rag intervenes between the person's hands and the animal's head, does that constitute a valid semichah, or does it constitute a chatzitzah that invalidates the act? The answer comes from a baraita: *uvilevad shelo tehei davar chotzetz beino levein hazavach* — there must not be any intervening object between the person and the animal. The hands must touch the animal's head directly.

### Location & Timing

### Reish Lakish's Derivation: Yado in Singular Context of Semichah Means Two Hands

The Mishnah states that semichah requires both hands. Reish Lakish derives this from the verse concerning Yom Kippur: *v'samach Aharon et shtei yadav* — and Aaron shall place his two hands. The word is written *yado* in the singular, yet the full phrase is *shtei yadav* — two hands. Reish Lakish establishes a paradigm: *kol makom shene'emar yado harei kan shtayim* — wherever the Torah writes *yado* in the context of semichah, it means both hands, until the Torah explicitly specifies one hand. This is a substantial chiddush: the verse governing semichah says *v'samach yado* — his hand, singular — and from this alone one would never infer two hands. Reish Lakish's drasha reverses the intuition.

### The Story of Rabbi Elazar: Taking Credit Without Attribution

Rabbi Elazar went and taught this drasha in the beit midrash without attributing it to Reish Lakish. Reish Lakish heard of this and was angered. In response, he confronted Rabbi Elazar: if every instance of *yado* in the singular means two hands, why does the Torah ever use *yadav* in the plural? He challenged him twenty-four times the Torah uses the plural form — *yadav tevi'ena*, *yadav rav lo*, *shikel et yadav* — and why would any of those have been necessary if *yado* already implies two? Rabbi Elazar had no answer and was silent.

### Reish Lakish's Challenge: Why Does Torah Ever Use Yadav in Plural?

After Reish Lakish calmed down, he told Rabbi Elazar what he should have said: *yada d'semichah ka'amri* — my drasha applies only to semichah. It is not a universal principle that *yado* means two wherever it appears. Rather, in the specific context of semichah on animals, *yado* means two hands. This is why the Torah never needs to say *yadav* in the context of semichah on animals — *yado* is sufficient to indicate two.

### Resolution: The Drasha Applies Only to Semichah on Animals, Not Universally

The Gemara raises a further challenge: but even in the context of semichah the Torah does write *yadav* in the plural — *vayismoch et yadav alav vayitzaveihu*, when Moshe performs semichah on Yehoshua. Reish Lakish narrows the drasha still further: *semicha d'behema ka'amri* — the principle applies only to semichah performed on animals. When it is semichah on a person, the Torah does use the plural. Within the specific context of semichah on animal korbanot, however, *yado* in the singular means both hands, and the verse never needs to say *yadav* in that context.

### Semichah Shechita

### The Mishnah's Statement: Semichah Happens Where Shechita Happens

The Mishnah concludes: *uv'makom shesomchin shochtin* — in the place where semichah is performed, the shechita is performed. The Gemara asks what the Mishnah is teaching with this formulation — is it two separate rules or one?

### Immediate Succession: Shechita Follows Immediately After Semichah

The Gemara explains: *hachi ka'amar* — this is what the Mishnah means: you must perform semichah in the same location where the shechita will occur, and the reason is *shetechef l'semichah shechitah* — because the shechita must immediately follow the semichah. The location requirement and the timing requirement are therefore connected: since shechita must follow immediately, you perform semichah precisely where the shechita will take place, so that no movement of the animal is required after semichah.

### The Meaning: The Relationship Defined Through Semichah Immediately Translates to Offering

The juxtaposition of semichah and shechita is not merely procedural. Whatever relationship is being articulated through the semichah — the personal identification with the korban, the designation of its purpose, the connection of the owner to this offering — is immediately, without interruption, translated into the act of bringing the korban. The semichah defines the meaning of what is about to occur, and the shechita immediately actualizes it. The two acts together constitute a single continuous gesture: this is my korban, and now it is being offered.

---

---

# Menachot 94

## Smicha vs. Tenufa

### Smicha Weightier

The *daf* opens with a *mishnah* that systematically compares *smicha* — the pressing of hands upon a sacrifice — with *tenufa*, the ritual waving performed with certain offerings. The *mishnah* identifies ways in which each practice is more demanding than the other, and the *gemara* then unpacks the textual and logical foundations for these distinctions.

### Individual Duty

The first and central way in which *smicha* is weightier is stated in the *mishnah* itself: *shehayachid manif l'chol chaverav v'ein echad somech l'chol chaverav* — one person waves on behalf of all his partners, but no single person performs *smicha* on behalf of all his partners. When a *chabura*, a group of partners, brings a *korban* jointly, only one member of the group performs *tenufa*, whereas every individual member of the group must perform *smicha* personally. As the *gemara* will explain, the physical constraints of *tenufa* make it impossible for all partners to wave simultaneously or sequentially. *smicha*, by contrast, can be done sequentially, and each person is required to do so. This reflects the underlying character of *smicha* as an expression of personal ownership and connection to the sacrifice — an act that demands each individual's direct participation. From the *mishnah*'s framing, this universal individual requirement is presented as a stringency: *smicha* imposes a greater demand precisely because it cannot be delegated.

### Tenufa Weightier

The *mishnah* then turns to identify the ways in which *tenufa* is weightier than *smicha*.

### Tenufa Scope

*Tenufa* has a far broader scope of application. The *mishnah* states: *shetnufa noheget b'korbanos hayachid u'v'korbanos hatzibbur* — *tenufa* applies both to individual offerings and to communal offerings. Among individual offerings, one performs *tenufa* with the breast and thigh of a *shelamim*. Among communal offerings, *tenufa* is performed in the context of the *zivchei shalmei tzibbur* that accompany the *shtei halechem* on *shavuot*. Furthermore, *tenufa* is performed both with living animals — as with the lambs brought on *shavuot*, which are waved alive — and with slaughtered animals — as with the breast and thigh of every *shelamim* after *shechita*.

### Animate/Inanimate

Beyond the distinction between living and slaughtered animals, *tenufa* extends even to objects that have no life at all: *u'v'davar she'ein bo ruach chayim* — with things that possess no living spirit. This includes the breads that accompany the lambs of *shavuot*, the loaves of the *todah* offering, and, as Rashi notes, even the *nesachim*, the libation offerings that accompany the *korban*. *smicha*, by contrast, is performed only upon a living animal; it does not apply to non-living objects, nor to animals after *shechita*.

---

## Textual Sources

### Baraita Smicha

The *gemara* now proceeds to examine the textual basis for these principles, beginning with a *baraita* that addresses the rule requiring every individual owner to perform *smicha*. The *baraita* cites the verse *korbano* — "his offering" — with its emphasis on personal possession, to derive that every co-owner of a *korban* must personally perform *smicha*. The language of individual ownership, *korbano*, demands an individual act.

### Kal V'Chomer

But the *baraita* does not simply assert this conclusion — it first confronts a seemingly compelling argument in the opposite direction. One might have thought, the *baraita* reasons, that a *kal v'chomer* should lead us to the reverse conclusion. *tenufa*, which is weightier and broader in scope — applying even to *shchutim*, slaughtered animals — and yet is nonetheless restricted when it comes to a *chabura*, requiring only one person to wave on behalf of all. If *tenufa*, with its greater scope, demands only one representative from the group, then *smicha*, which is narrower and less broadly applied, should surely require no more — and perhaps even less — of each participant. By this logic, one person's *smicha* should suffice for the entire group.

This argument has genuine force. There is something counterintuitive about saying that the narrower *mitzvah* imposes a greater individual burden. Yet the *kal v'chomer* itself is what the *baraita* is setting aside, and the *mishnah*'s framing — treating universal individual participation as a *stringency* of *smicha* — reflects exactly this tension.

### Korbano Proof

The *baraita* concludes that the *kal v'chomer* is overridden by the explicit verse: *talmud lomar korbano* — the Torah's insistence on "his offering" teaches that every individual who is a co-owner of the *korban* must personally perform *smicha*. *l'rabot kol ba'alei korban l'smicha* — to include all owners of the offering in the obligation of *smicha*.

### Reverse Logic

Having established that every partner must perform *smicha*, the *baraita* then asks: can the same reasoning be extended to *tenufa*? If *smicha* — the narrower practice — requires every individual, should not *tenufa* — the broader and weightier practice — equally or even more so require every individual? The *kal v'chomer* now runs in the opposite direction: *u'ma smicha she-lo nitrabta b'shechutin*, *smicha*, which does not extend to slaughtered animals and is thus more limited in scope, nonetheless requires every individual. *tenufa*, which does extend to *shchutim* and is broader, should certainly require each individual as well.

### Chatzitza Problem

The *gemara*'s answer is striking: there is no textual rebuttal. The reason all partners do not perform *tenufa* is simply *mishum d'lo efshar* — because it is physically impossible. If all were to wave simultaneously, *havi chatzitza* — the hands of one person would interpose between another person's hand and the object being waved. *tenufa* requires direct contact with the object, and with multiple hands, that contact cannot be maintained for every participant. The possibility of sequential waving, on the model of *smicha*, is rejected for a different reason.

### Singular Form

The exclusion of sequential *tenufa* rests on a linguistic observation: *tenufa Rachmana v'lo tenufot* — the Torah uses the singular abstract noun *tenufa*, "a waving," not the plural. This indicates that only a single *tenufa* may be performed. The verb used in connection with *smicha*, by contrast, carries no such singular restriction — it is expressed as an action rather than a counted noun — and so multiple sequential acts of *smicha* are perfectly permissible.

---

## Smicha Shechutim

### Question Posed

The *gemara* now challenges the principle that *smicha* does not apply to animals after *shechita*. The challenge comes in the form of a question: *u'smicha b'shechutin leita?* — is it truly the case that *smicha* does not apply to slaughtered animals?

### Kohen Gadol Case

The *gemara* cites a *mishnah* as a potential refutation. The *mishnah* describes the procedure followed when a *kohen gadol* wished to perform the *avoda* of burning the limbs of an *olah* upon the *mizbe'ach*. The *kohen gadol* always retained the prerogative to participate in the *avoda* if he so chose, and the *mishnah* describes the ceremonial procedure that was arranged to honor him in this role.

### Relay Procedure

When the *kohen gadol* ascended the *kevesh*, the ramp leading to the *mizbe'ach*, the *segan* — the deputy *kohen gadol* — would stand at his right hand. Upon reaching the midpoint of the ramp, the *segan* would grasp the *kohen gadol*'s right hand and help him to the top, suggesting that the *kohen gadol* required assistance and that the *segan* lent him support in the manner of an honor guard.

Once at the top, an elaborate relay would unfold. The first *kohen* in the sequence would extend to the *kohen gadol* the *rosh veharegel* — the head and foot of the *olah*. The *kohen gadol* would then perform *smicha* upon them and throw them onto the fire.

### Smicha & Throwing

The second *kohen* in the sequence would then hand his portions — the two forelegs — to the first *kohen*, who in turn would pass them to the *kohen gadol*. The *kohen gadol* would again perform *smicha* and throw them onto the *mizbe'ach*. The second *kohen* would then withdraw, and the process would repeat: a third *kohen* would approach, pass his portions through the same chain, and the *kohen gadol* would perform *smicha* and throw them on. If the *kohen gadol* wished, he could perform the *smicha* himself while allowing others to do the throwing; the procedure was flexible in that regard. The result was a grand ceremonial production, with multiple *kohanim* participating in an elaborate chain, all to give honor to the *kohen gadol* in his role at the altar.

The apparent difficulty is clear: the *kohen gadol* was performing *smicha* on portions of a slaughtered animal — *shechutim* — which the principle under discussion holds to be inapplicable.

### Honor Exception

Abaye resolves the difficulty directly: *amar Abaye hatam mishum kevodo dekohen gadol* — what is described there is done purely for the honor of the *kohen gadol*. This *smicha* carries no *halachic* significance; it is not a fulfillment of any obligation, but rather a ceremonial gesture whose entire purpose is the dignity and splendor of the *kohen gadol*'s participation. The principle that *smicha* does not apply to slaughtered animals therefore remains intact.

---

## Ben Sira Account

### Emergence Glory

Before the *gemara* moves to the next *perek*, a remarkable digression is warranted. The procedure described in the *mishnah* — the *kohen gadol* ascending the ramp, receiving portions from his *kohen* brethren in a grand relay, and offering them on the *mizbe'ach* — is not only preserved in Rabbinic literature. It finds an ancient parallel in the Wisdom of Ben Sira, a work composed in the second century before the Common Era, whose fiftieth chapter contains a celebrated description of the *kohen gadol* Shimon ben Yochanan in all his glory.

The passage opens: *mah nehedar behashkifo me'ohel uvetzeito mibeit haparochet* — how glorious was he when he visited the Tent and when he emerged from the *kodesh hakodashim*.
