Ben Sira then lavishes a series of luminous comparisons upon the *kohen gadol*: like a star of light among clouds, like a full moon at the season of the festival, like the sun blazing upon the sanctuary of a king, like a rainbow seen in clouds, like a flowering branch in days of appointed times, like a lily upon flowing waters, like a flower of Lebanon in days of summer, like fire of frankincense upon the meal offering. This sequence will sound immediately familiar: the *pizmon* sung on *yom kippur*, *mah nehedar mareh Kohen Gadol betzeito mibeit Kodesh Hakodashim*, appears to draw its inspiration ultimately from this very passage of Ben Sira, making that liturgical poem far more ancient than one might otherwise suppose.

### Receiving Portions

Ben Sira continues with a description that maps directly onto what the *mishnah* records. The text states: *be'aloto al mizbeach hod veyehedar ezrat mikdash bekabelo netachim miyad achiv* — when he ascended upon the glorious *mizbe'ach* and honored the courtyard of the sanctuary, receiving the portions from the hands of his brothers, the other *kohanim*. This is the identical relay procedure described in the *mishnah*: the *kohen gadol* at the top of the ramp, receiving the *netachim*, the limbs of the *olah*, passed to him by his priestly colleagues.

### Priestly Splendor

Ben Sira then describes the surrounding scene: *saviv lo ateret banim keshtilei arazim balevanon veyakifuhu kearvei nachal kol benei Aharon bichvodam* — surrounding him was a crown of sons, like saplings of cedars of Lebanon; all the sons of Aharon in their glory encircled him. *ve'ishei hashem beyadam* — the fire offerings of the Lord were in their hands, *neged kol kehal Yisrael ad kalot sheret hamizbeach lesader maarachot elyon* — before all the congregation of Israel, until he finished his service at the altar, arranging the firewood piles on high. The entire tableau — the *kohen gadol* at the center, ringed by the *kohanim* in full ceremonial array, the fire offerings passing through their hands toward the altar — is preserved with striking fidelity in this ancient text.

### Fire vs. Blood

This passage invites a broader theological observation. Throughout *masechet zevachim*, the halachic focus of animal sacrifice falls overwhelmingly on the blood: *ki hadam al hamizbe'ach hu yechaper*, for the blood upon the altar effects atonement. The burning of the limbs upon the altar, the *olah* ascending in flame, has seemed throughout that discussion to be secondary — almost incidental — to the central atonement function of the blood. In *menachot*, the burning of the *ketoret* and the *kometz* assumes greater prominence, but even there the paradigm differs. Yet here, in both the *mishnah*'s description of the *kohen gadol*'s *avoda* and in Ben Sira's account, it is the act of placing the *netachim* upon the fire that receives all the attention and ceremonial elaboration. The *torah* itself devotes substantial language to the *ishei rei'ach nicho'ach*, the fire offerings of pleasing aroma, and to the act of raising and burning the parts of the sacrifice upon the altar. What emerges from the *mishnah* and from Ben Sira is that the offering of the limbs to the fire carried its own distinct weight of sanctity and splendor in the lived experience of the *beit hamikdash* — one that stands alongside, and does not simply reduce to, the atoning function of the blood.

---

## Shtei Halechem

### Mishnah Text

With the conclusion of *perek shtei middot* — *hadran alach shtei midot* — the *gemara* opens the next *perek* and returns, at least briefly, to the subject of *menachot* proper. The *mishnah* states: *shtei halechem niloshot achat achat vene'afot achat achat* — the two loaves of *shavuot* are kneaded individually and baked individually.

### Lechem Hapanim

By contrast, the *lechem hapanim* — the twelve showbreads — follows a different rule: *niloshot achat achat vene'afot shtayim shtayim* — each loaf is kneaded individually, but they are baked in pairs, two at a time.

### Mold Stages

Because the *lechem hapanim* was required to assume a precise and elaborate shape, molds were essential to its production at every stage. The *mishnah* records that three separate molds were used. First, while the dough was still raw, it was placed in a mold to give it the proper form. Second, when transferred to the oven, a separate mold was used during baking so that the shape would be maintained throughout the firing process — presumably because a different material was required for oven use. Third, upon removal from the oven, the loaf was placed into yet another mold to prevent it from crumbling or losing its form as it cooled: *kedei shelo yitkalkel*, so that it should not be ruined. The experience of bakers who work with shaped breads or molded cakes will be familiar with the importance of each of these stages in preserving the integrity of the final form.

---

## Textual Basis

### Isaron Measure

The *gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei?* — what is the textual basis for these rules? A *baraita* is cited that derives each principle from specific verses. The starting point is the verse pertaining to the *lechem hapanim*: *shnei esronim yihye hachala ha'achat* — two *esronim* shall be for each single loaf. Each of the twelve loaves of *lechem hapanim* thus contained two *esronim* of flour — a notably large quantity, given that a standard *mincha* consists of one *isaron*, and that the loaves of the *todah* offering, though individually smaller, comprise one *isaron* distributed across ten loaves.

### Individual Kneading

From the phrase *hachala ha'achat* — "the one loaf" — the *baraita* derives that each loaf is treated as an individual unit: *melamed shenilosha achat achat*, this teaches that they are kneaded one by one. The singular emphasis in the verse — "the one loaf" — establishes individual processing at the kneading stage. The extension of this rule to the *shtei halechem* is derived from the superfluous word *yihye* in the same verse.

### Paired Baking

The rule that the *lechem hapanim* are baked in pairs is derived from a different verse: *vesamta otam* — you shall place them. The word *otam*, "them," is interpreted as referring to a placement in the oven — as Rashi explains, *sima rishona she'ata ose mehen dehainu batanur*, "the first placing you do with them, which is in the oven." The word *otam* carries a minimum plural value of two, establishing that two loaves are placed in the oven together.

### Otam Exclusivity

One might then ask whether the same paired-baking rule applies to the *shtei halechem* as well. The *gemara* considers this possibility and rejects it on the basis of the very same word *otam*: *talmud lomar otam* — the word "them" carries an exclusionary force, indicating that it is specifically these loaves — the *lechem hapanim* — that are baked in pairs, and not the *shtei halechem*.

The *gemara* anticipates the obvious objection: how can the word *otam* serve double duty — first to establish paired baking, and then to exclude the *shtei halechem* from it? The answer lies in the grammatical form of the verse. Had the Torah simply written *vesamtam* — "and you shall place them" — the plural would already have been conveyed by the verb conjugation alone, and the minimum of two would follow automatically. The fact that the Torah writes the separate word *otam* — making "them" a distinct term — indicates that this word is doing additional work: *shma mina tarti*, we derive two things from it. The placement is two at a time, establishing the minimum; and it is *otam* specifically — only the *lechem hapanim* — that follows this rule, excluding the *shtei halechem*.

### Three Molds

The *baraita* continues with the three-mold requirement. The *gemara* grounds this in the verse *vesamta otam*, which it reads as referring to a placing in a mold: if you want to bake these loaves in a precise and prescribed shape, a mold is required, and the *baraita* identifies three distinct stages at which a mold was necessary. The first mold shaped the dough before baking. The second mold, in the oven, maintained the shape during baking. The third received the loaf upon its removal from the oven.

### Expansion Problem

A natural question arises: if you already had a mold before baking and a different mold inside the oven, why not simply return the baked loaf to the original pre-baking mold rather than using a third? The *gemara*'s answer is straightforward: *keivan de'aphi nafcha* — once the bread was baked, it expanded. The baked loaf was larger than the raw dough had been, and it would no longer fit in the original mold. A third mold, sized to accommodate the expanded loaf, was therefore required.

---

## Shape Debate

### Open Box View

The *gemara* then turns to a dispute regarding the precise shape of the *lechem hapanim*. Rabbi Chanina holds that the *lechem hapanim* was shaped *kemin teiva perutza* — like an open box. On this view, the loaf consisted of a flat base with walls rising up on two sides, forming a U- or box-like cross-section, open at the top.

### V-Shaped View

Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, holds that the loaf was shaped *kemin sefina rokedes* — like a racing boat or a shaking boat. Rashi describes this as a vessel whose hull narrows to a V at the bottom, enabling it to move rapidly through water. According to Rashi, the cross-section of the loaf came to a pointed or V-shaped bottom. Tosafot qualifies this somewhat, suggesting that the walls above the V-bottom may have continued upward at right angles, but for the purposes of the *gemara*'s analysis, the essential feature is the pointed or angled lower profile.

### Frankincense Placement

The *gemara* now tests each view against the practical requirements of the *lechem hapanim*. The Torah commands that two dishes of frankincense — *zichin* — be placed *al hamaarachot*, upon the stacks of bread, which the *gemara* understands to mean upon the topmost loaf of each of the two columns. According to the open-box view, this presents no difficulty: *hainu dehavu yasvi b'zichin* — the flat base of the open box provides a natural surface on which the frankincense dishes can rest securely. This is a clear advantage of Rabbi Chanina's position.

### V-Shape Fix

The V-shaped view, however, faces an apparent difficulty: *heichi havu yasvi b'zichin?* — how would the frankincense dishes rest on a V-shaped bottom? There is no flat surface to receive them. The *gemara* answers that one would make a place for them — *makom avid lah* — either by flattening a small area within the V, or by creating a niche in one of the walls into which the dish could be inserted, or by allowing the dish to be suspended and supported by the two rising sides of the V. Some adjustment to the bread's form would accommodate the placement, and the requirement could be met.

---

## Support Structure

### Box Rod Support

The *gemara* now turns to a more elaborate analysis of how the panels (*snifin*) and rods (*kani*) of the *shulchan* apparatus functioned under each view of the bread's shape, and how each shape resolves some structural problems while creating others.

On the open-box view, the rods separating successive loaves in the stack would rest on the thick walls of the loaf below. The perpendicular side-walls of the open box have a certain thickness at their upper edge, and the rods can lie across those edges, spanning from one side-wall to the other. This provides a natural and stable resting place for the rods: *hainu dehavi yasvi kani* — this is how we understand where the rods would sit.

### V-Shape Rod Support

Under the V-shaped view, however, the walls narrow as they converge toward the point at the bottom, and the upper edges of those walls — wherever they terminate — may not offer sufficient flat surface to support the rods. The *gemara* addresses this: *mosha avid lehu* — one would fashion a protrusion from the dough itself. A small amount of dough would be built out at the appropriate height, creating a ledge or extension — *davka* — specifically to provide a resting surface for the rods that would lie above.

### Box Stability

The *gemara* then raises a stability question that bears directly on the open-box view. If the bread is a flat-bottomed box whose width extends fully across the table, how do the panels keep the stack of twelve loaves — six to a column — in place? The panels are meant to support the bread from the sides, preventing lateral movement, but if the open box fully occupies the width of the table at its base, it is not immediately clear how there is any room for panels along the sides, or how the panels engage the bread to steady it. This is a pointed structural difficulty.

### Weight Distribution

The *gemara* then asks why the open-box view would need panels at all. If the bread has a flat stable base, why not simply stack the loaves directly one upon another, without the elaborate apparatus of panels and rods? The answer is: *agav yukra delachma chals* — because of the sheer weight of the bread, the loaves below would be crushed under the accumulated weight of those above. The panels and rods serve not primarily to prevent the stack from toppling, but to distribute the load — to interpose a structural framework that transfers weight away from the bread itself so that the lower loaves are not damaged. Under the boat-shaped view, by contrast, the entire apparatus of panels and rods is essential simply to keep the V-shaped loaves from toppling at all, quite apart from the weight distribution problem.

### Panel Placement

The structural difference between the two views extends to where the panels are physically positioned. Rabbi Abba bar Memel articulates this explicitly. According to the view that the bread is shaped like a racing boat, *snifin algabei shulchan munachim* — the panels rest on the surface of the table itself. Because the V-shaped bread narrows to a point at the bottom, there is physical space between the base of the bread and the edges of the table, and the panels can be erected beginning from the table's surface, rising alongside the bread as it widens upward. According to the view that the bread is like an open box, however, *snifin algabei karka munachim* — the panels rest on the ground. Since the flat-bottomed box occupies the full width of the table from its base upward, there is no room on the table's surface for the panels; they must be built from the floor and rise up along the outer edges of the table to frame the stack from without.

### Mutual Support

Finally, the *gemara* asks how the principle stated by Rabbi Yehuda fits into this debate: *halechem ma'amid et hasnifin vehasnifin ma'amidin et halechem* — the bread supports the panels and the panels support the bread. This reciprocal or mutual tension — where bread and panels press against one another, each holding the other in place — accords with the view that the bread is shaped like a racing boat. On that view, the structural arrangement is one of tension and counter-pressure: the V-shaped loaves, suspended on angled rods and surrounded by panels, exert lateral force against the panels while the panels prevent the loaves from splaying outward. Rashi explains that the bread's pressure on the bent rods pushes against the panels, while the panels in turn hold the bread from collapsing — a system of mutual structural tension. On the open-box view, by contrast, the relationship between bread and panels is less obviously reciprocal in this way: the weight of the bread bears down on the rods, and the panels prevent lateral displacement, but the sense of the bread actively pressing against and sustaining the panels is less clear. As the lecturer acknowledges, the precise mechanics of Rabbi Yehuda's principle as applied to the boat-shaped view remain somewhat difficult to fully visualize, but the *gemara* aligns his formulation with that opinion.

---

---

# Menachot 95

## Tanur Structure

### V-Shape Debate

We begin at the very top of 95a, with the word *meitivei* — a challenge to the view that the Tanur was shaped like a boat, a V-like shape. A Baraita is cited: *k'min kaveiret haya l'matnur* — the Tanur was like a *kaveiret*. A *kaveiret* literally means a beehive, but it also referred to a kind of wicker basket or hollow tube-like vessel. So the Tanur was not exactly like a *kaveiret*, but similar to one in shape.

### Kaveiret & Squared

The Baraita continues: *v'domeh k'min tavla meruba'at* — however, it resembled a squared tableau. This sounds very much like a description of a box shape, not a V-shape. The Gemara responds: *eima upia domeh k'min tavla meruba'at* — do not read it as saying the entire structure was square; rather, only the opening was square-shaped. This is the first we hear of such a qualification, since the V-shape as previously described would taper at the ends and could not naturally be described as square.

### Tosafot Reconciliation

Tosafot suggests — not only to explain this Gemara but to reconcile numerous other sources that speak of folding up the edges and having them rise straight up — that after the V-shaped lower portion, the walls did in fact continue vertically upward. This would fit with the squared-opening description. Nevertheless, as we have seen throughout, so many sources point toward the box-like shape, and that remains clearly the dominant position.

### Sideboards Theory

A second Baraita is now quoted: *tanya ke-man de-amar k'min sefina rokedet* — we have a Baraita that supports the position of a boat-shaped, V-shaped Tanur. *de-tanya arba'ah snifim shel zahav hayu sham* — there were four golden *snifim*, sideboards, that supported the bread. *mifutzalim merosheihem k'min dakranim hayu* — and they spread out at their heads like palm fronds. So there was some manner in which the tops of these sideboards opened and spread outward, making them less like solid walls and more like something resembling a fork whose tines splay open at the top.

### Merosheihem Meaning

The word *merosheihem* — meaning "at their heads" or "at their tops" — raises a question about what exactly was spreading and where. One reading is that the sideboards ran the full height of the structure but were not solid; rather, they were lattice-like, resembling sticks with many branches, *k'min kanim ha-dokranim kanim she-yesh ba-hem anafim harbeh*, as Rashi describes. This reading, while somewhat supported by Rashi, is challenged by the word *merosheihem*, which implies the spreading occurred specifically at the top.

Tosafot therefore suggests that perhaps the sideboards extended only to the height of a single loaf of bread, and then spread out at their tops — *merosheihem* referring to the top of the sideboards, which reached only to the height of the first bread — in order to support that bottom loaf while the remaining loaves rested above. This reading accounts for why the spreading was needed: it was to stabilize the structure from below upward. The Baraita concludes by stating explicitly that the bread was *she-domeh kemin sefinah rokedet* — like this rocking, unstable boat shape — which strongly supports the V-shaped opinion. The two opinions thus stand unresolved.

### Rambam Box Shape

As one would expect, the Rambam rules that the box-shaped interpretation is far superior. It simply works better with the sources and is easier to understand physically. The V-shape, while supported by certain Baraitot, creates difficulties that the box-shape does not.

---

## Lechem HaPanim & Masa'ot

### Question Posed

We now turn to a more halachic discussion. *ibaia lehu* — the following question was raised: *lechem haPanim nifsal be-masa'ot o einu nifsal be-masa'ot?* Does the Lechem HaPanim become disqualified during the journeys of the camp or not? This question is obviously pressing: the bread is supposed to remain on the Shulchan throughout the week. Yet whenever the camp moves, if there is no longer a standing Ohel Moed, the bread is effectively outside the Ohel Moed — and bread removed from the Ohel Moed should become *pasul* as *yotzei*. The counterargument is that the bread is still physically on the Shulchan. That tension is precisely what the Gemara now explores.

### Becomes Pasul View

Rebbi Yochanan and Rebbi Yehoshua ben Levi debate this question. The one who says it becomes *pasul* derives it from the verse *ka'asher yachanu kein yisa'u* — as they encamped, so they traveled. *mah bi-chaniyatan nifsal be-yotzei af bi-nesiato nifsal be-yotzei* — just as when encamped, removing the bread from its proper place renders it *pasul*, so too when traveling, the same rules apply without special dispensation. Since the Ohel Moed has been dismantled, the bread is effectively outside the Mikdash and thus *pasul*.

### Remains Kosher View

The one who says it does not become *pasul* derives from the verse *ve-lechem ha-tamid alav yihyeh* — the bread should constantly be upon it. Since the Torah itself commands that the bread remain on the Shulchan, as long as it remains in place, how can we say that following the Torah's command constitutes a problem? And as for the verse *ka'asher yachanu kein yisa'u*, he reads it *le-idach gisa* — in precisely the opposite direction. *mah bi-chaniato ki lo yatza mi-mekomo lo nifsal* — just as when encamped, if the bread was not removed from its place, it is not *pasul*, so too *af bi-nesiato ki lo yatza mi-mekomo lo nifsal* — when traveling, if nothing was removed from its place, it is equally not *pasul*. The key question is how one conceptualizes the problem: is it that bread becomes *pasul* whenever it is outside the Mikdash, or only when it has been actively removed from its proper place? According to the second view, no removal occurred here — the Ohel Moed changed around it, but the bread itself remained where it belongs.

This second view is additionally supported by its core proof-text: *lechem ha-tamid alav yihyeh*, which commands the bread to remain on the Shulchan constantly. Since it does remain there, it is in its proper place and does not become *pasul*.

One might ask how the bread could remain stable while being transported on the Shulchan amid all those elaborate stacking arrangements. This must have been among the miracles associated with the Mishkan. And if the journey lasted beyond a week — a genuine question — we recall that a Baraita already stated *afilu yamim harbeh*, that even for many days the bread on the Shulchan does not become *pasul* through *linah*.

### Rav Dimi Reframe

The Gemara then says: actually, you are right, the verse *ve-lechem ha-tamid alav yihyeh* is quite persuasive. The back-and-forth has become compelling enough that the Gemara opts to reframe the debate entirely. *ki ata rav dimi* — when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reformulated the debate as follows: *bimesudar kuli alma lo peligi* — when the bread is arranged on the Shulchan, nobody debates that it does not become *pasul* during travel. It is where it is supposed to be, even if the Ohel Moed has been dismantled. *ella ki peligi bimesulak* — the debate concerns bread that has already been removed from the Shulchan.

How does this scenario arise? On Shabbat, the old bread is removed and the Kohanim are supposed to eat it that day. The new bread goes on immediately — there is no concern about the new bread. The question is about the bread that was removed: the Kohanim may eat it halachically through Saturday night. If the camp begins traveling Saturday night, when there is no longer an Ohel Moed standing, does that removed bread become *pasul* as *yotzei*? The one who says it becomes *pasul* holds that no special dispensation exists: just as when encamped, bread outside the Mishkan is *pasul*, so too when traveling. The one who says it does not become *pasul* holds that the verse *venasah ohel moed betoch hamachanot* — and the Ohel Moed shall travel in the midst of the camps — indicates that even while traveling and not yet erected, the Ohel Moed retains its status as Ohel Moed.

### Practical Stability

This discussion raises further questions. Once we are speaking of bread removed from the Shulchan, the same problem should apply to all *kodshei kodashim*, not just to the Lechem HaPanim. After all, *kodshei kodashim* may not leave the environs of the Ohel Moed — so where exactly is the Ohel Moed when the camp is moving? The Leviim traveled as groups in a particular order: Bnei Gershon and Bnei Merari went ahead to prepare the structure, while Bnei Kehat came later with the actual *keilim*. If they traveled in a line, it becomes quite difficult to identify where, physically, the space of the Ohel Moed would be during transit.

One could argue that if they traveled as a compact unit, as some opinions hold, it would be easier to define where one could eat *kodshei kodashim*. But the plain reading of the verses — which describe first one group traveling, then another — suggests a more linear arrangement. The Gemara itself does not resolve precisely where the physical space of the Ohel Moed is during travel, nor does it specify exactly how the Kohanim would have eaten their bread while on the move, though one might note that the Kohanim were associated with the section of the camp where they traveled and could have eaten during the journey itself.

The Gemara returns to the opposing view — that traveling the Ohel Moed means the status of Ohel Moed persists — and addresses the challenge posed by *ka'asher yachanu kein yisa'u*. The response is *lishiteih d'idach*: the verse goes the other direction entirely. *mah bi-chaniyato ki lo mafik lei lo misal* — when encamped, if you did not remove it from its place, it is not *pasul*; *af bi-nesiato ki lo mafik lei lo misal* — so too during travel, if it was not removed from its place, it is not *pasul*. And more fundamentally, since the Ohel Moed is still called Ohel Moed even in transit — *af al pi shenasah Ohel Moed hu* — there is no *yotzei* problem at all.

The two sides then debate the meaning of *venasah ohel moed betoch hamachanot*. One says this verse is merely narrative, describing when the Ohel Moed travels, not granting it halachic status as Ohel Moed during travel. The other responds that the verse *mimachaneh haLeviim betoch hamachanot* already covers the narrative; the reason the Torah specifically calls it *ohel moed* here rather than simply the Levite camp is precisely to teach that it retains the status of Ohel Moed during travel.

---

## Kodashim & Masa'ot

### Zevachim Baraita

With the debate framed, the Gemara now introduces a Tosefta from Zevachim: *besha'at siluk masa'ot* — when the camps were moving — *kodshim nifsalim b'yotzei* — the *kodashim* become *pasul* through *yotzei* — and yet *vezavim u'metzora'im mishtalhin chutz limechitzatam* — Zavim and Metzora'im must still be sent outside their respective boundaries. The Torah commands that a Metzora be sent outside all three camps and a Zav be kept outside Machaneh Leviyah, and this remains in effect even while traveling. So the Tosefta is indicating that while the camp retains the status of Machaneh Leviyah and Machaneh Yisrael during travel, it does not retain the status of the Mikdash itself — and therefore *kodashim* become *pasul*.

### Apparent Contradiction

This creates a direct problem. If *kodashim* become *pasul* during travel because there is no longer an Ohel Moed, then there is no room for any debate about whether the Lechem HaPanim remains *kasher* when removed from the Shulchan. The bread is simply another case of *kodshei kodashim*: once the Ohel Moed is dismantled, it is outside its proper place and is *pasul*. So where does the debate go?

### Two Cases Solution

The Gemara answers: *ella ki ata ravin amar — mar amar bimesudar u'mar amar bimesulak velo paligi* — when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reframed the dispute. There is in fact no debate at all. The one who said it does not become *pasul* was discussing the bread still on the Shulchan, where, as we argued from the verse *lechem ha-tamid alav yihyeh*, it remains in its proper place and does not become *pasul*. The one who said it does become *pasul* was discussing the bread removed from the Shulchan, where, as the Tosefta shows, *kodshei kodashim* in general become *pasul* — and the removed Lechem HaPanim is no different. These were not competing positions but descriptions of two separate cases.

### Night Travel Inference

From this reframing, Abaye draws an inference: *shema mina yesh siluk masa'ot balaila* — from this entire debate, we learn that the camps would travel at night. Why? If they never traveled at night, the question about the removed bread would never arise. The bread is taken off the Shulchan on Shabbat; the Kohanim are supposed to eat it that day. If the camp could only begin moving in the morning — Sunday morning at the earliest following a Shabbat departure — the bread would already be *pasul belina*, having remained overnight in a state of *kedushah* without being placed back on the Shulchan. The *yotzei* question would be moot, preempted by the *linah* disqualification. The fact that the Amoraim debated whether the bread becomes *pasul beyotzei* — not *pasul belina* — proves they understood that the camp could depart Saturday night, when the bread was still *kasher* but the Ohel Moed had been dismantled.

The Gemara objects: *peshita* — obviously they could travel at night! The verse *lalekhet yomam valaila* — to travel by day and by night — says so explicitly. The Gemara replies: one might have thought that the verse means only that once a journey was begun by day, it could be continued through the night; but perhaps the camp could not initiate a journey at night. Therefore, from the debate itself we learn that the Amoraim understood the camp could begin traveling at night as well.

The Gemara then raises a further challenge: *huglelu haparochet* — when the Parochet of the Kodesh HaKodashim was rolled up, *hutar l'zavim u'l'metzora'im likanes lesham* — Zavim and Metzora'im were permitted to enter. This implies that once the Parochet was removed, the Ohel Moed entirely lost its status, and not even the *machaneh* boundaries remained — Zavim and Metzora'im no longer needed to be expelled. Yet the earlier Tosefta said that during travel, even with *kodashim* becoming *pasul*, Zavim and Metzora'im still had to remain outside their respective boundaries. This is a direct contradiction. One might also ask why it is specifically the rolling up of the Parochet that triggers this loss of status — why not the dismantling of the courtyard walls, or the removal of the Aron?

### Rabbi Eliezer View

The Gemara resolves this through Rav Ashi: *ha rabbi eliezer, ha rabbanan* — these two statements reflect a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages. A Baraita is cited in which Rabbi Eliezer addresses the following scenario: if, during a *pesach ha-ba be-tum'ah* — a communal Pesach offering brought in a state of *tum'at meit* — Zavim and Metzora'im forced their way into the Azarah, *dachaku*, are they liable? The Torah did not extend them the license granted to *tamei meit* on such occasions. Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse *v'yishalhu min ha-machaneh kol tzarua ve-chol zav ve-chol tamei la-nefesh* — send out from the camp all those afflicted with *tzara'at*, every Zav, and every person *tamei* for a dead body — that the expulsion of Zavim and Metzora'im is conditional on the expulsion of *tamei meitim*: *besha'at she-tme'ei meitim mishtalhin zavim u-metzora'im mishtalhin; ein tme'ei meitim mishtalhin ein zavim u-metzora'im mishtalhin* — when *tamei meitim* are sent out, Zavim and Metzora'im must also be sent out; when *tamei meitim* are not sent out, Zavim and Metzora'im need not be sent out either.

This is directly applicable to the *siluk machanot*. When the camp travels, what is missing? Machaneh Shechinah — the Ohel Moed no longer stands. A *tamei meit* is only prohibited from Machaneh Shechinah itself — this is derived from the fact that Moshe carried the bones of Yosef *immo bi-mchitzato*, within the Levite camp, demonstrating that a *tamei meit* may be in Machaneh Leviyah. Since during travel there is no Machaneh Shechinah, *tamei meitim* are not being sent anywhere — and by Rabbi Eliezer's principle, therefore Zavim and Metzora'im need not be sent out either. This is precisely the position of the Baraita that says *huglelu haparochet* removes all obligations.

The Sages, by contrast, hold that the obligation to expel Zavim and Metzora'im is not contingent on the status of *tamei meitim* in the same way. Even without Machaneh Shechinah, the status of Machaneh Leviyah and Machaneh Yisrael remains intact and the expulsion requirements remain in force — which is why the Tosefta from Zevachim says that even during travel, Zavim and Metzora'im must be sent outside their boundaries.

### Three Purity Levels

The three levels of *tum'ah* restrictions operate as follows. A *tamei meit*, despite contracting one of the more far-reaching forms of *tum'ah* — lasting seven days, requiring the *parah adumah*, and transferring with unusual severity — is nonetheless prohibited only from Machaneh Shechinah, the Mikdash itself. This is because the *tum'ah* is contracted externally, from contact with death, and is therefore seen as less definitively altering the person's status. A Zav, by contrast, is prohibited from Machaneh Leviyah — equivalent in contemporary terms to Har HaBayit — but may remain within Machaneh Yisrael, i.e., Yerushalayim. A Metzora is expelled from all three camps entirely.

The deeper question this raises is whether the status of Machaneh Yisrael as a place where *kodashim kalim* may be eaten is itself dependent on the presence of the Mikdash — functioning, as it were, as the suburbs of the Mikdash. If so, once the Ohel Moed is dismantled during travel, perhaps even *kodashim kalim* would become *pasul*, since there are no longer any operative suburbs. On the other hand, the obligation to expel *tme'im* might be an intrinsic feature of the camp's status, independent of the Mikdash's presence. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages turns precisely on this distinction.

---

## Bread Preparation

### Mixed Location View

We now turn to the next Mishnah, which addresses both Shtei HaLechem and Lechem HaPanim together — two communal *menachos* that share the feature of containing no oil, which becomes significant shortly. The Mishnah states: *lishatan va'arichatan bachutz* — the kneading and shaping of both were done outside the Beit HaMikdash, meaning they had not yet acquired *kedushat haguf* at that stage. *ve'afiyatan mibifnim* — but their baking was done inside the Beit HaMikdash. The Mishnah's assumption is that the oven was a *kli sharet* located in the Azarah. Since there is no oil in these offerings, there is no *kli sharet* involved in the measuring — the *midot lach*, the liquid measures, were sanctified, but here only flour and water are used, and water was not measured. Flour uses only dry measures. So the entire process up to baking could be conducted without encountering a *kli sharet*. The baking stage, however, in the Mikdash oven, would confer *kedushat haguf*. *ve'einan dochot et haShabbat* — and the baking does not override Shabbat, since one simply bakes before Shabbat.

### Lina Problem

This is precisely where the Gemara's problem lies. *alma tanur mekadesh* — if the oven sanctifies, then baking before Shabbat means the bread acquires *kedushat haguf* on Friday. Now it is Shabbat, the bread has been sanctified, and it has not yet been placed on the Shulchan. It therefore becomes *pasul belina* — disqualified by having remained overnight in its sanctified state without being put in its proper place. Once the oven confers *kedushah*, you cannot bake before Shabbat and then place it on the Shulchan on Shabbat; the bread would be *pasul* by then. So if the oven is a *kli sharet*, the baking must occur on Shabbat — which means the baking *does* override Shabbat, in direct contradiction to the Mishnah's statement. This is the strong question attributed to Rav Sheshet, which Rabbah praises: *hiksha adam kasheh shehu kasheh kevarzel* — a hard question asked by someone as strong as iron.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

Rav Ashi attempts a resolution: *dilma mai bifnim? bemakom zerizim* — perhaps "inside" does not literally mean within the Azarah, but rather in a place where zealous, scrupulous personnel are overseeing the process. On this reading, the oven is not a *kli sharet* and does not confer *kedushah*; "inside" simply means under supervision — perhaps in the *ezrat nashim* or a side chamber — to ensure, for instance, that the Lechem HaPanim does not become *chametz*. This would explain why the baking does not override Shabbat: since the oven is not a *kli sharet*, no *kedushat haguf* is conferred at the baking stage, and the bread can be baked before Shabbat without any *linah* concern.

### Refutation

The Gemara dismisses this: *ha deRav ashi bruta hi* — what Rav Ashi said is simply wrong. *avi afiyah be'inan zerizim lishvira nami be'inan zerizim* — if zealous overseers are needed during the baking to prevent *chametz* or ensure proper procedure, the same concern applies equally during the kneading and shaping. *ve'ei l'lisha va'aricha lo be'inan zerizim, afiyah nami lo be'inan zerizim* — and if you trust people without zealous oversight during the kneading, you cannot claim the baking requires a different standard. There is no principled basis for distinguishing the two stages in this way. The Gemara therefore concludes that Rav Ashi's interpretation is untenable; *bifnim* must mean literally inside, and the difficulty remains. Tosafot notes — not in this immediate context, but in an earlier passage — that the Gemara's resolution is essentially to recognize that the line *ve'einan dochot et haShabbat* in the Mishnah represents a different opinion from the voice that said baking occurs inside. Specifically, that line reflects the position of Rabbi Shimon, whose view appears at the end of the Mishnah, as will now become clear. It is, in effect, a misplaced line belonging to Rabbi Shimon's position — *mi sheshana zu lo shana zu*.

### Rabbi Yehuda: All Inside

Rabbi Yehuda says *kol ma'aseihen mibifnim* — all stages of preparation were done inside the Mikdash. He presumably holds that even the dry measures were sanctified *klei sharet*, so that the entire process from kneading onward occurred within the Mikdash and conferred *kedushah* from the outset.

### Rabbi Shimon: All Outside

Rabbi Shimon states the opposite: *shtei halechem u'lechem haPanim ksheira ba'azarah u'ksheira b'beit pagi* — whether prepared in the Azarah or in Beit Pagi, which Rashi explains as referring to all of Yerushalayim, or by some readings even outside Yerushalayim entirely, both were valid. On his view, not even the oven was a *kli sharet*. The sanctification of the Lechem HaPanim occurs only when it is placed on the Shulchan; the sanctification of the Shtei HaLechem occurs through the slaughter and blood-sprinkling of the *kivsei atzeret*. Until that point, the bread has no *kedushat haguf* regardless of where or how it was prepared. This is why, on Rabbi Shimon's view, there is no *linah* problem and no need for the baking to override Shabbat — the bread acquires no *kedushah* from the oven at all.

We are thus left with three positions: the Mishnah's first opinion holds that the dry measures were not sanctified but the oven was, so the process began outside and was completed inside, and on that view the baking does override Shabbat (the *ve'einan dochot* line not belonging to this voice). Rabbi Yehuda holds that even the dry measures were sanctified and everything was done inside. Rabbi Shimon holds that nothing was sanctified until the bread reached the Shulchan or the *korban*, and the entire preparation could be done outside.

---

## David & Lechem HaPanim

### Same Verse Source

Rabbi Abbahu bar Kahana observes: *ushneihem mikra echad darshu* — both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon derive their positions from the same verse. The verse is *v'hu derech chol af ki hayom yikdash bakeli* — spoken in the episode in which David HaMelech came to Nov, the city of the Kohanim, and asked for bread.

### Biblical Narrative

The episode unfolds as follows. David says to the Kohen: *ma yesh tachat yadcha chamisha lechem tena beyadi o hanimtza* — give me five loaves of bread, or whatever you have. *vaya'an haKohen et david vayomar ein lechem chol el tachat yadi* — the Kohen answers that he has no *lechem chol*, no ordinary unsanctified bread. *ki im lechem kodesh yesh* — only sacred bread. *im nishm'ru hane'arim ach me'isha* — if the young men have kept apart from women, they may have it. David responds that his men are pure. *v'hu derech chol af ki hayom yikdash bakeli* — and the matter of *derech chol*: even if today it would be sanctified through the vessel. The next verse clarifies: *vayiten lo haKohen kodesh ki lo hayah sham lechem ki im lechem haPanim hamusarim milifnei hashem lasum lechem cham beyom hilakcho* — the Kohen gave him sacred bread, for there was no bread there except for the Lechem HaPanim that had been removed from before God, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it was taken. This is also the source for the teaching that the Lechem HaPanim remained fresh like the day it was placed on the Shulchan.

### Rav Yehuda Reading

Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse as follows: *bechol ashkecheinhu d'ka-afei lehu* — David found that they had baked the bread on a weekday, i.e., without it being in the Mikdash. David then said to the Kohen: *derech chol ka-afeitu leh?* — you baked this as *chol*, in a non-sanctified way? *af ki hayom yikdash bakeli v'ipsulei belinah* — it was already sanctified through the holy vessels when baked, and therefore it has now become *pasul belina*, since it sat overnight after having been sanctified in the oven. David's point is that the bread was always sanctified by the sacred vessel at the time of baking — which is precisely Rabbi Yehuda's position that the oven is a *kli sharet* and confers *kedushah* from the moment of baking.

### Rabbi Shimon Reading

Rabbi Shimon reads it differently: *beShabbat ashkecheinhu d'ka-afei lehu* — they had baked it on Shabbat. David said to them: *lo derech chol be'itu lema'avdeih?* — could you not have done it *derech chol*, baked it on a weekday using non-sanctified vessels? Since on Rabbi Shimon's view the bread does not acquire *kedushah* from the oven, there is no need to bake it on Shabbat at all. Baking on a weekday in unsanctified vessels would have been entirely sufficient, with sanctification occurring later upon placement on the Shulchan. David's complaint is thus that they violated Shabbat unnecessarily.

### Me'ila Issue

The Gemara then questions whether this reading of the narrative is correct. *umi matsit amart d'beshat afeiyah ashkecheinhu?* — was David present when the bread was being baked? The verse says the bread had already been *hamusarim milifnei Hashem* — removed from before God — which implies it had long since been baked and was no longer on the Shulchan. David was not speaking to a situation of fresh baking. Rather, the Gemara clarifies, what David was addressing was the *me'ila* question. The Kohen had told him he had *lechem kodesh* — sacred bread — that had just come off the Shulchan. David responded: *lo miba'ei hai* — I have no question about that bread. *dekivan deka nafik lei mime'ila* — since this bread has left the realm of *me'ila*: once *kodashim* become fit for human consumption by *kohanim*, the prohibition of *me'ila* — the misappropriation of sacred property — no longer applies. Thus, *derech chol hu* — it is now in the domain of ordinary human use, and giving it to non-Kohanim presents no *me'ila* concern. There remains the separate prohibition of a *zar* eating *kodesh*, but *me'ila* is not at issue.

### Pikuach Nefesh

Having addressed the bread already removed from the Shulchan, David continues: *afilu ha'ich nami d'hayom yikdash bakeli* — even the bread that was sanctified today through the vessels and placed on the Shulchan today, which does still carry *me'ila* concerns — *havu li d'lechol*, give it to me as well. Why? *mesukan hu* — because there is a matter of *sakanat nefashot*, danger to life. *pikuach nefesh* overrides all. David's statement thus operates on two levels: better to give the bread already off the Shulchan, where no *me'ila* applies; but even the fully sanctified bread currently on the Shulchan may be given when lives are at stake.

The Gemara concludes that the verses in this passage are therefore not about the method of sanctification — whether through the oven, the dry measures, or the Shulchan — but about the *me'ila* question and the principle of *pikuach nefesh*. And as for the actual dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, the Gemara notes: *tnan nami d'katani, rabbi shimon omer, le'olam hevei ragil lomar...* — Rabbi Shimon's formulation, "teach yourself always to say," indicates that he is transmitting a tradition rather than expounding a verse. This in turn confirms that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon are not engaged in exegetical debate about those verses but are transmitting different received traditions about how the bread was prepared. *shema mina* — so we learn.

The three positions therefore stand as distinct traditions: the first opinion that the dry measures were not sanctified but the oven was, such that preparation began outside and concluded inside; Rabbi Yehuda that all preparation was conducted inside the Mikdash with sanctified dry measures throughout; and Rabbi Shimon that the entire preparation could be performed outside, with sanctification occurring only upon placement on the Shulchan or the offering of the *kivsei atzeret*.

---

---

# Menachot 96

## Chavitei Kohen Gadol

### Preparation Steps

The daf opens with a mishna concerning the chavitei Kohen Gadol — the special mincha that the Kohen Gadol was required to bring every day, half in the morning and half in the evening. To arrive at this mincha, a series of preparatory steps was necessary: the wheat had to be ground, sifted, kneaded (lisha), shaped (arichah), and baked (afiyah). As the mishna states, lishatan, va'arichatan, ve'afiyatan bifnim — the kneading, shaping, and baking had to be performed inside, that is, within the azara of the Beit HaMikdash. These final steps also vedochot et hashabbat, override Shabbat, since this is a minchat tamid that must be performed each day without exception, including on Shabbat.

### Work Location

However, not all steps carry the same status. Techinatan veharkadatan einan dochot et hashabbat — the grinding of the flour and the repeated sifting through multiple sieves do not override Shabbat. These preliminary steps could and should have been completed before Shabbat arrived.

### Rabbi Akiva's Rule

This distinction leads to a general principle articulated by Rabbi Akiva: kol melacha she'efshar la'asotah me'erev Shabbat einah dochah et HaShabbat, veshe'ee efshar la'asotah me'erev Shabbat dochah et HaShabbat. Any labor that could have been performed on erev Shabbat does not override Shabbat; only labor that could not have been done beforehand may be performed on Shabbat itself. An analogous principle applies to Yom Tov: one may cook on Yom Tov, but one may not harvest and grind grain on that day, since those preparatory steps could have been done in advance. In the case of the chavitim, it is from lisha ve'eilach — from the kneading onward — that the work is docheh et HaShabbat. The reason is practical: you could not knead the dough in advance and have it sit overnight without refrigeration, and in any event the flour itself could not be placed until the day it was needed, since the issaron had to be divided in half on that day. The grinding and sifting, by contrast, could easily be completed beforehand.

### Vessel Requirement

The mishna then states: kol haminchot yesh bahen ma'aseh kli bifnim ve'ein bahen ma'aseh kli bachutz — all minchot require the action of a kli sharet performed inside, and none of the required work may be done outside. There is some ambiguity as to the precise scope of this statement. It may be a general principle applying to every mincha without exception, or it may be a continuation of the discussion of the chavitim and similar offerings such as the Lechem Hapanim and Shtei HaLechem. Either way, the chiddush is at minimum twofold: first, that a kli sharet is required, and second, that these actions must take place inside the azara. This does not necessarily exclude all preliminary steps from being done elsewhere — it was established elsewhere that, for instance, measuring and sifting could be done outside — but from lisha onward, the work had to be done inside the azara, in a kli sharet.

The Gemara then asks how we know this, and Rabbi Zira derives it from a pasuk in Yechezkel: Vayomer elai zeh hamakom asher yevashlu sham hakohanim et ha'asham ve'et hachatat, asher yofu et hamincha levilti hotzi el hachatzer hachitzonah. The verse describes the place where the kohanim cook the chatat and asham, and states that the mincha too must be baked there, so as not to bring it out to the outer courtyard. Since the mincha is mentioned in the same context as the chatat and asham, we derive by comparison: just as those offerings require a kli and must be performed inside, so too the mincha requires a kli and must be performed inside.

---

## Shtei HaLechem

### Dimensions

With the setting established, the daf turns to a topic that demands both careful textual attention and some spatial reasoning — the dimensions of the Shtei HaLechem and the Lechem Hapanim. The Shtei HaLechem, brought on Shavuot, had the following dimensions: arkan shiva tefachim — length of seven tefachim — verachban arba — width of four — vekarnoseihen arba etzbaot, with corners four etzbaot high. These loaves were rectangular, not braided, with a definite thickness, and their raised corners gave them a distinctive appearance resembling horns, hence the term karnot.

The Lechem Hapanim — the Showbread placed on the shulchan each week — was larger: arko yud tefachim, verachbo chamisha tefachim, vekarnosav zayin etzbaot. That is, ten by five tefachim, with corners seven etzbaot high.

To help remember these two sets of dimensions, Rabbi Yehuda provides a mnemonic: shelo titeh, zad-yah-z. The first set (for the Shtei HaLechem) yields 7-4-4, and the second set (for the Lechem Hapanim) yields 10-5-7. Rabbi Yehuda was known for such mnemonics — he similarly constructed detzach adash be'achav in the Haggadah — though he does not tell us which set of numbers belongs to which offering; the mnemonic simply ensures you remember the numbers themselves.

### Ben Zoma

Ben Zoma comments on the verse venatata al hashulchan lechem panim lefanai tamid, interpreting it to mean lechem panim sheyihiyu lo panim — the bread must have a panim, a face. At first glance this statement is cryptic, and Ben Zoma offers no elaboration. His comment is best understood as an introduction to the opinions that follow in the mishna, which will describe how the bread was positioned and folded so as to present multiple surfaces or "faces." That explanation will emerge from the discussion below.

### Table Dimensions

The shulchan's dimensions are given as amatayim orko ve'amah rochbo — two amot in length and one amah in width. To work with these measurements alongside the bread's dimensions in tefachim, one must know the conversion rate. Here there is a machloket: an amah is either five or six tefachim. If an amah is five tefachim, then two amot (the table's length) equal ten tefachim, and one amah (the width) equals five tefachim. If an amah is six tefachim, then two amot equal twelve tefachim and one amah equals six tefachim. This conversion will be decisive in understanding the two opinions about how the bread was placed on the table.

---

## Bread Placement

### Rabbi Yehuda

The central spatial challenge is this: the Lechem Hapanim is ten tefachim in length, but the width of the shulchan (the dimension against which the bread's length was aligned) is only five tefachim according to Rabbi Yehuda's measure of the amah. The bread was not placed lengthwise along the length of the table; rather, noten arko keneged rochvo shel shulchan — the length of the bread was placed against the width of the shulchan. This means a ten-tefach loaf had to fit within a five-tefach space. The solution was to fold up the edges. Since you must do the same thing on both sides, the five tefachim of width are distributed as follows: two and a half tefachim are folded up on one side, two and a half on the other, with the base of the bread corresponding exactly to the width of the table. As the mishna states: vechofel tefachim umechetza mikan vefachim umechetza mikan nimtza arko melo rochvo shel shulchan, divrei Rabbi Yehuda. The length, once folded, exactly fills the width of the shulchan.

### Rabbi Meir

Rabbi Meir holds that an amah is six tefachim. Under his measure, the table is twelve tefachim long and six tefachim wide. The bread's dimensions remain unchanged: ten tefachim in length, five in width. But now the bread's length must fit within a width of six tefachim rather than five. This allows for a different folding arrangement: tefachayim mikan vefachayim mikan, two tefachim folded up on each side, and then vetechayim revach be'emtza — two tefachim of open space in the middle — kedei shetehei haruach menashevet bahen, so that air can circulate and the bread will not become moldy. As for the length: if the table is twelve tefachim long and each stack of bread is five tefachim wide, the two stacks placed side by side leave a gap of two tefachim between them down the length of the table.

This also explains Ben Zoma's remark about the bread having panim: once folded up on two sides, the loaf presents multiple faces — a bottom, two folded sides, and openings — giving it a distinctly three-dimensional, faced appearance.

### Abba Shaul

Abba Shaul introduces a related point: sham hayu notnim shenei bezichei levona shel lechem hapanim. According to his view, the two cups of levona — frankincense — that accompanied the Lechem Hapanim were placed in that space of two tefachim between the stacks. The levona served both a practical purpose, since it was offered on the mizbeach together with the Lechem Hapanim, and an aromatic one.

### Frankincense

An objection is raised: the verse says venatata al hama'aracha levona zacha — place the levona on the ma'aracha, the pile or stack, not between them. How then does Abba Shaul put it in the space between the stacks? Abba Shaul responds by citing the verse ule'vinyamin amar yedid Hashem yishkon lavetach alav, where the language of "on" or "upon" clearly does not mean literally on top of, but rather near. So too, al hama'aracha means near the stack — that is, in the adjacent space between the two stacks. The response is compelling: "upon" in such contexts is a common idiom for proximity rather than literal placement atop.

---

## Table Structure

### Golden Panels

The mishna describes ve'arba'ah snifin shel zahav hayu sham — four golden side panels flanking the stacks of bread, two for each side. These snifim served as supports for the structure. The word mefutzalim merosheihem is the subject of debate: one interpretation holds that the tops of these panels were split like the tines of a fork; another holds that they had small protruding pegs, like dowels on a coat rack. On this second interpretation, the half-hollowed reeds (kanim) that were inserted between the loaves would be placed with their hollow ends resting on these pegs, keeping them in place. A third interpretation holds that holes were bored into the panels themselves, and the rods were threaded through from one side to the other.

### Reeds and Rods

The mishna states: ve'esrim ushmonah kanim kechatzi kaneh chalul — twenty-eight rods, each like a half-hollowed reed. With two stacks of bread on the shulchan (fourteen loaves per stack, split into two ma'arachot of six each), there were fourteen rods per side and fourteen for the other, totaling twenty-eight: ve'arba'ah asar laseder zeh ve'arba'ah asar laseder zeh.

### Erev Shabbat Work

Lo sidur kanim velo netilatan docheh et HaShabbat — neither the arrangement of the reeds nor their removal overrides Shabbat. Instead, ela nichnas me'erev Shabbat veshomtan venotnan le'orko shel shulchan: on erev Shabbat, one would enter and slide the reeds out, placing them along the length of the shulchan. The exact nature of the melacha involved — whether it constitutes mefarek, makeh bapatish, or something else — is not resolved here. Part of the reasoning is practical: the reeds needed to be removed in order to extract the bread, since the bread had been baked with indentations corresponding to the rods, and removing the loaves without first withdrawing the rods was not possible. The detailed order of operations for erev Shabbat is a subject the Gemara takes up elsewhere.

### Vessel Orientation

A general principle is stated: vechol hakelim shehayu bamikdash orkan le'orko shel bayit — all the vessels of the Mikdash were aligned with their length running along the length of the building. This statement is mentioned here in connection with the reeds being placed le'orko shel shulchan, and the shulchan itself being aligned accordingly.

---

## Height Calculations

### Yehuda Height

Rabbi Yochanan now turns to calculating the height of the stacked bread. According to the opinion that each loaf was folded two and a half tefachim on each side (Rabbi Yehuda's position), the height of a single loaf as it stands on the table corresponds to two and a half tefachim. With six loaves stacked per ma'aracha, the total height is six times two and a half, which yields fifteen tefachim: nimtza hashulchan mekadesh chamisha asar tefachim lemalah.

### Meir Height

According to the opinion that each loaf was folded two tefachim on each side (Rabbi Meir), the height per loaf is two tefachim. Six loaves stacked yields twelve: nimtza hashulchan mekadesh yud-beis tefachim lemalah.

### Rod Embedding

One might object: ve'haika kanim — what about the rods inserted between the breads? Won't they add to the total height? The answer is sheku'ei meshaka lehu — the rods were embedded in the bread, meaning when the loaves were baked, indentations were formed on the underside to receive the rods.

This answer immediately raises a further question: mai ta'ama mishum demapish lehu — if the reason for the rods was to allow air to circulate so the bread would not spoil, and the rod is entirely buried in the bread, then what purpose do the rods serve? If the breads are sitting directly on each other, there is no airflow. The answer is demagbah lei purta — the rod was embedded only partially. The indentation was shallow, so the bread rested on the rod but retained a small airspace between each loaf. That minimal airspace, while technically adding to the height, is treated as ve'ika purta aval k'man de'leita dami — so slight that it is negligible and does not affect the round numbers.

### Corner Height

The Gemara now asks: ve'ika bezychim — what about the cups of levona? According to Rabbi Meir, who placed them between the stacks in the open space of two tefachim, they lie beside rather than atop the bread and do not add to the height. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who placed them on the bread itself, the Gemara explains: l'gabbei d'lechem havei yatbei, ul'hadei lechem havei kaimei — they were set into a hollow in the top loaf, so they did not add height beyond the loaf itself.

Ve'ika karnot — and what about the corners? Recall that the Lechem Hapanim had karnot seven etzbaot high. Converting: seven etzbaot equal one and three-quarters tefachim. Now consider what the total width of the bread amounts to when accounting for its thickness and karnot. The bread had a thickness of one tefach. Folded up on each side, the folded portion includes: one tefach of thickness, then one and three-quarters tefachim for the keren, then another one and three-quarters for the other keren, and then another tefach of thickness on the other side. The total: one plus one and three-quarters plus one and three-quarters plus one equals five and a half tefachim. But under Rabbi Yehuda's system, an amah (the table's width) is only five tefachim. There is half a tefach too many. How does it fit?

### Curved Corners

Karnot l'gabbei lechem kaif lehu u'lechem aleihu nayach — the corners were curved inward. Rather than standing straight up, the karnot bent inward toward each other, each side curving in by a quarter of a tefach, accounting for the surplus half tefach in total. The bread then rested on these curved corners without the total width exceeding the five tefachim of the table. This was accomplished through the use of a baking mold that shaped the bread accordingly.

---

## Table Frame

### Biblical Source

The Gemara now considers another structural feature: ve'ika misgarto — and what about the misgeret, the frame of the shulchan? The relevant pesukim state: ve'asita shulchan atzei shittim — the table was to be made of acacia wood — amatayim orko ve'amah rochbo ve'amah vachetzi komato; vetzipita oto zahav tahor, ve'asita lo zer zahav saviv; ve'asita lo misgeret tefach saviv; ve'asita zer zahav lemisgarto saviv. The table was to be overlaid with pure gold, fitted with a zer zahav (a golden crown) around its edge, and given a misgeret one tefach wide, itself crowned with a second zer zahav.

The question is: what is this misgeret, and where was it positioned relative to the tabletop?

### Frame Position

There are two opinions. The misgeret may have been the structural element connecting the four legs beneath the tabletop — the crosspieces that stabilize the legs and form the lower frame, upon which the daf (the flat tabletop panel) rested above. This is called misgarto l'mata — the frame was below. Alternatively, the misgeret may have been a raised border above the surface of the tabletop, forming a kind of fence around its perimeter. This is misgarto l'ma'ala — the frame was above.

### Angled Bread

If the misgeret was below, there is no problem: the bread was placed on top of the panel, and the frame adds no height to the bread stack. But ul'man d'amar misgarto l'ma'ala haichi hava — according to the opinion that the misgeret was above, you now have an extra tefach of height before the bread even begins, and that tefach cannot be dismissed as negligible rounding. The answer given is d'peruktei hava mefarkta v'lichma gabei d'shulchan hava yasiv — the misgeret was sloped or angled rather than a full vertical tefach, and the bottom loaf was similarly angled to rest in the groove created by this slope. The bottom bread was thus not raised a full tefach above the surface but rather slid into the angled misgeret, sitting at the level of the table itself. The total height was therefore not affected.

### Rabbi Yosei

A baraita introduces a third view: d'tanya Rabbi Yosei omer lo hayu sham snifin — Rabbi Yosei holds that there were no side panels (snifim) at all. Rather, misgarto shel shulchan ma'amedet et halechem — the misgeret of the shulchan itself held the bread in place. The misgeret stabilized the lowest loaf, and the remaining loaves were stacked above it with the assistance of the rods. The response in the Gemara is amar leih misgarto l'mata hayta — the misgeret was indeed present, but it was positioned below, and therefore the snifim were needed to support the stacks from the sides. According to the view that the misgeret was below, there is no surface feature above the tabletop to support the bread, making the snifim indispensable.

---

## Ritual Impurity

### Transportable Status

Rabbi Yochanan raises a question: according to the one who says the misgeret was below, the daf — the flat tabletop panel — can be reversed and placed either way, which would make it a movable object. According to the one who says the misgeret was above, the daf is essentially fixed in one orientation. But underlying this entire inquiry is a prior question: ke'ilu shulchan bar kibbul tumah hu — the assumption is that the shulchan is susceptible to tumah. Is that assumption warranted?

The difficulty is that kli etz ha'asui lenachat hu — a wooden vessel that is meant to remain stationary is not mekabel tumah. The principle derives from the pasuk mikol kli etz o beged o or o sak: medumiya desak, mah sak mittaltel malei vereikan af kol mittaltel malei vereikan — just as a sack is taken up whether full or empty, so too any vessel capable of tumah must be something one transports in both states. The shulchan, however, was not generally a portable object. It sat in the Beit HaMikdash and stayed there. Accordingly, one might argue it cannot be mekabel tumah at all.

### Reish Lakish

The answer is that the shulchan was in fact moved: shulchan nami mittaltel malei vereikan, kid'Reish Lakish. Reish Lakish derives this from the verse: mai d'cheitiv al hashulchan hatahor. The verse calls it the "pure" shulchan — tahor miklal de'ika tamei, implying that tumah is a real possibility. Furthermore, and more concretely, it teaches: ella melamed shemaggbihin oto le'olei regalim umarin bo lechem ve'omrin lahem reu chibatchem lifnei HaMakom. On the Regalim, the priests would lift the shulchan and carry it out to show the assembled pilgrims, saying: "See how beloved you are before God." The showbread — lechem hapanim, sometimes rendered as "showbread" precisely because of this display — was exhibited to the people. Since the shulchan was indeed transported on these occasions, it qualifies as a movable vessel and is therefore susceptible to tumah.

### Miracle of Bread

This practice prompts a related teaching: de'amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi nes gadol na'asa belechem hapanim — a great miracle was performed with the Lechem Hapanim, shenemar lasum lechem cham beyom hikalcho, that on the day it was taken off the table it was still warm, as fresh as the day it was placed. The Lechem Hapanim was placed on Shabbat and replaced the following Shabbat. The bread had been on the table for a full week — potentially exposed to conditions that would make it stale, cold, or moldy — yet when it was shown to the pilgrims, it appeared and felt freshly baked, steaming hot. The pilgrims saw this and were moved: God's love for Israel was manifest in the miraculous freshness of the bread brought before Him.

### Gold Plating

Having established that the shulchan could become tamei, the Gemara asks: vetipok lei mishum tzipui — why not resolve the entire question more simply, based on the gold plating? If the gold covering determines the character of the object, then the shulchan would be considered a metal vessel — and metal vessels are certainly mekabel tumah, regardless of whether they are transported or stationary.

The relevant principle is examined from a mishna: mi lo tnan hashulchan vehadofleki shenifchetu o shechipan beshayish veshayer bahem mekom hanachat kosot tamein — a table or bench that was broken or covered with marble (or another material) but still retains a portion large enough to place goblets upon it remains tamei. The principle derived is shayer in, lo shayer lo: if some of the original surface remains, it retains its original identity; if none remains, then no. Since the shulchan was completely gold-plated, nothing of the wood surface was left exposed. It would therefore take on the identity of the gold covering, which is metal, which is mekabel tumah.

A further nuance is raised: perhaps it depends on whether the tzipui omeid — whether the covering is firmly attached — or she'eino omeid — whether it is only loosely applied, abutted rather than bonded. Reish Lakish was asked this question by Rabbi Yochanan, and the answer was: lo shana tzipui omeid velo shana tzipui she'eino omeid — it makes no difference whether the plating is firmly attached or not. In either case, the plating determines the identity of the vessel. And whether the rims (livzivin) were plated or not was similarly irrelevant.

Given all this, why can't we simply say the shulchan is mekabel tumah because it is gold-plated metal? Perhaps because vchi teima achti chashivi velo batli — if the underlying material is itself of great value or importance, it may not be nullified by the plating. Reish Lakish held that this exception applied only to kelim from Alexandria that came from overseas; ordinary vessels, even valuable ones, are nullified by their plating. But Rabbi Yochanan held that even locally made valuable vessels are nullified. On his view, then, one should have a clear answer that the gold-plated shulchan is treated as metal.

### Torah's Term

The resolution is: shani shulchan d'rachmana karyei eitz — the shulchan is different, because the Torah itself calls it wood. The verse states, shenemar hamizbeach eitz shalosh amot gavoah ve'arko shtayim amot umiktze'otav lo ve'arko vekirotav eitz vayedaber elai zeh hashulchan asher lifnei Hashem. What begins as a description of the mizbeach made of wood concludes with "this is the shulchan that is before Hashem." The verse calls it eitz — wood — even though it was in fact gold-plated. The Torah's own characterization of the shulchan as wood overrides the general principle that plating determines identity. Therefore, even under Rabbi Yochanan's view that plating normally nullifies the underlying material, the shulchan retains its identity as a wooden vessel, and the question of whether its daf can be mekabel tumah remains live.

---

## Agada

### Altar Teaching

The daf closes with a striking observation of aggadic import. The verse just cited begins with the mizbeach and ends with the shulchan: patach bamizbeach vesiyem bashulchan. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both teach: kol zman sheBeit HaMikdash kayam mizbeach mechaper al ha'adam, ve'achshav she'ein Beit HaMikdash kayam shulchano shel adam mechaper alav. When the Beit HaMikdash stood, the mizbeach brought atonement for a person. Now that it no longer stands, a person's own table brings atonement. This is the source for the well-known teaching that one's dining table is like a mizbeach — through Birkat HaMazon, divrei Torah spoken at the table, and the hospitality shown to guests, the table assumes the atoning and sanctifying role that once belonged to the altar. The transition from mizbeach to shulchan within a single verse is thus read as a deliberate divine hint, embedded in the Torah itself, anticipating the time when the Temple would no longer stand and the table of every Jewish home would carry the weight of the sacred.

---

---

# Menachot 97

## Four Poles/Shulchan

### Pasuk Source

The mishna on daf 97 describes what was on top of the shulchan — the framework for the lechem hapanim — including, as it states, *arba snifin shel zahav hayu sham*: there were four poles of gold. These are the vertical pieces of the framework. The Gemara asks: *menalan hanei milei?* What is the source for these?

Rav Katina answers that the pasuk states: *ve'asita ke'arotav vekapotav ukesotav umenakiotav* — and you shall make its dishes, its spoons, its frames, and its rods.

### Vessel Interpretation

The Gemara does not read this pasuk according to its simple translation. Rather: *ke'arotav* — the dishes — *elu dfusin*, these are the frame-molds. *kapotav* — the spoons — *elu bezichin*, these are the spoons used for the levona. *kesotav* — *elu snifin*, these are the poles of the framework we are discussing. *umenakiotav* — *elu kanim*, these are the rods that separate the loaves of lechem hapanim from one another. The phrase *asher yusach bahen* — with which you cover — refers to the kanim, *shemesach'chin bahen et halechem*: with which you cover the bread.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava raises a difficulty. We have a principle: *lo sidur hakanim velo netilatan docha et hashabbat* — neither the arranging of the rods nor their removal overrides Shabbat. Now, the lechem hapanim was replaced every Shabbat, and everything required for the avodah in the Beit Hamikdash does override Shabbat. If the kanim are described explicitly in the Torah as part of the apparatus of the shulchan — and thus part of the avodah — why would arranging them not override Shabbat? This seems to undermine the claim that *kesotav* and *umenakiotav* refer to Temple vessels of Torah-level status.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava then retracts his challenge: *lav milta hi* — that was not a valid argument. He cites the principle stated by Rabbi Akiva in a mishna: *kol melacha she'efshar la'asotah me'erev shabbat einah docha et hashabbat* — any labor that could have been performed before Shabbat does not override Shabbat even when it is required for the avodah. The kanim could be arranged before Shabbat. Why? Because the purpose of the rods is *delo liy'apesh lechem* — to prevent the loaves from becoming moldy when stacked against one another. But *behei shi'ura lo mi'apesh* — over the short span of Shabbat itself, the loaves would not have time to become moldy. Therefore, the rods can be removed before Shabbat and replaced afterward, and there is no need to perform this act on Shabbat at all.

### Rod Procedure

A baraita describes the precise procedure. On erev Shabbat, the kohen would enter and remove the rods from beneath the loaves, placing them along the length of the shulchan. After Shabbat, he would return, lift the edge of each challah, and slip a rod underneath — *magbi'a rasha shel challah umachnis kaneh tachteha* — repeating this for each loaf. In this way, the loaves would be without the rods for only half a day at most — from the time the new loaves were placed until after Shabbat — which is insufficient time for them to become moldy.

### Rods Per Loaf

The baraita continues with further detail. The lechem hapanim was arranged in two stacks of six loaves each. Of the loaves in a given stack: *arba challos tzerichos shelosha shelosha kanim* — four of the loaves required three rods each beneath them. *ha'elyonah einah tzerichah ela shenayim* — the topmost loaf required only two rods, *lefi she'einah lah masoi* — because it bears no additional weight on top of it. *hatachtonah einah tzerichah kol ikar* — the bottom loaf requires no rods at all, *lefi shehu munach al taharo shel shulchan* — because it rests directly on the shulchan itself. Rashi explains *taharo shel shulchan* as indicating that the golden table is cool, and it is the contact of warm bread against warm bread that risks mold; contact with the cold metal surface does not present the same concern. The Shita Mekubetzet similarly explains: *shulchan d'karir* — the table is cool.

---

## Mizbeiach Measures

### Rabbi Meir Position

The Gemara now digresses from the details of the shulchan to the mizbeiach. A mishna elsewhere records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about the amot used in the Mikdash. Rabbi Meir says: *kol amos she'hayu bamikdash beinoniyos* — all the amot used in the Mikdash were the medium measure. We will shortly encounter amot of five tefachim, six tefachim, and seven tefachim; for now we deal with five and six. The beinoni, according to Rabbi Meir, is the six-tefach amah. The exceptions are: *chutz m'mizbeach hazahav* — the inner golden altar for the ketores — and the keren of the mizbeiach ha'olah, the sovev, and the yesod. Those specific elements were measured not with the six-tefach amah but with a five-tefach amah.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. He draws the distinction differently: *amas binyan shisha tefachim* — for construction purposes the amah is six tefachim, *v'shel kelim chamisha* — but for the assembly of the kelim and klei shares, the five-tefach amah was used.

### Single Pasuk Source

Rabbi Yochanan observes: *misheneihem mikra echad darshu* — both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda derive their positions from the same single pasuk. That pasuk is in Yechezkel: *v'eileh middos hamizbeiach ba'amos amah amah vatofach v'cheik ha'amah v'amah rochav u'gevulah el sfatah saviv zeres ha'echad v'zeh gav hamizbeiach* — these are the measurements of the mizbeiach in amot: an amah and a tefach; and the cheik ha'amah; and an amah of width; and its border to its edge all around is one zeret; and this is the gav hamizbeiach.

### Yechezkel Parsing

The Gemara proceeds to parse this pasuk, and it must be said that this is Yechezkel — one must suspend ordinary reading expectations. In a preliminary reading: *v'eileh middos hamizbeiach ba'amos* — these are the measurements of the mizbeiach in amot — the Gemara will interpret *ba'amos* as referring to medium amot. *amah amah vatofach* — the Gemara understands this as: a standard amah is five tefachim, and the medium amah is that five plus one tefach, equaling six. *cheik ha'amah* will be interpreted as the base. *ve'amah rochav* concerns a width of an amah. *u'gevulah el sfatah saviv* — the distance from the border to the edge — refers to the keren. *zeres ha'echad* — that width is one zeret, which is half an amah. *v'zeh gav hamizbeiach* — this is the top of the mizbeiach.

Rabbi Meir understands *zeh gav hamizbeiach* as: these specific measurements of the mizbeiach — those just enumerated — use the five-tefach amah, while all other kelim in the Mikdash used the six-tefach amah. Rabbi Yehuda reads the same phrase *zeh gav hamizbeiach* differently: just as this mizbeiach was measured with five-tefach amot, so too the other kelim likewise used five-tefach amot for their assembly.

---

## Mizbeiach Height

### Initial Calc

The Gemara now attempts to work through these measurements. The initial assumption is: *mi'yesod ve'ad sovev be'ama bas chamisha begova* — from the base to the sovev, the middle section of the mizbeiach, we are using five-tefach amot for the vertical measurement. The phrase *cheik ha'amah ve'amah rochav* is interpreted as follows: from the base (*mecheik ha'amah*) until you reach a horizontal surface (*ve'ad rochav*) — that is, as you ascend the vertical face until arriving at the ledge — that stretch uses the five-tefach amah. The first horizontal surface encountered is after the yesod. The yesod is one amah high, and then the exposed horizontal surface of the yesod appears before the body of the mizbeiach rises further to the sovev. The sovev is five amot above the yesod, so the total run from the base to the top of the sovev is six amot, all measured in five-tefach amot. Above the sovev the remaining height is four amot measured in six-tefach amot.

### 54 Tefachim

With this interpretation, the total height of the mizbeiach is: six times five equals thirty tefachim, plus four times six equals twenty-four tefachim, for a total of fifty-four tefachim. *palga d'mizbeach kamah haveh esrin v'shiv'ah* — the halfway point of the mizbeiach is twenty-seven tefachim. This matters because certain matnos dam had to be applied to the upper half of the mizbeiach and others to the lower half, and there was a red line — *chut shel sikra chogro b'emtza* — painted around the mizbeiach at the halfway mark to distinguish *damim ha'elyonim* from *damim hatachtonim*.

From the top of the karnot down to the surface of the sovev is four amot of six tefachim each, equaling twenty-four tefachim. The difference between twenty-four and twenty-seven is three tefachim — meaning the surface of the sovev is three tefachim above the halfway mark of the mizbeiach.

### Baraita Problem
