At this point the Gemara raises a difficulty from a baraita concerning olas ha'of, the bird elevation offering, whose blood must be applied to the upper portion of the mizbeiach. The procedure: the kohen ascends the ramp, turns off at the sovev, proceeds to the southeast corner, performs the melika, and *umamatze es damo al kir hamizbe'ach* — squeezes the blood against the wall of the mizbeiach. Since he is standing on the sovev, he is already above the halfway mark.

But the baraita then states: *ve'im asah l'mata meraglav afilu amah achas kesherah* — if he applied the blood below his feet, even a full amah below the surface of the sovev, it is still valid. This is the problem. Under our current calculation, the halfway mark is only three tefachim below the sovev. A full amah — whether five or six tefachim — brings him well below the halfway mark. *hacha yehei elyona lemata mishnei tefachim* — under this calculation the kohen would be placing blood two tefachim below the halfway point and calling it valid. Our calculations must therefore be wrong, and the interpretation of the pasuk must be revisited.

### Reinterpret Horizontal

The Gemara therefore reinterprets: *cheik ha'amah kenisa* — when the navi says *cheik ha'amah*, the base was an amah of indentation, meaning a horizontal measurement, not vertical. Similarly, *amah rochav kenisa* — the width of an amah is also an indentation, a horizontal measure. The five-tefach amah, on this reading, governs horizontal measurements — the width of the exposed ledge at the yesod and at the sovev — not the vertical height of the mizbeiach.

---

## Revised Calcs

### 60 Tefachim

With all vertical measurements now in six-tefach amot, the total height of the mizbeiach is ten times six, equaling sixty tefachim. *palga demizbeach kama havei sheloshim* — the halfway point is now thirty tefachim. From the top of the karnot to the surface of the sovev is four amot of six tefachim, equaling twenty-four. The gap between the sovev surface and the halfway mark is therefore thirty minus twenty-four, which is six tefachim.

### Baraita Fit

The baraita's ruling now fits perfectly. If the kohen stands on the sovev and applies the blood even one full amah — six tefachim — below his feet, he is still exactly at the halfway mark. *detanya mesulak lemata meraglav va'afilu amah achas kesherah* — the ruling that even one amah below the sovev surface is valid is precisely accounted for by the corrected calculation.

### Surface Area

The Gemara, however, now faces a different complication. Having established that horizontal measurements use the five-tefach amah while vertical measurements use the six-tefach amah, we must reckon with the surface area dimensions of the mizbeiach — and this is where the analysis becomes intricate.

### 32x32 to 24x24

A baraita states: *mizbeach haya lamed-bet al lamed-bet* — the mizbeiach was thirty-two amot by thirty-two amot at its base. It then goes up one amah and indents one amah — *ala ama vekanas ama zehu yesod* — that is the yesod. In ordinary six-tefach amot, this should leave thirty by thirty. But the Gemara notes: *nimtza lamed veshenei tefachim havei* — what actually remains is thirty amot plus two tefachim. The reason is that the indentation of the yesod uses a five-tefach amah, not a six-tefach amah. So instead of removing two full six-tefach amot (one from each side), we remove two five-tefach amot — leaving two extra tefachim unaccounted for in our standard reckoning.

The mizbeiach then rises five amot and indents one amah — *ala hamesh vekanas ama* — this is the sovev. Again, in standard terms this should bring us to twenty-eight by twenty-eight. But the Gemara protests: *esrim u'shmona v'arbaa tefachim havu* — it is actually twenty-eight plus four tefachim, because now we have accumulated four extra tefachim from the two non-standard horizontal indentations. The Gemara suggests that the mishna simply does not bother counting partial amot — it rounds down. This is admittedly unsatisfying but is offered as a response.

Continuing, the karnot occupy one amah on each side, reducing the surface to twenty-six by twenty-six. And beyond that, one amah on each side is the walkway for the kohanim, leaving twenty-four by twenty-four as *makom hamaaracha* — the location of the actual fire. But here the Gemara calculates that the actual figure is not twenty-six but twenty-seven, since we have now lost a full amah's worth of tefachim through three applications of the non-standard measure. The Gemara again answers *lo dak* — the mishna is not being precise. These are acknowledged as unsatisfying answers.

### Ariel 12 Center

The Gemara then raises a more serious problem. The navi in Yechezkel states: *v'ha'ariel shteim esreh orech b'shteim esreh rochav ravuah el arbaat rivav* — the ariel, the top surface of the mizbeiach, was twelve by twelve, square to its four sides. One might think this means it was literally only twelve by twelve amot — but we have established that the maaracha surface was twenty-four by twenty-four. The resolution: *keshehu omer el arbaat rivav melamed she'be'emtza hu moded* — when it says "to its four sides," it teaches that the measurement is from the center. Twelve from the center in each of the four directions yields twenty-four by twenty-four measured from the outside — *shteim esreh l'chol ruach v'ruach*.

Here one cannot appeal to imprecision; the navi's words are deliberate. Accordingly, the Gemara considers whether six of the amot used in the overall calculation might themselves be five-tefach amot, which would make the arithmetic work. But this is immediately rejected: *rav kol ha'azarah* — it creates a problem with how the mizbeiach fits within the azarah.

---

## Mizbeiach/Azarah

### Azarah 187x135

A mishna records the dimensions of the entire azarah: *kol ha'azarah haysah orech me'ah ushmonim vesheva al rochav me'ah ushloshim vechamesh mimizrach lema'arav* — the azarah was 187 amot in one direction and 135 amot east to west.

### Space Breakdown

The 187 amot are accounted for as follows: eleven amot for the walking space of the Yisraelim; eleven amot for the walking space of the kohanim; thirty-two amot for the mizbeiach; twenty-two amot between the ulam and the mizbeiach; one hundred amot for the heichal itself; and eleven amot behind the beis hakappores — the space between the back of the kodesh hakodashim and the wall of the azarah. The total is 11 + 11 + 32 + 22 + 100 + 11 = 187. The mizbeiach is listed here explicitly as thirty-two amot. This constrains any interpretation that would enlarge its dimensions.

### Final Interp

The Gemara's final resolution: *cheik ha'amah begovah* — the phrase *cheik ha'amah* refers to height, the first amah of the base measured vertically, and that amah is a five-tefach amah. *amah rochav kenisah* — the next phrase, *amah rochav*, refers to the width of the horizontal indentation of the yesod, which is also a five-tefach amah. As for *gevulah el sfatah saviv* — the border of the keren — the Gemara says *lo shanah hachi velo shanah hachi*: it does not significantly affect the calculation either way. The conclusion is that the mizbeiach's total height is fifty-eight tefachim — eight amot of six tefachim each, plus two amot (the bottom yesod and the top keren) of five tefachim each: 8 × 6 + 2 × 5 = 58.

The halfway mark is therefore twenty-nine tefachim. From the top of the karnot down to the sovev is four full amot plus one small amah: 4 × 6 = 24, plus approximately half of 5, giving roughly 23 tefachim from the karnot to the sovev. The gap between the sovev surface and the halfway mark is six tefachim — one full six-tefach amah. *detanya mesulak lemata meraglav va'afilu amah achas kesherah* — the baraita's ruling that blood applied one full amah below the sovev is valid is confirmed: one amah below the sovev is exactly the halfway mark. *dayka nami dechsiv cheik ha'amah ve'amah rochav* — this is further corroborated by the phrasing of the pasuk itself, which describes both a vertical base-amah and a horizontal width-amah, corresponding precisely to the two applications of the five-tefach measure.

---

## Standard Amot

### Six Tefach

The Gemara asks: *vekamah amah beinonis* — how large is the medium amah? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *shisha tefachim* — six tefachim. Rav Yosef bar Avin adds that we find this confirmed in the mishna itself. Rabbi Meir states that the shulchan was twelve tefachim long and six tefachim wide. We know from the Torah that the shulchan measured two amot by one amah; since Rabbi Meir gives those dimensions as twelve by six tefachim, each amah equals six tefachim. This is the amah beinonis.

The Gemara then notes: *michlal dehavi amah denfisha minah* — if there is a middle measure, there must be a larger one as well. Indeed there is.

### Two Sticks

The mishna states: *shtei amos hayu bishushan habira* — there were two measuring sticks kept in the chamber known as Shushan Habira within the Beit Hamikdash. One was in the northeast corner and one in the southeast corner. The one in the northeast corner was *yeseira al shel moshe chatzi etzba* — half a finger-breadth longer than the amah of Moshe, which was presumably used for the measurements of the Mishkan and served as the foundational standard. The one in the southeast corner was a further half-etzba longer still — thus a full etzba longer than Moshe's amah.

Why were two standards maintained? The mishna explains: *kdei sheyiyu haumnim notlin biktana umachzirim bigdola* — so that craftsmen would submit their cost estimates based on the smaller (slightly enlarged) measure but would be required to deliver based on the larger (even more enlarged) measure. The actual standard of Moshe served as the basis for cost estimates, and delivery was measured against one of these enlarged standards. The Gemara adds that this was instituted *kdei shelo yavo'u lidei meila* — so that craftsmen would not inadvertently commit meila by delivering slightly less than required and thus shortchanging the Mikdash. Rashi and Tosafot discuss whether this constitutes technical meila in the strict halachic sense or simply the moral equivalent of misappropriating Temple property.

### Two Rationales

One might ask why two distinct enlarged standards were necessary rather than one. *tartei lama li?* The Gemara answers: *chada lchaspa vedahava* — one was for gold and silver work, *vechada livinyana* — and one for building materials. Since precious materials are costly, it would be unduly burdensome to require craftsmen working with gold and silver to over-deliver by a full etzba; therefore the half-etzba standard was used for such work. For ordinary building materials — wood, plaster, and the like — the additional cost of a full etzba's surplus is negligible, so the larger standard was applied there.

---

## Shushan Picture

### Location

The mishna also records that *sha'ar hamizrach alav sushan habira tzura* — the eastern gate bore an engraving or picture of Shushan Habira. This is a striking detail — a foreign city's image permanently affixed to the Temple. It also explains why the chamber housing the measuring sticks was called Shushan Habira.

### Remembrance/Fear

A dispute is recorded between Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi over the reason. One holds: *kdei sheyeidu meheichan ba'u* — so that the people would know and remember where they had come from. Rashi elaborates: *kdei sheyeidu veyeira'u meheichan ba'u* — they would see the image of Shushan and recall that they had returned from Persian exile, *v'yitnu hoda'ah lamalchut shehotzi'am misham* — and give acknowledgment to the Persian government that permitted their return to Eretz Yisrael. This is a political statement of gratitude. The Maharsha understands the gratitude as directed toward God, who moved the Persian authorities to permit the return; Rashi's language, however, points to the Persian government itself. This is the context of the second Beit Hamikdash.

The other opinion holds that the image was placed there not for gratitude but *kdei shetehei eimat malchut aleihen* — so that those who saw it would maintain a healthy fear and respect for government authority.

### Fear Government

This second rationale leads into a broader statement: *amar rav yannai le'olam tehei eimat malchut alecha* — one should always maintain fear of governmental authority.

### Textual Support

Rav Yannai derives this from the incident of the tenth plague. When Moshe warned Pharaoh, he said: *ve'yardu kol avadecha eileh elai vehishtachavu li leimor* — all your servants will come down to me and bow before me. He said "your servants" — he did not say "you yourself will come down." *v'ilu ledidi lo ka'amar lei* — he did not address Pharaoh directly in this way, as an expression of *eimat malchut*, a show of deference to the king even in the moment of confrontation.

Rabbi Yochanan derives the same principle from a different pasuk: *veyad Hashem hayetah el Eliyahu vayeshannes matnav vayaratz lifnei Achav ad bo Yizreel* — the hand of God came upon Eliyahu and he girded his loins and ran before Achav all the way to Yizreel. Rashi explains that Achav was riding and it would not have been proper conduct toward the king for Eliyahu simply to let him pass; therefore Eliyahu ran as an escort before the royal chariot for the entire distance, as a demonstration of respect for *malchus*.

---

---

# Menachot 98

## Leaves that Heal

### Pasuk & Dispute Intro

The Gemara on this daf opens with what appears at first to come out of left field — a dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi that, while unconnected to the immediately preceding discussion, mirrors the structure of an earlier dispute between those same two Amoraim. The Gemara cites the pasuk from Yechezkel, *va-alehu li-trufa* — "and its leaves are for healing" — referring to the Messianic vision of a spring flowing out from beneath the Kodesh Hakodashim, with trees growing along its banks. This is one of those idyllic visions of the end of days, where the Mikdash serves as the source of water, healing, and renewal for the entire world.

### Upper vs. Lower Mouth

The dispute centers on the precise nature of the healing described in the pasuk. *chad amar le-hatir pe shel ma'ala* — one opinion holds that these leaves will open the mouths of those who are mute, restoring the power of speech. *ve-chad amar le-hatir pe shel mata* — the other holds that they will open the lower mouth, that is, they will cure the barrenness of women who are unable to conceive.

### Chizkiya & Bar Kappara

The Gemara then cites a parallel dispute that is more explicit in its formulation. Chizkiya says the leaves serve *le-hatir pe ilmim* — to open the mouths of the dumb. Bar Kappara says *le-hatir pe akarot* — to open the womb of barren women. These two pairs of opinions, while stated separately, clearly correspond to one another.

---

## Twelve Loaves Setup

### Three Details Explained

From here the Gemara transitions to the laws governing the arrangement of the Lechem HaPanim on the Shulchan. The Gemara cites the relevant pesukim: *ve-lakachta solet ve-afita otah shtem esrei chalot* — you shall take flour and bake twelve loaves, each made of two esronim of flour, which amounts to a remarkably large loaf. The subsequent pasuk then commands: *ve-samta otam shtayim ma'arachot shesh hama'arechet al hashulchan hatahor lifnei Hashem* — you shall place them in two stacks, six in a stack, on the pure table before God. The specification is tripartite: twelve loaves, two stacks, six in each stack.

### Why Three Details Needed

The Gemara proceeds to demonstrate why each of the three details is indispensable. Had the pasuk stated only that there were twelve loaves in two stacks — without specifying six in a stack — one might have thought the division could be four and eight, or any other uneven split. Therefore the Torah specifies *shesh hama'arechet*, six in a stack. Conversely, had the pasuk stated only two stacks of six without specifying a total of twelve, one might have concluded there were three stacks of six, yielding eighteen loaves. Therefore the Torah specifies twelve. And had the pasuk specified only twelve loaves in stacks, without stating that there were two stacks of six, one might have arranged them as three stacks of four. The Gemara concludes: *ha ad shelo yomeru gimel mikra'ot hallalu lo lamadnu* — had all three specifications not been stated, we would not have known the correct arrangement.

### Valid Arrangement

The operative ruling is therefore: *noten shtei ma'arachot shel sheish sheish* — one places two stacks of six each. If one placed them four and eight, *lo asah* — the arrangement is invalid. This question is in some sense theoretical, since once the wooden frame is constructed to hold the loaves in position, there is really only one way to stack them properly.

### Seventh Loaf Question

The Gemara then raises a more interesting edge case: what if one placed two stacks of seven each, for a total of fourteen loaves? Within those fourteen, the required twelve are still present, arranged as two stacks of six, with one extra loaf resting on top of each stack. *rabbi omer ro'in et ha-elyonah ke-ilu einah* — Rabbi rules that the extra loaf on top is simply disregarded, as though it were not there. It does not invalidate the six loaves beneath it. Notably, the Gemara does not at this point raise the issue of *bal tosif* — the prohibition against adding to the commandments — which one might have expected to be relevant here. The classic cases of *bal tosif* involve something like adding a fifth parchment to one's tefillin or extending a festival by an extra day. Whether placing a seventh loaf on the Shulchan rises to that level is left unaddressed, with Rabbi's ruling apparently treating the extra loaf as simply extraneous to the mitzvah itself.

### Frankincense Problem

The Gemara challenges Rabbi's ruling, however, from a different angle. The pasuk states *venatata al hama'arechet levonah zachah* — you shall place frankincense on the stack. The Gemara's understanding is that the frankincense must rest directly on top of the mitzvah bread. If there is a seventh loaf sitting on top of the six, then the frankincense is resting on bread that is not part of the mitzvah — it is resting on the extraneous loaf, not on the six. This creates a significant problem for Rabbi's ruling.

### Al Means Near

The Gemara resolves this by invoking Rabbi's consistent interpretive position. Rav Chisda said to Rav Hamnuna — or according to an alternative tradition, Rav Hamnuna said to Rav Chisda — *rabbi le-ta'ameih*, that Rabbi's ruling is internally consistent, because he holds that the word *al* in the pasuk does not mean directly upon, but rather *besamuch* — in proximity to. According to Rabbi, *venatata al hama'arechet levonah zachah* means the frankincense is placed near the stack, not necessarily resting directly upon the top of the mitzvah bread.

### Paroches as Proof

The Gemara then asks: how do we know that *al* can mean near rather than directly on? Perhaps *al mamash* — it means literally on top. The Gemara answers from the pasuk regarding the Paroches: *ve-sachos al ha-aron et ha-paroches* — the curtain is to be spread *al*, upon, the Aron. Yet we know that the Paroches was not draped over the Aron; it stood upright as a curtain dividing the Heichal from the Kodesh Hakodashim. Nevertheless the pasuk uses the word *al*. We thus have proof that *al* can indicate proximity rather than direct placement, and Rabbi's position is fully coherent.

---

## Vessel Orientation & Ark

### All Vessels East-West

The Gemara now turns to the question of how the vessels of the Mikdash were oriented within the space. The Mishkan — and by extension the Mikdash — was oriented along an east-west axis. The general rule established by the Gemara is: *kol ha-keilim she-ba-Mikdash orkan l'orkan shel bayis* — all the vessels in the Mikdash were oriented in the same direction as the building itself, that is, east-west.

### Ark North-South

There is one prominent exception: *chutz mei-aron* — except for the Aron, *she-orko l'rochbo shel bayis* — whose length was oriented along the width of the building, that is, north-south. The Aron thus ran north-south within the Kodesh Hakodashim. And correspondingly, *kach hayu badav munachim* — and that is how its carrying poles were placed.

### Poles Stretched Out

The Gemara asks: how do we know that the poles ran east-west? *detanya* — as we have a Braita: *vayarikhu habadim* — the poles stretched outward. One might think that they simply extended without touching the Paroches, but the Gemara cites the pasuk in Melachim Aleph 8:8: *vayera'u rashei habadim min hakodesh al pnei hadvir* — the tips of the poles were visible from the Kodesh, looking toward the Dvir, i.e., the Kodesh Hakodashim. Yet another phrase indicates they were not visible from outside. This seems contradictory.

### Poles Bulge Paroches

The resolution is: *dochakin uvotin baparochet* — they pressed against and bulged through the Paroches. The poles did not pierce or tear the curtain, but they pushed against it from behind, creating visible protrusions. From inside the Heichal, one could see where the poles were pressing against the curtain, yet they were not exposed to view from outside. The Gemara invokes the imagery of Shir Hashirim: *domim kishnei dadei isha* — they resembled two breasts. *shenem'ar tzror hamor dodi li bein shadai yalin* — "my beloved is to me like a bundle of myrrh that lies between my breasts." On Yom Kippur, the Kohen Gadol would enter the Kodesh Hakodashim with the incense, which is the *mor*, and the image of the incense resting between the twin protrusions of the poles pressing through the Paroches gives rise to this striking use of the verse from Shir Hashirim.

### Pole Placement Logic

The Gemara then asks: from where do we know that the poles were on the long sides of the Aron rather than the short sides? The dimensions of the Aron were two and a half amot long by one and a half amot wide. *amar rav yehuda: trei gavrei b'amta u'palga lo mistagei* — two people cannot fit side by side in a space of only one and a half amot. The Gemara's assumption is that when the Aron was carried, two people stood at each end of the poles, walking within the space between the poles. If the poles were on the short side, only one and a half amot would be available for the carriers to stand abreast — not enough room. But on the long side, two and a half amot are available, which is sufficient for two carriers to stand side by side. Therefore the poles must have been placed on the long sides, oriented east-west.

### Four Carriers

Finally, the Gemara asks: how do we know that there were four carriers total — two on each side? *de'ketiv: u'nas'u ha'kehatim nosei ha'mikdash* — it is written that the Kehatim, the *nosei*, the carriers of the Mikdash — referring to the Aron as the holiest object — carried it. *nosei* is plural, implying at least two. *nosei ha'mikdash* — another plural — implies another two, yielding four carriers in total.

---

## Tables & Menorot

### Solomon's Ten Tables

The Gemara now discusses an important historical development in the layout of the Mikdash. *asarah shulchanot asah shlomo haMelech* — King Shlomo made ten tables when he built the Beit HaMikdash. The pasuk in Melachim records this explicitly. These tables were placed in the Heichal, five on the right and five on the left. One might think this means five on the right side of the building and five on the left — but that cannot be correct, because the Torah mandates that the Shulchan be placed on the north side. The phrase "right and left" therefore means: the original table of Moshe stood in the center, with five of Shlomo's tables to its right and five to its left, forming two rows flanking the original.

### Solomon's Ten Menorot

The same structure applies to the Menorah. *esser menorot asah shlomo* — Shlomo also made ten Menorot, as stated explicitly in the pasuk. He placed them in the Heichal, five on the right and five on the left. Again, this cannot mean five on the south side and five on the north side, because the Torah requires *ve-et ha-menorah nochach ha-shulchan* — the Menorah must be opposite the Shulchan, on the south side. The arrangement is therefore analogous: Moshe's Menorah in the center, five of Shlomo's to the right and five to the left.

### Location Dispute

There is a Tannaitic dispute regarding where precisely in the Heichal these tables and Menorot were placed. One Tanna says *michatzi ha-bayit u'lifnim* — they were positioned within the inner half of the building. Another says *meshlish ha-bayit velifnim* — within the inner third. The Gemara explains that this is not actually a contradiction. The Heichal was forty amot long and the Kodesh Hakodashim was twenty amot. The Tanna who says "half" is calculating half of the entire sixty-amot space — half of sixty is thirty, which puts them within the back thirty amot. The Tanna who says "third" is speaking only of the Heichal's own forty amot — a third of sixty is also twenty — placing them within the back twenty amot of the Heichal. Both opinions arrive at the same physical location.

### Rabbi East-West

The question of orientation now becomes central. *mizrach u'maarav hayu munachim, divrei rabbi* — they were oriented east-west, in the opinion of Rabbi. Rabbi derives the orientation of the Shulchan from the Menorah: just as the Menorah was oriented east-west, so too were the tables. And how do we know the Menorah was east-west? *midechtiv: bener ma'aravi ya'aroch oto aharon lifnei hashem* — because the pasuk specifies a western lamp, one of the seven lamps designated as the primary one. If the Menorah were oriented north-south, all lamps would be equally close to the west, equally close to the Kodesh Hakodashim. The fact that there is specifically a *western* lamp — one that is more westerly than the others — demonstrates that the Menorah was aligned east-west, with one lamp closer to the Kodesh Hakodashim than the rest. Rashi understands the western lamp to be the westernmost one; Tosafot understands it to be the second from the east, i.e., the first one encountered as you move westward. In any case, the point is established: the Menorah ran east-west, and so did the Shulchan.

### R. Elazar North-South

Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon disagrees. *tzafon vedarom* — he holds both the Menorah and the tables were oriented north-south. He derives his position from the Aron: just as the Aron was oriented north-south, so too were the vessels of the Heichal. The Gemara asks: why doesn't Rabbi also learn from the Aron? The answer is that we apply the principle *danin chutz michutz ve'ein danin chutz mibifnim* — we derive the law of an item in the outer sanctum from another item in the outer sanctum, not from something in the inner sanctum. The Aron was in the Kodesh Hakodashim; the Menorah and Shulchan were in the Heichal. Rabbi therefore derives one from the other, keeping the comparison within the same space. Conversely, the Gemara asks why Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon does not learn from the Shulchan, which might appear to have been east-west. His reply is that the Menorah itself was also north-south — he does not concede the east-west orientation of either vessel.

### Wicks Lean Center

This raises an obvious question: if the Menorah ran north-south, how can the pasuk speak of a specifically *western* lamp? Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon answers: *mitzadadi lehu itzdudei* — the wicks were angled. Even if the body of the Menorah ran north-south, the wicks could be tilted to face toward the center, and thus the central lamp's wick could be tilted specifically toward the west, creating a functionally westernmost lamp even within a north-south orientation.

### Middle Lamp Superior

A Braita is cited in support: *el mul pnei ha-menorah yairu shivat ha-nerot* — the seven lamps shone toward the face of the Menorah. *melamed shehayu metzadedim pneihem klapei ner emtzai* — this teaches that all the lamps had their faces, their wicks, angled toward the central lamp. *amar rabbi natan: mikan she'emtzai meshubach* — from here Rabbi Natan derives that the central lamp is the most distinguished of the seven. This accords with the structure of the Menorah, where the central shaft is the primary column from which the six branches extend.

---

## East-West Spacing Problem

### N-S Fits Easily

Having established the two opinions, the Gemara now examines whether the physical dimensions of the Heichal actually permit each arrangement. *bishlama l'man d'amar tzafon vedarom shapir* — according to Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon's north-south orientation, there is no difficulty. The ten tables of Shlomo plus Moshe's table total eleven, arranged in two rows of five with Moshe's table in the center. The depth of the space available along the north-south axis easily accommodates five tables oriented with their width running north-south, since there is ample room in that dimension.

### E-W Space Calc

But a serious problem arises for Rabbi's view that the tables ran east-west. Here the challenge is not the length of the rows but the width — how much space is consumed across the north-south axis. Working through the calculation: the table had to be set two and a half amot from the wall, because two Kohanim needed to walk side by side alongside it during the exchange of the Lechem HaPanim, just as two carriers were needed for the Aron. The table itself was one amah wide. Then two and a half amot of space between that row and Moshe's central table. Another amah for Moshe's table. Another two and a half amot between Moshe's table and the second row. And another amah for the second row. Adding these together: 2.5 + 1 + 2.5 + 1 + 2.5 + 1 = 10.5 amot. But the available north-south space on the north side of the Heichal was only ten amot, meaning the arrangement would spill half an amah into the south side, where the Menorah was required to stand. This is a genuine spatial impossibility under Rabbi's east-west arrangement.

### Moshe Table Front

The Gemara resolves this: *mi savrat chad dara havo* — who says there was a single row arrangement with Moshe's table in the middle between two parallel rows? *trei darei havo* — there were two rows, yes, but Moshe's table was not positioned between them in the center of the north-south space. Rather, it was positioned *lifnim*, up toward the front, closer to the entrance of the Heichal, offset from the two rows so that it did not occupy the space between them. With Moshe's table moved to the front, the two rows of five could be placed close enough to each other that the total north-south width fit within the available ten amot: 2.5 + 1 + 2.5 + 1 + 2.5 = 9.5 amot for the two rows and their clearances, which fits within ten.

### Teacher-Student

The positioning of Moshe's table toward the front, with the two rows of Shlomo's tables behind it, is described evocatively: *k'talmid hayoshev lifnei rabo* — like a student sitting before his teacher. Moshe's table is the teacher; the two rows of tables extending behind it are the students arranged at his feet. The spatial and hierarchical arrangement reinforce one another.

---

## Functional Use

### One Table Opinion

The Gemara now turns to the question of whether Shlomo's ten tables were actually used or were merely ornamental. The first Tanna holds: *v'lo hayu mesadrin ela al shel Moshe* — the Lechem HaPanim was arranged only on Moshe's table, not on any of the ten tables Shlomo constructed. The proof is from Melachim, which refers in the singular to *ha-shulchan asher alav lechem hapanim* — the table upon which was the Lechem HaPanim. The singular implies that only one table bore the bread. Similarly, with respect to the Menorot: *v'lo hayu madlikin ela beshel Moshe* — only Moshe's Menorah was actually lit. Again, the proof is from Melachim, which refers in the singular to *menoras hazahav* being lit in the evening.

### All Tables Opinion

Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua takes the contrary position: *al kulam hayu mesadrin* — bread was arranged on all of them, and *uv'kulan hayu madlikin* — all the Menorot were lit. His proofs come from Divrei Hayamim, which uses the plural forms: *es hashulchanos va'aleihem lechem hapanim* — the tables with the Lechem HaPanim on them — and *es hamenoros v'neroseihem leva'aram* — the Menorot and their lamps that were kindled. The Gemara notes that this is one of the well-known instances where Melachim and Divrei Hayamim present differing versions of the same events.

### Three Functional

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda offers a third position. He agrees with the first Tanna that the Lechem HaPanim was placed only on Moshe's table, but he offers a different explanation of the plural references in Divrei Hayamim. *elu sheloshah shulchanos shehayu ba-mikdash* — the plural refers to three functionally active tables that existed in the Mikdash. *shenayim shehayu ba-ulam mifnim lepesach ha-bayis* — two of these were located in the Ulam, the antechamber, just inside the entrance to the Heichal, where the outer altar stood. These two tables served a specific ceremonial function during the weekly exchange of the Lechem HaPanim.

### Silver & Gold

One of the two Ulam tables was silver and one was gold. *al shel kesef nosein lechem hapanim bichnisaso* — on the silver table, the fresh bread was placed upon entering, that is, when the new loaves were brought in to replace the old ones. *v'al shel zahav biyitziaso* — and on the gold table, the removed bread was placed upon exiting. The procedure was thus: fresh bread was set on the silver table in the Ulam; the old bread was removed from Moshe's table inside the Heichal and placed on the gold table in the Ulam; then the fresh bread was brought in and placed on Moshe's table. This accounts for the plural "tables" in Divrei Hayamim — it refers not to Shlomo's ten ceremonial tables but to these two functional exchange tables together with the primary golden table inside the Heichal.

---

## Status Elevation

### Ascend Not Descend

The choice to place the fresh bread on the silver table rather than the gold, and the old bread on the gold rather than the silver, is governed by the principle of *ma'alin bakodesh v'lo moridin* — in matters of sanctity, we ascend rather than descend. Gold is more precious than silver. Fresh bread that is about to enter the sacred space and be placed on the golden table inside begins its journey on the less prestigious silver table, ascending from silver to gold. The bread that has already rested on the golden interior table and is being removed maintains its elevated status by being placed on the gold table, not demoted to silver. The principle operates in two directions: the fresh bread ascends, and the removed bread is not degraded.

This is a striking application of the principle. There are two dimensions to *ma'alin bakodesh v'lo moridin*: one concerns the reuse of sacred objects — a vessel that has served a holy purpose may only be used for a purpose of equal or greater sanctity. The other concerns how one treats such objects — even when they are being retired from active service, they must be treated with the same dignity they had when in use.

### Erecting Mishkan

The Gemara then asks: *u'minalan d'ma'alin bakodesh v'lo moridin* — from where do we derive this principle? One proposed source is the pasuk describing Moshe's erection of the Mishkan: *vayakem Moshe et ha-mishkan vayiten et adanav vayasem et krashav vayiten et brichav vayakem et amudav* — Moshe erected the Mishkan, placed its sockets, its planks, its bars, and its pillars. The argument, apparently, has something to do with the use of the more elevated word *vayakem* appearing at particular points in the verse, though the connection is admittedly difficult to understand clearly and the explanations offered are not fully satisfying.

### Fire Pans Example

A far more compelling proof is offered by Rabbi Yochanan bar Yaakov. The pasuk says: *et machtot hachata'im ha-eleh b'nafshotam* — referring to the fire pans used by the 250 men who joined Korach's rebellion. Those men brought their fire pans into the Mishkan as commanded, and were destroyed. God then commanded Moshe to collect those pans and hammer them into sheets to overlay the altar: *v'asu otam riku'ei pachim tzipui lamizbeach ki hikrivum lifnei Hashem vayikdashu* — they had been brought before God and thereby become sanctified. *b'tchilat tashmishei mizbeach* — initially these pans were accessories used in service of the altar. *v'achshav gufo shel mizbeach* — now they were elevated to become part of the altar itself, forming its outer overlay. This is *ma'alin bakodesh* made concrete: objects that had served as vessels were elevated to become the body of the sacred structure itself. The application of this principle here is powerful.

### Broken Tablets

Another proof is drawn from the Luchos. *asher shibarta v'samtem ba-aron* — the broken tablets that Moshe had shattered were placed in the Ark alongside the second, intact tablets. *tani rav yosef: melamed shehaluchot v'shivrei luchot munachim ba-aron* — it teaches that both the complete second Luchos and the broken fragments of the first Luchos were kept in the Ark. This too reflects the principle: even in their broken state, the first Luchos retained their sanctity and were not discarded but rather preserved in the holiest vessel in the Mishkan, alongside the whole tablets.

### Talmid Chacham

The Gemara concludes with an application of this principle to human beings. *mikan l'talmid chacham sheshachach talmudo machmat onso she'ein nohagim bo minhag bizayon* — from here we learn that a talmid chacham who has forgotten his learning not through negligence but through circumstances beyond his control — declining health, advancing age — must not be treated with disdain. He retains his stature and must be accorded the respect due to a scholar. The broken Luchos in the Ark serve as the paradigm: even sacred things that have lost their original form or function are not to be degraded. They ascend; they do not descend.

---

---

# Menachot 99

## Reish Lakish: Tablets

### Negation as Foundation

The daf begins at the final line of 99a, picking up from the preceding *aggadeta* concerning the *aron*, which taught that the broken *luchot* and the whole *luchot* were carried together — establishing that a *talmid chacham* who forgets his Torah through no fault of his own is not to be treated with disrespect. From this point, Reish Lakish offers a series of related teachings.

*Amar Reish Lakish*: *pe'amim shebitulah shel Torah zo hi yesodah* — there are times when the negation of Torah is precisely the laying of its foundation. The proof text is *asher shibarta* — the verse in which God says to Moshe, "which you broke." The Gemara reads God's response as an expression of approval: *yashar kochacha sheshibarta* — well done that you broke the *luchot*. There was a moment when breaking the *luchot* actually allowed the relationship between God and *Bnei Yisrael* to be preserved and ultimately healed.

### Rashi's Explanation

What exactly does Reish Lakish mean when he says *bitulah zo hi yesodah* — that negating Torah is its foundation? Rashi explains: *shebitulah shel Torah kegon shemevatel Torah lehotza'at hamet ulehachnasat kallah* — one who suspends Torah study in order to perform a *mitzvah* that the entire community should participate in, such as accompanying the dead or bringing a bride to the *chupah*. And this, says Rashi, *zehu yesodah* — is its very foundation, because Torah must ultimately lead to action. One receives credit *ke'ilu yoshev umeyasdah* — as though one were sitting and laying its foundation. The point runs deeper than simply not losing out for *bitul Torah*: in some sense, the very doing of *mitzvot* constitutes a form of *osek baTorah*.

The textual basis in the *pasuk* lies in the tone of *asher shibarta* — God mentions the breaking of the *luchot* matter-of-factly, without anger or rebuke: *shelo amar lei belashon ka'as*. From this one derives that God consented, that the *shechina* agreed with Moshe's action, since he acted for the good — *kivan deniskaven letovah*.

### Broader Interpretations

It is worth noting that the phrase is frequently quoted not as *bitulah zo hi yesodah* but as *bitulah zo hi kiyumah* — its negation is its fulfillment. As a formulation, *kiyumah* works more naturally as an antonym: the opposite of *bitul* is *lekayem*, to fulfill. In the *yeshiva* world the phrase is often invoked to justify stepping away from the *beit midrash* — taking time for rest, exercise, or a short break — on the grounds that *bitulah zo hi kiyumah*: the brief respite allows one to return with renewed energy and thereby sustain the learning.

There is also a more radical reading, one that Rashi is certainly not advancing and which Reish Lakish likely does not intend either: that sometimes actually violating something is necessary for its *kiyum* — the concept the Gemara elsewhere calls *aveirah lishmah*. This is a genuinely dangerous idea and is treated as such, but it does surface in other contexts in the Gemara.

---

## Fallen Scholars & Forget…

### Honoring Fallen Scholars

Reish Lakish continues with a second teaching in the same spirit as *shivrei luchot*. *Ve'amar Reish Lakish*: *talmid chacham shesarach ein mevazin oto befarhesia* — if a *talmid chacham* has gone off course — *sarach*, like meat that has gone rancid — one does not shame him publicly. The proof text is *vechashalta hayom vechashal gam navi imcha layla* — if you stumble today, and even the *navi*, the person of great religious standing, stumbles at night, then conceal it as the night conceals. The teaching speaks to protecting the dignity of someone who was once a person of great Torah stature. The concern is real, of course, that such a principle can be misused to cover up genuine wrongdoing — *chas veshalom* — but absent matters of *bein adam lechavero*, the principle of protecting people's dignity stands.

### Forgetting Torah

*Ve'amar Reish Lakish*: *kol hamishakeach davar echad mitalmudo over belav* — whoever intentionally causes himself to forget even one thing from his learning violates a negative prohibition. This is distinct from the *talmid chacham* discussed at the end of 99a who loses his Torah *machmat onso* — through no fault of his own, because he could not retain everything. Here we are speaking of one who goes out of his way to forget what he learned.

The proof text is *hishamer lecha ushmor nafshecha me'od pen tishkach et hadevarim* — guard yourself and watch your soul greatly, lest you forget the things you witnessed. In context, the verse refers to the experience of *Ma'amad Har Sinai*, but Reish Lakish reads it as an admonition to retain all of Torah received at that revelation. Intentional forgetting thus constitutes a violation.

### Number of Violations

The Gemara then records a dispute about how many negative prohibitions are violated. The background principle is that of Rav Avin in the name of Rabbi Ila: *kol makom shene'emar hishamer pen ve'al, eino ela lo ta'aseh* — wherever the Torah uses the language "guard yourself," "lest," or "do not," it is the language of a negative prohibition.

Ravina counts two violations: *hishamer lecha* and *pen tishkach* — two distinct negative formulations in the verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak goes further and counts three *lavin*, pointing to the three verbs of admonition in the full verse — *hishamer lecha ushmor nafshecha me'od pen tishkach*. The Torah's repetition of warning here is notably emphatic.

### Intent vs. Circumstance

The Gemara asks whether this prohibition might apply even to one who forgets *machmat onso* — through unavoidable circumstances, simply because one cannot retain everything. The verse itself answers: *ufen yasuru milevavecha* — "lest they turn away from your heart" — implies an active removal, a deliberate turning away. *Bimesira milev hakatuv medaber* — the verse speaks of an intentional distancing from the heart.

Rabbi Dostai beRabbi Yannai raises a further case: what if *takfa alav mishnato* — the material proved too difficult for him to master? Rashi explains this as *shelo yachol le'amid girsato* — he simply could not hold the learning, whether due to difficulty or to the sheer volume he was trying to retain. The verse again provides the limit: *rak* — the limiting word — narrows the prohibition to cases of genuine intention to forget. Both the case of one who forgot because he could not remember everything and the case of one for whom the material was beyond his capacity are exempted from the prohibition.

---

## Forty Days Teaching

### Torah & Soul Formation

Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar together state: *Torah nitna be'arba'im veneshama notzra be'arba'im* — the Torah was given over forty days, referring to *Ma'amad Har Sinai*, and the soul takes form over forty days. This reflects the well-known teaching of *Chazal* that for the first forty days of gestation a fetus is regarded as *maya be'alma* — like water — and only on day forty does it begin to take the shape of a human being, *tzurat havlad*, and this is also when *yetzirat haneshama* — the formation of the soul — occurs. The parallel between Torah and soul, both formed over forty days, sets up what follows.

### Protecting Torah & Soul

*Kol hameshamer toraso, nishmaso mishtameret* — whoever protects his Torah, his soul is protected. The act of *shemirat Torah* — actively guarding what one has learned, through review, through mnemonics, through disciplined effort — is placed in direct parallel with the protection of one's soul. And conversely: *ve'chol she'eino meshamer et hatorah, ein nishmaso mishtameret* — one who does not guard his Torah does not guard his soul. There is clearly also a deeper sense here: the more diligent one is in Torah, the more one protects one's religious wellbeing, and neglect exposes one to spiritual danger.

### Bird Parable

The school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a *mashal*: *mashal le'adam shemasar tzippor dror le'avdo* — it is like a person who gave a wild bird to his servant. The master says to the servant: if you lose it, do not think you will merely pay the price of a bird — *nishmascha ani notel mimcha* — I will take your life. The image is apt: a wild bird that wants to fly free, that you must actively hold and restrain. Torah is like that bird — it strains to escape the mind and must be actively protected. Lose it, and you pay not with the cost of a pet but with something far more fundamental.

---

## Two Tables Setup

### Marble & Gold Tables

The next *mishnah* opens: *shnei shulchanos hayu ba'ulam* — there were two tables in the *ulam*, the antechamber that preceded the *heichal* and then the *Kodesh Kodashim*. Unlike the *Mishkan*, which had no *ulam*, the *Beis Hamikdash* had a full structure of *ulam*, *heichal*, and *dvir*. The *heichal* was where the *shulchan*, *menorah*, and *mizbe'ach hazahav* stood; the *ulam* was the outer chamber.

The two tables were *mibifnim al pesach habayis* — on the inner side, at the rear of the *ulam* near the opening to the *heichal*: *echad shel shayish ve'echad shel zahav* — one of marble and one of gold. Tosafot notes that in many manuscripts the reading is *echad shel kesef* — one of silver — and attempts to reconcile the two versions, while Rashi suggests that marble and silver have a similar appearance. The arrangement was as follows: on the marble table they placed the *lechem hapanim* upon its entry — when the priests brought the new bread in on *Shabbat* to place it in the *heichal*. On the gold table they placed the bread upon its exit — when the old bread was removed and set aside in the *ulam* while the *levonah* was being burned on the outer *mizbe'ach* before the *kohanim* would eat it.

### Ascending Holiness

The principle governing this arrangement is *ma'alin bakodesh velo moridin* — one ascends in sanctity and does not descend. Rashi notes that there was no strict halakhic requirement to set the bread on the marble table on the way in, but it was done in order to embody this principle: by passing through an intermediate stage of marble or silver before reaching the gold *shulchan* in the *heichal*, the entire process was given more layers of ritual and reverence. And on the way out, since the bread was already associated with the gold *shulchan* inside, it could not be placed on something of lesser sanctity — yet it also could not go higher than gold. The solution: it remains on a gold table. One does not descend; one may stay level.

### Gold Table & Showbread

*Ve'echad shel zahav mibifnim* — and then of course there was the gold table inside the *heichal* itself, *she'alav lechem hapanim tamid* — upon which the *lechem hapanim* rested constantly. This is the central *shulchan* of the Temple service.

---

## Showbread Ceremony

### Four Priests Enter

*Ve'arba'ah kohanim nichnasim* — four *kohanim* would enter: *shnayim beyadam shnei sdarim* — two of them holding the two columns of bread, six loaves stacked upon each other in a column, and *shnayim beyadam shnei bazichin* — two holding the two dishes of *levonah*. In terms of the workload, those carrying the bread carried something considerably bulkier and more difficult to manage; those carrying the *bazichin* had a far simpler task.

### Four Priests Precede

*Ve'arba makdimim lifnehem* — four additional *kohanim* would go in ahead of them, whose role was to remove the existing bread and *levonah* as the new contingent placed the new ones. Two were assigned to take out the two columns of bread and two to take out the two dishes of *levonah*.

### Positioning & Coordinati…

The spatial choreography was precise. *Hamachnisim omdim batzafon upnehem ladarom* — those bringing the new bread stood in the north, facing south. Since the *shulchan* was itself positioned in the north, these four were positioned between the northern wall and the *shulchan*, facing inward toward the table. *Hamotzim omdim badarom upnehem batzafon* — those removing the old bread stood to the south, in the more open space of the *heichal*, facing toward the *shulchan*.

*Elu moshchin ve'elu manichim* — the ones on the outside pull away the old bread while those between the table and the wall place the new bread into the cleared spaces. *Vetfacho shel ze keneged tfacho shel ze* — one *tefach* is directly opposite the other *tefach*, meaning the movements are so closely coordinated that the hands of the two groups are at virtually the same distance from the table at every moment.

### Continuous Presence Deba…

This choreography is driven by the requirement of *lefanai tamid* — constantly before Me. For the *Tanna Kamma*, *tamid* means there cannot be even a single moment when the table holds no bread. The simultaneous pulling-away and placing-on, with hands within a *tefach* of one another, ensures that at no instant is the *shulchan* left bare.

*Rabbi Yose omer*: even if the old bread is removed before the new is placed — *afilu elu notlin ve'elu manichim* — it still constitutes *tamid*. The Gemara will elaborate on how far Rabbi Yose extends this position.

### Transfer & Division

After the ceremony, *yatzu venatnu al shulchan hazahav* — those who removed the old bread carried it out to the *ulam* and placed it on the gold table mentioned at the outset of the *mishnah*. Then *hiktiru habezichim* — the two *kohanim* who had taken the *bazichin* burned the *levonah* on the outer *mizbe'ach*. Only once the *levonah* had been offered were the *chalot* divided among the *kohanim*.

---

## Yom Kippur on Shabbat

### Timing Issues

*Chal Yom HaKippurim lihyot beShabbat* — if Yom Kippur fell on *Shabbat*, the priests could not divide and eat the bread on *Shabbat* itself. *Hachalot mitchalkot la'erev* — the *chalot* would be divided and eaten *Motzei Shabbat*, which is also *Motzei Yom Kippur*. This does not constitute *linah* — overnight disqualification — since *linah* does not apply until the following morning.

If Yom Kippur fell on *erev Shabbat*, a further complexity arose: *se'iro shel Yom HaKippurim ne'echal la'erev* — the goat offered as *chatat* on the outer *mizbe'ach* on Yom Kippur — not the *se'ir la'azazel* sent to the wilderness, nor the goat whose blood was sprinkled inside, but the ordinary external *chatat* whose meat was to be eaten by the *kohanim* — would need to be eaten that night, *Motzei Yom Kippur*, i.e., Friday night, to avoid it becoming *notar*. But it went directly from Yom Kippur into *Shabbat* with no opportunity to roast or cook it.

### Babylonian Priests

*Vehavliyim ochlim oto keshehu chai* — and the Babylonian priests would eat it raw. *Mipnei sheda'atan yafa* — because, the *mishnah* says euphemistically, "they have a refined temperament." This is clearly ironic: they were willing to eat raw meat, which is in fact an expression of coarseness. The Gemara will shortly identify who these "Babylonians" actually were.

---

## Rabbi Yose's View

### Morning Removal/Evening…

The Gemara now examines Rabbi Yose's position. A *baraita* states: *Rabbi Yose omer afilu silek et hayashan shacharit vesider et hachadasha aravit, ein bakach klum* — even if the old bread was removed in the morning and the new bread was not arranged until the evening, it is not a problem at all — not even *bedi'avad*. For Rabbi Yose, the requirement of *tamid* is not violated by a daytime gap.

---

## Rabbi Yose's View (II)

### Reinterpretation of Tamid

*Ela mah ani mekayem lefanai tamid* — how then does Rabbi Yose interpret the word *tamid* — "constantly"? *Shelo yalin shulchan belo lachem* — the table should not pass the night without bread. What is prohibited is an overnight gap, not a momentary or even a lengthy daytime absence. The word *tamid*, for Rabbi Yose, means something like continuity across days — no night should pass without bread having been on the table — rather than an unbroken moment-by-moment presence.

---

## Rabbi Ami Derivation

### One Chapter AM/PM

From Rabbi Yose's position, Rabbi Ami draws a halakhic lesson for Torah study. *Afilu shana adam ela perek echad shacharit u'perek echad aravit* — even if a person studied only one chapter of Torah in the morning and one chapter in the evening, *kiyam mitzvat lo yamush sefer haTorah hazeh mipicha* — he has fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *lo yamush sefer haTorah hazeh mipicha*, the commandment that this *sefer Torah* shall not depart from your mouth. The verse continues *vehagita bo yomam valailah* — you shall meditate in it day and night. Just as Rabbi Yose holds that *tamid* is satisfied by continuity without an overnight gap rather than by every-moment presence, so too *yomam valailah* is satisfied by some learning in the day and some in the night. There is always something of one's day that is Torah — and that continuous thread is enough.

---

## Kriyas Shema Fulfillment

### Shema AM/PM

Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai goes a step further: *afilu lo kara adam ela kriyat shema shacharit ve'arvit, kiyam lo yamush* — even if a person only recited *kriyat shema* morning and evening, he has fulfilled *lo yamush*. This is not as surprising as it might initially appear. The *psukim* of *shema* are themselves *psukim* of Torah; the *bracha* of *ahavat olam* that precedes *shema* functions as *birchat haTorah*; and the text of *shema* itself — *velimadetem otam et beneichem vedibarta bam beshivtecha beveitecha*, *beshachbecha uvekumecha* — speaks directly about the constant engagement with Torah, about *talmud Torah* as a way of life, from lying down to rising up. When one recites *kriyat shema* morning and evening, fulfilling *beshachbecha uvekumecha*, one is also fulfilling a sense of *yomam valailah* — there is Torah at the start of one's day and Torah at the close.

### Yochanan vs. Rava

However, Rabbi Yochanan adds: *vedavar zeh assur l'omro bifnei amei ha'aretz* — this teaching should not be said in front of the *amei ha'aretz*. If an *am ha'aretz* — someone not oriented toward serious Torah study — hears that *kriyat shema* alone fulfills *lo yamush*, he will simply conclude that there is nothing more required of him and will use it as an easy exemption. The teaching is meaningful only for *talmidei chachamim* who already learn extensively and for whom it is merely an interesting theoretical point; for those who would be affected by it in practice, it is better left unsaid.

Rava disagrees: *mitzvah l'omro bifnei amei ha'aretz* — it is a *mitzvah* to say it to the *amei ha'aretz*. Hearing this, they will feel valued, feel that their Torah matters, and may well be inspired to do more. Rashi elaborates: if even *kriyat shema* earns such extraordinary reward — the verse concludes *ki az tatzliach et derachecha*, then you will be greatly successful — how much more so if one were to learn all day? The generosity of the reward should serve as an enticement toward greater learning, not as a ceiling. This is a genuine pedagogical dispute: does it serve people better to tell them what they have already accomplished, or to communicate the full weight of what remains?

---

## Greek Wisdom Prohibition

### Ben Dama's Question

Ben Dama, the nephew of Rabbi Yishmael, posed a question to his uncle: *kegon ani shelamadti kol haTorah kullah, mahu lilmod chochma yevanit* — someone like me, who has learned the entire Torah — can he now learn Greek wisdom?

### No Time for Other Studies

Rabbi Yishmael responded by citing the very verse under discussion: *lo yamush sefer haTorah hazeh mipicha vehagita bo yomam valailah* — this sefer Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall study it day and night. *Tze u'vedok sha'ah she'eina lo min hayom velo min halaylah u'lemad bah chochmat Yevanit* — go find a time that is neither day nor night, and in that time you may study Greek wisdom. For Rabbi Yishmael, the verse addressed to a *talmid chacham* cannot be read in the lenient manner of Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Yochanan. For someone at Ben Dama's level, *yomam valailah* means what it says: every moment of day and every moment of night belongs to Torah. If you can identify a moment that is neither, that is when you may learn something else. Since no such moment exists, there is simply no room.

This raises the question of what *chochmat Yevanit* actually means. The attractive reading is Greek philosophy or secular studies more broadly. There is, however, a narrower and more historically specific interpretation: the Gemara elsewhere records a *gezeirah* that one may not teach one's son *chochmat Yevanit*, and in that context it may refer to something more specifically dangerous — perhaps a form of secret code language or a set of ideas particularly associated with Hellenistic religious subversion — rather than general secular learning. The *mishnah* in context probably points to that more specific danger, though the verse Rabbi Yishmael cites has been applied broadly across the tradition.

---

## Mitzvah or Blessing?

### Blessing Not Obligation

*U'fliga d'Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* — this entire discussion of whether *lo yamush* imposes a strict obligation or can be satisfied minimally is challenged by Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, who says in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *pasuk zeh eino lo chovah velo mitzvah ela brachah* — this verse is neither a *chovah* nor a *mitzvah* but a blessing. This is probably the *pshat* of the verse. The setting is the beginning of *Sefer Yehoshua*: after Moshe's death, God speaks to Yehoshua. Rather than imposing an obligation, God is blessing him.

### Divine Enticement

Why? *Ra'ah haKadosh Baruch Hu et Yehoshua shedivrei Torah chavivin alav beyoter* — God saw that Torah was extraordinarily dear to Yehoshua. The proof: *umesharto Yehoshua bin Nun naar lo yamish mitoch ha'ohel* — his servant Yehoshua son of Nun, a young man, never departed from the tent, understood as the tent of *talmud Torah*. *Amar lo haKadosh Baruch Hu*: Is Torah so beloved to you, that you are always reaching for it — *kol kach chavivin alecha divrei Torah*? Then I bless you: *lo yamush sefer haTorah hazeh mipicha* — may this Torah never depart from your mouth.

### Not a Burden

The school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a formulation that attempts to hold both dimensions in tension: *divrei Torah lo yihiyu alecha chovah, ve'ee atah rasha'ee liftor atzmecha mehen* — the words of Torah should not be an obligation upon you, yet you are not permitted to exempt yourself from them.

### Torah & Worldly Life

Rashi reads this as a single coherent statement: don't treat Torah like a debt — the attitude of *matai efra'enu ve'epater*, "when can I discharge this and be done?" — because you cannot discharge it and be done. You are never exempt; the study must always continue. For Rashi, both clauses say the same thing from different angles: don't treat it as a burden you can satisfy.

Tosafot reads the two clauses differently. *Lo yihiyu alecha chovah shelo ta'asok ela bahen* — do not make it so all-encompassing an obligation that you do nothing but Torah. *Ve'ee atah rasha'ee liftor atzmecha mehen* — but you cannot exempt yourself from them entirely either, *shelo ta'asok bahen klal*. The conclusion: *ela yafeh talmud Torah im derech eretz* — Torah study combined with worldly occupation is the ideal. Tosafot also offers an additional reading: *lo alecha hamelacha ligmor* — you are not obligated to complete all of the Torah — echoing the teaching in Avot — but *ee atah rasha'ee liftor atzmecha*, you cannot opt out. Do what you can, but you cannot choose nothing.

The reading perhaps most aligned with the spirit of the formulation is: do not approach Torah as a burden. It is an obligation, yes, but the attitude should not be one of discharging a debt. Rather, treat it as an opportunity — an approach reminiscent of what Rav Soloveitchik articulated about *tefillah*: *tefillah* is indeed *keva*, it is fixed and obligatory, yet one must not *approach* it as *keva* — as a rote obligation to discharge. One should approach it as *tachanunim lifnei hamakom*, as pouring out the heart before God. The same reframing applies here: Torah study is obligatory, but the disposition toward it should be one of opportunity, not burden.

---

## Gehinnom Midrash

### Human vs. Divine

Rav Chizkiya expounds the verse *ve'af hesitcha mipi tzar rachav lo mutzak tachteiha* — "He has enticed you from a narrow place, wide and unconfined beneath." *Shelo kemidat haKadosh Baruch Hu midat basar vadam* — the ways of God are not like the ways of flesh and blood. *Adam mesit et chaveiro midarchei chayim ledarchei mita* — when a human being seduces his fellow, he leads him from the path of life toward the path of death, away from the straight and narrow toward destruction. *Vehakadosh Baruch Hu mesit et ha'adam midarchei mita ledarchei chayim* — but when God seduces and entices a person, He draws him away from the path of death toward the path of life. *Ve'af hesitcha mipi tzar* — God entices you from the narrow place, which is *Gehenom*, *shepiha tzar* — whose opening is narrow.

### Gehinnom Description

The image of *Gehenom* presented here is striking: its entrance is narrow but its interior is deep and wide. *She'ashana tzavur betocha* — its smoke is all contained within it, which is why the narrow opening gives no sense of the vastness inside. The Gemara anticipates the objection: perhaps since the opening is narrow, the interior too is small and constrained — *keshem shepiha tzar kach kula tzara*. The verse answers: *he'emik hirchiv* — it is made deep and wide. The opening is deceiving; within, there is vast space for fire and punishment.

### Gehinnom Assurances

The *midrash* continues with a series of reassurances — or warnings, depending on how one reads them. *Veshema tomar lemelech lo hukan* — perhaps you will say it is not prepared for a king, meaning a *talmid chacham* (as Rashi explains) — perhaps someone of Torah stature is exempt. The verse answers: *gam hi lemelech hukan* — it is prepared even for a king. *Veshema tomar ein ba eitzim* — perhaps you will say there is no wood there, that the fire is not sustained. The verse answers: *medurata esh ve'eitzim harbeh* — its conflagration is fire and abundant wood. And lest one think the entire reward of Torah is merely escape from *Gehenom*: *venachat shulchancha male dhashen* — your table will be set full of richness. The ultimate reward of Torah is not merely the avoidance of punishment but the abundance of life and blessing.

---

## Babylonians vs. Alexandr…

### True Identity Revealed

Returning to the *mishnah*'s reference to the "Babylonian priests" who ate the *se'ir* raw, the Gemara provides a clarification. *Amar Rabbah bar Bar Chana amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *lo Bavliyim hem, ella Alexandriiyim hem* — they were not actually Babylonians but Alexandrians, Greeks from Alexandria. *Umitoch shesonim et haBavliyim korin otam al shem Bavliyim* — and because the sages of Israel had such antipathy toward "the Babylonians," when they wanted to describe someone as coarse and barbaric in their eating habits, they reached for the term "Babylonian" as a slur. A *baraita* confirms this: Rabbi Yose states the same — they were Alexandrians, called Babylonians as a term of derision.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Relief

*Amar lo Rabbi Yehuda: tanuach da'atcha shenachata et da'ati* — Rabbi Yehuda said to him: may your mind be at ease, for you have set my mind at ease. The reason, as Rashi explains, is that Rabbi Yehuda's own family was from Babylonia — *mishpachat Rabbi Yehuda miBavel hayeta* — and he was therefore relieved to learn that this attribution of coarse behavior to "Babylonians" was not an actual slur against Babylonian Jews but rather the use of "Babylonian" as a byword for something else entirely.

It is worth noting the somewhat ironic undertone: that the sages of *Eretz Yisrael* used "Babylonian" as a curse word reflects a degree of inter-communal tension. One possible reading that softens this is that *haBavliyim* referred not to the Jewish community of Bavel but to native Babylonians — the gentile population — and that the *kohanim* of Alexandria were being compared, unfavorably, to them. That reading would make the dynamic less internally contentious, though the usage remains a pointed one.

---

---

# Menachot 100

## Lechem HaPanim Setup

The daf opens at 100a, still within the *mishnah* treating *lechem hapanim*. The *mishnah* presents three distinct scenarios of procedural failure in the arrangement of the showbread and its accompanying frankincense, and the Gemara examines the consequences of each.

### Bread Sat, Incense Sun

The first case: the *kohanim* placed the bread on the *shulchan* on *Shabbos* but delayed placing the frankincense (*levona*) until Sunday. When the *bezichin* — the two bowls of frankincense — were then offered up on the following *Shabbos*, the offering is *pasul*. As Rashi explains: *demichusar zman hu shelo haya al hashulchan ela shishi yamim* — it is lacking in its proper time, since the frankincense had rested on the table for only six days rather than the required seven. A prerequisite for the *bezichin* to be offered is that they have remained on the *shulchan* for a full week. Because this condition was not met, the *levona* was not brought as a valid *matir*, and consequently the bread never attained the status of being permitted for consumption. The *mishnah* therefore rules that *ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul notar vetamei*: a *pigul* intention at the time of offering has no effect, since *pigul* applies only when the *matir* was offered *kemitzvaso*; *notar* does not apply since the bread was never rendered fit to be eaten; and a *tamei* person who consumed it incurs no *kares*, since *kares* for eating sacred food applies only when the food had attained a state of permissibility — which this bread never did.

One might ask: why not simply offer the *bezichin* on Sunday, giving them a full week before the following *Shabbos*? The answer is two-fold. The *bezichin* may only be offered on *Shabbos*, not on a Sunday. Furthermore, since the bread was placed at the correct time — on *Shabbos* — it would no longer be valid by the time a Sunday *bezichin* offering could complete the required seven-day period from the bread's placement.

### Both Sat, Incense Late

The second case: both the bread and the *bezichin* were placed on the *shulchan* correctly, on *Shabbos*, but the frankincense was then offered late — *l'achar hashabbos*, after *Shabbos* had ended. Again the verdict is *psula*: the *matir* was not offered *kemitzvaso*, and the same consequences follow regarding *pigul*, *notar*, and *tumah*.

### Both Sun, Wait Solution

The third and most instructive case: both the bread and the *bezichin* were placed on the *shulchan* on Sunday — that is, entirely after *Shabbos*. If one then attempted to offer the *bezichin* on the following *Shabbos* (six days later), the offering would again be *pasul*, since the full seven days had not elapsed. Here, however, the *mishnah* offers a resolution: *yani'chenu l'Shabbos haba'ah* — leave the bread on the table until the *Shabbos* after that. And *she'afilu hi al hashulchan yamim rabim ein bekach klum* — even if it sits on the *shulchan* for many days, that causes no problem.

This ruling requires careful explanation. It does not mean that extended time on the *shulchan* is unconditionally harmless. Rather, since the bread was placed on Sunday — *shelo bizmano*, at the wrong time — the *shulchan* never sanctified it and the clock never began ticking. The clock only begins when the bread is placed on *Shabbos*, which is its proper time. Therefore, when the bread sits through that first *Shabbos* without having been placed correctly, only at the next *Shabbos* does its placement become meaningful, the *shulchan* sanctify it, and the seven-day count commence. The *bezichin* can then be offered on the *Shabbos* following that — thirteen days in total from the original Sunday placement.

This stands in contrast to the first case. There, the bread was placed on *Shabbos* and the clock began immediately. No amount of waiting past the initial *Shabbos* could remedy the *bezichin* being placed a day late. Here, the clock never started, so waiting costs nothing and the next *Shabbos* provides the proper initiation point.

---

## Tamid Timing & Prep

### Daylight Check

The *Gemara* quotes a *mishnah* from Tamid: *amar lahem hamemuneh, tze'u ur'u im higiya zman shechita* — the overseer would send someone out to verify that the time for *shechita* of the daily *tamid* offering had arrived. When the scout reported that the east had become light, he would say *barkai* — an expression evoking the breaking light of dawn. *Matia ben Shmuel* is quoted as saying that when he himself served as overseer, he would ask the scout: *he'ir pnei kol hamizrach ad shebeChevron* — has the entire eastern sky brightened, as far as one can see toward Chevron? Only upon receiving confirmation would he proceed. This was a deliberate double-check, not an impulsive reaction to any flash of light.

### Moonlight Mistake

The reason for such caution is historical. On one occasion, *me'or halevana* — the moonlight — rose brilliantly and the *kohanim* mistook it for dawn. They slaughtered the *tamid*, only to discover the error. The offering had been *shechted* at night and was therefore invalid; it had to be taken out to *beit hasreifah* to be burned. In addition, the *kohen gadol* was brought to *beit hatvilah* — a detail that Rashi understands as most likely reflecting a *Yom Kippur* context — though that matter is tangential here.

### Temple Purity

The general rule that then follows describes the purity standards maintained in the *Beis HaMikdash*: any *kohen* who had defecated was required to immerse in a *mikvah*, while one who had urinated was required to wash his hands and feet. This was not a strict *halachic* requirement triggered by *tumah* per se, but rather the standard of preparation that was observed before performing the *avodah* in the Temple.

---

## Mincha at Night

### Night Slaughter

The father of Rabbi Avin (*avuha d'Rabbi Avin*) taught a *braita*: *lo zo bilvad* — not only is an animal slaughtered at night invalid, but *afilu olas ha'of shenimleka balaila umincha shenikmitza balaila taitzei leveit hasreifah* — even a bird offering whose *melikah* was performed at night, or a *mincha* whose *komets* was taken at night, must go out to *beit hasreifah*. The *Gemara* accepts the ruling about the bird without difficulty: *mishum delo efshar lehahadura* — there is no way to undo a *melikah* and restore the bird to life. But the *mincha* presents a genuine question. Why can one not simply return the *komets* to its vessel and take it again by day?

### Handful Sanctification

The answer given by the same authority who taught the *braita* is: *klei sharet mekadeshin shelo bizmanam* — the service vessels sanctify even outside their proper time. When the *kohen* placed the *komets* into a *kli sharet* at night, even though night is not the valid time for this act, the vessel nonetheless imparted a degree of sanctification to the *komets*. As a result, the *komets* has been designated and can no longer simply be returned to the *mincha* and re-taken. Without this principle, one could have argued that when the *kli sharet* is used *shelo bizmano*, nothing meaningful has occurred and the *komets* retains no distinct status. The *chiddush* is that this assumption is wrong.

### Temurah Challenge

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from a teaching in Temurah: *kol hakarev bayom kadosh bayom* — whatever is offered in the day is sanctified in the day; *balaila kadosh balaila* — if an offering is valid at night, it is sanctified at night; *bein bayom uvein balaila* — if it is valid either way, the vessel sanctifies it either way. The plain implication is that the *kli sharet* functions precisely when the offering can be brought: for a normal daytime *korban*, the vessel works by day but not by night. This directly contradicts the claim that vessels sanctify *shelo bizmanom*.

### Vessel Timing Rule

The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *eino kadosh l'hikarev aval kadosh l'hipasel* — the *komets* taken at night is not sanctified to the degree that it may be offered, but it is sanctified to the degree that it may be rendered *pasul*. This is, as the analysis frankly acknowledges, the worst of both worlds. Because the act was performed at the wrong time, the *komets* cannot be offered up. But because it was placed in a *kli sharet*, it has nonetheless acquired its identity as a designated *komets* — a *komets psula* — and may no longer be returned to the *mincha* for a fresh taking by day. The vessel did not elevate the offering to fitness, but it did lock in its identity and its disqualification.

---

## Bread Vessel Rules

### Zeira Challenge

Rabbi Zeira now raises a sharp challenge that brings the discussion back to our *mishnah* about *lechem hapanim*. He returns to the third case: bread and *bezichin* placed on the *shulchan* on Sunday, and the *bezichin* offered on the following *Shabbos* — invalid, because only six days have elapsed. The *mishnah*'s solution was to wait until the *Shabbos* after that, noting that bread sitting on the *shulchan* for many days creates no problem, because the clock never started ticking when the bread was placed *shelo bizmano*.

Rabbi Zeira's challenge: if we accept the principle that *klei sharet mekadesh shelo bizmanom* — at least to the extent of rendering something *pasul* — then why does the Sunday placement not begin the clock? The *shulchan* is itself a *kli sharet*. When the bread is placed on it on Sunday, even though that is the wrong time, it should nonetheless sanctify the bread sufficiently to render it *pasul*, just as the *komets* vessel rendered the nighttime *komets* unable to be re-taken. If so, by the time the bread has been on the table for eight days, it should be considered to have already been designated and subsequently disqualified — which would mean that even the "wait until next *Shabbos*" solution collapses.

Rava acknowledges that the question is excellent: *man dekamosif shapir kamosif* — the one who raises this addition raises it well. Nevertheless, he notes that the father of Rabbi Avin was citing an established *braita*, not inventing a position. That *braita* unambiguously states that a *mincha* taken at night cannot be rectified — which only makes sense on the assumption that the *kli sharet* functions *shelo bizmano* at least to create disqualification. So both the *braita* and the *mishnah* must somehow be reconciled.

### Night vs Days

The resolution: *kasavar laila ein mechusar zman, hayamim mechusarin zman* — night is not considered "lacking in its proper time," whereas the intervening days are considered fully lacking. Night, specifically the night leading into the day on which an offering could be brought, is close enough to the proper time that when the *kli sharet* operates at night, it operates within a period that is conceptually adjacent to the day of *avodah*. The offering is *pasul* because *avodah* cannot be performed at night, but it is not *mechusar zman* — not so far removed from proper time that the vessel's act is entirely without meaning. Therefore, the nighttime taking of the *komets* locks in the *komets*'s identity.

By contrast, placing the bread on the *shulchan* six days before *Shabbos* is *mechusar zman* in the full sense. The *shulchan* is not acting *shelo bizmano* in a mild way — it is acting at a completely wrong time, and therefore no sanctification of any kind occurs. The clock does not start, no disqualification takes hold, and the bread waits inertly until it reaches a proper *Shabbos*.

### Friday Night Problem

This resolution, however, generates a new problem. If we say that "the days" lack proper time but "night" does not, then consider what happens as the bread sits on the *shulchan* from Sunday through the week. By the time Friday night arrives — the night of *erev Shabbos* — the bread has been on the table for six days, and Friday night is the nighttime preceding the very *Shabbos* on which the bread ought to have been placed. That night is not *mechusar zman*, by the logic just established. So why does Friday night not begin the clock — sanctifying the bread, starting the seven-day count, and causing it to become *pasul* before the second *Shabbos* that the *mishnah* relies upon?

### Clock Prevention

Two answers are offered. Rava says: *beshekodmo v'silayko* — in practice, before Friday night arrived, the *kohanim* would remove the bread from the *shulchan* temporarily, preventing Friday night from triggering any sanctification. They would keep it elsewhere and return it to the *shulchan Shabbos* morning, ensuring that the first *Shabbos* on which the bread rested on the table was the second *Shabbos* after its placement — the one the *mishnah* intends.

Mar Zutra, and some say Rav Ashi, offers an alternative: *afilu tayma beshelo kodmo v'silayko* — even if the bread was never removed before Friday night, *keivan desiduro shelo kemitzvato naaseh kemi shesidro hakof* — since the original placement was so far removed from its proper time, the entire act of placement is treated as though it were performed by a monkey, that is, as entirely meaningless.
