The bread on the *shulchan* from Sunday is not the product of a valid act of *sidur*; it is simply present there without consequence. The *kli sharet* cannot operate on something whose placement was so fundamentally improper as to be considered no act at all.

This second answer illuminates a deeper principle. In the case of the *mincha* at night, the act of taking the *komets* was close enough to its proper time — the night immediately preceding the day — that it was a meaningful act. The *kli sharet* responded to that meaningful act by imparting at least the sanctification of *pasul*. But an act so far removed from its proper time — like placing the bread six days early — is not merely *shelo bizmano* in a technical sense. It is so disconnected from any notion of proper performance that it registers as no act at all, and no *kli sharet* can respond to a non-act.

---

## Two Loaves Duration

### Two Loaves Timing

The final *mishnah* of the *perek* turns to two related topics: the *shtei halechem* of *Shavuos* and the *lechem hapanim*. Regarding the *shtei halechem*: they are eaten no fewer than two days after baking and no more than three — *ein pachos mishnayim v'lo yoter al shlosha*. The *mishnah* explains: since baking does not override *Yom Tov* — *eino docheh Yom Tov* — the loaves must be baked on *erev Yom Tov*, yielding a minimum of two days (baking day and eating day). If *Yom Tov* falls on Sunday, one cannot bake on *Yom Tov* or on *Shabbos*, so baking must occur on Friday — yielding three days: Friday, *Shabbos*, and Sunday.

It should be noted: the clock for the *shtei halechem* does not begin when the loaves are baked. It begins when the accompanying *korban* is *shechted*. Similarly, the baking itself does not trigger sanctification that would create a problem of *linah* or premature disqualification.

### HaPanim Timing

The *lechem hapanim* follows the same structural logic but with a longer duration: *ein pachos mitish'ah* — no fewer than nine days from baking, *velo yoter al echad asar* — no more than eleven. The same principle applies: baking is not *docheh Shabbos*, so it must be done on *erev Shabbos*, and the loaves are eaten the following *Shabbos*. Counting both the day of baking and the day of eating gives nine days.

If *Yom Tov* falls on *erev Shabbos* (Friday), one cannot bake on that *Yom Tov*, so baking is moved to Thursday — yielding ten days. If *Rosh Hashanah* falls on Thursday and Friday, baking cannot occur on either day of *Yom Tov*, so it is done on Wednesday, and the bread is eaten the following *Shabbos* — eleven days total.

Rashi notes that when *Rosh Hashanah* is Thursday-Friday, the *Shabbos* on which the bread is eaten falls out on *Yom Kippur*, and asks how the bread can be consumed then. His answer is that it is eaten on *motzaei Shabbos*, still within the eleven-day window since the bread does not become *pasul* until Sunday morning. Tosafot takes a different approach: at the time of the *Beis HaMikdash*, when *Rosh Hashanah* was observed over two days, the second day of *Rosh Hashanah* was the first of *Tishrei*, making the arithmetic work differently — though that is a broader discussion.

The *mishnah* concludes this section by stating explicitly: *ve'eino doche lo es haShabbos velo es Yom Tov* — baking neither the *shtei halechem* nor the *lechem hapanim* overrides *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov*. That the *lechem hapanim* baking does not override *Shabbos* is self-evident; the case of *Yom Tov* is more interesting, particularly regarding the *shtei halechem*, which are to be eaten on *Yom Tov* itself.

### Shimon Exception

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then quotes Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan with a dissenting view: *doche es haYom Tov ve'eino doche es Yom Tzom* — baking does override *Yom Tov*, but it does not override *Yom Kippur*. According to this opinion, one may bake the *shtei halechem* on *Shavuos* itself to eat them on *Shavuos*. Furthermore, this applies even to the *lechem hapanim*: if *Yom Tov* falls before *Shabbos*, one may bake on *Yom Tov* in preparation for a *Shabbos* as many as eight or nine days later. The one exception is *Yom Kippur*, which cannot be overridden even for this purpose.

---

## Baking Override

### Offerings Category

Ravina offers an analytical framework to understand why, according to the first opinion in the *mishnah*, one cannot bake the *shtei halechem* on *Yom Tov*. One might have supposed that the prohibition is only *miderabanan*: biblically, cooking for food (*ochel nefesh*) is permitted on *Yom Tov*, and the *shtei halechem* will ultimately be eaten by the *kohanim*, so perhaps it qualifies. The *Rabbanan*, on this reading, would have prohibited it out of concern that people would defer their obligations — *shema yishehe* — postponing their *nedarim* and *nedavot* until *Yom Tov* if *Yom Tov* baking for a *korban* context were permitted. But Ravina argues that the prohibition is *mid'oraita*, not *miderabanan*: when an act of cooking or baking is done fundamentally for the purpose of a *korban* — even if the *kohanim* will eat the result — it is not classified as *lachem*, "for you," and therefore does not fall within the *Yom Tov* permit of *ochel nefesh*. The *Torah*'s permission is for cooking that is oriented directly toward human eating; something performed as a *korban* act, with eating as a downstream consequence, does not qualify.

### Shavuot Proof

The proof for this reading is the *shtei halechem* themselves. The concern of *shema yishehe* — postponing one's obligations — would have no relevance to the *shtei halechem*, since they can only be brought on *Shavuos* and there is nowhere to defer them. If the prohibition were merely *miderabanan* for reasons of *shema yishehe*, no such prohibition could logically apply to the *shtei halechem*. Yet the *mishnah* plainly states *ve'kasani eino doche lo es haShabbos velo es Yom Tov* — the *shtei halechem* baking does not override *Yom Tov*. This can only be explained if the prohibition is *mid'oraita*: baking for a *korban* purpose is categorically outside the *Yom Tov* permission, regardless of any rabbinic concern about deferral.

What makes the position of Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan particularly striking is its breadth: he permits not only baking on *Yom Tov* for *Yom Tov* itself, but also baking on *Yom Tov* in preparation for a *Shabbos* that falls many days later. Beyond the question of baking a *korban* item on *Yom Tov*, this also touches on the principle — parallel to the concerns addressed by *eiruv tavshilin* — of cooking from *Yom Tov* for *Shabbos*.

---

## Mincha Redemption

### Pre-Vessel Redemption

A new *mishnah* opens the next *perek*: *hamenchos v'hanesachim shenitme'u ad shelo kidshu b'kli yesh lahem pidyon* — if a *mincha* or *nesachim* became *tamei* before being placed into a *kli sharet*, they may be redeemed. At this stage, the flour, oil, or wine has been designated for sacred use but not yet placed in a service vessel. The sanctity it holds is *kedushat damim* — sanctity of monetary value. Just as one who declares his animal or property consecrated to the Temple creates an obligation to transfer that item's monetary value to the sanctuary treasury, so too these offerings, before the *kli* step, are sanctified only in terms of their worth. Something with only *kedushat damim* can be redeemed: its *kedushah* transfers to the redemption money, and the original item is released.

### Post-Vessel No Redemption

Once the *mincha* or *nesachim* have been placed in a *kli sharet*, the situation changes entirely: *mishekidshu b'kli ein lahem pidyon* — after sanctification by the service vessel, they cannot be redeemed. The vessel's sanctification elevates them to *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic sanctity. At this level, the item's sacred identity is not merely a matter of monetary value; the item itself is sacred in a substantive sense. Something with *kedushat haguf* cannot be redeemed. Even if it subsequently becomes *tamei* — making it impossible to offer — it still cannot be redeemed. The questioner cannot say: since I cannot use it in its *tamei* state, allow me to redeem it and purchase replacement ingredients. The *mishnah* answers: no. Once in the *kli*, the door to redemption is closed.

### Exception List

The *mishnah* then lists a separate category: *ha'ofot v'ha'etzim v'halevona v'chlei sharet* — birds, wood, frankincense, and service vessels themselves. These *mishenitme'u ein lahem pidyon* — once they become *tamei*, they cannot be redeemed. The stated reason is *shelo ne'emar pidyon ela bevehema* — the Torah's language of redemption was stated only in the context of animals.

This list, placed in the middle of the *mishnah*, appears somewhat puzzling at first glance. The opening and closing of the *mishnah* fit together coherently: *minchos* and *nesachim* before a *kli sharet* can be redeemed, after the *kli sharet* they cannot, because the *Torah* only provided a redemption mechanism for an animal with a *mum*. But why single out birds, wood, *levona*, and *kli sharet* in the middle? The *Gemara* will clarify this.

---

## Why Vessel Matters

### Shmuel Position

Shmuel teaches: *va'afilu hein tehorim nifdim* — the *minchos* and *nesachim* may be redeemed before being placed in a *kli sharet* even if they are *tahor*, even if no *tumah* has occurred. The *mishnah* framed the case in terms of *tumah* — the items became *tamei* before being placed in the *kli* — but that framing should not be read as establishing *tumah* as a prerequisite for redemption. The *Gemara* itself immediately notes: *pshita, nitmu tnan* — is this not obvious? The *mishnah* already states that *tamei* items can be redeemed before the *kli* step. The implicit question is, what is Shmuel adding?

Shmuel's point is a careful reading of the *mishnah*'s structure. One might have read the opening clause as establishing a *chiddush* in the other direction: specifically when the items have become *tamei* before being put in a *kli sharet*, they may be redeemed — but if they are *tahor*, even before the *kli* step, perhaps they may not. Shmuel rejects this. The *mishnah* uses the *tamei* scenario not because *tamei* is the threshold, but because it wants to contrast it with the *sefa*: *mishekidshu b'kli ein lahem pidyon* — once in the *kli*, no redemption, even if they are now *tamei*. In order to create that contrast, the *reisha* phrases its case in terms of *tamei* items. But in actual *halacha*, before the *kli* step, *kedushat damim* items can be redeemed regardless of *tumah* status.

*Va'idi dekaba'i lemisni seifa* — since the *mishnah* needed to teach the *sefa*, which is the genuine *chiddush* — namely, that even *tamei* items cannot be redeemed once they have acquired *kedushat haguf* through the *kli sharet* — it correspondingly framed the *reisha* in the *tamei* scenario for parallel structure. But Shmuel clarifies the actual rule.

### Body Sanctity

The *Gemara* then asks: is it not obvious that once the items are in the *kli sharet* they cannot be redeemed? *Pshita, kedushat haguf ninhu* — they have intrinsic sanctity; of course they cannot be redeemed. The *Gemara* answers: *itzterich* — no, this needed to be stated. One might have argued as follows: consider an animal sanctified as a *korban*. It has *kedushat haguf* from the moment of sanctification. Yet if it develops a *mum*, it can be redeemed. So perhaps, by analogy, these items — which also have *kedushat haguf* after the *kli* step — can likewise be redeemed when they develop a problem analogous to a *mum*, namely *tumah*. After all, in both cases the item with *kedushat haguf* has become unfit for use. Why not permit redemption in both situations?

The *mishnah* answers by rejecting the analogy. The allowance for redeeming an animal with a *mum* is a specific Torah provision; it does not establish a general principle that any item with *kedushat haguf* may be redeemed when it becomes unfit. The language the *Torah* uses regarding redemption was addressed specifically to animals — *shelo ne'emar pidyon ela bevehema* — and does not extend to *minchos*, *nesachim*, or the other items in the list.

### Animal Blemish

The distinction between animals and other sacred items runs deeper. An animal sanctified as a *korban* acquires *kedushat haguf* immediately upon the verbal act of designation, well before any service vessel is involved. When the animal is later *shechted*, the knife — itself a *kli sharet* — is applied, but the animal's *kedushat haguf* preceded this. Strikingly, however, something that acquires its *kedushat haguf* through placement in a *kli sharet* — like a *mincha* in a service bowl — cannot be redeemed once that *kli* step has occurred, even if it subsequently becomes *tamei*. The animal, despite having *kedushat haguf*, remains redeemable when blemished; the post-*kli* *mincha* does not. The *Gemara* acknowledges a certain asymmetry here: why should the *kli sharet* step be more restrictive for a *mincha* than the equivalent stage is for an animal? The *Gemara* notes that it simply takes this as given — *dimekli sharet lo ashkachan demifrak* — we have never found anything that was redeemed after its sanctification by a *kli sharet*. The animal's *kedushat haguf* exists prior to any *kli sharet* involvement, so the redemption provision for *ba'al mum* applies there; once anything, animal or otherwise, enters the *kli sharet* stage, redemption is foreclosed.

### Textual Basis

The *mishnah*'s conclusion — *shelo ne'emar pidyon ela bevehema* — points to the *pasuk* in Vayikra 27 as the source for the entire framework. The verse that provides for redemption of sacred animals is the textual basis from which the Rabbis derive that redemption is limited to animals. Everything else with *kedushat haguf*, whether *minchos*, *nesachim*, birds, wood, *levona*, or *kli sharet*, is outside the scope of that provision.

### Blemish Derasha

The *Gemara* concludes by identifying precisely where the *Torah* calls a blemished animal *tamei*. The relevant *pasuk* reads: *ve'im kol behema tmeia asher lo yakrivu mimena korban l'Hashem* — if it is an impure animal from which a *korban* cannot be brought to God. The *Gemara* asks: is this verse speaking about an actually *tamei* animal, such as a non-kosher species, or is it speaking about a blemished animal?

A nearby verse already addresses a genuinely *tamei* animal: *ve'im babehema hatmeia ufada be'erkecha* — if it is an impure animal, it may be redeemed at its assessed value. Since that verse already covers the literally *tamei* case, the first verse must be serving a different purpose. The phrase *asher lo yakrivu mimena korban l'Hashem* — from which a *korban* to God cannot be brought — is the key. This describes not a non-kosher species (for which the prohibition needs no elaboration), but rather a kosher animal that has become unfit for the *mizbe'ach* due to a *mum*. The animal belongs to a species that could normally be offered, but *this particular animal* cannot be brought — because it is blemished. That is what the *Torah* means by calling a *ba'al mum* "impure."

A further limitation is derived from the phrase *asher lo yakrivu*: the prohibition must be absolute — "from which they will not bring." This excludes a *mum over*, a transient blemish that will heal. Since such an animal *can* eventually be offered, it does not meet the criterion of absolutely not being *karev*, and therefore the Torah's redemption provision does not apply to it. Only a permanent *mum* — one that definitively prevents the animal from ever being brought as a *korban* — allows for redemption of a sanctified animal.

The *Gemara*'s identification of the *pasuk* and the *derasha* that follows thus ties the entire discussion together: the Torah's redemption mechanism was constructed specifically for blemished animals and does not carry over to *minchos*, *nesachim*, or the other categories listed in the *mishnah*. The contrast between animals and everything else is not a rabbinic fence but a biblical boundary, and the *mishnah*'s enumeration of birds, wood, *levona*, and *kli sharet* as a separate group will be parsed further in the next *daf*.

---

---

# Menachot 101

## Shmuel's Redemption Rule

### Sanctity Levels

The daf begins approximately fifteen lines down, at the word *lemachar*, picking up with the challenge of Rav Huna bar Manoach. To understand that challenge, it is necessary first to recall the position that Shmuel has advanced: if one sanctifies *menachot* and *nesachim* — the flour, oil, and libations that require sanctification in a *kli sharet* before being offered on the *mizbe'ach* — but they have not yet been placed in a *kli sharet*, one may redeem them even though they are *tahor*.

### Kedushat Damim vs. Haguf

The basis of Shmuel's position is a distinction between levels of sanctity. At the stage before placement in a *kli sharet*, these items possess only *kedushat damim* — their monetary value is sacred — but they have not yet attained *kedushat haguf*, the sanctity of the object itself. Shmuel holds that at the *kedushat damim* stage, redemption is available even without *tumah*. The *mishna*'s reference to *tumah* as a trigger for redemption, in his reading, applies only to items already in a *kli sharet*: once they have been sanctified in a vessel and attained *kedushat haguf*, they can no longer be redeemed even if they become *tamei*.

### Animals vs. Mum

This distinguishes such items from animal sacrifices. An animal possesses *kedushat haguf* and yet may be redeemed if it develops a *mum* — a disqualifying blemish. However, that avenue is specific to animals. Other items that acquire *kedushat haguf* through the *kli sharet* cannot be redeemed when *tamei*, even though *tumah* might seem analogous to a *mum* in rendering the item unusable. That is the framework Shmuel erects, and it is this framework that the *gemara* now proceeds to challenge.

---

## Rav Huna's Challenge

### Middle List Problem

Rav Huna bar Manoach raises an objection from the middle portion of the *mishna*, which presents a notably puzzling list. The *mishna* states: *ha-ofot ve-ha-etzim ve-ha-levonah ve-khlei sharet shenitme'u ein lahem pidyon* — birds, wood, frankincense, and *kli sharet* that became *tamei* cannot be redeemed. The reason offered by the *mishna* is *shelo ne'emar pidyon ela be-vehemah* — the concept of redemption applies only to an animal with a *mum*.

### The Specific Items

This list is genuinely difficult to understand. Alongside birds, the *mishna* groups wood, frankincense, and *kli sharet* — none of which are animals, and none of which have been placed in a *kli sharet* (indeed, a *kli sharet* cannot be placed inside another *kli sharet*). The challenge this poses to Shmuel is clear: if items with only *kedushat damim* and no *kli sharet* sanctification can normally be redeemed, what is the *mishna* telling us by listing these objects as non-redeemable?

### No Redemption When Tamei

The *gemara* proposes that this list must be conveying something about the general conditions for redemption. The very fact that these items — which should, on Shmuel's account, be redeemable — are listed as non-redeemable suggests that the operative principle is broader than Shmuel allows. The *gemara* will develop this.

---

## Tahor Status Theory

### Birds Analysis

The *gemara* begins its analysis: *bishlama ofot kedushat haguf ninhu* — it is understandable why birds cannot be redeemed, since birds are *kedushat haguf*. They are offered directly as sacrifices, and their slaughter is performed by the *kohen*'s fingernail rather than with a knife, so there is no *kli sharet* involved. They are thus comparable to animals with *kedushat haguf*, and only an animal with a *mum* may be redeemed. That much is clear.

### Wood & Frankincense

But what of wood, frankincense, and *kli sharet*? These items do not possess *kedushat haguf* and have not been placed in a *kli sharet*. Why, then, can they not be redeemed? The *gemara* proposes that the answer lies in the nature of these items: *ela lav mishum de-tehorim be-alma ein nifdim* — the principle must be that items that are fundamentally *tahor* cannot be redeemed. These items are listed because *af al gav de-nitme'u ke-tehorim damu* — even when they become *tamei*, they are effectively still *tahor*.

The *gemara* elaborates. Wood and frankincense are *lav benei ashvuyei okhla* — they are not genuinely edible, and therefore they should not ordinarily be susceptible to *tumah*. It is only the special rule of *hibat ha-kodesh* — the heightened treatment of temple-related objects — that causes them to be treated as if they were food and thus capable of receiving *tumah*. But this is a legal fiction, not a genuine food-status.

Moreover, wood becomes fit to receive *tumah* only once it has been smoothed and prepared as logs for the *mizbe'ach*. Until that stage — *kama de-la mashfei lehu le-gizrin* — the wood is *lo makhshiri*, not yet prepared for *tumah* susceptibility under biblical law. This rule is derived from the verse *ve-ha-basar*, which the *gemara* uses to include wood and frankincense in the laws of *tumah*, but only when they have reached the requisite state of readiness.

### Kli Sharet Purification

Similarly, *levona* does not become fit for *tumah* until it has been sanctified in a *kli sharet*. And a *kli sharet* itself — the third item in the list — presents yet another reason why its *tumah* is not truly definitive: *ho'il ve-is lehu tahara be-mikvah* — since it can be purified by immersion in a *mikvah*, its *tumah* is not a permanent condition and is therefore not the kind of *tumah* that would justify redemption.

### Fundamentally Tahor

The *gemara*'s initial theory, then, is that the middle list in the *mishna* is there to teach a general principle: items that are fundamentally *tahor* — either because they are not genuinely susceptible to *tumah*, or because their *tumah* can be reversed — may not be redeemed. This, on this reading, directly contradicts Shmuel's position that items with only *kedushat damim* may be redeemed even when *tahor*.

---

## Rarity Explanation

### Shmuel Rejects Theory

The *gemara* rejects this first reading: *lo* — no. *Le-olam eima lach tahor be-alma nifdin* — in truth, Shmuel is correct that *tahor* items may in principle be redeemed. The middle list does not establish a general principle that *tahor* items cannot be redeemed. Rather, *ve-hanei mishum de-lo shechichi hu* — the reason these particular items cannot be redeemed is that they are uncommon.

### General Redemption Rule

Shmuel's position is thus defended: the general rule permits redemption of items with *kedushat damim* even when *tahor*. The middle list represents a specific rabbinic restriction, not a general principle. The Rabbis did not want these uncommon items to be redeemed — they wanted them to reach the *Beit Hamikdash*. If someone has finally sanctified some frankincense, the Rabbis did not want that sanctification undone. But this is a limited exception, not a categorical rule against redeeming *tahor* items.

### Rarity Exception

The *gemara* then examines each item on the list. *Bishlama levona ve-khlei sharet lo shechichi* — frankincense and temple vessels are indeed uncommon, and it is understandable that once sanctified, the Rabbis would want them to remain consecrated. But then the *gemara* raises a difficulty: *ela etzim meshkach shechichi* — wood, however, is common. Why would the Rabbis apply the same restriction to wood?

### Wood Rarity

The *gemara* answers: *etzim nami keivan de-amar mar kol etz she-nimtza bo tola'at pasul le-gabei mizbe'ach* — even wood is not so common in its usable form, because we learn that any wood in which a worm is found is disqualified for the *mizbe'ach*. Wood that is fit for use on the *mizbe'ach* is therefore sufficiently rare that the same rabbinic concern applies. The conclusion is that these two readings of the middle list represent two distinct approaches to understanding why these items cannot be redeemed — one holding that *tahor* items are generally non-redeemable, and the other holding that this is a specific rabbinic restriction grounded in the rarity of these items and the desire to channel them to the *Beit Hamikdash*.

---

## Temimim Challenge

### Mizbe'ach Principle

The *gemara* now presents a challenge from Rav Papa. He cites a *baraita*: *ha-matfis temimim le-vedek ha-bayit ein podin osam ela le-mizbe'ach* — if one dedicates an unblemished animal to the general temple fund (*bedek ha-bayit*) rather than as a sacrifice, when the *Beit Hamikdash* comes to sell it, it may only be sold to someone who will use it as a *korban*. The sanctity will then transfer to the money received, and the animal will be resanctified as an offering.

### Animal Redemption

The reason for this rule is *she-kol ha-rauy le-mizbe'ach eino yotzei mi-yedei mizbe'ach le-olam* — anything fit for the *mizbe'ach* must never be permitted to escape the *mizbe'ach*. The animal was sanctified, it could serve as a *korban*, and therefore we ensure that it ultimately does so, even if the nature of the sanctification was for *bedek ha-bayit* rather than as a direct offering. *Ve-af al gav de-kedushat damim ninhu ve-ein nifdim* — even though it has only *kedushat damim*, it cannot be redeemed in a manner that would take it away from the *mizbe'ach*.

### Parallel Logic

Rav Papa argues that the same logic should apply to *menachot* and *nesachim*. These were sanctified directly for the *mizbe'ach*, they are *tahor*, and they can be placed in a *kli sharet* and offered. The principle that nothing fit for the *mizbe'ach* should escape it ought to mean that one cannot redeem them when they are *tahor*. The *baraita* thus seems to challenge Shmuel directly.

### Shmuel Consistent

The *gemara* defends Shmuel: *velo hi* — it is not so. Shmuel is familiar with this *baraita* and did not reverse his position. The reason is that on Shmuel's account, the explanation for the middle list in the *mishna* — wood, frankincense, and *kli sharet* — is that these items are rare, and the Rabbis wanted to ensure they made it to the *Beit Hamikdash*. *Lav amrat hatam kevan de-lo shechichi lo mifriki* — since those items are uncommon, we do not allow them to be redeemed when *tahor*. By contrast, *hacha nami kevan de-shechichi mumim de-paslei be-vehemah* — since blemishes that disqualify animals are common — *de-afilu be-dukin she-ba-ayin nami paslei*, even a film over the eye disqualifies an animal — *hilkhakh lo shechichi*, it is therefore not common to have a genuinely unblemished animal. And because an unblemished animal fit for the *mizbe'ach* is rare, the Rabbis similarly wanted to ensure that when one such animal was sanctified, even if for *bedek ha-bayit*, it should find its way to the *mizbe'ach*. The *baraita* about unblemished animals thus operates on the same logic as the middle list — it is not a general rule but a specific restriction applied to rare items. Wine and flour, which are common, can be redeemed freely.

---

## Tamei vs. Tahor

### Rav Kahana Position

Rav Kahana takes a categorical position against Shmuel: *tamei'im nifdim, tehorim ein nifdim* — only *tamei* items may be redeemed; *tahor* items, even those with only *kedushat damim*, may not be redeemed. This is the reading of the middle list in the *mishna* that flows from the *gemara*'s first proposed explanation, and it is also consistent with the *baraita* about unblemished animals.

### Rabi Oshaya Agrees

*Ve-khen amar Rabi Oshaya* — Rabi Oshaya expressed the same view: *tamei'im nifdim, tehorim ein nifdim*.

### Alt: Tahor Redeemable

However, there is an alternative version of Rabi Oshaya's position: *ika de-amri amar Rav Oshaya afilu tehorim nifdim* — some report that he said even *tahor* items may be redeemed. On this version, Rabi Oshaya aligns with Shmuel's fundamental position, with specific exceptions for rare items.

### Minchat Chatai Exception

Rabbi Eliezer offers a position that largely agrees with the restrictive view — *kulam tamei'im nifdim tehorim ein nifdim*, all may only be redeemed when *tamei* — but with one notable exception: *chutz me-asirit ha-eifah shel minchat chotei* — the *mincha* brought as part of the sliding-scale *korban* (*oleh ve-yored*) may be redeemed even when *tahor*.

---

## Minchat Chatai Rules

### Oleh V'Yored System

The *minchat chotei* arises within the *korban oleh ve-yored* system described at the end of Parshat Vayikra. For certain categories of sin, the Torah prescribes a graduated scale of offerings: one who can afford it brings an animal; one who cannot brings birds; and one who cannot even afford birds brings a *mincha*. The scale is designed to ensure that the obligation of *kaparah* is accessible at every economic level.

### Movement Between Levels

The Torah uses the phrase *me-chata'to al chata'to* to convey that the level of obligation tracks the sinner's current financial situation, not the level at which the obligation was originally incurred. If one set aside money for the higher-level offering and subsequently became impoverished, one may redirect a portion of those funds toward the lower-level offering appropriate to one's current means. Conversely, *al chata'to* teaches that if one sanctified a *mincha* — the lowest level — and subsequently became wealthier, one is obligated to step up to the higher-level offering.

### Minchat Chatai Redemption

This is why redemption of a *minchat chotei* is permitted even when *tahor*: the Torah itself demands flexibility in this system. If the person has become wealthier after sanctifying the *mincha*, they must be able to redeem it and bring a bird instead. The Rabbis' general restriction against redeeming *tahor* items was not applied to this case, because the Torah's own framework of *oleh ve-yored* requires the ability to move up and down the levels of obligation. The operative consideration is not the state of the *mincha* but the current financial status of the obligant.

---

## Piggul Food Status

### Piggul in Mincha

Rabi Oshaya introduces a further teaching: *shamati pigul be-mincha le-Rabi Shimon eino metamei tumat ochlin* — he heard that according to Rabi Shimon, a *mincha* that has become *piggul* — through a disqualifying intention entertained during the *avodah* — does not contract *tumah* as food (*tumat ochlin*). This is a striking and counterintuitive claim, and the *gemara* will need to explore both its basis and its apparent implications.

### Assur Behenaa Rule

The underlying principle is that for Rabi Shimon, something must be edible — or at least capable of being benefited from by someone — in order to bear the status of "food" for purposes of *tumat ochlin*. A *mincha* that has become *piggul* is forbidden not merely in eating but in any benefit (*assur be-hana'ah*), and therefore, under Rabi Shimon's reasoning, it lacks the status of food entirely.

---

## Assur Behenaa Dispute

### Tanna Kamma View

The *gemara* now grounds this discussion in a *mishna*. The *mishna* lists items that are *assur be-hana'ah* — forbidden even for benefit — including: *orlah* and *kilai ha-kerem*; the ox that is sentenced to stoning (*shor ha-niskal*) and the *egla arufa*; the birds of the *metzora* used in the purification ritual; a firstborn donkey whose neck is broken rather than redeemed; and *basar be-chalav* — meat cooked in milk. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that all of these are nonetheless capable of contracting *tumat ochlin* — food-related impurity. Even though they are forbidden in benefit, they retain the legal status of food for purposes of *tumah*.

Rashi notes that by the time the *shor ha-niskal* or *egla arufa* is stoned or has its neck broken, it would in any case be a *neveilah* and *tamei* on that basis. The relevant scenario, therefore, is one where the animal was *shechted* rather than dispatched by the prescribed method — even so, if it is in a state of being *assur be-hana'ah*, the *Tanna Kamma* holds that it is still considered food for *tumah* purposes.

### Rabbi Shimon Exception

*Rabi Shimon omer kulam ein metame'im tumat ochlin* — Rabi Shimon disagrees and holds that none of these items can contract *tumat ochlin*, because they are *assur be-hana'ah* and therefore not "food" in the legally operative sense.

### Basar Bechalav Case

However, Rabi Shimon himself concedes one case: *u-modeh Rabi Shimon be-vasar be-chalav she-metamei tumat ochlin* — he agrees that *basar be-chalav* can contract *tumat ochlin*. The reason is *ho'il ve-hayetah lo sha'at ha-kosher* — because it had a prior moment of fitness. The meat and milk each existed separately as permitted foods. Even after they were soaked together, before being cooked, they remained permitted. Only after cooking do they become *assur be-hana'ah*. Because at an earlier stage in their existence they were permissible food, they retain food-status even after becoming *assur be-hana'ah*.

All the other items on the list, by contrast, never existed as foods without the prohibition already in place. Even a live cow, before it became a *shor ha-niskal*, was not food — you cannot eat a living animal. So from the moment these items came into existence as the forbidden object in question, they were already *assur be-hana'ah*. They therefore never had a *sha'at ha-kosher*, and Rabi Shimon holds they cannot be considered food.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan Explains

### Pesuk Interpretation

Rav Assi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *mah ta'ama de-Rabi Shimon?* — what is Rabi Shimon's textual basis? The source is the verse *mi-kol ha-ochel asher ye'achel* — "from all food that can be eaten" — which the Torah employs in the context of a *sheretz* rendering food *tamei*.

### Food Definition

From this verse, Rabi Shimon derives: *ochel she-atah yakhol le-achilo la-acherim karui ochel* — food that you can feed to others is called food. The standard need not be that a Jew may personally eat it; it suffices that it can be given to non-Jews, or to a dog, so that some person or creature may derive benefit from it. If that threshold is met, the item bears the status of food for *tumah* purposes.

### Assur Behenaa Not Food

*Ochel she-ei attah yakhol le-achilo la-acherim eino karui ochel* — but if you cannot feed it to anyone, because it is *assur be-hana'ah*, then it is not called food. This is Rabi Shimon's position in its simplest form.

A question arises — one that Tosafot addresses in the name of Rabbi Eliezer mi-Mitz, the *Yere'im* — why, given the verse *asher ye'achel*, does Rabi Shimon only exclude items that are *assur be-hana'ah*, rather than excluding all items that are *assur ba-achilah* (forbidden to eat)? In another context (*Perek Kissui ha-Dam*), Rabi Shimon uses the same phrase *asher ye'achel* to exclude even *tereifah* from the obligation of covering the blood, meaning that there he excludes things forbidden to eat, not merely things forbidden in benefit.

Tosafot's answer: the verse here says *mi-kol ha-ochel* — "from all food" — with the word *kol* indicating an expansive category. Since the verse suggests inclusion broadly, if something is to be excluded, it must be only the most severely restricted items — those forbidden in any benefit at all. Other items that are merely *assur ba-achilah* but *muttar be-hana'ah* would still fall within the scope of "food."

---

## Basar Bechalav Challenge

### Basar Bechalav OK

The *gemara* now raises a question regarding Rabi Shimon's treatment of *basar be-chalav*. Before invoking the *sha'at ha-kosher* principle — that it had a prior moment of fitness — there is a more immediate reason why *basar be-chalav* poses no difficulty for Rabi Shimon at all: according to his own ruling, *basar be-chalav* is not *assur be-hana'ah* in the first place.

A *baraita* records: *Rabbi Shimon Yehuda omer mishum Rabi Shimon: basar be-chalav assur ba-achilah muttar be-hana'ah* — meat cooked in milk is forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit. The proof is a *gezeirah shavah* from the word *kadosh*: the verse regarding *basar be-chalav* calls Israel *am kadosh* — a holy people — while another verse calls them *anshei kodesh*, in the context of *tereifah*, where *assur ba-achilah* but *muttar be-hana'ah*. The parallel implies that *basar be-chalav* likewise is only *assur ba-achilah* and not *assur be-hana'ah*. (This is not the normative ruling, but it is Rabi Shimon's position.)

### Two Reasons

If so, asks the *gemara*, why did Rabi Shimon need to invoke the *sha'at ha-kosher* reasoning for *basar be-chalav*? The *gemara* answers: *chada ve-od ka'amar* — he is offering two independent reasons. First, *de-ochla de-ata yakhol le-achilo la-acherim hu* — his own personal position is that *basar be-chalav* is *muttar be-hana'ah*, so it can be fed to others and is therefore unambiguously food. Second, *le-didi nami haytah lo sha'at ha-kosher* — even for one who holds (unlike Rabi Shimon) that *basar be-chalav* is *assur be-hana'ah*, Rabi Shimon would still agree that it is food, because it had a *sha'at ha-kosher* — a prior moment of fitness before the prohibition came into effect. So he is saying: I have two independent grounds for treating *basar be-chalav* as food.

---

## Piggul-Notar Problem

### Notar Before/After

The *gemara* now raises a challenge from a *baraita* that quotes Rabi Shimon himself making a distinction regarding *notar* — sacrificial meat left over beyond its permitted time of consumption. Rabi Shimon states: *yesh notar she-metamei tumat ochlin ve-yesh notar she-eino metamei tumat ochlin* — there is *notar* that can contract *tumat ochlin* and there is *notar* that cannot.

### Notar Before Zerika

The case of *notar* that cannot contract *tumat ochlin*: meat that stayed overnight *lifnei zerika* — before the blood was ever sprinkled. From the moment this meat existed — from *shechita* — it was never fit to be eaten, because its permissibility to be eaten depends on the blood being sprinkled. Since the blood was never sprinkled, the meat moved directly from being *not yet fit* to being *notar*, without ever passing through a stage of fitness. It therefore never had a *sha'at ha-kosher* and is not food.

### Notar After Zerika

The case of *notar* that can contract *tumat ochlin*: meat that stayed overnight *le-achar zerika* — after the blood was properly sprinkled. Once the blood was sprinkled, the *kohanim* became permitted to eat the meat. It had a genuine *sha'at ha-kosher*. If they then failed to eat it before the deadline and it became *notar*, it retains its food-status and can contract *tumat ochlin*.

### Sha'at Hakoasher

This *baraita* confirms Rabi Shimon's consistency: what determines food-status is whether the item ever had a *sha'at ha-kosher* — a moment during which it was genuinely fit to be eaten. The same principle that governs *basar be-chalav* governs sacrificial meat, and by extension, it will govern the *mincha*.

---

## Oshaya-Shimon Issue

### Growing Sanctification

The *gemara* now brings the earlier teaching of Rabi Oshaya into focus in light of this framework. Rabi Oshaya's claim that a *mincha* that became *piggul* is not food according to Rabi Shimon requires explanation — after all, the *mincha* existed as flour and oil before it was sanctified, and flour and oil are edible. The *gemara* resolves this by specifying the scenario: *de-hikdishanu bi-mchubar* — the olives and the wheat were sanctified while they were still attached to the ground, still growing.

### No Sha'at Hakoasher

Because the sanctification took effect from the very beginning — from the moment when these were still raw agricultural produce attached to the earth and not yet edible in any meaningful sense — the resulting *mincha* never had a *sha'at ha-kosher*. By the time the wheat was harvested, milled into flour, and the olives were pressed into oil, and the material was processed into a proper offering, the *kedushah* had already attached. There was never a moment when it existed as ordinary, edible food free of sanctification and available to be eaten.

### Theoretical Redemption

This is admittedly a somewhat forced reading of Rabi Oshaya's statement, but the *gemara* proceeds on this basis. The question then becomes: in this scenario, does the theoretical possibility of redemption change the analysis?

---

## Potential Redemption Iss…

### Redemption Logic

Even in this unusual scenario — sanctified while still growing — the *gemara* points out that redemption is theoretically available. The *mincha* has *kedushat damim*; depending on the position one adopts about *tahor* items, it could be redeemed. If it can be redeemed, then through redemption it would once again become ordinary food, theoretically edible. Should that theoretical possibility not count as a *sha'at ha-kosher*? The *gemara* engages this question directly.

This entire inquiry is now explicitly connected to the earlier dispute: *hani — le-hakh lishna de-amar Rav Oshaya tamei'im nifdim tehorim ein nifdim* — according to the version in which Rabi Oshaya holds that only *tamei* items may be redeemed, the question does not arise. If the wheat-and-olive *mincha* cannot be redeemed while *tahor*, there is no theoretical redemption-path and therefore no *sha'at ha-kosher*. *Shapir* — that works cleanly. But *ela le-hakh lishna de-amar afilu tehorim nifdim* — according to the version that says even *tahor* items may be redeemed, *ve-lifrikinhu* — why can't we simply redeem it? And if we could redeem it, then shouldn't it be considered food?

### Could/Is Principle

The *gemara* first offers a narrow answer: *ha-shta mi-hah lo parik* — right now, in practice, it has not been redeemed. We judge things by their actual state, not by theoretical possibilities. But the *gemara* immediately pushes back on this, because it emerges that Rabi Shimon himself holds *kol ha-omed li-fdot ke-fadu dami* — anything that stands to be redeemed is considered as if it has been redeemed. That is, for Rabi Shimon, the theoretical possibility of redemption is not merely hypothetical — it carries normative weight in determining status.

### Para Aduma Case

The *gemara* cites the source for this principle: a *baraita* in which Rabi Shimon states that a *parah adumah* — the red cow used for purification — can contract *tumat ochlin* as food. This is striking, since the *parah adumah* is sanctified for burning, not for eating. But Rabi Shimon holds *hayetah lo sha'at ha-kosher* — it had a moment of fitness. What moment? Reish Lakish explains: *Rabi Shimon haya omer para nifdit al gabei ma'arachta* — Rabi Shimon would say that the *parah adumah* can be redeemed even when it is already on the woodpile, ready to be ignited. Since it can theoretically be redeemed at any moment, and since redemption would restore it to ordinary food-status, it is considered food even now. And Rabi Shimon explicitly formulates the rule: *kol ha-omed li-fdot ke-fadu dami* — what stands to be redeemed is treated as redeemed.

If Rabi Shimon holds this principle explicitly, then why doesn't the same logic apply to the wheat-and-olive *mincha* that can theoretically be redeemed?

---

## Para vs. Menachot

### Para Always Redeemable

The *gemara* draws a sharp distinction: *hachi hashta — bishlama para omedet li-fdot hi* — the *parah adumah* is not merely theoretically redeemable; it genuinely and continuously stands in a state of potential redemption. The possibility of being redeemed is always live, always in the foreground, always operative.

### Better Para Search

*She-im matza acheret na'ah mi-menah mitzvah li-fdotah* — because if one finds a more beautiful *parah adumah*, there is a *mitzvah* to redeem the first one and use the superior animal. There is thus an ongoing obligation to seek a better animal and to redeem the first if one is found. This is not merely a legal technicality; it is an active religious imperative. The *parah adumah* is therefore genuinely "standing to be redeemed" in the full sense — we are, in effect, always looking for a reason to redeem it.

### No Menachot Search

*Ela hani menachot — mitzvah li-fdotan?* — but when it comes to *menachot*, is there any such ongoing search or imperative to redeem them and find a better offering? There is not. The scenario of a *mincha* sanctified while still growing is a narrow, unusual case, and there is no analogous institution of constantly seeking a superior *mincha* and redeeming the first. Therefore, the *mincha* does not enjoy the same status as the *parah adumah* under Rabi Shimon's principle. The *mincha*'s theoretical redeemability does not generate a genuine *sha'at ha-kosher*.

---

## Notar Contradiction

### Meat Unsprinkled

The *gemara* now identifies an internal tension within Rabi Shimon's own position. Rabi Shimon said that meat that stayed overnight *before zerika* is not food. But from *shechita* until the moment of *zerika*, there is a *mitzvah* to sprinkle the blood — and if you had sprinkled it, the meat would have become fit to eat. Why doesn't the obligation to do the *zerika* — like the theoretical possibility of redeeming the *parah adumah* — count as a kind of standing readiness that makes the meat food even before the *zerika* is performed?

### Missing Earlier Case

The *gemara* presses this further in a formal way: if Rabi Shimon's rule is that once there is an opportunity to do the *zerika* the meat is considered food, then the *baraita* should have presented a more subtle internal distinction within the category of meat that stayed overnight *lifnei zerika*. It should have said: *bameh devarim amurim* — when does this meat *not* count as food? *She-lo haytah she'ut ba-yom* — only when the animal was slaughtered with insufficient time remaining in the day to perform the *zerika* (e.g., immediately before sunset). *Aval haytah lo she'ut ba-yom — metamei tumat ochlin* — but if there was ample time during the day to perform the *zerika* and it was not done, then it would be food. The *baraita* does not say this; it simply says that meat before *zerika* is not food, full stop. This seems to imply that the theoretical ability to do the *zerika* does not affect the status.

### Opportunity vs. Obligati…

The *gemara* formally resolves this by saying *hachi nami ka'amar* — yes, that is in fact what is meant. The *baraita* is to be read as implying that if there was sufficient time to perform *zerika* and it was not done, the meat would be considered food. The distinction is between having had no opportunity at all (*shelo haytah she'ut ba-yom*) versus having had the opportunity. This resolution is forced — the *baraita* does not actually say this explicitly — and the *gemara* acknowledges the awkwardness by reading it into the text. But the upshot is: Rabi Shimon is understood to hold that the theoretical possibility of *zerika* does constitute a kind of *sha'at ha-kosher*, much as the possibility of redemption does for *parah adumah*.

---

## Piggul in Animals

### Piggul at Zerika

The *gemara* now applies this framework to *piggul* in animal sacrifices. If *piggul* was enacted at the moment of *zerika* — meaning the *kohen* had a disqualifying intention when sprinkling the blood — then between *shechita* and *zerika* there was an obligation to perform the *zerika* correctly, and the meat was theoretically fit to be eaten. Consistent with the principle just developed, this should mean that the meat is considered food, and *piggul* by *zerika* should be *metamei tumat ochlin*.

### Baraita Contrast

The *gemara* then asks: if this is the case — if *piggul* by *zerika* would make the meat food — why does Rabi Shimon's *baraita* contrast *piggul* in animal sacrifice (which is not food) with *piggul* in a *mincha* (which is food)? It would have been more instructive to make an internal distinction within animal sacrifice itself: *piggul* at *shechita* (not food) versus *piggul* at *zerika* (food). Why bring in the *mincha* at all?

The *gemara* answers: *piggul bi-mincha itzterikha lei* — the *baraita* specifically wanted to teach the case of *piggul* in a *mincha*, and the reason is to highlight a specific parallel. The *gemara* wanted to contrast *shechita* of an animal (not food when *piggul*) with *kmitza* of a *mincha* (food even when *piggul*). The *kmitza* — the taking of the handful — is structurally analogous to *shechita* in animal sacrifice: both are the initial act that separates the portion destined for the *mizbe'ach* from the remainder.

### Shechita-Kmitza

Even though *kmitza* is analogous to *shechita*, the *mincha* is different because the flour and oil existed as ordinary food before the *kmitza* took place — indeed, before the entire process of offering began. The *mincha* therefore had a genuine *sha'at ha-kosher* from its earliest existence, even if at the moment of *piggul* (the *kmitza*) it was no longer fit. The *baraita* therefore made the contrast between *shechita*-of-animal and *kmitza*-of-mincha in order to highlight this structural parallel and the crucial difference in prior food-history. *Aval ein hachi nami* — and nonetheless, *piggul* by *zerika* in an animal sacrifice would also be *metamei tumat ochlin*, for the reasons just discussed.

---

## Rav Ashi Resolution

### Redeem vs. Sprinkle

Rav Ashi offers the most satisfying resolution to the tensions that have accumulated throughout this discussion. He reported: *aminah la-shema'ta kamei de-Rav Nachman* — I stated this analysis before Rav Nachman. The core principle: *de-ei ba'ei parik amrinan; ei ba'ei hava zarik lo amrinan* — the fact that you could have redeemed it, we say; the fact that you could have thrown the blood, we do not say. This is the fundamental distinction that organizes Rabi Shimon's entire approach.

### Verbal vs. Act

The difference between these two cases is not merely technical. Rashi (ten lines down in the narrow column) explains: *de-mechusar pidya lav ke-ma'aseh dami — devarim be-alma ninhu* — the act of redemption lacks the character of a formal act; it consists of words alone. To redeem something from *hekdesh*, one simply declares the transfer of sanctity from the object to money. There is no complex physical procedure, no intervening steps, no new ritual act required. The potential to redeem is therefore present here and now, fully accessible, needing only a verbal declaration.

### Here and Now

Because redemption requires only words — *devarim be-alma* — the potential to redeem is genuinely alive in the present moment. Rabi Shimon therefore treats what stands ready to be redeemed as if it has already been redeemed. The *sha'at ha-kosher* is visible, real, and immediate. It is not a hypothetical contingent on a future act; it is as present as a spoken word.

### Without Performance

By contrast, *de-ei ba'ei zarik lo amrinan* — the potential to sprinkle the blood is not treated in the same way. Sprinkling the blood is a full ritual act: it requires catching the blood at *shechita*, carrying it to the *mizbe'ach*, and performing the *zerika* correctly. Until that act is performed, the meat remains in its current state — not yet fit to be eaten, not yet food. The mere possibility that one could perform the *zerika* does not alter the present status of the meat, because the possibility is contingent on a complex act that has not yet occurred. If grandma had wheels she'd be a trolley car — the conditional is real, but the present reality is assessed as it actually stands.

Rav Ashi's resolution thus unifies the entire sugya. When Rabi Shimon says *kol ha-omed li-fdot ke-fadu dami*, he means it specifically for cases where the change in status requires only words. In those cases, the potential is treated as present reality. When the change requires a complex act — *zerika*, or any other ritual procedure — the potential is not treated as present reality until the act is actually performed. With this distinction in place, all the apparent contradictions within Rabi Shimon's position resolve cleanly, and the analysis of the *parah adumah*, the *mincha*, *piggul*, and *notar* all fall into coherent alignment.

---

---

# Menachot 102

## Rabbi Shimon & Possibili…

### Reu'uy Principle

We pick up approximately fifteen lines down on 102a, at the line beginning with the word *havi* — *havi zorik lo amrinan* — in the middle of the discussion concerning Rabbi Shimon's position on *tum'as ochlin*. The question at stake is what counts as food for the purposes of susceptibility to *tumah*. Rabbi Shimon holds that if something is halachically prohibited from being eaten or from which benefit may be derived — *asur b'hana'ah* — it does not qualify as food. However, he carves out an important exception: something that was *ra'uy*, fit or theoretically capable of being eaten at some point, retains its status as food. His examples include *basar b'chalav* where the meat and milk were each independently edible before mixing, the flour of a *mincha* before it was sanctified, and even something consecrated such as the *parah adumah* that could have been redeemed. In all these cases, the theoretical availability of permitted consumption is sufficient to confer the status of food.

### Pigul & Blood-Throwing

The debate now turns to a sharper question: does Rabbi Shimon extend this principle of *ra'uy* to cover cases where something would require an affirmative act — specifically, the throwing of blood — in order to become fit for consumption? Consider a *korban* that was *shechted* and whose blood, when sprinkled on the *mizbeiach*, was accompanied by a thought of *pigul*. Such an animal could never be eaten: not as a living animal, not as meat after *shechita* once the blood was thrown with *pigul* intent. Yet there was a brief window — between *shechita* and the invalid sprinkling — during which one could theoretically have thrown the blood correctly. The question is whether *i bei zorik*, the theoretical possibility that the blood could have been thrown properly, is sufficient under Rabbi Shimon's framework to consider this animal food.

### Rav Ashi's Distinction

Rav Ashi reports that he presented this discussion before Rav Nachman and offered the following resolution: even granting Rabbi Shimon's position in its broadest form, there is a meaningful distinction between two kinds of theoretical possibility. When redemption is effected verbally — *i bei porik*, if one could simply redeem it with words — that trivial accessibility is enough to establish the item as *ra'uy* and thus as food. But when becoming fit for consumption would require an actual transformative act, such as the proper throwing of blood, we do not apply the principle of *i bei havi zorik*. Mere theoretical feasibility of blood-throwing does not suffice to confer food status.

---

## Me'ilah & Sha'at Heter

### Sha'at Heter Principle

The Gemara now challenges Rav Ashi's position by invoking a general rule stated by Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Yehoshua articulates a broad principle: *kol shehayesa lo sha'as heter lakohanim ein mo'alin bo* — anything that had a period during which it was permissible for the *kohanim* to eat it is no longer subject to *me'ilah*; and conversely, anything that never had such a period remains subject to *me'ilah*. The relevance is immediate: just as the question of food status for *tum'as ochlin* turns on whether something was fit to be eaten, so too the question of *me'ilah* turns on whether something was permissible to the *kohanim*. And in both cases, the operative question is whether we require actual permissibility or whether theoretical possibility suffices.

### Examples of Heter

Rabbi Yehoshua's rule is then illustrated with examples. What constitutes a case where something *had* a period of being permitted to the *kohanim*? The Gemara answers: *she-lana, she-nitme'ah, she-yatz'ah* — meat that slept overnight and became *notar*, or that became *tamei*, or that was taken outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. In each of these scenarios, the meat was at some point — after the *zericas hadam*, the proper sprinkling of blood — genuinely permissible for the *kohanim* to eat, even though something subsequently rendered it forbidden. Conversely, a *korban* that was *shechted* with a thought of *pigul*, or slaughtered outside its proper time or place, or whose blood was received or thrown by disqualified *kohanim*, never passed through such a window of permissibility.

### Theoretical vs. Actual

The Gemara raises the possibility that the phrase *sha'as heter lakohanim* — "a time when it was permitted to the *kohanim*" — does not require that the blood was actually thrown and the meat was genuinely accessible. Rather, the *sha'as heter* might mean only that it was theoretically possible: *i bei havi zorik*, had the blood been thrown correctly, it could have been eaten. On this reading, even a case where the blood slept overnight without ever having been sprinkled could qualify, because in theory one could have thrown the blood. This would directly challenge Rav Ashi's contention that theoretical blood-throwing does not suffice.

### Actual Throwing Required

The Gemara says: *lo* — no. And it explains: *re'uyah latzet, re'uyah letamei, re'uyah lelin* — the cases of *yetzia*, *tumah*, and *linah* should be understood as cases where the meat was in a state where it was susceptible to those *pesulim*. Rashi explains this to mean that in the cases cited by Rabbi Yehoshua, the blood was actually thrown. The meat had become fully *kasher* — genuinely fit for consumption by the *kohanim* — and it was only subsequently that a *psul* of *linah*, *yotze*, or *tumah* occurred. The language *she-lana, she-nitme'ah, she-yatz'ah* refers to those *pesulim* occurring at a stage when the meat was legitimately available, which presupposes that the blood had already been sprinkled. This is, admittedly, a somewhat difficult read of the text, and Rashi and Tosafot each work to unpack it — but the essential point is that the Gemara understands the *Mishnah* to be describing scenarios where blood-throwing actually occurred, not merely where it could hypothetically have occurred.

It is also worth noting that the Gemara implicitly assumes Rabbi Yehoshua's principle must be consistent with Rabbi Shimon's framework — a point that itself warrants reflection, though the Gemara does not develop it further.

### Grammar & Hypothetical

The Gemara then pushes further on the language. If the determining factor is whether the blood was *actually* thrown — making the meat genuinely permissible to the *kohanim* at that moment — then Rabbi Yehoshua's formulation is curious. He says *kol shehayesa lo*, "anything that *had* a time," using the past tense. If actual permissibility is what matters, why phrase it in the past? The formulation should have been *kol sheyesh lo sha'as heter*, "anything that *has* a time" — framing the moment of permissibility as the operative present fact rather than a past historical occurrence. The past tense, the Gemara suggests, sounds more like a hypothetical: something that *could have had* such a time, not something that was actually and concretely permissible. Rashi reads this grammatical nuance as an argument that the Gemara was initially tempted to read *sha'as heter* as covering merely theoretical possibility. On that reading, the past tense captures a moment that was available in principle but never actualized. Based on this grammatical pressure, the Gemara is inclined to concede that by *me'ilah*, theoretical possibility may well suffice — while maintaining that the case of food status for *tum'as ochlin* operates differently.

---

## Me'ilah vs. Food Status

### Kedushah & Possibility

Rav Ashi responds to this challenge directly: *me'ilah tuma ramit* — can you really draw a comparison between *me'ilah* and *tumah*? These are categorically different questions. *Me'ilah* depends on the degree of *kedushah* the object carries. Once the *kedushah* is lowered — *depaka lei kedushtei*, once the sanctity flies off, so to speak — *me'ilah* ceases. And once lost, that *kedushah* level does not return: *u-vemai hadra rachva lah*. The crucial point is that the theoretical possibility of blood-throwing is sufficient to weaken the *kedushah*. The moment it becomes conceivable — within human reach — that the blood could be thrown and the meat could be eaten, the *kedushah* begins to slip from its highest register. And once it has slipped, there is no mechanism to restore it. So by *me'ilah*, theoretical possibility changes the status in a real and permanent way.

### Food Requires Actuality

When it comes to *tum'as ochlin*, however, the question is categorically different: *mishum ochla velav ochla hi* — we are asking whether this is food. The *girsa* in the *Shita Mekubetzes* and the emendation offered by the *Bach* help clarify the text here: the principle as Rav Ashi intends it is that only where the blood was actually thrown — *d'izrik* — is the meat rendered food. Where the blood has not been thrown, the theoretical possibility that it *could* have been thrown does not suffice to grant food status. The formulation *kol heicha de'i ba'ei zarku mashvei lei ochla* would read as "wherever one could have thrown, that makes it food," which proves too much; the corrected reading is that actual throwing is what makes it food, and without it, it remains non-food regardless of theoretical accessibility.

### Losing vs. Gaining States

Rashi articulates the underlying principle that explains the asymmetry: it is easier to *lose* a state than to *gain* one. Something that is *kadosh* and sits at a high level of *kedushah* — as soon as the door is opened, as soon as it becomes conceivable that the blood could be thrown and the meat could be accessed, the *kedushah* begins to descend. That theoretical opening is enough for the item to slip from its elevated status. But to *gain* the status of food — for something that is not actually edible to be reclassified as food — mere theoretical possibility is insufficient. One cannot simply say that because the blood *could* have been thrown and the item *could* have been eaten, it therefore counts as food. The asymmetry between losing and gaining a halachic state explains why *me'ilah* responds to theoretical possibility while food status does not.

---

## Asham Talui Case

### Asham Discovery Case

The Gemara now introduces a *Mishnah* from Kerisot as a potential challenge. Someone brings an *asham talui* — the contingent guilt offering brought when one is uncertain whether he committed a sin requiring a *chatas*. The classic case: two pieces of meat were before him, one permitted and one forbidden *cheilev*, and he ate one without knowing which. In a state of genuine doubt, he is obligated to bring an *asham talui* to atone provisionally, with the understanding that if he later discovers he did eat the *cheilev*, he must bring a full *korban chatas*. He sanctifies an animal for this purpose. Now suppose that before the *shechita*, he discovers that in fact he did not sin — someone clarifies which piece he ate, and it was the permitted one. In that case, *im ad shelo nishchat noda lo*, if the discovery comes before *shechita*, Rabbi Meir says: *yeitzei veyeireh ba'eder* — let the animal go back into the flock. The sanctification was made in error. Since the *asham talui* was only ever predicated on the state of doubt, and that doubt is now resolved, the sanctification retroactively has no basis. The Sages, however, disagree: *yeireh ad sheyista'eiv veyimmacher veyipelu damav lindava* — the animal retains its *kedushah*, must be allowed to develop a blemish, be sold, and the proceeds directed to a voluntary *olah*. Their reasoning is that at the moment of the vow, one presumably intended to bring a *korban* in any eventuality, even if ultimately it would take the form of a donation rather than an obligatory offering.

### Nullification Post-Shech…

Rabbi Eliezer takes yet a different approach: bring it regardless. Since an *asham talui* does not require a highly specific concrete possibility of sin — and since people inevitably have some exposure to undetected transgression — the animal may serve as *asham talui* for some other potential sin. After the *shechita*, however, the situation changes. If one discovers *after* slaughter that he had not sinned, *hadam yishafeich vehabasar yisaref* — the blood is spilled and the meat is burned. The reason is that it is now essentially *chullin b'azarah*. Even according to the *chachamim*, who hold that the animal retains *kedushah*, Tosafot in Kerisot explains that the sanctification was never for the animal itself to serve as an *olah* but rather for its proceeds to go toward one; and since it was *shechted* as an *asham* without valid obligation, and its alternative identity as an *olah* does not apply to the animal itself, it is in any case a *korban pasul*. Alternatively, Tosafot suggests that once *shechita* takes place with the identity of an *asham*, that identity cannot be retroactively changed — even if the worshipper had in mind that it might alternatively serve as an *olah*.

### Rabbi Yosei's Position

If, however, the blood was actually sprinkled on the *mizbeiach* before the discovery — *nizrak hadam* — and only afterward does one learn he had not sinned, then *habasar yeiachel* — the meat is eaten. This is because at the moment of *zerikah*, the offering was being brought in a genuine state of doubt, and was therefore brought under valid obligation. The post-facto discovery does not invalidate what was properly done. Rabbi Yosei goes further: *afilu hadam bekos yizraik vehabasar yeiachel* — even if the blood is still in a cup and has not yet been thrown, and even though the discovery has now revealed that there was no obligation, one may nevertheless proceed to throw the blood and eat the meat. This is the striking position that now engages the Gemara.

### Rava's Attribution

Rava explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning by attributing it to the school of Rabbi Shimon: *Rabbi Yosei b'shitas Rabbi Shimon amar, de'amar kol ha'omed lizrok k'zaruk dami* — Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that anything that is positioned to be thrown is considered as if it has already been thrown. On this reading, the moment the blood is in a cup and the *zerikah* could technically be performed, it is treated halachically as if the *korban* has already been properly offered, and the meat may therefore be eaten. This would represent a robust application of Rabbi Shimon's principle — and notably, it would apply to *gaining* a status, not merely losing one. If the possibility of throwing makes it as though the *korban* has been brought, then the meat gains the status of something that may be eaten. This constitutes a challenge to the distinction Rav Ashi drew between losing *kedushah* (where theoretical possibility suffices) and gaining food status (where it does not).

---

## Kli Sharet Alternative

### Kli Sharet Receives Blood

The Gemara responds by offering an alternative explanation of Rabbi Yosei's position that does not rely on Rabbi Shimon at all. *Midi taima* — the real reason, as transmitted in the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, is not the principle of *kol ha'omed lizrok k'zaruk dami*, but rather: *dikesavar klei shares mikadshin et hapsulin l'chatchila likarev* — Rabbi Yosei holds that a *kli shares*, a sanctified service vessel, has the capacity to sanctify even *pesulim*, at least in certain configurations, sufficiently to permit the offering to go forward.

### Safety in Kli Sharet

Rashi qualifies this as applying specifically to a relatively *weak* or attenuated *psul* — such as the one that pertains here, where the *asham* was brought in genuine doubt and only afterward did one discover there was no obligation. The *psul* that affects this offering is not a *psul* of the animal itself or of the act of *shechita*, but rather a change in the worshipper's obligation status. In such a case, once the blood has been caught in the *kli shares*, it is considered, in Rashi's framing, to have "arrived home safely." The *kli shares* creates a kind of protective threshold: now that the blood is properly contained within the vessel, even the subsequent emergence of a *psul* does not prevent the *zerikah* from proceeding. This is analogous to the principle that certain *pesulim*, once an offering has ascended the *mizbeiach*, do not require it to be brought down. Here too, once the blood is in the *kli shares*, one proceeds to complete the *avoda*. On this explanation, Rabbi Yosei's position does not commit us to Rabbi Shimon's broad principle, and the scope of *kol ha'omed lizrok k'zaruk dami* remains in question.

---

## Notar & Parah Adumah

### Burn Obligation Problem

Rav Ashi then raises a further problem. If one grants that Rabbi Shimon really does hold *kol ha'omed lizrok k'zaruk dami* in its fullest sense — that something fit to have its blood thrown is treated as if the blood has been thrown — then by parallel logic one might also say *kol ha'omed lisrof k'saruf dami*, that something which must be burned is treated as if it has already been burned, i.e., as if it is already ash. This creates an immediate difficulty: *notar* and *parah adumah* each carry an obligation to be burned, yet we said earlier that both are susceptible to *tum'as ochlin* — they are treated as food. If the obligation to burn them makes them theoretically equivalent to ash, why should they count as food at all? *Afra b'alma nihu* — they should be considered mere dust.

### Chibat HaKodesh Solution

Rav Ashi responds: *chibas hakodesh machshartan* — the special relationship of sanctity that pertains to things within the *Mikdash* confers upon them a food-like status that overrides normal considerations. Even where something would not ordinarily qualify as food — whether because it is theoretically equivalent to ash or for some other reason — the elevated association with the *Mikdash* is itself sufficient to render such items susceptible to *tumah*. This principle was already encountered several *dapim* earlier in the tractate, in the context of wood, *levonah*, and other items that acquire susceptibility to *tumah* by virtue of their sanctified context rather than by their intrinsic edibility.

### Tamei vs. Pasul Question

Ravina asks a pointed follow-up question to Rav Ashi: *mihedi mehani lei chibas hakodesh lifsulei d'gufei* — I can understand that *chibas hakodesh* operates to make something more susceptible to *tumah* such that if a *tamei* object contacts it, it becomes *pasul*. But would you go so far as to say it becomes genuinely *tamei*, capable of transmitting *tumah* onward — to count *rishon* and *sheni* degrees of *tumah* removal? These are two distinct categories in the laws of *tumah v'taharah*: *tamei* means the object has absorbed *tumah* and can transmit it further; *pasul* means it is disqualified but the chain of transmission stops there. If *notar* and *parah adumah* are only considered food-like by virtue of *chibas hakodesh*, and not intrinsically, the strong language of *metamei tumas ochlin* — *transmitting* food *tumah* — seems to overclaim.

### Reish Lakish Resolution

Ravina observes that this question connects to one already posed by Reish Lakish: *tzarid shemen menachot* — if a *mincha* offering dried out and the oil never reached a portion of the flour, that dry flour was never rendered susceptible to *tumah* through contact with liquid in the ordinary way. Yet by virtue of *chibas hakodesh*, it gains susceptibility. Reish Lakish's question was: when this flour becomes *tamei* through *chibas hakodesh*, does the transmission proceed as *rishon* and *sheni* — i.e., is it genuinely *tamei* in the full sense — or does the chain stop, making it only *pasul*? If we could resolve the question about *notar* and *parah adumah* — accepting that *chibas hakodesh* renders them truly *tamei* in the language of *metamei tumas ochlin* — that would appear to answer Reish Lakish's question as well.

### D'Rabbanan Level

The Gemara declines to accept this resolution. Reish Lakish was asking about the status *d'Oraisa* — whether at the level of Torah law, *chibas hakodesh* produces genuine *tumah* with full transmission capacity. The answer being discussed here, the Gemara clarifies, operates only at the *d'Rabbanan* level: *ki ka'amina d'Rabbanan* — whatever the precise Biblical framework, at the Rabbinic level we are willing to say that *chibas hakodesh* renders an item genuinely *tamei* in the full sense, including transmission. This resolves the apparent tension in using the language *metamei tumas ochlin* for items whose food status derives only from their sanctified context: at the Rabbinic level, that context is sufficient to activate the full vocabulary of *tumah* transmission, even if the Biblical analysis might operate differently.

---

## Mincha Vow Cases

### Vessel Type Mismatch

The Gemara transitions to the next *Mishnah*, which was cited already at the beginning of the tractate. The *Mishnah* presents a series of cases involving the specification of a *mincha* offering. In the first, someone takes a vow — *harei alai* — to bring a *mincha* in a *machavat*, a shallow pan, and instead brings it in a *marcheshet*, a deep pan, or vice versa. The ruling: *mah sheheivi heivi veyedei chovato lo yatza* — what he brought was brought as a valid offering, but he has not fulfilled his vow. The *mincha* is accepted as a valid donation; the vow obligation remains outstanding. The vow was specific as to the vessel type, and bringing a different vessel type — even with the same amount of flour — does not satisfy it.

### Sanctification Mismatch

The second case: if he says *zo lehavi bamachavat* — I am sanctifying *this* flour to bring as a *minchat machavat* — and then brings it as a *minchat marcheshet*, or the reverse, *harei zo pesula* — it is invalid. When the flour itself is sanctified with a specific designation, using it in a manner inconsistent with that designation creates a mismatch between the *kedushah* and its execution. The result is not merely an unfulfilled vow but an invalid offering.

### Quantity Mismatch Unfulf…

Similarly, if someone takes a vow to bring two *esronot* of flour in two separate vessels — two *menachot* of one *issaron* each — and instead brings both in one vessel, or takes a vow to bring them in one vessel and brings them in two, the ruling again is *mah sheheivi heivi veyedei chovato lo yatza*: the offering brought is valid on its own terms as a donation, but the obligation remains unfulfilled. The specificity of the vow — both the number of *esronot* and the number of vessels — is part of its definition, and a departure from either dimension means the obligation is not discharged.

### Sanctified Configuration…

When, however, the flour itself is sanctified with a specific configuration — *elu bikli echad*, this flour to be brought in one vessel, and one then brings it in two, or the reverse — *harei elu pesulim*, the offerings are invalid. This is somewhat surprising. One might have thought that the question of one vessel versus two is a procedural detail without substantive halachic import. The *Mishnah* teaches otherwise. Rashi explains: if you said two *menachot* and brought one, you have effectively presented a *mincha yeteira* — an oversized offering — since what should have been two separate *menachot* with two *kematzim* burnt on the *mizbeiach* now has only one *komets* taken from a combined mass. And if you said one and brought two, each offering is a *mincha chaseira* — each is half of what it was supposed to be. These structural changes mean the offering is fundamentally different from what was sanctified, and it is therefore *pasul*. This is admittedly a *chiddush*: the configuration of vessels is treated as part of the essential identity of the sanctification, not merely a technical preference.

### Reminder Reframes Vow

The final case in the *Mishnah* is the most intriguing. Someone takes a vow to bring two *esronot* in one vessel and then, while walking to the *Beis Hamikdash*, places them in two vessels instead. A bystander says to him: *b'kli echad nadarta* — you vowed to bring it in one vessel. He ignores the comment and proceeds to offer it in two vessels. The ruling: *pesulim* — invalid. And conversely, if someone vowed two *esronot* in two vessels and was bringing it in one, and a bystander says *bishnei keilim nadarta* — you vowed two vessels — and he proceeds to offer it in one, it is similarly invalid. Yet if, upon hearing the reminder, he corrects his approach and aligns the offering with his vow, it is *kasher*.

Rashi's explanation of why the reminder creates invalidity is that the bystander's statement frames the act in the context of the vow. The worshipper's silence and continuation are interpreted not as a statement that this is an independent offering disconnected from the vow, but rather as an implicit acknowledgment that he is attempting to fulfill his vow — improperly. What he brings is thus assessed as an attempted fulfillment of his vow, and since it does not conform to its terms, it is not merely an unrelated valid donation but an invalid offering.

This explanation, it must be admitted, is puzzling. The vow was about the worshipper's personal obligation, not about the flour. The flour was sanctified for a *mincha* without any designation of one vessel or two. How can the intervention of bystanders retroactively impose an identity on the offering that makes it *pasul*? If someone vowed a sheep *olah* and brought a cow *olah*, we would say: thank you for the cow *olah*, it is valid, but your obligation for a sheep *olah* remains. Why, here, does the verbal reminder transform a valid offering into an invalid one? This remains an open question, as Rashi and Tosafot do not provide a fully satisfying resolution.

---

## Vow vs. Sanctification

### Both Cases Necessary

The Gemara opens its analysis of the *Mishnah* by asking why both the vessel-type case (*machavat* versus *marcheshet*) and the quantity case (one vessel versus two) are necessary. The answer follows a standard Talmudic pattern: each case teaches something the other does not. *Iy ashmi'inan hach kmaisa* — had we only been taught the first case, one might have thought the invalidity results specifically because the type of pan is integral to the character of the *mincha*: a *minchat machavat* and a *minchat marcheshet* are defined by the Torah as distinct offerings with their own *parshiyos*, and vowing one and bringing the other is therefore inherently a mismatch. One might then suppose that when someone vows a *mincha* of a certain quantity in a certain number of vessels, the number of vessels is not so defining — after all, *idi v'idi machavat* and *idi v'idi marcheshet*, the flour is being prepared in the same type of pan either way — and the quantity configuration is merely incidental. *Eima de-nidron nami yeitzei* — perhaps the vow is substantially fulfilled. The second case teaches that even the number of vessels is sufficiently integral to the vow that a departure from it means the vow is not fulfilled. Conversely, had only the quantity case been taught, one might have thought the deficiency results specifically because altering the number of vessels changes the amount of flour being offered in each unit, making each *mincha* either oversized or undersized.
