But in the case of *machavat* and *marcheshet*, where the total amount of flour is unchanged, perhaps the vow is fulfilled. The *Mishnah* therefore needs both cases to teach that each dimension — vessel type and vessel number — independently defines the vow.

### Kli Sharet Non-Sanctifyi…

A *baraita* is then cited that bears on the case where flour is sanctified with a specific configuration. The *baraita* states that the *kli shares* does not sanctify the flour with a fixed identity prior to the offering. The relevance: if someone designated flour as *elu bikli echad* — this flour in one vessel — and then placed it in two vessels, why not simply recombine it before the *avoda*? The *baraita* suggests that the *kli shares* does not yet lock in its identity in a way that would prevent correction. The implication seems to be that even after placing the flour in an incorrect vessel, the situation could be remedied.

### Abaye's Position

Abaye reconciles the *baraita* with the *Mishnah*'s ruling of *pesulim*: *lo kadshem likarev aval kadshem lipassel* — the *kli shares* does not make the offering *kasher* for presentation, but it does fix its identity sufficiently to establish invalidity. This is a well-known distinction in halachic analysis. Once the flour is in the *kli shares*, its identity is crystallized — it cannot be reconfigured without that configuration becoming its defining characteristic. If that configuration is misaligned with how it was sanctified, the *kli shares* has locked in the misalignment, making it *pasul*, even though it has not yet made it valid for offering in the positive sense.

### Time of Neder Fixes Iden…

Abaye adds a further important principle: *lo shanu ela shekeva'am besha'as neder* — the rule that misalignment creates invalidity applies only when the specific configuration was established at the time of the *neder* itself. *Aval besha'as hafrasha lo* — but if the configuration was specified only at the time of separating the flour (*hafrasha*) and not at the time of the original vow, then that subsequent specification does not define the identity of the offering in the same binding way. The reason: the *neder* is the generative act that defines the obligation, and the identity it creates is what governs. When someone vows simply to bring a *mincha* and then, at the time of *hafrasha*, specifies that it will be a *marcheshet* or a *machavat* or will be in two vessels, that specification at *hafrasha* does not carry the same halachic force. If the offering is ultimately brought in a different configuration than specified at *hafrasha* but consistent with what was left open at the time of the *neder*, there is no *psul*. This principle is confirmed by a parallel transmission: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yosei in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states the same rule — *lo shanu ela shekeva'am besha'as neder aval besha'as hafrasha lo, ka'asher nadarta velo ka'asher hifrashta*.

### Reminder Problem Unresol…

This principle makes the final case of the *Mishnah* all the more perplexing. In that case, the worshipper took a personal vow obligation — he never sanctified the flour in a specific configuration. He vowed to bring two *esronot* in one vessel or two vessels and then walked toward the *Beis Hamikdash* with the flour arranged differently. The bystander's reminder framed the act as an attempt to fulfill the vow, and the Gemara rules it *pasul* as a result. But if the time of *neder* is what fixes identity, and the *neder* here was simply a personal obligation without a specific flour-vessel designation, how does the bystander's oral comment at the time of delivery suddenly impose a specific identity on the offering — one that then makes it *pasul* for being misaligned? The flour was never sanctified with any configuration. The vow was abstract. Nothing at the time of *neder* fixed a vessel identity. Why should what amounts to a verbal exchange at the moment of approaching the *mizbeiach* now redefine the nature of the *mincha* and render it invalid? Rashi and Tosafot do not resolve this difficulty, and we leave it as an open question.

---

---

# Menachot 103

## Mishnah Intro

### Cases Overview

The daf opens at the *mishnah* approximately six lines from the top of 103a. The subject is a person who takes a vow (*neder*) to bring a *minchah* — a meal offering — but formulates the vow in terms that do not match any recognized category of voluntary *minchah*. The question throughout is: what are the consequences? Is the person bound, and if so, to what?

The *mishnah* presents a series of such cases. One who says *harei alai minchah min ha-se'orim* — "I obligate myself with a *minchah* of barley" — must nonetheless bring a standard *minchah* of wheat flour, since there is no voluntary *minchah* of barley (barley *menachot* are limited to the *minchat choteh* and the *minchah* of the *sotah*). Similarly, one who vows a *minchah* of bran (*kemach*) must bring fine flour (*solet*). One who says *belo shemen u-velo levonah* — without oil and without frankincense — must bring it with oil and frankincense, since those are indispensable components. In each of these cases, the impermissible specification is set aside and the person is bound to bring a proper *minchah*.

### Invalid Specifications

What unites these cases is that the person specifies something that cannot be part of a voluntary *minchah* — whether the wrong grain, the wrong grade of flour, or the omission of required ingredients. The *mishnah* in each instance directs that we ignore the defective specification and hold the person to the underlying obligation of a *minchah*. The central question, which the *Gemara* immediately raises, is why: why should we not simply say that the vow, as stated, is meaningless, and release the person entirely?

### Half-Issaron Case

The *mishnah* adds two further cases involving the *issaron*, the standard unit of flour for a *minchah*. One who says *chatzi issaron yavi issaron shalem* — "I obligate myself in half an *issaron*" — must bring a full *issaron*, since *menachot* can only be brought in whole *issaron* units. This is relatively straightforward by analogy to the earlier cases: ignore the "half" and obligate in the minimum valid quantity.

The most striking case, however, is the last: *issaron u-mechtzah yavi shnayim* — if one says "I obligate myself in an *issaron* and a half," one must bring two full *issronot*. This goes well beyond anything the earlier cases suggest. In all the prior examples, one can explain the rule by simply cutting off the defective portion of the vow and relying on what remains — the word *minchah* standing alone. But here, how do we get from "an *issaron* and a half" all the way to two full *issronot*? That is the crux the *Gemara* will grapple with at length.

*Rabbi Shimon* dissents and exempts in all these cases: *shelo hitnadev k'derech ha-mitnadbim* — the person did not take a vow in the manner of those who make vows. Since the complete statement the person uttered does not describe any valid *minchah*, *Rabbi Shimon* treats the entire vow as void.

---

## Why Binding?

### Neder Upitcho Imo

The *Gemara* opens with a sharp question: *amai?* — why is the person bound at all? The principle invoked is *neder upitcho imo* — a vow whose very utterance contains within it an opening for annulment. *Rashi* explains: since the person said, for instance, *minchah min ha-se'orim*, and everyone knows there is no *minchah* of barley, we may read the specification as a signal that the person already regrets the vow or never genuinely meant to obligate himself. Either way — whether we understand it as attempted retraction or simply as a meaningless formula — why should it be binding?

### Tafos Lashon Rishon

*Chizkiyah* answers: the *mishnah* follows *Beit Shammai*, who hold the principle of *tafos lashon rishon* — seize the first language. The moment the person said *harei alai minchah*, those words bound him. Whatever followed — "of barley," "of bran," "without oil" — is irrelevant. The first word *minchah* was already out of his mouth, and nothing said afterward can redefine or retract it. The second portion of the statement is simply ignored; the obligation that attached at the first word remains.

### Beit Shammai vs Hillel

The *Gemara* cites the *mishnah* in Nazir as the locus of this dispute. One who says *hareini nazir min ha-gerogerot u-min ha-deveilah* — "I am a *nazir* from pressed figs and pressed dates" — is formulating a *neziroot* in terms the *Torah* does not recognize. *Beit Shammai* say he is nonetheless a *nazir*: we ignore everything after the first word and he is bound by *hareini nazir*. *Beit Hillel* say he is not a *nazir* at all.

This makes the structure of our *mishnah* noteworthy: it appears as a *stam mishnah* — an unattributed ruling — aligned with *Beit Shammai*, with *Rabbi Shimon* being the sole dissenting voice. That is *Chizkiyah's* reading.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan

### Assumed Intent

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees and maintains that the *mishnah* can in fact be read in accordance with *Beit Hillel*. His explanation turns on the following: *b'omer ilu hayiti yodea she'ein nodrin kach lo hayiti noder kach ela kach* — the case is one where the person would say, "Had I known that one cannot make a vow in this form, I would not have vowed this way, but rather in the straightforward way." That is, had the person realized that a *minchah* of barley is impossible, he would simply have obligated himself in a plain *minchah*.

The question naturally arises whether this requires actually asking the person, or whether we simply assume it. The *mishnah* does not say "if he declares that this is what he meant," which suggests that the point is not to query the person but to assume his intent based on the circumstances. *Rabbi Yochanan's* approach is therefore best understood as an objective inference from the nature of the case: when someone says "I want to bring a *minchah* of barley," the specification of barley is a relatively minor modification — perhaps a cheaper alternative — and it is reasonable to infer that, had the person known it was unavailable, he would have accepted the standard obligation. We can therefore treat the vow as if he had said simply *harei alai minchah*, because that is plausibly what he would have meant.

This contrasts with the case of *neziroot*: one who says "I am a *nazir* from figs and dates" cannot be assumed to have intended full *neziroot* had he known the rules, since *neziroot* entails abstinence from wine, haircuts, and corpse impurity — a substantially different and more demanding commitment than what he described. There we cannot make that assumption, and *Beit Hillel* therefore exempts him entirely. But in the *minchah* cases, where the modification is minor and the core intent clear, *Beit Hillel* can bind him on the basis of his presumed intent.

### Binding Without Words

There remains, however, a serious difficulty with *Rabbi Yochanan's* approach — one that is most acute in the last case of the *mishnah*. Even granting that we can infer the person's intent, a *neder* requires actual words to be binding. If the person said *issaron u-mechtzah*, and we conclude that what he would have meant had he known the *halachah* is two full *issronot* — the inference may be entirely correct, but he never actually said "two *issronot*." There is no verbalized *neder* to anchor that obligation. This remains an open question at this stage, to be resolved later in the *Gemara*.

---

## Barley vs Lentils

### Chizkiyah's Limit

*Chizkiyah* draws a distinction: the rule of the *mishnah* — that the person is bound — applies specifically when he says *minchah min ha-se'orim*, a *minchah* of barley. But if he says *minchah min ha-adashim* — a *minchah* of lentils — he is not bound, because everyone knows one cannot bring a *minchah* of lentils, and the utterance therefore cannot be read as anything other than a meaningless statement.

### Challenge to Chizkiyah

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this distinction. *Chizkiyah* explained the *mishnah* according to *Beit Shammai*, whose principle is *tafos lashon rishon* — we simply seize the first word. *Beit Shammai* do not inquire into what the person was thinking; they focus mechanically on the first term uttered. If so, what difference does it make whether the person said "barley" or "lentils"? In either case, he said the word *minchah*, and that word binds him. The subsequent specification — barley or lentils or anything else — is simply ignored.

### Chizkiyah Reverses

Confronted with this objection, *Chizkiyah* reverses his position. He concedes that the barley-versus-lentils distinction does not work within the framework of *Beit Shammai*, and accordingly adopts *Rabbi Yochanan's* reading: the *mishnah* follows *Beit Hillel*, and the operative question is what the person genuinely meant and would have intended had he known the *halachah*.

### Rava's Inference

*Rava* identifies what drove *Chizkiyah* to reverse himself: *matnitin kashyateih* — the language of the *mishnah* itself pressed the point. *Rava* asks: why does the *mishnah* choose the example of barley, which is precisely the kind of mistake a person could plausibly make? Why not teach a more striking *chiddush* — that even if one said "a *minchah* of lentils" one is still bound? The fact that the *mishnah* illustrates the rule with barley and not lentils indicates that the rationale is *mishum de-ta'ei* — because the person made a reasonable mistake. This is the framework of *Beit Hillel*: we ask what the person really intended, and we hold him to that intent only when the error was plausible. By barley — a grain associated with other *menachot* — one could genuinely have thought a voluntary *minchah* was possible. By lentils, that is plainly absurd: *bi-se'orim ta'ei, de-adashim lo ta'ei*. Since lentils cannot be explained as a reasonable mistake, there is no presumed underlying intent to bring a *minchah*, and the vow is void. The *mishnah's* choice of example thus implicitly endorses *Beit Hillel's* intent-based approach.

---

## Lentils Dispute

### Yochanan: Even Lentils

In a striking reversal of expected positions, *Rabbi Yochanan* now asserts that even a vow of *minchah min ha-adashim* — a *minchah* of lentils — would bind the person, at least according to the reading of the *mishnah* he is addressing. This might seem inconsistent with his own intent-based approach, which appears to require that the mistake be reasonable.

### Lentils Obvious

The *Gemara* resolves this by clarifying that *Rabbi Yochanan* is speaking *li-devarav de-Chizkiyah* — within *Chizkiyah's* original framework, addressing him on his own terms. *Rabbi Yochanan* is saying: you can maintain your original position that the *mishnah* goes like *Beit Shammai*, and even so you need not retract the distinction you drew. According to *Beit Shammai*, even lentils would bind the person — and the *mishnah* does not say lentils precisely because lentils is *obvious* according to *Beit Shammai*. When someone says "a *minchah* of lentils," that is so clearly absurd that it functions as an open retraction or a second statement entirely distinct from the first. *Beit Shammai's* rule of *tafos lashon rishon* applies with full force: the retraction is ignored and the first word *minchah* binds. Of course lentils yields an obligation — that is self-evident. But why does barley yield an obligation? That is less obvious, because one might have thought that when the second part of the statement shows the person's genuine mistaken intent — as opposed to a clear retraction — *Beit Shammai* might treat the entire statement as a unit and invalidate the whole thing.

### Intent vs Retraction

*Rabbi Yochanan's* point is therefore a refinement of *Beit Shammai's* position. One might have supposed that *tafos lashon rishon* operates only when the second part of the statement is a clear retraction — "I changed my mind" — in which case we ignore the retraction and hold to the first word. But when the second part reveals what the person always had in mind, perhaps *Beit Shammai* would weigh the entire statement together and find it defective. To this *Rabbi Yochanan* responds: *afilu hachi tafos lashon rishon* — even so, *Beit Shammai* ignores the second half absolutely. Whether the second part is a clear retraction (lentils) or an expression of original mistaken intent (barley), it is equally disregarded. *Beit Shammai's* rule is categorical. The *mishnah* mentions barley rather than lentils only because barley requires the novel ruling; lentils was already obvious.

To summarize the final state of the debate: the *mishnah* can be read either as *Beit Shammai* or as *Beit Hillel*. According to *Beit Shammai*, the binding force of the vow depends entirely on the first word uttered, regardless of what follows or what the person intended — and accordingly lentils would also bind. According to *Beit Hillel*, we ask what the person genuinely would have meant, and only where a reasonable mistake accounts for the mismatch do we impose an obligation — so barley binds but lentils does not.

---

## Zeriri's Condition

### Mincha Word Required

At the top of 103b, *Zeriri* introduces a further condition. The principle that the *mishnah* applies — under whichever rationale, *Beit Shammai* or *Beit Hillel* — only holds *lo shanu ela de-amar minchah*: where the person actually said the word *minchah*. If he did not say the word *minchah* — for instance, if he said merely *harei alai min ha-se'orim* or *harei alai min ha-kemach*, leaving *minchah* only implied — he is not bound.

Working within the *Beit Shammai* framework, the logic is clear: *tafos lashon rishon* requires an actual first word to seize. If the person said *minchah min ha-se'orim*, we discard *min ha-se'orim* and grab *minchah*. But if he said only *min ha-se'orim*, there is nothing to grab; the word *minchah* is not present. Similarly, *minchat se'orim* — written in the construct form — does not give us a freestanding *minchah*: *minchat* is the *minchah* of, and it pulls the word *se'orim* along with it as an inseparable unit. Only when *minchah* stands alone as a discrete word can *Beit Shammai* seize it. According to *Beit Hillel*, one could argue that even without the explicit word, if we know the person meant a *minchah*, we could obligate him — but *Zeriri's* condition, at minimum as applied to *Beit Shammai*, requires the word.

### Rava Challenges

*Rava* challenges this by reading through the cases in the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* says *kemach yavi solet* — bran, bring fine flour — without explicitly stating *minchah min ha-kemach*. Is this not a case where the person did not say the word *minchah*? Similarly, *belo shemen u-velo levonah yavi shemen u-levonah* makes no mention of the word *minchah*. And *chatzi issaron yavi issaron shalem* — again, no explicit *minchah*. *Rava* presses: does the *mishnah* not thereby contradict *Zeriri's* requirement that the word *minchah* must be stated?

### Mincha Implied

The *Gemara* deflects each challenge by insisting that in each case the person did in fact say the word *minchah* — the *mishnah* simply abbreviates. *Kemach yavi solet* means he said *minchah min ha-kemach*; the fuller formulation is understood. And so with each case: the *mishnah's* shorthand does not indicate that the word *minchah* was absent; it is present in each instance, as *Zeriri* requires.

---

## Half-Issaron Crux

### One Word Binds

The challenge that remained from the opening discussion now comes into sharp focus. According to *Beit Shammai* — where we work with the words themselves and need the word *minchah* to anchor the obligation — consider the case of *issaron u-mechtzah*. If the person says *minchah issaron u-mechtzah*: the word *minchah* obligates him in one *issaron* (the minimum valid *minchah*). The word *issaron* that follows is consistent with *minchah* and confirms the obligation. But then he says *chatzi* — half — and that word *chatzi* carries no obligating force on its own. So he remains bound to one *issaron*, and we never arrive at two. How, under *Beit Shammai's* logic, does this case yield the obligation of two *issronot*?

### Reversed Order

The *Gemara* resolves this with a creative structural move: *lo tzericha de-amar harei alai minchah chatzi issaron ve-issaron* — the case in the *mishnah* is not where the person said "an *issaron* and a half," but where he said it in reverse order: a *minchah* of "half an *issaron* and an *issaron*." This changes the analysis entirely.

When the person says *minchah*, he is obligated in one *issaron* — the minimum. When he then says *chatzi issaron*, that phrase carries no halakhic weight: *lo klum ka-amar* — it says nothing binding. It is a meaningless specification in this context and is discarded. But then he says the final word *issaron*, standing on its own. That word *issaron* is itself a valid specification and obligates him in an additional *minchah* of one *issaron* — *meisi issaron achrina*, a second *issaron* is brought. The result: two *issronot*, one anchored by the initial word *minchah* and one anchored by the final word *issaron*, with the intervening *chatzi issaron* discarded as inoperative.

### Two Statements

The *Gemara* thus presents this case as structurally comprising two separate obligating statements: the word *minchah* generating one obligation and the concluding word *issaron* generating a second. It is only this reversed-order formulation — *minchah chatzi issaron ve-issaron* — that produces the two-*issaron* result under *Beit Shammai's* framework.

---

## Rabbi Shimon

### Whole Statement

This resolution, however, raises a difficulty regarding *Rabbi Shimon's* position. If the formulation is *minchah chatzi issaron ve-issaron* — which sounds like two distinct components, one of which (the final *issaron*) is fully valid on its own — why does *Rabbi Shimon* exempt entirely? The final *issaron* should at least obligate him, even if the *chatzi issaron* in the middle is discarded. *Rabbi Shimon's* stated reason is *shelo hitnadev k'derech ha-mitnadbim* — he looks at the whole statement and finds it does not constitute a valid vow. But when the statement clearly contains what sounds like two components, one of which independently works, should *Rabbi Shimon* not at minimum obligate him in the one valid *issaron*?

### Rabbi Yosi Position

*Rava* explains: *Rabbi Shimon b'shitat Rabbi Yosi amarah* — *Rabbi Shimon* follows the position of *Rabbi Yosi*, who holds *af be-gmar devarav adam nitpas* — a person can be bound even by the conclusion of his statement, by the final words he utters. The implication of *Rabbi Yosi's* position, as *Rava* applies it, is that the entire utterance from beginning to end is treated as a single unit.

### Same Sentence Rule

When *Rabbi Yosi* says that the end of one's statement is also binding, *Rabbi Shimon* derives from this a broader principle: even where a single sentence contains what might appear to be two logically separable sub-statements, they are treated as one integrated unit. One does not parse the sentence into its components and evaluate each independently; rather, the whole is assessed together. Since the whole formulation — *minchah chatzi issaron ve-issaron* — does not constitute a valid voluntary *minchah*, *Rabbi Shimon* invalidates the entire vow. The final *issaron* does not stand alone; it is part of the same utterance as the *chatzi issaron* that preceded it, and together they form an incoherent vow that is wholly rejected.

---

## Sixty-Issaron Limit

### Sixty-One Split

A new *mishnah* establishes that a person may voluntarily bring a *minchah* of up to sixty *issronot* in a single vessel: *mitnadev adam minchah shel shishim issaron u-meivi bi-khli echad*. If he explicitly vows a *minchah* of sixty, it is brought in one vessel. But if he vows *shishim ve-echad* — sixty-one — the *mishnah* rules: *meivi shishim bi-khli echad ve-echad bi-khli acher* — sixty is brought in one vessel and the additional one in a separate vessel. The vow is not simply fulfilled as a single unit of sixty-one; rather, it is split.

### Communal Sacrifice

The *Tanna Kamma* explains the basis for the sixty-*issaron* limit by reference to the communal sacrifice. There exists one situation in which the communal offerings of a single day involve a combined *minchat nesachim* totaling sixty-one *issronot*: when the first day of *Sukkot* falls on *Shabbat*. *Rashi* works out the calculation in detail. The thirteen bulls of the *Sukkot musaf* each require three *issronot*, yielding thirty-nine. The fourteen sheep each require one *issaron*, yielding fourteen — bringing the total to fifty-three. The two rams each require two *issronot*, yielding four, for a total of fifty-seven. The two *tamidim* add two more, as do the two lambs of the *Shabbat musaf*, bringing the grand total to sixty-one. Since the community can bring a total of sixty-one *issronot* in a single day's sacrifices, the principle is *dayo le-yachid she-yipaches min ha-tzibbur echad* — it suffices for an individual to bring one fewer than the community. The individual's maximum is therefore sixty.

### Not Mixed

*Rabbi Shimon* objects to this rationale. The sixty-one *issronot* of the communal sacrifice are never brought as a single *minchah*: some are for the bulls, some for the rams, some for the sheep, and some are the *tamid* offerings brought at different times of day. *Velo, harei elu la-parim ve-elu la-kvasim, ve-einan nivlalin zeh im zeh* — these are for bulls and these are for sheep, and they are never mixed together, since the bulls' *minchah* has a different proportion of oil per *issaron* than the sheep's, and the two cannot be combined. The community therefore never in fact brings sixty-one *issronot* as a unified *minchah*; the figure of sixty-one is only an aggregate. Accordingly, it cannot serve as the benchmark for an individual's *minchah*.

---

## Mixing Requirement

### Cannot Mix

*Rabbi Shimon* offers the real reason for the sixty-*issaron* limit: *ad shishim yecholim le-hibalel* — up to sixty *issronot*, the flour can be properly mixed with the oil. Beyond sixty, it cannot mix well. This explanation requires a specific understanding of the oil requirement. *Rashi* notes that the ruling follows *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*, who holds that no matter how much flour a voluntary *minchah* contains, only one *log* of oil is used. Under that view, one *log* of oil is sufficient to mix with up to sixty *issronot* of flour, but sixty-one *issronot* exceeds what one *log* can properly permeate.

### One Difference

The Sages press *Rabbi Shimon*: *beshishim nivlalin, be-shishim ve-echad ein nivlalin?* — does one *issaron* really make the difference? If sixty can be mixed, surely sixty-one can also be mixed?

### Sages' Measures

*Rabbi Shimon* responds: *kol middot chachamim ken* — that is always the nature of the Sages' measures. All *halakhic* thresholds work this way. One must draw a line somewhere, and below that line the rule applies while above it the rule does not, regardless of the fact that the difference at the margin is small.

### Parallel Examples

*Rabbi Shimon* illustrates with two parallel examples. A *mikveh* requires forty *se'ah* of water: with forty *se'ah* one may immerse; with forty *se'ah* minus a *kortov* — a thimbleful — one may not. The difference at the margin is negligible, yet the rule is absolute. Similarly, a piece of cloth three *tefachim* by three *tefachim* is susceptible to *tumat midras* — the impurity transmitted by a *zav*, *zavah*, or *niddah* sitting or leaning upon it; three *tefachim* by three *tefachim* minus a single thread is not. The *Sages* set precise measures and they are honored as such. The same applies here: sixty *issronot* is the limit of what can be mixed with the prescribed quantity of oil, and that is the cutoff.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Question Posed

The *Gemara* records that the following question was raised in the presence of *Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai*: what is the source for the rule that one who vows a *minchah* of sixty-one *issronot* must bring sixty in one vessel and one in another — that is, why do we not simply treat a sixty-one-*issaron minchah* as a single valid offering?

### Bar Ilai Speaks

*Patach Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai* — *Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai* opened the discussion. The *Gemara* notes that he held the distinction of *rosh ha-medabrim be-khol makom* — the one who had the right to speak first in every gathering. The *Gemara* in Shabbat relates the background: when the Sages convened and *Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai* praised the achievements of Rome, this apparently secured for him — perhaps at Roman insistence — the privilege of opening all public discussions.

### Communal Debate

*Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai* advanced the same argument as the *Tanna Kamma* in the *mishnah*: the community brings sixty-one *issronot* when the first day of *Sukkot* falls on *Shabbat*, and it suffices for the individual to bring one fewer. *Rabbi Shimon* replied with his objection in more elaborate form: some of those *issronot* are for the bulls (*parim*), some for the rams (*eilim*), some for the sheep (*kevasim*). The bulls and rams have a thicker mixture (*belilatan avah*) — two *log* of oil per *issaron* — while the sheep have a thinner mixture (*belilatan rakah*) — three *log* of oil per *issaron*. Moreover, some offerings are brought in the morning (*shacharit*), others in the afternoon (*bein ha-arbayim*), and they are never combined: *ve-ein nivlalin zeh im zeh*. The community's sixty-one *issronot* therefore cannot serve as a model for an individual's single *minchah*.

### Final Answer

The Sages told *Rabbi Shimon*: if you reject the communal argument, you supply the reason. *Rabbi Shimon* responded with the verse: *ve-khol minchah belulah ba-shemen ve-charevah* — any *minchah* mixed with oil or dry. The *Torah* itself demands *bilul* — mixing — and this means there must be a *minchah* that is capable of being mixed with oil. More than sixty *issronot* cannot be mixed properly with the oil. The Sages again challenged him — sixty works but sixty-one does not? — and *Rabbi Shimon* gave the same answer as in the *mishnah*: *kol middot chachamim ken hen*, with the same examples of forty *se'ah* and the cloth of three by three *tefachim*.

---

## Rabbi Zeira

### Mixing Not Required

A final question is raised. If the *Torah* requires *bilul* — mixing — the entire edifice of *Rabbi Shimon's* argument depends on that requirement. But we have a tradition that teaches: *im lo balal kasher* — even if one did not actually mix the oil with the flour, the *minchah* is still valid after the fact. If mixing is not strictly required in practice, why should the theoretical capacity to mix determine the valid quantity?

### Potential Mixing

*Rabbi Zeira* resolves this with a fundamental principle: *kol ha-ra'ui le-vilah ein vilah me'akevet bo* — anything that is fit to be mixed, the actual failure to mix does not invalidate it.

### Theoretical Capacity

The principle works as follows: once we know that the quantities are such that mixing is theoretically possible — that is, that the flour and oil are in proportions that could be combined — then the post-facto failure to carry out the mixing does not render the *minchah* invalid. The *Torah's* demand of *bilul* is satisfied by the theoretical capacity for mixing, even if that mixing was not actually performed.

### Cannot Mix Fails

Conversely: *ve-khol she-eino ra'ui le-vilah, vilah me'akevet bo* — if the quantities are such that mixing is not even possible in principle, then the requirement of *bilul* is inherently unmet, and the offering is invalid. In this case, the failure to mix is not a mere procedural omission; it reflects that the offering was never constituted in the manner the *Torah* demands.

*Rabbi Zeira's* principle thus elegantly resolves the apparent tension. The rule that *im lo balal kasher* — non-mixing does not invalidate — applies only where mixing was possible. Where mixing was never possible because the quantities are wrong, the *Torah's* demand of *belulah ba-shemen* remains unsatisfied at the most basic level, and the offering is defective. It is this principle that undergirds the sixty-*issaron* limit: sixty *issronot* are fit for mixing (*ra'uy le-vilah*) and therefore valid even without actual mixing; sixty-one are not fit for mixing, and no amount of post-facto leniency can remedy what is structurally impossible. The *Gemara* notes that while *Rabbi Zeira's* principle is entirely coherent in its original context, the *Gemara* elsewhere sometimes abstracts it as a general rule — that whenever a requirement can be theoretically satisfied, its non-satisfaction in practice is excused. The question of when that abstraction is legitimate and when a requirement must actually be met in practice is its own broad topic, and not one the *Gemara* pursues further here.

---

---

# Menachot 104

## Dam Neveilah Tumah

### Dead Mule, Revi'it Blood

The daf opens by picking up from the very bottom of 103b, where we had just encountered an important statement of Reb Yehuda, who was ראש המדברים בכל מקום — Rosh Hamedabrim Bechol Makom — who held the right to speak first in any gathering, followed by Reb Shimon, concerning the sixty עשרונות and the principle that the rabbis' שיעורים must have firm cut-off points. A new story now follows, and we will see how it does or does not connect to what came before.

אמר רב ביבי — Rav Bibi said, citing Reb Yehoshua ben Levi: there was a case involving a mule from Rebbi's household that died — מעשה בפרדה אחת שמתה — and the Sages measured its blood and found that it contained a רביעית of blood. A רביעית is roughly three to three and a half ounces, the same minimum measure used for a כוס of קידוש. Presumably this was a very young mule.

The reason the Sages measured it was as follows. A dead animal's carcass communicates טומאת נבילה — impurity — and the assumption is that this would apply not only to the meat but to the blood as well. The operative principle is that the relevant quantity of blood is the amount which, were it to congeal, would equal the size of a כזית — an olive's bulk — because a כזית of flesh is the minimum quantity of an animal's body that communicates impurity. A רביעית of liquid blood, when congealed, becomes approximately a כזית of solid matter. That is why the Sages measured the blood: to determine whether a רביעית was present and whether it would therefore communicate impurity.

### Eduyot: Blood is Pure

מתיבי רב יצחק בר ביסנא — Reb Yitzchak bar Bisna raised an objection from Mishnah Eduyot. The Mishnah states: העיד רבי יהושע ורבי יהושע בן בתירא על דם נבילה שהוא טהור — Reb Yehoshua and Reb Yehoshua ben Beteira testified that the blood of a נבילה is pure. According to their testimony, no quantity of blood from a carcass communicates impurity; only the flesh does so. This stands in direct tension with the story of Rebbi's mule, where the blood was measured precisely to assess its impurity.

### Lions Stadium Story

Reb Yehoshua ben Beteira's testimony in Mishnah Eduyot was not merely a theoretical ruling — he supported it with an account of actual practice. מעשה והיו נוחרים ארדיות לאריות באסטרייא — there was a case where animals were slaughtered, through נחירה rather than through שחיטה, for the lions in the stadium — אסטרייא likely referring to the Roman amphitheater in the land of Israel. והיו עולי רגלים שוקעים עד ארכובותיהם בדם ולא אמרו להם דבר — and when pilgrims would come up for one of the three major festivals, they would be wading up to their knees in the blood of these carcasses, and no one ever said anything to them about impurity. Had dam neveilah communicated טומאה, someone would certainly have objected — these pilgrims were coming to the Temple. The fact that no objection was raised is compelling evidence that the blood was considered pure.

One may also wonder what precisely these pilgrims were doing in the vicinity of the stadium, but apparently visiting such attractions was part of the culture of the city during the festival period.

### Rav Bibi's Poverty

אישתיק — Rav Bibi fell silent. He had no response. Rav Zerika then asked him: מאי טעמא לא קמהדר מר — why did you not give an answer? Rav Bibi replied: היכי אהדר ליה — how could I be expected to respond?

His explanation is striking. He cited a teaching of Reb Chanina, who interprets the verse in the curses of Devarim: והיו חייך תלוים לך מנגד — your life will hang suspended before you. Reb Chanina explains that this refers to someone who must purchase grain from year to year rather than growing his own. As Rashi notes, the verse says לוקח — one who purchases — specifically indicating someone without land, for a landowner has a sense of security in his ability to provide for himself, while a purchaser does not, even if he has enough money this year. The verse continues: ופחדת לילה ויומם — you will fear day and night. This, explains Reb Chanina, refers to someone who can only purchase grain from week to week, anxious each day whether he will have the money to buy next week's supply. Finally, the verse concludes: ולא תאמין בחייך — you will have no faith in your own life — meaning someone who relies entirely on the baker's daily charity for his bread, not knowing each day where his next meal will come from.

Rav Bibi then said: and that man — meaning himself — על פלטר סמך, I rely on the baker every day. He had absolutely no livelihood, no security, and lacked the ישוב הדעת — the presence of mind — to formulate an adequate response to the challenge.

### Beit Hillel: Blood Tamei

מאי הוי עלה — so what is the resolution? Two traditions stood in conflict: one in which the blood of a carcass communicates טומאה, and one in which it does not.

אמר רב יוסף — Rav Yosef resolved the matter. רבי יהודה מוריינא דבי נשיא הוה — Reb Yehuda served as the halachic authority in the house of the Nasi. Rashi explains that מוריינא means he served as the posek for Rebbi's household. ואורי ליה כשמעתיה — and he ruled for Rebbi's household according to his own teaching. It was therefore not Rebbi himself who determined that the blood was impure; it was Reb Yehuda ruling for Rebbi's household in accordance with his own position.

What is Reb Yehuda's position? The Gemara cites a Mishnah: רבי יהודה אומר ששה דברים מקולי בית שמאי ומחומרי בית הלל — Reb Yehuda says that there are six matters in which Beit Shammai is lenient and Beit Hillel is strict, the reverse of the usual pattern. One of those six is דם נבילה. Beit Shammai holds that dam neveilah does not communicate טומאה — only the flesh does. Beit Hillel holds that it does communicate טומאה. Since we rule like Beit Hillel even when they are strict, dam neveilah is tamei. Reb Yehuda ruled accordingly for Rebbi's household when measuring the blood of the mule.

The story in Mishnah Eduyot, with the pilgrims wading through the blood at the stadium, reflects the opposing position — that dam neveilah is pure — and thus represents a different opinion.

### Revi'it Congeals Kezayit

The Gemara adds a further nuance. אמר רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה — Reb Yosi the son of Reb Yehuda said: אף כשטימאו בית הלל לא טימאו אלא ברביעית — even when Beit Hillel ruled that dam neveilah is tamei, they only ruled so for a quantity of a רביעית, הואיל ויכול להקריש ולעמוד על כזית — because that is the amount of blood that can congeal to the size of a כזית. The logic is that blood does not communicate טומאה as blood in its own right; rather, it communicates טומאה as a form of meat — as an extension of the category of flesh. The threshold for flesh is a כזית, a solid measure. The liquid measure of a רביעית is therefore the operative standard for blood, because that is precisely the volume of blood whose congealed form equals a כזית.

### Shiurim Connection

Rashi explains that this passage appears here because the end of yesterday's daf involved a broad discussion of the rabbis' שיעורים — the precise measurements they established for various halachic categories — and this story presents a closely related issue about how blood is measured against the standard of meat. Tosafot adds a further connection: yesterday we noted that Reb Yehuda was ראש המדברים בכל מקום, and today we learn that he also served as the halachic authority in Rebbi's household — perhaps indicating a relationship between his precedence in public discourse and the role he played in that domestic context.

---

## Nesachim Quantities

### Mishnah: Log Limits

The Mishnah now before us teaches: אין מתנדבים לוג שנים וחמשה אבל מתנדבים שלשה וארבעה וששה ומששה ולמעלה — one may not donate two or five לוג of wine, but one may donate three, four, or six לוג, or any quantity above six.

### Wine Denominations

The framework of this Mishnah presupposes that the wine may be brought as a separate, independent sacrifice — a נדבה of wine — even when not accompanying an animal sacrifice. This category is called מנחת נסכים, the libation offering. The Mishnah's permitted quantities are derived from the wine that accompanied animal sacrifices, since that is the only model available. The quantities of wine brought with the various animals are stated in the מוסף prayer: חצי ההין לפר — half a הין for a bull — שלישית ההין לאיל — a third of a הין for a ram — and רביעית ההין לכבש — a quarter of a הין for a lamb.

A הין consists of twelve לוג. Half of twelve is six לוג for a bull, a third of twelve is four לוג for a ram, and a quarter of twelve is three לוג for a lamb. Accordingly, the valid denominations for an independent wine donation are three, four, and six. One לוג is excluded because it falls below the minimum of three. Two לוג is excluded for the same reason. Five is excluded because it is not itself one of the three denominations. As for quantities above six: seven can be composed of three and four; eight of four and four; nine of six and three; ten of six and four — and so on. Any whole number above six can be composed of some combination of three, four, and six. That is the basis for the Mishnah's ruling that from six and above all quantities are permitted.

### Keva L'Nesachim?

איבעיא להו — the Gemara raises a question: יש קבע לנסכים או אין קבע לנסכים — is there a fixed unit for nesachim donations, or is there no fixed unit?

The practical stakes of this question are illustrated through a concrete case. Suppose one has sanctified five לוג of wine. The Mishnah rules that five is an impermissible quantity. What is to be done? If there is no fixed unit — אין קבע לנסכים — then the five לוג need not be offered as a single unit. One could extract four לוג from the five, offer those four לוג as the denomination appropriate for a ram, and the remaining one לוג would be treated as a separate donation — given to another individual who needs an extra לוג to complete his own sacrifice. If, however, there is a fixed unit — יש קבע לנסכים — then the five cannot be subdivided. One would be obligated to add a sixth לוג and offer all six together as the denomination for a bull.

### Six Shofarot Boxes

אמר אביי — Abaye proposed a proof from the institution of the Temple collection boxes. In the Temple there were thirteen essentially tzedakah-style boxes into which people would deposit leftover funds from various types of sacrifices — money that had been sanctified for an obligation, partially used, and left over with no further application to the original purpose. These funds would be drawn upon on slow days at the altar to purchase communal burnt offerings, maintaining the appearance of an active Temple service.

Of these thirteen boxes, six were designated לנדבה — for free-will donations. The Mishnah asks: וכנגד מי — what do these six represent? Each of the six corresponds to a distinct category of leftover obligatory funds: מותר חטאת — money left over from a sin offering; ומותר אשם — from a guilt offering; ומותר אשם נזיר — from the guilt offering a Nazirite brings at the conclusion of his period of nezirut, which is not an atonement offering but a rite of termination; ומותר אשם מצורע — from the guilt offering of a person with tzaraat who underwent a process of purification; ומותר קינים — from bird sacrifices; and ומותר מנחת חוטא — from a sin-mincha offering.

The common denominator among all six categories is that the funds had been designated for an obligatory sacrifice of a specific type. Once that obligation was discharged, the leftover money could not be redirected toward fulfilling the same obligation, but it also had no other designated use, and so it was transferred to these Temple funds and used to sustain the altar's activity.

Abaye's argument runs as follows: if it were true that leftover wine from nesachim donations created a distinct and commonly occurring scenario — specifically, if one who donated five לוג could not subdivide them and instead had an unavoidable remainder — then we would have expected a seventh שופר box dedicated to מותר נסכים. The absence of such a box implies that the leftover-wine scenario does not commonly arise as a distinct category, which would be explained if the wine could always be subdivided and redistributed without remainder.

### Leftover Wine Pooled

The Gemara rejects Abaye's proof. הנך לנדבת ציבור אזלי — those boxes and their funds are used for communal burnt offerings. הני שכיחי — those other categories are common in the sense that the leftover money genuinely has nowhere else to go. But leftover wine is different: אפשר דמצטרפי דמר ודמר בהדי הדדי — it is easily possible for the leftover wine of one person to be combined with the need of another. Since almost every animal sacrifice requires wine as part of its nesachim, a person who has slightly less wine than he needs can readily receive the leftover לוג from someone else. The leftover wine need never become a stranded surplus at all; it is instantly reabsorbed into the system. There was therefore no need for a dedicated שופר box for this category, and Abaye's proof from the absence of such a box is inconclusive. וקרבי — and it would simply be offered as part of someone else's sacrifice.

### Ezrach: Independent Wine

אמר רבא — Rava offered a different approach, now seeking a proof from the scriptural basis for the very institution of independent wine donations. The verses in the Torah regarding nesachim deploy the word אזרח — citizen — which is an unusual term in this context and is therefore read as expanding the scope of the law. What does it expand to teach? מלמד שמתנדבין נסכים — it teaches that one may donate wine as an independent sacrifice. וכמה — and how much? שלושה לוגין — the minimum is three לוג, which is the smallest denomination that accompanies any animal sacrifice.

The verse also contains the word יהיה — shall be — which broadens the law further. ומניין שאם רוצה להוסיף יוסיף — how do I know that one may add more than three? From that word. And the word כך — thus or in this manner — excludes the possibility of bringing less than three: יכול יפחות — one might have thought one could bring less than three לוג — תלמוד לומר ככה — the Torah says no, it must be this way. From these words we derive all the principles of the Mishnah: wine may be given as an independent sacrifice, but only in the prescribed denominations and not below the minimum of three לוג.

### Yosef = Five Log

The Gemara now presses the analysis of the word יוסיף in the verse — "one may add." מאי יוסיף — what does "may add" mean? If it means that one may donate the other standard denominations alongside three — namely four and six לוג — that would be unnecessary, since those denominations are already established by the same principle that permits three לוג. Just as three is permitted because it is the denomination for a sheep, four and six are permitted on the same basis for a ram and a bull respectively. The word יוסיף therefore cannot be teaching those standard units.

אלא לאו — rather, it must mean something beyond the standard denominations. Since the Mishnah specifies that five is forbidden, the word יוסיף must be teaching that one can bring five. But if five is permitted, how does one offer five? Only by extracting four from the five and using the remaining one לוג in some other way. ושמע מינה — this implies אין קבע לנסכים — there is no fixed unit, and therefore a five-לוג donation can be subdivided and partially offered.

### Rav Ashi: Five = Two

אמר רב אשי — Rav Ashi objected. ואנן לא תנן הכי — this does not accord with our Mishnah. The Mishnah states: אין מתנדבין לוג שנים וחמשה — one may not donate two or five לוג. קתני חמשה דומיא דשנים — by listing five alongside two, the Mishnah implies that the problem with five is analogous to the problem with two. מה שנים דלא חזו כלל — just as two לוג cannot be brought to the altar at all because the minimum denomination is three, אף חמשה נמי דלא חזו כלל — so too five לוג cannot be brought at all. One must wait until a sixth לוג is added to reach the denomination of six. This would suggest that five is entirely unusable as offered, implying יש קבע — there is a fixed unit.

### Different Grounds

The Gemara dismisses Rav Ashi's objection. מידי איריא — the parallel does not hold. הכי איתא והכי איתא — each case operates on its own terms. Two and five are both listed as forbidden, but they are forbidden for entirely different reasons. Two לוג simply do not reach the minimum; there is no way to offer any part of a two-לוג donation. Five לוג, however, may well be subtractable: perhaps four can be extracted and offered, with the one remainder handled separately. Listing them together in the same sentence does not mean they share the same legal mechanism. The proof from the Mishnah's grouping therefore fails.

### Eleven Log Problem

אמר אביי — Abaye now turns the question in a different direction. אם תמצא לומר אין קבע לנסכים — if one concludes there is no fixed unit, then the question is entirely resolved and no further difficulties arise. But אם תמצא לומר יש קבע לנסכים — if one concludes that there is a fixed unit and a donor must offer his entire vowed quantity without subdivision, a new question emerges.

עד עשרה פשיטא לי — for any vowed quantity up to ten לוג, the answer is obvious. Seven can be composed of three and four; eight of four and four; nine of six and three; ten of six and four. All of these are clean combinations of the standard denominations. But חד עשר מיבעיא לי — eleven לוג presents a difficulty. Can eleven be composed of the standard denominations? Four, four, and three — that is indeed eleven — but this is not a clean two-unit combination; it requires two units of one denomination and one of another. Is such a combination valid?

One possibility is that the person who vowed eleven was mentally aiming for twelve — two sixes, the denomination for two bulls — and simply fell short. In that case, גברא לשני פרים קמיכוין — he had two bulls in mind — ועד דמלא להו לא קרבי — and until the full twelve לוג are assembled, nothing may be offered. The other possibility is that he intended two rams and one sheep — two fours and a three — which total eleven exactly. Is it valid to interpret a vow as combining two of one denomination with one of another? תרי מחד מינא וחד מחד מינא אמרינן או לא — do we say such a combination is acceptable, or is the asymmetry of the combination problematic?

### Teiku: Eleven Log

תיקו — the question is left unresolved. The underlying question of whether יש קבע לנסכים or אין קבע לנסכים itself remains open, and this specific application — the eleven-לוג vow — is likewise left without an answer.

---

## Oil Donation Debate

### Akiva vs. Tarfon: Oil

The Mishnah now addresses the question of oil. We have established that wine may be donated independently as a free-will sacrifice. The question arises whether the same is true of oil alone. Both oil and wine accompany animal sacrifices — with the animal come both flour mixed with oil and a separate measure of wine. May one donate just oil, as one may donate just wine?

מתנדבין יין ואין מתנדבין שמן — one may donate wine as a free-will sacrifice but not oil, דברי רבי עקיבא — this is the position of Rabbi Akiva. רבי טרפון אומר מתנדבין שמן — Rabbi Tarfon says one may donate oil independently.

### Tarfon: Oil Like Wine

Rabbi Tarfon's argument by analogy: מה מצינו ביין שהוא בא בחובה ובא בנדבה — just as we find that wine comes as an obligation when accompanying an animal sacrifice and also comes as a voluntary free-will offering, אף שמן — so too oil: just as wine can come independently, oil should be able to come independently as well.

### Akiva: Oil Not Alone

Rabbi Akiva rejects the analogy. אם אמרת ביין שכן קרב עם חובתו בפני עצמו — wine, when it accompanies the obligatory animal sacrifice, is brought as a discrete unit in its own right. It is a separate measure of wine, standing alone. That is why wine can also be given as an independent free-will offering — there is a model of wine standing alone. תאמר בשמן שאינו קרב עם חובתו בפני עצמו — but can you say the same of oil? Oil never comes by itself even when it accompanies an obligatory sacrifice. It always comes as a flour-and-oil mixture, a מנחה. There is no model of offering pure oil independently. Since oil never comes alone even in its obligatory form, there is no basis for saying it may come alone as a voluntary donation.

### Minchat Nesachim Daily

אמר רבא — Rava draws an inference from the very structure of the debate. מדברי שניהם — from the positions of both Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon — נלמוד — we can infer — מתנדב אדם מנחת נסכים בכל יום — that a person may donate minchat nesachim, the flour-and-oil mixture that accompanies animal sacrifices, as an independent free-will sacrifice at any time.

The reasoning is as follows. Rabbi Akiva's very argument against oil turns on the fact that oil does not come alone — it always comes as a flour-and-oil mixture. This implicitly concedes that the flour-and-oil mixture itself may be donated independently. And Rabbi Tarfon, who permits oil alone, would certainly permit the mixture. So both opinions, from their respective angles, imply that minchat nesachim can be brought independently.

One might object: of course minchat nesachim can be donated, since a מנחה can generally be given as a free-will offering. What is new here? The answer is that there is a difference. The מנחות listed in ויקרא have a specific ratio of flour to oil. The minchat nesachim uses a different ratio — the ratio that accompanies the animal sacrifices. One might have thought that only the מנחות explicitly catalogued in the Torah may be brought independently, and that the nesachim ratio is not among them.

### Explicit Nesachim Mincha

פשיטא — the Gemara initially reacts: is this not obvious? The response is that it is not. מהו דתימא — one might have argued — מנחת נדבה גלי בה רחמנא — the Torah made explicit which מנחות may be donated voluntarily — הני חמשה מנחות — those five types of מנחה prepared by different methods listed in ויקרא — טפי לא — and no others. Wine, the Torah never discussed as an independent sacrifice, and so we derive that permission through the drasha on אזרח. But מנחה — the Torah did discuss explicitly — and the listed five might be exhaustive. One might then have said that the flour-and-oil mixture in the nesachim ratio falls outside this list and therefore cannot be donated independently.

קא משמע לן — therefore this teaches us: הני מילי בסתמא — this exclusion applies only when a person donates a מנחה without specifying what type. In that case, we assume he means one of the five established types. אבל היכא דפריש פריש — but if he explicitly specifies that he wishes to donate a מנחה according to the nesachim ratio — the ratio that accompanies animal sacrifices — he may do so.

---

## Nefesh: No Mincha Partner

### Mishnah: No Joint Mincha

The פרק concludes with a ruling that closes the Mishnah: אין שנים מתנדבין עישרון אחד — two people may not jointly donate a single עישרון, the minimum measure of a מנחה, as a partnership offering. אבל מתנדבין עולה ושלמים — they may, however, jointly donate a free-will עולה or שלמים. ועוף — they may even jointly bring a bird as an עולה, אפילו פרידה אחת — even a single bird, though normally birds come in pairs in the Torah. Any animal sacrifice, however small, may be jointly donated. A מנחה may not.

### Nefesh = Individual

The Gemara asks: מאי טעמא — what is the reason? The initial proposal is that the Torah uses the singular form תקריב — you shall bring — when speaking of the מנחה, implying that only an individual may bring it. But this proposal fails because עולה also uses the singular יקריב. The response is that for עולה, another verse uses the plural לעולותיכם — for your עולות — indicating that multiple people may be jointly involved. If so, the same argument should apply to מנחה, since a similar verse uses the plural למנחותיכם — for your מנחות. There is no difference in grammatical structure between the two.

אלא משום דכתיב ביה נפש — rather, the reason is the specific word used in the מנחה passage. When the Torah introduces animal sacrifices it says אדם כי יקריב מכם קרבן — a person who offers a sacrifice. But when it introduces the מנחה it says ונפש כי תקריב — and if a נפש — a soul — brings a מנחה. This shift from person to soul carries halachic weight: the נפש implies a single individual, reflecting the utter individuality and uniqueness of a soul.

### Baraita: Mincha Alone

תניא נמי הכי — a Baraita confirms this ruling. The verse says that one will bring his sacrifice for all of their vows and free-will offerings that they bring to God, moving from the singular to the plural. הכל באים בשותפות — this teaches that all sacrifices may come in partnership. לא סילקה הכתוב אלא מנחה שנאמר נפש — the Torah excludes only the מנחה, because it uses the word נפש — a soul — requiring that the מנחה come from a single individual.

### Poor Person's Nefesh

אמר רבי יצחק — Rabbi Yitzchak asks: מפני מה נשתנית מנחה שנאמר בה נפש — why is it specifically the מנחה for which the Torah uses the word נפש? The answer lies in asking: מי דרכו להביא מנחה — who is it that typically brings a מנחה rather than an animal sacrifice? The answer is evident: עני — a poor person who cannot afford an animal. For a poor person, the flour-and-oil offering is not a diminished substitute but the fullest expression of what he can give. Therefore, says Rabbi Yitzchak, God declares: מעלה אני עליו כאילו הקריב נפשו לפני — I regard it as though he has offered his very soul before Me.

This is in fact one of the places in the Talmudic literature where the principle of אחד הממעיט ואחד המרבה ובלבד שיכוון לבו לשמים is invoked — it does not matter whether one does much or little, what matters is that one's heart is directed toward heaven.

### Five Preparations Parable

אמר רבי יצחק — Rabbi Yitzchak continues: מה נשתנית מנחה שנאמר בה חמשה מיני טיגון הללו — why does the Torah describe the מנחה in five different forms of preparation? One may be baked, one pan-fried, one deep-fried — all from the same flour and oil. Why this elaborate variety for what is, in objective terms, a simple inexpensive offering?

משל למלך בשר ודם שעשו לו אוהבו סעודה — it is like a king whose close friend prepared a meal for him. ויודע בו שהוא עני — but the king knew his friend was poor and could not provide extravagant delicacies. So the king said to him: אמר לו עשה לי מן חמשה מיני טיגון כדי שאהנה ממך — please prepare for me five different types of pastries and confections from what you have. Not because the king needed the food, but because this gave the poor friend the fullest possible opportunity to express love and honor for the king within the constraints of his means — to do everything he was capable of doing, and to do it with care and variety. The five methods of preparation are the Torah's gift to the poor person: they allow him to bring something elaborate and meaningful, something that genuinely expresses devotion, rather than something that feels like the minimum.

### Dignity of Poor's Gift

This theological understanding of the מנחה — that it is the gift of the poor person's very soul, and that the Torah goes out of its way to give it dignity and meaning — illuminates, perhaps, why partnership is forbidden. If one may form a partnership of any size — two people, ten people, twenty people — then the offering loses its character as the full, personal gift of a single individual. The whole point of the מנחה, in Rabbi Yitzchak's reading, is that when a poor person brings it he has truly given something. He has brought everything he was able to bring; this is his soul.

If we say — well, find a partner, bring half of one together — we are in effect saying that even this small gift can be subdivided further, made lighter, reduced to a fraction of what it already was. It becomes performative rather than meaningful. As the principle goes: it is not the quantity that matters but the direction of one's heart toward heaven. But that principle depends on the giving being genuine and whole. A gift halved indefinitely ceases to carry that weight. The מנחה must come from a single soul — because its entire significance lies in the fact that it is the full expression of that one soul's devotion.

---

---

# Menachot 105

## Mincha Vows: Quantity

### One Isaron

The new *perek* — the final *perek* of Masechet Menachot — opens with a series of cases governing vows of *minchot*, beginning with the most basic. The *mishnah* states: *harei alai isaron* — if someone takes upon himself a vow to bring an *isaron*, the standard measure of flour for a *mincha*, he brings one *isaron*. This is, as the *Gemara* will note, entirely self-evident.

### Two Isaronot

If someone says *isaronot* — the plural form — implicitly vowing a *mincha* of *isaronot*, he brings two, since two is the minimum the plural can denote. One cannot obligate the person in more than the minimum implied by his words.

### Uncertain Quantity

The third case is where the genuine *chiddush* lies. If someone says *perashti ve-eini yodea ma perashti* — "I specified a quantity but I do not remember what I specified" — *yavi shishim isaron*: he brings a *mincha* of sixty *isaron*. We have already established in earlier portions of the tractate that sixty is the maximum; no *mincha* may exceed that amount. He therefore brings sixty and declares: however many *isronot* I vowed, those are for my vow, and anything beyond that — sixty minus the amount I actually vowed — is a free-will *mincha*, a *nedavah*. The *mishnah* leaves open, for the moment, the question of whether this is brought as a single large *mincha* in one vessel or in separate vessels, a matter the *Gemara* will address.

---

## Type Specification

### Five Mincha Types

The *mishnah* continues: *harei alai mincha* — if one simply vows to bring a *mincha* without specifying which type, *yavi eizo she-yirtze*, he may bring whichever of the five varieties enumerated at the beginning of *Vayikra* he wishes. These five are: *solet* (fine flour with oil), *machavat* (a flat pan), *marcheshet* (a deep pan), and the two forms of *ma'afeh tanur* (oven-baked offerings) — *challot* (loaves) and *rekikin* (wafers). Since he did not specify, he retains his choice.

### Rabbi Yehuda: Solet Defa…

*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees. He holds that one who vows an unspecified *mincha* must bring *minchat solet*, because it is *meyuchedet she-be-menachot* — it is, in some sense, the distinctive or designated *mincha* among the *menachot*. The *Gemara* will explore the precise meaning of this characterization.

---

## Mincha Vows: Quantity…

### Rabbi's Separate Vessels

Before turning to *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position, the *Gemara* returns to the quantity cases. The *mishnah*'s last case reads: *perashti mincha shel isaronot ve-eini yodea kama perashti* — "I vowed a *mincha* of *isaronot* but do not remember how many." This closely resembles the earlier case of *perashti ve-eini yodea ma perashti*, where one simply said *isaronot* without the word *mincha*. The *Tanna Kamma* holds the same rule applies: bring sixty *isaron*, with the vowed portion designated for the *neder* and any excess as *nedavah*.

*Rebbi*, however, states: *yavi menachot shel isronot me-echad ve-ad shishim* — one must bring sixty separate *menachot*, one of one *isaron*, one of two, one of three, and so on up to sixty. The *Gemara* naturally asks: why does *Rebbi* not dispute the earlier case in the *mishnah* as well, where one said only *isaronot* without specifying *mincha*?

*Chizkiyah* resolves this by stating that the *Tanna Kamma*'s ruling in the first case — where one simply said *isaronot* and forgot the quantity — is not like *Rebbi* at all; *Rebbi* would dispute it.

*Rabbi Yochanan*, however, maintains that *Rebbi* could even agree with the first case. The distinction is: *be-omer perashti isronot aval lo kafiti bi-kli* — when one said only *isaronot* and did not say *mincha* of *isaronot*, he made no specification that they all constitute a single unit in one vessel. By contrast, when one says "a *mincha* of *isaronot*," the word *mincha* implies a single offering in a single vessel, and therefore the amount must be exact — it can be neither more nor less. In that case, *Rebbi* holds that one must bring every possibility from one to sixty, each in its own vessel, so that whichever was the actual amount vowed is fulfilled precisely. But when one merely said *isaronot* — not a *mincha* of them — perhaps that implies multiple *menachot* or multiple vessels, and therefore sixty individual *isronot* in sixty separate vessels can serve as *nedavah* for whatever the amount beyond the vow actually was.

---

## Solet Default: Rationale

### First Mentioned Challenge

The *Gemara* now examines *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position. A *baraita* explains his reasoning: *ho'il u-fatach bo ha-katuv techilah* — because *solet* is the type the Torah introduces first. Indeed, *Vayikra* opens the laws of *mincha* with *venefesh ki takriv mincha korban mincha la-Hashem solet yihiye korbano* — if one brings a *mincha*, it shall be *solet* — and only afterward introduces the variants of *ma'afeh tanur*, *machavat*, and *marcheshet*.

The *Gemara*, however, challenges this reasoning with a sharp rhetorical counter. *Ela me-ata* — if the logic is simply "the Torah mentions it first," then: *ha-omer harei alai olah yavi ben bakar ho'il u-fatach bo ha-katuv techilah* — one who vows an *olah* without specifying should have to bring from the cattle, since the Torah in *Vayikra* opens the laws of *olah* with *im olah korbano min ha-bakar*. Similarly, *min ha-tzon yavi keves*, one who vows an *olah* from the flock should have to bring a sheep, since sheep are listed before goats. And *min ha-of yavi torim*, from birds one should have to bring turtle doves, since they appear before the young pigeons. Yet the following *mishnah* rules otherwise — *harei alai olah yavi keves*, one who vows an *olah* simply brings a lamb (the minimum obligation), and *Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah* says he may bring from birds. Being first-mentioned is plainly not the operative criterion there.

Moreover, *Rabbi Yehuda* does not dispute the ruling regarding *olah* — he does not argue there that one must bring from the cattle. So why does he invoke the "first mentioned" logic for *mincha* if he does not apply it to *olah*?

### No Descriptor Name

The *Gemara* therefore steps back: *ella mai meyuchedet she-be-menachot delait leh shem levai* — what does it truly mean that *solet* is the distinctive *mincha*? It means that *solet* is the only *mincha* that carries no qualifying descriptor name. Every other type requires an appended designation: *minchat machavat*, *minchat marcheshet*, *korban mincha ma'afeh tanur*. But *solet* is introduced simply as *korban mincha* — a *mincha* — with *solet* functioning merely as a description of the substance (flour), not as a categorizing title. It is, in other words, the default: it requires no further qualification to specify what it is.

The *Gemara* then asks: but the *baraita* itself says *patach bo ha-katuv techilah* — the reason given is that the Torah opens with it. How then can we say the real reason is the absence of a descriptor name? The *Gemara* answers: *hachi ka-amar* — this is what the *tanna* means. Which *mincha* is the one without a qualifying descriptor name? It is the one the Torah lists first. The fact of being listed first is not itself the reason; it is the identifying marker — a *siman be-alma* — to help you locate which *mincha* bears no adjective. The actual logic is that an unspecified vow of *mincha* defaults to the one called simply *mincha*, not *minchat X*. The first listing in the Torah is merely a pointer to that type.

### Olah vs Mincha

The distinction from *olah* is, the lecturer notes, actually quite elegant and deserves appreciation independent of the *Gemara*'s resolution. The Torah's presentation of *mincha* is fundamentally different from its presentation of *olah*. For *olah*, the Torah says *adam ki yakriv mikem korban la-Hashem min ha-behema min ha-bakar umin ha-tzon takrivu* — the offering can come from any of several categories, and then *im olah korbano min ha-bakar* presents the cattle option as one branch among equals. The structure is genuinely open-ended. By contrast, the *mincha* passage says *venefesh ki takriv mincha korban mincha la-Hashem solet yihiye korbano* — "if you bring a *mincha*, it shall be *solet*" — presenting *solet* not as one option but as the statement of what a *mincha* is, with the other types introduced as variations. The Torah's framing itself signals that *solet* is the default.

---

## Minei Mincha Debate

### Rav Papi's Question

The *mishnah* teaches further: *mincha o min ha-mincha yavi achat* — if one vows "a *mincha*" or "from a type of *mincha*," he brings one. *Menachot o min ha-menachot yavi shtayim* — if he uses the plural, "types of *menachot*," he brings two. *Rav Papi* then poses a question: *minei mincha mahu?* — what is the law if one says *minei mincha*, pluralizing the word for "type" (*minei*) but leaving *mincha* in the singular? On one reading, *keivan de-amar minei tarti ka-amar* — since he said "types" in the plural, he means two. And the singular *mincha* simply denotes the category, as indeed the Torah uses the singular when referring to the entire category of *menachot* — *vezot torat ha-mincha* — meaning not a single *mincha* but the genus. But on another reading, *keivan de-amar mincha chada mincha ka-amar* — since he said *mincha* in the singular, he means only one. And *minei mincha* then means: from among the types of *mincha*, I obligate myself in one — *miminei mincha chada mincha alai*.

### Baraita Evidence

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this from the *mishnah* itself. The cases of "one" all involve every word in the singular — *mincha*, *min mincha* — suggesting that any use of a plural would produce an obligation of two. So *haminei mincha shtayim* — if "types" is plural, it should mean two. But the *Gemara* counters: *eima seifa* — look at the second half of the *mishnah*. The cases that produce an obligation of two all feature *menachot* in the plural. *Haminei mincha chada* — the fact that "types" was used without pluralizing *menachot* might mean only one. Neither reading can be proven from the *mishnah* alone, which is precisely why the question was being asked in the first place.

The *Gemara* then brings a *baraita*: *min menachot alai yavi shtei menachot m'min echad* — "a type of *menachot* on me" requires bringing two *menachot* of the same type. This resolves a matter that was only implicit in the *mishnah* — namely, that when one says "a type" in the singular but pluralizes *menachot*, the two must be of the same type. Further, the *baraita* continues: *haminei mincha* — if one had said *minei mincha* (types in the plural, *mincha* in the singular), the implication seems to be only one *mincha*. The *Gemara* initially considers this a proof.

But the *Gemara* deflects: *dilma lo* — perhaps *minei mincha* does not mean one, but rather two of two *different* types, as opposed to *min menachot* which is two of the *same* type. And yet, *ve-halo tanya hachi* — the *baraita* continues explicitly: *minei menachot alai yavi shtei menachot mishnei minim* — "types of *menachot* on me" produces two *menachot* of two different types. If *minei mincha* already conveyed two *menachot* of two different types, it would have been unnecessary for the *baraita* to introduce *minei menachot* for that purpose. The very fact that the *baraita* reserves *minei menachot* for the case of two of two different types seems to imply that *minei mincha* means only one.

### Minei Mincha Unresolved

The *Gemara* responds: *dilma ha mani Rabbi Shimon hi* — perhaps this *baraita* follows *Rabbi Shimon*, who holds that a *ma'afeh tanur* can be brought as a combination of *challot* and *rekikin*. According to *Rabbi Shimon*, a single *mincha* can contain two types — *mincha de-it bah terei minei*. Therefore *minei mincha* according to *Rabbi Shimon* means two types within one *mincha* — namely, the *ma'afeh tanur* that is part *challot* and part *rekikin*. That is why the *baraita* can reserve *minei menachot* for two separate *menachot* of two types. But according to the Rabbis, who hold that *ma'afeh tanur* must be either entirely *challot* or entirely *rekikin* and cannot be divided, there is no single *mincha* with two types. In that case, *minei mincha* might indeed mean two *menachot* of two types. The question of *Rav Pappa* therefore remains unresolved.

---

## Uncertain Type: Five Opt…

### Five Types Standard

The *mishnah* then rules: *perashti ve-eini yodea eizeh mehem perashti yavi chameshtan* — if one vowed a *mincha* of a specified type but does not remember which of the five types he vowed, he must bring all five, playing it safe. One of them fulfills his vow and the others are free-will offerings.

### Non-Rabbi Shimon

*Rabbi Yirmiyah* observes: *de-lo ke-Rabbi Shimon* — this ruling follows a position other than that of *Rabbi Shimon*. For *Rabbi Shimon* holds that a *ma'afeh tanur* can be half *challot* and half *rekikin*, or indeed any distribution of the ten units between the two types. Therefore, one who does not remember what type of *mincha* he vowed would, according to *Rabbi Shimon*, need to consider not five but potentially fourteen possibilities: the three base types (*solet*, *machavat*, *marcheshet*) plus eleven possible distributions of *challot* and *rekikin* within the *ma'afeh tanur* (all ten as *challot*, nine *challot* and one *rekikin*, eight and two, and so on through all ten as *rekikin*). Working with *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position of ten units, that is eleven internal permutations, yielding fourteen total. (Under *Rabbi Meir*, who holds twelve units, it would be sixteen.)

---

## Rabbi Shimon: Permutatio…

### Half-and-Half Mixing

*Abaye*, however, says: *afilu teima Rabbi Shimon* — even according to *Rabbi Shimon*, one need only bring the five types, not fourteen. This is because *Rabbi Shimon* allows one to bring an offering and attach a stipulation. *Rabbi Shimon*'s allowance to stipulate means that one can bring the standard five — including all ten *challot* and all ten *rekikin* — and declare that whichever combination of *challot* and *rekikin* constitutes one's vow is the *neder*, and the remainder is *nedavah*.

### Fourteen Possibilities

The logic bears careful articulation. If one does not remember whether he vowed *challot*, *rekikin*, or some mixture, he need not bring eleven separate *menachot* of *ma'afeh tanur* to cover every permutation. Instead, he brings the *challot* and *rekikin* together and stipulates.

### Abaye's Stipulation

This works because *Rabbi Shimon* is known to permit stipulation-based hedging in cases of doubt, as *Abaye* demonstrates from an explicit *baraita*. We know *Rabbi Shimon* says: *meisi u-masni* — one brings and stipulates. The case establishing this principle follows immediately.

---

## Metzora Stipulation Case

### Asham or Shelamim

The *baraita* cited is the case of a person whose status is uncertain — he may be a *metzora* who requires specific *korbanot* for his *tahara*. *Rabbi Shimon omer le-machar mevi ashamo ve-logo imo* — *Rabbi Shimon* says: the following day he brings his *asham* and his *log* of oil together and declares the following stipulation: *im metzora hu zehu ashamo vezehu logo* — if he is indeed a *metzora*, this is his *asham* and this is his *log* and the *tahara* procedure is to be performed accordingly. *Ve-im lav, asham ze yehe shalmei nedava* — and if he is not a *metzora*, this *asham* should become a *shelamim* of free will.

The practical execution is then spelled out. *Ve-oto asham ta'un shechita ba-tzafon* — the animal must be slaughtered in the north, since it might be an *asham*, which is *kodshei kodashim* and requires *shechita* in the north, even though a *shelamim* may be slaughtered anywhere. *U-matan behonot* — the blood is applied to the thumb, toe, and ear as required for the *tahara* of a *metzora*. *U-smicha* — he performs *smicha* on the animal, as required for a *shelamim*. *Tosafot* notes that *smicha* applies to an *asham* as well, though whether it is *de-oraita* for an *asham* is debated; in any case, *smicha* is unambiguously required for a *shelamim*. *U-nesachim* — *nesachim* are brought, as is done for a *shelamim*. The *asham metzora* itself actually carries *nesachim* as well, as studied earlier in the tractate, but other *ashamot* do not; the emphasis here is that this offering will have *nesachim*. *U-tnufat chazeh va-shok* — the *chazeh* and *shok* are waved, as is done for a *shelamim* but not an *asham*. All the actions appropriate to one or the other possibility are performed.

*Ve-ne'echal li-zichrei kehuna le-yom ve-layla* — it is eaten only by male *kohanim*, and only for a single day and night. If it turns out to be a *shelamim*, this is a restriction, since *shelamim* may normally be eaten by anyone in *Yerushalayim* over two days. This means one risks the possibility that the *shelamim* will have to be burned before it otherwise would need to be.

### Eating Limitations

The *Gemara* — self-referentially noting a discussion in the *Kodashim* tractates — asks: when does *Rabbi Shimon* allow one to bring an offering and stipulate in this fashion *lechatchila*? The answer: *le-takkunei gavra* — to restore this person to normal life. A *metzora* cannot remain in that state indefinitely; he must be returned to a normal state.

### Metzora Exception

The implication is that in general, *Rabbi Shimon* would not ordinarily permit stipulation *lechatchila*; ordinarily, *be-di'avad in, lechatchila lo* — after the fact it may be acceptable, but one would not set out from the start to hedge with stipulations in this way. The special leniency for the *metzora* is precisely because there is no other way to restore him to normal life.

### Minchot: No Destruction

The *Gemara* then clarifies why the *metzora* case requires a special justification while the *mincha* case does not.
