The particular problem in the *metzora* case is *hanei milei gabei shelamim de-kamam'it ba-achilatan de-havu lehu kodashim le-veit ha-pasul* — one risks treating what might be a *shelamim* as though it were an *asham*, limiting its eating to one day and to *kohanim* only, thereby potentially causing it to be burned before it needs to be. That destructive consequence requires special license to override, and the license is the *metzora*'s need to return to normalcy.

By contrast, *aval menachot afilu lechatchila* — with *menachot*, nothing is being limited or destroyed by the stipulation. One is simply designating one portion as *neder* and another as *nedavah*, neither of which involves any degradation or premature burning of the *mincha*. Therefore *Rabbi Shimon* would permit this stipulation *lechatchila* with no special justification needed.

---

## Double Portions Strategy

### Two Isaronot, Two Log

*Rav Pappa* then poses a question to *Abaye*: according to *Rabbi Shimon*, who says that a *ma'afeh tanur* can be half *challot* and half *rekikin*, if one plays this out in practice, one would be bringing one *isaron* out of two *isronot* and one *log* out of two *logim*. That is, to cover all the permutations within *ma'afeh tanur*, one would bring two *isronot* — one that will become the *challot* and one that will become the *rekikin* — together with two *logim* of oil.

### Neder/Nedavah Split

One then stipulates: of this, the amount needed for my *neder* is my *neder*, and the remainder is my *nedavah*. Whichever combination of *challot* and *rekikin* I vowed, those units are my *neder*, and the balance — the ten minus x from the *challot* and the ten minus y from the *rekikin* — is a free-will *mincha*.

### Rav Pappa Clarification

*Rav Pappa* confirms this works, noting that we know *Rabbi Shimon* holds that if someone brought two *isronot* and two *logim* and said the part needed for his *mincha* should count, *yatza* — it is valid. The stipulation of taking one *isaron* from two *isronot* and one *log* from two *logim* is precisely what *Rabbi Shimon* endorses in principle.

---

## Kemitza Oil Problems

### Kemitza Uncertainty

The discussion then pivots to the *kmitza* problem. How does one perform *kmitza* when the type of *mincha* is uncertain? This is not a trivial procedural question. If the *mincha* is all *challot*, the *kmitza* must be taken entirely from *challot*. If it is all *rekikin*, entirely from *rekikin*. If it is a mixture of *challot* and *rekikin*, presumably the *kmitza* must reflect that mixture — it must contain the appropriate proportion of both types, or at least some of each.

### Two Kemitzot

The proposed solution is to take two separate *kmatzim* — one entirely from the *challot* and one entirely from the *rekikin*. One then stipulates: *ei chalot lachudaihu ve-rekikin lachudaihu* — if I vowed all *challot*, the *kmitza* from the *challot* is for my *neder* and the *kmitza* from the *rekikin* is for the *nedavah*. If I vowed all *rekikin*, the reverse. But what if I vowed some mixture — *mechtza rekikin u-mechtza challot*, or any other proportional split?

The stipulation is: *deka kamatzna me-chalot lihavei amar mechtza challot u-mechtza rekikin* — the *kmitza* taken from the *challot*, let it stand for the *challot* portion of my *neder*; and the *kmitza* from the *rekikin*, let it stand for the *rekikin* portion of my *neder*. The remainder of each — *ten minus x* from the *challot* and *ten minus y* from the *rekikin* — is the *nedavah*. In this way, each *kmitza* is said to "work for" the relevant proportion of the vowed and free-will portions simultaneously. This looks like it resolves the question, and yet the *Gemara* raises a difficulty: by taking one *kmitza* from all *challot* and one from all *rekikin*, you are effectively applying the *challot* *kmitza* to the *rekikin* portion of the *neder* as well, and the *rekikin* *kmitza* to the *challot* portion of the *neder*. That is, *ve-ka kamitz me-chalot a-rekikin u-me-rekikin achalot* — you are taking a *kmitza* of *challot* and directing it over the *rekikin* and a *kmitza* of *rekikin* and directing it over the *challot*.

### One Kemitza Works

At this point, the *Gemara* reveals that what appeared to be a series of devastating objections are in fact all resolvable by appeal to known positions of *Rabbi Shimon*. *Shmia lei le-Rabbi Shimon de-amar im kamatz be-yado me-chad al sheneihem yatza* — we know *Rabbi Shimon* says that if one took a *kmitza* from one of the two types in a mixed *mincha* of *challot* and *rekikin*, it is valid for both types. Therefore taking one *kmitza* from the *challot* and one from the *rekikin*, and then stipulating that each works for the correct proportional share of the *neder* and the *nedavah*, is fully consistent with *Rabbi Shimon*'s position.

The dialectical arc, then, is this: it initially appeared that *Rabbi Shimon*'s position would require fourteen separate offerings to cover all permutations. *Abaye* argued that one need only bring the standard five and stipulate. *Rav Pappa* elaborated the mechanics — two *isronot* and two *logim* with a *neder*/*nedavah* split — and this was confirmed to be *Rabbi Shimon*'s view. The *kmitza* difficulty was raised and shown to be resolved by *Rabbi Shimon*'s own ruling that a *kmitza* from one type in a mixed *mincha* is valid for both.

### Remainder Oil

However, one more problem remains: *ve-ha ikka motzar shemen* — what about the remainder of the oil? The issue is this. For a *mincha* that is all *challot*, the oil is mixed directly into the loaves — *challot* require a heavy, integral application of oil. For a *mincha* that is all *rekikin*, the *rekikin* receive only a smear of oil, and the remainder of the oil stays separate and is eaten by the *kohanim*. But if the *mincha* is half *challot* and half *rekikin*, *motzar shemen machziru la-challot* — the leftover oil from the *rekikin* portion is poured back into the *challot*. This creates a problem for the stipulation strategy: if the *mincha* turns out to be all *challot* or all *rekikin*, the remainder oil for the *rekikin* stays separate; if it is a mixture, that remainder must be poured back. One cannot both pour and not pour the oil at the same time.

### Oil Chi Pattern

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda*. *D'tanya Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda omer mishum Rabbi Shimon* — *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda* said in the name of *Rabbi Shimon*: even when a *mincha* is half *challot* and half *rekikin*, one does not pour the remainder oil back into the *challot*. Instead, *moshcham ke-minchu* — one applies the oil in the pattern of a chi (the Greek letter), making an X-shaped smear across the *rekikin*, and *motzar shemen ne'echal le-kohanim* — any remaining oil is eaten by the *kohanim*. According to this version of *Rabbi Shimon*'s opinion, the treatment of the oil is identical whether the *mincha* is all *challot*, all *rekikin*, or any combination: the *challot* receive their oil mixed in, the *rekikin* receive a smear in the chi pattern, and any leftover oil goes to the *kohanim*. There is no scenario in which the oil must be poured back. Therefore the stipulation strategy works perfectly even with regard to the oil — nothing changes in the treatment of the oil across all the permutations.

---

## Minchat Nesachim Excluded

### Different Category

Having established that even according to *Rabbi Shimon* the answer is five types with stipulation, the *Gemara* then addresses a challenge raised by *Rav Kahana* to *Rav Ashi*: *ve-ika le-ispukei be-minchat nesachim* — but there is a sixth possibility one should have to account for. *Rava* has stated that *misnadiv adam minchat nesachim be-chol yom* — a person may voluntarily bring a *minchat nesachim* every day, independently of an animal sacrifice. This *minchat nesachim*, unlike the five *menachot* enumerated at the beginning of *Vayikra*, has a different ratio of oil to flour. Should one not have to bring it as well when uncertain which type of *mincha* was vowed?

### Five Distinctions

The *Gemara* responds with a series of categorical distinctions. *Ki ka mistafqa lei, be-ba'ah be-yachid, be-ba'ah be-tzibur lo mistafqa lei* — when someone is uncertain what type of *mincha* he vowed, he would only consider a *mincha* brought by private individuals. A *minchat nesachim* can be brought by the *tzibur* as well, making it categorically distinct from the five standard types. *Ki ka mistafqa lei be-ba'ah be-fnei atzma, be-ba'ah im ha-zevach lo mistafqa lei* — one would only be uncertain about a *mincha* that normally stands alone, whereas a *minchat nesachim*, even if it can be brought independently, standardly accompanies an animal sacrifice. *Ki ka mistafqa lei te'una levona, she'eina te'una levona lo mistafqa lei* — standard *menachot* require *levona*; a *minchat nesachim* does not. *Ki ka mistafqa lei ba'ah be-log, ba'ah be-shlosha login lo mistafqa lei* — standard *menachot* come with one *log* of oil per *isaron*, whereas a *minchat nesachim* uses a substantially greater proportion of oil — two or three *logim* per *isaron* — making it sufficiently anomalous that one would not think of it as a default vow. *Ki ka mistafqa lei te'una kmitza, she'eina te'una kmitza lo mistafqa lei* — standard *menachot* require *kmitza*, the removal of a handful; a *minchat nesachim* is entirely burned and has no *kmitza*.

### Not Default Option

These five distinctions establish that a *minchat nesachim* is so categorically different from the standard five *menachot* of private individuals — in terms of its bringing by individuals versus the public, its independence versus its accompaniment to an animal, its *levona*, its oil ratio, and its *kmitza* — that when someone vows an unspecified *mincha* and then cannot remember which type, a *minchat nesachim* simply would not have been what he had in mind. Therefore there is no need to add it as a sixth option, and the ruling to bring five types — or, according to *Rabbi Shimon*, five types with appropriate stipulation — stands.

---

---

# Menachot 106

## Unspecified Mincha

### Mishnah Setup

Today's *daf* is *Menachot* 106. We pick up on 106a about halfway down the page, at the words *perashti minchah shel esronim* — "I designated a *minchah* of *esronim*." The case is one where a person vowed to bring a *minchah* of *esronim* but cannot remember how many *esronim* he specified. Because he said a *minchah* — singular — of *esronim*, the assumption is that it must be one *minchah* of X *esronim*. The *mishna* resolves the uncertainty by bringing sixty, since that is the maximum number of *esronim* a single *minchah* can contain. According to the *Chachamim*, he stipulates that whatever amount satisfies his *neder* is his *neder*, and the remainder is a *nedavah* — a free-will offering. According to *Rebbi*, however, the amount must be exact: since he said a specific number, he must bring every possible amount from one to sixty, each in its own vessel, covering all possibilities.

### Tanu Rabbanan

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* that elaborates on the *mishna*: *Tanu Rabanan* — the Rabbis taught: *Perashti minchah v'kavati b'kli echad shel esronim v'eini yodeia mah perashti* — "I designated a *minchah* and specified it in one vessel of *esronim*, and I do not know how many *esronim* I specified." When the person says a *minchah* singular, it is either explicit or implicit that the entire amount is in one vessel — as opposed to the possibility discussed earlier of bringing a *minchah* across multiple vessels.

*Yavi minchah she-shishim esronim Divrei Chachamim* — according to the *Chachamim*, one brings sixty *esronim* in a single vessel and stipulates: whatever is needed for my *neder* is the *neder*, and the rest is a *nedavah*, an additional *minchah* brought as a free-will offering. *Rebbi omer yavi menachot shel esronim me-echad v'ad shishim* — *Rebbi* says one brings separate *menachot* of *esronim* from one through sixty. And if the person also does not know which of the five types of *minchah* he vowed, or how many *esronim* he intended — *v'eini yodeia mah perashti v'eizo mehem perashti v'eini yodeia kamah perashti* — the phrase *kamah perashti* addresses how many, *eizo mehem* addresses what type, and *mah perashti* encompasses the whole uncertainty — then *yavi chamesh menachot she-shishim esronim Divrei Chachamim*: the *Chachamim* require five sets of sixty *esronim*, one for each type of *minchah*, and *Rebbi omer yavi chamesh menachot she-shishim esronim me-echad v'ad shishim*: *Rebbi* requires bringing all five types, each multiplied across all amounts from one to sixty.

### Sum 1–60

This raises the arithmetic: what is the total number of *esronim* according to *Rebbi*? Adding all integers from one to sixty yields 1,830 — *she-hen elef u-shmoneh me'ot u-shloshim*. *Tosafot* provides an elegant method for this calculation: *keitzad kach b'yadcha me-echad v'ad shishim v'tzaref techilatan v'sofan ad ha-emtza k'gon echad v'shishim hen shishim v'echad* — take the numbers from one to sixty and pair each from the beginning with one from the end: one plus sixty equals sixty-one, two plus fifty-nine equals sixty-one, and so on, until the middle pair of thirty and thirty-one. That yields thirty pairs of sixty-one, and thirty times sixty-one is 1,830. This same method is attributed to the mathematician Carl Gauss, who reportedly discovered it as a young boy when a teacher assigned him to sum all integers from one to one hundred. Whatever the history, *Tosafot* records the identical insight centuries earlier.

### Rabbi's Count

According to *Rebbi*, if the person also forgot the type of *minchah*, he must bring all five types, each covering amounts from one to sixty. The total is therefore 1,830 multiplied by five: *she-hem tishat alafim u-me'ah va-chamishim* — nine thousand one hundred and fifty *esronim*.

### Core Debate

Now that the arithmetic is clear, the *Gemara* asks: *b'mai kamifligi* — what is the underlying dispute? Why can *Rebbi* not accept the *Chachamim*'s solution? If everything must be in one vessel, why not place sixty *esronim* in that vessel, stipulate that whatever amount corresponds to the *neder* is the *neder*, and treat the remainder as a *nedavah*? What precisely prevents mixing the obligatory portion with an additional free-will offering in the same vessel?

## Chullin in Azarah

### Chullin Entry

*Rav Chisda* proposes the following framework: *b'muttar lehachnis chullin la'azarah kamifligi* — the dispute concerns whether one is permitted to bring non-sanctified matter, *chullin*, into the Temple courtyard, the *azarah*. The logic, strange as it sounds, is that the extra flour beyond the amount of the *neder* would not be designated as a *nedavah* but would simply remain *chullin*. The question would then be whether a vessel can be brought into the *azarah* when part of its contents may be *chullin*.

### Rabbi Forbids

According to *Rav Chisda*'s initial framing, *Rebbi savar assur lehachnis chullin la'azarah* — *Rebbi* holds that it is forbidden to bring *chullin* into the *azarah*, and therefore each amount must be placed in its own separate vessel. In a separate vessel, the donor can designate the exact sanctified amount as the *neder* and anything additional as a *nedavah*, without the problem of *chullin* in the *azarah*.

### Chachamim Allow

By contrast, *v'rabbanan savri muttar lehachnis chullin la'azarah* — the *Chachamim* permit bringing *chullin* into the *azarah*, and therefore have no objection to a single vessel containing both the obligatory and the possibly non-sanctified portions. This position is admittedly difficult to understand: if some of the flour is *chullin*, a handful will need to be taken and the offering placed on the altar — it is hard to see why the *Gemara* would initially prefer this arrangement over simply designating the extra as a *nedavah*.

### Rava Corrects

*Rava* rejects this framework entirely: *dechulei alma assur lehachnis chullin la'azarah* — obviously everyone agrees that *chullin* may not be brought into the *azarah*. The initial framing was misguided; no one would wish to have *chullin* mixed with a *korban*. The true dispute is something else: *vehacha bemuttar le'arev chovah binedava kamifligi* — here they disagree about whether it is permitted to mix an obligatory offering, the *chovah*, with a free-will offering, a *nedavah*, in a single vessel. *Rabbanan savri muttar le'arev chovah binedava* — the *Chachamim* permit combining them. *Rebbi savar assur le'arev chovah binedava* — *Rebbi* forbids it. It is striking that the *Gemara* initially seemed more comfortable with the idea of *chullin* in the *azarah* than with mixing *chovah* and *nedavah*; *Rava* now corrects course and makes clear that the real issue is the latter.

## Kometz Mixture

### Two Kematzim

*Abaye* now raises a practical difficulty with the *Chachamim*'s position to *Rava*. If *chovah* and *nedavah* are mixed together in one vessel, *le'Rabbanan de'amri muttar le'arev chovah binedava*, then you have a problem: *ha ba'inan sheni kematzim* — you need two *kematzim*, one for the *neder* and one for the *nedavah*. You cannot know in advance whether the sixty *esronim* are entirely a *chovah* (if you vowed sixty) or partly a *chovah* and partly a *nedavah* (if you vowed less). The *Gemara* answers: *dekometz vehadar kometz* — fine, you take two *kematzim*, one after the other.

### Mixed Kematzim

But a further problem immediately arises: *veha kometz mechovah anedava uminedava achovah* — when you take each handful, it will contain a mixture drawn from both the *chovah* portion and the *nedavah* portion, since everything is in one vessel and the two are not physically separated. How then can the first *kematz* serve properly as the *kematz* of the *chovah* and the second as the *kematz* of the *nedavah*?

### Kohen's Intent

The *Gemara* resolves this: *detali lei bedaat kohen* — the matter is made to depend on the intention of the *kohen*. The stipulation is formulated as follows: *kol heicha dematya yadeih dekohen hashta chovah* — wherever the *kohen*'s hand reaches now as he takes his first handful, that section of the flour is designated as the *chovah*. He is thus taking entirely from the *chovah* portion. Then, assuming there is a *nedavah* portion — meaning the person vowed less than sixty — the second section into which the *kohen* reaches is designated as the *nedavah*: *hashta chovah ulevasof nedavah*. The two *kematzim* are thereby kept distinct through designation, even though the physical flour is intermingled.

### No Nedava Problem

However, a more serious difficulty now presents itself. If the person did in fact vow sixty *esronim*, then the entire sixty constitutes the *chovah* — there is no *nedavah* at all. Yet a second *kematz* will have been taken. The *Gemara* asks: *veidach heichi maktar* — how do you then burn this second *kematz*? The *Gemara* explores the possible order of operations. *Liktar nedavah bereisha* — should you burn the second *kematz* first, treating it as the *nedavah*? The *Gemara* objects: *dechovah heichi maktar lah* — how would you then subsequently burn the first *kematz* as the *chovah*? *Dilma kullah chovah hi* — perhaps the entire sixty is the *chovah*, in which case offering that first *kematz* would be burning the *kometz* after you have already removed and burned what might be the *shirayim* — the remnant. And the rule is: *shirayim shechasru bein kemitzah lehaktarah ein maktir kometz aleihem* — if the *shirayim* were diminished between the taking of the *kematz* and the burning of it, you cannot then burn the *kometz*.

The *Gemara* therefore reverses the order: *liktar chovah bereisha* — burn the first *kematz*, the one designated as the *chovah*, first. But then the difficulty shifts: *denedavah heichi maktir lei* — how do you subsequently burn the second *kematz*, the one designated as the *nedavah*? *Vedilma kullah chovah hi* — perhaps the entire sixty was the *chovah*, and there is no *nedavah* here at all. *Vechol shehu mimenu leishim harei hu beval taktir* — and the rule derived from the verse *ki kol seor vechol devash lo taktiru mimenu isheh l'Hashem* is that anything from which a portion has already been offered on the altar, its remainder may not itself be offered on the altar. If there is no *nedavah*, that second *kematz* consists entirely of *shirayim* of the *chovah*, and burning it on the altar violates this prohibition.

### Fuel Solution

The resolution is offered by *Rav Yehuda brei d'Rav Shimon ben Pazi*: *d'maseik lehu l'shum etzim* — you place the second *kematz* on the altar and treat it not as a ritual burning of an offering but simply as fuel, as firewood. The stipulation is: if a *nedavah* exists here, this *kematz* is its proper *kometz* and is being offered as such; but if the entire sixty was the *chovah* and there is no *nedavah*, then this flour — which should rightfully be eaten by the *kohanim* — is being placed on the altar fire as mere kindling, not as a sacrificial act. This is permitted, and does not violate the prohibition of *lo taktiru*, since it is not being offered *l'reach nichoach*, as an act of sacrifice. This solution invokes the principle of *Rabbi Eliezer*, as cited in a *baraita*: *D'tanya Rabbi Eliezer omer l'reach nichoach ee atah ma'aleh aval atah ma'aleh l'shum etzim* — *Rabbi Eliezer* says one may not offer it up as an act of *reach nichoach*, but one may place it on the fire as fuel. The verse *al hamizbeach lo ya'alu l'reach nichoach* prohibits only the former, not the latter. That is how the *Chachamim*'s position, permitting the mixture, is made technically workable. *Rebbi*, by contrast, simply forbids the mixture outright — though we have not yet fully explained the reason.

## Rav Acha's View

### Alternate Framework

*Rav Acha brei d'Rava* now proposes an alternative way of understanding the entire debate to *Rav Ashi*: *v'dilma d'kulei alma mutar l'arev chovah b'nedava* — perhaps everyone actually agrees that mixing *chovah* and *nedavah* is in principle permitted. *V'hacha b'd'Rabbi Eliezer kamiflagi* — the real disagreement is whether to accept *Rabbi Eliezer*'s fuel doctrine. *Derabbanan it lehu d'Rabbi Eliezer* — the *Chachamim* accept *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position, and therefore, even if the second *kematz* turns out to be *shirayim*, it can be placed on the altar as fuel. *V'Rebbi leit lei d'Rabbi Eliezer* — *Rebbi* rejects *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling, and therefore has no way of properly disposing of the second *kematz* if the entire sixty was the *chovah*, making the whole arrangement unworkable.

### Objection to Acha

The *Gemara* objects to this proposal: *ee salka dach'takh l'Rebbi mutar l'arev chovah b'nedava* — if *Rebbi* in principle permitted mixing *chovah* with *nedavah* and his only problem were the technical difficulty of the second *kematz*, then a technical solution could be found, and the objection based on *Rabbi Eliezer* alone would not explain why *Rebbi* requires sixty separate vessels.

### Touching Vessels

The technical solution is as follows: *efshar d'mayti shitin b'chad mana* — take sixty *esronim* in one vessel, and also take one additional *esaron* in a separate vessel, *v'chad b'chad mana u'maga lehu* — and bring the openings of the two vessels together so they are touching, with a continuous surface of flour between them. *U'maga lehu v'kometz* — and then take the *kematz*.

### Nedava Guarantee

Here is how this solution works. The first *kematz* is taken from the large vessel of sixty and designated as the *chovah*. Then the stipulation is made: if the vow was for sixty, the sixty constitutes the *chovah*, and the separate *esaron* in the second vessel is the *nedavah* — and you take the second *kematz* from that separate vessel. If the vow was for less than sixty, then everything beyond the vow in the large vessel, plus the entire second vessel, constitutes the *nedavah*, and you still take the second *kematz* from the second vessel. The problem that motivated *Rabbi Eliezer*'s ruling was that if the person vowed sixty, there would be zero *nedavah* remaining and nothing valid to take a *kometz* from. By ensuring a separate *esaron* is always present, there is always a guaranteed *nedavah* portion from which the *kometz* may be taken. This is an elegant solution, which means *Rebbi*'s objection cannot be merely technical — it must reflect a principled opposition to mixing *chovah* with *nedavah* in any form.

## Oil Proportion

### Rava's Answer

*Rava* now offers yet another explanation: *d'kulei alma mutar l'arev chovah b'nedava* — everyone agrees that mixing *chovah* and *nedavah* is permitted, *v'kulei alma it lehu d'Rabbi Eliezer* — and *Rabbi Eliezer*'s fuel doctrine is not a point of contention either. *Vehacha bepelugta deRabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov veRabbanan kamipalgi* — the actual dispute at the heart of the *machloket* is the well-known debate between *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* and the *Chachamim* regarding the amount of oil required for a *minchah*.

### Oil Mishnah

The *Gemara* cites the relevant *mishna*: *afilu minchah shel shishim isaron noten la shishim log* — even a *minchah* of sixty *esronim* receives sixty *log* of oil, according to the *Chachamim*, who hold that oil is always proportional, one *log* per *esaron*. *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov omer afilu minchah shel shishim isaron ein la ela loga* — *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* says that regardless of how large the *minchah* is, it receives only one *log* of oil, based on the verse *shenemar laminchah velog shemen* — "for the *minchah* and one *log* of oil" — which implies a fixed quantity of one *log* for any *minchah*.

### One Log Problem

The practical implication is now clear. If you do not know the amount of your *neder*, and you place everything in one vessel, you face a fundamental uncertainty about the oil. *Velo yadinan ei chada mincha hi desagi la bechad log* — is this entire vessel one *minchah* requiring only one *log* of oil? *Ei shtei menachot ninhu deva'ayan shtei lugin* — or is it in fact two *menachot*, a *neder* and a *nedavah*, each requiring its own *log*? There is no way to know, and no way to fulfill the oil requirement correctly.

### Chachamim vs. Eliezer

*Rabbanan savri keRabbanan de'amri shishim log* — the *Chachamim* hold like the majority view that oil is proportional to the number of *esronim*. Therefore, whether the vessel contains one *minchah* or two, *vechol chad vechad isaron log ka shakil* — each *esaron* takes its proportional *log* of oil, and there is no difficulty in having a *neder* and a *nedavah* in the same vessel. *Rebbi savar keRabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov de'amar ein la ela log* — *Rebbi* holds like *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* that only one *log* is required per *minchah* regardless of size. Since it is unknown whether this is one *minchah* or two, the oil requirement cannot be determined, and it is therefore impossible to fulfill the *korban* in a single vessel. This, according to *Rava*, is the true reason *Rebbi* requires every amount to be brought separately.

## Exact vs. Minimum

### Ashi's Framework

*Rav Ashi* proposes yet another framework for the debate: *bekatan vehevi gadol kamipalgi* — perhaps the dispute turns on a different question altogether: whether a vow for a specific amount means that amount exactly, or whether it merely establishes a minimum. That is, if a person said "I obligate myself to bring a *minchah* of X *esronim*," does bringing more than X satisfy the vow, or does it not?

### Minimum View

*Rabbanan savri katan vehevi gadol yatza* — the *Chachamim* hold that if you vowed a small amount and brought a larger one, you have fulfilled your obligation. Under this view, you need not specify the minimum amount separately at all: you bring sixty *esronim*, and since sixty certainly exceeds whatever you vowed, your *neder* is fulfilled, and nothing is left over as a distinct *nedavah*.

### Exact View

*VeRebbi savar lo yatza* — *Rebbi* holds that a vow means the exact amount specified, and bringing more does not satisfy it. Therefore, the excess beyond the vowed amount is not part of the *neder* and creates a situation of mixing obligatory and free-will offerings, with all the attendant problems already discussed.

### Verified Debate

The *Gemara* notes that this exact debate is already documented elsewhere: *detnan katan vehevi gadol yatza Rebbi omer lo yatza* — there is a later *mishna* that records this same dispute regarding an animal sacrifice: if someone vowed to bring a small animal and brought a large one, the *Chachamim* say he has fulfilled his obligation, while *Rebbi* says he has not. *Umi paligu beha zimna* — is it not already known that they disagree on this? *Tzricha* — nevertheless, both instances are necessary.

### Why Mincha Differs

*De'i itmar beha beha qa'amri Rabbanan mishum de'eidi ve'eidi qomzo* — if only the *minchah* case were stated, one might say the *Chachamim* permit bringing more because regardless of the size of the *minchah*, at the end of the day the same act occurs: one *kometz* is taken and offered on the altar. Whether the *minchah* has three *esronim* or thirty, it is still one *kometz* being burned. The quantity offered on the altar is identical in form, so one might say that a larger amount simply and naturally satisfies the vow. *Eima modi leh leRabbi* — one might then think that even *Rebbi* would agree in this case. The *tzricha* tells us that *Rebbi* does not.

Conversely, *ve'i itmar beha ika le-meimar le-Rabbi* — if only the animal case were stated, *Rebbi*'s position there makes intuitive sense, since a larger animal has more *imurin* — internal organs — placed on the altar, which is a fundamentally different act in quantitative terms, not merely the same act performed on a larger substrate. *Aval be-ha* — but in the case of a *minchah* where regardless of size it is always one *kometz* being offered, *eima modu le-Rabbanan* — one might think *Rebbi* would concede to the *Chachamim*. The *tzricha* confirms that he does not, and the debate applies equally in both contexts.

### Bottom Line

To summarize: according to *Rav Ashi*, *Rebbi*'s requirement to bring sixty separate vessels rests on his position that a vow for X means exactly X — not a minimum of X. Bringing more does not satisfy the vow but rather creates a mixture of a *neder* and a *nedavah*, and that mixture, combined with all the difficulties of oil proportionality or the prohibition on mixing obligatory and free-will offerings, is why *Rebbi* insists on strict separation.

## Wood & Metals

### Wood Rules

The *Gemara* moves to the next *mishna*. *Harei alai etzim* — if someone obligates himself to bring wood to the altar. Wood, as will be seen, may be vowed as a voluntary offering to be placed on the altar. *Lo yifchot mi-shnei gzirin* — the minimum is two logs of wood. *Tosafot* adds: *ve-davka ki amar etzim aval ki amar etz maytei gzir echad* — this specifically applies when you say "wood" in the plural; if you say "wood" in the singular, one log suffices.

### Frankincense

*Harei alai levonah* — if someone obligates himself to bring frankincense. *Lo yifchot mi-kometz* — the minimum is one *kometz* of frankincense. There are five standard *kematzim* of frankincense mentioned in context: *ha-omer harei alai levonah lo yifchot mi-kometz* — one who vows to bring frankincense must bring no less than a *kometz*; *ha-menadev mincha yavi ima kometz levonah* — one who brings a voluntary *minchah* brings with it a *kometz* of frankincense; *ha-ma'aleh et ha-kometz ba-chutz chayav* — one who burns a *kometz* of frankincense outside the Temple is liable; and *shnei bzichin te'unim shnei kmatzim* — the two dishes accompanying the showbread each require a *kometz* of frankincense. *Tosafot* notes that one of the novel points about the case of *ma'aleh ba-chutz* is that one is liable even for burning only one of the two dishes, though it represents only half the total amount.

### Precious Metals

*Harei alai zahav lo yifchot mi-dinar zahav* — if one obligates himself to bring gold, the minimum is one gold *dinar*. *Kesef lo yifchot mi-dinar kesef* — silver, not less than one silver *dinar*. *Nechoshet lo yifchot mi-ma'ah kesef* — copper, not less than the value of one silver *ma'ah*, which is one-sixth of a silver *dinar*. To put this in perspective: a gold *dinar* is worth twenty-five silver *dinarin*, and each silver *dinar* contains six *ma'ah*. Thus, when one says gold, the minimum is a gold *dinar* worth twenty-five times a silver *dinar*; when one says silver, the minimum is a silver *dinar*; and when one says copper, the minimum is copper valued at one-sixth of a silver *dinar*. Finally: *perashti ve-eini yode'a mah perashti* — if one specified a type of donation but forgot how much, *mevi ad she-yomar lo le-kach nitkavanti* — one brings increasingly larger amounts until one can say, "I certainly did not intend that much."

## Frankincense Default

### Default is Frankincense

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraita*: *Tanu Rabanan* — if someone says *harei alai la-mizbeach* — "I obligate myself to bring something to the altar" — without specifying what, *yavi levonah* — he must bring frankincense. The reason given is: *she-ein lecha davar she-karav legabei mizbeach ella levonah* — there is nothing that is offered directly on the altar except frankincense. This is a startling statement that immediately demands explanation — what about all other *korbanot*? The *Gemara* will address this shortly.

The *baraita* also addresses a further case: *perashti ve-eini yode'a mah perashti* — if one said explicitly that he is obligating himself to bring something to the altar and cannot remember what, *yavi mi-kol davar she-karav legabei mizbeach* — one must bring from every category of offering that is placed on the altar: an *olah*, a *shelamim*, a *minchah*, and so forth. Every possible fulfillment must be covered.

### Frankincense Kometz

The minimum quantity for a vow of frankincense is one *kometz*, derived from the following verse: *veherim mimenu vekomzo misolet hamincha umishamnah ve-et kol halevona* — "and he shall raise from it his handful of the fine flour of the *minchah* and its oil, and all the frankincense." *Maquish levona le-harama de-mincha* — the frankincense is hereby equated to the taking of the *kometz* of the *minchah* itself. *Mah harama de-mincha kometz af levona nami kometz* — just as the standard unit of the *minchah* offering is a *kometz*, so too the standard unit of frankincense is a *kometz*. The *Gemara* here is explaining not how we know one can vow frankincense in the first place, but how we know that the unit of frankincense — once vowed — is measured in *kematzim*.

## Wood & Metals…

### Uncertainty Rule

If a person declared *harei alai la-mizbeach* but forgot what he had in mind, *yavi mi-kol davar she-karav legabei mizbeach* — he must bring from every category of permitted altar offerings. Since he cannot determine which type of offering he intended, he covers every possibility.

## Frankincense Default…

### Why Frankincense

Returning to the claim that frankincense is the only offering placed on the altar: *v'tu lo* — is that really so? *Ve-ika olah* — what about a burnt offering, which is entirely consumed? The *Gemara* responds: *or le-kohanim* — the hide of the animal goes to the *kohanim*, so not everything goes to the altar. *Ve-ika olat ha-of* — what about a bird burnt offering, where everything is thrown on the altar? The *Gemara* responds: *ika mur'ah ve-notzah* — the crop and feathers are removed and do not go on the altar.

### Exceptions Discussed

Continuing into 107a: *ve-ika nesachim* — what about wine libations, which go entirely on the altar? *Le-shitin azli* — the wine pours into the underground channels, *shitin*, beneath the altar; it is assumed that when someone says *la-mizbeach* he means to be burned on the altar fire, not poured into channels. *Ve-ika minchat nesachim* — what about the *minchat nesachim*, the meal offering accompanying libations, which is entirely burned? The *Gemara* responds: *keivan de-ika mincha de-achli kohanim minah, lo paskinah beh* — since *menachot* in general are eaten by *kohanim*, when a person declares he is bringing something fully to the altar, the category of *minchah* does not come to mind as a wholly burned offering. Even though a specific type of *minchah* would indeed satisfy that description, the mental default image of a *minchah* is one that the *kohanim* eat.

### Mental Default

The upshot is this: *Tosafot* further asks, why not include oil — at least according to the view in an earlier chapter that oil may be vowed on its own and fully burned? The answer is the same: *keivan de-ika shemen de-achli Kohanim lo paski leh* — since oil is also eaten by the *kohanim* when mixed with a *minchah*, it does not register as a wholly altar-consumed offering. *Tosafot* also asks about wood, noting that even according to *Rebbi* who requires a *kemitzah* from it, all of it goes on the altar — yet it is not listed. The answer is that *levonah* is the paradigmatic mental image of something wholly consumed by the altar fire. When a person says *harei alai la-mizbeach* without specification, frankincense — the one substance that exists solely to be burned on the outer altar — is what he must have meant.

## Metal Precision

### Gold Coin

The *Gemara* now examines the metal vow rulings in greater detail. Regarding the gold minimum of one gold *dinar*: *ve-dilma naska* — perhaps when one said gold, he meant a gold ingot or bar rather than a coin? *Amar Rabbi Elazar de-amar matbe'a* — *Rabbi Elazar* explains that we interpret the vow as referring to a gold coin, not an ingot. *Tosafot* discusses the further question of whether an ingot would be considered more or less than the minimum, though that is not resolved here.

### Silver Coin

*Ve-dilma priti* — perhaps the person meant small change, like a small gold piece? *Amar Abaye priti de-dahava lo avdi inshi* — *Abaye* responds: people do not make gold small change. Gold simply does not come in the denomination of small coins; the standard unit of gold currency is the *dinar*, and that is what one intends.

*Kesef lo yifchos mi-dinar* — for silver, the minimum is likewise a silver *dinar*. *Ve-dilma naska* — perhaps a silver ingot was intended? *Amar Rabbi Elazar de-amar matbe'a* — again, *Rabbi Elazar* rules that a coin is intended. *Ve-dilma priti* — perhaps silver small change?

### Regional Context

*Amar Rav Sheshes be-asra lo sagi priti de-kaspa* — *Rav Sheshes* qualifies: this ruling applies in a place where silver small change is not commonly used for transactions, where people use copper coins for that purpose. In such a locale, when one says silver, one certainly means a silver *dinar*, not small change. The implication is that in a place where silver small change is prevalent, the ruling might differ.

### Copper Fork

*Nechoshes lo yifchos mi-ma'ah kesef* — copper must be worth at least a silver *ma'ah*. A *baraita* records: *Tanya Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov omer lo yifchos mi-tzinnora ketana shel nechoshes* — *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* says the minimum is not less than a small copper fork or tine. *Le-mai chazei* — what is this used for? *Amar Abaye she-mechattin bo pesilos u-mekanchin bo neros* — *Abaye* explains that it is used to clean out lamp wicks and maintain lamps. *Tosafot* specifies that this is not referring to the Temple *menorah* specifically, but to ordinary lamps. Thus, for copper, rather than specifying a monetary value equivalent, the *baraita* describes a concrete minimum object made of copper that people actually produce and use.

### Iron Spike

Finally, the *mishna*'s category of iron: *Tanya hachi nami lo yifchos mi-kila orev* — a *baraita* likewise teaches that the minimum for an iron vow is no less than the amount of iron needed to make a spike for warding off ravens. *Ve-kamma* — how large is this? *Amar Rav Yosef amma al amma* — an *amma* by an *amma* of iron. Some versions of the text read: *ika de-amri lo yifchos me-amma al amma* — others record this as "not less than an *amma* by an *amma*." *Le-mai chazei* — what is such an iron piece used for? *Amar Rav Yosef le-kila orev* — for the spike used to drive away ravens. The Temple rooftop would attract ravens drawn by the smell of the sacrificial meat, and iron spikes were installed to prevent them from perching. This serves as the standard unit of iron, much as the copper fork serves as the standard unit for copper.

---

---

# Menachot 107

## Wine & Oil Vows

### Wine Vows Intro

The *mishna* on 107a opens a series of cases in which individuals undertake vows (*harei alai* — "I hereby obligate myself") to bring various inanimate offerings to the altar. The first *mishna* of this section deals with someone who says *harei alai yayin* — "I obligate myself to bring wine." The underlying *chiddush* — that one may indeed bring wine as a standalone offering, in the manner that wine accompanies the *minchat nesachim* (the flour, oil, and wine that accompany animal sacrifices) — has already been established. The *mishna* now focuses on the minimum quantity required.

### Wine Minimum

*Lo yifchot mi-shlosha lugim* — the offering may not be less than three *log*, because that is the minimum amount brought as *nesachim*. The *pasuk* states *revi'it ha-hin la-keves yayin* — a quarter of a *hin* of wine for a lamb. A *hin* is twelve *log*, so a quarter of a *hin* is three *log*. That is the floor below which one may not go.

### Oil Offering Debate

*Shemen* — if one obligates himself to bring oil on its own (a position whose permissibility was itself debated earlier in the *mishna*, with Rabbi Tarfon's view being that one may indeed do so), how much must he bring? *Lo yifchot mi-log* — no less than one *log*, because one *log* is the amount of oil that accompanies a standard *mincha*. *Rabbi omer shlosha lugim* — Rabbi, however, says three *log*, because the conceptual basis for this type of offering is the *minchat nesachim*, where the minimum quantity of oil is three *log*. If one said a quantity but cannot recall the precise amount — *perashti ve-eini yodea mah perashti* — *yavi ke-yom merube* — he brings the amount appropriate to the largest day of offerings, as will be explained.

### Wine Source Pasuk

A *baraita* is then cited: *Tanu Rabbanan* — the Rabbis taught. The *pasuk* says *kol ha-ezrach yaaseh kacha* — "every citizen shall do thus," an apparently superfluous verse following the section on *nesachim*. This extra verse teaches, *melamed she-mitnadvin yayin* — that one may bring wine as a voluntary standalone offering, separate from any animal sacrifice. *Ve-kama* — and how much? *Shlosha lugim* — three *log*, the minimum quantity of *nesachim*.

### Wine Increase

*U-minyan she-im ratza le-hosif yosif* — and how do we know that one may bring more than three *log*? *Talmud lomar yihye* — the verse says *ke-chachem ka-ger ka-ezrach yihye* — the word *yihye* implies that additional amounts are permitted. And lest one think one may bring less than three *log* — *yachol yifchot* — *talmud lomar kacha* — the word *kacha* ("thus," i.e. exactly as specified) teaches that the minimum is fixed. One must bring no less than three *log*, but may bring any greater amount.

### Derash Methodology

The *Gemara* turns to the *machloket* between the Rabbis and Rabbi regarding oil. *Be-mai ka-miflegi* — what is the precise nature of their dispute? *Amru rabbanan kamei de-Rav Pappa* — the rabbinic students offered an explanation before *Rav Pappa*: *be-don minah u-minah u-ve-don minah ve-oki be-atrah ka-miflegi* — they are debating the hermeneutical principle of *don minah u-minah* versus *don minah ve-oki be-atrah*.

The distinction is this: when one derives a law by analogy from a source case, does one import the original context of the source ("source formatting," so to speak) — that is *don minah u-minah* — or does one apply the law but anchor it in the contextual norms of the destination case — that is *don minah ve-oki be-atrah*, "learn from it but place it in its [destination] location"?

### Rabbanan Position

The Rabbis held *don minah u-minah* — learn from the source and carry its original context with you. The reasoning: *mah mincha mishtandvin af shemen nami mishtandvin* — just as one can voluntarily dedicate a *mincha* to the altar (derived from *adam ki yakriv mikem korban lashem* and *ve-nefesh ki takriv korban mincha lashem*, where the word *korban* serves as the textual basis for the permissibility of a standalone oil offering), so too one can bring oil on its own. And *u-minah* — carry the source context with you: *mah mincha be-log af shemen be-log* — just as a standard *mincha* has one *log* of oil, so too standalone oil is one *log*.

### Rabbi Position

Rabbi, by contrast, held *don minah ve-oki be-atrah* — learn from the source, but anchor the ruling in its destination context. *Mah mincha mishtandvin af shemen nami mishtandvin* — the word *korban* from the *mincha* verse is indeed the textual hook that permits standalone oil. *Ve-oki be-atrah* — but place it in its destination: *ke-nesachim* — like the *nesachim*. Because the operative model for bringing oil not mixed into a flour offering — the model of liquids brought independently — is the *nesachim*, where wine is the paradigmatic standalone liquid offering. The *nesachim*, then, serves as the anchor or destination context. *Mah nesachim shlosha login af shemen nami shlosha login* — just as the minimum quantity of oil in *nesachim* is three *log*, so too standalone oil is three *log*.

### Rav Pappa Resolve

*Rav Pappa*, however, rejected the students' framing. *Ei mi-mincha gamar lah le-Rabbi de-chulei alma lo pligi dominu mino* — if it is truly agreed that the source text for Rabbi is the *mincha* verse, then everyone would agree to apply the source context directly, and the minimum would be one *log*. There would be no basis for three *log* if you are genuinely deriving from a *mincha* context. Rather, *Rav Pappa* said, *ela Rabbi me'ezrach gamar lah* — Rabbi derives the permissibility of standalone oil not from the *mincha* verse at all, but straight from the *ezrach* verse — *kol ha-ezrach yaaseh kacha* — the same verse that teaches the permissibility of standalone wine. On this reading, Rabbi learns from *minchat nesachim* directly, and the minimum is therefore three *log*. This is a more elegant solution: in both the standard *mincha* and the *minchat nesachim* the oil is mixed with flour; the *ezrach* verse, by contrast, speaks to items brought independently alongside a sacrifice, making it a more natural source for a standalone oil offering.

### Rav Huna Challenge

*Rav Huna berei de-Rav Natan* challenged *Rav Pappa*: *umi mazit amrat hachi* — how can you say that? *Ve-ha-tanya* — has it not been taught in a *baraita* that the word *korban* from the standard *mincha* verse teaches that one may bring standalone oil — *melamed she-mitnadvin shemen* — *ve-kama shlosha login* — and the minimum is three *log*? Now, the position of three *log* is Rabbi's position — *man shamat lei de-amar shlosha login Rabbi* — and yet this *baraita* derives it from the word *korban* in the *mincha* verse, not from *ezrach*. This directly contradicts *Rav Pappa*'s reconstruction, which held that Rabbi does not derive from the *mincha* verse at all. *Rav Pappa* replied: *ei tanya tanya* — if that is what the *baraita* says, so it is. He conceded that if the *baraita* explicitly roots Rabbi's position in *korban* from the *mincha* verse and yet arrives at three *log*, then the students' original framing — that the dispute is about *don minah u-minah* versus *don minah ve-oki be-atrah* — must be correct after all, however conceptually awkward it may seem.

### Oil Uncertainty

As for the case of *perashti ve-eini yodea mah perashti* — one who specified an amount of oil but cannot recall what he said — *yavi ke-yom merube* — he brings the maximum amount corresponding to the largest day. The *tanna* specifies: *ke-yom tov ha-rishon shel chag she-chal lihyot be-Shabbat* — the first day of *Sukkot* that falls on *Shabbat*, when the greatest number of communal *korbanot* are brought and thus the greatest quantity of *minchat nesachim* accompanies them. That total quantity of oil is the maximum one could have had in mind, and it is therefore what must be brought.

---

## Olah Vows

### Olah Lamb Default

The next *mishna* takes up the case of *harei alai olah* — one who obligates himself to bring an elevation offering without further specification. *Yavi keves* — he brings a lamb, the smallest of the standard animal *olot*.

### Olah Birds Debate

*Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah omer o tor o ven yonah* — Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says one may fulfill the obligation with either a turtledove or a young pigeon, which are objectively even smaller than a lamb. All of these appear in the opening passages of Vayikra as valid forms of *olah*. The apparent basis of the dispute is whether the default interpretation of an unspecified *olah* vow refers to the minimum within the standard mammalian category, or to the absolute smallest *olah* possible — which would be a bird. The *Gemara* will clarify, however, that the dispute is not really about this, but rather a matter of regional pricing: *ve-lo pligi, mar ki atreih u-mar ki atreih* — they do not actually disagree in principle; in one locale, lambs were cheapest, and in another, birds were. (The *Gemara* thus explains the dispute as one of local custom and cost rather than a principled disagreement about the nature of the obligation.)

A *baraita* then elaborates: *Tanu Rabbanan* — if one says *harei alai olah be-sela la-mizbeach* — I obligate myself to bring an offering on the altar for one *sela* — *yavi keves she-ein lecha davar she-karev be-sela le-gabei mizbeach ela keves* — he brings a lamb, because there is nothing offered on the altar that costs exactly one *sela* other than a lamb, as established in the *mishna*. If one said he specified something but cannot recall what — *perashti ve-eini yodea mah perashti yavi mi-kol davar she-karev be-sela le-gabei mizbeach* — he must bring every possible item that in its entirety costs a *sela*, since he committed to a specific item at that price and must cover all possibilities.

### Cattle Uncertainty

*Peirashti min ha-bakar ve-eini yodea mah peirashti* — if one said his *olah* would be from the cattle but cannot remember which, *yavi par ve-egel* — he brings both an ox and a calf, since an *olah* must be male, and he may have intended either.

### All Mammals Uncertainty

*Min ha-behemah ve-eini yodea mah peirashti* — if one said from the mammals generally but cannot recall the species, he must bring all types: *yavi par ve-egel, ayil, sa'ir, gedi u-taleh* — an ox and a calf, a ram (adult sheep), an adult goat, a kid goat, and a lamb. The assumption is that had he remembered, he would have specified among these distinct categories, so since he cannot, he must bring all of them.

If the uncertainty is even broader — *peirashti ve-eini yodea mah peirashti* — he said he was bringing some kind of *olah* but does not know whether it was an animal or a bird — *mosif aleihem tor u-ven yonah* — in addition to all the mammals, he must also bring a turtledove and a pigeon, covering the possibility that he vowed a bird *olah*.

---

## Todah & Shelamim

### Todah Lamb Minimum

*Harei alai todah u-shlamim* — if one says "I obligate myself in a thanksgiving offering or a peace offering," what is the minimum? *Yavi keves* — a lamb. Unlike *olah*, there is no bird option for a *todah* or *shelamim*; the minimum is a lamb.

### Todah Cattle Gender

*Peirashti min ha-bakar ve-eini yodea mah peirashti* — if one specified cattle but cannot remember which type. Unlike *olah*, which is exclusively male, a *shelamim* or *todah* may be either male or female. Therefore — *yavi par u-parah, egel ve-eglah* — he must bring an ox and a cow, and a male calf and a female calf, covering all possibilities of gender and age within the cattle category.

### Todah All Mammals

*Min ha-behemah ve-eini yodea mah peirashti* — if one said mammals generally but cannot remember which type, he must bring every species in both genders: *par u-parah, egel ve-eglah, ayil ve-rachel, sa'ir u-se'irah, gedi u-gediyah, taleh u-tlayah* — an ox and cow, a male and female calf, a ram and an adult female sheep, a male and female adult goat, and a male and female kid.

---

## Sacrifice Pricing

### Ox Price

The *mishna* now specifies the standard monetary values assigned to each type of animal sacrifice together with its *nesachim*. *Harei alai shor* — one who says "I obligate myself in an ox" — *yavi hu ve-nesachav be-maneh* — must bring it together with its *nesachim* for the total cost of one *maneh*, which is one hundred *dinar*.

### Calf Price

*Egel* — a calf — *yavi hu ve-nesachav be-chamesh* — he brings it with its *nesachim* for five *sela*, which is twenty *dinar*.

### Ram Price

*Ayil* — a ram — *yavi hu ve-nesachav bi-shtayim* — with its *nesachim* for two *sela*, which is eight *dinar*.

### Lamb Price

*Keves* — a lamb — *yavi hu ve-nesachav be-sela* — one *sela*, which is four *dinar*. To appreciate the scale: a lamb costs four *dinar* and an ox costs one hundred *dinar*, twenty-five times as much. *Rashi* notes that these valuations derive from tradition (*halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*), while *Tosafot* raises the possibility that they simply reflect the standard market prices of the time.

### Price Excludes Nesachim

When one does not specify an amount, the stated figure covers the entire bundle — the animal plus its *nesachim*. But if one explicitly names both the animal type and the price — *shor be-maneh yavi be-maneh chutz me-nesachav* — an ox at a *maneh*, he brings an ox costing one *maneh* and the *nesachim* are separate and additional. *Egel be-chamesh yavi be-chamesh chutz min ha-nesachim* — a calf at five *sela*, the five *sela* goes to the calf alone, not including the *nesachim*. *Keves be-sela yavi be-sela chutz min ha-nesachim* — and similarly for a lamb.

---

## Exact Specification

### Two Animals Fail

The *mishna* now turns to cases of exact specification and what happens when the fulfillment does not match the vow precisely. *Shor be-maneh ve-hevi shnayim be-maneh lo yatza* — if one vowed an ox for one hundred *dinar* and brought two oxen whose combined cost is one hundred *dinar*, he has not fulfilled his obligation — he vowed a single ox at that price. *Ve-afilu zeh be-maneh chaser dinar ve-zeh be-maneh chaser dinar* — even if each of the two oxen cost ninety-nine *dinar*, so that together he spent nearly double the vowed amount, he has still not fulfilled his obligation, because he specified a single ox worth one hundred *dinar* and did not bring one.

### Color Specificity

*Shachor ve-hevi lavan, lavan ve-hevi shachor* — if one specified a black animal and brought white, or a white and brought black, the obligation is not fulfilled.

### Size Dispute

The *mishna* then addresses size: *gadol ve-hevi katan lo yatza* — if one vowed a large animal and brought a small one, the obligation is not fulfilled. Here arises a *machloket*:

### Tanna Kamma: Large OK

*Katan ve-hevi gadol yatza* — if one vowed a small animal and brought a large one, the Tanna Kamma holds that the obligation is fulfilled. The apparent reasoning is that when one says "small," one means at minimum something small — not an exact size — so a larger animal satisfies the obligation.

### Rabbi: Large Fails

*Rebbi omer lo yatza* — Rabbi says the obligation is not fulfilled even in this direction. Rabbi's position is conceptually coherent: a large ox is not simply a small ox with something added; it is a categorically different type of animal. One might note that the argument for Tanna Kamma is stronger in the case of meal offerings — when one vows a certain number of *isronot* of flour and brings more, the larger amount literally contains the smaller amount within it. With animals, that containment is less obvious.

---

## Size Debate Resolution

### Gemara Question

The *Gemara* now raises a difficulty. Recall that the *mishna* ruled: *peirashti min ha-bakar ve-eini yodea mah peirashti yavi par ve-egel* — if one said his offering would be from the cattle but cannot remember which, he must bring both an ox and a calf. The *Gemara* asks: *amai* — why? *Ve-leihavei par min ha-munach* — just bring an ox. If one vowed a calf and brings an ox, and Tanna Kamma holds that *katan ve-hevi gadol yatza* — bringing a larger one fulfills a vow for a smaller one — then an ox should discharge even the possibility that he vowed a calf.

The answer is immediate: *ha mani Rebbi hi de-amar katan ve-hevi gadol lo yatza* — this ruling in the *mishna* follows Rabbi, who holds that if you vowed a small animal and brought a large one, you have not fulfilled your obligation. Therefore even if he vowed a calf, he cannot discharge that obligation with an ox; he must bring a calf in any case.

### Mixed Opinions

The *Gemara* then pauses: *ei Rebbi eima seifa* — but if the ruling about cattle follows Rabbi, look at what the *mishna* says further on: *shor be-maneh ve-hevi shnayim be-maneh lo yatza... shachor ve-hevi lavan, lavan ve-hevi shachor, gadol ve-hevi katan lo yatza, katan ve-hevi gadol yatza* — and then the *mishna* itself states the Tanna Kamma's position that bringing a large animal fulfills a small vow, followed by *Rebbi omer lo yatza* at the very end. So the opening (*reisha*) of the *mishna* would follow Rabbi, the middle (*metzi'ata*) would follow the Rabbis, and the end (*seifa*) would return to Rabbi? *Reisha ve-seifa Rebbi, metzi'ata Rabbanan?*

### Rabbi Position

The *Gemara* confirms: *ein, reisha ve-seifa Rebbi, metzi'ata Rabbanan* — yes, that is precisely how the *mishna* is to be read. *Ve-hachi ka'amar* — and this is what the *mishna* means: The opening, which requires bringing both a calf and an ox when the vow was for an unspecified type of cattle, follows Rabbi — an ox does not discharge a calf vow. The middle section then states the general *machloket* between Rabbi and the Rabbis — the Rabbis hold *katan ve-hevi gadol yatza*, Rabbi holds *lo yatza* — and the final ruling *Rebbi omer lo yatza* is Rabbi's position within that debate.

### Debate Framework

The broader implication is that the question of size substitution — whether a larger animal can discharge a vow for a smaller one — is the heart of a comprehensive dispute between Rabbi and the *Rabbanan*, and the structure of this entire *mishna* reflects that disagreement, with the earlier section being attributed to Rabbi's position and the middle to the *Rabbanan*'s.

---

## Temple Treasury Boxes

### Six Horns Intro

The *Gemara* now cites a *mishna* from *Shekalim*: *shisha l'nedava* — there were six horns (*shofarot* — the narrow-topped collection boxes in the Temple) designated for voluntary elevation offering funds. Money that could not be used for its original purpose was redeemed, and the proceeds placed in these boxes; from them, *olot* were funded to keep the altar active during quiet periods. The question is: *keneged mi* — corresponding to what? Why specifically six boxes rather than one?

### Six Families Theory

*Chizkiyah* offered one explanation: *keneged shisha batei avos ha-kohanim she-tiknu lahem chachamim she-yishalom zeh im zeh* — corresponding to the six priestly family units (*batei avos*) within each weekly rotation (*mishmar*) of priests. The twenty-four *mishmarot* each served one week; within each *mishmar*, the six *batei avos* each took a day of the week (Sunday through Friday, with *Shabbat* shared by all). Each *beit av* served on its designated day, and on quiet days when few private *korbanot* were brought there would be less revenue from hides and other perquisites. By having a separate box for each day, each *beit av* could draw supplemental funds only from its own box — the day's designated *shofar* — rather than from a communal pool. This avoided resentment: had there been a single box, a *beit av* on a busy day might have bristled at a slower-day *beit av* drawing communal funds to sponsor extra *olot* and profit from their perquisites. The word *keneged* here, *Chizkiyah* implies, points not merely to symbolic correspondence but to the practical purpose that motivated the arrangement.

### Coin Preservation

*Rabbi Yochanan* offered a different practical rationale: *mitoch she-nedava meruba tiknu lahem shofarot merubos kedei she-lo yis'afshu ha-maos* — because the volume of donations was large, multiple boxes were instituted so that the coins would not sit too long and deteriorate. Copper coins left in a single large box for an extended period would rust or become moldy; distributing the funds across six boxes meant each box turned over more quickly.

### Animal Types Theory

*Zeiri* gave a third explanation: *keneged par ve-egel, keves ve-gedi ve-sa'ir* — corresponding to the six types of mammalian *olah* offerings: an ox, a calf, a ram, a lamb, an adult goat, and a kid goat. Each box was designated for a particular animal type, and donors could earmark their funds accordingly.

### Rabbi Connection

*Ve-Rebbi hi de-amar katan ben gadol lo yatza* — and this explanation follows Rabbi's position, who holds that a smaller animal vow is not discharged by a larger animal. Because Rabbi maintains that each animal type constitutes a categorically distinct offering — a calf is not merely a small ox — it is coherent to have six separate boxes, one for each distinct mammalian *olah* type. Were they interchangeable, there would be less reason to maintain separate accounting for each. The juxtaposition of this *mishna* from *Shekalim* with the preceding discussion of Rabbi's position is thus not incidental; the six-box structure of the Temple treasury itself reflects Rabbi's fundamental view of how these six animal types relate to one another.

---

---

# Menachot 108

## Six Shofrot Origins

### Shofrot Purpose

The *daf* opens in the middle of 108a, eight lines from the top, beginning with the words *v'Shmuel amar*. The discussion concerns why there were six extra collection boxes (*shofrot*) in the *Beis HaMikdash* — thirteen in total — into which money was deposited for the *olah l'keitz hamizbeach*, a communal burnt offering brought when there was insufficient activity to keep the altar occupied. Much of the money directed to this fund was originally designated for various *korbanot* that could not ultimately be brought — certain types of *chataot*, *ashamot*, and the like — and the question is what accounts for exactly six such *shofrot*. One earlier answer attributed to *Bar Padda* explained the six in terms of the different species of animals with which donations could have originally been made. Now the *Gemara* presents the view of *Shmuel*, whose answer focuses on different categories of *korbanot* rather than different species of animals.

### Shmuel's Categories

*Shmuel* explains: *keneged motar chataot u'motar asham u'motar asham nazir u'motar asham metzora u'motar minchat chote u'motar asirit haeifah shel kohen gadol* — the six *shofrot* correspond to leftover money from six distinct sources: the *chatat*, the *asham*, the *asham nazir*, the *asham metzora*, the *minchat chote*, and the daily *minchat chavitin* of the *kohen gadol*. The *halacha* for the first two is that leftover money designated for a *chatat* or an *asham* — situations where money was sanctified for such a sacrifice but not all of it was consumed — goes toward the *olah l'keitz hamizbeach*.

The three categories of *ashamot* are distinguished because each serves a distinct purpose. The *asham metzora* is brought as part of the purification process of one afflicted with spiritual impurity, with its blood applied to the ear, thumb, and toe; the *asham nazir* similarly marks a transition of status, enabling renewed *nezirut* in a state of purity. Both of these are therefore unlike the classic *asham*, which addresses sins such as theft with false denial (*asham gezelot*) or misuse of consecrated property (*meilah*). That gives four categories: one *chatat* and three types of *ashamot*. The fifth is the *minchat chote*, the sinner's *mincha* brought in cases of *olah veyored* — when the *Torah* permits a lesser-cost substitute for a *chatat* — which parallels the *chatat* but in *mincha* form. The sixth is the leftover money from the *minchat chavitin*, the daily tenth of an *eifah* brought by the *kohen gadol*, which a verse in *Yechezkel* calls a *chatat*, leading to the assumption that leftover money from it follows the same rule of redirection toward the *olah l'keitz hamizbeach*.

*Shmuel*'s list thus comprises one *chatat*, three *ashamot*, a *mincha*-equivalent *chatat*, and the *minchat chavitin* — six distinct sources.

### Rabbi Oshaya List

*Rabbi Oshaya* presents an alternative list: *keneged motar chatat u'motar asham u'motar asham nazir u'motar asham metzora u'motar kinnim u'motar minchat chote* — he agrees with the first four sources (*chatat* and the three *ashamot*), agrees with the *minchat chote* (though he places it last), but replaces the *minchat chavitin* of the *kohen gadol* with the *kinnim*, the bird sacrifices. This substitution is natural enough: bird sacrifices are indeed a classic form of *chatat*, brought, for instance, by a woman after childbirth (*yoledet*) in her purification offering. The five sources *Rabbi Oshaya* endorses are thus: the ordinary *chatat*, the three types of *ashamot*, the bird *chataot*, and the *minchat chote*.

### Bird Sacrifice Omission

A question is raised: *v'Shmuel mai ta'ama lo amar k'Rabbi Oshaya* — why did *Shmuel* not include bird sacrifices (*kinnim*), which are a most natural category? The answer is: *Kinnim tana lei reisha* — the *Mishnah* that lists all thirteen *shofrot* already specifies one of the first seven as designated explicitly for bird sacrifices, where a woman wishing to contribute money for her obligatory bird offerings could deposit directly into that box, with the *kohanim* then bringing the appropriate sacrifices on her behalf. Since one of the first seven *shofrot* already serves *kinnim*, *Shmuel* has no reason to include a category for leftover *kinnim* money among the final six.

### Kinnim Shofrot Split

The *Gemara* then addresses the implicit tension in *Rabbi Oshaya*'s position. One might suppose that *Rabbi Oshaya* simply did not have *kinnim* in his version of the opening seven *shofrot*, and so he needed to include it among the six. The *Gemara* raises this: *v'hatani Rabbi Oshaya* — but did not *Rabbi Oshaya* himself teach a *Mishnah* that includes *kinnim* in the first seven? The answer is: *chad l'kinnim v'chad l'motar kinnim* — there is no contradiction. The *shofar* among the first seven designated for *kinnim* receives money designated *l'chatchila* for the purpose of purchasing bird sacrifices, with the *kohanim* bringing offerings on behalf of whichever women deposited that money. The *shofar* in the second six, by contrast, receives leftover *kinnim* money — funds originally designated for a bird sacrifice that ended up not being fully used, and which must now be redirected to an *olah*. These serve distinct purposes and thus require distinct *shofrot*. This resolves *Rabbi Oshaya*'s position; the lecturer notes, however, that it does not fully explain why *Shmuel* rejected *kinnim* as one of his six, beyond the formal answer already given.

---

## Leftover Money Rules

### Money Rot Principle

The *Gemara* now asks: *v'Rabbi Oshaya mai ta'ama lo amar k'Shmuel* — why did *Rabbi Oshaya* exclude the *minchat chavitin* of the *kohen gadol* from his list? While one could answer simply that he already has six without it, the *Gemara* proposes a principled objection: *savar lei k'man d'amar mosar shel asiris haeifah shel kohen gadol yirakeiv* — *Rabbi Oshaya* holds that the leftover money of the *kohen gadol*'s daily *minchat chavitin* must be allowed to rot. The reasoning is as follows: on one hand, since *Yechezkel* calls it a *chatat*, it cannot simply be repurposed toward another *chatat*-type offering — the general rule is that what was used for a *chatat* cannot be redirected back to its own purpose in this way. On the other hand, *Rabbi Oshaya* does not regard it as a standard *chatat* whose leftover money redirects to an *olah*. The result is a middle category with no valid destination, leaving no choice but to let it rot.

### Baraita Interpretation

A *baraita* is cited: *mosar minchas nedavah, mosar minchah yirakeiv* — leftover money of a freewill *mincha*, the leftover *mincha* shall be let to rot. As the *Gemara* immediately asks, *mai kamar* — what does this even mean? The statement is nearly incomprehensible as stated. *Rav Chisda* explains: *mosar minchas chotei nedavah nedavah* — the *baraita* means that leftover money of a *minchat chote* goes to a *nedavah*. The word *nedavah* here refers to the communal *nedavat tzibbur*, that is, the *olos keitz hamizbeach* — which is precisely what both *Shmuel* and *Rabbi Oshaya* agreed upon. So the first part of the *baraita* is uncontroversial and consistent with both views.

The second clause — *mosar asiris haeifah shel kohen gadol yirakeiv* — states that the leftover money of the *minchat chavitin*, the *kohen gadol*'s daily tenth of an *eifah*, must be let to rot. It is called a *chatat* in *Yechezkel*, but because it is not a standard *chatat* brought for a sin, its leftover money cannot go toward an *olah*; yet it cannot go back toward another *chatat*-type offering either. So it must rot. *Rav Chisda* thus reads the *baraita* as containing two distinct propositions: the *minchat chote*'s leftovers go to *nedavah*, while the *minchat chavitin*'s leftovers rot.

### Rabbah's Ruling

*Rabbah* now offers a third position: *afilu mosar asiris haeifah shel kohen gadol nami nedavah* — even the leftover money of the *kohen gadol*'s daily *mincha* goes to *nedavah*, i.e., to the *olos keitz hamizbeach*. *Rabbah* sides with *Shmuel*, rejecting the *baraita*'s conclusion that this money rots. If there must be something that rots according to the *baraita*, *Rabbah* redirects that ruling: *ella motar lachmei toda yerakev* — rather, it is the leftover money from the *lachm* of the *todah* offering that must rot. The bread of a *todah* has no independent sanctified status; it exists solely to accompany the *todah* sacrifice itself and cannot be transferred to any independent *korban*. Leftover money for it therefore cannot be redirected and must be let to rot.

### Kohen Gadol Debate

The *Gemara* confirms that this question — what to do with the leftover money of the *kohen gadol*'s *minchat chavitin* — is an established dispute among *Amoraim*: *Rabbi Yochanan amar nedavah*, it goes toward the communal *nedavah* of the *olos keitz hamizbeach*, in keeping with the positions of *Shmuel* and *Rabbah*; *Rabbi Elazar omer yerakev*, it must rot, in keeping with the position of *Rabbi Oshaya*.

### Shekalim Mishna

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from a *Mishnah* in *Shekalim*: *mitivei — Motar shekalim chulin umotar asirit haeifah umotar kinei zavim vekinei zavot vekinei yoledot vechatatot vashamot motreihem nedavah* — leftover money from *shekalim* contributions is non-sanctified (*chulin*) and may even be used for non-sacred purposes; but leftover money from the tenth of an *eifah*, from bird sacrifices of a *zav*, a *zava*, and a *yoledet*, from *chataot*, and from *ashamot* — all of these go to *nedavah*. This *Mishnah* explicitly states that the *motar asiris haeifah* goes to *nedavah*, which appears to be a clear proof for the position of *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Shmuel*.

The lecturer notes that this *Mishnah* is actually a hybrid of the two lists: it includes both the bird sacrifices (which *Rabbi Oshaya* mentioned but *Shmuel* did not) and the *asiris haeifah* (which *Shmuel* mentioned but *Rabbi Oshaya* did not). This reflects the actual substance of the *machloket*: everyone agreed about the *halacha* regarding leftover bird sacrifice money — that it goes to the *keitz hamizbeach* — and the real debate was specifically about the *asiris haeifah*. The *Mishnah* in *Shekalim* thus appears to settle the matter firmly in favor of *nedavah*.

The *Gemara* asks: *mai lav motar asirit haeifah shel kohen gadol* — does "tenth of an *eifah*" not refer to the *kohen gadol*'s *minchat chavitin*? The *Gemara* offers a deflection: *lo motar minchat chote* — no, it refers to leftover money of a *minchat chote*. While *asiris haeifah* ordinarily calls to mind the *kohen gadol*'s daily offering, a standard *mincha* is also a tenth of an *eifah*, and so the term can be applied to the *minchat chote* as well. *Rabbi Oshaya* therefore reads this *Mishnah* as perfectly matching his own list of six sources: the *chatat*, the three *ashamot*, the bird sacrifices, and the *minchat chote* (referred to here as *motar asiris haeifah*). The surface reading, however — that the *Mishnah* refers to the *kohen gadol*'s offering — still supports *Shmuel*'s position.

### Non-Standard Chatat

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* weighs in: *mistavera k'man d'amar mosar asiris haeifah shel kohen gadol yerakev* — it stands to reason that the leftover money must rot. He brings proof from a *baraita*: *lo yasim aleha shemen v'lo yiten aleha levonah ki chatas hi* — this is the verse regarding the *minchat chote*, specifying that no oil and no frankincense are placed upon it, because it is a *chatat*. *Rabbi Yehuda* comments on this verse: *hi k'ruyah chatas v'ein acheres k'ruyah chatas* — the *minchat chote* is the *mincha* called a *chatat*, and no other is called a *chatat*. The implication is that even though *Yechezkel* calls the *kohen gadol*'s daily offering a *chatat*, the verse in the *Torah* is teaching that that designation does not apply with full legal force to any other offering.

### True Chatat Standard

*Rabbi Yehuda*'s principle illuminates the underlying debate. The *baraita* continues: *limed al asiris haeifah shel kohen gadol she'einah k'ruyah chatas* — this teaches that the *kohen gadol*'s *asiris haeifah* is not truly called a *chatat*. *V'te'unah levonah* — and consequently, since it is not a real *chatat*, it requires frankincense (*levonah*), because the prohibition on *levonah* applies only to a genuine *chatat* (*lo yasim aleha levonah*). *U'mide'einah k'ruyah chatas mosarah yerakev* — and because it is not a real *chatat*, its leftover money must rot.

This resolves the entire debate with precision. The position that says leftover money goes to *nedavah* holds that since *Yechezkel* calls it a *chatat*, any leftover funds follow the *chatat* rule and are redirected to *nedavah*. The position that says it rots holds that *Yechezkel*'s terminology notwithstanding, this is not a genuine *chatat* as established by the *Torah* verse — it therefore receives *levonah* (contrary to the *chatat* rule), and its leftover money cannot be redirected to an *olah*. Caught between the two, with no valid destination available, the money must be let to rot.

---

## Blemished Animals

### Ox Quantity Change

The *Gemara* now moves to a new *Mishnah*. *Shor zeh olah v'nistayev* — if someone said "this ox is an *olah*," thereby sanctifying the animal itself rather than undertaking a personal obligation, and then the animal developed a blemish rendering it unfit for the altar, it must be redeemed. *Im ratzah yavi bedamav shenayim* — if he wishes, he may use the redemption money to purchase two oxen, offering both. *Shenei shevarim elu olah v'nistavu* — if he said "these two oxen are an *olah*" and both developed blemishes, *ratzah yavi bidmeihem echad* — he may use the combined redemption money to bring a single large ox. In both cases, the *Mishnah* permits these transfers, because the issue is not satisfying a specific personal vow but rather properly channeling the existing sanctity. There is no designated obligation to fulfill — just a *halacha* that sanctity of an *olah* must be transferred to a valid *olah*, and the number or size of animals is unrestricted.

*Rebbi* forbids. The question is whether *Rebbi* forbids only the second case (two to one) or both.

### Sheep-Ram Transfers

The *Mishnah* continues: *ayil zeh olah v'nistayev im ratzah yavi bedamav keves* — if one said "this ram is an *olah*" and it developed a blemish, he may bring a sheep in its place, even though it is smaller — perhaps it was simply more expensive. Similarly, *keves zeh olah v'nistayev im ratzah yavi bedamav ayil* — if one said "this sheep is an *olah*" and it developed a blemish, he may bring a ram. *Rebbi oser* — *Rebbi* forbids. Since *Rebbi* clearly forbids even the last case of sheep to ram, which is going from small to large, it follows that *Rebbi* is opposed to any change — not merely to a deterioration in quantity or size.

### Sanctification vs. Vow

The *Gemara* opens 108b by noting the apparent tension with an earlier ruling: *v'amarta reisha shor be-maneh v'hevi shenayim be-maneh lo yatza* — we established previously that if one takes a personal vow to bring an ox worth a *maneh* and instead brings two animals together worth a *maneh*, the vow is not fulfilled. How then can the *Mishnah* here permit going from one ox to two? The *Gemara* answers: *shor zeh u'nistaiv shani* — the case of "this ox" (sanctifying the animal itself) is different. Here there is no personal obligation to be satisfied; the sanctity already rests on the animal and must simply be transferred to a valid recipient. The question of whether a specific vow has been fulfilled does not arise — only the question of where the sanctity must go. Therefore, no restriction applies to number or size.

### Rabbi No Changes

The *Gemara* then takes up *Rebbi*'s position. Why does *Rebbi* forbid? *Mishum de-have lei gadol ve-hevei katan* — because one started with something large (two oxen are always considered greater than one, regardless of individual cost) and is bringing something small (one). This mirrors the rule of personal vows, where one may not obligate oneself in something large and discharge with something small. *Ve'af al gav de-nistaiv lechatchila lo shari Rebbi* — and even though a blemish intervened, *Rebbi* does not permit it even *lechatchila*, applying the personal vow standard to cases of sanctification.

The *Gemara* then asks: *v'liflog nami be-resha* — if *Rebbi*'s principle is to pattern sanctification after personal vow rules, why does he not also object to the first case, going from one to two? *Rebbi a'kula milta palig* — *Rebbi* does forbid both cases. *Venatru rabbanan ad demaseik miltei vehadar mifalg aleihu* — he let the Rabbis finish stating their position across both cases and then registered his dissent, which applies to the entire *Mishnah*. Thus, *Rebbi oser* at the end of the *Mishnah* is to be read as rejecting both the case of one to two and two to one.

### Vow Pattern Logic

The *Gemara* elaborates on *Rebbi*'s reasoning: *lechatchila* one must treat the sanctification of an animal as subject to the same constraints as a personal vow.
