In the earlier discussion of personal vows, *Rebbi* held that even going from a small animal to a large one does not satisfy the vow — any deviation, upward or downward, is impermissible. *Rebbi* applies this same standard to cases of sanctification: the blemish does not free the owner to transfer in any direction he chooses. Even though there is no specific obligation to satisfy, *Rebbi* requires *lechatchila* that the transfer not involve any change of quantity or magnitude, patterning the sanctification rules after the personal vow framework.

### Proof Both Cases

*Teida d'katani* — to confirm that *Rebbi* forbids both directions, the *Gemara* points to the structure of the *Mishnah* itself. The final cases are: *ayil ze olah v'nistav ratza yavi b'damav keves* — a ram to a sheep; and *keves ze l'olah v'nistav ratza yavi b'damav ayil* — a sheep to a ram. *Rebbi oser* covers both. The second case explicitly involves going from small to large (sheep to ram), and *Rebbi* forbids it. *Shma mina* — we learn from this that *Rebbi* forbids any change: large to small, small to large, one to two, two to one. The *Mishnah*'s structure confirms that *Rebbi oser* at the end applies to both preceding cases, and the principle is that *lechatchila* no changes are permitted, based on the personal vow framework.

### Species Change Query

The *Gemara* now raises a new question: *ibayi l'hu — mimina l'mina mai* — they raised the question of cross-species transfer. The earlier discussion was about changes in number or size within the same species. What if one transfers the sanctity not within the same species but from one species to an entirely different one — say, from a cow to a ram? Can that be done?

### Cost Equivalence Rule

*Ta shema* — come and hear. A *baraita* states: *shor ze olah v'nistav lo yavi b'damav ayil* — if one said "this ox is an *olah*" and it developed a blemish, one may not bring a single ram in its place. This might seem to indicate a species change is forbidden, but the *baraita* immediately clarifies: *aval mavia b'damav shenei eilim* — but one may bring two rams. The concern is not the species difference per se, but rather that a single ram is of lesser value than an ox; one must not shortchange the *Beis HaMikdash* by transferring to an animal of significantly lower cost. Two rams together may be of equivalent value, and that transfer is permitted. Thus, cross-species transfer is in principle allowed by the Rabbis, as long as the final animals are roughly equivalent in cost. *Rebbi oser* — but *Rebbi* forbids, *lefi she'ein bila* — because there cannot be mixing.

### Bila Principle

What does "cannot be mixing" mean? When one brings two rams, each requires its own accompanying *minchat nesachim* — the *mincha* that accompanies an animal offering. The result is two separate *menachos*, which makes clear to all observers that something substantially different is happening from what was originally vowed. *Rashi* explains that while transferring sanctity from one animal to another is understood as a transfer of *kedusha*, producing two separate *menachos* confuses the matter and signals a departure from the original act. This is *Rebbi*'s concern with the one-to-two transfer.

The *Gemara* then challenges this reading of *Rebbi*: *ha yesh bila, shari* — if the two *menachos* could be mixed together, would *Rebbi* permit it? That seems to recast *Rebbi*'s objection as limited to the *bila* problem, as if he has no fundamental objection to going from one animal to two. But this is difficult: *v'hatnan ayil ze olah v'nistav ratza yavi b'damav keves keves ze olah v'nistav yavi b'damav ayil* — we already read in the *Mishnah* that going from ram to sheep or sheep to ram is forbidden by *Rebbi*, and those are single-animal cases involving no *bila* problem at all. *Rebbi*'s objection there has nothing to do with the mixing of *menachos*. So *bila* cannot be *Rebbi*'s only concern.

### Two Tannaic Views

The *Gemara* resolves the tension: *trei tana'ei v'aliba d'Rebbi* — there are two *tannaim* who represent different understandings of *Rebbi*'s position. Our *Mishnah* holds that according to *Rebbi*, any change — in number, size, or direction — is forbidden *lechatchila*, because sanctification is patterned entirely after personal vow rules, and just as no deviation is tolerated in a personal vow, none is tolerated here. The *baraita*, by contrast, represents a different *tanna*'s understanding of *Rebbi*, according to which *Rebbi* objects only when there is a *bila* problem — i.e., when the transfer creates two separate *menachos* that cannot be properly merged. Under this second view, going from a single animal to another single animal (even of a different species) would in principle be permissible for *Rebbi*, and the *baraita* thus records a more limited version of *Rebbi*'s restriction.

### Personal Vow Standard

The *baraita* concludes: *uv'tehorim, egel veheivi par, keves veheivi ayil, yatza* — in cases of pure, unblemished animals, meaning cases of a personal vow, if one vowed to bring a calf and brought a full-grown ox, or vowed a sheep and brought a ram, one has fulfilled the obligation. This is the Rabbis' position: *stam k'Rabbanan* — going from small to large in a personal vow satisfies the vow. This is to be contrasted with *Rebbi*, who holds that even small-to-large does not discharge a personal vow, and who carries that same stringency into the laws of sanctification as well.

To summarize the positions: according to the Rabbis, when a sanctified animal develops a blemish, the owner may transfer the sanctity across changes in number, size, and species, provided the *Beis HaMikdash* is not shortchanged in terms of value — and at least one *tannaic* reading of the Rabbis' position introduces this cost-equivalence requirement. According to *Rebbi*, there are two layers of restriction: first, his fundamental principle that in a personal vow one may not deviate in any direction, and second, his application of that principle to cases of sanctification, such that *lechatchila* no changes are permitted — neither one to two, nor two to one, nor small to large, nor large to small. Two *tannaim* interpret this second principle differently: one holds that *Rebbi* forbids all changes without exception, while the other holds that *Rebbi*'s concern is specifically the *bila* problem, i.e., the improper appearance created when a single animal is replaced by two that generate separate, unmixed *menachos*.

---

---

# Menachot 109

## Kedusha Transfer

### Sanctification Types

We begin slightly back on 108b, at the passage before the mishna: *רצה יביא בדמיהם שנים* — one may bring two animals with the redemption money. The context is the transfer of kedusha: when a person sanctifies an animal and it subsequently develops a mum, the kedusha is transferred through redemption, and the proceeds may then be applied to other animals for an olah.

Rav Menashya bar Zavid said in the name of Rav: this applies only when one says *שור זה עולה* — "this ox is an olah." In that formulation, the kedusha adheres directly to the animal. If the animal develops a mum, one redeems it and may apply the proceeds to any other suitable animal for an olah — even a different species or a different number of animals. However, if one says *שור זה עלי עולה* — "this ox is upon me as an olah" — then *הוקבע*, it is fixed. The phrasing creates a personal obligation, not merely a sanctification of the object, and one would therefore be required to bring a single ox of the same kind when transferring the kedusha.

### Alai Lehavio Read

The Gemara is not satisfied with this distinction. It asks: *ודילמא עלי להביאו קאמר* — perhaps even when one says "upon me," one means "upon me to bring this particular one." That is, the two formulations are being conflated: saying "this ox upon me as an olah" occupies a middle ground between the purely personal obligation ("I obligate myself to bring an ox") and the direct sanctification ("this ox is an olah"). But in either case, once the animal develops a mum and can no longer be brought, the obligation cannot be satisfied by that animal anyway, and thus the flexibility of transfer should apply regardless.

The Gemara therefore reformulates the teaching. Rav Menashya bar Zavid said in the name of Rav: the rule permitting flexible transfer applies whether one says *שור זה עולה* or *שור זה עלי עולה* — in both cases, since the specific animal is named and cannot be brought once blemished, the kedusha may be transferred to whatever one wishes. The process is not a direct exchange but a two-step redemption: one first redeems the blemished animal with money and then designates that money for a new animal.

### Animal vs. Value

The case where transfer is restricted is a different formulation altogether: *שור זה ודמיו עלי עולה* — "this ox and its monetary value I accept upon myself to bring as an olah." Here, by explicitly including the value of the animal in the obligation, one has undertaken to bring a korban equivalent in value to a single ox. If the animal develops a mum, the kedusha must be transferred to something of comparable value — not to two sheep or two oxen of lesser value than the original — because the obligation has been fixed both to the animal and to its value. This concludes the final mishna of the previous discussion, and we move on to a new topic.

---

## Ambiguous Designation

### Two vs. Three Animals

The next mishna introduces a related but distinct question. If someone says *אחד מכבשי הקדש* — "one of my sheep is hekdesh" — or similarly for oxen, but does not specify which animal, how do we interpret the declaration?

If the person has two animals, the mishna rules: *הגדול שבהן הקדש* — the larger one is hekdesh. The assumption is that a person who sanctifies does so generously, giving the more valuable gift. If the person has three animals, the mishna rules: *בינוני שבהן הקדש* — the middle one is hekdesh. This is initially puzzling. If we assume generous intent, why not always assume the most expensive? The Gemara will need to address this tension.

The mishna then introduces another case: if one explicitly specified which animal was meant but has forgotten — or if one's father, on his deathbed, said he had sanctified one of his animals but died before clarifying which — and the person has a number of animals in the herd, the ruling is *הגדול שבהן הקדש* — the largest is hekdesh. This appears to contradict the three-animal case and requires explanation.

The Gemara observes: *אלמא מקדיש בעין יפה מקדיש* — from the two-animal case we see that one who sanctifies does so with a generous eye, giving the most valuable. But from the three-animal case: *אלמא מקדיש בעין רעה מקדיש* — one who sanctifies does so with a stingy eye, giving only the middle one. How are these reconciled?

### Shmuel's Explanation

Shmuel resolves the tension: *חיישינן אף לבינונית דלגבי קטן עין יפה הוא* — we are also concerned for the possibility that the middle one was intended, because the middle one is generous relative to the worst. The ruling does not mean we are certain the person meant only the middle animal. Rather, when there are three animals, the statement is genuinely ambiguous — we cannot be certain whether the person meant the second or the first. What we can say is that the person meant something better than the worst, and therefore the smallest is excluded. The middle animal and the best animal are both live possibilities.

### Blemish Technique

This raises the practical question: *היכי עביד* — what does one actually do? Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said: *ממתין לו עד שיומם* — one waits until the middle animal develops a blemish. Once it is blemished, one transfers its kedusha to the larger animal: *ומחליא לקדושתיה אגדול*. One then brings the large animal as the korban.

The logic is elegant. If the original declaration referred to the middle animal, then now that it has a mum, one may transfer its kedusha to the large animal and bring the large one. If the original declaration referred to the large animal, then the transfer is superfluous but harmless — one brings the large animal in any case. Either way, the large animal is brought.

One cannot simply exchange one animal directly for another, because the Torah prohibits *תמורה* — direct substitution of a sanctified animal: *לא ימיר אותו טוב ברע ורע בטוב*, and the Gemara understands *רע בטוב* to include even a blemished animal being replaced by an unblemished one. The workaround is indirect: one redeems the blemished animal with money and then designates the money for the new animal. This is entirely permissible.

Rav Nachman said in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: this entire discussion about the middle animal applies only when one says *אחד משורי הקדש* — "one of my oxen." But if one says *שור בשורי הקדש* — "an ox from my oxen" — the ruling is simply that the largest is hekdesh, because the phrase *תורא בתוראי קאמר* — you are saying "the choice ox of my oxen," and the most prominent member of the herd is implied.

The Gemara challenges this: surely the same reasoning should apply to the case of a house? If someone says *בית בביתי אני מוכר לך* — "I am selling you a house from among my houses" — one might think this means the finest house. Yet we rule that one may point to the attic (*עלייה*) and say that is what was sold. An attic is a valid *bayit* but is less desirable than the ground floor. So the phrase "a house from my houses" does not mean the best house. Why then does "an ox from my oxen" mean the best ox?

### Mixed-Up Animals

Before resolving the house case, the Gemara raises a further challenge. A *baraita* discusses a case where an ox designated as hekdesh becomes mixed up among other oxen so that one cannot identify which one was sanctified. The ruling is: *הגדול שבהן הקדש* — the largest is given to hekdesh. This seems analogous to the case of "an ox from my oxen," since in both situations one cannot isolate which animal is meant. Yet in the mixed-up case, additional steps are required: *וכולן ימכרו לצרכי עולות ודמיהן חולין* — all the remaining animals are sold to people who intend to use them for olot, while the proceeds of those sales may be kept by the original owner as ordinary funds.

The mechanism is as follows: suppose the sanctified ox was mixed with ten others. One brings the largest as the designated korban. But perhaps the original sanctified animal was not the largest. In that case, one sells the remaining nine to someone who will bring all of them as olot, ensuring that even if the actual sanctified animal is among the nine, it will be brought as a korban. One is not transferring kedusha away from those animals — they remain hekdesh — so the proceeds from selling them can be used as ordinary funds.

The Gemara resolves the tension by distinguishing between the two cases in the scope of their rulings. When one says "an ox from my oxen," one means the best, and one simply brings that animal without concern for the others. When an animal becomes mixed up in a herd and one cannot identify it, not only does one bring the best, but one must also ensure all the others are used for korbanot. They are textually parallel only in that both involve bringing the largest — not in all the surrounding details.

### House Among Houses

Returning to the house case: the Gemara cites a *baraita* that states if one says "I am selling you a house from my houses" and one of the houses subsequently collapses, one may point to the collapsed ruin and say that was the one sold. Similarly, if one says "I am selling you a slave from my slaves" and one of the slaves dies, one may say that was the slave sold. This demonstrates that in the context of a commercial sale, the seller retains the right to designate the worst item as the one transferred, and the buyer cannot demand better.

This is counterintuitive at first: one might have thought that "a house from my houses" implies the seller is presenting himself as owning many properties and the buyer should receive a proper one. But the Gemara explains:

### Seller's Prerogative

*שאני לוקח דיד בעל השטר על התחתונה* — a purchaser is different, because the one holding the document of sale always has the weaker hand. Until the sale is completed, the property belongs to the seller. The buyer, by producing a document of sale, is making a claim against the seller's property. Any ambiguity in the terms of the contract is resolved against the claimant — against the buyer. The buyer must prove that the contract refers to the better property; failing that, the seller may designate the lesser one.

This principle — *יד בעל השטר על התחתונה* — is a significant rule in contract law. It applies particularly to real estate and slaves, where the transfer is effected by the document or by money rather than by physical possession. Because the transaction can occur without the specific item being present, ambiguities of identity arise, and they are always resolved against the party seeking to extract.

The Gemara then adds: *השתא דאתית להכי* — now that we have established this principle, we can even explain the earlier case of the attic. Even if *עלייה* means the attic — the less desirable upper floor — the seller can legitimately point to it, because *יד בעל השטר על התחתונה*.

This is fundamentally different from hekdesh. In hekdesh, there is no party trying to extract property from another. The question is how we as a legal system choose to interpret the declarant's words. There the Gemara chooses to interpret in the direction of generosity — not necessarily the maximum possible generosity, as the three-animal case shows, but at least something better than the minimum.

This points to a broader theme running through the recent mishnayot: the distinction between trying to recover a speaker's subjective intent and making a legal determination about how to interpret ambiguous language. When we know what was said but not which option was meant, we read the language with a certain generosity — not necessarily maximally, but not minimally either. When no text survives — as in the final case of the mishna, where a father declared something before dying and no one knows what he said — we ask what he probably meant, and since people giving to hekdesh probably give their best, we assume the largest animal.

---

## Beit Chonyo Vows

### Olah in Beit Chonyo

The next mishna introduces an entirely different subject. *הרי עלי עולה יקריבנה במקדש* — someone says: I accept upon myself an olah, to bring it in the Beit HaMikdash. If such a person brings it in Beit Chonyo instead, *לא יצא* — the vow is not fulfilled. Beit Chonyo was an alternate Jewish place of sacrifice established in Alexandria, Egypt. We have independent historical corroboration of its existence from sources such as Philo and Josephus. Beyond not fulfilling the vow, the person also transgresses the biblical prohibition of *שחוטי חוץ* — bringing korbanot outside the Beit HaMikdash.

### Vow Fulfillment

The more striking part of the mishna follows: *הרי עלי עולה שיקריבנה בבית חוניו* — if someone says "I accept upon myself an olah that I will bring in Beit Chonyo," what then? The mishna says: *יקריבנה במקדש* — one should bring it in the Beit HaMikdash, and: *ואם הקריבה בבית חוניו יצא* — if one brought it in Beit Chonyo, one is yotzei.

This is striking. On one reading, the person has brought a korban outside the Beit HaMikdash, which is an act for which one is *חייב כרת* — yet the mishna frames the outcome with the word *יצא*, suggesting fulfillment. At minimum, the mishna conspicuously omits mentioning the karet liability. The Gemara will become harsher, but the mishna itself speaks very softly.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *אין זה עולה* — this is not an olah at all. One cannot make a binding vow to bring a korban in Beit Chonyo; such a vow is simply invalid, and there is nothing to fulfill and nothing to transgress.

The mishna then discusses the parallel nazirite case. *הריני נזיר יגלח במקדש* — if one vows to be a nazir and stipulates that the concluding rituals will take place in the Beit HaMikdash, but then brings the hair-cutting and korbanot in Beit Chonyo, *ולא יצא* — one has not fulfilled the nezirut. And if one vows nazirut specifying that the concluding rituals will take place in Beit Chonyo, but then performs them in the Beit HaMikdash, *יצא* — the nezirut is ended. But if one actually performs the rituals in Beit Chonyo: *יצא*. This is deeply puzzling, because nezirut can only be concluded by bringing the prescribed korbanot in the legitimate Beit HaMikdash. Rabbi Shimon again says: *אין זה נזיר* — no such vow of nezirut exists at all.

### Rav Hamnuna's Read

The Gemara challenges the Chachamim's ruling that one is *yotzei* by bringing in Beit Chonyo: *המיסת קטליה* — you have killed it, meaning that a korban brought outside the Beit HaMikdash has no status as a korban whatsoever.

Rav Hamnuna answers: *נעשה כאומר הרי עלי עולה על מנת שלא אתחייב באחריותה* — we reinterpret the vow as though the person said "I accept an olah upon myself on condition that I will not be liable for replacing it." Normally, if one sanctifies an animal for a korban and the animal dies or is lost, the obligation remains and one must bring a substitute. Here, by specifying Beit Chonyo, the person is in effect saying: my obligation extends only as far as the act of bringing this animal in Beit Chonyo. Once I have done that, even though halachically it does not constitute bringing a korban, my personal obligation is discharged. We thus reinterpret the word "Beit Chonyo" to delimit the scope of the obligation rather than to identify a legitimate place of sacrifice.

### Nazirite Difference

Rava challenges Rav Hamnuna's interpretation from the nazirite case. For a nazir, it is not just a matter of personal liability — *כמה דלא מייתי קרבנותיו לא מיתכשר* — until one brings the korbanot properly, the nazir status simply does not end. It is a matter of objective halachic standing, not personal obligation. Even if one could argue that a person's liability for the sacrifices ends upon performing the rituals in Beit Chonyo, the nazirite status itself cannot be terminated by an act that has no halachic validity. The mishna's statement that one is *yotzei* in the nazirite case cannot be explained by Rav Hamnuna's approach.

### Rava's Conditional Read

Rava offers an alternative interpretation of the entire mishna: *אדם זה לדורו נתכוון* — this person genuinely intended to give a gift to God. He is not acting in bad faith; he simply believes, perhaps as a diaspora Jew living in Egypt surrounded by fellow Jews who bring sacrifices to Beit Chonyo, that this is a legitimate way to fulfill the obligation. His vow should be interpreted as follows: *אי סגי בבית חוניו טרחנא* — if it works in Beit Chonyo, I will go to the trouble of bringing it there. *טפי לא מצינא לאיצטעורי* — but I am not able to go to the effort of traveling to Jerusalem.

On this reading, the vow is implicitly conditional: I intend this to be binding only if Beit Chonyo constitutes a valid place of sacrifice. Since it does not, the vow was never binding in the first place. When the mishna says *יצא*, it does not mean "fulfilled a binding vow" — it means there was never a vow to fulfill. And when it says that if one brings it in the Beit HaMikdash one is *yotzei*, the meaning is that if one chose to go to Jerusalem, that choice reveals that one was in fact prepared to fulfill the obligation properly, and the vow is retrospectively binding and fulfilled.

The same logic applies to the nazirite case: the person wanted to afflict himself as a nazir, but only conditionally — *אי סגי בבית חוניו טרחנא* — if it works in Beit Chonyo I will take on the nezirut. If told it does not work there, he did not want to be a nazir at all. If he goes to the Beit HaMikdash, that action reveals genuine intent, and the nezirut is binding.

The difference between Rava's reading and Rabbi Shimon's is therefore subtle. Both agree that the specification of Beit Chonyo is halachically void. Rabbi Shimon holds that this voids the entire declaration absolutely: there is no vow at all, and one can never retroactively validate it. The Chachamim, as read by Rava, hold that the choice to bring it in the Beit HaMikdash reveals that the person did fundamentally intend to be obligated, and that intent can be honored.

Rav Hamnuna responds to Rava: in the nazirite case, he concedes that Rava's reading is necessary, since there is no way to dissolve a nazirite status short of saying the vow was never binding. But in the olah case, there is more room to say the animal was genuinely sanctified, and the mention of Beit Chonyo only limits personal liability rather than nullifying the entire vow — which is a stronger reading of the declarant's words.

### Rav Yochanan's Ruling

The Gemara notes that Rav Yochanan holds like Rav Hamnuna. Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rav Yochanan: if one said *הרי עלי עולה שאקריבנה בבית חוניו* and one brought it not in Beit Chonyo but in the Land of Israel outside the Beit HaMikdash — *יצא ואינו בכרת* — one is yotzei and is liable for karet. This formulation makes clear: *yotzei* because on Rav Hamnuna's reading, the animal was genuinely sanctified regardless of the Beit Chonyo specification, and the obligation is discharged whenever the animal is slaughtered — wherever that occurs. Liable for karet because the animal was genuinely sanctified and was slaughtered outside the Beit HaMikdash, constituting shichutei chutz.

A *baraita* confirms this ruling: one who vows to bring an olah in the wilderness brings it in Ever HaYarden — *יצא ואינו בכרת*. Rashi notes that the person perhaps thought the wilderness retained sanctity from the days of the Mishkan. The Gemara interprets: we do not take the specification of the wilderness or of Beit Chonyo literally. The meaningful halachic content of such a declaration is: I am sanctifying this animal but limiting my personal liability to replacing it if it is lost or dies. Any subsequent slaughter of the animal — wherever it occurs — discharges that obligation. But because the animal was genuinely sanctified, slaughtering it outside the Beit HaMikdash carries karet.

This produces a clear three-way map of positions. Rabbi Shimon holds the entire vow void. The Chachamim, on Rava's reading, hold the vow conditionally binding — binding if performed in the Beit HaMikdash, non-binding if performed in Beit Chonyo. The Chachamim, on Rav Hamnuna's and Rav Yochanan's reading, hold the vow unconditionally binding — the animal is genuinely sanctified from the moment of declaration, and Beit Chonyo merely limits personal replacement liability.

---

## Kohanim Disqualification

### Disqualification Rule

The next mishna rules: *הכהנים ששימשו בבית חוניו לא ישמשו במקדש שבירושלים* — kohanim who served in Beit Chonyo may not serve in the Beit HaMikdash in Jerusalem. *ואין צריך לומר לדבר אחר* — it goes without saying that kohanim who served in avodah zarah are excluded entirely. A pasuk from Yechezkel supports this: *אך לא יעלו כהני הבמות אל מזבח ה' בירושלים* — the kohanim of the *bamot* may not ascend to the altar of Hashem in Jerusalem, but *כי אם אכלו מצות בתוך אחיהם* — they may eat *matzot* among their brothers. The Gemara explains: *הרי אלו כבעלי מומים חולקין ואוכלין ולא מקריבין* — they are like kohanim with physical blemishes: they receive a portion of the sacrificial foods but may not perform the service. Their disqualification is a spiritual *mum*, a religious blemish — not complete exclusion, but permanent removal from active service.

The implicit point of the mishna's formulation — *it goes without saying* regarding avodah zarah — is that Beit Chonyo is not itself a house of avodah zarah. The *baraita* later confirms: *תניא כמאן דאמר בית חוניו לאו עבודה זרה היא* — we taught in accordance with the opinion that Beit Chonyo was not avodah zarah.

### Shechita Exception

Rav Yehuda rules: a kohen who slaughtered an animal for avodah zarah and subsequently did teshuvah — *קרבנו ריח ניחוח* — his subsequent korban in the Beit HaMikdash is accepted. The act of shechita for avodah zarah does not disqualify him. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi derives the disqualification of kohanim who actually served avodah zarah from a pasuk in Yechezkel: *יען אשר ישרתו אותם לפני גלוליהם* — because they performed service before their abominations — *ולא יגשו אלי לכהן לי* — they may not draw near to Me to serve as priests.

The key word is *ישרתו* — they performed *sheirus*, priestly service. Shechita, however, is *לאו שירות* — it is not categorized as a priestly service, since a non-kohen may also serve as a *shochet*. Therefore, although slaughtering for avodah zarah is a grave sin, it does not besmirch one's kehuna in the specific way that performing priestly service for avodah zarah does. After teshuvah, such a kohen may resume service.

### Zrika Debate

The Gemara now turns to a more complex case: a kohen who performed *zrika* — the sprinkling of blood — for avodah zarah, but did so *bishogeg*, unintentionally. Rav Nachman rules: *קרבנו ריח ניחוח* — his korban is subsequently accepted; he is not disqualified. Rav Sheshet rules: *אין קרבנו ריח ניחוח* — he is disqualified.

Rav Sheshet's source: the pasuk reads *והיו לבית ישראל למכשול עון* — they shall be a stumbling block of sin. *מכשול* refers to an unintentional act (*shogeg*) and *עון* to a willful one (*meizid*). Since both are listed, even a shogeg in zrika disqualifies. Rav Nachman reads *מכשול דעון* as a single phrase — the stumbling that is of a willful kind — meaning only meizid disqualifies.

Rav Nachman adduces support from a *baraita*: *כהן שעבד עבודת כוכבים בשוגג — קרבנו ריח ניחוח* — a kohen who worshipped avodah zarah bishogeg, his korban is subsequently accepted. The baraita adds that he must have done teshuvah. Now: if the case were shogeg, why would teshuvah be needed to restore his status? A shogeg who was never invalidated obviously does not require teshuvah to be re-accepted. Therefore the baraita must be discussing meizid — and yet it says that after teshuvah he is accepted. And if the case were zrika bemeizid — the most severe form — teshuvah would be irrelevant, since he has performed a priestly act in service of avodah zarah and is irrevocably excluded. Therefore the case must be shechita bemeizid: willful slaughter for avodah zarah, after which teshuvah restores full status.

### Rav Nechman Lenient

Rav Nachman's position can now be stated precisely: shechita for avodah zarah — even bemeizid — never invalidates, and teshuvah is required only as a matter of general repentance, not to restore kehuna status. Zrika for avodah zarah bishogeg also does not invalidate. Only zrika bemeizid irrevocably disqualifies.

### Rav Sheshet Strict

Rav Sheshet interprets the baraita differently. He reads the case as shechita bishogeg. Why does teshuvah matter? The baraita is saying: *אם שב מעיקרו* — if he remained in a state of teshuvah from the outset, meaning if his act was genuinely inadvertent throughout, then *קרבנו ריח ניחוח* — he is accepted. If not, *אין קרבנו ריח ניחוח* — he is not. On this reading, even shechita bishogeg can be invalidating unless one maintained genuinely inadvertent intent. Rav Sheshet's consistent position: shechita bemeizid invalidates, not because it is a priestly act, but because one who willfully serves avodah zarah — *נעשה משרת לעבודת כוכבים* — has become identified as a servant of idolatry, and that identity is incompatible with kehuna service regardless of the particular act.

The Gemara notes: *ואזדו לטעמייהו* — they go according to their own reasoning consistently. Rav Nachman says: shechita bemeizid for avodah zarah — *קרבנו ריח ניחוח*, because one did not perform a priestly act. Rav Sheshet says: *אין קרבנו ריח ניחוח*, because one has become a willing servant of avodah zarah.

### Other Avodah Zarah Acts

The Gemara extends the dispute to further cases. If a kohen bowed down — *השתחוה לעבודת כוכבים* — Rav Nachman says *קרבנו ריח ניחוח*: bowing is not a priestly act in the Beit HaMikdash context, and therefore does not besmirch the kehuna. Rav Sheshet says *אין קרבנו ריח ניחוח*: any willful service of avodah zarah disqualifies. If a kohen merely accepted an idol as his deity — *הודה לעבודת כוכבים* — without performing any act of worship, Rav Nachman still says *קרבנו ריח ניחוח* and Rav Sheshet still says *אין קרבנו ריח ניחוח*.

The Gemara explains why all three cases must be stated: had only the zrika case been taught, one might have thought Rav Sheshet is strict only there because it is a genuine priestly act, but would be lenient by shechita. The shechita case teaches that he is strict even there. Had only the shechita case been taught, one might have thought that at least shechita involves an act performed in the Temple context — but hishtachava, which is not a Temple-related act at all, Rav Sheshet might accept. The hishtachava case teaches otherwise. Had only hishtachava been taught, one might have thought that verbal acceptance — *hoda'ah*, which is only words — would not suffice to disqualify. Hence all cases must be stated.

On the other side, Rav Nachman's consistent leniency is clear: only the narrowly defined misuse of priestly service — zrika bemeizid — disqualifies. Every other act, however serious a personal sin, does not carry over into the domain of kehuna invalidation.

The Gemara then notes a discussion in Tosafot relevant to contemporary application. Tosafot cites a work called Sefer HaZahir — a Geonic text, not the Zohar — which holds that a kohen who apostatized and returned should not perform nesi'at kapayim, drawing an analogy from these cases. Rashi, in a responsum, disagrees sharply. Rashi argues that the mishna describes even kohanim who served in Beit Chonyo — which was not avodah zarah — as being like *ba'alei mumim*. A ba'al mum, however, does perform nesi'at kapayim. Moreover, the Gemara's exclusion pertains to service in the Beit HaMikdash; birkat kohanim outside the Temple is a separate matter. There is also a related discussion in Sotah about a kohen who killed someone, where the consideration of *takanas hashavim* — the enactment for penitents — plays a role: to what degree does permanently barring a returnee from his former status push people away rather than bringing them close?

---

## Chonyo-Shimei Story

### Shimon's Prophecy

The Gemara establishes from the mishna's formulation that Beit Chonyo was not regarded as a house of avodah zarah. A *baraita* then begins the narrative of how it came to be founded. In the year that Shimon HaTzaddik died, he emerged from the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur and said to those around him: this year, he himself would die. They asked how he knew. He told them: every Yom Kippur, when I entered the Kodesh HaKodashim, I would encounter an elderly man dressed entirely in white, wrapped in white, who would enter and depart with me. This year I saw an elderly man dressed entirely in black, wrapped in black, who entered with me but did not come out with me — a sign of mourning and departure.

After Sukkot he became ill, lingered seven days, and died. Following his death, his fellow kohanim ceased to pronounce the *shem haMeforash* — the explicit divine name — in birkat kohanim, since the level of piety required to utter that name safely was no longer present among them.

### The Garb Trick

At the moment of his death, Shimon said: *חוניו בני ישמש תחתי* — my son Chonyo shall serve in my place as Kohen Gadol. Shimei, Chonyo's brother, was jealous — *שהיה גדול ממנו שתי שנים ומחצה* — because Shimei was two and a half years older and had been passed over. He approached his younger brother and said: come, let me teach you the order of the Temple service. He dressed Chonyo in a cloak (*unkeili*) and girded him with a belt (*tziltzul*) — both garments associated with women — and stationed him at the altar. He then turned to the other kohanim and said: look at what this man vowed and fulfilled for his beloved wife — he said that on the day he would serve as Kohen Gadol he would wear her robe and her belt.

Tosafot notes a difficulty: if Chonyo had been designated as Kohen Gadol, how could he have been duped into thinking this was a normal inauguration ceremony? Tosafot offers two answers. First, he may have been chosen for his exceptional piety rather than his knowledge of Temple procedure, so he was genuinely unfamiliar with the inauguration rites. Second, perhaps he had never witnessed the inauguration of a Kohen Gadol and believed this was the unusual ceremony involved.

### Two Versions

This is Rabbi Meir's version. The fellow kohanim, outraged at the perceived mockery of the kehuna, sought to kill Chonyo. He fled; they pursued him. He went to Alexandria of Egypt. *ובנה שם מזבח והעלה עליו לשם עבודת כוכבים* — and he built an altar there and offered upon it for the sake of avodah zarah. The rabbis, hearing of this, commented: one who was never given the office, and was so consumed by jealousy that it led to this, how much more so one who actually holds a position of power — *המבקש לירד לה על אחת כמה וכמה* — will go to terrible lengths to seize or retain it.

Rabbi Yehuda offers a completely different version. In his account, it was Chonyo who declined the appointment — *לא קיבל עליו חוניו* — out of deference to his older brother Shimei, saying Shimei was the elder and should serve. Shimei became the Kohen Gadol. Nevertheless, Chonyo was jealous of the brother whose advancement he had himself enabled. He approached Shimei and said: come, let me teach you the inauguration procedure. He dressed Shimei in the same female garb, stationed him at the altar, and announced to the assembled kohanim: look at what this man vowed and fulfilled for his beloved wife — on the day he would serve as Kohen Gadol he would wear her robe and her belt.

The other kohanim now wanted to kill Shimei. Shimei explained what had actually happened and turned the anger back toward Chonyo. They then sought to kill Chonyo. *כל הרואה אותו אומר זהו זהו* — everyone who saw him called out that he was the one. He fled to the king's palace, then to Alexandria.

### Alexandria Altar

According to Rabbi Yehuda's version: *ובנה שם מזבח והעלה עליו לשם שמים* — and he built an altar and offered upon it for the sake of Heaven. He was pursuing power through devious means, but his original motivation had been piety — he initially declined the appointment — and he was now fleeing his own deviousness rather than fleeing a rejection of himself. The story reads differently when the founder of Beit Chonyo was someone who set it up as a genuine house of worship, even if driven to Egypt by unworthy jealousy.

Rabbi Yehuda provides a scriptural basis for the founding of an altar in Egypt: *ביום ההוא יהיה מזבח לה' בתוך ארץ מצרים* — on that day there shall be an altar to Hashem in the midst of the land of Egypt; *ומצבה אצל גבולה לה'* — and a pillar at its border to Hashem (Yeshaya 19:19).

When the rabbis heard of it, they commented: *ומה זה שברח ממנה כך* — this person who ran away from the position of greatness, who did not seek it — and yet jealousy still led him to such lengths. *המבקש לירד לה על אחת כמה וכמה* — how much more so will one who actively pursues authority go to improper lengths to acquire or defend it.

### Power Danger Lesson

A *baraita* records Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachiah's personal statement: *בתחילה כל אומר עלי לה אני כופתו ונותנו לפני אריה* — originally, if anyone had told me to take a position of authority, I would have bound him and thrown him before a lion. He regarded the pursuit of office as a dangerous thing to be avoided at all costs.

### Shaul Parallel

*עתה כל האומר לי לירד ממנה אני מטיל עליו קומקום של חמים* — now, having taken such a position, anyone who tells me to relinquish it, I would throw a flask of hot water upon him. The lesson: *שהרי שאול ברח ממנה* — just as Shaul fled from kingship — as we read in this week's haftarah — *ועלה ביקש להרוג את דוד* — and once he was in the position, he sought to kill David to protect it. The desire for status and the fear of losing it can transform even a person of admirable initial humility.

### Five Cities Alternative

Mar Kashisha son of Rav Chisda asked Abaye: according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that Chonyo built his altar for avodah zarah — what does he do with the verse that Rabbi Yehuda uses to justify it (*ביום ההוא יהיה מזבח לה' בתוך ארץ מצרים*)? A *baraita* answers: after the fall of Sancherib, Chizkiya went out and found royal princes seated in golden wagons. He seized the opportunity to spread recognition of God and made them swear not to worship avodah zarah. This is referenced in the verse: *ביום ההוא יהיו חמש ערים בארץ מצרים מדברות שפת כנען ונשבעות לה' צבאות* — on that day there shall be five cities in Egypt speaking the language of Canaan — Hebrew — and swearing allegiance to Hashem of Hosts. Those princes and their followers went to Alexandria and built an altar and offered upon it *לשם שמים* — for the sake of Heaven.

Thus, according to Rabbi Meir, the verse from Yeshaya refers not to Beit Chonyo but to the altar built in Alexandria by those whom Chizkiya had brought to acknowledge God, centuries before Chonyo's time. For Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that Beit Chonyo was built *leshem shamayim*, the same verse applies to both.

---

---

# Menachot 110

## Beit Chonyo

### House of Onias

Daf 110 brings us to the conclusion of the *perek* and the conclusion of Menachot as a whole. We are in the midst of a discussion of *Beit Chonyo* — the house, the temple, of Onias — which was built in Egypt. According to the Gemara it was in Alexandria, though historically it was located in a different part of the Nile Delta known as the land of Onias. It was founded by a son or descendant of Shimon HaTzadik, and the central question is whether it constituted a house of *avodah zarah* or a house of legitimate worship of God. Rabbi Meir held it was *avodah zarah*. Rabbi Yehuda held it was genuine worship of God, though still forbidden as *shechutei chutz* — bringing *korbanot* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* — yet far better than *avodah zarah*. Rabbi Yehuda adduced a verse from Yeshayahu in support: *ba'yom hahu yiheyeh mizbe'ach l'Hashem b'toch eretz Mitzrayim u'matzeva etzel gevulah l'Hashem* — on that day there will be an altar to God in the midst of the land of Egypt and a pillar at its border for God. This appears to prophesy an altar to God in Egypt, lending support to the view that *Beit Chonyo* was legitimate worship.

### Isaiah 19 Reading

The Gemara then asks: what does Rabbi Meir do with that verse? He reads that verse together with the verse immediately preceding it — Yeshayahu 19:18 — not as referring to *Beit Chonyo* at all, but as referring to events in the time of Chizkiyahu. When the Assyrian forces of Sancheriv were defeated, the foreign princes in his camp were made to swear that they would not worship *avodah zarah*, and when they subsequently went to Egypt, they actually worshipped God.

### Alexandria Altar

We pick up at the top of daf 110 with the conclusion of that point:

> *Halchu l'Alexandria shel Mitzrayim u'vanu mizbe'ach v'he'elu alav l'shem shamayim* — they went to Alexandria of Egypt and built an altar and offered upon it *l'shem shamayim*. As it is written: *ba'yom hahu yiheyeh mizbe'ach l'Hashem b'toch eretz Mitzrayim*.

So according to Rabbi Meir, the verse refers not to *Beit Chonyo* but to an entirely different historical episode. The Gemara then turns to the phrase earlier in that verse — *Ir HaHeres ye'amer l'achat mehen* — the city of destruction will be said about one of them. The full verse (Yeshayahu 19:18) reads: *ba'yom hahu yiheyu chamesh arim b'eretz Mitzrayim medabrot sfat Kna'an* — on that day five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan, meaning Hebrew — *v'nishba'ot l'Hashem Tzeva'ot Ir HaHeres ye'amer l'achat mehen* — and swear by the Lord of Hosts; the city of *heres* will be said of one of them.

What does *Ir HaHeres* — the city of destruction — mean here? *K'targum Rav Yosef* — as Rav Yosef translates it: *Kartei d'Beit Shemesh d'atid l'michrav it'amar dehi chada mi'hon* — the city of *Beit Shemesh* that will in the end be destroyed, it will be said that it was one of them. The reference appears to be not to the *Beit Shemesh* in the Land of Israel but to some other city bearing that name — the House of the Sun — since the context is the land of Egypt. The word *heres* appears to mean "sun," yielding the reading "City of the Sun," which will ultimately be destroyed and called the City of Destruction.

The Gemara then asks: *u'mimai d'Ir HaHeres lishana d'shimsha hu?* — how do we know that *heres* means sun? *De'chtiv h'omer l'cheres v'lo yizrach* — as it is written in Iyov, God commands the *cheres* and it does not shine forth. In context, *cheres* clearly refers to the sun. It may be noted that in the Septuagint, the Greek translation renders *Ir HaHeres* as something like "the City of Splendor."

---

## Exiles & Nations

### Sons & Daughters

Since the discussion has been touching on Jews in Egypt and their worship of God in exile, the Gemara now proceeds to quote verses relating to the Jewish people in dispersion. The verse is: *Habii vanai merachok u'venotai miketze ha'aretz* — bring My sons from afar and My daughters from the ends of the earth (Yeshayahu 43:6). Why the distinction between sons and daughters? *Amar Rav Huna elu galuyot she'be'Vavel* — these are the exiles in Babylonia — *she'daatam meyushevet aleihem* — whose minds are settled upon them. *U'venotai miketze ha'aretz elu galuyot she'she'ar aratzot she'ein daatam meyushevet aleihem* — "My daughters from the ends of the earth" refers to the exiles in all other lands, whose minds are not settled, who do not have tranquility or peace of mind. Rashi explains the underlying assumption: those in Babylonia, where the primary Torah communities were concentrated, are like sons whose minds are settled; those in the other lands of exile are like daughters whose minds are less settled.

### Tyre-Carthage

The Gemara continues with a further teaching. *Amar Rabbi Abba bar Rav Yitzchak amar Rav Chisda, ve'amri lah amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav* — with variant traditions as to who transmitted this in whose name. The teaching is: *mitzor vead Kartigigi makirin Yisrael ve'et avihem she'bashamayim* — from Tyre to Carthage, they recognize the Jewish people and they recognize their Father in Heaven. The implication is that because the non-Jewish nations from Tyre to Carthage have encountered the Jewish people, they have come to understand the idea of a single God. Rashi explains *va'avihem she'bashamayim* as meaning that they affirm belief in God and are not given over to *avodah zarah* — at minimum they are *makirim*, they recognize what the Jewish people represent and the faith they embody.

*U'Mitzor klapei ma'arav u'miKartigigi klapei mizrach ein makirim et Yisrael ve'lo et avihem she'bashamayim* — but from Tyre toward the west, and from Carthage toward the east, they do not recognize the Jewish people and do not recognize their Father in Heaven. The implied reason is that the Jewish people were not exiled into those regions, and therefore those nations have no knowledge of the Jewish people or of the idea of a single God. One must acknowledge, however, that the geographic directions as stated are difficult to follow: Carthage lies considerably to the west of the Land of Israel along the Mediterranean, so one would expect the formulation to be reversed — from Carthage to the east and from Tyre to the west lies the territory between them where they *do* recognize Israel. An examination of all available manuscripts yields no variant reading that resolves this, and the directions remain puzzling.

### Geographic Challenge

*Eitiveih Rav Shimi bar Chiya le'Rav* — Rav Shimi bar Chiya challenges Rav's position with the following verse: *mimizrach shemesh vead mevo'o gadol shemi ba'goyim, u'vechol makom muktar mugash lishmi u'mincha tehorah* — from the rising of the sun to its setting, My name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is being offered and brought to My name, and a pure *mincha* (Malachi 1:11). This seems to say that everywhere in the world the nations recognize God — not merely between Tyre and Carthage.

*Amar lei* — Rav replied to him: is that a question worthy of you? What the verse means is *d'karai lei Elaha d'Alahaya* — they call God the God of Gods. They acknowledge the existence of a supreme divine power even while worshipping other gods beneath it. But this prompts a further difficulty: the earlier statement was not about whether the nations actually worship God rather than *avodah zarah*, but about whether they are *makirim* — whether they recognize Israel's Father in Heaven. If they call God "the God of Gods," why does that not count as *makirin avihem she'bashamayim*?

The Maharsha explains that part of truly recognizing God through the lens of the Jewish people is not merely acknowledging an all-powerful supreme being but recognizing God's *hashgacha pratis* — His direct involvement in history and in the lives of individuals. This is perhaps evoked by the very phrase *avihem she'bashamayim* — Father, one who cares. The nations beyond the boundary may acknowledge a supreme God in the abstract while worshipping lesser gods underneath, but they do not know the God of the Jewish experience — the personal, caring Father. That is the distinction Rav is drawing.

---

## Torah = Korban

### Learning = Incense

The Gemara now returns to the end of the verse from Malachi: *u'vechol makom muktar mugash lishmi* — and in every place incense is offered to My name. *U'vechol makom salka daitach?* — in every place? Can it really mean that incense is offered to God everywhere in the world? Surely they are not worshipping God everywhere, and even if we are speaking of Jews, *korbanot* cannot be brought outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. *Amar Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yochanan* — these are *talmidei chachamim ha'oskim baTorah b'chol makom* — Torah scholars who engage in Torah in every place. *Ma'aleh ani aleihem k'ilu maktirim u'magishim lishmi* — I account it to them as though they are burning incense and offering up to Me.

This is a striking statement, and one that is entirely apt at the conclusion of Menachot. We have just completed the two great *masechtot* on *korbanot* — Zevachim and Menachot — and we no longer have *korbanot*. The answer given here is that the learning of Torah in any place counts as the offering of *korbanot*. And indeed, the Torah's mode of service is in certain respects more expansive: it can take place anywhere, not only in the *Beit HaMikdash*.

The Gemara then asks what *u'mincha tehorah* — and a pure *mincha* — means in this context. *Zeh ha'lomed Torah b'taharah* — this is one who learns Torah in purity. How does one achieve this purity? *Nosei isha v'achar kach lomed Torah* — one first marries and then learns Torah, so that one is not distracted by wayward thoughts and is able to learn with full concentration and purity of mind.

### Night Learning

The Gemara continues on the theme of Torah as equivalent to temple service. The verse reads: *Hinei barchu et Hashem kol avdei Hashem ha'omdim b'veit Hashem baleilot* — behold, bless God, all servants of God who stand in the house of God at night (Tehillim 134:1). But *baleilot* — at night? *Korbanot* are not performed at night. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan* — these are the Torah sages *ha'oskim baTorah ba'laila* — who engage in Torah at night. *Ma'aleh aleihem ha'katuv k'ilu oskim ba'avodah* — the verse accounts it to them as though they are engaging in the temple service. Here again the transcendence of limitation is emphasized: Torah learning at night — something impossible for *korbanot* — is reckoned as equivalent to the temple service, and it can take place in any location.

### Supernal Altar

The Gemara then brings the verse from Divrei HaYamim in which Shlomo declares: *Hineni boneh bayit l'shem Hashem Elokai l'hakdish lo l'haktir l'fanav ketoret samim u'ma'arechet tamid v'olot la'boker v'la'erev l'shabbatot v'lchodashim u'lmo'adei Hashem Elokeinu l'olam zot al Yisrael* — I am building a house for the name of the Lord my God, to sanctify it, to burn incense before Him, and the continual arrangement, and burnt offerings morning and evening, on Sabbaths and new moons and appointed times of the Lord our God — this is forever upon Israel. But is it truly forever? There is no *Beit HaMikdash* now. *Amar Rav Gidel amar Rav: zeh mizbe'ach banui u'Michael sar ha'gadol omeid u'makriv alav korban* — this refers to an altar that is built in heaven, where the great angel Michael stands and offers *korbanot* upon it. Even without the physical *Beit HaMikdash*, the supernal *Beit HaMikdash* endures in heaven, and the service continues there, perpetually maintained. This is a powerful image about the metaphysical necessity of *korbanot* — somehow the spiritual health of the world depends upon this service, and even when the earthly Temple is destroyed, it continues above.

### Laws Rebuild Temple

*Rabbi Yochanan amar: elu talmidei chachamim oskim b'hilchot avodah* — these are Torah scholars who engage in the laws of the temple service. *Ma'aleh alav ha'katuv k'ilu nivneh mikdash be'yameihem* — the verse accounts it to them as though the *Beit HaMikdash* were built in their days. This is the meaning of *l'olam*: through the study of the laws of the *avodah*, the Torah scholar in effect rebuilds the Temple. This teaching reinforces and extends the earlier pattern: Torah study transcends all limitations — of place, of time, of the absence of the *Beit HaMikdash* itself.

---

## Lev 7:37 Derash

### No Need Sacrifices

*Amar Reish Lakish: mai d'chtiv — Zot HaTorah l'olah la'minchah v'lachatat v'la'asham* — this is the Torah of the *olah*, of the *mincha*, of the *chatat*, and of the *asham* (Vayikra 7:37). The verse concludes the section in *Tzav* that lays out the basic parameters of the *korbanot*. Reish Lakish reads it to teach: *kol ha'osek baTorah k'ilu hikriv olah mincha chatat va'asham* — whoever engages in Torah it is as though he offered an *olah*, a *mincha*, a *chatat*, and an *asham*.

*Ve'amar Rava* — but Rava offers a different reading. The verse, he observes, does not say *torat olah* or *torat mincha* — the Torah of the *olah*, the Torah of the *mincha* — as one might expect. It says *l'olah la'mincha* — for the *olah*, for the *mincha*. *Ela amar Rava: kol ha'osek baTorah eino tzarich lo olah v'lo mincha v'lo chatat v'lo asham* — whoever engages in Torah does not need an *olah*, does not need a *mincha*, does not need a *chatat*, does not need an *asham*.

How does this differ from what Reish Lakish said? Both seem to be saying that Torah study is equivalent to offering sacrifices. The grammatical point Rava is making is significant: the prefix *la-* in Mishnaic Hebrew and in related Semitic usage can function as a negative — *la* meaning "not." So Rava reads the verse as: this is the Torah — *la-olah*, you do not need an *olah* — *la-mincha*, you do not need a *mincha*. The statement is substantively different, not merely stylistically so. The earlier teachings — including the image of Michael offering *korbanot* in heaven — frame *korbanot* as the ideal, the model, with Torah study being credited *as if* one performed them. Rava is saying something else entirely: Torah and *korbanot* are different and independent modes of serving God. If you learn Torah, *korbanot* become simply unnecessary; Torah is not a substitute for them, it is a parallel — perhaps superior — track. This is a genuinely different theological claim.

### All Four Sacrifices

*Amar Rabbi Yitzchak: mai d'chtiv — Zot torat ha'chatat v'zot torat ha'asham* — this is the Torah of the *chatat* and this is the Torah of the *asham* (Vayikra 7:37, read in *semichut* with the specific offerings). This teaches: *kol ha'osek b'torat chatat k'ilu hikriv chatat, v'kol ha'osek b'torat asham k'ilu hikriv asham* — whoever engages in the laws of the *chatat* it is as though he offered a *chatat*, and whoever engages in the laws of the *asham* it is as though he offered an *asham*.

The Maharsha notes a subtle distinction between Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching and those preceding it. Reish Lakish was saying that learning Torah generally — learning any topic — is reckoned as having offered *korbanot*; the Torah as a whole is a mode of serving God analogous to the *avodah*. Rabbi Yitzchak is saying something more precise: the Torah study of a specific *korban* counts as that specific *korban* — not that general Torah learning is equivalent to sacrifices generically, but that learning the laws of a *chatat* counts specifically as a *chatat*, and learning the laws of an *asham* counts specifically as an *asham*. This is a deeply embedded idea in traditional practice. It underlies the custom of reciting passages describing the *korbanot* before *Pesukei d'Zimra*, with a *yehi ratzon* prayer that the recitation of these verses and the learning of these laws should count as though one actually offered those sacrifices.

### Tosafot & Prayer

At this point it is worth examining the Tosafot on *Michael sar gadol*, which opens a striking window onto the liturgy. Tosafot notes that there are different *midrashim* regarding what Michael is actually offering on the supernal altar. One view holds that it is *nishmotehem shel tzaddikim* — the souls of the righteous — that are being offered, as though the *tzaddikim*, upon their death, have their souls brought as an offering before God. This is a vivid and to some degree arresting image, one that becomes all the more poignant when considered in the context of Jewish martyrdom throughout history. A second view, evidently more comfortable with the metaphorical register, says *kvasim shel esh* — lambs of fire — keeping the image entirely in the heavenly domain: a heavenly *mizbe'ach*, a heavenly angel, a heavenly sacrifice, preserving the formal structure of the *avodah* without personalizing it in the same way.

Tosafot then connects this directly to the *Shmoneh Esrei*: *v'hainu d'amrinan b'Shmoneh Esrei b'avodah, v'ishei Yisrael u'tefilatam meherah b'ahavah tekabel b'ratzon* — this is why we say in the *Retzei* blessing, "and the fire offerings of Israel, accept their prayer with love and favor." What are the *ishei Yisrael*, the fire offerings of Israel, that we invoke each day in *davening*? According to this reading, it is the ongoing heavenly *avodah* that Michael continues to perform. We are asking that those offerings — the celestial service that continues even in the absence of the earthly Temple — be accepted with love.

Tosafot then records a dissenting view: *v'yesh omrim d'kai ad'le'il* — some say that *v'ishei Yisrael* does not modify *u'tefilatam tekabel b'ratzon* but rather attaches to the preceding sentence — *hashev et ha'avodah lidvir beitecha v'ishei Yisrael* — restore the service to Your holy sanctuary and the fire offerings of Israel. In this reading, we are not asserting that fire offerings are currently taking place and asking God to accept them; rather, we are asking God to restore them. Some even read *ishei* here as *anshei* — restore the Jewish people to Your sanctuary. The precise meaning of this phrase that we recite every single day remains genuinely open.

This moment is an opportunity to reflect on something quite striking in the broader picture. The entire discussion in Berachot establishes that *tefillah* is *keneged* the *korbanot* — the three daily prayers correspond to the daily *tamid* offerings and to *Musaf*. Yet remarkably, nowhere in the *Shmoneh Esrei* is the word *korban* ever explicitly mentioned. Even in the *Retzei* blessing — where the word *ratzeh*, with its unmistakable connotations of sacrificial acceptance, points entirely toward *korbanot* — no sacrifice is named. The emphasis falls on *tefilatam tekabel be'ratzon*, accept our prayer, and *ishei Yisrael* remains, as we have seen, semantically indeterminate. This silence appears deliberate. If *tefillah* were framed explicitly as a substitute for *korbanot*, it would perpetually signal its own inadequacy — we are only doing this because we cannot do that. Better to say, in the spirit of Rava, that Torah and prayer are independent paths of *avodat Hashem*. A related statement appears in the name of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai — that *tefillah* is not merely *keneged* *korbanot* but is their equivalent, perhaps even superior. And this idea is foreshadowed in the very verse with which we open *Shmoneh Esrei*: immediately following *Hashem sefatai tiftach u'fi yagid tehilatecha* in Tehillim, the next verse reads *ki lo tachpotz zevach ve'ettenah olah lo tirtzeh — zivchei Elokim ruach nedava, lev nishbar ve'nidkeh Elokim lo tivzeh* — what God desires is the generous spirit; a broken and contrite heart God will not despise.

---

## Sacrifice Theology

### Heart to Heaven

The final *mishnah* of Menachot draws together the threads of the entire *perek* in a theologically resonant way. The *mishnah* observes that the Torah uses the same phrase — *ishei rei'ach nicho'ach* — a fire offering of pleasing scent — for the *olat behemah*, the animal burnt offering; for the *olat of*, the bird burnt offering; and for the *mincha*, the grain offering. This is deliberate: *lomar lecha echad ha'marbeh ve'echad ha'mam'it u'vilvad she'yechaven libo lashamayim* — to tell you that whether one brings much or little, what matters is that one directs one's heart to Heaven. The quantity is irrelevant; the intention is everything.

### Sleep Reward

In the Gemara, Rabbi Zeira asks: *mah kra* — what verse supports this principle beyond the parallel phrasing that the *mishnah* itself relies upon? He cites a verse from Kohelet: *metuka shenat ha'oved im me'at ve'im harbeh* — sweet is the sleep of the worker whether much or little. Applied to our context: the one who brings a *korban* and goes home to sleep — his sleep is just as sweet and his reward just as full whether he brought much or little.

### God Sees Intent

*Rav Adda bar Ahava amar me'hacha* — Rav Adda bar Ahava supports the principle from a different verse, from Mishlei: *birbot ha'tova rabu ochleha, u'mah kishron la'ba'aleha ki im re'ot einav* — with the increase of goodness those who eat it increase, but what benefit is it to the master except the sight of his eyes? More sacrifices means more *kohanim* eating from them, which is fine. But as far as God, the *ba'al* in the ultimate sense, is concerned, it is *ki im re'ot einav* — only what His eyes see, meaning the intent behind the offering, that matters.

### Divine Names

*Tanya amar Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai: bo re'eh mah katuv be'parshat korbanot she'lo ne'emar bahen lo El v'lo Elokim ella Hashem* — come and see what is written in the portion of the *korbanot*: throughout the relevant passage of Vayikra, the names *El* and *Elokim* do not appear; only the divine name *Yud Kay Vav Kay* is used. The purpose is *she'lo liten pitchon peh laba'alim lachlok* — so that no adversary should have an opening to argue that the *korbanot* were being brought to pagan deities, since both *El* and *Elokim* could in principle refer to other powers. By using only the ineffable divine Name, the Torah forecloses any such misreading.

### Psalm 50 Meaning

The *baraita* continues: *ne'emar b'shor ha'gas ishei rei'ach nicho'ach, u'v'of ha'dak ishei rei'ach nicho'ach, u'va'mincha ishei rei'ach nicho'ach* — the formula *ishei rei'ach nicho'ach* is used for the large ox, for the small bird, and for the *mincha* — reiterating the principle of *echad ha'marbeh ve'echad ha'mam'it u'vilvad she'yechaven libo lashamayim*.

But now the *baraita* confronts a deeper theological question. *Ve'shema tomar la'achilah hu tzarich* — perhaps one might think that God actually needs the sacrifices to consume, that this is *lechem Elokav*, the bread of God, that He smells the *ishei rei'ach nicho'ach* and requires it. *Talmud lomar: im erva lo omar lach, ki li tevel u'melo'ah* — therefore the verse states: were I ever hungry I would not tell you, for the world and all its fullness is Mine (Tehillim 50:12). God self-evidently does not need to be fed, and even if He did, you could not provide it. *Ki li kol chaito ya'ar behemot b'harerei alef, yadati kol of harim ve'ziz sadai imadi* — for Mine is every animal of the forest, the cattle on a thousand mountains; I know every bird of the mountains, and the creatures of the field are with Me. *Ha'ochal basar abirim ve'dam atudim eshteh* — do I eat the flesh of mighty beasts and drink the blood of goats? The rejection of the pagan model — in which the gods are hungry and the sacrifices feed them — could not be more explicit.

*Lo amarti aleichem zivchu kedei she'tomar e'eseh retzono ve'ya'aseh retzoni* — I did not say to you to bring sacrifices so that you can reason: I have done God's will, now God will fulfill mine. This is not the exchange economy of paganism. *Lo lirtzoni atem zovchim ella lirtzonchem atem zovchim* — you are not sacrificing for My sake but for your own sake. By performing *mitzvot*, you are the beneficiary. God has given you these commandments for your benefit, not His. The verse states *lirtzonchem tizbachu* — for your sake you shall sacrifice.

This teaching invites comparison with the Rambam's famous position, according to which sacrifices represent a divine concession to the human psychological need to worship in a manner familiar from the surrounding pagan culture. The Rambam holds that the Torah redirected this pre-existing form of worship toward the service of God as a means of weaning Israel away from idolatry. One may frame the point more broadly: the verse is saying that *I* do not need your *korbanot* — this is for your sake, not Mine. It is a *mitzvah* given for your benefit. This is at minimum what the verse teaches, and it is not a long step from there to the Rambam's reading.

### Intent Requirement

The final *halacha* of the tractate returns from these theological reflections to a point of law. *Davar acher: lirtzonchem tizbachu, lirtzonchem zivchu* — reading the verse as: for your will, your desire, you shall sacrifice. *Lida'atchem zivchu* — with your intentionality you shall sacrifice. This is the context of a question that Shmuel posed to Rav Huna: *minayin le'mitasek be'kodashim she'hu pasul* — from where do we derive that if one engages in the *shechita* of a sacrifice without awareness that one is doing so — in a *mitasek* fashion, almost in passing — the act is invalid? *She'ne'emar ve'shachat et ben ha'bakar* — as it is written, you shall slaughter the calf — *she'tehei shechita le'shem ben bakar* — meaning the *shechita* must be performed with the awareness that this is a calf and that this is a sacrifice. Rav Huna replied: that the *shechita* should ideally be performed with such intentionality we obviously know — but *le'akev minayin*, from where do we know that without it the act is actually invalid and not merely deficient? *Talmud lomar lirtzonchem tizbachu* — only a slaughter accompanied by your intentional will counts; without it, the act does not constitute a valid *shechita* for a sacrifice.

It is fitting, in a way, that Menachot closes with a discussion of *shechita* rather than with a *mincha*, even as the tractate's final theological reflections concern the purpose of sacrifice and the relationship of Torah to *korbanot*. *Hadran alach Isaron, ve'slika lach masechet Menachot.* Yashar koach to all who have now completed learning Menachot.

---

---

# Hullin 2

## Intro to Hullin

### Name & Scope

We begin Masechet Chullin, daf 2a. The masechet is traditionally called Shechitas Chullin, in contrast to Zevachim, which is Shechitas Kodshim. The name reflects its primary subject matter, though the masechet is by no means limited to shechita alone.

### Masechet Topics

The masechet is extremely well organized, covering all the steps involved in eating meat that is not a korban. It opens with two perakim on shechita, then treats treifos — the examination for punctures and wounds. It then addresses the mitzvos relating to kisuy hadam, covering the blood. Notably, this obligation applies only to birds and chayos such as deer, but not to behemos, since the blood of domesticated animals normally goes on the mizbeach. The masechet continues with the prohibition against slaughtering an animal and its mother on the same day, and then addresses the removal of blood, gid hanasheh, and forbidden fats, concluding with the prohibition of cooking meat with milk. The masechet thus traces the entire sequence of what one must do in order to eat meat.

---

## Hakol Shochtin Mishnah

### Anyone May Slaughter

Our perek opens with the mishnah: *hakol shochtin* — anyone may slaughter — *veshechitasan kesheira* — and their shechita is valid.

### Cheresh Shoteh VeKatan

The mishnah then provides an exception: *chutz mecheresh shoteh vekatan* — excepting the cheresh, shoteh, and katan. This is the standard triad of individuals who, in halachah, are considered to lack da'as — the mature, functioning intellect required to effect halachically significant acts. The cheresh is a deaf-mute; the shoteh is one who is functionally unaware of his surroundings or the significance of his actions (with the technical parameters discussed in Masechet Chagigah); and the katan is a minor, a boy under thirteen or a girl under twelve.

Typically, such individuals are categorically excluded from acts that are not merely physical but require intent and awareness of the act's legal significance — a business transaction being the classic example, where even if an observer could confirm that all the technical steps were performed, the transaction still would not take effect, because the transaction is constituted by the parties' knowledge and intent, not merely by the physical exchange.

### Not Categorical Exclusion

What is striking here is that the mishnah does not treat the exclusion of cheresh shoteh vekatan as categorical. The mishnah explicitly spells out the reason: *shema yekalkelu es shechitasan* — lest they ruin their shechita. The concern is not that they are constitutionally incapable of effecting a halachic act, but rather that they may not execute the physical act correctly — they may not have the sufficient attention or awareness to ensure proper technical performance. This is therefore not a categorical exception but a concern about performance.

### Observed = Valid

Accordingly, the mishnah concludes: *vechullan sheshachatu ve'acherim ro'im osam, shechitasan kesheira* — if any of them slaughter while being observed by others, their shechita is valid. Since the exclusion was never categorical but only a concern about technical execution, the presence of an observer who can verify proper performance suffices to render the shechita valid.

This contrasts sharply with cases where cheresh shoteh vekatan are categorically excluded — such as performing a mitzvah on someone else's behalf, or executing a sale. In those contexts, even a perfectly observed performance would not suffice, because the deficiency is not in the physical act but in the legal capacity of the actor.

### Cheresh in Modern Law

One might ask: why should a cheresh, whose physical coordination is entirely intact, lack the requisite awareness for shechita? The answer lies in the assumption, operative in the Talmudic period when there were no means of communication with a deaf-mute, that such a person was effectively outside the normal frameworks of society — unable to receive information or to communicate in any meaningful way — and therefore lacked the focused awareness required to perform the act reliably.

Contemporary poskim have engaged seriously with whether this assumption still applies. One approach is to argue that the reason for the exclusion no longer obtains in the modern world. This approach is often considered halachically problematic, since halacha tends to focus on the defined parameters of a category rather than the underlying reasons, which would otherwise allow for too much flexibility in redefining categories. The more common approach, therefore, is to argue at the level of the parameters themselves: the cheresh was excluded because he could not speak. Today, a person who communicates through writing or sign language may well be considered to speak through those means and therefore might not fall within the technical definition of cheresh at all. There is a substantial body of contemporary teshuvos addressing this question.

---

## Hakol: L'chatchila?

### L'chatchila vs B'diavad

The Gemara opens with an observation about the mishnah's language. *hakol shochtin* — anyone may slaughter — implies that *lechatchila* anyone may do so. Yet the subsequent phrase *ushechitasan kesheira* — their shechita is valid — sounds like a post-facto endorsement, implying that certain people should not have done it *lechatchila* but that *bediavad* it is acceptable. The two halves of the mishnah appear to be in tension.

Rav Acha brei deRav poses this to Rav Ashi: *vechol hakol lechatchila hu?* — Is it always the case that the word *hakol* implies *lechatchila*? Perhaps *hakol* simply means that whoever does it produces a valid result, without implying that all such people are equally preferred *lechatchila*.

The Gemara then surveys a range of mishnayot that open with the word *hakol*, in order to determine whether *hakol* normally implies *lechatchila* or only *bediavad*. It should be noted that in Masechet Erchin a parallel discussion examines *hakol* from a different angle entirely — asking whom the word is coming to include. Here in Chullin, the Gemara takes a different tack, asking not who is included but whether their inclusion is *lechatchila* or merely *bediavad*.

### Temura Challenge

The first challenge comes from Masechet Temura: *hakol memirin* — anyone can effect a temura. Temura is the act of attempting to transfer the kedusha from one korban to another. The Torah explicitly prohibits this: *lo yachlifenu velo yamir oso, tov bera o ra betov* — do not exchange it, do not transfer it, good for bad or bad for good. If you attempt it, both animals become kadosh — the kedusha does not leave the original, but the replacement animal also acquires sanctity. *hakol memirin* means that everyone who attempts temura succeeds in effecting it. But can this mean that it is permitted *lechatchila*? Clearly not, since doing so is a biblical prohibition.

### Temura Answer

The Gemara answers: *hatam kidekatani ta'ama* — there, the mishnah in Temura itself explicitly qualifies the statement. The mishnah says *lo she'adam rashai lehamir* — this is not to say that a person is permitted to perform temura — *ela she'im hemir mumar* — but that if he did, it takes effect. And it adds *vesofeg es ha'arba'im* — and he receives the forty lashes. The fact that the mishnah in Temura had to explicitly state that *hakol memirin* does not mean *lechatchila* is itself proof that *hakol* normally does mean *lechatchila*. Here in Chullin, where no such qualification appears, *hakol shochtin* should indeed be read as *lechatchila*.

### Erchin Challenge

The Gemara continues with a challenge from the opening mishnah of Masechet Erchin: *hakol maarichin vene'erachin, nodrim venidrim* — everyone can pledge an erech and be the subject of an erech; everyone can make a neder and be the subject of one.

To understand the challenge, it is necessary to explain the two modes of valuation described at the end of Sefer Vayikra. If one says *dmei ploni alai* — the monetary value of that person is upon me — one obligates oneself to give the market value of that person to the Beis Hamikdash. Since a person has no market value in ordinary circumstances, this is determined by asking what that person would be worth if sold as a slave. If one instead uses the technical term *erech* — which also means value but functions as a terminus technicus — the obligation is fixed by the schedule the Torah itself provides: male or female, within various age ranges, each carries a specified amount. The word *erech* thus bypasses market value entirely and substitutes a Toraitic list.

The word *hakol* in that mishnah comes to include, among others, a *mufla samuch le'ish* — a minor within a year of adulthood who understands the significance of vows, whose vows are binding. *vene'erachin* — being the subject of an erech — includes even one who is terminally ill or unable to do any labor and thus has no market value: when the word *erech* is used, one pays the fixed Toraitic rate regardless. *nidrim* — being the subject of a neder of market value — includes even a newborn, who has no erech since the Toraitic list begins at one month, but who may have a market value.

### Vow Debate: Meir/Yehuda

The Gemara now challenges the inference that *hakol* implies *lechatchila* from this mishnah in Erchin: *vehaktiv vechi techdal lindor lo yihiyeh vecha chet* — the verse says that if you cease to make vows there will be no sin in you, implying that vowing is something to be avoided. And the famous verse in Kohelet: *tov asher lo tiddor mishetiddor velo tishalem* — better not to vow than to vow and not to fulfill. So how can *hakol maarichin* imply that vowing is *lechatchila* permitted?

This opens the celebrated debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda. A baraisa teaches: *tov mizeh umizeh she'eino noder kol ikar* — better than either of them is not to vow at all. This is the position of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says: *tov mizeh umizeh noder umeshalem* — the best is to vow and to fulfill. Rabbi Meir's position is clear: even if you intend to fulfill your vow, you should not vow, because you are opening yourself to the risk of violation. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds that vowing and fulfilling is praiseworthy.

### Yehuda Read Narrowly

One might think that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the mishnah in Erchin could be read as *lechatchila*. The Gemara, however, chooses to read Rabbi Yehuda very narrowly: *ve'afilu Rabbi Yehuda lo ka'amar ella be'omer harei zeh* — even Rabbi Yehuda's lenient position applies only when one actually sanctifies a specific object, saying "this animal" or "this sum of money" is hereby donated. In that case there is no personal obligation: one has sanctified the object itself, not taken upon oneself a personal duty to produce a payment. If the object is lost without negligence, there is no personal liability, since the obligation resided in the object rather than in the person. What Rabbi Yehuda would not permit, under this reading, is a personal vow — one where the person takes upon themselves an obligation to pay — since that always carries the risk of non-fulfillment. Under this reading, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda converge: both agree that a personal vow is always potentially problematic. Rabbi Yehuda's permissive ruling applies only to the sanctification of an object, not a personal commitment.

With this, the challenge to *hakol* meaning *lechatchila* is reinstated: according to both Rabbi Meir and this narrow reading of Rabbi Yehuda, there is never a straightforward *lechatchila* basis for making a personal vow. So *hakol maarichin* cannot mean *lechatchila*.

### Why Make Vows?

This naturally raises the question of why the Torah describes vowing as a category at all, if it is always better not to vow.
