The answer lies in the psychological reality that people are sometimes seized by intense religious motivation — at a moment of inspiration or thanksgiving, they want to give expression to that feeling and to commit themselves to acting on it. A vow channels that motivation and creates a binding obligation that makes it more likely the person will actually follow through. Without the vow, the impulse may simply dissipate: one thinks, "I should give some money," and by the time one returns home, the feeling has passed and nothing happens. The vow is the mechanism by which the feeling translates into action.

The tension, then, is that the same mechanism that spurs action also opens the door to sin if the vow is not fulfilled. The Gemara's concern is with that downside risk, and that is why — at least according to Rabbi Meir and the narrow reading of Rabbi Yehuda — a personal vow is never straightforwardly recommended *lechatchila*.

It is also worth noting that the Torah never formulates a mitzvah to donate money to the Beis Hamikdash. It describes the phenomenon of such donations and legislates the laws of vows at the end of Vayikra, but it does not command it. The analogous commandments are tzedakah and support for the Levi'im. Capital donations to the sanctuary were clearly a major and ancient phenomenon — ancient synagogues bear inscriptions attesting to donors — but they are not themselves a mitzvah in the technical sense. The institution of vows taps into the deep religious motivation people feel to give, while the Gemara's restraint reflects the real risks that accompany formal commitment.

### Smicha Challenge

The Gemara continues. Having argued back and forth, it now tries the opposite position: perhaps *hakol* never means *lechatchila*. To test this, the Gemara cites: *hakol somchin* — everyone may perform smicha, the act of pressing one's hands on a korban. The verse says *vesamach yado venirtzah* — and he shall press his hand and it will be desired for him — which clearly establishes smicha as an obligation, something one should do *lechatchila*. Can *hakol somchin* be read as only *bediavad*? Surely not.

### Hakol: Either Way

The Gemara therefore concludes: *ika hakol lechatchila ve'ika hakol bediavad* — sometimes *hakol* means *lechatchila* and sometimes it means *bediavad*, depending on context. Since *hakol* can mean either, the original question dissolves: even if *ushechitasan kesheira* implies *bediavad*, *hakol shochtin* need not mean *lechatchila*. Perhaps the entire mishnah is speaking *bediavad*.

### Manufactured Problem

At this point the Gemara introduces what can only be described as a deliberately manufactured tension. It says: the real difficulty for me was the phrase *shechitasan kesheira* — since that implies *bediavad*, the opening *hakol shochtin* must mean *lechatchila*, for otherwise why use two phrases both meaning the same *bediavad* thing? Simply say *shechitasan hakol kesheira* and be done with it. Since the mishnah employs both phrases, the first must be conveying something different — *lechatchila* — which then creates a contradiction with the *bediavad* implication of the second phrase.

This is frankly a strange piece of reasoning. Having already established that *hakol* can mean *bediavad*, the simplest reading would be to accept the mishnah as consistent throughout. The Gemara instead insists on reading the two halves as saying different things in order to introduce a tension — and it is through resolving that tension that the Gemara will now read a host of additional cases into the mishnah's few words. The manufactured quality of the problem is the point: the Gemara is using it as an opportunity to expand what the mishnah is teaching.

### Smicha & Women MSS

Before moving on, a textual point regarding the smicha case. The Gemara here reads *hakol somchin, echad hanashim ve'echad ha'anashim* — whether men or women. This is striking, because a marginal note in the printed text — attributed to the scholar responsible for the cross-references, Yehoshua Boaz — states: *chipasnu bechol hamakomot velo matzanu ken beshum makom bashas* — we searched everywhere and found this formulation nowhere else in the entire Talmud. On the contrary, *ve'adaraba ipecha matzanu* — we found the opposite: that women are excluded from smicha. Even Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon, who permitted women to perform smicha, held only that it was *reshus* — permissible if they wished — not that women are obligated at the same level as men. The inclusion of *echad hanashim ve'echad ha'anashim* in the context of smicha, which in every other place in the Talmud is described as not obligatory for women, is an outlier. A check of the *dikdukei soferim* confirms that this phrase does not appear in some manuscripts, making it quite plausible that it entered the text as a copyist's error.

---

## Tamei Shochet Reading

### Tamei in Chullin

Rabbah bar Ula now proposes a reading of the mishnah that resolves the manufactured tension and simultaneously introduces new material. He says: *hachi katani* — this is how the mishnah should be read. *hakol shochtin* — anyone may slaughter — means that even a tamei person may slaughter *lechatchila*. Why would one have thought otherwise? Because the mishnah is referring to chullin shena'asu al taharat hakodesh — non-sanctified food that is being treated with the purity standards of kodesh.

This practice had a historical reality. There was a group known as the *chaverim* who were scrupulous about maintaining purity even for their ordinary food, treating their chullin with the same level of taharah ordinarily required for kodshim. This practice existed both during and after the period of the Beis Hamikdash. The question therefore arises: if you are part of such a group and you are tamei, may you slaughter your meat?

One might assume that since you are treating your food like kodesh, you ought not slaughter it while tamei, just as you would not handle actual kodshim while tamei. The mishnah therefore tells us: *hakol shochtin* — even a tamei person may slaughter *lechatchila*. The Gemara's initial objection — *tamei bechullin mai le'meimra*, why would we need to be told that a tamei person may slaughter ordinary chullin? — is answered precisely by this specification: we are not talking about ordinary chullin, but chullin al taharat hakodesh, where the tamei status is a relevant concern.

### Long Knife Solution

Even for chullin al taharat hakodesh, however, the tamei shochet must take care: *mevi sakkin arucha veshochet bah, kedei shelo yigga babasar* — he brings a long knife and slaughters with it, in order not to touch the meat. Tosafot raises a question about the mechanics of this concern, noting that for food to contract tumah it must have first been in contact with a liquid — and the blood of shechita does not serve as the requisite *machshir* to render the meat susceptible to tumah. Tosafot raises this question in the context of chullin al taharat hakodesh, though the full resolution of that question is not pursued here.

### Tamei Kodshim B'diavad

While a tamei person may slaughter chullin al taharat hakodesh with a long knife *lechatchila*, the case of actual kodshim is different: *uvemukdashim lo yishchot shema yigga babasar* — a tamei person should not slaughter a korban *lechatchila*, lest he touch the meat. However, *ve'im shachat ve'omer bari li shelo nagati, shechitatho kesheira* — if he did go ahead and slaughter, and declares with certainty that he did not touch the meat, the shechita is valid *bediavad*.

### VeChullan Referent

With this framework, the full mishnah takes on a more complex reading. *hakol shochtin* — everyone may slaughter *lechatchila*, including even a tamei person slaughtering chullin al taharat hakodesh with a long knife. *ushechitasan kesheira* — and *bediavad* it is valid — refers to the tamei person who slaughtered actual kodshim: even though *lechatchila* he should not have, if he did and did not touch the meat, the korban is valid.

*Chutz mecheresh shoteh vekatan* — excepting the cheresh, shoteh, and katan — means that even *bediavad*, if they slaughtered even ordinary chullin, their shechita is not valid: *shema yishhu, shema yidresu, shema yachlidu* — lest they have paused, applied pressure, or displaced the simanim. These are categorical concerns about technical performance that apply to the plainest case of chullin.

Then *vechullan sheshachatu ve'acherim ro'im osam* — if anyone slaughtered while being observed — does not refer back solely to the cheresh shoteh vekatan, but primarily to the tamei person slaughtering kodshim. If he was observed, even if he cannot himself report that he did not touch the meat, the observation suffices to establish that he did not, and the shechita is valid. This reading explains why the mishnah uses the broad *kol* rather than simply saying "and if cheresh shoteh vekatan slaughtered and were observed": the phrase is carrying a different referent, namely the tamei shochet of kodshim.

### Tosafot: Where Standing?

Tosafot raises a pointed practical question about the scenario of a tamei person slaughtering kodshim. A tamei person is prohibited from entering the Beis Hamikdash. Now, a person who is tamei meis — who contracted tumah through contact with a corpse — is permitted, according to biblical law, to enter the Ezras Nashim; only the Mikdash proper is off-limits. One could imagine him standing at the threshold of the Ezras Yisrael, with the korban just inside, and slaughtering it with a long knife. However, the problem is that by rabbinic enactment, even a tamei person was not permitted to be anywhere in the Ezras Nashim. And the Ezras Nashim is 135 amos — approximately 200 feet — in length. It is difficult to imagine a knife 200 feet long. Tosafot therefore suggests two possibilities: either the scenario refers to shechita on the bamos, the altars used outside of Jerusalem before the Beis Hamikdash was built, rather than to the Beis Hamikdash proper; or alternatively, it might depend on precisely where one was standing relative to the various entrances to the Temple complex.

### Women Shecht L'chatchila

On this point Tosafot cites a ruling from a Geonic work called Hilchos Eretz Yisrael to the effect that women should not perform shechita because *daatan kalos* — they are of insufficiently serious and focused mind. Tosafot rejects this categorically. In Tosafot's view, not only may women slaughter chullin, they may slaughter even kodshim *lechatchila*. The verse in Zevachim, to be discussed shortly, explicitly lists women among those who may perform shechita on sacrifices, and the word *lechatchila* is appropriate. *hakol shochtin* thus clearly includes women — and not merely in a *bediavad* sense, but fully *lechatchila*, even for kodshim. There are in fact one or two known historical cases of women who served as shochtos, and there is contemporary interest among women in studying Hilchos Shechitah. The halachic sources are unambiguous that gender is no barrier to shechita; only cheresh shoteh vekatan are excluded.

### Why Repeat Here?

The Gemara now raises an objection to Rabbah bar Ula's reading: *hai tamei bemukdashim me'hacha nafka?* — is the law about a tamei person and kodshim derived from here? It is derived from the explicit mishnah in Masechet Zevachim: *kol hapsulin sheshachatu shechitasan kesheira* — any invalid persons who slaughtered, their shechita is valid — *she'shechitah kesheira bezarim, banashim, uba'avadim, uvetmei'im, ve'afilu bekodshei kodashim* — for shechita is valid when performed by non-kohanim, by women, by slaves, and by tamei persons, even with the most holy sacrifices — *uvilvad shelo yihyu tme'im nogim babasar* — provided that the tamei persons do not touch the meat. This mishnah in Zevachim already teaches everything Rabbah bar Ula reads into our mishnah. Why would the law need to be repeated here?

### Zevachim Primary Source

The Gemara offers two answers. The first: *hacha ikar* — the primary teaching is actually here, with Zevachim's inclusion being secondary. The second, which the Gemara identifies as the better answer: *hasam ikar* — the primary teaching is indeed in Zevachim, where the context is kodshim and the ruling fits naturally. *debekodshim kai* — since Zevachim is speaking about korbanot, that is where the ruling about a tamei shochet properly belongs. Our mishnah, however, since it is discussing tamei and chullin, also implicitly brings in the case of tamei and kodshim alongside it. The case is not the primary teaching of our mishnah; it is carried along by the discussion. What makes this exchange remarkable is that the discussion in our Gemara is a lengthy elaboration of two short phrases — *hakol shochtin ushechitasan kesheira* — from which an entire framework regarding tumah and shechita has been constructed, including then an inquiry into why that which was never stated needed to have been stated.

---

## Ramban on Vows

### Yaakov's Vow

Before closing, it is worth pausing on the issue of vows. The Ramban poses a difficulty: the very Torah figures held up as models of piety made vows. *vayidor yaakov neder leimor* — Yaakov made a vow. *vayidor yisrael* — Yisrael made a vow. And we have the exhortation *nidru veshalmu la'Hashem Elokeichem kol sevivav* — make vows and fulfill them to Hashem your God, all those around Him. How is all of this reconciled with the discouragements of vowing found in Kohelet and in the Gemara?

### Vow in Distress

One answer the Ramban cites is *dibe'shaat tzarah shani* — in times of distress it is different, and vowing is specifically permitted. This fits within Ramban's broader framework, in which prayer too is commanded specifically in times of distress rather than as a daily obligation. In moments of crisis, making a vow is a legitimate expression of one's appeal to and reliance on God.

### Vows for Tzedakah OK

The Ramban then adds his own view, which he finds the more fundamental point: *veli yeira'eh shelo asru ella bekodshei mizbeach* — it seems to me that the prohibition applies specifically to vows concerning korbanot brought on the mizbeach — *shema yavo lidei takalah* — lest one come to violate the vow — *ve'ein bekorbanot tzorekh gavoah* — and because God has no need of your korbanot, as the verse states, *hinei shemoa mizevach tov* — behold, obedience is better than sacrifice. Since the korban is ultimately for the benefit of the person bringing it, not for God, and since there is the risk of non-fulfillment, vowing to bring korbanot carries particular danger.

However, *aval litzedakah ulevahapish issar la'aniyim* — if you are making a vow to give charity or to give money to the poor — *ve'ein tzorekh lomar lekayem*, and certainly to fulfill other mitzvot — *nishba'in venodrin* — it is appropriate to make such vows. Vows in service of genuine good in the world — giving to the poor, supporting those in need, fulfilling important obligations — are not subject to the same critique. The problem was always vowing in the context of korbanot, where the utility was personal and the risk of sin was real. Vowing in order to do good in the world is another matter entirely.

This is a fascinating Ramban, offering what amounts to a critique of korbanot as a category — not that they were wrong, but that they served human needs rather than divine ones — in a way that resonates with the conclusion of Masechet Zevachim itself, where the Gemara similarly notes that God does not need our korbanot. Vows that actually produce benefit in the world, that spur us to give tzedakah and to do mitzvot, stand on different ground entirely.

---

---

# Hullin 3

## Mishnah Structure & Them…

### L'chatchila/B'diavad Int…

We pick up on the bottom of Daf 2b. The first discussion in the Gemara may have felt somewhat frustrating, in that it created what seems like an artificial question about the Mishnah — is it talking about le'chatchila or be'di'avad? — and then forced itself toward the answer that the Mishnah is addressing both: le'chatchila and be'di'avad. That said, it is worth stepping back to appreciate what the Gemara is doing here, because the answer illuminates a great deal about what is to come.

### Opening Sugya Pattern

This is a classic move at the beginning of a masechet. The Gemara will often focus on what appears to be a side issue — sometimes purely linguistic, sometimes a question that does not seem to demand much attention — and use it as a vehicle for introducing major themes that will recur throughout the masechet. One finds this pattern across numerous masechtos. The beginning of Bava Kamma, for instance, uses the question of arba avos and tolada as an occasion to survey all the categories of nezikin. In some cases, one has the sense that the opening sugya was constructed quite late, specifically for this introductory purpose.

That is precisely what is happening here. We insisted that the Mishnah first indicates something le'chatchila and then something be'di'avad, and we are going to use that framework to examine four or five different answers — each of which lays out a different understanding of the le'chatchila and be'di'avad of shechita. Taken together, they serve as an introduction to the central questions of the masechet: who can shecht, under what circumstances, what constitutes le'chatchila, what constitutes be'di'avad, and where the debates lie. That is the agenda for the remainder of this daf.

---

## Tamei & Tuma Mechanics

### Tamei Source & Distincti…

We are wrapping up the first explanation, which held that the le'chatchila and be'di'avad in the Mishnah concerned a person who is tamei. Le'chatchila, such a person may shecht chullin — even chullin treated with the purity standards of hekdesh — but may not shecht hekdesh itself. Be'di'avad, if he did shecht hekdesh and did not touch it, the shechita is valid. Now the Gemara asks: hai tamei de-itma be-mai — this tamei person who is performing the shechita, how did he become tamei?

### Cherev ke-Chalal Princip…

The Gemara raises the case: ileima de-itma be-meis — if he became tamei through a met, a dead body. And here the Gemara cites the halakhic principle of cherev harei hu ke-chalal, derived from the pasuk be-chalal cherev, at the top of Daf 3a. This is a special rule in Hilchot Tumas Meis. Normally, tuma descends in level as it transfers from one object to another. The corpse itself occupies the highest level, avi avot hatuma — the granddaddy of tumot. The person who touches it becomes an av hatuma; what that person touches becomes a rishon, then a sheni, and so on. But by tumas meis, there is a remarkable exception: a metal object that contacts a met does not descend a level — it retains the status of avi avot hatuma. And by extension, if a person who is an av hatuma by virtue of having touched a met then touches a metal object, that metal object retains av hatuma status rather than descending to rishon.

How does this bear on our case? We are assuming a metal knife is being used for shechita, which is the natural assumption. If the shochet became tamei through contact with a met, he is an av hatuma. He then takes his metal knife to shecht — and by the principle of cherev ke-chalal, that knife does not descend a level; it too is an av hatuma. Even if the shochet never directly touches the meat, the knife is touching the meat, and an av hatuma contacting food renders it tamei. How then can we say that the shechita is permissible?

Both Rashi and Tosafot note that the special rule about metal is not even strictly necessary to generate the problem. Even with a non-metal knife, the shochet as av hatuma would render the knife a rishon, and the knife touching the meat would still make the meat tamei. The Gemara acknowledges this: letamyei lesakin vetimtei lebasar — the knife will be rendered tamei and the knife will render the meat tamei. So how does it help that the shochet does not personally touch the meat?

### Tamei via Sheretz

The Gemara's first answer: de'itmei besheretz — he did not become tamei through a met, but through a sheretz, a dead rodent or animal carcass. In that case, the animal is an av, not an avi avot — only tumas meis begins at that elevated level. If I touch a sheretz, I become a rishon. And a rishon cannot be metamei a kli — a vessel. So if I touch my knife, I cannot render the knife tamei at all. Consequently, the knife remains tahor and there is no problem.

### Shechita Objects

The second answer takes a different route: ve'iba'it eima, le'olam de'itmei bemeis — even if he did become tamei through a met, the case is ukegon shebadak kerumit shel kaneh veshachat bah — he checked a reed, like a hard bamboo reed, sharpened it sufficiently, and used it to shecht. And here the Gemara takes the opportunity to cite a braita: bechol shochtin — you may shecht with anything — bein betzur bein bizchuchit, whether a rock or a piece of glass, bein bikrumit shel kaneh, or a reed — as long as it is sharp and smooth and does the job.

This is already significant in its own right: you do not need a knife per se. There are no formal requirements as to what object you must use. It simply has to be sharp enough and smooth enough to perform the shechita.

### Kli Requirement Debate

Tosafot raises an important question here. There is a principle, derived from the pasuk concerning Avraham and Yitzchak — vayikach es hama'achelet lishchot es beno — that shechita requires a kli. Tosafot asks two things. First: the objects listed in the braita — a sharp rock, a piece of glass — are not recognized as kelim for the purposes of tuma law. They do not carry the formal halakhic designation of a vessel. So if we say shechita requires a kli, we evidently do not mean a kli in the technical sense recognized in other legal contexts. We just mean something fashioned to serve the purpose — which renders the requirement nearly circular, because it reduces to: the object has to be capable of doing the job. For all practical purposes, there is no formal specification of what the shechita implement must be. There is no defined "shechita knife" with prescribed characteristics; it only needs to be sharp and smooth.

Second, Tosafot questions whether even for shechitat kodashim, where the pasuk of the ma'achelet might impose stricter requirements, the implement must qualify as a kli shareit. Tosafot finds this genuinely difficult, noting that some of the objects that appear to be valid for shechita would not normally qualify as kli shareit. This is also not fully settled in the Rambam. The question is complicated further by other Gemarot that speak of the shechita knife as mekadesh — sanctifying — the animal, which would suggest a more formal status for the implement. The matter remains unresolved, but the key practical point is established: for ordinary shechita, there is no prescribed knife and no requirement that the implement be a formally recognized vessel.

---

## Abaye: Kuti & Supervision

### Kuti Status & Concern

Abaye now offers his reading of the Mishnah, moving away from tuma entirely and toward the more central question of who may perform shechita. He focuses on the person doing the shechita: Abaye amar hachi katani — here is how you read the Mishnah. Hakol shochtin, everybody may shecht — va'afilu Kuti, even a Samaritan.

The Kuti here is used literally, not as a euphemism. There are several distinct questions surrounding the Samaritan's status. The first is whether Samaritans are Jewish at all. The book of Yirmiyah records that Nevuchadnezzar settled the Samaritans in the Land of Israel, and that they worshiped both their own god and God. Whether they genuinely converted or not is a matter of halakhic dispute. The second question is: even granting that they are Jewish, can we trust that they follow the same system of shechita laws as we do? It was well-known that Samaritans kept many Jewish laws throughout the Second Temple period, and so this is a reasonable assumption. But the third and most pointed concern is this: even if they follow the same shechita laws for themselves, do they care about causing other people to sin? Given the well-documented antagonism between the Samaritans and the Jewish community, one cannot simply assume that a Kuti shechting meat for non-Samaritan Jews will be careful about their interests. He might not hold by the prohibition of lifnei iver lo titein michshol — the prohibition against placing a stumbling block before others. He may not feel any obligation to prevent them from eating treif, and may even, in some cases, wish to do so.

So the concern is not that the Kuti does not know the laws or is technically incompetent. The concern is one of intent and motivation when shechting for others.

### Supervision & Salvage Te…

With that background, Abaye parses the Mishnah as follows: hachi katani — hakol shochtin, everybody may shecht, va'afilu Kuti, even a Samaritan. B'meh devarim amurim — when is this true? Kshe'Yisrael omeid al gabav — when a Jew is standing over him, in direct and constant supervision. Under those conditions, even though the Kuti's motivations might be suspect, the direct observation ensures he is performing the shechita correctly. That is the le'chatchila. Aval yotzei v'nichnas lo yishchot — but if the supervision is merely yotzei ve'nichnas — the supervisor popping in and out at intervals rather than maintaining constant presence — that is not sufficient le'chatchila.

### Meat-Eating Test

Then the be'di'avad: ve'im shachat — if he went ahead and shechted without the required constant supervision, there is still a mechanism to salvage the shechita. Choteich kezayit basar, you cut a piece of the meat, v'nosein lo, and offer it to the Kuti himself. Achal lo — if he eats it, mutar le'echol mishchitato — you may eat the rest of the shechita. Lo achal lo — if he refuses to eat it, assur le'echol mishchitato — you may not. The logic is precise: we assume the Kuti knows the laws and is technically competent; the only concern is whether he would willfully feed others treif. If he himself eats from it, we know he performed it correctly, because he would not eat neveilah.

### Cheresh Shoteh Katan

Chutz mecheresh shoteh vekatan — excluded from this dispensation are the deaf-mute, the mentally incompetent, and the minor. For them, even if there is no direct supervision, the meat-eating test will not work. Ve'afilu be'di'avad nami lo — even after the fact, there is no way to salvage it. Why? Shema yish'hu shema yidresu ve'shema yachlidu — we are concerned that they may have paused, applied pressure, or performed the shechita in such a way as to invalidate it. The distinction is fundamental. For the Kuti, the concern is one of motivation and honesty — he knows what to do, and the question is whether he will do it faithfully for others. For the cheresh, shoteh, and katan, the concern is one of technical competence — they may have committed a technical violation without even knowing it. Therefore, even the meat-eating test is irrelevant, since their own assessment of what they did carries no weight.

### Vechulan Difficulty

The final phrase of the Mishnah — vechulan sheshachatu ve'acherim ro'in otam, anyone who shechted while others directly observed is valid — creates a difficulty for Abaye. Ilema cheresh shoteh vekatan — if this phrase is referring to cheresh shoteh vekatan, we were just discussing them; it should have simply said ve'im shachatu. Ela akuti — so perhaps it refers back to the Kuti. But ha amart kesheyisrael omeid al gabav shachat afilu le'chatchila — Abaye himself already established that with direct supervision the Kuti's shechita is good even le'chatchila. Why then restate it in a way that makes it sound like this is only a be'di'avad dispensation? Kashya — this is a difficulty that Abaye's reading cannot fully resolve.

---

## Rava: Yotzei Ve-Nichnas

### Wine Precedent Question

Rava now uses Abaye's position as an opportunity to challenge the threshold of required supervision. Amar Rava: ve'yotzei ve'nichnas le'chatchila lo? — are you really saying that periodic supervision is insufficient? Ve'hatnan — we have a Mishnah regarding yayin nesech: ha'maniach oved kochavim be'chanuto ve'yisrael yotzei ve'nichnas — if you leave a non-Jew in your wine store and you yourself are simply popping in and out, mutar — the wine remains permitted. Periodic supervision is enough to keep the non-Jew honest, since you might catch him in the act at any moment. So Rava asks: why does Abaye demand omeid al gabav for the Kuti performing shechita, when yotzei ve'nichnas evidently suffices in the wine case?

### L'chatchila vs B'diavad

The Gemara responds on Abaye's behalf: mi katani maniach? — does the Mishnah say you may leave him there le'chatchila? Ha'maniach katani — it says "he left him," describing a post-facto situation. Perhaps be'di'avad yotzei ve'nichnas suffices, but le'chatchila even in the wine case you would require more direct supervision. Rava presses further with an additional source: eino shomer tzarich lihyot yoshev umeshamer, ela af al pi shehu yotzei venichnas mutar — the watchman does not need to sit and watch continuously; even if he is merely going in and out, it is permitted. And there the language sounds le'chatchila. So Rava maintains that yotzei ve'nichnas is sufficient le'chatchila, and he disagrees with Abaye's more stringent demand for constant supervision.

### Guarding vs Processing

The key distinction that emerges, which explains Abaye's position, concerns both opportunity and the nature of the task. In the wine case, the non-Jew has no legitimate basis for handling the wine. It belongs to someone else. If he were caught opening a barrel or touching the wine, he would have no excuse — it is immediately apparent that he is doing something wrong. Yotzei ve'nichnas works precisely because the illicit act is easy to catch and there is no pretext for it. In the shechita case, the situation is entirely different: the Kuti has been given the animal to shecht. He has every right to be handling it. Any error — whether deliberate or negligent — can happen in a single instant, in the moment when the supervisor steps out. There is no opportunity to catch him red-handed. Additionally, in the shechita case the person actually processing the food has a direct role in the outcome; the potential for impropriety is woven into the very act he has been assigned to perform. This is why Abaye holds that yotzei ve'nichnas cannot suffice for shechita even if it suffices for wine storage.

### Rava's Re-Reading

Rava accordingly re-reads the Mishnah on his own terms. Ela amar Rava, hachi katani: hakol shochtin va'afilu kuti — everybody may shecht, even a Samaritan. B'meh devarim amurim — when? Keshe'yisrael yotzei ve'nichnas — when a Jew is periodically checking in. That, says Rava, is sufficient le'chatchila. Aval ba umatza sheshachat — if you arrived and found that he had already shechted, with no supervision at all, then chotech kezayit basar ve'nosein lo — you cut a piece of the meat and give it to him. Achlo — if he eats it, mutar le'echol mishchitato. Lo achlo — if he refuses, assur. Chutz mecheresh shoteh vekatan — de'afilu be'di'avad nami lo, with the same reasoning as before. And the final phrase vechulan sheshachatu again generates the same difficulty under Rava's reading that it did under Abaye's — kashya.

---

## Rav Ashi: Mumar

### Mumar Types & Neveilot

Rav Ashi now offers a third reading: Rav Ashi amar hachi katani. Hakol shochtin va'afilu Yisrael mumar — everybody may shecht, even a Jew who is a mumar, a habitual violator. In the Gemara's usage, mumar does not mean heretic in the theological sense; it refers to someone who regularly transgresses a particular law. There are two types. A mumar le'te'avon violates out of desire and appetite — he simply cannot resist the temptation, or finds it economically convenient, even while being otherwise careful about halacha. A mumar lehach'is, by contrast, has no particular desire for the forbidden thing but does it out of spite — as an ideological act of defiance against God. The mumar lehach'is is categorically worse, because his violation reflects an active axe to grind, which may translate into other behaviors as well.

The specific violation in question here is eating neveilot — non-shechted meat — and this is directly relevant to shechita. If a person is willing to eat meat that has not been shechted properly, that raises an immediate concern about his reliability as a shochet. The question is: can we trust such a person to shecht correctly for others?

### Mumar Le'Te'avon

The Gemara cites a statement of Rava: Yisrael mumar ochel neveilot le'te'avon — a Jew who habitually eats neveilot out of desire — bodek sakin ve'nosein lo, u'mutar le'echol mishchitato — if you check the knife, ensure that it is sharp and smooth, and give it to him, you may eat from his shechita.

The reasoning is elegant. A mumar le'te'avon only violates when there is some gain — the meat tastes good, or it is cheaper, or there is some other benefit to eating the non-kosher over the kosher. Here, you have pre-checked the knife and handed it to him. The most demanding part of a shochet's responsibility — ensuring the knife is in proper condition — has been taken off his hands. He has no effort to exert, and no incentive to do the shechita incorrectly, because doing it incorrectly provides him no benefit. Since he would just as readily do it correctly, and since he knows the laws, we can trust that he did. This is a striking ruling. We are speaking of a person who is a known regular violator of the laws of shechita — who eats non-shechted meat — and yet we are prepared to designate him a shochet, without supervision, provided only that the knife has been checked beforehand.

### Post-Facto Knife Check

Aval lo badak ve'natan lo — but if the knife was not pre-checked and the responsibility was left to him, lo yishchot — he should not shecht le'chatchila, because checking a knife is an effort, and he might not be motivated to do it properly. Ve'im shachat — if he did shecht, bodek sakino acharav — you check the knife afterwards. The knife can only become worse in the process of shechita, never better — it can become duller or nicked, but it cannot become sharper or smoother on its own. So if the post-shechita inspection finds the knife in good condition, it was certainly in good condition before and during. Nimtza sakin yafeh — mutar le'echol mishchitato. Ve'im lav, assur le'echol mishchitato — and if the knife is not good afterwards, or if it cannot be located to be checked, the shechita is invalid. The unavailability of the knife for post-facto checking thus creates a serious problem that even direct supervision cannot remedy: if you do not have the knife, even if you observed the physical motions of the shechita perfectly, you cannot rule out the possibility that the knife had a nick — dilma be'sakin pguma ka'shachat.

### Cheresh Shoteh Exclusion

As in the previous readings, cheresh shoteh ve'katan are excluded — de'afilu be'di'avad nami lo. Even with a pre-checked knife, even with direct supervision, the concern for the cheresh, shoteh, and katan is not one of motivation or honesty but of technical performance. Shema yish'heh shema yidros ve'shema yachlid — they may have paused, applied downward pressure, or driven the knife laterally in an invalid manner, without knowing it.

### Vechulan Difficulty Again

The final phrase of the Mishnah — vechulan sheshachatu — poses the same difficulty as before. Ilima cheresh shoteh ve'katan — if it refers to the cheresh, shoteh, and katan, halo ka'amar, ve'im shachatu mibei lei — it should have said ve'im shachatu. Ella Yisrael mumar — so it must be referring to the mumar with direct supervision. But ai d'badak sakina ve'yahiv lei, ha amart shochet le'chatchila — if the knife was checked, Rav Ashi already said he may shecht le'chatchila even without direct supervision. And if the knife was not checked, then direct observation of his physical technique does not solve the knife problem: d'leita le'sakina, ki acherim ro'in oto mai havei — if the knife is not available to check, what does it matter that observers watched him? Kashya — this too remains difficult.

---

## Ravina: Expertise & Expe…

### Ravina I: Expertise

Ravina now offers a fourth reading of the Mishnah, one that does not focus on unusual categories of people — tamei, Kuti, mumar — but on the general requirements that apply to any person who wishes to shecht. Ravina proposes two distinct criteria, each representing a separate version of his statement. The first is that of the mumcheh — expertise in the law. Ravina amar hachi katani: hakol shochtin, hakol mumchin shochtin — everybody may shecht who is mumcheh, expert in the laws of shechita. Ve'af al pi she'ein muchzakin — even without experience, provided that knowledge is established.

B'meh devarim amurim — when is this true? She'yodim bo she'yode'a lomar hilchot shechitah — when it is known that he can articulate the halachot of shechita, meaning he has been tested and demonstrated his knowledge. Aval ein yodim bo she'yode'a lomar hilchot shechitah — if his expertise has not been established, lo yishchot — he may not shecht.

### Testing Mechanism

Ve'im shachat — if he shechted without prior testing, bodkin oto — you test him after the fact. Im yode'a lomar hilchot shechitah — if he passes the test, mutar le'echol mishchitato. We assume he did not learn the laws in the last ten minutes, so passing the post-facto test is meaningful evidence that he knew the laws at the time of the shechita. Ve'im lav — if he fails the test or cannot be tested at all, assur le'echol mishchitato.

### Cheresh Knowledge Gap

Chutz mecheresh shoteh ve'katan — ve'afilu be'di'avad nami lo. And here there is a notable twist: even if the cheresh, shoteh, or katan could somehow pass a knowledge test, their shechita remains invalid. Shema yish'eh shema yidros shema yachlid — for them, we are not merely concerned with what they know abstractly, but with what they are capable of doing in practice. Their age or disability makes it specifically likely that they will be unable to execute the shechita technically even if they can articulate the laws. This is a meaningful distinction: they might pass the exam in flying colors, yet still not be trusted to hold the knife.

### Vechulan Under Ravina

On Ravina's reading, the final phrase vechulan sheshachatu ahai — what does it refer to? Ilima cheresh shoteh ve'katan — it cannot mean them, because we were just discussing them. Ella she'ein mumchin — it refers to someone who has not been tested as an expert. Be'bodkin oto sagi — for him, post-facto testing suffices. But de'leika kaman de'livdekei — if he is no longer around to be tested, then direct observation of his shechita is sufficient. And here is an important principle: someone who was not tested beforehand or afterward is no worse than a cheresh, shoteh, or katan in this regard. As long as the shechita was directly observed and performed correctly, it stands. An implicit assumption throughout is that the act of shechita, when directly observed, yields sufficient information to determine whether it was done correctly — in combination, of course, with checking the knife.

Tosafot raises a sharp question here: the Gemara speaks of a case where the shochet cannot be found afterward. But it does not discuss a more extreme case — where the shochet is found and fails the test. Tosafot points out that the Gemara should have noted this even more obvious case: if direct observation of the shechita is what saves the situation when the person cannot be tested at all, then surely it would save the situation even when he was tested and failed. Tosafot does not fully resolve this, but the implication seems to be that direct observation works for all cases where the concern is knowledge-based — which would include the adult who does not know the laws — just as it works for the cheresh, shoteh, and katan.

### Ravina II: Experience

Ika de'amri — others say a different version of Ravina's statement: hakol muchzakin shochtin — everybody who is experienced may shecht. Muchzakin af al pi she'ein mumchin — experience suffices even without formal knowledge testing. This is the inverse of the first version: where the first version said knowledge without experience is sufficient, the second says experience without verified knowledge is sufficient.

The Gemara is careful to explain what muchzak means here: she'shachtu lefanenu shtei ve'shalosh pe'amim, ve'lo nitalef — they have shechted before us two or three times and did not faint in the process. The concern about fainting is specific: if a shochet faints during the shechita, the interruption itself invalidates the shechita through the prohibition of shehiyah — pausing. So the requirement for witnessed prior experience is designed to establish that this person can see the shechita through without losing composure.

### Experience Witnessed

Aval lo shachat lefanenu shtei ve'shalosh pe'amim — if prior experience has not been witnessed, lo yishchot — he should not shecht, shema yitalef — lest he faint. The concern is not only about the dramatic case of full unconsciousness; even a momentary loss of control or a reflexive recoil upon first confronting the act could cause an invalid pause or pressure.

### Self-Report Be'diavad

Ve'im shachat ve'amar bari li she'lo nitalafti — if he went ahead and shechted and declares, "I know I did not faint," shechitato kesheira — his shechita is valid be'di'avad. We take his word for it. This is a considerable chiddush. Someone presents himself to shecht — we have not tested his knowledge, and we have not witnessed his prior experience — he shechts, and he reports that he performed correctly without fainting. Be'di'avad, we trust him. The underlying principle the Gemara will invoke momentarily is rov hametzuyim eitzel shechitah mumchin hein — most people who have the confidence to step forward and shecht actually know what they are doing. Nobody would typically approach a large animal with a knife unless they had at least some grounding in the laws and practice. This rov provides the baseline of reliability that makes the self-report meaningful.

Chutz mecheresh shoteh ve'katan — de'afilu be'di'avad nami lo, shema yish'hu shema yidresu ve'shema yachlidu. For them, the concern is not whether they fainted but whether they are capable of performing the technical act correctly at all — and that cannot be resolved through their own report.

Ve'chulan sheshachtu ve'acherim ro'in otan — and anyone who shechted with direct observation is valid. The same difficulty about this phrase recurs. Ilima cheresh, shoteh, ve'katan lo kai — we were discussing them. Ela ashe'eino munchzak — it is referring to someone who is not known to be experienced. Ve'amarta be'bari li sagi — his self-report would suffice if he were present. D'leita d'nishaylei — but if he is no longer around to report, direct observation suffices.

---

## Reconciliation & Debate

### Tuma'ah Rejection

The Gemara now turns to explain why each Amora did not adopt the approaches of the others. Ravina and Rabbah bar Ulla — the latter having offered the first answer regarding tuma — did not use the readings of Abaye, Rava, and Rav Ashi because, as we noted, the phrase vechulan remained difficult in all of those readings. As for why the others did not say like Rabbah bar Ulla's tuma answer: le'hach lishna de'amart hacha ikkar — according to the version that says the tuma ruling is primarily located here, the response is addaraba hatam ikkar — on the contrary, it properly belongs in Zevachim where kodashim are discussed. And le'hach lishna de'amart hatam ikkar — according to the version that says the tuma ruling belongs in Zevachim and was brought here only incidentally — ve'hacha aidi de'tana tamei be'chullin tana nami tamei be'mukdashim — the deeper problem is that tamei be'chullin gufah lo itztaricha leh. There is no need for the Mishnah to address a tamei person shechting chullin at all. Even chullin she'na'asu al taharat kodesh — chullin treated with the purity standards of hekdesh — lav ke'kodesh dami. It does not attain the halakhic status of kodesh. There is no genuine prohibition for a tamei person to engage with it. The entire tuma framework is simply not relevant to chullin, which is why the others found that answer uninteresting and inapplicable.

### Ravina Rejection I

As for why the others did not adopt Ravina's readings — le'hach lishna de'amar mumchin in she'ein mumchin lo — according to the version that knowledge is required and must be verified: rov metzuyin eitzel shechitah mumchin hein. Most people who present themselves to perform shechita do in fact know the laws. It would be extraordinary for someone to step forward and attempt to shecht without any knowledge of what is required. We therefore operate with the presumption that knowledge exists and do not require formal testing to establish it. The other Amoraim agree that knowledge is essential — they simply do not agree that we must actively verify it. The presumption suffices.

### Ravina Rejection II

Le'hach lishna de'amar muchzakin in she'ein muchzakin lo — according to the version that experience must be witnessed — le'allufei lo chashinan — we are not concerned about fainting. This is, frankly, the most surprising of the conclusions. It holds that someone who has mastered the laws of shechita may be handed a knife and entrusted to shecht an animal for the first time — with no prior observed practice — and his shechita is valid. The reasoning is that knowledge of the law implies practical competence. If someone truly knows what is required at every stage of the shechita, we trust that he will be able to execute it correctly. The concern about fainting or loss of composure is not applied to someone who is established as knowing the laws. This is a far-reaching chiddush: the knowledge criterion and the experience criterion are not independent — knowledge is held to entail practical ability, at least to the degree the halacha requires.

### Rav Ashi on Kuti

Rav Ashi did not adopt the approaches of Abaye or Rava regarding the Kuti: kasavar Kuti gerei arayot hein — he holds that Kutim are not genuine converts but gerei arayot, converts motivated by fear of the lions, as recorded in Yirmiyahu. They are therefore not Jewish. If they are not Jewish, they are categorically excluded from shechita regardless of supervision level, and the entire framework built around the Kuti's reliability is irrelevant.

### Abaye on Mumar

Abaye did not adopt Rav Ashi's reading about the mumar: lo svira lei haderava — he does not hold like Rava's ruling that pre-checking the knife suffices to render the mumar's shechita trustworthy. Abaye holds that a person who regularly eats non-kosher meat cannot simply be handed a pre-checked knife and trusted to shecht for others. The removal of the incentive through the pre-checked knife is insufficient in Abaye's view; direct supervision remains necessary.

### Rava's Polemic

Finally — ela Rava, mai tama lo amar kishmayse? — why did Rava himself not explain the Mishnah as being about the mumar, as Rav Ashi did, given that Rava was the one who stated the original ruling about the mumar and the pre-checked knife? The Gemara answers: lidvarei de'Abaye ka'amar velei lo svira lei — Rava was speaking polemically, responding to Abaye's position. Rava's argument about yotzei ve'nichnas was directed at Abaye, challenging his requirement for constant supervision in the Kuti case. Rava was not laying out his own preferred reading of the Mishnah in that context, but arguing against Abaye's framework. Had Rava been presenting his own reading of the Mishnah independently, he would have explained it as Rav Ashi did — in terms of the mumar and the pre-checked knife. In that reading he personally agrees, but his contribution to this sugya was a polemical one, responding to what he saw as an overreach in Abaye's supervision requirements.

What has emerged from today's daf is a comprehensive introduction to some of the central concerns of Masechet Chullin. Through the fiction of explaining the Mishnah's le'chatchila and be'di'avad structure, the Gemara has surveyed the formal requirements of the shechita implement, the question of who may shecht, the degree of supervision required to establish reliability, and the interplay between knowledge, experience, and presumption in determining who may be entrusted with the act of shechita.

---

---

# Hullin 4

## Samaritan Shechita

### Hakol Shochtin Overview

Daf 4 opens by returning to the Mishna's phrase *hakol shochtin* — "all may slaughter" — and the range of interpretations that phrase invites. The most consequential cases are those involving two categories of people whose trustworthiness is not assured: the Samaritan (*kuti*) and the Jew who is indifferent to *kashrut*. Beyond the question of trustworthiness, there is also the prior question of basic qualification: must a slaughterer be tested for knowledge? Must he have demonstrated prior experience? These questions will be taken up in turn.

### Samaritan Slaughter Rules

The Gemara opens with a *tanu rabbanan*: *shechitas kuti muteres* — the slaughter of a Samaritan is permissible. This is qualified immediately: *bameh devarim amurim? keshe-yisrael omeid al gabav* — when does this hold? Only when a Jew is directly standing over him and supervising. But if a Jew came after the fact and found that the Samaritan had already slaughtered — *avo u'metza'o sheshachat* — then a test is required. The operative concern is that a Samaritan may slaughter properly for his own consumption but may not trouble himself to do so when slaughtering for others. To resolve this, one takes a *kezayis* of the meat and offers it to the Samaritan himself. If he eats it, one may eat from his *shechita*; if he refuses, one may not.

### Testing Samaritan Trust

The *braisa* then extends this principle to a parallel case: *matza beyado dikuy shel tzipporim* — if a Jew finds in the Samaritan's possession a bundle of slaughtered birds. Here too, one cuts off the head of one of the birds and offers it to the Samaritan. If he eats it, the entire batch is permitted; if not, it is forbidden. On its surface this seems identical to the meat case, but as the Gemara will explain, the bird case introduces complications that make it considerably more interesting.

---

## Abaye-Rava Debate

### Excluded Middle

The *braisa* has now established two clear cases: direct supervision (*yisrael omeid al gabav*), which renders the *shechita* permissible, and no supervision at all, which requires the eating-test. But a middle case is conspicuously absent — what about a Jew who pops in and out periodically (*yotzei venichnas*) without standing over the Samaritan continuously? The *braisa* addresses the two extremes and leaves the middle open. This is what Aristotle might call the excluded middle: the *braisa* says nothing about the intermediate case, and that silence becomes the ground for dispute between Abaye and Rava.

### Abaye: Direct Only

*Abaye dayik mei'reisha* — Abaye draws his inference from the beginning of the *braisa*. The *reisha* states that the *shechita* is permitted only *keshe-Yisrael omeid al gabav*, when a Jew is directly standing over the Samaritan. From this, Abaye infers: *ta'ama deYisrael omeid al gabav, aval yotzei venichnas lo* — the reason it is permitted is specifically because of direct standing supervision; anything less, even *yotzei venichnas*, would not suffice.

### Rava: Periodic OK

*Rava dayik mei'seifa* — Rava draws his inference from the end of the *braisa*. The *seifa* tells us that a problem arises only when a Jew *came and found* the meat already slaughtered — *ba u'metza'o sheshachat* — with no prior oversight whatsoever. From this, Rava infers: *ta'ama deba u'metza'o sheshachat, aval yotzei venichnas shapir dami* — only total absence of supervision is disqualifying; anything better than that, including periodic supervision, is acceptable.

### Abaye Explains Seifa

The Gemara challenges each position in turn. *ul'abaye kasha seifa* — how does Abaye account for the *seifa*, which seems to imply that anything better than no supervision would be acceptable? Abaye responds: *yotzei venichnas nami bo matzo kare lei* — popping in and out is effectively equivalent to having come and found the meat already slaughtered. It is, in Abaye's view, tantamount to no supervision at all, and that is precisely why the *seifa* does not need to address it separately.

### Rava Explains Reisha

*Ul'Rava kasha reisha* — how does Rava account for the *reisha*, which speaks of *omeid al gabav* and seems to require direct supervision? Rava responds symmetrically: *yotzei venichnas nami k'omed al gabav dami* — periodic supervision is equivalent to direct standing supervision. The *reisha* did not need to enumerate *yotzei venichnas* explicitly because that case is obviously subsumed within the category of adequate supervision. In the end, the *braisa* describes only the two poles. Each *amora* reads the missing middle through his own interpretive lens: Abaye assimilates it to the bottom, Rava to the top.

This dispute has practical resonance for questions of *hashgacha* in the contemporary world. *yotzei venichnas* and *mashgiach temidi* represent two distinct models of supervision, and which is required depends on the level of concern — both intentional and unintentional — in any given setting. The distinction between *fleishig* and *milchig* restaurant supervision, for instance, tracks this same logic, even if no single line in the Gemara maps directly onto that contemporary ruling.

---

## Bird Head Test

### Birds Example

Returning now to the case of the bundle of birds: *kiyotzei bo* — similarly, if a Jew finds a Samaritan holding a bundle of slaughtered birds, one cuts off the head of one and offers it to him to eat. If he eats it, the entire bundle is permitted.

### One Head Problem

The Gemara raises an obvious difficulty: *leichush dilma hai hu dehavi shachit shapir* — perhaps the Samaritan slaughtered some birds properly, intending them for himself or his family, and slaughtered others improperly, intending them for others. If so, how can eating one head tell us anything reliable about the rest of the batch? The Samaritan could simply know which bird he slaughtered properly and eat that one strategically.

### Rav Menasha Hiding

*Amar Rav Menasha* — Rav Menasha resolves the difficulty: *bemachnisam tachat kenafav* — one hides all the birds under one's cloak, concealing them from the Samaritan's view, then extracts a single head without the Samaritan seeing which one was selected. Since he cannot know which bird is being tested, if he is willing to eat it, one can infer that all the birds were slaughtered properly.

### Mark Problem

The Gemara presses further: *vedilma simana hava yaiv leh begaveh* — perhaps the Samaritan anticipated this and placed a hidden mark on the properly slaughtered birds, allowing him to identify the good ones even when their heads are presented to him. The concealment alone would then be insufficient.

### Mashing Solution

*Amar Rav Mesharshaya* — Rav Mesharshaya provides the final answer: *demimasmas leh mimusmei* — one mushed the head thoroughly into an undifferentiated mass before presenting it. Any mark the Samaritan may have made would be obliterated, and only then, having eliminated the possibility of strategic identification, can one present the head to him and draw a reliable inference from his willingness to eat it.

---

## Samaritan Standards

### Written vs. Oral

The Gemara now shifts to a deeper question underlying all of the above. The assumption throughout has been that if a Samaritan slaughters for himself, he does so correctly — the only concern was whether he would extend that care to meat intended for others. But what is the basis for that assumption? A new challenge is raised: *vedilma kasavri Kutim ein shechitah le'of min HaTorah* — perhaps Samaritans believe there is no biblical requirement of *shechita* for birds at all. The concern is rooted in the nature of Samaritan authority: they defer to the written *torah* rather than to rabbinic tradition. With respect to large animals, the *torah* explicitly uses the verb of slaughter — *vezavachta*. But for birds, no such verb appears. Given that Samaritans are thought to be more careful about matters that are written than those that depend on oral tradition, perhaps they do not recognize any laws of *shechita* for birds at all — even when slaughtering for their own consumption.

### Five Defects

The Gemara's rebuttal begins by taking stock of the five major ways in which a *shechita* can be rendered invalid: *shehiyah* — pausing mid-stroke before the cut is complete; *drasah* — applying downward pressure rather than allowing the sharpness of the blade to do the cutting; *chaladah* — tunneling, meaning inserting the knife between the trachea and esophagus rather than cutting them from the outside; *hagramah* — slaughtering too high or too low along the neck; and *ikkur* — uprooting, tearing out one of the *simanim* before severing it. These are the essential technical requirements of valid *shechita*.

### All Unwritten

The Gemara's rebuttal is then put sharply: *aboch veta'amech* — if your concern is that Samaritans disregard laws that are not explicitly written in the *torah*, then this concern applies universally. *shehiyah, drasah, chaladah, hagramah, ve'ikkur — mi ketivan?* Are any of these written? None of these laws appear explicitly in the *torah*. Yet we assume that Jews who accept the oral tradition observe them. If the concern about the unwritten renders all *shechita* laws suspect for Samaritans, then we could never trust their *shechita* for any animal whatsoever.

### Embrace Principle

The resolution is: *keivan de'achziki behu achziki* — once a community has embraced a practice, the fact of that embrace is what grounds our trust, regardless of whether the practice is explicitly written. The principle is applied here: just as Samaritans have embraced the general laws of *shechita* for animals, so too, if they have embraced *shechita* for birds, that embrace is sufficient grounds for trusting them. The question thus becomes not whether something is written, but whether it has been adopted in practice — and that question, the Gemara now reveals, is itself the subject of a *tannaic* dispute.

---

## Samaritan Matza Debate

### Matza Permitted

The Gemara cites a *braisa*: *matzas Kuti muteres* — Samaritan *matza* is permissible — *ve'adam yotzei bah yedei chovaso b'Pesach* — and one may even fulfill the biblical obligation of eating *matza* on the *seder* night with it. This is not as obvious as it sounds. One might have thought that while Samaritan *matza* is not *chametz*, it nevertheless lacks the *shimur* — the intentional watching to prevent leavening — that is required for *matza* used to fulfill the *mitzvah* on the *seder* night. The *tanna kamma* holds that their *matza* has even this quality and may be used *l'chatchila*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Strict

*Rabbi Eliezer oser* — Rabbi Eliezer forbids it outright. His reasoning is that Samaritans are not expert in the precise details of *mitzvah* observance — *lfi she'ein beki'in bedikdukei mitzvot* — and therefore one cannot trust that they exercise the scrupulousness necessary to prevent the *matza* from becoming *chametz* in the first place. The Gemara notes that the formulation *lo beki'ei* — they are not expert — is technically imprecise as a characterization of Rabbi Eliezer's position. His actual view, as consistently understood, is more sweeping: even in areas Samaritans do observe, one can never be assured they observe them with the full level of care required by *halacha*, precisely because they operate outside the rabbinic system and do not submit to its authority. The problem is not ignorance of specific rules; it is the inability to verify scrupulousness in any instance.

### Rabban Shimon Lenient

Then comes the most striking position in the *braisa*: *rabban shimon ben gamliel omer, kol mitzvah she'hechziku bah kutim harbeh medakdekin bah yoter mi'yisrael* — any *mitzvah* that the Samaritans have embraced as their own, they observe with greater scrupulousness than Jews. This is a remarkable statement. The explanation is not difficult to understand psychologically: when a community does not observe everything, the areas it does observe can take on heightened significance. Those who observe fewer things may observe each one with an intensity that those who observe everything cannot always maintain. The phenomenon is recognizable.

### Core Debate

The Gemara notes that the positions of the *tanna kamma* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appear at first to be identical — both permit Samaritan *matza* — and asks what distinguishes them. The answer requires the Gemara to construct the underlying logic of each position.

### Tanna Kamma Position

*Ika beinaihu delo ketiva ve'achziku bah* — the difference lies in a case where a law is not written in the *torah* but Samaritans are known to have embraced it, or conversely, where it is written but they are not known to have embraced it. *tanna kamma savar keivan dechtiva, af al gav delo achziku bah* — the *tanna kamma* holds that what is written in the *torah* may be trusted even without confirmed embrace; since it appears in the written text, one may assume Samaritans observe it. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the opposite: *ei achziku ein, ei lo achziku lo* — only what is demonstrably embraced may be trusted, and whether it is written is irrelevant. Conversely, something not written but demonstrably embraced may be trusted according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel but not according to the *tanna kamma*.

The Gemara thus frames the core dispute: the *tanna kamma* anchors trust in the written *torah*, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel anchors it in demonstrable practice.

### Why Clear Rules

This raises an obvious challenge: once one is prepared to trust Samaritans at all — as the *tanna kamma* clearly is — why not simply do the fact-finding and determine what they actually embrace, as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel proposes? The empirical approach seems more accurate. One possible answer is that *halacha* often prefers clear, stable rules over case-by-case fact-finding. What Samaritans embrace can vary from community to community and from generation to generation. A random sample may not be representative. Written *torah* provides a fixed, verifiable criterion. The trade-off is that the rule will not always track the facts, but clear rules have their own value in a legal system. It may even be the case that the *tanna kamma* requires both: that a law be written *and* that Samaritans be known to have embraced it — a reading that would make the *tanna kamma*'s position somewhat more intelligible, combining the clarity of the written criterion with the empirical grounding of the embrace criterion.

---

## Mumar Ochel Nevelot

### Rava: Check Knife

*Gufa* — the Gemara now turns to the other major case: the Jew who is personally indifferent to *kashrut*. *amar rava: yisrael mumar ochel nevelot l'teiavon* — a Jew who has abandoned observance of *kashrut* not out of ideological rejection but out of appetite and indifference, eating non-*shechted* meat when it is convenient or cheaper — *bodek sakin venosen lo* — one checks his knife and gives it to him, and *mutar le'echol mishchitato* — one may eat from his *shechita* without even standing over him.

### Heter vs. Issur Logic

*Mai ta'ama?* — what is the reason? *keivan d'ika heter ve'issura, lo shavek heiteira ve'achil issura* — since there are two options before him, one permitted and one forbidden, and all other things being equal he has no reason to prefer the *issur* over the *heter*, we assume he will not abandon the *heter* for the *issur* without some incentive. This man eats non-*shechted* meat when it is cheaper or more convenient. But when there is no advantage to doing so — when the *shechita* itself costs him no additional effort — we assume he will do it correctly.

### Effort Threshold

The Gemara presses: if the principle is that all things being equal he will prefer *heter*, then why is a knife-check necessary at all? Why not simply trust him even without it? The answer: *mitrach lo tarach* — he will not exert himself. Without being given a pre-checked knife, he may not take the trouble to ensure his knife is sharp and nick-free. That is an effort, and if an effort is required, the *lo shavek heiteira* logic no longer applies. But given a properly checked knife and no added burden of care, the correct *shechita* is essentially the default — once one knows how to do it properly, there is no greater muscular or practical effort involved in doing it correctly than incorrectly. Under those conditions, we rely on the presumption that he will choose the *heter*.

---

## Chametz After Pesach

### Chametz Permitted

The students bring a *braisa* as support for Rava's position: *chamtzan shel ovdei aveirah achar haPesach mutar* — the *chametz* belonging to Jews who kept *chametz* in their homes throughout *pesach* is permitted after *pesach*. This is striking because *chametz she'avar alav haPesach* — *chametz* that remained in Jewish possession over *pesach* — is in principle prohibited after the fact. Yet the *braisa* declares it permitted.

### The Swap Logic

The reason given is: *mipnei shehein machlifin* — because these violators exchange their *chametz* for a neighbor's *chametz* after *pesach*. The reasoning reveals a remarkable psychology. These are Jews who transgressed *chametz* on *pesach*, a violation carrying the penalty of *kares*. Yet after *pesach*, when the stake is considerably lower — perhaps only a rabbinic prohibition — they go out of their way to swap their *chametz she'avar alav haPesach* for ordinary post-*Pesach chametz*, so that what they eat carries no halachic taint at all. The *lo shavek heiteira* principle operates here with no effort required: swapping *chametz* costs nothing additional, and so they do it. This corroborates Rava's position that those who are indifferent to *halacha* in one context will nonetheless choose the *heter* over the *issur* when no effort is required.

### Gemara Precision

The Gemara initially assumes this *braisa* follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that *chametz she'avar alav haPesach* is a biblical prohibition, and reasons that if we trust these violators even for a biblical matter, this supports Rava all the more. The Gemara then considers whether the *braisa* might follow Rabbi Shimon, who holds this prohibition is only rabbinic, and asks whether the *lo shavek heiteira* principle would then be limited to rabbinic matters only. The Gemara responds that if that were so, the text would have employed the phrase *shani omer* — "I would say" — indicating a permissive assumption despite uncertainty. Instead, the *braisa* states *mipnei shehein machlifin* — *because* they swap — asserting it as a known fact, not a convenient presumption. Since it says they *definitely* swap, and they do so even for what might be a rabbinic prohibition, this establishes the principle a fortiori for biblical matters: *bedioraita lo kol sheken* — how much more so for a biblical prohibition will a person prefer the *heter* when no effort is required.

### Knowledge vs. Presumption

A distinction emerges from this analysis. There is a difference between saying *shani omer* — I will presume without certainty — and saying *machlifin* — they factually do this. In the former, the leniency would rest on a legal fiction adopted for practical purposes; in the latter, we are asserting something we genuinely hold to be true. The Gemara here insists we are doing the latter. Whether or not an actual investigation was conducted in any individual case, we are asserting as a matter of established fact that this is the behavior, not merely granting ourselves permission to assume it without knowledge.

---

## Tosefta Cases

### Tosefta List

The Gemara now cites a *tosefta* that reads as a direct commentary on the Mishna's *hakol shochtin*: *hakol shochtin, ve'afilu kuti, ve'afilu arel, ve'afilu yisrael mumar* — all may slaughter, including a Samaritan, including an uncircumcised Jew, and including a Jewish *mumar*. The *tosefta* thus enumerates three of the cases the Gemara has been analyzing. What it adds is the category of the *arel* — the uncircumcised Jew.

### Arel Case

*Hai arel heichi dami?* — what type of uncircumcised Jew does the *tosefta* mean? If it refers to someone whose brothers died as a result of circumcision — a family pattern of what we would today recognize as hemophilia — then he was halachically exempt from circumcision, and *hai Yisrael maya hu* — he is a perfectly ordinary Jew whose *shechita* raises no question at all. The *tosefta* must therefore be speaking of someone who deliberately remains uncircumcised despite having no medical exemption — a *mumar l'areilus*.

### One Area Principle

The implicit reasoning of the *tosefta* is: *mumar l'davar echad lo havei mumar l'chol ha-Torah kullah* — rejection of one area of *halacha* does not render a person a *mumar* with respect to the whole *torah* or with respect to any other specific area. The principle reflects a realistic understanding of human psychology: people compartmentalize. A known violator in one domain may be entirely reliable in another, even if the violated domain is technically more severe. The *tosefta* therefore permits this person's *shechita lechatkhila*.

### Mumar L'Kashrut

The Gemara then asks what the *tosefta* adds by mentioning the *yisrael mumar* separately, since that case would appear to be subsumed under *mumar l'davar echad*. The answer is that the *tosefta* must be referring to a *mumar l'oso davar* — someone who has specifically rejected *kashrut* itself. This is then read as a support for Rava's position: that even a Jew who himself eats non-*shechted* meat may be trusted to slaughter for others, provided the knife is checked and no additional effort is required.

---

## Sin Becomes Heter

### Repeat Sin

The Gemara rejects this reading of the *tosefta* as support for Rava. *le'olam eima lach mumar l'oso davar lo* — in fact, a *mumar* who has rejected *kashrut* specifically cannot be trusted for *shechita*, and the *tosefta* must be referring only to rejection of an unrelated area. The Gemara's objection to Rava strikes at the psychological premise underlying his entire position.

### Two Sins Erase

*Keivan d'dash bei k'heteira dami leh* — once a person has repeatedly transgressed, the transgression begins to feel like a *heter* to him. Rava's logic assumed that even the person who eats *neveilot* still maintains some internal distinction between *issur* and *heter* and, all things being equal, will choose the *heter*. But the Gemara says this is not psychologically accurate. The Gemara elsewhere states: *aveirah d'adam over bah ve'shonah, na'aseis lo k'heter* — a sin that a person commits twice becomes like a *heter* in his mind. Once the categories of *issur* and *heter* have collapsed in this domain, there is no longer a preference for *heter*, because he no longer perceives the act as *issur* at all.

### Salanter Coda

Rav Yisrael Salanter added a coda to this principle: do it twice and it becomes like a *heter*; do it three times and it becomes like a *mitzvah*. The capacity of human rationalization is such that repeated behavior is not merely normalized but eventually embraced as positive and proper.

### Cannot Trust Mumar

The consequence for *halacha*: one cannot trust the *shechita* of a *mumar ochel nevelot* precisely because, in his own mental framework, the distinction between kosher and non-kosher meat no longer exists as *issur* and *heter*. He is not a person choosing *heter* over *issur* when the choice is costless — he is a person for whom the category of *issur* in this domain has ceased to exist. Rava's premise therefore does not apply to him.

---

## Mumar Avodas Kochavim

### Idolater Trusted

*Ella mumar l'avodas kochavim* — the *tosefta*'s reference to a *mumar* whose *shechita* is trusted must be referring to a Jew who practices idolatry. *ve-ki-d'rav anani, d'amar rav anani amar shmuel: yisrael mumar l'avodas kochavim mutar* — as Rav Anani said in the name of Shmuel, a Jew who is a *mumar* with respect to *avodas kochavim* may still have his *shechita* trusted. This is a striking ruling: a Jew who worships idols may be trusted for *kashrut* purposes.

### Separate Areas

The logic follows the *mumar l'davar echad* principle in its most striking application. Rejection of one religious domain — even one as fundamental as the rejection of idolatry — does not necessarily entail any change in behavior or attitude in another domain. A Jew who practices idolatry may nonetheless keep a fully kosher home, not because idolatry is treated lightly, but because the categories are conceived as genuinely separate. Just as rejecting *brit milah* does not make one suspect regarding *kashrut*, rejecting monotheism in practice does not in itself alter one's relationship to the laws of *shechita*. The discussion will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Hullin 5

## Mumar & Shechita

### Mumar Categories

We begin at the very last line of 5a. The Gemara arrives at תיובתא דרבנן תיובתא — a decisive refutation of the Rabbinic position — in light of a Baraita establishing that a mumar can serve as a shochet. Two explanations had been offered for this Baraita. The first is that the mumar in question is a mumar ochel neveilos leteavon — someone who violates kashrus out of appetite rather than ideological defiance. The second explanation would have accommodated even a genuine mumar, including an idolater. That second explanation was ultimately rejected by the Gemara on the basis of another Baraita that places the public violator of Shabbat in the same categorical exclusion as an idolater — both are treated as fundamentally invalidated in their personal status. We are therefore left with the first explanation: a person who violates in a single area, even if that area is kashrus itself, is not categorically excluded and may, under the right circumstances, be trusted to perform shechita. This is the position that governs halacha.

### Source for Mumar Exclusi…

The Gemara now raises a pointed question: do we actually derive the exclusion of a mumar from bringing sacrifices from the verse about מכם — "from you," excluding those who have departed from the community — or do we derive it from a different source entirely? In fact, the Gemara notes, there is another pasuk: מעם הארץ, "from the people of the land." The letter mem there is read as partitive — not all members of the people of the land qualify — and this serves as the basis for excluding a mumar, a habitual violator and rebel, from bringing a sin offering.

### Willful Violator Doctrine

Rabbi Shimon Yossi then teaches in the name of Rabbi Shimon a distinct principle derived from the verse, "that which should not be done was done in error, and he is guilty." From this verse, Rabbi Shimon derives that only someone who, had he known the facts, would have refrained from the act — הַשָּׁב מִידִּיעָתוֹ, one who returns upon gaining knowledge — brings a korban for his unintentional sin. But someone who would have sinned anyway even with full awareness — אֵינוֹ שָׁב מִידִּיעָתוֹ — does not bring a korban. The logic is stark: if a person habitually eats treifa and on a given occasion eats meat he believed to be kosher that turned out to be treifa, he brings no korban, because even had he known it was treifa, he would have eaten it regardless.

### Rav Hamnuna's Case

The Gemara then asks: what is the practical difference between the two exclusions — the mumar excluded by virtue of his category, and the person excluded because he would have sinned willfully anyway? Rav Hamnuna answers: the difference emerges in the case of a mumar le'echol cheilev — a habitual eater of forbidden fat — who now accidentally consumes blood. As Tosafot notes, cheilev and dam occupy closely related territory: both are prohibited by the Torah in parallel fashion, both are associated with the korbanot, and both carry the penalty of karet. They belong to the same cluster of behaviors, even though the specific violation differs.

The Gemara does not spell out the analysis explicitly, but the distinction between the two positions is as follows. According to Rabbi Shimon's principle — that the issue is whether this person would have done it anyway — a habitual eater of cheilev can still bring a korban for accidentally eating blood, since for blood specifically he would not have sinned willfully. He eats fat out of habit; blood he avoids. Since he would have refrained had he known, the inadvertent transgression is a genuine shgaga, and he brings a korban. But according to the mumar category — the position that a person's status as a habitual violator in a related domain disqualifies him entirely from bringing a sin offering in that cluster of behaviors — even this person does not bring a korban. Since he is a habitual violator in the sphere of cheilev, and dam belongs to the same halachic family, he is excluded from the sin-offering framework for that entire cluster.

Tosafot is careful to point out that we are not speaking here of the categorical disqualification reserved for idolaters and Shabbat violators. A habitual violator of kashrus does not, as a general matter, lose his personal status in the way an idolater does. What he does lose is his standing to bring a sin offering within the halachic sphere in which he is a willful violator. The two frameworks — categorical disqualification and domain-specific exclusion — operate differently, even if both result in the mumar being barred from bringing a korban.

### Two Exclusion Grounds

Having established these two bases for excluding a mumar, the Gemara asks: why do I need both derivations? Why does the Torah need to teach me the mumar exclusion twice — once from מֵעַם הָאָרֶץ and once from the verse about the willful violator? The Gemara answers: חַד בְּחַטָּאת וְחַד בְּעוֹלָה וּצְרִיכָא — one exclusion applies to a chatat, the sin offering, and the other to an olah, the elevation offering, and both are necessary.

Had the Torah only excluded the mumar from a chatat, one might have argued: a chatat is about atonement, and a willful violator simply does not deserve atonement — that is why he is excluded. But an olah is a gift to God; perhaps even a sinner should be permitted to bring a gift, and the exclusion would not apply. Conversely, had the Torah only excluded the mumar from an olah, one might have argued: an olah is a voluntary offering, and since the mumar has no obligation to bring it, we say he is not entitled to. But a chatat is obligatory — the mumar has sinned, even if inadvertently, and incurred an obligation; perhaps we should accept it, and, as Rashi adds, we should not allow the mumar to benefit from his own sinfulness by being released from an obligation. Therefore both exclusions are necessary, each teaching something the other could not.
