Returning to the issue at hand: the category of person who is categorically excluded in the general halachic sense — from shechita and other areas — is the idolater and the public Shabbat violator. A person who sins in a particular area, even in kashrus, is not globally invalidated. Given appropriate circumstances, even such a person may be trusted to perform shechita.

---

## Behemah Terminology

### Behemah & Insult

The Gemara now pauses to examine a lexical question that arises from the Baraita cited earlier. That Baraita had interpreted the word בְּהֵמָה in a verse about those who may bring korbanot as a reference to sinners — people who are as bad as animals. The Gemara asks: does the word behemah always carry this pejorative meaning?

### Humble Behemah

A counter-example is immediately raised: אָדָם וּבְהֵמָה תוֹשִׁיעַ ה' — "man and beast the Lord will save" — and here the term behemah is clearly used in a positive context, since the verse promises salvation. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains: this verse refers to people who are clever in their intellect, ערומים בדעת, and yet humble themselves like an animal — מַשִּׂימִים עַצְמָן כִּבְהֵמָה — unpretentious and non-arrogant. In this verse, then, behemah carries an admirable connotation.

### Context of Reference

How do we reconcile the two uses? The Gemara distinguishes on the basis of context: הָתָם כְּתִיב אָדָם וּבְהֵמָה, הָכָא בְּהֵמָה לְחוּדֵיהּ כְּתִיב — there, the verse writes "man and beast" together, and since the two are linked, behemah is interpreted in a positive light, as a type of person who shares the animal's quality of humility while retaining human intelligence. Where behemah appears alone, unlinked from adam, it is interpreted negatively, as referring to someone who has degraded himself to an animal-like level through sin.

### Planting Verse

The Gemara, however, will not let the principle stand unchallenged. It raises another verse: וְזָרַעְתִּי אֶת בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע אָדָם וְזֶרַע בְּהֵמָה — "I will plant the house of Israel, the planting of man and the planting of beast." Here adam and behemah appear together, yet the Gemara, drawing on its interpretation in tractate Sotah, reads זֶרַע בְּהֵמָה as a reference to those who are not learned in Torah — an unflattering characterization. Does this not refute the principle that the paired usage is always positive?

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by a close reading: חַלְּקֵי קְרָא — the verse separates the two. It does not say זֶרַע אָדָם וּבְהֵמָה in a single conjoined phrase, as the earlier verse did; rather, it treats them as distinct categories — the planting of man, and separately, the planting of beast. Because they are not syntactically linked but placed in parallel as separate items, the word behemah in this verse stands alone in meaning, and is thus interpreted negatively. The principle is thereby preserved: genuine linkage of adam and behemah yields a positive interpretation; separation — even in apparent proximity — permits the negative reading.

---

## Kuti Shechita

### Rabban Gamliel's Ban

The Gemara returns to the central thread of shechita and the question of who qualifies as a valid shochet. The mumar has been addressed; now the Kuti — the Samaritan — is revisited. Rabbi Chanan said in the name of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, who said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara: רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וּבֵית דִּינוֹ נִמְנוּ עַל שְׁחִיטַת כּוּתִי וְאֲסָרוּהָ — Rabban Gamliel and his beit din took a formal vote and reassessed the status of the Kuti, and they forbade it. The earlier framework, which had permitted reliance on Kuti shechita under certain conditions, was now overturned by a formal rabbinic ruling.

### Observation Question

Rabbi Zeira addressed Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi directly with a pointed question. He asked: שֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁמַע רַבִּי אֶלָּא בְּשֶׁאֵין יִשְׂרָאֵל עוֹמֵד עַל גַּבּוֹ — perhaps the ruling you are reporting applies only when there is no Yisrael standing over the shochet, i.e., no direct observation? The earlier framework had always required either direct observation of the Kuti's shechita or ensuring that the Kuti himself would eat from the same meat. Perhaps, Rabbi Zeira suggested, this ruling of Rabban Gamliel did nothing more than reaffirm that without such observation the shechita is invalid — and stopped short of invalidating Kuti shechita even when directly observed.

### Sharp Response

The response was withering. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi replied: it appears that this rabbi has never properly learned anything in his life. בְּשֶׁאֵין יִשְׂרָאֵל עוֹמֵד עַל גַּבּוֹ לְמֵימְרָא בָּעֵי? — Would that need to be stated at all? The requirement of direct observation when dealing with a Kuti is elementary and universally accepted. If someone is transmitting a ruling attributed all the way back to Rabban Gamliel and his beit din to the effect that Kuti shechita is invalid, the ruling cannot be addressing the already-obvious case of unobserved shechita. It must be addressing direct observation — the only case in which the ruling would tell us something new. The implication is remarkable: Rabban Gamliel and his beit din were declaring the shechita of a Kuti invalid even when a Yisrael stands directly over him and observes every movement. And as the Gemara makes clear, there is really only one category in all of halacha where such a ruling makes sense — a non-Jew, whose shechita is categorically invalid regardless of technical correctness. The implicit conclusion is that Rabban Gamliel's beit din had reclassified the Kutim as non-Jews.

### Later Acceptance

This ruling notwithstanding, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reported in the name of Rav Assi: אֲנִי רָאִיתִי אֶת רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שֶׁאָכַל מִשְּׁחִיטַת כּוּתִי — I saw Rabbi Yochanan eating from the shechita of a Kuti. And Rav Assi himself similarly ate from the shechita of a Kuti. These were later Amoraim, operating after the ruling of Rabban Gamliel and his beit din, yet they consumed meat slaughtered by a Kuti without apparent hesitation.

### Zeira's Confusion

Rabbi Zeira was astonished. He proposed two possible explanations for their behavior. Either — לֹא שְׁמִיעַ לְהוּ — they never received the report of Rabban Gamliel's ruling, and had they heard it they would certainly have accepted it and refrained. Or — שְׁמִיעַ לְהוּ וְלֹא קַבְּלוּהָ — they heard the ruling and deliberately rejected it, holding that the shechita of a Kuti remained valid. Rabbi Zeira did not initially know which of these alternatives was correct.

The Gemara then records that Rabbi Zeira resolved the question for himself: מִסְתַּבְּרָא דִּשְׁמִיעַ לְהוּ וְלֹא קַבְּלוּהָ — it is more plausible that they had heard the ruling and rejected it. The reasoning rests on a principle the Gemara now invokes.

### Tzadikim Principle

The Gemara argues as follows. If Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi had never heard the ruling of Rabban Gamliel, and had they heard it they would have accepted it and treated the meat as treif, then they were in fact eating what they themselves would have considered forbidden food — through no fault of their own, simply because the report never reached them. But this leads to a deeply uncomfortable consequence: הֵיכִי מִסְתַּיְּיעָא מִילְּתָא לְמֵיכַל אִיסּוּרָא — how could God have allowed this to happen, that these righteous figures would eat forbidden food?

The Gemara grounds this reasoning in an explicit principle: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵבִיא תַּקָּלָה עַל יְדֵיהֶם — God does not bring about stumbling through the hands of the righteous. The illustration is the celebrated story of the donkey of Pinchas ben Yair, which refused to eat untithed grain — something the Gemara will return to later on the daf. If God takes such care that even the animals of tzadikim do not consume forbidden food, how much more so — צַדִּיקִים עַצְמָן לֹא כָּל שֶׁכֵּן — would God not allow the tzadikim themselves to inadvertently eat issur. It follows that if Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi did eat from Kuti shechita, it cannot be that they were eating something they would have considered forbidden. They must have heard the ruling and consciously ruled against it — holding that Kuti shechita remained valid.

This principle is significant and, as Tosafot notes, requires careful delimitation. The Gemara does not claim that tzadikim never sin or never err. Tosafot points out that there are cases in the Gemara where tzadikim make mistakes in other domains. The principle as deployed here — and as it will recur later in the daf — is specifically about forbidden food. And this narrow application reflects a broader halachic orientation: that the consumption of forbidden food is not simply a sin like other sins, but carries some additional dimension — physical, spiritual, or both — that makes it a category apart. This is why, for instance, the question of feeding infants non-kosher food is treated differently from allowing infants to perform other prohibited acts before the age of chinuch: treif food may be understood to have a corrupting effect that goes beyond the technical prohibition, an effect that the Gemara treats as an objective concern independent of culpability.

### Final Acceptance

The Gemara then draws the final inference about Rabbi Zeira's own position. Had Rabbi Zeira maintained his initial suggestion — that Rabban Gamliel's ruling only addressed unobserved Kuti shechita — he would have had no difficulty explaining why Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi ate the meat. He could simply have said: they ate it when directly observing, and the ruling says nothing about that case. The very fact that Rabbi Zeira was troubled, that he was forced to consider whether they had never heard the ruling or had rejected it, demonstrates that he had already abandoned his earlier position. He accepted the sharp rebuttal — that Rabban Gamliel's ruling clearly speaks to direct observation as well — and therefore could not simply wave aside the behavior of Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi. אֶלָּא לָאו שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ קִבְּלָהּ מִינֵּיהּ — we therefore conclude that Rabbi Zeira accepted the ruling as applying even when a Yisrael stands directly over the Kuti shochet.

The overall picture that emerges from this extended sugya is layered. There is a firm ruling, attributed to Rabban Gamliel and his beit din, that Kuti shechita is invalid under all circumstances — a ruling that implicitly treats Kutim as non-Jews. Rabbi Zeira ultimately accepts this ruling in its full scope. Yet even generations later, prominent Amoraim such as Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi ate from Kuti shechita, having apparently concluded that the ruling should not be followed. The sugya thus presents a halachic controversy that did not resolve uniformly across all authorities, even well after Rabban Gamliel's formal decree.

---

---

# Hullin 5b

## Mumarim & Sacrifices

### Mumar Explanations

We resume at the very last line of Amud 1, where the Gemara presents a Baraita establishing that a Mumar can serve as a Shochet, and offers two explanations for this ruling. The first explanation is that we are dealing with a Mumar Ochel Nevelot Le-Te'avon — someone who simply does not care about Kashrut and eats forbidden meat for his own pleasure. The second explanation involves a full-fledged Mumar, even one who worships idols.

### Idolaters & Shabbat

The Gemara ultimately rejects the second explanation based on a Baraita that places the public violator of Shabbat in the same category as the idolater. This reflects the well-established principle that an idolater and a public Shabbat violator are categorically excluded from a range of Mitzvot, their very personal status having been fundamentally compromised. We are therefore left with the first explanation: a person who violates a single area — even Kashrut — retains sufficient standing to perform Shechita under the right circumstances. The Ochel Nevelot Le-Te'avon has not been categorically excluded, while the idolater and public Shabbat violator have been, and that is indeed where the Halacha stands.

### Source of Exclusion

Picking up at the very last line, the Gemara raises a pointed question: *ve-ha me-hakha naffka me-hatam naffka?* — do we really derive the exclusion of a Mumar from bringing sacrifices from this particular verse about *mi-kem*? The Gemara notes that the exclusion appears to come from elsewhere entirely. The verse in the context of the sin offering reads *me-am ha-aretz* — "from the people of the land" — where the word *mem* signals a limitation: *prat le-mumar*, excluding a habitual violator or rebel from bringing a sin offering.

### Two Exclusions

A second source of exclusion is derived from the verse *asher lo te-asena bi-shgaga ve-ashem* — "which should not be done, and he did so in error and is guilty." From this the Gemara derives: *ha-shav mi-da'ato mevi korban al shigagato* — one who, had he been aware of what he was doing, would have refrained and corrected himself, is obligated to bring a Korban for his unintentional sin. But *eino shav mi-da'ato* — one who would not have changed his behavior even had he known the facts — does not bring a Korban for that error. The logic is stark: if a person routinely eats treif and this time happened to eat something non-kosher by accident, he cannot bring a Chatas, because even had he known it was forbidden, he would have eaten it anyway. So we have two categories of exclusion: the Mumar whose habitual sinning disqualifies him, and the person who would have sinned deliberately regardless.

### Rav Hamnuna Case

The Gemara then asks *mai beinaihu* — what practical difference exists between these two categories of exclusion? After all, both seem to say that a habitual sinner does not bring a Korban. Rav Hamnuna answers: *mumar le-ekhol chelev ve-hevi korban al hadam ika beinaihu* — the difference emerges in the case of someone who is a habitual violator in one area but accidentally sins in a related but distinct area. Take a person who regularly eats Cheilev — forbidden fat — but never eats Dam, forbidden blood. This time he accidentally consumed blood.

As Tosafot point out, Cheilev and Dam are a closely linked cluster of prohibitions: the Torah addresses both in a similar manner, both are associated with the sacrificial rites, and both carry the penalty of Karet. They inhabit the same halachic universe, even though they are distinct. Now, does such a person bring a Korban for his accidental consumption of blood? According to the reasoning of *eino shav mi-da'ato* — "he would have done it anyway" — this person would actually be *obligated* to bring a Korban, since he would *not* have eaten blood intentionally; his habitual violation is of fat, not blood. But according to the reasoning of categorical Mumar status, since his ongoing sinful pattern falls within this cluster of related behaviors, his status as a Mumar in that domain excludes him from the sin offering even for errors in the adjacent area.

### Status vs Unworthiness

This distinction carries real weight. Tosafot emphasize that the categorical Mumar exclusion — the kind we have been discussing in the context of idolaters and Shabbat violators — does not apply here. This person is not globally invalidated on account of eating Cheilev. What he is, rather, is excluded from bringing sin offerings within this specific cluster of behaviors. The two exclusions thus operate differently: one is a broad disqualification of personal status, and the other is a targeted exclusion from the Korban process in a particular domain of conduct.

One might ask how such a status would even be established — would it require testimony before a Beit Din? Would it have to be "public" in some formal sense? There is indeed discussion in Halacha about exactly these questions, particularly concerning the Shabbat violator and what "in public" requires. But it is clear that the category does not require any formal proclamation or public marking of the person.

### Chatas vs Olah

The Gemara then asks: since we now have two overlapping exclusions of Mumarim from Korbanos, why do we need both? The answer is *chad be-chatas ve-chad be-olah u-tzricha* — one exclusion applies to the Chatas and one to the Olah, and both are necessary.

Had the Torah only taught the exclusion regarding a Chatas, one might have said: the Chatas is denied because *mishum de-chapparah hi* — it is an instrument of atonement, and an unrepentant sinner does not deserve atonement. But an Olah, which is *de-doron hu* — a gift to God — might perhaps still be accepted even from a habitual violator; there seems less affront in offering a gift. Had the Torah only taught the exclusion regarding an Olah, one might have argued: the Mumar is excluded from an Olah because *de-lav chovah hu* — he has no binding obligation to bring it, so there is no reason to force the issue. But a Chatas is *de-chovah hu* — it is an obligatory offering — and one might think we should still insist that he bring it. Moreover, as Rashi notes, we do not want the sinner to benefit by being let off the hook from an obligation simply because of his sinful status. Hence *tzricha* — both exclusions are needed.

Tosafot further notes that these are not truly parallel exclusions: one involves categorical disqualification of personal status (as with the idolater or Shabbat violator), while the other is a more specific exclusion rooted in the inappropriateness of bringing a Korban when one is a willful violator in the relevant area. Regardless, both exclusions together establish the full scope of who is barred from the Korban process.

To return to the application for Shechita: the type of person categorically excluded in all matters is the idolater and the Shabbat violator. But a person who sins in a particular area — even Kashrut itself — may under the right circumstances still be trusted to perform Shechita properly.

---

## Behemah Terminology

### Behemah Meanings

The Gemara pauses at this juncture to address a point raised by the earlier Baraita. That Baraita had derived from the word *behemah* in the verse about Korbanos that even people who are sinners, described as being "like animals," may still bring sacrifices. But does the word *behemah* necessarily carry a negative, derogatory connotation? The Gemara challenges this assumption: *ve-hakesiv Adam U'Behemah Toshiya Hashem* — the verse in Tehillim states "man and beast God will save," and surely that is a positive context, not a pejorative one.

The Gemara resolves this by citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *eilu bnei adam she-hen arumim be-da'as u-mesimin atzmam ke-behemah* — this verse refers to people who are clever in their intellect but nonetheless conduct themselves with the humility and lowliness of an animal, suppressing arrogance. Here *behemah* is unambiguously positive. So why does the earlier Baraita interpret it negatively as referring to sinners?

### Context Matters

The Gemara draws a clean hermeneutical line: *hasam kesiv Adam u-Behemah, hacha Behemah lechudei kesiv* — there, the verse links Adam and Behemah together, so we read the animal as a type of human being: humble, non-arrogant, like an animal. Here, where the word Behemah stands alone, we interpret it negatively, as referring to sinners.

The Gemara presses the point further: is it always the case that where the verse says "man and beast" together the meaning is positive? A counter-example appears in Yirmiyahu: *ve-zarati es Beis Yisrael zera adam ve-zera Behemah* — "I will plant the house of Israel, the planting of man and the planting of beast." The Gemara in Sotah interprets this verse as referring to people who are learned in Torah alongside those who are not — meaning *behemah* there refers to ignoramuses, which is not a flattering characterization. Yet this is a verse that pairs *adam* and *behemah*!

The Gemara answers: *hachalki kra, zera adam lechudei ve-zera Behemah lechudei* — examine the verse more carefully and you will see that it does not actually fuse the two; it enumerates them separately — "the planting of man" and "the planting of beast" — unlike the earlier verse which said *adam u-behemah* in a single unified phrase. Where they are truly linked, *behemah* takes on a positive human connotation; where they are listed separately, the word reverts to a negative register.

---

## Kutim Shechita

### Rabban Gamliel Ban

Returning to the central theme of the sugya — who is and is not acceptable as a Shochet — the Gemara now revisits the case of the Kuti, the Samaritan. Earlier discussion had explored the degree to which Kutim could be trusted: whether they observe the laws, whether they observe them with sufficient scrupulousness, and whether one needs to guard against them deliberately sabotaging the Shechita even while personally observing it. The working assumption had been that under certain conditions a Kuti's Shechita was acceptable.

Now a significant new tradition is introduced: *amar rabbi chanan amar rabbi yaakov bar idi amar rabbi yehoshua ben levi mishum bar kappara* — Rabban Gamliel and his court convened, reassessed the situation of the Kutim, and issued a ruling forbidding their Shechita.

### Zeira's Question

Rabbi Zeira responds to Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, through whom this tradition was reported, with a question: *shema lo shama Rebbe ella be-shein Yisrael omed al gabav* — perhaps this ruling applies only when there is no direct Jewish observation of the Shechita? We had already established that trusting a Kuti requires either direct observation (*yisrael omed al gabav*) or compelling him to eat from his own meat. Rabbi Zeira was suggesting that perhaps Rabban Gamliel's prohibition was not an across-the-board ban but merely a reiteration — or a sharper formulation — of the requirement for supervision.

### Yaakov Response

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's reply is stinging: *dami hai me-rabbanan ke-dlo gmir inash shma'ata* — "this rabbi seems like someone who has never learned anything in his life." His point: if the ruling merely meant that an unobserved Kuti's Shechita is forbidden, there was never any need to say it. That requirement has always been in place. For Rabban Gamliel and his entire court to formally convene and issue a ruling, they must be saying something new — namely, that the Shechita of a Kuti is invalid even under direct observation.

### Kutim as Non-Jews

This conclusion carries a weighty implication. We know of only one category of individuals whose Shechita is invalid even under complete, direct Jewish supervision: the non-Jew. Even a Cheresh, Shoteh, or Katan — a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor — can perform valid Shechita when directly supervised. If Rabban Gamliel's ruling extends to cases of direct observation, the only coherent explanation is that Kutim are being classified as non-Jews, whose Shechita is categorically invalid regardless of supervision. That is precisely the direction in which the Gemara will develop the discussion.

### Later Amoraim Eat

Against this ruling stands the testimony of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, who reports in the name of Rav Assi: *ani ra'isi es rabbi yochanan she-achal mi-shechitas kuti* — "I saw Rabbi Yochanan eat from the Shechita of a Kuti." This was clearly after the ruling of Rabban Gamliel and his Beit Din, and yet Rabbi Yochanan was prepared to eat from it. Similarly, Rav Assi himself ate from the Shechita of a Kuti.

### Zeira Bewildered

Rabbi Zeira was astounded. He posed the question in two directions: *lo shemia lehu* — perhaps Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi simply never received the tradition of Rabban Gamliel's ruling; had they heard it, they would certainly have accepted it and refrained. Or alternatively — *shemia lehu ve-lo kiblu* — perhaps they did hear it and consciously rejected it, ruling that the Shechita of a Kuti remained permissible.

The Gemara then reports that Rabbi Zeira himself resolved the dilemma: *mistavra de-shemia lehu ve-lo kiblu* — it is more reasonable to conclude that they heard and did not accept. Why? Because if they had never heard the ruling, and would have accepted it had they heard it, then in practice they were eating meat that they themselves would have considered forbidden. And that scenario is theologically untenable.

### Tzaddikim Principle

The Gemara invokes a striking principle: *hashta behematan shel tzaddikim ein ha-kadosh baruch hu mavi takala al yadam, tzaddikim atzmam lo kol sheken* — if God does not even allow the animals of tzaddikim to stumble into wrongdoing, how much more certainly does He prevent tzaddikim themselves from stumbling. The paradigmatic case is the donkey of Pinchas ben Yair, which refused to eat anything it was not supposed to eat — a story the Gemara will return to later. If God protects even the animals of tzaddikim from consuming something forbidden, He would assuredly prevent tzaddikim themselves from unknowingly eating non-kosher food. Since Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi in fact ate from the Kuti's Shechita, they must have done so deliberately, having ruled that it was *mutar*. They heard the ruling and disagreed with it.

### Zeira Accepts Ban

This resolution also tells us something critical about Rabbi Zeira's own position. Recall that Rabbi Zeira had initially raised the possibility that Rabban Gamliel's ruling applied only without direct observation. If he still held to that reading, he would have had a simple answer when confronted with Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi eating from the Kuti's Shechita: they were simply eating under direct observation, which was always permissible even by Rabban Gamliel's ruling. The fact that Rabbi Zeira had no such simple resolution — that he was genuinely troubled and needed to conclude they heard and rejected the ruling — proves that he himself had by this point accepted that Rabban Gamliel's ban extended even to cases of direct observation. *ela lav shma mina kibla minei* — from this we infer that he did accept the response, and with it the broader scope of the prohibition.

The picture that emerges, then, is that there are two valid positions in the tradition: the ruling of Rabban Gamliel and his Beit Din, accepted by Rabbi Zeira, that the Shechita of a Kuti is invalid in all circumstances — implying their classification as non-Jews — and a dissenting position maintained by Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Assi, who held that Kuti Shechita remained acceptable.

### Forbidden Food Effect

The invocation of the principle that God protects tzaddikim from eating forbidden food warrants a closer look, since this same idea will resurface later in the daf. Tosafot raises an obvious objection: the Gemara in other places records cases where tzaddikim did in fact sin — even grievously — so how can we claim that God prevents tzaddikim from erring? Tosafot answers sharply: this principle applies specifically, and exclusively, to the consumption of forbidden food. The argument of *behematan shel tzaddikim tzaddikim atzmam lo kol sheken* is only ever invoked in the context of eating something that is *assur*.

The underlying reasoning appears to be that forbidden food is not simply a sin like other sins. When something forbidden enters the body, it is not merely a transgression of a command — it is understood to carry some form of corrupting effect, whether physical or spiritual, upon the person who consumes it. This is a qualitatively different kind of wrong: not only a sin but an objective contamination of the body. That framing carries significant halachic implications. For instance, the question arises whether one may permit an infant below the age of Chinuch to eat non-kosher food — after all, one does not stop such an infant from inadvertently violating Shabbat. Is food different? Is treif food seen as having a harmful, corrupting effect that overrides the usual leniency toward pre-Chinuch children, independent of any formal prohibition? That is a genuine area of halachic discussion, and it is precisely this notion — that forbidden food acts upon the person in a way that transcends mere sin — that drives it.

---

---

# Hullin 6

## Samaritan Shechita & Ido…

### Dovecote Idol at Har Ger…

We begin on 6a, four lines from the top, with the question of the shechita of a Kuti. By the time of Rabban Gamliel, such shechita had been forbidden even when performed under direct observation, and the Gemara now seeks to understand why.

The Gemara asks: u'mai ta'ama gazru bo rabbanan — what was the reason the Rabbis issued this ruling against Kuti shechita? The answer is introduced through the following episode. Rabbi Meir sent Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar — shadreih Rabbi Meir le'asuyei chamra mi'beit kuta'ei — to bring wine from the house of Kutim, either because wine had been stored there or for purposes of purchase. While on this errand, a certain elder found him — ashkecheih hahu saba. Tosafot notes that when the Talmud refers anonymously to "a certain elder" in this manner, it may well be a reference to Eliyahu HaNavi. In any event, the elder is someone whose words carry great weight. The elder quoted the pasuk: vesamta sakin beloecha im ba'al nefesh ata — "you should put a knife in your throat if you are a person of soul" — effectively warning Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that he should not be drinking this wine.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar then returned and told Rabbi Meir what had transpired — ve'siper devarim lifnei Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Meir heard the account and, presumably after some investigation, issued an edict — vegazar leih — forbidding the wine of Kutim. The logic here is important: the prohibition was not grounded in any technical deficiency in how the Kutim handled the wine. Rather, the ruling treated them as non-Jews. And once their wine is forbidden on those grounds, it becomes clear why their shechita is likewise invalid: even if technically performed and directly observed, we are treating Kutim as non-Jews, and that categorically excludes them — as was established in yesterday's daf — from performing valid shechita.

### Rabbi Meir's Minority Co…

The Gemara continues to press the explanation. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides the factual basis: demut yona matzu lahen berosh Har Grizim — they found a form, some type of statue of a dove, at the summit of Har Gerizim, the Samaritans' holy mountain — she'hayu ovdin otah — and they worshipped it. The Samaritans, in other words, had become idolaters.

The Gemara then adds: Rabbi Meir letamei — Rabbi Meir acts in accordance with his characteristic reasoning — dechayesh lemi'uta — he is concerned even for minority cases. This principle appears elsewhere in Rabbi Meir's rulings. One classic example involves yibbum: if the deceased husband's brother seeks to perform yibbum with a minor widow, Rabbi Meir objects on the grounds that she might eventually turn out to be sterile, in which case she would not be subject to yibbum, and the marriage would constitute a violation of the prohibition of eishet achiv. Even though only a small minority of women are sterile, Rabbi Meir requires that we account for the possibility.

Applying this same principle to the Samaritans: even if only a subset of them — say, those living near Har Gerizim — worshipped the idol, Rabbi Meir concluded that we must be concerned about all of them. Hence: vegazar ruba atu mi'uta — he extended the prohibition to the majority on account of the minority. All Samaritans were to be treated as suspected idolaters. It bears noting, however, that this does not necessarily mean Rabbi Meir considered them non-Jews. As was discussed yesterday, there is an intermediate category — a Jewish idolater — who is treated as a non-Jew for purposes of halacha without literally being assigned the status of a non-Jew. So what Rabbi Meir may have been saying is that Samaritans are Jewish idolaters, and on that basis their wine is forbidden.

### Rabban Gamliel's Extensi…

Rabban Gamliel u'beit dino — k'Rabbi Meir svira lehu — agreed with Rabbi Meir's underlying reasoning and extended it to shechita as well. This extension represents a genuine progression in the logic. The prohibition on wine is specifically linked to idolatry concerns — yayin nesech flows directly from the worry that wine was used in idolatrous worship. But Rabban Gamliel then reasoned: if we are already treating Kutim as idolaters, that designation is not confined to laws relating directly to idolatry. Rather, as we saw yesterday, being classified as an idolater constitutes a categorical exclusion across the board — including shechita, which has nothing to do with idolatry per se. So the stages are: they are suspected idolaters, therefore their wine is forbidden; and because they are categorically excluded as idolaters, their shechita is likewise invalid.

Importantly, as we have already seen, this ruling was not immediately or universally accepted. There were Amoraim who resisted it, likely because the idolatrous practice was demonstrably limited to a subset of the Samaritan population and did not apply to all Kutim equally.

---

## Knife in Your Mouth

### Verse Interpretation

Having cited the pasuk vesamta sakin beloecha im ba'al nefesh ata in the context of warning against Kuti wine, the Gemara pauses to ask parenthetically: pashte dikra bemai ktiv? — to what does the simple sense of that verse actually refer? Because in the story above it was deployed as a warning against drinking problematic wine, but surely that is not its original context.

The Gemara answers: betalmid hayoshev lifnei rabbo — the verse speaks of a student sitting before his teacher. A Baraita taught by Rebbi Chiya elaborates on the full pasuk: ki teshev lachom et moshel — when you sit down to contend with a ruler — bin tavin et asher lefanecha — understand what is before you — vesamta sakin beloecha im ba'al nefesh ata — and put a knife in your throat if you are a person of soul.

The Gemara interprets: im yodea talmid birabbo sheyodea lehachzir lo ta'am — if a student knows that his teacher is capable of answering his questions and offering him substantive responses — bin — then he should go ahead and ask. Ve'im lav — but if he knows his teacher cannot adequately answer him — tavin et asher lefanecha — he should understand his situation and refrain from asking questions that will only frustrate him and embarrass the teacher. Vesamta sakin beloecha — put a knife in your throat — meaning, hold your tongue and do not ask. Im ba'al nefesh ata — if you are a person of real intellectual drive and desire to learn — perosh mimenu — then leave him and find another teacher. But do not subject the teacher to questions he cannot answer.

The real plain meaning of the verse, by contrast, is a more general counsel about knowing your audience: if you are going to dispute with a person of power, exercise discretion, because the stakes are high.

### Pshat Terminology

This discussion presents an opportunity to clarify a point about terminology. The Gemara uses the phrase pashte dikra — the pshat of the verse. We commonly translate pshat as the "simple sense" of the verse, but that is not actually what the word means. Pshat means the official or accepted interpretation of the verse. This distinction is illuminated by the Talmudic phrase pshuto kemashmao — the pshat is what it sounds like. If pshat already meant "the simple sense," then pshuto kemashmao would be tautological. Rather, pshat denotes the authoritative reading, and mashmao — what it sounds like — is a separate claim being made about that reading. So when the Gemara here asks pashte dikra bemai ktiv, it is asking: what is our accepted way of understanding this verse? — not merely what the words superficially seem to mean.

---

## Later Acceptance of Ban

### Rabbi Isaac's Wine Incid…

We now return to the question of Kuti wine and shechita, because as we have seen, not everyone was prepared to accept the new status assigned to the Kutim. A second incident is now recorded that is strikingly parallel to the first. Rebbe Yitzchak ben Yosef was sent by Rebbe Abbahu — shadrei Rebbe Abbahu la'asuyei chamra mibei kusai — to bring wine from the Kutim. Again, an elder found him: ashkachay hahu saba — and said: leis kan shomrei Torah — it seems that people here are not keeping Torah. The reference was presumably not to the Kutim themselves but to those who were going to purchase wine from them, people who, if they truly cared about halacha, should not have been doing so.

Rebbe Yitzchak did not complete the errand. He returned — azal Rebbe Yitzchak vesiper devarim lifnei Rebbe Abbahu — and reported what the elder had told him. The episode then cascaded upward: ve'azal Rebbe Abbahu vesiper devarim lifnei Rebbe Ami — Rebbe Abbahu went and told Rebbe Ami. The fact that the account of one elder's remark set off such a significant chain of consultation is itself notable, which is presumably why Tosafot entertains the possibility that this "elder," like the one in the earlier story, may have been Eliyahu HaNavi.

### Ami & Assi's Declaration

The consultation ultimately reached Rebbe Ami and Rebbe Assi. V'lo zazu misham — they did not move from that place — ad she'asa'um ovdei kochavim gemurim — until they had declared Kutim to be full-fledged idolaters, with all the halachic consequences that entails: their wine, their shechita, everything.

The Gemara then asks: lemei — for what halacha precisely did they need to make this declaration? Ilima shechita v'yein nesech — if it is about their slaughter and their wine — that had already been addressed by Rabbi Meir and Rabban Gamliel. The Gemara's answer: inhu gazru v'lo kiblu minayhu — they made the ruling but it was not accepted by their generation. Atu Rabbi Ami v'Rabbi Assi — Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi came along — gazru v'kiblu minayhu — and when they reiterated the ruling, it was finally accepted. So this was not a more expansive ruling but rather a reaffirmation of an existing one, now successfully implemented.

### Rashi on Habit & Change

This raises an obvious question: why was the ruling of Rabbi Meir and Rabban Gamliel — authorities far greater than Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi — not accepted in their own time, while Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi succeeded? Rashi addresses this directly with a fascinating sociological observation. Lo she'elu gedolim mehem — it is not that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi were greater authorities — ela shebdoro shel Meir lo ratzu lekabel mehem lifrosh min haKutim lefi shehayu regilim bahem: in the generation of Rabbi Meir, people were already deeply habituated to trusting Kutim and treating them with full Jewish status. They were not prepared to reverse their well-entrenched behaviors and attitudes.

By the time of Rabbi Ami, says Rashi — ubdoro shel Rabbi Ami hayah efshar lifrosh — it had become possible to enforce the separation. People were increasingly aware that Kutim could not be trusted and were beginning to view them differently. It was therefore finally possible for the ruling to take hold. The lesson here is a striking one about the relationship between correct halachic rulings and the social conditions required for their acceptance: even if a ruling is halachically sound, its implementation may have to await a moment when the community is psychologically and culturally ready to receive it.

### Gerizim Temple Context

Steinsaltz offers a complementary historical perspective. Apparently, a temple was actually built on Har Gerizim in the wake of the Bar Kokhba rebellion, representing a concrete and visible intensification of Samaritan idolatrous practice. This may well be what stands behind the Gemara's account of discovering the dovecote idol — the Dositheana's worship at Har Gerizim may be connected to this actual construction. The timing aligns with the generation of Rabbi Meir, explaining why the campaign against Kuti wine and shechita began precisely then. As for why acceptance awaited the generation of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, Rashi's sociological explanation remains the more compelling answer — though the historical confirmation of actual idolatrous worship on Har Gerizim lends the initial ruling its firm empirical footing.

---

## Idolaters vs. Non-Jews

### Status Distinction

The Gemara declares that Kutim were made ke-ovdei kochavim gemurim — like full-fledged ovdei kochavim. The phrase ovdei kochavim, however, is ambiguous: it can mean either non-Jews or idolaters. Given that up to this point the assumption has been that Kutim were geirei emet — genuine converts — the most coherent reading would be that they are now classified as Jewish idolaters. A Jew who is oved avodah zarah is categorically excluded from performing shechita and his wine is forbidden, as was established yesterday. This accounts for all the practical consequences without requiring us to strip them of Jewish status entirely.

### Rambam on Tumah

There is, however, a striking indication in a Rambam in one location in the Peirush HaMishnayot that the matter may go further. There is a Mishnah in Niddah that deals with the bloodstains of Kuti women — the stains of niddah, menstrual bleeding. The Rambam there rules that such stains do not convey tumah, because Chazal made Kutim like ovdei kochavim. This is remarkable on several levels.

The laws of niddah tumah apply to Jewish women, not to non-Jewish women — but they do apply even to a Jewish woman who is an idolater. The exclusion entailed by being classified as an idolater pertains to functional matters like shechita and wine; it does not reassign a person's fundamental halachic identity for purposes of tumah. So when the Rambam says their bloodstains do not convey tumah, he appears to be treating Kutim not merely as Jewish idolaters but as actual non-Jews.

What makes this even more striking is the direction of the ruling: here the Rambam is being meikel — lenient. In every other context, treating Kutim as ovdei kochavim was a stringency: don't drink their wine, don't eat their meat. But to say that their niddah bloodstains are tahor because they are not Jewish — that is a leniency. It is genuinely difficult to understand how, if they were truly Jewish, their status could be so comprehensively transformed. The Rambam's ruling raises the serious question of whether the Rabbinic declaration meant that Kutim were treated as idolaters or actually reclassified as non-Jews — and the Rambam's position in Niddah seems to point toward the latter.

---

## Eruv & Reshus

### Eruv Mechanics

Having established that Kutim are treated as full ovdei kochavim, the Gemara asks: mai ovdei kochavim gemurim — in what halachic area does this designation matter beyond shechita and wine, which were already addressed earlier? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers: l'vattel reshus u'litten reshus — with respect to annulling and giving one's domain in the context of eruv.

Some clarification of the mechanics is helpful here. What is commonly called an eruv — the string and posts surrounding a neighborhood — is technically a tzurat hapesach, a virtual doorway that creates a notional enclosure. The actual eruv, in the strict sense, refers to eruv chatzerot: the joining of separate domestic domains. Because each household owns its own property, the space within the enclosure is subject to chiluk reshuyot — a division of domains — which prevents it from functioning as a single private domain. To address this, residents join together in a communal share of food, typically a box of matzot held in one household, establishing a fictive joint ownership. Since everyone now has a share in that one household, the entire space is treated as a single unified domain.

### Annulling vs. Renting

What happens if someone forgets to participate in the communal box of matzot and Shabbos arrives? If the person is a Jew, the solution is straightforward: he can verbally declare that he is annulling his domain — reshusi mevutela lach — or transferring it to others. Ve'ein tzarich lizkos — no formal act of acquisition is required; the verbal declaration alone suffices, and the eruv is thereby preserved.

For a non-Jew, this mechanism is unavailable. A non-Jew is not part of the collective framework that makes this verbal fiction operative. Accordingly, if there is a non-Jew in the shared space, one cannot simply have him declare his domain annulled. Instead, his domain must actually be rented from him — a real transaction, not merely a verbal declaration — in order to incorporate his space into the shared domain.

### Samaritans in Eruv

The practical question this raises for the modern eruv — how to address non-Jewish-owned property within the enclosure, whether through municipal agreements, the doctrine of eminent domain, or other mechanisms — is a separate and complex matter. The relevant principle established here is that a Kuti, now that he has been declared ke-ovdei kochavim gemurim, falls into the same category as a non-Jew for purposes of eruv. His verbal annulment of reshus is ineffective, and his domain must actually be rented from him. Notice, however, that this does not technically require that he be a non-Jew — only that he be treated like one. The same rule applies, as the Baraita will demonstrate, to a Jewish public violator of Shabbos. It is a matter of halachic status, not necessarily of ethnic or religious identity.

---

## Baraita: Mumar & Shabbat

### Mumar Respecting Shabbat

The Gemara cites a Baraita that elaborates on these distinctions. The Baraita begins: Yisrael mumar — a Jew who is non-observant in certain respects — meshameir Shabatto bashuk — but who keeps Shabbos in public, in the marketplace. The phrase here is bashuk rather than the more familiar b'farhesia, but the meaning is the same: this person publicly respects Shabbos observance even if his private conduct is not fully consistent. Such a person retains full Jewish halachic status. Accordingly: mevattel reshus v'notein reshus — he can annul his domain or give it, and his verbal declaration on Shabbos is effective for eruv purposes.

### Public Shabbat Violator

She'eino meshameir Shabatto bashuk — one who does not keep Shabbos in public, meaning a mechalel Shabbos b'farhesia, a public Shabbos violator — eino mevattel reshus v'notein reshus. His verbal annulment is ineffective. To incorporate his space into an eruv, his domain must be rented from him, exactly as one would have to rent from a non-Jew.

### Jewish Verbal Annulment

The Baraita then articulates the general principle: Yisrael notein reshus u'mevattel reshus — a Jew who forgot to participate in the eruv can verbally give or annul his domain on Shabbos itself. Reshusi knuya lach, reshusi mevutela lach — my domain is acquired by you, my domain is nullified — and that verbal act alone is sufficient; v'ein tzarich lizkos, no physical act of acquisition is needed.

The conclusion that follows is that not only a non-Jew, but also a public Shabbos violator — and now, by extension, a Kuti — requires actual rental rather than verbal annulment. The eruv must treat the Kuti's domain as it would treat that of a non-Jew or a mechalel Shabbos b'farhesia.

---

## Inn Incident & Tzadikim

### Eggs & Wine Mixture

The Gemara now shifts to a different narrative, returning to the theme — which appeared earlier in the tractate — of whether God allows tzadikim to accidentally eat forbidden food. Rabbi Zeira and Rav Assi came to an inn — ikla'u lefundaka deYa'i, in a place called Ya'i. There, eggs that had been cooked together with wine were brought before them — aisu lekameihu beitzim hametzumakos beyayin. Rabbi Zeira did not eat. Rav Assi ate.

Afterward, Rabbi Zeira said to Rav Assi: velo chayish mar leta'aroves demai? — were you not concerned about the mixture of demai? The category of demai refers to agricultural produce purchased from an am ha'aretz, a Jew who is not learned or careful in the observance of halachic requirements. Because such a person may not have taken terumot u'ma'asrot — tithes and priestly portions — from his produce, one must suspect that the product remains tevel, with the separations not yet made. Demai is this doubtful status. The eggs themselves presented no problem, but the wine mixed with them presumably came from an am ha'aretz innkeeper, and might well have been demai. How, then, could Rav Assi have eaten it?

Rav Assi replied: lav adaitai — I simply was not thinking about it. I saw eggs and did not focus on the wine mixed in.

### Tzadikim Protected

Rabbi Zeira found this answer difficult to accept. He said to himself: efshar gazru al ta'aroves demai — is it really possible that the Rabbis forbade something merely because it is mixed with demai? Ve'istaiya milsa deRav Assi lemichal issura — and it would have come to pass that Rav Assi ate something forbidden? He could not accept this. Even granting that Rav Assi had simply not been thinking, Rabbi Zeira could not countenance the idea that a tzadik of that stature would have inadvertently eaten even a rabbinic prohibition — for that is all demai is, a rabbinic concern.

His reasoning was drawn from a well-known principle: hashta behemton shel tzadikim ein hakadosh baruch hu meivi takala al yadam — if the Holy One, blessed be He, does not cause even the animals of tzadikim to stumble into transgression — tzadikim atzman lo kol shekein? — certainly He would not allow the tzadikim themselves to do so. Rabbi Zeira thus went out — nafik — to investigate whether there is in fact any prohibition on a ta'aroves of demai.

---

## Demai Mixtures

### Raw Ingredients Rule

Rabbi Zeira investigated and found the following Baraita: halokei'ach yayin lases lesoch hamoryas o lesoch ha'aluntis — one who purchases wine from an am ha'aretz, intending to put it into moryas, some type of prepared dish, or aluntis, a mixture of wine and oil and other ingredients. Or o karshinim la'asos mehen tchinim — one who buys karshinim, apparently some type of leek, intending to make a prepared dish from it. O adashim la'asos mehen resisin — lentils to make a different type of mixture. In all of these cases, the person is purchasing a raw agricultural product of demai status, with the intention of mixing it into a dish rather than eating it directly.

The Baraita rules: chayav mishum demai — one is nonetheless obligated to take terumot u'ma'asrot on account of the demai laws. Ve'ein tzarich lomar mishum vadai — and needless to say, if the seller explicitly states that separations were not made, one must certainly take. The obligation is triggered by the initial encounter with the raw product, and the fact that one intends to mix it does not exempt one.

### Prepared Dish Exemption

However, the key ruling follows: vehein atzman mutarin — if, however, one encounters the product not as a raw ingredient but as a prepared dish in which the demai has already been incorporated, one does not need to take terumot u'ma'asrot. Mipnei shehein ta'aroves — because it is a mixture. This distinction is crucial: the obligation is created at the moment one first confronts the original product in its raw state. If one never encounters it in that form — if it arrives already embedded in a dish — the obligation never crystallizes.

### First Encounter Rule

This Baraita was precisely what Rabbi Zeira needed. The case at the inn was exactly analogous: the eggs and wine were presented to them already combined as a prepared dish. Rav Assi never encountered the wine as a standalone raw ingredient; he encountered it only as part of the mixture. The Baraita says that in such a case, there is no obligation and no prohibition. Rabbi Zeira could now rest easy: Rav Assi had not eaten anything forbidden, since the rabbinic concern of demai does not apply when one first encounters the product as a prepared mixture. His confidence in divine protection of the righteous was vindicated — not overridden — by the halacha.

The Gemara then presses the question: v'lo gazru al ta'aroves demai? — is it truly the case that the Rabbis placed no prohibition on a mixture of demai? The Gemara raises a Baraita that appears to complicate this: hanosenes leshchentah issa le'ofos — a woman who is a chaver, someone scrupulous in terumot u'ma'asrot, gives dough to her neighbor, an am ha'aretz, to bake. Or ukdeirah levashel — a pot to cook. Einah chosheshas l'se'or vetavlin shebah — she need not be concerned about the sourdough or spices in it, lo mishum shevi'is velo mishum ma'aser — neither for shevi'is nor for ma'aser laws. Meaning, she does not suspect that the neighbor will swap the product, so she can assume she gets back what she gave.

Ve'im amrah lah asi li mishelach — but if she explicitly tells her neighbor: please bake using your own dough, please add your own spices — then chosheshas l'se'or vetavlin shebah mishum shevi'is umishum ma'aser. Now she must be concerned, because the neighbor's own products may be shevi'is produce or may lack terumot u'ma'asrot.

The apparent difficulty is this: in the case where the neighbor adds her own spices or sourdough, the resulting food is still a mixture — the majority of the stew is not problematic. Why should a minority admixture of demai spices or sourdough create an obligation?

---

## Sourdough & Spices

### Additive vs. Dominant

The Gemara resolves the difficulty in two ways. The first answer is: shani hassam — there it is different — keivan d'amrah lah asi li mishelach — since you explicitly told the neighbor to add her own ingredients — keman d'arvah b'yadayim dami — it is as though you yourself mixed them in with your own hands. And if you personally add an ingredient, you have encountered the original product in its raw state at the moment of incorporation. The exemption for ta'aroves applies only when one first encounters the product already embedded in a prepared dish. Here, the explicit instruction to add the ingredient is tantamount to personally handling the raw product, and so the exemption does not apply.

Rafram offers a second, independent answer: shani se'or vetavlin d'leta'ama avid — sourdough and spices are different because they are added for taste and leavening, and as such they are not merely incidental additives. Sourdough makes the bread rise; spices define the character of a dish. In these cases, the problematic ingredient is not simply one of many components — it is dominant. When the Rabbis said that a ta'aroves of demai is not a problem, they meant a case where the demai item is genuinely subordinate and not the defining element. V'ta'ama lo batil — something that gives the dish its essential taste or function is not nullified. This is not the ordinary law of bittul — which would require sixty times the volume — but rather a distinct principle: if the demai ingredient is dominant by taste or function, it is not considered a mere mixture, and the exemption does not apply.

---

## Swapping Food Risk

### Mother-in-Law Case

The Gemara raises a further question: v'chilufei lo chashinan — is it truly the case that we are not concerned that someone will swap the food entrusted to them? The Baraita above stated that a woman who gives her neighbor dough to bake need not suspect that the neighbor will exchange it for her own. But a Mishnah appears to complicate this. Ha-noten lachamoto ma'asser et shehu noten lah ve'et shehu notel himmenah — a man whose mother-in-law is an am ha'aretz, not careful in terumot u'ma'asrot, who gives her something to cook or bake, must take ma'aser both from what he gives her and from what he gets back.

Why must he separate from what he gives her? Because if she swaps the food on him, the product he has given her — which he has not yet separated from — will be eaten by her as tevel. He would be party to causing her to eat something non-kosher, and therefore he must take terumot u'ma'asrot from what he gives her before handing it over. And why must he separate from what he gets back? Because she may have swapped it, and what he receives may be her own food, which has not had terumot u'ma'asrot taken. So the concern about swapping cuts in both directions.

### Embarrassment Motive

This Mishnah appears to contradict the earlier principle that we do not suspect food-swapping as a general matter. The Gemara resolves the tension: hatam kedei tanya ta'ama — there, the reason is as taught in a Baraita. Amar Rabbi Yehuda: rotzah hi betakanat bittah u'bushah mechamiah — the mother-in-law wants her daughter's household to be well-served, and she is embarrassed before her son-in-law. These family dynamics create a specific and identifiable motivation for swapping. If the food burns or is ruined, the mother-in-law will not hand back the ruined dish. Out of embarrassment, she will prepare a fresh dish using her own ingredients and present that instead. The swap is not motivated by dishonesty but by the desire not to disappoint her son-in-law.

It is precisely this particular social dynamic — the combination of wanting to benefit one's daughter and fearing the son-in-law's disapproval — that creates the reasonable suspicion of swapping in this case. As a general rule, when one entrusts food to a neighbor or acquaintance, no such specific motivation exists, and we do not suspect that they will exchange it. The mother-in-law case is the exception, not the rule, defined by the Baraita's explicit psychological explanation.

---

---

# Hullin 8

## White-Hot Knife

### Sharpness Precedes Heat

We open on 8a with the statement of Rav Zeira in the name of Shmuel. Having concluded the earlier digressions about tzaddikim and treif food, the Gemara returns to its central theme of shechita — and begins to focus not merely on who may perform it, but on the act itself. The ruling is as follows: *liben sakin veshachat bah* — if one heated a knife white-hot and then used it to shecht, the shechita is nevertheless valid, *shechitato kesheira*. The reason given is *chiduda kodem lelibuna* — the sharpness of the knife precedes the heat. In other words, even though the knife is white-hot, the cutting edge makes contact with and severs the throat before the heat has any material effect. It is therefore a valid shechita.

### Heat Burning the Simanim

The Gemara immediately raises a difficulty. One might well grant that as the knife first enters the throat, the sharpness does its work. But as the knife continues through the cut — moving laterally through the trachea and esophagus — the heat of the blade is burning the inner walls of the opening it has created. Is this not burning the simanim before the cut is complete, potentially rendering the animal a treifa? At the very least, the heat seems to be acting upon the animal in a problematic way before the shechita is finished.

### Wound Opens (Mivrach)

The Gemara responds: *beit hashechita mivrach ravach* — the place of the cut opens up as the shechita proceeds. When one draws the knife through the throat, the wound naturally spreads open, so that the sides of the blade — which carry the bulk of the heat — are no longer in direct contact with the flesh. Only the cutting edge itself, the very tip that is making contact, is touching the skin at any given moment, and that edge is doing the work of sharpness, not of heat.

### Blood Sealing

This explanation prompts a further observation worth noting: the heat might in principle be sealing the wound as the knife passes through, preventing blood from flowing. But this does not invalidate the shechita. The halachic requirement of shechita is specifically the severing of the trachea and esophagus — the simanim — and not the draining of blood. While cutting the carotid artery facilitates the subsequent removal of blood, it is not part of the formal requirement of *hechsher shechita*. The blood-sealing concern would therefore not passel the shechita itself; it might complicate the later stages of preparing the meat, but the act of shechita stands as valid.

---

## Hot Poker & Tzara'at

### Shechin vs. Michva

The Gemara now introduces a related question by way of analogy: *liben shipud vehika bo* — if someone heats a poker white-hot and strikes another person with it, is the resulting lesion classified as a *shechin* (a wound) or as a *michva* (a burn)? These two categories are drawn from the Torah's discussion of tzara'at, where lesions arising from either a wound or a burn are treated in specific ways. The question is which classification applies when an injury involves both impact and heat simultaneously.

### One Week Rule

The practical difference is established through a braita: *shechin umichva metama'im beshavua echad bishnei simanim bese'ar lavan uvifisyon* — both a shechin and a michva are assessed over only one week, not two. In most cases of tzara'at, if the appearance of the spot is indeterminate at the end of the first week, it is closed up for a second week of observation. But for lesions arising from a wound or a burn, there is only one week, and two signs are looked for: the growth of white hair and the spreading of the lesion.

Now, if shechin and michva carry the same law, one might ask why the Torah devotes separate passages to each. The answer is *she'ein mitztarfin ze im ze* — they do not combine with one another. The minimum size for a leprous spot is *k'gris*, the size of a lentil bean. If a person has two adjacent spots, each half a gris, one a shechin and one a michva, they cannot be combined to satisfy the minimum size. Each must independently meet the threshold. This is why the distinction between the two categories matters at all.

### Shechin Definition

The Gemara proceeds to define each category. A shechin is produced when one is struck or burned by something that is not fire. The mishna gives examples: being struck by wood or stone (*laka b'etz b'even*), being exposed to *gefet* — the lees of olives, which generate heat through organic decomposition — or to the hot springs of Tiberias (*chamei Tverya*). The principle is captured in the phrase *u'vchol davar shelo ba machamat ha'or* — anything whose heat is not derived from fire. This category also includes, according to one reading, metal in its naturally heated state at the point of mining — Rashi appears to indicate that certain metals, such as lead, are hot when first extracted from the ground, and some have suggested this refers to molten ore or naturally heated mineral deposits.

### Michva Definition

A michva, by contrast, requires heat that originates from fire. The mishna gives examples: being burned by a coal (*gachelet*), by hot ashes (*remetz*), by boiling plaster heated by fire (*sid roteach*), or by *gafsit* — another type of plaster that has been heated. The governing principle is *u'vchol davar haba machamat ha'or* — anything whose heat derives from fire, including water that has been heated by fire (*chamei ha'or*). It is specifically the origin of the heat — fire versus non-fire — that determines the classification.

### Last Status Rule

When a single lesion involves both categories — for example, when there is first an impact and then a burn, or vice versa — the halacha follows the last status. A braita states: *im shechin kodem l'michva, batla michva et hashechin* — if the wound came first and the burn came afterward, the michva status nullifies and supersedes the shechin. Conversely, *im michva kodemet l'shechin, batla shechin et hamichva* — if the burn came first and the wound followed, the shechin status prevails. The most recent stage of the lesion's origin determines how it is classified.

### Half-Gris Lesions

This priority rule creates the specific scenario the Gemara has been building toward. Suppose a person already had a spot on his skin — a shechin that was exactly half a gris in size, insufficient on its own to constitute a leprous lesion. Now someone heats a poker and strikes him near that spot, and a new half-gris spot appears adjacent to the first. Combined, the two would satisfy the minimum size requirement — but do they combine?

The answer depends on how the poker strike is classified. If the impact comes first and is then overlaid by the heat, the last status is michva. The new spot is therefore a michva. Now we have a shechin and a michva side by side — and as established, they do not combine. But if the heat comes first and the impact follows, the last status is shechin. Both spots are now shechin, and they do combine. The question — *chavata kadim* (does the wound precede) or *havala kadim* (does the heat precede) — is therefore halachically determinative.

The Gemara notes that this question is distinct from the white-hot knife case. There, one could argue with confidence that the sharpness of the blade acts first, since the cutting edge is specifically designed to sever. But in the case of a blunt or even pointed poker, there is no obvious a priori reason to prefer one over the other. If anything, one might reason that the skin reacts to heat more immediately than to blunt impact, and that the black-and-blue of blunt trauma develops only afterward — which would suggest heat comes first. This is the tension the Gemara is working through.

### Back to Sharpness

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing the ruling with which this entire sugya opened. Since Rav Zeira said in the name of Shmuel that *chiduda kodem lelibuna* — the sharpness precedes the heat — perhaps this proves that in general, physical impact precedes heat, and therefore the wound comes first even in the poker case. The Gemara rejects this inference: *chidud shani* — sharpness is different. A knife is specifically constructed to cut, and the geometry of the blade ensures that the cutting action makes contact before the heat can spread. That tells us nothing about a blunt impact.

### Pointed Poker

The Gemara then cites an explicit braita: *liben shipud vehika bo, nidon mishum michvas eish* — if one heated a poker and struck with it, it is classified as a burn. This would seem to prove that the heat precedes the wound. But the Gemara is not satisfied and qualifies the braita: *d'barzi marza, d'hainu chidud* — the case in the braita involves a poker with a sharpened, pointed tip. In that case, just as with the knife, the point punctures the skin before the heat has its effect, and the last stage is therefore the heat. This is analogous to the knife case, and equally unhelpful for resolving the blunt-force question.

### Blunt vs. Heat

The Gemara ultimately leaves the question open. When a blunt white-hot object strikes the skin, does the physical force or the heat register first as the causative agent of the wound? The question is left unresolved. The practical stakes — whether the resulting half-gris lesion is a shechin or a michva, and therefore whether it combines with an adjacent half-gris lesion of the other type to produce actionable tzara'at — remain without a definitive answer.

It is worth noting, as the Gemara itself seems to register, why this digression into tzara'at is the vehicle of choice rather than some other case. The tzara'at framework offers a precise legal question that maps onto the same binary the shechita case presents: which of two simultaneous forces is the operative one? The narrow issue the Gemara cares about — not the macro consequences of an act, but the specific causal priority between impact and heat at the point of contact — is best isolated in the tzara'at context, where classification of a single lesion carries halachic consequence.

---

## Idolatry Knife

### Kilkul vs. Tikun

The Gemara now shifts to a series of rulings about knives that have been used in problematic contexts, each raising distinct kashrus concerns. Rav Nachman said in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: a knife used for avoda zara — idolatry — may be used to shecht with, but may not be used to cut meat. The operative distinction is *kilkul* versus *tikun*: shechita is considered a *kilkul*, a destruction or degradation, while cutting already-slaughtered meat is a *tikun*, an improvement or benefit. Since one may not derive benefit from objects used in avoda zara, using the knife as a cutting implement is forbidden. But using it to shecht is permitted, because shechita is not considered an act of deriving benefit.

### Agricultural Context

This ruling is striking to the modern sensibility, since the entire meat industry exists to profit from the slaughter of animals. The answer lies in the agricultural context presupposed by the Gemara. In an agrarian economy, animals are kept primarily for their ongoing productivity — for milk, eggs, wool, and labor. Slaughter is not the productive use of the animal; it terminates that productivity. One would only slaughter an animal for a special occasion or when it had outlived its agricultural utility. Shechita, in this context, represents the end of the animal's value, not the realization of it. Cutting meat into usable portions, by contrast, transforms a carcass into something directly edible and is therefore a clear *tikun*.

This framework is admittedly difficult to internalize given the reality of modern industrial meat production. Yet the Gemara is operating from a coherent, internally consistent economic logic in which the living animal — not the slaughtered carcass — is the primary asset.

### Ill Animal Exception

Rava introduces nuance: *pe'amim sheshochet assur* — there are times when shechita itself becomes forbidden with the knife, because it constitutes a genuine benefit. This is the case of a *mesukenet*, a dangerously ill animal that is on the verge of dying on its own. In this situation, shechita is actually an economic salvage operation: if the animal dies without being shechted, even its meat cannot be used. By shechting it in time, one rescues the value of the animal. Here, shechita is unambiguously a tikun and not a kilkul — and therefore forbidden with the avoda zara knife.

Rava also notes the converse: *umchatach muttar* — there are times when cutting meat is actually permitted, because it constitutes a degradation rather than an improvement. This would be the case of fine whole cuts of meat that are suitable to be presented as gifts — for example, a whole thigh or rib roast — where cutting them into smaller pieces actively diminishes their value. The classification of an act as kilkul or tikun is therefore context-dependent and not intrinsic to the act itself.

### Kashering by Heat

The Gemara then raises a separate concern that operates independently of the avoda zara prohibition: *shamnunit de'issura* — the residue of forbidden substances on the knife. Even setting aside the question of deriving benefit, a knife that has been used to slaughter animals for idolatry would presumably be coated with fat and residue from those animals, which are neveilah. Using such a knife to shecht kosher animals would transfer that residue to the place of the cut.

The Gemara resolves this by positing two possible answers. The first is that the knife was used for *gazra* — chopping wood for idolatrous purposes — and therefore has no meat residue on it at all. This is acknowledged as an *okimta*, a qualifying deflection rather than a principled resolution. The second answer is that the knife, although previously used with forbidden meat, has been kashered: *beyeshana shelivna ba'or* — it was an old knife that was heated white-hot in fire, thereby burning off all absorbed or surface residue. This kashering method — *libun* — removes the concern about transferred taste and renders the knife fit for use. With this, the Gemara transitions from the avoda zara framework into the broader questions of taste absorption and transfer in kashrus.

---

## Non-Jewish Knife

### Peeling vs. Rinsing

The Gemara now introduces a new but closely related case: *ha-shochet be-sakin shel ovdei kochavim* — one who shechts with a knife belonging to non-Jews. The phrasing is deliberately distinct from the earlier case of *sakin shel avodat kochavim* (a knife of idolatry). There, the primary issue was deriving forbidden benefit; here, the idolatry concern is absent, and the sole question is the transfer of non-kosher residue. A knife that has been used by non-Jews to cut their meat will have non-kosher fat and residue on it. When used to shecht a kosher animal, does that residue transfer to the *beit hashechita* — the specific area of the neck where the cut is made — in a halachically significant way?

Rav rules: *koleif* — one must peel away the surface layer of the meat at the site of the cut before eating. Rabba bar Bar Chana rules: *madiach* — it suffices to rinse the area with water. Both positions accept that some transfer occurs; the debate is whether the residue penetrates beneath the surface or remains on it.

### Heat & Absorption

The Gemara explores what underlying disagreement drives this dispute. One possibility is that Rav holds *beit hashechita roteiach* — the site of the slaughter is halachically hot, i.e., hot enough to cause absorption of taste into the flesh — while Rabba bar Bar Chana holds *beit hashechita tzonen*, that it is cold, and therefore no absorption occurs. Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that both may agree the site is hot; the one who rules that rinsing suffices can still explain his position by arguing *aidi de-tridi simanim le-apukei dam lo bali* — since the simanim are occupied, so to speak, with expelling blood at the moment of shechita, there is no capacity for simultaneous absorption of external matter.

### Knife Pressure

A further possibility inverts the previous one: perhaps both Rav and Rabba bar Bar Chana actually agree that the beit hashechita is cold. On that reading, Rabba bar Bar Chana's ruling that rinsing suffices follows naturally. But Rav's requirement of peeling demands explanation: why would peeling be necessary if there is no heat? The Gemara answers: *agav duchka de-sakina bala* — because of the pressure of the knife itself, absorption occurs even without heat. The physical force of the blade pressing through the flesh drives the surface residue inward, bypassing the normal requirement of heat for taste transfer.

### Yad Soledet Bo

This sugya gives rise to two significant halachic discussions. The first concerns the definition of *yad soledet bo* — the threshold of heat required for halachic absorption of taste, relevant both to shabbat and to kashrus. Several Rishonim assume that the heat needed for taste absorption in kashrus is identical to the standard of yad soledet bo. Since the Gemara here presents a debate about whether the beit hashechita is hot or cold, some authorities reason that this site must be near the borderline of that threshold — otherwise there would be no debate — and attempt to translate that into a quantifiable temperature. The figure arrived at is quite low, perhaps around 102–106 degrees Fahrenheit.

However, a number of other Rishonim reject this line of reasoning entirely, arguing that yad soledet bo is a shabbat category and that the heat required for taste absorption in kashrus may in fact be lower. On that view, this Gemara is irrelevant to establishing the yad soledet bo threshold, and the debate about the beit hashechita operates on a different scale.

The second halachic issue concerns *duchka de-sakina* — whether the pressure of a knife can by itself transfer taste into food, independent of heat. The Gemara raises this as a possibility, but Tosafot argues, based on other Gemarot, that pressure alone is insufficient. Rather, what produces absorption in the relevant cases is a combination of heat that is close to — but perhaps just below — the formal threshold, together with the added factor of knife pressure. Whether knife pressure entirely without heat can drive absorption into food remains unclear from this Gemara alone.

These two principles have direct practical application to the question of purchasing fish from a non-kosher counter. If one can confirm the species by visible signs — scales, skin pattern — the remaining concern is whether the knife used to cut it transfers non-kosher residue into the fish. According to the stricter view, one should koleif — scrape away the surface at the cut. According to the more lenient view, rinsing suffices. If the fish store uses separate knives or demonstrably cleans its blade, there may be further grounds for leniency. The separate and more significant concern is the intentional mislabeling of fish species, which is a distinct problem unrelated to the knife question.

---

## Treifa Knife

### Rav Aha & Ravina

The Gemara now turns to an analogous but distinct scenario: a knife that has been used to shecht a treifa animal. This is not a hypothetical — it happens in the normal course of shechita, since an animal may turn out to have had a treifot only after the shechita is completed. The fat and meat residue on the knife are now from a treif animal. Rav Aha and Ravina debate how such a knife must be kashered. One holds that it requires heat — *bachamin* — implying that the forbidden matter has been absorbed into the metal of the knife itself. The other holds that cold water suffices — *b'tzonin* — implying that the residue is only on the surface.

### Surface-Level Only

The halacha is ruled in accordance with the lenient position: *afilu b'tzonin* — cold water is sufficient. Moreover, if one has a material such as steel wool with which to scrub the surface, that alone suffices even without water, since the concern is only surface residue and not absorbed matter. The underlying principle is that the knife does not become heated to the point where it absorbs the forbidden taste from the animal into its metal. The forbidden matter remains on the surface and can be removed mechanically or by rinsing.

### Blood Adhesion

Rashi raises a pointed question: if we are concerned about the knife absorbing treif fat and meat, why are we not equally concerned about the blood that flows over the knife with every shechita? Blood is, after all, a forbidden substance, and it is always present at the site of the cut. Rashi's answer is that blood is substantially less adhesive than fat and meat; it does not cling to or penetrate the metal in the same way. The concern for residue on the knife is specifically about fat and meat, which tend to coat and adhere to the surface. Blood, by contrast, slides off and presents no comparable risk of transfer.

### Heat During Penetration

The Gemara then addresses a subtle but important question. If one holds that absorption into metal does occur through heat — the position that was rejected as halacha but is worth understanding — one might ask: even when the animal is kosher, doesn't the knife absorb the taste of the flesh as it cuts through? The Gemara responds: *eimas d'ka chamima, l'chi gamra shechita* — the moment at which the knife is surrounded by the heat of the animal is only when the blade is fully embedded deep within the neck, and that is precisely when the shechita is already complete. The absorption, if any, would occur after the animal has already been rendered kosher.

### Post-Shechita Absorption

This logic resolves a potential circularity. One might have worried that the very beginning of the shechita — before it is complete — involves the knife contacting flesh that is still *eiver min hachai*, meat from a living (or not-yet-shechted) animal, which is itself forbidden. The Gemara addresses this directly: the heat that would drive any absorption is only present when the knife has penetrated deeply into the neck. But by that point, the shechita is already complete and the animal is permissible. There is therefore no moment at which the knife is simultaneously hot enough to absorb and in contact with forbidden meat — the two conditions never coincide in the shechita of a kosher animal.
