The overall picture that emerges from these final sugyot is one of carefully calibrated physical and halachic reasoning: the metal of the knife is less absorbent than flesh; blood is less adhesive than fat; the heat at the beit hashechita is at or near the borderline of halachic significance; and the sequencing of events within the shechita itself ensures that the knife's moment of deepest heat exposure is also the moment of the animal's permissibility. Two halachic principles of broad application — the definition of yad soledet bo and the question of duchka de-sakina — emerge from this discussion as live and contested matters among the Rishonim and Poskim.

---

---

# Hullin 9

## Three Knives

### Knives for Meat/Fat

We begin in the middle of 8b, where the Gemara continues its focus on knives. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: the butcher — הטבח — requires three separate knives. The first, אחת ששוחט בה, is used exclusively for shechita, and must be maintained with particular precision. The second, ואחת שמחתך בה בשר, is used for cutting the meat. Clearly one would not use the shechita knife for chopping meat, as that would ruin the precision instrument required for shechita. The third knife, ואחת שמחתך בה חלבין, is used for cutting the chelev — the forbidden fat.

It is worth clarifying what chelev is. The fat one sees marbled throughout a cut of meat is not chelev; that is שומא, shuma, and is permitted. The chelev that the Torah forbids — with the severity of karet, equivalent to the prohibition of blood — is the fat that surrounds the internal organs, remaining distinct and separate from the meat itself. It lays atop or around the organs rather than being integrated into the tissue. This fat, though forbidden for consumption, is permitted for benefit, and so the butcher would cut it up to sell in the marketplace to non-Jews. That is why the Gemara speaks of cutting the chelev rather than merely removing it — it is being processed for sale.

### Cross-Contamination Risk

The Gemara asks: why not use a single knife for both the cutting of meat and the cutting of fat? After all, the shechita knife is obviously kept separate — using it for chopping would ruin it. But why maintain two distinct chopping knives? The Gemara answers: גזירה שמא יחתוך חלבין ואחר כך בשר — we are concerned that the butcher will cut the fat and then, without properly cleaning the knife, proceed to cut the meat, thereby transferring the chelev to the meat and causing cross-contamination.

### Knife Marking

One might ask: if we require two separate knives, won't the butcher simply confuse which is which — מיחלף ליה — and inadvertently use the fat knife for the meat? The Gemara answers: כיון דצריכינו תרי אית ליה היכירא — precisely because we demand that he maintain two distinct knives, he will take care to mark them and keep them identifiable. If he has two knives to track, he will develop a system to distinguish them. The concern about confusion therefore does not override the requirement for separation.

## Two Wash Vessels

### Separate Vessels

Rav Yehuda said again in the name of Rav: the butcher requires two separate vessels of water — שני קיתונין של מים. One, אחד שמדיח בו בשר, is used to rinse the meat itself, and the other, ואחד שמדיח בו חלבים, is used to rinse the fat. The plain reading of the Gemara is that the meat and fat themselves are being washed in these vessels. Once a vessel has been used to rinse one type of item, the water is no longer clean — it contains residue of either meat or chelev — and washing the other type of item in the same water risks transferring the forbidden fat to the meat.

### Order Concern

The Gemara asks: why not maintain a single vessel and establish a careful sequence — first rinse the meat, then the fat? One could even assume that all the meat is processed before any of the fat, or that between animals the vessel is emptied and refilled. The Gemara responds: לא, גזירה שמא ידיח חלבים ואחר כך בשר — no, we are concerned that the butcher will forget the established order, reverse the sequence, or move on to a second animal without cleaning the vessel. The risk is too great to rely on a single vessel and a remembered procedure.

### Vessel Distinction

As with the knives, one might ask whether having two vessels simply doubles the chance for confusion. The Gemara answers identically: כיון דצריכינו תרי אית ליה היכירא — since we require two separate vessels, the butcher will label or otherwise distinguish them, and confusion will be avoided. The underlying principle in both cases is the same: a formal requirement of separation creates the conditions for vigilance, while a single shared implement invites error.

## Fat on Meat

### Kipli Flanks

Meimar said in the name of Rav Pappa: לא ליסחף איניש קיפלי אלווי בשרא — a person should not place the כפלי, kiflei, atop the meat. Rashi identifies the kiflei as the flanks of the animal in the region of the kidneys — the area where the forbidden fat of the kidneys sits. This fat, tarba, is the same chelev forbidden by the Torah. The concern is that when these fat-laden flanks are placed on top of other meat, gravity will cause the fat to flow downward — דדייץ תרבא ובלע בשרא — and be absorbed into the meat below.

### Gravity Concern

The Gemara challenges this ruling: if we are concerned that the fat will flow from the kiflei into the meat when placed on top, then we should equally be concerned when they are placed side by side — כי טריצי נמי דייב תרבא ובא לבישרא — for the fat will dissolve and flow even in that configuration. Why should the prohibition be limited to placing them on top of one another?

### Membrane Barrier

The Gemara answers: קרומא מפסיק מתתאי — there is a membrane surrounding the fat that acts as a barrier. When the fat-laden portions are merely placed adjacent to the meat, the membrane contains the fat and prevents transfer. The Gemara then asks: but if there is a membrane, why is placing them on top more concerning? Even in that position the membrane should provide a barrier. The Gemara answers: איידי דממשמשא ידיה דטבחא מיפתח — because when the butcher handles the portions and lays them atop the meat, the physical handling causes the membrane to rupture. It is the combination of gravity and the pressure of handling that creates the risk of the fat escaping the membrane and flowing into the meat below. Placing portions side by side involves less handling-induced pressure, and the membrane remains intact. Precisely how the act of placing something on top differs from placing it alongside in terms of membrane integrity is not entirely resolved, but the Gemara understands that the combination of factors creates a meaningfully greater risk.

## Three Skills

### Core Skills

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: תלמיד חכם צריך שיהא למוד שלשה דברים — a student of the sages must know three practical skills: כתב, שחיטה, ומילה — writing, shechita, and milah. These are not conventional rabbinic disciplines in the sense of textual analysis, but practical skills essential for a rabbi serving a community, particularly one in a far-flung locale without ready access to specialists. A rabbi must be able to write, since even basic literacy was not universal; he must be able to perform shechita, since a remote community may have no access to a trained shochet; and he must be able to perform milah, since a community may have no mohel.

### Writing/Ktav

The word כתב, ktav, admits of several interpretations among the Rishonim. Rashi understands it simply as the ability to sign one's name — something not everyone knew how to do — since a talmid chacham might sit on a beit din and be required to sign documents. The עיטור, Ittur, interprets ktav as knowledge of שטרות, shtaros — the ability to draft legal documents — which makes considerable practical sense for a communal rabbi. The מהרש"א, Maharsha, understands it as the ability to write a Sefer Torah. The ים של שלמה, Yam Shel Shlomo, suggests it means the ability to write in a literate and articulate style — a reading that is difficult to derive from the word כתב alone. In any case, the list reflects a curriculum of practical rabbinic competence: whatever you know in learning, you must arrive in a community equipped with skills the community will actually need.

## Ritual Skills

### Tfillin/Tzitzit

Rav Chanina bar Shlamya said in the name of Rav: אף קשר של תפילין, וברכת חתנים, וציצית — in addition to the three already mentioned, one must also know how to tie the knot of the tfillin, how to recite the sheva brachos, and how to attach tzitzit. These are three further practical skills that a community might rely upon its rabbi to perform.

### Rabbi's Role

The inclusion of ברכת חתנים, birchas chasanim, is particularly striking. There is a question throughout halachic literature regarding who recites the sheva brachos — whether it is the chasan or members of the community. The Rambam holds that under the chupah the chasan recites the brachos, while at the meals they are recited by community members. The fact that this Gemara specifically requires the rabbi to know birchas chasanim implies that the rabbi is the one who will be reciting them — and further implies that the rabbi serves in the role of mesader kiddushin. This is one of the few places in the Gemara where such a role for the rabbi is suggested.

On the question of the knot of tfillin: there is a debate in Tosafos about whether the knot must be retied daily. One of the Baalei Tosafos reads the verse וקשרתם, vkshartam, literally as requiring the knot to be redone each day. Tosafos itself cites the fact that this Gemara singles out the knot of tfillin as a skill the rabbi must know as proof against that opinion — for if every person were required to redo the knot daily, everyone would already know how to do it, and there would be no special need to mention it as a rabbinic skill.

### Essential vs. Common

The Gemara asks: why does the first authority list only ktav, shechita, and milah, and not the three additional skills of tfillin, birchas chasanim, and tzitzit? The answer: ואידך הני שכיחי — those latter three are commonplace. Everyone knows how to make birchas chasanim, tie tzitzit, and make the knot of tfillin. The first three skills are the greater חידוש, chiddush — they are specifically the skills that are not naturally assumed and that must be deliberately acquired.

## Shochet Knowledge

### Knowledge Required

Returning now to themes central to the beginning of the masechta, Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: כל טבח שאינו יודע הלכות שחיטה אסור לאכול משחיטתו — any shochet who does not know the laws of shechita, one may not eat from his shechita.

### Five Halachos

The Gemara specifies the five primary halachic concerns of shechita: שהייה — pausing in the middle of the shechita; דרסה — applying pressure to the knife rather than drawing it; חלדה — tunneling, meaning inserting the knife between the trachea and esophagus and cutting from the inside rather than from without; הגרמה — shechting in the wrong location, too high or too low; and עיקור — a term whose precise meaning is debated. Rashi understands ikur as the physical tearing out of one of the simanim — the trachea or esophagus — rather than cutting it. Tosafos objects that this would simply mean the siman was not cut, not that a separate psul occurred, and therefore cites another opinion: that ikur refers to a situation in which one of the simanim has been displaced from its normal anatomical position in the animal while still alive — not enough to render the animal a treifa, but such that the shechita requires the simanim to be in their original locations or it is pasul.

### Knowledge Gap

The Gemara asks: is this ruling not obvious? These five categories are all taught in later Mishnayos — of course a shochet must know them. The Gemara responds: לא צריכא — it is necessary in a specific case. The case is where we have witnessed the shochet perform shechita two or three times with evident skill and precision — ושחט שפיר — and one might therefore assume that since he performs so flawlessly in practice, it does not matter whether he possesses the theoretical knowledge. The Gemara teaches that this assumption is wrong. Even if we observe perfect performance, if he does not know the laws — כיון דלא גמר — we cannot trust him. Why? זימנין דשהי ודריס ולא ידע — there will be occasions where he pauses or applies pressure and will not know that he has done anything wrong. A person who does not know the halachic parameters cannot recognize his own deviations from them, and therefore will never report a problem.

### Competence Presumption

The Gemara earlier established two distinct categories: גמיר, gamir — one who has been tested on the laws — and מומחה, mumcheh — one who has demonstrated practical experience. The present ruling addresses the case where we positively know the shochet does not know the laws: in that case, experience alone is insufficient. But there is a third category: what if we simply do not know whether the shochet knows the laws, and had no opportunity to ask or test him? The Gemara earlier established the principle of רוב מצויין אצל שחיטה מומחין הם — those who regularly engage in shechita may be presumed competent, meaning that a person performing shechita is presumed to know what he is doing. Thus: if we have tested the shochet and confirmed knowledge, the shechita is valid; if we have confirmed that he does not know the laws, the shechita is invalid regardless of his practical skill; and if we simply do not know, we may rely on the presumption of competence.

## Inspect Simanim

### Check Organs

Rav Yehuda also said in the name of Shmuel: הטבח צריך שיבדוק בסימנים לאחר שחיטה — after performing shechita, the butcher must inspect the trachea and esophagus to verify that the cut was clean and properly executed. The primary concern is a nick in the knife, which would cause tearing rather than cutting, rendering the shechita invalid.

### Inspection Time

Rav Yosef noted that this obligation is implicit in a Mishnah: רבי שמעון אומר אם שהה כדי ביקור — Rabbi Shimon says that an invalid pause during shechita is defined as a pause long enough to allow for ביקור, inspection. The very fact that a duration called "inspection time" exists implies that there is a recognized practice of inspecting — and Rav Yosef understood this inspection to refer to checking the simanim, the trachea and esophagus.

### Knife Check

Abaye challenged this reading. He cited Rabbi Yochanan: כדי ביקור חכם — the time in question is the time it takes to have a sage check the knife, not the time to check the simanim. The practice was that when a new rabbi arrived in a community, all the shochtim would bring their knives to him for inspection, as an implicit acknowledgment of his authority. The method of checking a knife for nicks is to run one's fingernail along the blade — any hesitation or catch indicates a nick and renders the knife unusable. Those with greater expertise check the blade with the tip of the tongue.

The Gemara then raises a practical objection to the interpretation of ביקור חכם: אם כן נתת דבריך לשיעורין — if the measure of time is how long it takes to have the sage inspect the knife, this is not a fixed duration. It depends on how far away the sage lives, how long the ceremony takes, and so on. The Gemara therefore refines: the measure is not the time to travel to a sage for a formal ceremony, but rather the time required for the shochet himself — who is a knowledgeable practitioner — to check the knife: כדי ביקור טבח חכם. This is a fixed and practical standard.

### Resolution

Although the Gemara could not conclusively prove from the Mishnah that ביקור refers to inspection of the simanim, the halakhic requirement to inspect the simanim after shechita nonetheless stands as stated by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel.

## Uninspected Status

### Treifa Status

The Gemara now asks: לא בדק מאי — if the shochet did not inspect the simanim, what is the halachic status of the animal? Rabbi Eliezer ben Antigonos citing Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Yannai rules: טרפה ואסורה באכילה — it is treifa and forbidden to eat. This is a striking ruling. One might have assumed that the requirement to inspect is only lechatchila and that bedi'avad, after the fact, the animal is permitted — the shochet is experienced, the knife was checked beforehand. Yet the Gemara does not take this position. Without verifying the simanim, we cannot confirm the shechita was valid, and the animal is therefore forbidden.

### Nevela Status

A braita goes further: נבילה ומטמאה במשא — the animal is not merely treifa but nevela, and conveys tumah through carrying. The distinction between treifa and nevela is significant: treifa refers to an animal that was shechted correctly but had an internal defect — a ruptured organ, for example — rendering it non-kosher; nevela refers to an animal that was not shechted correctly at all, whether because it died on its own, was killed in another way, or the shechita was invalid, such as due to a nick in the knife causing tearing. Both are forbidden to eat, but only nevela conveys tumah. If the shechita was not confirmed to be valid, then if it was indeed invalid, the animal would be a nevela — and the braita holds that without confirmation, we treat it as such.

### Chazaka Debate

The Gemara frames the dispute between the treifa ruling and the nevela ruling as reflecting a disagreement about the principle of Rav Huna: בהמה בחייה בחזקת איסור עומדת — while alive, an animal stands in a presumptive status of issur, forbidden to eat. This status persists עד שיודע לך במה נשחטה — until you know how it was shechted. Once a proper shechita is established, the animal moves to a חזקת היתר, a presumptive status of permissibility, and remains there unless you know it became a treifa.

The question is: what does chazaka track? One position holds that chazaka follows the physical facts. The animal was not shechted — that is the factual status quo. Since we cannot confirm it was shechted correctly, we must treat it as though it was not, and an animal not properly shechted that dies is nevela. The other position holds that chazaka follows the halachic status rather than the physical details. The animal's halachic status while alive was: forbidden to eat, but not tamei. Now it is dead and we are uncertain whether the shechita was valid. We retain its prior halachic status: forbidden to eat, not tamei. What category of non-kosher animal is forbidden to eat but does not convey tumah? A treifa — not a nevela. Therefore, without any indication of an internal defect, the animal is categorized as treifa purely on the basis of continuing its prior halachic status. Tosafos notes that this latter reasoning is somewhat strained, and assumes the treifa position is derabbanan — at a biblical level the animal would be considered permitted — which allows the reasoning to operate with greater flexibility.

## Chazaka Principle

### Initial Status

The Gemara now examines Rav Huna's statement in its own right. Rav Huna declares: בהמה בחייה בחזקת איסור עומדת — a live animal stands in a presumptive status of being forbidden. One cannot consume a live animal, and one cannot rip off a limb from a living creature. This forbidden status persists until one establishes that a proper shechita was performed. Chazaka, then, works לחומרא here: the presumption of being forbidden remains until affirmatively overridden by knowledge of a valid shechita.

### Kosher Status

Once proper shechita has been confirmed, the animal acquires a new chazaka — חזקת היתר — a presumptive status of being permitted. This chazaka now works לקולא: the animal is presumed kosher unless there is positive knowledge that it became a treifa. This is why in practice we do not inspect every internal organ after shechita. Most organs present no commonly occurring defects, and relying on the chazaka of heter is sufficient. The only exception is the lungs, where tears and perforations are a relatively common occurrence — a מיעוט המצוי, miyut hamatzui — which obligates inspection. For all other organs, since the defect would be a מיעוט שאינו מצוי, miyut she'eino matzui — a rare occurrence — there is no obligation to investigate.

### Fox Case

The Gemara presents the following scenario, posed by Rabbi Abba to Rav Huna: you shechted an animal, the organs are laid out, and a wolf came and snatched some of them. May we assume the organs were unpunctured? The Gemara immediately clarifies: if the organs were simply carried away, הא ליתנהו — they are not before us, and we need not concern ourselves with them. The question refines itself: suppose the animal grabbed a piece, punctured it, and returned it — or carried it off and returned with a hole evident in it. The concern is: was there a hole in the organ before the animal bit it, perhaps now concealed by the bite mark? The Gemara answers on the basis of chazaka: once proper shechita has been performed, the animal stands in a chazaka of heter. This chazaka persists unless one can positively establish a treifa condition. A doubt raised by a fox's bite — without being able to confirm whether a hole predated it — does not override the chazaka, and the animal remains permitted.

## Hazard Exception

### Snake Concern

The Gemara poses a challenge from a case of real-world danger. If one saw a bird pecking at a fig or a weasel gnawing at a melon, the ruling is חוששין שמא במקום נקב נקב — we are concerned that the bite may be covering a hole left by a snake. The Gemara was consistently concerned that snakes might eat from exposed food and leave behind venom. The fact that you observe the weasel making a hole does not eliminate the concern, because the weasel may have bitten precisely where a snake had bitten previously. The question is: why don't we apply chazaka here? The fig had a chazaka of being intact and unpoisoned; why does a doubt override that chazaka?

### Issur vs. Sakana

The Gemara answers: מי קמידמי איסורא לסכנתא — how can you compare a question of issur, of halachic status, to a question of sakana, of real-world danger? סכנתא שאני — danger is categorically different. The principle חמירא סכנתא מאיסורא captures part of this, but the deeper point is that formal halachic mechanisms like chazaka are appropriate for resolving questions about halachic status. Chazaka is a legal tool — it tells us how to treat something in the halachic framework. It does not actually tell us anything about physical reality. When the question is one of health — is there poison in this food — what matters is the actual state of affairs, not a formal legal presumption. Chazaka is therefore simply irrelevant to health concerns. Real-world danger operates by percentages and probabilities, not by legal status quo.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava challenged this answer: מאי שנא ספק סכנה לחומרא — why is a doubt regarding danger treated strictly, ספק איסורא נמי לחומרא — if so, should a doubt regarding prohibition not also be treated strictly? Rava does not see a principled distinction; both involve doubt, and strictness seems to apply in both domains.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye responded: ולא שני בין איסור לסכנתא — are you saying there is no difference between issur and sakana? He demonstrates the difference with a compelling example. The rule is ספק טומאה ברשות הרבים ספיקו טהור — a doubt about tumah in a public domain is resolved leniently, the status is tahor. Yet ספק מים מגולים אסורין — a doubt about uncovered water is treated strictly. Here we have two parallel cases of doubt, and the outcomes are opposite. For halachic tumah, we have a formal rule directing leniency; for health concerns about exposed water, we are strict regardless. This proves that the two domains operate under fundamentally different principles.

## Sota Rules

### Tumah Criteria

Abaye's proof is challenged: perhaps the leniency regarding tumah in the public domain is not based on the general principle of chazaka at all, but on a specific law derived from the case of Sotah. The Torah employs the phrase ונסתרה ונטמאה — she was secluded and she became defiled — in the context of the suspected sotah. From this phrase, the Sages derived that a doubt about tumah is treated as definite tumah only when two criteria are met: it occurred in a private domain, and there was present a party who in theory could know what happened. When either criterion is absent — when the doubt arises in a public domain, or when no party capable of reporting was present — the doubt does not generate a presumption of tumah. This is not chazaka; it is a formal derivation from the laws of sotah.

### Vessel Rules

The Gemara further illustrates this framework with the case of a vessel used to store water for the Parah Adumah purification ritual. If one left a pitcher uncovered and returned to find it covered, one must be concerned that a tamei person entered and covered it — and the vessel may therefore be tamei. Conversely, if one left it covered and returned to find it uncovered, the concern is not about human agency but about animals: could a weasel or snake have drunk from it, rendering the water invalid for use in the Parah Adumah ritual? As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains: מפני שדרכן של שרצים לגלות ואין דרכן לכסות — because the nature of small animals and insects is to uncover vessels, not to cover them. When the vessel was found covered, a human being must have been involved, raising the concern of tumah. When found uncovered, only animal access is suspected, and that raises no tumah concern — only the separate question of whether the water has been invalidated for ritual use.

### Stricter Scrutiny

Rav Ashi concludes the discussion: שמע מינה חמירא סכנתא מאיסורא שמע מינה — conclude from this that danger is treated more strictly than issur. Throughout the extended discussion, the Gemara has demonstrated that doubts resolved by chazaka and formal halachic rules in the domain of issur and tumah are not resolved the same way in the domain of health and danger. When the question is one of halachic status, legal mechanisms — chazaka, formal rules derived from Sotah, the principle of rov — are fully adequate tools. When the question is one of real-world danger, those tools are beside the point. What matters is the actual state of affairs on the ground: is there poison here, did a snake drink from this water. A legal status quo cannot answer that question. Health concerns demand scrutiny of actual probabilities; they cannot be managed by formal legal presumptions.

---

# Hullin 10

## Mayim Megulim

### Three Liquids Assur

The Gemara opens this section with a Mishnah cited from elsewhere: three types of liquids are forbidden if left exposed — *mayim v'yayin v'chalav*, water, wine, and milk — due to the concern that a snake may have drunk from them and left behind venom. The question then becomes: how long must the liquids have been left unattended before they become forbidden? The answer given is *k'dei she'yeitzei harachash mimakom karov v'yishteh* — enough time for a crawling creature, specifically a snake, to emerge from a nearby place and drink. The Gemara then asks how nearby is "nearby," and Rabbi Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda answers: enough time for a snake to emerge from beneath the handle of a vessel, drink, and return to its hole. The logic is straightforward: you cannot simply measure the time for the snake to slither out and drink, because if it had only done that much, you would still see it upon turning back. Therefore, the time threshold must account for the full round trip — slither out, drink, and return.

### Snake Timeline

The Gemara's formulation — *ela yishteh veyachzor lechoro* — establishes that the operative concern is the complete sequence: emergence, drinking, and retreat. This is the window during which one must have left the liquid unattended for the prohibition to apply.

### Tosfos on Snakes

Tosfos cites the Yerushalmi, which takes an even stricter approach. The Yerushalmi mentions a variety of snake called a *shfiphon* that is as thin as a hair, and states that *reshus nitna lekarka lehibakeia lefanav* — permission is granted for the ground to crack open before it. This means that even if no visible hole is present near the vessel, one cannot confidently rule out the snake's access, since it can apparently find or create an entry point in the earth that is invisible to the observer. Consequently, the time threshold must account for this more expansive possibility, and the standard of concern is accordingly heightened.

### Ashkenazi Practice

Despite the explicit and early halakhic formulation of *mayim megulim* — appearing at the Tannaitic level with the language of *assur* and with detailed parameters — Tosfos in several places states that this halakha is not practiced among Ashkenazim. His reasoning is that the entire prohibition is grounded in a concern for *sakana*, specifically the prevalence of dangerous snakes, and that this environmental condition no longer applies in the communities where Ashkenazim live. This is why many are unfamiliar with the law that leaving one's drink unattended renders it forbidden. The Rambam, however, rules it straightforwardly, and the Shulchan Aruch similarly appears to rule it for Sefardim.

### Health-Based Laws

This situation closely parallels the halakha of *mayim acharonim*, where the Gemara requires washing one's hands at the end of a meal on account of the salt residue left on one's fingers — a concern rooted in the heavy salting used to preserve meat in the Talmudic era, compounded by the absence of forks, which were not introduced into European usage until roughly the 14th century. Here too Tosfos states that the practice is not required in his day, though his precise reasoning is less transparent given that salted meat preservation was still practiced in his time. The Rambam and Shulchan Aruch continue to rule *mayim acharonim* as obligatory. What is striking about the comparison between these two halakhot is that *mayim megulim* employs far stronger halakhic language — *assur*, with detailed Tannaitic parameters — and yet Tosfos sets it aside, just as he does with the Amoraic, and in some ways more modest, formulation of *mayim acharonim*. In both cases, the principle that underlies the halakha — a health concern — is treated by Tosfos as the operative factor that determines the law's ongoing applicability.

### Halacha Obsolescence

One might ask: who decides which halakhot have become obsolete, and by what authority? The general principle holds that even when the underlying reason for a halakha no longer applies, the halakha itself does not change. However, matters of health and *sakana* occupy a somewhat distinct category. The Rambam, for instance, readily sets aside Talmudic medical remedies — and even the Gemara's prohibition of eating fish and meat together, which also uses the language of *assur* — on the grounds that the scientific assumptions underlying those rulings were simply incorrect. So specifically in the domain of health, one can argue that such statements were never purely halakhic in the same sense as other prohibitions and are therefore more susceptible to revision based on changed circumstances.

### Rambam/SA Ruling

The Rambam's approach is nonetheless inconsistent, retaining some health-based halakhot while discarding others. The Rambam rules *mayim megulim* and *mayim acharonim* while dismissing certain Talmudic medical prescriptions — reflecting that even within this domain there is no single clean criterion.

### Tosfos Method

An important methodological point about Tosfos bears emphasis here, one that is sometimes misunderstood. Tosfos does not proceed by examining a halakha, reasoning that its underlying rationale no longer applies, and concluding that the community need not observe it. Rather, Tosfos almost invariably begins from the observed fact that the halakha was *not* being practiced in his community and then works backward to explain why this practice — or non-practice — might be correct. He is reconciling the fact on the ground with the Talmudic text, not abolishing laws from the top down. This is a characteristically Ashkenazic and community-oriented halakhic posture: assume the community's practice may be defensible and seek the justification, rather than assume the community is wrong. It is worth emphasizing that one cannot find a case in all of Shas where Tosfos says: "although the community observes this halakha, since the reason no longer applies we may abandon it." The directionality always runs the other way.

---

## Knife Nick After Slaught…

### Case Setup

The Gemara now turns to what becomes one of the central and most analytically rich cases of this section. *hashochet besakin venimtset peguma* — one slaughtered with a knife, having checked it beforehand, and upon completing the shechita discovered that the knife was nicked. The question is: when did the nick occur? Before the shechita, rendering the animal non-kosher, or after?

### Rav Huna Position

Rav Huna rules: *afilu shiber bah atzamot kol hayom pesula* — even if after the shechita the knife was used to chop bones the entire day, the shechita is invalid. The reasoning is *chaishinan shema ba'or nifgama* — we must be concerned that the nick occurred at the very beginning of the shechita, in the outer skin of the animal's neck, before the cut was completed. This is admittedly a worst-case scenario — it is far more plausible that a nick found after extensive bone-chopping was caused by the bones. Nevertheless, Rav Huna holds that once you observe that the status quo has changed — the knife, which was checked and known to be good, is now nicked — you must be concerned that the change occurred as early as possible, not as late as possible.

To appreciate the stakes here, it is important to distinguish this case from the cases discussed previously. Before, the principle of *chazakah* was invoked to say: we had a status quo and a doubt arose — we dismiss the doubt and maintain the status quo. Here, by contrast, the status quo has demonstrably ended. The knife was good; now it is not. The question is no longer whether a change occurred — it did — but *when*. And the question of when a chazakah ends, and whether one can assume it held as long as possible, is the crux of the dispute.

An instructive parallel is the case of a *sefer torah* being read and a letter found to be cracked mid-reading. The ruling is that only the last *aliyah* must be repeated, because we assume the crack occurred at the last possible moment and not during an earlier *aliyah*. This suggests that in some contexts the principle of extending the chazakah until the last possible moment does apply. Whether that principle governs the shechita case — where, crucially, the animal begins with a chazakah of being non-kosher — is precisely what Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute.

### Rav Chisda Position

Rav Chisda rules: *keshera* — the shechita is valid. His reasoning introduces a distinct halakhic principle: *etzem vadai pogem, o safek pogem safek lo pogem* — a bone will definitely cause a nick, while whether the animal's skin would cause a nick is a genuine doubt. This invokes the principle of *safek v'vadai*: *ein safek motzi miyedei vadai* — a possibility does not displace a certainty. If there is a definite cause to which the nick can be attributed, namely the bone-chopping that occurred after the shechita, then the speculative concern that it was caused by the skin during the shechita is insufficient to undermine the definite explanation. The Gemara notes that this is a strong argument: the bone-breaking definitively, or at minimum far more plausibly, accounts for the nick, and there is no reason to abandon that explanation in favor of a far-fetched alternative.

### Mikvah/Chatzitza Case

The Gemara records that Rava attempts to marshal support for Rav Huna from a parallel case: *taval v'ala v'nimtza alav davar chotzetz* — one immersed in a mikvah and upon emerging discovered a *chatzitza* on one's body. The ruling is that even if one worked with the very material that could have caused the *chatzitza* — for example, cement, which could easily lodge under fingernails — the entire day after the immersion, the *tevilah* is invalid unless one can state with certainty, *bari li*, that the obstruction was not present beforehand. The parallel to the knife case seems precise: in both instances, there is a post-facto discovery of a problem, and there is a plausible explanation attributing it to activity that followed the act in question, yet that explanation is insufficient.

### Competing Chazakos

The Gemara responds to this parallel by noting that in the *tevilah* case there are two competing *chazakot*. The person had a chazakah of not having a *chatzitza* on their body, but they also had a prior status of being *tamei*. The principle established earlier applies: *ha'amed tamei al chazakato* — maintain the person's status of *tum'ah* until you know with certainty that it changed. Any doubt, even a doubt supported by a plausible alternative explanation, is insufficient to change a status that begins as *tamei*. Similarly, the Gemara suggests, the animal begins with a chazakah of being non-kosher, and one cannot assume the shechita was valid unless there is complete certainty. Rav Huna is consistent: he applies this principle across both cases.

### External vs. Intrinsic

To defend Rav Chisda's position — which is lenient about the shechita but presumably would be strict in the *tevilah* case — the Gemara offers a formal distinction: *sakin itra'ei beheima lo itra'ei* — the doubt pertains to the knife, not to the animal. In the *tevilah* case the doubt concerns the person's own body, which is the very subject of the status change from *tamei* to *tahor*. Because the *chatzitza* doubt is intrinsic to the person himself, it cannot be set aside. In the shechita case, the locus of doubt is the knife — external to the animal — and therefore the animal's shechita can be evaluated independently: the act was performed, the *simanim* appeared correct, and the problematic question is an extrinsic one about the instrument.

### Tosfos Critique

Tosfos finds this distinction deeply unsatisfying. In what way does the formal location of the problem — knife versus animal — change the halakhic reality? If the knife was nicked, the shechita was invalid regardless of whether we call the doubt "external" or "intrinsic." The question of validity still reduces to whether the knife had a nick at the time of shechita, which is precisely the doubt. Tosfos therefore offers an alternative reading: in the knife case there is a *double* doubt. First, it is uncertain when the nick occurred. Second, even if it is assumed the knife had a nick, the nick might have been located on a part of the blade that did not actually contact the *simanim* during the cut — a long knife could conceivably be nicked at one point while the shechita was performed with a different portion of the blade. This double doubt, he argues, is what actually distinguishes the case from the *tevilah* scenario, which involves only a single doubt.

### Inspection Evidence

A cleaner explanation, however, may lie in the distinction between what can be directly inspected after the fact. In the shechita case, as the previous daf established, one examines the *simanim* — the trachea and esophagus — after the fact, and that direct inspection provides affirmative evidence that the cut appears to have been performed correctly. This post-facto examination constitutes meaningful evidence that the shechita was valid, giving substance to the claim that the knife was likely fine at the moment of the cut and the nick occurred later. In the mikvah case, by contrast, emerging wet from the water provides no equivalent evidence. One cannot inspect the immersion retroactively the way one can inspect the *simanim*. The person's being wet shows that they dunked, not that they dunked without a *chatzitza*. In this reading, the Gemara's phrase *harei shechuta l'fanecha* — here the slaughter is before you — refers precisely to this: the visible evidence of the *simanim* supports the presumption of validity. By contrast, *harei tavul l'fanecha* carries no such evidentiary weight. This explanation may in fact be embedded in the Gemara's own language, rendering the Gemara's distinction less purely formalistic than it at first appears.

---

## Bird Trachea Case

### Baraita on Trachea

The Gemara cites a Tannaitic case to probe the question further. *shachat es haveshet ve'achar kach nishmata hagargeres* — one slaughtered the esophagus of a bird and then found that the trachea had been displaced from its proper location. To be clear on the anatomy: *veshet* is the esophagus and *gargeres* is the trachea. For a bird, only one of the two *simanim* must be cut, but both must be in their correct anatomical position at the time of shechita, lest the cut constitute an *ikkur* — a dislodgment that invalidates the shechita. If the trachea was already displaced before the shechita, the shechita is invalid; if it moved afterward, it is valid. The case arose in practice — *zeh hayah ma'aseh* — and the ruling was issued: *kol safek bashechita pasul* — any doubt in shechita renders it invalid.

### Doubt Principle

The Gemara asks what the word "any" in *kol safek bashechita pasul* comes to include. The answer is that it includes even cases where there might be contextual reason to assume validity — the broad formulation sweeps in doubts that might otherwise seem resolvable. The implication seems to be that even in the knife case, where bone-breaking provides a plausible alternative explanation for the nick, the principle of *kol safek* would still invalidate the shechita, thereby supporting Rav Huna.

### Animal vs. Knife Doubts

The Gemara responds: *lo le'asuyei safek she-hasafek daras* — the broad principle of *kol safek* is directed at standard categories of doubt about the act itself, such as *shehiyah* (pausing mid-cut) or *derisah* (applying pressure rather than cutting), not at the specific case where one has a definite causal explanation attributable to something that occurred after the shechita. Furthermore, the Gemara reasserts its earlier distinction: *hasam israyei be'reisha bavehema* — in the trachea case, the locus of doubt is the animal itself, its own physical condition and the act performed upon it. *sakin israyei beheima lo israyei* — in the knife case, the doubt concerns the knife, which is external to the animal.

### Principle Agreement

At this point the Gemara clarifies that both Rav Huna and Rav Chisda actually agree on the general principle of *kol safek bashechita pasul*. Their dispute is not about whether doubts are generally disqualifying — both agree they are — but rather about whether the specific configuration of the knife case, particularly when there is bone-breaking to attribute the nick to, constitutes the kind of resolved situation that removes it from the category of genuine doubt. The Gemara's distinction between doubts about the animal and doubts about the knife is the formal mechanism by which that resolution is achieved, at least according to Rav Chisda.

---

## Resolution & Halacha

### Hilcheta Rav Huna

The Gemara renders its final ruling in two parts. *v'hilchata kevastei de-rav kahana* — the halakha follows Rav Huna when no bone-breaking took place. If one slaughtered an animal, found a nick in the knife afterward, and had not used the knife on bones in the interim, the shechita is invalid. The reasoning is that without a definite cause to attribute the nick to, the concern that the nick was present at the time of shechita — that it arose *ba'or*, in the skin — cannot be dismissed, and we rule stringently consistent with the animal's initial chazakah of being non-kosher.

### Hilcheta Rav Chisda

*V'hilchata kevastei de-Rav Chisda* — when bone-breaking did occur, the halakha follows Rav Chisda and the shechita is valid. The presence of bone-breaking constitutes the *vadai* to which the nick can be attributed, and the principle of *ein safek motzi miyedei vadai* operates to permit the animal. The Gemara then works through the full range of the debate between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda, clarifying what each position holds even in cases they did not explicitly address. Rav Chisda, understood as invoking the chazakah of the knife and assuming the problem occurred at the last possible moment, would logically attribute the nick to the spine at the conclusion of the very last shechita — meaning all animals in a sequence would be valid. Rav Huna, applying worst-case assumptions throughout, would say even the first animal is compromised. The Gemara resolves that in a case without bone-breaking we follow Rav Huna; with bone-breaking, Rav Chisda.

### Rav Yosef Case

The Gemara records a practical case: *havah uvda* — such an incident occurred, and Rav Yosef *taraf* — declared non-kosher — thirteen animals after a nick was found in the knife at the end. The Gemara asks: according to whose opinion did Rav Yosef rule? If it is like Rav Huna, then even the first animal is invalid, which would account for all thirteen. But if it is like Rav Chisda, then thirteen animals are too many to explain, since Rav Chisda should allow you to attribute the nick to the very last moment.

### Nick Attribution

The Gemara considers the possibility that Rav Yosef ruled like Rav Chisda but in the version where the nick is attributed not to the very last shechita but to the backbone of the first animal, meaning all subsequent animals after the first are invalid — which would yield twelve invalid animals, not thirteen, unless the first is also counted, arriving at the same number. The Gemara then entertains an alternative: *v'ee ba'is ayma l'olam k'Rav Huna* — actually, Rav Yosef ruled entirely like Rav Huna, and all thirteen animals are invalid including the first, because Rav Huna's position is that once the chazakah of the knife is undermined by visible evidence of a nick, the concern reaches all the way back. If Rav Chisda's leniency were truly operative, one would logically extend the best-case attribution to the very last shechita and declare all thirteen valid — since *micdei matlee taleenan*, if we are going to project a best-case scenario, why attribute the nick to the first spine rather than the last? The fact that Rav Yosef declared all thirteen invalid confirms he ruled like Rav Huna.

### Practical Solution

Rav Acha son of Rava reported to Rav Ashi that Rav Kahana's practice was *mashich bedikuta beyn kol chad v'chad* — to extend the checking of the knife between each and every animal. This is the practically prudent approach: if a nick is discovered, the damage is contained to at most the most recently slaughtered animal, rather than retroactively invalidating an entire sequence. By checking the knife after each shechita, the shochet limits the range of uncertainty and avoids the disaster of invalidating a large batch.

### Knife Inspection

The Gemara observes that this practice of intermediate checking resembles the standard pre-shechita inspection before a sage — raising the question of whether each intermediate inspection also requires showing the knife to a *chacham*. The Gemara responds to this question by invoking Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: *lo amru l'har'ot sakin l'chacham elah mipnei kvodo shel chacham* — the requirement to show the knife to a sage was never a halakhic prerequisite for valid shechita but was instituted for the honor of the sage, to acknowledge rabbinic authority and oversight over the process. Once that obligation is discharged — as when all the *shochtim* in a community present their knives to a newly arrived authority — the ongoing intermediate checking can be done by the shochet himself.

### Self-Checking

This is grounded in the principle *eid echad ne'eman b'issurin* — a single witness is trusted in matters of kashrut. Just as one trusts one's butcher or household members regarding the status of food, the shochet is trusted to inspect his own knife competently. Accordingly, after the initial formal presentation to the sage, the shochet may check his own knife between animals without requiring external validation, and that intermediate self-inspection is halakhically sufficient to establish the knife's status at each stage of the shechita process.

The practical upshot: we rule like Rav Huna in cases without bone-breaking, meaning a nick discovered at the end creates retroactive doubt about all animals slaughtered since the last verified inspection. The solution is to check the knife after each animal so that any problem is isolated. If one was chopping bones in the interim, we rule like Rav Chisda and the shechita is valid. Rashi records that this question was raised in practice and that his teacher Rabbeinu Yaakov ben Rabbi Yitzchak ruled the animal *assur* in a case involving a bird — consistent with the ruling like Rav Huna.

---

## Source of Chazaka

### Derivation Question

Having applied the principle of chazakah extensively, the Gemara now steps back and asks the foundational question: *mena hani mili d'amri rabanan okminhu a'chezkateh* — from where do the Rabbis derive the very principle of chazakah, that one establishes something upon its prior status and assumes that status to persist until one knows otherwise?

### Tzara'at Source

Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: we learn it from the *pasuk* regarding *tzara'at* of a house. The Torah states *veyatza hakohen min habayit el pesach habayit vehisgir et habayit shivat yamim* — the kohen exits to the doorway of the house and seals it for seven days. The implicit question is: how can the kohen declare the house *tamei* if he is not directly observing the spot at the very moment of declaration? From the instant he saw the spot until the moment he steps outside and pronounces the declaration, perhaps the spot shrank below the minimum size required for *tum'ah*. The fact that the Torah enables this declaration at all demonstrates that we rely on chazakah — we assume the spot is still the same size it was when last observed, and the kohen acts on that assumption.

### Backward Walking

Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges: perhaps the source tells us nothing about chazakah at all. Perhaps the kohen walks out of the house *backwards*, keeping his eyes on the spot the entire time, so that he is in fact directly observing it as he exits. If so, there is no gap between observation and declaration, and no need to invoke any principle of assuming status quo.

### Abaye's Answers

Abaye offers two responses. First, *yetziah derech achorav lo shemah yetziah* — walking backwards does not constitute a normal departure; when the Torah says the kohen "exits," it means he exits in the normal fashion, facing forward. Second, even if one were to allow backward walking, what happens when the spot is behind the door? If the door opens outward and the spot is on the wall behind it, the kohen cannot see the spot as he exits regardless of which direction he faces. One might suggest cutting a window into the door to allow a line of sight, but here Abaye invokes another ruling: *bayit afel ein potchin bo chalonot lir'ot et nigo* — for a dark house one does not open windows to see the spot, because the standard is *l'chol mareh einei hakohen*, what the kohen can see under natural conditions. The house is assessed as it naturally stands, not as artificially illuminated. By analogy, one would not cut a window into a door solely to maintain visual contact with a spot.

### Rava Response

Rava counters Abaye on both points. Regarding backward walking not constituting a valid exit: *kohen gadol b'Yom HaKippurim yochiach* — the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur proves the contrary. The Torah describes him as exiting the Holy of Holies (*veyatza*), and we know from the Mishnah that *yatza u'va lo derech knisato* — he exits the way he entered, which is understood to mean he walked backwards to avoid turning his back on the Holy of Holies. Yet the Torah uses the language of *yetziah* for this backward exit, demonstrating that backward departure is indeed called leaving.

Regarding the dark-house ruling: *hani mili heichah d'lo itchazek itchazek* — that rule applies before a spot has been established. When no spot has yet been formally identified, one does not open windows to try to find or better see one. But *aval heichah d'itchazek itchazek* — once a spot has been established and its size confirmed, it may be permissible to open a window to continue observing it as the kohen exits. So Rava maintains that the backward-walking scenario, supplemented by a window, remains a viable alternative interpretation of the verse.

### Baraita Rules

The Gemara resolves the back-and-forth by citing a Baraita that rules definitively against the backward-walking reading. The Baraita derives from the Torah's phrasing that the kohen must fully exit the house — *ad sheyeitzei min habayit kulo* — he may not stand under the lintel when making the declaration. Rather, *omed b'tzad hamashkof u'masgir* — he stands just outside, near the lintel, and seals the house from there.

### Post-Facto Sealing

Crucially, the Baraita continues: *u'minayin she'im halach l'soch beiso v'hisgir* — how do we know that if the kohen deviated from the procedure and went all the way home before declaring the house sealed, or even remained inside the house and declared it from within, *she'hisgir u'musgar* — the house is still considered sealed and has its halakhic status? From the phrase *vehisgir et habayit* — "and he shall seal the house" — *mikol makom*, regardless. This is the decisive proof: the kohen can be entirely at home, with no visual contact with the spot, and yet the declaration is valid. This is only possible if we apply chazakah — we assume the spot retained its qualifying size, precisely because we maintain the status quo until we know otherwise.

### Final Challenge

Rav Acha bar Yaakov makes one final attempt to deflect the proof, suggesting that perhaps the kohen received a relay of reports — *k'gon d'kaimi dara d'gavrei v'amri k'dikay kai* — a row of people standing between the house and the kohen's home, each confirming that the spot is still present, passing the information along so that the kohen acts on real-time knowledge rather than on presumption. Of course, by the time the information traveled down the chain of people, there would still be a moment of lag between the final observation and the declaration, but the Gemara treats this as the last serious objection before conceding the point.

### Chazaka Conclusion

In the end, the Gemara concludes: the principle of chazakah — assuming that an established status persists until one knows definitively otherwise — is derived from the *tzara'at* passage. The kohen can seal the house and declare it *tamei* based on his earlier observation of the spot because we presume things to remain as they were last known to be.

### Tosfos on Chazaka

Tosfos raises two further refinements. First, one might object that the *tzara'at* source only demonstrates chazakah being applied stringently — to render a house *tamei*. How do we know the principle also operates leniently, to permit something or preserve a status of *taharah*? Tosfos responds that once the principle is established as a mechanism for resolving uncertainty, it applies symmetrically to both strict and lenient outcomes; we do not distinguish between the two. He also notes that leniency is implicitly present even in the *tzara'at* case, since the kohen who declares the house sealed is thereby enabling the bringing of a *korban* at the conclusion of the process — a leniency of sorts, since permitting a *korban* to be brought by someone who is not a genuine *metzora* would itself be a problem. Second, Tosfos addresses the question of chazakah when there is a later *rei'uta* — an undermining development. If the kohen returns and finds the spot has shrunk below the minimum size, we do not retroactively assume it was already undersized when the house was sealed. Rather, we assume it remained at the qualifying size until it was observed to have shrunk, meaning the chazakah held for its full duration and only ended at the point of observed change. This maps directly onto the question about the nicked knife discussed at length earlier in the shiur.

With this, the principle of chazakah has been fully established and sourced. Tomorrow's daf will turn to the next foundational principle: *rov*.

---

---

# Hullin 11

## Intro to Rov

### Chazakah Review

Daf 11 opens by moving from the principle of chazakah, which occupied the preceding days, to an equally fundamental principle: rov, going by the majority. The discussion of chazakah established that status quo creates a high threshold to prove that things have changed — you assume an object or situation retains its prior status until you can prove otherwise. Two dimensions of chazakah were examined: first, the basic rule that one must demonstrate that the knife used for shechitah was valid, that no chatzitzah was present, and so forth; and second, the question of itra chazakah — what happens when the chazakah is disrupted? When a nick is found in the knife, when a bad letter appears in a Sefer Torah, do you use the status quo to determine that the change occurred at the latest possible moment or not? The Gemara derived the principle of chazakah from the laws of tzara'at, where one assumes the size of a spot has remained constant.

The new topic, rov, is in many ways the more intuitive principle. It directs us to go by the likelihood of something having occurred, using that likelihood to guide behavior when the facts are not known with certainty. Both chazakah and rov are tools for navigating doubt — acknowledging that while we would always prefer to know the facts, life often demands that we act without certainty, and the halachic system provides principled direction for doing so.

### Mina Ha-Milta

At the top of 11a, the Gemara asks: mina ha-milta — where is this well-established principle derived from? The question is not whether rov is rabbinic in origin, since the Gemara will immediately derive it from psukim and apply it to biblical prohibitions; rather, it asks where in the Torah this broadly accepted principle — zil batar ruba, go by the majority — is grounded. The Gemara answers: dechtiv acharei rabim lehatot, the verse in Shemot that instructs us to incline after the majority.

### Acharei Rabim Limit

The Gemara immediately qualifies this answer. The verse acharei rabim lehatot provides a clear source only for ruba de-ita kaman — a majority that is present before us, such as tesha chanuyot, the case of nine stores, or the vote of a Sanhedrin. In those cases, the derivation is unproblematic. The real question — ki kamiba'ya lan — is whether we can rely on rov in the case of ruba de-leisa kaman, an abstract or statistical majority not physically present before us, such as the case of katan ve-ketanah in the context of yibbum. From where do we know that principle?

---

## Ita vs. Leisa Kaman

### Nine Stores Example

The distinction between ruba de-ita kaman and ruba de-leisa kaman is worth spelling out carefully. Ruba de-ita kaman means that the majority is actually present and identifiable before you. Consider a case of three pots of meat, two of which are kosher and one of which is neveilah. If one accidentally ladles from one of them and cannot recall which, the question of what to assume is grounded in a concrete, present set: two out of three are fine. One can attribute one's action to the majority because the items that constitute that majority are right there.

The classic Talmudic formulation of this is tesha chanuyot — nine kosher butcher stores and one non-kosher store. A piece of wrapped meat is found on the street, evidently dropped from one of the stores. Since nine out of ten are kosher, one may assume the meat is kosher. This is not merely an abstract 90% probability; it is a judgment made against a known, present set of possibilities. One is attributing the item to the majority of a set that is actually in front of one — that is ruba de-ita kaman.

### Leisa Kaman & Yibbum

Ruba de-leisa kaman, by contrast, involves general statistical probabilities not anchored in any present, identifiable set. The Gemara's example is the case of yibbum involving a katan or ketanah. When a man dies without children, the mitzvah of yibbum or chalitzah applies — but only if there is the possibility of children, since the entire purpose of yibbum is le-hakim shem achiv ha-met, to perpetuate the brother's name. If either party is sterile, the mitzvah does not apply, and their union would instead be a biblical prohibition.

If one of the parties is a minor, there is no way to determine whether they will grow up to be fertile or sterile. The question is whether one may proceed with yibbum based on the likelihood that the minor will turn out to be fertile. This is not a question about which item from a known set a given object belongs to; it is a pure question of general population probabilities. What percentage of minors grow up to be sterile? Presumably very few — perhaps one in a hundred or one in a thousand — but there is no present, identifiable set from which one is drawing this inference. That is ruba de-leisa kaman.

### Formal vs. Probability

One might ask why this distinction should matter at all. In both cases the question ultimately reduces to likelihood: what is more probable? The Gemara's insistence on the distinction, however, points toward something deeper. As was seen in the discussion of chazakah, halacha does not operate purely as a probability-calculating machine. Chazakah is a formal rule — assume status quo until you know otherwise — and does not claim to tell you what the actual likelihood is that something has changed. Similarly, the Gemara's treatment of rov suggests that it is not simply about percentages.

When dealing with ruba de-ita kaman, one can do something more than calculate probabilities: one can associate the item in question with one of two present, distinguishable groups — the majority or the minority. There is a formal act of attribution occurring. With ruba de-leisa kaman, all one has are abstract percentages, and the question is whether halacha permits acting on the basis of pure probability alone. The Gemara's framing implies that this is the harder case, and the rest of the passage is devoted to finding a source that proves ruba de-leisa kaman is also operative.

### Sanhedrin & Birur

The Gemara includes Sanhedrin voting within the category of ruba de-ita kaman, and this is a striking inclusion. When a court takes a vote and twelve judges say one thing and eleven say the other, the majority determines the ruling — this is the halacha of acharei rabim lehatot in its most direct application. But it is immediately apparent that this is categorically different from inferring where a piece of meat came from. When one says the majority of stores were kosher, there is at least a sense in which one is making a claim about the real-world origin of the meat. When a Sanhedrin votes, however, no one is claiming that the majority vote tells us anything about the actual facts of the case. The majority vote is a procedural mechanism for reaching a decision, not a truth-tracking device.

The Gemara's inclusion of Sanhedrin voting in the same discussion as the case of the nine stores is therefore highly revealing. It signals that the principle of rov is not solely about resolving factual uncertainty by identifying the most probable truth. Sometimes it is about providing rules for how one lives and acts within a space of unresolved doubt. This is the distinction the contemporary yeshiva world frames as birur versus hanhaga: is rov a clarification of the facts, or is it a guideline for action even when the facts remain unresolved? Chazakah is clearly a hanhaga — it does not tell you the facts, it tells you how to proceed. The question is whether rov functions similarly, or whether it actually purports to establish the facts.

The inclusion of Sanhedrin voting suggests that rov has at least a hanhaga dimension. When the court does not know the truth, the system provides a rule: go by the majority vote. By extension, when the source of a piece of meat is unknown, the system provides a parallel rule: associate it with the majority. In both cases, the underlying doubt may not be resolved, but there is a principled framework for action.

### Birur vs. Hanhaga

This leads to a nuanced theoretical point. One might argue that birur does not require absolute certainty, only that a sufficient evidentiary threshold has been crossed. On this reading, when one says the piece of meat probably came from the kosher stores, one is not claiming certainty — one is claiming that the threshold for treating the matter as established has been met. Whether one frames this as "we have established the facts sufficiently" or "we have a rule for acting in the absence of established facts" may turn on precisely how one defines the concept of birur and what level of certainty it requires.

The connection to ruba de-ita kaman is particularly suggestive here. The reason ruba de-ita kaman is conceptually more tractable is that it allows one to replicate, in a sense, the structure of the Sanhedrin vote — there are nine stores versus one store, and one can treat that as a formal majority determination the same way a court vote is a formal majority determination. This provides a procedural basis for action that does not depend solely on raw probability. Ruba de-leisa kaman, dealing only in abstract percentages, raises the harder question of whether pure probability is sufficient to ground a halachic determination.

---

## Proofs from Korbanos

### Olah Brain Proof

Having established the question, the Gemara proceeds to search for a source for ruba de-leisa kaman. Rabbi Elazar says: atya me-reisha shel olah — one learns it from the head of a korban olah. The Torah states venisach otah lintacheha — the olah is cut into its parts and burned on the mizbe'ach. The Gemara derives from the phrase otah lintacheha velo netacheha lintachim that while the animal is divided into its constituent parts, one does not cut those parts into sub-parts. The head is thus offered whole; it is one of the sections placed on the mizbe'ach without further subdivision.

The problem is that one of the known treifot is a hole in the krum shemoach, the membrane surrounding the brain. If the head is offered whole and one is not permitted to break it open, how can one ever verify that the animal being brought as a korban olah is not a treifah on account of a perforated brain membrane? The only explanation is that one relies on rov — the majority of animals do not have perforated brain membranes — and that this rov must function even though the items are not present before us in a formal ruba de-ita kaman sense. This would constitute proof for ruba de-leisa kaman.

### Olah Refuted

The Gemara immediately challenges this proof. Mimai — how do you know the brain is not actually inspected? Perhaps one does crack open the skull to examine the membrane — dilma de-palyei u-vadkei. And if the concern is the rule that the parts may not be cut into sub-parts, hani milei heicha de-chatchei legamrei — that would only apply if one were to fully separate the skull into two distinct pieces. Aval heicha de-liyeif, if one merely cracks it open while keeping the two sides connected at the bottom, leis lan bah, that may not violate the prohibition. The proof from the olah is thus rejected: perhaps the brain is routinely inspected before the head is placed on the mizbe'ach, and no reliance on rov is necessary.

### Pesach Bone Proof

Mar breih d'Ravina tries another proof: atya mishvirat etzem d'be-Pesach, from the prohibition against breaking bones of the korban Pesach. The Torah states ve-etzem lo tishberu bo — not a single bone of the Pesach offering may be broken. Since the skull is a bone, one can never crack it open to inspect the brain membrane. Yet the korban Pesach must be valid and not a treifah, and the animal is brought and consumed. The only explanation is that one relies on rov — again, ruba de-leisa kaman.

### Coal Refutation

The Gemara refutes this as well. Dilma de-manach gumra alei ve-kalyu lei u-vadik lei — perhaps one places a hot coal on the skull, allows the heat to burn through it, and then inspects the brain through the resulting opening. This would not constitute active bone-breaking, and indirect burning through a coal is not shvirat etzem. A Baraita is cited in support: hamichatech begidin vehasoref be-atzamot ein bo mishum shevirat etzem — one who cuts through sinews or burns through bones does not transgress the prohibition of breaking a bone. Thus the korban Pesach case also fails to prove that rov must be operative, since an alternative method of inspection is available.

### Alyah Spine Proof

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a proof from the alyah — the fat tail of the sheep that is burned as part of the korban. The Torah says chelbo ha-alyah temimah — the entire fat tail must be offered. The fat tail is removed from a point along the spine — specifically, as the Gemara explains, le-umat ha-atzeh, opposite the atzeh, meaning at the level of the kidneys, since makom she-haklayot yo-atzot, the kidneys are the seat of counsel and wisdom, so the fat tail is severed at the point where it connects to the kidneys. This means the fat tail that is offered includes a section of the spine within it.

One of the treifot is nifzak chut hashidra — a severed spinal cord. If the fat tail must be offered whole — temimah — how can one inspect the portion of the spine concealed within it? One has no way of checking for this treifah. The inevitable conclusion is that one relies on rov, on the majority of animals not having severed spinal cords. This would once again be ruba de-leisa kaman.

### Alyah Refuted

The Gemara raises two possible rebuttals. First, demitata pasik lei — perhaps one cuts the fat tail off below the point where the spine runs through it, so that the offered portion of the fat tail contains no spine at all. The Gemara dismisses this: the verse says le-umat ha-atzeh, at the level of the kidneys, which situates the cut at a point where the spine is present. Second, even granting that the spine is included, dilma de-fatach lei u-vadak lei — perhaps one does cut open the fat tail and inspect the spine, and ve-i mishum temimah, if the concern is the requirement that it be whole, heicha de-chatcheh le-gamrei, that would only apply if one cut it into two entirely separate pieces. Aval heicha de-laf, if one opens it while keeping it connected, leis lan bah, perhaps that does not violate temimah. The proof from the alyah is therefore also rejected.

### Eglah Arufah Proof

Rav Sheshet breih de-Rav Idi says: atya me-eglah arufah, one learns it from the calf whose neck is broken in the wadi when a murder victim is found and the killer is unknown. The verse describes the eglah arufah using the term ha-arufah, from which the Gemara derives keshei sheleimah tehei — the calf must remain whole. The ritual requires breaking its neck and leaving it untouched thereafter; it cannot be cut open or inspected.

Before proceeding, the Gemara establishes why the eglah arufah cannot be a treifah. Kaparah ketiv bah — the verse employs the language of kappara, atonement: kaper le-amcha Yisrael. The house of Rabbi Yannai teaches that since it is associated with kappara like kodashim, it is ke-kodashim, and just as sacrifices cannot be treifot, the eglah arufah cannot be a treifah. Yet if it must remain whole — sheleimah — there is no way to inspect its internal organs. How can one ever perform this ritual without concern that the animal was a treifah? The answer must be that one relies on rov.

Tosafot notes that one might ask why the Gemara does not raise the same rebuttal here as it did with the olah — namely, that one can crack it open without fully severing it. The Gemara apparently understands that the term sheleimah, as distinct from temimah used in the alyah case, means genuinely whole and untouched. Moreover, unlike the olah and the alyah, where the animal is actively cut up as part of the offering process, the eglah arufah is killed and then simply left — there is no further handling. This stronger emphasis on complete non-interference makes the proof more compelling, and the Gemara seems to accept it as a meaningful advance in the argument.

### Parah Adumah Proof

Rabba bar Shila brings a parallel proof from the parah adumah, the red heifer. The Torah states ve-shachat ve-saraf — it is slaughtered and then burned. The drasha is: mah shechitatah ke-shehee shleimah, just as at the moment of slaughter it is whole, af srefiatah ke-shehee shleimah, so too at the moment of burning it is whole. The same term shleimah appears here as in the eglah arufah, and the emphasis is similarly on the animal remaining completely untouched and unhandled other than the act of killing. No cutting, no internal inspection is possible.

The question then arises: how can one ever perform the parah adumah ritual without concern that the animal was a treifah? And who says a parah adumah cannot be a treifah? Chatat karyah rachmana — the Torah calls it a chatat, a sin offering. There are extensive sugyot in Shas debating the precise status of the parah adumah — it is performed outside the Beis Hamikdash, yet the blood is sprinkled toward it, and in many respects it is treated like a korban. But for present purposes, the Gemara grants that since it is called a chatat, it has sufficient korban-like status that it cannot be a treifah. Yet since it must be whole and untouched, there is no way to inspect it, and one must rely on rov — ruba de-leisa kaman.

---

## Rov in Capital Law

### Paternity & Rov

Rav Mari shifts the discussion away from korbanos and korban-adjacent laws entirely and brings a proof from capital law: atya mi-makeh aviv va-imo. The Torah mandates the death penalty for one who strikes his father or mother, understood as drawing blood. The immediate problem is: how do we know who the father is? V-leichosh dilma lav aviv hu — perhaps the man assumed to be the father is not actually the biological father. Are we prepared to execute someone for striking his presumed father when paternity cannot be established with certainty?

The Gemara answers: ela lav mishum de-amrinan zil batar ruba — we go by majority. V-rov beilos achar ha-ba'al — the majority of sexual acts that a wife engages in are presumed to be with her husband, and therefore the child is attributed to the husband. On this basis, the presumed father is treated as the legal father for purposes of this capital offense.

### Rov vs. Chazakah Nature

This proof raises a fundamental question. The Gemara's initial rebuttal is: dilma kegon she-haya aviv ve-imo chavushin be-veis ha-asurin — perhaps the Torah only permits prosecution in a case where the parents were held together in jail, such that the wife had no opportunity to commit adultery and paternity was certain? The Gemara dismisses this: afilu hachi, ein apitropus la-arayos — even in that case, there is no absolute guarantee, since when the sexual drive is involved, normal assumptions about behavior cannot be made with certainty. The Gemara invokes this as a general principle: one can never completely rule out the possibility of adultery based on circumstantial controls alone.

One might press further and ask whether rov beilos achar ha-ba'al is genuinely a rov at all. When the Gemara speaks of the likelihood that an animal is not a treifah, there is at least a theoretical empirical basis — one can observe many animals, determine what percentage have internal defects, and derive a percentage. But in the case of paternity, there is no analogous population study. The claim that most of a wife's sexual acts are with her husband is not derived from any statistical survey; it is a presumption about human behavior and social norms.

This is indeed better described as a chazakah — but a different kind of chazakah than the status quo chazakah discussed in earlier sugyot. The Gemara elsewhere uses the phrase chazakah ein adam meiz panav bifnei ba'al chovo — there is a presumption that a person will not be so brazen as to explicitly deny a debt he owes. Similarly, rov beilos achar ha-ba'al is essentially a presumption of human nature: we presume that a married woman's sexual life is primarily with her husband, not because we have counted, but because that is the operative social and moral assumption. The Gemara itself uses the language of rov here, but as noted, this is the kind of rov that is grounded in and functions more like a chazakah of human nature. It is telling that this case is being included in a discussion of rov, since it blurs the line between the two categories.

### Murder Victim Treifah

Rav Kahana says: atya mi-horeg et ha-nefesh — one learns it from the execution of a murderer. The Torah mandates that a murderer be put to death. But v-leichosh dilma treifah hava — perhaps the person who was killed was a treifah, in which case the killer cannot be executed.

This requires some elaboration. Unlike the case of a terminally ill patient, where murder remains retzichah regardless of prognosis, the halacha treats the case of a treifah differently. If a person has an internal injury that renders him a treifah — meaning that due to this specific injury he will die — then killing such a person is not considered full murder in the halachic sense, and the killer cannot be executed. This principle applies bein biydei adam bein biydei shamayim, whether the injury was caused by human action or by natural causes. The question of how one acquires the status of a treifah in halachic terms is discussed extensively in the relevant sugyot.

The problem for our Gemara, then, is that one can never know whether the murder victim was a treifah. If there is any possibility he was, how can the murderer ever be executed? The answer must be ela lav mishum de-amrinan zil batar ruba — we go by majority, and we assume the victim was not a treifah.

### Autopsy & Kevod Hamet

The Gemara raises the possibility: v-chi teima, dibadkinan lei — perhaps we do perform an autopsy on the victim and determine whether he was a treifah? The Gemara responds: ha ka menavel — that would constitute a nivul, an indignity to the dead body, which is prohibited on account of kevod ha-met.

The Gemara immediately counters this objection: v-chi teima, mishum ibud neshamah d-hai — one should be willing to tolerate the indignity to the corpse in order to protect the life of the murderer. If the victim was indeed a treifah, the murderer should not be executed, and ninvalei — we would allow the autopsy in order to protect his life. This is a meaningful digression, as it touches on the question of what circumstances permit autopsy and override the concern for kevod ha-met.

However, even granting that an autopsy would be performed, it still cannot resolve the uncertainty. V-neichosh shema bi-mkom sayaf nekev havah — perhaps exactly where the sword pierced the victim's heart, there was already a pre-existing hole.
