If the victim was killed by a sword through the heart, an autopsy would show a perforated heart — but one cannot determine whether that perforation existed before the murder or was caused by the sword itself. There is no way to rule out the possibility that the victim was a treifah in precisely the location where he was killed. Thus, regardless of whether an autopsy is performed, one cannot achieve certainty, and one must rely on rov.

### Edim Zomemim Proof

Ravina says: atya me-eidim zomemin. The Torah states va-asitem lo ka-asher zamam — one does as the conspiring witnesses planned to do to the person they testified against. If two witnesses falsely testified that Reuven killed someone, intending to have Reuven executed, they are themselves executed. But v-leichosh dilma hai d-ashidu bei treifah havah — perhaps the person they were testifying against was himself a treifah. If they were only trying to have a treifah killed, their scheme, while wicked, was not aiming at the destruction of a full life in the halachic sense. Can one then execute them?

The answer must be ela lav mishum de-amrinan zil batar ruba — we assume the person they sought to have killed was not a treifah.

The Gemara raises the obvious rebuttal: d-nivdkei — let us inspect the person they were trying to kill. He is still alive; why not examine him and determine whether he is a treifah? The Gemara responds with a Baraita: lo haragu neheragin — the eidim zomemin are only executed if they did not succeed in having the person killed; if they did succeed, ein neheragin, they cannot themselves be killed. Since the person they sought to have killed is still alive, one might think an inspection is possible. But a live person cannot be cut open for an autopsy — so there is genuinely no way to determine whether the intended victim is or is not a treifah. One must therefore rely on rov.

### Shechitah Rov Proof

Rav Ashi returns the discussion to the opening topic of the masechet. Atya mi-shechitah atzmah — the proof comes from shechitah itself. The Torah states shechot ve-echol — slaughter and eat. V-leichosh shema bi-mkom nekev ka-shachit — perhaps right at the site of the cut, where one severed the trachea and esophagus, there was already a pre-existing hole. If so, the animal was a treifah before the shechitah was performed. The only reason one may eat the meat is ela lav mishum de-amrinan zil batar ruba — one goes by majority and assumes no pre-existing hole was present.

---

## Efshar Le-Varer

### Shimi's Challenge

Rav Ashi reports that he transmitted this entire discussion to Rav Kahana, who in turn transmitted it to Rav Shimi, and Rav Shimi responded with a fundamental challenge: dilma heicha de-efshar efshar, heicha de-lo efshar lo efshar — perhaps where checking is possible, one must check and cannot rely on rov; where checking is not possible, one may rely on rov.

This is the principle the Rishonim frame as efshar le-varer — can one use rov and chazakah as tools even when one has the ability to obtain more information? Rav Shimi is suggesting that all the proofs brought so far share a common feature: in each case, it was impossible to perform the relevant inspection, whether because of the laws of the korban, because the evidence had been destroyed, or because the facts were simply not ascertainable. Maybe the license to rely on rov is only granted when there is no alternative, and when one can check, one must check.

### Rabbi Meir & Miut

The Gemara responds with a powerful reductio. L-Rabbi Meir d-chaish le-miuta — Rabbi Meir holds that one must be concerned about the minority; he does not permit relying on rov and ignoring the miut at a rabbinic level. If Rav Shimi's principle is correct, then Rabbi Meir's position would extend further: even when checking is possible, one would have to check, and even then there are things that cannot be checked. Hacha nami d-lo achil bisra — would one conclude that Rabbi Meir simply never ate meat? Because there is always the possibility that the trachea had a pre-existing hole precisely at the site of shechitah, and there is no way to verify this after the fact.

V-chi teima, hacha nami — perhaps Rabbi Meir was indeed a vegetarian? The Gemara dismisses this: pesach ve-kodashim mai eika le-meimar — Rabbi Meir still lived under the obligation to eat korban Pesach and, in the time of the Beis Hamikdash, to participate in the eating of korbanos. He could not have been a vegetarian in any complete sense. Therefore, even Rabbi Meir would concede that where there is genuinely no alternative, one cannot remain in a state of perpetual abstention. This demonstrates that the distinction between possible and impossible checking cannot be the operative line.

### Rashi Halacha Misinai

The Gemara does not resolve this tension explicitly in the text, but Rashi, at the end of 11b and the beginning of 12a, provides the resolution. Looking at the first narrow column of Rashi on 12a: ella vadai — since one cannot prove from any of the evidence brought that rov applies even when checking is possible, one must instead say halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai — ha de-samchinan a-ruba afilu heicha de-efshar. There is a transmitted tradition that one may rely on rov even when the facts could theoretically be ascertained. Alternatively, Rashi adds, one returns to the verse acharei rabim lehatot — mashma bein ruba de-ita kaman bein ruba de-leisa kaman, and regardless of whether checking is possible, de-mai shna hai me-hai, there is no basis for distinguishing.

### Lungs Matzui Rule

Rashi then states the practical bottom line: de-ha milta samchinan — we rely on the fact that one goes by rov even when more information could be obtained, velo badkinan kol yud-chet trefos, and we do not check for all eighteen categories of treifot. The one exception is nekuvat ha-reia — the possibility of holes in the lung. Mishum de-shachi bei re-uta — because it is common, shachi'ach, to have problems in the lung. Hatam badkinan — there we check.

Rashi also addresses the case where inspection of the lung becomes impossible: ve-heicha de-ishtachach de-avda reia velo badak, if the lung was lost and one did not check it, michla achila, one may eat the meat, since even then one falls back on rov. The requirement to check applies only when checking is possible and the defect is shachi'ach; if inspection is no longer possible even for the lungs, rov suffices.

### Matzui vs. Eino Matzui

The Rishonim's distinction between miut ha-matzui and miut she-eino matzui — a likely minority possibility and an unlikely one — is not stated explicitly in the Gemara but provides the conceptual framework for the ruling. In practice, the threshold is generally understood to be around five percent: a defect that occurs in five percent or fewer cases is considered miut she-eino matzui; more than that is miut matzui.

The underlying logic of this distinction is illuminating. When a problem arises in fewer than five percent of cases, one might say that halacha itself defines this as vadai — certainty. The question is not how certain one must be in a psychological sense, but what threshold the halachic system sets for treating something as established. If ninety-five percent certainty counts as established fact, then a sub-five-percent minority does not even rise to the level of a recognized safek — doubt. On this understanding, when the miut is she-eino matzui, there is no doubt to address, and no further investigation is warranted. No reliance on rov is even needed, strictly speaking, because the category of doubt has not been triggered.

When the miut is matzui, by contrast, the doubt is genuine and acknowledged. Here one does have a safek that must be addressed, and if one can obtain more information, one must do so. This creates two distinct logical modes in which rov operates: in the case of miut she-eino matzui, rov functions by effectively dissolving the doubt — there is no recognized uncertainty. In the case of miut matzui, rov acknowledges the doubt and provides a basis for action despite it — but when the doubt is acknowledged and resolution is available, one is obligated to pursue it.

This is the final conceptual architecture of the sugya: one goes by rov in all cases, but the nature of that reliance differs depending on whether the minority possibility is matzui or not. And in the practical realm of hilchot treifot, the consequence is clear — one checks only the lungs, where problems are shachi'ach, and relies on rov for all other organs.

---

---

# Hullin 12

## Rov Metzuyin Principle

### Intro: Who Can Shecht

We pick up today with daf 12, four lines from the top, near the two dots. We have just finished laying down the foundation of the two major principles for dealing with areas of doubt: chazakah, which is the principle of status quo, and rov, which is the principle of majority. The discussion touched in particular on the question of efshar levareir — whether one may rely on these principles when the facts could be independently ascertained — and on two types of mi'ut, a common and an uncommon likelihood, which bears directly on the question of which organs require examination for treifa. We now return to the major theme of the Mishnah: who may perform shechita, and when do we assume the shechita was done correctly.

### Ra'ah Ruling

Rav Nachman said in the name of Rav: ra'ah echad sheshachat — if you directly observed a person performing a shechita from beginning to end, you may eat from it. If you did not directly observe the full act, you may not eat from it. This statement requires unpacking, and the Gemara immediately asks: what is the case?

### Expert/Non-Expert Cases

The Gemara identifies three possible scenarios. If you know the person performing the shechita is knowledgeable — that he knows the laws — why would you need to observe him at all? And if you know he does not know the laws, it is obvious that you cannot eat from his shechita without observation; we have already established that even a person with extensive experience cannot be trusted if he does not know the laws, since he may err and not realize he has done so. That leaves the middle case: you simply do not know whether he knows the laws or not.

### Unknown Status, Use Rov

The Gemara presses further. If you do not know whether the person knows the laws, why not rely on the principle of rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein — that the majority of people who take up a knife to slaughter an animal know what they are doing? Here the discussion connects naturally to the preceding pages' treatment of rov, since we are using a rov to override the chazakah that the animal is not kosher. The animal begins with a chezkat issur, and the rov is being invoked to establish that the shechita was performed correctly. That is a noteworthy step.

### Chicken in Market Baraita

The Gemara introduces a Baraita in support: if you find a slaughtered chicken in the marketplace — say, your chicken wandered off and you find it shechted — or you told your messenger to go slaughter and found the animal already slaughtered when you arrived, the rule is chazakato shechuta: you may assume it was done correctly. This demonstrates that we do indeed say rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein, and that we assume any person who performs a shechita without known disqualification knew what he was doing.

### Rov vs. Chezkat Issur

This principle is striking. We are allowing a rov to override the chazakah that the animal was forbidden. One might raise the point that the Baraita speaks of a chicken, which is a far more commonly slaughtered animal than large livestock, and that the skill involved is correspondingly more widespread. The Gemara does not explicitly draw this distinction, and appears to proceed on the assumption that the logic of rov metzuyin applies regardless of the type of animal — though the argument is certainly more intuitive in the case of chickens.

### One Siman, Then Left

The Gemara ultimately resolves its question by locating Rav Nachman's ruling in a very specific case: we know the person does not know the laws. How can there still be any question? The case is one where you watched him perform one of the simanim — say, the trachea — correctly, and then you turned away before he completed the second siman. One might have thought: since he began the process correctly, I can assume the rest followed suit. The Gemara rejects this.

### Correct Start Not Enough

The Gemara teaches: perhaps the first siman was done correctly by chance — even a stopped clock is right twice a day — while the second siman was done with a shehiya or a derasa, errors he would not recognize because he does not know the laws. Even a correct beginning does not guarantee a correct finish when the person is known to be ignorant of the halachic requirements. This underscores what was established earlier: experience alone is insufficient. If we know the person does not know the laws, we cannot trust even a technically convincing start.

### Rov vs. Standards

This creates what appears to be an interesting tension. We permit reliance on rov metzuyin when we find an animal shechted and know nothing about who did it — even though the chezkat issur of the animal would seem to demand certainty. Yet when we know a person has failed the test, we do not permit reliance on his extensive experience or even on a correctly performed first siman. The resolution appears to lie not purely in the logic of rov, but in the regulatory framework of shechita: we set requirements — passing a test, checking the simanim — and when those requirements are violated, we do not permit eating from the shechita even where rov might theoretically support leniency. Where we simply do not know who performed the shechita and no standard has been violated, rov metzuyin applies in full. The two situations are structurally different: one is about applying standards, the other is about making reasonable inferences in the absence of information.

---

## Shaliach & Rov Metzuyin

### Shaliach Shechita Query

Now that the principle of rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein has been introduced, the Gemara records a question posed by Rav Dimi bar Yosef to Rav Nachman: if a person tells his shaliach to go and slaughter, and then finds the animal already slaughtered, what is the status? Rav Nachman responds: chazakato shachut — you may assume it was done correctly.

### Shaliach Terumah Query

Rav Dimi bar Yosef then poses a parallel case concerning terumah: if one tells his shaliach to go and separate terumah from his grain, and finds upon arrival that the terumah has already been separated, what is the status? Rav Nachman rules: ein chazakato tarum — you may not assume it was done correctly.

### Shaliach Contradiction

Rav Dimi bar Yosef immediately points out the apparent contradiction. The principle at issue is chazakah shaliach oseh shlichuto — the presumption that a messenger performs the task he was assigned. It is worth noting that this use of chazakah is entirely different from the chazakah of status quo discussed earlier; this is a chazakah about human behavior, a presumption about how people act. If we hold chazakah shaliach oseh shlichuto, both the shechita and the terumah cases should be valid. If we do not hold it, neither should be valid. How can Rav Nachman rule differently in the two cases?

### Ein Chazakah + Rov

Rav Nachman responds with the Aramaic idiom lichi tichol ala kor demilcha — an expression indicating that the questioner should have thought more carefully before asking. The answer is: le'olam ein chazakah shaliach oseh shlichuto. We do not presume that a messenger has performed his task; we cannot assume it without confirmation. The shechita case is valid not because of any presumption about the messenger, but because rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein applies regardless of who performed the slaughter. Even if a random person heard the instruction and stepped in to do the owner a favor, that person's shechita is valid under rov metzuyin. The identity of the slaughterer is irrelevant — any person who performs a shechita is presumed to know what he is doing.

### Torem Shelo Mida'at

The terumah case is fundamentally different. Even if someone performed the separation with full technical competence, if it was done by a random person who heard the owner's instructions and acted on his own initiative, that constitutes torem shelo mida'at — separating terumah without the knowledge and authorization of the owner. Ve-hatorem shelo mida'at ein trumaso trumah: terumah separated without the owner's authorization is not valid. The halacha of terumah requires that it be separated by the owner himself, or by someone formally empowered by the owner to do so. Technical correctness does not suffice.

### Agency for Terumah

This raises the question of whether a blanket authorization can be given for terumah. The answer is that a person can in principle declare that anyone who hears his instruction is authorized — kol hashomeia koli — but the key point is that terumah requires proper shlichut, the formal transfer of agency from the owner. If that formal authorization was not given, a random person's act is invalid regardless of how carefully it was performed. The distinction between shechita and terumah thus lies not in technical competence but in the nature of the respective acts: shechita is validated by the physical performance alone, while terumah is bound up with the owner's personal authority over his grain and requires formal empowerment of an agent.

### Shaliach in Gittin

The practical stakes of the question of chazakah shaliach oseh shlichuto extend well beyond the present context. As the citation in the margin of the daf indicates, this principle appears in Gittin 64 in connection with the question of whether a man who sends a shaliach to deliver a get to his wife — or a woman who sends a shaliach to receive one — may assume the act has been accomplished without receiving confirmation. When the shaliach reports back, there is of course no question. The issue is whether an assumption can be made in the absence of such a report. That is where the question of chazakah shaliach oseh shlichuto carries its full halachic weight.

---

## Rov Metzuyin Debate

### Tannaitic Dispute Intro

Having established and applied the principle of rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein, the Gemara now asks whether this principle is itself subject to Tannaitic dispute.

### Lost Animals Baraita

A Baraita is cited: if one's kid goats or chickens went missing and were found slaughtered — perhaps someone found them, slaughtered them thinking they were his, realized the mistake, and left them — Rabbi Yehuda forbids eating them, while Rabbi Chanina the son of Rabbi Yose HaGlili permits. This appears to be precisely the dispute about whether we apply rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein. It is worth noting, as raised in the discussion, that the Baraita is speaking of chickens and small goats, animals whose slaughter is a common and widespread skill, which only strengthens the case for applying rov metzuyin. One would have thought that if rov metzuyin applies anywhere, it applies here.

### Rebbi's Split Ruling

Rebbi offers a nuanced ruling. The position of Rabbi Yehuda — that the animals are forbidden — seems correct when they were found in a garbage dump, since one would naturally infer that they were discarded because the shechita was invalid. The position of Rabbi Chanina the son of Rabbi Yose HaGlili — that the animals are permitted — seems correct when they were found inside a house. This appears to suggest that both opinions are correct in their respective circumstances.

### First Reading of Dispute

The Gemara's initial reading of the Baraita is that the fundamental disagreement is over whether we apply rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein at all. Rabbi Chanina holds that we do; Rabbi Yehuda holds that we do not.

### Rav Nachman: Narrow Disp…

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative reading. There is no need to say that anyone disputes the principle of rov metzuyin. Everyone agrees that we apply rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein. The dispute is narrower: it concerns only the case of a private garbage dump.

### Neveilah in Home Garbage

The logical basis of the dispute, under this reading, is a factual question about human behavior. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a person will ordinarily discard a neveilah — an invalidly slaughtered animal — into his private garbage dump. If that is so, then finding the animal in one's private garbage is evidence of invalidity, and one cannot rely on rov metzuyin to override it. Rabbi Chanina the son of Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds that a person would not leave a neveilah in his private garbage dump, since it would attract vermin and create a hygiene hazard; if one were truly discarding an invalid animal, one would take it to the public garbage dump. Therefore, finding it in the private garbage is ambiguous and rov metzuyin still applies.

### Rebbi's Contradiction Re…

Under this reading, Rebbi's statement — which seemed to split between the two positions — must be re-examined. If the debate covers only the private garbage dump, then Rebbi's statement cannot mean he rules like Rabbi Yehuda in some cases and like Rabbi Chanina in others, since their dispute is confined to a single scenario. The Gemara resolves this by re-reading Rebbi's statement entirely. Rebbi is not splitting his vote; he is defining the boundaries of what is not in dispute. When Rebbi says "the words of Rabbi Yehuda appear correct when found in the garbage dump," he means that in the case of a public garbage dump, everyone agrees the animals are forbidden — even Rabbi Chanina would concede this. When Rebbi says "the words of Rabbi Chanina appear correct when found in the house," he means that in the case of an animal found inside the house itself, everyone agrees it is permitted — even Rabbi Yehuda would concede this. The entire debate is confined to the private garbage dump, which is the ambiguous middle case. Rebbi is identifying the undisputed extremes, not adjudicating between competing positions.

### Summary: Shechita Requir…

The upshot of this entire discussion is that rov metzuyin etzel shechita mumchin hein is a firmly accepted principle, not a matter of Tannaitic dispute. It is worth reviewing what the full set of requirements for valid shechita looks like in light of all that has been discussed. A shochet must have passed the requisite examination — if he is known not to know the laws, his shechita is invalid even with extensive experience and even if the process appeared to begin correctly. Where we simply do not know who performed the shechita and no standard has been violated, we apply rov metzuyin, and this rov suffices to override the chezkat issur of the animal. That is a noteworthy ruling, particularly given that in other contexts — such as checking the simanim — rov does not substitute for the required standard. The distinction, as noted, appears to be that rov metzuyin operates in the space where no standard has been breached and no information is available; where halachic requirements have been established and violated, rov does not rescue the shechita.

---

## Cheresh Shoteh veKatan

### Mishna: CSvK Restriction

The Gemara now returns fully to the Mishnah's treatment of who may and may not perform shechita. The Mishnah states: chutz micheresh shoteh ve-katan — anyone may shecht with the exception of the cheresh shoteh ve-katan — shema yekalkelu shechitatan — lest they ruin the shechita. If they shecht under direct observation, however, the shechita is valid.

### Rava: No Animals Lechatc…

Rava draws an inference from the precise language of the Mishnah. The Mishnah does not say "lest they have ruined" — it says "lest they will ruin." This indicates we are not speaking about a fait accompli; we are speaking prospectively. Rava therefore rules: zot omeret ein mosrin lahem chullin lechatchila — one may not give animals to a cheresh shoteh ve-katan to slaughter in the first place, even lechatchila.

### Rashi: Even With Observe…

Rashi explains that this prohibition applies even when others are present and intend to observe the shechita. Even if you are planning to watch, we are so concerned that they will ruin the shechita that it is irresponsible to give them the animal to begin with. The halachic consequence might not be severe if something goes wrong — the shechita is simply invalid — but there is a concern of wasting a good animal. As Rashi puts it: afilu chullin lechatchila ve-afilu acherim omdin al gaban.

### Rabbenu Tam Extension

Rabbenu Tam extends the prohibition further. Even if one intends the animal for non-kosher use — for dog food or to be sold to non-Jews — one should still not give it to a cheresh shoteh ve-katan to slaughter. The reason is ma'arit ayin: observers may see the shechita being performed and draw the incorrect conclusion that one may rely on the shechita of a cheresh shoteh ve-katan in general.

### Bedieved If Observed

The Mishnah continues: if they did slaughter and others were observing them, the shechita is kosher bedieved. The Gemara asks: which Tanna holds this position?

### Physical Act, Not Da'at

The implicit assumption requires examination. Why are the cheresh shoteh ve-katan not categorically excluded from performing shechita entirely? In many halachic contexts these individuals are disqualified, but that is typically because the relevant act is not merely a physical performance but an effecting of a change of status — marriage, divorce, commercial transactions, freeing of a slave. Such acts require a bar da'at, a legally competent adult who is empowered to effect the change. Shechita, by contrast, is fundamentally about a physical act performed correctly. The Torah does not use the word ish in the context of shechita, and the halachic validity of the act turns on its physical execution rather than on the status of the one performing it. It is for this reason that the cheresh shoteh ve-katan are not categorically excluded — their shechita, if physically correct, is valid bedieved when observed.

### Knife Throw Case

Rava cites, in the name of Oshaiya Zeira of Chavraiya, a Baraita that bears on this question. If a person throws a knife intending to embed it in a wall — playing darts, as it were — and the knife passes by an animal's neck and performs a technically valid shechita, what is the status? Rabbi Natan rules it is valid; the Chachamim rule it is invalid. Avuya, who taught this Baraita, adds: halacha ke-Rabbi Natan — the ruling follows Rabbi Natan.

### Halacha: Rabbi Natan

The Gemara raises an objection: shechita requires the molich u-meivi, the back-and-forth motion of the knife. A knife thrown in a single direction cannot satisfy this requirement. The Gemara responds: shehalchu bah kedarka — the knife traversed the neck in both directions. Either it bounced off the wall and came back — which would require the animal to have been standing very close to the wall — or, more plausibly, the knife was twice the width of the animal's neck, so that a single pass accomplished the equivalent of the required double motion.

### Da'at vs. Kavanah

With the ruling of Rabbi Natan established, the Gemara opens a deeper analytical question. There are two distinct categories of intention that must be kept apart. The first is da'at: the legally competent intention required to effect a change of status — to sell, to marry, to divorce, to separate terumah. This is what the cheresh shoteh ve-katan categorically lack, not because they are incapable of thought, but because halacha designates adult competence as the precondition for exercising such legal powers. The second is kavanah: the intention relevant to physical acts, and in particular to acts of mitzvah. The question of mitzvot tzrichot kavanah — whether one must intend to fulfill a mitzvah in performing a mitzvah act — is a distinct issue. But even on the more lenient view that mitzvot do not require kavanah, there remains a lower threshold: the act must not be mitasek. Mitasek means the act was entirely incidental — one did not even intend to do what was physically done. The example given is someone blowing through a shofar to clean it, with no intention of producing a blast at all. Even if mitzvot do not require formal kavanah, one cannot be yotzei on an act that was completely incidental.

### Ma'aseh Shechita Defined

The central question raised here is whether shechita requires more than physical correctness. Does the act need to be defined as a ma'aseh shechita — formally intended as an act of slaughter — or is it sufficient that the physical criteria were met? When the knife is thrown as a dart and happens to cut through the simanim correctly, the physical act was performed correctly. But the person was doing an act of playing darts, not an act of shechita. Does the halachic validity of shechita depend solely on the physical reality, or does it require that the act be constituted as a ma'aseh shechita? The existence of technical requirements such as shehiya and derasa, which define what constitutes a valid act of shechita, suggests that there is a formal halachic definition of the act, not merely a physical description. The debate between Rabbi Natan and the Chachamim turns precisely on this question, and the ruling follows Rabbi Natan: the physical correctness of the act suffices.

### Automated Shechita/Koach…

A related question arises concerning automated shechita — whether a mechanical device could perform a valid shechita. This question is structurally similar to the knife-throw case but introduces an additional consideration independent of kavanah: koach gavra, the requirement that the act proceed through human power and agency. Even if kavanah is not required, and even if the physical criteria are met, there remains the question of whether the act derives from a human being's physical force. If a person presses a button and the rest proceeds mechanically, or if the energy of running water turns a mechanism, the question is whether that still counts as koach gavra. These issues are discussed in the relevant halachic literature, but they represent a separate dimension of the analysis from kavanah alone.

---

## Katan's Machshava

### Rabbi Yochanan's Query

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports a question posed by Rabbi Yochanan: katan yesh lo machshava o ein lo machshava? Does a minor have machshava — halachically relevant intention? This question can be read as a potential critique of the earlier sugya. If we rule that cheresh shoteh ve-katan can perform valid shechita bedieved because the act requires only physical correctness and not da'at, one might ask whether they can even supply kavanah. Rabbi Yochanan is pressing on exactly this point: is the intention of a minor halachically meaningful?

### Rabbi Ami: Ask Ma'aseh F…

Rabbi Ami challenges Rabbi Yochanan's formulation. Why ask about machshava? Ask about ma'aseh — about whether their acts are halachically significant. The question about thought should not even arise, since the Mishnah already demonstrates that their acts are meaningful.

### Tinokot Hollowing Gourds

The Mishnah cited is the following. If tinokot — minors — hollowed out gourds, acorns, or pomegranates to use as vessels for measuring dirt or as pans for a scale, the vessels are tamei: they can become ritually impure and are therefore halachically recognized as vessels. The reason given is mi-pnei she-yesh lahem ma'aseh ve-ein lahem machshava: because they have acts but do not have thought. Their physical act of fashioning the item into a vessel is halachically significant. Their intention standing alone — seeing a naturally hollowed object and deciding to use it as a bowl without any act of fashioning — would not be significant. The act, accompanied by the intent that guided it, constitutes the vessel. The thought alone does not.

### Tension With Earlier Sug…

This Mishnah creates an implicit tension with the earlier discussion. If a minor's act accompanied by intent is halachically significant enough to render a vessel susceptible to tumah, why would we assume they lack the kavanah necessary to constitute a ma'aseh shechita? The Gemara appears to be working toward a distinction, but the Mishnah seems to suggest that a minor's acts are indeed meaningful and are understood to be accompanied by the guiding intention that shapes them. If they can hollow out a gourd with the intent to make it a vessel, and that act is valid, it is difficult to see why their shechita should be disqualified on grounds of lacking kavanah.

### Preview: Tomorrow's Gema…

The exact question being posed and the way the Gemara resolves it will be clarified in tomorrow's shiur.

---

---

# Hullin 13

## Cheresh, Shoteh, Katan

### Physical Act vs. Intenti…

The daf opens by returning to the Mishna's ruling that a cheresh, shoteh, and katan may perform shechita, provided that an observer confirms the technical correctness of the act. This ruling immediately raises a foundational question: is shechita fundamentally a physical act, or does it require kavana — intention, the awareness that one is actually slaughtering an animal?

On one level, the Mishna itself seems to answer this question. The cheresh, shoteh, and katan are not bnei daat — not because of any simple assessment of their intellectual capacity, but because halakha does not recognize them as legal agents capable of effecting a halakhic change, entering into transactions, or altering status through an act of the mind. Yet shechita, perhaps, is different: it may be categorically a physical act, not an act of daat at all. If so, there would be no difficulty in allowing a cheresh, shoteh, or katan to perform it. But the Gemara presses further: even if daat is not required, does shechita require kavana? And kavana is distinct from daat.

### Non-Agency & Halakhic St…

The distinction deserves emphasis. Daat, in the halakhic sense, is not merely describing the presence or absence of thought. It refers to a threshold category of legal agency — the recognized capacity to effect changes of halakhic status, to be a party to a transaction, to function as a full agent within the law. Cheresh, shoteh, and katan are categorically excluded from this category. They are not bnei daat, and no act they perform that fundamentally depends on this kind of legal personhood will be recognized by halakha, regardless of whether they are physically capable of performing it.

### Daat vs. Kavana

Kavana is different. Kavana refers to intention in a narrower, more immediate sense — awareness of what one is doing, directedness toward a specific act. The question the Gemara is exploring is whether shechita requires this, and whether a cheresh, shoteh, or katan can supply it. These are two separate inquiries. The prior analysis, which implied that perhaps shechita requires no intention at all, was one possible answer. But the Gemara now wants to examine more carefully what the law does and does not acknowledge from these individuals when it comes to something more specific than full daat — namely, the question of machshava, of intention in the sense of directed thought or purpose.

---

## Three Categories

### Intention Alone

The Gemara (13a) opens with a clarifying exchange. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yochanan, reports that the question being raised is not about machshava gureita — naked, bare intention alone — as distinct from action. That case is already explicit in the Mishna: the intention of a cheresh, shoteh, or katan standing alone, without being embodied or expressed in an action, is not halakhically significant. Lo ka mibaya lei — that was never Rabbi Yochanan's question.

### Self-Evident Action

The Mishna regarding vessels made from gourds already established a clear distinction: yesh lahem maaseh, ve-ein lahem machshava — they have action but they do not have machshava. The implication is that when a cheresh, shoteh, or katan performs an act, that act carries halakhic weight, while their intention stated independently does not. What constitutes a meaningful act? According to Tosafot's reading, an action has halakhic significance when it is maaseh atzmo mevuat — when the purpose of the action is self-evident from the action itself. If a katan hollows out a gourd, the question of what he intended is not the issue; the action of hollowing out a gourd is objectively and unambiguously an act of fashioning a kli. We look at the action and classify it on its own terms.

### Ambiguous Action

Rabbi Yochanan's actual question concerns the middle case: machshavto nikeret mitoch maasav — where the intention is evident from the action, but the action is not completely self-evident. The example that follows involves a korban olah. A korban olah, as a kodshei kodashim, must be slaughtered in the north of the Beit HaMikdash. If the animal is standing in the south and the cheresh, shoteh, or katan brings it to the north and slaughters it there, the action strongly suggests that he knows it is an olah and is performing shechitat olah. But it is not entirely unambiguous — perhaps he moved it north simply because there was insufficient room in the south. The action points toward a specific intention, but does not definitively establish it. This is the middle case.

### Tosafot's Framework

Tosafot's interpretation of this entire discussion has a coherent inner logic that deserves careful articulation. According to Tosafot, when the Mishna says ein lahem machshava — they do not have machshava — it means that halakha categorically declines to give any weight to their stated intentions. It does not matter what a katan says he intends, nor does it matter that he says it while performing an action. His words about his inner state are simply not acknowledged. Halakha cannot take that route.

What halakha can do, however, is observe the action itself and classify it objectively. When someone hollows out a gourd, we do not need to know what he was thinking; the action, viewed in context, is self-evidently an act of making a kli. This classification has nothing to do with entering the mind of the katan — it is about describing the type of action being performed. That is what "they have an action" means: the action can be defined as an intended action of a certain type, based on the action's objective character, without any reliance on what the katan claims he was thinking.

This framework resolves a deeper question about the nature of kavana requirements in halakha generally. Whenever halakha requires kavana for a particular act — whether to validate a kli, a shechita, or an offering — one must ask: is that kavana an independent criterion alongside the action, or is it a criterion for defining the type of action being performed? Tosafot's position, as reflected in this sugya, is that kavana is not an independent requirement but is rather what defines the nature of the act. We do not require, as a second separate datum, that the person be thinking a certain thought simultaneously with the action. We require that the action be classifiable as an action of a certain type — and it is that classification that kavana enables when applied to adults. For a katan, since we cannot acknowledge his stated kavana at all, we rely entirely on the objective analysis of the action itself. If the action is unambiguous, it has full halakhic weight. If there is some ambiguity — if the action probably indicates a certain purpose but the matter is not entirely clear — that is the middle case, which Rabbi Yochanan is asking about.

### Rashi's Framework

Rashi frames the question differently. For Rashi, the issue is not a categorical refusal to acknowledge a katan's intention, but rather a question of evidentiary credibility: when can we believe that a katan's stated intention represents his genuine mental state? If he merely states an intention without performing any corresponding action, we do not believe him. If he states his intention and then performs an action that substantiates it — that corresponds to and confirms what he said — then we do believe him, and halakha acknowledges that intention. The middle case, for Rashi, is when a katan performs an action without a corresponding verbal statement of intention. In that circumstance, it is uncertain whether we can infer his intention from the action alone.

For Rashi, then, the three cases are: stated intention alone (not believed), stated intention accompanied by a confirming action (believed and halakhically valid), and action alone without a stated intention (uncertain). The distinction is less categorical than Tosafot's; for Rashi it is genuinely a question of what evidence allows us to conclude what the katan was thinking.

---

## Fruit on Roof Case

### Case Setup

The Gemara now reports that Rabbi Yochanan had already addressed a version of this middle-case question on a prior occasion, citing a Mishna about fruit brought to a rooftop. The case is as follows. Harvested fruit does not become susceptible to tumah until it comes in contact with liquid — and even then, only if the owner either actively placed the liquid on the fruit or desired that the liquid be there. The operative phrase from the Torah is ki yutan mayim al zera — if water is placed upon seed (Vayikra 11:38). If someone brings fruit up to his roof in order to protect it from infestation, and dew subsequently falls upon it overnight, the dew does not render the fruit susceptible to tumah, because the owner placed the fruit there for protection, not for moisture. The fruit is therefore einam bekhiyutan — not in the category of ki yutan.

### Adult's Intention

For an adult, however, pure intention — even without any accompanying action — can change this status. If the owner, having brought the fruit to the roof, subsequently thinks to himself that the dew would be beneficial and desires it, that mental act of desiring the liquid is sufficient to render the fruit susceptible to tumah. Ve-im niskavven lekach — harei hem bekhiyutan. Bare intention, for an adult, has full biblical weight.

### Minor's Intention

When a cheresh, shoteh, or katan brings the fruit to the roof, however, the situation is categorically different. The Mishna states: af al pi sheniskayvnu lekach, einam bekhiyutan — even if they intended it, even if they explicitly desired the dew, the fruit does not become susceptible to tumah. The reason given is: mipnei sheyesh lahem maaseh ve-ein lahem machshava — because they have action but do not have machshava.

According to Tosafot, the critical point here is that bringing the fruit to the roof is not a self-evident action with an unambiguous purpose. Even if we knew an infestation had driven them to the roof, there are multiple reasons one might bring fruit to a rooftop. The act of carrying the fruit upstairs does not objectively and unambiguously express any particular intention regarding moisture or dew. Therefore, even if the katan states an intention regarding the dew, that stated intention is irrelevant — we look only at the action, and the action does not carry clear enough meaning to classify it as an act of intending moisture for the fruit.

### Middle Case Example

Rabbi Yochanan's qualification introduces the middle case. Lo shanu ela shelo hipech bahen — the ruling that the cheresh, shoteh, or katan's action is relevant applies only if he did not flip the fruit over after the dew had fallen. But if the dew fell on the fruit this morning, and then the cheresh, shoteh, or katan went and turned the fruit over — why else would one flip fruit already exposed to dew if not to ensure that dew falls on the other side as well? That action, while not completely unambiguous — perhaps he turned it for sun, or for fear of infestation — strongly suggests an intention to expose the fruit to more moisture. Harei zeh beki yutan: in this case, Rabbi Yochanan indicates, even the cheresh, shoteh, or katan's action has significance. But how much significance? That is what Rabbi Yochanan was asking about — whether this middle case has biblical weight or only rabbinic weight.

---

## Action vs. Intention Lev…

### Action Biblically Valid

A second version of this same discussion is transmitted by Rav Zevid bar Yitzchak. In this formulation, the question is framed as: katan yesh lo maaseh o ein lo maaseh — does a katan have an action or not? Rabbi Ami objects: why ask whether he has an action? The Mishna already says yesh lahem maaseh — they have action. And why ask whether he has machshava? The Mishna already says ein lahem machshava. So what is left to ask?

The answer is: de'oraisa o derabanan — is the weight of these categories biblical or only rabbinic? The Gemara then resolves the question. Yesh lahem maaseh ve-afilu mide'oraisa: their action — when it is self-evident, unambiguous action — has full biblical weight, even to be lenient, even to validate a shechita or a kli.

### Intention Never Valid

Ein lahem machshava ve-afilu miderabanan: their intention alone — machshava gureita, without any action — has no weight whatsoever, not even rabbinically, not even to be strict.

### Middle Case Level

The middle case — machshavto nikeret mitoch maasav, where the intention is evident from the action but with some degree of ambiguity — occupies an intermediate position. Mide'oraisa ein lo: it has no biblical weight. Miderabanan yesh lo: it does carry rabbinic weight. According to Rashi's reading, this means that in the middle case we would be strict rabbinically — we would treat the fruit as susceptible to tumah, for instance — but we would not rely on it for biblical leniencies.

### Kavana's Role

This is a central Gemara — not only regarding the specific laws of cheresh, shoteh, and katan, but regarding halakhic categories of broad applicability. Three concepts emerge in sharp relief. Daat is the threshold category of full legal agency, through which one effects halakhic changes by virtue of one's recognized legal personhood; cheresh, shoteh, and katan are categorically excluded. Kavana is the narrower question of directed intention within an act; this is where the nuanced analysis of action versus machshava applies. And the philosophical question underlying it all — whether kavana is an independent criterion or merely the definer of the type of action being performed — is, as Tosafot frames it, resolved in favor of the latter. Halakha, when dealing with a katan, does not attempt to enter his mind. It observes the objective character of his action and classifies it accordingly. If that classification is unambiguous, it has full force. If it carries some ambiguity, it has only rabbinic force. If there is no action to classify, there is nothing halakhically to acknowledge at all.

---

## Offerings & Intention

### Mitasek Definition

The Gemara now introduces a related question concerning korbanot. Shmuel asked Rav Huna: minayin le-mitasek be-kodashim she-hu pasul — from where do we know that one who acts as a mitasek with respect to kodashim has invalidated the korban? What does mitasek mean here? According to Rashi, it refers to a case where one is not even aware that one is slaughtering an animal — as if throwing a knife at a wall and incidentally performing shechita. Even though we said that for shechitat chulin, a completely incidental act might suffice for the physical act of shechita, the question is how we know that by kodashim this is invalid.

### Korban Requirement

The Gemara cites a verse: ve-shachat et ben habakar — you shall slaughter the cattle. The derash is: shetehei shechita leshem ben bakar — the shechita must be performed with the awareness that one is slaughtering an animal. For a korban, unlike for chulin, it is not sufficient to have performed the physical motions of shechita incidentally; one must know that one is performing an act of shechita on an animal. The verse is then cited to establish not merely a lechatchila requirement but also that bedieved — after the fact — if this awareness was absent, the korban is invalid: lirtzonchem tizbachu — leda'atchem zivchu, slaughter it with your knowledge.

### Minor & Korban

This generates a further question: can a katan perform shechitat kodashim? That question folds back into the entire analysis of machshavto nikeret mitoch maasav and yesh lo maaseh. If, through the objective analysis of the action, it is self-evident that the katan knows he is slaughtering an animal — for instance, because the action itself makes this unmistakable — then according to the framework developed above, that self-evident action would have biblical weight and might suffice even for kodashim.

### Kedoshim Intent

Tosafot extends the analysis further. The requirement by kodashim is not only that one know one is slaughtering an animal, but that one know one is slaughtering a korban — a kodesh — and not treat the act as though it were shechitat chulin. If the shochet thought the animal was unconsecrated — chulin — then from the perspective of korbanot this is a completely incidental act: it is not shechitat kodashim at all. This is the broader meaning of mitasek in the context of kodashim according to Tosafot: not only that one was unaware of performing shechita, but that one was unaware one was dealing with a korban. The contrast with chulin is thus sharpened: by chulin the act may be purely physical; by kodashim one must be aware at least that one is performing shechita on an animal, and perhaps additionally that the animal is a korban.

---

## Non-Jew's Slaughter

### Neveilah Status

The Gemara transitions to the Mishna's ruling regarding shechitat oved kochavim. The Mishna states: shechitat oved kochavim neveilah — the slaughter performed by a non-Jew is neveilah. Even if the shechita was technically perfect in every physical respect — the knife was checked, the simanim were cut correctly — it is as though the animal was never slaughtered at all. U-metamei be-massa: and as neveilah, it imparts tumah through carrying.

### Categorical Exclusion

The non-Jew is categorically excluded from the role of shochet. This is not a question of intention — the analysis of cheresh, shoteh, and katan showed that intention can be parsed and evaluated. Nor is it a question of technical competence — if one observes the non-Jew performing the shechita correctly, that changes nothing. The Torah simply does not recognize a non-Jew as someone who can perform a ritual act of shechita. This is a categorical exclusion of legal capacity, not a judgment about the mechanics of any particular slaughter.

### Avodah Zarah Concern

The Gemara immediately notes: neveilah in — yes it is neveilah — issur hana'ah lo — but it is not forbidden in benefit. This raises a concern: since the Gemara is dealing with a world saturated with paganism, where animal sacrifice was ubiquitous, should we not be concerned that when a non-Jew slaughters an animal, he intends it as an act of worship to his god? If so, the animal would be a sacrifice offered to avodah zarah and would be forbidden in benefit, not merely neveilah. The Mishna is not concerned with this, and the Gemara asks: who is the tanna who holds this position?

---

## Rabbi Eliezer View

### Eliezer's Assumption

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: the Mishna does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. De-tani Rabbi Eliezer — for Rabbi Eliezer holds: stam machshavas oved kochavim la-avodah zarah — we assume that the default intention of a non-Jew, at least in the context of slaughtering an animal, is toward his idolatry. Even if he is slaughtering your animal, he will avail himself of the opportunity to dedicate the act to his god. According to Rabbi Eliezer, the slaughter of a non-Jew would therefore be forbidden in benefit.

### Objection to Intent

The Gemara raises an objection: ve-ha niscaven al davar she-lo shelo — he intended it upon something that is not his. Even if the non-Jew states an intent to dedicate the animal to avodah zarah, that mental act does not effect a physical change in the status of the animal. The animal belongs to someone else; a private intention, however sincere, is not an action that alters the halakhic status of another's property.

### Mainstream View

The mainstream view — not Rabbi Eliezer's — is that we do not assume stam that a non-Jew intends avodah zarah when slaughtering. Rabbi Ami, citing Rabbi Assi, proposes a more precise reading of the Mishna: shechitat oved kochavim neveilah — the ordinary non-Jew's slaughter is neveilah, not avodah zarah. But the Mishna is implicitly contrasting this with the case of a min — a Jew who has apostatized and committed himself to idol worship. Ha de-min ka-amar la-avodah zarah: the slaughter of a min is indeed considered to be for the sake of avodah zarah. A Jew who has actively embraced idolatry is presumed to be directing his acts toward his avoda zarah, and his shechita would therefore be forbidden in benefit.

The Gemara then cites a Braita confirming this reading: shechitat min la-avodah zarah — the slaughter of a min is indeed treated as an idolatrous offering. The consequences are comprehensive: his bread (pito) is like the bread of Samaritans (pas kuti); his wine is yein nesech; his sifrei Torah are like books of sorcery; his fruit is suspect as tevel; and some say even his children must be suspected of mamzerut. Tosafot notes that in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, Ezra, Zerubbavel ben She'altiel, and Yehoshua ben Yehotzadak excommunicated the Samaritans through a solemn ceremony involving three hundred kohanim, three hundred children, three hundred sifrei Torah, and the blowing of shofarot accompanied by Levitical song, concluding with the declaration that whoever eats the bread of a Kuti is as one who eats pork. This historical background illuminates the severity of the language used here — the framing of the Kuti comparison is not merely a technical halakhic disqualification but carries the weight of a formal, sweeping social and religious exclusion.

---

## Minim Question

### Minority Concern

Having established that the ordinary non-Jew's shechita is neveilah but not avodah zarah, the Gemara raises a further concern. Even granting that most non-Jews are not sincerely devoted to idolatry, should we not be worried about the minority who are — the committed idolaters, perhaps priests — and treat their shechita as forbidden in benefit? Ve-nechush shema min hu — perhaps this particular non-Jew is a min, a genuinely devout idolater.

### No Minim Among

The Gemara answers in the name of Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha: ein minim be-umot ovdei kochavim — there are no minim among the nations of idolaters. At first glance this seems an extraordinary claim, and the Gemara immediately challenges it: ve-ha ka-chazinan de-ika — we actually observe that there are such committed non-Jewish idolaters. The Gemara qualifies: ein rov ovdei kochavim minim — the majority of non-Jews are not minim. Since they are not the majority, we need not be concerned about the possibility.

### Custom vs. Belief

This qualification is grounded in the position of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: nochrim she-be-chutz la-aretz lav ovdei kochavim hein — non-Jews who live outside of the Land of Israel are not genuine idolaters. Ella minhag avoteihen bi-yadeihem — they are simply following the custom of their ancestors. Their religious practice is rote and cultural, not a matter of sincere theological commitment. This observation was made in the context of the late Roman world, where pagan religion had become increasingly pro forma, and where the intellectual and spiritual ground was being prepared — precisely because of this shallowness — for the rise of monotheistic alternatives.

### Medieval Application

This ruling was invoked extensively by the medieval authorities, including Tosafot, to address the practical impossibility of observing the restrictions of Masechet Avodah Zarah in their dealings with Christian neighbors — and in some cases, even in selling objects that served Christian liturgical purposes. The argument was that the principle of minhag avoteihen — that non-Jews practice their religion as mere inherited custom rather than sincere belief — applies to medieval Christianity as well, rendering it less than full avodah zarah in the operative halakhic sense. Whether this accurately described the religious reality of medieval Christians is a separate question; the principle functioned as what one might call a halakhic framework, applied to resolve genuinely difficult practical problems, even where the empirical conditions of the original ruling no longer clearly obtained.

---

## Minim & Sacrifices

### Context-Specific

The Gemara (continuing the discussion of minim) now refines the halakhic meaning of the statement ein minim be-umot by specifying the context in which it operates. Rabbi Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Nachman states: ein minim ba-umot ovdei kochavim as a halakhic ruling — but for what purpose does this apply? The Gemara considers whether it means that a non-Jew who appears to be a committed idolater is not treated as a min for purposes of shechita — that is, his shechita is not considered to be la-avodah zarah even if he seems to be a religious devotee. But this seems counterintuitive: if the shechita of a Jewish min is forbidden in benefit because we assume it is la-avodah zarah, a kal vachomer would suggest that the same, or more so, should apply to a non-Jew who is a min.

### Execution Rule

The Gemara then considers whether the ruling applies to the other law concerning minim — that one is obligated to cause their death. Here the kal vachomer runs in the same direction: if a Jewish min is subject to this, certainly a non-Jewish min would be. So the ruling cannot be introducing a distinction on that basis either, since no difference would make sense.

### Sacrifices Allowed

The operative application is narrower: likabel mehem korban — whether we may accept a sacrifice brought by a non-Jew who is a min. The Gemara cites a Braita: the word mikem — "from you" — in the verse governing offerings is interpreted to distinguish: among Jews (bachem chalakti), I have distinguished between who may and who may not bring a korban. A Jewish mumar or min may not bring a korban. But v'lo b'ovdei kochavim — no such distinction applies to non-Jews. Even a non-Jew who is a committed idolater may bring a korban. The Gemara confirms this from a second Braita: the repetition of ish ish — "any person, any person" — in the verse comes to include ovdei kochavim, teaching that non-Jews may bring nedarim and nedavot, free-will offerings, just as Jews do, with no distinctions drawn among them. A Jewish min, by contrast, cannot bring a korban until he has done teshuvah. Thus within this narrow domain — the acceptance of sacrifices — the principle ein minim ba-umot operates: even a non-Jew sincerely devoted to idolatry is not halakhically classified as a min in a way that would disqualify his korban.

---

## Idolatry & Tumah

### Tumah Levels

The Gemara concludes by returning to the Mishna's statement that shechitat oved kochavim u-metamei be-massa — the non-Jew's slaughter, being neveilah, causes tumah through carrying. Rava points out that this statement is doing more than stating the obvious. It is drawing a contrast: the shechita of a non-Jew causes tumah only through carrying (massa), but there is a worse category — v'yesh lecha acheret she-hi metama afilu be-ohel — something that causes tumah even in a tent, meaning even without direct contact or carrying, simply by virtue of being under the same roof as the object. What is that worse category? Tikrovet avodah zarah — an actual idolatrous sacrifice, an animal offered as an act of pagan worship, which carries a more severe level of tumah than ordinary neveilah.

### Rabbi Yehuda View

This leads to a debate. According to one version of Rava's reading, the Mishna is teaching that the non-Jew's shechita causes tumah be-massa, and that tikrovet avodah zarah causes the greater tumah even be-ohel — and this would accord with the position of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira. According to the other version of Rava's reading, the Mishna is teaching that the shechita of a non-Jew causes tumah be-massa, and that tikrovet avodah zarah is comparable — it too only causes tumah be-massa — which would be the view that does not follow Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira.

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira's position is stated in a Braita: minayin le-tikrovet avodah zarah she-hi metama be-ohel — from where do we know that an idolatrous offering causes tumah even in a tent? The verse (Bamidbar 25:3) says: va-yitzmadu le-Vaal Pe'or va-yochlu zivchei meitim — they cleaved to Baal Pe'or and ate the sacrifices of the dead. The comparison of idolatrous sacrifices to sacrifices of the dead establishes the analogy: mah meit metama be-ohel af tikrovet avodah zarah metama be-ohel — just as a corpse causes tumah in a tent, so too an idolatrous offering causes tumah in a tent. Whether the Mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beseira — treating the idolatrous sacrifice as carrying corpse-level tumah — or whether it assigns it only the tumah of neveilah through carrying, is the final unresolved question with which the daf closes.

---

---

# Hullin 15

## Shechita Shabbat, Eating…

### Review: Lighting & Blood

The shiur on Daf 15 begins by picking up from the bottom of 14b. After the Mishnah had covered who may perform shechita, the Gemara turned to the question of *when* shechita may be performed. Two cases were addressed: nighttime — where shechita is valid only b'di'eved if lighting is insufficient — and Shabbat, where a violation of Shabbat does not invalidate the shechita.

Tosafot drew two striking observations from this ruling. First, the slaughterer is not classified as a *mumar l'chalal Shabbos* — a habitual Shabbat violator — whose shechita would be invalid, because that status requires habitual, not one-time, Shabbat desecration. Second, Tosafot raised the question: granted one might not cook the meat, but what of the blood absorbed within it? Tosafot's answer is that blood which remains absorbed within the meat is not yet legally considered "blood." One may therefore eat raw meat without first removing the blood through salting. The reason we salt meat is specifically because cooking causes the blood to be released and reabsorbed; for raw consumption or broiling, the salting requirement does not apply. These are two important principles derived from the Mishnah, though the Gemara's own focus was on Rav's statement — attributed to the opinion of Rebbi Yehuda — that one may not eat this meat on Shabbat itself.

### Muktzeh Machmas Mius

The bulk of the previous daf was devoted to identifying which ruling of Rebbi Yehuda underlies Rav's statement. The Gemara now continues that investigation. Rav Sheshes, the son of Rav Idi, proposes that the relevant position is Rebbi Yehuda's ruling about lamps — *rebbi yehuda d'neros*. A Baraita teaches: *metaltelin ner chadash aval lo yashan divrei Rebbi Yehuda* — one may move a brand-new lamp on Shabbat but not an old one. The old lamp, blackened and oil-soaked after repeated use, is considered *ma'us* — disgusting — and falls into the category of *muktzeh machmas mius*, muktzeh on account of disgust. The proposal is that Rebbi Yehuda's sensitivity to this category would similarly apply to the animal: since it could not be used when Shabbat began, it would be muktzeh.

### Muktzeh Machmas Issur

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *eima deshamat leih l'rebbi yehuda b'muktzeh machmas mius — muktzeh machmas issur mi shamat leih?* When did we ever hear that Rebbi Yehuda extends his stringency to *muktzeh machmas issur*? These are distinct categories. The Gemara then answers its own challenge by citing a Mishnah at the top of 15a: Rebbi Yehuda rules that all metal lamps may be moved on Shabbat. This implies that the restriction on certain lamps is not merely about disgust but about the lamp's status as something engaged in a prohibited act — *muktzeh machmas issur* — when Shabbat began.

The nature of this category, however, requires some unpacking. A cow on Shabbat is *muktzeh machmas issur* in a clear sense: there is no permitted use for it on Shabbat — one cannot slaughter it, one cannot plow with it. But a candle presents a different conceptual picture. A candle is not inherently prohibited; one may light a room with it. What makes it *muktzeh machmas issur* is either that it was actively performing a *melacha* — burning — when Shabbat began, or that the very act of moving it raises concerns: moving a burning candle risks extinguishing it or altering the rate of combustion, either of which is prohibited. These distinctions have practical relevance today for questions such as whether one may reposition a halogen lamp that is on during Shabbat.

The Gemara then adds a further complication. The proposal had been that the cow falls into this category of *muktzeh machmas issur*. The Gemara now pushes back: *v'dilma shani hasam d'hu dachai lei b'yadayim* — perhaps the lamp case is different because when one lights a candle before Shabbat, one actively pushes it away, making a conscious act of setting it beyond reach for Shabbat. A cow that was never actively designated as off-limits — it simply happens to be prohibited by virtue of Shabbat — may not carry the same status.

Tosafot, however, notes that this is a *dehuya b'alma* — a forced deflection. If Rebbi Yehuda has a problem with *muktzeh machmas mius*, he most certainly has a problem with *muktzeh machmas issur*, and of course a cow is muktzeh on Shabbat. The Gemara's resistance to confirming this does not reflect genuine doubt about whether a cow is muktzeh, but rather a technical failure to prove it from the specific sources cited in connection with Rebbi Yehuda. The upshot is that the Gemara brackets the muktzeh explanation and turns to an entirely different basis for why the meat cannot be eaten on Shabbat itself.

### Candle vs. Cow Logic

The Gemara's resistance to the muktzeh argument — specifically the claim that the lamp case involves actively pushing the object away before Shabbat — leads to a reframing of the question. The discussion so far had operated on the assumption that the problem with eating the shechted meat on Shabbat is a muktzeh problem. The Gemara has now established that this cannot be proven decisively from Rebbi Yehuda's statements about lamps, and therefore a different explanation must be found. It is worth noting, as Tosafot makes clear, that this does not mean there is no muktzeh problem — there almost certainly is — but the Gemara is not satisfied to ground Rav's ruling there.

---

## Ma'aseh Shabbat Principle

### Rav Ashi: Cooking Rule

Rav Ashi proposes an entirely different approach: *rebbi yehuda d'mevashel hi* — the relevant opinion of Rebbi Yehuda is not about muktzeh at all but about the category of *ma'aseh Shabbat*. The principle here is distinct from muktzeh: if a person performs a *melacha* on Shabbat and thereby changes the status of an object — rendering it fit for use or consumption — one may not derive benefit from that act of violation on Shabbat itself. According to most Tannaim this prohibition is rabbinic in origin, grounded in the concern that one not benefit from a Shabbat violation lest it encourage future violations. According to Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar, as we will see, it rises to a biblical level. The relevance to our case is direct: if one slaughtered an animal on Shabbat, the shechita — though technically valid — constitutes a Shabbat violation, and to eat the meat on that same Shabbat would be to derive benefit from that violation. Waiting until after Shabbat eliminates the benefit, since one could simply have slaughtered the animal after Shabbat in any case.

### Rebbi Yehuda: Cooking

The Gemara cites the relevant Mishnah: *hamevashel b'shabbos b'shogeg yochal b'meizid lo yochal divrei rebbi meir* — if one cooks on Shabbat unintentionally, one may eat it; if intentionally, one may not — this is Rebbi Meir's position. Rashi explains that Rebbi Meir is the most lenient: an unintentional violation carries no consequence whatsoever, even for the perpetrator on Shabbat itself. A willful violation means that nobody may eat from it — though only until after Shabbat.

Rebbi Yehuda then states: *b'shogeg yochal l'motzei Shabbos* — if unintentional, it may be eaten, but not on Shabbat itself; only after Shabbat. *b'meizid lo yochal olamis* — if willful, it may never be eaten; that is a permanent prohibition in the nature of a *knas*, a fine imposed on the perpetrator. This is precisely the position relevant to Rav's ruling: even an unintentional violation prohibits eating on Shabbat itself.

### Rebbi Yochanan Strict

Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar goes further still. He rules: *b'shogeg yochal l'motzei Shabbos l'acherim v'lo lo* — if unintentional, others may eat after Shabbat, but the perpetrator himself may never eat it. *b'meizid lo yochal olamis lo lo v'lo l'acherim* — if willful, it may never be eaten — not by the perpetrator and not by anyone else. The stringency here is derived from the verse *kodesh hi lachem* — Shabbat is holy to you — and Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar understands this to mean that the products of a willful Shabbat violation take on a kind of prohibited sanctity, off-limits to all. A willful sin creates an object that is permanently forbidden to the entire world, not merely to the sinner.

One critical element is absent from the statements of both Rebbi Meir and Rebbi Yehuda: the distinction between the perpetrator and others. Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar explicitly introduces this distinction, but the earlier Tannaim do not state it directly. This omission generates a significant dispute among the Rishonim as to how to read their positions on this point.

Regarding the broader question of what constitutes "deriving benefit" in Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar's framework — the answer is that any personal gain from the violation is prohibited. Giving the food to a non-Jew with no expectation of reciprocity might be permitted, but selling it would not be.

### Tosafot Mnemonic

Tosafot offers a useful mnemonic for keeping these positions straight: each authority is precisely one step stricter than the one before. Rebbi Meir's case of *meizid* — willful violation, where no one may eat on Shabbat itself — is identical in its consequence to Rebbi Yehuda's case of *shogeg* — unintentional violation. And Rebbi Yehuda's case of *meizid* — where the perpetrator may never eat — is identical in its consequence to Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar's case of *shogeg* — unintentional violation, where the perpetrator himself may never eat. The entire structure shifts one category at a time, with each Tanna treating the more lenient case of the previous authority as the basis for his more stringent ruling.

### Mishnah via Yom Kippur

The Gemara now explains what motivated Rav to say that the meat cannot be eaten on Shabbat itself. The Mishnah mentions both Shabbat and Yom HaKippurim together: *dumya d'Yom HaKippurim* — the case of Shabbat is analogous to Yom Kippur. On Yom Kippur, it does not matter whether the shechita was performed *b'shogeg* or *b'meizid* — one cannot eat the meat regardless, because eating itself is forbidden. By analogy, on Shabbat too, one cannot eat the meat on that day regardless of whether the violation was intentional or unintentional.

Now, who holds that even *b'shogeg* one cannot eat the product of a Shabbat violation on Shabbat itself? That is Rebbi Yehuda. And who holds that *b'shogeg* is eventually permitted to everyone, consistent with the Mishnah's language that *shechitaso k'sheira* — the shechita is valid and the meat is ultimately fit for consumption? Also Rebbi Yehuda. According to Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar, the perpetrator could never eat from it even after Shabbat, which would conflict with the implication that *shechitaso k'sheira* means the shechita produces meat that is ultimately available to all. The Gemara is therefore satisfied: the Mishnah reflects the position of Rebbi Yehuda.

### Shogeg Assumption

One might object: the Mishnah says *af al pi shemitchayev b'nafsho* — even though the violator is liable with his life — which implies a willful violation, a *meizid*, since the death penalty applies to intentional Shabbat desecration. If so, should we not say the Mishnah reflects the position of Rebbi Meir, who addresses *meizid*?

The Gemara resolves this: *af al pi d'b'meizid mitchayev b'nafsho — hacha d'b'shogeg shechitaso k'sheira* — the Mishnah is saying that although this *type* of violation carries capital punishment when performed willfully, in our case it was done *b'shogeg*. It is the kind of act that *would* be a capital offense if done intentionally, but since it was done unintentionally, the shechita is valid and the meat may be eaten after Shabbat. This reading preserves the attribution to Rebbi Yehuda: the case is *shogeg*, and Rebbi Yehuda rules that even unintentional violators must wait until after Shabbat.

A further question arises: why not attribute the Mishnah to Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar, who also prohibits eating on Shabbat itself regardless of *shogeg* or *meizid*? The Gemara answers that Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar differs in his treatment of *motzei Shabbat*: according to him, the perpetrator who acted *b'shogeg* can never eat from the meat. But our Mishnah says *shechitaso k'sheira*, implying that the shechita is ultimately valid for everyone — including the one who performed it. That fits only Rebbi Yehuda, not Rebbi Yochanan HaSandlar.

---

## Rav's Authority Choice

### Rav Silences Tanna

The Gemara reports: *tani Tanna kamei d'Rav* — a Tanna recited in front of Rav the following formulation: *hamevashel b'Shabbos b'shogeg yochal b'meizid lo yochal* — if one cooks on Shabbat unintentionally it may be eaten; if willfully it may not. This is Rebbi Meir's lenient position. Yet *u'mashtikei lei Rav* — Rav silenced him.

The Gemara considers an initial explanation: perhaps Rav silenced him because Rav holds like Rebbi Yehuda and did not want Rebbi Meir's more lenient ruling publicized. But the Gemara immediately rejects this: *man d'svira lei k'Rebbi Meir mashtikei lei?* — Just because you personally rule like Rebbi Yehuda, do you silence someone presenting Rebbi Meir's view? Moreover, the Gemara challenges the premise itself: do we even know that Rav rules like Rebbi Yehuda? In fact, from what Rav Chanan bar Ami reports, Rav rules like Rebbi Meir.

### Rav's Public/Private

The Gemara introduces a fascinating distinction: *ki morei lehu Rav l'talmidei morei lehu k'Rebbi Meir* — when Rav would instruct his private students, he would rule leniently like Rebbi Meir. *v'chi darash b'pirka darash k'rebbi yehuda* — but when he would deliver a public lecture, he would expound Rebbi Yehuda's stricter position. The reasoning was that his students were sufficiently scrupulous that they could be trusted with the leniency without sliding into carelessness; the general public could not be given the same ruling in a public forum without risk of misapplication.

This phenomenon has a very recognizable contemporary parallel. The popular halakhic handbooks in English typically present the strictest positions, with leniencies occasionally buried in Hebrew footnotes — on the apparent assumption that those who can read the Hebrew and navigate the scholarly apparatus are the ones who can be trusted with the nuance. There is something both familiar and uncomfortable about this structure. The *b'di'eved* that a posek communicates privately to one individual has a way, once publicized, of becoming a *l'chatchila* in practice. The concern is real. And yet the alternative — controlling the information entirely — raises its own questions.

### Control of Info Debate

This phenomenon of differential rulings — one position for students, a stricter one for the public — raises genuine tension. On one hand, the Gemara itself invokes the language of *mishum amei ha'aretz* — on account of the unlearned — as the rationale for the stricter public ruling. On the other hand, whether this constitutes responsible leadership or a kind of paternalistic arrogance depends entirely on whether the assessment is accurate.

Those who find it troubling would argue that treating the public as incapable of handling nuanced rulings ultimately infantilizes them and may drive some people away from observance altogether when they encounter standards they cannot sustain. Those who defend the practice would point to the observable dynamic in which leniencies, when publicized, tend to expand far beyond the circumstances that justified them — a *b'di'eved* heard publicly is experienced as a *l'chatchila*. Rabbis regularly encounter this reality when a carefully qualified private ruling becomes their public reputation.

There is also a distinction within the Gemara's own narrative worth noting. The Gemara itself has no difficulty presenting Rebbi Meir's lenient position as legitimate data — as a Tannaitic opinion — even as Rav apparently resisted its public dissemination in the context of practical ruling. The category of *halacha v'ein morin kein* — a ruling that is technically correct but not to be announced publicly — is a distinct phenomenon, and operates even with respect to students in some cases. Here, the issue is different: it concerns what gets announced in the context of a public *drasha* versus what gets taught in the beit midrash.

The word *darash* itself is worth noting. A *drasha* in the amoraic period was not simply a halakhic ruling delivered from the pulpit. Based on early works like the *sheiltot*, it appears that the standard format involved beginning with a halakhic or aggadic topic, weaving in a *drasha* on the weekly *parasha*, and then circling back to the practical ruling. The information emerging from such a public setting had a different character and reach than private instruction.

### Cooking vs. Slaughter

The Gemara ultimately resolves why Rav silenced the Tanna. It was not because the Tanna was presenting Rebbi Meir's position — that would have been no reason at all. Rather, *tana shochet kamei* — the Tanna had changed the category: instead of teaching *hamevashel b'Shabbos*, he was teaching *hashochet b'Shabbos*. He had applied Rebbi Meir's ruling about cooking to a case of slaughter. Rav objected: that is incorrect. Rebbi Meir's leniency does not extend from *bishul* to *shechita*.

### Meat Not Edible Raw

The Gemara explains the distinction: *ad kan lo kashari Rebbi Meir ela b'mevashel d'ra'ui l'kos* — Rebbi Meir permits benefiting from the unintentional cooking precisely because the food being cooked was *ra'ui l'kos* — fit to be eaten raw, even if one would not normally do so. Vegetables or meat are at least theoretically chewable in their raw state. Therefore they are not *muktzeh* — they were fit for use when Shabbat began — and the only issue is *ma'aseh Shabbat*. Since the violation was *b'shogeg*, Rebbi Meir permits it entirely. But *aval shochet d'ein ra'ui l'kos* — in the case of slaughter, the living animal cannot be eaten; it is not fit for consumption in any form when Shabbat begins. Therefore, in addition to any question of *ma'aseh Shabbat*, there is an independent *muktzeh* problem.
