And that *muktzeh* problem — about which the Gemara has now come full circle — applies even where *ma'aseh Shabbat* does not.

---

## Sick Person Cases

### Rebbi Meir: Sick Plan

The Gemara now asks: given that the Mishnah attributes a ruling to Rebbi Meir — specifically the implication that according to Rebbi Meir, one may eat the meat even on Shabbat itself — how is that possible if there is a muktzeh problem? The Gemara answers: *k'gon shehaya lo choleh mi'be'od yom* — for example, a case where someone in the household was critically ill when Shabbat began. Because there was a seriously ill person present from before Shabbat, the owner recognized that this animal might need to be slaughtered on Shabbat to provide fresh meat for the patient. The animal was therefore mentally designated for possible slaughter on Shabbat, and that designation removes the *muktzeh* status. Under those circumstances, the *muktzeh* problem is eliminated, and the only remaining question is *ma'aseh Shabbat* — deriving benefit from a Shabbat violation. According to Rebbi Meir, if the violation was *b'shogeg*, there is no problem even on Shabbat itself.

But if the animal was not muktzeh only because there was a *choleh* — a sick person — from before Shabbat, how does a prohibition of *ma'aseh Shabbat* then enter the picture? After all, slaughtering for a *choleh* whose life is at risk is permitted on Shabbat. The Gemara introduces the case of *shehaya lo choleh v'hipri* — the person was ill when Shabbat began, so the animal was not muktzeh, but then the person recovered before the slaughter was performed. With no longer any justification to slaughter on Shabbat, the person went ahead and did it anyway. In this case there is no muktzeh problem — that was set aside when Shabbat began — but there is a Shabbat violation, and the question of *ma'aseh Shabbat* is fully operative. It is precisely here that Rebbi Yehuda's rule becomes relevant: even if the violation was *b'shogeg*, one must wait until after Shabbat.

### Sick & Healthy Eat

Rav Achah bar Ada, and some say Rebbi Yitzchak bar Ada, rule in the name of Rav: *hashochet l'choleh b'Shabbos assur l'bari* — if one slaughters for a sick person on Shabbat, a healthy person may not eat from the meat. The reason is muktzeh: since the sick person's condition arose during Shabbat — the animal was not designated for this purpose before Shabbat began — it remains muktzeh for anyone other than those for whom the shechita was permitted.

By contrast, *hamevashel l'choleh b'Shabbos mutar l'bari* — if one cooks for a sick person on Shabbat, a healthy person may eat from it. The distinction turns on *ra'ui l'kos*: food that is being cooked was at least theoretically edible in its raw state when Shabbat began and is therefore not muktzeh. The living animal, however, was not fit for any form of consumption when Shabbat began, and so it is muktzeh to all but those for whose benefit the shechita was halachically permitted.

This distinction has a vivid practical application: if one is spending Shabbat with a patient in a hospital and the patient is brought hot food but is too ill to eat it, may the visitor eat from it? There is no concern of deriving benefit from a Shabbat violation, since the cooking was done for the patient's sake. The question turns entirely on whether the food was of a type that was edible before Shabbat began — if so, there is no muktzeh concern and the visitor may eat.

Rav Pappa adds a further observation: there are circumstances in which even a case of *shechita* permits a healthy person to eat, and circumstances in which even *bishul* forbids it. Shechita is permitted to a healthy person when the animal had been designated from before Shabbat for a person who was ill — as discussed above. Cooking is forbidden to a healthy person when, for example, a *delaat* was cut from the ground during Shabbat: either it was muktzeh for an independent reason, or — as Tosafot suggests — it was a variety so hard as to be entirely inedible without cooking, and therefore had the status of *eino ra'ui l'kos* when Shabbat began.

### Halacha Summary

Rav Dimi of Nehardea states the practical halacha: *hashochet l'choleh b'Shabbos mutar l'bari b'umtsa* — if one slaughters for a sick person on Shabbat, a healthy person may eat from it raw, provided that the sick person was ill when Shabbat began so that the animal was not muktzeh. One may not cook it, but one may eat it raw. The reason is formulated as follows: *keivan d'efshar l'kezayis basar belo shechita — ki shachit adaata d'cholah kashachit* — since it is impossible to obtain even an olive's worth of meat without slaughtering an entire animal, any additional meat that results from the shechita was incidentally produced in the course of acting for the patient's benefit. The healthy person consumes what was in effect an unavoidable byproduct; no additional *melacha* was performed on his behalf.

### Gezeirah Shema Yarbe

The ruling on the cooking side is the inverse. If one cooks for a *choleh* on Shabbat, *assur l'bari* — a healthy person may not eat from it — even though there is no muktzeh problem and no personal violation of Shabbat. Why? *gezeirah shema yarbe bishvilo* — a rabbinic safeguard against the risk that the cook, knowing someone else will benefit, will cook more than is strictly required for the patient. Perhaps consciously, perhaps unconsciously, the knowledge that the healthy person will eat from the food will lead to additional cooking. To eliminate that risk entirely, the Sages categorically forbade the healthy person from eating from what was cooked for the *choleh*. The ruling is structural, not personal: the cook did nothing wrong, and the food is not prohibited as a product of sin — but the potential for abuse is real enough to warrant the rabbinic fence.

The halacha as ruled by the *shulchan aruch* follows Rebbi Yehuda: even a *b'shogeg* Shabbat violation prohibits the violator and others from eating on Shabbat itself, and the food must wait until after Shabbat. The *mishnah berurah* notes, however, that *b'sha'at had'chak* — in a pressing situation — one may rely on the position of Rebbi Meir, since a significant group of Rishonim, including Tosafot, rule leniently. In practice, this becomes relevant in common situations such as when a guest in someone's home has a Shabbat violation committed on one's behalf, or when refusing to eat would cause offense or result in having no food for the Shabbat meal. The separate question of how to define *shogeg* — and how to treat someone who knows the orthodox prohibition but personally rejects its authority — remains a matter requiring independent analysis.

---

## Shechita Instruments

### Acceptable Tools

Having dealt with *who* may perform shechita and *when* it may be performed, the Mishnah turns to the instrument. *hashochet b'magal yad b'tzur u've'kaneh — shechitaso kesheira* — one who slaughters with a hand sickle, a sharpened rock, or a sharpened reed produces a valid shechita. The latter two cases establish that shechita does not require a formal *kli* — a designated utensil — so long as the implement is sufficiently smooth and sharp. The hand sickle is more complicated: it has serrated edges on the interior. The ruling is that since the inner edge is serrated but the outer edge is smooth, and one uses only the smooth outer edge, no *gezeirah* is enacted and the shechita is valid.

### Three Principles

The Mishnah then introduces a summary formulation: *haKol shochtin, u'le'olam shochtin, u've'chol shochtin* — everyone may slaughter, one may always slaughter, and one may slaughter with anything. These three phrases encapsulate the entire discussion to this point: the first addresses who may perform shechita, the second addresses when, and the third addresses what instrument may be used. It is possible that these three words represent an early, compressed teaching that predates the elaborations recorded in the surrounding Mishnayot — a terse original formulation that the Mishnah then proceeded to unpack in detail.

### Forbidden Tools

The summary Mishnah immediately introduces exceptions. *chutz mi'magal katzir ve'ha'magera ve'ha'shinayim ve'ha'tzipporen* — one may not use a harvest sickle, a saw, animal teeth removed from the animal, or a fingernail. Most of these share a common defect: they are serrated. The Mishnah provides the unifying explanation: *mipnei she'hen chonkin* — because they strangle. A serrated or nicked instrument does not cut cleanly; it tears. The entire requirement of a smooth, nick-free blade is grounded in this principle: shechita must be accomplished by the sharpness of the knife, not by tearing or pressure. Any implement that tears rather than cuts causes *chanikah* — strangulation — which invalidates the shechita. The fingernail differs slightly in the nature of its disqualification, but the result is the same.

One might ask: does a kohen not use his fingernail for *melikah* of a bird? Yes, but *melikah* is performed from the back of the neck, not through the throat, and it would constitute a *neveilah* in any other context — it is permitted only as an exception specific to *korbanot*.

### Attached vs. Detached

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's language — *hashochet* — suggests these instruments are valid only *b'di'eved*, after the fact, but not *l'chatchila*, at the outset. The Gemara is puzzled by the hand sickle: *bishlama b'magal yad* — that one is understandable as a *b'di'eved* case, since we are concerned that using the smooth outer edge might lead one to mistakenly use the serrated inner side. But why would a rock or reed be valid only *b'di'eved*? There is no such slippery-slope concern.

The Gemara then raises a counter-source: a Tosefta states *b'chol shochtin* — one may slaughter with anything — and proceeds to enumerate rocks, glass, and the hard outer shell of a reed, all described as permissible even *l'chatchila*. If so, why does the Mishnah imply a *b'di'eved* limitation?

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: *kan b'talush kan b'mechubar* — the distinction is whether the object is detached from the ground (*talush*) or still attached to it (*mechubar*). If the rock or reed is detached and held in the hand, it is valid even *l'chatchila*. If it is still attached — a boulder with a sharpened edge, or a reed growing from the ground — the status changes. The Mishnah's language of *b'di'eved* refers to the case of something still attached, where one must bring the animal's neck to the object rather than the object to the animal. The Tosefta's permissive formulation refers to detached objects.

### Rebbi vs. R. Chiya

Rav Kahana reports a dispute: *hashochet b'mechubar l'karka — Rebbi possel, v'Rebbi Chiya machshir* — if one slaughters with something still attached to the ground, Rebbi invalidates the shechita even after the fact, while Rebbi Chiya validates it *b'di'eved*. Rav Kahana adds that Rebbi Chiya's validation is only *b'di'eved* — not *l'chatchila*.

### Baraita All Methods

A Baraita, however, teaches that one may slaughter with anything, *bein b'talush bein b'mechubar* — whether detached or attached — and it uses permissive language that appears to extend even to *l'chatchila*. The Baraita further specifies that shechita is valid whether the knife is above and the animal below (i.e., the animal is on the ground), or the knife is below and the animal above (i.e., the animal stands and the knife is applied from beneath). The concern in the latter case — that the weight of the animal's neck pressing down on the knife might constitute *derasah* rather than clean cutting — is dismissed.

The Gemara is now troubled: this Baraita, which validates even attached objects *l'chatchila*, seems to match neither Rebbi nor Rebbi Chiya. Rebbi invalidates *mechubar* even *b'di'eved*; Rebbi Chiya validates it only *b'di'eved*, not *l'chatchila*. If neither authority accounts for the Baraita's leniency, *manni* — whose opinion is it?

The Gemara resolves this as follows: the Baraita does in fact follow Rebbi Chiya. *v'afillu l'chatchila* — Rebbi Chiya actually holds that even an attached object is valid *l'chatchila*. The reason Rav Kahana described Rebbi Chiya's position as only *b'di'eved* was to show how far Rebbi would go in the opposite direction — he invalidates even *b'di'eved*. But Rebbi Chiya's own position is permissive even at the outset.

This still leaves the Mishnah unexplained, since the Mishnah's *b'di'eved* language fits neither Rebbi (who invalidates even *b'di'eved*) nor Rebbi Chiya (who permits even *l'chatchila*). The Gemara therefore returns to the same answer: *l'olam Rebbi Chiya* — it is indeed Rebbi Chiya — *v'matnisin d'ktani hashochet Rebbi* — and the Mishnah that implies *b'di'eved* reflects Rebbi's view. But this creates an internal contradiction in Rebbi's position: does Rebbi invalidate *mechubar* even *b'di'eved*, or does he validate it *b'di'eved*?

*Lo kashya* — it is not difficult. The resolution turns on a distinction of great practical significance in many areas of halacha: *kan b'mechubar meikara — kan b'talush u'lisof chibro* — there are two distinct categories of "attached." Something that was always attached to the ground from the beginning — a natural rock, a growing plant, a tree — has the full status of *mechubar*. Something that began as a detached object and was later attached — a knife inserted into a wall and plastered over, a beam built into a structure — retains a different status despite being physically connected. When Rebbi invalidates the shechita even *b'di'eved*, he refers to an object that was always attached from the outset, *mechubar meikara*. When Rebbi permits *b'di'eved*, he refers to something that was once detached and only subsequently attached, *talush u'lisof chibro*. Rebbi Chiya, by contrast, permits even *mechubar meikara* at least *b'di'eved*, and according to the Gemara's final reading, even *l'chatchila*. This three-way structure — Rebbi's complete invalidation of original attachment, Rebbi's post-facto validation of secondary attachment, and Rebbi Chiya's across-the-board permission — will be developed further in the discussion that continues on the following daf.

# Hullin 16

## Attached vs. Detached

### Opening

We pick up six lines from the bottom of 15b, at the words *u'mina teima*. The Mishnah had established that one may slaughter with any instrument — including a rock or a reed — provided it is sufficiently smooth. This ruling leads the Gemara into a discussion of whether one may use something that is attached to the ground.

### Mishnah & Gemara

The position of Rabbi (Rebbi) is that an instrument attached to the ground is not valid. The Mishnah implies as well that *lechatchila* it is not valid; use of such an instrument is acceptable only *bedievid*, post facto. We also established that Rabbi would permit *bedievid* a case where the instrument began as detached and was subsequently attached — *talush u'levasof chibur* — as distinct from something that was always attached, *mechubar me'ikara*. The Gemara now asks: how do we know to draw this distinction between the two categories?

### Rabbi's Position

Rabbi holds that an instrument *mechubar me'ikara* — always attached to the ground — is invalid even *bedievid*. By contrast, something that is *talush u'levasof chibur* — first detached and only later attached — is not fully considered attached. According to Rabbi, at least *bedievid*, such an instrument is valid. *lechatchila* it remains problematic, since one might confuse the two cases, but post facto it is not treated as genuinely attached.

### Proof Needed

The Gemara asks: *u'mina teima d'shani lan bein mechubar me'ikara l'talush u'levasof chibur* — from where do we know to distinguish between something always attached and something that was detached and then attached?

### Baraita Evidence

*D'tanya*: A baraita is cited. *ha'shochet b'muchni shechitato keshera* — if one slaughters with a knife driven by some type of wheel mechanism, the shechita is valid. *bimechubar l'karka shechitato keshera* — if the knife is attached to the ground, it is valid. *natatz sakin bakotel v'shachat ba shechitato keshera* — if one took a knife and lodged it into a wall and slaughtered with it, the shechita is valid.

Here an important point must be noted. If these instruments are attached to the ground, how does one actually perform the shechita? Rashi, in a brief but critical comment, explains: *v'holich v'heivi tzavar habeheima aleha* — one does not move the knife at all; instead, one moves the neck of the animal back and forth over the knife. This is a striking observation. We naturally assume that one must move the knife, but in fact, since all motion is relative, as long as there is a proper cutting motion between knife and animal, even if the motion is applied to the animal rather than the knife, the shechita is valid.

The baraita then continues: *hatzoer yotzei min hakotel* — if a rock protrudes from a wall, *o kaneh oleh me'eilav* — or a reed growing naturally from the ground, *v'shachat bo shechitato pesula* — and one slaughtered with it, the shechita is invalid.

### Resolution

*Kashya ahadadei* — the two halves of the baraita contradict one another. The resolution: *ela lav shema mina shani bein mechubar me'ikara l'talush u'levasof chibur* — there is a difference between something always attached and something that was once detached and later attached. *shema mina* — this is a sound proof. The case of *mechubar l'karka* in the baraita refers to something attached by human agency — *talush u'levasof chibur* — which *bedievid* is valid. The case of the reed growing naturally or the rock protruding from a cave wall — something always attached — is invalid.

One might pause at the phrase *tzoer yotzei min hakotel* — a rock coming out of a wall — since a wall is presumably man-made and constructed. The Gemara will later clarify that the reference here is to a natural wall, such as the wall of a cave, so that such a rock was always attached and never detached. This distinction — between always-attached and detached-then-attached — will occupy much of the discussion on this daf.

---

## Koach Gavra

### Wheel Contradiction

The baraita stated that one who slaughters with a knife powered by a wheel — *ha'shochet b'muchni shechitato keshera* — the shechita is valid. Yet a parallel baraita states that in this same case the shechita is invalid: *shechitato pesula*. The Gemara must resolve this contradiction.

A clarification about the mechanics: the wheel does not mean the knife moves in a circle, which would obviously be impossible for shechita. Rather, the energy of a turning wheel is transformed through a mechanism into a vertical cutting motion. The question is whether such a mechanism produces valid shechita.

### Pottery vs. Water

*Lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. *ha be'sadna de'pakhra, ha be'sadna de'maya* — one case refers to a pottery wheel and the other to a water wheel. A pottery wheel is driven by the operator's leg pushing a pedal, which spins the wheel to shape clay. A water wheel is driven by the rush of water. The distinction is consequential: in the case of the pottery wheel, the energy ultimately derives from the human operator — the mechanism is powered by the person. In the case of the water wheel, the energy comes from the rushing water itself, not from the person.

This introduces a fundamental criterion for shechita: *koach gavra* — human energy. Even if intention is not required for *ma'aseh shechita*, the energy animating the act must derive from a person. A knife blown by the wind onto an animal's throat would not constitute shechita. *ma'aseh shechita* requires human energy even where intention may not be required. A water wheel, driven by natural forces, lacks *koach gavra*; a pottery wheel, driven through a person's physical effort, possesses it.

### First vs. Second Power

The Gemara then proposes an alternative resolution: *v'ibayit eima, ha ve'ha be'sadna de'maya* — both contradictory baraitot may involve a water wheel, yet one permits and the other forbids. How? *lo kashya: ha be'koach rishon, ha be'koach sheni* — the difference lies in whether we are dealing with *koach rishon*, the first power, or *koach sheni*, the second power.

The question is how the water wheel came to be turning. One may imagine a river flowing nearby, with a sluice gate controlling whether the water diverts into one's channel and turns the wheel. Who opens that gate? If the person opens the gate and the water immediately rushes through and turns the wheel, that initial turning is a product of *koach rishon* — the direct consequence of the person's act. As the river continues to push the wheel on its own afterward, that is *koach sheni* — a derivative power no longer traceable directly to the person.

### Sluice Gates Example

*Ki ha de'amar Rav Pappa* — Rav Pappa illustrates the principle with a case of murder. *hai man de'kaftei le'chavrei ve'ashkelei bidka de'maya u'mit chayav* — if a person bound his fellow and placed him in front of sluice gates over a rushing river, and then opened the gates so that the water came crashing down and killed the bound man, the perpetrator is liable. *mai ta'ama? giray didei ninhu* — they are his arrows. Although the physical energy was in the water, since the water burst through as a direct consequence of his opening the gates, it is as though he fired an arrow. The initial crash of the water is attributed to him.

However, the statement continues: *v'hanei milei be'koach rishon* — this is only true for *koach rishon*, the first, direct impact. *aval be'koach sheni, grama b'alma hu* — if it is the second power, it is merely indirect causation, *grama*.

As Rashi explains, the distinction is one of physical position. If the victim stands directly at the base of the sluice gate, the crashing water strikes him immediately — that is *koach rishon*, and the person is fully liable. But if the victim stands several feet away, the water first crashes down at the base and only then flows onward to drown the man standing further back — that derivative flow is *koach sheni*, and the perpetrator is exempt from formal liability, though the Gemara notes he remains *chayav b'dinei shamayim*, liable before Heaven.

### Application

This principle has ramifications across many areas of halacha. The distinction between direct action and *grama* — indirect causation — is not merely about physical causation in a philosophical sense, but about whether one's energy is the operative force.

One instructive application is the familiar question of closing an electrical circuit on Shabbat. At a micro level, one who switches on an incandescent light closes a circuit, causing electrons to flow and heat a filament. Although the person did not personally heat the filament, the result is so instantaneous that it is treated as *koach rishon* — as though the person performed the act directly. The immediacy collapses the intervening steps, and the action is considered a *ma'aseh*, not a *grama*. This analysis applies *l'chumra*, where what matters is not merely that one set a process in motion, but that when the result follows immediately, it is attributed to the person as their own act.

An analogous but distinct question arises in other contexts — for example, whether machine-made matzah is produced *lishma* — where the relevant criterion is not *koach gavra* but *kavana*. There, what transpires after the initial activation of the machine is arguably no longer the operator's direct action. In any event, the principle is established: shechita requires *koach gavra*, which is satisfied either by directly imparting one's physical energy or by releasing energy in such a way that the immediate result is attributed to that release — as in *koach rishon* of the water wheel.

---

## Defining Attachment

### Three Generations

*Yativ Rav achorei d'Rabbi Chiyya, v'Rabbi Chiyya kammai d'Rabbi* — Rav sat behind Rabbi Chiyya, who sat before Rabbi. This scene captures three pivotal generations in the transition from Tannaim to Amoraim: Rabbi — Rebbi — the editor of the Mishnah; Rabbi Chiyya, who edited the Tosefta and the baraitot; and Rav, the first of the Amoraim. Their respective positions are likewise arranged: Rabbi holds that the knife must be detached; Rabbi Chiyya holds that attachment to the ground does not invalidate the shechita.

### Abraham & the Knife

Rabbi, sitting before them, offers a proof for his position: *minayin l'shechita shehu betalush?* — from where do we know shechita requires a detached instrument? *she'ne'emar, vayikach et hama'achelet lishchot et b'no* — as the verse says, he took the knife to slaughter his son. The word *ma'achelet* — a proper knife — implies something that functions as a vessel, as a detached implement.

It should be noted that Rabbi is not claiming shechita requires a formal *kli* — a recognized vessel. A detached rock or reed carries no status as a vessel, yet Rabbi would permit it. For *kodashim*, a different verse may demand a recognized *kli*, perhaps even a *kli sharet*, but for ordinary shechita, the inference from *ma'achelet* is only that the implement must be detached.

Rav, seated behind Rabbi Chiyya and too far to hear clearly, asks: *mai ka'amar?* — what is Rabbi saying? Rabbi Chiyya replies: *vav deketiv a'uptza ka'amar* — he is writing a *vav* on a ridge. This is an idiomatic expression for making an argument on broken ground, like trying to draw a straight line across a series of bumps — the line will be uneven and the argument does not hold together.

The Gemara then clarifies why the proof fails: *lo kra l'zrizutei d'Avraham kamma'shma lan* — the verse is not stating a legal principle; it is describing the alacrity of Avraham, who prepared himself carefully before the *akeidah* and took along a knife. As Rashi explains, Avraham may have been concerned that he would not find a suitable instrument at the site of the *akeidah*. But one cannot derive from Avraham's choice of implement a binding principle about what constitutes a valid instrument for shechita. The Torah is offering a narrative detail, not a legal prescription. Had Avraham wished, he could have sharpened a detached rock — or pulled a rock from the ground.

### Avodah Zarah Case

Rava states: *peshita li — talush she'basof chibro l'inyan avodat kochavim havei talush* — it is obvious to me that something once detached and subsequently attached to the ground is treated as detached for purposes of *avodah zarah*, idolatry.

### House Forbidden

The operative principle in *avodah zarah* is *ha'mishtachaveh l'vayit shelo assaro* — one who bows down to one's own house renders it forbidden in benefit. Two conditions underlie this rule. First, *ein adam oser davar she'eino shelo* — one cannot render another person's property forbidden through one's own actions, absent a physical change to the object. Bowing down to a neighbor's house, unlike slaughtering a neighbor's animal for idolatrous purposes, involves no physical transformation, and therefore cannot alter its status. Second, and more relevant here, the object must be considered detached — *metaltelin* — in order to be rendered forbidden.

The basis for this second condition is the verse in Devarim: *eloheihem al he'harim, v'lo he'harim eloheihem* — their gods that are upon the mountains, but the mountains themselves cannot be their gods. The Gemara in *avodah zarah* states plainly that one who bows to a mountain has committed an act of *avodah zarah* and is *chayav mita*, yet the mountain itself does not become a forbidden object. This makes practical sense: if mountains and the earth itself could be rendered *avodah zarah* and forbidden in benefit, vast portions of the globe would be prohibited.

The underlying concept is that something must be capable of having its identity designated — and that capacity belongs only to things that are, in some sense, under human dominion. The earth itself, being permanently fixed, cannot have its identity designated in this way.

Now, one who bows to one's own house does render it forbidden. This demonstrates that a house — which began as individual stones and timber that were *talush*, detached — even after being constructed and attached to the ground, is treated for *avodah zarah* purposes as *talush*. It is not the ground itself, even though it is affixed to it.

*V'ei salka da'atach havei mechubar* — if you would say that something detached and later attached is now considered fully attached, the house could not become forbidden, since like a mountain it would be immune. Yet the halacha is that the house does become forbidden. This confirms that *talush u'levasof chibur* — detached-then-attached — is treated as *talush* for *avodah zarah*.

### Seeds & Water

*U'l'inyan hechsher zera'im* — when it comes to making agricultural produce susceptible to *tumah*, the Gemara notes that the matter is a debate among Tannaim: *tanna'ei hi*.

By way of background: water that comes into contact with food renders that food susceptible to *tumah* — *huchshar*. But this applies only once the food has been harvested; food still attached to the ground is not susceptible. Importantly, for the water to render food susceptible, the water itself must have been desired — the principle of *ki yutan*. If the water fell upon the food unwanted, it does not render it susceptible.

The question of relevance here is this: if you desire water for the sake of something that is *talush u'levasof chibur* — detached and now attached — does your desire for that water activate the *ki yutan* principle and render food susceptible? The issue is whether such an object is treated as *talush*, in which case wanting water for it constitutes a desire for something not attached to the ground, or as *mechubar*, in which case it does not.

*D'tenan* — a Mishnah is cited. *ha'kofeh ke'arah al ha'kotel bishvil she'tudach* — one who places a vessel against a wall because one wants the rain to clean it out: *harei zeh be'chi yutan* — this is in the category of *ki yutan*, and the water can render food susceptible. *bishvil shelo yilkeh ha'kotel* — if one placed the vessel against the wall merely to protect the wall from the rain, *eino be'chi yutan* — the water is not desired and does not render food susceptible.

The Gemara identifies an internal contradiction within this Mishnah. From the first clause, the implication is that if one wanted the water for the wall itself — not to clean the vessel, but to wash the wall — that would be *eino be'chi yutan*, since wanting water for the wall is wanting it for something attached. But from the second clause, the implication runs the other way — that wanting the water for the wall is *be'chi yutan*, sufficient to make food susceptible.

*Amar Rabbi Elazar: tavrah* — Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by splitting the Mishnah. *mi she'shanah zu lo shanah zu* — whoever taught the first half did not teach the second half. The middle case — wanting water for the wall — is actually a disagreement between two anonymous Tannaim, one representing each half of the Mishnah.

### Wall Types

Rav Pappa disagrees: *kulei chad tanna hu* — the entire Mishnah is the position of a single Tanna. *ha be'kotel me'arah, ha be'kotel binyan* — the two halves are implicitly discussing two different types of walls. One involves the wall of a cave — a natural, always-attached formation — and the other involves a constructed wall.

The reading then runs as follows: if one places a vessel against a wall to have it cleaned, the water renders food susceptible. If, however, one only wanted the water for the wall, and it is the wall of a cave — always attached, genuinely *mechubar* — the water does not render food susceptible. But if the wall is a constructed wall — made from materials that began as *talush* — then even wanting the water for the wall suffices, since a constructed wall is treated as *talush u'levasof chibur*, not as true ground. Only if one was trying to keep the water away entirely, to protect the constructed wall, does the water fail to render food susceptible.

### Summary Across Areas

We now have three domains in which the status of *talush u'levasof chibur* has been analyzed. For shechita, although the matter remains somewhat open, at least according to Rabbi it appears that detached-then-attached is treated as *talush*. For *avodah zarah*, Rava states plainly that it is considered *talush*. For *hechsher zera'im*, Rav Pappa's resolution treats a constructed wall — a paradigmatic case of *talush u'levasof chibur* — as *talush* as well.

A possibility arose, however, that different areas of halacha might treat this category differently. The Gemara opens this question: might *talush u'levasof chibur* be treated as *talush* for *avodah zarah* but as *mechubar* for *hechsher zera'im*? And what of shechita?

At the top of 16b, Rava poses the question explicitly: *talush ul'sof chibro l'inyan shechita mai?* — what is the rule for shechita? The Gemara attempts several proofs. The baraita stating that a rock protruding from a wall or a naturally growing reed renders shechita invalid is resolved: *hacha b'mai askinan? B'kotel me'arah* — we are dealing with a cave wall, something always attached, not a constructed wall. The inference is supported by the comparison to the naturally growing reed — *deika nami d'katani dumya d'kaneh oleh me'eilav* — just as the reed was never detached, so too the rock. *shema mina.*

The baraita that permits a knife lodged in a wall — *na'atz sakin b'kotel v'shachat, shechitato kesheira* — is rejected as proof: *shani sakin d'lo mevatlei* — a knife is different because one never fully commits it to the wall; one always intends to retrieve it. It therefore never truly assumes the status of something permanently attached. One would need a case where materials genuinely become part of a structure — like constructed walls — to pose the question properly, and that remains unresolved.

### Conceptual Framework

It is worth pausing to reflect on why different areas of halacha might treat *mechubar l'karka* differently. The conceptual issue is one of categories. At the extremes, there is *karka* — the earth itself — and *metaltelin* — movable chattels. The middle category is *mechubar l'karka*: attached to the ground, but not itself the ground.

Some halachot are organized around the distinction between *karka* and everything else, such that the question is whether something qualifies as the ground itself. In *avodah zarah*, the operative verse is *eloheihem al he'harim v'lo he'harim eloheihem* — the mountains do not become gods. The principle is that actual earth, as part of the created landscape, cannot be rendered an object of worship. A constructed house, even though attached to the ground, is not *karka* — it is not the earth itself — and therefore can be rendered forbidden. The category that matters there is whether something is truly *karka* or merely attached to it.

Other halachot, however, are organized around the distinction between *metaltelin* and everything else. For shechita, according to Rabbi, the inference from *ma'achelet* points toward requiring something that functions as a movable implement. Something permanently attached to the ground fails not because it is the earth, but because it is not *metaltelin*. In those frameworks, *mechubar l'karka* may follow the laws of land not because it is land but because it is not chattel — and *talush u'levasof chibur* might or might not share that status depending on how the particular halacha conceptualizes the operative boundary.

This framework is consistent with the law of transactions: a house is bought and sold through the mechanisms of land acquisition, not *meshicha*, because it is not *metaltelin* — not true chattel. There, what matters is that it is not movable, and *mechubar l'karka* falls on the land side of that divide. The precise location of *talush u'levasof chibur* within this spectrum thus legitimately varies by context.

---

## Knife in Wall

### Moving the Animal

The Gemara returns to the baraita: *natan sakin bekotel v'shachat bah shechitato kesherah* — a knife inserted into a wall and used for shechita is valid. As Rashi established earlier, this works by moving the animal's neck over the knife rather than moving the knife itself.

### Position Requirements

*Amar Rav Anan amar Shmuel: lo shanu ela she'sakin l'malah v'tzavar behemah l'matah* — Shmuel rules that this is valid only when the knife is positioned above and the animal's neck is below. One must always cut toward the front of the throat — not from behind, which would break the spine and render the animal a *treifah* first. The question here is whether the animal lies with the knife pressing from above or stands with a knife pointing upward from below. In the case of an attached knife, Shmuel requires the knife to be above and the throat below.

*Aval sakin l'matah v'tzavar behemah l'malah* — if the knife points upward and the animal's throat is above it, and the animal is being moved back and forth over the upward-pointing knife, this is invalid. *chaishinan shema yidros* — we are concerned that the operator may press down on the animal while moving it, causing the cut to result from pressure rather than the knife's sharpness. This is the defect of *derisah*, which invalidates shechita.

### Contradiction

The Gemara notes a baraita that appears to contradict this: *bein she'sakin l'matah v'tzavar behemah l'malah, bein she'sakin l'malah v'tzavar behemah l'matah* — whether the knife is below and the throat above, or the knife is above and the throat below, the shechita is valid either way.

### Two Cases Resolved

*Amar Rav Zevid: l'tzedadin katani* — Rav Zevid resolves the contradiction by reading the baraita's two halves as addressing separate cases. The clause permitting the knife below and the throat above applies to a *talush* — a free, detached knife. There, the shochet moves the knife with a single smooth motion and, even if the animal's throat is above, the natural weight of the animal does not create a *derisah* problem. The clause requiring the knife above applies to a *mechubar* — an attached knife. When the knife is fixed and one must move the animal instead, there is a much greater risk of pressing down on the animal and causing *derisah*. Therefore, when the knife is attached to the wall, it must be positioned above with the throat below.

### Birds Exception

*Amar Rav Pappa: be'ofa dekallil* — Rav Pappa notes an exception. If one is slaughtering a bird — which is light — the concern about *derisah* does not apply in the same way. A bird can be held in one hand and moved with a smooth, controlled motion comparable to moving a knife. Consequently, even with an attached knife, it does not matter which is above and which is below; the lightness of the bird makes *derisah* a non-concern.

---

## Reeds & Splinters

### Five Restrictions

*Amar Rav Chisda amar Rav Yitzchak, v'amrei lah bematnita tana: chamisha devarim ne'emru bekrumei shel kaneh* — five laws were stated regarding the reed. One may not use it for shechita, for *bris milah*, to cut meat, to pick one's teeth, or to wipe one's hands. The concern underlying most of these is that reeds splinter: a reed used for shechita may produce splinters that cause tearing in the animal and invalidate the shechita; a reed used for *milah* presents obvious dangers; a reed used to cut meat may leave splinters in the flesh that cut the person eating; a reed used to pick teeth may produce splinters that lacerate the gums; a reed used to wipe the hands may leave splinters in the skin.

### Reed Types

This prohibition on shechita with a reed appears to contradict an earlier teaching: *bekol shochtin bein betzur bein bizchuchit bein bekrumei shel kaneh* — one may slaughter with anything, whether a rock, glass, or even a reed. *amar rav pappa: besimona de'agma* — Rav Pappa distinguishes between types of reeds. The reed that is permitted for shechita is a specific variety that grows in swamps, hard and rigid, without the tendency to splinter. The reed prohibited is the common type prone to producing splinters. There is no contradiction; the two sources are discussing categorically different materials.

### Contextual Meat Cutting

The prohibition on cutting meat with a reed was not universally applied in practice. *rav pappa mitchatech bah karbei dagi* — Rav Pappa himself used a reed to clean the innards of fish. *dezigi* — fish are relatively translucent, so any splinter dislodged in the flesh would be visible and could be removed before eating. *rabbah bar rav huna mitchatech bah ofa* — Rabbah bar Rav Huna used a reed to cut poultry. *derachich* — bird meat is soft, and he was therefore not concerned that the cutting would cause splinters to break off. Each authority assessed the specific context and material and determined that the concern did not apply.

### Witchcraft Concern

The prohibition on using a reed to wipe one's hands rests on a different basis entirely. *ha'menakayach bedavar she'ha'or sholetet bo shinav noshrot* — one who cleans oneself with something flammable will suffer the falling out of teeth. *mekaneach* here refers to using material for toilet purposes, and the concern is not splinters but witchcraft: material that has come into contact with one's body in such intimate circumstances can serve as a medium through which harmful forces — or witchcraft — can take hold. The expression *shinav noshrot* — his teeth fall out — is understood to refer to serious physical deterioration in the affected area.

*Amar Pappa: l'kinuach d'maka ka'amrina* — Rav Pappa clarifies that the prohibition being extended here, based on splinters, applies to wiping in other contexts — cleaning a wound or drying one's hands. There, the witchcraft concern is inapplicable, but the concern about splinters entering the skin remains. The two prohibitions thus operate on separate rationales.

---

## Perpetual Permission

### Mishnah Summary

The Mishnah concludes with the phrase *hakol shochtin u'l'olam shochtin* — all may slaughter and one may always slaughter. As a likely summary of the preceding Mishnayot, *hakol shochtin* recalls the earlier discussion of *cheresh, shoteh v'katan* and the question of non-Jews; *u'l'olam shochtin* recalls the discussions of nighttime, Shabbat, and Yom Kippur — occasions when shechita is halachically impermissible but, performed in violation, is nonetheless valid *bedievid*. It is even possible that this phrase was the original kernel of the tractate — the earliest teaching — and that the preceding Mishnayot represent elaborations of its two components: who may slaughter and when may one slaughter.

### All Require Shechita

The Gemara, however, reads the Mishnah differently. *hakol shochtin* is reinterpreted as *hakol b'shechitah* — all things require shechita. The specific *chiddush* is *v'afilu of* — even birds. Fish require no shechita; birds require a less stringent form of shechita than large animals, needing only one of the two organs to be cut rather than both. There is even an opinion that birds require shechita only rabbinically, not biblically. The Mishnah comes to establish that birds, too, require shechita biblically. Correspondingly, *u'l'olam shochtin* is reread as a statement that one must always slaughter — one must always perform shechita.

### Rabbi Yishmael View

*Amar Rava: Rabbi Yishmael hi* — Rava identifies this reading as representing the position of Rabbi Yishmael. A baraita teaches: *ki yarchiv Hashem Elokecha et gevulcha ka'asher diber lach v'amarta ochla vasar ki ta'aveh nafshecha l'echol vasar b'chol avat nafshecha tochal vasar* — when God will expand your borders as He promised and you will say, I wish to eat meat, because you desire meat, with all your desire you may eat meat. This verse in Devarim addresses the transition from the desert to the Land of Israel. In the desert, all slaughter had to be performed as a *shelamim* offering brought to the *mishkan*; one who simply slaughtered an animal for meat outside that framework violated a prohibition. The Torah here permits, upon entering the Land, the slaughter and eating of meat independent of any sacrificial framework — *basar ta'avah*, meat of desire.

*Rabbi Yishmael omer: lo ba hakatuv ela l'hatir lahem basar ta'avah* — Rabbi Yishmael says the verse comes only to permit meat of desire. *she'batchila ne'esar lahem basar ta'avah* — meat of desire was originally forbidden in the desert; *mishenichnesu l'aretz hutar lahem basar ta'avah* — upon entering the Land, it became permitted.

### Rava's Inference

Rava, working from Rabbi Yishmael's framework, draws a further inference: *v'achshav shegalu, yachol yachzor l'issuran harishon* — now that Israel is in exile, one might think they should revert to their original state of prohibition. After all, in the desert, meat of desire was forbidden; perhaps exile — also a time of displacement — reimports that prohibition. *l'olam shochtim* — the Mishnah therefore comes to teach that one may always slaughter and eat meat, including in the present age of exile. The word *l'olam* specifically counters the possibility that the exile-era prohibition could be reinstated.

This reading carries an implicit theology: the permission to eat meat is tied, in some way, to the existence of the Temple and the sacrificial order. When korbanot are brought, they validate — or at least accompany — the general permission to eat meat. One might have thought that in exile, without the Temple, this validation is absent and the original prohibition returns.

### Rav Yosef Objects

*Matkif lah Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef challenges this reasoning on two counts. First, if the *chiddush* of *l'olam shochtim* is that one remains permitted to eat meat in exile, the Mishnah should have said *l'olam shochtim v'ochlim mibei lei* — one may always slaughter and eat — since the point is the eating, not the shechita. The Mishnah's formulation focuses on the act of shechita, not on the permission to eat meat.

Second, and more fundamentally: *me'ikara mai ta'ama itassar?* — why was meat of desire originally forbidden in the desert in the first place? *mishum d'havu mikravi l'mishkan* — because the Israelites were encamped directly around the *mishkan*, so close to it that they were expected to bring their animals as *shelamim* rather than slaughter them for ordinary consumption. *u'l'vasof mai ta'ama ishtari?* — why then was meat permitted upon entering the Land? *d'havu mirchaki m'mishkan* — because they were distant from the Temple and it was not feasible to bring every slaughter as a korban. The permission to eat *basar ta'avah* is thus a function of distance and inaccessibility, not of any deeper theological condition.

If that is the logic, then *v'kol sheken, hashta, d'itcharku tefei* — now, in exile, they are far more distant still. There is no Temple at all. Of course meat is permitted; the rationale for permitting it applies with far greater force in exile than it did in the Land. The Mishnah cannot be telling us something so obvious. And since the Mishnah also does not say *v'ochlim*, the eating of meat cannot be the *chiddush*. What the Mishnah does mean by *l'olam shochtim* remains to be explained, and that discussion will continue in the next shiur.

---

---

# Hullin 17

## Intro & Mishna Overview

### Opening

The daf opens at the very first line of 17a. The discussion at this point has been centered on a phrase in the Mishnah stating that one may always shecht. Unquestionably, the simple sense of this phrase refers back to an earlier ruling that one may shecht at night. However, the Gemara has chosen to interpret this phrase differently.

### Reinterpretation

The Gemara's first interpretive move was to read this phrase in light of Rabbi Yishmael's position. According to Rabbi Yishmael, Bnei Yisrael in the midbar were not permitted to eat meat unless they brought it as a korban. Once they entered Eretz Yisrael and the Beis Hamikdash was distant, they were told they could eat meat without bringing it as a korban. The Mishnah, on this reading, would be teaching that even though we are no longer in Eretz Yisrael in that same context, the allowance still applies — one may still shecht at all times.

### Challenge to Yishmael

The Gemara, however, challenged this reading on two grounds. First, if this were the Mishnah's intent, the emphasis should have been on eating meat, not on the act of shechting. Second, it is entirely obvious that one may shecht meat nowadays, since the entire problem in the midbar stemmed from the requirement to bring meat as a korban. If a korban cannot be brought — as is the case when one is far from the Beis Hamikdash, and certainly nowadays when there is no Beis Hamikdash at all — it should go without saying that meat is permitted. The Gemara therefore rejected this interpretation and now turns to a variation of it.

---

## Rabbi Akiva Position

### Rav Yosef Intro

At the top of 17a, Rav Yosef introduces a new possibility: *ela amar rav yosef* — the Mishnah follows the position of Rabbi Akiva, who disagrees with Rabbi Yishmael.

### Baraita & Basar Nechira

A Baraita is cited: *ki yarchiv hashem elokecha et gevulcha ka'asher diber lach ve'amarta ochla vasar ki te'aveh nafshacha leechol basar bechol avat nafshacha tochal basar. ki yirchak mimcha hamakom asher yivchar hashem elokecha lasum shemo sham vezavachta mivekarcha umitzonecha.* This is the same verse Rabbi Yishmael discussed: when you enter the land of Israel and the place where God has chosen to rest His name is distant, you shall slaughter from your cattle and from your sheep wherever you are. Rabbi Yishmael reads this as granting permission to eat meat as basar ta'ava — the meat of desire — without requiring it to be brought as a korban, when the Beis Hamikdash is far away. Rabbi Akiva, however, reads it in a startling way: *lo ba hakatuv ela le'asor lahem basar nechira* — the verse comes to forbid for them, upon entering the land of Israel, meat that was killed through nechira.

### Nechira Explained

The word *nechira* denotes a method of killing an animal other than through proper shechita. It may refer to stabbing into the neck rather than slicing across it, or it may refer to a vertical slicing motion from the direction of the nostrils downward, rather than the lateral motion that constitutes valid shechita. Whatever its precise meaning, nechira denotes killing without ritual slaughter. Rabbi Akiva's position is therefore a remarkable one: the Torah's discussion of slaughtering animals upon entering the land — when the Beis Hamikdash is distant — implies that prior to entering the land, when they were in the midbar, Bnei Yisrael were permitted to eat meat without any act of shechita at all.

### Akiva Logic

This position is, as one must frankly acknowledge, wild. What could possibly be the logic? In the midbar, the Mishkan was close at hand and the opportunity to bring a korban was always available. If one chose not to bring a korban and simply wished to eat meat, there was apparently, according to Rabbi Akiva, no ritual requirement whatsoever associated with the killing of that animal. The one rationale that might be offered — though it is admittedly not fully satisfying — is the following: the primary ritual associated with meat was clearly the act of bringing a korban. Rabbi Akiva agrees with Rabbi Yishmael on this point. Since the Mishkan was always present and the opportunity for korbanot was constant, even when one did not avail oneself of it, perhaps all the rituals associated with meat — including the manner in which the animal is killed — were understood to exist entirely within the framework of korbanot. Once Bnei Yisrael entered Eretz Yisrael and korbanot were infrequent on account of the distance of the Beis Hamikdash, additional rituals became regularly associated with the consumption of meat — specifically, the requirement of shechita. This is, as stated, a strange position whose underlying theology is difficult to fully articulate.

### Contemporary Context

The Baraita continues: *ve-achshav she-galu, yachol yachzeru le-heteiran ha-rishon* — now that Israel has gone into exile, one might have thought they revert to the earlier state, as if returning to a pre-Temple condition where shechita was not required. The Mishnah therefore teaches: *le-olam shochtin* — one must shecht at all times, even nowadays. This too is, as the Gemara acknowledged earlier, a bizarre inference. By what logic would the absence of the Temple in exile restore a permission that had been revoked when entering the land? The Gemara is, apparently, not troubled so long as the argument is not self-evidently wrong. The argument that one might think meat cannot be eaten at all in exile — analogous to the wilderness restriction — was self-evidently wrong, since the entire reason for that restriction was the proximity of the Mishkan. Here, however, the argument that exile might restore an earlier, less restrictive regime is not obviously absurd, however strange the underlying premise. The Mishnah, according to Rabbi Akiva's reading, comes to teach that shechita is still required even now.

---

## Core Debate

### B'mai Miphligi

The Gemara now steps back to analyze the root of the dispute: *b'mai miphligi* — what exactly are Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael arguing about?

### Yishmael: Meat Permitted

Rabbi Yishmael holds *basar ta'ava lo ishtari klal* — basar ta'ava, meat eaten outside the context of korbanot, was never something the Torah would have permitted without restriction. The Torah's distinction between the midbar period and entry into the land must therefore pertain to whether one is permitted to eat meat at all. What changed upon entering the land was that eating meat outside of a korban became permitted — basar ta'ava became allowed once the Beis Hamikdash was distant.

### Akiva: Shechita Required

Rabbi Akiva holds the opposite: *basar nechira lo ishtarei klal* — nechira, killing without shechita, was something the Torah would never have permitted. Therefore the Torah's distinction between before and after entering the land cannot be about whether one is permitted to eat meat — that was always permitted. Rather, the distinction is about whether shechita is required as the method of killing. In the midbar, it was not. Upon entering the land, it became mandatory. The Gemara notes that this framing does not truly explain the debate so much as restate it; nevertheless, it sets the stage for the textual analysis that follows.

---

## Verse Analysis

### Yishmael Verse

The Gemara now examines how each position handles the verses. According to Rabbi Yishmael, everything fits: *bishlama le-Rabbi Yishmael, hainu d'chtiv ha-tzon v'ha-bakar yishachet lahem* — when Moshe speaks to God about providing the people with meat, he describes slaughtering the flocks and cattle. This demonstrates that in the midbar, eating meat required shechita.

### Akiva Response

But according to Rabbi Akiva, who says there was no requirement of shechita in the midbar, what does this verse mean? The Gemara presses: *mai ha-tzon v'ha-bakar yishachet lahem* — why does it say they will be slaughtered? If shechita was not required, it should have said *yinacher lahem* — they will be killed without ritual. Rabbi Akiva's answer is: *nechirata shelahem zu hi shechitatan* — their form of nechira was their form of shechita. That is to say, in that period, the word *shechita* had not yet acquired the specific technical connotation of ritual slaughter. It simply meant killing. This is, upon reflection, a genuine textual point: reading the word *shechita* in the Torah as necessarily implying a defined halakhic ritual is itself an assumption. The word means slaughter, and there is nothing intrinsically in the word that demands a formal ritual. It is only through our pre-existing knowledge that such a ritual exists that we read it that way. Rabbi Akiva is therefore arguing that prior to entry into the land, the word *shechita* was purely descriptive, devoid of the formal requirements that would later be imposed.

### Terminology Resolution

The question remains: how does Rabbi Akiva know that when the Torah subsequently commands *ve-zavachta mi-bekarcha umitzonecha* — and you shall slaughter from your cattle and from your flocks — upon entry into the land, this constitutes a formal command of ritual shechita rather than merely a description? The answer, it appears, lies in the nature of the verse itself. Prior to this point, all references to killing animals are descriptive. The first time the Torah actually issues a command in the context of non-kodashim, non-sacrificial meat, is in this verse in Devarim. It is the only pasuk that can be read as commanding the act of slaughter specifically for non-sacrificial meat. The shift from *shachat* to *zavachta* may also carry additional weight in Rabbi Akiva's reading. But the essential point is that this is the first and only instance where the Torah commands, rather than merely describes, a form of killing in the context of eating non-sacrificial meat — and from that point forward, the act acquires a formal ritual dimension.

As for the verse *ve-shachat et ben ha-bakar* in the opening of Parshat Vayikra, the Gemara already addressed this: *kodashim shani* — sacrifices are different. Rabbi Akiva never claimed that korbanot could be killed in any manner; they always required ritual shechita. His claim was only that non-sacrificial meat in the midbar period had no such requirement.

### Verse Structure Support

The question was also raised regarding the verse *ha-tzon v'ha-bakar yishachet lahem* in relation to deer and other wild animals. According to Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that eating meat outside of a korban was forbidden in the midbar, why does the Torah use the deer and the hart as an example of something permissible — *ach ka'asher ye'achel et ha-tzvi v'et ha-ayal ken tochlenu* — if those animals were also presumably forbidden? The Gemara addresses this directly: *ki asar Rachmana beheima dechazya lehakerava* — when the Torah restricted the eating of meat outside of a korban in the midbar, that restriction applied only to animals that were fit to be brought as sacrifices. Wild animals such as deer, which cannot be brought as korbanot, were never subject to that prohibition. Therefore the Torah can legitimately invoke them as a model of freely permitted meat.

---

## Blood Covering Case

### Mishna on Blood

The Gemara now turns to a Mishnah regarding improper slaughter and the obligation of kisui ha-dam — covering the blood. The Torah requires that after shechting a chaya or an of — a wild animal or a bird, not cattle — one must cover the blood. The Mishnah rules that this obligation applies only when the shechita was performed correctly. If one performed shechita improperly — whether by pressing rather than cutting (*hashochet v'nitnavla b'yado*), by performing nechira (cutting lengthwise), or by uprooting one of the simanim (the trachea or esophagus) prior to cutting them — one is exempt from covering the blood: *patur mil'chasot*.

### Yishmael Consistency

According to Rabbi Yishmael, this ruling is straightforward. When the Torah commanded kisui ha-dam, that command was given before Bnei Yisrael entered the land — indeed, all the Torah's commandments were given before entry into the land. At that time, according to Rabbi Yishmael, there was already a meaningful distinction between correct and incorrect shechita: killing an animal without proper ritual meant the animal was not validly slaughtered. When the Torah commanded covering the blood, it could therefore have specified — and did specify — that the obligation applies only when the animal was slaughtered correctly.

### Akiva Challenge

According to Rabbi Akiva, however, a difficulty arises. At the time the command of kisui ha-dam was given, Bnei Yisrael were still in the midbar, and at that time there was no concept of ritual shechita for non-sacrificial meat. How the animal was killed was irrelevant. The Torah still commanded covering the blood — and at that time, that command would have applied regardless of the method of killing. Why, then, do we now say the obligation applies only when shechita was performed correctly?

### Retroactive Revision

The Gemara's answer is: *hoil ve'itztar itztar* — once the Torah subsequently imposed the requirement of ritual shechita upon entry into the land, everything was revised retroactively. When there was no concept of ritual shechita and any killing was valid, the obligation of kisui ha-dam applied in all cases. But now that the meat is only halachically valid when killed through proper shechita, the entire framework was revised: kisui ha-dam now applies only when the ritual is performed correctly. The introduction of the shechita requirement effectively restructured the entire system surrounding the consumption of meat.

---

## Yishmael Verses

### Redemption Verse

The Gemara returns to examine the verse that supports Rabbi Yishmael's reading. The verse *ach ka'asher ye'achel et ha-tzvi v'et ha-ayal ken tochlenu* refers to a sacrificial animal that became invalid and was subsequently redeemed. The Torah says one may slaughter it in one's gates — notwithstanding that it was once designated as a sacrifice — just as one eats the tzvi and the ayal, the deer and the hart. The point is that the redeemed animal is no longer subject to the sanctity of a korban, just as the deer and hart are freely permitted. This verse supports Rabbi Yishmael's reading: the Torah is teaching that basar ta'ava — meat that was once restricted because it should have been brought as a korban — now becomes permitted.

### Chaya Question

As noted above, the Gemara addresses the question of why deer and hart function as the Torah's example of freely permitted meat according to Rabbi Yishmael, given that he holds meat was restricted in the midbar. The answer, established in the Gemara itself, is that *ki asar Rachmana beheima dechazya lehakerava* — only animals fit for korbanot were subject to the restriction. Animals that could not be brought as korbanot, like deer, were never restricted, and so the Torah can legitimately invoke them as an example of something that was always freely available.

### Basar Ta'ava Reading

Rabbi Yishmael's approach, it must be said, gives the simplest reading of the relevant verses. The standard reading of those passages — that there was a presumed prohibition against basar ta'ava in the midbar, that one could not eat meat outside the context of a korban when the Mishkan was close, and that upon entering the land and building a distant Beis Hamikdash, basar ta'ava became permitted — is precisely Rabbi Yishmael's position. This reading also fits coherently with contemporary attitudes toward meat consumption: the idea that eating meat began as an exclusively religious act, within the framework of korbanot, and that permission to eat it otherwise was a concession to human weakness — *basar ta'ava*, an allowance to desire — reflects a view that the consumption of meat is not something to be taken for granted. This theme recurs in rabbinic literature, with Chazal sometimes suggesting that meat should be eaten only sparingly. Rabbi Akiva's reading, by contrast, is difficult to understand on any theological or philosophical level. Why the Torah would have dispensed with ritual slaughter specifically in the midbar, of all places and times, is genuinely puzzling.

---

## Pre-Entry Meat Issue

### Yirmiya Question

Rabbi Yirmiya raises a question: according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that shechita was not required in the midbar, what is the law regarding meat killed through nechira that Bnei Yisrael carried with them into the land — *evrei basar nechira she-hichnisu Yisrael imahen la-aretz mahu*? Imagine that just before entering the land, an animal had been killed without shechita, and pieces of that meat were brought across. Since at the time of the killing, nechira was entirely permitted, does such meat receive a grandfathered status? Or does it become forbidden once the requirement of shechita took effect upon entry?

### Seven Years Conquest

The Gemara initially asks: when exactly is this question being posed? If it refers to the seven years during which Bnei Yisrael were conquering the land, the question seems moot. During that period, they were permitted to eat even non-kosher food: *u'vatim malei'im kol tuv* — they would find houses filled with all good things, and the Gemara cites Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba in the name of Rav that this included even *kitzlei d'chazirei* — dried pork found in the houses they conquered. If they could eat that, is there any question that they could eat meat killed without shechita?

### Booty Exception

The Gemara clarifies: what was permitted during the seven years of conquest was not a general waiving of the laws of kashrut. Rather, what was permitted was specifically the *shalal shel ovdei kochavim* — the booty of the non-Jewish inhabitants of the land they were conquering. Their own food — *did-hu lo ishtarv* — was not subject to any relaxation of kashrut requirements. This distinction is significant. The permission to eat non-kosher booty was not simply a matter of *sakana* — wartime exigency — for if that were the reason, it would not require a special statement; general pikuach nefesh principles would suffice. The Gemara seems to be saying something more specific: as part of the entitlement to benefit from the spoils of conquest, God granted them permission to eat whatever food was in the homes they conquered, even if it was not kosher. This is itself a remarkable idea — a targeted, contextual suspension of kashrut in order to allow full benefit from the booty — but it was limited to that specific category. It was not a blanket permission for the entire conquest period.

### Teiku

The question therefore remains with regard to meat killed through nechira in the midbar, carried into the land after the period of conquest. Does such meat get grandfathered in, since it was permissibly killed before the requirement of shechita took effect? The Gemara concludes: *teiku* — the question is left unresolved.

---

## Rava Reinterpretation

### Problem with Explanation

At this point Rava steps back and reconsiders the entire interpretive approach that has been applied to the Mishnah. The Mishnah contains three parallel phrases: *hakol shochtin*, all may shecht; *le-olam shochtin*, one may shecht at all times; and *bechol shochtin*, one may shecht with all things. The Gemara's earlier readings had interpreted *hakol shochtin* as meaning all animals must be shechted, and *le-olam shochtin* as meaning that the requirement of shechita applies even today — readings that are, as acknowledged throughout, forced and convoluted. Rava points out a further difficulty: if one reads the first two phrases not as referring to the act of shechita but rather to what is subject to it, then the third phrase *bechol shochtin* — you may shecht with all things — would also have to refer not to the instruments of shechita but to the objects upon which it is performed, which clearly makes no sense.

### Rava Simple Reading

Rava therefore proposes the natural reading: *ela amar rava — hakol shochtin*, all people may shecht. *le-olam shochtin*, one may shecht at all times — whether by day or by night, whether on a rooftop or on a boat. *bechol shochtin*, one may shecht with all things — whether with a rock, with glass, or with a reed (*bein betzur bein bizchuchit bein bikrumit shel kaneh*). This reading simply echoes the structure of the earlier Mishnayot in the tractate, as one would naturally have assumed from the outset.

### Repetition Purpose

The reason the Mishnah repeats material already covered in earlier chapters is not, on Rava's reading, a signal to pursue exotic interpretations. Rather, each repetition subtly expands a category. *hakol shochtin* was already stated — but perhaps it only covered a *kuti*. By repeating it, the Mishnah now includes even a *yisrael mumar*, a habitual sinner. *le-olam shochtin* was already stated for day and night — but what about an unusual location such as a rooftop or a boat? The second statement includes those as well. *bechol shochtin* was already stated for a rock — but what about a reed or a piece of glass? The repetition extends the earlier ruling. The three phrases are not advancing a novel halakhic theory about the historical status of shechita; they are providing incremental expansions of the practical rules, following the natural structure of earlier Mishnayot.

---

## Prohibited Instruments

### Serrated Edges

The Mishnah then states: *chutz mimagal katzir vehamigerah* — one may not use a harvesting scythe or a saw. The fundamental rule is that the cutting instrument must have a sharp, smooth edge; anything with serrations or teeth is disqualified. The problem with such instruments is that their serrated edges tear rather than cut.

### Shmuel Father Test

The Gemara records that the father of Shmuel would make specific nicks in knives — *pagam veshadar, pagam veshadar* — and send them to Eretz Yisrael, evidently seeking guidance on what types of nicks render a knife unfit for shechita. The response that came back was: *kimagaira shaninu* — we were taught that the problem exists only when it is like a saw. This response sets up the core analytical question of what exactly makes a nick analogous to a saw.

---

## Nick Types

### Saw Response

The key distinction, as the Gemara will develop, concerns the geometry of the nick. The problem of a saw derives from the fact that its teeth have edges on both sides of the point — a V-shape that catches and tears in either direction of movement. By contrast, a nick that rises sharply on only one side will cause tearing only when the knife moves in one particular direction.

### V vs One-Directional

The critical difference is therefore between a bump that has a rise on both sides (analogous to the V-shape of a saw tooth) and a bump that rises sharply on only one side. If the nick is V-shaped, every movement of the knife — in either direction — will encounter a rising edge, first weakening the tissue and then tearing it: *d'mursha kamma machlish umursha basra baza* — the first inclination weakens and the second tears. If, however, the nick rises on only one side, it will be a problem only when moving in the direction that encounters the rise.

The Gemara immediately challenges even this more lenient case: even a one-directional bump should be problematic, since *churpa d'sakkina machlish* — the sharpness of the knife itself already weakens the tissue as it cuts through the flesh toward the trachea and esophagus. By the time the bump comes in contact with the exposed simanim, should not even a one-directional bump be sufficient to tear them? The Gemara's answer: the bump is located at the very beginning — *d'kayim a-reisha d'sakkina* — at the heel of the blade. When the bump first contacts the animal's neck, it is touching only the skin and outer flesh, not the simanim. The damage it causes is at that outer layer, not at the critical internal structures. The Gemara then raises a further objection: even so, if one moves the knife back in the other direction, the knife will by then have exposed the simanim, and the one-directional bump will now encounter them on the return pass. The answer, as one student noted during the discussion, is: *kigone she-holich velo heivi* — like a case where one passes the knife in only one direction and does not bring it back. That is, one uses a sufficiently long knife to traverse the entire width of the animal's throat in a single pass, without reversing direction.

### Multiple Bumps

While a single one-directional bump at the heel of the blade may theoretically be permissible under these narrow conditions, the Gemara rules that multiple such bumps render the knife unfit regardless: *sheyesh bah pgimos harbe, kidon kimagaira* — a knife with many nicks is like a saw. Even if each individual bump is of the gentler, one-directional variety, the cumulative effect of multiple bumps will weaken and eventually tear the tissue. The combination of repeated weakening impacts means the skin will be torn even if no single bump would suffice on its own.

---

## Knife Defect Types

### Ogeres Type

Rava now presents a formal classification of three types of knife characteristics. The first is the *ogeres* — a gathering bump. Rashi explains that the name derives from the image of skin gathering into a crevice. This denotes a nick that is V-shaped, with a rise on both sides. *lo yishchot v'im shachat shchitah p'sula* — one may not shecht with such a knife, and if one did so, the shechita is invalid even after the fact.

### Mesuchsachet Type

The second type is the *mesuchsachet* — a rubbing bump, one that rises on only one side. This is the more lenient variety: *lo yishchot bah* — one should not shecht with it *le-chatchila*, for one is clearly inviting trouble. But *v'im shachat, shechitah kesheira b'di-eved* — if one did shecht with it, and the conditions described above were satisfied (a single bump, at the heel of the blade, knife traversed in one direction only), the shechita is valid after the fact.

### Mesuchsachet Questions

The Gemara records a clarificatory exchange: Rav Huna the son of Rav Nechemia said to Rav Ashi that he had reported in the name of Rava that *mesuchsachet* is invalid. But had not Rava himself stated — and this was also the ruling of a Baraita — that *mesuchsachet kesheira*? The resolution: *lo kashya, kan she-holich ve-heivi, kan she-holich velo heivi* — there is no contradiction. When Rava said it is invalid, he meant a case where the knife was passed back and forth; when he said it is valid, he meant a case where the knife passed in only one direction. The principle is precisely as discussed: on the return pass, the one-directional bump now encounters the exposed simanim from the problematic side, causing tearing.

There is also the question of whether a single nick (*niktza*) on a knife is problematic. Based on the analysis above, a single nick that is of the *mesuchsachet* type remains acceptable only under the very narrow conditions outlined — at the heel, single direction, long knife. In practice, the net result of all this analysis is that virtually any nick is disqualifying. The case of a permissible *mesuchsachet* is so hedged with conditions that it is almost theoretical.

### Oleh V'Yored

The third type is *oleh v'yored* — a gradual elevation. This describes a knife that is not perfectly straight, but whose variations in surface are gentle curves with no sharp angles or actual notches. There is nowhere for anything to catch, nowhere for the tissue to be grabbed or torn. Such a knife may be used *le-chatchila* — *oleh v'yored besakin shochet le-chatchila*. The practical image is of a hilly surface as opposed to a cliff — gradual undulation that presents no tearing risk.

### Sasa'a Knife

A further type is raised: Rav Acha the son of Rav Avya asked Rav Ashi about a knife that resembles a *sasa'a* — the fine strands of a barley plant — which seems to refer to a blade that is not perfectly smooth but whose surface roughness consists only of extremely fine, shallow irregularities, with no actual notches at all. *man yahiv lan mibishra ve'achlinan* — Rav Ashi responded that he would be the first to eat from the meat shechted with such a knife; it presents no problem whatsoever. According to the commentary, this type has finer surface variation than even *oleh v'yored*, the texture being more akin to slight roughness — as one commentator explains, one would feel it if rubbing a finger along the edge but there are no actual notches — while *oleh v'yored* involves more perceptible bumps, like gentle hills.

---

## Checking Knife

### Torah Source

The Gemara shifts to the requirement of *bdika* — checking the knife before shechita. Rav Chisda asks: *minayin l'vdikat sakin min haTorah* — from where in the Torah do we derive the requirement to check the knife? He cites a verse from Shmuel in which the phrase *ve-zavachtem bazei ve-achaltem* appears — you shall slaughter with this and eat — implying that the knife was inspected and declared fit before being used.

### Objection Resolution

The Gemara objects: *pshita* — is this not obvious? Since a nick in the knife would render the shechita invalid and the animal a treifa, of course one must check it. There is no need for a special derivation. The Gemara resolves this: the question was not about checking the knife per se, but about the requirement to show the knife to a *chacham* — a halachic authority — for inspection. That requirement is derived from the verse in Shmuel.

### Rabbinic Authority

The Gemara then cites Rabbi Yochanan: *lo amru le-harot sakin le-chacham ela mipnei kvodo shel chacham* — the requirement to show the knife to a sage was instituted not as a strict halakhic necessity but as a way of honoring the sage. Accordingly, this requirement is only rabbinic in force, and the verse from Shmuel serves as an *asmachta b'alma* — a support or allusion in the biblical text, rather than a true Torah-level derivation.

### Regional Methods

Different regions developed different methods for checking the knife. In the West — Eretz Yisrael — *badki lei b'shimsha*: they would check using sunlight, examining the knife against the sun, perhaps using the shadow to detect any deviation from straightness, as contrast makes irregularities more visible. In Nehardea, *badki lei b'maya* — they used water. Rashi offers two explanations: one involves drawing the edge of the knife across the water surface and observing any disruption in the flow; the other involves placing a drop of water on the blade and watching whether the drop descends in a straight line or hesitates at a nick. Rav Sheshet — who was blind — checked the knife *b'reish lishna*, with the tip of his tongue, an extraordinarily sensitive instrument capable of detecting the slightest nick, though obviously requiring great care. Rav Acha bar Yaakov used *chut ha-sa'arah* — a strand of hair — held perpendicular to the edge and drawn across it, which would catch on any imperfection.

### Sura Approach

In Sura, the approach was different: *bisra achla bisra livdika* — the knife is for cutting meat, so test it with meat. This means using the fingertip — a practical and appropriately calibrated test, since the shechita is performed on meat and the test need not be more sensitive than the task. A nick detectable only by tongue or hair might not be significant enough to affect the actual shechita.

---

## Flesh & Nail Protocol

### Rav Pappa Rule

Rav Pappa ruled: *tzricha bdika a-bisra v'atufra* — the knife requires checking both with the flesh of the finger and on the fingernail. Some add: *v'atlata ruchta* — and on three sides, meaning not only the very cutting edge itself, but also the two angled faces where the blade is sharpened down toward the edge.

### Sides Clarification

This formulation was the subject of a clarificatory exchange. Ravina reported to Rav Ashi that Rav Sama the son of Rav Mesharshiya had cited Rav Ashi himself as requiring the check on the flesh, the nail, and all three sides.
