Rav Ashi confirmed that he required testing on the flesh and the nail, but denied having stated the requirement for all three sides.

An alternate version of the exchange is also recorded: some say Rav Ashi confirmed all three elements — flesh, nail, and three sides — but denied that he had stated this in the name of Rava; it was his own ruling.

### Rav Ashi Approval

Practical confirmation of the three-part protocol came when someone brought a knife before Rav Ashi for inspection. Rav Ashi handed it to Rav Acha the son of Rava and instructed him to check it. Rav Acha checked it on the fingernail, on the flesh of the finger, and on all three sides. Rav Ashi responded: *yiasher koach* — well done — and confirmed that this is exactly what Rav Kahana ruled as well.

### Rav Yemar Dissent

Rav Yemar disagreed. He held that the fingernail and the flesh are required, but the three sides are not — only the actual cutting edge need be tested, not the angled faces on either side.

### Hot Knife Proof

Rav Yemar's position draws on a ruling of Rav Zeira in the name of Shmuel: *liben sakkina ve-shachat bah shechitatah kesherah* — if one heated a knife until it was white hot and shechted with it, the shechita is valid, because *she-chidudah kodem le-libunah* — the sharpness of the blade precedes the burning, so the cut is made by the edge before the heat can cause damage. A difficulty was raised: even if the initial cut is made by the sharpness, as the blade travels through the throat the white-hot sides of the blade will still burn the tissue — why is this not a concern? The answer: *beit ha-shechitah mirvach ravach* — as the blade cuts through the throat, the incision opens up, so the sides of the blade are not in contact with the surrounding tissue. Applying this to the question of checking three sides: if the sides of the blade are not in contact with anything during the shechita, there is no need to check them — only the cutting edge itself matters.

Despite this reasoning, Rashi notes that the accepted practice is to check the sides as well, not only the primary edge.

### Nail Purpose

One might ask: why test the knife on the fingernail in addition to the flesh? If the principle from Sura is that the knife should be tested in the same medium in which it will be used — i.e., meat — why add the harder surface of the fingernail? Tosafot explains: the knife must also cut through the trachea, which is considerably harder than flesh. The fingernail serves as a proxy for the hardness of the trachea. Testing the knife on the fingernail therefore evaluates whether the blade will perform correctly when it reaches and cuts through the hard cartilaginous tissue of the trachea, ensuring that no nick will cause tearing at that critical juncture.

---

---

# Hullin 18

## Three Types of Nicks

### Opening & Rav Huna

Daf 18 begins at the bottom of 17b, where the Gemara turns to the real details of the act of shechita itself. The opening statement is that of Rav Huna bar Kattina, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

### Three Pegimot Categories

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish declares: *shalosh pegimot hen* — there are three types of nicks that are related to one another in terms of what defines a nick and where a nick constitutes a halachic problem.

The first is *pegimat etzem bapesach* — a nick in a bone on Pesach. The Torah states *kol etzem lo tishberu vo*, that no bone may be broken. Surprisingly, one might have thought that breaking a bone meant snapping it in two; in fact, even nicking a bone constitutes a violation of this prohibition. The second is *pegimat ozen babechor* — a nick in the ear of a bechor, which constitutes a mum and thereby permits the animal to be slaughtered and eaten outside the Beit Hamikdash. The ear is mentioned because it appears first in the list of mumim applicable to a bechor. The third is *pegimat mum bekodashim* — a nick that creates a blemish in kodashim, rendering the animal unfit to be brought as a korban and requiring a transfer of kedusha.

A fourth opinion is then introduced: *veRav Chisda amar af pegimat sakkin* — Rav Chisda adds that a nick in a knife is equally governed by the same standard. The Gemara notes that the earlier tanna did not include the knife because that discussion pertained to non-kodashim contexts. The essential point of grouping all of these together is not merely that nicks are problematic in various domains, but that they all share the same definition of what constitutes a nick: *vechulam pegimatan kedei pegimat hamizbe'ach* — in every case, the standard is that of the nick of the altar.

### Rashi on Bechor vs. Koda…

One might ask why bechor and kodashim are listed separately, given that a bechor is itself a type of sacrifice. Rashi offers two reasons. First, bechorot are exclusively male, and there are certain mumim — particularly in the genital area — that apply only to females and are therefore only relevant to kodashim. Second, and more significantly, Rashi addresses what might have been a *hava amina*: one might have thought that even if a blemish disqualifies an animal from being brought as a korban, a greater degree of blemish might be required before a bechor may actually be slaughtered and eaten outside the Beit Hamikdash. Unlike kodashim, where a blemished animal can have its kedusha transferred and a replacement korban brought, a bechor with a mum is simply slaughtered outside the Beit Hamikdash — and one might have imagined that to reach that stage requires a more severe blemish. The answer is that this is not the case, and that is precisely why both bechor and kodashim are stated: to exclude the possibility of any such intermediate threshold.

### Restatement of Three Nic…

The common thread uniting all of these nicks — the bone on Pesach, the ear of the bechor, the blemish in kodashim, and the nick in a knife — is that their shared definition derives from the standard of the altar: *kedei shetachgor bah tziporen*, that the nick is of sufficient size that a fingernail running across it would catch. That is the operative measure in every one of these contexts.

---

## Nick Definition & Altar

### Altar Nick Definition

Having established that the standard for all these nicks is that of the altar, the Gemara now asks: *kama pegimat hamizbe'ach* — what exactly is that standard? The answer given is *kedei shetachgor bah tziporen* — that if you run your finger across it, it gets caught. This is precisely the standard that had been discussed in connection with knives used for shechita: any nick sufficient to catch a fingernail is considered a nick in the altar, and thereby constitutes the operative measure for all related domains.

### Baraita: Tefach vs. Keza…

The Gemara raises a challenge from a Baraita. The Torah states *avanim shelemot tivneh et mizbach Hashem Elokecha* — the altar must be built of whole stones — and *lo tanif aleihem barzel* — no iron tool may be used upon them. Given the standard of *shetachgor bah tziporen*, the question becomes: how large must a nick in the altar actually be? Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says a nick must be a full *tefach* to be considered a disqualifying nick; Eleazar ben Yaakov says it need only be the size of a *kezayit*.

### Plaster vs. Stones

The Gemara resolves this apparent contradiction without difficulty: *ha besida ha be'avna* — one ruling applies to the plaster and the other to the stones. The Torah's requirement of *avanim shelemot* applies specifically to the stones of the altar. With respect to those stones, even the slightest nick — sufficient to catch a fingernail — renders the stone incomplete. However, the plaster used between the stones is not subject to the Torah's requirement of *shelemot*, and therefore a nick in the plaster only becomes halachically significant when it reaches a more substantial size, whether a *tefach* or a *kezayit*.

### Tosafot's Building Quest…

Tosafot raises the obvious difficulty: how was the altar ever built to meet such a demanding standard if iron tools were forbidden? Tosafot frames the question precisely: *ve'im tomar veheich banu hamizbe'ach* — how could they build it? *ve'anna yimtze'u avanim belo pegima* — where would they find stones without any nicks? And if they were to smooth the stones with iron, there is a biblical prohibition of *lo tanif aleihem barzel*.

### Shamir & Cement Mold

Tosafot anticipates and then dismisses the popular answer involving the shamir, the legendary worm said to have the ability to cut stone without iron tools. Tosafot argues that even the shamir could not have produced a surface smooth enough that no fingernail would catch on it. A more compelling answer, which emerges from the Gemara in Zevachim 54, is that the altar was constructed not by laying individual cut stones but by pouring a mixture — essentially cement — into a mold. This method would produce a surface that, being formed by the mold, could be extremely smooth. It also raises the question of whether such a construction goes by the standards applicable to stones or to plaster in terms of how significant a nick must be.

### Tosafot's River Pebbles

Tosafot arrives at a somewhat different formulation. Citing the sugya in the perek of *eizehu mekoman*, Tosafot suggests that the altar was built using very small, smooth stones — *chalukei avanim shel nachal*, smooth river pebbles — that by their nature have no nicks, having been smoothed by the water of a riverbed. These pebbles were then held together by cement and plaster. On Tosafot's reading, one still looks at the individual stones, but since those stones are themselves perfectly smooth, the standard of *shetachgor bah tziporen* is satisfied. In practice, however, since the bulk of the surface consists of the plaster holding the stones together, only a nick of *tefach* or *kezayit* in that plaster would be problematic. This represents a realistic resolution to what would otherwise seem like an impossible standard.

---

## Butcher & Knife Display

### Rav Huna's Cherem

The Gemara continues with a ruling of Rav Huna: *hai tavcha d'lo sar sakina kamei chacham* — a butcher who does not show his knife to a sage is placed in cherem. Rashi explains that the reason is *mishum afkirootah* — because of disrespect. The word *apikoros*, as the Gemara in Sanhedrin explains, does not here mean heresy but rather refers to one who is disrespectful of authority, specifically rabbinic authority. The butcher who refuses to show his knife is acting with *chutzpah*, failing to show proper deference, and is therefore subject to this sanction.

### Rava's Deposition

Rava goes further: *maavirin lei* — one removes him from his post entirely — *umachrizinan abisreih detreifa* — and publicly announces that all of his meat should be considered treifah. This is a significantly more severe consequence.

### Reconciling Rav & Rava

The Gemara moves to reconcile these two positions: *velo peligi* — they do not actually disagree. The distinction is whether, upon examination, his knife was found to be acceptable or not. If the knife ultimately was found to be in good condition, then his only failing was a lack of deference to the sage, and for that he is placed in cherem — a serious but not permanent sanction from which he can presumably emerge through teshuvah. If, however, his knife was not in good condition, then he was not merely disrespectful but actively deceptive, attempting to conceal the fact that he was performing shechita with a defective knife. In that case, his meat is announced as treifah and he is removed from his post.

### Ravina's Extra Penalty

Ravina adds a still more severe layer. Where the knife is found to be defective — meaning not only disrespect but actual deception — one does not stop at the natural halachic consequence of declaring the meat treifah. Rather, *memarmesinan lei beparta* — one would literally drag the meat through dung — *de'afilu le'ovdei kochavim nami lo mizdaben* — to prevent him even from selling it to a non-Jew. The reasoning is twofold: not only has he produced treifah meat, but he has done so knowingly and deceptively. Accordingly, not only the obvious halachic consequence must follow, but additional punitive measures must be taken to prevent such conduct in the future.

According to Ravina's framework, then, Rava's position — deposing the butcher from his post and declaring his meat treifah — applies to the case where the butcher refused to show the knife but the knife was in fact acceptable. Even in that case, the disrespect alone warrants removing him from his post. If the knife was actually defective, Ravina would add the additional penalty of preventing any sale even to non-Jews.

### Rabbinic Authority Discu…

This raises an obvious difficulty: the case where the butcher's knife is entirely acceptable and yet he is deposed from his post and his meat publicly declared treifah — even though it is not — seems quite severe. There is an inherent tension in applying such heavy penalties purely on grounds of disrespect toward rabbinic authority, as opposed to any substantive halachic failing.

One might ask whether this is a matter of personal honor or of communal culture. The answer lies in recognizing that the culture of respecting rabbinic authority is itself a prerequisite for the effective functioning of halachic observance. The Gemara in Sanhedrin is full of cases where niduy is imposed specifically for disrespect of rabbinic authority, and the concern is not personal but systemic: if a culture develops in which a butcher feels he need not show his knife to the rav, then when rabbinic authorities attempt to enforce genuine standards — whether in kashrus or in other areas — they have no basis of authority from which to do so. This point is reinforced by historical examples where butchers who wished to evade kashrus standards did so precisely by undermining the authority of the supervising rabbi.

At the same time, the discussion has real contemporary resonance in the area of hashgacha. A community may restrict itself to a single hashgacha even where another is halachically sound, and the dynamics of rabbinic authority — and the limits on how far that authority may appropriately extend — are very much alive in this sugya. The Gemara's concern, it would seem, was genuinely about creating the conditions for halachic observance rather than about personal prestige, though the line between the two is not always easy to draw in practice.

---

## Butcher Story

### Rabba's Deposition

The Gemara now presents a narrative that crystallizes these tensions. There was a butcher who refused to show his knife to Rabba Bar Bar Chana. Rabba Bar Bar Chana, following the more severe position, placed him in cherem, removed him from his post, and announced that the meat was treifah.

### Investigation Requested

Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi subsequently came to visit Rabba Bar Bar Chana, who asked them to look into the case — *de'talu bei taflei*, because the butcher had many children dependent on him. Despite having acted as he believed he was required to act, the matter weighed on his conscience, and he asked the visiting scholars to investigate whether something could be done.

### Knife Found Acceptable

Rav Ashi examined the knife and found it to be acceptable — *ve'nimtzas yafa*. He thereupon declared the shechita kosher and permitted the butcher to return to work. Mar Zutra then challenged Rav Ashi: was he not concerned for the elder — *velo leichush Mar l'Saba* — meaning that by taking the more lenient position he was effectively overriding the ruling of Rabba Bar Bar Chana, who had proceeded on the assumption that the butcher should be deposed regardless of the knife's quality?

### Rav Ashi's Justification

Rav Ashi replied: *shlichutei avdinan* — I am carrying out his instructions. Rabba Bar Bar Chana himself had asked them to find a way to help this man. Rav Ashi found that the knife was acceptable and could therefore rely on the position that, where the knife is in fact good, the appropriate response is cherem rather than deposition from his post — and on that basis he reinstated him.

### Niduy vs. Cherem

A note on terminology: the term *cherem* has been used loosely throughout this discussion. In practice, what is more typically invoked in cases of disrespect toward rabbinic authority is *niduy* — a lighter form of social and personal sanction — rather than full *cherem*. Niduy involves certain practices that the individual must adopt, resembling in certain respects the practices of aveilus, but is less focused on communal exclusion. It is also not a permanent state; if the person does teshuvah, it can be lifted.

### Authority & Enforcement

This narrative is difficult to read in isolation from all the factors it leaves unspecified. The personal dimensions — the relationship between a specific butcher and a specific rabbi, the presence of dependent children, the involvement of additional rabbinic figures — all complicate any attempt to draw clean conclusions. What is clear is that the story illustrates the Gemara's sensitivity to the severity of these penalties and the need for proportionality. On the other side of the ledger, the history of kashrus enforcement is replete with cases in which the meat industry sought to evade oversight, and in which the absence of a culture of rabbinic deference enabled real halachic violations to persist undetected. A mashgiach who is not respected has very little ability to ensure compliance even when the stakes are genuinely matters of kashrus.

---

## Teeth & Fingernails

### Detached Tools Valid

The Gemara returns to the Mishna's discussion of the tools with which shechita may be performed. Raba bar Rav Huna states that a detached tooth — *sheit shluchos* — and a detached fingernail — *tziporen tlushah* — may be used for shechita, and indeed may be used *lechatchila*, at the outset. The logic is straightforward: one may use a rock or a reed for shechita, and these items, once detached, are no different in principle.

### Mishna: Prohibition

The Mishna, however, states that a harvest sickle, a saw, teeth, and a fingernail may not be used for shechita — *mipnei shehein chonkin* — because they cause the animal to choke rather than cut cleanly. The various items listed are serrated and produce a choking effect rather than the clean incision required.

### Attached vs. Detached

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction. With respect to the tooth: *shein ashein lo kashya, ha b'chada ha b'tartei*. The Mishna uses the plural *shinayim* — teeth. If two attached teeth are used together, the gap between them creates a serrated, uneven surface even if each individual tooth has been smoothed. With respect to the fingernail: *tziporen atziporen lo kashya, ha bitlusha ha bimchuberet* — the distinction is between a detached nail and an attached one. A detached fingernail may be used; an attached one presents the same problem as an implement attached to the ground — which, per the principle articulated by Rebbi that only a detached implement is valid, would render the shechita invalid.

---

## Harvest Sickle Debate

### Sickle Direction Debate

The Mishna presents a case involving a harvest sickle with serrated teeth. The question is: what is the halacha if shechita is performed with this sickle moving in its normal direction — *b'derech halichatah*? Beis Shammai invalidates such a shechita; Beis Hillel permits it. This appears at first to contradict the earlier Mishna, which listed a harvest sickle among the prohibited implements.

### Rashi on Angle

Rashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that this involves a very particular type of serration: teeth that lie at such a shallow angle to the cutting surface that when the knife moves in the direction aligned with the serrations, the entire surface is effectively smooth. The serrations only create a cutting or snagging effect when the motion goes against them — much as a surface that is completely smooth in one direction can be highly abrasive in the other. On this reading, the earlier Mishna's prohibition addressed serrations that create a problematic surface regardless of direction, while this Mishna addresses a case where the direction of movement renders the serrations inert.

### Smoothed Teeth

The Mishna adds that if the teeth of the sickle are smoothed entirely — *ve'im hechliku shineha* — then it is equivalent to a knife — *harei hi k'sakin* — and all would agree that shechita performed with it is valid, presumably even Beis Shammai.

### Neveilah Exemption Only

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yochanan, offers a restrictive reading of Beis Hillel's position: *af keshemachshirin Beis Hillel, lo hechshiru ela l'taharah midei neveilah* — even when Beis Hillel declares such a shechita valid, they only mean that the animal does not attain the status of neveilah. The meat is still forbidden for consumption. On this reading, Beis Hillel's concern was that permitting shechita in one direction might lead people to perform it in the other direction as well, where the serrations fully engage. Beis Hillel therefore issued a rabbinic prohibition against eating the meat, while declining to treat it as a full neveilah. Beis Shammai goes further, treating the animal as an actual neveilah — whether because they regard the act itself as halachically invalid, or because they extend the rabbinic prohibition to impose neveilah status as well.

### Language Analysis

Rav Ashi notes that the language of the Mishna supports this reading: the Mishna uses *poslin* and *machshirin* — invalidate and validate — rather than *osrin* and *matirin* — forbid and permit. This suggests that the debate concerns not the permissibility of eating the meat but some more ritual dimension. The language of *pasul* and *kasher* refers to a status rather than a straightforward prohibition, pointing toward a discussion of neveilah for purposes of tumah rather than eating.

### Rejection of Chiya

The Gemara rejects Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's position. The Gemara points out that if the debate were truly about tumah and tahara, the Mishna should have used the terms *mitamin* and *mitaharin* — declares tamei and declares tahor. Since it does not, the language of *poslin* and *machshirin* is simply equivalent to *osrin* and *matirin*, referring to the act of shechita itself and its consequence for permissibility of the meat. On the Gemara's rejection, Beis Hillel holds that the shechita is actually valid and the meat is genuinely permitted. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's motivation for his reading was apparently the difficulty of permitting any serrated implement at all, given the emphasis in the prior discussion on avoiding serrations — but in the end his position is rejected, and Beis Hillel's ruling is that the shechita is fully *kasher lechatchila*.

---

## Shechita Location

### Trachea Anatomy

Having concluded the discussion of the implements used for shechita, the Gemara turns to the question of where in the neck the shechita must be performed. The trachea — *kanah* — has a distinctive anatomical structure: it is surrounded by cartilaginous rings that are visible and palpable. Near the top there is a large ring — a substantial structure beneath which the epiglottis sits — and beneath it are a series of smaller individual rings that do not extend entirely around the circumference of the trachea. The valid zone for shechita extends from somewhere within this large top structure all the way down to the lungs.

### Kosher Shechita Area

The Mishna addresses the case of shechita performed within the top ring. The kosher zone for shechita extends from this large top ring down to the lungs. The discussion that follows focuses on shechita performed at the very upper limit of this zone, and what happens when the cutting motion reaches or crosses that boundary.

### Rashi: Top Ring

Rashi reads the Mishna's phrase *hashocheit mitoch hataba'at* — shechita within the ring — as referring specifically to this large top ring. The significance of this reading becomes clear in the context of the psul known as *hagrama*.

---

## Hagrama Problem

### Tanna Kamma Position

The psul of hagrama occurs when the knife moves outside the valid shechita zone during the act of shechita. The scenario under discussion is as follows: the shochet is performing shechita at the very top edge of the valid zone, directly at the limit of the *makom hashechita*. The question concerns what happens when the majority of the siman — the trachea — has been cut within the valid zone, but the shochet's knife then moves beyond the upper boundary before the cut is complete.

To understand what "majority" means here: the relevant measure is not the thickness of the walls of the trachea but the diameter of its hollow. One must cut through more than half the hollow of the tube. If the first fifty-one percent of this cut is performed within the valid zone and the remaining minority is completed outside it, does the shechita remain valid?

The tanna kamma holds that the entire cut is relevant: even if the majority was performed properly, finishing the cut in an invalid location constitutes hagrama and disqualifies the shechita.

### Rubo Kechulo

This dispute turns on a fundamental question about the principle of *rubo kechulo* — whether majority is treated as a complete substitute for the whole. Does the requirement of cutting the siman mean that one must cut fifty-one percent, with the remainder being irrelevant? Or does it mean that in principle the entire siman must be cut, and the rule of rov permits one to rely on the majority as though the whole were cut — meaning that what happens in the remaining minority still matters, since we are treating it as though it were the whole? If the latter, then performing the last minority improperly introduces a disqualifying factor even though the majority was done correctly.

### Rabbi Yose Position

Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda takes the lenient position: *melo chut al pnei ruba* — as long as the majority of the ring was cut within the valid zone, the shechita is valid even if the knife moved out of the valid zone for the remaining minority. He holds that once the majority is completed properly, the shechita is done, and what occurs in the last minority does not affect its validity.

### Rav & Shmuel Ruling

The Gemara records that Rav and Shmuel both rule like Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda: *halacha keRabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda*. This ruling makes shechita more manageable in practice, as the shochet need not be concerned about where the knife finishes once the majority of the siman has been cut in the valid zone. The question then arises whether this ruling of leniency applies uniformly to all the other psulim of shechita — such as shehiya and drasa — in their final minority; that question will be addressed separately.

---

## Lower Rings Shechita

### Top Ring Only

The Gemara adds a qualification: *ve'af Rabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda lo amar ela betaba'at hagedola* — even Rabbi Yose beRabbi Yehuda stated his lenient ruling only with respect to the large top ring, *ho'il umakefet et kol hakaneh* — because that ring completely encircles the trachea. With respect to the other, lower rings, his ruling does not apply.

### Rashi: Not Part Trachea

Rashi, in a manner he acknowledges is somewhat unusual, considers multiple readings of this statement. The explanation Rashi ultimately favors is that since the lower rings do not completely encircle the trachea, they are not considered part of the trachea itself. On this reading, shechita performed in one of these lower rings is as though the shochet were not cutting the trachea at all — and therefore the valid location for cutting is specifically the skin between the rings, not the ring itself. This would mean that a shochet performing shechita in one of the lower rings would have to cut between rings rather than through them — a remarkably demanding practical standard.

### Tosafot: Majority Trachea

Tosafot proposes what is arguably a more compelling reading. On Tosafot's view, the issue is not that the lower rings are not considered part of the trachea, but rather that doing the majority of a lower ring does not constitute doing the majority of the trachea. This is almost analytically self-evident: since the lower ring does not extend all the way around the trachea, cutting through the majority of the ring's arc does not translate into having cut through the majority of the trachea's hollow. Therefore, while Tosafot agrees that shechita can be performed in the lower rings, the measure of "majority" must be calculated against the trachea itself, not against the individual ring. To have a valid shechita in the lower rings, one must cut the majority of the trachea — not merely the majority of the portion of trachea covered by that ring.

There is a third reading that Rashi acknowledges as a possible reading of the Gemara — that the requirement to remain within a ring applies not just to the top ring but to any ring in which the shechita is being performed, such that the knife must not leave the ring before the cut is complete. Rashi rejects this reading both because it lacks an obvious conceptual basis and because it would make valid shechita practically very difficult to achieve. However, it does render certain passages of the Gemara more readable.

### Baraita Support

The Gemara introduces a Baraita in support of the view that shechita in the lower rings is valid. Rabbi Yosef beRabbi Yehuda says: *hashocheit bishar taba'ot* — one who performs shechita in the other rings — *af al pi she'ein makifot et kol hakaneh* — even though those rings do not entirely surround the trachea — *ho'il umakifot rov hakaneh* — since they do surround the majority of the trachea — *shechitatu keshera* — the shechita is valid. This supports Tosafot's reading: the relevant measure for the lower rings is whether the majority of the trachea is encircled — and since it is, shechita there is valid, provided the cut achieves the majority of the trachea.

The Baraita also notes: *umugremet pesulah* — hagrama is still a disqualifying psul. This means that even according to those who permit shechita in the lower rings, if the knife moves outside the valid zone during shechita, it remains disqualified.

### Chanina Testimony

Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos testified that *mugremet keshera* — hagrama is valid. This appears strikingly absolute. The resolution is that Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos holds a different definition of where the *makom hashechita* ends. He believes the valid zone extends higher than the standard position, such that what others would call hagrama — moving outside their defined upper boundary — falls within the valid zone as defined by Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos. He does maintain the psul of hagrama, but applies it at a different, higher location. Thus his testimony is not as absolute as it sounds; it represents a substantive difference in defining the upper limit of the valid shechita zone.

---

## Rabbi Zeira Story

### Zeira Eats Mugremet

When Rabbi Zeira made aliyah to Eretz Yisrael, he ate meat from an animal whose shechita would have been considered *mugremet* — and therefore invalid — according to the ruling of Rav and Shmuel. The practice in Eretz Yisrael was not to treat such shechita as invalid, and Rabbi Zeira accordingly ate it there without concern.

### Zeira Doubts Report

The people of Eretz Yisrael challenged him: was he not from the community of Rav and Shmuel? How could he eat this meat? Rabbi Zeira replied: *man amrah?* — who actually said that Rav and Shmuel took this position? The tradition had been reported by Yosef bar Chiya — that is, Rav Yosef — but Rabbi Zeira questioned whether Rav Yosef had really received this directly from Rav and Shmuel, implying that he may have simply heard it circulating and not from a direct transmission. Rabbi Zeira's implication was that he had never been fully persuaded that Rav and Shmuel actually said this, and therefore had never adopted it as a firm ruling — which would mean he may not have been strictly following this position even when he was in Bavel.

### Yosef Defends Source

Rav Yosef heard that his transmission was being questioned and was deeply offended: *ana mi-chulei alma gamina?* — did he receive his traditions from people on the street? He declared: *ana mi-Rav Yehuda gamirna* — he received this directly from Rav Yehuda, who was himself a student of Rav and Shmuel. Furthermore, Rav Yehuda was so precise in his traditions that even when he had a doubt as to which of his teachers had said something, he recorded that doubt explicitly, as evidenced by the formula: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba — *safek mishmei de-Rav safek mishmei de-Shmuel* — possibly in the name of Rav and possibly in the name of Shmuel. The very fact that Rav Yehuda would record such uncertainty demonstrates the meticulousness of his transmission, and therefore to suggest that his report of Rav and Shmuel's position was unreliable was deeply insulting.

### Bechor Blemish Ruling

The reason this chain of tradition is cited at all is parenthetical: it was Rav Yehuda's practice to record exactly what he heard and from whom, and the example cited — *shlosha matirin et ha-bechor be-makom she-ein mumche* — is incidental to establishing that practice. The ruling itself is that if there is no qualified expert available to examine a blemish on a bechor, three ordinary people may constitute a beit din to rule on the matter, even without the specialized expertise normally required.

---

## Local Custom Rules

### Custom Question

Having established that Rav and Shmuel did in fact rule that mugremet shechita is invalid, the Gemara addresses why Rabbi Zeira felt free to eat such meat in Eretz Yisrael. The general principle is that when traveling, one must observe *chumrei hamakom sheyatza misham* — the stringencies of the place one left — *vechumrei hamakom shehalach l'sham* — and the stringencies of the place one has arrived. If Rabbi Zeira had followed the ruling of Rav and Shmuel in Bavel, why did he not maintain that stringency in Eretz Yisrael?

### Abaye's Distinction

Abaye answers that the rule of following the stringencies of both one's place of origin and one's destination applies only to travel within the same country — from one part of Bavel to another, or from one part of Eretz Yisrael to another — or alternatively even when traveling from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel.

### Bavel to Israel

However, when traveling from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael, a different principle applies: *keivan d'anan kaifinan lehu avdinan kevataiyu* — since we, the Babylonians, are subservient to them, when we are in Eretz Yisrael we follow their practices entirely. This is a remarkable statement to appear in the Bavli: Bavel acknowledges that Eretz Yisrael constitutes the ultimate authority, and when a Babylonian is in Eretz Yisrael he does not retain his Babylonian practices but fully adopts those of Eretz Yisrael.

### Ashi's Condition

Rav Ashi qualifies this ruling: even the principle that one retains the practices of one's place of origin applies only *heicha d'da'ato lachazor* — where the person intends to return. If one plans to return to Bavel, one retains Babylonian practices even while in Eretz Yisrael. But if one does not intend to return, one fully adopts the practices of wherever one has gone.

### Zeira's Permanent Move

In the case of Rabbi Zeira, *ein da'ato lachazor* — he did not intend to return to Bavel. Rabbi Zeira made aliyah permanently and settled in Eretz Yisrael. Accordingly, even on Rav Ashi's more qualified formulation, Rabbi Zeira was fully entitled to adopt the practices of Eretz Yisrael and to eat the mugremet meat without concern for the ruling of Rav and Shmuel.

---

## Authority Relationship

### Eretz Yisrael Authority

This sugya raises the broader question of the relationship between the halachic authority of Eretz Yisrael and that of Bavel. There are other Gemaras that appear to point in the opposite direction, suggesting that Bavel had greater practical authority — including the authority to enforce its rulings — owing to the greater political support accorded to Jewish leadership by the Babylonian Sassanian government. Tosafot addresses this tension by drawing a distinction between political authority and ultimate religious authority. While it may be true that Babylonian Jewish leadership had greater capacity to enforce its decisions and was backed by a more powerful governmental structure, ultimate religious authority remained in Eretz Yisrael.

### Calendar & Semichah

The clearest expression of Eretz Yisrael's primacy was its exclusive jurisdiction over *kiddush hachodesh* — the sanctification of the new month and the determination of the calendar. Rashi also mentions the question of semichah and the capacity to adjudicate *knasot* — monetary penalties — both of which remained functions of the Eretz Yisrael rabbinic establishment. As long as these critical religious functions were centered in Eretz Yisrael, it retained ultimate religious authority even if Bavel had greater political leverage.

### Geonic Period Shift

The decisive shift came in the Geonic period. A major dispute arose between the Babylonian and Eretz Yisrael Geonim over the calendar — specifically, over when Rosh Hashanah fell. The Eretz Yisrael Geonim asserted their primacy as the ultimate religious authority. The Babylonian Geonim countered that while Eretz Yisrael's authority might be presumed when all other things are equal, the greater scholarship concentrated in Bavel meant that Babylonian authority prevailed. In the end, the Babylonian position won out — not only because of the argument on its merits, but because the center of gravity of the entire Jewish world had shifted decisively to Bavel. The Babylonian Geonim's ruling on Rosh Chodesh prevailed, and this represented the *makeh b'patish* — the decisive final blow — that settled the question of Bavel's authority over Eretz Yisrael.

### Why Bavli Authority

This historical development has direct bearing on the canonical authority of the Bavli over the Yerushalmi. The reason we follow the Babylonian Talmud, and why Daf Yomi studies the Bavli, is rooted in this same historical process: the shift of communal and scholarly gravity to Bavel during the Geonic period ultimately established the Bavli as the authoritative halachic document for the Jewish world.

---

## Halachic Pluralism

### Mechuza Opinion

Abaye reports to Rav Yosef that the rabbis who came from Mechuza — a Jewish community in Bavel — say in the name of Rav Zeira, citing Rav Nachman, that *mugremet keshera* — mugremet shechita is kosher. This is striking, because it means that even within Bavel itself, in Mechuza, the practice was to permit what Rav and Shmuel had ruled impermissible. The question thus arises not only as a dispute between Bavel and Eretz Yisrael, but as a disagreement among communities within Bavel itself.

### Nahara Nahara

Rav Yosef responds with the celebrated phrase: *nahara nahara u-pashtei* — every river and its tributaries. This phrase encapsulates a fundamental principle of halachic pluralism.

### Regional Pluralism

Rashi explains the phrase with a vivid image: even one river, as it branches off into tributaries, may have cold water in one place and warm water in another, salty water here and fresh water there. The same river flows differently in different channels. So too, within a single broad community or even a single region, different communities may legitimately maintain different practices. Even within Bavel, some communities ruled that mugremet was invalid and some ruled that it was valid, and Rav Yosef's response is not that one side is simply wrong but that each community's practice follows its own established course.

### Conclusion

The sugya concludes, then, with a recognition of legitimate halachic pluralism — *nahara nahara u-pashtei* — operating not only between Eretz Yisrael and Bavel, but among communities within Bavel itself. The specific halachic question that generated this entire discussion — whether shechita that is mugremet, whether understood as cutting outside the large top ring or as cutting only the majority of a lower ring rather than the majority of the trachea, is valid — finds different answers in different communities, and the Gemara's response is not to adjudicate between them definitively but to affirm that each community follows its own established practice, as each river runs its own course.

---

---

# Hullin 19

## Reish Lakish & Hagrama

### Reish Lakish Ruling

On Daf 19a the Gemara continues its discussion of the practical parameters of שחיטה, with a particular focus on the upper boundary of the valid shechita zone and the problem of הגרמה — moving the knife above the top cartilage ring of the trachea. The preceding sugya had established that Rav and Shmuel objected to shechita in the ring itself, preferring the spaces between the rings, while others disagreed, and the discussion concluded with the celebrated principle of נהרא נהרא ופשטיה — every river follows its own course — acknowledging that differing local practices all draw from the same halachic source.

The Gemara now introduces the position of רבי שמעון בן לקיש. Reish Lakish ruled that the shechita is valid even if performed בחודא דכובעא — at the very tip of the hat. The anatomical image at work here is of the upper portion of the trachea, which, when viewed from the side, resembles a hat with a rising slope and a tip at the very top. Reish Lakish permitted shechita even at that uppermost point, well above the topmost ring. This position is framed against the background of רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס, whose opinion — as the Gemara will later develop — was that הגרמה presents no problem, meaning not that there is no upper limit whatsoever, but that the valid zone extends considerably higher than the other tannaitic opinions allow. The question driving much of this portion of the sugya is precisely how far upward that zone extends, and whether the fleshy, muscular area just below the tip is included or excluded.

### R. Yochanan Objects

Rabbi Yochanan objected to Reish Lakish's position, dismissing it with the word גיסא גיסא — too much, too far. Even granting that shechita above the top ring is permissible, the very tip of the hat is excessive. Rav Papa in the name of Rava provides the technical explanation: פגע בחיטי טרפה — if one encounters the strings, the muscular or ligamentous strands in that upper zone, the shechita is a טרפה. The concern, in other words, is not merely elevation in a general sense, but specifically whether the knife reaches into or above this band of fibrous tissue that sits just beneath the tip of the hat.

### Pagah Debate

The Gemara raises the question: what precisely does פגע mean in this context? Is it פגע ונגע בהן — that you actually touch and cut through the strings, as suggested by the verse וַיִּפְגַּע בּוֹ וַיָּמָת, which implies physical contact and impact? Or is it פגע ולא נגע — that you merely encounter the area without making contact, analogous to וַיִּפְגְּעוּ בוֹ מַלְאֲכֵי אֱלֹהִים, where the angels of God met Jacob without necessarily touching him? The halachic stakes of this question are whether the stringy area itself is included in the kosher zone or whether only cutting above that zone without touching it renders the shechita invalid.

### Shiyur B'Chite

An authoritative tradition is then transmitted in multiple chains: שיור בחיטי כשרה — if one leaves some of the strings remaining, it is kosher. This means that cutting through that muscular zone is permissible as long as one does not cut above it entirely. The tradition is confirmed by Rav Papa in the name of Rava, corroborated by Rav Meimar bar Mar Yenuka who heard the same ruling from Rav Chiya the son of Rav Avya, and further attested in a report that Ravina told Rav Ashi: Rav Sheman mi-Suvra reported that Mar Zutra came to their locale and expounded publicly that שיור בחיטי כשרה. This convergence of traditions reinforces the ruling. Mar bar Rav Ashi, however, states the matter in a formulation that Tosafot's reading presents as: פגע בחיטי כשרה שיור בחיטי טרפה — if the knife encounters the strings and cuts through them, it is kosher; if one leaves the entire string area above, having cut above it, it is a טרפה. The version of Rashi reverses the girsa, but following Tosafot, the principle is that penetrating into that muscular zone is the lower threshold of acceptable practice, while remaining entirely above it crosses into invalidity.

### Hilchata Ruling

The Gemara delivers its ruling: והלכתא משיפוע כובע ולמטה כשרה — the halacha is that shechita is kosher only from the slanting of the cap downward, and this is consistent with the principle of שיור בחיטי — that one must at minimum cut through that stringy zone below the tip. The top of the cap, where Reish Lakish permitted shechita, is excluded. The practical upshot is that while the position of רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס permits a substantially larger zone than the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda who limit one to the top ring and below, even that expanded zone does not reach all the way to the very tip of the anatomical structure. Shechita begins to be valid only from the point where the hat begins to slope.

## Rav Nachman

### RN Allows Cap

The Gemara then records: רב נחמן אכשר משיפוע כובע ולמטה — Rav Nachman permitted shechita from the angling of the cap downward, which is the same ruling just delivered as the halacha. One might wonder why the editor placed the final halachic ruling before Rav Nachman's statement, but the substance of their positions is identical.

### Fitting Opinions

Rav Chanan bar Rav Kitina challenged Rav Nachman: כמאן — like whom? This position, permitting the entire structure above the top ring, does not align with either of the two tannaitic positions in the Mishnah. Neither the Rabbis nor Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda would sanction shechita so high up, since both of their debates concern the top ring itself, and anything above that ring — which is this entire structure — they consider הגרמה.

### Tradition Defense

Rav Nachman responded with the celebrated declaration: אנא לא חילק ידענא ולא בילק ידענא אנא שמעתא ידענא — I know neither chilek nor bilek, I know my tradition. As Rashi explains, after entertaining the possibility that chilek referred to the Rabbis and bilek to Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda based on the connotations of those roots, he ultimately concludes that these are simply idiomatic expressions akin to "I don't know Joe, I don't know Schmoe" — I am not going to resolve the tannaitic dispute, I am simply transmitting what I received. And what he received, passed through Rabbi Chiya bar Zavda who said it in the name of Rabbi Chanina, and also transmitted as Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi said it in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, is: משיפוע כובע ולמטה כשרה — from the slanting of the cap downward it is kosher.

### Fitting Amoraim

The Gemara then proceeds to integrate the amoraic tradition with the tannaitic framework through the voice of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi himself: מוגרמת דרבנן כשרה לרבי יוסי ברבי יהודה — what the Rabbis define as invalid הגרמה is kosher according to Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda. And what even Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda considers invalid — שחיטה conducted entirely above the top ring — is kosher according to Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus. The Gemara objects: פשיטא, this is obvious! The response is that one might have assumed that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, who rejects הגרמה, was only rejecting the Rabbis' definition of הגרמה, not extending beyond Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's position. The Gemara teaches that he goes further than all of them — his rejection of הגרמה encompasses every definition of that disqualification that any tanna articulates.

A further objection is raised: perhaps Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus indeed goes only as far as Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda? The Gemara answers: if so, when the Mishnah reported that Rabbi Yose bar Chanina testified regarding הגרמה and repeated that term, it would have said that he testified on "it" — meaning specifically the case of הגרמה as defined by one particular opinion. The use of הגרמה in a general sense implies that he dismissed every tanna's definition of הגרמה, giving a far wider zone for valid shechita than anyone else. Thus the position from the slanting of the cap downward corresponds to following Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, who is the most lenient of the tannaim on this question.

## Majority Debate

### Majority Principle

The Gemara now shifts from anatomical location to a more abstract conceptual question. Rav Huna said in the name of Rav Assi: מחלוקת בששחט שני שליש והגרים שליש — the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda concerns the case where one has already shechted the first two-thirds of the trachea correctly and then, for the final third, moved the knife above the valid zone. The question is whether what occurs after the valid majority of the cut has been completed can invalidate the shechita retroactively.

It is important to remember that the measurement here is depth — how far through the hollow of the trachea the knife penetrates — not the linear length of the stroke. The שחיטה is halachically defined as cutting through the majority of the inner hollow of the trachea, and so the debate is framed in terms of what portion of that hollow was cut correctly.

### Rabbis Whole Act

The Rabbis hold: כולי שחיטה בעינן בטבעת גדולה — we require that the entire act of shechita be performed within the proper zone. Although it is true that performing the majority of the trachea's depth suffices to render the animal halachically slaughtered, if one is going to perform the entire act, every part of that act must be done correctly. Doing the majority correctly and then moving into the disqualified zone taints the shechita.

### RY Majority Stands

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda applies the principle of רוב ככולו — the majority is treated as the whole. Once the majority of the trachea has been cut through a valid act of shechita, the shechita is complete and whatever occurs afterward is legally irrelevant. The conceptual question underlying this debate, which has broader application across multiple פסולי שחיטה such as שהייה and דרסה, is whether the principle of "majority suffices" means that majority is all that is required — making everything after the majority legally invisible — or whether it means that majority serves as a stand-in for the whole, in which case if the whole thing is being done, the entirety of it must be performed correctly.

### Two-Thirds Good

This framing allows for the following resolution: in the case where the first two-thirds were done correctly and the final third was too high, that is the case of their debate. But if one considers the reverse scenario — beginning incorrectly — the analysis shifts entirely.

### First Third Bad

If the first third was too high and the final two-thirds were done correctly, דברי הכל פסול — everyone agrees it is invalid.

### Nafakat Chayuta

The reason is: דכי נפיק חיותא בעינן רוב בשחיטה וליכא — when the life-force of the animal departs, meaning at the moment when the majority of the trachea has been severed, we require that the majority have been cut through a valid act of shechita, and here it was not. When the knife reached the fifty-one percent mark — the point at which the animal's חיות leaves — half of the trachea had been cut through invalid הגרמה and half through valid shechita. The majority of the trachea had not been cut correctly at that critical moment, and so the shechita is universally invalid. The entire dispute, on this reading, is confined to the case where the majority was already done correctly and only the final portion was deficient.

## Chisda Challenge

### Reverse Case

Rav Chisda challenges this framing directly: אדרבה, say the opposite. Perhaps the debate between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda concerns precisely the case where the first third was incorrect and the last two-thirds were done correctly — and it is the other case, where the first two-thirds were correct and the last third was not, that is universally agreed upon.

### Hole Analogy

According to Rav Chisda's reversal, Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda would say that beginning incorrectly is valid, and his reasoning is: מידי דהוי אחצי קנה פגום — it is analogous to a case where the trachea had a pre-existing natural injury occupying half its width. The halacha, as we will encounter, is that while small holes in the trachea generally render an animal a טרפה, the trachea is an organ that can sustain a natural cut of up to half its circumference without becoming a טרפה. If such a natural injury exists, and the shochet then cuts the remaining fraction needed to cross the fifty-one percent threshold, that constitutes a valid shechita — even though the shochet performed only a small portion of the cutting. The rationale is that the existing opening is incorporated into the act of shechita, redefining the trachea's remaining intact tissue as the relevant measure. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda applies the same logic to the case where the first third was cut above the valid zone: that invalid portion is comparable to the pre-existing hole, and the valid cutting of the remaining two-thirds, which does cross the majority threshold in the correct zone, suffices.

### Right Place Cut

The Rabbis disagree and draw a crucial distinction: התם מקום שחיטה — there, in the case of the natural pre-existing hole, the cut exists in the correct zone where shechita must take place. Even though the shochet only contributed the final increment, the majority of what was severed lies within the valid zone. הכא לאו מקום שחיטה — here, however, when the first portion of the cut was made above the valid zone, the cut in the invalid zone does not count. When the knife reaches the fifty-one percent depth of the trachea, the right zone has not yet had the majority of its width severed — only half of the correct area has been cut. The principle the Rabbis assert is not merely that the majority of the trachea must be cut, but that the majority of the trachea must be cut correctly, meaning in the right place. Starting above the zone and finishing below it leaves the valid zone only partially incised even at the moment the fifty-one percent depth is crossed.

Under Rav Chisda's reversal, it would follow that if one did the first two-thirds correctly and the final third too high, everyone would agree it is valid — since the principle of רובו של אחד כמוהו, the majority of a סימן counts as the whole, would mean we disregard entirely what happened after the majority was correctly performed.

## Rov Concept

### Part of Day

This conceptual divide — whether "majority suffices" means majority is the complete requirement or merely a substitute for the whole — has broad implications across halacha. An instructive parallel is the principle of מקצת היום ככולו, part of a day counts as a whole day. Consider the practical application in the laws of נידה: since women today are treated with the stringency of a זבה, who must count seven clean days, the beginning of the seventh day can halachically count as though the day is complete. A woman could therefore immerse in the mikvah at the beginning of the seventh day. Yet the practice is to wait until nightfall. The reason is that if she immerses during the day and then sees blood later that same day, the immersion is retroactively nullified — since the day did not in fact end cleanly, the beginning of the day never counted. This is a precise analogue to the question here: does the part-counting-as-whole work absolutely, rendering subsequent events irrelevant, or does it remain provisional and subject to invalidation by what follows?

### Majority Exclusive?

Rav Yosef raises a pointed question regarding Rav Chisda's reversal and the conclusion that if the first two-thirds were done correctly everyone would agree it is valid based on the principle of רובו של אחד כמוהו. מאן לימא לן דהוא רובא דהתם לרבי יוסי בר יהודה קתני לה — who says that this ruling about majority is not exclusively the position of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda? Perhaps it is only Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda who says that once the majority is done we disregard what follows, and the Rabbis would say we continue to care about the entirety of the act.

### Shechita Debate

Abaye responds: אטו כל רובי דאמר רבי יוסי בר יהודה קתני להו — does every invocation of majority throughout Shas reflect only Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda's position? The principle of majority is a broad and fundamental principle of halachic reasoning applied across countless contexts. The rejoinder is: אנא רובי דשחיטה קאמינא — I am speaking specifically about majority within the domain of shechita. There we explicitly know that the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda debate this very question. Perhaps different areas of halacha treat the concept of majority differently, but within shechita, the dispute over how majority functions is between these two positions, and so the question of whether the Rabbis would accept the principle of disregarding post-majority deficiencies remains genuinely open.

## Lishna Achrina

### Begin Wrong

The Gemara presents a לישנא אחרינא, a second formulation of Rav Huna's statement in the name of Rav. In this version, the debate is framed from the outset as: מחלוקת שהגרים שליש ושחט שני שליש — the dispute concerns the case where the first third was performed incorrectly and the last two-thirds were performed correctly. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda says it is valid: מידי דהוה אחתיכה דפגא — analogously to a pre-existing cut in the trachea, the invalid opening in the beginning is treated as though it were a natural wound, and the valid cutting of the remainder suffices. The Rabbis say it is invalid: התם מקום שחיטה הכא לאו מקום שחיטה — there, the pre-existing wound is in the proper location; here, the initial cut was not in the proper location. In the end the valid zone was not cut through its majority even though the majority depth of the trachea was reached.

## Middle Third Case

### Good-Bad-Good

The second formulation then posits: if the first two-thirds were performed correctly and only the final third was above the zone — אבל שחט שני שליש והגרים שליש, דברי הכל כשרה — everyone agrees it is valid, because the principle of רובו של אחד כמוהו applies and we do not concern ourselves with what occurred after the majority was correctly executed.

## Lishna Achrina (II)

### First Two OK

On this reading of the second formulation, the universal agreement on the validity of the case where the first two-thirds were correct is grounded in a precise reading of the phrase רובו של אחד כמוהו. One might note that the formulation says כמוהו rather than ככולו. Possibly the דיוק is that כמוהו means that the majority counts as itself — as sufficient — rather than as a stand-in for the whole, implying that once majority is achieved, the requirement is discharged and nothing thereafter can undermine it.

## Middle Third Case (II)

### Life at Middle

A further case now presents itself: הגרים שליש ושחט שליש והגרים שליש — the first third was too high, the middle third was performed correctly, and the final third was again too high. Here only one third of the entire act of shechita was in the valid zone, and that one valid third was confined to the middle. The majority of the cutting was done incorrectly. Yet crucially, the middle of the trachea — the fifty-one percent line — was crossed during the valid portion of the cut. Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: כשרה — it is valid. The reasoning is: כי נפק חיותא בשחיטה קנפק — when the life-force of the animal departed, meaning when the knife passed the midpoint of the trachea, it was doing so through a valid act of shechita. The fact that the majority of the total cutting was performed in the wrong zone is subordinated to the fact that the critical moment — the crossing of the midpoint — occurred correctly.

### Majority Needed

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: טרפה — it is invalid. בעינן רובא בשחיטה וליכא — we require that the majority of the trachea be cut through a valid act of shechita, and here it was not. Only one-third of the trachea was cut correctly. The crossing of the midpoint alone is insufficient; what matters is not the midpoint but the majority of the trachea's depth, and most of that depth was severed in the wrong zone.

### Bad-Good-Bad

The Gemara then presents the mirror image of this case: שחט שליש והגרים שליש ושחט שליש — the first third was performed correctly, the middle third was above the zone, and the last third was performed correctly again. Here the majority of the cutting was done correctly but the middle third — where the fifty-one percent line sits — was crossed in the wrong zone.

### RY Reverses

Rav Yehuda now says: כשרה — it is valid. He reverses his ruling from the previous case. Since for him what matters is the majority of the trachea being cut correctly, and here the majority of the cutting was indeed in the valid zone, the shechita is good. The fact that the fifty-one percent line was crossed during the invalid middle portion does not matter to him.

### RN Objects

Rav Yehuda heard that Rav Huna ruled the opposite — טרפה for this mirror case — and was offended, saying: when I say טרפה, he says כשר; when I say כשר, he says טרפה. Rav Huna acknowledged that Rav Yehuda was right to be offended: שפיר קא מקפיד. He offered two reasons. First, חדא איהו שמיע ליה מיניה דרב ואנא לא שמיע לי — in one of these cases, Rav Yehuda transmitted the ruling in the name of Rav, while Rav Huna did not; Rav Yehuda had the authority of a direct tradition from Rav. Second, ועוד האיכא רובא בשחיטה — moreover, in the mirror case where Rav Huna declared טרפה, there is actually a majority of the trachea that was cut correctly, and Rav Huna should have acknowledged that. The implied criticism is that Rav Huna's position commits him to a standard inconsistent with his first ruling.

### Don't Reverse

Rav Chisda then stepped in to warn Rav Huna: לא תהדר בך — do not reverse yourself. His caution is precise: דאם כן מסתרת לה לקמייתא — if you reverse yourself on this case, you implicitly undermine your first position. Rav Huna's first ruling, that the case with the valid middle third is כשר, was premised on the principle that כי נפק חיותא בהכשר קנפיק — when the life-force departed, meaning when the fifty-one percent line was crossed, it was crossed through a valid act of shechita. That is what makes it valid, not the majority of the cutting. Now in the mirror case, where the first and last thirds are valid and the middle is not, כי נפק חיותא באגרמה קנפיק — when the life-force departed, the fifty-one percent line was crossed during the invalid middle portion. If Rav Huna's criterion is whether the midpoint is crossed correctly, he must say this mirror case is invalid. To say otherwise would be to abandon his own rationale. Rav Chisda urges him: be consistent; do not let the pressure of Rav Yehuda's offense lead you to reverse a well-reasoned position.

## Comb Shechita

### Asked RN

When Rav Nachman visited Sura, the scholars there posed to him the question of שחט שליש והגרים שליש ושחט שליש — the first and last thirds in the valid zone, the middle third above it.

### Masreik Position

Rav Nachman responded: לאו היינו דרבי אלעזר בר מניומי — is this not the case of Rabbi Elazar bar Minyumi? Rabbi Elazar bar Minyumi had said: שחיטה העשויה כמסרק כשרה — a shechita performed like a comb, meaning with an up-and-down jagged motion, is valid. Rav Nachman applies this to the case at hand, where the knife moved in and out of the valid zone in a comb-like pattern, and rules it kosher.

### Kosher Zone Only

The Gemara challenges this analogy: ודילמא במקום שחיטה — perhaps Rabbi Elazar bar Minyumi's ruling about comb-like shechita refers only to a case where the jagged motion remained entirely within the kosher zone? That would not address a case where the knife moved outside the valid zone. The Gemara then asks: if comb-like shechita within the valid zone were the entire teaching, what would be the חידוש? One might have thought that בעינן שחיטה מפורעת — a valid shechita requires an exposed, straight, unobstructed cut, such that a jagged line within the zone where portions of the cut are recessed and not directly visible in a straight line would be invalid. The ruling teaches that this is not required, and an irregular line within the kosher zone is acceptable. But this leaves open the question of a case where portions of the cut are outside the kosher zone entirely.

## Pre-Existing Cuts

### RK Questions

Rabbi Abba was sitting in the back row while Rav Kahana sat before Rav Yehuda in a shiur. Rav Kahana posed the following sequence of questions to Rav Yehuda regarding pre-existing cuts in the trachea.

### Front vs Back

Rav Yehuda responded to Rav Kahana's questions as follows: שחט במקום נקב — if the shochet cut in the place where there was already a pre-existing hole in the front of the trachea, such that he simply extended what was already there and crossed the majority threshold — שחיטתו כשרה, it is valid. שחט ופגע בו נקב — if, however, the shochet was cutting from the front and encountered a pre-existing hole in the back of the trachea, meaning the knife reached the midpoint by meeting the back hole rather than by cutting through the front wall to beyond the center — שחיטתו פסולה, it is invalid. Rabbi Abba then went and reported this distinction to Rabbi Elazar, who brought it before Rabbi Yochanan.

### Goy Analogy

Rabbi Elazar offered an explanation of why the front hole makes it valid while the back hole makes it invalid: שחט במקום נקב נעשה כמי ששחט עובד כוכבים וגמר ישראל — when one cuts where there is already a front hole, it is as if a non-Jew began the shechita and a Jew finished it. The first half of the opening was not the act of the shochet; he picked up from the midpoint and completed the majority correctly. So long as the critical crossing of the fifty-one percent line was done by the shochet in the valid zone, the shechita is valid. שחט ופגע בו נקב — if one encountered a back hole, נעשה כמי ששחט ישראל וגמר עובד כוכבים — it is as if a Jew began and a non-Jew finished. The shochet cut up to the midpoint, but the midpoint was crossed by connecting with the back hole rather than by a genuine cutting act through the valid tissue. The fifty-one percent line was not crossed by the shochet, and so the shechita is invalid.

### Reject Analogy

Rabbi Yochanan was unimpressed: עובד כוכבים עובד כוכבים — goy, goy. As Rashi notes, this was a rhetorical dismissal rather than a personal insult to Rabbi Elazar; Rabbi Yochanan was mocking the analogy as inadequate, telling him not to explain it to him with this kind of reasoning.

### Whole Act Defense

Rava explains why the objection is well-founded: שפיר קרי ליה עובד כוכבים עובד כוכבים — it was correct to taunt him, because the analogy is genuinely flawed. In the actual case of a non-Jew and Jew, the invalidity is clear: מדאית ליה לישראל למשחט רובא ולא שחט — the Jew was obligated to shecht the majority and did not, and so when the life-force departed, כי נפקי חיותא בידא דעובד כוכבים קא נפקי — it departed through the act of the non-Jew, who cut the fifty-one percent line. The non-Jew's act brought the animal to its death.

But here, by contrast, מכדי שוחט שחיט ליה — the shochet himself performed the entire act. There was no other actor. מה לי במקום נקב מה לי פגע בו נקב — what is the difference to me whether the shochet cut through a front hole or encountered a back hole? In both cases the shochet did everything, and there is no other actor whose intervention could be said to have taken over the act. The analogy to a non-Jew and a Jew breaks down precisely because in the pre-existing hole cases, a single person performs the complete act of shechita, meaning the existing hole should be incorporated into that actor's shechita regardless of whether it is in the front or the back. This creates a logical tension with Rav Yehuda's own earlier rulings, since if what matters is the majority of the trachea being cut correctly, and the shochet personally cut the majority of the trachea correctly in the front-hole case (even though he only added a small amount), the legal framework would need to treat the existing hole as part of his act of shechita — and that logic should apply equally to the back hole.

## Shechita vs Melikah

### Side Shechita

The Gemara closes this amud with a Mishnah that introduces a systematic contrast between שחיטה and מליקה. השוחט מן הצדדים — one who shechts from the sides of the neck — שחיטתו כשרה, the shechita is valid, because cutting from the side reaches the trachea and esophagus without severing the spine or otherwise creating an additional בסיס פסול. המולק מן הצדדים — one who performs מליקה from the sides — מליקתו פסולה, it is invalid. Melikah is the act performed by the כהן with his thumbnail on bird sacrifices, and it specifically requires cutting from the back of the neck through the spine; the side is not the correct location for that act.

### Back Melikah

Correspondingly: השוחט מן העורף — one who shechts from the back of the neck, the עורף — שחיטתו פסולה, the shechita is invalid, because cutting from the back breaks through the spine, creating an independent פסול of a broken spine. המולק מן העורף — one who performs מליקה from the back of the neck — מליקתו כשרה, it is valid, because that is precisely the required method.

### Front Shechita

השוחט מן הצוואר — one who shechts from the front of the throat — שחיטתו כשרה, obviously valid; this is the paradigmatic act of shechita. המולק מן הצוואר — one who performs מליקה from the front — מליקתו פסולה, it is invalid.

### Summary

The Mishnah draws the governing principle: שכל העורף כשר למליקה — the entire back of the neck is valid for מליקה, וכל הצוואר כשר לשחיטה — the entire throat, which the Mishnah implies includes the sides as well, is valid for שחיטה. The conclusion: כשר בשחיטה פסול במליקה — what is valid for שחיטה, meaning the throat and sides, is invalid for מליקה; כשר במליקה פסול בשחיטה — what is valid for מליקה, meaning the back of the neck, is invalid for שחיטה. This Mishnah opens a series of mutually exclusive categories that will be the subject of the discussion going forward.

# Hullin 20

## Oref & Melika Location

### Shechita vs. Melika Intro

The Mishnah on 19b contrasts the act of shechita with the act of melika. Melika is valid only from the back of the neck, while shechita is valid from the throat — whether the front or the sides. The basic reason is that there is no topographically specific location required for shechita in terms of the throat; the trachea and esophagus must be cut within a certain space, but shechita is not restricted to any particular side of the neck. The reason shechita cannot be performed from the back is that doing so would break the backbone and sever the spinal cord, rendering the animal a treifa before the simanim are cut. Melika, by contrast, is specifically required to be performed from the back.

### What Is Oref?

The Gemara now opens by asking: mai oref — what does "oref" mean as used in the Mishnah? The Gemara entertains the possibility that oref means literally the back of the head — that small area at the posterior of the skull where the head meets the neck. If so, then ileima oref mamash, mai irya shocheit — why would only shechita be invalid from there? Afilu moleik nami — even melika would be invalid. Why? Because the pasuk says mimul orpo — opposite the oref — not the oref itself. Hence the Mishnah's use of "oref" must mean not the back of the skull but rather its opposite: the back of the neck. The Mishnah is therefore using the term loosely, and this is confirmed by the continuation: kol ha-oref kasher le-melika — the entire oref is valid for melika. The phrase "the entire oref" implies a length, a span — something that would not apply to the small area at the base of the skull. Oref in the Mishnah, therefore, refers to the back of the neck proper.

### Kol Ha-Oref Kasher

The Gemara anchors this in the relevant pasuk: u-malako mimul orpo — the kohen performs melika from what is mimul orpo, opposite the oref. The Mishnah is describing the offering of a bird korban, specifically the act by which a bird is slaughtered for the altar. The pasuk itself is understood to refer to the oref as the back of the head, and mimul orpo accordingly refers to the back of the neck — the place that faces, or is in the direction of, the oref.

### Mimul Orpo Drasha

The Gemara then asks: minah haini milei — how do we know this location? The Baraita teaches: mimul orpo — mul ha-ro'eh es ha-oref — facing what sees the oref. That is, the melika must be done at the place that is, as it were, facing the oref from below: the back of the neck. This is supported by the verse ve-hu yosheiv mimuli — "he sits opposite me" — where mimul clearly means facing, or in front of. So if the oref is the lower back of the skull, then mimul orpo is the back of the neck, the area immediately beneath it and oriented toward it.

### Oref Opposite the Face

The Gemara then cites a second verse to establish the meaning of oref itself — for without knowing where the oref is, we cannot know what is mimul it. Ve-chi teima oref gufei lo yadnan heicha — we don't know where the oref itself is located. Ta shema: ki fanu eilai oref velo fanim — "they turned to me their oref and not their face." Miklal de-oref la-hadei fanim — this shows that the oref is directly opposite the face. If the face is the front, the oref is the back of the head, and mimul oref — opposite or facing the oref — is the back of the neck.

### Am Keshei Oref

This prompts a brief observation: the classic phrase am keshei oref — the stiff-necked people — takes on an unexpected dimension. If oref itself refers to the back of the head rather than the neck, what does it mean to have a stiff oref? A stiff neck suggests an unwillingness to turn, to do teshuvah — but a stiff back of the head is a less intuitive image. The question is noted without a clear resolution.

## Machzir Simanim Debate

### Bnei R' Chiya Position

Amari bnei Rabbi Chiya — the sons of Rabbi Chiya, Yehuda and Chizkiya, stated: mitzvas melika — the proper performance of melika — is accomplished by machazir simanim achorei ha-oref u-molayk: moving the trachea and esophagus to behind the spinal cord and then performing the melika. The concern is the same problem that makes shechita from the back invalid — one would break the backbone and the spinal cord before reaching the simanim, rendering the animal a treifa first. To avoid this, the bnei Rabbi Chiya hold that one physically manipulates the simanim, relocating them to the posterior of the spinal cord so that the melika cuts through the trachea and esophagus before encountering the backbone. In the case of a bird olah, only one siman need be cut, while for a chattas both must be severed — and the use of the hand to reposition the simanim may be understood accordingly.

### Davka vs. Af Machzir

Two versions of this position are transmitted. Ika de'amrei: af machazir — even moving the simanim is acceptable, but it is not required. Ve-ika de'amrei: machazir davka — according to others, moving the simanim is the exclusive valid method of melika according to the bnei Rabbi Chiya, because only this prevents the bird from becoming a treifa midway through the act. U-mistabra ke-man de'amar af machazir — the Gemara registers that the af machazir reading seems more plausible. The question is how to prove this.

### Proof from Mishnah

The proof comes from a reading of our Mishnah: ha-shochet min ha-oref shechitaso pesulah — one who performs shechita from the back of the neck, the shechita is invalid. Ve-ha-moleik min ha-oref melikaso kesheirah — but one who performs melika from the back, the melika is valid. On daf 20a the argument proceeds: ve-i salka da'atach machazir davka — if the only valid form of melika requires first relocating the simanim behind the spinal cord, such that the knife never contacts the backbone before the simanim, then mai irya moleik — why would only melika be valid from the back? Afilu shocheit nami — shechita from the back should equally be valid under those conditions. The Gemara takes as axiomatic that if the simanim are repositioned, there is no intrinsic reason why shechita from the back would be prohibited — the trachea and esophagus are encountered before the spinal cord regardless of the direction of approach. Since the Mishnah declares shechita from the back invalid while allowing melika, it must be assuming the standard case in which the simanim have not been relocated. This in turn demonstrates that the repositioning is not the required and exclusive mode of melika, but merely an additional acceptable option — ella lav shema minah af machazir. The Mishnah's ruling applies to a normal melika without any relocation of the simanim.

It is worth noting that melika is performed exclusively in the Beit HaMikdash as part of the korban service — the olah is not eaten while the chattas is. Outside the context of a valid bird korban, melika would render the bird a neveilah or treifa; it is only recognized as a legitimate act of shechita within the framework of a korban offering.

### Rav Yannai's Rejection

Rav Yannai is unwilling to accept even this concession. Yekablu ha-Rubim et teshuvatan — let the young men receive their response, he says, addressing the bnei Rabbi Chiya with pointed directness. He cites the end of the Mishnah: nimtza kasher bishchita pasul bi-melika, kasher bi-melika pasul bishchita — what is valid for shechita is invalid for melika and vice versa. Although on its surface this seems to merely summarize what came before — the throat is good for shechita but not for melika; the back of the neck is good for melika but not for shechita — the Gemara assumes this closing formulation is not merely recapitulating but extending to other cases as well. L'atuyei mai? What new case does it add? The Gemara takes it as given that relocating the simanim to the back would be valid for shechita — if the trachea and esophagus are moved to the posterior, there is no halakhic reason shechita performed from the back would be invalid. Therefore, what is valid for shechita is not valid for melika — and since machzir simanim would be valid for shechita, it follows that it is not valid for melika either. Rav Yannai thus rejects not merely the claim that machzir simanim is required for melika but the claim that it is even acceptable.

### Shen ve-Tzipporen

Amar Rabbah bar bar Chana — Rabbah bar bar Chana offers a different reading entirely. Perhaps the Mishnah's concluding formulation is not addressing the location of the simanim at all but the instrument of the act. L'atuyei shen ve-tzipporen — it comes to include the case of a tooth and a fingernail. The reasoning: what is valid for melika — using one's own fingernail — is invalid for shechita, since an attached fingernail cannot serve as a valid shechita implement according to Rabbi (who holds that attached objects, whether attached to the ground, to a person, or to an animal, cannot be used for shechita). The reverse applies as well. So the Mishnah's summary may be teaching about the instrument rather than the location.
