This reading is admittedly somewhat forced, since the plain sense of the Mishnah is clearly focused on the anatomical location of the act rather than the instrument. And one might ask why the phrase includes both shen and tzipporen together — the tooth alongside the fingernail.

### Melika With a Tooth?

Tosafot takes this seriously. The basis for using a fingernail for melika derives from the verse u-malako, which is expounded as be-atzmo shel kohen — the melika must be performed with the body of the kohen himself. If so, Tosafot reasons, perhaps the kohen's tooth is equally valid — after all, the requirement is that it be part of his own body, and the tooth qualifies. The only question Tosafot raises is whether the right-side requirement applies: every act performed by the kohen in the avodah must be done with the right hand. But a tooth does not have a right and a left, and Tosafot suggests that the requirement of using the right may apply only to a limb or appendage that possesses a right-left distinction. Where no such distinction applies, perhaps the right-side requirement does not operate. Tosafot therefore reads this Gemara as allowing, in principle, for melika to be performed with the kohen's tooth.

This raises in passing a further question: if melika can be performed with any part of the kohen's body, perhaps even his toenail is valid. The question of blood ingestion is noted as well — but the practical concern would be to spit it out, since the act of melika, as will be discussed, is a piercing rather than a cutting motion, and could in theory be executed with sharp teeth biting through the neck. Rashi, for his part, consistently emphasizes the fingernail and reads the Mishnah's reference to shen as part of a paired citation rather than as an independent endorsement of the tooth as a valid melika instrument. The word kegon in Rashi appears in the context of what is pasul bishchita — the tooth is included among those things — but when Rashi gets to kasher bi-melika, he mentions only the fingernail. Tosafot, however, is willing to read the Gemara literally and remains open to the tooth as a valid option.

### Molich u-Mevi Excluded

The Gemara objects to the Rabbah bar bar Chana reading as well: shen ve-tzipporen be-hedya katani le-hu — the tooth and the fingernail are stated explicitly in the earlier Mishnah, so the concluding formulation would not be needed to convey that point. Ella amar Rabbi Yirmiya: lema'utei molich u-mevi — rather, the Mishnah's concluding statement comes to exclude the back-and-forth motion. By shechita, the valid act is performed molich u-mevi — a horizontal, sawing, back-and-forth motion. By melika, the valid act is a piercing, downward cut — not a horizontal motion. The horizontal motion by melika would constitute hadrassa, a form of pressure, which is invalid for shechita precisely because it does not involve the sharp cutting action required. Conversely, the piercing motion that is valid for melika is invalid for shechita. This formulation — what is valid for shechita is invalid for melika and vice versa — cleanly captures the distinction between these two modes of motion.

### Bnei Chiya & Molich u-Me…

The Gemara then reasons: henicha le-man de'amar molich u-mevi bi-melika pasul — this reading of the Mishnah works perfectly if we hold that the back-and-forth motion is invalid for melika. But ela le-man de'amar kasher — if we hold that the back-and-forth motion is actually valid for melika, then Rabbi Yirmiya's reading collapses, and we would need to revert to the reading that the Mishnah is excluding machzir simanim. Benei Rabbi Chiya savrei lah ke-man de'amar molich u-mevi bi-melika pasul — the bnei Rabbi Chiya would hold that the horizontal sawing motion is invalid for melika. Therefore, from their perspective, the Mishnah's concluding formulation is not addressing the machzir simanim case at all; it is addressing the motion — what is valid for shechita (the horizontal cut) is invalid for melika, and what is valid for melika (the piercing motion) is invalid for shechita. This allows their position on machzir simanim to remain technically intact, even if Rav Yannai has largely dismantled it from another direction.

### Melika vs. Shechita Summ…

At this point it is worth summarizing the several dimensions in which melika differs from shechita. First, location: melika must be performed from the back of the neck, which by shechita would render the animal a treifa or a neveilah by breaking the spinal cord before reaching the simanim. Second, motion: shechita requires the horizontal sawing motion of molich u-mevi, while melika requires the piercing, downward kotzetz ve-yored motion; these motions are mutually exclusive as valid acts for their respective procedures. Third, instrument: shechita requires a detached knife, and according to Rabbi, an attached object cannot serve; melika by contrast is performed with the kohen's own fingernail — or, according to Tosafot's reading, potentially with his tooth — which is precisely what would be invalid for shechita.

The open questions are whether melika could theoretically become kasher shechita if both problematic variables were corrected simultaneously — both relocating the simanim and performing a horizontal cut. The Gemara treats the two approaches as alternatives rather than as cumulative requirements, noting that whichever approach one takes, some element precludes melika from counting as kasher shechita. The conclusion is that standard melika — from the back, without relocating the simanim, using the piercing motion and the kohen's fingernail — is always what would otherwise constitute a neveilah, and its validity is entirely anchored in its unique status as a korban act.

## Kotzetz ve-Yored

### Rav Kahana's Ruling

Amar Rav Kahana: mitzvas melika — kotzetz ve-yored. Rav Kahana states that the prescribed method of melika is cutting downward, a piercing motion. Zu hi mitzvasam — this is the way the mitzvah is performed.

### Rav Ami vs. R' Yirmiya

Sevar Rav Ami lemeimar: kotzetz ve-yored — in, molich u-mevi — lo. Rav Ami assumed that Rav Kahana's formulation was exclusive: the piercing downward cut is valid, the horizontal back-and-forth motion is not. Amar lei Rabbi Yirmiya: kol shekein de-molich u-mevi bi-melika kasher — Rabbi Yirmiya pushes back, arguing that certainly the horizontal motion should be valid for melika. If the downward piercing is valid, the conventional cutting motion should be at least equally acceptable. U-mah zu hi mitzvasah — eima af zu hi mitzvasah: the statement "this is its mitzvah" means only that this is also an acceptable method, not that it is the exclusive one. This is a direct parallel to the earlier debate about machzir simanim — the same question of whether a formulation stating a preferred method implies that other methods are excluded (davka) or merely that they are also acceptable (af).

### Shmuel's Kasher Rule

Amar Rabbi Yirmiya amar Shmuel: kol ha-kasher bi-shchita, kenegdo ba-oref kasher bi-melika — anything that is valid for shechita, its counterpart at the back of the neck is valid for melika. The emphasis here is not on the instrument or the motion per se, but on the location within the animal's throat and neck. Wherever the anatomy of the throat would make shechita valid, the corresponding location at the back of the neck makes melika valid. What Shmuel is coming to include is that a range of positions along the length of the valid shechita zone, when transposed to the back of the neck, will each be valid for melika.

### Pasul Shechita = Pasul M…

The Gemara then extrapolates the inverse: ha-pasul bi-shchita pasul bi-melika — what is invalid for shechita is invalid for melika. Lema'utei mai — what is this coming to exclude? Ileima lema'utei ikur simanim — perhaps it comes to exclude the case where the simanim have been uprooted. The psul of ikur simanim is one of the invalidating conditions of shechita: if the trachea or esophagus has somehow been wrenched or detached from its natural embedded position within the flesh of the animal's throat — not merely torn through the cut, but physically displaced from where it sits — the shechita is invalid. Rashi in several places describes this as rendering the animal a treifa, though Tosafot argues cogently that we never find ikur simanim listed as a treifa condition, and that it is better understood as a psul she-chitah — a defect in the act of shechita itself, requiring that the simanim be in their proper anatomical position for the shechita to be valid. The question, then, is whether ikur simanim similarly invalidates melika.

### Ikur Simanim ba-Of

The Gemara rejects this: ve-hatanya Rami bar Yechezkel — ein ikur simanim ba-of — the uprooting of the simanim is not a problem by birds at all. If there is no psul of ikur simanim for shechita of birds, one cannot claim that Shmuel's principle is coming to extend this problem to melika, since the problem does not apply in this context to begin with.

### Hagrama in Melika

Amar Rav Pappa: lema'utei rosho — the head. The Gemara asks peshita — is that not obvious? The Torah says mimul orpo — opposite the oref — which is the back of the neck, velo ve-rosho — and not the head itself. The Gemara clarifies: what Rav Pappa means to exclude is shefui rosho — the slope of the head, the case of hagrama. If one begins the melika too high up, starting at the downward slope of the skull, and works downward until reaching the proper zone of the back of the neck, that is invalid — just as hagrama is a psul shechita when one begins the cut outside the valid zone and finishes inside it. This is confirmed by the rule transmitted by Rav Huna in the name of Rav Assi and discussed in the preceding daf: higram shelish ve-shachat shenei shelishim — if one performed the first third of the cut in the wrong zone and the final two thirds in the correct zone, the shechita is invalid. Rav Pappa holds that the same principle of hagrama applies to melika.

## Ikur Simanim & Birds

### Ikur if Shechita Rabbinic

Amar Rav Acha bereih de-Rava le-Rav Ashi: ha de-tani Rami bar Yechezkel ein ikur simanim ba-of — the statement that ikur simanim is not a problem by birds — lo amran ela le-man de'amar ein shechita la-of min ha-Torah. This principle applies only according to the view that shechita of birds carries no biblical requirement. The reasoning is clear: if shechita of birds is entirely rabbinic, the rabbis may well have constructed a more lenient framework, one that does not require the simanim to be in their anatomically proper position. The concept of ikur simanim as a psul shechita may simply not have been applied to birds because there is no biblical shechita mandate for them to begin with.

### Biblical Shechita & Ikur

The counterargument is stated: amar lei — adaraba, ipcha mistabra — the opposite is more logical. Le-man de'amar yesh shechita la-of min ha-Torah — if the requirement of shechita for birds is biblical, icha lemeimar de-hachi agmareih — this may be precisely what God taught Moshe: de-ein ikur — that ikur simanim is not a problem. The Torah gave birds a unique set of shechita laws distinct from those of beheimah. Just as birds require only one siman while animals require two, so too the Torah may have established that ikur simanim does not apply to birds as part of this independently transmitted framework. The phrase agmareih here evokes the image of halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai — a tradition given directly to Moshe rather than derived from a verse.

The reason this framing becomes significant is the very basis upon which biblical shechita of birds is claimed. The Torah never uses the word veshachatta in the context of birds. The word vezavachta, from which the requirement of shechita is derived for beheimah, does not appear in any pasuk about birds. The one passage where birds are mentioned in the context of eating — the covering of blood — speaks only of shefichat dam, not of shechita. Therefore, any claim of biblical shechita for birds cannot rest on a standard textual derivation but must rely on a tradition, or be learned from the verse zot torat ha-beheimah ve-ha-of, which links birds to the same legal framework as animals. Given this, the view that shechita of birds is biblical can accommodate birds having their own distinctive rules — including the absence of an ikur problem — because the very content of that tradition may include such distinctions.

### Rabbinic = Modeled on Be…

Ve-afilu le-man de'amar ke-beheimah — even according to the view that the biblical basis for bird shechita is derived from the verse linking birds to animals, it does not follow that every detail of shechita law is fully equated. The ikur principle might still not apply to birds even if the general shechita requirement is biblical. However, the inverse argument has force: ela le-man de'amar ein shechita la-of min ha-Torah, ela mi-divrei sofrim — if shechita of birds is only rabbinic, me-heicha gemiri lah — where would the rabbis have derived their model? From beheimah. Me-heicha gamiri lah mi-beheimah — they would have taken the laws of beheimah as their template and applied them to birds. If so, kuleihu nuscha ke-beheimah — all the details should follow the model of beheimah, including the psul of ikur simanim. Under this view, the lenient ruling of ein ikur simanim ba-of is harder to explain if shechita of birds is rabbinic, because a rabbinic ordinance modeled on biblical precedent would typically import all the attendant stringencies of that precedent.

### Ikur Only by Melika

Amar Ravina amar li Ravin bar Kisi: ha de-tani Rami bar Yechezkel ein ikur simanim ba-of — lo amran ela bi-mlikah. The statement that ikur simanim is not a problem by birds should not be read as a general ruling about bird shechita at all. It applies exclusively to melika. Since melika already operates by a set of anomalous rules — it breaks the spinal cord, it uses the kohen's fingernail, it is performed from the back — it is consistent that ikur simanim similarly presents no problem within the framework of melika. But for ordinary shechita of birds — aval bi-shchita, yesh ikur — the standard psul of ikur simanim applies, just as it does by beheimah.

### Conflicts with Shmuel

This position, however, stands in tension with the principle stated earlier by Shmuel: kol ha-kasher bi-shchita kenegdo ba-oref kasher bi-melika, ha poslo poslo — what is valid for shechita is valid for melika, and what is invalid for shechita is invalid for melika. If ikur simanim is a psul for shechita of birds but not for melika, this directly contradicts Shmuel's symmetry principle. Ha pligu — yes, Ravina's position is in explicit disagreement with Shmuel's rule. The two positions reflect genuinely competing frameworks for understanding the relationship between shechita and melika.

## Nishbera Mafreket & Neve…

### Shechita vs. Death Intro

A broader question lurks beneath all of these discussions: is shechita a legal definition of an act, or is it a definition of the moment of death? When the Gemara speaks of shechita and the categories that follow from it, is it determining only whether the required ritual act has been performed, or is it also determining when, halachically, the animal has died? This question has bearing on fundamental issues far beyond the laws of korbanot.

### Ben Noach & Eiver Min Ha…

An illuminating example is the following case discussed in the Gemara: if one performs shechita on an animal and the animal continues to thrash — which it will do for some time after a valid shechita — a Jew may take a piece of meat from that animal and eat it, because the animal is halachically shechted. However, if a Ben Noach were to take a piece of meat from that same animal while it is still thrashing, he would be liable for eiver min ha-chai — the prohibition against taking a limb from a living animal. The Jew is exempt because he operates within a halachic category of shechita; once shechita is performed, the meat is permissible. The Ben Noach has no such category; he has only the concepts of alive and dead, and from his perspective the animal is still alive.

This case raises a profound question: does shechita halachically constitute the death of the animal, such that for the Jew the animal is considered dead even while it thrashes? Or does the halachic category of shechita operate independently of life and death, rendering the meat permissible even if the animal is still technically alive? These are two very different frameworks. One says that death is a legal definition — and the Jew's definition of when death occurs differs from the non-Jew's. The other says that life and death are not the operative categories here; rather, shechita permits the meat regardless of the animal's biological status.

This bears directly on the brain death discussion. The question of when death occurs is not simply one of uncovering a metaphysical reality. In the gray zones — where some biological systems continue to function and others do not — it is a legal question: when does the law consider the person to have died? Just as the question of when life begins (in discussions of abortion) or when death occurs is, in those gray zones, fundamentally a legal determination rather than the identification of a pre-existing metaphysical fact, so too the halachic question of brain death requires establishing how the law defines death at its boundary — not merely reading off a biological datum.

### Zeiri's Neveila Ruling

Amar Zeiri: nishbera mafreket ve-rov basar imah — neveilah. If the mafreket — the upper portion of the spine, at the nape of the neck — is broken, and most of the flesh around it is severed as well, the animal is a neveilah. This means that even if one subsequently performs shechita, it is too late; the animal is not merely a treifa — an animal mortally wounded but halachically alive — but a neveilah, an animal killed without a valid shechita act.

This is a striking ruling. The expected category for a mortal wound prior to shechita would be treifa. Zeiri goes further: the animal is a neveilah, which halachically means it has already been killed — without shechita — before any shechita act was performed. And this is the case even though the trachea and esophagus have not been reached, and the animal may still be breathing.

### Melika b'Sakin = Neveila

Amar Rav Chisda af anan nami tanina — Rav Chisda finds a corroborating proof from the Mishnah. Malak be-sakin — if a kohen performed melika using a knife rather than his fingernail, the melika is invalid. The consequence: metame begadim be-veit ha-bliah — the bird imparts the tumah of a neveilah when swallowed, which is how a valid bird neveilah transmits its impurity. The bird is thus a neveilah, not a treifa. And what has happened here? The kohen has approached from the back of the neck and cut through, as one would in melika, but using a knife. Rav Chisda reasons: why does this produce the status of neveilah and not treifa? If the cutting through the back of the neck produced only a fatal wound — a treifa — and the subsequent cutting of the trachea and esophagus constituted a valid shechita of a treifa animal, then the animal should be a treifa, not a neveilah. The fact that it is a neveilah shows that by the time the knife reaches the trachea and esophagus, the animal has already been halachically killed — it is a neveilah — and the subsequent cutting of the simanim cannot serve as shechita because one cannot perform shechita on a neveilah. This supports Zeiri's ruling: cutting through the back of the neck constitutes killing the animal in a halachic sense, not merely mortally wounding it.

### Dores vs. Machlid Answers

The Gemara rejects this proof. Amri — hatam mishum de-lav shechita hi klal. When the kohen performs melika with a knife from the back of the neck, the reason the animal is a neveilah is not that it was already halachically killed before the simanim were cut. Rather, even when the knife reaches the trachea and esophagus, the act performed is not a valid shechita. Two explanations are offered.

Rav says: mipnei she-hu machlid — because the act involves machlid, burrowing. What is the psul of machlid? In its standard form, this psul occurs when one inserts a knife between the two simanim and cuts them from the middle outward, rather than cutting from the outside in. Rashi explains machlid in this context as follows: when the knife has already cut through the backbone, the bone now overlays the knife as it continues forward, causing the knife to be buried, hidden inside the neck, as it proceeds toward the simanim. The knife is not cutting cleanly from the outside in; it is burrowing within the neck, with the bone covering over it. This constitutes the psul of machlid. Tosafot explains machlid differently — as a problem of reversed order, cutting from top to bottom rather than in the proper direction — and reads the problem as one of procedure rather than of the knife's visual exposure.

Rava says: mipnei she-hu dores — because the act involves dores, pressure or stabbing. Melika requires a piercing motion; that piercing motion, when performed with a knife, constitutes not a valid shechita but the psul of dores — applying pressure rather than using the sharpness of a cutting blade. Therefore the bird is a neveilah not because it was already killed before the simanim were reached, but because the act of cutting the simanim itself was not a valid shechita. And if this is the explanation, one cannot use the case of malak be-sakin as proof that cutting through the back of the neck halachically constitutes killing the animal.

The Gemara then notes: man de-amar mishum machlid, mai ta'ama lo amar mishum dores? The one who says the problem is machlid — why does he not say the problem is dores? Kasavar molich u-mevi bi-melika kasher — he holds that the back-and-forth horizontal motion is valid for melika. If so, he cannot say that every stabbing motion in the context of melika with a knife constitutes the psul of dores, since he allows for the horizontal cutting motion as valid. Therefore he must locate the problem elsewhere — in machlid. U-man de-amar mishum dores, mai ta'ama lo amar mishum machlid? The one who says the problem is dores — why not machlid? Amar lach: chaluda heichi dami? The psul of machlid is like a weasel (chulda) burrowing under the foundation of a house — de-michasya, the knife is genuinely hidden, tunneling from the inside. Here — ha hacha migalya — the knife is exposed; it entered from the outside in, cutting through the back of the neck in a visible manner. The mere fact that the bone lies over the knife as it proceeds does not constitute the concealed burrowing that defines machlid. Therefore this opinion locates the entire problem in dores alone.

In either case, the proof from malak be-sakin fails: one cannot demonstrate from it that cutting through the back of the neck constitutes halachic death. The neveilah status results from a defect in the shechita act itself, not from prior death of the animal.

### Rava: Melika on Mesa?

Amar Rava: i kashya li, ha kashya li — if there is something in this sugya that troubles me, this is it. Veci meisa omeid u-molayk? And one stands and performs melika on a bird that is already dead (meisah)? Rava's question cuts to the heart of the issue. If we accept Zeiri's ruling — that breaking through the back of the neck and most of the surrounding flesh renders the animal a neveilah — then by the time the kohen reaches the trachea and esophagus to perform the melika, he is performing melika on an animal that is halachically meisah. How can melika be valid if the bird is already dead before the simanim are cut? And significantly, Rava uses the word meisah — dead — not merely neveilah, which underscores that in his framing the concern is not merely a formal halachic category but the actual status of the animal as living or dead at the moment the melika is performed.

### Abbaye's Olah Parallel

Amar lei Abbaye: ve-tukshei lach olat ha-of de-baya shenei simanim — and this question should trouble you equally with respect to an olat ha-of. A bird olah requires both simanim to be cut for the melika to be complete, even though ordinary shechita of a bird requires only one. Veci meisah omeid u-molayk — and one stands and performs melika on a bird that is already meisah? After the first siman is cut, the bird is halachically dead — so how can one proceed to cut the second siman as a valid continuation of the melika? Abbaye implies that this is a built-in feature of melika: you perform it even as the animal is halachically dying through the very act. That is simply the nature of melika as a chiddush, and the question of performing melika on an animal that has become meisah mid-act is not a disqualifying problem.

### Havdalah Not Shechita

Amar lei Rava: hasam kedei lekayem bah mitzvas havdalah — no, the second siman of the olat ha-of is not being cut as a shechita act at all. The Torah requires that for an olat ha-of the kohen perform havdalah — severing the head from the body. The verse by chattas says velo yavdil; by olah the requirement is the positive act of separating the head. Accordingly, cutting the second siman is not an attempt to perform melika on a dead bird; it is the performance of an independent mitzva of havdalah, the physical separation of the head. You are cutting a bird that is already dead — and that presents no problem, because the act is not shechita but the completion of the korban's procedure.

The Gemara then asks: if so, one should have to cut the outer skin of the neck as well for the havdalah to be complete. The answer: kol ha-me'akev bi-shchita me'akev be-havdalah — anything that is involved in the act of shechita, that is what must be severed for the havdalah requirement to be satisfied. Ve-chol she-eino me'akev bi-shchita eino me'akev be-havdalah — what is not part of the shechita act — such as the outer skin — is not required for havdalah. The Gemara then refines this formulation: kol she-yeshno bi-shchita yeshno be-havdalah — anything that can be part of a shechita act is part of the havdalah requirement — ve-chol she-eino bi-shchita eino be-havdalah. This reformulation accounts for the Rabbinically required complete severance of the trachea and esophagus for the bird olah, even though for shechita only a rov is needed — the potential inclusion of each part of those simanim in the shechita act means they are all required for havdalah as well.

### Rava's Melika Method

But we remain with Rava's original question about standard melika: if the bird becomes meisah once the back of the neck is broken through and most of the flesh severed, how can the kohen then perform melika on a dead bird? Miklal makom kashya. Amar Rava: eima ve-chen hu oseh — we must say that this is precisely what the correct procedure of melika requires. Rather than rejecting Zeiri's ruling that nishbera mafreket ve-rov basar is a neveilah, Rava instead revises our understanding of how melika is to be performed.

Chotech shidrah u-mafreket, belo rov basar — the kohen cuts through the spinal cord and the nape, but without severing most of the surrounding flesh. The melika must be performed as a precise, targeted piercing that gets through the backbone to the trachea and esophagus while carefully not tearing away the majority of the flesh that holds the neck together. If most of the flesh is severed, the bird becomes a neveilah before the simanim are reached, and the melika is invalid. But if the kohen cuts through the backbone without severing most of the flesh, the bird remains halachically alive — not yet a neveilah — until the simanim are cut. The act of melika is completed on a living bird, and the cutting of the simanim constitutes a valid melika.

This is a demanding halakhic requirement: a piercing cut through the backbone that reaches the trachea and esophagus without cutting away the majority of the surrounding flesh. The precise anatomical mechanics — whether the critical flesh surrounds the spinal cord or occupies a different part of the neck — remain somewhat unclear. But the principle is halakhically clear: the bird must be kept alive in a halachic sense until the moment of melika, and the procedure must be calibrated accordingly.

### Treifa Midway Is Normal

Rashi takes care to address an obvious question: the procedure just described involves cutting through the backbone, which creates a fatal wound — rendering the bird a treifa — before the simanim are cut. Why is that acceptable? Rashi explains that this is not a conceptual problem at all, because every act of shechita works this way. At any moment during a valid shechita, if one were to stop halfway, the animal would be a treifa. Part of shechita is necessarily passing through a phase in which the animal has a mortal wound but is not yet fully shechted. The act of shechita itself creates a treifa as it proceeds and then completes the act. What is unacceptable is performing shechita on an animal that is already a neveilah before the act begins. Being in a state of treifa midway through the act is inherent to shechita and does not invalidate it. The problem arises only if the animal has already been halachically killed — made a neveilah — before the melika reaches the simanim.

### Brain Death & Neveila

This sugya is cited by some in the context of the halachic debate over brain death, and it is worth examining both what it potentially establishes and where the argument has limits.

The scenario described by Zeiri — the spinal cord at the nape of the neck is broken, the brain is functionally disconnected from the body — is structurally analogous to brain death in one important respect: the brain is no longer communicating with the rest of the body. The animal's trachea and esophagus may still be intact; its lungs may still be moving. Yet the Gemara, following Zeiri, treats this as constituting a neveilah — and Rava himself uses the word meisah. Those who invoke this source in the brain death discussion point to the fact that the Gemara appears to define the severing of brain-body communication as death, even prior to cessation of breathing or heartbeat.

However, there are significant difficulties with this argument. First, the case requires not only the severing of the spinal cord but also the tearing away of most of the surrounding flesh — rov basar. The question of why that additional element is required, and why severing the spinal cord alone is insufficient to constitute a neveilah, is not easily answered if the theory is that brain disconnection from the body defines death. Severing the spinal cord without rov basar does not produce neveilah status; why not?

Second, and perhaps more fundamentally, there is the question of whether neveilah is the same thing as meisah. The Gemara uses the two terms in proximity and, at points, seemingly interchangeably. But when the Rambam codifies Zeiri's ruling, his language is notably more cautious. He writes: harei zo ki-neveilah le-chol davar — it is like a neveilah for all purposes. He does not say it is a neveilah in the strict sense; he says it is ke-neveilah. And earlier he writes af al pi she-lo meisah in parallel contexts — even though it has not died — which suggests that for the Rambam, the category of neveilah and the factual state of meisah may not be fully coextensive. Something could be ke-neveilah for halachic purposes without being considered an animal that has factually died.

This distinction is at the heart of the brain death question. Is neveilah a halachic definition of death — meaning the law treats this as death, period? Or is it a category that tracks death but can apply even in cases where the law recognizes that factual death has not yet occurred, as the Rambam's hedged language implies? If the latter, the Gemara's use of meisah alongside neveilah may be a somewhat loose application of the term rather than a precise halachic equation. The question of whether this source can ground a definition of brain death as halachic death thus remains genuinely open — the source is relevant and the structural parallel is real, but the equation of neveilah with meisah cannot be assumed without further analysis.

---

---

# Hullin 22

## Neveilah & Melikah

### Opening Review

Daf 22 opens in the midst of an ongoing discussion that has touched on definitions of neveilah and death — a topic with fascinating implications for contemporary questions about defining the moment of death, particularly in cases where the body remains partially functional. The sugya has now moved to a closely related area: the distinction between the chatat ha-of and the olat ha-of, specifically with respect to the act of melikah. Both bird sacrifices require melikah performed from the back of the neck, as established by our mishna. However, a fundamental difference exists in how much separation is required.

### Chatat vs Olat

By the chatat ha-of, the Torah states ve-lo yavdil — one does not fully separate the head from the body. By the olat ha-of, in contrast, separation is required. The question that occupies the Gemara is: how much separation?

### Tanna Kamma Position

The Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yishmael hold that by the olat ha-of, both simanim are severed fully, though one need not literally sever the skin itself. The basis for this position is the phrase u-malak ve-hiktir — the Torah states "he shall perform melikah and burn." Since we learn elsewhere that the head and body are burned separately, the assumption is that the melikah mirrors the burning: the head and body are treated as fully separate.

### R. Elazar Position

Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon disagrees, holding that even by the olat ha-of one need only cut through the majority of both simanim rather than severing them entirely. In his view, the olat ha-of retains a degree of similarity to the chatat ha-of — the head and body remain more connected — and therefore full severing is not required.

---

## Head-Body Connection

### Gemara Inquiry

The Gemara, two lines from the top of 22a, asks: what exactly does Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon mean when he says that by the chatat ha-of the head and body remain together?

### Blood Squirting

The Gemara answers: hachi ka-amar — this is what he means. Mah lehalan keshe-hu ochez ha-rosh ba-guf mazeh: just as by the chatat ha-of the kohen holds the head by means of the body when he squirts the blood — that is, the head and body are still connected at the moment of the blood-squirting — so too here, af kan keshe-hu ochez ha-rosh ba-guf mazeh, even by the olat ha-of, when the kohen squirts the blood the head and body are still connected. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon presumably would not dispute that by the time of the haktarah, the burning, the head and body are fully severed. But at the moment of the melikah itself and the subsequent squirting, he holds they must still be more connected, analogous to the chatat ha-of.

### One Siman Challenge

The Gemara presses further: if you are drawing a comparison between the olat ha-of and the chatat ha-of, why not go all the way? By the chatat ha-of it is only one siman, since the Torah says ve-lo yavdil — you are specifically commanded not to fully sever. By the same logic, perhaps the olat ha-of should also require only one siman.

### Ve-hikrivo Response

The Gemara answers: talmud lomar ve-hikrivo. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon agrees that when the Torah says by the olat ha-of "he shall offer it," this signals that its mode of offering is distinct from the chatat ha-of and cannot be fully identical. And because u-malak ve-hiktir does indicate a greater degree of severing for the olat ha-of, Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon navigates a middle position: on the one hand he acknowledges that the olat ha-of involves more severing than the chatat ha-of; on the other hand, it is not completely free of the association with the chatat ha-of. His compromise is that both simanim are cut but remain somewhat connected — the head and body are more separated than by the chatat ha-of, yet the connection is not entirely eliminated.

---

## Tanna Kamma Argument

### Full Severing Position

The Gemara now turns to the position of the Tanna Kamma, who holds that by the olat ha-of both simanim are fully severed. His reasoning flows from u-malak ve-hiktir: since burning is performed with the head and body separately, melikah too must fully separate them.

### Ve-hikrivo Question

The Gemara asks: if the Tanna Kamma can derive the full severing internally from the phrase u-malak ve-hiktir, why does the Torah need the word ve-hikrivo at all? What additional work does this phrase perform?

### Comparison to Chatat

The Gemara answers: ei lav ve-hikrivo, had the Torah not written ve-hikrivo, hava amina — I might have thought that kemishpat, the phrase "as is the law," refers to comparing the olat ha-of to the chatat ha-of, just as Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon reads it. On that reading, the head would need to remain more connected to the body.

### Top of Mizbeach

As for the verse u-malak ve-hiktir, the Gemara explains that without ve-hikrivo, I would have read that verse differently. Hava amina: mah haktara be-rosho shel mizbeach — just as the burning takes place at the top of the mizbeach (obviously, since one must place the offerings in the fire at the top), af melikah be-rosho shel mizbeach — so too melikah must be performed at the top of the mizbeach. On this reading, u-malak ve-hiktir would teach the location of melikah, not the degree of severing. This is worth pausing on: the laws of birds are in fact the reverse of those of animals. By animal sacrifices, the chatat is applied at the top of the mizbeach, since the kohen applies the blood with his finger at the horns of the altar; everything else is at the bottom. By bird sacrifices, it is reversed — the chatat ha-of is performed at the bottom, and the olat ha-of at the top.

### Severing Association

The role of ve-hikrivo, then, is first to sever the olat ha-of from the association with the chatat ha-of. Once that association is broken and one is not drawn to read kemishpat as a reference to the chatat ha-of, the Tanna Kamma is free to read u-malak ve-hiktir as teaching two things simultaneously: that melikah must be performed at the top of the mizbeach, and that just as the head and body are burned separately, so too melikah must fully separate them. Ve-hikrivo is thus a necessary first step that liberates the subsequent derivation from u-malak ve-hiktir.

---

## Learning from Animal Cha…

### What Do We Learn

The Gemara now asks: ha chatat behemah degamrinan mechullin menalan — since the Tanna Kamma was not comparing the olat ha-of to the bird chatat but to the animal chatat, what exactly do we learn from the animal chatat and how do we establish that comparison?

### Three Learnings

Rav Chisda identifies three things that are learned by comparing the bird olah to the animal chatat: first, that the bird olah may only be brought from non-maaser money, i.e., from chullin funds; second, that it must be brought during the daytime; and third, that the right hand must be used.

### Aaron's Offering

The source for the prohibition against using maaser money is the verse: ve-hikriv Aharon et par hachattat asher lo — "Aaron shall bring the sin offering that is his" (in the context of Yom Kippur). The phrase asher lo teaches mishelo velo mishel tzibbur — from his own resources, not from communal funds — velo mishel ma'aser, and not from any maaser funds. Although one might in principle use maaser sheni money for a voluntary korban eaten in Yerushalayim, one cannot exempt oneself from an existing obligation through money already designated for another purpose.

### Tosafot Explanation

One might ask: since this verse speaks specifically of Aaron's offering on Yom Kippur, how do we derive a general principle from it applicable to all chatat offerings? Tosafot raises precisely this question and offers a compelling answer. The par hachattat of Yom Kippur was burned entirely — its meat was not eaten. Since the entire basis for the potential leniency regarding maaser money is that one eats the meat in Yerushalayim, there was never any reason to think Aaron's offering could be brought from maaser money in the first place. The verse would therefore be superfluous if it applied only to Yom Kippur. Its very inclusion forces us to read it as teaching a general principle applicable to all chatat offerings. And once we apply it to the animal chatat, we extend it through the comparison to the bird olah as well.

---

## Daytime & Right Hand

### Daytime Requirement

The second item learned from the animal chatat — that the bird olah must be brought during the daytime — might seem to require the comparison. However, the Gemara notes that we actually derive the daytime requirement for all korbanot from a general verse: zot ha-torah la-olah vela-mincha vela-chatat vela-milu'im... bayom tzivoso et b'nei Yisrael l'hakriv et korbaneihem — "This is the law of the olah, the minchah, the chatat, and the miluim... on the day He commanded the children of Israel to offer their korbanot." From the word bayom we derive that all korbanot must be brought during the day. Since this is derivable from a general principle, the Gemara remarks kidi nasba — it was simply added to the list incidentally, without being necessary to learn specifically from the animal chatat.

### Right Hand Requirement

The third item — that the right hand must be used — is attributed to the teaching of Rabba Bar Bar Chana in the name of Reish Lakish: kol makom shene'emar etzba o kehuna, eino ela yamin — wherever the Torah mentions either the word "finger" (etzba) or "priesthood" (kehuna) in the context of sacrificial service, it implicitly requires the right hand. The source is a verse by the metzora that specifies the right finger explicitly: ve-lakach ha-kohen be-etzba'o ha-yemanit. From this we generalize that any mention of etzba in a sacrificial context implies the right hand.

### Finger vs Kohen

However, the Gemara refines this principle. One might have thought that merely the word kohen always indicates the right hand. The Gemara rejects this: kehuna ba'ia etzba, etzba lo ba'ia kehuna — the word kohen requires the additional word etzba to imply the right hand, but the word etzba on its own, without kohen, does already imply the right hand. It is therefore not sufficient to simply read the word kohen and assume right; one also needs the word for finger.

### Melikah Technique

Because of this qualification, one does need to learn the requirement of the right hand from the animal chatat and apply it to the bird olah. Particularly relevant is the melikah itself, which must be performed with the kohen's right hand. And here it is worth recalling a related discussion from Tosafot: the source that the kohen uses his fingernail for melikah is the drasha of be-atzmo shel kohen — with the body of the kohen himself. This drasha does not specify any particular finger or thumb, which is what led Tosafot to raise the celebrated question of whether, in principle, the kohen could use his teeth, since the drasha focuses on his body rather than his hand.

---

## Melikah Source

### Melikah Location

A further question arises: if the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon do not compare the olat ha-of to the chatat ha-of (which is how Rabbi Yishmael derived that melikah is from the back of the neck), where do they learn that melikah must be performed from the back of the neck? This is stated explicitly by the chatat ha-of but not by the olat ha-of.

### Verbal Analogy

The Gemara answers: gamri melikah mi-melikah — they derive it through a verbal analogy, a gezerah shavah on the word melikah itself. Since both the chatat ha-of and the olat ha-of use the same term melikah, and melikah is described by the chatat ha-of as coming from the back of the neck (mimul orfo), melikah by definition always means from the back of the neck — regardless of whether one employs the categorical comparison of kemishpat.

---

## Mutually Exclusive

### Location Contrast

To summarize the discussion: shechitah is performed from the front and the sides of the neck; melikah is performed only from the back. One cannot perform melikah from the front, and shechitah from the back does not constitute valid slaughter. The two categories are, in the language of our mishna, mutually exclusive: what is valid for shechitah is not valid for melikah, and what is valid for melikah is not valid for shechitah.

### Pattern Introduction

This pattern — what is good for A is not good for B, and vice versa — is precisely the structural theme that the mishna has established and that will now drive the remainder of this perek. The next series of mishnayot will apply this same framework of mutually exclusive categories to a range of cases. We turn now to the first of these.

---

## Turtledoves & Pigeons

### Age Requirement

The mishna states: kasher b'torin pasul b'vnei yonah — what is valid for turtledoves is invalid for young pigeons, and vice versa. When the Torah permits bird sacrifices it always mentions either torim or bnei yonah. The word bnei, "children of," implies that the acceptable pigeons must be young and immature, while the torim — turtledoves — must be adults. What is kosher for the turtledove (adult stage) is invalid for the pigeon (which must be young), and what is kosher for the pigeon (immature stage) is invalid for the turtledove.

### Golden Feathers

The mishna adds: techilat ha-tziyuv baze uvaze pasul — the beginning of the yellowing, or golden coloring, of the neck feathers renders the bird invalid for both categories. At this stage the bird is too old to be considered bnei (young pigeons) but not yet old enough to be a full adult turtledove. This is the excluded middle: an adolescent stage that satisfies neither category.

### Tanna's Ruling

The Baraita elaborates: torim gedolim — adult turtledoves, gedolim kesherim, adults are valid, ketanim pesulim, the young are invalid. Bnei yonah: the opposite applies — the young are valid, ketanim kesherim, gedolim pesulim, adults are invalid.

### Kal Vachomer

One might have attempted a kal vachomer: if bnei yonah — which are not valid as adults — are valid as children, then surely turtledoves, which are valid as adults, should certainly also be valid as children. Part of what makes this kal vachomer at least plausible is that the word tor by itself might be read as a generic term encompassing any age, while bnei yonah specifically emphasizes youth. If the more restricted category (valid only as children) is valid, certainly the more expansive one should also be valid even in its younger form.

### Response to Kal

The Gemara rejects this: talmud lomar bnei yonah — the Torah's explicit use of the phrase bnei yonah limits the valid pigeons to children only. This phrase forecloses the kal vachomer by anchoring the pigeon category exclusively to young ones, leaving no room to extend the argument to turtledoves.

---

## Argument from Silence

### Torah Consistency

The Gemara now asks: but where do we derive that torim means only adults and not children as well? On what basis do we read the word tor as an exclusively adult category? Rava answers: lo lishtameit kra lichtov min bnei ha-torim o min ha-yonah. The Torah, across all the many verses that discuss bird sacrifices, never reverses the pairing. It always says torim and bnei yonah in the same order and with the same meaning. One will never find a verse saying bnei torim or simply yonah in place of bnei yonah. This consistent usage, never once varying, is itself the proof.

### Lo Lishtameit

This is the principle of lo lishtameit: the text would not have systematically omitted a formulation if that formulation were ever valid. Given the sheer number of verses dealing with bird sacrifices and the total absence of any alternative phrasing, we infer that the categories are precise and exclusive. Rashi explains that because so many verses speak about bird sacrifices and yet the phrasing never shifts, we are meant to infer that tor refers to adults only, and bnei yonah to children only.

### Halakha Precedent

This is an important moment to note the broader halakhic significance of the phrase lo lishtameit. Arguments from silence are of course treated with appropriate caution — the mere absence of evidence is not itself evidence. But when the circumstance is one in which, if something were true, one would fully expect it to appear somewhere, and yet it is entirely absent across two thousand years of halachic literature — that absence becomes meaningful. The phrase lo lishtameit kra (the verse would not have remained silent about this), or lo lishtameit Tanna, or lo lishtameit shum posek, is invoked precisely in these situations: if this ruling or this ruling or this leniency were valid, it would have appeared somewhere in our tradition. The fact that it has never appeared is itself a form of counter-evidence.

### Parallel Categories

Tosafot adds that this principle would apply even if there were only a single verse with this consistent formulation, not just many. The mere fact that the verse could have been written differently and was not is sufficient to draw the inference.

---

## Limiting Kal Vachomer

### Generic Term Question

The Gemara asks: perhaps torim is simply a generic term that includes both young and adult, and the kal vachomer that young turtledoves should also be valid cannot be dismissed simply by pointing to the word bnei yonah?

### Parallel Derivation

The Gemara responds: the exclusivity of one category is established by parallel derivation from the other. Just as bnei yonah means only young ones and not adults, so too torim means only the adult category and not the young. As Rashi frames it, echoing the structure of the mishna: just as bnei yonah can only be young and not adult, so tor can only be adult and not young. The two categories mirror each other as mutually exclusive, and the restriction of one implies the equal and opposite restriction of the other.

---

## Adolescence Debate

### Hypothetical Vow

The Gemara now poses the central question of this section through the inquiry of Rabbi Zeira: ha'omer harei alai olah min ha-torim o mi-bnei ha-yonah ve-heivi techilat ha-tzihuya shebaze v'shebaze mahu — suppose a person declares, "I will bring a bird olah," and specifies that either a tor or bnei yonah will satisfy his vow. He then brings both a tor and a bnei yonah that are each at the stage of techilat ha-tzihuya, the initial onset of the yellowing. Has he fulfilled his vow?

### Own Category Theory

If adolescence is its own independent category — neither adult nor child — then he has failed to fulfill his vow on either count. The tor he brought was not a valid adult tor, and the bnei yonah he brought was not a valid young bnei yonah. He brought neither.

### Doubt Theory

If, on the other hand, adolescence is merely a state of uncertainty — we simply do not know whether this stage counts as adulthood or childhood, but it is definitively one or the other — then one of the two animals he brought must have been correct. Either this stage constitutes adulthood, in which case the tor was valid, or it constitutes childhood, in which case the bnei yonah was valid. In that case, he has satisfied his vow.

### Rava's Argument

Rava attempts to resolve the question from the verse itself. Ta shema: prat le-techilat ha-tzihuya shebaze v'shebaze shepasul — we have a verse that explicitly excludes the adolescent stage. Rava reasons: ei amrat bishlamah berya havei — if you say adolescence is its own distinct state, then the verse is readily understood. You might have thought that since this stage is adjacent to adulthood it can count as an adult, or since it is adjacent to childhood it can count as a child. The verse therefore needed to exclude it explicitly.

### No Verse Needed

Ela ei amrat sveika havei — but if adolescence is merely a safek, a doubt from our perspective, then why would God need a verse to exclude it? If the Torah says bring a valid tor or a valid bnei yonah and we ourselves have a doubt as to which category this bird falls into, it is self-evident that we do not bring it. We bring only what we know to be valid; we do not bring things we are doubtful about. The verse would be entirely superfluous on the doubt-theory. Consequently, the fact that a verse was needed to exclude this stage must mean it is genuinely its own category — not a doubt, but a distinct state — which one might otherwise have thought to be valid, and the verse comes to disqualify it.

### Asmachta Response

The Gemara, however, does not accept this proof. Ki itztrich kra lemi'utei nirva ve-ne'evad — the verse is actually needed to exclude birds rendered invalid for other reasons entirely, such as a bird used in an act of bestiality or one that was worshipped as an idol. The exclusion of the adolescent stage was not the primary purpose of the verse; that exclusion is only an asmachta. Since the verse was genuinely needed for these other disqualifications, one cannot infer anything about whether adolescence is a safek or a biryah from the existence of the verse. The question of Rabbi Zeira therefore remains unresolved.

---

## Broader Implications

### Other Cases

This unresolved question — whether an undefined middle state constitutes its own independent category (biryah) or merely a safek between two known categories — is not unique to the case of turtledoves and pigeons. The Gemara will go on to apply it in multiple contexts. One parallel is the androgynos: is a person with both male and female characteristics their own halakhic category, or are they either male or female with an unresolved doubt? Another parallel is bein hashmashot: is twilight a middle state between day and night, neither one nor the other, or is it definitively one of the two and we simply do not know which? And there is the question of the palgas — the adolescent animal in the context of kodshim — which carries its own version of this debate.

### Philosophical Question

Underlying all of these cases is a profound conceptual question: when the world has been divided into two categories and something falls in between, does that middle thing force us to abandon the dichotomy and recognize a third category? Or do we maintain the dichotomy and treat the middle case as simply one of the two, acknowledging only our ignorance of which?

### Context Dependence

Critically, the answer may differ from case to case. Bein hashmashot may resolve one way, androgynos another, and tzihuya potentially a third. The question is not settled by any single universal principle but must be addressed in each context on its own terms. This discussion will continue on the next daf, extending across multiple areas of Shas, with the possibility that each domain yields a different answer.

---

---

# Hullin 23

## Middle Categories

### Excluded Middle Overview

The sugyot of Daf 23 continue the broader theme running through the Mishnayot of this Perek: what is valid for A is not valid for B, and what is valid for B is not valid for A. The Gemara's deeper concern, however, is with the space between A and B — what Aristotle called the excluded middle. The opposite of A is not B; the opposite of A is "not A." If the world is defined in terms of chocolate and vanilla, one must ask: what about everything that is neither? This is the animating question of the daf, and it plays out across several distinct domains.

### Bird Adolescence

The specific case that opened this discussion involves bird korbanot. Torim (turtle doves) must be adults, and Bnei Yona (young pigeons) must be juveniles. What then is the status of a bird in the transitional stage — Tchilat Hatzihuv, when the feathers begin to brighten or yellow? Is this adolescence simply a state about which we are uncertain (is it adulthood or childhood?), or is it a genuine third category, neither adulthood nor childhood?

The Gemara framed its question through a case: if someone vows to bring a korban of either Torim or Bnei Yona and then brings both species, each at the stage of Tchilat Hatzihuv, can we say that definitively one of them was valid — that at least one was either fully adult or fully juvenile — or must we say that both were invalid because that middle stage belongs to neither category? The Gemara had attempted to prove that Tchilat Hatzihuv is its own distinct category from the fact that a Pasuk is required to exclude it. The reasoning: if it were merely a doubt about categorization, no Pasuk would be needed — we would simply apply normal rules of doubt resolution. The need for a Pasuk implies a positive, independent category requiring explicit exclusion.

## Pasuk Purpose

### Gemara's Question

The Gemara now challenges that inference. It asks: Ki itztarich kra — for what was the Pasuk actually needed? Perhaps the Pasuk was not needed to exclude Tchilat Hatzihuv at all. Perhaps it was either an Asmachta, or its primary purpose was to exclude an entirely different set of problematic birds, in which case the exclusion of adolescent birds might rest on a different basis entirely — perhaps on genuine doubtful categorization rather than on their constituting a third category.

### Hashchata Midrash

The Gemara proposes: Lemiutei nirva vene'evad — the Pasuk is needed to exclude birds that were used in an act of bestiality or that were worshipped as idols. These are well-established grounds for invalidating large animals as korbanot. But why would one think they might not apply to birds? The answer begins with the Pasuk concerning blemishes in animals: Ki moshchatam bahem mum bam — because their corruption is in them, their blemish is in them. The Midrash of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches: Kol makom shene'emar hashchata — wherever the Torah uses the root hashchata (to corrupt), it refers to one of two things: devar erva (illicit sexual behavior) or avodat kochavim (idolatry).

How do we know hashchata refers to illicit sexual behavior? Because the Torah says before the Flood: Ki hishchit kol basar et darko al ha'aretz — all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth. The emphasis on kol basar, on flesh, and the broader context of midrashic tradition, associates the sin of the generation of the Flood with sexual transgression. How do we know hashchata refers to idolatry? Because the Torah says: Pen tashchitun va'asitem lachem pasel — lest you act corruptly and make for yourselves an image.

### Two Forms Avoda Zara

This is a striking point that deserves careful attention. The Torah uses two distinct imageries when describing the prohibition of idolatry. The first is zenut — the language of adultery and fornication. The Torah says: Vekam ha'am hazeh vezanah acharei elohei nechar ha'aretz — this nation will go astray after the gods of the foreign lands. God is described as El Kana, a jealous God, like a husband whose wife is suspected of infidelity. In this imagery, the sin is one of abandonment — leaving one's true partner and consorting with another. This is the framework of lo yihyeh lecha elohim acherim: the betrayal of the covenantal relationship by turning to other gods entirely.

The second imagery is that of hashchata — corruption. This appears in a different context entirely: the passage in Devarim reminding the people that at Har Sinai they saw no image, and therefore they must not act corruptly and fashion an image of God. Here the sin is not the worship of a foreign god but rather the attempt to represent and worship the true God through physical form — as in the sin of the Golden Calf, where the text says ki shicheit amcha. This is not abandonment of God but a corruption of the manner of His worship: one is still directed toward God, but in a fundamentally distorted way.

These are thus two conceptually distinct forms of Avoda Zara. The zenut imagery applies to the wholesale rejection of God in favor of other deities. The hashchata imagery applies to the corruption of God's own worship through the making of images or representations.

### Nirva v'Ne'evad

Returning to the Gemara: the Pasuk by animal blemishes reads moshchatam bahem mum bam — their hashchata is in them, their mum is in them. The Gemara understands this as an equation: the Torah likens hashchata to mum, and therefore the grounds that render animals unfit for the altar are not limited to physical blemishes but extend to hashchata in its two forms — erva and idolatry. Thus an animal used in an act of bestiality (nirva) or worshipped as an idol (ne'evad) is rendered unfit, as though it bore a moral blemish comparable to a physical one.

From this equation, one might draw the following inference: Kol shemum posel bo devar ervah va'avodat kochavim posel bo — wherever a physical mum disqualifies, these moral disqualifications also apply. Vechol she'ein mum posel bo, ein devar ervah va'avodat kochavim posel bo — wherever a physical mum does not disqualify, perhaps these moral disqualifications also do not apply, since they are derived through comparison to mum.

### Birds Physical Blemishes

This inference becomes relevant to birds. The Gemara states: Ho'il velo paslei behu muma — since physical blemishes do not disqualify birds. The source is the principle that tamut vezachrut bebiheimah ve'ein tamut vezachrut be'ofot — the Torah requires that animals be tamim (unblemished) and zachar (male) in various contexts, but when it speaks of bird offerings, it never invokes these requirements. The word tamim never appears in connection with birds; nor does the Torah ever specify that a bird offering be male or female. It is therefore understood that these standards simply do not apply to birds. If so, one might reason by analogy that the moral disqualifications — used in bestiality or idolatry — should also not apply to birds, since all of these are derived through comparison to physical blemishes.

### Moral Blemishes Priority

This, then, is why the Pasuk is needed: to teach that nirva and ne'evad do disqualify birds, notwithstanding the fact that physical blemishes do not. Kamashmalan — the verse teaches us otherwise. The conclusion is, in a certain sense, striking: physical blemishes are not a disqualifying factor for birds, but moral and religious blemishes are. The categories that one might think are weightier — an animal's physical integrity — turn out to be less determinative for birds than the categories rooted in moral corruption.

One might find this counterintuitive, particularly given the broader emphasis in the laws of korbanot on physical perfection. The entire institution of mum, applying with considerable detail to both animals and Kohanim, might suggest that external, physical categories are what the Torah primarily cares about. Here, the Gemara surfaces a corrective: by birds, at least, what we might call moral or religious blemishes remain operative even when physical blemishes do not. If one were a strict literalist, relying only on those Pesukim that explicitly address blemishes, one might have concluded that the Torah concerns itself only with the physical. The requirement of a verse to import nirva and ne'evad into the context of birds reveals that these considerations are, in this respect, of greater weight.

A parenthetical observation is worth noting: the Torah never specifies that bird offerings must be male or female. This is not merely a legal technicality but reflects a genuine biological reality — determining the sex of birds is notoriously difficult, and indeed certain species offer no external markers of sex at all. The Torah's silence on this point may reflect an awareness of this difficulty.

There remains a potential objection: is it truly accurate to say that physical blemishes never disqualify birds? There is a known category of mechussar eiver — missing an entire limb — which does apply even to birds. The resolution depends on how one understands mechussar eiver. Rashi, though Tosafot disputes this, holds that the disqualification of a bird missing a limb is not derived from the laws of mum at all, but rather from the verse hakrivehu na le'pachatecha — would you present this as a gift to an official? It is not a technical mum but an independent standard of appropriateness. Alternatively, mechussar eiver may constitute its own distinct category that does not overlap with the mum framework, which is why its existence does not undermine the principle that mum, as such, does not apply to birds.

## Palgas Debate

### Vow Scenario

Having established that the Pasuk was needed not to exclude the adolescent stage of birds but to exclude nirva and ne'evad, the Gemara returns to the underlying question about middle categories. Reb Zeira poses a parallel case in the domain of animal korbanot. He asks: Omer harei alai olat behema min ha-ayil o min ha-keves — if someone declares, "I hereby obligate myself to bring a burnt offering from either a ram or a sheep," and then brings a palgas — what is the law?

The palgas is the animal in its transitional month, between twelve and thirteen months of age. Below twelve months it is a keves (sheep); from thirteen months onward it is an ayil (ram). The one-month interval between them is the palgas, the adolescent animal. Presumably, this interval corresponds to a genuine transitional period in which the animal is developing the physical characteristics of a ram but has not yet fully matured — in other words, a recognizable period of adolescence. The question is whether this stage is simply a state of uncertainty (it is really either a ram or a sheep, we merely cannot determine which), or whether it constitutes its own independent category, neither ram nor sheep.

### Palgas Libations

An additional dimension of the question arises from the laws of minchat nesachim — the flour and wine libations that accompany animal korbanot. The Torah, as read that Shabbat in Parashat Pinchas, specifies different quantities based on the type of animal: a sheep requires one issaron of flour and a quarter of a hin of wine (three log), while a ram requires two isronot of flour and a third of a hin of wine (four log). What libations does one bring with a palgas?

Notably, the Gemara does not seem troubled by the question of whether a palgas is even a valid korban at all. One might have thought: if the Torah permits bringing a keves or an ayil, and a palgas is neither, perhaps it cannot serve as a korban in the first place. The Gemara appears to assume it is kasher as a korban — it simply does not satisfy any vow or obligation, since a vow obligating one in a keves or an ayil is not discharged by something that is neither. What remains uncertain is the type of minchat nesachim required.

### Rabbi Yochanan

The Mishnah teaches: if one brings a palgas as a korban, ma'aleh alav niskei ayil — one brings the libations appropriate for a ram (the larger quantity). Ve-ein oleh lo mizivcho — but the obligation or vow is not discharged, since one required a keves or an ayil and a palgas satisfies neither.

Rabbi Yochanan explains the source for bringing the ram's libations: the verse says o la'ayil — "or for a ram" — and this extra formulation serves lerabbos es hapalgas, to include even that which is not yet fully a ram. The logic parallels the earlier inference from the birds: if the verse itself addresses the palgas as a distinct case, this implies it is its own category. A mere doubt about which existing category it belongs to would not require scriptural address — that would be a matter of doubt resolution. The fact that the verse legislates for the palgas specifically indicates that it is a biryah, its own independent state, to which the Torah assigns the ram's libations.

### Bar Pada Doubt

Bar Pada takes a different view: maisei umasnei — one brings the libations and makes a stipulation. According to Bar Pada, we do not know whether the palgas is a ram or a sheep. Therefore one brings the larger quantity of flour and wine and declares: if this animal is a ram, then the full libation is the minchat nesachim of the ram; if it is a sheep, then the portion appropriate for a sheep serves as the minchat nesachim, and the remainder is an independent voluntary gift to the mizbei'ach. Bar Pada thus treats it as a safek — a genuine doubt between two existing categories — rather than as a biryah.

Tosafot raises a difficulty with this formulation: the proportions of flour to oil differ between a sheep and a ram, so the libations are not simply a larger and smaller version of the same mixture. They are qualitatively different. Tosafot resolves this by saying one brings both types of mixture with the stipulation: if it is a ram, the larger mixture serves as the korban's minchat nesachim and the smaller is an independent gift; if it is a sheep, the smaller mixture is the minchat nesachim and the larger is an independent gift.

### Unresolved Doubt

For Rabbi Yochanan, the matter is clear: the palgas is a biryah, its own state, and the verse assigns it the ram's libations. For Bar Pada, the palgas is a safek. But here the Gemara raises a further question: Ki tiba'ei lach aliba de-Bar Pada — when we ask what Bar Pada's position means, the issue is this. When Bar Pada stipulates "if it is a ram, this; if it is a sheep, that" — does his stipulation encompass only those two possibilities, or does it also include the possibility that the palgas is a biryah — its own category?

Mi amrinan ayil vekeves masna, bevirya lo masna — do we say he stipulates for ram or sheep but not for the case that it is an independent entity? Or dilma bevirya nami masna — does his stipulation include that possibility as well? If Bar Pada does acknowledge the possibility of biryah, what would follow? Without a verse like Rabbi Yochanan has, what would one do if the palgas truly belongs to no category? The Gemara suggests: De'amar, ei birya havei lehavei kula nedava — if it is its own category, all the flour and wine I am bringing should be treated as a pure voluntary gift, since the Torah assigned no minchat nesachim to this animal at all. Teiku — the Gemara leaves this unresolved.

## Se'or Bread

### Todah Vow

Reb Zeira poses yet another case in the same analytical framework. Haomer harei alai lachmei todah min hachametz o min hamatzah vehevi se'or mahu — if someone declares he will bring the bread of a Todah from either chametz or matzah, and he proceeds to bring se'or (sourdough, the beginning stage of fermentation), what is the law?

The Todah offering is accompanied by forty loaves: thirty of matzah and ten of chametz. The case constructed here involves someone who vowed specifically regarding one of these sets. If the ten loaves he brings are fully matzah, or fully chametz, he has satisfied his obligation with respect to that portion. If he brings se'or — which is in a state between matzah and chametz — the question is whether he has satisfied his obligation at all, or whether se'or is neither chametz nor matzah and therefore counts for nothing.

### Se'or Definition

In contemporary practice, the chametz question has been converted primarily into a matter of time — eighteen minutes of leaving dough unworked determines leavening. The Gemara, however, works from physical appearance. When dough begins to crust over, that is one stage; when that crust develops cracks, that is a later stage. These correspond to the positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.

Rabbi Meir is strict. He holds that se'or begins as soon as the dough crusts over, and further, that eating this se'or on Pesach incurs malkot (lashes), though not karet. Rabbi Yehuda is lenient in two respects: he holds that there is no issue at all until the crust actually cracks, and even once it has cracked, eating it on Pesach incurs no lashes — it is forbidden, but without the consequence of lashes. The question about se'or's status — whether it is chametz, matzah, or a middle state — will thus yield different answers depending on which view one adopts and at which stage one is examining.

### Rabbi Meir Se'or

The Gemara works through the combinations. If one asks about Rabbi Meir's stage — the crusted-but-not-cracked state — from Rabbi Yehuda's perspective: matzah malyasa hi — it is entirely matzah, since Rabbi Yehuda does not even consider this stage problematic. No question arises. Conversely, if one asks about Rabbi Yehuda's stage — the cracked state — from Rabbi Meir's perspective: chametz hu — it is unambiguously chametz. Again, no interesting question arises.

The question becomes interesting when one asks about Rabbi Meir's stage from Rabbi Meir's own perspective: since one incurs lashes for eating it on Pesach, midelaki lei chametz hu — the Gemara concludes that the receipt of lashes establishes it as chametz. The logic is: lashes are a consequence of a biblical prohibition, and the biblical prohibition on Pesach targets chametz specifically. If one incurs lashes, one has eaten something the Torah prohibits as chametz. Therefore it is chametz.

Tosafot is not satisfied with this. Tosafot objects: if it were truly chametz, one should incur karet, not merely lashes. The failure to incur karet suggests that this is not full chametz — perhaps it is precisely the middle state the question is trying to isolate. Rashi attempts to answer differently: one should indeed incur karet, but the technical reason one does not is that the se'or at this stage is not yet rauy le'achilah — not fit for consumption as food. It is still raw, sour dough, and therefore the prohibition is not fully triggered even though the leavening is technically complete. The chametz status is complete in terms of fermentation; what is lacking is the food-fitness that would complete the biblical violation.

Tosafot, however, is not persuaded by this resolution and offers a different approach: perhaps the Torah applies a broader definition of chametz specifically in the context of Pesach. Because Pesach's prohibition is more expansive, se'or at this stage triggers lashes under the Pesach rules, but that does not mean it would be classified as chametz in other halachic domains. The broader category generates lashes while the more standard category — which would trigger karet — requires a stricter threshold. Tosafot acknowledges that this answer is weaker than the question, but the point he draws is significant: the classification of a borderline state may differ depending on the halachic domain in question. Adolescence might count as childhood in one context and adulthood in another; se'or might be chametz for certain purposes and not for others. There is no single objective answer that applies uniformly across all areas of halacha.

### Rabbi Yehuda Se'or

This is why the Gemara ultimately frames the question within Rabbi Yehuda's own position: ela de'Rebbi Yehuda le'Rebbi Yehuda. At Rabbi Yehuda's stage — when the crust has cracked — Rabbi Yehuda himself says it is forbidden to eat on Pesach but does not incur lashes. Mai? What does this mean? If one incurs lashes, the Gemara has established, there is at minimum a clear chametz element, and the se'or is certainly not matzah. But if one does not incur lashes, the question remains genuinely open. Is this a case of safek — it is either chametz or matzah but we cannot determine which — in which case Rabbi Yehuda forbids it because it might be chametz but does not give lashes because it might be matzah? Or is it a biryah — a genuine middle state, neither chametz nor matzah — and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling reflects that: forbidden because it is not matzah, no lashes because it is not chametz?

### Se'or Todah

The Gemara now asks how the vow scenario could even be constructed, since bringing the full complement of Todah bread — thirty matzah and ten chametz — would make a doubtful item useless. If one does not know which category the se'or exempts one from, one would still be obligated to bring all forty loaves. Rav Huna teaches: ha-omer harei alai lachmei todah meivi todah ve-lachmah — if one obligates himself in the bread of a Todah, he implicitly obligates himself in the Todah as well, and that requires bringing thirty matzah and ten chametz with certainty. Doubtful items do not resolve his obligation.

The Gemara therefore reconstructs the case: not that the person obligated himself in his own Todah bread, but rather de'amar harei alai challah li-ftor todato shel ploni — he declared he would bring loaves to exempt someone else from their Todah obligation. I will bring ten of the loaves owed by another person. The Gemara still objects: even here, if the se'or is only a safek, the person bringing the Todah still does not know which portion of his obligation has been addressed, and his full obligation remains. He must still bring all forty.

### Se'or Vow Unresolved

The Gemara therefore narrows the case further: lo, tzricha delo amar liftoor — the person did not say he would exempt the other from his obligation; he simply vowed to bring ten of the other's loaves. No exemption was promised, only a contribution. In this formulation, the question becomes: mapik yedei nidro, nafik o lo nafik — did this person satisfy his own vow or not?

If the se'or is a biryah — a genuine middle state, neither chametz nor matzah — then it does not count as any of the loaves of the Todah, and his vow to bring ten of those loaves has not been satisfied. If it is a safek — truly either chametz or matzah but unknown — then objectively he has brought ten loaves toward the other's Todah obligation, even though the other person still cannot know which ten. His own vow, in that case, would be satisfied, since he did bring ten loaves; which ten they are remains unclear, but the contribution itself was real. Teiku — the Gemara leaves this unresolved.

The parallel to the birds and the palgas is clear. In all three cases, a middle stage sits between two defined categories, and the same fundamental question is posed: is this an uncertainty about which of the two categories applies, or is it a genuinely independent state? The consequences differ as well. By birds in Tchilat Hatzihuv, the animal appears to be invalid as a korban entirely. By the palgas, it is apparently a valid korban but does not satisfy any vow or obligation. By the se'or loaves, the question is whether they count toward a vow at all.

## General Middle States

### Compare Middle States

Comparing these three cases — birds, sheep, and bread — reveals both the consistency of the underlying question and the divergence in consequences. In each case, the Gemara asks whether the middle stage is a doubt about categorization or a biryah. The answer has different practical implications in each domain, and what constitutes a valid korban, a satisfied obligation, or a discharged vow may depend on how one resolves this question in each particular sphere.

### Other Middle States

This question is not unique to korbanot. The same structure appears in many other areas of halacha. Bein hashmashot — the period of twilight between sunset and the emergence of stars — is a paradigmatic example. Is dusk simply a period of uncertainty (is it night or day, we cannot tell?), or is it its own halachic state, neither night nor day? If it is genuinely its own state, it requires its own set of halachot, since it cannot be fully subsumed under the rules of either day or night. Similarly, the period between the morning star and sunrise — dawn — presents a parallel question.
