Rav Soloveitchik, for example, held that this period is not merely rabbinic in its special status but reflects a genuine parallel to bein hashmashot: it is a transitional state with its own character, neither night nor day, and therefore certain day-mitzvot may not be performed lechatchilah during this period, even though bedieved they are fulfilled.

### Category vs Doubt

The key question across all these cases is whether a middle state constitutes its own halachic category or merely represents our epistemic uncertainty about how to classify something that objectively belongs to one of the two established categories. If it is the former, one must determine what halachic rules govern this independent state. If it is the latter, one applies normal rules for cases of doubt. The answer may differ not only from domain to domain but potentially even within a single domain, as Tosafot's analysis of se'or suggests: a borderline state might be classified differently for the purposes of lashes than for the purposes of karet, or differently in the context of Pesach than in other areas. How a middle state is resolved may thus be an inherently context-sensitive question.

## Parah vs Eglah

### Two Rituals

The daf now moves to the Mishnah that continues the chapter's theme of mutual exclusivity: what is valid for one is invalid for the other. The two cases here are the Parah Adumah (the Red Heifer) and the Eglah Arufah (the heifer whose neck is broken when an unidentified murderer cannot be found). Both involve bovines used in rituals outside the Mikdash. The method of their respective rituals, however, is categorically different: the Parah Adumah is killed through shechita — ritual slaughter with a knife — while the Eglah Arufah undergoes arifah — the breaking of the neck.

### Mishnah Teaching

The Mishnah and the Tanna teach: kasher beparah pasul be'eglah, kasher be'eglah pasul beparah. What is valid for the Parah — shechita — is invalid for the Eglah. What is valid for the Eglah — arifah — is invalid for the Parah. These two rituals are entirely distinct, and the method appropriate to one cannot be imported into the other.

### Kal Vachomer

The Gemara immediately constructs a kal vachomer: Vedeha parah kesherah ba'arifah mikal vachomer — why should one not be able to perform arifah on a Parah Adumah through a kal vachomer? The argument runs: Umah eglah shelo huchsharah bishchitah huchsharah ba'arifah — the Eglah Arufah, which cannot be slaughtered through shechita, is nonetheless valid through arifah. Parah shehuchsharah bishchitah, eino din shehuchsharah ba'arifah — the Parah Adumah, which can be killed through shechita, should certainly also be valid through arifah. If the more restricted case (the Eglah, which is limited to arifah alone) is valid through arifah, surely the less restricted case (the Parah, which permits shechita) should also be valid through arifah.

### Pasuk Limitation

The Gemara answers: Amar kra, veshachat vechukah — the verse states explicitly that the Parah Adumah is to be slaughtered (shachat), and the same verse describes this as a chok, a divine statute. Bishchitah in, ba'arifah lo — only shechita, not arifah; the verse confines the valid method to precisely what it states, and the characterization as chok signals that the logic of the kal vachomer cannot override the statutory prescription. The Gemara will continue this discussion on the following daf.

This is characteristic of a certain category of frustrating kal vachomer arguments in the Gemara — the kind where the logical inference seems compelling, yet the Torah's formulation blocks it. Each of these rituals is unique to its own context, and the assumption that what applies in one domain should apply to a structurally analogous domain is precisely what the term chok forecloses. The statute stands on its own terms, immune to analogical extension.

# Hullin 24

## Parah vs. Eglah

### Intro: Two Rituals

Daf 24 opens by comparing two rituals performed with bovines outside of the Mikdash: the Parah Adumah and the Eglah Arufah. One is performed through shechitah; the other through arifah, the breaking of the neck — and not vice versa. We know that the Parah Adumah requires specifically shechitah because the Torah says veshachat and also employs the word chukah — zot chukat hatorah — indicating that the method is precisely prescribed.

### Chok Principle

The Gemara opens on daf 24a by asking: wherever the Torah writes chukah, do we say lo darshinan kal vachomer — we cannot derive through a kal vachomer? Recall that chok was a term used extensively in Zevachim to indicate that a given criterion is meakeiv, that it must be fulfilled and cannot be bypassed. But that is different from saying one cannot use a kal vachomer to propose alternatives or additions. The question here is not whether shechitah can be forfeited, but whether a kal vachomer from the Eglah Arufah might allow arifah as an additional valid method for the Parah Adumah.

### Yom Kippur Case

The Gemara demonstrates that chok does not block a kal vachomer by citing Yom HaKippurim, where the Torah uses the language chukat olam. Anyone who has learned Yoma knows that word chok is used there to establish that many of the details of Yom Kippur are meakeiv. And yet, as a braita shows, we do attempt a kal vachomer in the context of Yom Kippur. Specifically, the Torah states vehayetah zot lachem le-chukat olam in connection with the two goats: veasahu chattat — it is the goral, the drawing of lots, that determines which goat becomes the chattat and which is sent to the cliff as the la-azazel, and not a verbal declaration.

### Lots vs. Declaration

The braita raises the possibility of a kal vachomer: umah bemakom shelo kideish hagoral kideish hashem — where lots do not sanctify, verbal declaration does work (as Rashi illustrates with the case of two birds brought as a chattat and olah, where declaration designates which is which). If in that case declaration works but lots do not, then by the goats of Yom Kippur — where lots do work — how much more so should verbal declaration also function? The braita rejects this kal vachomer through the verse veasahu chattat, which teaches that only the goral designates the chattat, and not a verbal declaration: hagoral oseh chattat, ve'ein hashem oseh chattat.

The Gemara then draws the crucial conclusion: ta'ama — the reason we do not follow the kal vachomer — is dichsiv rachmana veasahu chattat, because the verse explicitly established that only the lot creates the designation. Halo hachi, had that verse not existed, we would have used the kal vachomer even in the presence of chok. This establishes that chok does not itself prevent a kal vachomer; only an explicit contrary verse does.

Returning to the original question: how then do we know that arifah cannot be performed for the Parah Adumah? If chok alone does not block the kal vachomer, the Gemara needs another source.

### Parah Cannot Use Arifah

The Gemara answers: mi'eit rachmana gabi eglah ha-arufah — the Torah minimizes the applicability of arifah through the language it uses by the calf whose neck is broken.

### Definite Article Exclusi…

The Torah uses the expression eglah ha-arufah banachal — the calf, the one with the broken neck. The definite article heh identifies this animal uniquely: zot ba-arifah ve'ein acheret ba-arifah — this one undergoes neck-breaking, and nothing else does. This excludes even the Parah Adumah from the method of arifah.

### Eglah & Shechita

Having established that the Parah Adumah cannot use arifah, the Gemara attempts the kal vachomer in the reverse direction: v'tehei eglah kesheirah be-shechita mi-kal vachomer? Since the Parah Adumah, which cannot use arifah, is nevertheless valid through shechitah, then the Eglah Arufah, which can use arifah, should certainly be valid through shechitah as well. Indeed, one might ordinarily assume that shechitah — the standard ritual method of slaughter — should be at least as acceptable as neck-breaking in any ritual context.

### Limiting Arifah

The Gemara rejects this: amar kra v'arfu ha-eglah — the Torah says "they shall break the neck of the calf." Rashi notes that the decisive point is the repetition: the Torah had already indicated that arifah is performed, and when it states ve'arfu ha-eglah a second time, this repetition is limiting — ba-arifah in, be-shechitah lo — only through neck-breaking, not through shechitah. The Gemara notes that Tosafot is quite troubled by the underlying logic of these hava amina arguments — why would one have assumed in the first place that one distinctly prescribed ritual method could substitute for another? Tosafot attempts several approaches, but the hava amina remains difficult.

---

## Kohanim vs. Leviyim

### Initial Statement

The Gemara transitions to another case of inverse rules. The braita states: Kohanim be-mumin psulin, be-shanim ksheirin — Kohanim are invalidated by physical blemishes, but age presents no disqualifying limit. The reverse holds for Leviyim: be-mumin ksheirin, be-shanim psulin — blemishes present no problem, but age does, since the Torah establishes that Leviyim serve between the ages of 30 and 50, and upon reaching 50, yashuv mitzva ha-avoda velo ya'avod od — he shall return from the army of his service and no longer serve.

What makes this case different from the previous ones — and genuinely surprising — is that here the potentially transferable disqualifications are not arbitrary ritual characteristics of objects but substantive personal conditions: physical deficiency on one hand, age-based incapacity on the other. Moreover, both Kohanim and Leviyim serve in the Mikdash, and a Kohen is in fact a subset of the tribe of Levi. One might well have argued that if blemishes disqualify Kohanim, they should certainly disqualify Leviyim as well — and that if age disqualifies Leviyim, it should at least disqualify Kohanim.

### Leviyim Age Derived

The Gemara asks, mena hani milei — where does this come from? The braita cites the verse zot asher la-Levi'im and connects it with the verse umiben hamishim shanah yashuv, establishing that years disqualify Leviyim. The relevant pesukim are in Behaalotecha, where after describing the ritual dedication of the Leviyim the Torah states: miben chamesh ve-esrim shanah va-ma'alah yavo litzvo tzava ba-avodat ohel mo'ed — from 25 and above they shall come to serve in the army of the Ohel Mo'ed — and then umiben hamishim shanah yashuv mitzva ha-avoda velo ya'avod od. The imagery of military service — litzvo tzava — applied to the Leviyim mirrors the language used when Bnei Yisrael were counted for the actual army from age 20 onward.

From here the braita establishes: lamadnu la-Levi'im shehashanim poslim bahem — we learn that years disqualify Leviyim.

### Rejecting Kal for Leviyim

Once age is established as a disqualifier for Leviyim, the braita raises the question: yachol mumin poslim bahem — perhaps blemishes also invalidate Leviyim? The kal vachomer would run: Kohanim, for whom age is not a problem, are nonetheless disqualified by blemishes — how much more so should Leviyim, for whom age is a problem, be disqualified by blemishes? The Torah preempts this inference with the phrase zot asher la-Levi'im: this — and only this — is the disqualifying criterion for Leviyim. Ve'ein acheret la-Levi'im — there is no additional criterion. Blemishes are excluded.

### Age & Kohanim

The braita then attempts the reverse. Yachol yehu ha-Kohanim psulin ba-shanim — perhaps Kohanim are also disqualified by age? The kal vachomer: Leviyim, for whom blemishes are not a problem, are nonetheless disqualified by age — how much more so should Kohanim, for whom blemishes are a problem, be disqualified by age? This argument is reinforced by the fact, raised in the discussion, that Kohanim are a subset of Leviyim — if anything, one would expect them to carry at least as many, if not more, disqualifications.

### Reject Reverse Kal

The Torah again blocks this inference: asher la-Levi'im — this is for Leviyim — velo asher la-Kohanim. The age-based disqualification belongs to Leviyim alone and does not extend to Kohanim.

### Ohel Moed Only

The Gemara now raises a crucial limitation that was not stated in the Mishnah itself: yachol af be-Shilo uve-Veit Olamim ken? Perhaps the age restriction for Leviyim applies even in Shilo and in the permanent Beit HaMikdash in Yerushalayim? The verse teaches otherwise: la'avod avodat avodah va-avodat masa — the service designated for the 30-to-50 age range combines the avodat avodah, meaning the singing that accompanies the korbanot, together with avodat masa, the carrying of the Mishkan. The Gemara derives from this juxtaposition: lo amarti ela mizman she-ha-avoda ba-katef — this age restriction applies only when the service includes physical carrying.

### Carrying Requirement

Once the Jewish people entered the land and established a permanent or semi-permanent sanctuary — first in Shilo, then in Yerushalayim — the Leviyim were no longer required to transport the Mishkan on their shoulders. Consequently, the age restriction no longer applies. The capacity to carry was the functional rationale behind requiring a certain age range, and once carrying ceased to be part of the service, age ceased to be the operative criterion. It is notable that once they are above 50 and exempt from service, the Torah does say that they may still serve in mishmar, guard duty, as the Rambam explains — guarding the Mikdash is a form of showing honor and respect to a sacred place, much as important institutions post sentries as a mark of dignity.

### 25 vs. 30 Years

A textual problem must be addressed. The Torah in Naso and Bamidbar counts the Leviyim from 30 to 50 — miben shloshim shanah ve-ad ben hamishim shanah kol haba litzvo tzava ba-avodat ohel mo'ed — the exact same phrase litzvo tzava used in Behaalotecha, where the starting age is 25. These two figures appear to be in direct contradiction.

The resolution: kaf-hei lilmod u-shloshim la-avodah — at 25 one begins studying and training; at 30 one enters active service. There is a five-year apprenticeship period. The Gemara even notes a subtle textual hint in the choice of language: when referring to age 25, the verse uses yavo litzvo, connoting coming toward a future entry, whereas the counting from 30 describes those already fully engaged in the service — though as the Gemara itself notes, the exact same phrase litzvo tzava appears in both contexts, so this linguistic distinction may not be definitive.

What is clear is that the resolution is: five years of training and practice, followed by twenty years of active service from 30 to 50.

### Five-Year Mastery

The Gemara draws a broader principle from this five-year training period: letalmid shelo ra'ah siman yafeh be-mishnato chamesh shanim, shuv eino roeh — a student who has not shown positive progress in mastering a subject within five years will not succeed in it. The implication is practical: if after five years of serious study one has not achieved command of the material, it is likely time to consider a different direction.

### Three vs. Five Years

Rabbi Yossi disagrees with the five-year figure: he holds that three years is the threshold — as derived from the verse in Daniel, u-legadlam shanim shalosh, referring to the three-year program in which the captive nobles of Jerusalem were taught sefer and leshon Kasdim, the literature and language of the Chaldeans. If mastery is not achieved in three years, Rabbi Yossi holds, it will not come.

The Gemara reconciles the two opinions: shani lashon Kasdim de-kalil — the language of the Chaldeans is relatively easy to acquire and therefore requires only three years; while shani hilchos avoda de-tkifin — the laws of the Temple service are particularly demanding and therefore require a full five years. The baseline for most areas lies somewhere between them, with the five-year rule applying to more complex disciplines and the three-year rule to simpler ones. One might have thought the Leviyim required little time to master their duties — after all, their service was singing and playing instruments, not the intricate halachic performance of the Kohanim — yet the Gemara uses the language hilchos avoda de-tkifin, suggesting that the full mastery of their service was considered genuinely demanding.

---

## Conceptual Framework

### Kohen as Kli Kodesh

Having established the halachic rules, the Gemara's discussion invites us to consider what underlying conceptual distinction drives this difference. The Rambam, in his Mishneh Torah, groups the laws pertaining to Kohanim together with the laws of klei hamikdash vehamishartim bo — the sacred vessels of the Mikdash and those who serve within it. The Kohanim are treated, in an important sense, as klei kodesh — holy vessels. This is not merely a metaphor. The Torah describes the Mikdash as a place of overwhelming aesthetic and ritual perfection: everything is gold, silver, and beautiful; the korbanot are unblemished; every object that participates in the service of the Mikdash is required to be free of blemish. The Kohen, as one of the functioning elements of the Mikdash, participates in this same demand for perfection.

Many details of halachah reflect this conception of the Kohen as a kind of sacred vessel: the Kohen does not wear shoes in the Mikdash because the ritzpa mekadeshes — the sanctity of the floor connects through his bare feet to him, and through him to the korban. The concept of be-atzmo shel Kohen — the body of the Kohen as a site of sacred status — appears in multiple contexts, including the bedikos. It is the Kohen's very person that must conform to the standard of unblemished holiness required of the Mikdash's sacred contents.

### Levi as Servant

The Levi, by contrast, is never cast in those terms. Although the Torah does wave the Leviyim as a kind of korban during their dedication — treating them in some respect like a sacrificial offering — the Torah uses the word kodesh far less for them than it does for Kohanim. What dominates the description of the Leviyim is the language of service and assistance: netunim netunim hem lo — they are given over, designated to assist the Kohanim. The very name Levi connotes attachment and service. They are not presented as holy vessels but as capable servants.

What disqualifies a servant is not aesthetics but incapacity. The Levi's disqualifying criterion is therefore functional: can he perform the service he is assigned to? When the service involved carrying the Mishkan — physically demanding, requiring strength and endurance — age was the relevant criterion. A Levi too young had not yet reached full physical maturity, and one past 50 was presumed to have declined in physical capacity. When the service no longer involved carrying but was limited to song and musical accompaniment, the relevant criterion became the voice: ve'afilu mumin poslim bahem, a defective voice would disqualify — not because of any concern for the aesthetics of the Mikdash, but because he cannot perform the job he is there to do.

### Soloveitchik

Rav Soloveitchik in his Shiurim le-Zecher Abba Mari develops this distinction at length. His formulation is that the Levi's service is fundamentally role-based, while the Kohen's service involves being fully given over — a total sanctification of his person. He adduces a striking illustration: if a Kohen declares that he objects in principle to any one aspect of the kehunah — that he finds some element of it distasteful or refuses it — he is not a valid Kohen. The Kohen must be entirely surrendered to the whole of the service; any reservation undermines the totality of the dedication.

By contrast, the Levi's service is explicitly divided by role. Some Leviyim are assigned to the gates; others to the singing. A Levi designated for one role may not perform the other. Rav Soloveitchik sees in this precisely the contrast: the Kohen's service flows from a state of total sanctification — any crack in that totality compromises the whole. The Levi's service is about assignment to a specific function, and it is the ability to discharge that function that alone determines his fitness. This framework illuminates why mumin disqualify the Kohen — because he must be an unblemished kli kodesh — while shanim, age, disqualifies the Levi — because it determines whether he is capable of the work he has been assigned.

---

## Specific Requirements

### Kohanim Age Range

The Gemara now spells out the precise parameters. Kol mi she-hevi shtei searot ad she-yazkin — a Kohen is kasher for service from the time he reaches halachic adulthood, marked by the appearance of shtei searot, two pubic hairs, until he becomes old. U-mumin poslin bo — and blemishes disqualify him throughout. There is no fixed upper age limit, as there was for Leviyim in the Ohel Mo'ed; rather, the criterion is a functional one determined individually.

### Leviyim Age 30–50

Ben Levi mi-ben shloshim ve-ad ben hamishim kasher la-avodah — a Levi is fit for service from 30 to 50, in the context of the Ohel Mo'ed in the midbar. Ve-shanim poslin bo — age disqualifies, both as too old and by implication too young, since only from 30 onward is one counted.

### Leviyim Voice Only

Bameh devarim amurim — when does this apply? Be-Ohel Mo'ed she-ba-midbar — only in the Ohel Mo'ed in the desert. Aval be-Shilo u-Veit Olamim — but in Shilo and in the permanent Beit HaMikdash, ein nifsalim ela be-kol — they are disqualified only on account of their voice. This is the elegant internal logic of the Levi's functional criterion: when the service was about carrying, the criterion was physical capacity as measured by age. When the service is about singing, the criterion is vocal capacity. If the voice remains strong, age is no disqualifier.

### Voice Requirement

Amar Rav Yossi: mai kra — what verse establishes that even elderly Leviyim may sing as long as their voice is good? Vayehi ke-echad la-mechatztzerim vela-meshorerim le-hashmia kol echad — they were like one, the trumpeters and the singers together, producing a single unified voice. Rashi explains that the emphasis of vayehi ke-echad is to include even those who are older, who join in the unified choral sound. The verse encompasses them because they are still capable of contributing to the kol echad. Notably, this verse also addresses the playing of musical instruments alongside the singing — a point relevant to the broader discussion of which roles belong specifically to the Leviyim and how central each is to their designated service.

### Trembling Criterion

Returning to the Kohanim, ad she-yazkin — until he becomes old — raises the question: ad kama, how old is too old? Amar Rabbi Ila amar Rabbi Chanina: ad she-yiratev — until he trembles. There is no fixed year cutoff; the criterion is physical infirmity manifest as unsteadiness. Each person's fitness is assessed individually.

This prompts the Gemara to juxtapose a related discussion from another context. A braita teaches: baal keri she-taval velo hetil mayim — someone who had a seminal emission and immersed in the mikvah but did not urinate afterward — u-le-cheshe-yatil tamei — when he subsequently urinates, he is tamei, because a residual drop of semen is assumed to emerge with the urine. Rabbi Yossi qualifies: be-choleh u-ve-zaken tamei — this concern applies only to a sick person or an elderly person, whose full seminal discharge cannot be assumed. Be-yeled u-be-viri, tahor — for a young and healthy person, we assume complete discharge.

Yeled ad kama — how young qualifies as yeled for this purpose? Amar Rabbi Ila amar Rabbi Chanina: kol she-omed al raglo achat ve-choletz minalo ve-noel minalo — anyone who can stand on one foot and remove and put on his shoe. This is a test of balance and physical stability. Amru alav al Rabbi Chanina she-haya ben shemonim shanah ve-haya omed al raglo achat ve-choletz minalo ve-noel minalo — it was said of Rabbi Chanina himself that at 80 years of age he could stand on one foot and take off and put on his shoe. He attributed this to the hot water and oil with which his mother anointed him in his youth: chamin ve-shemen she-sachtani immi be-yalduti hen amdu li be-et ziknuti — they stood by him in his old age. The test in this braita, while not directly parallel to the Kohen's service, illustrates the same principle: fitness is assessed individually based on demonstrated physical capacity, not by a fixed numerical cutoff.

### Kohen Ritual Roles

The Gemara presents another braita on the theme of age and service. Nitmalei zikno — when a person's beard is filled out, raui laasot shaliach tzibbur — he is fit to serve as shaliach tzibbur, veleired lifnei ha-teivah — to lead davening, velisa et kapav — and if he is a Kohen, to perform Nesi'at Kapayim, the priestly blessing. Rashi explains that shaliach tzibbur in this context is not limited to leading prayer; it encompasses communal leadership roles more broadly: litkoah shofar — blowing the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, velinot — pronouncing excommunication, velimnot parnas — being appointed as a lay communal leader. In all of these functions, a mature appearance is a prerequisite — not a technical halachic threshold so much as a social requirement of communal respect. The lists found in various Gemarot discussing the qualifications of a chazan mention age, marital status, and communal acceptance — but conspicuously do not explicitly require a fine voice, though this is addressed separately.

### Rebbi's 20-Year Rule

On the question of when a Kohen may begin his service, the Mishnah states misheyavi shtei searot — from the time he achieves halachic adulthood. Rebbi, however, says: omer ani, ad ben esrim — I say, not until age 20. Rav Chisda explains Rebbi's source: the verse vayaamidu et ha-Levi'im miben esrim shanah va-malah le-natzeach al melechet Beit Hashem — the Leviyim were appointed from the age of 20 to oversee the work of Beit Hashem. Rashi interprets lenatzeach here as referring to physically demanding service that requires great fortitude and strength. The implication drawn is that service in the Mikdash in general requires this level of maturity.

The Gemara then asks: but this verse is written about Leviyim — how can it be applied to Kohanim? This is resolved through the principle stated by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: be-esrim ve-arba mekomot nikru Kohanim Levi'im — in twenty-four places in the Torah, Kohanim are referred to as Levi'im. This is one of them — as illustrated by the verse veha-Kohanim ha-Levi'im bnei Tzadok, where Tzadok was unmistakably a Kohen, yet described as a Levite. Rashi adds that the name Levi itself can connote service — v'ani shamati lashon Levi'im shamashim, citing kmo ve-yilavu alecha ve-ishartucha — they shall accompany and assist you — so that calling Kohanim Levi'im underscores their role as servants and assistants in the Mikdash. Against Rebbi's position, the Gemara raises the objection that this verse specifically concerns a particular kind of overseer work — likely the physical construction work in the time of Ezra — rather than the standard service of Kohanim in the Mikdash.

### Respect vs. Invalidity

The Gemara presents a final ambiguity about the status of a Kohen younger than twenty. Aval echav ha-Kohanim ein manichin oto la-avodah ad she-yehei ben esrim — his fellow Kohanim will not allow him to perform the avodah until he is twenty, out of respect for the dignity of the service.

The Gemara records two views: ika de-amri ha Rebbi hi — some say this reflects Rebbi's position that twenty is a genuine requirement; ve-afilu psul de-rabbanan leit leh — and even so, Rebbi would hold that less than twenty is not even a rabbinic invalidity, only a social convention among the Kohanim. Ve-ika de-amri — others say that Rebbi does hold twenty is a genuine rabbinically-imposed invalidity; and the ruling that fellow Kohanim prevent the younger one from serving reflects the view of the other Rabbis, for whom it is merely a matter of lechatchilah — they prefer not to allow it, but bedi'eved avodato ksheirah — after the fact, the service is valid.

This discussion illuminates a distinction that runs through the entire treatment of age as a criterion: some age thresholds are hard halachic invalidities, while others are expressions of communal respect and dignity. Just as one might feel that it is inappropriate for a very young person to lead the Yamim Noraim davening for a community — even if they have a beautiful voice — the Torah and rabbinic tradition reflect an awareness that who represents and serves a community carries weight beyond the technical question of minimum capacity.

Tosafot raises a practical question arising from all of this: since children accompany their fathers to the duchan for Birkas Kohanim, and these children are clearly below Bar Mitzvah age, how does this square with the requirement of shtei searot? Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing between going up alone and going up alongside adults: when adults of proper age are already performing the mitzvah, a younger Kohen may join them. The concern about communal respect is satisfied by the presence of the qualified adults; the child's accompanying participation does not compromise the blessing. However, this leniency appears to apply to Birkas Kohanim specifically; in the context of actual Temple service, the age threshold of thirteen — or twenty per Rebbi — appears to be treated more strictly, with or without other Kohanim present.

---

## Pottery & Tumah

### Initial Rule Reversal

The Mishnah presents yet another case of inverse rules: tahor bikli cheres tamei bechol ha-keilim, tahor bechol ha-keilim tamei bikli cheres — what renders a pottery vessel tahor is what renders other vessels tamei, and what renders other vessels tahor is what renders a pottery vessel tamei.

### Space vs. Contact

The operative distinction is this: for all ordinary vessels, tumah is transmitted through contact — a sheretz or other source of tumah that touches the vessel, whether on its exterior or interior surface, transmits tumah. For pottery vessels, the mechanism is entirely different: what matters is not contact but presence within the contained airspace — the avir — of the vessel. If a tamei object is suspended in midair within a pottery vessel without touching its walls, the vessel becomes tamei. Conversely, if that same object touches the outside of a pottery vessel, the vessel remains tahor entirely. The back of a pottery vessel — gabo — is impervious to tumah; avir kli cheres tamei, gabo tahor.

The reverse applies to ordinary vessels: avir kol ha-keilim tahor, gaban tamei — presence in the interior airspace of a non-pottery vessel does not transmit tumah, but external contact does.

### Kol Asher Betocho

The Gemara asks, vahani mili mena lan — what is the scriptural basis? The braita cites the verse kol asher be-tocho — everything that is within it — said in connection with a pottery vessel. The verse makes tamei anything inside the vessel, ve-af al pi shelo naga — even if it did not touch. The question is whether the verse means merely that an object inside that is also touching becomes tamei, or whether mere presence — without physical contact — suffices.

### Two Verses Proof

Rabbi Yonasan ben Abtolmos resolves this through a textual comparison. The Torah uses the word tocho in two related contexts: one describing objects within a pottery vessel that become tamei, and another describing the vessel itself becoming tamei because of what is within it. He argues: mah tocho ha-amur leitamei — when the Torah says that the presence of a tamei object inside the vessel makes the vessel tamei — af al pi shelo naga — even if that object did not actually touch the vessel walls. Therefore, af tocho ha-amur letamei — when the Torah says objects inside the vessel become tamei, the same logic applies: af al pi shelo naga — even if those objects do not touch the vessel walls.

### Mustard Seed Example

The practical force of this principle is illustrated by an example. The Torah testified that a pottery vessel transmits tumah to things within it ve-afilu malei chardal — even if it is filled with mustard seeds — tiny seeds, like poppy seeds. Consider: if a pottery vessel is filled with such seeds and a tamei object enters it, only those seeds at the very surface might be said to touch anything at all. Yet the Torah indicates that all of the seeds inside — potentially millions of them — become tamei. This cannot be explained through contact, since the overwhelming majority of seeds are not in contact with the tamei object, and moreover tumah does not continue to spread from food to food indefinitely once the first degree of transmission is reached. The only coherent explanation is that the mechanism is presence within the enclosed space of the vessel, not physical contact. And since we know that the millions of seeds inside a sealed pottery vessel become tamei through presence alone, we similarly conclude that the pottery vessel itself becomes tamei through the presence of a tamei object within its airspace — regardless of whether contact occurs.

# Hullin 25

## Pottery Vessels Interior

### Pottery vs Other Vessels

The daf opens at 25a with the declaration of Rav Adda bar Ahava to Rava. Before engaging the new sugya, it is worth setting out the foundational distinction that frames the entire discussion. Normal vessels become tamei when a source of tumah — such as the carcass of a dead animal — touches them, whether it touches their exterior or interior. The operative mechanism is contact. A kli cheres, however, is governed by an entirely different principle. The Torah states, *asher yippol mehem el tocho* — "that which falls into its interior." For a pottery vessel, what matters is the presence of a source of tumah within the interior. If the tumah-source is suspended inside the vessel without touching it, the vessel becomes tamei; if it touches the pottery from the outside, without entering the interior, the vessel does not become tamei.

The Gemara demonstrates this from the very opening of 25a: *veafilu malei chardal* — even if the vessel is filled with mustard seed, everything inside it becomes tamei. This is striking. If tumah transmission in a pottery vessel operated through contact, only the mustard seeds directly touching the walls of the jar would become tamei; the remainder, separated from the vessel's surface by intervening seeds, could not be reached. Since the Torah declares that everything inside becomes tamei, the mechanism must be presence in the interior rather than physical contact. This is how a kli cheres differs: it receives and transmits tumah through interiority, not touch.

### Kal Vachomer Challenge

Having established this distinction, the Gemara immediately faces a challenge from Rav Adda bar Ahava. He poses a kal vachomer: let a kli cheres become tamei *migabbo* — from its back, meaning its exterior, through contact — by the following reasoning. All other vessels, which do not receive tumah through their interior, do nevertheless become tamei through contact with their exterior. A pottery vessel, which has the stronger capacity of becoming tamei through something merely present in its interior, should *a fortiori* also become tamei through direct contact from the outside.

The argument is not without force. Contact is the most natural and obvious mode of tumah transmission — it is how virtually everything else in the world of tumah operates. If a pottery vessel possesses the enhanced capacity to receive tumah through presence in the interior, without even touching, one might indeed expect it to receive tumah through the more basic mechanism of contact as well.

### Sealed Vessels Refutation

The Gemara responds by citing a verse: *vechol kli patuach asher ein tzamid patil alav tamei hu* — "every open vessel upon which there is no tightly sealed cover, it shall be tamei." This verse concerns vessels found in an ohel hamet, a dwelling in which a human corpse lies. Under a roof shared with a corpse, everything present becomes tamei. Yet the Torah declares that a pottery vessel with a tightly sealed cover remains tahor.

The Gemara asks: how can a sealed cover protect a pottery vessel from tumah? Everything under the roof becomes tamei. The answer is clear: if the pottery vessel receives tumah exclusively through its interior, and the seal prevents access to the interior, then the interior is not exposed to the ohel hamet and the vessel remains tahor. But if the pottery vessel's exterior is also exposed — which it obviously is — and if exterior contact sufficed to convey tumah, the seal would be meaningless. The fact that the Torah attributes complete protection to the sealed cover demonstrates that a pottery vessel is not susceptible to tumah from its exterior at all. The exterior of the pottery vessel, even in an ohel hamet, simply does not count.

The Gemara draws this conclusion through a play on language: *eizu kli shetumato kodemet lepitcho* — which type of vessel is it that tumah arrives, as it were, at its opening? The answer: *hevei omer zeh kli cheres* — this is the pottery vessel. The tumah enters specifically through the opening, through the interior, and through no other route.

### Tumah Nature Debate

This discussion naturally prompts a deeper question: why should pottery vessels operate so differently from other vessels? One notes that in the laws of kashrut, the porous nature of pottery — its capacity to absorb taste and its inability to be fully purified through conventional means — provides a rationale for special treatment. But for tumah, the distinction seems to lack any physical justification. Tumah appears to be a purely ritualistic designation.

A further consideration: the Torah does not permit pottery vessels to be purified in a mikvah. Other vessels — wood, metal — can be immersed and rendered tahor. For pottery, once it becomes tamei, it must be broken. This consequence is far more severe. It may therefore be that the Torah, precisely because the consequences of tumah for pottery vessels are so severe, sought to limit the avenues through which they become tamei. Restricting tumah reception to the interior — and specifically reading *tocho* as an alternative to contact rather than an addition to it — serves a protective function. Sealing the interior is far simpler than guarding every exterior surface. This gives practical relief to anyone in whose home a person died, which in ancient times would have been a common occurrence.

This, of course, raises the inverse question: why cannot pottery vessels be purified in a mikvah in the first place? That remains without a fully satisfying answer. But at minimum, the two features — restricted modes of tumah reception and inability to purify — form a coherent pair, even if neither is individually explained from first principles.

The question of whether tumah is a purely ritualistic designation or something with metaphysical or quasi-physical reality is one the Gemara itself does not resolve, and it reflects two fundamentally different orientations. One approach understands tumah as a kind of real, spreading phenomenon — something that actually moves through space, that bursts upward from a corpse, spreads under a roof, and reaches whatever lies beneath it. On this view, the laws of tumah describe a kind of physics of impurity. The other approach treats tumah not as a thing in itself but as a description of the relationship between a person or object and a source of impurity. One becomes tamei not because something called tumah physically reached him, but because of his proximity or relational exposure to the source. Both approaches have their proponents, and neither is without difficulty. The case of a kohen flying at great altitude over a cemetery is equally hard to explain on either account — tumah spreading thirty thousand feet upward is as difficult to conceptualize as a relationship with a source thirty thousand feet below.

### Reversed Kal Vachomer

Having established that pottery vessels receive tumah exclusively from their interior, the Gemara attempts the reverse kal vachomer. If pottery vessels, which do not become tamei from their exterior, do become tamei from their interior — then all other vessels, which do become tamei from their exterior, should *a fortiori* also become tamei from their interior, through mere presence of a tumah-source within them.

The Gemara rejects this by appeal to the word *tocho* — "its interior" — used in the Torah in the context of pottery vessels. *tocho shel zeh*, the interior of this one — the pottery vessel — *ve-lo tocho shel acher*, and not the interior of any other type of vessel. The word *tocho*, with its possessive construction, teaches that interior-based tumah reception is the exclusive property of the pottery vessel and is not extended to metal, wood, or any other class of vessel.

One clarification is worth making explicit. Although the Gemara frames the contrast as interior versus exterior, this is a simplification. Other vessels, if something touches their interior, do also become tamei — but that is because of the touch, not because of presence within the interior. The Gemara is distinguishing between two modes of reception: contact (which governs other vessels) and presence-in-the-interior (which governs pottery alone).

There is then a further attempted argument: perhaps other vessels require both conditions simultaneously — contact with the interior specifically, so that neither contact with the exterior alone nor presence in the interior alone would suffice. The Gemara rejects this as well by returning to *vechol kli patuach*. That verse demonstrates that in an ohel hamet, sealed pottery vessels are tahor and all other vessels are tamei regardless of whether they are sealed — meaning other vessels become tamei through their exterior exposure, with no interior requirement whatsoever.

### Four Derashot Tocho

At this point the Gemara raises an objection: if *tocho* is being used to teach that interior-based tumah applies only to pottery and not to other vessels, how can that usage be legitimate? The word *tocho* has already been deployed for other purposes.

The Gemara answers: *arba tocho ketivei* — effectively, we extract four derashot from the word *tocho*. The Torah uses the root *toch* twice in the relevant passages, and since the Torah could have expressed the idea differently — Tosafot notes that the text could have said simply *bo*, "into it," rather than *tocho*, "into its interior" — the specific language of *toch* is itself an addition that licenses interpretation. Thus we have four derashot.

The first, *chad l'gufei*, is the peshat meaning: a tumah-source that falls into the interior of a pottery vessel renders it tamei. The second, *chad l'gezeirah shavah*, teaches through a parallel derivation that just as the vessel transmits tumah to everything inside it — hence the case of mustard seeds where every single seed becomes tamei — so too it receives tumah from whatever is present in its interior, even without contact. The third, *chad* — *tocho shel zeh ve-lo tocho shel acher* — teaches that interior-based tumah is exclusive to the pottery vessel and does not apply to other vessels. The fourth remains.

### Vessel Within Vessel

The fourth derashah is *tocho ve-lo toch tocho* — the interior, but not the interior of the interior. This teaches a principle of spatial containment: *ve-afilu kli shetef* — and this applies even with respect to non-pottery vessels (*kli shetef* being the term for vessels that can be purified through immersion in a mikvah, that is, all non-pottery vessels).

The principle operates as follows. If one vessel is placed inside another — imagine a smaller vessel sitting within a larger pottery vessel — then what is inside the inner vessel is considered to be located in the inner vessel and not in the outer one, provided that the walls of the inner vessel extend higher than those of the outer vessel. This has two practical consequences. First, if a tumah-source is in the inner vessel, the outer pottery vessel does not become tamei, because the tumah-source is considered to be located in the inner vessel, not in the pottery vessel. Second, if the outer pottery vessel is tamei, food inside the inner vessel remains tahor, because that food is considered to be in the inner vessel, not in the outer one.

Why does the inner vessel not itself become tamei when surrounded by a tamei outer vessel, thereby passing tumah to its contents? Rashi explains that pottery vessels communicate tumah only to foods; they do not make other vessels tamei. So the inner vessel itself remains tahor, it operates as an independent location, and what is inside it is protected accordingly.

One might ask: why should the food in the inner vessel care? Even if the inner vessel is tahor, once a tamei outer pottery vessel surrounds everything, should the food not be considered to be in the outer vessel as well? The derashah answers precisely this. Even though the inner vessel is physically inside the outer one, what is inside the inner vessel — when its walls extend higher — is considered to be in the inner vessel only, not in the outer one. The principle of *tocho ve-lo toch tocho* is specifically about the food and other contents, not about the vessel itself.

This question of how to locate an object that is in one thing which is itself inside another thing recurs throughout the Gemara. A well-known parallel involves the principle of *keilav shel lokeach*: if a buyer's vessel is sitting in the seller's courtyard and the seller places the merchandise inside the buyer's vessel, does the buyer acquire it? The object is in the buyer's vessel, but the vessel is in the seller's domain — so which is the operative location? The pottery vessel case resolves its version of this problem by applying the rule of *tocho ve-lo toch tocho*: when the inner vessel's walls stand higher, what is inside it is exclusively in that inner vessel.

---

## Wood vs Metal Vessels

### Wood/Metal Intro

The Mishnah now introduces a new pairing. *tahor b'khlei etz tamei b'khlei matachot; tahor b'khlei matachot tamei b'khlei etz* — what is pure for wood vessels is impure for metal vessels, and vice versa. The subject here has shifted from the mode by which tumah is received to the question of what constitutes a vessel in the first place — that is, what state of completion a vessel must achieve before it becomes susceptible to tumah at all.

The distinction is this: wood vessels require a *kibbul* — a receptacle, a hollowed-out interior capable of containing something — in order to be susceptible to tumah. This is derived from the verse *kol kli etz o beged o or o sak* — just as a sack is defined by its capacity to contain things, so a wood vessel must have a receptacle. A wood knife, for example, is entirely functional but has no receptacle; it does not become tamei. Metal vessels, by contrast, do not require a receptacle — a metal knife does become tamei. What metal vessels require instead is *gemar melacha*, the finishing of the work, the completion of every last step of manufacture.

### Unfinished Wood

The Gemara elaborates with a Baraita. *golemi klei etz* — the word *golem* here means an unfinished product, evoking the image of the famous unformed creature of Jewish legend, a lump not yet fully made. Unfinished wood vessels are nonetheless tamei, provided they have a receptacle. *peshuteihen* — flat wood vessels without a receptacle — are tahor. For wood, the question of whether the object is finished or unfinished is irrelevant; what matters is only whether it has a hollowed interior.

The Gemara then provides examples of what "unfinished" means for a wood vessel: anything that still requires polishing (*lashuf*), the addition of filigree or engraving (*leshabetz*), scraping or sanding (*legarer*), carving (*lekarkev*), or sealing with an oil or fish-skin coating (*lehatiach betunas*). Furthermore, a vessel lacking a base (*mechusar kan*), or without a lip (*mechusar ogen*), or without handles (*mechusar ozen*) — all of these are still considered tamei if they have a receptacle, because for wood, it is the receptacle that defines vessel status.

### Receptacle Incomplete

A question arises: if a wood vessel is lacking the carving-out altogether — *mechusar chatita* — it is tahor. This seems obvious. The Gemara clarifies that the case is not obvious: *lo tzericha dechaka kafiza bekava* — the vessel is intended to hold a full kav, but so far only a smaller receptacle has been carved. The vessel does have some receptacle, but the intended receptacle has not yet been completed. In this case, the incomplete intention matters. Even though a functioning, if shallower, receptacle exists, the fact that the maker intends a deeper receptacle and has not yet finished carving it out means the vessel is not yet complete as a receptacle and remains tahor.

This introduces an element of intentionality even into the wood vessel analysis, where ordinarily we emphasize objective function. It is a notable qualification.

Tosafot raises a tension with another Gemara, in the second chapter of Sanhedrin, which states that a kneading trough and a bed — *ha'arisa vehamitah* — become susceptible to tumah only after being smoothed with fish skin (*misheyishufam be'or hadag*). This seems to contradict the Baraita here, which says that even if a wood vessel has not yet been smoothed, it is tamei if it has a receptacle. Tosafot resolves this cleanly: the smoothing referred to in Sanhedrin means removing large splinters that would injure someone using the vessel. Without that, the object is not yet truly usable and so has not achieved vessel status at all. The polishing mentioned here in our Gemara, however, refers to purely aesthetic finishing — making it look nicer and smoother — which does not affect usability. Thus: removing hazardous splinters is a prerequisite for function; decorative polishing is not.

### Unfinished Metal

For metal vessels the rule is reversed. *golemi klei matachot* — unfinished metal vessels — are tahor. A vessel missing its polishing, its filigree, its final engraving, its final hammer blow (*lehakish bekurnas*), is not yet susceptible to tumah. The concept of *makeh bepatish* — the final hammer blow — is well known from the laws of Shabbat as the paradigm of the finishing touch, and it applies here directly. A metal vessel that has not received this final completion, this last stage of manufacture, is not yet a vessel for purposes of tumah.

Noteworthy is what does not matter for metal: *mechusar kan o ogen o ozen* — if a metal vessel is missing its base, its lip, or its handles, it is nonetheless tamei already, because those attachments are considered separate objects, not integral parts of the vessel itself. Conversely, *mechusar kisuy* — if it is merely missing a cover — it is tamei, because the cover is similarly a separate object and not part of the vessel's completion.

### Honor vs Expense

The Gemara now poses a question that is unusual in this type of sugya: *mai shna hani u-mai shna hani* — what is the reason for this distinction? Why does metal require finishing but not receptacle, and wood require receptacle but not finishing? Two amoraim offer competing rationales.

Rabbi Yochanan explains: *ho'il u-lechavod asuyin* — metal vessels are made for use in contexts of honor and respect. One brings out metal vessels when receiving distinguished guests; metal belongs to the domain of the elevated and the ceremonial. Because of this association, a metal vessel must be in a fully finished, presentable state before it attains vessel status. An unfinished metal vessel is incongruous with the honored purpose for which metal is used; it has not yet become what it is meant to be. Wood vessels, being common and ordinary, carry no such expectation, and thus their mere functionality — having a receptacle — suffices.

Rav Nachman disagrees. His reasoning is *hovu de-damei yakarim* — they are expensive. Metal costs more, and someone paying a significant price for a metal vessel expects to receive a finished product. The consideration is not the social context of use but the economic investment and the expectation that comes with it. An unfinished expensive item is not yet worth what it should be worth; it has not yet been completed in the sense that matters to its owner.

### Bone Vessels

The practical difference between these two rationales is identified through the test case of bone vessels (*klei etzem*). Bone vessels were presumably expensive — worked bone is a costly material. However, bone vessels are not specifically associated with contexts of honor and ceremony in the way metal vessels are; they are used by ordinary people in ordinary contexts.

On Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning, bone vessels would not require finishing, since they are not vessels made for honored occasions. On Rav Nachman's reasoning, bone vessels would require finishing, since they are expensive items and the criterion is cost rather than social context.

The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman follows his own reasoning: *ve'azal Rav Nachman leta'amei* — Rav Nachman rules that bone vessels are like metal vessels and require finishing before they become susceptible to tumah.

### Bone Biblical Tumah

The Gemara observes that this entire discussion implies — *miklal* — that bone vessels are susceptible to tumah at the biblical level, since the debate about their status appears to be conducted at the level of biblical law. A Baraita then confirms this. Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka asks: what does the verse *vechol ma'aseh izim titchata'u* — "all things made of goats you shall purify" — teach? The straightforward reading would limit biblical tumah susceptibility to things made from goat hair. But the Baraita expands: *lehavi davar haba min ha'izim* — to include things that come from other parts of the goat, *min hakarnayim* — from the horns — and *umin hatalpayim* — from the hooves. Worked horn and hoof, which are essentially bone-like materials, are thus biblically susceptible to tumah.

How do we know this extends beyond goats to other animals? The verse also says *vechol ma'aseh* — "all acts," in a broader formulation. If so, why mention goats specifically? *perat le'ofot* — to exclude bird bones. Something made from bird bones would not become tamei, either because they are too fragile or too insignificant. Only things made from the bones, horns, or hooves of land animals are included.

---

## Agriculture & Commerce

### Nuts Obligation

The Mishnah now shifts entirely, moving from the domain of tumah and tahara to that of Zeraim — agricultural law. The pairing follows the same structural pattern: *hachayav bishkedim hamarin patur bimetukin, hachayav bimetukin patur bamarin* — one who is obligated with respect to bitter almonds is exempt with respect to sweet ones, and vice versa. The question is when something is considered food and thus obligated in trumot u'ma'asrot.

Two varieties of nuts are contrasted. Bitter almonds are edible and palatable when they are small and immature; once they reach full maturity they become bitter to the point of inedibility. Sweet almonds follow the opposite trajectory: when immature they are not yet edible, but once fully developed they are desirable food. Obligation in trumot u'ma'asrot tracks edibility. Thus the small, immature bitter almonds are obligated; the mature bitter almonds are exempt. The mature sweet almonds are obligated; the immature ones are exempt. What makes something obligated in one case exempts it in the other, and vice versa.

The Gemara cites a Baraita elaborating this principle: *shkedim hamarin ktanim chayavin, gdolim pturin; metukin gdolim chayavin, ktanim pturin*. Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yossi then introduces a dissent in the name of his father: *zeh vezeh liphtur* — both forms of the bitter almond are exempt — and some say *zeh vezeh lachiyuv* — both are obligated. The view that both forms of the bitter almond are exempt is intelligible: even the immature bitter almond, though subjectively edible, is not yet an objectively developed fruit and might therefore be exempt on grounds of not having reached a recognizable stage of agricultural completeness. Rabbi Chanina is cited as ruling in practice according to the view that both are exempt.

### Processing via Fire

The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that both forms of the bitter almond are obligated — including the mature, bitter ones — how can the mature bitter almonds possibly be considered food? They are inedible in their raw state.

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *ho'il veyachol l'matkan al yedei ha'or* — since they can be rendered edible through cooking, through the application of fire, they are considered food. The potential for edibility through processing is sufficient to confer the status of food and trigger the obligation in trumot u'ma'asrot. Even something that is not presently edible raw may be obligated if it can be made edible through a recognized culinary process.

### Temed Wine

The Mishnah moves to another case of threshold classification: *ha-temed*. Temed is produced by adding water to grape lees — the residual grape matter remaining after pressing — and allowing the water to absorb the remaining juice. The result is a diluted, weaker form of wine-like liquid.

The question is whether temed is classified as water or as wine, and the Mishnah identifies the moment of fermentation as the decisive threshold. *ad shelo hechmit* — before it has fermented — temed is considered water. As water, it has two legal consequences. First, *eino nikach b'kesef ma'aser* — it cannot be purchased with ma'aser sheni money, since ma'aser sheni funds may only be spent on food and drink products of agricultural origin, not on mere water. Second, *u-posel et ha-mikvah* — if drawn temed is added to a mikvah that has not yet reached its required measure of forty se'ah, it invalidates the mikvah, since it is drawn water rather than rainwater or spring water.

*Mishe-hechmit* — once it has fermented — temed is reclassified as wine. It may then be purchased with ma'aser sheni money, and if it flows into a mikvah, it does not invalidate it, since wine is not drawn water for these purposes.

This connects to a broader structural point about modern mikvah construction. Standard mikva'ot maintain a sealed pit (*bor*) of forty se'ah of rainwater that no one ever enters, connected to the bathing pool from which water is regularly changed and cleaned. The entire legitimacy of the usable pool depends on its connection to that sealed bor, which never falls below the required minimum. Once the minimum is fully present, the addition of drawn water does not invalidate.

### Brothers Partners

The final Mishnah takes yet another turn, now addressing a question of civil and communal law that bears on the concepts of partnership and corporate unity. *ha-achim ha-shutfim* — brothers who are partners — can exist in two distinct legal configurations, and their obligations differ accordingly.

When brothers inherit a father's estate and then divide it between themselves before re-entering into a partnership, they are thereafter two separate individuals who happen to be in a joint business arrangement. In this configuration, each brother giving his annual half-shekel contribution is treated as a separate person giving a separate coin. They are therefore *chayavin b'kalbon* — obligated in the kalbon, the small additional fee paid to the money changer for breaking a full shekel into a half-shekel. However, because they are treated as independent individuals whose flocks are jointly owned through partnership, they are *pturim mi-ma'aser behemah* — exempt from the animal tithe, since ma'aser behemah applies to individually owned flocks, not to flocks held in partnership.

When brothers have not divided the estate and thus hold it as an undivided inheritance, the estate itself functions as a unified entity. One entity gives one full shekel — no half-shekel transaction, no money changer's fee. They are therefore *pturim min hakalbon*. But precisely because the flock belongs to a single unified entity rather than to separate individual owners, they are *chayavin b'ma'aser behemah* — obligated in the animal tithe.

This Mishnah touches on a conceptual question of considerable practical importance. Halacha recognizes partnership — a joint arrangement between two individuals who each retain their separate identities — but does not generally recognize the corporation as a legal entity distinct from its owners. The closest analogue in classical halachic thinking to what we would call a corporation is the undivided inherited estate. In that case, the estate itself is treated as a unified juridical entity, and the brothers are its owners but not individual partners in the ordinary sense. This distinction — between partnership and unified estate — is directly relevant to contemporary questions about the halachic status of corporations, where the inherited estate model serves as the primary point of comparison.

A concluding note from yesterday's discussion. Both Rashi and the Rambam — though the Gemara itself does not state it explicitly — assume that the twenty-four rotational groups (*mishmarot*) used for kohanim also applied equally to levi'im. The Mishnah in Ta'anit indicates that levi'im served on the same rotation, and the implication is that they were similarly divided into twenty-four groups, each serving roughly two weeks per year, with further subdivision by day within each week. In practice, any individual levi might have served as few as two days per year. On the separate question of a levi whose voice had deteriorated due to age or infirmity — and whether such a levi could continue in any role — the Rambam, employing the phrase *yeiraeh li* (indicating a conclusion without an explicit source), rules that a levi who can no longer sing may still serve in the other functions of the levitical role, such as gatekeeping. This accords with the principle discussed yesterday: the levi'im are defined by their service and their roles, and the loss of capacity in one role does not disqualify them from others.

---

---

# Hullin 26

## Survey of Six Orders

### Structure Overview

We pick up with the Gemara right after the Mishnah at the bottom of 25b. Before proceeding, it is worth noting something about the structure of the remaining Mishnayot in this perek. Throughout, we have been dealing with propositions of the form "what is true for A is not true for B, and what is true for B is not true for A." The Mishnah we just read — concerning water that has been soaked in grape leaves and is in the process of fermenting — does not quite fit that classical structure. It is not two different objects or two different spheres being compared; it is one thing undergoing a process, with the Mishnah saying that at one stage it is still water and at a later stage it is wine. Rashi points this out. So while there is a structural similarity — here these characteristics apply and not others — it is slightly different from what we have been seeing, and we will encounter that pattern in several of the later Mishnayot as well.

### All Six Orders

There is a second observation worth making about the structure of the perek as a whole. The Mishnayot in this section, taken together, appear to conduct a deliberate survey of all six Sedarim of Shas, and what is striking is that they are not mixed together — each Seder is treated in its own separate unit.

So far, we have covered Kodashim — dealing with which type of bird one brings as a sacrifice, Parah Adumah, Eglah Arufah, and related matters — followed by Taharot, concerning wooden, metal, and pottery vessels. Then came Zeraim, with questions about nuts and the stages at which they are considered bitter, and our present Mishnah about when something is considered wine, which touches on the obligation of Terumos UMa'asros and the eligibility for purchase with Kesef Ma'aser — and though it also touches on Mikvah law, it remains fundamentally a Zeraim question. That accounts for three Sedarim.

Looking ahead, the end of the perek's Mishnayot cover the remaining three. The question of brothers who inherit an estate and when it is treated as one or two estates may at first seem like a stretch, but Achim HaShutafim is a very common question in civil law — so that represents, at some level, Nezikin. The next Mishnah deals straightforwardly with Nashim, concerning at what stage certain legal categories apply to a girl. And the final Mishnah comes from Mo'ed. It appears highly intentional that all of Shisha Sidrei Shas — Kodashim, Taharot, Zeraim, Nezikin, Nashim, Mo'ed — are each dealt with separately and in sequence. It is not by chance.

### Metamed Water-Wine

With that introduction, we turn to the Gemara, which addresses the case of water that has absorbed some grape juice and the question of when it is considered water and when it is considered wine.

---

## Fermentation Debate

### Maasrot Mishna

The Gemara opens by asking: Mani Matnitin? Who authored our Mishnah? Lo Rebbe Yehuda Velo Rabbanan — it is neither Rabbi Yehuda nor the Rabbanan as we know them from a Mishnah in Maasrot. The Mishnah in Maasrot discusses the following case: HaMetamed VeNatan Mayim BeMidah — someone performing the process of metamed, soaking water in grape skins or leaves to produce a weak wine, puts in a measured quantity of water and UMatza Kedei Midato — finds upon removing the liquid that the quantity is exactly equal to what was put in. The significance is that whatever grape juice entered the water was not detectable through any increase in measured volume, suggesting the grape content is negligible. So is the result considered water or wine?

The Mishnah rules Patur — it is exempt from Terumos UMa'asros, meaning it is treated as water. Rabbi Yehuda Mechayev — Rabbi Yehuda obligates, holding that it is considered wine and therefore Chayav in Terumos UMa'asros regardless of the quantity measurement.

Now, note that neither opinion in the Maasrot Mishnah discusses fermentation at all — they debate whether there has been a measurable increase in quantity. Our Mishnah, however, makes fermentation the determining criterion. So the Gemara asks: how can our Mishnah be reconciled with the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan? Ei Rabbanan — if our Mishnah reflects the Rabbanan, the difficulty is that the Rabbanan seem to require a measurable increase in volume, not merely fermentation; af al gav de-hichmit, even if it fermented, without an increase in quantity they call it water. Ei Rebbi Yehuda — if our Mishnah reflects Rabbi Yehuda, the difficulty runs the other way: af al gav de-lo hichmit, Rabbi Yehuda seems to require no fermentation at all, since he calls it wine even without any measurable increase. So our Mishnah, which pivots entirely on the question of fermentation, appears to fit neither position.

### Rav Nachman: Hichmit

Amar Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha — the first resolution, appearing at the top of 26a, is as follows: Beshe-hichmit machloket — the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan applies specifically when the metamed has already fermented. This explains the logic of each position: the Rabbanan can acknowledge that fermentation has occurred, yet maintain that without a measurable increase in volume there is insufficient evidence of genuine grape content to call it wine. Rabbi Yehuda, for his part, does not require that measurable increase — fermentation itself is sufficient for him to call it wine. The Mishnah in Maasrot is therefore about a case that has fermented, and UMatnisin Rebbi Yehuda — our Mishnah, which does not mention any criterion of quantity and focuses solely on fermentation, follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yehuda does not add the criterion of increased quantity; he requires only fermentation, and that is precisely what our Mishnah says. Vecho'en amar Rebbi Yose b'Rebbi Chanina — Rabbi Yose the son of Rabbi Chanina made the same statement: Beshe-hichmit machloket, the dispute applies when it has fermented; otherwise, how could one even understand Rabbi Yehuda's position in calling it wine?

### Potential Fermentation

V'amar Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha — a further ruling from the same authority: if someone purchased temed with Kesef Ma'aser — as our Mishnah states is permitted once it has fermented — but purchased it before it fermented, and Uv'esof hichmit, in the end it did ferment, then Kana Ma'aser — the Kesef Ma'aser acquired it retroactively, meaning the sanctity of the Ma'aser money transferred validly to this liquid. The implicit reframing here is significant: although our Mishnah speaks of actual fermentation as the criterion, what this ruling suggests is that the real key is the capacity to ferment. If it will ferment in the future, that determination can be made retroactively. As the Gemara explains: Iglay milta lemafrea depeyra hu — the matter has been revealed retroactively that it was fruit, that it was already wine. Since it ultimately fermented, we see that at the time of purchase it was already on the path to fermentation and therefore already carried the status of wine.

The Gemara immediately challenges this. Our Mishnah states: dektani hichmitz in, lo hichmitz lo — if it fermented, yes; if it did not ferment, no. The criterion appears to be actual present fermentation. But according to Rabbah bar Avuha, the Gemara objects, Dilma ishavte havei machmitz — perhaps if you had simply waited, it would have fermented eventually. How then can the Mishnah make any ruling based on whether it has fermented right now? The same problem applies to both legal consequences in our Mishnah: whether the metamed invalidates a Mikvah and whether it can be purchased with Kesef Ma'aser. According to Rabbah bar Avuha, the criterion should be will it ferment, not has it already fermented — so how does our Mishnah permit a determination based solely on its present state?

### Sample Test

Amar Rabba — Rabba resolves this by reinterpreting what our Mishnah is describing. Kesheshayer mimenu bekos velo hichmitz — the Mishnah is addressing a case where one set aside a small sample in a cup in order to monitor whether it will ferment. The determination is not made by looking at the liquid at a single moment and declaring it wine or water on the basis of current fermentation. Rather, one holds over a sample and checks that sample after some time to see whether it ferments. If the sample ferments, the ruling is that the original liquid was wine at the critical moment — when it fell into the Mikvah or was purchased with Kesef Ma'aser. If the sample does not ferment, the ruling is that it was water. The language of the Mishnah — "has it fermented?" — is therefore not asking about the liquid's present state at the moment of the event, but about the result of a prospective test conducted on a retained sample.

The underlying logic, as one participant helpfully articulated, is perhaps best framed not merely as "will it ferment" in some abstract future sense, but "is it currently in the process of fermenting?" — which is a state already underway and measurable, even if not yet apparent to the eye. The result of the sample test reveals what was already happening at the critical moment. This is admittedly not the plain pshat of the Mishnah; the plain reading speaks of has it fermented. But Rabbah bar Avuha reinterprets the criterion to be will it ferment, or more precisely, is it in the fermentation process, and Rabba reads that back into the Mishnah by positing that the Mishnah refers to a test conducted on a held sample, whose result retroactively determines the status at the critical time.

---

## Appearance & Taste

### Water-Milk Mixture

The Gemara now introduces an entirely different approach to our Mishnah. Rav amar hamani Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri hi — Rav says our Mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. The basis for this is a Mishnah in Mikva'ot: Gimmel lugin mayim chaser kortov shenafal letochan kortov yayin — three log of water missing a kortov, into which a kortov of wine fell, and umarean kemarei yayin — it looks like wine. The Mishnah rules lo pasul — it does not invalidate a Mikvah. This is the straightforward case: there are two independent reasons not to be concerned. First, it does not actually contain three log of water — only 2.99 log — and the full shiur of drawn water is required to invalidate; anything less is insufficient. Second, it no longer looks like water but like wine.

The Mishnah then presents the more difficult case: Gimmel lugin mayim chaser kortov — the same 2.99 log of water — shenafal letochan kortov chalav — into which a kortov of milk fell. Umarean kemarei mayim — and it looks like water. Now what? In terms of actual composition, it does not contain three log of water; it contains only 2.99 log of water. But it looks like three log of water. The question is whether we determine status by what it actually is or by what it appears to be.

The first opinion rules Shenafal lemikvah lo pasul — it did not invalidate the Mikvah — because actual content determines identity, not appearance. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri omer: Hakol holech achar hamareh — everything follows appearance. If it looks like water, it has the status of water regardless of its actual composition.

### Rav's Position

The principle of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri is that identity is determined not solely by what a substance factually is, but by the characteristics it exhibits — preeminently, its appearance. The Gemara now applies this principle to our Mishnah: Lav amar Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri batar chazuta azlinan? Does not Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri say that we define things based on how they appear?

### Appearance & Taste

Hacha nami zil batar chazuta v'taima — here too, go by appearance and taste. The Gemara here introduces taste alongside appearance, which is worth pausing over. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's Mishnah spoke only of appearance. Why does the Gemara feel comfortable adding taste?

The answer lies in an important structural point. For Kashrut questions, the primary criterion of identity is taste — ta'am. If a drop of chazir falls into a soup, the question is whether its taste is detectable; that is the operative standard for food matters. For non-food identity questions, such as whether something invalidates a Mikvah, appearance is more primary because that is how we ordinarily perceive and categorize things. The metamed case, however, straddles both spheres: whether it can be purchased with Kesef Ma'aser is a food-related determination, while whether it invalidates a Mikvah is a general identity question. One might have said the criteria differ depending on which sphere one is addressing, but the Gemara proceeds on the assumption that the same standard applies across both. Therefore, since Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri bases identity on exhibited characteristics rather than on what something objectively is, the Gemara extends his principle to include taste alongside appearance — both are relevant exhibited characteristics, and the Gemara feels justified in importing taste into his framework.

### Applied to Metamed

V'chazuta d'hai maya ninhu — the appearance of this temed that is going to ferment but has not yet fermented is that of water. The same is true of its taste. On any experiential basis — how we see it and how we taste it — it presents itself as water. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri does not care what something is in some objective, compositional sense; he cares about how it appears, how it tastes, and what characteristics it actually exhibits. Since this metamed does not yet look like wine and does not yet taste like wine, he is not prepared to call it wine. Our Mishnah, which demands that it actually have fermented before receiving the status of wine, is therefore Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position.

This stands in contrast to the position attributed to Rabbah bar Avuha, who says the criterion is what the substance objectively is undergoing — and something in the process of fermentation is, in that objective sense, wine, regardless of how it presently appears or tastes. The debate can thus be conceptualized as a fundamental question: is identity determined by what a substance objectively is or by how we experience it? Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri insists that our experienced reality — primarily through appearance but also through taste — defines identity, not some standard that is inaccessible to ordinary perception. The Rabbanan in the water-milk case are, by contrast, measuring actual ingredients, and Rabbah bar Avuha in the fermentation case is measuring what process the substance is undergoing irrespective of perception. What unites Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri across both cases is the consistent appeal to experienced characteristics as the determinant of legal identity.

---

## Rabbi Elazar

### Before Fermentation

Ufleiga d'Rabbi Elazar — this entire framework, which assumed that the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan in Maasrot concerns a case that has already fermented, is disputed by Rabbi Elazar. D'amar Rabbi Elazar: hakol modim she-ein mafrishin alav mi-makom acher ela im ken hechmitz — everyone agrees, both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan, that one cannot take Terumot uMa'asrot from another place to exempt this metamed unless it has actually fermented. The significance of this statement is that Rabbi Elazar assumes the debate in Maasrot takes place when the metamed has not yet fermented — the opposite of what Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yose ben Rabbi Chanina assumed above. On this reading, the question Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbanan are disputing is whether the temed has wine status even before fermentation has occurred.

### Rabbinic Status

This makes Rabbi Yehuda's position considerably more difficult to understand. If it has not yet fermented and the volume has not measurably increased, on what basis does he call it wine? The Gemara explains: Kasavar belo hichmit machloket — Rabbi Elazar holds that the debate applies precisely when it has not yet fermented.

Accordingly, Rabbi Elazar qualifies Rabbi Yehuda's position: Ve'ad kan lo mechayev Rebbe Yehuda ella minei u'vei — Rabbi Yehuda's obligation is only to take Terumot uMa'asrot from the metamed itself, on itself. His position is not that the temed is fully and genuinely wine; it is at most a stringency — perhaps a rabbinic one — to treat it as requiring tithing. Aval me'almah lo — but one cannot take from real wine to exempt this, or from this to exempt real wine. The reason is straightforward: Dilma ati la'aprushei min hachiyuv al haptur min haptur al hachiyuv — genuine wine is fully obligated in Terumot uMa'asrot, whereas this temed that has not fermented is not fully obligated, only rabbinically so at most. Taking from one to exempt the other would therefore involve taking from a patur on a chayav or vice versa, creating miscalculations in every direction. So Rabbi Elazar's contribution is to say: the debate in Maasrot is at the pre-fermentation stage, and even Rabbi Yehuda who calls it wine does not treat it as genuinely and fully wine — only enough to require tithing from itself, rabbinically.

---

## Mikvah Application

### Metamed Mikvah
