Tanu Rabbanan — a Baraita: Hatemed ad shelo hichmis — temed that has not yet fermented — Mashiko bemayim — can be brought to kiss the waters of a Mikvah. This is the process by which tamei water can be purified: since a Mikvah operates on water, tamei water placed in contact with a kosher Mikvah becomes absorbed into the Mikvah's water and thereby becomes tahor — not because the Mikvah purified it in the way it purifies a person or vessel, but because it becomes part of the Mikvah water itself. This process, however, works only for water. For other liquids there is no such mechanism. Therefore, if one's temed became tamei and one wishes to make it tahor, the determination of whether it is still water is essential. As long as it has not yet fermented, it retains the status of water and can be brought into contact with the Mikvah. Mishehichmitz — once it has fermented — ein mashkiko bemayim — it can no longer be brought to kiss the Mikvah water, because it is now wine.

### Pure Water Only

Amar Rava lo shanu ela shetimdo bemayim tehorim venitme'u — Rava qualifies: this ruling — that pre-fermentation temed can be brought to the Mikvah — applies only when the water was originally pure and then became tamei after the grape material was added. Aval temei mei ikara lo — but if the water was tamei from the outset, it cannot be brought to the Mikvah even before fermentation. Tosafot explains the distinction: because it was never in a state of being simply pure water before the process began, it no longer has the straightforward status of pure water that has become tamei; its identity has been complicated from the start.

### Rav Ashi's Q

Ata Rav Gaviha mi-bei Katil amra lishmayta kamei de-Rav Ashi — this ruling was reported before Rav Ashi, who raised a challenge. Mai shna mi-temei mei ikara? What is the difference between water that became tamei originally and water that was pure and only became tamei after the grape material was added? In both cases, before fermentation, it should still have the status of water — so why should the original purity of the water matter?

### Density Separation

De-amrinan idi de-maya yakiri shachni tata'ei u-peira kafi mei-eila — the answer lies in the physics of the mixture: water is denser than the grape juice product and therefore settles at the bottom, while the juice product floats on top. When one brings the vessel of liquid into contact with the Mikvah water, only the surface of the liquid in the vessel actually touches the Mikvah water. If the juice component has separated and risen to the top, then it is only the juice layer that makes contact with the Mikvah — not the water beneath it. Ve-lo salka lah hashkaka le-maya — and the process of hashkakah, of the water kissing the Mikvah water, cannot take effect for the water below, because the water itself never actually touched the Mikvah.

Rav Ashi then asks: Ei hachi tehorim desof mitmu nami — if that is the reason, then even in the case of originally pure water that subsequently became tamei, the same separation problem should apply. The answer is: Mevalbeli — one stirs and mixes the liquid before placing it in the Mikvah, so the water and juice are fully blended and the separation has not yet occurred. Hacha nami mevalbeli — and in the case of originally tamei water, one should equally be able to stir it first and thereby solve the problem. Rava's distinction between originally pure and originally tamei water is thus rejected, and the resolution is simply that in any case one must stir the mixture before bringing it to the Mikvah.

It is worth noting that the Gemara does not pursue the fascinating later portion of the Mishnah dealing with the concept of brothers who inherit an estate and when that estate is treated as a single entity — a striking application of something like a theory of corporate identity in Halacha. The Gemara passes over it, and we move on.

---

## Nashim: Sale & Fine

### Mutual Exclusion

We have now covered Kodashim, Taharot, Zeraim, and something of Nezikin in the brothers-and-estate question. We turn now to Nashim — the order of women's law — and then to Mo'ed, which will bring the perek to its conclusion as a survey of all of Shas.

Kol makom she-yesh mecher ein knas ve-chol makom she-yesh knas ein mecher — where there is mecher, the right of a father to sell his underage daughter into a form of servitude, there is no knas; and where there is knas, the fine imposed upon a man who seduces or rapes a na'arah, there is no mecher. These two legal categories are mutually exclusive.

The term na'arah requires some unpacking. As the Rabbis understand it, na'arah refers to a young woman who has halachically become an adult — she is twelve years old with two pubic hairs — but who has not yet become a bogeret, a full adult, which occurs six months later. The Torah's obligation of knas for one who rapes or seduces applies to a na'arah specifically. The father's right of mecher, by contrast, applies while she is a ketanah — underage, less than twelve years old.

It is natural to ask: if there is no knas for a ketanah, does she have no legal protection? The Gemara's answer is that knas is not the only consequence. The Rabbis derive that pitui ktanah ones — seduction of an underage girl is treated as rape in any case — and rape carries obligations of personal-injury payments: tza'ar for pain and suffering, boshet for humiliation, and pegam for physical injury. These obligations exist even absent a formal knas. Additionally, the Rambam is explicit: the fifty kesef of knas is for the illicit pleasure of the act itself, and the seducer owes boshet and pegam beyond the knas; the rapist additionally owes tza'ar. As for who receives these payments, the Rambam is clear that the three payments of the seducer and the four of the rapist belong to the father — kol shevach neurim la-av — because all the enhancement of her youth belongs to the father. If there is no father, they go to the girl herself. And if the matter goes to court after she has already become an adult, she receives the payments at that point.

### Rabbi Meir

Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav zu divrei Rabbi Meir — this principle of mutual exclusion between mecher and knas is the position of Rabbi Meir alone. As the Baraita elaborates: Ketanah mi-bat yom echad ad she-tavi shtei se'arot — from one day old until she has two pubic hairs — yesh lah mecher ve-ein lah knas. During this period of being a ketanah, there is mecher but no knas. Mi-she-tavi shtei se'arot ad she-tivager — from the time she has two pubic hairs until she becomes a bogeret, that is, from twelve years and a day to twelve years and six months — yesh lah knas ve-ein lah mecher. She is now a na'arah and no longer a minor, so there is knas but no mecher. Divrei Rabbi Meir — she-hayah Rabbi Meir omer: kol makom she-yesh mecher ein knas ve-chol makom she-yesh knas ein mecher. According to Rabbi Meir, these are strictly non-overlapping windows.

### Sages' Overlap

Va-chachamim omrim yesh knas bimkom mecher — the Sages disagree and hold that there is an overlap: knas applies even while mecher applies. Ketanah mi-bat shalosh shanim ve-yom echad ad she-tivager yesh lah knas — from three years and a day all the way through adulthood, the girl is subject to knas. The lower bound is not birth but age three, because only from that age is the act halachically classified as an act of sexual intercourse. Before age three, even if the same physical events occur, the Rabbis do not consider it a halachic act of sex, and therefore no knas is triggered. So for the Sages, from one day to three years there is only mecher and no knas; from three years to twelve years and a day there is both mecher and knas simultaneously; from twelve years and a day to twelve years and six months there is knas but no mecher; and from twelve years and six months onward, there is neither.

---

## Miun & Chalitzah

### Mutual Exclusion

Kol makom she-yesh miun ein chalitzah ve-chol makom she-yesh chalitzah ein miun — where there is the right of miun, there is no chalitzah; where there is chalitzah, there is no miun. Chalitzah is the ceremony by which a woman releases her deceased husband's brother from the obligation of yibum, and it requires that both parties be halachic adults; a minor cannot perform chalitzah. Miun is the institution by which a girl who has been married off by her mother and brothers — not her father — can reject that marriage at any time before she becomes an adult. This institution is entirely rabbinic, a takanah enacted because of the social reality of needing to provide for daughters when no father is present. When she reaches adulthood she is no longer a minor, so miun is unavailable — but chalitzah becomes available. The two categories, according to one position, occupy mutually exclusive windows.

### Rabbi Meir

Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav zo divrei Rabbi Meir — this strict mutual exclusion is again Rabbi Meir's position. A Baraita spells it out: ad matai habat mima'enet — until when can a girl reject the marriage? Ad shetavi shtei se'arot divrei Rabbi Meir — until she has two pubic hairs, meaning until she becomes an adult. Once she reaches twelve years and a day, miun is no longer available for Rabbi Meir, and chalitzah begins.

### Sages' Overlap

Aval Chachamim omrim yesh miun bemakom chalitzah — but the Sages say there is a period of overlap, when a girl can perform both miun and chalitzah. That period is when she is a na'arah — twelve years and a day to twelve years and six months. She is halachically an adult and can therefore perform chalitzah, but she can also still exercise miun to reject this rabbinic marriage, as long as she has not confirmed the marriage through sexual relations as an adult.

This is the position of Rabbi Yehuda in the Baraita: ad sheyirbeh hashachor al halavan — until the more developed adult state — understood by the Gemara not as an abundance of pubic hair but as the growth of particularly long pubic hairs, marking her transition to bogeret. According to Rabbi Yehuda, as long as she has not yet become a full bogeret and has not had conjugal relations as an adult in this marriage, she retains the right of miun even though she is already a na'arah and could perform chalitzah. Once she becomes a bogeret or once she has had sexual relations as an adult within the marriage — which constitutes kiddushei biah and fully confirms the marriage — miun is no longer possible.

---

## Tekiah & Havdalah

### Mutual Exclusion

Kol makom sheyesh tkiyah ein havdalah ve-chol makom sheyesh havdalah ein tkiyah — where there is tekiah there is no havdalah, and where there is havdalah there is no tekiah. The background: on erev Shabbat the shofar was blown to signal to people to cease melachah. On motzei Shabbat, havdalah is recited to formally permit melachah once again. Tekiah marks the transition into a more restrictive state; havdalah marks the transition into a more permissive one. They are therefore categorically opposed.

### Yom Tov Erev

Yom Tov shechal lihyot be'erev Shabbat — when Yom Tov falls on erev Shabbat: Tok'in — one blows the shofar, as one does at the entry of any sanctified day, marking the transition to increased restriction. Lo mavdilin — one does not make havdalah, because one is not moving from a more restricted state to a less restricted one; Yom Tov entering Shabbat moves from one level of restriction to a heavier one.

### Yom Tov Motza'ei

When Yom Tov falls on motzei Shabbat, it is the reverse: Mavdilin v'lo tok'in. Havdalah is recited because one is transitioning out of Shabbat — moving from a more comprehensive prohibition of melachah to a less comprehensive one — and havdalah marks that opening of permission. But tekiah is not performed, because tekiah accompanies the forbidding of melachah, and while Yom Tov is not entirely permissive, one is not moving into a more restricted state.

### Tekiah Method

Heikhi toke'a — how exactly is the tekiah performed when Yom Tov transitions into Shabbat, given that it must be somehow distinguishable from the standard erev Shabbat tekiah, which consists of a tekiah and a teru'ah?

Amar Rav Yehuda: toke'a u'mevi'ah mitoch hateki'ah — one blows the tekiah and it transforms from within itself into a teru'ah. There are not two discrete blows; rather the tekiah flows into the teru'ah without separation.

Rav Assi omer: toke'a u'mevi'ah b'neshimah achat — one produces both sounds in a single breath, so they are distinct sounds but without the pause of taking a new breath between them. Itkin Rav Assi b'Hutzal k'shmaiteh — and Rav Assi enacted in Hutzal to practice as he had ruled.

A challenge is raised from a Baraita: Yom tov shechal lihyot b'erev Shabbat tok'in v'lo mari'in — you blow tekiah but not teru'ah. Does this not mean no teru'ah at all, contradicting both Rav Yehuda and Rav Assi? The Gemara resolves that each Amora defends his position on his own terms: Rav Yehuda metareitz l'taameh — lo mari'in bifnei atzmah, ella mitoch hateki'ah: you do not blow a teru'ah as a separate, independent blow; the teru'ah emerges from within the tekiah. Rav Assi metareitz l'taameh — lo mari'in b'shtei neshimot, ella b'neshimah achat: you do not produce the teru'ah with a separate breath; the two sounds are produced together in one breath.

### Havdalah Text

Uv'motzei Shabbat — when Shabbat ends and Yom Tov begins, and one must recite havdalah, a question arises about the text. The standard havdalah formula contains the phrase hamavdil bein kodesh l'chol — "who separates between holy and mundane." But if Shabbat is being followed by Yom Tov and not an ordinary weekday, the transition is not to chol. One cannot say that God separates between kodesh and chol when the day being entered is itself kodesh. What does one say?

The ruling is hamavdil bein kodesh l'kodesh. Amar Rav Yehuda b'chatimatah — Rav Yehuda rules that this modified phrase is said only in the chatimah, the closing blessing formula, not at the opening. V'chein amar Rav Nachman b'chatimatah — Rav Nachman agrees: only at the close. Rav Sheshet breih d'Rav Idi says af bifitichatah — even at the opening one should say bein kodesh l'kodesh. V'leit hilkhata k'vathieh — and we do not rule like him. The standard text bein kodesh l'chol is retained at the opening, as Rashi explains, because that text reflects biblical language: the Torah itself uses the formulation of separation between the holy and the mundane.

As for Rav Dosa, who would have one say bein kodesh chamur l'kodesh kal — between the heavy holiness of Shabbat and the light holiness of Yom Tov — v'leit hilkhata k'vathieh as well. Rashi explains it is disrespectful to characterize Yom Tov as a kal, a lighter kedushah, and we therefore do not say it.

This brings us to the final ruling of the perek. Amar Rav Zeira: Yom tov shechal lihyot b'emtza Shabbat — when Yom Tov falls in the middle of Shabbat, meaning one is making havdalah on Yom Tov itself as Shabbat ends — what does one say? It might strike one as peculiar to recite bein yom hashevi'i l'sheshet yemei hama'aseh — "between the seventh day and the six days of work" — when there is no weekday in sight. Nevertheless, Rav Zeira rules that one says the standard formula: hamavdil bein kodesh l'chol, bein or l'choshech, bein Yisrael l'amim, u'vein yom hashevi'i l'sheshet yemei hama'aseh.

Mai taama — why? Seder havdalot hu moneh — because one is simply reciting the ordered list of the traditional havdalot, the separations that are mentioned in the Torah itself. Rashi specifies: vayavdeil bein ha'or u'vein hachoshech is the source for bein or l'choshech; v'avdil etchem min ha'amim is the source for bein Yisrael l'amim; and the sanctification of Shabbat in the account of Creation is the source for bein yom hashevi'i l'sheshet yemei hama'aseh. All the clauses of our havdalah are drawn from the Torah. Therefore, even in a context where the transition is not from Shabbat to an ordinary weekday, we retain the biblical nusach in its entirety. And with that, the perek concludes.

---

---

# Hullin 27

## Intro & Basic Rules

### Perek Bet Overview

The second perek of Masechet Chullin opens on 27a and takes up where many students might have expected the first perek to begin: with the act of shechita itself — what is required, where it must be performed, and how much must be cut. The first perek, as we know, focused on the kasherim and psulim, addressing who may perform shechita, with what instrument, and under what conditions. Here, by contrast, we finally turn to the mechanics of the act itself. That said, the Gemara does not remain purely technical; it uses the occasion as an opportunity for a range of abstract and conceptual inquiries, as we shall see.

### Mishnah: Simanim

The Mishnah opens with the rule: ha-shochet echad ba-of u-shnayim ba-beheimah — one who slaughters one siman, either the trachea or the esophagus, in birds, or two simanim in animals (more precisely, mammals), shechitato kesherah — the shechita is valid. The Mishnah then adds: v'rubo shel echad kamo-hu — the majority of one siman counts. One need not cut the full trachea or full esophagus; a majority suffices, as has been discussed previously and will be revisited again. The Mishnah continues with the ruling on half: if one cut exactly half — not a majority — of a siman in a bird, or one full siman and half of another in a mammal, shechitato pesulah — the shechita is invalid. This second case is notable: even though cutting one full siman plus half of another amounts to one and a half simanim cut in total, which exceeds the combined majority of each (roughly 1.2), since one did not cut a majority of the second siman it remains invalid. The Mishnah then restates the affirmative: rov echad ba-of v'rov shnayim ba-beheimah — a majority of one in a bird, a majority of two in a mammal — the shechita is valid.

### Rabbi Yehuda & Vridim

Rabbi Yehuda adds: ad she-yishchot et ha-vridim — one must also shecht the blood vessels in the neck, which are presumably the major vessels responsible for draining the blood, either the jugular vein or the carotid arteries. The precise identity of the vridim merits clarification: the word vridim is suggestive of veins, Rashi speaks of there being one on each side of the neck, and various anatomical illustrations identify them as both the jugular veins and the carotid arteries — a contradiction that requires further investigation. What is clear is that they are a major blood vessel in the neck, and it is worth noting that we actually pasken like Rabbi Yehuda, making this not merely an academic question.

The interesting question already in the Mishnah is whether Rabbi Yehuda considers the cutting of the vridim to be part of the act of shechita itself — implied by his use of the verb yishchot and by the apparent consequence that the shechita is invalid without it — or whether he is addressing a separate concern about removing blood from the meat before consumption. The language of the Mishnah strongly suggests that it is part of shechita, but the Gemara will rule otherwise: for Rabbi Yehuda, the cutting of the vridim is not part of the act of shechita but addresses a distinct problem of ensuring adequate removal of blood. The Gemara acknowledges that this reading is not intuitive from the Mishnah's formulation, and it grapples with that tension directly.

Additionally, the Gemara will limit Rabbi Yehuda's requirement to birds, not to mammals — which is somewhat counterintuitive, since one might have supposed that mammals, with their greater volume of blood, would require more rigorous blood removal. The Gemara's discussion of this follows.

### Majority Requirement

The Gemara opens by noting that the verb ha-shochet — one who slaughters — implies a b'di-eved context: post facto the shechita is valid, but le-chatechila something was lacking. This raises an immediate question: what could be le-chatechila deficient when one has cut the full two simanim in a mammal? One might understand a le-chatechila concern regarding birds — perhaps ideally one should cut both simanim even in a bird. But what more could one have been expected to do when one has cut both the kaneh and the weshet in their entirety?

The Gemara offers two resolutions. The first: eiba'it eima echad ba-of — the implication of b'di-eved is directed at the bird, meaning that le-chatechila one should cut both simanim in a bird as well, even though one suffices. The second resolution, which appears to be the Gemara's primary focus: eiba'it eima a'rubo shel echad kamo-hu — the le-chatechila concern is not with the first clause of the Mishnah at all but with the second, which permits a majority. That is, le-chatechila one should cut the entire siman; b'di-eved a majority suffices.

Rashi explains this le-chatechila requirement as a rabbinic concern: since the boundary between a majority and exactly half can be difficult to gauge with precision, one is asked le-chatechila to cut the entire siman so as to avoid any doubt. There is, however, a deeper conceptual question lurking here that has bearing not only on this halacha but on broader questions in shechita. How do we understand the fundamental obligation: is one's basic duty to cut fifty-one percent, with the majority being the baseline requirement? Or is the baseline obligation to cut the entire siman, with a majority counting as halachically equivalent to the whole — rubo shel echad kamo-hu? If the latter framing is correct, then even the act of cutting more than fifty percent is conceptually a stand-in for cutting the full siman. This in turn bears on the question of le-chatechila, because if conceptually the obligation is to cut the entire siman and the majority merely fulfills it in a diminished form, then of course le-chatechila one should do the full thing. It would also be relevant to cases where a psul — such as shehiya or derasah — occurs in the final forty-nine percent after the majority has already been cut: does that psul affect the shechita, or was the shechita effectively completed at the fifty-one percent mark?

---

## Location: The Neck

### Rav Kahana: Shach

Having established the basic rules, the Gemara turns to an entirely different question: how do we know that shechita must be performed at the neck or throat? This question has two dimensions: first, why not some other part of the animal entirely — why not stab it in the heart or the back? Second, within the neck, how do we know it must be the front of the throat rather than the back of the neck? Tosafot's reading of the entire subsequent sugya is largely organized around this second question.

Rav Kahana opens: minayin lishchita shehi min hatzavar — from where do we know that shechita is at the neck or throat? He cites the verse: ve-shachat et ben ha-bakar — he shall slaughter the calf, which appears in the context of a korban. From this he derives through a play on words: mi-makom she-shach chata'ehu — from where it bows, there you shall cleanse or validate it. The word shach evokes bowing or inclining, and if one observes a cow standing normally, its neck is angled downward — that is the part of its body that inclines. The word chata'ehu is read as meaning to cleanse or purify, with an analogy to other usages of the root chet-tet-alef in the sense of purification — as in ve-chite et ha-bayit from the purification of a house, or techate'eni be-ezov ve-etaher from the sprinkling of ashes of the Parah Adumah. The reading is therefore: from the place where the animal inclines, there you shall make it kasher or cleanse it.

### Shach Challenged

The Gemara challenges this derivation on multiple grounds. First: perhaps it refers to the tail, which also hangs downward perpetually. The Gemara responds: sach mi-klal she-zakuf — the word sach, which suggests bending, implies that this is a body part that is sometimes upright and sometimes bent. The tail is always hanging down and therefore cannot be the referent. The Gemara then asks: perhaps the ear? Animals can apparently bend their ears downward. The Gemara responds: be'inan dam ha-nefesh ve-leika — in the context of korbanot, the Torah emphasizes that shechita produces the blood of the soul, and cutting the ear would not produce that effect. The Gemara presses further: perhaps one starts at the ear and continues cutting until one reaches the blood of the soul? Here the Gemara shifts register. Tosafot reads the text as continuing with the word ve-le-ta'ameich — according to your own reasoning — rather than the standard ve-tu. The point becomes: if you challenge this derivation, you will have to concede that it fails. And if it fails, how do you know any of the laws of shechita from the Torah? How do you know the prohibitions of derasah, chaladah, hagramah, and ikkur? The answer: ela Gemara — we know them from tradition. And therefore: shechita min ha-tzavar nami Gemara — the requirement that shechita takes place at the neck is likewise a matter of tradition and cannot be derived from a verse.

### Chateihu & Gistra

If the verse cannot teach us the requirement of the neck from first principles, the Gemara asks: ve-kra le-mai ata — what, then, does the verse teach us? The answer: de-lo le-shaveih gistra — not to sever it completely in two, meaning not to chop through the backbone and divide the animal into two parts. Rashi explains this as a warning not to continue cutting after the simanim until the entire backbone is severed. Tosafot reads this differently and more consistently throughout the sugya: according to Tosafot, once we know from tradition that the shechita takes place at the neck, the verse comes to specify that it must be at the throat — the front of the neck — and not from the back of the neck, i.e., not gistra. Since the verse emphasizes where the animal inclines and connects this to the cleansing or removal of blood, it directs us to the throat, from which blood will flow most directly, rather than to the back of the neck.

It is worth pausing to note a striking irony that runs through all of these drashot: the deriving of the location of shechita is consistently oriented around blood — where the blood is, where it flows, how it is cleansed — and yet shechita in its technical halakhic form is about the trachea and esophagus, not about blood. One could in theory perform a perfectly valid shechita that produces very little blood, if the animal were to die of asphyxiation following the severing of the trachea. The Rabbanan do not make blood a formal requirement of shechita at all. Rabbi Yehuda introduces blood as an additional concern, but the Gemara will even bracket his position as relating not to the act of shechita itself but to a separate concern about preparing the meat. And yet the drashot that locate shechita at the throat are all built around the premise of blood flow. This tension is notable and unresolved.

### Rav Yeimar: Flow

Rav Yeimar offers a second derivation. The verse says ve-zavachta — you shall slaughter. He derives from a different play on words: mi-makom she-zav — from where it flows — chateihu — there cut it. Here the word chateihu is spelled with a tav rather than a tet, and the Gemara establishes that this root means to break or sever — as in the verse al tira ve-al techas, do not fear and do not be broken, where the root is read as connoting trembling or collapsing. So: from where the blood flows, there cut it, i.e., the throat. Once again the emphasis is on blood.

The Gemara challenges this as it challenged the previous derivation. Perhaps the nose — mucus flows from the nose? The Gemara responds: zav al yedei chitui ba'inan — we need something that flows as a result of being cut, not something that flows spontaneously. Perhaps the heart — if you want to ensure blood flows, cut at the heart? Again the Gemara invokes ve-le-ta'ameich and returns to the same conclusion: you cannot derive it from a verse, and we know it from tradition. The verse then teaches de-lo le-shaveih gistra — not to sever the animal from the back, but to proceed from the throat. Tosafot's consistent reading holds here as well: tradition gives us the neck; the verse refines this to the front of the throat, based on the emphasis on blood flow.

### Rabbi Yishmael: Sachat

A third derivation is offered from the school of Rabbi Yishmael. The verse says ve-shachat — do not read it as ve-shachat, slaughter, but as ve-sachat. The word sachat can mean squeeze, again evoking the release of blood. Alternatively, the drasha reads: mi-makom she-sach — from where the animal speaks, i.e., its throat — chateihu — there cut it. The Gemara challenges this as before: perhaps cut the tongue, since that is even more directly the organ of speech? The Gemara responds: be'inan dam ha-nefesh ve-leika — the context of korbanot demands blood of the soul, and cutting only the tongue will not produce that. The Gemara presses further — begin at the tongue and continue until you reach the blood of the soul? The same conclusion follows: we cannot derive the throat from a verse, and we know it from tradition. The verse teaches only that one must cut from the throat and not from the back of the neck.

What distinguishes this drasha from the previous two, however, is that it does not rely solely on the theme of blood. The trachea is the organ centrally associated with speech and with the act of shechita — the trachea being one of the two simanim. So at least this drasha, unlike the others, points toward the actual anatomical focus of shechita rather than blood removal, even if it arrives at the same conclusion about the front of the throat.

### Rabbi Chiya: Olah

Rabbi Chiya offers yet another derivation, this time from a ברייתא: minayin lishchita min ha-tzavar — how do we know shechita is from the neck? He cites a verse about the olah: ve-archu bnei Aharon ha-kohanim et ha-netachim et ha-rosh ve-et ha-pader — the kohanim shall arrange the pieces and the head and the fat. The question arises: why does the verse single out the head? The head is merely one of the pieces of the animal — it should be included in the general category of netachim. The Torah describes the process: flay the olah, cut it into pieces, place the pieces on the fire. But the head, as Rabbi Chiya argues, was not part of the same process of flaying and dismemberment. The head was already separated in the act of shechita, and therefore it conceptually falls outside the category of netachim produced by the subsequent flaying and severing. Hence the Torah must single it out explicitly to tell us that it too goes on the fire.

The Gemara then draws the inference: mi-klal de-shechita min ha-tzavar — evidently shechita is from the neck, since otherwise the head would not have been treated as already separately processed. The reasoning is not circular, despite initial appearances. The question is: why would the Torah ever need to single out the head from the other pieces? The only compelling explanation is that the head was already in some sense separated prior to the dismemberment process. And the only way that could be true is if shechita occurred at the neck, creating a significant degree of separation between the head and the body. Rashi acknowledges that the head is not fully severed — the backbone is not cut through — but argues that the degree of detachment is sufficient to render it conceptually separate.

The Gemara then resolves an internal tension in the ברייתא: the opening cites one verse about the head and fat, while the conclusion cites a slightly different verse using the possessive form its head and its fat. The resolution is that the two verses each teach something distinct. The first teaches that the head, despite not being dismembered together with the rest of the animal, is nonetheless placed on the fire. The second teaches that the head and fat are placed on the fire first, based on the juxtaposition of et rosho ve-et pidro ve-arach. And why does each verse mention fat alongside the head? A third ברייתא teaches: chofeh et ha-pader al beit ha-shechita uma'alehu — one covers the place of the severing with the fat before placing the head on the fire. The exposed site of the cut is not aesthetically fitting to be offered to God as is, and so the fat is used to cover it. Ve-zeh derech kavod shel ma'alah — this is a respectful manner of presenting it.

This drasha from the olah is more satisfying than the preceding word-plays. It requires no forced etymology; it reasons directly from the structure of the sacrificial procedure. One limitation Tosafot notes is that this drasha does not distinguish between the throat and the back of the neck — it tells us the neck, but not which side. The earlier drashot, for all their awkwardness, at least attempted to address that further specification through the emphasis on blood flow.

---

## Spectrum Model

### Torah Links Birds

The Gemara now presents a ברייתא concerning the verse zot torat ha-beheimah ve-ha-of — this is the law of the mammal and the bird — which appears in the context of tumah. The ברייתא asks: in what respect are mammals and birds ever comparable in terms of how they impart tumah? In fact, they are not comparable at all. A dead mammal — a nevela — conveys tumah through maga and masa, touch and carrying. A dead bird does not convey tumah in that way. Conversely, a dead bird that has not been slaughtered properly conveys tumah be-vet ha-bli'a — when it is swallowed and passing through the esophagus — and this tumah extends even to the garments one is wearing at the moment of swallowing, making them a rishon. A dead mammal does not convey tumah in this manner.

So the ברייתא asks: since the tumah laws of mammals and birds are so different, why does the Torah use a single heading — this is the law of the mammal and the bird — as if they share a common law? Lomar lach: mah beheimah bi-shechita af of bi-shechita — just as mammals require shechita, so too birds require shechita. And this is where the verse connecting them becomes relevant: in the context of tumah, a corpse is no longer a nevela if it has been properly slaughtered. The same holds for both mammals and birds. Shechita is the link.

One might then ask: should the equation be complete? Perhaps birds too require two simanim, exactly as mammals? Talmud lomar: zot — this, the limiting word, indicates that the equation is not total. Shechita is required for birds, but not in the identical manner as for mammals. This is the first of two readings of the verse; it establishes that birds require shechita but does not specify what shechita means for birds and does not provide a new source for the idea of shechita at the neck.

Rabbi Eliezer reads the same verse differently. He too asks: in what way are mammals and birds similar? And he answers: mah of hechshero min ha-tzavar af beheimah hechsheirah min ha-tzavar — just as the validation of a bird is from the neck, so too for a mammal. Where do we know that shechita for a bird is from the neck? From melikah. The Torah explicitly describes an act of ritual slaughter in only one place — the melikah of bird offerings, where it says u-malak oto mi-mul orpo — you shall perform melikah from the back of its neck. This is the single instance in which the Torah overtly describes a killing procedure for a korban. Rabbi Eliezer uses it as a model: since melikah is from the neck, and birds and mammals are linked in the verse, the same applies to mammalian shechita — it too is from the neck. Might we then say it must be from the back of the neck, as in melikah? The Torah distinguishes: the verse about melikah singles out that one — the bird korban — as being from the back of its neck, implying that other forms of slaughter are not from the back of the neck, but from the throat. Rabbi Eliezer's drasha is considered the most compelling of all those presented, because it is the one case in which the Torah does explicitly describe a slaughter procedure, and the derivation by analogy has real force.

The Gemara then asks: what does Rabbi Eliezer do with the limiting word zot in the verse? He uses it to prevent the complete equation from running in the other direction: without zot, one might have said — since we are equating birds and mammals — that just as a bird requires only one siman, so too a mammal requires only one siman. The word zot prevents this: the equation is only for the requirement of shechita at the neck, not for the number of simanim. The mammal remains at two.

### Bar Kappara: Spectrum

Bar Kappara taught a sweeping conceptual framework grounded in the same verse: zot torat ha-beheimah ve-ha-of, and the end of the pasuk adds u-ve-chol nefesh ha-chayah ha-romeset ba-mayim — and all living creatures in the water. The verse thus lists three categories: mammals, birds, and fish. Bar Kappara derives from this ordering a spectrum of shechita requirements. The Torah placed birds between mammals and fish. To require two simanim of a bird, as with a mammal, is impossible — shekevar hukash le-dagim — because on one side birds are linked to fish, and fish require no shechita at all. To exempt birds entirely from any shechita is equally impossible — shekevar hukash le-beheimah — because on the other side birds are linked to mammals. Ha keitzad — how does one resolve this? Hechshiro be-siman echad — one falls in the middle of the spectrum, and thus one siman suffices for a bird.

This is an elegant and systematic piece of reasoning, but it rests on two premises that still need to be established: that fish require zero shechita, and that mammals require two simanim. These endpoints define the spectrum. The Gemara will address the first; the second, as we shall see, remains grounded ultimately in tradition.

### Fish & Asifa

How do we know fish require no formal shechita? The Gemara cites the verse in which Moshe speaks to God about feeding Bnei Yisrael: ha-tzon u-vakar yishachet lahem ve-im et kol degei ha-yam ye'asef lahem u-matza lahem — if you slaughter all the cattle and flock for them, and if you gather all the fish of the sea for them, will it be enough? The parallel structure is telling: cattle and flock are slaughtered; fish are merely gathered. Ba-asifa be-alma sagi lehu — gathering alone suffices for fish.

The Gemara challenges this: the word gather is also used in connection with the slav — the quail — as in va-ya'asfu et ha-slav. Would we then say quail requires no shechita? The Gemara distinguishes: in that case, the word gather does not appear in parallel to slaughter performed on other creatures. Here, by contrast, the gathering of fish is explicitly set against the slaughtering of cattle and flock. The parallel is the point; gathering in the verse about fish is the functional equivalent of what slaughter is for mammals. Therefore, ba-asifa be-alma sagi lehu — for fish, mere gathering from the water is sufficient, and no formal shechita is required.

Some have playfully entertained the question of whether the act of asifa — gathering from the water — is itself the required act for fish, raising the theoretical puzzle of what one's status would be if one were to eat a fish directly in the water without ever removing it. The simple reading of the Gemara, however, is unambiguous: lav bnei shechita ninhu — fish are simply not subject to the concept of shechita at all.

### Birds: One Siman

With fish established at zero and mammals understood to require two simanim — a point that, as the Gemara will acknowledge, is itself ultimately rooted in tradition — Bar Kappara's framework is complete. Birds, positioned between these two endpoints by the Torah's own formulation in the verse, require one siman. The framework is clean and appealing, though the Gemara will note tomorrow that the mammals-require-two end of the spectrum is likewise not derivable from a verse and must be learned from tradition.

---

## Birds from Mud

### Galilean Drasha

An itinerant Galilean preacher — an over Gelila'ah, a transient darshan whose name is not even recorded — offers a theological grounding for the same spectrum. His framework is not hermeneutical but cosmological: the number of simanim required reflects the substance from which each creature was created. Behemah shenivret min ha-yabashah — mammals were created from solid earth — and therefore require two simanim; they possess the most substantial and robust form of life. Dagim shenivru min ha-mayim — fish were created from water — and are the least substantial, and therefore hechshiran be-lo klum — require nothing. Of shenivra min ha-rakak — birds were created from mud, a mixture of earth and water — and therefore occupy a middle position, requiring one siman. The shechita requirement tracks the ontological weight of the creature.

### Scales on Legs

Rav Shmuel Kaputka adds an empirical observation in support of the claim that birds were created from mud: teida she-harei ofot yesh bahem kaskeset be-ragleihem ke-dagim — you can verify this because birds have a type of scales on their legs, similar to fish scales. The legs of a chicken, for instance, exhibit a scaly texture reminiscent of fish scales — a visible remnant of the birds' dual origin from earth and water, the same mud that was their source of creation.

It is worth pausing at this juncture to note another conceptual puzzle raised in passing. The continuum framework — more substantial life requires more simanim — raises a question about the esophagus specifically. Cutting the trachea produces rapid death through asphyxiation. But cutting the esophagus, in isolation, does not directly kill the animal; death would follow only after a prolonged period of starvation. The connection between shechita and immediate killing is therefore not fully symmetrical across both simanim. The Gemara appears to assume that greater vitality demands more cutting, but the mechanism by which the esophagus contributes to death as part of the shechita act is not self-evident from a biological standpoint. This is not a question the Gemara resolves here, but it is worth holding in mind.

### Two Narratives

The Gemara now presents the origin of the claim that birds were created from mud, through a story about Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai. A certain Roman official — referred to as a hēgemōn — posed to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai a contradiction between two verses in Bereishit. Perek 1 states: va-yomer Elokim yishretzu ha-mayim sheretz nefesh chaya ve-of ye'ofef — God said let the waters teem with living creatures, and birds flying above. This verse clearly implies that birds were created from water. Perek 2, however, states: va-yitzer Hashem Elokim min ha-adama kol chayat ha-sadeh ve-et kol of ha-shamayim — God formed from the ground all the animals of the field and all the birds of the sky. This verse attributes the creation of birds to the ground.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's initial answer was: min ha-rakak nivre — they were created from mud, which is a mixture of water and earth, thereby harmonizing both verses. But when his students looked at one another in astonishment — apparently finding this answer dismissive — Rabbi Yochanan explained himself. He told them: kasha be-eineichem she-dachiti et oyvi be-kaneh — is it troubling to you that I dismissed my antagonist with a reed, a straw? The implication is that he gave the hēgemōn a deflecting answer rather than his real one.

### Mud Resolution

The real answer, which Rabbi Yochanan gave his students, is that the two narratives in Bereishit are serving different purposes. Perek 1 describes the process of creation and is specific: birds emerged from the water. Perek 2, by contrast, is a narrative centered on man — ve-lama hevi'an el ha-adam? likro lahem shem — it describes how God brought the animals and birds to man so that man could name them. Perek 2 is not offering a precise account of how each creature came into being; it is describing the relationship between man and the created world. Therefore, the phrase min ha-adama in perek 2 need not be taken as a precise statement of how birds were formed, and there is no contradiction.

However, the Gemara then records a minority view that reverses the attribution of the two answers: vi-yesh omrim, some say that Rabbi Yochanan gave the mud answer to his students as the genuine resolution, not as a dismissal. According to this view, since perek 2 does say that God formed from the ground — and this cannot simply be ignored with respect to birds — the truth is that both texts are correct in their own way: perek 1 says water, perek 2 says ground. The resolution is mud. Birds were created from the rakak, the muddy swamp, that mixture of earth and water in which the two elements combine. And it is precisely this hybrid origin that places birds in the middle of the ontological spectrum, between the earth-rooted mammals and the water-born fish, and that grounds the requirement of one siman — the middle point between two and zero.

---

---

# Hullin 29

## Half vs. Majority Debate

### Majority of Siman Intro

Today's daf begins several lines before the wide lines on 28b, precisely at the start of a new topic. Having established that mammals require shechita of two simanim, birds of one, fish of none, and having addressed Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding the cutting of the major blood vessels — understood by the Gemara not as a requirement of shechita per se but as a means of draining the blood — we now arrive at the final section of the Mishna, which states that it is not necessary to sever the entire siman. Cutting the majority of it, or the majority of both simanim in the case of a mammal, is sufficient. From here, the Gemara opens a broader conceptual inquiry into the nature of the principle of majority.

### Rav: Half = Majority

The Gemara introduces a dispute: *itmar* — it was taught. Rav said *mechtza al mechtza ke-rov*: exactly half is like the majority. The Mishna, it seems, addressed this case directly — it said majority yes, half no — but we will bracket that for a moment. The question being raised is: when the Mishna says majority suffices, does it mean a true majority, or is exactly half sufficient to qualify as a majority? Rav maintains that half suffices. The chain of reasoning runs as follows: *rubo ke-kulo*, the majority is like the whole, and half is like the majority — so by that chain, exactly half counts.

### Rav Kahana: Half ≠ Major…

Rav Kahana disagrees: *mechtza al mechtza eino ke-rov*, half is not like the majority. The Gemara frames the disagreement by presenting each position as a kind of divine mandate communicated to Moshe, which is the Gemara's way of articulating how we understand the underlying requirement of shechita. Rav says: *hachi amar lei Rachmana le-Moshe* — this is what God said to Moshe: *lo tishayer rubo*, do not leave the majority remaining. Do not leave too much of the siman uncut. How much is too much? A majority. Rav Kahana, by contrast, says God told Moshe: *shchot rubah*, slaughter the majority — cut the majority. The criterion is positively defined: you must cut the majority.

### Defining Valid vs. Inval…

This debate reflects a fundamental conceptual distinction: are we positively defining the criteria required to make the shechita valid, or are we positively defining the conditions under which it is invalid? The one you are defining creates the higher standard, and anything that falls into a grey area goes on the other side of the definition.

A useful illustration: consider an etrog with a broken pitam. One could say the pitam must be complete — in which case half-broken is not complete and the etrog is invalid. Or one could say if the pitam is broken it is pasul — in which case something ambiguously broken might still be acceptable, since we are defining what makes it bad rather than what makes it good.

Precisely that distinction is at work here. Rav understands the Torah as defining the invalidity: don't leave the majority over. If I leave less than the majority uncut — including exactly half — then I have not violated that criterion, and the shechita is valid. Rav Kahana understands the Torah as defining what makes the shechita valid: you must cut the majority. Anything less than a true majority, including exactly half, fails to satisfy the positive requirement.

It is important to note that this question could in principle yield different answers in different areas of halacha. Majority could be sufficient for shechita for one reason, and sufficient for other contexts for entirely different reasons. But here the Gemara is specifically examining how the requirement of shechita should be conceptualized — and it will soon broaden this inquiry significantly.

### Mishna's Answer: Rabbini…

The Gemara raises the obvious objection from our own Mishna: *tnan*, we learned — *chatzi echad be-of ve-echad ve-chatzi be-veheimah*, if one cut exactly half by a bird, or one full siman plus half of another by a mammal, the shechita is *psulah*, invalid. The Mishna seems quite clear: half is invalid. If Rav holds that half counts as majority, why would the Mishna declare it invalid?

The Gemara responds: *miderabbanan*. The Mishna's ruling may be only rabbinic. The concern is that if we permit exactly half, a shochet will come to do slightly less than half. Therefore, rabbinically, we require a true majority to ensure that at minimum a half is achieved. But biblically, Rav's position holds: exactly half would still be valid.

### Tanur & Letzamtzem

Rav Katina now attempts a proof from a different area of halacha entirely — and this is where the Gemara makes a striking move, implicitly treating the question of whether half counts as majority as a universal principle rather than a context-specific rule of shechita. The case concerns a pottery vessel — specifically a tanur, an oven — that becomes tamei. A pottery vessel cannot be immersed in a mikvah to become tahor; it can only become tahor if it is considered broken, which requires that the majority of it is no longer present. What if the oven is split exactly in half?

The passage reads: *chilko lishnayim ve-heim shavin* — if it was divided into two exactly equal halves, *shneihem tme'in* — both halves retain their tumah. Why? *lefi she'i efshar letzamtzem* — because it is impossible to determine with certainty. This introduces the principle of *ai efshar letzamtzem*: we cannot measure with perfect precision, and therefore we cannot know with certainty which half is actually larger.

This principle extends beyond the question of exactly half — it applies to any situation requiring real precision. The classic example is twins born simultaneously: did they really emerge at exactly the same moment, or do we simply lack the ability to determine which came first? The question of *efshar letzamtzem* or *ai efshar letzamtzem* — whether perfect simultaneity or exact halves are even possible — is itself a significant dispute. Tosafot address this at length, raising, among other factors, the distinction between *bidei adam*, where human action controls the situation and precision is more achievable, and *bidei shamayim*, where we are not in control and exact precision is more doubtful.

The Gemara presses: if we did know with certainty that the halves were exactly equal, what would the ruling be? It cannot be that one is tamei and the other tahor, since they are identical — it would have to be that both are tahor. But why tahor? If half counts as majority, each half should count as if the majority of the tanur is still present and both should be tamei. So the implication of the ruling — that both would be tahor in the hypothetical of certainty — seems to support Rav Kahana: half does not count as majority.

### Rav Papa: No Two Rovs

Rav Papa responds: *trei rubei be-chad mana leika* — you cannot have two majorities in one vessel. This answer is significant and, as Tosafot explains, it represents a shift in how the Gemara conceptualizes the entire dispute.

Up to this point, the debate was framed as a question of definitional orientation: are we defining what makes the shechita valid or what makes it invalid, such that the grey case falls on one side or the other? Rav Papa's answer shifts the framing. The Gemara is no longer asking which criterion is being defined. Instead, it is making a more universal claim: when we say majority suffices, we mean that fifty percent is close enough to majority that it counts *as if* it were the majority — *rubo ke-kulo*, majority is like the whole, and fifty percent is close enough to majority to count accordingly.

This universalized framing explains why the Gemara felt free to move from shechita to tumah and pottery vessels: if the claim is a general one — fifty percent counts as majority — then it applies across domains. And Rav Papa's response follows logically: if fifty percent counts as majority, you cannot simultaneously say that both halves count as majority, because that would require the same object to be simultaneously mostly present and mostly absent. The logical contradiction rules out both being tahor on that basis. But this also raises a further difficulty: even for one of the halves, it is unclear which half should count as the majority. The Gemara's move here is somewhat strange logically, and the earlier framing — which criteria are we defining — was in many ways more satisfying. But by universalizing the question, the Gemara has recast it in a way that will carry through the subsequent discussion.

### Universal Half=Majority…

The force of Rav Papa's response is that the Gemara has now committed to a more general position: the question of whether fifty percent counts as majority is not merely a local question about how to define the requirements of shechita. It is a universal question about how the concept of majority functions. Once framed that way, the Gemara will need to contend with cases in other areas of halacha where the answer appears to differ — and that tension will drive the next section.

---

## Shehiya, Treifa & Half

### Half + Shehiya Proof

The Gemara continues: *ta shema* — come and hear. If one cut half the trachea and then paused — *shehiya* — for the amount of time it would take to perform another shechita, and then completed the cut, the shechita is valid. The reason this works requires some explanation. Normally shehiya, pausing in the middle of the act of shechita, is a psul. But in this case, the argument runs as follows: since cutting exactly half the trachea does not render the animal a treifa — because the majority has not been cut — we can view the initial half-cut as an incidental cut, not an act of shechita. The animal now has a half-cut trachea but is not yet a treifa. When the shochet returns and completes the cut, that is treated as a new, independent act of shechita, and the shehiya in the middle is irrelevant because the two acts are not part of a single continuous process.

The Gemara asks: but if half counts as majority, then the initial half-cut already renders the trachea as if the majority were cut, making the animal a treifa. And if the animal is a treifa, the shochet cannot then save the situation by completing the cut and treating the second act as a new shechita — because the animal is already treifa. This would seem to support Rav Kahana's position.

### Bird vs. Animal Shehiya

The Gemara responds: *mi savrat be-behemah* — why do you assume this case concerns a cow? *lo — be-of*, it concerns a bird. And *miman nafshach* — either way you go: if half counts as majority, then when one cut half the trachea of a bird, that already constitutes the majority of the one siman required for shechita of a bird, and the shechita is complete. If half does not count as majority, then cutting exactly half neither constitutes valid shechita nor renders the bird a treifa, since the trachea is only considered a treifa when the majority is cut. The animal therefore remains in a neutral state — not yet shechted and not yet treifa — and the shochet can return and complete the act, with the second cut constituting the actual shechita.

The reason this distinction between bird and animal matters is that a mammal requires both simanim. For a mammal, if one says half counts as majority, cutting half the trachea makes it as if the majority of the trachea is cut, rendering the animal a treifa. The shochet is then trapped: the only way out is to treat the shechita as one continuous process, but doing so incorporates the shehiya in the middle, generating a psul of shehiya. For a bird, by contrast, there is only one siman, and the situation resolves cleanly either way.

### Pre-Cut Trachea Proof

The Gemara offers another case: *harei shehaya chatzi kaneh pagum* — suppose half of the trachea was already cut prior to the shechita, through some other means, not by the shochet's own act. This half-cut does not render the animal a treifa, since the majority has not been cut. The shochet then added a tiny increment beyond that half — moving from fifty percent to fifty-one percent — and completed the shechita. The ruling is that the shechita is valid.

The Gemara presses: if half counts as majority, then the pre-existing half-cut should already have made the animal a treifa, and the subsequent shechita would be shechting a treifa. The fact that the shechita is valid implies that the pre-existing half-cut did not render it a treifa — suggesting that half does not count as majority in the context of treifa. But here we have moved to a third domain: the laws of treifa are distinct from shechita, and distinct from the laws of tumah governing pottery vessels. If the Gemara is going to apply the question universally, it must address why the answer seems to differ in the context of treifa.

### Treifa: Rov Hanikar

Rava responds: *shani l'inyan treifa de-beinan rov hanikar l'einayim* — treifa is different, because by treifa we require a majority that is visibly discernible, a real majority, not merely a formal or virtual one. The claim is that for treifa, where the question is ultimately about the biological viability of the animal — whether it will survive the injury — one cannot apply legal fictions. When we say that an animal is a treifa because the majority of its trachea is cut, we mean a real, actual majority, not a situation where fifty percent is deemed equivalent to majority through a halakhic construction. Real biological questions demand real biological answers.

It is worth noting that *rov hanikar l'einayim* could be read in different ways — it might mean simply a true fifty-one percent majority, rather than something that must be dramatically or obviously more than half. In context, the meaning seems to be a genuine majority rather than a constructive one: fifty percent does not suffice even if we might elsewhere rule that fifty percent counts as majority.

### Abaye Kal Va-Chomer

Abaye objects with a *kal va-chomer*: *velo kol shekein hu?* Is it not all the more so? By treifa, sometimes even a tiny wound renders the animal treifa — a *mashehu* — because in certain organs even a minuscule puncture is fatal. And yet, Rava says, when treifa requires a majority, it must be a real, visible majority, not a virtual one. How much more so, then, by shechita — where small cuts are never themselves a problem and you need to achieve cutting the majority — should we require a true majority rather than relying on the construction that fifty percent counts as majority?

This argument turns the reasoning on its head: the very feature that makes treifa stringent in one direction — that biological reality governs — also makes it stringent in the other direction when majority is the operative threshold. And if treifa demands a real majority, shechita should demand no less. The kal va-chomer appears quite strong, and it pushes the Gemara toward a conclusion that in fact even in the context of shechita, fifty percent is not sufficient.

### Debate = Pesach Only

The Gemara responds: *ela, de-kuli alma mechtza al mechtza eino ke-rov* — in fact, everyone agrees that for shechita, and indeed for most other areas of halacha, fifty percent is not majority and majority means a real majority. *ve-chi itmar de-rav u-de-rav kahana* — when the dispute of Rav and Rav Kahana was stated, *le-inyan Pesach itmar* — it was stated in the context of the korban Pesach. This is a striking move by the Gemara, and it raises an important point that is worth pausing on: the original statements of Rav and Rav Kahana — *mechtza al mechtza ke-rov* and *mechtza al mechtza eino ke-rov* — were formulated without specifying their context. The Gemara is now suggesting that the original context was entirely different from what was initially assumed. From an academic perspective, this is a fascinating illustration of how the Gemara attributes and recontextualizes statements whose internal evidence does not make the original setting clear.

### Pesach: Half Tamei/Tahor

The Pesach case is as follows: *harei she-hayu Yisrael mechtza tehorim u-mechtza temeim* — suppose the Jewish people were exactly half tahor and half tamei. The governing principle is that if a majority of the people are tamei, the korban Pesach is brought be-tumah; if a minority are tamei, the tamei individuals are deferred to Pesach Sheni. What happens if it is exactly fifty-fifty? And here, crucially, this is a case where one can obtain an exact count — it is a whole number, and a precise fifty-fifty result is possible. Rav says: *mechtza al mechtza ke-rov* — fifty-fifty counts as majority, so the half that is tamei counts as if the majority is tamei. Rav Kahana says: *mechtza al mechtza einah ke-rov* — the tamei minority goes to Pesach Sheni.

### Ish Nidcheh, Not Tzibur

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama de-Rav* — what is Rav's reasoning in this case? *de-chtiv: ish ish ki yihyeh tamei la-nefesh* — the verse says: a person who is tamei brings the korban at Pesach Sheni. *ish nidcheh* — only an individual is deferred, *ve-ein tzibur nidchin* — but not a tzibur. At fifty percent, the tamei group is no longer a mere minority of individuals. They are half of Klal Yisrael, and at that level they cannot be treated as simply *ish*, individuals. The logic is structurally the same as the earlier conceptual debate: if I am defining when individuals are deferred, the moment the tamei group reaches fifty percent, they are no longer individuals and cannot be deferred. The fifty percent falls on the other side of the definition.

In general, however, the Gemara concludes that Rav would not say fifty percent counts as majority universally — the specific ruling here is anchored in a pasuk that refers to individuals, and fifty percent falls outside the definition of individuals.

### Tosafot's Contradictions

Tosafot note a significant difficulty: there are other gemarot where fifty percent does in fact count. The classic example comes from Eruvin, in the context of mechitzot and carrying on Shabbat. If a fence has spaced poles — without relying on *lavud* — and the question is whether the majority of the perimeter must be sealed for it to qualify as a mechitzah: the Gemara there comes out that fifty-fifty is acceptable. Tosafot are troubled because the Gemara here universalized the question of whether fifty percent counts as majority, and that universalization was the very thing that drove the Gemara to restrict the Rav-Rav Kahana debate to the narrow context of the korban Pesach. Yet in other places, the answer differs. The problem is not merely that different areas of halacha yield different conclusions about fifty percent — that would be unremarkable. The problem is that the Gemara's universalization of the issue, and the framework it built on that universalization, sits in tension with the variation found in other tractates.

---

## Chulin vs. Kodshim Rov

### Hoshaya: Chulin/Kodshim

The Mishna both opens and closes with the statement that majority suffices — majority of one by a bird and majority of two by a mammal. This repetition raises the question: why state it twice? Rav Hoshaya answers: *echad be-chulin ve-echad* — one statement refers to non-sanctified animals (chulin) and one refers to sacrifices (kodshim). *ve-tzricha* — both are necessary.

### Blood in Kodshim

The Gemara explains the need for both statements. If the Mishna had only taught majority suffices by chulin, one might have thought: that is because by chulin you are not concerned with obtaining blood from the animal. But by kodshim, where the blood is central — you need the blood for the *zerikah*, the sprinkling — perhaps you must cut fully through the simanim in order to ensure the blood flows out. Therefore the Mishna teaches that even by kodshim, majority suffices. Conversely, if the Mishna had only taught majority suffices by kodshim, one might have thought: that is because you need the blood, so naturally the Torah demanded you cut the majority to ensure blood flow. But by chulin, where blood is not the concern, perhaps fifty percent suffices. The Mishna therefore teaches both: majority is required by chulin and majority is sufficient by kodshim.

One might note that the connection between cutting more of the trachea and esophagus and obtaining more blood is somewhat indirect — more blood is obtained by cutting the major blood vessels, as per Rabbi Yehuda's position, not by cutting deeper into the simanim. The Gemara nonetheless works with the idea that cutting the majority of the simanim is what was thought to drive greater blood flow, and it clarifies that in any case the rule is the same: majority for both chulin and kodshim.

### Hashochet vs. Hamolek

Having established that one mention refers to chulin and one to kodshim, the Gemara now asks which is which. Rav Kahana argues: *mistabra reisha be-chulin ve-seifa be-kodshim* — the beginning of the Mishna refers to chulin and the end to kodshim. His proof comes from the verb used. The Mishna opens with *hashochet* — one who slaughters — and the term for slaughtering by knife is shechita. If the beginning referred to kodshim, it would have said *hamolek*, the term for the special avian offering where the neck is severed by the kohen's thumbnail rather than a knife, which is how birds are handled in the context of kodshim. Since the beginning uses the verb hashochet, it cannot be referring to kodshim and must be referring to chulin.

The end of the Mishna lacks a new verb and simply says the majority of one by bird and the majority of two by behemah, the shechita is valid — *shechitato kesherah*. The Gemara raises: according to you, if the end refers to kodshim, it should have said *melikato kesherah* in the case of the bird. The Gemara responds: this is not difficult. Since the Mishna just discussed the behemah — the last topic before the concluding formula — it naturally used the term shechita, which applies to behemah. But as for the beginning, the first siman mentioned is the bird, and for birds in kodshim the term should have been hamolek, not hashochet.

### Olat Ha'of Two Simanim

Rav Shimi bar Ashi offers a different proof that the beginning of the Mishna refers to chulin. The Mishna says cut one by a bird. If the beginning referred to kodshim, this would be inaccurate, because there exists the *olat ha'of* — the avian burnt offering — which requires cutting both simanim, not just one. The Gemara responds: could one not say the end of the Mishna also refers to kodshim, specifically *seifa be-kodshim*, with the ruling that the majority of one by a bird suffices? There the same problem arises — the olat ha'of requires two. The Gemara replies that this can be resolved: *mai rov echad* — what does "majority of one" mean? It could be read as *rov kol echad ve-echad* — the majority of each one, whichever applies. The phrase is deliberately ambiguous: by the chatat ha'of, one siman suffices, and by the olat ha'of, both are required, but cutting the majority of each one that is required is sufficient. So the end of the Mishna can be read to cover both cases, framed in a way that accommodates either one or two simanim depending on the offering. The beginning, however, straightforwardly says one by a bird — which excludes the olat ha'of and therefore must be referring to chulin.

### Rav Papa: Jugular Proof

Rav Papa offers yet another proof. He derives from the fact that the Mishna records the debate with Rabbi Yehuda — Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the *vridin*, the jugular vein or carotid artery — while the Rabbis disagree. If the beginning of the Mishna referred to kodshim, why would the Rabbis ever argue with Rabbi Yehuda's requirement there? By kodshim, obtaining the blood is the entire point of the sacrifice — *hu atzmo le-damo hu tzarich* — and so of course one would need to cut the vessels to draw blood. The fact that there is a live dispute, with the Rabbis rejecting Rabbi Yehuda's requirement, indicates that the discussion is about chulin, where there is room to argue that cutting the blood vessels is not part of the shechita requirement.

### Two Heads & Tizbach

Rav Ashi's proof comes from the upcoming Mishna, which states: *hashochet shenei rashim ke-echad shechitato kesherah* — if one slaughters two animals simultaneously with one stroke, the shechita is valid. The verb *hashochet*, combined with *kesherah*, carries the implication that it is valid only *di'avad* — after the fact — but not *lechatchila*. If the end of the Mishna refers to kodshim, then this explains why it is only bedi'avad: because Rav Yosef taught a drasha from the word *tizbach* — you shall slaughter — in the context of sacrifices. The word is written without the expected *vav*, yielding a singular form — *tizbachuhu* — which is expounded to teach two things: *shelo yihyu shnayim shochtim zevach echad*, no two people should perform the shechita of one animal simultaneously, and *shelo yehei echad shochet shenei zevachim*, one person should not shecht two animals simultaneously. Both flow from the interplay between the written and read forms of the word. This is a pasuk specifically about kodshim and explains why shechting two animals at once is only bedi'avad when dealing with sacrifices. But if the end of the Mishna referred to chulin, there would be no such restriction and shechting two animals simultaneously should be entirely permitted lechatchila. The fact that it is treated as bedi'avad confirms that the end of the Mishna refers to kodshim.

### Reish Lakish: Yom Kippur

Reish Lakish offers a different explanation for the repetition altogether. He points out that the Mishna teaches elsewhere about Yom Kippur: *hevi'u lo et ha-tamid*, they brought the tamid to the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur, *tzirtzo*, he began the shechita, *u-mireik acher shechitato*, and another person completed the shechita on his behalf. From this one might infer: perhaps by kodshim if one does not complete the cut the shechita is invalid — perhaps the Kohen Gadol's completion by another person was only possible because the finishing is not required. But perhaps the implication runs in the other direction and majority is not sufficient for kodshim. Therefore the Mishna reiterates: *rov echad be-of ve-rov shnayim be-behemah* — majority of one by bird and majority of two by behemah is sufficient, affirming that even by kodshim majority is enough.

### Mitzva to Complete Cut

The Gemara then refines the analysis of the Yom Kippur case. Could one have thought that the Kohen Gadol needed to complete the shechita himself? If completing the cut were biblically required, it could never have been done by another person, since *kol avodat Yom Kippur einam kesherot ella bo* — all the service of Yom Kippur is valid only when performed by the Kohen Gadol himself. So the concern cannot have been a biblical requirement. But perhaps it is rabbinically required? The Gemara answers: *yacho yihyeh pasul mide-rabbanan* — indeed, one might have thought there is a rabbinic invalidity if the cut is not completed. Therefore the Mishna reiterates that majority suffices, to exclude even a rabbinic invalidation. Since there is not even a rabbinic invalidity — *afilu psulah de-rabbanan leika* — why then did someone complete the shechita for the Kohen Gadol? The Gemara answers: *mitzva lemareik* — it is a mitzvah, an ideal, to complete the cut. Not an invalidation of any kind, but a positive ideal that by kodshim one should complete the shechita fully.

Whether this ideal extends to chulin as well is left somewhat open. The question of whether majority suffices only bedi'avad or even lechatchila — which surfaced at the very beginning of the Gemara's discussion — remains somewhat unresolved for chulin. But what is established clearly is that neither biblically nor rabbinically does any more than a majority invalidate the shechita.

### Summary of Principles

Before turning to the practical discussion, it is worth summarizing the major principles established. Mammals require shechita of two simanim; birds require one, with a debate as to whether this is biblical or rabbinic; fish require none. The majority of each required siman suffices. Whether fifty percent counts as majority was debated by Rav and Rav Kahana, but the Gemara ultimately concludes that this debate concerned only the case of the korban Pesach, where the question was whether the tamei half of the population must wait for Pesach Sheni. In general, majority means a real majority and not merely fifty percent. The Mishna's repetition of the majority rule addresses both chulin and kodshim: neither more nor less than majority is required by either, though by kodshim there is a positive ideal to complete the cut. And while in kodshim blood is the central purpose of the sacrificial act, the requirement to cut the blood vessels — per Rabbi Yehuda — is separately addressed and is not itself a part of the shechita requirement even there, though the rationale for cutting them is particularly compelling in the sacrificial context.
