## Shechita Demo & Kabbala

### Aaron's Kabbala Intro

At this point in the shiur, Aaron Braund joins — someone who has been studying for his kabbala in shechita over the past several months. What follows is a practical discussion of the art and halacha of shechita as it is actually practiced. Aaron notes at the outset something important: much of what the Gemara discusses, while normative halacha, is not always followed with the precision one might expect from the text alone. For instance, the question of fifty percent versus majority: in practice, a visibly discernible majority is required, and the Simlah Chadasha — the major work on the laws of shechita — indicates this is approximately sixty percent. Most shochtim do not measure; they rely on trained eye. A small minority of authorities, including a position cited in the Simlah Chadasha, do permit measurement, but this is not general practice.

### Chalaf Construction

The chalaf — the shechita knife — is flat on one side, with a double-edged blade. In America it is typically made from raw, unpolished metal, while in Israel it is more common to find knives that are shined and polished, reflecting a Chassidic minhag. The handle is constructed with a fiber grip in American-made knives; Israeli versions sometimes resemble molded plastic handles of the kind found on commercial cutlery. The tang — the metal portion extending from the blade into the handle — must pass sufficiently through the handle so that when the shochet grips the knife, he is in effect holding the metal itself, ensuring the knife functions as a single unified implement. A Nakiri knife, which resembles the chalaf in shape, is typically disqualified because either the tang does not extend adequately through the handle, or the knife is too heavy.

The weight of the knife is a significant practical concern. The heavier the knife, the greater the risk of derisah — pressing down rather than drawing back and forth — which is one of the five psulim of shechita. This is one reason why the increasingly large knives now fashionable in some communities have been a source of discomfort among experienced shochtim. For small birds (dakot), a smaller knife is used; for large animals (gasot), the knife must be at least twice the width of the animal's neck, unless the shochet goes back and forth across the neck multiple times.

### Knife Bedika Methods

The chalaf must be examined before and after each shechita. This is not a case where one relies on a chazakah of a previously checked knife — the knife must be actively checked each time, particularly given how readily a blade of this sharpness can be damaged. In principle, the check involves twelve examinations: the blade has three edges — the two flat sides and the actual cutting edge — and each is examined twice with the fingernail and twice with the pad of the finger, never checking two edges simultaneously. In current practice in America, finger-checking has largely been set aside; the nail check remains standard.

There are additional methods for difficult cases. If a slight drag is felt during the nail check and one is uncertain whether it reflects a pegimah — a nick that would invalidate a shechita performed with it — several supplementary checks exist. One method involves holding the knife up to the sun; contrary to what is commonly assumed, this refers not to looking at the blade itself but at its shadow, where the magnifying effect of shadow projection makes small irregularities more visible — a technique described by Rishonim. Another method is running water down the blade and observing whether the stream is deflected where a nick might be. A third method, employed when neither of the above is available and the knife is very clean, is the tongue test: the distinct metallic taste that a nick produces on the tongue — similar to the sensation of touching a metal fork to aluminum — allows the shochet to detect even small irregularities. Stropping the blade before and after shechita removes fibers and static-charge debris that accumulate during the cut.

The sides of the blade are also worth checking — not merely the edge. Aaron recounts detecting a scratch on the side of his blade that he had not noticed at the top, which his instructor was subsequently able to feel at the top as well, a defect that could have constituted ikkur.

### Sharpening the Chalaf

The primary sharpening stone used for the chalaf is known as the green stone. Unlike the practice in general knife sharpening, oil-based whetstones are prohibited for a shechita knife: oil fills a pegimah and prevents the shochet from detecting it during the bedika, making the check unreliable. Only water-based stones are used. The green stone is used for routine maintenance once the knife has already been brought to its proper sharpness; coarser stones are used for initial shaping. A chalaf of this kind requires approximately fifty hours of sharpening work before it reaches the standard required for shechita.

The resulting sharpness is extraordinary — sufficient to catch on paper and acquire fiber from it, though this is more a consequence of the static charge the knife builds up during repeated honing than a demonstration that paper causes a genuine pegimah. The knife is so fine that the case in which it is stored must be constructed so the blade does not contact the interior walls. The practical test for sharpness used in training — not described as such in the Simlah Chadasha — involves drawing the blade lightly across the surface of the skin; if it catches two or more layers, the blade is sharp enough.

### Holding the Chicken

Restraining the bird correctly is essential both for the validity of the shechita and for the animal's welfare, since the shochet bears responsibility for the pain and suffering of the animal. The technique, handed down as practical tradition, involves first layering the wings — the right wing is placed over the left — and inserting the left hand beneath both wings into the armpits of the bird. This, combined with gentle downward pressure, causes the bird to go limp almost immediately; a bird that is struggling will go quiet when held this way. The shochet then quickly pulls the skin from the back of the head and neck and flips the bird, which ends up lying calmly on the back of the hand with the head separated forward and a clear red zone at the throat where the shechita is performed.

The point at which birds typically react is precisely when the skin at the back of the head is pulled, which is why speed matters at that stage. Once positioned, the bird is entirely limp and the shochet has a clear working area.

### Act of Shechita

The bracha — *asher kid'shanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu al ha-shechita* — is recited once at the beginning of a session, with the kavvanah that all birds brought during that session are covered under the bracha, provided there is no interruption. It is not recited before each individual bird.

The shochet then draws the chalaf from his mouth — where it rests during restraint of the bird — and performs a *holacha ve-hava'ah*, a back-and-forth motion, quickly and without downward pressure. Speed is essential: a slow cut invites the bird to begin moving, forcing the shochet to withdraw and potentially creating a shehiya. The knife is held perpendicular to the throat, at a slight angle, and the cut must stay within the defined zone between the shipui hakova — the small triangular projection beneath the bird's beak — and the spine.

After the cut, the knife is returned to the mouth and the shochet checks for ikkur ha-simanim by pressing on the shipui hakova and pushing toward the cut. If the shechita was properly performed, the kaneh — the trachea — will pop out clearly. The softness of the esophagus means it does not protrude in the same manner, but the trachea's rigidity makes it a reliable indicator of a clean cut. The bird is then placed in a traffic cone positioned over a container with dirt at the bottom, both to facilitate drainage by gravity and for kisuy hadam.

### Trachea & Esophagus Cut

In practice, the shochet aims to cut both the trachea and the esophagus. The esophagus, being soft and longer than the distance it must travel, typically falls in front of the trachea in the living bird, but when the skin is pulled back during restraint, the rigid trachea is drawn upward to its full extent while the soft esophagus falls behind it. The cut therefore passes through the esophagus and then the trachea in sequence.

The working window is narrow. One must not cut into the spine — getting into the spine without actually severing it is permissible, but cutting through the spine is treated as derisah because it cannot be reached without exerting improper downward force. The shochet must know from the length and weight of his particular knife how far a given stroke will travel and calibrate accordingly. The zone that is valid for shechita is the area between the shipui hakova above and the junction with the body below, and the entire hagramah concern relates to cutting above or below this zone.

### Blood Vessels & Rubashkin

As discussed in the Gemara, cutting the blood vessels — the jugular vein or carotid artery — is not itself part of the shechita requirement but is necessary for the blood to drain while the animal is still alive, without which salting will not be effective in drawing the blood. The practical requirement is that the vessels must be cut while the bird's heart is still pumping. In most properly performed shechitot, the stroke that cuts the simanim also severs the blood vessels simultaneously. However, there are cases where the vessels are not cut in the stroke, and then the shochet must nick them while the heart is still active.

This is the practice that drew controversy in the Rubashkin case, where footage showed shochtim cutting the blood vessels of cattle after the initial shechita, causing the animals to appear to vocalize and move. What appeared alarming to outside observers was in fact a normal post-shechita phenomenon: the sound is air escaping through the severed trachea, not vocalization, and the movement reflects post-shechita muscle activity. The cutting of the vessels afterwards is required precisely because by large animals the stroke does not always catch them — the vessels tend to fall behind when the kaneh is grabbed and pulled forward — and ensuring blood drainage while the heart still pumps is a halachic necessity.

Halachically, after shechita has been performed, a Jew may in principle immediately eat from the bird — the shechita renders it permitted. But the animal is not yet *dead* in any broader sense: for a non-Jew, shechita does not constitute death, and the animal is forbidden to them under the prohibition of ever min ha-chai until the pirkus is complete. The Simlah Chadasha states plainly that Jews do not treat the bird as permitted for cutting before death in order not to be less stringent than non-Jews in this regard.

### Five Psulei Shechita

The five psulim of shechita — recalled by the mnemonic *ashi-chad*: ikkur, shehiya, hagramah, chaladah, and derisah — each present practical challenges. Shehiya applies not only to stopping and resuming; it also applies if the blade is momentarily arrested on something outside the zone of shechita — for example, if the shochet accidentally cuts his own finger during the stroke, the blade has paused and the shehiya invalidates the shechita. Derisah — downward pressure — is a constant concern and is one reason heavy knives are problematic. It is also considered derisah to press one's finger against the back of the blade during the stroke. Cutting through the spinal column is treated as derisah because reaching it implies the application of downward force beyond what is appropriate.

Hagramah requires that the cut be made within the valid zone. Chaladah — burrowing, beginning a cut from within the neck rather than at the surface — is addressed practically by the flat, non-pointed back of the chalaf, which prevents the knife from being inserted beneath the simanim. For small animals (behemah dakah), the animal is typically suspended and the head is pulled upward so the shochet can see what he is doing; cutting with the animal simply standing would risk chaladah by blocking the shochet's view of the stroke. Ikkur — tearing the simanim from their connections — manifests primarily when there is a pegimah in the knife, causing the blade to catch and tear rather than cut. It can also occur if the simanim are detached from above or below; pressing the shipui hakova and confirming the trachea pops out is the practical check for this.

A note on the scythe (magal) discussed in the Mishna: the issue raised there concerns ikkur from serrations — cutting against the grain of serrations tears rather than slices. In practice, such a shechita is not considered kosher even bedi'avad.

### Kisuy Dam & Non-Jewish

After the bird is placed in the cone and bleeds out, the blood that collects must be covered with earth — *kisuy hadam*. The container prepared beneath the cone is filled with dirt for this purpose, fulfilling the mitzvah as the blood drains.

Pirkus — the death rattle, the final convulsive movements — is a phenomenon that in healthy birds is not itself a halachic requirement; the shechita is valid regardless. The practical determination of when the bird has died is generally clear in the context of chicken shechita — it happens quickly. The theological and legal nuance is that for a Jew, shechita constitutes the act that renders the bird permitted for consumption; for a non-Jew, the animal is not considered legally dead until the pirkus has ceased. For a non-Jew to consume from the bird before that point would constitute eating ever min ha-chai, which is one of the seven Noachide prohibitions.

Non-Jewish methods of slaughter differ substantially. Chickens in industrial settings are suspended upside down by their legs, passed through an electrified water bath, and then through a scalding bath that removes the feathers. For cattle, the standard industrial method involves a captive bolt pistol — originally a fixed piston device that fractured the skull and struck the brainstem, now increasingly a pull-down pneumatic gun — which stuns rather than kills. The animal must still be killed by cutting the major blood vessels, since the heart must be pumping for the blood to drain; stunning followed by exsanguination is the industry standard. The difference between this and shechita, beyond the quality and precision of the knife and the care taken, is primarily the absence of prior stunning.

### Giraffe Shechita Problem

A question naturally arises about giraffes, which are a kosher species. The practical difficulty with shechita of a giraffe is not the biblical requirement — bedi'avad, as long as one does not cut above the shipui hakova or below the junction with the body, one has twelve feet of valid zone to work with. The problem is that *lechatchila*, the Simlah Chadasha requires cutting in the middle of the neck, and the traditional method for identifying the middle is to bend the animal's ear downward — the tip of the ear, when pressed to the neck, points to the precise midpoint. This method works reliably for cows and several other animals for which there is an established tradition.

For the giraffe, however, there is no established minhag for where to cut. One could theoretically measure the neck and find the midpoint geometrically, and one side of the modern debate holds that measurement should suffice. But the ear-bending method — the traditional way of establishing the midpoint — fails entirely for a giraffe, since the giraffe's ear is small relative to its neck length and does not reach past the jawline. This leaves the giraffe in a state of lacking a recognized tradition for lechatchila shechita, which is the basis for the position that giraffe shechita is practically problematic despite being theoretically valid.

The question is largely academic given that giraffes are endangered and not available for consumption. Deer, by contrast, are regularly shechted in America and are available in some kosher restaurants, including establishments in the northeastern United States. Turkey presents a similar historical question about the establishment of a minhag for a new-world species, but there is a well-established tradition for turkey shechita today.

### Kaddish DeRabbanan

The shiur closes with Kaddish DeRabbanan.

# Hullin 29b

## Shechita Timing

### Reish Lakish vs. R. Yoch…

We begin on 29b with one of the central conceptual questions of the entire masechta. The Gemara presents a foundational dispute about how to conceptualize the act of shechita as a process. Reish Lakish said in the name of Levi Sava: *eino li-shechita ela be-sof* — shechita occurs only at the end. The final cut or the final moment that completes the majority of the simanim is what constitutes the act of shechita. Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, says *yeshno li-shechita mi-techilah ve-ad sof* — it spans from the very beginning to the end.

This is a genuinely interesting conceptual question. A process only finishes at the end, but that does not tell us whether we consider the entire process to be the act itself, or only its culminating moment. The logic strongly favors Rabbi Yochanan's position. If one said that shechita occurs only at the very end, one must grapple with an obvious problem: what happened before the end? By the time you reach the final cut, the animal is already a treifa — you have already severed part of its neck. Clearly something of significance occurred before the final moment. Furthermore, the Gemara elsewhere recognizes a pesul of shehiya — a pause during the cutting — which would be entirely inexplicable if nothing halakhically meaningful were happening until the last instant.

These are excellent questions, and the Gemara is aware of them. To make sense of the position that shechita is only at the end, one must reframe the debate. The question is not whether one is *in the process* of shechting — that everyone would agree is true from the beginning — but whether one has yet performed a *completed act* of shechita. According to the view that shechita is only at the end, one is in the process of shechting throughout, which is why the animal is not a treifa and why shehiya is a pesul, but one cannot yet say that shechita *has been performed* until the process is complete. According to Rabbi Yochanan, even at an intermediate stage one can already be said to have done shechita, even if incompletely. This framing makes the first position more internally coherent, though it admittedly makes the second position somewhat harder to understand.

### Rava's Agreement Cases

Rava begins by identifying scenarios where both opinions would agree on the outcome. *ha-kol modim heicha di-shachat siman echad oved kochavim ve-siman echad yisrael she-hi pesulah* — if a non-Jew cut the first siman and a Jew cut the second, everyone agrees it is invalid. This requires no appeal to the debate about when shechita occurs. Even if one says the act of shechita is only at the end, by the time the Jew arrives, the animal is already a treifa. The non-Jew's act rendered it a treifa; it is not the non-Jew's shechita that is the problem but the prior physical state of the animal.

Similarly, regarding an olas ha-of — a bird brought as an olah — if one cut one siman at the bottom of the altar and one siman at the top, and an olah bird must be performed at the top, everyone agrees it is pesulah. One might have thought: according to the view that shechita is only at the end, the act performed at the bottom does not yet count as shechita, so no violation has occurred there. But that reasoning fails. Even if the cut at the bottom is not yet a shechita act, it does constitute *ma'aseh chatas ha-of lemata* — it is an act equivalent to the shechita of a bird chatat performed at the bottom, which is precisely how a chatat bird is treated. By doing that at the bottom of the altar, one has treated the olah as a chatat, which everyone agrees is an invalidation. So both of these cases are not disputed regardless of which position one holds.

### Shechuting Outside

Where then is the practical difference between the two opinions? *lo nechelku ela kegon she-shachat siman echad ba-chutz ve-siman echad bi-fnim* — the original framing of the debate is a case where one shechted one siman of a korban outside the Beit Hamikdash and completed the second siman inside. One who shechts a korban outside the Beit Hamikdash transgresses the prohibition of shochtei chutz. According to Rabbi Yochanan, who says the process begins at the beginning, one has already performed a shechita act outside — one is chayav. According to Reish Lakish, one has only begun a process; no shechita has yet been done, and one is not chayav.

However, Rava bar Shimi reports in the name of Rav Yosef that this framing is incorrect. *heicha di-shachat siman echad ba-chutz ve-siman echad bi-fnim, nami pasul* — even according to the view that shechita is only at the end, everyone would agree that shechting one complete siman outside transgresses the prohibition, because cutting one siman is sufficient for a bird chatat, and thus it constitutes a complete act relative to that category of korban. Accordingly, the proper framing of the debate must involve a lesser act.

*Lo nechelku ela kegon she-shachat miyut simanim ba-chutz u-gmaro bi-fnim* — the debate applies where one shechted only a minority of a siman outside and completed the rest inside. According to the view that shechita begins at the beginning, even cutting 30 percent of the trachea outside counts as the beginning of a shechita act, and one is chayav. According to the view that shechita is only at the end, one has not yet performed shechita; one was merely in the middle of a process and is not chayav.

### Rav Yosef Refines

Rav Yosef's refinement thus limits the practical scope of the dispute. The debate only surfaces in a case of *miyut simanim* — a minority of the siman cut outside. Only there does the question of whether the process-beginning constitutes an act become determinative. A full siman cut outside generates liability regardless, because it independently constitutes a complete act for the category of chatat ha-of.

---

## Parah Adumah

### Parah Tumah Rules

Rabbi Zeira raises a challenge to the preceding debate from a Mishnah concerning the parah adumah. The Torah states that all who engage in the process of the parah adumah become tamei. The Mishnah teaches that this tumah — strong enough to cause one's clothing to become tamei — applies to anyone involved *mi-techilah ve-ad sof*, from the beginning of the process to the end. The first ritual act upon the parah adumah is the shechita; prior to that, everything is preparatory. Additionally, performing any other melacha simultaneously with any stage of the parah adumah process invalidates the parah entirely.

### Pesul During Shechita

The Mishnah then addresses cases of invalidity. If some form of pesul occurred during the shechita — either the shechita itself was performed incorrectly, rendering the animal a neveilah, or, according to Tosafot, a simultaneous melacha was performed — then both those involved before the pesul and those involved after the pesul do *not* become metamei begadim. The reasoning is: if the shechita is ruined, it was never a shechita at all; if it was never a shechita, the process of parah adumah never commenced; and if the process never commenced, no involvement in it can generate tumah.

### Pesul During Haza'ah

The rule differs when the invalidity occurs at the stage of haza'ah — the sprinkling of the blood of the parah. Here, the distinction is temporal: one who was involved before the pesul *does* become metamei begadim, because at the time of that involvement the process was still valid. One who becomes involved after the pesul does not become tamei. This contrast — full preclusion of tumah when shechita fails versus partial preclusion keyed to the timing of the pesul when haza'ah fails — sets up the Gemara's central question.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava poses a sharp question: *ve-lei aflog nami bi-shchitata* — if the shechita process begins at the beginning, why does the Mishnah not draw the same before/after distinction for the shechita stage that it draws for haza'ah? If shechita is a process that begins from the start, then someone involved before the pesul occurred during shechita should become tamei, and someone involved only after the pesul should not. Why does the Mishnah treat the shechita stage as a complete non-event for purposes of tumah?

### Rava's Response

Rava himself resolves the challenge: *niskalkela shechita ka'amrat? — shani hatam, d'igla milta le-mafrea d'lav shechita hi klal* — when the shechita itself is ruined, it has been retroactively revealed that no shechita ever took place. The key qualifier is that the position *yeshno li-shechita mi-techilah ve-ad sof* — that shechita begins at the beginning — only applies when the process is successfully completed. Once it is complete, we look back and say the process began from the first cut. But if the shechita ends in failure, there is retroactive revelation that nothing was ever being done. It was not a process of shechita in the first place; it was merely an attempt. Accordingly, no one involved in the failed shechita becomes tamei, and there is no before/after distinction to draw.

Rashi understands the pesul as referring to a ruined shechita that produced a neveilah. Tosafot takes the pesul as referring to a simultaneous melacha. For Rashi, the point is straightforward: since the shechita failed, we retroactively read back that there was never a shechita occurring. For Tosafot, the argument is slightly more nuanced: since the parah adumah process was not validly executed — because an extraneous melacha was performed — the process of *shechitat parah adumah* never commenced, even if the physical cutting was technically valid.

### Two People Shechting

Rava raises an additional question: given the debate between the two positions, why does the Mishnah on parah adumah not illustrate its point with a simpler case? Even in a fully valid, uninterrupted parah adumah shechita, one could distinguish when tumah attaches by positing two people shechting — one cutting the first siman and one cutting the second. According to the view that shechita is only at the end, only the second person would become tamei; the first would not. Why doesn't the Mishnah discuss this scenario to illustrate the principle?

Rav Yosef responds: *trei gavrei be-chad zivcha ka'amarta* — two people with one sacrifice? The verse *tizbach* — you shall slaughter — is read without the vav, in the singular, indicating that only one person may slecht a given sacrifice. Since the parah adumah has quasi-sacrificial status and is called a chatat, this rule applies to it as well. Accordingly, the scenario of two people shechting the parah adumah is impossible, and the Mishnah cannot use it.

### Abaye's Handkerchief

Abaye objects: this exclusion of two people from shechting a parah adumah is the view of Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Shimon, who is the stam author of that Mishnah, but the Chachamim permit two people to shecht one sacrifice. So the question stands: why not use the two-person scenario according to the Chachamim?

And, continues Abaye, even according to Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Shimon who prohibits two people, one can construct an equivalent scenario with one person and two garments. *k'gon she-shachat chad gavrah bi-shnei sudarin* — if the shochet was wearing one garment at the beginning of shechita and a different garment at the end, the first garment was only present during the beginning of the process and not at its completion. According to the view that shechita is only at the end, only the final garment would become tamei. This scenario requires only one person and could have been stated by the Mishnah to illustrate the principle.

### Gemara Clarifies

The Gemara acknowledges the force of Abaye's question but explains why the Mishnah does not use such scenarios: *ela be-psulah de-para ka'amiri, bi-cheshirah lo ka'amiri* — the Mishnah was discussing cases where the parah adumah process was invalidated; it was not interested in exploring scenarios where the process was completed validly and the question is only which garment one was wearing. The structural focus of the Mishnah is on when invalidity disrupts the process and how that affects tumah. Exploring the nuances of which moment during a valid shechita generates tumah was simply not the Mishnah's concern. In principle, however, Abaye is correct: if shechita is only at the end, only the garment worn at the end would become tamei.

---

## Pesach Timing

### Pesach on Chol Hamoed

The Gemara introduces a new challenge from a passage concerning the korban pesach. The rule is well known from Zevachim: a korban pesach shechted not on the fourteenth of Nisan, and shechted with a different designation in mind, is reclassified as a shelamim. There is also a prohibition derived from the verse *lo tishchat al chameitz dam zivchi* — one may not slecht a sacrifice while one possesses chametz. This applies not only to the korban pesach itself but to any valid korban during Chag Hamatzos when chametz is present.

The Mishnah states: *u-ve-moed li-shmo patur, she-lo li-shmo chayav* — if on Chol Hamoed Pesach one slechts what was designated as a korban pesach *li-shmo*, with the intent to bring it as a pesach, one is exempt from the violation of slaughtering over chametz, because the sacrifice is invalid. If one slects it *she-lo li-shmo*, consciously redesignating it as a shelamim, it is a valid sacrifice and one is chayav.

### Auto Identity Change

The Gemara asks: the reason one is chayav when acting *she-lo li-shmo* implies that if one acts *stam*, with no particular intent, one would be patur — meaning the korban would still function as a pesach and be invalid. But does a pesach not automatically become a shelamim when brought at the wrong time? If so, even with no intent, it should be a valid shelamim and one should be chayav.

The inference is that a pesach outside its proper time does *not* automatically change identity; it requires conscious *akira* — an active uprooting of its original designation — in order to become a shelamim. Without such akira, it remains a pesach at the wrong time and is invalid.

### R. Chiya Context

Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda clarifies the context. This ruling was taught in a setting where the reason the pesach had not been brought on the fourteenth of Nisan was that the owners were temei meitim — ritually impure from contact with a corpse. They are therefore eligible to bring a pesach sheini, a second pesach on the fourteenth of Iyar. Since their animal is still earmarked for pesach sheini, its identity as a pesach remains active and compelling; it does not automatically shift to shelamim. Only through a deliberate act of redesignation would it become a shelamim. In a case where there is no prospect of pesach sheini — a pesach brought during the rest of the year with no upcoming opportunity — the animal automatically becomes a shelamim without any conscious akira.

---

## Pesach Mum

### Mum Changes Identity

The Gemara now applies the earlier debate about shechita timing directly to this case. *ei amrat bishlama yeshno li-shechita mi-techilah ve-ad sof* — if shechita begins at the beginning, then from the very first moment one starts cutting the animal, one has begun a shechita act upon a pesach. It is already being shechted as a pesach at the wrong time, and it is immediately invalid. The framework is coherent.

But *ei amrat eino li-shechita ela be-sof* — if shechita is only at the end — then when one begins cutting the animal, one has not yet performed any shechita act. One has merely made a cut, which creates a mum. As soon as the animal has a mum, it can no longer be brought as a pesach sheini next month. As soon as it can no longer serve as a pesach sheini, why should it not automatically be redesignated as a shelamim — even without conscious akira — since its future as a pesach is foreclosed the instant one starts cutting? If so, by the time one finishes the shechita, the animal is already a shelamim, not a pesach, and one should be chayav even without any intent. The Mishnah's ruling that *stam* intent leads to exemption becomes inexplicable.

This is a penetrating question and highlights the recurring difficulty with the view that shechita is only at the end. As has been noted throughout this sugya, if nothing has been halakhically accomplished until the very last moment, then the earlier cuts must be characterized as mere physical damage — creating mum, making the animal a treifa — which would seem to have implications for the animal's status. Yet the proponents of *eino li-shechita ela be-sof* must somehow bracket those implications for most halakhic purposes while invoking them selectively. This tension runs through the entire discussion and is left without complete resolution.

### Pesach Category Remains

Abaye provides the response: *nehi d'id'chayei lah mi-pesach* — it is true that from the moment one begins cutting, the animal can no longer be brought as a pesach sheini in its current form. *bi-dmei pesach mi id'chayei* — but it has not been removed from the *category* of pesach entirely. Even after acquiring a mum, the animal could be redeemed: its kedusha could be transferred to money, and that money could be used to purchase an animal for the pesach sheini. Therefore, the animal has not been fully uprooted from its pesach identity. It remains within the ambit of pesach, and without a conscious act of akira it will not become a shelamim.

One might object: once one has begun shechita, can the animal still be redeemed? The verse requires that the animal be stood before the kohen and evaluated while alive — *ha'amada ve-ha'aracha* — which would seem to foreclose redemption once shechita has begun. Abaye responds: the animal is not yet dead when shechita begins, and the Mishnah elsewhere teaches that even after two simanim have been cut, as long as the animal is still *mefarchesets* — convulsing, showing signs of life — it retains a degree of halakhic vitality. Therefore, theoretically, even during an ongoing shechita the possibility of redemption has not been entirely foreclosed, and the animal remains within the pesach category.

The broader discussion is admittedly frustrating at a conceptual level. If one defines the two positions as: (a) one is *in the process of shechita* from the beginning versus (b) the *act of shechita* is only complete at the end, then in some sense both positions ought to be simultaneously true — one is always in the process from the beginning, and the act is always complete at the end. The only meaningful debate would be whether being in-process is itself halakhically significant for specific purposes, such as triggering chiyuv for shochtei chutz or generating tumah in the context of parah adumah. That framing helps make both positions intelligible, but it does not fully eliminate the difficulties around why the animal is not a treifa or ba'al mum for most halakhic purposes even according to the view that nothing counts until the end.

---

## Multiple Locations

### Shechita in 2-3 Places

The Gemara introduces a new halacha: *ha-shochet bi-shnayim u-vi-shloshah mekomot, shechitato kesherah* — if one shechted in two or three places, the shechita is valid. The scenario envisioned is one where the knife did not trace a single continuous path across the siman but rather cut 40 percent at one location, then 20 percent at a different location, such that combined they constitute the required majority, yet no single contiguous cut covers the full majority. The question is whether this is valid or whether a single exposed, unbroken cut is required.

When this ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav was reported to Shmuel, he disagreed: *beinan shechita meforaat ve-leika* — we require *shechita meforaat*, an exposed cut, and this case lacks it. A valid shechita must produce a cut that is open and visible as a single line, comparable to the straight path of an arrow.

### Arrow Analogy

Reish Lakish provides the textual source for the requirement of shechita meforaat. The verse states *chetz shachut leshono mirma diber* — their tongue is like a sharpened arrow when they speak treachery. The same verb *shachut*, cutting, that appears in the verse describing an arrow's straight path, applies to shechita. Just as an arrow cuts in a straight, unimpeded line, so must shechita produce a straight, unimpeded cut.

### Two Knives Case

Rabbi Elazar challenges this requirement from a Mishnah: *bi-shnayim ochazim be-sakin ve-shochtim* — two people holding knives and shechting, *afilu echad mi-lema'ala ve-echad mi-lemata, shechita kesherah* — even if one is working from above and one from below, the shechita is valid. This appears to describe exactly the scenario of shechita in two separate locations, with each person contributing part of the cut at a different place on the siman. Why would that be valid if shechita meforaat is required?

### One Knife Two Handles

Rabbi Yirmiah resolves the apparent contradiction: *mishnatenu be-sakin echad u-shnei bnei adam* — our Mishnah is not describing two separate knives cutting at separate locations. It describes two people holding the two handles of a single knife, operating it like a two-handled saw. In this configuration, the cut is indeed a single path — it is just being drawn by two sets of hands from opposite ends. The requirement of shechita meforaat is therefore not violated.

### Angled Cutting

Rabbi Avin raises a further question. A Mishnah states that if one shechted the veshet below and the kanah above, or the veshet above and the kanah below, the shechita is valid. This describes cutting at an angle — the blade passes through the siman diagonally such that the cut across the veshet is at a different vertical point than the cut across the kanah. Is this not a case of shechita in two separate locations? If shechita meforaat is required, how can an angled cut qualify?

### Quill Edge

Rabbi Avin himself answers the question: *bi-shechita de-siki de-kumsa* — it is like the edge of a quill. The cutting edge of a quill feather is not perpendicular but diagonal — it forms a flat, angled plane. An angled cut of the veshet and kanah similarly produces a single exposed plane of cutting, visible in its entirety when the beit ha-shechitah is opened. This is not a case of the knife jerking to a different location; it is a single diagonal stroke. The requirement of shechita meforaat is satisfied because the entire cut is visible and continuous, even if not perpendicular. What remains genuinely unresolved is whether a knife that truly does jerk — cutting in one location and then an entirely separate location — would be valid. That is the underlying question the sugya has been circling.

### Cow Story

A practical story is brought to illustrate how this was handled in practice. A cow was shechted in two or three separate locations — presumably exactly the case of genuinely discontinuous cuts on the siman. The matter was brought before Rav Yosef bar Shmuel bar Marta. He proceeded to take the choicest portions of the meat for himself — a pointed practical ruling that the shechita was entirely kosher and required no further deliberation.

### Rav Zeira Infers

Rav Zeira draws an inference from this ruling: *limadatenu rabbeinu, mishnatenu bi-shnei sakinim u-vi-shnei bnei adam* — from Rav Yosef bar Shmuel bar Marta's action, one can infer that the Mishnah describing two people shechting should indeed be understood as referring to two separate knives cutting at two separate locations on the siman, not merely two handles on one knife. His lenient ruling on the cow with multiple cuts supports the reading that genuinely discontinuous shechita in two locations is valid.

The overall ruling of this passage appears to be lenient: shechita meforaat as an absolute requirement for a single unbroken line may not be as strict as Shmuel suggested, and shechita in two or three locations can be valid. The rishonim debate the precise parameters of this case, and the practical ruling is also disputed, though the Gemara's trajectory is clearly toward leniency.

---

## Chaldah

### Chaldah Definition

The Gemara introduces the pesul of chaldah — burrowing. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *hechlid et ha-sakin bein siman le-siman u-fesako, pesulah* — if one inserted the knife between the two simanim and then cut through them, it is invalid. The proper method of shechita requires cutting from the outside inward; one may not begin in the interior, between the simanim and the spinal cord, and then work outward. This is why, as discussed earlier in the masechta, the front edge of a shechita knife is flat rather than pointed — so that it cannot burrow through and pierce from the middle.

### Tachat Ha-Or Valid

An important distinction is immediately introduced: *tachat ha-or, kesherah* — if one inserted the knife not between the simanim themselves but between the simanim and the outer skin, and then proceeded to cut the simanim in the normal outward motion, this is valid. Inserting the knife beneath the skin is not considered chaldah, because the burrowing that is prohibited is specifically entering the interior space between the simanim and the spinal cord. Beginning beneath the skin while still cutting from the outside toward the simanim and beyond does not constitute the prohibited form of burrowing.

### R. Yeshevav vs. Akiva

The Gemara notes that there is already a Mishnah addressing a related case: *o she-hechlid et ha-sakin tachat ha-sheni u-pesakah* — if one inserted the knife above the second siman and then cut downward. Rabbi Yeshevav says this produces a neveilah; Rabbi Akiva says it is a treifa. The distinction between neveilah and treifa here will be addressed elsewhere in the masechta.

### Cutting Direction

The Gemara clarifies what the new ruling adds beyond the Mishnah. One might have thought that the problem of burrowing above the second siman is specifically because one is cutting in the wrong direction — moving away from the spinal cord rather than toward it, which is the natural direction of shechita. Perhaps burrowing is only a pesul when one cuts in the wrong direction. If so, inserting the knife between the simanim but then cutting toward the spinal cord — the correct direction — might be valid.

The ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that even burrowing in the correct direction is invalid. Even if one inserts the knife between the two simanim and cuts in the direction of the spinal cord — the correct shechita motion — this is still chaldah and the shechita is pesulah.

### Cloth Wool Cases

The passage then raises a series of unresolved questions. The school of Rav held that *tachat ha-or eini yodea* — they were uncertain whether inserting the knife beneath the outer skin, as described above, is in fact valid or not. And building on this uncertainty, the Gemara asks two further questions that remain in teiku. *tachat ha-matlit mahu* — what if there was a cloth wrapped around the neck of the animal and one inserted the knife beneath the cloth? The cloth is not part of the animal at all, yet if beginning beneath even the skin of the animal is already suspect, perhaps beginning beneath an external cloth is equally or more problematic.

*O tachat tzemer mesubach mahu* — or what if it is a sheep whose wool covers the area of shechita, and one begins cutting beneath the wool? The wool at least belongs to the sheep and grows from its body, so it is not as external as a cloth, but it is also not the skin proper. Both questions — burrowing under cloth and burrowing under wool — remain unresolved.

The underlying structure of the pesul of chaldah is now clear. What is prohibited is beginning the cutting from the interior of the neck — between the simanim and the spinal cord — and working outward. This is chaldah regardless of direction. What is permitted is beginning from outside the neck entirely and cutting inward in the normal fashion. The gray area, which the Gemara leaves undecided, is how far "outside" one must truly begin: does the very outer edge of the skin suffice, or must one begin even before the skin? And if one begins beneath a cloth or beneath the wool of the sheep, has one begun "outside" in the required sense? These questions are left for further analysis.

---

---

# Hullin 31

## Rashi vs. Rabbeinu Tam

### Rav Papa's Question

The present daf, 31b, brings to a close a series of discussions concerning the *psulim* of *shechita* — the various ways in which the act of slaughter can be rendered invalid. Among those discussed in the preceding material was *chalada*, the defect of "burrowing," which occurs when the knife does not begin cutting from the outside but instead penetrates between the *simanim* (the trachea and esophagus) and cuts in the wrong direction, or begins from the interior. On this note, the *gemara* closes with a brief but significant question posed by Rav Papa: *ki chalda bemiut simanim mah* — what is the *halacha* if the act of *chalada* occurs only in the minority of the *simanim*? The *gemara* leaves this unresolved with the word *teyku*.

On its surface, this seems unremarkable. But the question opens onto one of the most important debates between the Rishonim, one to which we have referred in earlier sessions and which now demands careful examination.

### Rashi's View

According to Rashi, the question of *chalada bemiut simanim* is really a manifestation of a much broader conceptual problem that runs through several passages in this *masechta*. To understand it, consider the following scenario: in the case of a *behema*, one has already cut the first *siman* and sixty percent of the second — which constitutes the *rov*, the majority. At the point where *rov* has been accomplished, the *shechita* is in principle complete. *rubo kekulo* — the majority counts as the whole. But now the *shochet* goes ahead and finishes the remaining forty percent, and does so improperly — through *chalada*, or through *shehiya* (a pause in cutting), or through *hagrama* (cutting in the wrong location). What is the *halacha*?

For Rashi, this question is not unique to *chalada*. He explicitly ties it to earlier discussions in the *gemara* about *hagrama* and to a question that appears on the following daf concerning *shehiya bemiut batra* — a pause that occurs in the final minority of the cutting. In all these cases, Rashi identifies the same underlying conceptual question: once the *rov* has been accomplished, does the act of *shechita* effectively end? Or does the halachic act continue, such that if one goes ahead and completes the remaining portion incorrectly, that completion becomes retroactively incorporated into the act of *shechita* and can invalidate it?

Rashi frames this as a genuine dispute about the meaning of *rubo kekulo*. Is *rov* simply the minimum threshold required — after which *halacha* is satisfied and anything further is legally immaterial? Or does *rubo kekulo* mean that the *rov* is treated *as if* the whole were done — meaning that in principle, the act encompasses the full one hundred percent, and if the remaining portion is completed with a *psul*, that *psul* is part of the act and invalidates it? Since the *gemara* resolves none of this — leaving it as *teyku* — Rashi rules that we must be stringent.

### Rashi's Ruling

This stringency has practical implications that Rashi himself spells out in his commentary to the following daf. Suppose a *shochet* has already completed *rov* of the *simanim* and the animal is clearly dying, but it is taking time and suffering. A natural instinct would be to complete the *shechita* to hasten the animal's death. Rashi says: do not do it. Going back and completing the remaining minority of the *simanim* now — after a pause — would constitute *shehiya bemiut batra*, a *shehiya* in the final minority, and since that final minority may be part of the act of *shechita*, the *shehiya* could invalidate the entire *shechita*. If one wishes to end the animal's suffering, Rashi says to accomplish this by other means — severing the neck from behind, for example — but not by continuing the *shechita* itself.

### Rabbeinu Tam

*Tosafot* cites Rabbeinu Tam, who rejects Rashi's understanding entirely. According to Rabbeinu Tam, once the *rov* of the *simanim* has been accomplished, the act of *shechita* is complete. Anything that happens thereafter — any further cutting, any further contact of the knife with the *simanim* — is simply not part of the *shechita* act. It cannot affect what has already validly occurred. The problem of *shehiya bemiut batra*, or any other *psul* in the final minority, is thus a non-issue according to Rabbeinu Tam.

How, then, does Rabbeinu Tam read Rav Papa's question? He interprets *chalada bemiut simanim* as a different scenario entirely — not about completing the remainder after *rov*, but about a knife that penetrates *into* a *siman* (rather than between the two *simanim*) and cuts with only a *miut* of that *siman* lying beneath the blade. Is that considered *chalada* or not? That is the question according to Rabbeinu Tam, and it is entirely distinct from Rashi's formulation.

The debate thus comes into sharp focus. Rashi holds that *rubo kekulo* is a legal equivalence — the *rov* stands in for the whole, meaning the whole act remains in play, and completing it improperly can invalidate. Rabbeinu Tam holds that *rubo kekulo* means *rov* is simply sufficient — *halacha* requires only *rov*, and once achieved, the act ends there. What follows is legally irrelevant. This is one of the central conceptual disputes about the meaning of *rubo kekulo* in all of *halacha*, and it emerges here from a single ambiguous line of *gemara*.

---

## Multiple Heads & Knife

### Two Heads & Two People

The *gemara* turns to the next *mishna*, which addresses several related scenarios. *hashocheit bishnei roshim ke-echad* — one who slaughters two animal heads simultaneously. If the knife is long enough and the animals are positioned properly, one can slaughter in a single motion without applying pressure to either neck, and the *shechita* is valid. Similarly, *shnayim ochazim basakin veshochtim* — two people holding opposite ends of a knife together, as if using a saw, and slaughtering — *shechitatan kesheira*, it is valid. This is true even if one person is on one side of the neck and the other is on the other side — *afilu echad lemala ve'echad lemata* — or even if they are using two separate knives, one at each position.

### Head Severed

The *mishna* then addresses a more complex case: *hitiz et harosh bebat achat* — if the head was entirely severed in one motion. The presumptive concern is *drisa*, the *psul* of applying pressure. If the entire head is chopped off in one stroke, we suspect that this occurred through force and pressure rather than through the proper horizontal cutting motion. Therefore, under ordinary circumstances, such a *shechita* is *pesulah*.

However, the *mishna* provides an exception: *haya shocheit vehitiz et harosh bebat achat, im yeish basakin mlo tzavar, kesheira* — if one was actively slaughtering with a horizontal cutting motion and the head was severed, if the knife had the length of a neck (*mlo tzavar*), it is valid.

The *gemara*'s explanation of this phrase is that the knife must measure the length of the animal's neck *plus* an additional neck length — that is, double the length of the neck. The logic is as follows: in a normal *shechita*, the knife travels back and forth, meaning the neck is effectively cut in two passes. A knife of double length, even in a single forward motion, covers the equivalent of two passes across the neck, making it possible to cut cleanly without pressure. If the knife achieves that double coverage through a single horizontal motion, we are not concerned that the severing of the head is evidence of *drisa*.

### Back and Forth Motion

The *mishna* then introduces the contrasting case: *im holich veheivi* — if the *shochet* was moving the knife back and forth — *afilu kol shehu afilu be'izmel kesheira* — even the tiniest blade, even an *izmel* (which Rashi identifies as a kind of scalpel or awl), is valid. This is a striking *chiddush*. The requirement for a double-length knife applies only when the *shochet* is performing a single directional motion. When cutting back and forth, even a blade of minimal width suffices, since the back-and-forth motion itself generates sufficient cutting across the *simanim* without recourse to pressure.

This point is worth pausing over. In principle, a *shochet* could perform *shechita* with a blade so small that it requires many back-and-forth passes to sever the *simanim* entirely. As long as no pressure is being applied, this would appear to be valid *shechita*. The concern about *drisa* is not triggered by the repetition of motion, only by the application of force or by evidence — such as the head being severed in a single motion with an insufficiently long blade — that force was applied.

### Source: Shachut

The *gemara* asks: where is the textual source for the principle that *shechita* must be accomplished through the sharpness of the blade — through horizontal cutting — rather than through pressure? The answer is attributed to Shmuel, who derives it from the verse *chetz shachut leshonam mirma diber* (Jeremiah 9:7): their tongue is like a *shachut* arrow — an arrow that cuts by moving horizontally through the air by the sharpness of its edge, not by stabbing or pressing. The *tana debe-rabi yishmael* further derives it from the word *veshachat* in the Torah itself: *ein veshachat ela umashach* — *shachut* means to draw horizontally. Additional support comes from the verse *zahav shachut* — spun gold drawn into threads — which likewise conveys the image of a horizontal drawing motion.

The *gemara* notes that one might have thought *zahav shachut* is not derived from the same root as *shechita* — perhaps the *shin* is not part of the verbal root and the word simply means gold shaped into threads. Therefore the verse about the arrow (*chetz shachut*) is also cited, to confirm the association with horizontal cutting.

### Arrow Story

The *gemara* now narrates a striking story. Rava would inspect the arrows of Rabi Yona bar Tachlifa — a hunter — and Rabi Yona bar Tachlifa would use these arrows to kill birds *bahadi deperach*, as they were flying. The edge of the arrow, presumably checked by Rava to be free of nicks and to have the appropriate sharpness, would cut through the neck of the bird in flight.

The *gemara* immediately raises the concern: *udilma avad lei chalada* — perhaps the arrow burrowed through the neck, entering point-first rather than cutting with its edge? The *gemara* answers: *chazinan gidfei de'miframmei* — we can inspect the neck feathers and see that they were cut from the outside in, confirming that the edge of the arrow, and not the point, performed the cutting.

The *gemara* then raises the question of *kisui ha-dam*. Since this is a bird (*of*), the blood must be covered. *ve'amar rabi zeira amar rav*: one who slaughters must place dirt below the blood and dirt above it, as derived from the verse *vechisahu be'afar* — "and he shall cover it in the dirt" — the preposition *be* indicating that dirt must be beneath as well as above. The solution offered for Rabi Yona bar Tachlifa's practice is that he would spread dirt across the entire valley where he hunted, so that wherever the bird fell, its blood would land on the prepared earth and could be covered from above.

The discussion in the shiur naturally raises the question of whether the arrow constitutes a sufficient act of *shechita* given that the hunter is no longer holding it when it cuts the bird. This leads directly into the subject of *koach gavra*, which will be addressed explicitly in the next *mishna*. Theoretically, the *gemara* will clarify, valid *shechita* does not require the *shochet* to be physically manipulating the knife at the moment of cutting — it requires that the act issue from human energy (*koach gavra*), not that the human hand be in contact throughout. An arrow released from a bow, like a knife released from the hand, still carries the energy of the one who propelled it.

This also occasions a broader discussion about how far *koach gavra* can be extended in principle. If one's energy is communicated through a mechanical chain — pedaling a bicycle that drives a machine — that seems clearly to qualify. If one presses a button and the energy that performs the act travels through electrical wires, the question becomes considerably more complex. The degree of separation between the human actor and the act itself is not always easy to measure, and such questions recur throughout *halacha* wherever the concept of *koach gavra* is operative.

---

## Knife Fell

### Knife Falls

The following *mishna* states: *nafla sakin veshachata* — a knife fell and in the process performed *shechita*. Even though it slaughtered the animal correctly — *af al pi sheshachata kedarka* — the *shechita* is *pesulah*. The *mishna* derives this from the verse *vezavachta ve'achalta*: "you shall slaughter and you shall eat" — what *you* slaughter, *you* may eat. The act of *shechita* must be a human act, not merely an event that happens to cut the *simanim*.

The *gemara* extracts from the *mishna* an implied leniency: *ta'ama denafla* — the *mishna's* reason is that the knife fell on its own; *ha hipila*, if the person caused it to fall — even by simply releasing it — the *shechita* is valid. This establishes that *koach gavra* does not demand that the knife be actively held at the moment of cutting; it is sufficient that the cutting is the product of the human's energy, even if communicated indirectly.

The *gemara* further notes: *ve'af al gav dela michavein* — and this is so even though the person had no intention for the *shechita* to occur. This introduces a second, independent question: does *shechita* require *kavana*, intent?

### Throwing Knife

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* taught by the younger Oshaya: *zarak sakin linoatza bakotel* — if one threw a knife at a wall, intending to stick it there, and the knife passed by an animal and slaughtered it *kedarka* — properly — *rabbi natan machshir*, Rabbi Natan declares the *shechita* valid. *vechachamim poslin*, the Sages invalidate it.

Here the situation is clearly one of *koach gavra* — the knife was propelled by human energy — but there is obviously no intention whatsoever to perform *shechita*. Rabbi Natan holds that *shechita* does not require intention. The Sages hold that it does. The *gemara* reports: *halacha ke-Rabbi Natan* — we rule like Rabbi Natan. *shechita* of *chullin* does not require *kavana*.

### Two Criteria

The *gemara* reflects on the analytical structure underlying these two *mishnayot*. Normally, for an act to be halachically operative, we presume two criteria: first, it must be a human act — it must issue from human energy (*koach gavra*); second, it must be intentional — if it is entirely incidental, it is treated as *mitasek*, something that simply happened without the person's agency. Rabbi Natan's ruling is striking precisely because it disaggregates these two criteria. *koach gavra* is required; *kavana* is not.

### Both Mishnayot

One might ask: given that Rabbi Natan's principle is stated explicitly in the *baraita* about the thrown knife, why did Rava find it necessary to identify Rabbi Natan's view in connection with the earlier *mishna* about the *cheresh, shoteh, ve-katan* (the deaf-mute, the insane person, and the minor) as well? The *gemara* answers: *tzricha* — both statements are necessary.

Had Rava only cited the earlier *mishna*, one might have explained the permissibility of the *cheresh, shoteh, ve-katan* on narrow grounds: those individuals are, in some sense, *intending to cut*. As *tosafot* notes, they are aware that they are cutting the trachea and esophagus. Their lack of *kavana* is therefore narrow — they may not have the capacity to intend the halachic implications of *shechita*, but they have some intention. In that case, the *chiddush* of the earlier *mishna* is not about *kavana* at all, but about whether *shechita* requires an actor who has full halachic standing (*ben da'at*). One might then have thought that a person of full standing throwing a knife with no intention at all would not suffice, since there is truly zero *kavana*. The *baraita* of Rabbi Natan is therefore needed to teach that even in that case, *shechita* is valid.

Conversely, had Rava only cited the *baraita* about throwing the knife, one might have concluded that *kavana* is not required but *koach gavra* must come from a halachically competent adult. The earlier *mishna*, which validates the *shechita* of a minor or deaf-mute when observed by others, adds the complementary *chiddush*: the act need not issue from someone with full halachic standing. Together, the two teachings establish that *shechita* of *chullin* requires *koach gavra* — but neither *kavana* nor a fully competent actor.

---

## Intent Required?

### Nidda Case

The *gemara* now broadens the discussion from *shechita* to the general question of when *halacha* requires *kavana* and when it does not. The springboard is a case involving a *nidda* (a woman in the state of ritual impurity): *nidda shene'ensa vetavla* — a *nidda* who was compelled and immersed in a *mikveh* without intent. Is this a valid *tevilah*?

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *tehora leveisa* — she is permitted to her husband; *ve-asura leochol bitruma* — but she may not eat *teruma*. The distinction rests on the principle, established elsewhere, that immersion for the purpose of eating *kodshim* or *teruma* requires specific intent. Without that intent, the *tevilah* does not achieve purification for those purposes. But for the lesser status — her relationship with her husband, which is a matter of *chullin* — no such intent is needed.

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *af leveisa lo tehora* — she is not even permitted to her husband. For Rabbi Yochanan, the entire framework of *tumah ve-tahara* requires intent, and one cannot split the package.

Rava challenged Rav's position before Rav Nachman: if this *tevilah* suffices to lift the *karet* prohibition (the severe prohibition of a man being with a woman who is a *nidda*), why would it not lift the lesser prohibition associated with eating *teruma*, which carries only the penalty of death by divine hands (*mita*) rather than *karet*? Rav Nachman responded: the distinction is not about the relative severity of the prohibition. *ba'alah chullin hu* — her husband belongs to the sphere of *chullin*, of lay matters. *uvechullin lo ba'ei kavana* — when it comes to *chullin*, intent is not required. *teruma*, by contrast, belongs to the sphere of sanctified obligations, where intent is required.

This formulation — *chullin lo ba'ei kavana* — becomes the operative principle. When a halachic act serves to change a status in the domain of ordinary, non-sanctified matters, that act does not require *kavana*. The requirement of *kavana* is limited to the domain of *kodshim* — of sanctified objects and elevated halachic categories — and even there it may be rabbinic in origin.

### Wave Case

The *gemara* seeks textual support for the principle that *chullin* does not require *kavana*, citing a *mishna*: *gal shenitlash uvo arbaim se'ah* — a wave that detaches from the sea containing forty *se'ah* (the minimum measure for a valid *mikveh*) and falls upon a person and vessels standing on the shore. *tehorim* — both the person and the vessels are rendered *tahor*.

The *gemara* attempts to prove from this case that *tevilah* without intent is valid: just as the vessels have no intention when the water strikes them, so too the person's immersion should be valid without intent — and thus *chullin* does not require *kavana*.

### Intent Objection

The *gemara* deflects this argument: *dilma beyoshev umetzappeh askinan* — perhaps the *mishna* is speaking of a person who is sitting and waiting for the wave, anticipating its arrival, effectively having *kavana* in advance. And if the person had intent, perhaps the vessels are analogous — they were placed there intentionally by someone who wanted the wave to strike them. If so, the *mishna* would not prove anything about the absence of *kavana*.

The *gemara* then asks: if both the person and the vessels had intent, what is the *mishna's chiddush*? The answer is that the *mishna* is teaching that one need not be concerned about confusing this act with immersion in the arc (*kif*) of a wave rather than in its head (*rosh*). The head of a wave — the part that strikes the ground — constitutes a valid *mikveh*; the arc of the wave, suspended in midair, does not, because *she'ein matbilin ba'avir* — one cannot perform *tevilah* in midair. A separate *mishna* teaches: *matbilin berashim ve'ein matbilin bekifin*. The *chiddush* of the wave *mishna* may thus be entirely about this distinction, leaving the question of *kavana* unresolved.

A subtle additional point deserves mention. Even if one were to posit that the person in the wave case had *kavana* — sitting and waiting for the wave — this raises a conceptual difficulty about how *kavana* functions. Normally, *kavana* accompanies an intentional *act*: I lower myself into the *mikveh* with intent; I move the knife with intent. Here, the person performs no action — the wave acts upon them. Even if one stipulates that the person's waiting constitutes an act of some kind, the extension of *kavana* to this setting — particularly for the vessels, which are inanimate objects placed passively on the shore — is conceptually strained. The *gemara* does not press this point further, but it is a genuine difficulty.

### Fruit Case

The *gemara* therefore seeks a cleaner proof and cites another *mishna*: *peiros shenafalu toch ammat ha-mayim* — fruit that fell into a water channel. A person who was *tamei* stuck his hands into the water to retrieve the fruit: *yadav tehoros* — his hands are *tahor* — *upeiros einam beki yutan* — and the fruit is not rendered susceptible to *tumah* through the water.

The logic of the *mishna* is as follows: the hands, having been submerged in water, are purified — yet the person had no intention to purify his hands; he merely wanted to retrieve the fruit. The fruit, meanwhile, is not rendered susceptible to *tumah* because there was no desire (*ratzon*) for the water to be on the fruit — contact with water only renders produce susceptible to *tumah* if the owner desired that contact (*ki yutan*). In this case there was no such desire.

The *mishna* then provides a contrasting case: if the person wanted his hands to be cleaned, then *yadav tehoros* — his hands are *tahor* for the obvious reason — *upeiros beki yutan* — and now the fruit is also susceptible, because his desire to have his hands washed constitutes sufficient desire for the water, which was in contact with the fruit.

The proof for present purposes is the first case: the person's hands were purified without any intention to purify them. This demonstrates, at least in the domain of *netilat yadayim*, that a halachic change in status can occur without *kavana*.

### Rav Nachman

Rava challenged Rav Nachman with a seemingly contradictory teaching: *taval lechullin vehuchzak lechullin asur lema'aser* — if a person immersed in a *mikveh* intending the *tevilah* to work for *chullin* and was established for *chullin*, he is forbidden to eat *maaser*. This seems to imply that only by virtue of having intent does the *tevilah* count for *chullin* — *huchzak in, lo huchzak lo* — with establishment it works, without it does not.

Rav Nachman reinterpreted the teaching: *af al pi shehuchzak lechullin asur lema'aser* — the point is that even if one intended the *tevilah* for *chullin* and was established for *chullin*, one still cannot eat *maaser*. It does not mean that intent is a prerequisite for *chullin*; it means that having established oneself for *chullin* does not automatically extend to *maaser sheni*.

Rava pressed further with another formulation: *taval velo huchzak ke'ilu lo taval* — if one immersed without being established for a particular level, it is as if one did not immerse at all. Rav Nachman explained: *ke'ilu lo taval lema'aser* — it is as if one did not immerse with respect to *maaser*, but *aval taval lechullin* — it does work for *chullin*. Rava, thinking this answer was evasive, went and searched and found an explicit *baraita*: *taval velo huchzak muttar lechullin ve'asur lema'aser* — one who immersed without establishing intent is permitted for *chullin* and forbidden for *maaser*. This confirms Rav Nachman's position explicitly: *tevilah* without intent is valid for *chullin*.

### Rabbi Yonatan

At this point, Abaye asked Rav Yosef whether this *baraita* constitutes a definitive refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's position that *kavana* is required even for *chullin*. Rav Yosef responded that Rabbi Yochanan could be understood as ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef.

A *baraita* records Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's position: in analyzing the double use of the washing requirement (*tichabbeis*) for garments afflicted with *tzara'at*, he derives through a *hekesh* (analogical derivation) that just as the first washing is performed with the intent of the *kohen* who commands it, so too the second washing — the purification — requires intent. And this is true even though we are not dealing with *kodshim*. Thus Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef explicitly holds that *kavana* is required for *tahara* in a context of *chullin*.

The *gemara* then questions whether Rabbi Yochanan could really have held this position, given that Rabbi Yochanan himself ruled that *halacha* follows every *stam mishna* (an anonymous *mishna* representing the majority view). And the *stam mishna* about the knife that fell — from which we derived that dropping a knife intentionally constitutes valid *shechita* even without *kavana* — appears to operate as a *stam mishna* ruling against the requirement of intent.

### Resolution

The resolution is that *shechita* is a special case — *bishechita afilu Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef* would agree that *kavana* is not required, even according to the opinion that otherwise mandates intent for *chullin*. The proof is derived from the Torah's own language regarding *shechitat kodshim*: the Torah explicitly states that one who acts as *mitasek* — who inadvertently performs what would otherwise constitute *shechitat kodshim* without realizing it — has not performed a valid *shechitat kodshim*. The *gemara* draws the inference: *michlal delachullin lo ba'inan kavana* — the very fact that the Torah singles out *kodshim* as requiring intent implies, by contrast, that for *chullin*, *kavana* is not required.

Thus the conclusion is nuanced and carefully calibrated. By *shechitat chullin*, everyone agrees — even Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef — that *kavana* is not required. The broader question, whether *chullin* generally requires *kavana* for acts that change halachic status (such as *tevilah*), is where the debate lies. We will continue from this point in the next session.

---

---

# Hullin 32

## Kavana Requirements

### Intro: General Framework

Our discussion picks up on 31b, where the *gemara* had been addressing whether *shechita* is valid without intention and had broadened this into a larger question about whether non-sacred, non-*kodshim* acts require *kavana* at all. The *gemara* had extended the analysis to *tevilah*, raising the question of how far such a generalization ought to reach. It had established, moreover, that even those who require *kavana* for *tevilah* concede that *shechita* is governed by a distinct verse, and that verse indicates *kavana* is not required there. We now turn to a more precise question: what *type* of intention is, or is not, being discussed?

### Rabbis' Position

The passage opens with the position of the *rabbanan*, who hold that intention *is* required for *shechita*. They were the ones who ruled that throwing knives at a wall does not constitute valid *shechita*. How, then, do they account for the Torah's implicit message that *kodshim* demand *kavana* while non-sacred acts do not? Their response is precise: *nechee delo ba'inan kavana lizevicha* — granted, one need not intend for the act to constitute *zevichah*, formal ritual slaughter — *l'chatichah ba'inan*, but one must at least intend the act of cutting.

The scope of this requirement for *kavana l'chatichah* is itself a matter of discussion. It might mean no more than a general intention to cut *something* — so that if one believed one was cutting a gourd and instead cut a chicken's neck, that would suffice. Or, as *tosafot* suggests, it might mean that one must know one is cutting the *simanim* — the trachea and the esophagus — even without intending that this act will carry the *halachic* force of *shechita* and render the meat permissible.

### Kavana Levels

This range of *kavana* levels parallels the *gemara*'s broader treatment of *mitzvos tzrichos kavana*. The classic illustration involves someone walking behind a *shul* who hears a *shofar* being blown. If he intended, he has fulfilled his obligation. But the *gemara* clarifies: this may mean only that he recognized the sound as a *shofar* and not as the braying of a donkey — not that he directed his mind toward fulfilling the *mitzvah*. So too with eating *matzah*: the minimal requirement might be only that one be aware one is eating *matzah* and not a cracker, without any conscious intention to discharge an obligation.

At the furthest extreme lies the category of *mitasek* — acting in complete incidental unawareness of the physical nature of what one is doing. A person in this state does not even know at the physical level what is occurring; the act is entirely disconnected from any conscious engagement. Beyond that threshold, one knows physically what one is doing but need not grasp its *halachic* import. The *rabbanan* stake out a middle position: full *kavana* — intending that this act serve as *shechita* — is not required, but one must at least be consciously performing the act of cutting, or perhaps specifically cutting the *simanim*. Below that level lies *mitasek*, and *mitasek* is insufficient.

### Rabbi Natan Extreme

The striking position belongs to *rabbi natan*, whom the *gemara* ruled we follow. He maintained that even completely incidental action is valid — if one accidentally drops a knife and it performs a *shechita*, or if one is throwing darts and happens to sever the *simanim*, the *shechita* is good. These are precisely the cases we would ordinarily classify as *mitasek*, where what occurred was wholly incidental to any intention of the actor. And yet *rabbi natan*, whom the *halacha* apparently follows, holds that such an act is valid. This is a tremendous *chiddush* — that for *shechita*, *zero* intention is required, not even intention for the physical act.

### Rava's Challenge

*Rava* now advances a sharp logical challenge. *mi ksiv vechatachta?* — the Torah never wrote "and you shall *cut*." *vezavachta ktiv* — it wrote "and you shall *slaughter*." The verse demands a full act of *shechita*. So one should either require *kavana* for the complete *halachic* act of *shechita* — *kavana* that one's cutting is intended to render the meat permissible — or one should require no *kavana* at all. What is the justification for this intermediate position of *kavana l'chatichah*? Either the verse's demand for a *zevichah* imports full intentionality, in which case the *rabbanan* should require *kavana* even for the *shechita's* legal effect; or it does not, in which case there is no basis for requiring *kavana* even for the physical act of cutting.

The implicit response — consistent with the *gemara*'s broader treatment — is that without any *kavana* for even the physical act, the deed does not connect to the actor at all. One has become entirely *mitasek*. It is entirely coherent to say: at minimum, the actor must have performed *some* act; perhaps he did not define it as *shechita*, did not think about *shechita*, but he consciously performed the cutting. The *gemara*'s challenge, however, is that once we concede the Torah's demand is an act of *shechita*, there is no principled stopping point short of full *kavana* for the *halachic* act.

### Tevilah Parallel

The *gemara* now returns to the case of a *niddah* who immersed without intention. The question is raised: what exactly is this case? If a friend physically grabbed her and threw her into the *mikveh*, the *gemara* suggests that the friend's *kavana* substitutes for hers — *kavana dechavarta kavana mealya hi*. This is not self-evidently true. If the Torah demands that *she* perform a conscious act of *tevilah*, it is not obvious that someone else's intention to immerse her satisfies that requirement, since she has gone from being the subject of the act to being its object. Yet the *gemara* operates on the assumption that *kavana* can be transferred in this way, analogous to the earlier discussion in which one person's *kavana* was said to apply to another's vessels.

The *gemara* supports this from a *mishnah* listing a woman who is a *chereshet*, a *shoteh*, or *suma* — deaf-mute, unsound of mind, or blind — as well as a woman whose mind became temporarily disturbed. The *mishnah* states that if they have sound companions, those companions can assist them and arrange for them to eat *terumah*. The *gemara* reads this as establishing that another's intention and assistance can render the *tevilah* valid on behalf of someone whose own *kavana* is insufficient.

The *gemara* then turns to *rav pappa*'s formulation for *rabbi natan*'s position: the paradigmatic case of *tevilah* without *any* intention — not even for the physical act — is a woman who fell off a bridge into a river that would have qualified as a *mikveh*. She did not intend to enter the water at all. And for the *rabbanan*, the parallel case is a woman who went into a river to cool off — she intended the physical act of entering the water but had no *kavana* for *tevilah* as such.

This elegantly demonstrates how the *gemara* abstracts and generalizes the debate. The argument over *kavana* in *shechita* is understood to reflect a broader dispute about what level of intention is necessary for acts that change status in the non-*kodshim* realm. For *rabbi natan*, zero intention suffices — the act may be entirely incidental, what we would ordinarily classify as *mitasek* — and this is a position of enormous scope. For the *rabbanan*, intention for the physical act is the minimum threshold.

---

## Parah Adumah Case

### Rule: One Animal

*Rava* now introduces a distinct application that, while not strictly a *kavana* question, illuminates the *kavana* debate in a revealing way.
