There, we accept the *bat kol* not as a substantive halachic ruling but as a procedural resolution to an otherwise irresolvable logjam.

The Gemara then returns to the original difficulty: even after all this, how did Rava rule as he did? *amar rav tavos: kulei k'rava avda* — the answer is that Rava's ruling actually follows a coherent single position, because there is another tradition of Rav's view. Rami bar Yechezkel testified: do not follow what Yehuda my brother reported in Rav's name; here is what Rav actually said: *veshet natnu bo chachamim shiur* — the sages established a defined boundary for the *veshet*, beyond which it is no longer considered the *veshet* for *halacha*. That upper zone — the *turbatz* — is therefore not a *makom shechita*. But Rav never retracted his ruling that a *mashehu* hole in the *turbatz* constitutes a *treifah*. On this tradition, Rav himself held both positions simultaneously: the *turbatz* is not a *makom shechita*, and yet a tiny hole there renders the animal a *treifah*. There is no logical contradiction in holding both, because there are other organs for which a *mashehu* suffices for *treifah* even though they are not the *veshet*. So Rava was not grafting two contradictory authorities; he was faithfully transmitting a single coherent position of Rav.

The Gemara has thus resolved the practical ruling — but it is worth noting that it does not offer an alternative route of saying that Rava was entitled to combine the stringencies independently because they are not logically contradictory. The Gemara specifically requires Rav himself to have held both positions. This implies that the standard is not merely logical non-contradiction but consistency of authority: one must follow a *posek* consistently, not simply adopt whatever positions happen not to contradict each other.

---

## Esophagus Boundaries

### Upper Boundary

The Gemara now examines how far the *veshet* extends in each direction. *lema'la ad kama* — how high up does the *veshet* go? Rav Nachman answers: *ad kedei tfisas yad* — until the span of a hand-grip. Rashi suggests this means roughly three to four fingers' breadth, though another reading yields two fingers. The question being addressed here is not primarily the *makom shechita* — that has largely been covered — but rather the upper boundary for purposes of *treifah*: beyond a certain point upward, a hole no longer constitutes a *treifah* because the tissue is no longer considered *veshet*.

### Lower Boundary

*Lemata ad kama* — and how far downward? Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: *ad kedei sheyis'ar* — until it becomes hairy. This refers to the anatomical distinction between the esophagus and the stomach (*keres*): the upper portion of the stomach near the esophageal junction is lined with a rougher, felt-like hairy texture, while the lower stomach is smooth. Where the tissue begins to exhibit that hairy character, the stomach has begun and the esophagus has ended. This is not merely an anatomical observation; it is a halachic boundary. Below that point, the rules governing the *keres* apply rather than those governing the *veshet*.

### Stomach Sections

The Gemara qualifies this with a statement of Ravina citing Kineva in Rav's name: *tefach ba-veshet samuch la-keres zehu keres ha-penimi* — a handbreadth of the esophagus right near the stomach is considered the inner stomach (*keres ha-penimi*). The Gemara immediately corrects the reading: it does not mean a handbreadth of esophagus is reclassified as stomach — that would be anatomically strange — but rather a handbreadth of *stomach* nearest the esophagus constitutes the inner *keres*. This is the hairy zone visible near the esophageal junction, which the Gemara identifies as the *keres ha-penimi* referenced in the Mishnah. The outer *keres* is the smooth portion of the stomach further from the esophageal inlet. The distinction matters because the Mishnah assigns different *shiurim* for the hole-size that constitutes *treifah* in each section.

What emerges is a layered anatomy: the *veshet* proper, the hairy band of *keres ha-penimi* immediately adjacent to the esophageal inlet, and then the smoother *keres ha-chitzon* beyond. The halachic boundary between *veshet* and *keres* is located where the hairy texture begins.

### Animal Variations

The Gemara notes a complication specific to one type of animal. *ki kama rav be-tura de-mas'ir tfeh* — Rav's statement about the hairy boundary applies to an ox (*tura*), which grows this hairy texture particularly well, beginning already at the very bottom of the esophagus or near it. In other animals such as goats and sheep, the corresponding texture does not appear at the base of the esophagus — there, the esophagus proper extends all the way to its terminus, and only the stomach itself exhibits the hairy characteristic. The practical implication is that in an ox, what might appear to be esophageal tissue near the juncture may already be classified as *keres ha-penimi*, while in smaller ruminants the same tissue would still be classified as *veshet*.

The Gemara additionally notes the related topic of *simanim she-nildedu* — displaced or dislocated *simanim* (trachea and esophagus) — which constitutes a *treifah* or at minimum invalidates a *shechita*. The cases of the *turbatz* having been removed from the jaw (*nital lechi ha-tachton kashar*) and the question of *ikur simanim* are distinguished: surgical removal in which the *simanim* remain embedded in surrounding tissue does not constitute *ikur simanim*, while a violent dislocation in which they are wrenched free does. Similarly, being "peeled" gently from the skin differs from being "yanked" away: the latter produces a *treifah* because it cannot heal, while the former, when limited to a majority rather than total separation, may be treated more leniently.

---

## Trachea Cut Standard

### Trachea Majority Rule

The Gemara now turns to the *gargeret* (trachea). The Mishnah established that a *treifah* in the *gargeret* requires *pesikah* — a cut — of the majority. A hole alone does not suffice; there must be a significant severing. The Gemara asks: *kama psukat ha-gargeret? — b'ruba* — what constitutes "cut"? The majority. And how do we measure majority?

### Measurement Methods

Here the Gemara introduces a fundamental dispute about the unit of measurement. Rav says *rov ovya* — the majority of its thickness, meaning the majority of the material of the tracheal wall measured as solid matter. Others report Rav as saying *rov chalala* — the majority of its hollow, meaning one has cut through the majority of the interior space of the tube.

The difference is consequential because the trachea is not geometrically uniform: one side of the tracheal wall is substantially thicker than the other. If we measure by the total thickness of the solid material — *rov ovya* — we reach the majority threshold before we have cut through half of the actual interior space. This makes *rov ovya* the more stringent standard. If we measure by how much of the hollow has been traversed — *rov chalala* — we require more cutting before declaring a *treifah*, making that the more lenient standard.

### Rav's Case

A case came before Rav himself: *hahi psukat ha-gargeret de'atai lekamei de-Rav, yativ ve-kabdik lei b'rov ovya* — he sat and examined it using the *rov ovya* standard (majority of thickness), which is the more stringent measure. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi then told him: *rabbenu, you taught us* that the standard is *rov chalala* (majority of hollow). The existence of two versions of what Rav said may itself reflect this episode: Rav was inconsistent, or at least ambivalent, and his students had received different traditions. Faced with their reminder, Rav sent the case to Rabbah bar bar Chana for a further opinion.

### Rabbah's Ruling

Rabbah bar bar Chana examined the trachea using the *rov chalala* standard — the more lenient measure — and declared it *kasher*. Once it was declared *kasher*, he purchased meat from it for thirteen *istarei pshitei* — the value of thirteen coins of some denomination, essentially a regular purchase. This purchase then becomes the springboard for the Gemara's extended discussion of procedural *psak* in the following section.

---

## Overriding Rulings

### Non-Overriding Principle

*V'heichi avid hachi* — how could he have done this? The Gemara cites the well-known rule: *chacham she-timah, ein chavero rashai le-taher; assar, ein chavero rashai le-hatir* — if one sage declared something *tamei*, a colleague may not declare it *tahor*; if one declared it forbidden, a colleague may not permit it. One *posek*'s ruling cannot be overridden by another.

At first glance, the question seems puzzling — Rav himself had not yet issued a final ruling but had simply begun applying a standard, and the case was then forwarded to Rabbah bar bar Chana. But the Gemara's answer clarifies the exact scope of the principle.

### No Ruling Exception

*Shani hacha de-Rav lo assar meissar* — the case of Rav is different because Rav never actually issued a ruling (*psak*) of forbidden. He was examining the animal using a measuring standard that would have led to a ruling of *treifah*, but he had not yet declared it so. Since no *psak* was formally issued, there was nothing for Rabbah bar bar Chana to override. The principle against overriding applies once a ruling has been given; before a ruling is issued, referring the matter to another authority is entirely legitimate.

This carries an important implication: even if a *posek* who has issued a *psak* wishes to have it reconsidered, he cannot simply invite a colleague to override him. He may reconsider and reverse himself, but a different authority cannot issue a contrary ruling — even at the original *posek*'s invitation.

### Benefit from Psak

The Gemara then raises a second question: even if Rabbah bar bar Chana's ruling was procedurally valid, how did he allow himself to benefit by purchasing the meat? *v'kivan de'orei bah chacham heichi achal minei* — once a sage had issued a *psak* on an animal, how may he eat from it?

### Yechezkel's Standard

The Gemara invokes Yechezkel: *hinei nafshi lo metuma'ah, u'neveilah u'treifah lo achalti mine'urai, v'ad atah lo ba befi besar pigul* — Yechezkel declared that his soul was never defiled, that he never ate *neveilah* or *treifah*, and that no *pigul* ever entered his mouth. The Gemara parses this: the claim not to have eaten *treifah* cannot be taken at face value — of course Yechezkel did not eat *treifah*. Rather, *shelo achalti mibeheimah shehorah bah chacham* — he never ate from an animal that had required a rabbinic ruling. Any meat that had been a *shailah* — that needed a *posek* to determine its status — he would not eat.

The Gemara also records a parallel reading in the name of Rav Nasan: Yechezkel's declaration meant he never ate from an animal whose *matnos* (priestly gifts) had not been properly set aside. Both interpretations are preserved. The *yechezkel* standard is presented as an ideal — stringent and difficult to maintain practically — not as a binding norm.

### Judgment vs. Tradition

*Hani milei milsa de-talya be-svara* — this scruple applies specifically when the ruling was a matter of judgment (*svara*), an assessment call where the *posek* weighed the evidence and reached a conclusion that another equally competent authority might have reached differently. There one can reasonably worry that the ruling was mistaken. But *rabbah bar bar chana agmarei samich* — Rabbah bar bar Chana's ruling was not a matter of his own judgment; it rested on a received tradition (*gemara*) that the standard is *rov chalala* rather than *rov ovya*. When a ruling is simply the application of a received tradition rather than a personal assessment call, the concern about error does not apply in the same way, and the *yechezkel* standard is not invoked.

### Suspicion Concern

A further concern is then raised: *v'sipok lei mishum chashada* — even apart from the *yechezkel* standard, should he not refrain from purchasing the meat to avoid the appearance of impropriety? The *braita* teaches: *dan et ha-din, zikey ve-chiyev, timei ve-tiher, assur ve-hitir... kullan resha'in likkach* — a judge who ruled on a property dispute, a sage who declared something *tamei* or *tahor*, *assur* or *muttar*, may technically engage in commerce with the party they favored. But *aval amru Chachamim, harchak min ha-kiyur u-min ha-domeh lo* — the sages say: distance yourself from what is ugly and from what resembles it. The concern is the appearance that the ruling was influenced by anticipated personal benefit — that the *posek* declared the animal *kasher* precisely because he wanted to buy the meat cheaply.

### Rava's Defense

The Gemara resolves: *hani mili be-midei de-mizben be-shuma* — this concern applies when the item is sold by estimated valuation, where it is plausible that the *posek* received a favorable estimate. *hacha be-matkla muchach* — in this case, the meat was sold by weight, a fully objective measure. No special deal could have been extended, and so there is no appearance of impropriety.

The Gemara then closes with a parallel story to illustrate the principle. Rava permitted an animal on a question of *treifah* and then purchased meat from it. His wife, the daughter of Rav Chisda, challenged him: her father, when he would permit a *bechor* by ruling that it had a *mum* (blemish) sufficient to permit it for ordinary consumption, would never purchase the meat from it. Why are you doing so?

Rava replied: *hani mili bechor de-vishuma mizdaben* — with a *bechor* that is sold by estimated valuation, there is genuine reason for concern that the ruling and the subsequent purchase look collusive. *hacha be-matkla muchach* — here, where it is sold by weight, it is demonstrable that no advantage was obtained. His wife pressed: even buying by weight, might he not have received a choice cut — *umtza malya* — a particularly desirable piece? Rava replied simply: *kol yoma umtza malya zavni li* — the butchers always give me the best cut because I am the rabbi. That raises other concerns about the relationship between rabbis and the marketplace, he acknowledged, but it does not raise concerns about the appearance of corrupt *psak*, which is the relevant issue here.

Tosafot notes a further nuance: the principle that a *posek* may technically benefit after issuing a ruling may be limited to contexts where multiple judges are involved, since collusion among several judges is less plausible than in a case of a single judge ruling alone. Whether a sole *posek* is even theoretically permitted to benefit from his ruling — or whether it is formally prohibited rather than merely discouraged — remains, in Tosafot's view, genuinely unresolved.

---

---

# Hullin 44b

## Talmid Chacham & Honesty

### Honest Ruling Definition

The sugya opens with a statement of Rav Chisda: *eizehu talmid chacham? zeh haroeh treifah le'atzmo* — who is considered a genuine *talmid chacham*? One who rules honestly on his own animal's *treifot*. The placement of this teaching is initially jarring: it appears amid five lines of *aggadata* before the Gemara returns to the technical laws of *treifot*, and the transition feels abrupt. Yet the statement itself repays careful attention.

### Intellectual vs. Honesty

Rashi explains that a true *talmid chacham* is someone so honest and truthful that he is comfortable ruling on questions of *kashrut* affecting his own animal, because he knows that if the animal is *treif*, he will say so without flinching. The implicit corollary is striking: the standard being celebrated here is not intellectual prowess at all, but moral integrity. This raises an obvious and somewhat unsettling question. Is the definition of a *talmid chacham* really so low a bar? Should we not take honesty entirely for granted in a person of learning?

The discomfort runs deeper still. In our world we tend to measure a *talmid chacham* by how much he knows, not by whether he is honest. That sad observation may itself be the Gemara's point. The Gemara is deliberately pushing our buttons, forcing us to confront the relationship between intellectual mastery and moral character — and implying that the two are not nearly as conjoined as we might assume. Historically, the stakes were real: meat was expensive and rarely eaten; the one time a family *shechted* an animal and discovered a potential *treifah*, the temptation to rule leniently — particularly on one's own animal — must have been enormous. The Gemara also recalls a parallel passage in *zevachim* where the Sages found that adding *tumah* as a consequence of *notar* and *pigul* was more effective as a deterrent than the much graver consequence of *karet* — suggesting that different forms of concern operated differently on people, and that financial or quasi-superstitious consequences could be more practically motivating than purely religious ones.

### Tosafot's Solution

Tosafot are similarly bothered by the conflation of intellectual standing with personal honesty. They resolve it by pointing to the Gemara in *bava metzia*: ordinarily a lost object is returned only upon the presentation of a *siman*, yet the Gemara there allows a *talmid chacham* to recover a lost object on the basis of *tvi'at ayin* alone — recognition by sight. The premise underlying that leniency is precisely that a *talmid chacham* known to be religiously honest can be trusted in financial matters as well. The two domains are thus connected: reliability in *issur ve-heter* is the foundation for reliability in *mamon*. This is how Tosafot explain why the Gemara defines *talmid chacham* in terms of honesty rather than erudition.

### Soneh Matanos Connection

The Gemara then records a second teaching of Rav Chisda: *eizehu soneh matanos yichyeh* — who truly fulfills the verse in *mishlei* that "one who hates gifts will live"? Again the answer is *zeh haroeh treifah le'atzmo*. The logic of the connection is as follows: a person who is scrupulously honest even when honesty costs him money — declaring his own animal *treif* at personal financial loss — is precisely the kind of person who is not driven by material gain. Such a person would naturally refuse gifts, and would fulfill *soneh matanos yichyeh* at the highest level. The Gemara is thus drawing a portrait of integrated character: honesty about *treifot* is not an isolated virtue but flows from, and expresses, a broader orientation toward financial disinterest.

---

## Learning Framework

### Three Learning Stages

The Gemara continues with a teaching of Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Chisda: anyone who *koreh*, *shoneh*, and *meshamesh talmidei chachamim*, and who rules honestly on *treifot* affecting his own animals — of such a person the verse says, *yegia kapecha ki tochal, ashrecha ve'tov lach*. The three-part formula — *koreh*, *shoneh*, *meshamesh talmidei chachamim* — invites interpretation. The most natural reading maps it onto the three levels of Torah study: *koreh* is *mikra*, *shoneh* is *mishnah*, and *meshamesh talmidei chachamim* is *talmud* — meaning, in the plain sense, attendance upon Torah scholars to observe and absorb their way of life.

Rashi, however, takes a characteristically consistent if surprising position. Throughout *shas*, wherever the phrase *shimush talmidei chachamim* appears, Rashi interprets it not as literally serving or accompanying scholars in their daily lives, but as learning *gemara* — that is, listening to *talmidei chachamim* debate halacha. For Rashi, the three stages are therefore *chumash* and *mikra*, *mishnah*, and *gemara*. Most *rishonim* take the literal reading: being around *talmidei chachamim* and learning from how they conduct themselves. Rashi dissents, maintaining the parallel with the other two stages: all three are forms of textual study. The question of which form of learning yields more — sitting with a great scholar and observing how he lives, or laboring over the *gemara* itself — is one that the passage raises without quite answering.

### Reward Pesukim

The verse cited as the reward for this threefold path — *yegia kapecha ki tochal, ashrecha ve'tov lach* — is one that *chazal* return to repeatedly, and the very fact that they must reinterpret it is itself noteworthy. On its face, *yegia kapecha ki tochal* extols self-sufficiency and the dignity of physical labor: eat from the fruit of your own hands. *chazal* were not entirely comfortable leaving it at that. A verse that praises manual labor without mentioning Torah or virtue seemed to them incomplete as a statement of Jewish values, and so they consistently read *yegia kapecha* metaphorically: the "labor of your hands" refers to the intellectual and spiritual toil of learning *mikra*, *mishnah*, and *gemara*, and the capacity that labor produces — the ability to *pasken* on *treifot* with both competence and integrity.

The closing phrase *ashrecha ve'tov lach* then receives its standard *chazalic* reading: *ashrecha ba'olam hazeh, ve'tov lach la'olam haba* — happiness in this world and goodness in the world to come. This formulation appears again in the Gemara's citation of Razvid, who renders it: one who follows this path inherits both worlds.

### Ascetic Examples

To illustrate the ideal of *soneh matanos yichyeh*, the Gemara presents two figures. Rabbi Elazar would refuse any gift sent from the *nasi*'s household, and would likewise decline any invitation to dine there — maintaining total financial independence from communal patronage. Rav Pinchas ben Yair was similarly cited in this vein, as an exemplar of extreme self-sufficiency grounded in the rejection of gifts.

### Social Compromise

Rav Zeira adopted a more moderate position. When gifts were sent to him, he too would refuse them — consistent with *soneh matanos yichyeh* — but when he was invited to a meal, he would accept. His reason, however, was not primarily social. He explained: *ityakura hu de-mityakru bi* — they are honored by my presence. The invitation creates honor for the host rather than a benefit for the guest, and therefore accepting it does not compromise the principle of rejecting gifts. One might note the irony: the strictest reading of *soneh matanos yichyeh* taken literally forces one back to *yegia kapecha ki tochal* in its most literal sense — live entirely from what you earn — which is precisely the interpretation *chazal* were trying to move beyond. The two teachings circle back upon each other.

---

## Trachea Defects

### Two Treifah Types

The Gemara returns to the *gargeret* — the trachea — and the conditions that render it *treif*. The *mishnah* establishes two categories. The first is *nifsakah ha-gargeret*: if the trachea has suffered a substantial split along its length, it is *treif*. The second is a hole: if the trachea is pierced with a hole of the size of an *issar* — a particular coin — that too renders it *treif*. These are two distinct standards, one measured by the length of the trachea (majority), and one by the circumference of a circular hole.

### Combining Small Holes

The Gemara raises a question that recurs throughout discussions of *treifot*: what happens when, instead of one large hole or one long split, the trachea is punctured with many small holes, each individually too small to constitute a *treifah*? Do they combine? And if so, toward which standard — toward the length of a *rov* of the trachea, or toward the circumference of a *k'issar*?

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules: *nikva k'napa* — if the trachea is perforated like a sieve, *mitzstarfin le-rovah* — the holes combine toward the majority of the trachea's length. This is the initial ruling. But the Gemara immediately notes a parallel case that seems to point in the opposite direction.

### Skull Analogy

The parallel case involves a skull that contains multiple small holes. The halacha is that if a skull is perforated with holes equivalent in total to the size of a *k'mlo makdech* — the width of a doctor's drill bit — the skull has begun to disintegrate and no longer conveys *tumah*. Crucially, even multiple small holes may combine to reach that circular measurement. This appears to be the converse of what the Gemara just ruled regarding the trachea. There, small holes combine toward the standard of *rov* — the length of a split. Here, small holes combine toward the standard of *k'mlo makdech* — a circular hole.

### Yirmiya's Challenge

Rav Yirmiya poses the challenge explicitly. In the case of the skull, even multiple small holes combine toward the circular measurement — *k'mlo makdech*. The reasoning seems to be: since the standard for a skull is a hole of that circular size, all holes combine toward that standard. By the same logic, since the standard for the trachea being *treif* via a hole is *k'issar*, should not small holes in the trachea combine toward *k'issar* rather than toward *rov*? Why does the Gemara apply one standard for combination in one place and the opposite standard in another?

### Chisaron Answer

The Gemara answers by citing a ruling in the name of Rav Chelbo quoting Rav Chama bar Guria quoting Rav: it depends on the nature of the holes. *nekavim she-yesh bahen chisaron* — holes in which there is actual *chisaron*, meaning tissue has been removed from the wall of the trachea — *mitzstarfin k'issar*: they combine toward the circular measurement of the *issar*. *she-ein bahen chisaron* — holes in which there is no *chisaron*, meaning the wall was pierced but no flesh was actually removed (the tissue was merely pushed aside) — *mitzstarfin le-rov*: they combine toward the majority standard of a split.

The logic, as best as anatomical terminology allows, seems to be that a hole accompanied by *chisaron* is structurally more similar to a cut-out hole, and so combines toward the *k'issar* measurement. A hole without *chisaron* behaves more like an elongated crack or split, and so its accumulation is measured against the *rov* standard. Whether this distinction reflects a coherent physiological principle or partakes of *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — since the line between the two hole-types may seem arbitrary to an untrained eye — is not resolved. The Gemara simply presents the distinction as normative.

This yields three operative rules for the trachea: a split along the majority of its length renders it *treif*; a single hole the size of an *issar* renders it *treif*; and multiple small holes combine either toward the *rov* standard or toward the *k'issar* standard depending on whether they involve *chisaron* or not.

### Repetitive Question

Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani subsequently poses the question *nekava k'nafa mai hi* — what is the law if the trachea is perforated like a sieve? — before the Gemara, which has just answered precisely this question. The response, *harei amru*, is delivered with unmistakable impatience: "They have already said!" The Gemara repeats the ruling — holes with *chisaron* combine toward *k'issar*, holes without *chisaron* combine toward *rov* — as though the earlier discussion had settled the matter entirely. The tone of the exchange is notable: the Gemara's *harei amru* reads less like a polite citation and more like a rebuke for inattention.

### Coin Measurement

The Gemara proceeds to ask: *u-vemah meshaarin* — how does one actually measure a hole in the trachea of a bird? Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports a practice he received from Rabbi Elazar directly: one folds the excised piece of flesh and places it — *manicho al pi ha-kana* — over the opening of the trachea. If it covers the majority of the circumference of the tracheal opening, the animal is *treif*; if not, it is *keshera*. Rav Pappa adds a mnemonic: *nafya* — a sieve placed over a frame — to illustrate the visual image of a piece of tissue draped over the circular opening of the trachea. The measurement is thus not abstract but concretely geometric: does the hole, when laid flat over the opening, cover its majority?

For a hole that lacks *chisaron* — where the flesh remains but is merely slit open — the standard becomes slightly different. Since the flesh is still present and provides some structural protection, the hole must be large enough that an *issar* coin can pass through it comfortably, meaning the opening must be slightly larger than the coin's exact circumference. Rashi understands the coin to be measured standing upright — its width fitting through the slit — while Tosafot understand it as lying flat, the coin's face passing through the opening. These produce different practical thresholds, one more *chamur* and one more *kula* than the other.

### Hole Coverage Test

The Gemara introduces the case of *niftachah ke-deles* — the hole is open like a door, meaning the flesh is splayed open rather than removed. Rav Nachman rules on the applicable *shiur* in this configuration. The principle governing all of these cases is that different physical configurations of the same wound carry different thresholds: complete removal of tissue, mere perforation without removal, and a flap-like opening each engage their respective standards.

### Tracheal Cracks

The Gemara then turns to *nisdeka* — a crack in the trachea, as opposed to a hole or a split. A crack runs differently from a split: where a split runs along the length of the trachea and is through-and-through, a crack runs across the bands of the trachea and is not necessarily through-and-through. Since a lengthwise crack is more likely to heal on its own — the animal's neck movements do not force it further open the way a widthwise split would worsen — the Gemara treats it differently.

### Minimal Intact Ends

Rav initially states that even if the trachea is cracked along nearly its entire length, as long as one full *chulya* — one intact ring or band of the tracheal structure — remains at each end, the animal is *keshera*. The *chulyot* are the small ring-like segments that make up the trachea's length.

When this ruling was repeated before Rabbi Yochanan, he rejected it with impatience: *ma chulya uma chulya de-ka'amar Rav* — what is all this talk of *chulyot*? Rabbi Yochanan rules that no intact band is required. Rather, *mashu le-mala u-mashu le-mata* — a mere *mashu*, a minimal intact piece at each end of the crack, suffices to preserve the trachea's *kashrut*. The crack may extend along almost the full length of the structure, so long as something — however minimal — remains at each pole.

When the same ruling was reported before Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yonatan — that only a *mashu* is required — Rabbi Yochanan expressed admiration: *yadein chavrein Bavla'ah le-parsha ke-hai ta'ama* — our Babylonian colleagues know how to explain this properly. The compliment is backhanded in the way characteristic of the ongoing Eretz Yisrael–Bavel tension, but it is genuine: Rabbi Yochanan affirmed that Rabbi Yonatan had arrived at the correct and well-reasoned ruling.

---

## Neck-Lung Boundary

### Shechitah Range

The Gemara now addresses the anatomical question of where the neck ends and the lung begins — a question relevant for *shechitah* and for the laws of *treifot*, and as the Gemara will note, also for *chazeh ve-shok*. Rav Chiyya bar Yosef taught before Rabbi Yochanan: *kol ha-tzavar kulo kasher li-shechitah* — the entire neck is valid for *shechitah*, from the *tabaat ha-gedolah* — the large ring at the top of the trachea — *ad kanfei reiah ha-tachtonah*, until the lower wings of the lung.

### Anatomical Orientation

Rava immediately clarifies what "lower" means, since the orientation of the animal changes depending on whether it is standing or hanging: *tachtonah she-hi elyonah* — the "lower" wings of the lung are those that are lower when the animal is hung upside down after *shechitah* for skinning, which are in fact the frontal wings when the animal is walking normally. The trachea is thus considered neck until it reaches the point parallel to those wings. The Gemara's diagram of the lung, with its multiple *unot* of different sizes arranged around the central structure, helps clarify which wings are in question.

### Stretched Neck Issue

A complication arises from the fact that the neck can be stretched. When a shochet slaughters, the demarcation line is invisible — the animal is intact, and the lung is not exposed. Moreover, an animal can extend its neck considerably beyond its resting position. Does a shechitah performed on the stretched portion of the neck remain valid?

### Grazing Stretch Test

Rav Ashi establishes the governing principle: *kol she-posheitet tzavarah ve-ro'eh* — any portion of the neck that the animal naturally extends when grazing counts as neck for the purposes of *shechitah*. This is a functional definition: wherever the animal's own neck reaches in the normal course of grazing is halakhically considered neck. The limiting condition is: *u-vilvad she-lo te'anes* — so long as the stretch was not forced. If the shochet or another person pulled the animal's neck to extend it artificially, the stretched portion does not qualify.

### Teiku on Self-Stretch

Rav Chanina raises a further question that is left unresolved: *onsa atzmah mai hu* — if the animal itself stretched its own neck, even without external compulsion, does that stretched portion count as valid neck? The Gemara leaves this as *teiku*. The question is subtle: Rav Ashi's rule already stipulates that the animal's natural stretching in grazing counts as neck. The residual question apparently concerns a stretch that is self-initiated but not part of the animal's ordinary grazing movement — some intermediate case of the animal extending its neck for reasons of its own, not while actually grazing. Whether such a stretch is sufficient to extend the zone of valid *shechitah* remains undecided.

### Below-Chest Rule

The Gemara applies the demarcation principle to *treifot*: once the trachea crosses the threshold into the zone treated as lung, defects in that portion of the trachea are judged by the standards of the lung, not the trachea. *nikva ha-kaneh le-mata min ha-chazeh* — if the tracheal tube is punctured below the chest — *nidon ke-rei'ah*: it is treated with the same *treifah* standards as the lung.

### Priestly Portions

The question of where neck ends and chest begins has a second halakhic application: the priestly portions of a *korban shelamim*. When bringing a *shelamim*, one must give the *kohen* the *chazeh* and the *shok*. The Gemara asks: *eizehu chazeh* — what counts as the breast? The answer is: *ze ha-ro'eh et ha-karka* — the part of the animal that faces the ground, from the forward end up to the neck and from the top end back to the stomach. The shochet cuts two ribs and two panels on each side — and that constitutes the *chazeh* given to the *kohanim*. The demarcation of neck from chest thus governs both *shechitah* validity and the boundaries of the priestly gift.

---

## Brain Anatomy

### Two Membranes

The Gemara turns to the brain — *mo'ach* — and the law of *nikav krum shel mo'ach*: a perforation of the brain's membrane. Two membranes surround the brain according to rabbinic anatomy, an outer and an inner. Rav and Shmuel both hold — *d'amri tarveihu* — that perforation of the outer membrane alone, even if the inner membrane remains intact, renders the animal *treif*. A second opinion holds that the animal is not *treif* unless the inner (*tata'ah*) membrane is also perforated — *ad de-inkiv tata'ah*.

The underlying question is whether a perforation in the outer membrane necessarily signals a disease process that will progress to the inner membrane, or whether the enclosing protection of the skull makes healing more likely and the two membranes must therefore be evaluated independently. Since the brain, unlike the lung or trachea, is enclosed within bone, there is a stronger argument that a wound in the outer membrane will not inevitably spread inward. This mitigating factor is what generates the dispute.

### Brain Sac Siman

Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani offers a *siman* to help identify these two membranes anatomically: *chayata de-manach beih mocha* — the sac in which the brain rests. The sac itself, as a bounded vessel, helps conceptualize how two distinct membranes can surround a single organ.

### Testicle Analogy

Rav Chana bar Papa in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds a practical teaching: *kenegdo be-veitzim nikar* — the two membranes can be seen more clearly by analogy with the testicles. *chazal* were aware that the two layers of membrane are not easily distinguished when examining the brain directly. The testicles, however, display two clearly distinct encasing membranes visible to the naked eye. One who wants to train his perception of what two separate membranes look like should study the structure of the testicles first. (The Gemara uses *beveitzim* as the standard rabbinic euphemism, a word that has since shed any euphemistic quality through long familiarity.)

### Skull-Cord Boundary

Rav Shimon ben Pazi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara establishes the boundary between brain and spinal cord. *mo'ach kol mah she-be-kedeira* — everything within the skull, which the Gemara calls *kedeira* (lit. "pot") as a somewhat colorful anatomical metaphor — is treated as brain and governed by the halachot of brain. *hitchil limshoch* — once the matter begins to extend outward and thin into a cord — *nidon ke-chut ha-shidrah*: it is treated as spinal cord and its halachot change accordingly. The two — brain and spinal cord — have different *shiurim* for holes and different halachic consequences for defects, and so a clear anatomical boundary is legally necessary.

### Polin Markers

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports directly from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi the specific anatomical marker: *ke-min shnei polin yesh munachin al pi ha-kedeira* — at the very opening of the skull there are two *polin*, two gland-like structures, sitting at the junction between skull and spinal canal. *min ha-polin u-lifnim* — inward from the *polin*, on the skull side — is treated as brain. *min ha-polin ve-lachutz* — outward from the *polin*, on the spinal side — is treated as spinal cord.

### Polin Classification

The Gemara then raises the natural residual question: *ee polin atzmah* — what is the halachic status of the *polin* themselves? Are they classified as brain or as spinal cord? The Gemara answers: *ani yodeia* — I do not know. It then adds: *u-mistavra ke-lifnim* — it is more logical that they should be classified as brain, on the inner side. Why this is the more logical conclusion, given that this is a question of anatomy rather than pure legal reasoning, is not fully explained. When the Gemara says *mistavra* in the context of a scientific question, it is invoking something like functional logic — perhaps that the *polin* serve as a threshold structure still within the containing framework of the skull, and therefore align structurally with the brain rather than with the elongated spinal cord. The question remains, in the strict sense, without a definitive resolution.

### Bird Brain Verification

Rabbi Yirmiya investigated whether the same anatomical structure applies to birds. *rabbi yirmiya badak ba-of* — he examined the brain of a bird — *ve-ashkach ke-min shnei polin munachin al pi ha-kedeira*: he found the same two gland-like structures at the opening of the skull in birds as well. The same boundary therefore applies to birds as to animals, and the halachic framework of brain versus spinal cord operates identically in both.

---

## Heart & Vessels

### Heart Chamber Hole

The Gemara turns to the heart. *nitkav ha-lev le-veit challalo* — if a hole in the heart reaches the heart's chamber — the animal is *treif*. This is the basic principle.

### Chamber Size Dispute

Rav Zeira immediately asks: *le-veit chalal katan o le-veit chalal gadol* — does this mean that even a hole reaching only one of the minor chambers of the heart renders the animal *treif*, or only if the hole penetrates the main central chamber?

### Lung-Heart Comparison

Abaye challenges the question itself. He points to the halacha of the lung: there, the ruling is that the animal is *treif* only when the hole reaches *le-veit ha-simponot* — the primary chamber housing the main bronchi. Presumably, he argues, the heart should follow the same principle: only the main chamber should count. The question therefore appears to answer itself.

### Language Distinction

The Gemara rejects Abaye's argument and defends Rav Zeira's question by identifying a critical difference in formulation. Regarding the lung, the language is *le-veit ha-simfonot* — "to the house of the bronchi," an expression pointing emphatically to the central, primary source. This is reinforced by Rabbah bar Tachlifa citing Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba citing Rav: *ad she-tinakeiv le-simpon gadol* — only when the hole reaches the main bronchus. The word *beit* before *simponot* indicates the ultimate source, the convergence point of all the bronchi.

Regarding the heart, by contrast, the language is *le-veit challalo* — "to its chamber." *beit chalal* is a general term: a chamber is a chamber, large or small. *mah li chalal gadol, mah li chalal katan* — what difference does it make whether the chamber is large or small? The formulation itself includes minor chambers. The two laws are therefore not analogous, and Rav Zeira's question stands as a genuine one: the language of the Mishnah regarding the heart encompasses any chamber, not only the primary one.

### Aorta Hole Standard

The Gemara next considers the *kaneh ha-lev* — the pipe of the heart, understood to be the aorta — as distinct from the heart itself. If the aorta is perforated, what is the *shiur*? Rav says *be-mashehu* — any perforation at all renders the animal *treif*. Shmuel says *be-rubo* — only if the majority of the aorta is perforated. The practical question of how an animal could survive a majority perforation of the aorta is acknowledged as pressing, though the Gemara does not resolve it on anatomical grounds.

### Aorta Location

The Gemara asks: *hai nihu kaneh ha-lev* — where exactly is the *kaneh ha-lev* located? Rav bar Yitzchak says in the name of Rav: it is embedded within the fat on the wall of the animal — *cheilev she-al gabei d'fanot*. The Gemara objects: *d'fanot salka da'atach* — you mean the stomach walls? That makes no anatomical sense when discussing the heart. The answer is corrected: it is embedded in the wall of the lung — *she-al gabei dophnei rei'ah*. The *kaneh ha-lev* is thus located within the lung's surrounding structure rather than the heart itself.

### Three Tracheal Pipes

The Gemara now introduces a teaching attributed to Amimar in the name of Rav Nachman that is among the most anatomically challenging passages of these *sugyot*. *tlati kani havei* — there are three pipes extending from the trachea. *chad parash le-liba* — one extends to the heart. *ve-chad parash le-rei'ah* — one to the lung. *ve-chad parash le-kavda* — one to the liver. The literal reading of the Gemara is that these three organs each receive a pipe directly from the trachea. This conflicts substantially with modern anatomical understanding, and commentators such as the *sichas chullin* invest considerable effort in demonstrating that *chazal* did not mean this literally — that the language refers to proximity or parallelism rather than direct anatomical connection. The literal Gemara text, however, states the three-pipe structure plainly.

### Pipe Standards

The halakhic consequence flows directly from the anatomical claim: each pipe takes on the *treifah* standards of the organ it serves. *d'rei'ah k'rei'ah* — the pipe going to the lung is judged by the laws of the lung. *d'kavda k'kavda* — the pipe to the liver by the laws of the liver. *d'liba* — the pipe to the heart was already the subject of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding *be-mashehu* versus *be-rov*.

### Reversed Standards

Mar bar Chiya transmits the opposite ruling. The pipe leading to the lung is governed by the standards of the *liver*, and the pipe leading to the liver is governed by the standards of the *lung*. The logic of this reversal is not explained in the Gemara, and the inversion is startling. In any other *sugya* one might say that a ruling so counterintuitive must contain a layer of meaning one is simply not grasping. In the domain of *treifot*, however, where the rules do not always yield to pure logical deduction and where *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* often underlies the distinctions, the absence of stated reasoning is less surprising, even if the content remains puzzling.

### Rav's Credibility

The discussion closes with a scene that crystallizes the difficulty of *treifot* as a field of study. Rav Chiyya bar Yosef reported Rav's position — that even a *mashehu* perforation of the *kaneh ha-lev* renders the animal *treif* — before Shmuel. Shmuel's response was withering: *ei hachi amar Abba* — if Abba (Rav's familiar name) really said that — *lo yada be-treifot*: he has no understanding of *treifot*. Shmuel's position, that the standard is *be-rov*, is what he takes to be self-evidently correct, and Rav's *be-mashehu* standard strikes him as simply wrong.

The exchange is a fitting conclusion to these sugyas. *treifot* is a domain where the normal tools of Talmudic reasoning — *kol va-chomer*, analogy, logical inference — often fail to generate determinate answers, where the standards seem to resist systematic derivation, and where even great *amoraim* find themselves in sharp disagreement. Shmuel's dismissal of Rav is not merely polemical; it reflects a genuine frustration with the subject matter itself — a frustration the Gemara invites every serious student to share.

---

---

# Hullin 46

## Spinal Cord

### Opening

The daf under discussion is 45b, picking up six lines down in the wide lines at the phrase *nishbar hashidra* — "the spine is broken." We are working through the various *trefot*, having dealt with the heart the previous day. The *mishna* lists the spine and the spinal cord together, but the *gemara* makes clear that it is really the spinal cord that is the operative concern. If the spine itself is broken but the spinal cord remains intact, that is not a *treifa*; the spine is essentially irrelevant. The entire discussion therefore centers on the spinal cord.

### Moach vs. Oro

The *gemara* opens with a *baraita*: *chut hashidra shenipsak derubo* — if the majority of the spinal cord is severed, it is a *treifa*. That is the view of Rabbi. Rabbi Yaakov holds more stringently: even a hole in the spinal cord suffices to render it a *treifa*. The *gemara* notes, strikingly, that when an actual case came before Rabbi himself, he ruled like Rabbi Yaakov — more strictly than his own recorded position in the *mishna*. This is a remarkable observation, since the principle of *maaseh rav* — that a scholar's practical ruling carries even greater weight than his theoretical position — would ordinarily reinforce Rabbi's strict ruling. Yet the *gemara* ultimately rejects that practical precedent in favor of Rabbi's stated *mishna* position.

Why Rabbi would rule against his own *mishna* in practice is genuinely difficult to explain. What is worth noting, however, is how frequently this *perek* presents not merely theoretical debates but actual narratives of *psak* — cases that came before sages, how they ruled, what they sent for further examination, how they proceeded differently in practice than in theory. It is no coincidence that this is the traditional tractate studied for *semicha*; the intersection of methodology and practice of *halachic* decision-making is on vivid display throughout.

Returning to the substantive question: the *baraita* speaks of the majority of the spinal cord being severed, but what exactly constitutes the *moach* and the *oro* of the spinal cord? The spinal cord is not a simple structure. It consists of multiple layers: an outer protective layer, a gap, a web-like inner layer, another gap, and finally the *dura mater*, which adheres directly to the nerve itself and is quite thin. The *gemara*'s term *moach* — literally marrow — refers to some portion of this inner content, perhaps the *dura mater* or the second protective layer, while *oro* refers to the outer skin of the cord.

### Majority Definition

With this anatomical picture in mind, the *gemara* records a debate. *rav amar rov oro* — Rav holds that a *treifa* requires the majority of the outer skin of the spinal cord to be severed. The alternative position, *amrei lah rov mocho*, holds that a *treifa* requires the majority of the inner content to be severed — meaning one must cut deeply enough to reach and sever the majority of the *moach*, not merely the outer layer. If the *moach* is the *dura mater*, then severing its majority is tantamount to severing the nerve itself. If it is the second protective layer, then the debate is about how deep one must cut before the animal becomes a *treifa*, with the outer-skin position holding that once the outer protection is compromised, the cord is ultimately doomed.

### Rava's Logic

Rava draws an important logical inference from this dispute. According to the opinion that requires *rov mocho* — severing the majority of the inner content — it follows *kal v'chomer* that severing the majority of the outer skin would certainly also render it a *treifa*: if the inner content matters even though the outer skin still protects it, surely the outer skin itself matters. This may seem counterintuitive — one would expect that cutting deeper, closer to the nerve, would be the more serious concern — but the *gemara* reasons that an intact outer skin provides meaningful protection and enhances the animal's survival prospects. Thus severing the outer skin, which eliminates that protection, is at least as serious as severing the inner content with the outer still present.

The converse question then arises: according to the opinion that only requires *rov oro* — severing the majority of the outer skin — what is the status if only the *moach* is severed? The *gemara* brings a ruling: *amar Rav Huna*, the majority that the sages spoke of refers to the majority of the *oro*, the outer skin. *moach zeh lo maaleh velo morid* — the inner *moach* makes no difference either way.

### Rav Huna Ruling

This ruling of Rav Huna is itself somewhat surprising. One might have expected the inner content — which is directly protective of the nerve — to matter most, analogous to how marrow is the living material within a bone. The *gemara* may be reasoning along the lines of how bone structure works: the bone itself gives structural integrity and the marrow, while functionally important in its own right, does not bear on the integrity of the bone as bone. So too, perhaps, the *gemara* understood the outer skin of the spinal cord as providing the essential structural function, while the inner material, however physiologically significant, does not determine whether the cord will hold together or collapse. The phrasing *lo maaleh velo morid* — it neither adds nor detracts — does seem extreme if one considers what the inner layers actually do, but this is where the *halacha* lands. The broader point, frequently encountered in this *perek*, is that the determinations of *chazal* regarding *trefot* are not negotiated on scientific grounds by later generations; they are received and applied as authoritative.

### Dissolution

A new question arises: what if the *moach* is not severed but rather dissolved? Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *nitmare'ach pasul, nitmasmes pasul* — if the inner content is dissolved in either of two distinct ways, the animal is invalid. *nitmare'ach* refers to a more complete liquefaction — according to Rashi, it becomes like water. *nitmasmes* refers to something less complete, perhaps best described as having a jelly-like consistency: the material has lost its firmness but has not fully liquefied.

### Types of Dissolution

The *gemara* sharpens these definitions. *hamramtses* — the more liquefied form — means that it would spill out like a pitcher if cut open; the insides are fully liquid. *hamemasmes* means it cannot stand upright: the cord loses its rigidity; held in the hand, it would simply flop over. Both of these render the animal *pasul*. A further question is posed by Rav Yirmiya: what if the cord cannot stand not because its inner content has jellied but because it is somehow top-heavy and therefore unsteady despite retaining some degree of rigidity? The *gemara* leaves this in *teiku* — unresolved.

The house of Rav adds a further distinction: *nitmasmesa pasul*, but *nitmazmeza kasher* — a third, lesser category, described as *nitmazmeza*, is still valid. Rashi understands this to mean that some of the inner content has been displaced or lost, but the material has neither been severed, fully liquefied, nor fully jellied. That lesser disruption does not render the cord invalid.

A *baraita* is then cited that appears to challenge this, as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that an animal whose *moach* has been *nitmazmeiz* is *treifa*. The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by emending the reading: the correct *girsa* in that *baraita* is *nitmasmes*, not *nitmazmeiz*, and thus there is no contradiction.

### Levi Story

A further challenge to the leniency of *nitmazmeza* is raised from a narrative involving Levi. Levi was sitting in a bathhouse when he witnessed a man strike his head violently. Levi declared: *nitmazmeiz mocha dedein* — this man's brain has been *nitmazmeiz*. The implication of the story, as the *gemara* reads it, is that this is a serious, life-threatening condition. If *nitmazmeiz* of the brain portends death, why should *nitmazmeiz* of the spinal cord's inner content be treated as harmless?

### Abbaye's Position

Abbaye resolves this by explaining that Levi's remark does not mean the man will die but rather that he will no longer be able to father children. Rashi, citing a physiological belief of the *gemara*, explains that the spinal cord branches downward through the thigh area and one branch enters the reproductive organ, affecting virility. A disruption of the brain or spinal cord *moach* — even without being fatal — could therefore impair fertility. Thus Levi's exclamation in the bathhouse concerned the man's reproductive capacity, not his life expectancy, and this does not contradict the ruling that *nitmazmeza* does not render the animal a *treifa*.

It is worth pausing on the broader theoretical difficulty lurking behind this entire discussion. The category of *treifa* is traditionally understood in terms of *treifa eina chayah* — a *treifa* cannot live. Yet an animal with a severed spinal cord would in many cases be paralyzed rather than dead; a domesticated animal that is fed by its owner might survive for a considerable time. This difficulty is never explicitly resolved in the *gemara*. Similarly left unaddressed is the noted parallel with yesterday's discussion, where the *gemara* described branches of the trachea feeding into the heart and liver — reflecting an ancient physiological model in which the heart functions as an organ of respiration rather than as a circulatory pump. That understanding is directly relevant to how certain *rishonim* and later authorities cited *gemara* passages in discussions of the definition of death and the significance of circulation — though all such analysis proceeds from the *gemara*'s own framework.

---

## Extent of Spinal Cord

### Bein HaParshiyot

Having established the law of the spinal cord, the *gemara* asks: *ad heichan* — until where along the spine does the rule apply? This is particularly pressing given the suggestion that the spinal cord branches off and connects to other parts of the body at lower points. After a certain level, the cord presumably diminishes in criticality. Where is that lower boundary?

### Shmuel's Teaching

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *ad bein haparshiyot* — until the *bein haparshiyot*. Rashi offers three possible explanations of this term, preferring the following: after the main ribcage ends, smaller ribs continue branching off from the vertebrae down the lower spine. The *bein haparshiyot* refers to the area of these smaller ribs — specifically the spaces between the points where these mini-ribs branch off from the spine. Shmuel's tradition then adds detail: until the first such branching point it is still unambiguously *treifa*; from the third branching point onward it is unambiguously *kesheira*; and the second branching point is uncertain.

### Rav Dimi Story

The *gemara* relates a telling story. Rav Dimi bar Yitzchak wished to travel to Be Khuzai, a district in Babylonia. He came before Rav Yehuda — presumably to take his leave. Before letting him go, Rav Yehuda asked: *lechevi li mar bein haparshiyot heicha* — show me where the *bein haparshiyot* is located. The subtext, as the story reveals, may well have been a test of whether Rav Dimi bar Yitzchak was truly ready to leave his teacher's presence.

Rav Dimi replied: bring me a goat and I will show you. A fat goat was brought. Rav Yehuda said: *bliya tefei* — it is too fatty; the relevant area is absorbed and concealed and cannot be clearly identified. A skinny goat was then brought. Rav Yehuda said: *belit tefei* — it is too protruding; the hip bone obscures the location. (Rashi alternatively suggests the animal was still alive in this second case, which would make the difficulty more understandable.) Unable to demonstrate the location satisfactorily either way, Rav Dimi bar Yitzchak did not pass the test. Rav Yehuda then said: come, let me teach you the tradition — *hachi amar Shmuel*: until the first one it is *treifa*, at the third it is *kesheira*, and at the second I do not know.

### Inclusive Language

The *gemara* then asks a series of increasingly precise questions. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua asks: when Shmuel says "until the first," does he mean *ad ve'ad bichlal* — up to and including the first branching point — or *ad velo ad bichlal* — up to but not including it? Although the practical stakes might seem modest given that the entire zone up through the second point is at minimum a *safek treifa*, the question is still posed.

Rav Pappa then asks: *im timtzi lomar ad velo ad bichlal* — if you conclude that the first point itself is not included in the *vadai treifa* zone, what is the status of *pi parasha* — the very opening of that space? We are now debating a matter of perhaps a centimeter or less.

Rabbi Yirmiya's question goes in the other direction: *im timtzi lomar ad ve'ad bichlal* — if you conclude that the first point is included in the *vadai treifa* zone — what is the status of the *parasha atzma*, the separation itself? On the first reading of Rashi, this refers to the actual small rib bones that branch off. But on a more satisfying reading, it refers to the *space* between the first and second branching points. If the first point is *vadai treifa* and the second is *safek*, is the intervening space treated as *vadai* or as *safek*?

### Bones Insignificant

The *gemara* addresses whether the bones of the mini-ribs themselves matter. A ruling is cited: *haparasha kidon k'basar* — the separation itself is treated like flesh, meaning the bones have no intrinsic significance; only the spinal cord matters. The *gemara* initially reads this as applying to the first and second separations, but then concludes it refers to the third — at the third point the bones, if they break, are irrelevant. The unresolved questions about the first and second points, including what happens in the intermediate spaces, remain in *teiku*. As throughout this section, the question of why the spinal cord constitutes a *treifa* at all — given that its severance causes paralysis rather than death — is noted but left unanswered.

---

## Spinal Cord in Birds

### Rabbi Yannai vs. Reish L…

The *gemara* turns to birds: until where along the spine does the *treifa* of the spinal cord apply in a bird? Rabbi Yannai says *l'mata min ha'agapayim* — below the wings, meaning the concern extends throughout the region where the wings are attached, all the way to where the wings end. Reish Lakish says *ad bein ha'agapayim* — until between the wings, meaning only until where the wings begin to be attached; from that point downward, it is no longer a concern. This is a substantial disagreement. Tosafot raises the further question of whether "below the wings" means the bottom of where the wings attach to the body or the bottom of where the wings lie against the body — which would extend the zone considerably lower.

### Ulla & Rav Pazzi

Ulla relates: I was present before Rav Pazzi when a bird with a question about possible *treifa* was brought before him. He examined the bird for a severing, checking from the neck downward until the space where the wings begin. At that point, a messenger arrived from the house of the *nasi* and Rav Pazzi left to respond, having never rendered an explicit ruling on the bird. Ulla reflects: I do not know whether Rav Pazzi stopped because he considered his examination complete — meaning one need not check beyond where the wings begin, and the bird was effectively declared kosher by his departure — or whether he stopped only because of the obligation to respond immediately to the *nasi*, intending to return and finish the examination.

This story has an additional point of interest. If Rav Pazzi was actively checking the bird, it implies there was some reason to suspect a severance — perhaps the bird fell, or was found in a compromised condition. This is relevant to the broader question of which defects require routine examination and which do not. The question of what triggered the examination here is left open, though it seems plausible that some incident had given reason for concern.

---

## Liver

### Liver Contradiction

The *gemara* now addresses the liver. The *mishna* states that if the liver is removed and nothing remains, the animal is *treifa* — the implication being that if even a small amount (*mashehu*) remains, it is kosher. A later *mishna*, however, states explicitly: *nital hakaved venishtayer mimenu kezayit kesheira* — if a *kezayit* of liver remains, it is kosher. These two *mishnayot* contradict each other: does one need a *kezayit* or does any minimal amount suffice?

### Two Opinions

Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya* — it is not difficult; the two *mishnayot* reflect different opinions. One corresponds to Rabbi Chiyya and one to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi — that is, to the son of Rabbi, who was Rabbi's own child, while Rabbi Chiyya was Rabbi's nephew.

The *gemara* illuminates the dispute through a telling detail about their eating habits. Rabbi Chiyya would simply discard the liver; he did not eat it. Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi would dip the liver and eat it — treating it as something of an appetizer. A mnemonic for remembering who held which view: *ashirim mekamtzin* — wealthy people are frugal. Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, being from the *nasi*'s household and correspondingly wealthy, did not want to waste anything, including the liver. Rabbi Chiyya, not wealthy, had no interest in the liver.

What does eating practice have to do with *halachic* status? Rashi explains that vital organs — those recognized as central to the life force of the animal — were eaten for their perceived health properties. Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, who ate the liver, evidently regarded it as a genuinely vital organ and therefore demanded a *kezayit* for it to continue its essential function. Rabbi Chiyya, having no interest in the liver, clearly did not view it as a vital life force, and therefore held that any minimal amount (*mashehu*) suffices — or, as Rashi goes further to explain, the minimal amount is needed not even to perform the liver's own function but merely to cover the point where the liver connects to the gallbladder, preventing an exposed hole there. On this reading, Rabbi Chiyya essentially denies that the liver itself plays a critical life-sustaining role.

The *gemara* had already indicated in a previous passage, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, that the *halacha* requires a *kezayit*, and the present discussion confirms that we rule in accordance with the second *mishna* — corresponding to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi.

### Troop Story

A *gemara* narrative sets the context. A certain army troop (*pulmasa*) came to Pumbedisa. Concerned about conscription or other dangers, Rabba and Rav Yosef fled. Rabbi Zeira, who had connections with the authorities and could move about freely, encountered them and called them *arukai* — deserters — a somewhat pointed remark given his own liberty of movement. It is in this context that Rabbi Zeira then states the ruling: *kezayit she'amru bimkom mara* — the *kezayit* that the sages required must be located specifically where the gallbladder is.

Another authority, Afah bar Ahva, says *bimkom shehi chayah* — where the animal lives. This somewhat unusual phrase is explained by Rashi as referring either to the lobe of the liver — the distinctive flap-like section visible in a picture of a liver — or to the location where the liver is embedded between or beneath the kidneys.

### Rav Pappa Ruling

Rav Pappa rules: *hilchach ba'inan kezayit bimkom mara uba'inan kezayit bimkom shehi chayah* — since we cannot decide between the two opinions, we require a *kezayit* in both locations: both where the gallbladder is and where the liver is embedded. This is a practical *chumra* born of unresolved dispute.

### Kezayit Form

Rabbi Yirmiya raises a series of questions about the form the *kezayit* must take. *milaket mahu* — what if the required amount is not concentrated in one place but consists of scattered bits here and there that together combine to a *kezayit*? *keritua mahu* — what if it is stretched into a long thin strip, connected but lacking any concentrated mass? Rav Ashi adds: *kezayit merudad mahu* — what if it is present in the required volume but spread as an extremely thin, flat film? Technically there is a *kezayit* of material, but there is no thickness to it; can it perform any function? The *gemara* leaves all these in *teiku*.

A final query comes from Rav Zerika, who asks Rav Ami: *niddaldela kaved ume'ura betarpesheih mahu* — what if the liver has been loosened and separated from its proper position but is still being held in place by its surrounding membrane? Rav Ami replies that he has no idea what this question is about — meaning it is not a recognized halachic category at all. As long as the liver is still there in its location — whether measured from the gallbladder or from where it lives — it counts. The fact that it has become loosened is of no significance.

---

## Conclusion

### Adhesions Intro

Having completed the discussion of the liver, the shiur turns to the lungs — the most practically significant organ in the laws of *treifot*, because the lungs are the site of the most frequently encountered problems, centered above all on *sirchos*, adhesions. The term *glatt* — now familiar in common usage — literally means smooth, referring to lungs free of adhesions. Adhesions are fibrous connections that link the lung either to the inner wall of the ribcage or to adjacent lobes of the lung itself.

### Why Adhesions Matter

Why are adhesions a problem? The dominant explanation, adopted by Rashi and the subject of a major *tosafot* that will be encountered when the daf is turned, is that an adhesion is a sign that there was previously a hole in the lung and the adhesion has formed over it, concealing it. The concern is thus that a hole exists beneath the adhesion. Tosafot also entertains the possibility that the adhesion might not reflect a pre-existing hole but could itself cause a hole to develop — but this alternative is bracketed, and the working assumption throughout is that an adhesion signals a covered-up perforation.

In practice, *glatt* does not mean that the animal has absolutely no adhesions — virtually no animal's lungs are entirely free of them — but rather that it falls within a more stringent threshold of permissible adhesions, accepting only very thin adhesions that peel away easily. Non-*Glatt* practice tolerates a broader range of adhesions, relying on testing methods — including the water test and the blowing test — to verify whether a hole exists beneath an adhesion. Those tests and the full details of the adhesion laws will be taken up in the next session.

---

## Lungs - Holes

### Lung Membranes

The *gemara* opens the discussion of lung *trefot* with a fundamental question: *ha-reiah she-nikvah* — a lung that has been pierced. Three *amora'im* — Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Assi — weigh in, some saying the *treifa* requires that the *kruma ila'ah*, the outer membrane, be pierced, while others say the *kruma tata'ah*, the inner membrane. The structure of the lung involves multiple layers: an outer wall, a gap between the outer and inner walls, and an inner wall that is closer to the hollow of the lung itself. The debate concerns which layer must be pierced before the animal becomes a *treifa*.

Unlike the membrane surrounding the brain, the lung's membranes were not explicitly discussed in the *mishna*. Yet the *gemara* here does not require the piercing to reach all the way to the hollow interior of the lung — even a hole in one of the outer membranes can suffice, depending on which opinion is followed.

### Red Cloak

Rav Yosef bar Miyumi said in the name of Rav Nachman, with a mnemonic to aid recall: *ke-chituna de-varda de-mancha bei reiya* — like a red cloak that lies within the lung. This is a description of the inner membrane surrounding the lung, which has a distinctly reddish appearance. The ruling embedded in the mnemonic is that it is the inner membrane — this red cloak — that is the decisive layer. A hole that penetrates only the outer layer is not sufficient to render the animal *treifa*; the inner, red membrane must be pierced. This parallels the *gemara*'s earlier discussion of the membrane around the brain, where similarly the inner membrane was the determining layer.

### Peeled Lung

This ruling is confirmed and amplified by Rava: *hai reiya de-iglid de-atya sumka* — if a lung has been peeled of its outer membrane and the result looks like a red date, it is nonetheless *kesheira*. The red appearance is precisely that inner membrane which remains intact and continues to protect the lung. The removal of the entire outer membrane, while certainly a significant alteration to the lung's surface, does not compromise the inner membrane and therefore does not constitute a *treifa*.

### Inner vs. Outer

This raises a converse question. We have established that if the outer membrane is pierced but the inner is not, the inner protects — that is the clear implication of the ruling about the red cloak. But what if it is the inner membrane that is pierced while the outer remains intact? Does the outer protect even when the inner has a hole?

Rav Acha and Ravina debate this. One holds that the outer membrane does not protect if the inner has been breached; the other holds that it does. The *halacha* is that the outer membrane does protect: *hilchata magin*. Thus both membranes must be pierced for the animal to be *treifa* — a hole only in the inner membrane, with the outer intact, is not sufficient.

### Avsha Test

Rav Yosef states: *hai reiya de-avsha* — if a lung makes a whistling sound. This refers to a testing procedure: after removing the lung from the animal, one blows into it as one would inflate a balloon, and listens for escaping air. If a whistling sound is heard, a hole is present somewhere. The question is then how to locate it.

If one knows where the sound is coming from, the procedure is: place a feather (*gadfa*), spittle (*roka*), or a thin straw (*gila*) over that spot and blow again. If the feather flutters or the spittle bubbles, air is escaping through that point to the outside, and the lung is *treifa*. If there is no movement, the lung is *kesheira* despite the sound.

If one does not know where the sound originates, one cannot apply the spot-test. In that case, the procedure is the water test.

### Water Test

*Meisinei mitikla d'maya, pshurei* — one takes a vessel filled with lukewarm water, inflates the lung, and submerges it. Specifically, the water must be lukewarm: not hot (*bachamimei lo*), because hot water causes the tissue to constrict and would compress a hole shut, concealing it; and not cold (*bekarimei lo*), because cold water hardens the tissue and might actually cause a hole to be created artificially. Lukewarm water alone preserves the lung's natural state. Once the inflated lung is submerged, one blows further and observes: if air bubbles emerge, the lung is *treifa*; if no bubbles appear, it is *kesheira*.

### Sound Explanation

But if no air is actually escaping to the outside, why was there any sound at all? The *gemara* explains: *tata inkiv ila lo inkiv* — the inner membrane was pierced but the outer was not. The air escapes from the hollow of the lung through the hole in the inner membrane and enters the space between the inner and outer walls. That trapped air is what produces the whistling sound. But because the outer membrane is intact, the air goes no further, and the lung is still *kesheira* — consistent with the ruling that both membranes must be pierced.

This analysis implies a structural picture in which the two membranes function as a genuine double wall, with a real space between them. A hole in the inner wall allows air to seep into that interstitial space, producing an audible sound; a hole in the outer wall is necessary to allow that air to escape entirely to the exterior. Only when both walls are compromised is the animal a *treifa*. One might also ask: what if there is a hole in the inner membrane in one location and a hole in the outer membrane in a different location? That question is not explicitly addressed, though the emphasis on requiring that air escape all the way to the outside suggests the concern is with continuity of the penetration.

---

## Lung Defects

### Lung Redness

Rava states: *reia she-hidima miktzata kashira, kula treifa* — if a lung shows redness (*hidima*) from a wound in part of it, it remains *kesheira*; if the entire lung is reddened, it is *treifa*. The redness here is not the natural red of the inner membrane, as discussed earlier, but the redness of a wound — blood collecting beneath the surface from broken blood vessels, without having escaped to the exterior, much like a bruise or contusion.

### Ravina Challenge

Ravina challenges Rava: if part of the lung being reddened is *kesheira* because *d'hadar barya* — it will heal — why should the entire lung being reddened be any different? Surely the entire lung can also heal. He supports this with a *baraita* about the laws of *shabbat*.

### Shabbat Context

One of the *melachot* of *shabbat* is causing blood to flow. This applies even when the blood does not exit the body — if blood collects beneath the skin as a result of a wound (*nitzrar ha-dam af al pi she-lo yatza*), a prohibited act has been performed. The *gemara* distinguishes between different categories of animals: large animals certainly have real skin such that subcutaneous blood collection counts as a *melacha*. Regarding the eight rodents (*sheratzim*) enumerated in the Torah as sources of *tumah*, they too have real skin and subcutaneous reddening counts. Regarding other small creatures, they lack what is considered real skin and the reddening does not constitute a *melacha* unless the blood actually exits.

Ravina argues from this: if the lung's reddening is to be treated like the eight *sheratzim* — as real subcutaneous wounding that does not naturally heal — then even a partial reddening should be *treifa*. And if it is to be treated like the other creatures — as insignificant because the wound will heal — then even a complete reddening should be *kesheira*. Either way, the distinction between partial and complete reddening seems incoherent.

The *gemara* responds: *ela lo shna* — in fact there is no difference. Rashi is inclined toward the lenient reading: either way it is *kesheira*. Tosafot, however, cites Rabbeinu Tam who says either way it is *treifa*. Interestingly, this is one of several cases in this *perek* where Rashi tends toward leniency and Rabbeinu Tam toward stringency. Tosafot notes that Rabbeinu Gershom's *hilchos trefos* aligns with one reading, and that Rabbeinu Tam himself authored a work called *hilchos gedolos* on this subject — indicating how early the practice began of composing specialized handbooks on the laws of *kashrus*, stretching back at least to Rabbeinu Gershom's time. On the specific question of *hidima*, Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam coincide in ruling *kesheira*, though they diverge in other cases.

### Dried Lung

Rava further states: *reia she-yavsha miktzata treifa* — a lung of which part has dried out is *treifa*, even if only part. How dry must it be to qualify? Rav Pappa reports in the name of Rava: *kedei she-tiparech be-tziporen* — so dry that it would crumble if snapped with a fingernail. This is an advanced degree of desiccation — extremely brittle.

### Rabbi Yossi Position

The *gemara* notes: *ke-man* — whose opinion does this follow? It corresponds to Rabbi Yossi ben HaMeshullam. The comparison arises from a parallel debate in the laws of *bechor*, the firstborn animal. To establish a *mum* in a firstborn — a physical defect that exempts it from being brought as a *korban* and permits the *kohen* to eat it outside the *beit haMikdash* — the *mishna* discusses a dried limb, particularly a dried ear. What counts as dried? *nitnakev ve-eino motzi tipat dam* — if pinpricked and no blood emerges, it is considered dry, according to the Sages. Rabbi Yossi ben HaMeshullam is more stringent: *yeveshah kedei she-tehei niphrechet be-tziporen* — it must be brittle enough to crumble when snapped with a fingernail.

The *gemara* initially implies that it imports the more lenient standard (no blood emerges) into the lung case as well, then compares it to Rabbi Yossi ben HaMeshullam's crumble standard.

### Redness Resolution

The *gemara* provides the resolution: *ela lo shna* — the two cases are ultimately not to be distinguished. The lung being *kesheira* even when all of it is reddened is because the redness indicates that healing can occur; the blood is collecting but not escaping. Whether the reddening is partial or total does not change this.

### Ear vs. Lung

The reason the dried-lung standard is pegged to crumbling rather than the lower threshold of no blood emerging upon pinprick is explained by the *gemara* through a structural distinction. *gabei ozen bechor d'ka shalit bei zika* — the ear of a firstborn is exposed to the open air. Because it is exposed, once blood ceases to flow through it (*lo hadra bari*), it will not recover. Hence the lower threshold — no blood emerging — suffices to declare it a *mum*. *aval reia d'lo ka shalit bah avira* — the lung, however, is protected inside the body and is not exposed to the air.
