The ruling regarding *aveilus* pertains to a Mishnah in which the question arises as to when a late-arriving mourner joins the household's *shiva* count. The Mishnah establishes: during the first three days, if the newly arrived mourner comes from *makom karov* — a nearby place, defined as within a day's journey — he counts together with the household (*moneh imahem*) from the day of death, even if he personally only learned of the loss later. If he comes from *makom rachok* — a distant place — he counts *shiva* on his own from the day he finds out. The underlying concept is that the household constitutes a unit: if the mourner could theoretically have heard within time, he is treated as if he did hear and is conceptually part of the mourning household from the outset.

After the first three days, the Mishnah rules that even one arriving from *makom karov* counts *shiva* on his own. Rabbi Shimon, however, extends the joining principle: *afilu be-yom ha-shevi'i, ba mi-makom karov moneh imahem* — even if he arrives on the seventh day and comes from a nearby place, he counts together with the household and his *shiva* concludes with theirs. Tosafot raises the practical question of what it means to arrive on the seventh day, since by the morning of that day the mourners have already risen. Tosafot explains that this refers to arriving before the consolers have departed, since the *shiva* formally concludes only when the consolers leave.

Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that we follow Rabbi Shimon in this matter of *aveilus* is part of the same transmitted tradition. It is said in the name of a certain unnamed individual (*man d'hu* — what's-his-name, as Rashi explains that the *ba'alei ha-gemara* knew the story but had forgotten whose name to attach to it) that he once said: *iski v'eisik v'gamru shema'atei mi-pumei d'mara* — I wish to go up to *eretz yisrael* and hear this ruling directly from the one who taught it. This theme of traveling to verify the *mesorah* and hear things *mi-pumei d'mara* — from the mouth of the master — is a recurring and striking motif in these *dapim*.

### Mesorah Check

This unnamed person resolved to ascend to *eretz yisrael* precisely to verify the tradition. The desire to confirm the *mesorah* at its source, rather than rely on reported transmission, reflects how seriously the *amoraim* treated the accuracy of attributed rulings, especially in matters as consequential as *treifos*.

### Correction

When he arrived in *eretz yisrael*, *ashkechei le-Rabbi Abba breih de-Rabbi Chiya* — he found Rabbi Abba the son of Rabbi Chiya — and asked him directly: did you really say we rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding *treifa*, that the mucus seals holes? Rabbi Abba's reply is startling: *ha ein halachah amri* — no, I said we do *not* rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding *treifa*. The version of the tradition that had reached Bavel was simply inverted. The mucus does not seal holes according to the final ruling.

### Final Aveilus

The questioner then asks: what is your ruling regarding Rabbi Shimon in the matter of *aveilus*? Rabbi Abba responds that this is itself subject to debate: *pelugta ninhu* — it is disputed. Rav Chisda rules that we follow Rabbi Shimon (*halachah*), and similarly Rabbi Yochanan himself says *halachah*. But Rav Nachman rules that we do not follow Rabbi Shimon (*ein halachah*). The Gemara then concludes: *v'ein halachah ke-Rabbi Shimon* — and the law does not follow Rabbi Shimon on the *treifa* question — but *v'halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon ba-avel* — we do rule like Rabbi Shimon in the matter of *aveilus*, in accordance with the principle *halacha ke-divrei ha-mekil be-avel* — in matters of mourning, we rule like the more lenient position, as stated by Shmuel.

The result is precise: the *treifa* ruling is rejected — the mucus of the organ does not constitute a valid hole-sealer — while the *aveilus* ruling is affirmed — a mourner arriving from a nearby place even on the seventh day joins the household's count and his *shiva* concludes with theirs. The anonymous concluding voice of the Gemara, associated with the *stam* of the *shas*, presents this as the definitive ruling. The entire episode once again demonstrates how dramatically a transmitted tradition could diverge from what was actually taught, and how the *amoraim* took extraordinary steps to correct such errors.

---

## Hole Dating

### Comparison Test

The Gemara introduces a significant *kula*: *amar Rav Shimi bar Chiya: makifin bifnei me'ayim* — one may make comparison holes in the inner organs. The procedure is as follows: when a hole is found in an organ, if there is reason to suppose — or simply a desire to explore whether — it may have occurred after *shechita* rather than when the animal was alive, one may take the same organ, make a fresh hole in another location, and compare the two side by side. If the existing hole resembles the freshly made hole, one may conclude that the original hole was made after *shechita*, and the animal is *kasher*. If they look different, one must assume the hole antedates *shechita* and the animal is a *treifa*. This is a striking *kula*: notwithstanding all the stringencies regarding holes in organs, the Gemara provides a practical experimental method to attribute a hole to a post-mortem cause and thereby rescue the animal's *kashrut* status.

### Rava's Case

The Gemara records an incident. Certain inner organs were brought before Rava with holes in them. *akfinhu* — he made a comparison hole — but the two holes did not look similar, and Rava accordingly ruled the animal a *treifa*, concluding that the hole had been made while the animal was alive.

### Handling Effect

At that point, *ata Rav Marshorshie brei* — Rav Marshorshie's son arrived. He took the freshly made comparison hole, *mimashmesh bahu* — rubbed and handled it with his hands — and after that handling, *v'idmi* — it now looked just like the original hole. He then pointed this out to Rava: *kama yadei mimashmeshu behani mikami d'leito l'kamei d'mar* — how many hands must have handled this organ before it was even brought before you? The original hole had been handled extensively before Rava saw it. When he made his comparison hole, it was fresh and untouched, and naturally looked different. Once he handled the comparison hole to simulate what the original had undergone, the two appeared identical — and therefore one could conclude that both holes were made after *shechita*.

### Brilliance Praise

Rava's response was unrestrained admiration: *chakim brei b'treifos k'Rabbi Yochanan* — my son is as brilliant in the laws of *treifos* as Rabbi Yochanan. Rashi explains this either as a general superlative — Rabbi Yochanan being the gold standard of *talmidei chachamim* — or more specifically, since Rabbi Yochanan was known as a particular expert in the laws of *treifos*. The practical consequence was that the animal could now be permitted based on the son's insight.

### Lung Comparison

Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both rule: *makifin b'reia* — the comparison test applies even to the lung. Rashi explains this is noteworthy because even in a place where one would not normally attribute the hole to the *shochet's* handling, the comparison test may still be employed. If the hole in the lung resembles a freshly made hole, one may assume the original hole occurred after *shechita* — perhaps from a knife flying during the butchering process or from some other post-mortem cause — and the animal remains *kasher*.

One might wonder about cases where the hole was made by a needle: would a post-mortem needle hole really look different from a pre-mortem one? The Gemara does not address this directly, but the broader principle seems to be that when there is genuine doubt as to when the damage occurred, the presumption of *chezkat kashrut* operates more forcefully, and reasonable grounds for attributing the hole to a post-mortem cause are sufficient to permit. Where the cause of the hole is established with certainty, on the other hand, the relevant *treifa* rules apply without exception.

### Same Row

Rava introduces a limitation on the comparison test for the lung: *lo amru ela b'osah arugah* — the comparison is valid only within the same row or section of lung tissue. *aval me'arugah l'arugah lo* — one may not make a comparison hole in a different row of the lung and compare it to a hole in this row, since different sections of the organ may have different textures and appearances.

### Cross-Row

However, the *hilchata* — the final ruling — is more lenient: *afilu me'arugah l'arugah*, even from one row to another within the same lung, the comparison is valid. Furthermore, *midaka l'daka u'migasa l'gasa* — one may make the comparison hole in an entirely different animal of the same type: small animals (sheep and goats) may be compared to other small animals, large animals (cattle) to other cattle. One takes a healthy organ from a different animal of the same species, makes a fresh hole in it, and uses that as the comparison point. What is not permitted is *lo migasa l'daka v'lo midaka l'gasa* — one may not compare a hole in a cow's organ to a freshly made hole in a sheep's organ or vice versa.

### Trachea

Abaye and Rava both rule: *makifin b'kaneh* — the comparison test applies also to the trachea. This is somewhat more complex to visualize, since the trachea is only rendered *treifa* by a cut through the majority of its circumference, but the same principle applies: if such damage is found, one may make a comparable cut elsewhere and compare. Pappa rules that this comparison is valid only *b'oto chulya* — within the same ring section of the trachea's cartilage. *aval mechulya lechulya lo* — from one ring section to another is not a valid comparison.

The *hilchata*, however, again overrules this restriction: *afilu mechulya lechulya* — even from one ring section to another, *u'mivar chulya levar chulya* — and even from one *bar chulya* to another. The *bar chulya*, as Rashi explains, refers to either the soft membrane between the cartilage rings or the softer posterior portion of the cartilage ring where the hard material gives way to softer tissue. The one restriction that remains is that one may not compare a hole in the hard cartilage to a hole in the soft inter-ring membrane or vice versa — *aval lo mechulya levar chulya velo mivar chulya lechulya* — since these different materials will naturally look different and no valid comparison can be drawn between them.

---

## Chacholet/Keres

### Chacholet Kosher

The Gemara now turns to the *chacholet*, the rectum. *amar zeiri: chacholet shenikva, kesheira* — the rectum that has been perforated is *kasher*. The Mishnah had not enumerated the *chacholet* among the organs whose perforation renders an animal a *treifa*, and Zeiri makes explicit why: *hoil v'yerechayim ma'amidot otah* — since the animal's thighs hold it in place and support it, the functional concern that gives rise to *treifa* status for other perforated organs does not apply here with the same force. Rashi elaborates that the waste matter passing through the rectum is already dry and hard, making it highly unlikely that it would actually exit through a hole in the rectal wall.

### Thigh Support

*Amar Rabbi Ila amar Rabbi Yochanan*: the leniency is calibrated by location. *mekom hadevek berubo* — where the thighs actually adhere to the *chacholet*, even if the majority of the rectal wall is missing or torn, the animal is *kasher*. *shelo bimekom hadevek, bemashehu* — where the thighs do not adhere, even a *mashehu*, the slightest perforation, renders the animal *treifa*.

### Rav Nachman

The Rabbis reported this ruling before Rava in the name of Rav Nachman. Rava pushed back sharply: *lav niamina lechu, lo titlu beih buki sariki* — have I not told you not to attribute empty and mistaken ideas to Rav Nachman? Here again we encounter the recurring Talmudic theme of correcting inaccurate *mesorah*. *hachi amar rav nachman* — this is what Rav Nachman actually said: *mekom hadevek afilu nital kulo kasher* — where the thighs adhere, even if the entire *chacholet* is removed, the animal is *kasher* — provided that *vehu shenishtayer bo kedei tfisa* — enough remains to be grasped, i.e., there is some minimal remnant.

### Finger Width

The Gemara asks: *v'chama* — how much is *kedei tfisa*? Abaye answers: *kemalei bitda betura* — as much as a finger-width in a large ox. Even if only a finger's breadth of the rectal wall remains, the animal retains its *kasher* status. This is a remarkable ruling. One might expect that an animal whose rectum has been almost entirely removed would be a *treifa* on physiological grounds, but the *halacha* does not follow physiological intuition here; the rule of the thighs' support overrides what one might expect.

### Inner Keress

The Gemara transitions to the *keres*, the first of the four stomach compartments. The Mishnah had distinguished between the *keres hapnimi* — the inner stomach — and the *keres hachitzon* — the outer stomach. A hole in the inner stomach renders the animal a *treifa* even at the level of *mashehu*, while the outer stomach requires a tear of *rov* (majority). The critical question — generating multiple competing opinions — is what exactly constitutes the inner and outer *keres*.

By way of anatomical orientation: the *keres* is the large first chamber, the rumen, where ingested matter initially enters. From there it passes to the *mesas*, then to the *beis hakosos*, where it is regurgitated and rechewed, and finally to the *keivah*. The *keres* itself is an enormous organ.

### Sanya Divi

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: Natan bar Shila, the head butcher of Tzipori, testified before Rebbi in the name of Rebbi Natan — *eizehu hi hakeres hapnimi? Sanya Divi* — what is the inner *keres* where even a *mashehu* perforation is a *treifa*? It is *sanya divi*, literally "that which is hated by foxes" — a term understood to refer to the cecum, a separate appendage into which waste matter and indigestible material passes. The cecum earns its epithet because even animals will not eat it, given its contents. It is anatomically distinct from the *keres* proper, though in context it is categorized as the "inner" portion of the stomach complex. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Karcha agrees: *sanya divi*.

### Alt Definitions

Rabbi Yishmael offers a different definition: *istomcha dekarsa* — the stomach of the *keres*, which in ancient usage likely meant the opening or mouth of the organ, perhaps the juncture where the *keres* opens into the next chamber. Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says: *makom tzar yesh ba-keres ve-eini yodeia eizehu hu* — there is a narrowing within the *keres* and I do not know exactly where it is, and that narrowing is the inner *keres*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak wryly observes: *nafal karsa be-beira* — your *keres* has fallen into the well — an echo of the expression *nafla pita be-beira*, meaning: what good is a ruling if you cannot identify what it describes? Rav Acha bar Rav Avya, explaining Rav Assi's position, says: *min ha-meitzar ulematah* — from where the narrowing begins and below, that is the inner *keres*.

Rabbi Yaakov bar Nachmani in the name of Shmuel defines the inner *keres* as *makom she-ein bo milat* — the place where there is no felt-like material. The *keres* has a particular texture at one end — likened to felt — and where that texture stops and smooth wall begins, that is the inner *keres*. This corresponds roughly to the area sheltered beneath the full rib cage, in contrast to the more exposed portion. Rabbi Avina, in the name of Geniva, citing Rav, gives yet another definition: a *tefach* within the *keres* near the esophagus is the inner *keres* — a position that seems geographically anomalous relative to all the others, since it locates the "inner" *keres* at the entry end rather than the far end of the organ.

### EY Position

The position of *eretz yisrael*, transmitted by Rav Ami in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, is the most sweeping: *kol ha-keres kulo zo hi keres ha-pnimit* — the entire *keres* in its entirety is the inner *keres*, where even *mashehu* is a *treifa*. If so, what then is the outer *keres* that requires *rov*? *basar ha-chofeh et rov ha-keres* — the flesh that covers the majority of the *keres*. This is not the *keres* itself but the abdominal muscles running underneath it. These muscles extend across the underside of the *keres* — not beneath the entire organ, only beneath the majority of it — and a tear in those muscles requires a *rov* before it constitutes a *treifa*. The *keres* proper, on this view, is entirely inner and maximally stringent; only the external musculature receives the more lenient *rov* standard.

This is a strikingly *machmir* position: it means any hole anywhere in the *keres* is a problem, and the leniency of *rov* applies only to the abdominal muscles outside the *keres* entirely. The location of these abdominal muscles can be seen clearly in butchering context — they run along the underside of the carcass and are visible once the animal is opened.

### Exposure Test

*Amar Rabba bar Rav Huna: mafrata* — the demarcation is where it is torn open. Rav Avia explains: *heicha de-pro atvacha* — where the butchers tear open the animal when they begin the slaughtering and processing. When the carcass is hung and cut down the middle, whatever area is immediately exposed constitutes the inner *keres*, while what remains concealed beneath the full rib cage is the outer *keres*. This criterion aligns naturally with the *milat* definition: the area under the full rib cage, sheltered by the ribs, is not exposed when the animal is opened and corresponds to the area with the felt-like texture.

In Nahardea they ruled according to Rabba bar Rav Huna — that is, the inner *keres* is defined by what is exposed during butchering.

### Superset

Rav Ashi asked Ameimar — who was from Nahardea — *kol hani shema'ateta de-mai?* — what do you do with all those other opinions? The question seems to express surprise that Nahardea would rule like a single position when the matter was so extensively debated. Ameimar replied: *kulhu shaychan be-de-Rabba bar Rav Huna* — they are all subsumed within Rabba bar Rav Huna's criterion. That is, all the other definitions — the narrowing, the area without felt-like texture, the cecum, and so forth — are included within the area exposed during butchering. The exposure test is the broadest definition of inner *keres*, a superset encompassing all the other definitions, and therefore the most *machmir* position among those that still distinguish inner from outer.

Rav Ashi pushes further: and what about the positions of Rav Assi (narrowing) and Rav Avina (near the esophagus) and the position of *bnei Ma'arava* (entire *keres* plus only the abdominal muscles as outer)? Ameimar concedes: *hani vadai pligi* — those clearly disagree with how we rule. The position of *bnei Ma'arava* in particular — where the entire *keres* is inner and the outer is only the external muscles — is distinct from and more stringent than Rabba bar Rav Huna in one direction, while Rabbi Avina's placement near the esophagus is entirely different. The Nahardean practice does not encompass all opinions but does encompass most.

One might ask whether this diversity of practice implies that there was no uniform standard of *kashrut* throughout the Talmudic period. The question is apt: until the *gemara* established *hilchata* rulings, and those rulings were very late indeed — associated with Rav Ashi and Ameimar — wide regional variation existed. *treifos* are matters that only arise when the situation actually presents itself, so such variation would have had practical consequences only when a particular question came before a given authority. The *gemara* clearly tolerated a range of practice while simultaneously striving toward a definitive ruling.

### Size Rules

*Rabbi Yehuda omer bigdola* — Rabbi Yehuda says: for a large animal, a *tefach* tear in the outer *keres* renders it a *treifa*; for a small animal, the majority (*rov*). Rav Binyamin bar Yephet in the name of Rabbi Elazar explains: "large" and "small" are not absolute terms referring to the physical size of the animal per se. Rather, *lo gdola gdola mamash velo ktana ktana mamash* — "large" means an animal whose outer *keres* is large enough that a *tefach* tear does not yet constitute a majority, so that a *tefach* is the earlier threshold; "small" means an animal whose outer *keres* is small enough that the majority is reached before one achieves a *tefach*. The practical upshot: *rov* or *tefach*, whichever comes first, is the measure of *treifa*. For a large-stomached animal the smaller threshold will be the *tefach*; for a small-stomached animal the smaller threshold will be the *rov*.

### Majority Case

The Gemara objects: *ruba velo havei tefach, peshita* — if we are dealing with a case where the *rov* is torn and it has not yet reached a *tefach*, is that not obvious? Once we have established that any tear is a problem (which is the premise of these discussions), surely a majority of the organ is problematic. The Gemara answers: *lo tzricha dehavei tefach b'mashehu* — the case that requires teaching is one where a majority has been torn, and the addition of just a tiny bit more (*mashehu*) would bring it to a *tefach*. One might have thought to insist on waiting for the full *tefach* before declaring a *treifa*, and the Mishnah teaches that no — we go by *rov*, and majority suffices. Tosafot questions this *havah aminah* as strange — if majority always matters, why would we ever have thought to demand more? — and offers an alternative reading of the Gemara, though the discussion here stays with Rashi's understanding.

### Sela Size

*Amar Gneva amar Rav Assi: niktra k'sela, treifa* — if a window-like hole (*niktra* implies a shaped, cut-out perforation rather than a mere puncture) the size of a *sela* coin is made in the outer *keres*, the animal is a *treifa*.

### Circle Math

The relationship between the *sela* and the *tefach* standard is then explained. The *tefach* standard for a straight tear means a tear of one handbreadth in a straight line. A circular hole the size of a *sela* — meaning a circle whose circumference equals a *tefach* — is the equivalent, since the circumference of a circle the size of a *sela* is a *tefach*. Therefore such a hole constitutes the required threshold. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba adds that this was explained to him directly in the name of Gneva by the bridge of Nahardea: exactly the size of a *sela* is *kasher*, even slightly larger is *treifa* (*k'sela kesheira, yeter mik'sela treifa*). The practical question is then: how much is "a little bit larger"?

### Date Pit Test

*Amar Rav Yosef: kegon d'ayel tlat kashyata betzipa beducheka* — it is like a hole through which three date pits, with the thin layer of date flesh still attached, can be inserted tightly. If three date pits with their flesh can be pushed through the hole under pressure, the hole is large enough to be *treifa*. Conversely, *b'lo tzipa b'revach* — if three bare date pits without any flesh can pass through easily and with room to spare, that too is a hole of sufficient size to constitute a *treifa*. This concludes the daf.

---

---

# Hullin 51

## Masess & Beit Hakosot

### Four Stomachs Intro

The sugya opens with a brief orientation to the anatomy under discussion. Ruminants possess, in effect, four stomach compartments. The first and largest is the *keres* (rumen), where food initially passes and begins to be ground down. From there it enters the *masess* and the *beit hakosot*, two intermediate chambers where further grinding occurs. Food deemed sufficiently processed moves on to the *keivah* — the true stomach, analogous to the human stomach — where digestion takes place; food that requires more processing is pumped back up through the esophagus to be chewed again.

### Holes: Between vs. Outsi…

The halachic framework for these two intermediate chambers differs from other organs precisely because of their functional relationship to one another: since food naturally passes between the *masess* and the *beit hakosot* in both directions depending on the stage of processing, the membrane dividing them is effectively permeable. A hole in the wall *between* the two chambers is therefore not a concern — it does not render the animal a *treifa* — because food traverses that wall in the normal course of digestion. It is only a hole that penetrates from the inner cavity of the *beit hakosot* all the way through to the outside that constitutes a *treifa*, and as we shall see, that wall is itself double-layered, introducing additional nuance.

---

## Holes in Beit Hakoso (II)

### Needle Perforation Rules

The *Gemara* at the top of 51a continues with a *baraita*: if a needle is found embedded in the wall of the *beit hakosot*, the ruling depends on how far it has penetrated. The *beit hakosot* has two concentric layers of wall. If the needle has gone through only one of those layers — *mitzad echad*, from one side — the animal is *kesherah*. Only if it has passed through *both* walls, fully bridging the cavity to the outside, is it a *treifa*. This mirrors the general principle applied to many organs: a hole must traverse the entire thickness of the wall to disqualify the animal.

### Blood Evidence

Even when a needle has penetrated both walls and would otherwise constitute a *treifa*, there remains the question of *when* the hole was made. Throughout the past several days of learning, we have encountered a recurring principle: if the perforation occurred after *shechita*, it cannot retroactively render the animal a *treifa*. The *Gemara* now applies this to the needle case. If a drop of blood (*koret dam*) is found on the needle, this is considered proof that the piercing occurred before *shechita* — when blood was still coursing freely through the animal — and the *treifa* ruling stands.

### No Blood = After Shechita

Conversely, if no blood is found on the needle — *lo nimtsa lah koret dam* — this is taken as evidence that the hole was made *after shechita*, and the animal is permitted. This is a striking conclusion. Even with direct physical evidence of a foreign object having created the hole, the absence of blood adhering to it suffices to attribute the piercing to the post-*shechita* period, when far less blood is in active circulation through the tissue. The logic will be elaborated shortly, but the practical upshot is already clear: the absence of blood on a foreign object is a powerful exculpatory indicator.

---

## Scab & Mekach Taot

### Scab Evidence

The *baraita* continues: *higlit pi hamaka* — if the opening of the wound has formed a scab. A scab's formation is taken as evidence that the hole is at least three days old, since it takes approximately three days for that kind of natural crust to develop. This establishes not only that the hole predated *shechita* but also that it was already present for at least three days prior.

One might ask: once we know the hole predates *shechita*, the animal is a *treifa* regardless — why does the three-day timeframe matter? The answer becomes apparent when we consider the commercial context. If someone purchased an animal within the last three days and then slaughtered it only to discover a *treifa*, the presence of a scab is direct evidence that the defect existed at the time of purchase. This opens the door to a claim of *mekach ta'os* — a defective sale — and a demand for reimbursement.

### Burden of Proof

This brings the *Gemara* to a remarkable halachic discussion. If a seller sells a cow to a buyer who proceeds to slaughter it and discovers it is a *treifa*, can the buyer demand the money back? The answer seems counterintuitive at first glance: yes, in principle the buyer can — even if the seller had no knowledge of the defect and there was no misrepresentation. The principle of *mekach ta'os* can operate even without deceit; if the item was clearly not fit for the purpose for which it was purchased, the sale may be voided.

This seems deeply problematic from a commercial standpoint. A seller of livestock would be assuming enormous risk: a meaningful percentage of animals are *treifos*, and if every such case entitled the buyer to a refund of a slaughtered animal (now worth only what can be sold to non-Jews, not at kosher prices, and certainly not returnable alive), the business would be untenable.

The resolution, for the vast majority of cases, is the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — the burden of proof falls on the one seeking to extract from another. If the buyer has already paid and now wants the money back, it is the buyer who must prove that the defect existed at the time of purchase. In most cases this is impossible, and so the claim fails. The seller can simply say: how do you know the animal did not become a *treifa* in your possession, after I sold it to you?

### Kan Nimtza Kan Haya

*Tosafot* introduces an additional dimension. Beyond the question of who holds the money, there may be an independent presumptive principle: *kan nimtza kan haya* — where the defect was discovered, there it is presumed to have originated. Under this logic, if the *treifa* was found in the buyer's possession, we presume it arose during that time, regardless of who holds the money. The scab case is the exception: the scab is direct evidence that the hole is at least three days old and therefore predates the purchase, shifting the presumption.

This produces a somewhat unusual system. The default assumption, even when a defect is discovered, is that it arose under the current owner's watch — and only concrete evidence, like a scab, overrides that. Without such evidence, *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* protects the seller (if payment has been made), or *kan nimtza kan haya* supplies the presumption (as *Tosafot* would have it), leaving the buyer without recourse in most cases.

### Seller's Risk

There is an additional variable: the timing of payment. Since halachic acquisition (*kinyan*) takes effect when the buyer takes possession of the animal — independent of whether payment has been made — it is possible that the buyer takes possession and has not yet paid. In that case, the seller is now the one trying to extract money from the buyer. If the buyer then claims the animal was a *treifa* at the time of sale, it is the seller who bears the burden of proof. Similarly, the buyer's intended use matters: if it is clear that the buyer was a butcher purchasing the animal for *shechita*, the seller cannot later claim he assumed the animal was being purchased for plowing. But if the buyer's intended use is ambiguous, that too may factor into the analysis.

The underlying commercial reality is stark: in a world where a certain percentage of animals will inevitably be *treifos*, the seller is, in effect, assuming that risk in most cases where the buyer can make a showing. The principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* rescues the seller in the majority of situations, but it does not eliminate the exposure entirely.

---

## Holes in Beit Hakoso (II)

### Needle vs. Natural Holes

The *Gemara* now returns to address a question that had been left implicit: why, in the needle case, can we use the absence of blood as a basis for ruling the animal permitted? In other cases of holes — naturally occurring perforations — even without blood we would not feel comfortable attributing the hole to the post-*shechita* period. What makes the needle different?

The *Gemara* explains: *hasam leka midi lemisrach* — in cases of naturally occurring holes, there is no foreign object for the blood to adhere to. *Hacha*, here, since there is a needle, *ei isa dekodem shechita hu* — if it truly was pierced before *shechita*, when blood was freely flowing through the living animal, blood would necessarily have adhered to the metal. The needle provides a surface for the blood to stick to. Therefore, if the needle is clean, one can conclude with confidence that the piercing occurred after *shechita*, when circulation had largely ceased.

This crystallizes an important structural principle running through this entire section: holes in internal organs are not solved primarily by membranes or fat occluding them, though those mechanisms exist. They are solved, far more commonly, by attributing them to the post-*shechita* period through various evidentiary means — yesterday through comparison wounds made by the *shochet*, and now through the physical properties of whatever foreign object caused the hole. A hole made by a foreign object that leaves no blood behind is, in this framework, presumptively post-*shechita*.

---

## Rav Avira's Story

### Needle Half-Through Story

Rav Safra says to Abaye: there is a certain student of the Rabbis who came from Eretz Yisrael — *mima'arava*, from the West — and said his name is Rav Avira. This Rav Avira reported the following incident: a case came before *Rabbi* — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — involving a needle found in the wall of the *beit hakosot* that had penetrated only *one* of the two layers. And yet, Rav Avira reported, Rabbi declared it a *treifa*.

This is deeply troubling. The *baraita* we have just been learning makes unambiguous that a needle through a single wall is *kesherah*. For a needle that penetrated both walls — fully through — it is a *treifa*. Abaye, hearing this, is understandably unsettled: this appears to be a direct contradiction of established *halacha* in the name of the foremost authority of the Tannaitic period.

### Abaye's Investigation

Abaye sends word to Rav Avira requesting that he come and discuss the matter. Rav Avira declines to come. Abaye, rather than letting the matter drop, goes to him. He finds Rav Avira up on the roof engaged in some task. Abaye asks him to come down so they can sit and speak. Rav Avira refuses to descend. So Abaye climbs up to him.

The scene is worth pausing on. Here is Abaye — a leading *amora* of his generation — climbing onto someone's roof because this person has information he needs, despite the fact that the man has refused every invitation to simply come and talk. The episode reflects something important about Abaye's character: the imperative to get the facts straight overrides considerations of personal dignity.

Once on the roof, Abaye says: *eima li gufa de'uvda heichi hava* — tell me the details of the incident, exactly how it unfolded. Rav Avira explains that he was the *maftir* — the one who would assemble and dismiss Rabbi's students, the gatherer and releaser of the congregation before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi the Great. Sitting before Rabbi at the time were two otherwise unknown figures: Rav Huna of Tzippori and Rabbi Yosi of Medea (or a similar locale). It is worth noting that the chronology here is somewhat strained: Abaye lived roughly from 278 to 338 CE, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi flourished around 200 CE. For Rav Avira to have personally served in Rabbi's academy and still be alive and accessible to Abaye would have required him to have been quite young in Rabbi's time and quite elderly when Abaye sought him out — the timeline just barely works, but it is pushing it.

Rav Avira continues: the case that came before Rabbi was indeed a needle in the wall of the *beit hakosot* from one side only — *mitzad echad*. And Rabbi declared it a *treifa*.

### Blood Drop Resolution

At this point, Rav Avira reveals the crucial detail that had been lost in transmission. Rabbi examined the wall and turned it over — *hafcha* — and on the other side found a drop of blood, *koret dam*. Even though no visible hole could be seen on the far side, the drop of blood established that the needle had in fact penetrated all the way through. The presence of blood on the far wall was the evidence that the perforation was complete — the needle had traversed both layers. On *that* basis, Rabbi declared it a *treifa*. The ruling was never about a needle through only one wall. It was always about a needle that had in fact gone all the way through, as established by the blood evidence on the other side.

As Rav Avira himself explains: *im ein sham maka koret dam minalan* — if there were no perforation going all the way through, how would a drop of blood have gotten to the far side at all?

### Broken Telephone

Abaye's reaction is exasperation. *Tarach tarchai v'hahu gavra* — you made me go through all that effort for this? The ruling is simply our *mishnah*: a needle that goes through to the outside is a *treifa*. Rabbi merely inferred that it had gone all the way through from the presence of the blood drop. There was no novel ruling, no departure from established *halacha*, no precedent that a one-sided perforation could disqualify an animal.

The episode is a vivid illustration of the problem of *broken telephone* in the transmission of traditions. A story circulates that Rabbi declared a one-sided needle a *treifa* — and that, taken at face value, appears to overturn well-established law. The reality, once Abaye goes through the considerable effort of extracting the full details, is that the ruling was entirely conventional; the dramatic detail — Rabbi turned the wall over and found a blood drop on the far side — had simply dropped out of the transmission. The lesson drawn is not about the specific law of needles and walls, but about the imperative to pursue the full factual record of any tradition rather than accepting a summary that may have lost something crucial in the retelling. There is also, as noted, something quietly powerful in the image of Abaye climbing onto a stranger's roof in pursuit of that record, regardless of what it cost him in effort or dignity — even if he permitted himself a moment of frustration when it turned out to have been unnecessary.

---

## Nefulah & Risuk Eivarim

### Nefulah Definition

The *sugya* now turns to a new category of *treifa* that does not depend on finding any specific lesion or perforation in any organ: *nefulah*, the fallen animal. The *mishnah* states simply *nafla min hagag* — it fell from the roof — and declares it a *treifa*. This is a fundamentally different type of disqualification. Unlike holes in the lung or perforations of the stomach, the *treifa* here is not identified by pointing to a damaged organ. Rather, the very event of the fall is itself the disqualifying factor, under the category known as *risuk eivarim* — the shattering or loosening of the limbs.

The *Gemara* will make two significant additions to the bare *mishnah*, one stringent and one lenient. The stringent addition: even if you were to check all of the internal organs and find nothing abnormal, that bedika would be insufficient to permit the animal. The *risuk eivarim* is itself a form of *treifa*, not merely a presumption that some other *treifa* lurks inside. The lenient addition — which we will reach later — is that the problem can be resolved if the animal subsequently gets up and walks around, or survives for twenty-four hours. This leniency is hinted at in a parallel *mishnah* regarding birds, which speaks of an animal that survives *me'eis le'eis*, twenty-four hours, after a traumatic impact.

On the question of how severe a fall is necessary to trigger this concern: the *Gemara* in *Bava Kamma* establishes that the threshold is ten *tefachim*, roughly three feet. That may not sound dramatic, but the angle and manner of landing obviously matter enormously.

### Found Below Rule

Rav Huna introduces a significant qualification: *hiniach behemah l'maalo u-va u-matsah l'mato* — if you left an animal on a roof and returned to find it at the bottom, we are not concerned about *risuk eivarim*. The reason is epistemic: we do not know *how* it got down. Perhaps it climbed down. Perhaps it jumped rather than fell. Since we cannot establish that it actually fell in the problematic manner, we do not impose the concern.

### Goat Skylight Story

This ruling is immediately tested by a case from Ravina's household. Ravina had a goat that apparently caught sight of barley visible through a skylight in the roof. The goat jumped from the roof to the ground below in order to get at the barley. The case came before Rav Ashi. Ravina's question was whether Rav Huna's ruling — that finding an animal below without witnessing the fall is not a concern — applies here, where the mechanism of descent is known. The goat did not climb down; it leaped through a skylight. Does Rav Huna's principle help here, and if so, why?

### Amda Nafsha Principle

Rav Ashi identifies two possible rationales for Rav Huna's ruling, and the choice between them determines the outcome in the goat case.

The first rationale: perhaps the animal is not a concern because when descending from a wall, it may have gripped the edge of the wall — *midi lemisrach*, something to adhere to — and thereby broken its fall. If this is the reason, it would not apply to the goat, which leaped through a skylight in the middle of a roof with nothing to grip on the way down.

The second rationale: *amda nafsha* — the animal assessed its own strength. An animal that willfully jumps knows its own capabilities and is able to orient itself for landing; it knows whether it can make the leap safely, and it will land on its feet and absorb the impact. If this is the reason, then the goat case is not different at all — the goat also made a voluntary leap and assessed what it was doing.

Rav Ashi's answer is that the latter rationale is correct: *mishum d'amda nafsha*, because the animal gauged itself, *v'hai nami amda nafsha*, and the same is true of this goat. A voluntary jump is categorically different from an accidental fall, and it does not trigger the *risuk eivarim* concern regardless of whether there was anything for the animal to grip on the way down.

---

## Ramming & Impact

### Mutual Ramming Rule

Rav Huna rules that rams engaging in their characteristic mutual ramming behavior — *dichrei hamenagchin zeh et zeh* — are not a concern for *risuk eivarim*, even when the impact is strong enough to make them groan in pain. The groaning, the *Gemara* explains, reflects the exertion involved, not a genuine traumatic injury of the kind that would loosen limbs. As long as neither animal is thrown to the ground, the violence of the ramming does not rise to the level of concern.

However, *i nefal l'ara* — if as a result of the impact one animal is thrown down to the ground — then we are indeed concerned. Even without a fall from a height, the impact of hitting the ground after being knocked down by a ram is sufficient to raise the question of *risuk eivarim*.

### Thieves Throwing Rams

Rav Menasheh addresses a case that captures something of the texture of everyday life in the rabbinic period: thieves who steal rams by throwing them over walls. This would presumably render the rams subject to *risuk eivarim*, since they are being thrown and falling. Rav Menasheh rules that we are not concerned. The reason: *amatzvayei shadi lehu* — the thieves throw them so that the rams land on their feet (literally "on their sides," but meaning feet-first). The thieves' practical interest dictates the manner of the throw: they want the animal to land and start running so they can make their escape. A ram thrown feet-first can absorb the landing and will not suffer *risuk eivarim*.

### Theft Return Cases

The situation changes when the thieves throw the animal back. If they hear the authorities approaching and hastily toss the ram back over the wall to avoid being caught — *mechamat yira*, out of fear — we are indeed concerned, because in their panic they are not careful about how the animal lands.

But if the thieves act out of genuine *teshuvah* — they made their escape, and subsequently, moved by remorse, they return the animal — then we assume they acted with care, *teshuvah maliyuta hi de-avdi*, they are doing a sincere *teshuvah* and would not have thrown the animal carelessly. In that case, we assume they returned it carefully and we are not concerned. How one determines after the fact whether the return was driven by fear or by repentance is not specified explicitly; presumably the timing and circumstances would provide some indication — a return well after the fact, with no imminent danger, more readily suggests genuine *teshuvah*.

### Stick Striking

Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: if one strikes an animal on its head with a long stick — long enough that the length of the stick spans the full length of the animal from head to tail — and the impact travels toward the tail, or conversely, one strikes at the tail and the motion carries toward the head along the full length of the spine, we are *not* concerned about *risuk eivarim*. The reason is that when a stick of such length comes down along the length of the animal, the force is distributed and attenuated; the tip of the stick is actually doing relatively little work at any one point. The impact does not create the kind of concentrated trauma to the spine that would cause *risuk eivarim*.

However, if the stick is shorter and its impact terminates at the midpoint of the animal's back — *palga de-gaba* — then we *are* concerned, because the force of impact is concentrated at a single point along the spine and can cause real damage.

Additionally, even a long stick causes concern if it has knots — *kitrei* — the protruding nodes where branches once joined the trunk. These knots create localized points of impact, so that when the stick comes down, even a distributed blow delivers concentrated force at each knot. Similarly, if one strikes the animal *a-pitya* — width-wise, perpendicular to the length of the animal — that is a direct impact on the spine at a single concentrated point, and we are again concerned.

In all these cases of concern, the underlying problem — *risuk eivarim* — remains to be addressed. As will become clear shortly, subsequent movement by the animal is the key to resolving it. Notably, the *Gemara* has been building an extensive catalogue of concerning scenarios without yet stating how they are resolved, and the resolution — walking, standing — will only be articulated at the end.

---

## Birth & Recovery

### Birth Not Traumatic

Rav Nachman rules: *beis harechem ein bo mishum risuk eivarim* — the womb is not a source of *risuk eivarim*. The experience of being born does not constitute the kind of traumatic impact that would classify the newborn animal as a *treifa* under this category. Rava supports this with a *mishnah*: a one-day-old infant boy can become a *zav* if he has a penile emission. The laws of *zav* require that the emission be a genuine pathological flow, not one caused by external trauma — *mibsaro v'lo mechamat onso*. If birth itself were the kind of physical trauma that could cause *risuk eivarim* in an animal, we would have reason to say that a newborn's emission is a product of that trauma, and he would not qualify as a *zav*. The fact that a one-day-old boy *can* become a *zav* implies that we do not regard birth as that kind of externally imposed physical trauma.

The *Gemara* pushes back: perhaps this proof is limited to cases of *derech dofen* — cesarean section — where the infant was simply removed from the womb without passing through the birth canal. Perhaps natural birth *is* traumatic, and it is only the cesarean case where the *zav* status applies cleanly. The argument from the newborn *zav* would then be insufficient to prove that natural birth is not a cause of *risuk eivarim*.

### Cesarean Section

The *Gemara* then considers a second proof: *egel shenolad b'yom tov shochtin oso b'yom tov* — a calf born on *Yom Tov* may be slaughtered on that same *Yom Tov*, since it is not *muktzeh*. The reasoning is that even while still in the womb before *Yom Tov* began, the fetus was in principle fit to be eaten (had the mother been slaughtered), and thus the calf is not newly fit on *Yom Tov* in a way that would make it *muktzeh*. But if birth caused *risuk eivarim*, how could one slaughter the calf on the day of its birth? It might be a *treifa*! The *Gemara* again deflects: perhaps this refers to a calf born by cesarean section — *derech dofen* — which is not subject to the physical trauma of natural birth.

The second variant of the proof involves a *bechor* — a firstborn animal — born on *Yom Tov* already bearing a blemish (*mum*). Both sides of the *muktzeh* debate agree that such an animal, born with its *mum*, can be slaughtered on *Yom Tov* because it was fit to be eaten from the moment of birth. Here the *Gemara* attempts the same deflection — perhaps it was born by cesarean section — but this is immediately foreclosed. An animal born *derech dofen* cannot have *bechor* status at all. As *Tosafot* emphasizes, the entire concept of *bechor* depends on *peter rechem* — emerging naturally from the womb — and Rabbi Yochanan states explicitly that even Rabbi Shimon, who holds that cesarean birth creates *tumah* obligations for the mother in the context of human childbirth, would agree that for purposes of sacrifices the animal is not sanctified. Since the case must involve a *bechor*, it must involve natural birth, and yet slaughter on the day of birth is unproblematic. This would seem to prove definitively that natural birth does not cause *risuk eivarim*.

### Standing Up Evidence

The *Gemara* offers a final escape: *shehifris al gabi karka* — perhaps the case is one where the animal had already gotten to its feet. This finally introduces, even if only implicitly, the principle that subsequent movement resolves the *risuk eivarim* concern. *Rashi* suggests that even the beginning of the process — the animal moving into position to stand — is sufficient. The significance of this deflection is that it points toward the resolution that will be stated explicitly in the next section: what the animal does after the traumatic event determines whether the *risuk eivarim* concern remains.

### Slaughterhouse Casting

Rav Nachman adds a parallel ruling: *beis hamatbechayim ein bo mishum risuk eivarim* — the slaughterhouse casting procedure does not cause *risuk eivarim*. When an animal is brought down for slaughter — through tumbling machines or other means of flipping it to expose the neck — even though this might seem like the kind of impact that triggers the concern, it does not.

The *Gemara* illustrates with a graphic incident: an ox was cast down, and its groaning could be heard from a distance. Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta nevertheless slaughtered it and took the choicest cut of meat — a demonstration that it was permitted. When questioned by the other rabbis about his basis, he cited Rav: *tzippornav no'etz ad shemagia l'aretz* — the animal digs in its hooves as it is being brought down, resisting the fall. That resistance, that instinctive bracing against the ground as the animal is pushed down from a standing position, breaks the impact. It is categorically different from falling from a height without preparation or control. The animal, in effect, partially controls its own descent, and that is sufficient to eliminate the *risuk eivarim* concern.

The description is deliberately unflinching: the animal is in evident pain, its distress audible from a distance. Yet the legal analysis is entirely technical — not whether this constitutes *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*, but whether the specific biomechanics of the impact meet the threshold for *risuk eivarim*. The *Gemara* throughout this discussion is concerned with *kashrut*, not with suffering, and the two analyses are kept entirely separate.

---

## Movement Resolution

### Standing Rule

Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: *amda eina tzricha me'eis le'eis* — if the animal stood up after the fall, it does not require waiting twenty-four hours. This is the first explicit statement that standing up resolves the problem, and it implicitly confirms that waiting twenty-four hours also works — it simply turns out not to be necessary if the animal stands. The parallel with the *mishnah* by birds, which speaks of surviving *me'eis le'eis* after a traumatic impact, has been in the background throughout this discussion; here it is quietly confirmed and then superseded by the standing criterion.

However, *bedika badei ba'ya* — standing up, while eliminating the twenty-four-hour requirement, does not eliminate the need for a *bedika* of the internal organs after *shechita*. The animal gets out of the specific *risuk eivarim* status, but *shechita* must still be followed by an internal examination.

### Walking vs. Standing

The optimal outcome is walking. *Halacha* dictates that if the animal walked, *eina tzricha bedika* — no internal examination is required. Walking is the clearest and most complete evidence that no serious internal damage occurred, and it removes all residual concerns. Standing alone resolves the *risuk eivarim* concern but leaves the *bedika* requirement in place.

### Partial Movement

Rav Yirmeya bar Abba says in the name of Rav: *pashta yada l'amod* — even if the animal merely stretched out a foreleg in an attempt to stand, *af al pi shelo amda*, even without actually achieving a standing position, that suffices as equivalent to standing. Similarly, *akra ragla l'halech* — if it moved a hind leg in preparation for walking, even without actually walking, *af al pi shelo halcha*, that also counts. Rav Chisda goes further: *niera l'amod* — even if the animal only shifted its body weight in a motion suggesting it was trying to stand, without extending any limb, that suffices as standing.

### Final Halacha

The concluding *halacha* — likely a Geonic addition to the text — synthesizes the discussion. If an animal fell from a roof unknowingly, meaning it neither jumped willfully nor broke its fall: if it subsequently stood up without walking, *tzricha bedika v'eina tzricha me'eis le'eis* — a *bedika* is required after *shechita*, but there is no need to wait twenty-four hours. If it walked, *afilu bedika nami lo tzricha* — even the *bedika* is waived entirely.

Notably, the final *halacha* does not adopt the more lenient positions of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav Chisda: mere stretching of a limb or shifting of the body does not qualify as "standing" for these purposes. The animal must actually stand or actually walk. Partial movement, however indicative of life and recovery, is not sufficient under the final ruling.

---

---

# Hullin 52

## Fallen Animals & Bedikah

### Amemar: Bedikah Focus

The daf opens at the bottom of 51b, picking up from a discussion that had introduced a principle not found in earlier treatments: if an animal that fell from a roof gets up and walks around afterward, it is presumed unharmed. If, however, it merely stood without walking, or if twenty-four hours elapsed, it may still be permissible but requires an internal inspection — a *bedikah*. The Gemara now turns to the precise scope of that *bedikah*.

Amemar said in the name of Rav Dimi from Nehardea: when we say that a *nefulah* — a fallen animal — requires *bedikah*, what must be examined? *Keneged bnei mei'ayim* — the internal organs, to verify that the fall did not puncture or tear them. This is intuitive: a fall might cause a rupture that is not externally visible, and such damage would render the animal a *treifah*.

Rashi, it should be noted, had understood the *bedikah* differently at an earlier stage of the discussion: he assumed the examination was directed at the bones, specifically to check whether the ribs had shattered or the spinal cord severed — each of which constitutes an independent *treifah*. On Rashi's reading, the concern for *piruk atzamot* (dislocation or loosening of the bones as a general category) is resolved by the fact that the animal stood up; what remains is to rule out those more specific skeletal *treifot*. Amemar's formulation, by contrast, focuses on the organs.

### Mar Zutra & Rav Pappa

Mar Zutra responded with a tradition in the name of Rav Pappa: the *bedikah* must cover the entire inner cavity — *kol beit halal kulo*. Two questions arise from this formulation. First, does *beit halal* mean the organs throughout the cavity, including heart and lungs, or does it refer — as Rashi suggests — to the bones, ribs, and vertebrae that form the structure of the cavity? Second, is Rav Pappa supplementing Amemar or contradicting him — broadening the scope of inspection beyond the digestive organs, or redirecting it entirely?

Neither question yields a clean resolution. Rashi's reading of *beit halal* as emphasizing the skeletal structure connects to the *treifot* of shattered ribs and a severed spinal cord; the alternative reading, that it means every organ within the cavity, is perhaps more natural linguistically. The relationship between the two opinions remains open.

### Rav Ashi: Simanim

A question was then posed to Rav Ashi by Huna Mar the son of Rav Nechemiah: what of the *simanim* — the trachea and esophagus? Must one also check whether these were damaged in the fall?

Rav Ashi replied: *simanim kashim heim eitzel nefilah* — the *simanim* are resistant, hardy with respect to falling. They are not the kind of structures that sustain damage from the impact of a fall. One need not check them. The concern for a *bedikah* after a fall is directed at the bones and internal organs, not the trachea or esophagus, which are not vulnerable to that type of immediate trauma.

---

## Bird Impact Types

### Bird in Water Test

The Gemara transitions to birds, drawing on a principle articulated by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. For large animals, the test of walking resolves the concern for *risuk eivarim* — internal organ rupture from impact. For birds, an analogous test is needed.

If a bird was hurled against the surface of the water — *nichbat al pnei hamayim* — and one cannot readily perform the walking test, the Gemara provides a substitute: *keivan she'shat melo komato dayo* — as long as the bird swims the length of its own body, that is sufficient, equivalent to a large animal walking. However, a critical qualification applies: this works only when the bird is swimming *against* the current — *mi-mata l'ma'ala*. If it is carried along *with* the current, the movement proves nothing, as the water is simply moving it. If the water is still, the question of current is moot, and any swimming is probative.

An additional nuance: if there are pieces of wood floating downstream with the current, and the bird is moving faster than those pieces, that is evidence of the bird's own locomotion — and that suffices.

### Taut Cloaks & Nets

The Gemara now surveys which surfaces, when a bird strikes them, constitute a harsh impact sufficient to create concern for *risuk eivarim*, and which do not. A cloak spread taut — whether hung like laundry perpendicular to the ground or otherwise stretched — creates concern (*chaishinan*) if the bird smashes into it, because the surface is unyielding. If the cloak is not taut, we are not concerned, even if it arrested the bird's flight. A cloak that is folded double, even if taut, similarly does not produce a harsh enough impact — *lo chaishinan*.

A tightly-knotted net — one where the knots are close together — creates concern: the bird may strike directly against a knot, producing a hard impact. If the knots are spread apart, we are not concerned.

### Flax & Bundle Types

Flax arranged in bundles (*d'avid bituni*) creates concern, because the bundle is firm. However, if the bird strikes at the edges of the bundle — on either side — where the structure is less rigid, we are not concerned.

A bundle of wood similarly creates concern. Flax that has been beaten and combed — with the hard seed vessels removed — is soft, and we are not concerned. Flax that has been soaked but not yet had its outer layers removed retains those harder components, and we are concerned. If the flax is bundled together with knots (as opposed to being loose), the knots themselves create the hard surface of impact, and we are concerned. If the outer husks themselves have been removed and then crushed finely, they are no longer a hard surface — *lo chashinan*.

A processed vine-like fiber (*nivra*) that has not yet been worked into its final form remains hard and creates concern; once processed into its finished, soft state (*timchasa*), it does not.

### Sand, Ash, Straw

Sifted ashes (*kitma nehila*) create concern, because the sifting process results in a compressed, densely packed pile; unsifted ashes, which contain more air and are looser, do not. Fine sand (*chol ha-dak*) does not create concern; coarse, pebbly sand (*chol ha-gas*) does. Dust compacted on a roadway (*avak drachim*) creates concern — Rashi explains this as dust that has been gathered and compressed underfoot. Straw formed into bundles is a concern; loose straw piled without being bundled is not.

Wheat and harder grains create concern. Barley and similar softer grains do not — notably, the Gemara here breaks the alternating *chaishinan / lo chaishinan* pattern by listing them separately, implying a meaningful distinction in hardness.

### Legumes & Slip Rule

All types of *kitniyot* — legumes — do not involve *risuk eivarim*. The Gemara's phrasing here shifts tellingly from the *chaishinan / lo chaishinan* idiom to the more absolute *ein bahem risuk eivarim*. Rashi explains this is not merely because legumes are soft, but because they do not hold together — they slip against one another, such that impact against them is scarcely an impact at all.

An exception is noted for *rubaya* (fenugreek), which does hold its shape and compact. Another substance, *chamtzei* (likely peas), also slips and does not stack, and therefore is not a concern. *Chaptzei* (chickpeas, according to Artscroll), which is not circular and does stack, does present concern for *risuk eivarim*.

The Gemara then articulates the general principle: *kol midi demishrak ein bo mishum risuk eivarim* — anything that slips does not produce *risuk eivarim*. Anything that does not slip does.

### Glued Trap Dispute

The Gemara addresses a particular type of bird trap in which pieces of wood were coated with glue. When a bird landed, its wing — or wings — would stick to the wood, and when it tried to fly off, it would crash to the ground. The question is whether such a fall constitutes *risuk eivarim*.

Rav Ashi permitted; Rav Amimar forbade. A first version of the dispute holds that if only one wing is immobilized, everyone agrees the bird is permitted — one free wing cannot fly the bird but can cushion its fall enough that the impact is insufficient to cause concern. The dispute applies when *both* wings are stuck: the one who forbids argues that the bird cannot control its descent at all; the one who permits argues that the bird can still brace itself on the heel of the wing where it joins the body, and this partially breaks the fall.

A second version of the dispute inverts the structure: when both wings are immobilized, everyone agrees the bird is forbidden — it has no means to soften its crash. The dispute applies when only *one* wing is stuck. The permitting opinion holds that one free wing allows the bird to flap and control its fall sufficiently; the forbidding opinion holds that since it cannot fly with the stuck wing, the one free wing also becomes functionally useless, as the bird cannot coordinate flight — *keivan debehai lo matzya parchah, behai nami lo matzya parchah*.

The *halacha* is: two wings stuck — forbidden; one wing stuck — permitted.

---

## Broken Ribs Debate

### Amemar: Rib Majority

The Gemara returns to the *mishnah*, which speaks of *rov tzaloteha* — the majority of the ribs being broken as a *treifah*. The ribs relevant to this discussion are the large ribs that form the ribcage — those that have marrow. Rashi holds that there are eleven such ribs on each side, for a total of twenty-two. The majority of twenty-two is twelve. It may be noted that anatomists count thirteen pairs of ribs in these animals, but Rashi's number apparently reflects only those with marrow — possibly the top eleven pairs — with the remaining ones excluded as non-qualifying.

The *Tanna'im* teach: *eilu hein rov tzalot* — what constitutes the majority? Either six ribs from each side, or eleven from one side and one from the other — and by implication, any distribution in between. What matters is that twelve ribs in total, drawn from these eleven pairs, are broken. The distribution between the two sides is irrelevant, so long as the overall number reaches twelve.

### Zeiri: Upper Half Rule

Zeiri adds a qualification: the break must occur in the half of the rib *toward the spinal cord* — *mechetzayan klapei shidra*. A break in the lower half of the rib, toward the front of the animal and away from the spine, does not constitute a full break for the purposes of this *treifah*. Only fractures in the upper, spinal half of the rib count.

Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that throughout this discussion, we are speaking of *tzalot gedolot* — the large ribs that have marrow — eleven on each side.

### Ben Zakkai vs. R. Yochan…

Ulla cites Ben Zakkai (not to be confused with the Tanna Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, given the generational distance, but some other Sage of that name): *ne'ekru b'rov tzad echad* — if the ribs are not merely broken but *uprooted* — fully detached from where they join the spinal column — then a majority of *one side* suffices. Six uprooted ribs from one side would render the animal a *treifah*. If, however, the ribs are merely *broken* (*nishtabru*), the majority must span *both* sides — twelve ribs total.

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: whether uprooted or broken, one always requires the majority of both sides combined — twelve ribs. The uprooting of ribs is not inherently more severe in terms of the threshold required.

### Rav: Rib + Vertebra

Rav goes further: *ne'ekra tzela v'chulya imah* — if a rib is uprooted together with its vertebra, *v'afilu achat treifah* — even a single such rib renders the animal a *treifah*. Until now we have been discussing ribs broken or uprooted from their articulation with the spine; here Rav speaks of a rib removed entirely along with the vertebra to which it is attached.

### Challenge: Opposing Ribs

Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged Rav: what of a case in which a rib from each side — an opposing pair — is uprooted, but the vertebra in the middle remains intact? They assumed this was a case Rav had not yet addressed — more severe than just a rib, but perhaps less than a rib with its vertebra, since the vertebra itself is present.

Rav's response was striking: *gistera ka ramitu* — "You are presenting me with a *gistera*?" The *gistera* is an animal split in half widthwise; even while still alive, such an animal is considered a *neveilah* — not merely a *treifah* but a carcass outright. Rav apparently regarded the removal of an opposing pair of ribs as equivalent to splitting the animal in half — a remarkable and, one might say, counterintuitive leap.

### Gemara Resolution

The Gemara then presses: but Rav himself already said a rib with its vertebra is a *treifah*. If removing one rib pulls the vertebra with it, then the rib on the other side would also detach. How is Rav's case not already more severe than the one Rav Kahana and Rav Assi proposed?

The Gemara resolves this: Rav did not mean the rib with the *entire* vertebra. He meant the rib with *half* a vertebra — *tzela v'chatzi chulya* — the half to which that rib attaches. The other half of the vertebra, where the opposing rib connects, remains in place. That is Rav's case: one rib and half a vertebra. Rav Kahana and Rav Assi were asking about two opposing ribs removed, without any part of the vertebra. Rav treated that as obviously worse than his own ruling — indeed, as a *neveilah*.

The Gemara then reconciles this with Ben Zakkai's and Rabbi Yochanan's positions, which had seemed to require a majority even for uprooted ribs. The key distinction is *buchna v'asita* — ball and socket. When the earlier Sages discussed uprooted ribs requiring a majority, that was ribs uprooted without any portion of the socket — the joint structure that anchors the rib to the vertebra. When Rav Kahana and Rav Assi asked about opposing ribs that also carried the socket, that is qualitatively different and constitutes *gistera*.

Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that even for uprooted ribs one needs twelve poses an apparent challenge: if you require twelve ribs from both sides, at least some opposing pairs are inevitable — either six-and-six or eleven-and-one. If any two opposing ribs together amount to *gistera*, how could Rabbi Yochanan require a majority? The answer: Rabbi Yochanan spoke of ribs uprooted without the socket — *buchna belo asita*. Only when the socket is removed with the rib does the opposing-pair case become *gistera*.

### Inquiry Strategy Debate

A final question remains: if Rav Kahana and Rav Assi had not heard Rav's ruling about one rib with half a vertebra, why did they ask about two opposing ribs rather than starting with one rib — the simpler, foundational case?

The Gemara explains their reasoning: they believed that asking about two would yield both answers simultaneously. If Rav said two opposing ribs (with the socket) are permitted, they would know by inference that one rib is certainly permitted. If he said it is forbidden, the tone of his response would tell them whether one rib is similarly forbidden or only two. The logic is that if he answers with outrage — "Two? Of course two is forbidden!" — one can infer that even one is forbidden. If he answers straightforwardly, one can infer that the single case is permitted.

Indeed, Rav did respond with what amounted to exasperation: *gistera ka ramitu* — "You're asking about a *gistera*?" — and the Gemara confirms: *hainu rathichei* — that very tone of agitation was the signal they anticipated, from which they could infer that even the single-rib case was a *treifah*.

---

## Amoraic Treifot

### Shmuel's Three Treifot

The Gemara now records three *treifot* transmitted by Rabba bar bar Shila in the name of Rav Matna in the name of Shmuel. These belong to the corpus of Amoraic *treifot* that supplement the *mishnah*'s list. The three are: *ne'ekra tzela me'ikara* — a rib fully uprooted from its base; *gulgoles shenichbesa beruba* — a skull bashed in over the majority of its surface (without necessarily cracking through); and *basar hofe et rov hakeres beruba* — the abdominal muscle covering the majority of the *keres* (the rumen), if the majority of that muscle is torn.

### Rib vs. Vertebra

The Gemara immediately raises a challenge to the first item — one uprooted rib as a *treifah* — from a *baraita* concerning *tumah* in an *ohel*. How much of the spinal column must be missing for a human skeleton to lose its status as a complete skeleton (and therefore no longer convey *tum'at ohel*)? Beit Shammai: two vertebrae. Beit Hillel: one vertebra. Shmuel himself is reported to have taught that the same threshold applies to *treifah* in an animal: whatever level of skeletal incompleteness prevents the skeleton from conveying *tumah* also means an animal cannot survive — and is thus a *treifah*. That ruling is about vertebrae, not ribs. How then does Shmuel add "one uprooted rib" to the list?

The Gemara resolves this cleanly: the two rulings address different cases. *Hacha tzela belo hulya* — here we speak of a rib without a vertebra: a rib uprooted from its joint, carrying no portion of the vertebra. *Hatam hulya belo tzela* — there we speak of a vertebra without a rib: a vertebra removed from a location where there is no rib attached (as in the lower portion of the spinal column). Either alone renders the animal a *treifah*. Two new additions to the list thus emerge: an uprooted rib (without the vertebra), and a removed vertebra (without a rib).

Rashi reads *ne'ekra tzela me'ikara* as meaning a rib with no part of the vertebra — but this conflicts with what was established on 52a, where even half a vertebra sufficed for Rav's ruling. Tosafot therefore reads the phrase as meaning a rib with *part* of the vertebra, not the full vertebra.

The Gemara also notes: it is straightforward to imagine a rib uprooted without taking the vertebra entirely; but how does one remove a vertebra without the rib coming with it? The answer is that in areas of the spine where no ribs are attached — the floating vertebrae lower in the spinal column — a vertebra can indeed be removed without any rib.

### Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

An objection is raised by Rav Hoshaya: given that Shmuel's teaching about vertebrae and *treifah* derives from the *tumah* debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, why is this not listed among the well-known cases of *kulei Beit Shammai* and *chumrei Beit Hillel* — the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel? In the context of *tumah*, Beit Shammai is *machmir* (two vertebrae must be removed before the skeleton loses its status) and Beit Hillel is *meikel* (one suffices). But if we apply the same logic to *treifah*, the positions reverse: Beit Hillel becomes *machmir* (one vertebra already renders the animal a *treifah*) and Beit Shammai becomes *meikel* (two must be removed). This would be a case of Beit Hillel being strict — a reversal of the usual pattern.

Rava responds: the original debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel was framed entirely in the context of *tumah* — specifically, the *tum'at ohel* of a human skeleton. In that framing, Beit Shammai is indeed stringent and Beit Hillel lenient. Shmuel then extrapolated the same principle to *treifah*, at which point the positions with respect to stringency and leniency swap. But the debate itself was not framed as a *treifah* debate, and therefore it does not appear in the canonical lists of *kulei* and *chumrei*. This, incidentally, is the classic model of a ruling that is consistent in its internal logic even as it appears to produce reversed stringency across two domains.

### Skull Height or Circumfe…

The second item on Shmuel's list — *gulgoles shenichbesa beruba*, the skull bashed in over its majority — prompts a question from Rami bar Ami: when we say "majority," do we measure *rov govha* — the majority of the skull's height — or *rov heikeifa* — the majority of its circumference? Rashi notes that the circumference is larger than the height; the two measures therefore yield meaningfully different thresholds. Rashi locates the midpoint of the height at approximately the level of the eyes — a consideration familiar from the anatomy of the face, where the eyes fall at the midpoint of the skull's vertical dimension. The Gemara offers no resolution: *teiku*.

### Abdominal Muscle Torn

The third item — the abdominal muscle covering the majority of the *keres* — prompts a parallel question from Rav Ashi: does *beruba* mean the majority of the muscle is *torn* (*rov karua*), or the majority is *removed* (*rov natul*)? The latter would be a far more expansive standard.

The Gemara attempts to resolve this from the *mishnah*, which speaks of the outer *keres* being torn over its majority. A tradition from Eretz Yisrael in the name of Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina identifies the entire stomach as the *keres hapnimis* — the inner stomach — and the *keres hachitzona* as the abdominal muscle itself. If that reading is correct, the *mishnah* already addresses this case, and "majority" there clearly means *torn*, not *removed*.

However, Shmuel himself explains the outer *keres* differently: it refers to the part of the stomach wall where the felt-like inner lining ends. On Shmuel's own reading, the abdominal muscle is not mentioned in the *mishnah* at all — it is a genuinely new *treifah* he is introducing. If it is a new category, the *mishnah*'s language about "torn" cannot resolve the question of what "majority" means for this muscle. The question remains unresolved.

---

## Animal Attack Treifot

### Rav Yehuda: Wolf & Netz

The *mishnah* turns to *derusah* — the damage caused by an animal attack. The Gemara understands the concern here to involve not simply the physical wound but something transmitted through the attack — perhaps a venom-like substance, or more plausibly some form of infection introduced through violence to the body. It is worth noting that the later *mishnah* will establish that poison alone, without bodily assault, does not render an animal a *treifah*; what is at issue here is a combination of attack and toxic consequence.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav establishes: for large animals (*behemah*), the attacker must be a wolf or larger to create a *treifah* concern. For birds, it must be a *netz* — a sparrow hawk — or larger.

### R. Yehuda: Lion vs. Wolf

The Gemara asks what novel ruling this adds, since the *mishnah* already establishes that a wolf is the relevant attacker. One suggestion: perhaps Rav Yehuda is teaching that a wolf is sufficient for *all* large animals, including oxen — one might have thought a wolf's attack on a large bovine would be inconsequential. But this suggestion is challenged by Rabbi Yehuda's position in the *mishnah* itself: *drusas haze'ev bedaka* — a wolf is only the threshold for small animals like sheep and goats; for large animals, one requires a lion (*ari*).

A tannaitic tradition from Rabbi Binyamin bar Yafes in the name of Rabbi Ila holds that Rabbi Yehuda was not disputing the *Tanna Kamma* but merely clarifying: the *Tanna Kamma*'s wolf applies only to small animals, and Rabbi Yehuda is specifying what is required for large ones. If that is so, Rav Yehuda's ruling simply aligns with that clarification — stating explicitly that a wolf suffices for all animals, *against* Rabbi Yehuda's position.

The Gemara offers a second resolution: Rav Yehuda's ruling excludes not a large animal from the wolf's reach, but a *cat* from below the wolf. The *mishnah* mentions a wolf — perhaps because wolves were the typical attacker of sheep, one might generalize that any large predator capable of injuring sheep would suffice. Rav Yehuda teaches that the threshold is specifically the wolf, no smaller.

### Rav Chisda: Cat & Weasel

Rav Amram in the name of Rav Chisda adds further detail: an attack by a *chatul* (cat) or *nemiyah* (weasel or marten) on *kivshim u'gedayim* — young lambs or kid goats — does constitute a *derusah* concern. The relevant variable is not only the species of attacker but the size of the prey. Against the adult versions of these animals, a cat or weasel would not suffice; but against their young, these smaller predators can inflict the kind of attack that creates the *treifah* concern. Similarly, an attack by a *chuldah* (weasel) against birds is sufficient.

### Baraita: Organ Piercing

A *baraita* is cited that appears to contradict this: *drusas chatul netz u'nemiyah* — attacks by a cat, *netz*, or *nemiyah* — are not a concern for *derusah* unless they also pierce an inner organ (*tinakev l'chalal*). The attack alone, without such piercing, does not render the animal forbidden. The *baraita* seems to say explicitly that these animals do not create *derusah*.

The Gemara notes one apparent internal problem: the *mishnah* includes the *netz* among those that do create *derusah* by birds, yet the *baraita* places the *netz* in the list of animals that do not.
