This is resolved cleanly: the *mishnah* addresses the *netz* attacking birds; the *baraita* addresses the *netz* — and cat and *nemiyah* — attacking other animals. But the ruling of Rav Chisda remains in tension with the *baraita*, since Rav Chisda says cats and weasels do create *derusah* against young goats and lambs, while the *baraita* says they do not.

### Birebbi: Rescue Factor

The Gemara resolves this by citing a *tanna* known as *Birebbi*, who offers a principle that reframes the entire discussion. *Lo amru ein drusa ela b'makom she'ein matzilim* — the ruling that these animals do not create *derusah* applies only in a situation where there is no prospect of rescue intervention. When a cat, weasel, or similar predator attacks and is not afraid that anyone will intervene to save its prey, it attacks in a relatively measured, controlled way — and that kind of attack does not produce the *drusa* effect that creates a *treifah*.

*Aval b'makom she'yesh matzilim* — but where there is prospect of intervention, the predator attacks more urgently and viciously, knowing it may be deprived of its prey. In that case, *yesh drusa* — there is *derusah*. The violence of the attack, and whatever toxic or infectious consequence flows from it, is directly proportional to the threat perceived by the attacker.

This distinction elegantly reconciles Rav Chisda with the *baraita*. When Rav Chisda says cats and weasels create *derusah* against young goats and lambs, he speaks of a domestic or farm setting — precisely the context where human rescue is likely, prompting a more ferocious attack. The *baraita*'s ruling that they do not create *derusah* applies to an open field or unguarded setting, where no rescuer is anticipated and the attack is less severe.

The Gemara breaks off at this point, with the full elaboration of this principle to be taken up in the following session.

---

---

# Hullin 53

## Derusah Mechanism

### Derusah Principle

The daf begins five lines from the bottom of 52b, at the words *bemakom she-ein matzilin ein derusah* — "where there is no one to intervene, there is no *derusah*." The background to this passage is the discussion introduced on the previous daf: smaller animals such as a cat or weasel can render a victim *treif* through an act of *derusah*, which involves attacking a smaller animal in a manner that injects poison and thereby condemns the prey. The Mishnah had spoken of a wolf as the paradigmatic predator, but the Gemara extended this concern to smaller predators attacking proportionally smaller prey — young sheep, young goats, and the like. A *brayta* had complicated this picture by appearing to deny *derusah* to these smaller animals altogether. The resolution offered was that these animals attack viciously, injecting their poison, specifically when they fear that their prey will be saved by intervention. When no such intervention is anticipated, they do not inject their poison with the same force.

### Chicken & Cat Case

The Gemara now challenges this resolution with a case from the house of Rav Kahana. A cat was chasing a chicken, which fled into an interior chamber — the word *indara*, an uncommon Aramaic term, is helpfully glossed by the marginal note with a reference to the Targum on the verse where Yosef withdraws to an inner room. The door was slammed shut in the cat's face, leaving it alone with the chicken. The cat then struck the door with its claws, and five drops of blood were found on the door — apparently one per claw — indicating that poison had been injected. But if the entire concern is about the fear of intervention, and here the cat was utterly alone with its prey in a sealed room, why would it have injected its poison?

The Gemara answers: *hatzalat atzmah nami ke-hatzalat acharina dami* — the chicken's potential escape from its own predicament is treated like a rescue by an external party. The cat knew that people were pursuing it, and that it had been chased into the room precisely because of human intervention. It was therefore in a heightened state of agitation and acting vicious even within the sealed chamber.

### Tanna Kamma vs Rebbi

The Gemara then records a second version of this entire discussion — *ika de-amri*, some say — in which the positions of *tanna kamma* and Rebbi are reversed. In the first version, the view that small animals *do* cause *derusah* under certain conditions was attributed to Rebbi, while *tanna kamma* denied it. In the second version, it is *tanna kamma* who holds that small animals always cause *derusah*, and Rebbi who restricts the concern to cases where the predator fears intervention. The substantive ruling is identical; only the attribution changes.

The same story of the cat and chicken in Rav Kahana's house is then recruited to challenge Rebbi's position in this second version — if Rebbi says there is no *derusah* when there is no one to intervene, how do we explain the five drops of blood? The Gemara gives the same answer: the cat's self-protective agitation constitutes a form of concern equivalent to fear of external intervention.

The Gemara also addresses the view of the Sages who deny *derusah* entirely to these smaller animals, even in light of the physical evidence of blood. Their response is *zei'ah ra'itah ve-lo kali zikei* — what was observed was not genuine poison but merely a form of excretion; the small animal's venom does not burn with sufficient intensity to cause the kind of damage that would render an animal *treif*.

---

## Rav Kahana Questions

### Cat & Weasel Debate

The Gemara now transitions to the top of 53a, where Rav Kahana posed a series of questions to Rav. He asked: is there *derusah* for a cat, or is there no *derusah* for a cat? Rav replied cryptically: even a weasel, which is smaller, causes *derusah* — implying that the cat question is trivially obvious. Rav Kahana then asked: is there *derusah* for a weasel? Rav replied: there is not even *derusah* for a cat — implying the opposite, that the question is equally trivial but in the other direction. Finally Rav Kahana combined the questions: do a cat and weasel have *derusah* or not? Rav answered: for a cat yes, for a weasel no.

### Rav's Answers

The apparent contradiction resolves once the Gemara introduces a third variable — the nature of the prey. When Rav said that even a weasel causes *derusah*, he was speaking of birds (*b'ofot*), against which even the smaller weasel is effective. When he said that even a cat does not cause *derusah*, he was speaking of large sheep (*b'imrei ravrevei*), against which neither animal is effective. When he split his ruling — cat yes, weasel no — he was addressing an intermediate category: young goats and young lambs (*bi-g'dayim u-t'layim*). Tosafot elaborates on why Rav chose to answer cryptically, effectively encoding all three cases within three sequential responses. The key principle is that *derusah* depends not only on which predator is attacking but also on what it is attacking. The size of the prey is as determinative as the species and capacity of the predator.

---

## Birds of Prey

### Non-Kosher Birds

Rav Ashi asked a further question: what about other non-kosher birds — birds of prey other than those explicitly mentioned in the Mishnah? The Mishnah had mentioned the *netz* (sparrowhawk) and the *gas* (buzzard). Do other predatory birds also cause *derusah* when they attack smaller birds? Rav Hillel responded in the name of Rav Kahana: yes, other non-kosher birds of prey do cause *derusah*. One might object from the Mishnah's specific language, which singles out the sparrowhawk — but just as in the parallel case of the wolf, the Mishnah's specificity serves not to exclude other capable predators but to convey something particular about the species mentioned, while larger predators are certainly included.

### Sparrowhawk Superior

The Gemara then explains the precise significance of the Mishnah's mention of the sparrowhawk. According to the first version (*ika de-amri*): the sparrowhawk causes *derusah* even in birds of comparable size (*bidekhvateih*), while other birds of prey cause *derusah* only in birds smaller than themselves. According to the second version: the sparrowhawk causes *derusah* even in birds larger than itself (*bidarabi mineih*), while other birds of prey cause *derusah* only in birds of comparable size. In both versions the sparrowhawk is distinguished as the more formidable attacker; the question is whether its superior capacity extends to equal-sized prey or to prey larger than itself.

---

## Fox Derusah

### Fox No Derusah

Rav Kahana then transmitted in the name of Rav Shimi bar Ashi: there is no *derusah* for a fox. This is striking. We have just established that a cat and weasel — smaller animals — can cause *derusah* against appropriately sized prey. A fox is a larger and more powerful animal. The basis for the distinction, as will become clearer, is that *derusah* is about clawing and the injection of poison through the claw, and the relevant animals are those whose claws carry this poison. A fox, despite its capacity to cause serious injury through biting, may not share this particular mechanism.

### Bathhouse Story

The ruling is immediately challenged. When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael he reported: there was a story of a fox and a ewe in a bathhouse of Beit Heini — *ma'aseh be-shual ve-rachel be-mirkhatz shel Beit Heini* — and the case came before the Sages, who ruled that there is a problem of *derusah*. This appears to directly contradict the position that a fox cannot cause *derusah*.

The Gemara then presents a competing version of both the ruling and the story. According to the first version, Rav Kahana had said there is *no* *derusah* for a fox, and the bathhouse ruling had confirmed *derusah*. According to the second version (*ika de-amri*), Rav Ashi had actually said there *is* *derusah* for a fox, and the bathhouse story had ruled that there is *no* *derusah*. Both the transmitted ruling and the story are each reported in contradictory forms.

### Fox vs Cat

In each version, Rav Safra offers a resolution by identifying the animal in the bathhouse story not as the species assumed. In the first version — where it was ruled that *derusah* applies and this contradicts the denial of fox *derusah* — Rav Safra says: that bathhouse animal was not a fox but a cat. In the second version — where *derusah* was denied despite Rav Ashi holding that fox *derusah* applies — Rav Safra says: that animal was not a fox but a dog (*kalba*). This last identification points ahead to the next major topic: dogs do not cause *derusah* because *derusah* is specifically about clawing, not biting, and dogs lack the relevant claws. The canine family — foxes and wolves among them — presents the interesting puzzle that the Mishnah treats the wolf as the paradigmatic *derusah* predator, yet the fox is contested. Both, in zoological terms, are canines. The resolution must lie in the specific mechanism of poison injection through the claw.

---

## Nature of Derusah

### Foreleg Claws

Rav Yosef states as an operating principle: *ein derusah le-chelev* — dogs do not cause *derusah*. Abaye then articulates the structural logic underlying all of the preceding discussions: *ein derusah ela beyad* — *derusah* is only through the foreleg, not the hind leg; and *ein derusah ela be-tziporen* — only through the claw, not through the teeth (*la'apukei shen dlo*). This is why dogs are excluded: despite their capacity for serious injury, dogs do not attack primarily through retractable claws that inject poison, and so the mechanism of *derusah* does not apply to them.

One might have thought teeth would be more dangerous from the standpoint of poison injection — after all, snakes inject venom through their bite. But the Gemara's assumption is that the specific poison of these predatory animals is delivered through the claw. This is why the concern is limited to the foreleg (where retractable claws are located), to the claw itself, and to certain species identified as carrying this poison: cats, weasels, wolves, and certain birds of prey.

It is worth noting that if a dog bite or any other attack caused a wound that in turn raised concern about perforation of an internal organ, that would be a separate *treif* problem — not *derusah* but a question of *nekuva* or *drusah* in a different sense. The *derusah* discussed here is specifically the concern about clawing and poison injection.

### Intent & Withdrawal

The Gemara continues to define precisely when *derusah* applies. *ein derusah ela mida'at* — *derusah* requires that the animal consciously and intentionally attack with its claw (*la'apukei shelo mida'at dlo*). If the claws were extended and the animal accidentally made contact with another animal, no poison would be transmitted. *ein derusah ela mi-chayyim* — *derusah* requires that the attacking animal be alive at the time of the attack, not that a dead animal with extended claws fell upon another.

The Gemara notes that the ruling about death seems superfluous: if we already know that the animal must be acting intentionally, a dead animal obviously cannot act intentionally, and so the case of the dead animal would already be excluded. The Gemara therefore clarifies that the case being addressed is where the animal clawed another, and then its foreleg was severed. The animal itself is still alive, but the severed limb is functionally dead. One might have thought that the poison was injected in the act of clawing and so would have been transferred during the clawing motion itself. The Gemara teaches: *be-hide de-shalif shadi zeharei* — the poison is deposited not as the claw enters but as it is *withdrawn*. Since the severed limb cannot be withdrawn in a living, intentional way, no poison is injected, and there is no *derusah*.

---

## Lion Among Oxen

### Detached Nail

Rabbah bar Avuna citing Rav presents the following scenario: a lion entered among oxen, and afterward a claw (*tziporen*) was found embedded in the back of one of them. Should we be concerned that the lion attacked that ox, rendering it *treif* through *derusah*?

The Gemara rules: we are not concerned. Two reasons are offered. First, *rov arayos dorsin u-mi'utan ein dorsin* — Tosafot explains this not as a claim that most lions actually attack at any given moment, but that most lions have the capacity to cause *derusah*, while a minority are not vicious or capable in this way. The mere presence of a lion does not establish that this particular lion attacked. Second, *ve-chol ha-dores ein tziporen nishmemet* — any animal that actually claws another does not leave its claw behind in the process. The very evidence being offered — a claw in the ox's back — counts against the hypothesis of clawing, because clawing does not produce detached claws.

### Wall Rubbing

The Gemara then introduces an alternative explanation for how the claw came to be embedded in the ox: *eimar be-kosel nis-chatech* — perhaps the lion was scratching itself against a wall, and in the process its claw became detached and fell. This detached claw then somehow came to be lodged in the ox's back. The argument is that lions do sometimes shed claws in this way, and the claw's presence in the ox does not require the hypothesis of attack.

### Resolve Nail

The Gemara then reverses course and argues the other direction: *adarabba* — in fact, one could argue from the same evidence that the ox *was* attacked. The counter-argument runs as follows. *rov shvarim mis-chatchin u-mi'utan ein mis-chatchin* — most oxen do rub their backs against walls, but not all. And even those that do, *ein tziporen yosheves lo be-gavlo* — rubbing against a wall does not result in a claw becoming embedded in the ox's back. Similarly, clawing an animal does not result in the claw being left behind. Neither mechanism produces the observed evidence cleanly, yet the ox does have a claw in its back. So one could argue from this that the lion must have attacked.

The Gemara concludes: *ika le-meimar hachi ve-ika le-meimar hachi* — arguments can be made in both directions. When evidence admits of competing interpretations, the principle is *okmei milta a-chazakah* — we maintain the animal in its presumptive status. The animal has a *chazakah* of fitness; this is a case of *safek derusah*, and Rav holds *ein chosheshin le-safek derusah* — in doubtful cases we rely on the *chazakah* of fitness and do not declare the animal *treif*.

This raises a broader question about the Gemara's overall approach: in many cases concerning *treifot*, the Gemara appears extremely stringent, refusing to permit reliance on a membrane covering a hole or other mitigating factors. Yet here it is lenient based on *chazakah*. These approaches are not contradictory. Where a problem is established — a hole is known to exist — the Gemara does not easily permit the assumption that it has been resolved by other means. But where the question is whether a problem ever arose in the first place, the Gemara consistently permits reliance on *chazakah* to conclude that it did not. The strictness is reserved for cases where an issue is known; the leniency operates before a problem has been formally established. There is also a further question about the nature of *chazakah* here — whether it describes a physical state (the animal began its life without being attacked) or a halachic state (the animal began its life as forbidden). The Gemara is clear that once the animal has been properly slaughtered, it carries a *chezkat hetter*.

The Gemara then introduces a qualification in the name of Bivi: *lo amru ela tziporen* — the leniency where we find a detached claw applies specifically when the claw is found protruding. But *mekom tziporen* — if one finds a hole clearly shaped by a claw, one is obviously concerned. Furthermore, even a protruding claw is only dismissed if it is moist (*lacha*); a dried claw (*yevesha*) might have been naturally shed. And even a moist claw: if only one is found, it is dismissed, but two or three claws found together (*tarti ve-tlat*), especially if they are arranged in the pattern of claws on a paw (*de-kaymi be-dardei de-chuchpa*), constitute clear evidence of having been attacked.

---

## Safek Derusah

### Rav Chazakah

The Gemara now presents the formal dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding *safek derusah* in general. Rav says: *ein chosheshin le-safek derusah* — in doubtful cases of *derusah*, we are not concerned; we rely on the *chazakah* of the animal's fitness. The practical implication is that unless there is clear evidence of an attack, the animal is presumed undamaged.

### Shmuel Concern

Shmuel says: *chosheshin le-safek derusah* — we are concerned even in cases of doubtful *derusah*. Once there is sufficient basis to raise the doubt, the *chazakah* of fitness does not override it.

### Limit Debate

The Gemara works to define the precise boundaries of this dispute. Certain cases are excluded from the debate because they do not rise to the level of a genuine *safek*. If it is unknown whether the predator even entered the herd, *de-kulei alma safek al safek lo al* — everyone agrees that a doubt compounded upon a doubt does not require concern. This is understood through the concept of *leidat ha-safek* — the formal "presentation" of a doubt that obliges us to address it. A doubt that is too remote — we do not know if the lion entered, and even if it did we do not know if it attacked — is not a sufficiently concrete *safek* to trigger halachic concern. Similarly, if it is unknown whether the animal in question was a dog or a cat, and it is only a cat that causes *derusah*, then since we do not even know there was a cat present, the doubt has not formally presented itself.

The Gemara then adds a case with more contextual texture: the predator entered among the sheep and simply sat there (*aylei ve-yativi beineihu*) — perhaps, as Rashi notes, they had been domesticated to coexist, or perhaps, in a striking image, the lion lay down with the lamb. That alone does not create concern. Even if the lion decapitated one animal — which is certainly a *neveilah* — Shmuel would not require concern about the remaining animals merely because a violent lion was present. The case that does generate the debate is more specific.

---

## Lion & Sheep

### No Attack

The cases examined so far — the lion merely present, the lion making noise, the lion that decapitated one animal — do not reach the threshold that even Shmuel would consider a *safek*. The Gemara considers the scenario of a lion that has actively roared and the sheep that have responded with distressed sounds, and rules: *meva'atei ahadadei* — they are frightening each other; the sounds indicate mutual fear, not necessarily an actual attack. None of these scenarios suffice to trigger Shmuel's concern.

### Silent Lion

The case that divides Rav and Shmuel is identified at the top of 53b: *de-ihu ka shatik ve-inhu ka mekarkeran* — the lion is silent while the sheep are bleating. The dispute is in the interpretation of the sheep's cries. One authority holds *maisa ka'avid* — the lion is clearly doing something to them; the silence of the lion combined with the distress of the sheep indicates active attack. The other holds *be-machmat bi'uta hu de-ka'avid* — the sheep are bleating from sheer terror at the lion's presence, not because they are being attacked. It is this specific, nuanced circumstance — a silent predator and distressed prey — that constitutes the case where Rav and Shmuel disagree about whether to apply the *chazakah* of fitness.

---

## Practical Ruling

### Amemar Rules

Amemar rules: *hilchata kavatei de-choshishin le-safek derusah* — the *halacha* follows Shmuel's position, and in cases that present a sufficient basis for doubt (of the kind delineated above), we are concerned about *safek derusah* and do not simply rely on *chezkat hetter*.

### Ashi Questions

Rav Ashi challenged Amemar: what about Rav's opposing position that we do not worry about *safek derusah* and do rely on *chazakah*? How can one simply rule against Rav without addressing his view?

### Amemar Response

Amemar replied: *lo shmia li* — I have not heard of Rav's position. The Gemara immediately glosses this: *k'lomar, lo sevira li* — "I have not heard it" is a way of saying "I do not find it persuasive." The idiom is that of a student who is technically aware of the teaching but simply declines to give it weight. Amemar is not claiming ignorance; he is registering disagreement.

---

## Rav Reversal

### Basket Birds

The Gemara raises the possibility that Rav himself reversed his position: *hadar bei Rav legabei Shmuel* — Rav ultimately came around to agree with Shmuel. The evidence offered is that a certain basket (*sharkafa*) — Rashi explains this as a basket of birds — that presented a question of *safek derusah* was brought before Rav, and Rav sent it to Shmuel. The argument is: if Rav still held that *safek derusah* is not a concern, why would he send it to Shmuel, who was his disputant on precisely this question?

### Shmuel Action

Shmuel received the basket and acted decisively: he strangled the birds and threw them into the river — *chankinhu ve-shadinhu be-nahara*. As noted elsewhere in the Gemara, a *posek* who rules that an animal is forbidden and physically feeds it to dogs thereby takes responsibility for the financial loss. Shmuel's act of strangling and discarding the birds effectively constituted such an act, and he did so in keeping with his consistent ruling that *safek derusah* is a genuine concern.

The Gemara then challenges the inference that Rav reversed himself: *aval mah hadar bei* — even if he did reverse himself, why send it to Shmuel? If Rav now holds it is forbidden, he should simply rule it forbidden himself. The Gemara responds: *asrei de-Shmuel hava* — it was in Shmuel's locale, his city. Rashi presents two readings of this answer. In the first, the answer simply deflects the proof: because it was Shmuel's city, Rav sent the question to him out of deference to the *rav ha-makom*, and we therefore cannot infer anything about Rav's own ruling. In the second — which Rashi presents as more striking — the deference to the local authority does not override the financial interests of the questioner, and therefore if Rav had genuinely held the birds were permitted, he would have ruled so even in Shmuel's city to save the person from a loss. The fact that he sent it rather than ruling leniently shows that he had reversed himself. Rashi ultimately favors the *p'shat* that we cannot determine whether Rav reversed himself; the sending of the basket is explained by the fact that it was Shmuel's locale.

### Publicity

The Gemara then asks why Shmuel specifically strangled the birds and threw them into the river, rather than using simpler methods. Could he not simply have thrown them into the river without strangling? The birds would have flown away and been eaten by unknowing individuals. Could he not have waited and sold them to non-Jews? The concern there is *asi lizvinehu le-Yisroel* — the non-Jews might resell them to Jews who would not know of the problem. Could he not simply have thrown them in the garbage or fed them to dogs? The Gemara's answer: *ela le-farsumei milsa d'isura* — Shmuel wanted to publicize the seriousness of the prohibition. As Rashi explains, *derusah* is not always easy to detect, and Shmuel's dramatic action was a one-time measure designed to make clear to everyone that this category of doubt is genuine and serious. It is not presented as a general policy recommendation.

### Twelve Month Test

The Gemara raises the question of why Shmuel did not simply observe whether the birds lived for twelve months. The principle is that any animal that is genuinely *treif* will not survive a full year; if an animal of *safek* status lives out twelve months, this demonstrates retroactively that it was not *treif*.

### Why Not Wait

The answer is *asi behu lidei takala* — holding a basket of birds for twelve months would lead to others stumbling, as someone would inevitably eat one before the year was out. The twelve-month test, while theoretically available, was not practically viable in this case given the number of birds and the difficulty of maintaining control over them for so long.

---

## Goose Case

### Goose Incident

A goose belonging to the household of Rav Ashi went into the reeds (*al beini kanya*) and returned with a bloody neck (*nafak ata ki mimasmas kovei d'may*). The question arose: was the neck injured by a cat lurking among the reeds, which would create a concern of *derusah*, or was it cut by the sharp reeds themselves?

### Reeds Injury

Rav Ashi resolved the case: *lo amran safek chavsa ve-shunra eimar chavsa* — in a case where one does not know whether the culprit was a dog or a cat, even Shmuel would agree that the doubt has not formally presented itself, because we have no established evidence of a cat being present. Similarly here: *safek kanya safek shunra* — it is uncertain whether the wound was caused by the reeds or by a cat among the reeds. *eimar kanya amchayei* — it is reasonable to conclude that it was the sharp reeds that struck the neck. The doubt therefore does not reach the threshold of a *safek* requiring concern, even according to Shmuel's more stringent position.

---

## Inspection Methods

### Check Organs

The sons of Rabbi Chiya taught: *derusah she'amru tzricha bedikah keneged bnei me'ayim* — the *derusah* referred to by the Sages requires inspection opposite the area of the inner digestive organs. If an animal was attacked by a predator, one checks whether the outer skin opposite the stomach and intestinal area has turned red. Rashi explains the mechanism: the concern with *derusah* is that the poison injected through the claw is acidic in nature and will eat its way through to the inner organs, creating a hole. The relevant location to inspect is therefore the skin opposite those organs, since that is where the damage will manifest. If, upon inspection, that area shows no redness, the animal is not condemned. The language of the teaching — *tzricha bedikah*, "requires inspection" — sounds like a demand rather than a leniency, but both Rashi and Tosafot read it as providing a mechanism to *permit* the animal: even in a case of known *derusah* or *safek derusah*, a clean inspection can establish fitness.

### Shmuel Method

Rav Yosef notes that this teaching of the sons of Rabbi Chiya had already been articulated by Shmuel: *d'amar Shmuel mishum Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos, derusah she'amru tzricha bedikah keneged bnei me'ayim* — in the name of Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos, Shmuel had taught the identical rule about inspecting opposite the digestive organs.

### Neck Area

Ilfa raised two distinct questions. First: *yesh derusah la-simanim o ein derusah la-simanim?* — is there *derusah* when the attack was at the neck, in the area of the *simanim* (trachea and esophagus), rather than the abdominal area? Rabbi Zeira replied that this had already been answered by Rav Chanan bar Rava in the name of Rav: the inspection must cover not just the area opposite the digestive organs but *keneged beit ha-chalal kulo* — the entire body cavity, including, by implication, the area of the *simanim*.

Ilfa's second question is formally separate but is presented in the same context: *simanim she-nidaldelu be-ruban mahu* — when the *simanim* have been uprooted from their proper position in the flesh of the neck for the majority of their length, what is the ruling? Rabbi Zeira replied that Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Shmuel had already addressed this: if the *simanim* are uprooted (*nidaldelu*) from their proper place for the majority of their length, it is a disqualifying condition.

---

## Reddened vs Rot

### Bloody Flesh

Rabbi Ami raised a question about flesh that is *martema* — somewhat bloody or reddened in appearance. In the context of evaluating *derusah*, when one inspects the area opposite the inner organs, what is the significance of flesh that appears bloody or discolored? Rabbi Zeira replied that this too had already been explained — the Gemara here continues the pattern of *kvar pirshah*, "this was already explained."

### Reddened Evidence

The explanation comes from Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *bi-drusah, ad she-ya'adim basar keneged bnei me'ayim* — in a case of *derusah*, the determining evidence is that the flesh opposite the inner organs has actually turned red (*ya'adim*). Redness of the skin in this location is the indicator that poison has penetrated and is working its way toward the inner organs. Rashi explains that the redness signals that the acidic poison has reached that level of the body wall, and from there it will continue to the organs. This is what makes *derusah* dangerous and what the inspection is designed to detect.

### Rotting Treatment

A separate but related question concerns flesh that has *nitmasmeis* — that has decomposed, become putrid, or is dissolving. The rule is: *ha-basar ro'enu k'ilu einu* — such flesh is treated as if it were not present, as if it had been removed. The inquiry then shifts from *derusah* specifically to a general question about *treifot*: if that flesh were removed entirely, would the animal be *treif* or not? *derusah* operates through the mechanism of poison penetration, so evidence of redness in a particular location of the outer wall indicates ongoing danger to the inner organs. Rotting flesh operates differently: one simply assesses whether the animal, absent that flesh, would be *treif* based on the standard criteria for the affected area.

---

## Rotting Definition

### Medical Removal

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua defines rotting flesh precisely: *kol she-rofe godro u-ma'amido al basar chai* — any flesh that a physician would surgically excise in order to expose and treat the healthy tissue beneath. Flesh in this condition has the halachic status of removed flesh, and the animal is evaluated as though that flesh had been cut away.

### Lung Example

Rav Ashi reported that while he was in the house of Rav Kahana, a lung was brought before them. When placed on a table it appeared normal, but when lifted, it would crumble and fall apart in pieces. Rav Kahana ruled it *treif* (*ve-tarfina lah*) on the basis of Rav Huna's principle. A lung with a hole is *treif*; this lung's tissue was so decomposed that it would disintegrate upon handling, meaning the substance of the lung was functionally absent in those areas. Since the rotting tissue is treated as if removed, the lung is evaluated as having openings — and a lung with openings is not fit.

---

## Derusah vs Puncture

### Thorn Perforate

Rav Nachman articulates a crucial distinction: *be-kotz, ad she-tenakev le-chalal* — if a thorn or needle pierced the animal's body wall, it is only a concern if it penetrated all the way through the abdominal wall into the inner cavity. A thorn merely embedded in the outer flesh, without reaching the cavity, is not a problem. The rationale is straightforward: a thorn is simply a sharp object causing mechanical injury, and the danger is only if it actually reaches the inner organs.

### Claw Reddening

The case of *derusah* is categorically different: *bi-drusah, mishe-ta'adim basar keneged bnei me'ayim* — if the skin opposite the inner organs has turned red, that is sufficient evidence of a problem, even if the claw did not physically penetrate all the way through the body wall. The claw's poison, injected into the tissue upon withdrawal, is not a purely mechanical injury. The redness indicates that the poison is actively working through the tissue, and the assumption is that it will continue through to the organs. Thus the evidentiary threshold for *derusah* is lower than for a thorn: redness suffices, while full perforation is not required.

### Simanim Exception

Rav Zavid teaches a qualification regarding the *simanim*. In the case of *derusah* to the body generally, redness of the outer skin opposite the inner organs is the evidentiary standard. But when the concern involves the *simanim* specifically — the trachea and esophagus in the neck — the *simanim* themselves must turn red (*ad she-ta'adimu simanim atzamam*). The outer skin of the neck alone turning red is insufficient; one needs to see the redness in the *simanim* themselves. The reasoning is that these structures are more robust and are not as immediately affected by the poison spreading from the outer layers. Throughout all of this, the question persists — noted by both Rashi and Tosafot — whether the inspection method applies only to *safek derusah*, as a way to determine whether an attack actually occurred, or whether it applies equally to a *vaday derusah*, as a means of establishing that despite the confirmed attack, the poison has not reached the critical organs and the animal remains fit.

---

# Hullin 54

## Derusa & Inspection

### Derusa Overview

The daf opens at the very bottom of 53b, in the midst of the *gemara*'s treatment of *derusa* — the notion that certain animals inject a harmful substance through their claws, rendering the prey a *treifa*. The *gemara*'s underlying assumption, that this clawing mechanism transmits something lethal through the wound site, does not correspond to modern zoological knowledge; indeed, only the platypus possesses a genuinely venomous claw, and even that is confined to a hind spur. Attempts to reconcile the *gemara*'s framework with contemporary science — whether by invoking rabies or the bacteriological dangers of cat-scratch fever — founder on the internal details of the *sugya* itself, which stipulates that the problem arises only when the predatory animal acts willingly and retracts its claws, not merely when they make contact. Whatever the underlying reality, that is the halakhic framework we are working within.

### Skin Inspection

The *gemara* has been discussing how *derusa* is investigated. The operative principle established in the preceding discussion is that if one inspects the wound site and finds no redness of the skin, there is no problem. The assumption is that the absence of reddening at the site indicates that no harmful substance was injected, and the animal is therefore permitted. The case of the trachea and esophagus, however, is treated differently: for those organs, the organs themselves must show redness, since a hole in either — however small — constitutes a *treifa* in its own right. Reddening of those organs indicates that the clawing has created an effective problem at that location.

### Trachea vs Esoph.

With this framework in place, Rav Pappa reports a question raised by Rav Bibi bar Abaye. The starting point is a known distinction between the two *simanim*: a hole in the esophagus, however minute — *b'mash'hu* — renders the animal a *treifa*. It follows that if *derusa* affected the esophagus and redness appears upon inspection, even the smallest red spot constitutes a problem. But the trachea operates by a different standard: a hole in the trachea is a *treifa* only if it amounts to a majority of the trachea's circumference, or if an actual cutaway hole reaches the size of an *issar*, a coin of specific dimensions. The question Rav Bibi bar Abaye raises is therefore: when *derusa* manifests on the trachea — not a hole, but a red spot on the outer surface of the trachea discovered upon inspection — what is the minimum size of that red spot to create a *treifa*? Should it mirror the standard for a hole in the trachea, requiring a full *issar*-sized marking? Or does some other consideration apply?

### Poison Burns

After raising the question, Rav Pappa then resolves it. The answer is that both the esophagus and the trachea share the same standard in the context of *derusa*: even a minimal red spot — *b'mash'hu* — is problematic. The reasoning is captured in the phrase *zihara mikla kali v'azil*: the harmful substance burns and continues to spread. The *gemara*'s model here is not poison in the systemic, bloodstream sense, but something more akin to an acid — a locally acting corrosive agent. Rashi explains that the assumption is one of local, progressive destruction. A small site of redness on the trachea is not merely a small injury; it is an ongoing process of burning that will continue to erode the tissue until a significant hole results. Therefore, even a tiny red spot on the trachea is sufficient to render the animal a *treifa*, because that small mark represents the beginning of what will inevitably become a larger lesion. This comparison to flesh-eating bacteria — a locally destructive process that spreads inexorably from its point of origin — captures something of what the *gemara* appears to be describing.

It is also worth noting that the *gemara*'s treatment of *derusa* in general significantly limits the practical scope of this *treifa* category. Just as the case of *nefila* — an animal that falls from a roof — was progressively limited by the conditions that the animal must have jumped rather than fallen passively, and must subsequently be able to stand and walk, so too *derusa* is hemmed in at every turn: questions of which predatory animals are included, whether the action was intentional, whether it involved the insertion or the retraction of the claws, and now the entire inspection mechanism by which redness at the wound site can exculpate the animal. For those troubled by these two categories that sit uneasily with modern understanding, it is worth observing that the *gemara*'s cumulative effect is to restrict their application considerably.

### Abdominal Check

The *gemara* continues: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta was sitting before Rav Nachman and stated that when a case of *derusa* arises, the required inspection — *bedika* — must be conducted opposite the *benei mei'ayim*, the abdominal organs. The logic is that *derusa* creates a *treifa* specifically by causing holes in internal organs, and the organs most vulnerable are those of the gastrointestinal tract, which sit below the ribcage with less bony protection than the heart or lungs. The inspection is therefore targeted: one examines the outer skin of the animal in the area of the *benei mei'ayim*, looking for those telltale red spots. Rashi and Tosafot both understand *benei mei'ayim* to refer primarily to the gastrointestinal organs — stomach, intestines, and the like — rather than to the entire inner cavity. If no redness appears at that location, one may assume that no harmful substance was injected into those organs and the animal is permitted. Clawing elsewhere on the body — the limbs, for instance — would not in any case produce a *treifa* even if redness appeared there, because *treifa* is generated by injury to the internal organs, and those areas do not directly threaten the vulnerable organs.

### Full Body Check

Rav Nachman, upon hearing this teaching, responded with an emphatic exclamation — *ha Elokim!* — expressing surprise or even mild reproach. He cited Rav's teaching that the inspection must extend *mikafo ad atama*, from the *kaf* to the *atama*, the thigh socket. The *gemara* immediately raises a question: what does *kaf* mean here? If it means the palm of the hand, the range described — shoulder to thigh — would be essentially equivalent to the *benei mei'ayim* area, adding nothing. Rashi understands *kaf* here not as the palm of the hand but as the shoulder joint, a large bony structure that can loosely be described by that term. But even understood as the shoulder, Rashi and Tosafot both note the problem: the range from shoulder to thigh encompasses the entire internal cavity including the lungs and heart, which the *gemara* elsewhere refers to not as *benei mei'ayim* but as *kol hachalal kulo*, the entire inner cavity. Tosafot suggests that in bovine anatomy this bone may extend further, such that the shoulder-to-thigh range in cattle aligns with what the *gemara* means by *benei mei'ayim*. The *gemara* ultimately resolves that *kaf* here refers to *kafa demoucha* — the brain pan, the bony cup that houses the brain — making the range extend from there all the way down to the thigh. Crucially, this range includes the neck area, which contains the trachea and esophagus. What Rav's teaching therefore adds, beyond the earlier statement about *benei mei'ayim*, is that the neck region — where those *simanim* are located — must also be inspected, even though as we discussed, those organs are somewhat more resistant and have their own separate inspection standards.

The practical upshot of this discussion is a clarification of which regions of the body require inspection when the site of clawing is unknown. The answer is not the entire body, since clawing in many areas would never produce a *treifa* regardless. But neither is it limited to the abdominal area alone. The inspection must cover the full range from the brain pan down to the thigh socket, including the neck.

---

## Shmutat/Shchitat

### Rav's Position

The *gemara* now shifts to a teaching reported in connection with Rav. The narrative that follows involves Rav Chiya bar Yosef's journey from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael, where he found Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish sitting together and articulating the rule that a *derusa* requires inspection opposite the *benei mei'ayim*. Rav Chiya bar Yosef informed them that Rav had extended this range from the *kaf* to the *atama*. Resh Lakish's response was striking: *manu Rav u'manu Rav?* — "Who is this Rav? I don't know anyone named Rav." Rabbi Yochanan then intervened to remind Resh Lakish of that same student who had sat in their presence in the *yeshiva* — who had actually occupied the more prestigious position of sitting while the younger Rabbi Yochanan himself had stood — and who had been great in all respects, in Torah and in *chesed* alike. Once Resh Lakish was reminded, he conceded: *beram zachor oto ha'ish l'tov*, "that person should indeed be remembered favorably," for at least people had reported teachings in his name — she'amru shmuah mipiv.

It is worth noting how reluctant Resh Lakish's acknowledgment is: he refers to Rav throughout as *oto ha'ish*, "that man," and frames his concession around the fact that others have cited teachings in his name, rather than offering any direct tribute to the greatness of those teachings. There may be a geographic dimension to this reluctance — the feeling, perhaps, that Rav had taken his formidable Torah to Babylonia and built it up there when he might have remained in Eretz Yisrael. And the fact that Resh Lakish did not know him at all likely reflects the chronology: Rav had already departed for Babylonia by the time Resh Lakish came onto the scene, and if Rav was indeed an honorific rather than a given name, Resh Lakish may genuinely have been encountering this appellation for the first time.

The teaching that Rav is credited with — and that Resh Lakish acknowledges for this reason — is the following: *shmuta v'shchuta keshera*. If an animal's *siman* — let us say the trachea — was cut during *shechita* and was subsequently found to be dislodged from its proper position, the animal is nevertheless *keshera*. The reasoning is *she'i efshar lishmuta she'teaseh shchuta*: it is impossible for a *siman* that was dislodged before *shechita* to have been cut by the *shechita*, because if the trachea had already been displaced from its anatomical position, the blade of the *shochet* would never have reached it. Therefore if we see that the trachea has been cut, we know that the cut occurred while it was in its proper place; the dislocation must have happened afterward, and is therefore not a disqualifying defect.

### Yochanan's Test

Rabbi Yochanan, however, disagrees with this simple inference. He rules that one cannot rely on that logical argument alone — *yatvi v'yakbi*, one must sit and establish through a comparison test. The procedure Rashi describes is this: one makes a second cut in the trachea in its now-dislodged position and compares the appearance of that test cut with the appearance of the original *shechita* cut. The underlying assumption is that a cut made while the trachea is in its normal anatomical position will look different from a cut made while it is displaced. If the original *shechita* cut resembles the test cut made when the *siman* is dislodged, one must conclude that the original cut also occurred when the *siman* was out of position — meaning the *shechita* was invalid. Only if the two cuts look different can one accept that the original cut occurred properly.

### Nachman's Limit

Rav Nachman then qualifies Rav's teaching further. He states: *lo shanu ela shelo tafas b'simanin* — Rav's ruling applies only in the case where the *shochet* was not gripping the *simanim* during the act of *shechita*. In that case, the logic holds: if the trachea was displaced before the cut, the blade would not have reached it. But *aval tafas b'simanin v'shachat* — if the *shochet* was holding the *simanim* together in his hand while performing the *shechita*, then it is entirely possible that the trachea was already displaced before the cut and the *shochet* was holding it in place manually, such that the cut reached it even though it was not in its natural anatomical position. In that case, one cannot make Rav's inference and the animal may well be a *treifa*. The effect of these two qualifications — Rabbi Yochanan's comparison test and Rav Nachman's limitation to cases where the *shochet* was not gripping the *simanim* — is that by the time Resh Lakish has begrudgingly acknowledged Rav's teaching as worth remembering, two immediate and significant restrictions have already been placed upon it.

---

## Tradition vs Science

### Enumerated List

The final line of the first *mishna* had stated: *zeh ha-klal, kol she'ein kamohah chayah, treifa* — "This is the general rule: any animal with such an injury that it cannot live, is a *treifa*." The *gemara* asks what this *zeh ha-klal* comes to include. The answer given is that it comes to include the seven teachings — *sheva shmaitata* — of *amoraim* who added to the list of *treifot*. This seems to suggest that the category of *treifa* is open-ended: any injury the sages demonstrate will cause the animal's death can be added to the list.

### Hunter Evidence

The *gemara* now challenges this apparent openness with two stories. First, from the house of a man known as Yosef the hunter: hunters would strike animals in the *gid hanasha*, the sciatic nerve region, and those animals would die as a result of that wound. Rashi suggests the hunters would hit the hindquarters to bring the animal down and then *shecht* it, but if they failed to do so in time, the animal would perish from that wound alone. The *gid hanasha* injury, however, is not on the list of *treifot*. They brought this evidence to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. His response was categorical: *ve'chi l'hosif al treifot yesh? Ein lecha ela mah she'manu chachamim* — Are you trying to add to the list of *treifot*? You have only what the sages enumerated.

A parallel case is then presented. Rav Pappa bar Abba was also a hunter. He would strike animals in the kidneys and they would die. Notably, the very next *mishna* will state explicitly that an animal whose kidneys are removed is not a *treifa*. Yet here is direct evidence that a blow to the kidneys kills the animal. They brought this observation to Rabbi Abba, who responded identically: *ve'chi l'hosif al treifot yesh? Ein lecha ela mah she'manu chachamim*.

### Medicine Response

The *gemara* then presses the point: *ve'ha ka'chazinan de'ka meita* — but we see with our own eyes that the animal dies! How can one simply invoke the authority of the enumerated list and dismiss the empirical evidence? The *gemara*'s response is: *gemiri, ee badri lah samma chayah* — it is a tradition that if one were to apply a certain medicine to that wound, the animal could survive. That is to say, the animals in question did not die because the injury is inherently lethal; they died only because no treatment was applied. Were the appropriate remedy administered, the animal would live. Therefore, these wounds do not actually belong on the list of injuries from which an animal cannot survive.

### Philosophy

This is a striking *gemara* that raises significant questions about the relationship between the list of *treifot* and empirical reality. The tension is immediately apparent: the *gemara* began by saying that *zeh ha-klal* comes to include the *sheva shmaitata*, implying that the *amoraim* could and did add to the list. Yet now the *gemara* insists the list is closed and cannot be augmented by new observations. How are these reconciled?

The resolution lies in understanding how the *gemara* itself treated the *sheva shmaitata* when they were introduced at the beginning of the *perek*. The *gemara* went to considerable lengths to fit those seven teachings within the original enumerated eighteen — not simply to acknowledge them as independent additions, but to demonstrate that they were subsumed within categories already present. This treatment reveals the *gemara*'s understanding that even those *amoraic* additions were not novel discoveries made by individual rabbis based on observation, but rather long-standing traditions that happened to be transmitted through the *amoraim*. The *gemara* thus presents a coherent position: the list of *treifot* is based entirely on tradition — *halakha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* — and not on empirical determination. Empirical observation cannot add to or subtract from the list. As for injuries not on the list that appear to cause death, the *gemara* responds that some remedy exists, whether or not we know what it is. And as for injuries that are on the list where an animal might appear to survive, one does not revise the list on that basis either.

This framework provides protection against the constant challenge of new scientific discovery. Every generation might observe something new that seems to argue for revising the list. By grounding the list entirely in tradition, one insulates it from that pressure. The cost of this position, however, is a degree of tension with the very principle underlying *treifa* — that the animal cannot survive — since the list and the underlying rationale no longer perfectly track one another.

### Rishonim Views

The Rambam and the Rashba both grappled with this tension and ultimately came down on the side of protecting the list. When confronted with evidence that animals survive injuries that are on the *treifot* list, or die from injuries that are not, they maintained the list's authority and sought ways to discount the empirical challenge rather than yield to it. The Chacham Tzvi, by contrast, took a notably different position in at least one famous case — involving an animal believed to have had no heart — arguing that it would be absurd and even harmful to the integrity of the halakhic system to consistently reject what we demonstrably know about how the world works. The Chacham Tzvi's concern was that a system that cannot engage with observable reality becomes intellectually untenable.

The discussion naturally extends to the broader question of how *halakha* relates to scientific knowledge in other areas. Rav Moshe Feinstein addressed a striking case: a man who underwent a testicular biopsy for the purpose of treating infertility, and who, according to the explicit language of the *gemara*, would be classified as a *krut shofcha* — a status that would bar him from marriage. The *gemara* is unambiguous that even the removal of a tiny amount of tissue creates this status. Rav Moshe argued, however, that the category of *krut shofcha* is grounded in the assumption of resultant infertility. Since we now know that a limited testicular biopsy does not produce infertility, the underlying rationale is absent and the man is not in fact a *krut shofcha*. Crucially, Rav Moshe was explicit that this mode of reasoning — revisiting a halakhic category in light of updated scientific understanding of its underlying rationale — is in principle applicable across *halakha*. What makes *treifot* different and immune to such reinterpretation is precisely the halakha's own insistence that the list is *halakha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*, not derived from the principle of non-survival but transmitted as a fixed tradition that the principle of non-survival only approximates.

This position is not without its difficulties. The *gemara*'s response that medicine might exist does not sit entirely comfortably as a categorical assertion — one could read it not as a blanket dismissal but as a specific factual claim that in these particular cases, effective treatment does exist. Under that reading, the *gemara* would not be foreclosing revision of the list in principle, but only contesting whether these particular cases truly meet the standard of inevitable death. That reading was not, however, the general approach adopted by the *poskim*. The dominant tradition in this area — specific to *treifot* — is that the list is authoritative as received, not subject to revision based on new observation.

---

## Kosher Conditions

### Full List

The *gemara* now turns to the second *mishna*, which enumerates conditions that do not render an animal a *treifa*. *v'eilu kashrot b'beheimah* — the following are kosher in a large domesticated animal.

A hole in the trachea — *nikva hagargeret* — that does not sever the majority of the trachea is not a *treifa*. Nor is a crack — *nisdeka* — running along its length, provided it does not extend all the way through. If material is actually removed from the trachea, how large a lacuna is problematic? Rabban Gamliel says: the size of an Italian *issar*, a specific Roman coin. Anything smaller is not a *treifa*.

If the skull is cracked open — *niftecha hagulgoles* — but the membrane surrounding the brain is not pierced, the animal can survive and is not a *treifa*. A hole in the heart — *nikav halev* — that does not penetrate the inner chamber is not a *treifa*. The spine — *hashidra* — may be broken, provided the spinal cord itself is not severed. The liver may be substantially removed, provided a *k'zayit* of liver tissue remains — the *gemara* ultimately rules in favor of this *mishna* against an earlier suggestion that any remaining amount suffices. The two middle stomachs — *hemases u'veit hakosos* — may have a hole in the wall between them without creating a *treifa*, since food passes through a permeable membrane between them in any event. The spleen may be removed; the kidneys may be removed — though this is medically remarkable, since survival without kidneys requires dialysis today, a consideration the ancients could not have anticipated, and there is a possibility that kidneys were understood more metaphorically, as the seat of wisdom, which an animal does not need. The lower jaw may be removed provided the *simanim* remain in place. The womb — *ha'eim*, literally "mother," a striking usage — may be removed. If the lung is hardened but the hardening occurred through natural causes rather than human intervention — *charuta bidei shamayim* — the animal is not a *treifa*.

Finally, the *mishna* records the case of *hagluda* — an animal whose skin has been removed while alive, whether through disease or human action. Rabbi Meir rules the animal *machshir*, kosher; the Sages rule it invalid. According to the Sages, this case thus falls into the category of *treifot*, even though it does not appear on the first *mishna*'s list.

### Excluded Middle

The *gemara* now raises what is essentially the excluded middle problem. The two lists — the first *mishna*'s enumeration of *treifot* and this *mishna*'s enumeration of kosher conditions — together do not obviously exhaust all possibilities. There will be cases that appear on neither list. The question is which list is *davka* — exclusive and definitive — such that anything not explicitly included in it falls into the opposite category.

*Itmar*: a dispute is reported. Rabbi Yochanan says the first *mishna* is *davka* — these are the *treifot*, and only these. Anything not on the first list is therefore not a *treifa*. Resh Lakish says the second *mishna* is *davka* — these are the kosher conditions, and only these. Anything not on the second list is therefore a *treifa*. Note the logic: whichever list is *davka* is the smaller, more restrictive category, and everything outside it falls into the other. Rabbi Yochanan, by treating the first list as *davka*, makes the category of *treifa* smaller and the category of *kosher* open-ended — a *kula*. Resh Lakish, by treating the second list as *davka*, makes the category of *kosher* smaller and the category of *treifa* open-ended — a *chumra*.

### Dislocated Thigh

The practical case that falls between the two lists, and thus determines which position is correct, is the statement of Rav Masna: *hai buka d'atama d'shaf miduchtei, treifa* — an animal whose thigh socket has been dislocated from the hip joint is a *treifa*. This case appears on neither *mishna*. Under Rabbi Yochanan's position, since it is not on the first *mishna*'s list of *treifot*, it cannot be a *treifa*; the first list is *davka*, so Rav Masna's case must be kosher. Under Resh Lakish's position, since it is not on the second *mishna*'s list of kosher conditions, it must be a *treifa* — consistent with Rav Masna's ruling.

The *gemara* explains each position's internal reasoning. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the first *mishna* taught the *treifot* and then stated *zeh ha-klal*, anticipating that people would want to include cases like Rav Masna's under the general principle that "an animal which cannot survive is a *treifa*." After all, a dislocated thigh is somewhat similar to cases of organ removal — *nitulei* — in that the thigh has been removed from its proper position. The *tanna* therefore stated *eilu treifot* — these and no others — to exclude Rav Masna's case. Even if someone wanted to include it under *zeh ha-klal*, the word *eilu* signals that the list is limited and this case falls outside it.

Resh Lakish holds that the second *mishna* anticipated that Rav Masna's case was a gray area — it was not clearly similar enough to any of the established *treifot* categories to be automatically included under *zeh ha-klal*. It is not quite like a hole in an organ — *nikuv*; not quite like a severed organ — *psukei*; and not quite like a removed organ — *nitulei* — because the thigh has not been fully removed, just displaced. Since it was ambiguous whether it belonged on the *treifot* list, the *tanna* of the second *mishna* stated *eilu kashrot* — these are the kosher conditions, and only these — signaling that anything ambiguous falls into the category of *treifa*, not kosher. Rav Masna's case, being ambiguous, is therefore a *treifa*.

### Ligament Severance

The *gemara* then returns to Rav Masna's case directly. Rav Masna ruled it a *treifa*; Rava rules it *kesheira*. Rava draws a distinction, however: *ifsak nivei* — if the ligament connecting the thigh to the hip socket is cut — that is a *treifa*. The *gemara* then rules: *v'hilkhasa, ifsak nami kesheira* — even if the ligament is cut, the dislocated hip is not a *treifa*, until — *ad d'mis'achla it'achulei* — the ligament is completely dissolved or decomposed. The *gemara* may be operating with the assumption that even a severed ligament can heal unless it has fully disintegrated. This distinction also clarifies why the dislocated thigh is not simply assimilated to the category of *nitulei*, removed organs: the thigh is never fully removed, it is roughly in position and may even retain some ligamentous connection, making it genuinely distinct from an organ that has been extracted entirely.

---

## Work & Respect

### Craftsmen & Sages

At this point the *gemara* records an account that begins with an incidental observation by Rabbi Chanana, a money changer, who reported the following. Rabbi Bar Nafcha came to his table and requested a *dinar kurdina* — a specific coin from Babylonia that he wished to use to gauge the size of a hole in a trachea for *treifa* determinations. As Bar Nafcha approached the table, Rabbi Chanana wished to rise and honor him. Bar Nafcha stopped him and said: *sheiv beni sheiv* — sit, my son, sit. He then articulated the principle: *ein ba'alei umniyot resha'im la'amod bifnei talmidei chachamim b'sha'ah she'oskim b'melachtam* — craftsmen are not permitted to stand before Torah scholars while they are engaged in their work.

The word *resha'in* here does not mean "forbidden" in an absolute sense but, as Tosafot explains, means "not obligated." The question of why is addressed differently by Rashi and Tosafot. Rashi invokes a *tosefta* that limits the case to someone working in a partnership arrangement — where the worker receives a commission but a partner or employer is also depending on the proceeds. Since the craftsman is not solely working for himself, he cannot choose to interrupt his work, even for the honor of a sage, without effectively stealing from his partner. Rashi extends this to say that even a shopkeeper who merely sits inattentively rather than engaging customers is derelict in his duty to his employer. Tosafot suggests the case may apply even to someone working solely for himself, reading *ein resha'in* as "not obligated." Even without an employer's interests at stake, the person engaged in productive work is not obligated to interrupt it to stand for a sage — the honor is waived by the sage, as the sage understands the importance of one's livelihood.

This reflects a noteworthy ethic present elsewhere in the *gemara* as well — the *mishna* in *berakhot* shortens the permitted length of prayer for workers during working hours, out of respect for their responsibility to their employer.

### Bikkurim Honor

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge from a *mishna* about *bikkurim*. When the people of Israel would travel from their towns to bring their first fruits to Jerusalem, they would pass through villages along the way. At those villages, *kol ba'alei umniyot omdim mipneihem* — all the craftsmen would stand before the *bikkurim* pilgrims, and would greet them warmly: *acheinu bo'achem b'shalom*, "our brothers, come in peace." This standing was clearly done during working hours, yet no objection is raised in the *mishna*. How, then, does Bar Nafcha say one need not stand?

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the apparent contradiction: *mipneihem omdim* — yes, one stands for the *bikkurim* pilgrims, *mipnei talmidei chachamim ein omdim* — but one need not stand for Torah scholars in the same circumstances. A Torah scholar's honor can be waived; the scholar understands the craftsman's situation and releases him from the obligation. But the *bikkurim* occasion is different.

### Mitzva Timing

Rav Yosef bar Abba explains why: *kama chaviva mitzvah b'sha'atah* — how beloved is a *mitzva* performed at its proper time. The *bikkurim* pilgrims are doing something that happens at a specific, designated moment — the appointed season, the single annual opportunity to bring firstfruits. This is not something the scholar can do for them at another time; it is a *mitzva* that, if not performed now, cannot be performed at all for another year, and perhaps not by that same individual ever again. The uniqueness and time-bound urgency of the *mitzva* elevates it above the ordinary honor due to a scholar, who will always be there to be honored another time. One rises not for the person but for the act — for the *mitzva* being performed in its proper moment.

### Communal Welcome

The *gemara* then offers a second, more pragmatic explanation. Perhaps the craftsmen rose not purely from a sense of halakhic honor, but *kedei shelo tehei nimtza machshilan l'atid lavo* — so as not to be found causing them to stumble in the future. If the pilgrims traveled great distances, making significant effort to bring their *bikkurim*, and were met along the way with indifference or silence, they might conclude that the effort was not worth repeating and decline to make the journey in subsequent years. But if the villages rose to greet them warmly, asking after their welfare and welcoming them as brothers, the pilgrims would feel the communal significance of what they were doing and would be encouraged to return. The warmth of communal welcome thus serves not only as an expression of present honor but as an investment in future *mitzva* performance. It is left open whether the primary reason is the intrinsic value of the time-bound *mitzva* or this pragmatic communal consideration.

---

## Ad v'Lo Ad B'Chlal

### Exact = Upper

The *gemara* concludes the daf with a brief but important principle articulated by Rav Nachman. The context is the various size-thresholds encountered throughout the laws of *treifot*: a hole in the trachea the size of an *issar* is a *treifa*; a hole in the skull the size of a *sela* creates a problem; and so on. The question arises: what is the ruling when a hole measures exactly the stated size — neither more nor less? Is it treated as belonging to the upper (prohibited) category or the lower (permitted) category?

Rav Nachman rules: *k'sela kiyetar misela* — if it is the size of a *sela*, it is considered like more than a *sela*. *k'issar kiyetar me'issar* — if it is exactly the size of an *issar*, it is considered like more than an *issar*. In both cases, the exact measurement falls into the upper, prohibited category. An animal with a hole in its trachea exactly the size of an *issar* is a *treifa*, not because it exceeds the threshold but because the exact threshold itself is included in the prohibited category.

### Until Not Incl.

The underlying principle is *ad v'lo ad b'chlal*: when the sages say that something is permitted "until" a certain size, they mean up to but not including that size. The moment the object reaches the stated threshold, it is already beyond the zone of permission. The word "until" in the sages' usage excludes the limit point itself from the permissive ruling. This *sugya* of *ad v'ad b'chlal* versus *ad v'lo ad b'chlal* — whether boundary measurements are included within the stated limit or fall just beyond it — will continue to be developed on the next daf.

---

---

# Hullin 56

## Tereifos Ba'Of

### Intro: Birds List

The daf opens with a new *mishna* — *v'eilu tereifos ba'of* — which presents the list of *tereifos* specific to poultry. Having completed the extensive discussion of *tereifos* in large animals (*behemot*), spanning many pages and *dapim* of *gemara*, we now turn to birds. What is immediately striking is how much shorter this list is. The *mishna* covering *tereifos* in large animals is considerably more elaborate; birds, by contrast, receive a more compressed treatment. As we will see, this is not because fewer rules apply, but because a general principle — articulated by Levi — holds that whatever applies to large animals applies to birds as well, unless anatomy or explicit teaching dictates otherwise.

### Esophagus & Trachea

The first two items in the list are familiar: *nikuvat haveshet*, a hole in the esophagus, and *phuskat hagargeres*, a split trachea. By now the rules governing these organs are well established. A hole in the esophagus renders the bird a *tereifah*. A split trachea requires that the cut extend at least halfway through the circumference, as we learned from the discussion concerning large animals.

### Weasel Attack

The *mishna* then introduces *hiksa chuldah al rosha* — if a weasel struck the bird on its head, *makom she'oseh osah tereifah*, in a place where that blow could render it a *tereifah*. This formulation is notable: the mere fact of an attack is insufficient. The blow must have been in a location capable of causing a hole in the membrane surrounding the brain (*krum shel moach*). It is worth pausing on why the *mishna* frames the rule this way for birds when, in the context of large animals, the concern was stated more abstractly as a hole in the *krum*. The answer is practical: for chickens and other small birds, the realistic scenario for such a wound is precisely a weasel attack. The imagery is concrete and recognizable.

Rashi adds an important clarification. Although *hiksa* sounds like the sort of blow one might deliver with a hand or a claw — and indeed *derusah* (the *tereifah* of being clawed) involves a very different mechanism — this is explicitly not a case of *derusah*. Rather, *hiksa* here refers to a weasel attacking with its teeth. This matters halachically: the weasel bites, it does not claw. The concern is not the poison that *derusah* involves but the mechanical penetration of the skull and potentially the membrane.

### Gizzard & Organs

The *mishna* continues: *nikav hakorkovan*, a hole in the gizzard. The anatomy of the bird is relevant here. Unlike ruminants, birds have no multiple stomachs. Their digestive process involves two distinct organs: the *zefek* (crop), where food goes first, and the *korkovan* (gizzard), which comes second and grinds the food before it reaches the stomach. Artscroll's anatomical illustration is helpful here: one can see the esophagus descending into the crop, which then connects to the gizzard, followed by the small intestines. A hole in the *korkovan* is a *tereifah*; a hole in the *zefek*, as we will see in the next *mishna*, is not.

The list continues: *nikvu hadakin*, a hole in the small intestines, renders the bird a *tereifah* as well.

### Fire Damage

*Naflu la'ur venichmeru bnei mei'eha* — if the bird fell into fire and its inner organs became shriveled. The *mishna* adds a critical distinction: *im yerukim psulim*, if the organs turned green, the bird is *pasul*; *im adumim ksheirim*, if they remain red, it is *kosher*. The *gemara* will unpack this considerably, including the counterintuitive case where organs that are naturally a different color change in the opposite direction.

### Trampling Impact

Finally, the *mishna* discusses *darsa vetarfa bakosel* — if the bird was trampled or thrown against a wall, and *o she-retzatza behema u-mefarkeset* — or if an animal crushed or stomped on it, and the bird is still thrashing about (*mefarkeset*). This is a case of *risuk evarim* — the same blunt-force impact we encountered in the *mishna* about a large animal falling off a roof. There, the *gemara* had to borrow the concept of a twenty-four hour waiting period from the birds; here the *mishna* states it explicitly: *ve-shahata me-et le-et ve-shachata keshera* — if it survived for twenty-four hours and then was slaughtered, it is *kosher*. As we will revisit below, surviving the twenty-four hours does not entirely resolve the question; an internal organ check is still required.

---

## Weasel Testing

### Brain Push Test

Having established that the concern with a weasel attack is whether the *krum shel moach* has been pierced, the *gemara* now asks how one determines whether this occurred after the bird has been slaughtered. Rav, Shmuel, and Levi all agree on the same method: *machnis yado lifnim u-vodek* — you insert your hand from below, into the skull, and push the brain upward toward the hole that the weasel made. *im mevatzetz ha-moach treifah ve-im lav keshera* — if brain matter comes up through the hole, the membrane has been pierced and the bird is a *tereifah*; if nothing comes through, the membrane is intact and the bird is *kosher*.

### Brain Membranes

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty with this test. *ha nicha le-man de-amar ad de-mankiv kruma tata'ah* — this test works well according to the opinion that a *tereifah* requires that the inner (*tata'ah*) membrane be pierced. If that is the standard, then if nothing comes through the hole, it means neither membrane has a hole, and the test is definitive. But what about the opinion that *nikav ila'ah af al gav de-lo nikav tata'ah* — that even a hole in the outer membrane (*ila'ah*) alone suffices to render the bird a *tereifah*, even if the inner one is intact? In that case, one might worry: *dilma ila'ah nikav ve-tata'ah lo nikav* — the outer membrane has a hole but the inner one does not, so nothing comes up through the hole, yet the bird is still a *tereifah*.

The *gemara* resolves this: *tata'ah agav ruchya mifsek pasak* — when you apply pressure from below, if the outer membrane already has a hole, the pressure you generate will cause the inner membrane to tear as well, and brain matter will indeed come up through the hole. Therefore, if you push and nothing comes through, it is reliable proof that even the outer membrane is intact. The logic is that the experimental conditions are slightly altered by the act of pushing — but this actually works in the test's favor: it ensures that even a partial perforation of the outer membrane will be detected.

One might observe that this reasoning cuts in a particular direction. If you require only the outer membrane to be pierced, the test catches everything. If you require both membranes, the test still catches it — but in that case, a result showing brain matter might reflect only a hole in the outer membrane that was torn through by the pressure of the test itself, not a pre-existing hole in the inner one. So the test does have a potential for false positives under the two-membrane standard, even if it avoids false negatives. The *gemara* appears to accept this.

### Zeiri Position

Against this backdrop, *amar Zeiri: ein bdika l'chulda* — Zeiri declares that there is simply no valid method of inspection for a weasel attack. Once the skull has been struck, the bird must be treated as a *tereifah*. The reason offered is *mipnei sheshineha dakot* — because the weasel's teeth are very thin and therefore a visual inspection cannot detect the wound.

### Diagonal Holes

The *gemara* asks on Zeiri's position: *vechi shineha dakot mai havay* — so what if the teeth are thin? We have just described a test that does not rely on visual inspection at all. Rav Oshaya provides the answer: *mipnei sheshineha dakot ve'akumot* — the teeth are not only thin but also angled. A diagonal bite creates a hole in the skull that does not correspond directly to the hole in the membrane below. The hole in the membrane will be located at an offset position from the skull perforation. Therefore, even if you push from directly beneath the skull hole, you may be pushing at the wrong angle and will not drive brain matter through the membrane hole, even if one exists. The test is unreliable precisely because the path of the wound is not straight.

### Zeiri Retraction

The matter does not end there. *ki salik l'nahardea* — when Zeiri subsequently traveled to Nahardea, he sent a message back to his students: *devarim she'amarti lifneichem ta'ut hem beyadi* — what I previously taught you was a mistake; I retract it. He then transmits a ruling in the name of Reish Lakish: *bodkim l'chulda beyad aval lo bemachat* — one may indeed inspect for a weasel attack using one's hand (the pushing method), but one may not use a nail. It is worth noting the irony: Zeiri is visiting Nahardea, a Babylonian center of learning, and bringing back a teaching from Reish Lakish, who was of course an Eretz Yisrael authority — and this despite the earlier *gemara* in which Reish Lakish refused even to acknowledge Rav's authority when his teachings were cited to him.

### Hand vs. Nail

Why would a nail be considered as a testing instrument at all? The nail method works differently from the hand method: rather than pushing from below, one runs the tip of a nail along the surface of the brain membrane itself to feel whether it catches on a perforation. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar take a more permissive position, ruling *afilu masmer* — even a nail may be used — because we are not concerned that the nail itself will create a hole. The *gemara* traces this dispute back to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemiah: *chad badik beyada vechad badik bemachata* — one tested with a hand and one with a needle.

### Testing Trade-offs

The exchange between the two positions is memorable. The one who used the hand challenged the one who used the needle: *ad matai ata mechaleh mamonam shel Yisrael* — how long will you continue to squander the money of the Jewish people? The needle test produces too many false positives — the needle itself creates holes — and so many animals are being declared *tereifah* unnecessarily, causing financial loss to their owners.

The response from the needle camp is equally pointed: *ad matai ata ma'achil leYisrael nevelot* — how long will you feed the Jewish people forbidden food? The hand test produces too many false negatives; animals with genuine perforations are being passed as *kosher*. The *gemara* notes, with characteristic precision, that the word *nevelot* is imprecise here, since the bird was in fact properly slaughtered — *veha shechutah hi* — and so the correct charge is *tereifot*, not *nevelot*. But the substance of the accusation stands.

This exchange crystallizes a tension that recurs throughout halachic literature: the concern for *mamonam shel Yisrael* — not placing undue financial burdens on people — weighing against the concern for rigorous protection of the law's integrity. Both poles have their own internal logic, and neither can be dismissed.
