The *gemara* concludes that it was Rabbi Yehuda who employed the hand test, as confirmed by a *baraita*: *bodkim lechulda beyad aval lo bemasmer* — test with the hand, not with a nail.

That same *baraita* adds a puzzling line: *nishbar ha'etzem af al pi shelo nikav krum shel moach* — a broken skull renders the bird a *tereifah* even if the membrane was not pierced. But if that is so, what is the entire purpose of the inspection? The *gemara* resolves this with a crucial clarification that will occupy the next section.

---

## Waterfowl Exception

### Thin Membranes

The *gemara* addresses the apparently contradictory final line of the *baraita* — that a cracked skull is a *tereifah* even without a pierced membrane — by explaining: *seifa atan le'of hamayim*, that ruling pertains to waterfowl. The principle is *ho'il ve'ein lo krum* — since waterfowl lack a membrane. The *gemara* immediately questions this on biological grounds: *ein lo krum salka daitach* — do you really mean to say it has no membrane at all? Of course it does. The *gemara* corrects: *ela ho'il vekrumo rach* — rather, its membrane is very thin and delicate. The consequence is that once the skull of a waterfowl is breached, one can assume that the membrane will inevitably tear as well, or alternatively, as Rashi suggests, one assumes that the membrane has already been compromised. Either way, for waterfowl, a hole in the skull alone suffices to create *tereifah* status; no inspection of the membrane is needed or possible.

### Levi's Rule

This section also introduces explicitly the teaching of Levi that serves as the foundational principle for the entire discussion of *tereifos* in birds: *treifos shemanu chachamim bebeheimah kenegdan ba'of* — whatever *tereifos* the Sages enumerated for large animals apply equally to birds. *yeser aleihen of* — birds have additional *tereifos* beyond those of large animals. Chief among these additional stringencies: *nishbar ha'etzem af al pi shelo nikav krum shel moach* — a skull fracture is a *tereifah* even without membrane penetration. This, as we have just seen, refers to waterfowl specifically. For other birds, the rules parallel those of large animals, and an intact membrane means the bird is *kosher* — with the hand-inspection available as the testing method.

### Case Study

The practical stakes of this distinction emerge in a concrete case. A chicken in the house of Rav Chana was apparently struck by a weasel. Rav Chana sent it to Rav Matna for a ruling. The facts were: *nishbar ha'etzem* — the skull was fractured — *velo nikav krum shel moach* — but the membrane was intact. Rav Matna declared it *kosher*. Rav Chana challenged this, citing Levi's principle: if birds have the additional stringency that a skull fracture alone is a *tereifah*, how can this bird be *kosher*? Rav Matna replied: *hasam be'of hashamayim* — that stringency applies to waterfowl, whose membranes are thin. For a regular chicken, the same standard as large animals applies: so long as the membrane is intact, the animal is *kosher*.

The question arises: if Rav Chana knew about this teaching and was concerned it made the chicken a *tereifah*, why did he send it to Rav Matna rather than simply rule himself? A plausible answer is that he felt genuinely conflicted — he was aware of traditions permitting inspection and traditions suggesting inspection was futile, and he could not resolve the tension. Sending the case to another authority and then pressing for an explanation of the ruling is a recognizable dynamic: one may not feel positioned to *pasken*, and once someone else has ruled, one can then engage the question analytically.

### Sun & Water Tests

The *gemara* records that different authorities employed different techniques for detecting membrane perforations. Rav Shizbi tested by holding the membrane up to sunlight, presumably to observe how light reflected off or through the tissue in a way that would reveal a hole. Rav Yeimar tested with water. Rashi offers two possible explanations of the water test. One is that the brain is scooped out of the membrane sac, which is then filled with water to observe whether any leaks through — though Rashi acknowledges this is difficult to execute given the delicacy of the tissue. The other explanation is that water is poured into the skull through the hole and then poured out: if the water comes out clear, the membrane is intact; if it comes out cloudy with brain matter, the membrane was breached. Rav Acha bar Yaakov used a thin tailor's needle run along the surface of the membrane. Notably, the language of testing with the sun and testing with water recalls the techniques used for inspecting the slaughtering knife for *pgima* — the very same terms applied to entirely different types of inspection.

### Geese Status

Rav Shizbi adds a taxonomic observation: *hani avazi didan ke'of hashamayim damyan* — our geese are classified like waterfowl. This is somewhat puzzling. If geese spend all their time in water, why the qualifying language *damyan* — "are like" — rather than simply saying they are waterfowl? Rashi suggests that geese are described as being *always in the water*, which would make the statement tautological. Perhaps the statement reflects a specific population of geese that were less aquatic in habit but were nevertheless treated halachically as waterfowl for these purposes. The word *damyan* — resembling — does retain a note of approximation rather than full identity, and this remains a point of some difficulty.

---

## Fire Organ Damage

### Green Amount

The *gemara* now turns to the rules governing organs that have changed color as a result of the bird falling into fire. Rabbi Yochanan teaches in the name of Rabbi Yosi ben Yehoshua: *ha-yirukatam ke-shier nikuvatan* — the amount of discoloration required to create a problem is the same as the amount of a hole that would create a *tereifah*. *mah nikuvatan b'mashehu* — just as even the smallest hole in the relevant inner organs is a *tereifah*, *af ha-yerukatam b'mashehu* — so too the slightest greening of those organs is a problem. The logic is consistent: a green spot is understood as an eventual rupture; if even a pinhole is fatal, then even the smallest discoloration matters.

### Liver Evidence

The son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi posed a question to his father: *horika kaved keneged bnei mei'ayim mahu* — if the liver turned green in the area where it rests against the other inner organs, what is the ruling? The significance of the question is that the liver in general is a less essential organ halachically — the loss of most of the liver is not a *tereifah* — so one might think its discoloration is similarly less significant. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled: *treifah*.

The reasoning is supplied by Rava: *kivan she-horika kaved keneged bnei mei'ayim, beyadua she-nafelu la'ur ve-nechamru bnei mei'ayim* — since the liver is green precisely at the point where it contacts the other inner organs, we may infer that those other organs have also been affected by the heat, even if we cannot see the discoloration on them directly. The liver is lying on top of those organs; the green on the underside of the liver, at the interface, is evidence of damage in the tissue opposite it. Even though a hole in the liver alone would be permissible, the liver's discoloration here functions as forensic evidence of damage to the organs beneath.

This raises a broader and important question: does the problem arise only when you know that the bird fell into fire, and then you look for these green spots? Or does the presence of a green spot, even without prior knowledge of a fire incident, itself create a presumption that the bird fell into the fire and the organs were damaged? The final line of Rava's ruling — *beyadua she-nafelu la'ur* — says "we know that it fell into the fire," which suggests the green spot alone is sufficient to establish that fact. If so, any green spot on the relevant organs, regardless of what you know about the bird's history, would render it a *tereifah*. This question is practically significant and the text leaves some ambiguity on this point.

### Intact Organs

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi himself had a chicken that he sent to Rabbi Elazar Hakapar b'Rabbi. Rabbi Elazar ruled *kosher*, despite the organs appearing green. The objection is immediate: the *mishna* says *yerukim pesulim* — green is the problematic color. Rabbi Elazar's ruling is explained by a limiting principle: *lo ameru yerukim pesulim ela bekorkevan uvalev uvakaved* — the rule that green discoloration is a *tereifah* applies only to three specific organs: the gizzard, the heart, and the liver. This is confirmed by a *baraita*: *be-eilu bnei mei'ayim amru* — it is specifically regarding these three organs that the rule of greenness applies.

### Color Reversals

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef had a chicken that he sent to Rabbi Abbahu. In this case, the organs were red — *adumim havhu* — yet Rabbi Abbahu declared it a *tereifah*. The objection is now the mirror image of the previous: *adumim kesherim* — red is the kosher color according to the *mishna*! Rabbi Abbahu explains: *adumim she-horiku ve-yerukim she-edimu* — organs that are naturally red turning green is a problem, and equally, organs that are naturally greenish (or flesh-toned) turning red is also a problem. The *mishna*'s formulation is not exhaustive; it describes the paradigmatic case (naturally red organs remaining red is fine; naturally red organs turning green is not), but Rabbi Abbahu extends this symmetrically. *lo ameru adumim kesherim ela balev bekorkevan uvakaved* — only the heart, gizzard, and liver are being discussed. The intestines and other organs have a more neutral, orangeish hue, and a shift in their color in either direction is the relevant concern for those organs.

The *artscroll* anatomical illustration is actually helpful at this point: the heart and liver appear in a clear deep red; the gizzard, similarly; the intestines, by contrast, show a more orangeish-neutral tone. The color distinction that the *gemara* is drawing is visually recognizable.

### Boiling Test

Shmuel bar Chiya in the name of Rav Mani introduces a further nuance: *adumim she-horiku veshalokan vechazru ve-edimu kesherim* — if organs that should be red turned greenish, but you then cooked them in boiling water and they reverted to their normal red color, they are *kosher*. The reason: *kutra ai behu* — the discoloration was caused by smoke, not by organic damage to the tissue. The boiling process removes the external contaminant and reveals the organ's natural and healthy state. The color change was superficial rather than indicative of structural damage.

### Testing Limits

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak extends this logic in the opposite direction: if you can use the boiling test to rescue an animal that appeared problematic, should you not also apply the test to an animal that appears fine? If you boil what look like healthy, properly-colored organs and they turn the wrong color, that change reveals their true condition — *igla bahita'iyu*, their defect has been exposed.

Rav Ashi takes the logical conclusion to its extreme: *lo leichol inish ela be-shalka* — no one should eat a chicken unless the organs have been subjected to this boiling test. This is a striking statement. At face value, it seems to mandate universal testing before any bird may be consumed. But the *poskim* consistently interpret this as operating within the context already established: the bird is known or suspected to have fallen into fire. The boiling test is triggered only in that context, not as a universal requirement for every chicken slaughtered.

### No Presumed Defects

The *gemara* itself closes this discussion with the decisive limiting principle: *velo hi — achzukei rei'ata lo machzekinan* — we do not presume defects. The term *rei'ata* derives from *ra*, meaning bad; the principle is that we do not go looking for problems where none are apparent. If the organs present well visually, we do not then subject them to further testing in the hope of uncovering hidden problems. If something looks bad, one may attempt to demonstrate through testing that it is actually fine. But one does not take something that looks fine and subject it to tests designed to reveal possible defects. The *chazaka* is in favor of the animal being *kosher*, and we require a concrete *leidas ha-safek* — an actual precipitating concern — before that presumption is disturbed.

---

## Blunt Force Impact

### Internal Check

The *gemara* returns to the case of *darsa vetarfa bekosel* — the bird that was trampled or thrown against a wall. Rabbi Elazar ben Antignus rules in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Yannai: *bein kach uvein kach tzericha bedika* — in either case, whether the bird survived twenty-four hours or not, an internal organ inspection is still required after slaughter. The twenty-four hours establishes a baseline — an animal that does not survive twenty-four hours is a *tereifah* even without internal organ damage — but survival does not completely resolve the question of *risuk evarim*. One must still examine the internal organs.

### 24-Hour Rule

The broader picture is worth noting. When the earlier *mishna* discussed a large animal (*behemah*) falling off a roof, there was no explicit mention of the twenty-four hour rule. The *gemara* there borrowed the concept from this very *mishna* about birds. Here, the rule is explicit: *ve-shahata me-et le'et ve-shachata keshera* — if it waited twenty-four hours and was then slaughtered, it is *kosher*, provided the organ inspection is clear. If the bird got up and walked around (or in the case of a bird, flew), even the organ inspection may be waived. These are the parameters of *risuk evarim* as applied in both contexts.

---

## Kosher Conditions

### Minor Damage OK

The following *mishna* presents the *kosher* counterpart: *eilu k'sheiros ba'of*. A hole in the trachea (*nikva ha-gargeres*) is acceptable, as is a crack running along its length that does not extend to the very top or bottom. These are less than the disqualifying injuries already described. Similarly, if the weasel attacked the head *makom she-eino oseh tereifah* — in a place where, even if the membrane were reached, it would not correspond to the brain — the bird remains *kosher*. Whether such a location exists anatomically is left somewhat open, but the *mishna* contemplates it.

### Missing Crop

*Nikav ha-zefek* — a hole in the crop — does not render the bird a *tereifah*. And then *rebbi* goes further: *afilu nital* — even if the crop is entirely removed, it is still *kosher*. How this is anatomically possible is not straightforward. Looking at the diagram, the esophagus flows directly into the crop, which flows into the gizzard; removing the crop without disrupting the esophagus seems difficult to execute without causing a hole in the esophageal passage. The *ran* and *beer ha-golah* address this by clarifying that "removed" does not mean fully excised, but rather that enough of the crop remains to allow food to pass to the gizzard. The functional criterion — that the food pathway remains viable — is what determines the ruling.

### Protruding Organs

*Yatzu bnei me'eha velo nikvu* — if the internal organs protruded from the body cavity but sustained no punctures or holes, the bird is *kosher*. This is a notable ruling: an open body cavity with organs hanging out is not itself a *tereifah* condition, so long as the organs themselves are intact. *nishtabru gapeha* — broken wings, *nishtabru ragleha* — broken legs: these are all *kosher*. External structural injuries, even severe ones, do not render a bird a *tereifah* absent internal organ damage.

### Feather Loss

*Nimretu knafeha* — if the bird's outer feathers have been pulled out, it is still *kosher*. But *rabbi yehuda* introduces a distinction: *im nitla ha-notza pesula* — if the *notza*, the down feathers closest to the skin, have been removed, that is a *tereifah*. The down is what insulates and protects the bird, and Rabbi Yehuda holds that without it the bird cannot survive. The outer feathers, by contrast, are not essential to the bird's viability. This parallels a discussion earlier in the tractate about skinning a large animal, where Rabbi Meir permitted and the *chachamim* prohibited. It is tempting to identify that *bar plugta* dispute as reflecting the same underlying disagreement — Rabbi Yehuda arguing for the *tereifah* status, Rabbi Meir for *kosher* — although the framing here presents Rabbi Yehuda's position as the *da'as yachid*, the minority view.

---

## Anatomy & Analogy

### Simai & Tzadok

A *baraita* records that Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Tzadok traveled to participate in a calendar intercalation convocation at Lod, spending Shabbos along the way in Ono. A case involving the *tarpachat* — a term for the womb — was brought before them, and they ruled *ke-Rebbi be-zefek*, like Rebbi ruled in the case of the crop. That is, the same way Rebbi had ruled that a missing crop does not render a bird a *tereifah*, they ruled that a missing womb does not render a large animal a *tereifah*. The analogy rests on the principle that some organs are not essential to the animal's survival: the crop is one such organ, and the womb, they argued, is another.

### Teiku Question

The *gemara* raises a question about how to read this *baraita*: *iba'ya lehu* — it is uncertain. Rashi's *girsa* reads: did they rule stringently about the womb (*le-issura*), with the phrase *ke-Rebbi be-zefek le-heteira* referring to a separate, second ruling they issued on the crop itself? Or does the phrase mean that they ruled leniently about the womb (*le-heteira*), using Rebbi's crop ruling as their analogy, but without necessarily indicating their own view on the crop?

The practical upshot of this ambiguity is significant: the *baraita* might serve as evidence that Rebbi's lenient ruling on the crop was accepted and followed — or it might be that the *baraita's* author is merely drawing an analogy for descriptive purposes, without implying that Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Tzadok endorsed Rebbi's position on the crop itself. The *gemara* concludes: *teiku* — the question stands unresolved.

### Crop-Esophagus Line

A related anatomical question is raised by Rabbah (some say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi): *gago shel zefek nidon ke-veshet* — the "roof" of the crop is treated as part of the esophagus. Looking at the anatomical diagram, the esophagus descends and opens into the crop; there is a point at which the tube transitions into the sac-like crop. The upper portion of that transition — the "roof" — is treated halachically as continuous with the esophagus, meaning a hole there is a *tereifah*, not a permissible crop injury.

### Stretching Test

Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye specifies the criterion: *kol she-nimtach immo* — any tissue that stretches together with the esophagus when pulled is considered part of the esophagus. Rashi explains this as referring to the point where the walls of the crop begin to be pulled taut into the esophageal tube — that is where one draws the line. Below that boundary is the crop, where a hole is permissible; above it is the esophagus, where any perforation is a *tereifah*.

---

## Organ Positioning

### Fallen Organs

We return to the case of *yatzu bnei me'eha* — the organs that fell out of the body cavity without being punctured.

### Wrong Order

Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak introduces a critical qualification: *lo shanu ella she-lo hiphech bahen* — this ruling (that protruding organs without holes are *kosher*) applies only if the organs have not been disturbed in their natural arrangement. *aval hiphech bahen, tereifah* — if the organs were turned over or repositioned in the wrong order, it is a *tereifah*. This could occur when someone, attempting to help the animal, pushes the organs back into the body cavity but inadvertently reverses their natural arrangement relative to one another.

### Divine Design

The *gemara* grounds this ruling in a verse: *hu ascha vayechonenecha* — from *devarim*, in *ha'azinu*, describing how God made and established Israel. *melamed she-bara hakadosh baruch hu koneni'ot ba'adam* — this teaches that God fashioned specific chambers within living creatures, such that *sheim nefalech echad mehem eino yachol lychayot* — if any one of them were to be situated in the wrong position, the creature could not survive. The *gemara* draws a parallel to the *bracha* of *asher yatzar*, with its recognition that *im yipatei'ach echad mehem o yisateim echad mehem* — if any opening were to close or any sealed space were to open, life could not be sustained. The wonder of the body's design is that every component is precisely where it must be. And from this theological reflection, the *gemara* draws a direct halachic conclusion: organs repositioned in the wrong order have been removed from the configuration God designed, and the animal cannot survive — hence, *tereifah*.

### Midrash Nation

Rabbi Meir reads the same verse — *hu ascha vayechonenecha* — differently, in a national rather than anatomical register. *ke'am karcha dekula bei* — God has made Israel like a self-sufficient city, containing within itself everything it requires: *mimeinu Kohanim mimeinu Nevi'im mimeinu sarav mimeinu melachav* — from within Israel come priests, prophets, officers, and kings. The verse speaks of completeness and self-sufficiency — *mimeinu pina mimeinu yated*, the cornerstone and the foundation both come from within. This *midrash* is applied to Israel as a nation, not to the physiology of the chicken. The *gemara* applies the first interpretation — the anatomical one — to the halachic ruling about organ positioning, while Rabbi Meir's *drasha* stands as a separate homiletical reading of the same verse.

### Life-Saving Surgery

The daf concludes with a striking narrative. A non-Jew witnessed a person fall from a roof, his abdomen burst open, with his internal organs spilling out but remaining unruptured and attached. The non-Jew devised an extraordinary intervention: he brought the injured man's son before him and, through an illusion (*beachizat einayim*), made it appear as if he was killing the son. The shock caused the injured man to faint (*ingid ve'itnach*), at which point the non-Jew replaced the organs inside the man's body, restoring them to their proper arrangement, and then sutured the abdomen closed. The man survived.

The story is told here in the context of the ruling that organs replaced in the wrong order render an animal a *tereifah* — the corollary being that organs replaced in the correct order do not. And indeed, as Rashi notes in closing, even for human beings the principle holds: organs that have fallen out and are restored in their correct anatomical order can allow the person to live. The divine engineering of the body is both the halachic foundation of the *tereifah* ruling and, as this story demonstrates, the basis for the possibility of restoration and recovery.

---

---

# Hullin 57

## Harlequin ducks & sinews

### Inkurei birds identified

The daf opens two lines from the top, continuing the discussion of conditions affecting birds that do not render them a *tereifah*. Having already addressed cases such as the intestines falling out but remaining attached, or the stomach rupturing, the Gemara now turns to further scenarios. The case at hand involves a basket of birds: *hahu tsana de'inkurei*, a basket of *inkurei* birds that came before Rava. The term *tsana* ordinarily means basket, but the identity of the *inkurei* birds requires explanation.

Rashi, citing the responsa of the Geonim, describes these birds as black waterfowl with white splotches on the forehead — *of shakhor hu*, a black bird, *veshel mayim hu*, a waterfowl, *uve-mitskho khavarbarot levanot*, with white markings on its forehead. Rashi explains that the name *inkurei* derives from a root meaning spotted or splotched, likening the appearance to puncture marks against the black background. He adds, remarkably specifically, *u-ve-ir ha-zot yesh mehem* — in this very city, referring to his location in France, such birds are found. ArtScroll identifies these as harlequin ducks, a description consistent with Rashi's characterization.

### Rava checks sinew cluster

The Gemara records that Rava examined these birds: *badke Rava bi-tsomet ha-gidim*, Rava checked the cluster of sinews in the bird's leg. Apparently some broken leg bones were present among the birds, bringing the discussion into the orbit of our sugya. *va'achshereih* — and he declared them kosher, meaning the cluster had not been severed. The implication, of course, is that had the cluster been severed, there would have been a halachic problem even in the case of a bird.

### Sinew cluster anatomy

To understand what is at stake, it is necessary to appreciate the anatomy of the *tsomet ha-gidim* and how it functions as a potential *tereifah* in mammals. By cows, sheep, and other large animals — although curiously absent from the *mishnayot* that enumerate the various *tereifot* in our chapter, though alluded to elsewhere in the Gemara and destined to become a central focus in the next *perek* — there exists a *tereifah* involving the broken hind leg. The relevant break is *min ha-arkuva u-lemala*, from the lower knee joint and above. In four-legged animals there are effectively two hinge points in the hind leg; the *arkuva* refers to the lower joint, essentially the ankle. A bone broken at or above that point renders the animal a *tereifah*, which is itself somewhat surprising since it does not appear to be a gravely serious injury, and it is not listed explicitly among the enumerated *tereifot* of our chapter. Nevertheless, this is what emerges from the *mishna* in the next *perek*.

Alongside the broken bone, there is a second *tereifah* in this anatomical region: *tsomet ha-gidim*, the cluster of sinews located near this lower ankle joint. If this cluster has been severed or removed, even without a break in the bone itself, the animal is a *tereifah*. Thus there are two overlapping *tereifot* in this region of the animal: the fractured hind leg above the ankle and the severed sinew cluster. The question that now drives the Gemara's analysis is whether these same *tereifot* apply by analogy to birds, given the general principle that whatever renders a mammal a *tereifah* likewise renders a bird a *tereifah*.

---

## Dislocated leg rules

### Rav Yehuda's teaching

The Gemara now introduces the teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *shmutat yad bivehemah kesherah, shmutat yerech bivehemah tereifah*. A dislocated forearm of a large animal is kosher, but a dislocated hind leg is a *tereifah*. This was in fact mentioned earlier in the sugya as one of the *sheva shmaytata* — the seven teachings — with the phrase *buka de'atma deshaf miduchteih*, the hind thigh bone that was dislocated from the hip. Thus the dislocated rear leg of a *behemah* is a *tereifah*.

### Application to birds

By logical extension, *shmutat yerech be'of tereifah* — a dislocated thigh bone of a bird is likewise a *tereifah*. Here a point of anatomical interest arises. Birds do not have both forelegs and hindlegs as quadrupeds do; rather, their wings correspond to the forelimbs, and their feet correspond to the hind legs. The thigh bone of a bird connects remarkably high — essentially near the spinal cord — which is anatomically coherent given that the hip joint in all vertebrates represents the base of the spinal structure. Thus the *tereifah* of the dislocated hind leg has been applied to the bird's leg by analogy to the cow's hind leg, just as the bird's wing corresponds to the cow's foreleg.

### Dislocated wing

The Gemara then extends the discussion to the wing: *shmutat gaff be'of tereifah*, a dislocated wing renders a bird a *tereifah*. This is immediately surprising. A dislocated foreleg in a mammal is kosher, and the wing is the bird's analog to the foreleg — so why would a dislocated wing be a *tereifah*?

The answer is that it is not intrinsically problematic, but rather: *chayshinan shema nikvah hareiah*, we are concerned that the dislocation of the wing may have punctured the lung. Given that the wing is located in roughly the same region of the body as the lung, the violence of the dislocation may have caused such a puncture. It is therefore not an independent *tereifah* but a concern about a secondary consequence.

This immediately raises a question: the *mishna* did not mention lungs as a concern for birds. Nor did it list many of the additional *tereifot* we have been discussing. The position that whatever applies to a *behemah* applies to a bird — itself largely absent from the explicit text of the *mishna* — enormously extends the list, and even within that framework the Gemara is now applying *tereifot* involving hind legs, which had not been explicitly enumerated even for mammals in this context. The remainder of this daf will challenge several of these applications.

Since the concern about a dislocated wing is only a potential secondary consequence — the lung may or may not have been punctured — it is possible to resolve the question empirically. And so: *shmuel amar tivdeik*, Shmuel says, check the lung. *v'chen amar rebbe yochanan tivdeik*, and Rabbi Yochanan likewise says, examine it. Do not declare it a *tereifah* outright; inspect the lung and rule accordingly.

---

## Do birds have lungs?

### Chizkiya vs. Yochanan

At this point the Gemara introduces a startling statement: *chizkiya amar ein reia l'of*, Chizkiya said that birds have no lungs. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *yesh lo*, they do have a lung, *v'yeshna k'aleh shel vered*, and it resembles a small rose leaf. It is located *bein agapayim*, between the wings.

### Lungs protected by ribs

The Gemara asks: *mai ein reia l'of?* What exactly does Chizkiya mean when he says birds have no lungs? If he means literally that birds possess no lungs whatsoever — *ilima d'leis lei klal* — that is empirically refuted: *ve'ha qhazina d'is lei*, we can see that they have them. Anyone who has ever cut open a chicken can observe the lung.

Perhaps then Chizkiya means that the lung is halachically irrelevant — *ela d'lo mitreifei* — that we do not apply lung-related *tereifot* to birds? But this too is untenable, since Levi's comprehensive teaching explicitly states that *treifa she'manu chachamim b'vehema k'negdan b'of*, all the *tereifot* enumerated for large animals apply equally to birds, and birds even have additional *tereifot* beyond those.

The Gemara therefore reinterprets Chizkiya: *ela hachi ka'amar, ein lo lo linpol v'lo l'chamer*. He must mean that in two specific scenarios one need not worry about the bird's lung. When an animal falls from a height and we require examination of the internal organs, perhaps one need not examine the lung of a bird, since the rib cage forms a protective dome around it. Similarly, when an animal is exposed to fire and the concern is *l'chamer* — whether the organs have become shriveled or discolored from heat — perhaps the ribs protect the lung sufficiently that it need not be examined. As Rav Chana explains: *ho'il v'rov tzaloteha m'ginot aleha*, because the majority of its ribs protect it, and Rashi notes that the ribs create an actual structural gap between themselves and the organs within, a protective dome rather than merely a physical barrier.

However, the Gemara objects: since Rabbi Yochanan responds to Chizkiya by specifying that the bird *does* have a lung, and that it looks like a small leaf located between the wings, it seems clear that Chizkiya was in fact claiming that birds have no lung at all. *miklal d'chizkiya savar d'leis lei* — by implication, Chizkiya truly believed birds lack lungs.

### Chizkiya dismissed

The Gemara then delivers its verdict. They say in the West — in Eretz Yisrael — in the name of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina: *midivrei shel Rebbe nikar she'eino baki b'tarnigolei* — from the words of this great *rebbe*, it is apparent that he was not well-versed in the anatomy of chickens. This is quite a striking formulation. The Gemara goes out of its way to preserve and then dismiss Chizkiya's opinion, and one can speculate as to how such an error arose. One possibility is that Chizkiya was entirely book-learned on this matter: noting that the extensive lists of *tereifot* by animals include lung-related conditions while the parallel discussion for birds does not, he may have inferred that birds simply have no lungs. Alternatively, even if he examined a bird, without knowing what to look for — having been accustomed to the large, prominent lung of a cow — he may have looked at a chicken and failed to recognize the small, leaf-like structure for what it was. As Rabbi Yochanan's description implies, someone who did not know what he was looking for could easily overlook it.

What is particularly instructive is that the Gemara records this opinion at all. Perhaps it does so precisely because others might make the same mistake, whether from insufficient anatomical knowledge or from reading the texts without looking at actual animals. The quick and unequivocal rejection — he simply did not know his chickens — stands as an important corrective.

---

## Dislocated thigh debate

### Rav Huna: kosher

Having resolved the digression about bird lungs, the Gemara returns to the core question of the dislocated leg. *amar rav huna amar rav: shmutat yerech be'of keshera* — Rav Huna said in the name of Rav that a dislocated thigh bone of a bird is in fact *keshera*, kosher. This directly contradicts the earlier statement that by analogy to a *behemah*, a dislocated thigh of a bird should be a *tereifah*. The Gemara now undertakes an extended analysis: do we compare birds to *behemot* in this regard, or not?

### Different traditions

Raba bar Rav Huna confronted his father with a conflicting tradition: *ve-ha-rabbanan de-atu mi-Pumbedita amar Rav Yehuda mishmeih de-Rav* — the sages who came from Pumbedita transmitted a teaching of Rav Yehuda in Rav's name stating precisely the opposite: *shmutat yerech be'of treifa*, that a dislocated thigh in a bird is a *tereifah*. Thus two traditions circulate in Rav's name, one permitting and one forbidding.

### Rivers metaphor

Rav Huna responded to his son: *beri, nahara nahara u-pashtei* — my son, every river and its tributaries. This phrase, encountered earlier in the Gemara (18b), typically conveys a form of halachic pluralism: different places maintain different practices, each rooted in legitimate authority, and we should be tolerant of that diversity. The difficulty here is that this is not a case of two communities following different authorities — it is a case of two traditions claiming to report what the same authority, Rav, actually said. To invoke *nahara nahara u-pashtei* here is somewhat unusual, since only one tradition can accurately reflect what Rav said.

Rashi attempts to reconcile this by proposing that Rav genuinely held that a dislocated thigh was kosher, consistent with Rav Huna's tradition. The competing tradition from Pumbedita reflects not a different ruling by Rav, but rather Rav's tolerance of communities that had adopted the stricter practice — he did not override their custom. Rashi thus frames it as a matter of *minhag*, though one must acknowledge that the term here is better understood as *nihug*, adopted practice, rather than custom in the narrow sense. What one community treated as *tereifah* and another treated as *kasher* is not merely a divergence of custom but of substantive halachic practice. And the difficulty Rav's son identified is real: these are not simply different practices in different places, they are different reports of what Rav himself said.

### Rabbi Abba's inquiry

The narrative continues with Rabbi Abba, who encountered Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba examining the *tsomet ha-gidim* of a bird. Rabbi Abba challenged him: *lama lei l'mar kulei hai* — why are you troubling yourself with this? Rav Huna said in Rav's name that a dislocated thigh of a bird is kosher, which would seem to imply that we do not draw the analogy between birds and *behemot* with respect to the hind leg, and therefore the *tsomet ha-gidim* of a bird should likewise present no concern.

Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba responded: *ana matnita yadana* — I know our *mishna*. The *mishna* states that *behema shenichtechu ragleha min ha'arkuva ulemata kesheira, min ha'arkuva ulemala pesula* — an animal whose leg is severed below the ankle joint is kosher, above the ankle is invalid — *vechen shenital tzomet hagidim*, and similarly if the cluster of sinews has been removed. And he possessed a tradition that Rav himself had said *vechen ba'of* — the same applies to birds. Thus Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba held that the comparison to *behemot* was operative, and if so, a severed *tsomet ha-gidim* is a problem in birds.

This creates an apparent internal contradiction within Rav's teachings: on one hand, Rav supposedly said that a dislocated thigh of a bird is kosher — implying we do not draw the analogy to *behemot*; on the other hand, Rav supposedly said that the severed *tsomet ha-gidim* of a bird is a *tereifah* — implying we do draw that analogy. Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba fell silent, unable to resolve the contradiction.

### Dislocated vs. severed

Rabbi Abba himself then proposed the resolution: *dilma shani leih bein shmuta l'chatucha* — perhaps for Rav there is a distinction between dislocated and severed. The analogy to *behemot* is not applied uniformly across all hind-leg *tereifot*. When it comes to a dislocated thigh, we do not draw the parallel to *behemot*, and therefore a dislocated thigh of a bird is kosher. When it comes to the severed *tsomet ha-gidim*, we do draw the parallel, and that remains a *tereifah* even in a bird. The application of mammalian *tereifot* to birds is thus selective rather than categorical in this domain.

### Rav's explicit rule

Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba then challenged Rabbi Abba: *v'at mefaraish shemateta d'Rav* — you are speculating about Rav's position based on your own *sevara*? To which Rabbi Abba responded: Rav did not need to be reconstructed through logical inference. *befeirosh amar rav: shmuta kesheira, chatucha pesula* — Rav explicitly stated this very distinction: dislocated is kosher, severed is *pasul*. And, Rabbi Abba adds, *v'al titmah* — do not be astonished by this. One cannot make a *kal v'chomer* argument from one type of injury to another: *chatucha mikan u'metah, chatucha mikan v'chayah* — you can sever an animal in one location and it will die, sever it in another location and it will survive. The biology of death from injury is not amenable to simple hierarchical inference, and so the distinction Rav drew is coherent on its own terms.

---

## Abba reports to Zeira

### Full recapitulation

When Rabbi Abba subsequently made his way up to Eretz Yisrael, he found Rabbi Zeira sitting and teaching: *amar Rav Huna amar Rav, shmutat hayerech b'of tereifa* — that a dislocated thigh in a bird is a *tereifah*. Rabbi Abba addressed him: *chayei d'mar, m'yoma d'salik mar l'hacha* — by the life of the master, from the day you made *aliyah* and left us in Bavel, let me tell you what transpired. *hevei lan pitcha puma kamei d'rav huna* — we had the opportunity to open our mouths before Rav Huna, to put the question to him directly. And *v'shailneih*, we asked him — and he told us *shmutat yerech ba'of kesheira*, that it is kosher.

Rabbi Abba then recounts the entire sequence of events: the encounter with Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba examining the *tsomet ha-gidim*; his challenge based on Rav Huna's ruling; Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba's counter-appeal to the *mishna* and his tradition that Rav said *vechen ba'of*; the silence that followed when the contradiction within Rav's teachings was pointed out; Rabbi Abba's own proposal that Rav distinguished between dislocated and severed; and finally the revelation that this was not merely logical inference but Rav's explicit formulation — *befeirosh amar Rav: shmuta kesheira, chatucha pesula*. The conclusion reached in Bavel was clear: the *tsomet ha-gidim* is a problem, but a dislocated thigh is not. What is striking throughout is the recurring theme of competing traditions — not merely halachic debates between authorities, but different reports claiming to represent what the same authority said.

### Zeira's traditions

Rabbi Abba then turned to Rabbi Zeira: *ve'at mah beyadecha* — and you, what traditions have you accumulated here in Eretz Yisrael? For his part, Rabbi Zeira reported two traditions. First: *rav chiya bar ashi amar rav, shmutat yerech ba'of treifa* — yet another tradition in Rav's name declaring a dislocated thigh to be a *tereifah*. Second, and moving beyond the debate about Rav: *rabbi yaakov bar idi amar rabbi yochanan, shmutat yerech ba'of treifa* — Rabbi Yochanan himself held that a dislocated thigh in a bird is a *tereifah*.

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi added a remarkable comment: *ilmalei havei Rabbi Yochanan be'atreih dechorei bah chavruta lehatiro, lo parchi* — had Rabbi Yochanan been present in the place where his colleagues ruled to permit it, he would not have resisted — meaning, had he been in the presence of authorities of sufficient stature who ruled leniently, he would have deferred to them. The implication is that those who permitted it were of such weight that Rabbi Yochanan would have yielded.

### Chanina's chicken

This leads to the identification of those greater authorities. *de'amar rabbi chanina amar rebbi: shmutat yerech ba'of kesheira* — Rabbi Chanina transmitted a ruling of *rebbi* himself, the editor of the *mishna*, that a dislocated thigh is kosher. And this was not merely a theoretical position: Rabbi Chanina once had a chicken whose thigh was dislocated, he brought it before *rebbi*, and *rebbi* declared it permissible. Rabbi Chanina preserved the chicken in salt and used it as a teaching tool, taking it out before his students and saying *zeh hitir li Rebbi, zeh hitir li Rebbi* — this is the chicken that *rebbi* declared permissible for me. The concrete, tangible demonstration — here is the actual chicken — reflects something about the nature of halachic transmission, and about Rabbi Chanina's commitment to anchoring abstract rulings in physical, teachable reality.

Given all of this — the tradition from Rav's own explicit statement, the story of *rebbi*'s ruling, and the implication that Rabbi Yochanan would have deferred had he been present at such a ruling — the Gemara would seem to be heading unmistakably toward the conclusion that a dislocated thigh is kosher.

---

## Ruling: treifah

### Widespread practice

And yet: *leis hilchasa k'chol hani shmaatsa* — we do not rule in accordance with any of this entire preceding discussion.

### Trachea hole sizes

The Gemara pivots to a related discussion that illuminates the principle underlying this reversal. Rabbi Yossi ben Nehorai asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *kideira kama b'kama* — how large a hole in the trachea constitutes a *tereifah*? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi replied that it is an explicit *mishna*: up to the size of an Italian *issar* coin is acceptable; beyond that it is *pasul*.

### Sheep survival case

Rabbi Yossi ben Nehorai then challenged this with an empirical case: did we not have a young sheep in our neighborhood that had a hole in its trachea, and they fashioned for it a kind of reed covering to bandage the hole, *v'chayesa* — and it survived? How can an animal with a hole in the trachea above the permissible size be a *tereifah*, when this one lived even with such a hole?

The challenge rests on a principle that the Gemara has previously asserted: if an animal is truly a *tereifah*, it cannot survive even with medical intervention. Indeed, earlier in the Gemara, when discussing why a hunter's strike that kills an animal in a certain location does not generate a *tereifah* designation, the Gemara responded that if one were to apply medicine the animal would live — implying that a genuine *tereifah* cannot be saved by medicine. Here then is an animal with a textbook *tereifah* wound that was treated and survived.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's response is to cite the case of *rebbi shimon ben chalafta* and his chicken with the dislocated thigh, similarly treated with a reed splint and surviving. That case is a *halacha ravacha b'Yisrael* — a widespread practice throughout Israel — that a dislocated thigh in a bird is a *tereifah*, regardless of the empirical evidence of survival. How do we deal with the survival? *ela mai is lach l'meimar: toch shneim asar chodesh havei* — one must say it died within twelve months.

### Twelve-month rule

This is where the Gemara formally introduces and crystallizes the principle of the twelve-month timeframe: a *tereifah* does not necessarily die immediately. The claim is that a *tereifah* animal will not survive beyond twelve months. Thus when an animal that is halachically a *tereifah* is observed to have survived for some period, the response is not that the *tereifah* status is wrong, but that it will die within a year. *hacha nami toch shneim asar chodesh havei* — the same answer applies to the sheep with the tracheal hole: it survived for a time, but we must assume it died within the year.

This ruling carries significant weight beyond the specific case. After all of the extensive discussion — multiple traditions in Rav's name, the explicit ruling attributed to Rav himself, the story of *rebbi* and Rabbi Chanina's salted chicken — the Gemara nonetheless reverses course. The driving force appears to be not the theoretical halachic analysis but rather *halacha ravacha b'Yisrael*, the widespread established practice. The phrase *b'Yisrael* is telling: it suggests not merely rabbinic *psak* but something that has become the deeply embedded communal norm. How such a practice became entrenched — whether through cautious rabbis ruling *l'chumra*, through communities asking *shailos* that consistently produced stringent answers, or through some other dynamic — is not always easy to determine. But the tension between theoretical analysis and accepted practice is real, and the Gemara here strongly weights the latter.

The twelve-month rule itself opens a further layer of complexity. The Gemara's position seems to be that a *tereifah* animal will die within twelve months without exception. This is not merely a statistical claim — it appears to be treated as absolute. The implication is that no individual animal can be an exception, and that medical intervention cannot change the outcome. These positions will generate serious challenges, particularly from the *rishonim*, who will encounter animals with apparent *tereifah* conditions surviving well beyond a year, with and without intervention. The appropriate response to such evidence is already prefigured here: the Gemara does not entertain the possibility of exceptions, and dismisses the contrary evidence by assuming death occurred within the year. That methodological stance — the rejection of empirical counter-evidence in favor of halachic authority — will define the field of *tereifot* for the next two thousand years.

---

## Shimon tests halacha

### Down feather test

The Gemara introduces a character sketch: *amru alav al Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta she'askan bidvarim haya* — they said of Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta that he was deeply involved in testing things out, that he wanted to subject claims to empirical examination. The Gemara illustrates this with two episodes. The first concerns a position of Rabbi Yehuda stated in our *mishna*: *nitla hanotzah pesula* — if a bird has lost its down, it is *pasul*, a *tereifah*. Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta set out to disprove this.

He had a chicken from which the down had been removed. He kept it near the oven to maintain warmth, and covered it with a smelter's apron — a thick, heavy material used by ironworkers — to keep the bird warm and protected.

### Chicken survives

*Vegidlah knafayim acharonim yoseir min harishonim* — the chicken grew new feathers that were superior to the original ones, and it survived. From this Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta concluded that Rabbi Yehuda was wrong: a bird missing its down is not a *tereifah*, in support of the *chachamim* who disagreed with Rabbi Yehuda's position.

### Treifah improving

The Gemara raises a challenge to this line of reasoning: *vedilma kasavar Reb Yehuda treifa meshabbachas* — perhaps Rabbi Yehuda holds that even a *tereifah* animal can improve in some respects. If so, the chicken's recovery would not disprove *tereifah* status; it would merely demonstrate that a *tereifah* can experience improvement. The Gemara rejects this: *im kein bimidi dimitrefah bah* — even granting that other parts of a *tereifah*'s body might compensate for the original defect, no one would maintain that the specific organ or feature that defined the *tereifah* condition can be restored to a state better than it was originally. Here, the very feathers that were the supposed basis of the *tereifah* were restored in superior form. This goes beyond *treifa meshabbachas* in other dimensions of the animal's health — the injury itself reversed and improved upon itself. On what basis, then, can one call it a *tereifah* at all?

It is worth noting that in this episode, Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's empirical test served to support the *chachamim* against Rabbi Yehuda — he was not attempting to overturn an established halachic consensus, but rather to vindicate one rabbinic position over another. The second episode is of a rather different character.

---

## Ant king experiment

### Proverbs experiment

The verse in *mishlei* (Proverbs) instructs: *leich el nemala atzel, re'ei deracheiha, vehocham* — go to the ant, O lazy one, see its ways and become wise. The verse then specifies: *asher ein lah katzin soteir umosheil* — it has no officer, judge, or ruler; yet it prepares its food in the summer without anyone commanding it. This is presented as a *mashal* about industriousness in the absence of external authority. Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta — *askan bidvarim* that he was — decided to test whether the premise of the verse was empirically accurate: *eizel achzei i vadai hu delais lah malka*, let me go and verify whether ants truly have no king.

### Scout ant tagged

*Azal bitkufas Tammuz* — he went in the summer season. He spread his cloak over an anthill to create shade on a sunny day. One ant emerged — a scout — and Rabbi Shimon tagged it with a distinguishing mark, much as a scientist might tag an animal for tracking purposes. The ant returned to the colony, and based on what followed, one can infer it communicated to its fellows that the area outside was shaded and safe: *nefalti tulla*, it's shady out there.

### Scout killed

All the ants emerged from the hill. At that moment Rabbi Shimon removed his cloak, exposing them all to direct sunlight. The ants, discovering they had been misled, turned on the scout: *nafalu lei v'katlei* — they fell upon it and killed it. From this, Rabbi Shimon concluded: *sh'ma mina, leis lehu malka* — ants have no king. The lynching proceeded without any judicial process or royal sanction. Had there been a king, *harman d'malka l'va'u* — the ants would have required a royal decree before executing the offending scout.

### Challenges to proof

Rav Acha the son of Rava challenged Rabbi Shimon's inference before Rav Ashi with three objections. First: *v'dilma malka hava behadayhu* — perhaps the king was himself among the mob that executed the scout, and thus royal authorization was implicitly present. Second: *harman d'malka hava nekita* — perhaps a standing royal decree already existed authorizing immediate execution of any ant that caused harm to the colony. Third: *bein malka l'malka hava* — perhaps the colony happened to be in an interregnum, a period between kings, accounting for the absence of formal royal process. This last challenge is underscored by the verse: *bayamim hahem ein melech b'Yisrael, ish hayashar b'einav ya'aseh* — in those days there was no king in Israel; each man did what was right in his own eyes. A system may normally have kings and law, but in the gaps between rulers, anarchy can prevail.

---

## Trust authority

### Trust Solomon

*S'moch a-heimnusa d'Shlomo* — just trust King Solomon. The Gemara's answer to Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta is not to refute his experiment on its merits, but to question whether the experiment was necessary at all. If Solomon said it, trust him. Do not conduct empirical tests to verify what authoritative tradition has already established.

The designation *askan bidvarim* — deeply involved in things, one who tests things out — carries a sense that is less than entirely complimentary. It reflects a disposition that the Gemara here seems to view with some ambivalence: a scholar who feels the need to verify received knowledge through direct observation. The Gemara's response to this disposition is fundamentally pre-empirical: knowledge comes from authority, and the authority of a Solomon or of the sages does not require experimental confirmation.

### Tosafot explains

Tosafot, however, reads Rabbi Shimon's motivation more charitably. He says: *shani hacha sheba levarer ulehodia eich yada Shlomo* — this case is different, because Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta came not to disprove Solomon but to confirm him, to demonstrate *how* Solomon knew what he knew. He was not a skeptic with an axe to grind; he accepted the truth of the verse and simply wanted to understand and illustrate the mechanism by which it was true. Even so, the Gemara's response holds: empirical confirmation is unnecessary. Even if you are trying to confirm rather than refute, you should simply trust authority without needing to verify it experimentally.

### Student mocks sages

A parallel case reinforces this point. In *masechet ta'anit*, a student hearing Rabbi Yochanan describe the wonders of the messianic era expressed doubt — implying that without seeing it he could not believe it. Subsequently, the student encountered something in the natural world that seemed to confirm the possibility of Rabbi Yochanan's description. Rabbi Yochanan rebuked him: *im lo ra'isa lo he'emanta, m'lagleg al divrei Chachamim ata* — if you could not believe without seeing it, you are a mocker of the words of the sages. The demand for empirical proof before accepting the teaching of sages is itself presented as a form of disrespect.

The contrast between this student and Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta is the contrast between skepticism and enthusiasm: the student doubted the sages until proven right; Rabbi Shimon accepted them and wanted to confirm them. Yet both are told the same thing: trust, and do not require empirical validation.

### Authority vs. observation

This brings into sharp relief a tension that runs through the entire daf and indeed through the halachic tradition more broadly. The field of *tereifot* as it developed over the following centuries proceeded precisely as the Gemara here would have it: empirical counter-evidence was routinely dismissed, animals that survived in apparent contradiction of *tereifah* status were assumed to have died within the year, and medical intervention was treated as halachically irrelevant. The *rishonim* would struggle with this when confronted with unavoidable empirical challenges — animals with textbook *tereifah* conditions surviving well beyond twelve months, with and without treatment — and they did so within the same methodological framework: not by revising the halachic categories based on new observations, but by finding ways to reconcile or deflect the observations in favor of the inherited tradition.

That framework is precisely what the Gemara here articulates and defends. The twelve-month rule, which the Gemara has now formally introduced as the operative timeframe for *tereifah* survival, will receive further development in the material ahead. The discussion to this point has established the rule's existence and its function as a bulwark against empirical challenge; the next section of the Gemara will examine more closely the specifics of that timeframe and what it demands of us as a halachic category.

---

---

# Hullin 58

## Treifa Lifespan

### Rav Huna's Standard

The daf begins at the bottom of 57b, where the Gemara takes up a question that had been alluded to earlier in the chapter: in what timeframe does a *treifa* die? The issue had already surfaced when empirical evidence arose that an animal had not died, and the response offered was that it must have died within the year — that being sufficient for *treifa* status. Now the Gemara addresses the question directly.

*Amar Rav Huna: siman le'treifa yud-beis chodesh* — Rav Huna teaches that twelve months is the indicator for a *treifa*. This does not mean that any animal dying within twelve months was a *treifa*, since it may have died from other causes entirely. Rather, the ruling operates in the reverse direction: if there is a *safek* whether an animal is a *treifa* and it survives for twelve months, one may conclude it is not a *treifa* — and proceed to *shecht* it. The twelve-month threshold thus has practical relevance specifically in cases of *safek treifa*.

### Tosefta Debate

The Gemara immediately challenges this with a *meteiv* from a *tosefta* that presents multiple different indicators for determining *treifa* status. The first opinion in the *tosefta* states: *siman le'treifa kol she'eina yoledes* — an indicator of a *treifa* is that it does not give birth. This formulation is admittedly imprecise, since many animals cannot give birth for reasons entirely unrelated to being a *treifa* — old age or independent fertility problems, for instance. The teaching must therefore be read in its positive form: when an animal *does* give birth, that is evidence it is *not* a *treifa*.

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabban Gamliel offers a different indicator: *meshabbachas ve'holechet beyadua she'hi keshaira* — if after an injury the animal's health progressively improves, it is kosher. Conversely, *misnavveves ve'holechet beyadua she'hi treifa* — if the animal's health continues to decline, it is a *treifa*. Notably, Rabban Gamliel does not specify that the animal will die, which raises a broader question about the underlying logic of these opinions.

One must ask: are these indicators — inability to give birth, declining health — simply diagnostic tools for identifying that a wound was indeed fatal? That reading would be consistent with the principle that a *treifa* cannot survive. Alternatively, perhaps these opinions do not accept that principle at all, and instead define *treifa* by functional criteria: an injury that causes infertility, or that causes progressive deterioration. The difficulty with the infertility criterion, however, is that the Gemara elsewhere is explicit that an animal missing a womb is *not* a *treifa*. It therefore cannot be that any injury leading to infertility constitutes a *treifa*. The simpler reading remains that all opinions agree in principle that a *treifa* will die; what they debate is how to determine whether a particular doubtful injury is fatal, and these physiological markers — fertility and health trajectory — serve as the practical tests.

### Rabbi Meir

A third opinion in the *tosefta* is attributed to *rebbe* or, in some versions, to Rabbi Meir: *siman le'treifa shloshim yom* — if the animal does not die within thirty days, it is not a *treifa*. This raises an obvious difficulty.

### Empirical Challenge

The Gemara records the objection directly: *ve-lo harbeh miskayyemes shtayim ve-shalosh shanim?* — are there not many animals that survive two or three years? This is the empirical challenge. Importantly, those raising this objection are not proposing two or three years as an alternative timeframe; they are arguing that since animals with such injuries sometimes survive that long, no single fixed period can serve as a reliable threshold. The implication may be that one should rely instead on qualitative indicators — does the animal's health improve, can it give birth — rather than on a specific duration.

This brings the problem back to Rav Huna. Even if thirty days is too short, how can Rav Huna assert twelve months when some animals demonstrably survive their injuries for two or three years?

### Seasonal Theory

The Gemara answers: *tannai hi* — it is a dispute among *tannaim*, meaning yet another *braita* is brought to bear. The *braita* records a case cited by Rabbi Yosi ben HaMeshullam: in a place called Invo, a person suffered a perforated skull. Medical intervention was applied — Rashi explains a hardened gourd was used as a kind of covering, a plaster of sorts — and the person survived. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar dismisses the proof: *misham raya?* — that was in the summer, *yemos hachamah haya*, and *de'keivan de'asa alav yemos hageshamim miyad mes* — once winter came upon him, he died immediately.

This is the basis for Rashi's explanation in support of Rav Huna's twelve-month standard: any injury that constitutes a *treifa* will necessarily prove fatal when the seasons turn. A particular season may not exacerbate the wound, but over the course of a full year every season will arrive, and one of them will. After twelve complete months, if the animal has survived, it has weathered every seasonal condition and thus demonstrated it is not a *treifa*.

This explanation gives rise to a noteworthy question raised by later *poskim*: if the twelve-month rule is about seasonal exposure, then in a leap year (*ibur*) with thirteen months, should one wait thirteen months rather than twelve? The Gemara consistently says twelve months, not a *shanah*, suggesting the number itself — rather than the concept of a full seasonal cycle — is determinative. What the answer would be in a climate with effectively no seasonal variation, like certain consistently temperate regions, is left unresolved.

---

## Treifa Fertility

### Rav Acha Position

*Amar Rav Acha bar Yaakov: halacha treifa yoledes u'meshabbachas* — the ruling is that a *treifa* can give birth and can improve in health in other respects. This is a striking ruling. It means that observing an animal giving birth or seeing its health improve cannot serve as evidence that it is not a *treifa*, since these phenomena are consistent with *treifa* status.

Before proceeding, it is worth clarifying what this discussion does and does not mean. It does not mean that when an animal's health improves or it gives birth with no evidence of injury, one should suspect it of being a *treifa*. Nor — and this is crucial — does it mean that if an animal clearly has a *treifa* injury (a punctured lung, for instance) and then survives twelve months, gives birth, or improves in health, one can retroactively declare it kosher. The *rishonim* themselves were confronted with empirical evidence of animals with established *treifa* conditions surviving, and no authority suggested that such evidence could override the established category. A *ma'aseh nissin* — a miraculous exception — does not alter the *halacha*. (The Maharshal does suggest that perhaps ninety-nine percent of animals with *treifa* injuries will die, and there is a small percentage of outliers, which reconciles the principle with contrary evidence without disturbing the ruling.)

The only context in which these tests are halachically operative is where there is genuine doubt — a *safek treifa* — such as when an animal was clawed (*drusa*) and it is unknown whether the membrane was punctured. In such cases, if the animal survives or gives birth, that evidence resolves the *safek*.

There is also a significant and somewhat surprising ruling that emerges from the *poskim*: if there is a dispute among halachic authorities (*machlokes haposkim*) whether a particular type of injury constitutes a *treifa*, one may invoke empirical evidence — that animals with this injury consistently survive twelve months — to rule in favor of those authorities who hold it is not a *treifa*. This is not overriding an established Talmudic *treifa* category; it is using evidence to adjudicate between positions in an unresolved halachic dispute. What one cannot do is use such evidence to override something that has been established by tradition as definitively a *treifa*.

### Ameimar Eggs

*Amar Ameimar: hanei beiei d'treifa* — Ameimar addresses the case of eggs from a hen that is a *treifa*. The general principle is that a food product from an animal that is not kosher — even a kosher species rendered non-kosher by being a *treifa* — is itself not kosher. Milk from a *treifa* cow and eggs from a *treifa* hen are both forbidden.

### First Cluster

*Shachala kama asira* — the first cluster of eggs is forbidden. The reasoning: when the hen was attacked and became a *treifa*, it was already carrying eggs. Those eggs, carried within the hen at the moment she became a *treifa*, are treated as part of her body and therefore take on her status. The first cluster is forbidden.

### Later Eggs Permitted

*Mikan v'eilach havi lei zeh v'zeh goreim u'mutar* — from that point forward, however, subsequent eggs fall under the principle of *zeh vezeh goreim* and are permitted. This principle applies to fertilized eggs — where the concern would be the developing chick. What causes the chick to develop? Both the contribution of the mother and the contribution of the father. Even though the mother is a *treifa*, the father is not, and when there are two contributing causes — one forbidden, one permitted — the product is not considered exclusively a product of the forbidden source. This is *zeh vezeh goreim mutar*: two causes, and therefore permissible.

One might object that the mother remains a *treifa* throughout and continues producing *treifa* ova. But the point is that when fertilized eggs are in question and one is interested in the developing chick, what creates the chick is the combined contribution of both parents. Having one *treif* contributor and one non-*treif* contributor is not the same as mixing a *treif* ingredient into a non-*treif* food. This is something entirely new, caused by both a *treifa* origin and a non-*treifa* origin, and the ruling of *zeh vezeh goreim* is that it is permitted.

The counterintuitive element here is worth noting. One might have thought the logic runs the other way: the eggs the hen was carrying *before* becoming a *treifa* should be fine, since they were in a kosher hen; the eggs produced *after* she became a *treifa* should be forbidden, since they are growing in a *treifa* hen. The Gemara rejects this intuition, applying something analogous to *ubar yerech imo*: the egg being carried at the moment the hen became a *treifa* is treated as part of the mother, just as a *shechita* of the mother covers the fetus. But what comes afterward is viewed in the context of the developed chick and the father's contribution — hence *zeh vezeh goreim* applies and those later eggs are permitted.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

*Aisi Rav Ashi l'Amemar* — Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar from the well-known agreement between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the egg of a *treifa* hen. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about an egg found in a *neveilah* — a hen that was killed without *shechita* and is therefore *neveilah*. When such a hen is opened and a fully formed egg is found inside — complete enough that, as the Gemara describes, *kemosa nimkeres bashuk*, it could be sold in a marketplace — is it considered part of the mother and thus *neveilah*, or is it so complete that it is already independent of the mother and therefore kosher? That is the *machlokes*.

However, they agree — *veshavin beveitzas treifa she'asura* — that the egg of a *treifa* hen is forbidden. Why is the *treifa* case worse than the *neveilah* case? *mipnei shegadla be'issur* — because it grew while the hen was in a state of prohibition. Meaning: when the hen was attacked and became a *neveilah* — dead on the spot — the egg stopped developing at that moment. But when the hen became a *treifa* and then continued living for days or weeks before being slaughtered, the egg continued to grow inside a *treifa* hen. It is precisely that continued growth during the period of prohibition that makes it forbidden.

But if *zeh vezeh goreim* applies to later eggs, why does it not apply here as well? Why can one not invoke the father's contribution to permit these eggs?

### Egg Types

*Hasam desafna me'ara* — the Gemara answers that the case where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree the egg is forbidden involves an *unfertilized* egg. The Gemara's idiom is that the egg "became fertilized from the ground" — a circumlocution for an egg that has no paternal contribution. An unfertilized egg has only one cause — the mother alone — and *zeh vezeh goreim* has no application where there is only a single source. *d'chad gorem hu* — it is only one cause, and therefore forbidden.

This also resolves a question about the formulation. The Gemara says the egg is forbidden because it *grew* when the hen was already *asura*. One might have assumed the relevant case is an egg she was already carrying when she became a *treifa* — which, as we said, is part of the mother anyway. But the language "*gadla* be'issur" — that it *grew* in the prohibited state — implies the egg came into being after she became a *treifa*. The Gemara presses this point: if the intended case were an egg already present at the time of the injury, the *braita* should have said *gamra be'issur* — that it *completed* growing — not that it grew during the prohibition. The use of *gadla* therefore indicates even a newly generated egg, and the reason it is forbidden despite arguably having a paternal contribution is that it is unfertilized, making it a case of only one cause.

---

## Treifa Offspring

### Sacrifice Question

The Gemara now raises the debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about *vlad treifa* — the offspring of a *treifa* animal — and whether such offspring may be offered on the *mizbei'ach*. Rabbi Eliezer holds *lo yikarev l'gabei mizbei'ach* — it may not be brought as a *korban*. Rabbi Yehoshua holds *yikarev* — it may.

The question is: what is the case? *b'shenitrefa u'levasof ibra* — the animal first became a *treifa* and afterward became pregnant. And then the question becomes one of *zeh vezeh goreim*: the mother is a *treifa*, the father is not, and the offspring results from both. Rabbi Eliezer holds *zeh vezeh goreim assur*: when there are two contributing causes — one forbidden — the product is forbidden. Rabbi Yehoshua holds *zeh vezeh goreim mutar*: two causes renders it permissible.

The Gemara then asks: *ad d'mifligi l'gavoa, liflego l'hedyot?* — why do they only debate whether it may be used as a *korban*? Why not debate whether a layperson may eat it? The Gemara answers: *koach d'heiteira adif lei* — it is a greater *chiddush* to declare something permitted than to declare it forbidden. Forbidding something requires no special justification — it is always the cautious position. It takes real halachic courage, so to speak, to go so far as to permit something. Therefore the *tanna* chose to teach the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua in its most expansive form: that the offspring is *so* unproblematic it may even be offered on the *mizbei'ach*. Symmetrically, one might have framed Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in terms of a layperson to demonstrate how far his stringency extends — that not only may it not be a *korban*, a layperson may not eat it either. But the Gemara's answer is that the *tanna* always prefers to demonstrate the reach of the permissive position.

Implicitly, then, there is no middle ground: the Gemara frames the debate as all-or-nothing. An offspring of a *treifa* via *zeh vezeh goreim* is either fully permissible (permitted even as a *korban*) or fully forbidden (even for a layperson). A middle position — forbidden as a *korban* but permitted for a layperson — is not entertained.

---

## Ravina Position

### Ravina Rejects

*Ravina lo savar lah k'Rav Acha bar Yaakov* — Ravina does not accept Rav Acha bar Yaakov's position. Ravina holds that a *treifa* cannot give birth at all. This fundamentally reframes the halachic application of the fertility test: rather than *zeh vezeh goreim*, the question of whether an animal produces subsequent eggs becomes a diagnostic tool for determining whether the animal was ever a *treifa* in the first place.

### Ameimar Doubt Test

Accordingly, Ravina presents an entirely different version of Ameimar's teaching. In Ravina's version, Ameimar was speaking about *safek treifa* — a doubtful *treifa*. The formulation is: *hanei bei d'safek treifa* — eggs of a hen that is a *doubtful* *treifa*.

### First Cluster Test

*D'shichla kama* — the first cluster of eggs poses a problem, because the hen may have been carrying them before the doubtful injury occurred, making it impossible to determine from those eggs alone whether she is a *treifa*. The Hebrew *shichla* (which Rashi renders *pushta*) appears to refer to a cluster of developing eggs at various stages — a hen carrying multiple eggs at once, depositing them successively as each reaches completion.

So how does one resolve the *safek*? *mashinan lehu* — one puts those eggs aside and waits. *ei hadra v'tana sharainan* — if the hen subsequently produces another cluster of eggs after the injury, then one permits even the first cluster, since her continued egg production demonstrates she was not a *treifa*. *v'ei lo asiran* — if she never produces more eggs, the first cluster is forbidden as well, because the absence of subsequent eggs suggests she was indeed a *treifa*.

### Safek Resolution

This version of Ameimar's ruling uses fertility not as *zeh vezeh goreim* but as evidence to resolve a *safek treifa* from the outset. The halachic force is entirely different: it is not that the offspring of a *treifa* is permissible because the father also contributed; rather, subsequent egg-laying demonstrates that the hen was never a *treifa*, making even the eggs from the first cluster permissible in retrospect.

---

## Treifa Offspring (II)

### Case Reconstruction

Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar (in this second version, per Ravina's reading) from the ruling of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel that the egg of a *treifa* is forbidden. If a *treifa* cannot give birth, how is it possible for a *treifa* hen to have an egg that grew while she was already forbidden? The Gemara answers: *hasam b'shichla kama* — that ruling speaks not of new eggs produced after she became a *treifa*, but of the cluster she was already carrying when she became one. Those eggs continued developing inside a *treifa* hen, and are therefore forbidden.

The Gemara presses further: the *braita* says the egg is forbidden because it *grew* while she was *asura*, which sounds as though the egg came into being during the period of prohibition. If it were merely an egg already present at the time, the *braita* should have said *gamra* — it *completed* growing — not *gadla*, it grew. The Gemara accepts this: *tani gamra* — read the *braita* as saying *gamra*, or understand *gadla* to mean *gamra* in this context. The case is eggs already present when she became a *treifa*, and their continued development inside a *treifa* hen is what makes them forbidden.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Now the Gemara returns to the debate of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about *vlad treifa* — but the case must be reconstructed differently under Ravina's position that a *treifa* cannot become pregnant. If she cannot become pregnant after becoming a *treifa*, then the case of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua cannot be *b'shenitrefa u'levasof ibra* (first became *treifa*, then became pregnant). That scenario is impossible according to Ravina. The case must instead be *k'she'ibra u'levasof nitrefa* — she was first pregnant, and then became a *treifa*.

Under this reconstruction, *zeh vezeh goreim* drops out entirely — the father's contribution occurred before the *treifa* status arose, and he is out of the picture by the time she becomes a *treifa*. The question is solely: does the mother's *treifa* status extend to the fetus she is carrying? Rabbi Eliezer holds *ubar yerech imo hu* — the fetus is like a limb of the mother. Since the mother became a *treifa*, the fetus became a *treifa*.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua holds *ubar lav yerech imo hu* — the fetus is not part of the mother. The mother's becoming a *treifa* does not extend to the fetus. The debate, on this reading, has nothing to do with *zeh vezeh goreim* and is entirely about the principle of *ubar yerech imo*.

### Egg Agreement

The Gemara then notes that even though Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate the status of the fetus, they agree regarding the egg of a *treifa*: *gufa hi* — it is simply part of her body. The egg does not have its own life force. Whereas the fetus, even inside the womb, manifests its own independent vitality — and that is what makes *ubar yerech imo* debatable — the egg has no such independent existence. Tosafot elaborates further on this distinction: physically, the egg is entirely embedded within the hen; the fetus in a mammal is connected to the mother through the placenta and has visible signs of its own life. It is therefore more intuitive to treat the egg as part of the mother than to treat the fetus as part of the mother, and accordingly the egg's status is undisputed by both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

To summarize the two frameworks that have emerged: According to Rav Acha bar Yaakov, a *treifa* can give birth, and the question of whether the offspring of a *treifa* is permitted involves *zeh vezeh goreim*. According to Ravina, a *treifa* cannot give birth, and egg-laying after an injury serves not as *zeh vezeh goreim* but as a diagnostic test for *safek treifa*. Where all agree is that unfertilized eggs — exclusively the product of the mother — are forbidden, as are eggs carried within the hen at the time she became a *treifa*, on the grounds that they are effectively part of her body.

---

## Final Ruling

### Halacha Summary

*Ve-hilchesa: bezachar kol shneim asar chodesh; benekeva kol she'eina yoledes* — the *halacha* follows: for a male, the standard is twelve months; for a female, the indicator is failure to give birth — or more precisely, giving birth demonstrates it is not a *treifa*.

### Phrasing Issues

The formulation is admittedly imprecise. As stated, *kol she'eina yoledes* — all that does not give birth — would be the negative indicator, which is not quite the operative rule; the positive form, *kol she'yoledes*, all that does give birth, is what matters practically. The Gemara articulates it in the negative, which creates some ambiguity. Furthermore, the ruling as stated does not make explicit that for females as well, surviving twelve months is sufficient. One would assume this, but it goes unstated until the *shulchan aruch*, and the *shach* is the one who makes it explicit: of course twelve months for a female is also sufficient, but the Gemara means to add that giving birth within twelve months suffices as well, even before the full year has elapsed.

### Poskim Debates

The *halacha* is that we rule a *treifa* cannot give birth, and therefore a female's producing offspring resolves a *safek treifa* in her favor.
