This generates two related questions debated among the later *poskim*. First, since we rule *treifa aina yoledes*, do we also rule *treifa eino molid* — that a male *treifa* cannot impregnate? This parallel is not discussed in the Gemara and is disputed among the *poskim*. Second, when the Gemara says *aina yoledes*, does it mean a *treifa* cannot become pregnant at all (*aina me'uberes*), or that it cannot carry to term and give birth? The impression from the Gemara is the more expansive reading — she will not even conceive — but this too is somewhat debated.

### Evidence Use

The *poskim* also address the use of empirical evidence more broadly. As noted above, if there is a *machlokes haposkim* about whether a particular injury constitutes a *treifa* — not an established Talmudic category but an unresolved halachic question — and there is empirical evidence that animals with this injury consistently survive twelve months or give birth, one may invoke that evidence to rule in accordance with the lenient *poskim*. One cannot use such evidence to override what has been definitively established as a *treifa* by Talmudic tradition. But for unresolved questions, the evidence is admissible.

The practical context for these tests — twelve months for a male, fertility for a female — is primarily cases of *safek drusa*, *nefula*, and similar situations where the animal sustained an injury of uncertain severity and the internal examination is inconclusive.

### Rambam Exception

The Rambam makes a notable remark in this context. As a general rule, *safek* in *treifos* is treated leniently — animals have a *chazaka* of being permitted, and various grounds exist to resolve doubts favorably. The one area where the *poskim* are distinctly stricter about *safek* is *safek drusa* — an animal that may have been clawed, with possible internal injection of venom. The Rambam explains that *drusa* is the paradigmatic *treifa* of the Torah itself. The classical *treifa*, after all, is an animal mauled by a predator — the Torah's own example. The Rambam's point is that this foundational case carries a stringency that other *safek treifa* situations do not, and therefore greater scrutiny applies to *safek drusa* than to other doubtful *treifa* categories.

---

## Invertebrates

### No Bones Rule

*Amar Rav Huna: kol biryah she'ein bo etzem eino miskayeim yud-beis chodesh* — any creature that has no bones cannot survive twelve months. The Gemara presents this as a related teaching from Rav Huna, extending his twelve-month principle beyond *treifos* to the biological domain of invertebrates generally.

### Wormy Fruit

*Amar Rav Pappa: shma mina mi'deRav Huna* — Rav Pappa derives a practical halachic ruling from Rav Huna's principle, based on a teaching of Shmuel.

The background: the Torah forbids *sheretz hashoretz al ha'aretz* — a creeping creature that crawls on the ground. This is understood to mean that insects found in fruits or vegetables are only forbidden if they have at some point been on the ground. If an insect develops inside a fruit after it has been picked from the tree and never contacts the ground, it is permissible. However, if the insect developed while the fruit was still attached to the tree and growing, then the insect is considered to have been moving in something connected to the ground — and it is forbidden.

Shmuel's ruling: *kishus she'hisli'ah be'avi'ah asura* — a gourd that became wormy while it was still growing on the vine is forbidden, because the worm's movement occurred while the fruit was connected to the ground. The mechanism of detection: since invertebrates cannot survive twelve months (per Rav Huna), any live worm found in an already-harvested fruit must have developed after it was picked, and therefore never was on the ground.

### Date Test

*Hanei tamrei de-chada* — if one has dates that have been sitting in a bowl for more than twelve months (*le-basar treisar yarchei shata*) and then discovers live worms inside them, those worms must have developed after the dates were picked — since any worm present at the time of harvesting could not have survived the intervening year. Therefore *sharyin* — they are permissible.

### Fly Dispute

*Amar Rav: leit baka bar yoma* — Rav states that a *baka* (a type of fly or gnat) does not survive even a single day. *v'leit didva bar shata* — a *didva* (another type of flying insect) does not survive a year.

Rav Pappa then cites a popular folk-tale to challenge the first claim. The story: *sheva shani de'amrah bakta l'bakra* — for seven years, the female *baka* was arguing with the male. She had seen a wealthy man from *mechuza* bathe in the river, emerge, wrap himself in sheets — and the male *baka* had sat upon him and drawn his blood without telling her. How could he have deprived her of this feast? The story implies the *baka* lives for seven years. Is this not a challenge to Rav's claim that it does not survive a day?

The Gemara is unimpressed: *u'letaameich*, if you want to bring proofs from folk-tales, the same tradition says sixty *mane* of iron hung from a mosquito's stinger. *mi ika ihu gufa kama hvei?* — how much does the mosquito itself weigh? Such tales cannot be taken literally. Rather, *b'shani didei* — the seven years is in "mosquito years," and the sixty *mane* is in "mosquito measures," analogous to noting that an ant can lift one hundred times its own weight. In the mosquito's frame of reference, it is seven years; in human terms, it does not live a day.

---

## Extra Limbs

### Hind Leg Rule

*Tnan hatam: behema ba'alat hamesh raglayim, o she'ein la ela shalosh, harei ze mum* — the Mishnah elsewhere rules that an animal with five legs or only three legs has a *mum* and may not be brought as a *korban*. Rav Huna now extends this: *lo shanu ela shechisar v'yiter b'yad* — this *mum* ruling applies only to the foreleg. *aval chisar v'yiter b'regel* — if the hind leg is missing or extra, it is not merely a *mum* but a *treifa*.

A missing hind leg making an animal a *treifa* is already established, since a dislocated hind leg does so. But an *extra* hind leg as a *treifa*? That requires explanation.

### Yiter Principle

*Kol yiter k'natul dami* — anything extra is considered as if it were missing. Therefore, an animal with an extra hind leg is treated as though it were missing a hind leg, and a missing hind leg is a *treifa*.

### Rishonic Problem

This ruling generated significant difficulty for the *rishonim*, who had clear empirical evidence of animals with extra limbs living and not dying as *treifos* are supposed to die. The Rashba suggests a possible resolution: perhaps the principle of *yiter k'natul* does not operate on the same basis as other *treifos*. All other *treifos* rest on the empirical claim that such animals cannot survive. *yiter k'natul* is instead a legal-conceptual principle — extra counts as missing — which does not necessarily carry the prediction of death. Under this reading, the animal may well survive; it is still forbidden as a *treifa* because the legal construct applies. The Rashba himself, however, is not fully satisfied with this resolution and acknowledges the empirical problem remains serious.

### Sani D'Avi

*Hahi chayuta d'havu lah tartei sani d'evi* — there was an animal with two of what is called *sani d'evi*, a chamber near the first stomach where waste accumulates. The case was brought before Ravina, who declared it a *treifa* — *mi-dei d'Rav Huna*, on the basis of Rav Huna's principle: since a missing *sani d'evi* would make it a *treifa*, an extra one does as well.

### Stomach Tubes

However: *v'ei shaphichan l'hadadi, kesherah* — if the fluids flow between the two chambers, it is kosher. When the two chambers are hydraulically continuous, they are effectively one, and there is no extra chamber to invoke *yiter k'natul*.

A subsequent case: *hahu gufsa d'hava nafka mibei kassi l'huvelila* — there was a tube connecting the *beit hakosot* (the second or third stomach) to the next stomach. Rav Ashi wanted to declare it a *treifa*. Huna Mar bar Chiya told him: *kol hanei chivei b'varai hachi it lehu* — this is common in animals; it does not indicate a defect.

---

## Dual Rectums

### Nassan Testimony

*Heid Nassan bar Shila Rav Tavchaya di'Tzippori lifnei Rebbi* — Rav Nassan bar Shila, who served as head butcher in Tzippori, testified before Rebbe: *al shenei benei me'ayim hayotzim min habeheimah ke'echad she'hi tereifah* — if an animal has two large intestines whose waste exits at once, meaning the animal has two rectums, it is a *treifa*. This is striking given that the Gemara elsewhere establishes that certain problems with the rectum — holes in it, for instance — do not constitute a *treifa*. Nevertheless, a fully duplicated exit is treated differently. *u'kenegedam b'of kesherah* — the equivalent in a bird, however, is kosher.

### Exit Proximity

*Bameh devarim amurim sheyotzim bishnei mekomot* — this *treifa* ruling applies only when the two intestines exit through two separate openings. *aval yotzim bemakom echad vekalyan ad ke'etzba kesherah* — but if they exit through the same place and converge to the width of one *etzba*, it is kosher.

### Fusion Debate

*Palgi bah Rav Ami ve'Rav Assi* — Rav Ami and Rav Assi debate what it means for the two to share a single exit. One opinion: *ha d'hadrei ve'arbei* — the two tubes actually reconnect internally, inside the animal, before reaching the exterior, and therefore constitute a single continuous passage. The other opinion: *af al gav d'lo hadrei ve'arbei* — even if they do not reconnect internally, if they exit in such proximity that together they span only an *etzba* in width, that suffices to render it kosher.

The Gemara notes the internal tension: the first opinion integrates naturally with the language *ad ke'etzba* — the tubes reconnect inside and thus exit as a single passage of *etzba* width. The second opinion must interpret *ad ke'etzba* differently: the two separate exits lie side by side — not one below the other — and together measure no more than an *etzba* across. The case of the tube connecting the *beit hakosot* to the *kares* (first stomach) — *hahu gufsa d'hava ma'avra mibei kassi l'karsa* — Mar bar Rav Ashi wanted to permit this by analogy to the previously permitted tube connecting the second and third stomachs. Rav Oshaya rejected the analogy: *atu kulhu b'chada machta machtinhu?* — do you think all cases are decided in the same batch? *heicha d'itmar itmar, heicha d'lo itmar lo itmar* — where it was taught, it was taught; where it was not taught, it was not taught. The first tube was explicitly identified as common and therefore kosher; this tube was not, and the absence of such identification means it is treated as an aberration and constitutes a *treifa*.

The discussion of the principle that extra is like missing — *yiter k'natul* — thus continues to generate challenging applications, and as noted, it has posed significant difficulties for the *rishonim* that remain without fully satisfying resolution.

---

---

# Hullin 59

## Notzah/Down of Birds

### R. Yehuda & Notzah

The daf actually begins a few lines before the *mishnah* on 58b. There the Gemara records: *rabbi yehuda omer im nitlah hanotzah pesulah* — Rabbi Yehuda said that if the down of a bird is missing, it is *pesulah*. This appears in the context of things that are not ordinarily considered *treifah* defects. The term *pesulah* here is understood to mean *treifah* — that missing down, according to Rabbi Yehuda, renders the bird a *treifah*. The Gemara notes that this position was contested, and the story of Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta, who performed an experiment to refute Rabbi Yehuda, is cited in this connection.

### R. Yochanan's Comparison

Rabbi Yochanan draws a comparison: *rabbi yehuda v'rabbi yishmael amru davar echad* — Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael essentially said the same thing with respect to the *notzah* of birds. Rabbi Yehuda's position, just stated, is that the *notzah* is necessary and its absence creates a *treifah* condition. Rabbi Yishmael's parallel view appears in a *mishnah* in *taharos*: *rabbi yishmael omer hanotzah mitztarefet* — the down combines. The question is: combines for what?

### Rashi on Pigul

Rashi understands this *mishnah* in *taharos* as referring to *pigul*: if a *kohen* intends to eat the meat of a bird *korban* together with its down, the down is treated as flesh, and such intent constitutes *pigul*. This reading parallels Rabbi Yehuda's position in the sense that both treat the down as functionally analogous to flesh. Rashi further connects this to the issue of a *gluda* — a skinned cow — which was discussed at the *mishnah* earlier. Just as skin is compared to flesh in the context of *pigul* (though not perfectly equivalent, since skin itself does not create *pigul*), so too missing down is analogous to a removed skin. This is where Rashi makes the comparison: if down is considered like flesh in this limited sense, its removal is akin to the animal having been stripped of its skin.

### Tosafot: Shomer

Tosafot disagrees with Rashi's reading. The *mishnah* in *taharos*, Tosafot argues, is not about *pigul* at all but about the laws of *tumah* — specifically, the minimum size requirement of *k'beitzah* for food to become *tamei*. If one has meat from a bird that does not amount to a full *k'beitzah*, can the down combine with the meat to reach that minimum? Tosafot notes that under the laws of *tumah*, a *shomer* — a protective element such as a nutshell around a nut — can combine with the food it protects to reach the required measure. Rabbi Yishmael is therefore saying that the down qualifies as a *shomer* for the flesh, protecting it, and may thus combine with the meat to reach the required size. The down cannot count on its own; it must be protecting actual flesh, and it is the meat that must constitute the majority. On this reading, the comparison to Rabbi Yehuda's position about *treifah* is more intuitive: in both cases, the down is not itself flesh, but it performs a necessary protective function for the flesh.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava then asks whether Rabbi Yochanan's comparison is actually sound: *dilma lo* — perhaps they are not saying the same thing at all. *ad kan lo ka'amar rabbi yehuda hacha ela l'inyan treifa d'leika midi d'magein alah* — Rabbi Yehuda only applies his position in the context of *treifah*, where without the down nothing is protecting the living bird. But when it comes to *pigul*, he may agree with the rabbis that the down is not considered meat. Conversely, *v'ad kan lo ka'amar Rabbi Yishmael hatam ela l'inyan pigulei* — Rabbi Yishmael only says his position regarding *pigul*, that the down is considered edible like meat. But when it comes to *treifah*, he might say *agonei lo magnei* — it does not protect — and therefore would not render the bird a *treifah*.

This is Rashi's version of Rava's answer. On Rashi's reading, the distinction is clear: being like meat (*pigul*) is a different question from whether the down protects (*treifah*), and the two cannot be compared. According to Tosafot, however, the *mishnah* in *taharos* is already about *shomer* — protection — which seems to make it a closer parallel to the *treifah* discussion. Tosafot's answer is that the concept of *shomer* in *tumah* law refers to something that protects the food *now*, after slaughter, as it lies there as an edible item. Rabbi Yehuda's position about *treifah*, by contrast, concerns the down's role in protecting the *living* bird. The Gemara's resolution is therefore that what serves to protect the animal while alive is not necessarily the same as what constitutes a *shomer* for the meat once the animal has been slaughtered. Hence the two cases remain distinguishable even on Tosafot's reading.

It is worth noting that Rashi's text apparently read *pigulei* at a key juncture in the Gemara — indeed, Rashi himself writes *pigulei garsinan*, signaling either that he is affirming his own version against an alternate text or that he actively emended the reading. Tosafot clearly worked with a different text, and the two *rishonim* are therefore not only offering different analyses but operating from different versions of the Gemara.

---

## Fatal Non-Treifah

### Final Mishnah Intro

The final *mishnah* of this entire section addresses a point that has underlain the discussion throughout: *treifah* does not simply mean that an animal will die. An animal can die from old age or illness without being a *treifah*. The category of *treifah* is specifically tied to a fatal type of wounding or injury, and this *mishnah* draws the distinction explicitly.

### Fatal Conditions List

The *mishnah* enumerates several conditions that may prove fatal to an animal yet do not constitute a *treifah*: *achuzas ha-dam* — a blood clot; *ha-me'ushenes* — inhalation of smoke; *ha-metzunenah* — chills or frostbite; eating *hordufni* — some type of plant that burns through the inner organs; eating *tzoas tarnegolim* — chicken dung, presumably a concern about parasites or bacteria; and drinking *mayim ra'im* — bad water. All of these can lead to the animal's death, but they involve no wound or injury. Therefore, in all these cases, the animal remains *keshera* — it is not a *treifah*.

### Poison & Snake Bite

The *mishnah* then contrasts these with two further cases. If the animal ate *sam ha-maves* — a deadly poison — or was bitten by a snake, it is *muteres mishum treifah* — the animal is not rendered a *treifah* on account of these events, since again there is no wound of the *treifah* type. Nevertheless, *ve'asurah mishum sakanat nefashot* — it is forbidden to eat such an animal because of the health risk to humans. The poison may remain in the meat and endanger whoever consumes it.

This raises an interesting implicit distinction. The earlier cases — bad water, chicken dung, and the like — are apparently not considered a danger to humans who eat the animal, only to the animal itself. The *mishnah* seems to assume that when an animal consumes something harmful to itself, a human who eats that animal will not be poisoned. The snake bite and *sam ha-maves* cases are different: there the poison can remain in the flesh and endanger the human consumer directly. This juxtaposition is striking when placed alongside the Talmudic concern about *mayim megulim* — exposed water — which is always treated as a potential snake-poison risk. The *mishnah* here apparently holds that water contaminated through means other than direct snake contact, even if it sickens or kills the animal, does not constitute a human health risk.

---

## Chiltit & Spices

### Shmuel on Chiltit

The Gemara now proceeds to analyze specific items from the *mishnah*'s discussion of fatal conditions. Shmuel teaches: *hilitah chiltit treifah* — if an animal swallowed *chiltit* (asafoetida), it is a *treifah*. The reasoning is *d'minkevu lehu lemayeha* — because it burns holes in the animal's inner organs. This is a significant ruling: unlike the other items in the *mishnah*'s list, *chiltit* does not merely cause illness and death but actually creates an internal wound, which is precisely the type of injury that generates *treifah* status. The spice is understood to be so acrid that it perforates the intestines.

### Rav Shizbi's Kashya

Rav Shizbi challenges Shmuel from a *beraita* that elaborates on the *mishnah*. The *beraita* lists: blood clots, smoke inhalation, eating *hordufni*, eating chicken dung, drinking bad water — and then adds: *ve'hilitah ti'ah chiltit ve'pilpelin* — and if it swallowed *ti'ah*, *chiltit*, and peppers (presumably hot peppers). It then adds: *o sam ha-maves* — or if it ate poison. In all these cases: *kesherah* — it is kosher. It may die, but it is not a *treifah*. The *beraita* explicitly lists *chiltit* among the non-*treifah* fatal conditions, directly contradicting Shmuel's ruling that *chiltit* creates a *treifah*.

The *beraita* then continues: *hikisha nachash o she'nashcha kelev shoteh* — if the animal was bitten by a snake or by a mad dog, it is not a *treifah* but is forbidden because of *sakanat nefashot*. The question of whether rabies can be transmitted through inadequately cooked meat is genuinely unresolved, and that concern underlies the health-risk prohibition here.

The Gemara therefore identifies a double contradiction: *kashya chiltit achiltit* — there is a conflict regarding *chiltit*, since Shmuel renders it a *treifah* while the *beraita* does not; and *kashya sam ha-maves asam ha-maves* — there is also an apparent conflict regarding poison, since the *mishnah* treats it as a health risk while the *beraita* appears to permit the animal.

### Leaves vs. Seeds

The resolution of the *chiltit* contradiction is: *kan be'alin kan bekartin* — in one case we are speaking of the leaves, and in the other of the seeds. The leaves of *chiltit* may be harmful and ultimately fatal, but they do not perforate the organs and therefore do not create a *treifah* condition. The seeds, however, are so intensely concentrated that they burn through the intestinal walls, creating an actual hole — and it is the seeds that Shmuel has in mind when he rules *treifah*. The analogy to chili peppers is instructive: the flesh of the pepper has a certain sharpness, but the seeds are capable of causing searing burns on contact.

### Animal vs. Human Poison

The contradiction regarding *sam ha-maves* is resolved differently: *ha deidah ha de'adam* — in one case the animal consumed a poison harmful to animals, while in the other it consumed a poison harmful to humans. Certain substances are toxic to animals but pose no health risk to humans who eat the animal's flesh. In such a case, the animal is not a *treifah* and may even be eaten. But if the animal consumed something that is a human poison, then while it still does not create a *treifah* condition, eating the meat is forbidden on account of the health risk. The Gemara then notes: *sam ha-maves debehemah haynu herdufni* — animal poison is essentially the *hordufni* already mentioned in the *mishnah*. The Gemara therefore clarifies that the *beraita*'s reference to *sam ha-maves* in the context of permitted animals denotes animal-specific poisons, of which *hordufni* is one type and other substances are others: *trei gavnei sam ha-maves* — there are multiple categories of animal poison.

### Tea (Tiah) ID

The Gemara asks: *mai ti'ah* — what is this *ti'ah* listed among the harmful substances? Rav Yehudah says it is *ikra demarirta* — the root of *marirta* (or, in some versions, *maridta*), some species of bitter herb. Rashi identifies it as the root of *torah*, though the precise botanical identification remains uncertain.

---

## Dangerous Foods Tales

### Three Measures Warning

Rav Yehudah issues a cautionary ruling: *hai man de'achal tlata taklei chiltit aliba reikanya* — anyone who eats three measures of *chiltit* seeds on an empty stomach, *mishtalach mashchei* — will suffer to the point that his skin falls off. The physiological premise is consistent with the Gemara's earlier understanding that this substance perforates inner organs.

### Rav Avahu's Experience

Rav Avahu reports a personal experience: *uvedidi havah uvda* — this happened to me. He consumed only a single measure of *chiltit*, and *ilu dela yatvi bemaya, mishtalach mashchai* — had he not immediately immersed himself in water, his skin would have come off. He applies to himself the verse *hachochmah techayeh be'aleha* — wisdom keeps its master alive: he may not have been wise enough to avoid eating it in the first place, but he was wise enough to know the remedy.

### Rav Yosef on Sterility

Rav Yosef teaches: *hai man de'achal shitsar beyei ve'arba'in guzei vesheva butita defarchi veshati revi'ta deduvsha bitkufas Tamuz aliba reikana* — one who eats sixteen eggs, forty nuts, seven caper berry seeds, and drinks a *revi'it* of honey, all in a single meal, on an empty stomach, in the summer — *mitakar taya d'liba* — the membranes or sinews around the heart become uprooted, which apparently can cause some form of cardiac trauma or dislodgement.

### Reish Galuta Deer

The Gemara now introduces a narrative: *hahu bar tavia d'ata l'vei Reish Galusa* — a certain deer that was brought to the house of the *reish galuta*, the political head of the Jewish community in Babylonia — *d'hava nifsak karaia basraisa* — whose rear legs were cut or broken. The precise nature of the injury is left somewhat open: it was not necessarily a complete amputation, and the subsequent inspection makes clear that the concern centered on the area of the *tzomas ha-gidin*, the nexus of sinews at the lower knee joint.

### Rav's Inspection

Rav examined the *tzomas ha-gidin* and found it intact — the sinews had not been severed at that critical juncture, and the injury appeared to be below that point. He therefore declared the animal *keshera*, ruling it fit. *savar l'meichal minei b'umtza* — he then proposed to eat from the meat immediately, either raw or very lightly prepared. This in itself is telling: eating from an animal one has just *pasken*ed on demonstrates genuine confidence in the ruling.

### Shmuel's Snake Bite Warn…

At this point Shmuel intervened: *lo chaish mar l'neshichusa* — is my master not concerned about snakebite? His point was that the cut in the leg might not have resulted from a physical blow or amputation but from the bite of a snake, in which case venom could have been injected into the flesh. This is not a *treifah* concern — the organs were not perforated, and the *drusa* category (clawing by a predatory animal) does not apply to biting — but it does implicate the prohibition of *sakanat nefashot*. Rav asked: *mai takansa* — what should be done? Shmuel replied: *naspeiya b'sanura* — put it in an oven. Cook it thoroughly. *d'ihu badik nafshiya* — it will test itself; the result of the baking will reveal whether poison is present.

It is worth pausing on why snake bite does not constitute *drusa*. The category of *drusa* — which does render an animal a *treifah* — is the clawing of a predatory animal with presumed injection of venom through the tearing of the outer skin. The defining feature of *drusa* appears to be the clawing action itself. A snake bite, by contrast, transfers venom through a puncture but without clawing, and it therefore falls outside the *drusa* category. If the bite actually perforated an inner organ, it would create a *treifah* through that separate mechanism. But a bite that penetrates only the outer flesh creates no *treifah* condition — the health risk alone remains.

### Oven Test Result

The meat was placed in the oven: *nafal tilchi tilchi* — it fell to pieces. The disintegration of the flesh confirmed that poison had indeed been present in the meat. Rav was thereby saved from eating it.

### Rav & Shmuel Praise

*Kari Shmuel alei d'Rav* — Shmuel said of Rav: *lo ye'uneh l'tzaddik kol aven* — no harm shall befall the righteous. The providential timing — that Shmuel happened to be present at precisely the moment Rav was about to eat — was understood as divine protection. *kari rav alei d'shmuel* — Rav then reciprocated, saying of Shmuel: *kol raz lo anis lach* — no secret is hidden from you. Shmuel had both the foresight to consider the possibility of poison and the practical knowledge of how to test for it. The mutual praise between these two great contemporaries also illuminates the mode of address: Rav had called Shmuel *mar*, a term used between colleagues, not merely a student addressing a master.

With this narrative the entire *treifos* section draws to a close. The daf has traced *treifos* of *behemos*, *treifos* of birds, and the category of conditions that are fatal but not *treifah*. The final *mishnah* and its Gemara culminate in the principle that *treifah* is defined by the nature of the injury, not merely by whether the animal will die — and that some conditions, even lethal ones, fall entirely outside that category while nonetheless triggering a health-risk prohibition of their own.

---

## Kosher Species ID

### Simanim Intro

Having concluded the discussion of *treifos*, the Gemara now transitions to a *mishnah* that in some ways precedes all the previous material conceptually: before one can inquire into whether an animal is *treifah*, one must first establish that it belongs to a *kosher* species. The *mishnah* opens: *simanei behema vechaya ne'emru min hatorah* — the identifying characteristics of domesticated and wild mammals are given explicitly in the Torah (split hooves and cud-chewing). *vesimane ha'of lo ne'emru batorah* — but the Torah provided no such characteristics for kosher birds; it simply listed the non-kosher species. This creates a significant practical problem: since the identities of the non-kosher birds are no longer known with certainty, and since no positive *simanim* are given, the permissibility of any unfamiliar bird depends entirely on received tradition.

### Kosher Bird Signs

The *mishnah* records: *aval amru chachamim kol of ha-dores tamei* — the Sages declared that any predatory bird is non-kosher. The precise definition of *dores* — predatory — is a matter of dispute among the *rishonim*. Three interpretations are offered: that the bird swoops and seizes its prey; that it holds its prey with one foot while tearing at it with the other; and that it eats from its prey while the prey is still alive. The shared core is that the bird attacks living creatures rather than foraging. Note that the word *dores* is the same root as *drisa*, the clawing that generates *treifah* status — the connection is not incidental.

By contrast, the *mishnah* provides three positive *simanim* for a kosher bird: *kol sheyesh bo etzba yeteira vezefek vekorkavano niklaf tahor* — any bird that has an extra finger, a crop, and a gizzard whose inner lining can be peeled is kosher. What "extra finger" means is itself debated: Rashi identifies it as the opposable rear talon — the small thumb-like protrusion at the back of the foot — while others hold it refers to the elongated middle finger that is disproportionate to the others.

This raises the broader question of whether possessing these three signs is *sufficient* to establish a bird as kosher, or whether the absence of the predatory character (*dores*) is also independently required. This question bears directly on the permissibility of turkeys and other birds for which there is no longstanding tradition — a matter the Gemara will address.

### Split Fingers Sign

Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok adds a negative indicator from the bird's perspective: *kol of ha-holek et raglav tamei* — any bird that splits its toes evenly — two in front and two behind — is non-kosher. This configuration characterizes birds of prey, which require the bilateral grip to seize and hold their prey. The normal kosher bird configuration, by contrast, has three toes forward and one behind.

### Grasshoppers & Fish

The *mishnah* then turns to other species. For grasshoppers: *kol sheyesh lo arba raglayim ve'arba knafayim ve'chartzulayim veknafav hofin et rubo* — four legs, four wings, jumper legs, and wings that cover the majority of the body's length. Rabbi Yossi adds the requirement that it be called a *chagav* — that it belong to the tradition-recognized category of *chagav* — which introduces the same dependency on transmitted tradition that applies to birds.

For fish: *kol sheyesh lo snapir vekaskeset* — fins and scales. Rabbi Yehudah specifies a minimum of two scales and one fin, though what species might possess only those minimum quantities is unclear.

---

## Derived Simanim

### Cud & Upper Teeth

The Gemara introduces a *beraita*: *kol behemah shema'alah gerah, beyadu'a she'ein lah shinayim lema'alah, vetehorah* — any animal that chews its cud, you may know that it has no upper front teeth, and it is kosher. The observation is empirically striking: ruminants lack upper incisors, as one can readily see by looking at a cow, which has lower front teeth but a hard upper palate where front teeth would otherwise be. The claim seems to imply a shortcut: if you observe an animal without upper front teeth, you know it is a ruminant, and if it is a ruminant, it is kosher.

### Camel Exception

The Gemara immediately raises a challenge: *vaharei gamal, dema'aleh gerah hu, ve'ein lo shinayim lema'alah, vetamei* — what about the camel, which chews its cud, and seemingly lacks upper front teeth, yet is not kosher? The Gemara answers: *gamal nivei is lei* — the camel does in fact have those long front teeth, sometimes called fangs or incisors — which is why it is non-kosher. Rashi notes that horses similarly have prominent upper front teeth.

### Statement Correction

The Gemara now recognizes that the original statement was imprecise and inverts it. The statement was not meant to say that cud-chewing tells you about upper teeth. The point is precisely the opposite: *kol behemah she'ein lah shinayim lema'alah, beyadu'a shehi ma'alat gerah umafriset parsah* — any animal lacking upper front teeth, you may know that it chews its cud *and* has split hooves. This is a *siman* that works as a shortcut to the Torah's two criteria: one need only examine the front upper teeth. Since animals without upper front teeth are ruminants with split hooves, the absence of those teeth is sufficient to establish kosher status — subject to knowing the exceptions.

The Gemara also addresses the objection from *shafan* and *arnevet* (the hyrax and the hare), which the Torah lists as chewing their cud yet having no split hooves. These animals, the Gemara notes, do have upper front teeth — consistent with the revised formulation that no upper teeth signals both cud-chewing *and* split hooves. One might note parenthetically that modern zoology questions whether these animals are true ruminants in the technical sense, but the Gemara takes their cud-chewing as given.

### Young Camel Issue

The *ben gamal* — the young camel — presents a genuine difficulty. A young camel has not yet developed those characteristic incisors. It therefore lacks upper front teeth but is not kosher. This is the single exception to the rule. The Gemara responds by invoking the *beraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *v'es hagamal ki ma'aleh gerah hu* — the Torah specifies the camel precisely because it is the *only* cud-chewing animal that does not have split hooves (along with the other species enumerated there: hyrax, hare, and the few others). *shalit b'olamo yodeia she'ein lecha davar shema'aleh gerah vetamei ela gamal* — the Master of the Universe knows that the only cud-chewing non-kosher animals are those explicitly listed. Since those are the only exceptions, and since within that category the only animal whose young would lack upper incisors is the camel, the sole exception one must know in applying the teeth test is the young camel. As long as you can confirm the animal is not a young camel, the absence of upper front teeth is a reliable indicator of kosher status.

### Rav Chisda Scenario

Rav Chisda formalizes this as a practical ruling: *hayah mehalech b'midbar umatz'a behemah sheparsosav hatuchot* — you are traveling in the wilderness, you find an unknown animal, and its hooves have been severed. You cannot apply the Torah's primary *siman*. What do you do? *bodek b'piv* — examine its mouth. *im ein lo shinayim lema'alah, biyadu'a shehi tehorah* — if it has no upper front teeth, it is kosher. *im lav, biyadu'a shehi temei'ah* — otherwise, it is non-kosher. *u'vilvad sheyakir ben gamal* — provided you can identify a young camel and confirm the animal is not one.

This principle is theoretically elegant, though one might ask whether it actually holds empirically across all mammalian species. Rabbi Natan Slifkin, among others, has examined this question and noted that the Torah's lists are not necessarily exhaustive — there are in fact ruminants without split hooves beyond those the Torah enumerates. The Gemara's claim, premised on the *d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* tradition, asserts divine authority for the completeness of those lists; the scientific question remains separate.

### Split Hooves Test

When the animal's teeth cannot be examined — its mouth has been damaged or removed — Rav Chisda provides the next level of the inquiry: *badik b'parsoteha* — examine its hooves. *im parsoteha sedukot, biyadu'a she'hi tehorah* — if split hooves, it is kosher. *u'vilvad sheyakir chazir* — provided you can recognize a pig.

### Pig Exception

Here again the school of Rabbi Yishmael is invoked: *v'es hachazir ki mafris parsa hu* — the Torah specifies the pig because it is the *only* animal with split hooves that does not chew its cud. *shalit b'olamo yodeia she'ein lecha davar shemafris parsa vetamei ela chazir* — the Master of the Universe knows that the pig is the unique exception. This assertion — that the pig is the *only* split-hooved non-ruminant — is in fact supported by modern zoology, unlike the parallel claim about cud-chewers.

### Meat Grain Direction

Rav Chisda provides a final tier of the analysis, for the extreme case where neither teeth nor hooves are available: *badik bivshara* — examine the flesh itself. *im mehalech sheti va'erev, biyadu'a she'hi tehorah* — if the grain of the meat runs in two directions (as one who cuts against the grain in cooking would discover), it is kosher. The musculature of kosher animals runs in multiple directions, creating the characteristic cross-grain pattern.

### Wild Donkey Exception

As before, the Gemara raises the concern: once you admit there is a single exception — the *arod* (wild donkey), whose flesh apparently runs in one direction despite being non-kosher — are there not other potential exceptions? The Gemara responds: *gemiri* — we have a tradition — that the wild donkey is the *only* exception to the meat-grain rule. Unlike the previous two rules, which had scriptural backing through the *d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* tradition, this one rests on received tradition alone, since the direction of meat grain is not a Torah *siman* at all. *avaye* adds that the place to examine this is toward the rear flanks of the animal, where the directional pattern is most pronounced.

---

## Chaya vs. Behema

### Chaya/Behema Intro

The *mishnah* had stated that *simanim* for both *behema* and *chaya* are given by the Torah. The Gemara asks: why are we now discussing *simanim* that distinguish *chaya* from *behema*? For *kashrus* purposes, both are governed by the same criteria. The Gemara explains: *chaya bekhlal behema hi lesimanim* — true, for *kashrus* they are equivalent, but the distinction matters for two other halachos. First, the fat (*chelev*) of a *chaya* is permitted, while that of a *behema* is forbidden. Second, the blood of a *chaya* requires covering (*kisui ha-dam*). Therefore, the *simanim* here are not about *kashrus* but about identifying something as *chaya lehattir chelvah* — a wild animal whose fat is permitted.

### Horns & Hooves

The *beraita* states: *kol sheyesh lah karnayim utlafim* — any animal with horns and hooves is a *chaya*. Rabbi Dosa qualifies this: *yesh lah karnayim, i attah tzarikh lachzor al hatlafiym* — if it has horns, you need not check the hooves; *yesh lah tlafim, tzarikh attah lachzor lekarnayim* — if it has hooves alone, you must also check the horns. For Rabbi Dosa, the horns are the primary indicator.

Why mention hooves at all? According to Rashi, the reference to hooves in the *beraita* serves not to distinguish *chaya* from *behema* but to exclude non-kosher wild animals — like bears — that lack hooves entirely. An animal must have kosher-type hooves to be a valid *chaya*. Rabbeinu Tam offers a different reading: "hooves" here refers specifically to the *chaya*-type hoof — long and slender, like a deer's, as opposed to the broad, compact hoof of a cow. On this reading, the distinctive hoof shape is itself a marker of *chaya* status. Either way, the Gemara's focus in what follows is almost entirely on the horn characteristics.

### Goat Counterexample

The Gemara challenges the sufficiency of horns: *vaharei ez deyesh lo karnayim utlafim, vechelban assur* — a goat has horns and hooves, yet its fat is forbidden because it is a *behema*, not a *chaya*. The Gemara therefore cannot accept the bare presence of horns as sufficient; the horns must have specific characteristics.

### Bundled Pattern

The Gemara proposes: *keruchot beinan* — the horns must be bundled, meaning they grow in layered rings, one layer deposited upon the previous as the horn extends. Looking at these horn cross-sections, one sees concentric growth rings — visually resembling the growth rings inside a tree. This, the Gemara initially suggests, is the hallmark of a *chaya*.

### Ox Counterexample

But: *vaharei shor dekeruchot, vechelban assur* — an ox's horns also grow in this layered, bundled manner, yet it is a *behema* whose fat is forbidden. Bundled growth alone is therefore insufficient.

### Ridged Texture

The Gemara proposes: *charukot beinan* — the horns must be ridged. Certain horns have visible, pronounced ridges running along their length, in contrast to smooth horn surfaces.

### Goat Ridged Issue

The problem recurs: *vaharei ez decharukot, vechelban assur* — a goat has ridged horns and yet is a *behema*. Ridging alone is also insufficient.

### Branched Structure

The Gemara proposes: *mefutzalot beinan* — the horns must be branched, like antlers. The paradigmatic image here is the antlered deer — or more dramatically, the moose — whose horns extend and divide into multiple branches. Moose, like deer, are indeed *chayot* whose fat is permitted, and they are fully kosher.

### Deer Counterexample

But now the exception runs in the other direction: *vaharei tzvi de'ein mefutzalot vechelban muttar* — a deer does not have branched horns, yet it is a *chaya* with permitted fat. Rashi himself acknowledges difficulty here, writing *lo yadana mai ka'amar d'avadei mefutzalot hein* — he does not know what the Gemara means, since deer's horns are in fact branched. Rashi then offers: *venira be'einai* — it seems to him that what we call *tzvi* is not what the Talmud called *tzvi*; the Talmudic *tzvi* may have been what is called in his day a *steinbuck* (identified variously as an ibex-type animal or a South African antelope), whose horns are ridged but not branched. The author of *sichat chullin* adds that Middle Eastern deer in the land of Israel have non-branched antlers, so the identification may simply refer to the indigenous Israeli deer species rather than requiring Rashi's more exotic identification.

### Pointed Tips

The Gemara therefore proposes a fourth criterion: *chadurot beinan* — the tips must be pointed, or according to another reading of Rashi, the base must be perfectly circular. Rashi suggests two possible meanings: either that the horn narrows to a fine point at its tip, or that it is perfectly round in cross-section at its base, unlike the more irregular cross-sections of *behema* horns. Looking at deer antlers, the pointed tips are indeed characteristic.

### Synthesis & Rules

The Gemara synthesizes: *heicha demiftzala, lo dina velo dayana* — if the horns are branched, there is simply no question; it is a *chaya*, full stop. *heicha delo miftzala, beinan keruchot chadurot vecharukot* — if the horns are not branched, then all three remaining criteria must be satisfied: bundled growth, pointed tips, and ridged texture. Furthermore, *vehu demivla chirkayhu* — the ridges must be overlapping, close together, not widely spaced.

### Karchos Goats

This synthesis leads directly into the famous case of the goats of Karchos: *hahi iza dekarchos dehavi bei Reish Galusa* — there were goats of Karchos in the household of the *reish galuta*, from which an entire basketful of fat (*chelev*) had been extracted. The question was whether these were *chaya* or *behema* — could the fat be eaten? Their horns were presumably of the non-branched variety, triggering the requirement to satisfy all three other criteria. The ridges were present but the question was whether they were sufficiently overlapping.

### Karchos Resolution

*Rav Acha asar* — Rav Acha ruled the fat forbidden, treating the animals as *behema*. *shmuel breih deRabbi abbahu achal minei* — Shmuel the son of Rabbi Abbahu ruled it permitted and, true to form, ate from the fat himself to demonstrate his genuine conviction. He applied to himself the verse *mipri pi ish tisba bitno* — from the fruit of your mouth your stomach will be satisfied: his own ruling enabled him to benefit. A ruling was subsequently sent from Eretz Yisrael: *hilchata kevasei deShmuel breih deRabbi Abbahu* — the *halacha* follows Shmuel the son of Rabbi Abbahu, and the goats of Karchos are *chaya*, their fat permitted.

### Respect for Rav Acha

Yet the message from Eretz Yisrael added: *vehizaharu beRabbeinu Acha* — nonetheless, show respect to Rabbeinu Acha. Do not rule against him flagrantly, and certainly not in his presence. *shemeir einei golah hu* — he is the one who illuminates the eyes of the diaspora. The honorific *meir einei ha-golah* — which would later be famously applied to the Maharam of Rothenburg — conveys the stature of a figure whose authority over the diaspora community demands deference even when the formal *halacha* runs against his ruling.

---

# Hullin 60

## Bei Ilai Creatures

### Keresh Overview

The daf begins, picking up from 59b at the dividing point in the middle of the page, with a ruling about a creature called the *keresh*. The *gemara* had previously been engaged in distinguishing between *chaya* and *behema* based on features of the hooves and the horn, and had noted in passing that there exists an animal called the *keresh* — variously pronounced — which possesses only a single horn and whose identity no one can precisely determine, yet which is nonetheless *kosher*. The ruling at the two dots reads: *keresh af al pi she-ein lo ela keren achat mutar* — the *keresh*, even though it has only one horn, is permissible.

### Tagris Lion

Rav Yehuda identifies the *keresh* as *tabya d'Bei Ilai* — a deer from a place called *bei ilai*, which Rashi identifies as a certain forest. The *gemara* then introduces another creature associated with this same place: the *tagris*. Rashi acknowledges that he does not know the original context in which the *tagris* had been mentioned, but proceeds to define it as *arye d'Bei Ilai* — a lion from *bei ilai*.

### Lion Dimensions

Rav Kahana states: *tesha amot havei bein una le-una de-arye d'Bei Ilai* — there are nine *amot* between one ear and the next of the lion of *bei ilai*, a distance of roughly fifteen feet. It is clear from this description that the lion of *bei ilai* is no ordinary creature but something of a mystical nature. This raises an interesting question: if the lion of *bei ilai* is plainly mystical, why do the commentators not similarly treat the *keresh* as a mystical creature rather than laboring to identify it as an actual *kosher* species? The answer lies in the fact that the *keresh* appears in a *halakhic* context, and so identifying it with a real animal becomes obligatory for those who wish the ruling to carry practical force.

Rav Yosef adds that *shit-sar amot havei mashchei d'tabya d'Bei Ilai* — sixteen *amot*, approximately twenty-four feet, is the length of the skin or the body of the deer of *bei ilai*, i.e., the *keresh* with its single horn.

### Giraffe Theory

This dimension of twenty-four feet brings to the fore the suggestion found in the *sichat chullin* that the *keresh* may in fact be a giraffe. The animal is called a *tabya*, a deer, and indeed if one were to describe a giraffe without access to that term — noting its deer-like body structure, its relatively thin and horse-like frame — one would likely say it resembles a deer with a remarkably long neck. Giraffes stand up to nineteen feet and weigh between two thousand four hundred and four thousand pounds, making the identification with a sixteen-*amah* animal at least plausible. The spotted skin might also suggest comparison to a leopard, though the body structure points more toward a deer or horse. The suggestion is, in any case, a fascinating one, even if the identification cannot be established with certainty. As for the lion of *bei ilai* — no comparable naturalistic identification is offered, and Rashi himself confesses he does not know what it is.

---

## Caesar Dialogues

### Lion Comparison

The *gemara* now transitions to a series of exchanges between a Roman Caesar and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya was a second-generation *tanna*, student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, whose colleagues included Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh and whose students included Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael. He thus lived in the period immediately following the *churban*, a historical detail that becomes significant when we consider the nature of these exchanges.

The underlying theme of all these encounters is that the Roman Caesar, operating within a pagan framework of multiple and anthropomorphic gods, consistently attempts to fit the Jewish God into a pagan conceptual framework. He takes seriously and literally language about God that the Jewish tradition understands metaphorically.

The Caesar opens the first exchange: *eloheichem k'aryeh masil* — your God is compared to a lion, as the verse states, *aryeh sha'ag mi lo yira, Hashem Elokim diber mi lo yinavei* — a lion has roared, who shall not fear? The Lord God has spoken, who shall not prophesy? The verse compares the irresistibility of God's speech to the roar of a lion. The Caesar's response is dismissive: *parasha katil aryeh* — a horseman can kill a lion. What is so impressive about your God if He is merely like a lion?

Rabbi Yehoshua responds: *lo k'hai aryeh masil, k'aryeh d'Bei Ilai masil* — He was not compared to just any lion but to the lion of *bei ilai*, which is of a wholly different order. The Caesar declares: *be'ina d'machzis li nihalei* — I want you to show me this lion. Rabbi Yehoshua replies: *lo matzi chazis lei* — you cannot see it. The Caesar insists — *ivra chazina lei* — in truth, I will see it.

### Lion's Roar

Rabbi Yehoshua prayed, and the lion was uprooted from its place. When the lion was four hundred *parsei* from Rome, it let out a single roar: every pregnant woman in hearing distance miscarried, and the walls of Rome fell. This is the meaning of *hashem elokim diber mi lo yinavei* — who shall not be compelled when God speaks. When it had advanced another three hundred *parsei* closer, it let out a second roar: the molars and incisors of all men fell from their mouths, and the Caesar himself fell from his throne to the ground. The Caesar immediately implored Rabbi Yehoshua: *b'matusa minach, bei rachamei alei d'lihadar l'duchsei* — by your entreaty, please pray that the lion return to its place. Rabbi Yehoshua prayed, and the lion returned.

The exchange makes vivid what was meant by comparing God to the lion of *bei ilai* rather than to an ordinary lion. There may also be a pointed subtext here: the Romans were famous for parading exotic animals, including lions, through Rome after military victories in distant lands. To the Roman Caesar, a lion was a trophy, something subdued and displayed. Rabbi Yehoshua's response — that there exist creatures before whom even Rome is helpless — is thus a response on the Caesar's own terms.

### Invisibility Proof

In the next exchange, the Caesar says: *be'ina d'ichzei lei l'elokeichu* — I want to see your God. Rabbi Yehoshua responds with the verse *lo yirani ha'adam vachai* — no man can see Me and live. The Caesar again insists: *ivra chazina lei*. Rabbi Yehoshua then led the Caesar outside and stood him before the sun at the height of summer, the *tekufat Tammuz*. He instructed him: look directly at the sun. The Caesar replied: *lo matzina* — I cannot; the light is too intense.

Rabbi Yehoshua replied: *yoma d'chad mishamshei d'ka'i kamei Kudsha Berich Hu, amart lo matzina l'istakulei bei, Shechina lo kol shekhen* — the sun, which is merely one of the servants that stands before God, you cannot look at directly; how much more so the *shechina* itself.

The Maharsha develops this argument further, noting that the point is not simply that the sun is bright. Rather, light is the least physical of all physical things — it is in a sense the boundary of the material world. If even that which is barely physical cannot be looked upon directly, how much more so that which transcends physicality entirely. This gives the argument its real philosophical force: it is not merely an argument from scale but an argument from the nature of the non-physical.

One might also ask about the use of the term *shechina* here, since this term does not appear in the *torah* or *tanach* as a divine name — only the verbal form, that God *shochein*, dwells. The answer may be that *shechina* specifically denotes God's presence as it is accessible within the world; it is thus precisely the right term to use in this context, since if anything could in principle be perceived, it would be the *shechina*. That even the *shechina* cannot be seen is the ultimate conclusion of the argument.

### Banquet Attempt

The Caesar now raises a third challenge: *be'ina d'a'avid lei nahama l'eloheichem* — I want to prepare a banquet for your God. One commentator, likely the Maharal, observes that the consistent logic of these three challenges is to place the Jewish God within a pagan framework. The first challenge took the lion metaphor literally; the second assumed God was the sort of entity that could be seen; and now the Caesar assumes that God, like the pagan gods, can be fed. This assumption is not entirely without basis even in Jewish thought: the *korban* is described in the *torah* as *lechem isheh*, a fire-offering, a *reiach nichoach*, a pleasing aroma. The difference is that Jewish tradition takes this language metaphorically while the Caesar takes it literally.

The parallel to the challenge about seeing God is instructive. The verse says *lo yirani ha'adam vachai*, and the *rambam* reads this as expressing God's utter non-physicality; but the simple meaning of the verse does not say God cannot be seen in principle, only that seeing Him results in death. Similarly, the *korban* language could, on its plain reading, support the pagan reading. The consistent theme of these exchanges is thus that the Caesar is reading the *pesukim* in their more literal, physical sense, and Rabbi Yehoshua is correcting him by applying the deeper theological understanding.

Rabbi Yehoshua's response to the banquet proposal is: *nefishi chiluvasei* — His troops are so numerous that one could not possibly feed them, let alone God Himself. He is again responding within the Caesar's own conceptual framework rather than directly dismantling it. He then instructs the Caesar to go to the banks of the river Revisa — a wide, open space — and prepare the feast there. The Caesar labored for six months of summer to prepare. Then *ata zika* — a wind came, Rashi explains, as part of Rabbi Yehoshua's plan all along, and *kanshenhu l'yama* — swept it all into the sea. The Caesar spent the next six months of winter preparing again, and then *ata mitra* — the rain came and *tavyei b'yama* — washed it all away.

When the Caesar demanded an explanation, Rabbi Yehoshua said: *hani knushai v'zulchai d'asu kamei* — these are the sweepers and dusters that go before God's troops, as a king's processional retinue would sweep the road and sprinkle water to settle the dust before the king passes. The wind and the rain are merely the sweepers; the main retinue of God has not even arrived. The Caesar acknowledged: *lo matzina* — I certainly cannot prepare a banquet for God if even His sweepers consume a full year's worth of preparation.

The argument here is somewhat indirect; it does not frontally assert God's non-physicality, but it gestures toward the total inadequacy of any physical offering to encompass the divine. The deeper argument — that feeding God is simply a category error — remains implicit, perhaps because Rabbi Yehoshua was meeting the Caesar on his own terms at each stage rather than asking him to abandon his entire theological framework at once.

---

## Daughter's Challenge

### Carpenter Argument

Having concluded the exchanges with the Caesar, the *gemara* now records a separate exchange between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the Caesar's daughter. She said to him: *eloheichem nagra hu* — your God is a carpenter, as the verse says, *hamakareh bamayim aliyotav* — He who lays the beams of His upper chambers upon the waters, building His heavens. If He built His heavens, He is a craftsman, a carpenter.

There is an implicit subtext here, noted in *bereishit rabbah*: the argument that God did not create the world *yesh me'ayin*, from nothing, but rather worked with pre-existing materials — the *tohu*, the *vohu*, the *choshech*, the *mayim* — none of which are explicitly stated to have been created by God. The *torah* says *shamayim va'aretz* but does not specifically record the creation of *tohu va-vohu* or *choshech*. So the daughter's challenge is not merely mockery but carries a theological argument: your God, like any craftsman, had materials to work with.

### Leprosy Curse

She concluded by saying: tell your God *d'na'avid li chada mistorisa* — let Him make me a spool, a small item, just to see what He can actually do. Rabbi Yehoshua replied: *amar lachai* — let it be so. This is already a shift in tone from the Caesar dialogues, where Rabbi Yehoshua resisted being tested. Here he acquiesced, perhaps because her request was less a genuine theological inquiry and more a mockery.

He prayed — *bei rachamei aleh* — and she was struck with leprosy. The *gemara* clarifies what happened next: she was placed in the marketplace of Rome with a spool, because the practice in Rome was that anyone afflicted with leprosy — the medical condition, not the *tzara'at* of the *torah* — would sit in the marketplace with a spool, wrapping and unraveling thread, so that people could see the condition and pray for them. She had asked for a spool; she received one, in the most pointed way imaginable.

### Spool Gift

One day Rabbi Yehoshua was passing through the marketplace and saw her sitting there with her spool. He said to her: *shapirta mistorisa d'yahav lach Elohayich* — is it a beautiful spool that your God has given you? She responded: *eima leh l'Elahach lishkol mai d'yahav li* — tell your God to take back what He gave me. He replied: *elaha didan mehav yahiv mishkal lo shakil* — our God gives but does not take back.

This story is the most cryptic of the three. The Caesar dialogues were clearly organized around the theme of the pagan conceptualization of God. Here the point is harder to locate. One reading is that her challenge was not a sincere theological confrontation but a taunt — she was, so to speak, testing God — and the response therefore took a different form than the careful philosophical engagement of the earlier exchanges. The lesson, if there is one, may have to do with the irreversibility of divine action: unlike the lion that was sent and then recalled, what God gives in the course of providential events is not simply undone on request.

---

## Ox vs Donkey

### Ox Traits

Moving away from the *aggadic* material about *bei ilai* and the Caesar, the *gemara* records a series of practical descriptions attributed to Rav Yehuda. He states: *shor karsetan* — an ox has a wide body, *ufarsatan* — wide hooves, *rav reishia* — a large head, and *rav genovtei* — a large tail.

### Donkey Traits

In contrast, *v'chilufa b'chamra* — the donkey is the opposite in all of these respects: a smaller body, narrower hooves, a smaller head, and a smaller tail.

### Market Knowledge

The *gemara* asks: *lemai nafka mina* — why does this matter? The answer is *lemekach u-mimkar* — for commercial purposes. Rashi explains that this is less about challenging a completed transaction and more about practical buyer's guidance: if you are in the marketplace looking to purchase an ox or a donkey, you should know the characteristic features of each animal, so that if an animal lacks the expected features you know something is amiss. One might also suggest a narrower application: if animal parts are being sold separately — say, an ox tail for cooking — a knowledgeable buyer can distinguish ox parts from donkey parts by their size and shape. In any case, the Talmud's standard approach when physical descriptions do not yield an obvious *halakhic* application is to assign them commercial relevance: knowing what the world looks like is valuable in the realm of commerce and transactions.

---

## Adam's Offering

### Single Horn

The same Rav Yehuda now returns to a theme introduced earlier — the one-horned *keresh* — and connects it to a *midrashic* tradition about Adam HaRishon. Rav Yehuda states: *shor she-hikriv Adam HaRishon keren achat hayeta lo b'mitzcho* — the ox that the first man offered to God had a single horn in the middle of its forehead. This offering is not mentioned in the *pesukim* but is drawn from *midrash*, understood to have occurred after Adam confronted his sin before God. The prooftext is *va-teitav l'Hashem mi-shor par makrin mafris* — it shall be more pleasing to God than an ox, a bull, *makrin mafris*, with horns and hooves. The *gemara* asks: *mai makrin* — the word *makrin* with a *yud* implies two horns. But Rav Nachman responds: *mikeren ketiv* — the word is written without a *yud*, implying a single horn, and read in the context of Adam's offering, this is the animal with one horn.

### Horn Precedence

Rav Yehuda adds a further detail: *karnav kadmu lefarsotav* — the horn preceded the hooves. This is striking because normally a newborn animal is born with its hooves but grows its horns only later in life. This animal, however, came into being with its horn first. The same verse supports this: *makrin mafris* — horns first, then hooves.

### Full Stature Creation

This detail, the *gemara* notes, supports the teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *kol ma'aseh bereishit bekomatan nivreu, l'da'atan nivreu, b'tzivyonam nivreu* — all of the acts of creation were formed in their full stature, with their knowledge or desire, and in their full appearance or beauty.

"Full stature" means that Adam was not created as an infant or fetus but as a fully formed adult, and similarly, the ox of Adam was not born and then grown — it emerged fully formed. If an animal rose up fully formed from the ground in an upright position, its horn, being at the top of its head, would emerge first — hence the horn preceded the hooves.

*L'da'atan* — Rashi explains this either as meaning the creatures were created already possessing developed intellect and instinct, rather than with an infant's undeveloped mind, or that in some sense God consulted the creatures about their form of creation. For animals, the former reading is more natural: the question of where animals' instincts come from is answered by saying they were created with those instincts already present.

*B'tzivyonam* is harder to distinguish from *l'da'atan*. Rashi glosses it as *le-tzivyonam be-dmutan she-bacharu lahem* — in the appearance they desired for themselves. The Maharshal and others note a triple play on the root *tzvi*: *tzvi* as glory (*tzvi hu l'chol ha-aratzot*), as beauty (*u-ltzvi u-letifaret*), and *tzave* in Aramaic meaning desire. The prooftext is *va-yechulu ha-shamayim ve-ha-aretz ve-chol tzeva'am* — read not as *tzeva'am*, their hosts, but as *tzivyonam*, their desire.

---

## Vegetation Logic

### Kal VaCheomer

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa expounds the verse *yehi chevod Hashem le-olam, yismach Hashem b'ma'asav* — God's glory will be forever, God will rejoice in His works — and identifies it as the verse said by the *sar ha-olam*, the officer of the world. Several commentators identify this figure with the angel *metatron*, understood in *chazal* as the angel charged with overseeing the affairs of this world — God's appointed agent over worldly matters. This concept of an angel with such a degree of authority is one that many find theologically uncomfortable from a strong monotheistic standpoint, but it does appear periodically in the *gemara*.

When did the *sar ha-olam* say this verse? *be-sha'ah she-amar haKadosh baruch hu l-mineihu ba-ilanot* — at the moment when God commanded the trees to come forth each according to its own kind. At that moment, *nas'u desha'im kal va-chomer b'atzman* — the grasses and vegetation made a *kal va-chomer* argument among themselves:

*Retzono shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu be-irvuvya* — if God wanted things mixed together, *lama amar l-mineihu ba-ilanot* — why did He demand that trees come forth each according to their kind? *ve-od, kal va-chomer* — and moreover, we can make an inference: *u-mah ilanot she-ein darchan latzet be-irvuvya* — trees, which by their nature tend to stand apart from one another with space between them, and yet God insisted *le-mineihu* — each according to its own kind; *anu al achat kamma ve-chamma* — we, grasses and vegetation, which naturally grow commingled and close together, how much more so should we come forth each according to its own kind. And so *miyad kol echad ve-echad yatza le-mino* — immediately each one came out according to its own species.

This *midrash* extends the earlier theme that creatures participated willingly — and even actively — in the process of creation. Here the vegetation does not merely acquiesce; it reasons from first principles, constructs a *kal va-chomer*, and acts on that inference.

### Officer's Praise

At this moment, *patach sar ha-olam ve-amar* — the officer of the world opened and declared: *yehi chevod Hashem le-olam, yismach Hashem b'ma'asav* — God's glory will be forever, God rejoices in His works. The occasion for this declaration was the spectacle of God's creatures figuring out on their own what God's will was, and acting accordingly.

### Grafting Kilayim

Ravina then poses a question building directly on this *midrash*: *hirkiv shenei desha'im zeh al gav zeh* — if someone grafts two different types of grass or vegetation together, what is the law? Tosafot notes that *kilayim*, the *torah*'s prohibition of forbidden mixtures, applies when one plants two different species of seeds together — wheat and barley, or different vegetable species. But the question here is about grafting vegetation as one grafts trees, and whether that would also constitute *kilayim*.

Rav Chanina bar Pappa's formulation poses two possibilities. On the one hand, *keivan d'lo ketiv behu le-mineihu, lo mechayev* — since the *torah* did not command vegetation to be *le-mineihu*, since that requirement was stated only regarding trees, perhaps there is no prohibition. On the other hand, *keivan d'hiskim yadeihu, ke-man d'chtiv behu le-mineihu dami* — since God expressed approval of what the vegetation did, it is as if it had been commanded, and therefore grafting it together might constitute *kilayim*. The *gemara* concludes *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

This is a striking passage. Not only does it deploy a *midrashic* narrative as the basis for a *halakhic* question, but it invokes the narrative of *ma'aseh bereishit* — the story of creation itself — to determine the scope of *halakhic* categories. The *kilayim* prohibition is explicitly linked in the *torah* to the concept of *le-mineihu*, and here the *gemara* is asking whether the *midrashic* account of how the world was created in its original separateness can expand the application of that prohibition beyond its explicit textual scope.

Tosafot raises an even more interesting possibility: perhaps the question is not about grafting vegetation per se, but about whether this prohibition applies as one of the *sheva mitzvot b'nei Noach*, the seven Noahide laws. There is an opinion that *kilayim* belongs among the Noahide prohibitions, derived from the verse *et chukotai tishmoru* — keep My statutes — understood as referring to statutes already established before Sinai, meaning the original order of creation in which each species was to remain according to its kind. In that reading, the question from *ma'aseh bereishit* becomes even more natural, since Noahide law inherently draws on the order established at creation. This makes the use of the *midrashic* narrative to determine a *halakhic* category considerably more elegant.

---

## Moon-Sun Story

### Co-Kings Problem

Rav Shimon Pazi raises a textual contradiction. One verse says *vaya'as Elohim et shenei ha-me'orot ha-gedolim* — God made the two great luminaries. Yet immediately the same passage reads *et ha-ma'or ha-gadol le-memshelet ha-yom ve-et ha-ma'or ha-katan le-memshelet ha-laila* — the great luminary to rule the day and the small luminary to rule the night. First both are called great, then one is great and one is small. The famous *midrash* resolves this:

*Amra yareiach lifnei HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — the moon said to God: *ribono shel olam, efshar lishnei melachim she-yishtamshu b'keser echad* — Master of the universe, is it possible for two kings to share one crown? The kings here are the sun and the moon themselves, both designated by the *torah* with dominion — *le-memshol*, to rule — and thus both kings. The partnership is inherently unstable because sovereignty is by nature singular. The moon's complaint is that this arrangement cannot stand.

### Dominion Division

God responded: *lechi u-ma'ati et atzmech* — go and make yourself smaller; you will be the subsidiary king. The moon objected: *hoil va-amarti lefanecha davar hagun, amait et atzmi* — because I raised a valid point, I should be the one to suffer? God then offered a consolation: *lechi u-mishli ba-yom u-va-laila* — you will have dominion in both the day and the night, since the moon can sometimes be seen during daylight hours. The moon replied: *deshraga b'tihara mai ahani* — what good is a candle in the daytime? To be present but invisible is no consolation.

### Calendar Role

God then offered a second consolation: *zilu limnu bach Yisrael yamim ve-shanim* — the Jewish people will count their days and years by you. The Jewish calendar operates primarily according to the lunar cycle, and months are reckoned by the moon. The moon, however, was still not fully satisfied, pointing out that the sun too plays an irreplaceable role in the calendar — the seasons are solar, and the calendar is periodically adjusted to reconcile the lunar months with the solar year. The verse itself concedes this: *va-yiheyu l'otot u-le-moadim u-le-yamim ve-shanim* — the *moadim*, the seasons, correspond to the sun, and even there the *moadim* is mentioned first.

The Maharsha notes, and it is worth following his observation, that a subtext runs throughout this *midrash*: the moon represents the Jewish people and the sun the nations of the world. The other nations count their calendar by the sun; the Jewish people by the moon. The moon waxes and wanes, is most prominent at night, and only occasionally visible in daylight — a metaphor for the rhythm of *galut* and the Jewish people's place in the world. The Jewish people's calendar, like the moon, has its periods of fullness and its periods of diminishment.

### Righteous Names

God offered a third consolation: *zil likru tzadikei bishmech* — the righteous will be named after you. *yaakov ha-katan, shmuel ha-katan, david ha-katan* — very often the greatest *tzadikim* bear the epithet "the small one," the humble one. Humility, the quality of making oneself small, is the mark of genuine greatness. There is also an implicit message here for the moon — and, in the metaphorical reading, for the Jewish people — that smallness in this world is not a deficiency but a distinguishing mark of the righteous.

### Divine Atonement

The *gemara* then records: *chazyei d'lo ka mitvatva da'atah* — God saw that the moon was still not appeased. And so God declared: *heviu kapara alay she-mi'ateti et ha-yareiach* — bring an atonement for Me, because I diminished the moon. This is the teaching of Reish Lakish: *ma nishtana se'ir shel Rosh Chodesh she-ne'emar bo la-Shem* — what is different about the goat offering of *rosh chodesh* that the verse calls it a *chatat la-Shem*, a sin offering for God? God says: *se'ir zeh yehei kapara al she-mi'ateti et ha-yareiach* — this goat shall be an atonement for the fact that I diminished the moon.

This is a striking *midrash*. Read with full literal force, it says that God sinned. Even softening the language — understanding it as God acknowledging that something necessary in the ordering of the world nonetheless caused harm, and that a form of reparation is therefore owed — the statement remains remarkable. The *gemara* deploys it to explain the unusual phrasing of *chatat la-Shem* at *rosh chodesh*: the atonement of *rosh chodesh* is not only Israel's atonement but, in some sense, God's own.

In the larger metaphorical reading, this passage suggests that even when the diminishment of the moon — the suffering of the Jewish people — is in some sense necessary or correct, it is not without moral weight. A reckoning is owed. The *rosh chodesh* offering becomes the vehicle through which that reckoning is expressed, month after month, with the moon's renewal.

---

## Prayer Creation

### Timeline Contradiction

Rav Ashi raises a further textual contradiction in the narrative of creation. The third day of creation records *va-totzei ha-aretz desha* — the earth brought forth grass and vegetation. Yet the second chapter of *bereishit* states *ve-chol siach ha-sadeh terem yihyeh ba-aretz* — all the vegetation of the field had not yet come forth, because there was as yet no man to work the ground and no rain had fallen. The vegetation seems to have come forth on the third day, but the second chapter implies it had not yet emerged even before Adam was created on the sixth day.

### Adam's Prayer

The *gemara* resolves: *melamed she-yatzu desha'im ve-amdu al petach karka* — the grass and vegetation came forth from the ground but stood at the very lip of the earth, *ad she-ba Adam HaRishon u-vikesh aleihem rachamim va-yardu geshamim va-tzmchu* — until Adam came and prayed for them, and rain fell, and they grew. The vegetation emerged on the third day but did not complete its growth until Adam prayed.

*Lelamedcha she-HaKadosh Baruch Hu mit'aveh li-tfilatam shel tzadikim* — this teaches that God desires the prayer of the righteous. God created the world in such a way that certain processes remained incomplete, awaiting the prayer of a righteous person to complete them. Adam was created precisely so that he would recognize the need for rain and pray for it, and only through that prayer would the creation be brought to its fullness.

### Nachman's Garden

This principle is illustrated by a practical example: *rav nachman bar papa havi lei ha'i ginasa* — Rav Nachman bar Papa had a garden, *shadi bei bizruni* — he sowed seeds in it, *v'lo tzmach* — and they did not sprout. *ba'a rachamei* — he prayed, *ata mitra* — rain came, *v'tzmach* — and they grew. The parallel to Adam's situation is explicit: seeds sown, no growth, prayer, rain, growth. The story of creation is not merely a cosmological narrative but a pattern that recurs in the lives of the righteous.

### Prayer Mechanism

The Maharsha connects this passage to a deeper *midrashic* tradition. God initially intended to create the world governed entirely by *middat ha-din*, strict justice — the first chapter of *bereishit* uses only the name *elokim*. But God saw that the world could not survive on justice alone, and so the second chapter introduces *hashem elokim*, the divine name that combines justice with compassion. The same phrase, *hashem elokim*, appears in the passage about the vegetation waiting for man to work and pray.

The theological point is that *tefillah* — prayer — is the mechanism through which God introduced compassion into a world structured by justice. The world runs according to its laws; those laws belong to *middat ha-din*. But God built into creation the possibility of prayer, so that through prayer *middat ha-rachamim* can override the strict operation of those laws. Rain is the paradigmatic expression of this: it comes from above, it gives life, and it is not mechanically determined but responsive to the prayer of one who recognizes the need and calls out.

God did not simply want man to exist in the world. God wanted man to look at the world, perceive its incompleteness, and pray. Creation reaches its fullness not through any automatic process but through the encounter between human prayer and divine response. This is, in the end, both the lesson of Adam's first act and the lesson of every garden that waits for rain.

---

---

# Hullin 61

## Shisuah & Torah

### Shisuah Definition

The daf is 61, though the shiur begins a page earlier on 60b. Approximately ten to twelve lines down, the Gemara records a statement of Rav Chana bar Rava concerning the *shisuah*. The *shisuah* appears in the Torah's list of non-kosher animals: *ach et zeh lo tocheilu mima'alei hageirah umimafrisei haparsah hashisuah* — do not eat from those that chew the cud and have split hooves: the *shisuah*, the camel, the hare, and so on. The Gemara elects to read *hashisuah* not as an adjective modifying *mafrisei haparsah* but as the first noun in the list of forbidden animals — a creature unto itself. And what is it? *Beryah bifnei atzmah hi* — it is an independent creature. *Yesh lah shnei gavim ushnei shidra'os* — it has two backs and two spinal cords. Whatever exactly it is, it belongs to that category of animals we have never encountered.

### Moshe's Knowledge

The Gemara then asks: *v'chi Moshe Rabbeinu kanigi hayah o balistri hayah?* Was Moshe Rabbeinu a trapper or a hunter? The word *balistri* derives from the same root as "ballista" — one who hurls projectiles — and *kanigi* is a word for a hunter. The question is pointed: how did Moshe know to include in his list of non-kosher animals a creature so bizarre that he could never have observed it in the natural world? The answer follows: *mikan teshuvah l'omer ein Torah min hashamayim* — here is a refutation of anyone who claims the Torah was Moshe's own composition. Had he invented it himself, how would he have known to mention the *shisuah*?

### Loanwords: Kanigi & Bali…

Having heard this *drasha*, Rav Chisda said to Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi: *zil kesov kanigi uvalistri b'aggadetecha* — go and write down the words *kanigi* and *balistri* in your *aggadeta*, *uperashah* — and make sure you explain them. These are foreign loanwords — Greek, in fact — and not everyone who encounters this *aggadeta* will know what they mean. Presumably when these teachings originated in Eretz Yisrael, the Greek terms were familiar to the audience. But for those transmitting the tradition in Babylonia, a marginal note or an explanation alongside the text was essential so that the unusual vocabulary would not become an obstacle to understanding.

---

## Philistines & Ivim

### Five Leaders, Six Named

In the spirit of recording strange vocabulary with care, the Gemara moves to a related case.
