The book of Yehoshua speaks of *chamesh sarnei Plishtim* — the five Philistine leaders — and then lists six: the Azzati, Ashdodi, Ashkeloni, Gitti, Ekroni, *v'ha'Ivim*. The text announces five and then enumerates six. How is this reconciled? Rav Yonasan says: *arunki shelahen chamishah* — their true, prominent leaders number only five. The word *arunki* is not Hebrew or Aramaic; it is a foreign term, with some manuscript variants reading *adindiki* or similar. The appearance of this foreign loanword is precisely the occasion for what follows.

### Arunki Explanation

Again Rav Chisda said to Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi: *kesov Arunki b'aggadetecha uperashah* — write down this word *arunki* in your collection of *aggadetos* and make sure to explain it. Like *kanigi* and *balistri*, this is a term that could easily become opaque in transmission, and the care taken to record and gloss such foreign expressions reflects the broader commitment to preserving the intelligibility of *aggadeta* across generations.

### Ivim from Teiman

Having raised the *drasha*, it is worth noting how Tosafot resolves the underlying textual difficulty. The verse immediately following the list of the six names reads: *miteiman kol eretz haKna'ani* — from Teiman, the whole land of Canaan. Tosafot points out that the period, so to speak, falls before the word *v'ha'Ivim*: the five are the five leaders of the Philistines, and the *Ivim* belong to the next verse — they came from Teiman, which is a territory associated with a grandson of Esav. This reading is reinforced grammatically: the five Philistine leaders each carry a *yud* at the end of their designation — *ha'Azzati*, *ha'Ashdodi*, *ha'Ashkeloni*, and so on — a form suggesting "leader of such-and-such." But *ha'Ivim* lacks that final *yud*; it does not follow the same grammatical pattern and therefore does not belong to the same list.

The Gemara confirms this with a *Baraita*: *Ivim miTeiman bau* — the Ivim came from Teiman. Why are they called *Ivim*? The *Baraita* offers several explanations. *She'ivtu et mekomam* — they either perverted or abandoned their place. Rashi understands this to mean they left their original land, which was either destroyed or abandoned. A second explanation: *she'ivu lelohut harbe* — they craved many gods, reading *Ivim* with an *alef*, meaning they lusted after the idolatrous practices of the Philistines and were drawn after them. A third: *shekol haro'am ochazato avit* — anyone who sees them is seized by trembling. Whatever the precise etymology, the upshot is clear: the Ivim were not originally Philistines at all but descended from Esav through Teiman, and this reading resolves the discrepancy between five and six.

---

## Torah's Hidden Meaning

### Ivim Description

Rav Yosef adds a vivid detail about the Ivim: *d'is lehu shitsa darei shinei lechol chad vchad* — each one of them has sixteen rows of teeth. This detail returns us to the theme of describing extraordinary creatures and beings encountered in the *aggadeta*. And it sets the stage for a broader point made by Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish teaches: *harbe mikra'ot she're'uyin lisrof* — there are many verses that to an unlearned eye would seem fit to be discarded. They appear trivially historical, antiquarian digressions with no obvious relevance to *halacha* or theology. And yet upon closer examination they turn out to be *gufei Torah* — the very body of the Torah, central to critical ideas. What follows illustrates this principle through the very passage about the Ivim.

### Avimelech Covenant

The verse in Devarim reads: *v'ha'Ivim hayoshvim b'chatzerim ad Aza* — the Ivim who dwelt in Chatzerim until Gaza. One might dismiss this as mere geographical background. *Mai nafka lan minah* — what does it matter? The Gemara answers: it matters enormously. The reason goes back to the covenant between Avraham and Avimelech, in which Avraham swore: *im tishkor li velini ulenachdi* — you shall not deal falsely with me, nor with my children, nor with my grandchildren. Avraham had bound himself and his descendants not to betray Avimelech and the Philistines.

### Kaftoriim & Conquest

If the Ivim were Philistines — which, as we have seen, is the first *drasha* — then Bnei Yisrael would have been unable to conquer their territory, bound as they were by Avraham's oath. God therefore arranged a solution: *leisu Kaftorim lifku me'Ivim* — let the Kaftoriim come and displace the Ivim. The verse itself says: *Kaftorim hayotzim miKaftor hishmidum vayeshvu tachtam* — the Kaftoriim who came from Kaftor destroyed the Ivim and settled in their place. Once the Kaftoriim occupied that land, it was no longer Philistine territory. *Ve'leisu Yisrael velifku miKaftorim* — and then Israel came and took the land from the Kaftoriim, at which point there was no longer any oath-violation involved.

This is why the Torah bothers to record the seemingly irrelevant history of the Ivim: without it, one might think Bnei Yisrael had violated the covenant with the Philistines. The history reveals that the land had already passed through an intermediate conquest, severing any connection to the original oath. As to who exactly the Kaftoriim were: some identify Kaftor with Crete, which is historically interesting given that archaeologists have concluded that the later Philistines — the Plishtim of the conquest period — were themselves of Aegean or Greek origin. This could be precisely the point: a later Greek people displaced the earlier Ivim, themselves tied to the Philistine territory, so that when Israel arrived the land had already changed hands.

---

## Conquest Principle

### Sichon's Conquest

A parallel case follows. The Torah states: *ki Cheshbon ir Sichon melech Emori hi vehu nichlam bemelech Moav harishon* — Cheshbon was the city of Sichon king of the Emorites, and he had fought against the first king of Moav. Again the reaction is: *mai nafka minah* — who needs this history? The answer is the same in structure. God had commanded Israel: *al tatzar et Moav* — do not oppress Moav, for they are descendants of Lot, our kinsmen. Had Cheshbon remained Moavite territory, Israel could not have taken it. But God arranged that Sichon would conquer it from Moav first: *leysei Sichon leyfuk mi-Moav* — let Sichon come and seize the land from Moav, *veleysei Yisrael veleysei mi-Sichon* — and then let Israel come and take it from Sichon. Once Sichon had conquered it, the land was no longer Moav's, and the restriction against taking from Moav no longer applied.

This is why Rav Pappa states: *Amon u-Moav tiharu be-Sichon* — Amon and Moav were "purified" by Sichon. The territory that had originally belonged to Amon and Moav became permissible to Israel because Sichon had conquered it, breaking the chain of ownership. The Torah's seemingly tedious historical digression is in fact indispensable to the legal analysis of why Israel was permitted to settle those lands.

### Kibbush Milchamah

From this principle the Gemara in Gittin derives the broader concept of *kibbush milchamah* — territorial acquisition through warfare. One might have argued that conquest is simply theft on a national scale. But the Gemara's position is that conquest in war carries a recognized legal effect: territory captured in war genuinely belongs to the conqueror. It no longer belongs to its former owners. This is precisely what made Israel's possession of those transjordanian territories legitimate — not despite the original prohibitions against taking from Amon, Moav, and the Philistines, but consistent with them, because *kibbush milchamah* had already transferred ownership before Israel arrived.

---

## Chermon Names

### Siryon & Senir

Still in the spirit of explaining why the Torah records seemingly trivial historical details, the Gemara cites another example. The verse states that the Tzidoniim call Chermon *Siryon*, and the Emoriim call it *Senir*. Why does the Torah bother telling us what foreign nations call this mountain?

### Geography Reverence

The Gemara teaches: *Senir ve-Siryon meharei Eretz Yisrael* — Senir and Siryon are names of mountains in Eretz Yisrael. The nations built great cities for themselves on Mount Chermon, but when they named it, they borrowed the names of mountains from the Land of Israel. Just as Vilna was called the Jerusalem of Eastern Europe, or as people might describe a notable peak as the Alps of some other region — they are honoring a new place by associating it with the paradigmatic one. *Melamedkha she'afilu harei Eretz Yisrael chavivin al umot ha-olam* — this teaches that even the mountains of Eretz Yisrael are beloved to the nations of the world. That is why the Torah records the foreign names: to convey the esteem in which the geography of Israel was held even among those who never lived there.

---

## Yosef & Egypt

### Yosef's Compassion

A final example from this series: the verse states that Yosef *ve'et ha'am he'evir oto le'arim* — relocated the Egyptian population from city to city during the years of famine, after he had already taken their wealth and their persons. *Mai nafka minah* — why does the Torah record this administrative detail of Egyptian history? The Gemara explains: *delo likru achav galvusa* — so that the Egyptians would not call Yosef's brothers exiles or foreigners. If the Egyptians all remained rooted in their ancestral cities while Yosef's family arrived as newcomers, the Egyptians could say: you are strangers here, you do not belong. By relocating the Egyptians to new cities, Yosef ensured that they too would feel themselves displaced, and could not look down upon the family of Yisrael as foreign interlopers. This was an act of forethought on behalf of his brothers' dignity — and that is why the Torah saw fit to record it.

This concludes the *aggadeta* section of the shiur. It is also worth noting, as was observed in discussion, that the pattern of these *derashot* carries some contemporary relevance: the passages make clear that the territory of Gaza is within the borders of Eretz Yisrael, whereas the status of Mount Chermon is less straightforward from the Gemara's own presentation, even if the boundaries drawn at the end of Bamidbar would seem to include it.

---

## Bird Simanim Intro

### Simanim Not Explicit

With the *aggadeta* concluded, the Mishnah at the bottom of 60b — which is where the official daf of 61 properly begins — turns to the question of kosher and non-kosher birds. The Mishnah states: *simanei ha'of lo ne'emru* — the identifying characteristics of birds were not stated explicitly in the Torah. The Torah lists the non-kosher birds by name but does not articulate a set of formal *simanim* the way it does for animals (split hooves and chewing cud) or fish (fins and scales). The Mishnah then proceeds to offer some practical guidance: birds that are *dores* — predatory birds of prey — are non-kosher; birds that have certain positive characteristics are kosher.

### Nesher's Traits

The Gemara immediately challenges the Mishnah's premise. A *Baraita* is cited: consider the *nesher* — the bird most likely to be a vulture rather than an eagle, based on other descriptors. *Ma nesher meyuchad she'ein lo etzba yeteirah ve'zefek ve'ein kurkevano niklaf ve'dores* — what is distinctive about the *nesher*? It lacks an *etzba yeteirah* (an elongated or extra finger), it has no *zefek* (crop), its gizzard (*kurkavan*) cannot be peeled, and it is *dores* — a predatory bird. *Tamei* — it is non-kosher. *Af kol kayotzei bo tamei* — anything with those four characteristics is likewise non-kosher.

The *Baraita* continues with the *torim* — turtle doves or pigeons, the birds offered as *korbanot* — which display the opposite profile: they have an *etzba yeteirah*, a *zefek*, a gizzard that can be peeled, and they are not *dores*. *Tehorin* — they are kosher. *Af kol kayotzei bahem tehorin* — anything with all four positive characteristics is likewise kosher.

This *Baraita* appears to contradict the Mishnah's claim that the *simanim* were not stated — here they are being stated and used quite explicitly. Moreover, there is a striking gap: the *Baraita* describes the extreme cases, the bird with all four non-kosher characteristics and the bird with all four kosher characteristics. But the vast middle ground — birds that have some mix — is left unaddressed. Both of these issues require resolution.

---

## Simanim by Sofrim

### Torah vs. Rabbinic

Abaye resolves the contradiction between the Mishnah and the *Baraita* with precision: *lo ne'emru peirushan midivrei Torah ela midivrei Sofrim* — the Mishnah does not mean that no characteristics exist at all; it means that the characteristics were not made explicit in the Torah. The Sages had to come and identify which features are the operative ones. The *simanim* are real and usable for *halachic* determination, but they are a rabbinic inference, not an explicit biblical articulation.

This clarification matters enormously for the larger question the Gemara is building toward: can one determine whether an unknown bird is kosher on the basis of these characteristics alone, without being able to identify it by name against the Torah's list? Or is the list itself the only operative criterion, with the *simanim* being merely descriptive? Abaye's statement opens the door to the former position — the characteristics are substantive enough to adjudicate — while still acknowledging that they are a product of rabbinic analysis rather than explicit scriptural text.

---

## Bird Simanim Intro (II)

### Dores Definition

Before addressing the central gap in the *Baraita*, it is worth pausing on the meaning of *dores*. Rashi (*hakuntres*) explains: *she'ocheiz betzipornav umagbiha min hakarka ma she'ochel* — it grabs with its talons and lifts from the ground what it intends to eat. Tosafot objects that this description would apply even to domestic chickens, which also pick up food with their feet. Rabbeinu Tam therefore offers an alternative definition: *dores ve'ochel mechayim ve'eino mamtin ad shetamos* — it preys upon and eats living creatures, not waiting for them to die first. This distinguishes a true bird of prey from a scavenger.

The discussion is complicated by the fact that some birds that would seem to qualify as *dores* under at least one of these definitions are in fact kosher. Ducks, for example, are kosher, yet they plunge their heads into water and swallow live fish. This reinforces the possibility — which the Gemara will shortly develop at length — that *dores* is not the definitive criterion for non-kosher status; it is one of four *simanim*, and the interplay among all four is what ultimately determines a bird's status. The connection to *derusah* — one of the categories of *treifos*, an animal whose flesh has been clawed by a predator — is also worth noting, as the same root *d-r-s* underlies both concepts.

---

## Middle Category Birds

### One Siman Suffices

With this background established, the Gemara turns to the central problem: the *Baraita* describes only the two extremes. What about everything in between? Rabbi Chiya teaches: *of ha'ba b'siman echad tahor* — a bird that presents even one kosher *siman* is kosher. His reasoning: *lefi she'ein domeh la'nesher* — such a bird does not resemble the *nesher*. The *nesher* has no kosher *simanim* whatsoever — *nesher d'leis lei klal hu d'lo teichul* — and that is what makes it non-kosher. *Heicha d'is lei chad teichul* — if a bird has even one kosher *siman*, it may be eaten.

### Why List All Birds?

The Gemara immediately pushes back: but the *Baraita* describes the *torim* as having all four kosher *simanim*. Why not learn from the *torim*? Just as the *torim* are kosher by virtue of possessing all four positive characteristics — *mah torin d'ika kullu arba* — perhaps the rule is that only a bird with all four kosher *simanim* is kosher, and any single negative *siman* disqualifies it.

The Gemara's response is decisive: *im ken she'ar ofot teme'im d'kasav Rachmana lama li* — if a single non-kosher *siman* were sufficient to disqualify a bird, why would the Torah have needed to list the twenty-four non-kosher birds at all? If the rule were that simple — one non-kosher *siman* and you are out — then any bird with a non-kosher *siman* would obviously be prohibited, and there would be no need to enumerate them by name. The fact that the Torah provides a detailed list implies that the rule is not so straightforward, and that many birds with some non-kosher *simanim* remain kosher — which is why the list of exceptions was necessary.

This is a more radical claim than most people would intuitively assume. The lay assumption tends to be that all twenty-four non-kosher birds share the predatory characteristic of *dores* and perhaps other common features, and that the list simply identifies which birds these are. What emerges from the Gemara's analysis is something quite different: the *simanim* do not map cleanly onto the list. A bird could in principle be *dores* and still be kosher; a bird could be non-*dores* and still be non-kosher. The list functions as a set of exceptions to a general rule that needs to be derived from the *nesher* — and deriving that rule is the work of the extended Talmudic discussion that follows.

Tosafot's lengthy treatment of this passage makes two striking points explicit: first, that a predatory bird could be kosher if it is not on the list and has one positive *siman*; and second — and more startling — that the majority of the twenty-four non-kosher birds may not even be birds of prey at all. Tosafot infers from the Gemara's own distribution that twenty of the twenty-four actually possess three of the four kosher *simanim*, and argues that not being *dores* is one of those three positive characteristics they retain. This is admittedly difficult to square with the ornithological identifications typically proposed for those birds, but it is the logical consequence of the Gemara's framework, and Tosafot follows it through consistently.

---

## Inferring the Rule

### Two or Three?

The Gemara now works through the logical possibilities systematically. Assuming the Torah's list is not simply a brute enumeration but carries evidential weight for inferring a general rule, one might reason as follows. The majority of the listed birds — twenty of the twenty-four — apparently have only one non-kosher *siman* (equivalently, three kosher *simanim*). Why not infer from them that one non-kosher *siman* is sufficient to disqualify a bird? The Gemara's response: if that were true, the Torah would not have needed to mention the *orev* (raven), which has two non-kosher *simanim*. Once we know one suffices, why mention a bird with two? The presence of the *orev* on the list is superfluous under that hypothesis, and the Torah does not write superfluously.

Fine, says the Gemara — perhaps learn from the *orev* instead. Let the rule be two non-kosher *simanim*: *mah hatam trei lo af kol trei lo* — just as the *orev* with two cannot be eaten, so anything with two or more non-kosher *simanim* cannot be eaten. The Gemara objects: *im ken peres ve'ozniyah de'chasav Rachmana lama li* — if two sufficed, why would the Torah have mentioned the *peres* and *ozniyah*, which, according to the Gemara's tradition, have three non-kosher *simanim*? If the rule were two, those birds would be obviously non-kosher without needing to be named.

The argument advances one further step: let the rule be three, derived from the *peres* and *ozniyah*. The Gemara objects: *nesher de'chasav Rachmana lama li* — then why mention the *nesher*, which has all four non-kosher *simanim*? If three sufficed, the *nesher* would be redundant. The pattern is consistent: at every proposed threshold, the Torah's mention of birds with more non-kosher *simanim* than the threshold requires renders the proposed rule superfluous. The only threshold that avoids this problem is four — and at four, the *nesher* is the paradigm case, not a redundancy, because it is the only bird that fully embodies the rule.

A deeper difficulty underlies all of this, however. The Gemara was using the list of twenty-four birds as evidence from which to infer a general rule. But there is a well-established hermeneutical principle: *shenei kesuvim habaim ke'echad ein melamdin* — when the Torah provides two examples that yield the same rule, you cannot derive a general law from them, because the repetition itself signals that these are exceptional cases rather than paradigmatic ones. If the rule were, say, one non-kosher *siman*, then among twenty-four birds there would inevitably be multiple examples that each exhibit the same single non-kosher *siman* — and the presence of two examples of the same characteristic should label them as exceptions, not as evidence of a rule.

### Shnei Kesuvim

The hermeneutical principle of *shenei kesuvim habaim ke'echad* thus threatens to undermine the entire inference. If the Torah repeats any given characteristic among multiple birds — and with twenty-four birds and only four possible *simanim*, repetition is inevitable — then by this principle we should conclude that no general rule can be derived from any of them. The force of *binyan av*, paradigmatic inference, requires a singular example; repeated examples cancel each other's evidentiary weight.

The Gemara anticipates this objection and acknowledges its theoretical force, but then introduces a tradition that resolves it.

### Distribution Pattern

*Gmiri* — we have a received tradition. Of the twenty-four non-kosher birds, twenty of them each have three kosher *simanim* (one non-kosher *siman*). The *orev* has two kosher *simanim* (two non-kosher). The *peres* has one kosher *siman* (three non-kosher). The *ozniyah* also has one kosher *siman*, but crucially — *de'ika behai leka behai* — the *siman* it possesses is a different one from the *siman* possessed by the *peres*. The *peres* and the *ozniyah* each have three non-kosher *simanim*, but their three are not the same three.

This distribution matters enormously for the hermeneutical argument. The tradition establishes that among the twenty-four non-kosher birds, the *simanim* are distributed in such a way that certain combinations appear only once. In particular, if we label the four kosher *simanim* A, B, C, and D, then the twenty birds at the base level all possess A, B, and C (lacking D). The *orev* possesses A and B (lacking C and D). The *peres* possesses, say, A (lacking B, C, and D). The *ozniyah* possesses D — and D appears nowhere else on the list. This means there is no second example of a bird whose only kosher *siman* is D. The principle of *shenei kesuvim habaim ke'echad* is therefore not triggered for that combination: there is a single case, from which a rule could in principle be derived.

One might therefore have reasoned: let the *ozniyah* serve as a singular paradigm. Since it is the only bird with kosher *siman* D and no other kosher *siman*, infer the rule that any bird lacking A, B, and C (possessing all three of those as non-kosher *simanim*) is non-kosher. This is what the Torah forestalled by explicitly listing the *nesher*.

---

## Four = Non-Kosher

### Unique Combinations

The tradition establishes something quite precise: the distribution of *simanim* across the twenty-four non-kosher birds is not arbitrary. The various combinations are arranged so that for any given sub-threshold set of non-kosher *simanim*, it is either the case that there are multiple birds sharing that combination — in which case *shenei kesuvim* blocks inference — or there is a single unique example, but the Torah's inclusion of the *nesher* overrides any rule one might have derived from it. The *ozniyah*'s unique possession of kosher *siman* D (while lacking the other three) is the key: it represents the only potential singular paradigm from which one might have derived a rule of three non-kosher *simanim* being sufficient. But the Torah writes the *nesher* — which lacks all four kosher *simanim* — to preempt that inference.

### Nesher Proves Rule

The *nesher* is thus the definitive paradigm. *Nesher deleis lei klal hu delo teichol* — only a bird with no kosher *simanim* whatsoever, no A, no B, no C, no D, represents the general rule of non-kosher status. *Ha'ee de'is bei chad* — any bird that has even one kosher *siman* is, as a general rule, potentially kosher. *V'ela ta'ama de'chasav Rachmana nesher hava amina leilaf miperes ve'ozniyah* — had the Torah not written the *nesher*, we would have tried to derive the rule from the *peres* and *ozniyah*, concluding that three non-kosher *simanim* suffice. The Torah writes the *nesher* to preempt this, establishing that only the complete absence of kosher *simanim* defines the general rule.

---

## Three Bird Categories

### All Kosher Simanim

The Gemara's analysis yields a clean three-part structure. First: a bird that possesses all four kosher *simanim* — an *etzba yeteirah*, a *zefek*, a peelable gizzard, and not being *dores* — is definitively kosher. This is what we learn from the *torim*. Such a bird is certainly not among the twenty-four on the Torah's list, and one need not consult the list at all to establish its status. Four kosher *simanim* is a sufficient and self-contained determination of *kashrut*.

### Zero Kosher Simanim

Second: a bird that has none of the four kosher *simanim* — the profile of the *nesher* — is definitively non-kosher. This follows from the general rule that the Torah establishes through the *nesher* as paradigm. Here too, the list is irrelevant; the *simanim* alone determine the outcome.

### Mixed Simanim

Third: a bird that has some mix of kosher and non-kosher *simanim* — somewhere between zero and four on the kosher scale — occupies the ambiguous middle category. This is where the Torah's explicit list of twenty-four non-kosher birds becomes indispensable. The list consists entirely of birds in this middle category: birds that have at least one kosher *siman* but are nonetheless non-kosher because the Torah specifically names them. Conversely, any bird in this middle category that does not appear on the Torah's list is kosher. To know whether a particular bird with mixed *simanim* is or is not on the list, one requires either a reliable identification of the bird's name or a received tradition about it.

This structural conclusion has direct practical implications for the famous question of birds that have entered Jewish communities without a pre-existing tradition — such as the turkey — and whether possession of all four kosher *simanim* suffices to permit them. The Gemara's framework suggests that if all four kosher *simanim* are present, the bird is kosher regardless of whether its name appears in any received list. The list is only relevant for the middle category, where a mix of *simanim* leaves the determination open. A bird with a complete set of positive *simanim* falls outside the domain where the list operates at all.

---

---

# Hullin 63

## Bird Simanim Review

### Simanim Recap

The present daf continues a multi-day discussion of the kosher and non-kosher status of birds. By way of review: the *gemara* concluded that any bird possessing none of the kosher *simanim* — or, stated differently, possessing all four non-kosher *simanim* — is definitively non-kosher. The *nesher* (the eagle, or more probably the griffon vulture) was cited as the clearest example. A bird possessing all four kosher *simanim* is definitively kosher. Where a bird exhibits a mixture of kosher and non-kosher *simanim*, its status depends on whether it appears on the Torah's enumerated list of forbidden species. The preceding session refined this framework further, analyzing specific birds with only one or two kosher *simanim* and asking whether, by process of elimination, one could determine that such a bird was nonetheless kosher. The general conclusion was that possessing all four kosher *simanim* is sufficient to establish permissibility, a ruling with real practical significance today.

### Swamp Hen & Mesorah

A case raised at the end of the prior discussion deserves closer attention. The *gemara* cited the instance of the *tarnegolta de-agma*, the hen of the swamp, which had been presumed kosher on the basis of its apparent *simanim*. Upon subsequent observation, however, it was discovered that this bird was in fact a *dores* — a bird of prey — a characteristic that had not previously been detected. The ruling was accordingly reversed, and the bird was declared non-kosher.

From this brief episode, Rashi draws a sweeping conclusion: one cannot eat any bird without an established *mesorah*, a reliable tradition of identification. Since one of the kosher *simanim* is the absence of predatory behavior, and since this characteristic may not always be evident, any assumption of permissibility based solely on observed *simanim* remains vulnerable to being overturned by later discovery. Rashi's position is not stated explicitly in the *gemara* itself, and it raises the question regarding birds of the New World, such as the turkey, for which no *mesorah* existed at the time of first contact. Even within Rashi's framework, one might ask whether a centuries-long, well-documented record of a bird's behavior could substitute for traditional *mesorah* — particularly if it conclusively established that the bird was not a *dores*. The question is complicated further by observations, such as the fact that wild turkeys are known to consume rodents and small animals, which raises the subsidiary question of precisely how *dores* is to be defined.

### Tosafot: Birds of Prey

A further clarification is needed regarding a point that had been stated imprecisely in an earlier session. One might have inferred from the *gemara*'s discussion that a bird of prey could theoretically still be kosher under certain circumstances. Tosafot, however, is emphatic on this point and derives from an explicit statement in the *mishnah* that every bird of prey, without exception, is non-kosher. This is a categorical rule for Tosafot: *dores* status renders a bird definitively forbidden regardless of what other *simanim* it may possess. Conversely, if a bird is not a *dores* but exhibits some non-kosher *simanim* without all four, its status then depends on whether it figures in the Torah's list. This represents an important corrective to a reading that might have emerged from the *gemara* alone.

---

## Shakitna & Species ID

### Shakitna Characteristics

The *gemara* at the second line of 63a opens with a statement of Rav Yehuda regarding a bird called the *shakitna*. Whether this bird is kosher or non-kosher depends on a set of observable characteristics. If it has *arichi shaki* — long legs, literally long thighs — and is *sumki*, reddish in color, it is *shari*, permissible. If, however, it has *gutzei*, short legs, even though it is reddish, it is *assiri*, forbidden. If it has long legs but is *yeroki* — green or yellow, depending on how that term is understood in context — it is likewise forbidden.

### Mnemonics: Murzma

Each ruling is accompanied by a mnemonic. For the long-legged, reddish bird that is permissible: *murzma murzma*, the name of a familiar kosher bird that was reddish and long-legged, providing a mental image of the permissible type. For the short-legged bird that is forbidden: *nanos pasul*, a midget is disqualified from performing the *avodah* in the *Beis Hamikdash*, since short stature constitutes a physical blemish. For the long-legged but greenish or yellowish bird: *yerokin pesulin*, recalling the rule that if a bird falls into fire and its internal organs turn greenish or yellowish, it is rendered a *treifa* and invalidated. Crucially, these are not reasons but memory devices — mnemonics designed to aid retention, not to supply legal justification.

### Mixed Simanim Birds

A broader difficulty underlies the entire discussion. If a bird has some kosher and some non-kosher *simanim*, its permissibility depends on whether it appears on the forbidden list — and that in turn depends on its name. This is why slight variations among similar-looking birds can matter: variations in leg length or coloration might be precisely what determines whether a bird falls under one species name or another, and thus whether it is included on the list.

### Species Definition

One might ask whether the variations described here — long versus short legs, reddish versus greenish coloration — genuinely distinguish different species or merely represent natural variation within a single species. The *gemara* does not address this directly, but one possibility is that these distinguishing traits correlate with behavioral differences, perhaps including whether the bird is in some sense a *dores*. Another possibility is simply that they are what define the species name, which is the operative category for determining the bird's listing status.

---

## Torah Birds ID

### Nesher ID

The *gemara* now turns to identifying the specific birds mentioned in the Torah's own list. This task carries halachic urgency: since the status of a bird with mixed *simanim* depends on whether it appears on the list, one must know what the listed names actually refer to. The *nesher* has already been mentioned throughout this discussion. Although it is conventionally translated as "eagle," Yehuda Feliks, in his authoritative work on the flora and fauna of the Torah, identifies it with the griffon vulture — the largest bird found in the Land of Israel — based on multiple converging indicators.

### Shalach ID

Rav Yehuda states that the *shalach* is *zeh ha-sholeh dagim min ha-yam* — the one that scoops up fish from the sea. The root *shal* is embedded in the name itself. As to the precise identification: Feliks suggests a fish owl; others propose the cormorant, a bird well known for diving into water to catch fish; Aryeh Kaplan in *The Living Torah* translates it as the cormorant. Artscroll's translation, both here and in its Torah commentary, declines to translate these bird names at all, so as not to mislead readers regarding the halachic implications. The caution is well founded, given the difficulty of mapping ancient nomenclature onto modern ornithological taxonomy.

### Duchifat & Shamir

The *duchifat* is identified through a play on its name: *she-hodo kaffut*, its glory or crest of feathers is folded or bent over. This likely refers to the hoopoe, a bird whose distinctive crown of feathers can be erected or folded flat. A *baraita* confirms this derivation and adds an aggadic note: *ve-zeh she-hevi shamir l'Beis Ha-Mikdash*. The *gemara* recalls the account in Tractate Gittin of the *shamir*, a worm capable of cutting through stone, which was needed for the construction of the *Beis Hamikdash* because the Torah prohibits using iron tools on the stones of the altar. The *duchifat* made use of the *shamir* to break open stones in order to access prey concealed within them, and thus served as the means by which the *shamir* was brought. Onkelos, in his Aramaic translation of the Torah, renders *duchifat* as "breaker of stones," reflecting this tradition.

### Yochanan's Drasha

The *gemara* records that when Rabbi Yochanan would observe the *shalach* — the fish-catching bird — he would recite the verse: *mishpatecha tehom raba*, "Your judgments are in the great depths." And when he saw an ant, he would say: *tzidkascha k'harrei El*, "Your righteousness is like the mountains of God."

Rashi offers two interpretations of this pairing. The first, which he attributes to his teachers: the fish dwelling in the depths of the sea are nonetheless subject to divine judgment and cannot escape it; even the smallest creatures, the ants, receive divine sustenance, and this reflects God's great righteousness. The second interpretation, which Rashi himself prefers: the *mishpat*, the strict justice, is reflected in the *shalach*, which must labor intensely, diving into the sea for its food — it earns what it receives. The ant, by contrast, finds its food more easily, raiding a pantry or a picnic, as it were — and this reflects divine *tzedaka*, a more generous, charitable dispensation. Rashi himself notes a certain tension in the word *tzedaka* here, observing that *tzedek* and *mishpat* are closely related terms, often paired in Scripture.

---

## Ambiguous Birds

### Custom & Peres

The *gemara* shifts to a new statement: *likni u-vitni sharyin* — birds called *likni* and *bitni* are kosher. But what of *shiknai* and *bitnai*? The answer given is: *makom she-nahagu le-echol ochlin, makom she-nahagu she-lo le-echol ein ochlin* — where there is a local custom to eat these birds one may eat them; where the custom is to refrain, one may not. The *gemara* pushes back immediately: *atu be-minhaga talya milsa?* Is this really a matter of custom? This is a legal question, not merely a matter of practice. The *gemara* answers: yes, and it is not difficult to explain.

### Peres ve-Ozniya

The key to understanding this ruling lies in the *peres* and *ozniya*, two species of non-kosher birds that Feliks identifies as variants of the vulture family. These birds are extremely rare in inhabited areas. Because they possess only a single kosher *siman*, and because they are so rarely encountered in settled areas, there is ordinarily no reason to worry that a bird one has identified as kosher might in fact be a *peres* or *ozniya*.

However, where *peres* and *ozniya* are locally common — *b'atra de-shechiach peres ve-ozniya* — the concern arises that a bird believed to be a kosher species might actually be one of these forbidden birds. In such a location, one must not eat the *shiknai* or *bitnai*, because they might be confused with the *peres* or *ozniya*. In a place where these non-kosher species are not found — *b'atra de-lo shechiach peres ve-ozniya* — there is no basis for concern, and one may eat the bird without restriction.

### Geography & ID

This raises a question regarding the formulation *where there is a custom to eat*. If the concern is purely geographic — the presence or absence of the *peres* and *ozniya* — why is it phrased as a matter of custom rather than of fact? Some *rishonim* address this by suggesting that perhaps one location had a *mesorah* regarding the bird's identity and another did not. But that explanation has a difficulty: if one location possessed a reliable *mesorah*, that *mesorah* should suffice for others as well, and the ruling should not appear to be a mere matter of local custom. The fact that it is framed in terms of *minhag* suggests that the distinction is indeed geographic, not testimonial.

---

## Abaye's Lists

### Kuai Birds

Abaye now introduces his own list of specific birds. Birds called *kuai* and *kakuai* are forbidden. The *kakuasa*, however, is permissible.

### Regional Disputes

Strikingly, in *Eretz Yisrael* — *be-ma'arava* — the *kakuasa* was not merely considered forbidden but was considered so definitively forbidden that those who ate it were given *malkot*, lashes. Furthermore, the bird was known by a different name there, *tachvasa*. This radical discrepancy — a bird considered clearly permissible in one region and clearly forbidden in another, to the point of warranting physical punishment — is difficult to explain if the dispute hinged solely on the *simanim*. One would expect that the *simanim* would be equally observable in both locations. The more likely explanation is that the dispute concerned whether this bird was subsumed under the name of a forbidden species on the Torah's list, with the different regional nomenclature (*kakuasa* versus *tachvasa*) perhaps driving different legal conclusions.

---

## Tinshemet

### Bird & Sheretz

The *gemara* now turns to the *tinshemet*, one of the birds listed in the Torah's roster of forbidden species. A *baraita* defines it as *ba'ut she-ba-ofot* — the "screecher" or "howler" among birds. Rashi elsewhere identifies this term as meaning something that shrieks, and renders the *tinshemet* variously as an owl or a bat, with some inclination toward the bat. The word *tinshemet* also appears in the Torah's list of forbidden *sheratzim*, the creeping creatures. Rashi there identifies that creature as a mole, and notes the resemblance: a bat, he observes, looks somewhat like a mole with wings, which may explain why the same name attaches to both.

There is also a possible textual variant to consider: the word *ba'ut* may in some versions be *bava'at*, reflecting the Aramaic *bava'at* used by Onkelos in translating this word, which involves the reversal of an *alef* and a *vav*. Feliks identifies the *tinshemet* bird as a barn screech owl and the *tinshemet* *sheretz* as a chameleon. One etymology connects the name to the word *neshamah* — breath — suggesting that the creature breathes in a distinctive manner; another, cited in the *Arukh*, takes *ba'ut* to mean something fearful or repugnant, suggesting that both animals — the owl or bat, and the mole or chameleon — inspire a particular revulsion.

### Context Principle

The *baraita* poses a question: since the word *tinshemet* appears in both the list of forbidden birds and the list of forbidden *sheratzim*, how do we know which is being referred to in each context? The answer invokes one of the thirteen hermeneutical principles — *davar ha-lamed me-inyano*, a matter is interpreted according to its context. When *tinshemet* appears in the portion dealing with birds, it refers to a bird; when it appears in the portion dealing with *sheratzim*, it refers to a *sheretz*. This same reasoning is then applied in the reverse direction by an analogous *baraita* dealing with *sheratzim*: one might have thought the *tinshemet* mentioned there refers to the bird of the same name, but context establishes that it refers to a creeping creature.

### Tinshemet = Kipuf

Abaye then provides identifications in the vernacular known to his contemporaries. The *tinshemet* among birds is the *kipuf*, which again Rashi renders as either a bat or an owl. The *tinshemet* among *sheratzim* is the *korpadai*, which Rashi identifies as a mole.

Rav Yehuda then identifies the *ka'at* — another bird on the list — as the *kuk* or *kik*, which Feliks identifies as the tawny owl. Rashi supplies a French gloss whose precise meaning is difficult to recover. The *racham* is identified as the *sherakrak*, the shrieker or crier.

Rabbi Yochanan then asks: why is this bird called *racham*? Because *keivan she-ba racham ba'u rakhamim la-olam* — when the *racham* arrives, compassion (*rakhamim*) comes to the world. The bird is a harbinger of the rainy season, and rain in the Land of Israel is understood as a divine expression of mercy and providential care. Identifying the specific bird has proven difficult: Feliks says it is an Egyptian vulture; Aryeh Kaplan and some traditional commentaries suggest the magpie; Artscroll has proposed the roller, partly on the basis of Rashi's description. Rav Bibi bar Abaye adds a qualification: the sign of impending rain is specifically when the bird sits on something elevated and performs its characteristic cry. But there is an even more extraordinary tradition: if the bird sits on the ground itself and cries out, that is a sign not merely of rain but of the coming of *mashiach*, as the verse in the prophets says *eshreka lahem va-akabtzem* — "I will call out to them and gather them." Rav Adda bar Shimi raised an apparent objection to Mar bar Rav Idai: there was a case of a bird sitting among cabbages and crying out, and rather than presaging the *mashiach*, a boulder came and crushed its head. The response: *hahu kadba hava* — that was a false messenger, a false herald. The boulder crashing down was itself the evidence that the signal was fraudulent.

---

## Raven & Kite ID

### Orev Varieties

The *gemara* now proceeds to a *baraita* identifying further species. *Orev zeh orev* — the *orev* is the *orev*. The *gemara* finds this unhelpfully circular, noting that the *baraita* ought to be more specific since it is distinguishing the canonical *orev* from related subspecies. The *gemara* therefore amends the reading: the *orev* referred to is specifically *orev uchma*, the black raven or crow, as implied by the verse in *Shir Ha-Shirim*: *kvutsotav taltalim shekhorot ke-orev*, "his locks are curled, black as a raven."

The *orev ha-amaki*, "the one of the valleys" or "the deep one," is described as white or whitish. The connection to the word *amok* (deep) here draws on a verse concerning the *tsara'at* affliction: a leprous spot whose appearance is *amok min ha-or*, deeper than the surrounding skin. Rashi and other commentators explain that a lighter-colored spot appears visually deeper than darker skin surrounding it — a claim that the Ramban famously challenges, noting that it contradicts ordinary visual experience, where a darker area appears closer and a lighter area further away. The *gemara* draws an analogy: the appearance of sunlit pavement appears deeper, further receding from the viewer, than the shade nearby — though this too is a counterintuitive claim that resists easy verification.

The third variety, *orev ha-ba be-roshei yonim*, might seem to mean a raven that flies at the head of a flock of doves. Rav Pappa corrects this: *de-dami reshei le-yona*, its head resembles that of a dove.

Raven and crow are not the same species, though they are closely related. Feliks identifies the *orev afur* as the hooded crow and the *orev shachor* as the raven — and it is possible that exactly these two categories, one darker and one lighter, correspond to the *orev uchma* and *orev ha-amaki* discussed in the *gemara*.

### Hatz & Variants

The *baraita* then addresses the *netz*, the sparrowhawk according to Feliks. The text states simply *zeh ha-netz* — this is the *netz* — and then adds that its species (*l'minehu*) includes the *bar chirya*, a related species. Abaye identifies the *bar chirya* in the vernacular as the *shurinka*.

### Chasida = Daya

Rav Yehuda identifies the *chasida* as the *daya levana*, the white *daya*, or white kite. This identification immediately introduces a terminological complexity that will drive the remainder of the day's discussion, since the Torah's list includes both *daya* and *ayah*, and the *gemara* will need to determine how these terms relate to one another. Feliks identifies the *chasida* as the stork, while identifying the *da'ah* and *dayah* as the black kite — which would make the *chasida* and the *dayah* distinct species, though both fall under the general family name.

### Chasida Meaning

Why is this bird called *chasida*, a name derived from the root *chesed*, kindness? Because *she-osa chasidut im chavroteha* — it performs acts of kindness with its companions, sharing its food with members of its own group. A well-known homiletical observation notes the apparent paradox: if the reason non-kosher birds are forbidden is because they embody predatory or morally deficient traits, why is this bird — which is explicitly named for its kindness — among the forbidden species? The answer given is that its *chesed* is confined to its own kind; it shares food only with members of its own flock, not with outsiders. Kindness that extends only to one's own circle, rooted in group interest rather than genuine moral concern, is not true *chesed* — and indeed may be understood as a form of self-interest in communal form.

### Anafa Meaning

The *anafa* is identified as the *daya ragzanit*, the angry *daya*. Why is it called *anafa*? Because *she-mena'efet im chavroteha* — it quarrels with or becomes enraged at its companions. A textual variant — *she-mna'anefet*, from the root *alef-nun-peh*, meaning anger — may actually be more coherent with the name *anafa*, since *ve-hi'anef* means to become wrathful (as in Moshe's words that God became angry with him). The current received text, *mna'efet*, carries the meaning of adultery, which is also attested as a behavior among certain birds — but the linguistic connection to *anafa* is cleaner if one reads *mna'anefet*.

---

## 24 Birds Count

### Count Intro

Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda cites a tradition in the name of Rav Chisda, who cites Rav, which holds that there are twenty-four species of non-kosher birds. Now that the *gemara* has done its best to identify what is on the list, it turns to the problem of actually counting to twenty-four and resolving apparent discrepancies in the number by conflating certain species.

### List Discrepancy

Rav Chanan, who had transmitted this tradition from his father, turns back to ask him directly: *v'heicha?* How do you actually arrive at twenty-four? If one counts the names in the list in Vayikra, there are twenty. If one counts the list in Mishneh Torah — the list in Devarim which we encountered in the preceding day's portion — there are twenty-one. Even if one adds the one bird, *da'ah*, that appears in Vayikra but not in Mishneh Torah, and adds it to the twenty-one in Devarim, the total is only twenty-two. How does one reach twenty-four?

His father responds with what he says was transmitted from Rav: the word *leminehu* ("of its kind"), which appears multiple times in the lists, carries halachic weight, extending each category to include related species. Counting the instances of *leminehu* in Devarim — four occurrences — and adding them to the base count of twenty yields twenty-four. (The *Toldot Aharon* cites three from Vayikra and one from Devarim, but the *gemara* here is counting from Devarim.)

### Da'ah = Ra'ah

The *gemara* immediately objects: if there are twenty-one base species in Devarim and one adds the *da'ah* from Vayikra, that is twenty-two base species, plus four *leminehus*, which is twenty-six — not twenty-four. How does one return to twenty-four?

Abaye answers: *da'ah ve-ra'ah achat hi* — the *da'ah* and the *ra'ah* are one and the same species. The alignment of the two lists makes this easy to see: Vayikra has *da'ah* and *ayah*, while Devarim has *ra'ah*, *ayah*, and *dayah*. The *da'ah* and *ra'ah* occupy the same position on their respective lists, and the words differ only in that one begins with a *dalet* and the other with a *resh*. They are different names for the same bird.

### Mishneh Torah Adds

This conflation is further supported by a structural principle: *Mishneh Torah le-osufi hu de-ata* — the list in Devarim is understood as coming to add to the list in Vayikra, not to diminish it. That is, everything in the Vayikra list must also be present in the Devarim list, and the Devarim list may only expand upon it. If *da'ah* and *ra'ah* were distinct species, then since Devarim replaces *da'ah* with *ra'ah* and does not include both, the Devarim list would contain *less* than the Vayikra list — which violates this principle. Therefore, they must be the same species. The Devarim list simply uses a different name for the same bird — presumably so that someone who heard the bird called by one name would not think that only that name was forbidden while the other was permissible.

### Aya = Daya

Abaye continues: just as *ra'ah* and *da'ah* are the same, so too *ayah* and *dayah* are the same. This is a bolder conflation: both *ayah* and *dayah* appear on the same list in Devarim — *ra'ah*, *ayah*, *dayah* — so here the Torah uses two different names for the same species within a single list.

The proof again comes from the principle of addition. In Vayikra, the word *leminah* ("of its kind") is appended to *ayah*, indicating that the *ayah* category is broad and encompasses related species. In Devarim, *leminah* is attached to *dayah*, but *not* to *ayah*. If *ayah* and *dayah* are distinct species, then the Devarim list has applied *leminah* to *dayah* while removing it from *ayah*, leaving *ayah* as a narrower category than it was in Vayikra. That would mean Devarim reduces the scope of a prohibition established in Vayikra — again violating the addition principle. The only solution is that *ayah* and *dayah* are the same species, and so it makes no difference to which of them *leminah* is attached; they are interchangeable.

### Multiple Names

Why, then, does the Torah use two names for the same species within a single list? The *gemara* cites Rebbi: *ekra ani ayah, dayah lama ne'emar?* Since *ayah* was already stated, why was it necessary to add *dayah*? The answer: *kedei she-lo titen pitchon peh le-va'al din lachlok* — so as not to give grounds for a disputant to draw distinctions. One person calls the bird *ayah*, another calls it *dayah*, and the disputant claims that only one of those names appears in the Torah's prohibition. By including both names, the Torah forecloses that argument and makes clear that whatever one calls this bird, it is forbidden.

### Addition Resolved

The *gemara* then raises a challenge from the *baraita* that discusses why the Torah repeated the list in Devarim at all. By mammals, the repetition was to introduce the *shisua*, a novel animal — an apparently new species of cloven-hoofed creature — thereby genuinely adding to the Vayikra list. By birds, the *baraita* states that the repetition was *mipnei ha-ra'ah* — because of the *ra'ah*, implying that the *ra'ah* is itself a new species not found in Vayikra. This directly contradicts Abaye's conflation of *ra'ah* and *da'ah* as a single species.

The *gemara* resolves this: by mammals, the repetition was genuinely additive (*le-osufi*); by birds, however, the repetition was explanatory (*le-frushei*). The Devarim list does not introduce the *ra'ah* as a new species but clarifies that what Vayikra called *da'ah*, Devarim refers to as *ra'ah* — they are the same creature, and the second mention serves to prevent future ambiguity or legal dispute.

---

## Rav Abbahu

### Ra'ah = Aya

Rav Abbahu offers an alternative harmonization that diverges significantly from Abaye's. Where Abaye identified *da'ah*/*ra'ah* as one pair and *ayah*/*dayah* as another, Rav Abbahu says: *ra'ah zu ayah* — the *ra'ah* is the *ayah*. His basis is etymological and descriptive: why is this bird called *ra'ah* (which can mean "seeing")? Because *she-ro'ah bi-yoter* — it can see at an extraordinary distance. A verse from Iyov lends support: *nesiv lo yeda'o ayit ve-lo shezafatto ein ayah* — "a path unknown to the *ayit* (vulture), unseen by the eye of the *ayah*" — invoking the *ayah*'s renowned visual acuity. Thus the name *ra'ah* is simply a descriptor applied to the *ayah* because of this characteristic, and the two names refer to a single bird. A *baraita* confirms the remarkable sharpness of this bird's vision: *omedet be-Bavel ve-ro'ah neveilah be-Eretz Yisrael* — it can stand in Babylonia and spot a carcass all the way in the Land of Israel, then swoop down to consume it. This aligns with what we know of large raptors and vultures, which soar at great heights and can detect carrion from extraordinary distances.

### Addition Test

The *gemara* examines Rav Abbahu's position against the same addition principle it applied to Abaye. If *ra'ah* and *ayah* are the same, then Rav Abbahu implicitly leaves *da'ah* and *ra'ah* as distinct species — he has not claimed that *da'ah* equals *ra'ah*, only that *ra'ah* equals *ayah*. But this creates the same problem: Vayikra has *da'ah*, Devarim does not — it has *ra'ah* in its place. If they are not the same, then Devarim's list is missing something from Vayikra's, violating the addition principle. Rav Abbahu must therefore also accept that *da'ah* and *ra'ah* are the same — and since *ra'ah* equals *ayah*, it follows that all three, *da'ah*, *ra'ah*, and *ayah*, are the same species.

### All One Species

The *gemara* then presses further. If *ra'ah* and *ayah* are the same, then presumably *dayah* remains a distinct species. But we saw in Abaye's discussion that *ayah* and *dayah* must also be the same, on account of the *leminah* problem: Vayikra attaches *leminah* to *ayah*; Devarim attaches it only to *dayah*; they cannot be distinct, or Devarim would narrow the *ayah* category below what Vayikra established. Therefore, Rav Abbahu too must conclude that *dayah* is the same as *ayah* — and since *ayah* equals *ra'ah* which equals *da'ah*, all four names — *da'ah*, *ra'ah*, *ayah*, *dayah* — refer to a single species.

This means Rav Abbahu's position yields a list of only twenty-three non-kosher species, one fewer than the standard count of twenty-four. By combining four names into one species rather than two pairs of two, he arrives at a smaller total than the framework Abaye constructed.

---

## Kosher Infinite

### Infinite Varieties

A *baraita* records the view of Avimi bar Rav Abbahu: there are seven hundred species of kosher fish, eight hundred species of kosher grasshoppers, and of kosher birds there is no number — they are infinite. This is not an exaggeration from the standpoint of modern taxonomy, which recognizes thousands of species in many animal families.

### Why 24 Works

The *gemara* challenges this: we have just spent considerable effort establishing that there are exactly twenty-four species of non-kosher birds — so how can kosher birds be infinite? The answer is direct: the twenty-four refers to non-kosher birds; kosher birds, being everything that does not appear on that list, are indeed without number, because they comprise the totality of all bird species minus the twenty-four forbidden ones. The structure of the Torah's enumeration — listing only the forbidden species — is precisely what makes this possible: by bounding the non-kosher category at twenty-four, the kosher category is left open and unlimited. Whether Avimi's statements about fish and grasshoppers similarly refer to the kosher varieties of those species is left as an open question.

---

## Torah Lists

### Shorter List

A *baraita* records Rebbi's explanation for what might otherwise seem like an inconsistency: by mammals, the Torah lists the kosher species; by birds, it lists the non-kosher ones. Why the difference? *Galui ve-yadu'a lifnei mi she-amar ve-hayah ha-olam* — it is known to God that non-kosher mammals far outnumber kosher ones. Therefore the Torah provides the shorter list, which is the list of kosher mammals. Conversely, it is known that kosher birds vastly outnumber non-kosher ones. Therefore, by birds, the Torah provides the shorter list, which is the list of the twenty-four non-kosher species. In each case, the Torah teaches by enumerating the smaller category and leaving the larger one to inference.

### Short Teaching

The pedagogical principle underlying this practice is stated explicitly by Rav Huna in the name of Rav — and some versions of the attribution add "in the name of Rabbi Meir" — *le-olam yishaneh adam le-talmido derekh ktzarah*: one should always teach one's student in the shortest way possible. The Torah's alternating methodology — listing kosher by mammals, non-kosher by birds — is itself a demonstration of this principle: in each domain, it says as little as necessary to convey the maximum amount of information.

---

## Mesorah Suffices

### Tradition Works

Rav Yitzchak states: *of tahor ne'echal be-mesoret* — a kosher bird may be eaten on the basis of tradition. This statement must be understood carefully. Rav Yitzchak is not requiring a *mesorah* as an absolute precondition; he is affirming that a *mesorah* is sufficient. The context is practical: all of the preceding discussion about identifying species, conflating names, and knowing which birds appear on the forbidden list makes clear how technically demanding the determination of a bird's permissibility can be. When one does not know with certainty whether a bird has all four kosher *simanim*, and when one faces the question of whether a bird with some non-kosher *simanim* might nonetheless be permissible because it does not appear on the list — the answer is that a reliable tradition of identification suffices to establish permissibility. This is the *gemara*'s position; it is only in the later period, beginning with Rashi, that the *mesorah* becomes not merely sufficient but necessary, on the grounds that one can never be fully certain whether a bird is a *dores* without a long-standing tradition.

### Hunter Testimony

The *gemara* applies this principle to a specific case: *ne'eman ha-tzayad lomar of zeh tiher li rabbi* — a hunter is believed when he testifies that a given bird is kosher, provided that his master taught him so. The hunter's tradition — received from someone with practical expertise in bird identification — constitutes a valid basis for consuming that species.

### Know Birds & Names

Rabbi Yochanan qualifies this rule: *ve-hu she-baki bahen u-vi-shmotseihen* — the ruling applies only if the master who transmitted the tradition was genuinely expert in both the birds themselves and their names. Both components are essential. Knowledge of the bird's physical characteristics is necessary to know what one is dealing with; knowledge of its name is necessary because, as established earlier in this discussion, a bird bearing the name of a forbidden species may be forbidden even if its *simanim* appear kosher — on the grounds that it may be a taxonomic extension of that forbidden species. Without knowledge of both appearance and nomenclature, the tradition cannot be relied upon. This caveat also addresses a perennial concern about oral traditions: that knowledge transmitted without grounding in empirical reality gradually loses accuracy as each generation repeats what it has heard without being able to verify it against the facts on the ground.

### Teacher vs Hunter

Rabbi Zeira raises a pointed question: when the *gemara* says "his master taught him," does this refer to a Torah teacher — a *chacham*, a *talmid chacham* — or to a master hunter?

### Hunter's Tradition

The resolution comes from Rabbi Yochanan's qualification itself. If we require that the transmitter of the tradition be *baki bahen u-vi-shmotseihen* — expert in the birds and in their names — then consider: if it were a Torah teacher being discussed, one could readily understand that he knows the *names*, since names are transmitted through textual study. But *baki bahen*, expert in the birds themselves, in their physical characteristics and appearance? *Ela inhu mi yada?* — do Torah scholars typically possess that kind of practical, empirical expertise in birds? The phrasing of the requirement — that the master must know both the birds and their names — only makes sense if the master in question is a hunter, precisely the kind of person one would not normally assume to be expert in the legal and textual dimension of the names. The requirement that he know *both* aspects, the empirical and the nominal, is what makes the specification necessary, and it only makes sense when applied to a hunter. Therefore: *shema mina rabo tzayad* — the tradition in question is that of a master hunter.

The conclusion is both surprising and significant. The operative tradition that establishes a bird's permissibility need not come from a *talmid chacham* or rabbinic authority. It suffices if it comes from a knowledgeable, God-fearing craftsman — a hunter who truly knows his birds and has received a tradition regarding their status from those who came before him. The tradition is reliable not because of the scholarly credentials of its bearer, but because of his practical mastery and the authenticity of what he received.

This brings the day's discussion to its natural conclusion. To summarize the full framework: a bird with all four kosher *simanim* is definitively kosher. A bird with a mixture of *simanim* may still be kosher if it does not appear on the list of twenty-four forbidden species, and a reliable tradition — even one stemming from a master hunter rather than a rabbinic sage — suffices to establish that it does not appear on that list. And according to Rashi, given the difficulty of ever being fully certain that a bird is not a *dores*, a *mesorah* is ultimately not merely sufficient but necessary.

---

---

# Hullin 64

## Eggs from Non-Jews

### Basic Permissibility

The daf opens with a *baraita*: *locḥin beitzim min ha'ovdei kokhavim bechol makom* — one may purchase eggs from non-Jews wherever one finds them. The concern of *neveilah* — that the eggs came from birds that died without proper *shechita* — does not apply, nor does the concern of *tereifah* — that the bird had some internal injury rendering it *tereif* and its eggs consequently forbidden — because the overwhelming majority of eggs come from live, healthy birds. These concerns are therefore statistically negligible.

### Merchant's Claim

The *Gemara* immediately raises a sharper question: *vedilma d'of tamei ninhu* — perhaps these eggs came from a non-kosher bird? Something derived from a non-kosher animal is itself forbidden, and a bird being alive does not address whether it belongs to a forbidden species. The answer, attributed to Avuha deShmuel, the father of Shmuel, is that we are speaking of a case *be'omer shel of ploni tahor* — where the non-Jewish merchant explicitly states that the eggs come from a particular identified kosher species. Rashi clarifies why the specification must name a particular species (*ploni*) rather than merely asserting "these are from a kosher bird." If the merchant only made a general claim, he could always escape scrutiny by saying, "Well, I don't remember exactly which kosher bird, but it was some kosher bird." By naming a specific species, however, his claim becomes falsifiable: one can always take a known sample of that species and compare.

### Testability Standard

This leads naturally into one of the central principles underlying *kashrus* credibility: under what circumstances can one trust the statement of a person — especially a non-Jew, who is outside our halakhic framework, and especially a merchant with a financial stake in the sale? Two distinct mechanisms are sometimes invoked in such cases. The first is *masiach lefi tumo* — the speaker volunteers information innocently, with no vested interest in the halakhic outcome. That is clearly not the situation here, where the merchant is consciously telling the buyer what the eggs are in order to make a sale. The second is *uman lo marei umnutei* — an expert will not say something that undermines his professional reputation. This principle applies somewhat differently: it is less about dishonesty resulting in lost sales and more about an expert whose claim of expertise can be directly tested.

### Avida Legluya

The more precise principle operating here is *milsa d'avida legluya* — a matter that is easily and publicly verifiable. When a claim can be readily tested and disproven, the person making it has a powerful incentive not to lie, because exposure would be swift. By specifying the particular species, the merchant's claim becomes just such a testable assertion — one can always procure a sample of that species and compare the eggs directly. The *Gemara* will later refine how these factors interact, but the implicit logic at this stage is that testability provides sufficient assurance.

---

## Egg Indicators

### Fish Egg Parallel

Having established that the merchant's specific claim is required, the *Gemara* asks: why rely on the merchant at all? Why not simply examine the eggs themselves? After all, the *Gemara* introduces a *baraita*: *ke'simanei beitzim kach simanei dagim* — the indicators for eggs are like the indicators for fish. The *Gemara* immediately parses this: surely one cannot look for *snapir* and *kaskeset* — fins and scales — on bird eggs. Rather, the statement means that the indicators used to identify kosher fish eggs (*ovrei dagim*) are parallel to the indicators used for bird eggs. That is, the same type of morphological examination that reveals whether fish eggs come from a kosher species also applies to bird eggs.

### Shape Indicators

The *baraita* then specifies: *kol shekoderet ve'algulgelet* — any egg that is spherical and rounded. Rashi explains that both terms are really conveying a single idea: *algulgelet* alone might suggest roundness in only two dimensions, like a lentil or a wheel of cheese, whereas *koderet* adds depth, indicating that the egg is spherical in three dimensions — not perfectly spherical, as we know, but genuinely ovoid. Then: *rosha echad kad, ve'rosha echad chad* — one end of the egg is like a *kad*, a pitcher, meaning rounded and blunt, and one end is sharp and pointed. If an egg has one rounded end and one pointed end, it is *tehorah* — kosher. If *shnei rasheha kadin* — both ends come to a point — or *shnei rasheha kadin* in the opposite direction, both ends are rounded, *tme'in* — it is from a non-kosher species.

### White/Yolk Test

The *baraita* continues: *chelbon mibachutz ve'chelmon mibifnim* — if the albumin (*chelbon*) is on the outside and the yolk (*chelmon*) is on the inside, the egg is *tehorah*, kosher. A useful mnemonic: *chelbon* sounds like *chalav* — milk — which aids in remembering that it refers to the white. Whether this criterion is independent of the shape indicator or must accompany it is not explicitly resolved at this point in the *Gemara*, but the implication is that both are relevant indicators. It is worth noting that this test of albumen-outside and yolk-inside applies only to bird eggs. Fish eggs, having no such internal structure, are assessed purely on the basis of shape.

### Non-Kosher Indicators

Conversely: *chelmon mibachutz ve'chelbon mibifnim* — if the yolk is on the outside and the white on the inside, the egg is *teme'ah*, non-kosher. Whether this inversion ever actually occurs in nature is left open, but it is stated as a negative indicator. More significantly: *chelmon ve'chelbon me'uravin zeh bezeh* — if the white and yolk are thoroughly intermingled, *beyadu'a she-hi beitzat ha-sheretz* — one may assume with confidence that this is the egg of a *sheretz*, a creeping or crawling creature. The *sheratzim* of the Torah are not merely insects but include small reptiles, rodents, lizards, chameleons, and the like. These creatures' eggs apparently contain no distinct albumin, the entire content being essentially yolk — or, as the ArtScroll footnote suggests, what would normally be the white's constituents are incorporated into the yolk, producing the appearance of intermingling.

### Scrambled Egg Ban

If these indicators exist, why must one rely on the merchant's testimony at all? The *Gemara* works through a series of scenarios. If the eggs are chopped and cooked (*dechatuchot*), one cannot assess their shape — but perhaps the white-yolk arrangement can still be seen. If, however, they are *betrufot beke'arah* — scrambled together in a bowl — neither shape nor internal arrangement can be examined. Yet at this point a striking *baraita* intervenes: *ein mochrin beitzat tereifah le-nochri ela im ken trufah beke'arah* — one may not sell the egg of a *tereifah* bird to a non-Jew lest he resell it to a Jew, unless it has been scrambled in a bowl. Only when scrambled will no Jew purchase it, because a Jew encountering scrambled eggs from a non-Jew knows there are no indicators to check. Consequently, *ein locḥin mimenu beitzim trufot beke'arah* — one may not purchase scrambled eggs from a non-Jew, because the very fact that the eggs have been scrambled raises suspicion: perhaps they were scrambled precisely because they were *tereifah* eggs being sold off. So the *Gemara* has arrived at a closed circle: if the eggs are intact and unscrambled, the indicators should suffice — so why need the merchant's claim? And if they are scrambled, one cannot buy them at all.

---

## Simanim Framework

### Lav De'oraita

This impasse leads Rabbi Zeira to state the governing principle: *simanim lav de'oraita* — the egg indicators are not sufficient at the biblical level (*de'oraita*) to serve as a basis for determination. It is important to clarify what this means. It does not simply mean that these indicators are not written explicitly in the Torah, because the indicators for identifying kosher birds — the *doresh*, the extra toe, the *korkovan nikshal*, and so forth — are likewise not written in the Torah but were derived by the rabbis, yet they are fully sufficient for *de'oraita* purposes. Rather, *simanim lav de'oraita* here means that the indicators for egg kashrus are not a sufficiently reliable basis on which to make a biblical-level determination, because they are not one hundred percent definitive. They are useful but not conclusive.

The phrase itself is borrowed from a major *sugyia* in the second *perek* of *Bava Metzia*, which discusses the return of lost objects. There the question is whether the identifying characteristics (*simanim*) given by a claimant are a biblically valid basis for returning the object. The debate of *simanim de'oraita o lav de'oraita* in that context provides the vocabulary, but the application here is specific: egg indicators, unlike the full morphological indicators of the birds themselves, cannot by themselves settle questions that have biblical-level stakes.

### Eight Birds Problem

The *Gemara* illustrates this principle with a compelling proof. Rav Assi had stated that there were eight birds of uncertain status — the rabbis did not know definitively whether they were kosher or not, the question turning on whether their gizzard was of the peelable kind. One might suppose that this uncertainty could be resolved elegantly: simply examine the eggs of these birds and see whether the eggs display kosher indicators. If these indicators were fully reliable for *de'oraita* purposes, this would be an obvious solution. The very fact that the *Gemara* never proposes this solution — and indeed that the eight birds remain uncertain — proves that *simanim lav de'oraita*: the egg indicators cannot resolve questions of biblical-level bird kashrus.

### Negative vs Positive

The *Gemara* then articulates the precise role these indicators do play: *elu hen simanei beitzim* in their negative capacity are absolutely reliable. If an egg has *two* rounded ends, or two pointed ends, or the yolk is on the outside rather than the inside, that egg is *vadai teme'ah* — certainly non-kosher, and no testimony from any merchant can override it. The negative indicators are conclusive. However, the positive indicators — one rounded end, one pointed end, white on the outside and yolk inside — are necessary but not sufficient. They rule out obvious non-kosher eggs, but they do not by themselves establish that the egg is from a kosher species. Positive indicators in combination with a merchant's testable claim (*veamar lach shelo ploni ve'tahor hu*) together permit reliance. Without the merchant's claim, even a perfectly shaped egg with the correct white-yolk arrangement — *bistama*, without specification — one may not rely on the indicators alone.

### Raven-Dove Problem

### Combined Evidence

Why not? Because *de'ika de'urva dedami leyona* — there are raven eggs that resemble dove eggs. The ArtScroll notes that raven eggs and dove eggs actually do share a similar morphology in terms of the rounded-pointed shape, even though they typically differ in color — and since color has not been mentioned as a criterion in this *baraita*, shape alone is insufficient to distinguish them. If even such a similar case of confusable eggs exists, it stands to reason that other non-kosher bird eggs may share the positive indicators of kosher bird eggs. This is precisely why the indicators cannot stand alone. What is required is both: the positive indicators confirming that nothing is obviously wrong, *and* the merchant's specific, falsifiable claim naming the particular species. The indicators on their own do not suffice because some non-kosher eggs look like kosher ones; the merchant's claim alone would not suffice either, since those same misleading similarities exist. It is the convergence of the two — clean indicators plus a testable, specific claim — that generates sufficient reliability to permit purchase.

This analysis raises broader questions about the role of non-Jewish testimony in *halakha* generally. Some authorities read this *Gemara* as establishing that even when a claim is easily testable and thus subject to *milsa d'avida legluya*, it may still require corroborating physical evidence. Others note that the specific requirement for corroboration here may arise from the unusual circumstance that even the corroborating evidence itself is imperfect — because raven eggs can look like dove eggs, the physical evidence alone is compromised, and so neither strand of proof is sufficient by itself. Whether this *Gemara* establishes a general rule that non-Jewish testimony always requires corroboration, or whether it reflects the particular weakness of these specific indicators, remains a matter of halakhic discussion.

---

## Tosafot Practical Rules

### Majority Principle

How did the *rishonim* actually conduct themselves in a world without formal certification? Tosafot addresses this directly and with great frankness. He notes that the practice in medieval Europe was to purchase eggs from non-Jewish sellers without ever asking them to specify the species — the very step the *Gemara* seemed to require. His justification: *anu somkhim al rov beitzim she-metzuyim beineinu de-shel ofot tehorim hem* — we rely on the fact that the overwhelming majority of eggs found among us come from kosher birds. Just as in discussions of *chalav Yisrael* the question arises whether one need worry when the only available milk is certainly from kosher animals, so too here: where there is no realistic population of non-kosher bird eggs in the marketplace, one may rely on the majority without requiring the merchant's verbal corroboration.

### Mixed Products

Tosafot then extends this analysis to the more complex case of baked goods — *oblias* and *kantias*, various types of pastries and breads that the Jews of medieval Europe regularly purchased from non-Jews, all of which were made with eggs. Here the concern is twofold: the eggs are incorporated into the dough and cannot be individually inspected, and the final product resembles scrambled eggs in that the whites and yolks are no longer distinguishable. Tosafot distinguishes this from the prohibited scrambled egg purchase of the *Gemara*: in that case, the very fact that a non-Jew was selling eggs already mixed and scrambled raised a specific suspicion that they had been scrambled to hide their *tereifah* origin. When a baker incorporates eggs into bread dough, however, no such suspicion attaches — eggs are simply an ingredient in the recipe, and there is nothing suspicious about their appearing in mixed form. *Lo damya* — the two cases are not comparable. One then applies a double reliance: *rov beitzim* that the eggs are from kosher species, and the further likelihood that even among those, the overwhelming majority are not from *tereifah* birds.

### Contextual Leniency

Tosafot also addresses the blood-spot question in this context: *ve-lo chashinan shema haya ba-hem dam* — we do not worry that perhaps there were blood spots in the eggs used for baking, because *rov beitzim ein ba-hem dam* — most eggs simply do not have blood spots. What is striking about Tosafot's entire treatment is that he begins not from abstract legal analysis but from existing practice, and works backward to justify it.
