If it then migrates from pit to flesh, has it left its original habitat in a way that changes its status?

### Fruit-to-Fruit

*Mitimrei letimrei mahu* — what if an insect passes from one date into an adjacent date, without ever passing through open air, when two dates were pressed together?

### Teiku Conclusion

The Gemara answers all of these questions with a single word: *teiku* — they remain unresolved. These cases illustrate just how difficult it is to draw precise lines once one commits to the principle that separation from the original medium is the operative trigger. In an era when produce inspection is easier and stricter standards are routinely applied, these unresolved questions carry correspondingly greater weight; when the easier path was simply to find a basis for permission, the ambiguities were tolerable.

---

## Animal Worms

### Kokiani Forbidden

Rav Sheshes son of Rav Idi rules: *kokiani assiri* — the *kokiani* worms, found in the lungs and liver of an animal, are forbidden. The reason: *me'alma asu* — they came from outside the animal; they did not grow within it originally.

### Rav Ashi Challenge

Rav Ashi challenges this immediately. If the *kokiani* truly came from outside — presumably swallowed with the animal's food — why are they found in the lungs and liver? They should have passed through the digestive tract and be found in the intestines or the stomach. Their presence in the lungs and liver is difficult to explain if they entered through the mouth.

### Formed From Flesh

An alternative view is then presented: some say Rav Sheshes son of Rav Idi originally ruled *kokiani shari* — the *kokiani* are permitted. Why? *minei gavli* — they are formed from the flesh of the animal itself. Here the Gemara makes explicit the ancient assumption about spontaneous generation: the flesh literally becomes the bug. Since these organisms arise from the animal's own tissue and not from any external source, they would — on the analogy of bugs formed within a fruit — be permitted.

### Nostril Entry

Rav Ashi then provides the resolution that leads to the final ruling. The entry route is neither the mouth nor spontaneous generation from the flesh: *minyiraya ayili be'ushi* — they enter through the nostrils during the animal's breathing. When the animal inhales, these tiny organisms enter through the nose, travel through the passages connected to the lungs, and from there reach the liver — which the Gemara treats as connected to the lungs. This explains why they are found in the lungs and liver and not in the digestive tract.

### Final Ruling

*Vehilchesa kokiani assiri* — the final *halacha* is that *kokiani* are forbidden. Because they enter from outside via breathing, they are external organisms that have entered the animal, not creatures formed from the animal's own substance. They are therefore subject to the prohibition applicable to external insects.

---

## Meat vs. Fish

### Beast Worms

*Toloy darna de-bisra assiri* — worms found in the flesh of a beast are forbidden. This ruling will require explanation, since one might have supposed that such worms, growing within the flesh of a properly slaughtered animal, should be analogous to bugs within a fruit — and thus permitted.

### Fish Worms OK

By contrast, *dichvurei de-chayei ha-yamim* — worms found in the flesh of fish — *sharyin*, are permitted.

### Hide & Eat

Ravina offered his mother practical guidance on this point: if you find such worms in the fish, hide them from my sight — I would rather not see them and be disgusted — but I will eat the fish, because *halacha* permits it.

### Origin Theory

Rav Mesharsheya son of Rav Aha explains the distinction by posing the question: how is this different from what a *braisa* teaches, that *et nivlatam tishketzu* — you shall treat their carcasses as abominable — comes to include the *darnim* found in the flesh of a beast, which are forbidden? Why are worms in beast flesh forbidden while worms in fish flesh are permitted?

### Shechita Theory

The answer introduces an entirely new conceptual framework, distinct from the question of whether the organism came from outside or grew within. *behema bi-shechita hu de-mishtaryia* — a beast becomes permitted only through *shechita*. These worms, the Gemara assumes, are formed from (*gavlin* — grew out of) the flesh of the beast itself. They began as beast meat. Meat of a beast requires *shechita* to be permitted. At the moment *shechita* was performed, these organisms were already in their worm-form and distinct from the meat — and so *shechita* did not render them permitted. *be-issuraiyu kaimi* — they remain in their forbidden state: not forbidden as insects, but forbidden as beast meat that was never subject to *shechita*. They are, in effect, a piece of the beast that was transformed *after* the slaughter had already taken effect on the rest of the animal, leaving them outside the scope of the *shechita*.

Fish, however, do not require *shechita*; fish flesh is permitted through mere gathering — *asifa*. Thus even if the worms grew from (*gavlin*) the fish's own flesh, that flesh was already entirely permitted at the moment of gathering. *ki gavlin be-hetera gavlin* — they grew into being within something that was already permitted, and so they too are permitted.

---

## Creeping Things

### Belly Crawlers

The Gemara now turns to a systematic enumeration of the other categories of forbidden creeping things on land. *holech al gachon* — that which goes on its belly — this is the snake (*nachash*). The verse's inclusive language (*kol*) extends to other creatures similar to the snake, *de-domeh le-shilshul* — anything resembling a slithery crawling thing, including various types of worms.

### Four-Legged

*Al arba* — that which goes on four legs — this refers to the scorpion (*akrav*), which moves in its distinctive shuffling gait. The inclusive language again extends to *hachipushit* and anything similar to it. Rashi honestly acknowledges that he does not know precisely what a *chipushit* is; in modern Hebrew the word is used for a ladybug.

### Multi-Legged

*Marbe raglayim* — that which has many legs — this is the *nadal*. Rashi explains: *me'at raglayim korin lo* — they call it the hundred-legged creature — that is, the centipede.

### Inclusive Rule

*Lerabot et ha-domeh ve-et ha-domeh le-domeh* — to include anything similar and anything similar to what is similar. The principle is a sweeping one: any creature not falling within the categories of a *kosher* mammal (split hooves, chewing cud), a *kosher* fish (fins and scales), or a *kosher* bird is forbidden. Every other creeping, crawling, or multi-legged creature is included within these prohibitions.

---

## Livyatan

### R. Yossi Opinion

A final *braisa* closes the perek with an aggadic teaching. Rabbi Yossi ben Durmaskit declares: the *livyatan* — the great sea creature whose flesh will be served at the banquet for the righteous in the World to Come — *dag tahor hu*, is a *kosher* fish.

### Biblical Support

The source is a verse from Job: *ga'ava afikei maginim tachtav chadudei cheres* — pride of the channels of shields is upon it, underneath it are the sharp shards of pottery. *afikei maginim* — the channels of shields — *ellu kaskasim* — these are the scales; the things that protect it like shields are its scales. *tachtav chadudei cheres* — under it are the sharp shards of pottery — *ellu snapirim* — these are the fins; they are like shards of pottery in the way they cut through the water, enabling the creature to swim. Since the *livyatan* has both scales and fins, it possesses the *simanim* of a *kosher* fish, and the righteous may eat it at the great feast to come.

With that, the *hadran* is recited and we close on *elu tereifos*.

---

## Treifot Intro

### Beast Treifot

The third perek opens with its *mishna*: *elu treifot be-behema* — these are the *treifot* in a large domesticated animal.

### Key Defects

The Mishna lists the foundational cases of *treifa*. *nekuvat ha-veshet* — a perforation of the gullet. *pesukat ha-gargeret* — a severed windpipe. *nikav krum shel moach* — if the membrane of the brain was punctured. *nikav ha-lev le-veit chalalo* — if the heart was punctured to its internal cavity. *nishberah ha-shedrah ve-nifsek ha-chut shelah* — if the spinal column was broken and its spinal cord was severed.

### Liver Rule

*Nitlah ha-kaved ve-nishtayer heimena kezayit, harei zu kesheira* — if the liver was removed and there remains of it at least a *kezayit*, the animal is *kosher*. The rule is not merely that some liver must remain; the minimum is a *kezayit*. If even that much remains intact, the animal is valid.

### More Defects

*Nikav ha-mases u-veit ha-kosot la-chutz* — if the omasum or the reticulum were punctured through to the outside. *naflah min ha-gag* — if the animal fell from a roof. *nishtabru rov tzaloteha* — if the majority of its ribs were broken.

### Mauling Rules

*U-derusat ha-ze'ev* — and the mauling of a wolf renders the animal a *treifa*. Rabbi Yehuda qualifies: *derusat ha-ze'ev ba-dekah* — the mauling of a wolf applies to small cattle, for that is within a wolf's power to inflict lethal damage. *u-derusat ha-ari ba-gasah* — the mauling of a lion applies to large cattle. *derusat ha-netz be-of ha-dak* — the mauling of a hawk in small birds. *u-derusat ha-gas be-of ha-gas* — the mauling of a larger predatory bird in large birds. The criterion, in other words, is scaled to the relative strength of predator and prey.

### General Rule

*Zeh ha-klal: kol she-ein kamohah chayyah, treifah* — this is the general rule: any animal that cannot survive as it is, is a *treifa*. This overarching principle encompasses all the specific cases enumerated, and serves as the conceptual foundation for the entire perek to follow.

---

---

# Hullin 68

## Ben Pakua & Shechita

### Opening Remarks

We begin the fourth *perek* of Masechet Hullin, Daf 68. The previous *perek*, *eilu treifos*, was a major accomplishment — spanning some thirty *daf* and covering critical topics in *treifos*, including highly challenging material involving biology and anatomy, as well as questions of which species are *kosher*. All of that was directly and practically relevant to everyday *kashrus*. This fourth *perek*, by contrast, is occupied with more theoretical discussions and interesting conceptual questions before the tractate returns to more practical concerns.

### Ben Pakua Concept

The *perek* opens with a scenario involving *shechita* in the field: one slaughters an animal and wishes to eat its meat, but must consider the status of a potential *ubbar* — a fetus — found in the mother's womb at the time of *shechita*. This fetus is called the *ben pakua*, and the governing principle is that the *shechita* of the mother works for the *ubbar*, because until the fetus is born it is considered part of the mother. However, as the opening *mishna* will make clear, this is not entirely equivalent to any other limb of the mother. The *perek* therefore addresses a range of questions: at what stage is the fetus considered to have been born, such that the mother's *shechita* no longer covers it?

### Mishna: Limb Out

The *mishna* opens: *behema hamaksha leiled* — an animal experiencing difficult labor, meaning it is actively in the process of giving birth. *hotzi ha-ubbar yado vehechzira* — the fetus extended a limb, literally its arm, and then pulled it back in. After this, the mother is slaughtered. *mutar baachila* — the result is permissible to eat.

The *mishna* here leaves open what precisely is permissible. The obvious implication is that the fetus itself may be eaten — but does the word *mutar* extend also to the limb that briefly protruded? This question will occupy the *gemara* at length.

### Mishna: Head Born

The *mishna* continues: *hotzi et rosho* — if the fetus extended its head out of the womb, *af al pi shehecheziro* — even if it was then pulled back in, *harei zeh k'yalud* — it is considered as though it has already been born. In that case, the mother's *shechita* does not cover the fetus.

The working assumption is that this applies when the majority of the head (*rubbo*) has emerged. The *mishna*'s primary focus here is establishing the criterion for birth: not the extension of a limb, but the emergence of the head — and, critically, once the head has emerged, even if it is pulled back, that status of birth is irrevocable.

### Fetus vs. Spleen

The *mishna* then introduces an illuminating contrast. *chotech me-ubbar shebim'eha* — if someone dismembered the fetus while it was still inside the mother's womb and then slaughtered the mother, the *shechita* of the mother still works and the pieces of the fetus are permitted. The fetus's dismembered parts remain within the animal, and the *shechita* covers them.

However, *min hat'chol umin haklayos* — if a person reached into a living animal and detached the spleen or the kidneys — and this case uses specifically the spleen and kidneys because, as established in the previous *perek*, detaching them does not render the animal a *treifa* — those organs, now disconnected and sitting in the body cavity, become *asur baachila*. Slaughtering the animal afterward does not render the spleen and kidneys permissible.

### Fetus Not True Limb

We thus have a striking contrast: a dismembered fetus inside the mother is covered by the mother's *shechita*, while a detached organ of the mother itself is not. The reason lies in the nature of the prohibition of *ever min hachai* — a limb severed from a living animal. When an intrinsic organ such as a spleen or kidney is cut from a living animal, that organ immediately acquires the status of *ever min hachai*, a detached limb from a living creature. Subsequent *shechita* of the mother cannot retroactively undo that status.

The fetus, though we speak of it as *ubbar yerech imo* — as though it were a limb of the mother — is not truly and intrinsically a limb of the mother. It has its own independent vitality, its own developing existence, merely sustained within the mother. Therefore, dismembering the fetus within the womb does not constitute severing a limb from the mother in the halachic sense, does not create *ever min hachai*, and the *shechita* of the mother continues to cover what remains within her.

The *mishna* closes with a *klal*: *davar shegufah asur* — something that is genuinely part of the animal's own body, when severed while the animal is alive, is forbidden as *ever min hachai*. *veshe'eino gufah mutar* — something that is not literally a part of the mother, such as the fetus, is permissible, because the mother's *shechita* still works for it. This closing principle elegantly encapsulates the entire *mishna*: the *shechita* of the mother operates on behalf of the fetus, but we are not asserting that the fetus is in every respect identical to a limb of the mother.

---

## Rav Yehuda's Ruling

### Limb Forbidden

The *gemara* opens with a statement attributed to Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *v'ever atzmo asur* — the limb itself is forbidden. This is an entirely new idea, not found in the *mishna* at all. Rav asserts that when the fetus extends a limb out of the womb, the act of that limb's protrusion renders it forbidden — and it remains forbidden even after it is pulled back in.

This is striking. One might naturally have assumed that while the limb is protruding, the mother's *shechita* simply cannot reach it — it is outside the womb and therefore outside the domain of the *shechita*. But one would also have assumed that if the limb is pulled back in before *shechita*, everything returns to normal: the fetus and all its limbs are now inside the mother, and the *shechita* covers them. Rav rejects this. He holds that the limb, once it has gone out, remains forbidden — not only will the mother's *shechita* fail to cover it, but even if the fetus were subsequently born alive and then slaughtered in its own right, this particular limb would remain forbidden. It has acquired a permanent prohibited status from the moment of its protrusion.

### Basar Basadeh

Where does this principle come from? The *gemara* cites a *pasuk*: *u'vasar basadeh tereifah lo tocheilu* — "and meat of a field that is torn, you shall not eat." Ordinarily, halachic attention falls on the word *tereifah* and the word *basadeh* is passed over. But here the *gemara* draws attention to *basadeh*: *keivan sheyatza basar chutz limechitzato* — once meat goes out beyond its rightful boundaries, like meat exposed out in the field, *ne'esar* — it becomes forbidden. The word *basadeh*, "in the field," is understood as representing the idea of being outside one's zone, beyond one's proper domain.

### Sacrificial Meat

This principle finds its most natural application in the laws of *korbanot*. *kodshei kodashim* — sanctified offerings of the highest degree, such as a *chatat* — may be eaten only within the Temple precincts proper, not even on the *har haBayit* but within the *beis haMikdash* itself. *kodashim kalim* — lesser sanctified offerings, such as *shelamim* — may be eaten throughout Jerusalem. If the meat of a *shelamim* is taken outside Jerusalem, or the meat of a *chatat* is taken outside the *beis haMikdash*, one might wonder: can it simply be brought back and eaten? The answer derived from this *pasuk* is no. Once the meat has left its permitted zone, it becomes forbidden — the sanctity has been, in some sense, violated by its displacement.

### Field Metaphor

This logic is now applied by Rav to the fetus. The proper zone for the fetus — the zone which allows the mother's *shechita* to function on its behalf — is the mother's womb. When a limb protrudes, it is, from the perspective of the *shechita*'s ultimate effect, out of bounds. If the animal is eventually slaughtered and the fetus is to be permitted via the mother's *shechita*, then the relevant domain is the inside of the womb. A limb that has gone outside that domain has, in the framework of *basar basadeh tereifah*, stepped out of bounds. And as Rav frames it: once out of bounds, one cannot return to the play. Even if the limb is pulled back in, it remains forever stamped with the status it acquired when it was outside.

This is a genuine *chiddush*, and admittedly a conceptually unusual one. The idea that a piece of the fetus, which was not yet *ever min hachai* and which is now physically back inside the mother, nonetheless carries a permanent prohibition — this requires the full force of the *basar basadeh* derivation to sustain it.

---

## Gemara Challenges

### What Is Permitted

The *gemara* now turns to examine the *mishna* itself as a potential challenge to Rav's position. The *mishna* says: the fetus extends its limb and pulls it back, the mother is slaughtered — *mutar baachila*. The *gemara* asks: *mai lav eivar* — does this not mean the limb itself becomes permissible? If so, that directly contradicts Rav, who holds the limb remains forbidden. The *gemara* responds: *lo ha-ubbar* — no, the *mutar* refers to the fetus, not the limb. The *mishna* is teaching that the extension of a limb does not constitute a birth event, so the fetus remains covered by the mother's *shechita*.

### Mishna's Point

The *gemara* presses further. If the only point is that the fetus is permissible, *mai irya dehachziro* — why does the *mishna* specify that it pulled the limb back? The conclusion that the fetus is not yet born would hold even while the limb is still extended. The mention of the retraction seems purposeful.

The *gemara* grants the point: *hu hadin af al gav delo hechzir* — yes, even without pulling the limb back, the fetus would not be considered born. The reason the *mishna* mentions the retraction is structural: since the *mishna* wants to conclude with the case of the head being extended and pulled back — and there, the pulling back is the pivot of the law, because once the head emerges the fetus is considered born even if pulled back — the *mishna* mirrors the language in its opening clause as well, mentioning the retraction of the limb to parallel the retraction of the head. The *mishna*'s real *chiddush* lies in the closing case, not in the opening one. The *gemara* therefore maintains that the *mishna* teaches nothing about whether the limb is permitted or forbidden; it is exclusively focused on the threshold of birth.

### Birth Definition

The *gemara* continues: *umai kamashma lan seifa* — so what is the *mishna* actually teaching in its closing section, that when the head emerges the fetus is considered born? The *gemara* responds that this already appears to be known from elsewhere, and it should not be necessary to teach it again. The source cited is from *masechet bechoros*: *eizehu bechor lenachalah ve'eino bechor lekohanim* — what constitutes a firstborn for the purposes of inheritance but not for the purposes of *pidyon haBen*?

To understand this, one must distinguish between the two aspects of *bechora*. The double portion in inheritance goes to the father's firstborn viable son — the first *ben kayama*, the first child who actually survived and was considered viable. The *pidyon haBen* obligation, by contrast, is triggered by *peter rechem*, the first breaching of the womb, regardless of viability. A child born after miscarriages or stillbirths is thus a firstborn for inheritance — he is the first viable child — but not a firstborn for *pidyon haBen*, because the womb was already breached.

The *gemara* adds the case of an eighth-month child — a child born after only eight months of gestation. In the *gemara*'s framework, such a child was considered non-viable regardless of whether it appeared to be living at birth; only a nine-month child was presumed viable. Such a child would count for *pidyon haBen* purposes as having breached the womb, but would not count as the viable firstborn for inheritance. The *mishna* in *bechoros* therefore states: *af al pi sheyatza rosho chai* — even if this non-viable child came out alive, or *ben tesha sheyatza rosho met* — a fully gestated child that was stillborn — in either case, the subsequent child is the firstborn for inheritance but not for *pidyon haBen*.

From this *mishna* the *gemara* infers: *ta'ama derosho met* — the reason the stillborn child did not count for inheritance is because when its head came out it was already dead. The implication is that *ha rosho chai* — had its head emerged alive, it would have been considered born and viable for the inheritance calculation, and the following child would not have received the double portion. This inference establishes that birth is reckoned from the emergence of the head.

### Human vs. Animal

One might object that this evidence comes from the laws of human birth, not animal birth. The *gemara* acknowledges the distinction: *de'adam mibeheima lo yalif* — one cannot draw a direct inference from animals to humans, because *de'ein prozdor libeheima* — animals do not have a *prozdor*. The word *prozdor* ordinarily means an antechamber or vestibule. Rashi and Tosafot acknowledge that this is its standard meaning but find it difficult to understand why the presence or absence of such a canal should alter the threshold of birth.

Their explanation points in a different direction. For a human female, the anatomy is such that the birth canal is not directly exposed; as the fetus emerges, it must be drawn from between the mother's legs, and to the observer the emergence is less immediately visible. One might therefore have thought that more of the fetus must appear before it is considered born. For a female animal, by contrast, the relevant opening is directly exposed, and the emergence of the head is immediately perceptible. Therefore one might have applied the rule of the head more readily to animals than to humans, and it would have been necessary to state both cases.

Conversely, *de'chashiv partzuf panim didei* — for humans, the face carries special significance; the human face represents the entire person in a way that has no animal parallel. One might therefore have thought that specifically for humans, the emergence of the face constitutes birth, while for animals a different standard — perhaps the majority of the animal's body — applies.

Since neither inference would travel safely in either direction, it was necessary to state the rule in each domain independently. Hence the *mishna* in *bechoros* cannot serve as a prior source for the animal case in our *mishna*, and the *gemara* must look further.

---

## Placenta Evidence

### Placenta Proof

The *gemara* finds an additional source in a *mishna* dealing with placentas. The case is one in which a placenta emerges from an animal without any visible fetus accompanying it. Since a placenta necessarily implies a fetus, the *halacha* concludes that a fetus must have been present but dissolved or miscarried. The question is whether the placenta itself may be eaten after the mother is slaughtered, and when.

The *mishna* states: *shilya she-yatzta miktzasa* — if even part of a placenta emerged, *asura baachila* — none of the placenta may be eaten. The reasoning is: *kesiman vlad be-isha kach siman vlad bevehema* — what serves as a sign of birth for a human woman serves equally as a sign of birth for an animal. Since the placenta implies the presence of a fetus, and part of the placenta has emerged, we must assume that the fetus has been born — meaning that the head of the fetus, along with the placenta, has already come out. The *shechita* of the mother therefore no longer covers this placenta-fetus unit, and it is forbidden.

The *gemara* uses this *mishna* to demonstrate that even within the context of animal law, the emergence of the head constitutes birth. The reasoning, admittedly, involves some inference: from the partial emergence of a placenta we assume the head of the fetus came out, and from that we conclude that birth has occurred. The jump from placenta to head is acknowledged to require careful unpacking — Tosafot notes the difficulty — but the *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that partial placenta emergence can only signal birth if we connect it to the standard criterion of the head. Furthermore, none of these cases about the placenta address the scenario of pulling the head back, so the primary *chiddush* of our *mishna* — that once the head has emerged, pulling it back does not undo the birth — may still be a genuine novelty not derivable from these prior sources.

---

## Makom Chataach

### Limb Pulls Back

The *gemara*, having pressed these arguments, introduces the resolution of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak. His principle is: *lo nitzrecha ela lemakom chataach* — the *mishna* is needed only to teach about the *makom chataach*, the place of cutting — the boundary line itself. This concept will be elaborated more fully later, but the kernel of the idea is as follows. When a limb extends out of the mother's womb, there is a portion of that limb that is unambiguously outside, a portion that is unambiguously inside, and a portion right at the line itself — neither in nor out. According to Rav, the part that was outside remains forever forbidden. But the part that was precisely at the line, being neither inside nor outside, does not fall under the *basar basadeh* prohibition. If the limb is pulled back in, that boundary portion — the *makom chataach* — is now fully inside the mother, and the mother's *shechita* covers it. The *mishna* teaches that this boundary portion becomes permissible when the limb is pulled back. This is a narrow reading, but it allows Rav's position to stand: the part that was outside remains forbidden, while the part on the line becomes permissible upon retraction.

---

## Placenta Evidence (II)

### Braita Parallel

The *gemara* now examines a *braita* that parallels the *mishna*. The *braita* describes an animal in difficult labor where the fetus extends a limb and pulls it back — and the mother is then slaughtered: *mutar baachila*, permissible. Once again the question of what is permissible arises.

### Limb Forbidden

The *braita* continues: if the mother was slaughtered while the limb was extended and only then was the limb pulled back, *asur baachila* — it is forbidden. Here the contrast between the two cases — limb pulled back before *shechita* versus pulled back after — suggests that whether the limb is in or out at the moment of *shechita* determines its status.

### Cutting Limb

The *braita* then introduces two further cases. If the limb was extended and cut off while in that state, *shebechutz tamei* — what was cut off outside is considered *tamei*, and indeed constitutes *ever min hachai* — a limb severed from a living creature — which carries *tumah* and is forbidden. The fetus remaining inside, *tahor umutar*, is *tahor* and permissible. If, on the other hand, the mother was slaughtered while the limb was extended and only afterward was the limb cut, the question becomes the status of that extended limb: Rabbi Meir holds it is like *neveilah* — meat that never had the benefit of *shechita* at all — while the Sages hold it is like *maga tereifah shechuta*, in contact with a *tereifah* that was slaughtered, since there was a *shechita* but it simply did not apply to this limb. This is an interesting dispute: does one say there was no *shechita* whatsoever on the limb, making it *neveilah*, or does one say the *shechita* occurred but failed to cover the limb, making it more analogous to a *tereifah*?

---

## Makom Chataach (II)

### Boundary Solution

Returning to the core question, the *gemara* presses the *braita*: the opening clause says that if the fetus extended its limb and pulled it back and then the mother was slaughtered, *mutar baachila*. *mai lav haeiver* — does this not mean the limb itself is permissible? The *gemara* tries to say *lo ha-ubbar* — no, it means the fetus. But this is immediately challenged: *ei ha-ubbar amai asur* — if we are talking about the fetus, why does the closing clause say that when the mother was slaughtered with the limb extended and then the limb was pulled back, it is *asur*? The fetus never becomes forbidden merely because of the limb's extension. Clearly, the subject of both clauses is the limb, not the fetus. And if so, the *braita* explicitly says the limb becomes permissible when pulled back — a direct contradiction to Rav.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer is again: *lo nitzrecha ela lemakom chataach* — the *braita*'s permissibility and prohibition attach not to the limb proper, but to the *makom chataach*, the boundary portion. When the limb is pulled back, that boundary portion moves inside the mother and is covered by the *shechita* — hence *mutar*. When the limb is not pulled back, that boundary portion remains outside or on the line and the *shechita* does not cover it — hence *asur*. The limb itself, on this reading, remains perpetually forbidden as Rav maintains. This is admittedly a significant inference to draw from what appears to be a straightforward statement about whether the limb is in or out, but it is the resolution the *gemara* offers.

### Hoof Braita

A further *braita* is introduced, brought by Avimi who had studied in the *beis medrash* of Bei Chuzaei. This *braita* offers a *drasha* on the *pasuk* that establishes the permissibility of the *ben pakua*: *kol behemah mafreset parsah veshashat shesa shetei parasot maalat gerah babehemah otah tocheilu* — an animal within an animal may be eaten. The *pasuk* uses both the singular *parsah* (hoof) and the plural *parsot* (hooves), and the *braita* derives from this: *parsah hechezir echol* — if it pulls back its hoof, you may eat; *parasot hechezir echol* — if it pulls back its hooves, you may eat. The apparent implication is that pulling the extended limb back renders it permissible.

The *gemara* resists this reading: *lo ha-ubbar* — you can eat the fetus, not the hoof. But then pulling back the hoof would be irrelevant to eating the fetus, and the *gemara* demands: *mai irya hechezir, afilu lo hechezir nami* — if it is about the fetus, why does pulling back matter? Here again Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supplies the answer: *lo nitzrecha ela lemakom chataach* — one reference teaches about the *makom chataach*, the boundary line. The *gemara* then asks why we need two formulations, singular *parsah* and plural *parasot*. Could one not teach both lessons from a single reference? The *gemara* answers: *chad lemakom chataach* — one instance teaches about the boundary line. *vechad lekolat bidmei parah* — the other teaches about a calf born from a cow whose hooves are not cloven, what the *gemara* calls *kalut ben parah*. Rabbi Shimon holds that such an animal, once born into the world, is forbidden — it lacks the characteristic of split hooves that defines a *kosher* species. However, while it remains within the mother's womb, it is still covered by the mother's status. The word *parsah* in the singular — a hoof rather than split hooves — teaches that even a fetus without cloven hooves is permissible while in the mother, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon's view. Thus both the singular and plural forms carry independent teachings, and neither supports the reading that the limb itself becomes permitted.

---

## Ulla Disagrees

### Limb Permitted

Having worked through all the *braitatot* under the framework of Rav's position and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution, the *gemara* now explicitly surfaces the opposing view. *ulla amar rebbi yochanan* — Ulla, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, states: *v'eiver atzmo mutar* — the limb itself becomes permissible when pulled back. This is the position that has been lurking behind all of the *gemara*'s challenges: that there is simply no concept of permanent prohibition attaching to a limb that protrudes and retracts. The only issue while the limb is out is that the *shechita* cannot cover it in that state; once it is pulled back, the *shechita* covers it fully.

### Rav Yehuda Challenge

Rav Yehuda confronts Ulla directly: *veha Rav uShmuel de-amri taryehu, eiver atzmo assur* — but both Rav and Shmuel say the limb remains forbidden. This is significant — we had previously heard the ruling in Rav's name alone, and now we learn that Shmuel concurred.

### Ulla's Response

Ulla's response is celebrated. *man yahiv lan mei'afar deRav uShmuel umalina einan* — who could give us from the dust of where Rav and Shmuel walk, and I would place that dust in my eyes. It is a statement of profound veneration: Ulla holds Rav and Shmuel in the highest esteem. Yet despite this reverence, he maintains: *ela hacha amar Rebbi Yochanan* — nonetheless, here is what Rabbi Yochanan says, and I stand by it.

---

## Rebbi Yochanan

### Chatat Only

Ulla then transmits the full reasoning of Rabbi Yochanan. *hakol hayu bichlal basar basadeh tereifah* — in principle, the verse *u'vasar basadeh tereifah lo tocheilu* communicates a broad idea: meat that exits its proper zone becomes forbidden. This would theoretically encompass *kodshei kodashim* taken outside the *beis haMikdash*, *kodashim kalim* taken outside Jerusalem, and — as Rav extrapolated — the limb of a fetus protruding from the mother's womb. However, *keshepierat lecha hakatuv gabei chatat* — when the Torah explicitly specified this rule in the context of the *chatat*, stating that if it goes outside its boundaries and returns it is nevertheless forbidden — *chatat hu depirat Rachmana bah* — it is specifically by the *chatat* that the Torah made this detail explicit. Rabbi Yochanan concludes that this principle, once particularized to the *chatat*, applies only there. *aval kol mili, keivan dehader, shari* — for everything else, once the meat or limb returns to its proper domain, it becomes permissible.

### Fetus Not Sacrifice

The implication is far-reaching. Even *kodashim kalim* — lesser sacred offerings taken outside Jerusalem — would, according to Rabbi Yochanan, become permissible if brought back. Certainly a fetus's limb, which is not a *korban* at all, does not fall under this stringency. The extension of the *basar basadeh* principle beyond the domain of the *chatat* is, in Rabbi Yochanan's view, an unwarranted extrapolation.

### Moshe's Inquiry

Where does Rabbi Yochanan find that the *chatat* specifically is governed by this rule? It is derived from Moshe's inquiry on the eighth day of the *milu'im*. The goat sin-offering of that day was burned, and Moshe asked why. *chazal* read the *pasuk* — *hen lo huva et dama el hakodesh pnimah* — as conveying two propositions: the blood was not brought into the inner sanctuary, and the meat remained *pnimah*, inside. Moshe was demonstrating that there was no basis to burn it, since neither condition that would have warranted burning applied. The implication drawn is that had the meat been taken outside the *mishkan*, it would have been burned — i.e., it would have been rendered permanently forbidden. This establishes specifically for the *chatat* that departure from its permitted space creates an irremediable prohibition. Rabbi Yochanan limits the rule to this case.

---

## Final Braita

### Braita Rule

A *braita* is now adduced as a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's position. The *braita* expounds on the *pasuk* *u'vasar basadeh tereifah lo tocheilu*: *mah talmud lomar* — what does the verse come to teach? *lefi shematzinu bemaaser sheni uvikurim* — because we have found in the context of non-sacrificial sanctified items such as *maaser sheni* and *bikurim*, which must be consumed in Jerusalem, that if taken outside Jerusalem and brought back they remain permissible — *sheaf al pi sheyatziu chutz lemchitzatan vechazru mutarin* — perhaps even meat that exits its zone and returns would also be permissible. Therefore the verse says *tereifah*: *mah tereifah keivan shenitrefa shuv ein lah heter* — just as a *tereifah* once rendered *treif* has no path back to permissibility, so too meat that exits its zone, *keivan sheyatza chutz lemchitzato shuv ein lo heter* — once it has gone beyond its boundaries, it does not regain its permitted status.

This *braita* states the principle broadly, applying it to meat beyond the specific context of the *chatat*, and thus appears to contradict Rabbi Yochanan's narrower reading.

---

## Rebbi Yochanan (II)

### Maaser Sheni

Rabbi Yochanan's position finds support in the very contrast the *braita* draws. The *braita* itself acknowledges that *maaser sheni* and *bikurim*, which are sanctified but not sacrificial, do become permissible when taken out and brought back. This is precisely Rabbi Yochanan's point: the stringency of permanent prohibition upon departure from the permitted zone applies only to the *chatat* and similarly restricted *kodshei kodashim*, not to lesser sanctified items and certainly not to a fetus's limb.

---

## Final Braita (II)

### Favors Rav

Nonetheless, the *gemara* concludes with *tiyuvta de-Ulla tiyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation of Ulla. The final posture of the *gemara* is to weigh in favor of Rav's position: once the limb has protruded from the womb, it remains forbidden even upon retraction. All of the evidence from the *mishna* and various *braitatot* that seemed to indicate that the limb becomes permissible when pulled back is resolved through Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's principle of *makom chataach* — each time, the leniency applies only to that precise boundary portion that was neither inside nor outside, not to the limb proper.

This is a striking outcome. The weight of straightforward readings throughout the *sugia* consistently pointed toward the permissibility of the limb upon retraction, and the argument from *basar basadeh tereifah* had to work hard against that current. Yet the *gemara* ultimately endorses Rav — and with him Shmuel — that the limb, having once stepped outside the domain which the mother's *shechita* defines, acquires a permanent prohibition that no subsequent retraction can undo.

---

---

# Hullin 70

## Fetus Shechita

### Minalan

The *gemara* opens with a fundamental question: *minalan* — from where do we know that the *shechita* of the mother renders the fetus permitted for consumption? The *mishna* had established this principle as settled law, but the *gemara* now seeks its scriptural basis. The discussion begins from the *pasuk*: *v'chol behemah mafreset parsa* — "and any animal that has a split hoof..." — and concludes with the phrase *babeheimah otah tochelu*, "amongst those animals that one you may eat."

### Behemah Be-Behemah

The initial *drasha* proceeds as follows. The word *behemah* appears at both the beginning and the end of the *pasuk*. Reading these two appearances together yields the formulation *behemah ba-behemah* — an animal within an animal. If there is an animal inside another animal, then slaughtering the mother renders the inner entity permitted *l'rabos ha-vlad*, including the fetus.

### Temurah Difficulty

The *gemara* immediately presses this *drasha*: *ela me'ata yamiru bo* — if the fetus is called a *behemah*, an actual animal, why then cannot it serve as the object of *temurah*? The laws of *temurah* — the forbidden exchange of one consecrated animal for another — operate on the phrase *lehamir behemah b'vehemah*, one *behemah* for another *behemah*. If the fetus qualifies as a *behemah*, the act of *temurah* performed with a fetus should be effective.

Yet the *mishna* states explicitly: *ein memirin lo evarim b'ubarim* — one cannot perform *temurah* using limbs against fetuses, nor fetuses against limbs, nor limbs or fetuses against whole animals, nor whole animals against limbs or fetuses. If any of these combinations are attempted, the act of *temurah* is not legally effective: no transgression has occurred and no sanctity is conferred on the second animal. How can this be, if the fetus is already being called a *behemah*?

### Vechol Behemah

The *gemara* concedes the point and abandons the *behemah ba-behemah* reading. A new *drasha* is proposed. The *pasuk* begins *v'chol behemah* — "any animal" — and the word *v'chol*, "anything," is read expansively: it is almost as though the verse had said *v'chol b'vehemah*, anything within an animal. Under this reading, we are not calling the fetus a *behemah* in its own right. Rather, the verse permits anything located within the animal *l'rabos ha-vlad*, to include the fetus.

### Shleimah Requirement

This inclusive reading immediately generates a problem: if *anything* within the animal is permitted through the *shechita* of the mother, then why does the *mishna* rule that one who cuts away the spleen or the kidney while the animal is still alive — leaving them detached but still inside the body cavity — finds those organs forbidden even after the mother is subsequently slaughtered? According to the expansive reading, they too are "anything in the animal" and should be permitted.

The *gemara* resolves this by reading the word *otah* — "that one" — as a restriction: *shleimah v'lo chaseirah*, only something that constitutes a complete entity in itself, not a part of something larger. The fetus qualifies as a self-contained whole. The spleen and kidney, by contrast, are parts of the mother and have been severed from their context; they are not permitted by the *shechita* of the mother. Something that is a fragment of a larger entity does not fall under the permit.

### Dmut Yonah Case

The *gemara* then tests this position with a further case. *rabbi yochanan* rules: *hashochet et habeheimah u-matza bah dmut yonah assur ba'achilah* — if one slaughters a *behemah* and finds inside it something that resembles a dove, it is forbidden, because the *shechita* of the mother does not work for it. This makes intuitive sense: the *shechita* of the mother works for something that is a natural extension of the mother's reproductive process, not for something aberrant. Whether the *gemara* means this literally — that a genetically alien creature is growing inside the animal — or whether it refers to a fetal stage at which the phenotype does not yet resemble a cow, the ruling stands: only something that presents as an animal-like entity is covered.

But how does this fit the *drasha*? If the verse permits "anything in the animal," there is no basis to exclude something that happens to look like a bird. It is a complete entity (*shleimah*), it is inside the animal — why is it forbidden?

### Hoofs Requirement

The *gemara* answers by invoking another word in the *pasuk*. The verse reads in full: *v'chol behemah asher hi mafreset parsah v'shosa'at shesa shtei frasot babeheimah otah tochelu* — "any animal that splits the hoof and has two split hooves, among those animals that one you may eat." The *drasha* "anything in an animal" still draws on *v'chol b'vehemah*, but the word *parsot* — hooves — limits what qualifies. Only something with hooves, something that resembles a *behemah* in that respect, is covered. This excludes the dove-like entity.

The *gemara* then asks: according to this reasoning, *kalut b'mei parah leiaser* — should a fetus with an unsplit hoof, resembling a camel's hoof rather than a split cow's hoof, also be forbidden? The *gemara* answers: *ha tani d'vei Rabbi Yishmael k'Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai*. The school of *rabbi yishmael* taught in accordance with *rabbi shimon ben yochai*, whose *drasha* uses both the singular *parsah* and the plural *parsot* present in the verse. The singular *parsah* permits a fetus with an unsplit hoof — inside the mother — while the plural *parsot* permits one with split hooves. Note carefully that *rabbi yishmael*'s school treats the fetus with an unsplit hoof as permitted only while in the mother; once born, such an animal would be forbidden.

At this point, the *gemara* has navigated to the following position: the fetus is permitted through the *shechita* of the mother not because it is called a *behemah* in its own right, but because it is a complete entity (*shleimah*) inside the mother that possesses either a split or unsplit hoof — close enough in form to a *behemah* — and is therefore covered by the inclusive term *v'chol*, qualified by *otah* and *parsot/parsah*.

### Rabbi Ashimi Solution

*Rav Ashimi bar Ashi* now proposes returning to the original *drasha*. He says: *le'olam kede'kamart me'ikara* — in truth, let us restore the original formulation of *behemah ba-behemah*. This is a far more elegant *drasha* and naturally accounts for the requirement that the fetus resemble an animal: it must be a *behemah* inside the *behemah*. The one outstanding objection — why *temurah* does not work — he undertakes to answer directly.

### Temurah & Ma'aser

*Rav Ashimi* responds: *ha mani Rabbi Shimon hi de-makish temura le-ma'aser* — the *mishna* that says *temurah* cannot be performed with fetuses reflects the position of *rabbi shimon*, who derives the laws of *temurah* from *ma'aser behemah*, the tithing of animals. The verse governing *temurah* in the context of *ma'aser* reads: *ha'asiri yiheyeh kodesh la-Shem, lo yachalifenu v'lo yamir oto betov bera'* — the tenth shall be sacred to God, do not exchange or substitute it. The Torah repeats the prohibition of *temurah* in the context of *ma'aser*, and *rabbi shimon* draws legal conclusions from that juxtaposition.

One such conclusion: the *ma'aser* verse says *asher ta'avor tachat ha-shavet* — "that passes under the staff" — meaning the animal must walk on its own accord. A fetus cannot walk under a staff. Therefore, just as *ma'aser* does not apply to fetuses, *temurah* — which is compared to *ma'aser* by *rabbi shimon* — likewise does not apply to fetuses. In the *gemara*'s formulation: *ma ma'aser eino noheg be'evarim uve'ubarim, af temura einah noheget be'evarim uve'ubarim*. The same exclusion applies to limbs, for the same reason.

So the position of the *mishna* is entirely coherent: the fetus is called a *behemah*, justifying the *drasha* of *behemah ba-behemah*, but *temurah* still does not apply because *rabbi shimon* derives the inapplicability of *temurah* to fetuses from the *ma'aser* comparison. The *drasha* of *behemah ba-behemah* is thus restored.

### Rabbi Yosi Disagrees

The *gemara* now proves that the *mishna* excluding *temurah* for fetuses reflects *rabbi shimon* by pointing to the dissent recorded at the end of that same *mishna*. *rabbi yosi* says: *v'lo be-mukdashim* — and is the law not otherwise even by consecrated animals? He argues that one can sanctify a limb, and by doing so the sanctity spreads to the entire animal (*kulah olah*). If sanctifying a limb can transform the whole animal, then an act of *temurah* performed on a limb — *raglah shel zu tehei zu tachat zu* — should likewise be effective, making the whole animal a *temura* in exchange for the consecrated animal. *rabbi yosi* holds that *temurah* can indeed be performed on limbs, and presumably on fetuses as well.

### Proving Tanna Kamma

The *gemara* now asks: to whom is *rabbi yosi* directing his argument? *leman ka-mahadar lei?* His proof rests on the premise that sanctifying a limb transforms the entire animal. But *rabbi meir* and *rabbi yehuda* do not accept that premise. For them, sanctifying a limb results in only the limb bearing sanctity, not the whole animal. Therefore *rabbi yosi* cannot be arguing with *rabbi meir* or *rabbi yehuda*. He must be addressing someone who shares his premise — and that person is *rabbi shimon*. This proves that the *tanna kamma* of the *mishna* who holds that *temurah* cannot be performed on fetuses or limbs is *rabbi shimon*, which is precisely what *rav ashimi* asserted.

### Limb Sanctification

A *baraita* makes the positions explicit. *yachol omer raglo shel zo ola tehei kulo ola* — one might think that if one declares "the leg of this animal is an *ola*," the entire animal becomes an *ola*. The verse says: *kol asher yiten mimenu la-Shem yiheyeh kodesh* — whatever one gives from it to God shall be sanctified. The word *mimenu* — from it — implies that only part becomes sanctified, *v'lo kulo kodesh*: not the whole animal becomes holy. But then can the leg simply be redeemed? No, because the verse adds *yiheyeh* — "shall be" — meaning *be-havayato tehei*, it retains its status. Since it cannot be redeemed without a *mum* and cannot be brought as a *korban* on its own, the practical resolution is *mocher le-tzorchei olot*: one sells the whole animal to someone who needs to bring an *ola*, at a discount excluding the value of the already-consecrated limb, and that person brings the whole animal. This, the *baraita* states, is the position of *rabbi meir* and *rabbi yehuda*.

*Rabbi Yosi* and *rabbi shimon*, however, derive from the word *yiheyeh* the opposite conclusion: *lirabos kulo*, the whole animal becomes an *ola*. If one sanctifies a limb, the entire animal is transformed. This is the shared premise between *rabbi yosi* and *rabbi shimon* that makes *rabbi yosi*'s argument regarding *temurah* legible only as addressed to *rabbi shimon*. The identification of the *tanna kamma* as *rabbi shimon* is thus confirmed.

### Rabbi Yosi's Logic

The *gemara* qualifies the proof. The final conclusion is *lo* — not quite. *rabbi yosi ta'ama de-nafshei ka'amar*: *rabbi yosi* is not necessarily addressing *rabbi shimon* at all. He is simply articulating his own reasoning. His position is: I hold that *temurah* can be performed on a limb, for the same reason I hold that sanctifying a limb transforms the whole animal. These two views are logically connected in *rabbi yosi*'s own system. He is not attempting to persuade *rabbi meir* and *rabbi yehuda*, who reject his first premise; he is simply explaining the inner coherence of his own position. From this reading, the identity of the *tanna kamma* remains somewhat open, though the *drasha* of *behemah ba-behemah* remains the most naturally elegant and most frequently cited basis for permitting the fetus through the mother's *shechita*.

### Spleen & Kidney

Before proceeding, it is worth pausing on a point that the *gemara* never explicitly addresses. Why exactly are the spleen and kidney forbidden after the mother's *shechita*? One might have assumed the reason is *eiver min ha-chai* — that by cutting them away from the living animal, one created a limb severed from a living creature, which remains forbidden regardless of subsequent *shechita*. But strikingly, this *gemara* never once invokes the concept of *eiver min ha-chai* in that discussion.

The *gemara*'s reasoning is rather that the *shechita* of the mother simply does not extend its permit to them. They are fragments of the mother, not complete entities, and the *drasha* — whether *behemah ba-behemah* or *v'chol b'vehemah* qualified by *otah* — covers only what qualifies as a whole thing. Once severed, the spleen and kidney are pieces of flesh inside the body cavity, no longer part of the mother and not covered by any *drasha* to include them. Their status would then be that of *neveila* — meat that did not undergo *shechita* — rather than *eiver min ha-chai*. The practical difference is significant: a non-Jew could consume them, and they would not generate *tumah*. This reading emerges organically from the *gemara*'s own logic, even if never stated outright.

---

## Bechor & Childbirth

### Mivakeret Case

The next *mishna* shifts from the laws of *shechita* to the laws of *bechor*. The case is *hamivakeret ha-maksheh liyaled* — an animal giving birth for the first time (*mivakeret*, in the *hif'il*, meaning the one causing a firstborn to be born) that is experiencing difficulty in childbirth (*maksheh*). In such a situation one may cut the fetus limb by limb to save the mother's life. The *mishna* rules: *mechatich eiver eiver u-mashlich la-klavim* — one may cut it limb by limb and throw the pieces to the dogs.

The reasoning is that *bechor* sanctity attaches only at birth, and birth has not yet occurred. Each limb, as it emerges, is severed before the fetus is considered born, and therefore carries no *bechor* sanctity. Since the pieces have no sanctity, they may be discarded.

### Bechor Emergence

When precisely does the fetus become a *bechor*? The *mishna* implies two triggers: emergence of the head, or emergence of the majority (*rubo*) of the body. If the birth is headfirst, the head's emergence confers *bechor* status. If the birth is not headfirst — which is precisely the dangerous scenario motivating the intervention in our *mishna* — then the *rov*, the majority, must emerge for the *bechor* sanctity to attach. This is why, with each limb emerging, the act of cutting prevents the *bechor* from ever being "born" in the legally operative sense.

### Majority & Exemption

The *mishna* continues: *yatza rubo, harei zeh yikaver* — once the majority has emerged, the animal now bears *bechor* sanctity. Even if pieces continue to be cut at that point, what is being cut carries *bechor* sanctity and must be buried rather than discarded; it is a *korban* that has died and may not be used. Furthermore, *u-niftar min ha-bechora* — this birth exempts subsequent offspring from *bechor* status. Even a birth accomplished through the piecemeal collection of limbs until a majority has emerged constitutes a birth for *halachic* purposes, such that the next animal born to this mother will not be a *bechor*. *tosafot* draws an explicit parallel: a human *mishna* similarly holds that once a majority of the fetus emerges — even piecemeal — the mother is considered a *yoledet* and acquires the relevant *tumah*, a ruling that confirms that majority need not emerge at once.

### Piecemeal Status

The *mishna*'s language on this point is somewhat ambiguous — does *yatza rubo* refer to a majority that emerged all at once, or one that accumulated through the piecemeal dismemberment? *tosafot* clarifies that the logic applies to the accumulated majority as well, consistent with the parallel *mishna* concerning human birth and *tumat leidah*. The practical halachic question of how to measure "majority" — whether by volume, by number of limbs (*rov minyan u-vinyan*), or by some other standard — is left for further discussion, though the presumption is that it tracks the volume majority of the fetus.

---

## Selling to Non-Jew

### Third Sold Case

The *gemara* now presents a more complex scenario: *yatza shalish u-machro le'oved kochavim* — a third of the fetus emerged and was sold to a non-Jew. Since a *bechor* must be entirely owned by a Jew to bear *bechor* sanctity, selling even a portion to a non-Jew, in principle, exempts the animal from *bechor* status. The sale here was not of the fetus while still entirely in the womb (a known device for avoiding *bechor*), but of that portion that had already emerged. Then *vachazar v'yatza shalish acher* — the rest came out, bringing the total to a majority. What is the status? Has the sale to the non-Jew successfully prevented *bechor* sanctity from attaching?

### Rav Huna View

*Rav Huna amar kadosh* — it is sanctified as a *bechor*. The sale was ineffective. His reasoning: *kasvar lemafrei'a kadosh* — once the majority emerges, the *bechor* sanctity takes effect retroactively. *de-keivan de-nafik lei rubei, iglai milta lemafrei'a de-me'ikara hava kadosh* — since the majority has now come out, the matter is revealed retroactively, and we understand that the sanctity in fact began from the moment the birth process commenced. *u-mai de-zavin lav klum zavin* — and since it was already sanctified from that earlier moment (viewed retroactively), the sale of a *bechor* is invalid, and the non-Jew acquired nothing. This is the *lemafrei'a* principle: halachic retroactivity that reaches back to the beginning of the process once the legally operative moment — emergence of the majority — is achieved.

### Rava View

*Rava amar eino kadosh* — it is not sanctified. His reasoning: *kasvar mikan u-lehaba kadosh* — the sanctity of *bechor* takes effect only from the moment of majority emergence going forward, not retroactively. *u-mah de-zavin shapir zavin* — the sale made before the majority emerged was therefore a valid sale. Once the majority does emerge, *bechor* sanctity would ordinarily attach, but now part of the fetus is already owned by a non-Jew. A *bechor* that is partly non-Jewish owned does not become a *bechor*, and therefore the sanctity does not apply.

### Sale Validity

The practical divergence is sharp. Under *rav huna*, the retroactive view, the sale of the third to the non-Jew is nullified by the *bechor* sanctity that is deemed to have existed from the beginning; the non-Jew acquired nothing, and the animal is a full *bechor*. Under *rava*, the forward-looking view, the sale was valid at the time it was made, the third remains in non-Jewish ownership, and the *bechor* sanctity never fully attaches.

---

## Cesarean & Natural

### Mixed Emergence

The *gemara* now presents a second scenario that tests the same underlying debate. *yatza shlish derech dofen u-shenei shlishim derech rechem* — a third of the fetus emerged through the wall of the womb (i.e., via Cesarean section), and then two-thirds emerged through the normal birth canal. Birth — in the halachically operative sense, *peter rechem* — requires emergence through the natural opening, not through a surgical incision in the uterine wall. So a third came out in a non-birth manner, and then the remaining two-thirds came out naturally, at which point the majority had been reached. Is the animal a *bechor*?

### Rav Huna: No Sanctity

*Rav Huna amar eino kadosh* — it is not sanctified. True to his *lemafrei'a* approach, once the majority emerges, he looks retroactively to the beginning of the process. The beginning of the process here was a Cesarean extraction — a non-birth. Since the process began through the wall of the womb and not through the natural opening, the entire birth process is tainted. *u-rubba kama leisa be-rechem* — and that initial portion was not from the normal birth canal. The retroactive view requires that the beginning of the process qualify as genuine birth, and here it does not.

### Rava: Sacred

*Rava amar kadosh* — *rava* says it is sanctified. *rava le-tameih de-amar mikan u-lehaba kadosh* — consistent with his forward-looking position, *rava* does not retroactively examine the process. He asks only: what is in front of us now? *u-rubba derech rechem nafka* — the majority emerged through the natural birth canal. That is the operative fact. The Cesarean third is simply ignored; it does not corrupt the analysis. Since the majority came out through the natural opening, *rava* considers the animal born and the *bechor* sanctity fully operative.

This pairing of positions produces an intriguing reversal of the practical outcome. In the first scenario (selling to a non-Jew), *rav huna*'s retroactive view leads to the *stringent* conclusion (the animal is a *bechor*, the sale failed), while *rava*'s forward-looking view leads to the *lenient* conclusion (no *bechor*). In the second scenario (Cesarean plus natural birth), *rav huna*'s retroactive view leads to the *lenient* conclusion (not a *bechor*), while *rava*'s forward-looking view leads to the *stringent* conclusion (is a *bechor*). Neither *amora* is simply playing it strict or lenient; each is applying a consistent analytical principle.

### Need Both Cases

This observation is itself the subject of the *gemara*'s closing discussion. *utzricha* — it is necessary to state both cases. Had the *gemara* only reported the first case, one might have supposed that *rav huna* adopts the retroactive view only because doing so there produces a *stringent* result (*le-chumra*), and perhaps in the second case, where retroactivity produces a *lenient* result, he would concede to *rava*. Conversely, had the *gemara* only reported the second case, one might have supposed that *rava* adopts the forward-looking view only because it is strict in that scenario, and in the first case perhaps he would agree with *rav huna*. By recording both cases, the *gemara* establishes that each *amora* holds his position consistently regardless of whether it leads to stringency or leniency in the particular case at hand. Their dispute is principled and systematic, not outcome-driven.

---

---

# Hullin 70b

## Intro & Overview

### Context & Transition

The opening pages of this *perek* have dealt with *shechita* and *kashrus*-related questions surrounding the mother and her fetus: when slaughtering a mother cow, one may eat the fetus found inside, with attendant discussions about protruding limbs and the status of a firstborn. Now the *daf* pivots to an entirely different domain—*tumah v'taharah*—while retaining the same underlying phenomenon of the mother and the fetus within her womb.

### Mishnah: Fetus Status

The *mishnah* at the top of 70b opens: *behemah shemeisah v'ubar b'toch me'eha*—an animal that has died while its fetus is still in the womb, a stillborn. Were such a fetus to have been born and died on the outside, it would be a *nevelah*, and one who touches it would become *tamei* at the level of a *rishon*. The question the *mishnah* poses is whether that *tumah* exists while the fetus remains inside the living mother's womb.

The shepherd—*Tosafot* notes that the one assisting in the birthing of cattle is referred to in the masculine because of this very term—reaches his hand inside and touches the dead fetus. The *mishnah* rules: *bein b'vehemah tme'ah bein b'vehemah tehorah, tahor*—whether the mother is a kosher or non-kosher animal, the one who touches the fetus is *tahor*. The dead fetus in the womb, regardless of species, does not yet communicate *tumah*.

This ruling stands in direct contrast to the subsequent *mishnah*, which discusses a human stillbirth: there, if a midwife reaches her hand into the womb and touches the fetus, she becomes *tme'ah*, treated as though she has touched a corpse even before the fetus has been delivered. The underlying distinction turns on the concept of *balua*—literally "swallowed up," absorbed within another body. From the perspective of the mother, the fetus is still entirely contained within her and has not yet entered the outside world. But from the perspective of the midwife or shepherd who inserts a hand into the womb, the situation is different: that person is now in direct contact with the fetus in a shared space, not separated from it by any intervening body. Nevertheless, the *mishnah* holds that for an animal fetus, even this direct contact does not produce *tumah*, whereas for a human fetus it does—and the *gemara* will explain why.

## Tanna Kamma vs. R. Yose

### R. Yose: Kosher/Non-Kosh…

*Rabbi Yose HaGlili* dissents from the anonymous first opinion: *b'tme'ah tamei, uv'tehorah tahor*—by a non-kosher animal, such as a horse, touching the dead fetus in the womb renders one *tamei*; by a kosher animal, such as a cow, it does not. This distinction, which might initially seem strange given that both a dead horse and a dead cow generate the same *tumah* of *nevelah*, becomes intelligible upon reflection.

### Logic: Shechita & Edibil…

The key consideration is what would happen if the mother were slaughtered. If the mother cow were subject to *shechita* while the dead fetus was inside her, that fetus would be treated as a piece of meat belonging to the mother and could be eaten—this was precisely the ruling discussed earlier in the *perek*. By a horse, of course, *shechita* is irrelevant because the animal can never be eaten in any case.

Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position therefore rests on the following logic: since the dead fetus inside a kosher mother cow could, through the mother's *shechita*, become permissible for consumption—regarded simply as a piece of meat attached to the mother—we cannot yet classify it as an animal corpse. And if it cannot yet be called a *nevelah*, it cannot communicate the *tumah* of a *nevelah*. This reasoning is also why the logic of the *mishnah* is not trivial: once you assert that the dead fetus in the mother's womb is not a *nevelah*, that status cannot suddenly reverse itself. The only way the mother's *shechita* can render the fetus permissible is if one maintains from the outset that a dead fetus in the womb is not yet a *nevelah*. The two positions are interdependent.

### Tanna Kamma: All Equal

The *tanna kamma* agrees with Rabbi Yose HaGlili's reasoning for the kosher animal but goes further, extending the same ruling to the fetus of a non-kosher animal. The *tanna kamma* holds that since kosher and non-kosher animals are treated identically for *tumah* purposes—both corpses being classified as *nevelah* and generating the same *tumah*—what is true of one must be true of the other. If the dead fetus of a kosher animal in the womb is *tahor*, the same applies to the dead fetus of a non-kosher animal.

## Rav Chisda: Kal VaChomer

### Kal VaChomer Logic

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama d'Tanna Kamma*—what is the reasoning of the *tanna kamma* who says that even the dead fetus of a non-kosher animal does not cause *tumah*? Rav Chisda answers: it is a *kal vachomer*. The argument proceeds in two steps, the first of which also supports Rabbi Yose HaGlili.

The *kal vachomer* is formulated as follows: *im ho'il imo lehatirah ba'achilah, lo to'il lo letaharo midei nevelah*—if the mother is capable of making this dead fetus permissible for eating, should she not certainly be able to remove it from the status of *nevelah* for purposes of *tumah*? The point is that rendering something fit for consumption is in some sense a more demanding standard than simply determining *tumah* status. If the mother's *shechita* can achieve the more demanding result of permitting the fetus for consumption, how much more so should it prevent the fetus from being classified as a *nevelah* that causes *tumah*. This is the *kal vachomer* that explains why the dead fetus of a kosher animal in its mother's womb does not render one *tamei*.

### Kosher Animal: Tahor

The *gemara* thus establishes: *ashkachan behemah tehorah*—we have accounted for the kosher animal. This is the basis for Rabbi Yose HaGlili as well as the *tanna kamma* with respect to the kosher species. The next question is how to extend this ruling to the non-kosher animal.

## Non-Kosher Fetus Derivat…

### Q: Non-Kosher Status

*Behemah tme'ah minayin*—and from where do we know this ruling applies to the non-kosher animal? In the case of a horse or other non-kosher species, the mother's *shechita* is irrelevant; the fetus inside can never be rendered permissible for eating. The *kal vachomer* does not apply. So why would the dead fetus of a non-kosher animal also be *tahor* in the womb?

### Pasuk: Vechi Yamut

The *gemara* cites a *pasuk*: *v'chi yamut min habehemah asher hi lachem l'ochlah, hanogea b'nivlatah yitma ad ha'arev*—"and if it dies from the animal that is for you to eat, one who touches its corpse is *tamei* until evening." This verse addresses the *tumah* of a *nevelah* of a kosher animal. The *gemara* now applies a *drasha* to this verse: although the verse concludes with *asher hi lachem l'ochlah*—"which you may eat"—one may pause at the phrase *min habehemah*, "from an animal," which can encompass any animal, kosher or non-kosher. Thus: *min habehemah*—*zu behemah tme'ah*, a non-kosher animal as well; *asher hi lachem l'ochlah*—*zu behemah tehorah*, a kosher animal.

### Hekesh: Kosher/Non-Kosher

This reading creates a *hekesh*: it links kosher and non-kosher animals together with respect to the *tumah* of an animal corpse. The *gemara* then spells out the implication: *mah behemah tehorah ubaratah tahor*—just as by a kosher animal the dead fetus inside is *tahor* (since, as demonstrated by the *kal vachomer*, it could become permissible through the mother's *shechita*), *af behemah tme'ah ubaratah tahor*—so too, by a non-kosher animal, the dead fetus in the womb is *tahor*.

The structure of the argument is now clear. Logically, one can only prove on independent grounds that the dead fetus of a kosher animal does not cause *tumah*—that is Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position. The *tanna kamma* goes further by using this *hekesh* to extend the ruling to the non-kosher animal: since *tumah* of *nevelah* is identical for both species, we compare them and apply the same rule to both fetuses. Rabbi Yose HaGlili does not accept this extension, maintaining the distinction. The *tanna kamma*'s position depends entirely on the *hekesh* to cross that line.

## Refining Hekesh Criteria

### Challenge: Hooves vs. Ko…

The *gemara* is not yet satisfied. The verse used by the *tanna kamma* to create the *hekesh* does not actually speak in terms of kosher versus non-kosher. Rather, it invokes the language of *mahalchei kapayim*—things that walk on paws. This raises an immediate question: should the relevant criterion be kosher status, or the physical characteristic of having split hooves versus non-split hooves?

The *gemara* explores this problem through a series of cases. The first is *kalut b'mei para*—a cow with non-split hooves (*kalut*), an aberration, found as a fetus within its mother. Would one say that because this fetus walks on paws—non-split hooves—even though it is the fetus of a kosher animal, it would cause *tumah* within the womb? According to the logic that the *pasuk* speaks about paws, one might think so: *d'mahalchei kapayim b'chayah hu*—it is a paw-walker inside of an animal.

### Holech BeChol Holech

The *gemara* responds by attending to the full verse: *v'chol holech al kapav b'chol hachayah haholechet al arba*. The phrase *haholechet al arba*—"that goes on four"—at the end of the verse is significant. A cow with split hooves is considered to be going, in effect, on eight, since each split hoof counts as two. Therefore, *tumah* is only generated when a paw-walker is found inside of a four-footed creature—that is, one whose hooves are not split. A non-split-hooved fetus inside a normal cow, which is "eight-footed," would not fall under this rule: *v'hai mahalchei arba v'mahalchei shmonah hu*—it is a four-footed within an eight-footed, and the verse requires four-within-four.

### Further Cases

The *gemara* now pushes further. *para b'mei gamal*—a fetus resembling a cow, with split hooves, found within the womb of a camel. The camel has no split hooves and is thus "four-footed." The cow-like fetus with split hooves would be "eight-footed." So here we have an eight-footed within a four-footed. Is this covered by the *pasuk*?

The *gemara* answers: *holech b'chol holech*—the verse says not merely "that goes" but "everything that goes," *v'chol*, which extends the rule to include even this aberrant case. The inclusive language of the verse thus covers a split-hooved fetus inside a non-split-hooved mother.

But the *gemara* is still not satisfied, because the analysis still tracks hooves rather than kosher status. It therefore poses the case of *kalut b'mei kelutah*—a fetus with non-split hooves inside a mother that also has non-split hooves, an aberration of a kosher animal. This is a case of four-footed within four-footed, which fits the verse precisely—and yet both mother and fetus are kosher animals. According to the hoof-based reading, this should cause *tumah*. The *gemara* responds: here, one returns to Rav Chisda's *kal vachomer*. Since this is ultimately a kosher fetus inside a kosher mother, the mother's *shechita* could render the fetus permissible for eating, and therefore it cannot be treated as a *nevelah* causing *tumah*. The *kal vachomer* overrides the apparent implication of the verse.

### Rav Achtva'i Objection

At this point, *rav achtva'i bar ami* raises a decisive objection. The entire discussion has been struggling to locate a case where the hoof-based criterion yields the same result as the kosher/non-kosher criterion. But, he notes, there is an obvious counterexample that has been overlooked: the pig. A pig has split hooves but is not kosher. Therefore, *chazir b'mei chazirta*—the fetus of a pig inside a sow—presents the case of a split-hooved creature inside a split-hooved creature: *d'mahalchei shmonah meimalchei shmonah hu*, an eight-footed within an eight-footed. According to the hoof-based reading, this case *should not* cause *tumah*. But there is no logical basis for saying that the dead fetus of a pig in its mother's womb is *tahor*—neither the *kal vachomer* (which depends on the mother's *shechita* being effective) nor any other consideration applies. This demonstrates conclusively that the dividing line cannot be hooves; it must be kosher versus non-kosher status.

## Rav Nachman: Vayikra Sou…

### Pasuk Omission Analysis

Having established that the hoof-based approach fails, the *gemara* turns to a different source. *ela amar rav nachman bar yitzchak me'hacha*—rather, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives the ruling from a different verse. The verse in question is from the beginning of *vayikra*, in the context of the *korban oleh v'yored*: *nefesh ki tiga b'chol tamei, o b'nivlat chayah tme'ah, o b'nivlat behemah tme'ah, o b'nivlat sheretz tamei*—"a soul that touches anything *tamei*, or the corpse of a non-kosher wild animal, or the corpse of a non-kosher domesticated animal, or the corpse of a *sheretz*." This verse lists various categories of *tumah* that trigger liability. Strikingly, what the verse does *not* mention is the corpse of a *kosher* animal.

The *gemara* asks the obvious question: *v'chi nivalat behemah tme'ah metamei, u'tehorah lo metame'ah*—does only the corpse of a non-kosher animal cause *tumah*, while the corpse of a kosher animal does not? Of course not—there is an explicit verse elsewhere that establishes the *tumah* of a kosher animal's corpse. Why, then, is the kosher animal's corpse absent from this passage?

### Fetus-Specific Teaching

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer is elegant: the omission is intentional. There exists precisely one context in which the corpse of a non-kosher animal creates *tumah* but the corpse of a kosher animal does not—and that is the case of the fetus in the womb. The verse, by listing only non-kosher animals, is specifically teaching about fetal status.

### Resolution: Non-Kosher O…

*Ela eizehu zeh—ubar she'bitme'ah tamei u'vitehorah tahor*: which case is this? This is the fetus—where the fetus of a non-kosher animal causes *tumah* and the fetus of a kosher animal does not. This is the position of Rabbi Yose HaGlili, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's verse provides a clean *scriptural* basis for it: the *torah* itself encodes the asymmetry between kosher and non-kosher fetuses precisely in this *parshah* by mentioning only the non-kosher animal's corpse.

## Both Verses Needed

### Purpose of Hooves Verse

The *gemara* now raises a natural follow-up: *ume'achar denafkah lei mi'd'Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, d'Rabbi Yitzchak lamah li*—once we can derive the whole ruling from Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's verse, what is still the purpose of the verse used by Rabbi Yitzchak, which spoke about paw-walkers inside of animals? If Rav Nachman's *pasuk* already establishes that only the non-kosher fetus causes *tumah*, why do we need Rabbi Yitzchak's verse at all?

### Combined Verses: Distinc…

The *gemara* answers: *ei lav d'Rabbi Yitzchak, hava amina kullah k'Rabbi hu de'asa*—had it not been for Rabbi Yitzchak's verse, one might have concluded that the entire point of the verse in *vayikra* that mentions non-kosher animals is not to address the question of fetuses at all, but rather to convey a different *drasha* attributed to *rabbi* (whose teaching will be encountered shortly). Without Rabbi Yitzchak's verse drawing our attention to the possibility that a fetus within a mother might have distinct *tumah* status, we would not have known to read the *vayikra* verse in the way Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes.

It is the *combination* of both verses that does the work. Rabbi Yitzchak's verse, which speaks of a creature inside another creature (*bechol hachayah*), alerts us to the possibility of differential fetal *tumah* status. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's verse then provides the textual demonstration that this differential exists and that the dividing line is kosher versus non-kosher. Neither verse alone is sufficient; together they establish that fetuses of non-kosher animals cause *tumah* while fetuses of kosher animals do not.

## Behema/Chaya Terminology

### Terms Introduced

The preceding discussion involved verses that speak of any *behemah* that dies or any *chayah* that dies, and this brings the *gemara* to a brief but illuminating digression concerning the terms *behemah* and *chayah* in *tanach*. These terms can be used in a technical sense—where *behemah* refers to domesticated animals and *chayah* to non-domesticated ones—or in a non-technical sense, where both terms simply mean "animal" in general. The *gemara* now explores how this ambiguity affects the determination of which animal corpses cause *tumah*.

### Tanya: R. Yonatan/Ben Az…

A *braita* is introduced: *amar Rabbi Yonatan, namti lo l'Ben Azzai*—Rabbi Yonatan said, I spoke to Ben Azzai. Rabbi Yonatan recounts that he told Ben Azzai: we have learned that the corpse of a kosher *behemah* causes *tumah*—this is explicit in the verse *v'chi yamut min habehemah asher hi lachem l'ochlah, hanogea b'nivlatah yitma ad ha'erev*. We also know that the corpse of a non-kosher *behemah* causes *tumah*, and that the corpse of a non-kosher *chayah* causes *tumah*—both are stated explicitly in the *vayikra* passage.

### Gap: Kosher Chaya
