What is missing from all of these explicit sources is the corpse of a *kosher chayah*—a deer, for example. The *torah* gives us the *tumah* of a kosher *behemah*, a non-kosher *behemah*, and a non-kosher *chayah*, but never explicitly states that a dead kosher *chayah* causes *tumah*. Rabbi Yonatan asks Ben Azzai: *nevelat chayah tehorah lo lamadnu—minayin*, from where do we know that a kosher wild animal's corpse also causes *tumah*?

## Ben Azzai's Derasha

### Ben Azzai's Logic

Ben Azzai responds by citing the verse: *kol haholech al kapav b'chol hachayah haholechet al arba*—"everything that goes on its paws among all the *chayot* that go on four." Ben Azzai reads *b'chol hachayah* as introducing an additional category: not merely the paw-walkers, but any *chayah* that goes on four—including kosher *chayot* such as a deer. The dead corpse of any such *chayah*, he argues, causes *tumah*, as derived from the conclusion of the verse: *kol hanogea b'nivlatam yitma ad ha'erev*.

### R. Yonatan Rejects

Rabbi Yonatan rejects this *drasha*. He says: *v'chi ne'emar v'chol chayah—halo lo ne'emar ela b'chol hachayah*—the verse does not say "and every *chayah*"; it says "among all the *chayah*." The straightforward *pshat* of the verse is that it speaks of one category—paw-walkers—found among all the *chayot* that go on four. The phrase *b'chol hachayah* is not introducing a separate, additional category of animals; it is a qualifier indicating context. *lemahalchei kapayim b'chayah hu de'asar*—the verse is only forbidding the paw-walking animals found in that context. There is no second category being included. Rabbi Yonatan insists that this *drasha* is not *pshat*, and therefore he does not accept it.

## R. Yishmael Approach

### R. Yishmael Offered

Ben Azzai, recognizing that his *drasha* has been rejected, turns to Rabbi Yonatan and asks: *u'mah Yishmael omer ba'davar hazeh*—what does your teacher, Rabbi Yishmael, say about this question? The exchange is telling: Ben Azzai comes from the school of Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yonatan is aligned with the school of Rabbi Yishmael. The implicit tension is between the more expansive hermeneutic approach associated with Rabbi Akiva—willing to derive additional categories from unusual phrasing—and the more *pshat*-oriented approach associated with Rabbi Yishmael, which Ben Azzai's rejected *drasha* exemplified.

Rabbi Yonatan then conveys Rabbi Yishmael's answer. He cites once more: *v'chi yamut min habehemah asher hi lachem l'ochlah*—and this is where Rabbi Yishmael's *drasha* operates. The phrase *min habehemah* indicates even a non-kosher animal, and *asher hi lachem l'ochlah* indicates a kosher one. But this does not yet account for the *chayah*.

### Inclusion Principle

The key principle Rabbi Yishmael employs is: *chayah bichlal behemah u'vehemah bichlal chayah*—wherever the *torah* speaks of a *behemah*, this includes a *chayah*, and wherever it speaks of a *chayah*, this includes a *behemah*, unless the text explicitly draws a distinction between them. This is not a *drasha* in the narrow sense of finding a hidden inclusion; it is a broader hermeneutic principle about how biblical language operates. The *torah* uses these terms fluidly, and absent a clear distinction, one implies the other.

### Application to Categories

The practical application follows directly: *chayah tehorah bichlal behemah tehorah*—a kosher *chayah* is included in the category of a kosher *behemah*. *chayah tme'ah bichlal behemah tme'ah*—a non-kosher *chayah* is included in a non-kosher *behemah*. And conversely, *behemah tme'ah bichlal chayah tme'ah* and *behemah tehorah bichlal chayah tehorah*—the relationship runs in both directions. Thus, whenever the *torah* records the *tumah* of a *behemah*'s corpse, the *chayah* is included, and vice versa. The apparent gap—the missing source for the *tumah* of a dead kosher *chayah*—is no gap at all; it is covered by the explicit *tumah* of the kosher *behemah*, since the two categories are interchangeable unless otherwise specified.

This approach reflects Rabbi Yishmael's general orientation toward a more fluid, contextual reading of biblical language, as opposed to a hyper-precise parsing of each word. The Torah says *behemah*; it means any animal. It says *chayah*; it also means any animal. The technical distinction between domesticated and non-domesticated exists, but it applies only when the context demands it.

## Ben Azzai's Regret

### Lament & Conclusion

The *braita* closes on a poignant note. Ben Azzai, having heard Rabbi Yonatan transmit Rabbi Yishmael's approach, exclaims about himself: *chaval al Ben Azzai shelo shimash et Rabbi Yishmael*—woe to Ben Azzai, that he never had the opportunity to learn directly from Rabbi Yishmael. He regrets that his entire formation was within the school of Rabbi Akiva, which led him toward a different hermeneutic—one that Ben Azzai now recognizes as potentially too limiting. Rabbi Yishmael's approach, with its principle of *chayah bichlal behemah* and its comfort with non-technical usage of biblical terminology, offered an answer that was both more elegant and more grounded in *pshat* than Ben Azzai's own proposed *drasha*. It is a rare and striking moment of self-criticism from one of the great Tannaim, acknowledging that a different master's path might have served him better.

# Hullin 71

## Chayah & Behemah

### Intro: Inclusion

The Gemara on 71a opens by establishing, through explicit *psukim*, that the categories of *chayah* and *behemah* are mutually inclusive — each can fall under the rubric of the other depending on context. The question *chayah bichlal behemah minalan* — how do we know that *chayah* is included within *behemah* — is answered from the verse *zos habehemah asher tocheilu* (Devarim 14:4–5), which opens with the heading of *behemah* and proceeds to enumerate species such as *shor*, *seh chesavim*, and *seh izim* — ox, sheep, and goat — but then continues to list *ayal*, *tzvi*, and *yachmur* (deer, gazelle, and fallow deer), which are plainly *chayah*. The fact that the verse subsumes these *chayos* under the heading of *behemah* demonstrates that *behemah* can function as a generic term inclusive of *chayah*.

The converse is established from a separate verse: *v'zos hachayah asher tocheilu mikol habehemah asher al ha-aretz* — "and this is the *chayah* that you may eat from among all the *behemah* on the land" — which inverts the terminology, subsuming *behemah* under the heading of *chayah*. The *pshat* is clear: these words are not always category-specific; they function as general terms that can encompass each other. With this mutual inclusion established, the Gemara proceeds to identify four distinct halachic applications, two in each direction, encompassing both *tahor* and *tamei* species.

### Kosher Inclusion

The first application: *chayah tehorah bichlal behemah tehorah l'simanim* — a kosher *chayah* is subsumed under the category of kosher *behemah* with respect to the identifying signs of permitted consumption. The verse that specifies the *simanim* — split hooves and cud-chewing — frames them in terms of *behemah*. Since *chayah* is included within *behemah*, the same *simanim* apply to *chayah* as well, even though the verse does not enumerate them separately for wild animals.

### Non-Kosher Cross-breed

The second application concerns non-kosher animals: *chayah temeiah bichlal behemah temeiah l'harva'ah* — a non-kosher *chayah* is included within *behemah* for the prohibition of cross-breeding (*kilayim*). The verse *behemtecha lo tarbi'ah kilayim* prohibits cross-breeding one's *behemah*, but says nothing explicit about *chayah*. Since *chayah* is included in *behemah*, the prohibition extends to wild animals as well, whether of kosher or non-kosher species.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The third application reverses the direction: a non-kosher *behemah* is included within *chayah* — *behemah temeiah bichlal chayah temeiah* — and this is relevant to what Rebbi taught in a *braisa*. Rebbi asks: the verse that addresses the case of one who touches the corpse of a non-kosher animal and then enters the *beis hamikdash* or eats consecrated food — why does that verse mention both *chayah* and *behemah*? Since *chayah* already includes *behemah*, the explicit mention of *behemah* is redundant and therefore available for a *gezeirah shavah*. Rebbi leverages this: the word *behemah temeiah* appears here and also later in *vayikra* in the context of prohibiting the eating of *korbanos* while in a state of *tumah*. The shared language creates a *gezeirah shavah* — *mah lehalan tumas kodesh, af kan tumas kodesh* — teaching that the transgression under discussion is specifically eating sacred food while *tamei*. The case thus requires the mutual inclusion not as a source of new law, but as the precondition that renders the explicit mention of *behemah* in the first verse formally superfluous and available for the hermeneutic derivation.

### Formation & Miscarriage

The fourth application: *behemah tehorah bichlal chayah tehorah liyetzirah* — a kosher *behemah* is included within *chayah* with respect to *yetzirah*, the act of formation or creation. This rests on the verse in *bereishis*: *vayeitzer hashem elokim min ha'adamah kol chayas hasadeh v'es kol oph hashamayim* — God fashioned from the earth all the living creatures of the field and all the birds of the sky. The verse uses the word *chayah*, yet it plainly refers to all animals, including *behemah*. The halachic relevance emerges from a *mishnah* in *niddah*: *hamapeles min behemah chayah va'oph* — if a woman miscarries a fetus that resembles a *behemah*, a *chayah*, or a bird, whether of a *tahor* or *tamei* species, she is nonetheless treated as *temeiah leidah*. If the fetus appears male she observes the impurity of bearing a male child; if female, the longer impurity of a female; if indeterminate, she takes on both stringencies. This is *divrei Rebbi Meir*.

The reasoning of *rebbi meir* is that since all creatures — human, *chayah*, and *behemah* — are included together in the verse of *vayeitzer*, even a fetus resembling a non-human animal is considered a sufficient act of birth to impose *tumat leidah* on the mother. The question then arises: where does *rebbi meir* derive the inclusion specifically for a fetus that resembles a *behemah*, given that the *bereishis* verse mentions only *chayah* and *oph* explicitly? The answer is precisely the principle established above — *behemah bichlal chayah* — since *behemah* is encompassed within *chayah*, the verse in *bereishis* covers *behemah* as well.

The *chachamim* disagree, holding *kol she'eino mitzurat adam eino valad* — if it does not appear human, it does not impose *tumat leidah*. The Gemara notes that since the *chachamim* reject *rebbi meir's* ruling here, they must find another use for the verse demonstrating *behemah bichlal chayah* — and indeed, *rebbi* in the previous case (*lehalan*) uses it for the derivation concerning *tumah* of the non-kosher *behemah*.

What emerges from this entire sugya is that the mutual inclusion of *chayah* and *behemah* is not merely a lexicographic observation but has operative halachic consequences across domains ranging from the *simanim* of permitted eating, to the *kilayim* of cross-breeding, to the complex hermeneutics of *korbanos*, to the *tumah* status of a miscarried fetus. It also reflects a broader methodological disagreement between *rebbi yishmael*, who views the interchangeability of *chayah* and *behemah* as straightforward *pshat* — the *torah* simply speaks in general terms — and others who derive legal content from the same interchangeability through formal *drashos*.

---

## Tumah Bluah

### Fetus in Womb

The *mishnah* that brings us into the next sugya introduces a case that initially appears straightforward but conceals one of the more technically involved principles in these chapters: *ha'isha shemeit valadah betoch me'eha* — a woman whose fetus died in her womb. *ufashtah chayah et yadah* — the midwife (the *chayah*, literally "the one who gives life") extended her hand inside to assist in delivery, *venag'ah bo hachayah tmeiah tumat shivah* — and touched the dead fetus; she contracts seven-day *tumah* from corpse contact. *veha'isha tehorah* — and the mother remains *tehorah* until the fetus exits the womb.

The operative principle here is *tumah bluah* — literally, swallowed or absorbed *tumah*. Something enclosed within a body is not considered to exist in the wider world as an independent source of *tumah*. To appreciate this, consider the analogous case that the Gemara will develop: a *neveilah* — the corpse of a non-kosher animal or any animal that died without proper *shechita* — that has been swallowed and is sitting in a person's stomach. Does it continue to cause *tumah*? The answer is no: absorbed within a body, it is no longer present in the world in a halachically operative sense.

This principle explains the asymmetry in the *mishnah*. From the mother's perspective — and from the perspective of everyone outside — the fetus is *bluah*, enclosed and absorbed, and thus does not function as a corpse causing *tumah*. The midwife, however, has inserted her hand into that space and is making direct contact with the fetus. From *her* perspective, it is not *bluah* at all — she is accessing it and touching it. Hence she contracts *tumat shivah* while the mother remains *tehorah*.

One might ask: what about the space itself — if the midwife's hand is within the womb but not yet touching the fetus, should not the proximity within that enclosed space itself create *tumah*, given that a corpse ordinarily projects *tumah* to all persons sharing an *ohel*? This is a genuine question, and the *mishnah*'s formulation — emphasizing *touching* — implies that the *bluah* status is only removed when there is actual handling contact, not mere presence in the same enclosed space. Until the fetus is physically handled, it retains the status of *bluah*.

The question of how a midwife could know with certainty that the fetus was already dead at the moment of contact is addressed practically: in any case of doubt, the same *halachah* applies *misafek* — she would be *temeiah tumat shivah misafek*.

A striking dimension of this *mishnah* is its implicit position on the status of the unborn. However varied the halachic opinions on abortion may be — ranging from those who view a fetus as having virtually no independent status, through positions that recognize partial life, to the stringent view of *rav moshe feinstein* based on the *rambam* that considers abortion akin to a form of killing — this *mishnah* treats a fetus that dies in the womb as a *met* in the full sense, capable of conveying *tumat meit*. It does not say the fetus lacks corpse-status because it was never born alive. The question of how early in development this applies is separately addressed in the *mishnah* in *niddah*, where the threshold of *tumat meit* from a fetus requires that it have reached a sufficient stage of development — specifically, a head of a size comparable to the warp-spool — and not merely the 40-day mark that governs *tumat niddah* in cases of questionable discharge.

### Rava's Principle

*Amar Rava*: just as absorbed *tumah* does not cause *tumah* — *keshem she-tumah bluah einah metame* — so too *tahara bluah*, something *tahor* that is absorbed inside a person, does not become *tamei* — *kach tahara bluah eina mitame*. This is a paired principle: the absorption effect runs symmetrically in both directions.

### Neveilah Proof

The Gemara then asks: *tumah bluah minalan* — from where do we derive that absorbed *tumah* does not cause *tumah*? The source is the verse *ve-hochel mi-nivlatah yechabes begadav* — one who eats from a *neveilah* must immerse his garments. The Gemara reasons: are we not discussing a case where a person ate this *neveilah* close to sunset — *samuch lishkias hachamah* — immersed in the *mikvah*, and emerged *tahor*, even though the *neveilah* is still inside his stomach? *ve-amar rachmana tahor* — the Torah declares him *tahor*. Despite the continued presence of the *neveilah* within him, he is not *tamei*. This is the proof that absorbed *tumah* does not cause *tumah*.

Rashi makes a critical methodological observation here that will carry weight throughout the subsequent discussion. One might have thought the reason the person is not *tamei* is simply that he is not in contact with the *neveilah* — invoking the principle of *negiat beit hastarim*, that touching something with an internal part of the body (a hidden part not exposed externally) does not constitute halachic contact. If so, the proof would only establish the absence of *tumah* from non-contact, not the full principle of *tumah bluah*. Rashi explains, however, that this objection does not apply here, because a *neveilah* transmits *tumah* not only by touch but also by carrying — *masa*. If the *neveilah* in the stomach were still halachically operative, the person carrying it would be *tamei* without any touching at all. The fact that he is *tahor* therefore cannot be attributed to the absence of touch; it must reflect that the absorbed *neveilah* is simply no longer present in the world as a *neveilah*. Similarly, in our *mishnah*, the dead fetus projects *tumah* to all in the room if it is exposed — but while within the mother, it does not, precisely because it is *bluah*.

### Reuiah Le-Ger

The Gemara raises a challenge: perhaps the reason the *neveilah* in the stomach does not cause *tumah* is not the principle of *tumah bluah* at all, but rather because it is no longer *reuiah lager* — fit for the *ger* (the stranger or non-Jew in one's community). The Torah instructs *lager asher bisharecha titnena* — give the *neveilah* to the stranger in your midst. The designation of an animal carcass as a *neveilah* is tied to its edibility; if it is no longer something a person would consume, perhaps it loses its halachic status as a *neveilah* entirely, not because it is hidden but because it is no longer edible.

The Gemara resolves this by invoking the position of *rabbi yochanan*, who holds that *neveilah* retains its status so long as it is fit for a dog — *achad zu ve-achad zu l'kelev*. Fitness for canine consumption is the operative threshold for *tumah*; human edibility is not required. Since a *neveilah* inside a person's stomach, if regurgitated, would certainly be eaten by a dog, it retains its status as *neveilah*. The only reason it does not cause *tumah* while in the stomach, therefore, must be *tumah bluah*.

The Gemara further notes that even for the position of *bar pada* — who holds that *neveilah* loses its severe *tumah* once unfit for human consumption, though it retains a lesser *tumah* until unfit even for a dog — the objection can still be deflected. The Gemara argues: *ledidei delo chazi be'anpei, aval shelo bifanav mechazi chazi leih* — while a person would not eat it if they saw it laid out before them and knew what it was, if they were unaware of what they were consuming, there is no reason to assume it is literally unpalatable. The repulsion is aesthetic, not intrinsic. Thus the *neveilah* in the stomach is still halachically edible to the person carrying it, and its failure to cause *tumah* can only be explained through *tumah bluah*.

### From Below

Having established *tumah bluah* for the case of swallowing — absorption from above — the Gemara asks: *beluah dilmata minalan* — from where do we know that the same principle applies to absorption from below, i.e., something entering through the lower orifices, including the case of the fetus in the womb? The Gemara answers with a *kal vachomer*: if absorption from above — through the mouth, which is not the primary site of digestion — nevertheless grants *bluah* status and protects from *tumah*, then absorption from below — *she'oseh ichul*, where the digestive process is more intensive — certainly should. The Gemara anticipates the objection that digestion below only occurs because of what came from above, and responds that despite that dependency, *ichul dilmata nafish* — the degree of processing that occurs further down the digestive tract is in any case greater, making the *kal vachomer* stand.

### In Behemah

With the principle of *tumah bluah* established for human beings — both from above and from below — the Gemara extends the inquiry: *beluah debeheimah minalan* — how do we know that something absorbed within an animal also has *bluah* status? This is directly relevant to the preceding *mishnah* about the fetus in an animal's womb, where the shepherd who inserted a hand and touched the fetus became *tamei* while the mother did not. The Gemara answers again with a *kal vachomer*: *umah adam shemetame mechayim matzil be-valua* — a human being, who is susceptible to *tumah* even while alive (through *zivah*, *baal keri*, *niddah*, *yoledet*, *metzora*, and the like), nevertheless protects things absorbed within him from operative *tumah*. *behemah she-einah metamma'ah mechayim* — an animal, which does not transmit *tumah* while alive, is far less susceptible to *tumah* overall. *eino din she-tatzil be-valua* — how much more so should it protect things absorbed within it.

### Tzaraat House

The Gemara counters that there is one domain in which an animal is *more* susceptible to *tumah* than a human, which might undermine the *kal vachomer*. The case involves a *beit hamenuga* — a house afflicted with *tzara'at*. The Torah teaches that one who enters such a house and eats there — which the *chazal* understand as meaning one who tarries there the duration of eating a *pras* (roughly half a loaf of wheat bread, eaten while reclining with a dip, at a leisurely pace — *rashi* measures this as eight eggs' volume, the *rambam* as nine) — causes even his worn garments to become *tamei*. If however one entered but did not tarry, one becomes *tamei* personally but the clothes one is wearing remain *tahor* until the required duration has passed. This special protection of worn garments applies specifically to human beings. Garments being carried (on the shoulder, in the hand) become *tamei* immediately — as the *mishnah* teaches: *hanichnas le-veit hamenuga*, if one entered carrying one's clothes, one's sandals in hand, and one's ring in hand rather than wearing them, then both the person and all these objects become *tamei mi-yad*. Only when wearing them — *haya lavush kelav, ve-sandalav beraglav, ve-tabato be-etzbao* — are the garments protected initially, becoming *tamei* only after tarrying.

This protection of worn garments does not apply to animals. If a *behemah* enters a *beit hamenuga*, whether it is wearing anything or not, the animal and everything on it become *tamei* immediately. In this respect, the animal is *less* protected than a human, and one might argue that this lesser protection undermines the *kal vachomer* — if the *behemah* is less shielded in this domain, perhaps it also cannot generate *bluah* protection for what is inside it.

### Tosafot Resolution

The Gemara's response is that the *beit hamenuga* case is not truly a domain where the animal is conceptually more *susceptible* to *tumah* — it is rather a structural difference in how *tumah* is transmitted *through* a human subject versus objects. The Gemara notes that the difference between worn and carried garments applies equally to humans: carried garments become *tamei mi-yad* for humans as well. The unique protection of worn garments exists because *tumah* reaches them *through* the person who wears them; they are treated as an extension of his subjectivity. An animal, by contrast, does not function as a halachic subject through whom *tumah* is mediated — everything associated with it, worn or carried, is treated as a direct object of *tumah*.

*Tosafot* draws out this point precisely: even if a *behemah* were wearing garments — say, a collar or a saddle or whatever constitutes apparel for an animal — those garments still become *tamei mi-yad*, because the *tumah* is considered to reach them directly, not through the animal as an intermediary subject. This is not evidence that the *behemah* is more susceptible *internally*; it reflects only the fact that the animal is not a legal subject through whose personality *tumah* is mediated. Since the *bluah* principle concerns what is *inside* the body — what is absorbed and enclosed — and not how external garments are affected, the *beit hamenuga* asymmetry is irrelevant to the *kal vachomer*. The fundamental point remains: a human, who is more susceptible to *tumah* in the personal sense, protects what is absorbed within him. A *behemah*, which is less susceptible, does so equally.

### Mishnaiyot Evidence

The Gemara closes this section with a remark that cuts the discussion short in a different way. *rava* had stated both *tumah bluah* and *tahara bluah* as if they required demonstration. The Gemara responds: *tarvaihu taninu* — both of them are explicit in *mishnayot*. *rava* need not have derived either principle.

For *tumah bluah*: *bala tabaat teme'ah* — someone swallowed a ring that had contracted *tumat meit* (having touched a corpse, and being metal, it is treated as the corpse itself — *cherev ke-chalal* — such that touching it would ordinarily confer seven-day *tumah*). This person *tovel ve-ochel bi-terumah* — immerses in the *mikvah*, completes the process of *taharah*, and may eat *terumah*, with no concern that the *tamei* ring in his stomach continues to cause *tumah*. And if he subsequently regurgitates it — *hetia, temeia* — the ring is still *tamei*; it never lost its *tumah*. It simply did not project that *tumah* while absorbed within him. This is an explicit *mishnah* proving *tumah bluah*.

For *tahara bluah*: *bala tabaat tehorah* — one swallowed a *tahor* ring. *ve-nichnas le-ohel ha-met* — then entered a room containing a corpse, through which *ohel* contamination one normally contracts *tumah*. The person underwent the complete process of *taharah* — *ve-hiza ve-shina ve-taval* — the sprinkling of *mei chatat* on the third and seventh days, followed by immersion. Then *ve-hitia* — he regurgitated the ring — *harei hi ke-mah she-hayata* — and it remains *tahor*, just as it was. The ring was never *metamei*, because while inside his body it was insulated from the *tumah* of the *ohel*. That is *tahara bluah*. Both principles, *rava's* statement notwithstanding, are fully documented in the *mishnayot* of *mikvaot*. The Gemara will address tomorrow why *rava* found it necessary to articulate what is already explicit in *mishnah*.

---

---

# Hullin 72

## Tumah Beluah

### Swallowed Rings

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion of *tumah beluah* — the principle of absorbed impurity. When something *tamei* is inside a body, whether a person's or an animal's, its *tumah* is effectively suspended. It does not radiate outward. Even a dead fetus inside its mother's womb, which would ordinarily cause *tumah* in an enclosed space, does not do so while it remains within the mother. Conversely, if something *tahor* is inside a body, it remains unaffected even if the person carrying it becomes *tamei*. This principle was established by Rabba, who demonstrated it from various *pesukim* and from an explicit *mishnah* in *mikvaot* involving a ring — *tamei* or *tahor* — that was swallowed. If the principle was already stated in that *mishnah*, one might ask: what was Rabba's *chiddush*?

### Two Rings Case

The *gemara* answers by specifying Rabba's novel case: *kegon shebala shtei tabaot* — someone swallowed two rings sequentially, one *tamei* and one *tahor*. Rabba's innovation is the ruling that *dilo metamaya la mitmea letehora* — the *tamei* ring does not render the *tahor* ring *tamei*, even though they may well be touching inside the stomach. This is a striking *chiddush*: *tumah beluah* does not merely prevent impurity from radiating outward to people on the outside; it means that once something is absorbed within a body, it is as though it does not exist even from the perspective of other objects sharing that same interior space. Even contact occurring entirely inside the body is halakhically inert.

Tosafot raises the natural follow-up: where does Rabba derive this principle if it is not explicit in prior *mishnayot*? Tosafot answers that the source is a case mentioned earlier in which someone who had swallowed a *tamei* object was permitted to eat *terumah*. The implicit concern would be that the *terumah*, upon being swallowed, would enter the stomach and contact the *tamei* object there. That this is not treated as a problem demonstrates that even within the body, a *tamei* object does not render a *tahor* one *tamei*. Once absorbed in a body, the *tumah* does not exist even from the inside.

### Fetus-Midwife Problem

This principle, however, appears to conflict directly with an established *mishnah*. That *mishnah* discusses a dead fetus inside a woman's womb: the mother remains *tehorah* because the fetus is *beluah*, but the midwife who inserts her hand and touches the fetus becomes *temei'ah*. The midwife's hand inside the womb is in precisely the same situation as the second ring inside the stomach — both are in the same interior space as the *tamei* object. Yet in the midwife's case, *tumah* is transferred. The *gemara* at the top of 72a formulates the contradiction directly: *keshtei tabaot dami* — the fetus and midwife case is analogous to two rings in a stomach — *vekamitamela ubar lachaya*, and yet the fetus does render the midwife *temei'ah*.

The *gemara* initially suggests that the fetus is different because *sofo latzeis* — it is destined to emerge. But this cannot be the distinction, since a swallowed ring is equally destined to exit the body by a different route. The *gemara* acknowledges this and abandons that line of reasoning.

### Rav Yosef Resolution

The *gemara* then says that the explanation is known to the Pumpeditans — *umanhu Rav Yosef* — and it is Rav Yosef. In the chain of transmission Rav Yosef amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel, the ruling is stated: *tumah zu einah mi-divrei Torah ella mi-divrei Sofrim* — the *tumah* of the midwife is only rabbinic. This resolves the contradiction entirely. Rabba is correct that *tumah beluah* suspends *tumah* even for things sharing the same interior space, including the midwife's hand inside the womb. The reason the midwife is *temei'ah* in that *mishnah* is not because of a biblical principle, but because the rabbis enacted a special *gezeirah*.

The *gemara* notes that the formulation "it is not from *divrei Torah* but from *divrei Sofrim*" is doing more than simply declaring the ruling rabbinic. It is preemptively addressing the position of Rabbi Akiva — whom we will encounter shortly — who holds that a dead fetus inside its mother *does* cause *tumah* biblically. One might have thought that our *mishnah* reflects Rabbi Akiva's view. Rav Yosef's statement is therefore saying: even according to Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that the fetus is *tahor* while still in the womb, the rabbis nonetheless imposed *tumah* on the midwife.

### Midwife Stricture Logic

The *gemara* then asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for this rabbinic *gezeirah*? Rav Hoshaya explains: *gezeirah shema yotzi pevah rosho chutz l'prozdor* — it is a precautionary decree lest the fetus's head emerge beyond the *prozdor*, the birth canal, and the midwife fail to notice. Once the head emerges, the fetus is no longer *beluah* and causes *tumah* biblically. Since the midwife is in the process of delivering the baby and may not notice the precise moment of emergence, the rabbis ruled that from the moment she is handling it inside the womb, she is already considered *temei'ah*.

The *gemara* then asks: if so, why not also impose this *gezeirah* on the mother herself? The answer is *margeshes b'atzmah* — the mother will sense when the baby has emerged. The *gemara* then asks: but could the mother not simply inform the midwife? The answer is *trida* — she is preoccupied and cannot reliably be expected to communicate the precise moment of emergence. Hence the rabbinic stringency applies specifically to the midwife.

The upshot of all this is striking: the principle of *tumah beluah* applies even when two objects are in the same interior space, such as two rings in a stomach or a midwife's hand touching a fetus in the womb. The midwife's *tumah* is an exceptional rabbinic enactment born of a specific practical concern about the moment of emergence, not a reflection of any inherent limitation of *tumah beluah* itself.

---

## Rabbi Akiva vs. Yishmael

### Biblical Sources

The *gemara* now spells out the debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael regarding whether a dead fetus inside its mother causes *tumah* biblically. A *baraita* is cited. The verse in *parashat chukat* states: *vechol asher yiga al p'nei hasadeh* — anyone who touches something on the open field, whether someone slain by the sword or a dead body, is *tamei* for seven days.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva reads the phrase *hanogei bemeit benefesh* — one who touches a dead body *be-nefesh* — as referring to a dead body *within* another person, i.e., a fetus inside its mother. The word *benefesh* is read not as a qualifier of the corpse but as indicating the location: the dead body is inside another soul. *eizo meit shebenefesh shel adam* — what is a dead body inside a person? *hevei omer zeh ubar she-be-mei isha* — this is the fetus in the mother's womb. According to Rabbi Akiva, touching such a fetus causes *tumah* biblically.

### Rabbi Yishmael Position

Rabbi Yishmael reads the same phrase differently. The verse's phrase *al p'nei hasadeh* — on the open field — indicates that *tumah* applies only to what is out in the world and exposed. This *lehotzi* — comes to exclude — a fetus inside the mother's womb. Since it is not in the open field, it does not cause *tumah*. As for *hanogei bemeit benefesh*, Rabbi Yishmael does not use this phrase to teach the fetus case; he uses it instead to derive that even a *revi'it* of blood from a corpse causes *tumah* — *dam hu hanefesh*, blood is the soul, and so a quantity of blood representing a *nefesh* carries the same *tumah* as the body itself. The amount of a *revi'it* was understood by the rabbis to represent the quantity of blood initially present in a newborn, and hence the threshold of blood upon which life depends.

Rabbi Akiva, for his part, derives the rule about a *revi'it* of blood from a different verse — *ve'al kol nafshos meis lo yavo* — which uses the plural *nafshos*, teaching that even a *revi'it* of blood combined from two separate corpses causes *tumah*. Rabbi Yishmael disagrees with that position as well, holding that *benefesh adam* in the singular means the blood must derive from a single corpse.

### Tosafot on Stages

Does Rabbi Akiva then reject *tumah beluah* entirely? Tosafot offers the most cogent resolution. There are distinct stages to consider. When the fetus is in the uterus, it is genuinely *beluah* — absorbed deeply enough within the body that it does not exist for *tumah* purposes even vis-à-vis the mother and even for the midwife touching it (absent the rabbinic *gezeirah*). But once the fetus begins descending through the birth canal, it is no longer *beluah* — it is no longer hidden in the deep interior of the body — while it is also not yet *born*, since birth occurs only when the head emerges. This intermediate stage — in the birth canal but not yet born — is the point of contention.

*Beit hastarim* refers to a surface or space that is hidden but not necessarily *beluah* in the strict sense. Something inside the mouth is *beit hastarim* but not *beluah*; one could open the mouth and expose it. *beluah* requires a deeper level of absorption, inaccessible without intervention.

### Debate Summary

According to Tosafot's resolution, Rabbi Akiva holds that once the fetus is in the birth canal, it is no longer *beluah*, and since it is dead, it causes *tumah*. The verse does not need to exclude it because it is no longer absorbed in the sense that triggers *tumah beluah*. Rabbi Yishmael, however, holds that there is a special rule regarding a fetus: as long as it has not yet been born — head not yet emerged — it does not cause *tumah*, even when it is in the birth canal and thus no longer strictly *beluah*. The *chiddush* is thus Rabbi Yishmael's, not Rabbi Akiva's. Rabbi Akiva follows the ordinary logic that once something is no longer *beluah* it can cause *tumah*; Rabbi Yishmael introduces a special exclusion applying to the fetus specifically.

Our *mishnah*'s ruling that the mother is *tehorah* until birth follows Rabbi Yishmael. And the three stages are: in the uterus (*beluah* — *tahor* according to everyone); in the birth canal (debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael); emerged (*tamei* according to everyone).

---

## Protruding Limb Case

### Limb Cut Before

The *gemara* now turns to a case discussed in the *mishnah*: *behema hamaksha leyeled* — an animal experiencing a difficult labor — and the fetus extends a limb out of the womb. Someone cuts off this limb in order to assist the delivery. What is the status of the limb and the mother's meat?

If the limb was cut off and afterwards the mother was slaughtered — *vehotzi ubar yado, vechatacha, ve'achar kach shachat et imo* — the meat of the mother is *tahor*. The limb itself is *ever min hachai*, a limb severed from a living animal, which is forbidden. However, since it was severed while the mother was alive, it did not confer *tumah* on the mother (living animals do not become *tamei*), and the subsequent *shechita* of the mother renders all her meat *tahor*. The limb had no effect on the mother's status.

### Limb Cut After

The more complex case is when the mother was slaughtered first and the limb was cut off afterwards — *shachat et imo ve'achar kach chatacha*. The *shechita* of the mother was effective for the fetus inside but not for the protruding limb. The limb was outside, beyond the scope of the *shechita*. What is its status?

Two categories present themselves. A *neveila* is an animal that never had a *shechita* performed, or died without *shechita*; it causes *tumah*. A *tereifa* is an animal whose *shechita* was performed but was not halakhically effective to render it fit for eating; it does not cause *tumah*. The question is which of these two categories applies to this limb. Was there *shechita* for the limb — in which case it is like a *tereifa*, no *tumah* — or was there no *shechita* for it at all, making it a *neveila* that does cause *tumah*?

### Rabbi Meir Debate

Rabbi Meir rules: *maga neveila* — the meat is treated as having touched a *neveila*, meaning the limb is a *neveila* and causes *tumah*. The *chachamim* rule: *maga tereifa shechuta* — it is treated as having touched a slaughtered *tereifa*, which does not cause *tumah*.

The *chachamim* reason by analogy: *ma matzinu betereifa sheshechitatah metaheratah* — just as we find that a *tereifa* animal's *shechita* prevents it from becoming a *neveila*, so too the *shechita* of the mother, even though it did not make the limb permissible, is sufficient to prevent the limb from carrying the status of *neveila*. An act of *shechita* was performed; it simply was not effective for the limb.

### Meir's Argument

Rabbi Meir responds: the comparison does not hold. When a *tereifa* animal is slaughtered and is thereby prevented from becoming a *neveila*, that is because *davar she'be'gufah* — the *shechita* was performed on its very body. One may say an act of *shechita* was done to this animal. But to say that the mother's *shechita* should purify the limb — *davar she'eina gufah* — something that is not part of the mother's body? That is a different matter entirely.

Rabbi Meir's argument is grounded in the principle of *yesh leida l'eivarim* — the limb that has protruded is treated as if it has already been born, as if it has already left the mother. Once it is regarded as no longer part of the mother, the mother's *shechita* has no relevance to it, and since no *shechita* ever applied to the limb, it is a *neveila*. The *chachamim* presumably disagree with one of two premises: either they hold that the limb is still considered *gufah* — part of the mother's body — or they concede it is not *gufah* but maintain that its physical attachment and dependence on the mother is sufficient for the mother's *shechita* to relate to it. The *gemara* does not fully articulate which of these two positions the *chachamim* are taking.

---

## Tereifa Shechita

### Mishnah Logic

The *mishnah* now uses the preceding debate as an opportunity to establish on what basis a *tereifa*'s *shechita* prevents it from acquiring *neveila* status — a principle everyone in the preceding argument accepted. The *mishnah* poses the question in the form of a logical challenge: *behema tmei'a asura ba'achila* — a non-kosher animal may not be eaten; *af treifa asura ba'achila* — a *tereifa* may not be eaten. If we say about a non-kosher animal that its *shechita* does not make it *tahor* — it still causes *tumah* as a *neveila* — perhaps we should say the same about a *tereifa*.

### Non-Kosher vs. Tereifa

The *mishnah* responds: *im amarta be-behema tmeah she-lo hayta lah sha'at ha-kosher* — a non-kosher animal was never in the category of something that could be eaten. The concept of *shechita* is simply irrelevant to it; the entire institution of *shechita* exists to render kosher animals permissible, and it has no meaning for a species that cannot be eaten under any circumstances. A *tereifa*, by contrast, began life as an animal that could in principle have been eaten. *she-hayta lah sha'at ha-kosher* — it had a time when it was fit. Since *shechita* is a meaningful and operative act for its species, and the *shechita* was performed, that is sufficient to remove it from the category of *neveila*.

### Born Tereifa

The *mishnah* then presses further: what if an animal was born with a defect that rendered it *tereifa* from the very moment of birth? It never had a *sha'at ha-kosher*. Should it not be treated like a non-kosher animal? The *mishnah* answers: *she-ken ein be-minah shechita* — for a non-kosher species, *shechita* has no relevance whatsoever to any member of that species. For a kosher animal, even one born as a *tereifa*, *shechita* remains a conceptually meaningful act for its *min*. Because *shechita* is meaningful for the species, the performance of *shechita* is sufficient to prevent even a *tereifa* born as such from acquiring *neveila* status. The *mishnah* acknowledges this is a basis for distinction rather than a proof, but on that basis concludes that *shechita* of a *tereifa* prevents *tumah* regardless of whether it was born *tereifa* or became one later.

### Eighth-Month Animal

The *mishnah* concludes with an exceptional case: *ben shmonah chai* — an animal born in the eighth month of gestation. The rabbis understood such an animal to be nonviable, effectively stillborn even if it appears alive. Because it is considered as though already dead, *shechita* has no effect on it — *ein shechitatu metaharatu, lefi she-ein be-mino shechita*. The *mishnah*'s formulation — that there is no *shechita* in its *min* — is somewhat imprecise, since it is still a cow and the species is certainly subject to *shechita*. The more accurate understanding, as the *gemara* implies, is that *shechita* has no meaning when performed on something already effectively dead. Just as *shechita* on an animal that has already died accomplishes nothing, so too with an eighth-month animal whose viability has not been established: the act of *shechita* is halakhically inert, and such an animal carries the status of *neveila*.

---

## Hidden Surface Impurity

### Hidden Contact Problem

The *gemara* now raises a sharp difficulty within Rabbi Meir's position. If the protruding limb is a *neveila* and the fetus is *tamei* by virtue of touching it, the question is: where exactly are they touching? The limb is attached to the fetus. There is no exposed surface at the point of attachment — it is all one continuous body. The surfaces that are in contact are hidden, interior surfaces — *beit hastarim*. And the principle is that *negiyat beit hastarim* — contact at a hidden surface — does not transfer *tumah*. The act of touching must occur at an exposed surface. How then does the *neveila* limb render the fetus *tamei*?

### Self-Touching Theory

The *gemara* suggests that perhaps Rabbi Meir's ruling is consistent with a position he holds elsewhere — that an object can be considered to be touching itself.

### Splitting Seat Case

The *gemara* cites a *mishnah*: a cloth that is *shlosha tefachim al shlosha tefachim* in size — large enough to serve as a seat — is *tamei* as *midras* if a *zav* sat upon it, since *mishkav u'moshav* makes the seat an *av hatumah*. If this cloth is then torn in half, each half is no longer large enough to be a seat and loses its *midras* status. The question is whether the remnant cloth retains some *tumah* through having "touched" the *midras* as it was being torn.

Rabbi Meir rules: *tahor min hamidras, aval tamei maga midras* — it is no longer *tamei* as a *midras*, but it has the *tumah* of something that touched a *midras*, one degree removed. Rabbi Yose challenges this: *vechi be'eizeh midras naga zeh* — what *midras* did this piece of cloth touch? It did not touch a *midras*; it *was* a *midras*. The only way to say it touched a *midras* is to say it touched itself — that one half of the cloth is considered to have touched the other half. Rabbi Yose rejects this and says: if a *zav* had both touched the cloth and sat upon it, then upon tearing it loses its *midras* status but retains the *tumah* of having touched a *zav* — that *tumah* survives the splitting. But if the cloth only ever had *midras* status and was never *tamei* through contact, tearing it in half simply ends its *tumah* entirely.

So Rabbi Meir holds that something can be considered to be touching itself — two parts of a single object are treated as touching one another — while Rabbi Yose does not. If Rabbi Meir's view governs our case of the limb and fetus, then even the hidden, interior contact between the attached limb and fetus can transfer *tumah*, resolving the *beit hastarim* problem.

### Ulla's Distinction

The *gemara* does not settle for this resolution, because Ulla draws a distinction within Rabbi Yose's own view. Ulla says: *lo shanu ela shlosha al shlosha shenechlak* — the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose applies only to the case where a cloth that was exactly the minimum size for a seat was torn in half, so that the seat ceased to exist in the process. In that scenario, Rabbi Yose says: the original *midras* went out of existence as you tore it, so there is no ongoing *midras* to be the source of transferred *tumah*.

But, says Ulla, *aval shlosha al shlosha haba mibeged gadol* — if you tear a piece of three-by-three *etzbaot* (large enough to be *tamei* but not large enough to be a seat) off of a large cloth that itself remains a full *midras*, then *besha'at perishatan me'avihen mekablot tumah me'avihen* — as the piece separates from its source, it receives *tumah* from its source. In this case, even Rabbi Yose would agree that the torn-off piece is *tamei*, because the original *midras* still exists and is still a source of *tumah* at the very moment of separation.

And this, says Ulla, is precisely the case with the fetus and the protruding limb. When the limb is cut from the fetus, the fetus itself continues to exist and continues to be subject to *tumah*. It does not go out of existence in the cutting. Therefore, as the limb is being separated, the fetus receives *tumah* from the limb — *besha'at perisha me'eiver mekabel tumah me'eiver* — even according to Rabbi Yose. The *mishnah*'s ruling is thus not dependent on Rabbi Meir's unique principle of self-touching at all.

Rashi explains this mechanism as not requiring that contact occurred while the limb was wholly attached, which would be *beit hastarim*. Rather, as the limb is physically cut away, there will necessarily be a moment where the cut surface of the limb comes into contact with the exposed surface of the fetus — a fleeting but genuine surface contact at an exposed place. It is that moment of contact, during the process of separation, that transfers the *tumah*.

### Ravina's Approach

Ravina offers an independent resolution. He distinguishes between a cloth and a protruding limb with respect to the very concept of self-touching. *beged lav lechaticha kai* — a cloth is not in a state of readiness to be cut. Even if you have a large cloth, there is nothing about the cloth itself that tells you to cut it; you see it as one integral unit. The notion that one part of the cloth is "touching" another part is therefore conceptually strained.

*Ubar lechaticha kai* — the protruding limb of a fetus, by contrast, stands to be cut. The limb cannot be eaten while the fetus can; it is already recognized as something that must be removed. Because it is already conceived of as something that will necessarily be severed, we treat it *halakhically* as though it has already been cut: *kol ha-omed lachtokh ke-khatukh dami* — anything that is destined to be cut off is considered as already cut off. Once it is conceptualized as already cut off, its surface is considered exposed, and the contact between the limb and the fetus is no longer *negiyat beit hastarim* but ordinary surface contact between two adjacent objects. The *tumah* is therefore transferred directly, without need for the moment of physical separation. The *gemara* will continue with this principle on the following daf.

---

---

# Hullin 73

## Fetal Limb Status

### Debate Setup

The Gemara opens on 73a with the question *keman* — according to whom? — probing the tannaic dispute regarding a fetal limb that protrudes from the womb at the moment the mother is slaughtered. The central question is whether such a limb is classified as a *neveilah* or as a *treifah*. These two categories carry a crucial conceptual distinction: *neveilah* describes an animal upon which no valid *shechitah* was performed, while *treifah* describes an animal upon which *shechitah* was performed but was halachically ineffective. Applied to the protruding limb, the question becomes: did the *shechitah* of the mother relate to the limb at all — making it, at worst, a *treifah* — or did the *shechitah* not apply to the limb whatsoever, leaving it a *neveilah*? Underlying this is the question of *gufah*: whether the limb is considered part of the mother's body. The practical stakes are primarily in the realm of *tumah*, since a *neveilah* conveys ritual impurity while a *treifah* does not.

### Rabbi Meir Position

According to Rabbi Meir, the protruding limb has the status of a *neveilah* and therefore conveys *tumah*. His position is that the limb is not *gufah* — not part of the mother — and therefore the *shechitah* of the mother did not apply to it at all, leaving it as if it died without *shechitah*. Consequently, Rabbi Meir holds that the limb renders the remainder of the fetus *tamei*.

### Tumah Transmission

A difficulty immediately arises, however. The limb that protrudes from the womb is not touching the rest of the fetus on an exposed surface; it touches only through the *beis hastarim*, the concealed surface. How then does it transmit *tumah* to the fetus? The Gemara resolves this by invoking Rabbi Meir's own principle: since the limb is destined to be cut off — one would not eat it in any case, as it is forbidden, and would naturally remove it — it is considered as though it already stands to be cut. And the operative rule is *kol ha-omed lachatoch ke-chatuach dami*: something that stands to be cut is legally regarded as though it has already been cut. Thus, there is already, in legal contemplation, an exposed surface, and the limb is treated as if it is in contact with the fetus through that surface.

### Mikvaos Analogy

The Gemara traces this principle to a *mishnah* in *mikvaos*. If a vessel has an unusually long handle that its owner intends to shorten by cutting, one need not immerse the entire handle in the *mikveh* — only up to the point that will be retained. The reasoning is that the excess portion, since it stands to be cut off, is already regarded in law as though it has been severed; it is no longer considered part of the vessel. This is the position attributed to the *tanna kamma*, identified with Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, holding that until the handle is actually cut, it remains part of the vessel and must be immersed in its entirety.

The same principle functions differently in our context. Whereas in the *mikvaos* case it operates as a leniency — exempting one from immersing the surplus handle — here it can serve as a stringency: the limb is considered already severed, an exposed surface exists in legal contemplation, and *tumah* is therefore transmitted to the fetus through that virtual contact.

### Food Logic

The Gemara then extends this reasoning beyond Rabbi Meir alone. *afilu teima rabbanan* — perhaps even the Rabbis would agree in the case of the fetal limb. The principle invoked here is *chiburei ochlin ke-man de-mifrash dami* — items that are foodstuff are more readily regarded as already separated than solid vessels. The logic is that food is inherently in the process of being consumed and destroyed; it lacks the structural unity of a vessel. Since both the fetus and the limb are, in principle, food, and since the limb is destined to be discarded or given to dogs, it is easier to regard the limb as already detached from the fetus. Even the Rabbis might therefore concede that the limb is considered as though already cut off, rendering it in virtual contact with the fetus and capable of transmitting *tumah* — whereas by a vessel, where the integrity of the whole is more pronounced, only Rabbi Meir would apply this logic.

### Ulla vs Ravina

Two distinct explanations emerge for the mechanism by which the limb transmits *tumah* to the fetus. The first, associated with Ulla, holds that *tumah* is transmitted at the moment of actual severance. When the limb is physically cut off, an exposed surface is created; in that very instant of separation, the surfaces make contact and *tumah* passes. This explains why the *mishnah* uses the formulation *chatacha* — "if one cut it" — because the transmission occurs at that moment of cutting. The second explanation, Ravina's, holds that the legal fiction of *ke-chatuach dami* is sufficient: since the limb is considered already cut, the surfaces are already deemed to be touching, and the *tumah* is transmitted even before any physical severance. On this view, the *mishnah*'s use of *chatacha* is merely stylistic, following the language of the earlier clause which discussed actually cutting the limb prior to *shechitah*.

The conceptual irony here is worth noting. Ordinarily one might suppose that the very unity of a body would be the conduit of *tumah* — that things that are fully joined would more readily convey impurity to one another. Yet the opposite is true: it is precisely because the limb and the fetus are one continuous whole that no *tumah* passes between them. *tumah* requires one object to come into contact with another. Only when there is a demarcation — actual or legal — does contact and transmission become possible.

### Tosafot Paradox

*Tosafot* raises a striking difficulty. In the *mikvaos* analogy, the principle is that the excess handle need not be immersed because it is treated as already cut off — it is not considered part of the vessel. Fine. But consider the implication: if the excess handle is treated as already severed and now lies against the vessel, it would cover the virtual surface at the cut point, creating a *chatzitzah* — an interposition — that might block the *mikveh* waters from reaching the vessel's own surface. Can one apply the *ke-chatuach* logic selectively? Can one say it is cut for purposes of not requiring immersion of the extra portion, yet not cut for purposes of *chatzitzah* — so that the virtual exposed surface at the cut point is not treated as covered?

*Tosafot* finds this untenable and resolves the problem by stipulating that the handle in question is not a solid wooden or metal handle but a chain-link handle. Because the links of a chain allow water to pass between them, even when the excess portion remains physically attached, the *mikveh* water can reach every part of what is being retained. There is therefore no *chatzitzah* concern regardless of how one applies the *ke-chatuach* principle. This solution is ingenious, but the underlying question remains conceptually significant: when we say something is *ke-chatuach*, how thoroughgoing is that fiction? Is it sufficient to generate some legal consequences — exemption from immersion — while not generating others, such as treating a virtual cut surface as obstructed?

---

## Sages Response

### Treifah Model

Having established Rabbi Meir's position, the Gemara turns to the view of the Sages. The Sages hold that the protruding fetal limb is not a *neveilah* but a *treifah*. Their reasoning is that the *shechitah* of the mother did apply to the limb; it simply was not effective in permitting the limb to be eaten. The practical consequence is that the limb does not convey biblical *tumah*. The Gemara notes that a slaughtered *treifah* ordinarily carries no *tumah* at all. If the Sages mean only that touching such a limb is like touching a slaughtered *treifah* — which conveys nothing — why does the *mishnah* invoke the *treifah* comparison rather than simply declaring the limb *tahor*? The Gemara resolves this by citing the position of Abaye's father, Shmuel's father, who held that a *treifah* that was slaughtered carries a rabbinic degree of *tumah* with respect to sanctified objects and items of the Temple. The *mishnah* thus invokes the *treifah* analogy not to declare full biblical *tumah* but to acknowledge this limited rabbinic impurity.

### Braita Exchange

The Gemara then presents a *braita* that reconstructs the full exchange between Rabbi Meir and the Sages in greater detail, filling in what the *mishnah* left elliptical.

Rabbi Meir opens: *ve-chi mi tiharuhu le-eiver zeh midei neveilah* — what has purified this limb from the category of *neveilah*? The Sages respond: *shechitat imo* — the *shechitah* of the mother applies to it. Rabbi Meir presses: if so, *tatirenu ba'achila* — why not permit the limb to be eaten? The Sages respond: *treifah tochich* — the *treifah* case proves the point. A *treifah* that is slaughtered is purified from the category of *neveilah* by virtue of the *shechitah*, yet it cannot be eaten. There is therefore an established category of an act of *shechitah* that removes the designation of *neveilah* without rendering the animal permissible. The same applies here: the *shechitah* of the mother applied to the limb and removed it from the category of *neveilah*, even though it cannot be eaten.

Rava notes — and some attribute the observation to the text anonymously — that the exchange in the *mishnah* was abbreviated, *chisorei mechasra*, and that the *braita* supplies the missing steps.

### Conceptual Basis

Rabbi Meir responds to the Sages' *treifah* analogy by drawing a sharp conceptual distinction. He says: I accept that the *shechitah* of a *treifah* can remove the *neveilah* designation even though the animal cannot be eaten, because in that case the *shechitah* was performed upon the *gufah* — the body of the animal itself. The *shechitah* genuinely related to the *treifah* as its subject. But the limb protruding from the fetus is *she-einah gufah* — not part of the body. If the limb is not part of the mother's body, then the *shechitah* of the mother was simply not performed upon the limb at all. One cannot say the *shechitah* applied but was ineffective; it never applied to begin with. And if no *shechitah* applied, the limb is a *neveilah*.

This exchange clarifies the precise point of contention. Rabbi Meir holds that *shechitah* can only relate to a subject that is *gufah* of the slaughtered animal. If something is not *gufah*, no act of *shechitah* can be said to have been done to it. The Rabbis must therefore be maintaining either that the limb is still *gufah*, or that *shechitah* can relate to something even if it is not strictly *gufah*.

### Fetus vs Organs

The *braita* continues with the Sages' rejoinder, which demonstrates that *shechitah* can indeed function more effectively for something that is *not* integral to the body than for something that is. *harbe matzinu she-eino gufah yotzei mi-gufah* — we find many instances where *shechitah* is more efficacious for something that is not part of the body than for something that is.

The proof is from the first *mishnah* of the *perek*: if one dismembers a fetus inside the mother's womb and then slaughters the mother, the dismembered fetus pieces are permitted for consumption. But if one cuts off the spleen or kidney from the inside of the mother and then slaughters the mother, those organs cannot be eaten. Here is the paradox: the inner organs, which were entirely and integrally part of the mother, lose the benefit of the mother's *shechitah* once they are severed from her body. But the fetus, which was never fully *gufah* of the mother, retains the benefit of the mother's *shechitah* even after being dismembered.

This demonstrates that the Sages' position does not require the fetus to be *gufah* for *shechitah* to apply to it. *shechitah* can relate to something connected to the mother even if it is not an intrinsic part of her body. The underlying question is whether the *shechitah*'s efficacy for the fetus is because the fetus is *gufah* — which would be the position assumed by Rabbi Meir — or whether it is because the fetus is sufficiently connected to the mother even without being *gufah*, which is the Sages' position. The proof from the dismembered fetus shows that even after severance, the *shechitah* of the mother reaches it — indicating that the rationale was never *gufah* in the strict sense.

Importantly, however, the Sages' response does not directly address why the protruding limb cannot be eaten. Rabbi Meir challenged: if the *shechitah* applies, eat the limb. The Sages' rejoinder about the dismembered fetus shows that *shechitah* can apply to something that is not *gufah*, but does not explain what prevents eating the limb. The Rabbis presumably hold that there is some independent prohibition — perhaps derived from the verse *u-vasar basadeh treifah lo tocheilu* — that disqualifies the limb without negating the application of *shechitah*. Rabbi Meir, by contrast, may maintain that the limb's disqualification flows entirely from its not being *gufah*, and that the same fact that disqualifies it also negates the application of *shechitah* entirely.

### Meir Rejoinder

Rabbi Meir's final response in the exchange, as preserved in the *braita*, insists that the categories are mutually exclusive. If the limb is not *gufah* and that is why *shechitah* does not work for it, then one cannot simultaneously claim that *shechitah* did apply but was ineffective — that is only coherent when the *shechitah* was genuinely performed on the subject, as with a *treifah*. The Sages' appeal to the dismembered fetus does not persuade him, because from his perspective the fetus *is gufah* — that is precisely why *shechitah* works for it. For Rabbi Meir, *shechitah* works for the fetus because the fetus is considered part of the mother's body. It follows that the only reason *shechitah* fails for the protruding limb is that the limb is no longer considered part of the body — and once that conclusion is reached, the *shechitah* cannot be said to have applied to the limb at all.

### Hanging Limb Intro

Within this *braita* exchange, a new case is introduced: *ever ha-meduldal*, the hanging or dangling limb of the animal itself. This is distinct from the fetal limb; here we are discussing a limb of the mother animal that has been partially severed — torn perhaps by a predator or other trauma — yet remains attached by some ligament, hanging but not fully detached. Rabbi Meir, in the course of his argument, concedes that the *shechitah* of the mother works for the dangling limb. His reasoning: *davar she-hu gufah* — the dangling limb is part of the body of the animal itself. This concession will be significant for the subsequent analysis. The dangling limb is poised between two statuses: it is not yet *eiver min ha-chai*, since that requires complete detachment, yet it is not fully integrated either. What is its status after *shechitah*, and what happens to it if the animal dies naturally? These questions carry over into the next section.

---

## Dangling Limbs

### Lakish vs Yochanan

The Gemara now presents a dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan concerning whether the controversy between Rabbi Meir and the Sages over the fetal limb extends equally to the *ever ha-meduldal*, the dangling limb of the animal. Reish Lakish maintains: *ke-machlokes be-ubarim kach machlokes be-evarim* — just as Rabbi Meir and the Sages debate the fetal limb, so too they debate the dangling limb of the animal. Rabbi Yochanan initially appears to say that the debate is confined to the fetal limb, while concerning the dangling limb of the animal *divrei ha-kol shechitah osa nipul* — all agree that *shechitah* makes it as though the limb has fallen off, rendering it an *eiver min ha-chai*. The Gemara will eventually reverse Rabbi Yochanan's formulation, but the tension is first worked through analytically.

### Pull Back Logic

Rav Yosef bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning as follows. With respect to the fetal limb, there remains a theoretical possibility that the limb could be pushed back into the womb and the mother could then be slaughtered, permitting the entire animal including the limb. This possibility — *takanta be-chazarah*, the remedy through retraction — means that the protruding limb remains, in some sense, within the ambit of a valid *shechitah*. The Rabbis therefore say the *shechitah* relates to it, even as it protrudes. The dangling limb of the animal, by contrast, can never be restored. Once it is dangling and partially severed, no retraction is possible; it will never be fully permissible. For this reason, Rabbi Yochanan reasons, the Rabbis would concede that the *shechitah* does not apply to the dangling limb in the same way, and all would agree it becomes *nipul* — as though it had fallen.

### Meir Concedes

The Gemara challenges this reading from the *braita* itself. There, Rabbi Meir explicitly says — in addressing the Sages — that *shechitah* applies to the dangling limb (*ever ha-meduldal*) because it is *davar she-hu gufah*, part of the body of the animal. This appears to contradict both Reish Lakish and the initial formulation of Rabbi Yochanan, since both had suggested the dangling limb is subject to dispute. If Rabbi Meir himself concedes the dangling limb, how can it be said that the Sages dispute it?

### Resolution

The Gemara resolves the difficulty for Reish Lakish as follows. Rabbi Meir's concession in the *braita* was dialectical: *le-divreichem ka-amar* — he was speaking according to the Sages' own premises, not expressing his own view. Rabbi Meir's personal position, *lidi*, is that whether it is the fetal limb or the dangling limb, the *shechitah* does not apply to either and both are *neveilah*. He said *le-divreichem*: even according to your logic, I might grant you the dangling limb — since at least that is *gufah* of the animal — but I cannot grant you the fetal limb, which is not. Reish Lakish thus maintains that the true debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages encompasses the dangling limb as well; Rabbi Meir's concession was rhetorical only.

### Yochanan Position

For Rabbi Yochanan, however, the Gemara acknowledges a problem and concludes that his statement was transmitted in inverted form. The corrected version is: the debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies only to the fetal limb. Regarding the dangling limb of the animal, *divrei ha-kol ein shechitah osa nipul* — all agree that *shechitah* does *not* make the limb as though it fell off. All agree that the *shechitah* of the mother applies to the dangling limb, removing it from the category of *neveilah*, and making it, at worst, like a *treifah* — forbidden for consumption but not *tamei*. As Rashi clarifies: *de-tahor mi-letamei af al pi she-assur be-achilah* — it is pure from conveying *tumah*, even though it is forbidden to eat.

This gives Rabbi Yochanan's position a clean logic. The dangling limb is precisely the case that the Sages invoke to prove their point against Rabbi Meir. Since the dangling limb is clearly *gufah* of the mother, everyone agrees the *shechitah* applies to it — yet everyone also agrees it cannot be eaten. This is exactly the Sages' model: *shechitah* can relate to something and yet not render it permissible. Rabbi Meir himself concedes this in the *braita*. The remaining debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages concerns only the fetal limb — whether *shechitah* can apply to something that is not *gufah* at all.

---

## Death vs Shechitah

### Death Principle

Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that there is universal agreement on two related principles concerning the dangling limb. The first is *mita osa nipul* — natural death makes the limb as though it has fallen off. When an animal with a dangling limb dies naturally, the process of dying is treated as completing the limb's detachment. This is admittedly a strange idea: the limb becomes *eiver min ha-chai* precisely at the moment the animal ceases to be alive. But this is the established rule, and it applies regardless of the debate between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about the fetal limb.

### Shechitah Principle

The second universal principle is *ein shechitah osa nipul* — *shechitah* does not make the limb as though it has fallen off. When one slaughters an animal with a dangling limb, the act of *shechitah* does not cause the limb to be treated as fully detached. The *shechitah* relates to the limb, removes it from the category of *neveilah*, and makes it — at worst — like a *treifah*. It does not complete the detachment in the way that natural death does.

### Mishna Evidence

The Gemara asks: if these two principles are universally agreed upon, what *chiddush* does Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef add? Both points are already explicit in a *mishnah* — one that appears much later in the tractate, at 127b. The *mishnah* there states: *meta ha-behemah* — if the animal with the dangling limb died naturally — *ha-basar tzarich hechsher* — the meat of the animal requires susceptibility through contact with liquid — *ve-ha-eiver metamei mishum eiver min ha-chai* — and the limb conveys *tumah* as an *eiver min ha-chai* — *ve-eino metamei mishum eiver min ha-neveilah divrei Rabbi Meir* — but it does not convey *tumah* as a *neveilah*, according to Rabbi Meir.

This explicitly establishes *mita osa nipul*: the limb becomes *eiver min ha-chai* when the animal dies. The difference between *eiver min ha-chai* and *eiver min ha-neveilah* in this context is a matter of the type of *tumah* conveyed. *neveilah* conveys *tumah* through its flesh alone — a *kezayis* of *neveilah* meat is *tamei*. *eiver min ha-chai* conveys *tumah* as a whole limb — if the flesh is separated from the bone, it no longer conveys *tumah*, since it is no longer a complete limb. This distinction is not merely academic; it determines whether separating flesh from the dangling limb creates an independent source of *tumah*.

### Huchsharu Proof

The same *mishnah* continues: *nishchata ha-behemah huchsharu be-dameha divrei Rabbi Meir* — if the animal was slaughtered, the animal and the limb become susceptible to *tumah* through its blood. Rabbi Meir holds that the blood of *shechitah* functions as the liquid that renders the slaughtered animal's meat susceptible to becoming *tamei*. The significant word is *huchsharu* — "they became susceptible," in the plural. If the dangling limb were itself a *neveilah* — already *tamei* — there would be no reason to say it "became susceptible," since it would already be in a state of *tumah*. The use of the plural therefore implies that the limb itself is not *tamei*, that it is susceptible but not yet *tamei*, which in turn means the *shechitah* did apply to it and it is not a *neveilah*.

### Meat vs Limb

The Gemara pushes back. Perhaps *huchsharu* does not refer to the dangling limb at all, but to two types of meat: flesh that separates from the animal's body (*basar ha-poresh min ha-behemah*) and flesh that separates from the dangling limb itself (*basar ha-poresh min ha-eiver*). The *mishnah* might be teaching that both of these become susceptible through the blood of *shechitah* — not that the dangling limb itself is non-*tamei*.

The Gemara further imagines why one might have thought these two types of meat require separate mention: since flesh that separates from an *eiver min ha-chai* was at one moment itself a source of *tumah chamura* by virtue of being attached to the *eiver*, one might have thought it remains susceptible to *tumah* even without contact with liquid — that its prior connection to a *tamei* source exempts it from the ordinary requirement of *hechsher*. The *mishnah* therefore informs us this is not the case; even such flesh requires contact with liquid before it can become *tamei*.

The Gemara acknowledges this is a possible reading of the *mishnah*. The conclusion is that on its own, the *mishnah* might not have been sufficient to establish *ein shechitah osa nipul* with respect to a genuine limb; one might have argued the *mishnah* speaks only of dangling meat, and that a true dangling limb might still be treated as having fallen off upon *shechitah*. Nevertheless, taken together — and ultimately with the explicit statement of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef in Rabbi Yochanan's name — both principles are established: death makes the limb *nipul*, and *shechitah* does not.

### Flesh Susceptibility

The analysis concludes with a clarification about flesh removed from an *eiver min ha-chai*. Such flesh — once separated from the limb — is no longer a *tamei* object in its own right, since *tumah* of *eiver min ha-chai* requires a complete limb with its associated bone and tissue. The separated flesh, however, is susceptible to becoming *tamei* and requires *hechsher* like other foodstuffs. The prior association with a *tamei* object does not grant it an automatic susceptibility independent of liquid contact. This point is established by the *mishnah* and is itself a *chiddush* worth noting.

---

## Eating Prohibition

### Braita Source

Having established that *shechitah* applies to the dangling limb and does not render it *neveilah*, the Gemara turns to the question of why the dangling limb cannot be eaten. The *braita* derives the prohibition from the verse *u-vasar basadeh treifah lo tocheilu* — flesh in the field that is *treifah* you shall not eat. This verse was already invoked in the discussion of the fetal limb. The *braita* extends it: *lehavi es ha-eiver ve-es ha-basar ha-miduldalin bi-behemah u-vi-chayah u-va-of* — to include the dangling limb and hanging flesh of an animal, wild animal, or fowl. Even if one slaughters the mother — *she-hen asurin* — they remain forbidden.

### Dangling Forbidden

Rabba bar bar Chana records this ruling: the dangling limb of the animal, even after valid *shechitah* of the mother, remains forbidden for consumption. The *braita* associates this prohibition with the verse of *basar basadeh treifah*, placing the dangling limb in the same category as the fetal limb in terms of the prohibition against eating it.

### Rabbinic Severity

Rabbi Yochanan, however, as cited by Rabba bar bar Chana, draws a critical distinction between the two cases. When it comes to the dangling limb — *ein bahem ela mitzvas peirush bilvad* — the prohibition is merely a matter of appropriate conduct, a rabbinic-level requirement to refrain. Although the *braita* invokes a biblical verse, Rabbi Yochanan maintains that at the biblical level the *shechitah* of the mother is fully effective for the dangling limb; one could technically eat it. The prohibition against doing so is rabbinic in character — the dangling limb presents as something that should not be eaten, and the Rabbis accordingly prohibited it, but there is no biblical disqualification.

The fetal limb, by contrast, involves a genuine biblical dispute. Rabbi Meir holds it to be *neveilah* at the Torah level; the Sages hold it to be a *treifah*-like case that is biblically forbidden. Either way, the fetal limb's prohibition is of biblical severity. The dangling limb, in Rabbi Yochanan's view, stands apart: *shechitah* is fully effective for it, it is not *tamei*, and its prohibition is entirely rabbinic. This distinction — between biblical severity for the fetal limb and rabbinic severity for the dangling limb — is the concluding conceptual point of the *sugya*.

---

---

# Hullin 74

## Dangling Limbs

### Dangling Limbs Overview

The daf opens by continuing the discussion of *eiver talui* — a limb hanging from a slaughtered animal, in a manner analogous to the arm protruding from a fetus when the mother is slaughtered. In the case of the fetus, the protruding limb is forbidden on account of the verse *basar basadeh tereifah*. The *gemara* now applies the same concern to the dangling limb of a slaughtered animal: it cannot be eaten. However, the *gemara* introduces a qualification: *ein bahem ella mitzvas poresh bilvad* — there is only, as it were, a requirement to abstain, a *mitzvas poresh*, and not a full-fledged prohibition.

### Mitzvas Poresh

What does *mitzvas poresh bilvad* mean? The standard interpretation, shared by Rashi and Tosafot, is that the prohibition against eating the dangling limb is merely rabbinic in force. This is striking, given that the *gemara* anchors the prohibition in a biblical verse and treats the dangling limb in the same category as the protruding limb of a fetus. Yet Rashi and Tosafot read the phrase as signaling that unlike the fetal limb — which carries a biblical prohibition — the dangling limb is only a rabbinic concern.

### Rambam on Mitzvas Poresh

The Rambam offers an alternative reading. In his view, *mitzvas poresh bilvad* applies equally to the dangling limb and the fetal limb alike. Even where the Torah derives a prohibition from the verse, it does not carry the full weight of a standard negative commandment. The Torah is, in effect, instructing avoidance — *mitzvas poresh* at the biblical level — but without the legal consequences that accompany a classic biblical prohibition. It is a directive to separate from something that is not appropriate to eat, but it is not the kind of prohibition that generates *malkos*.

### Eating Dangling Limbs

The practical consequence of this distinction surfaces when one asks: what happens if someone eats the dangling limb?
