The *gemara* is about to rule that one does not receive *malkos* for eating the dangling limb. By contrast, some *rishonim* hold that eating the fetal limb does incur *malkos*, either for violating *basar basadeh tereifah* or, according to the Ra'avad, because the limb has the status of *tereifah* — an act of *shechitah* was performed that was ineffective, leaving the limb in a state from which one could receive *malkos* for eating a *tereifah*. The Rambam, however, draws no such distinction and holds that neither the dangling limb nor the fetal limb exposes the consumer to *malkos*.

### Dangling Limbs & Tumah

A further consequence follows from this: since the dangling limb is not so severely prohibited, it certainly does not convey *tumat neveilah*. The *shechitah* was effective enough to prevent the animal — and by extension this limb — from acquiring the status of *neveilah*. Its status is closer to that of a *tereifah* than to that of a *neveilah*, which was the substance of the preceding discussion. A *neveilah* and a *tereifah* both carry *malkos* if eaten — they represent distinct negative prohibitions — but the *shechitah* of the animal ensures that the dangling limb does not generate *tumah* as a *neveilah* would.

---

## Rav Yosef Dispute

### Rav Yosef's Position

The *gemara* reports that Rav Yosef was sitting before Rav Huna and stated the following tradition: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav — *achalo l'zeh lokeh* — if one eats this limb, one does receive *malkos*. This is seemingly surprising, because it was Rav Yosef himself, just the day before, who cited the ruling of *mitzvas poresh bilvad*, which implies no *malkos*.

### Anonymous Objection

An anonymous member of the assembled group — designated only as *hahu me-rabbanan*, one of the other rabbis present — immediately spoke up and said: do not listen to Rav Yosef. He then cited a competing tradition: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta said in the name of Rav — *achalo l'zeh eino lokeh* — if one eats this, one does not receive *malkos*, consistent with the principle that it is only *mitzvas poresh bilvad*.

### Rav Huna's Question

Rav Huna, faced with two traditions both transmitted in the name of Rav, responded by saying: *anan amai nishmoch* — upon whom should we rely? He appeared to weigh the two traditions against each other, treating them as equally credible competing reports. Rav Yosef turned his face away — *ahadrei Rav Yosef l'appei* — a gesture of offense. Rashi explains that he turned away in anger, *b'kaas*. One might wonder why the presence of a competing tradition would provoke such a reaction; the *gemara* is replete with disputes. It seems Rav Yosef was offended on two counts. First, the competing tradition came from an unnamed individual of no apparent stature, and Rav Huna was according it equal weight with his own. Second, and perhaps more pointedly, Rav Yosef felt that Rav Huna had assumed there was a contradiction in the first place rather than simply asking him for clarification — a reasonable expectation when two traditions bearing the same authority appear to conflict.

### Clarification: Death vs.…

Rav Yosef then explained himself: *mai kashya* — what difficulty did you see? When I said in the name of Rav that one receives *malkos*, I was speaking *b'misah* — when the animal died naturally. What happens when an animal dies with a limb dangling from it? The death of the animal causes the limb to be treated as though it had already fallen off — *d'ahosei nipel* — rendering it *ever min hachai*, a limb from a living animal, for which one does indeed incur *malkos*. The other tradition, the one this anonymous figure cited in the name of Rav, speaks *bishchitah* — the case in which the animal was slaughtered. There, the *shechitah* does not cause the limb to be treated as having fallen off, and one does not receive *malkos*; the prohibition is only the *mitzvas prosh* discussed earlier. The two traditions are therefore not in conflict at all — they address entirely different scenarios.

### Reconciliation

The reconciliation that Rav Yosef offers is thus fully consistent with his position from the previous day. When the animal dies naturally, the dangling limb is treated as *ever min hachai* — a limb detached from a living animal — and eating it carries *malkos*. When the animal is slaughtered, the *shechitah* does not produce this effect of *nifol* — of treating the limb as fallen — and the prohibition remains in the lesser category of *mitzvas poresh bilvad*, without *malkos*. The key conceptual distinction underlying the entire discussion is thus: *misah osei nifol, shechitah eino osei nifol* — natural death creates the legal effect of a fallen limb, *shechitah* does not.

---

## Misah Osei Nifol

### Rava's Question

Rava now presses further: *minah m'yosaf d'amru Rabbanan* — what is the source for this principle that death creates the effect of *nifol* while *shechitah* does not? The principle has been invoked and relied upon, but where does it originate?

### Verses on Shratzim

The *gemara* answers from a verse concerning dead *shratzim* — the small creeping creatures listed as sources of *tumah* in the Torah. The verse states: *v'chol asher yipol alav meihem b'mosam yitma* — whatever falls upon them from among them in their death shall become *tamei*. The *gemara* reads this verse creatively. The word *b'mosam*, "in their death," might appear redundant, since the verse already uses the word *mi-nivlatam*, "from their carcasses," earlier. The question becomes: what does the additional phrase *b'mosam* exclude or add?

If the answer were simply that something falling from a live creature does not cause *tumah*, that would already be derivable from *mi-nivlatam* — "from their carcasses," implying only when dead. So the word *b'mosam* must be teaching something else. The *gemara* therefore derives: *misah osei nifol, v'ein shechitah osei nifol* — death creates the legal status of a fallen limb; *shechitah* does not. The word *yipol*, which normally means "falls upon," is read here as referring to something that falls off the creature — *asher yipol meihem* — a limb that falls from them. And this occurs *b'mosam*, in their death. The implication is that natural death is what generates the legal fiction that the dangling limb has already fallen off, whereas *shechitah* does not produce this effect.

### Rav Ada's Challenge

Rav Ada bar Abba objected to Rava: *veha k'ra b'shratzim ksiv* — but this verse speaks about *shratzim*, creatures that cannot be subject to *shechitah* at all! They are never *kosher*, so there is no meaningful contrast between dying naturally and being slaughtered. How, then, can one derive from this verse any distinction between death and *shechitah*?

### Applying to Animals

Rava responded: *einu inyan l'shratzim d'lav bnei shechitah ninhu* — you are correct that the teaching cannot be applied to *shratzim* themselves, since *shechitah* is simply irrelevant to them. But precisely because the verse's contrast has no application there, *t'neihu inyan l'vehemah* — apply the teaching to animals, where *shechitah* is a meaningful category. The verse's emphasis on death as the operative moment is thus redirected to teach us something about animals, where *shechitah* presents a genuine alternative to natural death.

### Ke-ein Mitah

At this point, a further question arises. The word *bemotam* is also needed to teach another principle regarding *tumah*: *ke-ein mitah* — the creature must be in a state resembling the moment of death in order to convey *tumah*. Concretely: *lachim metamin, yeveshin ein metamin* — moist dead creatures convey *tumah*, but desiccated ones do not. A dead creature that has completely dried out is no longer in the condition it was at the moment of death, and so it no longer generates *tumah*. This principle is also derived from the word *bemotam*.

### Double Bemotam

The *gemara* resolves this by noting that the word *bemotam* appears twice in the relevant verses. One instance teaches *ke-ein mitah* — the moisture requirement for *tumah*. The second instance teaches *misah osei nifol, shechitah eino osei nifol* — the principle that death creates the status of a fallen limb while *shechitah* does not. Each usage of *bemotam* carries its own independent teaching.

---

## Dead vs. Live Fetus

### Rav Chisda's Rule

Rav Chisda now introduces a distinction that applies specifically to the case of a fetus with a limb protruding from the mother's womb when the mother is slaughtered. He differentiates between a live fetus and a dead fetus in this scenario.

### Live Fetus Limb

When the fetus is alive and a limb is protruding, and the mother is then slaughtered, a debate among the *rishonim* concerns the status of that limb. Some hold the limb is *neveilah*, while others hold it is more analogous to *tereifah*. The precise categorization carries consequences for *tumah*, *malkos*, and related questions, and this is the substance of the earlier discussion the *gemara* has been working through.

### Dead Fetus Limb

The case of the dead fetus is treated differently. If the fetus has already died in utero, and a limb is protruding, and the mother is then slaughtered — according to Rav Chisda, in this case *divrei hakol shechitah osei nipul* — all opinions agree that even the *shechitah* of the mother creates the effect of *nifol* with respect to that limb. The reasoning is that since the fetus itself is already dead, the limb is attached to something whose natural death already occurred; the *shechitah* of the mother cannot undo that, and the limb is treated as though it had already fallen off, acquiring the status of *ever min hachai*.

### Rava's Disagreement

Rava disagrees with this conclusion. In his view, *kemachlokes be-zeh kach machlokes be-zeh* — whatever dispute exists regarding the live fetus applies equally to the dead fetus. The principle of *misah osei nifol* refers to the natural death of the animal being discussed — the mother. The fetus's prior death does not change the analysis when the mother is then slaughtered. *shechitah* of the mother never creates the effect of *nifol*, regardless of whether the fetus itself was alive or dead at the time. The practical stakes of this dispute, as throughout these discussions, concern primarily whether the limb generates *tumah* as a *neveilah* or *ever min hachai*, not whether one may eat it — eating it is forbidden in any case.

---

## Eight-Month-Old

### Eight-Month Non-Viable

The *gemara* now turns to the case of the *ben shemonah* — an eight-month-old fetus, which the *gemara* assumes to be non-viable. When such a creature is born and then slaughtered, the *shechitah* does not help. It retains the status of *neveilah*, not *tereifah*. The underlying assumption is that since the eight-month-old baby is effectively already dead — it will not survive — the *shechitah* performed on it has no more effect than *shechitah* performed on a corpse.

This assumption reflects the *gemara*'s settled view, found in other contexts as well, that an eight-month-old baby is entirely non-viable. So certain was this assumption that the *gemara* rules one may not even pick up such an infant on *shabbos*, because it is treated as *ke-even* — like a stone — *muktzah* and without the status of a living being. Contemporary practice departs from this position, accommodating the reality that medical technology can sustain premature infants, but the *gemara*'s halachic framework proceeds on the assumption that an eight-month baby categorically cannot survive.

### Baraita Challenge

A *baraita* challenges this framework. The *baraita* invokes the case of the *ben shemonah* as proof that *shechitah* being relevant to a species does not automatically exempt the animal from causing *tumah* upon death. The *baraita* states: *ben shemonah chai yochiach* — an eight-month-old baby should prove the point. For even though *shechitah* is applicable within its species (*she-af al pi she-yesh bemino shechitah*), *shechitah* performed on this creature does not purify it from *tumah* (*ein shechitato metaharato*).

The larger context here is the question of how we know that a *tereifah* that was slaughtered does not cause *tumah* as a *neveilah* would. The *mishnah* reasoned: at least for this species, *shechitah* is meaningful, and therefore it is effective enough to prevent *tumat neveilah*. The *baraita* presses back: an eight-month-old baby is a case where *shechitah* is applicable to the species, and yet *shechitah* of this particular creature does not protect it from *tumah*. Why, then, should the argument work for *tereifah*?

### Ein Bemino Shechitah

The *mishnah*'s position answers this challenge by treating the eight-month-old as a species unto itself — *ein bemino shechitah*. Since this type of creature can never be rendered *kosher* through *shechitah*, it is classified like a non-*kosher* species for which *shechitah* is simply irrelevant. It therefore presents no counter-example to the principle that *shechitah*, when relevant to the species, protects against *tumat neveilah*.

### Shechitah of Mother

The *baraita*, however, rejects this classification. Rav Kahana explains: *yesh bemino shechitah agav imo* — there is *shechitah* applicable to this type of creature by virtue of its mother's slaughter. When the eight-month fetus is still in utero, *shechitah* of the mother renders it permitted. Thus *shechitah* is not entirely without application to this *min* — it can take effect upon the creature indirectly. The *baraita* therefore contends that the eight-month-old cannot be classified as *ein bemino shechitah*, and it does present a legitimate counter-example: here is a creature to which *shechitah* is in principle applicable, and yet slaughtering it does not protect from *tumah*. The dispute between the *mishnah* and the *baraita* thus turns on whether *shechitah* that operates only through the mother counts as *shechitah* applicable to the species of the eight-month-old itself.

### Trefah & Shechitah

The *gemara* asks: according to the *tanna* of the *baraita*, who accepts the eight-month-old as a counter-example, how does he know that a *tereifah* that is slaughtered does not cause *tumah*? The answer is derived from a verse. The Torah states *v'chi yamut min ha-behemah* — when one of the animals dies. The *gemara* reads *min ha-behemah* as implying that only some animals cause *tumah* upon dying. The distinction is not between species but between manners of death: *zo tereifah she-shachatah* — a *tereifah* that was slaughtered does not cause *tumah* upon its death. The verse itself thus provides the source, independent of the eight-month-old analogy.

---

## In Utero Shechitah

### Rav Hoshaya's Question

Rav Hoshaya poses a striking question: what if a *shohet* inserted his hand into a mother's womb and slaughtered the fetus while it was still in utero? This is understood as a thought experiment — it does not require resolving the practical impossibility of the act. The question is conceptual: can *shechitah* be meaningful for a fetus while it is still within the mother? Or, at that stage, is the fetus simply not yet its own animal, such that *shechitah* has no purchase on it?

### Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbanan

Rav Hoshaya notes that the question can be posed both according to Rabbi Meir and according to the *rabbanan* — the debate we will encounter in the *mishnah* regarding whether the mother's *shechitah* is effective for the fetus. According to Rabbi Meir, who holds that the fetus requires its own *shechitah* upon being removed from the womb, one might reason that Rabbi Meir recognizes the fetus as a sufficiently independent entity such that *shechitah* is relevant to it. But this recognition could cut either way. One might say: Rabbi Meir views the fetus as independent enough that once it enters the world, its own *shechitah* is necessary — but while still in utero, even he would agree it is not yet sufficiently its own entity for *shechitah* to be meaningful. Alternatively, one might argue: even according to the *rabbanan*, who hold that the mother's *shechitah* suffices, perhaps the Torah provided four *simanim* — two for the mother, two for the fetus — such that either pair can serve as the operative *shechitah*. In that case, the fetus's own *shechitah* in utero might also be valid. The question thus remains unresolved.

### Born Treifah

Rava resolves the question by means of a *baraita*. The *baraita* discusses an animal that was born as a *tereifah* from birth — *harei shenolad trefah min habeten* — a creature that was never permissible to eat. If it were possible to slaughter a fetus in utero, Rava points out, there would have been a moment prior to its emergence from the womb during which such an in utero *shechitah* could theoretically have been performed, and the animal would at that point have been permissible. The *baraita* would then be inaccurate in stating that the creature never had a moment of permissibility — *sha'at kosher*.

Rava resolves this by emending the scenario: *tani shenotzra trefah min habeten* — the *baraita* must be speaking of an animal that was a *tereifah* from conception, not merely from birth. This is possible in the case of an animal born with five legs — *ba'alat hamesh raglayim* — a congenital defect that constitutes a *tereifah* from the very moment of conception. In such a case, there was never a moment, even in utero, at which the animal was permissible. This resolves the challenge and implies that in utero *shechitah* is in principle possible; otherwise, there would be no need to specify that the animal was a *tereifah* from conception in order to eliminate any moment of permissibility.

---

## Mishnah Debate

### Case 1: Non-Viable

The *mishnah* now lays out the various cases systematically. *hashochet et habehemah umatza ba ben shemonah chai o met* — if one slaughters a mother animal and finds within it an eight-month-old baby, whether alive or dead — *o ben tisha met* — or a nine-month-old that is dead. In all of these cases, the creature is either not viable or not alive, and in every such case, all opinions agree: the mother's *shechitah* is effective for it. It is treated as a limb of the mother. The practical consequence is *koro umotzi et damo* — one tears it open and removes the blood, just as one would do for any other limb of the animal, and then it may be eaten. The requirement to remove the blood is no different here than with any other part of the slaughtered animal.

### Rabbi Meir Position

If, however, one finds a nine-month-old viable baby alive — *matza ben tisha chai* — then, says Rabbi Meir, *taun shechitah* — it requires its own *shechitah*. The mother's *shechitah* does not work for it. Furthermore, *vechayav be'oto ve'et beno* — one must not slaughter it and the mother on the same day, because this fetus is its own independent animal for whom *shechitah* is both required and significant. The prohibition of *oto ve'et beno* applies.

### Rabbanan Position

The sages disagree: *shechitat imo metaherato* — even for a nine-month-old viable fetus, the mother's *shechitah* is fully effective. The fetus is treated as part of the mother, and no separate *shechitah* is required.

### Rabbi Shimon Shezuri

Rabbi Shimon Shezuri goes further: *afilu ben chamesh shanim vechoresh basadeh* — even if this viable nine-month-old fetus was allowed to grow up, becoming a five-year-old cow plowing in the field, the *shechitah* of its mother from five years earlier still renders it permitted — *shechitat imo metaherato*. He is not disputing the *chachamim* but elaborating on the extent of their position: the leniency is not limited to the period immediately after birth; it follows the animal throughout its life.

### Mother Not Slaughtered

Where all opinions converge is in the case where the mother was not slaughtered. If the fetus was removed by Caesarean section and the mother was not subject to *shechitah*, then the viable nine-month-old fetus requires its own *shechitah* — everyone agrees. The permissibility of the fetus is entirely contingent on the mother's *shechitah* having been performed; in its absence, the fetus stands as its own animal and requires its own act of *shechitah*.

---

## Chelev & Gid

### Rabbi Elazar

The *gemara* now asks whether the leniency that extends to the fetus — the *shechitah* of the mother working for it — applies also to other prohibitions associated with the animal: specifically *chelev* (forbidden fat) and *gid hanasheh* (the sciatic nerve). Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: *lo hilchu bo ella al iskei shechitah bilvad* — the leniency applies only to matters of *shechitah*, not to the *chelev* or *gid* of the fetus. Those remain forbidden.

### Baraita on Chelev

The *gemara* immediately challenges this. It cites a *baraita*: *gid hanasheh noheg beshlil vechelbo assur divrei Rabbi Meir* — the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* applies to the fetus and its fat is forbidden, says Rabbi Meir. *rabbi yehuda omer eino noheg beshlil vechelbo mutar* — Rabbi Yehuda says the *gid hanasheh* prohibition does not apply to the fetus and its fat is permitted. This is an explicit debate — they are not in agreement. So how can Rabbi Elazar say the leniency is confined to *shechitah* when it seems to extend, at least according to Rabbi Yehuda, to *chelev* and *gid* as well?

### Logic of Dispute

The *gemara* explains that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda are each following their own positions consistently. Rabbi Meir holds that the nine-month-old viable fetus requires its own *shechitah* — he views it as an independent animal — and therefore its *chelev* and *gid hanasheh* are subject to the standard prohibitions. Rabbi Yehuda (who aligns with the *chachamim*) holds that the fetus is treated as a limb of the mother. If that is so, then the *chelev* forbidden by the Torah is only fat found in specific locations on the animal — around the kidneys and so forth. The fat in this limb, embedded in the uterus, is not in those locations. Similarly, the *gid hanasheh* prohibition applies to the sinew in the animal's own hind leg — not to the corresponding sinew in some limb that happens to be inside the mother. Therefore, if it is treated as a limb, neither the *chelev* nor the *gid hanasheh* is a problem. Blood, on the other hand, is always a problem — blood in any limb must be removed.

### Clarification

The *gemara* clarifies that the debate in the *baraita* concerns the *chelev* that surrounds the *gid hanasheh* — a separate question about the fat around the sciatic nerve in a normal animal — and not, as might first appear, about the general status of fetal *chelev*. An independent *baraita* records a dispute on this specific question: Rabbi Meir holds one must dig after all the fat surrounding the *gid hanasheh* and remove it from its very root, whereas Rabbi Yehuda holds one need only skim the surface fat — the deeper fat is not forbidden. In either case, the question of fetal *chelev* and the question of fat around the *gid hanasheh* are distinct debates that should not be conflated.

### Kashrut Issues

The *gemara* therefore revises Rabbi Elazar's formulation. What he meant was not that the leniency applies only to *shechitah* in the narrow sense, but rather: *lo hilchu bo ella al iskei achila bilvad* — the leniency applies only to matters that relate to eating, to *kashrut*. This includes the question of *shechitah* itself, and also *chelev* and *gid hanasheh*, all of which relate to the permissibility of the food. It does not extend to matters that have nothing to do with eating.

---

## Blood Issues

### Resh Lakish

Resh Lakish now addresses the blood of the fetus. He states: *l'divrei hamatiri b'chelbo matiri b'damo* — according to those who permit the *chelev* of the fetus (i.e., those who follow Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim*), they also permit its blood. Conversely, *v'divrei ha'oser b'chelbo oser b'damo* — those who forbid the *chelev* also forbid the blood. This appears to contradict what was established earlier, namely that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the blood of the fetus must be removed (*koro umotzi et damo*), as the *mishnah* itself states.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan objects to Resh Lakish: even according to those who permit the *chelev*, the blood should still be forbidden. The reasoning is straightforward: even if the fetus is treated as a limb of the mother, blood in any limb remains prohibited. The *mishnah* makes precisely this point. *af l'divrei hamatiri b'chelbo oser b'damo* — even by those who permit the fat, the blood is forbidden.

### Rav Zeira

Rav Zeira resolves the apparent contradiction between Resh Lakish and this obvious point. Resh Lakish was not saying the blood is outright permitted. What he meant was: *lomar she'ein eno kareis* — the blood does not carry the punishment of *kareis*. The distinction is between *dam hanefesh* — the lifeblood, the blood that flows at the moment of slaughter, for which *kareis* is incurred — and blood absorbed within the limbs, which is forbidden by a negative prohibition but not subject to *kareis*. Resh Lakish's point was specifically about *kareis*, not about whether the blood is forbidden at all.

### Fetus Blood & Kareis

This resolution requires one further step. Rabbi Yehuda holds, in a *baraita*, that even *dam hatamtzis* — the residual blood that remains in the flesh, not the lifeblood — carries *kareis*, derived from the verse *v'chol dam lo socheilu* ("and all blood you shall not eat"). If so, how can Resh Lakish say there is no *kareis* for the fetal blood even according to Rabbi Yehuda?

Rav Yosef, son of Rav Salla Chasida, explains before Rav Pappa: Rabbi Yehuda derives *kareis* for residual blood from *v'chol dam* — "all blood" — but this extension depends on the concept of lifeblood. *kol heicha d'mechayev adam hanefesh* — wherever *kareis* applies to the lifeblood, the prohibition extends also to cover the residual blood of the limbs with *kareis*. But *v'chol heicha d'lo mechayev adam nefesh* — wherever *kareis* does not apply to the lifeblood, the residual blood of the limbs also does not carry *kareis*. In the case of this fetus, since it is treated as a limb of the mother and the *shechitah* of the mother rendered it permitted, there is no concept of *dam hanefesh* — lifeblood — for the fetus itself. Without a *dam hanefesh* context, even Rabbi Yehuda's extension to residual blood does not apply. Therefore, the blood of the fetus is forbidden, and must be removed as the *mishnah* states, but eating it does not incur *kareis*. The mother's *shechitah* works for the fetus; within the logic of permissibility, the fetus is treated as a limb, and since a limb has no lifeblood of its own, *kareis* does not attach to its blood.

---

## Pidyon Bechor

### Question Posed

The *gemara* now raises a question about a *ben pakuah* — the name given to a fetus found alive in the womb when the mother is slaughtered. According to the *chachamim*, the mother's *shechitah* renders it permitted, and it is treated as a limb of the mother for food purposes. The question is: can one use a *ben pakuah* of a sheep to redeem a firstborn donkey? The Torah requires that a firstborn donkey be redeemed with a sheep (*seh*). Is a *ben pakuah* sheep sufficiently a *seh* to serve this purpose?

### Rabbi Meir's View

According to Rabbi Meir, there is no question. Since Rabbi Meir holds that the fetus requires its own *shechitah*, it is unambiguously its own independent animal — *seh ma'alyahu* — a proper sheep. One may certainly redeem a firstborn donkey with it.

### Rabbanan Debate

The question arises only according to the *rabbanan*, who hold that the mother's *shechitah* works for it. If it is treated as a limb of the mother — effectively as *basar b'dikula*, meat in a pot — then perhaps it is not sufficiently an independent animal to function as the *seh* required for redemption. On the other hand, the *gemara* notes with characteristic directness: *keivan d'rahit v'azil v'rahit v'ati* — since it runs back and forth, one can hardly call it merely meat; it is a living, running creature, and perhaps *seh karina beih* — we can still call it a sheep.

### Mar Zutra

Mar Zutra holds that one cannot redeem a firstborn donkey with a *ben pakuah*.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet holds that one can.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi addresses Mar Zutra's reasoning. Mar Zutra's position is apparently based on a *gezeirah shavah* — a verbal analogy — connecting the word *seh* used in the context of redeeming a firstborn donkey to the word *seh* used in the context of the *korban pesach*. Just as a *ben pakuah* cannot serve as a *korban pesach* — since it is already in a state of *shechitah* and one cannot bring something already slaughtered as a *korban* — so too it cannot be used for *pidyon*. Rav Ashi presses back: if you apply the *gezeirah shavah* fully, you would require the sheep used for redemption to be *zachar tamim uven shanah* — male, unblemished, and one year old, as the *korban pesach* must be. Since no one applies those conditions to *pidyon*, the *gezeirah shavah* cannot be used this comprehensively. The answer is that the word *tifdeh tifdeh* — the doubled language of redemption in the Torah — broadens the obligation to include any type of sheep. And yet the *gezeirah shavah* must serve some purpose; it cannot be entirely discarded. Its function, according to this analysis, is precisely to exclude the *ben pakuah* — not by importing the specific requirements of *korban pesach*, but by establishing that the *ben pakuah* falls outside the category of *seh* usable for this purpose.

### Conclusion

The *gemara*'s final position resolves cleanly with the principle established throughout this discussion. For matters of *kashrut* — for food — the *ben pakuah* is treated as meat; the mother's *shechitah* has rendered it permitted and it is considered a limb of the mother. For other halachic purposes — *kil'ayim*, bestiality, plowing with disparate animals, and, as the *gemara* concludes here via the *gezeirah shavah*, *pidyon bechor* — the *ben pakuah* is considered an animal in its own right. The leniency of *shechitat imo* is bounded: it governs matters of eating and *kashrut*, but it does not dissolve the creature's independent legal existence in other domains.

---

---

# Hullin 75

## Fetus Tumah Status

### Recap: Mother's Shechita

The daf opens at 74b, where we have been discussing the case of a fetus found alive in its mother's womb after the mother has been *shechted*. We have already established the dominant rabbinic position — against Rabbi Meir — that the mother's *shechita* works for the fetus. The *gemara* then probed how completely the fetus is treated as meat: on one hand, its fat (*chelev*) and the *gid hanasheh* are not forbidden as they would be in an independent animal, since the fetus is treated like a limb of the mother; on the other hand, there is a prohibition of blood. For matters outside the domain of food — such as plowing with a donkey, or questions of redeeming a firstborn donkey — the fetus is treated as a live animal in its own right. With that background in place, the *gemara* now takes up a further dimension of the same underlying question.

### Tumah: Rishon or Sheini

The *gemara* asks: *mahu limnos bo rishon v'sheini* — once the mother has been *shechted* and both she and the fetus are dead, do we treat them as one unit or two for purposes of *tumah*? Concretely: if the mother's carcass comes into contact with something *tamei* and becomes a *rishon* (a first-degree derivative of *tumah*), what is the status of the fetus? Is it also a *rishon*, as part of the same body? Or is it a *sheini*, because it is a separate entity that the mother is merely transmitting *tumah* to?

The analogy to a single animal body is instructive. If a *shechted* cow touches something *tamei*, every part of that animal — head, torso, tail — becomes *tamei* as a *rishon*. One does not say the head is a *rishon* and by the time *tumah* reaches the tail it has descended to a *sheini* or *shelishi*. Everything is one unit. The question here is whether the fetus inside the mother participates in that same unity.

One clarification is in order. If the fetus were still alive, it could not become *tamei* in any case, since the concept of *tumah* as applied to food presupposes that the item is fit to be eaten, and a living animal — even one that does not require *shechita* — is not currently food in the relevant sense. So the question arises only when both mother and fetus are dead.

### RY vs. RL Dispute

Rabbi Yochanan rules that *monin bo rishon v'sheini* — one does count down, the mother is a *rishon* and the fetus is a *sheini*. They are separate enough that *tumah* must pass from one to the other in a graduated way. Reish Lakish rules the opposite: *ein monin bo rishon v'sheini* — one does not count down degrees; the fetus and mother are treated as a unified whole and the fetus receives *tumah* directly, not as a second-degree transmission.

### Nut Analogy & Shomer

The reason Reish Lakish offers is not that mother and fetus are literally one body — indeed, earlier evidence suggests they are not fully unified. Rather, Reish Lakish invokes the principle of *shomer*: a protective covering that surrounds an item is considered sufficiently bound up with that item that *tumah* touching the covering reaches the item inside directly, without losing a degree. His analogy is *na'aseh ke'egoz hamitkashkesh bekliptah* — it is like a nut rattling around inside its shell (think of a pistachio or acorn, where the inner nut can be felt to move within the outer shell). If something *tamei* touches the shell, one does not say the shell is a *rishon* and the nut inside is a *sheini*. Because the shell functions as a *shomer* — a protector and extension of the nut — the *tumah* is considered to have reached the nut directly; the nut becomes a *rishon* just like the shell. Similarly, says Reish Lakish, the mother's body and womb function as a *shomer* for the fetus. Even granting that the fetus is not strictly one unit with the mother, the mother nonetheless envelops and protects the fetus sufficiently that *tumah* reaching the mother reaches the fetus as a *rishon*, without stepping down to a *sheini*.

### Pregnant Cow Challenge

Reish Lakish then challenges Rabbi Yochanan from a different angle, raising the issue of *hechsher* — the requirement that food come into contact with liquid before it can become susceptible to *tumah*. The *gemara* cites the case of a limb protruding from the womb at the time of *shechita*. Rabbi Meir says that limb is a *neveilah*, and the body of the fetus connected to it has therefore touched a *neveilah*. But for the fetus to have become *tamei* through that contact, it must first have been rendered susceptible (*huchshar*) through contact with liquid. When the mother is *shechted*, blood flows and contacts the mother's exterior, rendering the mother susceptible. If the fetus is considered one body with the mother, then that same *hechsher* applies to the fetus. But if — as Rabbi Yochanan insists — they are two separate bodies, what made the fetus susceptible? Reish Lakish presses: for me it works well, since I say they are *chad gufa* for *tumah* purposes, and the blood of the mother renders the fetus susceptible as well. But according to you, Rabbi Yochanan, how did the fetus become susceptible?

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *bi'shchita k'Rabbi Shimon* — through the act of *shechita* itself, following the position of Rabbi Shimon, who held that *shechita* renders meat susceptible to *tumah* even without any blood making contact, since the act of *shechita* that converts the animal into food substitutes for the usual *hechsher*. The *shechita* worked on the mother and worked on the fetus; that act itself made the fetus susceptible, with no need to appeal to the mother's blood. This answer, Rabbi Yochanan maintains, says nothing about whether the fetus is a separate unit.

Rabbi Yochanan then challenges Reish Lakish from a *baraita*: a pregnant cow is *shechted*, a live fetus is found inside — one that now does not require its own *shechita* — and later this grown-up fetus walks through a river (*avar b'nahar*) and thereby becomes susceptible (*huchshar*), then enters a cemetery and becomes *tamei*. The remarkable feature of this case is that even as a live animal, this *ben pakua* can become *tamei* as food. But the key point Rabbi Yochanan draws from it is that the fetus needed to pass through a river to become susceptible — meaning the blood of the mother at the time of *shechita* did not render it susceptible. This proves the fetus was a separate body, not united with the mother for *tumah* purposes, which is Rabbi Yochanan's position. For Reish Lakish — who holds they are one body — the fetus should already have been rendered susceptible through the mother's blood at *shechita*; why would it need the river?

Reish Lakish answers that the *baraita* is dealing with a case of *shechita yaveshta* — a miraculous dry *shechita* in which no blood was produced at all — and moreover, not according to Rabbi Shimon, so neither the blood nor the act of *shechita* rendered it susceptible. Hence the need for the river. The *gemara* notes that this is a difficult resolution: the case of a bloodless *shechita* is already nearly impossible to imagine, let alone to assume that the *baraita* was taking it for granted. The straightforward reading of the *baraita* thus supports Rabbi Yochanan: the fetus is a separate unit from the mother.

### Living Fetus Tumah

The *baraita* introduces something striking beyond the *hechsher* debate: the fully grown *ben pakua* can become *tamei* as a live animal. The *gemara* at the top of 75a asks: who is the *tanna* that holds a live animal can become *tamei* as food? Rabbi Yochanan answers: it is Rabbi Yose HaGlili.

A *baraita* records Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yose HaGlili: this live *ben pakua* that has grown up *metamei tumat ochlin* — it can become *tamei* with the *tumah* of foodstuff — and it does require *hechsher* (contact with liquid) first. The Sages, however, disagree: *eino metamei tumat ochlin*, *mipnei shehu chai* — it does not become *tamei*, because it is alive, and anything alive (*v'chol shehu chai*) does not become *tamei* as food. For *kashrus* purposes, the *shechita* of the mother defined this animal's identity as a limb of the mother — so no *shechita* is required, no *chelev* prohibition applies, no *gid hanasheh*. But for *tumah v'taharah*, one cannot ignore the plain fact that this is a breathing, living animal. Just as we said for other domains — plowing with a donkey, for instance — the live animal must be treated as a live animal.

Rabbi Yochanan then connects Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position to a parallel dispute: *Rabbi Yose HaGlili u-Veit Shammai amru davar echad* — Rabbi Yose HaGlili and Beit Shammai said the same thing. The parallel is the question of when a fish becomes susceptible to *tumah* as food, since fish require no *shechita* and can be eaten alive. The *mishnah* in *Uktzin* records the dispute: Beit Shammai says *mishe'yitzadu* — from the moment they are caught in a net they are already considered food, even while still alive and in the water. Beit Hillel says *mishe'yamutu* — they must actually die before they become food. Rabbi Akiva offers a middle position: *mishe'she'ein yecholim lichyot* — they must reach a point at which they can no longer survive, even if they have not yet died.

The *gemara* asks what distinguishes Rabbi Akiva from Beit Hillel. Rashi understands the question to concern the case between Rabbi Akiva and Beit Hillel. Rabbi Yochanan answers: *dag mikarteia* — a fish that is thrashing. Rashi explains this as a fish in its last throes, still alive and moving, but already dried out to the point that it cannot be revived even if thrown back in the water. Tosafot reads the question differently — as distinguishing Rabbi Akiva from Beit Shammai — and explains that vigorous thrashing is Beit Shammai's indicator that the fish is already fully under human control and irrevocably destined for consumption, while Rabbi Akiva requires something stronger: the fish must be past the point of survival. Either way, the underlying question is a fascinating one: something can be edible while alive, and yet the question remains whether it counts as food for purposes of *tumah*.

Beit Hillel's position maps directly onto the Sages' ruling about the *ben pakua*: as long as it is alive, it is not food and cannot become *tamei*. Beit Shammai's position maps onto Rabbi Yose HaGlili's: something edible while alive is already considered food.

The *gemara* then raises a further question prompted by the discussion of fish survival: *noldu bedagim simanei treifa mahu* — what is the law if a fish displays signs of a *treifa* injury? This question is novel; the entire earlier section of *Chullin* discussed *treifos* by cattle and sheep, but never by fish. The reason it matters here is that according to Rabbi Akiva, the threshold for the fish becoming food is whether it can survive. If a fish has a *treifa*-type injury, perhaps it cannot survive, and would therefore already be considered food. The *gemara* explores this from both angles: according to those who hold *treifa chaya* — a *treifah* animal can survive — perhaps the fish's lesser vitality (*denafish chayusa*) means the same injury that a cow could survive would be fatal for a fish. And according to those who hold *treifa einah chaya* — a *treifah* cannot survive — perhaps the concept of *treifa* is simply inapplicable to fish since they have no *shechita*, and so the list of *treifah* injuries has no traction there. The *gemara* leaves this as *teiku* — unresolved. The discussion also illuminates something about the nature of the *treifah* list itself: even those who hold *treifa chaya* seem to admit that the listed injuries carry a high likelihood of death, even if not an absolute certainty, which is why the *treifa* injuries remain relevant even on that view.

## Fetus Status: Birth/Gest…

### Miscarriage Case

The *gemara* now turns to a different case: *hetila nefel* — the mother miscarries a fetus. This fetus emerges dead — a stillbirth — and the question is whether its *chelev* is forbidden like the *chelev* of a *beheima* (a domesticated animal), or not. If this fetus has attained the status of an independent animal, then cutting and eating its fat would violate the prohibition of *chelev*. If it has not, the fat is unrestricted (though the flesh itself would still be problematic as a *neveilah* or as *basar min hachai* from the living mother — the *gemara* does not suggest the fetus is entirely ownerless meat, but rather whether it has its own fully realized identity as a *beheima*).

Rabbi Yochanan says *chelbo ke-chelev beheima* — its fat is like the forbidden fat of an animal. His reasoning: *avira garam* — the air causes it. The moment the fetus exits the womb and enters the air, it acquires independent status as its own *beheima*, and its fat is forbidden.

Reish Lakish disagrees: *chelbo ke-chelev chayah* — its fat is like the fat of a *chayah* (a wild animal), which is not forbidden. The fetus is not yet a fully formed *beheima*. Why? *Chadashim garmu* — the months of gestation determine its status, not the act of birth. This fetus was miscarried before completing its gestation, and since the months were not completed, it cannot be called a *beheima* regardless of the fact that it was born.

It is worth pausing on the larger implications: Rabbi Yochanan holds that birth is the decisive moment of independent identity, while Reish Lakish holds that full gestation is what matters, and birth alone is insufficient. Both agree that before gestation is complete, nobody considers the fetus a *beheima* — that is the uniform position. The debate concerns either a miscarried but incompletely gestated fetus (first version of the dispute) or — in a second formulation — a fully gestated fetus.

### In-Womb Fat Case

The *gemara* records a second version of the dispute (*ika d'amri*), in which the two sides agree that an ungestated fetus is clearly *lav klum hu* — nothing whatsoever, not to be considered a *beheima* — and the debate concerns a more extreme thought experiment: *hoshit yado l'mei beheima v'talash chelev shel ben tish'ah chai* — one reaches a hand into the womb of a living mother and tears out the fat from a fully gestated, living fetus still inside the womb, and eats it. Is that fat forbidden as the fat of a *beheima*?

According to Rabbi Yochanan in this version, *chadashim garmu* — the months of gestation are decisive. Since the fetus has completed its full nine months, it is already its own *beheima*, and its fat is forbidden *chelev*, even though it has not yet been born and remains inside the mother. According to Reish Lakish, *chadashim v'avira garmu* — you need both full gestation and birth. A fully gestated fetus that has not yet been born is still not an independent *beheima*, and its fat carries no special prohibition.

The human parallel here is impossible to ignore: at what point does the fetus attain its own identity? Upon birth, as Rabbi Yochanan holds, or upon completed development in the womb, as Reish Lakish holds in this version? And both agree that well before completion of gestation, there is no independent identity to speak of.

### Asham Proof

Rabbi Yochanan now challenges Reish Lakish from a *baraita* in the *Torat Kohanim* (the *Sifra* on *Vayikra*): *mah chelev ushtei kelayot ha'amur ba'asham mutza miklalo shel ubar* — the fat and two kidneys mentioned in connection with the *asham* offering are entirely excluded from any discussion of a fetus. The *asham* is by definition a male animal; it has no fetus. The *baraita* uses this to derive that in all cases — even female animals that could in theory contain a fetus — the fat of a fetus is never brought on the altar and is never forbidden.

Rabbi Yochanan argues that this verse requires explanation only according to his own position. If, as he holds, the fat of a fully gestated fetus in the womb is forbidden *chelev*, then there is indeed something to exclude — the verse must tell us that even though in theory such fat could be forbidden, it is not to be placed on the altar and (in the *korban* context where the mother was *shechted*) is not subject to the *chelev* prohibition. The verse is needed because there is a genuine case where the fat has significance. But according to Reish Lakish, who holds the fat never has significance under any circumstances, why would the verse need to exclude it at all? There is nothing to exclude.

Reish Lakish responds: *hai teima didi nami hacha* — that is precisely where he derives his principle from. He would have thought, like Rabbi Yochanan, that the fat had some significance; the verse teaches him that it does not, and that is his proof that even a fully gestated in-womb fetus has no status as a *beheima*.

The *gemara* then records the reverse version (*v'ika d'amri*), in which Reish Lakish uses the same *baraita* to challenge Rabbi Yochanan: if the fat of the fetus truly has significance in your system, why is it never brought on the altar? Rabbi Yochanan responds with *midi d'hava a'mechusar zman* — it is no different from an animal less than eight days old. Even a valid animal that has genuine sacrificial potential is not offered before its time is ripe. Similarly, the fat of the fetus, while perhaps forbidden in theory if extracted from the womb, is nonetheless not yet in a state fit for the altar. The *gemara* notes that this answer is somewhat strained, since in the actual *korban* scenario both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree the mother's *shechita* renders the fetus's fat fully permitted — so the question of why that fat is not offered on the altar answers itself. But that is the exchange as the *gemara* records it.

## Treifa Mother's Fetus

### Rav Chisda Case

The *gemara* now introduces what Rabbi Ami frames as a problem: *hashochet et hatreifah umatza bah ben tisha chai* — one *shechts* a mother animal that is a *treifa* and finds inside it a live, fully gestated nine-month fetus. What is the status of this fetus?

The difficulty is this. According to Rabbi Meir, the mother's *shechita* never works for a fetus — the *shechita* is irrelevant to the fetus's identity. In that case, the situation here is straightforward: the *shechita* of the *treifa* mother was always irrelevant, and you simply have a live fetus; proceed to *shecht* it independently. But according to the Sages, who hold that the mother's *shechita* does work for the fetus — and that is the dominant view — a problem arises. The *shechita* took place and it did act on the fetus, but the *shechita* was that of a *treifa*, which means the animal is not *kosher*. The fetus may now be defined by that *shechita* — as already *shechted* — but in a way that rendered it non-*kosher*. And one cannot simply *shecht* it again.

Rabbi Ami thus says: *lidivei oser matir, lidivei matir oser* — the position that normally forbids (Rabbi Meir, who says the mother's *shechita* does not work) here permits, since the *shechita* never applied and you can *shecht* the fetus anew. The position that normally permits (the Sages, who say the mother's *shechita* does work) here forbids, since the *shechita* of the *treifa* mother has defined the fetus's status and locked it into non-*kashrut*.

### Rava: Arba Simanim

Rava disagrees: *lidivei dematir nami mutar* — even according to the Sages, the fetus can be eaten. Why? *Arba simanim achshar beih Rachmana* — the Torah provided four *simanim* for it. This pithy formulation — memorable precisely because it is somewhat imprecise — means the following: the *shechita* of the mother is not the only avenue through which a fetus can be permitted. The mother's *shechita* can work for the fetus, but it is not compulsory that it do so. There is an alternative: *shecht* the fetus independently, with its own *shechita* (two *simanim*), in addition to or instead of relying on the mother's *shechita*. The fetus is not so completely fused with the mother that only the mother's *shechita* can ever define it. It retains its own independent potential for *shechita*.

This principle connects back to the broader debate about whether the fetus is a unitary part of the mother or a connected-but-distinct entity. Rava's position is that the fetus is connected but not fully absorbed — it can be defined by the mother's *shechita* when that *shechita* is valid, but when it is not, the fetus can stand on its own. In the *treifa* mother case: the mother's *shechita* is not efficacious for purposes of *kashrut*, so the fetus is simply treated on its own terms, and one *shechts* it independently.

Rav Chisda then elaborates: *hashochet et hatreifah umatza bah ben tisha chai, te'un shechita* — the fetus requires and can receive its own *shechita*, and accordingly, once that *shechita* is performed, one incurs the obligation of giving the priestly gifts (*zero'a, lechayayim, u'keiva*). Since the mother's *shechita* did not define the fetus's *shechita*, when one now performs a genuine *shechita* on the fetus, it is a full act of *shechita* with all attendant obligations. One could add that *chelev* and *gid hanasheh* would presumably be forbidden in this case as well, since the mother's *shechita* did not impart its special limb-of-the-mother status. Furthermore: *v'im meis tamei v'metamei b'masa* — if the fetus subsequently dies, it is not a *neveilah* but rather has the status of a *treifa*, since the mother's *shechita*, while not defining its *kashrut*, did exist and can be relevant when the animal ultimately dies: the *shechita* of a *treifa* mother means the fetus's death is not the death of an un-*shechted* animal.

### Baraita Contradiction

Rava (or, as the *gemara* suggests, Rabba — since Rava already spoke) challenges Rav Chisda: *te'un shechita, keman ke-Rabbi Meir?* — saying it requires *shechita* sounds like Rabbi Meir, who denies that the mother's *shechita* ever works. Yet *v'im meis tamei v'metamei b'masa*, which says the fetus's death is not a *neveilah* (because the mother's *shechita* already defined it to some extent), sounds like the Sages. How can you hold both simultaneously?

Rav Chisda's reply: the identical formulation appears verbatim in a *baraita* of Rabbi Chiya — *hashochet et hatreifa*, *u'matza bah ben tesha chai, te'un shechita, v'chayav b'zroa v'lechayayim u'v'keiva, v'im meis tamei v'metamei b'masa* — word for word what he said. So why challenge him? Ask the same question on Rabbi Chiya's *baraita*.

Tosafot notes wryly: if the *baraita* says this, why did Rav Chisda state it as his own ruling rather than simply quoting the *baraita*? That is a broader phenomenon in the *Bavli* — *amoraic* statements are sometimes followed by a *baraita* that says the identical thing (*tanya nami hachi*) — and scholars have puzzled over what precisely is happening in such cases.

The questioner responds: the *baraita* itself is not difficult, because *Rabbi Chiya im kevar matzo meis ka'amar* — Rabbi Chiya was speaking of a case where the fetus was already dead when found inside the *shechted treifa* mother. In that case, both halves of the ruling make sense without contradiction: there is no *shechita* question for a dead fetus, and the dead fetus takes on *treifa* status (not *neveilah*) from the mother's *shechita*. There is no tension. The problem is specifically with Rav Chisda's formulation, in which the fetus was found alive, grew up, and then died — and yet Rav Chisda says it is a *treifa* and not a *neveilah*. That suggests the mother's *shechita* remained relevant even for a fetus that walked around independently. But if the mother's *shechita* was relevant, how could one perform a new *shechita* on it in the first place?

### Zeira-Assi Exchange

Rava resolves the apparent tension, restating the principle: *arba simanim achshar bei Rachmana* — the Torah gave four *simanim*. The mother's *shechita* is not the exclusive means of defining the fetus's status; one can perform an independent *shechita* on the fetus. When the fetus is then alive and walking, you *shecht* it and it is fully *kosher*. When it dies without having been *shechted*, the mother's *shechita* — which always existed in the background — kicks in: it is not a *neveilah* but a *treifa*. The two halves of the ruling are fully consistent because the two eventualities draw on different operative principles.

This resolution is confirmed by a report from Rabbi Zeira. When Rabbi Zeira went up to Eretz Yisrael, he found Rabbi Assi *yasiv v'ka'amar lah le'hai shamaita* — sitting and teaching over precisely this principle: that when the mother is a *treifa*, the fetus is not locked into the status of a *treifa*; one can *shecht* the fetus and eat it. Rabbi Zeira said to him: *yasher koach* — well done, that is a sound ruling — *v'chen amar Rabbi Yochanan*, and Rabbi Yochanan holds the same way.

The *gemara* then asks: since you cited Rabbi Yochanan, did Reish Lakish disagree? Rabbi Assi explains: *mesha hava shehi lei v'shatik lei* — Reish Lakish was delayed in responding and fell silent, and Rabbi Assi left before hearing what Reish Lakish would say. An alternate version: *mishtei hava sheti lei v'shatik lei* — Reish Lakish was in the middle of drinking when the statement was made and could not immediately respond. Rashi adds that Reish Lakish had a practice of waiting before voicing any disagreement with Rabbi Yochanan — to make sure he had thought through his position fully, and to see whether Rabbi Yochanan would reconsider on his own. In any case, Rabbi Assi reports only Rabbi Yochanan's position; whether Reish Lakish agreed or disagreed remains unknown.

## Ben Pekua Maris Ayin

### Shimon Shezuri Debate

The *mishnah*'s second striking statement — that even if the *ben pakua* grew up and was plowing the fields for five years, the mother's *shechita* is still effective and no new *shechita* is required — is now subjected to scrutiny. The *gemara* asks: is that not identical to the position of the first *tanna*, who already established that the mother's *shechita* works?

Rav Kahana answers: *hiphis agavi karka ika beineihum* — the difference is whether the animal's hooves (*parsah*) have touched the ground, i.e., whether the animal has actually stood up and walked around. The first *tanna* says no new *shechita* is required in principle; Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says even when the animal has been walking around for years, still no *shechita* is needed. The implication is that the first *tanna* does require *shechita* — at least rabbinically — once the animal has walked around, because of *maris ayin*: it no longer looks like a piece of meat, it looks like a full-grown animal, and slaughtering it without *shechita* creates a problematic appearance of impropriety. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri dismisses this concern entirely.

It is thus a dispute about *maris ayin*. Does the *ben pakua* that has grown up and been walking around require *shechita* to avoid giving the wrong impression to onlookers who will not know its unusual history? The Sages say yes; Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says no.

### Hybrid Ben Pekua

The *gemara* introduces a further complication: *Rav Mesharshaya* reports that according to the view that we are concerned about paternal lineage (*chosheshin lezera ha'av*) — meaning that the identity of an animal's father carries *halachic* implications — a *ben pakua* that has mated with a non-*ben-pakua* female produces offspring whose status is irresolvable. The offspring is half *ben pakua* (from its *ben pakua* father, whose *shechita* is already defined and irrelevant) and half normal animal (from its non-*ben-pakua* mother, whose *shechita* is still required). You cannot forgo *shechita* on account of the *ben pakua* father, since the mother's side demands it. But performing a *shechita* on account of the mother's side is meaningless on the father's side, since the father was already *shechted* and the *shechita* for this offspring is considered to have already been performed from that lineage. The result: *ein lo takana* — there is no remedy for this animal.

### Abaye Exception

Abaye qualifies the debate about *maris ayin*: *hakol modim bekalut ben pakua* — everyone agrees that a *ben pakua* born with unsplit hooves (*kalut*) can be eaten without *shechita* even when fully grown. The rationale: *kol milta detmiha midkeri inshi* — anything that is astounding, people remember. An animal with conspicuously fused, unsplit hooves is so unusual that all who see it will recall its peculiar status and will not mistake it for an ordinary animal requiring *shechita*. The concern about *maris ayin* evaporates when the animal's bizarre appearance ensures it will be remembered.

A second version of Abaye's ruling (*ika d'amri*) is more restrictive: only a *kalut ben keluta ben pakua* — a *ben pakua* that had unsplit hooves, and that itself gave birth to another *ben pakua* that also had unsplit hooves — generates sufficient memory. Two astounding things compounding across generations (*tartei tmihei midkeri inshi*) are what people remember; a single astounding feature may not be enough. Rashi clarifies that this second version describes a *ben pakua* with unsplit hooves whose own offspring — itself a *ben pakua* by virtue of its mother being *shechted* — was also born with unsplit hooves. That doubled rarity is what triggers the universal exemption.

### Final Ruling

Rabbi Zeira cites Rav Chanina for the *halacha*: *halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon Shezuri* — we rule like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, and moreover, the general principle is that wherever Rabbi Shimon Shezuri appears in our *mishnah*, the *halacha* follows him.

The case of Adda bar Chavu tests this. He had a *ben pakua*; a wolf attacked it and rendered it a *treifa*. He came before Rav Ashi. Rav Ashi told him: go and *shecht* it. His instruction was twofold in its implication: (a) *shechita* is required — ruling like the *Rabbanan* against Rabbi Shimon Shezuri for *maris ayin* purposes — but (b) the *treifa* injury from the wolf does not prohibit eating it, since the *ben pakua*'s exemption from the *treifa* category is a genuine *halachic* benefit of its status, not merely a procedural nicety. Adda bar Chavu objected: don't we rule like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri? No *shechita* should be needed at all.

Rav Ashi replied: the ruling *halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon Shezuri* applies only in the two specific cases where Rabbi Yonatan explicitly invokes it — *b'mesukan u'vitrumat ma'aser shel demai* — and not in our case. We rule like the *Chachamim*: *shechita* is required for appearances.

The final *halacha*, as codified by both the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, follows this ruling of the *Chachamim*. Once the *ben pakua* has stood up and walked around, *shechita* is required — but only for *maris ayin*, not because the animal is genuinely subject to the full range of *shechita* concerns. Accordingly, the *ben pakua* retains its distinctive *halachic* benefits: one need not worry about *treifa*, *chelev*, or *gid hanasheh*. The *ben pakua* farm is thus not the revolutionary enterprise that the Torah's plain permission might suggest — no onlooker will accept seeing an animal slaughtered without any *shechita* at all — but it retains real *halachic* advantages: the burdens of checking for *treifos*, avoiding *chelev*, and removing the *gid hanasheh* are entirely eliminated.

---

---

# Hullin 77

## Nishbar Ha-etzem

### Bone Break Covered

Daf 77a picks up several lines into the page, at the word *yachid*, near the end of the line, with the topic of *nishbar ha-etzem* — the broken bone. This case was introduced in the *mishnah*: if the leg bone of an animal broke and the limb was left dangling, the halachic status of that limb depends on the nature of the break. Under ordinary circumstances, a break high enough up the leg renders the animal a *treifah*, or at least prohibits the consumption of that dangling limb even after *shechitah* of the animal. However, the *mishnah* establishes an exception: if the break is covered by the surrounding flesh, the break is not halachically significant. The Gemara now continues probing exactly how to define adequate coverage.

### Bone Chipped Off

The Gemara introduces a specific incident: *hahu nishbar ha-etzem ve-yatza lachutz* — there was a case where a bone broke and protruded outward — and *ve-ishtakeil korta minei* — a small fragment of the bone had actually chipped off. This case differs from what the *mishnah* addressed directly, which spoke of a break, not of a bone fragment falling away. Nevertheless, the flesh apparently still covered the area. The question was whether that additional factor — the chipped fragment — undermined the protection of the flesh covering.

### Abaye & Rava

This case came *ata lekamei de-Abaye* — before Abaye — who *shehayah telasa riglei*, held it over for three *regalim*, apparently hoping that the gatherings of scholars at festival times would yield an answer. There is something arresting about this: what happened to the meat in the interim? Presumably it was salted and preserved. And there is also something to note about the fact that in Babylonia, the *regalim* had ceased to be pilgrimage occasions, yet the gatherings they occasioned still served as opportunities for broader rabbinic consultation.

Eventually, *Rav Adda bar Matna* said — and Rashi notes that he was speaking to the owner of the animal, not to Abaye — *zel lekamei de-Rava breih de-Rav Yosef bar Chama*, go before Rava son of Rav Yosef bar Chama, *de-charifa sakinah*, whose knife is sharp — a metaphor for Rava's penetrating analytical ability — since Abaye had not been able to resolve the matter. One might ask whether it is proper to seek a second ruling when a first posek has not yet decided; since Abaye rendered no *psak*, however, there was no ruling to be bound by, and the questioner was free to seek another opinion.

### Mishnah Analysis

The owner went before Rava, who said: *michdi, nishbar ha-etzem ve-yatza lachutz tenan* — our *mishnah*, or at least the *baraita*, says simply that the bone broke and protruded, and the question is whether the break is covered by flesh. *Mah li nafal mah li issa* — what difference does it make whether a fragment of bone broke off or not? The *mishnah* draws no such distinction. The implication is clear: as long as the flesh covers the area of the break, the outcome is the same regardless of whether a splinter of bone has fallen away. This is, admittedly, a somewhat less pyrotechnic resolution than one might expect given Rava's reputation for sharp analysis — the argument amounts simply to pointing out that the *mishnah* does not distinguish. Yet Rava found it sufficient, and the ruling stands: even when a piece of the bone has chipped off, if the flesh surrounds the break, that coverage is effective.

---

## Flesh Coverage Variants

### Ravina's Questions

The Gemara then turns to a series of questions posed by Ravina to Rava. These questions are no longer about whether a bone fragment has broken off, but about the nature and condition of the flesh itself that is supposedly covering the break.

*Mislaket mahu* — what if the flesh covering the break is discontinuous, meaning it surrounds the break in scattered patches with gaps in between, rather than in one contiguous area? The *mishnah* does not say the coverage must be uninterrupted, but one might think that only contiguous flesh provides meaningful protection.

*Mishrosos mahu* — what if the flesh is thinned? It may surround the break, but it has worn down to only a very thin layer rather than full-thickness flesh.

*Mismasas mahu* — what if the flesh is rotting away, though still in place? The Gemara clarifies this case: *heichi dami mismasas*? What does this mean precisely? *Kol she'arofe kodro* — flesh that a doctor would excise, that is, flesh so far gone that a physician would remove it as necrotic tissue. Does such flesh still count as coverage?

*Nikev mahu* — what if there are holes in the flesh? Even granting that the majority of the flesh is present and surrounding the break, the flesh is perforated. Rashi notes that this may refer even to a hole that has not removed any flesh, simply a perforation.

*Niklaf mahu* — what if the flesh has been peeled away from the bone, so that it sits above the break without adhering to the bone itself? This case is intuitively more significant: flesh resting loosely atop the break, with no actual adhesion to the bone, seems to offer far less structural support.

*Nisdak mahu* — what if the flesh is cracked? This is similar to the question of holes: the flesh is present but fissured, and one might worry that such cracks will propagate and eventually cause the flesh to detach entirely.

*Nitosh tlisha tachton mahu* — what if the bottom third of the flesh has been removed? This is more severe than the *niklaf* case: not only is the flesh unattached to the bone, but a portion of its thickness has been excised, leaving the flesh sitting atop the break with neither full thickness nor adhesion.

To none of these questions does the Gemara provide a direct answer.

### Skin Adheres to Bone

The Gemara then introduces a possible resolution by analogy, citing a ruling of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan from a prior discussion: *or harei hu kevasar* — skin counts as flesh. That is, if skin covers the break even where there is no overlying flesh, that skin coverage is sufficient. This was established yesterday, and now the Gemara asks whether this ruling sheds light on our questions.

If skin alone — which is thinner and lighter than flesh, and which, at certain points on an animal's body, lies directly against the bone — constitutes adequate coverage, might that not tell us something about cases where flesh is present but compromised, whether thinned, cracked, or peeled away?

The Gemara rejects the analogy. There is a fundamental difference: *dilma dekana mashka didei* — perhaps the reason skin counts is that in the places where skin bears directly on the bone, it is naturally adhering to the bone, it has effectively grown onto it. This is true of the skin over a knee, a shin, an ankle, or a nose — anywhere that one can feel the bone directly through the skin, because there is no intervening fat or muscle. In such places, the skin is *mamash* upon the bone, directly and naturally. But our questions concern cases where flesh is present and presumably was once fully in place, but has been disturbed: peeled back, thinned, cracked, or allowed to rot. That is a different situation from naturally adherent skin. The *or kevasar* principle, therefore, does not resolve the questions about compromised flesh.

### Ring-Shaped Hole

Rav Ashi reports that when he was in the academy of Rav Papi, a further question arose: *nikdar k'min tabaat mahu* — what is the status of a ring-shaped hole in the flesh, a hole of significant size? Rashi notes that even in this scenario we are still assuming the majority of the break is covered; the question is whether a large ring-shaped perforation, while leaving much of the flesh intact, nonetheless so fundamentally disrupts the coverage that it can no longer be said to protect the break.

The answer came from a statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, who said: *davar zeh sha'alti lachachamim u'larofim* — I asked both sages and physicians about this. The question was whether flesh with such a hole can heal. Their answer: *mesarto b'etzem u'ma'ala arucha* — if you scratch the area with a bone and cause it to bleed, the resulting scabbing and regeneration can actually heal the wound and fill the hole over time. This is a mechanism of healing. By contrast, using a metal knife to attempt the same thing — *aval parzla, mizraz zarif* — would actually cause incisions and be counterproductive. The implication of this ruling is that since even a large ring-shaped hole can, under appropriate treatment, heal and regenerate, the flesh in such a case is still considered to constitute coverage of the break.

### Flesh Adhesion

Rav Papa adds a crucial qualification: *v'hu dekana garma didei* — this applies only as long as the flesh is still adhering to the bone. If the flesh has separated from the bone and is merely sitting atop it without cleaving to it, it would not carry the same protective effect. Rashi adds that one should also look for signs that the flesh is in the process of scabbing and healing around the area of the hole.

---

## Dangling Limb

### Limb Status

At this point the Gemara steps back to orient us within the broader structure of the *perek*. The entire discussion of *nishbar ha-etzem* — the broken bone and the coverage of flesh — arose because the *mishnah* in this *perek* is concerned with the status of dangling limbs. The *perek* as a whole addresses the halachic status of a fetus inside an animal when the mother is *shechted*, and what happens to limbs growing out of the fetus or hanging from it. The *mishnah* introduces the parallel case of a dangling limb of the mother animal itself: if an animal's leg bone has broken and the limb is hanging, and you then *shecht* the animal, the dangling limb cannot be eaten. However, if the break is covered with flesh, that counteracts the problem.

It is this last clause — the flesh covering — that has occupied the Gemara's attention, leading to all the cases just discussed: what counts as covering, how much, under what conditions, and what happens when the flesh is discontinuous, thinned, rotted, perforated, or peeled.

The *mishnah* also raised what appears to be a new category of *treifah*: if the hind leg breaks high enough up, the animal is rendered a *treifah*. This is striking because it does not appear explicitly in the chapter of *eilu treifos*. Notably, the *mishnah* itself does not use the word *treifah* but rather *pesulah* — disqualified — and yet the Gemara treats it as a *treifah*, a category of invalidation with broad consequences. The entire treatment of flesh coverage is bound up in trying to determine when such a break is halachically neutralized by the presence of covering flesh — and Rashi's commentary here, one should acknowledge, is especially extensive and essential. Without Rashi — and in places even with Rashi — the graphic anatomical detail of this passage calls for visual aids that the ancient commentators, needless to say, did not supply.

---

## Shilya Emerging

### Placenta Alone

The final *mishnah* of the *perek* opens: *hashochet et habeheimah umatzah bah shilya* — one who slaughters an animal and finds inside it a *shilya*. The word *shilya* is commonly translated as placenta, though there is a significant question — to which we shall return — as to whether it might more precisely refer to the amniotic sac. Either way, the scenario is that you find this *shilya* without any visible fetus. The animal has apparently miscarried or dissolved the fetus prior to *shechitah*, and all that remains is this remnant. What is its status?

### Placenta Impurity

The *mishnah* rules: *nefesh hayafa tochalennah* — the finicky may decline, but the non-squeamish person may eat it, since the *shechitah* of the mother renders everything inside her permissible. Then the *mishnah* adds: *ve'eino mitamei lo tumat ochlin velo tumat neveilot* — it does not cause *tumah* of foodstuff, and it does not cause *tumah* of a *neveilah*.

The logic of these two rules: it does not cause *tumat ochlin* because it is not normally eaten, and an item must be normally consumed food to become susceptible to or transmit *tumah* as food. It does not cause *tumat neveilah* because the *neveilah tumah* attaches to the actual flesh of a carcass, not to organs that are not meat — just as bones, teeth, and horns of a dead animal do not carry *tumat neveilah*, neither does the *shilya*, which is not meat.

If, however, *chishav alav* — one planned to eat it — *metamei tumat ochlin aval lo tumat neveilah*: by intending to eat it, one has reclassified it as food and it can now receive and transmit *tumat ochlin*. But it can never become a *neveilah*, because that status is reserved for actual meat, which this is not.

### Placenta Emerges

*Shilya sheyatza miktzatah asurah be'achilah* — if part of the *shilya* has emerged from the womb, it is forbidden to eat. The reason is that the *shilya* is *siman vlad ba'ishah ve-siman vlad ba-behemah* — its emergence is a sign of birth for a woman and for an animal alike. Since there is no *shilya* without a fetus having existed, the emergence of the *shilya* raises the concern that the dissolved fetus is coming out with it.

This is a genuinely striking ruling. One might have assumed that a dissolved fetus is simply biological matter — like a discharge — with no ongoing halachic status. Yet the *mishnah* treats the dissolved fetus as though it were a stillbirth. If an actual stillborn calf had emerged head-first, it would be considered born, and since it is dead and *shechitah* is impossible, it could not be eaten. The same logic applies here: if the dissolved fetus is treated as having been born, and born in a state that precludes *shechitah*, then the flesh is forbidden.

One can raise the conceptual difficulty: if the fetus was viable and the head emerged, we say it has been born. That is coherent when dealing with an actual formed animal. But why should dissolved material carry that same status? The Gemara's answer is that the logic of *siman vlad* — the sign of birth — extends even to this dissolved state, and the *mishnah*'s ruling follows accordingly.

Moreover, once the head of the fetus has emerged, even the portion remaining inside the womb cannot be eaten — the whole fetus is treated as born. The *mishnah* here applies the same principle to the *shilya*: when any part of it emerges, the entire *shilya* is forbidden, not merely the emerged portion.

There is an extended discussion of the precise meaning of *shilya* versus *shapir*. Artscroll translates *shilya* as the amniotic sac rather than the placenta — the reverse of the common assumption, which holds *shapir* to be the amniotic sac and *shilya* the placenta. It is worth noting that the *sugya* coheres considerably more naturally if *shilya* denotes the amniotic sac: the concern that the dissolved fetus is "coming out with it" is much more intuitive if the sac is what is emerging, since the fetus would have been contained within it. The Steinsaltz commentary at this point describes the *shilya* as a large, blood-vessel-filled mass attached to the uterine wall within which the fetus is washed — language that supports the amniotic sac reading. This is a matter that warrants further investigation in other contexts.

### Sacred Placenta

*U'vimukdashim titkaver* — if this *shilya* was expelled from a sanctified animal, it must be buried. The reasoning is that whatever was inside — dissolved or not — would have borne the sanctity of a *korban*, since offspring of sanctified animals, male or female, carry that sanctity. Since we treat the emergence of the *shilya* as a birth, the dissolved contents retain their sacred status, and the *shilya* must therefore be buried rather than discarded. This is not because it is a discharge, but because we treat it as a birth — the same logic that makes it forbidden to eat when it emerges, and that makes it subject to *kedushah* when it comes from a sanctified animal.

### Firstborn Miscarriage

*Ha-mevakeret she-hipila shilya yashlichenah la-klavim* — if an animal that has never yet given birth miscarries and produces only a *shilya*, you may simply give it to the dogs. This is because the dissolved contents might or might not have been a firstborn male with the sanctity of a *bechor*. The Gemara will explain this further: since only a male firstborn carries *kedushat bechor*, and since there is a small subset of male firstborns that nonetheless do not carry that *kedushah* — the *nidmeh* case, to be discussed — the probability that this dissolved *shilya* contains a valid *bechor* is technically less than fifty percent. By *rov*, therefore, one need not treat it as a *bechor*.

---

## Siman Vlad

### Textual Source

*Mena hani milei* — where is the scriptural source for the permissibility of eating the *shilya*? A *baraita* derives it from the verse *kol behema tochlu* — you may eat any animal — which is read to include the *shilya* found inside a slaughtered animal. The *baraita* then raises the possibility that even if part of it has emerged it should still be permitted — *yachol afilu yatza miktzatah* — and the verse responds *otah velo shilyatah*: "it" — the animal itself — but not its *shilya* once the *shilya* has partially emerged.

### No Placenta Alone

The Gemara then questions why we need a verse at all for the prohibition once it has partially emerged: *ein shilya belo vlad* — there is no *shilya* without a fetus. If a *shilya* is present, a fetus certainly existed at some point, and if the *shilya* is emerging, the dissolved fetus is presumably coming with it. The answer is: *kra asmachta be'alma* — the verse is only an *asmachta*, a scriptural support; the reasoning is logically derivable even without it.
