Here, Rabbi Meir permits slaughtering the offspring on the same day — a position that initially seems startling, because perhaps the first *shechita* was valid, in which case slaughtering the child is a violation of *oto ve'et beno*. The *chachamim*, however, prohibit slaughtering the offspring that day.

### Active vs. Passive

The distinction between the two cases of the *mishna* rests on the difference between action and inaction. When one covers the blood, one is performing an act that sends a clear message — here is a valid *shechita*. When one simply refrains from slaughtering the offspring that day, no such message is sent. A bystander who sees that no *shechita* is occurring today has no particular reason to conclude that the earlier *shechita* was valid; one might simply not be hungry, or prefer a different food. The absence of *shechita* is invisible and sends no signal. Thus the *chachamim* can prohibit covering the blood — because the act carries a message — without being inconsistent in declining to prohibit refraining from *shechita*.

### Prohibition Overrides

A second and perhaps more fundamental distinction applies. Covering the blood is a positive *mitzvah*. The rabbis are empowered to instruct a person not to perform a positive *mitzvah* when circumstances warrant — and saying one is *patur* from the *mitzvah* is, in effect, such an instruction. But in the case of *oto ve'et beno*, the concern is the possible violation of a prohibition. Even if one were worried about sending the wrong message by refraining from *shechita*, the rabbis cannot grant license to possibly transgress a *lav*. When there is a genuine concern about violating a prohibition, one must be strict and refrain, regardless of any messaging considerations. Hence the *chachamim* say: do not slaughter the offspring today.

The *mishna* concludes with a point on which all agree: *she'eino sofeg et ha'arba'im* — if one did slaughter the offspring on the same day after the unobserved *shechita* of the *cheresh shoteh vekatan*, one does not receive the forty lashes. Since there is doubt whether the first *shechita* was valid, there is no certainty of a prohibition having been violated, and one is not lashed for a *safek*.

---

## Reisha and Seifa

### Apparent Contradiction

The *gemara* asks: *rabanan mai shena reisha delo paligi u'mai shena seifa depaligi* — why do the rabbis take a position in the opening clause of the *mishna*, ruling that the blood need not be covered, but then also take a position in the closing clause, ruling that the offspring may not be slaughtered? The two rulings seem to operate on different principles. In the first case, the rabbis act as if the *shechita* was definitively invalid, refusing to cover the blood. In the second case, they act as if it might be valid, forbidding the slaughter of the offspring. The *gemara* explores whether these positions are internally consistent.

The *gemara* presses the point. In the first case — covering the blood — one might say: cover the blood without a *beracha*, since it is a *safek*. But the rabbis say do not cover, apparently because doing so would send the message that the *shechita* was good and people would eat the meat. But if that logic applies in the first case, why does it not apply in the second? If the rabbis say do not slaughter the offspring, does that not equally send the message that the first *shechita* was valid and thereby lead people to eat from that meat?

The *gemara* attempts to deflect: perhaps by not slaughtering, no message is sent — *amrei bisra delo ka mibaya lei*, he simply does not want meat today. But then the *gemara* presses from the other side: in the first case too, perhaps covering the blood sends no unambiguous message — one might be cleaning up the yard. The *gemara* counters: if someone comes to the rabbi and asks whether to cover the blood, and the rabbi says yes, that ruling clearly sends the message that it was a valid *shechita*. Symmetrically, if someone asks whether to slaughter the offspring today and the rabbi says no, that ruling also sends the message of a valid first *shechita*. The cases seem perfectly parallel, and the *gemara* cannot find a principled distinction between them using the messaging rationale alone.

### Rabbis Ignore Messages

The resolution the *gemara* reaches is elegant: *ela rabbanan a'kulhu pligi* — the rabbis in fact argue against Rabbi Meir's entire framework, and they do not concern themselves with the messaging question at all. The rabbis treat the *shechita* of a *cheresh shoteh vekatan* as a genuine *safek* — a doubt — in both directions. Because it is a *safek*, they act consistently and strictly in both directions: cover the blood, because it might have been a valid *shechita*; do not slaughter the offspring, for the same reason. They do not exempt from covering the blood in order to send a message of invalidity, and they do not worry that not slaughtering the offspring sends a message of validity. Messages are simply not part of their calculus.

The *mishna* as we read it presented what appeared to be Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* arguing only in the second clause, with agreement in the first. The *gemara* now explains that in fact, the *mishna* let Rabbi Meir complete his entire position before recording the rabbis' dissent: *d'shavkuhu l'Rabbi Meir ad d'masik lei l'miltei, v'hadar pligi alei* — they allowed Rabbi Meir to finish his full presentation and only then recorded their dispute. The apparent agreement in the first clause does not represent the rabbis' actual view; it represents Rabbi Meir's position being stated, and the dispute with the rabbis extends to everything.

### Rabbi Meir's Rov

What, then, is Rabbi Meir's position? Rabbi Yaakov said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Meir would hold that one who eats from the meat of an unobserved *shechita* of a *cheresh shoteh vekatan* is liable as if having eaten *neveilah* — the *shechita* is considered definitively invalid, not merely doubtful. The basis is *rov*: the majority of cases in which a *cheresh shoteh vekatan* performs an unobserved *shechita* are cases where they do it incorrectly. Following the majority, Rabbi Meir rules the *shechita* invalid. On the basis of that definitive ruling, he permits not covering the blood and permits slaughtering the offspring on the same day.

---

## Minority & Chazaka

### Meir's Minority Concern

A sharp challenge immediately arises. Rabbi Meir is famously the authority who is *choshesh l'miyuta* — who gives weight to minority cases and rules strictly even when a minority of situations present a concern. If so, even if the majority of *cheresh shoteh vekatan* perform *shechita* incorrectly, there is still a significant minority who do it correctly. Rabbi Meir's characteristic stringency should lead him to attend to that minority and forbid eating the meat on account of the minority possibility that it was valid — not to discard the minority and declare the meat definitively prohibited as *neveilah*. The argument seems to run in exactly the wrong direction.

### Rov Cannot Change

The *gemara* resolves this with a subtle but important principle: *semoch miyuta l'chazaka ve'itrei lei rova* — attach the minority to the *chazaka*, the presumptive status quo, and the majority is undermined. Here is the logic. Before it was slaughtered, the animal had a *chazaka* — a presumptive status — of not being a valid *shechita*, of being a living non-*shechted* animal. Changing that status requires an effective act of *shechita*. Now, even if the majority of cases in which a *cheresh shoteh vekatan* slaughters unobserved result in a valid *shechita*, Rabbi Meir gives weight to the minority. That minority possibility, that the *shechita* was invalid, combines with the pre-existing status quo of the animal: it had not been validly slaughtered, and the minority possibility that it remains so is enough — combined with the *chazaka* — to prevent the majority from changing its status. *Rov* alone cannot overcome *chazaka* when the minority possibility has independent weight.

This is the productive irony of Rabbi Meir's position. His characteristic stringency in attending to minority possibilities is precisely what generates this result. By taking the minority seriously, he ensures that a *rov* cannot simply override a status quo. Normally one might think: most cases are valid, therefore assume validity. But Rabbi Meir says: the minority cannot be ignored, and a *rov* that faces a *chazaka* reinforced by the minority is not strong enough to change that status.

### Infant & Dough

The *gemara* finds a proof for this principle in a *mishna* regarding *tumah*: *tinok shenimtza b'tzad ha-issa u'vatzek b'yado* — an infant found next to a batch of dough with a piece of dough in its hand. The *chachamim* rule the dough *tamei*, because the majority of infants pat and touch everything around them, and since the infant is *tamei* (Rashi: because the infant touched an insect; Tosafot: because the infant's mother, who typically handles the infant, is most often a *niddah*, rendering the infant *tamei*), the majority dictates that the infant touched and contaminated the rest of the dough. Rabbi Meir, however, rules the dough *tahor*. His reasoning: true, the majority of infants touch everything around them, but there is a minority who do not. And the dough began in a status of *taharah*. Attaching the minority possibility to the *chazaka* of *taharah*, one cannot allow the majority to change the status quo. The dough remains *tahor*.

### Ruling vs. Action

The *gemara* presses: if Rabbi Meir says the *chazaka* combined with the minority suffices to render the dough *tahor* by the infant case, why in our case does the *gemara* say Rabbi Meir needs the *majority* to have done the *shechita* badly? Even if only a minority of *cheresh shoteh vekatan* did it badly, combined with the *chazaka* that the animal was not validly slaughtered, that should be enough for Rabbi Meir to rule the *shechita* definitively invalid.

The *gemara* answers: *im amru safek tumah letaher, yomru safek issur lehatir?* Just because a *safek* in *tumah* can result in a lenient ruling does not mean that the same logic licenses a lenient ruling when it comes to potential prohibitions. There is a categorical difference. By the dough, the ruling is simply about the status of the dough itself: it retains its existing status of *taharah*. By the *cheresh shoteh vekatan* and the offspring, the question is not merely maintaining the status of the slaughtered animal, but actively licensing a new act — going ahead and slaughtering the offspring today. Allowing some new behavior based on this logic is a larger step than simply affirming a status quo, and the *gemara* treats it as categorically different.

### Tosafot on Tahara

Tosafot adds a further distinction. The laws of *tumah ve'taharah* operate according to their own internal logic, including certain leniencies that apply specifically to that domain — particularly the well-known rule that a *safek tumah birshut harabbim* is *tahor*. It is possible that for Rabbi Meir, the *chazaka* plus minority amounts to a kind of fifty-fifty, which in the domain of *tumah ve'taharah* is enough to be lenient. But in other areas of law, where such specific leniencies for *safek* do not apply, a fifty-fifty doubt does not automatically generate a lenient outcome. Tosafot thus suggests that it is the peculiar rules of *tumah ve'taharah* that allow Rabbi Meir's logic to produce a lenient ruling for the dough, while the same logic does not transfer to permit slaughtering the offspring.

The upshot: certainly if Rabbi Meir holds that the majority of unobserved *shechitot* by a *cheresh shoteh vekatan* are invalid, he can confidently rule the *shechita* definitively not good and draw all the resulting consequences — no obligation to cover the blood, permission to slaughter the offspring on the same day, and liability for *neveilah* if one eats the meat.

---

## Rabbi's Final Ruling

### Conflicting Rulings

The *gemara* now reports that Rabbi issued rulings in both directions. On one occasion he ruled like Rabbi Meir — treating the unobserved *shechita* as definitively invalid. On another occasion he ruled like the *chachamim* — treating it as a genuine *safek* requiring strict treatment in both directions. This is not without precedent; great authorities sometimes issue different rulings to different questioners or at different stages of their lives.

### Which is Achreita?

The question raised in the *beis medrash* is: *hei mineihu debatrayta* — which ruling was Rabbi's last, and therefore his authoritative, final position? This is a standard question in *halachic* methodology: when a *posek* issues conflicting rulings, the later one is presumed to supersede.

### Missed Opportunity

The *gemara* recounts: Rav Abba the son of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and Rabbi Zeira were standing in the marketplace of Caesarea, outside the entrance to the *beis medrash*. Rabbi Ami came out and reproached them for not being inside during *beis medrash* hours — someone might need help with a difficult topic and would be left without guidance. Rabbi Zeira listened and went in. Rabbi Abba did not. Later, those inside the *beis medrash* were grappling with precisely this question of Rabbi's final ruling. Rabbi Zeira said: *lo shvakitun li de'isha'il lesaba* — had I known this was the question, I would have asked the elder, referring to Rabbi Abba who had remained outside. Why would Rabbi Abba know? Because he might have heard from his father, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, who was the student of Rabbi Yochanan and reviewed his learning before Rabbi Yochanan every thirty days — a relationship of constant, meticulous review. Through that chain, the tradition might have been preserved.

### Elazar's Message

The answer eventually came from another source. Rabbi Elazar sent word to the exile: *hora Rabbi k'Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Meir. Since we also have a tradition that Rabbi ruled like the *chachamim*, the *gemara* concludes: *shma mina hada achreita* — since this was the ruling sent abroad by Rabbi Elazar (which typically reflects the authoritative, final position), this ruling like Rabbi Meir was Rabbi's last and definitive ruling. The result is somewhat surprising: although common intuition might have assumed the *shechita* of a *cheresh shoteh vekatan* is a *safek*, the authoritative ruling is that it is considered definitively invalid when unobserved. Consequently, one does not cover the blood, and one may even slaughter the offspring on the same day.

---

## Multiple Animals & Blood

### Single Covering

The *gemara* closes the daf with a brief but important *mishna* on the mechanics of *kisuy hadam*. If one slaughtered a hundred *chayot* in the same place, *kisuy echad lekulan* — a single covering suffices for all of them. One need not cover each animal's blood separately. The blood collects together and is covered collectively.

### Mixed Animals

Similarly, if one slaughtered a hundred birds in the same place, a single covering suffices. The *mishna* further extends this: if one slaughtered a *chaya* and a bird — for example, a deer and a chicken — in the same place, *kisuy echad lekulan*, one covering may serve for both.

### Rabbi Yehuda's View

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with this final ruling. He holds: *shachat chaya yachasena ve'achar kach yishchot es ha'of* — one should first cover the blood of the *chaya* and only then proceed to slaughter the bird. His reasoning is that the Torah, in addressing *kisuy hadam*, mentions *chaya* and *of* separately — *shachat chaya o of*, using the disjunctive *o*, implying that each requires its own distinct act of covering. Since the Torah distinguishes between them, the covering for a *chaya* and the covering for a bird must be separate acts; one cannot serve as the covering for both simultaneously.

---

---

# Hullin 87

## Chaya & Oph Coverage

### Multiple Animals

The Mishnah on 87b addresses a scenario in which one slaughters multiple animals — multiple *chayot* or multiple birds — at the same time. The ruling is that one covers the blood only once, at the end. There is no obligation to cover between each animal. A dispute arises, however, when one slaughters both a *chaya* and *oph* together, where Rabbi Yehuda holds that the bloods must be covered separately.

### Linguistic Analysis

The *Gemara* opens with a *baraita*: the word *chaya* in the verse is understood as a class term — *kol mashma chaya*, meaning whether one or many. Similarly, *oph* — fowl — *kol mashma oph*, whether many or few. From this linguistic analysis the *baraita* derives its ruling: if one slaughtered a hundred *chayot* in one place, *kisui echad l'kulam* — one covering suffices for all. The same applies to a hundred birds, and even if one slaughtered *chaya* and *oph* together in the same place, a single covering covers them all. Rabbi Yehuda, however, dissents: if one slaughters a *chaya*, one must cover it, and only thereafter slaughter the birds — for the verse states *chaya o oph*, using the word *o* (or) to indicate that they are to be treated separately.

### Scriptural Source

The Sages respond to Rabbi Yehuda by citing the verse *ki nefesh kol basar damo b'nafsho hi* — the soul of all flesh, its blood is in its soul — which appears immediately after the verse commanding the covering of blood, addressed to *bnei yisrael* collectively. The intent is to establish that the obligation of covering blood is addressed to the entire community of Israel — *azhara lechol yisrael* — not merely to a single individual acting in isolation. The communal dimension of the *mitzvah* flows directly from this formulation.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Or

The question immediately raised is: what kind of a response is this? How does citing *ki nefesh kol basar* address Rabbi Yehuda's position? The *Gemara* clarifies that the Sages are challenging his use of the *o*. Rabbi Yehuda reads *chaya o oph* as mandating separate coverings. The Sages counter: that *o* is needed to teach *l'chaleik* — to inform us that the obligation applies even when only a *chaya* is slaughtered and even when only *oph* is slaughtered, not solely when both are present together.

Rabbi Yehuda's rejoinder is that we already know this from the singular *damo* — "its blood" — which teaches that even a single animal requires covering. Since the singular form already handles that lesson, the *o* is freed to teach that *chaya* and *oph* require separate coverings.

The Sages respond that *damo* does not necessarily mean only one animal's blood. The word can function collectively, as demonstrated by the very same verse — *ki nefesh kol basar damo b'nafsho hi* — which uses the singular possessive while referring to all flesh universally. Since *damo* alone could not have taught us that either *chaya* or *oph* individually obligates, the *o* is required for precisely that lesson. Rabbi Yehuda, left without an alternative source for the *o*, uses it to mandate separate coverings.

---

## One Bracha Question

### Rabbi Chanina

The *Gemara* continues with a teaching of Rabbi Chanina: *modeh hayah Rabbi Yehuda l'inyan beracha she'eino mevareich ela beracha achas* — Rabbi Yehuda concedes that for the purpose of the *beracha*, one recites only a single blessing, even according to his own position. This is striking. One might have assumed that if the nature of the *mitzvah* according to Rabbi Yehuda demands two separate acts of covering, each would require its own *beracha*. Rabbi Chanina teaches otherwise.

This invites a broader question: what precisely defines the relationship between *mitzvos* and the *berachos* recited over them? One might frame it in two ways. Perhaps even when two *mitzvos* are performed sequentially, one immediately after the other, a single *beracha* suffices. Or, more simply, Rabbi Yehuda understands the entire obligation — covering *chaya* blood separately from *oph* blood — as constituting a single *mitzvah*, the nature of which merely requires that the coverings be performed in a particular order. On that reading, there is only one *mitzvah* and therefore only one *beracha*.

### Ravina's Question

The *Gemara* then records that Ravina said to Rav Acha son of Rava — and some say Rav Acha son of Rava said to Rav Ashi — *mai shna me-hamidei de-Rav*, why is this any different from the following story involving the students of Rav? The question is not a conceptual one about whether we view the two coverings as a single *mitzvah*, but a practical one. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the person actually performs an intervening act — covering the blood of the *chaya* before proceeding to slaughter the *oph*. Should that act of covering not constitute a *hefsek*, an interruption, between the two? And if so, even if we call the entire process one *mitzvah*, the first *beracha* cannot carry over past a *hefsek* to cover the second act.

### Hefsek Concern

The comparison is to a case involving students of Rav. Rav Bruna and Rav Chananel were seated at a meal, with Rav Yeba Saba serving as the *shamash*. They said to him *havu nvarech* — come, let us bentch — perhaps intending to include him in the *zimun*. They then changed their minds and said *havu nishrei*, wait, bring us more wine. Rav Yeba Saba told them: this is what Rav ruled — *keivan de-amru havu nvarech*, once you said "come let us bentch," *itzlei le-mishtei chamra* — you may no longer drink wine. The statement constituted a *hefsek*. You cannot simply retract it and resume drinking without consequence.

### Bentching Story

The implication for our case is as follows: here too, *keivan de-itzlei le-kisui ichayev lei be-bracha* — once you were obligated to attend to covering the blood, you have effectively signaled the end of one stage, and the next covering should require a new *beracha*. The *Gemara* presses the comparison: just as declaring "let us bentch" constituted a *hefsek* that precluded drinking wine without a new blessing, so too the first covering should interrupt the sequence and require a new *beracha* for the second.

---

## Hefsek Resolution

### Simultaneity Argument

The *Gemara* rejects the comparison: *hachi hashta* — what kind of comparison is this? *Hatam, mishtei u-vruchei be-hadei hadadi lo efshar* — there, one cannot drink wine while simultaneously making the *beracha*. One cannot talk while eating. Saying *rabosai nevarech* necessarily sets aside the drinking, because one physically cannot do both at once. *Hacha, efshar de-shachi be-chada u-mechasi be-chada* — here, if one is ambidextrous, one can be slaughtering with one hand while covering with the other. The covering is therefore not a contradiction to the ongoing process of *shechita*, and is not a *hefsek*.

### Ambidextrous Act

Taken literally, the *Gemara*'s reasoning is purely physical: if it is not physically possible to perform two activities simultaneously, then one activity signals the conclusion of the other. Since declaring intent to bentch makes drinking physically impossible at that moment, it constitutes a *hefsek*. Covering blood, however, is theoretically compatible with simultaneous *shechita*, and therefore cannot constitute a decisive break.

### Tosafos Signals End

Tosafos is uncomfortable with this purely physical reading of the *Gemara*, and offers a more conceptual interpretation. He raises a challenge: suppose in the middle of eating one rose to *daven* — to pray. One cannot eat and *daven* simultaneously. Does returning to eating after *davening* require a new *beracha*? According to the physical logic of the *Gemara*, it should. Similarly, if one heard thunder during a meal and paused to make a *beracha* on the thunder, would resuming the meal demand a new *beracha* merely because one cannot eat and speak simultaneously? Tosafos finds this problematic.

Tosafos therefore reframes the *Gemara*'s reasoning. The critical point is not physical simultaneity but what an activity *signals*. Bentching is the formal conclusion of a meal — it is what one does when eating is finished. When one says *rabosai nevarech*, one has declared, in effect, that eating is over. That declaration is what constitutes the *hefsek*, independent of any physical impossibility.

On this reading, one might have thought the same logic applies to covering blood. After all, covering blood comes at the end of *shechita*, just as bentching comes at the end of eating. Tosafos says this is precisely what troubled the *Gemara*, and it is why the *Gemara* made the comparison in the first place. The *Gemara*'s answer is that since covering blood is at least theoretically compatible with ongoing *shechita* — one could cover and slaughter simultaneously — the act of covering does not carry the same decisive finality that bentching carries relative to eating. Bentching admits of no ongoing eating whatsoever, whereas covering does not fully exclude the continuation of *shechita*. Therefore, covering blood is not a *hefsek* of the same order.

### What Is Hefsek

The upshot of Tosafos's reading is that a true *hefsek* — one that demands a new *beracha* — must consist of an activity that genuinely signals the conclusion of the prior process, in the way bentching signals the end of eating. A physical pause alone, or an activity that does not carry such conclusive significance, does not rise to that level. Because covering blood does not fully exclude the continuation of the *shechita* process, it does not constitute an interruption, and a single *beracha* suffices throughout.

This opens onto a broader discussion. Regarding *tefillin*, for instance, if one interrupts between the *shel yad* and the *shel rosh*, a new *beracha* is required. Even Ashkenazim who recite a separate *beracha* on the *shel rosh* — *al mitzvat tefillin* — must nonetheless also recite *lehaniach* on the *shel rosh* if there was an interruption, because the *beracha* of *lehaniach* on the *shel yad* can only extend to the *shel rosh* without interruption. Yet in other contexts — *bedikas chametz*, for example — once one has begun, even a pause or an exchange of words in the service of the *mitzvah* does not demand a new *beracha*. The same *beracha* continues to govern subsequent acts throughout the process.

Tosafos is inclined to treat *tefillin* as the exception: there it is one *mitzvah* where even a small interruption severs the connection between the *beracha* and the second act. In other extended processes or in *mitzvos* that comprise multiple sequential acts, the standard for *hefsek* is considerably higher. The same questions apply to a *shochet* who *shechts* throughout the day: does going to the bathroom, stopping for a meal, or answering a call constitute a *hefsek* sufficient to require a new *beracha*? Tosafos raises these questions but does not resolve them with finality.

One further distinction is worth noting. The *beracha* discussed in the parallel case of the students of Rav was a *beracha* on the drinking, and the bentching was what interrupted and terminated it. Here, by contrast, the *beracha* is not on the *shechita* — it is on the *kisuy* itself. What the *Gemara* would therefore have to establish is not that covering interrupts the *shechita* that preceded it, but rather that the *shechita* between the two coverings does not constitute a *hefsek* between the first covering and the second. The conceptual structure is not perfectly parallel, but the *Gemara*'s distinction still holds.

---

## Arvus Principle

### One Slaughters

The next Mishnah establishes: *shachat velo kisa* — if one slaughtered and did not cover the blood, *vera'ahu acher chayav lechasot* — and another person saw the exposed blood, that other person is obligated to cover it. The obligation does not reside exclusively with the *shochet*. This raises a fundamental question about the structure of the *mitzvah*: certain obligations are personal, binding the individual who performed the triggering act; others inhere in a state of affairs that demands rectification regardless of who created it. Here, exposed blood that has not been covered creates a condition that obligates the broader community to address it.

### Spiller Must Cover

A *baraita* teaches: *veshafach vechisa* — you shall spill and cover. From the juxtaposition of these two acts, the *Sages* derive *mi sheshafach yechaseh* — the one who spills is the one who should cover. That is the primary obligation. But if he slaughtered and did not cover, and another person saw it, the *baraita* asks: from where do we know that the other person is obligated to cover? The answer derives from the verse *va'omar livnei yisrael* — and I said to the children of Israel — which places the declaration in the context of a collective address to *Klal Yisrael*. From this the *Gemara* establishes *azhara lechol yisrael*: the obligation of *kisuy hadam* carries a communal dimension. The primary obligation rests with the *shochet*; if he fails to discharge it, the obligation devolves upon others.

### Respectful Covering

A second *baraita* derives an additional lesson from *veshafach vechisa*: cover with the same implement used to spill — *shelo yechasenu beregel*, do not cover the blood with one's foot. Kicking dirt over the blood may be physically effective, but it is disrespectful. *Shelo yiheyu mitzvos bezuyos alav* — one should not treat *mitzvos* with contempt. Even when performing a *mitzvah* in a technically sufficient manner, it must be done with appropriate dignity. A shovel would be acceptable; one's foot would not.

### Jumped Ahead Story

A third *baraita* returns to the primary obligation: *mi sheshafach hu yechasenu* — the one who spills is the one who should cover it. The *baraita* then records a case: *ma'aseh be'echad sheshachat vekadam chaveiro vechisa* — someone slaughtered and another person jumped ahead and covered the blood before the *shochet* had a chance to do so. Rabban Gamliel obligated this person to pay ten gold coins to the one from whom the *mitzvah* was seized.

### Fine Question

The *Gemara* raises the question: *sechar mitzvah o sechar beracha* — is the payment for stealing the *mitzvah*, or for stealing the *beracha*? The practical difference is illustrated by analogy to *birchas hamazon*: if someone stole the opportunity to lead the bentching for a *zimun*, that involves four *berachos*. If the fine is per *mitzvah*, the payment is ten gold coins for one *mitzvah*. If the fine is per *beracha*, the calculation shifts — and the *Gemara* implies a figure of forty gold coins.

The *poskim* note that the fine cannot be understood as applying to any *stam* stolen *beracha*, particularly in light of the principle that *gadol ha'oneh yoser min hamevarech* — greater is the one who answers *amen* than the one who makes the *beracha*. Two explanations are offered: either the *beracha* was recited quietly so no one could answer *amen*, making the loss more acute; or, more persuasively, the number of *berachos* associated with a *mitzvah* serves as an index for measuring the weight of the *mitzvah* itself. The fine is not literally about the *beracha* as a discrete act but about the severity of the theft, which is calibrated by how many *berachos* attended the stolen *mitzvah*. This reading avoids the difficulty of imposing a fine merely for stealing a *beracha*, which would seem disproportionate, and frames the *beracha* count as a measure of the *mitzvah*'s weight.

---

## Min Debate

### Mountains & Wind

The *Gemara* introduces a remarkable aggadic passage. A certain *min* said to Rebbi: *mi she'yatzar harim lo bara ruach* — the one who fashioned the mountains did not create the wind, and the one who created the wind did not fashion the mountains. His proof: the verse reads *ki hinei yotzer harim u'vorei ruach* — behold the fashioner of mountains and the creator of wind — using two distinct verbs with two distinct grammatical constructions, implying two distinct creative agents.

### One Creator

Rebbi's response was immediate: *shoteh* — idiot. *Shfil l'seifa de'krah* — go look at the end of the verse: *Hashem tzevaot shemo* — the Lord of hosts is His name. The verse itself resolves the apparent duality by attributing both acts to a single name. One senses that the theological stakes in this exchange were considerably higher than a grammatical dispute. The use of *borei* — a term associated with creation *yesh mei'ayin*, from nothing — alongside *yotzer* — formation and fashioning — may itself be part of the provocation, suggesting distinctions in the nature or hierarchy of divine acts. The broader context of such debates in the Talmud, particularly involving *minim*, suggests that arguments for divine plurality or a compound godhead were very much in the background.

### Three Days Fast

The *min* responded: *nekos li zimna tlati yomei u'madveina lach tyuvta* — give me three days, and I will come back to you with a challenge. Rebbi, clearly concerned, sat in three consecutive fasts — *yasiv Rebbi tlata ta'anisa* — that this person should not be able to construct an effective rebuttal. The echoes of medieval *vikuach*, religious disputation with all its attendant dangers, are unmistakable here.

### Good News

When Rebbi finally reached the end of his fasts and was about to eat, people came to the door and announced that a *min* was there. Rebbi quoted the verse *vayitnu bivrosi rosh* — they have put poison in my food — expressing his dismay at being interrupted precisely at the moment he was ready to eat. But the *min* at the door was not his adversary. *Mevaser tovos ani lacha* — I bring you good news, he said. *Lo matza teshuvah oyvecha* — your enemy found no answer for you — *v'nafal min hagag v'met* — and he fell from the roof and died.

### Cup of Bracha

Rebbi then extended an invitation: *retzoncha shetis'ad etzli* — would you like to eat with me? The *min* accepted. After they ate and drank, Rebbi offered him a choice: *kos shel beracha ata shoteh* — would you drink the *kos shel beracha* — or *arbaim zuzim ata notel* — would you take forty gold coins? The *min* chose the *kos shel beracha*.

Tosafos notes that Rebbi was not eager to extend the *kos shel beracha* to this individual, but felt a certain obligation to acknowledge the man's good deed. The offer of forty gold coins was an attempt to buy him out of the honor while still showing respect. The man's preference for the *kos shel beracha* over a substantial sum of money demonstrated the depth of his reverence for Jewish practice.

There is also a textual nuance worth noting. The *Gemara* says *kos shel beracha ata shoteh* — will you drink the cup of blessing — rather than *kos shel beracha ata notel*, will you take it. Rashi understands this as an invitation to remain present for the bentching, to hear the *berachos*, and to answer *amen* — *schar arba brachos she'ani achreihem amen*, the reward of the four *berachos* to which he answered *amen*. On this reading, the *min* was not leading the bentching but participating as one who answers. That interpretation, however, creates its own difficulty: would the opportunity to answer *amen* truly be weighed against forty gold coins? And the broader question arises regarding whether it was appropriate to include a *min* in a *zimun* at all. These questions are noted in the discussion, with the observation that exclusion on grounds of theological deviance, while prominent in the *Rambam*, is far less prominent as an operative principle in the *Gemara* itself.

### Heavenly Voice

*Yatzta bat kol v'amra* — a heavenly voice went forth and declared: *kos shel beracha yishveh arbaim zuzim* — the cup of blessing is worth forty gold coins. Rabbi Yitzchak adds that the family of that *min* survives to this day among the prominent families of Rome, known as the house of Bar Lavyanus.

The *bat kol* here is understood not as a one-time supernatural pronouncement but as the articulation of what became the received wisdom — the moral that everyone drew from the story, a principle that entered common discourse. And indeed, the matter is brought *le-halakhah*: the question of what fine is owed to one from whom a *mitzvah* is stolen is discussed in the *Shulchan Aruch*. Some understand the figure of ten gold coins as a fixed fine; others hold it subject to the assessment of a *beit din*. Further questions arise regarding whether contemporary Jewish courts retain authority to impose fines of this punitive nature as distinct from purely compensatory damages.

Tosafos also addresses the scope of the principle: the *mitzvah* must belong to the person from whom it was seized. If a father intended to perform the *milah* on his son himself and another person performed it without authorization, the *mitzvah* was stolen from the father. But if the father assigned a *mohel* to do it and a second *mohel* pushed him aside and performed the *milah*, the father retains a grievance against the interloper, but the first *mohel* does not — for the *mitzvah* never belonged to him in the first place. It was always the father's *mitzvah*, merely delegated. Similarly, Tosafos holds that being called for an *aliyah* does not vest a proprietary claim in the *mitzvah* — if another person takes it, the one called has been denied an honor, but has not had a *mitzvah* stolen from him in the sense that triggers this fine.

---

## Re-exposure Cases

### Covered Then Exposed

The *Gemara* now turns to several cases involving blood that was covered and subsequently uncovered. The Mishnah rules: *kisa venisgala* — if one covered the blood and it became exposed again, *patur milachasot* — one is exempt from covering it a second time. The *mitzvah* was performed; that it was undone by subsequent events does not reimpose the obligation.

### Lost Objects

Rav Achai son of Rava poses a challenge to Rav Ashi: why should this be different from *hashavat aveida* — returning a lost object? The verse commands *hashev* — return — and from this the *Sages* derive that one must return even *afilu me'ah pe'amim*, even a hundred times over, should the object keep getting lost. Perhaps the same should apply here: if the covered blood becomes exposed again, one must cover it again.

The reply is that by *hashavat aveida* there is no limiting word in the verse. Here, however, the verse reads *vechisahu* — and cover it — which carries an implicit restriction: you cover it once, and once it has been covered the obligation is discharged. The word itself signals that a single performance of the *mitzvah* completes the obligation, and re-exposure does not reimpose it.

### Wind Coverage

By contrast, if the blood was covered by the wind — *kisa'u haruach* — the *mitzvah* was never performed at all, and therefore *chayav lechasot* — one is still obligated to cover. But a natural question arises: if the blood is already covered, what does covering it accomplish? Rabbah bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo shanu ela shechazar venitkaleh* — the obligation applies only if the wind-covered blood was subsequently revealed again. If it was covered by the wind and remains covered — *lo chazar venitkaleh patur milachasot* — one is exempt, because there is nothing to cover. The obligation arises only when there is exposed blood that has never had the *mitzvah* performed upon it.

### Ein Dichuy

The *Gemara* then pushes further: *vechi chazar venitkaleh mai havei* — so what if it was revealed again? During the period that it was covered by the wind, was it not effectively *nidcheh* — pushed away — from the scope of the *mitzvah*? By analogy to *korbanot*, where an animal that was disqualified and then becomes eligible again remains invalid due to the principle of *dichuy*, perhaps the same should apply here: since there was a period during which the blood could not be the subject of the *mitzvah*, it should remain ineligible even when it is re-exposed.

Rav Pappa draws the decisive distinction: *zot omeret ein dichuy etzel mitzvot* — from this case we learn that the principle of *dichuy* applies to sacrifices but not to *mitzvos*. A *mitzvah* is not pushed away permanently by a period of ineligibility. When the condition that triggers the *mitzvah* returns — exposed blood that has never been covered — the obligation returns with it.

---

## Blood Mixtures

### Blood & Water

The Mishnah deals with blood mixed with various liquids. The first case: *dam shenitarav bemayim* — blood mixed with water. The rule: *im yesh bo mareh dam chayav lechasot* — if the mixture has the appearance of blood, one must cover it. Tosafos raises the question of what exactly *mareh dam* means in this context. Does the mixture merely need to have a reddish tint, or must it genuinely look like blood — deep in color and viscosity, not merely detectable? Tosafos holds that it must truly look like blood, reasoning that if the non-blood ingredient were in the majority, we would apply the laws of *bittul* and the blood would be nullified. Therefore, these cases assume that the other ingredient is in the minority, and even then the mixture must look not merely reddish but actually like blood.

### Blood & Wine

The next case: *nitarav beyayin* — blood mixed with wine. Since both are red, one cannot simply observe color. The rule is *ro'eh oto ke'ilu hu mayim* — one imagines the wine as if it were water and asks: would the blood still look like blood in that water? If yes, one must cover. If the dilution would be sufficient to render it not blood-looking, one need not cover.

### Blood Mixtures

Two further cases: blood mixed with *dam behemah* — the blood of a domesticated animal, which does not require covering — or with the blood of a living animal. The same test applies: treat the other blood as if it were water. If the *chaya* or *oph* blood would still appear as blood against that background, one must cover.

### Dam Lo Mevatel

Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *ein dam mevatel dam* — blood does not nullify blood. Since both substances are of the same type — *min bemino* — one does not nullify the other. Accordingly, the blood of the *chaya* or *oph* retains its status regardless of how much other blood surrounds it, and the obligation to cover remains.

### Splattered Blood

The final case in the Mishnah: *dam hanitaz veshel hasakin* — blood that has spattered away from the main collection point, or blood remaining on the knife, *chayav lechasot* — must be covered. Rabbi Yehuda qualifies: *eimatai*, when does this apply? *Bizman she'ein sham dam ela hu* — only when there is no other blood present to which the *mitzvah* can be applied. *Aval yesh sham dam shelo hu, patur milachasot* — if there is a main collection of blood to which the *mitzvah* is directed, one need not separately cover the spatters or the knife blood. This raises the question of whether one must cover every drop of blood or whether covering the main collection discharges the obligation — Rabbi Yehuda's position suggests the latter.

---

## Zevachim Parallel

### Zevachim Mishnah

The *Gemara* observes that nearly the same Mishnah appears in Zevachim, addressing sacrificial blood. *Dam shenitarav bemayim* — blood mixed with water — *im yesh bo mareh dam kasher* — if it has the appearance of blood it is *kasher* and may be sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach*. The parallel is almost word for word with the Mishnah in Chullin, the difference being that there the operative term is *kasher* rather than *chayav lechasot*. The wine case, the *behemah* blood case — all follow the same structure, and Rabbi Yehuda's position of *ein dam mevatel dam* appears there as well.

### Water Into Blood

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *lo shanu ella shenaflo mayim letoch dam* — all of the above applies only when water fell into the blood, gradually diluting it. In that scenario the blood is the dominant substance into which water is introduced, and the appearance of blood is assessed against that background.

### Blood Into Water

But *aval nafal dam letoch mayim* — if blood dripped into water, drop by drop — a different principle applies. *Rishon rishon battel* — each drop, as it enters, is nullified, because at that moment the blood does not appear as blood against the surrounding water. Even if ultimately enough blood accumulates so that the mixture looks like blood, the principle of *rishon rishon battel* means that each increment was neutralized at the point of entry. This is the concept of *chozer veni'or* — reawakening — a substance that was neutralized and then, as subsequent quantities accumulate, regains its effective status.

### Dichuy Distinction

Rav Pappa rules: *ul'inyan kisuy eino ken* — this rule does not apply when it comes to the *mitzvah* of covering blood. *Ein dichuy etzel mitzvot* — *mitzvos* are not subject to *dichuy*. Even if there was a period when the blood was neutralized — when it had, so to speak, lost its status — now that it has regained that status and the mixture appears as blood, the obligation to cover applies. The principle of *dichuy* that disqualifies a *korban* permanently after a period of ineligibility does not carry over to the domain of *mitzvos*.

The distinction is important on multiple levels. For *korbanot*, sanctity is a formal legal status; once compromised, it is not simply restored. For a *mitzvah* obligation like *kisuy hadam*, what matters is the present condition: is there blood that appears as blood and that has not had the *mitzvah* performed upon it? If the answer is yes, the obligation exists, regardless of any prior period of neutralization.

This principle has implications for *trefos* more broadly. Where prohibited substances accumulate drop by drop and each drop is *battel* upon entry, the question of whether the aggregate *chozer veni'or* — reawakens — is a significant practical question in the laws of *bittul*.

---

## Tumah Susceptibility

### Red Appearance

The *Gemara* cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *kol mareh admumit mechapperin* — any red appearance suffices for *kapparah*, for the use of sacrificial blood. And *umachshirin* — and such a mixture renders food susceptible to *tumah*, since blood is one of the seven liquids that confer susceptibility upon produce. And *v'chayavin bekisuy* — and one is obligated to cover such a mixture.

### Rainwater Question

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *mai ka mashma lan* — what is the novel point here? The rule that such a mixture is *kasher* for *kapparah* was already taught in the Mishnah of Zevachim. The rule that one must cover it was already taught in the Mishnah of Chullin. And as for *hechsher zerayim* — the susceptibility of produce — since the mixture contains either blood or water, either component would render produce susceptible to *tumah* anyway. What has Shmuel added?

The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzricha shenis'arvu b'mei geshamim* — the ruling is necessary for a case where the blood became mixed with rainwater. Rainwater does not confer susceptibility upon produce unless the owner desired that the water fall on the produce, or unless the water was designated for some use. Rainwater that falls naturally and unintentionally does not render produce susceptible.

### Natural vs. Intentional

The *Gemara* initially suggests that even rainwater, once consciously mixed with blood — *keivan d'shakil v'rami*, since one took it and poured it — has been given significance by the intentional act, and would therefore be *machshir*. But Shmuel's ruling is necessary for the case of *lo tzricha shenis'arvu mei'aleihen* — where the mixing happened entirely on its own, without any human intention. A vessel of blood was left out, rainwater fell into it naturally, and the mixture was then knocked onto produce. Treating the liquid as rainwater, one might think it could not render the produce susceptible, since no human intention was involved. Shmuel teaches that since the mixture still has the appearance of blood, it is treated as blood for all purposes — for *kapparah*, for *kisuy*, and for conferring susceptibility upon produce — regardless of whether the mixing was intentional or accidental.

---

---

# Hullin 88

## Blood & Water Mixtures

### Rabbi Assi: Clear Serum

The daf opens by continuing a discussion from 87b concerning the nature of blood and blood mixtures — specifically, when a substance retains the halachic status of blood. The preceding context had established that as long as a blood mixture still appears red, it functions as a *machshir zera'im*, rendering food susceptible to *tumah*. The Gemara had objected that if blood is mixed with water, the water alone would suffice to *machshir*, so what is the novelty? The answer had been that the case involves blood mixed with rainwater.

Continuing into 88b, Rabbi Assi mi-Naharville states that even the *tzilusah d'dama* — the clear serum of blood — qualifies as a *machshir zera'im*. As Rashi explains, if blood is allowed to sit undisturbed, the denser matter collects toward the center while a clearer, more watery liquid settles at the edges. Rabbi Assi teaches that even this clear component, though it no longer appears deeply red, retains sufficient connection to blood to render food susceptible to *tumah*.

### Rabbi Yirmiyah: No Karet

Rabbi Yirmiyah mi-Difti then states: *ein bo karet* — this component does not carry liability for *karet*. The question is whether this statement addresses the case of blood mixed with water discussed just above, or the immediately preceding line concerning the *tzilusah d'dama*. Rashi is somewhat ambiguous, but Tosafot understands it as bearing on both cases. Tosafot maintains that one incurs *karet* even for the watery component of blood, since it was originally entirely blood and has merely separated into its constituent parts — though only if a *kezayis* of actual blood is present.

This qualification requires attention. Of course, a *kezayis* of blood is ordinarily required for *karet* — so what is the novelty? The *chiddush* seems to lie in the following: if the blood has separated such that only the clear serum remains in the quantity consumed, and the genuinely red, solid component amounts to less than a *kezayis*, one does not incur *karet*. The analogy is straightforward — if one consumes a stew containing *chazir* mixed with vegetables, liability attaches only if one has ingested a *kezayis* of the forbidden substance itself, not merely of the mixture as a whole.

What makes this particularly striking is the potential middle position it implies. The *tzilusah d'dama* may retain enough of the character of blood to function as a *machshir zera'im*, yet lack sufficient density to trigger the prohibition of eating blood or to carry the liability of *karet*. This would be an unusual intermediate status — connected enough to blood for one purpose but not another.

### Tannaim: Blood & Tumah

A *baraita* then teaches that a blood mixture causes *tumah* in an *ohel* — provided a full *revieis* of blood is present. Again, the same analytical question arises: does this concern blood mixed with water, or the watery component that has separated from the blood itself? If it concerns blood mixed with water, the ruling is intuitive — human blood from a corpse causes *tumas ohel* when present in a tent, and naturally a *revieis* of actual blood must be present within the mixture, not merely a *revieis* of the diluted combination. If, however, the statement addresses the *tzilusah d'dama*, it effectively becomes a limiting ruling: only the red, dense component of blood generates *tumas ohel*, while the clear separated liquid — though connected enough to the blood to *machshir zera'im* — is insufficient to transmit *tumah*.

On this reading, the Gemara emerges with a finely calibrated hierarchy: the clear serum of blood carries enough of blood's identity to render food susceptible, but not enough to impose *karet* on the one who consumes it, nor to cause *tumas ohel*.

### Corpse Liquids & Blood

The Gemara now cites a related source. Though the marginal notation indicates *Tosefta*, and Rabbi Shimshon (the *Rash*, one of the *Ba'alei HaTosafot* who composed a commentary on the Mishnah) notes that all manuscripts read *tnan* — suggesting a *mishnah* — the passage in fact appears in no *mishnah* and belongs to the *Tosefta* alone. The Gemara acknowledges this kind of imprecision elsewhere.

The passage states: *kol mashkei meis tehorim chutz midamo* — all liquids of a corpse are *tahor* except for its blood. The blood of a corpse, as just established, causes *tumah* and even *tumas ohel*. The passage continues: *v'chol marei admumit shebo metam'in b'ohel* — any reddish appearance within the liquid also causes *tumah* in the *ohel*. This formulation could mean, consistent with what was said earlier, that a blood-water mixture causes *tumas ohel* as long as it retains a red appearance; or it could mean that even blood that is not deeply red — perhaps the partially separated, more liquidy component — still qualifies as blood for this purpose. All other liquids of the corpse, however, are *tahor* and carry no *tumah* of the corpse.

---

## Impure Liquids & Tumah

### Corpse Exception

The Gemara now raises a challenge from a different source. A *mishnah* teaches that liquids emerging from a *tamei* person are treated as though that person touched them — rendering such liquids *tamei* themselves. The question posed is whether this principle extends even to liquids emerging from a corpse, which is the gravest source of *tumah*. If so, the teaching that all non-blood liquids of a corpse are *tahor* seems contradicted.

### Tevul Yom Status

Before resolving this tension, the Gemara introduces an important distinction. A *tevul yom* — someone who has immersed in a *mikvah* on that day but whose purification is not yet complete until nightfall — carries the halachic status of a *sheni l'tumah*. The *mishnah* teaches that liquids emerging from a *tevul yom* are treated as though he touched them. Since a *tevul yom* is in transition out of *tumah*, the Rabbis did not extend the rule that a *sheni* who touches liquid elevates it to a *rishon*. Consequently, *v'eilu v'eilu ein metamin* — these liquids do not cause *tumah* at all.

To appreciate this ruling, one must understand the general principle: when a *sheni* touches a liquid, that liquid rises to the level of a *rishon*. This is why the hands, which are rabbinically considered *sheni*, must be dried after *netilat yadayim* — lest the liquid on them become *rishon* and, upon touching food, elevate it as well. It is also the basis for the custom of washing one's hands before dipping *karpas* on Seder night, since the liquid on the *karpas* would otherwise be elevated by contact with *sheni* hands. For the *tevul yom*, however, who stands on the threshold of *taharah*, the Rabbis made no such extension.

For all other *tamei* persons — whether light (*kalin*), such as one who touched a *sheretz* and is thereby a *rishon*, or grave (*chamurim*), such as a *zav* who is an *av hatumah* — liquids emerging from their bodies are treated as though they touched those liquids, rendering the liquids *rishon l'tumah*. The only exception: certain bodily fluids of those whose very *tumah* derives from their bodily emissions — the *zav*, the *zavah*, and the *niddah* — are themselves *avot hatumah*. Specifically, their spit, urine, and semen (based on the verse *v'chi yarok*, "and if he spits," from which the Gemara extends to all fluids that collect within the body before being discharged) are *avot hatumah* in their own right. Blood and tears, by contrast, do not satisfy this criterion even for these individuals — they would be *rishon* but not *av*.

### Zav vs. Corpse Logic

With this background established, the Gemara returns to the apparent contradiction. The *mishnah* teaches that even low-level *tamei* persons (*kalin* — those who touched a *sheretz*) have their liquids treated as *rishon*, and even *chamurim* (the *zav*, an *av hatumah*) generate *tamei* liquids. Yet the corpse — the *avi avot hatumah*, the most severe source of *tumah* — has all non-blood liquids declared *tahor*. The irony is striking: the weightiest source of *tumah* in the Torah generates no *tumah* in its liquids, while a comparatively minor *tamei* person does.

The Gemara resolves this with a sociological observation. A *zav* — Rashi notes — is not visibly distinguishable from any other person. People do not naturally distance themselves from him, do not recoil, and often do not even know he is a *zav*. Given this proximity and the likelihood of inadvertent contact, the Rabbis extended the *tumah* decree to his emitted liquids as well, to prompt greater vigilance. The corpse, by contrast, is known to all and is naturally avoided by anyone concerned with maintaining *taharah*. Since the Rabbis' protective decree was unnecessary for the corpse situation, they made no extension — leaving non-blood corpse liquids *tahor*.

Tosafot raises a further question: why are we speaking of this as rabbinic in the first place? A liquid that emerges from a body is touching that body; should it not become *tamei* biblically through contact? Tosafot offers two answers. The first, admittedly highly technical, posits the case where some kind of conduit was used such that the liquid never actually made surface contact with the corpse's skin. The second answer — more structurally significant — observes that only the canonical seven liquids (*yayin, shemen, dvash, shemen zayit, mayim, dam, tal* — as encapsulated in the mnemonic *yad shachat dam*) formally qualify as liquids in the halachic sense. Tears, urine, and similar bodily fluids are not among them. Since they are not biblically recognized as liquids, even contact with the corpse would not transmit *tumah* to them; hence the *tumah* applicable to them in the case of a *zav* is purely rabbinic in origin.

### Seven Liquids Rule

This leads to a clarifying discussion of the seven liquids themselves. The question is raised why tears, for example, are not subsumed under *mayim* — water — since they clearly have a water component. The answer is that the Gemara's list of seven liquids was not constituted by chemical composition. The very fact that dew (*tal*) required explicit inclusion — despite being entirely water — demonstrates that the category *mayim* was not simply "anything containing water." The seven liquids are a defined, closed category, and fluids such as tears and sweat, whatever their composition, fall outside it.

---

## Covering Sacrificial Blo…

### Damo Debate

The Gemara now transitions to the final *mishnah* of the perek, which concerns the obligation of *kissuy hadam* — covering blood after *shechita*. A *baraita* is cited: *v'chissahu* — "and he shall cover it" — teaches that the blood which splatters (*hanitaz*) and the blood remaining on the knife must also be covered. Rabbi Yehuda, however, qualifies: *eimasai* — when does this apply? Only when there is no other blood present. If the main pool of blood is available to be covered separately, one is exempt from covering the splattered blood and the blood on the knife. A second *baraita* teaches that one must cover *kol damo* — all the blood, including what splatters on the walls of the slaughterhouse (*agafayim*), which would require scraping or applying earth to the walls themselves.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then articulates a different position: the obligation is conditioned on whether one has covered *dam hanefesh* — the life blood, the blood that flows immediately upon *shechita*. If that blood has been covered, one is exempt from covering the rest, regardless of where it may have landed.

The Gemara presents this as a three-way debate turning on the interpretation of the word *damo* in the biblical verse. The rabbis read *damo* as *kol damo* — all of its blood, with no qualification. Rabbi Yehuda reads *damo* as *afilu miktzas damo* — any portion of its blood suffices, so covering some blood discharges one of any obligation regarding the remainder. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reads *damo* as *damo hameyuchad* — its most distinguished blood, namely the life blood.

### Pesak & Practice

The question of how we rule is debated among the *rishonim*. Ordinarily, when Rabbi Yehuda employs the phrase *eimasai* — "when does this apply?" — the convention is that he is not dissenting but clarifying the position of the *tanna kamma*. Here, however, the Gemara frames it as a genuine three-way disagreement, which complicates the application of that principle. A number of *rishonim*, including the Rambam and what appears to be the dominant position in Tosafot, hold that Rabbi Yehuda is indeed clarifying, and we rule accordingly. The Ra'avad, by contrast, maintains that Rabbi Yehuda represents a dissenting view and we rule with the *chachamim*, requiring all the blood to be covered.

A practical observation emerges: even those who accept Rabbi Yehuda's ruling do not frame it as permission to cover only a token amount and be done. The consistent formulation is that if there is blood one cannot practicably cover, one is exempt from that remainder — but one should still cover as much as possible. Whether at the biblical level Rabbi Yehuda means only that *miktzas* suffices minimally or that he also envisions covering as much as one can, even if not all, is not fully resolved.

In practice, *shechita* as conducted today involves covering the primary flow of blood as it emerges — the *pirkus* stage — and thereafter the knife is cleaned in a sink rather than in earth. One cannot realistically rule like the *chachamim* requiring all blood to be covered; it would be practically impossible in a slaughterhouse setting. The operative ruling therefore follows either Rabbi Yehuda or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, with Rabbi Yehuda representing the more lenient position since, read literally, any amount of blood covered would suffice.

---

## Materials for Kissuy

### Granular vs. Thick

The *mishnah* now addresses the question of *bameh mechassin u'bameh ein mechassin* — with what may one cover the blood, and with what may one not? The items with which one may cover include: *zevel hadak* (thin manure), *chol hadak* (thin sand), *sid* (lime or plaster), *charsit* (pottery material), *leveinah* (brick), and *magufah* (barrel seals) — provided the latter two have been ground (*she-ketashan*) into a granular form. One may not cover with thick manure, thick sand, nor with the brick or barrel seal that has not been ground. And one may not simply place a vessel over the blood — *lo yichpeh alav et ha-keli*.

Two criteria emerge from the *mishnah*: the covering material must be granular in character, and it must be of the type from which vegetation can grow. These are conceptually distinct. Rashi emphasizes that the very act of "covering" — *kisui* — requires something granular rather than solid. When one places a vessel or a solid object over something, the covering is removable and external; something granular, by contrast, integrates itself into the surrounding ground and stays. The covering must therefore be like *afar*, earth, not only in what it is made of but in how it covers.

The imagery here is also evocative. When blood is spilled in violence and injustice, leaving it exposed cries out to heaven — *kol d'mei achicha tzo'akim eilai*, the voice of your brother's blood cries out from the earth. When blood is spilled legitimately through *shechita*, the obligation is to cover it — not to expose and display it. There is a meaningful inversion: the crime of murder is to cover up the blood, while the *mitzvah* after valid *shechita* is to cover it properly.

### RSBG: Growth Principle

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel articulates a general principle: *davar she-megadel bo tzmachim mechassin bo* — anything in which vegetation grows may be used as a covering; anything in which vegetation does not grow may not. At first glance, this appears to merely restate or synthesize the specific cases of the *mishnah* rather than add a new criterion. Yet a closer look reveals that "growth" and "granularity" are not identical. A clump of manure or a solid block of soil is also presumably fertile ground — yet it is excluded. The *mishnah* thus seems to require both characteristics simultaneously: the material must be granular in form *and* capable of sustaining plant life.

One perspective raised during the shiur is that the emphasis on growth may carry a deeper resonance: the blood is itself a life-source, and covering it with something that can itself generate life creates a kind of continuum — life returning to life, the ground sustaining new growth from what was once a source of vitality. This contrasts with the purely structural reading that *megadel tzmachim* is simply a proxy for "resembles earth." Both dimensions may be operative.

### Potter's Standard

The Gemara then asks: what precisely is *chol hadak* — thin sand? Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: any sand that a potter does not need to grind before using in his clay. Conversely, *chol hagas* — thick sand — is sand that the potter must grind before incorporating into the clay.

A parallel formulation is offered: alternatively, the teaching clarifies the *seifa*, the latter clause — defining thick sand as that which requires grinding. The Gemara then asks: what is the practical difference between these two formulations? The answer is a borderline case — sand that can be crumbled by hand (*demifrach parich*) but does not strictly require grinding. Under the definition of thin sand as "not requiring grinding," such sand qualifies as thin, since one need not grind it. Under the definition of thick sand as "requiring grinding," the same sand might qualify as thick, since in some sense it does benefit from grinding. The formulation chosen therefore affects how borderline cases are classified.

---

## Klal u'Prat Analysis

### Klal Tzarich l'Prat

The Gemara proceeds to a *baraita* that analyzes the verse hermeneutically. The verse says *v'chissahu* — "and he shall cover it" — and then *be'afar* — "with dust." One might think that covering with stones or placing a vessel on top would suffice; therefore, the verse says *be'afar*. But then one might think that only actual *afar* — earth — is permitted. How, then, do we permit thin manure, thin sand, ground stone, ground pottery, thin flax fibers, thin sawdust, lime, brick, and barrel seals that have been ground? The verse says *v'chissahu*, which is inclusive.

Conversely, one might think the inclusive *v'chissahu* extends to thick manure, thick sand, ground metal vessels, unground brick and barrel seals, flour, and bran. Against this, the verse says *be'afar* to exclude them. The operative distinction is: those things that are *min afar* — of the nature of earth, granular in character and capable of sustaining growth — are included; those that are not *min afar* are excluded.

At this point the Gemara raises the obvious hermeneutic challenge: why not apply *klal u'prat* here? *V'chissahu* would be the *klal* — the general inclusive statement — and *be'afar* would be the *prat* — the limiting particular. Under the principle *klal u'prat ein baklal ela mah shebaprat*, one would be restricted to earth alone, excluding all other materials. Why, instead, does the Gemara proceed by *ribuy u'miut* — inclusion followed by limitation, yielding the broader class of earth-similar materials?

Rav Mari answers: because this is a *klal hatzarich liprat* — a *klal* that requires the *prat* to clarify it. The general rule is that a *klal hatzarich liprat* is not subject to the standard *klal u'prat* analysis.

### Rashi & Tosafot

Rashi and Tosafot differ on what *klal hatzarich liprat* means in this context. Rashi explains that the *klal* here — the word *v'chissahu* — does not stand on its own as a clear general statement. The verb itself is ambiguous: "covering" can refer to placing a vessel or blanket over something (a removable, external cover), or it can refer to the granular, earth-like embedding that is actually required here. Since the verb does not independently convey a well-defined class of objects or actions, the *prat* is not functioning as a limiting exception to an otherwise understood *klal* — rather, it is the *prat* that gives the *klal* its meaning in the first place. A *klal* that needs the *prat* for its very intelligibility cannot be processed through the standard *klal u'prat* analysis.

Tosafot offers a simpler interpretation. The word *tzarich* in *klal hatzarich liprat* means that the *prat* — the word *be'afar* — was needed to communicate a separate piece of information: that earth must be placed both beneath and above the blood. Since the *prat* was needed to serve this other purpose, it cannot simultaneously be understood as a purely restrictive term that limits the *klal* to *afar* alone. The *prat* is doing double duty; therefore, it does not function as a standard *prat* in a *klal u'prat* derivation.

In summary: Rashi locates the problem in the ambiguity of the *klal* itself; Tosafot locates it in the *prat* having been drafted for a separate legal point. Both arrive at the conclusion that *klal u'prat* does not apply here.

### Ribuy u'Miut Method

The Gemara notes that one could alternatively frame the interpretation as *ribuy u'miut* — a broad inclusion followed by a narrowing exclusion — rather than *klal u'prat*. The *ribuy* would be the general word *v'chissahu*, and the *miut* would be *be'afar*, yielding anything similar to the narrower term. Since the entire community operates on the reading that this case is *klal u'prat* rather than *ribuy u'miut*, the Gemara works within that framework. Under *ribuy u'miut*, one arrives at anything that shares the relevant properties of *afar*, without being restricted to *afar* alone — which is precisely the conclusion the Gemara reaches through the alternative analysis. The difference between the two methods would manifest in other cases, but here the practical outcome is the same.

---

## Desert & Sea Cases

### Gold Coin Case

Having established the general framework, the Gemara now addresses extreme circumstances. If one is traveling in the desert and has no *afar* available with which to cover the blood — and the context of the *baraita* already used to establish the exclusion of desert sand makes clear that sand from the desert floor is not valid, since planting into it yields nothing — one may grind a gold coin and use the gold dust as a covering.

This is surprising given what was said earlier: ground metal (*shchikat klei mateches*) was among the items explicitly excluded. How then can gold dust be used?

### Tallit Ashes

The parallel emergency case involves traveling by sea. If one has no *afar* available on board, one may burn one's *tallit* and use the ashes as a covering. This too raises questions given the earlier discussion, since ashes are not obviously organic in all cases, and their capacity to support plant growth is not self-evident.

### Ashes & Gold Dust

The Gemara resolves these cases through textual derivation. Regarding ashes: *bishlama soref taliso umechasen, ashkechan eifer d'ika* — we find that ashes are called *afar*, as the verse says regarding the *parah adumah*, *velakchu latamei me'afar sreifat hachatat* — they shall take for the *tamei* person from "the dust of the burning of the purification-offering." The word *afar* is used explicitly to describe what is in fact ash. Since the Torah calls ash *afar*, it qualifies as a covering material.

Regarding gold: Rav Zeira cites the verse *ve'afrot zahav lo* — "and he had gold dust" — which uses the word *afrot* (dust) in the context of gold. Since the Torah applies the term *afar* to gold dust, gold dust is classified as *afar* for the purpose of *kissuy hadam*. This represents a category of permitted materials that rests not on the physical properties of *afar* — granularity, capacity for growth — but on the Torah's own application of the label *afar* to those substances.

---

## Shammai v. Hillel

### Core Dispute

A *baraita* records a tannaitic dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai holds: *ein mechassin ela be'afar* — one may cover the blood only with actual earth, nothing else. All the permitted materials discussed above — ground pottery, sand, thin manure, ashes, and the rest — are rejected by Beit Shammai. Only dirt qualifies.

Beit Hillel responds: *matzinu eifer shekarui afar* — we find that ashes are called *afar*, as proven from the verse about *parah adumah* cited above. Beit Shammai counters that that verse says *afar sreifah* — the dust of burning — which is a compound phrase modifying *afar* with the word "burning." It does not prove that plain *afar* in the verse of *kissuy hadam* extends to ashes in general; it merely gives a specific name to a specific substance. Plain *afar*, used without qualification, refers only to earth.

This debate maps neatly onto the two categories that have emerged across the entire discussion: materials that possess the *properties* of *afar* (granularity, capacity for plant growth), and materials to which the Torah *applies the label* of *afar* (gold dust, ashes). Beit Shammai refuses both extensions; Beit Hillel accepts at minimum the extension via label.

### Added Materials

The *mishnah* adds further materials that were subsequently permitted: ground charcoal (*shachor*), eye salve (*kachol*), and the dust that accumulates in a mill (*nikris pisulin*, as Rashi identifies it — though whether this derives from the wheat being ground or from the millstones themselves is uncertain, given that flour was explicitly excluded earlier). Some authorities add even *zarnich*, identified by Rashi as some form of metallic powder and by others as related to antimony or a similar cosmetic substance. The precise logic of these inclusions — and how some metallic substances come to be permitted despite the exclusion of ground metal vessels earlier — is not fully resolved by the Gemara, and the lines of distinction remain, at minimum, not entirely transparent.

---

## Abraham's Reward

### Avraham's Statement

The Gemara concludes the perek with an *aggadic* statement from Rava. Because Avraham Avinu said to God, during his intercession on behalf of Sodom: *ve'anochi afar va'eifer* — "and I am dust and ashes" — expressing profound humility before the Divine, his descendants were privileged to receive two *mitzvot* that correspond to those very words: *eifer parah* — the ashes of the *parah adumah*, which purify the *tamei* — and *afar sotah* — the earth placed into the water that the *sotah* drinks.

### Why Not Kissuy

The Gemara immediately anticipates the obvious question: given that this entire perek has been devoted to *kissuy hadam* — which itself requires *afar* — why is that *mitzvah* not included in Avraham's reward?

The answer: *hasam hechsher mitzvah ika, hana leka* — there, in the cases of *parah adumah* and *sotah*, there is a genuine benefit that results from performing the *mitzvah*, in addition to the merit of the *mitzvah* itself. The *parah adumah* restores the *tamei* person to *taharah*; the *sotah* process resolves the husband's suspicion and enables the couple to reconcile — *oseh shalom bein ish l'ishto*. Thus those *mitzvot* carry both spiritual credit and concrete, tangible benefit. *Kissuy hadam*, by contrast, is a *mitzvah* whose performance does not produce any such additional benefit — the meat may be eaten regardless of whether the blood is covered. The *mitzvah* is its own reward, without a corresponding consequential benefit; and for that reason, it does not rise to the level of a reward that mirrors Avraham's humility in the same way.

The observation is striking: paradoxically, one accumulates *mitzvah* credit by performing *kissuy hadam*, yet does not receive credit of the same quality as performing *sotah*. The *sotah* process yields no *mitzvah* points for the individuals involved — it is a process of clarification and resolution, not an affirmative act of piety — yet it yields a concrete benefit. The reward of Avraham, it emerges, was specifically in the dimension of *benefit*, not merely *mitzvah performance*. This closes the perek, with the *aggadata* of the final daf to be continued.

---

---

# Hullin 89

## Kisuy HaDam & Humility

### Intro & Materials

We begin on the last line of 88b, with the intention of completing the discussion of *kisuy hadam* and then moving into the next prohibition relating to the eating of meat, namely *gid hanasheh*. Before turning to the *aggadeta*, it is worth noting a practical observation that arose in connection with the previous session's discussion of valid materials for *kisuy hadam*. The question had been what distinguishes valid materials from invalid ones — why, for instance, can one not use flour or metal filings? The suggestion offered was that invalid materials fall into one of two categories: those that are entirely non-absorbent, such as metal, and those that are so absorbent that they are transformed in the process, such as flour, which simply clumps together. Valid materials, by contrast, absorb without being fundamentally altered — dirt being the paradigmatic example. This framework, while not explicitly articulated as such in the *mishna*, does seem to align with the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the dominant view in the *gemara*.

### Abraham's Merit

The *gemara* now resumes with an *aggadic* passage, noting that while its original locus is in Masechet Sotah — where it arose naturally in context — it is quoted here because of its thematic connection to the *aggadeta* already introduced in our *sugya*. Rava says: in the merit of what Abraham our father said — *im michut ve'ad seroch naal*, "if from a thread to a shoe-strap" I will take nothing of yours (Genesis 14:23), his descendants merited two *mitzvot*: the blue thread of *tzitzit* (*chut shel techeilet*), which corresponds to the "thread," and the strap of *tefillin* (*retzuah shel tefillin*), which corresponds to the "shoe-strap."

The *gemara* continues by asking what kind of benefit is conferred by these *mitzvot*, since the broader context of the discussion has emphasized *mitzvot* from which a person derives some tangible benefit in this world.

### Tefillin Benefit

The *gemara* says: *bishelama retzuah shel tefillin* — the strap of *tefillin* is understandable. As the verse states, "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of God is called upon you" (Deuteronomy 28:10), and we learned in a *baraita* that Rabbi Eliezer the Great said: this refers to the *tefillin shebarosh*, the head-*tefillin*, which bears the divine Name in the form of the letters *shin* and *dalet* on the *bayit* and the *kesher*. The end of that verse reads, *ve'yaru mimcha* — "and they shall fear you." The benefit, then, is that wearing *tefillin* causes the nations of the world to stand in awe of the one who bears them.

### Techeilet & Throne

The *gemara* then asks: but what is the benefit of the blue thread of *tzitzit*? Where is the practical benefit in this world? The *gemara* cites a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Meir: why was *techeilet* chosen over all other colors? Because *techeilet* resembles the sea, the sea resembles the sky, the sky resembles sapphire (*even sapir*), and sapphire resembles the *kisei hakavod*, the heavenly throne.
