The verse says, "And they saw the God of Israel, and under His feet was like the work of sapphire stone, and like the very heavens for purity" (Exodus 24:10) — showing that the heavens are like sapphire. And another verse says, "like the appearance of sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne" (Ezekiel 1:26) — establishing that sapphire is the color of God's throne.

Rashi understands the *gemara* as asking about practical worldly benefit, and answers that since the color of *techeilet* corresponds to God's throne, God, ever present upon His throne, continuously recalls the merit of *tzitzit* and that merit accrues to Israel. However, there is another and perhaps more natural reading: that the emphasis here is not on practical benefit but on the quality that makes these two *mitzvot* particularly meaningful — namely, their expression of an intimate connection between Israel and God. The name of God is upon us through *tefillin*; the color of God's throne is upon us through *techeilet*. This sense of direct relationship arguably fits the theme of Abraham more naturally, given that a central motif of Abraham's covenant is God's declaration, "I will be your God." Rashi's reading emphasizes practical benefit, but the *gemara* may simply be asking what makes these *mitzvot* stand out among all *mitzvot* — and the answer is that profound quality of closeness to the divine that they embody.

One student noted that the *midrash* also teaches that the *luchot* were made of sapphire — a point that could have reinforced the chain of associations but is not invoked here. Another observation raised is the degree of anthropomorphism in the passage — speaking of what stands beneath God's feet and the color of His throne. The *gemara* does not recoil from these images; they appear in the *Torah* itself and the *gemara* treats them straightforwardly. The point, though, seems ultimately to be about the spiritual reality of a connection to the divine, not a visual or physical description in any pagan sense.

### Stolen Property

Rabbi Abba says: *kasheh gezel hanachal* — stolen property that has already been consumed is particularly difficult. When one steals an object that remains intact, restitution is straightforward: return the object. But when the stolen item has already been used up or consumed, and the thief now feels genuine remorse and wishes to make restitution, the practical and psychological difficulty of doing so is enormous. The money may already be spent. The object no longer exists. Even the most righteous of people find themselves unable to make full restitution in such a case — *afillu tzadikim gemurim ein yekholin lehachazira*.

The proof-text is the verse in which Abraham, after refusing all the war booty, adds an exception: *biladai rak asher achlu hane'arim* — "only what the young men have eaten." The simple reading of the verse is that the fighters were entitled to their sustenance as wages of war. But the *gemara* reads it more sharply: Abraham was acknowledging that what his retinue had consumed was something he could not return, and so he was releasing the king of Sodom from any claim rather than being able to make whole. The language implies that this consumption had the quality of *gezel* — and even Abraham could not undo it.

### Humility Drasha

The *gemara* introduces the next passage with the statement of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili: whenever you find the words of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili in *Hagada*, make your ear like an *arparcheset* — a collecting bin into which grain is thrown in the mill — meaning, open yourself to receive everything he has to say. The *drasha* that follows is evidently the one being quoted in his name.

The verse reads: *lo merubchem mikol ha'amim chashak Hashem bachem* — "Not because you are greater than all the peoples did God desire you; rather, you are the fewest of all the peoples" (Deuteronomy 7:7). The *drasha* reads: God said to Israel, I desire you because *she'afilu besha'ah she'ani maspia lachem gedula*, even when I give you greatness, *atem mamitim atzmechem lefanai*, you make yourselves small before Me. The verse is re-read: God desires you not because you are *rav* — great — but because *ki atem hame'at* — you make yourselves *me'at*, small. Even when greatness is bestowed upon you, you do not treat yourselves as elevated. You remain humble.

The *gemara* enumerates the proof-cases. God gave greatness to Abraham, and Abraham said, *ve'anochi afar va'efer* — "I am dust and ashes." God gave greatness to Moses and Aaron, and they said, *venachnu mah* — "What are we? We are nothing." God gave greatness to David, and David said, *ve'anochi tola'at velo ish* — "I am a worm and not a man."

The idolaters are then contrasted. God gave greatness to Nimrod, and Nimrod said, "Come, let us build a tower to reach the heavens" — in *chazal*'s reading, it was Nimrod who led the *migdal bavel*. God gave greatness to Pharaoh, and Pharaoh said, *mi Hashem* — "Who is God that I should listen to Him?" God gave greatness to Sennacherib, and he said, "Who among all the gods of the lands has stood against me?" God gave greatness to Nebuchadnezzar, and he said, *e'eleh al bamotei av* — "I will ascend upon the high cloud." God gave greatness to Hiram king of Tyre, who had collaborated with Solomon in building the *beit hamikdash*, and he said, *moshav elohim yashavti belev yamim* — "I have sat in the dwelling of God, in the heart of the seas."

The pattern is striking: give the nations greatness and they believe themselves divine; give Israel greatness and their great ones speak of their own nothingness.

### Moshe & Aaron Merit

Rava — and some say Rabbi Yochanan — states: *gadol shene'emar beMoshe veAharon yoter mishene'emar beAvraham*. "Greater is what is said of Moses and Aaron than what is said of Abraham." The word "greater" here means more profound in its humility. Abraham called himself *afar va'efer* — dust and ashes — which at least is something. Moses and Aaron said *venachnu mah* — "What are we?" — nothing at all. Nothing is less than dust and ashes.

Rava — and some say Rabbi Yochanan — further states: *ein ha'olam mitkayem ela bishvil Moshe veAharon* — the world endures only on account of Moses and Aaron. The proof is a *gezeirah shavah*: the verse says *venachnu mah*, and the verse about creation says *toleh eretz al belimah* (Job 26:7) — God suspends the earth on *belimah*, which is read as *beli mah*, on "nothingness." Moses and Aaron said *mah* — we are nothing — and the world is suspended on that same *mah*, on their nothingness, on the merit of their humility.

A question arises: we invoke *zechut avot* on Rosh Hashana, but not typically *zechut Moshe veAharon*. The distinction is worth drawing carefully. *Zechut avot* is deeply intertwined with *brit avot* — the covenant God established with the Patriarchs, and God's repeated declaration *zacharti et briti*. It is a relational concept rooted in the foundational relationship between God and the Jewish people. The notion of *zechut tzadikim* — the merit of the righteous — is a different concept entirely, more akin to a spiritual endowment that future generations inherit and draw upon. Both are genuine concepts in the *gemara*, but they operate in different registers.

This passage also raises the question of the extreme nature of the humility being praised here. It is worth pausing over the fact that the *gemara* presents *venachnu mah* as surpassing *afar va'efer* in its humility — as if Abraham's expression was itself insufficient. The Rambam, deeply influenced by Aristotelian ethics in most areas of character development, makes an explicit exception when it comes to humility. Whereas Aristotle counseled a golden mean between pride and self-abasement, the Rambam in his *Hilchos Deos* and *Peirush HaMishnayot* explicitly calls for going to the extreme: *me'od me'od hevei shefal ruach*. This is not a Western value, and the *gemara* here reflects precisely that non-Western orientation. At the same time, this kind of humility does not mean denying one's accomplishments or pretending they did not occur. *Moshe anav mikol adam* — Moses was the most humble of all men — yet Moses did not deny what he had done. The humility the *gemara* speaks of is fundamentally about one's orientation toward God: not attributing greatness to oneself, not seeing oneself as the center of attention, acknowledging that whatever one has accomplished flows from gifts not of one's own making.

### Silencing Self

Rabbi Ila'a says: *ein ha'olam mitkayem ela bishvil mi shebolem et atzmo bish'at merivah* — the world endures only on account of one who stops his mouth at a time of quarrel, who does not give back an angry retort when someone says something hurtful. The proof-text is again *toleh eretz al belimah* — the world is suspended on *belimah*, on the one who is *bolem*, who seals his mouth.

Rabbi Abbahu says: *mi shemesim atzmo k'mi she'eino* — the world endures on account of one who makes himself as if he does not exist. The verse cited is *umitachat zero'ot olam* (Deuteronomy 33:27) — those who place themselves *mitachat*, underneath, who allow others to walk past them, they are the *zero'ot olam*, the everlasting support of the world.

### Valley Drasha

Rabbi Yitzchak asks: what is the meaning of the verse *ha'umnam elem tzedek tedaberun, mesharim tishpetu bnei adam* — "Is it indeed in silence that you speak righteousness; with justice do you judge the children of men?" (Psalms 58:2)? The *drasha* reads *ha'umnam* not as "in truth" but as a related form of *umanut* — craft, vocation. *Ma umanuto shel adam ba'olam hazeh?* What should be the primary endeavor of a person in this world? *Yasim atzmo ke'ilem* — make yourself like a mute person. Swallow the retort, don't engage in every quarrel.

One might ask: should one be silent even regarding *divrei Torah* — matters of Torah? The *gemara* answers: the verse says *tzedek tedaberun* — speak righteousness. Torah is called *tzedek*, and therefore one must speak up for Torah. And should one feel a sense of pride or self-satisfaction if he successfully defended the honor of Torah in an argument? Here the verse adds *mesharim tishpetu bnei adam* — and Rashi explains *mesharim* through the word *mishor*, a plain or valley: make yourself like a valley, low and level. Even when you must speak up for Torah, do not emerge from that exchange with a sense of superiority or self-righteousness.

## Ir Hanidachat & Kissing

### Ir Hanidachat Dust

Rabbi Zeira — and some say Rabba bar Yirmia — states: *mechasin be'afar Ir HaNidachat* — one may cover the blood using the dust of an *ir hanidachat*, a city condemned for communal idolatry, whose entire contents are to be burned. The question that immediately presents itself is that objects of an *ir hanidachat* are *isurei hana'ah* — forbidden for use or benefit — and we have been assuming throughout this *sugya* that one may not use objects that are *asurim behana'ah* even for the purpose of performing a *mitzvah*.

### Dirt vs. Ashes

*Ziri* clarifies: when we speak of *afar ir hanidachat*, we do not mean the ashes of things that were burned inside the city. Earlier in the *gemara* the words *afar* and *efer* were shown to be used interchangeably in certain contexts, so one might have assumed this refers to the burned residue. No — we are speaking of the ordinary dirt of the condemned city, not of its ashes.

### Disconnected Items

Why is the dirt of the city not itself forbidden in benefit? The verse says, *ve'et kol shelalah tikbotz el toch rechovah vesarafta* — "gather all of its spoil into the public square and burn it" (Deuteronomy 13:17). The principle derived is: only that which requires merely gathering and burning is included in the prohibition. The dirt of the city, however, would require uprooting (*telisha*), then gathering, then burning — it is not something that one simply gathers and burns. Moreover, there is a general principle that objects still connected to the ground cannot become *asurim*: if one worshipped the ground as *avodah zarah*, the ground itself does not become forbidden. The verse does say *vehayetah tel olam lo tibaneh* — the city shall never be rebuilt — but that does not extend to an outright prohibition on deriving all benefit from the soil. Accordingly, the dirt of an *ir hanidachat* is not *asur behana'ah*, and one may use it for *kisuy hadam*.

### Mitzvot Lav Lehanot

Rava, however, takes a different position. He holds that we are speaking of the ashes of objects that were burned, and yet the covering is valid. His reasoning: *mitzvot lav lehanot nitnu* — *mitzvot* were not given for the purpose of deriving benefit. This principle is not primarily a metaphysical statement about the nature of *mitzvot*; it is, more precisely, a statement about the nature of *isurei hana'ah*. When the Torah prohibits benefit from an object, it prohibits a certain kind of real-world, physical or monetary benefit — not religious or spiritual benefit. Fulfilling a *mitzvah* is not the kind of benefit that the prohibition of *hana'ah* is meant to prevent.

### Benefit Definition

To illustrate: there is a question whether one may study from a cadaver in order to acquire medical knowledge — is that "deriving benefit" from a *met*? The general answer is no, because the prohibition of *hana'ah* addresses physical or monetary benefit, not intellectual benefit. Similarly, the credit one receives for performing a *mitzvah* — the spiritual fulfillment — is not the kind of benefit that *isurei hana'ah* target. One can therefore, according to Rava, even use ashes from an *ir hanidachat* to cover blood.

It is worth noting a distinction that arises at the margins: smell is generally considered a form of physical pleasure and is treated as a form of *hana'ah* on some level. But aesthetic or auditory pleasure is not biblically prohibited. When we are speaking of objects with *issur hana'ah*, the operative definition of forbidden benefit is firmly in the domain of the physical and the monetary.

## Shofar & Lulav

### Shofar/Lulav Prohibition

Ravina was sitting and repeating this teaching of Rava. Rav Rechumi raised an objection. A *baraita* teaches: *shofar shel avodah zarah lo yitka bo* — do not blow a *shofar* of *avodah zarah*. Similarly, *lulav shel avodah zarah lo yitol* — do not take a *lulav* of *avodah zarah*. Both prohibitions exist as initial instructions.

### Non-fulfillment

The *gemara* initially understands the language of "do not" (*lo yitka*, *lo yitol*) to imply that if one did perform these actions, one would not have fulfilled the *mitzvah* — and this seems to be a direct contradiction of Rava's principle. If *mitzvot lav lehanot nitnu*, then using these *isurei hana'ah* objects for a *mitzvah* should be permitted, and one should fulfill the obligation. The *gemara* notes that there is also a *baraita* that says explicitly: *taka lo yatza, natal lo yatza* — if one did blow, one did not fulfill the obligation; if one did take the *lulav*, one did not fulfill the obligation.

One might ask: if this is a contradiction to Rava's position, why doesn't the *gemara* simply say that one does fulfill the *mitzvah* and simultaneously transgresses the prohibition of *hana'ah*? The answer is that when the law presents a choice — either you fulfilled the *mitzvah* and transgressed, or you didn't fulfill the *mitzvah* and didn't transgress — we prefer the latter. It is better not to fulfill the *mitzvah* than to both sort of fulfill it and transgress. Hence the presumption in the *baraita* is non-fulfillment.

### Shiur Distinction

Rav Ashi resolves the apparent contradiction. *Hachi hashta* — how can you compare these cases? *Hasam shiura ba'ina* — there, by *shofar* and *lulav*, a *shiur* is required. A *shofar* must be a certain minimum size; a *lulav* must be a certain minimum length. An object dedicated to *avodah zarah* is subject to the rule *kol ha'omed lisreifah kesaruf dami* — everything that is destined to be burned is considered already burned. Or, framing it differently without relying on that principle: part of what a *shiur* demands is not merely a quantitative threshold, but that the object carry some significance. An object that is supposed to be destroyed — that is slated for the flames — has no significance whatsoever. It therefore cannot serve as a proper *mitzvah* object, not because of the *issur hana'ah*, but because its destined destruction undermines its halachic significance as an object.

### Blood Covering Logic

Here, by *kisuy hadam*, the situation is entirely different: *kol mah demichatat malei lechisui* — the more it is burned or ground up, the better it serves for covering the blood. The material used to cover blood has no requirement of *shiur* and no requirement of significance. Dirt, ashes, and excrement are all valid materials. The object used for covering has no independent halachic status as a *mitzvah* object in the way a *shofar* or *lulav* does. Therefore, the fact that it is slated for burning is no disqualification.

Rashi and Tosafot add a further dimension. Even in the case of *shofar* and *lulav*, the *gemara* indicated that one should not use them even *lechatchila* — initially — and even where the initial prohibition was resolved, there might still remain a concern of *bizuyot alav*, of treating the *mitzvah* in a disparaging manner, if one were to use an object that had been an object of *avodah zarah*. However, for *kisuy hadam*, no such concern arises. The material used to cover blood does not function as a *mitzvah* object in any dignified or formal sense. Dirt is dirt; the covering material does not require *kavod* as a *tashmish mitzvah*. There is therefore no reason to say that using dirt that was once the ground of an idolatrous site is a *bizayon* to the *mitzvah* — and if it was the actual ground itself that was worshipped, there would still be no problem using that soil for *kisuy hadam*.

### Church Conversion

This analysis has direct practical resonance today: there are many occasions when churches are converted into synagogues. The question of what may be used and what is prohibited within such a building — whether the *aron kodesh*, furnishings, the structure itself — is extensively discussed in *halacha*. God willing, when we reach the third *perek* of Megillah, where this topic arises, we will have the opportunity to explore it in depth.

## Gid HaNasheh Intro

### Gid HaNasheh Scope

We now turn to the new *perek* and the prohibition of *gid hanasheh*. The *mishna* opens by establishing the broad applicability of the prohibition: *noheig ba'aretz uvechutz la'aretz* — it applies both in the Land of Israel and outside it; *bifnei habayit veshelo bifnei habayit* — whether the Temple stands or not; and *bechullin uvemukdashim* — whether the animal is non-sanctified or a sanctified offering.

It is worth pausing to note the dramatic preamble that the sequence of this chapter represents. The *sugya* has been progressing through the entire process of preparing meat for consumption: first, the *shechita* had to be performed correctly; then one had to check for *tereifot*; then one had to determine whether there was a fetus in the womb; then, following *shechita*, one had to cover the blood if the animal was a *chayah* or a bird, not a *behemah*; and earlier, the prohibition of *shechting oto ve'et bno* on the same day had to be heeded. Now, having gotten through all of that, there remains one more prohibition before the meat may be eaten: the *gid hanasheh* must be removed. And following *gid hanasheh*, the *perek* after this will bring us to *basar bechalav*. It is curious, incidentally, that there is no *perek* directly dedicated to the removal of blood or the removal of *chelev* — perhaps because *chelev* was considered sufficiently obvious to identify and the blood-removal process sufficiently well known, but their absence from explicit *mishnayot* is notable.

### Anatomy & Location

The *mishna* continues: *beyerech hayamin uveyerech hasmol* — the prohibition applies to both the right and the left thigh. This will be the subject of debate. *Ve'eino noheig be'of* — it does not apply to birds. The reason is *mipnei she'ein lo kaf* — a bird does not have the *kaf hayarech*, the rounded socket of the hip joint that is referenced in the verse *asher kaf hayarech*. While birds do have the corresponding sinew, the anatomical structure that defines the prohibition — the rounded thigh-socket — is absent in birds.

### Fetus Dispute

The *mishna* states: *venoheig bashalil* — it applies to the fetus; *Rabbi Yehudah omer eino noheig bashalil* — Rabbi Yehudah says it does not. This dispute apparently concerns a nine-month fetus, where the *tanna kamma* — presumably Rabbi Meir — holds that a nine-month fetus has its own independent halachic status, and therefore its *gid hanasheh* is the *gid hanasheh* of a separate animal. Rabbi Yehudah disagrees, holding that even a nine-month fetus remains legally part of the mother and is not yet an independent animal, and therefore its sinew carries no separate prohibition.

### Butcher Trust

The *mishna* then states: *ve'ein hatavachim ne'emanim al gid hanasheh* — butchers cannot be trusted when they say they removed the *gid hanasheh* — in the words of Rabbi Meir. This is a striking ruling, because normally the principle of *ed echad ne'eman be'isurin* applies: one reliable person is trusted regarding matters of *kashrus*, even if they have a financial interest in the outcome. The reason butchers cannot be trusted here is that removing the *gid hanasheh* is exceptionally difficult and time-consuming. The labor involved in properly tracing and removing the sinew and all its tributaries is so demanding that the concern is not simply dishonesty but the practical reality that even a well-intentioned butcher may not have done it fully. The financial temptation compounds the problem. It should be noted that even where one cannot simply take the butcher's word, the alternative is not necessarily constant supervision — it may simply mean inspection after the fact. The anatomical complexity of the *gid* makes visual inspection challenging, particularly once the meat has been cut into pieces, but the principle is that one needs more than the butcher's assurance.

### Supervision Dispute

The *sages* disagree with Rabbi Meir: *vachachamim omrim ne'emanim alav ve'al hachelev* — butchers are trusted regarding the *gid hanasheh* and also regarding the removal of *chelev*, the forbidden fat. This ruling implicitly reminds us that the prohibition of *chelev* also requires active removal, even if no *perek* of this tractate is formally dedicated to it.

### Anatomy Display

The anatomy of the *gid hanasheh* is worth pausing over. The sinew is extremely long, running down the length of the thigh. What makes its removal so laborious is not just its length but its numerous tributaries — branching extensions that penetrate deep into the surrounding tissue — as well as a secondary branch that we will discuss as the *gemara* proceeds. One can readily understand why the *gemara* frames the removal as something that even committed and well-meaning butchers may fail to complete properly.

## Gid & Sanctified

### Sacrifices Question

The *mishna*'s inclusion of *mukdashim* — sanctified offerings — in the scope of *gid hanasheh* seems, at first glance, unremarkable. Tosafot observes, however, that there ought to be a *chiddush* — a novel teaching — in each clause of the *mishna*. What new information does the inclusion of *mukdashim* convey? The fact that *gid hanasheh* applies to an animal does not disappear simply because you sanctified that animal. The prohibition was already there. Why would sanctification change anything?

### Taste Question

The answer hinges on a question that will recur throughout this entire *perek*: does the *gid hanasheh* impart taste (*yesh begidim benoten taam*), or does it not (*ein begidim benoten taam*)? The question has significant practical and theoretical implications. On the practical side: if one cooked the thigh together with the *gid hanasheh*, may one remove the *gid* afterwards and eat the surrounding meat? This depends on whether the *gid* gave off sufficient taste to render the meat forbidden. On the theoretical side: if an animal is a *korban*, its flesh is forbidden to ordinary consumption. If the *gid* has taste, then eating the *gid* of a *korban* is not only a violation of *gid hanasheh* but also a violation of the prohibition against eating from a *korban*. If the *gid* has no taste, eating it provides no actual benefit from the *korban*, in which case — like eating the horn or hoof of a *korban* — the *korban* prohibition may not be violated.

### Interpretation

One possible reading of the *mishna* is that the *tanna* holds *yesh begidim benoten taam* — the *gid* does impart taste — and the *chiddush* of *mukdashim* is therefore: since the *gid* of a *korban* has taste, eating it means benefiting from the *korban*, and the *mishna* is telling us that the prohibition of *korbanot* now applies to the *gid* as well. If that is the *chiddush*, however, the *mishna* phrased it incorrectly. It should have said: the prohibition of *mukdashim* applies even to the *gid* — not that *gid hanasheh* applies to *mukdashim*. The *mishna*'s formulation (*noheg bemukdashim*) places the emphasis on the *gid hanasheh* prohibition, not on the *mukdashim* prohibition. This suggests the *tanna* holds the opposite: *ein begidim benoten taam* — the *gid* has no taste — and therefore eating the *gid* of a *korban* does not constitute deriving benefit from the *korban*. The *chiddush* is thus: even in *mukdashim*, where the entire animal is sanctified, the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* alone applies to the *gid*, and the *mukdashim* prohibition does not.

### Taste Evidence

But can the *tanna* really hold *ein begidim benoten taam*? The *gemara* notes that the very next *mishna* in this tractate — apparently by the same *tanna* — states: *yerech shenitbashal bah gid hanasheh, im yesh bah benoten taam harei zo asurah* — if you cooked a thigh together with the *gid hanasheh* and the *gid* imparted its taste, the thigh is forbidden. This *mishna* clearly presupposes that the *gid* can and does impart taste. So the *tanna* cannot hold *ein begidim benoten taam* as a categorical principle. The *gemara* must therefore find an alternative way to explain the *chiddush* of the *mukdashim* clause.

## Fetus in Sanctified

### Fetus Context

The *gemara* proposes a new reading: *ela hacha bivladot kodashim askinan* — we are dealing here with the offspring (*vlad*) of a sanctified animal. The scenario is as follows: a female animal is sanctified as a *korban* while already pregnant, or becomes pregnant after being sanctified. The fetus grows within a sanctified mother. According to the position that *vladot kodashim bimei iman hen kedoshim* — the offspring of sanctified animals are sanctified from the moment they begin to develop in the womb — the fetus acquires *kedushat korban* from the very earliest stage of its formation.

Now, if *gid hanasheh* applies to a fetus (following the *tanna kamma* against Rabbi Yehudah), and if both prohibitions — *gid hanasheh* and *mukdashim* — arise simultaneously at the moment the fetus begins to form, then the *chiddush* is clear: one might have thought that when two prohibitions arrive at exactly the same moment, one of them will be displaced. The *mishna* teaches that both apply — the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* takes effect along with the *mukdashim* prohibition.

James raises a sharper observation: the even more powerful *chiddush* would be if the *mukdashim* prohibition arrives *first*, and only later does the *gid hanasheh* prohibition take effect — because in that case, one might invoke the principle of *ein issur chal al issur* (a later prohibition cannot take effect upon an already-existing prohibition) and argue that the *gid* prohibition fails to apply. The *gemara* will indeed arrive at precisely this scenario.

### Fetus Clarification

The *gemara* raises a difficulty with the fetus reading. The *mishna* itself, in its later clause, introduces the application of *gid hanasheh* to a *shalil* as a matter of dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehudah. The fact that it is mentioned separately at the end of the *mishna* implies that the earlier clause about *mukdashim* was not already talking about a *shalil*. The *gemara* resolves this: we should understand the *mishna* as saying that while the preceding analysis does indeed concern a fetus of a *korban*, this is itself part of the very dispute — and the reader should be aware that Rabbi Yehudah disagrees with the underlying premise that *gid hanasheh* applies to a fetus at all.

### Corpse Evidence

The *gemara* then demonstrates from a *mishna* elsewhere that the scenario where *mukdashim* precedes *gid hanasheh* is not merely hypothetical — it is anatomically real. The *mishna* in the context of a *nazir* teaches that a *nazir* becomes obligated to shave and recommence his *nezirut* upon contact with a corpse. The list in that *mishna* includes both *al hames* (the whole corpse) and *al kezayit min hames* (a *kezayit* from a corpse). The question was asked there: if a *kezayit* suffices to generate *tum'ah*, then surely the whole corpse — which is many times larger — should also. Why state both? Rabbi Yochanan answers: the case of the whole corpse is necessary because there can exist a corpse that is smaller than a *kezayit*. How? A very early miscarriage — *lo nikre'u eivarav begidim*, the limbs have not yet been formed with sinews. At that stage, the entire fetus may be smaller than a *kezayit*.

What is critical for our discussion is the embedded teaching: at the very early stages of fetal development, the *gidim* — the sinews — do not yet exist. This means that when a fetus begins to develop within a sanctified mother, *kedushat korban* attaches to it from the outset, but the *gid hanasheh* prohibition cannot yet apply because the sinew does not yet physically exist. The order is therefore precisely what James anticipated: first the *korban* prohibition, then, later, the *gid* prohibition.

### Gid Timing Question

This creates a conceptual difficulty: if the *gid hanasheh* prohibition is supposed to apply to this fetus, but at the moment the fetus is sanctified the *gid* does not yet exist — how and when does the *gid* prohibition take effect? And once the *korban* prohibition is already in place, can the *gid* prohibition come and take effect upon it, given the principle of *ein issur chal al issur*?

## Ein Issur Chal

### Principle Stated

The principle of *ein issur chal al issur* states that a second prohibition cannot take effect upon an object already subject to a prior prohibition. If an object is already forbidden, a subsequent *issur* cannot "land" on it — it has nowhere to add, since the object is already prohibited.

### Application to Gid

The *gemara* arrives directly at this question in the scenario under discussion. The fetus is first sanctified as a *korban*. Then — anatomically and developmentally — the *gid hanasheh* comes into existence. At the moment the *gid* forms, can the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* take effect? Or does *ein issur chal al issur* prevent it, since the fetus is already *asur* as a *korban*?

### Pre-Sinai Weight

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty: *af al gav de'issur mukdashim kodem, asi issur gid chal alaihu* — even though the *korban* prohibition comes first, the *gid hanasheh* prohibition still takes effect. The reason: *sheken issuro noheg bivnei Noach* — the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* carries a special weight because it applied to *bnei Noach*. More precisely: it is not that *gid hanasheh* currently applies to non-Jews, but that it was in force *before Matan Torah*, prohibited to our ancestors when they were still in the category of *bnei Noach*. This pre-Sinaitic status gives it a unique weight — a kind of categorical primacy — that allows it to take effect even when a subsequent prohibition has already landed on the object.

### Tosafot Question

Tosafot raises a sharp question: the whole analysis assumes that the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* applies to the fetus while it is still developing inside the sanctified mother. But we know from the earlier discussion of the *mishna* that there is a broad consensus — including both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah — that if the mother is *shechted*, the fetus is treated as a limb of the mother and the *gid* of the fetus carries no independent prohibition. So how can we say that the *gid* of the fetus is prohibited by *gid hanasheh* at all, given that as long as the fetus is in the mother's womb and the mother is eventually *shechted*, the fetus-*gid* will be permitted?

### Retroactive Application

Tosafot answers that the determination of whether the fetus is treated as an independent entity or as a limb of the mother depends on what ultimately happens to the mother. If the mother is *shechted* while the fetus is inside her, the *shechita* of the mother extends to the fetus, which is then treated retroactively as a limb of the mother throughout its development — and the *gid* prohibition never applied. But if the mother was never *shechted* — whether because the fetus was born alive after nine months, or because it was miscarried, or because it was removed — then since the mother's *shechita* never encompassed the fetus, the fetus is regarded retroactively as having been an independent entity throughout. In that case, looking backwards, the *gid* prohibition applied from the moment the sinew came into existence within the womb. The independence or dependence of the fetus is not determined at any single frozen moment during gestation, but is resolved by what ultimately happens at the time of the mother's *shechita* — or its absence.

---

---

# Hullin 91

## Gid Hanasheh: Both or On…

### Mishna vs. Rabbi Yehuda

We begin on 91b, picking up the discussion of whether the *gid hanasheh* applies to both thighs or only one. Our mishna rules that it applies to both, and this is the normative *halacha*. The Gemara opens by noting that our mishna does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, as a *braita* teaches: Rabbi Yehuda says the prohibition applies only to one of the thighs, and *hada'at machra'at* — the reasoning inclines, or the Torah's reasoning indicates — that it is the right one. It is worth noting in passing that the phrase *da'at machra'at* is one of the early appearances of the concept later associated with *da'at Torah*, though the meaning here is quite different: it simply means that if one examines the Torah carefully, the evidence points to the right side.

### Certainty vs. Doubt

This leads to the *ibaya*: is it *pshita* to Rabbi Yehuda — does he know with certainty which thigh is prohibited? Or does he merely say *sfukei m'sapka lei* — that he genuinely doubts whether it is the right or the left, and the phrase "the reasoning inclines" means only that logic leans in one direction without definitive evidence? This question has real *halachic* consequences, as we will see.

### Korban Pesach Proof

The Gemara attempts to resolve this from a *braita* concerning the *korban pesach*: the bones, sinews, and any *notar* — leftover meat — must be burned on the sixteenth of Nisan. Burning on the fifteenth is impossible because one may not burn *kodashim* on *yom tov*, even *pasul kodashim*, so one waits until after *yom tov*.

The Gemara then asks: what is the *chiddush* of mentioning the sinews? If they are edible sinews, one should simply eat them — why burn them? And if they happen to be left over, they are already *notar* — the verse has already covered them. The Gemara concludes that the reference must be to inedible sinews, such as those in the neck. But then another problem arises: if they are not meat at all — if they are physically inedible — they carry no obligation of eating in the context of the *korban*, and therefore they are not *notar*. They should simply be discarded; why must they be burned?

### Rav Chisda's Answer

Rav Chisda resolves this: the *chiddush* refers specifically to the *gid hanasheh* according to Rabbi Yehuda. In this case, the sinew is not inedible for physical reasons but because it is halachically prohibited. Now the Gemara from the previous daf is relevant: something prohibited by law does not carry the *mitzvah* of eating within the *korban* context, and therefore it should not be *notar* either — just discard it.

But here the Gemara explains: *if* Rabbi Yehuda holds that there is genuine doubt about which thigh is the *gid hanasheh*, the case becomes clear. You cannot eat either *gid* because one of them is definitively the *gid hanasheh* — though you do not know which one. That is precisely the situation: one is the quarter, so to speak, and the other is the *gid*. You cannot eat the right or the left because one of them is certainly prohibited. But you must also burn them, because the one that is not the *gid hanasheh* was supposed to be eaten, and since you do not know which that is, you must burn both rather than eat either. This creates the unusual scenario of passively transgressing the prohibition of *lo totiru* — leaving meat over from the *korban* until morning — rather than actively transgressing the prohibition of *gid hanasheh*. The principle applies: it is preferable to transgress passively than actively.

This scenario makes sense only if Rabbi Yehuda harbors genuine doubt. If he *knew* which side was prohibited, there would be no difficulty: eat the permitted one, discard the prohibited one. There would be no grounds for burning anything.

### Avika's Resolution

Avika bar Chanina offers a different resolution. Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda does in fact know which side is the *gid hanasheh* — it is definitively the right. The *braita* about burning, however, is dealing with a case where you originally knew which was the right thigh and which was the left, but then they became mixed up. In such a scenario, even if Rabbi Yehuda knows with certainty that it is the right *gid* that is prohibited, since the two *gidim* are now indistinguishable, you cannot eat either — and since one of them was obligated to be eaten, you burn both. This resolution preserves the view that Rabbi Yehuda has no doubt about which side is prohibited, while still explaining why burning is required.

---

## Why Burn the Gid?

### Rav Ashi: The Fat

We now turn to the top of 91a for two alternative explanations that have nothing to do with Rabbi Yehuda's position. Rav Ashi says: *lo nitzrecha ela leshumno* — the *chiddush* of burning the sinew of the *korban pesach* concerns not the *gid hanasheh* itself but the fat surrounding it. The term used here is *shuman* rather than *chelev*, because the fat around the *gid hanasheh* is not forbidden *chelev*; at most it is rabbinically restricted. A *braita* supports this: *shumno mutar* — the fat around the *gid* is biblically permitted — but *Yisrael kedoshim nahagu bo issur* — because the Jewish people are holy, they have adopted the practice of refraining from it.

The *chiddush* is therefore as follows: you did not eat this fat because of widespread *minhag*, but since the Torah permits it biblically, it legally remains *notar* — meat that was supposed to be eaten — and it must therefore be burned rather than discarded. This case raises a striking observation: a *minhag* is causing a person to passively transgress a biblical prohibition of *notar*. The Gemara itself does not raise this as a difficulty and simply takes for granted that the *minhag* stands and the consequence is burning rather than eating. Nevertheless, the tension is genuinely remarkable, particularly since one could construct a scenario where someone has not yet eaten a *kezayit* of the *korban pesach*, and the only remaining meat is this rabbinically restricted fat — in which case the question of whether to eat it to fulfill the *mitzvah* becomes exceedingly pointed.

### Ravina: Two Sinews

Ravina offers yet another answer. He cites Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *shnei gidim hem* — there are actually two sinews running through the thigh. The inner one, *pnimi samuch l'etzem* — close to the thigh bone — is the biblical *gid hanasheh*, and one who eats it is *chayav*, liable for the biblical transgression. The outer one, *samuch l'basar* — closer to the fleshy part of the thigh on its outer side — is only rabbinically prohibited, and one is not biblically liable for eating it.

Looking at a diagram of the thigh's anatomy, this distinction becomes clearer: the inner sinew running alongside the thigh bone for the full length of the thigh is the biblical *gid hanasheh*; the outer sinew — known as the *gid hachitzon* — which runs only partway down is the rabbinic one. According to Ravina, the *braita* about burning the sinew of the *korban pesach* concerns this outer, rabbinic sinew. Since the Torah biblically permits it — one is merely rabbinically forbidden — it remains legally obligated to be eaten and therefore qualifies as *notar*, requiring burning rather than simple disposal. The rabbis said not to eat it, so you did not; but since the Torah says you could have eaten it, it is *notar* and must be burned.

This again raises the question of a *minhag* — or here a rabbinic enactment — causing a passive biblical transgression of *notar*, and even the possibility of someone who has not yet fulfilled his *kezayit* of *korban pesach* being left with only this outer sinew. The Gemara does not address these questions but proceeds to the next stage of the discussion.

---

## Which Side? Right or Bot…

### Eating Both Thighs

We return to the core question: does Rabbi Yehuda know which side is the prohibited *gid*, or does he not? The Gemara cites another source that was encountered just a few days earlier. If one ate a *kezayit* of the *gid* from the right thigh and a *kezayit* from the left thigh, the Rabbis say he receives eighty lashes — two sets, one for each transgression — assuming he was warned separately for each. Rabbi Yehuda says he receives only forty lashes, one set.

The Gemara now examines the logic. If Rabbi Yehuda knows which side is prohibited — and we will see it is the right — then the ruling is straightforward: you transgressed on the right and receive one set of lashes; you did not transgress on the left and receive no lashes there. That is perfectly coherent.

But if Rabbi Yehuda genuinely doubts which side is prohibited, a different problem arises. How can you receive even one set of lashes? Before eating each *gid*, the warning (*hatra'ah*) would have been doubtful — *hatra'at safek* — because at the moment of warning, you did not know whether this particular act would constitute a transgression. Rabbi Yehuda himself, as established from a *braita*, holds that *hatra'at safek lo shemah hatra'ah* — a doubtful warning does not count as warning. The *braita* discusses a man who does not know which of two men is his father, strikes one and then the other, curses one and then the other. Rabbi Yehuda rules that if done sequentially, he is exempt, because even though by the end we know he has certainly struck his father, before each individual act the warning could not be unequivocal.

This would mean that if Rabbi Yehuda truly doubts which *gid* is prohibited, no lashes could be administered at all — not even forty. The ruling of forty lashes, then, is difficult to explain on the assumption of doubt.

The Gemara resolves this tension: *hai tanna savar lah ke'idach tanna deRabbi Yehuda* — the *tanna* who recorded the ruling of forty lashes holds by a different version of Rabbi Yehuda's position, one that says *hatra'at safek shemah hatra'ah* — even doubtful warning suffices, as long as by the end of the act we know a transgression occurred. The *braita* on *notar* supports this: the verse says do not leave over; if you do, burn it. The Torah gave a positive commandment after the negative, signaling that there are no lashes for the transgression — Rabbi Yehuda's view — because the positive *mitzvah* of burning provides a remedy. Rabbi Yaakov disagrees and says the reason for exemption from lashes is simply that it is a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — a passive transgression, which never carries lashes. Notably, neither gives *hatra'at safek* as his reason, suggesting that in this context Rabbi Yehuda does not object to doubtful warning as grounds to exempt from lashes. Accordingly, the ruling of forty lashes can coexist with Rabbi Yehuda's doubt about which side is prohibited.

### Two Animals Scenario

The Gemara attempts one more proof, and this one is quite elegant. The source states: if one ate two *gidei hanasheh* from two thighs from two different animals — meaning the same *side* from two separate animals — the Rabbis say eighty lashes and Rabbi Yehuda says forty. The Gemara observes: why did the source need to specify two different animals? Why not simply present the scenario of the right and left from the same animal? The only reason to insist on two animals is if it matters which side we are discussing — because if both sides were equally prohibited, any two *gidim* would suffice for the scenario, including right and left from the same animal. The fact that the source took care to specify two animals of the same side demonstrates that this scenario was constructed specifically to satisfy Rabbi Yehuda's position that only one particular side is prohibited, and to ensure that both *gidim* in the scenario are indisputably forbidden even according to him.

This proves, even before analyzing the ruling, that Rabbi Yehuda knows which side is the prohibited one. The scenario *had* to be drawn this way to make it work within his framework.

Now, if Rabbi Yehuda knows the prohibited side and both of these *gidim* are from that side, why does he give only forty lashes? One might expect eighty. The Gemara answers: the case involves two *gidim* each of which lacks a *kezayit* individually. The *braita* records a debate: the Rabbis hold that eating an entire *gid*, even if it lacks a *kezayit*, constitutes a full transgression — this is the principle of *beriah*, that eating a whole entity creates liability regardless of volume, since the prohibition is against eating *the* sinew, not a quantity of it. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: one is only liable if a *kezayit* is present. In this scenario, each *gid* lacks a *kezayit*, but together they contain a *kezayit*. According to the Rabbis, eating two whole *gidim* is two transgressions — eighty lashes. According to Rabbi Yehuda, since neither individually contained a *kezayit*, there is effectively only one combined transgression — forty lashes. The debate about right and left is deliberately bracketed, and what is isolated here is the separate dispute about the quantity required.

We have now established that Rabbi Yehuda knows which side is the prohibited one. The remaining question is: which side, and why?

### Rabah: Textual Proof

Rabah derives it from the verse itself. The Torah uses the phrase *asher al kaf hayarech* — that which is on the *kaf* of the thigh — with the definite article ה (*hei*): *ha-yarech*, *the* thigh, not simply *a* thigh. The use of the definite article singles out one particular thigh, and the assumption is that we attribute primacy to the right side, which is called *hamyumenet shebaYarech* — the more important or distinguished of the thighs. Thus the right *gid* is the prohibited one.

### Rabbis' Explanation

The Rabbis, who hold that both thighs are prohibited, explain the definite article differently. They read *ha-yarech* not as singling out one side but as identifying which of the two sinews within each thigh is the biblical *gid hanasheh* — namely, the one that extends (*pashit*) across the full length of the thigh, *lihafukei chitzon d'lo* — to the exclusion of the outer sinew that does not traverse the entire thigh. Thus the verse is describing the nature of the sinew rather than specifying a particular side.

### Wrestling Narrative

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi offers a different proof for the right side, deriving it directly from the narrative of the wrestling match. The Torah says *behe'avko imo* — in his grappling with him. The word suggests, in the manner of one who embraces another (*chovek*), that the angel was grasping Jacob from behind, with his arm going around Jacob's right side. As Rashi explains: when you reach your arm around someone in a wrestling grip, your right arm reaches your opponent's right side. Therefore, the *gid* that was displaced was on Jacob's right thigh. The fact that the wrestling match lasted the entire night and the displacement apparently occurred toward its conclusion makes the reconstruction of their physical positions somewhat speculative, but that is the reasoning the Gemara presents.

### Non-Jew Narrative

Rabbi Yishmael bar Nachmani offers another approach: *ke'oved kochavim nidmeh lo* — the angel appeared to Jacob in the guise of a non-Jew, perhaps representing Esav. There is a ruling from elsewhere (*Avodah Zarah*) that if a Jew is walking with a non-Jew on the road, he should position the non-Jew on his right — *toflo leyamino* — so that the non-Jew cannot easily draw a sword with his dominant right hand and strike. This was a precaution given the real dangers of life under Roman occupation. Since the angel appeared on Jacob's right, he had access to Jacob's right thigh — which is why the right *gid* was affected.

This is a striking derivation: we are determining which *gid* was displaced by reconstructing how two people would have stood at the outset of the encounter, even though the actual displacement occurred at the very end of a night-long fight.

### Torah Sage Narrative

An alternative tradition: Rav Shmuel bar Acha in the name of Rava bar Ulla says the angel appeared to Jacob *ketalmid chacham nidmeh lo* — as a Torah sage. There is a principle that one who walks to the right of his teacher is an *am ha'aretz*, a boor. Out of deference, Jacob would have positioned himself to the angel's left, placing the angel on the right. This again placed Jacob's right thigh within reach of the angel.

Once more, as with the previous account, this describes the initial positioning and does not easily explain what occurred at the climactic moment of the fight — but these are the Torah sage's terms of analysis.

### Both Sides Moved

The Rabbis, who hold that both thighs are prohibited, explain the narrative differently: *me'achorei ata ve'nashyei* — the angel came from behind Jacob and attacked from the rear, displacing both *gidim* simultaneously. *Ve'nashyei betarvaihu* — he caused both sides to move. This is what underlies the Rabbis' ruling that both thighs are prohibited.

The Gemara then asks: what do the Rabbis do with the verse *behe'avko imo*, which Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi used to derive the right side? They use it differently: *melamed she'alu avak margelotam ad kisei ha'kavod* — it teaches that the dust (*avak*) raised by their feet during the struggle rose all the way to the heavenly throne. The verse is linked to another verse describing God's throne, *ve'anan avak raglav* — a cloud of dust beneath His feet. For the Rabbis, the word *be'he'avko* relates not to grasping but to the cloud of dust, signaling the cosmic significance of the struggle. Jacob and Esav, in the broader rabbinic framework, represent the perennial religious and historical confrontation between Israel and Rome — or later, Christianity — and perhaps the image of dust rising to the heavenly throne captures the eternal, transcendent nature of that struggle.

---

## Etymology & Sources

### Nasheh: Moved

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks: why is the sinew called the *gid hanasheh*? What does the word *nasheh* mean? He answers: *shenasha mimekomo* — it moved from its place, it was displaced. The word *nasheh* denotes removal or movement, as evidenced by a verse in another context: *nashta gevuratam hayu lenashim* — their strength has been removed, they became like women. The name *gid hanasheh*, then, memorializes the fact that the sinew was dislodged in the course of Jacob's struggle.

### Jacob's Legacy

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina connects the *gid hanasheh* to a verse in Yeshayahu: *davar shalach Adonai beYaakov venafal beYisrael* — a matter God sent through Jacob, and it fell among the Jewish people. The *davar* — the matter or thing — sent through Jacob is the *gid hanasheh*, the only prohibition that we have specifically inherited through Jacob, apart from *davening maariv* according to another Gemara. The second half of the verse, *venafal beYisrael*, describes how this practice spread and became universal among the entire Jewish people, originating with Jacob himself but becoming the obligation of all Israel.

### Joseph & Brothers

Rav Yosef bar Rabbi Chanina expounds another verse: when Joseph instructed his household manager to slaughter an animal and prepare the meal for his brothers, the verse says *tevo'ach tevach ve-hachen* — slaughter and prepare. The *drash* reads *para lahen beit ha-shechita* — expose to them the place of slaughtering so they can inspect and confirm the *shechita* was performed properly. And *ve-hachen* — prepare the meat: *tol gid hanasheh bifneihem* — remove the *gid hanasheh* in their presence. Why specifically in their presence? Because, as we learned in the first *mishna*, one cannot simply trust a butcher to remove the *gid hanasheh*; it must be done visibly. This reading fits with the opinion that the sons of Jacob were already obligated in the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* — *gid hanasheh ne'esar livnei Noach* — meaning not all of humanity, but specifically Jacob's sons, before they formally became the Jewish people at *Matan Torah*.

One could ask how it helps that the slaughter was performed by Egyptians, since *shechitat nochri* is generally invalid. Perhaps the answer is that since everyone present — slaughterer and eaters alike — was at that historical moment a non-Jew in terms of formal *halachic* status, the considerations differ. In any case, the picture conjured by this *drash* is extraordinary: Joseph, concealing his identity, nevertheless ensuring that his brothers can verify every aspect of the *kashrut* of the meal he sets before them.

---

## Jacob's Righteousness

### Small Vessels

The Gemara now turns to a series of *aggadic* passages about Jacob, spending the remainder of the daf on the narrative surrounding his wrestling match with the angel. The Torah says *vayivater Yaakov levado* — Jacob was left alone. Why was he alone? Rabbi Elazar teaches: *she-nishtayer al pachim ketanim* — he had gone back to retrieve some small, inexpensive pottery vessels that had been forgotten when the household crossed. The *chiddush* is formulated thus: *mikan le-tzaddikim she-chaviv aleihem mamonam yoter mi-gufam* — from here we learn that the righteous care for their property more than their own bodies, in that Jacob was willing to remain alone and exposed to danger in order to retrieve some trivial vessels. Why such care over small things? *She-ein poshtim yedeihem be-gezel* — because they never reach out their hands to take what is not theirs. Those who respect property — their own and others' — treat every object with conscientiousness. The person who says "it's only a little thing, leave it behind" may not be the same person who is careful about the line between his and another's.

This is worth pausing over, because there is a conventional reading of the verse *u-vchol me'odecha* — with all your possessions — that treats excessive attachment to property as somehow secondary to other virtues. Yet here, the *tzaddik*'s care for even small possessions is presented as a mark of his character, not a failing.

### Not Alone at Night

Rabbi Abba bar Kahana derives from the same episode — Jacob left alone as the angel arrived — that a Torah sage should not go out alone at night. *Tosafot* notes that there is also the concern of *mazikim*, harmful spiritual forces that attack Torah sages in particular; in any event, night carries greater danger, whether from people or from supernatural forces, and the angel's insistence on leaving at daybreak is itself a sign that the night domain operates differently. Three additional proof-texts are adduced: Naomi knew Boaz would remain in the field overnight rather than walk home alone; Abraham rose early in the morning before setting out; Jacob's brothers were sent to check on the flocks during daylight; and the verse *vayizrach lo ha-shemesh* — the sun shone upon him — tells us that the fight with the angel only ended at sunrise, meaning the entire episode was a nighttime event.

### Folded Geography

There is a narrative about how Jacob came to sleep at this particular place. The Torah says *vayeitzei Yaakov mi-Beer Sheva vayelech Charana* — Jacob left Beer Sheva and went toward Charan — and then says *vayifga ba-makom* — he encountered the place. The word *vayifga* sounds like an unexpected encounter. The Gemara explains: Jacob actually did arrive in Charan, and then realized he had passed by the place where his forefathers had prayed — identified with *Har ha-Bayit* in Jerusalem, since the location of the ladder (*sha'ar ha-shamayim*, the gateway of heaven) is understood by the Rabbis to be none other than the Temple Mount — and had not stopped to pray there. He said: *efshar avarti al makom she-hitpalelu avotai va-ani lo* — how could I have passed the very place where my fathers prayed and not done so myself? He turned to go back, and *kafetzah lei are'a* — the land leaped up to meet him. He encountered the place through *kefitzat haderech*, the miraculous folding of distance, and was suddenly back at the holy site. The word *vayifga* thus carries both the meaning of an unexpected encounter and, as the Rabbis elsewhere note, the meaning of prayer.

The apparent contradiction between the narrative happening both at *Beit El Luz* and at Jerusalem is resolved by this same folding: when Jacob turned back toward Luz, the land of Israel folded beneath him so that *Har ha-Bayit* came to meet him at Luz. Geography itself became fluid. This also connects thematically to what will come later on the daf — the land folded under Jacob as a promise that it would be easy to conquer.

### Sun Set & Rise

Once Jacob prayed at the holy site, he wanted to leave and continue to Charan. But God said: *tzaddik zeh ba le-veit meloni ve-yipatr be-lo linah* — this righteous person came to My inn, My resting place, and he would depart without spending the night? So God caused the sun to set early, compelling Jacob to stay and sleep. This is the meaning of *ki va ha-shemesh* — the sun came, it set unexpectedly — creating the conditions for the dream of the ladder.

Now, back to the verse *vayizrach lo ha-shemesh* at the end of the fight: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the sun which had set early for Jacob now rose early for Jacob — *shemesh ha-ba'ah ba'avuro zarcha ba'avuro*, the sun that had been summoned to set on his account now rose on his account. Having borrowed time from him earlier, it now repaid the debt. The sunrise ended the wrestling match. These two episodes — the sun setting early at Beit El and rising early after Penuel — form a pair, and God is the author of both.

A question arises: if Jacob arrived in Charan before setting out back toward Jerusalem, how does this interact with the tradition that Jacob *instituted* *davening maariv*, the evening prayer? The verse *ki va ha-shemesh* is cited in another context as the source for *maariv*. If the sun set miraculously early and Jacob prayed, does that constitute the institution of *maariv*? The *pashut peshat* of the Torah never mentions prayer here; the tradition of prayer is from the *midrash*, and the full details of the interplay between these traditions remain for another discussion.

### Gathering Stones

The Torah says Jacob took from *the stones of the place* — plural — and placed *the stone* under his head — singular. Rabbi Yitzchak teaches: *melamed she-niskabetzu kol osan avanim le-makom echad* — all those stones gathered themselves into one place. *Ve-chol achas ve-achas omeret: alai yanich ha-tzaddik ha-zeh rosho* — each stone declared that the righteous one should rest his head upon it. Because they all competed for the honor, *tana ve-chulan nivlu be-achas* — they were all absorbed into a single stone. That is how the many became one: they merged in shared devotion.

---

## Ladder & Throne

### Ladder Width

The Gemara asks: how wide was the ladder? *Shemonat alafim parsa'os* — eight thousand parsangs. The calculation proceeds as follows. The Torah says *malachei Elokim olim ve-yordim bo* — angels of God were ascending and descending upon it. *Olim* is plural: at least two angels were ascending. *Yordim* is plural: at least two were descending. Since these were different angels going up and coming down, and since they would have to pass each other at some point, at the moment of passing there would be four angels on the ladder simultaneously. And from another verse, a single angel's physical span is described as *k'Tarshish* — like Tarshish — and it is received tradition that Tarshish is 2,000 parsangs wide. Four angels at 2,000 parsangs each gives 8,000 parsangs.

### Jacob's Heavenly Image

The angels would ascend the ladder and look at the image above — the *diyukan shel ma'alah* — the image on the heavenly throne. In rabbinic tradition, the face of the man among the four faces on the divine throne is the face of Jacob. The word *diyukan* derives from the Greek for icon, meaning image or likeness. Then the angels would descend and see Jacob sleeping below — *ve-yordim u-mistaklin be-diyukno shel mata* — and recognize that it was the same face. Realizing that a human being bore the image inscribed on the heavenly throne, they were seized with jealousy and wanted to harm Jacob — *ba'u le-sak'nah* — to injure him.

### God's Protection

Immediately, *ve-hinei Hashem nitzav alav* — God stood over Jacob. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish notes: *ilmalei mikra kasuv iy efshar le'omro* — were it not written in the verse, it would be impossible to say such a thing. What does it mean for God to stand over someone protectively? *Ke-adam she-meif al bino* — like a person fanning over his child. The image is of a parent standing over a sleeping child, fanning away insects or the heat, hovering in attentive care. The *Maharsha* suggests it could specifically mean fanning away flies. The point is not the specific motion but the intimacy of the care: had the verse not written it, such language applied to God would be unthinkable.

### Land Folded

*Ha-aretz asher atah shochev aleha* — the land upon which you are sleeping, I will give to you. The plain meaning seems to promise only the small plot on which Jacob lay. But Rabbi Yitzchak teaches: *melamed she-kipel Hakadosh Baruch Hu kol Eretz Yisrael ve-hinichah tachat Yaakov Avinu* — God folded the entire land of Israel and placed it beneath Jacob, *she-tinoach le-hikaivesh le-vanav* — to show that it would be easily conquered by his descendants. The promise was not merely of territory; the folding of the land beneath him was a tangible sign that the conquest would be, in some sense, as natural as sleeping upon it.

---

## Angel's Turn to Sing

### Final Opportunity

Returning to the conclusion of the wrestling match: the angel says to Jacob *shalcheni ki alah ha-shachar* — send me free, for the dawn is rising. Jacob responds with a challenge: what kind of creature are you, afraid of daylight? You must be a burglar or — and here *Tosafot* in another tractate notes — a card player, someone who does his questionable work under cover of night. The angel replies: *malach ani* — I am an angel — and explains his urgency: *u-miyom she-nivreiti lo higi'a zemani lomar shirah ad achshav* — from the day I was created, I had never yet had my turn to sing praise to God until this very moment. He must go now because his opportunity has finally arrived.

### Angels' Rotations

This statement is supported by Rav Chanana citing Rav: *shalosh kitot shel malachei ha-shareit omrot shirah bechol yom* — three groups of heavenly angels take turns singing praise every day, constantly rotating. Each group gets its moment. The angel could not delay; it was finally his turn after an eternity of waiting.

Israel, by contrast, is told: *Yisrael omrim shirah bechol sha'ah* — Israel may sing to God at any hour. We pray three times a day; we are not confined to a single assigned moment. How rare is the angel's opportunity? The Gemara offers a range of opinions: once a day, once a week, once a month, once a year, once every seven years, once every fifty years, and — most dramatically — once in an entire cosmic lifetime, *pa'am achat be-olam*. This last view fits the angel's urgency best: he has waited since creation itself for this single moment of *shirah*, and he cannot miss it.

The most natural reading of these opinions is that each *individual* angel receives an opportunity at one of these intervals — not that *all* angels collectively sing only that rarely, which would be a peculiar way to describe a theology of ongoing angelic praise. The theme reinforces the contrast: any individual Jew can praise God at any moment, whereas any individual angel must wait for his assigned turn across vast stretches of time.

### Israel vs. Angels

Beyond the frequency of *shirah*, there is another dimension in which Israel surpasses the angels. *Ve-Yisrael mazkirin et Hashem achar shtei teivot* — Israel mentions the name of God after two words: *Shema Yisrael — Hashem*. The angels, by contrast, *ein mazkirin et Hashem ela achar gimel teivot* — do not mention God's name until after three words: *Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh — Hashem Tzeva'ot*. Moreover, Israel does not even begin its *shirah* above until Israel has first sung from below: *be-ron yachad kochvei voker* — with the rejoicing of the morning stars (understood as Israel), and only then *va-yari'u kol bnei Elohim* — do all the heavenly beings shout out. The angels wait for Israel to lead.

### Three Kadoshes

This last point, however, creates an apparent difficulty. The Gemara described three groups of angels: one says *kadosh*, one says *kadosh*, and one says *Kadosh Hashem Tzeva'ot*. The third group mentions God's name after only one word — not three. How is this consistent with the rule that angels mention God's name only after three words?

The Gemara resolves this: the division into three groups does not mean each group says one *kadosh* independently. Rather, the groups build upon one another: the first group says *kadosh*, the second says *kadosh kadosh*, and the third — having inherited what the previous two said — says *kadosh kadosh kadosh Hashem Tzeva'ot*, completing the full proclamation. The third group thus pronounces all three *kadoshes* and only then reaches the name of God. This preserves the rule: even the last group of angels says three words before mentioning God's name. Israel, reciting *Shema Yisrael Hashem*, mentions God's name after just two words — and in that small asymmetry, the Gemara finds the superiority of Israel over the angels.

*Chazak chazak ve-nischazek.*

---

---

# Hullin 92

## Israel vs. Angels

### Shema vs. Kadosh

The *aggadata* section of this *daf* concludes with a striking comparison between Israel and the angels in their praise of God. The *Gemara* had established that Israel surpasses the angels because Israel invokes God's name after only two words — *Shema Yisrael Hashem* — whereas the angels do so only after three, as in *Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh*, the refrain from the vision in *Yeshayahu*. One might ask, however: after *Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh*, the angels say *Baruch kevod Hashem mimkomo* — that too invokes God's name after only two words. How then does the original claim stand?

### Ophanim Hierarchy

The *Gemara* resolves this by distinguishing between classes of heavenly beings: *baruch ophanim hu de-amri lei* — it is specifically the *ophanim*, the heavenly wheels described in the prophetic vision, who say it after two words, not the ordinary *malachim*. The ordinary angels require three words of *Kadosh* before they may invoke God's name. On this reading, Israel stands above the ordinary *malachim* and is on a par with the *ophanim*, the higher class. The *Tosafot* and *Maharsha* address this hierarchy at length for those who wish to explore it further.

### License & Holiness

The *Gemara* offers an alternative answer as well: *kivan de-yehaiv reshut yehaiv* — once the angels have already begun with *Kadosh Kadosh Kadosh* and have thereby been granted license to invoke God's name, the subsequent invocation may come more readily. But the initial permission requires three acknowledgments of God's holiness. This is deeply ironic, and that irony is precisely the *Gemara*'s point. One would expect the angels, who are perpetually and intimately aware of God's holiness, to require *less* preparation before invoking His name — yet Israel does so more readily. The *Gemara* seems to suggest that Israel's awareness of how God's presence is expressed within the actual world gives them a distinctive form of closeness, or perhaps that God wishes to grant Israel a special capacity to connect to Him that the angels, who have no need of it, do not possess. The element of free will and existential struggle that defines human religiosity — in contrast to the angels' unfree servitude — hovers behind this discussion, even if the *Gemara* does not spell it out explicitly.

---

## Jacob's Struggle

### Ambiguous Pronouns

The *Gemara* now turns to the *psukim* in *Hoshea* that poetically retell the story of Yaakov's wrestling with the angel: *vayasar el malach vayuchal, bacha vayitchanen lo* — he strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and supplicated to him. The problem is that the antecedents of the pronouns are entirely ambiguous. Without knowing the backstory from *Bereishit*, one cannot determine from *Hoshea* alone who prevailed over whom, and who was weeping and supplicating to whom. *Eini yodea mi nasa sar l'mi* — I do not know who became master over whom.

### Jacob as Sar

The *Gemara* resolves the ambiguity through cross-reference. The verse in *Bereishit* — *ki sarita im Elokim* — says explicitly: *you*, Yaakov, strove with angels. *Hevei omer*: Yaakov was the one who became a *sar*, a prince, over the angel — he was the victor. And as for the weeping and supplication — *eini yodea mi bacha l'mi* — again the *Hoshea* text is unclear. But the verse *vayomer shalcheni* — "send me free" — makes clear who was in the position of begging to be released. The angel was crying and supplicating to Yaakov. This is not new exegesis so much as a demonstration that the poetic retelling in *Hoshea* cannot stand alone; it requires the narrative of *Bereishit* to be intelligible.

### Two Princes

The *Gemara* now interprets the phrase *ki sarita im Elokim ve'im anashim* — you have striven with angels and with men. *Amar Rava*: the angel hinted to Yaakov that two future authorities would descend from him — *mimenu rosh golah she-beBavel*, the head of the exile in Bavel, and *veNasi she-beEretz Yisrael*, the *Nasi* in the land of Israel. The very fact that Yaakov would need two separate figures of authority — one in Bavel and one in Israel — was itself a hint at the coming exile. Two centers of authority imply a people divided between two lands.

### Religious Authority

Where is this encoded in the verse? *Sarita im Elokim* — you will have a prince among *Elokim*. The term *Elokim* in rabbinic reading denotes judges and courts vested with legal authority; indeed, the *Torah* uses *el haElokim yavo devar shneihem* when referring to bringing a case before a court. The *Nasi* in *Eretz Yisrael* — *Rebbi Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi* — held both religious and political authority, and this corresponds to *sarita im Elokim*. *Ve'im anashim* — and with men — refers to secular authority. The *Resh Galuta*, the exilarch in Bavel, was often a figure whose household conduct was not fully consistent with *halacha*, making him a secular rather than religious authority. So the verse encodes both: a religious authority and a secular authority, both descendants of Yaakov. One may note, as was observed in the discussion, that this also provides a historical precedent for the existence of a Jewish political authority that is not itself a religious institution — a point that has not been lost on subsequent generations.

---

## Three Branches

### Sarei Ge'im

The *Gemara* moves to interpret the vision of Pharaoh's wine steward, in which a vine bore three branches — *uvagefen shlosha sarigim*. *Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Abba amar Rav*: the word *sarigim* evokes *sarei ge'im* — princes of great power and influence — who emerge from the Jewish people in every generation. Sometimes two such figures are found in Bavel and one in *Eretz Yisrael*, and sometimes the reverse — two in *Eretz Yisrael* and one in Bavel. The *Gemara* notes that the rabbis directed their gaze toward Rabana Ukva and Rabana Nechemya, the sons of Rav's daughter, apparently wealthy and prominent men of their day.

### Sarei Goyim

*Rava amar*: *sarigim* alludes to *sarei goyim* — princes of the nations, powerful non-Jewish figures *she-melamdin zechut al Yisrael bechol dor vador* — who argue merit on behalf of the Jewish people in every generation. *Rashi* interprets these as heavenly angels of the other nations who advocate on Israel's behalf before God — an interpretation reinforced by the phrase *melamdin zechut*, which typically connotes pleading a case before the divine tribunal. One might alternatively read the passage as acknowledging those human gentile figures who throughout history have occasionally come to the defense of the Jewish people, but *Rashi*'s reading of heavenly advocates carries its own poignant irony: it is the angels of the very nations that have often oppressed Israel who stand in their defense before God.

### Avos & Imahos

A *braita* presents *Rabbi Eliezer*'s interpretation: *gefen zeh ha-olam* — the vine represents the world; *shelosha sarigim zeh Avraham Yitzchak ve-Yaakov* — the three branches are the three *avos*. *Ve-hi ke-forachat alta nitzah* — the blossoming — *elu ha-imahos*, those are the matriarchs. *Hivshilu eshkeloteiha anavim* — the clusters that ripened to grapes — *elu ha-shevatim*, those are the tribes. Here at least the imagery is coherent: the vine of the world gives rise to the patriarchs, the matriarchs, and ultimately the tribes, the fruit of the whole.

### Future vs. Past

*Amar lo Rabbi Yehoshua*: but what would be the point of showing someone a vision of things that had already occurred? The *avos*, the *imahos*, the tribes — all of these already existed in Yosef's time. *De-lo omerim le-adam ela mah she-atid li-heyos* — visions are shown only of what is yet to come, not of established historical facts. Therefore, *Rabbi Yehoshua* proposes: *ela gefen zeh Torah* — the vine is the *Torah*; *shelosha sarigim eilu Moshe Aharon u-Miriam* — the three branches are Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam; *elu Sanhedrin* — the blossoming is the *Sanhedrin*; and *eilu ha-tzaddikim she-bechol dor va-dor* — the ripened grapes are the righteous of every generation. It is worth noting that Miriam appears here among the primary three who emerge from the vine of *Torah* — a striking inclusion.

This interpretation, however, leaves something to be desired thematically. While *Moshe*, *Aharon*, and *Miriam* as the foundational leaders, the *Sanhedrin* as the institutional framework, and the *tzaddikim* of each generation as its fruit are all admirable Jewish ideals, they do not cohere around the specific motif of *Torah* in any obvious way — at least not without understanding *Torah* in a very broad sense as encompassing the full ideal of Jewish religious life. The *Maharsha* does not appear to resolve this tension.

*Rabban Gamliel* then remarks: *adayin tzerichim anu la-Modai* — we still need the *Modai*, a phrase that both names *Rabbi Eliezer HaModai* specifically and signals more generally that someone with genuine skill in *aggadata* interpretation is needed here. The present interpretations are not fully satisfying.

### Jerusalem Focus

*Rabbi Eliezer HaModai omer*: *gefen zu Yerushalayim* — the vine is Jerusalem. *Shelosha sarigim ze mikdash melech ve-chohen gadol* — the three branches are the Temple, the king, and the *kohen gadol*. At least these three belong together; they are all centered in Jerusalem and represent both the religious and political heart of the Jewish world. The blossoming — *elu pirchei kehuna* — are the young *kohanim* who serve in the *Beit HaMikdash*, a connection reinforced by the word *ke-forachat* evoking *lifroach*, to blossom, a rabbinic term for junior priests. The ripened clusters — *elu nesachim* — are the wine libations offered in the *Beit HaMikdash*, which creates at least a direct visual connection with grapes and the act of pressing them into wine. Everything here is geographically and institutionally centered on Jerusalem, even if the thematic coherence is not perfectly tight — the king, for instance, sits somewhat uneasily alongside the *kohen gadol* and the *nesachim*.

The broader question of why the *Gemara* dwells so extensively on interpreting the wine steward's dream is itself worth noting. The dream plays a limited narrative role in the *Yosef* story and would seem to have no lasting theological resonance. The *Gemara* appears determined to find in it an enduring message about the Jewish people — yet the interpreters themselves acknowledge, through *Rabban Gamliel*'s remark, that none of the available interpretations fully satisfies.

### Desert Gifts

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* interprets the passage as referring to gifts God gave the Jewish people: *gefen zu Torah* — the vine is the *Torah*; *shelosha sarigim ze be'er amud anan u-man* — the three branches are the three gifts of the desert: the miraculous well of water, the pillar of cloud, and the *manna*. The blossoming — *elu ha-bikkurim* — represents the first fruits; and the ripened clusters — *elu nesachim* — the wine libations. *Rashi* notes that in each case God provides the gift so that Israel may then return it to God. This interpretation carries perhaps the most satisfying internal logic: God gives, Israel receives, Israel returns. The *manna* was placed in a container by the *aron*; the well was acknowledged through song in the *Torah* — *be'er chafaruha sarim, ali be'er enu lah*; and the pillar of cloud, at least according to one opinion, is what we recognize and acknowledge on *Sukkot*. The *amud anan* fits somewhat less naturally into the pattern of return, but the overall imagery of the vine giving forth its bounty to be offered back does create a more coherent parallel to Pharaoh's steward pressing out the grapes into Pharaoh's cup.

### Egypt & Redemption

*Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba* reads the passage through the lens of the Exodus: *gefen elu Yisrael* — the vine is the Jewish people, as the verse says *gefen miMitzrayim tasi'a* — a vine from Egypt You lifted up. *Shelosha sarigim elu shlosha regalim* — the three branches are the three pilgrimage festivals, *she-Yisrael olin bahem bechol shanah va-shanah*.
