The connection to the Exodus is apt: *Pesach* and *Sukkot* both explicitly commemorate it, and *Shavuot* — understood by *Chazal* as the time of *Matan Torah* — is likewise bound up with that redemptive moment. The blossoming — *alta nitzah* — represents *higia zmanam shel Yisrael lifrot ve-lirbot*, the moment when the time came for Israel to be fruitful and multiply in Egypt. *Vayishretzu* — they swarmed — and then *alta nitzah*, the blossom rose up, signifying *higia zmanam shel Yisrael lehiga'el* — the time for Israel to be redeemed had arrived. The verse from *Yeshayahu* — *vayeiz nitzcham al bgadai* — is connected through the word *nitzcham*, linking the blossoming imagery to the blood of the Egyptians splattered on God's garments during the act of redemption.

### Three Cups

The ripened clusters — *hivshilu eshkeloteiha anavim* — represent the moment when *higia zmanam shel Mitzrayim lishtot et kos ha-tareilah* — the time came for Egypt to drink the cup of poison. *Ve-haynu de-amar Rava*: the three cups mentioned in this very dream — *kos Paroh* appears three times in the steward's vision — correspond to three moments of Egypt's punishment. The first is *kos she-shatah bi-mei Moshe*, the punishment Egypt suffered at the Exodus. The second is *she-shatah bi-mei Paroh Necho*, when *Nevuchadnetzar* swept through and Egypt was overrun. The third is *she-atid lishtot im kol ovdei chochavim* — the punishment Egypt will share with all the nations at the future time of reckoning, having already received particular punishment for subjugating Israel, they will nonetheless join in the universal judgment.

This interpretation achieves a coherence the earlier ones approached but did not quite reach. The connection to Pharaoh and his drinking is direct and visceral: the steward presses grapes into Pharaoh's cup in the dream, and the *Gemara* reads this as Pharaoh — Egypt — drinking the cup of punishment. The imagery of blossoming as redemption, of spring and new life, ties naturally to *Pesach*, and the punishment of Egypt follows organically from the Exodus narrative. *Rav Abba* confirms to *Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba* that when *Rav* himself interpreted these verses in *aggadata*, his interpretation matched this one exactly.

---

## Vine Metaphor

### Nation Structure

*Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish*: this nation has been compared to a vine — *uma zu ke-gefen nimshala*. Now the *Gemara* steps back from the specific vision of the wine steward's dream and reflects more broadly on the vine as an image of the Jewish people and its internal structure. The branches — *zemoros* — are the *ba'alei battim*, a term that in the *Gemara* connotes not merely homeowners but people of wealth and means: those whose resources sustain the community. The clusters — *eshkolos* — are the *talmidei chachamim*, the Torah sages, for the clusters are the true purpose of the vine, just as *Torah* scholarship is the highest fruit the nation produces. The leaves — *alim* — are the *amei ha'aretz*, the working people who farm, trade, and perform the practical labors of society; just as leaves protect the clusters, so these people provide the material conditions that allow *Torah* study to flourish. Finally, the *knoknot* — the small protrusions that branch off without bearing fruit — are the *reikanim she-b'Yisrael*, the empty ones who contribute little to the life of the community.

There is an unmistakable elitism in this hierarchy, though it is entirely consistent with the *Gemara*'s general orientation. The *talmidei chachamim* are the fruit — the ultimate purpose of the vine. The *Rambam* develops a parallel argument in his philosophical writings: the world requires enormous numbers of people performing mundane labors — planting, harvesting, weaving, building — precisely so that the philosophers who contemplate ultimate truths can be sustained. The *Gemara* here is less extreme, but the underlying logic is similar: a complex and productive society is necessary precisely so that its highest spiritual achievements become possible.

### Leaves Support

*De-haynu de-shalchu mi-tam* — this is what they sent from the land of Israel as a message: *liba'ei rachamei itkala al ilaya* — the clusters should pray for the leaves, *de-imallei alaya lo miskayimei itkalya* — for without the leaves the clusters would not survive. This is a remarkable statement. The *talmidei chachamim*, highest in the hierarchy of value, are instructed to acknowledge a genuine dependence on those below them — not merely on the wealthy *ba'alei battim* who write the large checks, but on the *amei ha'aretz*, the ordinary working people who sustain the material fabric of society. The elitism of the hierarchy is real, but it is tempered by a requirement of genuine gratitude and recognition of mutual dependence.

---

## Righteous Survival

### 15th of Nisan

*Ve-achra li be-chamishah asar kasef* — and I purchased for me with fifteen pieces of silver. The *Gemara* pivots to a passage about redemption and the righteous, which connects to the preceding theme of the vine's fruit and those for whose sake the community survives. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yozadak*: *ein kirah ela lashon mechira* — the word *kirah* here denotes purchase, as in *be-kivri asher karisi li*, the grave that I purchased for myself. *Be-chamishah asar* — fifteen — is *zeh tet-vav be-Nisan*, the fifteenth of Nisan, *she-bo nigalu Yisrael mi-Mitzrayim* — the night Israel was redeemed from Egypt. *Kasef* — silver — *elu tzaddikim*, these are the righteous. The verse in *Mishlei* — *tzror ha-kesef lakach be-yado* — depicts God as having taken the bundle of silver, meaning the *tzaddikim*, with Him, leaving the community exposed. The meaning here: God redeemed Israel on the fifteenth, on *Pesach*, by virtue of the *chamishah asar kasef* — the fifteen righteous.

### 45 Righteous

The verse continues: *chomer se'orim ve-letech se'orim* — a *chomer* of barley and a *letech* of barley. A *chomer* is 30 *se'ah* and a *letech* is 15 *se'ah*, for a total of 45 *se'ah*. *Elu mem-heh tzaddikim she-ha'olam mitkayem bahem* — these are the 45 righteous people in whose merit the world is sustained. This figure of 45 is not the one that has lodged most powerfully in the Jewish imagination — that would be the *lamed-vav tzaddikim*, the 36 righteous of other *Gemaras* — but this *Gemara* is explicit: 45. *Ve-eini yodea im sheloshim kan ve-tet-vav be-Eretz Yisrael* — I do not know whether 30 are here in Bavel and 15 in Israel, or the reverse. This is a notable bookend to the earlier discussion of the *sarei ge'im*, the figures of influence divided between Bavel and Israel in a two-to-one ratio. Here too there is a two-to-one ratio, and the *Bavli* itself concludes — from the verse *ve-ekcha sheloshim ha-kasef ve-ashlich oto beit Hashem* — that the 30 are in *Eretz Yisrael* and the 15 are in Bavel. The *Bavli* thus acknowledges that the greater number of righteous are found in the land of Israel, not in the diaspora community whose *Talmud* we are studying.

### Tuti Afsa

*Amar Abaye*: *ve-rubaiyu mishtach'chi be-vei knishta de-Tuti Afsa* — most of the righteous of Bavel can be found in the synagogue of *Tuti Afsa*. *Rashi* explains that *Afsa* may denote a kind of alcove or recessed space within the synagogue. One sharp observation made in discussion is worth noting: the *tzaddikim* here are found not in the most prominent location but in an unassuming corner — which may itself be an implicit comment on what true righteousness looks like, as opposed to its surface appearances.

### Zechariah Vision

*Ve-haynu de-chtiv* — and this is what is meant by the verse in *Zechariah*: *im tov be-eineichem havu schari ve-im lo chadalu va-yishklu et schari sheloshim kasef* — if it is good in your eyes, give me my fee; if not, cease; and they paid me thirty pieces of silver. This is a vision in *Zechariah* in which God, figured as a shepherd, removes His protection from the other nations. *Rashi* reads the passage as God reclaiming His thirty righteous, who had in some sense been present among the nations, and now placing them within the Jewish people — so that the nations, stripped of this protective merit, are exposed to punishment.

### Thirty Righteous

*Rabbi Yehuda omer*: these thirty righteous are in fact *tzaddikei umot ha-olam* — righteous people among the non-Jewish nations themselves — *she-umot ha-olam mitkayimim aleihem*, in whose merit the nations survive. This reading keeps the thirty righteous *among* the nations rather than removing them.

### Bnei Noach

*Ulla omer*: these thirty are not thirty righteous individuals but thirty *mitzvot* that the *bnei Noach* accepted upon themselves — *ve-ein mekayimim ela shelosha*, but they only keep three of them. The thirty *mitzvot* are not enumerated elsewhere in the *Gemara*, and *Rashi* acknowledges that they are not specified. The three they do keep are identified as follows. First: *she-ein kotvim ketubah le-zecharim* — they do not formalize male homosexual unions in the institution of marriage, even if the underlying prohibited behavior may occur. This connects to other *Gemaras* about *ma'aseh Mitzrayim* — the Egyptian practice of institutionalizing such unions — and remains a *sugyah* of ongoing relevance for contemporary discussions. Second: *she-ein shoklim besar ha-meit be-makolin* — they do not sell human flesh in the marketplace. Third: *she-mechab'dim et ha-Torah* — they honor the *Torah*, meaning they recognize and accord dignity to the Jewish people and their tradition, an influence presumably mediated through the spread of scriptural religion into the wider world.

The overall arc of this section moves from the 45 righteous who sustain Israel, to the 30 righteous in *Eretz Yisrael* and 15 in Bavel, to the role of righteous among the nations, to finally a somewhat deflating conclusion: the nations had thirty *mitzvot* and kept only three. Whatever merit the nations possessed — the protection figured in the *Zechariah* vision — has been substantially eroded by their failure to fulfill the obligations they accepted.

---

## Gid HaNasheh

### Birds Exception

The *Gemara* now returns to the *halacha* of *gid hanasheh*, the sciatic nerve. The *Mishnah* had established that *gid hanasheh* does not apply to birds — *de-ein noheig be-of*. This seems puzzling: *de-ha chazeinan de-it lei* — we observe that birds do have such a sinew. The *Gemara* explains: *it lei ve-lo agil* — they have it, but it is not situated in a rounded part of the thigh. The *Torah* specifies *asher al kaf ha-yerech* — the rounded, bowl-like hollow of the thigh — and birds lack this anatomical feature; their thighs are not structured in that curved, ladle-like form.

*Ba'ei Rabbi Yirmiyah*: what if you were to find a bird whose thigh happened to be rounded in the relevant way — or conversely, a *beheimah* whose thigh lacked the rounded shape? *Mai* — what is the law? Does one go by the anatomy of the individual animal — *batar didei azlinan* — or by the anatomical norm of the species — *batar minei azlinan*? One might expect this to be obvious: the *Torah* legislates for species, not individual anatomical variations. Nevertheless the *Gemara* concludes with *teiku*, leaving the question unresolved, which means one must be strict in both directions. A bird whose thigh is rounded would require attention to the laws of *gid hanasheh*.

### Fetus Debate

*Amar Shmuel*: when the *Mishnah* says *ve-chelbo mutar* — the fat is permissible — this applies universally. *Mutar le-divrei ha-kol*. The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: which fat is Shmuel speaking of? If it is the fat of the fetus itself, surely that is disputed — the same debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* that applies to *gid hanasheh* in a fetus applies equally to its fat. *De-tanya*: we learned in a *braita* that *Rabbi Meir* says *gid hanasheh* applies to a fetus and its *chelev* is forbidden, while *Rabbi Yehuda* says *gid hanasheh* does not apply and its fat is permissible. *Ve-halach Rabbi Meir le-shitato ve-Rabbi Yehuda le-shitato* — each follows his own reasoning consistently. *Rabbi Meir* holds that a nine-month viable fetus is an independent legal entity, so it has its own *gid hanasheh* and its own *chelev*. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds it is legally part of its mother, and therefore the *shechita* of the mother covers the fetus and neither *gid hanasheh* nor *chelev* applies independently.

### Meir vs. Yehuda

Reframing the question: perhaps *Shmuel* is not speaking about the fetus at all, but rather about the fat surrounding the *gid hanasheh* itself. Does that fat have an independent prohibition? *Ve-ela chelbo de-gid? Ha-miflag paligei bah* — but they dispute that too. *De-tanya*: *Rabbi Meir* says *mechateit achrav be-chol makom she-hu* — you must dig after the *gid hanasheh* wherever it branches and spreads, and *ve-choteich shemano me-ikaro* — you must cut away the fat from its very root. Note the language carefully: the *braita* uses *shemano* — *shuman*, permitted fat — not *chelev*, which is the term for biblically forbidden fat. This is not accidental.

### Fat Status

*Rabbi Yehuda omer*: *gummo im ha-shofeh* — cut it off at the surface. *Tosafot* understands *Rabbi Yehuda* as making two separate claims: first, one need not dig after the minor branches of the *gid* at all — only the main sinew at the surface requires removal; and second, the fat is entirely permissible, not even subject to *minhag*. *Rashi* reads *Rabbi Yehuda* as acknowledging some surface fat must be removed but not requiring one to dig deeply. The debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* therefore operates on two axes: the extent to which one must dig after the branches of the *gid*, and the status of the surrounding fat. On the fat, both agree that it is not biblically forbidden — they use the word *shuman*, not *chelev*. The question is whether there is a rabbinic prohibition or merely a *minhag*.

The *Gemara* resolves *Shmuel*'s statement accordingly: *l'olam chelbo de-gid* — Shmuel is indeed speaking of the fat surrounding the *gid hanasheh*, not the fetus. *U-modeh Shmuel d'mederabbanan assur* — Shmuel acknowledges that even though it is biblically permissible, there is a rabbinic prohibition. A *braita* supports this: *ve-shumano mutar, Yisrael kedoshim nahagu bo issur* — the *shuman* is permissible, but the holy people of Israel have adopted the practice of treating it as forbidden. Whether *nahagu bo issur* connotes a *minhag* or a full rabbinic enactment is itself a matter of discussion, but the bottom line is clear: the fat around the *gid hanasheh* is biblically permitted and at most rabbinically or customarily restricted.

The *Gemara* then confirms that this reading is tied to *Rabbi Meir*: for *Rabbi Yehuda*, according to *Tosafot*, there is not even a *minhag* — the fat is entirely permissible. For *Rabbi Meir*, there is at minimum a rabbinic concern, and the language of *Yisrael kedoshim nahagu bo issur* reflects that elevated practice.

### No Taste Issue

*Amar Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta amar Rav*: *lo asra Torah ela knoknot she-bo* — the *Torah* only forbade the branching extensions of the *gid hanasheh*, not the main sinew itself. Why? Because the main *gid* itself — *eitz hu* — is like a piece of wood; it has no taste whatsoever. Yet the *Torah* nonetheless obligated one concerning it — *ve-rachmana chayveih*. This is a striking position: it relocates the primary prohibition from the main sinew to its branches, precisely because the branches have some slight taste while the main sinew has none.

### Main Sinew

*Amar Abaye*: the position of *Ulla* is more compelling. *De-amar Rav Sheshet amar Rav Assi*: the sinews that run through *chelev* — forbidden fat — are themselves forbidden, but one does not incur *chiyuv* for them. Why not? *Alma chelev amar rachmana ve-lo chutin* — the *Torah* says *chelev*, meaning fat, not the stringy tissues running through it. So too here: *hachi nami gid amar rachmana ve-lo knoknot* — the *Torah* says *gid*, meaning the main sinew, not its branches. The fact that the *gid* has no taste does not justify relocating the prohibition to the *knoknot*; the *Torah* specified the *gid*, and the *gid* it means.

The resolution is thus the reverse of what the earlier position proposed. The main sinew is indeed what the *Torah* prohibits — even though it is like wood and has no taste — while the branches are precisely what may not be subject to the biblical prohibition at all. This is in fact what underlay the *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* debate about the branches: if the *knoknot* are not the primary locus of the prohibition, there is reason to debate how far the rabbinic extension reaches. And the question of whether the *gid* has taste or not connects to a later debate in the *Gemara* — one that *Tosafot* analyzes in relation to these positions. Unsurprisingly, those who are troubled by the tastelessness of the main *gid* and wish to relocate the prohibition to the branches have a greater stake in insisting that the *gid* does have taste. Those who accept that the *gid* has no taste are more naturally comfortable affirming that it is precisely the main sinew — taste or no taste — that the *Torah* forbids.

---

---

# Hullin 94

## Butchers & Gid HaNasheh

### Trust in Butchers

The daf proper begins slightly before 94a, picking up at the Mishna on 93b. The Mishna presents a dispute regarding whether butchers may be trusted to have properly removed the *gid hanasheh* (sciatic nerve) from meat they sell. Rabbi Meir holds that they cannot be trusted, while the *Chachamim* hold that they can — reasoning that the removal is not particularly demanding and butchers can therefore be relied upon to perform it.

### Rabbinic Opinion Shift

Against this backdrop, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: *chazru lomar ne'emanim* — the Rabbis reversed their position and declared that butchers are indeed trustworthy. This statement of reversal, however, immediately draws a sharp challenge.

### Rav Nachman's Challenge

Rav Nachman responds with a pointed rhetorical question: *achshurei darei*? Do you really think that people have gotten frummer — that the generations have improved? This is a striking piece of *mussar*, particularly apt for *Erev Rosh Hashanah*: the assumption that people tend, over time, toward greater religious rigor runs against the grain of how the *Gemara* generally understands the direction of history.

### Meir to Yehuda Shift

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty by reconstructing the historical trajectory. Originally, the ruling followed Rabbi Meir, who required digging after the *gid hanasheh* to remove all its tiny branches. Under this demanding standard, *me'ikara savruha k'Rabbi Meir*, butchers could not be trusted — the task was simply too exacting. Eventually, the ruling shifted to follow Rabbi Yehuda, whose standard required only the removal of the main *gid* without pursuing all the smaller branches. With this far simpler standard in place, butchers could indeed be trusted: *u'vesof savri k'Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Yehuda to Meir Reverse

A parallel version of this discussion is applied to the end of the Mishna, where the *Chachamim* state that butchers are trusted both regarding the *gid* and regarding the *chelev* (forbidden fat). Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan again, but this time in reverse: *chazru lomar ein ne'emanim* — they reversed their position and said butchers cannot be trusted. Then Rav Nachman adds that *bizman hazeh*, in the present era, *ne'emanim* — they can once again be trusted, returning to the original lenient standard. Rav Nachman's objection resurfaces: *achshurei darei*? How does one explain a return to a more lenient standard without implying that the generations have become more observant?

The *Gemara* explains: originally the ruling followed Rabbi Yehuda's easier standard, so butchers were trusted. Subsequently, the ruling shifted to follow Rabbi Meir's more demanding standard — *v'hashta savruha k'Rabbi Meir* — and butchers were no longer trusted.

### Old Guard's Memory

What makes this shift psychologically and sociologically interesting is the mechanism the *Gemara* identifies. Even after the ruling formally shifted to Rabbi Meir's standard, a segment of the butchering community still remembered the era of Rabbi Yehuda's leniency — *kamei dehava dechirei leih l'Rabbi Yehuda*. These older butchers, consciously or not, continued to perform only the minimal removal they had always known. They were unwilling or unable to adapt to the new and more demanding standard. As a result, during this transitional period, butchers as a class could not be relied upon: some were meeting Rabbi Meir's standard while others were quietly operating according to the older and lighter practice.

### Forgotten Mesorah

Only once sufficient time passed — once the old guard died out and the lenient *mesorah* was no longer actively remembered — could butchers again be trusted. *V'hashta d'anshivah l'Rabbi Yehuda*: now that Rabbi Yehuda's teaching has been forgotten, the only standard any butcher knows is Rabbi Meir's, and therefore they can be assumed to be following it. The lenient *mesorah* was lost — and paradoxically, its loss is what enables trust to be restored.

### Halachic Ruling

This analysis carries significant *halachic* weight. The first version of the history concludes that the ruling is like Rabbi Yehuda — the easier standard — and therefore butchers can be trusted because the task is manageable. The second version, as explained, concludes that the ruling is like Rabbi Meir, with the more demanding requirement to dig after all the branches. This is a substantial *nafka mina*. It is worth noting that as a general rule in *Shas*, when Rabbi Meir disputes another *Tanna* by name, the *halacha* almost never follows him — which makes this outcome surprising.

The discussion raises the broader question of *yeridat hadorot* — the decline of generations. Rabbi Yochanan is a major voice throughout *Shas* on this theme, and the *Gemara*'s evident discomfort with the notion that a generation could become more observant than its predecessors reflects how deeply this assumption is embedded. One might ask how broadly *yeridat hadorot* applies: does it refer to intellectual capacity, to observance, or both? What is clear from this passage is that the *Gemara* treats generational improvement as inherently improbable.

The practical ramifications extend to our own time. The custom among Ashkenazim not to eat the hindquarters at all — rather than attempting removal of the *gid* — likely reflects a ruling in accordance with Rabbi Meir's demanding standard, which made the process impractical. More broadly, the discussion here illuminates the logic of *hashgacha* in contemporary kashrut. The Mishna's general presumption — that where a task is not difficult, a butcher with financial interest may nonetheless be trusted on the basis of *ed echad ne'eman b'issurin* — already surprised earlier readers. The *Gemara*'s own caveat, that *metzius* (contemporary reality) can compel a reassessment of such presumptions, is what underlies the modern institution of *mashgichim*. Even a religiously observant Jewish-owned establishment requires external supervision — which effectively means that *ed echad ne'eman b'issurin* is not applied in contexts where financial interest and the difficulty of certain requirements create structural incentives for noncompliance. The *Gemara* acknowledges this explicitly: the *halachic* standard must track reality, not merely the theoretical framework.

---

## Fat Dispute

### Fat Trust Question

The Mishna's closing statement about *chelev* raises a natural question. The formulation implies that Rabbi Meir holds butchers cannot be trusted regarding the fat, while the *Chachamim* say they can be trusted regarding both the *gid* and the fat. One might initially wonder which fat is being discussed: is this the fat surrounding the *gid hanasheh* itself, or forbidden *chelev* generally?

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* addresses the question directly. Rabbi Yehuda's position, as discussed earlier in the tractate, is that there was never even an established *minhag* regarding the fat of the *gid hanasheh* — it is simply permitted. If so, the debate about whether butchers can be trusted in this regard would be meaningless. *Tosafot* therefore reads the dispute as concerning the removal of *chelev* in general. On this reading, however, the connection between the two debates becomes less obvious: the question of whether butchers are trusted regarding the *gid* turns on how demanding the removal process is, whereas the question about *chelev* involves a prohibition that all authorities agree exists.

### Linking Disputes

*Tosafot* acknowledges the difficulty in explaining precisely how these two disputes are organically linked. The best explanation seems to be that Rabbi Meir's skepticism about butchers is not purely a function of the difficulty of any particular task but reflects a broader disposition: either he sets higher standards for what constitutes adequate performance or he is more skeptical about whether butchers will actually meet those standards, even when the task is not inherently difficult. His position on *chelev*, applied even where the obligation itself is uncontested, fits this characterization — it is an expression of a general stance rather than a precise extension of the argument about digging after the *gid*.

---

## Sending to Non-Jew

### Mishna Statement

The Mishna on daf 94a introduces a new case: *sholeach adam yerech lenachri vegid hanasheh besocha mipnei shemekomo nikar* — a person may send a thigh to a non-Jew without first removing the *gid hanasheh*, because the location of the *gid* is clearly visible. Since the *gid* is obvious, any Jew who subsequently encounters the meat will recognize that it has not been removed and will handle it accordingly.

### Treifa Concern

The Mishna implicitly draws a distinction from the case of *treifa* meat. If a kosher butcher slaughters an animal and it is found to be *treif*, may he sell it to a non-Jew? The concern is that the non-Jew will resell the meat to a Jew, and since there is no outward indication that the animal is non-kosher, the Jew will purchase it without suspicion. The *gid hanasheh* case is different: because the *gid* remains plainly visible in a whole thigh, any Jew who might try to purchase the meat from the non-Jew will immediately see the *gid* and understand that it requires removal. The absence of the *gid*'s removal does not create a hidden kashrut problem — it creates a visible one that the next buyer can address.

### Community Context

The broader social context is important for understanding the Mishna's logic. The scenario envisions a community in which the kosher butcher is the sole or primary source of meat. In such a setting, if a non-Jew possesses a piece of meat, the natural assumption is that it came from the kosher butcher. A Jew who sees meat at a non-Jew's home or stall might therefore feel comfortable purchasing it, on the reasoning that the non-Jew acquired it locally from the only available source. This assumption, however, also creates the risk: if the butcher sold the non-Jew *treifa* meat, and there is no way for the community to know, the Jew may purchase what he believes to be acceptable meat. The Mishna's permission to send the thigh with the *gid* intact depends on this communal context — precisely because the *gid* is visible, the Jew is protected even if he buys the meat back from the non-Jew.

---

## Gemara Analysis

### Whole vs. Chopped

The *Gemara* opens by sharpening the Mishna's rule. The Mishna permits sending a whole thigh to a non-Jew — but why does this not extend to chopped meat? The *Gemara* frames the question: *shleima in, chatukha lo* — a whole thigh, yes; a chopped one, no. The question then becomes: what precisely is the context in which this distinction operates?

### Announcement Explanation

The *Gemara*'s first move is to identify what kind of community we are dealing with: *bemakom shemachrizin* — a place where announcements are made. These announcements are public notifications to the Jewish community that *treifot* have been sold to non-Jews on a given occasion. The practical effect is that community members know not to purchase meat from non-Jews for a reasonable period following such an announcement, until it can be safely assumed the non-kosher meat has been consumed.

### Announcement Details

In a community that makes such announcements, the baseline rule is that Jews *may* buy from non-Jews — the announcement system provides the safeguard. When no announcement is in effect, residents can proceed on the assumption that any meat a non-Jew possesses came from the kosher butcher and has not been flagged as *treif*.

### First Case Logic

Given this framework, the *Gemara* asks: if the community makes announcements, why is there any restriction on selling chopped meat to a non-Jew? In a place with announcements, when no announcement has been made, Jews may freely buy from non-Jews. If the non-Jew then possesses chopped meat, a Jew may purchase it. And since Jews may purchase from non-Jews in this community, one cannot casually sell them meat with a *gid hanasheh* intact — because Jews will buy it back without detecting the *gid*. But then, the *Gemara* presses, why is whole meat permitted? If the non-Jew can simply chop the whole thigh himself and resell the pieces, the protection of the visible *gid* dissolves.

### No Announcements Case

The *Gemara* therefore shifts to the second scenario: *bemakom she'ein machrizin* — a place where no announcements are made. In such a community, Jews never know whether non-Jews are in possession of *treifot*, and therefore Jews never buy from non-Jews at all. If Jews will never purchase from non-Jews regardless, then the entire concern about resale evaporates. One may freely sell a whole thigh — with or without the *gid* removed — because there is no realistic risk that a Jew will buy it back.

But this too generates a difficulty: if Jews never buy from non-Jews in this community, why does it matter whether the sold meat is whole or chopped? In a place where Jews categorically do not purchase from non-Jews, one could sell the non-Jew chopped meat as readily as whole meat. The restriction on chopped meat therefore demands a different explanation.

The first resolution the *Gemara* offers — *makom shemachrizin* — addresses the whole-versus-chopped distinction through the observational capacity of a knowledgeable buyer. In a community with announcements, when no announcement is in effect, Jews do buy from non-Jews. If the non-Jew possesses a whole thigh, a Jew who buys it will see the *gid hanasheh* and know to remove it. If, however, the meat has already been chopped, the *gid* is no longer visible. Moreover — and this is key — there was in that era a recognizable difference between the way Jewish butchers and non-Jewish butchers cut meat. If a Jew saw that pieces had been cut in the manner of a non-Jew, he would recognize that the butchering was done by a non-Jew and would accordingly be on guard: perhaps the *gid* was never removed. By contrast, if the whole thigh was purchased from the non-Jew, the Jew will see the *gid* clearly and act accordingly. This distinction operates in a community already attuned to such distinctions — precisely the kind of community that maintains an announcement system.

The second resolution — for *bemakom she'ein machrizin* — operates differently. Here, no Jew ever buys from non-Jews in general. But there is a special case: a Jew might be standing in the butcher shop at the very moment a sale is made to a non-Jew. He sees the butcher carve a particular cut and hand it to the non-Jew. Because he witnessed the transaction, and because he can see that the animal from which it came was used to supply Jewish customers as well, he might feel comfortable turning immediately to the non-Jew and purchasing that specific piece. In this narrow scenario, if the piece was sold whole, the Jew will see the *gid*; if it was sold already chopped, he will not, and will assume — incorrectly — that the *gid* has been removed.

### Gneivat Da'at Reason

The *Gemara* then introduces a third and entirely different explanation: *mishum dekaganiv lei leda'atei* — the concern is one of *gneivat da'at*, of misleading the non-Jew. This explanation sets aside the kashrut dimension entirely. In a community where Jews never buy from non-Jews — *makom she'ein machrizin* — there is no risk of resale. Yet the restriction on selling chopped meat remains. Why?

The non-Jew who receives meat from a Jewish butcher will naturally understand the social meaning of the transaction. When a Jewish butcher sends a whole thigh with the *gid* still intact, the non-Jew understands that he is receiving the piece the butcher could not sell to Jewish customers. The *gid* is visible; it is clearly the reason the piece has been redirected. The non-Jew has a realistic picture of what he has received and feels a proportionate sense of gratitude. If, however, the butcher sends chopped pieces from which the *gid* has not been removed but where its absence is no longer detectable, the non-Jew may believe he has received something the butcher could have sold to Jewish customers. He feels a greater degree of gratitude — a gratitude that is, in fact, undeserved, since the butcher was simply disposing of meat he could not sell. This creation of false gratitude is *gneivat da'at*, forbidden even toward a non-Jew.

The *Gemara* anchors this principle in a statement of Shmuel: *assur lignov da'at ha-beriyot va'afilu da'ato shel oved kochavim* — it is forbidden to mislead people, including a non-Jew. This ruling was not stated explicitly by Shmuel but inferred from a story: Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry and instructed his attendant to do something kind for the ferryman in appreciation. The attendant apparently gave the ferryman a *treifa* chicken — or, according to another version of the story, instructed him to give the ferryman a drink of *anpaka* (undiluted wine or a healthful beverage) but gave him diluted wine instead. Shmuel was displeased.

### Third Explanation

The *Gemara* notes that the source for Shmuel's position was *inferred* from a story rather than stated directly, and that this matters — because the story is susceptible to alternative interpretations. According to Abaye, the story involved a *treifa* chicken given to a non-Jewish ferryman: Shmuel's displeasure was because the attendant created the impression that the chicken was a premium gift when in fact it was a discard. According to Rava, the story involved the *anpaka* drink: the attendant was told to give a particular beverage and gave a lesser substitute instead. In Rava's version — on one reading of Rashi — Shmuel's complaint was not about misleading the non-Jew at all, but simply about the attendant's failure to follow instructions. If so, the *Gemara* leaves open the possibility that Shmuel's position on *gneivat da'at* toward non-Jews cannot be definitively established from this story.

The *Rambam*, however, rules definitively that *gneivat da'at* is forbidden even toward non-Jews. Interestingly, the *Rambam* places the prohibition not in *Hilchot Gneiva v'Gzeila* but in *Hilchot De'ot* — the laws concerning character traits. This reflects a deeper point: the prohibition is not simply about the harm done to the other party by engineering false gratitude; it is about the character of the person who engages in systematic deception. The *Rambam* emphasizes that the problem is what such behavior does to oneself — to one's honesty and integrity as fundamental traits of character.

This framing also sheds light on a broader tension in the *sugyot* of *Bava Kamma* regarding the differential treatment of Jews and non-Jews in monetary law. It is notable that the *Gemara* seems in some respects more prepared to extend *gneivat da'at* to non-Jews than it is to extend certain other prohibitions — perhaps precisely because the primary locus of the prohibition, as the *Rambam* frames it, is one's own character rather than an obligation to the other party. The concern about what deceit does to a person applies regardless of who is being deceived.

---

## Gneivat Da'at

### Pressuring to Eat

A *tanya* introduces a series of teachings in the name of Rabbi Meir on the theme of *gneivat da'at*. Rabbi Meir teaches: a person should not press his friend to come eat with him *veyodeia bo she-eino so'ed* — when he knows that the friend is unable to accept the invitation. The critical factor is not whether the invitation is sincere in some general sense, but whether the host knows for certain that the friend cannot come. There is no prohibition against inviting someone to a celebration even knowing they will likely decline, if one genuinely wishes they could attend. The problem arises when the host issues the invitation knowing with certainty it will not be accepted, purely to generate an unearned sense of being honored or cared for.

### Unwanted Gifts

Similarly, a person should not send a large number of gifts *veyodeia she-eino mekabel* — knowing the recipient will not accept them, but expecting the recipient to feel a sense of gratitude or indebtedness nonetheless from the gesture itself.

### Pre-Sold Barrels

A person should not open barrels of wine for a guest when those barrels are already pre-sold to the shopkeeper — unless he informs the guest of this fact. The context is the following: opening a fresh barrel is a significant gesture of hospitality. Wine exposed to air after a barrel is opened begins to degrade; to open an entire barrel for the sake of a guest represents a real cost to the host. A guest who sees a barrel opened in his honor accordingly feels a deep sense of gratitude. But if the host has already pre-arranged to sell that barrel — or the remainder of it — to a shopkeeper, the economic loss is negligible or nonexistent. The grand gesture conceals the fact that the host has sacrificed nothing. If the host informs the guest of this arrangement, the gratitude adjusts accordingly: the guest understands exactly what he has and has not received. Without disclosure, the guest is left with a false impression of the host's generosity.

### Empty Vessel Cases

A person should not go to a mourner's house carrying a *lagin* — a container of wine — that is audibly or visibly not full, presenting it as a gift. And a person should not fill such a container with water and present it as wine. In both cases, the recipient will eventually discover the deception — in the second case almost immediately upon tasting. This raises a genuine analytical question: if the deception is so quickly exposed, what exactly is the *gneivat da'at*? The *Gemara* seems to be working with one of two possibilities: either even a momentary false impression of generosity constitutes *gneivat da'at*, since the recipient experienced an unearned gratitude however briefly; or the concern is that the recipient, being a mourner in a vulnerable state, will charitably assume the giver made an honest mistake, and some residual sense of goodwill therefore survives even after the discovery.

### Honor Exception

An important exception is introduced: *im bishvil kevodo mutar* — if the gesture is done for the recipient's honor, it is permitted. The classic illustration is opening a pre-sold barrel publicly, in front of assembled guests, so that the honoree is seen to be treated with great distinction. Even though the host suffers no real economic loss from the gesture, the guest receives something genuine and tangible: the public honor of being seen as important enough to warrant a freshly opened barrel. The benefit conferred is real, even if its cost to the host is zero. On this reading, the *bishvil kevodo* exception does not require disclosure — the honor being given is itself the substance of the gift, and the recipient benefits from it regardless of the economic mechanics.

### Ulla & Yehuda Story

The *Gemara* raises a challenge: was it not the case that Ulla came to the house of Rav Yehuda, and Rav Yehuda opened barrels that had already been pre-sold to the shopkeeper? This appears to violate the rule just stated. The *Gemara* resolves the challenge in two ways.

### Alternative Explanation

The first resolution: *oduei odaiei* — Rav Yehuda told Ulla about it. Since Ulla was informed, there was no *gneivat da'at*. The second resolution: *shani Ulla dechaviv leh leRav Yehuda* — Ulla was especially beloved to Rav Yehuda, such that *debilav hachi nami patach leh* — he would have opened a new barrel for Ulla regardless of any pre-sale arrangement. If the host would have incurred the cost anyway out of genuine affection, the fact that circumstances made the gesture economically costless does not create a problem of *gneivat da'at*. The gratitude the guest feels is fully merited, since the host's willingness to sacrifice was real even if no actual sacrifice was made.

This second resolution raises an interesting practical question. A host who discloses such an arrangement to a guest — saying, for instance, "I want you to know I had already sold this wine, so opening it is no loss to me" — might inadvertently diminish the warmth of the moment rather than enhance it. Those who are *machmir* about *gneivat da'at* in such circumstances and make the disclosure are doing so out of genuine scruple, but it is worth appreciating the interpersonal complexity involved.

### Dead Animal Sandal

The *Gemara* cites a *braita*: a person should not sell his friend a sandal made from the leather of an animal that died naturally (*shel metah*), presenting it as leather from a properly slaughtered healthy animal (*bichlal shel chayah*). Leather from an animal that died on its own is of inferior quality compared to leather taken from a slaughtered animal.

### Sandal Reasons

The prohibition rests on two distinct grounds: first, *mipnei shemat'eihu* — it is straightforward misrepresentation, closer to commercial fraud than to *gneivat da'at* in the interpersonal sense; and second, *mipnei hasakana* — there is a concern about physical danger, since the body of an animal that died naturally may harbor disease or other harmful matter that could transfer to the wearer's foot through the leather.

### Oil on Wine Deception

A person should not send his friend, as a gift, a barrel of wine with a layer of oil floating on top — *chavis shel yayin v'shemen tzaf al piha*. Oil is more expensive than wine; oil also floats on wine, just as it floats on water. A recipient who opens such a barrel will see the oil on top and assume he has received a barrel of oil — a valuable gift. Only when he works through the barrel will he discover that it is predominantly wine. Once again the question arises: since the deception will ultimately be discovered, what exactly has been achieved? Several possibilities suggest themselves. One is that the recipient had the false impression for a period of time and acted on it — perhaps inviting guests, as in the story below, on the basis of the anticipated windfall. Another is that even once discovered, some residue of the initial positive feeling remains. A third, consistent with the *Rambam*'s framing, is that the problem is the act of deception itself — the engagement with dishonesty — regardless of whether it ultimately succeeds in producing lasting false gratitude.

### Oil-Wine Tragedy

The *Gemara* records a case in which someone sent a friend a barrel of wine with oil on top. The recipient, believing he had received a barrel of oil, went and invited guests to a feast — bread and oil being a fine and fitting meal. When the guests arrived and the barrel was broached, it became clear the contents were wine, not oil. The host, overcome with shame and anguish at the embarrassment, strangled himself. Rashi explains that this is not a figure of speech — the man took his own life. This and the stories that follow drive home the *Gemara*'s point about the severity of these seemingly technical prohibitions.

### Guest Giving Rules

The *Gemara* transitions to a related category: guests may not give from the food placed before them to the children of the host — *ella im ken natlu reshut miba'al ha-bayis* — unless the host has explicitly granted permission. The reasoning is straightforward: the host has taken care to provide particular food for the honored guest, often at greater expense and effort than what the household children receive. The guest's food belongs, in a social sense, to the occasion and to the guest-host relationship. Redirecting it to the children without permission violates the host's intentions and the social meaning of the gesture, even if the food is technically in the guest's hands.

### Egg Tragedy

The *Gemara* records a devastating illustration. Someone invited three guests during a time of famine. All he had to offer each was a single egg — at a time of famine, a not-insignificant provision. The host's son approached. One of the guests, moved by the child's apparent hunger, shared his egg with the boy. The child then went to the second guest and received his egg as well, and then to the third. When the father of the child returned, he found his son clutching two eggs in his hands and eating a third — and realized that the child had taken the guests' entire meal. The father struck the child in his rage, and the child died. The mother, seeing her child killed, climbed to the roof and threw herself off. The father, in despair at the loss of his entire family, did the same.

### Yaakov's Conclusion

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov concludes: *al davar zeh nehergu gimel nefashot m'Yisrael* — because of this transgression, three Jewish lives were lost. The *Gemara* asks: surely this is self-evident from the story just told, so why does Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov bother stating it? The answer: his statement is not meant to add new information but to attribute the entire *braita* to Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, establishing him as its author by giving him the final word. This is the *Gemara*'s way of signaling that the teaching as a whole is his.

---

## Selling Meat Rules

### Friend Meat Rules

A *braita* now revisits the rules regarding the *gid hanasheh* in the context of sending meat to a friend. If one sends a whole thigh to a Jewish friend, he need not remove the *gid hanasheh* before sending it — the *gid* is visible in a whole thigh and the recipient will see it and understand that he must remove it himself before consumption. If, however, the thigh is sent chopped, the sender must remove the *gid hanasheh* first. Once the meat is cut into pieces, the *gid* may no longer be visible, and the recipient will naturally assume that a seller or sender who provides pre-cut meat has already handled any necessary preparations. Sending him chopped meat without removing the *gid* therefore creates the false impression that the *gid* has been removed.

### Non-Jew Exception

For a non-Jew, the rule is different: *bein chatukha bein shleima eino tzarich litol heimenu gid hanasheh* — whether whole or chopped, one need not remove the *gid hanasheh* before sending or selling. The *braita* takes this as its baseline, the explanation for which the *Gemara* will shortly work out. The presumption appears to be that we are operating in a context where Jews do not purchase from non-Jews, so there is no risk that a Jew will receive the meat and be misled.

### Treifa Prohibition

The *braita* then states: there are two reasons one may not sell *neveilot* (animals that died without proper slaughter) or *treifot* to non-Jews. The first reason is *mipnei shemat'eihu* — one misleads them, creating the false impression that they are receiving normal, sale-worthy meat when in fact they are receiving the butcher's discards. The second reason is *shema yachzor v'yimkarenah l'Yisrael acher* — one fears the non-Jew will turn around and sell it to another Jew. Here, in this *braita*, the *gneivat da'at* rationale appears explicitly alongside the resale concern — confirming that the concern about misleading the non-Jew regarding the quality of the gift is indeed operative.

### Don't Send Non-Jew

Finally, the *braita* states: a person should not send a non-Jew to a Jewish butcher with money to purchase meat on his behalf. Two concerns underlie this prohibition. First, *mipnei ha'anasim* — the concern about coercion: in the specific social context of the *braita*, where Roman domination was a reality, a non-Jew might use his position to compel the store owner to give him the meat without actually paying, pocketing the money for himself. Second, *shema yimkru lo neveilot u'treifot* — the butcher, seeing that the buyer is a non-Jew, may sell him non-kosher meat; the non-Jew will then bring that meat back to the Jew who sent him, who will consume it thinking it is kosher.

---

## Harmonizing Braita

### Contradiction Problem

The *Gemara* now observes that the *braita* just cited creates a set of apparently contradictory assumptions. Three consecutive clauses make incompatible presuppositions about whether Jews purchase meat from non-Jews — and the *Gemara* lays out the contradiction with precision.

### Case One Logic

The first clause permits sending a non-Jew a whole thigh without removing the *gid hanasheh*. For this to make sense — that is, for there to be no concern that a Jew will subsequently buy the meat from the non-Jew and be misled by an unremoved *gid* — the operative assumption must be that Jews do *not* buy from non-Jews. The clause only works in a community where Jews never purchase from non-Jewish sources.

### Case Two Logic

The second clause prohibits selling non-kosher meat to non-Jews, with one stated reason being the fear that the non-Jew will resell it to a Jew. For this concern to be operative, Jews must buy from non-Jews. The clause therefore presupposes a community in which Jews *do* purchase from non-Jewish sources.

### Case Three Logic

The third clause — prohibiting a Jew from sending a non-Jew to the butcher — includes as one of its concerns the fear that the butcher will sell the non-Jew *neveilot* or *treifot*, which will then be brought back to the Jew who commissioned the purchase. For this to be a real worry, Jews must actually receive and consume meat purchased by non-Jews on their behalf. Again, this implies that Jews are in practice obtaining meat through non-Jewish intermediaries — which assumes that Jews do buy from non-Jews.

The *Gemara* thus has before it a *braita* in which the first clause assumes Jews do not buy from non-Jews, and the second and third clauses assume they do.

### Abaye Resolution

Abaye accepts that the *braita* is genuinely inconsistent in its underlying assumptions and resolves it by assigning each clause to a different social context. The first and last clauses — the *reisha* and *seifa* — describe a community *bemakom she'ein machrizin*: a place where no announcements are ever made regarding *treifot* sold to non-Jews. In such a community, Jews never know whether the non-Jew possesses *treifa* meat, and therefore they never buy from non-Jews as a matter of policy. In this context, there is no risk of resale — which is why one may sell a non-Jew the *gid hanasheh* without removal; and there is no announcement system — which is why the butcher might attempt to sell the non-Jew non-kosher meat without community knowledge. The middle clause — the *metziata* — describes a community *bemakom shemachrizin*, where announcements are made and Jews ordinarily do buy from non-Jews when no announcement is in effect. In that context, one may not sell non-kosher meat to a non-Jew, because when no announcement is in effect, a Jew may purchase from the non-Jew and receive the *treifa* unknowingly.

### Rava Resolution

Rava offers a different resolution, one that does not require assigning different clauses to different communities. He holds that the entire *braita* describes a single community *bemakom shemachrizin* — a place where announcements are made. The variation among the clauses is not about place but about timing. The *reisha* and *seifa* describe situations in which an announcement *has been made* and is currently in effect. When the announcement is active, Jews know not to buy from non-Jews, and accordingly one may sell to non-Jews without fear of resale. The *metziata* — the middle clause about not selling *treifot* — describes a situation in which no announcement is currently in effect. At such a time, Jews are buying from non-Jews, and therefore one may not sell the non-Jew *treifa* meat, since it may find its way back to a Jewish buyer.

### Rav Ashi Resolution

Rav Ashi offers a third approach, holding that the entire *braita* refers to a community *bemakom she'ein machrizin* — no announcements are ever made, and Jews categorically do not buy from non-Jews. On this reading, the first and last clauses are straightforward: since Jews do not buy from non-Jews, one may sell them a *gid hanasheh* without removal; and the store owner, not being constrained by the announcement system, may sell non-kosher meat to the non-Jew without community awareness. The middle clause — the prohibition on selling *treifot* — is then explained differently: it is a *gezeira*, a rabbinic precautionary decree. Even though in principle Jews in this community never buy from non-Jews, one should not sell *treifot* to a non-Jew because of the fear that a Jew might happen to see the transaction and draw incorrect conclusions.

### Rashi Distinction

Rashi elaborates on Rav Ashi's approach by identifying the precise mechanism of the *gezeira*. The key, Rashi notes, is the distinction between *giving* (privately, typically through an intermediary, away from the bustle of the market) and *selling* (in the store, a public transaction witnessed by many). The *reisha* permits sending meat to a non-Jew — a private gift, sent through a messenger, not conducted openly. The *metziata* prohibits selling *neveilot* and *treifot* in the store. A sale in the market is a visible, public act. Even in a community where Jews ordinarily never buy from non-Jews, if another Jew sees a butcher openly selling meat to a non-Jew in the store, he may assume that the non-Jew obtained the meat through the normal channels, that the meat is therefore kosher, and that he himself may purchase it from the non-Jew. The private gift circumvents this concern; the public sale does not. The upshot is that the *gezeira* against selling applies to the public commercial context — not because there is a direct risk of resale in communities that never buy from non-Jews, but because public visibility creates the conditions in which such an assumption could arise.

---

---

# Hullin 98

## Ta'am vs. Shishim

### Gid Hanashe & Ta'am

To situate today's daf properly, it is worth summarizing the central conceptual terrain covered on the previous page, since it underlies everything that follows. The *mishna* opened with a discussion of the prohibition of *gid hanashe* in the context of cooking, and the principle that emerged from it was *ta'am ke'ikar* — taste is legally equivalent to the thing itself. If a forbidden substance imparts its taste to a permissible mixture, the mixture is prohibited. This principle is broadly accepted as biblical in force, such that the forbidden taste carries the same legal weight as the forbidden substance from which it derived.

### Methods of Transfer

The *Gemara* then explored the mechanisms by which taste is transferred. The *mishna* had mentioned cooking, and Shmuel added three further modes: roasting, salting, and pickling. Roasting, in Shmuel's view, does not transfer taste throughout the entire dish; Tosafot and other *rishonim* clarify that it does transfer taste to a thin surface layer immediately adjacent to the roasted item — though it does not spread further unless the item is particularly fatty, which raises its own practical questions. Salting, Shmuel says, operates like roasting — it transfers taste, but only to a limited degree, akin to direct heat without liquid. Pickling, by contrast, involves liquid and therefore functions like cooking, transferring taste throughout.

### Two Models

The deeper question the *Gemara* addressed is how one determines whether taste has been imparted when two substances are cooked together. The *mishna* itself mentioned taste as the criterion, and offered a conceptual model: imagine the forbidden item were meat and the permissible mixture were turnips — would the taste spread? Rabbi Yochanan introduced a further model, using onions as a stand-in for the forbidden substance on the grounds that onions have a particularly penetrating flavor, making this approach inherently stringent. Alongside this experiential, taste-based approach stands a second model: the quantitative rule of *shishim* — sixty. If the permissible portion is sixty times the volume of the forbidden substance, no concern of taste impartation remains. This serves as a universal, calculable substitute for the otherwise contextual and subjective determination of taste.

### Non-Jewish Taster

Rabbi Yochanan introduced a third approach: when the forbidden substance cannot be tasted directly — either because it is non-kosher or because one cannot identify its flavor — a non-Jewish taster may be relied upon. Later *poskim* debated the precise conditions under which such reliance is valid, including whether the taster's professional reputation must be at stake or whether it matters if they are aware their judgment is being used halachically. Rava then demonstrated how all three approaches may be integrated. If the admixture involves a kosher substance, a Jew may taste it directly. If it involves a non-kosher substance, a non-Jewish taster may be employed. And when neither option is available — or when the nature of the mixture makes taste determination impossible — one falls back on the measure of *shishim*.

### Sephardic vs. Ashkenazi

This integration of approaches reflects the Sephardic ruling, which follows the *Gemara's* graduated logic: the taste of a Jew for *heter*, the taste of a non-Jew for *issur*, and *shishim* as the fallback when tasting is unavailable. Ashkenazic practice, by contrast, largely dispenses with contextual taste determinations and applies *shishim* as the standard rule in virtually all cases, though in principle a Jew's tasting of a permissible substance remains valid even according to Ashkenazim. The practical distinction between these approaches has less to do with *how* one measures and more to do with the question of whether a given prohibition is *de'oraita* or *derabanan* in character — a point that will become significant below.

---

## Eggs & Taste

### Eggs & 60

The *Gemara* now turns to the case of non-kosher eggs mixed with kosher eggs. The principle stated is: *beitza beshishim* — an egg requires sixty times its volume to be nullified — and the egg itself does not count toward that sixty. This latter point is simply the standard rule: one always requires sixty against the forbidden item, and the item itself is not part of the count.

### Hard Shells Argument

Rav Idi bar Avin poses a challenge to Abaye: the assumption that an egg imparts taste when cooked with other eggs seems questionable on its face. Eggs have hard shells that would seem to block the transfer of flavor, and the *Gemara* invokes a common expression — *k'maya d'bei'ei b'alma*, "like mere egg water" — used precisely to describe something utterly flavorless. The expression itself is evidence that the liquid produced by cooking eggs was understood to convey almost no taste whatsoever. So why should a non-kosher egg cooked with kosher eggs be a concern?

### Chick Exception

The *Gemara* resolves this by specifying the case: *bebeitat efroach* — we are dealing with an egg that contains a developing chick. Such an egg is prohibited not merely because it derives from a non-kosher species but because it contains what is effectively an unhatched living creature, with a status akin to *neveilah*. That kind of egg does give off taste. By contrast, an ordinary egg from a non-kosher bird — without any developing chick — does not give off taste and would not be a concern. The *Gemara* accordingly transitions to discussing a *baraita* that describes mixing kosher and non-kosher eggs.

### Baraita Clarification

The *baraita* states that if one boiled kosher eggs together with non-kosher eggs, and the non-kosher eggs impart taste, the entire mixture is forbidden. A challenge arises: if this first clause refers to eggs from non-kosher species rather than eggs containing chicks, and such eggs can apparently impart taste, then the second clause of the *baraita* — which introduces the case of eggs found to contain a chick — would be entirely redundant.

The *Gemara* first attempts to resolve this by saying the *baraita* is not presenting two distinct cases but one case explained in two parts: the second clause clarifies what "non-kosher egg" means in the first — namely, an egg with a chick inside. The first clause describes the prohibition; the second tells you what category of egg produces it.

However, a counter-reading is raised: the more natural reading of the *baraita* is that it presents two separate cases. The first case refers to an egg from a non-kosher bird (without a chick), and the second introduces the case of a chick specifically, so that you know the first case is distinct from it — and yet even the first case, the egg from a non-kosher bird, could in theory impart taste and be a concern. The *Gemara* ultimately leans on real-world knowledge to resist this reading. Given that normal eggs, even from non-kosher species, do not meaningfully impart taste, the *Gemara* is willing to read the *baraita* as presenting a single case: only an egg containing a chick is a genuine concern. An egg from a non-kosher bird, absent a chick, does not give off taste and would not render the mixture forbidden.

### Absorption Question

A further question — raised in the course of this discussion — is whether the hard shell of an egg also prevents it from *absorbing* taste from a forbidden medium, not merely from imparting it. The *Gemara's* discussion here addresses the "giving off" side, not the "absorbing" side. Yet the *Gemara* does appear to assume that eggs are capable of absorbing taste — that the shell does not fully seal the interior against external flavors. Whether eggs absorb through the shell when cooked in a non-kosher vessel remains a live practical question, and one that the *Gemara* here does not definitively resolve. What is clear from this passage is that the leniency regarding eggs is specifically about their not imparting taste outward, not about their being impervious to absorbing taste inward.

---

## Fat in Meat

### Pot Absorption

The *Gemara* introduces a new scenario: a *kezayit* of forbidden fat (*chelev*) fell into a pot of meat. Rav Ashi considered being lenient by measuring not the current contents of the pot against the fat, but rather including what the pot had absorbed over the time since the fat fell in. His reasoning: by the time the question was brought before him — perhaps an hour after the fact — some of the meat had been absorbed into the walls of the pot, and if one could credit that absorbed meat toward the sixty, the ratio might become sufficient to nullify the fat.

### Proportional Absorption

The rabbis rejected this reasoning. Their objection is precise: just as the pot absorbed some of the permissible meat over that hour, it likewise absorbed some of the forbidden fat proportionally. The ratio of permissible to forbidden in the pot's walls mirrors the ratio in the pot itself at any given moment. Therefore, one cannot artificially increase the count of the permissible by adding what the pot absorbed, because the pot absorbed from both sides equally. The proper approach is to assess the current proportions in the pot, which reflect the original proportions when the fat first fell in. There is no basis for a leniency here.

---

## Half K'Zayit

### Thirty Halves Proposal

A related but distinct scenario: half a *kezayit* of forbidden fat fell into a pot of meat. Mar bar Rav Ashi proposed that in this case, thirty half-*zayit* portions of permissible meat would suffice to nullify it — that is, thirty against a half, rather than the standard sixty. His reasoning appears to have been that since a half-*kezayit* does not carry the full biblical penalty of lashes — it is below the minimum *shiur* for punishment — perhaps it rises only to the level of a rabbinic prohibition, and rabbinic prohibitions may be handled with a more lenient measure.

### Rav Ashi Rebuke

His father Rav Ashi rebuked him sharply: do not be lenient with rabbinic *shiurim*. The phrase *d'rabbanan* in this context carries ambiguity — it could modify the prohibition (which may be only rabbinically prohibited because it involves a sub-*shiur* quantity) or it could modify the measure of sixty itself (which many understand to be a rabbinic standard, a worst-case-scenario stand-in for taste). Rav Ashi's rebuke addresses both possibilities simultaneously. Furthermore, Rav Ashi adds: taste is not always negated at sixty — sometimes things are tasted even below that proportion. Sixty is a conservative outer bound, a *worst-case scenario*, precisely so that one need not investigate taste case by case. To start reducing it to thirty in certain situations undermines the entire function of the standard.

### Chatzi Shiur Asur

Moreover, Rav Ashi invokes Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: *chatzi shiur asur min haTorah* — even a half-measure of a forbidden substance is biblically prohibited. One does not incur lashes for less than the full *shiur*, and one certainly does not face the penalty of *karet*, but the act of consumption is itself a biblical prohibition. This means Mar bar Rav Ashi's premise — that a half-*kezayit* of fat is only rabbinically forbidden — was mistaken from the outset. The *Gemara* notes parenthetically that whether a half-*shiur* of an *issur karet* is more severe than a half-*shiur* of a mere *issur lav* is a question the Ramban raises elsewhere, but that discussion belongs to a different *sugya*.

---

## Sixty vs. 61 Eggs

### 60/61 Tradition

A tradition is cited from the school of the *nasi* in the name of Rabbi Yaakov, transmitted through a long chain of authorities ultimately going back to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi via Bar Kappara: *beitzah beshishim asurah, beshishim ve'achat muteret* — if there are sixty eggs (against the forbidden one), it is forbidden; if there are sixty-one, it is permitted. On its face this seems to simply restate the standard rule of sixty, but the phrasing is subtly ambiguous and gives rise to a difficulty.

### Counting Ambiguity

Rav Zeira presses Rav Shimon bar Abba on this tradition. The problem is that the formulation draws a line between permitted and forbidden, and whenever a tradition establishes such a boundary it must be precise. In this case, it was not. Two great authorities of the generation — Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani — both transmitted this ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, yet they themselves were uncertain as to its precise meaning. The question they could not resolve: does "sixty-one permits" mean sixty-one total eggs including the forbidden one — which is the standard rule, since one need sixty *against* it plus the item itself equals sixty-one — or does it mean sixty-one *in addition to* the forbidden egg, for a total of sixty-two? The latter reading would represent an unusual stringency by eggs, requiring not sixty against the forbidden item but sixty-one. No explanation is given in the *Gemara* for why eggs would carry this extra stringency, and the *rishonim* offer various suggestions. What is notable is that the *Gemara* entertains this possibility despite having already established that eggs are if anything *less* of a taste concern than other substances — one might have expected leniency with eggs, not stringency.

### Yitzchak's Clarity

Rav Yitzchak the son of Rav Yehuda then provides a definitive statement: *beitzah beshishim u-mah hi asurah, beshishim ve'achat ve-hi muteret* — an egg with sixty others is forbidden, sixty-one including the egg itself and it is permitted. According to Rashi's reading, this formulation actually means sixty-one against it plus the egg for a total of sixty-two — confirming the stringency. By this reading, an egg requires one more against it than the standard rule would demand. The number sixty was clearly emerging as the dominant standard in the Amoraic period, but as these discussions reveal, its precise application — including or excluding the forbidden item, and whether certain categories warrant deviation from the norm — was still being worked out.

---

## Evolution to 60

### Forty-Seven/45

The *Gemara* now traces how the number sixty crystallized historically. Someone came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi with a case involving a certain proportion of forbidden to permissible substance. Rabban Gamliel responded: my father would not accept forty-seven as sufficient — and you want me to accept forty-five? The force of the statement is clear: if the previous authority held firm even when the proportion was more favorable, there is no basis to be lenient now with a less favorable one.

### 45/43

A parallel case: someone came before Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi. He replied: my father would not accept forty-five as sufficient — and you want me to accept forty-three? The same structure, the same reasoning, one step further along.

### Lenient Reading

Rashi, however, reads these same passages in precisely the opposite direction. According to Rashi, the language *abba lo shi'er* — "my father did not measure it" — means not that the father forbade the case with the larger proportion, but that the father *permitted* it with that proportion without even requiring more. Thus: my father permitted it with forty-seven, therefore I can permit it with forty-five; my father permitted it with forty-five, therefore I can permit it with forty-three. On this reading, these authorities were actually ruling *more leniently* than sixty, not working toward it. Either way — whether the tradition records stringencies or leniencies — the key observation is the same: sixty was not yet the fixed number. The precise proportion had not yet crystallized.

### From Taste to Numbers

This historical picture is exactly what one would expect from the trajectory the *Gemara* has been describing. The process began with the biblical concept of taste — does the forbidden substance impart its flavor? — and then developed practical tools for measuring that taste: stand-in models such as onions, the use of a non-Jewish taster, and eventually quantitative thresholds. The move toward numbers is a move toward universality and predictability. A universal number like sixty does not require one to know what the forbidden item was, what the permissible mixture was, or to find a taster. One simply counts. But it takes time for any such universal standard to crystallize, and these traditions from the children and students of Rabbi reflect that transitional moment.

### Thirty Question

A final vignette from this period: someone came before Rabbi Chiya with a case. Rabbi Chiya responded: *klum yesh shloshim?* — is there even thirty? The remark was not a ruling that thirty would suffice. As Rabbi Chanina clarifies, it was an exaggeration — a rhetorical dismissal. The proportion was so evidently inadequate that Rabbi Chiya did not even engage with the specific number. He simply noted that there was not even thirty, meaning the case was obviously problematic, and there was nothing to discuss.

---

## Sixty/100 Drash

### All by 60

The *Gemara* now moves from the historical development to scriptural grounding. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, in the name of Bar Kappara: *kol issurin she-ba-Torah beshishim* — all Torah prohibitions are measured by sixty. This statement distills the entire preceding discussion into a single universal principle: regardless of what the forbidden item is or what the permissible mixture is, sixty is the measure.

### All by 100

A second tradition, also in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi via Bar Kappara — but transmitted through a different chain — states the opposite: *kol issurin she-ba-Torah beme'ah* — all Torah prohibitions are measured by one hundred. One hundred does appear in *mishna* contexts, specifically in tractates of *Zeraim* concerning agricultural prohibitions such as *terumah* and *orlah*, where a higher threshold applies. But as a universal standard for general taste-based prohibitions, it is a striking claim. The *Gemara* identifies a single source from which both sixty and one hundred are derived — the case of the ram's foreleg offered in connection with the *nazir's* sacrifice — and explains how the two traditions emerge from different ways of analyzing that case.

---

## Ram's Foreleg

### Nazir's Ram

The case is as follows: a *nazir* who completes his period of abstinence brings a ram as a *shelamim* offering. The foreleg of that ram — the *zeroa* — is designated for the *kohen* and may not be eaten by non-*kohanim*. The foreleg is cooked together with the rest of the ram. The question is: how can a non-*kohen* eat the rest of the ram, given that the foreleg — which is forbidden to non-*kohanim* and functions in status like *kodshei kodashim* — was cooked in the same pot? Should not its taste transfer to the rest of the meat and render it forbidden? The answer offered by the *Gemara* is that the proportions of the foreleg to the rest of the ram are such that taste is nullified — and this proportional relationship becomes the model for the universal standards of sixty and one hundred.

### Cooking Methods

A *baraita* is cited on the question of how the foreleg is cooked. One view holds that *bisheila* means the foreleg is cooked whole and intact with the ram. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai reads *bisheila* to mean specifically that it is cooked together with the ram in the same pot. The precise tannaitic dispute concerns the procedure: one opinion holds that the foreleg is severed first and then cooked together with the rest of the ram in the same vessel; another holds that it is all cooked together first and then the foreleg is separated; a third possibility is that the foreleg is cooked in a separate pot entirely. The *Gemara* notes that according to the first approach, the *Gemara's* derivation applies according to all opinions, since in every case the foreleg ends up cooked together with the rest of the ram. According to the second approach, the derivation applies only according to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, since the view that the foreleg is cooked separately would eliminate the very scenario from which we are learning.

### 60 vs. 100

The dispute between sixty and one hundred now resolves itself as a disagreement about which proportions to measure. The opinion that sixty is the standard holds: *basar va'atzamot bahadei basar va'atzamot misha'arinan* — we measure meat and bones against meat and bones. When you compare the total mass of the foreleg (meat and bone together) to the total mass of the rest of the ram (meat and bone together), the ratio is approximately one to sixty. The opinion that one hundred is the standard holds: *basar bahadei basar misha'arinan* — we measure meat against meat alone. The foreleg, like a chicken's drumstick, has a relatively high ratio of bone to meat compared with the rest of the animal. If you strip out the bones and compare only the meat of the foreleg to the meat of the rest of the ram, the proportional meat in the foreleg is smaller — and the ratio of the rest of the ram's meat to the foreleg's meat comes out to approximately one hundred.

### Bones Question

Rashi raises the underlying question that drives this dispute: do bones absorb taste, and do bones give off taste? There is marrow in bones; they may well contribute to and absorb flavor to some degree. If one includes bones as taste-active, one measures the full mass of bone and meat against bone and meat, yielding sixty. If one treats only meat as taste-active — whether because bones neither give nor absorb significantly, or because they do so at a different rate — then one measures meat against meat alone, yielding one hundred. Ordinarily, the *Gemara* assumes a rather inclusive approach to what counts toward the sixty: everything in the pot, including liquids, solids, and even the walls of the vessel, in principle contributes. But the question of bones specifically — and whether the bones of the forbidden substance itself are counted, and whether the marrow within them is treated as taste-active — is a live issue that this *Gemara* directly engages.

---

## Exception or Rule

### Exceptional Status

Having established the foreleg as the model for sixty and one hundred, the *Gemara* raises a fundamental objection: the foreleg case is described in a *baraita* as *heter ha-ba mi-kol issur* — something permissible that derives from what would otherwise be an exceptional category of prohibition. In other words, the *baraita* itself signals that this case is unusual. If it is unusual, how can we learn universal rules of sixty and one hundred from it? The concern runs in both directions: if it is an exception, perhaps the Torah was more lenient here than the general rule, in which case sixty or one hundred may not actually be sufficient in ordinary cases.

### Rabbi Yehuda Exception

Abaye offers the first answer. The *baraita's* characterization of the foreleg case as exceptional applies specifically to the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that *min bemino* — a substance mixed with its own kind — is never subject to *bitul* regardless of proportions. Blood mixed with blood, meat mixed with meat: for Rabbi Yehuda, the identical nature of the two substances means the forbidden component can never be considered nullified, no matter how small it is. The foreleg is meat cooked with meat; under Rabbi Yehuda's principle, it should never be *batel*. The Torah nonetheless declares it *batel* at sixty or one hundred — and that is the *chidush*, the innovation. This case represents the Torah making an exception to Rabbi Yehuda's principle.

### Yom Kippur Parallel

The *Gemara* establishes the basis for Rabbi Yehuda's general principle: the verse concerning the Yom Kippur service says to take from the blood of the ox *and* from the blood of the goat, mix them, and then sprinkle — which implies that even after mixing, both bloods retain their distinct identities and neither is ever nullified by the other, despite the obvious quantitative disproportion (an ox produces far more blood than a goat). This establishes Rabbi Yehuda's *din*: same-kind mixtures are never subject to *bitul*. The foreleg case thus represents a specific scriptural exception to that principle.

### Learning Stringencies

This then resolves the *Gemara's* concern about deriving a general rule from an exceptional case.
