There is a principle that one does not learn leniencies from exceptional cases — *chidush lo gamrinan*. But sixty and one hundred are not leniencies learned from the foreleg. They are *stringencies*. Biblically, a minority is ordinarily nullified by a majority — *de'oraita beruba batel*. According to Rashi, this is because taste itself is not a biblical concern, and without a concern of taste, a simple majority suffices. According to Tosafot, the reason is different: in a case of *min bemino*, where everything tastes the same, there is no taste-impartation concern at all, and therefore a simple majority would be sufficient even if one accepts taste as a biblical category. Either way, requiring sixty or one hundred rather than a simple majority is a *stringency* relative to the biblical baseline. And stringencies may be learned from exceptional cases. The foreleg teaches us to be more demanding than the raw biblical minimum — and that teaching applies universally.

---

## Ta'am by Kodashim

### Ta'am Exception

Rava offers an alternative framing of what makes the foreleg case exceptional. The *baraita* describes it as an exception, Rava says, because the Torah here sets aside the concern of *ta'am ke'ikar* — the principle that taste is legally equivalent to the substance itself. In all other contexts of *kodashim*, *ta'am ke'ikar* applies and creates a prohibition. Here, the Torah permits despite the potential transfer of taste. The exception is not about *min bemino* per se, as Abaye suggested, but about the suspension of *ta'am ke'ikar* in this specific context.

### Rashi Position

Rashi draws from Rava's formulation a significant implication: if *ta'am ke'ikar* is described as a problem specifically "by *kodashim*," this implies that it is not a biblical problem in ordinary, non-*kodashim* contexts. In other words, Rashi reads this *Gemara* as grounding a position that taste-based prohibitions are rabbinic in origin, not biblical, when it comes to ordinary food mixtures. The biblical mechanism of *bitul* is then fundamentally quantitative — about proportional insignificance — and not primarily about whether flavor has been imparted. This is why sixty and one hundred can be derived as independently meaningful thresholds, not merely as practical proxies for taste.

### Tosafot Position

Tosafot vigorously rejects this reading. In Tosafot's view, *ta'am ke'ikar* is unambiguously a biblical prohibition in all contexts, as demonstrated by numerous *sugyot* elsewhere. The foreleg case does not prove that taste is only a rabbinic concern in ordinary cases; it simply presents a situation where *ta'am ke'ikar* in its ordinary sense is not triggered, because all the material in the pot is of the same kind and tastes the same. The entire *sugya* is therefore not overturning the biblical status of taste, but rather addressing what happens when the taste concern is neutralized by identity of species.

### Residual Taste

Tosafot offers a more precise reading of what Rava means by describing the foreleg case as an exception regarding *ta'am ke'ikar*. What the foreleg case sets aside is not full *ta'am ke'ikar* — which would require actual discernible flavor transfer — but something more subtle: *ta'am she'ein mishtaneh*, residual taste that lingers even when nothing qualitatively distinct can be detected. In *kodashim*, even such imperceptible residual transfer of taste-properties is normally a concern and creates *kodashim*-level restrictions on whatever absorbed it. The foreleg case is lenient specifically regarding this category of residual taste, not regarding the mainstream prohibition of *ta'am ke'ikar*. And since this is a leniency, it cannot be extended beyond the specific case.

### Chatat Absorption

The *Gemara* grounds the normal *kodashim* stringency regarding residual taste in a verse: *kol asher yigga biv'sarah yikdash* — anything that touches the flesh of a *chatat* becomes holy. This is interpreted to mean that if a *korban* absorbs the juices of a *chatat*, it takes on the stringencies of the *chatat*: if the *chatat* was invalid, the absorbing *korban* is treated as invalid; if the *chatat* was valid but subject to a one-day eating restriction, a *korban* that would normally be eaten over two days and absorbed from the *chatat* may only be eaten for one day. This applies even when the two *korbanot* are the same kind — *min bemino* — and even when the quantity transferred is minimal and qualitatively indistinguishable. It demonstrates that in *kodashim*, residual taste transfer is a real and operative concern, which is precisely what the foreleg case sets aside as an exception.

### Conclusion

The *Gemara* completes its argument symmetrically. One might ask: if the foreleg case is an exception that sets aside residual-taste concerns, why not learn from it a general rule that residual taste is always inconsequential? The answer is the same as before: we do not learn leniencies from exceptional cases. And one might further ask: if the case is entirely exceptional, how can we derive from it the standards of sixty and one hundred? Again: because sixty and one hundred are stringencies relative to the biblical baseline. Without the foreleg, one would say that a simple majority suffices — either because taste is not biblically operative (Rashi) or because in a same-kind mixture there is nothing to taste (Tosafot). The foreleg demands more than a majority, and that greater demand is a stringency we extend universally. The extraordinary nature of the case, then, does not prevent us from learning stringencies from it — and it is precisely from the proportions of that cooked arm to the rest of the ram that the measures of sixty and one hundred are derived and applied to all forbidden admixtures throughout the Torah.

---

---

# Hullin 99

## Ta'am vs. Shishim

### Two Models of Bitul

The sugya of Hullin 99 sits at the heart of some of the most fundamental questions in practical *kashrut* — the twin criteria of *ta'am* (taste) and *shishim* (one-in-sixty) as measures for *bitul*. To appreciate where we are picking up, it is worth briefly recalling the two models that the *gemara* has been developing.

The first model is taste-based. The *mishna* raises the question of the *gid hanasheh* cooked in the thigh: the criterion is whether the forbidden substance can still be tasted. When *min b'mino* — like mixed with like — makes tasting impossible, the *mishna* suggests an analogy: evaluate it as one would evaluate meat cooked with turnips, treating the permissible meat as a stand-in for the *gid* and assessing whether the taste can be detected. The *gemara* extends this approach, introducing the model of imagining every forbidden substance as if it were an onion, so that its potential contribution to taste is treated stringently. Rabbi Yochanan goes further, opening the possibility of relying on a non-Jewish taster — a professional cook, for instance — to determine whether *ta'am* is present, or, if the food is otherwise *kosher*, even a Jewish taster.

The second model is quantitative. Unable or unwilling to rely on tasting in every case, the *gemara* develops the *shiur* of sixty — a ratio at which the forbidden substance is presumed to be *battel*. This ratio emerged as a stand-in for *ta'am*: when *ta'am* cannot be assessed directly, one-in-sixty serves as a proxy. The *gemara* noted that earlier traditions had fluctuated — one-in-thirty for certain rabbinic prohibitions, one-in-forty-five or forty-seven in some contexts — but one-in-sixty eventually became the operative standard.

### Sefardi vs. Ashkenazi

These two models map, broadly, onto the divergence between Sephardic and Ashkenazic practice. The Sephardic approach holds that when *treif* material is mixed with *kosher* food, one may and indeed should invite a non-Jew to taste it under appropriate conditions — namely, circumstances where there is no concern that the taster is trying to mislead. If the non-Jew cannot detect the forbidden substance, the food is permitted. Only when *ta'am* testing is unavailable — whether because there is no suitable taster or because the mixture is *min b'mino* and taste cannot distinguish — does one fall back on the *shiur* of one-in-sixty.

The Ashkenazic approach, by contrast, adopts a unified standard. Rather than adjudicate each case individually, Ashkenazic practice follows one-in-sixty as the universal rule — what one might describe as the "keep it simple" principle, which in practice means adopting the most stringent applicable standard. The Ashkenazic authorities do not in principle deny that *ta'am* is the underlying concern, but they prefer a fixed numerical threshold to case-by-case evaluation.

### Rashi: Quantitative Requ…

This brings us to a striking dispute between the *rishonim* about the nature of the *shiur* itself. Rashi reads the *gemara's* derivation from the *psukimm* — the *zroa beshelah*, the cooked arm of the ram brought as part of the *shelamim* offering — as establishing an independent biblical requirement. On Rashi's view, there is a quantitative threshold that operates independently of *ta'am*: even if *ta'am k'ikar d'oraisa* is itself subject to debate, the Torah independently requires that the forbidden substance be quantitatively insignificant. One-in-sixty, or according to another opinion one-in-a-hundred, is not merely a stand-in for taste but a self-standing biblical criterion.

### Tosafot: Asmachta Model

Tosafot disagrees sharply. According to Tosafot, the *gemara's* use of those *pesukim* is an *asmachta* — a supporting textual peg for what is, at its core, a rabbinic enactment. The one-in-sixty rule is a rabbinic substitute for the *ta'am* test, and the *pesukim* lend it a textual anchor without making it a genuine biblical derivation. On this reading, the fundamental Torah-level concern remains *ta'am*, and the numerical standard is an instituted rabbinic proxy.

---

## Ravina: Makom Chatech

### Leniency at Cut Site

Having surveyed those two positions, the *gemara* now turns to a lingering problem. Earlier, the *gemara* had cited the *zroa beshelah* — the arm of the ram cooked for the *shelamim* — as the source from which to derive the *shiur* of sixty or a hundred. But a complication arose: the *gemara* had also noted that this case was described as a special leniency, which raises the question of what the leniency pertains to and whether one can legitimately derive general *bitul* rules from it.

Ravina resolves this by arguing that the special leniency of the *zroa beshelah* has nothing whatsoever to do with *bitul* and therefore cannot undermine the derivation. The leniency, he says — *lo nitzrecha ela limkom chatech* — concerns the place of cutting: *d'amar makom chatech batar amma shadi*. Normally, the exact point at which a forbidden thing is severed from the permitted is treated with stringency. Here, in this particular case, the Torah is lenient about that precise boundary zone.

### Fetus & Arm Boundary

To appreciate Ravina's point, one must recall a well-known *gemara* concerning a fetus whose arm protrudes from the womb during birth. That arm cannot be eaten — it lies outside the mother, and the mother's *shechitah* does not render it permitted. But if one cuts off the protruding arm, what is the status of the tissue at exactly the point of severance — the material that is neither clearly inside the womb nor clearly outside it, precisely at the thickness of the womb wall? The conceptual question the *gemara* poses is: is it the being-outside that renders the limb forbidden, or is it the failure to be inside the womb that disqualifies it from the protection of the mother's *shechitah*? At the precise boundary, one might think stringency demands treating that tissue as part of the forbidden exterior.

In the case of the *zroa beshelah*, similarly: when the Kohen receives the arm of the ram, one might imagine that the exact flesh at the joint of connection should also be given to the Kohen, lest it be considered part of the arm. The leniency is that we are not strict about this grey zone — we do not extend the obligation to the precise place of attachment. That is the special ruling here, and it has no bearing on proportional *bitul*.

### Tosafot: Remove & Give

Tosafot adds that this principle is not unique to the *zroa beshelah* but applies across *kodashim*. Whenever the Torah commands giving a specific portion to the Kohen — the breast, the thigh, the arm from the *shelamim* — the operative instruction is simply: remove this and give it. The Torah's language of "remove and give" implicitly and naturally excludes that grey zone of exact connection from the obligation. On Tosafot's reading, one does not even need a special *pasuk* for this. The instruction *remove the arm and give the arm to the Kohen* means just what it says — the identifiable arm, not the ambiguous tissue at the point of severance. The case thus requires no special leniency, and the *gemara's* identification of it as a leniency is, for Tosafot, simply a function of what the Torah's own ordinary language implies.

---

## Abaye's Challenge

### Rav Dimi's Report

With Ravina's resolution of the *zroa beshelah* difficulty in place, the *gemara* now records a separate exchange. Rav Dimi was sitting and relating this entire discussion — the attempt to ground a *shiur* of one-in-sixty or one-in-a-hundred in *pesukim* as an independent requirement for *bitul*. Abaye challenged him directly: how could there be any opinion requiring one-in-a-hundred for ordinary *issurim* across the board?

### Orlah Mishna Analysis

To press the point, Abaye invokes a *mishna* — specifically the *mishna* in *Orlah*. The *mishna* asks: in what circumstances do the rules of *mechametz* (leavening), *metabel* (seasoning), and *medameh* (simple mixture — here in the context of *terumah*) apply to create a stringency? The answer it gives is: *lehachmir min b'mino* — the stricter numerical threshold applies when like is mixed with like. But by *min vesheino mino* — unlike mixed with unlike, apples and oranges — the rule cuts both ways: it can be strict and it can be lenient. The *mishna* then explains: for unlike items, taste governs exclusively. If the forbidden substance can be tasted, it is forbidden; if it cannot be tasted, it is permitted — and this is true regardless of whether there is or is not a ratio of one-in-a-hundred. The numbers are simply irrelevant when it is apples and oranges.

This, says Abaye, proves that across the *mishnyot*, there is no numerical threshold for ordinary *issurim* — only taste. Numbers of the type one-in-a-hundred belong to a specialized domain: certain agricultural prohibitions like *terumah* and *orlah*. They have never appeared as a standard for ordinary *issurim*, where the measure has always and only been *ta'am*.

### Min B'Mino Framework

Before examining how the *gemara* responds, it is worth dwelling on the conceptual framework of *min b'mino* and *min b'she'eino mino*, because the relationship between them is somewhat counterintuitive.

For *min b'she'eino mino* — unlike with unlike, apples and oranges — there is always a natural measure of identity: can the forbidden substance still be tasted? If it can be tasted, its identity persists; if not, it has been fully absorbed and has lost its identity. The analogy is to someone who has completely acclimated to a surrounding culture — they no longer look or feel different. Taste is king here, and since taste measures identity in this category, we cannot demand more of an unlike mixture than the loss of taste. To do so would be incoherent: if it cannot be tasted, its identity is already gone.

For *min b'mino* — like with like, apples and apples — there is no such natural measure, because the taste test is inherently unavailable. This creates two polar possibilities. At one extreme, one could say that since there is no distinct taste to detect, a simple majority of *heter* suffices to render the forbidden substance *battel be'rov*: the forbidden apple has no way to make its presence felt, so it simply vanishes into the majority. At the other extreme, one could say — as Rabbi Yehuda does — that since the forbidden substance never loses its identity (it is always apples), it is never *battel* at all. A middle position, broadly associated with the *Rambam*, holds that the forbidden substance becomes nullified through its extreme quantitative insignificance — *battel me'otzem mi'uto* — not through being untasteable, but through being quantitatively trivial, which requires a fixed ratio rather than a simple majority.

This dual character of *min b'mino* explains what would otherwise seem paradoxical: in the world of *terumah* and *orlah*, where we demand elevated numerical thresholds to effect *bitul*, those stringent thresholds apply specifically and only to *min b'mino*, not to *min b'she'eino mino*. For unlike-with-unlike, the identity is already demonstrably lost when taste is absent, and one cannot demand more. For like-with-like, precisely because taste is unavailable as a measure, we can impose — and in the context of particularly stringent prohibitions, do impose — a demanding numerical standard such as one-in-a-hundred.

---

## Orlah Mishna Deep Dive

### Split Peas Example

The *gemara* now examines the *seifa* of the *mishna* in detail. The case presented is split peas (*grisin*) and lentils (*adashim*) cooked together — two types of legume that, while perhaps not as divergent in flavor as, say, meat and fish, are considered different enough to constitute *min b'she'eino mino* for these purposes. One of them is *terumah* and the other is ordinary produce. What is the rule?

The *mishna* states: if you can taste it, it is forbidden, regardless of whether the ratio reaches one-in-a-hundred-and-one or not. Conversely, if you cannot taste it, it is permitted — again regardless of whether the ratio is one-in-a-hundred-and-one or not. In other words, for *min b'she'eino mino*, the numerical threshold of one-in-a-hundred is entirely irrelevant. Taste governs exclusively and completely.

### Gemara's Inference

Here the *gemara* makes a striking move. One might have thought that if taste is absent, that is simply the end of the matter — no further criterion need be satisfied. But the *gemara* now operates from a different assumption: it takes for granted that a *shiur* must be in play, that there is always some numerical standard lurking in the background. On this assumption, the *mishna's* statement that the food is permitted without a hundred-to-one ratio must mean that a different, lower number is operative. And since the only alternative number the *gemara* knows of is sixty, it infers: *lav b'shishim* — must it not be sixty? This *mishna* would thus prove that the correct *shiur* is sixty rather than a hundred, since it explicitly excludes the stricter threshold of a hundred for the case of *min b'she'eino mino*.

The *gemara* challenges this inference: perhaps the number that applies in this lenient case is still a hundred, just as in the strict case. But this creates an immediate problem: if the lenient case of apples-and-oranges also requires a hundred, it is no different from the strict case of apples-and-apples, and the *mishna's* distinction between the two collapses. The *gemara* therefore responds: *rישא וסיפא be-me'ah* — perhaps both the *reisha* and *seifa* operate with a hundred, but a different kind of hundred.

### Yeast Example

To understand this response, the *gemara* directs attention to the *reisha* of the *mishna*, the strict case. The example given is *se'or shel chittin she-nafal le-issat chittin* — sourdough starter made of wheat that fell into wheat dough. This is a classic case of *min b'mino*: it is all wheat, there is no possibility of tasting one against the other. The *mishna* states: if the *se'or* has enough to cause fermentation (*kedei lechametz*), then it is forbidden — regardless of whether there is a ratio of one-in-a-hundred-and-one or not. And the converse: if it does not have enough to cause fermentation, it is also forbidden if the ratio of one-in-a-hundred-and-one is not present.

This requires unpacking. The logic is as follows: for *min b'mino* where the *shiur* is one-in-a-hundred, there are two independent conditions that must both be satisfied for the mixture to be permitted. First, the forbidden substance must be unable to make its impact felt — in this case, it must be unable to cause fermentation. Second, there must be a ratio of at least one-in-a-hundred of *heter* against the *issur*. Conversely, the mixture is forbidden if either condition is unmet: if the *se'or* can still cause fermentation, no ratio saves it; and if the ratio is insufficient — even if in theory the fermentation ability is absent — it is still forbidden.

The reason both conditions are necessary is that, by *min b'mino*, the measure of taste is replaced by these two surrogates: the numerical ratio and the functional impact (here, the ability to ferment). Fermentation is, in a sense, the analogue of tasting for *min b'mino* — it is the only way the forbidden substance's presence can be felt when it is indistinguishable by flavor. Crucially, this framework also explains how you can have a concept of *ta'am* even with *min b'mino*: the fermenting ability functions as the equivalent of taste, since it is a detectable impact on the mixture.

### Hundred vs. 99

The *gemara* now offers its resolution: *lo, reisha be-me'ah ve-chad, ve-seifa be-me'ah*. The key is what "a hundred and one" means in each context. In the strict case of *min b'mino* by *terumah*, one-in-a-hundred-and-one means the forbidden object plus a hundred opposite it — a hundred parts *heter* against the *issur*. In the lenient case of *min b'she'eino mino*, according to the opinion that demanded a numerical threshold for ordinary *issurim*, "a hundred" means a hundred in total: one of *issur* and ninety-nine of *heter*. The difference between the strict and lenient cases is therefore: the strict case demands a hundred of *heter*, while the lenient case requires only ninety-nine.

This answer, it must be said, is not a satisfying one, and it is hardly surprising that the opinion requiring a hundred for ordinary *issurim* is effectively set aside. The whole thrust of the *gemara's* analysis is that a threshold of one-in-a-hundred belongs to the world of *terumah*, *orlah*, and *kil'ayim* — the agricultural prohibitions where elevated *shiurim* are explicitly known. It has no place in the ordinary world of *issurim*, where the *mishnayot* know only taste. The most that can be justified for ordinary *issurim* is one-in-sixty, and even that is either an independent rabbinic enactment (Tosafot's position) or a biblically-grounded independent standard (Rashi's position), but never the heightened threshold of a full hundred-to-one.

---

## Exceptions: Pungent Items

### Se'or Special Case

Having resolved the dispute about sixty versus a hundred, the *gemara* raises a different kind of question — one that cuts against the entire project of reducing *bitul* to a single numerical standard. The *gemara* confronts the following difficulty: if sourdough starter has enough fermenting power to leaven the dough but there is a hundred-to-one ratio against it, why is it still forbidden? Surely its presence is trivial if it is one part in a hundred. The questioner is silenced — he does not know how to respond — and his interlocutor suggests: *dilma shani se'or de-chimutzo kasheh* — perhaps *se'or* is different because its fermenting power is exceptionally strong. Even at one-in-a-hundred dilution, sourdough starter may genuinely retain real leavening capacity.

### Fermentation Exception

This suggestion prompts Rav Yosef bar Chanina to articulate a broader principle: *lo kol hashi'urin shavin* — not all *shi'urim* are equal. The derivation of a standard *shiur* of sixty (or a hundred) does not mean that this threshold functions identically in every case. Where a substance is exceptionally pungent, possesses unusual fermenting power, or produces a detectable impact by some mechanism other than ordinary flavor, the numbers cannot simply be applied mechanically and treated as dispositive. This is, in essence, a reminder that the underlying concern is always *ta'am* — the perceptible impact of the forbidden substance — and the numerical threshold is a proxy for that concern, not a replacement for it. Where the perceptible impact demonstrably survives the numerical threshold, the threshold alone cannot create *bitul*.

This principle has obvious practical implications. Spices, artificial flavors, natural flavor additives — all of these are substances whose impact is disproportionate to their quantity. The entire purpose of adding a tiny amount of a flavor concentrate is precisely that it can be tasted even at a minute proportion. The numerical *shiur* cannot simply override what is perceptually present.

### Tzir & Ze'iva B'Alma

A related case is *tzir* — fish brine. The *gemara* states that for *tzir*, the *shi'ur* required for *bitul* is close to two hundred: *shi'uro karov l'masayim*. The source is a *mishna* stating that the brine of a non-*kosher* fish is forbidden. Rabbi Yehuda gives the *shiur* as a *revi'is* in *sasayim* — approximately a quarter-*log* in two *seah*, which works out to a ratio of roughly one-in-192. This is a remarkable stringency.

The *gemara* then raises a complication: Rabbi Yehuda is the same authority who holds that *min b'mino lo batil* — like-with-like is never nullified. So presumably this *mishna* concerns brine mixed with brine, i.e., *min b'mino*, and his stringency is consistent with his general position. But then the *gemara* notes: *shani tzir de-ze'iva b'alma hu* — Rabbi Yehuda is in fact lenient about *tzir*, because brine is only *ze'iva b'alma*, a mere secretion or sweat of the fish, not the fish itself. Therefore, even Rabbi Yehuda is willing to allow *bitul* for it, and his leniency is expressed through the relatively accessible (for a substance so pungent) standard of one-in-192.

Two observations are worth making here. First, Tosafot notes the broader question of whether brine or juices flowing off forbidden substances are themselves biblical prohibitions. If *ta'am k'ikar* is biblical, one might expect the brine to carry the same prohibition as the fish itself, since it carries the same flavor. But there may be gradations — whether the flowing juices constitute the identical *issur* or a derivative one — and those gradations affect the *shiur* required. The *gemara* in fact records a *pasuk* that treats the brine of non-*kosher* fish as a biblical prohibition, even though an argument exists that it is *ze'iva b'alma*.

Second, the question of *ze'iva b'alma* recurs in a context familiar from discussions of *Pesach*: grain alcohol. Some authorities argue that alcohol derived from grain is *chametz gamur*, full and complete *chametz*, while others contend it may be *ze'iva b'alma* — a mere secretion of the grain, comparable to flavor rather than substance — and potentially subject to different rules. Whether *ze'iva* is analogous to the general questions of *ta'am k'ikar* is itself a distinct discussion in the *poskim*.

One further puzzle deserves mention. The entire framework of exceeding the *shiur* because of pungency or residual impact seems to presuppose *min b'she'eino mino* — cases where taste is the operative measure and one's concern is that the detectable taste survives the *shiur*. But for the case of brine with brine — *min b'mino* — how can one speak of pungency or perceptible taste at all? If it all tastes the same, by definition the forbidden substance's presence cannot be tasted. And if the brine tastes different from the other liquid, it is *min b'she'eino mino* and not subject to a fixed numerical standard in the first place. This leaves the conceptual basis of Rabbi Yehuda's *shiur* for *tzir* somewhat unclear, and a fully satisfying answer is not readily available.

---

## Summary & Principles

### Practical Story

The foregoing analysis can be drawn together through a vivid practical illustration. At a large *simcha*, a substantial quantity of food was inadvertently rendered potentially *treif* when forbidden material fell in. The question was whether the mixture contained a ratio of one-in-sixty or not, and it was uncertain. What could be done?

First, a non-Jew was brought and asked to taste the food. He reported that he could not detect any foreign flavor. For a Sephardic *posek*, this was sufficient: the Sephardic position is that a non-Jew may be relied upon to determine the absence of *ta'am*, and if no *ta'am* is present, the food is permitted. Having established this, the Sephardic rabbi ate from the dish. This then created a new possibility for the Ashkenazic guests. The Ashkenazic authorities, while they do not rely on a non-Jew's tasting, do accept — at least *be'di'eved* — the testimony of a Jew regarding *ta'am*. The Sephardic rabbi, a Jew, had now tasted the food and confirmed no foreign flavor was present. On that basis, the Ashkenazic guests were also able to eat.

This anecdote illustrates not merely legal ingenuity but the structural logic of the entire sugya. The fundamental concern of both Sephardic and Ashkenazic practice is *ta'am* — the presence or absence of a detectable flavor. The Ashkenazic preference for one-in-sixty as a universal standard is not a rejection of the primacy of *ta'am* but a simplification designed to avoid case-by-case adjudication. Where *ta'am* can be demonstrated to be absent through a mechanism Ashkenazic authorities do credit, that underlying concern is equally resolved.

There is also a broader cultural dimension to the Sephardic willingness to rely on a non-Jew's tasting. One might wonder whether the different historical experiences of Sephardic and Ashkenazic Jewry shaped their respective attitudes toward non-Jewish testimony in *kashrut* matters. Sephardic Jewry in its classical period, particularly under Islamicate rule, lived in a relatively hospitable environment, whereas Ashkenazic Jewry endured centuries of hostile Christian Europe, including the Crusades. That said, it would be an oversimplification to attribute the Ashkenazic reluctance primarily to mistrust of non-Jews per se. At its core, the Ashkenazic approach is about standardization: one fixed rule, one-in-sixty, applied universally, without the complexity of evaluating individual circumstances of tasting or the identity of the taster.

---

## Meat-Turnip Analogy

### Taste Model Setup

Having resolved the larger theoretical questions about *ta'am* and *shishim*, the *gemara* returns to the concrete problem with which the *sugya* opened: how does one determine in practice whether a *gid hanasheh* cooked in the thigh has imparted *ta'am*?

Rav Huna offers a practical model: evaluate it *ke'basar be'roshei liftot* — as one evaluates meat cooked with the heads of turnips. In other words, take a reference case of meat cooked with turnip heads (or roots, depending on one's reading), and use that as the taste-standard for assessing whether the *gid* has imparted flavor to the surrounding meat and broth. In this model, the meat represents the *gid* and the turnip represents the rest of the pot. There is a dispute between Rashi and Tosafot about whether the *reisha* (top) or the *ikkar* (root) of the turnip is more effective at absorbing and dispersing taste — which in turn affects whether the model is being applied stringently or leniently — but the core principle is clear: a structured analogy serves as a practical instrument for assessing *ta'am* when direct tasting is unavailable or inapplicable.

---

## Baraita Gid Dispute

### No Taste Position

The *gemara* now introduces a *tanna* whose position stands at odds with the *stam mishna's* assumption that the *gid hanasheh* does pose a potential *ta'am* problem. A *beraita* records the view of Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Yochanan ben Beroka: *ein be'gidim b'nosein ta'am* — *gidin* have no taste. Accordingly, if a *gid hanasheh* is cooked in the thigh together with the surrounding meat, one need not concern oneself with *ta'am* at all. The *gid* simply did not impart any flavor, and therefore no question of *bitul* arises.

It is worth noting that this position is analytically separable from a different claim that appears earlier in the *sugya* — namely, the opinion that since *gid* has no taste, what the Torah forbade must be limited to its identifiable branches (*knoknot*). Rabbi Yehoshua's *beraita* does not directly adjudicate what is or is not forbidden as *gid hanasheh*; it simply asserts a factual claim about taste. One can hold, as the *gemara* elsewhere suggests, that *etzu ve-Torah asarto* — yes, it is like wood, tasteless, but the Torah forbade it nonetheless — while simultaneously accepting that since it has no taste, cooking it with meat creates no secondary *ta'am* problem. These are distinct questions.

---

## Rabbi Chanina Incident

### Initial Inquiry

### Chanina's Response

The *gemara* now relates a narrative that brings the halakhic pluralism latent in this dispute vividly to life. Someone came before Rabbi Chanina with a question — evidently the classic scenario of a *gid hanasheh* that had been cooked together with the surrounding meat. Rabbi Yehuda bar Zvina was sitting at the doorway of Rabbi Chanina's house, and when the questioner emerged, Rabbi Yehuda asked him: *mai amar lach* — what did he say to you? The questioner replied: *sharya ni alei* — he told me it was permitted. Presumably Rabbi Chanina had ruled *ein be'gidin b'nosein ta'am* and told him not to worry.

Rabbi Yehuda bar Zvina was not satisfied with this answer, and he instructed the questioner to go back inside and ask again, as if perhaps he had misunderstood. The questioner did so. Rabbi Chanina's reaction was sharp: *man hai de-ka meitzarei li* — who is this that is troubling me? He then said to the questioner, in effect: go tell whoever is sitting out at the doorway — *zil eimal lei leman de-yasiv b'vava* — that *gidin* have no taste and the food is permitted. That is my ruling. I am not changing it because someone finds it surprising or unwelcome, and I am not going to be pressured into reversing a *psak* simply because it is being second-guessed from the doorstep.

The incident is instructive on several levels. Rabbi Chanina is following the position of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who held that *gid hanasheh* has no *ta'am*. He is fully confident in this ruling and resists the implicit pressure — communicated through the returned questioner — to adopt a more stringent position.

---

## Pluralistic Halakhic (II)

### Referral to Lenient Posek

The *gemara* then shifts to a different scene. When people — the *gemara* uses the plural *ki asu*, suggesting this was not a rare occurrence, since many people forgot to remove the *gid hanasheh* from the thigh before cooking — came before Rabbi Ammi with this question, he did not answer them directly. Instead, *meshader lehu lekamei de-Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chalov* — he sent them to Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chalov — *de-mori ba le-heteira k'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* — because Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chalov rules leniently, following Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that the *gid* presents no *ta'am* problem.

### Public vs. Private Posit…

And then the *gemara* states the striking conclusion: *ve-lei lo seveira lei* — but Rabbi Ammi himself did not agree with this position. Rabbi Ammi personally held that the mixture was *assur*, yet he consistently referred questioners to Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chalov who would permit it.

### Eilu V'Eilu Pluralism

This *gemara* is, in a certain sense, one of the most remarkable statements of halakhic pluralism in the entire *Talmud*. What Rabbi Ammi is demonstrating is not merely the theoretical acknowledgment that there exist multiple legitimate opinions — something we mouth whenever we note that Ashkenazim and Sephardim follow different rulings. What he is demonstrating is that one can hold a specific *psak* with full conviction while simultaneously recognizing that a different *psak* is also within the legitimate range of *halakha*, to the point where one can actively refer questioners to a *posek* who holds that other position without any compromise of personal integrity or institutional authority.

Normally, *eilu v'eilu divrei Elokim chayim* — "both these and these are words of the living God" — functions as a theoretical statement, quickly followed by *ve-halakha ke-divrei Beit Hillel*: in theory both are legitimate, but in practice one rules. Rabbi Ammi's conduct goes further. He is saying: I know what I hold, I hold it sincerely, and yet I also acknowledge that there is another position that is equally within the range of legitimate *halakha*, and the person in front of me may be better served by consulting the *posek* who holds that position. This is not a compromise of his *psak*; it would be a compromise to rule against his own position. But to acknowledge the legitimacy of another view and to refer accordingly — that, Rabbi Ammi demonstrates, requires no compromise at all.

This implicit acknowledgment operates constantly in any community where Ashkenazic and Sephardic practice coexist, or where different *poskim* are known to hold different positions on the same question. But it is relatively rare to find it stated so consciously and directly within a single community and by a single authority. Rabbi Ammi is not rabbi-shopping; he is a *posek* who, out of a principled recognition of the breadth of legitimate *halakha*, declines to impose his own view on questioners who would be served by hearing a different one.

---

## Summary & Principles (II)

### Gid Hanasheh Ruling

The operative *halakha* is stated plainly: *ve-hilch'ta ein be'gidin b'nosein ta'am* — the *gid hanasheh* has no taste, and if it is cooked in the surrounding meat, one is not required to apply numerical *bitul* standards. The practical ruling is simply to remove the *gid*; the concern that it may have imparted *ta'am* to the meat or broth during cooking does not stand.

This conclusion is, as noted, somewhat surprising against the backdrop of the *stam mishna*, which seemed to assume that *ta'am* from the *gid* was a genuine concern worth elaborate discussion. The *halakha* sets that concern aside entirely.

Rashi limits the ruling somewhat: he notes that the fat (*cheilev*) surrounding the *gid* does have taste, and if the fat was present and cooked, its contribution to the mixture remains a concern unless the *cheilev* was also removed. Tosafot, however, argues that we cannot apply greater stringency to the fat of the *gid* than to the *gid* itself. If the operative *halakha* is that *gidin* impart no *ta'am*, we do not separately reintroduce a *ta'am* concern via the surrounding fat. On Tosafot's view, the ruling *ein be'gidin b'nosein ta'am* covers the full scenario: remove the *gid* and the surrounding fat, and no *ta'am* problem remains.

A further implication, noted by Tosafot, follows from a *sugya* in *Psachim*. That *gemara* reasons that if *gid hanasheh* has no taste, logic would seem to push toward the conclusion that it is *assur be'hana'ah* — forbidden to derive benefit from it. (The *Rambam* apparently does not accept this implication and does not follow the *Psachim* reasoning, but Tosafot engages it directly.) If we accept that *gid hanasheh* is *assur be'hana'ah*, a question arises about giving an unremoved thigh to a non-Jew: does the presence of the *gid* constitute a kind of indirect benefit to the one handing it over, since the non-Jew may be more pleased to receive the complete thigh? Tosafot essentially dismisses this concern — what would the non-Jew care whether there is a *gid* in the thigh? — but he acknowledges the question.

---

## Pluralistic Halakhic (II)

### Rabbi-Shopping vs. Exper…

The incident involving Rabbi Ammi's referral raises a question worth examining directly: is this not simply rabbi-shopping — the very practice the principle of *asei l'cha rav* is often invoked to prohibit?

The answer requires distinguishing carefully between different phenomena. *Asei l'cha rav*, as a phrase from *Pirkei Avot*, is fundamentally about religious integrity and submission to halakhic authority — the *gemara* elsewhere applies a *pasuk* about necromancy to draw the inference *kol hameikel lo yagid lo*: one who seeks out whoever will be lenient for them is in a certain sense not truly submitting to *halakha* at all. They have already decided what they wish to do and are searching for someone to validate that decision. This is not a failure to follow a particular rabbi; it is a failure to follow *halakha* itself, using the formal structure of asking a *shayla* while avoiding any genuine submission to the answer.

This is fundamentally different from what Rabbi Ammi does, and different from several legitimate forms of consulting different authorities. If one follows a particular rabbi in questions of *kashrut* and a different rabbi in questions of family purity law, because one has genuine confidence in each respective *posek's* expertise and outlook in their area, this is a matter of appropriate specialization and differentiated trust — not shopping for leniency. Similarly, if one encounters a question outside one's usual *posek's* primary area of expertise, seeking a more expert opinion is not rabbi-shopping. And some questions are genuinely sensitive to a *posek's* values and perspective: the weighing of competing concerns in *hilchot nidda*, for example, may be deeply influenced by how a *posek* understands the underlying human and religious stakes involved, and there it may be entirely appropriate to seek a *posek* whose framework one trusts for that particular set of concerns.

The test, in the end, is one of religious integrity rather than formal compliance. Rabbi Ammi refers questioners elsewhere not because he wants them to hear a lenient answer, but because he consciously acknowledges the legitimacy of that answer within the range of *halakha* — and that acknowledgment itself reflects a profound intellectual honesty about what *eilu v'eilu divrei Elokim chayim* means when taken seriously as a living principle rather than a theoretical disclaimer.

---

---

# Hullin 100

## Daf 100 Overview

### Completion & Preview

Daf 100 of *Chullin* marks a milestone — one hundred *dapim* completed — and it also closes what has been an extended and intensive treatment of *kashrus* that will not resume until the next *perek*. The framing context throughout has been the prohibition of *gid hanasheh*: what happens when one inadvertently cooks the *gid* together with permitted meat? That question opened a much broader discussion of *ta'am* (taste), *min bemino* and *min beino mino*, and the role of sixty in nullification.

### Previous Topics Review

To situate the present *sugya*, it is worth recalling the terrain already covered. The *Mishnah* addressed how to determine whether forbidden taste has dispersed through a mixture, the distinction between *min bemino* (like and like, as when forbidden meat falls into permitted meat of the same species) and *min beino mino* (unlike items, such as forbidden fish among permitted meat), and the standard of *shishim* — sixty — as the measure by which absorbed taste is rendered insignificant. Today's *daf* concludes that discussion and then returns the *perek* to the laws of *gid hanasheh* proper.

## Bitul Exceptions

### Mishnah vs. Gemara

The *Mishnah* taught that if a *gid hanasheh* was cooked together with other *gidim* and cannot be identified, none of them may be eaten. Similarly, if a piece of *neveilah* or non-kosher fish became mixed with other pieces of permitted meat and cannot be identified, none of the mixture may be consumed. The plain implication of the *Mishnah* is that *bitul* — nullification — does not operate when the forbidden object is a discrete, independent item rather than a dispersed substance. The *Gemara*, however, pushes back forcefully on this reading.

The *Gemara*'s established principle is that *bitul* functions not merely to negate absorbed taste but to negate the thing itself. One might have been willing to concede *bitul* in cases of thorough admixture — as when blood disperses into water or wine, losing its discrete identity in a homogeneous mass — while still arguing that independent pieces retain their individual integrity and therefore cannot be nullified. After all, when one picks up a single chunk from a pile of chunks, one may be picking up the forbidden piece and nothing else. That is precisely the logic that the *Mishnah* appears to endorse.

### Yavash/Lach Types

The *Rishonim* give this distinction its technical terminology. A homogeneous mixture — whether literally liquid or reduced to a uniform mass in a blender — is called *lach belach*, wet with wet. Discrete, identifiable objects that retain their individual form are called *yavash beyavash*, dry with dry. The *Mishnah*'s apparent ruling is that *bitul* does not work for *yavash beyavash*, since each item retains its integrity.

### Three Exceptions

The *Gemara* rejects that reading entirely. It asserts that *bitul* applies even to *yavash beyavash* — even to separate, independent objects — and that the reason the *Mishnah*'s cases are forbidden is not because *bitul* is categorically inapplicable to discrete items, but because those particular cases fall under specific exceptions. The *Gemara* thereby reformulates the *Mishnah*: rather than establishing a general principle that independent objects cannot be nullified, the *Mishnah* is presenting instances of three recognized exceptions to *bitul*: *berya* (a whole, intact object), items *darko limnot* (customarily sold by count), and *chaticha harauya lehitchabed* (a piece of meat of sufficient quality to be served to honored guests).

### Berya Exception

The first exception is *berya*. The *Gemara*, at the very end of 99b, poses the question with remarkable economy: if *bitul* works even for *yavash beyavash*, then *u-livatel berubbah* — let the *gid* be nullified by a majority of other *gidim*! The answer, in two equally spare words, is *beryah shani* — a *berya* is different. The *gid hanasheh* is a whole object: the Torah's prohibition attaches to the *gid* as an entire, intact entity, and it is that wholeness which prevents it from losing its identity. It should be noted that this applies specifically when the entire *gid* is cooked — if only a segment of the *gid* were involved, it would in principle be subject to *bitul*. But a complete *gid* possesses the halachic status of a *berya*, and a *berya* cannot be negated regardless of how many permitted items surround it.

### Sold by Count

The second exception is the category of *darko limnot* — items customarily sold by count. The *Gemara* at the top of 100a turns to the case of a piece of *neveilah* mixed with other pieces of permitted meat: *v'tibatel berov* — let it be nullified by a majority! The *Gemara*'s response here is more complex and introduces a fascinating tannaitic dispute over the text of a *Mishnah* in *Orlah*.

That *Mishnah* in *Orlah* establishes that certain items are not subject to *bitul* because they are sold by number rather than by weight or volume. The logic is that items sold individually — by count — have significance as independent objects, and that significance prevents them from losing their identity. Items sold by weight or in bulk, by contrast, lack that individual significance; what matters is the quantity, not the particular object.

There is, however, a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish over how to read the operative phrase in that *Mishnah*. Does it read *et shedarko limnot shaninu* — "that which is [exclusively or primarily] sold by count" — meaning the category is limited to items for which counting is the standard mode of sale? Or does it read *kol shedarko limnot shaninu* — "anything whose way it is [even occasionally] to be sold by count"? The practical difference is considerable. A piece of meat, for example, is primarily sold by weight; one pays by the pound. Yet one can certainly imagine a butcher selling an individual rib chop by the piece. According to the broader reading — *kol shedarko limnot* — even that occasional practice suffices to give the piece individual significance. According to the narrower reading — *et shedarko limnot* — meat, which is primarily a commodity sold by weight, would not qualify.

The *Gemara* notes that the question has direct bearing on the *Mishnah*'s case of a piece of *neveilah* among permitted meat. If we follow the broader reading, meat might qualify as *darko limnot* since it is sometimes sold by piece. If we follow the narrower reading, meat does not qualify, and we need another reason to explain why the *Mishnah* forbids the entire mixture.

### Chaticha Exception

That other reason is the third exception: *chaticha harauya lehitchabed*. The *Gemara* states: *shani chaticha, ho'il v're'uyah lehitkabed bah lifnei ha'orchim* — a cut of meat is different, because it is the kind of thing one would present before honored guests. A dignified cut of meat carries a social and honorific significance that prevents it from dissolving into anonymity even when surrounded by a majority of permitted pieces. This is the *Gemara*'s answer even according to the opinion that *et shedarko limnot* — that meat does not qualify as an item primarily sold by count: its status as a fitting presentation piece provides an independent basis for retaining its identity and resisting *bitul*.

### Chaticha Parameters

The *Rishonim* engage in considerable discussion about what precisely qualifies as *chaticha harauya lehitchabed* and what falls outside that category. One question concerns the degree of processing required: does a whole side of beef qualify, even though one would not present it before guests in that form? What about an unplucked chicken — clearly unfit to serve as is, but potentially serviceable after processing? Some hold that the potential for the piece to become presentable is sufficient; others insist that the piece must be fit to serve in its current state.

A related question concerns size and form. Some *Rishonim* hold that a very small piece, or meat that has been reduced to ground meat, would fall outside this category, since neither is typically placed before an honored guest. A larger, intact cut, by contrast, would retain this status regardless of whether it happens to be an inexpensive cut. There is also a nuanced textual difference that carries halachic weight: the phrase *chaticha harauya lehitchabed* — meaning "a piece that is fitting to be honored with" — implies that not all pieces meet this standard, only certain ones. The *Rambam*'s formulation, however, treats a standard cut of meat as presumptively *rauya lehitchabed*, such that the ordinary *chaticha* of meat is assumed to fall into this category without requiring case-by-case assessment. The upshot of the *Gemara*'s analysis is this: even *yavash beyavash*, independent discrete objects, are generally subject to *bitul*. The *Mishnah*'s cases involve exceptions — *berya*, *darko limnot*, and *chaticha harauya lehitchabed* — each of which confers upon the forbidden item a significance, whether legal or social, that allows it to resist nullification.

## Four Quadrants

### Chopped Meat Example

Before examining the precise structure of the *bitul* framework, a clarifying case helps ground the analysis. Consider three separate packages of ground hamburger meat: two kosher and one *neveilah*. The packages have been inadvertently mixed together so that they are indistinguishable. Because the meat is ground, it is not *chaticha harauya lehitchabed*; because it is sold by weight, it is not *darko limnot*; and because it is not intact, it is not a *berya*. None of the three exceptions apply. The question is therefore purely one of *bitul* in the ordinary case of *yavash beyavash*.

The *Gemara*'s ruling — and the view of nearly all *Rishonim* — is that a simple *rov*, a majority, suffices in this case. One may eat all three packages. Some *Rishonim* suggest that the three packages should be eaten separately rather than combined, since eating them together would mean knowingly consuming *issur*; but even those authorities agree that one may make three separate portions and eat each in turn, applying *rov* to each one. Indeed, certain *Rishonim* explain *bitul* here in terms of probability: each time one takes a package, the odds favor its being one of the two kosher ones. But the more fundamental understanding is that when a forbidden item is lost within a majority of permitted items, the *Halachah* treats it as having lost its identity entirely — it is subsumed by the majority and ceases, legally, to exist as the forbidden object.

### Quadrant 1: Rov Enough

This case corresponds to what may be envisioned as the upper-left quadrant of a conceptual grid organizing the four possible combinations of the *yavash/lach* and *min bemino/eino mino* variables. The upper-left quadrant is *yavash beyavash* combined with *min bemino* — separate objects of the same species. Here, the items are not cooked together, so there is no dispersal of taste; and because they are of the same kind, even if cooked together there would be no perceptible alien taste. This is the most lenient quadrant: *rov* alone suffices, both biblically and rabbinically. The three packages of hamburger meat are the paradigm case.

### Quadrant 2: Shishim

The upper-right quadrant is *yavash beyavash* combined with *min beino mino* — separate objects of unlike species. The items are still discrete and not mixed together, so the immediate concern of taste dispersal does not arise. However, because they are of unlike kinds, there is a potential concern: were they to be cooked together, the unlike tastes would interact. This rabbinic concern imports a requirement of *shishim* even for the *yavash beyavash* configuration when the items are *min beino mino*.

### Quadrant 4: Taam Keikar

The lower-right quadrant — *lach belach* combined with *min beino mino* — is the most severe. Here, unlike items are fully mixed together in a liquid or homogeneous medium, and the forbidden taste disperses throughout the entire mixture. This is the biblical problem of *ta'am ke'ikar*: taste is treated as equivalent to the substance itself. One needs *shishim* to nullify that taste, and this requirement is biblical in origin.

### Quadrant 3: Shishim

The lower-left quadrant is *lach belach* combined with *min bemino* — like items cooked together in a liquid medium. In this case, since the items are of the same species, the taste of the forbidden substance is indistinguishable from the taste of the permitted ones; there is no alien flavor to detect. Nevertheless, because the mixture is a homogeneous *lach belach*, there is a theoretical concern that taste could disperse, and one cannot be certain it has not. A rabbinic requirement of *shishim* therefore applies even here. This is precisely the discussion that occupied the previous several *dapim*: even meat cooked with meat of the same type requires sixty when they are combined in a *lach belach* mixture.

The one quadrant that is fully rescued — where *rov* alone suffices and there is no *shishim* requirement, even rabbinically — is the upper-left: *yavash beyavash*, *min bemino*. That is the case of the three separate hamburger packages. They are discrete, not homogeneous; and they are the same species. The forbidden item is furthest from the paradigm of problematic taste dispersal, and thus the ordinary principle of *rov* operates without supplementation.

## Q&A on Bitul

### Cooking Together Q

A natural question arises from the *Mishnah* itself, which discusses *chaticha shel dag* — a piece of fish — cooked together with other pieces. Once items are cooked together, do not their juices exude and intermingle? The answer is yes — and indeed that is exactly what the *Mishnah* addresses. The *Mishnah* requires determining whether taste has been imparted, and if one cannot identify the offending piece, the entire mixture is forbidden. The *Gemara*'s discussion of *bitul* via *rov* pertains to a scenario in which the items are not actually cooked together — where the only problem is one of identity, not of taste dispersal. In that case, absent one of the three exceptions, *rov* suffices. But once items are cooked together in a common pot, one moves into the *lach belach* quadrants, where *shishim* applies.

### Monsey Incident

This framework has direct contemporary application. In the Monsey chicken scandal, a butcher was found to have been selling non-kosher chicken alongside kosher product. One of the halachic questions that arose was whether the pots and equipment of consumers required *kashering*. The observation was made — and credited to Rabbi Tendler's ruling — that since the butcher was simultaneously selling a large quantity of certified kosher chicken alongside the non-kosher product, the principle of *bitul* might apply to the absorbed taste in the cookware, particularly given that any taste absorbed over time is *derabbanan* in status, and a day-old absorbed taste (*nat bar nat*) weakens the stringency further. This is not the place to adjudicate that ruling in full, but it illustrates that the principles under discussion here — *bitul* of *ta'am ke'ikar*, proportionality, and the conditions of *bedieved* leniency — are operative in contemporary *psak*.

### Nine Pieces Q

One might ask whether the case of nine separate pieces of meat drawn from nine different sources — the classic case of *rov* discussed elsewhere in the *Gemara* — is conceptually superior to, inferior to, or equivalent to the three packages of hamburger meat. The answer is that the cases are at least as good as each other, and the hamburger package case may actually be stronger. In the nine-pieces case, one must consume each piece separately while consciously relying on *rov* with each selection, and one must ultimately accept that one has, in fact, consumed a piece of *treifa*. In the hamburger case, by contrast, *bitul* operates as a categorical principle: the forbidden item loses its halachic identity within the majority, and one need not reckon with having consumed *issur* at all.

### Separate vs. Mixed

This distinction highlights a conceptual difference between *rov* and *bitul*. When applying *rov* to a sequence of individual choices — as in the nine-pieces case — the logic is probabilistic: each individual selection is most likely from the permitted majority. But the halachic mechanism of *bitul* goes further. It declares that the forbidden item has ceased, as a matter of law, to exist as a forbidden object within the mixture. The permissibility is not merely probabilistic but ontological: the *issur* has been subsumed.

### Penguin Metaphor

The underlying intuition can be captured by an image: imagine a vast ice floe filled with thousands of identical penguins, save for one who is dancing and insisting on his individual identity. Lost in the crowd, that penguin's distinctiveness evaporates — he is absorbed into the collective mass, indistinguishable from any other. So too with a forbidden item in a mixture: once surrounded by a majority of permitted items with which it is indistinguishable, it loses its individual halachic identity. The exceptions — *berya*, *darko limnot*, *chaticha harauya lehitchabed* — are precisely the cases where the forbidden item is, so to speak, the dancing penguin: it possesses some intrinsic significance, legal or social, that enables it to retain its identity even within the crowd.

### Intentional Mix Q

It must be emphasized, however, that all of the above applies only after the fact — *bedieved*. One is not permitted to deliberately create a nullifying mixture in order to render a forbidden substance permissible. This is the principle of *ein mevatlin issur lechatchilah*: one may not intentionally nullify a prohibition. The cases under discussion all arise from accidental admixture; the leniency of *bitul* is a *bedieved* remedy, not a *lechatchilah* strategy.

### Tomato Sauce Q

A practical illustration: suppose one pours tomato sauce into a stew and then discovers that the sauce contains meat as an ingredient and bears no *hechsher*. One calls the rabbi to ask whether the stew is permissible. The rabbi's analysis will center on proportion — how much non-kosher meat was in the sauce relative to the total volume of the stew — and whether the amount of forbidden substance is sufficient to impart taste. If the proportion is small enough, *bitul* applies and the stew is permitted *bedieved*. The consumer may find this counterintuitive — after all, one is effectively eating something that contains *treifa* — but that is precisely the *chiddush* of *bitul*: the *Halachah* declares the forbidden substance to have lost its identity, and therefore one is no longer, in any halachic sense, eating *treifa*.

### Pork & Beans Q

A further question concerns the mechanics of taste transfer without heat. If, for example, one were to serve foods containing non-kosher ingredients on a plate alongside kosher items, but without any heat involved, does taste transfer from one to the other, or from either into the plate? The governing principle is that taste transfers halachically only through heat: *kavush*, soaking, and *irui*, pouring of hot liquid, are their own discussions, but simple adjacency of cold foods does not cause halachic taste transfer. The plate and the kosher items on it would therefore not be rendered non-kosher merely by proximity, absent the application of heat.

## Chatichah Natah

### Raba's Principle

Continuing on the case of *chaticha shel neveilah*, the *Gemara* records an exposition by Raba bar bar Chana: a piece of *neveilah* or non-kosher fish does not render the rest of the pot forbidden until it has imparted taste into the sauce (*rotev*), the residue (*kippa*), and the other pieces together. This reaffirms the earlier point that the measure of *shishim* applies against everything in the pot collectively — the liquid, the vegetables, the sediment at the bottom — and only if the total quantity is insufficient does the mixture become forbidden.

Raba then wished to qualify and sharpen this ruling in a specific case, and had his *amora* — his designated announcer, whose function was to project the *Amora*'s words to the assembled public in the beit midrash, much as the *tanna* (with a lowercase *tav*) served as a living repository and oral transmitter of tannaitic traditions — stand over him and proclaim the following: *keivan she-natan ta'am be-chaticha, chaticha atzma na'aseit neveilah ve-oseret kol ha-chatichot kulam mipnei she-hen minah* — once the non-kosher piece has imparted its taste into one permitted piece, that piece itself becomes *neveilah*, and it in turn renders all the other pieces forbidden, because they are all of the same kind (*min bemino*) and, according to Rav Yehuda, like-and-like is not nullified.

The case Raba has in mind involves two stages: a piece of non-kosher meat — call it N — is first cooked together with a single piece of kosher meat (piece 1), and only afterward are both placed into the larger stew. In the first stage, N imparts its taste to piece 1. The question is what the halachic status of piece 1 now is when it enters the stew.

### Chanan Term

This principle is of such cardinal importance in the laws of *kashrus* that it has acquired its own shorthand in *beit midrash* parlance: *chanan*, an acronym for *chatichah atzmah na'aseit neveilah* (or *chatichah natah neveilah* in some formulations). When students and *poskim* speak of *chanan*, this is the concept: a piece of permitted food that has absorbed the taste of a forbidden substance does not merely become a carrier for that taste — rather, its entire halachic identity is transformed. It becomes, in law, a new unit of *neveilah* in its own right. Piece 1 is no longer simply a kosher piece with traces of forbidden taste; it has become N-prime — a second unit of *neveilah*.

The contrast with *ta'am ke'ikar* is instructive. *Ta'am ke'ikar* establishes that taste is treated as the substance itself, so that absorbed taste renders a vessel or food forbidden. *Chanan* goes a step further: it is not that piece 1 merely carries a trace of forbidden substance, but that piece 1 itself has become forbidden as an independent unit — with the full weight of *neveilah*.

### Need 120 Now

The practical consequence is significant. When N and N-prime are both placed into the stew, one does not need sixty times N alone. One needs sixty times the combined volume of N and N-prime — that is, 120 rather than 60. The forbidden presence in the pot is now two units, not one, and the *bitul* calculation must account for both.

### Rav Safra Q

This generates an immediate objection from Rav Safra to Abaye: *Rav k'man amrah lishmatei* — whose position is Rava following? Evidently Rav Yehuda's, since the ruling that piece 1's becoming N-prime renders all the other pieces forbidden assumes that *min bemino lo batel* — like-and-like is never nullified, which is Rav Yehuda's position. But if that is so, *mai irya ki natan ta'am* — why does any of this depend on whether N first cooked together with piece 1? Even without that preliminary stage, if N falls directly into the stew surrounded by other pieces of meat, Rav Yehuda would say none of them can nullify it — *min bemino lo batel*. The entire exercise of piece 1 becoming N-prime seems superfluous.

### Answer: Original Removed

The *Gemara* answers: *hacha b'mai askinan b'she-kadam v'silko* — the case is one in which the original N was removed from the pot before the stew was assembled. After N cooked with piece 1 and imparted its taste, N itself was discarded. Only N-prime — piece 1, now transformed — was placed into the stew with the other pieces of kosher meat. In this scenario, if piece 1 were merely a carrier for N's taste, one might reason as follows: N is gone; what remains is only absorbed taste, which might be nullified by the surrounding meat and liquid. But because piece 1 has become N-prime — a full unit of *neveilah* — and because the surrounding items are all of the same species (meat), Rav Yehuda's *min bemino lo batel* prevents any nullification. The case for *chanan* is therefore precisely the scenario of preliminary cooking followed by removal of the original forbidden item: without *chanan*, there would be a basis for leniency; with *chanan*, the transformed piece is treated as a full unit of *neveilah* and cannot be nullified by like-kind items.

## Chatichah Natah (II)

### Rava's Formulation

Rava offers a further formulation of the same principle that applies even without the removal of the original N. Even when N remains in the pot alongside the other pieces of meat and the vegetables and liquid, the presence of N-prime matters. According to Rav Yehuda, the pieces of kosher meat are irrelevant to the nullification calculus — *min bemino lo batel* renders them halachically invisible for purposes of negating the *issur*. What remains to negate N and N-prime are the *eino mino* elements: the potatoes, carrots, liquid, and other non-meat components. Rava's point is that once N has transformed piece 1 into N-prime, you now have two units requiring negation by the *eino mino* components, not one. If you had exactly 60 units of potatoes and liquid, that would suffice against N alone but not against N and N-prime together. You now need the *eino mino* components to equal 120, not 60.

### Ashkenazi/Sefardi

Whether this ruling is normative is itself the subject of a major dispute among *Rishonim* and between the Ashkenazi and Sefardi traditions. The *Tosafot* occupy considerable space with the position of Rabbeinu Ephraim and others who hold, for cogent reasons, that this *Gemara* is not the operative ruling — at least outside the context of *basar b'chalav*, where a separate *Gemara* establishes *chanan* independently and more clearly. The practical upshot is a *machlokes* between *Sefardim* and *Ashkenazim*: *Sefardim* are lenient and do not rule in accordance with this *Gemara* in the *neveilah* context; they require only sixty times the original trace amounts of forbidden substance. *Ashkenazim* rule in accordance with this *Gemara* and hold that if the forbidden substance first imparted taste into a separate piece before both entered the pot, one requires sixty times the volume of the combined units — 120 rather than 60.

### Liquid Application

This ruling generates highly practical questions when the forbidden substance is not a solid piece of meat but a liquid product. Suppose a non-kosher canned tomato sauce — which itself contains meat as an ingredient — is poured into a stew. If the meat in the tomato sauce was already *batel* within the can before it ever reached one's kitchen, then even *Ashkenazim* agree: the *chanan* principle does not reactivate a *bitul* that has already taken effect. The question is when the meat in the sauce was not *batel* in the can — for instance, if the non-kosher meat constituted more than 1/60th of the sauce. In that case, according to *Ashkenazim*, one may need to treat the tomato sauce itself as the forbidden object: the relevant question is not merely whether the trace amounts of non-kosher meat are less than 1/60th of the stew, but whether the entire tomato sauce, having absorbed the forbidden taste, must now be treated as N-prime. Whether a liquid product functions as a *chaticha* for purposes of *chanan* — since *chanan* classically applies to a discrete solid piece — is itself disputed, and the parameters are worked out in the *poskim*. But the operative question in any *sha'ilah* involving a non-kosher product mixed into another dish is precisely this: does *chanan* apply, or does one reckon only with the original trace amounts of forbidden substance?

## Gid in Kosher

### Mishnah Rule

The *Gemara* now returns to the *Mishnah* governing the laws of *gid hanasheh* proper. The *Mishnah* states: *noheig bitehorah ve'eino noheig bitmeiah* — the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* applies to kosher animals and does not apply to non-kosher animals. The intuitive rationale is that the Torah's prohibition is directed at the *gid* of an animal one is otherwise permitted to eat: the Torah allows the animal, permits its flesh, but reserves the *gid*. If the animal itself is *tamei* — non-kosher — the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* adds nothing meaningful, since one may not eat any part of it in any case.

A related question lurks in the background: does the *gid* itself have taste — *yesh bigidim binoten ta'am* — or is it tasteless? This matters for the question of whether eating the *gid* of a non-kosher animal triggers any prohibition at all. If the *gid* has no taste, one who eats the *gid* of a camel has not violated the prohibition of eating camel, since the *gid* contributes nothing in terms of flavor; and since *gid hanasheh* does not apply to non-kosher animals, one would violate no prohibition whatsoever — just as eating a hoof or horn of a camel violates nothing. If, however, the *gid* does have taste, one who eats it has consumed camel flesh, triggering one set of lashes, while remaining exempt from a second set since the *gid* prohibition does not, according to the *tanna kamma*, extend to non-kosher animals.

### Tanna Kamma/RY

The *tanna kamma* holds that *gid hanasheh* applies exclusively to kosher animals. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *af bitmeiah* — it applies to non-kosher animals as well.

### RY's Argument

Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: *vahalo mivnei Yaakov ne'esar gid hanasheh ve'adayin behemah tmeiah muteres lahen* — was it not to the children of Yaakov that the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* was given? And at that time, non-kosher animals were still permitted to them. The children of Yaakov were not yet commanded regarding the broader dietary laws that would distinguish kosher from non-kosher animals. Therefore, when the Torah said "do not eat the *gid hanasheh*," it was necessarily speaking of all animals — including those that would later be classified as non-kosher — since at the time there was no distinction. The prohibition therefore extends to non-kosher animals even after the categories of *tahor* and *tamei* were established.

### Har Sinai Response

The *chachamim* respond: *besinai ne'emar* — that verse, *al ken lo yochlu bnei Yisrael*, was given at Har Sinai, not in the time of Yaakov. When Moshe wrote the *Sefer Torah*, he embedded the verse in the narrative context of Yaakov's encounter, *ela shenichtav bimkomo* — because the divine instruction was to record it in its narrative location. But the *mitzvah* itself was commanded to the Jewish people as a nation, at Har Sinai. And *bnei Yisrael* in that verse means the children of Israel as a people — Israelites — not the literal sons of Yaakov the patriarch. Consequently, one cannot draw conclusions about the scope of the prohibition based on what was or was not forbidden in Yaakov's time.

This position is undergirded by an important principle articulated by the *Rambam* in his *Peirush Hamishnayot*: everything that Jews observe today as obligatory has its source in Matan Torah and not in any earlier precedent. The fact that Avraham performed *bris milah* is not the basis for our obligation; the fact that Yaakov's sons abstained from *gid hanasheh* is not the basis for ours. We are commanded as a people who stood at Har Sinai — whatever preceded that event is historically and spiritually significant but is not the source of our halachic obligations.

### Noahide Q

This principle raises a corollary theological question: are Jews also included in the category of *Bnei Noach* and thereby bound by the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach* as a separate basis of obligation? The *Rambam*'s answer is clear: no. The reason Jews observe prohibitions such as *eiver min hachai* — tearing a limb from a living animal — is not because they are members of humanity commanded as *Bnei Noach*, but because they were specifically commanded at Har Sinai. The two obligations run in parallel — both *Bnei Noach* and Jews are forbidden to eat *eiver min hachai* — but the source of each group's obligation is distinct. Jews observe what they observe because of their covenant at Sinai, not because of any Noahide framework.

## Multiple Issurim

### Ein Issur Chal

The *Gemara* now examines Rabbi Yehuda's position through the lens of a technical halachic principle: *ein issur chal al issur* — one prohibition cannot take effect upon an object that is already subject to another prohibition. The *Gemara* notes that this principle ought to generate a structural problem for Rabbi Yehuda's view. The question is not merely whether logically the Torah's prohibition of *gid hanasheh* was intended to encompass non-kosher animals, but whether the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* can even take effect on an animal that is already forbidden as a non-kosher species.

### Gid on Camel

Applied specifically: a camel is forbidden as a *tamei* animal. When does the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* take effect? If it takes effect after the prohibition of *tamei* animal is already operative, then *ein issur chal al issur* would seem to block it. One prohibition cannot layer on top of another. How then can Rabbi Yehuda hold that eating a camel's *gid* carries two separate sets of lashes — one for *tamei* and one for *gid hanasheh*?

### No Taste Answer

One proposed answer draws on the question of whether *gidin* have taste. If the *gid* has no taste — *ein bigidin binoten ta'am* — then a person who eats the *gid* of a camel has not technically consumed camel, since tasteless matter is not considered consumed flesh for halachic purposes. In that case, there is no competition between the two prohibitions: the *tamei* prohibition has not been violated (since the tasteless *gid* is not camel flesh), while the *gid hanasheh* prohibition could independently apply. The two prohibitions would occupy distinct domains and would not interfere with one another.

### Refutation: Two Lashes

This proposal is immediately refuted. A *beraita* explicitly records Rabbi Yehuda as ruling that one who eats the *gid hanasheh* of a non-kosher animal — a camel — *mechayev shtayim*, is liable for two sets of lashes: one for eating camel and one for eating *gid hanasheh*. This demonstrates unambiguously that Rabbi Yehuda holds *yesh bigidin binoten ta'am* — the *gid* does have taste and it does constitute a violation of the prohibition on eating camel. The neat resolution through tastelessness is therefore unavailable. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, holds *poter* — one is entirely exempt — which may reflect either the view that the *gid* is tasteless, or a different analysis of the overlapping prohibitions. But Rabbi Yehuda clearly holds both that the *gid* has taste and that both prohibitions apply simultaneously.

### In Utero Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the structural problem differently: *kasavar noheig bishilya* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* takes effect already *in utero*, as the fetus forms. In that case, the prohibitions do not arise sequentially — with the *tamei* prohibition established first and the *gid* prohibition attempting to layer on top afterward. Rather, both come into being simultaneously, at the moment the fetus begins to form. If both prohibitions arise at the same moment, *ein issur chal al issur* is not triggered, since that principle applies only when one prohibition precedes the other chronologically.

### Sequential Prohibition

The *Gemara* immediately presses this resolution. A *Mishnah* about *nezirut* is adduced: a *nazir* becomes *tamei* upon contact with a corpse, even one composed of less than a *k'zayis*, if it is an early miscarriage — *shelo nitkashru eivarav begidin*, meaning that the sinews of the fetus had not yet formed. The implication is clear: sinews form later in fetal development, after the basic structure of the fetus has already been established. Therefore, even if the *gid hanasheh* prohibition applies *in utero*, it cannot arise simultaneously with the *tamei*-animal prohibition. The fetus exists first, and is forbidden as a camel from the moment it begins to form in the womb; only weeks later do the sinews form, at which point the *gid hanasheh* prohibition would theoretically come into being. The prohibition of *tamei* therefore precedes the prohibition of *gid hanasheh*, and the problem of *ein issur chal al issur* returns.

### Override via Weight

The *Gemara*'s final resolution: *af al gav de'issur tumah kadim, asi issur gid chayal alai* — although the prohibition of *tamei* animal precedes the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* in time, the *gid hanasheh* prohibition nonetheless takes effect on top of it. The basis is that the *gid hanasheh* prohibition is in a certain sense weightier: *shekein issur noheig bivnei Noach* — its reach extends even to the period before Matan Torah, having been operative for the children of Yaakov before the Torah was given at Sinai. When a later prohibition is more encompassing or more weighty than an earlier one, it can take effect even upon an object already subject to that earlier prohibition.
