The *Gemara* notes that this reading is consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's own formulation in the *Mishnah*, where he invokes the children of Yaakov as the basis for the prohibition's scope: it is that very pre-Sinaitic antiquity and breadth that gives *gid hanasheh* the halachic weight to override the principle of *ein issur chal al issur* and take effect upon an already-forbidden camel.

---

---

# Hullin 101

## Gid Hanasheh & Non-Kosher

### Rabbi Yehuda's Position

The daf opens with the position of Rabbi Yehuda in the Mishnah, who holds that *gid hanasheh* applies to non-kosher animals. His argument is partly historical: since the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* predates the giving of the Torah, it applied already to the children of Yaakov, which would include all animals they ate—kosher and non-kosher alike.

### Rambam's Approach

The Rabbis in the Mishnah dispute this, arguing that *bnei Yisrael* refers to the Israelites—a national designation that did not exist before Har Sinai—and not to the children of Yaakov. Consistent with this, the Rambam holds emphatically that nothing binding upon us today derives from pre-Torah practice. On this reading, the verse was given at Har Sinai but was inserted into the narrative of Yaakov's struggle with the angel in order to provide historical context—to tell us *why* the prohibition exists—rather than to indicate that it was operative at that earlier moment.

### Issur Chal Problem

The Gemara raises a separate concern: even setting aside the historical question, how does Rabbi Yehuda avoid the problem of *issur chal al issur*—one prohibition taking effect on top of a pre-existing one? If we eat the *gid hanasheh* of a camel, the prohibition of eating camel surely pre-exists; how can the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* then take effect upon it?

### Timing of Prohibitions

The Gemara's answer exploits the biological fact that the *gid* only forms in the fetus some weeks into gestation. Thus it is already forbidden as part of a non-kosher animal before the *gid* as such even exists. The Gemara then repurposes Rabbi Yehuda's historical claim—originally a point about when the prohibition began—to resolve this halachic concern.

### Bnei Noach Scope

The reframing works as follows: Rabbi Yehuda's line in the Mishnah, which speaks of the prohibition applying to *bnei Yaakov*, is now understood (or at least suggested) to refer to *bnei Noach*—non-Jews as well. If *gid hanasheh* has a broader scope, applying even to non-Jews, then it constitutes an *issur kolel*, a prohibition with wider reach, which is one of the recognized exceptions to the rule that one prohibition cannot take effect upon another. Because the prohibition applies to a larger group of people, it can take effect even on top of a pre-existing prohibition.

### Lashes Debate

According to Rabbi Yehuda, one who eats the *gid hanasheh* of a camel therefore receives two sets of lashes—one for eating camel and one for eating *gid hanasheh*. Rabbi Shimon, however, exempts entirely. And that is puzzling: even if one accepts that *issur chal al issur* prevents the *gid hanasheh* prohibition from taking effect, at a minimum one should receive lashes for eating camel. How does Rabbi Shimon arrive at zero?

---

## Rabbi Shimon Zero

### Dilemma Setup

The Gemara poses the dilemma directly: *mah nafshach*—make up your mind. If Rabbi Shimon holds that one prohibition does take effect upon another (*issur chal al issur*), he should agree with Rabbi Yehuda and impose two sets of lashes. If he holds that one prohibition does not take effect upon another, then at least the pre-existing prohibition—the prohibition of eating a non-kosher animal, which preceded the *gid*—should generate lashes. How does he arrive at zero?

The Gemara entertains one possible resolution: perhaps Rabbi Shimon holds that *gidim* have no taste (*ein begidim noten ta'am*). If the *gid* has no taste, it would not be defined as meat, and one would not receive lashes for eating camel on account of it. But this only explains why there are no lashes for camel; it does not explain why there are no lashes for *gid hanasheh* itself. After all, the rule that *gid* has no taste is relevant to questions of mixture—whether cooking a *gid* in meat renders the meat forbidden—but it does not by itself exempt one from the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* on a kosher animal. If anything, one freed from liability for camel should now be liable for *gid hanasheh*. The question remains.

### No Taste Theory

The Gemara continues to probe whether the absence of taste in *gidim* can account for the zero-lash result. As noted, this principle explains why one does not transgress for eating camel—the *gid* is not considered meat in that context—but it does not automatically discharge the *gid hanasheh* prohibition itself. The two directions of the dilemma seem to cancel each other out, leaving Rabbi Shimon's zero-lash position unexplained on purely logical grounds.

### Rava's Solution

Rava resolves the difficulty. He says: indeed, Rabbi Shimon holds that *gidim* have no taste, and that is why there are no lashes for eating camel. But the reason there are also no lashes for *gid hanasheh* has nothing to do with *issur chal al issur*. Rather, it follows from the verse itself.

### Exclusion Logic

The Torah states: *al ken lo yochlu bnei Yisrael et gid hanasheh*—"therefore the children of Israel shall not eat the *gid hanasheh*." Rava reads this verse as implicitly limiting its own scope. The prohibition of *gid hanasheh* applies to animals *whose meat you are otherwise permitted to eat*. The verse defines the category: an animal from which the *gid* is forbidden is one from which the meat is permitted. This creates a reciprocal exclusion: if the meat of an animal is forbidden, the *gid* of that animal is outside the scope of the *gid hanasheh* prohibition entirely.

### No Transgression

It follows that if one eats the *gid hanasheh* of a camel, one commits no transgression whatsoever—not for camel, because the *gid* has no taste and is thus not considered meat in the relevant sense, and not for *gid hanasheh*, because the Torah's prohibition of *gid hanasheh* simply does not apply to animals whose meat is forbidden. This is the source of Rabbi Shimon's position. It is worth noting the irony: the verse that establishes the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* simultaneously, by implication, limits its application.

---

## Taste & Food Status

### Gid as Meat?

This raises a conceptual question: if the *gid* has no taste, in what sense is it considered food at all? And conversely, if it is not considered food in the taste-based sense, why should it be forbidden under *gid hanasheh* even on kosher animals?

### Yotze Min HaTameh

The answer requires distinguishing between different bases for a prohibition. There is a principle—*yotze min hatameh tameh*—that something which comes from a non-kosher source is itself forbidden, even if it is not itself meat. Milk from a non-kosher animal, for example, is forbidden not because it is meat but because of this principle. So the absence of taste does not automatically exempt something from being prohibited.

### Hoof Example

However, this principle does not extend without limit. Consider the hoof of a camel. A hoof is hard, indigestible, and utterly devoid of taste. Eating it would not constitute a violation of *yotze min hatameh*, because it is not considered food at all. It is not a matter merely of having no taste; it is that the combination of physical properties—hardness, indigestibility, absence of taste—removes it entirely from the category of *ma'aseh achilah*, of eating as the Torah contemplates it. One who chews on a rock has not "eaten" in any legally cognizable sense.

### Taste & Properties

The *gid*, being a sinew, shares some of these properties. It is physically unlike meat; it does not dissolve or digest in the ordinary way. In this physical respect, it resembles a bone without marrow. Now, if a bone has no marrow but somehow retained some taste, one might consider whether it constitutes food. But if it has no taste and no ordinary food-like physical properties, it is simply not food—like eating a rock. The *gid*'s lack of taste, combined with its nature as a sinew, is what removes it from the category of non-kosher meat. Taste, in this analysis, functions as a decisive factor given the *gid*'s physical reality: it is the presence or absence of taste that determines whether a substance with unusual physical properties crosses the threshold into "food."

### Gelatin/Rennet

These principles bear directly on contemporary questions such as the status of gelatin derived from pig's bones and rennet derived from non-kosher animals. With respect to gelatin specifically, two distinct arguments arise. First, there is a question whether the industrial transformation of bones into gelatin is so complete that the product no longer retains its original identity at all. Second, even if it does retain some identity, the question becomes whether pig's bones—stripped of marrow and converted into an essentially tasteless, physically altered substance—ever qualified as food in the first instance. The analysis of the *gid*'s status, and of the camel's hoof, maps directly onto this debate.

---

## Meir Neveila Case

### Setup: Healthy→Dead

The Gemara now presents a related scenario involving a kosher animal. A healthy, properly kosher animal has a *gid hanasheh*, which is forbidden. It then dies without proper *shechita* and becomes *neveilah*. The *gid hanasheh* prohibition pre-existed; the *neveilah* prohibition came later. Does the *neveilah* prohibition take effect on top of the *gid hanasheh* prohibition? This is again the question of *issur chal al issur*.

### Meir: Two Lashes

Rabbi Meir holds that one who eats the *gid hanasheh* of such an animal receives two sets of lashes—one for *gid hanasheh* and one for *neveilah*. In his view, the *neveilah* prohibition does take effect on top of the pre-existing *gid hanasheh* prohibition.

### Sages: One Lash

The Sages disagree. They hold *ein issur chal al issur*—one prohibition does not take effect on another—and therefore only one set of lashes applies, presumably for *gid hanasheh*, which was the first prohibition. The *neveilah* prohibition did not take additional hold on the *gid*.

### Olah/Niskal Case

However, the Sages concede to Rabbi Meir in a different case. If the animal was initially sanctified as an *olah* (a burnt offering) or if it gored and killed a person and thereby acquired the status of *shor haniskal* (an ox condemned to be stoned), they agree that two sets of lashes apply. In these cases, even the Sages say the second prohibition takes effect on top of the *gid hanasheh* prohibition.

### Asur BeHana'ah

What distinguishes the *olah* and *shor haniskal* from plain *neveilah*? Both *olah* and *shor haniskal* are *asur beHana'ah*—forbidden not merely to be eaten but forbidden in any form of benefit. The ordinary *neveilah* prohibition is a prohibition on eating; the prohibition of *olah* and *shor haniskal* extends to deriving any benefit whatsoever. This added dimension—a prohibition that is not merely broader in scope but weightier in character—is what, in the Sages' view, allows the second prohibition to take hold.

---

## Kolel & Mosif

### Two Exceptions

The Gemara in Kerisot recognizes two categories of exceptions to the general rule that one prohibition does not take effect upon a pre-existing one: *issur kolel* and *issur mosif*.

### Kolel Defined

*Issur kolel* refers to a prohibition whose scope of affected objects or people is larger than that of the pre-existing prohibition. Because the new prohibition takes effect on other things or people not previously covered, it is considered to "bring along" the original item as well, and thus takes effect even on what was already forbidden.

### Neveila Example

*Neveilah* is a classic illustration of *issur kolel* in the dimension of objects. Before the animal died, only the *gid* was forbidden. When it became *neveilah*, every part of the animal—all the meat—became forbidden. Since the *neveilah* prohibition takes effect on the meat, it also takes effect on the *gid*. The *gid* is "brought along" by virtue of the prohibition's larger reach. This is Rabbi Meir's logic: because *neveilah* is an *issur kolel* that applies to the meat, it can also apply to the *gid*, and therefore double liability obtains.

An *issur kolel* in the dimension of persons would arise when the new prohibition applies to a wider group of people than were previously bound. For example, if a prohibition that previously applied only to Jews now also applied to *bnei Noach*, the wider personal scope would constitute an *issur kolel*.

### Mosif Defined

*Issur mosif* is more contested. The term suggests a prohibition that "adds" something—but adds what, exactly? The Gemara uses the related term *issur chamur* (a weightier prohibition), and Rashi throughout this sugya conflates the two, treating a more weighty prohibition as equivalent to an *issur mosif*. In this reading, if the new prohibition is more severe than the pre-existing one, it can take effect.

### Chamur Factor

The example at hand is again the *olah* and *shor haniskal*. These impose not merely a prohibition on eating (*issur achilah*) but a prohibition on benefit (*issur hana'ah*). The new prohibition is thus weightier—*chamur*—than what pre-existed.

### Rashi vs. Rishonim

Rashi's conflation of *issur mosif* with *issur chamur* is not accepted by most Rishonim. They maintain that *issur chamur* is a distinct and secondary consideration—an added factor—and that the primary mechanism permitting *issur chal al issur* is always a question of scope, whether *kolel* or *mosif*. The precise distinction between *issur kolel* (larger scope of objects or persons) and *issur mosif* (larger scope of the prohibition itself) is nuanced and debated among the Rishonim, and *issur mosif* as an independent category does not arise explicitly in our immediate sugya. For present purposes, the operative distinction is this: *issur kolel* is clear—a wider reach over objects or people—while *issur chamur*, a weightier prohibition, functions as an added factor that may augment the force of *issur kolel* but does not alone suffice.

---

## Neveila Analysis

### Meir's Kolel Logic

With that framework in place, we can now read Rabbi Meir's position precisely. He holds that *neveilah* is an *issur kolel*—it applies to the meat of the animal, which was not previously forbidden—and therefore it takes effect even on the *gid hanasheh*, which was already forbidden. The logic of *kolel* is that because the prohibition reaches new territory (the meat), it is not merely piling onto a pre-existing prohibition; it is a genuinely broader prohibition that sweeps in everything, including what was already forbidden. Two lashes follow.

### Sages' Position

The Sages reject this. *Issur kolel* alone is not sufficient for *issur chal al issur* to operate. However, when the second prohibition is both *kolel* (larger in scope, applying to the meat) and *chamur* (weightier, prohibiting benefit as well), they agree that it takes effect. Hence their concession in the *olah* and *shor haniskal* cases: there the prohibition is not merely broader but also more severe, and both factors together permit the second prohibition to take effect on the *gid*.

### Mystery Tanna

The Gemara now searches: who is the *tanna* that rejects *issur kolel* alone (refusing to say *issur chal al issur* when the second prohibition is merely broader in scope) but would accept it when the second prohibition is both broader and weightier (*kolel* plus *chamur*)? Rabbi Shimon is not a candidate: he is explicit that he rejects *issur chal al issur* in all cases, regardless of whether the second prohibition is *kolel* or *chamur*. We need someone more nuanced—someone who rejects *kolel* alone but might accept *kolel* combined with *chamur*. The Gemara will now propose a candidate.

---

## Rabbi Yosi HaGelili

### Tamei/Kodesh Mishna

Rava identifies Rabbi Yosi HaGelili as this figure. The relevant source is a Mishnah: a *tamei* person who eats *kodesh* (consecrated meat) is liable to *karet*. But what if the *kodesh* itself had already become *tamei*? Rabbi Yosi HaGelili says: if the person was *tamei* and ate *tahor kodesh*, he is liable (*chayav*). But if he ate *tamei kodesh*—consecrated meat that had already been defiled—he is exempt (*patur*), because the meat's sanctity had already been compromised.

### Contradiction Raised

The Rabbis challenge Rabbi Yosi HaGelili. They point out that even in the case he says generates liability—a *tamei* person eating *tahor kodesh*—by the time the meat reaches the person's mouth, he will have touched it and made it *tamei*. Every case of a *tamei* person eating *tahor kodesh* inevitably passes through a moment where the person renders the meat *tamei* before swallowing it. If eating *tamei kodesh* is always exempt, then liability would never arise. This appears to collapse Rabbi Yosi HaGelili's distinction.

One could construct an artificial scenario in which the meat was never rendered susceptible to *tumah* (*huchshar lekabel tumah*) or in which a *tahor* party placed it in the person's mouth. Tosafot acknowledges this possibility, but notes that the Gemara is operating under the assumption of a normal case and that Rabbi Yosi HaGelili would need to explain how liability arises in the standard situation.

### Order Matters

Rava resolves the difficulty by attending to the order of events. The question is not simply whether the meat was *tamei* at the moment of consumption, but which status—the person's *tumah* or the meat's *tumah*—came first.

### Person First: Agree

If the person became *tamei* first, and then picked up *tahor* meat to eat it—thereby rendering it *tamei* in the act of eating—all opinions agree he is *chayav* and receives *karet*. The reason: the *issur karet* (the prohibition with *karet*-level severity) attached to him the moment he became *tamei*, in relation to all *tahor kodesh*. The fact that he subsequently defiled the meat in the act of eating does not dissolve the pre-existing *issur karet*. The meat's *tumah* came second, after the prohibition was already operative.

### Meat First: Debate

The debate concerns the reverse scenario: the meat became *tamei* first, and then the person became *tamei*. Now the meat is already forbidden with a *lav*-level prohibition (eating *tamei kodesh*)—a lesser prohibition than *karet*. The question is whether the person's becoming *tamei* adds an *issur karet* on top of that pre-existing *lav*.

### Sages: Kolel Works

The Rabbis hold that it does, on the basis of *issur kolel*. When a person becomes *tamei*, the scope of his prohibition is larger than just this one piece of *tamei* meat: he is now forbidden from eating all *korban* meat, including *tahor kodesh* throughout the world. Because his *tumah* prohibition applies to *tahor kodesh* generally, it also takes effect on this particular piece of *tamei kodesh*. The logic is: *migu demichayev achatechos tehoros* (since he would now be liable for eating other *tahor* pieces), *michayev nami achatecha temeiah* (he is also liable for eating this defiled piece). The wider scope pulls the pre-existing lesser prohibition up into the larger prohibition.

### Yosi: Kolel Fails

Rabbi Yosi HaGelili rejects this. He does not accept the *migu* logic—that because the prohibition reaches *tahor* pieces, it also reaches this *tamei* piece. The meat was already forbidden before he became *tamei*; the fact that his *tumah* creates new prohibitions elsewhere does not give it the power to redefine the status of something already prohibited. *Leit lei issur kolel*: he does not hold of *issur kolel* as a valid mechanism.

The Gemara's reframing is thus significant. What initially appeared to be Rabbi Yosi HaGelili's position—that eating defiled *kodesh* is simply a lesser offense and less deserving of *karet*—is reconceived as an *issur chal al issur* position. His real concern is whether a new prohibition can take effect on a pre-existing one. When he was *tamei* first, there is no *issur chal al issur* problem: the *issur karet* pre-existed and remains. When the meat was defiled first, the new prohibition (*karet*-level) would have to take effect on top of the prior *lav*, and Rabbi Yosi HaGelili says it cannot, even via *issur kolel*.

The Gemara then asks: why not say that Rabbi Yosi HaGelili would at least admit when the second prohibition is not only *kolel* but also *chamur*—as the Sages require? After all, the person's *tumah* does create liability with *karet*, which is weightier than the *lav* of eating *tamei kodesh*. The Gemara answers via Rav Ashi: it is not obvious that the person's *tumah* is the weightier prohibition. One could argue that the meat's *tumah* is in some sense more severe—*deleit lei taharah bemikvah*—because the meat cannot be purified by immersion in a *mikvah*. The meat will remain *tamei* permanently; the person's *tumah* is theoretically transitory, curable by *mikvah*. So even though the person's *tumah* carries the heavier formal punishment (*karet*), the meat's *tumah* is "weightier" in the sense of being irremediable. Because the weightier-prohibition determination is ambiguous, Rabbi Yosi HaGelili cannot be said to have admitted the principle even for *kolel* plus *chamur*.

---

## Shabbat & Yom Kippur

### Setup: Double Day

The Gemara now turns to a case directly relevant to the present moment: Shabbat and Yom Kippur falling on the same day. A *Mishnah* asks: if someone accidentally performs *melacha* on a day that is simultaneously Shabbat and Yom Kippur, how many *korbanot* does he bring? Each of these days, taken alone, would independently generate liability for a *korban* for inadvertent *melacha*. The question is whether both can apply simultaneously, or whether one prohibition is subsumed into the other.

### Yosi: Two Korbanos

One opinion holds that two *korbanot* are required—one for Shabbat and one for Yom Kippur—since each day retains its independent force. The verse says *Shabbat hi* (it is Shabbat) and *Yom HaKippurim hu* (it is Yom Kippur), implying that even when they coincide, each maintains its own distinct status.

### Akiva: One Korban

The opposing opinion holds that only one *korban* is required. On this view, the second prohibition does not independently take hold, and liability is singular.

### Yom Kippur Scope

The Gemara's framing suggests that if one accepts *issur kolel* as a valid mechanism, Yom Kippur would take effect on top of Shabbat, because Yom Kippur has a wider scope: it prohibits not only *melacha* (as Shabbat does) but also *achilah* (eating). Since Yom Kippur makes its impact felt in a broader domain—the eating prohibitions—it can also take effect in the *melacha* domain, and therefore a second *korban* would be required.

### Name Reversal Issue

The Gemara initially identifies the opinion requiring two *korbanot* with Rabbi Yosi HaGelili and the opinion requiring only one with Rabbi Akiva. But this creates an immediate problem: given everything the Gemara has established, Rabbi Yosi HaGelili does *not* hold of *issur kolel*. He should be the one saying only one *korban* applies. If the logic for two *korbanot* rests on *issur kolel*—the wider scope of Yom Kippur—then Rabbi Yosi HaGelili should reject it, not endorse it. The attribution appears to be internally contradictory.

### Ravin's Correction

The resolution comes from a transmission sent by Ravin from Eretz Yisrael, in the name of Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina. The names in the Mishnah are simply reversed (*ipoch*). Rabbi Yosi HaGelili is the one who says only one *korban* is required—consistent with his rejection of *issur kolel*—and Rabbi Akiva is the one who says two are required, holding that Yom Kippur's wider scope (*kolel*) allows it to take effect on top of Shabbat. With this reversal, the positions are internally consistent.

---

## Mixed Intent Scenarios

### Forgot Shabbat

The Gemara now examines a series of sub-cases arising from Shabbat and Yom Kippur coinciding. In the first scenario, a person forgot that it was Shabbat but remembered that it was Yom Kippur, and willfully performed *melacha*.

### One Korban Shabbat

He brings one *korban* for Shabbat—because his violation of Shabbat was inadvertent (*shogeg*), which is the condition for *korban* liability—but no *korban* for Yom Kippur, because his violation of Yom Kippur was willful (*mezid*), for which there is no *korban*. The result: one *korban* for Shabbat.

### Forgot Yom Kippur

In the reverse scenario: the person knew it was Shabbat and willfully violated it, but forgot that it was Yom Kippur.

### No Korban

He brings no *korban* at all. For Shabbat, there is no *korban* because he was *mezid*. For Yom Kippur, even though he was *shogeg*, according to Rabbi Yosi HaGelili the Yom Kippur *melacha* prohibition did not take effect on top of the Shabbat prohibition. If the *melacha* prohibition of Yom Kippur does not independently exist as a distinct prohibition in the presence of Shabbat, then there is nothing to be *shogeg* about with respect to Yom Kippur.

### Abaye: Shabbat Prior

Abaye explains the underlying principle: *Shabbat kevia ve-kayama*—Shabbat is fixed and standing. It occurs every week with complete regularity. Yom Kippur, by contrast, is set by *Beit Din* each year based on the sanctification of Rosh Chodesh Tishrei. Until witnesses testified and *Beit Din* declared Rosh Chodesh, the precise day of Yom Kippur was not determined. When they sanctified Rosh Chodesh Tishrei, they effectively "placed" Yom Kippur on top of Shabbat after Shabbat's prohibition was already fixed. Therefore, Shabbat is treated as pre-existing, and Yom Kippur's *melacha* prohibition does not add to it.

### Rava Objects

Rava objects to Abaye's reasoning. Whatever was true during Elul, at the actual moment when Friday night arrives—*sof sof tarveihu bahadi hadadi ka-asu*—both Shabbat and Yom Kippur take effect simultaneously. Since they take effect at exactly the same moment, there is no sense in which one pre-exists the other, and the problem of *issur chal al issur* should not arise. If they take effect simultaneously, each should operate independently without one subordinating the other.

### Rava: Shmad Case

Because Rava rejects Abaye's framework, he reinterprets the entire discussion. He says that the case under discussion involves a *shmad*—a year of persecution in which the non-Jewish authorities issued a decree forbidding Jews to observe Yom Kippur. In that year, Yom Kippur did not actually fall on Shabbat; it fell on another day. But the Rabbis instructed the community to observe it on Shabbat, since abstaining from food on Shabbat would not attract the attention of the authorities in the way that ceasing *melacha* on a weekday would. For this special, Rabinically-reassigned Yom Kippur on Shabbat, no *korban* liability would apply for violating what was not a real Yom Kippur in the ordinary halachic sense. This is an extraordinary scenario, not a standing ruling about the normal calendar.

### E.Y. Agreement

This reading is confirmed by a transmission from Eretz Yisrael: *ki ada de-yoma de-kippura de-hai shata shabta hava*—the Yom Kippur of that year was observed on Shabbat. When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael together with others who had made the journey to Bavel, they all confirmed Rava's understanding. The scenario is exceptional, not normative, and therefore does not constitute a general ruling about the interaction of Shabbat and Yom Kippur when they coincide in the regular calendar.

---

## Bnei Yisrael Debate

### Yehuda's Claim

The Gemara now returns to Rabbi Yehuda's position in the Mishnah: that *gid hanasheh* was prohibited to the *bnei Yaakov* already before the Torah was given. This historical claim underpins his view that the prohibition applied in some form to non-kosher animals from the outset.

### Sages Object

The Rabbis object: the verse does not say *bnei Yaakov*. It says *bnei Yisrael*. These are different things.

### Sinai Proof

*Bnei Yisrael* is a national term—the Israelites—a designation that did not exist until the people stood at Har Sinai. Therefore, the verse must have been given at Har Sinai. It cannot be read as referring to an earlier period in history when the children of Yaakov were not yet a nation called Israel.

### Narrative Placement

The Rabbis acknowledge that the verse appears in the narrative of Yaakov's struggle with the angel—seemingly in the wrong place for a law given at Sinai. They explain: the verse was indeed given at Sinai, but it was written here, in the narrative of the struggle, in order to communicate the reason for the prohibition. The Torah is providing historical context: *this* is why Bnei Yisrael were later commanded not to eat the *gid hanasheh*—because of what happened to Yaakov. The verse is inserted into the narrative as explanation, not as the legal moment of the prohibition's inception. In this, the Torah departs from its usual pattern (stating a law and then connecting it to its historical basis) and instead embeds the law in the story.

### Rava's Proof

Rava challenges the Rabbis' argument that *bnei Yisrael* is necessarily a post-Sinaitic term. He cites the verse *vayisu bnei Yisrael et Yaakov avihem*—"and the children of Israel carried Yaakov their father" (to Egypt). There, the phrase *bnei Yisrael* clearly refers to the sons of Yaakov, not to the nation of Israel. So the term can evidently be used to mean Yaakov's children even in an earlier context.

### Name Change Timing

The Gemara responds: that verse appears *after* Yaakov's name had already been officially changed to Yisrael by God. Once God ratified the new name, the children could appropriately be called *bnei Yisrael* in the sense of "sons of Yisrael/Yaakov." But in the passage about the struggle with the angel, Yaakov's name change had not yet been ratified by God—only the angel had given him the name, and that is insufficient for official use. Therefore, at that moment in the narrative, calling his children *bnei Yisrael* would be premature; the verse must be understood as referring to a later period.

### Rav Aha Query

Rav Aha the son of Rava presses the point to Rav Ashi: perhaps from the moment that God did officially rename Yaakov as Yisrael—in a later episode—the verse should be understood as taking effect from that point forward? Perhaps the prohibition applied from the moment of God's ratification of the name, not only from Har Sinai?

### Rav Ashi Reply

Rav Ashi rejects this. The Torah is not given piecemeal. There is no halachic mechanism by which a heavenly communication at one point in the patriarchal narrative generates a binding commandment. A commandment binds when it is given as part of the formal reception of Torah at Har Sinai. Neither the moment of the struggle with the angel nor the moment of God's subsequent renaming of Yaakov was a *shat matan Torah*—a moment of Torah-giving. Therefore neither occasion could have been the binding moment for the *gid hanasheh* prohibition.

### Final Resolution

The conclusion is as the Rabbis maintained all along: *bnei Yisrael* means Israelites; the prohibition of *gid hanasheh* was given at Har Sinai; and the verse was inserted into the narrative of the struggle with the angel not because it was given then, but in order to embed its reason within the story. The prohibition belongs to the world of Sinai, not to the world of Yaakov and his children.

---

---

# Hullin 102

## Ever Min HaChai Intro

### Definition & Scope

The daf under discussion is 102, though the material begins at the bottom of 101b with the words *tana rabanan*. Having previously examined the debate concerning whether *gid hanasheh* applies to non-kosher animals, the Gemara now turns to a parallel — though distinct — discussion regarding *ever min hachai*.

The *braita* opens: *ever min hachai noheg bivehemah chayah ve'of bein tme'in bein tehorin divrei Rabbi Yehudah* — the prohibition of *ever min hachai* applies to domesticated animals (*behemah*), wild animals (*chayah*), and even birds, whether kosher or non-kosher. This is the position of Rabbi Yehudah. The same Rabbi Yehudah who holds that *gid hanasheh* applies to non-kosher animals maintains the same position regarding *ever min hachai*. Without being stated otherwise, the discussion presupposes a Jewish audience, though the application to *bnei Noach* will emerge shortly.

One implication of Rabbi Yehudah's view is that when a Jew eats an *ever min hachai* from a non-kosher animal, two prohibitions are simultaneously violated — the prohibition of non-kosher food and the prohibition of *ever min hachai*. This raises the question of *issur chal al issur*, which the Gemara will address in turn.

### Verse Derivation

Rabbi Yochanan teaches that both Rabbi Yehudah and his disputants are interpreting a single verse: *rak chazak levilti achol hadam ki hadam hu hanefesh velo tochal hanefesh im habasar* — "Only be strong not to eat the blood, for the blood is the life force, and you shall not eat the life force with the meat" (Devarim 12:23). This verse is understood as the source for *ever min hachai*, and indeed for *basar min hachai* as well.

Notably, the prohibition is not stated in terms of a limb explicitly; rather, *nefesh* — life force — is read as referring to the limb. Rashi explains this by noting that just as life, once lost, does not return, so too a limb severed from an animal does not regenerate. The verse thus prohibits eating the *nefesh* — understood as the limb — *im habasar*, while the life force remains in the meat, i.e., while the animal is still alive.

A subtler point emerges from the structure of the verse. The word *vav* connecting *velo tochal hanefesh im habasar* to what precedes it is significant: without the *vav*, one might read the clause as an independent prohibition concerning blood. With the *vav*, the phrase is connected to the blood prohibition, and the shift in the referent of *nefesh* — from blood in the preceding clause to the limb or life force in the following clause — becomes the crux of the interpretive debate. The reading *lo tochal hanefesh im habasar* is taken to mean: do not eat the limb when the life force is still in the animal, which is the prohibition of *ever min hachai*.

### Yehudah & Eliezer

The Gemara records: *vedivrei Rabbi Yehudah veRabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer joins Rabbi Yehudah in holding that *ever min hachai* applies to non-kosher animals. The reasoning: *kol she'atah metzuveh al damo atah metzuveh al evarav* — any animal whose blood one is prohibited from eating, one is likewise prohibited from eating its limbs when torn off alive. Since the blood of non-kosher animals is prohibited — the prohibition of blood applies across the board, including to non-kosher species — it follows that *ever min hachai* from non-kosher animals is equally prohibited. There is no categorical exclusion, and no insuperable problem of *issur chal al issur* stands in the way, for reasons that will be spelled out.

### Rabbis' Position

The Rabbis (*chakhamim*) disagree. They focus on the concluding phrase of the verse: *lo tochal hanefesh im habasar* — do not eat the soul with the meat. Their reading: *ela basar lechuda* — the meat alone, eaten when the soul is no longer in the animal. The prohibition is therefore only incumbent in a case where the meat would otherwise be permissible: *kol shebasaro muttar atam metzuveh al evarav* — where the meat is permitted, one is bound by the restriction on limbs; *v'chol she'ein basaro muttar ein atah metzuveh al evarav* — where the meat is not permitted in the first place, the prohibition on limbs does not apply.

This is a categorical exclusion closely analogous to the Rabbis' position by *gid hanasheh*: just as the prohibition of the *gid* applies only to animals whose meat may be eaten, the prohibition of *ever min hachai* applies only to animals whose flesh is otherwise permissible. The underlying logic is not merely technical. The Torah's concern is with imposing additional restrictions upon what one is already permitted — do not eat the *gid*, do not eat a limb torn from a living animal — within the domain of permissible food. For animals that are already categorically forbidden, that logic does not obtain. One is not going to be eating non-kosher animals in any capacity, so there is no need for a special prohibition on their limbs. The restriction is meaningful precisely within the space of what is permitted, not outside it.

---

## Why Need Verse

### Yehudah Needs No Verse

Having established the positions of Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Eliezer on one side and the Rabbis on the other, the Gemara raises a question specifically about Rabbi Yehudah: *lama li kra*? Why does Rabbi Yehudah need a verse to establish that *ever min hachai* applies to non-kosher animals? The Gemara suggests that he should not need one at all. *Leiti issur eiver liychol al issur tumah* — the prohibition of *ever min hachai* should simply take effect on top of the pre-existing prohibition against non-kosher food without any special scriptural mandate, because the second prohibition is broader in scope than the first. The argument: *sheken issur noheig bivnei Noach* — *ever min hachai* is a prohibition that applies to *bnei Noach*, to all non-Jews, and therefore encompasses a wider group of people than the prohibition of non-kosher food, which applies only to Jews. Since the second prohibition (*ever min hachai*) has a larger scope than the first (the prohibition of non-kosher animals, which burdens only Jews), it qualifies as an *issur kolel* and should be able to take effect even where the first prohibition already exists, without requiring a special verse.

### Verse for Eliezer

The Gemara resolves the question: *ein hachi nami* — indeed, you are correct. According to Rabbi Yehudah, no verse was needed; the larger scope of *ever min hachai* is sufficient to allow it to take effect even on non-kosher animals. *V'chi itzterich kra l'Rabbi Eliezer* — the verse is needed for Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Eliezer's general view regarding *issur chal al issur* is not independently established; we cannot assume he would ordinarily permit one prohibition to take effect on top of another even on the basis of larger scope. Hence a special scriptural derivation is required in his case, linking the prohibition of *ever min hachai* to the prohibition of blood and thereby extending it to non-kosher animals just as the blood prohibition extends to them.

### Issur Kolel/Mosif

This analysis invites a fuller consideration of the categories that permit *issur chal al issur*. The basic principle is that one prohibition generally does not take effect upon an item already subject to another. However, there are recognized exceptions.

The first is *issur kolel* — a more inclusive prohibition. This can mean that the second prohibition encompasses more objects than the first: for instance, on *Yom Kippur*, not only is non-kosher meat forbidden, but all food is forbidden. When I become ritually impure (*tamei*), not only is the specific meat before me prohibited, but all *korban* meat is now prohibited to me. In both cases, the second prohibition sweeps in a wider category of objects and therefore takes effect even where the first prohibition already applies.

The case at hand — *ever min hachai* applying to non-kosher animals — illustrates a different dimension of *issur kolel*: not more objects but more persons become subject to the prohibition. *Ever min hachai* applies to all *bnei Noach*, and therefore when a limb is torn from a non-kosher animal, the prohibition applies to all people. This wider scope of persons subject to the second prohibition is what enables it to take effect on top of the first. A comparable example would be if a man's sister subsequently married; she was already forbidden to him, but now, as a married woman, she becomes forbidden to all men — a broader prohibition applies, and that breadth is what creates the additional prohibition for him as well.

The second category, *issur mosif*, is related but distinct. Rashi understands it as a weightier prohibition, while the more broadly accepted understanding is that it refers precisely to the category of more persons becoming prohibited — the very category illustrated above. These represent the two primary categories — *issur kolel* and *issur mosif* — under which one prohibition can ordinarily take effect on top of another. A third consideration, *issur chamur*, involves a prohibition that is weightier in some other sense: it may be forbidden in benefit (*hana'ah*), it may carry *kares*, or it may have applied to the children of Yaakov prior to Sinai. These are secondary considerations; the primary operative categories are those of larger scope.

The Gemara's conclusion is that even for one who does not generally accept Rabbi Yehudah's position regarding *gid hanasheh* and the weight of *bnei Noach*-era prohibitions, and even for one uncertain about whether larger scope suffices on its own, here by *ever min hachai* in a non-kosher animal there are two grounds for the prohibition to take effect: the larger scope (*issur kolel* of *bnei Noach*) and a special verse linking the prohibition to blood, which extends it to non-kosher animals just as the blood prohibition extends to them.

---

## Braita & Bnei Noach

### Braita Text

The Gemara brings a *braita* in support: *ever min hachai noheg b'vehema chaya v'of bein tmeia bein tehora* — *ever min hachai* applies to domesticated animals, wild animals, and birds, whether kosher or non-kosher. The verse adduced: *rak chazak l'vilti achol hadam* — and from there the principle: *kol she'atah mtzuvah al damo atah metzuveh al evarav* — any creature whose blood is prohibited, its limbs are likewise prohibited when torn off alive. This includes non-kosher animals and even birds, since the blood prohibition extends to birds. Conversely, *ve-chol she-ei atah metzuveh al damo ei atah metzuveh al evarav* — for creatures whose blood is not prohibited, such as fish and grasshoppers, there is no prohibition of *ever min hachai*. This teaching is attributed to Rabbi Eliezer — and the Gemara notes this pointedly, since it is precisely for Rabbi Eliezer that the verse is needed, as established above. Rabbi Yehudah requires no verse; the *braita* clarifies the *drasha* and identifies its primary recipient.

The Rabbis' counter-position is stated in the same *braita*: *velo tochal hanefesh im habasar* — *ela basar le-chud*, and since the prohibition is framed around eating the meat when the life force remains in the animal, it is limited to *kol she-besaro mutar* — animals whose meat is otherwise permissible. *Kol she-ein besaro mutar ein atah metzuveh al evarav* — by non-kosher animals, no such prohibition applies. This is, again, less a matter of *issur chal al issur* and more a categorical exclusion grounded in the plain sense of the verse: the Torah's restriction on *ever min hachai* is addressed to what one eats, and non-kosher animals were never within the domain of permissible eating.

### Rabbi Meir Limits

The Gemara now introduces a third position. Rabbi Meir holds that *ever min hachai* applies not only to kosher animals but specifically to kosher *behemah* — domesticated animals — to the exclusion of *chayah* (wild animals) and birds. His reasoning is textual: the verse introducing the entire passage reads *ve-zavachta mi-be-karecha u-mi-tzoncha* — "and you shall slaughter from your cattle and from your flock." The prohibition of blood and the prohibition of *ever min hachai* derived from this context are therefore limited to the species explicitly mentioned in the introduction: cattle and sheep. Birds and wild animals are excluded, not because of any philosophical argument, but because the verse's own framing does not encompass them.

The Rabbis, by contrast, read *dibra hatorah bahoveh* — the Torah speaks in the customary manner; the mention of cattle and sheep does not restrict the verse's reach. The blood prohibition is not limited to cattle and sheep, and neither is *ever min hachai*.

### Bnei Noach Apply

Rav Gidel citing Rav states: *machloket beYisrael* — the entire debate about whether *ever min hachai* applies to non-kosher animals pertains to Jews. *Aval bivnei Noach divrei hakol muzar le-tme'im ke-tehorim* — but for non-Jews, all opinions agree that *ever min hachai* applies to non-kosher animals just as to kosher ones. For *bnei Noach*, there is no issue of *issur chal al issur* with respect to non-kosher animals, since non-kosher animals are not prohibited to them in the first place. And the verse's implied logic — that the restriction applies only to animals one is otherwise permitted to eat — poses no obstacle either, since for *bnei Noach*, non-kosher animals are entirely permissible. There is therefore no reason to exclude non-kosher animals from the scope of *ever min hachai* for *bnei Noach*.

This does not mean that *bnei Noach* are in a stricter position than Jews in any absolute sense. A Jew who eats *ever min hachai* from a camel violates the prohibition against eating camel. A non-Jew who does the same violates the prohibition of *ever min hachai*. Each receives one prohibition; neither receives two. The *braita* confirms this: *ben Noach muzar lo al ever min hachai al hatme'im ketehorim* — a *ben Noach* is prohibited in *ever min hachai* from non-kosher animals just as from kosher ones. *VeYisrael eino muzar ela al hatehorin bilvad* — and a Jew is subject to *ever min hachai* only regarding kosher animals, in accordance with the position of the *chakhamim*.

A textual variant in the *braita* is noted: some versions read *tehorah* (singular), which would align the ruling for Jews with Rabbi Meir's position — limiting *ever min hachai* to domesticated kosher animals only. Other versions read *tehorim* (plural), aligning with the *chakhamim*, who include all kosher animals: birds, cattle, sheep, and deer alike.

---

## Non-Kosher Bird Mishna

### Mishna Text

Rav Shizvi notes that the following *mishna* supports the foregoing discussion. The *mishna* states: *achal ever min hachai mimena eino sofeg arba'im* — one who ate an *ever min hachai* from a non-kosher bird does not receive forty lashes. Furthermore, *ve'ein shechitata metahareta* — slaughtering it does not render it *tahor*.

Two difficulties arise immediately. First, why does one not receive lashes for eating the non-kosher bird itself? Second, the phrase *ein shechitata metahareta* requires clarification — does it refer to *tumah* (ritual impurity) or to *kashrus*?

### Jews vs Bnei Noach

The Gemara works through these questions. If the *mishna* is addressing a Jew (*ileima beYisrael*), then the statement that *shechita* does not render it *tahor* is trivially obvious — no one imagines that slaughtering a non-kosher bird makes it kosher. And the *tumah* reading is equally unavailable: a non-kosher bird does not carry the *tumah* of *neveilah* in the first place. The *tumah* of birds — a distinctive and unusual category — applies only to kosher birds that died without proper *shechita*, and only upon being swallowed. A non-kosher bird carries no *tumas neveilah* regardless of how it died. So *ein shechitata metahareta* cannot be read as a statement about *tumah* if we are discussing a non-kosher bird, and it cannot be a meaningful statement about *kashrus* if we are talking about Jews. The *mishna* must therefore be addressing *bnei Noach*.

For *bnei Noach*, the question is concrete: they are permitted to eat non-kosher animals, but they are prohibited in *ever min hachai*. What is the status of *shechita* in resolving that prohibition? This leads directly to the next subsection.

### Shechita Effects

The question of *shechita*'s effect on *ever min hachai* differs between Jews and *bnei Noach*. For a Jew, the moment an animal is slaughtered, it is considered halachically dead and permissible to be eaten; even if the animal is still flopping about, a limb taken after *shechita* is not *ever min hachai*. For a *ben Noach*, by contrast, the animal is not considered dead until it has actually ceased moving; *shechita* alone does not suffice to remove the prohibition of *ever min hachai*. The animal must be biologically and physically still.

This raises a further question: if a Jew slaughters a kosher animal and it is still flopping, may a *ben Noach* eat a limb from it? Some hold that since for the *ben Noach* the animal may not yet be considered dead, such a limb would remain prohibited to him as *ever min hachai*. This creates a potential paradox — something permissible for the Jew but forbidden to the *ben Noach*. As a result, some authorities hold that since the animal is treated as dead for purposes of Jewish law (the *shechita* having taken effect), it is treated as dead for the *ben Noach* as well, and he may eat the limb. Others go the opposite direction and impose the stricter standard even on the Jew. The resolution is not uniform.

For a non-kosher animal — say, an ostrich — the situation is different. *Shechita* does not render the ostrich permissible to the Jew in any case. And therefore, *shechita* does not remove the *ever min hachai* prohibition from the ostrich for the *ben Noach* either. *Ein shechitata metahareta* — the *shechita* does not render it permissible to the *ben Noach* so long as the animal is still alive. Only when it is fully dead does the *ever min hachai* concern cease.

### Proof from Mishna

The Gemara now draws out the proof: *ella lav biBnei Noach michlal de'assur* — if the only coherent reading of the *mishna* places it in the context of *bnei Noach* and a non-kosher bird, then we see from the *mishna* itself that *bnei Noach* are prohibited in *ever min hachai* from non-kosher animals. This confirms Rav's ruling: *mach'loket beYisrael* — but for *bnei Noach*, the prohibition of *ever min hachai* extends to non-kosher animals universally.

The contradiction between the beginning and the end of the *mishna* — the opening, which speaks of not receiving lashes, seemingly implying no prohibition of *ever min hachai* by non-kosher birds, and the conclusion, which implies the opposite — is resolved by Rav Mani bar Patish: *reisha b'Yisrael v'seifa b'Bnei Noach*. The opening of the *mishna* addresses Jews, for whom *ever min hachai* does not apply to non-kosher animals and who therefore do not receive lashes for that prohibition (though the question of why they also do not receive lashes for the non-kosher prohibition is addressed separately). The conclusion of the *mishna* addresses *bnei Noach*, for whom *ever min hachai* does apply to non-kosher animals, and for whom *shechita* does not resolve the prohibition as long as the animal continues to move.

---

## Shiur for Transgression

### Rav's Position

Having concluded the discussion of which animals are subject to *ever min hachai*, the Gemara turns to the question of the *shiur* — how much must one eat to transgress. Rav states: *ever min hachai tzarich kezayis* — one must eat a *kezayis* to transgress the prohibition of *ever min hachai*, just as is the rule for all other food prohibitions. The reason: *achila kesiva bah* — the verse employs the language of eating (*lo tochal*), and eating in halachic contexts requires a *kezayis*.

### Rav Amram's Challenge

Rav Amram challenges this from the *mishna* cited earlier. The *mishna* states that one who eats *ever min hachai* from a non-kosher bird does not receive lashes. The question: if Rav is correct that a *kezayis* is required, then in the scenario the *mishna* describes, the person has eaten a *kezayis* worth of the limb — so why does he not receive lashes for eating a *kezayis* of a non-kosher bird? *V'isalka daatach be'inan kezayis teipok lei d'achal kezayis* — if the scenario involves eating a *kezayis* of the *ever*, one ought to be liable for eating a *kezayis* of a non-kosher bird regardless. The fact that the *mishna* says no lashes are incurred suggests that the *ever min hachai* scenario does not necessarily involve eating a *kezayis* of the animal's meat, which in turn implies that a *kezayis* of meat is not what is required.

### Meat vs Limb

The Gemara resolves this tension by invoking an explanation attributed to Rav Nachman. *Bemashu basar gidim ve-ha'atzamot* — the limb in question contains only a small amount of actual meat, while the rest of its *kezayis* is composed of sinews and bones. The *kezayis* required for *ever min hachai* is a *kezayis* of the *ever* as a whole — meat, sinews, and bones combined — not a *kezayis* of meat alone. The prohibition of non-kosher food, by contrast, requires a *kezayis* of meat specifically. Therefore, it is possible for a limb to constitute a *kezayis* for purposes of *ever min hachai* (meat plus bone together reaching a *kezayis*) while not providing a *kezayis* of meat (since the meat component alone is less than a *kezayis*). In such a case, one would transgress *ever min hachai* without incurring lashes for the non-kosher prohibition — exactly what the *mishna* says.

---

## Whole Unit Principle

### Living Bird Case

The Gemara brings a further teaching from Rav: *achal tzipor tehora be-chayeha be-chol shehu* — if one ate a whole living kosher bird, one transgresses even with the smallest amount. The entire bird, eaten alive, constitutes an *ever min hachai* violation without any *kezayis* requirement, because eating the whole unit is sufficient.

### Dead vs Non-Kosher

If the bird is dead, the analysis changes. *U-ve-mitata be-kezayit* — a dead bird creates a *neveilah* concern, and for *neveilah* a *kezayis* is universally required. The Torah does not identify the dead animal as a specific unit that is forbidden; rather, the prohibition of *neveilah* concerns the meat generically, and therefore the standard *kezayis* measure governs.

If the bird is non-kosher, the rule is different in the other direction: *bein be-chayeha bein be-mitata be-mashehu* — whether alive or dead, the smallest amount suffices. A non-kosher bird is forbidden as a unit — *al tochal* applies to the specific entity — and the principle of *biryah* (an entire creature) applies. If one ate the entire non-kosher ant, or the entire non-kosher bird, regardless of whether the quantity is less than a *kezayis*, one transgresses, because the Torah prohibits the entity itself.

The distinction can be stated as follows. The principle of *biryah* — that a whole entity suffices even without a *kezayis* — depends on whether the Torah identifies the forbidden item as a specific unit. When the Torah says do not eat non-kosher birds, it identifies the bird as the unit, and eating the whole bird transgresses even if it is tiny. When the Torah says do not eat from a *neveilah*, it refers to the flesh generically, not to any specific creature, and therefore the standard *kezayis* applies. *Ever min hachai*, when the whole living bird is eaten, is treated like the former: the *ever* or the unit is identified as what is prohibited, and the whole suffices.

### Small Bird Debate

A *braita* introduces a further case: *natal tzipor she-ein bo kezayit ve-achalo* — one took a bird that does not contain a *kezayis* in the entire bird and ate it. Rabbi (Rebbe) holds one exempt; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds one liable. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon argues by way of *kal vachomer*: *al ever mimena chay al kula lo kol shekein* — if one is liable for eating even a limb torn from a living animal, one is certainly liable for eating the whole animal alive. Rebbe's position, by implication, is that the prohibition of *ever min hachai* is specifically addressed to a limb removed from a living animal; eating the entire living animal whole is a different act, not captured by the prohibition of *ever min hachai*. Rashi suggests that eating the whole animal would still constitute *basar min hachai*, for which a *kezayis* of meat would be required.

If one strangled the bird and then ate it — *chanka ve'achla* — all agree that a *kezayis* is required, since at that point the prohibition is *neveilah* rather than *ever min hachai*.

### Limb Division Question

The Gemara frames the debate between Rebbe and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon as turning on a conceptual question: *bechayei evarim omedet, u-mar savar bechayei lav evarim omedet* — does one regard a living animal as already subdivided into its constituent limbs, or does one regard a living animal as a unified living creature not yet conceived of as limbs? If the animal is conceptually already divided into limbs while alive, then eating the whole thing is eating all the limbs together, and one transgresses *ever min hachai*. If the animal is regarded as a single living entity rather than as a collection of limbs, then eating it whole does not constitute eating an *ever*, and one does not transgress *ever min hachai* on those grounds.

Crucially, the Gemara notes that on one matter all agree: *lo ba'inan kzayis* — no *kezayis* is required. The case in the *braita* involves a bird with no *kezayis* in the whole bird, yet Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds one liable and Rebbe holds one exempt — not because of the *kezayis*, but because of the question of whether the whole constitutes an *ever*. Neither party is troubled by the absence of a *kezayis*. This itself is a significant implication: eating an *ever*, or an entire unit equivalent to an *ever*, does not require a *kezayis*.

---

## Kezayit Resolution

### Limb Kezayit Reinterpret…

At this point the Gemara attempts to reconcile all of this with Rav's original statement that *ever min hachai* requires a *kezayis*. The resolution offered is a reinterpretation: when the *braita* says the bird does not contain a *kezayis*, it does not mean the bird has no *kezayis* at all. It means there is not a *kezayis* of meat alone — *bemashu basar, gidim va'atzamot* — only a small amount of meat, with the remainder being sinews and bones. The *kezayis* of the *ever* (meat plus bone and sinew together) does exist; what is absent is a *kezayis* of meat in isolation. This allows Rav's position — that a *kezayis* of the *ever* is required — to remain intact.

The Gemara is candid that this reinterpretation is a stretch. The simple sense of the *braita* and the proofs adduced is that an *ever*, as a whole unit, suffices even without a *kezayis*. Rav's position requires a more contrived reading of the sources, and the Gemara's resolution consistently employs the same device: interpreting "no *kezayis*" to mean no *kezayis* of meat, while maintaining that there is a *kezayis* of the whole limb.

### Kalanisa Bird

The Gemara presses the scenario further. If one holds that a *kezayis* of the limb is required — meaning even bone and sinew count toward the *kezayis* — then the case of eating a whole bird involves a bird where the entire bird has a *kezayis* (otherwise no transgression would occur), yet has no *kezayis* of meat. Furthermore, the *braita* indicates that if one eats a limb, all agree one transgresses, which on Rav's view means the limb has a *kezayis*. We are therefore describing a bird where a single limb has a *kezayis* and yet the entire bird has no *kezayis* of meat. This would be a remarkably bony and spare bird. Rav Shiviya confirms that such a bird exists: the *kalanisa*, a notoriously bony bird with very little meat, such that one limb might constitute a *kezayis* (of bone, sinew, and flesh together) while the whole bird yields less than a *kezayis* of meat.

### Kalanisa Kosher

The Gemara immediately notes a difficulty: the *kalanisa* is a non-kosher bird. And Rav himself stated that for a non-kosher bird — whether alive or dead — one transgresses with the smallest amount (*be-mashehu*), because the *biryah* principle applies. The entire framing of the *braita*, where the debate between Rebbe and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon hinges on whether one needs a *kezayis*, presupposes that the bird in question is kosher. For a non-kosher bird, there is no debate — one transgresses as a *biryah* regardless of size. The Gemara therefore concludes: *ela k'ein kalanisa* — not the *kalanisa* itself, which is non-kosher, but a kosher bird of similar characteristics: extremely bony, with minimal meat, where one limb reaches a *kezayis* but the whole bird provides less than a *kezayis* of meat. Whether such a kosher bird actually exists is uncertain, but the Gemara treats the description as not entirely impossible.

---

## Intent & Limbs

### Rava's Intent Theory

The Gemara turns to a striking application of subjective intent. Rava proposes: *im timtza lomar savar Rebbi machsheves ochalim shemah machshavah* — were one to say that Rebbe holds that the way one thinks about one's eating (*machsheves ochalim*) has legal significance, then the following would follow. *Chisheiv le'ochlah eiver eiver ve'achlah kullah k'chayyei* — if, while the bird is still alive, one thought to oneself specifically about eating it limb by limb (for instance, thinking about the leg while the bird is still walking), and then swallowed the whole bird alive, Rebbe would concede that one has transgressed *ever min hachai*. The reason: one's subjective framing has already divided the animal into limbs in one's mind, and therefore when one ate it, the act is treated as having eaten an *ever* rather than a whole living unit.

This connects to a broader principle of *machsheves ochalim* — the significance of how one defines what one is eating. The related concept of *achshavei* (found elsewhere in the *poskim*, particularly in contexts of *Pesach* and matters of medicine) concerns elevating something ordinarily unfit for eating to the status of food by virtue of consuming it. The present case is different: it is not about whether something counts as food at all, but about whether a living animal is treated as subdivided into limbs or as a unified creature. Nevertheless, both share the feature of allowing subjective intent to shape how one defines the object of one's eating.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye objects: *umi ika midi d'ilu achla acher lo mechayev v'achla hai mechayev* — is there anything where if another person ate it they would not be liable, yet if this person eats it they would be liable? Abaye finds it deeply problematic to allow individual subjective intent to determine whether a halachic transgression occurs. The bird is what it is; its status should not vary based on what different people happen to be thinking. If one person's *machshavah* makes the bird into limbs while another person's neutral state of mind does not, then the same bird is simultaneously divided and undivided depending on who is looking at it — a result Abaye finds untenable.

### Rava's Response

Rava's response is direct: *zeh lefi machshavto v'zeh lefi machshavto* — each person's transgression is determined by his own perspective. For the person who had the *machshavah* dividing the animal into limbs, the act of eating is treated as eating *ever min hachai*. For another person with no such intent, the act is treated as eating a whole living creature. Rava is not troubled by the divergence; each individual's subjective framing governs his own halachic reality.

### Reverse Case

Rava then applies the same logic in the opposite direction. *Im timtza lomar savar Rebbe Elazar bar Rebbe Shimon machsheves ochalim shemah machshavah* — if Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon also holds that *machsheves ochalim* is legally significant, the following would follow in reverse. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's general position is that a living animal is already conceptually divided into its limbs. But if *machshavah* matters, and if the person eating the bird was thinking about it in the mode of its eventual death — planning how he would slaughter and prepare it, not thinking of its living limbs at all — *chishev l'ochlah misa*, then *v'achla chaya patur* — if he then ate the whole bird alive, he would be exempt. His subjective intent has un-divided the animal in his mind; he was not treating it as a collection of limbs, and therefore eating the whole does not constitute eating an *ever*.

Abaye objects identically: *umi ika midi d'ilu achla acher mechayev v'achla hai patur* — how can it be that for anyone else who eats this bird (they being in the default state of treating it as limbs, per Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view) the act is a transgression, yet for this specific person, who was thinking about it differently, the act is exempt? Rava responds again: *zeh lefi machshavto v'zeh lefi machshavto* — each goes according to his own perspective.

It bears noting that the weight of halachic tradition sides with Abaye on this point. The general principle in *halacha* is that objective standards govern, and it is uncommon for individual subjective intent to redefine the halachic nature of an act for that person alone. Rava's position represents a genuinely striking departure from the norm.

---

---

# Hullin 103

## Sources: Ever/Basar

### R. Yochanan's Sources

The Gemara opens near the bottom of 102b, with a debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish concerning the scriptural sources for two related prohibitions: *ever min hachai* (a limb from a living animal) and *basar min hachai* (flesh from a living animal).

Rabbi Yochanan identifies each prohibition with a distinct verse. The source for *ever min hachai* is the verse *lo tochal hanefesh im habasar* — "you shall not eat the soul with the meat" (Devarim 12:23). Rashi explains that *nefesh* here signifies the limb, something that possesses a kind of independent vitality, a piece that, once severed, does not regenerate. Hence, do not eat the limb while the *nefesh chayah* is still animating the flesh. The source for *basar min hachai*, by contrast, is a separate verse: *uvasar basadeh treifah lo tochelu* — "do not eat flesh torn in the field" (Shemot 22:30). Although this verse is, of course, the primary source for *treifah*, Rabbi Yochanan reads it simultaneously as a prohibition against flesh torn from a living animal, since *basar treifah* denotes flesh that has been violently ripped.

The practical distinction between the two prohibitions is also worth noting. For *ever min hachai*, one transgresses even by consuming less than a *kezayis* — certainly if the limb includes bones that together constitute a *kezayis* — whereas *basar min hachai* is only transgressed upon eating a *kezayis* of flesh.

### Reish Lakish's Sources

Reish Lakish agrees that *lo tochal hanefesh im habasar* is the source for *ever min hachai*, but he departs from Rabbi Yochanan regarding *basar min hachai*. For Reish Lakish, the very same verse — *lo tochal hanefesh im habasar* — also prohibits *basar min hachai*. The reading is natural: do not eat the meat while the soul is still within the animal, meaning eat meat only after the animal has been slaughtered and its soul taken. By this reading, the verse *uvasar basadeh treifah lo tochelu* refers exclusively to the laws of *treifah*, with no additional derivation for *basar min hachai*.

### Debate Implications

The practical consequences of this dispute come into focus when one examines the rules governing multiple sets of lashes (*malkot*). The Gemara operates on the assumption that transgressions learned from the same verse — even if they are conceptually distinct — yield only a single set of lashes when committed simultaneously in a single act.

If one ate *ever min hachai* and *basar min hachai* together with a single warning (*azharah*), Rabbi Yochanan would hold him liable for two sets of lashes, since they derive from separate verses. Reish Lakish would hold him liable for only one set, as both are derived from a single verse. The Gemara notes that this is not the same as the principle of *lav shebichlalus* — a prohibition whose verse is so broad and nonspecific as to preclude lashes entirely. Here, the verse is specific; it is simply interpreted in two ways. Still, simultaneous transgression of two applications of the same verse yields only one set of lashes.

A more striking implication involves eating *basar min hachai* together with *basar min hatreifah* — undeniably distinct prohibitions, one concerning meat ripped from a living animal and the other concerning a slaughtered *treifah*. Yet according to Rabbi Yochanan, who derives *basar min hachai* from the same verse as *treifah* (*uvasar basadeh treifah*), if both were eaten simultaneously, only one set of lashes would result. For Reish Lakish, who assigns *basar min hachai* to a different verse, two sets of lashes would apply. Finally, if one ate *ever min hachai* together with *basar min hatreifah* — the two extremes of the spectrum — everyone agrees these derive from separate verses, and two sets of lashes apply regardless of the debate.

---

## Ever + Treifah Case

### Live Treifah Scenario

The Gemara now opens 103a with a new and more intricate case: *achal ever min hachai min hatreifah* — one ate a limb taken from an animal that is both alive and a *treifah*. Rabbi Yochanan holds him liable for two transgressions; Reish Lakish holds him liable for only one.

At first glance, the ruling of Rabbi Yochanan poses no difficulty: *ever min hachai* and *treifah* are derived from universally agreed-upon separate verses, so two sets of lashes are expected. The difficulty lies with Reish Lakish. Since those two prohibitions come from distinct verses — something everyone concedes — why does Reish Lakish say only one set of lashes?

The resolution offered by Rav Yosef is that the earlier discussion concerned two separate animals — one forbidden as *ever min hachai*, the other as *treifah* — eaten simultaneously. With two animals and two verses, everyone agrees on two sets of lashes. But the present case concerns a single animal, and here the complications of *issur chal al issur* — one prohibition taking effect on top of another — come into play. When the same piece of meat must be doubly categorized, the question is no longer merely which verse applies, but whether both prohibitions can simultaneously be in force on the very same object.

### Born Treifah Case

Abaye proposes the first specific scenario to illustrate what the debate might actually be about. The animal was born as a *treifah* — it emerged from the womb already carrying the defect that renders it mortally ill. At the moment of birth, both the prohibition of *treifah* and potentially the prohibition of *ever min hachai* came into being simultaneously.

This scenario depends on a further halachic question we have already encountered: does the principle of *beheimah bechayeha le'eivarim omedet* apply — is a living animal already considered, in halachic terms, as subdivided into its limbs? If it is, then the prohibition of *ever min hachai* begins the moment the animal is born, since it is already "seen" as constituent limbs. If so, both *treifah* and *ever min hachai* take effect simultaneously at birth, and there is no prior prohibition to block the other.

According to this reading, Rabbi Yochanan holds that *beheimah bechayeha le'eivarim omedet* — the animal is considered subdivided from the moment it lives — and therefore both prohibitions arose at the same time, both take full effect, and two sets of lashes apply. Reish Lakish holds the opposite: the animal is not considered subdivided into limbs while alive. The prohibition of *ever min hachai* only arises at the moment the limb is actually severed. Since the animal began its life already as a *treifah*, the *issur treifah* was already in place when the limb was torn off, and the subsequently arising *issur ever min hachai* cannot take effect upon it — *ein issur chal al issur*.

Tosafot raises the natural objection: is not *ever min hachai* an *issur mosif*, a prohibition of larger scope — since it applies even to non-Jews (*bnei Noach*)? And does not larger scope allow a later prohibition to take effect on a pre-existing one? Tosafot acknowledges that not everyone accepts the principle of *issur mosif* in this way. At least one position simply does not grant the later-arising prohibition the power to take effect, even when its scope is broader.

### Larger Scope Debate

The Gemara then offers a second way of understanding the debate. In this reading, everyone would agree that *beheimah bechayeha lav le'eivarim omedet* — the animal is not considered subdivided into limbs from the moment of birth. There is no dispute on that question. The dispute instead concerns whether the *issur ever min hachai*, which arises later (when the limb is severed from an animal already established as a *treifah*), can nonetheless take effect by virtue of its larger scope.

The argument for allowing it to take effect is straightforward: *ever min hachai* is an *issur mosif* — it applies to a broader category of persons, namely *bnei Noach* — and therefore it ought to be able to take hold even on top of a pre-existing *issur treifah*. One opinion accepts this; the other does not, perhaps questioning whether the fact that non-Jews are additionally prohibited constitutes a sufficient basis for *issur mosif*, given that non-Jews exist in an entirely separate legal framework.

### Reverse Order Case

The Gemara entertains a third possibility. Here, everyone agrees that *beheimah bechayeha le'eivarim omedet* — the animal is considered subdivided from birth — but the temporal sequence of the prohibitions is reversed. The animal was born healthy; from the moment of birth, it was already subject to the prohibition of *ever min hachai*. Only later did it develop the defect that rendered it a *treifah*. Now the question is inverted: can *treifah* take effect on top of a pre-existing *ever min hachai*?

This is a far harder case to justify. *Treifah* has no claim to larger scope in this context; if anything, it has a narrower or equal scope relative to *ever min hachai*. How then could it take effect on top of a pre-existing prohibition? The Gemara states the debate: one opinion holds that *issur treifah* can indeed come and take effect (*ati vichayela*); the other holds it cannot.

The possibility that *treifah* can take effect on pre-existing prohibitions is not without precedent, and the Gemara will spell this out later in connection with *chelev* — but it is previewed here as the possible rationale for the opinion that allows *treifah* to override.

### Single Act Both

Rava presents a fourth and particularly elegant scenario. The animal was healthy, and the act of tearing off the limb was itself the event that rendered the animal a *treifah* — for example, the hind leg was torn off, and this very act created the *treifah* condition. In this case, the question is not about which prohibition arose first, since both *ever min hachai* and *treifah* would seem to arise at the identical moment of tearing.

One might think this eliminates the problem of competing prohibitions entirely — if they arise simultaneously, both should take effect, and two sets of lashes should result. But the Gemara shows that even here, the debate depends on the question of *beheimah bechayeha le'eivarim omedet*. The opinion that holds the animal is not considered subdivided into limbs while alive would say that *ever min hachai* only begins at the moment of tearing — and therefore, at that same moment, both *issur ever* and *issur treifah* arise together (*bahadi hadadi kasu*), both take effect, and two transgressions result. The opinion that holds the animal is already considered subdivided while alive would say that *issur ever* preceded the tearing — the limb was already subject to *ever min hachai* while the animal was walking around — and when the tearing now creates *treifah*, that prohibition is trying to take effect on an already-forbidden object, which it cannot do. Hence only one transgression.

---

## Chelev Cases

### Chelev as Eiver?

The Gemara now brings a statement of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: one who ate *chelev* (forbidden fat) from a live *treifah* animal is liable for two transgressions. The Gemara pauses on this formulation, because it apparently treats the *chelev* as an instance of *ever min hachai* — but since when is *chelev* considered a limb?

The underlying question is significant. The prohibition of *ever min hachai* normally applies to a limb — an *eiver* — which is conventionally understood as a structure that includes bone, flesh, and sinew. *Chelev* is fat; it has none of these components in the ordinary sense. A number of *Rishonim* grapple with this. The Ramban establishes that if a limb naturally has a bone, the bone must be present for the *ever* designation; but if a limb by its nature has no bone — such as the ear or nose — then it can constitute an *ever* without one. From here, the Rashba extends the argument: if *ever min hachai* can apply to internal organs (which also have no bones), and if the *chelev* is associated with an internal organ such as the kidney — lying in its crevice, in some sense belonging to it — then the *chelev* might itself be categorized as an *eiver*. The Rashba goes further to suggest that *chelev*, considered on its own terms as a discrete anatomical unit, could constitute an *eiver*. This is admittedly difficult, since the precise boundaries of a mass of fat are not self-evident, but that is the direction of the analysis.

Given this, in the scenario under discussion, you have a *treifah* animal from which you have removed *chelev* while it is still alive. Three prohibitions are in play: *chelev*, *ever min hachai*, and *treifah*. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan as saying two transgressions — and immediately Rabbi Ammi challenges him: why only two? I myself say three. And indeed, another tradition is cited in which Rabbi Abbahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan as saying three. So there are now competing traditions about Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling.

### Two vs. Three Versions

The Gemara directly confronts these competing traditions of Rabbi Yochanan — two lashes versus three. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba transmits a tradition of two; Rabbi Abbahu transmits a tradition of three. Rabbi Ammi, pressing on behalf of the three-lash tradition, challenges Rabbi Chiya's report. The Gemara asks: *bimai kamifligi* — what is this debate actually about?

### Timing Resolution

The Gemara explains the two versions by applying the framework already developed. The scenario involves an animal that became a *treifah* at the moment of birth (*kegon shenitrefa im yetziat rubba*).

The tradition of three lashes relies on the principle of *beheimah bechayeha le'eivarim omedet*. If the animal is considered subdivided into limbs from the moment of birth, then at the very instant this animal emerged, the prohibition of *chelev* began (since *chelev* of a fetus does not apply, it begins at birth), the prohibition of *ever min hachai* began, and the prohibition of *treifah* began — all simultaneously. When all three prohibitions take effect at precisely the same moment, all three apply in full, yielding three sets of lashes.

The tradition of two lashes applies the opposite principle: *beheimah bechayeha lav le'eivarim omedet*.
