# Hullin 105

## Washing & Order

### Kinuach Definition

Before turning to the topic of the waiting period, it is worth correcting a slight misstatement from the previous session regarding the requirement of *kinuach* and *hadachah* between meat and dairy. When the Gemara uses the term *kinuach*, both Rashi and Tosafot understand it to mean not one or the other, but both wiping and washing the mouth. The Gemara's formulation *mediach af mekaneach, mekaneach af mediach* reinforces this: each act implies the other, so that the requirement is conjunctive, not disjunctive. This is practically significant when one is transitioning from cheese to meat — the obligation is to do both, not merely to choose between them.

A further clarification concerns the framing of yesterday's passage. The Gemara's earlier reference to washing hands and cleaning the mouth was presented as applying when cheese comes first and meat second. That framing was offered as a way to reconcile the passage with our practice. However, it is worth noting that the original statement of *Iggur* uses the formulation *of u-gevina* — poultry first. Taken literally, this would suggest that even when poultry precedes cheese, washing hands and cleaning the mouth is sufficient, without requiring a waiting period. That nuance will bear on the discussion that follows.

### Waiting Period Intro

The Gemara now turns to the question of the waiting period between meat and dairy. Rav Assi poses the question to Rabbi Yochanan: *kama yisheh bein basar le-gevina* — how long must one wait between meat and milk? Rabbi Yochanan answers: not at all. Rav Assi expresses surprise — *eini* — is that really so? He raises the ruling of Rav Chisda: *achal basar assur le-echol gevina, gevina mutar le-echol basar* — if one ate meat, one is forbidden to eat cheese afterward; but if one ate cheese first, one is permitted to eat meat afterward. Given this asymmetry, the question is reframed: how long must one wait between cheese and meat? To which Rabbi Yochanan replies: not at all.

### Order Matters

The Gemara then presents the ruling of Rav Chisda directly: *achal basar assur le-echol gevina, gevina mutar le-echol basar*. Order matters. Meat first creates a prohibition that requires some form of separation before eating cheese; cheese first imposes no waiting period before eating meat.

### Meat Between Teeth

Rav Acha bar Yosef poses a question to Rav Chisda: *basar she-bein ha-shinayim mahu* — what is the status of meat that is lodged between one's teeth? Is it considered as though one still has meat in one's mouth, even if it has been sitting there for some time? Rav Chisda responds by citing the verse *ha-basar odenu bein sheneihem* — the meat was still between their teeth — indicating that meat between the teeth retains its status as meat.

### Waiting Purpose

This question opens a window onto the underlying rationale for the waiting period. One reading of the ruling is that as long as meat remains lodged between the teeth, the prohibition continues, and the waiting period begins only once the meat is removed. More broadly, the question points toward one of two explanations offered by the *Rishonim* for why waiting is required at all: either because meat gets stuck in the teeth and lingers there, or because meat is fatty and its residue remains in the mouth and throat even after swallowing. These two explanations are not merely theoretical — they have practical implications for cases such as liquid meat dishes like chicken soup, which would not lodge between the teeth. Nevertheless, the *Rishonim* and later authorities do not draw practical distinctions based on these differences, treating the prohibition uniformly. The asymmetry between meat first and cheese first — which is the more stringent direction — is connected to both of these explanations, since cheese is neither as fatty as meat nor as likely to lodge in the teeth.

---

## Duration Dispute

### Mar Ukva Practice

The Gemara now addresses how long the waiting period actually lasts. Mar Ukva introduces the topic with characteristic humility: *ana le-ha milta chala bar chamra legabei abba* — for this matter I am like vinegar the son of wine compared to my father. His father, when he ate meat, would not eat cheese *ad lemachar ad hashta* — until the following day at the same time, a full twenty-four hours later. Mar Ukva himself, by contrast, waits only until the next meal: *be-ha seudata hu de-la achilna, aval le-seudata achrita achilna* — he would not eat cheese at the same meal, but at a subsequent meal he would.

### Tosafot: Meal Change

Tosafot's interpretation of Mar Ukva's statement is significant and precise. The *le-seudata achrita* does not refer to the standard gap between the morning and evening meals, which could span many hours. Rather, Tosafot understands it to mean a formally different meal, even if that next meal begins very shortly thereafter. As Tosafot writes: *afilu lealtar im silek ha-shulchan ve-veirach mutar* — even immediately, if one has cleared the table and recited *birkat ha-mazon*, one may eat dairy at the next meal. The criterion is a change of meal context, not elapsed time.

### Rambam: Six Hours

The Rambam takes a different position. He requires *ke-shesh shaot* — approximately six hours — understanding the gap between meals to be defined by a measure of time rather than by the formal act of concluding one meal and beginning another. The *kaf* of approximation (*ke-shesh*) is noted by some as leaving room for minor variations, though the basic requirement is understood as roughly six hours.

### Conceptual Framework

The conceptual underpinning of this dispute is worth examining carefully. The question is: what is the waiting period actually accomplishing? If the concern were purely about removing the physical reality of meat from one's mouth — the fatty residue, the fibers lodged between teeth — then a new meal, without elapsed time, would accomplish nothing. One would still have the meat in one's mouth. The fact that Tosafot considers a new meal immediately after the previous one to be sufficient indicates that, in Tosafot's framework, the waiting period is not primarily about physical removal at all. Rather, it is about a formal halakhic definition of eating together. The Rabbis were concerned about the possibility of coming to cook meat and milk together; they therefore redefined what it means to "eat together." Just as having one at the table while eating the other renders them halakhically eaten together, so too does the lingering taste or experience of one create a connection to the other that makes them halakhically continuous. But if one clears the table, recites *birkat ha-mazon*, and begins a new meal, then even with some residual taste, one has not eaten them together — they belong to formally distinct meals. Tosafot's approach is thus about defining the boundary of a meal rather than about the physical state of one's mouth.

The Rambam, who requires the passage of time, appears more concerned with the reality of the situation — that the actual experience of the meat meal genuinely persists in the mouth, and starting a new meal does not adequately address that physical reality. Accordingly, sufficient time must pass for the taste and fatty residue to dissipate.

### Custom Variations

Practically speaking, the *Shulchan Aruch* rules like the Rambam, requiring six hours. The *Rema* notes that technically, for Ashkenazim, a new meal would suffice, but records the *minhag* or *chumra* to wait six hours like the Rambam. In practice, different communities have arrived at different customs. Dutch Jews wait one hour — essentially translating Tosafot's position into a minimal unit of time rather than a pure meal-change standard. German Jews wait three hours, which is harder to explain theoretically, though it may reflect the practical spacing of meals in those communities, with breakfast around nine and the midday meal around noon or twelve. Some who follow the Rambam but take the *kaf* of *ke-shesh shaot* seriously wait five hours and a few minutes, or five and a half hours, though the rationale for stopping short of six is not entirely clear. The most widely observed practice among Ashkenazim is to wait the full six hours, following the stringent position even though their authorities technically permit less.

---

## Cheese & Mouth Clean

### Cheese First Rule

Returning to the question of washing and mouth-cleaning, Tosafot offers a reconciliation of yesterday's passage with the framework established here. The requirement to wash one's hands and clean one's mouth — without a waiting period — applies specifically when cheese is first and one wishes to eat meat afterward. This is consistent with the general principle that the cheese-first direction is more lenient, requiring only a physical cleaning rather than a temporal separation.

### Rabbeinu Tam Leniency

Tosafot also records a more lenient position, attributed to Rabbeinu Tam and the *Behag*. According to this view, the option of washing hands and cleaning the mouth is not limited to the cheese-first case. Even when meat is first, one could in principle wash one's hands and clean out one's mouth in lieu of waiting an extended period. On this reading, Mar Ukva's father who waited twenty-four hours, and Mar Ukva himself who waited until the next meal, were doing so only because they preferred not to go through the procedure of washing and cleaning. This is admittedly a striking position — why would Mar Ukva's father wait a full twenty-four hours rather than simply wash his mouth? But Rabbeinu Tam's view demonstrates just how far certain Ashkenazic approaches could extend leniency. In practice, the accepted approach treats yesterday's Gemara about washing and cleaning as applying to the cheese-first direction, and this Gemara's waiting period as governing the meat-first direction, with Ashkenazim maintaining that a new meal suffices even in the latter case.

### Convert Hardship

A practical consideration worth noting is the particular difficulty the waiting period poses for those new to observance or for converts. Keeping *Shabbos* and basic *kashrus* involve changes one makes to one's life context. The waiting period, by contrast, is one of the few halakhic obligations that actively constrains one's future choices every time one eats meat — foreclosing dairy options for the next six hours. This can feel like a uniquely heavy burden. The *poskim* do recognize that under special circumstances — such as medical considerations where a person has been advised to consume significant amounts of dairy — it is possible to rely on the more lenient positions. This is not a general license but an ad hoc consideration for genuine need.

### Hard Cheese Practice

One further development concerns hard cheese. The Maharam MiRothenburg, the great thirteenth-century Ashkenazic *posek* and teacher of the Rosh and the Mordechai, once found that a piece of hard cheese had become lodged between his teeth during a meal, much as meat does. As a result, he adopted a personal stringency not to eat hard cheese without waiting — as one would after meat — before eating meat. He explicitly stated this was his own practice and not a ruling for others. Nevertheless, among some of his followers, this personal practice developed into an actual *halakha*, giving rise to the widespread practice of waiting after hard cheese in the same manner as after meat. The definition of "hard" in this context — questions of aging, consistency, mold, and so forth — became the subject of later discussion, but the key point is that this practice originated as an individual stringency with no basis in the Gemara itself, and only gradually assumed the character of binding practice in certain communities.

---

## Property Supervision

### Samuel's Teaching

The Gemara now takes what it introduces as a digression — though the connection to the preceding passage is the shared phrase *chala bar chamra*, vinegar the son of wine. Shmuel employs that same expression in a different context: *ana le-ha milta chala bar chamra legabei abba* — for this matter I am like vinegar the son of wine compared to my father. His father would conduct a tour of his property twice a day, *terei zimnei beyoma*, while Shmuel himself managed only once. Shmuel then elaborates on the principle behind this practice: *man de-sayar nichsei kol yoma mishkach astira* — whoever visits his property once a day will find a coin. The idea is not necessarily that literal coins will be discovered lying on the ground, but that regular supervision yields financial benefit: problems are caught early, losses are prevented, and workers are kept honest.

### Abaye Catches Theft

Abaye followed this teaching and would visit his property every day. On one occasion, he encountered his sharecropper carrying a bundle of wood — clearly intending to take it for himself. When Abaye challenged him, asking where he was taking the wood, the sharecropper claimed he was bringing it to Abaye's house. Abaye replied: *kevar kadmucha rabanan* — the rabbis already beat you to it, meaning that Shmuel's teaching had brought him there in time to catch the would-be theft before it was completed.

### Rav Assi Flood

Rav Assi similarly visited his property daily, though he complained that he had yet to find any of the coins Shmuel had promised. One day, he noticed that an irrigation pipe on his land had burst and was about to flood his fields. He took his cloak, wrapped it up, and used it to plug the hole, then called out for help. The townspeople came and repaired the breach properly. Rav Assi then declared that he had found all the coins Shmuel had promised him — the single visit had saved him from a potentially catastrophic loss.

---

## First & Last Washing

### Obligation Levels

The Gemara turns to the laws of hand-washing at meals. Rav Idi bar Abin in the name of Rav Yosef bar Ashi establishes the foundational distinction: *mayim rishonim mitzvah, ve-acharonim chovah* — the washing before eating bread is a *mitzvah*, while *mayim acharonim*, the washing after the meal, is a *chovah*, an obligation. The reason *mayim acharonim* is considered more weighty is the health concern associated with *Melach Sedomit*, a salt that can cause blindness if it reaches the eyes — a matter of physical danger takes priority over a religious *mitzvah*. A practical *nafka mina* offered by Tosafot: if one finds oneself in a situation of duress with only enough water for one washing — such as wartime conditions — one must prioritize *mayim acharonim* because of the health concern.

### Brachah Difference

At the same time, Tosafot draws a further distinction between the two in the opposite direction. Despite being weightier as an obligation, *mayim acharonim* lacks the religious and spiritual character of a *mitzvah*. It is performed purely for health or protective reasons, not as an act of religious significance in its own right. This explains why a *brachah* is recited over *mayim rishonim* but not over *mayim acharonim* — the latter, though mandatory, lacks the quality of religious value that would warrant a blessing.

The middle washing, *mayim emtzoyim*, performed between courses during a meal, occupies a different category entirely: *amtzei reshut* — optional. It is done purely for cleanliness. This creates an apparent terminological tension: if *mayim acharonim* is called a *chovah* (obligation) while *mayim rishonim* is called a *mitzvah*, how can *mayim emtzoyim* also be called a *chovah* relative to the others? The answer is that the terminology is relative: compared to something that is entirely optional (*reshut*), even a *mitzvah* can be called an obligation. But when distinguishing between *mayim rishonim* and *mayim acharonim* themselves, the terms carry distinct valence.

### Rishonim Rules

The Gemara now enumerates the practical rules governing each type of washing. For *mayim rishonim*: *rishonim notnin bein bi-kli bein al gabei karka* — one may wash so that the water runs either into a vessel or directly onto the ground. A practical note for *Shabbos*: if one is outdoors and washes directly onto grass, one would be watering the grass, which is forbidden. However, since *gerama* — an indirect cause — is permitted on *Shabbos*, one may wash onto a concrete or paved surface and allow the water to run off from there onto the grass; that suffices.

### Acharonim Rules

For *mayim acharonim*, the rule is stricter: *acharonim ein notnin ela bi-kli* — one may not wash directly onto the ground; the water must go into a vessel. The reason is that since the water has been in contact with *Melach Sedomit*, which is dangerous, one does not want it left on the ground where others might come into contact with it. There is also a mystical dimension that the Gemara introduces: a *ruach ra'a*, an evil spirit, resides over this water, and one does not want that spirit to be released onto the ground. A further view within the Gemara holds that the water should not be poured onto the ground, though it need not necessarily go into a vessel — pouring it onto wood chips, for instance, might suffice on this view since it does not go directly onto the ground, even if it is not enclosed in a vessel. The practical difference between these two positions concerns intermediate surfaces such as wood chips: the first view requires an actual vessel; the second merely prohibits the bare ground.

As for temperature: *mayim rishonim* may be performed with either hot or cold water. For *mayim acharonim*, only cold water may be used. This is somewhat counterintuitive — one might think that hot water would be more effective at removing grease and salt. The concern, however, is that hot water without soap and without running water can cause the fatty residue to rise to the surface of the skin without actually removing it, or as Rashi explains, cause it to be absorbed further into the hand. The result would be that the *Melach Sedomit* would remain on the hands in a more accessible form rather than being removed.

### Yad Soledes

The Gemara refines the rule regarding temperature. Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rav Yanai specifies: when the Gemara says *mayim rishonim* may be used with hot water, this applies only when the water is not *yad soledes* — not so hot that holding one's hand in it for a few moments would force one to withdraw it. The threshold of *yad soledes* is approximately 105 to 112 degrees Fahrenheit, though the exact measure is subject to discussion. Rashi offers a striking interpretation of why water that hot cannot be used even for *mayim rishonim*: water at the level of *yad soledes* has ceased to be considered water in the halakhic sense — *bitlu ve-nistalku mi-toras mayim* — and therefore does not fulfill the washing requirement at all.

A second version of this ruling in the Gemara applies Rav Yanai's statement to *mayim acharonim* instead, yielding a more lenient conclusion: even warm water — short of *yad soledes* — may be used for *mayim acharonim*. This is more permissive than the simple reading of the rule that only cold water is permitted. And by inference from this formulation — *michlal de-rishonim*, it follows — even water at the level of *yad soledes* would be permitted for *mayim rishonim*, though this seems a strange case to optimize for in practice.

### Middle Washing Optional

The *mayim emtzoyim*, the middle washing between courses, is entirely optional and done solely for cleanliness purposes. There is no halakhic requirement to wash between ordinary courses of a meal.

### Meat-Milk Washing

Rav Nachman, however, introduces an important qualification: *lo shanu ela bein tavshil le-tavshil* — the rule that the middle washing is optional applies only between one cooked dish and another. But *bein tavshil le-gevina*, between a meat dish and cheese — *chovah* — one must wash one's hands. This is the final ruling touching on the meat-dairy separation, and it carries implications for how we understand the entire framework of *basar be-chalav*. The passage appears to suggest that between a meat *tavshil* and dairy, washing one's hands suffices — without a waiting period, without the requirement of a separate meal. Tosafot acknowledges this, affirming that the passage does essentially say this, and sees here once again the principle that even a relatively small act of separation can suffice when the experience of eating them together is sufficiently attenuated.

This points to a broader conceptual pattern. If the concern were purely about the physical reality of meat in one's mouth or hands, it would be hard to explain why the form in which the food appears — *be'eyn*, in its own recognizable form, versus dissolved into a stew — should make any halakhic difference. Yet the Gemara does draw such distinctions: a meat *tavshil* is treated differently from meat *be'eyn*; cheese in a dish is treated differently from cheese standing alone. The more that the meat or dairy component is embedded in a mixture and therefore not presenting itself as a distinct food item, the less the experience registers as eating meat and dairy together. The concern, it seems, is about the phenomenological experience of combining them — the more hidden the component, the less the act reads as a violation. These distinctions are ultimately flattened in the *Shulchan Aruch*, which requires the same six-hour wait across the board, but they are present in the Gemara and clearly reflected in Tosafot's analysis.

The practical halakhic upshot is illustrated by a common case: one who eats food prepared in a *fleishig* restaurant where the dishes and equipment are presumed *fleishig* — even if the food itself contains no meat — technically, if it is a genuine *tavshil besari* situation, washing the hands and cleaning the mouth may suffice. Similarly, food that is cooked in clean *fleishig* vessels but contains no meat does not require a waiting period at all, since the principle of *noten ta'am bar noten ta'am de-heteira* applies: the flavor absorbed into the pot from *fleishig* food is one degree removed, and the flavor absorbed from the pot into the parve dish is two degrees removed, and since all the components are individually permitted (*heter*), this double-removed absorbed flavor is treated as halakhically negligible. If the resulting dish were then mixed with *milchig* food, however, that would be a different question, since it would no longer be merely a case of absorbed pot flavor. These distinctions will be addressed more fully in a later *sugya*.

---

## Melach Sedomit

### Salt Danger

The Gemara now focuses specifically on the rationale for *mayim acharonim*. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Chiya states: *mipnei mah ameru mayim acharonim chovah* — why did the Rabbis declare *mayim acharonim* obligatory? *She-melach Sedomit yesh she-mesama et ha-einayim* — because *Melach Sedomit* exists, a salt that can blind the eyes. Abaye adds that this salt is present in only a tiny concentration — *ke-kurta be-kora*, like one small kernel in a large barrel — yet even at that minute concentration it is considered dangerous.

### Salt Preservation Theory

What exactly is *Melach Sedomit*? The evocative name, with its association with the city of Sodom and the Dead Sea, tends to conjure images of some mysterious and powerful substance. But technically speaking, *Melach Sedomit* is simply sea salt — the term is connected to *melach mischart*, mineral salt — and the name reflects the association with the Dead Sea region. The Gemara's concern is real but mundane: this is the salt with which meat was heavily preserved, and when one handled salted meat, one's hands would become coated with it. Touching one's eyes with salt-covered hands could cause serious harm.

This understanding suggests a compelling explanation for Tosafot's ruling that *mayim acharonim* need not be observed today: it is not because *Melach Sedomit* has ceased to exist as a substance, but because the circumstances that led to hands being heavily coated with it have changed. One theory is that in the colder climates of northern Europe, meat may not have required the same heavy salt preservation as in warmer regions — in extreme winters, the cold itself could serve a preserving function. A second theory concerns the handling of food more generally: before the introduction of forks as personal eating utensils in Europe, food was handled directly with the hands, meaning that salt-preserved meat would regularly come into direct contact with fingers that might later touch the eyes. The widespread adoption of table napkins — documented as nearly universal throughout France by the twelfth century — may have been the more directly relevant factor: once napkins were in use, hands were wiped during the meal and were less likely to retain dangerous salt residue by the meal's end. This would explain why Tosafot, writing in France, no longer considered the requirement operative. The practice had fallen away, and Tosafot found the justification in the changed material circumstances. Whatever the precise reason, the simple meaning of the Gemara points to sea salt used in meat preservation as the source of the danger.

### Practical Concern

Abaye explains the prohibition against washing *mayim acharonim* directly on the ground as being due to *zuhama* — filth. Even after the salt is dissolved and washed away, the greasy, salt-laden water is disgusting and potentially harmful to others who might step in it.

### Spirit Concern

Rabba, however, corrects Abaye's practical explanation and offers a deeper rationale: *mishum de-sharya ruach ra alaihu* — it is because an evil spirit rests upon the water. It is this concern about the *ruach ra'a* inhabiting the wash water that drives the prohibition against releasing it onto the ground. This correction by Rabba initiates a remarkable extended passage in which Abaye recounts a series of practices he had originally understood through practical, rational lenses, each of which Rabba reframes in terms of spiritual dangers and other-worldly concerns.

---

## Practical Mysticism

### Removing Dishes

Abaye recounts: he used to explain the practice of not removing a dish from before a person while that person is holding a cup to drink as a practical concern — *shema ye-arei davar kalkala bi-seudah* — perhaps the person will try to object or speak while drinking and will choke. Rabba corrects him: *mishum de-kasha l'ruach tzerada* — it is because such an act opens one to the spirit *Tzerada*, apparently associated with epilepsy.

### Dish Removal Rules

The prohibition on removing dishes, however, is not absolute. The Gemara qualifies it carefully. It applies only if the dish is taken outside of *arba amos* — four cubits — from the person eating. Within that distance, there is no concern. Furthermore, the prohibition applies only if the dish is removed and not returned; if it is taken and brought back, there is no issue. Finally, it only matters if the item being removed is something that is needed for the *seudah*; items that are not part of the meal may be removed freely.

### Mar bar Rav Ashi

Mar bar Rav Ashi went further than most. He would not allow even the mortar and pestle used for grinding spices to be removed from the table during a meal, because of this same concern about the spirit. Even an empty mortar and pestle — something not itself food — was treated as part of the *seudah's* equipment and therefore protected under the same prohibition. His reasoning was presumably that such items are things one might wish to use during the meal to season the food, and their removal creates the same spiritual vulnerability.

### Crumbs & Poverty

Abaye continues his recitation. He used to explain the practice of sweeping crumbs after a meal as being motivated by cleanliness — *mishum nakiuta*. Rabba corrects him: it is because leaving crumbs on the floor exposes one to the spirit of poverty, *sar d'aniyuta*. Failing to sweep invites this spirit; sweeping it away removes the opening through which poverty might enter.

### Crumb Vigilance

The Gemara illustrates this with a story. A certain man was being pursued by the spirit of poverty — the spirit had been sent, so to speak, to bring destitution upon him — yet was unable to find a foothold *de-zahir a-nashvara tuva*, because this man was extraordinarily careful about crumbs. One day the man went on a picnic and ate bread on open ground. The spirit thought its opportunity had finally arrived: how could a person be careful about crumbs at a picnic, with no table to sweep and crumbs falling directly into grass? But after the man finished eating, he took a shovel, uprooted all the grass from the area where he had eaten so that the crumbs embedded in it would be removed, and threw it all into a river. He would not leave a single crumb. The spirit was heard lamenting: *vai d'afkinhu hai gavra m'beiteih* — woe, this man has driven me from my home, I cannot reach him.

### Foam Danger

Abaye further relates: he used to explain the practice of not drinking the foam from a cup as being due to *miusa* — it is simply disgusting. Rabba clarifies: *mishum de-kasha l'kartzem* — drinking foam causes *kartzem*, a runny nose. An additional nuance: if one blows the foam off the cup, that is bad for the head and causes headaches. If one pushes it away with one's hand, that exposes one to poverty. The connection between careless treatment of food and vulnerability to the spirit of poverty is a recurring motif in this passage.

### Foam Remedies

If one has drunk foam and thereby contracted *kartzem* — the runny nose condition — there are remedies, though they depend on what was drunk. If the foam was from wine, one should drink beer. If the condition arose from the foam of beer, one should drink water. If it arose from the foam of water — there is no remedy.

### Poverty Follows

This brings the Gemara to a proverb: *batar anya azla anyuta* — poverty follows the poor. Water, being the humblest and least prestigious of drinks, is the most problematic: it is associated with destitution, and its foam-caused condition cannot be cured. The pattern of the poorest having no remedy mirrors the social reality that the poor have the fewest resources to address their misfortunes.

### Vegetable Bundle

Abaye continues: he used to say that the reason one should not eat a vegetable pulled directly from the bundle — before unwrapping it, rinsing it, and preparing it properly — is *mishum de-michzei ke-ravtanuta*, because it looks like ravenous hunger, like one cannot wait to eat and is grabbing food in an undignified manner. Rabba offers the corrective: *mishum de-kashi la-kshafim* — it exposes one to witchcraft. This type of undignified behavior with food renders one vulnerable to those who would use *kshafim* against a person.

This ruling is dramatized in a story involving Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna, who were traveling by boat. A certain matron — apparently a non-Jewish woman of some authority — asked to board with them. They refused. She spoke an incantation and caused the boat to stop. They responded with their own words and released it. She then told them that no witchcraft could touch them because they did not expose themselves to it through the behaviors that create vulnerability. Among the practices she cited was the very one under discussion: *ve-lo achlitu yarka mikisha de-asri ginai* — they did not eat vegetables directly from the bundle that the gardener had tied together.

### Fallen Vegetable

Abaye adds: he used to say that the reason one should not eat a vegetable that has fallen from the plate onto the tray is *mishum meisuta* — it is simply disgusting. His mother's teaching offered a different reason: *mishum de-kashi le-rei'ach ha-pah* — because somehow eating such a fallen vegetable causes bad breath.

### Drain Pipe Danger

Finally, Abaye recounts: he used to say that the reason one should not sit beneath a drain pipe or rain gutter is the practical concern about water *mishum shofchin* — the water may spill on one from above. His mother's teaching provides the deeper explanation: *mishum de-shichichi mazikin* — because *mazikin*, dangerous spirits, are known to frequent that location.

---

## Barrel & Spirit

### Barrel Explodes

The Gemara relates a story that illustrates this final teaching about the drain pipe. A group of schleppers — porters carrying a barrel of wine — stopped to rest and set the barrel down underneath a drain pipe. The barrel exploded. The porters came before Mar bar Rav Ashi seeking remedy.

### Cherem Applied

Mar bar Rav Ashi took out a *shofar* and placed the spirit that had destroyed the barrel under *cherem* — rabbinic excommunication. Remarkably, the authority of such a sanction is presented as effective even against a spirit of this kind.

### Spirit's Defense

The spirit appeared before Mar bar Rav Ashi and requested a formal *din Torah* — a legal proceeding. It argued on its own behalf: *heichi aeivid, de-otveih be'odnai* — what was I supposed to do? They placed the barrel right against my ear. I was sleeping there. They disturbed me by placing their cargo on top of me while I was in my resting place. Why should I bear responsibility?

### Ruling & Payment

Mar bar Rav Ashi rejected the spirit's defense: *at be-duchta de-shichichi rabim mai bayit* — you should not have been in a place frequented by the public. Sleeping in a public thoroughfare, where people regularly pass and rest their loads, was the spirit's own error. *Ihu de-shannit* — it was you who behaved irregularly by resting in a public space. Therefore: *zil shalleim* — go and pay these porters for the barrel you destroyed. The spirit asked for time to gather the funds — it would need to do so by appropriating goods from others, which raises its own questions — and Mar bar Rav Ashi granted a deadline.

### Spirit Limitations

When the deadline arrived, the spirit came late. Mar bar Rav Ashi asked why it had not appeared on time. The spirit explained: *kol milli de-tzayar ve-chayil ve-chatim u-mani, leit lan reshuta le-mishkal mineih* — anything that is bound, knotted, measured, or counted, we have no permission to take from it. I can only appropriate items that are left unguarded, uncounted, and essentially treated as ownerless or neglected. Finding such items took more time than anticipated. I had to search until I found *midi de-hefkeira* — something treated as ownerless or sufficiently unprotected.

### Mistreatment Theme

The concluding theme that emerges from this entire passage is coherent: the spirits and dangers described throughout — poverty, epilepsy, witchcraft, the *mazikin* under the drain pipe — all find their foothold through a common mechanism. It is the careless, disrespectful, or undignified treatment of food, objects, and one's surroundings that creates openings for these forces. Crumbs left on the floor, foam carelessly drunk, vegetables grabbed from the bundle, dishes removed without care, property left unguarded and unmeasured — all of these represent a failure of attentiveness and respect toward the material world. Conversely, those who count their goods, protect their belongings, and treat even minor items with proper care are described as inaccessible to these harmful forces. The spirit itself confirms this principle in its own words: it cannot touch what is properly bounded, measured, and guarded.

# Hullin 106

## Mayim Stories

### Abaye's Assumption

The *gemara* opens with a statement of Abaye: *meireisha hava amina*, I used to assume that a certain widespread practice was motivated by purely practical concerns. The practice in question is *hai dishadi maya mipuma dechatzba* — the custom of pouring off the top layer of water from a barrel or jar before drinking. Abaye had assumed this was done *mishum tzip tza*, because of small impurities — splinters of wood and the like — that would float to the surface and needed to be removed. Rava, however, corrected him: no, it is done *mishum zika demaya hara'im*, because of "bad water" — evil spirits were believed to drink from the top layer, leaving a harmful spiritual residue there, which is why one pours it off before use. This is a striking juxtaposition: the same observable act carries either a prosaic hygienic explanation or a spiritual one, and Rava insists the latter is the real reason.

### Bar Shida Story

A brief but vivid narrative follows. There was a certain *bar shida* — a minor shade or spirit — who was employed in Rav Pappa's household, apparently due to a shortage of human workers. Rav Pappa sent him to fetch water from the river, *azal le'atuyei maya minhara*, and the spirit took an unusually long time. When he returned, the members of the household asked him why he had delayed. He replied: *ad dechalfei maya hara'im* — I had to wait for the bad water to pass, so that I could bring you clean water.

Upon his return, however, he observed the household members doing *dekishadu maya mipuma dechatzba* — pouring off the top layer from the pitchers themselves. He then said: had I known that this was your regular practice, I would not have delayed. I would have brought the water immediately, knowing you would handle the purification yourselves at home. *Tosafot* notes the natural question of why the spirit had not simply told them about this practice: the answer given is that he did not want to alert other spirits and provoke their hostility.

### Rav Dimi Account

The *gemara* now transitions away from the world of *shedim* and toward a series of cautionary reports about the practical consequences of neglecting *mayim rishonim* and *mayim acharonim*. When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported two cases: *mayim rishonim he'echilu basar chazir* — failure to wash before the meal caused someone to be fed pork; and *mayim acharonim hotziu et ha'ishah miba'alah* — failure to wash after the meal caused a woman to be needlessly divorced.

### Ravin's Account

When Ravin arrived from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported versions of both cases that were worse: *rishonim he'echilu basar neveilah* — the first case involved *neveilah* rather than *chazir*; and *acharonim hergu et hanefesh* — the second case resulted not in divorce but in death.

The *gemara* provides a mnemonic for keeping the versions straight: Rav Dimi came first, so in his version the woman was divorced — she could still be divorced at that point. Ravin came later, so in his version she was killed — one cannot divorce a woman who is already dead. Rabbi Abba, for his part, combined the worst elements of both accounts: *chazir* in the first case and death in the second.

The question naturally arises: why is *chazir* worse than *neveilah*? Both carry a *lav*. *Rashi* notes that *chazir* involves two prohibitions, though he does not specify which two. One possibility is that unkosher meat, including *chazir*, would typically also carry the prohibition of *dam*, since there would be no reason to salt non-*shechted* meat — though one could construct a scenario involving *neveilah* from an animal that had been salted before the *shechita* was discovered to be invalid, in which case *dam* would not apply to the *neveilah*. Beyond the technical analysis, however, it is simply true historically that *chazir* has always carried an outsized visceral weight relative to other prohibitions: archaeologists excavating ancient sites in *Eretz Yisrael* can identify a Jewish settlement by the absence of pig bones alone, even when no other marker of Jewish identity survives.

### Stories Analysis

The question of what exactly happened in each case requires some reconstruction. *Rashi* fills in the narrative: someone arrived at an inn and ordered meat but did not wash *mayim rishonim* before eating. The innkeeper — a Jewish innkeeper who served both kosher and non-kosher food to Jewish and non-Jewish customers respectively — concluded from the absence of *mayim rishonim* that the guest was not Jewish and therefore served him *treif* meat. This is the mechanism behind the first case.

The *mayim acharonim* story is traced to a fuller narrative found in *Yoma*, involving Rabbi Meir and the innkeeper named *Kidor*. Rabbi Meir, who was attentive to the meaning of names, did not trust this man — deriving from the verse *ki dor tahapuchot heima* that the name *Kidor* bespoke an untrustworthy character — and so did not entrust his wallet to him. The other Sages were less cautious. When Kidor denied having taken their wallets, they noticed lentils caught in his beard, indicating what he had eaten for breakfast. They went to his wife, gave the detail of the lentils as a *siman*, and retrieved the wallets. When the husband learned of this, he either divorced or killed his wife. The connection to *mayim acharonim* is that had he washed properly after the meal — which in the time of the *gemara* constituted a thorough washing that would have included cleaning the beard — there would have been no lentils caught there, and the *siman* would not have worked.

This observation has an important implication: *mayim acharonim* in the *gemara*'s era was not the highly ritualized, minimal act familiar today — a small silver vessel, a few drops of water, performed almost as a formality. It was a genuine washing-up after the meal, and apparently included the face and beard. The reason, as the *gemara* has made clear, is *melach Sedomit* — the concern about Sodomite salt, which could blind if left on the fingers and brought to the eyes. That concern no longer obtains in the same practical sense today, which explains why the ritual has contracted into something more ceremonial.

Both stories together speak to something beyond their immediate subject: they raise questions of *identity*. In the first case, the person was identified — or misidentified — as non-Jewish precisely because he did not wash *mayim rishonim*. In the second, the entire catastrophe hinged on a question of identity and whether one could be trusted. It is striking that the absence of *mayim rishonim* was sufficient to mark someone as non-Jewish — this implies that there was *no* other visible marker of Jewish identity that would have given the innkeeper a different impression. The person was not wearing a distinctive Jewish garment; he carried no other immediately visible sign. From this, several late *rishonim* and early *acharonim* derived that there was no binding requirement for Jews to dress in a manner that distinguished them from their non-Jewish surroundings — since if there had been, the question of *mayim rishonim* would have been superfluous as an identifier.

The *psukim* the *gemara* elsewhere associates with these practices — *vehiskadishtem viheyitem kedoshim*, "you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy" — assign *vehiskadishtem* to *mayim rishonim* and *viheyitem kedoshim* to *mayim acharonim*. This framing suggests that beyond whatever specific physical reasons motivated these practices, there is also a dimension of identity and sanctity: the way one conducts oneself at the table is a statement about who one is and what kind of life one aspires to.

---

## Halachic Basis

### Heated Water Debate

The *gemara* now turns to the technical question of which types of water may be used for *mayim rishonim*. The case under discussion is *chamei ha'ur* — water that has been heated by fire. Chizkiyah says: *eino notlin leyadayim* — one may not use it for *netilat yadayim*. Rabbi Yochanan says: *notlin leyadayim* — one may use it.

Rabbi Yochanan then relates: *sha'alti et Rabban Gamliel bno shel Rabbi* — I asked Rabban Gamliel, the son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who was known as someone who ate his *chullin betahara*, and he told me that *kol gedolei Galil osim ken* — all the great personages of the Galilee do this; they use heated water for *mayim rishonim*.

The significance of the reference to *ochlei taharos* — those who ate their non-sanctified food with purity — will be unpacked shortly. But it is worth pausing here to ask why the *gemara* does not specify the reason hot water is problematic. *Rashi* gestures toward an explanation rooted in the distinction between water in its natural state and water that has been altered. The previous *gemara* had already established that one cannot use water that is *yad soledet bo* — hot enough to scald — for *mayim rishonim*, with two opinions as to whether the prohibition applies to any hot water or only water at that threshold of heat. The present *gemara* seems to address a question about *how* the water was heated rather than *how hot* it is, though the exact contours remain somewhat unclear.

### Hot Springs Issue

The *gemara* then turns to *chamei Tveriah* — the natural hot springs of Tiberias, water that is hot not because of fire but by virtue of the geological heat of the earth. Here the analysis becomes more nuanced.

Chizkiyah maintains: *eino notlin leyadayim* — one cannot use this water for *netilat yadayim*. Yet he concedes that *matbilin bahen et yadayim* — one may immerse one's hands in it and fulfill *tevilat yadayim*. This distinction is significant. *Tevilat yadayim* is the alternative to *netilat yadayim* available when one finds oneself without a convenient place to pour water — near a river, a pond, or some other body of water — where one may dip one's hands in lieu of pouring. It requires that the water be in its natural location, analogous to a *mikvah*, and contain at least *arbaim se'ah*. Since the hot springs of Tiberias are in their natural state — the heat is intrinsic to them, not an external alteration — they function as a valid *mikvah* for this purpose.

Rabbi Yochanan takes a different and at first seemingly contradictory position: *kol gufo tovel bahen* — you may immerse your whole body in them — *aval lo panav yadav veraglav* — but you may not do just the hands. *Tosafot* notes that the mention of face and feet alongside hands is *lav davka*; in practice, when the *gemara* discusses partial body washing, it conventionally lists hands, face, and feet as the standard units of washing for cleanliness, but the ritual concern here is specifically about the hands. So Rabbi Yochanan is saying: the springs are a valid *mikvah* for full immersion, but *tevilat yadayim* specifically — immersing only the hands — is not permitted.

The *gemara* immediately raises the obvious objection: *hashtah kol gufo tovel bahen panav yadav veraglav lo kol sheken* — if one can use these waters for full-body immersion, how much more so should one be able to dip just the hands? Rav Pappa resolves this by reframing the entire dispute. When the water is *bimkoman* — in its original location, still flowing from the spring — *dechulei alma lo pligi desharei*: all opinions agree it is permitted for *tevilat yadayim*. When water has been removed with a vessel — *mishku mineihu bimana* — all agree it is forbidden. What, then, is the dispute? *Depaskinehu be'vatz biertza* — a small channel or eddy that has been cut off from the main flow, a little sidepool fed by the springs but no longer fully part of the main body of water. One opinion holds that we apply a safeguard — *gazrinan vatz biertza atu mana* — and treat this sidepool as if it were water removed in a vessel, lest people confuse the two situations. The other holds that no such safeguard is imposed — *lo gazrinan*.

*Rashi* makes an interesting observation about the logic of Rabbi Yochanan's position as it relates to heated water: Rabbi Yochanan, who was lenient about water heated by fire for *netilat yadayim*, is apparently strict about naturally hot water used in a vessel for *tevilat yadayim*. *Rashi* suggests this is because water heated by fire began its existence as normal water and its prior identity as ordinary water continues to obtain. Water that has been hot from its very origin — like the springs of Tiberias — is in a different category: it has never had *sha'at hachosher*, a moment of being ordinary water, and so lacks that prior identity.

### Purpose Serach Terumah

The *gemara* then provides the key statement about the purpose of *mayim rishonim* for *chulin*: *netilat yadayim l'chulin mishum serach terumah* — we wash our hands before non-sanctified bread because of a *serach*, a vestige or semblance, of the concern for *terumah*. The background: eating *terumah* required *kohanim* to have ritually pure hands. Unlike full-body *tumah*, which required full immersion in a *mikvah*, the rabbinically decreed *tumah* that applies specifically to hands could be remedied by *netilat yadayim* alone. Over time, those who ate their *chulin betahara* — who maintained purity standards even for non-sanctified food — adopted the same practice. The ritual washing before bread that we observe today is a carry-through from that world.

### Mitzvah to Listen

The *gemara* adds: *ve'od mishum mitzvah* — and also because it is a *mitzvah*. The immediate question is: what *mitzvah*? Abaye answers: *mitzvah lishmo'a divrei chachamim* — it is a *mitzvah* to heed the words of the Sages.

### Cleanliness Holiness

*Tosafot* probes this further: if the whole institution goes back to the concern of *terumah*, what does the *ve'od* add? *Tosafot* proposes that the additional dimension is *mishum nekiyut* — cleanliness. The rabbis also simply wanted people to have clean hands before sitting down to eat. This is a striking observation. *Mayim acharonim*, as noted, has an explicit cleanliness rationale in the concern about *melach Sedomit*. If *Tosafot* is correct, *mayim rishonim* shares this dimension as well.

This connects to the *pasuk* the *gemara* elsewhere cites for both practices: *vehiskadishtem viheyitem kedoshim* — sanctify yourselves and be holy. According to that *gemara*, *vehiskadishtem* refers to *mayim rishonim* and *viheyitem kedoshim* to *mayim acharonim*. There is a sense in which both practices are about maintaining a kind of holiness at the table — treating oneself with the dignity appropriate to someone who eats in the awareness that food comes from God and that the act of eating carries religious weight.

This connects to a broader theme: the table as *mizbeiach*, the act of eating as sustained within a framework of purity and sanctity. It is no accident that the same *gemara* that discusses *netilat yadayim* invokes the concept that deriving benefit from this world without a *bracha* is like *me'ilah* — misappropriating property of *hekdesh*. The deliberate choice of the *Beis HaMikdash* term *me'ilah* rather than simply *gezel* from God is telling: the framework is one in which eating takes place within the conceptual world of sanctified property, and *netilat yadayim* is one of the practices that anchors the ordinary meal within that world. The *ochlei chullin betahara* were those who took this aspiration most seriously and lived it most completely; the retention of *netilat yadayim* in the absence of the *Beis HaMikdash* is a way of sustaining at least a trace of that orientation — accessible to everyone, not requiring the full rigor of *chulin betahara* — and affirming that something of the world of *tumah vetahara* persists even now.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Derivation

### Zav Verse

Rava adds his own formulation: *mitzvah lishmo'a divrei Rabbi Eliezer ben Arach* — it is a *mitzvah* specifically to heed the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Arach. What teaching? The verse states: *v'chol asher yiga bo hazav, v'yadav lo shataf bamayim* — and whatever the *zav* touches, and his hands have not been washed with water, becomes *tamei*. At first glance, this is puzzling: a *zav* is *tamei* in his entirety and must immerse his whole body in a *mikvah* to become *tahor*. Why does the verse single out his hands and the rinsing of water, as if rinsing alone would suffice? The answer normally given is that this is a synecdoche — the verse mentions hands as a part representing the whole, meaning he has not immersed.

### Literal Reading

Rabbi Eliezer ben Arach, however, takes the verse more literally and derives from it: *mikan samchu chachamim l'netilat yadayim min hatorah* — here is the Scriptural basis, the *asmachta*, for the rabbinic institution of washing hands.

### Rava Challenge

Rava presses Rav Nachman on the precise reading: *mai mashma* — how do you derive it? *D'ksiv yadav lo shataf bamayim* — the verse writes that his hands were not washed with water. Implication: *hashataf*, once you rinse them, *tahor* — he becomes *tahor*. But that cannot be correct — *ha'tvilah bei*, a *zav* is required to immerse his whole body. Rinsing the hands alone would not make him *tahor*.

### Unwashed Hands Tumah

The resolution is a different reading of the verse. *Ela hachi kamar* — this is what the verse actually means: *v'chol asher yiga bo hazav* does not refer to the *zav* himself but to a person whom the *zav* has touched. Such a person becomes *tamei* at one degree of remove — a *rishon l'tumah*. And *v'yadav lo shataf bamayim* — a different person, one whose hands have simply not been washed — is also *tamei* and conveys *tumah* to *terumah*. Both such individuals — the person touched by a *zav* and the ordinary person with unwashed hands — produce the same result when they contact food. From here, the rabbis derived that unwashed hands transmit *tumah*, lending Scriptural support to the institution of *netilat yadayim*. The support is an *asmachta*, a reading into the verse, but it is the *peg* on which the institution is hung.

---

## Bread vs Fruit

### No Fruit Requirement

Rabbi Eleazar citing Rabbi Yehoshua teaches: *lo amru netilat yadayim l'peirot* — they did not require *netilat yadayim* before fruit. *Ela mishum nekiyut* — the only reason to wash one's hands before eating fruit is if one wishes to be clean; there is no rabbinic ritual obligation. The reason is structural: *terumah* was drawn primarily from grain, and the purity obligation pertained principally to bread. The *serach terumah* rationale does not extend to fruit.

The students initially understood Rabbi Yehoshua to mean that while there is no *chovah* — no strict obligation — there remains a *mitzvah*, a religious value, in washing before fruit. Rava corrects this: *lo chovah v'lo mitzvah ela reshut* — there is neither obligation nor *mitzvah*; it is entirely optional. If one wishes to be clean, one may wash, but there is no religious dimension to the act.

### Rava Arrogance

Rav Nachman goes further still. *Hanoteil yadav l'peirot einu ela migasei haruach* — one who washes before eating fruit is displaying arrogance: "I am so refined that I must wash even before fruit." Washing before fruit is not merely neutral — it signals a kind of haughtiness that is inappropriate. The progression is notable: from a possible *mitzvah* on the grounds of cleanliness, to a merely optional act, to something verging on spiritual vanity.

---

## Bread vs Fruit (II)

### Rabba Bar Chana Story

Rabba bar bar Chana reports: I was in the presence of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi. They had a basket of fruit brought before them, *achlu v'lo mishu yadayhu* — they ate without washing their hands. Furthermore, *lo yahavu li midi* — they did not offer him any fruit. And *varich chad chad l'chudei* — each of them recited *birkat acharona* separately rather than together.

The *gemara* derives three conclusions: first, *ein ta'un netilat yadayim l'peirot* — one does not require *netilat yadayim* before fruit. Second, *ein mezamnin al hapeirot* — one does not do *zimun* after eating fruit, since if *zimun* applied, they would have offered him some so as to have a quorum of three. Third, *shnayim she'achlu mitzvah l'chaleik* — when two people eat, it is preferable for each to bench separately rather than together. The last inference is derived from the fact that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, even as two people, chose not to bench jointly. *Tosafot* raises a difficulty with this inference: the rule about two people benching separately is a rule about bread, where *zimun* applies at three; but fruit does not generate a *zimun* obligation even for three, so of course two would not bench together on fruit. The *gemara* is making a jump from fruit to bread, and *Tosafot* goes through considerable difficulty trying to justify it. The question is in many ways more compelling than the answer.

A supporting *baraita* confirms: *shnayim she'achlu mitzvah l'chaleik* — when two people eat, the proper practice is to bench separately. *Bamei devarim amurim* — when does this apply? When both are *sofrim* — when both are literate and capable of benching for themselves. But if one is literate and the other is *bur* — unlettered and unable to bench independently — then the one who knows benches aloud and the other fulfills his obligation thereby: *sofer mevarech v'bur yotzei*. The *zimun* obligation creates a communal structure; absent that structure, individuality in expression is preferred, unless dependence makes joint recitation necessary.

---

## How Much to Wash

### Baraita Levels

A *baraita* lays out a tiered structure: *netilat yadayim lechulin* requires washing *ad haperek* — up to one joint; for *terumah*, up to a higher joint; and *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim bamikdash* — the washing of hands and feet by the *kohanim* in the *Beis HaMikdash* — extends to yet a higher joint still. *Rashi* specifies: for *chulin*, up to the middle knuckle; for *terumah*, up to the joint where the fingers meet the palm; for the *Mikdash*, up to the wrist.

### Rav Opinion

Rav rules: *ad kan l'chulin, ad kan l'trumah* — here for *chulin*, here for *terumah* — consistent with *Rashi*'s reading of distinct requirements for each.

### Shmuel Stringency

Shmuel rules: *ad kan bein l'chulin bein l'trumah l'chumra* — the same level for both *chulin* and *terumah*, but on the strict side. According to *Rashi*, this means the joint where the fingers meet the palm for both.

### Rav Sheshes Leniency

Rav Sheshes rules: *ad kan bein l'chulin bein l'trumah l'kula* — the same level for both, but on the lenient side, meaning the middle knuckle applies even for *terumah*.

### Wrist Practice

Bar Hadaya reports that he observed Rav Ami rule strictly — the same joint for both *chulin* and *terumah*. The *gemara* cautions against attributing this stringency solely to the fact that Rav Ami was a *kohen* who might have felt personally bound to the higher standard. The proof: Rav Meisha bar bei d'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was a *Levi*, not a *kohen*, and he too ruled strictly.

The practical *halacha* that emerges: *Rashi*'s reading, combined with the dominant stringent opinions, would require washing up to the joint where the fingers meet the palm. *Tosafot*, however, reads the *gemara* as requiring washing until the wrist. The *Shulchan Aruch* brings both opinions and recommends doing the full wrist. One may rely on the more lenient position if necessary, but *lechatchila* the accepted practice is to wash the entire hand up to and including the wrist.

---

## All Day Coverage

### Piksa Valley

Rav says: *notel adam shtei yadav shachrit u'matneh aleihem kol hayom kulo* — a person may wash their hands at *shachrit*, in the morning, and rely on that washing for the entire day, provided they maintain attention to their hands and do not allow them to become dirty or *tamei* in the interim. In principle, a single morning washing can cover all subsequent meals throughout the day.

Rav Avina applied this rule concretely: he instructed the people of the valley of Piksa that since they had limited access to water — no plumbing, no nearby wells — *m'shu yadaychu mi'tzafra v'atnu aleihu l'chulei yoma* — wash your hands in the morning and rely on that washing for the whole day.

### Distress Requirement

A dispute arises over the scope of Rav Avina's ruling. Some say he only permitted this because of the particular circumstances — *b'sha'at hadechak*, a time of pressing need — but without such need the all-day extension would not be permitted. This reading would place Rav Avina's ruling in tension with Rav's more general statement.

### Morning Washing

Others say Rav Avina's ruling was not conditioned on *sha'at hadechak* at all — it is permitted under any circumstances — and this is consistent with Rav. The practical *halacha* is that one may rely on morning washing for the entire day, provided one maintains care with one's hands. The key mechanism is *hesech hada'at* — once one ceases to pay attention to one's hands, the principle of *yadayim askaniyot hen* reasserts itself: hands are "busy" and always potentially touching something, and as soon as they fall out of one's attentive awareness, a new *netilah* is required. Conversely, if one maintains mindful attention throughout the day, the morning washing remains in effect.

---

## Koach Gavra

### Irrigation Channel

Rav Pappa introduces one of the defining structural requirements for *netilat yadayim*: *koach gavra* — human agency. The case is *arisa d'dilu'ei* — an irrigation channel. Water is drawn from a river by a person operating a bucket, poured into a channel, and flows down that channel for some distance. If one places one's hands into that flowing water at a point far enough downstream, *d'lo atu mikoach gavra* — the water is no longer reaching one's hands through direct human force — it does not qualify for *netilat yadayim*. The water is moving of its own momentum, not by virtue of the human act of pouring.

### Bucket Proximity

However, *v'i mikrav legabei dula* — if one places one's hands right at the point where the bucket empties — *d'ka'atu mikoach gavra* — where the water is directly flowing from the act of human pouring — *notlin mimenu l'yadayim*: this does qualify for *netilat yadayim*. At that proximate point, the human force is still operative and the requirement of *koach gavra* is satisfied.

Two distinct requirements govern *netilat yadayim*: *koach gavra* — that the water arrives at the hands through direct human agency — and the use of a *kli* — a vessel. These are separate and both must be met. If one opens a faucet and places one's hands directly underneath the initial flow, there is a basis to argue that the opening of the faucet constitutes *koach gavra*; the energy of the water pressure released by the initial act of turning the tap might be attributed to the human agent. However, leaving the faucet running continuously removes this connection — the ongoing flow is no longer attributable to the original human act. The question of the *kli* requirement in that context remains a separate discussion.

### Bucket Hole

A final case: *u'vazya dula b'choness mashkeh* — if the bucket has a hole large enough for water to enter (*kones mashkeh* is the halachic measure for an aperture through which liquid can pass into a vessel). In this scenario, the bucket is drawn from the river and poured into the channel immediately adjacent, but there is a hole in the bucket through which water streams back into the river, creating a continuous connection between the river and the contents of the bucket and channel. *Milef layef u'matev beita yadeya* — through that connection, the water in the channel retains its link to the river, and one may perform *tevilat yadayim* by dipping one's hands in it, because it is treated as still connected to the natural body of water — functionally equivalent to dipping one's hands in the river itself.

The overarching principle anchoring this entire discussion is thus: for water to function in *netilat yadayim* — as opposed to *tevilat yadayim* in a connected natural body — it must arrive at the hands through direct human force. Without *koach gavra*, the *netilah* is invalid.

---

---

# Hullin 107

## Vessel & Revi'is

### Rava's Vessel Rule

The sugya opens with a ruling of Rava: *kli she'ein bo revi'is ein notlin mimenu l'yadayim* — a vessel that does not contain a *revi'is* of water (approximately three and a half ounces) may not be used for *netilas yadayim*. The Gemara immediately notes a second, slightly different formulation of Rava's statement: *kli she'eino machzik revi'is ein notlin mimenu l'yadayim* — a vessel that cannot *hold* a *revi'is* may not be used. The distinction between these two versions is significant. The first formulation demands that the vessel actually contain a *revi'is* of liquid; the second demands only that the vessel be capable of holding that volume, even if the liquid present is less than a *revi'is*. According to the second version, the decisive criterion is the capacity of the vessel, not the quantity of water inside it at the moment of use.

This introduces two distinct requirements: the requirement of a *kli* — a proper vessel — and the minimum measure of a *revi'is*. The connection between them is not incidental. Some *Rishonim* note that the very word *netila* in the blessing *al netilas yadayim* reflects the Aramaic *natla*, meaning a vessel, so that the *kli* is in fact central to the entire institution. A vessel smaller than *revi'is* capacity would not be considered a meaningful vessel at all, and thus the size requirement is itself the basis for the *kli* requirement.

### Revi'is & Remnant

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the two formulations by distinguishing between one person washing and two people washing: *lo kashya — ha l'chad, ha l'trei*. The vessel must begin with a full *revi'is* of liquid, but once it has been used for *netilas yadayim* by one person, a second person may wash from whatever remains, even if it is less than a *revi'is*. A *Baraisa* is cited in support: *mei revi'is notlin l'yadayim l'echad v'afilu l'shnayim* — a *revi'is* of water suffices for *netilas yadayim* for one person and even for two. The fact that two people can share three and a half ounces is striking in itself, and points toward a conception of *netilas yadayim* that may require only minimal coverage — perhaps the fingertips or a single pouring.

The Gemara then qualifies this further: *v'lo hi — shani hasam mishum d'ka'asi mishirei tahara*. The case where the second person may use less than a *revi'is* is not a general dispensation from the quantity requirement; it is a special case because the remaining water derives from *shirei tahara* — the remnant of water that was already used for *taharah* purposes, having originally met the *revi'is* standard. That prior association with *taharah* lends the remnant its efficacy.

### Rav Sheshes' Questions

Rav Sheshes then posed a series of questions to Ameimar, pressing on each of the criteria that had been established. His first question: *kapdisu amana* — do you actually care about the vessel itself? Rashi explains this as asking whether the vessel must be whole, or whether a broken vessel would suffice. The answer was *in* — yes, the vessel matters. His second question: *achazusa* — do you care about the appearance of the water? Recall that certain types of water — extremely hot water, or water that does not look like water — may be disqualified; Ameimar confirmed that the appearance of the water is indeed a requirement. His third question: *ashi'ura* — do you care about the minimum quantity, the *revi'is*? Again, the answer was yes.

A second version of this exchange is also cited. According to that version, Ameimar's response was more selective: *amana v'achazusa kapdinan — ashi'ura lo kapdinan* — I care about the vessel and the appearance of the water, but I do not require a strict *shiur* of liquid quantity. This alternative reading is consistent with the earlier conclusion that the second person may wash from less than a *revi'is*, and the Gemara brings the same *Baraisa* — *mei revi'is notlin l'yadayim l'echad v'afilu l'shnayim* — as support for the view that no fixed quantity is required, as long as the water originated from a *revi'is* used for *netilas yadayim*.

### Standard Measures

The Gemara records that Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pakod established a standard glass vessel — a *natla bas revi'isa* — that held exactly a *revi'is*, which people could use as a reference to determine whether their own vessels were large enough for *netilas yadayim*. This was a form of communal standards: a bureau of measures by which people could calibrate the capacity of their vessels. Similarly, Rav Ashi in Hutzal established a *kuza bas revi'isa* — a pottery vessel holding a *revi'is* — for the same purpose. The practical message was reinforced by the physical standard: the vessel had to hold a *revi'is*, and people should know what that looks like.

### Acceptable Vessels

Rava further teaches that one need not use an elaborate or purpose-made vessel. *Magufas chavit she-tiknah notlin mimena l'yadayim* — if one takes the stopper of a barrel, carves out an indentation capable of holding liquid, and it meets the *revi'is* capacity, one may wash *netilas yadayim* from it. Similarly, a *cheimasa* or *kifiza* — types of flask or water skin — if properly adjusted, may be used for *netilas yadayim*. The point is that a wide range of objects can qualify as a *kli* for this purpose, as long as they meet the functional criteria.

### Disqualified Items

On the other side of the line stand objects that, despite being capable of containing liquid, are not classified as proper vessels for *netilas yadayim*: *sak v'kuppa — af al pi d'mekablin, ein notlin mehem l'yadayim*. A sack used for storing grain and a box, though they may physically hold liquid, cannot be used for *netilas yadayim*. Their primary function is not as liquid vessels; they are not defined as *kelim* in the relevant sense. This raises a genuine line-drawing question: what exactly distinguishes a vessel that qualifies from one that does not? The answer is not purely functional — it is definitional. The object must be recognized as a type of vessel associated with liquid, not merely something that happens to hold water in a given circumstance.

---

## Wrapping & Washing

### Wrapping Question

The Gemara now takes up a different question: *mahu le'echol b'mappa* — what is the law if one eats bread wrapped in a napkin, or with one's hands wrapped in cloth? The underlying premise of *netilas yadayim* is connected to the world of *tumah v'taharah*: hands were declared *sheniyos l'tumah* and thus capable of rendering food *tamei* upon contact. The Rabbis, however, attached the requirement specifically to the act of eating rather than to touching alone — one can handle bread without washing, but once one sits down to eat, washing is required.

The Gemara's question here is the inverse: if touching is the concern, what happens when eating occurs without touching? If bread is wrapped and one's hands never come into contact with it, is *netilas yadayim* still required? The question is framed practically — *mi chashinan dilma naga bei* — are we concerned that one will inadvertently touch the bread even if it is wrapped? Or is *netilas yadayim* a formal requirement that attaches to the act of eating regardless of any concern about contact?

### Rabbi Tzaddok Case

A *Baraisa* is brought from the tractate of Sukkah: when they gave food to Rabbi Tzaddok, he ate less than a *kabeitzah*, took it in a *mappa* — a cloth — ate it outside the *sukkah*, and did not recite *Birkat Hamazon* afterward. The case illustrates that eating less than a *kabeitzah* does not obligate one to eat in the *sukkah* and does not require *Birkat Hamazon*, because the sense of *seudat keva* requires at least a *kabeitzah* — the full satisfaction of *v'achalta v'savata*. Rabbi Tzaddok also did not wash his hands, apparently on account of the fact that the bread was wrapped.

### Size vs Wrapping

The Gemara asks: *mai lav* — does this not suggest that the *kabeitzah* measure is what triggers the requirement of *netilas yadayim*? On this reading, it would only be the smaller quantity that exempted him, not the wrapping. The Gemara counters: *dilma* — perhaps not; perhaps the *kabeitzah* measure addresses only the *sukkah* and *Birkat Hamazon* obligations, and it was specifically the fact that the bread was wrapped that exempted him from *netilas yadayim*. The case remains inconclusive, but it leaves open both possibilities: that the wrapping itself is sufficient to exempt, or that the relevant factor was the quantity of bread.

---

## Shiur of Bread

### Kabeitzah Measure

The discussion of Rabbi Tzaddok's case raises the broader question of what minimum amount of bread triggers the requirement of *netilas yadayim*. One reading of the case suggests that a *kabeitzah* is the threshold — below that, no *netilas yadayim* is required — which would parallel the *kabeitzah* as the threshold for *Birkat Hamazon* and for eating in the *sukkah*, rooted in the concept of genuine *seudah* and *seviyah*. If *netilas yadayim* is tied to the eating of bread as a meal, it would make sense that only a *kabeitzah* — a quantity that rises to the level of meaningful eating — would trigger the obligation.

### Kezayit Ruling

The *halacha* as ruled by most authorities, however, is that *netilas yadayim* is required already from a *kezayit*. This is consistent with the ruling regarding *Birkat Hamazon*, where a *kezayit* is sufficient to require *benching*, at least *mi-d'rabbanan*, even though the biblical obligation of *Birkat Hamazon* may require the fuller satisfaction of a *kabeitzah*. The parallel logic applies to *netilas yadayim*: most authorities require it from a *kezayit* onward.

### Practical Halacha

Nonetheless, there remains a dispute regarding the status of bread between a *kezayit* and a *kabeitzah*. There is an opinion that holds the *kabeitzah* to be the proper *shiur* for *netilas yadayim*, either because that is the genuine *shiur* of a *seudah* or because the minimum quantity that can become *tamei* at a biblical level is a *kabeitzah*. The practical ruling, as recorded in the *Mishnah Berurah*, is that for less than a *kabeitzah* one should perform *netilas yadayim* without a *bracha*, though many authorities hold that once there is a *kezayit* or more, the *bracha* is recited.

---

## Wrapping & Washing (II)

### Rav & Shmuel Case

The Gemara returns to the question of wrapping. Shmuel found Rav eating with his bread wrapped in a cloth. Assuming that Rav had not washed his hands and was using the wrapping as an alternative, Shmuel challenged him: *avdin kadein* — is this how one behaves? Rav replied: *da'ati katzra alai* — I am simply fastidious and do not like to handle bread directly, but of course I did perform *netilas yadayim*. The episode establishes clearly that both Rav and Shmuel hold that even when bread is wrapped, *netilas yadayim* is required.

### Rabbi Zeira's Finding

When Rabbi Zeira went up to Eretz Yisrael, he found Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi eating with their bread wrapped in worn rags. He assumed they were using this as an alternative to *netilas yadayim* and challenged them: *trei gavi raberavi kevaseichu ritu de-Rav u-Shmuel* — two such great scholars, are you departing from the established position of both Rav and Shmuel? In his own view, and as established from the story above, both Rav and Shmuel held that wrapping does not exempt one from *netilas yadayim*.

### Wrapping Terumah

Rabbi Zeira's challenge, however, was itself mistaken. He had overlooked a teaching transmitted by Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel: *hitiru mappa l'ochlei terumah v'lo hitiru mappa l'ochlei taharos* — wrapping one's hands is permitted for those eating *terumah*, but it is not permitted for those eating ordinary food who wash merely as a rabbinic requirement. Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi were *kohanim* eating actual *terumah*, and for *kohanim* eating *terumah*, who are punctilious about the laws of *tumah v'taharah*, the wrapping of the hands is a recognized alternative to *netilas yadayim*. The seriousness of *terumah* and the care that *kohanim* take in its consumption provide the justification for leniency there. For ordinary eating of bread, however, no such alternative is available, and wrapping remains insufficient.

It is worth noting the broader context: the discussion of *terumah* in the Gemara's time reflects the reality that at least some *kohanim* in the period of the *Amoraim* were actually eating *terumah*, at least *mi-d'rabbanan*. While in principle all of us today are assumed to be *tamei meis* and thus unable to eat *terumah*, the Gemara's cases reflect a different reality, in which the laws of *tumah v'taharah* were actively observed. Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi, as *kohanim*, were operating within that framework, and for them the wrapping was entirely permissible.

---

## Eater vs Feeder

### Being Fed

The Gemara raises a new question: *ochal machmas ma'achil — tzarich netilas yadayim o lo* — if one is eating because another is feeding him, placing bread directly into his mouth, does the person being fed require *netilas yadayim*? This question sharpens the fundamental issue. It is one thing to debate wrapping when there is some residual possibility of incidental contact; here, the concern about contact is all but eliminated. If the feeder is placing the food directly into the mouth of the one eating, the eater's hands need never come near the bread. Does *netilas yadayim* still apply?

### Rav Hamnuna Case

A story is brought: Rav Huna bar Sachorah was attending Rav Hamnuna and fed him meat, and Rav Hamnuna ate it. Rav Huna bar Sachorah remarked: *ila'v de-Rav Hamnuna at, lo sefina lach* — were you not Rav Hamnuna, I would not have fed you without ensuring you had performed *netilas yadayim*. The implication seems to be that Rav Hamnuna's exceptional reliability — the confidence that he would not touch the bread — was what justified feeding him without *netilas yadayim*. The Gemara, however, rejects this reading: *lo — d'zaris kadim u'mashi yadei me'ikara*. The statement did not mean that because Rav Hamnuna could be trusted not to touch, he did not need to wash; it meant that Rav Hamnuna, with characteristic alacrity, had already washed his hands in advance. The feeding was done only because Rav Hamnuna had already performed *netilas yadayim*, not as a substitute for it.

### Waiter Rule

A further teaching is cited, transmitted by Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav: *lo yitein adam prusa l'soch piv shel shamash ela im kein yodeia bo shenatal yadav* — one may not place a piece of bread into the mouth of a *shamash* — a waiter — unless one knows that he has already performed *netilas yadayim*. This seems to settle the matter quite clearly: even a person who is being fed and not handling the bread himself must have performed *netilas yadayim*. The Gemara, however, notes a possible qualification: *shani shamash d'tarid* — the *shamash* may be different because he is constantly distracted, constantly handling many things, and is therefore liable to inadvertently touch the bread even when being fed. Perhaps the *shamash* requires *netilas yadayim* for this practical reason, but a person in circumstances where there is truly no possibility of touching would not.

The Gemara then records a related ruling: *v'hashamash mevarech al kol kos v'chos v'eino mevarech al kol prusa u'prusa* — the *shamash* must recite a new *bracha* for each cup of wine offered to him, since such offers are infrequent and he cannot presume more will come, but he need not recite a new *bracha* for each piece of bread, since people commonly offer the waiter bread and he may assume the offers will continue. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and holds that even for bread, each piece requires a new *bracha*.
