Rav Papa reconciles the two positions: when there is an *adam chashuv* — an important person — at the table, the host will want to appear generous and will feed the *shamash* more regularly, so he may presume subsequent offers of bread; when there is no such person present, each offer is uncertain and a new *bracha* is required. This reconciliation resolves the dispute about *brachos* but does not resolve the underlying question about *netilas yadayim*.

### Shmuel's Case

The Gemara at last brings a decisive story. The father of Shmuel found Shmuel crying. When he asked why, Shmuel explained that his teachers had rebuked him, shaming him for having fed his child without performing *netilas yadayim* — *kasafis livrai velo mashis yadach*. Shmuel's father responded: why did you not wash? Shmuel replied: *hu achil va-ana mashina* — he is the one eating; do I have to wash? *Netilas yadayim* belongs to the eater, not to the feeder. His father's response was pointed: *lo mistayei delo gemiri — bimemcha nami machu?* It is not enough that these people are ignorant of the *halacha*; they are also berating you for it? The point being that those who do not understand the nuance are precisely the ones who raise the loudest protest.

### Halachic Conclusion

The Gemara concludes with an explicit ruling: *d'hilchata — ochal machmas ma'achil tzarich netilas yadayim, ma'achil eino tzarich netilas yadayim*. The one being fed requires *netilas yadayim*; the feeder does not. This conclusion is coherent with the entire trajectory of the sugya. *Netilas yadayim* was instituted not as a response to the act of handling bread but as a response to the act of eating it. Touching without eating does not require it; feeding without eating does not require it; but eating — even when the bread is wrapped, even when someone else places it in one's mouth — requires it. The requirement attaches to the eater alone, and this may reflect not only the *tumah v'taharah* origins of the institution but also a deeper logic: the act of eating itself, the *achat*, is what demands the sanctification that *netilas yadayim* provides, in the spirit of *ve-hitkadashtem vi'heyisem kedoshim*.

---

## Meat & Milk Table

### Wrapping Meat/Cheese

After the lengthy digression into *mayim rishonim* and *mayim acharonim*, the Gemara returns to the topic of separation between meat and milk. The *Mishnah* teaches: *tzorer adam basar u-gevina b'mitpachas achas u-vilvad she-lo yihyu nogi'im zeh va-zeh* — one may wrap meat and cheese together in a single cloth, provided they do not touch. This ruling is notable: on the same table during a meal, one cannot have meat and milk present simultaneously, yet here, wrapping them together in a cloth is permitted, so long as there is no contact between them. The distinction may rest on the context of eating — at the table, one might inadvertently share or consume from both; in a cloth, one is simply storing or transporting, and the concern of accidental consumption does not arise. Alternatively, as the discussion develops, the concept of the prohibition may be tied to what constitutes eating together in a meaningful sense, not mere physical proximity.

### Strangers Rule

The *Mishnah* continues with a ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *shenei achsanaim ochlin al shulchan echad — zeh basar ve-zeh gevina — v'ein chosheshin* — two *achsanaim*, strangers or chance guests, may eat at the same table, one eating meat and the other eating milk products, and there is no concern. Since they do not know one another, there is no risk that they will inadvertently offer food to one another or take from one another's plate. The prohibition of eating meat and milk at the same table is rooted in the concern for inadvertent sharing, and where that concern is absent, so is the prohibition.

### Cold vs Heat

The Gemara first addresses the *Mishnah*'s opening clause about wrapping meat and cheese in a single cloth. The question is raised: *ve-chi noge'a zeh va-zeh mai havei* — if they do touch, what is the harm? They are cold — *tzonin be-tzonin hu* — and cold-to-cold contact does not transfer taste. Abaye answers: granted, *kelipa* — the removal of a surface layer — is not required when foods are cold. Nevertheless, *hadacha mi lo ba'ei* — rinsing is still necessary. The concern is not taste transfer through heat but the presence of greasy residue on the surface of the food, which can transfer from one to the other even without heat. A rinse suffices to address this. This principle has practical implications wherever cold meat and dairy foods come into physical contact: no *kelipa* is needed, but rinsing with attention to any fatty residue may be required.

### Strangers Requirement

The Gemara then turns to the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rav Chana bar Avmi reports in the name of Shmuel: *lo shanu ela she'ein makirim zeh et zeh* — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's dispensation applies only when the two diners do not recognize one another at all; they are genuine strangers. *Aval makirim zeh et zeh — assur* — if they know one another, even without being close friends, eating meat and milk at the same table is forbidden. A *Baraisa* is cited in confirmation: two guests at the same inn, one coming from the north and one from the south — true strangers — one carrying meat and the other carrying cheese, may eat at the same table without concern.

### Tfisa Achat

The *Baraisa* adds a crucial formulation: *v'lo asru ela b'tfisa achat* — the prohibition was only imposed in the case of *tfisa achat*, one bundle. The Gemara immediately asks: *tfisa achat salka da'atach* — do you literally mean that the prohibition requires the two foods to be physically bundled together? That would be an absurdly narrow reading. The Gemara therefore clarifies: *ela ke'ein tfisa achat* — the meaning is *like* one bundle. What this denotes is a situation where the two people eating are connected in some sense — they know one another, there is a shared dimension to their meal — not merely that they are physically at the same table. The prohibition on eating meat and milk at the same table requires some sense of common eating, some social or relational dimension that creates the concern for inadvertent sharing.

### No Distinctions

Rav Yeimar bar Shalmiya posed a question to Abaye: what about two brothers who know each other well but are in the midst of a feud and are stringent with one another — *makpidin zeh al zeh* — refusing to share food? Since there is no social connection and no possibility of sharing, would the prohibition apply? Abaye's response invokes the principle of *lo plug*: *yomru kol ha-serikin asurin ve-serikei Baitos mutarin* — if we permit this case, people will say all decorative *matzot* are forbidden yet the designs of Baitos are permitted. The principle of *lo plug* holds that once a formal category has been established, we do not make exceptions within it based on particular circumstances, even where the underlying rationale does not apply. The distinction between strangers and non-strangers is workable; assessing the degree of social connection or animosity within the category of non-strangers is not. Even feuding brothers, therefore, may not eat meat and milk at the same table.

A challenge is raised: the Gemara in Moed Katan (in the name of Rav Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan) permits one who owns a single garment to launder it on *Chol ha-Moed*, even though laundering is generally forbidden. Is this not also a case of making an exception within a general rule — a violation of *lo plug*? The response, attributed to Mar bar Rav Ashi, is that in that case, *izoro mochiach alav* — his belt tells the story. When a person strips off his only garment to wash it, he does so visibly, in plain view; everyone can see why the exception applies. When an exception is self-evidently justified and apparent to all, it does not open the door to other exceptions, because the exceptional nature of the case is transparent. Other cases, however — such as brothers who happen to be feuding — involve facts that are not visible or verifiable, and cannot form the basis for categorical distinctions.

### Separations

Tosafot seizes on the Gemara's language of *ke'ein tfisa achat* to argue that even when two people know one another, the prohibition may not apply if there is some form of separation between them. Tosafot and the *Rishonim* discuss two types of separation: a physical barrier that would prevent someone from reaching across and inadvertently taking from the other's food, and a *siman* — a reminder — that signals to the participants that they are eating separately. Even without a physical barrier, something that marks off one person's eating as distinct from the other's — a placemat, a piece of paper, or any visible indicator — can serve as a sufficient reminder. The logic tracks the concept of *tfisa achat*: once it is clear that the two are not eating together in any meaningful sense, the concern that animates the prohibition does not apply.

### Table Types

The practical latitude offered by Tosafot is also informed by a basic historical observation. The *shulchan* of the Gemara and the *Mishnah* was not the large communal table of modern experience. In the world of the Talmud, eating was done Roman-style: individual trays were brought before each diner, and the *shulchan* referred to that personal tray. When the *Mishnah* in Pesachim speaks of the *shulchan* being brought before the *seder* participants containing the *matzah* and other foods, it refers to this individual tray. To eat at the same *shulchan* in that sense was to eat quite literally from the same surface, in close and intimate proximity. In contemporary life, where a large shared table serves many diners, the sense of *ke'ein tfisa achat* is considerably weaker even without any formal separation. It is on this basis that the ruling emerges that nowadays, some form of separation — whether a physical barrier or a visible *siman* — suffices to permit two people sitting at the same large table to eat meat and milk respectively.

---

---

# Hullin 108

## Intro & Mishna

### Transition to Basar

With Daf 108a, the tractate transitions away from the rabbinic concerns about eating forbidden and permitted foods together and moves into the weighty biblical prohibitions of *basar bechalav* — meat and milk cooked together. Notably, the Gemara has not yet introduced the question of which types of meat, which types of milk, or which species of animals are subject to this prohibition; that discussion belongs to a later Mishna. For now, the focus is the core biblical concern: the prohibition of cooking meat and milk together.

### Tipat Chalav

The Mishna at the top of 108a opens with the following case: *tipat chalav shenafela al hachaticha* — a drop of milk falls onto a chunk of meat sitting in a stew pot. This Mishna will sound familiar to anyone who studied the Mishna in the chapter of *Gid HaNasheh*. There, however, the *gid* itself was the forbidden substance falling among permitted pieces; here the meat is entirely permitted and the drop of milk is what triggers the concern.

### Taste Determines Status

The Mishna rules: *im yesh ba benotein ta'am b'ota hachaticha asura* — if the milk is detectable by taste in that piece of meat, the piece becomes forbidden as *basar bechalav*. The underlying general rule, which the Mishna expresses qualitatively rather than numerically, is that if the milk constitutes more than one-sixtieth of the meat it imparts a detectable taste and the meat is forbidden; if less than one-sixtieth, the taste is not detectable and the meat remains permitted. How detectability is assessed in practice — whether by estimation from an analogous case or by asking a non-Jewish taster — is a separate matter. What the Mishna establishes is that taste is the operative criterion. Strikingly, even though meat and milk have technically been cooked together, if the milk cannot be tasted in the result, the Torah does not treat it as though they were cooked together, and the meat is not forbidden.

### Stirred Pot

The Mishna continues: *ni'er et hakedira* — if the pot was stirred, then *im yesh ba benotein ta'am b'ota kedira asura* — if the taste is detectable throughout the entire pot, the entire pot is forbidden.

### Two Readings

The natural reading of this clause is that we are measuring whether the taste of the milk has spread throughout the pot. On this reading, the Mishna is making essentially the same point twice: milk must be tasteable in the meat for it to be forbidden, and after stirring, milk must be tasteable throughout the pot for the whole pot to be forbidden.

There is, however, a second way to read the Mishna. On this reading, after the milk fell and was absorbed into the original piece of meat, that piece of meat became *basar bechalav* — forbidden in its entirety, as if it were *chazir*. Now, when this piece of forbidden meat is stirred into the rest of the pot, it is not the taste of milk that is spreading throughout the pot, but the taste of a fully forbidden piece of meat. The forbidden substance being measured is now the entire piece of meat, not merely the original drop of milk. On this reading, the pot becomes forbidden if the taste of that forbidden piece of meat spreads throughout, and the taste in question is the taste of the meat — measured in full units of that piece — not just the taste of the original drop of milk. The Gemara will develop this reading further.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### Abaye's Position

The Gemara opens with a statement of Abaye: *ta'amo v'lo mamasho be-alma d'oraita* — the principle that taste without substance is a biblical concern. This is the principle known as *ta'am k'ikar*, that taste is like the essence of the forbidden thing. The paradigmatic case of *ta'amo v'lo mamasho* is when a piece of *chazir* falls into a kosher pot, the taste disperses, and then the piece is removed. One is left with taste of *chazir* but not the substance itself. Is this a biblical prohibition or only rabbinic? Abaye argues it is biblical, and he derives this from the laws of *basar bechalav*.

His proof: *d'ee salka datach d'rabbanan* — were you to suppose that taste-without-substance is only a rabbinic concern, why can we not prove that taste is a biblical concern from *basar bechalav*? After all, in the case of *basar bechalav*, a drop of milk gives taste to the meat and that makes the meat forbidden — demonstrating that taste is what the Torah cares about.

### Learning from Basar

This argument, however, is already known to the Gemara elsewhere (in tractates *Nazir* and *Pesachim*, among others) and is rejected: *dechidush hu* — *basar bechalav* is an exceptional case, a *chiddush*, and we cannot derive general principles from exceptional cases.

### Exception Theory

The reason *basar bechalav* is exceptional, the objection runs, is that the prohibition is not simply about taste — it is about having cooked them together. Consider: if one soaks cold meat in cold milk until the meat absorbs the milk's taste, this would not be biblically forbidden, even though the taste of milk is thoroughly present in the meat. This demonstrates that *basar bechalav* is not merely about taste but about the act of cooking. Since it is not purely a taste-based prohibition, one cannot cite it as proof that taste is a biblical concern in general.

### Abaye's Proof

Abaye responds to this objection directly. He grants that cooking is a necessary condition for the biblical prohibition. But, he argues, if the focus were entirely on the act of cooking rather than on taste, then *ei chidush hu* — if that were the logic — *af al gav d'leika notein ta'am nami* — even if the milk gave no detectable taste to the meat, you should still be biblically forbidden, because you cooked them together. Yet our Mishna demonstrates otherwise: if the milk is not detectable by taste, the meat is not forbidden. This means that the biblical prohibition is not simply triggered by the bare act of cooking; taste must be present. Since taste is what determines whether the prohibition applies, Abaye concludes that taste is indeed a biblical concern.

### Intermingling Concept

There is a genuine conceptual distinction at stake here. When meat and milk are cooked together, a chemical transformation occurs — the two substances merge into something that is genuinely a new combination, a true intermingling of tastes. By contrast, cold meat soaking in cold milk produces two tastes sitting alongside each other, not genuinely merged. As Rav Soloveitchik famously frames it: the cold scenario produces *basar vechalav* — meat *and* milk, with a *vav* — two separate things coexisting. The cooking scenario produces *basar bechalav* — meat *in* milk, a genuine mixture. Abaye's position is that the Torah requires cooking because cooking effects this true intermingling of tastes, but it is ultimately the intermingling of the tastes that is the problem.

### Rava's Position

Rava disagrees: *derech bishul asra Torah* — the Torah forbade the way of cooking, the act of cooking together, and taste is not itself the prohibited matter. Why then is the prohibition limited to cases where the milk is detectable by taste? Because without detectable taste, the act of cooking was not a *classic* act of cooking — you would not normally cook something with an ingredient that fails to impart any taste. So the taste threshold functions as a limiting condition that defines what counts as genuine cooking, not as evidence that taste per se is what is prohibited. On Rava's account, what is forbidden is not the presence of the intermingled taste but the historical act of having cooked them together.

It should be noted that although Rava appears to reject the biblical status of taste, many *Rishonim* suggest he may be doing so purely for the sake of argument. The overwhelming consensus of *Rishonim* is that *ta'am k'ikar* is indeed a biblical concern. Rashi, however, does read Rava as genuinely rejecting the biblical status of taste.

### Definition of Cooking

Beyond the question of taste, this debate has significant practical consequences for how one defines *bishul* at the biblical level. If, like Rava, the emphasis is on the act of cooking itself, one might be inclined to define cooking formally and narrowly. Other methods of applying heat — roasting, steaming, smoking — might then fall short of the biblical prohibition of *bishul*, at least at the Torah level. If, like Abaye, the emphasis is on the intermingling of tastes effected by heat, the formal category of cooking matters less; what matters is whether the heat produced a genuine merging of tastes. This debate between the *Rishonim* and *Acharonim* about which forms of heat application constitute biblical *bishul* in the context of *basar bechalav* flows directly from this disagreement between Abaye and Rava.

---

## Chaticha Neveila

### Rav's Ruling

The Gemara now opens what will be the central *sugya* of this section: *chaticha naaseit neveilah* — the piece becomes forbidden. Rav rules: *keivan shenatan ta'am b'chaticha, otah chaticha naaseit neveilah* — once the milk gives taste to that original piece of meat, that piece of meat becomes entirely forbidden, as if it were *neveilah*, as if it were *chazir*. The piece transforms in its entirety.

### Min Bemino

Rav continues: *v'oser kol hachatichot kulam mipnei shehen minah* — and if this piece is then cooked along with the other pieces in the pot, all the other pieces are forbidden, because they are of the same *min*, the same type. This invokes the principle of *min bemino lo batel* — a forbidden substance does not become *batel* among substances of the same type, no matter how many there are. The practical consequence is striking. Suppose you had one unit of milk and fifty units of meat. Ordinarily, sixty times the milk would suffice to render the milk *batel*. But once the milk gives taste to the meat, you no longer have one unit of forbidden milk among fifty units of kosher meat. You now have fifty units of forbidden *basar bechalav*. If that forbidden meat now continues cooking with other pieces of meat, the other pieces of meat are the same *min* as the forbidden piece, and *min bemino lo batel* applies — you cannot negate one piece of meat among a thousand other pieces of meat.

### Forbidden as Meat

There is an additional and subtle dimension to Rav's ruling. One might have supposed that meat cooked with milk becomes forbidden not as meat and not as milk but as a new, hybrid category — something in between. If that were so, the forbidden piece would be *eino mino*, a different type, relative to the plain kosher meat in the pot, and *bitul* might apply in the normal fashion. Rav is telling us otherwise: meat cooked with milk is forbidden *as meat*. Its *min* is meat. The forbidden piece is not some third category; it remains meat, simply meat that has been rendered forbidden. Consequently, it and all the other pieces of meat in the pot are the same *min*, and *min bemino lo batel* renders all the other pieces forbidden as well. This, incidentally, is fully consistent with Rava's understanding of *basar bechalav*: what is forbidden is the act of having cooked them together, not some new hybrid taste. The meat remains meat, categorically.

### Negation Question

This raises an obvious question. The forbidden piece falls into the pot. The pot contains not only other pieces of meat but also vegetables, water, and other ingredients. Even if the other pieces of meat are the same *min* as the forbidden piece and cannot negate it, why can't the *other* ingredients — which are a different *min* — negate it? According to Rava's principle stated in the context of *Gid HaNasheh*: *salek et mino k'mi she'eino, u'she'eino mino rabah alav u'mevatlo* — set aside the same-type items as if they weren't there, and if the different-type items are sufficient in quantity, they can negate the forbidden piece. So why, in a stew full of vegetables and water, can the vegetables not negate the forbidden piece of meat?

### Thick Stew Answer

The Gemara answers: *ei d'nafal berotev rakah hachi nami* — if it fell into a *thin* stew, you would be right. *Hacha bemai askinan d'nafal berotev avah* — the case under discussion is one in which it fell into a *thick* stew. Rashi explains that a *rotev avah* here means a stew that is predominantly meat with very little liquid or other ingredients. There is simply not enough of the non-meat ingredients to constitute sixty times the forbidden piece and negate it. But the Gemara explicitly acknowledges: had there been sufficient vegetables and water, they could indeed negate the forbidden piece, notwithstanding the meat's *min bemino* status relative to the other pieces.

---

## Efshar Lesochto

### Reversal Question

The Gemara now raises a fundamental conceptual question about Rav's ruling: *u'mai kasavar* — what does Rav hold regarding the theoretical possibility of reversing the forbidden status of the piece of meat? The question is: *ei kasavar efshar lesochto mutar* — if Rav held that were you to squeeze the milk back out of the piece of meat, the piece would revert to being permitted, then how can he maintain that the piece becomes a full *neveilah* and remains forbidden?

### Two Positions

The Gemara formulates the dilemma sharply. *Efshar lesochto mutar* — if in principle the milk could be removed and the status reversed, then the moment the piece of meat continues cooking in the pot and the milk disperses out of it, the original piece of meat should revert to being permitted, and the entire pot should be fine. *Efshar lesochto assur* — only if even theoretically squeezing the milk back out would not restore the piece to being permitted can Rav's ruling stand.

### Status Stickiness

There are two distinct conceptual frameworks for understanding why the piece might remain forbidden even after the milk is removed. The first framework is what might be called the stickiness of status: once a piece of meat has acquired a forbidden status, that status adheres and is not easily reversed. As long as any trace of milk remains — even if it is too small to have originally caused the prohibition — the status persists. Only if every last trace were removed, *efshar lehafrido*, might the piece conceivably revert; even then, the *Acharonim* debate whether it would.

The second framework connects directly to the conceptual debate between Abaye and Rava. If one holds, like Abaye, that the prohibition is about the mixture of tastes, then in principle reversing the mixture — removing the taste — might restore the status. But if one holds, like Rava, that the prohibition is the historical act of having been cooked together, that historical fact cannot be undone. The meat was cooked with milk. That is a fact that persists regardless of the current state of the milk in the pot. On this view, the meat remains forbidden not because of what it currently contains but because of what was done to it.

These three ideas — *chaticha naaseit neveilah*, that the piece remains forbidden as *meat* (not as a hybrid), and *efshar lesochto assur* — are mutually reinforcing and all point toward the same underlying understanding: the problem in *basar bechalav* is the act of cooking, not the resulting mixture of tastes.

### Majority View

The Gemara records that this debate is between major Amoraic authorities. Rav, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi Yochanan all hold *efshar lesochto assur* — even if the milk is squeezed out, the piece remains forbidden. Shmuel, Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, and Resh Lakish hold *efshar lesochto mutar* — if the milk is removed, the piece reverts to being permitted. The more authoritative line — Rav and Rabbi Yochanan — takes the stricter position, and this is the ruling that governs the *sugya* going forward.

---

## Meat in Milk Pot (III)

### Meat Falls in

The Gemara now reverses the scenario. Until now, the case was milk falling into a pot of meat. Now consider: *kezayit basar shenafal l'tokh yoreh shel chalav* — a *kezayit*-sized chunk of meat falls into a pot of hot milk.

### Rav's Ruling

Rav rules: *basar assur v'chalav mutar* — the meat is forbidden, and the milk is permitted. This ruling is logical on its face. The meat has absorbed the taste of milk and is therefore forbidden as *basar bechalav*. The milk, however, contained a thousand units of milk and only one unit of meat. The taste of meat in the milk is negligible — one part in a thousand — and the milk remains permitted.

---

## Meat in Milk Pot (III)

### Status Problem

This ruling, however, appears to be in tension with Rav's own position that *efshar lesochto assur*. If the status of the forbidden piece does not revert even when the forbidden ingredient disperses out of it, then consider what is happening here. The milk enters the meat. The meat becomes forbidden. The meat also imparts taste to the milk, but that is trace and not a problem. But now: the milk that entered the meat — which became, as it were, forbidden milk, *basar bechalav* as milk — when that milk goes back out of the piece of meat and disperses back into the pot of milk, why doesn't that forbidden milk render the entire pot of milk forbidden? After all, milk among milk is *min bemino*, and *min bemino lo batel*. So why does Rav say the milk pot is permitted?

---

## Efshar Lesochto (II)

### Milk Challenge

This challenge is precisely the parallel of the one raised against *chaticha naaseit neveilah*. There, the forbidden meat remained forbidden even as the milk dispersed out of it. Here, the forbidden milk that entered the meat and then dispersed back into the pot — if status is sticky and the milk retains its forbidden character — should render the entire pot forbidden through *min bemino*. The parallel seems exact: just as the forbidden meat cannot become permitted when the milk leaves it, so too the forbidden milk should not become permitted when it disperses back into the pot.

### Torah's Focus

The Gemara resolves this with a ruling that is striking in its precision. *D'amar kra: lo tvashel gdi b'chalav imo* — the Torah says: do not cook a kid in its mother's milk. *Gdi asra Torah v'lo chalav* — the Torah forbade the *gdi*, the meat, and not the milk. This is a remarkable statement. The Torah's focus in the prohibition of *basar bechalav* is on the meat. What is forbidden is cooking the meat in the milk. What becomes prohibited as a result is the meat. The milk is never the primary subject of the Torah's prohibition. Therefore, while the milk that entered the meat does contribute to the meat's forbidden status, that same milk, when it disperses back into the pot, does not itself become a new unit of *basar bechalav* that can in turn forbid the milk pot. The milk is simply not the thing the Torah is addressing.

This ruling is again deeply consistent with the underlying conceptual position: it is the act of cooking the meat that is prohibited, and it is the meat that bears the consequence. The milk is merely the medium. One might note how radical this sounds — milk cooked with meat being entirely permitted — yet the internal logic is coherent given the framing.

The Gemara then immediately raises an objection to the more extreme version of this position. If the Torah truly only forbids the *gdi* and not the milk at all, consider: *chatzi zayit basar v'chatzi zayit chalav shebishlan zeh im zeh* — if one cooked a half-*kezayit* of meat with a half-*kezayit* of milk. Now there is a full *kezayit* of *basar bechalav* — half meat, half milk. *Amar Rav loke al achilato* — Rav says one receives lashes for eating it. But if the Torah only forbids the meat and not the milk, then the person has only consumed a half-*kezayit* of meat, which is *chatzi shiur* and does not incur lashes. The Gemara concludes: *ela olam kasvar Rav chalav nami assur* — in fact, Rav holds that the milk is also forbidden. The statement that the Torah forbade the *gdi* and not the milk is not absolute; it explains why, in the specific case of meat falling into a milk pot, the milk pot is not rendered forbidden by *min bemino*. It is not a general statement that milk can never be forbidden as *basar bechalav*.

---

## Half-Kezayit Debate

### Half-Kezayit Case

The Gemara now examines the ruling about half-a-*kezayit* of each more carefully. The case: *chatzi zayit basar v'chatzi zayit chalav shebishlan zeh im zeh* — half a *kezayit* of meat and half a *kezayit* of milk cooked together.

### Rav's Position

Rav rules: *loke al achilato, v'eino loke al bishulo* — one receives lashes for eating the combined *kezayit*, but does not receive lashes for the act of cooking it. The reasoning: for eating, one has consumed a full *kezayit* of *basar bechalav* — it is true that it is half meat and half milk, but both halves are *basar bechalav* and they combine to a full *kezayit*, incurring lashes. For cooking, however, Rav does not impose lashes.

---

## Meat in Milk Pot (III)

### Boiling Pot Answer

Returning to the challenge about the milk pot: the Gemara resolves it by noting that the scenario involves a *yora rotachat* — a boiling vat of milk. *Demivla bala miplat lo palit* — in a boiling vessel, the meat absorbs the milk but does not release it back out. The milk flows in but does not flow back out while the vat is actively boiling. Therefore, the problematic scenario — forbidden milk dispersing back into the pot and rendering it forbidden through *min bemino* — simply does not occur. The meat absorbs the milk but retains it.

The Gemara then raises a follow-up: *ki nayach hadar palit* — surely when the pot cools and stops boiling, the meat will then release the milk back out. The Gemara answers: *kadam vesilko* — one removes the piece of meat from the pot before it cools. This is the practical scenario: the meat falls into the boiling pot, absorbs milk but does not release it while boiling, and is then removed. The milk in the pot has only trace amounts of meat taste — one in a thousand — and remains permitted. The milk that entered the meat has not been released back into the pot. The meat is forbidden. The milk is permitted.

---

## Half-Kezayit Debate (II)

### Inconsistency

The Gemara returns to the half-*kezayit* ruling and presses an internal inconsistency in Rav's position. *Mima nafshach* — make up your mind. *I mitztarfin abishul nami lilki* — if the half-*kezayit* of meat and half-*kezayit* of milk combine, then they should combine for cooking as well, and one should receive lashes for the act of cooking. *V'ei lo mitztarfin, achila nami lo lilki* — and if they do not combine because they are fundamentally distinct things, then one should not receive lashes for eating either.

### Combination Logic

The Gemara resolves: *leolam lo mitztarfin* — in fact, they do not combine. *Uvaba miyora gedola* — the ruling about lashes for eating refers not to a case of half-a-*kezayit* of each cooked in isolation, but to a different scenario: *b'ba miyora gedola* — coming from a large pot. Rashi explains that this means the following. The Gemara's challenge was not merely an abstract analogy; it was more pointed. If in the act of cooking a half-*kezayit* of meat with a half-*kezayit* of milk one has not transgressed — because neither constitutes a full *kezayit* of the relevant substance — then how does the *product* become forbidden? Given Rav's position that the prohibition is about the act of cooking, if no transgression occurred, the cooking act did not create forbidden food.

The Gemara's answer: Rav's ruling that one receives lashes for eating applies only where the forbidden act of cooking had in fact occurred. Specifically: imagine pot B, which contains a large quantity of meat into which sufficient milk fell — enough to constitute a full act of cooking and create forbidden *basar bechalav*. And imagine pot C, which contains a large quantity of milk into which sufficient meat fell — similarly a full and forbidden act of cooking. From pot B one takes a half-*kezayit* of forbidden meat; from pot C one takes a half-*kezayit* of forbidden milk. Combining and eating these two halves gives one lashes, because each half is already fully forbidden *basar bechalav* from its respective pot in which a complete, prohibited act of cooking occurred. In such a case, the two halves do combine for eating.

By contrast, if one takes a half-*kezayit* of raw meat and a half-*kezayit* of raw milk and cooks them together — where neither constitutes a full *kezayit* of its respective substance — no complete forbidden act of cooking occurred, the product is not forbidden, and one would receive neither lashes for cooking nor lashes for eating.

The essential principle: what makes *basar bechalav* forbidden is the prohibited act of cooking. Where that act was complete, the product is forbidden and can combine with other forbidden products for the purpose of eating. Where that act was incomplete — because neither substance reached the threshold of a *kezayit* — the product carries no forbidden status at all.

### Levi's View

Levi disagrees with Rav's limiting condition. *Af lo ke'al bishulo* — even in the case of a half-*kezayit* of each cooked together, one does receive lashes, and one need not reach the threshold of a full *kezayit* of each. Levi taught this in a *Mishna* (*matnisin*): just as one receives lashes for eating a half-*kezayit* of each, so too for cooking a half-*kezayit* of each.

### Cooking Standard

The Gemara adds one further qualification, attributed in context to this discussion: *ve'eizeh bishul amru — bishul she'hem ochlin oto machmat bishulo* — and what cooking did they mean? They meant cooking to a degree that others would actually eat it. This is significant. Even according to the view that the prohibition is about the act of cooking rather than merely the mixture of tastes, there is a qualitative standard for what constitutes a prohibited act of cooking. Initial heating that begins to mix tastes but does not produce food that others would eat does not qualify. This minimum standard of *bishul* — producing something edible — must be met before a biblical prohibition is incurred and before lashes apply. Rabbinic prohibition may of course begin earlier.

---

## Baraita & Tannaim

### R. Yehuda's View

The Gemara now demonstrates that the debate over *efshar lesochto* and *chaticha naaseit neveilah* is rooted in a Tannaitic dispute. A *Baraita* is cited: *tipat chalav shenafela al hachaticha* — a drop of milk falls on a piece of meat in the pot. *Keivan shenatan ta'am bachaticha, hachaticha atzmah naaseit neveilah ve'oseret kol hachatichot kulam mipnei shehen minah, divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — once it gives taste to that piece, the piece becomes entirely forbidden and renders all the other pieces of meat in the pot forbidden, because they are of the same *min*. These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda. This is word for word the ruling attributed to Rav, establishing that Rav's position follows Rabbi Yehuda.

### Sages' View

*Vachachamim omrim* — the Sages say otherwise. *Ad shetitein ta'am berotev uvakippa uvachatichot* — the pot is not forbidden unless the taste of the milk spreads and is detectable throughout the entire pot: in the liquid, in the residue (*kippa*), and in the pieces of meat. According to the Sages, the piece of meat does not transform into a new unit of forbidden food that then renders all other pieces of meat forbidden through *min bemino*. Rather, one measures only whether the original drop of milk is detectable throughout the pot.

One might assume that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages is simply about *min bemino* — whether same-type items can negate each other. But the Gemara does not read the dispute that way, because the next statement of Rebbi suggests that the deeper question is about the status of the piece of meat itself.

### Rebbi's Split

Rebbi — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi — offers a nuanced ruling: *nirin divrei Rabbi Yehuda beshelo ni'er veshelo kissa, vedivrei chachamim besheni'er vekhissa* — Rabbi Yehuda's position appears correct in a case where the pot was not stirred and not covered; the Sages' position applies where the pot was stirred and covered.

Rebbi is effectively ruling like Rabbi Yehuda, but limiting the scenario in which Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies. The distinction is about whether the milk initially concentrates into the original piece of meat or immediately disperses throughout the pot. If the pot was stirred and covered from the outset, the milk never settles on a single piece — it disperses immediately throughout the pot, and one measures only whether the original drop of milk gives taste to the whole pot. If the pot was not stirred and not covered, the drop of milk first settles on and absorbs into the original piece of meat, which then becomes fully forbidden as *basar bechalav*, and only subsequently is that forbidden piece stirred into the rest of the pot.

### Timing Question

The Gemara clarifies what Rebbi must mean. One might think *lo ni'er velo kissa* means the pot was never stirred and never covered at any stage. But then the original piece of meat becomes forbidden, yet no taste ever spreads from it to the other pieces, since nothing is ever stirred. In that case, why should the rest of the pot be forbidden? The Gemara explains: Rebbi must mean that one did not stir initially but did stir later — *lo ni'er bitchila ela besof* — the pot was not stirred at the beginning, allowing the milk to absorb into the original piece and make it forbidden, and only afterward was the pot stirred, causing the taste of that now-forbidden piece to spread to the rest of the pot.

### Gemara Challenge

With this reading in place, the Gemara raises an objection. Once the pot is stirred, the milk that was absorbed into the original piece of meat disperses back out into the pot. The proportions then reverse: the piece of meat, which originally had a full unit of milk giving it taste, now has only a tiny fraction of milk remaining. The milk has mostly left the piece. Should the piece of meat not then revert to being permitted? If so, it should not render the rest of the pot forbidden, and Rebbi's ruling is difficult to maintain.

### Final Answer

The Gemara answers: *kasavar efshar lesochto assur* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that *efshar lesochto assur*. Even when the milk disperses out of the original piece of meat and the piece now has only trace amounts of milk, the piece does not revert to being permitted. It acquired a forbidden status at the moment the milk gave it taste; that status is permanent. The piece remains forbidden as *basar bechalav*, forbidden as meat, and when stirred into the pot, it renders all the other pieces of meat forbidden through *min bemino*. The ruling of Rav, which follows Rabbi Yehuda, and the principle of *efshar lesochto assur* are thus mutually entailing: both are required for Rabbi Yehuda's position to be coherent, and both are confirmed by the *Baraita*. The *sugya* will continue on the first day of Yom Tov.

---

---

# Hullin 112

## Nat Bar Nat Summary

### Nat Bar Nat Principles

Today's daf is 112, and we resume from where we concluded on Shabbos: the discussion of *nat bar nat* — taste that is two degrees removed. Before proceeding to the new material, a brief summary of the practical *halacha* is in order.

The Gemara's foundational ruling is expressed in the phrase *dagim she'alu b'kara mutar le'ochlan b'kutach* — fish that rose in a *fleishig* plate may nonetheless be eaten with milk. Even if the plate was *fleishig* and the fish were hot, the fish themselves are not considered *fleishig*, because the taste transfer is two degrees removed: from the meat into the plate, and from the plate into the fish. This is called *nat bar nat de-hetera* — two degrees removed where the original substance was itself *heter* — and it remains *heter*.

This is sharply distinguished from *nat bar nat de-issura*. The reason that using a pot that absorbed *chazir* renders food forbidden — even though the *chazir* went into the pot and the pot into the food, making it technically two degrees removed — is that once something carries a status of *issur*, that forbidden status, as it were, retains its "stickiness." It does not dissipate with distance. By contrast, *milchig* and *fleishig* by themselves are *heter*; they carry no forbidden status until they come into contact with the opposing category. Therefore, when the taste is weakened both practically and *halachically* by being two degrees removed from the original, the food retains no problematic status.

A further qualification: *nat bar nat de-hetera* is only *heter* when the second stage of transfer also remains *heter*. This is explicit in a *meforash* braisa: *k'deira she-bishal bah basar assur le-vashel bah chalav* — a pot in which meat was cooked may not be used to cook milk, because at the second stage — from pot to milk — one encounters meat and milk together. The *heter* of *nat bar nat* applies only where the outcome remains entirely within the *heter* realm.

### Parve in Fleishig/Milchig

What then is the practical status of *parve* food cooked in a *fleishig* or *milchig* pot — the familiar case of the "DE" (dairy equipment) designation on kosher products? The Gemara permits it: at that stage of transfer it is already *nat bar nat* and remains *heter*, and one may eat it together with the opposing category.

Yet if this ruling is straightforward, why do manufacturers label products "dairy equipment," and why the widespread stringency? The answer lies in a dispute among *Rishonim*. Based on Rashi and Tosafot, there is a serious question as to whether actual cooking over fire is comparable to the Gemara's case. The Gemara's ruling may have been limited to placing dry, hot fish on a dry plate — not to food cooked over flame, where the intensity of heat may effect a more direct transfer that does not reduce to a second degree. On the other hand, if cooking was done in water, the water may itself introduce a third degree, potentially restoring the leniency. These competing considerations generate the practical framework that follows.

### Ashkenazi vs Sefardi

For *Ashkenazim*, the upshot is: *lechatchila*, one may not cook *parve* food in a *milchig* pot with the intent to mix it with *fleishig*, nor may one *lechatchila* combine the two after the fact. To illustrate: if one wishes to serve spaghetti at a meal with meatballs, one may not cook those noodles in a *milchig* pot *lechatchila* if that combination is the plan. Even if the noodles were cooked without that intent and only afterward does one wish to add meat sauce, the *Ashkenazi* position remains that one should not mix them *lechatchila*, because perhaps cooking over fire does not reduce the transfer to a second degree.

However, if one did not realize and already combined them on the plate — *bedieved* — even *Ashkenazim* would permit eating what was already mixed. *Bedieved*, *nat bar nat de-hetera* is fully acceptable. *Sefardim* are more lenient: they permit the combination even *lechatchila*, provided it was not done with that intent from the outset.

Practically speaking, when advising people in this situation, one can indicate that eating the *parve* food and the *fleishig* at the same meal is acceptable, so long as they are kept separate on the plate and not mixed together. If they were inadvertently mixed, *bedieved* it is permitted. An additional point worth noting: eating food made in *dairy equipment* does not render one *milchig*, and eating food made in *fleishig* equipment does not render one *fleishig* — this is universally agreed upon.

There is also a broader issue with the OU's practice of labeling products as "dairy equipment" entirely. The concern motivating that label is that consumers will not know the *halachos* of dairy equipment and may mix it improperly. But as established above, even if such mixing occurs, it is *bedieved* permitted. There is a general principle in *halacha* that one does not enact *gezeiros* over situations that are in any case *mutar bedieved*. Calling a product "dairy" when it is at most "dairy equipment" goes beyond what the *halacha* requires.

### Ben Yomo Status

All of the above discussion applies when the *keilim* in question are *ben yomo* — used within the past twenty-four hours, so that the absorbed taste within them is still considered "good." When the *keilim* are *eino ben yomo* — more than a day old — the situation is considerably more lenient.

According to the Gra, if the vessel is *eino ben yomo* and the case involves *nat bar nat de-hetera*, one may cook the *parve* food in the *milchig* or *fleishig* pot *lechatchila* even with the intent to serve it at a meal where the opposing category will be present. Thus, if one's largest pot is a *milchig* pot and it is *eino ben yomo*, one may *lechatchila* cook spaghetti in it for a meat meal. The combination of *nat bar nat* with *eino ben yomo* status permits this even at the outset. That concludes the *regel achat* summary of *nat bar nat*.

### OU Gezeira Critique

As noted above, the OU's labeling of products as "dairy" when they are only made on dairy equipment reflects a self-imposed *gezeira*. The concern that consumers will be unaware of the relevant *halachos* is understandable, but it does not justify treating a *bedieved*-permitted product as if it were fully dairy. The principle is well established that where the underlying act is *mutar bedieved*, there is no basis for a rabbinic *gezeira* — and applying one in this case takes matters further than the *halacha* requires.

---

## Davar Charif Laws

### Radish & Knife Absorption

We turn now to a brief standing-on-one-foot summary of the knife and *davar charif* issues, which the Gemara addressed in just two lines but which carry enormous practical consequences. The Gemara's concern is that when one cuts a *tznon* — a radish — with a *fleishig* knife, the radish absorbs the *fleishig* taste from the knife.

### Clean vs Dirty Knives

A threshold question is whether the Gemara assumes a clean or dirty knife. The straightforward *pshat* of the Gemara is that the knives were dirty and greasy. Evidence for this is that the Gemara says that if one alternates between cutting the radish and cutting other items, it is not a problem. If the knife were clean and the issue were purely the power of the *davar charif* to pull out absorbed taste, it would be difficult to understand why cutting other things in between would alleviate the problem — the absorbed taste in the knife's walls would remain regardless. The simplest explanation is that there was grease on the surface of the knife, and cutting other items in between effectively removed that surface grease.

Tosafot reinforces this reading by noting that if even heat — which is a powerful mechanism of taste transfer — does not make *nat bar nat de-hetera* problematic, how can the *tznon* be more powerful than heat? If one cooked a *parve* item in a *fleishig* pot and the result is *nat bar nat de-hetera*, why would cutting with a *fleishig* knife create a greater problem? The implication is that the issue with the knife is the dirty grease on its surface, not the inherent power of the *davar charif* to extract deeply absorbed taste. On a clean knife, there would be no issue at all.

### Stringent Davar Charif

However, there is a competing reading of the Gemara, and it is this more stringent reading that forms the basis of the *Shulchan Aruch*'s ruling. According to this reading, even on a clean knife, the power of a *davar charif* is such that it actively pulls out the absorbed taste from within the knife — and crucially, it does so without heat and without reducing the taste to *nat bar nat*. In other words, the *davar charif* eliminates the "degree of removal" that would otherwise render the transfer a second-stage *heter*. The absorbed *fleishig* taste is pulled directly into the radish at full strength, as if it were a first-degree transfer.

### Combined Stringent Views

The analysis does not stop there. There is an additional Gemara in Avodah Zarah dealing with a particularly sharp substance — *kurtia de-chiltis* — which states that it enhances the taste of fatty foods. When this Gemara is combined with the stringent reading of our Gemara, one arrives at the most severe interpretation: a *davar charif* not only pulls out absorbed taste without heat and without reducing it to *nat bar nat*, but it will do so even from a knife that is *eino ben yomo* — used more than a day ago. The conclusion of this combined reading is that a completely clean *fleishig* knife, last used six weeks ago, renders the radish or onion cut with it fully *fleishig* — despite the knife being clean, despite it being *eino ben yomo*, and despite what would otherwise be the leniency of *nat bar nat de-hetera*.

This is the source of all the major stringencies associated with *davar charif* in practical *halacha*. Whether leniencies are available *bedieved* is a separate discussion, but as these are not the only possible readings of the Gemaras in question, there is room in extreme cases to explore such options.

### Davar Charif Examples

As for which foods qualify as *davar charif*: the Gemara mentions the radish explicitly; onions and garlic are natural additions to the list. Salt is also raised as a candidate, though whether salt operates identically to the classic *davar charif* is subject to debate.

---

## Salt & Sour Milk Vessels

### Salt Dish Placement

We now arrive at the actual beginning of today's daf, four lines down on 112a. *Ba'a minei Rav Dimi me-Rav Nachman* — Rav Dimi posed a question to Rav Nachman: *mahu lehaniach kada de-milcha gabi kada de-kimcha* — may one place a dish of salt next to a dish of *kutach*? *Kutach* was a sour-milk dip, used in their cuisine as a condiment. The salt in question was not a shaker but an open bowl from which one would pinch or sprinkle salt by hand. The concern is straightforward: both vessels are open, there is a risk of inadvertent cross-transfer, and a drop of the *milchig kutach* landing in the salt dish could then be transferred into *fleishig* food at a subsequent meal.

### Salt Forbidden, Vinegar…

Rav Nachman's response: *amar lei assur* — it is forbidden to place the salt dish beside the *kutach*. Rav Dimi then asked the follow-up: *dechala mai* — what if instead of salt, one has an open dish of vinegar next to the *kutach*? *Amar lei shari* — that is permitted. The difference prompted Rav Dimi to press further, and Rav Nachman, in an idiomatic response that is also a playful allusion to the very subject under discussion, invited him to measure out some salt before he would explain — a phrase meaning, essentially, think a bit harder.

### Retention & Dissolution

The reason is as follows: *hai ita issura be-hai ve-hai leita issura be-hai* — with the salt dish, the *issur* remains present in it, whereas with the vinegar dish, the *issur* does not remain present. The operative principle is one of retention versus dissolution. If a drop of *kutach* falls into the salt dish, it sits on top of or among the salt granules and remains there as a discrete presence. The next time one uses the salt and places it on meat, the *milchig* contamination is carried along with it. By contrast, if a drop of *kutach* falls into a dish of vinegar, it dissolves and disperses throughout the large volume of liquid, becoming *batel* — nullified — in the vast quantity of vinegar. There is no discrete remaining presence to be subsequently transferred. The principle emerging from this passage is that *bitul* operates only when the forbidden substance is genuinely dissolved and integrated, not when it retains its distinct identity within the medium into which it falls.

---

## Pigeon in Yogurt Case

### Rav Chinana Permits

A case is now presented: *hahu bar gozla denafal lakada detimcha* — a pigeon fell into a pitcher of *kutach*, that is, a yogurt-like sour milk dip. Here we have meat and dairy together, but without any apparent heat source to drive the taste transfer. *Sharya Rav Chinana brei deRav miParshunya* — Rav Chinana son of Rav Mishparshunya permitted it. *Amar Rava* — Rava remarked with evident admiration: *man chakim lemishrei ki hai gavna i lav Rav Chinana brei deRav miParshunya* — who would have been clever enough to find the basis for permitting this, if not for Rav Chinana? The implied question is why this case requires any particular ingenuity to permit. The pigeon had been salted, as all meat must be, and the principle *maliach ke-roteach* — salted is like boiled — would seem to trigger taste transfer even without heat. Why then is it permitted?

### Maliach K'Roteach Princi…

The answer is that Rav Chinana rules in accordance with a qualification of Shmuel's principle. *Ki amar Shmuel maliach harei hu ke-roteach* — when did Shmuel say that salting is equivalent to boiling? *Hani mili heicha de'eino ne'echal machamat milcho* — only where the food cannot be eaten because of its saltiness. *Aval hai kutcha* — but this *kutach*, *harei ne'echal machamat milcho* — is indeed edible despite its saltiness. It may be salty, but it is not at the threshold level of inedible saltiness that would trigger *maliach ke-roteach*. Therefore, the principle does not apply, and the pigeon is permitted.

The context that produces inedible saltiness is worth clarifying. There are two relevant scenarios: the saltiness of meat that is in the process of being kashered, with heavy salt still resting upon it before rinsing; and in earlier times, the heavy salting used to preserve meat before refrigeration. That is the level of saltiness Shmuel had in mind — salt so heavy that one would never eat the meat in that state.

### Rashi vs Tosafot Saltine…

Rashi and Tosafot disagree on the precise threshold. Rashi maintains that *eino ne'echal machamat milcho* refers to the extreme saltiness of preserved meat — the kind that would be buried in salt for preservation and would only become edible after rinsing. According to Rashi, this level of saltiness is almost never encountered in practice today, making *maliach ke-roteach* a rarely triggered principle. Tosafot disagrees and sets the threshold lower. According to Tosafot, *eino ne'echal machamat milcho* does not require complete inedibility of that extreme degree. Rather, it is sufficient that the food is as salty as *melach kadronit* — the salt used in the kashering process — meaning salty enough that a normal person would not eat the meat in that state without first rinsing off the salt. This is a lower and more common threshold than Rashi's. The practical *halacha* follows Tosafot.

### Ashkenazi Strict Saltine…

The matter does not end with Tosafot's ruling. True to the broader *Ashkenazi* approach of resolving uncertainty through stringency, the *Ashkenazi* position is that since we cannot precisely determine the exact point at which saltiness crosses the threshold of *eino ne'echal machamat milcho*, we apply stringency to all serious saltiness. This does not mean that a trivial pinch of salt used to season food is a concern — that level is not problematic. But once food becomes significantly salty, *Ashkenazim* treat it with the stringency of *maliach ke-roteach* out of concern that it may have crossed the threshold.

### Bahag Salt-Heat Equation

It is worth dwelling further on the underlying equation between salt and heat, because Tosafot frequently cites the *Bahag* — the *Ba'al Halachot Gedolot* — in connection with this principle, and the *Bahag*'s formulation illuminates much of what follows. The *Bahag* addresses a question the Gemara itself never directly answers: how long must meat be salted in order to complete the kashering process? The *Bahag*'s answer draws on Shmuel's equation of *maliach ke-roteach*: since salt works like heat, one salts the meat for as long as it would take for heat to draw out the blood when roasting the meat over an open fire. The comparison is made possible precisely because Shmuel equates the two mechanisms.

Tosafot builds on this to derive the type of saltiness that triggers taste transfer between pieces of food. Since it is the salt used for kashering — salt at the level equivalent to heat — that constitutes the operative degree of saltiness in Shmuel's principle, that same level of saltiness is what can drive taste transfer between adjacent foods. It is the saltiness that is equivalent to the application of heat, and that is why it has the legal effects of heat.

---

## Blood Extraction Law (II)

### Roasted vs Raw Meat

The Gemara now turns to the topic of blood extraction from meat during the roasting process, continuing the practical *halachic* discussion of the previous daf. *Ve-hani mili chai* — this is true, that the pigeon that fell into the *kutach* is permitted, only when it is raw. *Aval tzli, bei klipa* — but if it was roasted, one must remove an outer shell. Furthermore, *ve-ei is bei pili, kulei assur* — if the roasted piece has crevices and cracks throughout, the entire piece is forbidden.

What does "roasted" mean in this context? One reading is that the meat was roasted and still hot, and the heat drives taste transfer directly into the outer layer — hence the requirement to remove an outer shell, *klipa*. But a second and equally compelling reading of this Gemara is that "roasted" does not mean the meat is currently hot, but rather that once meat has been roasted, it becomes more physically absorbent. This point deserves serious consideration, because it engages the *metzius* — the physical reality — and not merely the legal framework.

### Absorbency Without Heat

Consider a piece of soft, well-cooked *cholent* meat that is no longer hot. If it fell into a pitcher of milk and sat there for six hours, one could not simply dismiss the concern on the grounds that there was no *yad soledes bo* — no heat sufficient to transfer taste. A substance that is highly porous and absorbent will take in liquids even at cold temperatures, not through taste transfer in the technical *halachic* sense of heat-driven absorption, but through physical penetration into its pores and crevices. This is what the Gemara means when it says that roasted meat requires *klipa*: not that the meat is hot, but that the roasting process renders it absorbent enough that even without heat, the outer layer will have drawn in the milk.

This is also distinguished from the principle of *kavush* — soaking — which operates over a twenty-four-hour period. What the Gemara describes here is a shorter-term absorption driven purely by the physical absorbency of the roasted meat, not by the extended immersion required for *kavush* to take effect.

If there are crevices in the meat — as in a very porous, well-cooked piece — the concern extends throughout the entire piece, and it is entirely forbidden. The Gemara adds: *ve'im tavlu betavlin* — if the meat has been seasoned with spices, it is similarly forbidden across the board, even without crevices, because the spices themselves increase the osmotic draw of the meat and cause greater absorption of surrounding liquids. The same osmosis principle that explains how salt draws out blood from meat during kashering explains how heavily spiced or salted meat draws liquid inward when immersed.

### Red Juices Status

The Gemara now addresses one of the most practically significant questions in this area: what is the status of the reddish juices that flow from roasted meat? Are they still blood — and therefore forbidden — or are they merely permissible gravy?

*Amar Rav Nachman amar Shmuel: kichra de-chatich alei bisra assur le-michlei* — if one cuts meat on a piece of bread, that bread is forbidden to eat. The concern is that the act of cutting causes juices to run off the meat and absorb into the bread, and those juices are suspected of being blood that was not fully extracted during the original process of salting or roasting.

A fundamental question immediately arises: if there is still blood in the meat, why is one permitted to eat the meat itself? The answer rests on the principle of *dama de-evarim shelo peirash* — blood that is absorbed within the substance of the meat itself and has not emerged. Blood that is genuinely dissolved within the tissue of the meat — not in a visible vein or organ but absorbed throughout the flesh — is halachically permissible as long as it has not separated and come out. Once it exits the meat, it assumes the status of forbidden blood. This is why one may in principle eat raw meat without kashering it: the blood is entirely within the meat and has not *peirash* — it has not separated. It is also why roasting, in contradistinction to cooking, does not create a problem even if not all blood is extracted: what stays in, stays in and is permissible; what comes out, comes out and must not be eaten. Cooking creates the additional problem that blood that emerges during cooking is re-absorbed back into the meat in a new, legally problematic form.

### Shmuel Forbids Red

Shmuel's ruling continues: *ve-hani mili de-asmik* — this is only a concern if the juice that came out is red; *ve-hani mili de-avrai* — and only if it appeared in sufficient quantity to have penetrated through the full thickness of the bread; *ve-hani mili de-afmichi* — and only if the bread is thick, such that the juice has truly soaked all the way through. But *aval klisha* — if the juice is thin and watery, *leit lan bah* — that is not a problem. Thick, red juice that permeates a substantial piece of bread is the scenario Shmuel considers forbidden; thin, dilute liquid is not in the same category.

The Gemara records that when this occurred in practice, Shmuel would throw the juice-soaked bread to his dog — it was not fit for him to eat, but the dog could benefit from it. Rav Huna, by contrast, would give it to his personal attendant, who was Jewish. This prompted the obvious objection: *mima nafshach* — make up your mind. If it is permitted, it is permitted for everyone; if it is forbidden, it is forbidden for everyone. The Gemara resolves this: *shani Rav Huna de-adinin datei* — Rav Huna was simply fastidious, an *istenis*. For him, it was a matter of personal aesthetic preference, not *kashrut*. The bread was entirely kosher; he simply did not wish to eat something stained with red juices. His attendant, who had no such sensibility, was welcome to eat it, and halachically there was nothing wrong with it.

### Rava Permits Red

Rava takes a fundamentally different position from Shmuel: *Rava achil lei* — Rava would eat it, and he called it *chamra de-vasra* — the wine of the meat. In Rava's view, once meat has been properly roasted for the requisite time, whatever red juices emerge afterward are no longer halachically blood; they are simply the natural juices and gravy of roasted meat. The roasting process, when carried out properly, is presumed to have extracted all the blood that is halachically significant. Anything left behind does not carry the status of *dam* — blood — in the legal sense.

Note that this entire discussion concerns roasting specifically, not cooking after salting. If one were to propose that some blood remained after salting and then cooked the meat, the very act of cooking would cause that blood to emerge and then be re-absorbed, creating a genuine problem. Roasting is the only scenario where one can plausibly argue that remaining blood stayed in throughout the process, and therefore the question of whether post-roasting red juices constitute blood is a meaningful one.

The practical ruling follows Rava: after proper roasting, the red juices are permissible. Shmuel's position that even after roasting there may be residual blood that exits under knife pressure is a minority view, though as the Gemara will show, it is internally consistent.

---

## Catching Juices While Ro…

### Vessel Under Roasting

The discussion now turns to the practical mechanics of collecting meat juices during the roasting process itself, without simultaneously collecting the blood that is being expelled. *Ein manichin kli tachat basar ad she-yichleh kol mareh admumit shebo* — one may not place a vessel beneath meat while it is roasting until all the reddish appearance in the juices has ceased. The concern is that while blood is still flowing out, catching the drippings will collect blood along with the gravy. One must therefore wait until the outflow of red juice has stopped before positioning a vessel to catch the drippings.

### Smoke as Indicator

The question is: *mena yadeinan* — how can one tell when all the redness has ceased? One cannot easily monitor all the individual drips falling from a large piece of meat over a fire. *Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Papa* says: *mishe-ya'aleh timrato* — when the smoke rises. Rashi offers two explanations of this indicator: either the meat itself begins to smoke, signaling that all moisture including blood has been expelled; or alternatively, the embers beneath the meat, which are suppressed from smoking as long as blood drips onto them, begin to smoke again once the dripping stops.

### Rav Ashi's Objection

Rav Ashi objects to this criterion: *dilma mitata mata ila lo mata* — perhaps the bottom is fully roasted but the top is not. If one is roasting multiple layers, the smoke indicator might reflect the state of the lower piece near the fire while blood is still flowing from the upper piece that is further from the heat. The smoke rising from the bottom tells us nothing definitive about the top.

### Two Mounds Salt Solution

*Ela amar Rav Ashi: leit leh takanta ela mishdei bah tarti galalei milcha* — the only reliable solution, says Rav Ashi, is to place two mounds of salt in the collection vessel. The principle, striking as it seems to modern sensibilities, is that blood is attracted to the salt and absorbed into it, while the meat juices remain separate and can be collected from around the salt mounds. The blood, being drawn to the salt, is contained within the mounds; what remains is permissible gravy.

### Tosafot Rejects Salt Met…

Tosafot cites the *Bahag* in rejecting the practical applicability of this method. The *Bahag* states explicitly that it must be precisely two mounds: *aval harbeh melach posek koach ha-dam* — if there is more salt than the prescribed amount, it breaks the power of the blood and the mechanism fails, presumably because excess salt disperses the blood throughout the liquid rather than drawing it in and containing it. Too little salt is equally insufficient. Since we are no longer able to determine with confidence the exact measure of two mounds — *ve-ein anu beki'in ba-davar*, we are not expert in this matter — neither more nor less is acceptable, and we therefore cannot rely on this method at all. This is the characteristic *Ashkenazi* formulation: when a precise measure is required and we cannot guarantee it, the entire practice is set aside.

---

## Blood Extraction Law (II)

### Shmuel's Contradictions

The Gemara now returns to Shmuel's position and confronts an apparent internal contradiction. *U-mi amar Shmuel hachi* — did Shmuel really rule that once the red stops coming out during roasting one may collect the drippings? But surely Shmuel himself was the authority who said that cutting meat on bread produces forbidden juice — implying that even after roasting, blood can still be present in the meat and emerge under the pressure of a knife. How can these two positions coexist? If Shmuel believes that roasted meat may still contain blood that exits under knife pressure, how can he simultaneously permit collecting the post-roasting drippings on the grounds that the red has stopped flowing?

The Gemara resolves this through a critical distinction: *shani hatam de-agav duchka de-sakina palit* — the case of the bread is different, because there it is the mechanical pressure of the knife that forces out blood that was otherwise trapped deep within the meat. The roasting process expels whatever blood is capable of flowing out freely, and once that flow has ceased, the remaining juices are permissible. But there is a separate category of blood that is trapped so deeply within the muscle tissue that it cannot emerge through roasting alone. The forceful compression of the knife at the moment of cutting can expel that residual blood, which roasting never reached. Therefore, Shmuel's two rulings are consistent: the cessation of red flow during roasting indicates that freely flowing blood has stopped, and the remaining drippings may be collected; yet even roasted meat may harbor pockets of blood that will exit only under knife pressure, rendering the resulting juice on the bread forbidden.

This is a characteristically nuanced Talmudic resolution. Shmuel does not hold that roasting fails to extract blood as a general proposition. He holds that roasting extracts blood that is capable of flowing under heat, while knife pressure extracts blood that is not. These are two distinct categories, and each ruling addresses its own category correctly.

---

## Salting Fish & Birds

### Fish-Bird Salting Ban

The Gemara presents a new case: *dagim ve-ofot she-melachan zeh im zeh, assur* — fish and birds that were salted together are forbidden. The issue is that the blood being extracted from the birds during kashering may transfer into the fish. In general, one may salt multiple pieces of the same type of meat together without concern that blood drawn from one piece will be absorbed into another. The question is why fish and birds are treated differently.

### Tosafot Explanations

Tosafot undertakes an extensive analysis of the multiple principles that explain why same-type meats may be kashered together without concern, and then demonstrates why fish constitute an exception.

Several principles are at work when same-type meats are salted together. The first is *aidi d'tarid l'miflat lo bala* — since the meat is occupied with expelling blood, it cannot simultaneously absorb. Because all pieces are actively expelling their own blood under the influence of the salt, none of them is in a state to absorb the blood flowing from the others. A potential weakness in this principle, as Tosafot notes, is that it might not account for the moment when one piece finishes expelling before another. Tosafot responds with a variant formulation: it is sufficient that a piece is busy expelling even its own juices — not just blood — to prevent absorption, and even when a piece finishes expelling its blood, it continues to expel juices for some time, which prevents any incoming blood from taking hold.

A third principle is *dam mishrak sharik* — blood is inherently slippery in quality. It does not adhere to surfaces; it glides off. Even if blood from one piece of meat contacts another, it does not penetrate and adhere, but slides away. This property of blood explains why, even setting aside the question of whether a piece is actively expelling, blood-to-meat contact during salting does not result in actual absorption.

### Vessel Must Have Holes

Before addressing why fish are an exception, the Gemara clarifies the precondition for any of this to work at all: *ei bikli she-eino menukav* — if the salting is done in a vessel without holes, so that all the expelled blood pools at the bottom and the meat sits in it, *afilu ofot ve-ofot nami assiri* — even two birds together are forbidden. All the foregoing leniencies depend on the blood draining away: either through a board set at an angle, or through a vessel with holes in the bottom. If blood is pooling and surrounding the meat, re-absorption is assumed, and same-type meats are equally problematic. The case of *bikli menukav* — a vessel with holes — is therefore the assumed background of any permissible kashering arrangement.

### Fish Absorbency Timing

Fish cannot benefit from the same leniencies as birds salted with birds. The reason is twofold. First, *mishum de-rafu karmaihu* — because the outer surface of fish is very soft and highly absorbent, unlike the surface of bird or animal meat, which has a tighter skin. Second, *kadmi ufalti* — fish complete the expulsion of their own juices before the birds have finished expelling their blood. The birds, *kimiti* — they hold back, meaning their blood comes out more slowly, tightly retained at first. *Batar d'naihu dagim, palti ofot* — only after the fish have gone quiet and finished their own expulsion does the bird blood begin to flow. *Ve-hadar bali mineihu* — and then the fish, no longer occupied with their own expulsion and possessing a highly absorbent outer surface, absorb the bird blood.

It follows that if fish were placed on top and birds on the bottom on a slanted board, the bird blood would drain away from the fish rather than into them, and the problem might be avoided. The Gemara's concern is precisely the scenario where the fish are positioned to receive the outflowing bird blood while they themselves are in an absorbent, passive state.

---

## Non-Kosher Mixed Salting

### Trefa-Kosher Mix

The Gemara now presents the case of Rav Mari bar Rachel: he had salted pieces of meat together, and one of the pieces turned out to be *trefa* — it was done unwittingly, as when meat is purchased and only afterward is a disqualifying defect discovered in the animal. The kosher pieces had been salted together with the *trefa* piece on the same platform.

### Non-Kosher Juices Forbid…

He brought the question before Rava. *Amar lei Rava: ha-teme'im, le-asor tsiran ve-rotban ve-kippa shelahen* — Rava cited the verse regarding forbidden animals: not only is the meat of a *trefa* forbidden, but its *tsir* — juices — and *rotev* — gravy — and the *kippa* — the residue or goop in the vessel — are equally forbidden. The great *chiddush* here is that the juices of a non-kosher item carry the same legal status as the item itself and are forbidden just as the meat is.

### Blood vs Juice Transfer

This ruling creates a tension with the earlier analysis of same-type salting. If salting two pieces of kosher meat together is permitted because blood does not transfer — either because the meat is busy expelling or because *dam mishrak sharik*, blood is slippery — why should the juices of the *trefa* piece transfer into the kosher piece?

The resolution is implicit in the distinction between blood and juices. The principle of *dam mishrak sharik* applies specifically to blood: blood is slippery by nature and does not adhere to or penetrate surfaces it contacts. Juices — *tsir* and *rotev* — do not share this property. They are stickier and do penetrate. When kosher and *trefa* meat are salted together, it is not the blood of the *trefa* that transfers into the kosher meat — blood would glide off — but the non-blood juices that are expressed along with the blood, which do transfer and are absorbed.

### Taste vs Thing Itself

This leads to a final observation. One might ask: why does the Torah need a specific verse to tell us that the juices of a non-kosher animal are forbidden? If the principle of *ta'am ke-ikar* — taste is equivalent to the substance itself — applies, then presumably any taste of the *trefa* meat absorbed into another food should be forbidden on that basis alone, without need of a special derivation. The answer appears to be that the juices of meat may not carry the full taste profile of the meat itself. If the juice is distinct enough in character from the flesh that *ta'am ke-ikar* would not straightforwardly apply, then a special verse is required to declare the juice halachically equivalent to the meat and equally forbidden. The verse fills the gap that *ta'am ke-ikar* alone might not cover.

---

---

# Hullin 113

## Salting & Taste Transfer

### Previous Case & Shmuel

The Gemara on 113a opens by returning to the previous discussion concerning the salting of *kosher* and non-*kosher* meat together. By way of review: when *kosher* meat is salted, the blood runs off in a slippery fashion — *dam mishrak sharik* — and does not get absorbed into adjacent pieces of *kosher* meat being salted alongside it. However, when *kosher* meat is salted together with fish or with non-*kosher* meat, the concern is not blood per se but rather the juices (*tzir verotav*) of the non-*kosher* item, which can be absorbed into the *kosher* one.

The Gemara now asks: when the Gemara sought to prove that salting *kosher* and non-*kosher* meat together presents a problem, why did it not simply invoke Shmuel's well-known principle — *maliach harei hu kerose'ach*, that salted food is like roasted food, and *kavush harei hu kemevushal*, that pickled food is like cooked food? If salted is like roasted, presumably Shmuel's statement was addressing precisely such a scenario, in which salting two items together causes a transfer of taste. Why not cite Shmuel directly?

The answer the Gemara provides is that Shmuel's principle alone would be insufficient. *Ee mi-Shmuel, hava amina hani mili daman* — from Shmuel alone, one would have concluded that his statement refers only to blood. That is, Shmuel tells us that salting causes transfer of taste, but the paradigm case he addressed was blood — for instance, meat sitting in a vessel without a hole, saturated in its own blood, or blood being absorbed into fish. His principle establishes the *mechanism* of transfer (salting is like roasting) but says nothing about whether the *juices* of non-*kosher* meat are themselves forbidden.
