One might have thought that *aval tziran verotvan lo* — the juices and brine of non-*kosher* meat would not be halachically prohibited. It therefore required the independent verse — *hatme'im* — to establish that those juices are indeed forbidden. The two sources thus complement one another: Shmuel establishes that salting transfers taste, and the *braita* derived from *hatme'im* establishes that the juices of non-*kosher* meat are subject to the prohibition.

Tosafot address an implicit question: given that the *braita* is a *midrash halacha* and thus *de'oraisa*, why would one prefer Shmuel's teaching over it? Tosafot answer that each source contributes a distinct component of the equation. The *braita* tells us that the juices are forbidden but does not establish that salting is a mode of taste transfer. Shmuel establishes the transfer mechanism. The Gemara's point is therefore that the *braita* alone is not a self-sufficient proof — one needs both.

### Salting vs. Heat

The Gemara proceeds to examine the precise mechanics of *maliach kerose'ach* and the ways in which salting differs from heat as a mode of taste transfer. When it comes to heat, it does not matter which of the two objects in contact is *kosher* or non-*kosher* — what matters at most is which object is on top and which is on the bottom, since heat rises. If the bottom object is hot, it will heat things up more effectively than if only the top object is hot. But the identity of the *kosher* versus *treif* item is irrelevant for heat-based transfer.

With salting, the analysis is fundamentally different, because the primary mechanism of salt is to draw out the juices of the object being salted. If one has salted *kosher* fish alongside non-*kosher* fish that has not been salted, there is no problem — the salt will only draw the juices out of the *kosher* fish; it will not pull anything out of the unsalted non-*kosher* fish. The crucial variable in salting, therefore, is specifically whether the *non-kosher* item has been salted. Only if the non-*kosher* item is salted will its juices be drawn out and potentially absorbed into the *kosher* item.

### Braita Ambiguity

The Gemara raises a challenge from a *braita*: *dag tahor shemalcho im dag tamei, mutar* — if one salted a *kosher* fish together with a non-*kosher* fish, it is permitted. The natural reading of this *braita* is that both fish were salted together, and yet the result is *mutar*. If so, this appears to contradict the position that salting both items together causes a forbidden transfer of taste.

The Gemara responds: *lo, kegon shehaya tahor maliach vetamei tafel* — no, the *braita* is describing the case where the *kosher* fish was salted and the non-*kosher* fish was *tafel*, meaning plain and unsalted. It is only *mutar* because the *treif* item was not salted and thus its juices were not drawn out. The case where both are salted would indeed be forbidden.

But the Gemara then complicates matters further. The *braita* continues: *haya tamei maliach vetahor tafel assur* — if the non-*kosher* fish was the one that was salted and the *kosher* fish was unsalted, it is forbidden. The implication of this formulation — *michlal dereisha shnayim meluchim askinan* — is that the first clause must have been discussing the case where both were salted, and even so it was *mutar*. This would undermine the position that salting both together is a problem.

### Non-Kosher Salted

The Gemara responds that the second clause of the *braita* is not a separate ruling but an explanation of the first: *perushei kamfaresh* — it is explaining what the first clause means. The *braita* states that salting a *kosher* fish together with a non-*kosher* fish is *mutar* — and then immediately clarifies: under what circumstance? When the *kosher* fish was salted and the non-*kosher* fish was *tafel*. It is only in that specific case that the ruling of *mutar* applies.

### Both Salted Problem

The Gemara acknowledges that if this reading is correct — that the first clause of the *braita* deals with the case where only the *kosher* fish was salted — then one might ask why the *braita* bothers to state the case at all. If both being salted were *mutar*, it would be unnecessary to state that only one being salted is also *mutar*. The Gemara therefore explains: *tana seifa legiluyei reisha* — the second clause was taught to clarify the first. Without the second clause, one might have read the first clause as referring to the case of both being salted. By specifying the case of *tahor maliach vetamei tafel*, the *braita* signals what it meant in the first clause. But this also means, the Gemara concludes, that one cannot derive from the *braita* an absolute ruling about what happens when both are salted.

The *sof davar* is that the *braita* cannot definitively prove whether two items being salted together is *mutar* or *assur*. The simple reading of the *braita* is that both being salted is *mutar*, but the Gemara demonstrates that it can be read otherwise. What does emerge clearly is that if only the non-*kosher* item is salted, it is forbidden — *tamei maliach vetahor tafel assur* — and if only the *kosher* item is salted, it is permitted. The case of both being salted remains unresolved by the *braita*, and thus the ruling established previously stands: a special principle applies to the *kashering* of meat with blood — *dam mishrak sharik* — but outside that specific context, even if both items are spewing out their juices simultaneously, the *kosher* item can still absorb from the non-*kosher* one, and two items salted together do present a problem.

The essential asymmetry between salting and heat thus remains in place: with heat, the *kosher* or *treif* identity of the hot object is irrelevant; with salt, the decisive question is specifically whether the *non-kosher* item is salted.

---

## Salting for Kashering

### Blood Release Principle

The Gemara now transitions from the question of taste transfer through salting to the laws governing the *melichah* process itself — the salting of meat to remove blood before cooking. This discussion is anchored by a statement of Shmuel: *eina basar yotzei midei damo* — meat does not fully release all of its blood on its own. The implication is significant: unlike roasting, where whatever blood comes out comes out and whatever remains inside is not a problem (since it is not going anywhere once the meat is cooked *berotav*), the *melichah* process requires that *all* the blood be extracted. The reason is that after salting, the meat will be placed in a pot and cooked, and if any blood remains, it will flow out into the liquid and then be reabsorbed. Therefore, salting demands a thoroughness that roasting does not.

### Salting Practice

Shmuel accordingly rules: *ela im ken molcho yafeh yafeh umadicho yafeh yafeh* — one must salt the meat very well and rinse it very well. Admittedly, this formulation — "very well" — is not particularly precise, which points to the importance of a *mimetic* tradition in the transmission of *melichah* practice. How much salt, how long, at what angle the board should be tilted — these are matters better learned in practice from a parent or teacher than deduced from a textual description. In fact, one can find the basic rules of *koshering* printed on the side of packaged *kosher* salt in the supermarket: rinse the meat, salt it, leave it on a slanted surface for approximately 18 minutes, then rinse it again.

### Rinse-Salt Order

A *tannaitic* dispute is then cited regarding the order of rinsing and salting. Rav Huna rules *moleach umadiach* — one salts and then rinses. A *baraita*, however, teaches *madiach umoleach umadiach* — one rinses first, then salts, then rinses again. The Gemara reconciles the two positions: *hada de-chalei beit tavcha* — Rav Huna's ruling applies to a case where the meat was already rinsed in the butcher's shop. If it arrived pre-rinsed, one need only salt and rinse. If it was not rinsed at the butcher, the full three-step process of the *baraita* applies.

### Pre-Salting Rinse

Why must one rinse the meat *before* salting? Since the entire point is to extract the blood, why does it matter that there is surface blood present at the start? The *rishonim* offer approximately eight distinct reasons, which cluster around two underlying concerns. One category of answer holds that blood already on the surface, rather than being drawn out by the salt, may actually be driven inward by it, making the *kashering* counterproductive for those surface areas. Another category holds that rinsing first softens the meat, making it more receptive to the salt and thus making the salting process more effective. The pre-salting rinse should not use water that is too hot, as hot water would itself drive blood into the meat.

### Rav Dimi & Organs

The Gemara records that Rav Dimi Mi-Nehardea would salt with *milcha galinata* — thick salt, effectively what we would call *kosher* salt — and then *u-menafitz lei*, he would shake it off, scattering the excess salt from the surface before rinsing. Rav Mesharshaya then adds a separate ruling: *ein machazikin dam bifnei mei-ayim* — one need not be concerned about blood in the inner organs. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to the rectum, stomach, and large intestine. Whatever the physiological explanation, these organs are not halachically considered to contain *dam* in the relevant sense and do not require the usual blood-extraction treatment.

### Salt Mechanics

Rashi's comment on *u-menafitz lei* illuminates the reason for using thick salt in *kashering*. He explains that shaking off the salt is necessary *le-milcha le-achar zman* — after the salting period, before rinsing, so that the blood-saturated salt does not get reabsorbed into the meat. He further notes that thin salt (*melach dakka*) would not require shaking off, since it dissolves and washes away on its own. This might suggest thin salt is preferable. In practice, however, thick *kosher* salt is used because its larger, flatter crystals cover more surface area, draw out blood more effectively by remaining on the surface without penetrating the meat, and result in a less excessively salty final product.

### Vessel Requirements

Shmuel rules: *ein manichin basar maliach ela al gabi kli menukav* — one may not leave salted meat on anything other than a perforated vessel. This ensures that the blood draining from the meat does not pool beneath the meat and get reabsorbed. The same principle underlies the requirement to use a slanted board — the blood must run off and away from the meat, not collect beneath it.

### Individual vs. Multiple

Rav Sheshet would salt each piece of meat individually — *garma garma* — rather than salting multiple pieces together. The Gemara asks why he did not salt multiple pieces at once. The answer: he was concerned that blood running off one piece would be absorbed by an adjacent piece — *mishum de-parish mei-hai u-vala hai*. The Gemara, however, dismisses this concern. Even a single piece of meat would present the same problem — blood runs off the top surface and is absorbed by the bottom — yet we do not concern ourselves with that. Rather, the principle is *lo shna*: while a piece of meat is actively being salted and expelling blood, it does not simultaneously absorb blood from an adjacent piece. Tosafot works through the precise mechanics of this principle at length, noting that even if a lower layer of meat has finished salting before an upper layer has been added and is still expelling blood, the blood will simply slide off. The Gemara's conclusion is clear: one may salt multiple pieces together without concern.

### Neck-Breaking Prohibition

Shmuel then rules in the name of Rabbi Chiya: *ha-shover mafrakta she-beheima kodem she-teitzei nafsha, harei ze machbid et habasar vegozel et habriot umavlia dam baeivarim* — one who breaks the neck of an animal that has been *shechted* but before its life has fully departed is doing three things wrong. First, the meat becomes heavier — *machbid et habasar* — because blood that would have flowed out remains inside. Second, this constitutes *gezel*, a form of robbery — *gozel et habriot* — because if the butcher sells the meat by weight, the purchaser is receiving less actual meat and more blood per pound than anticipated. Third, and most serious for our purposes, *umavlia dam baeivarim* — the blood becomes embedded in the organs and limbs.

This third point is critical because of the difference between roasting and salting established above. When roasting, the blood can flow out as the meat cooks, and not all of it needs to come out beforehand. But when salting, all the blood must be extracted before the meat goes into the pot. If the neck-breaking maneuver has caused blood to become embedded and unable to exit through normal salting, the *kashering* itself is compromised.

### Kashering Doubt

The Gemara raises a *ibaia lehu* — an unresolved question. When Shmuel says that breaking the neck weighs down the meat and is a form of robbery, does he mean that *kashering* is still theoretically possible but the blood content makes the meat heavier and thus the seller is cheating the buyer? If so, it would be permitted to do this for one's own use — *ledidei shapir dami* — since there is no *gezel* involved, and the meat can still be *kashered*. Or does Shmuel mean that the blood becomes so embedded that *kashering* is genuinely ineffective? If so, even for one's own use it would be forbidden, since the meat cannot be rendered *kosher* through salting.

The Gemara concludes with *teiku* — the question remains unresolved. The practical ruling is therefore not to do it in any case.

---

## Meat & Cheese Table

### Poultry & Cheese

The *Mishnah* now states: *hamaleh et ha'of im hagevinah al hashulchan eino over belo ta'aseh* — one who places poultry and cheese on the same table does not transgress a biblical prohibition. This *Mishnah* is clarifying the rabbinic nature of the restriction against having meat and cheese at the same table simultaneously. The setting of the table together is, at most, a rabbinic prohibition — it is not a violation of the Torah's prohibition of *basar bechalav*.

### Poultry Reading

The Gemara, however, attempts to read something more into the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* specifies that *ha'ochlo over belo ta'aseh* — one who *eats* them together transgresses a biblical prohibition. Might this imply that there is a *Tanna* who holds that eating poultry cooked with milk constitutes a biblical transgression? *Shema mina basar of bechalav de'oraita* — perhaps we can infer that chicken and milk is a biblical prohibition.

The Gemara rejects this reading: *eima hamaleh et of im gevinah al hashulchan eina ba lidei lo ta'aseh* — the *Mishnah* means only that having poultry and cheese on the table together can never even lead to a biblical prohibition, precisely because the biblical prohibition does not apply to poultry at all. As the subsequent *Mishnah* will make clear, the Torah says *lo tevashel gedi bachalav imo* — a kid in its *mother's* milk — and birds have no mother's milk. It is difficult to understand how birds could ever be included in the biblical prohibition. Nevertheless, the Gemara makes the attempt to read into the earlier *Mishnayot* the possibility of a *Tanna* who holds that birds are included — though this is never said explicitly by any named *Tanna*, and we do not rule that way.

---

## Meat & Milk Biblical

### Tanna Kamma Rule

The next *Mishnah* now sets out the scope of the biblical prohibition of *basar bechalav* directly. The *Tanna Kamma* states: *basar behemah tehorah bechalav behemah tehorah assur levashel ve'assur behana'ah* — the meat of a *kosher behemah* (a domesticated mammal such as a cow, sheep, or goat) cooked with the milk of such a *kosher behemah* is biblically forbidden to cook, and furthermore one may not derive any benefit (*hana'ah*) from it whatsoever. The prohibition thus extends beyond eating to all forms of benefit.

### Non-Kosher Species

The *Mishnah* continues: *basar behemah tehorah bechalav behemah teme'ah* — the meat of a *kosher* animal with the milk of a non-*kosher* animal, or *basar behemah teme'ah bechalav behemah tehorah* — the meat of a non-*kosher* animal with the milk of a *kosher* animal — *mutar levashal vemutar behana'ah*: it is permitted to cook them together and permitted to derive benefit from the result.

Of course, the meat or milk of a non-*kosher* species remains forbidden to eat for its own reasons — but it does not trigger the *basar bechalav* prohibition, not even rabbinically. The rationale is striking: once the non-*kosher* species is involved, the rabbis saw no need to add an additional prohibition of *basar bechalav* on top of an existing *issur*. The result is that one may even cook pig meat with cow's milk, or cow's meat with pig's milk, without violating *basar bechalav* — either biblically or rabbinically — and may derive benefit from the result.

It should be noted carefully, however, that this leniency applies specifically when the *species* is non-*kosher*. Non-*shechted* meat of a *kosher* species — *treif* cow's meat, for example — does not benefit from this leniency. Cooking non-*shechted* cow's meat with milk is still *assur bevishul ve'assur behana'ah*.

### Chicken Cooking

A separate question arises regarding poultry. Can chicken be cooked with milk? The *Rambam* derives from this *Mishnah* a broader principle: anything not biblically prohibited as *basar bechalav* may be cooked with milk and the result may be used for *hana'ah*. Other *rishonim* disagree, arguing that the *Mishnah*'s leniency with non-*kosher* species is a special case — it is because those items already carry their own independent *issur* that the rabbis did not pile on an additional *basar bechalav* prohibition. For something like chicken and milk, where the items are individually *kosher* but only *rabbinically* prohibited as *basar bechalav*, the rabbis would certainly have prohibited cooking them together.

Nevertheless, the ruling follows the *Rambam*: while one may not have chicken and cheese at the same table, one *may* cook chicken and milk together, provided one does not eat the result. One may cook the dish and give it to one's dog, give it to a non-Jew, or otherwise derive benefit from it.

This is admittedly counterintuitive and somewhat paradoxical. The biblical prohibition is stated in terms of *cooking* — *lo tevashel* — yet in practice the emphasis has shifted almost entirely to *eating*, such that we impose rabbinic restrictions around eating (including the table restriction) while not extending those restrictions to the act of cooking itself. Nonetheless, that is how the *Rambam* reads the *Mishnah* and how we rule.

### Benefit Prohibition

The prohibition of *hana'ah* from *basar bechalav* has significant practical implications that are not immediately obvious. A common contemporary example is dog food: much commercial dog food consists of meat cooked with milk-derived ingredients. If the meat is of a *kosher* species — even if it is not *shechted* — buying such dog food and feeding it to one's dog may constitute deriving *hana'ah* from cooked meat and milk.

One might think that since the meat is *neveilah* — not *shechted* — it would not be subject to the *basar bechalav* prohibition. But this raises the question of *issur chal al issur*: can the prohibition of *basar bechalav* take effect on meat that is already forbidden as *neveilah*? The question of *issur chal al issur* bears directly on whether such dog food becomes forbidden in *hana'ah* as well as in the act of cooking. This issue is somewhat debated, but the upshot is that one must exercise care when purchasing dog food or cat food that combines meat and milk ingredients.

---

## Chayah & Bird Debate

### Mother's Milk Limit

Rabbi Akiva adds his voice to the *Mishnah*'s discussion: *chayah ve'of einam min haTorah* — wild animals (*chayah*) and birds are not included in the biblical prohibition. His derivation is based on the three occurrences of the verse *lo tevashel gedi bachalav imo* in the Torah. The starting assumption is that the prohibition is general — it refers to meat and milk broadly. The word *gedi* (kid) appears three times to *limit* the scope: only meat that is analogous to a *gedi* is included. The three exclusions are: *prat lechayah* — to exclude wild animals, *ule'of* — to exclude birds, and *uvehemah teme'ah* — to exclude non-*kosher* domesticated animals.

### Neveilah Inclusion

Rabbi Yossi HaGelili takes a different approach. His derivation is built on a juxtaposition within the Torah itself. The verse reads: *lo tochlu kol neveilah... lo tevashel gedi bachalav imo* — "do not eat *neveilah*... do not cook a kid in its mother's milk." From the juxtaposition, Rabbi Yossi HaGelili derives: *et she'assur mishum neveilah assur levashel bachalav* — anything that falls under the *neveilah* prohibition is also subject to the *basar bechalav* prohibition. This would include not only domesticated mammals (*behemah*) but also wild animals (*chayah*) and even birds, all of which are subject to *neveilah* if not properly *shechted*.

However, the same verse that includes them also limits them: *bachalav imo* — the mother's milk. A bird has no mother's milk. *Yatza of she'ein lo chalav em* — birds are excluded because the verse explicitly requires mother's milk, and birds produce none. The debate between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, then, concerns *chayah*: Rabbi Akiva excludes *chayah* from the *biblical* prohibition along with birds; Rabbi Yossi HaGelili includes *chayah*, since they do have mother's milk and are subject to *neveilah*.

---

## Shmuel's Gedi Drasha (II)

### Gedi Broadening

Before presenting Shmuel's expansive *drashas* on the word *gedi*, the Gemara first establishes that *gedi* is not limited to a goat. Rabbi Elazar cites the verse *Vayishlach Yehudah et gedi ha'izim* — Judah sent a kid *of the goats*. The fact that the Torah specifies *gedi ha'izim* — a kid *goat* — implies that when it wishes to speak of a goat specifically, it says so explicitly. When it simply says *gedi* without qualification, the term is broader and refers to any young animal. *Hacol makom shenemar gedi stam afilu parah urechelah bemashma* — whenever *gedi* appears without further specification, it encompasses any young animal, including a calf or a lamb.

One might counter: perhaps the paradigm of *gedi ha'izim* teaches the opposite — that *gedi* always means a goat, and only with the addition of *ha'izim* is it explicitly a goat? The Gemara answers that there is yet another verse — *ve'et orot gedayei ha'izim* (the skins of kids of the goats, from the story of Yaakov) — that also specifies *ha'izim* explicitly. The existence of two verses that feel the need to specify *ha'izim* means that these are not functioning as normative paradigms but as *shnei ketuvim ha-ba'im ke'echad* — two verses arriving together to teach the same point, which paradoxically *cannot* serve as a normative paradigm according to one interpretive tradition. Rather, both are limiting the word in those verses to goats, which demonstrates that elsewhere *gedi* is more general.

### Inclusive Drashas

Shmuel derives three inclusive *drashas* from the three appearances of *gedi*. First, *gedi lerabot et hachelev* — the word *gedi* broadens the prohibition to include *chelev*, the forbidden fat of an animal. If one cooks *chelev* with milk, one transgresses the prohibition of *basar bechalav* in addition to the independent prohibition of eating *chelev* — fat is considered a form of meat for this purpose. Second, *gedi lerabot et hameta* — *gedi* includes an animal that died on its own (*neveilah*), even though it already carries its own prohibition. Third, *gedi lerabot et hashallil* — *gedi* includes the fetus of an animal.

### Exclusive Drashas

Against these three expansive *drashas*, Shmuel also derives three narrowing ones. *Gedi lehotzi et hadam* — blood is excluded; cooking blood with milk does not constitute *basar bechalav*. *Gedi lehotzi et hashilya* — the placenta or afterbirth is excluded; it is not considered meat. *Gedi lehotzi et hatmeia* — a non-*kosher* animal is excluded, consistent with the *Mishnah*'s ruling and the derivations of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yossi HaGelili.

---

## Meat Definition

### Mother's Milk Source

The Gemara adds a further set of exclusions derived not from the word *gedi* but from the phrase *bachalav imo* — in its *mother's* milk. This phrase yields three additional limits: *velo bechalav zachar* — the prohibition does not apply to milk that comes from a male animal (which, while physiologically unusual, can occasionally occur); *velo bechalav shechuta* — it does not apply to milk that is inside a slaughtered animal's udder, as in the case of *kachal*, which was discussed at length earlier in the tractate; and *velo bechalav teme'ah* — it does not apply to the milk of a non-*kosher* animal. In short, *bachalav imo* requires that the milk be from a living mother of a *kosher* species, produced naturally during her lifetime.

---

## Shmuel's Gedi Drasha (II)

### Drasha Resolution

Having established that Shmuel derives six *drashas* from the word *gedi* — three inclusive and three exclusive — the Gemara notes a difficulty: *aha tlata gedi ketivi veshisha darshinan* — but *gedi* only appears three times in the relevant verses. How can Shmuel extract six distinct *drashas* from three occurrences?

The Gemara's resolution is that three of those *drashas* were, strictly speaking, unnecessary. *De'issur chelev ve-neveilah mechada kra nafka* — the inclusion of *chelev* and *neveilah* can both be derived from a single verse, since both cases present the same underlying point: one *issur* takes hold upon another. Similarly, blood's exclusion from the category of *meat* does not require a verse — it is self-evident that blood is not meat. And the placenta's exclusion likewise needs no verse — it is simply refuse, not flesh. These three *drashas* were therefore not each consuming one of the three *gedi* occurrences in a meaningful way. The actual required *drashas* are: one for *chelev* and *neveilah* together (the principle of *issur chal al issur*), one to include the fetus, and one to exclude the non-*kosher* species.

### Issur Chal Al Issur

Shmuel's position that *issur chal al issur* — one prohibition can take hold upon another already-existing prohibition — is the linchpin of why he needs no separate verse to include *chelev* and *neveilah* in the *basar bechalav* prohibition. Since he holds this principle as a general rule, it is already understood that cooking *chelev* with milk creates a double *issur*: the independent prohibition of *chelev* and the additional prohibition of *basar bechalav*. Similarly with *neveilah*: the meat of a *kosher* animal that died without *shechitah* is already forbidden as *neveilah*, yet Shmuel holds that cooking it with milk adds the *basar bechalav* prohibition on top of it.

This principle also has direct bearing on the dog food question raised earlier. When non-*shechted* cow's meat is cooked with milk, the question is whether the *basar bechalav* prohibition — which includes a prohibition of *hana'ah* — can take effect on meat already forbidden as *neveilah*. That is a specific application of *issur chal al issur* that remains the subject of debate and will be continued in the next *shiur*.

---

## Meat Definition (II)

### Fat Blood Placenta

The Gemara closes with a clarification of the three-part distinction that Shmuel's analysis yields regarding what constitutes *meat* for the purposes of *basar bechalav*. *Chelev* — forbidden fat — is considered meat and is therefore included in the prohibition. *Dam* — blood — is not considered meat and is therefore excluded. *Shilya* — the placenta or afterbirth — is also not considered meat and is excluded. The fetus, by contrast, is included.

The underlying principle that emerges is that the category of *meat* for *basar bechalav* is not simply coextensive with everything that comes from an animal. Blood and placenta, despite being animal products, fall outside the definition. Fat, despite carrying its own independent prohibition, falls within it. These distinctions will continue to be developed in the subsequent discussion.

---

---

# Hullin 114

## Shmuel's Parameters

### Gedi & Imo Derivation

The daf begins at the bottom of 113b, several lines above where the text widens, at the line beginning with the word *behemah*. The preceding discussion had established that Shmuel derived various parameters of *basar be-chalav* from the words *gedi* and *imo* in the verse *lo tevashel gedi be-chalav imo*. Among the rulings Shmuel produced from this derivation is the rule that one is liable even when the meat was never properly slaughtered — that is, even *neveilah* — and even when the meat in question is *chelev*, forbidden fat. Although *chelev* already carries its own *issur*, Shmuel held that the prohibition of *basar be-chalav* takes effect upon it nonetheless, because the verse teaches that one *issur* can take effect on top of another.

### Issur Chal al Issur Deba…

This ruling immediately prompts the Gemara's challenge: *ve-savar Shmuel issur chal al issur?* Does Shmuel truly maintain that one prohibition takes hold upon another? For Shmuel himself is reported to have said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: how do we know that a *kohen tamei* who ate *terumah tme'ah* — impure *terumah* — is not liable to the more severe punishment of death at the hand of Heaven? The verse states *u-metu vo ki yechaleluhu*, "they shall die thereby if they desecrate it," which the Gemara understands as excluding the case where the *terumah* was already pre-desecrated — *she-mechulelet ve-omedet*. The logic, as the Gemara reads it at this stage, is that the new *issur* of the *kohen tamei* eating *terumah* does not take effect upon an object already rendered forbidden by its prior state of impurity. If Shmuel endorsed this position, how can he simultaneously maintain that *issur chal al issur* applies in the case of *basar be-chalav*?

### Three Resolutions

The Gemara offers three possible resolutions. The first: *be-alma issur chal al issur* — perhaps Shmuel's general position is that one prohibition does take effect upon another, and his ruling about *basar be-chalav* simply reflects that general principle. The exceptional case of *terumah tme'ah* is explained by the specific verse *u-metu vo ki yechaleluhu*, which carves out a special exclusion, limiting liability to cases where an act of genuine desecration occurs. That is a textual anomaly, not a window into Shmuel's broader jurisprudence.

The second resolution inverts this: perhaps Shmuel's general principle is that *ein issur chal al issur*, one prohibition does not ordinarily take hold upon another. His ruling regarding *basar be-chalav* is then explained by the redundancy of the word *gedi* — the Torah's deliberate repetition of that term serves to teach that even in cases of pre-existing *issur*, the prohibition of *basar be-chalav* takes effect. The case of *terumah tme'ah* reflects the general rule, while *basar be-chalav* is the exception made explicit by the extra word.

The third resolution dissolves the tension entirely: the opinion permitting *issur chal al issur* is Shmuel's own, while the ruling about *terumah tme'ah* was transmitted in the name of Rabbi Eliezer — a *tanna* who held otherwise. The two statements need not be reconciled because they represent different authorities. One observes that the Gemara does not invoke the familiar formula *Rav tanna hu u-falig* with respect to Shmuel, though in this context the difference in view is between Shmuel and his teacher's tradition, and the subject matter belongs to an established *issur ve-heter* dispute among the *Tannaim*, so Shmuel's position is not without grounding.

The practical stakes here are considerable. The question of whether *basar be-chalav* applies to *neveilah* — non-*shechted* meat — has direct relevance to the overwhelming majority of meat in commercial circulation, and raises downstream questions about whether one may derive *hana'ah* from, say, a cooked mixture of *neveilah* and milk. Even if *ein issur chal al issur* saves a person from *lashes* for eating such a mixture, the prohibition of *hana'ah* — which does not pre-exist in the mixture — would still take effect. These are questions with genuine practical import.

---

## Milk Parameters

### Pregnant Animal Milk

The Gemara moves to refine the parameters of what qualifies as *chalav* for purposes of *basar be-chalav*. The question posed — attributed in some versions to Rav and in others to Rava — is: *ha-mevashel be-chalav gedi she-lo hinika mahu?* What is the law if one cooks in the milk of an animal that has never nursed? Earlier discussion had already excluded milk found in the udder of a slaughtered animal, since milk that was never expressed during the animal's life is not considered *chalav aim* — the milk of a living mother. The present question concerns a different scenario: an animal that is heavily pregnant, already lactating, but has not yet given birth and therefore has never actually been a mother. The milk has physically left the body of the animal and is available, yet the animal has not yet crossed the threshold of motherhood.

### Female Milk Status

The answer given draws on Shmuel's own formulation, which had excluded only the milk of a male animal. The reasoning: *zachar hu de-lo atei le-chalav* — a male could never reach the status of a milk-producing mother, which is why its milk is excluded. But the pregnant female in question — *kivan de-ba lei le-chalav* — will in fact become a mother. She is on the threshold of that status. Therefore, her milk is *assur*. The criterion is not whether motherhood has already been actualized, but whether the animal belongs to the category of those that can be mothers. A female who has not yet given birth but is fully capable of doing so falls within the prohibition.

---

## Cooking vs. Eating

### Initial Lashes Question

The Gemara now turns to a question with both conceptual depth and practical urgency: *ha-mevashel chelev be-chalav* — one who cooks forbidden fat together with milk. We have already established that *chelev* is treated as a form of meat for purposes of *basar be-chalav*. So the question is not whether such a combination is conceptually covered by the prohibition, but whether one receives *malkot* — lashes — for performing the act of cooking.

### Ami & Assi Debate

Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi disagree. One holds *lokei* — liable to lashes; the other holds *eino lokei* — not liable. The Gemara's initial framing of the dispute casts it as turning on *issur chal al issur*: the one who says *lokei* holds that one *issur* takes effect on another, meaning the prohibition of *basar be-chalav* operates alongside the pre-existing *issur* of *chelev*, and since one would receive lashes for eating the mixture under *basar be-chalav*, one likewise receives lashes for cooking it. The one who says *eino lokei* holds that *ein issur chal al issur*, so *basar be-chalav* never takes effect on the *chelev* meat at all — and since there is no *basar be-chalav* liability for eating it, there is similarly none for cooking it.

### Primary Concern Framing

But the Gemara rejects this framing and offers a more penetrating alternative. It may be, the Gemara says, that *everyone* agrees that *ein issur chal al issur* — that for purposes of *eating* the mixture, one would not receive lashes under *basar be-chalav*, since the prohibition of *chelev* already pre-exists and the new prohibition does not take hold. The disagreement, says the Gemara, is exclusively about *bishul* — the act of cooking itself. This reframing forces a fundamental question about the relationship between the Torah's prohibition of cooking and the prohibition of eating *basar be-chalav*.

### Independence Theory

The dispute may hinge on whether *bishul* and *achilah* are independent concerns or whether one is derivative of the other. The Torah never says *lo tochal gedi be-chalav imo*. It says *lo tevashel* — do not cook. So one way of understanding the structure of the prohibition is that cooking is the primary concern, and eating is the derivative safeguard. From this perspective, one might compare the prohibition to that of *kilayim*: the Torah's fundamental concern is the improper act of creating the mixture, and any prohibition on enjoying or consuming the product would be a downstream consequence. When it comes to *bishul*, then, there is only a single *issur* involved — no doubling up — and therefore the one who says *lokei* is saying that cooking is entirely independent of the eating prohibition. Whether or not one will receive lashes for eating the mixture later is irrelevant to whether one transgresses in the moment of cooking.

### Derivative Theory

The other direction, however, is the one reflected in the way rabbinic tradition overwhelmingly relates to *basar be-chalav*: the focus is on the *eating*, and the prohibition of *bishul* is a safeguard erected to prevent one from coming to eat. This is also how the Rambam frames the prohibition — the Torah was so concerned that one not eat this combination that it legislated distance from it by prohibiting even the cooking. On this understanding, cooking is a function of eating; it is a protective hedge rather than an independent prohibition.

From this framing, the Gemara articulates the opinion that says *eino lokei* for cooking in the following terms: *le-hachi afkei Rachmana le-achilah bi-leshon bishul* — the Torah expressed the prohibition of eating in the language of cooking, and this teaches that the two are connected. *Keivan de-achilah lo laki, a-bishul nami lo laki* — since one does not receive lashes for eating the mixture (because *ein issur chal al issur*), one likewise does not receive lashes for cooking it, because cooking is a derivative of eating.

### Derivative Theory

The *ika de-amri* version of the Gemara reverses the framing entirely. Here, both opinions agree that *bishul* is independent and that one always receives lashes for cooking the mixture — that is the primary prohibition. The debate is then only about *achilah*. The one who says *eino lokei* for eating applies *ein issur chal al issur* in the normal way, with eating saved from *basar be-chalav* lashes by the preexisting *chelev* prohibition. But the one who says *lokei* for eating reasons in the opposite direction: *le-hachi afkei Rachmana le-achilah bi-leshon bishul* — the Torah's formulation of the eating prohibition in the language of cooking teaches that the connection runs the other way. *Keivan de-a-bishul laki, achilah nami laki* — since cooking is the primary concern and one transgresses there, the product of that cooking carries the prohibition through into eating as well, even in a case where one would normally say that the second *issur* does not take hold.

### Possible Resolution

The Gemara closes this sugya with a possible resolution: *mar chada u-mar chada ve-lo pligi* — one statement refers to *bishul* and the other to *achilah*, and they do not actually disagree. The practical upshot, which the Gemara never frames as straightforwardly permissible, is that lashes for the act of eating may be avoided in cases of doubling up — but the prohibition of cooking together remains in force regardless. The Rambam, notably, rules that one does receive lashes for cooking *neveilah* or *chelev* together with milk, reinforcing that the leniency from *ein issur chal al issur* operates, at most, with respect to eating, not to *bishul* itself. This is why the question of cooking *neveilah be-chalav* is a real and live concern for those learning in professional culinary settings, for instance, where the act of cooking such a combination — not merely eating it — is the act in question.

---

## Exemptions List

### Mei Chalav Exemption

The Gemara cites a *baraita* listing cases that are exempt from the *basar be-chalav* prohibition: *ha-mevashel be-mei chalav patur* — one who cooks with *mei chalav*, milk water, is exempt. The identity of *mei chalav* is the subject of a debate among the *Rishonim*. Some identify it as whey — the watery liquid that separates from curds during cheese-making. Others, notably the Rosh, hold that whey retains full biblical *chalav* status. The Rosh identifies *mei chalav* instead as the pure aqueous component of milk, the H₂O constituent that remains once all the substantive milk content has been removed — analogous to what one might think of as the water extracted in the production of powdered milk. Whatever the precise identification, the category is defined by a component of milk so attenuated that it no longer qualifies as *chalav* in the biblical sense.

### Blood Exemption

The *baraita* continues: *dam she-bishlo be-chalav patur* — blood cooked with milk is exempt. The reason is that blood is not considered meat. Just as *mei chalav* fails the milk requirement, blood fails the meat requirement.

### Inedible Parts

Similarly, *atzamot ve-hagidim ve-hakarnayim ve-ha-tlafahim she-bishlam be-chalav patur* — bones, sinews, horns, and hooves cooked with milk are exempt, because they too are not considered meat. The implicit qualification holds that this applies only when there is no marrow or edible content within the bones.

### Forbidden Meat Liable

In contrast: *ha-piggul, ha-nosar, ve-ha-tamei she-bishlam be-chalav chayav* — if one cooked *piggul* (a sacrificial offering invalidated by improper intent), *nosar* (sacrificial meat left beyond its permitted time), or ritually impure meat together with milk, one is *liable*. These are already forbidden categories of meat. The *baraita* thus makes clear that pre-existing forbidden status of the meat does not exempt from the *basar be-chalav* cooking prohibition.

### Baraita Analysis

One might think this *baraita* definitively proves that *bishul* is independent of *achilah*: even if one would not receive lashes for eating *piggul* cooked in milk — since the *issur* of *piggul* preexists — the *baraita* declares one liable for the cooking. But the Gemara deflects: *hai tanna savar issur chal al issur* — this *tanna* may hold that one prohibition does take effect upon another, and therefore also receives lashes for eating the mixture. The *baraita* thus does not prove that *bishul* is independent of *achilah* in a case where everyone agrees one would *not* receive lashes for eating. The question remains unresolved.

---

## Mei Chalav Distinction

### Mishna Mei Chalav

The Gemara notes that the *baraita*'s ruling about *mei chalav* supports a ruling of Reish Lakish. The foundation is a *mishna* that states *mei chalav harei hen ke-chalav* — milk water is treated as milk — as well as *mochel* (the residual liquid from olive pressing after the primary oil has been extracted) being treated as oil. This is stated in the context of *hechsher*: the seven liquids that render food susceptible to *tumah*. One of those seven is *chalav*, and the *mishna* holds that *mei chalav* qualifies as *chalav* for this purpose. Similarly, *mochel* qualifies as oil.

### Reish Lakish Limit

Reish Lakish, commenting on this *mishna*, draws a critical distinction: *lo shanu ela le-hachshir et ha-zra'im* — the ruling that *mei chalav* counts as *chalav* applies only for purposes of making foods and seeds susceptible to *tumah*, where the requirement is simply that a qualifying liquid come into contact with the food. For that purpose, *mei chalav* suffices. However, *aval le-inyan bishul basar be-chalav, mei chalav eino ke-chalav* — when it comes to the prohibition of cooking meat in milk, *mei chalav* does not count as real milk. Reish Lakish's comment distinguishes between the broad category of liquids sufficient for *hechsher* and the more specific requirement of *chalav* needed to trigger the *basar be-chalav* prohibition.

### Baraita Confirmation

The *baraita* examined above confirms Reish Lakish's ruling explicitly, since it exempts cooking with *mei chalav* from *basar be-chalav* liability. Whether Reish Lakish was unaware of the *baraita* and derived his ruling independently, or was paraphrasing its ruling, the two positions are aligned. One should note the Rambam's position in this area: while he holds that things not biblically prohibited may be cooked together without transgression, this leniency applies to categorical exclusions — such as *chazir* or, on his view, *chayah* — rather than to borderline cases that derive from the same species and context as the core prohibition. For items closely adjacent to the main prohibition, such as certain borderline *chalav* derivatives, rabbinic prohibition of cooking would still apply, and the Rambam's treatment of these cases warrants careful review.

---

## Expansion Logic

### Cross-Species Derivation

The Gemara now turns to a *baraita* that works through the logical extension of *basar be-chalav* beyond the literal verse. The *baraita* begins: *bachalav imo — ein li ela bachalav imo, bachalav para ve-rachel minayin?* From the verse's language of *chalav imo* I know only a *gedi* cooked in its own mother's milk. How do I know that the prohibition extends to a calf cooked in cow's milk, or a lamb cooked in sheep's milk — that is, same species but not the literal mother?

### Kal va-Chomer Mother

The *baraita* proposes a *kal va-chomer*: *u-mah imo she-lo ne'esra imo be-harba'ah ne'esra imo be-vishulo* — the mother is not forbidden in terms of *harba'ah*, crossbreeding with the offspring; animals of the same species may be mated even in a mother-child pairing without violating the prohibition of crossbreeding, which is restricted to mixing species. Yet despite this leniency in *harba'ah*, the mother is forbidden together with the offspring in cooking. A cow and a goat, by contrast, *are* forbidden to be crossbred. If the weaker case — same-species mother and child, where crossbreeding is permitted — is forbidden in cooking, then certainly a cross-species case, where the very mating would be prohibited, should all the more be forbidden in cooking. *Eino din she-ne'esar imo be-vishulo?*

### Species Expansion

Therefore, says the *baraita*, the verse *bachalav imo* must be teaching something additional — and one understanding is that it serves to include cow's milk and sheep's milk even beyond the literal goat-and-mother scenario. The verse anchors the prohibition broadly. The Gemara's reasoning here captures an important structural point: the Torah's prohibition simultaneously draws on two conceptual frameworks — the closeness of the mother-child bond on one hand, and the severity attached to cross-species combination on the other. The question of intermediate cases — same species but not the literal mother — lies between these two poles and must be addressed.

---

## Scripture Necessity

### Rav Ashi Objection

Rav Ashi raises a challenge: *lama li kra, ha atya lah* — why is the verse needed at all? The *kal va-chomer* just constructed appears sufficient to derive that cross-species cooking is forbidden without requiring a separate scriptural teaching.

### Counter-objection

The response is that one could challenge the *kal va-chomer* from its very premise — *me'ikara de-dina pircha*. The argument had proceeded: mother and child, where crossbreeding is permitted, are nonetheless forbidden in cooking — therefore cross-species, where crossbreeding is forbidden, is certainly prohibited in cooking. But one can ask: *mah le-imo she-ken ne'esra imo bi-shchita* — the mother has a particular severity with respect to slaughter; the Torah prohibits slaughtering a mother and child on the same day (*oto ve-et beno*). There is no such prohibition with respect to slaughtering a cow and a goat on the same day. So the mother-child case may be severe not because crossbreeding between them is permitted but because the mother-child relationship itself carries unique stringency, as seen in *shechita*. One cannot therefore automatically extend the prohibition to cross-species cooking, because the reason for the cooking prohibition in the mother case may be precisely this unique mother-child severity, which does not apply across species.

### Verse Necessity

Accordingly, *Talmud lomar bachalav imo* — the verse is necessary to teach that the prohibition extends even in the direction of cross-species cooking, where the mother-child relationship is absent. The verse provides the textual basis for what the *kal va-chomer* alone could not establish, given the objection about the particular severity of the mother-child bond as evidenced by the laws of *shechita*.

---

## Sister's Milk

### Older Sister Case

The Gemara introduces yet another *baraita*: *bachalav imo — ein li ela bachalav imo, bechalav achoto ha-gedolah minayin?* Having established same-species and cross-species cases, the *baraita* now asks about an intermediate scenario: cooking a kid in the milk of its older sister — another animal of the same species, but neither the mother nor a member of a different species.

### Ma'aser Logic

The *kal va-chomer* here operates differently. It argues from the mother: *u-mah imo she-nichnesa imo la-dir le-hit'aser ne'esra imo be-vishul* — the mother can enter the same pen as the child to be counted together for *ma'aser behema* (the tithe levied on newborn animals), since mother and child born in the same year may both be counted for that year's *ma'aser*. Despite this closeness — being in the same *ma'aser* cycle — the mother is forbidden in cooking together with the child. An older sister, *she-lo nichnesa imo la-dir le-hit'aser* — born in a prior year and therefore not countable for *ma'aser* at the same time as the kid — represents a greater degree of difference or distance. If even the closely-reckoned mother is prohibited, should the more-distantly-reckoned older sister not be prohibited all the more so? That is the *kal va-chomer*.

### Rav Ashi Second Objection

Rav Ashi again raises the objection: *lama li kra* — why does a verse need to teach this? The *kal va-chomer* would appear sufficient.

### Slaughter Difference

The counter-objection is the same as before: *mah le-imo she-ken ne'esra imo bi-shchita* — the mother carries a unique severity through the prohibition of *oto ve-et beno* that the older sister does not. *Tomar be-achoto ha-gedolah shelo ne'esra imo bi-shchita* — an older sister is not subject to any prohibition of being slaughtered together with the kid. Thus the *kal va-chomer* breaks down, and the verse *bachalav imo* is once again required to include this case.

### Common Denominator

At this point, the Gemara extracts the *tzad ha-shaveh* — the common denominator — from the combined cases: *shehu basar ve-assur le-vashel be-chalav*. The common feature of all the prohibited cases is simply that it is meat, and meat may not be cooked in milk. This is a pivotal moment in the Gemara's analysis. Beginning from the very specific and narrow formulation of *gedi be-chalav imo*, the Gemara has traced the logical and exegetical path by which the Sages abstracted the prohibition into the broad principle of *basar be-chalav* — any meat with any milk. It is not about the species of the meat, not about the species of the milk, not about the mother-child relationship, and not about cross-species mixing. It is about the fundamental pairing of meat and milk.

One might then ask: if we have already derived from the two established cases — mother and cross-species — that the prohibition is general, why was a separate verse needed for the older sister at all? The Gemara replies: *ein hachi nami* — correct, it was not strictly needed for older sister. The verse *bachalav imo* written a second time was needed for a different and more challenging case entirely, to which the Gemara now turns.

---

## Animal's Own Milk

### Self-Milk Question

The final question in the Gemara's chain of derivations is the most conceptually demanding: *atzma be-chalvah minayin?* — how do we know that cooking an animal in its own milk is forbidden? All prior cases involved at minimum two distinct entities: a piece of meat from one animal, and milk from another. Here, there is only one animal. It is simultaneously the source of the meat and the source of the milk. The question is whether the verse needed to be invoked to cover this case, or whether logic sufficed.

### Siblings vs. Mother

The first *kal va-chomer* attempt: *u-mah be-makom she-lo ne'esar pri im pri bi-shchita ne'esar pri im em bi-shchita* — there is no prohibition against slaughtering two siblings on the same day; yet, there is a prohibition against slaughtering a mother with its child. Translating this into the language of *bishul*: two offspring of the mother — meaning a calf and the milk, both understood as products of the mother — should the cooking prohibition not extend to them? *Ne'esar pri im pri be-vishul* — you cannot cook the child (the calf) with another product of the mother (the milk). *Eino din she-ne'esar pri im em be-vishul* — then certainly one should not be able to cook the milk together with the animal that produced it, its mother. That is, if you cannot cook the milk with the calf (because both are *pri* of the mother), you certainly cannot cook the milk with the mother herself — which would be an animal cooked in its own milk.

### Horse-Mule Case

This *kal va-chomer* is challenged through an analogy involving crossbreeding. Suppose a female horse mated with a donkey and with a stallion, producing a mule and a horse. *She-assur pri im pri* — the horse offspring cannot mate with the mule offspring, because that would constitute *kilayim*, crossbreeding of species. *U-mutar pri im em* — yet the horse offspring can mate with its mother, since horse with horse is not a species violation. Here is a case where *pri im pri* is forbidden but *pri im em* is permitted — the exact inverse of the *kal va-chomer*. Accordingly, the argument from *shechita* does not carry through; the relationship between the two categories is not fixed.

### Reverse Case

The Gemara then examines the reverse scenario: a female horse mated with a donkey, producing two mules. *She-mutar pri im pri* — the two mule siblings can mate with each other, since mule with mule is not a species violation. *Ve-assur pri im em* — yet neither mule can mate with the horse mother, since mule and horse are distinct species. Here the pattern reverses again: *pri im pri* is permitted while *pri im em* is forbidden. The Gemara concludes that the relationship between *pri im pri* and *pri im em* in crossbreeding follows the identity of the father's species, not the mother's. It is not a stable indicator of relative severity and cannot serve as a reliable basis for the *kal va-chomer*. Accordingly, this line of reasoning does not prove the case.

### Slave-Woman Analogy

Another attempt is advanced: a slave woman has two children; one is subsequently freed while the other remains a slave. *She-assur pri im pri* — the freed sibling (now a fully Jewish free person) may not engage in prohibited relations with the slave sibling. *U-mutar pri im em* — the slave child may engage in relations with someone of the same status as its mother, i.e., another slave. Again: *pri im pri* is prohibited while *pri im em* is permitted. Yet the Gemara again dismisses this: *hatam get shichrur hu de-ka garem* — it is the document of emancipation that determines the parameters, not the abstract sibling/mother relationship. The Gemara confirms this by presenting the reverse: a free woman's children, one of whom becomes enslaved, can now mate with a slave (someone of their own kind) but not with a free person (someone of the mother's kind). The pattern again inverts. Neither example establishes a fixed logical principle.

### Kilai Zera'im

One more attempt: *kilai zera'im* — crossbreeding seeds. You may not plant wheat and barley (*pri im pri*) together, but you may plant either grain into the ground (*pri im em*, the earth being the mother of all crops). Here *pri im pri* is forbidden and *pri im em* is permitted. The Gemara, however, deflects: *klum ne'esar pri im pri ela al yedei ha'em?* — is the crossbreeding of wheat and barley in the field not always by means of the mother, the earth? You cannot plant them side by side without involving the earth. Indeed, if you put wheat and barley in a bowl together, there is no prohibition. It is always the earth — the mother — that is the operative medium, so you cannot say the mother is uninvolved.

### One Body Principle

At last, Rav Ashi provides the decisive answer: *mah li pri mi-pri she-ken shnei gufim* — the *kal va-chomer* from calf-and-milk fails because in that case there are *two bodies* involved. The mother is one body, the calf is another body; the milk is one body, the calf is another body. Even in the case of milk and calf — both called *pri* of the mother — they are physically distinct entities. One could therefore argue that the prohibition requires the presence of two distinct bodies, two animals as it were, and that an animal cooked in its own milk — which is a single entity, *guf echad* — falls outside the prohibition.

### Verse Needed

*Tomar be-pri em she-ken guf echad* — you might indeed say that an animal with its own milk, being one entity, is excluded. *Mishum hachi itztarich kra* — it is for precisely this reason that the verse was necessary. The extra formulation *bachalav imo* in the verse comes to teach that even where only one body is involved — an animal cooked in its own milk — the prohibition of *basar be-chalav* applies. This is the final and most difficult case in the Gemara's systematic expansion of the prohibition from the literal *gedi be-chalav imo* to its full logical scope, and it required explicit scriptural support precisely because logic might have led us to exclude it.

# Hullin 115

## Intro: Meat & Milk

### Opening Remarks

The present daf continues a discussion that began on 114b, and which will occupy us for roughly the next daf and a half: how do we derive from the verses forbidding the *bishul* — the cooking — of meat and milk together that one is also prohibited from eating the mixture and even from deriving any benefit from it? This is a question that exercised the *tannaim* considerably, producing a remarkable variety of derivations. Contrary to the impression one might get from reading Rashi on the *parasha* — where he simply notes that the verse was repeated three times, once for cooking, once for eating, and once for benefit — the *tannaim* in fact offer close to a dozen independent approaches to these same questions, and only one of them corresponds to Rashi's familiar explanation.

## Intro: Meat & Milk (II)

### Problem Statement

The central problem is straightforward: the verse says *lo tevashel gdi bachalav imo* — do not cook a kid in its mother's milk. The explicit prohibition is of *bishul*, cooking. How do we know that the cooked mixture is also forbidden to eat? And how do we know one may not derive any monetary or physical benefit from it? These are the questions that animate the entire discussion from here through the end of the daf.

## Rav Ashi: Kol To'evah

### Product of Aveirah

The Gemara opens with Rav Ashi's teaching: *minayin lebasar bechalav she'asur ba'achilah* — from where do we know that *basar bechalav* is forbidden in eating? The verse states: *lo tochal kol to'evah* — do not eat any abomination (Devarim 14:3). The *derasha* is as follows: *kol she'ti'avti lecha harei hu beval tochal* — anything that I have rendered an abomination to you, you may not eat. If the Torah has rendered the act of cooking meat and milk together an abomination, then the product of that forbidden act must itself be considered an abomination, and therefore falls within the prohibition of *lo tochal kol to'evah*.

### Abbahu's Principle

The Gemara then continues: *ve'ein li ela ba'achilah* — this verse tells me only that the mixture is forbidden in eating. *Be'hana'ah minayin* — from where do I know that one may not derive benefit from it at all? The answer is *k'de'Rabbi Abbahu*: like the principle articulated by Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rabbi Elazar, which is developed at length in Pesachim.

Rabbi Abbahu's principle is that whenever the Torah employs the language of *lo ye'achel*, *lo tochal*, or *lo tochelu* — in any of its conjugations — the prohibition encompasses not only eating but all forms of benefit, whether physical or monetary. This holds *ad she'paret lecha hakatuv*, unless the verse explicitly carves out a permission to derive benefit. And the proof that this is the standard meaning of such language is precisely from the one place where the Torah did make such an exception explicit — namely, the case of *neveilah*.

### Neveilah Exception

The verse concerning *neveilah* — an animal that was not properly slaughtered — says: *lo tochlu kol neveilah lager asher bisharecha titnenah va'achalah o machor lenochri* — do not eat any *neveilah*; give it to the *ger* in your gates or sell it to the foreigner. The Torah thus explicitly permits giving or selling the *neveilah*, i.e., deriving benefit from it. The fact that the Torah needed to spell out this permission teaches us that without such explicit permission, *lo tochal* would have prohibited benefit as well.

A *baraita* then elaborates the scope of this permission. The verse seems to indicate only that one gives it to the *ger* and sells it to the non-Jew. From where do I know I may sell it to the *ger*? The verse says *lager titnenah o machor* — give it to the *ger* or sell it — connecting the verb of selling to the *ger* as well. From where do I know I may give it to the non-Jew? The same repositioning of the *o* — "or" — connects the giving to the non-Jew as well: *titnena o machor lenochri*. The conclusion is: *nimtza echad ger ve'echad oved kochavim bein bimchira bein binetina* — whether the *ger* or the non-Jew, one may give or sell to either.

It should be noted that the *ger* in this context is understood by the Sages as a *ger toshav* — a resident alien who accepts the seven Noahide laws and dwells among Israel, but who does not observe the full corpus of Jewish law, as evidenced by the fact that the Torah permits him to eat *neveilah*. Indeed, this individual is sometimes referred to in rabbinic literature as a *ger ochel neveilah*, precisely on the basis of this verse.

### Meir vs. Yehudah

This is the position of Rabbi Meir, who rules that one may give or sell the *neveilah* to either the *ger* or the non-Jew interchangeably. Rabbi Yehudah disagrees and holds *dvarim kichtavam* — the words must be taken as written, without the play of repositioning. According to Rabbi Yehudah, one gives it to the *ger* and sells it to the non-Jew, and the categories may not be crossed.

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama deRabbi Yehudah* — what is Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning? His argument is that if Rabbi Meir were correct that both options apply to both recipients, the Torah should have written the verse more explicitly, permitting all four combinations without ambiguity. The presence of the *o* — "or" — is therefore meant to separate the two clauses, not to combine their verbs. Give to the *ger*, sell to the non-Jew, and do not reverse the arrangement.

Rabbi Meir, for his part, reads the *o* not as a separator but as establishing a priority: one should give priority to bestowing the *neveilah* as a gift to the *ger* rather than selling it to the non-Jew, because there is a positive obligation to sustain the *ger toshav* in one's midst. Permission exists to do all of the above, but priority must be given to the welfare of the sojourner.

Rabbi Yehudah responds that no verse is needed to establish such a priority — it follows from *sevara*, plain logic: *ze ata metzuva lehachayoto veze i ata metzuva lehachayoto* — you are obligated to sustain the life of the resident sojourner, but you bear no equivalent obligation toward the foreigner. Priority needs no scriptural source. Therefore, the verse's only function must be to prohibit crossing the categories, which is precisely Rabbi Yehudah's position.

The upshot of this entire exchange, for purposes of the law of *basar bechalav*, is that all opinions agree the Torah had to go out of its way to permit benefit from *neveilah*, and that without such explicit permission, *lo tochal* would have encompassed *issur hana'ah* as well. The *halacha* follows the view that *lo tochal* means no benefit unless the Torah specifies otherwise, and by *basar bechalav*, no such exception appears.

It should be noted that there exists a lengthy *sugya* in Pesachim that catalogs the many instances where the Torah does permit benefit even after forbidding eating, demonstrating that in practice there are more exceptions to Rabbi Abbahu's rule than there are applications of it. Nevertheless, the principle stands, and *basar bechalav* is not among the exceptions.

### Tosafot: Trivial Benefit

Tosafot raises an important question on the *baraita*: the ruling that one must give the *neveilah* as a gift to the *ger* before selling it to the non-Jew seems to require a person to forgo profit in favor of charity. But a person is entitled to earn a livelihood — one has a *mitzvah* to sustain one's fellow Jew as well, and yet we do not require that all food be donated before it may be sold. Why should *neveilah* be different?

Tosafot's answer is that the entire discussion is predicated on a realistic assessment of what *neveilah* is: an animal that died on its own or was not properly slaughtered, more akin to a carcass than to market meat. What one could realistically hope to receive by selling such an item is a relatively trivial sum. Given that the monetary gain would be minimal, it is better to give it as a gift to the *ger toshav* and thereby fulfill the genuine obligation to sustain him, rather than to pocket a few coins in an open sale.

Tosafot makes explicit — in the lines immediately before the word *kederech* — that if a person actually wishes to sell something for its full value, he may certainly sell it to whoever wishes to buy, whether non-Jew or otherwise, without first being obligated to donate it. The priority of giving to the *ger* applies specifically in the case of *neveilah*, where the realizable monetary value is too trivial to outweigh the *mitzvah* of sustaining the sojourner.

## Challenges to Model

### Rashi's Defense

Having established Rav Ashi's model — that *basar bechalav* is forbidden as a *to'evah* because it is the product and embodiment of a forbidden act — the Gemara immediately raises a series of challenges. If the principle is that the product of a forbidden act is itself forbidden, why do we not apply this broadly? Why are the products of many other prohibitions entirely permissible?

Rashi's answer is this: *basar bechalav* is uniquely and directly the embodiment of the forbidden act itself. The prohibition of cooking meat and milk is constituted precisely by the combining of the two. The product — cooked *basar bechalav* — cannot exist without the commission of the *aveirah*; it *is* the *aveirah* in physical form. This stands in contrast to, say, cooking on *Shabbos*: the prohibition of *chilul Shabbos* is violated by the act of cooking, but the cooked meat is not in any sense an embodiment of *chilul Shabbos*. One could have cooked the same meat on Tuesday. The meat does not bear within it the stamp of the transgression. By *basar bechalav*, however, the cooked mixture of meat and milk is inseparable from the violation; there is no way to arrive at cooked *basar bechalav* without having done precisely what the Torah forbade.

This point connects to a broader conceptual question: is the prohibition of *basar bechalav* fundamentally about the act of *bishul* — with eating as merely a derivative consequence — or is it fundamentally about the eating, with *bishul* as a form of fence or precaution? The discussion here, particularly Rav Ashi's approach, seems to argue for the former: it is the *bishul* that is the core prohibition, and if one has already cooked them together, what one has produced is the very embodiment of what the Torah abhors. From that standpoint, the natural implication is that the product itself takes on the character of a *to'evah*.

One can also frame this in terms of what the *aveirah* of *basar bechalav* actually consists of. If the prohibition is understood as being about the commingling of tastes through cooking — the production of a hybrid flavor — then the cooked mixture is not incidental to the *aveirah* but is its very content. The Torah's concern, on that reading, is the existence of this hybrid taste-entity, and so of course the product that embodies it is itself forbidden.

### Kilayim Exception

The Gemara then asks: *kilay zerayim lissru* — the mixing of different seeds, which is also a form of forbidden mixture — why is its product not forbidden? The Gemara answers: *degali rachmana gabei kilay hakerem* — the Torah revealed, specifically in the case of *kilay hakerem* (mixed planting in a vineyard with grapes), that the product is forbidden. The verse *pen tikdash* is read as *pen tukad esh* — lest it be burnt in fire, meaning the mixture is *assur behana'ah*, forbidden in benefit. From the fact that the Torah singles out *kilay hakerem* for this stringency, one infers that ordinary *kilay zerayim* are permissible.

The Gemara then asks: but at a minimum, should *kilay zerayim* not be forbidden in eating even if they are permitted in benefit, given that they too are an embodiment of a forbidden mixture? The answer is that we know from a *heikesh* — an analogical link — to *kilay behema* (crossbreeding animals) that the products of such mixtures are permitted. And how do we know the products of crossbred animals are permitted? *Mi-de'asar rachmana kilayim legavoha* — since the Torah forbids bringing a crossbred animal as a *korban*, one can infer that for ordinary, non-consecrated purposes it is permitted. This inference then extends by analogy to mixed seeds: just as the product of crossbred animals is permitted to the layperson, so too mixed grains.

The Gemara thus works out a coherent picture: some products of forbidden mixtures are indeed forbidden — *kilay hakerem* and *basar bechalav* — while others, through explicit Torah permission derived by inference, are not. The exceptions are not arbitrary; they are derived through recognized hermeneutical tools.

### Mixed Animals

Similarly, the Gemara addresses the case of threshing with an ox and a donkey together — a violation of *kilay behema* — or muzzling a cow while it threshes. In both cases, a clear *aveirah* is committed, yet the grain produced is entirely permissible in eating and benefit. How can these cases be reconciled with the model that the product of a forbidden act is itself abominable?

The Gemara's answer is consistent with Rashi's framework: in these cases, the forbidden act is truly incidental to the product. The grain was not produced *by* the prohibition; the ox and donkey did not combine to create a hybrid product. The prohibition was in the use of those animals together, but the crushed grain bears no trace of the *aveirah*. It is not an embodiment of the prohibition in any meaningful sense.

### Mother & Child

The Gemara raises the case of *oto ve'et beno* — the prohibition against slaughtering a mother animal and its offspring on the same day. If one violated this prohibition, why is the meat of the second animal permissible? Should it not be considered the product of a forbidden act?

The Gemara answers: *mi-de'asar rachmana mechusar zeman legavoha* — since the Torah establishes the concept of *mechusar zeman* (an animal not yet eligible to be offered because of its age) as a prohibition specifically in the context of *korbanot*, one can infer that outside the context of consecrated offerings, slaughtering in violation of *oto ve'et beno* does not render the meat forbidden to the layperson.

Tosafot notes, however, that the Gemara could have given the same answer it gave elsewhere: the slaughtered calf is simply not an embodiment of the *aveirah* of *oto ve'et beno*. The calf could have been slaughtered the next day; nothing about a slaughtered calf intrinsically reflects the prohibition. The product here is entirely incidental to the transgression, quite unlike *basar bechalav*, where the cooked mixture cannot exist apart from the *aveirah*. Tosafot explains that the Gemara chose the answer it did because it was more readily available, not because the conceptual answer was unavailable.

### Shiluach Ha-Ken

The final challenge is the case of *shiluach ha-ken* — the obligation to send away the mother bird before taking eggs or chicks from a nest. If one violated this and took the mother bird, why is she not forbidden? Tosafot formulates this question slightly differently from the others: here it is not even clearly a case where one did an *aveirah* in the conventional sense. Rather, the Torah indicates that taking the mother bird is off-limits — *lo tikach ha'em al habanim* — and if the Torah has signaled that the mother bird is *ti'avti lecha*, something I have made off-limits to you, then should she not remain forbidden even after being caught and slaughtered?

The Gemara's answer is: *lo amrah Torah shalach letakalah* — the Torah would not have commanded sending the mother bird away in a manner that creates a *takala*, a stumbling block. If the sent-away bird were rendered permanently forbidden, then anyone who subsequently caught and ate her would be consuming forbidden food without any fault of their own. The Torah's command to send the bird away was plainly not intended to generate such a consequence. From this we learn that even where the Torah signals disapproval, the sent-away bird does not become permanently forbidden.

This case is particularly instructive for the conceptual framework being developed. The discussion across all these challenges illuminates a nuanced understanding of the relationship between *issur bishul* and *issur achilah* in the law of *basar bechalav*. The weight of Rav Ashi's approach is that it is the *bishul* that stands at the center — the core of what the Torah opposes — and the eating prohibition flows from the fact that the product of that *bishul* is itself a *to'evah*. Most products of forbidden acts do not carry this character. But *kilay hakerem* and *basar bechalav* do, because the forbidden act is not merely incidental to their existence — it is constitutive of it.

## Reish Lakish: Pesach

### Double Language

The Gemara now presents a second approach, that of Reish Lakish: *minayin lebasar bechalav she'asar* — from where do we know that *basar bechalav* is forbidden? The source Reish Lakish cites is the verse concerning the *Korban Pesach*: *al tochlu mimenu na uvashel mevushal* — do not eat the Passover offering raw or cooked in water. The double language of *bishul* — *uvashel mevushal*, cooked, cooked — is superfluous. Why does the verse not simply say *bashel*? The extra word *mevushal* comes to teach: *yesh lecha bishul acher she'hu kazeh* — there is another type of *bishul* that the Torah similarly prohibits eating. What is that? *Basar bechalav*. Thus the prohibition against eating the cooked mixture is derived from the double language of cooking in the *Pesach* verse.

### Yochanan Challenge

Rabbi Yochanan responds sharply to Reish Lakish: *ke'urah zu she'shana Rabbi* — is what Rabbi taught something disgusting to you? Meaning: why are you inventing a novel *derasha* from the *Korban Pesach* when the *Tanna* known as *Rabbi* — Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi — already had a well-established *derasha* on the same question? Why not follow that?

### Rabbi: Psulei Mukdashin

Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi's *derasha* is based on the passage concerning *pesulei hamukdashin* — animals consecrated as offerings that became invalid and were subsequently redeemed. The Torah in that context says: *bish'arecha tochlenu hatamei vehatahir yachdav katzvi ucheayal* — you may eat it within your gates, the ritually impure and pure alike, as you would eat the deer and the hart. Then it says: *lo tochlenu* — do not eat it — referring to the blood. But the verse's final repetition of *lo tochlenu* is seemingly redundant. Rabbi derives: *bebasar bechalav hakatuv medaber* — the verse is here speaking about meat and milk.

The Gemara then asks: how do we know the repeated *lo tochlenu* refers to *basar bechalav* and not to some other prohibition in the Torah? The answer is *davar halamed me'inyano* — context. The verse is dealing with something that involves *shnei minin* — two kinds. According to Rashi, the animal in question has a dual character: it was once a *korban* and retains vestiges of its sacred status, yet has now been redeemed and is treated as *chullin*. It is a hybrid of two statuses. By analogy, *basar bechalav* is similarly a hybrid of two substances, and the *lo tochlenu* warns against consuming such a hybrid.

Rabbi Yochanan then challenges Reish Lakish: if you learned from the *Korban Pesach* rather than from *pesulei hamukdashin*, it is because from *pesulei hamukdashin* alone you could not derive *issur hana'ah*. Blood — the main subject of that verse — is only forbidden in eating, not in benefit. If the *derasha* for *basar bechalav* is learned from the same verse as blood, one might conclude that *basar bechalav* too is only forbidden in eating, not in benefit. The *Korban Pesach*, by contrast, is forbidden not only in eating but in all benefit if the *korban* becomes invalid. That is why Reish Lakish derived from the *Korban Pesach* context — to include *issur hana'ah* as well.

*Ve'Rabbi behan'ah mna lei* — and where does Rabbi himself derive the prohibition of *hana'ah* from? *Nafka lei mehacha* — he derives it from the verse *ki am kadosh atah*, which appears in connection with *basar bechalav* in Devarim 14. This verse says that Israel is a holy people to Hashem. By *gezeirah shavah* — specifically a shared use of the word *kadosh* — the Torah's statement *velo yihyeh kadesh bivnei Yisrael* (there shall be no male prostitute among Israel) is invoked: just as there the *kedasha* context involves a prohibition of pleasure that goes beyond eating, so too here *kedushah* in connection with *basar bechalav* extends to all forms of benefit.

Tosafot notes that the verse concerning *achilah* was also needed independently — so that we should not think the *kedushah* verse addresses only *hana'ah* that is not *achilah*. Rather, there are two separate prohibitions: *issur achilah* derived from one source and *issur hana'ah* derived from another.

## More Derivations

### Eliezer: Neveilah

The school of Rabbi Eliezer (*Dvei Rabbi Eliezer*) offers yet another approach, derived from the proximity of *neveilah* and *basar bechalav* within the same verse. The verse reads: *lo tochlu kol neveilah lager asher bisharecha titnenah va'achalah o machor lenochri ki am kadosh atah laHashem Elokecha lo tevashel gdi bachalav imo*. The Torah, in commanding one what to do with the *neveilah*, says give it or sell it — and then immediately concludes with the prohibition of cooking *basar bechalav*.
