The *derasha* is: the Torah is teaching, when you sell or give away the *neveilah*, do not first cook it as *basar bechalav* and then sell it — because if you cook it as *basar bechalav*, it will have become *assur behana'ah* and you will no longer be permitted to sell it or give it away. Thus the prohibition of deriving benefit from *basar bechalav* is embedded in the juxtaposition of the two verses.

### Yishmael: Three-fold

Finally, the school of Rabbi Yishmael offers the approach familiar from Rashi's commentary on the *parasha*: *lo tevashel gdi bachalav imo* is written three times in the Torah (Shemot 23:19, Shemot 34:26, Devarim 14:21). Each repetition carries its own prohibition: one for *issur bishul* (cooking), one for *issur achilah* (eating), and one for *issur hana'ah* (benefit).

This prompts reflection on the structure of the three prohibitions and their interrelationships. Is the *issur achilah* an independent prohibition, or merely a corollary of the *issur bishul*? Is the *issur hana'ah* an extension of the *issur achilah*, as Rabbi Abbahu's principle would suggest, or is it a conceptually independent category derived from an entirely different source, as the *derasha* from *kadesh bifnei Yisrael* implies? These questions carry practical *halachic* implications — for example, whether the *issur hana'ah* applies in a case where the *issur achilah* of *basar bechalav* did not take effect, such as when the meat itself was already *neveilah* when cooked with milk.

Rabbi Yishmael's *derasha* of three repetitions can be read either way — it could indicate three fully independent prohibitions, or three dimensions of a single interlocking prohibition. In any case, as the Gemara makes clear, this is the simplest and most elegant derivation, which likely explains why Rashi selected it for his commentary on the *parasha*: it simultaneously explains why the verse was repeated and answers the question of how we know *basar bechalav* is forbidden in eating and benefit.

It is also evident, as one steps back from all these *drashot*, that in many cases the *tannaim* began with the received tradition — the *mesorah* — that *basar bechalav* is forbidden in eating and in benefit, and then worked backwards to identify the scriptural basis. This is a well-established phenomenon in rabbinic literature. The Ramban, for example, explains that the rule requiring a *gezeirah shavah* to be received from one's teacher means only that one has a tradition regarding the *halacha* and that it may be derived via *gezeirah shavah*; the *tanna* then constructs the specific *gezeirah shavah* accordingly. The diversity of *drashot* here strongly suggests that the bottom line — that one may neither eat nor derive benefit from *basar bechalav* — was the starting point, and the verse-based derivations were the varied scholarly attempts to ground that tradition in the text of the Torah.

### Issi: Am Kadosh

Issi ben Yehudah offers a further *derasha*: the verse *ki am kadosh atah laHashem Elokecha* appears both by *basar bechalav* and in connection with *tereifah* — *ve'anshei kodesh tihyun li uvasar basadeh tereifah lo tocheilu*. The concept of *kedushah* as expressed in the Torah is intimately associated with restraining from forbidden foods. Since the Torah employs the term *am kadosh* in connection with *basar bechalav*, just as it does in connection with *tereifah* where the prohibition is clearly one of eating, so too the *kedushah* of *basar bechalav* carries with it a prohibition of eating, not merely a prohibition of cooking.

## Kal V'Chomer Logic

### Setup

With the *issur achilah* established via the *derasha* of Issi ben Yehudah from *am kadosh*, the Gemara then turns to deriving the *issur hana'ah* through a *kal vachomer*: *umah orlah she'lo ne'evda bah aveirah assurah behana'ah, basar bechalav shene'evda bo aveirah eino din she'assur behana'ah* — if *orlah*, regarding which no transgression was committed, is forbidden in benefit, then *basar bechalav*, regarding which a transgression was committed, should certainly be forbidden in benefit.

### Objection

But the *kal vachomer* is immediately challenged: there are many things regarding which transgressions were committed whose products are nonetheless fully permitted — grain threshed with an ox and donkey together, produce of a cow that was muzzled while threshing. These are clear cases where a *sin* was done and the product remains permissible. How then can we use the fact that an *aveirah* was committed as a basis for the *kal vachomer*?

### Chometz B'Pesach

The Gemara addresses a further potential objection to the *kal vachomer*: one might say that *orlah* is different because it was never permitted — it was forbidden from the moment of planting, while *basar bechalav* was permissible before it was cooked together. Something that was once permitted perhaps cannot become forbidden in benefit. The Gemara responds: *chometz bePesach yochiach* — *chometz* on Pesach proves otherwise. Leavened bread is entirely permissible before Pesach, yet on Pesach it is *assur behana'ah*. Thus the fact that something was once permitted does not prevent it from subsequently becoming forbidden in benefit.

The Gemara then challenges this: *ma lachometz bePesach she-ken anush kares* — perhaps *chometz* is different because its prohibition is punishable by *kares*. This does not apply to *basar bechalav*.

### Three-Case Rule

To counter this deflection, *kilay hakerem* is introduced as a third case. *Kilay hakerem* is not punishable by *kares*, was presumably permissible before the seeds were planted, and nevertheless is forbidden in benefit. Once these three cases are assembled — *orlah*, *chometz bePesach*, and *kilay hakerem* — neither the argument that it was once permissible nor the argument that it lacks the weight of *kares* can be used to distinguish *basar bechalav*, since *kilay hakerem* shares neither of those characteristics and is still *assur behana'ah*.

### Two vs. Three Cases

The Gemara then asks why all three cases were necessary. Why not simply derive the rule from the *mah hatzad* — the common denominator — of *orlah* and *chometz bePesach* alone? The answer Rav Ashi gives, in the name of Reish Lakish, is that with only two cases, the *mah hatzad* argument can be dismissed by pointing out an obvious exception — namely, *neveilah*, which is *assur ba'achilah* yet *mutar behana'ah*. If *basar bechalav* is only known to be forbidden in eating, one cannot simply assert that everything forbidden in eating is forbidden in benefit, since *neveilah* disproves that.

This leads to the broader logical principle articulated here. When deriving a rule from the common denominator of two cases, even a trivial internal challenge suffices to dismiss the rule's application. When one argues from the model of a single paradigmatic case (*binyan av*), a good internal reason is needed to dismiss its application to a new case. And when one derives from a *mah hatzad* of three cases, the analysis becomes more nuanced. Rav Mordechai transmits in the name of Reish Lakish: *kol mah hatzad migufo parchinan, me'alma lo parchinan* — when arguing from a common denominator, one may only challenge internally, not by pointing to external counterexamples.

When drawing from two cases, even a trivial internal distinction suffices to deflect the rule. When drawing from a *mah hatzad* of three cases, the situation depends on how the argument is structured. If the conclusion still rests on the common denominator of all three, a trivial question still suffices to dismiss it. But if, as in our case, one of the three cases — *kilay hakerem* — itself serves as a direct example that shares none of the supposedly distinguishing characteristics, then only a *kula ve'chumra* argument, a genuine reason of leniency or stringency, can deflect the rule; a trivial dismissal no longer suffices.

The upshot is this: *basar bechalav* is known to be *assur ba'achilah* by virtue of the principle of *am kadosh*. From that foundation, the *kal vachomer* establishes *issur hana'ah* by comparing *basar bechalav* to *orlah*, *chometz bePesach*, and *kilay hakerem* — all of which are *assur ba'achilah* and *assur behana'ah*, and from whose common denominator, properly reinforced by three cases, we apply the rule to *basar bechalav* as well.

Throughout this discussion, the centrality of the concept of *kedushah* — holiness — as a value instantiated through the discipline of eating is brought into sharp relief. The verse *ki am kadosh atah* does not merely add a prohibition of cooking; it signals that Israel's sanctity is expressed, in significant part, through restraint from forbidden foods. When that verse is affixed to the law of *basar bechalav*, it communicates not merely that cooking is prohibited but that eating — and indeed all benefit — is incompatible with the holiness the Torah demands.

---

---

# Hullin 119

## Shomer & Yad from Pasuk

### Rav Chaviva on Neveilah

Today's daf is 119, though we begin by picking up in the middle of 118b. The Gemara has been engaged in a technical discussion of how we know the concepts of *shomer* and *yad* — deriving them from the *pesukim* that speak about something falling onto seeds, and concluding that the word *lachem* teaches us the idea of *yad*, and that the concept of *shomer* by seeds teaches that the *shomer* adds to the minimum size rather than bringing *tumah* in and out.

We begin with one final *drasha* before proceeding to the specific *halachos*. Rav Chaviva addresses the question raised at the end of the previous daf: if we have an extra *pasuk* about *shomer* by *neveilah*, how do we know to read it as teaching a *din* of *yad*? Perhaps it teaches a *halacha* about *shomer* instead?

Rav Chaviva answers: *sha'ani shomer de-neveilah* — the *shomer* of *neveilah* is different. Since we know that a *shomer* by *neveilah* cannot add to the minimum size — *neveilah* is not an agricultural product — the only *halachic* function this *shomer* can serve is that of a *yad*, bringing *tumah* in and out. Therefore we are entitled to apply the *pasuk* to the laws of *yad*, and from there we derive that *yad* both brings *tumah* in and brings *tumah* out.

### Beyond Zera Zerua

With the *drashot* complete, the Gemara proceeds to discuss the practical *halachos* of *yad* and *shomer*. At this point, Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel raises a challenge rooted in the *pesukim* themselves. The entire concept of *shomer* is derived from the phrase *al kol zera zerua asher yizarei'a* — the shell that protects a seed taken out for planting. The paradigm, in other words, is the seed planted together with its shell. But the laws of *shomer* seem to go well beyond this model.

The *Mishnah* teaches, for example, that the *pitema* of a pomegranate — the twig or protrusion connected to the fruit — functions as a *shomer* and combines toward the minimum size. Now, whatever the *pitema* precisely refers to (whether the point of attachment to the branch or the growth at the opposite end, a question debated by the *Rishonim*, and one that intersects with the famous dispute about the *pitema* of the *esrog*), it is clear that one does not plant a pomegranate together with its *pitema*. Rashi explains further that the leaf, by contrast, does not combine, because it is attached to the *pitema* rather than directly to the fruit — making it a *shomer al gabei shomer*.

So the challenge stands: if *shomer* is learned from the model of *zera zerua*, how does it apply to the *pitema* of a pomegranate, which no one plants along with the fruit? And the *Mishnah* also teaches that the skin combines with meat to reach the minimum size for *tumah*. Where does one derive that *shomer* applies to non-agricultural items at all?

### Three Verses Generalize

The Gemara answers: *ela tlata kra'ei ketivi* — there are actually three separate verses that establish and generalize the concept of *shomer*. The phrase *al kol zera zerua asher yizarei'a* uses the language of planting and seed three times over. Each usage extends the concept to a different category.

The first teaches *shomer de-zera'im* — the *shomer* of seeds, in the tight, intimate sense of something planted together with the seed. The second teaches *shomer de-ilanot* — the *shomer* of fruit, such as the *pitema* of a pomegranate, which protects the fruit even though it is not planted along with it. The third extends the concept even further to *shomer basar, beitzim, ve-dagim* — foods that come not from the ground at all, but from the animal world. Each step represents an abstraction and generalization of the core concept. So while *shomer* is indeed derived from *zera zerua*, the Torah itself provides the warrant to apply it far beyond that original model.

---

## Yad & Hechsher Debate

### Rav: No Yad Hechsher

Having finished the *drashot*, the Gemara turns to the specific parameters of *yad*. The first question: does the concept of *yad*, which we know applies to *tumah*, also apply to *hechsher*?

By way of background: food only becomes susceptible to *tumah* once it has been detached from the ground and has come into contact with liquid. The question is whether the liquid must touch the food directly, or whether it is sufficient if the liquid touches only the *yad* — the handle or protrusion. For example, does water touching the bone to which meat is attached render the meat *huchshar*?

Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav rules: *yesh yad le-tumah ve-ein yad le-hechsher*. The concept of *yad* applies to the transmission of *tumah* but not to *hechsher*. If liquid only touched the *yad* and never touched the food itself, the food does not thereby become susceptible.

### R. Yochanan: Yad Both

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *yesh yad le-tumah u-le-hechsher*. The concept of *yad* applies in both directions.

### Debate Basis

The Gemara then asks: *be-mai miflagi* — what is the basis for this debate? Two possibilities are offered: *iba'is eima kra*, the dispute may turn on textual interpretation of the *pasuk*; and *iba'is eima sevara*, it may turn on a conceptual point.

Taking the textual possibility first: the *pasuk* reads *ve-chi yutan mayim al zera ve-nafal mi-nivlatam alav tamei hu lachem* — if water falls on seeds and a carcass then falls on it, it is *tamei lachem*. The word *lachem* teaches the concept of *yad*. One *amora* holds that a *pasuk* can be read back one step — *mikra nidrash le-fanav ve-lo lifnei fanav* — and so *lachem* applies only to the immediately adjacent phrase about *tumah*, not to the earlier clause about water rendering food susceptible. The other holds that a *pasuk* can be read back two steps — *mikra nidrash le-fanav u-lifnei fanav* — and so *lachem* extends all the way to the beginning of the *pasuk*, reaching the laws of *hechsher* as well.

Alternatively, the debate may be conceptual. One view holds *hechsher techilas tumah hi* — *hechsher* is the beginning of the process of *tumah*, and therefore since *yad* is part of the world of *tumah*, it applies here as well. The other holds *hechsher lav techilas tumah hi* — although *hechsher* renders food susceptible, it has not yet initiated the process of *tumah* itself. The laws of *yad* may belong specifically to that process and not to what merely precedes it.

One might frame the underlying intuition as follows: *tumah* is normally conceived of as a quasi-metaphysical force — it spreads, it is contagious, it fills a space under an *ohel* — and perhaps even indirect contact can transmit such a force through a *yad*. *Hechsher*, by contrast, is not a force; it is a status-change, a determination that this food has now entered a new category. That kind of categorical shift may require actual contact with the food itself.

### Attached to Tree

A *beraita* is cited in support of Rabbi Yochanan's position: *keshem she-yesh yad le-tumah, kach yesh yad le-hechsher* — just as *yad* applies to *tumah*, so it applies to *hechsher*. The same *beraita* adds a parallel rule: just as produce does not receive *tumah* while it is still attached to the tree, so too *hechsher* does not take effect while it is still attached.

This parallel is not merely symmetry. Rashi explains the rule about *tumah* on logical grounds: were produce susceptible to *tumah* while still growing, one would have to assume that everything in the world was potentially *tamei* — for who can know what dead creatures may have come into contact with every tree? The Torah cannot have intended such an assumption. Tosafot, however, offers a different analysis: the very reason produce does not receive *tumah* while attached is that *hechsher* has not yet occurred, and *hechsher* itself only takes effect once the produce is detached. On this reading, the two rules are not merely parallel; one actually explains the other.

There is also a deeper point here. *Tumah* as a category relates to things that have entered the sphere of human life and civilization — just as vessels become susceptible only once fashioned by human hands, not while they remain raw sticks and stones. Food, similarly, only becomes part of that human world once it is plucked and brought under human control. And *hechsher* — the requirement of contact with water, specifically water that one desires to fall on the food — reflects that same principle. It is not the mere natural fact of contact with water that matters; it is a purposeful human act that brings the food into the world of *tumah*.

---

## Minimum Size Debate

### Rav: Kezayis & Kepol

With the question of *yad* and *hechsher* resolved, the Gemara proceeds to a different set of parameters: does *yad* or *shomer* require a minimum size of food in order to operate? Rav rules: *ein yad le-pachos mi-kezayis ve-ein shomer le-pachos mi-kepul*. The concept of *yad* does not apply to less than a *kezayis*, and the concept of *shomer* does not apply to less than a *kepol* — a large bean, understood to be approximately the size of a fava bean.

### R. Yochanan: No Minimum

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *yesh yad le-pachos mi-kezayis ve-yesh shomer le-pachos mi-kepul*. Both concepts apply even below these minimum sizes.

One might ask: what would it even mean to have a *yad* connecting to something smaller than a *kezayis*? Since *tumah* in food normally requires the size of a *ke-beitzah* to transmit or receive, why does it matter whether the *yad* applies to a *kezayis* or less?

Rashi's answer is that the *yad* attaches to a piece of food that is a *kezayis* in size, while that same piece is in contact with other pieces of food that together reach the *ke-beitzah* threshold — so that touching the *yad* ultimately produces *tumah* for the combined mass. Tosafot, however, objects that a pile of separate items touching each other does not combine for the minimum size of *tumah*. On Tosafot's reading, the scenario is one where a *kezayis* of food is barely attached to a larger piece — connected by only a thread — so that pulling the *yad* would simply detach the *kezayis* without moving the whole. In that case the *yad* relates only to the *kezayis*, but the *kezayis* itself remains attached to the larger piece and so there is a minimum size. There is also the possibility that the *ke-beitzah* requirement applies only to transmitting *tumah*, not to receiving it.

### Two Bones Case

The Gemara now challenges Rav's position. A *beraita* teaches: two bones from a human corpse, each bearing half a *kezayis* of flesh, were brought with their non-flesh ends under a roof. The house is *tamei*. The principle at work is that since touching the bone would cause one to manipulate the flesh — making the bone a *yad* — so too being under a roof above the bone is like being under a roof above the flesh, and the *tumah* is transmitted. Yet in this case each bone bears only a half *kezayis*, and together they combine to constitute a *kezayis*. This appears to be a case where *yad* operates on less than a *kezayis* — a direct challenge to Rav.

### Combine Halves?

The *Tanna Kamma* of the *beraita* holds that the house is *tamei*, apparently accepting that *yad* can operate on two half-*kezayis* portions. But Yehuda ben Nekusa, citing Rabbi Yaakov, objects: *heich shnei atzamos mitztarfin le-kezayis* — how can two separate bones combine for a *kezayis*?

It is worth noting the unusual framing here. The Gemara presents this as a *meitivei* — an objection — rather than the standard *leima k'tannai* — let us say the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan parallels a Tannaic dispute. Although in substance the Tannaic dispute seems to map directly onto the Amoraic one, the Gemara nevertheless chooses the form of a challenge, obliging both Rav and Rabbi Yochanan to locate their positions within this *beraita*.

The two bones are not touching each other; they are connected only through the shared airspace beneath the roof.

### Positions Aligned

The Gemara resolves the tension as follows. If this *beraita* is read simply — as a case of *yad*, the bone serving as a handle for the meat — then the first opinion presents a difficulty for Rav, who holds *yad* does not apply to less than a *kezayis*. If instead it is read as a case of *shomer* — where the marrow inside the bone is the significant substance, and the bone itself is the *shomer* around it — then Rav can accommodate the first opinion, since he allows *shomer* to operate on less than a *kezayis* (only requiring the *kepol* threshold). But then the second opinion becomes difficult: Rabbi Yaakov says a *kezayis* is required, which conflicts with Rav's position on *shomer*.

The Gemara resolves this cleanly: *iba'it eima beyad* — read it as *yad*, and Rav aligns with Rabbi Yaakov, who also requires a *kezayis*. *Ve-iba'it eima be-shomer* — read it as *shomer*, and Rav aligns with the *Tanna Kamma*, who allows less than a *kezayis*, consistent with Rav's own ruling on *shomer*. For Rabbi Yochanan: *kula beyad ve-hu de-amar ke-Tanna Kamma* — read it entirely as *yad*, and Rabbi Yochanan simply follows the *Tanna Kamma*, since he holds that *yad* works even below a *kezayis*.

### Thigh Bone Case

A second *beraita* is then adduced. Rabbi Yehuda says: a *kulit* — a large thigh bone — that has a *kezayis* of flesh on it, *goreret kula le-tumah* — it draws everything along for the purposes of *tumah*. Even if the meat is far from where you are touching the bone, touching any part of the bone transmits *tumah* to the meat; the bone functions as a *yad*. The *Acherim* (generally understood to be Rabbi Meir) say: even if there is only a *kepol* of meat on it — not even a *kezayis* — it still draws everything for *tumah*.

This maps onto the earlier debate: Rabbi Yehuda requires a *kezayis* for *yad*, which fits Rav. Rabbi Meir requires only a *kepol*, which fits Rabbi Yochanan at least partially — Rabbi Yochanan might agree that a *kepol* is required even if he does not require a *kezayis*.

Once again the Gemara asks how Rav accommodates both opinions within a single *beraita*. If it is a *yad* case, the *acherim* opinion is difficult for Rav, who requires a *kezayis* for *yad*. If it is a *shomer* case (marrow inside the bone, with the bone serving as the protective covering), then Rabbi Yehuda is difficult for Rav, who requires only a *kepol* for *shomer*, not a *kezayis*. As before, the Gemara offers two readings: *iba'it eima beyad ve-hu de-amar ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — it is *yad*, and Rav follows Rabbi Yehuda; or *iba'it eima be-shomer ve-hu de-amar ke-Acherim* — it is *shomer*, and Rav follows Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yochanan, meanwhile, reads it entirely as *shomer* and follows the *Acherim*.

It is worth pausing here over something the Gemara itself finds somewhat curious. At the point where Rabbi Yochanan says *kula beshomer ve-hu de-amar ke-Acherim*, one might have expected the Gemara to say *kula beyad ve-hu de-amar ke-Acherim* just as well, since Rabbi Yochanan holds *yad* operates below a *kezayis*. The Gemara seems to prefer reading the *beraita* as about *shomer* at this stage, and this connects directly to what the Gemara discusses next.

The Gemara then cites a passage from the *Mishnah* about the pod of a *pol* (which Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya holds does not function as a *shomer*, since the bean is large enough not to require protection) and the pod of *kitnit* (smaller legumes, for which the pod does function as a *shomer* because one desires to use it through the pod). A difficulty arises: if we are talking about *kitnit* — individual small beans — there is not a *kepol*'s worth of food in any single pod. How can the *shomer* apply?

Rav Acha the son of Rava answers: this passage is not about the pod acting as a *shomer* at all. Rather, we are talking about the branch or stalk to which all the pods are attached, and it is functioning as a *yad*. The word *bemishmushan* — which might mean "in feeling them" — means here *betashmishan*, using them, manipulating them via the branch. Through one branch one moves all the pods attached to it, and therefore the branch is a *yad* to the entire cluster. The total quantity of food across all the pods reaches the minimum size, and the *yad* operates for the whole. The shell of any individual pod is not functioning as *shomer* here; the stalk is functioning as *yad*.

A case is then raised of a single remaining bean in a pod. Even though there is only one bean, and it is smaller than a *pol*, the pod still matters. Again, the answer is that we are not talking about the individual shell as *shomer* but the stalk as *yad* — the individual shell, being smaller than a *kepol*, cannot serve as a *shomer*, and for *yad* we are looking to the stalk and the combined mass of all the beans.

### Whole vs Fragmented

A final proof to Rabbi Yochanan's view is brought from a *beraita* of the *Tanna d'vei Rabbi Yishmael*: the verse *al kol zera zerua asher yizarei'a* — as people take out for planting: wheat in its shell, barley in its shell, lentils in their shells. Here the *shomer* applies to a single grain of wheat, which is certainly smaller than a *kezayis* and arguably smaller than a *kepol* as well. This seems to directly support Rabbi Yochanan.

Rav's response is the principle of *biryah sha'ani* — the case of a complete, whole item is different. When you are dealing with an intact, whole agricultural item — a single kernel of wheat in its shell — no minimum size is required for either *yad* or *shomer*, because the wholeness of the item itself confers *halachic* significance. The minimums of *kezayis* for *yad* and *kepol* for *shomer* apply only when the food in question is fragmentary — a piece of meat, part of a carcass, something that does not constitute a *biryah*. In those cases, you need a threshold of substance before the *yad* or *shomer* rules apply. But when the entire item is intact, even a tiny complete item is governed by its own integrity, not by size thresholds. Rashi notes that this principle would also have resolved some of the earlier difficulties discussed, particularly the cases involving peas and pods.

---

## Multiple Shomerim

### No Shomer on Shomer

The Gemara now takes up a fresh question posed by Rabbi Oshaya: *shnei shomrim mahu she-yitztarfu* — can two separate *shomrim* combine?

Before reaching the actual question, the Gemara clarifies what is not being asked. The question cannot be about one *shomer* stacked on top of another, because the *Mishnah* has already established that there is no *shomer al gabei shomer*. As proof, Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about the three layers of an onion is cited. The innermost layer, which is actually the beginning of the onion's edible flesh, combines regardless of whether it is whole or punctured. The middle layer, which is a thinner papery shell directly around the body of the onion, combines if whole (since it functions as a *shomer*) but not if punctured (since it no longer protects). The outermost layer is *tahor* in all cases — *bein kach u-vein kach tehorah* — because it is a *shomer* on a *shomer*, and such second-level protection is not recognized as part of the food at all.

The conceptual point is this: a *shomer* functions as an extension of the food itself, and therefore it must be directly connected to the food. Something that protects the *shomer* rather than protecting the food directly cannot achieve that extension; conceptually it is too distant, like a *gezeirah li-gezeirah*.

It is worth distinguishing this from the parallel question about *yad*. A *yad* is about manipulation, not about being an extension of the food. Therefore a *yad* can function at two degrees of remove: the Gemara earlier described a branch serving as *yad* to pods that each contain beans — the branch does not touch the beans directly, yet it manipulates them. For *shomer*, however, the requirement of direct connection to the food is structural to the concept itself.

The question is also raised about the outer shell: when the *Mishnah* says it is *tehorah* in all cases, does that mean it also fails to function as a *yad*? The simple reading of *bein kach u-vein kach tehorah* would imply so. This raises a deeper question about *yad*: is something a *yad* because it enables manipulation, or only because it makes manipulation easier? If the former, it is hard to see why touching the outermost shell would not transmit *tumah*. If the latter, then perhaps when an inner *shomer* is intact, the outer shell adds nothing practically to one's ability to manipulate the food, and therefore fails even as *yad*.

### Split Shomer Q

With the rule about *shomer al gabei shomer* established, the Gemara clarifies what Rabbi Oshaya's question actually is: *shomer ochel she-chilko ka-mibaya lei* — he is asking about a *shomer* that has been split. The scenario, as Tosafot explains it, is a single piece of meat whose skin (the non-edible skin functioning as *shomer*) has been cut into two separate portions, while the meat underneath remains intact and continuous. Each portion of the skin is still attached to the meat, and each protects the section of meat directly beneath it. But neither portion protects the entire piece of meat.

The question is whether these two portions of *shomer* combine. On one hand, *keivan de-hai lo magin a-hai ve-hai lo magin a-hai* — since neither protects the other, perhaps they should not be counted together as a unified *shomer*. On the other hand, *keivan de-hai magin a-didei ve-hai magin a-didei mitztaref* — perhaps since each one protects its own portion of the meat, together they fulfil the protective function over the whole, and they should combine.

### Multiple Foods OK

The Gemara brings a *beraita* as a possible proof. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya declares *tahor* the pod of a *pol*, but *tamei* the pod of *kitnit* — because one desires to use the smaller legumes through their pods. The argument — developed above in the minimum size discussion — is that Rashi reads this as demonstrating that multiple *shomrim* over multiple separate pieces of food do combine: no single pod has enough food inside it to reach the minimum size, and so the only way the ruling makes sense is if all the pods and their beans are counted together.

The Gemara notes that this is a significant step: combining two separate *shomrim* that each protect their own food may differ from combining two half-*shomrim* that protect portions of a single piece of food. Nevertheless, Rashi treats the *beraita* as bearing on Rabbi Oshaya's question. Tosafot reads it differently, but that reading is not developed at length here.

### Multiple Foods OK → Grain Row Union

Before resolving the question, the Gemara pursues the *beraita* about *kitnit* further and offers a different solution: *be-kulcha u-mishum yad* — we are not talking about the shells as *shomrim* at all; we are talking about the stalk connecting all the pods, which is functioning as a *yad* (as discussed above in the minimum size section). Rabbi Oshaya's unresolved question about combined *shomrim* therefore cannot be resolved from that source.

A second proof is attempted from the *Tanna d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* passage about wheat and barley in their shells being taken out for planting. Again Rashi argues that the only way there can be a minimum size here is if multiple kernels with their multiple shells are being combined, demonstrating that multiple *shomrim* can combine.

The Gemara again deflects: *hacha nami be-shidra u-mishum shomer* — here too we are talking about an ear of grain, not separate seeds. On a stalk of wheat, every kernel's presence contributes to holding the other kernels in place. The top kernels would fall if the bottom ones were removed. Accordingly, all the kernels together form a single unified *shomer*, not multiple separate ones.

### Grain Row Union

The Gemara then scrutinizes this resolution. *Bishlama d'ila'ata tzricha l'tata'ata* — granted, the top row requires the bottom row (remove the bottom and the top falls). But *ela tata'ah mai tzericha le-ila'ah* — how does the bottom row require the top row? You can remove the top without destabilizing the bottom. So the claim that every kernel protects every other kernel cannot be symmetric.

The Gemara's answer is *be-chada dara* — we are talking about a single row of kernels, not multiple rows. In one row, every kernel's presence holds its neighbors in place, and the mutual support is symmetric. Removing any kernel from the row destabilizes the adjacent kernels.

### Shimon Wheat

But this raises an immediate problem: *umi ika ke-beitza ochel be-chada dara* — is there really a *ke-beitza*'s worth of food in a single row of an ear of wheat? The Gemara's whole assumption was that we need multiple items to reach the minimum size. A single row of wheat would not plausibly yield a *ke-beitza*.

The Gemara's answer is: *be-chitei de-Shimon ben Shatach* — we are speaking of the miraculous wheat of Shimon ben Shatach, grains of the kind the *meraglim* reportedly saw in the Land of Israel, where a single row could contain a *ke-beitza* of food.

The Gemara immediately notes that once one resorts to such miraculous dimensions, the need for even a single row is unnecessary: *chada chita nami be-chitei de-Shimon ben Shatach* — a single grain of wheat from Shimon ben Shatach's crop could itself be the size of a *ke-beitza*. The entire question of combining multiple *shomrim* via a single row becomes superfluous. The upshot is that the question of Rabbi Oshaya — whether two separate *shomrim* can combine — remains formally unresolved by the Gemara.

---

## Hair as Yad

### Bone as Yad Dispute

The Gemara now returns to the *beraita* about two bones, each with a half-*kezayis* of flesh, brought under a roof. This time the focus is not on the minimum size question but on a different dispute: what exactly can function as a *yad*?

### R. Lakish Position

Reish Lakish rules: *lo shanu ela etzem de-havah yad, aval nima lo havah yad* — this law applies only to a bone, which functions as a *yad*, but not to a hair. A hair does not constitute a *yad*. The rationale is that *yad* requires the ability to actually manipulate the object — to pick it up or move it — and a single hair, which will ordinarily simply pull out under tension, does not enable that kind of manipulation.

### R. Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *afilu nima nami havah yad* — even a hair functions as a *yad*. This is a striking claim. The Gemara immediately investigates how Rabbi Yochanan grounds it.

### Hair Proof

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from an explicit *beraita*: skin from an animal bearing a *kezayis* of meat from a *neveilah* — one who touches either the *tziv* (a protruding sinew or string of flesh) or the *se'ar* (a hair protruding from the skin) that comes out of it is *tamei*. This *beraita* explicitly includes hair as a vehicle for *tumah*.

### Shomer Problem

*Mai lav mishum yad* — does this not demonstrate that hair functions as a *yad*? Reish Lakish responds: *lo, mishum shomer* — no, the hair is functioning as a *shomer*, not a *yad*. Meaning, it is not transmitting *tumah* through manipulation but by being an extension of the meat.

But this answer is immediately problematic: *umi ika shomer al gabei shomer* — we have established that there cannot be a *shomer* on a *shomer*. The hair is on the skin, and the skin is on the meat. For the hair to be a *shomer* to the meat, it would have to be the skin's *shomer*, making it a *shomer al gabei shomer* — precisely what the rule forbids.

### Hair Penetrates

The Gemara resolves this with a surprising claim: *shachuyei mechalchal* — the hair penetrates downward through the skin, filling the follicle hole all the way to the meat beneath. On this view, the hair is not resting on the surface of the skin; it passes through the skin and is directly in contact with the meat. Therefore it is not a *shomer* on a *shomer* — it is a *shomer* directly on the meat. The skin and the hair are, in a sense, at the same level.

Admittedly, this is anatomically striking, particularly for thick cow hide. But the argument requires that the hair follicle extends below the skin layer into the flesh layer — that the hair fills that channel and is therefore, structurally, directly attached to the meat.

### Tefillin Challenge

Rav Acha bar Yaakov seizes on this claim. *Tefillin heichi katvinan* — if we accept that hair follicles create actual holes passing all the way through the skin (which becomes *klaf* for writing *tefillin*), how can *tefillin* be written on such parchment? The requirement of *ketiva tama* — complete, uninterrupted writing — would seem to be violated if the ink is being laid over microscopic holes at every follicle.

### Ink Covers Holes

The Gemara's first answer: *kol nekev she-ha-dio over alav eino nekev* — any hole over which ink passes continuously is not considered a hole. If the ink stroke is continuous and unbroken in appearance, the presence of a microscopic gap beneath it does not constitute an interruption in the writing. This is what is said in the West (*ma'arava*, meaning *Eretz Yisrael*), and Rav Acha had simply forgotten this principle.

### Multiple Hairs Yad

The Gemara offers a second resolution: *ve-iba'it eima, kulei mishum yad* — alternatively, the hair in that *beraita* is functioning as *yad* after all, not *shomer*. But then Reish Lakish's objection stands — he denies that hair functions as *yad*. The answer, citing a principle of Rav Illa, is that the rule applies specifically *bi-mloi she-bein ha-mlo'im* — when the hair is one among many, embedded within a full group of hairs. A single strand cannot manipulate anything. But when there is a dense covering of hair — as with the hairs on a wheat stalk or the full coat of hair on an animal — the entire mass of hair functions as a *yad*. In that case, even Reish Lakish would agree.

### Wheat Hairs Example

This brings the Gemara to Rav Illa's original context. The *mloi she-bein ha-shibolim* — the hairs of the stalks of wheat — *metamin u-metamin ve-ein mitztarfin*: they function as *yad*, transmitting *tumah* in and out, but they do not combine to add to the minimum size. They are *yad*, not *shomer*.

The question is then asked: *le-mai chazi* — what possible use is one individual strand of wheat hair? Rav Illa answers: *bi-mloi she-bein ha-mlo'im* — we are speaking of a hair within a group of hairs. The multiple strands together allow manipulation, and therefore the group functions as a *yad*. A single isolated strand, by contrast, cannot manipulate anything and would not function as *yad* even according to Rabbi Yochanan.

---

---

# Hullin 120

## Yad & Shomer

### Yad/Shomer Intro

The daf opens by completing a discussion that began at the very bottom of 119b — literally the final three words of that amud — concerning the concepts of *yad* and *shomer* as they relate to the communication of *tumah*. The fundamental question is whether certain things attached to food objects — handles, protective coverings, and the like — can serve as conduits for *tumah*, and whether they can combine with the food itself to constitute the minimum size required for the food to become *tamei*.

The background principle is straightforward: in order for food to receive and transmit *tumah*, it must meet a minimum size, typically the volume of an egg (*ke-beitzah*). The question is whether items connected to the food can contribute to that minimum. The *halacha* establishes two distinct categories. A *shomer* — a protective covering, such as the skin around meat or a shell around a nut — is treated as fully integrated with the food itself and therefore does add to the minimum size. Moreover, if something *tamei* touches the *shomer*, it communicates *tumah* both to the *shomer* and through it to the food. A *yad* — a handle or manipulator, something through which you can grasp or move the food — does not add to the minimum size, since it is not truly integrated with the food, but it does serve as a conduit: touching a *yad* communicates *tumah* in both directions.

### Hair as Shomer

With this backdrop, the Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish that is taught, according to one tradition, specifically in connection with the Mishnah of our chapter. The Mishnah lists various things that combine with meat to constitute the minimum food size for receiving *tumah*, including the skin (*ha-or*). Reish Lakish holds that while a bone or skin — items that genuinely function as protectors — qualify as a *shomer*, a hair (*nima*) protruding from a piece of meat does not: *lo havei shomer*. Since the hair does no meaningful work of protection, if something *tamei* contacts the hair, the contact is halachically irrelevant. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *afilu nima nami havei shomer* — even a hair qualifies as a *shomer*.

Reish Lakish immediately challenges Rabbi Yochanan: *u-mi ika shomer agav shomer?* Can one *shomer* rest on top of another *shomer*? The skin already protects the meat; the hair sits on top of the skin. The Gemara had established in an earlier session that a *shomer* atop a *shomer* does not qualify — analogous to the principle of *gezeirah li-gezeirah*, that a rabbinic safeguard built upon another rabbinic safeguard has no traction. A *shomer* is halachically meaningful only when it directly relates to the food itself; something two steps removed loses that connection.

### Tefillin Challenge

Rabbi Yochanan's response to Reish Lakish is that the hair does not merely rest on top of the skin — *de-kulei mechalchel* — it actually pierces through the skin and reaches the flesh below. Therefore the hair is directly connected to the flesh, not simply sitting atop a *shomer* of the skin, and qualifies as a *shomer* in its own right.

Rav Achai immediately challenges this: *ela me-ata tefillin heichi katvinan?* If the hair follicle truly penetrates all the way through the leather to the flesh beneath, then the leather used to write *tefillin* is riddled with tiny invisible holes. Given the requirement of *ketivah tamah* — that the writing of *tefillin* must be complete and uninterrupted — how can one write valid *tefillin* on such leather?

### Ink Passes Over

The Gemara resolves this difficulty by citing a ruling known in the West, in *Eretz Yisrael*: *kol nekav she-ha-dyo over alav eino nekav* — any hole over which ink can pass without interruption does not count as a hole for the purposes of *tefillin*. The hair follicles, being minuscule, do not cause any perceptible break in the flow of ink across the parchment, and therefore they do not invalidate the writing. The *tefillin* challenge dissolves.

### Hair Pierces Skin

Having defended his own position against Rav Achai's challenge, Rabbi Yochanan now turns the tables on Reish Lakish. He adduces a source: if a piece of skin (*or*) bearing at least an olive's worth (*ke-zayit*) of flesh from a *neveilah* is lying before you, and someone touches a strand (*tziv*) emerging from the skin — *hanogei'a ba-tziv ha-yotzei mimenu* — or, more pointedly, hair that is directly opposite the flesh (*u-vasar she-kenegdo*) — that person becomes *tamei*. This, Rabbi Yochanan argues, demonstrates that the hair communicates *tumah*, vindicating his position.

### Multiple Hairs

Reish Lakish responds by reframing the source: the reason touching the hair makes one *tamei* is not that the hair is a *shomer* — it is that the hair is a *yad*, a handle. But the Gemara immediately objects: *nima achas le-mai chazya?* A single hair is useless as a handle; if you try to lift the meat by one hair it will simply snap off. How can it be called a *yad*?

The Gemara resolves this by invoking a ruling of Rabbi Ila: the same logic applies to the fine strands (*melo'i*) at the top of a wheat stalk. No individual strand can be used to manipulate the wheat, yet Rabbi Ila teaches — *bimloi she-bein ha-mloi'im* — that it is precisely because they function collectively that each individual strand counts as a *yad*. When you have a full complement of strands, you can grasp the bundle and use it to move the wheat. Similarly, *hacha nami binima she-bein ha-nimim* — here too, among the hairs, since the plurality of hairs together can be used to manipulate the meat, each individual hair, in context, serves the function of a *yad*.

The Gemara then specifies where Rabbi Ila's ruling was originally stated. It is the *halacha* of the strands of a wheat stalk that they communicate *tumah* and receive *tumah* — *ha-metamin u-mitamin* — but they do not combine with the wheat to constitute the minimum size — *ein mitztarfin*. This is precisely the distinction between *yad* and *shomer*: a *yad* transmits *tumah* but does not add to the minimum size; a *shomer* does both.

### Yad/Shomer Summary

With this, the Gemara concludes the discussion of *yad* and *shomer*, a topic treated extensively in its own right in *Masechet Uktzin*, one of the more obscure tractates of the order of *Taharos*.

A brief review of the conceptual structure is in order. The *yad* and *shomer* framework exists because *tumah* requires a minimum quantity of food: typically a *ke-beitzah*. Items attached to the food may or may not contribute to that minimum. A *shomer* — a genuine protective covering — is fully integrated into the food and contributes to the minimum size; touching a *shomer* communicates *tumah* in both directions, but only when the *shomer* is directly opposite the food it protects. A *shomer* upon a *shomer* does not qualify, for the same reason a *gezeirah li-gezeirah* does not: it is too far removed from the original item. A *yad* — a manipulator — does not add to the minimum size, since it is not one with the food, but it does transmit *tumah*, even indirectly. Unlike a *shomer*, a *yad* can communicate *tumah* even when it is not positioned directly opposite the food. Several further questions were touched upon in the broader discussion: whether the concepts of *yad* and *shomer* apply not only to *tumah* but also to *hechsher* (the liquid-contact that renders food susceptible to *tumah*), and what minimum quantity of food is required before the *yad* or *shomer* framework can be invoked at all.

---

## Rotev Gravy

### What is Rotev

The Mishnah of our chapter lists a series of things that combine with meat to constitute the minimum food quantity required for *tumah*: the skin (*ha-or*), the gravy (*ha-rotev*), and the *kipah* — to be defined momentarily. The Gemara now turns to *rotev*. What exactly is *rotev*? Rava answers: *shumna* — the fat and the fatty liquids that run off of meat during cooking.

### Gravy Combining

Abaye immediately challenges this definition: if *rotev* is something substantive enough that a person could eat it directly, why does the Mishnah present it only as something that *combines* with the meat to reach the minimum size? It should constitute food on its own and become *tamei* independently.

The proper reading of the text, as confirmed by the textual tradition, replaces the potentially misleading word with *chala de-karish* — a clear liquid runoff from the meat that, crucially, has congealed. Two issues are now being raised simultaneously. The first is that *rotev* refers to something that no one would eat on its own — it is eaten only in conjunction with meat, the way one might pour gravy over a piece of chicken or dip bread into it, but would not consume it independently. This is precisely why the Mishnah says it *combines* with the meat: it is not an independent food source, but together with the meat it constitutes additional foodstuff. The second issue, which will occupy the Gemara at greater length, is the question of physical state: must the *rotev* be congealed (a solid) in order to combine with the meat (also a solid), or can a liquid combine with a solid to reach the minimum food quantity?

### Gelled vs. Liquid

Abaye asserts that the *rotev* must be *karish* — congealed — in order to combine with the meat. The Gemara challenges this requirement. Reish Lakish teaches that the juices running off a vegetable (*tzir she-al gabei yerek*) combine with the vegetable itself to constitute the minimum quantity on *Yom Kippur*: *mitztaref le-kikoseves be-Yom ha-Kippurim*. On *Yom Kippur*, transgression requires consuming the volume of a *kikoseves* (a dried date), and if one ate a vegetable slightly below that threshold but with its liquid runoff, the liquid and solid together may constitute the requisite amount. Here, then, liquid combines with solid — without any requirement of congealing. Why, then, does Abaye insist that *rotev* must be congealed in order to combine with meat?

### Yishuv Hadaat

The Gemara answers that the two cases operate under entirely different legal frameworks. The *Yom Kippur* case is governed by the principle of *yishuv ha-daat* — the negation of affliction. The *Torah* does not, by *Yom Kippur*, explicitly forbid eating or drinking as such; it commands *inuy*, affliction, and the rabbis define the transgression as neutralizing that affliction. The measure of the *kikoseves*, larger than the standard *ke-zayit* required for most eating prohibitions, reflects the fact that we are not defining an act of eating but rather asking what quantity of consumption is sufficient to counteract the subjective sense of *inuy*. Because the legal question is about the effect on the person — *yishuv ha-daat*, the settling of the mind and body — liquid and solid can work together toward that effect even without congealing. The Gemara puts it directly: *hasam mishum yishuv ha-daat hu; hacha mishum itztarufei hu* — there it is about settling the affliction, here it is about combining as food.

When we turn to the question of *tumah*, by contrast, the legal category is the object itself: we need a minimum quantity of *food*, of solid foodstuff, and liquids belong to a different category altogether. Liquids have their own minimum quantities for *tumah*, and they do not combine with solids to reach the minimum applicable to solids. The *rotev*, as a liquid, therefore does not combine with the meat unless it has congealed into a solid. That is Abaye's position, and the Gemara accepts it: *karish mitztaref; i lo karish lo mitztaref* — if it is congealed it combines; if not, it does not.

---

## Kipah & Tavlin

### What is Kipah

The Mishnah also mentions *kipah* as something that combines with meat to constitute the minimum food quantity. What is *kipah*? Rabba (or Rava) answers: *pirma* — the small remnants and thin pieces of meat that settle at the bottom of a pot. Rashi explains this as the residue left after the main meat has been removed, the sort of thing that a hungry person might scrape from the bottom of the pot.

### Tavlin Spices

Abaye again challenges: if *kipah* is simply small pieces of meat, they are food in their own right and should become *tamei* independently, not merely in combination with the main piece. Why does the Mishnah present *kipah* only as something that combines?

Rav Pappa answers: *tavlin* — the word *kipah* in the Mishnah refers not to meat remnants but to spices mixed into the pot. Spices are not eaten independently; one does not sit down to a bowl of spices. Therefore they are not food in their own right and would not become *tamei* on their own. But when they are mixed together with the meat in the pot, they are part of the ensemble of foodstuff that one eats, and they therefore combine with the meat to constitute the minimum size for *tumah*.

### Non-Food Items

What exactly counts as "spices" (*tavlin*) here is a question of context. Ground spices are clearly never eaten straight. Onions and garlic present a more ambiguous case — some people eat them independently, others only in combination with bread or meat. The operative principle is that something which is never consumed on its own, but which is always eaten as part of a larger food preparation, may combine with that preparation to contribute to the minimum food quantity. If it can be eaten independently, it would be *tamei* on its own. If it cannot, it combines. The spices of the *kipah* fall into the former category: they are not independent food, but in combination with meat they are part of the food.

---

## Liquefying Foods

### Blood Case

A *baraita* introduces a new set of cases that substantially expand the discussion: *hikpah et ha-dam ve-achalo o she-himcha et ha-chelev u-gema'o — chayav*. If one took blood and congealed it, converting it from its natural liquid state into a solid, and then ate it — one is liable. Or if one took forbidden fat (*chelev*) and liquefied it, converting it from its natural solid state into a liquid, and then drank it — one is liable.

The first case, blood, is relatively straightforward. The Torah prohibition on blood (*kol dam lo tochelu*) uses the language of eating. By congealing the blood and consuming it as a solid, one has performed an act of eating in the most classical sense — indeed, in an even more emphatic sense than merely drinking liquid blood. Furthermore, by congealing it, *achshuvei achshavei* — one has elevated its status, made it more significant. There is no difficulty here.

### Fat Case

The second case is the challenging one. The Torah says don't *eat* forbidden fat — *achilah ketiv beih* — yet here one is not eating it, one is drinking it. The fat has been liquefied and consumed as a liquid. Does one transgress?

This raises a broader question that *Tosafot* engages with directly. There is a general principle that *shtiyah bi-khlal achilah* — drinking is subsumed under the prohibition of eating. When the Torah says "do not eat," this ordinarily extends to drinking as well. But that principle typically applies when the item being consumed is naturally a liquid — as when the Torah prohibits blood, which is in its natural state a liquid. The present question is different: here we are talking about an item that is naturally a solid and has been artificially converted into a liquid form. Taking a piece of *chelev*, liquefying it, and drinking the result is a thoroughly bizarre mode of consumption. One might well argue that the Torah's prohibition of eating *chelev* does not extend to drinking liquefied *chelev* — that the *Torah* only prohibited conventional acts of consumption: eating meat, drinking wine, not drinking meat.

### Nefesh Includes

Reish Lakish resolves the question by pointing to a word in the relevant verse. When the Torah discusses *neveilah* — and, by analogy, similar cases — it uses the word *nefesh*: the *nefesh* that eats *chelev* shall be cut off. Rashi explains that *nefesh* points toward the inner experience, the holistic impact of consumption on the person, rather than to the specific physical act. In other words, the prohibition is framed in terms of what happens to the *nefesh* — and therefore it includes even drinking. *Nefesh le-rabot et ha-shoteh* — the word *nefesh* comes to include even one who drinks.

It is worth noting that scholars of Semitic languages observe that *nefesh* has a cognate meaning of "throat" in other ancient Near Eastern languages, a reading that has some resonance here: whatever passes through the throat — whether eaten or drunk — is included in the prohibition.

### Chametz Case

A *baraita* then teaches a parallel by *chametz*: *himchehu u-gema'o* — if one liquefied *chametz* and drank it, one is still punishable by *karet*. Again, the verse says *achilah* — eating — and drinking liquefied *chametz* is not eating in the conventional sense. Again, Reish Lakish invokes the word *nefesh* from the relevant verse as the basis for including drinking.

### Matzah Case

The same *baraita* teaches the parallel for *matzah*: if one liquefied *matzah* and drank it on *Pesach*, one does not fulfill the obligation. The rationale is different: the Torah says *lechem oni* — bread of affliction — and liquefied *matzah* is no longer bread. This is a striking asymmetry. Liquefying undermines the positive character of *matzah* as bread and therefore disqualifies it from fulfilling the *Pesach* obligation. But it does not undermine the negative character of *chametz* as a prohibited substance. The prohibition of *chametz* survives the liquefying; the fulfillment of *matzah* does not. The same physical transformation — converting a solid grain product into a liquid — has opposite effects depending on whether the legal question concerns a prohibition (where the *nefesh* verse extends coverage) or a positive act of fulfillment (where the requirement of *lechem* demands a bread-form).

### Dead Bird Case

The *baraita* also teaches the parallel case in *tumah*: the carcass of a permitted bird (*neveilat of tahor*) renders one *tamei* if eaten. If one liquefied the carcass over fire (*himchehu ba-ur*), one becomes *tamei* upon consuming it — *tamei*. But if one liquefied it in the sun (*be-chama*), one remains *tahor*.

Why the difference? *Be-chama isruchei yasreich* — liquefying by extended exposure to the sun takes a long time, and during that process the flesh decomposes, becomes rancid, and loses its essential character as the flesh of a bird. When something becomes thoroughly rancid, it is no longer recognizable as the original substance; it has lost its identity and therefore its status. Liquefying over fire, by contrast, is rapid and preserves the substance's identity. In that case, even in liquid form, consuming it renders one *tamei*, again derived from the word *nefesh* in the relevant verse: *nefesh le-rabot et ha-shoteh*.

### Three Cases

The Gemara now asks the expected question: given that all three cases — *chelev*, *chametz*, and *neveilat of tahor* — carry the same teaching (that liquefied consumption counts), why does the Torah need to state the principle three times? Could we not derive the rule from one or two of them?

The Gemara works through every possible reduction. Had the Torah written it only for *chelev*, we could not derive *chametz*: *she-kein lo hayta lo sha'at ha-kosher* — *chelev* was never permissible, whereas *chametz* was once permitted. Had it written it only for *chametz*, we could not derive *chelev*: *she-kein huhtra mi-kelalo* — *chelev* of a *chaya* (a deer) is permissible to a layperson, giving *chelev* a dimension of leniency from which we might have hesitated to derive the stricter case of *chametz*. Had it written it only for *neveilah*, we could not derive the others: *she-kein metam'ah* — *neveilah* has the additional stringency of causing *tumah*, which the others do not, so we could not use it as a model. And even combining two of the three in any pairing fails, because each of the remaining two can be identified as sharing a stringency absent in the third. Therefore the Torah had no choice but to write the principle explicitly in all three places.

The Gemara then raises the case of *shratzim* — forbidden rodents and insects — and their juices and the *kipah* at the bottom of the vessel. Could one not have learned the rule of liquid equivalence from the three cases just discussed, rather than needing a separate verse for the *shratzim*? The Gemara answers that one could not: the principle derived from the three cases operates with the minimum quantity of those prohibitions — a *ke-zayit* — but *shratzim* cause *tumah* and transgression at the size of a lentil bean (*ke-adasha*), smaller than an olive. Had the rule for *shratzim* been derived from the other cases, one might have applied a *ke-zayit* minimum even to the liquid form of *shratzim*, whereas the proper minimum is a *ke-adasha*. The separate verse for *shratzim* is therefore necessary to establish that the liquid of *shratzim* follows the rules specific to *shratzim*, including the smaller minimum quantity.

Conversely, could one not have written the liquids rule only by *shratzim* and derived the rest from it? No: *mah li-shratzim she-kein tumatam be-mashehu* — the very stringency of *shratzim*, that they cause *tumah* in a small amount, is a reason one might not have applied the logic to other prohibited items that require a larger minimum. Thus both directions of derivation fail, and the full set of verses is necessary to establish the principle across all categories.

It is worth noting, as *Tosafot* observes, that throughout this sugya the Gemara treats two conceptually distinct phenomena as roughly equivalent: (a) liquefying a solid substance and consuming it in liquid form, and (b) liquids that naturally run off from a substance. These are quite different. Liquefied meat is still the meat itself in altered form; the juices running off meat are a separate substance that emerged from the meat. One could in principle imagine different rulings for the two — and indeed, there is an argument that liquefied meat, as the very substance of the original item, should be *more* clearly prohibited, while runoff juices, which are not the item itself, might be treated differently. The Gemara, however, treats them as equivalent for purposes of this discussion.

---

## Ag Product Liquids

### Forbidden Items

The Gemara now applies the principle of liquid equivalence to a new set of cases. A *baraita* teaches: *ha-tevel ve-ha-chadash ve-ha-hekdesh ve-ha-shvi'it ve-ha-kilayim* — untithed grain (*tevel*), new grain before *Pesach* (*chadash*), sanctified items (*hekdesh*), Sabbatical year produce (*shvi'it*), and forbidden agricultural mixtures (*kilayim*) — *kulan mashkin ha-yotzin me-hen ke-motan*: the liquids that emerge from any of these items have the same status as the items themselves.

### Liquid Status

The rule appears straightforward in light of what has just been established: liquids from forbidden items share the status of the items. But the Gemara now asks — where does this rule come from? Can it be derived from the cases already discussed?

### Natural vs. Imposed

The problem is that the three cases of *chelev*, *chametz*, and *neveilah* all involve items whose forbidden status is entirely natural — their prohibition arises from what they inherently are. The cases of *hekdesh* and *kilayim*, however, involve an imposed status: *hekdesh* becomes sanctified through a human act of designation; *kilayim* acquires its forbidden character through the human act of cross-planting. One might argue that an imposed status, being less intrinsic to the object, would operate differently — perhaps it attaches only to the object in its natural form and does not extend to the liquids that emerge from it. This is the distinction: *issur ha-ba me-elav* (a prohibition that arises of itself, naturally) versus an imposed prohibition. Rashi understands the point in terms of *hekdesh*; *Tosafot* identifies *kilayim* as the primary example.

So the Gemara can derive the rule for naturally prohibited items from the earlier cases, but cannot derive it for items with imposed status. The cases where the prohibition arises naturally can draw on the precedent of *chelev*, *chametz*, and *neveilah*. The question is: what is the source for the imposed-status cases?

### Bikurim Model

The Gemara answers: we learn it from *bikurim*. *Bikurim* is not a natural state — one must actively designate produce as first-fruits — and yet the principle of liquid equivalence applies there. Therefore *bikurim* serves as the model for all cases of imposed status.

### Bikurim Source

Where do we know that liquid equivalence applies by *bikurim*? Rabbi Yosi teaches from the verse: the Torah says to bring *pri* — fruit — from the first of the land's produce. *Pri ata meivi ve-ee ata meivi mashke* — you bring fruit, not liquid; one does not bring mere juice to the *Beit ha-Mikdash* in lieu of the fruit. However, if one brought the fruit and subsequently pressed it into wine, a different verse — *tavi*, "you shall bring," interpreted inclusively — indicates that it retains its *bikurim* status even in transformed liquid form. So: first bring the fruit intact; but once it has been brought and designated as *bikurim*, transforming it into a liquid does not strip it of that status.

### Bikurim Weight

One might challenge the extension from *bikurim* to other cases: *mah le-bikurim she-kein te'unim kri'ah ve-hanacha* — *bikurim* is uniquely weighty, requiring a formal declaration (*kri'ah*) and placement before the altar (*hanacha*). Perhaps the principle of liquid equivalence reflects this heightened significance of *bikurim* and does not apply to lesser categories.

### Terumah Link

The Gemara therefore shifts to *terumah*. Like *bikurim*, *terumah* is an imposed status (the priest's portion is designated by human action). We learn liquid equivalence by *terumah* from its link to *bikurim*: the verse speaks of *terumat yadecha* — the *terumah* of your hand — and the rabbis identify this as a reference to *bikurim*. Thus *bikurim* are called *terumah*, and what is true of *bikurim* regarding liquids is therefore true of *terumah*.

### Terumah Weight

But *terumah* too is weightier than ordinary cases: one who inadvertently eats *terumah* is liable to pay the principal and add a fifth (*chomesh*), and eating *terumah* intentionally carries a penalty of death at heaven's hand (*mita bi-ydei shamayim*). Perhaps the principle of liquid equivalence by *terumah* reflects this stringency and cannot be exported to less weighty prohibitions like *kilayim*.

### Combined Cases

The Gemara's resolution is to combine cases. By taking *terumah* and *bikurim* together with one of the naturally-prohibited cases (such as *shratzim*, or *neveilah*, or *chametz*), we can establish the principle across all types of prohibitions: naturally arising and imposed, lightly penalized and heavily penalized. Each pairing addresses the challenge raised by the other member's unique stringency, and together they establish that liquid equivalence is a universal rule applying to all forbidden items, whether their status arises naturally or by human imposition.

---

## Terumah Liquids

### Terumah Examples

Having established that liquids emerging from *terumah* share the status of *terumah* itself, the Gemara cites a *mishnah* (actually a *baraita*) that applies this principle in practice, while revealing that there is a significant dispute about its scope. The *baraita* lists: honey made from dates (*devash temarim*), apple cider (*yayin tapuchim*), vinegar made from the bitter late-season grapes (*chometz sitvaniyot*), and other liquid products made from *terumah* fruits.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

Rabbi Eliezer rules that all such liquid products of *terumah* have full *terumah* status: one who eats them inadvertently must pay the principal (*keren*) plus the added fifth (*chomesh*) — *mechayev keren ve-chomesh*. In Rabbi Eliezer's view, the principle we have established — that liquids from *terumah* share the status of *terumah* — applies universally to all fruits designated as *terumah* and their liquid derivatives.

### Rabbi Yehoshua View

Rabbi Yehoshua exempts — *poter* — holding that these liquids do not carry *terumah* status. The dispute is not about the general principle that liquids can share the status of their source; both authorities accept that. The debate is about how to apply the derivation.

### Damino Mimo Debate

The Gemara explains: *be-damino mino u-be-damino ve-okei ba-asra paligi* — they dispute whether, when learning a rule from an analogy, one preserves the original context of the source (*damino mino*) or applies the context of the target case (*okei ba-asra*).

Rabbi Eliezer holds *damino mino*: we derived the liquid equivalence rule for *terumah* from *bikurim*. Just as by *bikurim* the Torah says *pri ha-adamah* — the fruit of the ground — and therefore the liquids of all types of fruit count as *bikurim* in liquid form, so too by *terumah*, the liquids of all types of fruit designated as *terumah* carry *terumah* status. We preserve the broad context of *bikurim* — all fruits — and carry it over to *terumah*.

Rabbi Yehoshua holds *okei ba-asra*: yes, we learn from *bikurim* that liquid equivalence applies. But now apply it within the specific context of *terumah*. What liquids does *terumah* biblically recognize? Only *tirosh* and *yitzhar* — wine and oil. The Torah's language for *terumah* is *dagan, tirosh, ve-yitzhar*: grain, wine, and oil. Other liquids are not mentioned in the biblical law of *terumah*. Therefore, when we learn the principle of liquid equivalence from *bikurim* and apply it to *terumah*, we apply it only to those liquids that *terumah* itself explicitly recognizes: wine and oil.

### Wine & Oil Only

The practical consequence of Rabbi Yehoshua's position, as *Tosafot* explains it, is that the only liquid products of *terumah* fruits that carry the full *terumah* status — requiring payment of principal and fifth if inadvertently consumed — are wine and oil. Honey of dates, apple cider, and other fruit juices, even from fruits that are unquestionably *terumah*, do not carry *terumah* status as liquids, because the Torah did not recognize such liquids within the framework of *terumah* law. Notably, this may extend even to liquids that run off of grain or barley, since the Torah by *terumah* highlights specifically the liquids of wine and oil, implicitly excluding others.

The daf thus closes at a turning point. The long arc of the discussion has established that liquids are generally treated as equivalent to the solids from which they derive — whether through liquefaction or natural runoff, whether the prohibition is natural or imposed. Yet that principle is now shown to have limits. For *terumah*, at least according to Rabbi Yehoshua, the recognized liquids are specifically wine and oil; other liquid derivatives of *terumah* produce do not carry full *terumah* status. The discussion of precisely where liquid equivalence applies and where it breaks down will continue into the next amud.

---

---

# Hullin 121

## Liquids: Wine & Oil

### Liquids Overview

The discussion opens at the very bottom of 120a and carries into 121a, examining whether liquids that emerge from solids—or that liquefy solids—possess recognized halakhic status. Much of the preceding daf had been occupied with verses suggesting that they do: *chelev* in liquefied form, *chametz* in liquid form, and similar cases. But the sugya now closes on a more qualified, even negative note, establishing that when it comes to *terumah*, at least one position holds that only wine and oil are recognized liquids—no other type of liquid, even one derived from grain that would be *terumah* on a biblical level, enjoys halakhic standing.

### Bikkurim Liquids

The Gemara introduces the point with a *mishnah*: *ein mevi'in bikkurim mashkeh ela hayotzei min ha-zeisim u-min ha-anavim*—one may only bring *bikkurim* in liquid form if that liquid is what comes from olives or grapes, meaning olive oil or wine. Earlier in the discussion, the sugya had noted that if fruit designated as *bikkurim* was subsequently pressed into liquid, that liquid is acceptable. But the *mishnah* here draws a sharp limit: the only liquid form that counts is oil or wine. The Gemara then asks: whose view does this reflect?

### R. Yehoshua Rules

The answer is: *Rabbi Yehoshua hi*—this follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who took the same position regarding *terumah*: only wine and olive oil possess recognized halakhic status as liquids; any other liquid, even one that derives from produce that is subject to *terumah* obligations, does not. The Gemara explains his derivation: *amar dami leh ve-kava lah*—he identifies an analogy between *terumah* and *bikkurim*, situating the rule within the context of *terumah*, where the Torah explicitly mentions wine and oil. Having established the rule for *terumah*, one then applies it back to *bikkurim* as well.

### Three Linked Cases

The Gemara then adds a third case—*ain sofgin et ha-arba'im mishum orlah ela ha-yotzei min ha-zeisim u-min ha-anavim*: one only receives lashes for violating *orlah* (the prohibition on fruit of the first three years) in liquid form if the liquid consumed is olive oil, wine, or grape juice. Any other liquid form does not incur lashes. Here too the Gemara attributes the view to Rabbi Yehoshua, using the same mechanism. First, *bikkurim* is linked to *terumah*: just as *terumah* is only wine and oil, so too *bikkurim* is only wine and oil. Then, the Gemara reports a *gezeirah shavah* from the shared term *pri*—the word *pri ha-adamah* appears in the context of *bikkurim*, and the same root appears in the laws of *orlah*—and from this verbal analogy, the limitation on *bikkurim* is extended to *orlah* as well.

So after an entire daf exploring how many obligations attach to liquefied or liquidified forms of produce, the conclusion reached in these three domains—*terumah*, *bikkurim*, and *orlah*—is that at minimum one significant position restricts recognized liquids to wine and oil alone.

### Zei'ah Be'alma

What gives this position even broader weight is a statement in *Pesachim*. The Gemara there cites the same rule—that lashes for *orlah* apply only to wine and oil—and uses it to ground the sweeping conclusion that the juice of fruits other than wine and oil is *zei'ah be'alma*, mere sweat, possessing no halakhic status whatsoever. This is not a limited exception carved out for one domain; it is a global pronouncement about the standing of fruit juice. And in practice, this is largely how *halakhah* treats the matter: for instance, the only act of squeezing for which one violates *Shabbos* on a biblical level is squeezing olives or grapes, because only those products are considered to produce something genuinely significant.

### Shabbat Squeezing

This principle has direct practical application on *Shabbos*. While squeezing many types of fruit is prohibited on *Shabbos*, the biblical-level prohibition—*de-oraita*—applies only to squeezing olives (for oil) and grapes (for wine or grape juice), because only those liquids are regarded as producing something with real halakhic significance. Other fruit liquids, by contrast, fall into the category of *zei'ah be'alma*. The same logic underlies the uncertainty about whether *terumos u-ma'asros* can be taken from produce after it has been pressed: since the resulting liquid may not count as the fruit itself, the obligations may not follow. In any event, wherever the category is fruit juice as distinct from, say, liquefied meat, the general rule appears to be that only wine and olive oil matter.

### Central Question

This raises the fundamental question of what is rule and what is exception. Is the general principle that a liquid form of something does not have the halakhic status of the thing itself—with a handful of specific exceptions such as *chelev* and *chametz*? Or is the general principle that it does, with fruit juice carving out its own specialized rule that only wine and oil count? Or perhaps the rule is domain-specific: by fruit juice, only wine and oil; by liquefied meat, a different analysis would apply. It is worth noting that the entire halakhic discussion took shape in a cultural context in which drinking orange juice was entirely foreign—nobody even drank milk routinely, which is why the Gemara discussing *basar b'chalav* always focuses on cheese rather than milk. Against that backdrop, the notion of fruit juice as a significant category was simply not intuitive.

### Ta'am K'ikar Problem

*Tosafot* sharpens the difficulty by raising a third problem that the discussion has not yet addressed: what about *ta'am k'ikar*—the principle that the taste of something counts like the substance itself? If one boils water together with *orlah* fruit, the taste of the fruit pervades the water, and that water should be forbidden on account of *ta'am k'ikar*. Why, then, would squeezing *orlah* fruit not produce juice that is forbidden for the same reason? Even if the juice is not technically regarded as the fruit itself, it carries the taste of the fruit, and *ta'am k'ikar* should render it prohibited. A possible answer is that the juice is indeed forbidden but at a lesser level of severity—one would not receive lashes for it because it is not the substance itself, but it could still be prohibited through *ta'am k'ikar*. The question, however, remains genuinely open.

### Unresolved Issues

Several issues thus remain unresolved. First, there is a logical distinction between liquefying something and liquids that merely run off of something—the Gemara largely conflated these two scenarios, but one could argue they deserve separate treatment. Second, even if the halakhic standing of the liquid is unclear, the question of *ta'am k'ikar* remains operative and complicates any clean resolution.

The most significant practical application of this cluster of unresolved questions involves the status of liquor on *Pesach*. Liquor is a liquid derived from grain, and three distinct positions emerge from the analysis. Some hold it is *chametz gamur*—fully prohibited grain—on the basis of the principle that a liquidified form retains the status of the original substance. Others invoke the Gemara in *Pesachim* and argue that since grain-derived liquor is *zei'ah be'alma*, it may in fact be permissible to drink on *Pesach*, having no halakhic status as *chametz*. A third position, following *Tosafot*, holds that even if it does not have the full status of *chametz*, it must at minimum be forbidden through *ta'am k'ikar*, since the taste of grain pervades it. The final answer remains genuinely unclear—multiple possibilities exist without a clean systematic resolution.

---

## Meat Combinations

### Alaw Definition

With the discussion of liquids concluded, the *mishnah* turns to a further category: things that combine with meat to count toward the minimum halakhic measure but are not themselves considered food when standing alone. The *mishnah* uses the term *alaw*. What exactly is this *alaw*? Rabbi Yochanan says it is *martka*. Rashi explains *martka* as a large structure—he calls it a *gid*, which literally means a ligament—running down the back and along the side of the neck. It turns out anatomically this is indeed a ligament (*ligamentum nuchae* in cattle), which holds up the head.
