It is something extremely difficult to eat on its own. *Tosafot* accepts the identification but adds a functional explanation: while one would not eat this ligament by itself, it might be cooked together with the surrounding meat, or one would encounter it as part of a piece and eat it along with the meat. *Tosafot* also cites Rabbeinu Chananel, who identifies the *alaw* differently—as a piece of rotting or decomposing flesh, which no one would eat on its own, but which, if it happened to be part of one's portion of meat, one would consume along with the rest rather than remove.

### Meat on Skin

Reish Lakish offers a competing interpretation: *basar she-paltoso sakin*, flesh that is "spit out" by the knife during the flaying process. When flaying an animal, the skin is removed with a blade, and in the same way that peeling a cucumber with a knife leaves some of the flesh adhering to the peel, the flaying knife leaves scraps of meat stuck to the hide. Normally this meat would be discarded along with the skin—it is meat, but nobody bothers to eat it. However, if someone does intend to eat it, they could scrape it off the skin and consume it with the rest. So this too is something that is not by itself treated as food, but might be eaten together with meat.

### Job Verse

The Gemara seeks to determine which definition applies by citing a verse. In the book of *Iyov*, among the speeches of Job's would-be comforters, it says: *ve-ulam atem toflei sheker rof'ei elil kulchem*—you are plasterers of lies, healers of an *elil* are you all. The *elil* is something that cannot be healed. The Gemara then tests each interpretation: *bishlama le-man de-amar martka*, if the *alaw* is indeed the ligament or the rotting flesh, it fits perfectly—a severed ligament cannot heal, and rotting flesh certainly cannot. But *ela le-man de-amar basar she-paltoso sakin*, if it is merely flesh scraped off during flaying, that is something that could conceivably heal if it were cut from a person's body, so why does the verse describe it as incurable?

The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between two usages of the term. The verse in *Iyov* uses one form of the word, and everyone agrees that in the verse it refers either to the rotting flesh or to the inedible ligament—there is no debate about the verse. The debate is about what the word means in the *mishnah*, because a *mishnah* need not use language identically to a biblical verse.

### R. Yehuda Tumah Rule

The *mishnah* then records Rabbi Yehuda's position: *ha-alu ha-mechunas—im yesh bo kezayit be-makom echad, chayav alav*. If one gathers together this *alu* into one place and there is a *kezayit* of it in that place, one incurs the consequences—meaning it carries the *tumah* of a *neveilah*. This is a significant statement: not only can the *alaw* combine with meat to constitute food susceptible to *tumah*, but if gathered together in sufficient quantity, it can itself function as a *neveilah* and be a source of *tumah*.

### Intentional Gathering

To this Rav Huna adds a critical qualification: *vehu she-kinso*—the *kezayit* must have been gathered intentionally. It is not merely that the pieces happened to accumulate in one spot; rather, a person deliberately collected them. That deliberate act of collection gives the scraps significance: it signals that the person regards them as worthwhile, that they intend to do something with them, presumably eat them. The intention, therefore, is what transforms these otherwise insignificant pieces into halakhically meaningful food.

### Inedible Problem

This leads to a pointed difficulty. If the *alaw* is *martka*—the inedible ligament or rotting flesh—then even if a person gathers a *kezayit* of it together, what difference does that make? *Etz be'alma hu*—it is like a piece of wood. You cannot confer halakhic status on something that is objectively inedible simply by collecting it. So how can Rabbi Yehuda say that gathering it makes it a *neveilah*?

### Meat on Skin Resolved

The Gemara therefore concludes: *aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda lo peligi*—when it comes to Rabbi Yehuda's position, there is no debate. For Rabbi Yehuda to make sense, the *alaw* in the *mishnah* must refer to the flesh left on the skin during flaying. That interpretation is internally coherent: the meat is objectively edible, it is simply attached to the hide and would normally be discarded. When a person deliberately scrapes it off and collects it, they demonstrate that they regard it as significant and intend to eat it. That intention is what gives it halakhic status and makes it susceptible to the *tumah* of a *neveilah*. Whether the *mishnah*'s *alaw* also extends to the *martka*—the ligament or rotting flesh—is the subject of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish among the *rabanan*, but for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling at least, the reference must be to meat on skin.

### Tosafot on Intention

*Tosafot* is careful to delineate precisely what role intention plays here. One might think that if intention can grant food status, it should also work in reverse—that a person's intention to discard meat would prevent it from having the status of *neveilah* or remove it from the category of forbidden food. *Tosafot* explicitly rejects this. Forbidden food status—*neveilah* and its prohibitions—does not depend on intention. Meat that is *neveilah* remains *neveilah* regardless of what the owner plans to do with it. The domain in which intention operates is *tumah*. The laws of *tumah* that apply to food are predicated on the item being treated as food. If a person intends to discard something, it does not qualify as food for purposes of *tumah*, and therefore would not ordinarily bear the *tumah* of a *neveilah*. But Rabbi Yehuda says: if you gather it together deliberately, that act of intentional collection demonstrates that you are treating it as food, and therefore it assumes the *tumah* of *neveilah* in the domain of *tumah* law. The distinction *Tosafot* draws is important: intention cannot remove the *issur* of eating *neveilah*, but it can determine whether an item is categorized as "food" for *tumah* purposes.

There is an interesting anatomical aside worth noting. The observation was raised that the "meat" people eat—a steak, a chicken drumstick—is in fact muscle tissue. Everything one eats from an animal's body is muscle; flesh is simply an imprecise lay term for that muscle. What distinguishes the *martka*, then, is not that it is "different from meat" in some obvious way, but that it is a ligament (or, in Rabbeinu Chananel's reading, decomposing tissue) rather than functional muscle—and thus not the sort of thing one would normally consume even as part of a meal.

### Constructed Scenarios

The deeper problem, however, is not which interpretation of *alaw* is correct, but how the *mishnah*'s case can be coherently constructed even according to Reish Lakish, who says the reference is specifically to flesh left on the skin. The Gemara poses the dilemma sharply: *iy de-chashiv leh*—if the person intends to eat the flesh on the skin, then it counts as food on its own and should be able to convey *tumah* even without being combined with other meat; *ve-iy de-lo chashiv leh*—if the person intends to discard it, then it has been negated entirely, and why would it combine with the meat one does intend to eat? Either it is food and counts on its own, or it is not food and cannot combine at all. How does the *mishnah* construct a middle scenario?

Two *amoraim*, Rav Avin and Rav Maisha, each offer a *heichi timtza*—a constructed scenario designed to make the case coherent. A *heichi timtza* is not a general principle extracted from the case but rather a specific factual construction that brackets the case and limits its scope.

The first answer: *miktzato chishav alav*—the person intends to eat only part of the flesh left on the skin. Suppose there is a *kezayit* worth of such flesh scattered in various places on the hide, and the person intends to scrape off only some of it, not all. In that case, the portion one intends to eat has food status, but it is not enough by itself to reach the minimum measure. However, when combined with the meat one is definitely eating, that small portion tips the scale and completes the minimum. The bottom line of the principle is the same: what you plan to eat is food, what you plan to discard is not. The *mishnah*'s case works only when some but not all of the flesh on the skin is intended for consumption, and the some-but-not-all is sufficient to combine with actual meat to reach the required measure even though insufficient on its own.

The second answer: *miktzato paltoso chayah miktzato paltoso sakin*—some of the flesh hanging off the hide was torn by an animal that attacked the cow (but did not render it a *tereifah*), and some was scraped off during flaying by the knife. The person would be more inclined to eat the flesh torn by the attack, and less inclined to eat the flesh left by the knife—or perhaps the opposite reasoning applies—and because the two pieces are indistinguishable, the person is uncertain which is which. Therefore neither piece on its own has fully established food status, but combined with other meat, even one piece is enough to complete the minimum measure. Again, the underlying principle remains identical: intention to eat confers food status, absence of such intention negates it, and the *mishnah*'s scenario depends on a constructed ambiguity.

According to Reish Lakish, then, the entire discussion of the *mishnah*'s case—that the *alaw* combines with meat but is not food on its own—is essentially a *heichi timtza*, a carefully engineered factual situation rather than a broadly applicable rule.

---

## Bird Parts & Horns

### Taharot Case

The Gemara now cites a related passage from the tractate *Taharos*: *tnan hatam*—we taught over there. The case involves a bird: *ha-chartom ve-ha-tzipornayim*—the beak and the claws. The *mishnah* teaches that they *metamme'in u-mitztarfin*—they transmit *tumah* and they combine to the minimum measure. The question this raises is obvious: who eats a beak or claws? The prior analysis established two mechanisms by which something can combine with food to complete the minimum halakhic measure: either by being *ochel*—food, even food that would not be eaten on its own but would be consumed together with other food—or by being a *shomer*, a protective covering that guards the food. Both a *shomer* and an *ochel* can contribute to the minimum size for *tumah* purposes.

### Beak/Palate

The Gemara immediately challenges the inclusion of the beak: *etz be'alma hu*—it is like wood! Nobody eats a beak, and it does not obviously serve as a *shomer* for any food. Rabbi Elazar resolves this by specifying: *be-chartom tachton*—the lower beak. But the Gemara presses: the lower beak is also like wood. Rabbi Elazar then clarifies further: *tachton shel elyon*—not the lower beak as such, but the underside of the upper beak, meaning the palate. The palate of a bird's upper jaw contains soft tissue that is edible. While one would not eat the palate on its own, if one is in any case consuming the bird's head, the palate is scraped off and eaten along with it. As something eaten together with food, it constitutes *ochel* and therefore combines with the minimum measure.

### Claws Embedded

The claws present a similar challenge. Rabbi Elazar specifies: *mekom ha-muvla'in ba-basar*—where the claws are embedded within the flesh, submerged beneath the skin at their base. When the claw is embedded in that way, it may be soft enough to be edible, and in any case it would be consumed along with the surrounding tissue when one eats the foot. Whether this is better understood as the claw functioning as *ochel*—food eaten together with other food—or as a *shomer* protecting the tissue beneath it is not entirely clear from the Gemara's formulation, but the practical result is that such embedded claws combine toward the minimum measure.

### Horns Analysis

The Gemara returns to the case from the earlier *mishnah*: *karnayim*, horns. What is the basis for horns combining with meat toward the minimum measure? Rav Pappa answers: *be-makom she-chotchin ve-yotzei mehem dam*—at the point where the horn is attached to the head, where blood vessels still run through it, such that if cut there, blood would flow out. Again, two possible explanations apply. One is that at this base of the horn, where blood vessels and possibly marrow are present, the tissue is edible and would be consumed together with the surrounding meat of the head, functioning as *ochel*. The other is that the horn serves as a *shomer*—a protective casing for the marrow within—and it is in that capacity as a guardian that it combines with the minimum measure. Either way, the horn at the point of attachment qualifies.

### Ochel & Shomer

With this the Gemara's treatment of these auxiliary body parts comes to a close. The organizing framework consists of two principles: *ochel*—something that even if not eaten on its own is nonetheless consumed together with food—and *shomer*—something that serves as a protective shell or casing for food. Both categories contribute to the minimum halakhic measure and participate in the *tumah* of *neveilah*. What *yad*—handle—and other structural categories contribute is left for the broader tractate of *Taharos*; for present purposes, the discussion has illustrated both principles through the cases of the beak/palate, the embedded claws, and the horns.

---

## Jew/Non-Kosher

### Mixed Scenarios

The second part of the *mishnah* addresses a set of more intricate cases involving *shechita* that is halakhically significant but not fully so. The framework rests on the observation that for different actors and different animals, *shechita* plays entirely different roles. For a Jew slaughtering a *kosher* animal, *shechita* is everything: from the moment the act of *shechita* is complete, the animal is permitted for consumption and is definitively not a *neveilah*. For a non-Jew, *shechita* is halakhically irrelevant: the animal does not become permissible until it actually dies, and the formal act of *shechita* changes nothing in his framework. Ordinarily, halakhic status is all-or-nothing. The *mishnah* is searching for middle scenarios—cases in which *shechita* is meaningfully operative but not fully determinative—by mixing the two categories.

### Case 1 Setup

The first case: a Jew performs *shechita* on a non-*kosher* animal—a pig—for a non-Jew. Because a Jew is performing the act of *shechita*, that act carries some halakhic significance. But because the animal is a pig, being slaughtered for a non-Jew, the *shechita* is not fully operative: from the non-Jew's perspective, the animal remains prohibited as *eiver min ha-chai* until it dies, because a non-Jew's framework requires actual death, not *shechita*, for permissibility. And from a Jewish perspective, it was never going to be permissible regardless—it is a pig.

So the result is a middle state: the act of *shechita* by a Jew confers food status on the animal in the halakhic sense—the same act of *shechita* that would make a *kosher* animal permissible and would render it susceptible to *tumah* as food—even though the animal is not yet dead and will eventually become a *neveilah* when it does die. At this intermediate stage, the animal is halakhically food but not yet a *neveilah*. This parallels the earlier case in the *mishnah* where an animal was slaughtered and is still *mefarkheset*, still thrashing, not yet fully expired.

There is a more fundamental issue underlying the whole discussion: why does *shechita* require a Jew at all? The Gemara never cites an explicit verse for this. The *Rosh* cites *ve-zavachta ve-achalta*, but the derivation is not fully worked out. The general principle is that when a formal halakhic act is required—where procedure matters rather than just outcome—the person performing it must belong to the relevant halakhic category. A *Sefer Torah* written by a non-Jew, a *get* delivered by a non-Jew—there are several such cases where membership in the relevant category is a prerequisite. Interestingly, the question of whether a non-Jew can perform *milah* is more open than the question of *shechita*; the analogy is asymmetric.

### R. Assi Teaching

Rabbi Assi formulates the rule: *Yisrael be-tum'ah ve-oved kochavim be-taharah tzrichin machshavah*—a Jew who slaughters an impure animal and a non-Jew who slaughters a pure animal—these are exactly the two mixed scenarios—require *machshavah*, intention. Because the result of the *shechita* is an animal in this middle state—considered food, but not fully *kosher*—the animal does not automatically become susceptible to *tumah*; the person handling it must intend to eat it in order for it to have the status of food. Additionally, says Rabbi Assi, *ve-hekhsher mayim mi-makom acher*—it requires the independent act of *hekhsher*, contact with liquid from somewhere other than the *shechita* site, to render it susceptible.

### Hekhsher Needed

The requirement of independent *hekhsher* might seem surprising. In the case of a fully valid *shechita*, the act itself substitutes for *hekhsher*: the blood of *shechita* flowing over the meat is itself the liquid contact that renders the meat susceptible. But that rule applies only to a fully valid act of *shechita*. Here—either because the *shechita* was done on a non-*kosher* animal or because it was done by a non-Jew—it is not a fully valid *shechita*, and therefore it cannot substitute for *hekhsher*. Nevertheless, the partial validity of the *shechita* is enough to confer food status, and once food status is established, the animal can become susceptible if it comes in contact with liquid from another source.

### Hekhsher Question

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *hekhsher lama li?* Why does *hekhsher* matter at all? *Sofo letamei tumah chamurah*—in the end this animal is going to cause a serious form of *tumah*, because when it dies it will be a *neveilah*. And a general principle governs this area: *ve-khol she-sofo letamei tumah chamurah lo ba'i hekhsher*—anything that is ultimately destined to become a source of serious *tumah* does not require *hekhsher* to become susceptible. Its eventual status as a source of *tumah* already places it within the ambit of *tumah*-related law, so that it is susceptible even without the intermediary step of contact with liquid.

### Tumah Rule

This principle emerges from the verse *ve-khi yutan mayim al zera*, which is the source for *hekhsher*: water coming upon seeds renders produce susceptible to *tumah*. The derivation by *tannai de-vei Rabbi Yishmael* is: just as seeds, which can never themselves become a source of serious *tumah*, require *hekhsher* before they can be rendered susceptible—so too anything that will never be a source of serious *tumah* requires *hekhsher*. But the converse applies equally: anything that will ultimately become a source of serious *tumah* does not require *hekhsher*.

### Zera Proof

The proof-text is explicit in its formulation. Seeds are the paradigm case of *hekhsher* because seeds can never themselves generate *tumah*; they can only receive it. The principle is therefore: only things that are in the same structural category as seeds—items that will never themselves be sources of *tumah*—require the triggering mechanism of *hekhsher*. Items destined to be sources of *tumah* are already effectively within the system.

### Dead Bird Case

The Gemara corroborates this with the case of *neveilat of tahor*—the carcass of a ritually pure bird. A dead *kosher* bird is unique in that it causes *tumah* specifically through the act of swallowing: one who eats it while it is in the throat becomes *tamei*. The rule is: *tzricha machshavah ve-einah tzricha hekhsher*—it requires *machshavah*, intention to eat it, to have food status, but it does not require *hekhsher*. Why not? *Mipnei she-sofo letamei tumah chamurah*—because this bird can ultimately be a source of *tumah*, namely when someone swallows it. Since it has the potential to function as a source of serious *tumah*, it does not require *hekhsher*. But it does require *machshavah* because, unlike a standard *neveilah*, the dead bird's *tumah* mechanism is so specific—swallowing—that without someone's intention to eat it, it does not have an operative food status.

Returning to the question: why does the pig being slaughtered by a Jew in this middle state require *hekhsher*? If it is destined to become a *neveilah* when it dies, the principle should exempt it from needing *hekhsher*.

### Chizkiyah Answer

Chizkiyah answers: *ho'il ve-yakhol le-gorereha u-le-ha'amidah al pachot mi-kezayit*—because it is possible to bring it about that the animal will never become a *neveilah*, or at least that the specific meat being touched will never become a *neveilah*. Here is the mechanism: while the animal is still *mefarkheset*—still thrashing around after *shechita*—one could begin dismembering it. If one removes flesh (without severing a complete limb—a complete limb removed while the animal is still alive would be *eiver min ha-chai* and would itself cause *tumah*, but partial flesh, *basar min ha-chai*, does not cause *tumah* though it is forbidden to eat) then that flesh, having been removed while the animal was still alive, will never attain the status of *neveilah* even after the animal dies. Only flesh still attached to the animal at the moment of death becomes a *neveilah*. So in theory, one could so thoroughly dismember the animal while it is still thrashing that the remaining flesh attached to the carcass is less than a *kezayit*—and that specific piece of meat one is touching might be removed while the animal is alive and will therefore never be a *neveilah*.

Because the meat in question is not necessarily destined to become a *neveilah*—since it could be removed before death—the exemption from *hekhsher* does not apply, and the meat therefore requires *hekhsher* to become susceptible to *tumah*.

### Yirmeyah Question

Rabbi Yirmeyah then asks Rabbi Zeira: *u-mi amar Chizkiyah hachi?* Did Chizkiyah truly reason this way? Is this Chizkiyah's view? Because there is another explicit statement attributed to Chizkiyah: in the case of *shachat bah shnayim o rov shnayim ve-adayin hi mefarkheset*—one performed a valid *shechita* of two *simanim* or the majority of them on a non-*kosher* animal, and the animal is still thrashing—what is the status of a limb removed from the animal at this stage for a non-Jew? Does *eiver min ha-chai* apply?

Chizkiyah said *einah la-eivarim*—there is no problem of *eiver min ha-chai* for a non-Jew from this animal. Rabbi Yochanan said *yeshnah la-eivarim*—there is indeed a problem of *eiver min ha-chai* for a non-Jew. Rabbi Yochanan's position seems to align with the *mishnah*: the *shechita* gives the meat food status for *tumah* purposes, but from the non-Jew's perspective the animal is not yet dead, so removing a limb at this stage is still *eiver min ha-chai*.

But if Chizkiyah holds *einah la-eivarim*, meaning that from a non-Jew's perspective the animal is already considered dead after *shechita*, then why is the animal not yet a *neveilah* at this stage? If the animal is "dead" for the non-Jew's purposes—permissible to eat, no longer *eiver min ha-chai*—then it should simultaneously be a *neveilah* for *tumah* purposes. And that would flatly contradict the *mishnah*, which says it is not yet a *neveilah* at this stage. How does Chizkiyah accept the *mishnah* at all?

### Middle State

The Gemara resolves this with the formulation: *yatzta mi-klal chayah u-le-khlal meisah lo basa*—it has exited the category of the living, but it has not yet entered the category of the dead. This is a striking Gemara. The concept of a genuine middle state—neither alive nor dead—is invoked to allow Chizkiyah's position to cohere. The animal is no longer living in the full sense: a non-Jew may eat from it, and its limbs are not *eiver min ha-chai*. But it is not yet dead in the full sense: it does not yet cause the *tumah* of *neveilah*. *Shechita* has moved it out of the living category without yet placing it in the dead category.

This is an extraordinary halakhic concept. One way to understand what Chizkiyah is saying is that *shechita* functions as a *matir*—a halakhic permissive act—even for the benefit of a non-Jew, releasing the animal from the restrictions applicable to a living creature without yet making it dead. Under this framework, it is not that *shechita* counts as death even for a non-Jew; rather, *shechita* creates a third state in which the animal is neither fully alive nor fully dead.

Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, takes the position that for a non-Jew the framework remains binary: the animal is either alive or dead, and it is not dead until it actually expires. *Shechita* by a Jew on a non-*kosher* animal can confer food status for *tumah* purposes—that the *mishnah* establishes—but it does not make the animal "dead" from the non-Jew's perspective. Therefore removing a limb at this stage is still *eiver min ha-chai* for the non-Jew. The Gemara records that Rabbi Elazar rules *nakot le-ha de-Rabbi Yochanan be-yadcha*—hold onto Rabbi Yochanan's position, and a *baraita* from Rabbi Oshaya confirms it.

The *baraita*: *Yisrael she-shachat behemah teme'ah le-ovdei kochavim, shachat bah shnayim o rov shnayim u-mefarkheset*—a Jew who performed *shechita* on a non-*kosher* animal for a non-Jew, cutting both *simanim* or the majority, and the animal is still thrashing: *metamei tumat ochlin, aval lo tumat neveilah*—it has the *tumah* of food, not yet the *tumah* of *neveilah*—everyone agrees on this. *Eiver ha-porish mimmenah ke-porish min ha-chai*—a limb removed from it at this stage is like a limb from a living animal for a *ben Noach*, and is therefore *eiver min ha-chai*, forbidden to *bnei Noach*. Even after the animal subsequently dies, that status does not change: what determines the status of the limb is when it was removed, not what subsequently happens to the animal.

The *baraita* thus confirms Rabbi Yochanan's position and rules against Chizkiyah on the practical question. Nevertheless, the conceptual framework of *yatzta mi-klal chayah u-le-khlal meisah lo basa* remains a remarkable formulation, and the Gemara does not simply dismiss it—it uses it to explain Chizkiyah's internal consistency. The concept has resonance beyond its immediate *halakhic* context, touching on the question of what constitutes death and whether the transition from life to death admits of intermediate stages. The Gemara elsewhere speaks of individual moments—*ad shetamut*, until it dies—but never definitively specifies what that moment is, and these *sugyot* about animals have long formed part of the background for broader discussions about the definition of death.

---

## Non-Jew/Kosher

### Case 2 Setup

The *baraita* continues with the reverse scenario: *ve-oved kochavim she-shachat behemah tehorah le-Yisrael*—a non-Jew who performs *shechita* on a *kosher* animal for a Jew. This is the mirror image of the first case. Here, everything about the animal and the intended beneficiary is *kosher*—it is a ritually pure animal being slaughtered for a Jew—but the person performing the act is a non-Jew, which means the *shechita* is not halakhically valid as a Jewish act of *shechita*. The result is the same middle state: the act has enough features of a valid *shechita*—right animal, right beneficiary—that it confers food status, but because it is a non-Jew performing it, it does not have the full force of *shechita*, and the animal will ultimately become a *neveilah* when it dies.

### Same Halakha

The halakhic result is identical: *metamei tumat ochlin, aval lo tumat neveilah, umefarkheset*—while the animal is still thrashing, it has food-level *tumah*, not *neveilah*-level *tumah*. The same logic applies: the act of *shechita* here is partially operative and confers food status, but the animal has not yet died and is therefore not yet a *neveilah*.

### Eiver Status

Following from this, *eiver ha-porish mimmenah ke-porish min ha-chai*—a limb removed from the animal at this stage has the status of *eiver min ha-chai*. The *shechita* was done by a non-Jew; from a halakhic standpoint it does not count as a valid act of *shechita* for purposes of rendering the animal dead. So the animal is still considered alive while it is thrashing, and taking a limb from a living animal is *eiver min ha-chai*. The rule *ve-asur li-vnei Noach ve-afilu achar she-teitzei nafshah*—the status of *eiver min ha-chai* is determined at the moment of removal, not by subsequent events—applies here as well. Even after the animal dies, a limb removed while it was still thrashing retains its *eiver min ha-chai* status.

### Invalid Shechita

If the *shechita* was not even a full *shechita*—*shachat bah echad o rov echad*, only one *siman* or the majority of one *siman*—then the act is not an act of *shechita* at all, and *einah metamei tumat ochlin*: there is no food status, there is no *tumah* at the intermediate stage. Similarly, if the animal was killed through some other means entirely—*nachrah*—it simply has no *tumah* until it dies and becomes a *neveilah* in the ordinary sense. The capacity to be treated as food before death, and to receive *tumah* as food before dying, exists only when there is at least the semblance of a valid *shechita*. An act that is not *shechita* at all—whether because only one *siman* was cut or because the animal was killed by another means—confers nothing.

Interestingly, the Gemara's presentation implies that failing to cut both *simanim* (cutting only one) is treated as a more fundamental failure than having the wrong person perform the *shechita*. A non-Jew who cuts both *simanim* properly has performed an act that resembles *shechita* in form; a Jew who cuts only one *siman* has not performed a full act of *shechita* regardless of personal status. This ranking is perhaps counterintuitive but follows from the structure of the *halakhah*: the technical requirements of the act are definitional, whereas the identity of the performer is a separate layer of validity.

### Started/Completed

The *baraita* continues with composite cases. *Hekhel ha-nochri u-gamar ha-Yisrael*—a non-Jew began the *shechita* and a Jew completed it. The *baraita* specifies: if the non-Jew cut part of the *siman* but had not yet cut enough to constitute a meaningful act and had not rendered the animal a *tereifah* by that partial cut, then the Jew's completion of the *shechita* without pause renders it *ksherah*. The non-Jew's partial cut, which did not yet count as an act of *shechita* and did not disqualify the animal, can be subsumed into the Jew's completed act.

### Jew/Non-Jew Order

The reverse: *shachat ha-Yisrael—bein be-makom she-oseh tereifah bein be-makom she-eino oseh tereifah—u-va oved kochavim ve-gamar*—whether or not the Jew's partial *shechita* rendered the animal a *tereifah*, if a non-Jew then completed the act, *shechitato pesulah*—the *shechita* is invalid. Because the final operative act of cutting—the act that completes the *shechita* and brings it to its conclusion—was performed by a non-Jew, the entire *shechita* is invalid. The critical point is who performed the decisive concluding act.

---

## Meat Before Death

### Health Practice

A practical application follows directly from the established middle state. The *baraita* records: *ha-rotzeh she-yochal mi-behemah kodem she-teitzei nafshah*—one who wishes to eat meat from the animal before it has fully expired. This was evidently considered medically beneficial: the meat taken from the animal in the immediate aftermath of *shechita*, while the animal is still thrashing, is saturated with blood that has not yet drained, and for some this was regarded as particularly healthful. The practical question is whether and how this is permissible.

### Salting/Rinsing

The procedure is: *choseich kezayit basar mi-beit shechitato*—one cuts a *kezayit* of meat from the site of the *shechita*, because that is the most accessible place immediately after the cut is made. Then *umolcho yafeh yafeh u-madicho yafeh yafeh*—one must salt it thoroughly and rinse it thoroughly, because the meat at that site is suffused with blood. The animal has not yet expelled all of its blood, and the blood concentration at the *shechita* site is especially high. A thorough job of salting and rinsing is therefore essential to remove the blood before the meat can be consumed.

### Waiting Requirement

Although technically the meat is permissible from the moment of valid *shechita*, the Gemara in *Sanhedrin* derives—at the level of *asmachta*—that one should not eat from an animal while it is still exhibiting signs of life. Therefore: *u-mamtin lah ad she-teitzei nafshah*—one waits until the animal has fully died. Only then does one eat the meat that was cut and prepared. The *halakhah* is technically satisfied from the moment of *shechita*, but propriety—and the rabbinic derivation—requires waiting for the animal to expire.

### Both Permitted

*Echad oved kochavim ve-echad Yisrael mutarin bahem*—this piece of meat, cut from the site of a valid *shechita* of a *kosher* animal, is permissible both for a Jew and for a non-Jew. This is the mirror image of the earlier case. When a non-Jew performs *shechita* on a non-*kosher* animal, or when a Jew performs *shechita* on a non-*kosher* animal, the flesh at the intermediate stage is *eiver min ha-chai* for a non-Jew—it cannot be consumed until the animal dies. But when a Jew performs *shechita* on a *kosher* animal, the *shechita* is fully valid, and the same way a Jew can technically eat from it before the animal expires, a non-Jew can eat from it as well. It is not *eiver min ha-chai* for a *ben Noach*, because the *shechita* has effectively resolved the status of the animal even from the framework of the *ben Noach*'s obligations. This point is corroborated by a teaching of Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashin, who formulates the same procedure—cut a *kezayit* from the *shechita* site, salt and rinse thoroughly, wait for the animal to die—as general guidance for someone who wants to be healthy.

---

## Technical Problems

### Shehah/Daras Q

The final question on the *daf*: Rabbi Elazar asks about cases where the *shechita* was technically defective. We established that what gives meat the status of food before the animal dies, in the mixed cases, is the act of *shechita*. A non-Jew's *shechita* of a *kosher* animal for a Jew is meaningfully operative even though it does not produce *kosher* meat; it is enough to confer food status. But suppose the *shechita* had a technical *pesul*—specifically *shehah* (pausing in the middle of the cut) or *daras* (pressing down with the knife rather than drawing it across). Does such a technically defective *shechita* still confer food status? Or does the technical flaw reduce it to the same level as not having performed *shechita* at all—meaning no food status until death?

### R. Yochanan Answer

An elder transmits Rabbi Yochanan's answer: *tzrichah hekhsher shechita ke-vehemah tehorah*—what is required for food status to be conferred is *hekhsher shechita*, a *shechita* that would be valid on a *kosher* animal. The act must be technically proper: it must meet all the requirements of a valid *shechita* as applied to a pure animal, even though the circumstances here—non-Jew performing it, or non-*kosher* animal—mean it will not produce *kosher* meat. Only if the act itself would have been valid *shechita* on a *kosher* animal does it confer the middle-state food status.

### Precision Required

Rav Shmuel Yitzchak sharpens this further: *ve-dayka salka*—the precision matters throughout. No pausing, no pressing, and even the knife must be checked beforehand. Every technical requirement of *shechita* must be met. The reason the mixed-genre cases (non-Jew performing *shechita*, or *shechita* on a non-*kosher* animal) still confer food status is not that they are some lesser form of *shechita*—they must be, in technical execution, perfect *shechita*. The only element that is excused is the one that cannot be supplied: in the case of the non-Jew, it is his personal status; in the case of the pig, it is the animal's nature.

### Only Kavanah Exempted

The conclusion: *kavanah* alone is waived. A Jew performing *shechita* on a *kosher* animal must have the proper intention—*kavanah*—for the *shechita* to be valid; one who performs *shechita* thoughtlessly, without intent, has performed a technically valid physical act that is nonetheless halakhically questionable. In the mixed cases, the person performing *shechita* (the non-Jew) cannot have the relevant Jewish *kavanah*, or the animal being slaughtered (the pig) is not the kind of animal for which *kavanah* is meaningful in the normal sense. That exemption—the non-Jew's lack of the relevant intention—is what the halakhah waives. Everything else—the knife's condition, the absence of *shehah*, the absence of *daras*, the proper drawing of the blade—must be present in full. Only once all those technical conditions are satisfied does the act constitute the kind of *shechita* that can confer food status in the middle-state cases.

---

---

# Hullin 122

## Non-Jew Shechita

### Shechita Defects

The daf opens by continuing a discussion that had distinguished between two fundamentally different types of problems in *shechita*. On one hand, there is a case where the act of *shechita* was performed perfectly in a technical sense, but the problem is extrinsic — namely, that the one who performed it was a non-Jew. On the other hand, there is a case where the act itself was defective: there was a pause, there was pressure applied, or the knife was not properly checked. These two categories carry different legal weight, and the *gemara* treats them distinctly before moving forward.

### Non-Jew Physical Act

The *gemara* then cites a ruling of Rav Shmuel Yitzchak. The relevant principle is that *shechita* must be physically performed by a Jew. If a non-Jew is present and instructs or supervises, but a Jew performs the act, the *shechita* is valid. Conversely, if the non-Jew physically performs the cut — even with a Jew observing — it is not valid. The physical execution of the act by the Jew is the operative requirement.

### Food Not Yet Dead

The *gemara* records a question posed by Rav Zeira to Rav Sheshes: *mahu she-tatzil balu'a she-betochah?* — what is the law regarding an item swallowed inside this animal after it has been *shecht*ed?

The background principle is that something which is *balu'a* — swallowed inside a living creature — is not susceptible to *tumah*. If, for example, a person swallowed a gold ring and then entered a house containing a corpse, the ring would not become *tamei*, because it is absorbed within the living body. Once the animal dies and becomes a *neveilah*, however, it is simply meat, and any item inside it is no longer protected by the concept of *balu'a* — it can become *tamei* like any object in contact with a *neveilah*.

The question Rav Zeira raises concerns an intermediate case: an animal that has been *shecht*ed but has not yet died, and is still thrashing. This could be a non-kosher animal *shecht*ed by a Jew, or a kosher animal *shecht*ed by a non-Jew. Such an animal has been ruled to have the status of food — it is already considered *ochel*, a foodstuff — yet it is not yet technically dead and has not yet become a *neveilah* in the full sense. Does it still retain the power of *balu'a* to protect what is swallowed within it, since it is still alive? Or, since it is now treated as food, has the animal been sufficiently objectified such that items within it are no longer shielded?

The *gemara* raises the tension sharply: if you say this animal causes *tumas ochlin* — the *tumah* of foodstuffs — and yet still protects what is swallowed, you are claiming contradictory things. Once you treat the meat as food that can become *tamei*, it seems incoherent to say it simultaneously still functions as a living body that shelters its contents.

### Swallowed Objects

Abaye rules definitively: *eina matzeles ela balu'a she-betochah de-metamei tumas ochlin* — it does not protect the swallowed item. Since this animal after *shechita* already carries the status of food and can become *tamei* as *ochel*, it no longer functions to protect what is absorbed within it. The status of *balu'a* depends on the creature being genuinely alive in the operative sense; once it has been reclassified as a foodstuff, even while still physically alive, it no longer provides that protection.

### Bestiality Case

The *gemara* buttresses this intermediate status with a striking case. It notes: *ve-arova chayav de-eino metamei tumas neveilah* — one who commits an act of *arayot* with such an animal after *shechita* would still be liable, because the animal is not yet a *neveilah*. It has not yet died fully; it is still alive in a relevant legal sense, even while it is simultaneously already classified as food.

This is a genuinely peculiar middle state. The animal is food — objectified, susceptible to *tumas ochlin*, no longer protecting its swallowed contents — and yet it is still alive, still subject to the prohibition of bestiality. These two statuses coexist without contradiction: because it is food, it no longer shelters what is absorbed within it; because it is still alive, it has not yet crossed into the full status of *neveilah*, and the prohibition of bestiality still applies. The case of bestiality thus serves as the proof that the animal genuinely remains alive in a halakhically meaningful sense, while the ruling of Abaye establishes that being alive in this sense does not prevent the loss of the *balu'a* protection once food status has been conferred.

---

## Meat on Hide

### Rabbi Yehuda Alal

The *gemara* now transitions to the end of the *mishna*, returning to the theme of items that combine with food to constitute a minimum measure, even when they are not themselves considered food independently. The *mishna* cites Rabbi Yehuda: *ha-alal ha-mekunas* — the *alal*, the scraps of meat left on the hide when an animal is flayed, if deliberately gathered together such that there is a full *kezayit* in one place, is considered food, and indeed Rabbi Yehuda says it carries the status of *neveilah* and causes *tumas neveilah*.

### Rav Huna Condition

Rav Huna qualifies this ruling: *v'hu she-kinso* — only if the person actively gathered the meat himself. This is not merely a procedural observation. Rashi explains the significance: the status of something as *ochel* can shift with one's subjective relationship to it, and one can go in and out of treating something as food. But regarding *neveilah* — once something ceases to have the status of *neveilah*, it cannot reacquire that status. Rashi therefore explains that meat left on the hide after flaying is normally assumed to have been mentally discarded, abandoned. If someone else came along and scraped it together, it would not matter — the meat had already lost its *neveilah* status. But if the same person who did the flaying then went and scraped the meat together, that act reveals retroactively that he had never truly abandoned it. He always intended to collect it. That continuous intention means it never lost the *neveilah* status in the first place, and Rabbi Yehuda therefore rules that it is *neveilah*.

Rav Huna adds a second ruling: *shnei chatzei zeisim she-yeishan agabi ha-or, ha-or mivatlam* — if you have two half-*zeisim* of meat sitting on a piece of hide, the hide negates them. They lose their status. This second statement brings the discussion into close contact with the famous dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva that the *gemara* will address in a *mishna* coming up shortly.

### Yishmael/Akiva

The *gemara* notes the structural tension: the *mishna* we are studying is coming up for debate in that later *mishna*, where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva argue about exactly this case — a hide flayed from an animal that is *neveilah*, on which there are two half-*zeisim* of meat. Everyone agrees that touching a half-*kezayit* here and a half-*kezayit* there separately does not render one *tamei*, since *tumah* requires contact with a full *kezayit* at once. But the question is: what if you carried this piece of leather on your back, thereby simultaneously carrying both half-*zeisim* at once? You have in effect carried a full *kezayit* of *neveilah*.

Rabbi Yishmael holds that you are *tamei*. The skin does not negate the two pieces of meat; they retain their status as *neveilah*, and together they constitute a full *kezayit* being carried. Rabbi Akiva holds that you are *tahor* — not because the carrying was somehow defective, but because the hide objectively nullifies each piece of meat that is less than a full *kezayit*. Each half-*zayit*, attached to the skin, has no independent significance; they are as if not present.

The *gemara* therefore asks: according to whom is Rav Huna's ruling formulated? *Aliba d'Rabbi Yishmael* — if it is according to Rabbi Yishmael, who says the skin does not negate the pieces of meat, then saying that the skin negates them seems to contradict him directly. *Ve-i aliba d'Rabbi Akiva* — if it is according to Rabbi Akiva, who says the skin does negate them, then Rav Huna's statement is obvious, *peshita*. What novel information is he providing?

### Yishmael Subjectivity

The *gemara* resolves: *le-olam aliba d'Rebbe Yishmael* — in fact we are proceeding according to Rabbi Yishmael, and a distinction within his position accounts for Rav Huna's ruling. When does Rabbi Yishmael say the skin does not negate the half-pieces of meat? *Hani mili she-platato chayah* — when the meat was torn off by a wild animal. *Aval platato sakin* — but if it came off in the course of your own flaying with a knife, *batil* — it is negated.

Rashi explains the logic: when you are actively flaying an animal, and meat comes off incidentally with the skin, you mentally discard it on the spot. It is like the piece of cucumber that goes off with the peel — you do not bother fishing it back out of the garbage. That implicit mental dismissal means you have subjectively negated the meat, and it loses its *neveilah* status. But if an animal tore the hide away and meat came with it, you had no role in that; you have not made any implicit decision to discard anything. The meat therefore retains its status.

The *gemara* then asks whether Rav Huna's ruling is consistent even under this reading of Rabbi Yishmael. The concern is as follows: Rabbi Yehuda in the *mishna* says that if you scrape together the scattered *alal*, it retains the status of *neveilah* — meaning that your subsequent act of gathering it reveals you never truly discarded it. This fits naturally with a reading of Rabbi Yishmael under which even knife-flayed pieces are not negated, and what matters is entirely your subjective relationship to the meat. If the skin never objectively negates anything, then gathering the scraps afterward simply shows you always cared about them, and they remain *neveilah*.

But if one reads Rabbi Yishmael as saying that knife-flaying does cause the skin to negate the pieces, then there is a difficulty: if the negation is based on the skin's objective relationship to the scraps, then Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that gathering them afterward preserves their status becomes incoherent — once objectively negated, subjective intent cannot restore them.

The *gemara* therefore rejects the reading that knife-flaying causes negation even according to Rabbi Yishmael. Rather, *le-olam* — truly and finally — according to Rabbi Yishmael, even knife-flayed pieces are *not* negated by the skin, *lo batil*. Everything under Rabbi Yishmael operates subjectively. When you flay and the meat falls away and you dismiss it, you have subjectively negated it. When you scrape it back together — as Rabbi Yehuda says — you have demonstrated that you never truly discarded it, and it retains its *neveilah* status. Both rulings of Rav Huna, and Rabbi Yehuda's position in the *mishna*, are all coherent within the framework of Rabbi Yishmael: nothing is objectively negated by the skin; it is entirely a matter of your subjective relationship to the scraps.

### Akiva Objectivity

With Rabbi Yishmael's position clarified, the *gemara* turns to Rav Huna's second statement — that two half-*zeisim* on a hide lose their status — and asks whether this simply restates Rabbi Akiva's position. Rav Huna is indeed ruling like Rabbi Akiva, and the *gemara* acknowledges the apparent redundancy: *peshita* — it is obvious, since Rabbi Akiva already says the skin negates them. What is Rav Huna adding?

One might have thought that Rabbi Akiva's principle applies specifically when the pieces were *platato sakin* — when human action, your deliberate flaying, produced the result, with the implicit act of discarding. One might therefore have thought that if an animal tore the pieces off and left them on the hide, even Rabbi Akiva would not say the skin negates them, since there was no human act of dismissal involved.

Rav Huna therefore teaches: *ta'ama d'Rabbi Akiva mipnei she-or mivatalan* — the reason Rabbi Akiva rules the skin negates the pieces is not about the psychological act of discarding at all. It is an objective reality. A piece of leather is a substantial object; pieces of meat amounting to less than a *kezayit*, attached to it, are simply insignificant relative to the leather. They are objectively nullified by it, regardless of how they got there. *Lo shna platata chayah, lo shna platata d'sakin* — it makes no difference whether it was torn off by a wild animal or flayed off by a knife. The objective principle is the same: the leather negates the significance of anything less than a full *kezayit* of meat attached to it.

The *seyfa* of the *mishna* on Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael — which the *gemara* notes is yet to be seen — states explicitly: *mipnei ma Rabbi Akiva metaher ba-or, mipnei she-or mivatalan* — Rabbi Akiva declares it *tahor* because the hide objectively negates them. This confirms that the operative principle for Rabbi Akiva is not subjective intent but the objective reality of the hide's dominance over insignificant scraps.

To summarize the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael rejects the idea that the leather can ever objectively negate the meat attached to it. For him, status is always determined by one's subjective relationship to the food. Flaying produces an implicit act of discarding; gathering it afterward demonstrates the absence of that intention. Rabbi Akiva holds that the objective relationship between the leather and small pieces of meat less than a *kezayit* determines their status — the leather renders them insignificant, irrespective of how they came to be there or what anyone intended. Rav Huna's statement clarifies that this objective principle of Rabbi Akiva applies equally whether the pieces arrived through human or natural means.

---

## Skins Like Meat

### Mishna Overview

The *gemara* now moves to the next *mishna*, which continues within the same broad thematic framework but introduces a distinct category of discussion. The preceding analysis concerned the hide of a large animal, which is not food and is not itself *neveilah* — only the meat matters. But there are certain animals, and certain parts of animals, where the skin is so thin, soft, and edible that it is genuinely like the meat itself. The *mishna* enumerates these cases, with primary attention to the implications for *tumah* and the status of *neveilah*:

*Elu she-oroteihen ke-vesaran* — the following things, whose skin is like their flesh:

*Or ha-adam* — the skin of a human being. In the context of *tumas meit*, a human corpse causes *tumah* and a minimum of a *kezayit* of flesh is required. If one has only a *kezayit* together — flesh combined with skin — the skin counts like the flesh for this purpose.

*Ve-or chazir she-yishuv* — the skin of a domesticated pig. Wild pigs presumably have much tougher hides, which would not be considered edible or meat-like. Rabbi Yehuda, however, says *af or chazir ha-bar* — even the wild pig's skin has the same status.

*Ve-or chatoteret shel gamal ha-rakah* — the skin of the hump of a young, soft camel. *Chatoteret* is the hump. Since the hump of a young camel is still soft, it is edible — at least for those who eat camel — and therefore has the status of meat for *neveilah* purposes.

*Ve-or harosh shel egel ha-rach* — the skin of the head of a young calf, the definition of which the *gemara* will discuss.

*Ve-or ha-parsos* — the skin of the area of the hooves.

*Ve-or beit ha-boshet* — the skin of the genital area of a female animal; even in a cow, the genital region is more exposed and flesh-like rather than tough leather.

*Ve-or ha-shilya* — the skin of a fetus. Even if the mother is a cow, an aborted fetus would have skin still soft enough to be meat-like.

*Ve-or shel tachat ha-alyah* — the skin beneath the fat tail of a sheep. The skin of a sheep generally would not have the status of meat, but directly beneath the fat tail it is soft, unworked, and effectively meat.

The *mishna* then adds certain lizard-like creatures from the *shemonah sheratzim*: *ve-or ha-anakah veha-koach veha-leta'ah veha-chomet* — these four from the second verse in the Torah listing the eight *sheratzim*. The *gemara* will explain how these lizard-like creatures are identified and why specifically this second group is listed.

The *mishna* concludes: *ve-chulan she-ibdan o she-hilach bahen kedei avodah, tehorin* — if one worked any of these skins, treating them as leather — by tanning them or by walking on them to flatten and harden them for a sufficient period — they lose their status as meat and become *tahor*. The exception is human skin: *chutz me-or ha-adam* — human skin, even after being worked and tanned, never loses its *tumah* status, for reasons the *gemara* will explain.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri offers a dissenting view: *shemonah sheratzim yesh lahen orot* — all eight *sheratzim* mentioned in the Torah have skin that is distinct from their flesh, and their skin does not cause *tumah*; only their flesh does.

The *mishna* raises the question of what exactly the line is between *sheratzim* and the larger animals — *chayot u-vehemot* — which cause *tumas neveilah* in their entirety when they die. All large animals that die without *shechita* cause *neveilah tumah*, but among *sheratzim* it is only the specific eight listed by the Torah in Parshat Shemini that cause *tumah* when dead. The practical differentiation appears to follow the criterion of proximity to the ground — crawling or ground-level creatures — though the exact biological boundary is not resolved in the *gemara* here.

### Human Skin

Ulla opens the *gemara*'s analysis with a striking statement: *devar Torah, or adam tahor* — biblically speaking, human skin is actually *tahor*. This requires explanation. Human bones cause *tumah*, unlike the bones of a *neveilah*; this is because with human *tumah* the concern is with the *nefesh adam*, the human soul, and the basis is not specifically the meat but a comparison to flesh in that it does not regenerate. Bones do not grow back and therefore carry *tumah*. The skin, however, is more ambiguous: when part of the skin is lost it may scar and partially heal. Moreover, since *tumas meit* does not require meat specifically the way *tumas neveilah* does, the skin's status is uncertain. Ulla therefore says that strictly from the Torah's perspective, human skin is *tahor*.

*Umah ta'am amru tamei?* — why then did the Rabbis declare it *tamei*? The answer is a *gezeirah*: *shema ya'aseh adam orot aviv ve-imo shetichin* — lest someone take the skin of his father or mother and fashion it into some type of leather mat. The image is profoundly disturbing, and Tosafot himself pauses to question why the Rabbis even entertained this concern. He notes that one is forbidden to derive *hana'ah* — material benefit — from a corpse in any case, so this would already be prohibited. Tosafot answers that because this particular act was so uniquely disturbing, the Rabbis felt it required an additional *gezeirah* beyond the general prohibition, to ensure that people maintain an especially marked distance from human remains in this regard. It may also be, as is suggested in the *gemara*, that there was something in the surrounding culture — perhaps Roman practices — that made this image a live concern for *Chazal* rather than a merely theoretical one.

There is a parallel image that appears even earlier than Ulla, in the *mishna* in Tractate Yadayim, in the context of the dispute between the Tzedukim and the Perushim over whether *kitvei ha-kodesh* cause *tumah*. There the Rabbis explain why the bones of a human cause *tumah* — lest a person take the bones of his father and mother and shape them into spoons or utensils. The concern about using the body of a parent for household implements runs through both sources, and the Dead Sea Scroll known as MMT — *Mikzat Ma'asei Torah* — shows that this very debate about whether bones of dead animal carcasses cause *tumah* was one of the explicit points of sectarian disagreement between the Qumran community and the halakhic authorities in Jerusalem.

The *gemara* then notes a variant formulation. Some transmit Ulla's statement in connection with the beginning of the *mishna*'s rule — that human skin, in its natural state, is only rabbinically *tamei*, not biblically. Others transmit it in connection with the *mishna*'s later clause, about skin that has been worked and tanned. Under this second version, Ulla is saying that once human skin has actually been processed into leather, it is biblically *tahor* — it is no longer flesh or skin in any meaningful sense. The *gezeirah* then applies specifically to prevent someone who actually converts human skin into leather from thereby rendering it *tahor*. The *gemara* notes the logical relationship between the two versions: if Ulla's statement is made about the beginning clause, then *a fortiori* it applies to the end clause, where the skin has been worked. If Ulla's statement is made about the end clause — worked skin is only rabbinically *tamei* — then the beginning clause, unworked skin, might carry biblical *tumah*, and the rabbinic *gezeirah* would apply only to the worked case where someone actually used it.

### Pig Skin

The *gemara* briefly resolves the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding pig skin: *mar savar hai ashun vehai rachich* — one holds that the wild pig's skin is tough and the domesticated pig's skin is soft and meat-like; *umar savar hai nami rachich* — the other holds that even the wild pig's skin is soft enough to be considered like meat. This is a straightforward factual dispute about the physical properties of the skin, without a deeper structural principle at stake.

### Young Camel

The *gemara* turns to the definition of *gamal ha-rakah* — a young or soft camel. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling is cited: *kol zman shelo ta'ana* — as long as the camel has never carried a load, it is still considered young and its hump-skin is soft like meat.

Rav Yirmiya poses one question: what if the camel has reached the age at which one would normally begin loading it, but it has not yet actually been loaded? Is the operative criterion the physical act of carrying a load, which toughens the hump, or is it age — once a camel reaches the natural age for bearing burdens, does the skin become classified differently regardless of whether it has actually been used? Abaye poses the reverse question: what if the camel has not yet reached that standard age, but was put to work early and already carried a load? Would that premature use toughen the skin and change the *halakha*? Both questions are left as *teiku* — unresolved.

The *gemara* then recounts two parallel anecdotes about the same question being posed to *amoraim* in two different settings. Reish Lakish asked the question; Rav Yishmael bar Abba reported in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi the ruling *kol zman shelo ta'ana*. Reish Lakish responded warmly: *tiv lekabli* — come sit next to me. He was pleased with the explanation and honored the one who provided it.

Rabbi Zeira posed the same question; Ravin bar Chinena reported the same ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi via Ulla. Ravin bar Chinena apparently began to repeat the answer, and Rabbi Zeira cut him off: *chada hava lach amartah* — you had one idea, you said it, move on.

The *gemara* appends an editorial observation: *tach chazi ma bein takifei de-Eretz Yisrael le-chasidei de-Bavel* — come and see the difference between the powerhouses of Eretz Yisrael and the *chasidim* of Bavel. Reish Lakish — a towering figure in his learning and his stature — responded to a straightforward but correct explanation with genuine warmth and honor. Rabbi Zeira — who was known throughout the tradition as a *chasid* of Bavel — nonetheless was dismissive and showed little respect to the one who answered him. The *gemara* notes this as a point of self-criticism: piety and scholarship do not automatically produce proper treatment of others, and Reish Lakish's conduct was more exemplary in this exchange.

### Young Calf

Regarding the *egel ha-rach*, the young calf whose head-skin is meat-like, Ulla says: *ben shnato* — one year old. Rabbi Yochanan says: *kol zman she-yonek* — as long as it is nursing.

The *gemara* asks how to read these two opinions in relation to one another. One possibility: Ulla means a year old *and* nursing — nursing is an implicit additional condition. Rabbi Yochanan then says only nursing matters, being more lenient and not requiring the year. The other possibility: Ulla means one year, period, whether nursing or not. Rabbi Yochanan then adds nursing as a further condition, being more stringent: the calf must be both within its first year *and* still nursing.

The *gemara* proves from the language that Rabbi Yochanan cannot be adding a stringency. He says *kol zman she-yonek* — as long as it is nursing. If he were adding a condition to Ulla's ruling, he would have said *vehu she-yonek*, "and it must be nursing" — adding to the prior standard. Since he frames it as an independent and complete criterion ("as long as it nurses"), he must be presenting nursing as *sufficient* on its own, making him more lenient than Ulla and setting aside the age criterion entirely.

### Yochanan Ruling

Reish Lakish then asks Rabbi Yochanan directly: does the skin of the head of a young calf cause *tumah* as *neveilah*? This question is, of course, answered straightforwardly by the *mishna* we are studying. Remarkably, Rabbi Yochanan answers *eino metamei* — it does not cause *tumah*. He rules against the *mishna*.

Reish Lakish presses him: *limadtanu rabbeinu* — but our teacher, you taught us the *mishna*, which explicitly lists the head-skin of the young calf among the things whose skin is like their flesh. How can you rule against it?

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *al taknitani* — do not press me on this point. *Bi-leshon yachid ani shoneh otah* — I teach that *mishna* as a minority opinion. It is not the consensus view. Although Rabbi Yochanan's general practice is to rule in accordance with the *stam mishna* — an unattributed *mishna* — here he believes the *stam* reflects only a single dissenting authority, and he does not rule accordingly.

### Baraita Pigul

The *gemara* identifies the source for Rabbi Yochanan's position in a *baraita* that discusses *pigul* — the disqualification of a sacrifice through an improper intention to consume it outside the proper time or place. *Pigul* applies only when one plans to eat something that is normally eaten; if a part of the sacrifice is not normally consumed, an intention regarding it does not create *pigul*. Whether a given skin counts as "normally eaten" therefore determines whether it falls within the *pigul* framework.

The *baraita* opens by discussing someone who *shochets* an *olah* with the intention to burn — *le-haktir* — a *kezayit* from the skin under the fat tail *chutz li-mkono* or *chutz li-zmano*. The wrong place renders it *pasul* without *karet*; the wrong time makes it *pigul* and one who eats it incurs *karet*. This recognizes the skin beneath the fat tail as *meat-like*.

Elazar ben Yehuda ish Avlom, reporting in the name of Rabbi Yaakov, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda ish Kfar Ikum, reporting in the name of Rabbi Shimon, extend the principle: not only the skin under the fat tail, but also the skin of the head of the young calf, the skin of the hoof area, *ve-chol she-manu chachamim gabei tumah she-oroteihen ke-vesaran* — and anything in the list that the Sages enumerated for *tumah* purposes as having skin like meat — all of these fall under the *pigul* framework as well. The *baraita* adds *le-havi or shel beit ha-boshet* — to include the skin of the female genital area, which was not mentioned in the context of the *olah* only because an *olah* is male.

The critical implication: this enumeration — which matches our *mishna* — appears as the *second* opinion in the *baraita*. The first opinion in the *baraita* recognizes only the skin under the fat tail, and by implication regards the skin of the calf's head, the hooves, and all the other parts listed in the *mishna* as having the status of ordinary leather, not meat. It is on the basis of this first opinion that Rabbi Yochanan rules: our *mishna* is a *da'at yachid*, a minority position. For the skin of a large animal, Rabbi Yochanan would recognize only the skin beneath the fat tail of a sheep as having the status of meat.

### Animal Parts

The *gemara* clarifies the two specific anatomical terms in the *mishna*. Regarding *beit ha-parsos* — the hoof area — Rav says it means the hooves literally. Rabbi Chanina says it refers to *rekuvnin* — the lower leg segment sold together with the head when an animal is marketed. Animals have a lower joint below which is a bone section extending to the actual hoof; that segment from the lower joint downward is conventionally sold with the head. The skin wrapping that lower joint and the lower leg area, Rabbi Chanina says, is what the *mishna* refers to, and it is soft and flesh-like enough to carry the status of meat.

---

## Sheratzim Skin

### Eight Sheratzim

The Torah mentions eight *sheratzim* in two separate verses in Parshat Shemini. The first verse lists the *choled*, *achbar*, and *tzav* with the phrase *le-mineihu* — according to their kinds — concluding the first group. The second verse lists *koach*, *leta'ah*, *chomet*, and *tinshames* and concludes with the verse *eileh ha-teme'im lachem* — these are the *tamei* ones for you. These latter four are all understood to be lizard-like creatures. Identifying them precisely is difficult; one appears to be a monitor lizard, another may be a skink, and at least one has been associated by commentators on the fauna of the Torah with something resembling a gecko or even, in Rashi's reading on the Torah, a frog.

The *mishna* states that the skin of *ha-anakah*, *ha-koach*, *ha-leta'ah*, and *ha-chomet* is like their flesh. A *baraita* is cited that grounds this in the verse: *eileh ha-teme'im* — the word *eileh* is read as expansive, teaching *le-rabbot oroteihen ke-vesaram*, to include their skins as like their flesh for *tumah* purposes. The question then arises: perhaps this inclusive language applies to the entire list of eight *sheratzim*, including the first group?

### Rav Verse

Rav answers: *l'mineihu hifsik ha-inyan* — the phrase *le-mineihu* at the end of the first verse creates a separation between the two groups. The verse reads: *ha-choled ve-ha-achbar ve-ha-tzav le-mineihu* — and then a new listing begins. The concluding phrase *eileh ha-teme'im lachem* therefore refers only to the second group, the lizards of the second verse. Rav accordingly uses the biblical verse to determine which *sheratzim* have skin that is like their flesh: it is the second group alone, because the verse refers only to them.

### Tinshames

The *gemara* immediately notes a problem with Rav's verse-based approach: if Rav is going strictly by the verse, the verse includes *tinshames* — the last item in the second verse — yet our *mishna* does not list *tinshames*. How can Rav reconcile this omission?

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the principle that *Rav tanna hu* — Rav has the status of a *tanna* and may transmit or teach a version of the *mishna* that differs from ours. The statement *dekani tinshames* — Rav does include *tinshames* in his version of the list. According to Rav, all four items of the second verse, including *tinshames*, have skin like their flesh, consistently following the verse.

### Yehuda Feel

But our *mishna* — which is the *mishna* of the standard *tanna didan* — does not include *tinshames*. It cannot therefore be operating from the same verse-based logic as Rav. The *gemara* cites Rav Sheshes the son of Rav Idi: *tanna didan savar lah ke-Rabbi Yehuda d'azil basar gishta* — our *tanna* follows the approach of Rabbi Yehuda, who goes after *gishta*, physical feel.

Rabbi Yehuda in the *mishna* had said that even the skin of *ha-leta'ah* does not have the status of its flesh — meaning Rabbi Yehuda does not rely on the verse but on the physical reality of whether the skin is practically distinguishable from and harder than the flesh. *Gishta* — feel, tactile physical reality — is his criterion. Our *tanna* similarly proceeds not from the verse but from the empirical question of which creatures have skin soft enough and indistinguishable enough from their flesh to warrant the same *tumah* status.

This produces two divergent approaches to the question of which *sheratzim* have skin like their flesh. Rav proceeds from the biblical verse: the second group, as delimited by *le-mineihu*, has the inclusive language *eileh ha-teme'im* applied to it, and therefore all four creatures of that group — including *tinshames* — have skin like their flesh. Rabbi Yehuda and the *tanna* of our *mishna* proceed from physical reality: the question is whether the skin is actually soft and flesh-like, and one can debate this empirically for specific creatures, just as one debated whether the wild pig's skin resembles its flesh. Under this approach, *tinshames* may be excluded because its skin is physically distinct enough from its flesh not to qualify, regardless of which verse it appears in.

The *mishna*'s final position — that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds all eight *sheratzim* have skin distinct from their flesh — is also explicable on either framework: one could read the verse as not applying *eileh ha-teme'im* to the skin question at all, or one could make a physical determination that in all cases the skin of *sheratzim* is different enough from the flesh to be treated separately.

---

---

# Hullin 123

## Processing Skins

### Skins Distinct from Meat

The daf opens at the very bottom of 122b, with the *mishna*'s discussion of skins that are considered functionally distinct from meat. Certain animal skins — such as those of lizards and similar creatures, or chicken skin — are ordinarily treated as meat-like, and therefore carry the status of food with respect to the laws of *neveilah* and *tumas ochlin*. The *mishna* establishes that once such skins are processed — tanned, worked into leather or parchment — they lose that meat-like status entirely.

### Walking on Leather

The *gemara* immediately focuses on one specific processing method: walking on the skin. It states *hilach in, lo hilach lo* — only if you walked on it does it lose its meat-like status; if you did not walk on it, the change in status has not yet occurred. The *gemara* then raises a challenge from a teaching of Rabbi Chiyya: if one takes the ear of a donkey and uses it as a cover or mat for one's box, that leather becomes *tahor* — it is no longer considered meat-like and can no longer receive *tumah*. This seems to suggest that actual use, rather than processing by walking, is what matters.

### Leather as Mat

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing two independent pathways. If one actually uses the leather in a particular capacity — for instance, spreading it over a box as a cover — then even without having walked on it, it exits the status of meat. Conversely, if one has not yet used it in such a way but has processed it by walking on it, that too suffices. Either processing or use, independently, is sufficient to transform the leather's status. It should be noted that while leather can in principle become *tamei* if fashioned into a receptacle, in these cases it would not.

---

## Four Mil Discussion

### Amount of Walking

How much walking is required to constitute sufficient processing? Rav Huna in the name of Rav Yannai states: *arba milin* — four *mil*. One *mil* takes approximately eighteen minutes to walk; four *mil* therefore corresponds to roughly seventy-two minutes of walking. This does not mean the piece of leather must be four *mil* long, but rather that seventy-two minutes' worth of walking upon it would constitute adequate processing, such that it is no longer considered meat but leather.

### Kneading Dough

This leads to a broader digression on other *halachic* contexts in which the measure of four *mil* appears. Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Reish Lakish states that four *mil* is the operative distance for three situations: *legabel* (kneading dough), prayer (*litfillah*), and washing hands (*linetilat yadayim*). Rashi explains the first case as follows: a laborer has been hired to knead dough *betahara*, and in order to do so properly he must immerse the vessels; if obtaining water for that purpose requires traveling more than four *mil*, he is not obligated to do so. Tosafos objects to this reading, noting that the other examples in the *gemara* concern a traveler, and it seems incongruous to allow the food to be prepared in a state of *tumah* merely because the distance is a burden, even in the case of a hired worker.

Tosafos therefore offers an alternative: one is traveling and normally eats one's bread *betahara* — that is, not merely with washed hands, but observing the full practice of *chullin betahara* — and the opportunity to obtain suitable *tahor* bread can be reached by continuing the journey. If that destination is within four *mil*, one should wait. If it is more than four *mil* away, one need not maintain the *betahara* practice for this meal.

### Prayer & Minyan

Regarding prayer, Rashi explains that the question is whether to wait and daven in a *shul*. Tosafos refines this: the issue is specifically about davening with a *minyan*. If a *minyan* is reachable within four *mil*, one should wait rather than daven alone. If it is more than four *mil* away, one may proceed to daven without one. This is better understood as a question of what is preferable and ideal, rather than a strict personal obligation — *minyan* is primarily a communal obligation rather than an individual one — but where it can be reached within that distance, it is the recommended course.

A more commonly applicable reading of the *tfilah* case ties it to the question of available water, which runs as a unifying theme through all three situations. If one needs to wash one's hands before davening and water is unavailable, and water can be reached within four *mil*, one should wait for it. If not, one may clean one's hands by other means — on wood, stone, or the like — and daven without water.

### Netilat Yadayim

The case of *netilat yadayim* is perhaps the most practically relevant. One is traveling, has packed food, and is hungry but has no water. Must one wait to wash hands before eating bread? The rule states: if water is reachable within four *mil*, one waits. If not, one need not wait, and may eat the bread wrapped so as not to touch it directly, thereby forgoing *netilat yadayim* altogether. This is noteworthy because when we studied *netilat yadayim* we learned that wrapping alone is not ordinarily a solution — even wrapped bread normally requires *netilat yadayim*. Here, however, where water is not readily available and waiting would require more than four *mil*, the *halacha* permits this alternative. This is a highly practical ruling applicable whenever one is traveling without access to water.

### Time vs. Distance

This raises an important question: is four *mil* measured as distance or as time? Four *mil* on foot corresponds to seventy-two minutes. On a donkey, the same distance takes less time. In a car, it might take only a few minutes. If the measure is purely distance, then even a rest stop thirty-two miles away would theoretically require waiting — which could be only minutes by car. It would seem more straightforward to measure by time, since the question is fundamentally about how long one must wait, not how far one must travel. According to this understanding, if water can be reached within approximately seventy-two minutes, one should wait; if not, one may employ the permitted alternatives. This question — time versus distance — is not resolved here, and while it is surely discussed in the *poskim*, it remains an open and practically pressing *sheilah*.

### Not Backtracking

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that the teaching was not attributed to Rabbi Abbahu but to *Evo*, and that he enumerated four things, not three — the fourth being the very case of our *mishna*, that processing leather by walking requires four *mil*. This rounds out the list.

Rabbi Yose the son of Rabbi Chanina introduces an important qualification: the rule of waiting up to four *mil* applies only when the water or the relevant resource lies *ahead* in one's journey. If one must retrace one's steps — traveling *backward* — even one *mil* is too much; one need not go back at all. The logic is clear: waiting while still advancing toward one's destination is merely a delay; backtracking means losing time and progress entirely. Rav Acha bar Yaakov infers from this that if it is less than one *mil* behind, one would in fact be required to turn back. So, practically: if one has just passed a rest stop and the next one is very far off, if the previous rest stop is within roughly eighteen minutes behind — and one can in fact turn back — one might be obligated to do so before eating without *netilat yadayim*.

---

## Army Tumah

### Troops & Tumah

The *gemara* cites a *baraisa*: if an army troop is passing through various cities and enters a house, one must assume everything in that house has become *tamei*. The reason: there is no army troop that does not have skulls among its members — apparently referring to the Roman practice of carrying the severed heads of defeated enemies.

### Rabbi Ishmael

The *baraisa* adds: *v'al titma* — do not be astonished by this — for the skull of Rabbi Yishmael rests in the palace of kings. This evokes the *Asara Harugei Malchus*, the Ten Martyrs commemorated in the *Yom Kippur* liturgy, and specifically the tradition about the flaying of Rabbi Yishmael's face.
