The connection to our *sugya* is not merely the general topic of *tumah* and *tahara*, but more specifically the theme of skin being removed from a body — a theme present in the *mishna* itself, which had mentioned the skin of humans and its use in making various vessels.

---

## Flaying Skin

### Flaying Overview

The *gemara* now turns to the next *mishna*, which concerns the flaying (*hafshata*) of animals and the question of when skin that is in the process of being removed is still considered *halachically* connected to the meat. The *mishna* opens: one who flays (*hamafshit*) a *behemah* or *chayah*, whether *tahorah* or *teme'ah* — meaning whether the animal is kosher or non-kosher — and whether it is a small animal like a sheep or a large one like a cow (*badakah uvigasah*) — the rules that follow apply equally to all.

The practical import: if the skin is still considered connected to the meat, touching the skin is *halachically* equivalent to touching the meat itself. If the animal is a *neveilah* (or is a non-kosher species, which is by definition a *neveilah*), a *tahor* person who touches the connected skin becomes *tamei*. Conversely, if something *tamei* touches the skin while it is still connected, the meat becomes *tamei* as well.

### Mat Usage

The first case: if one is flaying the skin with the intention of using it as a mat (*lishatiach*) — the kind of animal-hide floor covering one associates with traditional and indigenous cultures — then the skin is considered connected to the meat only for the measure of *kedei achizah*, the amount one can grasp in one's hand. Once the flayed portion exceeds that amount, the part that has been peeled away is no longer considered connected to the meat.

What exactly is *kedei achizah*? Intuitively one might say a *tefach*, the breadth of a hand, but the *gemara* will clarify that it is actually two *tefachim*. The practical image: the leather is being slowly peeled away from the meat. The portion still flush against the meat is obviously connected. The flap that has been peeled away and is hanging free — up to *kedei achizah* worth — is still considered connected and can communicate *tumah* in either direction. Once the flap exceeds that measure, touching that portion does not communicate *tumah* to or from the meat. The portion still attached to the meat remains connected; only the status of the peeled flap is in question.

### Water Skin

The second case: if the intention is to use the skin as a water skin — a leather flask or canteen, sewn without seams for maximum capacity — then the skin remains connected to the meat until one removes the chest area. This is because the preferred method for making a water skin, in order to produce a large, seamless container, is to peel the skin from the legs upward toward the head. This is considerably more difficult than the alternative method, and the chest area is the hardest portion to separate. Until one has managed to pull the skin away through the chest, the entire skin in progress is still considered connected and touching any part of it communicates *tumah*.

If one flays from the head toward the feet, the rule is the same: it is all considered connected until one passes the chest. The difference is practical: working from head to feet means one reaches the critical threshold of the chest approximately midway through the process, while working from feet to head means one must complete almost the entire flaying before reaching that threshold. In either case, the chest is the pivot point.

### Neck Skin Debate

What about the neck skin that remains above the chest, once the chest has been passed? Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that once you have gotten past the chest, the neck skin is no longer considered connected — *eino chibur*. The Sages disagree: it remains connected until the skin has been completely removed — *chibur ad sheyafsheet kulo*. Even though the neck skin will come off with minimal effort once the chest has been cleared — essentially in a moment — the Sages maintain it is still considered connected to the meat. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that such easy removability means it is effectively already detached.

### Shomer Principle

This entire *mishna* raises a fundamental question: on what *halachic* principle does the connectedness of the skin operate? The two relevant categories are *shomer* (a protector of food, which communicates *tumah* when directly covering it) and *yad* (a handle, which communicates *tumah* through manipulation at a distance). Rashi reads these cases as involving *yad*, but this is difficult: the *yad* principle concerns the ability to manipulate the food by means of the appendage, and it is hard to see why the difficulty or ease of removing skin should bear on that question.

Tosafos offers a more compelling reading. This *mishna* is about *shomer*. The *shomer* principle requires that the protector be directly covering the food. The question in our *mishna* is whether a flap of skin that is partially peeled away — no longer flush against the meat — retains sufficient connection to the meat still beneath it to be treated as though it remains one unit. According to Tosafos, the degree of physical connection and the ease or difficulty of removal are precisely the right criteria for this question. When the skin is still tightly bound and hard to remove, even the peeled flap is considered one with the meat beneath, and functions as a *shomer*. When the skin will fall away effortlessly, it is as though it has already been removed.

This reading makes excellent sense of the *mishna*'s structure. At the beginning of the *mishna*, even a portion that has been peeled is considered connected because it remains tightly bound and the rest of the skin is still firmly in place. At the end of the *mishna*, the neck skin that is effectively about to fall off on its own is treated by Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri as already disconnected. The degree of adhesion governs the *halacha*.

This analysis is well illustrated by practical observation. In the flaying of animals, some areas of skin are barely adhered to the flesh at all and will peel away, or even flop off, with no effort. Other areas — particularly around the pelvis and the chest — are firmly bonded, often with a thick fat layer beneath, and require not merely pulling but active use of a knife to separate. It is precisely these firmly bonded areas that the *mishna* identifies as the thresholds of connection.

---

## Connected Skin Analysis

### Beyond Kdei Achizah

The *gemara* now asks directly: *mikan va'eilach mai* — what is the status of the skin beyond the amount of *kedei achizah*? The specific question is about the *tefach* of skin that has been peeled away but remains closest to the meat. Even once you have pulled back more than *kedei achizah*, that first *tefach* adjacent to the meat is still very tightly bound — requiring active use of a knife — and might still be considered connected.

### Rav vs. Rabbi Assi

Rav holds: *tahor hamufeshat* — everything that has been peeled away is *tahor*, even the skin right next to the meat, once sufficient progress has been made in the flaying. Rabbi Assi disagrees: *tefach hasamuch labasar tamei* — the *tefach* immediately adjacent to the meat remains *tamei* and is still considered connected. Only the skin beyond that *tefach* is regarded as disconnected.

### Baraita Sources

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this dispute. A *baraisa* states: once one has flayed beyond the amount of *kedei achizah*, whoever touches any part of the flayed skin (*hanogea bamufshat*) is *tahor* — it does not communicate *tumah* in either direction. Does this not mean even the *tefach* closest to the meat? The *gemara* responds: no, the *baraisa* refers to the extended flap beyond that first *tefach*; the *tefach* adjacent to the meat would still be a *shomer* and would remain *tamei*.

A second *baraisa* is cited: touching the skin *shekeneged habasar* — opposite the meat — communicates *tumah*; conversely, the implication is that skin not directly opposite the meat would be *tahor*, which would seem to include the *tefach* closest to the meat. The *gemara* responds: the author of this *baraisa* treats the entire *tefach* closest to the meat as if it is equivalent to skin directly opposite the meat — calling it *or shekeneged habasar* — because it is so closely adhered that it is functionally part of the meat.

The *gemara* then cites a *Tosefta* that opens identically to our *mishna* and explicitly states: *vetefach hasamuch labasar tahor* — the *tefach* adjacent to the meat is *tahor*. This appears to support Rav directly. The *gemara* responds: the *Tosefta* is speaking about *tefach rishon* — the first *tefach*. What this means, according to Rashi, is that the first *tefach* after *kedei achizah* is still very difficult to remove, but once you get beyond that first additional *tefach*, everything comes off easily and is *tahor*. This explains the *Tosefta* as consistent with Rabbi Assi: it is saying that the *tefach* that is *tahor* is the one that has already been worked past, not the one immediately adjacent to the meat.

However, Tosafos notes that this reading is strained — if that first *tefach* is still hard to remove, that would be a greater reason for it to be *tamei*, not *tahor*. Tosafos cites a *girsa* of Rabbeinu Chananel that reads *tefach hasamuch labasar tamei*, directly supporting Rabbi Assi, with Rav's response being that he concedes the *tefach* immediately after *kedei achizah* is still connected — because it is still very tightly bound — but once one gets past that first additional *tefach*, everything thereafter, even the skin right up against the meat, becomes *tahor* because it will all fall away easily.

### Kdei Achizah Amount

How much is *kedei achizah*? One *baraisa* says a *tefach*; another says two *tefachim*. Abaye resolves this: when we say a *tefach*, we mean a doubled *tefach* — i.e., two *tefachim*. This is also consistent with Rav's position: *kedei achizah* (the initial grasping amount) corresponds to one *tefach*, and the next *tefach* beyond it remains considered connected because it is still tightly bound. Only beyond both of these — once more than two *tefachim* have been successfully peeled — does even the skin adjacent to the meat become *tahor*. The two *baraitot* thus refer to different thresholds: one to the *kedei achizah* proper, and one to the total amount including the adjacent *tefach*.

---

## Tallit Tearing

### Tallit Identity Loss

The *gemara* now introduces a digression that is, as we will see, directly connected to the question of when something is considered sufficiently separated or destroyed to lose its prior *halachic* identity. The *mishna* elsewhere states: a *talit* — here meaning an outer garment, not specifically a *tzitzit* garment — that has begun to be torn: once the majority of it has been torn, it is no longer considered a single unit (*eino chibur*), and it is *tehorah*. The mechanism here is the same as by vessels: destroying an object causes it to lose its identity, and with that loss of identity, its *tumah* falls away. One need not immerse it in a *mikvah*; tearing it past the majority achieves the same result. Less than that — even if the garment would not be worn in a torn state — there remains the possibility that it will be sewn up, and it is therefore still considered one piece and retains its *tumah*.

### Majority Concern

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha qualifies: this applies only to a *talit tevulat yom* — a garment that was already immersed in the *mikvah* that same day and is awaiting nightfall to complete its purification. Why would someone tear such a garment rather than simply wait until nightfall? The *gemara* explains: since this person had no concern for the garment's integrity — evidenced by the fact that they immersed it in the *mikvah* in the first place, an act that damages cloth — we can trust them to tear past the majority. *Lo chayeis lah ve-kara lah rubah*: since they did not care for the garment, they will not hesitate to tear it fully past the majority.

But by a *talit* that has *not* been immersed in the *mikvah*, tearing the majority does not suffice to render it *tahor*. Why? This is a rabbinic *gezeirah*: we are concerned that, since the person is protective of the garment and preferred tearing it (a repairable act) to immersing it (which damages it more permanently), they will not bring themselves to tear a full majority. They may tear only forty or forty-nine percent and convince themselves they have done enough. In that case we would mistakenly consider it *tahor* when it is not. Therefore, the rabbis require that the *entire* garment be torn before we permit relying on this method.

### Rava's Objections

Rava objects with two responses (*shtei teshuvot badavar*). First: you are making a *gezeirah* that perhaps he will not fully tear the majority. I counter with my own *gezeirah*: if a person immersed a garment in the *mikvah* and is then seen using the cloth on that same day, people will assume it is because the *mikvah* immersion alone rendered it *tahor* — they will not realize he also tore it. They will therefore conclude that *tevulat yom* (immersion without waiting for nightfall) is sufficient to render something *tahor*. In the case you permit, therefore, you create an equal or greater concern. It would be better not to use that method at all — and then people will understand that the cloth is being used *because* it was torn, which is the actual reason for its *taharah*.

Second: you claim we must be concerned that a person trying to do a majority will stop short and only do slightly less than a majority. But consider the case of *olas ha'of* according to Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon: when performing *shechita* of a bird *olah*, he requires cutting the majority of both *simanim* without severing the head entirely. If we were genuinely concerned that someone aiming for the majority would come to do too little, we should be equally concerned there that the *kohen*, in his caution not to sever the head, will fail to achieve the full majority. Yet we do not make such a *gezeirah* — evidently we trust people to achieve the required *shiur* precisely. Tosafos adds that Rava's argument may not require demanding the *entirety* be done, but at minimum one should require a *rov hanikar* — an obvious, clearly perceptible majority, say seventy percent — rather than 51%, so that there is no room for confusion between the threshold amount and slightly below it. If even that is not required, it clearly shows we trust people to execute a *shiur* accurately.

### Trust in Shiur

The *gemara* responds on behalf of the original position. To Rava's first objection — that people will confuse *tevulat yom* with full *taharah* — the answer is: *kra mochiach aleha*, the tear itself is visible. Although people saw the garment go to the *mikvah*, they will also see that it is torn, and they will understand that it is the tearing, not the immersion alone, that accounts for its current *tahor* status. This response is somewhat difficult, but that is the *gemara*'s answer.

To Rava's second objection from *olas ha'of*: *Kohanim zrizim heim* — *kohanim* are meticulous and punctilious in the performance of their service. We can trust them to achieve precisely the right amount — the full majority of both *simanim* — while simultaneously being careful not to sever the head entirely. That precision cannot be assumed of ordinary people handling garments. Rav Yosef adds that practically speaking, when performing *shechita* the practice is already to cut a *rov hanikar* — a clearly perceptible majority well beyond the technical 51% — so the concern about people confusing the threshold is already addressed in practice.

### No Gezeirah Here

The *gemara* now attempts to use our original *mishna* about flaying to resolve the broader question. The *mishna* states: once one has flayed beyond *kedei achizah*, touching the peeled skin does not communicate *tumah*. This raises the same structural question: why do we not impose a *gezeirah* requiring more than just *kedei achizah*? If we are generally worried that people will stop short of the required *shiur*, we should demand they peel away more than the minimum before declaring the flap disconnected. The *gemara* asks: *amai*, why allow it with exactly *kedei achizah*? Should we not be concerned that someone will believe they have peeled away enough when they have not, will then touch the skin, and will declare themselves *tahor* when they are not?

The *gemara* answers: if this were a case of *tumah deoraita* — biblical *tumah* — you would be correct, and we would make such a *gezeirah*. But what case are we actually discussing? A case of *tumah derabbanan* — rabbinic *tumah*. Something rabbinically *tamei* touches the skin, and the question is whether this communicates *tumah* to the meat beneath. For rabbinic *tumah*, we do not apply the same stringencies and we do not impose additional safeguards.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic Tumah

But one might object: the case in which a *tahor* person touches the skin of an animal that is a *neveilah* is certainly a *deoraita* concern. The *gemara* responds: *teinach tamei betahor* — it works when something rabbinically *tamei* touched *tahor* meat. But *tahor betamei* — when a *tahor* person touches the skin of a *tamei* animal — that is *tumah deoraita*. So why does the *mishna* not impose a *gezeirah* in that direction?

The answer: *bitreifa*. The *mishna*'s reference to a *teme'ah* animal does not mean a non-kosher species or a *neveilah*. It means a *treifa*. And a *treifa* that has been properly slaughtered is, biblically, *tahor*. There is, however, a rabbinic *tumah* for *treifa*, and therefore the entire *mishna* operates within the realm of rabbinic *tumah*, where no additional *gezeirah* is required.

### Treifa Tumah

The *gemara* then questions whether *treifa* carries any *tumah* at all, even rabbinic. The answer: yes — as taught by the father of Shmuel: *treifa sheshachta metamei bemukdashin* — a *treifa* that has been slaughtered, although it is *tahor* both biblically and rabbinically in ordinary contexts, is treated as *tamei* in the context of *kodshim*. If it comes into contact with *kodshim*, or if someone who has handled it wishes to eat *kodshim*, the *treifa* is considered *tamei* for those purposes. Thus, within the narrow world of *kodshim*-related concerns, the *treifa* carries a rabbinic *tumah*, and it is within that limited context that the *mishna* operates — allowing the *halacha* of *kedei achizah* to function without the imposition of a further *gezeirah*.

---

## Small Animals

### Shratzim Flaying

The *gemara* now introduces a further case. Rav Dustai ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon states: *hamafshit beshratzim* — when one flays one of the eight *sheratzim*, the skin is considered connected to the *sheretz* until the skin is completely removed (*chibbur ad sheyafsheet es kulo*). Whether because the skin is very closely adhered or because there is insufficient area for *kedei achizah* to begin with, the rule is that complete removal is required before disconnection can be said to have occurred.

### Camel Skin

If by *sheratzim* complete removal is necessary, the implication (*al kiddush hashem*) is that by other animals — for instance, a camel — less than total removal would suffice. A camel, being a non-kosher species, is a *neveilah*, and thus carries *tumah deoraita*. This would seem to undercut the *gemara*'s earlier answer that our *mishna* deals only with rabbinic *tumah*: if the analogous case of a camel — involving biblical *tumah* — also requires only less than full removal, then our *mishna* is not merely a rabbinic concern, and yet we still do not impose a *gezeirah* demanding more than *kedei achizah*.

### Neck Skin Resolution

The *gemara* resists this inference. Do not say that by a camel less than full removal suffices — *lo teima ha begamal eino chibur*. That is not accurate. By a camel, just as by a *sheretz*, one would indeed require complete removal. Rather, the implication of the contrast is more limited: by *sheratzim*, even the neck skin remains connected and must be fully removed; by other animals, the neck skin alone does not need to be fully removed — but everything else does.

This reading — that "less than all" means "all except perhaps the neck" — preserves the *gemara*'s position that in virtually every case of biblical *tumah* we would demand complete removal and would not permit relying on the lesser standard of *kedei achizah*. The cases in our *mishna* that permit less than complete removal are therefore consistently attributed to rabbinic *tumah* contexts. The *gemara* thus continues to resist the plain reading of the *mishna* that *kedei achizah* is a general and broadly applicable standard even for biblical *tumah*.

---

## Tallit Qualifications

### Bottom Cloth Remaining

Returning to the case of the *talit*, Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yossi adds a further qualification: *lo shanu* — when do we say that tearing the majority renders the *talit tahor*? Only when one did not leave at the bottom of the garment sufficient fabric to serve as a *ma'aforet* — a wrap or kerchief-like cloth. But if one *did* leave enough at the bottom to function as a wrap — *shiyer bah kedei ma'aforet* — then even the torn piece remains considered connected (*chibur*) and it is not yet *tahor*.

This too runs against the simple sense of the *mishna*, which permits majority without qualification. It is noted that Tosafos cites a *gemara* indicating this additional restriction is rabbinic in nature, which makes sense: biblically, once the majority is torn, the *talit* has lost its identity and is *tahor*, but rabbinically, if a usable remnant remains at the bottom, the garment is treated as still extant and still *tamei*.

### Leather vs. Cloth

Reish Lakish introduces a different qualification: *lo shanu ela talit* — the rule that tearing the majority renders the object *tahor* applies only to a cloth garment. But *aval or* — a leather garment — *cholim*, is strong and resilient. Because leather holds together better, tearing the majority of a leather garment does not sever its identity as a single unit in the same way, and therefore it does not become *tahor* by majority tearing. The reason appears to be one of the following: either that leather, even after the majority is torn, will not continue to tear naturally and still effectively retains its structural integrity; or, as Rashi explains, that when one sews up a torn leather garment it retains its integrity better than cloth.

### Leather Strength Challen…

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish: *afilu or nami lo cholim* — even leather is not particularly strong, and therefore the same rule as cloth should apply. He then cites a case that implicitly challenges the proposition that we never rely on less-than-full destruction for leather: a leather item that has become *tamei midos* — because a *zav* sat upon it — where the owner decides to cut it into strips for sandals or a belt. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the moment one places the awl to the leather — even before actually cutting it, merely beginning the transformation — it becomes *tahor*. The Sages say: not until the leather has been reduced to less than five *tefachim*. Tosafos notes that less than five *tefachim* of leather corresponds to less than the majority for cloth.

The point is that even by leather, there is a threshold below which the object is destroyed and becomes *tahor* — we do not say leather is so strong that it can never lose its identity through cutting. Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish is precisely this.

---

## Leather Transformation

### Awl Transformation

The *baraisa* at issue states: a leather item *tamei midos* — rendered *tamei* because a *zav* sat upon it, giving it the status of a seat or bed — where one intends to cut it into strips for sandals or leather bands. Rabbi Yehuda holds that as soon as one places the awl to the leather, the transformation has begun and it is *tahor*. This is a strikingly radical position — the mere initial act of beginning the cutting process suffices to change the object's *halachic* identity, even before any material change has occurred.

### Five Tefachim Rule

The Sages disagree: it becomes *tahor* only when it has been reduced to less than five *tefachim*. The reason is that five *tefachim* is the minimum size at which leather can serve as a usable garment or seat — below that threshold, the object can no longer function in the capacity that made it *tamei*, and so it is *tahor*. Tosafos draws the parallel: just as cloth becomes *tahor* when less than the majority remains, leather becomes *tahor* when less than five *tefachim* remain. The underlying logic is identical — it is no longer a functional object.

### Cut Direction

Finally, the *gemara* resolves the apparent tension with Reish Lakish's position by distinguishing between types of cuts. When does Reish Lakish say leather is strong and does not lose its identity so easily? *Heicha dekatzrei lei lehedya* — when one makes a straight linear cut, which can be sewn up and which allows the leather to retain its integrity. But the case in the *baraisa* — *bemekatz'o uvah derech sevivotav* — involves cutting all around the perimeter, creating strips in multiple directions, which leaves no possibility of restoring the object to its original form. For such cuts, even Reish Lakish would agree that the leather's identity is destroyed. The distinction therefore is between a straight cut (which leather can survive as a functional object) and circumferential or multiple-directional cutting (which irrevocably transforms it).

The *gemara* ends here, with the relationship between these cases — when a torn or peeled or cut object retains its identity versus when it loses it — forming the bridge that the *gemara* will continue to develop in the next daf.

---

---

# Hullin 124

## Leather & Flaying

### Flayed Skin Problem

The sugya picks up near the bottom of 123b, where Rabbi Yirmiya poses a challenge. The broader context is a statement attributed to Resh Lakish holding that the principle of a torn garment losing its *tumah* status applies only to cloth, not to leather — because leather is a strong (*chalim*) material and therefore retains its integrity even when the majority has been torn, unless it is completely rent. Rabbi Yirmiya challenges this from a *mishnah* dealing with one who flays an animal — a *behemah* or *chayah*, whether *tehorah* or *teme'ah*, large or small — for the purpose of making a mat (*l'shatiach*). The *mishnah* establishes that once the amount necessary for grasping (*k'dei achizah*) has been removed, the flayed portion is no longer considered connected to the remainder. The *Gemara* asks: why should that be so? Let us say that since the leather is strong (*chalim*), the flayed portion should still be regarded as connected to the rest of the skin — just as Resh Lakish's principle would suggest.

### Tosafot's Analogy

Tosafot is deeply troubled by the underlying analogy. The comparison that the *Gemara* appears to be drawing — between rending a leather garment and flaying skin from an animal — is, in Tosafot's view, fundamentally strained. When Resh Lakish says that a leather garment retains its integrity because of its strength, he is speaking of a garment that has been partially torn but remains connected at the bottom: the whole piece is still, in some sense, one unit. That is entirely different from the case of flaying, where skin is being actively separated from flesh. One cannot simply say that because skin will eventually become leather, the flayed portion is still to be considered "connected" to the meat beneath. Tosafot attempts an explanation of what the analogy might be, but ultimately acknowledges that it is a challenging comparison.

### Avin's Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty through Rabbi Avin's principle: *rishon rishon nafal* — as each piece is removed, it is as though it has already fallen off. Piece by piece, the flaying constitutes a continuous act of disconnection. The situation is thus categorically different from the case of the leather garment: there, the garment is being torn but remains a single connected unit at its base; here, each increment of skin removed has already, in effect, separated itself. This distinction, while perhaps somewhat circular, draws a meaningful line between a partial tear that leaves an intact remainder and an act of progressive removal that produces disconnection at each stage.

### Neck Skin Question

The *Gemara* then introduces a further challenge from Rabbi Yosef. The *mishnah* discusses the skin of the neck (*or shel tzavar*): if one has been flaying an animal from the feet upward and has reached the neck, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that the skin remaining on the neck is *not* considered connected (*eino chibur*). The *Gemara* asks: why not? Here the analogy to Resh Lakish may in fact be somewhat better — the skin is still physically attached to the flesh, and if leather is strong, surely what remains on the neck should be considered a single unit with the rest. Abaye, however, redirects the inquiry: rather than asking from Rabbi Avin's principle, look at the end of the *mishnah*, where the *chachamim* say the neck skin *is* considered connected (*chibur*) — which would indeed support Resh Lakish. Abaye then explains that the debate in the *mishnah* over the neck skin has nothing to do with Resh Lakish's principle at all. The question there concerns a *shomer* — the skin serving as a protective covering for the meat — that is of a kind that will detach on its own (*ha'asui l'natek me'elav*). Once the animal has been flayed all the way up to the neck, gravity and circumstance mean the remaining neck skin will naturally fall away even without continued effort. The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the *chachamim* is then about whether something that is still physically attached, but will inevitably detach on its own, counts as a *shomer*. One view holds that it is still a *shomer* because it remains connected now; the other holds it is not a *shomer* because its detachment is only a matter of time.

### Natural Detachment

What is striking about the *mishnah* as a whole, as Abaye's reading reveals, is the elegant tension between its two halves. The opening case involves skin that has already been physically removed, yet is still considered connected — because it is close to the flesh and part of one continuous piece, even the flayed section is treated as attached. The closing case involves skin that is still physically on the animal, yet is considered disconnected — because it will fall away on its own. The criterion throughout is not mere physical attachment but something closer to functional or meaningful connection, and the *mishnah*'s two rulings bracket that concept from opposite directions.

## Pottery Oven Case

### Oven Purification

Rabbi Yirmiya now introduces a new challenge to Resh Lakish's principle. If the previous analogy — leather garment to flayed skin — was strained by the similarity of material but difference of scenario, this new challenge operates in the reverse: similar scenarios of breaking a vessel, but involving very different materials. If one is going to say that leather is strong and therefore preserves its integrity even when partially damaged, the same logic might apply to pottery, which is also a strong material. The *mishnah* in *Keilim* that the *Gemara* now examines deals with a *tanur*, a clay oven of the kind common in the time of *Chazal*: a large pottery vessel, made separately and then plastered to the ground. Because it was originally fashioned as an independent object, a pottery *tanur* can become *tamei* — the *Torah* itself states, *tanur ve-khirayim yutatz, tme'im hem*, that an oven and stove are *tamei* and must be shattered.

The *mishnah* asks: if a *tamei tanur* is to be purified, how does one do so? The answer is: *chalko li-shlosha* — break it into three pieces. The reasoning is that if it were broken into only two pieces, one would constitute the majority and would retain the status of the original vessel. With three pieces, no single piece holds the majority, and the vessel's identity is dissolved. In addition, *ve-gorer et ha-tpila* — one must scrape away the plaster that attaches it to the ground — *ad she-yehei ba-aretz*, until it is fully released from the ground.

### Rabbi Meir's View

Rabbi Meir dissents. He holds that one need not remove the plaster or bring the oven down to the ground; it is sufficient to reduce the oven's interior measurement to less than four *tefachim* (*arba tefachim*). The minimum size for an oven to be considered a halakhically significant vessel is four *tefachim*; once the interior has been reduced below that threshold, the object no longer qualifies as an oven, and it loses its status. The measurement, Rabbi Meir specifies, is *mi-bifnim* — from the inside. This detail may reflect the principle that for clay vessels (*klei cheres*), susceptibility to *tumah* is measured from the interior, since pottery vessels become *tamei* only through their inner space.

The *Gemara* then asks directly: but according to Rabbi Meir, why is it sufficient to get the oven below four *tefachim*? One should say *chalim v'kai* — it is strong and retains its integrity — just as Resh Lakish would reason about leather. Even if you reduce it in size, pottery is still a strong material. Rava intervenes and reframes the entire discussion. He argues that in fact both the *chachamim* and Rabbi Meir agree, based on Resh Lakish's principle that a strong material requires complete rupture, that once an oven has become *tamei*, one must break it into three pieces and remove the plaster entirely to achieve *taharah*. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* is not about the method of purification once the oven is *tamei*; it concerns a different question entirely.

### Preemptive Purification

The question Rava identifies as the actual subject of the dispute is this: what must one do *before* the oven becomes *tamei* in order to prevent it from ever acquiring the status of a vessel? Suppose someone knows a *meit* will be brought into the house and wishes to ensure the oven never becomes *tamei* in the first place — is there a simpler way to strip the object of its identity as an oven before the *tumah* event occurs? The *chachamim* say no: even for that preventive purpose, one must break the oven into three pieces and remove the plaster. Rabbi Meir says that in this preemptive context, it is sufficient to reduce the size to below four *tefachim*, because an oven below that threshold never attains the identity of an oven to begin with. The asymmetry reflects the underlying principle: once *tumah* has been acquired by a fully formed vessel, Resh Lakish's logic requires complete destruction to undo it; but if the object was never fully constituted as a vessel, no complete destruction is necessary.

### Functional Identity

Implicit in Rabbi Meir's position is a significant conceptual claim: if an object cannot function for the purpose for which it was made, it has no identity as a *kli* at all. This is, as the *Gemara* acknowledges, a surprising proposition. The thirty chapters of *Masechet Keilim* are largely occupied with exactly this web of questions — how closely an object must resemble its original function to retain or acquire vessel-status, what role the maker's intent plays, and how different minimum-size thresholds operate at the stage of initial constitution versus after breakage. Rabbi Meir's position here is that functional incapacity is legally dispositive: an oven too small to cook in is simply not an oven, and Maimonides reads the law accordingly.

### Breaking Methods

The *Gemara* now examines a *braita* from *Keilim* that on its surface appears to contradict Rava's reframing. The *braita* states that a *tanur* whose initial minimum size is four *tefachim* also retains its status as long as its remnant (*shiyuro*) is four *tefachim* — this is Rabbi Meir's position. The *chachamim* qualify: the four-*tefachim* standard applies to a large oven; for a small oven, even the smallest size suffices from the outset, and the remnant retains its status as long as the majority remains. This *braita* appears to show the *chachamim* agreeing with Rabbi Meir that reducing an oven below four *tefachim* renders it *tahor* — which conflicts with Rava's claim that the *chachamim* require complete breaking regardless.

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between two methods of breaking. When the oven is cut *widthwise* (*tzalkei mitzlak*), the resulting piece retains functional utility — the bottom portion with its full circumference may still serve as an oven — and in that case the *chachamim* maintain their stricter position, requiring the oven to be broken into thirds rather than relying on the four-*tefachim* threshold. When the oven is cut *lengthwise* (*gistera*), what remains is far less functional, and there the *chachamim* concede that reduction below four *tefachim* suffices. It should be noted that Rashi reads the two cases in the opposite direction — he assigns the stricter requirement to the lengthwise cut and the more lenient standard to the widthwise — and his reasoning on this point is difficult to follow.

### Braita Measurements

The *braita* continues to specify: for a large oven, the standard of four *tefachim* governs both initial constitution and the size of the remnant after breakage. For a small oven, the *chachamim* say *techilato kol she-hu* — any size can constitute such an oven initially — and its remnant retains status as long as the majority remains. The *Gemara* asks: what is the practical minimum of *kol she-hu*? The school of Rabbi Yannai answers: *tefach* — even a single handbreadth. This invites an obvious question: what purpose could an oven of a single *tefach* possibly serve?

### Play Ovens

The *Gemara* answers: *she-ken osin tanurim benot tefach* — people make play ovens (*tanurim benot tefach*) the size of a *tefach*. This is a charming detail: children's play ovens, comparable in concept to the miniature kitchen sets familiar from later generations, were functional enough within the world of children's play that they were recognized as genuine *keilim* for the purposes of *tumah*. Rashi understands the word *benot* as referring to the oven itself — it is an oven of the daughter, i.e., a child's oven — and glosses it with the term *le-tinokot*, for children. Whether such an oven was genuinely usable in any practical sense, or whether its recognition as a *kli* rested entirely on its serviceability for the purpose for which it was made (children's play), is itself a conceptual question about the nature of vessel-identity: if it is made to serve as a real oven in the world of children's play, then play ovens have their own minimum size, and as long as the object functions for that purpose, it qualifies.

One might ask: if breaking the oven into three pieces causes it to lose its vessel-identity, why does not the first break already transfer *tumah* to the larger remaining piece, and then the second break to the larger of those two, and so on? The answer seems to be that even though the larger piece may technically retain the *tumah* of an oven, it is not clear that we would still call it an oven once it is non-functional as such. Moreover, one act of breaking can produce three pieces simultaneously, bypassing the question of sequential stages. The broader principle at work — that the minimum-size thresholds for initial constitution and for post-breakage significance may differ — is extensively treated in the preceding pages of the *Gemara*.

### Reconciling Views

The *Gemara* finally synthesizes the positions. The remnant of a small oven — one that started as small as a *tefach* — retains its status as long as the majority (*rubo*) remains. But then the *Gemara* asks: *ruba d'tefach l'mai chazi*? What can you actually do with the majority of a *tefach*-sized oven? It is completely non-functional even for children's play. Abaye clarifies: when the *chachamim* say the remnant is measured by majority, they are referring back to the earlier case of a *large* oven, not a small one. For a large oven, the *chachamim* hold that once the majority has been removed, the remainder loses its status. The apparent contradiction with the passage where the *chachamim* seemed to agree with Rabbi Meir's four-*tefachim* standard is resolved by distinguishing oven sizes: for an oven of nine *tefachim*, the *chachamim* hold it sufficient to have removed the majority even if the remnant exceeds four *tefachim*; for an oven of seven *tefachim*, reduction below four *tefachim* suffices. In this special context — where the oven is being broken widthwise (or, according to Rashi's reading, in the other orientation) — the *chachamim* are lenient and permit either standard, while Rabbi Meir always insists on the four-*tefachim* threshold regardless.

The entire discussion of the *tanur* was introduced to test Resh Lakish's principle. The *Gemara* ultimately holds that the pottery oven cases do not contradict him, because the debate between the *chachamim* and Rabbi Meir concerns preemptive action rather than post-*tumah* purification. Once *tumah* has been acquired, everyone agrees with the logic of Resh Lakish: a strong material requires complete destruction to be rendered *tahor*.

## Leather Importance

### Leather Retains Identity

The *Gemara* now presents an alternative formulation (*lashon acher*) of the same underlying principle. Rav Huna, citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose, restates the opening position: if a torn garment still retains enough material for a wrap (*k'dei ma'aforet*), it does not become *tahor* even if the majority has been rent. Resh Lakish then qualifies: this was said only about cloth (*tallit*), but leather (*or*) is *chashiv* — more significant — and therefore retains its identity by virtue of its importance rather than merely its physical strength.

### Leather vs. Cloth

The shift in language is worth noting. Earlier, the principle was framed in terms of leather being *chalim* — strong — which invited comparisons to other strong materials like pottery and led to a range of difficult questions. Here the language changes: leather is *chashiv*, important, a more significant material than cloth, one that people do not readily discard even when substantially damaged. Because of this significance, it is not regarded as having lost its identity until it is completely rent. This framing carries a somewhat different conceptual weight: the question is not merely physical durability but the object's standing in human use and valuation.

### Intent & Status

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Resh Lakish from a *mishnah*: a piece of *tamei* leather that had been used as a mat and acquired *tumah* from a *zav* sitting on it — once one intends to cut it into straps and sandals and applies a blade (*izmel*) to it, it immediately becomes *tahor*. This is the view of Rabbi Yehudah. The *chachamim* say one must reduce it to less than five *tefachim* before it becomes *tahor*. But in either case, the question arises: according to Resh Lakish, why does a single cut, or even reduction to five *tefachim*, suffice? If leather is so significant that it requires complete rending, surely it should retain its *tumah* until fully destroyed. The *Gemara* responds by distinguishing intent. Here, the owner has defined a very narrow, specific intended use for the leather — cutting it into straps and sandals — and that narrowly defined intent is sufficient to strip the object of its identity as a garment. A normal piece of leather, without such a clearly limited defined purpose, would retain its identity because of its importance, until completely rent. But when the owner mentally commits to a specific diminished use, that act of mind alone begins to dissolve the object's status as a significant leather item.

## Skin & Meat Significance

### Hair as Shomer

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *mishnah*. If a piece of skin (*or*) has on it a *kezayit* of meat from a *neveilah*, and one touches a strand of meat (*tziv*) trailing from it, or a hair (*sa'arah*) on the other side of the skin, one becomes *tamei*. This establishes the concept that even a hair or a trailing strand can serve as a *shomer* — a protector or connector — transmitting *tumah* from the meat through the skin, because it is considered meaningfully connected to the significant piece of meat on the other side.

### Rabbi Yishmael

The *mishnah* then addresses a more complex case: the skin has on it not a full *kezayit* but *shenei chatzei zeitim* — two half-*zeisim* — of *neveilah* meat. Rabbi Yishmael says: this combination renders *tamei* through carrying (*massa*) but not through touching (*maga*). The reason is that touching two separate pieces constitutes two separate acts of *maga*, and since neither half alone reaches the minimum measure of a *kezayit*, neither act of touching alone produces *tumah*. Carrying, by contrast, is a single act that moves both halves together, and since in total they equal a *kezayit*, one becomes *tamei* through *massa*.

### Rabbi Akiva's Principle

Rabbi Akiva takes a stricter position: the two half-*zeisim* on leather render *tamei* neither through touching nor through carrying. However, he himself concedes — and the *mishnah* makes this explicit — that if the same two half-*zeisim* were threaded on a twig (*kisom*) and one moved them, one *would* be *tamei*. This concession makes clear that Rabbi Akiva's leniency in the case of leather is not a general principle about two halves failing to combine. In general, Rabbi Akiva holds that two half-*zeisim* *do* combine to create *tumah*. The reason he is lenient specifically on the leather case is articulated by the *mishnah* itself: *mipnei she-ha'or mevatlan* — because the leather negates their significance. The leather is more substantial than the pieces of sub-*kezayit* meat resting upon it, and that material significance causes the leather to be *mevatel* the meat, rendering the halves as if they were not there.

### Bitul from Flaying

Ulla, citing Rabbi Yochanan, adds a further qualification: the significance of even small amounts of meat on leather is maintained only when the meat was torn away by an animal (*peletato chayah*). But if the meat remained on the skin as a result of flaying with a knife (*peletato sakin*), it is *batel* — negated — to the leather, and even Rabbi Yishmael would agree that such meat has no halakhic significance. The act of the knife, in this view, represents a kind of human discarding: the flesher removed what was meant to be removed, and what is left behind has been, in effect, abandoned to insignificance.

## Rav Nachman's Objection

### Extreme Bitul Rejected

Rav Nachman challenges Ulla sharply. He asks: did Rabbi Yochanan really say that *peletato sakin* — meat that came off by the knife — is *batel* to the leather, even if the quantity of meat is as large as a *tarta* (which Rashi identifies as a quarter of a *kav*, a substantial amount)? Ulla confirms: yes. Even if the quantity is as large as a *kenafya* — a large sieve used for sifting flour — would Rabbi Yochanan say it is *batel*? Again, Ulla confirms. At this, Rav Nachman declares: *chai Elokeim*, by God, even if I had heard this directly from Rabbi Yochanan's own mouth, I would not accept it. The claim that even a large, significant quantity of meat is *batel* simply because it came off the knife rather than from an animal's tearing strikes him as halakhically untenable. A *kezayit* of meat is a *kezayit* of meat; it should not lose its significance merely because of how it came to rest on the leather.

### Rabbi Ami's Reaction

When Rabbi Oshia traveled to Eretz Yisrael and related this exchange to Rabbi Ami — recounting what Ulla had said and how Rav Nachman had responded — Rabbi Ami was offended. He said: is it because Rav Nachman is the son-in-law of the house of the *Nasi* that he feels entitled to be so dismissive (*mezalzel*) of a teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan? The sharpness of Rav Nachman's rejection — "I would not accept it even from Rabbi Yochanan's mouth" — struck Rabbi Ami as an act of *chutzpah* that could only be explained by the social prestige Rav Nachman enjoyed through his family connection to the *Nasi*'s house. The story is notable for what it reveals about the social dynamics of the Babylonian *batei midrash* and the complex relationship between rabbinic authority and aristocratic standing.

### Yochanan Clarified

The story, however, does not end there. At a later occasion, Rabbi Oshia found Rabbi Ami teaching Rabbi Yochanan's statement — but this time applying it to the *seifa*, the second part of the *mishnah*, where the case involves two half-*zeisim* rather than a full *kezayit*. In that context, Rabbi Yochanan's claim that *peletato sakin* is *batel* makes perfect sense: it is only saying that when the meat left by the knife is less than a *kezayit* — specifically two half-*zeisim* in the case of the *mishnah* — it is *batel* to the leather. Rabbi Ami had understood Rabbi Yochanan's teaching to apply only in this limited register. Rabbi Oshia then says to him: you are teaching it on the *seifa*, on the case of less than a *kezayit* — but Ulla taught it on the *reisha*, on the case of a full *kezayit* or more. Rabbi Ami is startled. Now understanding just how extreme Ulla's transmission of Rabbi Yochanan's statement was, he declares: *HaElokim*, even if I had heard this from the mouth of Yehoshua bin Nun himself, I would not accept it. The same Rabbi Ami who had been offended by Rav Nachman's dismissiveness, once he grasped the actual content of the claim, made an even stronger declaration of rejection.

### Merudad Solution

When Ravin and the other scholars who came from the west (*nechusei yama*) arrived, they confirmed: yes, Rabbi Yochanan's teaching was indeed stated on the *reisha*, applying even to quantities larger than a *kezayit*. But they offered the key to understanding it: *k'damar Rav Pappa bimrudad* — as Rav Pappa would later explain, the case involves *merudad*, meat that has been spread thin. Rav Pappa's definition of *merudad* is meat that is technically a *kezayit* or more in total volume but is spread out so thinly across the surface of the leather — like the thin layer of flesh that clings to a peel when one peels a vegetable — that it has no practical significance as a discrete quantity of meat. In such a case, no matter how much it totals in the abstract, its thinness renders it *batel* to the leather beneath it. This resolution clarifies the outer limits of the principle: it is not that any quantity of meat left by a knife is automatically *batel*, but rather that meat which is spread so thin as to be practically invisible as a food substance loses its halakhic significance relative to the leather.

## Touching Sides Matter

### Front vs. Back Touch

Bar Padda introduces a distinction that refines the case of two half-*zeisim* on leather. He says: the ruling that touching does not render *tamei* was stated only with respect to touching from behind (*me'achorah*) — that is, touching the skin side rather than the meat. When one touches the skin side of the leather, the skin itself stands between the person and the meat, and since the skin is not a *shomer* for a mere half-*kezayit*, the touch does not communicate *tumah*. But if one touches from the front (*milfaneha*) — directly touching the meat itself — then, according to Bar Padda, two separate acts of touching (*yesh nogea ve-chozer ve-nogea*) do combine, and one would become *tamei*.

### Two Acts Don't Combine

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. He holds that *ein nogea ve-chozer ve-nogea* — there is no principle by which two separate acts of touching combine. Whether one touches the meat from the front or the skin from behind is irrelevant to the question of combination; two separate acts of touching two separate half-*zeisim* never produce *tumah*, regardless of which side is touched. The only act of conveyance in our *mishnah* that does combine two halves is *massa* — carrying — which is structurally a single act that moves both pieces together.

## Yochanan's Alignment

### Dosa's Case

Rabbi Yochanan further notes that his position aligns with an earlier parallel ruling. He states that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas said essentially the same thing. Rabbi Yishmael's position is what we have already seen: two half-*zeisim* touched separately do not combine. The parallel attributed to Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas comes from a case involving *ohel* — the *tumah* of a corpse spreading under a roof. If a *kezayit* from a corpse was divided into two halves and both halves were brought into a house, Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas rules the house remains *tahor*, while the *chachamim* say it is *tamei*. Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas reasons: just as one cannot become *tamei* by being *ma'ahil* — serving as a canopy — over one half and then the other half in separate acts, these two halves, even under the same roof, do not combine. This is analogous, in Rabbi Yochanan's view, to Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that two separate acts of touching do not combine.

### Tosafot's Challenge

Tosafot raises a sharp objection to this analogy. In our *mishnah*, everyone agrees that *carrying* two half-*zeisim* together renders *tamei*, because carrying is a single act that moves both pieces. One would think that being *ma'ahil* over two halves under one roof is far more similar to carrying — both are single encompassing acts — than to two separate acts of touching. Why then does Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas compare being *ma'ahil* over two halves to two separate touchings rather than to carrying? Tosafot's resolution is that the analogy is not really about "one act versus two acts" at all. For those who hold, like Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, that two half-*zeisim* do not combine, the ruling applies whether the act is a single one or multiple ones — whether touching, being *ma'ahil*, or anything else. The only exception is carrying, and that exception is not grounded in the logic of "one act" but in a specific *pasuk*. Even physically speaking, an act of carrying might be considered a single encompassing act just as being *ma'ahil* is — yet the *Torah* establishes a special rule for *massa* that overrides the general principle.

### Splitting Prevention

The deeper principle, on Tosafot's reading, is this: when a *kezayit* is split into two halves, those halves simply do not combine for *tumah* — whether by touching, by *ohel*, or by any other mode. The exception of *massa* is a *chiddush* derived from a specific verse, not a logical extension of any "single-act" theory. This reframing shifts the conceptual center of gravity: the question is not about counting acts but about whether a divided *kezayit* retains its power to transmit *tumah* in a given category of *tumah*-transmission. Only *massa* — by force of a scriptural derivation — treats the divided *kezayit* as still effective.

## Touching-Carrying Link

### Verse Comparison

The *Gemara* now turns to the scriptural basis for Rabbi Akiva's principle. The *Torah* uses two verbs side by side in the context of *neveilah*: *ha-nogea be-nivlatam* — one who touches their carcass — and *ve-hanosei et nivlatam* — one who carries their carcass. The juxtaposition of *maga* (touching) and *massa* (carrying) in the same context suggests a systematic relationship between the two categories.

### Akiva's Deduction

From this juxtaposition, Rabbi Akiva derives: *kol she-ba li-khlal maga, ba li-khlal massa; lo ba li-khlal maga, lo ba li-khlal massa* — whatever can make one *tamei* through touching can make one *tamei* through carrying; whatever cannot make one *tamei* through touching cannot make one *tamei* through carrying. Carrying, on this view, is conceptually a form of indirect touching — a more remote means of contact — and therefore requires the same potential for *tumah*-transmission through direct contact. If the object cannot render one *tamei* by being touched, it should not be able to render one *tamei* through the more attenuated act of carrying.

### Touching Meat Question

The *Gemara* now confronts this principle with a difficulty arising from Bar Padda's earlier distinction. Bar Padda had said that if one touches the meat of the two half-*zeisim* directly — from the front — one *does* become *tamei*. If that is so, then Rabbi Yishmael should be able to say: the two halves *can* render *tamei* through touching (from the front), and therefore Rabbi Akiva's principle should conclude that they render *tamei* through carrying as well. But Rabbi Yishmael says they *do* render *tamei* through carrying. So Rabbi Akiva's challenge to Rabbi Yishmael — that if you cannot become *tamei* through touching, you cannot become *tamei* through carrying — seems to have no force, since Rabbi Yishmael would agree that touching the meat directly does render *tamei*.

### Rava's Resolution

Rava resolves the difficulty by refining the principle. Rabbi Akiva's requirement is not merely that one *can* become *tamei* through touching the object from *some* side; it is that one must be able to become *tamei* by touching it *from any side* (*be-chol tzad*). If there exists even one side from which touching does not render *tamei* — specifically, the skin side in this case — then the condition for *massa*-*tumah* is not met, and one cannot become *tamei* through carrying either. The logical basis for this more demanding formulation is less immediately intuitive: why should the impossibility of becoming *tamei* from the skin side foreclose the possibility of *tumah* through carrying, if touching the meat directly *does* render *tamei*? Rava's resolution stands as the *Gemara*'s answer to defend Bar Padda's distinction, but the underlying reasoning requires careful study.

## Sealed Bone Case

### Sealed Marrow

Rav Avia Saba poses a question to Rabba bar bar Rav Huna that presses the principle of Rabbi Akiva to its limit. Consider a *kulis stuma* — a sealed thigh-bone with a *kezayit* of marrow inside it. The marrow is *neveilah* and would render *tamei* if one could touch it. But the bone is closed, uncracked, and intact; there is no way to touch the marrow without cracking the bone open. The question is: does carrying the bone render one *tamei* through *massa*? If one follows Rabbi Akiva's principle — that *massa* requires the potential for *maga* — and if it is literally impossible to touch the marrow (since the bone seals it completely), does that impossibility of *maga* foreclose *tumah* through *massa*? Or does Rabbi Yishmael reject that principle, holding that *massa* is an independent category that can render *tamei* even where *maga* is impossible?

The question is further sharpened by reference to Bar Padda's distinction. Bar Padda had said that Rabbi Yishmael is lenient on touching from the skin side but would agree that touching the meat directly renders *tamei* — and that this is precisely why Rabbi Yishmael says you are *tamei* through carrying: the potential for *maga* (from the front) still exists. On that reading, Rabbi Yishmael in fact agrees with Rabbi Akiva's principle; he just applies it differently. But in the case of the sealed bone, there is no side from which the marrow can be touched at all. So the question becomes: does Rabbi Yishmael agree with Rabbi Akiva that the complete impossibility of *maga* forecloses *massa*? Or does he hold that *massa* is a genuinely independent category that requires no *maga*-potential whatsoever?

### Evasion Story

Rabba bar bar Rav Huna's response to the question is memorable: *orba parach* — oh look, a bird flew by. He simply changes the subject. His son Rava is taken aback and rebukes him: is this not Rabbi Avia Saba of Pumbedita, whom you yourself regularly praise as a great *talmid chacham*? How can you dismiss his question so? Rabba bar bar Rav Huna explains himself: *ani hayom samchuni ba'ashishot* — today I have been supported by flasks (which Rashi reads as an expression of exhaustion). He had just delivered a major *drasha* — apparently a *Shabbat HaGadol* lecture — and was utterly spent. He simply did not have the mental energy at that moment to engage with a subtle question about whether Rabbi Yishmael accepts Rabbi Akiva's principle. The story has an appealing human quality: even the greatest scholars reach a point of exhaustion after intensive public teaching, and changing the subject to a passing bird is apparently a time-honored method of graceful evasion. The question about the sealed bone, for its part, is left unresolved by the *Gemara*.

## Ulla's Position

### Nosei Definition

Ulla now introduces a position that appears to stand in direct conflict with the *mishnah*. He asserts: *shenei chatzei zeitim she-thavan be-kisom, afilu molich u-meivi kol ha-yom kulo, tahor* — two half-*zeisim* threaded on a twig, even if one carries them back and forth all day, one remains *tahor*. Ulla's reasoning is derived from the word *nosei* in the verse — the *Torah* says *ve-hanosei*, one who carries. Ulla reads this to imply: *ba'inan nosei ve-hu de-nisai* — we require a form of carrying in which the object *carries itself*, i.e., in which the pieces are sufficiently connected that picking up one causes the other to come along by virtue of their natural connection. Two separate half-*zeisim* on a twig are genuinely distinct pieces; if one were to pick up one half alone (without the twig), the other would not follow. Therefore they do not meet the definition of *nosei* required for *massa*-*tumah*.

### Contradiction

The *Gemara* immediately objects: *tennan* — we have learned in the *mishnah* — *hayu alav shenei chatzei zeitim, metamei be-massa ve-lo be-maga, divrei Rabbi Yishmael*. Rabbi Yishmael explicitly says that two half-*zeisim* on leather *do* render *tamei* through *massa*. This is a flat contradiction of Ulla's position.

### Reconciliation Attempts

The *Gemara* attempts to reconcile: *Rav Pappa said, bi-merudad* — the case in the *mishnah* involves *merudad*, meat spread so thin across the leather that the two halves are in fact physically continuous along the surface. On that reading, they do constitute a single connected piece and therefore satisfy Ulla's requirement that the carried object *carry itself*. Tosafot, however, is dissatisfied: if the meat is genuinely *merudad* and continuous, it is no longer two separate half-*zeisim* in any meaningful sense, and it is difficult to understand why the *mishnah* would describe it in those terms. A second attempt is made from Rabbi Akiva's concession in the *mishnah*: *modeh Rabbi Akiva bi-shenei chatzei zeitim she-thavan be-kisom ve-hisitan she-hu tamei* — Rabbi Akiva agrees that two half-*zeisim* on a twig, when moved, render *tamei*. Again the *Gemara* objects: *amai? ve-ha lo nisai hu* — but they do not carry themselves, they are not one piece. And again the answer is *bi-merudad*. Tosafot raises the same difficulty: if it is *merudad*, why describe them as two halves? The *Gemara* then entertains the possibility that the entire question is itself a debate among *tannaim*: whether the *nosei* requirement demands that the object carry itself, or whether any act of physical conveyance suffices. On this reading, Ulla's position would reflect one *tannaitic* opinion, and the *mishnah* would reflect another. What is clear in any case is that Ulla's formulation of *massa*-*tumah* is striking, and the *Gemara*'s effort to avoid a direct contradiction with the *mishnah* is strained — with Tosafot explicitly noting that the proposed reconciliations do not fully succeed. Beyond Ulla's specific point, the *sugya* has now established two major questions: whether two half-*zeisim* combine for *tumah* by touching, by *ohel*, or by *massa*; and whether the capacity to become *tamei* through *maga* is a necessary prerequisite for *tumah* through *massa*. Both questions remain live as the *daf* concludes.

---

---

# Hullin 126

## Introduction & Setup

### Daf & Opening

We begin today's shiur a few lines back on 125b, at the passage commencing with the words *amar Rava mina amina lah* — "Rava said: from where do I derive this?" The overarching discussion concerns a *mishnah* that speaks of touching a bone from a corpse as a source of *tumah*. The question animating the preceding sugya is why the *mishnah* uses the language of touching rather than *ohel* — roofing or tenting — given that marrow inside a bone would seem to generate *tumas ohel* for anyone positioned above it. Rabbi Yochanan resolved this by arguing that in certain circumstances, touching and roofing (*ma'ahil*) are treated as equivalent categories, or more precisely, that a form of roofing is described by the term touching.

### Three Explanations

The *gemara* presents three distinct explanations for when roofing is considered equivalent to touching, each advanced by a different *amora*. Rabbi Zeira held that the equivalence obtains when the *tumah* is squeezed between two structures. Abaye held that it applies when one is within a *tefach* of the *tumah* — so close that the roofing is practically indistinguishable from contact. Rava, by contrast, held the broadest position: whenever one is directly above or below the *tumah*, that is equivalent to touching, and only when both parties are beneath the same shared roof — neither one above the other — does roofing remain a purely distinct category from touching. The *nafka mina* among these three positions concerns whether one can combine a *chatzi kezayit* of *tumah* that one roofs over with a *chatzi kezayit* that one touches, to produce a full *kezayit* and thereby incur *tumah*. We now turn to Rava's proof for his position.

---

## Rava's Proof

### Bed Ropes & Lattice

Rava cites the following *mishnah* as the source for his ruling: Rabbi Yosei says that *chavilei mitah* — the crisscrossed ropes forming the base of a bed frame — and *srigai chalonot* — lattice work — *chotzin bein ha-bayit la-aliyah*, serve as a partition between a lower story and an upper story of a building. When such lattice work is permanently installed and no longer functions as a vessel, it operates as a structural separator between the two floors. If there is *tumah* on the lower floor, it will not pass to the upper floor, even though the lattice has holes running through it.

### Separation Principle

The critical feature of this lattice work is that its openings are less than a *tefach* in width. The general principle is that an opening of a *tefach* or more allows *tumah* to pass through freely, while an opening smaller than a *tefach* does not. Once the lattice work is treated as part of the roof structure, those small holes are legally treated as if they do not exist — the lattice functions as a solid barrier. Accordingly, *tumah* arising directly beneath one of the holes is still considered to be under a solid roof, and it does not ascend to the upper floor.

### Lattice Over Corpse

The *mishnah* then shifts to a different scenario. The lattice work is not attached to any building structure but is suspended out in open air over a corpse — imagine a pole has been erected and the lattice placed above a body lying in a field. In this case, the unattached lattice does not have the full legal status of a roof, and the result is more nuanced: *ha-nogea ke-neged ha-nekev tamei*, one who touches opposite one of the holes in the lattice becomes *tamei*, because the *tumah* passes through the opening; *shelo ke-neged ha-nekev tahor*, one who touches opposite the physical material of the lattice itself is *tahor*, since the lattice matter itself blocks the *tumah* even without being structurally attached.

### Touching vs. Hole

This is the crux of Rava's proof. The *mishnah* uses the language *ha-nogea* — "one who touches" — in a context that describes someone holding a hand above the lattice work, which itself is suspended above the corpse. Rava argues that this person is not touching anything in the conventional sense; he is touching air. The *mishnah* would more naturally have said *ha-ma'ahil ke-neged ha-nekev* — "one who roofs opposite the hole." Instead it uses the verb *touch*, even in a scenario where the person is presumably above a *tefach*. Rava reads this as proof that in such a configuration — directly above the source of *tumah* — roofing is simply called touching, confirming his broad position.

---

## Abaye's Objection

### Within Tefach

Abaye rejects Rava's inference. He maintains that the *mishnah* must be describing a scenario in which the lattice work is within a *tefach* of the corpse, not above a *tefach*. On this reading, the *mishnah* uses the term "touching" because the lattice is so close to the body that something adjacent to it is, in the language of roofing law, essentially touching. The *gemara* probes this claim. It entertains the objection that if the lattice is within a *tefach* of the corpse, it should be treated like clothing on the body — *met kikesuto* — and disqualified as a partition entirely. But the *gemara* answers that the ordinary clothing analogy applies to garments one *mevatel* — incorporates — into the corpse itself, whereas this lattice work retains its independent character and is not subsumed into the body. It therefore may still function as a separator even within a *tefach*, at least opposite its solid portions.

### Buried Tumah Burst

However, the *gemara* raises a second, more forceful objection against Abaye's reading. There is a well-established principle: *tumah temunah* — *tumah* that is buried or enclosed without a *tefach* of airspace above it — *boka'at ve'olah*, bursts upward and is not contained by the physical barrier around it. This is treated as close to an iron rule of *tumas meis*: unless there is a *tefach* of airspace between the corpse and the covering above it, the *tumah* simply breaks through. If Abaye is correct that the lattice is within a *tefach* of the corpse, then why would the lattice stop the *tumah* at all? The *tumah* should burst straight through the lattice, reaching whoever is above, whether they are opposite a hole or opposite the solid lattice material.

### Yosei Rejects Burst

To preserve Abaye's reading, the *gemara* entertains a striking inference: perhaps Rabbi Yosei himself rejects the principle of *tumah temunah boka'at*. Perhaps Rabbi Yosei holds that any physical barrier — even one within a *tefach* of the corpse — stops *tumah* from ascending. This would be a remarkable departure from standard *halacha*. The practical implications would be enormous: if any physical covering stops *tumah*, even when less than a *tefach* above the body, the rules governing *kohanim* near cemeteries would be transformed entirely. But this is raised as a live possibility, and the *gemara* now turns to examine whether there is independent evidence for such a position in Rabbi Yosei's rulings.

---

## Cabinet Mishnah

### Cabinet Setup

The *gemara* cites a *mishnah* involving a *teivat migdal* — a large, immovable cabinet or dresser. An object so large and heavy that it is intended to remain in one place permanently does not attain the legal status of a vessel and cannot become *tamei*. The *mishnah* describes a scenario in which *tumah* — a small piece of a human corpse — is trapped beneath such a cabinet. The cabinet sits on the floor with a *tefach* of space between the floor and the bottom of the cabinet. This *tefach* causes the *tumah* to be treated as having a roof over it, so it spreads beneath the cabinet and out to the sides. However, the opening at the sides through which it could exit is less than a *tefach*. The *tumah* is, in principle, perfectly trapped: the *tefach* of space prevents it from bursting upward through the cabinet, while the narrow opening prevents it from spreading out into the room. The *mishnah* then states two rulings: if there is *tumah* beneath the cabinet, the house is *tamei*; if there is *tumah* in the house, whatever is enclosed beneath the cabinet is *tahor*.

### Sof Tumah Latzeit

The second ruling — that whatever is under the cabinet is protected from outside *tumah* — follows straightforwardly: there is no opening large enough for *tumah* to enter from the house into the space beneath the cabinet. The first ruling — that a corpse trapped under the cabinet makes the house *tamei* — requires explanation, since we just said the *tumah* cannot escape. The *gemara* explains it through the principle of *sof tumah latzeit*: the way of *tumah* is ultimately to go out. The practical meaning is that since any corpse or piece of a corpse will eventually be removed for burial, we treat it as though the removal has already occurred. We project forward to the inevitable moment of removal and count the *tumah* as having already traveled through the opening — even one smaller than a *tefach* — and entered the house. This principle is understood by the *gemara* to be rabbinic in origin, though many of the *mishnayot* that employ it do not make that explicit.

### Yosei's Exemption

Rabbi Yosei disagrees and says the house is *tahor*. His reasoning: *she-yachol hi le-hotzi chatza'im o lisrof bi-mekomah* — one can remove the corpse in half-pieces of a *kezayit* at a time, or could in theory burn it in place. Since there exists a mode of removal that does not involve passing the *tumah* through the opening of the house in a *kezayit*-sized amount at one time, we cannot be certain that the *sof tumah latzeit* principle will operate in the house-contaminating way the *tanna kamma* assumes. Tosafot notes that this reasoning applies specifically to a small piece of flesh; if there were a whole corpse inside, Rabbi Yosei would agree that it would be removed in the normal manner, and *sof tumah latzeit* would apply.

### Cabinet in Doorframe

The *mishnah* continues with a second case: the cabinet is positioned in the doorframe itself, with its opening pointing outward — toward the outside of the house. Now, whatever mechanism of *sof tumah latzeit* one applies, the imagined removal of the *tumah* would direct it outward, away from the house interior, not inward. Even granting the principle of *sof tumah latzeit*, the *tumah* goes out, not in. The house remains *tahor*, and whatever is enclosed under the cabinet is also *tahor* because the house is unaffected. The *mishnah* then appends: *Rabbi Yosei says tahor*.

---

## Contradiction & Clarific…

### Redundancy Problem

This final appended statement — *Rabbi Yosei says tahor* — immediately strikes the *gemara* as redundant. In the second scenario, where the cabinet is in the doorframe with its opening pointing outward, the *tanna kamma* already rules the house *tahor*. Why would Rabbi Yosei need to restate that it is *tahor*? If it applies to this second case, both opinions agree and there is no dispute to record. This forces the *gemara* to reconsider which case Rabbi Yosei's statement actually addresses.

### Resolution

The *gemara* resolves: Rabbi Yosei's appended statement must be referring back to the first scenario — the cabinet in the interior of the house with *tumah* trapped beneath it — where the *tanna kamma* ruled the house *tamei*. In that case, the *tanna kamma* relied on *sof tumah latzeit* to make the house *tamei*. Rabbi Yosei says the house is *tahor* even in that case. But now the *gemara* presses further: even aside from *sof tumah latzeit*, why would the *tanna kamma* assume the house is *tamei* in that first case? Because it is implicit in the *tanna kamma*'s framing that if there were *no* *tefach* between the corpse and the underside of the cabinet, the *tumah* would burst upward through the cabinet and fill the house — that case would be so obvious as to require no mention. The interesting case is precisely where there *is* a *tefach*, and the question is whether *sof tumah latzeit* then carries the *tumah* into the house.

### Yosei's Objections

Rabbi Yosei issues two rejections. First, against *sof tumah latzeit*: perhaps the piece is removed in sections or burned in place, so we do not apply the principle. Second, and more fundamentally, Rabbi Yosei also rejects the implicit premise of the *tanna kamma* — namely that *tumah temunah boka'at*, that *tumah* without a *tefach* roof above it bursts through. Rabbi Yosei holds *tumah temunah einah boka'at*: any physical barrier, even one within a *tefach* of the corpse, stops *tumah* from ascending. This is the position that the *gemara* is working to establish, and it is read into Rabbi Yosei's otherwise apparently redundant ruling of *tahor* on the second case — a ruling that, on closer examination, is his response to the *tanna kamma*'s implied assumption in the first case.

---

## Dog Stomach Case

### Dog & Flesh Setup

The *gemara* now introduces a further *mishnah* to test whether Rabbi Yosei consistently holds *tumah temunah einah boka'at*. The scenario: a dog ate flesh from a human corpse. While the dog is alive, the flesh causes no *tumah*, because *tumah belua* — *tumah* that is swallowed or absorbed within a living being — does not radiate outward; it is as though it does not exist. Once the dog dies, however, the principle of *belua* no longer applies. The flesh is now simply enclosed within a dead dog's body, and since it is no longer inside a living creature, it resumes its character as a source of *tumas meis*. If there is a *kezayit* of such flesh inside the dog's carcass, it becomes capable of causing everything beneath the same roof to become *tamei*.

### Doorstep Position

The *mishnah* then describes the dog lying on the threshold — the *iskoppa* — of a house, half inside and half outside the doorframe. The question is whether the corpse-flesh inside the dog's stomach renders the interior of the house *tamei*. One possibility is that the *tumah* travels through the dog's throat and esophagus, which functions as an *ohel*, and carries the *tumah* into the house. Another is that the *tumah* simply bursts through the walls of the dog's stomach wherever the stomach happens to be located, and one then examines where that location falls relative to the house. The *mishnah* records a four-way dispute.

### Rabbi Meir

Rabbi Meir rules: *im yesh be-tzavaro pote'ach tefach*, if the dog's throat is a full *tefach* in diameter, it brings the *tumah* into the house; if not, it does not. The esophagus functions as an *ohel* only when it has the minimum qualifying dimension of a *tefach*.

### Rabbi Yosei

Rabbi Yosei rules: *ro'in mi-keneged ha-mashkof u-lifnim ha-bayit tamei, mi-keneged ha-mashkof u-le-chutz ha-bayit tahor* — one inspects from opposite the *mashkof* inward and outward. The *mashkof* is the point in the doorframe where the door itself makes contact and stops — the interior striker-point, so to speak. Everything from that point inward is definitively under the roof of the house; everything from that point outward, though still within the outer dimensions of the doorframe, is not.
