Rabbi Yosei appears to reject the throat-as-*ohel* theory and instead looks directly at where the piece of flesh is located relative to this *mashkof* line, with *tumah* bursting through wherever the flesh sits.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *piv lifnim ha-bayit tahor* — if the dog's mouth faces inward, the house is *tahor*; *piv le-chutz ha-bayit tamei* — if the mouth faces outward, the house is *tamei*. Rabbi Eliezer apparently rejects the throat as a vehicle for *tumah* transmission, ruling the house *tahor* when the mouth faces inward, since the throat does not constitute a qualifying *ohel*. When the mouth faces outward, however, the rear of the dog is inside the house, and he applies *sof tumah latzeit* in an unusual form: the natural route of excretion for the *tumah* is through the rear, so we treat the *tumah* as though it has already passed out through the rear and thus entered the house. Tosafot notes that Rabbi Eliezer may not actually disagree with the possibility that the throat carries *tumah* — he may simply be addressing cases where the throat is not a *tefach* wide — but he adds the point about the rear and the direction of the dog.

### R. Yehuda ben Batera

Rabbi Yehuda ben Batera rules: *bein kach u-vein kach ha-bayit tamei* — whether the mouth faces inward or the rear faces inward, the house is always *tamei*. When the mouth faces inward, the throat carries the *tumah* into the house as an *ohel*; when the rear faces inward, *sof tumah latzeit* applies through the natural direction of excretion.

---

## Rava Reinterprets Yosei

### Initial Reading

The *gemara* initially reads Rabbi Yosei's ruling — *ro'in*, "you inspect" — as an instruction to examine where inside the dog the piece of corpse-flesh is actually located, and to check whether that location falls inside or outside the *mashkof* line. On this reading, Rabbi Yosei believes *tumah* bursts straight through the walls of the dog's stomach and spreads in all directions from wherever the flesh is, without any barrier stopping it. This appears to support the conclusion that *Rabbi Yosei does hold tumah temunah boka'at* — contradicting the position the *gemara* had tentatively attributed to him in the cabinet discussion. The *gemara* draws out the inference: *ki Rabbi Yosei u-shema minan tumah temunah boka'at* — from Rabbi Yosei here we derive that *tumah* buried or enclosed without a *tefach* bursts through.

### Cavity Requirement

Rava intervenes with a reinterpretation. When Rabbi Yosei says *ro'in*, he does not mean: inspect where the flesh is and assume it radiates straight through. Rather, he means: inspect whether the actual cavity — *challal* — of the esophagus is itself a *tefach* in diameter. There is a textual tradition cited in the name of Rav Acha son of Rava, who explicitly had the reading *ro'in et challal ha-tzavar* — "you inspect the hollow of the throat" — in his text of the *mishnah*. On this reading, Rabbi Yosei does not disagree with Rabbi Meir on the question of whether a *tefach*-wide throat carries *tumah*. He agrees that it does. What he disputes is what counts as *tefach*-wide: Rabbi Meir counts the entire anatomical throat, while Rabbi Yosei insists on measuring only the actual hollow passage within the esophagus.

### Meir vs. Yosei

Tosafot explains Rabbi Meir's logic by reference to a broader principle found elsewhere: Rabbi Meir in other *sugyot* holds that one can mentally project an object as carved out, treating a space as hollow even before any cutting takes place. Applied here, Rabbi Meir measures the full throat on the theory that if the meat surrounding the esophagus were cleared away, one would have a hollow of that full diameter. Rabbi Yosei rejects this and requires the actual hollow of the esophagus to be a *tefach*. In practice, this would be an extraordinary anatomical condition — imaginable perhaps for large animals like lions, but barely realistic for dogs. The theoretical possibility, however, is what the *halakha* must account for.

### Two Objections

Rava thus restates Rabbi Yosei's position as a dual objection against Rabbi Meir. First: where Rabbi Meir says the full throat being a *tefach* wide suffices, Rabbi Yosei says *anan batar challal azlinan* — we follow only the actual hollow. Second: where the *mishnah* appears to speak of any position within the doorframe as sufficient, Rabbi Yosei subdivides the doorframe at the *mashkof* line. The mouth of the dog being anywhere in the outer doorframe does not count; only from the *mashkof* inward is the dog's mouth considered to be beneath the roof of the house. On Rava's reading, then, Rabbi Yosei is not saying that *tumah* bursts straight through the dog's body from wherever the flesh is sitting. He is saying that the throat must have an actual hollow *tefach*, and even then, the right portion of the doorframe must be involved. Rabbi Yosei's position is thereby rescued from the apparent contradiction: he still holds *tumah temunah einah boka'at*.

---

## Rabbi Shimon

### Three Types

The *gemara* now turns to identify which *tanna* explicitly disputes the position we have been attributing to Rabbi Yosei — namely that some form of roofing is called touching. A *beraita* is cited: *Rabbi Shimon says: shalosh tumot porshot min ha-met* — three types of *tumah*-matter that derive from a corpse possess only two of the three standard modes of conveying *tumah*, lacking one mode each. Normally, a corpse or part thereof causes *tumah* in three ways: *maga* — touching it, *massa* — carrying it, and *ohel* — being beneath the same roof as it. Rabbi Shimon identifies three substances, each of which is deficient in one of these three modes.

### Decomposed Dust

*Melo tarvad rakev* — a ladle-full of decomposed corpse-dust — causes *tumah* through carrying and through *ohel*, but not through touching. The reason is that there is no practical way to touch all of the decomposed dust simultaneously; the material on the interior of one's cupped hand would never actually be in contact with one's skin. Since touching the entire quantity at once is impossible, the mode of *tumah* by touching does not apply. The *gemara* then asks: where, then, does one find a case of *tumah* through touching for this substance? The answer: in combination with one of the other two types listed, each of which does carry *tumah* through touching.

### Small Bone

*Etzem ke-se'orah* — a bone the size of a barley grain, without sufficient marrow to constitute a *kezayit* — causes *tumah* through carrying and through touching, but not through *ohel*. This connects directly back to our *mishnah*: a bare bone without marrow or flesh does not generate *tumas ohel*. Where does one find a case of *ohel* for this substance? Again, in combination with one of the other two types.

### Coffin-Boards

*Golel va-dofek* — understood by Rashi as the sideboard and headboard of a coffin, and by Tosafot as perhaps referring to the headstone of a grave — causes *tumah* through touching and through *ohel*, but not through carrying. Rashi attributes the *tumah* of *golel va-dofek* to *Halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, while Tosafot attempts to ground it in a *pasuk*. The absence of the carrying mode for the *golel* is what completes the symmetry of the three: one type lacks touching, one lacks *ohel*, one lacks carrying.

---

## Yosei vs. Shimon

### No Roofing-as-Touch

Having presented Rabbi Shimon's teaching, the *gemara* draws the key implication for our earlier discussion. Rabbi Shimon states explicitly that the *melo tarvad rakev* — the decomposed corpse-dust — does not cause *tumah* through touching. This is a definitive statement: for this substance, the mode of touching simply does not exist. Now, if Rabbi Shimon held that any form of *ohel* — any form of roofing — could be subsumed under the category of touching, he could not have made this ruling. Even if direct physical touching of all the material at once is impossible, there would remain a form of *ohel*-as-touching that would preserve some mode of *tumah* by touching for the decomposed dust. The fact that Rabbi Shimon categorically excludes touching as a mode for *melo tarvad rakev* proves that he does not recognize any equivalence between roofing and touching.

### Yosei's Proof

This stands in direct contrast to the *beraita* on 125b that served as the starting point for the whole discussion: Rabbi Yosei there says that one who roofs over the decomposed dust does become *tamei* through touching. The *gemara* had asked how one could possibly touch all of the decomposed material at once, and the answer was that Rabbi Yosei must be counting a form of *ohel* — a form of roofing or being directly above — as equivalent to touching. That is what enabled Rabbi Yosei to say that one becomes *tamei* through touching the *melo tarvad rakev*.

### Fundamental Dispute

The conclusion is that we have identified a genuine *machlokes* between two *tannaim*. Rabbi Yosei holds that roofing, under at least some conditions, is subsumed under or described as touching, so that one who roofs over the decomposed dust is *tamei* through touching. Rabbi Shimon categorically rejects any such equivalence: no form of *ohel* counts as touching, and therefore the decomposed dust lacks the mode of *tumah* by touching entirely. This was precisely the answer to the *gemara*'s question about which *tanna* disputes Rabbi Yosei's position — it is Rabbi Shimon.

---

## Bone Shomer

### Bone Rule

With the *ohel*-and-touching digression now concluded, the *gemara* returns to focus on the *mishnah*'s actual ruling, which concerns the bone of a *neveilah* — a carcass. The *mishnah* holds that a bone of a carcass causes *tumah* if touched or carried, but only when there is access to the marrow — even through a tiny hole. If there is no way to access the marrow at all, the bone is *tahor*.

### Shomer Concept

The governing principle is that of *shomer*: the bone serves as a guardian of the marrow. Touching the bone counts as touching the marrow, and carrying the bone counts as carrying the marrow, because the bone is the shell that protects and contains it. However, this *shomer* relationship only holds when it is at least theoretically possible to touch the marrow itself. If the bone is completely sealed and there is no opening whatsoever, the bone cannot function as a *shomer* and touching or carrying it causes no *tumah*.

### Source Analysis

The *gemara* derives this from the verse's language: *ha-nogea yitma* — "one who touches becomes *tamei*." The *talmud lomar* teaches that this applies only *she-efshar liga* — when it is possible to touch the actual flesh or marrow. If touching the flesh itself is impossible, *she-i efshar liga tahor* — one is *tahor*. The practical application to the bone of a *neveilah*: if there is a pinhole opening in the bone, it is possible to insert a hair and touch the marrow, so the bone functions as a *shomer* and one becomes *tamei* by touching the bone's exterior. If there is no hole, no such access is possible, and the bone is *tahor*.

---

## Challenging Shomer

### Rav Zeira's Q.

Rav Zeira poses a challenge to Abaye: if the principle is that one is *tamei* only when it is possible to touch the underlying flesh, how does touching a whole animal carcass — a standard *neveilah* — ever produce *tumah*? The animal has just died. Its skin is intact. There is no exposed meat anywhere on the surface. Yet it is universally accepted that touching a *neveilah* makes one *tamei*. This seems to contradict the rule that touching is only effective when the flesh is accessible.

### Abaye's Answer

Abaye answers without hesitation: *puch chazi kama kavvei it bei* — go see how many openings there are in a cow. An animal's body has natural orifices: the mouth, the nostrils. One can reach into the mouth and make direct contact with the flesh inside without touching the skin at all. Since it is possible to access the flesh through these openings, the condition is satisfied, and touching any part of the exterior — the skin, the bone — causes *tumah* because the flesh is accessible in principle.

### Rav Pappa's Q.

Rav Pappa raises a more refined challenge to Rava: if kidneys are surrounded by heavy fat — *cheilev* — and one were to pick up the kidneys, one would be handling the fat rather than the meat. Fat is not *metamei* in the same way meat is; the underlying kidneys are not directly accessible without first removing or penetrating the fat layer. How then does touching or carrying the kidneys cause *tumah* if the flesh itself is not reachable?

### Rava's Answer

Rava responds: *ta chazi kama chutin nimshachim heimena* — look and you will see that there are many thin strands of meat that run through the fat surrounding the kidneys. These strands are present throughout the fat layer and reach the surface. Since the meat is in fact accessible — it is exposed through and within the fat — the condition of *she-efshar liga* is satisfied, and touching the exterior causes *tumah*.

### Rav Ushaya's Q.

Rav Ushaya raises a more abstract question: what if one intends to drill a hole in the bone but has not yet done so? At the present moment, the bone is sealed and the marrow is inaccessible. But one is planning to make the hole. Does the intention to create access count as a form of potential accessibility — such that even now, without the hole, the bone functions as a *shomer* and causes *tumah*?

### Resolution

Rav Ushaya himself resolves the question: *mechusar nekiva lav ke-mechusar ma'aseh dami* — lacking a hole is not equivalent to lacking an action. The absence of a physical hole is simply a physical state; it does not have the legal status of an incomplete process the way an unmade transaction might. One requires actual, present physical accessibility. Intention to create future access does not transform the current sealed state of the bone into one where the marrow is reachable. The bone remains *tahor* until the hole is actually made. Strikingly, the *gemara* notes that Rav Ushaya reached this resolution by pure reasoning, without citing a text — an unusual feature worth noting.

---

## Reptile Eggs

### Sealed Egg

The *gemara* now applies the same inaccessibility principle to *beitzat ha-sheretz ha-merukemet* — an egg of one of the *sheratzim* species (here referring to the reptiles listed in the Torah, which lay eggs, in contrast to the mice and rats that are mammals) in which the embryo has taken form. Rashi specifies these as the *tzav*, *leta'ah*, and *chomet* — the reptilian members of the *sheratzim* group. If such an egg is intact and sealed, it is *tahor*. The developing fetus inside is not accessible; one cannot touch it from the outside. The same principle that governs the sealed bone of a *neveilah* applies: since touching the fetus itself is impossible, touching the shell does not constitute *tumah*-bearing contact.

### Hole in Egg

If the egg has even the smallest hole — *nikvah kol she-hu* — it becomes *tamei*. How small a hole? *Ke-chut ha-sa'arah* — the size of a hair. The *gemara* explains why: because even a pinhole-sized opening means one could, in principle, insert the hair of one's head — while it remains attached to one's body — through the hole and make contact with the fetus inside. That theoretical capacity for contact is sufficient to satisfy the condition of *she-efshar liga*, and the egg therefore causes *tumah* if touched. The connection back to the bone of a *neveilah* is explicit: the same derivation from *ha-nogea yitma* — possible touching renders one *tamei*, impossible touching does not — applies to both.

---

## Half-Flesh Mouse

### Basic Rule

The *mishnah* presents what the *gemara* treats as a genuine phenomenon: a mouse in mid-stage spontaneous generation, *achbar she-chetziyo basar ve-chetziyo adamah* — half flesh and half dirt. The presumption is that certain small rodents could be found in this intermediate state, partially emerged from the earth as living creatures. The governing rule of the *mishnah* is that if one touches the flesh half, one becomes *tamei*; if one touches only the dirt half, one is *tahor*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda extends the ruling: *af ha-nogea ba-adamah she-keneged ha-basar tamei* — even one who touches the dirt half, if that dirt portion is situated opposite or parallel to the flesh half, becomes *tamei*. Rabbi Yehuda treats the organism as a unified whole: once part of it is flesh and constitutes a *sheretz*, the entire form — including the still-earth portion directly adjacent to the flesh — is drawn into the *tumah* orbit of the whole creature.

---

## Reptile Eggs (II)

### Derivation

The *beraita* derives the rules about reptile eggs and bones from the verse: *ha-teme'im* — "those that are impure to you" — is expanded to include the egg of a *sheretz* and the *kulei* (thigh bone) of a *sheretz*. From the comparison *mah sheretz she-rakam* — just as a *sheretz* must be fully formed to cause *tumah* — the *gemara* derives that an egg only causes *tumah* if the embryo within is formed, *she-rikmah*. The verse *ha-nogea yitma* then limits the *tumah* to cases where touching is possible: *she-efshar liga tamei ve-she-i efshar liga tahor* — if it can be touched, one is *tamei*; if it cannot, one is *tahor*. And the minimum size of a hole that makes the interior touchable is *ke-chut ha-sa'arah* — the width of a single hair — because that is the smallest conduit through which meaningful contact can theoretically be made.

---

## Half-Flesh Mouse (II)

### Movement Condition

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi qualifies Rabbi Yehuda's ruling: *ve-hu she-hishritz pnei kulo* — Rabbi Yehuda's rule that touching the dirt half causes *tumah* applies only if the entire face of the creature has already begun to move, that is, if the organism has shown signs of life and locomotion. Without that sign of life, even the flesh half would not yet be considered a fully actualized *sheretz* for *tumah* purposes.

### Logical Inference

The *gemara* notes that this statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is attributed by some to the first clause of the *mishnah* — that is, to the basic rule that touching the flesh half causes *tumah* — and by others to Rabbi Yehuda's extension. The difference has a logical implication. If Rabbi Yehoshua's condition — that the creature must have begun to move — applies to the first clause, then it applies *a fortiori* to Rabbi Yehuda: if even the flesh half requires movement before causing *tumah*, certainly the dirt half that Rabbi Yehuda includes requires that the flesh half have begun to move. But if Rabbi Yehoshua's condition attaches only to Rabbi Yehuda's extension, then the first clause — touching the flesh half causes *tumah* — may hold even without movement having occurred, and only Rabbi Yehuda's more expansive ruling about the dirt half is limited to cases where the flesh has already stirred.

---

---

# Hullin 127

## Sheratzim Overview

### Opening & Prior Context

Daf 127 opens at the very bottom of 126b. Having spent considerable time on questions of skin and bone serving as a *shomer* — and, before that, on the laws of *tumas meis* and how the *tumah* of a corpse rises through the air, whether by contact or by *ohel* — we now turn to a new *mishna* treating an entirely different domain of impurity.

### Eight Sheratzim

The new *mishna* concerns *sheratzim* — the eight specific types of rodents and reptiles enumerated in the *Torah* that convey *tumah* upon death. These creatures, both small rodents and reptiles, are among the most familiar sources of *tumat maga* in the laws of purity, and the *mishna* opens up a series of questions about their precise scope and application.

### Reptile Eggs & Spontaneous Generation

The *mishna* also addresses the eggs of reptiles: because one does not have direct access to the developing fetus within, touching the egg renders one *tahor*, but if there is a hole in the shell, one becomes *tamei*. A striking and genuinely fascinating case then follows — one that can only be understood against the backdrop of ancient scientific belief. The rabbis understood that a certain *achbar*, a rat or mouse, could arise through spontaneous generation from the earth itself. At a particular stage of its development, the creature might be half soil and half flesh as it emerged from the ground. The *mishna* raises the question of whether that half-ground portion shares the *tumah* status of the rat itself. It bears emphasizing that spontaneous generation was not disproven until the seventeenth century, and the rabbis dealt with the best scientific understanding available to them.

---

## Sea Rat Dispute

### Tanu Rabbanan Sea Rat

The *Gemara* on 126b presents a *baraita*: *Tanu Rabbanan* — our rabbis taught. Since the *Torah* mentions *achbar* as one of the eight *sheratzim* that are *tamei* upon death, one might have thought this includes the sea *achbar* as well. There was a creature known as the sea rat — *achbar shebayam* — called by the same name. A *kal vachomer* or analogy might seem to support its inclusion. The *baraita* presents the argument as follows: the *Torah* states that both *chulda* (the weasel) and *achbar* are *tamei*. Just as the *chulda* is a creature of the land — *min hagadel al ha'aretz* — so too the *achbar* should be understood as referring only to land-dwelling animals, thereby excluding the sea rat.

### Chulda Analogies

The *baraita* immediately offers the counter-reading: *o kalech laderech zu* — or consider the alternative. The same analogy to *chulda* can be pressed in the opposite direction. One might argue that the term *chulda* applies to any creature called by that name — *kol sheshmo chulda* — without geographic restriction. The sea rat, called *achbar*, would then be included precisely because its name is *achbar*. The analogy from *chulda* thus cuts both ways, and neither direction is self-evidently correct.

### 'Al Ha'aretz Analysis

The *baraita* therefore turns to the verse itself: *talmud lomar* — *hasheretz hashoretz al ha'aretz*, that which creeps upon the ground. This phrase, the *baraita* argues, restricts *tumah* to land animals, not sea animals. But even this phrase admits of a further ambiguity: perhaps *al ha'aretz* refers not to the *type* of animal but to its *location* at the moment of contact. On that reading, if one touches a land rat while it is in the sea — say, a drowned rat floating in the ocean — one would be *tahor*, since the rat is not currently on the ground.

The *baraita* rejects this reading by adding *hashoretz — mikol makom sheshoretz*, wherever it creeps. This phrase comes to include even a land rat found in the sea, thus clarifying that *al ha'aretz* defines the *species*, not the *circumstance*. The phrase "on the land" tells us which type of creature is subject to the laws of *tumah*, not where that creature must physically be found when touched.

A further issue arises from the word *sheretz* itself. The verse could be read to mean that only a creature that procreates — *mashritz* — is subject to *tumah*, drawing on the related usage in *Shemot* where *vayishretzu* describes the Israelites multiplying prolifically. If so, the spontaneously generated rat, which does not procreate, might be excluded.

### Spontaneous Generation Inclusion

The *baraita* counters this by reading an inclusive *bet* in the word *basheretz* as extending the category to any creature called a *sheretz*, even one that does not procreate naturally. Through this exegetical move — somewhat opaque in its precise mechanism, as the lecturer notes — the spontaneously generated rat is brought within the scope of the verse's impurity laws.

### Analogy Reversal Question

At this point the *Gemara* on 127a records a challenge from one of the rabbinic students to *Rava*. The student asks: why not reverse the two rulings? Why not use *basheretz* to include the sea rat — interpreting it as applying to any creature that creeps, wherever found — and then use *al ha'aretz* to restrict *tumah* to cases where the creature is physically on land, thereby excluding both the sea rat in the sea and the land rat encountered in the sea?

This formulation would yield: sea rats are *tamei*, land rats only when on land, and spontaneously generated rats included by the name-based analogy. The student's question is whether the *baraita*'s chosen allocation of the exegetical resources is the only defensible one.

### Rava's Location Argument

*Rava* responds with a sharp logical observation: *me'achar deshaviteih layam mekom tumah* — once you have made the ocean a place where *tumah* can reside at all, by including sea rats, why would it make any sense to then exclude land rats found there? If the sea rat is *tamei* in the sea, then you have already conceded that the ocean is a venue where *tumah* operates. There is then no grounds to say a land rat found in the sea is *tahor*. The two positions are incoherent together. If, on the other hand, *al ha'aretz* defines species, then everything is consistent: land-type creatures are *tamei* wherever found, and sea-type creatures are excluded entirely.

---

## Safek Tumah Tzafa

### Floating Doubt Leniency

The *Gemara* then addresses a further implication of the phrase *al ha'aretz*: *vehai al ha'aretz miba'ei lei lehotzi safek tumah tzafa* — the verse is needed to exclude a case of *doubtful tumah* that is *floating* in the sea. *Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi* teaches: *al ha'aretz* — referring to what creeps upon the ground — comes to exclude *safek tumah tzafa*, a case of doubtful *tumah* floating in the ocean. In that case, one is *tahor*. Since the verse is needed for this purpose as well, the *Gemara* notes that *hasheretz al ha'aretz* is written twice, and one instance addresses the species question while the other addresses this special *safek* ruling.

### Tumah Domains & Ocean

This is one of the more strikingly arbitrary-seeming rules in the laws of *tumah*. The basic framework is familiar: if one has a doubt about *tumah* in a *reshut hayachid*, one is ruled *tamei*; in a *reshut harabim*, one is ruled *tahor*. Here, floating in the ocean constitutes its own halakhic category. If one touched an unidentified decomposed object in the ocean and cannot determine whether it was a dead *sheretz* or something else, one is *tahor* — a leniency that would not apply had the identical doubt arisen on land in a private domain.

The *tumah* of the *sheretz* itself, it should be noted, only applies to the creature after death — *asher yipol mehem bemotam yitma*, the *Torah* states explicitly. The special rule here concerns doubt: even where a land rat found in the sea would create *tumah* if one *definitely* touched it, the doubtful case is treated more leniently when the object is floating in the ocean. The precise logic underlying this leniency may be compared to the leniency in a *reshut harabim*, where the probability of inadvertent contact with *tumah* in a vast public space argues for leniency. The ocean, similarly, may function as a domain in which such doubts are resolved favorably. Whether this principle would extend to a private body of water — a private lake, for instance — is a question the *Gemara* does not resolve here.

---

## Tzav Species & Creation

### Reptile Species List

*Tanu Rabbanan* — the verse states *hatzav leminehu*, the *tzav* according to its kind. The *tzav* appears to be a type of lizard or chameleon. The phrase *leminehu* — "according to its kind" — is understood to include additional species within this category. These are: the *arod*, a type of lethal reptile (distinguished here from the wild donkey also called *arod* in some contexts, as noted by the *Gemara*); the *nifilim* (some versions read *uven hanifilim*); and the *salamandra*, the salamander.

The *arod* is the creature associated with the famous account in *Gemara Brachos* of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa: while he was in the midst of prayer at a hole in the ground, an *arod* bit him and died, since his prayer was so holy that the deadly creature could not harm him. The lesson drawn there was that it is not the *arod* that kills but sin.

### Rabbi Akiva's Praise

*Ubshaeh Rabbi Akiva megia lapasuk hazeh* — when Rabbi Akiva would reach the verse *hatzav leminehu* and reflect on the astonishing range of creatures included within it, he would say: *mah rabu maasecha Hashem* — how great and numerous are Your creations, O God. He used this verse as an occasion to reflect on the diversity of creation and on the specific ways in which each creature is fashioned to thrive within its particular environment.

### Environmental Adaptation

Rabbi Akiva's reflection unfolds as follows. *Yesh lecha briyot gedolot bayam v'yesh lecha briyot gedolot bayabasha* — there are enormous creatures in the sea and enormous creatures on the land. The sea creatures, if brought onto dry land, would immediately die. The land creatures — no matter how powerful, whether a lion or an elephant — if placed in the sea, would immediately perish. Similarly, there are great creatures of fire and great creatures of the air. The fire creatures, if brought into the air, would die immediately; the air creatures, if brought into fire, would immediately die.

*Mah rabu maasecha Hashem* — how great are Your creations. The wonder Rabbi Akiva is expressing is not merely the diversity of creation, but the exquisite specificity with which each creature is fashioned for its particular domain. The greatness lies not in universality but in the precise fit between creature and environment. The observation invites a question about amphibians and creatures that inhabit multiple domains, but the point of the *derasha* is the mutual incompatibility of the domains — and the marvel of the fact that each creature is made entirely to belong where it belongs.

### Salamander & Fire

The fire creatures Rabbi Akiva mentions are the salamanders. The rabbis believed that the salamander was a creature of fire — created from fire, according to *Rashi*, from fire and myrtle branches through some kind of process — and that anointing oneself with the salamander's blood would confer fireproof qualities. This is the creature included in the verse *hatzav leminehu*, which prompted Rabbi Akiva's exclamation of wonder.

---

## Regional Warnings

### Land-Sea Parallel

*Tanu Rabbanan* — our rabbis taught: every land animal has a sea counterpart, with the exception of the *chulda*, the weasel. Rabbi Zeira asks: *mai kra* — what is the scriptural basis for this? He cites the verse *ha'azinu kol yoshvei chaled* — hear, all who dwell in *chaled*. The word *chaled* is etymologically connected to *chulda*, and its usage in reference to dry land indicates that the *chulda* is specifically and exclusively a creature of dry land, with no sea counterpart.

### Narsh & Cherem

Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua then states: *bivrei deNarsh einam min hayishuv* — the people of the place called Narsh are not from the *yishuv*, not from civilized society. While *Rashi* interprets *bivrei deNarsh* as referring to the animals of Narsh being primarily sea creatures, *Tosafot* prefers a reading that fits the context better: these are people, and *einam min hayishuv* means that they are simply uncivilized. This sets the stage for a series of characterizations of various locales. Rav Papa, whose remark coheres with this reading, declares: *beshamta Narsh — tarbei mashchei ve'alifta* — let there be a *cherem* over Narsh, the fat, the skin, the fat tail — meaning all of them, every last one. The city is populated entirely by wicked people.

### Geographic Warnings

The passage continues with a series of terse warnings keyed to specific towns. *Eretz eretz eretz shimi devar Hashem* — land, land, land, hear the word of God — Rav Papa interprets this prophetic cry as addressed to the people of Narsh, who refused to listen. Rav Gidal in the name of Rav adds: if a person from Narsh kisses you, count your teeth — meaning, verify that your possessions are intact. If a person from Nahar Pekoda accompanies you, it is because he has noticed your fine cloak — watch your belongings. And if a person from Pumbedita accompanies you, change your inn immediately — he is trying to discover where you are staying in order to rob you at night. One wonders whether these characterizations applied to the non-Jewish inhabitants of these towns, or to the non-scholarly classes, rather than to the rabbinic community. In any event, the passages function as practical ethical warnings about certain locales.

---

## Arod Cross-Breeding

### Snake-Lizard Mating

The *Gemara* returns to the *arod* and to a remarkable firsthand account. Rav Huna bar Turta said: *paam achas hayisi l'vad* — once I attended a gathering (which *Rashi* identifies as a gathering where cross-breeding was practiced), *v'raisi nachash sheu karuch al hatzav* — and I saw a snake entwined with a *tzav*, a type of lizard. They were mating. *L'yamim yatza arod mibeineihem* — in time, an *arod* emerged from them — this lethal creature was the product of their cross-breeding.

### Divine Response Theory

When Rav Huna bar Turta brought this account to Rabbi Shimon HaChasid — a *Tanna* not often encountered in this form of address — the latter interpreted it theologically. *Amar HaKadosh Baruch Hu: heim heiviu birya shelo barasi b'olami* — they brought into existence a creature that I had not created in my world. *Af ani avia aleihem birya shelo barasi b'olami* — so I will bring upon them a creature that I had not created, meaning this dangerous *arod* is itself the divine response. Humanity tried to create something new and unnatural; the Holy One brought something equally unprecedented — but destructive — as the punishment.

### Cross-Breeding Objection

The *Gemara* raises a pointed objection. There is a principle: *kol she'ein tashmishan v'iburatan shaveh ein yoldin zeh mizeh* — any animals whose manner of copulation differs, whether front-to-front or front-to-back, or whose gestation periods differ, cannot produce offspring together. *V'kol she'ein tashmishan v'iburatan shaveh ein yoldin umigadlin zeh mizeh* — and they cannot nurse each other's young. A snake and a *tzav* differ dramatically in gestation period. How then could they have produced offspring at all?

### Double Miracle Explanation

The answer: *Rav nes b'toch nes* — it was a double miracle. First, a new creature came into being at all. Second, the cross-breeding succeeded despite the animals' biological incompatibility. The *Gemara* then asks: this is a negative event, a punishment — in what sense is it a *miracle*? The answer is: *mai nes b'toch nes l'puranusa* — it is indeed a miracle within a miracle, but a miracle administered as punishment. It is precisely as an expression of divine response that this impossible cross-breeding produced the dangerous *arod*.

---

## Genetic Engineering Ethics

### Torah Prohibitions

This passage opens into one of the more substantive halakhic-philosophical discussions of the tractate. There are explicit biblical prohibitions against cross-breeding animals — *kilayim* — and against cross-breeding seeds, as well as the prohibition of mixing wool and linen. These are grounded in specific verses. But the *Torah* contains no explicit prohibition of genetic engineering, cloning, or the contemporary forms of biotechnological intervention. The question then becomes: to what extent do the implicit values embedded in this *Gemara* inform those areas?

### Implicit Values Analysis

The language used by Rabbi Shimon HaChasid is striking: *birya shelo barasi b'olami* — a creature that I had not created in my world. This formulation seems to articulate a value of not fabricating new organisms that God has not brought into existence, at least within the animal kingdom. The story suggests that transgressing this boundary carries real moral weight, severe enough to warrant divine punishment through a new and dangerous creature.

### Innovation vs. Species Limits

And yet this sits in tension with other foundational values. The opening chapters of *Bereishit* command *v'chivshuha u'redu b'digat hayam* — human dominion over the natural world — and the opening of creation is marked throughout by the phrase *leminehu*, each species according to its kind. Human innovation is built into the structure of the world; keeping natural species distinct is equally built in. The challenge is that contemporary biotechnology often does not operate by crossing species in the traditional sense, which complicates any straightforward application of the *kilayim* prohibitions.

### Novel Applications Assessment

In areas not directly addressed by the *Torah*, the halakhic response must be case by case. This is not unique to genetic engineering: it is the general challenge of applying traditional halakhic categories to genuinely novel situations. Some *poskim* will seek to find the implicit values of the *pesukim* informative even where no explicit prohibition exists; others will resist ruling stringently in the absence of a direct source.

### Mule Precedent

The mule offers an instructive precedent. The act of cross-breeding a horse and a donkey is prohibited. Yet the mule itself is permissible — beneficial and indeed critical to pre-modern civilization. The *Torah* prohibits the act while not prohibiting the result. This asymmetry is important: the harm is not in the mule's existence but in the human act of deliberate species transgression that produced it.

### Shita Mekubetzet Reading

The *Shita Mekubetzet* offers an alternative reading of the *Gemara* that sheds further light on this. Rather than understanding the story as being about this particular act, the *Shita Mekubetzet* reads it more broadly. He cites the *pesukim* in the *Torah* that are understood to refer to the first instances of cross-breeding leading to mules — *hu matza et hayeimim bamidbar* — and suggests that from the time humans began to cross-breed at all, God decreed that this capacity could produce dangerous as well as beneficial outcomes. Read this way, the theological point is not a condemnation of any specific act, but a statement about the power that human beings unlock when they begin to manipulate natural boundaries. The potential for tremendous good and the potential for tremendous evil are released together.

### Human Responsibility

This reading speaks directly to the question of human responsibility in the face of novel creation. Once one has the power to produce something new — whether through cross-breeding, genetic engineering, or other biotechnological means — one cannot always anticipate what dangers may follow. The parallel to nuclear energy is instructive: the release of an enormously powerful force carries with it a corresponding magnitude of responsibility, and the inability to fully foresee consequences does not diminish that responsibility. The *Gemara* seems to say: you are playing with fire, and you must understand that even when the intent is constructive, the outcome may not be.

---

## Dangling Limb Status

### Dangling Limb Tuma

The *Gemara* transitions to the *mishna* governing the *eiver hamedulal* — the dangling limb or flesh barely connected to a living animal. The *mishna* states: *ha'eiver vehabasar hameduldalim bibehema — metam'in tumat ochlin bimkoman* — a dangling limb or dangling flesh from an animal conveys *tumat ochlin*, the impurity of food, while still in place. This is a case encountered earlier in the tractate: something that is in a middle status, not fully part of the living animal yet not fully detached, can already acquire the *tumah* classification of food. And yet — *u'tzrichin hechshier* — it requires *hechshier*, contact with a liquid, to become susceptible to *tumah*, since all foodstuffs require prior exposure to one of seven liquids before they can become *tamei*.

### Shechita as Hechshier

If the animal was subsequently slaughtered: *nishcheta habeheima huchshiru bedameha* — the act of *shechita* itself serves as *hechshier* for this dangling limb. This parallels a *mishna* treated earlier: the act of *shechita*, not merely the blood of *shechita*, functions as a *hechshier* that renders the animal's meat susceptible to *tumah* without any separate exposure to liquid. That principle applies equally to the dangling limb. Notably, one remains prohibited from eating this limb even after *shechita* — a prohibition derived from a verse, though some hold it to be rabbinic — yet the limb is considered edible enough to become susceptible to *tumah* through the *shechita*.

### Meir vs. Shimon

This is the position of Rabbi Meir: *divrei Rabbi Meir*. Rabbi Shimon disagrees — *Rabbi Shimon omer lo huchshiru* — the *shechita* does not render this dangling limb susceptible. Since the dangling limb cannot be eaten, the *shechita* does not extend to it for purposes of *hechshier*, and it would still require contact with a liquid.

### Death of Animal Case

The *mishna* then addresses the case where the animal simply dies rather than being slaughtered: *meta habeheima*. Here, the *mishna* distinguishes between the dangling meat and the dangling limb. Regarding the meat: *habasar tzarich hechshier* — the dangling flesh requires *hechshier* to become susceptible. The reason is notable. One might have expected the dangling flesh to become *nevela* along with the rest of the animal, but because it was not fully attached, it is not swept into *nevela* status with the animal's death. It is as though it had already fallen off before the animal died — and flesh that falls from a living animal is *basar min hachai*, which does not independently convey *tumah*. Therefore this flesh, once separated conceptually from the *nevela*, is simply detached meat that needs *hechshier*.

### Meir: Eiver Min Hachai

The limb presents a different issue. Rabbi Meir says: *ha'eiver metamei mishum eiver min hachai ve'eino metamei mishum eiver nevela* — the dangling limb conveys *tumah* as *eiver min hachai*, not as *eiver nevela*. The limb is conceptually understood as having fallen off at the moment of the animal's death — since it was never fully integrated, its separation is deemed to coincide with the animal's dying. Because it falls off in the course of the animal's dying, it is *eiver min hachai*, which carries its own *tumah*. The distinction between *basar min hachai* and *eiver min hachai* is that detached flesh does not independently convey *tumah*, whereas a detached limb does. Rabbi Meir therefore holds that the dangling limb conveys the *tumah* of *eiver min hachai*, not of *nevela*.

### Shimon: Entirely Tahor

Rabbi Shimon holds the more radical position: *Rabbi Shimon metaher* — the dangling limb is entirely *tahor*. It is neither *nevela* nor *eiver min hachai*. As the *Gemara* will examine, Rabbi Shimon's position apparently flows from his view that *shechita* does not apply to this limb at all, which has implications for how the limb's status is understood throughout.

---

## Gray Zone Detachment

### Tumat Ochlin Only

The *Gemara* opens its analysis of the *mishna*: *tumat ochlin ika, tumat nevela leika* — the dangling limb has *tumat ochlin* but not *tumat nevela*. A note is in order: *Tosafot* clarifies that *tumat nevela* as used here is not literal *nevela* — obviously the animal is still alive — but rather refers to *tumat eiver min hachai*, the *tumah* of a limb from a living animal. So: the dangling limb has the *tumah* of food, but not of *eiver min hachai*.

### Healing Capacity Test

*Heichi dami* — what precisely is the case being described? If the dangling limb could still heal and reattach — *ei demalina arucha* — it should not even be considered food; it is going to become integrated back into the animal. *Ve'ei de'ein malina arucha* — if it cannot heal, one would expect it to be treated as fully detached and therefore to convey *tumat eiver min hachai*. What kind of case yields the intermediate status of *tumat ochlin* only, without *tumat eiver min hachai*?

### Full Detachment Principle

The answer: *le'olam de'ein malina arucha* — we are speaking of a case where it cannot heal. *V'shani tumat nevela* — but *tumat eiver min hachai* is different. *Rachmana amar ki yipol — ad sheyipol*: the *Torah* requires that something actually *fall off* before it becomes *eiver min hachai*. Because there is still a point of connection, the limb has not yet fully fallen. This is the halakhically meaningful gray zone: the limb is detached enough from the living animal to be no longer considered part of it — and therefore can be categorized as food — but it has not yet physically fallen off, and therefore it has not crossed the threshold into *eiver min hachai* status.

### Hair Strand Connection

*Tanya nami hachi* — a *baraita* confirms this: if a dangling limb or flesh is still intertwined with the animal by even a single hair-strand — *ume'urin bechut hasa'ara* — one might think they already constitute *tumah* as a detached limb. The verse teaches: *yipol — ad sheyipol* — only when it actually falls off. The connection, however tenuous, prevents the full legal detachment needed for *tumat eiver min hachai*.

### Quasi-Food Status

Yet even so — *afilu hachi tumat ochlin metamei* — this limb, despite remaining connected, still conveys the *tumah* of food. This is the middle status: it is quasi-food, because it is regarded as no longer truly integral to the living animal; but it is not yet *eiver min hachai*, because it has not fully separated. The *Gemara* finds an analogy to support this principle.

---

## Dried Figs Analogy

### Rabbi Chiya Dried Figs

*Mesayeia lei leRabbi Chiya bar Ashi* — the *Gemara* notes that this point provides support for a teaching of Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi. *De'amar Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi amar Shmuel*: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi said in the name of Shmuel — *te'einim shetzamku be'avihen* — figs that have dried out on their stem while still on the tree. Here we have an analogous situation in the plant world. The fruit is dried out — no longer truly integrated into the tree as a growing, living part of it — and yet the stem connecting it to the tree has not dried out. The fruit is therefore in a middle state. The ruling: *hametamei tumat ochlin* — such a fig conveys the *tumah* of food; it is independent enough from the tree to be considered a food item. *V'hatolesh mehem beShabbat chayav chatat* — and yet, one who plucks such a fig on *Shabbat* is liable to bring a *chatat*, a sin-offering, because the act of *tolesh* — detaching from a living plant — still applies. The fig is still connected.

### Parallel Middle Statuses

The parallel between the two cases is precise. In both, something has reached a stage of quasi-independence: it is treated as food for the purposes of *tumat ochlin*, because it is no longer viewed as fully integrated into the parent body. Yet the remaining physical connection is halakhically real: in the animal case, the connection prevents the limb from being *eiver min hachai*; in the plant case, the connection means that removing the fruit on *Shabbat* remains a violation. The gray zone — between full attachment and full detachment — operates in the same way across both domains.

---

## Drying & Food Status

### Inedible When Dried

The *Gemara* now tests the boundaries of this principle through a series of cases. *Yerakot shetzimku be'iveihem* — vegetables that have dried out on their vine: specifically, *hakruv vehadilaat*, cabbage and gourd. *Ein mitamin tumas ochlim* — these do not convey *tumat ochlin*. The reason: a dried gourd becomes essentially wooden, and dried cabbage is similarly no longer edible. Since they are no longer fit to eat, they have lost their status as food entirely.

### Intent to Dry Exception

However: *katzatzan beyamshan* — if one cut them while still fresh with the *intention* of drying them, *mitamin tumas ochlim* — they do convey *tumat ochlin*. But the *Gemara* immediately clarifies: *de'amar Rabbi Yitzchak — be'almenas leyabshan* — this does not mean one literally cut them already dried out, which would be meaningless since dried gourd is essentially wood and not food. What it means is: one cut them while fresh, with the intention of drying them. At the moment of cutting they are still edible and therefore still food; the intention to dry them does not retroactively strip them of their food status. Since they are not yet dry, they remain food.

### Other Fruits Remain Food

The implicit reasoning here — *hashar peiros mitamei* — is that other fruits, which retain their edibility even when they dry out (unlike gourds or cabbage), would still be considered food even when dried on the vine and therefore still susceptible to *tumah*. A dried fig, a raisin — these remain edible even after drying, and therefore retain their food status.

### Twig Connection Implication

This raises a further question: if other fruits dried on the vine are still food, what does that mean for their connection to the tree? The *Gemara* asks whether the implication extends to saying that such dried fruit, because still connected by the twig, remains fully *mechubarin* — connected — for all purposes, including *Shabbat*. Would picking such dried fruit on *Shabbat* still constitute *tolesh*? And conversely, if we consider it detached enough for *tumah*, might we also consider it detached enough that picking it on *Shabbat* would not be a violation?

### Mishna's Main Point

The *Gemara* resolves the uncertainty by drawing back: *dechi katani amansi yavesh itztricha lei* — the point of the *mishna* is not the implied alternative at all. The *mishna*'s purpose is to state the case of the gourd cut while fresh with intent to dry: since it has not yet dried, it remains food and is susceptible to *tumah*. The *mishna* is not making any broader statement about other fruits dried on the vine, and we cannot draw halakhic conclusions about *Shabbat* or *tumah* from what might appear to be the implied alternative.

---

## Branch Severance

### Fruit on Cut Branch

A *baraita* is cited to clarify the distinction between severing a branch and drying fruit on a connected branch: *ilan shenifshach uvo peirot — harei hen ketlushin* — if a branch is broken off from a tree and it has fruit hanging from it, those fruits are considered *ketlushin*, fully detached, and are susceptible to *tumah* as food items. Cutting off an apple branch with apples attached renders those apples legally independent from the tree.

### Dried Fruit, Connected Branch

Conversely: *yaveshu — harei hen kemechubarin* — if the fruit dried out but the branch remains connected to the tree, they are still considered *mechubarin*, connected, for all purposes. The branch's continued connection to the tree preserves the fruit's legal status as attached, even if the fruit itself has dried.

### Categories Analysis

*Midi irya — ha kide'ita veha kide'ita* — these cases do not contradict one another; each operates according to its own category. When a branch is severed, the severing of the branch creates full legal detachment for the fruit, and this applies across all halakhic domains — both for *tumah* susceptibility and for *Shabbat*. When fruit dries on a connected branch, the branch's connection to the tree remains legally operative for all purposes. The two cases differ not by degree but by category: branch severance is a different halakhic event from fruit drying, and each carries its own complete set of consequences.

---

## Gray Zone Synthesis

### Middle Status Principle

What the *Gemara*'s extended discussion demonstrates — across the dangling limb, the dried fig, the gourd, and the severed branch — is that the category of *middle status* between connection and detachment is halakhically meaningful and not merely a transitional curiosity. The dangling limb that is no longer truly part of the animal but has not yet fallen off; the fig that has dried sufficiently to be food but is still connected enough that removing it on *Shabbat* is *tolesh* — these represent a genuine halakhic category, not a gap in the law. The *Gemara* is fascinated by precisely this gray zone, and the parallel between the animal and plant cases is deliberate.

### Impurity Despite Prohibition

A final, striking observation emerges. The dangling limb — whether *eiver min hachai* or simply dangling flesh — is prohibited for consumption by everyone. It is *eiver min hachai* or *basar min hachai*, forbidden not only to Jews but to *bnei Noach* as well. And yet it can be *tamei* with *tumat ochlin* — the *tumah* of food. The category of food susceptible to impurity does not require that the food be permitted to any human being. Something can be, for purposes of *tumah*, a food item — and therefore subject to all the rules of *tumat ochlin* — even when there is no one for whom it is *mutar* to eat it. This is, as the lecturer notes, quite a remarkable halakhic result.

---

---

# Hullin 128

## Dangling Limb Debate

### Intro & Mishna

The sugya on 128a opens by revisiting a theme that has recurred throughout this *perek*: the dangling limb — a piece of meat or a limb hanging loosely from a living animal. The halachic background established earlier in the *maseches* is as follows. While the animal is alive, the dangling limb has the status of food and can become *tamei*, even though it is technically neither fully part of the animal nor an *ever min hachai*. If the animal is *shechted*, the limb cannot be eaten — we learned this from the principle of *basar basadeh treifah* — yet it is not classified as *neveilah*; it retains the status of food and remains susceptible to *tumah*. The *mishna* thus presents the following question: does the act of *shechita* render this dangling limb susceptible to *tumah*? Does the *shechita* or its blood constitute *hechsher* — that which makes food susceptible to become *tamei* through contact with liquid?

By way of background: ordinarily, both the act of *shechita* and the blood that flows from it make the meat of a properly slaughtered animal susceptible to *tumah*. The question is whether that mechanism extends to this dangling limb. Rabbi Meir holds that it does; Rabbi Shimon holds that it does not. The *Gemara* now asks: *be-mai kamifligi* — what precisely is the conceptual point of dispute?

### Rabba's Yad Theory

Rabba frames the debate in terms of *yad* — the concept of a "handle." From the beginning of this *perek* we have been dealing with the notion that a bone attached to a piece of meat can serve as a *yad*, a conduit, for transmitting *tumah* to the meat. There was also a question raised earlier as to whether the concept of *yad* functions not only for transmitting *tumah* but also for *hechsher* — for making food susceptible through contact with liquid.

Rabba assumes that the concept of *yad* does apply to *hechsher*, and frames the debate accordingly. The question he raises is: can something vastly larger and more significant serve as a *yad* for something tiny and insignificant? Specifically: the blood of *shechita* contacts the cow's body. Can the enormous cow serve as a *yad* — a handle — for the tiny dangling limb, such that it is as though the blood touched the limb directly, thereby making the limb susceptible? One holds that *ein behemah na'asis yad le-ever* — the cow cannot serve as a *yad* for its own dangling limb — and therefore the limb is not rendered susceptible. The other holds *behemah na'asis yad le-ever* — even this asymmetric relationship qualifies as a *yad*, and the limb is thereby rendered susceptible.

### Abaye's Unity

Abaye offers an alternative framing that bypasses the *yad* concept entirely. He focuses instead on whether the limb and the cow constitute a single halachic unit. The key observation is asymmetric: if one were to lift the entire cow, the dangling limb would come along with it; but if one were to lift only by the dangling limb, the cow would not come along — it would simply break off. One position holds that even in a case where *ocheiz be-katan ve-ein gadol oleh imo* — you grasp the small part and the large part does not rise with it — the two pieces are nonetheless considered one unit. Under this view, there is no need for the *yad* concept at all; the liquid that contacts the cow contacts the whole cow, dangling limb included. The opposing position holds *eino kamosho* — this asymmetry disqualifies them from being considered a single unit — and therefore the *yad* question is moot; they are simply two separate entities.

### Yochanan's Contradiction

Rabbi Yochanan understands the debate in terms identical to Abaye's framing — the question of whether a small part's inability to pull the large part along means they are not a single unit. But he then raises an internal contradiction within Rabbi Meir's positions. In our *mishna*, Rabbi Meir holds that the *shechita*'s blood renders the dangling limb susceptible, which on Abaye's reading means Rabbi Meir considers them one unit even when the small piece cannot pull the large. Yet a *mishna* elsewhere (at the beginning of 108a) addresses an analogous case: a piece of bread in which one portion has separated and hangs connected by only a thin point of attachment. The same asymmetry applies — lift by the large piece and the small comes along; lift by the small piece and it breaks off. In that *mishna*, Rabbi Meir states *im ocheiz be-katan ve-gadol oleh imo harei hu kamosho* — it is one unit *only if* lifting the small piece brings the large piece along with it; *ve-im lav eino kamosho* — otherwise they are two separate units. In other words, in that *mishna* Rabbi Meir rules that the large will not follow the small means they are *not* one unit — the exact reverse of what he apparently holds in our *mishna*.

Rabbi Yochanan's response is *muchlefet ha-shita* — the positions should be reversed — though this is more a framing of the problem than a resolution. It should be noted that *Tosafot* observes that the text of that *mishna* as we have it actually has Rabbi Meir holding the reverse of what Rabbi Yochanan's version had, making the contradiction a non-issue according to our reading. Nevertheless, as Rabbi Yochanan had the text, Rabbi Meir appears to contradict himself.

### Tvul Yom Solution

The *Gemara* proposes a resolution: perhaps Rabbi Meir distinguishes between a *tvul yom* and other *tumot*. A *tvul yom* is a person who has immersed in a *mikvah* that day and will become *tahor* that evening; in the interim, he is a second-degree *tamei* who can render *teruma* into *shlishi*. The *mishna* about the bread involves precisely a *tvul yom* touching *teruma*. Perhaps Rabbi Meir considers this a weaker *tumah* and is therefore more lenient in the bread case, treating the two pieces as separate units. In the case of the dangling limb, where the *tumah* in question may be more severe, Rabbi Meir might be stricter and treat them as one unit.

At this point it is worth flagging a question that arises about the nature of *tvul yom tumah*. *Rashi* characterizes it as rabbinic in nature. The *Gilyon HaShas* — Rabbi Akiva Eiger — cites this and expresses astonishment: *ha tvul yom hu tumah d'oraisa b'posel terumah b'negi'ah* — the *tumah* of a *tvul yom* with respect to disqualifying *teruma* is biblical, not merely rabbinic. He notes that *Rashi* should have said the *tumah* is weak (*klisha*), not that it is rabbinic, and leaves the matter as *tzarich iyun gadol*. The proper framing, then, is not that we are being lenient where the law is only rabbinic, but rather that by other *tumot* we are stricter — the default halacha treats the pieces as two separate units, which applies when the *tumah* is merely the weaker (though still biblical) *tvul yom* level; when confronted with a more severe *tumah*, Rabbi Meir applies a stricter standard and considers them one unit.

The *Gemara* then challenges this resolution by citing a *braisa* in which Rebbi states that there is no distinction between *tvul yom* and other *tumot* with respect to this question of unity. The *Gemara* responds: perhaps that is Rebbi's view, but Rabbi Meir may well distinguish between them. Therefore, Rabbi Yochanan's position is refined by Rabbi Yoshiya: *according to Rebbi* — who insists there is no distinction — the contradiction within Rabbi Meir's positions stands, and the *shita* must be reversed.

---

## Yad Tumah/Hechsher

### Rava's Position

Rava frames the debate differently again. He proposes that the entire argument concerns whether *yad* applies not only to the transmission of *tumah* but also to *hechsher*. All parties would agree that the cow can serve as a *yad* for the dangling limb in the context of *tumah* — touching something *tamei* to the cow would convey *tumah* to the dangling limb. The question is whether *yad* also extends to *hechsher*: does liquid contacting the cow count as liquid contacting the limb, so as to make the limb susceptible? One holds *yesh yad l'tumah ve-ein yad l'hechsher* — the *yad* concept conveys *tumah* but does not convey the capacity for *hechsher*. The other holds *yesh yad l'tumah u'l'hechsher* — *yad* functions equally for both. This is a striking *Gemara* in that a single disputed *mishna* permits so many distinct and conceptually rich framings: whether a large body can be a *yad* for something smaller; whether something is one halachic unit or two when asymmetrically connected; whether *yad* extends from the domain of *tumah* to the domain of *hechsher*.

---

## Hechsher & Intent

### Why Intent Matters

Rav Papa offers yet another framing of the debate. He proposes that the *mishna* concerns *hechsher kodem machshava* — what happens when food comes into contact with liquid *before* there is any intention to eat it. Ordinarily, with food whose intended consumption can be taken for granted, the moment liquid contacts it the food becomes susceptible. But the dangling limb presents a problem: a Jew cannot eat it even after *shechita* (it remains prohibited as *basar basadeh treifah*). The only scenario in which anyone could eat it is if it is *shechted* and then given to a non-Jew. Moreover, had the animal died naturally, the limb would have become *ever min hachai*, forbidden even to a non-Jew. This limb, therefore, cannot be presumed to be intended as food. It only qualifies as food if someone has affirmatively decided to eat it or feed it to a non-Jew. What happens, then, if the blood of *shechita* contacted it — creating *hechsher* — before the owner ever formed that intention? Is that *hechsher* valid, or must the item first be defined as food (through intention) before *hechsher* can take effect?

### Rav Papa's Question

This question is formulated by Rav Papa as the subject of the dispute in the *mishna*, and the *Gemara* turns immediately to a *braisa* to provide context. The *Gemara* states: *amar Rav Yehuda kach haya Rabbi Akiva shoneh* — this is what Rabbi Akiva used to teach.

### Rabbi Akiva on Chelev

*Chelev shechuta bakfarim tzarich machshava ve-ein tzarich hechsher she-kevar huchshar bi-shechita.* The case involves *chelev* — forbidden fat — from a slaughtered animal in villages, where *chelev* is not normally consumed. *Rashi* suggests two possible reasons for this: either there is proportionally more meat per capita in villages and so the *chelev* is not in demand, or, conversely, *chelev* is a delicacy that only city-dwellers can afford. Either way, in the villages the *chelev* cannot be presumed intended for consumption. The only persons who would eat it would be non-Jews. Rabbi Akiva's original teaching was: the *shechita* renders the *chelev* susceptible (*huchshar bi-shechita*), and all that remains is forming the intention to eat it. That intention may come *after* the blood has already contacted the fat. In other words, the order — *hechsher* first, intention second — is acceptable.

### Ulshin Counterexample

Rabbi Yehuda responded to Rabbi Akiva: you have already taught us otherwise. He invoked the case of *ulshin* — a type of herb or bitter green (chicory, or perhaps endive) — that was plucked and rinsed for animal consumption, and only afterward was the owner's mind changed (*nimlach aleihem*) to use them for human consumption. In that case, Rabbi Akiva himself had taught that a second act of contact with liquid (*hechsher sheni*) is required, because the definition of "food" (i.e., human food) only came *after* the first contact with liquid. The *ulshin* teaches that *hechsher* requires the item already to be defined as food at the moment of contact; the intention cannot retroactively validate a prior *hechsher*. By the same logic, the *chelev* in the villages — which only becomes food once someone forms the intention to eat it — should also require that the intention precede the *hechsher*.

### Akiva Reverses

Rabbi Akiva accepted this argument and reversed his position to align with Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning. Both the pre-reversal and post-reversal positions are now on record, and the *Gemara* maps them onto the *mishna*: *mar savar lah ke-meikara* — one Tanna holds the pre-reversal position, that *hechsher* preceding intention is still valid — and that is Rabbi Meir. *U-mar savar lah ke-chazara* — the other holds the post-reversal position, that intention must precede *hechsher* — and that is Rabbi Shimon. Both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon were students of Rabbi Akiva, and there is nothing internally contradictory about Rabbi Meir maintaining the pre-reversal position: he may simply have judged it the more logically coherent of the two, or may not have been present when Rabbi Akiva retracted it.

---

## Shechita Timing

### Blood Splatter Case

Rav Ashi bar Rav Ika offers yet another framing, one that is admittedly a substantial *ukimta* — a forced reading of the *mishna* — but which allows the introduction of an important conceptual question discussed elsewhere. The scenario he proposes: during the *shechita*, blood splattered from the partially cut trachea and landed on the dangling limb. Before the *shechita* was completed, that blood was wiped off. Then the *shechita* was finished. Is the blood that came out and contacted the limb *during* the *shechita* — before the act was concluded — considered blood of *shechita*, which would make the limb susceptible? Or is it merely blood of a wound, which would not?

The underlying question is: only blood of *shechita* creates *hechsher*; blood flowing from a wound does not. The blood in this case came out between the cutting of the trachea and the cutting of the esophagus — before the *shechita* was complete. For the main body of the cow, there is no problem, since the cow will be covered by blood at the conclusion. But the dangling limb received only this early splatter, which was subsequently wiped away.

### Continuous vs. End-Defin…

This framing imports the earlier debate: *yeshno li-shechita mi-techilah ve-ad sof* — *shechita* is a continuous process from its beginning to its end — versus *eino li-shechita ela be-sof* — *shechita* is only formally defined at its conclusion. According to the first view, the blood that emerges mid-process is already blood of *shechita*, and therefore would create *hechsher*. According to the second view, the blood that came out before completion is merely blood of a wound.

### Retroactive Definition

This raises a conceptual difficulty. If *shechita* is truly only defined at the end, one cannot mean that only the final moment of cutting constitutes the act — that would mean one is *shechting* an animal that is already a *treifah* (having had its trachea severed without that act yet qualifying as *shechita*). The resolution must be: *eino li-shechita ela be-sof* does not mean the act occurs only at the final instant, but rather that we only *label* it *shechita* retroactively. While one is in the process of cutting, the act is not yet formally designated as *shechita* — it is only upon successful completion that one looks back and says: that entire process was *shechita*. If the act is never completed, it was merely an act of injuring and killing an animal.

This retroactive labeling is precisely what the *wiping away* of the blood illuminates. If *shechita* were defined prospectively from the outset, then the blood that contacted the limb during the cutting would already be blood of *shechita* at that moment — and it would have created *hechsher* regardless of whether it was later wiped away. The wiping away would be irrelevant. The only reason wiping away matters is if *shechita* is defined only at completion, looking backward. At that point of retroactive labeling, the blood is already gone — it is no longer present to create *hechsher*. Hence the debate turns on whether we look forward or backward at the act of *shechita*.

---

## Shechita vs. Blood

### Rav Ashi's Theory

Rav Ashi (in what the *Gemara* introduces as a separate formulation) frames the debate as follows: *be-shechita machsheret ve-lo dam kamifligi* — the argument concerns whether it is the act of *shechita* itself, without blood, that creates *hechsher*, or whether it is specifically the blood of *shechita*. This was itself a dispute discussed earlier in the *masechta*: one position held that the act of *shechita* alone — even if miraculously no blood flows — constitutes *hechsher*, and that conversely the *blood* of *shechita* does *not* independently create *hechsher*. Under that view, it is the act of *shechita* that transforms the animal into food, and that transformation constitutes the *hechsher*.

How does this play out for the dangling limb? The *shechita* did not transform the dangling limb into permitted food — even after *shechita*, the limb remains forbidden. Therefore, if the mechanism of *hechsher* is that *shechita* makes the meat fit for eating, that mechanism does not apply to the dangling limb at all. If, on the other hand, the mechanism is the *blood* of *shechita*, then the blood — which contacted the cow's body and can be attributed to the limb via *yad* or unity — would create *hechsher* for the limb as well. The debate in the *mishna*, on this reading, is precisely which mechanism operates: *shechita*-as-act-of-making-food, which excludes the dangling limb, or *blood*-of-*shechita*, which does not.

---

## Categorical Exclusions

### Living Cow as Yad

Having presented six distinct framings of the *mishna*'s dispute, the *Gemara* now turns to a series of fascinating questions about the limits of the *yad* concept. The first question is posed by Rava: *behemah be-chayeha mah shete'aseh yad le-ever* — can a living, breathing cow serve as a *yad* for its dangling limb? In the debate about our *mishna*, the cow was a dead animal; the question was whether the large body could be a *yad* for the small dangling piece. But now consider the case where the animal is still alive. We already know that while the animal is alive the dangling limb is considered food and can become *tamei*. But if liquid fell not on the limb but on the living cow, can that living cow serve as a *yad* to communicate *hechsher* or *tumah* to the limb?

*Tosafot*, following *Rashi*, notes that we already accept that a *yad* need not itself be susceptible to *tumah* — a bone can serve as a *yad* for the meat it is attached to, even though the bone itself is not food. But the cases we are about to encounter involve things that are categorically excluded in a more fundamental way — not merely inedible, but belonging to categories that may be so ontologically removed from the world of *tumah* that they cannot function as *yad* at all. A living, breathing animal is one such category. The *Gemara* answers: *teiku* — the question stands unresolved.

### Connected Cucumber

Abaye raises a parallel question rooted in a *mishna*. A cucumber planted in a sealed flower pot (an *atzitz* without a hole) is not considered *mechubar l'karka* — connected to the ground — and therefore the cucumber can become *tamei*. If the vine then grows beyond the edges of the pot and hangs over the ground, the portion suspended over the ground is considered *mechubar l'karka* and cannot become *tamei*; but the portion remaining within the pot retains the status of a detached item and can become *tamei*. The *Tanna Kamma* had held that the entire plant is *tahor* in such a case — presumably because the connected portion purifies the whole — but Rabbi Shimon rejects this: *ha-tamei be-tumato ve-ha-tahor be-taharato* — the part that can become *tamei* retains its susceptibility, and the part considered *mechubar* retains its *taharah*, independently.

Abaye's question: can the portion of the cucumber that is *mechubar l'karka* — which is categorically excluded from *tumah* by virtue of its connection to the ground — serve as a *yad* for the portion sitting in the pot? The two are physically and fully one organism; yet halachically one half is in the world of *tumah* and one half is outside it. Can the excluded half transmit *tumah* or *hechsher* to the susceptible half? The *Gemara* answers: *teiku*.

### Avodah Zarah Half

Rabbi Yirmiya raises yet another case. The *mishna* teaches that one who bows down and worships half of a gourd has rendered that half *avodah zarah*. *Avodah zarah* is forbidden in benefit — it cannot be eaten, sold, or used in any way that generates benefit, and therefore it lacks the status of food. Something that is not food cannot become *tamei*. Can the half-gourd that is *avodah zarah* serve as a *yad* for the other half that is not *avodah zarah* and retains the status of food? This case differs from an inedible bone: a bone is simply not food by its nature, whereas this half-gourd is physically edible — it is categorically excluded only because it is forbidden in benefit. Does that categorical exclusion remove it from the *yad* function entirely? The *Gemara* answers: *teiku*.

### Fig Branch Case

Rav Papa raises a case from a *mishna* about a fig tree. A branch has been broken but not fully severed — the bark still connects it to the tree. Rabbi Yehuda holds it is still considered attached to the tree and therefore *mechubar l'karka*, so the fruit on it cannot become *tamei*. The Rabbis distinguish: if the branch can still survive on the residual connection, it is considered attached and *tahor*; if not, it is considered severed and the fruit can become *tamei*, even though it remains physically attached by the bark. Rav Papa asks: can the tree — which is fully *mechubar l'karka* — serve as a *yad* for this halachically-severed branch? The *Gemara* answers: *teiku*.

### Cornerstone Half

Rabbi Zeira poses the final case of this series, drawn from the laws of *tzara'at* of houses. A cornerstone sits precisely at the boundary between two adjacent houses. When the house reaches the earlier stage of *tumah* requiring removal of stones (*chalitzah*), the entire cornerstone must be removed. But when it reaches the most severe stage requiring *netitzah* — shattering — one need only shatter the half of the stone belonging to the afflicted house; the half in the neighbor's house, which is *tahor*, may be left in place. Thus at the *netitzah* stage the stone is simultaneously half *tamei* and half *tahor*. Rabbi Zeira asks: can the *tahor* half of the cornerstone serve as a *yad* for the *tamei* half, such that one who touches the *tahor* half would become *tamei* through it? The *Gemara* answers: *teiku*.

All of these cases share a common structure: the *yad* candidate is not merely non-food or inedible, but is categorically excluded from the world of *tumah* in some more fundamental way — whether because it is a living organism, connected to the ground, forbidden in benefit, or halachically *tahor*. Whether such categorical exclusions strip something of the capacity to serve as *yad* remains, in each instance, unresolved.

---

## Death & Status

### Death Principle

The *mishna* now turns to a different scenario: the animal was not *shechted* but died naturally. Here the *mishna* invokes the principle of *misa oseh nipul* — death causes the limb to "fall." While the limb was dangling during the animal's life, it was food but was neither *neveilah* nor *ever min hachai*. If the animal died naturally, we treat the death as though the limb fell from the animal at the moment of death — that is, as though it separated from the animal while the animal was still in the process of dying. Consequently, the limb does not become *neveilah* (because it was no longer part of the animal when the animal died) but rather becomes *ever min hachai* — the status of a limb torn from a living animal.

### Meat vs. Limb

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ika bein ever min hachai le-ever shel neveilah* — what practical difference does it make whether we classify this dangling limb as *ever min hachai* or as *neveilah*? Both cause *tumah*. The answer: *ika beinaihu basar ha-porish mimenu* — the difference manifests when a piece of *meat* separates from this dangling limb after the animal has died. *Ever min hachai* means the *whole* limb — only the complete limb in its entirety conveys *tumah*. This is analogous to *basar min hachai*: if one tears a piece of flesh from a living animal, it is forbidden to eat but does not convey *tumah*, because *tumah* of *ever min hachai* requires the full intact limb, not mere flesh. A piece of meat that separates from an *ever min hachai* is not itself *tamei*. *Neveilah*, by contrast, causes *tumah* through the flesh itself — a piece of meat from a *neveilah* does convey *tumah*. Thus the practical consequence of the distinction: if meat falls from this dangling limb, it conveys *tumah* only if the limb's status is *neveilah*, not if it is *ever min hachai*.

### Pasuk Source

The *Gemara* then asks: *ever min hachai de-mitamei mai kera* — what is the biblical source for the *tumah* of *ever min hachai*? Rav Yehuda citing Rav derives it from the verse *ve-chi yamut min ha-behemah* — "and if one of the animals shall die." The *Gemara* reads *min ha-behemah* — "from the animal" — not as referring to the death of the entire animal but as indicating that even if only a *part* of the animal "dies" (i.e., is severed from it), that causes *tumah*. This same verse, however, was also used by Rav Yehuda citing Rav for a different teaching: *miktzas behemah metamei u-miktzas behemah eino metamei* — some dead animals convey *tumah* and some do not. A *treifah* that was *shechted* does not convey *tumah* of *neveilah* even though it may not be eaten, because the *shechita* removes the *neveilah* status. The word *min* — used as a separate prepositional word rather than a prefix — signals that both teachings can be derived from the same phrase: (1) not every carcass causes *tumah* (thereby excluding a *shechted treifah*), and (2) even something less than the full animal — a severed limb — causes *tumah*. Both rulings are contained in the single formulation *min ha-behemah*.

---

## Ever Definition

### Meat vs. Limb

Having established that *ever min hachai* conveys *tumah* while flesh alone (*basar min hachai*) does not, the *Gemara* now turns to the foundational question: how do we define what constitutes an *ever* for purposes of this *tumah*? The challenge it poses is direct: if *min ha-behemah* means "something from the animal died," why is it limited to a full limb? Perhaps even flesh alone that separates from a living animal should convey *tumah*? A *braisa* is invoked to address this.

### Yosei: Non-Replacement
