The *braisa* opens: *yakhol yehei basar ha-porish min ha-chai tamei* — one might have thought that flesh separating from the living conveys *tumah*. Therefore the verse teaches *ve-chi yamut min ha-behemah* — the separated item must resemble death. *Mah mitah she-ein lah chalifin* — just as death does not replace itself, so too only something that does not replace itself. A limb that is severed from an animal will not regenerate. Flesh that is removed may heal; the wound fills in and the animal recovers. Therefore only what is irreplaceable — a full limb — counts. This is the position of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

### Akiva: Animal Analogy

Rabbi Akiva derives from a different interpretive move. The verse says *min ha-behemah* — from the animal. Just as an animal (*behemah*) has not only flesh but also *gidim va-atzamot* — sinews and bones — so too only something that has sinews and bones qualifies as an *ever* for *tumah*. Mere flesh, which lacks bones and sinews, does not qualify.

### Rebbi: Adds Flesh

Rebbi agrees with the structural logic of Rabbi Akiva's derivation but extends the required elements: *mah behemah basar gidim va-atzamot* — an animal has flesh, sinews, and bones — *af kol basar gidim va-atzamot* — so too the qualifying *ever* must have all three. Flesh alone is insufficient, but so is a bone with sinews and no flesh. All three components are required.

### Arkuva Debate

What then is the practical difference between Rabbi Akiva and Rebbi? The *Gemara* identifies the *arkuva* — the lower joint of the leg, apparently characterized by an extreme paucity of meat (*rashi* describes it as having a lack of flesh, with the hard, sinewy structure predominating). Such a bone-and-sinew structure without meaningful flesh would qualify as an *ever* under Rabbi Akiva's requirement of sinews and bones, but would *not* qualify under Rebbi's requirement that flesh be present alongside the bones and sinews.

### Organs Test Case

The point of difference between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili is identified by Rav Papa: *kulya ve-nispataim* — kidneys and lips. These are organs that naturally lack bones. Under Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's criterion — that the separated item not replace itself — a kidney or lip, once severed, does not regenerate: it qualifies as an *ever*. Under Rabbi Akiva's criterion — that the item resemble a *behemah* in having sinews and bones — organs that naturally lack bones would arguably not qualify. *Tosafot* suggests that the question may really concern something that naturally possesses bones but is encountered in a boneless state; either way, the simple reading of the *Gemara* is that organs without bones are the operative test case between these two views.

---

## Sheratzim Extension

### Sheratzim Debates

The *Gemara* then teaches the identical three-way debate in the context of *sheratzim* — reptiles and rodents that convey *tumah* according to the Torah. The same question arises: does meat alone that falls from a living *sheretz* convey *tumah*, or only something that qualifies as an *ever*? The same three positions are restated. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from the word *be-motam* — "when they die" — the same logic of *mah mitah she-eino oseh chalifin*: only something that does not replace itself qualifies. Rabbi Akiva holds that it must resemble the *sheretz* itself by having sinews and bones. Rebbi adds the requirement of flesh. The *arkuva* distinction between Rebbi and Rabbi Akiva applies here as well, and Rav Papa's *kulya ve-nispataim* identifies the distinction between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

### Both Pesukim Needed

One might ask: is it necessary to state both laws — by *behemah* and by *sheratzim*? The *Gemara* demonstrates that each is needed, because each could have been argued to be more lenient by analogy to the other. Had only the *behemah* source been stated, one might have reasoned: the reason mere flesh of a *behemah* does not convey *tumah* is that *behemah* *tumah* has a stringency not shared by *sheratzim* — namely, that *behemah* does not convey *tumah* in the quantity of a lentil (*khadasha*) but only in the quantity of an olive (*kezayit*). Since *sheratzim* convey *tumah* in the smaller quantity of a lentil, one might think that *basar min hachai* from a *sheretz* would also convey *tumah*. Conversely, had only the *sheretz* source been stated, one might have said: *sheratzim* do not convey *tumah* through being carried (*massa*), and therefore we are not concerned that flesh alone conveys *tumah*. But a *behemah* does convey *tumah* through *massa* — its *tumah* is more powerful — and one might have concluded that flesh alone from a living *behemah* conveys *tumah*. Each source counteracts the potential inference from the other, and therefore both are needed. With this the *Gemara* concludes: by both *behemah* and *sheretz*, there is a *tumah* of *ever min hachai* and there is no *tumah* of *basar min hachai*.

---

---

# Hullin 129

## Meat from Dangling Limb

### Ever vs. Basar Status

Daf 129 is the final *daf* of this *perek*, which has dealt with the laws of dangling limbs, skin, meat, *tumah*, and *taharah*. We pick up at the bottom of 128b, where a *Tanu Rabanan* begins roughly four lines from the bottom.

The *braisa* returns us to the fundamental framework governing dangling limbs. When an animal dies, any limb that was dangling is treated as though it separated during the animal's lifetime, rendering it *ever min hachai*. As a whole limb from a living animal, it is a *source* of *tumah*. However, *basar min hachai* — mere flesh, as opposed to a complete limb — is not a source of *tumah*. The meat can, however, *receive* *tumah* as food, provided one has designated it as food through *chishev alav*, i.e., consciously planned to eat it. This designation is necessary because *ever min hachai* is ordinarily not eaten — neither by Jews nor, halachically, by non-Jews — and therefore without such intent it does not qualify as food.

### Cut Then Designate

The *braisa* presents the following case: one cuts a *kezayis* of meat from an *ever min hachai*. Rashi notes that for purposes of becoming *tamei* as food the relevant measure is actually a *kabeitzah*, but the core ruling stands regardless. The ever min hachai as a whole is a source of *tumah*; the question is whether the piece of meat cut away from it can itself *receive* *tumah*.

The ruling turns on the sequence of actions. If one first cuts the meat away and only afterward designates it as food — *chatcho ve'ach kach chishev alav* — it is *tahor*. The meat, once separated, is no longer part of a *tumah* source, and it has not yet been defined as food. When it is subsequently defined as food, it is no longer in contact with the limb and so receives no *tumah* from it.

If, however, one first designated the meat as food while it was still part of the limb, and only afterward cut it away — *chishev alav ve'ach kach chatcho* — it is *tamei*. The logic is as follows: at the moment of designation, the meat was still physically part of the *ever min hachai*, which is itself a *tumah* source. Once defined as food in that state, it was in contact with — indeed, was part of — the very source of *tumah*. When it is subsequently severed, it retains the *tumah* it absorbed while connected. It is no longer a *source* of *tumah*, but it carries the *tumah* it received.

### Assi's Challenge

Rabbi Assi had not been present in the *beis medrash* on the day this was discussed. He encountered Rabbi Zeira and asked what had been said, sensing from the context of the *sugya* that something in it was troubling. He cited the *braisa* — *chishev ve'ach kach chatcho tamei* — and raised the following difficulty, which we encounter at the opening of 129a: the contact through which the meat absorbed *tumah* from the limb was contact at an unexposed surface — *tumas beis hastarim*. And *tumas beis hastarim lo metamei* — contact at a hidden, non-exposed part of one's body does not transfer *tumah*. When a piece of meat is being cut away from a limb, it is in contact with the limb precisely at the point of severance, which is not yet exposed until the cutting is complete. Once the cut is made and the surface is exposed, the contact has ended. How, then, did the *tumah* transfer?

### Zeira's Answer

Rabbi Zeira responded that this very question had bothered him the previous day in the *beis medrash*, and he had posed it to Rabbi Abba bar Mamal. Rabbi Abba bar Mamal answered: *hani Rabbi Meir hi* — this *braisa* follows the position of Rabbi Meir, who holds that *tumas beis hastarim* does transfer *tumah*. The reference is to a case discussed roughly sixty pages earlier, involving a fetus that extended its limb outside the womb. If the animal was then slaughtered, that extended limb is considered a *neveila* rather than something rendered permissible by *shechita*, and it thus becomes a source of *tumah*. The question arose whether the fetus inside became *tamei* through contact with its own dangling limb — contact that occurred only at an unexposed surface. Rabbi Meir held that it did, and it is that position that underpins our *braisa*.

### Assi's Second Objection

Rabbi Assi, however, was not satisfied. He reported to Rabbi Zeira that Rabbi Abba bar Mamal had offered him this same answer on previous occasions, and that he had consistently rejected it. The cases are not comparable. In the fetus case, the *shechita* of the animal rendered the fetus itself susceptible to *tumah* without any need for prior *hechsher* — contact with liquid — because *dam shechita*, the blood of ritual slaughter, serves as *machshir*. In our case, by contrast, the meat was cut from an *ever min hachai*, an animal whose limb fell away without *shechita*. That meat never came into contact with any liquid that would render it susceptible to *tumah*. The concern is not only about the unexposed surface — that concern may indeed be resolved by invoking Rabbi Meir's position — but there remains an entirely separate problem: the piece of meat never underwent *hechsher*, and therefore how could it have become susceptible to *tumah* in the first place? The question stands.

One might wonder whether the blood produced during the cutting process could serve as *machshir*. The answer is no: only *dam shechita* renders food susceptible. Ordinary blood from a wound — *dam makah* — does not qualify as *machshir*, and so this avenue is closed.

### Rava's Principle

Rava responded to this second difficulty. Why is the absence of *hechsher* a problem? *De-neima de-huchshar* — one can simply posit that the meat did come into contact with liquid at some point. The circumstances of the *braisa* can be read to include that the meat was rendered susceptible before being cut away — that it was first designated as food, then came into contact with liquid, and then was severed. This is the sequence that produces the ruling of *tamei*.

### Alternative Principle

Rava bar Rav Chanan, however, offered a more fundamental answer. Why assume any *hechsher* is necessary at all? *Harei metamei tumah chamurah agav aviv* — this piece of meat, when it was part of the limb, was itself part of a weighty source of *tumah*. There is a principle that something which will become — or, even more powerfully, something that already *was* — a source of heightened *tumah* does not require prior contact with liquid to become susceptible. This meat began its existence as part of an *ever min hachai*, an *av ha-tumah*. That prior status as a *tumah* source should exempt it from any *hechsher* requirement; it is already so thoroughly embedded in the world of *tumah* that the liquid-contact requirement becomes superfluous.

---

## Ma'aseh Etz Doctrine

### Identity Change

Rava, however, objected to Rava bar Rav Chanan's principle. *Keshe-shimesh ma'aseh etz shimesh* — when this piece of meat served the limb, it was functioning as wood. That is, its identity then was not as *food*. The reason an *ever min hachai* is a source of *tumah* has nothing to do with its classification as food — as Rashi and Tosafot both note, an *ever* requires bone, sinew, and flesh together; what defines it as an *ever* is its identity as a *limb*, not its identity as something edible. When the piece of meat was part of the limb, it served in the capacity of a limb. That is a categorically different identity, to which Rashi applies the phrase *panim chadashot ba'u lechan* — a new face, a new identity, has arrived. As food, this meat never was a source of *tumah*. Its prior status as part of a *tumah* source was under a different identity entirely, and therefore it cannot exempt the meat — in its current identity as food — from the *hechsher* requirement.

This principle — *ma'aseh etz kimei shehayah*, that something functioning as wood, i.e., in a non-food identity, carries no relevance to its food-identity status — becomes the organizing principle for a series of cases the *Gemara* now works through, each asking why a particular food still requires *hechsher* if it once was or could become a weighty *tumah* source, and each receiving the same response.

### Hardened Dough Case

Abaye introduces the first case. The ruling states: a block of hardened leaven (*kupat se'or*) that was designated to be sat upon — *sheyichdah liyeshivah* — its *tumah* as food is negated (*batlah tumato*). It is no longer considered food and therefore is not subject to the *chametz* prohibition; simultaneously, since it now functions as a seat, a *zav* who sits upon it renders it *tamei* as a *midras* vessel.

### Abaye's Question

Abaye raises the question: if that *tumah* — the capacity of the hardened dough, now functioning as a seat upon which a *zav* sits, to become a weighty *tumah* source — were biblical, we would have established that any food can potentially become a source of *tumah chamurah*, since any food could in principle be hardened and repurposed as a seat. If that were sufficient to waive the *hechsher* requirement, food would never require *hechsher* at all. Since we know that conclusion is false, the status of this repurposed block as a *tumah* source must be only rabbinic.

The Gemara implicitly grants that there are two possible objections to Abaye's reasoning: certain foods are more naturally suited to becoming seats than others, and additionally, the principle waiving *hechsher* may apply only when becoming a *tumah* source is inevitable rather than merely theoretical. But Abaye assumes the theoretical possibility is sufficient, and on that assumption the conclusion follows.

### Ma'aseh Etz Response

The *Gemara*'s response is the same formula it will deploy throughout this series: *pirshu mishum ma'aseh etz*. Even if food is repurposed as a seat and thereby becomes a *tumah* source, in that role it is functioning as wood — as furniture, not as food. Its identity has changed entirely. The *panim chadashot* principle applies: as food it will never be a *tumah* source, and therefore it requires *hechsher* in its food identity. If it later becomes a seat, that is a new identity altogether, irrelevant to its current status. Tosafot raises the question of how it could then be permitted to own such an object on *Pesach* if its *tumah* status as a vessel is only rabbinic — but one answer may be that there is a middle category in which the object is sufficiently hardened and repurposed that it loses its *chametz* classification, without necessarily acquiring full biblical vessel status.

### Avodah Zarah Case

Abaye presents a second case. The ruling states that food offerings to *avodah zarah* (*tikrovet avodah zarah shel ochlin*) cause *tumah* under a covered space — *metamein be'ohel* — a form of *tumah* as severe as that of a corpse. If this were biblical law, then since any food could theoretically be offered to an idol and thereby become a weighty *tumah* source, food would never require *hechsher*. Abaye concludes that this *tumah* must be rabbinic.

The *Gemara*'s answer is again *tishmesh matzao ve-asao tishmesh* — when offered to an idol, the food functions in the capacity of a gift or tribute, not as food per se. One offers jewelry to an idol; one offers vessels; the fact that food is offered does not mean its identity as food is what gives the offering its significance. It is its identity as a dedicatory gift that matters. Therefore, whatever *tumah* status it carries in that role has nothing to do with its identity as food, and the *hechsher* requirement for food remains intact. It should be noted that the *Gemara* in *Shabbos* independently reaches the conclusion that *tumah* of *avodah zarah* offerings is rabbinic; what our *Gemara* adds is that in any case the identity-change argument would also preclude deriving any implications for the food-*tumah* system.

### Food in Vessels

Abaye presents a third case. The ruling states: *chiburei ochlin ke-keilim damu* — food that adheres to or is integrated into vessels takes on the status of the vessel itself. Rashi's example is food lodged in the cracks of a vessel, serving structurally as a kind of sealant. In such a case, the food is no longer independent; it is one with the vessel. Now: if such a vessel touches a *meis*, the vessel itself becomes an *av ha-tumah*. Food alone can never become an *av ha-tumah*. But food that has become integrated into the vessel can, through the vessel's contact with a corpse, attain that status. Were this biblical, any food could potentially be integrated into a vessel and thereby become an *av ha-tumah*, eliminating the *hechsher* requirement for all food. Hence this principle must be only rabbinic.

The answer is once again the same: when the food is integrated into the vessel, it is functioning as putty, as a structural filler — *ma'aseh etz*, serving in the identity of wood rather than food. That role is categorically distinct from its food identity, and no implications follow for the food-*tumah* laws.

### Fat/Kidney Case

Rav Papa addresses a fourth case. The ruling concerning fat (*chelev*) of a *neveila* notes that in villages, where such fat is not normally eaten, one requires both *machshava* (designation as food) and *hechsher* (contact with liquid) before the fat becomes susceptible to *tumah*. Rav Papa points out that the classic location of *chelev* is surrounding the kidneys. A kidney embedded in a mass of *chelev* is itself a *neveila* — since this is an animal that was not *shechted* — and is therefore a *tumah* source. The principle of *shomer* applies: the *chelev* that surrounds and protects the kidney functions as a *shomer* for it, meaning that touching the *chelev* is halachically equivalent to touching the kidney itself. The *chelev*, as *shomer*, thus effectively renders one *tamei* as though one had touched the *neveila* directly. This means the *chelev*, while connected to the kidney, was itself a source of *tumah* — not a derived or secondary one but one effective through the *shomer* principle. Why, then, should it require *hechsher* once separated and designated as food? The answer is the same: *keshe-shimesh ma'aseh etz shimesh* — when it served as *shomer* to the kidney, it was functioning in a structural, protective capacity, not as food. A *shomer* is conceptually analogous to a shell or husk — it is "wood." That identity is entirely distinct from its identity as food, and the *hechsher* requirement stands.

This entire series of cases establishes a principle while simultaneously demonstrating its limits. In every case where food might have been thought to be exempt from *hechsher* because it once was or could become a *tumah* source, the exemption fails because the *tumah* source role was not in the food's capacity *as food*. The one genuine application of the exemption is *neveilas of tahor* — the carcass of a *kosher* bird — which, when swallowed, renders one *tamei* from within. There the food *is* a *tumah* source in its capacity as food, and accordingly it does not require *hechsher*.

### Seeds/Roof Case

Rav Masna adds a fifth case. The ruling states: *beis she-tikho b'zraim taharu* — a house whose interior was covered with seeds (more precisely, with grain still in its stalks) and those stalks were designated for use as the roof, those seeds/stalks become *tahor*, losing their prior status as food, since they are now treated as attached to the structure and part of the ground. But as part of the house, if the house contracts *tzara'at*, the stalks become part of a *tumah* source — indeed, an *av ha-tumah*.

Were this biblical, any grain could eventually be placed on a roof, become part of a house with *tzara'at*, and thereby become an *av ha-tumah*, eliminating the *hechsher* requirement. Hence this must be rabbinic. The answer: *keshe-shimesh me'eitz shimesh* — when they became part of the roof, they were functioning as wood, as building material. Their *tumah* in that context is in their identity as structural components, not as food. The *hechsher* requirement for food is therefore unaffected.

Rashi notes, with evident candor, that in this last case he does not know the source from which the *Gemara* is drawing the ruling. In all the previous cases the *Gemara* cited identifiable *Mishnas* or *Braisos*, but here the cross-reference is absent, and Rashi acknowledges that the source of this accepted ruling is unclear to him.

---

## Shimon on Living

### Shimon's Case

With the *ma'aseh etz* doctrine established, the *Gemara* turns to the concluding statement of the *Mishnah* — Rabbi Shimon's ruling that the dangling limb is *tahor*. The context of the *Mishnah* involves three cases: the dangling limb while the animal is alive; the dangling limb after *shechita*; and the dangling limb after the animal dies naturally. Rabbi Shimon says *tahor*.

The *Gemara* opens with the striking observation: *man d'shach* — either way Rabbi Shimon's ruling is difficult. If death renders the limb as though it fell off during life (*misa osah nipul*), it should be *tamei* as *ever min hachai*. If death does not render it as though it fell off (*ein misa osah nipul*), the limb died with the animal and should be *tamei* as part of a *neveilah*. How can it be *tahor* under either reading?

The *Gemara* answers: *Rabbi Shimon areisha kai* — Rabbi Shimon is not referring to the final case of the *Mishnah* (the animal's death); he is going back to the first case — *ha'ever vehabasar hameduldalin bibeheimah* — the dangling limb while the animal is alive. The *Mishnah* rules that such a limb is susceptible to *tumah* as food and requires *hechsher*. It is to this ruling that Rabbi Shimon says *tahor* — this dangling limb, while the animal is alive, is not considered food.

### Yochanan's Explanation

Rav Assi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: what is Rabbi Shimon's reason? The verse says *mikol ha'ochel asher ye'achel* — from all food that will be eaten. *Ochel she'atah yachol lehachilo l'acherim karui ochel* — only something that you can feed to others, something that either a Jew or a non-Jew could eat and from which benefit can be derived, is called *ochel*. *Ochel she'ee atah yachol lehachilo l'acherim ein karui ochel* — something that cannot be fed to anyone is not called food. The dangling limb while the animal is alive is *ever min hachai*: it is forbidden to Jews, forbidden to non-Jews, and one may not derive any benefit from it whatsoever. Since it can be fed to no one and yields no permissible benefit, it cannot be called *ochel*, and therefore it is not susceptible to *tumah* as food.

### Zeira's Counter

Rabbi Zeira challenges this. Why invoke such a sophisticated explanation? Perhaps Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is far simpler: *dilma ta'ama d'Rabbi Shimon hasham mishum me'ura me'ura* — perhaps the reason is simply that the limb is still physically intertwined with the animal, still one unit with it. To classify a dangling limb of a living animal as *food* and therefore susceptible to *tumah* is already a conceptual stretch; Rabbi Shimon might simply be saying that physical attachment, however tenuous, renders it still part of the animal. Why is this more elaborate explanation needed?

### Tree Analogy

Rabbi Zeira supports this from a *braisa*: the case of a fig-tree limb that has cracked off but remains intertwined through its bark (*yichur shel te'enah she-nifshach u-me'ura b'klipatah*). Rabbi Yehuda rules that the fruit on such a limb is *tahor* — it is still considered attached to the tree. The Sages say: if the limb is capable of surviving and reconnecting (*im yachol lichyot, tahor*); if not, the fruit is *tamei*. And when the *Gemara* asks for Rabbi Yehuda's reason, the answer is *ho'il u-me'ura me'ura* — since it is still physically intertwined, it is considered one with the tree. If that principle applies to a cracked tree limb, the same *me'ura be-me'ura* reasoning should explain Rabbi Shimon's ruling about the dangling animal limb without needing to invoke the *ochel she'ee atah yachol lehachilo l'acherim* formula.

The *Gemara* concludes from this that Rabbi Yochanan's explanation — which invokes the food-definition argument — cannot have been offered for the first case of the *Mishnah* (the living animal), since the simpler *me'ura be-me'ura* explanation suffices there. This implies that Rabbi Yochanan's explanation was offered for a different case in the *Mishnah*, as will emerge.

---

## Shimon on Shechita

### Shechita Blood

The *Gemara* now moves to the middle case of the *Mishnah*: the animal has been slaughtered (*nishchata ha-behemah*). The *Mishnah* states that according to Rabbi Meir, the blood of *shechita* renders the dangling limb susceptible — *huchshara b'dameha*. Rabbi Shimon says the *shechita* blood did not render it susceptible (*lo huchshara*). Since the simpler *me'ura be-me'ura* explanation resolves Rabbi Shimon's position regarding the living animal, the *Gemara* proposes that the food-definition argument (*ochel she'ee atah yachol lehachilo l'acherim*) belongs here, in the middle case — where Rabbi Shimon denies *hechsher* by the *dam shechita*.

### Non-Consumable

Rabbi Yochanan's explanation in that context would be: the blood of *shechita* does not render this dangling limb susceptible because it is not *ochel*. Since it cannot be fed to anyone, it is not food, and the *hechsher* mechanism does not apply to it.

### Rejection

The *Gemara*, however, rejects this placement as well. *Dilma ta'ama d'Rabbi Shimon be-hai ika ke-Rabbi ika d'Rabbi Yochanan* — for the middle case there is already a full set of explanations debated earlier about why the *shechita* blood does or does not apply to a dangling limb; there is no need to invoke this entirely new food-definition argument. Positioning Rabbi Yochanan's explanation at the middle case is therefore also untenable.

---

## Shimon on Dead

### Dangling Meat

Having rejected both the first and middle cases as the home of Rabbi Yochanan's explanation, the *Gemara* concludes: *ela le'olam ha'seifa* — return to the simple reading, that Rabbi Shimon is addressing the final case, the animal's death. But the *Gemara* now refines which aspect of that final case is at issue. Rabbi Shimon cannot be arguing about a whole dangling *limb* when the animal dies — a whole limb presents the intractable *either-way* problem raised at the outset. Rather, he is arguing about dangling *meat* (*basar*). The case is thus: *lav a'ever ela a'basar* — not the limb but the flesh.

### Hechsher Problem

When an animal dies with dangling meat, the meat is *basar min hachai*: it is not a *tumah* source. As food, it could in principle become *tamei* if it had *hechsher*. The *Mishnah* teaches *meisa ha-behemah, ha-basar tzarich hechsher* — if the animal died, the dangling meat requires *hechsher* to become susceptible. On this ruling, Rabbi Shimon says *tahor* — even with *hechsher*, this dangling meat will never become *tamei*.

### Shimon's Answer

Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's position: *amar kra, mikol ha'ochel asher ye'achel* — the verse again. *Ochel she'atah yachol lehachilo l'acherim karui ochel; ochel she'ee atah yachol lehachilo l'acherim ein karui ochel.* The dangling meat when the animal died is *basar min hachai*. Nobody can eat it — it is forbidden to Jews, forbidden to non-Jews, and yields no permissible benefit. Since it cannot be fed to anyone, it is not *ochel*, and therefore even with *hechsher* it cannot become *tamei*.

### Chachamim's View

The *Chachamim* disagree. Their position is that the definition of food for purposes of *tumah* is determined by the physical capacity to be eaten, not by the halachic permissibility of eating. *Basar min hachai* is physically fit to be consumed — it is objectively edible as a physical matter, even if halachically forbidden. That physical capacity suffices to classify it as food for *tumah* purposes, and therefore it can become *tamei* upon *hechsher*.

This dispute echoes the fundamental question that has been present throughout this *perek*: is food defined by objective physical edibility or by halachic accessibility? Rabbi Shimon holds the latter; the *Chachamim* hold the former.

---

## Human Dangling Limbs

### Human Dangling Status

The *Mishnah* closes the *perek* by extending these laws to humans. *Ha'ever vehabasar hameduldalim b'adam tehorim* — a dangling limb or dangling meat of a human is *tahor*. This requires no elaborate explanation: a human being is not subject to *shechita*, the food-status framework does not apply to human limbs, and there is no basis on which to classify a dangling limb of a living person as *ochel*. While the person is alive, the dangling limb has no halachic status whatsoever.

### After Death

When the person dies, the *Mishnah* distinguishes between the two cases. *Ha-basar tahor* — the dangling meat remains *tahor*, because it is treated as having separated during the person's lifetime and is thus *basar min hachai* of a human, which is not a *tumah* source. *Ha'ever metamei mishum ever min hachai ve'eino metamei mishum ever min hameis* — the dangling limb, however, is *tamei* as an *ever min hachai*, since death causes it to be treated as though it separated during life, but it is not considered a limb of a corpse (*ever min hameis*).

The practical significance of this distinction is substantial. An *ever min hachai* requires the complete limb to be a *tumah* source; pieces that separate from it do not independently cause *tumah*. An *ever min hameis*, by contrast — as a component of a corpse — would cause *tumah* even through smaller pieces: a *kezayis* of flesh, or a bone the size of a barleycorn, can independently be *tumah* sources when they derive from a *meis*. By classifying the dangling limb as *ever min hachai* rather than *ever min hameis*, the *Mishnah* limits the *tumah* to the whole limb alone.

---

## Human Dangling Limbs (II)

### Logic Problem

The *Gemara* is troubled. If the dangling limb of a human who has died is *tamei* as *ever min hachai*, then what is the content of Rabbi Shimon's ruling that it is *tahor*? The same *either-way* problem arises: if death causes the limb to be treated as having fallen off (*misa osah nipul*), it should be *tamei* as *ever min hachai*; if not, it should be *tamei* as part of the corpse.

### Shimon's Real Position

The *Gemara* resolves this: *Rabbi Shimon be'alma kai* — Rabbi Shimon is not disputing whether the dangling limb itself is *tamei*. His *tahor* ruling is a response to the *tanna kamma*'s implicit position, not a direct negation of *ever min hachai* status. The *tanna kamma* states that the limb is *tamei* as *ever min hachai* and *not* as *ever min hameis* — implicitly establishing that an *ever min hameis* would *normally* be *tamei*. It is to that implicit premise that Rabbi Shimon objects. Rabbi Shimon holds: *ever min hachai* — agreed, *tamei*; but *ever min hameis be'alma lo metamei* — a limb from a corpse, when it lacks sufficient flesh or other components to cause *tumah* on its own, is *tahor*.

### Eliezer Position

The *Gemara* now brings a *braisa* that aligns Rabbi Shimon with Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Eliezer states: *shamati she'ever min hachai metamei* — I have received the tradition that a limb from a living person causes *tumah*. Implicitly, his tradition specifies *min hachai* — from a living person — and not *min hameis*, meaning that a limb from a corpse that lacks sufficient independent components would not cause *tumah*.

### Yehoshua's Logic

Rabbi Yehoshua challenges this with a *kal vachomer*: *ma chai she-hu tahor, ever ha-poresh mimenu tamei* — a living person is fundamentally *tahor*, yet a limb that separates from him causes *tumah*. *Meis she-hu tamei, lo kol sheken* — a corpse is *tamei* in its entirety; how much more so should a limb from a corpse, even without sufficient independent flesh, be *tamei*. Rabbi Yehoshua reinforces his argument by analogy to *Megillas Taanis*, which records that *Pesach Sheni* is a day on which one does not deliver a eulogy. One should not read this as implying that *Pesach Rishon* permits eulogies — it means even *Pesach Sheni*, the minor *Pesach*, carries this restriction. Similarly, Rabbi Eliezer's tradition that *ever min hachai* is *tamei* should not be read as excluding *ever min hameis*; it means even *ever min hachai* is *tamei*.

### Tradition Answer

Rabbi Eliezer's response is simply: *kach shamati* — this is what I received as tradition. The tradition specifies that a limb from a living person causes *tumah*, but a limb from a corpse — absent sufficient flesh — does not. The *kal vachomer* cannot override a received tradition.

---

## Practical Distinctions

### Whole vs. Pieces

The *Gemara* asks: once we have established that the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon disagree, what is the practical difference between *ever min hachai* and *ever min hameis* as the *Mishnah* frames it? The answer is *kezayis basar ve'etzem kesiorah ha-poresh me'ever min hachai ika beinaihu* — the difference concerns pieces that separate from the limb. For an *ever min hachai*, *tumah* attaches only to the complete limb; pieces that separate from it — a *kezayis* of flesh, a barleycorn-sized bone — are not *tumah* sources. For an *ever min hameis*, by contrast, considered part of the corpse, a *kezayis* of flesh or a barleycorn-sized bone is independently *tamei*. This distinction has real halachic consequences.

### Flesh Dispute

The *Gemara* cites a *Mishnah*: *kezayis basar ha-poresh me'ever min hachai* — a *kezayis* of flesh separated from an *ever min hachai* of a human. Rabbi Eliezer holds it *tamei*; Rav Nechunya ben HaKana and Rabbi Yehoshua hold it *tahor*. This is notable: by an animal, *basar min hachai* is simply not a *tumah* source. Here, some opinions hold that flesh from an *ever min hachai* of a human is *tamei*, indicating that the rules for human *ever min hachai* are stricter in certain respects than for animals.

### Bone Dispute

Regarding a bone: *etzem kesiorah ha-poresh me'ever min hachai* — a barleycorn-sized bone separated from a human *ever min hachai*. Here the positions shift: Rav Nechunya ben HaKana holds it *tamei*, while Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua hold it *tahor*. Again, regardless of the individual positions, the overarching point is that by an *ever min hachai*, even of a human, the pieces that separate from it are a matter of dispute — and at least according to some opinions, they are *tahor* — whereas by an *ever min hameis*, these quantities would be straightforwardly *tamei* as components of a corpse.

### Final Reconciliation

The *Gemara* concludes: *hasha de'asis le'hachi* — now that we have arrived at this framework of disputes about pieces separating from an *ever min hachai*, the scope of Rabbi Shimon's *tahor* ruling can be understood more narrowly. When Rabbi Shimon says the dangling limb is *tahor*, he need not be asserting the extreme position that an *ever min hameis* is entirely *tahor*. He may instead be disputing the *tanna kamma* regarding pieces that separate from an *ever min hachai* — the *tanna kamma* holding that at least flesh or bone pieces cause *tumah*, and Rabbi Shimon holding that only the whole *ever* causes *tumah* as *ever min hachai*, while any piece separated from it is *tahor*. Either way, the scope of Rabbi Shimon's *tahor* is limited: it applies to specific pieces or specific identity-classifications, not to a sweeping exemption of all dangling limbs.

*Hadarun lach or veharotev.*

---

---

# Hullin 130

## Gifts to Kohanim

### Priestly gifts intro

Today's *daf* is 130, the beginning of a new *perek*. The *perek* we just finished was, without question, the most challenging in *Chullin* — anatomical difficulties aside. We now turn to the last three chapters, which continue to address matters relating to animals but shift focus to the gifts derived from them: beginning with the shearing of sheep and the portions taken at *shechita* of cattle and sheep, and concluding with the commandment of sending away the mother bird. It is a welcome change of pace.

This *perek* opens with *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva* — the arm, the jaw, and the stomach. The *Torah* commands that when a person slaughters a cow or a sheep, he gives the arm, the jaw, and one of the stomachs to the *kohanim*. The relevant *pesukim* are in *Devarim* 18. The *Torah* first notes that the *kohanim* have no tribal portion and that they eat the fire-offerings of God: *lo yihyeh lakohanim halevi'im kol shevet levi chelek venachala im yisrael ishei Hashem venachalato yocheilun* — they have no inheritance; they live from the *korbanot*. But the *kohanim* were only present in the *Beit Hamikdash* roughly two weeks out of the year. What sustained them the rest of the time?

### Three gifts explained

The very next *pasuk* answers directly: *vezeh yihyeh mishpat hakohanim me'eit ha'am me'eit zovechei hazevach im shor im seh venatan lakohen hazroa vehalechayayim vehakeiva* — this shall be the law of the *kohanim* from the people, from those who slaughter an ox or a sheep: one gives the *kohen* the arm, the cheeks, and the maw. The *pasuk* continues: *reishit degancha tiroshcha veyitzharecha vereishit geiz tzoncha titein lo* — the first of the grain, the wine, the oil, and the first of the shearing of the flock shall be given to him.

There is a famous *Midrash* connecting these specific portions to *Pinchas*: he used his *zeroa* — his arm — to thrust the spear, and the spear passed through the stomach, *el hakuba* — *hakeiva*. Since *Pinchas* was a *kohen*, the *Midrash* sees these gifts as symbolically linked to his zealotry on God's behalf.

### Kohanim sustenance

The placement of these *pesukim* is deliberate. The *Torah* juxtaposes the gifts of the arm, jaw, and stomach, the *terumah* of grain, wine, and oil, and the first of the shearing, precisely because it is explaining how the *kohanim* sustain themselves. Grain is covered by *terumah*; clothing by *reishit hagez*; and meat by *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva*. The *kohanim* serve in a role of *avodat hakodesh* and are understood to function not only within the *Beit Hamikdash* but as teachers and religious leaders for the broader community — *yoru mishpatecha l'Yaakov*. The *Torah* accordingly provides for the full range of their material needs.

It bears noting that these gifts are not *kadosh* in the manner of *terumah*; they can be used and sold. The obligation to give them, however, applies in all times and in all places, as the *Mishnah* makes clear.

---

## Non-sanctified vs sacrif…

### Application scope

The *Mishnah* states: *noheg ba'aretz uvachutz la'aretz* — this obligation applies both within the Land of Israel and outside it — *bifnei habayit veshelo bifnei habayit* — whether the Temple stands or not. The gifts of *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva* are thus a perpetual obligation, independent of the *Beit Hamikdash*.

### Exclusion from korbanot

The *Mishnah* continues: *bechullin aval lo bemukdashin* — in non-sanctified animals but not in *korbanot*. When one brings an animal as a sacrifice, he does not separately give these portions as gifts to the *kohanim*.

### Kal vachomer setup

The *Mishnah* itself raises the question of why the gifts do not apply to *korbanot*. The argument that might have led us to think they should runs as follows: by *chullin*, ordinary non-sanctified animals, one does not give the *chazeh* and the *shok* — the breast and the thigh — as one does by a *shelamim*, and yet one does give *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva*. By *kodshim*, where one already gives the breast and thigh, one might reason *kal vachomer* — how much more so should these additional gifts apply. If a lesser obligation includes the gifts, surely a greater obligation should include them as well.

### Verse excludes korbanot

Against this *kal vachomer*, the *Torah* provides an explicit exclusion. The verse concerning the *shelamim* states: *ve'asain osam l'Aharon hakohen ulvanav l'chok olam* — I give these to Aaron and his sons as an eternal statute. The word *osam* — "them" — limits the priestly entitlement from *korbanot* to the *chazeh* and *shok* alone. The gifts of *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva* are not given from a *korban*; *ein lo ela mah shene'emar binyan* — one receives from the *korban* only what the verse explicitly designates.

---

## Blemish before sanctity

### Permanent blemish ruling

The *Mishnah* now turns to a question that, while only tangentially related to *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva*, is highly relevant to the larger category of when an animal is considered to have had the status of a *korban*. This passage, in fact, appears verbatim in *Bechoros* as well, because it defines the precise conditions under which an animal enters the *korban* category — which in turn determines whether it is excluded from *bechorah* and from the priestly gifts alike.

The principle: *kol hakodashim shekadam mum kavua lehekdesham* — if a permanent blemish preceded the sanctification of the animal. A *mum kavua* is a blemish that will not heal. If such a blemish already existed at the moment of sanctification, the animal could never have been designated as a *korban* in the first place, since it was already unfit. Consequently, whatever sanctity the animal received cannot be *kedushat haguf* — the sanctity of an object that is itself to be used as a sacrifice. Instead, it receives only *kedushat bedek habayit* — the sanctity of an object donated to the Temple treasury for its monetary value. The *Beit Hamikdash* owns its worth, not its identity.

The distinction is significant. *Kedushat bedek habayit* is, in essence, *kedushat damim* — the treasury cares only about the object's monetary value, not about what it is intrinsically. Just as one might donate a car to the *Beit Hamikdash* and the treasury simply assesses and sells it, so too this blemished animal: its identity as a cow or a sheep was never sanctified. It was merely property owned by the Temple for the sake of its price.

### Treasury property effects

Since this animal never possessed the sanctity of a *korban*, the *Mishnah* rules: *venifdu chayavim bivichorah uvematanot* — once redeemed, it is subject to the laws of *bechorah* and the priestly gifts. *Veyotzim lechulin lehiggazez ulehe'aved* — after redemption, it fully returns to the status of *chullin*; it may be shorn and worked.

This last point requires explanation. The *Torah* prohibits working or shearing an animal that was once a *korban* and was subsequently redeemed after acquiring a blemish. The principle is that even after redemption, the animal retains a residual *kedushah* of a former *korban*, and therefore may only be slaughtered and eaten — it cannot be put to secular use. But that residual sanctity applies only when the animal once genuinely had *kedushat korban*. Here, where the animal's sanctity was always only *kedushat bedek habayit*, redemption severs the relationship completely. There is no residual sanctity, because there was never *kedushat haguf* to begin with. The transaction is simply: the Temple owned it; now it does not. Accordingly, *vladan vechalban mutar* — its offspring and milk are permitted after redemption — and *lachtar pidyonam* — once redeemed.

Furthermore: *vehashochtan bachutz patur* — if one slaughters such an animal outside the *Beit Hamikdash*, one does not transgress the prohibition of offering a *korban* outside the Temple. That prohibition applies specifically to animals that possess *kedushat korban*. This animal may have been owned by the *Beit Hamikdash*, but it was never a *korban*, so no transgression is incurred — just as slaughtering an animal that was donated to the Temple treasury but was never a sacrifice does not constitute *shechita* of a *korban* outside the *Beit Hamikdash*.

*Ve'ein osin temurah* — the laws of *temura* do not apply. The *Torah* states that if one attempts to substitute a sanctified *korban* with another animal, both become *kadosh*: *vehaya hu utmurato yihye kodesh*. This principle of *temura* applies only to animals that possess genuine *kedushat korban*. An animal that was always only in the category of *bedek habayit* cannot generate *temura*.

*Ve'im mesu yifdu* — if such an animal dies, it may still be redeemed. By contrast, an animal that possessed genuine *kedushat korban* may not be redeemed after death. Two reasons underlie this: first, the principle of *ein podin et hakodashim l'hachilam l'klavim* — one does not redeem *korbanot* merely to use them as dog food. If the animal is dead, redemption would serve no licit purpose. Second, the *Torah*'s language for redeeming a blemished *korban* — *vehe'emido lifnei Hashem vehe'ericho lifnei hakohen* — requires that the animal stand and be assessed. Both *ha'amadah v'ha'arachah* — standing and valuation — are prerequisites that cannot be fulfilled by a dead animal. Neither consideration applies to an animal whose sanctity was only *bedek habayit*, and thus it may be redeemed even after death, if only to recover whatever monetary value remains.

### Bechor & maaser exception

The *Mishnah* records one exception to the rule that a pre-existing *mum kavua* prevents an animal from acquiring *kedushat korban*: *chutz min habechor umin hamaser* — except for the firstborn and the tithe animal.

Consider an animal born with a congenital blemish. Generally, if the blemish precedes the sanctification, the animal never achieves *kedushat korban*. Yet if this animal is a *bechor* — a firstborn male — the rule is different. The sanctity of *bechor* is not something actively conferred by a person through speech; it arises automatically and intrinsically from the act of birth. Because *kedushah* is imposed upon the animal by the *Torah* itself by virtue of being born firstborn, that identity as a *korban bechor* attaches regardless of any pre-existing blemish. The animal cannot be brought to the *mizbe'ach* because of its *mum*, but it nonetheless possesses the full *kedushah* of a *korban bechor*.

Similarly with *ma'aser behemah*: one gathers all newly born animals of the year, drives them into a pen, and counts them — *ha'asiri yihyeh kodesh*, the tenth is holy. If the tenth animal to emerge happens to have a blemish, it does not receive merely *kedushat bedek habayit*. Its sanctity as *ma'aser* is conferred automatically by the counting process, not by an act of verbal dedication on the owner's part. The *pesukim* teach that *ha'asiri yihyeh kodesh* regardless of a blemish. Accordingly, both *bechor* and *ma'aser behemah* acquire full *kedushat korban* even when the blemish preceded what would otherwise be considered their sanctification.

---

## Sanctity before blemish

### Sanctified then blemished

The *Mishnah* now presents the contrasting case: *kol shekadam hekdeshan es mumam* — where the sanctification preceded the blemish — or *mum over kodem hekdeshan* — where a *mum over*, a transient blemish, preceded sanctification. A transient blemish does not define the animal's identity, since it will heal; it does not bar the animal from *kedushat korban*, and it does not prevent the sanctity from taking hold. If the animal was then sanctified and only later developed a permanent blemish — *ve'achar kach nolad lahem mum kavua* — the permanent blemish occurred after the animal already possessed the full sanctity of a *korban*. As a result, all of the rules of *kedushat korban* apply.

### Post-redemption restrict…

For such an animal, once it acquires its permanent blemish and is redeemed, the following consequences obtain: *peturim min habechorahumin hamatnot* — it is exempt from the laws of *bechorah*, and one does not give *zeroa lechayayim vekeivah* from it after *shechita*. *Ve'einam yotzim lechulin lehiggazez ulehe'aved* — it does not fully return to *chullin*; it may not be shorn and may not be worked. *Uveladan vechalban assur le'achar pidyonam* — even after redemption, its offspring and milk are forbidden for benefit.

Furthermore: *vehashochtan bachutz chayav* — one who slaughters such an animal outside the *Beit Hamikdash* incurs liability, because the animal possesses *kedushat korban*. One might ask: if it has a permanent blemish, it cannot be brought as a *korban* in any event — how can one be liable for slaughtering it outside? The *Gemara* addresses this by confining the ruling to a specific type of blemish, such as a cataract of the eye, which is technically a *mum* sufficient to permit redemption and preclude normal offering, but which, if the animal were actually placed upon the *mizbe'ach*, would not be removed *bedi'eved*. Such a blemish allows the animal to be redeemed and bars it from ideal offering, but since *bedi'eved* it would be accepted, one is still liable for slaughtering it outside. *Ve'osim temurah* — the laws of *temura* apply, since the animal possesses genuine *kedushat korban*. *Ve'im mesu yikkaveru* — if such an animal dies before redemption, it must be buried; it cannot be redeemed, because of the requirements of *ha'amadah v'ha'arachah* and the prohibition of redeeming *korbanot* for use as dog food.

### Why restrictions apply

The underlying principle is that when an animal's identity was defined by *kedushat korban* — when the *kedushah* came first — that identity does not fully dissolve upon redemption. Even after the formal *kedushah* has been removed through *pidyon*, the animal retains a residual dimension of its former sanctity. The practical expression of this residual *kedushah* is that one may do nothing with the animal except slaughter it and eat it: one may not shear it, may not work it, may not benefit from its milk or its offspring. All the exclusions flow from this.

Contrast this with the first case: if the blemish preceded sanctification, the animal's identity was never defined by *kedushat korban* at all. The *Beit Hamikdash* owned it as property; redemption simply transfers that ownership back. No residual sanctity remains, because there was no *kedushat haguf* to leave a trace.

---

## 'Ze' and ownership

### Rav Chisda ruling

With the *Mishnah*'s framework now established, the *Gemara* turns to a remarkable ruling of Rav Chisda. The *Gemara* has already noted that when the *Torah* introduces the gifts of *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva*, it uses the word *ze* — *vezeh yihyeh mishpat hakohanim* — "this is the law of the *kohanim*." After establishing that this word *ze* excluded the *chazeh veshok* from non-*korban* animals (since the *chazeh veshok* is a *korban* ritual that cannot be replicated outside the *Beit Hamikdash* and cannot be performed inside with *chullin*), the *Gemara* asks: what further teaching does *ze* come to convey?

The answer is: *lichdirav Chisda* — it comes to support Rav Chisda's ruling. *Amar Rav Chisda: hamazik matnot kehuna o she'achalan patur milishalem* — one who damages gifts owed to a *kohen*, or who eats them, is exempt from payment. This applies to *hazroa vehalechayayim veakeiva*, to *reishit hagez*, and to analogous priestly gifts.

This is a striking ruling. One might assume that since the gifts are owed to the *kohanim* by *Torah* law, destroying them would obligate compensation. Rav Chisda says otherwise. The *Gemara* presents two possible rationales, each reflecting a fundamentally different understanding of the ownership of these gifts before they are handed over.

### Two explanations

*I ba'it eima mishum dehavei lei mamon she'ein lo tovin* — one may explain that the gifts, once separated, belong collectively to the *kohanim* as a class, but since there is no specific individual *kohen* who has a claim, no one can bring the damager to court. This is the principle of *mamon she'ein lo tovin* — property with no particular claimant. The damager has in fact injured the *kohanim*'s collective property, but since the injury cannot be attributed to any identifiable individual, there is no mechanism for legal recovery.

*Ve'i ba'it eima midikativ ze* — alternatively, the word *ze* teaches that the obligation to give the gifts exists only when they are physically present. If the gift has been destroyed, the obligation simply does not apply — not because the *kohanim* owned it and cannot collect, but because the *kohanim* never owned it to begin with. On this reading, the gift remains in the owner's possession until actually transferred. The owner has a *mitzvah* to give it; if he destroys it, he has subverted that *mitzvah*, but he has not damaged anyone else's property. He damaged his own.

These are two very different conceptual frameworks. The *mamon she'ein lo tovin* explanation acknowledges that the property already belongs to the *kohanim* as a collective; the obstacle is procedural. The *ze* explanation holds that the property never transferred — it belongs to the giver until the moment of actual delivery.

### 'Ze' means present

The word *ze* thus functions as a limiting principle: the obligation attaches only to that which is physically present, *ze* — this thing before you. If it is not here, there is no obligation to give, and consequently no liability for its destruction. The verb form of giving applies only to something that can actually be given.

---

## Verse & courts

### Court enforcement query

The *Gemara* now examines a *baraita* that appears to challenge Rav Chisda's ruling. The *baraita* states: *vezeh yihyeh mishpat hakohanim — melamed shehamatnot din* — "this is the law of the *kohanim*" teaches that the gifts have the status of *din*, meaning they are subject to the law of the courts. At first reading, this sounds as though the courts can compel payment or adjudicate claims relating to these gifts — which would seem to contradict Rav Chisda's ruling that one who damages them is exempt.

The *Gemara* asks: *lema'i hilchata? lav lehotzi'o bedayanim?* — For what practical purpose does the *baraita* say the gifts are a *din*? Is it not to say that one can collect compensation through the courts? Rashi notes that this might mean even the first *kohen* to file suit could collect. If so, the principle of *mamon she'ein lo tovin* would not apply here — even as a collective, the *kohanim* could bring a claim.

### Worthy kohanim rule

The *Gemara* rejects this reading. *Lo, lechulkan bedayanim* — the *baraita* does not mean courts can collect compensation for damaged gifts. Rather, it means that courts oversee the proper distribution of gifts. The *Gemara* invokes the teaching of Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani: one does not give the gifts of the *kohanim* — whether *terumah*, *zeroa lechayayim vekeivah*, or any other priestly gift — to a *kohen* who is an *am ha'aretz*, one who is not careful in his religious observance.

The source is a verse in *Divrei Hayamim*, cited in the context of the reign of Yehoshaphat. Yehoshaphat said to the people of Jerusalem: *latet menat hakohanim vehaleviyim lema'an yechezku betorat Hashem* — give the gifts to the *kohanim* and *leviyim* so that they will be strengthened in the Torah of God. The *Gemara* derives: *kol hamachzik beTorat Hashem yesh lo menat* — one who upholds God's Torah is entitled to receive; *veshe'eino machzik beTorat Hashem ein lo menat* — one who does not is not.

This is a *lekatchila* standard. Tosafot notes that *bedi'avad*, or where no other *kohen* is available, one may give to an *am ha'aretz kohen*. But when there is a choice, the obligation to give priestly gifts is bound up with the *kohen*'s role as representative and teacher of Torah. The *Beit Hamikdash* role and the communal religious-leadership role are intertwined; the gifts are meant to support the latter as much as the former. The court's oversight, then, is directed at ensuring that gifts flow to those *kohanim* who genuinely fulfill that role.

### Baraita ruling

The *Gemara* then examines a second *baraita* in which Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says: *mishpat — melamed shematanot din* — the word *mishpat* teaches that the gifts are subject to court law. *Yachol afilu chazeh veshok* — one might have thought this applies even to the *chazeh* and *shok* of a *korban*. *Talmud lomar ze* — the verse says *ze*, "this," excluding the *chazeh veshok* and restricting the principle to the gifts of *zeroa lechayayim vekeivah*.

The question then is: *l'mai* — for what purpose? *Ileima l'chulkan bedayanim* — if it means the courts oversee distribution to worthy *kohanim*, then why would the *chazeh veshok* be excluded? Presumably the same principle of giving only to deserving *kohanim* should apply to *korban* portions as well. The *Gemara* does not easily resolve this, and one might note that the *chazeh veshok* is in any case divided equally among the *kohanim* serving that week. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* here suggests another reading: the reference to courts is about the right to collect compensation — *lo tzivu bedayanim* — and it is that right that is specific to the gifts of *zeroa lechayayim vekeivah*.

### Possession requirement

To harmonize this with Rav Chisda's ruling that one who damages these gifts is exempt, the *Gemara* clarifies: *hacha bema'i askinan — de'asu liyadei* — the *baraita* is discussing a case where the gifts actually came into the *kohen*'s possession. *Le'asu liyadei betivlaihu* — specifically, a case where a *kohen* came and physically seized the whole animal — before the gifts had been formally separated — and claimed the *zeroa lechayayim vekeivah*. One might have thought he is not entitled to it since it was not yet separated and he was not given it. The *baraita* teaches, based on the principle that *matnot shelo hurmu kemi shehurmu damyan* — gifts not yet separated are treated as if already separated — that even in this case his possession is valid, and if someone subsequently damages those portions, the court can compel payment.

Why does this not apply to the *chazeh veshok*? Because the *chazeh veshok* is distributed to the *kohanim* serving that week's rotation. A *kohen* who was not on duty that week and burst in to seize the *chazeh veshok* would have no entitlement, and his seizure would not grant him ownership. The distinction, then, is that these priestly gifts — unlike *korban* portions — can be acquired through physical seizure even before formal separation, and it is that mode of acquisition that creates court-enforceable ownership.

Before the *kohen* takes possession, Rav Chisda's rule holds: one who damages the gifts is exempt, either because of *mamon she'ein lo tovin* or because of the *ze* principle. Once the *kohen* has validly taken possession, the ordinary laws of property damage apply.

---

## Poor gifts analogy

### Traveler taking poor gif…

The *Gemara* introduces a *baraita* from a related domain to test Rav Chisda's ruling. The *baraita* discusses a *ba'al habayit* — a person of means — who is traveling from place to place and finds himself with no funds or food. Being temporarily without resources, he is permitted to take *leket*, *shikcha*, *pe'ah*, and *ma'aser ani* — the agricultural gifts designated for the poor — even though he is not ordinarily eligible.

Rabbi Eliezer says: *notel hu vechesheyachzor yeshalem* — he takes them, and when he returns home, he repays. The implication is that there is some form of obligation to pay back on account of his having taken gifts he was not permanently entitled to.

### Repayment dispute

This seems to challenge Rav Chisda's ruling: if destroying or consuming gifts meant for the poor creates an obligation to repay, it would suggest that similar gifts — those of the *kohanim* — should also generate an obligation when consumed improperly. The *Gemara* raises this challenge and then considers how Rav Chisda might have responded.

The initial suggestion is that Rav Chisda would say *midat chasidut shanu kan* — what Rabbi Eliezer taught here is merely a matter of pious conduct, not a legal obligation. One is not compelled by the courts to repay; it is simply the right thing to do.

### Poverty timing test

Rava, however, objects to this framing. He argues: the word used is *yeshalem* — he shall pay — not a recommendation for piety. Rabbi Eliezer cannot be reduced to a counsel of *chasidut*. Moreover, Rava argues, the challenge to Rav Chisda should not have been drawn from Rabbi Eliezer's opinion at all — Rabbi Eliezer is a single *tanna* whose view is not authoritative.

Rava reframes the entire discussion. The real challenge comes from the *seifa* of the *Mishnah*, from the ruling of the *Chachamim*: *ani haya be'oto sha'ah* — he was poor at that moment. The *Chachamim* hold that the wealthy traveler, being temporarily without resources, was genuinely in a state of poverty at that time, and therefore was fully entitled to take the gifts. He owes nothing upon return.

The implication of the *Chachamim*'s reasoning is important: *ta'ama de'ani*, the reason he need not repay is that he was legally poor at the time. But if he were not poor — *ha'ashir meshalem* — if he had money available and simply helped himself to *leket shikcha pe'ah* and *ma'aser ani*, he would be obligated to repay. Why? *Lehavi kemazik matnot kehuna* — why should this be different from damaging gifts of the *kohanim*, where Rav Chisda says one need not pay?

It is to this question that Rav Chisda applies *midat chasidut shanu kan*. The *Chachamim*'s implication that the wealthy person who takes gifts of the poor must repay is not a court-enforceable obligation — after all, which *ani* will file suit? It is *mamon she'ein lo tovin*. But morally, since one took what was not rightfully his, it is more than *midat chasidut* — it is strongly the right thing to do to donate an equivalent amount to the poor.

### Final conclusion

The *Gemara* thus concludes with Rav Chisda's ruling intact. One who damages gifts of the *kohanim* — or priestly-analogous gifts such as those designated for the poor — before they are transferred is exempt from payment in court. Two explanations remain on the table, reflecting different understandings of ownership:

The first is *mamon she'ein lo tovin*: the property already belongs to the collective of *kohanim* or the collective of *aniyim*, but since no individual can assert a claim, there is no legal mechanism for recovery. The damage is real; the remedy is absent.

The second is the *ze* principle: the gift has not yet transferred. It remains the owner's property, and in destroying it he has deprived himself of the ability to fulfill his *mitzvah*, but he has not damaged anyone else's property. The obligation to give exists only when *ze* — this thing — is actually present.

These two explanations are not merely technical alternatives. They reflect fundamentally different understandings of the moment at which ownership of priestly and other obligatory gifts transfers from the giver to the recipient — a question the *Gemara* leaves instructively open.

---

---

# Hullin 131

## Rav Chisda's Ruling

### Rav Chisda Intro

The daf opens by returning to Rav Chisda's ruling that one who damages or destroys the priestly gifts — most prominently *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva*, but extending as well to classical gifts such as *terumah* and *ma'aser*, and by analogy to the gifts given to the poor such as *leket*, *shikcha*, and *pe'ah* — is not obligated to pay in a court of law.

### Mamon She'ein Lo

The reason for this exemption is that these gifts belong to no single identifiable claimant. This is the principle of *mamon she'ein lo tov'in*: property without individual claimants. The gifts are owned by the collective — the collective of *kohanim* or the collective of the poor — and since no particular person was harmed in any provable or assignable sense, no individual can file suit. This is distinct from a class-action scenario in secular law, where many individuals are each separately injured and combine their claims. Here, no specific person was deprived of anything that was demonstrably theirs. One person among the group lost out, but it cannot be proven which one.

### Ownership vs Mitzvah

A more radical explanation was also considered, grounded in the verse of *vezeh* — that the *kohanim* and *levi'im* do not own these gifts at all until the moment of formal separation or bestowal, and that the giver carries only a *mitzvah* obligation rather than a genuine proprietary debt. However, because the *gemara* has broadened the discussion well beyond *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* to encompass *terumah*, *ma'aser*, and the gifts to the poor, the primary analytical weight falls on the *mamon she'ein lo tov'in* explanation: ownership resides in the collective, not in any individual who could enforce a claim.

### Midat Chasidut

That said, the *gemara* concludes that one is not entirely off the hook in a moral sense. Even though no court can compel payment, there exists an obligation — at minimum the dimension of *midat chasidut*, and perhaps stronger than that — to make good to the collective. If these were funds of the poor, one ought to give to the poor; if they were funds of the *kohanim*, one ought to give them something in compensation. The enforceability is absent; the moral weight is not.

---

## Tevel Eating Case

### Tevel Braitah

The *gemara* now brings a *ta shema* — a challenge to Rav Chisda's position from a *braita*. The *braita* asks: from where do we know that a homeowner who ate his produce while it was still *tevel* — that is, without having first separated *terumot uma'asrot* — and similarly a *levi* who ate his *ma'aser* without having separated *trumat ma'aser* for the *kohen*, is exempt from monetary payment to the *kohen* or *levi* who thereby lost out?

The answer provided is the verse: *velo yechalelu et kodshei benei Yisrael asher yarimu l'Hashem* — "they shall not desecrate the sanctified things of the children of Israel which they shall separate off to God." The *braita* derives: *ein lecha bahen ela mishe'at harama va'eilach* — you, the *kohen* or the *levi*, have no standing in them until the moment of separation. Their ownership does not begin until the gift is actually set apart.

### Ukimta Distinction

The *gemara* immediately draws an inference from this *braita*: the verse establishes that *before* separation there is no ownership and no obligation to pay — but the implication (*ha mishe'at harama va'eilach*) is that *after* separation, if you were to eat or destroy the *terumah* or *ma'aser*, you would be obligated to pay. This seems to be a strong challenge to Rav Chisda's blanket rule.

The *gemara* responds with a notably narrow *ukimta*. The contrast being drawn in the *braita* is not, as one might have assumed, between *tevel* in the owner's hands versus separated *terumah* in the owner's hands. Rather, the *braita* is contrasting *tevel* in the owner's hands with *tevel* that has already been physically transferred to the *kohen*. The *tanna* here holds the view of *matnot shelo hurmu kemi shehurmu damyan* — that even before formal separation, the gifts are treated as though they have already been designated. What therefore determines liability is not whether separation has occurred, but rather whose possession the produce is in. Once the *kohen* has received the grain — even if it still has the status of *tevel* — he fully owns the *terumah* embedded within it, and if you were then to damage it, you would owe him.

### Tosafot Challenge

This *ukimta* is striking, because it fundamentally inverts the plain reading of the *braita*. The entire thrust of the passage was to draw a legal distinction along the axis of separation: before separation, no ownership; after separation, full ownership. The *gemara* replaces that axis entirely with the axis of possession. Tosafot is deeply troubled by this move and attempts to explain the *gemara*'s direction. This is a recognizable Talmudic pattern: Rav Chisda has made a ruling, a *braita* seems to contradict it squarely, and the *gemara* constructs an unusual or narrow framing to avoid a direct conflict — even when that framing cuts against the *braita*'s own internal logic.

---

## Royal Seizure Case

### Seizure Scenario

The *gemara* tries again with another *ta shema*. The case: the king seizes someone's entire granary — whether as payment for back taxes or through outright confiscation. Had that grain remained with the owner, he would have been obligated to separate *terumot uma'asrot* from it, including the *ma'aser* that would have gone to a *levi*. Does he still owe that *ma'aser* to the *levi*, even though the grain is gone?

### Debt vs Seizure

The *braita* draws a sharp distinction. If the seizure was *bechovo* — the owner genuinely owed those taxes, and the grain was taken as legitimate payment of a real debt — then he is *chayav le'aser*: he must give *ma'aser* from other grain to the *levi*. The *levi* was effectively cheated out of his portion because the owner used what would have been the *levi*'s *ma'aser* to satisfy his own debt. But if the seizure was *be'anparut* — an unjust, coercive taking, where the king simply grabbed the property without any real debt underlying it — then the owner is *patur*: he is exempt. Since he did not use the grain to discharge a legitimate obligation, and the grain was simply stolen from him, he is not required to compensate the *levi* from other resources.

This case seems to pose a powerful challenge to Rav Chisda, since it implies that there is a genuine monetary obligation to the *levi* that can be triggered even before any formal separation or transfer has taken place.

### Mishtarshe Leh

The *gemara* answers: *shani hatam dekamishtarshe leh* — that case is different, because there the benefit has taken root by him. This introduces a crucial halakhic concept. Even in the absence of a formal act of damage or theft or borrowing, there are situations where a person has concretely benefited from someone else's property, and that benefit is treated as though it has become embedded in his financial position. The *gemara* elsewhere offers analogous examples: if one's sheep falls from a roof and its fall is cushioned by another's grain, no formal damage has been committed — but the sheep owner derived a real benefit from the other's property, and that benefit is considered to have "taken root" in his ledger. Similarly, if a sheep ate grain in the public domain where no damage liability applies, the sheep owner nevertheless saved himself the cost of feeding the animal, and that saving constitutes a concrete benefit derived from the other's property.

In the royal seizure case, when the owner had a real debt and the king's seizure paid it off, the owner benefited by the amount of one box of *ma'aser*. He owed ten boxes but only had to use nine of his own; the tenth — which belonged conceptually to the collective of *levi'im* — covered his debt for him. That concrete financial benefit has "taken root" in his accounts. He cannot be taken to court by any particular *levi*, because no individual *levi* can prove it was his money — the principle of *mamon she'ein lo tov'in* still applies. But the abstract reality of having received a benefit from collective property generates an obligation to restore that benefit to the collective. This is the principle of *mishtarshe leh*, and the *gemara* emphasizes that it is a significant halakhic concept, whether its source is rabbinic or biblical.

### Tosafot Distinction

This answer, however, creates a problem that Tosafot raises directly. Recall that Rav Chisda's ruling extended not only to damaging the priestly gifts but also to eating them. If someone ate *matnot kehuna* before they were given, Rav Chisda says there is no obligation to pay. Yet eating also produces a benefit — one saved oneself a meal. Why does *mishtarshe leh* not apply to eating just as it applies to paying off a debt?

Tosafot's answer draws a meaningful distinction. When you eat something, the sense in which you have a concrete positive balance in your ledger is not straightforward. You might have gone without the meal; the benefit is diffuse and not precisely quantifiable. But when you pay off a real debt with property that wasn't entirely yours, the bottom line benefit is unmistakable and precisely calculable: you owed ten and only had to supply nine of your own. That elevated and concrete form of benefit — a genuine improvement to your financial position that can be measured — is what generates the *mishtarshe leh* obligation. Mere consumption, without that kind of clear positive ledger entry, does not rise to the same level. Hence Rav Chisda can maintain that eating does not obligate, while the debt-payment case does.

---

## Organ Purchase Case

### Organ Braitah

Another *ta shema*. The *braita* describes a case where a person approaches a butcher and says: sell me the internal organs of this cow. The organs include the *keivah*, the stomach, which is one of the gifts owed to the *kohen*. The buyer paid a flat price for all the organs. The ruling: *noten l'kohen* — the buyer must give the *keivah* to the *kohen* — *v'eino menakeh lo min hadamim* — and he cannot claim a refund from the butcher. The rationale is straightforward: if you purchase "the organs" as a category, you are on notice as a buyer that the *keivah* is among them and that you will not be able to keep it. The price was set for all the organs including the one you must give away, and you cannot claim to have been misled.

### Price vs Weight

If, however, the buyer purchased by weight — he asked for a quantity of organ meat, it was weighed out, and the *keivah* happened to be among the pieces — the ruling differs. He still must give the *keivah* to the *kohen*, but here *umenakeh lo min hadamim*: he can seek a refund from the seller for the weight of the *keivah*, since he had no particular reason to expect it would be included and he was charged for weight he cannot keep.

### Transfer Question

The *gemara* then poses its challenge: once ownership has transferred through the sale, why must the buyer give the *keivah* to the *kohen* at all? Let this be like the case of *mazik matnot kehuna* or *ochlan* — let it be as though the gifts have been consumed or destroyed, and since no individual *kohen* can demand compensation in that scenario, why should the buyer be obligated to give anything?

### Gifts While Exist

The *gemara*'s answer here is relatively straightforward: *shani hatam d'isnehu b'eineihu* — the case is different there because the gifts still exist. The entire question of Rav Chisda's ruling concerned situations where the gifts had been damaged or destroyed and nothing remained. Wherever the gifts physically exist, they must be given — the *mitzvah* to give them and the collective ownership of them by the *kohanim* remain intact regardless of whose hands the gifts have passed through. The sale does not extinguish the obligation; it merely shifts whose hands the item is in. The *gemara* notes that one possible reason to have thought otherwise would be the position grounded in the *pasuk* of *vezeh* — that the obligation is purely situational and tied to the original owner's possession — but even on that view, the ruling is that wherever the gifts exist, they must be given.

---

## Nine Gifts List

### Gift Enumeration

The *gemara* now cites a *braita* listing nine gifts of the *kohen* — though the text is subject to variant readings: Rashi's version reads fifteen, Tosafot's reads seven, and the precise enumeration has exercised the commentators considerably. Setting aside the question of why some gifts are included and others omitted, the focus here is on the list's purpose and what it teaches.

The gifts enumerated include *terumah*; *terumat ma'aser*, the tenth-of-the-tenth that the *levi* gives to the *kohen* from the *ma'aser* he receives; *challah*, the dough gift; *reishis hagez*, the first shearings; *umatanos*, the gifts of *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* from the slaughter of an animal; *hademai*, which is a rabbinic category — when one buys grain from an *am ha'aretz* whose *terumot uma'asrot* observance is uncertain, one separates *terumat ma'aser* and gives it to a *kohen*, since *ma'aser* itself is assumed to have been taken but *terumat ma'aser* cannot be assumed; *habikkurim*, the first fruits; and *keren vachomesh* — the principal and fifth paid back in the case where someone stole from a convert, swore falsely in denial, and the convert subsequently died without heirs. The Torah directs that in such a case the repayment goes to the *kohanim*.

### Nichsei Question

The question raised is: why does the *braita* call these gifts *nichsei kohen* — the property of the *kohen* — rather than simply calling them gifts to the *kohen*? The word *nichsei*, property, implies full ownership. Does this not suggest that the *kohen* owns them even before they have been physically given, such that if you damaged them you would have to pay him? Surely if calling them his "property" meant only that he owns them once he has received them, that would be patently obvious and not worth stating.

### Freedom of Use

The *gemara* answers: *lo* — that is not the point being made. The purpose of calling them *nichsei kohen* is explained by reference to a *mishna* in Bikkurim: *lama amru nichsei kohen* — why did they call them the property of the *kohen*? *Shekoneh bahen avadim vekarka'os uveheimah teme'ah* — to teach that the *kohen* has complete freedom in how he uses or spends the proceeds. Unlike certain sanctified things — such as the flesh of a *chatat* offering, which cannot be taken out of the *Beis HaMikdash* and cannot be exchanged for other goods — the gifts enumerated here, even those that carry *kedusha* such as *terumah*, may be freely used for any commercial purpose. The *kohen* can sell his *terumah* to other *kohanim*, use the proceeds to buy land, slaves, non-kosher animals, pay off debts, and a wife can collect her *kesuvah* from these goods. The emphasis of *nichsei kohen* is the *kohen*'s freedom of disposition, not a statement about pre-transfer liability. Rashi notes that the inclusion of a *sefer Torah* in the list is puzzling — if one may buy a pig with it, of course one may buy a *sefer Torah* — but regardless, the halakhic point stands: the phrase *nichsei kohen* does not constitute proof that one who damages these gifts before giving them is civilly liable.

---

## Levi Grabbing Case

### Levi Incident

At this point the *gemara* shifts direction somewhat. There was a certain *levi* who would hover near the butcher's stall, and as soon as an animal was slaughtered he would rush in and grab the *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva*.
