The problem is obvious: the gifts are designated for a *kohen*, not a *levi*.

### Rav's Complaint

People came and reported this behavior to Rav. Rav responded: *lo mistaya delo shaklina minei* — is it not enough that we do not take his own *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* away from him when he slaughters his own animals? We refrain from forcing him to give it, and that already represents a significant concession. *Ella miktaf nami khatif* — and he also goes and grabs other people's? This expression of moral outrage reflects Rav's view that the *levi*'s behavior is at minimum improper, and that his being spared from giving his own gifts already represents unusual leniency.

### Am Status Question

The *gemara* now unpacks the logic of Rav's statement and finds a tension within it. The question is whether *levi'im* are included in the word *am* — the people — in the verse *me'et ha'am*, "from the people," which establishes the obligation to give *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva*. There are many contexts in which *levi'im* stand apart from the general Israelite community: they receive no tribal land inheritance and are not counted among the fighting force. So does *me'et ha'am* include *levi'im* or not?

If *levi'im* are included in *am* and are obligated to give *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva*, the *gemara* asks: *mishkal nami lishklo minaihu* — why didn't Rav compel the *levi* to give his own gifts? And if *levi'im* are not included in *am* and are genuinely exempt — *Rachmana patreinhu*, the Torah exempted them — then why did Rav speak in a tone implying that there was something questionable about the *levi* keeping his own? If he is exempt, he is simply exercising his exemption; why frame it as a concession?

### Rav's Doubt

The *gemara* resolves this by saying: *mesafeka leh* — Rav was uncertain. He did not know whether *levi'im* are called *am* or not. Because of that doubt, Rav could not force the *levi* to give his own *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* — since in monetary matters the operative principle is *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'ayah*: the burden of proof lies with the one seeking to extract property from another. Since Rav could not prove the obligation, he could not compel payment. But it was not enough for this *levi* to benefit from that doubt — he then proceeded to grab gifts belonging to others entirely.

This raises the broader question of why we apply the civil framework (*hamotzi mechaveiro*) rather than the religious framework of *safek de'oraita le'chumra*. The answer — as discussed in the *Birchat Shmuel* — is that when the fundamental question is civil in nature (does one person owe another money?), we adjudicate it as a civil matter, and the religious dimensions of the obligation are understood through that civil determination. The *kohen* or *levi* seeking the gift bears the burden of proving entitlement; if they cannot, the holder is not compelled.

---

## Kohen Gifts Rules

### Rav Idi Question

Rav Pappa was sitting and presenting this entire discussion about Rav's doubt regarding the *levi*'s status. Rav Idi bar Avin approached Rav Pappa with an attempt to resolve the question by drawing on an analogy from the *braita* concerning gifts to the poor. The structure of the comparison — between how the gifts of the poor and the gifts of the *kohanim* are treated with respect to *tovat hana'ah* and compulsion — is meant to shed light on whether a *levi* would be obligated to give *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* to a *kohen*. This argument unfolds across the next section.

---

## Poor's Gifts

### Vineyard Gifts

The *braita* presents a systematic summary of the gifts given to the poor during the harvest season. In the vineyard there are four such gifts: *peret* and *olelot*, *shikcha*, and *pe'ah*. *Peret* corresponds to *leket* in a grain field — the individual grapes that drop from the hand during harvesting. *Olelot* are underdeveloped clusters: a normal cluster has a shoulder (*katef*) and a lower dripping section (*nataf*); a cluster that has formed without one of these characteristic features is considered an *olelot* and must be left for the poor. *Shikcha* refers to clusters that were overlooked and left behind after the harvest — things "behind you" that you forgot. *Pe'ah* is the intentional leaving of a corner section of the vineyard for the poor.

### No Choice Principle

Of all these gifts, the *braita* rules: *ein bahen tovat hana'ah le-be'alim* — the owners have no right to designate which poor person receives them. The reason, as the *gemara* will derive, is that the verse uses the language of *azivah* — abandonment: *ta'azov otam*, you shall leave them. The owner steps back; the poor come and take. He does not give to specific recipients of his choosing; he abandons the produce and the poor gather it. The classic imagery is precisely of an owner who is absent while the poor collect freely.

### Poor Give Too

A significant ruling follows: *ve'afilu ani she'be'Yisrael motzi'in oto miyado* — even a poor person who happens to own a small piece of a vineyard or a field is compelled to leave these gifts for other poor. He cannot reason that since he himself is poor, he will simply retain everything for his own use. The *gemara* derives this from the verse *v'leket k'tzircha lo telaket*, reading it as addressed to the *ani*: even you, the *ani*, shall not gather your own *leket*. You must leave it for others.

### Maaser Ani House

The rules differ, however, for *ma'aser ani* — the tithe given to the poor in the third and sixth years of the Sabbatical cycle — when it is distributed from within the owner's house (*hamitchalek be-toch beito*). Here the *gemara* rules: *yesh bo tovat hana'ah le-be'alim* — the owner does have the right to decide which poor person receives it. The reason is that the verse uses the language of *netinah* — giving: *ki titein*, you shall give. When you give, you are an active agent; you direct the gift to a specific recipient of your choice. This is in contrast to the *azivah* model, where you relinquish control entirely.

Tosafot, drawing on the Yerushalmi, makes a further distinction: there may actually be two different statuses of *ma'aser ani* depending on where the separation occurs. If separated at the threshing floor, it has the status of the field gifts — the owner abandons it and the poor come to take. But if brought into the house and then separated, the owner's connection to it is stronger, and the *netinah* model applies — he gives it actively to a recipient of his choosing. Tosafot also notes that even where the owner has *tovat hana'ah* and may designate the recipient, if a poor person comes and forcibly takes possession, the owner cannot recover it; the choice has been subverted but the taking is valid.

---

## Kohen Gifts Rules (II)

### Kohen No Choice

The *braita* continues: *ve-sha'ar matnot kehuna kegon zroa lechayayim vekeiva* — as for the other gifts of the *kehuna*, such as *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* — *ein motzi'in otan miyado*: you do not force a *kohen* to give them to another *kohen*. This stands in contrast to the poor, where we compel even a poor person to give to other poor. By the priestly gifts, a *kohen* who holds his own *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* is not forced to hand it over to another *kohen*.

### Levi to Kohen

The *braita* then adds — puzzlingly — *velo milevi l'levi*: nor do you compel a *levi* to give it to another *levi*. Since *levi'im* are not entitled to receive *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* in the first place, the statement seems odd on its face. But the *gemara* focuses on what this implies by contrast: if you don't force a *levi* to give it to another *levi*, the implication (*ha*) is that you would force a *levi* to give it to a *kohen*. This in turn would establish that *levi'im* are indeed obligated — they are included in *am* — and must give the gifts just as any *Yisrael* would. This constitutes a potential resolution of Rav's doubt. The *gemara* will now subject this inference to a series of interpretive challenges.

---

## Poor's Gifts (II)

### Field Gifts

The *gemara* turns to enumerate the scriptural sources for each gift. For the three field gifts — *leket*, *shikcha*, and *pe'ah* — the verse states: *uvkutzrechem et ketzir artzechem lo techaleh pe'at sadecha bekutzrecha* — do not finish the corner of your field in your harvesting (this is *pe'ah*); *v'leket k'tzircha lo telaket* — do not gather the droppings of your harvest (this is *leket*); and *ki tiktzor k'tzircha b'sadecha v'shachachta omer basadeh* — when you harvest and you forget a sheaf in the field (this is *shikcha*).

### Tree Gifts

For trees, the *gemara* establishes only two gifts: *shikcha* and *pe'ah*; there is no *leket* equivalent for trees. The source is: *ki tachbot zeitecha lo tefa'er acharecha* — when you beat your olive tree, do not *tefa'er* it afterward. Rav Levi explains that the word *acharecha* — "after you" or "behind you" — refers to *shikcha*, things left behind that were forgotten. The school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets *lo tefa'er* as meaning "do not strip it of its glory" — that is, leave some behind — which is the law of *pe'ah*. The word *tefa'er* is understood as a verb meaning to remove *pe'ah*, parallel to the way certain Hebrew verbs denote the removal of something rather than its addition. Having established both *shikcha* and *pe'ah* for olive trees, the *gemara* applies a *gezeirah shavah* from the word *acharecha* to derive the same two gifts for vineyards.

### Poverty Lesson

Returning to the ruling that even a poor person must give these gifts to other poor, the *gemara* notes the broader lesson embedded in this halakha. No one, however disadvantaged, is exempt from the obligations of giving. This reflects a profound principle: even those who are themselves recipients of communal charity remain full and equal members of a society structured around mutual obligation. The ability to give — even in small measure — carries its own dignity. It means something to be a contributor, not only a recipient. This is reflected as well in the concept of *maaser kesafim*: a person in genuine financial difficulty may direct much of his *maaser* toward his own needs, for *tzedaka* begins at home — but the framework of giving is never entirely suspended.

---

## Narrowing Attempts

### Ma'aser Rishon

The *gemara* now attempts to narrow the *braita* that implied *levi'im* are obligated, seeking to read it as not referring to *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* at all. The first reinterpretation: when the *braita* says "something like the *zeroa*" but not the *zeroa* itself — *kegon hazroa velo zroa* — perhaps it refers to *ma'aser rishon*.

The logic runs as follows. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya holds that *ma'aser rishon* may be given to a *kohen*, since *kohanim* are themselves members of the tribe of Levi. Rabbi Akiva disagrees, holding that *terumah* goes to a *kohen* and *ma'aser rishon* goes to a *levi*. If we follow Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya post-Ezra's *takana*, the picture shifts: Ezra was angered that the *levi'im* did not make *aliyah* during the Second Temple period, and — though not explicitly stated in the biblical text — the *gemara* understands that he instituted a fine: henceforth, do not give *ma'aser rishon* to the *levi'im*; give it to the *kohanim* instead, since they too are Levites.

Under this reading, the *braita*'s statement that you do not force a *kohen* to give to another *kohen* means: a *kohen* who receives *ma'aser rishon* need not pass it to another *kohen*. You do not force a *levi* to give to another *levi* — meaning the *levi* may keep his own *ma'aser* without being forced to share with another *levi*. And the implied case where you would force the gift — from *levi* to *kohen* — refers to the post-Ezra situation where *ma'aser* should be directed to *kohanim*.

However, the *gemara* objects: even granting Ezra's fine, it could only mean that we stop giving *ma'aser* to *levi'im* going forward — *d'la yahavinan lehu*. It could never mean that we forcibly extract *ma'aser rishon* from a *levi*'s hands and transfer it to a *kohen*. So this reading collapses: we cannot use the post-Ezra framework to generate a case where a *levi* is compelled to give *ma'aser* to a *kohen*.

### Reishis HaGez

The *gemara* therefore tries a second reinterpretation: *umai nihu reshit hagez* — the gift referred to is *reishis hagez*, the first shearings. The verse mandating *reishis hagez* does not use the word *am*, so this is a gift that any Israelite — including a *levi* — must give to a *kohen*. Under this reading, the *braita* means: a *kohen* who shears his own sheep need not give *reishis hagez* to another *kohen*; a *levi* who shears his own sheep need not give to another *levi* (who is in any case not entitled to receive it); but a *levi* who refuses to give *reishis hagez* to a *kohen* would be compelled to do so. This reading at least avoids the problems of the *ma'aser rishon* interpretation. But it still does not resolve the question of whether *levi'im* are obligated specifically in *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva*.

### No Kedusha Cases

A further *ta shema* is then brought, which states the rule in terms of *kedusha*: anything that has sanctity — *terumah*, *terumat ma'aser*, *challah* — you take out of a *levi*'s hands if he refuses to give it to a *kohen*, because it carries *kedusha* to which the *levi* is not entitled. Anything that does not have sanctity — such as *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* — you do not take out of the *levi*'s hands. At first glance, this seems to state directly that *levi'im* are exempt from *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva*. But the *gemara* applies the same move again: *kegon zroa velo zroa* — this is referring to something like the *zeroa* but not the *zeroa* itself, and *mai nihu* — what is it? *Ma'aser rishon* after Ezra's fine, which has no *kedusha*. Even post-Ezra, when *ma'aser rishon* is directed to *kohanim*, we would not forcibly extract it from a *levi*'s hands. The case of *zeroa lechayayim vekeiva* proper remains unresolved.

---

## Direct Proof

### Shechting Braitah

The *gemara* now brings what appears to be a direct and explicit proof. A *braita* states: *hashocheit l'kohen u'l'oveid kochavim patur min hamatanos* — one who slaughters an animal on behalf of a *kohen* or on behalf of a non-Jew is exempt from giving the gifts. The reason in the case of a *kohen* is obvious: the *kohen* himself receives and keeps the gifts. In the case of a non-Jew, the non-Jew has no obligation and when the slaughter is performed for his benefit the gifts do not apply. The *braita* then implies: *ha l'levi u'l'yisrael chayav* — if you slaughter for a *levi* or for a *Yisrael*, you are obligated to give the gifts. This seems to prove that a *levi* is included in the obligation just as a *Yisrael* is.

### Corrective Reading

The *gemara* responds: *lo teima ha l'levi u'l'yisrael chayav* — do not read it as "for a *levi* or a *Yisrael* you are obligated." Instead, *ela eima ha Yisrael chayav* — read it as "for a *Yisrael* you are obligated." The *levi* case remains unstated and therefore unresolved.

### Counter Argument

This corrective reading is met with an immediate objection. If the *levi* were in fact exempt, the *braita* would have said so explicitly — it would have listed the *levi* alongside the *kohen* and the non-Jew as cases of exemption: *hashocheit l'kohen u'l'levi u'l'oveid kochavim patur*. The fact that the *braita* only mentions the *kohen* and the non-Jew as exempt, and then lists the *levi* alongside the *Yisrael* as obligated, is strong evidence that the *levi* is indeed obligated. Furthermore, a second *braita* states explicitly: *l'levi u'l'yisrael chayav* — for a *levi* or a *Yisrael*, you are obligated. This is presented as a *tiyuvta d'Rav* — a formal contradiction of Rav's position.

---

## Am Inclusion Dispute

### Yom Kippur Verse

Rav, however, does not concede. He responds: *tannai hi* — this is a dispute between *tanna'im*, and there is a *tanna* who supports his position. The *gemara* cites a *braita* on the verse concerning the Yom Kippur atonement: *v'al hakohanim v'al am hakahal yechapper* — "and for the *kohanim* and for the people of the congregation it will atone." The *braita* expounds each word: *kohanim kemashmao* — the *kohanim* as the word implies; *am hakahal eilu yisrael* — the people of the congregation refers to the Israelites; *yechapper eilu haleviyim* — "and it will atone" — this extra word atones for the *levi'im*. The significance: the *levi'im* needed their own separate word for inclusion, meaning they are not subsumed under the term *am*. Had they been included in *am*, the word *yechapper* would have been superfluous.

### Tana Debate

Another *braita* reads the same verse differently: *yechapper eilu avadim* — "and it will atone" refers to slaves. This *tanna* would say the *levi'im* are included in the word *am* and need no separate word; it is slaves who require the extra inclusion. The *gemara* concludes: *mah lav beha kamiflgi* — is this not precisely the dispute? One *tanna* holds that *levi'im* are called *am* and are included; another holds that they are not called *am* and require a separate word for inclusion. This is a genuine *tannaitic* disagreement.

### Rav's Uncertainty

The final line of the *gemara* addresses Rav directly: if Rav holds like the *tanna* who says *levi'im* are included in *am*, let him rule accordingly and compel the *levi* to give the gifts; if he holds like the *tanna* who says they are not included, let him rule accordingly and declare the *levi* exempt. The *gemara* answers: *mesafeka leh* — Rav genuinely does not know. He cannot determine which *tanna*'s view is correct, and he therefore cannot resolve the question with confidence.

The practical consequence follows directly from *hamotzi mechaveiro alav hara'ayah*: the burden of proof falls on the one who seeks to extract a payment. Since the *kohen* cannot prove that the *levi* is obligated, the *levi* cannot be compelled to give. The evidence adduced in the *braita*ot strongly suggests that *levi'im* are indeed included in *am* and are obligated — but Rav maintains uncertainty, and that uncertainty is sufficient to insulate the *levi* from legal compulsion. Whether this uncertainty survives all the textual evidence brought against it is a question the *gemara* leaves open, to be taken up in the continuation.

---

---

# Hullin 133

## Exemption Framework

### Shochet & Ownership

The *mishnah* at the top of 132b opens with the ruling *hashochet l'Kohen ul'oved kochavim patur min hamatanot*: one who slaughters for a *kohen* or a non-Jew is exempt from the *matanot*. The *mishnah*'s phrasing, which focuses on the *shochet* rather than the owner, raises an immediate structural question: why frame the law around the act of slaughtering rather than around the ownership of the animal? After all, it is the ownership — or, more precisely, for whom the animal is being slaughtered — that determines whether an obligation exists.

The *gemara* navigates a subtle distinction here. The determination of *chiyuv* or *p'tur* turns on who owns the animal, or at least for whom the *shechitah* is being performed. Yet the person with whom the *kohen* deals to collect his gifts is the *shochet*, not necessarily the owner. One could well imagine a case where a *yisrael* owns a cow and hires a *shochet* to slaughter it: the obligation to give the gifts falls on the *shochet*, even though the *shochet* does not own the cow. Conversely, if the cow belongs to a *kohen* and the *shochet* is a *yisrael*, the *shochet* is exempt. The ownership of the animal — or the identity of the party for whom the slaughter is performed — governs the question of obligation, while the *shochet* is the relevant legal actor for purposes of fulfilling or defaulting on that obligation.

One might ask whether the question is truly about ownership at the moment of *shechitah* or about a more functional notion of "for whom" the animal is being slaughtered. The *gemara* never fully resolves this distinction, but working assumption throughout is that ownership at the moment of *shechitah* is the operative criterion.

### Rava's Exposition

The *gemara* asks pointedly: why does the *mishnah* say "one who slaughters *for* a *kohen*" rather than simply "a *kohen* and a non-Jew are exempt"? *Rava* answers: *zos omeres hadini im hatabach* — this teaches us that the legal relationship is with the butcher, the *shochet*. The *mishnah*'s formulation is deliberate. Had it stated that the *kohen* is exempt, one might have concluded that you pursue the owner of the cow. By framing it as "one who slaughters for a *kohen*," the *mishnah* locates the obligation squarely with the *shochet*.

*Rava* further derives this from a *derasha*. The verse states *me'eis ha'am* — "from the people" — excluding *kohanim*: a *kohen* need not give these gifts to a fellow *kohen*. What determines the obligation is for whom the animal belongs, not who performs the slaughter. As the verse adds, *me'izovchei hazevach* — "from those who slaughter the slaughtering" — this language encompasses even a *kohen* who serves as a butcher. The irony is precise: the determination of obligation depends on the ownership of the animal, but the person obligated is always the *shochet*.

## Exemption Framework (II)

### Partnership Strategy

This framework naturally gives rise to a strategy. If ownership by a *kohen* exempts the *shochet* from giving *matanot*, what if a *kohen* becomes a business partner in the butchery operation? Insofar as the *kohen* holds a share of the animals being slaughtered, those animals are — at least partially — being slaughtered for a *kohen*, and the *shochet* might claim exemption on that basis.

## Rav Tavla's Plan

### Partnership Proposal

The *gemara* presents a concrete case. *Rav Tavla* had a guest — a *kohen* — who was suffering financial hardship (*dachik lei milsa*). *Rav Tavla* advised him: *zil ishtatef bahadi tavchei Yisrael* — go and enter into a partnership with the Jewish butchers. The logic is that since you will be a partner with them, and they will thereby be slaughtering partly for a *kohen*, they will be exempt from giving the *matanot* (*d'migo d'miptari mimatnasa mishtatfi bahadach*). In exchange, the *kohen* receives a percentage of the business's profits — a more reliable income stream than occasionally collecting *zero'a lechayayim v'keiva* and waiting in line behind other *kohanim*.

The implicit assumption is that these butchers own the animals they slaughter — they purchase livestock, slaughter it, and sell the meat — so that at the moment of *shechitah* the animal is theirs, and the partnership with the *kohen* means part of it is being slaughtered on behalf of a *kohen*-owner. Even though the meat is immediately destined for sale to the general public, the ownership at the moment of *shechitah* appears to be what matters.

### Nachman's Rejection

*Rav Nachman* rejected the arrangement. When the butcher protested — *v'ha Rav Tavla patran*, "but *Rav Tavla* exempted us!" — *Rav Nachman* replied sharply: *zil afik*, go and give the gifts, *v'ei lo mafkina lach Rav Tavla m'oneich* — if you do not, I will remove *Rav Tavla* from your ear. The dismissiveness of the phrase is telling. *Rav Nachman* was not persuaded by the authority of *Rav Tavla*'s ruling and enforced the giving of *matanot* regardless.

*Rav Tavla* then came before *Rav Nachman* to ask why he had done this. *Rav Nachman* explained by citing a tradition brought by *Rav Acha bar Chanina* from the south, in the name of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*.

### South Elders' Rule

*Ziknei darom* — the elders of the south — ruled as follows: *Kohen tabach* — if a *kohen* is himself a butcher, meaning he owns the animals and is slaughtering them for sale, he is technically exempt from giving *matanot*, since at the moment of *shechitah* the animals are his. Nevertheless, *shtayim v'shalosh shabbatos patur min hamatnos* — for two or three weeks this exemption holds. *Mikan v'eilach chayav b'matnos* — from that point onward, he becomes obligated.

The reasoning is implicit but important. Technically, as long as the *kohen* owns the meat at the moment of *shechitah*, even with the intention of immediately reselling it to the public, he is exempt. The moment of slaughter is what matters, not the ultimate destination of the meat. However, once it becomes established that the *kohen* is operating as a butcher for the broader community — and that is what his business consists of — it is no longer appropriate or legitimate to claim the exemption. There is no biblical basis for the two-to-three week grace period, as *Tosafot* notes; it must be a rabbinic ruling. But the principle it reflects is that the exemption cannot serve as a vehicle for permanently avoiding the institution of *matanot*.

## System Protection

### Tosafot's Concern

*Tosafot* explicitly articulates the broader concern underlying *Rav Nachman*'s ruling. The worry is not merely about the individual *kohen* who happens to be a butcher, but about the systemic abuse of the exemption. As *Tosafot* states: *shelo yargilu tibchei Yisrael leshatef kohanim imahem lehipater min hamatnot* — we do not want Jewish butchers to make it a practice to partner with *kohanim* as a mechanism for evading *matanot* altogether. For the first two or three weeks, one cannot be certain whether the arrangement is a deliberate evasion or a genuine situation. After that point, the intent is clear, and the exemption is disallowed.

*Rav Nachman* added a further refinement to the storefront test. He explained: *hani mili d'lo kavia michtata* — this leniency applies only where the person does not have an established storefront. *Aval heicha d'ka-hacha kavia michtata* — but where there is a visible, fixed business operation, allowing the partnership exemption would obviously subvert the entire institution of *matanot*, since every butcher would immediately obtain a *kohen* as a nominal partner. The storefront is the dispositive marker: when the commercial operation is unmistakably running as a community-serving business, no partnership exemption is available.

### Chisda's Ban

*Rav Chisda* declared: *hai kahana d'lo mafrish matnata lei havei beshamta le-Elohei Yisrael* — a *kohen* who does not separate off the *matanot* is under a *ban* in the name of God. The phrase *beshamta le-Elohei Yisrael* is striking. The concern here, as clarified by the *Rif* and the *Rosh* cited in the commentaries, is the case of a *kohen* acting as a butcher where the animals are not owned by a *kohen* — and yet, because the *shochet* himself is a *kohen*, he declines to give the gifts. Against this, *Rav Chisda* imposes the *shamta*.

*Rava bar Rav Shila* then reports that the butchers of *Hutza* have been under *Rav Chisda*'s ban for twenty-two years.

### Compliance Not Punishment

One might read this statement as a critique of the ban's ineffectiveness, but the *gemara* draws a different conclusion. The question becomes: *le-mai hilchata* — what is the legal significance of this observation?

The suggestion that we should now lift the ban since it has clearly not worked is rejected by a *baraita*. The *baraita* distinguishes between punishment for a *lo ta'aseh* — a negative commandment — where one receives lashes and the matter is concluded, and a *mitzvas aseh* — a positive commandment. For a positive commandment, the principle is that we apply continuing pressure, *makin oto*, not as punishment for the past transgression but to compel future compliance. The ban on the butchers of *Hutza* is therefore not a punitive measure that has run its course. It is an instrument of compulsion, and the fact that it has persisted for twenty-two years without yielding compliance is not a reason to rescind it.

The *gemara* identifies a secondary legal implication of the twenty-two-year duration: *d'kansinan lehu belo asraisa* — we may now fine them without prior warning. They have had twenty-two years of warning. If it is now decided to shift tactics and begin imposing fines, no fresh warning is required. The *gemara* cites examples: *Rava* fined a butcher an entire thigh (*atma*) for refusing to give *zero'a lechayayim v'keiva*, awarding a larger cut to the *kohanim* as the penalty. *Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* went further and confiscated a *glima* — a cloak — underscoring that the fine need not be taken from the meat itself but can come from whatever is effective.

## Gift Protocol

### Proper Eating

*Rav Chisda* states: *matnot kehuna einan ne'akhalot ela tzali* — the gifts of the *kehunah* should be eaten only roasted, *v'ein ne'echelet ela bechardal* — and only with mustard. This is particularly evocative with respect to the tongue, which was included among the gifts along with the rest of the jaw area, and which would naturally be served roasted with mustard. The *gemara* asks for the basis of this requirement and cites the verse *lemoshcha* — meaning *ligdula*, for greatness. *Kederech shehamelachim ochlim* — the *kohen* should eat the way kings eat. The giving of these gifts is not a charity transaction. It is an act of honor, recognizing the *kohen*'s status as the religious representative of the people, performing the *avodah* on their behalf. The manner of eating should reflect that.

This raises an apparent tension with the *gemara* in *Zevachim*, where the rule is that *kohanim* may prepare *kodshim* however they like — roasted, boiled, or cooked. *Tosafot* addresses this directly. The ruling there (*resha'in hakohanim leshanot ba'achila lochelan tzloyim shluchin umevushalin*) grants discretion to the *kohen* to eat as he prefers. *Tosafot* explains: if roasting is genuinely how he most enjoys his food, he fulfills the intent by eating it roasted. But if all preparations are equally satisfying to him — if he has no strong preference — then *yochal tzli shehu gedula yoter*: he should eat it roasted, since that is the socially recognized mode of refined eating. The requirement is not an absolute override of personal preference but a default toward the manner of eating that signals honor and status to the broader community.

### Knowledge Requirement

*Rav Chisda* adds: *kol kohen she'eino baki bahen ein notnin lo matanah* — a *kohen* who is not expert in the twenty-four *matnot kehunah* does not receive a gift. *Rashi* interprets this in light of the preceding teaching: *heich din matanah heich ne'echalim bigdula* — "expert in them" means knowing how to eat them properly, understanding the nature and significance of the gifts and receiving them in the manner of honor. The *gemara* thus presents a coherent picture in which giving and receiving are both governed by an ethos of respect: the *shochet* is the one obligated to give, but the *kohen* too must understand the context in which he is receiving. The institution is not a mechanical transfer of meat but a social practice laden with religious meaning.

### Avodah Requirement

The *gemara*, however, immediately rejects this as the operative ruling. *V'lav milta hi* — that is not the *halacha*. In its place, a *baraita* is cited. *Rabbi Shimon* teaches: *kol kohen she'eino modeh ba'avodah ein lo chelek bakehunah* — any *kohen* who does not accept the *avodah*, who disclaims responsibility for or denies the legitimacy of the Temple service, has no portion in the *kehunah* and receives none of the gifts. The verse is cited: *hamakriv et dam hashelamim ve'et hachelev mivnei Aharon lo tihyeh shok hayamin lemana* — the one who offers the blood and the fat receives the thigh as his portion. From this the *gemara* derives that participation in and acceptance of the *avodah* is a prerequisite for receiving any priestly portion.

### Fifteen Services

The *baraita* then asks how we know this principle extends to all the *avodot* beyond the specific one mentioned in the verse. The answer is derived from the phrase *mivnei Aharon* — the service entrusted to the children of *Aharon*. Any *kohen* who does not accept his responsibility for the full range of that service has no portion. The *baraita* enumerates fifteen *avodot*: the *yetzikot* and *belilot* (the pouring and mixing of oil on *menachot*), the *ptitot* (breaking *menachot* into pieces), the *melichot* (salting the *korbanot*), *tnufot* and *hagashot* (waving and presenting to the altar), *kmitzot* (taking the handful), *ketoret* (burning incense or the handful on the altar), *melikot* (the *melika* for a bird), *mitzui hadam* (squeezing the blood of a bird), *kabalot* (catching the blood of an animal), *haza'ot* (throwing the blood), *hashka'at sotah* (administering the *sotah* waters), *arifat eglah* (breaking the neck of the calf in the *eglah arufah* ceremony), *taharat metzora* (the purification of the *metzora*), and *nesiat kapayim* (the lifting of the hands in the priestly blessing — *bein mibifnim bein mibachutz*, whether in the *Beit HaMikdash* or in the *beit hakeneset*).

The *gemara* draws a pointed conclusion from this. The original attractive idea — that you must know *how* to eat the gifts in a dignified manner — was rejected in favor of something more fundamental: you must accept the *chiyuv* of the *avodah* itself. *Ta'ama d'eino modeh bah* — the disqualification is because you reject the obligation. *Hamodeh bah*, af al gav *d'eino baki bahen* — if you accept it, even if you are not an expert in the details of the gifts, you are still entitled to receive them. The point is acceptance of responsibility, not technical mastery.

## Gift Mechanics

### Grabbing vs. Receiving

*Rav Yosef* posed a question to his students: *hai kahana d'chatif matnata* — a *kohen* who grabs the gift — is this an expression of *chivuv mitzvah*, eagerness to perform the *mitzvah*, or is it *mezalzel b'mitzvah*, a denigration of the *mitzvah*? The framing captures a genuine ambiguity. One could argue that running to grab the gift reflects zeal for the religious obligation. But there is an equally plausible reading: grabbing is undignified and undermines the very context of honor that should surround the giving and receiving of *matanot kehunah*.

The students resolved the question from a *pasuk*: *v'natan* — "and he shall give" to the *kohen* — *v'lo she-yitol me-atzmo*, which implies the *kohen* should not take it for himself. The verse specifies an act of giving by the *shochet* and receiving by the *kohen*, not a seizure. This both resolves the technical question — grabbing is impermissible — and reinforces the broader social meaning of the transaction: the giving of the gift is a relational act between two parties, not a unilateral appropriation.

### Abaye's Evolution

*Abaye*, himself a *kohen*, offers an unusually candid account of his own evolving practice. Initially, he would grab the *matanot* — *me-reisha hava chatifna matnasa* — telling himself *amina chivuvei ka-mechaveivna mitzvah*, that he was expressing love for the *mitzvah* by rushing to perform it. Once he heard the *drasha* on *v'natan v'lo she-yitol me-atzmo*, he stopped grabbing. Instead, *meimar amri havu li* — he would verbally request the gifts from the butcher, reasoning that at least he was not physically seizing them and was still expressing his desire to participate in the *mitzvah*.

### Shemuel's Sons

Then *Abaye* heard a *baraita* citing *Rabbi Meir* on the sons of *Shmuel*. The verse says *vayitu acharei habatza* — "and they turned after gain." *Rabbi Meir* explains: *bnei Shmuel chelkom sha'alu b'fihem* — the sons of *Shmuel* requested their portions verbally. The *gemara* operates with the assumption that *Shmuel* was a *levi*, and his sons would accordingly be entitled to their *matnos Levi'ah*. Yet their practice of asking for what was owed them is interpreted as "turning after gain" — pursuing material benefit. Even verbally requesting one's legitimate portion, rather than waiting for it to be offered, is read as a kind of avarice, since it signals that the desire for the material benefit is the dominant motivation. *Meimar nami lo amina* — *Abaye* therefore stopped asking as well. However, *i yahavu li* — if a butcher were to come and offer him the gifts spontaneously, *shaklina* — he would of course accept.

### Yom Kippur Exception

Even this final posture — accepting only when freely offered — was then called into question. *Abaye* heard a *baraita* about the *lechem hapanim* toward the end of the Temple period, when there was insufficient bread to go around among all the *kohanim*. The *tznu'im*, the modest ones, would step back and decline to take; the *gargaranim*, the gluttonous ones, would divide it up among themselves. *Tosafot* frames this in terms of deference to others with greater need: even to simply receive when other *kohanim* are present and may need it more is not the ideal posture. Therefore, *mishkal nami lo shaklina* — *Abaye* also stopped accepting the gifts.

There was, however, one exception: *levar mi-malei yoma d'kippurai* — except for *Erev Yom Kippur*. Why? *Lachazukei nafshai bi-khahuna* — to establish publicly that he is a *kohen*. On *Erev Yom Kippur*, when everyone is slaughtering and eating meat, all the *kohanim* are receiving their portions. If *Abaye* were the only one not receiving, people would assume he is not a *kohen* at all. To avoid that false impression — *v'illu lo hayah notel hayu omerim she'eino Kohen*, as *Tosafot* states — he would take on that occasion. The *gemara* then asks: why not instead do *birkat kohanim* to publicly establish his identity as a *kohen*? The answer is *anseiah leh idna* — his schedule prevented him from regularly attending *shul*. Whether due to illness, as some explain, or because his teaching obligations conflicted with the *minyan* time, as *Rashi* understands it, *Abaye* did not have a reliable opportunity to perform *nesiat kapayim*.

## Teaching & Transfers

### Transfer to Student

*Rav Yosef* rules: *hai kahana d'it leh tzurba merabbanan b'shivvavuteih v'dachika leh milta* — if a *kohen* has a *talmid chacham* in his neighborhood who is suffering financial hardship, *lizkei leh matnasa* — he should transfer his *matanot* to the *talmid chacham*. This is straightforward once the *kohen* has received the gifts; what is novel here is that the transfer can be effected even before the gifts come into the *kohen*'s physical possession.

How? The institution of *makirei kehunah u'leviya* makes this possible. When a *kohen* is an established recipient — when it is well known that a particular family consistently gives to him — his ownership of the forthcoming gifts is considered sufficiently certain that even before *shechitah* he can transfer that entitlement to another. Whether this operates as a form of *mechiras davar shelo ba l'olam* turns on a broader discussion in *Gittin* about whether one can sell something not yet in one's possession. The comparison is drawn to a case where a commodity is reliably available in the market: if I know I can obtain it immediately, there is an argument that a pre-sale is valid. Similarly, where the gifts will predictably be given to this *kohen*, the transfer in advance has legal effect.

### Rava & Safra Story

*Rava* and *Rav Safra* once came to the home of *Mar Yohana*, the son of *Rav Chana bar Adda* (or, in an alternative version, *Rav Chana bar Bizna*), who prepared for them an *egla tilsa* — a prized young calf. There is some dispute as to what *tilsa* means precisely: one interpretation is a third-grown calf, tender and young; another is the third calf born to the cow; a third understands it as three years old, though this last reading is flagged by *Jastrow* as incorrect. Whatever the precise meaning, it was understood as a special and honored dish.

*Mar Yohana*'s attendant was a *kohen*, and it was known that the master of the house customarily gave the *zero'a lechayayim v'keiva* to this attendant. *Rava* said to him: *zachi lan matnasa* — please transfer your gifts to us, *d'beina l'meichal lishna b'chardala* — I would like to eat the tongue in mustard. The attendant complied. *Rava* ate; *Rav Safra* declined to eat from the gift.

That night, the following verse was read to *Rav Safra* in a dream: *maade beged beyom karah*, *chometz al neter*, *v'shar beshirim al lev ra* — a worn cloak on a cold day, vinegar on mineral, singing to someone with a wicked heart. The implication seemed to be a rebuke for refusing to act on a valid teaching.

*Rav Safra* came before *Rav Yosef* and asked whether this was because he had gone against *Rav Yosef*'s ruling that a *kohen* may transfer *matanot* to a *talmid chacham*. *Rav Yosef* clarified: the ruling applies to an independent *kohen* who acts of his own free will — *b'acher, shama*. In the case of the attendant, however, *ba'al korcho masar* — he had no real choice. He was a servant in the household; when an honored guest like *Rava* asks him to transfer his portion, he cannot refuse. Such a transfer under duress is not what *Rav Yosef* had in mind. Moreover, *Rav Yosef* added: even the legitimate case applies only when the *talmid chacham* genuinely lacks means — *l'man d'lo efshar leih*. *Ha efshar leih* — but *Rav Safra* had means, so the transfer should never have been solicited from him in the first place.

The dream, then, was not directed at *Rav Safra*. It was meant for *Rava*, who had compelled the attendant and had sought a portion for a colleague who did not need it. *V'likriun l'Rava* — so why was it read to *Rav Safra* rather than to *Rava*? *Rava nazuf hava* — *Rava* was in a state of divine displeasure; heaven did not wish to engage with him directly. The verse was therefore delivered to *Rav Safra*, the intermediary. This precise dynamic is captured by the Yiddish expression: *der tochter zog ich, di shner mein ich* — I am speaking to my daughter, but I mean my daughter-in-law. Unable to address *Rava* directly, the rebuke reached him through *Rav Safra*.

### Yosef's Clarification

*Rav Yosef*'s clarification thus draws sharp parameters around the legitimate use of the transfer mechanism. It requires: a *kohen* who is an independent agent and gives willingly; a *talmid chacham* who is genuinely in need; and a genuine gift relationship — *makirei kehunah* — that gives legal force to the pre-*shechitah* transfer. Absent these conditions, the mechanism is inapplicable or worse — an abuse.

### Unworthy Students

The *gemara* then asks *Abaye* what the simple *peshat* of the verse that was read to *Rav Safra* is, and *Rav Dimi* answers: *b'shoneh l'talmid she'eino hagun* — it refers to one who teaches a student of bad character. This launches the *gemara* into a sharp discussion about the dangers of teaching Torah to an unworthy student.

*Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav*: *kol hashoneh l'talmid she'eino hagun nofel b'Gehinnom* — one who teaches an unworthy student will fall into *Gehinnom*. The danger is not merely that the Torah will be wasted, but that it will be weaponized. Teaching Torah to someone of genuinely bad character gives that person tools to undermine the Torah from within. The verse cited — *kol choshech tamun litzfunav tochlehu esh lo nupach yera sarid b'ohalo* — is interpreted with the phrase *eil sarid ela talmid chacham*. The *Maharsha* objects to reading *sarid* as the unworthy student; one would not call such a person a *talmid chacham*. He therefore reads the verse as referring to the *talmid chacham* doing the teaching: *yera b'ohalo* — it will be evil in his tent if he teaches such a person.

*Rav Zeira* in the name of *Rav* adds: *kol hashoneh l'talmid she'eino hagun k'zorek even l'markulis* — it is like throwing a stone at the *markulis*, the idol. The metaphor is explained by the *Maharsha*: throwing a stone at the *markulis* appears to be a hostile or denigrating act, but in fact it constitutes a form of worship of that idol. Similarly, teaching the unworthy student looks like the dissemination of Torah, but in reality it provides ammunition to those who will use it destructively. The verse cited: *k'tzror even b'margemah kein nosein l'ksil kavod* — like binding a stone in a sling is giving honor to the fool.

The *gemara* then resolves this with the general principle of *kol ha'osek b'Torah shelo lishmah* — that learning Torah not for its own sake can eventually lead to learning *lishmah*. *Tosafot* elsewhere distinguishes between two categories: one who comes to learning with fundamentally redeemable character, in whom the process of learning will itself effect transformation, and one who comes with deliberate malicious intent to use Torah destructively. It is the second category — clearly of bad character and bent on abuse — toward which these severe warnings are directed. The gray areas remain, and the tradition maintains the tension between an open approach that hopes learning will elevate and a more guarded approach that recognizes the dangers of arming those who will cause harm.

## Ownership Shares

### Marking Rule

The *mishnah* states: *hamishtatef imahem tzarich lirshom* — one who enters into a business partnership with a *kohen* or non-Jew must mark the animal. Since the partnership arrangement exempts the *shochet* from giving *matanot*, without a visible marker people observing the butcher not giving the gifts would be puzzled or misled. The mark communicates the reason for the exemption.

### Marking Distinctions

The *gemara* introduces a tension from a *baraita*: *hamishtatef im kohen tzarich lirshom* — partnership with a *kohen* requires marking, but *hamishtatef im ovdei kochavim u'psulei mukdashin* — partnership with a non-Jew, or animals that were once *hekdesh* and have been redeemed (*psulei mukdashin*), does not require marking. Why should there be a difference?

After several attempts to explain the distinction by appeal to various observable circumstances — whether the non-Jew is sitting visibly in the shop, whether he is counting the money, whether he is simply present at the counter — the *gemara* settles on a more pointed explanation. When the non-Jew is sitting at the counter, the *gemara* initially suggests he might be mistaken for a customer. But could people not equally mistake the *kohen* for a customer? The answer turns on trust: *ein heimuna b'oved kochavim*. *Rashi* is careful to soften this: *ein Yisrael regilim leha'amin bahem* — Jews are not accustomed to trusting non-Jews. It is not an evaluative claim about non-Jewish character, but a descriptive sociological observation: in that world, Jews did not typically entrust their business finances to non-Jews. Therefore, if a non-Jew is seen managing the money box, people immediately understand he must be a genuine partner, and no mark is needed. By contrast, when a *kohen* sits at the money box, people might assume the butcher simply trusts him — not that he is a legal partner — hence the need for a mark.

A second resolution is also offered: *stam oved kochavim mefap-peit* — the non-Jew partner will simply talk too much and be too visibly directive. If a non-Jew is sitting in the shop giving instructions about which piece to sell and at what price, it will be unmistakably clear to everyone that he is a business partner. No marking is required because the partnership is self-evident.

For *psulei mukdashin*, the *gemara* ultimately explains that the exemption-without-marking applies specifically to those animals — such as a *bechor* with a *mum* or an animal *ma'aser* — that must by law be sold from the home rather than in the marketplace, and weighed by the unit rather than by the pound. That distinctive mode of sale makes the animal's prior *hekdesh* status apparent to anyone who sees it. Where *psulei mukdashin* are sold in the ordinary way, in the marketplace and by weight (*yikru bahen nishchatin b'itliz v'nishkalin b'litra*), no one would know the animal's history, and a mark would be required. The resolution — *targema Rav Adda bar Ahava kammai d'Rav Pappa b'ozen hen nimkarin betoch habayis* — limits the "no marking needed" rule precisely to those cases where the manner of sale already broadcasts the animal's status.

### Huna's Rule

*Rav Huna* rules: *shutfut berosh patur min halechi* — if the *kohen* is a partner in the head, you are exempt from the cheek area. *Shutfut beyad patur min hazroa* — if he is a partner in the arm, you are exempt from the *zero'a*. *Shutfut bivnei meayim patur min hakeivah* — if he is a partner in the intestines, you are exempt from the *keivah*. The operative principle is that the *kohen*'s ownership must extend to the actual body part from which the gift is taken. Partial ownership of the rest of the animal does not suffice; the partnership must encompass the specific gift portion itself.

### Chiya's Rule

*Chiya bar Rav* stakes out a more expansive position: *afilu shutfut be'achat mehen patur mikulan* — even if the *kohen* is a partner in only one of the three gifts, he is exempt from all of them. On this view, the three gifts — *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah* — form a single halachic unit. Partial ownership in any one of them generates a blanket exemption from all three.

### Specific Exemption

The *gemara* challenges *Chiya bar Rav* from a *baraita*. The *baraita* distinguishes explicitly: *harosh sheli v'chulah shelcha* — if the *kohen* retains the head, even *afilu echad mimeah berosh* — even one percent of the head — *patur min halechi* — you are exempt from the jaw portion — *v'chayav bekulan* — but obligated in the remaining two gifts. Similarly, ownership only of the hand exempts only from the *zero'a* but not the others; ownership only of the intestines exempts only from the *keivah* but not the others. *Tiyuvta d'Chiya bar Rav tiyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation. The *halacha* is that the exemption is specific to the gift for which the *kohen* holds a portion.

*Rav Chisda* explains what led *Chiya bar Rav* to his erroneous position: *ha matnitin atisya l'Chiya bar Rav* — it was the following *baraita* that caused him to err. That *baraita* enumerates the twenty-four *matnot kehunah*, and in its enumeration counts *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah* as a single unit. *Chiya bar Rav* inferred from this that the three gifts are treated as one halachic entity. But the inference is mistaken. The same *baraita* counts the gift from the *todah* and the gift from the ram of a *nazir* as one unit (*muram mitodah v'eil nazir*), even though those are quite different: the *todah* involves the *chazeh* and *shok* with loaves of bread, while the *nazir* involves the *zero'a*. They are plainly distinct gifts. The reason they are counted as one is simply that they are similar in kind — both are *kodshim kalim* in which the *kohen* receives a part — *damyan lehadadi*, and so they are grouped together for the purposes of counting. The same is true of *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah*: they are similar to one another and grouped together for counting purposes, but that grouping carries no halachic implication that they form a unified entity for purposes of the exemption.

## 24 Matanot List

### 10 in Temple

The *baraita* enumerates the twenty-four *matnot kehunah* in three geographical categories. The first group, *eser bamikdash* — ten gifts given in the *Beit HaMikdash* and eaten there — comprises: the meat of the *chatat*; the meat of the *chatat ha'of*, the bird *chatat*; the *asham*, including both *asham vadai* (for a definite sin) and *asham taluy* (for a doubtful sin); *zivchei shalmei tzibur*, the communal *shlamim* brought on *Shavuot*; *log shemen shel metzora*, the remaining oil from the *metzora*'s purification; *shtei halechem*, the two loaves of *Shavuot*; *lechem hapanim*, the twelve loaves on the *shulchan*; *she'ar haminchot*, the remainder of individual *menachot*; and *minchat ha'omer*, which is the communal *mincha* and is listed separately for that reason.

### 4 in Jerusalem

The second group, *arba b'Yerushalayim* — four gifts eaten throughout all of *Yerushalayim* — consists of: *habechorah*, the firstborn animal; *habikkurim*, the first fruits (which are brought to the *Beit HaMikdash* but may be eaten throughout *Yerushalayim*); *muram mitodah u'me'eil nazir*, the priestly portions from the *todah* offering and the ram of the *nazir*, which are *kodshim kalim* and may be eaten anywhere in *Yerushalayim*; and *orot kodshim*, the hides of sacrificial animals, including the hide of the *olah*, which are given to the *kohanim* and may be used throughout *Yerushalayim*.

### 10 Throughout Israel

The third group, *eser bigvulin* — ten gifts distributed throughout all of *Eretz Yisrael* — includes: *terumah*; *terumat ma'aser* (the *terumah* separated by the *levi* from his *ma'aser*); *challah*; *reishit hagez*, the first shearings; *matanot* — meaning *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah*, counted here as one; *pidyon haben*, the redemption of the firstborn son; *pidyon peter chamor*, the redemption of the firstborn donkey; *sdei achuzah u'sdei charamim*, certain dedicated fields that revert to the *kohanim* at *yovel* or at other applicable times; and *gezel hager*, the restitution for theft from a convert who dies without heirs.

### Counting Convention

The fact that *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah* are listed as a single entry in this enumeration, despite being three distinct gifts, was what misled *Chiya bar Rav* into treating them as a single halachic unit. The *gemara* makes clear that this grouping is a counting convenience, not a substantive legal merger. The comparison to *muram mitodah v'eil nazir* — which are counted as one despite being structurally distinct — establishes that the counting convention reflects similarity of category rather than halachic identity. *Kivan d'damyan lehadadi chashiv lehu kechada* — since they resemble one another, they are counted as one; but for the purpose of determining the exemption through partnership, each gift stands independently. There is also an aesthetic dimension to the enumeration: the ten-four-ten structure is symmetrical and easy to remember, and achieving that symmetry required counting the three *matanot* as one unit. The grouping serves the purposes of enumeration and memorization, not legal derivation.

# Hullin 134

## Female Kohanim & Gifts

### Female Status

Before turning to the new daf, two points from yesterday's discussion deserve brief summary. The first concerns the twenty-four *matnot kehuna* and the surprising inclusion of the skins of the *korbanot* among the gifts eaten in Yerushalayim. Even the skin of an *olah* is given to the *kohanim*, yet we have never heard that this is limited to Yerushalayim. When the Rambam addresses this, he describes it as a gift *ba min hamikdash* — it comes from the Temple — but does not say it may only be used in Yerushalayim. One might suggest that ideally the *kohanim* would keep it there as a matter of respect, though the Rambam stops short of requiring it.

The second point concerns the status of female *kohanim* — *kohanos* — and female *leviyot* in receiving priestly gifts. The Gemara had emphasized, following Rashi, that *zroa lechayim vekeiva* carries no *kedusha*, and therefore the restrictions that apply to *kedusha*-bearing gifts — which belong specifically to male *kohanim* and their immediate households — do not govern it. A *kohenet* is entitled to *zroa lechayim vekeiva* and *reishit hagez* by virtue of her own personal status, not merely as a member of her father's household. This holds even if she is married to a non-*kohen*, even to a *Yisrael* — as the Gemara made explicit — since it is her own priestly identity, not her family affiliation, that creates the entitlement.

The Rambam extends this principle to a *leviyah* for *maaser*, since *maaser* likewise carries no *kedusha*, and a *leviyah* is independently entitled to it. The same logic applies to the question raised about *pidyon bechor*: since the Rambam groups all *bechor*-related gifts together, and since the *bechor* of an animal is restricted to male *kohanim* on account of its *korban* status, the *pidyon bechor* — both of a firstborn son and of a *peter chamor* — follows the same classification, even though those latter gifts carry no independent *kedusha*. The Rambam confirms this explicitly. The organizing principle is clear: gifts bearing *kedusha* follow the Torah's emphasis on male *kohanim* and their households; gifts without *kedusha* open the door to the independent status of *kohanos* and *leviyot*.

### Rambam on Terumah

The Rambam's position becomes considerably more striking when it comes to gifts that do carry *kedusha*. One might have expected that even if a *kohenet* is entitled to non-*kedusha* gifts in her own right, gifts like *terumah*, *terumas maaser*, and *challah* would remain the exclusive domain of male *kohanim* and their families. The Rambam, however, rules that a person may give *terumah* and *challah* directly to a *kohenet* — provided she is unmarried, since a *kohenet* married to a *Yisrael* cannot eat *terumah*. This has left commentators astounded, as it appears to run against numerous passages elsewhere in the Talmud.

The way the later authorities reconcile this is to note that the Rambam must be speaking of an unmarried *kohenet*, one who has no impediment to eating *terumah*. But even granting that qualification, it remains a remarkable extension: the Rambam is saying that even where the gift is a *kedusha*-bearing item like *terumah* or *challah*, a *kohenet* is entitled to receive it directly on the strength of her own status, not merely as part of her father's priestly household. Concretely, a person could, according to the Rambam, give his *terumah* to an unmarried *kohenet* as a direct fulfillment of the obligation. The same principle applies to a *leviyah* for *maaser*, which the Rambam states definitively, though there the absence of *kedusha* makes the case less surprising.

### Kedusha & Recipients

The underlying framework that ties these rulings together is the distinction between gifts that carry *kedusha* and those that do not. Gifts with *kedusha* — *korbanot*, *bechor* of animals, *terumah* when the question of eating is implicated, and the like — place particular weight on the category of male *kohanim* and their immediate families, as the Torah's formulations emphasize. Gifts without *kedusha*, including *zroa lechayim vekeiva*, *reishit hagez*, *pidyon bechor*, *pidyon peter chamor*, and *maaser* for *leviyot*, carry no such restriction, and the personal status of a *kohenet* or *leviyah* is sufficient to establish entitlement in her own right.

One further nuance emerges from the connection the Rambam draws between *zroa lechayim vekeiva* and *terumah* appearing in the same *pasuk*. The Rambam seems to read the juxtaposition as supporting the principle that wherever personal status suffices — wherever there is no overriding reason to restrict the gift to the male priestly household — the *kohenet* is entitled directly. It remains a daring ruling, and the commentators continue to wrestle with it, but the Rambam's internal logic is coherent.

---

## Partial Ownership

### Head vs. Body Split

The Gemara now poses the following question at the very bottom of 133b. A *kohen* who owns an animal says to a *Yisrael*: "The head is yours and the rest is mine." The *Yisrael* thus acquires only the head of the animal, and it is precisely in the head that the *lechayayim* — the jaw — is found. Does the *Yisrael* have to give that *matana* to a *kohen*? He owns only the part of the animal that contains the *matana*, but the main body of the animal belongs to the *kohen*.

This is the mirror image of the case discussed the previous day, where a *kohen* owning even a partial share of the *matana* portion was sufficient to exempt the *Yisrael*. Here the question runs in the opposite direction: does the *Yisrael*'s ownership of the specific portion that contains the *matana* — and only that portion — create an obligation to give it?

### Batar Chiyuva vs. Ikar

The Gemara frames the question as a dispute between two principles. *Batar chiyuva azlinan*: we follow where the obligation is located — that is, where the *matana* itself resides, which is in the *Yisrael*'s portion. If so, the *Yisrael* who owns that portion is obligated. Or *batar ikar behema azlinan*: we follow the main animal — the principal part of the *behema* belongs to the *kohen*, and therefore there is no obligation on the *Yisrael* who holds only a secondary portion.

The question is not merely technical. It turns on how we conceptualize the nature of the obligation: does it attach to whoever holds the specific anatomical gift, or does it require a relationship to the animal as a whole?

### Reishit Hagez Proof

The Gemara brings a proof from *reishit hagez*. If a *kohen* or a non-Jew gives his sheep to a *Yisrael* to shear, the *Yisrael* is exempt from giving *reishit hagez*, because the animal is not his — the obligation follows the owner of the sheep. And if a *Yisrael* purchases only the shearings — only the wool — without owning the sheep itself, he is likewise exempt. This establishes that by *reishit hagez*, the obligation depends on ownership of the whole animal, not merely ownership of the product. The principle operating there is *batar ikar behema*: you must own the animal, not just the gift that comes from it.

### Zroa Proof

But the Gemara then cites a *ברייתא* that teaches a contrast: *veze chamur bizroa uvelchayim uvekeiva yoter mireshit hagez* — there is a greater stringency by *zroa lechayim vekeiva* than by *reishit hagez*. The implication is that by *zroa lechayim vekeiva*, owning just the portion that contains the gifts is sufficient to create an obligation, even without owning the main animal.

### Zroa Resolution

The Gemara concludes: *shema mina batar chiyuva azlinan* — we learn from this that by *zroa lechayim vekeiva*, the operative principle is *batar chiyuva*, we follow where the obligation is located. The *Yisrael* who owns only the head — the portion that contains the *lechayayim* — is therefore obligated to give that *matana*, even though the main body of the animal belongs to the *kohen*. By *reishit hagez* the rule is different; there one must own the full animal. The two obligations are thus governed by distinct principles.

---

## Conditional Sale

### Chutz Exclusion

The Gemara now turns to a set of cases involving conditional language in the sale of an animal. The *Mishnah* states: if a *kohen* sells his animal to a *Yisrael* and explicitly says *chutz min hamatanot* — "except for the gifts" — meaning he is transferring ownership of the animal but retaining ownership of the *zroa lechayim vekeiva* — then the *Yisrael* does not have to give those gifts. He never acquired them.

### Al Menat Condition

Against this, the Gemara cites a *baraita* that appears to rule otherwise. If a *kohen* sells an animal to a *Yisrael* and stipulates *al menat shehamatnot sheli* — "on the condition that the gifts are mine" — the buyer may disregard the stipulation and give the gifts to whichever *kohen* he wishes. The *Yisrael* is not bound by the condition.

### Chutz vs. Al Menat

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing the legal structure of the two formulations. *Chutz* operates as a *shiyura* — a reservation. When the *kohen* says "except for the gifts," he is not transferring ownership of that portion to begin with. He is selling most of the animal while leaving part of it in his own possession, which is a perfectly valid mode of partial sale. The *Yisrael* never owns the *matanot*, so there is nothing to give.

*Al menat*, by contrast, is not a reservation. The *kohen* using *al menat* is selling the entire animal — lock, stock, and barrel — but attaching a condition to the complete sale. The animal changes hands entirely; the *kohen* is then attempting to impose a subsequent obligation on the buyer.

### Rabbinic Prevention

Why doesn't that condition hold? After all, contractual conditions are generally enforceable, and *Tosafot* notes that if a sale is made *al menat* and the condition is not fulfilled, the entire sale should arguably be voided. Some *Rishonim* accept that in principle the *Yisrael* is bound by the condition — but the Rabbis will not enforce it. The reason is the norm established earlier in the tractate: a *kohen* is not permitted to walk around demanding the gifts or positioning himself as entitled to receive them from a specific slaughter. The whole point of the obligation is that it is the *Yisrael*'s prerogative to decide which *kohen* to give the gifts to. A *kohen* who stipulates *al menat* is playing an entitlement game — using the language of contractual conditions to effectively demand what he should only be able to receive — and the Rabbis will not allow the machinery of contract law to be used toward that end.

### Ritva's View

The Ritva offers a different and more technical explanation. He argues that the outcome depends on the precise formulation. If the *kohen* had said *al menat shetitten li* — "on the condition that you give them to me" — that would be a real condition demanding a specific act, and the buyer would be obligated to fulfill it. But the formulation in our case is *al menat shehamatnot sheli* — "on the condition that they are mine." This is not a condition demanding action; it is a claim of fact. It is, in effect, a declaration that the *matanot* already belong to the *kohen* — which is either meaningless or factually incorrect, since the *matanot* do not yet belong to him. At most, he might receive them; they are not his as a matter of right. The Ritva therefore reads the stipulation as self-defeating: it purports to establish a factual state of ownership that does not exist, and therefore cannot be treated as a valid condition.

One might push back and say the statement sounds like an assertion of entitlement — a claim that the *kohen* retains control over them. But that is precisely the problem: the *kohen* has no such control, and if the stipulation were taken to its logical conclusion, it would mean the condition was never satisfied and the sale never went through. The cleaner explanation, and arguably the more satisfying one halachically, remains the first: the Rabbis simply will not permit this form of entitlement-claiming.

---

## Tannaitic Debate

### Opinion 1: Retention

The Gemara notes that there is in fact a Tannaitic dispute about the *al menat* formulation. The first opinion holds that *al menat* in this context means: I am not selling the *matanot*. Under this reading, the phrase functions similarly to *chutz* — it expresses the *kohen*'s intent not to transfer ownership of the gifts. Since he is understood to be retaining them, the *Yisrael* acquires the animal without the *matanot*, and the *kohen* keeps them.

### Opinion 2: Stipulation

The second opinion holds that *al menat* means precisely what it says: I am selling the whole animal but imposing a condition. Under this reading, the sale is complete and includes the *matanot*, but the *kohen* is attempting to attach an obligation to the buyer. As discussed, this stipulation is not enforced — the Rabbis decline to allow it to operate as a binding condition.

---

## Intestines Case

### Price Determination

The *Mishnah* concludes with the case of someone who buys the intestines from a butcher. If the buyer purchased all the intestines at a flat price, the *keivah* — the stomach — is included in what he acquired, and he must give it to a *kohen*. He receives no discount from the butcher, since he agreed to a fixed price and the stomach was part of the package; he should have known. If, however, he bought by weight, he still gives the stomach to the *kohen*, but he is entitled to a discount from the butcher equivalent to the weight of the *keivah*, since the butcher charged him for something he would never be able to keep.

### Rav: Butcher Liability

Rav qualifies this rule: *lo shanu ela sheshakal l'atzmo* — the distinction between flat price and by weight applies only if the buyer himself weighed out the intestines. But if the butcher did the weighing, then the *kohen* may deal with the butcher directly — *hadin im hatabach*. In that case, the butcher placed the stomach on the scale and charged for it, effectively appropriating something that belonged to the class of *kohanim*.

---

## Theft of Matanot

### Ramban: Benefit

This raises an immediate difficulty. Throughout the preceding discussion, the Gemara established that one cannot collect compensation for damaging *matnot kehuna* because they are *mamon she'ein lo tov'im* — money with no specific claimant who can sue. How then can a *kohen* go to the butcher?

The Ramban draws a crucial distinction. There was a case discussed earlier where the king's officers seized the gifts to satisfy debts, and there the ruling was that the owner must compensate the *kohen*. The reason it differs from ordinary damage is that the person who appropriated the *matanot* derived direct financial benefit from them. The benefit is still sitting, so to speak, in his account. The butcher did not merely destroy the stomach — he sold it and collected payment for it. That monetary gain belongs to the *kohanim*, and because it represents concrete, present benefit that was extracted from something not his to sell, he must give it back. It is not the same category as *mazik matnot kehuna*, where one simply diminishes or destroys something with no standing owner. Here there is ill-gotten gain, and that gain can be demanded.

The question of who exactly goes to the butcher remains somewhat open. The Ramban's framing suggests it is not a conventional lawsuit — *mamon she'ein lo tov'im* still means no specific *kohen* can compel the butcher in court. But the butcher bears the moral and legal responsibility. One possibility is that the case involves *makirei kehuna* — a known *kohen* to whom the gifts were designated — who would then have standing to demand compensation. Alternatively, a *kohen* might be able to demand it without being able to formally litigate it. The phrase *hadin im hatabach* — the law is with the butcher — sounds as though there is actionable liability, even if the Ramban's analysis moderates what that means in practice.

---

## Intestines Case (II)

### Rav Ashi: Buyer Only

Rav Ashi disagrees with Rav. Even if it was the butcher who weighed out the intestines, the sole responsibility rests with the buyer — *hadin im ba'al habayit*. The buyer is the one who now possesses the *keivah*, and it is he alone who must give it to the *kohen* or bear accountability for it. The butcher's role in the transaction does not shift the obligation to him.

---

## Theft of Matanot (II)

### Rav Chisda Rule

The Gemara now attempts to frame the dispute between Rav and Rav Ashi as a debate about Rav Chisda's principle. Rav Chisda rules: if someone stole an object and the original owners have not yet despaired of recovering it, and a second party then came and consumed or destroyed it — *ratza mizeh goveh ratza mizeh goveh* — the owners may collect from either the thief or the consumer, since each one committed a distinct wrong against them. The thief removed the object from their possession; the consumer destroyed it. The Gemara initially suggests that Rav follows Rav Chisda — the butcher who appropriated the stomach can be pursued, just as a thief can — while Rav Ashi rejects Rav Chisda and says only the person currently holding the object can be pursued.

### Abstract Ownership

The Gemara then complicates this picture by raising a more fundamental question: can *matnot kehuna* be stolen at all? This question has two distinct layers. First, does a *kohen* even own the *matanot* before they are formally separated and given? The *Yisrael* owns the animal until the moment of giving; the *matanot* are not yet the possession of any specific *kohen*, only of the abstract class of *kohanim*. If they are not yet owned by any individual, there may be nothing to steal in the classical sense. Second, even granting that they belong in some sense to the class of *kohanim*, the act of theft classically involves removing an object from someone's control and possession. But the *matanot* are not under the control of any particular *kohen* prior to being given — they are, as it were, owned by a category rather than by a person. If so, what does it mean to steal them? Moving the stomach from one place to another, or transferring it from one person to another, does not seem to dispossess any particular *kohen* who was holding it.

### Rav: Can Steal

Rav holds that *matnot kehuna* can be stolen. This is consistent with the earlier principle of *mamon she'ein lo tov'im* — a principle that, paradoxically, seems to acknowledge that the *kohanim* do own the *matanot* even before receiving them (otherwise the concept of "money with no claimant" would not apply). If there is ownership — even abstract, collective ownership — it is conceptually possible to steal. The butcher who intentionally gave the stomach to someone else rather than the *kohen* effectively took it away from the class of *kohanim*, and can therefore be pursued.

### Rav Assi: Cannot Steal

Rav Assi holds that *matnot kehuna* cannot be stolen. Since there is no specific possessor — no individual *kohen* from whose grip the object was removed — the act of appropriation does not constitute *geneivah* in the technical sense. Under this view, one can only pursue the person who physically has the object; there is no additional claim against the intermediary who set the process in motion.

### Principle Agreement

The Gemara resolves the framing: *de-chulei alma it lehu de-Rav Chisda* — everyone in principle accepts Rav Chisda's rule that one may collect from either the thief or the consumer when both committed wrongs. The debate between Rav and Rav Ashi is not about Rav Chisda's general principle at all. The real dispute is whether *matnot kehuna* constitute a stealable entity in the first place. Rav holds that they do, and therefore the butcher who appropriated them falls into Rav Chisda's category of a thief who can be pursued. Rav Assi holds that they do not, and therefore only the person with the object in hand can be held to account.

---

## Convert's Animal

### Shechita Timing

The next *Mishnah* takes up the case of a convert who owned an animal. If the animal was slaughtered before he converted, no *matnot* need be given — it is treated as the animal of a non-Jew, which is exempt. If it was slaughtered after his conversion, he is obligated. If the timing is uncertain — say, someone on his farm slaughtered the animal while he was in the process of converting — he is exempt: *safek patur*.

### Burden of Proof

The governing principle is *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-re'aya* — the burden of proof rests with whoever seeks to collect. A *kohen* who wishes to claim the gifts from the convert must prove that the animal was slaughtered after the conversion took place. Without that proof, the convert need not give anything.

This raises a tension that runs throughout the *perek*. Should we not approach this through the lens of *mitzvah* rather than civil liability — and say that since there is a possibility I owe a *mitzvah*, I should perform it? The Gemara's answer, as we will see, is that when the obligation is purely monetary, the civil standard of proof controls; it is only when there is an *issur* dimension that we say to be strict in cases of doubt. Here, failing to give *zroa lechayim vekeiva* does not render any food forbidden, so the civil lens governs, and the *kohen* who claims the gifts has the burden of proof.

---

## Doubt & Obligation

### Reish Lakish Proof

The Gemara reports that when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he conveyed the following exchange: Reish Lakish challenged Rabbi Yochanan from our *Mishnah*. Our *Mishnah* says *safek patur* — in cases of doubt, the convert is exempt, and we rule leniently when there is uncertainty about the *matnot*. But, Reish Lakish argued, this appears to conflict with how we treat doubtful gifts to the poor.

The case Reish Lakish cites is that of the holes made by burrowing animals in a wheat field. Wheat found in holes dug within the standing grain — before harvesting — belongs to the owner, since it clearly fell there before the harvest began. Wheat found in holes in the already-harvested area could have fallen there during harvesting, in which case it would be *leket*, belonging to the poor. The top layer of grain in such holes is given to the poor — *ha-elyonim la-aniyim* — as a safeguard, since it may have been dropped during the harvest. The bottom layer goes to the owner, since it must have accumulated earlier. And Rabbi Meir says: *hakol la-aniyim* — everything goes to the poor, for *safeik leket leket* — any doubt as to whether something is *leket* is resolved in favor of the poor.

Moreover, *Tosafot* notes that the question is not limited to Rabbi Meir's position: even the *Tanna Kamma* seems to agree that wherever there is genuine doubt, the grain belongs to the poor. The debate between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Meir appears to concern only whether the very bottom of the hole is actually in a state of doubt or not. On the underlying principle — that doubt about *leket* resolves in favor of the poor — everyone seems to agree. If so, how can our *Mishnah* say the convert is exempt when there is a doubt?

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan responded: *al taknitani* — "do not press me on this." He claims that the *Mishnah* which says doubtful *leket* goes to the poor reflects only a single, non-authoritative opinion — specifically that of Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra in the name of Rabbi Meir. Since it is a *da'at yachid*, we do not rule like it. The *baraita* records: *safeik leket leket, safeik shikcha shikcha, safeik peah peah* — each category of doubt about gifts to the poor is resolved in favor of the poor. But this, Rabbi Yochanan insists, represents only Rabbi Meir's minority view, not normative *halacha*.

### Reish Lakish: Tzedek Mishelcha

Reish Lakish was unmoved. He replied: even if it is an obscure opinion — even if it is attributed to someone as unknown as Ben Tada, as Rashi identifies him, essentially a nobody — I don't care. The opinion gives a compelling reason, and the reason should be examined on its merits. *Ve-ha-ta'ama ka'amar* — the reasoning stands on its own.

Reish Lakish then articulates his own independent derivation: what does the verse mean when it says *ani va-rash hatzdiku* — "give justice to the poor and the impoverished"? One cannot read it as a command to favor the poor in judicial proceedings, since the Torah explicitly says *vedal lo tehadar be-rivo* — do not show favor to a poor person in his lawsuit. Courts must be impartial. Rather, the verse means: *tzedek mishelcha veten lo* — if there is any doubt as to whether you owe something to the poor, tip the scales from your own resources and give it to them. Outside of formal adjudication, where you are weighing your personal obligations, the default should be generosity toward the poor. If you think you might owe them, give it to them.

This is reminiscent of the famous case in Bava Metzia where an *Amora*'s workers broke barrels and the judge, while technically ruling in the employer's favor, urged him to waive the payment and even pay their wages — an instance of *lifnim mishurat hadin*.
