The court must be objective, but your personal obligations, outside the courtroom, may pull you toward a higher standard of generosity toward those in need.

### Issur vs. Mamona

The Gemara ultimately provides the principled distinction. Rava formulates an initial answer: in the case of the convert, the cow began its life in a status of exemption — it belonged to a non-Jew, and we have a *chazakah* that it was not subject to *matnot*. We therefore presume it remains exempt unless proven otherwise. In the wheat field, by contrast, wheat owned by a Jew starts with an obligation to give the gifts to the poor, so we lean toward obligation when in doubt. Rava is thus reading our *Mishnah* as a narrow exception based on *chazakah*, while accepting Reish Lakish's general principle that doubt about gifts to the poor favors the poor.

But Abaye challenges this: the same *chazakah* logic would apply to the case of *challah*. A convert's dough, made before conversion, would also start with an exempt status. Yet we rule that if the timing is doubtful, the convert is *chayav* for *challah*. How does Rava explain that?

Rava's response — which the Gemara accepts as the authoritative resolution — is: *safek issura lechumra, safek mamona lekula*. When uncertainty involves an *issur*, we are strict; when it involves only money, we are lenient. The *challah* case involves an *issur*: if the dough was obligated in *challah* and none was separated, the remaining dough is *tevel* — forbidden to eat. You cannot eat from it. That is an *issur*, and so we rule strictly in cases of doubt. But *zroa lechayim vekeiva* and *reishit hagez* involve no *issur*. If you fail to give them, you do not thereby make any food forbidden; the only question is who owns the money. When it is purely monetary, *ha-motzi me-chavero alav ha-re'aya* controls: the claimant must prove his case.

### Eight Cases

This principle is illustrated and confirmed by Rav Chisda — and cited also by Rabbi Hiyya — who enumerates eight cases involving converts where uncertainty about the timing of conversion arises, four of which result in obligation and four in exemption.

The four cases of obligation all involve *issur* dimensions: the case of a convert's wife whose childbirth *korban* is uncertain (if she might need to bring a *korban* for a birth that occurred after conversion, and she doesn't, she may be eating *kodshim* while ritually impure); *challah* (where the dough would be *tevel* without separation); the firstborn of a pure animal (*bechor behema tehorah*, which carries *kedusha*); and the firstborn of a donkey (*peter chamor*, which remains forbidden in benefit until redeemed). In all four, failing to act when obligated leads to a prohibited state, so we rule strictly in cases of doubt.

The four cases of exemption are all purely monetary: *reishit hagez*, *zroa lechayim vekeiva*, *pidyon haben* (the redemption of a firstborn son, which is simply money paid to a *kohen* with no *issur* if not paid), and *pidyon peter chamor* — not the question of the donkey's forbidden status, which would be *issur*, but the question of the sheep used to redeem it, which now simply concerns whether the *kohen* gets the sheep as a monetary gift. In all four, no prohibition results from withholding, so the civil principle applies and the *kohen* has the burden of proof.

This resolves the apparent tension with the gifts to the poor. The case of the poor may be an exception — tipping the scales in their favor based on Reish Lakish's reading of *ani va-rash hatzdiku* — but that question remains a matter of debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. The main principle is settled: *safek issur lechumra, safek mamona lekula*. And under that framework, our *Mishnah*'s ruling that a convert in doubtful circumstances is exempt from *matnot* stands on solid ground.

---

## Poor vs. Kohanim

### Levi's Field

The Gemara now presents a case that sharpens the distinction between the two modes of giving. Levi planted his field in a place called Kishar. Grain was dropped during harvesting — potential *leket* — but there were no poor people in the area. The field was in a remote location, with no *aniyim* anywhere nearby.

### Rav Sheshet

Levi came before Rav Sheshet. Rav Sheshet ruled: *le'ani velager ta'azov otam* — "you shall leave it for the poor and for the stranger." The purpose of leaving *leket* is not to feed ravens and bats. If no poor person can actually reach the field and take the grain, you are not obligated to preserve it for them — and you may keep it for yourself. The obligation to give gifts to the poor is satisfied by leaving; if no one can come and take, there is nothing to leave and no obligation that remains unfulfilled.

### Terumah Transport

The Gemara challenges Rav Sheshet's ruling from the laws of *terumah*. There is a principle that one is not obligated to transport *terumah* from the threshing floor to the city, or from the wilderness to a settled area — the *kohen* comes to take it. But if there is no *kohen* available and the *terumah* would otherwise rot, one is required to hire an animal and bring it to the city — *socher parah umevia mipnei hefsed terumah* — because you may not allow *terumah* to go to waste. Here, then, you are obligated to actively transport the *terumah* even when no *kohen* is nearby. Why should the case of *leket* be different?

### Tevul Distinction

The Gemara answers: *shani terumah detavla* — *terumah* is different because it has *tevul* status. If you do not separate *terumah*, your produce is *tevel* and you cannot eat it. You are therefore obligated to separate *terumah* regardless of whether a *kohen* is available to receive it, and once separated, you must preserve it — even transport it — so that it does not rot. The obligation to preserve *terumah* is thus driven not by a duty to the *kohen* per se, but by the issur-dimension: you need to render your produce permissible, and the separated *terumah* must be given to a *kohen* eventually. Gifts to the poor carry no such *tevul* status; failing to give *leket* does not make any of your produce forbidden. Therefore the principle of *ta'azov* — leave it — controls entirely, and if the poor cannot come to take it, the obligation is not triggered.

The Gemara adds that the same reasoning now explains why *matanot kehuna* would seem to require active preservation: a *baraita* rules that if there is no *kohen* present when you separate the *zroa lechayim vekeiva*, you estimate its value, set that amount aside, and eat the gifts yourself — *ma'alin oto bedamim v'ochlan mipnei hefsed kohen* — so that the *kohen* does not lose out on the monetary value. Yet *matanot kehuna* also carry no *tevul* status. How is this different from *leket*?

### Nittina vs. Ta'azov

The Gemara provides the answer: *shani matnot kehuna denetina ketiva behu* — *matanot kehuna* are different because the Torah uses the language of giving. *Venatan* — you shall give it to the *kohen*. By the gifts to the poor, the Torah says *ta'azov* — you shall leave it. The language is not incidental; it defines the structure of the obligation. *Nittina* — giving — means the obligation is on you, the owner, to ensure the *kohen* receives it or its value. *Ta'azov* — leaving — means your job is only to make it accessible; the poor come and take it themselves. If they cannot come, your obligation is discharged by not interfering.

The same logic explains why *terumah* requires transport: the Torah there also uses the language of giving — *titen lo terumah* — and therefore it is your responsibility to ensure it reaches the *kohen*.

### Honor & Dignity

There is a deeper principle underlying this distinction. The entire discussion of *matanot kehuna* throughout this *perek* has emphasized that the gifts are given in a manner that reflects the honor of the *kohanim*: you give, they receive. It is an active gesture of acknowledgment. With the poor, the dynamic is deliberately reversed. The poor come and take; you do not hand it to them directly. This is not a lesser form of generosity — it is a more sensitive one. Giving directly to a poor person highlights their poverty and makes the interaction feel like a handout. Leaving it for them to take preserves their dignity; they exercise their own agency in coming to claim what belongs to them. Thus the Torah's choice of *ta'azov* versus *nettina* is not merely technical — it reflects two distinct conceptions of how one gives with respect. For the *kohen*, honor is shown through the act of giving. For the poor, dignity is preserved through the act of leaving.

---

## Sack of Dinari

### Rabbi Ami's Action

A concluding narrative ties together many of these themes. A sack filled with *dinari* — gold coins — was sent to the *beis medrash* as a gift to the *yeshiva*. Rabbi Ami, who served as *rosh yeshiva*, ran ahead and seized possession of the coins for himself — *kadim Rabbi Ami vezachi bahen*.

### Grabbing Gifts

The Gemara is puzzled. The entire preceding discussion has emphasized that gifts — and *matanot kehuna* in particular — should not be grabbed. The proper mode of receiving is that the gift is given to you; you do not run and snatch. The obligation involves *venatan* — giving — not grabbing. How could Rabbi Ami behave this way?

### First Answer

The first answer: *Rabbi Ami le'aniyim zachah bahen* — Rabbi Ami seized the coins on behalf of the poor, intending to distribute them as charity rather than keeping them for the *yeshiva*. Once the coins are understood as a gift for the poor rather than for a *kohen*-analog, the rules change. The applicable principle is *ta'azov* — the poor may take, they are supposed to come and claim what belongs to them. Rabbi Ami, acting as their agent, did precisely that.

### Adam Chashuv

The second answer: *adam chashuv shani* — a person of exceptional stature operates by different rules. The Gemara cites a *baraita*: the *kohen gadol* must be greater than his fellow *kohanim* in beauty, wisdom, and wealth. If he lacks wealth, *acherim omrim* — other authorities say — his fellow *kohanim* are obligated to contribute and make him wealthy, as the verse says *vehakohen hagadol me'echav* — *gadlehu mishel echav*, let his brothers make him great from their own resources. Since people have a responsibility to make the *kohen gadol* wealthy, he is in a sense entitled to claim resources that are being sent for that purpose. The *rosh yeshiva* — or the *adam chashuv* he represents — occupies an analogous position of institutional status, and the normal prohibition on grabbing does not apply to him.

This second answer is admittedly somewhat difficult to fully understand. There is a difference between whether money should go to a particular person and how one takes it. The whole point of the norm against grabbing is that even the person who is entitled to a gift should receive it graciously rather than seizing it. The first answer — that Rabbi Ami was acting for the poor, invoking *ta'azov* — is far more elegant and plays directly off the contrast developed throughout this sugya between how one gives to a *kohen* and how one gives to the poor. The second answer is noted by the Gemara as an alternative, but the first captures the deeper logic of the preceding discussion.

---

## Anatomy Lesson

### Zroa Definition

The final *Mishnah* of the *perek* defines the anatomical scope of each of the three gifts. The *zroa* — the arm — runs *miferek shel arkuva* — from the joint of the *arkuva*, the lower joint of the foreleg — *ad kaf shel hayad*, up to the shoulder. This comprises the two upper arm bones and all the meat on them. It is the same *zroa* that the Torah specifies when commanding that the arm of the ram be cooked for the *nazir*, and it corresponds anatomically to the *shok* — the thigh — given from a *korban shelamim*: the *shok* is the analogous pair of upper bones in the hind leg.

### Right Arm

The *Mishnah* and *baraita* establish that the *zroa* given as a *matana* is specifically the right arm — *hazroa zo zroa yamin*. This parallels the right thigh of the *shelamim*, and is derived through the same exegetical principle Rava applied to Rabbi Yehuda's position on the *gid hanasheh*: the "important" limb, *hamiyumenet*, is the right one — *hazroa hamiyumenet shebazroa*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Regarding the *shok* of a *korban*, Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with the majority about what the term encompasses. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the *shok* consists of only the single middle bone, not the two upper bones of the thigh. The *Mishnah* records his opinion: *shok miferek shel arkuva ad sof haregel* — the *shok* runs from the lower joint to the end of the leg, i.e., only the central bone, not the upper two. This is a minority view; the standard position includes the full upper pair.

### Lechayayim

The *lechayayim* — the jaws — are defined as the area *miferek shel lechi* — from the joint of the jaw — *ad pika shel gargoret* — until the covering of the esophagus at the back of the throat. This includes the tongue.

### Wool & Hair

A *baraita* teaches that the definite article *heh* of *v'halechayayim* in the verse extends the gift beyond the jaw itself. *Lehavi tsemer sheberosh kevasim* — it includes the wool on the head of sheep. Even though the *kohen* is only receiving the jaw as meat, he also receives the wool around the head of the sheep along with it. Similarly, *ve-sa'ar shebizkan tayashim* — the hair of the beard of goats is included as well.

### Keiva

The *heh* of *v'hakeivah* likewise extends the gift. *Lehavi chelev shel gabei hakeivah* — it includes not just the stomach itself, but the fat around the outside of the stomach. Although this fat is prohibited for eating, it may be used for benefit — for making leather, for burning, and similar purposes — and therefore belongs to the *kohen*. *Ve-chelev shebetoch hakeivah* — the fat inside the stomach is also included.

### Kohanim's Generosity

Rabbi Yehoshua adds: *kohanim nahagu bahen ayin yafah* — the *kohanim* practiced exceptional generosity when it came to the *keivah*, and *venatnu l'ba'alim* — they returned the fat to the owners. The Gemara notes that this was a voluntary practice, not a requirement: *ta'ama de-nahagu* — it is because of their customary generosity, but *ha lo nahagu, didehu* — had they not adopted this practice, they would have been entitled to the fat both inside and outside the stomach.

---

## Pinchas Derash

### Zroa Symbol

A section of *aggadata* closes the *perek*, introduced with the phrase *dorshei chamurot hayu omrim* — those who offer symbolic or *midrashic* interpretations of commandments said the following. The three *matanot* — *zroa*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah* — are understood as commemorating the act of Pinchas. The *zroa* represents the arm — specifically the right arm — with which Pinchas took hold of his spear: *vayikach romach beyado* — and he took a spear in his hand.

### Lechayayim Symbol

The *lechayayim* corresponds to prayer — *tefillah*. The verse in Tehillim says *vaya'amod Pinchas vayifallel*, which is read as *vayitpallel* — and Pinchas stood and prayed. The *lechayayim*, the site of speech and prayer, thus symbolizes his turning to God for strength before performing his act.

### Keiva Symbol

The *keivah* — the stomach — is *kemashma'ah*, its plain meaning: *ve-et ha-ishah el kuvatah* — and he thrust through the woman into her stomach. The spear passed through the bodies of Zimri and Cozbi at precisely that anatomical location. The Rambam in *Moreh Nevukhim* offers a different type of reason for these gifts — he sees them as representing something primary or first about the animal, the *zroa* as the first appendage, the *lechayayim* on the head, and so on — but the Gemara here clearly prefers the Pinchas parallel, which is a remarkably tight fit for two of the three gifts and a compelling homiletical framework for all three.

---

## Right Side Derivation

### Thigh Source

Having derived from the *aggadic* material that the *zroa* is the right arm, the Gemara now traces the technical textual basis for this. The *baraita* begins with the *shok* of a *korban shelamim*. The verse explicitly states *hayamin* — the right — in the context of the thigh given from a *shelamim*. From that case it is clear: the *kohen* receives the right thigh.

### Nazir Derivation

From the *shelamim* the Gemara then derives the *zroa* of a *nazir*'s ram. The verse there uses the term *terumah* — an extra word, or a word whose inclusion teaches something beyond its immediate context. The appearance of *terumah* implies that other items also characterized as elevated gifts to the *kohen* follow the same right-side rule. Therefore the arm of the *nazir*'s ram is the right arm.

### Regular Shechita

Finally, from the *nazir*'s ram the rule is extended to the *zroa* given in ordinary *shechita*. The verse uses the word *titnu* — you shall give — and this additional formulation is read as extending the right-side requirement to all priestly gifts of this type. Thus at every stage — the *shelamim*, the *nazir*, and regular slaughter — the gift is from the right side.

---

## Lechayayim Boundary

### Beit Shechita

The *Mishnah* defined the *lechayayim* as running from the jaw joint to the covering of the esophagus. A *baraita* complicates this: it says the jaw is taken along with the *beit shechita* — the place of slaughter. If the *shechita* takes place lower on the trachea or esophagus than the top, then the phrase "with the *beit shechita*" would seem to imply the jaw includes area that extends down to — or even includes — the site of slaughter, which would be lower than the top of the esophagus.

### Mugremet Debate

This leads to a Tannaitic dispute about whether *shechita* may be performed at the very top of the esophagus. *Mugremet pesulah* — slaughter performed in a *mugremet* position, meaning too high up on the esophagus, is invalid according to the standard view. Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, however, validates *shechita* performed at the *mugremet*, i.e., at the very top. The two opinions thus understand the *beit shechita* differently, and consequently have different views about where exactly the *lechayayim* ends.

### Resolution

The Gemara offers a resolution that sidesteps the Tannaitic dispute about *shechita* entirely. *Iba'it eima ha v'ha Rabbanan* — both opinions can actually be those of the Rabbis, who agree that *mugremet* is invalid. The phrase "with the *beit shechita*" does not mean the jaw is taken together with the place of slaughter. Rather, it means the jaw is separated *above* the place of slaughter — *imah d'behema*, the *beit shechita* remains with the animal. You take the jaw until the top of the esophagus; from there downward, where the actual *shechita* occurs, remains part of the *behema*. The *lechayayim* does not include the *beit shechita*; it ends just above it.

*Hadran alach zroa ulechayayim.*

---

---

# Hullin 135

## Reishit HaGez Intro

### Opening

With the penultimate chapter of Masechet Chullin, the Mishnah introduces *reishit hagez* — the first of the shearings — which represents the inaugural priestly gift derived from non-korbanot animals. Up to this point, the tractate has been occupied with *zroa lechayayim veKeivah*, the meat gifts taken from slaughtered animals. Now the subject shifts to wool, a gift that is structurally different and limited in scope.

### Mishnah Applicability

The Mishnah opens with a sweeping statement of applicability: *reishit hagez* applies both in *Eretz Yisrael* and outside of it, both when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands and when it does not. This broad applicability is unsurprising, since the obligation has no inherent connection to the Temple or to the Land. The Mishnah further specifies that the obligation applies only to non-sanctified animals (*chulin*), not to sanctified ones (*mukdashin*) — a ruling parallel to what we encountered with *zroa lechayayim veKeivah*.

### Zroa vs. Gez

Notably, the Mishnah does not here digress into the question of whether the animal was sanctified before or after it developed a blemish — a digression that did appear in the context of *zroa lechayayim veKeivah*. That discussion is deferred to Masechet Bechorot.

The Mishnah then enumerates the stringencies of *zroa lechayayim veKeivah* relative to *reishit hagez*. The meat gifts — the foreleg, jaw, and stomach — apply to both cattle and sheep (*bakar u-tzon*), and they apply even if one slaughters only a single animal, whether much or little (*be-merubeh u-ve-mu'at*). *Reishit hagez*, by contrast, applies exclusively to sheep (*rachelot*). Goat hair and cattle wool, even though they have their uses — and even in the *Mikdash* context — are not subsumed under the word *gez*, shearing. Shearing, as a halachic category, is reserved for sheep alone. Furthermore, *reishit hagez* requires a plurality of animals, which brings us to the next significant debate.

---

## Merubeh Debate

### Tzon Etymology

The Torah's formulation is *reishit gez tzoncha* — the first of the shearings of your flock. The word *tzon*, flock, is not the word for a single sheep. Just as "cattle" in English implies a group, *tzon* connotes a collective, a flock — not one lone animal. One would never refer to a single sheep as a *tzon*. Therefore, the obligation cannot apply to one sheep alone; by the very semantics of the verse, a plurality is required.

### Merubeh Requirement

The question then becomes: what is the minimum that qualifies as a *merubeh*, a plurality? The term "flock" is evocative but imprecise. How many sheep does one need to be obligated?

### Two vs. Five

*Beit Shammai* says two sheep suffice, as evidenced by the verse (Isaiah 7:21): *yichyeh ish egla bakar u-shtei tzon* — "a man shall raise a calf and two of the flock." The word *tzon* is applied there to just two, demonstrating that two animals can constitute a flock. In this instance, it is *Beit Shammai* who is more stringent, imposing the obligation even on a minimal flock of two.

*Beit Hillel* requires five, citing the verse (I Samuel 25:18): *chamesh tzon asuyot* — "five sheep ready," where the context of *tzon* appears alongside a quantity of five, laden with their wool. *Beit Hillel* finds the context more apt: not only does this verse invoke *tzon*, but the notion of animals laden with wool makes it specifically relevant to shearing.

### Rabbi Dosa View

*Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas* introduces an additional threshold. He agrees that five sheep are required, but he further demands that each individual sheep produce a minimum quantity of wool — specifically, one and a half *maneh* (a *peras* is a half *maneh*) — before the obligation is triggered. If a given sheep yields only a negligible amount of wool, it does not count toward the requirement in his view. The obligation arises only when the shearing is substantive: five sheep, each producing at least this minimum.

### Chachamim View

The Sages (*Chachamim*) disagree and hold that five sheep are sufficient regardless of the quantity each produces — *kol shehu*, any amount. Even the tiniest yield from each of five sheep creates the obligation. The Gemara will subsequently probe what exactly *kol shehu* means in practice.

---

## Amount & Wool Status

### Five vs. Ten Sela'im

Once the threshold of obligation is established, the Mishnah turns to the amount that must actually be given to the *kohen*. The minimum gift is defined by weight: the equivalent of five *sela'im* as measured in Judea, which equals ten *sela'im* in Galilee. The Judean *sela* was twice the weight of the Galilean one, so the underlying physical quantity is the same — roughly a modest but meaningful portion of wool, approximating what we will later see is enough to produce a small garment. When the Gemara reaches the detailed discussion of this measure, the proportional dimensions can be translated into more concrete terms; for now, it is sufficient to note that there is both a fixed minimum and, as the Gemara will explore, a proportional component that scales with larger shearings.

### Laundering Required

The Mishnah adds that the wool given to the *kohen* must be *meluban* — clean and laundered — and not in its raw, dirty state. Sheep wool comes off the animal in an unprocessed condition, having been exposed to the elements, mud, and general pastoral realities. One is not permitted to hand the *kohen* wool in that state; it must be cleaned first.

### Wool Cleaning

This raises a practical question about the cleaning process. Wool contains *lanolin*, a natural oil embedded in the fibers, which means simple washing may be insufficient. The cleaning of raw wool involves both washing and combing to produce usable material. Whatever the precise process, the halachic point is clear: the wool must be presented in a clean, processed form.

### Small Garment

The Mishnah anchors the minimum amount through a functional criterion: the gift to the *kohen* must be enough to make a small garment. As the verse states, *titen lo* — you shall give to him — implying a gift of real usability and significance. The *kohen* must be able to do something with what he receives; the minimum is therefore the smallest meaningful garment, something like a small belt.

### Dyed Before Gift

An important case: if the owner did not manage to give the wool to a *kohen* before proceeding to dye it — completing the cleaning process and then applying dye — he is *patur*, exempt. This ruling requires explanation.

### Dyeing Transforms

The exemption for wool that was dyed before the gift was given reflects the principle that dyeing constitutes a transformative act (*shinui*), a significant enough change to the object that it is treated halachically as if the original item no longer exists in its prior form. This principle appears in other contexts in the Mishnah: if one receives another's wool to clean and accidentally dyes it, the act of dyeing is considered significant enough to constitute a kind of conversion of the object — the original owner's claim is displaced, and the person who dyed it must compensate monetarily, but the wool in its changed form is now considered his.

In the context of *matnot kehunah*, the question of "stealing" a priestly gift is conceptually complex. Earlier in the tractate, there was discussion of whether the priestly gifts can be stolen at all, given that no specific *kohen* has yet acquired them. A butcher who gives the meat to one *kohen* rather than another is not considered a thief — he has simply moved the gift. But transformation is different. When the wool is dyed, it is no longer the same object. The Mishnah therefore concludes that dyeing the wool effectively removes it from the category of *matnot kehunah*: the original obligation is discharged — wrongly, but factually — and the obligation to give does not extend to the dyed product. One has undoubtedly done something wrong, but the dyed wool itself is no longer subject to the gift requirement.

### Clean Without Dye

By contrast, if the wool was laundered but not dyed, the owner is obligated to give it to the *kohen*. This is self-evident from the earlier ruling that the wool must be given in a *meluban* state. Laundering is not a transformation; it is merely the required preparation. The obligation therefore remains fully intact.

---

## Ownership Rules

### Non-Jew Owner

If one purchases the shearings of a non-Jew's sheep, one is exempt from *reishit hagez*. The Gemara will root this in the word *tzoncha* — your sheep — which implies that the sheep must be owned by a Jew. If the animals belong to a non-Jew, the obligation never attaches, regardless of who subsequently acquires the wool.

### Jewish Seller

If one purchases the shearings from a fellow Jew — a situation analogous to buying meat from a butcher after slaughter — the question is who bears the obligation. The rule is: if the seller retained some wool, the obligation falls on the seller. Just as the wool does not have a fixed recipient among the *kohanim* until designated, what matters is who holds the unseparated wool. If the seller kept even a small portion, that remaining wool is what he must designate for the *kohen*.

### No Remainder

If the seller sold all of his wool and retained nothing, he has nothing from which to fulfill the obligation. In such a case, the buyer becomes obligated and must give from his portion. This parallels the earlier principle that *matnot kehunah* cannot be discharged with monetary compensation — the physical item in whose possession the obligation resides is what matters.

### Wool Categories

The Mishnah introduces a further nuance. What if the seller had two distinct types of wool — for example, wool from black sheep and wool from white sheep, or wool from males and wool from females? These different categories apparently produce wool of different qualities or characters.

### Separate Categories

If the seller sold one category entirely — say, all the black wool — but retained the other category — say, all the white wool — one might think: the seller still has wool in his possession, so the entire obligation rests on him. The Mishnah rejects this. Because the two types of wool are considered distinct shearings, each category is treated independently. The buyer, who holds all the black wool, must give from his category; the seller, who holds all the white wool, gives from his. As the Mishnah formulates it: *zeh noten le-atzmo ve-zeh noten le-atzmo* — each one gives from his own.

One might ask whether a *shutafut*, a partnership in a single flock, creates any comparable complexity — specifically, does the word *tzoncha*, "your sheep," in the singular, require sole ownership and thereby exempt partners? This question is explicitly raised and will be taken up by the Gemara.

---

## Sanctified Exclusion

### Qedoshim Question

The Gemara opens its analysis by asking the obvious question: why does the obligation of *reishit hagez* not apply to *kodashim*, sanctified animals?

### Tzoncha Exclusion

The answer is derivational: the verse reads *tzoncha* — your sheep — which means sheep owned by the *baalim*, the lay owner, and thereby excludes *tzon hekdesh*, sheep owned by *hekdesh*, the Temple. The verse's singular possessive is interpreted to demand lay ownership.

### Why Verse Needed

The Gemara then asks why such a verse was necessary in the first place. Is it not obvious that one cannot shear sanctified animals? After all, the Torah explicitly states *lo tagoz bechor tzoncha* — you may not shear the firstborn of your sheep — and what applies to the *bechor* applies by extension to all sacrificial animals. The prohibition on shearing *kodshei mizbe'ach* is biblical. So why would anyone think the obligation of *reishit hagez* could apply?

### Kodshim Types

The answer introduces a critical distinction: there are two categories of sanctified animals. *Kodshei mizbe'ach* — animals sanctified as sacrifices — are indeed forbidden to be shorn. But *kodshei bedek habayit* — animals sanctified for the Temple treasury, whose value is donated rather than their bodies being offered on the altar — occupy a different legal space. Perhaps the Temple itself could shear such animals as a means of generating income, and the question would arise whether it must then give *reishit hagez* to a *kohen*.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

On this point, *Rabbi Eliezer* rules that even *kodshei bedek habayit* are forbidden to be shorn or put to work. However, the Gemara clarifies that *Rabbi Eliezer*'s prohibition is only rabbinic (*miderabbanan*), not biblical. The reason is likely concern about confusion with *kodshei mizbe'ach*. At the biblical level, shearing *kodshei bedek habayit* is permitted. Accordingly, if someone violated the rabbinic restriction and shorn such an animal, the question of whether *reishit hagez* must be given is a genuine one — and it is for that scenario that the verse is required.

---

## Sanctified Scenarios

### Redemption Solution

The Gemara now works through the precise scenario in which one might have thought the obligation of *reishit hagez* applies to sanctified animals. If someone violated the rabbinic restriction and shorn *kodshei bedek habayit*, perhaps the solution is: redeem the wool (by compensating the Temple treasury for its value), and then give a portion of the wool to the *kohen*. This would satisfy both the obligation to the Temple and the obligation of *reishit hagez*. Hence a verse is needed to tell us this is not required.

### Redemption Problem

The Gemara immediately raises a difficulty: how could one even redeem the wool? The Torah requires that when redeeming a sanctified animal, *ve-he'emido ha-kohen ve-he'erich oto lifnei Hashem* — the priest shall stand it up and assess it before God. The rabbinic understanding of this verse is that sanctified animals can only be redeemed when they are alive and able to be "stood up." Shorn wool, having been separated from the living animal, cannot be stood up, and therefore arguably cannot be redeemed. This difficulty arises specifically according to the opinion that the requirement of *ha'amada ve-ha'aracha* — standing up and assessment — applies even to *kodshei bedek habayit*, not only to sacrificial animals. According to the opinion that *kodshei bedek habayit* do not require *ha'amada ve-ha'aracha*, the redemption path remains open; but according to the other opinion, even that path is foreclosed. Either way, the redemption route seems unavailable.

### Rav Mani Solution

The Gemara resolves this impasse through a case constructed by *Rav Mani bar Patish* in the name of *Rabbi Yannai*. The operative scenario is one where the owner sanctified his animal to *bedek habayit* but explicitly excluded the wool from the sanctification: *makdish behemto le-bedek ha-bayit chutz mi-gizoteha* — "I am sanctifying my animal to the Temple treasury except for its shearings." By retaining ownership of the wool, the owner never transferred it to *hekdesh*. He then shears the wool — which he owns — and the question is whether he must give *reishit hagez* from that wool to a *kohen*.

### Own Wool Exempt

This is the scenario the verse addresses. Even though the owner retained possession of the wool, the sheep itself belongs to *hekdesh*. The verse *tzoncha* — your sheep — requires not only that the wool be yours but that the sheep be yours as well. Since the sheep is owned by the Temple treasury, the obligation of *reishit hagez* does not apply, even to the wool the owner legitimately retained. Hence the verse was needed.

---

## Kodshei Mizbe'ach

### Sanctity Spreads

Having established why the verse is needed in the case of *kodshei bedek habayit*, the Gemara asks: why not apply the same reasoning — sanctifying the animal but retaining ownership of the wool — even to *kodshei mizbe'ach*, sacrificial animals? If that were possible, the same question would arise and the same verse would be needed for the same reason, without having to invoke *bedek habayit* at all. The Gemara answers: *kachshi* — it weakens the animal. Shearing is a physically diminishing act; it causes some degree of debilitation to the sheep. If the animal is a sacrifice, one cannot perform an act that impairs it, as that would impinge on the sanctity of the sacrifice and potentially constitute *me'ilah*. Therefore, the scenario of retaining ownership of the wool while sanctifying the animal cannot be constructed for *kodshei mizbe'ach*.

### Shearing Weakens

One might then ask: if the owner retains ownership not only of the wool but also of the animal's diminishment — *chutz mi-giza ve-kechisha*, "except for the shearing and the weakening" — couldn't one construct the scenario even for a sacrifice? The Gemara addresses this directly: no. With a sacrifice, one cannot play these games of subdivided ownership. The sanctity of a *korban* is not merely a matter of who legally owns which portion; it defines the very identity and nature of the animal. Once an animal is consecrated as a sacrifice, its entire being is defined as a *korban*, and one cannot carve out a retained interest in its diminishment as if that were a separable portion.

### Temurah Proof

The Gemara grounds this principle in a debate in Masechet Temurah. *Rabbi Yose* rules: *ha-omer raglah shel zo olah kulah olah* — if one declares "the leg of this animal is an *olah*," the entire animal becomes an *olah*. The sanctity of a sacrifice, once applied to any part, spreads to the whole. Even *Rabbi Meir*, who disagrees in the specific case of the leg — arguing that the leg, since the animal can survive without it, does not carry the soul of the animal and therefore sanctifying it does not sanctify the whole — would agree that if one sanctifies a part upon which the animal's life depends (*davar she-ha-neshamah teluyah bah*), then the entire animal becomes sanctified. The upshot is clear: by *kodshei mizbe'ach*, the identity of the animal as a *korban* is total and indivisible. Ownership subdivisions that are permissible for *bedek habayit* simply do not function for sacrificial animals. This is why the Gemara is forced to develop the scenario through *bedek habayit*, and why the verse *tzoncha* was needed.

---

## Plural Override

### Challah Reishit

The Gemara now pivots to a broader inquiry. If *Rabbi Elai*'s principle is that a singular possessive in the Torah (*tzoncha* — your sheep) demands sole ownership and excludes partnership, does this principle apply uniformly across other agricultural and priestly obligations? The Gemara works through *challah*, *peah*, and *terumah*.

For *challah*, there is a potential analogy: the Torah uses the word *reishit* — "first" — both for *challah* and for *reishit hagez*. One might propose: just as *reishit hagez* excludes partnership (according to *Rabbi Elai*), so too should *challah* exclude partnership.

### Plural Challah

The response is that the Torah writes *arisoteichem* — your kneading troughs, in the plural — which overrides any exclusion of partnership. The plural possessive signals that even when multiple people are involved, the obligation applies.

### Trough Amount

The Gemara then asks: if the plural *arisoteichem* resolves the partnership question, what independent work does the word do? The answer is that *arisoteichem* comes to teach the minimum quantity that triggers the *challah* obligation — specifically, the amount equivalent to the *omer* of *man* that each person received in the wilderness (*omer le-gulgoles*). The Torah thus uses this word to anchor the size of the dough that obligates in *challah*.

### Peah Plural

For *peah*, the Torah says *sadcha* — your field — in the singular, which might suggest sole ownership is required and partnership is excluded. But elsewhere the verse reads *u-ve-kutzrechem et ketzir artzechem* — "when you harvest the harvest of your land" — in the plural, which overrides the singular and includes partnerships.

### Peah Non-Jew

Nevertheless, *sadcha* in the singular still does meaningful work: it excludes partnership with a non-Jew. If a non-Jew is a partial owner of the field, the Jewish partner is exempt from the obligation of *peah* for the non-Jew's portion.

---

## Kodshei Mizbe'ach (II)

### Part vs. Whole

The Gemara returns to sharpen the principle from Temurah. The debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yose* is more precisely framed: *Rabbi Meir*'s leniency applies only when the sanctified part is one from which the animal could be separated and still survive — such as a leg. That part lacks the *neshamah*, the life-force of the animal, and therefore sanctifying it alone does not define the whole.

### Korban Identity

But where the sanctified part is one upon which the animal's life depends — its heart, chest, or head — even *Rabbi Meir* agrees that the sanctity spreads to the entire animal. This is not merely a legal technicality of ownership spreading; it is a statement about the identity of a *korban*. A sacrifice is defined as a unified whole, an offering of the entire being. Once any life-sustaining part is consecrated, the animal's identity as a *korban* is total. This is why one cannot construct retained partial ownership in the context of *kodshei mizbe'ach* the way one can for *bedek habayit*.

---

## Plural Override (II)

### Terumah Concession

The Gemara introduces *Rava*'s formulation: *Rabbi Elai* concedes that *terumah* does not require sole ownership — partnership in *terumah* still obligates.

### Plural Terumah

Although the Torah writes *degancha* — your grain — in the singular, which by *Rabbi Elai*'s logic would exclude partnership, the Torah also writes *trumoteichem* — your plural *terumah* — which overrides the singular and includes partnership. The plural possessive functions as an explicit signal that the obligation extends to shared ownership.

### Non-Jew Excluded

The singular *degancha* is not therefore without purpose: it excludes partnership with a non-Jew. When a non-Jew is a part owner of the field, the Jewish partner's portion remains obligated in *terumah*, but the singular possessive excludes the non-Jew's portion from the obligation. This is the minimum work the singular can do once the plural has overridden its exclusion of Jewish partnerships.

---

## Rava's Wool Case

### Wool Sanctified

*Rava* introduces a distinct and simpler scenario: rather than sanctifying the animal to the Temple treasury while retaining the wool, what if a person sanctified only the wool itself — not the sheep at all — to *hekdesh*?

### Redeem Question

The Gemara asks: once the person wishes to shear the sheep, is he obligated to redeem the sanctified wool and then give a portion of that redeemed wool to the *kohen* as *reishit hagez*?

### Titen Excludes

The answer derives from the word *titen* in the verse *titen lo* — you shall give to him. The Gemara reads this as establishing: *mi she-ein mechusar ela giza u-netina* — only in a case where nothing stands between you and giving it to the *kohen* except shearing and giving is one obligated. This excludes *ze she-mechusar giza pidya u-netina* — a case where, in addition to shearing and giving, one must also first perform an act of redemption. Where an intermediate step of redemption is required before the gift can be transferred to the *kohen*, the obligation does not apply.

---

## Partnership Debate

### Partnership Q

The Gemara now addresses the central question raised by the Mishnah's wording: what does *tzoncha* — your sheep — exclude? Does it exclude partnership with a non-Jew, partnership with a fellow Jew, or both?

### Rabbi Elai View

*Rabbi Elai* holds that *tzoncha*, in the singular possessive, requires sole ownership. The singular implies: exclusively yours — not *tzonechem*, not shared. Therefore even partnership with a fellow Jew exempts one from *reishit hagez*. If two Jews jointly own a flock, neither is obligated to give *reishit hagez* from the shared shearings.

### Chachamim View

The *Chachamim* disagree. They read *tzoncha* more narrowly: the singular possessive excludes only partnership with a non-Jew, whose partial ownership renders the entire animal's status ambiguous in a way that discharges the obligation. Partnership with a fellow Jew, however, does not disrupt the obligation; both Jewish partners remain obligated, each giving from their respective portion.

### Reishit Separation

The Sages support their reading from the structure of the verse itself. The Torah uses the word *reishit* twice — once in the context of *terumah* (*reishit degancha*) and once here (*reishit gez tzoncha*). Had the two been meant to be read as a single continuous obligation, the Torah could have written simply *reishit degancha ve-gez tzoncha titen lo*. By repeating *reishit*, the Torah separates the two categories into independent subjects. Therefore, one cannot transfer the exclusions derived from *terumah* to *reishit hagez*; each stands independently, and *tzoncha* by the shearings does no more than exclude the non-Jew.

### Elai Counter

*Rabbi Elai* responds by invoking the *vav* that connects the two clauses: *ve-reishit gez tzoncha titen lo*. The conjunctive *vav* ties the law of *reishit hagez* back to the preceding discussion of *terumah*, allowing the exclusions already derived there — namely, that partnership with a non-Jew is excluded by *degancha* — to carry over to the case of shearings. Having already established the exclusion of non-Jewish partnership from *terumah*, when we reach *tzoncha* in the context of the shearings, that word is free to do additional work: it now excludes even Jewish partnership.

---

## Breira Debate

### Field Partnership

The Gemara now cites a *baraita* that examines a case of a Jew and non-Jew who jointly own a field and together harvest it. The central question is what happens to the *terumah* and *maaser* obligations of the grain they divide at harvest.

### Yesh Breira

According to *Rabbi* (here understood to represent the position of *yesh breira* — retroactive assignment), when the two partners divide the harvest and each takes his portion, we say retroactively that each partner's share was always "meant" to come from his portion of the field. The Jew's 50 bushels grew from the Jewish half of the field; the non-Jew's 50 bushels grew from the non-Jew's half. The result is that the grain is intermingled in terms of obligation: the Jew's portion consists of grain that is partly *tevel* (obligated in *terumot u-ma'asrot*) and partly fully exempt, because his portion grew partly from the Jewish-owned half and partly — by the logic of this view — the non-Jew's portion is carved out separately.

### Ein Breira

*Rabban Gamliel* holds *ein breira*: there is no retroactive assignment. The division at harvest is what determines ownership, and it is a clean division. Whatever the Jew took is fully in his possession, and since his ownership is total, his entire portion is obligated in *terumah* and *maaser*. The non-Jew's portion is entirely exempt. The two positions thus produce opposite practical outcomes: under *yesh breira*, the Jew's grain is a mixture of obligated and exempt; under *ein breira*, it is entirely obligated.

### Agreed Exempt

The Gemara notes that on one point all opinions agree: the non-Jew's portion is exempt from *terumah* and *maaser*, and the Jew's portion — to whatever extent it is his — is obligated. The dispute is only about whether we retroactively assign clean ownership boundaries (yesh *breira*) or whether the mixed-field reality means the Jew holds a grain supply that was always compositionally mixed (*ein breira*).

### Rashi Solution

There is a lengthy analysis here from *Rashi*, who works out how one actually fulfills the obligation under the position of *Rabbi* (*ein breira*). If the Jew holds 100 bushels that are conceptually 50% obligated and 50% not, he cannot simply give five bushels as *maaser* (a tenth of the obligated 50), because those five bushels are themselves 50% obligated and 50% not. Instead, *Rashi* explains, he should take grain from a different, entirely Jewish-owned field — grain that is 100% obligated — and use five bushels of that to serve as the *maaser* for his 50 obligated bushels mixed into these 100. This way, he gives only five rather than ten, since only 50 of his 100 are obligated. Under *Rabban Gamliel*'s view (*yesh breira*), all 100 are obligated, and he would give ten.

### Divisible vs. Unit

This discussion illuminates an important distinction that *Rashi* draws between grain and animals. For grain, the principle is that grain is inherently divisible: every kernel is its own unit, and the non-Jew's fractional ownership does not "contaminate" or define the Jew's portion as a whole — it merely means some of the grain is his and some is not, and these can, at least conceptually, be sorted out. Animals, by contrast, are indivisible units. A sheep or cow is one animal. If a non-Jew holds even a partial ownership in that animal, the non-Jew's ownership is not confined to a separable portion — it colors the whole animal. This is why, when a non-Jew is a partner in a sheep, the Jew is fully exempt from *zroa lechayayim veKeivah* and *reishit hagez*, whereas when a non-Jew is a partner in a grain field, the Jew's portion of the grain remains fully obligated. The conceptual divisibility of grain versus the indivisibility of an animal as a single halachic unit is the structural distinction *Rashi* identifies to reconcile these seemingly disparate rulings.

---

---

# Hullin 136

## Hefsek Taharah Basics

### Hefsek vs. Weekly Checks

The *hefsek taharah* is fundamentally different from the *bedikot* a woman performs throughout the *shiva nekiyim*. The distinction lies in purpose: the *hefsek taharah* is performed to establish that bleeding has ceased. The *bedikot* conducted during the seven clean days, by contrast, are performed to verify that nothing has occurred in the interim — that no bleeding took place since the previous check.

### Bedikot Theories

There is, however, a second and quite different way of understanding the function of the weekly *bedikot*. According to this view, the purpose of the *bedikot* is not primarily to detect any blood that may have emerged unnoticed, but rather to direct the woman's conscious attention to her bodily state at that moment. The very act of performing a *bedikah* creates a moment of mindful awareness: is anything coming out? Under this reading, the verse *v'safra lah shivat yamim* requires not merely that seven days pass, but that on each of those days the woman has been cognitively present — attentive, in some form, to whether she is bleeding. Even if something occurred between checks and was undetected, that is of secondary concern; what matters is that on each day there was a moment of focused awareness.

### Washing Protocol

This distinction between the two purposes produces a concrete *nafka mina* in practical law. Before performing a *hefsek taharah*, the woman should wash beforehand — cleaning internally and externally — so that any blood present from prior bleeding does not contaminate the check. Since the entire purpose is to confirm that bleeding has stopped *right now*, earlier blood is irrelevant, and we want nothing from minutes or hours prior to obscure the result. During the *shiva nekiyim*, however, washing immediately before a *bedikah* is problematic. The concern is not only whether bleeding is occurring at this precise moment, but whether any bleeding occurred at all that day. Washing right before could eliminate evidence of bleeding that happened that morning, which is precisely what we need to detect.

As a practical matter, a woman may wash or bathe during the *shiva nekiyim*, but she should wait approximately ten to fifteen minutes before performing the *bedikah*. If she is still bleeding, something will have emerged in that interval; if nothing does, it may be concluded that no bleeding occurred.

---

## Hefsek: D'Oraita or D'Ra…

### Source of Obligation

A threshold question must be asked: is the *hefsek taharah* — understood as a *bedikah*, performed as thoroughly as possible, reaching high internally and around the sides to ensure nothing is missed — required by Torah law? And more fundamentally: is the obligation of *hefsek taharah* at all a *d'oraita* requirement? On this question several distinct positions emerge.

### Niddah Needs Hefsek

One view holds that for a *niddah*, a *hefsek taharah* is required by Torah law for the following reason: the conclusion of the seven days of *niddah* does not by itself establish that bleeding has ended, because the woman may in fact have become a *zavah*. She may still be bleeding. Therefore, the Torah insists not only that the seven days have elapsed, but that she actively confirm the bleeding has stopped. The *hefsek taharah* is that confirmation. Without it, she cannot be certain she has exited the state of *niddah* and has not entered the state of *zavah*.

### Seven Days Suffice

Against this position, one can argue the converse: by a *zavah*, where she must count *shiva nekiyim*, the very structure of those seven clean days ultimately ensures she will know the bleeding stopped. If tomorrow she bleeds, she cannot count that day; if she does not bleed, she counts it. Eventually, by the time she completes seven clean days, she will know by default that the bleeding ended. Why, then, would she need to establish cessation at the outset before beginning the count? If blood appears tomorrow, the count does not begin anyway; if it does not, the count proceeds. The *hefsek taharah* appears superfluous for a *zavah*, since the *shiva nekiyim* themselves serve as ongoing verification.

### Zavah Needs Hefsek

The opposing view holds the exact reverse. For a *niddah*, the argument runs: *ve-chi le-olam tireh?* — is she going to bleed forever? This is the language of the Chatam Sofer, who traces it to Tosafot. A *niddah* bleeds for a predictable span — three days, four days, five days — and the seven days of *niddah* will certainly outlast that bleeding. There is no practical need for her to verify cessation, because cessation is a foregone conclusion well before the seven days are up. The Torah simply says: if you become a *niddah*, wait seven days. That suffices. If bleeding persists beyond seven days, we address that when it happens; but ordinarily, it is simply over.

For a *zavah*, however, the situation is fundamentally different. *Zivah* is, in the Ramban's framing, a form of illness — an abnormal physiological condition. Because the duration of *zivah* bleeding is uncertain and unpredictable, and because her *taharah* depends on counting *shiva nekiyim* — seven consecutive clean days — she genuinely needs to know that *today* ended without bleeding, so that *tomorrow* can count as day one. The *hefsek taharah* is, for the *zavah*, a prerequisite for initiating the count. The Ramban explains further why *niddah* requires only seven days while *zavah* requires *shiva nekiyim*: *niddah* is a natural biological process, and one need only wait out the maximum duration; *zavah* is unnatural, and the body must be shown to have fully recovered — hence seven consecutive clean days are required, and hence the need to establish clearly when clean days begin.

### Practical Nafka Mina

This dispute carries significant practical consequences. If *niddah* requires a *hefsek taharah* as a matter of Torah law, then leniencies are effectively unavailable. Even if we might otherwise invoke a *derabbanan* framework, a woman who is unambiguously a *niddah d'oraita* cannot benefit from such reasoning. Consider a case — not at all uncommon — where a woman has undergone a pap smear during the week of her *niddah*. She knows her period has stopped, but there is no possibility of performing a *bedikah* and finding it clean; the examination has caused bleeding that will persist for two or three days. Under this scenario, if *niddah* requires a *hefsek taharah d'oraita*, the posek has almost no room to maneuver. The standard *heterim* — those that apply to a *kesem*, or where there was no *hargashah*, or where blood derives from a wound — are simply unavailable for someone who is clearly a *niddah*.

If, on the other hand, we follow the view that *niddah* does not require a *hefsek taharah d'oraita* — because *ve-chi le-olam tireh*, she does not bleed indefinitely — then the *hefsek taharah* for *niddah* is only *derabbanan*. And since *zavah* in our day is always *derabbanan* as well — because a woman who observes *shiva nekiyim* every month can never be a *zavah d'oraita* (by *mima nafshach*, each month is either *niddah* or follows a previous *zavah* that was already resolved) — both the *niddah* dimension and the *zavah* dimension of the *hefsek taharah* are *derabbanan*. That opens the door to applying the range of *kulas* available when we are operating entirely within the *derabbanan* framework.

---

## Torah Level Hefsek

### Bedikot Requirement

Even granting that *hefsek taharah* is required at the Torah level — whether for *niddah* or for *zavah* — a further question must be asked: what precisely does the Torah require? Does it require *bedikot* — a physical internal examination? Or does it merely require that the woman know she has stopped bleeding?

The question deserves serious attention. Why should the Torah insist on a physical examination at all? Perhaps all that is needed is knowledge that bleeding has ceased. And how might a woman know that? By *hargashah* — by awareness in her body. If she has no sensation of bleeding, if she feels nothing emerging, perhaps that is sufficient *d'oraita*. She need not physically examine herself; she need only concentrate: is anything happening? If the answer is no, she has established, at the Torah level, that the bleeding has stopped.

Under this reading, the obligation of physical *bedikot* — the insertion of cloth, the reaching internally, the checking of all sides and crevices — is entirely *miderabbanan*. And once we are in the realm of *derabbanan*, the familiar tools of *pesika* become available: a wound, a *makkah*, the absence of *hargashah*, atypical circumstances — all of these can potentially be relied upon. The practical significance is considerable.

### Hargasha Approach

This is precisely the position of the Chatam Sofer and the Noda B'Yehuda, albeit arrived at through somewhat different conceptual routes. Both authorities maintain that what the Torah requires for *hefsek taharah* is not a physical examination but rather *hargashah* — the woman's concentrated, undistracted attention to whether she senses any bleeding. She must take a moment, clear her mind of all other thoughts, and focus solely on whether she feels anything. If she does not, she has performed a valid *hefsek taharah* at the Torah level.

The Chatam Sofer articulates this in vivid terms. His language, which he takes from the same *vein* as Tosafot, is *ve-chi le-olam tireh?* — was she going to bleed forever? The *niddah* stops bleeding; that is simply what happens. What the Torah requires is a moment of genuine, focused awareness that confirms this. *Chazal*, the Chatam Sofer adds, then mandated physical *bedikot* as a *d'rabbanan* overlay, because this degree of mental concentration is extraordinarily difficult to achieve — *bedika kasha me'od* — and so a physical examination was required as a more accessible substitute. But where physical examination is impossible, we may fall back on the Torah-level standard.

### Hargasha Definition

Despite their agreement on the basic principle, the Chatam Sofer and the Noda B'Yehuda in fact dispute what *hargashah* means — and this dispute explains why their positions diverge in certain cases.

The Chatam Sofer holds that *hargashah* is *pesicha pi ha-makor* — the sensation of the cervix or uterine opening opening. The Noda B'Yehuda holds that *hargashah* is *zivat davar lach* — the sensation of a liquid dripping or flowing. This difference in definition has precise implications for the *hefsek taharah* question. According to the Noda B'Yehuda, the *hargashah*-based method works for *hefsek taharah* as readily as for the weekly *bedikot*: if she feels no dripping, there is no *hargashah*, and the *hefsek taharah* is valid. According to the Chatam Sofer, however, a problem arises specifically at the *hefsek taharah* stage. During the *shiva nekiyim*, the method works well: if the cervix had closed when bleeding stopped, one would not feel it opening again unless bleeding resumed. But at the time of *hefsek taharah*, the cervix has been open throughout the days of bleeding — it may simply still be open, without any sensation of a new opening. How, then, can the woman confirm that the bleeding has stopped by attending to *hargashah*, if the very structure of *hargashah* as *pesicha pi ha-makor* cannot detect an absence of new bleeding from a cervix that was already open? That is the Chatam Sofer's objection. The Noda B'Yehuda's position does not encounter this difficulty, because *zivat davar lach* — the presence or absence of a dripping sensation — is relevant regardless of whether the cervix was already open.

### Makkah Case

The Chatam Sofer applies his position to a specific and practically significant case. A woman is a *niddah* and, at some point during or at the end of her *yemei nidosah*, develops a *makkah* — some internal wound or infection. The doctor has identified a problem, and performing a *bedikah* will inevitably yield blood from that *makkah*. What can be done?

The Chatam Sofer reasons as follows. Since for *niddah* there is no *hefsek taharah d'oraita* — because *ve-chi le-olam tireh?* — and since physical *bedikot* are only *derabbanan*, then when physical *bedikot* are impossible, we may fall back on the Torah-level alternative: the woman concentrates intently, clears her mind, and attends to whether she senses any bleeding. If she does not, that constitutes a valid *hefsek taharah* at the Torah level, and the *derabbanan* requirement of a physical *bedikah* is waived under these circumstances.

However, the Chatam Sofer himself raises a harder case. What if the *makkah* was already present *before* her period began, and she has been bleeding continuously — from both the *makkah* and the *niddah* — for an extended period? Now the problem is compounded: she does not even have a clear baseline of when her period began and ended. The Chatam Sofer expresses hesitation in applying the *hargashah*-based *hefsek taharah* in this situation, since the very uncertainty about the origin and duration of the bleeding complicates the assessment of cessation. Most later authorities, however, dispute this reservation. They argue that even in such a case, the woman typically knows her own body well enough to distinguish her period from the *makkah* bleeding, and knows when the periodic bleeding stopped. The concern the Chatam Sofer raises does not, in practice, undermine the reliability of the *hargashah*-based approach.

---

## Practical Solutions

### Rav Ovadia Position

Rav Ovadia Yosef rules decisively that one may rely on the broad consensus of *acharonim* who invoke *ve-chi le-olam tireh*. That principle — that a *niddah* does not bleed indefinitely and the cessation of her period is a known and predictable event — grounds a solid basis for permitting the *hargashah*-based *hefsek taharah* in difficult cases. Rav Ovadia specifically endorses the approach of the Chatam Sofer and the Noda B'Yehuda — the method of sitting, clearing the mind of all distraction, and concentrating entirely on whether one senses any bodily discharge. He holds that *ve-chi le-olam tireh* applies equally whether the *makkah* preceded or followed the onset of *niddah*, and that the Chatam Sofer's hesitation about the earlier *makkah* case need not be followed in practice.

---

## Torah Level Hefsek (II)

### Chazon Ish Method

The Chazon Ish approaches the same question from a different angle. Even if one accepts that the Torah requires some physical evidence of cessation — not merely mental concentration — it does not follow that the Torah requires an internal *bedikah* in the full *halachic* sense. The Chazon Ish suggests that repeated external wiping, performed at intervals over a sustained period, would constitute sufficient proof at the Torah level that bleeding has stopped. The logic is straightforward: if a woman wipes herself every several minutes over the course of half an hour (or at similarly regular intervals over some meaningful span of time), and finds nothing, the bleeding must have ceased. There is nowhere for the blood to go; if it were still flowing, it would appear. A single wipe might miss a drip that is still forming, or catch something that had been present earlier. But sustained, repeated wiping over time eliminates that concern. The Chazon Ish is clear that even by this standard, all the Torah ever required was knowledge that bleeding has ceased — and serial external wiping achieves that physically, without requiring an internal examination.

---

## Practical Solutions (II)

### Rav Moshe Ruling

Rav Moshe Feinstein is known to have ruled, at least in one case, that a woman should employ the Chatam Sofer's method: she should sit quietly, remove all other thoughts from her mind, and concentrate solely on whether she senses any bleeding. The Chatam Sofer's own language is precise on this point:

> *ela she-taamod sha'ah achas mesichas da'ata mikol hirhurim u-machshavot u-mashgicha al atzma ve-yoda'at she-lo niftach mekora*

She should stand — meaning remain still — for a period, completely withdrawn from all thoughts and preoccupations, attending only to herself and knowing that her *makor* has not opened. The Chatam Sofer acknowledges immediately that this is an extraordinarily demanding form of *bedikah* — *bedikah kasha me'od* — which is why *Chazal* required physical examination. But where physical examination is genuinely impossible, this is the fallback the Torah itself provides.

One might ask: if the Chatam Sofer's method is valid, does it not also eliminate the need for the weekly *bedikot* during the *shiva nekiyim*? The answer is that the Chatam Sofer himself holds that physical *bedikot* certainly work during the week, and the *hargashah*-based mental check works as well. In cases of difficulty — such as extra staining caused by an IUD, residual effects from a medical procedure, or other circumstances where normal *bedikot* are complicated — one might reduce the physical *bedikot* to one or two during the week, on days when examination is feasible, and rely on the mental *hargashah* check on other days. The Chatam Sofer's approach is a *b'dieved* fallback, not an ideal — but it is a genuine and grounded *halachic* option where the alternative is impossible.

### Pad Method Case

The following practical case illustrates how these principles come together. A woman preparing for marriage completed her seven clean days and performed *bedikot* during that week. When asked about her *hefsek taharah*, she realized she had never formally performed one. The question was whether she could proceed to the *mikvah*.

When asked how she had known her period stopped — that is, on what basis she had begun counting *shiva nekiyim* — she explained that she wears pads constantly, day and night. She had not seen anything on those pads since her period ended. Asked whether she checked the pads before discarding them, she confirmed that she had.

This constitutes, without question, a valid *hefsek taharah min haTorah*. It is no worse than the Chazon Ish's standard of repeated external wiping — indeed, it is arguably more comprehensive, since the pads were in continuous contact and she had attended to each one. The *hefsek taharah* is established *min haTorah*, and under the pressing circumstances of an imminent *chuppah* and the serious concerns associated with *chuppat niddah*, there is every reason to be *somech* on this. While it would be an overstatement to say that others explicitly rule this way, the ruling accords entirely with what the major authorities say about *hefsek taharah*, and *lechatchila* one should certainly perform the *hefsek taharah* formally with cloth.

### Tampon Usage

The question of a tampon as *hefsek taharah* is worth addressing directly. The standard *halachic* concern with internal examination is that the cloth or *bedikah* implement must reach the sides and crevices of the vaginal canal — not merely go straight up through the center — since blood may have dripped and caught on the sides. A tampon, being narrow and essentially cylindrical, might seem to miss those areas.

However, if the tampon is left in place for several minutes, it absorbs whatever discharges are present and expands, conforming to the surrounding tissue. This renders it functionally similar to a *moch dachuk* in its coverage, and it is therefore a valid medium for *hefsek taharah*. A woman who specifically intends to perform a *hefsek taharah* using a tampon should leave it in for approximately five to ten minutes.

Moreover, a tampon that was inserted during the day without any formal *kavana* of *hefsek taharah* — and was later found to be clean when removed — can retroactively serve as the *hefsek taharah*. The reasoning is that the very act of removing the tampon and examining it constitutes the *bedikah*; the woman obviously had the checking in mind at the moment she looked at it. That is precisely what *hefsek taharah* requires. If a woman returns home in the evening, reports that she never performed a formal *hefsek taharah*, but mentions that she had a tampon in all day and it came out clean — the tampon provides the *hefsek taharah*, and it was performed during the day, satisfying the timing requirement. *Lechatchila*, of course, a *hefsek taharah* should be performed deliberately and with *kavana*, with prior washing and with time for multiple attempts if necessary. But the tampon case is entirely valid *b'dieved*, and the *hefsek taharah* it represents occurred at the moment she removed and checked it.

---

## Timing of Hefsek

### Evening Timing

Turning to the question of timing: when should the *hefsek taharah* be performed? The *Mechaber* in siman 196 writes that the *shiva nekiyim* of the *zavah* begin on the day following the day she ceased bleeding, and that accordingly, on the day she stops, she examines herself in order to *tifsok b'taharah* — to conclude in a state of purity.

### Bein Hashmashot Role

The Vilna Gaon in his *Biur HaGra* explains that the requirement to perform the *bedikah* close to evening is a *chumra lechatchila*. The logic is as follows: what I want to establish is not merely that I found myself clean at some point during the day, but that nothing occurred between that examination and the onset of the next day. To achieve this most effectively, I should perform the *hefsek taharah* as close to *bein hashmashot* as possible. The reason I cannot do so *after* the onset of *bein hashmashot* is critical: if I wait until *bein hashmashot* has begun, I lose the day. The day of *hefsek taharah* must count as "yesterday" — a complete, clean day — so that tomorrow can begin as the first of the *shiva nekiyim*. If I wait until *bein hashmashot* is already underway, I cannot be certain that today, as a full day, was clean, and I cannot commence counting tomorrow.

Performing the *hefsek taharah* immediately before *bein hashmashot* solves this: all of today was unproblematic, and tomorrow begins — from the onset of *bein hashmashot*, *misafek* — as day one. The Beis Yosef had already noted that what the sources refer to is not *bein hashmashot mamash* but *samuch l'bein hashmashot* — in the vicinity of *bein hashmashot*, shortly before it begins.

---

## Timing of Hefsek (II)

### Morning Bedieved

The Rama rules that *b'dieved*, even if the woman examined herself only in the morning and found herself clean, that suffices. This ruling reflects a deeper truth about the physiology involved.

### Blood Flow Science

It is worth understanding why this is so. Prior to the discoveries of William Harvey regarding the circulatory system — that blood circulates through the entire body and returns via capillaries — it was commonly imagined that blood simply pooled and sloshed around within the body. The uterus, under this mental model, might have been conceived as something like a reservoir: full, it drips; emptied, it stops. Under such an image, one might indeed fear that the bleeding could stop at one moment and restart at another, as if a valve had opened and closed.

But this is not how uterine bleeding actually works. What we call menstrual flow is the atrophying of the uterine wall's vascular lining — a process by which blood vessels that had engorged in preparation for a fertilized egg gradually break down, releasing their contents through the cervix, which is normally open to approximately two millimeters. Once that process is complete, the blood does not "stop" in the sense of a valve closing; it is simply finished. There is no such thing as catching the precise moment of cessation. If the flow has stopped, it is because it is done. There is no closed/open dynamic to be monitored; the question is only whether the blood is dripping or not.

The Chatam Sofer already understood this reality. Given this understanding, the concern that undergirds requiring the *bedikah* close to *bein hashmashot* — namely, that something might have occurred between the morning examination and the evening — is largely theoretical. If the bleeding stopped, it stopped. A clean examination in the morning gives us genuine grounds to know that the next seven days will also be clean. The seven *bedikot* of *shiva nekiyim* are required not because the *hefsek taharah* might have missed something that later restarted, but because the Torah requires *shiva nekiyim* — seven days during which the woman is cognitively attentive to her status.

### Early Check Strategy

The practical conclusion from all of this is counterintuitive relative to the common practice of waiting until late afternoon. Doing the *hefsek taharah* as early as possible is actually advisable, because it leaves time to perform it again — and again, if necessary — if the first check does not come out clean. If a woman waits until immediately before *bein hashmashot* and that *bedikah* is problematic, she has no recourse. If she performs the *hefsek taharah* early in the afternoon and encounters a *shayla*, there is time to redo it. If it stopped bleeding today, it is done — and a clean examination at two in the afternoon is no less valid than one at six. The concern that drove the requirement of performing it close to evening was based on a model of uterine function that does not reflect reality. *Lechatchila* one certainly takes the *halachic* framework seriously, but *b'dieved* the morning is valid, and practically speaking, earlier is better.

There is an additional strategic consideration: in our day, a woman cannot begin counting *shiva nekiyim* until day five of the niddah period. But cessation of bleeding often occurs before then. Performing the *hefsek taharah* on day three or day four — even though counting will not begin until day six — has the advantage that if day five is cut off from the waiting period for any reason, that day five can be counted as day one of *shiva nekiyim*. There is no reason to delay the *hefsek taharah*; the cost of performing it early is negligible and the benefit is real.

---

## Moch Dachuk Discussion

### Why Moch Dachuk

Returning to the text of the *Mechaber* in siman 196, a further requirement is introduced. The *Mechaber* writes that a husband should instruct his household that the woman should perform her *hefsek taharah* using a *moch dachuk* — a tightly packed cloth insert — which should remain in place throughout *bein hashmashot*. The text reads:

> יִלְמַד אָדָם בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ שֶׁתְּהֵא בּוֹדֶקֶת בְּיוֹם הַפְסֵק טָהֳרָתָהּ בְּמוֹךְ דָּחוּק וְשֶׁיְּהֵא שָׁם כָּל בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת שֶׁזּוֹ הַבְּדִיקָה מוֹצִיאָה מִיַּד כָּל סָפֵק.

The function of the *moch dachuk* is to ensure that all crevices and folds of the vaginal canal are covered. Even after washing, a drop of blood may have dripped and lodged in a crevice in the interval between washing and inserting the *bedikah* cloth. A single *bedikah* with cloth going straight up the center might miss blood caught on the sides. The *moch dachuk* — tightly packed, expanding to fill the entire space — and left in place throughout *bein hashmashot*, addresses this comprehensively. As the *Mechaber* puts it, this examination removes all doubt.

### Moch Optional

The *moch dachuk* is, however, a *lechatchila* standard — an ideal, not an obligation. It is not required, and if it causes any discomfort, pain, or irritation, it should not be done. The practice creates a heightened standard of certainty, but it is not the baseline requirement; ordinary *bedikot* with cloth suffice.

### Against Moch Dachuk

After considerable experience with the questions (*shailos*) that the *moch dachuk* generates in practice, the conclusion of several authorities is simply: do not do it. The problems it creates outweigh the benefits. Blood from irritation caused by the *moch dachuk* itself creates new *shailos* about whether the woman has become *tamei*; husbands and wives come with questions that would never have arisen had the *moch dachuk* not been used. The *moch dachuk* is supposed to eliminate *safek* — but it generates more *sfeikot* than it resolves.

Rabbi Abadi, in his *Hilchos Niddah*, rules explicitly that the *moch dachuk* should not be done. It is a *chumra* that hurts people and causes complications, and despite its theoretical virtue of removing all doubt, the practical consequence is the opposite: it multiplies uncertainty. Similarly, Rav Tuvia Goldstein — a contemporary and close colleague of Rav Moshe Feinstein, and a major *posek* in his own right — when asked about the *moch dachuk*, responded simply that it causes irritation, conveying through that terse characterization his lack of enthusiasm for the practice. The practical recommendation is thus clear: *kallah* teachers should explain that the *moch dachuk* is strictly *lechatchila* and optional, and that if it is in any way uncomfortable or problematic, it should be avoided entirely.

---

## One-Day Bleeding

### One-Day Rule

An entirely different set of considerations applies when a woman has only a single day of bleeding. Ordinarily this is not the situation with *niddah*, but it can occur — for instance, with hormonal changes caused by a new contraceptive, which involves genuine hormonal activity and therefore genuine *niddah* blood rather than the blood of a *makkah*. If she ceased bleeding on that same day, the *Mechaber* rules in Halacha 2 of siman 196 that she must perform the *hefsek taharah* using a *moch dachuk* which remains in place throughout *bein hashmashot*. In this case, the *moch dachuk* is not merely *lechatchila* — it is required. The reason is that when bleeding occurred for only a single day, there is particular uncertainty whether that day concluded without bleeding. The full coverage of *kol bein hashmashot* is necessary to establish with confidence that the day ended cleanly, so that tomorrow can begin as day one of *shiva nekiyim*.

The Rama adds that *b'dieved*, if she examined herself *samuch l'bein hashmashot* and found herself clean, even without the *moch dachuk* remaining throughout *bein hashmashot*, this is valid. The reasoning is that *kol bein hashmashot* was never a *halachic* obligation that any authority actually imposed; it was acknowledged as an ideal — the Gemara's point is that if one were to require checking the entire *bein hashmashot*, that would be understandable, but no one ever required it. What Rav Yehuda required was *samuch l'bein hashmashot*, and it is that standard which applies *b'dieved* in the one-day case. The morning alone does not suffice here, because the one-day scenario generates genuine uncertainty not present when the bleeding has extended over multiple days.

### Kesem Leniencies

A further distinction applies when the single-day "bleeding" takes the form of a *kesem* — a stain — rather than clearly identifiable flowing blood. The *halachic* treatment of *kesamim* differs from that of significant bleeding.
