When the disruption of the *shiva nekiyim* was caused by a *kesem*, it is plausible to treat the discharge as residue from the earlier bleeding rather than as the onset of a new episode. If what was found is only a *kesem* — discovered on underwear or in toilet water rather than experienced as a clear flow — there is genuine room to be lenient and to hold that a *moch dachuk* is not required when counting resumes, particularly if the amount was not significant. Where there is clearly flowing blood, however, this distinction cannot be applied, and a new start with full requirements applies.

---

---

# Hullin 137

## Trefah Exemption

### Trefah Not Listed

The *mishnah* enumerated several ways in which *zroa u'lchayayim u'va'keiva* — the priestly gifts of the arm, cheeks, and stomach — has a broader application than *reshit ha'gez*, the obligation to give the first shearings. The most obvious distinction is that *reshit ha'gez* applies only to sheep and only when one owns at least five of them. The *Gemara*, however, observes that additional distinctions could have been listed, and asks why the *mishnah* omitted the fact that *reshit ha'gez* applies to a *trefah* animal, whereas the priestly gifts do not.

The *Gemara* takes it for granted that the gifts do not apply to a *trefah*. Rashi explains this on the basis of the verse *v'nasan la'Kohen* — "and he shall give to the Kohen" — which implies the gift must be suitable for the *Kohen* to eat. Since a *trefah* cannot be eaten by the *Kohen*, the gifts do not apply. Given this, why does the *mishnah* not list the *trefah* exemption as a point of difference, noting that *reshit ha'gez* applies to a *trefah* while *matanos* do not?

Ravina answers: the *mishnah* reflects the position of Rabbi Shimon. A *baraita* states explicitly that Rabbi Shimon exempts *trefos* from *reshit ha'gez* as well. From his perspective, there is no distinction to list: both *matanos* and *reshit ha'gez* are equally exempt from the *trefah*, so no contrast exists.

### Rabbi Shimon's Derivation

The *Gemara* asks: what is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning? The answer is that he employs a *gezeirah shavah*: he links the word *nesina* (giving) in the context of *reshit ha'gez* to the word *nesina* in the context of *ma'aser behemah*. Just as *ma'aser* does not apply to a *trefah*, so too *reshit ha'gez* does not apply to a *trefah*.

### Terumah Linkage Rejected

The *Gemara* immediately raises a challenge: if one is willing to derive a law through the shared word *nesina*, why not instead link *reshit ha'gez* to *terumah*? The consequence of such a linkage would be that just as *terumah* applies only in the Land of Israel and not outside it, so too *reshit ha'gez* would apply only in the Land of Israel — a position identified elsewhere with Rabbi Elazar, but not the position of the *mishnah*, which explicitly states that *reshit ha'gez* applies both in the Land of Israel and outside it.

The *Gemara* responds with a simple *ela*: that linkage is rejected precisely because of our *mishnah's* ruling that *reshit ha'gez* applies in *chutz la'aretz*. We therefore cannot learn from *terumah*. The reasoning of Rabbi Shimon must instead be grounded in the link to *ma'aser*.

The *Gemara* then explains the actual mechanism of Rabbi Shimon's derivation: he links *reshit ha'gez* to *ma'aser behemah* through the shared word *tzon* (flock). The verse establishing *ma'aser behemah* speaks of the flock, and *reshit ha'gez* likewise speaks of the flock. Just as *ma'aser* does not apply to a *trefah*, so too *reshit ha'gez* does not apply to a *trefah*.

The *Gemara* then asks: and how do we know that *ma'aser* itself does not apply to a *trefah*? After all, if the tenth animal that walks out of the pen has a *mum* (blemish), it does become sanctified as *ma'aser* and is eaten with its blemish rather than redeemed. Perhaps a *trefah* should be treated similarly? The *Gemara* answers from the verse *kol asher ya'avor tachas ha'shavet* — "whatever passes under the rod." Since a *trefah* cannot walk under the rod (some *trefos* are missing a limb), the verse excludes it. Tosafot notes a difficulty here: some animals that are not *trefos* also cannot walk under the rod, such as one whose hoof has been torn off. The *Gemara's* *drasha* thus focuses on the quality of being unable to walk as the operative exclusion, even though the category of *trefah* is broader than just those that literally cannot walk. That is the mechanics of the *drasha*, even if it is somewhat inexact.

### Ma'aser vs. Bechor

Having established the *tzon*-*tzon* link to *ma'aser*, the *Gemara* challenges: why not instead derive *reshit ha'gez* from *bechor* through the same shared word *tzon*? The verse regarding *bechor* also uses the word *tzon*. And since *bechor* does apply to a *trefah* — the firstborn is automatically sanctified by virtue of its birth, without any act on the owner's part — learning from *bechor* would lead to the conclusion that *reshit ha'gez* also applies to a *trefah*, reversing Rabbi Shimon's position.

### Reshit HaGez-Ma'aser Lin…

The *Gemara* responds that it is more logical to learn *reshit ha'gez* from *ma'aser* rather than from *bechor*, and proceeds to enumerate the points of connection between *reshit ha'gez* and *ma'aser*. First, *zecharim*: both *reshit ha'gez* and *ma'aser* are not limited to male animals, whereas *bechor* applies only to males. Second, *tmeim*: neither applies to non-kosher species, while *bechor* applies even to a donkey. Third, *bimrubim*: both require a minimum number of animals — *reshit ha'gez* requires five and *ma'aser* requires ten — whereas *bechor* applies even to a single animal. Fourth, *merachem*: neither *reshit ha'gez* nor *ma'aser* is sanctified from the moment of birth, unlike *bechor*, which is sanctified from the womb. Fifth, *adam*: neither applies to human beings, while *bechor* does. Sixth, *pashut*: crucially, both apply only to non-firstborns. An animal that is already a *bechor* is not subject to *ma'aser* and not subject to *reshit ha'gez*, since both apply only to ordinary, non-sanctified animals — the precise inverse of *bechor*. Seventh, *lifnei ha'dibur*: neither *reshit ha'gez* nor *ma'aser* existed as obligations before the Torah was given at Sinai, whereas *bechor* had a form of sacred status even in Egypt.

### Reshit HaGez-Bechor Cont…

The *Gemara* counters: *adrabah* — quite the reverse! Perhaps *reshit ha'gez* should be learned from *bechor*, since there are also numerous points of connection between them. The *Gemara* lists these in turn. *Yatom*: both *reshit ha'gez* and *bechor* apply to an orphan animal — one born after its mother died during delivery — whereas *ma'aser behemah* does not apply to such an animal, because *ma'aser* is bound by the rule that an animal must have been with its mother for seven days, a condition that cannot be fulfilled if the mother died at birth. *Shelakchu*: both apply to purchased animals. *Ma'aser behemah* applies only to animals born within one's own flock; if one purchases young sheep, one does not give *ma'aser*. But if one purchases sheep and shears them, one gives *reshit ha'gez*, and if one purchases a sheep and it gives birth to a firstborn, one gives *bechor*. *Beshutfut*: both apply in cases of partnership with another Jew, while *ma'aser behemah* applies only when the animals are solely owned. *Netano*: similarly, both apply to an animal received as a gift, which again is not born into one's own flock and thus not subject to *ma'aser*. *Bifnei Kohen* (or in the reading of Tosafot, *lifnei*): in the case of *ma'aser*, if one miscounts and designates the ninth or the eleventh animal as the tenth, those animals also acquire sanctity — *ma'aser* pulls in adjacent animals — whereas *bechor* and *reshit ha'gez* apply only to the specific animal itself, with no such spillover. *Kohen*: both *reshit ha'gez* and *bechor* are given to the *Kohen*, whereas *ma'aser behemah* is brought as a *korban* and eaten by the owner, not given to a *Kohen*. *Bikdushah*: neither *bechor* nor *reshit ha'gez* requires a formal act of sanctification, whereas *ma'aser* requires the act of designating and counting the tenth. *Mechira*: both *bechor* and *reshit ha'gez* may be sold, whereas the Torah states explicitly *lo yimacher* — *ma'aser behemah* shall not be sold.

### Pashut as Key Factor

Having presented a formidable list of connections to *bechor*, the *Gemara* acknowledges: *v'hani nifishei* — these points are even more numerous. Yet the conclusion remains that one should derive *reshit ha'gez* from *ma'aser* rather than from *bechor*. The decisive reasoning is: *pashut mipashut adif lei* — the connection of *pashut* (non-firstborn) is the most fundamental. The entire legal identity of *bechor* is that it is the firstborn; the entire legal identity of both *ma'aser* and *reshit ha'gez* is that they apply specifically to non-firstborns, to ordinary animals. *Bechor* is constitutively defined by being *bechor*; *ma'aser* and *reshit ha'gez* are constitutively defined by being everything that is not *bechor*. That structural correspondence outweighs the larger number of incidental shared features with *bechor*. Therefore, Rabbi Shimon correctly derives from *ma'aser* that *reshit ha'gez* does not apply to a *trefah*.

---

## Sheep Only

### Shearing Gezeirah

The *mishnah* teaches that *reshit ha'gez* applies only to *rechelim* — sheep — unlike the priestly gifts of *zroa u'lchayayim u'va'keiva*, which apply to both cattle and sheep. The *Gemara* at the top of 137a asks: from where is this derived?

Rav Chisda answers: we make a *gezeirah shavah* using the word *gez* (shearing). The Torah states *reishit gez tzonecha titen lo* — "the first shearing of your flock you shall give to him." And in the book of Iyov we find the verse *umigez kevasai yitchamam* — "and from the shearing of my sheep he warmed himself," where the same word *gez* appears specifically in the context of *kevasim*, sheep, not goats. The question naturally arises: why would one have thought to include goats in the first place, given that the verse mentions *tzon* (flock)? Tosafot addresses this by citing Bereishit 27, where Rivka tells Yaakov to go to the *tzon* and take *shenei g'deiyei izim* — two goats. There we see that goats can be included in the word *tzon*. Hence the need to exclude them through a comparison to the Iyov verse, which uses *gez* specifically by *kevasim*. Tosafot notes this is not a formal *gezeirah shavah* in the classical sense, but rather a textual inference that when the Torah speaks of shearing one's flock, it means shearing sheep, not goats.

### Goat Exclusion

The *Gemara* raises a further challenge: why not link the word *gez* (shearing) instead to the *bechor* context, where the Torah also uses the language of shearing flocks — *v'lo tagoz bechor tzonecha*, do not shear the firstborn of your flock. And the *baraita* there expands this prohibition to cattle as well, implying that shearing can be applied even to cattle. If shearing is broad enough to encompass cattle, perhaps the obligation of *reshit ha'gez* should likewise include goats and even cattle.

The *Gemara* responds with a verse: *titen lo* — "you shall give to him" — implies something suitable for the *Kohen* to wear personally, not merely for utilitarian purposes. This would exclude cattle hair, which is not used for clothing. But what of goat hair? Goat hair is used for certain textile purposes. The *Gemara* answers: *ba'inan geizah v'leika* — the Torah requires an act of *geizah*, actual shearing, and when one removes the hair of goats, one does not shear; rather, one plucks or removes it through a different process. Since the method of hair removal from goats differs from shearing, it does not qualify.

### Rabbi Yosi & Verbs

The *Gemara* then identifies the interpretive principle at stake and asks: who holds this position — that the word *geizah* means specifically an act of shearing and nothing analogous? This is the approach of Rabbi Yosi, who consistently interprets verbs in their narrow, precise sense and does not extend them abstractly to any act that achieves the same result.

However, the *Gemara* immediately complicates this: even according to Rabbi Yosi, who reads verbs narrowly, his principle is *modeh Rabbi Yosi b'midi d'orchei* — Rabbi Yosi concedes where the act in question is the normal, customary way of doing that thing for that object. Rabbi Yosi only excludes unusual or analogous methods when applied to the same object. But removing goat hair by plucking or by whatever method is standard for goats is the *normal* way of removing goat hair. It is not an unusual technique applied to goats — it is precisely the usual one. Therefore, Rabbi Yosi's narrow reading of *geizah* would not by itself suffice to exclude goats.

### Priestly Garment Test

The *Gemara* therefore invokes a different principle, attributed to the school of Rav Yehoshua ben Levi: the verse connecting *reshit ha'gez* to the *Kohen* uses the language *la'amod l'shareit* — to stand and serve — evoking the priestly service. This yields the requirement that the gift must be *davar harauy l'shirut* — something from which a garment suitable for the priestly service could potentially be made, i.e., *bigdei kehunah*. Wool meets this criterion, since wool was used in the *bigdei kehunah*. Goat hair was never used in the *bigdei kehunah* and therefore does not qualify. This principle — that the gift must be material suitable for priestly garments — will recur in the subsequent discussion to define both the type and the quantity of wool required.

### Hard Wool Exemption

With the *gezeirah shavah* to the Iyov verse no longer needed to exclude goats (since the *davar harauy l'shirut* principle accomplishes that independently), the *Gemara* asks: what purpose does the Iyov verse serve? It answers: *l'chadtani d'bei Rabbi Yishmael* — it comes to teach what was stated in the school of Rabbi Yishmael. The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: *k'vasim shetzamran kasheh peturin me'reishit ha'gez* — sheep whose wool is stiff and hard are exempt from *reshit ha'gez*. The basis is the very verse from Iyov: *umigez kevasai yitchamam* — "from the shearing of my sheep he warmed himself." The wool must be of the kind capable of producing warmth when fashioned into clothing. Wool that is too stiff and rigid to wrap around the body and provide genuine warmth does not qualify.

Rashi and the Rambam read this somewhat differently. Rashi appears to suggest a relative standard — that such wool is distinguished from ordinary sheep's wool — while the Rambam states the criterion in objective terms: wool that is categorically incapable of providing warmth as clothing is exempt.

This is a striking application. The thematic orientation of *reshit ha'gez* toward clothing and the *Kohen*'s personal use — an idea the Rambam himself introduces mid-*halacha* when he notes that the Torah provided the *Kohen* with grain through *terumah*, meat through *korbanot* and *matanos*, and clothing through *reshit ha'gez* — turns out to have concrete halachic consequences. It excludes goat hair, restricts the obligation to wool, and now further restricts it to wool that is genuinely fit for garment-making.

### Shearing vs. Bathing

The *Gemara* now addresses two apparently conflicting *baraitot*. The first *baraita* states: if one shears goats — which we have established is exempt — and if one *shotef* (rinses, passes through water) the sheep, one is exempt. The case of washing the sheep refers to the practice of driving flocks through a river or stream, which serves as a bath; in the course of this process, some wool may be torn off or separated from the sheep's body. The question is whether wool that detaches during bathing is subject to *reshit ha'gez*. The first *baraita* says no, this is exempt.

A second *baraita*, however, states: while shearing goats is exempt, *v'hashoteif et harechelim chayav* — one who bathes the sheep is *obligated*. The two *baraitot* thus appear to contradict each other directly regarding the wool that comes off sheep during bathing.

### Rabanan-Rabbi Yosi Debate

The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. One *baraita* represents the position of the *Rabanan* and the other represents the position of Rabbi Yosi. The dispute is precisely about how narrowly one reads the verb *gez*. According to Rabbi Yosi, *reshit ha'gez* requires a formal act of shearing; wool that separates during bathing is not the product of *geizah* and is therefore exempt. According to the *Rabanan*, who read the verb more broadly, any process that removes wool from sheep — including bathing, if wool detaches as a result — creates an obligation.

The *Gemara* at this point cites a *baraita* to illustrate Rabbi Yosi's broader hermeneutic: the Torah says *leket ketzircha* — the gleanings of your harvesting. Rabbi Yosi says *ein leket ela haba machamat katzir* — *leket* applies only to what falls as a direct result of using a scythe in the normal harvest process, not to grain that falls when one merely plucks stalks by hand. The *Gemara* notes that Rabbi Yosi here seems to say the same thing as the *tana kama*, and concludes that the *baraita* reads as Rabbi Yosi elaborating on the *tana kama*'s position: *kuli Rabbi Yosi* — it is all Rabbi Yosi.

Yet Rabbi Yosi is not entirely literalistic. A subsequent *baraita* shows that he extends *leket* to uprooting onions and plucking tomatoes, deriving this from the repetition of harvest-language in the relevant verses. His principle is *modeh Rabbi Yosi b'midi d'orchei*: he includes analogous acts that are the normal, standard method for that particular crop or object, even if they differ from scything wheat. He excludes only acts that are unusual or indirect — such as wool dislodging during bathing, or grain falling when one plucks stalks by hand. The crucial distinction is between what is genuinely *orchei* (customary practice) for a given subject and what is not.

Rav Acha the son of Rava makes this explicit to Rav Ashi, and a further proof is adduced from the *mishnah* concerning *pe'ah* and *malbinot betzalim shebein hayerek* — fields of onions interspersed among non-obligated vegetables. Rabbi Yosi there rules *pe'ah mikol achat v'achat* (one gives *pe'ah* from each separate row of onions), which presupposes that uprooting onions qualifies for *pe'ah* even though the verse uses the word *katzircha*. Since uprooting is the standard way of harvesting onions, Rabbi Yosi includes it. This confirms that his standard is functional normalcy, not strict literal identity with the verb.

---

## Wool Amount

### Sheep Count

The *mishnah* records a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the minimum number of sheep required to trigger the obligation of *reshit ha'gez*. Beit Shammai holds that two sheep suffice, while Beit Hillel holds that five are required. The *Gemara* notes that the position of Beit Shammai is not difficult: we know of a verse where two animals are called *tzon*, so two certainly constitute a flock. The difficulty is with Beit Hillel: there is also a verse where two are called *tzon*, so how can Beit Hillel require five and simply ignore that usage?

### Asuyyot Analysis

Rav Kahana answers by invoking the word *asuyot* in the verse cited by Beit Hillel, which describes five sheep as *asuyot*. The word *asuyot* — meaning "made" or "laden" — indicates, in the plural, that they perform (*osot*) two *mitzvot*: *reshit ha'gez* and *matanos*. When you own five sheep, you are positioned to fulfill both the obligation of giving first shearings and the obligation of giving the priestly gifts upon slaughter.

The *Gemara* challenges this: perhaps the two *mitzvot* are *bechorah* and *matanos* — the firstborn obligation and the gifts? The *Gemara* rejects this: one sheep is sufficient to be obligated in both the firstborn and the priestly gifts, so the number five would be irrelevant to that combination. The *Gemara* then turns the objection back: but similarly, one sheep suffices for *matanos*! Rav Ashi therefore reformulates the *drasha*: *asuyot* in the causative sense means that these five sheep impose an obligation on their owner — *she-ma'asot et ba'aleihem* — they compel him to perform the *mitzvah* of *reshit ha'gez*. The word *asuyot* thus signals that it is specifically when one owns five that this obligation is activated.

### Rabbi Yosi's Four

A third opinion is introduced from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: Rabbi Yosi's son cites his father as holding that four sheep are required, deriving this from the verse *v'arba tzon tachas ha'seh* — the Torah's requirement that one who steals and slaughters or sells a sheep repays four sheep in its place. That verse uses the word *tzon* (flock) to describe four animals, yielding the position that four constitutes a flock sufficient for the obligation.

### Rabbi Prefers Yosi

A *baraita* records that Rabbi (Rebbi Yehudah HaNasi) expressed a clear preference for the position of Rabbi Yosi. He states: even if Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai derived their positions from verses in the Torah, and Rabbi Yosi's position were derived only from a verse in *Nach*, the tradition (*kabbalah*) of Rabbi Yosi's school would be preferable. All the more so now, when in fact Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai are learning from verses in *Nach*, while Rabbi Yosi is learning from a verse in the Torah itself — how much more so should we follow Rabbi Yosi's ruling of four.

The *Gemara* asks what specifically attracts Rebbi to Rabbi Yosi's position. One might think he is drawn to it as a middle-ground compromise between the two and five of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. The *Gemara* rejects this reasoning, invoking the principle *ein hachra'ah shelishit machra'at* — a third opinion does not carry weight simply by virtue of situating itself between two others. Such weight applies only to a *da'at machria*, a position that actually splits its vote: where one *tanna* says a law applies in both Case A and Case B, and another says it applies in neither, a third who says it applies in A but not in B effectively sides with the first opinion in the dispute about A and with the second in the dispute about B, yielding a two-to-one majority in each direction. That is logically decisive. But a position that simply announces a new number — four, without any logical decomposition of the other positions — is merely a third opinion, not a tipping opinion.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that what drew Rebbi to Rabbi Yosi's position was not its middling character but its pedigree: *mipi ha'shemuah amrah* — he had it as a received tradition, *mipi Chaggai Zechariah u'Malachi*, from the last of the prophets. It should be noted that despite Rebbi's preference, the *Geonim* and the Rambam rule in accordance with Beit Hillel's position of five sheep, following the standard principle of *halacha* like Beit Hillel rather than privileging Rebbi's expressed preference, since a ruling in the *mishnah* does not in itself determine final *psak*.

---

## Amount to Give

### Dosetai's Position

The *mishnah* records the opinion of Dosetai ben Hurkenos, who holds that each of the five sheep must produce a *maneh u'pras* — one and a half *maneh* — of wool in order for the owner to be obligated. The *Chachamim* disagree and say *kol shehu* — even a small amount suffices. The *Gemara* immediately asks: how much is *kol shehu*?

### Rav's Unified Amount

Rav answers: *maneh u'pras* — the same figure as Dosetai ben Hurkenos, one and a half *maneh*. The difference is that whereas Dosetai requires one and a half *maneh* from each sheep individually, Rav requires one and a half *maneh* total from all five sheep combined. He adds the qualification *uvilvad sheyihyu mechumashot* — provided the total is equally distributed among the five sheep. This means each sheep must contribute its proportionate share: if one sheep produces its ninth of the total but another falls short, the obligation is not triggered. The floor per individual sheep is therefore one-fifth of one and a half *maneh*.

### Shmuel's Proportion

Shmuel states a different position: the flock must produce 60 *selaim* in total, and one *sela* is given to the *Kohen*. This introduces a proportional model — the gift is 1/60th of the total shearing, an idea recognizable from *terumah*. Shmuel's minimum of 60 *selaim* is likely derived by working backwards from the gift: since one must give something of significance — no less than one *sela* — and since the proportion is 1/60th, one must begin with at least 60 *selaim*. The minimum is generated by the logic of the proportion.

### Rabbi Yochanan's Minimum

Rabbi Yochanan, as reported by Rabbah bar bar Chana, disagrees with Shmuel on both points. He holds that the total shearing need only be six *selaim*, and the gift to the *Kohen* is five *selaim*. This reflects a fundamentally different framework: rather than a proportional obligation, Rabbi Yochanan posits an absolute minimum gift of five *selaim*. The basis for five as the minimum gift is presumably related to the *mishnah*'s language of *reishit* — the principle that *reishit sheyihyu she'reha nikarim*, that what remains after the gift is given must still be recognizable as a meaningful quantity. If the absolute minimum gift is five, then the minimum one must possess before giving is six: five to give plus something left over.

Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan are thus working from opposite ends. Shmuel fixes the proportion (1/60th) and derives the minimum from the smallest meaningful unit (one *sela*), arriving at 60. Rabbi Yochanan fixes the absolute minimum gift (five *selaim*) and derives the minimum holding from that floor, arriving at six.

### Conversion Clarified

The *Gemara* works with several units of measurement, and it is worth establishing the conversion table precisely. The correct equivalences are: one *maneh* equals 25 *selaim*, and one *maneh* also equals 100 *dinarim*, which means one *sela* equals four *dinarim*. With this corrected table, the positions may be restated: Dosetai ben Hurkenos requires one and a half *maneh* (= 37.5 *selaim*) per sheep, yielding a total of 187.5 *selaim* for five sheep — approximately eight pounds of wool. Rav requires 37.5 *selaim* total across all five sheep. Shmuel requires 60 *selaim* total. Rabbi Yochanan requires only six *selaim* total, which at the scale of roughly 100 *selaim* to four pounds amounts to approximately two-tenths of a pound — a very small quantity indeed. A useful shorthand for subsequent discussions: one *maneh* is approximately equivalent to one pound of wool.

---

---

# Hullin 138

## Mishnah Review

### Dosa vs. Hachamim

We begin on 137b, picking up the *sugya* dealing with *reishit hagez* — the obligation to give the first shearings to the *kohen*. The *mishnah* records a dispute about the minimum amount of wool required from one's sheep. Dosa ben Harkinas holds that the threshold is one and a half *maneh* per sheep. A *maneh*, it should be noted, equals 25 *sela*, which in turn equals 100 *dinar* — roughly a pound in modern terms. The *Hachamim*, by contrast, maintain *kol shehu*: any amount suffices. The *Gemara*, however, is unwilling to accept that *kol shehu* means literally any trivial quantity, and several substantive positions emerge from the attempt to define it more precisely.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel holds that the minimum unit relevant here is one *sela* — since there are 25 *sela* to a *maneh*, this amounts to roughly 4% of a pound. His reasoning is proportional: one must give a *sixtieth* of the total wool to the *kohen*, and since the minimum gift is one *sela*, working backwards, one must begin with at least 60 *sela* of wool. This is notably less than the one and a half *maneh* (37.5 *sela*) mentioned by the first opinion.

### Six Sela Minimum

A different approach dispenses with the proportional framework entirely and works from the absolute figure prescribed by the *mishnah* elsewhere: the *kohen* receives five *sela*. If five *sela* is the absolute minimum gift, then the minimum amount of wool one must start with is six *sela* — just enough to give five and retain a nominal remainder. On this view, the measure is always flat and absolute, not proportional.

---

## Ulla/R. Elazar

### Kol Shehu Statement

We now reach the line in the *Gemara* where Ulla reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *kol shehu shaninu* — when the *mishnah* says *kol shehu*, it means precisely that, any amount, however trivial. There is no minimum threshold of six, no minimum of sixty — any shearing at all triggers the obligation, and any amount may be given.

### Five Sela Problem

This immediately raises a difficulty from the very *mishnah* under discussion. The closing clause of the *mishnah* asks how much one actually gives the *kohen*, and answers: *mishkal chamesh sela'im biYehuda shehen eser sela'im baGalil* — five *sela* by the Judean standard, which equals ten *sela* by the Galilean standard (the *sela* of Judea being heavier). This is a prescribed minimum gift, stated in absolute terms.

### Kashya on Positions

The *Gemara* now formulates the objection. *Bishlama* — it is understandable — for Rav and Rabbi Yochanan, since Rabbi Yochanan explicitly said one gives a minimum of five *sela* in absolute terms, and Rav simply stated a threshold of one and a half *maneh* without specifying the gift amount. Both can accommodate a *mishnah* that prescribes five *sela* as the floor. But for Shmuel and Rabbi Elazar, there is a genuine *kashya*. Shmuel says one gives a *sixtieth*, which can be as little as a single *sela* — not five. And Rabbi Elazar, as cited by Ulla, says one may start with a *kol shehu*, in which case the gift will be trivially small — certainly not five *sela*. The *Gemara* further sharpens the problem: Rav himself, in another context, agreed to the principle that *reishit hagez* is measured as a *sixtieth*. If one begins with one and a half *maneh* — 37.5 *sela* — and gives a *sixtieth*, the result is well under one *sela*, far short of five.

The underlying tension is between two incommensurable modes of measurement: an absolute floor of five *sela*, and a proportional measure of one-sixtieth. They will not produce the same number except by coincidence, and when the proportional measure yields less than five *sela*, the two systems conflict directly.

---

## Resolution Approach

### Two Minimums

The *Gemara* now introduces a resolution attributed to Rav and Shmuel. The passage reads: *b'Yisrael sheyesh lo gizzin harbeh askinan* — we are dealing with a person who has a great deal of wool and intends to distribute it among multiple *kohanim*. On this reading, the five *sela* figure is not a minimum threshold for triggering the obligation. The fundamental measure of *reishit hagez* is indeed proportional — one-*sixtieth* — and that proportion could be very small or very large depending on how much wool one has. The five *sela* figure addresses a different question entirely: *kol chad v'chad lo tivtzar leh mechamisha sela'in* — when one is apportioning a large quantity among several *kohanim*, one must not give any individual *kohen* less than five *sela*. Five *sela* is thus a standard of dignified distribution, not a floor for the basic obligation.

### Giver/Receiver

This resolution is intellectually elegant and worth pausing over. Logically, one might have proposed that both minimums operate simultaneously — the obligation is a *sixtieth*, but it must never fall below five *sela*, whichever is higher. The *Gemara* does not take that route. Instead, it distinguishes the two measures by their respective functions. One governs the giver's obligation: give a proportion of what you have, so that the gift reflects the scale of the flock. The other governs the receiver's dignity: if you are subdividing a large gift, do not give any one *kohen* a disrespectfully small portion.

This framing resonates with earlier themes in the *sugya* regarding the dual perspective on these transactions. The obligation runs both ways — how appropriately one gives, and what constitutes a respectful minimum for the one receiving. A *kohen* who receives a trivial amount from someone who owns thousands of *sela* worth of wool has not been properly honored; and conversely, a *kohen* who receives less than five *sela* when a large gift is being divided has received something less than respectable. These are distinct concerns, and the *Gemara* assigns each concern its own measure.

One should also note that the *Gemara* does not say one is required to divide the gift among multiple *kohanim*. The rule is conditional: *if* one chooses to distribute the gift to several *kohanim*, then each must receive at least five *sela*. The decision to divide is the owner's; the standard of distribution, once that choice is made, is the *Gemara*'s.

---

## Terumah/Peah

### All Sixtieth

The *Gemara* now reports a broader principle in the names of Rav and Shmuel: *reishit hagez beshishim, terumah beshishim, pe'ah beshishim* — all three agricultural and pastoral gifts share the same proportional minimum of one-*sixtieth*.

### Terumah Kashya

This immediately invites a challenge from a *mishnah* regarding *terumah*. The *mishnah* there states that a generous measure of *terumah* is 1/40th, an average measure is 1/50th, and a stingy measure is 1/60th. Why would Rav and Shmuel cite the stingy measure as the standard? Would one not cite at least the average, if not the generous?

### Biblical/Rabbanic

The *Gemara* answers: *de'oraita beshishim* — biblically, a *sixtieth* is the required minimum. But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this as well: does Shmuel himself not say that a single grain of wheat exempts an entire granary? Biblically, *terumah* has no minimum whatsoever — even the most trivial designation removes the *tevel* status from a mound of grain. If that is so, how can one say the biblical minimum is a *sixtieth*?

The *Gemara* resolves this with a three-tier distinction. Biblically, Shmuel is correct — one grain suffices. The rabbinic minimum for biblically obligated produce (the five grains and similar crops) is 1/40th, with 1/50th as the standard and 1/60th as the floor one should not fall below. However, *derabbanan b'derabbanan* — for produce that is only rabbinically obligated in *terumah*, such as fruit and vegetables, the Rabbis were more lenient and set the standard at 1/60th. It is to this category that Rav and Shmuel refer.

This is a notable distinction that one does not often encounter explicitly: the rabbinic measure varies depending on whether the underlying obligation is biblical or rabbinic. For biblically obligated produce, the Rabbis raised the standard considerably; for rabbinically obligated produce, they kept the measure lower.

Several *Acharonim* have observed a related point about the nature of *terumah* itself. The act of designating *terumah* accomplishes two distinct things: it removes the *tevel* status from the grain, and it fulfills the *mitzvah* of giving to the *kohen*. The *Aruch HaShulchan* and others argue that while the *de'oraita* requirement for removing *tevel* is satisfied by even a single grain, the *mitzvah* of giving — *venatan*, as the verse puts it — requires an amount of genuine substance. Once, however, one has designated a trivial amount as *terumah*, that designation cannot be undone. The *kohen* receives the grain that was separated; one cannot subsequently add to it. If one wishes to fulfill the *mitzvah* of giving more ideally, one would need to separate additional *terumah* in the first instance.

### Peah Rule

The *Gemara* turns to *pe'ah*. Here too the claim is that the minimum is a *sixtieth*, yet a *mishnah* in *Pe'ah* explicitly teaches that *pe'ah* has no minimum measure at all — *ein lah shiur*. The *Gemara* resolves this as it did for *terumah*: *de'oraita ein lah shiur* — biblically there is no minimum — but *derabbanan b'shishim* — rabbinically the standard is a *sixtieth*. This is itself taught in a *mishnah*: *ein pochtin l'pe'ah mishishim*, one does not give less than a *sixtieth* for *pe'ah*, even though the Torah prescribes no minimum.

One might then ask: what *chidush* is Rav and Shmuel adding if the *mishnah* already states the *sixtieth* for *pe'ah*? The *Gemara* answers: *hatam b'aretz hacha b'chutz la'aretz* — the *mishnah* speaks of *Eretz Yisrael*, while Rav and Shmuel are teaching that even in the lands adjacent to Israel where certain agricultural obligations were rabinically applied, the standard remains a *sixtieth*. The principal *chidush* in Rav and Shmuel's statement remains, however, the application of the *sixtieth* to *reishit hagez* — where one might have expected an absolute measure from the *mishnah*'s language, Rav and Shmuel establish that the fundamental obligation is proportional.

---

## Isi bar Hini

### Grammar Correction

The *Gemara* now introduces a narrative about Isi bar Hini's visit to *Eretz Yisrael*. Rabbi Yochanan encountered Isi bar Hini while the latter was teaching his son the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* uses the word *rechelim* — female sheep — and Rabbi Yochanan corrected him: the proper form is *rachelot*, in the feminine plural as Mishnaic Hebrew employs it.

### Hebrew Standards

Isi bar Hini defended himself by citing a biblical verse: *rechelim matayim* — when Yaakov assembled gifts for Esav, the Torah uses the masculine plural form *rechelim* for female sheep. Rabbi Yochanan replied: *lashon Torah l'atzma lashon chachamim l'atzmam* — biblical Hebrew has its own grammar, and Mishnaic Hebrew has its own. The two are distinct literary registers, and one cannot import biblical usage into the Mishnaic context. Rabbi Yochanan, as a native of *Eretz Yisrael*, was fully fluent in spoken and Mishnaic Hebrew; Isi bar Hini, coming from Bavel, naturally fell back on biblical usage when uncertain — precisely as one who does not know the contemporary spoken form will reach for the classical source.

### Respect for Rebbi

Rabbi Yochanan then asked Isi bar Hini: *man reish sidra b'Vavel?* — who is the leading *rosh yeshiva* in Bavel? The question seems to carry an implicit criticism: if the head of your academy is as great as he is, why is your grammar so poor? Isi replied: *Abba Aricha* — Abba the tall one, which is Rav, whose full name was Abba.

Rabbi Yochanan was taken aback by the casual manner of address: *Abba Aricha karyat lei?* — you call him simply "Abba the tall one"? He then described his own memory of Rav: when Rav was still in *Eretz Yisrael* before departing for Bavel, he sat seventeen rows behind Rav in the academy of Rebbi. And as Rav and Rebbi exchanged words, *v'nafik zikukin d'nur mipumei d'Rav l'pumei d'Rebbi* — sparks of fire would emerge from Rav's mouth to Rebbi's mouth and back again, *v'la hava yadana mai ka'amri* — and Rabbi Yochanan could not understand a word of what they were saying. That is who Rav is. *V'at Abba Aricha karyat lei?* — and you refer to him so familiarly?

The correction here is not merely about titles. Rabbi Yochanan is making a point about how one speaks of one's teachers and of the great figures of one's generation. Twice in this exchange he corrects Isi bar Hini: once on grammar and once on respect. The way one speaks matters — in language, and in the reverence one conveys toward those who taught and shaped one's tradition.

### Reishit Debate

Isi bar Hini then turned the conversation to *halacha* and asked Rabbi Yochanan: *reishit hagez b'chama?* — what is the measure for *reishit hagez*? Rabbi Yochanan responded: *beshishim* — sixty, either meaning one must begin with sixty *sela* or that one gives a *sixtieth* (Rashi offers both explanations, though the reading of a *sixtieth* seems preferable in context).

Isi bar Hini challenged: but the *mishnah* says *kol shehu* — any amount! How can you impose a minimum of sixty? Rabbi Yochanan replied: *im kein ma bein li velach* — if all I can do is quote the *mishnah* at face value, then what distinguishes my role from yours? I too know how to read a *mishnah*. The point is that despite the *mishnah*'s language of *kol shehu*, there is more to be said, and Rabbi Yochanan maintains that the operative minimum is sixty, or a *sixtieth*, rather than a literal *kol shehu*.

---

## R. Yochanan Contradiction

### Two Versions

When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael* he reported: Rav says *beshishim* — sixty or a *sixtieth*; Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yannai says *beshesh* — six. This is the position we encountered earlier: one needs to begin with only six *sela* in order to give five as an absolute minimum.

### Abaye's Kashya

Abaye challenged Rav Dimi: *anachta lan chada v'aktasta lan chada* — one of these reports makes sense, the other is problematic. How can Rabbi Yochanan say both? In the exchange with Isi bar Hini just described, Rabbi Yochanan clearly maintained *shishim* — sixty or a *sixtieth* — yet here he is reported saying *shesh* in the name of Rabbi Yannai.

### Different Sources

The *Gemara* resolves the Rabbi Yochanan contradiction straightforwardly: *ha didei ha de-rabbei* — one statement is Rabbi Yochanan's own position (*shishim*), and one is what he transmitted in the name of his teacher Rabbi Yannai (*shesh*). There is no contradiction when the two statements belong to different authorities.

### Rav's Problem

But the difficulty with Rav remains. Here Rav is quoted as saying *shishim* — sixty — yet at the opening of the discussion Rav said the minimum is one and a half *maneh*, which equals 37.5 *sela*. These are not the same number, and they reflect different frameworks. How can Rav's position be internally consistent?

---

## Rav's Maneh

### Two Manahs

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction in Rav's position as follows: *mai mane de-ka'amar ben arba'im sela'im* — when Rav said one and a half *maneh*, he was not using the standard *maneh* of 25 *sela*. He was referring to a *maneh* of 40 *sela*.

### Rav Consistent

One and a half times forty equals sixty. *De-have leh b'shishim* — that comes out to sixty. Rav's statement of one and a half *maneh* and his statement of sixty are thus the same number, expressed in different terms. The *maneh* of 40 *sela* reconciles what appeared to be a contradiction.

### Shuttle Reference

One might wonder whether a *tanna* would ever use a *maneh* of 40 *sela* — it is an unusual measure. The *Gemara* confirms its existence by citing a *baraita* (preserved in the *Tosefta*) about a leather flask. The *baraita* discusses at what point a flask that has not yet been fully sewn acquires the status of a *keli* susceptible to *tumah*, and at what point a completed flask loses that status once it tears. Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov says that the relevant gauge is whether the hole is large enough that the shuttle used in weaving (*kefa'iyot shel shesi*, the implements used in the warp of a loom) would fall through. The *baraita* then specifies the size of this shuttle: *achas me-arba'ah be-mane ben arba'im sela'im* — one-quarter of a *sela* from a *maneh* that is made up of forty *sela*. This confirms that the forty-*sela* *maneh* appears in Talmudic sources, even if the speaker must explicitly clarify which *maneh* he means. Normally one assumes the standard *maneh* of twenty-five *sela*; but the forty-*sela* *maneh* exists and is referenced in authentic *tannaitic* material. With this, Rav's position is fully consistent: both his statements describe sixty *sela* as the minimum, and the apparent discrepancy dissolves.

---

## Five Sela Amount

### Raw Wool Rule

The *mishnah* asks *ve-kamah noten lo* — how much does one give the *kohen*? The answer given is five *sela*. A *baraita* clarifies that this does not mean one launders the wool first and then gives it: *lo she-yilbenenu ve-yitnenu lo* — one does not launder it and then give it. One gives the wool raw.

### After Laundering

The five *sela* figure refers to the value of the wool after processing. One must give enough raw wool that, after the *kohen* launders it himself, it will amount to five *sela* worth. The obligation is thus to give sufficient raw material, not a finished product.

This connects to the broader theme noted earlier: once the wool is separated for the *kohen*, it is in some sense already his, and one should not continue to handle or process it. If one were to dye it, for example, that would constitute a misappropriation — treating as one's own something that has effectively entered the *kohen*'s domain. Laundering it before giving it, while not as severe, would similarly overstep; the *kohen* receives the raw wool and processes it himself.

### Verse Source

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for this minimum? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers from a verse: *la-amod le-sharet* — God has chosen the *kohen* to stand and to serve. The gift must therefore be *davar she-hu ra'uy le-sheirut* — something fit for service in the *Beit HaMikdash*. The wool must be sufficient to produce a garment appropriate for priestly service.

### The Belt

What is the smallest priestly garment? The *Gemara* says: *avnet* — the belt. The wool that would go into the belt of a *kohen* during service amounts to five *sela*.

### Tafasta Rule

One might suggest the standard should be a larger garment, such as the *me'il*, the priestly robe. The *Gemara* rejects this with a well-known principle: *tafasta meruba lo tafasta, tafasta mu'at tafasta* — if you grab too much, you have not grabbed; if you grab a little, you have grabbed. The intent is: do not overreach. When the verse says a garment fit for service, and we do not know exactly which garment is meant, we take the minimum. If one claims it refers to a large garment, one may not be able to sustain that claim; if one claims it refers to the smallest garment, that claim is secure. The minimum here is the belt.

---

## Kippah/Tzitz

### Kippah Source

The *Gemara* now raises an alternative: perhaps the standard should be a small wool *kippah* worn by the *kohen gadol*, which might require even less wool than the belt. A *baraita* describes this: a small wool *kippah* was placed on the head of the *kohen gadol*, and the *tzitz* — the golden frontplate inscribed *Kodesh L'Hashem* — rested upon it. The verse says the *tzitz* was placed *al pesil techeiles*, on a blue thread; this *baraita* reads *pesil techeiles* as referring to the small blue wool *kippah* on which the *tzitz* sat. On this reading, the *tzitz* was not simply tied around the head with a string; rather, there was a small wool garment interposed between the gold plate and the forehead of the *kohen gadol*.

It must be noted that this description is unusual. The *Rambam* does not record it, and the standard understanding of *pesil techeiles* is a cord or string securing the *tzitz*. Artscroll renders it as a "ribbon," a translation that attempts to bridge the gap between a string and a *kippah* — something wider and more substantial than a string but not as full as a *kippah*. In any case, the *baraita* describes it as a small wool head-covering worn by the *kohen gadol* beneath the *tzitz*.

### Kohen Gadol Only

The *Gemara* raises a further objection: the verse *hu uvanav* — he and his sons — implies that the garment in question must be something equally worn by the *kohen gadol* and by ordinary *kohanim*. The *kippah* described above was worn only by the *kohen gadol*, not by other *kohanim*. It therefore cannot serve as the standard by which to measure the gift of first-shearings, which applies to all *kohanim*.

### Belt Materials

The *avnet*, the belt, presents its own complication. The *kohen gadol* on Yom Kippur wore a belt made entirely of linen. During the rest of the year, his belt was *shatnez* — a mixture of wool and linen. The belt of an ordinary *kohen* is subject to dispute: one view holds that it was the same as the *kohen gadol*'s Yom Kippur belt (all linen), while another view holds it was like the *kohen gadol*'s year-round belt (wool and linen).

### All Wear Belts

The *Gemara* resolves the issue as follows. If one holds that the ordinary *kohen*'s belt contained wool, then it was worn equally by the *kohen gadol* and by ordinary *kohanim*, and serves perfectly as the standard. If one holds that the ordinary *kohen* wore only a linen belt, then the wool element is confined to the *kohen gadol*'s garment — but all *kohanim* wear a belt of some kind. The principle is *shem avnet ba'olam* — the name "belt" applies universally. The verse requires a garment fit for priestly service, and the belt is the smallest garment worn by all *kohanim*. That at least one version of the priestly belt contains wool is sufficient to establish the wool measure. The five *sela* standard for *reishit hagez* is thus derived from the amount of wool required for the *avnet*.

---

## Gazaz U'Mechar

### Debate Position

The *mishnah* addressed in this section deals with *gazaz umachar rishona* — one who sheared the first sheep and sold it (in context, as Rashi clarifies, one who sheared and then sold the sheep itself) before completing the shearing of all five. The question is whether such a person is still obligated in *reishit hagez*, given that by the time all five shearings are complete, not all five sheep remain in the owner's possession.

### Chisda View

Rav Chisda rules: *chayav* — obligated. The fact that one sheared five sheep is the operative criterion, regardless of whether all five remained in one's possession throughout the entire process.

### Natan View

Rav Natan bar Oshaya rules: *patur* — exempt. His reasoning: *be-idna de-kamlei shiura*, at the moment the minimum threshold is completed — when all five shearings have been assembled — *be'inan tzoncha*, the flock must still be yours, *ve-leika*, and it is not, because some sheep were sold in the interim.

### Selling Sheep

Rashi's explanation confirms that the case involves selling the sheep themselves after shearing, not merely selling the shorn wool. The owner sheared each sheep and then sold it before proceeding to the next. By the time the fifth sheep was sheared, the first four had already left his possession. He holds all five shearings but no longer owns all five sheep.

### Timing Question

The question thus turns on when exactly the obligation of *reishit hagez* crystallizes. Does it attach at the moment of shearing each individual sheep — in which case the ownership condition was met for each at the time of shearing — or does it attach only when the minimum threshold (five shearings) is complete, by which time the flock has been partially dispersed? The *Gemara* leaves this as the substance of the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Natan bar Oshaya.

---

## Purchasing Wool

### Non-Jew Case

The *mishnah* rules that one who purchases the shearings of a non-Jew's flock is exempt from *reishit hagez*. The simple case is straightforward: the non-Jew already sheared and sold the wool; the buyer never owned the sheep, so no obligation attaches. Even if one purchased the wool while it was still on the sheep — effectively buying the shearings in advance and then performing the shearing oneself — one is still exempt, because the sheep were never *tzoncha*, one's own flock.

### Shearing Purpose

However, if one purchased the sheep themselves from a non-Jew — not for full ownership but specifically for the purpose of shearing — one would be *chayav*. The reason is that at the moment of shearing, the sheep are indeed one's own, and the act of shearing occurs under conditions of ownership.

### Friend's Residue

The more complex case involves purchasing the shearings of a fellow Israelite's flock — that is, buying the wool that is still on the sheep, before shearing takes place. If the seller retains even a small portion of his wool (and thus shears some himself), the obligation remains his. If he sells everything, the obligation passes to the buyer.

### Peah Analogy

Rav Chisda initially attempts to ground this ruling in an analogy to *pe'ah*. A *mishnah* in *Pe'ah* discusses one who sells individual trees growing in his grain field. Rav Yehuda rules: if the field owner retains even one tree for himself, he bears the *pe'ah* obligation for the entire crop — including the trees he sold. The same logic would apply here: if the seller retains any wool, he bears the entire *reishit hagez* obligation.

### Rava Objects

Rava objects to the analogy. Rav Yehuda's ruling in the *pe'ah* case applies only *ve-hu she-hitchil ba'al hasadeh liktzor* — only when the field owner had already begun harvesting before he sold the trees. The verse governing *pe'ah* reads *u-vekutzrechem et ketzir artzechem* — when you harvest — establishing that the obligation falls the moment harvesting begins. Once the owner began harvesting, the *pe'ah* obligation had already crystallized over the entire field; subsequent sale of individual trees does not divest him of that obligation. But in our case, the seller had not yet begun shearing before selling the wool. And unlike *pe'ah*, which attaches at the beginning of harvesting, *reishit hagez* attaches not at the start of shearing but at its conclusion — the verse says *gez tzonecha*, referring to the completed shearings, not to the act of shearing. If the obligation does not even arise until the shearing is complete, and if the seller was not yet obligated at the time of sale, how can the analogy to *pe'ah* sustain the rule?

### Never Sold

Rava therefore proposes a different foundation. He cites the principle established earlier in the tractate in the context of the stomach and other *matnot kohen*: *matnot de-kohen lo mizabin inish* — a person does not sell priestly gifts. When a butcher weighs out an animal and sells it, and the sale incidentally includes the stomach (which belongs to the *kohen*), we do not treat the stomach as genuinely sold. The butcher did not intend to sell it, and the buyer did not intend to purchase an obligation that was never his. Therefore, when the buyer gives the stomach to the *kohen*, he can recover its purchase price from the butcher.

### Butcher Case

The same interpretive principle governs the *reishit hagez* case. When the seller sold the wool on his sheep, we read his intentions generously: he never intended to transfer to the buyer the portion that would ultimately become *matnot kehunah*. The sale is real for everything else, but the *matnot* component is notionally excluded from what was transferred — even though the seller was not yet formally obligated at the time of sale.

### Final Rule

The operative rule that emerges is as follows. If the seller retains any residue of wool — even a small amount — then we say the buyer effectively told him: whatever *matnot kehunah* arise from this transaction, they come from your remaining portion. The seller remains obligated. If the seller sold everything and retained nothing, then the seller himself can say: I never sold you the *matnot* portion — meaning it was never genuinely transferred, and therefore it remains his to give to the *kohen*, even though legally the buyer now holds all the wool. In the latter case, Rava's interpretation ensures the obligation stays with the seller — the party who originally owned the flock — rather than passing entirely to the buyer who may never have contemplated taking on that responsibility.

---

---

# Hullin 140

## Shiluach Haken Intro

### Opening Context

The daf proper is 140, though the discussion opens at the very top of 139b, in the midst of the *mitzvah* of *shiluach haken*. The Gemara begins with the heading *chomer b'kisuy*, marking the transition into a new comparative discussion. The preceding material had explored the case of a mother bird that is *hekdesh* — consecrated property — and whether the *mitzvah* applies in such a circumstance. The Gemara there had worked through interesting questions about how ownership of a bird is dependent not merely on its creation but on its ongoing maintenance under one's control. With that as backdrop, the Gemara now proceeds.

### Ki Yikarei Drasha

Six or seven lines into the page, the Gemara introduces a *baraita*: *tanu rabanan* — our rabbis taught. The verse reads, *ki yikarei kan tzippor lefanecha* — "if a bird's nest chances upon you." The *baraita* asks: *mah talmud lomar* — what is the significance of this phrasing? Since the verse also states *shaleach tishalach es ha'eim v'es habanim tikach lach* — "you shall send away the mother and take the children for yourself" — one might have entertained the notion that there is an obligation to actively seek out this *mitzvah*, to go roaming through the mountains and hills in order to find a mother bird with eggs. After all, one might reason, should I not pursue all the *mitzvos* of the *Torah*?

The *baraita* dispels this reading: *talmud lomar ki yikarei* — the verse teaches, *bim'ora lefanecha*, that the obligation arises only when the situation presents itself before you. There is no requirement to go out and engineer these circumstances.

### Kan Mikol Makom

The *baraita* continues with the phrase *kan mikol makom* — the nest, in all cases. This inclusive reading addresses the variety of locations where a nest might be found. The verse's mention of *tzippor* implies, as the *baraita* will develop, that the bird must be *tehorah v'lo tmeiah* — kosher and not non-kosher. The word *lefanecha* — "before you" — points toward something within your domain or under your control. And *baderech* — "on the way" — extends the obligation to the public thoroughfare.

The *baraita* then asks: if we know it applies on the road and in your property, how do I know it applies in trees? *Talmud lomar b'chol etz* — "in any tree," as the verse continues. And how do I know it applies in a well or cave? *Talmud lomar o al ha'aretz* — "or on the ground," reading this expansively to include anything sunk into the ground. Once we have established that the obligation extends to any location a nest may be found, the *baraita* returns to ask: if so, why do the words *lefanecha* and *baderech* appear at all, since they seem to be limiting? The answer is: *mah derech she'ein kano b'yadcha af kol she'ein kano b'yadcha* — just as a path implies that the nest is not literally in your hand, so too the *mitzvah* applies only when the nest is not under your direct control.

## Lefanecha Baderech

### Property & Control

From this *drasha* of *baderech*, the *baraita* derives a practical rule. It lists cases that are still obligatory despite falling within one's property: pigeons of a dovecote (*yonei shovach*) and pigeons of an attic (*yonei aliyah*) that made their nest in protruding beams or in various structures; ducks and chickens that nested in a garden or orchard. In all these cases, even though the birds are on one's property, they are not sufficiently under the owner's control to exempt from *shiluach*. Rashi explains that the term *tafiach* refers to protrusions — places where birds might naturally nest — though some translate it as jars placed into walls for that purpose.

The principle at work is that *lefanecha* and *baderech* are both pointing to the same underlying condition: the nest must not be *b'yadcha* — in your hand, figuratively speaking. Being in one's yard or attic is not enough to constitute that level of control. A bird nesting on a balcony, for instance, that would fly away if one approached, falls squarely in this category of obligatory *shiluach* — the bird remains functionally free.

### Free vs. Captured

By contrast, the *baraita* exempts birds that nested inside the house itself (*kanenu betoch habayit*), and similarly the so-called Herodian doves (*yonei hordasiyot*), associated with the elaborate underground structures from the Herodian period — intricate networks of cavities where birds were kept in a manner that was fully captured and controlled. Such birds are *patur mishiluach* — exempt from the obligation.

The conceptual distinction, then, is not property versus public domain — it is freedom versus captivity. A bird in your orange grove, in your dovecote's open reaches, in your attic's rafters: still free, still obligatory. A bird kept in an enclosed cage, in a fully enclosed structure under your management: captured, exempt.

### Gemara Rejects Baraita

The Gemara then revisits the *baraita*'s logic. It notes: *ha lama li? Miki yikarei nafka* — why do I need *baderech* at all? We already learn the exclusion of a controlled bird from *ki yikarei* — "if it chances," implying it must not be something already designated and under your control. Furthermore, the Gemara asks: *ve'od lefanecha lama li* — and what then is the role of *lefanecha*, "before you"?

The Gemara answers: *ella lefanecha le'atuyei shehayu lefanav umardu* — rather, *lefanecha* comes to include a case where the bird had previously been under your control but escaped and returned to a wild state. Even though it once was "before you," now that it has reasserted its freedom and you are chancing upon it anew, you remain obligated. *Lefanecha* tells us that even former ownership does not create a permanent exemption once the bird is no longer under your control.

With *ki yikarei* excluding the currently controlled, and *lefanecha* including the formerly owned but now free, the Gemara sets aside the *baraita*'s reading of *baderech* as the source for exclusion, and instead takes *baderech* to serve a different function — which Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav will now explain.

## Baderech Extensions

### Ocean Case

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: if one found a nest floating in the ocean, *chayav beshiluach* — one is obligated to perform *shiluach haken*. The source: the verse states, *ko amar Hashem hanoten bayam derech* — "so says God who places a path in the sea." Since the *Torah* uses the word *derech* in connection with the sea, the *baderech* of the *shiluach haken* verse includes even this unusual location.

### Sky & Vulture

The Gemara pushes further: *ela me'ata matza kan bashamayim* — if so, what if one found a nest in the sky? Rashi explains this refers to a *nesher* — more accurately a vulture — carrying a nest in its talons while in flight. Perhaps one would be obligated there as well, since it says *derech nesher bashamayim* — "the way of the vulture in the heavens"?

The Gemara rejects this: *derech nesher ikri, derech stam lo ikrei* — in the sky, it is called "the way of the vulture," a qualified expression, not simply "a path." Only a plain, unqualified *derech* is included by the *baderech* of the *shiluach* verse. The ocean is called simply a *derech*; the sky is called only *derech nesher*. Hence the ocean qualifies, the sky does not.

One noted halakhic application of this distinction: the Rogatchover Gaon reportedly argued, based on this very *Gemara*, that one need not recite *Tefillat Haderech* upon an airplane flight, since *ba'avir* — through the air — is not categorized as *derech* but only as *derech nesher*.

### Nest on Head

The people of Papuna (*Papunai*) posed a question to Rav Masna: *matza kan berosho shel adam mahu* — what is the ruling if a bird made its nest on a person's head? The question has a whimsical quality to it — alongside the ocean and the sky, they are now asking about a human head — yet the answer is substantive. Rav Masna replied: *va'adama al rosho* — and the ground was upon his head, citing a verse about Shmuel. Rashi explains that the word *adama* — as opposed to *afar* (dust) or *aphar* (earth) — is used specifically for earth that is still connected to the ground. Since the verse applies the term *adama* to what is upon the person's head, it suggests the person himself is treated as being connected to the ground, and thus the nest is considered as resting upon the earth. Within the parameters of *ki yimatze ki yikarei lefanecha baderech*, such a case falls within the obligation.

This naturally raises the question of a nest found on a wagon or a moving vehicle — cases the Gemara does not address, but which the logic of the *Papunai* exchange would seem to leave unresolved.

## Biblical Hints Digr.

### Name Sources

The *Papunai* continued with a series of further questions to Rav Masna. *Moshe min haTorah minayin* — where is Moshe hinted at in the *Torah*? The answer: the verse in *Parshas Noach* reads *beshagam hu basar* — "for he too is flesh." The *gematria* of *beshagam* equals that of *Moshe*, and the continuation — *vehayu yamav me'ah ve'esrim shana* — "his days shall be one hundred and twenty years" — matches the lifespan of Moshe Rabbeinu exactly.

*Haman min haTorah minayin* — where is Haman hinted? From *hamina ha'etz* — "have you eaten from this tree?" — and indeed Haman was hanged from a tree. The allusion is not merely verbal but contextual: as Moshe's hint includes his lifespan, Haman's hint includes his end.

*Esther min haTorah minayin* — where is Esther hinted? From *ve'anochi haster astir* — "and I will surely hide my face from them on that day." Rashi notes that the hidden face of God — *hester panim* — is a central theme of the period of the Megillah: God's name does not appear in the Megillah, and the Jewish people faced a decree of annihilation. The continuation of that verse, *umatze'u tzaros rabbos vera'os* — "and they will find many great evils" — corresponds to the travails of that period.

*Mordechai min haTorah minayin* — where is Mordechai hinted? The verse speaks of *mar dror*, one of the spices of the *shemen hamishcha*, the anointing oil. *Umitargeminan mira dachya* — and we translate this as "pure myrrh," but *mira dachya* in Aramaic resembles *Mordechai*. Rashi notes that this hints at Mordechai's greatness — the association with something precious and aromatic foretells his ultimate honor.

### Maharsha Validation

The Maharsha offers a sophisticated framework for understanding why the Gemara bothers with these derivations. The underlying question, he explains, is whether these names — which are not originally Hebrew — can be said to be the proper, fitting names for these individuals. The *Torah*'s allusions to their names serve to validate them: even though Moshe was given an Egyptian name by Pharaoh's daughter, the *Torah* hints to that very name, showing it to be divinely appropriate. Similarly, the Persian names of Esther and Mordechai are ratified by their appearance in the text of *Torah*.

### Non-Hebrew Names

The Maharsha makes the striking observation that Moshe is indeed an Egyptian name — the suffix of Pharaoh's names (*Thutmose*, *Ramesses*) derives from the same root, meaning "son of." *Ki min hamayim meshisihu* — "for I drew him from the water" — was spoken by Pharaoh's daughter, who was speaking Egyptian, not Hebrew. Esther and Mordechai, the Maharsha further notes, are Persian names. He then cites a remarkable position of the Ibn Ezra: that God's name does not appear in the Megillah because the Megillah was written by Persians. This claim is startling — if Esther herself wrote it, as the verse *vatichtov Esther hamalka* implies, the Ibn Ezra's reasoning remains puzzling. And if the entire text were composed in Persian by non-Jews, why is it written in Hebrew? The Ibn Ezra's position is left as a curiosity without full resolution.

The connection of all this to the surrounding sugya is that these questions were posed by the *Papunai* to Rav Masna — seemingly as a collection of riddles or proofs, perhaps with a playful character, beginning with the nest on a person's head and continuing through a series of Torah allusions.

## Herodian Doves

### Rav Kahana Story

The Gemara returns to the case of *yonei hordasiyot* — the Herodian doves — as a paradigm of *mezuman*, fully controlled birds exempt from *shiluach*. Rav Kahana reported: *l'didi hazin* — I myself saw these birds — and they were arrayed in sixteen rows stretching across the width of a mile. The scale itself suggests something extraordinary. These birds would cry *kiri kiri*, and one among them refused to do so. Another bird turned to it and said, *suma* — "blind one," meaning fool — *imri kiri kiri*, say what you are supposed to say. The recalcitrant bird replied: *suma, imri kiri biri* — "say rather *kiri biri*." Rashi explains: *kiri* means master, and *biri* means slave. The birds had been trained to acknowledge Herod as their master, but this one declared that their master was himself a slave — a reference to the well-known tradition in the Gemara that Herod descended from slaves. So deeply embedded was this memory that even these birds, generations removed, carried it. *Asyuve veshachtua* — so they took the rebellious bird and slaughtered it, presumably Herod's household slaves who were still around.

### Rav Ashi Response

Rav Ashi reported in the name of Chanina that the story was *milat* — nonsense, or fabrication. The Gemara pushes back: would Rav Kahana simply make something up? *Ela eima bemilin* — rather, it was done through words, meaning through magic or incantation. Some interpret this to mean the birds were not speaking in human language, but in bird-speech, and Rav Kahana possessed knowledge of bird-speech. Either way, the Gemara openly acknowledges the fantastical character of the account.

## Herodian Doves (II)

### Mezuman Status

The story of the Herodian doves serves its halakhic purpose: they are the example of fully *mezuman* — captured and controlled — birds that are exempt from *shiluach haken*. The entire elaborate episode is the Gemara's illustration of what it means for birds to be so thoroughly under human dominion that the *mitzvah* does not apply.

## Of Tamei Debate

### Tzippor = Kosher

The Gemara turns to the explicit ruling: *of tamei patur belishloach* — a non-kosher bird, one need not send away. *Minani mili* — from where is this derived? Rabbi Yitzchak answers: from the verse *ki yikarei kan tzippor lefanecha*. The word *of* — bird in general — encompasses both kosher and non-kosher species, as evidenced by the verse *kol of tahor tocheilu* — "eat every kosher bird" — which implies that there is also an *of tamei*. But the verse of *shiluach haken* does not say *of*; it says *tzippor*. And *tzippor tahor ashkechan d'ikrei, tzippor tamei lo ashkechan d'ikrei* — we find kosher birds referred to as *tzippor*, but we never find a non-kosher bird described as a *tzippor*.

### Challenges to Rule

The Gemara systematically challenges this claim with a series of verses. First: *tavnit kol tzippor kanaf* — "the image of any *tzippor* of wing," the prohibition against making graven images. Surely this must include non-kosher birds. Second: *hachaya vechol habeheima, remes vetzippor kanaf* — the verse enumerating all creatures that praise God, which must include everything. Third: *kol tzippor kol kanaf* — all birds, all winged creatures entering Noach's ark, which was all-inclusive. Fourth: *ve'ata ben adam, emor letzippor kol kanaf* — "and you, son of man, say to the bird, to all of wing."

### Defense Sustained

In each case, the Gemara provides the same structural answer: *tzippor* refers to kosher birds, while *kanaf* — the additional modifier — extends the verse to include non-kosher birds and other winged creatures such as locusts (*chagavim*). The pairing is consistent: *tzippor* alone denotes the kosher species; *kanaf* or *tzippor kanaf* is the broader inclusive term.

One further challenge: *tzipparei shamaya* — birds of the heaven in the vision of Nevuchadnezzar, all of which dwelled in the great tree — surely this includes non-kosher birds. The Gemara responds: *tzipparei shamaya ikri, tzipparei stama lo ikrei* — "birds of the heaven" is a qualified expansive phrase; the plain word *tzippor* without qualification remains limited to kosher species. The pattern established here mirrors the earlier ruling about *derech*: a plain term has a narrower scope; a qualified compound expression has a broader one.

## Tehora Drasha

### Kosher Only?

The Gemara now brings a verse that seems more directly challenging: *kol tzippor tehora tocheilu* — "eat every pure bird." If *tzippor* already means only kosher birds, why does the verse need to add the word *tehora* — pure, or kosher? The very presence of that word suggests that *tzippor* on its own is not limited to kosher species, and *tehora* is what narrows it. This would imply there are non-kosher *tzipporim* — which contradicts Rabbi Yitzchak's entire position.

### Tehora Excludes

The Gemara's answer is elegant: *lo miklal de'ika issura* — the inference is not that *tzippor* includes non-kosher species, but that *tehora* excludes certain kosher-species birds that are nonetheless forbidden. What would that be? A *treifah* bird is one possibility, but that is explicitly prohibited elsewhere. More significantly: *bishchuta de'metzora* — the bird slaughtered as part of the *metzora* purification process. That bird is a kosher species, properly slaughtered, yet forbidden in consumption. The word *tehora* — eat the *tehora* — comes to exclude this specific case.

### Asei & Lo Ta'asei

The Gemara then asks: if *tehora* comes to exclude the *shechuta de'metzora*, then what does the other verse — *ve'zeh asher lo tochelu meihem* — come to add? The answer: the presence of both a positive commandment (*kol tzippor tehora tocheilu* — eat the kosher ones) and a negative commandment (*ve'zeh asher lo tochelu meihem* — do not eat these) creates a redundancy that is read as applying specifically to the *shechuta de'metzora*. Eating such a bird would violate both a *lo ta'asei* and an *asei*, making the prohibition doubly reinforced. This structure highlights the special status of the *metzora* bird among otherwise eligible kosher species.

## Metzora Birds

### Chayot Meaning

The Gemara now turns to the specific language of the *metzora* purification: *shtei tzipporim chayot* — "two living birds." The question is: *mai chayot* — what does the word *chayot* ("living" or "alive") come to add? The initial suggestion: *she'chayot be'ficha* — that they are alive in your mouth, meaning edible, which would imply *tzippor* on its own could include non-kosher species. This reading would mean *chayot* is what restricts the birds to those that can be consumed.

### Chayot vs Tehorot

The Gemara rejects that reading. *Ma chayot? She'chayot rashei evarim shelahem* — "alive" means that all their limbs are intact, alive and whole. For birds brought as *korbanot*, while there is no concept of *mum* (blemish) as with animals, there is the category of *mechusar eiver* — lacking a limb. Thus *chayot* establishes that the birds must be complete, not that they must be kosher species. That requirement — kosher species — comes from the separate word *tehorot* (pure), which appears in the full verse: *shtei tzipporim chayot tehorot*. The inference from *tehorot* would be that *tzippor* on its own could include non-kosher species; but as before, the Gemara rejects this inference by explaining that *tehorot* is not excluding non-kosher species but something else entirely.

### Machshir Mechaper

The Gemara invokes the principle taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *ne'emar machshir umechaper bifnim, v'ne'emar machshir umechaper bachutz* — just as inside the *Beis Hamikdash* the requirements for a *korban* that *machshir* (purifies) and one that *mechaper* (atones) are identical, so too outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, the things used for *machshir* and *mechaper* must meet the same standards. Inside, whether a *korban* is of a *zav* seeking purification or a *chatas* seeking atonement, all the same rules apply — no blemish, proper species, intact. Outside, the paradigmatic *machshir* is the *metzora* purification birds, and the paradigmatic *mechaper* is the *se'ir la'azazel* — the scapegoat. Since the *se'ir la'azazel* must be free of any disqualifying defect (for it could be designated for either purpose on *Yom Kippur* and thus must qualify for the *Beis Hamikdash*), the same standard applies to the *metzora* birds. They cannot be a *treifah*, and they must have all their limbs. This *limud* renders both *chayot* and *tehorot* available to exclude other things.

## Metzora Exclusions

### Avoda Zara Proceeds

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes: *l'ma'utei tzipporei ir hanidachat* — *tehorot* or *chayot* comes to exclude birds of an *ir hanidachat*, the subverted city condemned to destruction. This is a striking suggestion, for it implies that absent this verse one might have thought such birds could be used for a *korban* — which runs against intuition. Tosafot observes that the Gemara indeed seems to imply that birds of an *ir hanidachat* could otherwise have been valid for a *korban*, since the prohibition is against deriving benefit from them, and *mitzvot lav lehenot nitnu* — the performance of *mitzvos* is not considered personal benefit. The Gemara clarifies: such birds cannot be used for the *shiluach* bird (*lav deshiluach*) — this we would know independently, since the *Torah* would never command one to send away a bird that would then be found and impermissibly benefited from by another (*lo amrah Torah shalach letakalah*). Rather, it is the *shechitah* bird — the one slaughtered in the ritual — that *tehorot* comes to exclude.

Rav Pappa adds: *letzipporim shehichlifu betzipporei avoda zara* — birds obtained through exchange with idolatry, or purchased with proceeds of idol-selling. The verse states *vehayita charem kamohu* — it shall be banned like it; anything obtained through the proceeds of *avoda zara* is itself forbidden in benefit. One might have supposed that since using such a bird for *metzora* purification does not constitute personal *hana'ah*, it could still be used. The verse teaches otherwise. Again, the Gemara specifies it is the *shechitah* bird, not the *shiluach* bird, from which this is excluded — since sending away a forbidden-benefit bird is self-evidently impossible.

### Shor Haniskal

Ravina adds the case of a bird that has killed a person — *of sheharag es hanefesh*. Such a bird has the status of *shor haniskal* and is forbidden in benefit. One might have thought it could still be used for *metzora* purification prior to the formal judicial verdict (*kodem gmar din*), when it has not yet been formally condemned and killed. The Gemara asks: if the *gmar din* has already occurred, obviously it cannot be used. And before *gmar din*, the case for exclusion is this: one might have supposed that since there is a *mitzvah* to eliminate the dangerous animal (*uvi'arta hara mikirbecha*), shechting it for the *metzora* would serve that purpose at the same time. The verse *tehorot* comes to exclude this as well — only the *shechitah* bird, not the *shiluach* bird, since one would be obligated to bring the bird to court rather than send it away.

### Summary Tzippor

The cumulative picture is clear: *tzippor* — whether in the verse of *shiluach haken* or in the context of *metzora* birds — refers exclusively to kosher species. The word *tehorot* in the *metzora* passage does not come to reiterate what *tzippor* already establishes; it excludes specific, contextually relevant categories of disqualified birds: birds of an *ir hanidachat*, birds obtained with proceeds of *avoda zara*, and birds that have killed a person.
