Rashi explains the language of "bringing into *kedusha*" and "removing from *kedusha*" with reference to *Shabbat*: an animal under Jewish ownership has the opportunity to rest on *Shabbat*, which is itself a dimension of *kedusha*. When one sells the fetus to a non-Jew, the animal loses that opportunity. That is what Rashi means by removing from *kedusha*.

### No Knas Conclusion

The lesson — *ka-mashma lan* — is that despite the impropriety of the sale, no rabbinic *knas* is imposed. The exemption from *peter chamor* stands.

### Tosafot View

Tosafot offers a more contextually natural reading: the *kedusha* in question is *kedushat bechor* itself — the sanctity inherent in firstborn status. Under this reading, buying the fetus brings it into the orbit of potential *kedusha*, while selling it removes it. Tosafot acknowledges the difficulty, however: if the fetus is exempt because the non-Jew owns the mother, in what sense does buying the fetus create *kedusha*? Tosafot resolves this by noting that if the fetus turns out to be female, its future offspring would be subject to *bechor* obligations — so there is some residual proximity to *kedushat bechor*. There is nonetheless a pointed question about whether the term *kedushat bechor* is even appropriate in the context of *peter chamor*, where the redeemed sheep has no *kedusha*, the *kohen* simply owns it, and the *chamor* itself has no sacrificial dimension. This may be precisely why Rashi avoided Tosafot's reading, even though on the surface it seems more contextually fitting.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda View

### Partnership Case Need

The *Gemara* continues: *ve-ha-mishtatef lo lama li?* — why was the partnership case necessary? If we've already established that partial ownership in either the mother or the fetus creates an exemption, why add the case of joint ownership?

### R.Y. Exclusion

The answer: *le-apukei mi-Rabbi Yehuda* — to exclude the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

### R.Y. Partnership

Rabbi Yehuda holds: *shutafus oved kochavim chayevet bi-vchora* — a partnership with a non-Jew is still subject to the *bechora* obligation. In other words, Rabbi Yehuda takes the position that even where the non-Jew is a part-owner, the Jewish co-owner remains obligated for his share.

### Matnot Contrast

This stands in striking contrast to the other extreme we encountered earlier in the context of *matnot kehuna*, where one opinion held that even Jewish partnership exempts — that even a Jewish co-owner need not give *matnot kehuna*. Here, Rabbi Yehuda holds the opposite: even non-Jewish co-ownership does not exempt. The *mishna* therefore needs to include the partnership case explicitly, to make clear that we do not rule like Rabbi Yehuda — that *shutafut* with a non-Jew does exempt.

The logic of the first two cases — where the non-Jew owns the entire fetus or the entire mother — would be acceptable even to Rabbi Yehuda, since the Jewish party holds nothing of the relevant ownership. But in the partnership case, where both parties are co-owners in both the mother and the offspring, Rabbi Yehuda would say the Jewish partner is obligated for his half. The *mishna* comes to teach that the *halacha* does not follow that position.

---

## Maris Ayin Issue

### Consignment Opacity

The *Gemara* then asks: *ve-ha-mikabel lama li?* — why was it necessary to state the *kabala* case, where the non-Jew gives his donkey to the Jew to raise in exchange for a share of the offspring? Surely, if the non-Jew still owns the mother animal, the exemption is obvious.

The answer: the *mishna* needed this case not for its own sake but in order to introduce the far less obvious reverse case — *ve-ha-noten lo be-kabala* — where the Jew owns the mother but gives it to the non-Jew to raise, the non-Jew receiving half the offspring as his fee.

### Consequentialist View

*Salka daitach amina*: one might have thought to impose a rabbinic sanction in this case. Why? Because in the *noten* case, the Jew owns the mother, and the Jew is seen taking some of the offspring. The non-Jew also takes some, but *ho'il ve-ikar ha-behema de-Yisrael hi* — since the fundamental animal belongs to the Jew, a bystander observing the arrangement might reasonably conclude that the Jew is the sole owner of both the mother and the offspring. If the Jew is not giving *peter chamor*, this would appear to onlookers as a violation — as if a Jew who fully owns the animal is simply ignoring his obligation.

### Gezeira Rejected

One might therefore have thought that the Rabbis would impose a rabbinic *gezeira* — a decree compelling the Jew to treat the firstborn as if he were obligated, so that observers are not misled. The *mishna* teaches that no such *knas* is applied. The Jew is technically exempt and remains so.

### Confusion Risk

The precise nature of the concern is worth examining. The Jew owns the mother and receives half the kids. Observers see him taking offspring home and may not notice that the non-Jew also receives a share. Or they may notice that the non-Jew receives some offspring but assume he is merely a hired laborer being paid a daily wage, not an actual half-owner. In either case, the overall impression is that this Jew is the sole owner and is disregarding the *mitzvah* of *peter chamor*. One might further imagine the concern that observers could mistake the arrangement as one where the firstborn specifically goes to the Jew — precisely the case that would trigger the obligation — while the subsequent offspring go to the non-Jew as payment.

Despite all of this, *ka-mashma lan*: the Rabbis do not impose any rabbinic *gezeira* or *knas*. Since the Jew is technically exempt, he remains exempt.

---

## AZ Transition

### AZ Sources

Having established the framework of the *mishna*, the *Gemara* now pivots — and this pivot occupies essentially the rest of the *daf* — to the side point embedded in the *mishna*'s phrase *af al pi she-eino rashai*: the prohibition against selling animals to a non-Jew. The *Gemara* invokes the relevant *mishna* in *Masechet Avodah Zarah*: *tnan hosam* — it was taught there.

### R.Y. Broken Leg

In that *mishna*, Rabbi Yehuda *matir bi-shvura* — Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken-legged animal to a non-Jew, because the animal cannot perform *melacha*. If the entire basis of the prohibition is concern that the animal might be used for labor on *Shabbat*, then an animal that is physically incapable of labor presents no such concern.

### Ben B. Horse

*Ben Beteira matir be-sus* — Ben Beteira permits selling a horse to a non-Jew outright, even without any physical defect. His reasoning rests on the principle of *chai noseh et atzmo* — a living being bears its own weight. The primary use of a horse is carrying a rider, and since the rider is a living being who partially supports his own weight, riding is not classified as *melacha* at the biblical level. Therefore, the concern that a horse will be used for *melacha* on *Shabbat* in a biblically significant sense does not apply, and Ben Beteira holds that the decree against selling animals to non-Jews does not extend to horses.

The broader question of whether rabbinic restrictions on *melacha* also apply to the prohibition against letting one's animals work, and whether one would then be creating a *gezeira* atop a *gezeira* atop a *gezeira*, is a question that touches on deep issues in *Masechet Avodah Zarah*. What matters for present purposes is that Ben Beteira is carving out a narrow exception based on the nature of the animal's use.

### Fetus Question

*Iba'aya lehu* — the *Gemara* raises a question: what would Rabbi Yehuda say about selling a fetus? An animal in the womb clearly cannot perform *melacha* at present. Does Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning from the broken-leg case apply here as well?

### Reason vs. Unusual

The question is framed in two directions. *Ta'ama de-Rabbi Yehuda hosam de-shari mishum de-shvura* — is the reason Rabbi Yehuda permits the broken-leg case simply because the animal cannot work? If so, *ubar nami shavur hu* — a fetus also cannot work, and Rabbi Yehuda should permit it equally.

Or perhaps: *shvura lav hainu orchai* — a broken leg is not a normal state of affairs for an animal. It is an unusual and visually unmistakable condition. *Aval ubar, keivan de-hainu orchai, lav shavur hu* — but a fetus, since being in the womb is the normal developmental state of a living creature, is not analogous to something broken. Because it is *orchai* — normal — it does not stand out the way a broken leg does.

This distinction carries halakhic weight in two ways. First, a fetus, unlike a broken-legged animal, will eventually be born, grow, and be capable of performing *melacha* on *Shabbat*. The broken-leg exception holds only because the animal is presumed incapable of healing; a fetus presents no such permanence. Second, there is the question of *lo plug* — the rabbinic principle of not making fine distinctions. Rabbi Yehuda is willing to create an exception for the broken-leg case precisely because it is so patently obvious that the animal cannot work. A fetus, being a normal condition, does not present that same visual clarity, and therefore even Rabbi Yehuda might agree that *lo plug* applies — that we do not carve out exceptions for normal developmental states where the distinction would be unclear to an observer.

---

## Mishna Evidence

### Proof Source

*Ta shema* — the *Gemara* attempts to resolve the question about Rabbi Yehuda's position on the fetus by invoking our *mishna* itself as a source of evidence.

### Fetus Prohibition

The *mishna* states: *ha-mocher lo af al pi she-eino rashai* — if one sells the fetus to a non-Jew, even though one is not permitted to do so. The *mishna* thus establishes that selling the fetus is prohibited. The *Gemara* suggests that since Rabbi Yehuda does not object to this ruling in the *mishna*, he must implicitly agree that selling a fetus is forbidden.

### Silence Inference

*Ve-lo palig Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yehuda is not recorded as dissenting from this clause of the *mishna*. Can we infer from his silence that he agrees?

### No Inference Rule

The *Gemara* rejects this inference decisively. *U-letamecha* — by your logic, consider: the *mishna* also does not record Rabbi Yehuda as objecting to the cases of *mishtatef* and *kabala* — partnership and consignment. Yet we know from elsewhere that Rabbi Yehuda holds *shutafus oved kochavim chayevet bi-vchora* — a position that directly contradicts the *mishna*'s ruling in the partnership case. Clearly, Rabbi Yehuda disputes part of this *mishna* without the *mishna* recording his objection there.

The lesson: *ela palig ve-lo katani* — he disagrees, but it is simply not stated in this *mishna*. A *stam mishna* introducing a topic does not necessarily catalogue every dissenting opinion. One cannot draw conclusions from silence. The same may be true of the fetus prohibition — Rabbi Yehuda may disagree but the *mishna* does not record it. The evidential attempt fails.

---

## R.Y. Obligations

### Receive Consignment

The *Gemara* proceeds to cite a *braita* that lays out Rabbi Yehuda's affirmative positions on these cases. *Rabbi Yehuda omer: ha-mikabel behema mi-yad oved kochavim* — if one takes an animal from a non-Jew under a *kabala* arrangement, such that the Jew tends the animal and receives half the offspring, and the animal gives birth to a firstborn, *ma'alin oto be-shavin* — one assesses the animal's value, *ve-noten chatzi damav la-kohen* — and gives half of that value to the *kohen*.

### Half Value Obligation

This ruling is easier to understand in the context of a *chamor*: the obligation of *peter chamor* is discharged through a *se'eh* of redemption money — or a sheep — given to the *kohen*, without any *kedusha* attaching to the redemption. The Jew who is a half-owner in the offspring is obligated for his half, and the way he discharges that obligation is by giving the *kohen* half the assessed value of the animal. The case of *bechor behema* is more complex: a *bechor behema* is supposed to be brought as a *korban*, and it is difficult to conceptualize half an animal as a *korban* when the other half is owned by a non-Jew. Rashi understands we are dealing with small animals, and the solution is to give the *kohen* the monetary value of the half-share rather than the animal itself. Tosafot prefers to read the entire discussion as pertaining to the *chamor*.

It is worth pausing on a point raised in the course of the discussion: here, in the *kabala* case, the non-Jew owns the entire mother. The Jew owns only a half-share in the offspring — and specifically in the firstborn offspring. Yet Rabbi Yehuda holds that the Jew is still obligated. This is a striking implication of his position: ownership in the *ubar* alone — not in the mother — is sufficient to generate a *bechora* obligation.

### Owner Gives Case

The *braita* then presents the reverse: *ve-ha-noten lo be-kabala* — the Jew owns the mother and gives it to the non-Jew to raise, with the non-Jew receiving half the offspring as his fee. *Af al pi she-eino rashai* — even though one is not permitted to do this.

### Redemption Fine

*Konsin oto ad asara bi-damav* — the Rabbinical court imposes a fine: the Jew is compelled to buy back his share from the non-Jew, at up to ten times the value if necessary. The *Gemara* will later examine whether "ten times" is meant literally or hyperbolically. The severity of the fine reflects how strongly the Rabbis disapprove of this transaction.

### Full Value Penalty

Beyond buying back the share, the Jew is further required: *ve-noten kol damav la-kohen* — to give the full value of the firstborn to the *kohen*. Not half — the full value. This is a penalty imposed because the Jew acted improperly by creating this arrangement.

---

## Braita Clarification

### Violation Identification

The *Gemara* now subjects this *braita* to careful analysis. *Mai lav* — is it not the case that when the *braita* says the Jew violated by doing something he was *not rashai* to do, the violation refers to selling or conveying a share in the *ubar* — the fetus — to the non-Jew? If so, this would be direct evidence that Rabbi Yehuda holds selling the fetus is a violation of the prohibition against selling animals to non-Jews.

### Mother Violation

The *Gemara* rejects this: *lo, a-behema* — no, the real violation the *braita* is referring to is selling a portion of the mother animal itself. In the *kabala* arrangement as constructed, the Jew may have done more than simply arrange for the non-Jew to receive offspring — he may have effectively conveyed a share in the mother.

### Grammar Analysis

The *Gemara* challenges this reading on grammatical grounds: the *braita* uses the masculine form *damav* — "its value" — which would naturally refer to the *ubar* (fetus, a masculine noun), not to *behema* (animal, feminine). The *Gemara* responds: read *dameha* — with a feminine suffix — to refer to the *behema*. This is one of the moments in the *Gemara* where knowing grammar matters — and equally where the *Gemara* simply overrides the grammatical form by emending the *girsa*.

The *Gemara* then notes a further problem: the *braita* says *ve-noten kol damav la-kohen* — he gives all its value to the *kohen*. "All its value" in context plainly refers to the value of the *bechor*, not of the mother. What would a *kohen* have to do with the monetary value of the mother animal?

### Pregnant Animal

The *Gemara* therefore reframes the case: *kegon de-yahvei behema me'ubarta* — we are dealing with a case where the Jew gave the non-Jew a pregnant animal. The animal is already carrying a fetus, and the arrangement is not merely that the non-Jew will receive future offspring, but also that he receives a benefit-share in the animal itself.

### Fattening Rights

Specifically, the arrangement includes *l'ishtumei* — fattening rights. The non-Jew not only receives half of every offspring born but also benefits from the animal's increase in value through his tending, feeding, and fattening of it. This means he holds a partial economic stake in the mother animal — not just in the *velados*. When the arrangement includes benefit from the mother's increase in value, the Jew has effectively given the non-Jew a share in the mother itself, which is a clear violation of the prohibition against selling *behema gassa* to a non-Jew.

### Extension Logic

*De-migo de-kansinan leih a-behema* — since the court would impose a fine on the Jew for the violation regarding the mother, *kansinan leih a-ubar* — the court extends that fine to the fetus as well. The Jew is compelled to buy back both, and must give the full value to the *kohen*. The *braita*'s harsh consequences — buying back at up to ten times the value and giving the full amount to the *kohen* — flow from the violation concerning the mother. They then cascade onto the fetus as a further extension of the penalty.

The implication is significant: the *braita*, on this reading, does not establish that Rabbi Yehuda considers the fetus transaction itself to be a violation. The violation is the mother, and the fetus penalties are derivative. We therefore still lack a definitive answer from the *braita* alone about whether Rabbi Yehuda independently considers selling the fetus to be prohibited.

---

## Rav Ashi Logic

### Exception Rehash

At this point, Rav Ashi intervenes: *ta shema* — come and hear. He returns to the *mishna* in *Avodah Zarah* about Rabbi Yehuda's broken-leg exception.

### No Healing

Rav Ashi highlights a detail embedded in that ruling: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a broken-legged animal *because it cannot heal* — *einah yecholah le-hitrapot*. The exception is conditioned on the irreversibility of the injury.

### Future Capacity

This formulation carries an implicit corollary: *ha-yecholah le-hitrapot — assur* — if the animal could heal, it would be forbidden. The exception holds only when there is no future possibility that the animal will recover and become capable of *melacha*.

### Fetus Analogy

*Ve-ha ubar nami, de-hayecholah le-hitrapot dami* — and the fetus is precisely analogous to something that can heal. A fetus will be born, will grow, and will eventually be capable of working on *Shabbat*. In that sense, it is in exactly the category that Rabbi Yehuda himself would classify as forbidden — the category of conditions that are not permanent and from which the animal will emerge capable of labor.

### Conclusion

*Shema minah* — the *Gemara* is satisfied with this reasoning. The conclusion follows: Rabbi Yehuda holds that selling a fetus to a non-Jew does violate the prohibition. Our *mishna*, which says *af al pi she-eino rashai* regarding the fetus sale, does indeed reflect Rabbi Yehuda's view, not just that of the Sages.

---

## Alt Teaching Order

### Version Difference

The *Gemara* notes: *ve-ika de-matni lah a-matnitin* — there is an alternative version of the tradition in which this entire discussion is framed differently. While above the discussion arose in the context of learning *Masechet Avodah Zarah* — where someone cited our *mishna* in *Bekhorot* as relevant evidence — in this alternate version, the discussion begins from our *mishna* in *Bekhorot*, and someone cites the material from *Avodah Zarah* as relevant.

### Mishna Hypothesis

In this version, the starting point is the question: *leima matnitin dela ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — perhaps our *mishna* does not reflect Rabbi Yehuda's position at all? Since the *mishna* says you are not permitted to sell the fetus, and since Rabbi Yehuda allows the broken-leg case, perhaps Rabbi Yehuda would similarly permit the fetus — meaning our *mishna* does not accord with his view.

### Cross-Ref

The response is: *de-tnan, Avodah Zarah* — no, consider what is taught in *Masechet Avodah Zarah*: Rabbi Yehuda permits specifically the broken-leg case, and the reason, as will emerge, is precisely the *einah yecholah le-hitrapot* condition.

### Repeated Analysis

The *Gemara* then works through essentially the same analysis we already encountered: *shvura lav hainu orchai* — a broken leg is abnormal, while *ubar hainu orchai* — a fetus is a normal condition. Therefore, even Rabbi Yehuda would agree that the fetus falls under the general prohibition, not under his broken-leg exception. And the conclusion from Rav Ashi's point — *ha-yecholah le-hitrapot assur*, and the fetus is analogous — is reached again. The two versions of the tradition converge on the same conclusions through the same reasoning.

---

## Future Fetuses

### Question Posed

*Iba'aya lehu* — a new question is now raised: *mocher behema le-ubara mahu?* — what is the law if one sells the mother specifically in order to convey rights to its future offspring, to fetuses that do not yet exist and are not currently in the mother's womb? Does this constitute a violation of the prohibition against selling *behema gassa* to a non-Jew?

### Ownership Transfer

The conceptual mechanism being invoked here is the notion of *mocher behema li-veladoseha* — selling the animal for its offspring-rights. The principle at work is that while one cannot sell something that does not yet exist — *davar she-lo ba le-olam* — there is a recognized rabbinic concept by which one can transfer a defined dimension of ownership. The Rabbis have an analogous concept from the laws of trees: I can sell you a tree *li-feroteiha* — for its fruit. I am not selling you the fruit, which does not yet exist; rather, I am transferring to you that aspect of ownership in the tree which entitles the owner to receive its fruit. You retain the other aspects of ownership — the right to cut it down, to use the wood — while I now hold the fruit-rights.

---

## Future Fetuses (II)

### Non-Existent Rule

The doctrine of *davar she-lo ba le-olam* — that one cannot effect a legal transfer of something that does not yet exist — is a foundational principle of rabbinic property law. Ordinarily, a sale requires that the subject of the sale have present existence.

### Fruit Analogy

The tree-for-fruit model shows how this constraint can be worked around: ownership itself is not a monolithic concept. A single object can be owned in distinct, separable dimensions. By transferring one specific dimension of ownership — the entitlement to benefit from future fruit — while retaining all others, the parties accomplish a meaningful legal transfer without running afoul of *davar she-lo ba le-olam*. The buyer does not own nonexistent fruit; he owns a present, existing stake in the tree that will yield fruit.

### Rights Ownership

The same structure applies here: *livladoseha* — selling for offspring-rights. The seller retains the right to use the animal for work, to milk it, to shear it, to slaughter it. But the buyer acquires that dimension of the seller's ownership which entitles him to the offspring as they are born. This is a present transfer of a real ownership stake, not a sale of nonexistent animals.

---

## Whole Animal Debate

### Both Positions

*Tiba'ei le-Rabbi Yehuda, tiba'ei le-Rabbanan* — the question of selling for offspring-rights can be asked according to both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. Each has its own framework for determining what falls within the prohibition and what does not, and it is not obvious which direction the analysis points.

### Limited Exception

Considering Rabbi Yehuda first: *ad kan lo shari ela bi-shvura* — Rabbi Yehuda permits only the broken-leg case, and the reason, as established, is *de-lo ati le-ichlufei* — because a broken-legged animal will not be confused with a normal animal. It is visually distinct, obviously incapacitated, and therefore an exception can be made without creating confusing precedents. People can see that this is a special case and will not extrapolate to other situations.

### Visual Distinction

The logic of Rabbi Yehuda's exception rests on visual distinctiveness: the broken leg is observable and unmistakable. This is why *lo plug* does not apply — the distinction is so obvious that it does not invite confusion.

### Whole Confusable

*Aval shleima* — but a whole, healthy animal sold for its future offspring looks, externally, identical to a whole animal that has been fully transferred to the non-Jew. An observer sees the non-Jew with the animal in his possession or sees him receiving offspring and cannot tell from appearances whether the non-Jew owns everything or merely the offspring-rights. The visual distinction that justified Rabbi Yehuda's broken-leg exception is entirely absent here. Therefore, Rabbi Yehuda might well say that even this arrangement falls under the general prohibition — *lo plug* applies because there is no observable marker that would prevent confusion.

### Distinction Debate

On the other hand, the argument can be inverted. One could say: Rabbi Yehuda permits the broken-leg case even though the non-Jew takes the entire animal and severs all connection with the Jewish owner. The animal leaves the Jew's possession entirely. How much more so should Rabbi Yehuda permit the case where the animal remains fundamentally the Jew's property — where the Jew retains ownership, the animal stays in the Jew's domain, and only the offspring-entitlement has been transferred? The lesser degree of divestiture should more clearly fall outside the concern.

The same bifurcated argument applies to the Rabbis. They might argue: we only prohibit the broken-leg case — where the Jew fully divests himself of the animal — because the complete transfer looks like a full sale. But where the animal remains the Jew's property and only offspring-rights are conveyed, that is sufficiently distinct that we need not prohibit it. Or conversely: if we prohibit even the broken-leg case — which is visually obviously different from a normal sale — how much more so must we prohibit the case of a whole, healthy animal where the visual similarity to a full prohibited sale is even greater?

The *Gemara* leaves this as an unresolved question — *teku*.

---

## Concern Basis

### Rabbis' Reason

The *Gemara* now asks a foundational question that reframes the entire previous discussion: *ve-ta'amei de-Rabbanan mishum hachi hu?* — is it really true that the Rabbis' reason for disagreeing with Rabbi Yehuda is the *lo plug* concern — the worry about making confusing distinctions? Is that the actual basis of their position?

### Rabbis Respond

The *Gemara* invokes a *braita* in which the Rabbis respond to Rabbi Yehuda's broken-leg exception: *amru lo* — the Rabbis said to Rabbi Yehuda: even if this animal has a broken leg and cannot itself perform *melacha* on *Shabbat*, there is still a concern.

### Future Breeding

*Ve-halo marbi'in aleiha bnei veladot* — one may use this broken-legged animal for breeding. The non-Jew will have it mate with other animals, and the offspring will eventually be healthy animals that can and will be put to work on *Shabbat*. The concern is not limited to what this specific animal can do — it extends to what becomes possible through this animal's presence in the non-Jew's household.

### Initial Impression

The *Gemara* initially reads this as saying that the Rabbis have an independent concern: simply having young animals born into the non-Jew's possession is itself objectionable — *mishum ubra hu* — irrespective of any *Shabbat*-work calculation. If so, the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda are not even in the same conversation; the Rabbis' concern would be categorically different and could not be analyzed using Rabbi Yehuda's *lo plug* framework.

### Real Concern

The *Gemara* corrects this impression: *hachi ka'amar leh* — this is what the Rabbis are really saying to Rabbi Yehuda. Our concern is the same as yours — *ta'ama didan mishum de-ati le-ichlufei bi-behema* — we are concerned about *lo plug*, about people confusing permissible and prohibited cases. You say the broken-leg case is an exception because it is visually obvious. We say: it is not so obvious, because even a broken-legged animal will be kept around for breeding rather than immediately slaughtered. The animal stays in the non-Jew's possession, it is used, and observers will see what appears to be a Jew's animal in non-Jewish hands — and will not understand why the case is different.

### Lo Plug Focus

Rabbi Yehuda assumed that a broken-legged animal would promptly be slaughtered and would not remain in the non-Jew's home, making the exception visually clean. The Rabbis respond that this assumption is wrong — *marbi'in aleiha bnei veladot* — the animal may well be kept for breeding, and the visual clarity Rabbi Yehuda assumed will not materialize. Therefore, the Rabbis maintain *lo plug*: we do not permit even the visually differentiated cases, because the differentiation is not reliable.

Both positions, then, share the same underlying concern about appearances, *Shabbat*, and the risks of confusion. Their dispute is entirely about the reliability of the visual distinction in the broken-leg case. Rabbi Yehuda is convinced the distinction is patent enough to be an exception; the Rabbis are not. And since they share the same framework, the question about selling for future offspring-rights — whether there is a sufficiently reliable distinction — can legitimately be asked according to both positions.

---

## Oath Concern

### Partnership Banned

The *Gemara* now turns to the prohibition of *shutafut* — the concern about entering a business partnership with a non-Jew, as invoked above in explaining why the *mishna*'s *af al pi she-eino rashai* extends beyond the fetus-sale case. The teaching cited is from the father of Shmuel: *assur le-adam le-hishtatef im ha-oved kochavim* — it is forbidden for a person to enter into a partnership with a non-Jew.

### Oath Risk

The reason: *shema yitchayev lo shevuah* — perhaps in the course of the partnership, the Jewish partner will demand that the non-Jewish partner take an oath to verify his honesty in keeping the accounts or managing the business.

### Foreign God Oath

*Ve-nishba lo be-shem avodat kochavim shelo* — and the non-Jew will swear in the name of his deity. This is not a theoretical concern. In the ancient and medieval world, business partners who suspected misconduct routinely compelled oaths from one another, and those oaths were sworn by whatever god the swearer revered.

### Torah Prohibition

*Ve-ha-Torah amrah lo yishama al picha* — the Torah states that the name of other gods shall not be heard upon your lips. The formulation is notably passive or causative: not merely that one shall not personally invoke a foreign deity, but that one shall not be the cause of a foreign deity's name being uttered in one's presence or in one's business context.

### Causation Issue

The prohibition thus extends beyond active invocation: even causing a non-Jew to swear by his deity — by placing him in a situation where such an oath might be demanded — constitutes a violation of *lo yishama al picha*. The Jew who enters a partnership thereby creates the conditions under which such an oath might arise, and is therefore responsible for the resulting invocation.

---

## Partnership Omission

### Question Posed

*U-letamecha* — but if the concern about partnership is the oath prohibition, why does our *mishna* not explicitly say *af al pi she-eino rashai* — that one is not permitted — in the partnership case (*mishtatef*) as well? The *mishna* states the prohibition only in the context of selling the fetus.

### Mechira Teaching

The *Gemara* answers: *tana mechira avuha de-shutafut* — the *mishna* teaches the case of *mechira* — the sale — and that teaching implicitly encompasses *shutafut* and the other cases as well. Since *mechira* is mentioned and the *mishna* attached the *af al pi she-eino rashai* qualifier to it, the reader understands that other forms of prohibited dealings similarly carry the qualifier.

### Mechira Fundamental

*De-ikar mechira hi* — *mechira* is the foundational and prototypical case of these transactions. It is therefore the natural locus for the *mishna*'s explicit statement of prohibition.

### Tosafot View

Tosafot adds the simpler observation: *mechira* was mentioned first in the *mishna*, and the qualifier *af al pi she-eino rashai* was attached to that first case. It then carries forward implicitly to all subsequent cases. There was no need to repeat it. The *mishna* follows the standard practice of attaching a qualification to the first relevant instance, which then extends by implication.

---

## Critical Tosafot

### Actual Scope

This Tosafot on *shutafut* is notable not only for its immediate textual role but for what it signals about the practical scope of the partnership prohibition. The prohibition — based on the father of Shmuel's statement that one may not partner with a non-Jew lest one be brought to compel an oath — would, if applied broadly, impose severe economic constraints on Jews whose entire commercial lives were intertwined with non-Jewish neighbors and business partners.

### Oath Reality

Tosafot observes that across the Talmud there are numerous cases in which Jews and non-Jews do appear to enter partnerships and joint business arrangements, and not all *Tannaim* and *Amoraim* accept the father of Shmuel's prohibition in its full scope. The cases in *Gemara* that seem to presuppose joint arrangements — buying a field in partnership, splitting *orlah* produce, and others — constitute apparent counterexamples that Tosafot catalogues, noting *kol hanei uvdei pligi a-avuha de-Shmuel* — all of those cases imply disagreement with the father of Shmuel.

### Next Tosafot

The very next Tosafot — on the word *shema* — is one of the most halakhically significant *Tosafot* in the entire tractate. It engages directly with the question of whether, and in what circumstances, Jews and non-Jews could in fact have financial dealings with one another, given this oath concern.

### Christian Oaths

The question is whether the oath concern applies to Christians specifically. When a Christian takes an oath in business dealings, he does so in the name of Jesus or the saints. Does such an oath constitute swearing *be-shem avodat kochavim* — in the name of an idolatrous deity — such that a Jew who compels or enables such an oath has violated *lo yishama al picha*? Or is the status of Christian oath-taking different, given the theological character of Christianity's relationship to monotheism? This question has enormous practical implications for Jewish commercial life throughout the medieval period and beyond.

### Tomorrow Preview

This Tosafot is among the foundational texts for how the Rishonim and Acharonim think about the halakhic status of non-Jews in general, and of Christians in particular, in the context of commercial dealings, oaths, and *avodat kochavim*. We will begin with it first thing tomorrow.

---

---

# Bekhorot 3

## Tosafot: Non-Jews & Oaths

### Partnership Prohibition

The Gemara at the end of the previous daf cited a statement of Avuha DeShmuel that a person is not permitted to enter into a business partnership with a non-Jew. The concern, as the Gemara frames it, is that disputes over financial honesty would naturally be resolved by having the parties swear an oath. If a non-Jew were compelled to swear, he would do so in the name of his god, and the Jewish partner would thereby have caused the invocation of an idolatrous deity in a context expressing recognition and respect — transgressing the verse *lo yishama al picha*, "the name of other gods shall not be heard on your lips." The rabbis understand this verse to prohibit not merely the personal utterance of a foreign deity's name in a reverential context, but even causing others to utter such a name in that fashion. It is worth noting that this prohibition does not bar the mere mention of other gods' names in ordinary discourse — one may say "Zeus" without transgressing — but it does prohibit invoking them in any way that acknowledges them as genuine divine powers.

### Oath Problem

This prohibition creates a striking practical problem. The Tosafot on 70b, beginning with the word *shema*, takes up precisely this difficulty: if entering into business partnerships with non-Jews is forbidden due to the oath concern, how have Jews throughout the medieval period routinely formed such partnerships with Christians — and indeed, how have they allowed Christians to swear oaths in the course of those partnerships, oaths that typically invoke the names of saints and, alongside that, the name of God?

### Tosafot's Solution

Rabbeinu Tam, cited approximately ten lines from the bottom of the Tosafot in the passage beginning *lo hayu nizharin bahen*, first makes the general observation that other Gemarot suggest this prohibition was not rigorously observed even in the Talmudic period itself — raising the broader question of how a stated *halacha* interacts with widespread contrary practice. But the more consequential contribution follows immediately: *bizman hazeh kulam nishba'in bekadeshim* — nowadays, when Christians take oaths, they swear in the name of their saints, not in the name of Jesus. Since saints are not being accorded divinity — *ein tofsim bahem elohut*, their sanctity is acknowledged but they are not treated as gods — swearing in a saint's name is not swearing in the name of *elohim acherim*, another god.

A further complication arises from the fact that oaths typically combine the saint's name with the name of God. Rabbeinu Tam acknowledges this: *af al pi shemazkirim imahem shem shamayim*, even when they also say "God," *vekavanatam ledavar acher* — their intention when they say God differs from ours. Yet *mikol makom ein zeh shem avodat kochavim*, it is not the name of another god, *ki da'atam le'oseh shamayim va'aretz* — because when Christians say "God," they mean the creator of heaven and earth. Whatever the theological complications surrounding Jesus, when they appeal to God the Father in an oath, they are directing themselves to what is, in essence, the same concept of God as the creator that we ourselves invoke. So far, then, there is no problem of causing them to swear in the name of an idolatrous god.

A further issue remains: the oath combines God's name with another entity — the saint — and this constitutes a form of *shituf*, linking God's name with something else. A Jew cannot take an oath in this manner, because it places something created on the same level as God. Does causing the non-Jew to take such an oath violate the prohibition of *lifnei iver lo titein michshol*? Rabbeinu Tam answers: *debnei Noach lo huzharu akach* — non-Jews are not prohibited from this form of combined oath. And *lo ashkechan issur begram shituf* — there is no prohibition on us causing them to take an oath in that form. The prohibition of combining God's name with something else in an oath applies to Jews; we do not violate any prohibition by allowing a non-Jew to do it.

Read correctly, this Tosafot does no more than solve the specific practical problem of oaths and partnerships. In doing so, it also implicitly acknowledges a significant theological point: that within the Christian concept of God the Father, there is a genuine overlap with the Jewish understanding of the creator of heaven and earth. Christianity is still characterized as *avodah zarah* throughout the *rishonim*, but this Tosafot acknowledges the important domain of shared monotheistic conviction.

### Misinterpretation Issue

The historical influence of this Tosafot, however, derives largely from a misreading of it. When Rabbeinu Tam writes that there is no prohibition on non-Jews combining God's name with something else *in an oath*, if one drops the limiting phrase "in an oath," the statement transforms into a general theological dispensation: non-Jews are not prohibited from combining God and other concepts in their religious belief. Under this reading, the Trinity itself becomes permissible for non-Jews — not for Jews, for whom it remains *avodah zarah*, but for non-Jews, for whom a faith that combines an ultimate creator God with other divine figures presents no violation.

### Historical Impact

This misinterpretation was already institutionalized by the time of the Rema, whose rulings carry authoritative weight for Ashkenazic communities in the *Shulchan Aruch*, and it introduced what amounts to a dual standard for defining *avodah zarah*: for Jews, Christianity is *avodah zarah*; for non-Jews, it is not. This shift carried profound practical and attitudinal consequences. It allowed certain *halachot* to be applied less restrictively to Christians, and it fostered what might be called a quasi-pluralistic orientation — not a genuine theological pluralism, but at minimum a non-judgmental posture toward Christian belief. One can maintain the boundary — it is still *avodah zarah* for a Jew — without having to characterize Christians as *ovedei avodah zarah*. The misinterpretation of this Tosafot has entered so thoroughly into *halachic* discourse that the majority of *acharonim* today cite it without awareness that it represents a misreading of the original argument.

### Student Questions

One might ask why the oath concern ever arose at all, since parties could simply give their word without invoking any deity. The answer is that in the world in which Tosafot operated, an oath taken in the name of one's God was the operative mechanism for ensuring honesty in financial disputes. Where suspicions of fraud or dishonest bookkeeping arose, a sworn oath in the name of the relevant deity was the accepted instrument of resolution, and virtually no one in that era was in a position to substitute a purely secular affirmation. One might further ask whether the prohibition of partnership with non-Jews effectively became obsolete once sworn oaths ceased to be the standard mechanism for enforcing commercial honesty. This is a reasonable inference: if the oath concern dissolves, the prohibition grounded in it would logically fall away as well. What can be said is that by the time of the Tosafot the law had already been incorporated into the tradition, and by the time the oath mechanism itself began to lose its social force, the Tosafot's resolution was already deeply embedded in *halachic* literature — especially in its misread form.

---

## Non-Jewish Ownership

### Raising Animals Case

The Gemara now returns to the central topic of the *daf* — whether and how non-Jewish ownership of an animal affects the animal's status as a *bechor*. A *baraita* introduces the position of Rabbi Yehuda: *hamakabel behemah min ha'oved kochavim veyaldah* — if a person receives an animal from a non-Jew under a *kablanut* arrangement (taking the animal to raise, with the offspring to be split between them), and the animal gives birth, *ma'alin oto beshom venoten chatzi damav lakohen* — the animal is appraised and half its value is given to the *kohen* on account of the firstborn. This is Rabbi Yehuda's position: non-Jewish co-ownership does not exempt the animal from *bechor* status, so one must pay out one's share of the *bechor*'s value to the *kohen*.

The *baraita* adds a further ruling: if one gave the animal to the non-Jew under *kablanut* — transferring it to him to raise and take half the offspring — even though this is prohibited, *konsin oto ad asar bedamav* — we fine the person up to ten times the animal's value in order to compel the buyback of the firstborn, and *venoten kol damav lakohen* — because the person has transgressed, he must give the entire value of the firstborn to the *kohen*, not merely half. The Sages, by contrast, rule: *kol zman sheyad oved kochavim be'emtza, patur min habechorah* — as long as a non-Jew has a hand in it, meaning any co-ownership, the animal is fully exempt from *bechorah*.

The Gemara attempts to use this passage to resolve an open question from the previous daf: is selling a mother animal for the sake of her future offspring included in the prohibition against selling animals to non-Jews? Since the *baraita* describes a case in which the arrangement presumably transfers some right to future offspring, perhaps it proves that such an arrangement is forbidden. The Gemara rejects this: *lo, uvar* — the prohibition here concerns a case where the animal was already pregnant and the fetus itself was sold, not a sale of the mother contingent on future offspring. The question of selling a mother for her future offspring thus remains unresolved. What is confirmed, however, is that selling an existing fetus is included in the prohibition.

### Fine Amounts

The *baraita*'s mention of a fine — up to ten times the value — for one who has transgressed the prohibition of giving an animal to a non-Jew under *kablanut* sets the stage for a broader discussion about the nature and scope of these fines. It is also worth recalling the background prohibition here: the concern is that large working animals (*behemah gassah*) — cattle, horses, and similar — will be used for labor on *Shabbat*. Even if the non-Jew ultimately becomes the owner, there may be a period during which the animal is still technically the Jew's while already being worked, or it may continue to appear as a Jewish-owned animal to outside observers. For these reasons, the sale of large animals to non-Jews is prohibited.

### Reish Lakish Position

The Gemara cites a statement of Reish Lakish directly: *hamokher behemah gassah le'ovdei kokhavim konsin oto ad asarah be'dameha* — one who sells a large animal to a non-Jew is fined up to ten times its value in order to compel the buyback.

### Literal vs Exaggeration

The Gemara raises the question: *davka o lo davka* — is the figure of ten meant literally, or is it an exaggeration? Does it mean precisely ten, or does it mean "a very large amount, up to some high limit that we are rounding off as ten"? To resolve this, the Gemara appeals to a parallel teaching: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled that one who sells a slave to a non-Jew is fined *ad me'ah be'dameha* — up to one hundred times the slave's value in order to compel buyback. The concern with selling a slave is distinct: a slave in Jewish ownership who has undergone *brit milah* and *mikveh* is obligated in certain *mitzvot*, and transferring him to non-Jewish ownership removes that obligation.

### Slave vs Animal Fines

Rashi's argument is that if ten and a hundred were both mere exaggerations — rough ways of saying "a very high amount" — one would not use two different exaggerated numbers in two different contexts. The fact that one text says ten and another says one hundred indicates that they are both meant literally, and that there is a real and considered distinction between the two cases.

### Rarity Principle

The Gemara then explores what justifies the different amounts. One approach: the slave's case is more serious because *kol yoma ve'yoma mevatlei lei mi'mitzvot* — every single day the slave is being prevented from performing the *mitzvot* he is obligated in. That severity could justify a literally higher fine of one hundred. But perhaps "ten" by the animal is still merely an exaggeration.

A second version of the tradition presents the figures in reverse: Reish Lakish says a hundred for selling the animal, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says ten for selling the slave. The Gemara then draws a distinction to explain why the animal's fine is higher: *mekhirah paskah mineih* — when one fully sells the animal, one has completely divested oneself of it; the severance is total. In *kablanut*, by contrast, *lo paskah mineih* — the owner has not entirely separated himself from the animal, and so the fine is lesser. This resolves the contradiction between the hundred in Reish Lakish's ruling and the ten in the *mishnah* regarding *kablanut*.

When the fine for the animal is set at one hundred and the fine for the slave is set at ten, the Gemara offers yet another explanation for the gap: *shani eved delo hadar lei* — the case of the slave is different because the slave, once bought back, does not return to the owner's possession; as the Mishnah in Gittin teaches, once sold to a non-Jew, the slave must be freed upon buyback. Since the owner will ultimately lose the slave, the rabbis did not impose as heavy a fine. With the animal, which the owner recovers and keeps, one might think the fine should simply be one unit more than the slave's — you lose ten times its value and on the last payment you also receive the animal back. Why jump to a hundred? The Gemara answers: *eved milta delo shechicha hi* — selling one's slave to a non-Jew is an uncommon occurrence, and *kol milta delo shechicha lo gazru bah rabanan* — where something is uncommon, the rabbis did not press as hard with their legislative response. Selling large animals to non-Jews, by contrast, was a frequent and prevalent transgression, and the rabbis therefore imposed a much heavier deterrent.

---

## Ownership Threshold

### Scriptural Basis

Having established that the Sages exempt an animal from *bechorah* whenever a non-Jew holds any co-ownership, the Gemara turns to the underlying dispute: both the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda derive their positions from the same verse. The relevant text is *hikdashti li kol bechor b'Yisrael* — "I have sanctified for Me all the firstborn in Israel." The word *Yisrael* emphasizes Jewish ownership, and the word *kol*, "all," becomes the crux of the debate.

### Yehuda vs Sages

The Sages reason as follows: the word *bechor* by itself, without any modifier, would already have implied that even partial ownership (*miktzat bechor*) suffices to create the obligation. Therefore, when the verse adds *kol* — "all" — it must be coming to require that *the entirety* of the *bechor* be owned by a Jew before the obligation attaches. Any non-Jewish co-ownership therefore exempts.

Rabbi Yehuda reasons differently: *bechor* by itself would have suggested that the entire animal must be Jewish-owned, since the word *bechor* in its natural sense denotes the full animal. Therefore, when the verse adds *kol*, it cannot be adding something already implied. Rather, *kol* here must mean *afillu kol shehu* — even the slightest portion. That is, even if only a small fraction is Jewish-owned, the obligation attaches.

An alternative formulation proposes that everyone agrees *bechor* on its own implies the majority. Then the debate centers on what *kol* adds: one opinion holds that *kol* comes to expand — meaning the *entirety* must be Jewish-owned — while the other holds that *kol* comes to reduce the threshold — even a minimal Jewish portion creates the obligation. Either way, the practical outcome of the dispute is the same.

### Rav Huna: Ear Test

The question then follows: according to the Sages, who hold that any non-Jewish co-ownership exempts, how minimal can that ownership be? Rav Huna says: *afilu ozno* — even an ear. Even if the non-Jew owns only something as seemingly trivial as the animal's ear, that suffices for exemption. The implicit qualification is that the non-Jewish share must be at least enough that, were the non-Jew to take his portion, the animal would be left with a *ba'al mum* — a blemish. But even an ear satisfies that threshold.

It is worth noting the apparent curiosity here: even if an animal were genuinely born with a severed ear, it would still be given to a *kohen* as a *bechor* — a *ba'al mum* is still a *bechor*, simply one that cannot be brought to the altar. The exemption in the co-ownership case therefore does not derive from the fact that the animal is missing a part; it derives from the fact of non-Jewish ownership. The significance of the "ear" threshold is simply that the ownership must be of some meaningful, non-trivial portion.

### Nachman Objection

Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna's position. If the non-Jew owns only a specific, identifiable part of the animal — say, the ear — why can one not simply say to him: *shkol oznecha v'zil* — take your ear and go? The Jew would own the entire remainder of the animal, and that remainder would still be obligated in *bechorah*. Since the co-ownership is a specific anatomical portion that can in principle be separated, the Jew's remaining share ought still to be obligated. Rav Nachman's implicit conclusion is that so trivial a portion does not suffice for exemption, and this objection is left without a direct answer — signaling that in Rav Nachman's view, the "ear" standard does not hold.

### Chisda: Neveila

The Gemara now records two alternative positions. Rav Chisda holds: the non-Jew must own a part *she'oseh otah neveilah* — a part whose removal would render the animal *neveilah*. This means a vital organ whose removal would cause the animal's immediate death, or at minimum a part whose absence would make *shechitah* impossible, such as the trachea or esophagus. The reasoning is that only if the non-Jew owns a part so central to the animal's life — or its ability to be slaughtered — does his ownership rise to the level of genuine, significant co-ownership.

### Rava: Tereifa

Rava holds a more lenient standard: the non-Jew need only own a part *she'oseh otah tereifa* — a part whose removal would render the animal a *tereifah*, a fatally injured animal. This does not require the animal to die immediately, only that it sustain the kind of wound that would eventually be fatal.

### Tereifa Viability

The Gemara identifies the underlying disagreement between Rav Chisda and Rava as turning on the question of *tereifah chaya* — whether an animal with a *tereifah*-level injury can survive. According to Rava, *tereifah einah chaya* — such an animal will eventually die — and therefore if the non-Jew owns a part whose removal would cause a *tereifah*-level wound, he is a sufficiently significant owner that his co-ownership creates the exemption. According to Rav Chisda, *aval tereifah chaya* — an animal can survive such an injury — and therefore ownership of such a part is not considered sufficiently significant. Only ownership of a part whose removal would directly cause death or prevent *shechitah* altogether constitutes real co-ownership.

It bears emphasis that this debate applies specifically to the scenario where the non-Jew owns a *specific part* of the animal. Where the non-Jew simply owns a *percentage* of the whole animal — not any identified limb or organ, but a fractional interest in the entity as a whole — the discussion is largely uncontested: even a minute fractional co-ownership would seem to suffice.

### Reconciliation Attempt

Students in the academy attempted to reconcile the sweeping gap between Rav Huna's "ear" standard and the positions of Rav Chisda and Rava. Perhaps, they suggested, these camps do not actually disagree — *lav pligi* — and the different standards apply to different animals: the stringent standard of Rav Chisda and Rava may apply to the *bechor* offspring itself, while Rav Huna's lenient "ear" standard applies only to the ownership of the *mother* before birth. For the mother, even trivial co-ownership suffices to prevent the *bechorah* from taking effect.

### Pappa Refutation

Rav Pappa rejects this attempted reconciliation. By the offspring, if one claims that even an ear exempts, one must reckon with the verse's language: the Torah says *kol bechor* — the entirety of the *bechor* must be under Jewish ownership. If even an ear of the *bechor* is non-Jewishly owned, then by definition the *entirety* of the *bechor* is not Jewish-owned, and yet Rav Huna says it is exempt. But conversely, if one were to say that by the mother, the ear test applies — one can point to the verse *kol miknecha tizachar* — "all of your cattle, the males shall [be sacred]," where the word *kol* also appears. If *kol* means that even the slightest non-Jewish ownership of the mother exempts, then that logic applies equally to the offspring. There is no basis for splitting the two cases. Rav Huna's position therefore applies equally to both mother and offspring, and the attempted reconciliation fails.

This ruling is significant for practice: since we *pasken* essentially like Rav Huna, even a trivial ownership — such as selling the ear of the mother — suffices to exempt the offspring from *bechorah*, regardless of whether it is the mother or the *bechor* itself in question.

---

## Yochanan Rulings

### Slight Blemish Rule

Rabbi Elazar was once unable to attend the *beis medrash* and asked Rav Assi what had been taught there. Rav Assi reported two rulings in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. The first: *afilu mum kal* — even a slight blemish suffices to exempt an animal from the obligation of *bechorah*. This ruling essentially *paskens* like Rav Huna, with a clarifying qualification: the non-Jew's co-ownership must be of a portion that would leave the animal with at least some blemish — even a minor, permanent one. A hair or a toenail would not suffice, but anything that rises to the level of a recognized *mum*, however minor, does. This definitively sets aside the positions of Rav Chisda and Rava, which required ownership of a vital or life-threatening portion.

### Hybrid Offspring

Rabbi Yochanan's second ruling pertains to the *mishnah*'s teaching that a sheep which gives birth to an animal resembling a goat, or a goat that gives birth to an animal resembling a sheep, is exempt from *bechorah* since the offspring does not look like its mother. The *mishnah* adds, however, that if the offspring has *miktzat simanim* — some characteristics of its mother alongside characteristics of the other species — it is still *chayav*, still obligated as a *bechor*. Rabbi Yochanan adds his own *chiddush*: *mum kavua hu lishahet alav* — the hybrid nature of the animal itself constitutes a permanent blemish. It is still a *bechor*, it still has *kedushat bechor*, but its abnormal appearance is a *mum* — and therefore the *kohen* who receives it may slaughter and eat it without waiting for another blemish to develop.

### Abnormality Definition

The Gemara asks: is the novelty here really significant? Is it not already obvious from elsewhere that abnormality constitutes a *mum*? A *mishnah* already teaches that an animal whose mouth resembles that of a pig has a *mum*. Clearly something that looks like a different species is a blemish. So what did Rabbi Yochanan add?

The Gemara attempts a distinction. The case of the pig's mouth, one might argue, is understood as a blemish specifically because a pig is an animal that is *not* in the category of *bechorah* — it has a characteristic of a species entirely outside the *bechor* framework. But when a sheep has characteristics of a goat, and goats are also in the *bechorah* category, perhaps a mixed appearance between two *bechor*-eligible species is not considered a deformity at all. Rabbi Yochanan therefore comes to teach that even when the "foreign" characteristic belongs to a species also subject to *bechorah*, the abnormality relative to this animal's own species still constitutes a *mum*. This is the genuine *chiddush*.

### Animal vs Human Blemishes

A further difficulty arises from the parallel *mishnah* teaching about eye blemishes, which states that *eino achas gedolah ve'achas ketanah* — one eye significantly larger than the other — constitutes a *mum*. The Gemara analyzes what "significantly large or small" means: an eye as large as that of a calf, or as small as that of a goose. The case of the goose is understandable: a goose is not subject to *bechorah*, so an eye resembling a goose's eye represents a characteristic of a non-*bechor* species. But the case of the calf is more challenging: a calf *is* subject to *bechorah*. And yet, having one eye the size of a calf's eye is still classified as a *mum*. This confirms that even a characteristic drawn from a *bechor*-eligible species can constitute a blemish, vindicating Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

But this seems to eliminate the need for Rabbi Yochanan altogether — the calf-eye case already established the principle. The Gemara therefore refines: perhaps the different-sized-eye case is not an instance of a general principle about "abnormality," but rather a specific, named *mum* known as *sarua* — disproportionate limbs. The Torah, in listing the blemishes that disqualify a *kohen* from serving in the *Beis HaMikdash*, mentions *sarua*, which is understood to refer to limbs of unequal size or proportion. Perhaps the only reason different-sized eyes constitute a *mum* in animals is that *sarua* is a named blemish — not because of any general principle that abnormality equals *mum*.

### Abnormality Principle

The Gemara finds support for this interpretation in a crucial distinction between the blemish rules for animals and those for *kohanim*. For *kohanim*, the *mishnah* adds a category beyond what applies to animals: *shtaim gedolot shtaim ketanot* — both eyes abnormally large or both eyes abnormally small. For human *kohanim*, this disqualifies; for animals, it does not. Now: if the operative principle were simply "abnormality," then both-eyes-big and both-eyes-small would also be abnormal for an animal, and should similarly constitute a *mum*. The fact that they do not suggests that the principle is not general abnormality, but the specific *mum* of *sarua* — unequal, mismatched limbs. Two eyes both too big or both too small are not mismatched; *sarua* requires *disparity*.

For *kohanim*, the verse *ish ish mizerah Aharon* — any man from the seed of Aaron — is interpreted to require that the *kohen* be *shaveh* in his characteristics to other members of Aaron's line; even symmetric abnormality therefore disqualifies him. For animals, absent that verse and absent the specific *mum* of *sarua*, two symmetrically abnormal eyes do not constitute a *mum*.

The Gemara resolves the tension by maintaining that abnormality *is* in principle a category of *mum*, but with an important qualification. When both eyes are excessively large, one might attribute this to unusual good health: *im machmat bri'uta yitarta, travaihu ba'u lemevei* — if the animal were exceptionally healthy, both eyes would naturally be large. When both are too small: *im machmat kachishuta yitarta, travaihu ba'u lemichshei* — if the animal were malnourished or weak, both eyes would naturally be small. In either case, the symmetry allows one to say that this is still within the natural variation of the species. Only when one eye is large and the other small can one no longer attribute the disproportion to any natural cause affecting the entire animal; only then is it unambiguously characteristic of a different species, and therefore a genuine *mum*. This is what Rabbi Yochanan's ruling establishes as a principle, and it is a real *chiddush*: having characteristics that are genuinely abnormal for one's species — and that cannot be explained by within-species natural variation — constitutes a *mum* even when those characteristics are drawn from another species that also falls within the *bechorah* category.

---

## Rav Mari Case

### Mari's Strategy

The Gemara now introduces the case of Rav Mari bar Rachel. He owned animals and employed the following strategy: *hava maknei le'udnaihu le'oved kochavim* — he sold the ear of each animal to a non-Jew. Yet notwithstanding this sale, *ve'asar lehu begiza va'avoda* — he treated the firstborn offspring as if they were *bechoros*, forbidding their shearing and use for labor, *veyahiv lehu lekhahanei* — and giving them to *kohanim*. In the end, *vechalya chayuta deRav Mari bar Rachel* — all of Rav Mari bar Rachel's animals died. He was punished.

### Protective Motive

The Gemara asks the obvious question: if he was prepared to treat the animals as *bechoros*, forbid shearing, and give them to *kohanim*, why did he bother selling the ear to the non-Jew at all? His answer, as the Gemara explains, was *dilma ati lidei takala* — he feared that the *kohanim* might not be careful. He was willing to honor the *kedushah* of the *bechor*, but he worried that once the animal was in a *kohen*'s hands, the *kohen* might use it improperly — shearing it, working it, or slaughtering it before a proper *mum* had appeared. By selling the ear to the non-Jew, Rav Mari ensured that if a *kohen* were to misuse the animal, the *kohen* would technically not be transgressing, since the animal was not fully a *bechor*. His intent was protective — a safeguard against inadvertent transgression by others.

### Divine Punishment

Why, then, was he punished? The Gemara explains: *mishum demapkei lehu mikedushatayhu* — because he was removing these animals from their *kedushah* entirely. The act of selling the ear to a non-Jew, even with protective intent, stripped the animals of their status as *bechoros* in a way that denied them the *kedushah* they were entitled to bear.

### Blemish vs Kedushah

But this raises a challenge. Rabbi Yehuda rules that a person may insert his hand into the womb of a pregnant cow before birth and create a blemish in the *bechor* while it is still in utero — before *kedushah* attaches — so that it will emerge as a *ba'al mum*, exempt from the altar. If that is permitted, how is Rav Mari's strategy any different? He too acted before the *bechor* was born, preventing the full *kedushah* from attaching. The Gemara answers with a crucial distinction: *hatam mikedushat mizbe'ach kamapkei lei, mikedushat kohen lo mapkei lei* — when one creates a *mum* in utero, one exempts the animal only from the *kedushah* of the altar; the animal is still a *bechor* with the sanctity appropriate to a *kohen*'s property. It still may not be shorn or worked; it is still given to the *kohen* and still carries the full status of a *bechor* in every sense except sacrificial eligibility. In Rav Mari's case, however, *afilu mikedushat kohen kamafkei lei* — the sale of the ear excluded the animal entirely, removing it from all dimensions of *bechorah*, including its status as the *kohen*'s sanctified property.

### Misinterpretation Effect

A second explanation for the punishment is offered: Rav Mari bar Rachel *yadav laknuyei kinyan gamur* — he knew how to execute a transaction that would be fully and legally binding. His sale of the ear to the non-Jew was technically valid. But *vechazu lei inshei achrinei ve'azlu ve'avdu* — others observed what he was doing and imitated him, without knowing how to perform the transaction properly. They did it as a verbal transfer or in some other legally insufficient manner, meaning they had not genuinely transferred ownership to the non-Jew, yet they proceeded to treat the *bechor* as exempt. Rav Mari saw that people were executing these transactions sloppily, *ve'asi bohu lidei takala* — and this was leading them to transgression: they thought they had avoided *bechorah* when they had not. Because his practice was the catalyst for widespread error, Rav Mari was held responsible.

---

## Modern Exemption

### Shulchan Aruch Rule

The story of Rav Mari bar Rachel and his punishment might seem to foreclose the strategy of selling a portion of the animal to a non-Jew as a means of avoiding *bechorah*. In striking contrast, the *Shulchan Aruch* rules precisely the opposite: *bazman hazeh mitzvah leshatef im akum kodem sheyeitzei la'avir ha'olam* — in our time it is a *mitzvah* to make a non-Jew a co-owner in the mother before the firstborn emerges into the world, *kedei lifto'o min habechorah* — in order to exempt it from *bechorah*. And this remains true, the *Shulchan Aruch* continues, *af al pi shemafki'a kedushato* — even though doing so prevents the animal from ever attaining *kedushat bechor*.

### Modern Rationale

The reasoning represents a deliberate inversion of what might otherwise be expected. Rav Mari was punished in a context where the preferred religious path was to allow the *bechor* to attain its *kedushah*, wait for a *mum* to develop, and then give it to a *kohen* who would slaughter and eat it with appropriate care. In that world, one had the halakhic knowledge to assess blemishes properly, and the religious framework was intact enough to handle the obligations correctly. Today, the risks run in the opposite direction: lack of expertise in evaluating *mumim*, unfamiliarity with the detailed laws of *bechor*, and the likelihood that animals will be used improperly all combine to make the *kedushah* a source of transgression rather than sanctity. Under these circumstances, preventing the *kedushah* from taking effect is not a circumvention of the *mitzvah* — it *is* the *mitzvah*. It is better, the *Shulchan Aruch* rules, to remove the animal from *bechorah* entirely than to risk widespread violations of its laws.

### Transaction Mechanics

Nonetheless, the story of Rav Mari bar Rachel leaves a critical lesson intact: the transaction must be done properly. Those who copied Rav Mari incorrectly without executing a legally binding sale were led into transgression precisely because they assumed their informal or defective transactions had achieved the desired legal result. This concern is directly parallel to the laws of selling *chametz* before Pesach: in both cases the question of what form of transaction constitutes a legally binding *kinyan* between a Jew and a non-Jew — sufficient to transfer actual ownership in a *halachically* effective manner — is a matter of considerable complexity. The responsa literature on both topics is extensive, and the pages of the *Shulchan Aruch* in this area are surrounded by commentary running to dense columns of small print, all devoted to working through the conditions under which such a sale achieves genuine and binding effect. It is through this mechanism — a properly executed sale of co-ownership to a non-Jew before the *bechor* is born — that the obligation of *bechor* is avoided in practice today.

---

---

# Bekhorot 4

## Abaye: Animal Model

### Mishna Setup

The new *mishna* that opens our daf picks up immediately after the discussion of partnership with a non-Jew, whose important practical conclusion was that since even partial ownership of an ear exempts an animal from *bechor* status, it has become a *mitzvah* to sell the ear of the mother animal to a non-Jew—thereby avoiding all the complications of *kedushah* and *bechor*—and this is indeed the common practice today. The new *mishna* now turns to a different exemption: *kohanim u'levi'im peturin mi'kal vachomer*—Kohanim and Levi'im are exempt from redeeming the firstborn donkey, by means of a *kal vachomer*. The *mishna* states: *im piteru et shel Yisrael ba'midbar, din hu she'yifteru et shel atzman*—if they exempted those of the Israelites in the wilderness, it certainly follows that they should exempt their own.

### Kal Vachomer

Before we can accept this reasoning, however, a fundamental question must be confronted. The Torah states *behemot ha'Levi'im tachat behemotam*—the animals of the Levi'im in exchange for their animals. What exactly was the mechanism of exemption? Perhaps a Levi who happened to possess a sheep would thereby be exempt from the *peter chamor* obligation, since the sheep would stand in place of the firstborn donkey. But that is a very different claim from saying that by virtue of being a *kohen* or a *levi*, one's firstborn donkey is categorically exempt. The *gemara* therefore presses the point: is the exemption a function of personal status, or does it require the presence of a substitute animal?

### Abaye's Reading

The *gemara* opens with a sharp observation: *inu patrei*—did the Kohanim and Levi'im actually exempt the animals of the Israelites? No. *Adam, adam patar*—it was person opposite person. The *levi* as a person stood opposite the *bechor* of the Israelite. *Behemah, behemah patrah*—and the animals of the Levi'im stood opposite the firstborn animals of the Israelites. The verse makes this explicit: *kach et ha'Levi'im tachat bechor bi'vnei Yisrael ve'et behemot ha'Levi'im tachat behemotam*—take the Levi'im in place of the firstborn of the Israelites, and the animals of the Levi'im in place of their animals. If so, what entitles us to exempt the *levi*'s own *peter chamor* simply by virtue of his being a *levi*?

*Amar Abaye*—Abaye proposes a reading of the *mishna* that addresses this challenge directly. The *mishna*, he says, must be understood as: *kohanim u'levi'im peturin behemotam mi'kal vachomer*—it is their animals that are exempt, by means of a *kal vachomer*. The *kal vachomer* is: if in the wilderness the animals of the Levi'im exempted the firstborn animals of the Israelites, certainly they should exempt their own firstborn donkeys. In other words, Abaye insists that the exemption is mediated through an animal substitute. The Levi who possesses a sheep thereby exempts his *peter chamor*, on the model of what occurred in the *midbar*. The personal status of the *levi* does not, by itself, discharge the obligation.

### Raba Objects

Raba responds to Abaye with two objections. The first is textual: *ve'ha piteru inu katani*—the *mishna* uses the language "they exempt," referring to the *kohanim* and *levi'im* themselves, not to their animals. Abaye's reading requires inserting "their animals" into a text that does not say it. More importantly, there is an immediate practical difference: if the *kohen* has no animal other than the firstborn donkey itself, is he obligated or not? Abaye's model requires a substitute animal; Raba maintains the exemption is personal.

### Raba's Kosher Animal Que…

Raba's second objection cuts deeper. *Ve'od, im itta*—if it is truly the case that we derive the exemption of donkeys directly from the narrative model of the *midbar*, where animals of the Levi'im stood in place of animals of the Israelites, then why are Kohanim and Levi'im not also exempt from *bechor behemah tehorah*—the firstborn of kosher animals? This requires brief context: every listener knows that a *kohen* or *levi* is exempt from *pidyon haben*, but fewer may have paused to ask whether they are obligated in *peter chamor* or *bechor behemah*. Our *mishna* teaches they are exempt from *peter chamor*—but they are in fact obligated in *bechor behemah tehorah*. If a Kohen's sheep gives birth to a firstborn, he must still bring it as a *korban*; the exemption does not extend there. Yet Abaye's model, which reads the *midbar* exchange directly as a template for all animal firstborns, should logically extend the exemption to sheep and goats as well—since in the wilderness, the animals of the Levi'im stood opposite the firstborn animals of the Israelites, which certainly included kosher animals. The *mishna* itself, Raba notes, is explicit: *lo niftaru mi'bechor behemah tehorah ella mi'pidyon haben u'peter chamor*—they are only exempt from *pidyon haben* and *peter chamor*, not from the firstborn of a kosher animal. How does Abaye account for this?

---

## Raba: Status Model

### Raba's Reading

*Ella amar Rava*—rather, Raba proposes an entirely different reading of the *mishna*. The correct interpretation is: *kohanim u'levi'im pataru et shelahem atzmam mi'kal vachomer*—the Kohanim and Levi'im exempt *themselves*—that is, their firstborn donkeys are exempt by virtue of their own personal status—and the *kal vachomer* is built on a different foundation entirely.

### Levi Status & Substituti…

Raba's *kal vachomer* proceeds as follows: *im hifkia kedushatan shel Levi'im kedushat Yisrael ba'midbar*—if the sanctity of the Levi'im was able to substitute for the sanctity of the firstborn Israelites in the wilderness, then certainly it should uproot and replace their own *bechor* status. The model is now the person, not the animal. In the wilderness, the *levi* as a person, with his *kedushat Levi*, stood opposite and replaced the *kedushat ha'bechor* of the Israelite firstborn. We are not learning from what the animals did; we are learning from what the people did.

### Firstborn Levi'im

This leads to an important observation, implicit in the *gemara* but made explicit by Rashi in his commentary on the Torah. The Torah records that there were approximately 22,000 Levi'im counted against 22,273 firstborn Israelites, leaving 273 unredeemed who required five *sela'im* each. But when one adds up the Levi'im more carefully, the number exceeds 22,000—it comes to something like 22,300, meaning there were enough Levi'im that a genuine one-to-one substitution would have left no remainder at all. Rashi explains that those Levi'im who were themselves firstborns could not substitute for the firstborn of Israel, because their *kedushat Levi* was already serving as a substitute for their own *kedushat ha'bechor*. One *levi* who is himself a *bechor* cannot redeem another's *bechor*; his personal substitution is already "used" on himself.

This is precisely the conceptual engine behind why a *levi* does not require *pidyon ha'bechor* today. It is not merely a historical dispensation but a continuing structural reality: the *levi*'s very status as a *levi* substitutes for and replaces his status as a *bechor*. The *avodah* that was once carried out by the *bechorim* has been transferred to the *levi'im*, and so the *levi* who is a firstborn is, as it were, in a state of self-substitution.

### Gezerah Shavah

Having established that the personal status of the *levi* exempts him from *pidyon bechor* of humans, Raba then asks: *behemah teme'ah minalan*—how do we know the exemption extends to firstborn donkeys? The *gemara* answers by invoking a verse: *ach padoh tifdeh et bechor ha'adam ve'et bechor ha'behemah ha'teme'ah tifdeh*—you shall surely redeem the firstborn human and the firstborn of the non-kosher animal. The Torah places both in a single verse, linking the *mitzvah* of redeeming firstborn humans to the *mitzvah* of redeeming firstborn donkeys. This constitutes a *gezerah shavah*—a verbal-structural analogy—connecting the two obligations. Since the *levi* is exempt from the former, he is equally exempt from the latter.

### Kosher Animals Obligatory

This same reasoning explains why the exemption does not extend to *bechor behemah tehorah*. The *mitzvah* of *bechor behemah tehorah* is categorically different: it is not about redemption at all. When a kosher animal gives birth to a firstborn, the obligation is to retain its *kedushah* and bring it as a *korban* in the *Beit HaMikdash*. There is no payment, no exchange, no redemption in the ordinary sense. By contrast, both *pidyon ha'bechor* of a human and *peter chamor* of a donkey share the structure of redemption—*pidyon*, an act of paying to release a sanctified object from its obligatory status. The verse *padoh tifdeh* connects precisely these two, and it is within this shared category of redemption that the Levi's status creates an exemption.

### Final Raba Framework

The full framework that emerges from Raba is therefore: Levi'im—and Kohanim, who are counted among the Levi'im—are exempt from *pidyon bechor* of humans because their *kedushat Levi* structurally substitutes for *kedushat ha'bechor*. They are exempt from *peter chamor* by extension, because the Torah links the redemption of firstborn humans and firstborn donkeys in a single verse. They remain fully obligated in *bechor behemah tehorah*, because that *mitzvah* is not about redemption but about *korban*, and the structural logic of substitution does not reach there.

Tosafot adds an important clarification of why Abaye's model also does not extend to *bechor behemah tehorah*, even though he is learning from the animal substitution in the *midbar*.
