He explains that he counts it separately because the *mishna* explicitly refers to it as *mitzvas arifah* — the *mitzvah* of breaking the neck — suggesting it has independent standing. The *Ra'avad* objects forcefully: how can one call this a *mitzvah*? It is a consequence of failing to do what one should have done; it is the mechanism for dealing with a forbidden animal when the owner has neglected the proper *mitzvah*. Some *meforshim* respond that calling something a *mitzvah* does not necessarily mean it represents a positive or desirable act. There is, for example, a *mitzvah* governing how a man divorces his wife, though divorce itself may not be the ideal choice — the *mitzvah* prescribes the proper procedure for an act one has chosen to perform. *Arifah* functions similarly: given that redemption was not performed, here is the required procedure. Yet the *Ra'avad*'s discomfort with calling it a *mitzvah* even given this context remains striking, especially since the *mishna* itself uses that term.

### Mitzvot Priorities

The *mishna* continues with a series of analogous priority statements. *Mitzvas yi'ud kodemet lemitzvas pidyah* — the *mitzvah* of *yi'ud* takes precedence over the *mitzvah* of redemption. The context is a young Jewish girl sold by her father as a slave: the master may either designate her as a wife (*yi'ud*) or release her. The *mishna* states that *yi'ud* should come first. The underlying logic reflects the social and economic realities within which this institution was embedded: the goal of her sale was to ensure her protection and welfare, and marriage was the mechanism intended to achieve that. Redemption and release are appropriate only if the path to *yi'ud* is not taken. The verse corroborates: *asher lo ye'adah, vehefdah* — if he does not designate her as a wife, she shall be redeemed.

*Mitzvas yibum kodemet lemitzvas chalitzah* — *yibum* (levirate marriage) takes precedence over *chalitzah*. The *chalitzah* ceremony, in which the widow removes the shoe from her deceased husband's brother and spits before him, is described by the Torah as a mark of disgrace upon one who refuses to perpetuate his brother's name. This framing itself demonstrates that *yibum* is the preferred path. The *mishna* acknowledges, however, that this was true *barishonah* — in earlier times, when men performed *yibum* for the sake of the *mitzvah*. Now that *yibum* is often motivated by attraction to the widow's appearance or property rather than by *lishmah* intent, the ruling changed: *amru mitzvas chalitzah kodemet* — *chalitzah* now takes precedence. The *Gemara* in Yevamot goes as far as to suggest that *yibum* performed for improper motives borders on transgression, since the *mitzvah* of *yibum* redefines what would otherwise be a forbidden relationship — and if the defining intent is absent, the act falls closer to the category of *arayot* it was meant to transcend. It should be noted that *Sefardim* rule *mitzvas yibum kodemet* and practice *yibum* to this day, making this a live *machlokes* in practical *halakha*, to be discussed fully when we reach Yevamot.

*Mitzvas hage'ulah b'adon hu kodem l'chol adam* — one who consecrated property to the *Beis HaMikdash* has the first right to redeem it before others may do so, as the verse states *v'im lo yiga'el v'nimkar b'erkecha* — if he does not redeem it, the Temple treasury will sell it. The Temple is better served financially when the original owner redeems, because the owner must add one fifth to the redemption price; the owner also retains a prior right to reclaim what was his.

With these rulings the entire discussion of *peter chamor* concludes. As noted, virtually everything the *Gemara* has to say about *peter chamor* has been gathered within this *perek*.

---

## Bechora Tehora

### Non-Jew Ownership

The *Gemara* now transitions to the laws of *bechora tehora* — the firstborn of kosher animals. The new *mishna* closely parallels the opening *mishna* of the discussion of *peter chamor*. The governing principle is that non-Jewish ownership of either the mother or the offspring at any stage exempts the animal from the *bechora* obligation. The *mishna* lists the relevant cases: buying the fetus of a non-Jew's cow (where the non-Jew retains ownership of the cow itself); selling a fetus to a non-Jew (so that he is part owner of the firstborn); entering a partnership with a non-Jew; taking an animal from a non-Jew in *kabalut* (whereby one raises the animal and acquires a share of the offspring); or transferring an animal to a non-Jew in *kabalut*. In all these configurations, the non-Jew holds at least a partial ownership in either the mother or the firstborn, and that suffices for exemption. The verse provides the basis: *b'Yisrael* — the Torah sanctified firstborn animals specifically among Israel, *aval lo ba'acherim* — not among non-Jews.

---

## Bechora Tehora (II)

### Kohanim Status

The *mishna* continues: *Kohanim u'Leviyim chayavim* — *Kohanim* and *Leviyim* are obligated in the *bechora* of kosher animals, even though they are exempt from *pidyon ha'ben* and from *peter chamor*. The exemption of *Kohanim* and *Leviyim* from the redemption obligations derives from the swap in the desert, whereby the *Leviyim* were substituted for the firstborn Israelites, and the animals belonging to *Leviyim* were similarly substituted for the firstborn animals of Israel. That swap exempts them from the redemption-based *mitzvot*. However, it does not exempt them from the obligation regarding firstborn kosher animals, which are brought as *korbanos* — an independent and intrinsic sanctity (*kedushat haguf*) rather than a redemption-based one.

---

## Kinyan Methods

### Money vs. Meshicha

The *Gemara* now enters a discussion that, while framed as arising from the *mishna* about non-Jewish ownership, is one of the most practically consequential topics in the entire *perek*. At stake is the precise mechanism of acquisition when transacting with a non-Jew — a question central to the contemporary practices of selling the ear of a firstborn animal, selling *chametz*, and *heter mechira*. The discussion opens with a *baraita* cited by *Rav Gidel* in the name of *Rav* (also attributed to *Resh Lakish* in the name of *bar Kappara*): *Yisrael shenatan ma'ot la'akum b'behemtam b'dineihem* — if a Jew gives money to a non-Jew to purchase his flock in accordance with their laws, *af al pi shelo mashach kanah* — even though the Jew has not yet drawn the flock to him (i.e., taken physical possession), he acquires it through the giving of money, and the animal is obligated in *bechora* from that moment. Conversely, if a non-Jew gives money to a Jew for his flock, even without *meshicha*, the non-Jew acquires from the moment the money is given, and the animal is exempt from *bechora* thereafter.

### Peshat in Verse

The *Gemara* inquires into the meaning of *b'dineihem* — "in their laws." One possibility is that this phrase alludes to the law governing the acquisition of non-Jewish slaves, and that a *kal vachomer* can be constructed: if a Jew acquires a non-Jewish person through money (based on the verse *le'reshet achuza*, comparing a slave to a plot of land, and we know land is acquired through *kesef*, *shtar*, or *chazaka* — therefore *af eved kena'ani nikna b'kesef* — a non-Jewish slave is acquired through money), then certainly one may acquire their chattel through money. The *Gemara* rejects this: one cannot construct such a *kal vachomer*, as different types of property are acquired through different acts and those distinctions are not transferable by inference. Moreover, the comparison is disproven by the case of a Jew acquiring a fellow Jew as a slave — which is also done through money — whereas Jewish-owned chattel is acquired through *meshicha*, not money. If the *kal vachomer* were valid, Jewish chattel should also be acquirable through money. *Abaye* therefore provides the correct interpretation: *b'dineihem shepasak lahem Torah* — this is simply the law the Torah assigned for transactions involving non-Jews, as derived from the verse.

The verse states: *o kanei miyad amitecha* — "or if you purchase from the hand of your fellow." *Miyad amitecha* — from your fellow Jew — the emphasis on the hand implies physical transfer, i.e., *meshicha*, as the mode of acquisition. Therefore: *hu d'meshicha, ha miyad oved kochavim, b'kesef* — with a Jew, acquisition is through *meshicha*; with a non-Jew, the opposite applies, and acquisition is through *kesef*. *Tosafot* explains why only these two are in play: when transacting in cattle, there are two fundamental acts — one party gives money and the other takes possession of the object. These are the primary two modes, *kesef* and *meshicha*, and the verse addresses them specifically. When the Torah emphasizes that acquisition from a fellow Jew proceeds through *meshicha*, it necessarily implies that acquisition from a non-Jew proceeds through the other primary act: *kesef*.

### Kal VaChomer

The *Gemara* then addresses several alternative readings of the verse. Could one argue that nothing at all may be transacted with a non-Jew? A *kal vachomer* forecloses this: since one may acquire a non-Jew's person, *a fortiori* one may acquire his property. Could one argue that with a non-Jew, both *kesef* and *meshicha* must be performed? The *kal vachomer* again forecloses it: since acquiring a non-Jewish person requires only one act (*kesef*), it makes no sense that acquiring mere property should require two acts. Could one argue that with a non-Jew, either *kesef* or *meshicha* suffices? The *Gemara* says no — *dumya d'amitecha*: just as with a fellow Jew there is one exclusive mode of acquisition, so too with a non-Jew there is one exclusive mode. With a Jew it is *meshicha*; with a non-Jew it is *kesef*. The same sequence of arguments applies symmetrically to the reverse case — the non-Jew purchasing from a Jew — and the *Gemara* works through each step in identical fashion, concluding that money alone effects the non-Jew's acquisition.

### Non-Jew Buys

The *Gemara* examines the second half of the *baraita*: when a non-Jew purchases from a Jew, acquisition is likewise effected by the giving of money. The same derivation from *o kanei miyad amitecha* applies in this direction: when a Jew sells to a fellow Jew, the transaction is effected through transfer of possession (*meshicha*). When a Jew sells to a non-Jew, the transaction is effected through money. The same *kal vachomer* arguments are worked through: one cannot say no transaction with a non-Jew is possible, since a non-Jew can acquire a Jew as a slave (*mikessef miknato* — from the money of the purchase); one cannot require two acts for the non-Jew to acquire, since acquiring a person requires only one; and one cannot permit either act, since the parallel to the Jewish case demands exactly one exclusive mode.

### Ameimar Dispute

*Ameimar* dissents from the *baraita*'s conclusion: *meshicha b'oved kochavim konei* — it is *meshicha*, not *kesef*, that effects acquisition from a non-Jew. This dissent is not problematic in principle because, as the *Gemara* notes, there is an underlying unresolved debate about which mode of acquisition governs Jewish transactions at the biblical level. *Ameimar*'s position becomes coherent depending on which side of that debate one adopts.

If one holds like *Rabbi Yochanan* — *devar Torah ma'ot konot* — that biblically, for Jews, acquisition is through *kesef*, then *meshicha* is only a rabbinic innovation. The verse *miyad amitecha* therefore addresses a Jew and says acquisition proceeds through *kesef*; it implies that with a non-Jew acquisition proceeds through *meshicha* — and this is what *Ameimar* holds. The rabbis then reversed the Jewish rule from *kesef* to *meshicha* (to prevent the situation where purchased goods are lost before the buyer takes possession), so that in practice both Jews and non-Jews now operate through *meshicha* — one by rabbinic enactment, the other by biblical mandate.

If, however, one holds like *Resh Lakish* — *meshicha meforeshet min haTorah* — that *meshicha* is the biblical mode for Jews, then the verse implies the opposite for non-Jews, namely *kesef*. For *Ameimar* to say *meshicha* works for a non-Jew while holding like *Resh Lakish* would mean both Jews and non-Jews operate through *meshicha* — and *lama li le'amitecha*? What then does the verse's emphasis on *amitecha* accomplish? The *Gemara* resolves: *le'amitecha ata machzir ona ve'i ata machzir ona li'chnani* — the word *amitecha* is not addressing the mode of acquisition at all. Rather, it is the basis for the rule that the prohibition of *ona'ah* (overcharging) and the obligation to return excess payment applies to transactions with a fellow Jew but not to transactions involving a *kena'ani* (substituted in our printed text for the original *goy*). On this reading, *Ameimar* holds that acquisition from a non-Jew is through *meshicha*, in accord with *Rabbi Yochanan* that biblical Jewish acquisition is through *kesef*.

### Ona'at Akum

The *Gemara*'s discussion of *ona'ah* vis-à-vis non-Jews raises profound questions — moral, ethical, and historical — that cannot be fully addressed here. What should be noted is that already among the *Rishonim*, and continuing throughout the *kitvei Acharonim*, the apparent civil disparity between Jews and non-Jews with respect to *ona'ah*, *gezel*, and similar laws was subjected to significant qualification. Multiple *Rishonim* — not only the *Meiri* — held that these rules do not apply to contemporary law-abiding non-Jews. The *maskana* in Bava Kamma is that stealing from a non-Jew is forbidden. These modifications appear to reflect sincere legal and moral reasoning rather than mere concession to external pressure.

As for the formal *Gemara* text: the *Gemara* asks whether the verse's mention of *amitecha* is even necessary to exclude *ona'ah* with a non-Jew, given that the verse elsewhere says *al tonu ish et achiv* — do not overcharge a man his brother — which already implies that the prohibition is limited to a Jew. The answer is: *chad li'chnani v'chad le'hekdesh* — one exclusion addresses a non-Jew and the other addresses *hekdesh* (consecrated property), for which the prohibition of *ona'ah* likewise does not apply. *De'tzricha* — both are needed: without the second verse, one might have assumed that while overcharging a non-Jew is permitted, overcharging *hekdesh* is surely forbidden given the gravity of that relationship. The two verses work together to establish both exclusions.

The *Gemara* then notes: *hani'cha le'man de'amar gezelo assur* — this analysis works if one holds that stealing from a non-Jew is forbidden, because it then makes sense that a separate verse is needed to permit the lesser offense of overcharging. *Ela i savrat le'man de'amar gezelo mutar* — but if one holds that stealing from a non-Jew is actually permitted, no verse is needed to permit overcharging, since the lesser includes the greater. The conclusion follows: *al korchacha ke'Rabbi Yochanan sevira lei* — if *Ameimar* holds that stealing is forbidden, and therefore needs a verse to permit overcharging, and he also holds that *meshicha* governs acquisition from a non-Jew, then he must hold like *Rabbi Yochanan* that biblical Jewish acquisition is through *kesef* — since that is the only way the verse's *amitecha* is left free to address *ona'ah* rather than the mode of acquisition.

This debate — whether acquisition from a non-Jew is through *kesef* (per the *baraita* and *Rashi*) or through *meshicha* (per *Ameimar* and the overwhelming majority of *Rishonim*) — is of direct practical consequence for the *halakha* of *bechora*, *heter mechira*, and the sale of *chametz*. The accepted practice is to follow *Ameimar*: acquisition from a non-Jew proceeds through *meshicha*, and therefore when selling an animal's ear to exempt from *bechora*, the transaction must be effected through an act of *meshicha*. In practice many *poskim* recommend performing both *kesef* and *meshicha* to cover all positions. This question will continue to be explored in the *shiurim* that follow.

---

---

# Bekhorot 14

## Money vs. Meshicha

### Non-Jew Ownership

The daf opens in the middle of a discussion that began on 13b. The topic is the power of non-Jewish ownership to exempt an animal from the obligation of *bechor*. Having established this principle in the first *perek* with respect to donkeys, the Gemara now applies it to *bechor* of sheep, goats, and cattle. The prior discussion had established that a non-Jew acquires from a Jew through *kesef* — the exchange of money — though the opinion of Amemar had introduced the competing view that acquisition is effected through *meshicha*, the physical taking of possession. The practical consequences of this dispute are significant, and the Gemara now brings a challenge to resolve the question.

### Scrap Metal Case

The Gemara raises an objection (*meitivei*) from a *mishna* in Avodah Zarah — a text the same audience will have encountered when studying that tractate. The case involves someone who purchases scrap metal from a non-Jew and discovers an idol among the refuse. The *mishna* presents two scenarios: if the buyer performed *meshicha* — drew the metal toward himself — before paying, he may return the merchandise, presumably because the transaction had not yet taken effect. If, however, he performed *meshicha* after having paid the money, he may no longer reverse the sale; since he already owns the idol and may not benefit from it, he must take its monetary value and cast it into the Dead Sea. The structural logic of the *mishna* appears to require *both* payment and *meshicha* for the transaction to take effect — a position that fits neither the "money alone" view nor the "*meshicha* alone" view the Gemara had been developing.

### Meshicha Puzzle

The Gemara presses the difficulty directly. If one says that money (*maos*) effects the transaction, why does *meshicha* matter at all? The Gemara responds: the *braita* is discussing a case where the parties stipulated (*kibel alav l'dun dinei Yisrael*) that the transaction would follow Jewish law — that is, would be governed by *meshicha*. Hence the end of the *mishna* specifies that *meshicha* was performed. But then the beginning is troublesome: if *meshicha* works, why could the buyer back out when he had already performed *meshicha* without paying? The Gemara reformulates: even the beginning involves *meshicha*, and the *mishna* is saying that even where *meshicha* was performed, if money had not yet been paid, the transaction takes effect — but the buyer may still withdraw because the entire *mishna* is structured around *meshicha* as the operative act. Yet this reading immediately raises the inverse problem: *eima hachi kashya reisha* — if *meshicha* alone is what matters in both clauses, why does the end of the *mishna* mention money at all?

### Abaye's View

Abaye resolves the contradiction as follows: in both the beginning and the end of the *mishna*, the buyer has performed *meshicha* and the transaction has taken effect. The reason the buyer in the *reisha* may nonetheless reverse the sale is that it is a case of *mekach taos* — a purchase made in error. He never anticipated finding an idol among the scrap metal, and therefore he may undo the transaction. The *seifa*, by contrast, where money has already been paid, does not allow reversal. Rava immediately challenges this: if there is a *mekach taos* in the *reisha*, surely there is an equally valid *mekach taos* in the *seifa* — in both cases the buyer was surprised by the presence of the idol. The error is identical.

### Rava's View

Rava therefore offers his own resolution. He accepts that both clauses involve *meshicha* as the act that effects the transaction, and he accepts that both clauses technically involve *mekach taos*. The sole operative difference between the *reisha* and the *seifa* is whether money was paid. But the reason this makes a difference is not that money effects the transaction — it does not — but rather that it creates an *appearance* problem. In the *reisha*, where the buyer has not yet paid, reversing the sale does not look suspicious: since no money changed hands, onlookers will understand that the buyer simply backed out before completing the deal, and returning the merchandise does not look like selling an idol for profit. In the *seifa*, however, where money has already been paid, the object appears to be firmly in the buyer's possession. When he returns the idol and receives his money back, it looks to observers as though he is selling the idol — which is prohibited. The critical point is that what *effects* the transaction in both clauses is *meshicha*; money serves only to determine whether returning the object creates the problematic appearance of trading in idols.

One might ask: even in the *reisha*, a bystander could observe the idol being handed back. Rava's underlying assumption is that if no payment was made, observers will understand from the context that the buyer never truly finalized the acquisition and simply withdrew upon discovering the idol. Once money has exchanged hands, however, the perception of full ownership is stronger, and any subsequent return looks like a deliberate sale. The Rabbis, as with any functioning legal system, establish general rules rather than requiring case-by-case justification from each individual. The rule is calibrated toward the scenario most likely to produce misinterpretation.

Abaye's own alternative explanation of the monetary difference is also recorded. In the *reisha*, Abaye says it is a genuine *mekach taos* because the buyer had not yet paid and therefore bore no special responsibility to investigate. In the *seifa*, it is not treated as *mekach taos* — not because the error did not occur, but because once payment has been made, before performing *meshicha* the buyer ought to have examined the goods (*ki kamashich ibaei lei leyunei v'hadar limshoch*). Having already laid out his money, a buyer has greater incentive and responsibility to inspect what he is about to take possession of. His failure to do so shifts the risk to him — the principle of *caveat emptor*.

### Tosafot & Caveat

Tosafot raises a qualification: in ordinary cases of *mekach taos*, we do not apply the rule that prior payment obligates pre-*meshicha* inspection. That is a departure from standard halacha. Tosafot explains that purchasing from a non-Jew is genuinely different here: *shani lokeach me-oved kochavim de-ibaei lei le-asukei daateh tefei shema yesh bo avodas kochavim* — when buying from a non-Jew, a buyer should have anticipated the elevated possibility that idol-related items might be present. The scenario is therefore already close to the threshold where the likelihood of encountering the problematic item would, on its own, preclude any claim of *mekach taos* altogether. The payment tips the scales: it raises the buyer's duty of care to the level where he can no longer plead ignorance. Tosafot is careful to note that this logic applies only where the frequency of the risk is already high enough to make the claim of surprise relatively weak; if the risk were routine and well-known, no *mekach taos* claim would be available regardless of payment.

### Rav Ashi View

Rav Ashi offers the simplest reading of the entire *braita*. He argues that *meshicha* is irrelevant throughout: *midi de-reisha meshicha eina kona seifa nami meshicha eina kona*. In both the *reisha* and the *seifa*, *meshicha* does not effect the transaction. The only operative factor is the giving of money. The *reisha* permits reversal precisely because no money was paid; the *seifa* forbids reversal because money was paid. Why, then, does the *mishna* mention *meshicha* at all in both clauses? Simply because the *mishna* began by discussing *meshicha* in the *reisha* and carried the language through to the *seifa* — *v'aidi de-tana reisha mashach, tana nami seifa mashach* — but *meshicha* is substantively irrelevant. This reading aligns directly with the dominant position argued throughout the preceding discussion: what effects a transaction between a Jew and a non-Jew is the giving of money.

### Ravina View

Ravina takes the opposite position. Since in the *seifa* the outcome turns on *meshicha* — the *mishna* says that after paying and drawing the object close the buyer cannot reverse the sale — the *reisha* must be read the same way: *mi-de-seifa meshicha kana, reisha nami meshicha kana*. Under this reading, the *reisha* must be reinterpreted: the phrase *yachzir* means that the buyer may withdraw from his oral *commitment*, not from a completed transaction, since neither *meshicha* nor money had yet occurred. This reading introduces the concept of *mechusrei amana*, discussed next.

### Jew-NonJew Trust

The concept of *mechusrei amana* — breach of faith — holds that even though an oral undertaking to buy or sell has no binding legal force, withdrawing from such a commitment is nonetheless considered a form of faithlessness. Words of commitment carry moral weight; reneging on them, even when legally permissible, is regarded as a failing. The Gemara adds a notable qualification: *v'hani milei Yisrael mi-Yisrael d'kaimi b'diburaihu* — this concern for keeping one's word applies between Jew and Jew, where both parties are understood to stand behind their verbal commitments. Between a Jew and a non-Jew, however, the Gemara expresses a different view: *aval Yisrael mi-akum d'inu lo kaimi b'diburaihu* — the perception, at least as articulated in this Talmudic context, is that the standard of mutual verbal reliability does not hold in the same way, and therefore one is not equally bound by an oral commitment in a Jew–non-Jew transaction. This statement reflects the historical circumstances of the rabbinic period and the fraught relationship between the Jewish community and the surrounding non-Jewish authorities during that era; it should not be read as a timeless normative claim about interpersonal ethics.

### Halachic Summary

The dominant thrust of the entire discussion is clear: what effects a transaction between a Jew and a non-Jew is the giving of *kesef*, money — not *meshicha*. The Amora who argued for *meshicha* represents a dissenting view, and even within the *braita* that mentioned both *meshicha* and money, the various *amoraim* who sought to uphold the *meshicha* position did so by positing a special stipulation (*kibel alav l'dun b'dinei Yisrael*), not as the default rule. Rashi rules in accordance with the dominant *sugya*: the transaction is effected by money. The majority of *Rishonim*, however, reason differently. Since the general rule for Jews is that *kesef* acquires only by Torah law, while the Rabbis substituted *meshicha* in its place, the reverse principle applies for non-Jews: what the Rabbis substituted for Jews (*meshicha*) does not apply, and therefore *kesef* — the Torah-level mode — functions. Tosafot and most *Rishonim* therefore rule that *meshicha* is what effects the transaction with a non-Jew, contrary to the apparently dominant position of our *sugya*.

The practical consequence is enormous. The *halacha* governing the sale of *chametz* before Pesach, the transfer of land in *Eretz Yisrael* for *Shmita* purposes, and the transfer of a *bechor* to a non-Jew to avoid the obligation — all depend on what mode of transaction is operative. Since the *Rishonim* could not reach full consensus, the accepted practice is to perform both: to have the non-Jew give money *and* take physical possession. An additional mechanism widely employed is the rental of the land or premises on which the *chametz* or animal stands. Since all authorities agree that a non-Jew can acquire real property through money, and since an object resting on one's land is considered to be in one's possession, the combination of a monetary land-rental with constructive possession through location satisfies all opinions. Whether *chalipin* — a symbolic barter transaction using a handkerchief — also works is a further question debated among the authorities. This entire literature flows directly from the unresolved tension in our *sugya*.

---

## Blemish Before Sanctity

### Mishna Overview

At the top of 14a, the Gemara opens a new *mishna* — one that appears in *Chullin* as well, though without full analysis there, and which will receive extended treatment in *Temurah*. The *mishna* presents two contrasting cases involving sanctified animals and the timing of their blemishes.

### Blemish First

The first case: *kol hakodashim shekadmu mum kavua l'hekdeshan* — any sanctified animal that had a permanent, non-transitory blemish before it was sanctified. Suppose one takes a sheep with a broken leg — a fixed blemish — and declares it an *olah*. Since the animal was blemished at the moment of sanctification, it was never capable of attaining the sanctity appropriate to the altar. The attempt to confer *kedushat mizbeach* — altar sanctity — therefore produced only *kedushat damim*, value sanctity: the animal must be sold and the proceeds used to purchase a *korban*. This is categorically different from full *kedushat korban*, and it is also distinct from simple *kedushat bedek habayit* — sanctity for the temple treasury — since even here the proceeds are directed toward the altar rather than mere maintenance.

### No Korban Status

Because the animal never attained genuine *kedushat korban*, the *mishna* rules that after it is redeemed, its offspring are subject to the obligation of *bechor*, and when it is slaughtered, one must give the *matanot* — *zero'a, lechayayim v'keiva* — to the *kohen*. These obligations are waived only when an animal carries residual *kedusha*; this animal, having never possessed *kedushat korban*, retains no such residual status once redeemed. Furthermore, slaughtering it outside the *Beit HaMikdash* does not incur liability for the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*, since that prohibition applies only to animals with genuine *kedushat korban*.

### Post-Redemption Use

Once redeemed, the animal exits fully to the status of *chullin*: it may be shorn and worked — *ligazez v'la'avod* — without restriction. This stands in deliberate contrast to an animal that was sanctified while unblemished and subsequently became blemished: such an animal, even after redemption, retains residual *kedusha* and cannot be shorn or put to work. Here, by contrast, the sanctity is wholly extinguished upon redemption. The offspring and milk are likewise permitted — *ladan v'chalavan mutar* — after redemption. If the animal dies before redemption, it may still be redeemed, since the two grounds that ordinarily bar redemption of a deceased *korban* — the requirement to stand the animal before the priest (*he'emid oso hakohen*), and the rule that one may not redeem *kodashim* merely to feed the dogs — do not apply to an animal that never had *kedushat korban*.

Additionally, attempting to perform *temurah* — transferring the *kedusha* to another animal — produces no effect, since *temurah* is operative only for genuine *korbanos*.

### Bechor/Maaser

The *mishna* notes two exceptions to this first case: *bechor* and *maaser behema*. For both of these, even if the blemish preceded the *kedusha*, the animal still acquires a sanctity equivalent to *kedushat korban*. The reason is that in both cases the *kedusha* arises not from a human declaration but from a physical reality — birth and counting, respectively. A firstborn animal acquires its sanctity by virtue of being born; the tenth animal counted in the annual tally acquires its sanctity by virtue of being the tenth. In neither case does the timing of the blemish relative to the moment of sanctification matter, because the sanctity is imposed automatically by the Torah regardless of condition. The Torah states explicitly that the tenth animal is holy whether it is good or bad — that is, whether or not it is blemished. Similarly, a blemished *bechor* is not redeemed in the normal way; rather, the *kohen* slaughters and eats it outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, and it retains a quasi-*korban* sanctity throughout.

### Sanctity First

The second case: *v'chol shekodam hekdeshan mumam* — animals that were sanctified before they acquired their permanent blemish. Even if the animal had a transitory blemish at the time of sanctification, that is irrelevant; what matters is that a permanent blemish arose only after it had already been sanctified in an unblemished state. In such a case, the original sanctity was full *kedushat korban*. That *kedusha* does not dissipate when the blemish appears; it persists, and even after the animal is redeemed, a residual sanctity remains.

### Residual Status

Because of this residual *kedusha*, the *mishna* rules that even after such an animal has been redeemed, its offspring are exempt from *bechor* and one need not give *matanot* to the *kohen* when it is slaughtered. The residual *kedusha* — though it no longer renders the animal fit for the altar — is sufficient to suspend these obligations.

### Post-Redemption Limits

The animal also cannot be shorn or put to work even after redemption. The Torah's phrase *tizbach v'lo giza, v'achalta v'lo avoda* — you may slaughter it but not shear it, eat from it but not work it — is understood by the Sages to apply to *psulei mukdashin*, animals once destined for the altar that were redeemed on account of a blemish. Since this animal started as a proper *korban*, these restrictions continue even after redemption. Similarly, the offspring and the milk of such an animal remain forbidden even after redemption.

### Shechita & Temurah

Because these animals retain *kedushat korban*, two further consequences follow. First, if such an animal is slaughtered outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, one is liable for the prohibition of *shechutei chutz* — but only in the qualified case where the blemish is subtle enough that had the animal been brought to the altar, it would have been permitted to remain there *bedi'eved*, such as a cataract. Second, *temurah* is operative: if one attempts to exchange such an animal with an unblemished one, both the original and the substitute acquire *kedusha*.

### Redemption Test

The Gemara opens its analysis with a straightforward observation from the language of the first case of the *mishna*.

---

## Damim Sanctity

### Sanctity Exempts

The Gemara notes that the *mishna* specifies: *ta'ima d'nifdu* — the reason the animal is obligated in *bechor* and *matanot* is that it has been redeemed. The implication is that had it not yet been redeemed, it would still be exempt from *bechor* even though its sanctity was never *kedushat korban*. From this the Gemara infers: *kasvar kedushas damim madcha min habechora u'min hamatanos* — even a mere sanctity of value (*kedushas damim*), not altar sanctity, is sufficient to exempt an animal from the obligation of *bechor* and from the obligation of priestly gifts, as long as that sanctity remains in place.

This is a significant and precise point. The exemption from *bechor* is not contingent on an animal having full *kedushat korban*; it flows from the presence of *any* form of *kedusha*. So long as the animal is *kadosh* — even if only with *kedushas damim* — it is exempt.

### Donkey Example

This principle is illustrated with a case of an animal that could never enter the *korban* world at all. If one sanctifies a donkey for the temple treasury — *hekdesh*, but purely as a monetary contribution, not as a *korban* — and that donkey subsequently gives birth, the newborn animal is exempt from the *mitzvah* of *peter chamor*. Although the donkey's sanctity is purely *kedushas bedek habayit* and has nothing to do with the altar, the mere presence of *kedusha* is sufficient to prevent the offspring from being subject to the obligation of *peter chamor*. This reinforces the broader principle: while the animal carries any form of *kedusha*, the exemption holds.

### Shearing Prohibited

The Gemara then turns to another implication of the *mishna*: *ha lo nifdu assur b'giza v'avoda* — before redemption, even this animal that started with a blemish and never possessed *kedushat korban* may not be shorn or worked. This is puzzling. The prohibition on shearing and working applies to *korbanos*; it is derived from the verse *tizbach v'lo giza, v'achalta v'lo avoda*. But this animal is not a *korban*. Even the temple treasury could theoretically shear it and sell the wool for profit — that would seem to be entirely within the spirit of the animal's consecration for monetary purposes. Why, then, is shearing forbidden?

The Gemara notes that this ruling supports the position of Rabbi Elazar, who holds that *kodshei bedek habayit assur b'giza v'avoda* — even animals sanctified purely for the treasury may not be shorn or worked. The reason would presumably be an appearance-based prohibition: it looks too similar to what one does with a genuine *korban*, and permitting it would create confusion.

### Two Sanctity Types

However, the Gemara qualifies this immediately: the case of our *mishna* does not constitute strong support for Rabbi Elazar's position. Our case is fundamentally different from a straightforward *bedek habayit* animal, because here the owner attempted to sanctify the animal *for the altar* — he tried to declare it an *olah* or some other *korban*. What he achieved was a *kedushas damim l'mizbeach* — a value-sanctity directed toward eventual procurement of a *korban* — rather than a simple treasury sanctity. This animal is therefore much more likely to be confused with an actual *korban*, and the rabbinic prohibition on shearing and working it before redemption is readily understandable even without Rabbi Elazar's broader principle. A straightforward *bedek habayit* dedication — where the owner's intention was always purely monetary — might not generate the same degree of confusion, and therefore may fall outside the prohibition. The *mishna* thus does not prove Rabbi Elazar's view with respect to *kodshei bedek habayit* proper.

---

## Offspring & Milk

### Simple Case

The *mishna* also states that after redemption the offspring and milk of the first case — the blemished animal that was sanctified — are permitted. Before redemption, they are part of the *hekdesh* estate, since offspring and milk of a consecrated animal take on that animal's sanctity and belong to the temple.

### Pregnancy Test

The Gemara asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If the animal became pregnant and gave birth *after* redemption, the permissibility of its offspring and milk is self-evident — the *mishna* has already said it becomes *chullin* entirely upon redemption. The Gemara therefore specifies that the *mishna* is discussing the case where the animal became pregnant *before* redemption and gave birth *after* redemption. That is the meaningful case: the fetus was gestating while the mother was still *kadosh*, and one might have thought the offspring retains some residual *kedusha*. The *mishna* teaches that once the mother is fully redeemed — her *kedusha* extinguished entirely — the offspring born thereafter is also fully *chullin*, because the act of redemption removed the *kedusha* from mother and fetus alike.

### Redeemable?

This raises a further question. Before redemption, the offspring of such an animal also carry a *kedusha* — but what kind, and under what rules? Since the mother's *kedusha* was never *kedushat korban* and could never have led to this animal standing on the altar, the offspring likewise cannot be brought as a *korban*. Can such offspring — which are themselves unblemished — be redeemed without requiring a blemish? Under ordinary rules, a *korban* cannot be redeemed unless it is blemished. But these offspring are in a peculiar intermediate position: they have *kedusha*, but it is a *kedusha* that was always disqualified from the altar. Is the requirement for a blemish before redemption applicable to them?

### Source Teaching

An explicit teaching resolves the question: *hamakdish ba'alei mumim kev'u'im legabei mizbe'ach v'yaldu — yimachru v'ein tzerichim mum* — one who sanctifies animals with permanent blemishes for the altar and they give birth, those offspring may be sold without requiring a blemish. *She'ein kedusha chalah aleihem* — the altar sanctity does not attach to the offspring, since it never attached to the mother.

### Tafel Chamur

The principle underlying this ruling is stated explicitly: *v'shelo yehei tafel chamur min ha'ikar* — the derivative should not be more stringent than the source. Since the mother herself does not bear *kedushat mizbeach*, her offspring likewise do not, and imposing a blemish requirement on the offspring that does not apply to the mother would make the derivative stricter than the foundation — an inversion the *halacha* does not countenance.

---

## Sanctity Upgrade

### Upgrade Question

Having established that offspring of an animal with *kedushas damim l'mizbeach* can be redeemed without a blemish because the mother's *kedusha* limits theirs, the Gemara draws a contrast. What about the reverse situation? Suppose one takes a perfect, unblemished male animal — one that is fully eligible to be brought as an *olah* — and explicitly declares it sanctified only for its *monetary value* (*ledamav*), intending it to be sold with the proceeds directed to the temple treasury rather than brought directly as a *korban*. Does reality override intention? Since the physical animal is perfectly eligible to stand on the altar, does the verbal sanctification for treasury purposes automatically upgrade to full *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic altar sanctity?

### Rava's Rule

The Gemara concludes that this supports the position of Rava: *hikdish zachar ledamim kadosh kedushat haguf* — if one sanctifies a perfect male animal for its value, it nonetheless acquires intrinsic *kedusha* appropriate to a *korban*. The reasoning emerges from the contrast with the offspring case. When an unblemished offspring is born to a mother with limited *kedusha*, the limitation comes from the mother: her *kedusha* is confined, and the child's is equally confined. But when no mother is involved — when one simply performs a verbal sanctification — there is no external limiting factor. The animal is eligible for the altar; nothing prevents the full upgrade; and therefore the *halacha* shortcircuits the indirect route and recognizes the animal as a *korban* directly.

### Rashi Limit

Rashi qualifies the scope of this rule. The principle applies specifically to the middle category — *kedushas damim l'mizbeach* — where the *kedusha*, though expressed as a monetary sanctification, is inherently oriented toward the eventual procurement of a *korban*. In that case, if one says "I am sanctifying this animal to sell it and use the proceeds for a *korban*," the logic of upgrading is sound: the animal itself *is* the *korban*, so why take the indirect route? But if one intended straightforward *bedek habayit* sanctity — purely for temple maintenance with no connection to the altar — the same automatic upgrade would not apply. Rashi's reading confines Rava's principle to cases where the monetary sanctification is inherently directed toward a *korban* as its ultimate purpose.

---

## Blemish Korban

### Exempt Status

The discussion now turns to a broader series of halachic derivations. The general rule — as reflected in the first case of the *mishna* — is that if an animal has *kedushas damim* rather than *kedushat korban*, slaughtering it outside the *Beit HaMikdash* does not incur the liability of *shechutei chutz*. This is the baseline from which the Gemara proceeds.

### R. Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer dissents, invoking a private *bamah*. He argues that the verse in Devarim — *lo tizbach l'Hashem Elokecha shor va'seh... kol davar ra* — "do not slaughter to God an ox or a sheep with any blemish" — addresses a case that goes beyond the central sanctuary. The verse in Vayikra already enumerates all the blemishes that disqualify an animal from the *Beit HaMikdash*; the repetition in Devarim must therefore be teaching something additional. Rabbi Eliezer reads it as applying to a *bamat yachid* — a private altar operative during the period when such altars were permitted. Even on a private altar, bringing a blemished animal constitutes a transgression of a negative commandment. The majority of the *mishna*, reading the case as exempt, do not agree with Rabbi Eliezer's structural use of the verse — the *mishna* applies it to a period with a functioning *Beit HaMikdash* and the *mishna*'s own ruling is *patur*.

### Hermeneutics

The Gemara then conducts a careful hermeneutical exercise. If the extra verse in Devarim is not needed for the categories Rabbi Eliezer assigns it to, there must be a reason for its inclusion. The Gemara works through each category of animal that possesses *kedushat korban* independent of its blemish, asking in each case whether one might have thought the animal could be offered despite its blemish — and showing that each such case is excluded through its own verse or *gezera shava*.

For *bechor*: although a *bechor* acquires its sanctity regardless of whether the blemish preceded or followed birth, the Torah states explicitly — *piseiach o iver lo tizbachenu* — that a lame or blind *bechor* may not be offered. There is thus no need for an extra verse to establish that a blemished *bechor* cannot be brought. Similarly for *maaser behema*: the Gemara proposes that the extra verse might be needed to teach that a blemished *maaser* animal cannot be offered, since the Torah says the tenth is *kadosh* regardless of whether it is *tov* or *ra* — good or bad, that is, unblemished or blemished. But the Gemara deflects: *maaser* is linked to *bechor* through a *gezera shava* — both employ the word *haavara* ("passing under the rod" or "passing to") — and from the explicit rule about *bechor*, one derives the same for *maaser*. No additional verse is required.

The same logic applies to *temurah*: the Torah states that even if the substituted animal is *ra* — blemished — it still acquires *kedusha* (*v'lo yachlifenu v'lo yamir oto tov b'ra*). One might have thought that since the blemish does not prevent *kedusha* from attaching to the exchanged animal, the animal could also be brought with its blemish. But the Torah says *v'haya hu u'tmurato yihye kodesh* — the *temurah* has the same status as the original: just as the original *korban* cannot be brought with a blemish, neither can the *temurah*. The extra verse is therefore unnecessary for *temurah* as well.

Rav Zevid raises the case of *vladot kodashim* — offspring born to a *korban* animal that are themselves blemished. Since the mother's *kedushat korban* passes to the offspring even when the offspring is born blemished — the *kedusha* attaches *agav iman*, by virtue of the mother — one might have thought that such offspring could be brought despite their blemish. The Gemara responds with a *baraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *rak kodshecha asher yihyu lecha u'nedarecha* — "only your sacrifices and your vows" — is read to include *temurot* and *vladot*, placing them on equal footing with a regular vowed *korban*. Just as a vowed *korban* with a blemish cannot be brought, neither can a *temura* or a *vlad* that has a blemish.

### Unified Principle

Having worked through all these cases, the Gemara arrives at a unified principle: every animal that possesses *kedushat korban* — regardless of whether that *kedusha* attached in spite of a pre-existing blemish — is nonetheless entirely barred from being brought on the altar while blemished. The *kedusha* and the disqualification coexist: the animal is *kadosh* even with its blemish, but that *kedusha* cannot be realized through sacrifice until and unless the blemish is removed. This demonstration has the further consequence of freeing the extra verse in Devarim from having to teach any of these cases, leaving it available to support Rabbi Eliezer's position that bringing a blemished animal on a private *bamah* during the era when such altars were permitted likewise transgresses a prohibition.

The overall arc of this extended *sugya* has thus retraced and deepened the core distinctions of the *mishna* — between *kedusha* that attaches regardless of blemish and *kedusha* that requires an unblemished animal at the moment of sanctification — while establishing that across all categories, the presence of *kedusha* and the capacity to be offered are two distinct questions, and a blemish answers the second even when it cannot negate the first.

---

---

# Bekhorot 15

## Blemish & Non-Altar Sanc…

### Blemish Before Sanctific…

We pick up at the bottom of 14b, two lines before the lines widen. The subject is a *korban* that had a *mum* before it was sanctified. Because the blemish preceded the sanctification, the *kedusha* was never oriented toward the altar — never *kedushas mizbe'ach*. It was always destined to be redeemed, with the redemption money then directed toward the altar, but the animal itself was never going to be brought as an offering. We are thus dealing with *kedushas damim* — sanctity of monetary value only — and the *gemara* explores several consequences that flow from this non-altar sanctity.

### Temura from Verse

The first consequence stated is *ve'eino ose tmura*: one cannot effect an exchange (*tmura*) with such an animal. More precisely, if one attempts to exchange another animal for it, the second animal does not acquire *kedusha*. The laws of *tmura* simply do not apply. *Mai ta'ama* — what is the reason? The verse states *lo yachalifenu velo yamir oso tov b'ra o ra b'tov*: one may not exchange good for bad or bad for good. Now, in the context of *korbanos*, *Chazal* understand "bad" (*ra*) as the standard designation for a blemished animal. The *gemara* reasons: since the verse already tells us *ra b'tov* — you may not even exchange a blemished animal for an unblemished one — it is self-evident that *tov b'ra*, exchanging an unblemished animal for a blemished one, is likewise forbidden. Why then did the Torah state the prohibition of *tov b'ra* at all?

### Good vs. Bad from Start

*Ella* — the answer is that the phrase *tov b'ra* is not merely restating an obvious prohibition. It is defining the conditions under which *tmura* can operate at all. Only *tov me'ikara ose tmura* — only an animal that was originally unblemished, that began with *kedushas mizbe'ach*, can generate an exchange. Even if it subsequently acquired a *mum*, the original altar-sanctity it carried means that *tmura* can apply to it. But *ra me'ikara* — something that began with a blemish, as in our *mishna* — never had *kedushas mizbe'ach* to begin with, and therefore *eino ose tmura*: it cannot effect a *tmura* at all.

To state the reading precisely: even when the verse speaks of *ra b'tov* — a blemished animal potentially making a *tmura* — the qualifier from the opening phrase *tov* still applies. The blemished animal that can participate in *tmura* is only one that started as *tov*. If it started with a *mum* and its *kedusha* was never fit for the *mizbe'ach*, it stands entirely outside the category of *tmura*.

---

## Redemption & Alive Requi…

### Rabbi Shimon's Position

The *mishna* then moves to animals that had a *mum* from the start — *kedushas damim* — and teaches that if they die, they may still be redeemed. *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: this position reflects the view of *Rabbi Shimon*, who holds that *kodshei mizbe'ach hayu bichlal ha'amada veha'aracha* — altar-sanctified animals fall within the Torah's requirement of *ha'amada veha'aracha*, the obligation to stand the animal upright before the kohen for appraisal, which necessitates that the animal be alive at the time of redemption. This requirement, however, applies only to *kodshei mizbe'ach*. *Kodshei bedek habayis lo hayu bichlal ha'amada veha'aracha* — animals sanctified for the Temple treasury were never included in that verse's scope, and therefore even if they die, they can be redeemed.

A *mishna* in *Temura* makes this explicit: Rabbi Shimon says that *kodshei bedek habayis im mesu yipadu* — Temple-treasury consecrations may be redeemed even after death. And yet Rabbi Shimon *umodei b'ba'al mum me'ikara shenifda* — he concedes that an animal that began with a blemish and was then sanctified ostensibly for the altar, because it was blemished from the start and therefore never truly fit for the *mizbe'ach*, is treated like a treasury-consecration and may likewise be redeemed even dead. This is the underlying logic of our *mishna*: animals with original *kedushas mizbe'ach* must be alive for redemption; animals whose *kedusha* was only ever of monetary value may be redeemed in death.

The *gemara* asks for the verse that supports this distinction. The answer: the Torah uses the word *osah* — "it" — in the passage *ve'he'emid osah*, "and he shall stand it," to indicate that only a true *kedushas mizbe'ach* animal — one genuinely fit for the altar — is included in the requirement of being alive. An animal that was nominally sanctified for the altar but carried a blemish from the outset, and whose *kedusha* was therefore never really *kedushas mizbe'ach*, is excluded.

### Tana d'Bei Levi

The *gemara* then asks: who are the *chachamim* that disagree with Rabbi Shimon in the *Temura mishna*? The answer is that they are the tradition of *tana d'bei Levi*. The teaching of the House of Levi holds that *hakol hayu bichlal ha'amada veha'aracha* — everything is subject to the requirement of being alive for valuation and redemption, even *v'afilu ba'al mum me'ikara*, even an animal that began with a blemish. The scope of the verse extends not only to altar-sanctified animals but to all consecrated animals, even a *chaya*, even a bird — any creature sanctified even for the treasury must be alive in order to be redeemed. The question *v'haksiv osah* — but doesn't the Torah say "it," implying limitation? — is noted, and the *gemara* leaves it as a difficulty for the *tana d'bei Levi* without resolution.

### Sages' Position Clarified

The *gemara* then asks about the *rabanan* in that *Temura mishna* who argue against Rabbi Shimon — what exactly is their position? Could they be arguing in the same direction as our *mishna*, namely that blemished-from-the-start animals may be redeemed even dead? If so, our *mishna* would accord with the *rabanan* as well, and the statement "this is the position of Rabbi Shimon" would be incomplete.

*Rav* (as against *Rabbi Yochanan*) maintains that the *rabanan* who argue on Rabbi Shimon take precisely the reverse position: they say *kodshei bedek habayis hayu bichlal ha'amada veha'aracha, kodshei mizbe'ach lo hayu bichlal ha'amada veha'aracha* — treasury-sanctified animals require being alive, while altar-sanctified animals do not. That is the exact inversion of Rabbi Shimon's ruling. This cannot be the position of our *mishna*, which holds that an animal that *did* start with *kedushas mizbe'ach* cannot be redeemed dead — precisely because, as the *seifa* states, *im mesu yikaveru*, if they died they must be buried. Since the *rabanan*'s position would permit redeeming dead *kodshei mizbe'ach*, they are entirely incompatible with our *mishna*'s *seifa*. Therefore our *mishna* must indeed reflect the position of Rabbi Shimon.

The *gemara* raises the possibility of attributing our *mishna* to the *rabanan* by arguing that the prohibition on redeeming the dead *kodshei mizbe'ach* derives not from the verse requiring *ha'amada veha'aracha* but from a separate concern: *ein podin et hakodshim l'ha'achilan l'klavim* — one may not redeem consecrated animals to feed to dogs. If that is the reason, perhaps the *rabanan* could still maintain their reversed position on *ha'amada veha'aracha* while agreeing with our *mishna* on the practical outcome for *kodshei mizbe'ach* due to this secondary concern. The *gemara* challenges this: if that were the rationale, the *mishna* should have formulated the case using *treifah* — an animal that became a *treifah* — not one that died, since a *treifah* equally cannot be eaten and equally would implicate the prohibition of redeeming for dog food.

Ultimately, the *gemara* notes that *rav k'Rebbe Yochanan sevira lei* — one could resolve the matter by saying that Rav follows Rabbi Yochanan and that when we say "this is the view of Rabbi Shimon," we mean Rabbi Shimon *and his disputants* in that *mishna* — on the understanding that the *rabanan* there actually hold the same substantive position as Rabbi Shimon, differing perhaps only in formulation, and therefore our *mishna* does reflect both.

### Two Reasons Alive

This discussion clarifies that there are in fact two distinct reasons why a consecrated animal must be alive in order to be redeemed. The first is the *gezeiras hakasuv* of *ha'amada veha'aracha* — the Torah's requirement that the animal stand before the kohen for appraisal, which by definition requires it to be alive. The scope of this requirement is the subject of the debate: Rabbi Shimon limits it to *kodshei mizbe'ach*; the *tana d'bei Levi* extends it to all consecrated animals.

The second reason is independent of that verse entirely: *ein podin et hakodshim l'ha'achilan l'klavim* — one may not redeem consecrated property if the result will be that it is used as dog food. This concern differs from the first in several important ways. It may be in nature more of a *lechatchila* concern rather than a *bediavad* invalidation. It has a different scope: it applies even to a *treifah* — an animal that is alive and thus satisfies the requirements of *ha'amada veha'aracha*, but which, once slaughtered, cannot be eaten by a human and would wind up as dog food. Such an animal, on the grounds of the second concern, could not be redeemed. The first reason — the *gezeiras hakasuv* — would not apply to it because it is alive; but the second reason would. The practical difference between the two reasons thus emerges clearly: the verse about standing and appraisal speaks to whether the act of redemption is formally valid, while the prohibition against redeeming for dog food speaks to whether redemption is appropriate given the destination of the animal.

The *gemara*'s conclusion is that our *mishna*, which permits redemption of an animal that started with a blemish and forbids it for one that started unblemished, is most cleanly explained by Rabbi Shimon's position. When the *kedusha* was *kedushas damim* from the start — because the blemish preceded the sanctification — there is, according to Rabbi Shimon, neither the *ha'amada veha'aracha* requirement nor the dog-food concern in the same way. When the *kedusha* was *kedushas mizbe'ach*, both concerns apply in their full force.

---

## Residual Sanctity

### Deer/Hart Comparison

We now turn to the second category: an animal that was sanctified without a blemish — full *kedushas mizbe'ach* — and subsequently acquired a *mum*. This is *kedushas haguf*, genuine altar-sanctity. Once it is redeemed, it retains *residual kedusha* by virtue of having started as a true *korban*. The question is: what are the practical consequences of that residual sanctity?

A *braisa* is cited. The Torah states that one should eat this animal just as one eats the *tzvi* and the *ayal* — the deer and the hart. *Chazal* understand this verse as addressing *pesulei mukdashin* — animals with full original *kedusha* that were subsequently blemished and redeemed. The comparison to these wild animals yields two immediate *psurim*. First: *ma tzvi patur min habechora* — a deer is not subject to the firstborn (*bechor*) obligation, because *bechor* applies only to cattle, sheep, and goats. So too, *af pesulei mukdashin peturim min habechora*, even a redeemed blemished sacrifice is exempt from the *bechor* obligation. Second: one might have thought that we exclude only the *bechora*, since that has a narrower scope (*she'ein shaveh bakol* — it does not apply to all animals, only firstborn males). But *matanot* — the priestly gifts of the shoulder, cheeks, and stomach — have a broader scope (*shaveh bakol*, applying to all animals regardless of sex or birth order), and one might therefore not have excluded them. The Torah says both *tzvi* and *ayal*, and since we have two words for two distinct *chayos*, we derive from the second that *pesulei mukdashin* are also exempt from *matanot*: *af pesulei mukdashin peturim min hamatanot*.

### Limits of Comparison

The *braisa* continues: since we are comparing *pesulei mukdashin* to deer and hart, might we not go further and say *af pesulei mukdashin chelban mutar* — that their fat (*chelev*) is also permitted, just as the fat of a deer is permitted? The Torah responds with *ach* — "however" — indicating that the comparison should not be taken to its logical extreme. The fat of *pesulei mukdashin* remains forbidden.

What is striking is how seriously *Chazal* do take this comparison. There is in fact an opinion that if one mates two animals of *pesulei mukdashin* together, one would be liable for *kilayim* — the prohibition of interbreeding — because they are treated as a hybrid species akin to the *tzvi ve'ayal*. The verse is thus taken with great force, and the *hava amina* that fat might be permitted is not as far-fetched as it sounds. The *ach* is what draws the line.

*Rav Papa* then poses a sharper question to *Abaye*. If we take the comparison to *tzvi ve'ayal* seriously enough that we needed *ach* to exclude fat, why do we not also say *k'tzvi v'ayal ein oto v'beno noheig bahen* — the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day should not apply, since that prohibition (*oto v'beno*) is limited to *behemah* and does not apply to *chaya*? Surely we should apply the same verse to exclude *oto v'beno* from *pesulei mukdashin*?

*Abaye* responds: *l'mai midamset lah* — what are you comparing it to? This animal, wherever we place it, falls either in the category of *chulin* or in the category of *kodshim*. If it is like *chulin*, then *oto v'beno noheig bo*. If it is like *kodshim*, then *oto v'beno noheig bo* as well. Since *oto v'beno* applies in both categories, there is no way to use the *tzvi ve'ayal* comparison to exclude it. One should not take the comparison so far as to render this animal worse — more lenient — than *both* categories simultaneously.

### Rava's Solution

*Rav Papa* presses back on *Abaye*: if that argument were sufficient, it would have been equally sufficient for fat. Fat too is forbidden by both *chulin* and *kodshim* — so why did the *braisa* need the word *ach* at all? The Torah could simply have been silent and we would have known the fat is forbidden. Yet the *braisa* plainly takes the comparison seriously and requires *ach* to limit it. The same logic that requires *ach* for fat should require a verse to limit *oto v'beno*. *Aval lo mi amart ach velo chelbo* — we used *ach* to exclude fat; the same *ach* should then also exclude *oto v'beno*. This leaves a difficulty: can *ach* bear the weight of excluding both?

*Rava* then offers his resolution: *ach le'oto ve'et beno hu de'ata* — in truth, the word *ach* is coming to exclude *oto v'beno*, not fat. If so, how do we know that fat is forbidden? *Midamo nafka* — it is derived from the prohibition of blood. The Torah says *rak et damo lo tochal* — "only its blood shall you not eat." Now, it is puzzling why the Torah needs to prohibit the blood of *pesulei mukdashin*. Once the animal has been compared to *tzvi ve'ayal*, we already know its blood is forbidden — the blood of all animals is forbidden. So why state it?

*Mai damo* — the Torah cannot literally mean blood. *Ilima damo mamash, atu dama detzvi ve'ayal mi shari* — is the blood of a deer permitted? Obviously not. So the Torah's mention of "blood" must be pointing to something else. It means: the *chelev* — the fat — is being governed by the same rule as the blood. *Ma damo bekaret af chelban bekaret*: just as the prohibition of blood carries the penalty of *karet*, so too does the prohibition of fat in *pesulei mukdashin* carry *karet*. This is necessary because one might otherwise have reasoned from the comparison to *tzvi ve'ayal* that if fat is prohibited at all, it carries only a simple *lav* — since the classic *karet* prohibition of fat applies to *behemah* (*ki kol ochel chelev min habehemah*), not to deer. The Torah therefore uses the language of blood to signal that the fat here retains the full severity, including *karet*, of its original status.

The *braisa* is then reread in light of *Rava*'s interpretation: *ilu lo ne'emar damo, hayit omar ach velo chelban* — had the Torah not said "its blood," I would have used *ach* to exclude the fat. But since *damo* teaches us about the fat, *oto ve'et beno hu de'ata* — the word *ach* is freed to serve its true function of excluding *oto ve'et beno*. The *braisa*'s mention of fat and *ach* is thus a conditional reading: had we lacked the *damo* verse, *ach* would have done that work; since we have *damo*, *ach* addresses *oto ve'et beno* instead.

It is worth pausing on *Abaye*'s underlying logic, which at the end of the day captures the essential reason for the exemptions from *bechor* and *matanot*. The comparison to *tzvi ve'ayal* is the mechanism, but the deeper reason that *pesulei mukdashin* are exempt from *bechor* and *matanot* is that they retain residual *kedusha* — they have not fully descended into the category of *chulin*. The same way something genuinely *kadosh* is exempt from *bechor* and *matanot*, something with residual *kedusha* remains in that exempt category. That is the substantive point of our *mishna*.

---

## Post-Redemption Restrict…

### Slaughter & Eat Verse

We now reach the most direct expression of residual *kedusha*: after a *pesulei mukdashin* animal has been redeemed, one may not work it, shear it, or milk it. The only permitted act is *shechita* followed by eating. *V'einam yotzim l'chulin l'higazez ul'he'aved*.

The source: *d'tanu rabanan*, the sages taught from the verse *tizbach ve'achalta basar* — "you shall slaughter and eat the meat." *Chazal* read this as addressing *pesulei mukdashin*. One reading parses each word separately: *tizbach* — slaughter it — *belo giza*, without shearing; *basar* — you eat the meat — *belo chalav*, but not the milk; *ve'achalta* — and you shall eat it — *velo l'kalbecha*, not for your dog. From here, *mikan she'ein podin et hakodshim l'ha'achilan l'klavim*: one may not redeem consecrated animals for the purpose of using them as dog food. The only permitted use that justifies redemption is eating.

### Benefit After Slaughter

An alternative reading of the same verse: rather than parsing word by word, this second opinion reads *tizbach ve'achalta* holistically — slaughter and eat. The Torah is telling us that the only benefit permitted from *kodshim* that have been redeemed is benefit that comes *mishat zvicha ve'eilach* — from the point of slaughter onward. Before slaughter, while the animal is alive, no benefit is permitted — no shearing, no working, no milking. This reading, however, has a different implication for the dog-food prohibition: since benefit is only restricted while the animal is alive, once it is dead (or becomes a *treifah*) you might have thought it could be redeemed for dog food. The *gemara* explores this: if the animal is a *treifah* — alive but unable to be eaten by a human — there is no *ha'amada veha'aracha* issue since it is alive, but there is the concern of redeeming for dog food.

### No Redemption for Dog Fo…

This establishes the biblical basis for the principle that one may not redeem consecrated animals destined for dog food. As noted earlier, the distinction between this concern and the *ha'amada veha'aracha* requirement is meaningful: the former applies even to a *treifah*, which is alive but whose end use would be dog food; the latter applies even to an animal that is not a *treifah* but is dead. Both reasons are operative for *kodshei mizbe'ach*, and our *mishna*'s statement that *kodshei mizbe'ach* cannot be redeemed once they die reflects both underlying principles. For *kodshei damim* — the first case in our *mishna* — neither concern applies with the same force, which is why Rabbi Shimon permits their redemption even after death.

---

## Offspring & Milk Status

### Question on Prohibition

The *mishna* states that the offspring and milk of these animals (*pesulei mukdashin*) are forbidden even after redemption. This residual *kedusha* extends to what the animal produces. The *gemara* asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If both conception and birth happened entirely after the mother was redeemed, why should the offspring be forbidden? After all, the mother has been compared to a *tzvi ve'ayal* — a wild animal — and if a deer gives birth and produces milk, those are perfectly permissible. The residual *kedusha* restricts how one may *use* the mother, but should it really extend to offspring conceived and born after redemption?

### Conception Timing

The answer: *ela d'abar lifnei pidyon v'yalda l'achar pidyon* — the case is where the fetus was conceived before the mother was redeemed, but was born after redemption. In that case, the fetus shared in the mother's full *kedusha* during the period of gestation, and that *kedusha* remains in the offspring even after the mother is redeemed. It is this overlap between the period of full *kedusha* and the period of gestation that renders the offspring forbidden. If, however, conception occurred entirely after redemption, the offspring are not affected by the mother's residual *kedusha* and are completely unrestricted — *velad tzvi ve'ayal ninhu*, they are like the young of a deer.

### Offspring Born Before

What about offspring conceived and born entirely *before* the mother was redeemed — when the mother still had full *kedushas mizbe'ach*? *Ha lifnei pidyon mikdash nami kadshi* — it goes without saying that such offspring carry their own *kedusha*, and the question becomes what its precise nature is.

The *gemara* derives from the verse by *shelamim* — which states *zachar* and *nekevah*, male or female — that derivative *kedushos* are included. *Zachar l'rabot et havelad*: the word "male" extends to include the offspring of a consecrated animal; *nekevah l'rabot et hatmurah*: the word "female" extends to include an animal that was the subject of a *tmura* exchange. Both of these are derivative *kedushos*, and both carry full *kedusha* sufficient in principle to be brought as a *korban*. The same principle applies even where the mother subsequently acquired a *mum*: *im zachar l'rabot velad baalei mumin* — additional words in the verse include the offspring of an animal that has a fixed *mum*, as long as that *mum* came after the original consecration and thus did not compromise the foundational *kedusha*.

That said, there is a *machlokes* regarding such offspring. Some say *kadshi l'hakravah* — the offspring can actually be brought as a *korban*, reflecting full derivative *kedusha*. Others say *kadshi l'reia* — the offspring must graze until they acquire a *mum* and are then redeemed, the derivative *kedusha* not being strong enough to permit direct sacrifice. The simpler reading is that they do have full *kedusha* and can be brought as a *korban*, but the disagreement exists.

---

## Offspring After Redempti…

### Rav Kahuna's Ruling

The more complex and troubling case is offspring that were conceived before the mother was redeemed but born after. *Vladot she'le'achar pidyon mai te'hei aleihem* — what is their legal status? The problem is acute: *bema nafshach*, no straightforward approach resolves it. The offspring cannot be brought as a *korban* because they derive from *kedusha dchuya* — sanctity that was derailed when the mother was redeemed. *Mikoch kedusha dchuya ka'atu*: they come from sanctity that was pushed aside. One might think to redeem them — either directly or by letting them graze until they acquire a *mum* — but *lo alimi l'mispas pidyonam*: their sanctity is not robust enough to effectuate a transfer through redemption. The *kedusha* is so residual and so derailed that the formal mechanism of redemption, which requires a transfer of sanctity to a monetary substitute, cannot function.

*Amar Rav Kahuna*: *konsan l'kipa u'mesim* — they must be locked in a room and left to die. The well-known discomfort with *tzaar baalei chayim* is acknowledged: the *gemara*'s *rishonim* accept that where preventing transgression constitutes a sufficient overriding purpose, the principle of animal suffering does not override. This is one such case. The animal cannot be used, cannot be redeemed, cannot be sacrificed, and leaving it to roam freely would create risks of misuse. Locking it away is the only solution.

*De'heichi le'avid* — what other option is there? To bring it as a *korban*: impossible, *kedusha dchuya*. To redeem it: impossible, *lo alimi l'mispas pidyonam*. The *kedusha* that was in place while it was a fetus derived partly from the mother, and when the mother was redeemed, that derivative element was stripped away. The offspring is left with a form of *kedusha* that is neither functional enough to reach the altar nor transferable through redemption.

### In Utero Sanctification

The *gemara* then presents a solution attributed to *Ami*, *Mar*, and the school of *Eretz Yisrael* in the name of *Rabbi Chanina*: *samuch le'pidyon imam matpisan leshem oso zevach* — just before the mother is redeemed, one should sanctify the fetus in utero for the same type of sacrifice that the mother was intended to be. This is a brilliant intervention. The entire problem arises because the fetus's *kedusha* is derivative and becomes derailed once the mother is redeemed. But if, *before* that happens — before any derailment occurs — the fetus is given its own independent *kedusha* for the same purpose (a *shelamim*, say, if that was the mother's designation), then when the mother is subsequently redeemed, the fetus's status is entirely independent. It no longer relies on derivative *kedusha* from the mother; it has its own consecration. Once born, it is a *shelamim* in its own right.

The *gemara* initially questions this: we just established that the offspring cannot be redeemed. The response clarifies: the solution is not to redeem the offspring but to sanctify it *before* the mother is redeemed, thereby giving it an independent *kedusha* and preempting the problem entirely. Once that independent *kedusha* is established, when the mother is redeemed the fetus is unaffected.

Why then would anyone ever need the *kipa* solution? Because one must act before the redemption of the mother. If the mother has already been redeemed, it is too late — the *kedusha dchuya* is already in place, and once sanctity is *dechuyah*, it cannot be restored. The Talmudic principle is that *dichuy* is permanent: once something is pushed aside, it cannot return to eligibility. At that point, *kipa* is the only option.

A further question arises: why must we not graze the offspring, let it live its life and let things resolve naturally? The answer, attributed to *Rav Levi*, is *gezeirah shema yigadel me'hen adarim adarim* — a rabbinic concern that one might end up grazing entire flocks of such animals. These offspring would reproduce, their offspring would reproduce, and soon one would have large numbers of animals in this ambiguous status with no practical resolution and a significant risk of transgression. Swift resolution — either through in-utero sanctification or the *kipa* — is therefore mandated.

### Cannot Add Sanctity

*Ba'ei minei Ravina me'Rav Sheshet*: *Ravina* posed the following question. When we say that one sanctifies the fetus before the mother's redemption — does it matter what *type* of sacrifice one designates? May one designate it as an *olah* even if the mother was a *shelamim*? If we are giving it an independent *kedusha*, why not give it any *kedusha* one wishes?

*Rav Sheshet* replied: *ein matpisin* — no, one cannot do this. Why not? *Gemar bisharecha bisharecha mibechor* — there is a *gezeirah shavah* connecting the phrase "in your gates" by *pesulei mukdashin* and the same phrase by *bechor*. From the verse regarding *bechor* — *ach bechor asher yibaker laHashem bivehemah lo yakdish ish oto* — we know that one may not impose an additional, different *kedusha* upon a *bechor*. Even if one wished to keep the *kedusha habechor* intact and add a *shelamim* designation on top of it, this is prohibited. The verse says explicitly that you shall not sanctify the *bechor* for a different purpose.

The *gezeirah shavah* teaches that the same restriction applies to *pesulei mukdashin*: one cannot sanctify them for a different type of sacrifice. Since the fetus already has derivative *kedusha* from the mother — say, *kedushas shelamim* — one cannot now say "I am sanctifying it as an *olah*." Just as the *bechor* acquires its *kedusha* by virtue of the mother's womb, not because the mother was herself a *korban*, and yet receives no additional or different *kedusha*, so too here: the fetus has *kedusha* by virtue of the mother, and one may not impose upon it a *kedusha* of a different type. One may only give it an independent version of the *same* type of *kedusha* it already derivatively holds.

---

## Comprehensive Baraita Re…

### Blemish-Before Case

A *braisa* is now cited that systematically reviews both categories and serves as a comprehensive summary of the topics covered. *Tanya nami ke'vatah de'Rav Sheshet.*

*Kodshim she'kadam mum kavua le'hakdeshan* — if the blemish preceded the sanctification, and the animal was then redeemed, it is *chayav be'bechor u've'matanot*: the *bechor* and *matanot* obligations apply in full. There is no residual *kedusha* to exempt it. This applies both before and after redemption. Similarly, *hagozez ve'oveid bahen eino soveg et ha'arba'im* — if one shears or works with the animal before redemption, one does not receive the forty lashes, because there is no *kedushas haguf* here that makes those acts intrinsically prohibited. Before redemption, *moalin bahen* — there is *me'ila*, since the animal belongs to the Temple. After redemption, *ein moalin bahen* — no *me'ila* applies. It does not effect *tmura*. And *vladoseihem chol* — offspring born after redemption are completely *chulin*, entirely de-sanctified. Those offspring are *nifdim tmimim* — they can even be redeemed while unblemished, since their *kedusha* was never *kedushas mizbe'ach*. And *matpisin l'chol zevach she'yirtzeh* — once redeemed, one may dedicate the animal to any sacrifice one wishes. *Klalo shel davar harei hen k'chulin l'chol divreihem* — they are entirely like *chulin* in every respect. *Ein l'cha bahem ela mitzvas pidyon bilvad* — the only *mitzva* that applies to them is redemption; after that, nothing residual remains.

### Sanctification-Then-Blem…

*Aval kodesh hikdishan ba'al mum* — if the animal was sanctified first and then acquired a fixed *mum*, or if it had a transitory *mum* at the time of consecration and later acquired a fixed one, and it was then redeemed — this is the second category, the one with residual *kedusha*. The following rules apply:
