*Ptura min habechor u'min hamatanot* — exempt from *bechor* and *matanot*, both before and after redemption. *Hagozez ve'oveid bahen sofeg et ha'arba'im* — one who shears or works with the animal receives lashes, because the act itself is prohibited by virtue of the *kedushas haguf*, even after redemption; the residual *kedusha* is sufficient to generate this prohibition. It *oseh tmura* — effects a *tmura* both before and after redemption, the residual *kedusha* being sufficient for that as well. Before redemption, *moalin bahen* — full *me'ila* applies; after redemption, *ein moalin bahen* — but note that the absence of *me'ila* after redemption does not mean the animal is unrestricted. It means only that the *me'ila* framework no longer applies; the lashes-generating prohibitions remain. *Vladoseihem kodesh* — offspring are sanctified even if born after redemption. *V'ein nifdim tmimim* — they cannot be redeemed while unblemished.

### Residual Sanctity Final

The *braisa* then states its final and governing principle: *klalo shel davar harei hen k'hekdesh l'chol divreihem* — in every respect they retain the status of *hekdesh*. Even though they carry a *mum*, even after they have been redeemed, the residual *kedusha* is comprehensive. And the practical expression of that? *V'ein l'cha bahem ela heter achilah bilvad* — the only permission that exists for such an animal after redemption is the permission to eat it. Nothing more. All other uses — work, shearing, milking — remain forbidden by the force of that residual *kedusha*. The animal has traveled from full *kedushas mizbe'ach* through blemish through redemption, and what remains at the end of that journey is still genuine *kedusha* — just enough to restrict every use except the table.

---

---

# Bekhorot 16

## Klal Shel Davar

### Baraisa Review

Daf 16 opens by returning to the very end of 15b, where a *baraisa* had presented a comprehensive review of the *mishnah's* categories of sanctification, elaborating on the distinction between an animal that bore a *mum* before being sanctified and one that was first consecrated and subsequently developed a blemish. The *baraisa* concluded with two summary clauses — *klal shel davar*, general principles — one for each scenario. The *gemara* now turns to examine what additional legal content these summary clauses are meant to convey.

### Mum Before Kedushah

The first *klal* covers the case where an animal had a blemish before it was sanctified, with the result that it never possessed *kedushat mizbeiach*. Once redeemed, it is *chulin le-chol divreihem* — completely desacralized, with no residual *kedushah* of any kind. The *gemara* asks: *klal shel davar de-reisha l'atuyei mah* — what does this general principle come to include that was not explicitly stated? The answer is: *le-chulin she-shachtam ba-chutz de-patur* — that if one slaughters such an animal outside the *beit hamikdash*, one is exempt from liability. Of course, this animal was never possessed of *kedushat korban* even before redemption, so the exemption is self-evident. Nevertheless, since this case was not made explicit in the body of the *baraisa*, the *gemara* understands the *klal* to be extending the rule to cover it — operating on the assumption that whenever a *mishnah* or *baraisa* states "this is the rule," it is teaching a case not previously articulated rather than merely summarizing what was already said.

### Kedushah Then Mum

The second *klal*, on the other hand, addresses the animal that first acquired *kedushat korban* and then developed a *mum*. Even after redemption, such an animal retains residual *kedushah*. The *gemara* asks what novel case the *klal de-seifa* comes to include, and answers: *chalavo* — the milk of such an animal. Just as the offspring born to the mother after her redemption remain subject to certain restrictions because they derive from an antecedent *kedushah* — a topic the *gemara* spent the preceding daf exploring — so too the milk of that redeemed animal is treated under the same rubric of residual *kedushah*.

---

## Offspring Problem

### Baraita Restrictions

The *gemara* returns to examine the language of the *baraisa* itself. The relevant passage states: *ein pofdin temimim* — one may not redeem these offspring unblemished — and *v'ein matpisin le-chol zevach she-yirtzeh* — one may not designate them for whatever sacrificial category one chooses. The scenario under discussion is as follows: the mother possessed *kedushat korban*, then developed a *mum*, was redeemed, and subsequently gave birth. The offspring are thus in an impossible position. On the one hand, they cannot be redeemed without a blemish, since one never redeems an unblemished animal. On the other hand, the *kedushah* they inherit from the mother was a *kedushah dechuya* — a rejected sanctity, pushed away from actual sacrifice — and therefore they cannot be brought as a *korban* in their own right. The *baraisa* thus establishes that both routes are closed: no redemption without a *mum*, no designation as a different type of *korban*.

### Rav Chanina Solution

The *gemara* draws an inference from the *baraisa's* second restriction — *l'chol zevach she-yirtzeh hu de-lo matpisin*, you cannot designate them for any sacrifice you choose — which, by implication, suggests you *can* designate them for the same sacrifice as the mother. This is precisely the solution attributed to Rav Chanina. *Heichi mashkachat lah* — how does this actually work? Before the mother is redeemed, while the fetus is still *in utero*, one sanctifies it for the same type of *korban* as the mother. If the mother was a *shelamim*, the fetus is designated a *shelamim*. Once born, the offspring has its own independent *kedushah* — not merely derivative of the mother, but its own consecration — and can be brought as a *korban*. If it later develops a blemish, *venifdin bemuman*, it can be redeemed with that blemish. The implication of the *baraisa*, then, perfectly aligns with Rav Chanina's approach: designate the fetus in its mother's womb for the same *korban*, thereby giving it an independent standing that resolves the dilemma.

### Challenge Rav Huna

At this point the *gemara* notes a further inference from the *baraisa's* first restriction: *temimim hu de-lo mifreki* — it specifies that the offspring cannot be redeemed unblemished — *ha ba'alei mumim mifreki*, which implies that with a blemish they *can* be redeemed. This is a challenge to Rav Huna, who maintained that there is no solution whatsoever for these offspring — they must simply be confined and left to die. The *baraisa* seems to contradict his position by implying that redemption with a blemish is an available path.

### Rav Huna Reply

Rav Huna's response is that the *baraisa* has been misread. *Hu hadin de'afilu ba'alei mumin ein nifdin* — in truth, even with a blemish these animals cannot be redeemed; there is simply no viable path at all. Why then does the *baraisa* say one may not redeem them *unblemished*? Because of the structure of the *baraisa* itself. The *reisha* — the first case, where the mother never had *kedushat korban* — does allow redemption of the offspring even without a blemish, since those offspring never carried *kedushat mizbeiach*. Because the first case made a point of the option to redeem without a blemish, the *seifa* mirrors the language and says you cannot do so here unblemished. But this does not imply that a blemish would help; the reality is that no redemption is possible at all.

### Comparative Language

The same logic applies to the second inference. The *reisha* states that the offspring from a mother who was never truly consecrated may be designated for any *korban* at will. The *seifa* therefore uses the parallel construction — you cannot do so for any *korban* you choose — but this does not positively imply that designation for the same *korban* as the mother is permitted. Both restrictions in the *seifa* are simply mirror images of the *reisha's* permissive language, not affirmative statements about what is allowed.

The *gemara* thus acknowledges that the *baraisa* speaks somewhat imprecisely, employing language that echoes the first case without intending to suggest positive alternatives in the second. Rav Huna's position therefore remains that there is no solution, and these animals must be impounded and left to die. Nonetheless, the *gemara* notes that Rav Chanina's approach — sanctifying the fetus in the womb before the mother is redeemed — appears the more elegant resolution and remains unrefuted in substance. Rashi suggests that Rav Huna's reluctance to adopt Rav Chanina's method may stem from a concern that it would encourage the proliferation of such animals across many generations of offspring, eventually leading to inadvertent transgression; but the precise contour of Rav Huna's objection is not fully resolved.

---

## Shechita Chutz Mum

### Text Variant

The *gemara* now takes up another clause that appears either in a variant text of the *mishnah* or in the *baraisa* under continuing discussion. The clause reads: *ha-shochet bachutz patur* — one who slaughters such an animal outside the *beit hamikdash* is exempt. This stands in apparent tension with the text of our *mishnah*, which states *ha-shochet bachutz chayav* — one is *obligated*, meaning liable for having slaughtered a sacred animal outside its proper setting. On its face, the contradiction seems puzzling. Both clauses address an animal that was sanctified, then developed a *mum*, and was slaughtered outside. If the animal retains *kedushah* even after developing a blemish, how can one be exempt for slaughtering it outside? The answer proposed — and it is logically straightforward — is that liability for *shechita* outside the *mikdash* attaches only to animals that could in principle have been offered inside. An animal with a *mum* that renders it categorically unfit for the altar cannot give rise to such liability, even if it retains residual *kedushah* in other respects.

### Cataract Case

Rav Huna's version of the relevant text reads *chayav* — obligated — and he situates this ruling within a very specific factual scenario to resolve the apparent contradiction. *U-mokim lah be-dukin sheba'ayin* — he applies it to the case of a cataract of the eye (*dokin she-ba'ayin*). A cataract constitutes a *mum* that disqualifies the animal from being brought to the altar in the first instance; however, it is so subtle a blemish that Rabbi Akiva rules *im alu lo yerdu* — if such an animal was in fact placed on the altar, it need not be removed. Because *bedi'avad* this animal could remain on the altar, it retains a degree of functional eligibility for sacrifice. Accordingly, if one slaughters it outside the *beit hamikdash*, one is liable. Rav Huna thus holds that the ruling of *chayav* is not a general statement about all blemished sanctified animals, but applies specifically to this narrow case where the blemish is so minor that post-facto altar validity is recognized by Rabbi Akiva.

---

## Temura Problem

### Temura After Pidyon

The *gemara* now returns to another striking clause from the *baraisa* discussed on the previous daf: *bein lifnei pidyonan bein achar pidyonan oseh temurah* — whether before or after the animal has been redeemed, it is still capable of effecting a *temurah*. To appreciate why this is surprising, recall the structure of the case. An animal that once held *kedushat korban*, then developed a *mum* and was redeemed, does not become ordinary *chulin*. It retains residual *kedushah* — it may not be shorn or worked, and may only be slaughtered and eaten in the ordinary way. Given that it possesses only this attenuated *kedushah*, one might have thought that the mechanism of *temurah* — where one declares a second animal as a substitute for the first, causing the second to acquire *kedushah* — would be inoperative. The *baraisa* informs us otherwise: even the residual *kedushah* of a redeemed sanctified animal is sufficient to activate *temurah*.

### Must Die

Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha now addresses the practical consequence: *temurato le'achar pidyono meitah* — the animal designated as a *temurah* after the original was redeemed must be left to die. The structural logic closely parallels the discussion of offspring born after the mother's redemption. The *temurah* animal acquires a derivative *kedushah* from the original, but that derivative status places it in a legal no-man's-land. It cannot be brought as a *korban* because it derives from a *kedushah dechuya* — a sanctity that was already, as it were, rejected from the altar. It cannot be redeemed because redemption requires a robust *kedushah* that is capable of being transferred, and the residual *kedushah* of the original is too attenuated to support it.

Tosafot adds an important theoretical point here. Ordinarily, *temurah* operates by transferring the *kedushah* of the original to the second animal — it is derivative sanctity. But Tosafot argues that the act of *temurah* itself also contributes an element of *kedushah*: the owner's verbal designation of the second animal as a substitute constitutes a quasi-independent act of sanctification. This dual source of *kedushah* in the *temurah* animal — partly derivative from the original, partly from the owner's own act — explains both why the *baraisa* says *temurah* is effective at all despite the merely residual *kedushah* of the original, and why the *temurah* animal cannot simply be slaughtered and eaten as the original redeemed animal may be. Because its *kedushah* is not purely derivative, it cannot simply follow the more lenient track of the mother. Yet because it is also partly derivative of a rejected *kedushah*, it cannot be brought as a *korban*. It is caught in between. The *gemara* states: *l'kreivei? mikoch kedushah dechuya ka'ati* — to bring it as a *korban*? It derives from a rejected *kedushah*. *Lifreikei? Lo alima lemifrak pidyona* — to redeem it? The *kedushah* is too weak. *Hilkach meisa* — therefore it must die.

### Rav Amram Challenge

Rav Amram poses a sharp challenge: *v'teachel bemumah le-ba'alim* — why not simply wait for the animal to develop a blemish and then eat it? The model he appears to draw on is *bechor*. A firstborn animal carries *kedushah* but is not redeemed in the ordinary sense; when it develops a *mum*, it is eaten by the *kohen* outside the *beit hamikdash* without any formal redemption process. If this *temurah* animal similarly cannot be brought to the altar and cannot be redeemed, perhaps the solution is to wait for a *mum* and eat it analogously. Rav Amram strengthens this argument by citing a *mishnah*: *temurat bechor u-maaser hein veladav u-velad veladan ad sof kol ha-olam harei hen ke-bechor u-maaser, ve-yochlu be-mumam le-ba'alim* — the *temurah* of a *bechor* or *maaser beheima*, along with all their offspring to the end of time, carry the same status as *bechor* and *maaser* and are eaten with a blemish by their owners. Here is a direct precedent: the *temurah* of a *bechor* is eaten with a blemish without redemption. Why should our case be different?

### Abaye Response

Abaye's reply is incisive: *zeh shem imo alav ve-zeh shem imo alav* — each animal bears the name, the legal identity, of its source. In the case of *temurat bechor* and *temurat maaser*, the entire identity of the *temurah* is defined by *bechor* and *maaser* — *kulo temuras bechor maaser mikri*. The *halacha* of *bechor* and *maaser* is that they are eaten with a blemish by their owners, and since the *temurah* fully inherits that identity, the same rule applies: *af temuratan nochlin be-mumam le-ba'alim*. But the animal in our case — *temuras kodshim mikri* — bears the name and identity of a standard sanctified *korban*, be it an *olah* or *shelamim*. The rule for a blemished *olah* or *shelamim* is not to eat it with a blemish; it is to redeem it first — *ela be-pidyon*. Therefore the *temurah* of such a *korban* must follow the same track: it cannot be eaten with a blemish without redemption. The problem, of course, is that it also cannot be redeemed, because the *kedushah* is too weak. *Ha lo alima le-mitpas pidyona* — it is not strong enough to undergo redemption. And therefore we are back to the inescapable conclusion: it must die.

### Mixed Kedushah

The precise reason why the *temurah* animal cannot simply be slaughtered and eaten as the redeemed original may be — without any formal redemption — is not spelled out explicitly in the *gemara*. Tosafot, as noted, supplies the explanation: the *temurah* possesses a dual *kedushah* — derivative from the original's residual sanctity, and independently generated by the owner's own act of designation. This admixture means it cannot travel the simple path of the mother, who has only residual *kedushah* permitting ordinary slaughter and consumption. The *temurah* animal is thus trapped between an origin that disqualifies it from the altar and a mixed *kedushah* that disqualifies it from being treated as ordinary *pesulei mukdashim*. A parallel analysis would apply to the offspring born after the mother's redemption, discussed on the previous daf, where the child's inherited derivative *kedushah* places it in a similarly unreachable category.

---

## Chataim Meisos

### TAMNU'E Mnemonic

The *gemara* now cites a *baraisa* that seeks to establish the basis for the rule that the *temurah* of *pesulei hamukdashim* must die: *minayin le-temuras pesulei hamukdashim she-meita* — from where do we know this? The *baraisa* derives it from the verse: *mimafrisei ha-parsha tamei* — it is impure from among those with split hoofs — meaning that there exist kosher animals which are nonetheless forbidden and have no path to being eaten, comparable in that sense to non-kosher animals. But the *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: this verse is needed for another category entirely — the five *chata'os* that must die, *chamisha chata'os meisos*.

These five cases are taught in a *mishnah* in Tractate Temura and are encoded in the mnemonic *TAMNU'E* (ת, מ, נ, ו, ע): *taf* is *temuras chatas* — the *temurah* of a *chatas*; *mem* is *meisa ba'aleha* — the owner of the *chatas* died; *nun* is *nitkapru ba'alav b'acher* — the owners achieved atonement through a substitute *korban*, having lost the original and brought another; *vav* is *vlad chatas* — the offspring of a *chatas*; and *ayin* is *avra shnasah* — the animal passed its first year and is now too old. Each of these five scenarios renders the *chatas* unfit for its designated purpose of atonement and creates an animal whose *kedushah* cannot be discharged through any available mechanism — it cannot be brought, redeemed, or eaten. It must simply be impounded and left to die.

### Halacha MiSinai

The *gemara* observes that the rule of *chamisha chata'os meisos* is normally understood to be a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — a received tradition from Sinai — not derived from a biblical verse. If so, why is the verse being deployed here? The *gemara* considers whether to reassign the verse to yet another application: the *temurah* of an *asham*. An *asham* is closely analogous to a *chatas* — both are expiatory offerings — but follows a different track in parallel situations. The *gemara* replies: *temuras asham nami hilchata hi* — the law concerning the *temurah* of an *asham* is also a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. The principle is: *kol she-b'chatas meisa, b'asham ro'eh* — in any scenario that would cause a *chatas* to be left to die, the parallel *asham* is instead left to graze until it develops a *mum* and can then be redeemed. Both rules — the leniency for *asham* and the stringency for *chatas* — are encompassed within the same *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. Accordingly, neither *chata'os meisos* nor *temuras asham* requires the verse; each is already covered by tradition.

### Asham Difference

The *gemara* therefore returns to its earlier conclusion: *le'olam chamisha chata'os meisos* — the verse indeed addresses the five *chata'os* that must die — *v'itztrich kra v'itztrich hilchata* — and yet both the verse and the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* are independently necessary. Had only the verse been available, one might not have known to apply it specifically to the *chatas*, or might have concluded that even for a *chatas* in these circumstances one should simply wait for a blemish and redeem it. The *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* makes explicit: no, the *chatas* dies. Conversely, had only the *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* been available, one would know the procedural rule — these animals are confined and die — but one might have thought that transgressing this rule by eating such a *chatas* constitutes only a generic prohibited act, not a violation of a specific biblical prohibition. *Ka mashma lan* — the verse teaches that there is a formal *lav* involved: the verse's category of "forbidden from among those with split hoofs" imposes a real biblical prohibition on eating from such animals. The *gemara* also notes a further dimension: *le-akushei davar ha-ba mi-ma'aleh gerah le-davar ha-ba mi-mafris parsah* — the two halves of the verse are linked, so that each illuminates the other. The same fate — *meitah* — applies to both the *temurah* of *pesulei hamukdashim* and the *chamisha chata'os*. Each category confirms and clarifies the rule for the other.

### Caught In Between

The *gemara* thus reaches its conclusion. Whether an animal is the *temurah* of *pesulei hamukdashim* or falls within one of the five categories of *chata'os meisos*, it inhabits a kind of legal limbo. It cannot be brought as a *korban*, it cannot be redeemed, and it cannot be eaten. The only available course is to lock it in a room and allow it to die. This conclusion, as the *gemara* notes, is striking — a point to which we will return shortly.

---

## Animal Suffering

### Tza'ar Question

The ruling that one must confine certain animals and allow them to die naturally — without feeding or tending to them in a meaningful way, and without the quick relief of *shechita* — raises an obvious and important question: does *halacha* permit causing *tza'ar ba'alei chayim*, animal suffering, for the sake of satisfying ritual requirements? The question is all the more pointed given that these are cases where the ritual purpose cannot actually be fulfilled — the animal cannot be brought as a *korban*, the atonement cannot be achieved — and yet the animal must still endure a slow death because no other disposition is available.

### Ideal vs Reality

One might ask whether the transmitted laws here represent an ideal state of affairs, or whether there is a gap between what the tradition teaches in theory and what was actually practiced. The *gemara* never suggests any alternative to the rule it articulates; it presents the conclusion that these animals must die as the unambiguous *halacha*. At the same time, it is worth noting that by the time of the *gemara*, the entire world of *korbanos* and *pesulei mukdashim* was theoretical — these were discussions without a living institutional context. Nevertheless, the *gemara's* ruling is normative: it is not a description of what people did or did not do, but a statement of the law. And that law, by endorsing the confinement of an animal to a natural death in at least some circumstances, opens a conceptual space in which animal suffering is treated as a permissible cost for the sake of other religious values.

### Modern Tension

The *halacha* as it developed through the *rishonim* and the period of the *Shulchan Aruch* and thereafter permits *tza'ar ba'alei chayim* when animal suffering serves human need. This raises genuine moral complexity. On one hand, the principle that animal welfare may be overridden for human purposes underwrites practices ranging from animal experimentation for medical advancement to the industrial production of meat. On the other hand, an honest accounting must acknowledge the enormous scale of animal suffering involved in the contemporary meat industry — suffering that goes far beyond what was contemplated in the traditional framework. The discomfort one might feel with the *gemara's* ruling about confined animals dying slowly should, by the same logic, generate discomfort about the conditions under which most meat is produced today. The honest observer must reckon with a degree of inconsistency: objecting to the leniency of the ruling here while remaining indifferent to what occurs daily in industrial agriculture. The *halacha's* permission for animal suffering in service of human need is real, but its application requires a serious account of what genuinely rises to the level of "need" — and not every convenience or taste preference can bear that weight.

---

## Tzon Barzel

### Tzon Barzel Definition

With the discussion of *kodshim* complete for now, the *mishnah* turns to a new and more accessible topic: the laws of *tzon barzel*, the "iron flock" arrangement. *Ha-mekabel tzon barzel min ha-oved kochavim* — one who receives a *tzon barzel* contract from a non-Jew. The term *kibel* here does not simply mean "received" but rather denotes *kablanut* — contractual sharecropping. The arrangement works as follows: a non-Jew entrusts his flock to a Jew, and the parties agree to split the offspring. The flock is valued at a certain sum — say, a thousand dinars — and the Jew receiving the flock insures the principal. That is, if the animals die, depreciate, or are lost, the Jew must make up the difference to the non-Jew. This guaranteed-value structure is described as *tzon barzel*, the "iron flock," because the principal is, in a sense, as hard and secure as iron. The same concept appears in the laws of *ketubot*, where *nichsei tzon barzel* describes property a wife brings into marriage whose principal value is guaranteed by the husband.

### First Gen Exempt

The *mishnah* rules: *vladoteihen peturin min ha-bechorah* — the offspring of this flock are exempt from *bechor*. The exemption applies because the original animals belong, in a meaningful sense, to the non-Jew, and the *bechor* obligation requires Jewish ownership at the relevant moment. But the *mishnah's* statement goes further: it is not merely the offspring themselves who are treated differently; rather, those offspring *as future mothers* are exempt — meaning that when the first-generation offspring give birth, their young are also exempt from the laws of *bechor*. This requires explanation, since the non-Jew plainly does not own the first-generation offspring.

### Lien Theory

The *gemara's* approach is conceptually elegant. The Jew's obligation to guarantee the principal value of the original flock creates a right in the non-Jew to seize animals from the Jew's possession should a shortfall arise. If the original animals die or depreciate, and the Jew cannot produce the cash equivalent, the non-Jew may seize the offspring of the original flock to satisfy the debt. It is this right of seizure — a kind of intensified lien — that renders the first-generation offspring constructively subject to non-Jewish monetary interest. Since the non-Jew has a theoretical right to appropriate them at any time to cover the debt, they carry a quasi-non-Jewish presence, and their own offspring are therefore exempt from *bechor*.

### Substitute Animals

*He'emid vladoteihen tachat imoteihen* — if the original animals die and the Jew formally designates the first-generation offspring as substitutes for the originals in the *tzon barzel* arrangement, the entire structure shifts one generation forward. Rashi adds that even without the death of the originals, if the Jew explicitly stipulates that the non-Jew will have an immediate right to the offspring — not merely as a secondary collection option but as a designated principal — then the non-Jew's effective presence in those animals is treated as even more direct, again shifting the exemptions forward by one generation. The result is that the grandchildren of the original flock, now standing as the offspring of the designated substitutes, are exempt as future mothers, while only the great-grandchildren become obligated.

### Perpetual Lien

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules more expansively: *afilu ad asarah peturim, she'achrayutam le'ovdei kochavim* — even ten generations out, all offspring remain exempt, because the non-Jew's guarantee claim — his *achrayut* — extends indefinitely over all animals in the flock and its progeny. The logic is that the non-Jew can always, in principle, satisfy the debt by seizing animals from whatever generation is presently available. So long as that theoretical right to seize persists, no generation fully escapes the non-Jewish monetary presence, and all remain exempt from *bechor*.

---

## Ribbis Prohibition

### Usury Problem

The *gemara* now introduces a challenge from a different *mishnah*, one dealing with the laws of *ribbis* in Tractate Bava Metzia. That *mishnah* rules: *ein mekablin tzon barzel mi-Yisrael, mipnei she-hu ribbis* — one may not enter into a *tzon barzel* arrangement with a fellow Jew, because it constitutes forbidden interest. The very arrangement our *mishnah* permits with a non-Jew is, between two Jews, categorically prohibited.

### Object vs Money

Why is *tzon barzel* considered *ribbis* when applied between Jews? The analysis hinges on the distinction between a loan of an object and a loan of money. When I lend you my car and charge you rent, any natural depreciation that occurs during your use of the car falls on me, the owner — because it is still my car. I am renting you an object, not a monetary sum. But when you insure the value of the object — when you undertake to return not the object as it is but the full assessed value — you have, in effect, taken total possession of it and converted the transaction into a monetary loan. You owe me a thousand dinars. You will return a thousand dinars' worth of sheep, and you will also pay me half the offspring as a premium for having had use of my capital. That premium — the half of the offspring — constitutes *ribbis*. The arrangement is not the rental of sheep; it is the lending of money in sheep form.

### Abaye Distinction

Abaye attempts a resolution. He proposes that the *tzon barzel* of our *mishnah* — the one permitted with a non-Jew — is a special case in which the Jew *does not* accept full liability for loss and depreciation (*onsa u-zula*). By contrast, the *tzon barzel* that is prohibited between Jews is the classic form where the receiver fully insures the principal. In the case of our *mishnah*, Abaye suggests, the arrangement is one where the non-Jew still bears some of the risk of natural loss, and therefore the transaction remains in the category of an object-rental rather than a monetary loan. Since there is no conversion to a monetary loan, there is no *ribbis* problem — but there is also no transfer of full ownership to the Jew, which explains why the non-Jew retains sufficient legal presence to generate the *bechor* exemption. However, this distinction runs directly into an obvious problem.

### Rava Correction

Rava dismantles Abaye's proposal with two objections. First, *dekabel alei onsa u-zula tzon barzel kari lei* — if the original owner retains the risk of loss, how can you call this *tzon barzel* at all? The entire definition of *tzon barzel* is that the principal is guaranteed; an arrangement where the owner bears his own losses is simply not *tzon barzel* by any standard usage of the term. Second, if such a distinction existed, why does the *mishnah* in Bava Metzia not articulate it? The *mishnah* could easily have said: *when is it permitted between Jews? When the receiver does not insure against loss. When is it forbidden? When he does.* The fact that the *mishnah* simply prohibits *tzon barzel* from a Jew without qualification proves that no such intermediate category exists. *Tzon barzel*, by definition, always involves the guarantee of the principal — there is no version of it in which the original owner bears the risk. Therefore, Rava concludes, classic *tzon barzel* always involves the conversion of the loan into a monetary form, making it *ribbis* between Jews — but when the counterparty is a non-Jew, there is no *ribbis* prohibition, since interest between a Jew and a non-Jew is permitted. The *bechor* exemption in our *mishnah* must then be explained on different grounds entirely.

---

## Ownership Paradox

### Right vs Ownership

The apparent contradiction between the *ribbis* analysis and the *bechor* analysis now comes into focus. The *ribbis* discussion establishes that the Jew is the full owner of the flock — the *tzon barzel* converts the transaction into a monetary loan, the sheep are in the Jew's domain, and any profit generated belongs entirely to him. If so, why are the offspring exempt from *bechor*? If the Jew owns the sheep, the offspring should be entirely his and fully obligated. Rava's answer: *de'asi oved kochavim be-zuzei ve-lo yahiv lei, tafis lei le-behema; ve-i lo meshkach lei le-behema, tafsei lei le-vladoteiha* — when the debt comes due and the Jew cannot pay, the non-Jew will first seize the original animals, and if they are unavailable, he will seize their offspring. *De-harei yado be-emtza* — the non-Jew's hand is, in a meaningful sense, in the middle of things. And *kol yado be-emtza patur min ha-bechor* — any animal in which the non-Jew holds such a right of seizure is exempt from *bechor*. The exemption, in other words, is not grounded in actual ownership by the non-Jew; it is grounded in his legal right to appropriate the animals.

### Debt Mechanism

This distinction is important. One might have thought that since the *bechor* exemption requires non-Jewish ownership, and the *gemara* has just established that the Jew owns the flock, the exemption would be unavailable. Rava makes clear that the mechanism is different: it is not that the non-Jew *owns* the sheep, but that he holds a claim — a right to seize them in satisfaction of the debt — and that claim is sufficient to generate the *bechor* exemption. This is especially clear in the case of the offspring, where there was never even a *hava amina* of non-Jewish ownership; the non-Jew's right to seize the offspring is purely secondary, arising only if the original animals are insufficient to cover the debt. Yet this secondary right of seizure suffices to exempt the offspring from *bechor*, because it represents a genuine monetary stake in those animals.

### Tosafot Addition

Tosafot raises a further refinement based on a parallel discussion elsewhere in the *gemara*. There is a question whether a non-Jewish government's general right to tax or levy Jewish property — which in principle means the government could seize anyone's sheep to satisfy tax obligations — would similarly exempt Jewish flocks from *bechor*. One opinion suggests it would not. Tosafot asks: what is the difference between the government's general taxing authority and the non-Jew's right under a *tzon barzel* arrangement? The answer Tosafot offers is significant. A government's general taxing power is a generic, undifferentiated lien that rests on all property equally; it does not originate from any specific transaction involving these particular animals. In the *tzon barzel* case, by contrast, the non-Jew's right originates from the very transaction that created the flock arrangement. The animals themselves were the subject of the initial transfer; the non-Jew's claim is not merely a generic creditor's right but an interest that began with and attaches specifically to these animals. This is closer to a genuine quasi-ownership than to an ordinary lien. It is this initial transactional nexus — the fact that the non-Jew's right was born from his original ownership of these very animals — that creates a sufficiently robust non-Jewish presence to generate the *bechor* exemption, and that distinguishes the *tzon barzel* case from the mere possibility of governmental seizure.

---

---

# Bekhorot 17

## Non-Jew Rights & Bechor

### Sharecropping Setup

The daf begins at the bottom of 16b, continuing the discussion of a sharecropping arrangement involving the flock of a non-Jew. The scenario is essentially this: a Jew accepts a flock of sheep from a non-Jew under an arrangement in which the non-Jew retains rights in the principal. Because the non-Jew has rights in the principal animals, he may also seize the offspring to make up the value of the principal should any animals die. This right of seizure is what generates the exemption from *bechor*: since the offspring are, in a meaningful sense, available to the non-Jew, they cannot be fully consecrated as *bechor*.

### He'emid v'ladot

The Mishnah then presents a further case: *he'emid v'ladoteihem tachat imoteihem* — he designated the children in the place of the mothers. According to Rashi, this means the owner explicitly told the non-Jew that the children could be used to make up the difference; according to Tosafot, it means the original mother animals actually died and the children were substituted for them. Either way, the children now take on the primary status as if the non-Jew owns them, and this extends the non-Jew's rights one generation further. The Mishnah concludes: *v'ladei v'ladot paturin* — the grandchildren are exempt. In other words, when the children formally substitute for the mothers, the grandchildren of the original flock become the new exempt generation, and only the great-grandchildren would be obligated.

### Rav Huna Position

Rav Huna reads the Mishnah in its simplest sense. In the ordinary case, without the special designation, only the children (*v'ladot*) are exempt — the grandchildren (*v'ladei v'ladot*) are obligated. The *he'emid* case in the Mishnah introduces a one-generation extension, nothing more.

### Rav Yehuda Position

Rav Yehuda reads the Mishnah more expansively. He holds that even in the ordinary case, without *he'emid*, the grandchildren are also exempt; it is only the great-grandchildren who are obligated. His reasoning is that the non-Jew has inherently broader rights to seize future animals than Rav Huna acknowledges, extending naturally into the second generation.

### Rejection of Rav Yehuda

The Gemara attempts to refute Rav Yehuda's reading from the Mishnah itself. The inference is straightforward: the Mishnah says *ta'ama de-he'emid* — only because he designated the children as substitutes are the grandchildren exempt. *Ha lo he'emid* — without that designation — it would not be so; only the children would be exempt, not the grandchildren. This is a direct *tiyuvta* of Rav Yehuda.

Rav Yehuda responds with a difficult re-reading. He argues that in truth his position always held — even without *he'emid*, the grandchildren are exempt. The reason the Mishnah chose to state the case of *he'emid* is to teach something that might otherwise be missed: one might have thought that since a non-Jew's customary practice (*orchei d'ovdei kochavim*) is to seize offspring beyond what he is strictly entitled to, perhaps in the case of *he'emid* the non-Jew's rights extend yet further — to three or four generations. The Mishnah therefore informs us that even with *he'emid*, his rights do not exceed two generations, just as without *he'emid*. In Rav Yehuda's reading, the Mishnah is not drawing a contrast between *he'emid* and the ordinary case; it is drawing a ceiling on *he'emid* itself. The Gemara acknowledges this is a challenging re-read of the Mishnah, though it does not finally resolve the dispute.

The Gemara also cites a *braita*: *ha-mekabel tzon barzel min ha-akum, v'ladot paturin, v'ladei v'ladot lo* — in the *tzon barzel* arrangement with a non-Jew, the children are exempt but the grandchildren are not. This appears to be a direct contradiction of Rav Yehuda. Rav Yehuda responds by reinterpreting the word *v'ladot*: read it as *hein u-vladoteihen* — they and their children — meaning the children and their children are exempt. The Gemara records an alternative text that explicitly says *hein u-vladoteihen patur*, which would then instead challenge Rav Huna. Rav Huna reads that formulation as simply restating that the children (*hein*) are exempt and the grandchildren (*v'ladei v'ladot*) are obligated. The Gemara concludes without full resolution, though Rav Huna's reading remains the more straightforward understanding of the Mishnah. The operative principle accepted by all is that whatever generation the non-Jew retains the right to seize — that generation is exempt even in its capacity as future mothers.

### Ten Generations View

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, at the end of the Mishnah, declares: *afilu ad asara doros pturin* — even up to ten generations are exempt, because the non-Jew can always seize future offspring to make up the difference.

The Gemara observes that this position fits naturally with Rav Yehuda's reading: since Rav Yehuda already holds that the *tanna kamma* counts generations and reaches the second, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's contribution is to push against that limit and say it goes on indefinitely. There is a meaningful progression from two to ad infinitum that requires explicit statement.

But according to Rav Huna, who holds that the *tanna kamma* never counted generations at all — only said the children are exempt — what force does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement carry? Why must he say *ten generations* rather than simply say *it extends into the generations at all*?

The Gemara formulates this as a question on Rav Huna: *mai afilu ad asara doros* — once the first position does not even speak in terms of generations, a response saying it goes *into the generations* should be sufficient; why enumerate ten?

Rav Huna responds: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is specifically addressing the case of *he'emid*. Even Rav Huna concedes that in the *he'emid* scenario, the Mishnah does speak in terms of an additional generation — the *tanna kamma* there reaches the grandchildren. It is against that backdrop that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel needs to say not just *it goes further* but *it goes all the way to ten* — because once we are counting generations, there is a range of possible limits, and he must be explicit that there is no limit.

---

## Nidmeh Exemption

### Rabbi Meir Baraita

The Gemara now turns to the question of the *nidmeh* — an animal that does not resemble its mother. The earlier teaching established that if a sheep gives birth to something that looks like a goat, or a goat to something that looks like a sheep, it is exempt from *bechor*. Rav Hoshaya from Nehardea arrived with a *braita* in hand: *rachel bat ez v'ez bat rachel* — a sheep born of a goat or a goat born of a sheep — *Rabbi Meir mechayev v'chachamim potrin*. Rabbi Meir holds it is obligated; the Chachamim exempt it. This appears to invert our Mishnah's ruling, and the question immediately arises: in what category of law is Rabbi Meir declaring an obligation?

### Hoshaya Transmission

Rav Hoshaya posed the question to Rabba: when you go before Rav Huna, ask him — *Rabbi Meir mechayev l'mai* — to what law is Rabbi Meir's ruling of *chayav* addressed?

If it refers to *bechora*, this is difficult — does Rabbi Meir not accept the principle that the verse *ach bechor shor* requires that both the mother and the firstborn offspring must be an ox, i.e., they must resemble one another? The Gemara takes it as axiomatic that no one disputes this principle for *bechor*.

Could it then refer to *reishit hagez* — the obligation to give the first shearing of wool to the *kohen*? Here too there is a problem: the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that sheep with hard wool — the kind that does not retain warmth — are exempt from *reishit hagez*, based on the verse *u-migez kvasai yitchamam*, "from the shearing of my sheep he shall be warmed." A goat born of a sheep would have goat-like hair rather than proper wool, and would thus be exempt for that independent reason, quite apart from the *nidmeh* question.

Rabba then proposes that rather than sending the question to Rav Huna, they reason it through themselves — *nechzei anan*. He suggests a specific case: a sheep that gave birth to something resembling a goat, where the father was also a goat (*v'aviv tayish*). This is not a pure *nidmeh* case alone; it introduces the question of mixed parentage, a *kilayim*-adjacent concern.

### Father's Lineage Issue

The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim concerns the halacha of *oto v'et bno* — the prohibition against slaughtering an animal and its parent on the same day. And the underlying question is *choshshim l'zera ha-av* — do we give legal weight to the father's lineage in the animal world?

To clarify the term: *choshshim l'zera ha-av* does not mean we are uncertain who the biological father is. It means we are asking whether the father's biological relationship to the offspring carries any halachic significance in the animal world, where there is no family structure in the way there is for humans. Rabbi Meir holds *choshshim l'zera ha-av* — we do recognize the father's relationship. Therefore, since the father was a goat and the child resembles a goat, the child is connected to the father for purposes of *oto v'et bno*. The Chachamim hold *ein choshshim l'zera ha-av* — the father's lineage is irrelevant, and even in this case, the connection through the mother's species governs.

The Gemara then questions whether this is the right context for this debate: if Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim are really disagreeing about *choshshim l'zera ha-av*, why formulate the dispute specifically in the case of *nidmeh*? Let them argue it in the broader debate already conducted between Chananya and the Rabbis on that very question. The Gemara takes this objection as evidence that *nidmeh* is not the vehicle for the *choshshim l'zera ha-av* argument after all.

The Gemara therefore returns to the possibility that the dispute is indeed about *bechora*. The difficulty returns: how could Rabbi Meir say *chayav* for *bechor* when the child does not resemble the mother? The Gemara now offers a new case: *berachel bat rachel bat ez* — a sheep, whose mother was a sheep, whose grandmother was a goat. The child looks like the mother; but the mother herself was a *nidmeh*. The question thus becomes: is the *nidmeh* exemption a narrow halachic rule requiring only that the child resemble its immediate mother? Or is *nidmeh* a categorical label, such that once an animal is stamped as *nidmeh*, all its descendants carry that label indefinitely?

---

## Purity of Lineage

### Multi-Gen Definition

This question — whether *nidmeh* is a label attached to a lineage or simply a rule about resemblance to the immediate mother — opens into a broader discussion about how *nidmeh* is defined across generations.

One view holds *zil basar imei* — go after the mother. If the animal looks like its mother, that is sufficient; it is not a *nidmeh*, regardless of what the grandmother looked like. On this reading, *nidmeh* is not a permanent categorical designation.

The opposing view holds *zil basar imei de'imei* — you must trace back to the grandmother. If the grandmother was off-species, the mother was technically a *nidmeh*, and the grandchild inherits that status even if it now resembles its immediate mother.

A third formulation presents the inverse: *berachel bat ez bat rachel* — the sequence runs sheep, goat, sheep. The grandchild looks like a sheep, but its mother was a goat. On the one hand, the child does not resemble its mother and would seem to be a *nidmeh*. On the other hand, one could argue that the sheep-identity has reasserted itself — *chazra seyusa limkoman* — returning to the original species-line. Against this, the counter-view holds *lo chazra seyusa limkoman*: the genetic line, so to speak, remains tainted, and the child is still halachically classified as a *nidmeh* because it does not resemble its immediate mother, even if it has reverted to the appearance of its ancestral species.

---

## Purity of Lineage (II)

### Korban Chovah Requirement

Rav Yochanan now declares: *modeh Rabbi Meir b'se'ir shel Rosh Chodesh* — even Rabbi Meir concedes that the goat brought as a communal *chatat*, the *musaf* offering, requires that the animal be *ben se'ira*, born of a goat through a pure line. The verse says *v'se'ir izim echad l'chatat* — Rashi notes that *Rosh Chodesh* here is not to be taken literally; it refers to the goat of the *musafim* generally. The word *echad* is read as *hameyuchad uva misheshes yemei bereishit* — pure and distinct going back to the days of creation, with no interruption in the line. Even if at some point an ancestor merely *looked* like another species — not even a genuine crossbreed, just a *nidmeh* — the line is considered tainted and the animal is disqualified.

### Kilayim Exclusion

The Gemara then raises the question: is this requirement derivable from elsewhere? The verse states *shor o chesev o ez ki yivaled* — an ox, sheep, or goat when it is born. From this formulation we learn: *shor* — *perat l'kilayim*, to exclude a genuine crossbreed; *o ez* — *perat l'nidmeh*, to exclude even an animal that merely resembled the other species. And crucially, this applies not only to the animal itself but to any ancestor that was a *nidmeh* in the line.

The Gemara answers *tzericha* — both sources are necessary. Without the second verse, one might have thought the concern applies only when the animal itself is a *nidmeh*, not when it is a *nidmeh* several generations removed. Without the first verse, one might have thought the purity-of-line requirement applies only to communal obligatory offerings (*korban tzibur chova*) where standards are strictest, but not to free-will offerings (*nedavah*). Together, both sources are required to establish that across all categories of *korbanos*, neither a *nidmeh* animal nor one with a *nidmeh* ancestor anywhere in its line may be brought.

### Tzemmer Purity

The Gemara extends this logic to *shatnez*. The position is stated: *hakol modim she'ein lokin al tzemmer mishum kilayim* — universally, one is not liable for *kilayim* with wool that is impure in this sense. The verse *lo tilbash shatnez, tzemmer u-fishtim yachdav* — do not wear a mixture of wool and linen — is read with an analogy: *mah pishtan shelo nishtanah* — just as flax never undergoes this kind of change (the reason for which the Gemara will return to), *af tzemmer shelo nishtanah* — so too the wool must be of an unaltered line. Wool from an animal whose lineage was interrupted by a *nidmeh* at any stage does not qualify as halachic wool for the purposes of *shatnez*.

### Tzaraat Immunity

This same principle is then applied to *tcheiles* for *tzitzit* and *bigdei kehunah*. Rav Pappa declares: *hakol modim she-tzemmer pasul l'tcheiles* — universally, wool of a tainted line is unfit for *tcheiles*. The source is the juxtaposition of the verses *lo tilbash shatnez* and *gedilim ta'aseh lach* — do not wear *shatnez*, make for yourself fringes. Since *tzitzit* with *tcheiles* is placed adjacent to the *shatnez* prohibition, the wool requirement for *tcheiles* is bound by the same purity standard: *mah pishtan shelo nishtanah, af tzemmer shelo nishtanah*.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then states: *hakol modim she-ein tzemmer mitamei b'nega'im* — universally, such wool does not contract *tum'ah* from *nega'im*. The verse reads *b'veged tzemmer o b'veged pishtim* — in a garment of wool or linen. Once again: *mah pishtim shelo nishtanah, af tzemmer shelo nishtanah* — just as linen is pure and unaltered, the wool must likewise be pure to be susceptible to *tum'at nega'im*.

### Wine Purity

Rav Ashi joins the series: *af anu nomar* — let us also say the following. If one trained a grapevine to grow over a fig tree (*hidla hagefen al gabei te'enah*), the resulting grapes are presumably affected in flavor. Rav Ashi rules that *yeino pasul l'nesachim* — the wine from such grapes is disqualified for the *nesachim*, the wine libation accompanying *korbanos* on the *mizbe'ach*. The source is the verse *zevach u-nesachim* — the sacrifice and the wine offering are compared. Just as *mah zevach shelo nishtanah* — the animal must be of an unaltered line — so too *af nesachim shelo nishtanah* — the wine must be pure and unaffected.

### Ravina Objection

Ravina challenges Rav Ashi with a pointed objection: *hidla pishtan al gabei higah* — what if one trained flax around a thorn bush? Would that also mean the flax is no longer pure flax? If so, then *lo matzinu mah pishtan shelo nishtanah* — the very premise of all the foregoing analogies collapses. All the previous *drashos* — for *shatnez*, *tcheiles*, *tzaraat* — rested on the claim that flax is inherently unchangeable. If plant products can be altered by how they are grown, then flax is not a reliable baseline of purity, and the entire series of analogies breaks down.

Ravina's challenge is, in essence: you cannot use an admittedly alterable medium — plant products — as the anchor of a purity argument.

### Plant Nature Distinction

The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between different plants by their nature. *Amar lei zeh nishtaneh reicho v'zeh lo nishtaneh reicho* — this one, the grape, has its smell and taste affected; that one, flax, does not. Flax, by its intrinsic nature, cannot be affected by environmental manipulation short of an actual crossbreed. Its identity remains fixed regardless of what it is grown near or around. Therefore flax remains a valid baseline of purity, and all the preceding analogies hold.

Grapes, by contrast, are genuinely susceptible to the influence of what they grow alongside — as one can observe in the way wine takes on characteristics of the flowers or plants near which grapes are cultivated. It is therefore entirely coherent to say that a vine grown around a fig tree produces wine that has been altered in identity, rendering it unfit for *nesachim*, without undermining the foundational assumption that flax is invariably pure.

This entire sugya, it is worth noting, reflects something conceptually striking. The Gemara is operating with a category of *nidmeh* that functions beyond mere physical resemblance. Even if the animal is biologically a sheep, even if it functions in every practical respect as a sheep — if somewhere in the ancestral line an animal merely *appeared* different, the line is considered halachically tainted for *Mikdash* purposes. Whether the Gemara views *nidmeh* as a genuine biological deviation or purely a matter of appearance is left somewhat open; but the purity-of-line requirement for *korbanos*, *shatnez*, *tcheiles*, and *nega'im* all proceed from this premise.

---

## Nidmeh Exemption (II)

### Rav Ashi's Answer

Rav Ashi offers a simpler resolution to the original dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Chachamim regarding the *nidmeh* case. Rather than invoking multi-generational lineage questions or *choshshim l'zera ha'av*, he proposes that the case in the *braita* is simply one in which the animal in question bears *miktzat simanim* — some characteristics of the mother's species and some of the other. The animal partially resembles the mother.

On this reading, Rabbi Meir holds it is obligated because partial resemblance to the mother suffices. The Chachamim who exempt it are identified as Rabbi Shimon, who elsewhere required that *rosho v'rubo domeh l'immo* — the head and the majority of the animal must resemble the mother. A few resembling features is not enough for Rabbi Shimon; Rabbi Meir requires less. The debate, in Rav Ashi's framing, is straightforwardly about the threshold of resemblance required, not about lineage across generations or paternal identity. The Gemara accepts this as a viable resolution, noting that sometimes the same pair of positions — Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon — appear with one framed as the *stam* majority view and the other as the dissent, and sometimes with those roles reversed.

---

## Twins Simultaneity

### Twin Scenario

The Mishnah presents a new case: *rachel shelo bikhrah v'yalda shnei zacharim* — a sheep that has never previously given birth delivers two male twins simultaneously — *veyatze'u shnei rasheihem ke'echad*, their two heads emerging as one. Both are firstborns in the sense that neither preceded the other. Who receives them?

Rabbi Yose HaGlili rules: *shneihem la-kohen* — the *kohen* receives both. The verse says *ha-zacharim la-Shem* — the males are for God — and since it is possible for both to be *bechor* simultaneously, both are obligated.

The Chachamim rule: *iy efshar l'tzamtzem* — it is impossible to achieve or confirm such precision. Even if the births appeared simultaneous, one must have preceded the other, even if imperceptibly. Since we cannot determine which was first, the *kohen* cannot claim both. The Mishnah continues: one goes to the *kohen* and one is retained by the owner. Rabbi Tarfon says the *kohen* chooses the finer of the two. Rabbi Akiva says the value difference between the two is estimated and the *kohen* receives half that difference in addition to the lesser animal — effectively splitting the premium between them. The second animal must be left to graze until it acquires a *mum*, a disqualifying blemish, at which point it may be eaten as ordinary meat, since neither animal can be brought as a *korban* — doing so would risk bringing *chullin la-azara* — and neither can be formally consecrated.

### Yose HaGlili Position

Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position is that *efshar l'tzamtzem b'yedei shamayim* — precision is possible even in a natural event such as twin births. And *v'chol shekein b'yedei adam* — certainly when a human being constructs or controls the scenario. In natural events, the world itself can produce exact simultaneity, and halachically we may credit that. When a human agent is involved, there is even greater reason to accept precision.

### Chachamim Position

The Chachamim maintain the inverse. *B'yedei shamayim iy efshar l'tzamtzem* — in natural events, precision is impossible; we cannot trust the appearance of simultaneity and must assume one preceded the other. But a question arises: what do the Chachamim say about cases *b'yedei adam* — human-constructed or human-measured scenarios? Do they concede precision there?

Two distinct meanings of *b'yedei adam* are worth noting. One reading focuses on who constructed the scenario: if you deliberately engineered the situation to be simultaneous or equidistant, perhaps that earns halachic credit as precise. The other reading focuses on measurement opportunity: even if the event happened naturally, if you had the time and instruments to measure, perhaps that is sufficient. As will become apparent from the proofs brought below, it is the latter understanding — the availability of measurement, not the construction of the scenario — that the Gemara ultimately finds more compelling.

### Altar Line Proof

The Gemara attempts to bring evidence from the *mizbe'ach*. The altar in the *Beit HaMikdash* was girded at its midpoint with a red line (*chut shel sikra*) to divide the upper half, where certain sacrificial blood was applied, from the lower half, where other blood was applied. This line was drawn to demarcate the midpoint precisely. But if even human construction and measurement cannot be trusted, the line is useless — one might apply the blood of an upper-half *korban* just above the line, only to discover that due to imprecision the line was placed too high, and the blood was actually on the lower half.

The Gemara deflects: *d'marvach lei porta* — the line was made slightly thick, providing a buffer zone. Total precision is not claimed; the line's thickness itself creates the necessary margin. This answer does not establish that precision is achievable; it only shows that the system was designed to tolerate some imprecision.

### Best Effort Standard

The Gemara then raises a more fundamental challenge from the *shiurim* of the *Mikdash* vessels — the dimensions of the *shulchan*, the *menorah*, the *mizbe'ach* itself. The Torah specifies exact measurements. How can we ever say these requirements were met, if precise measurement is inherently unattainable?

The Gemara answers: *shani hatam d'rachmana amar avid, u-v'chol d'matzi l'me'avad nicha lei* — that case is different, because the Torah said *make it*, and by that it implicitly means: do the best you can. Whatever one is able to construct that matches the specified dimensions as faithfully as possible counts as having fulfilled the requirement. The accompanying verse — *ha-kol bi-chtav miyad Hashem alai hiskil*, all was revealed to me by the hand of God — suggests Divine communication of the standards in a manner compatible with human execution.

This answer is suggestive. One can read it as Rabbi Yose HaGlili's underlying position writ large: halacha does not demand scientific or metaphysical exactitude; it demands the best human effort. If to all observation and measurement the twins emerged simultaneously, halachically that counts as simultaneous. But the Gemara resists generalizing this principle, reserving it as a *davar she-tzarich* — applicable where the Torah explicitly commands the act, thereby implicitly accepting human-level execution, but not necessarily in other halachic contexts.

### Pottery Exception

Another attempted proof: if one breaks a pottery vessel into two pieces of apparently equal size, both pieces remain *tamei*, because we say *iy efshar l'tzamtzem* — you cannot be confident that the break was perfectly even. One piece might actually constitute the majority of the vessel, which would render it *tamei*, and the other the minority, which would be *tahor*. Since we cannot establish that either is truly the minority, both remain *tamei*. This is explicitly a *b'yedei adam* case — a human act — yet the Gemara rules *iy efshar l'tzamtzem*.

The Gemara responds: *shani kli cheres d'it bei gumot* — pottery is different because of its jagged edges. A pottery shard broken in two will have irregular, uneven fractures; no one could seriously maintain that such a break is perfectly equal. The case therefore does not demonstrate anything about situations where careful measurement is genuinely possible. It says nothing about human-made constructions that are controlled and measured in advance.

### Egla Arufa Case

The Gemara raises the case of *egla arufa*: if a slain body is found equidistant between two cities, Rabbi Eliezer rules that both cities bring a calf each. Now, if a body is found between two cities and the measurement comes out exactly equal, we could simply stipulate — if this city is closer, this is its calf; if that city is closer, that is its calf — and only one calf would need to be brought conditionally. The fact that Rabbi Eliezer requires *two* calves without qualification suggests he believes the body may genuinely be equidistant, and that each city is truly the closest, simultaneously. This implies *efshar l'tzamtzem b'yedei adam*.

The Gemara responds: this is the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds like Rabbi Yose HaGlili — *efshar l'tzamtzem* generally, both *b'yedei shamayim* and *b'yedei adam*. The question before the Gemara was what the Chachamim hold regarding *b'yedei adam*; this proof only tells us what Rabbi Eliezer holds, which is entirely consistent with his identification as a *tanna* who agrees with Rabbi Yose HaGlili.

### Measurement Opportunity

The final and most analytically productive observation concerns what makes the *egla arufa* case halachically classified as *b'yedei adam* at all. No human being placed the body there to be equidistant; the body was discovered where it fell. What makes the case *b'yedei adam* is not that a person constructed the scenario but that a person *had the opportunity to measure*. When investigators arrived at the scene, they could take out instruments and determine the distance. This is the meaningful distinction.

Accordingly, the Chachamim's position may be understood as follows: *b'yedei shamayim* — when an event occurs naturally and there is no opportunity for measured observation, such as the simultaneous birth of twins where you are a passive observer with no ability to instrument the measurement in real time — *iy efshar l'tzamtzem*, we do not credit apparent precision. But *b'yedei adam* — when you had the time and ability to measure — the question remains open: do the Chachamim say that even then, we cannot trust the measurement, or do they concede that a carefully measured equality is halachically credited as precise? The daf ends with this question unresolved, and the discussion will continue on the following day.

---

---

# Bekhorot 18

## Precision Debate

### Twins Simultaneity

The Gemara opens with the phrase *neima ketannai* — let us say that this is a dispute among *tanna'im*. The background is our *mishnah*, which discusses the case of two male twins born at precisely the same moment. Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds that both animals are *bechor*, while the Rabbis counter: *iy efshar l'tzamtzem* — it is impossible to be that precise. The Gemara now wishes to know whether the Rabbis would concede to Rabbi Yose HaGelili in a case of *bidei adam* — a humanly constructed or measured situation — as opposed to *bidei shamayim*, where things occur naturally without human control.

### Bidei Adam Types

There are two possible forms of *bidei adam*. The first is a case where one constructs the situation from the outset — as in the *gemara* about a line placed at the precise midpoint of the *mizbeach*, where patience and deliberate craftsmanship make precision achievable. The second form is where one does not construct the situation but has the opportunity and patience to measure it carefully afterward.

### Dead Body Case

The second form — measurement after the fact — is precisely what is at issue in the well-known case of a murdered body found between two cities. There, the body is not placed equidistantly by design; rather, one measures after the fact to determine which city is closest. And the Gemara had already seen a position requiring two *eglot* — one from each city — when the body is found exactly equidistant. This is significant: if the law were simply that there is a doubt about which city is obligated, one would bring a single *egla* jointly from both cities, stipulating that it belongs to whichever city turns out to be closest. The fact that two *eglot* are brought demonstrates that we accept the measurement at face value: the body genuinely is equidistant, both cities are equally "closest," and both are obligated. This is strong proof that *bidei adam*, where precise measurement is possible, is a case of *efshar l'tzamtzem*.

The Gemara initially proposes that the *egla arufa* dispute — between the *Tanna Kamma*, who says no *egla* is brought, and Rabbi Eliezer, who says both cities bring — maps directly onto the debate about *tzimtzum*. But the Gemara rejects this: if the *Tanna Kamma* truly held *iy efshar l'tzamtzem*, he would not say no *egla* at all; he would say bring one *egla* jointly, with a stipulation, since clearly one city must be closest, we simply do not know which. The fact that he says nothing is brought must mean he holds *efshar l'tzamtzem*, that the measurement can be precise — and his dispute with Rabbi Eliezer is purely about the verse. The Torah says *hakarov* — "the closest" city — in the singular. The *Tanna Kamma* reads this as excluding the case where two cities are equally close, since neither is singularly closest. Rabbi Eliezer reads *karov* as including *kerovot* — even two equally close cities qualify. Both *tanna'im*, then, agree that the measurement is reliable; they debate only the *din* when both cities are found to be equidistant.

### Physical Reality

One might ask what the Rabbis and Rabbi Yose HaGelili are really debating. One way to frame the question is whether, in physical reality, two things ever truly happen at the exact same moment. From a certain perspective, the answer is always no: one can always find a finer degree of measurement by which a difference will appear. As one participant noted, it is said that two objects never truly touch — their atoms only approach one another asymptotically. However refined the measuring instrument, there will always be some difference detectable in principle.

### Trust Measurement

But the more interesting and legally pertinent question — the one genuinely reflected in the distinction between *bidei adam* and *bidei shamayim* — is whether we can trust our measurements. The *chachamim*, on this reading, are saying: when you are simply observing, without having constructed or carefully measured the situation, you cannot say with confidence that two events were simultaneous. To call it simultaneous based on casual observation is to rely on something so rare as to be practically excluded from consideration. Rabbi Yose HaGelili disagrees: even a casual observation may be trusted. The further question is what happens when one does carefully measure. If the Rabbis say *iy efshar l'tzamtzem* even *bidei adam*, they appear to be saying that no measurement can ever be trusted to achieve true precision.

### Halacha Precision

This is a striking position, because one would think that *halacha* always operates on the basis of the best available measurement. When one measures a *kezayit* or a *tefach* or the ten *tefachim* required for various laws, we proceed on the basis of that measurement — not on the basis of some hypothetical more precise instrument that might reveal an error. So what would it mean to say that even *bidei adam*, even careful measurement, cannot be trusted to establish simultaneity or equidistance?

The only way to make sense of this, seemingly, is as follows: normally, we go by measurement because we are not trying to establish something practically impossible. Measuring a *kezayit* or a *tefach* is a realistic undertaking, and going by one's measurement is simply the *halacha*'s way of functioning. But claiming to have measured two events as perfectly simultaneous — or two distances as perfectly equal — is claiming to have achieved something so rare and so difficult that we must assume an error was made. It is not that measurements are generally distrusted; it is that this particular claim — perfect simultaneity or perfect equidistance — is so extraordinary that even after careful measurement the *chachamim* say we cannot accept it as established.

The Gemara's conclusion is that this itself is a *tannaitic* dispute. Our *mishnah* concerns *bidei shamayim*, but from the *egla arufa* case the Gemara draws evidence that there is a genuine dispute about *bidei adam* as well. The major *Tosafot* on the previous daf attempts to work through all the relevant *sugyot* in *Shas* to determine how we rule. The most logical position — that we follow the Rabbis in *bidei shamayim* cases but follow Rabbi Yose HaGelili in *bidei adam* cases — is treated by *Tosafot* as a serious possibility, though *Tosafot* also considers it possible that we rule like the Rabbis across the board, declining to accept any claim of perfect precision even when based on measurement.

---

## Two Animals

### Tarfon Picks

The *mishnah* now turns to the practical question: given that the Rabbis hold we cannot determine which of two animals emerged first, how does one proceed? If we do not know which sheep is *bechor*, which belongs to the *kohen*?

Rabbi Tarfon says: *hakohen boreir lo hayafa* — the *kohen* picks the nicer one.

### Tarfon Logic

The Gemara explains the logic: *kasavar hahu d'barya nafik beresha* — Rabbi Tarfon reasons that the stronger, healthier, and presumably larger animal was most likely the one that forced its way out first. Since being *bechor* depends on being first, and the nicer animal is presumed to have been first, the *kohen* is entitled to select it. It is worth noting that the Gemara does not clarify whether Rabbi Tarfon regards this as definitive proof — sufficient to allow the *kohen* to bring the animal as a *korban* — or merely as probabilistic evidence sufficient to award monetary rights while still requiring that the animal develop a *mum* before use. This may be because, as the Gemara will soon note, Rabbi Tarfon ultimately reversed his position.

### Akiva Splits

Rabbi Akiva says: *meshamnim beineihem* — one assesses the value between the two animals and, as the literal reading suggests, splits the difference.

### Yochanan Reads

However, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that this is not Rabbi Akiva's actual intent. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the *kohen* simply takes the lesser animal — *hakohen d'ati kachusha* — because of the principle *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya*: the one seeking to extract something from another's possession bears the burden of proof. Since the *kohen* cannot prove which is the *bechor*, he is entitled only to the lesser of the two.

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba raised the obvious question: the *mishnah* says *meshamnim beineihem*, which appears to mean they split the difference in value, implying some form of joint ownership in both animals. How can this language be read to mean simply "take the lesser one"? Rabbi Yochanan's response — rendered colloquially in the Gemara as a gentle rebuke that in the Land of Israel they had already worked this out while the Babylonians were occupied with other pursuits — is that one should look to the *seifa*, the end of the *mishnah*, to understand what the *reisha* really means.

### Contradiction

The end of the *mishnah* states: if one of the animals dies, Rabbi Akiva says *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* — the *kohen* is told to prove which one is his, and since he cannot, he receives the dead animal. Now, Rabbi Yochanan argues, if *meshamnim beineihem* truly meant equal joint ownership in both animals with the value split between them, then even when one dies, Rabbi Akiva should say the same thing: give me the lesser and half the difference. Why does Rabbi Akiva say the *kohen* gets nothing but the dead one? Clearly, Rabbi Akiva holds that the *kohen* has no rights in the more expensive animal at all — *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* — and this must be his position in the *reisha* as well.

The phrase *meshamnim beineihem*, then, must be reread. Rabbi Yochanan explains: *shuman yehei beineihem* — what lies "between" the two animals, what differentiates them, is the *shuman*, the fat, the premium value. The *kohen* receives the lesser animal, and the differential — the degree to which one animal is worth more — is precisely what separates their respective portions. It is admittedly a forced reading of the phrase, and Rabbi Yochanan himself acknowledges as much, saying he was compelled toward this interpretation by the logic of the *seifa*.

What makes this passage particularly striking is that Rabbi Tarfon's position, too, appears inconsistent between the *reisha* and *seifa* of the *mishnah*: in the beginning he says the *kohen* takes the nicer animal, yet at the end he says *yachloku* — they split. The Gemara, as we will see shortly, addresses this by saying Rabbi Tarfon reversed himself. Whether Rabbi Akiva similarly shifted, or whether there is some internal logic that explains why different principles apply once one animal has died, remains a genuinely open question. The Vilna Gaon is among those who sometimes attempts to interpret a *mishnah* on its own terms, independent of the Gemara's reading, and this might be a case where such an exercise is warranted.

To complete the picture: the *kohen*'s animal must still develop a *mum* before it can be used, as must the animal retained by the *Yisrael* — since we cannot be certain which is truly the *bechor*, neither may be brought as a *korban* or consumed without a blemish.

### Guarding Blemish

The *mishnah* states that the second animal — the one retained by the *Yisrael* — must be guarded until it develops a blemish, *yira'eh ad sheyista'ev*. Rashi notes that even the animal taken by the *kohen* requires a *mum*, though the *mishnah* treats this as understood. Furthermore, the *mishnah* rules *ve'chayav b'matanot* — one is obligated to give *matanot* from the animal one retains. Rabbi Yosei, however, exempts.

---

## Matanot Dispute

### Meir Both Sides

The Gemara asks: what is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir — identified as such because the parallel *mishnah* later on *amud bet* makes the attribution explicit — who holds one is obligated in *matanot*?

Rabbi Yochanan explains: *hava kohen ba lei mishnei tzdadim* — the *kohen* can come at the *Yisrael* from both sides. The *kohen* says: if the animal you retained is the *bechor*, *kuli didi hu* — give me the whole thing. And if it is not the *bechor*, then give me the *matanot* — the *zero'a, lechayayim, v'keiva*. Either way, whichever position the *Yisrael* adopts, the *kohen* is entitled to something from this animal. There is no escape from the *matanot* obligation.

### Yosei Sale

The Gemara then asks: what is Rabbi Yosei's reasoning for exempting?

### Rava Theory

Rava answers: *asu she'eino zocheh kezocheh* — they treated the one who did not actually acquire as if he had acquired. More precisely: *af al gav d'lo mati l'yadei k'man d'mati l'yadei, v'zavnei l'Yisrael b'mumei* — even though the larger, potentially more valuable animal never came into the *kohen*'s physical possession, it is as though it did come into his hand, and as though he then sold it to the *Yisrael* with a *mum*.

The logic requires unpacking. We have two animals. The *Yisrael* gives the *kohen* the lesser one, since *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* — the *kohen* cannot prove he deserves more. But the larger animal might in truth be the *kohen*'s. One cannot simply say the *Yisrael* has "paid off" the *kohen* with the lesser value as if it were a monetary claim, because the question is not only about money — it is about ownership of a specific object. The larger animal might be the wrong object entirely.

The resolution, on Rabbi Yosei's view, is as follows: since the *kohen* accepts the lesser animal and cannot extract more, we understand this as an implicit arrangement — the *kohen* is treated as having already taken possession of his potential ownership in the larger animal, and then as having sold that potential ownership back to the *Yisrael* in exchange for receiving the lesser one. Although no formal *kinyan* was performed, *chazal* constructed this as a legal fiction: *asu she'eino zocheh kezocheh* — they made it as though he had acquired and then sold. The result is that the larger animal, whatever its status, is now a *bechor* of a *kohen* that was sold to a *Yisrael* — and a *bechor* sold by a *kohen* to a *Yisrael* is exempt from *matanot*. Thus Rabbi Yosei exempts.

Importantly, Rabbi Yosei's exemption from *matanot* does not mean the *kohen* receives nothing. He receives the lesser animal. The question is solely whether *matanot* must also be given from the animal the *Yisrael* retains. On this, Rabbi Yosei says: no, because through the implicit exchange, the retained animal may be considered a *bechor* that passed through the *kohen*'s hands.

### Logic Question

The Gemara now asks whether Rabbi Yosei's logic is indeed this *chalufin* reasoning, or whether something else is driving his position.

### Elazar Agrees
