Rabbi Elazar claims that everyone — including Rabbi Yosei — would agree that if the *kohen* received nothing at all in exchange, *matanot* would be obligatory. What would such a scenario look like? Consider a case where the two births were a male and a female, and it is unknown which was born first. The *kohen* cannot claim the female as a *bechor* under any theory. If in such a case the *Yisrael* slaughters the male, must he give the *matanot*? Rabbi Elazar says yes, and that Rabbi Yosei would agree — because Rabbi Yosei's entire exemption rests on the *kohen* having gone home with something in exchange. If the *kohen* received nothing, there is no implicit sale, and *ממה נפשך* — whichever way one looks at it — the *kohen* is entitled either to the whole animal if it is a *bechor*, or to the *matanot* if it is not.

### Yosei Exchange

The Gemara accepts this framing but identifies what might have led one to think otherwise. One might have supposed that Rabbi Yosei's actual concern was a *gezeirah*: if one tells the *Yisrael* to give *matanot* from a *safek bechor*, he will conclude that this animal has been designated as a non-*bechor*, and will consequently treat it as fully his own — shearing it, working it, or even eating it without waiting for a *mum*. On this reading, Rabbi Yosei exempts from *matanot* to protect the *safek bechor* from misuse, not because of any *chalufin* theory.

If that were his reasoning, Rabbi Yosei would apply it even when the *kohen* went home empty-handed — in any case involving a *safek bechor*, he would say: do not give *matanot*, lest the *Yisrael* treat the animal as freely available. The Gemara rules out this reading: the explicit language of the later *mishnah*, where Rabbi Yosei says *kol shechalifin beyad kohen patur min hamatanot* — wherever the *kohen* has taken something in exchange, the *Yisrael* is exempt — makes unmistakably clear that the exemption is conditional on the *kohen* having received something. When the *kohen* goes home with nothing, Rabbi Yosei agrees that *matanot* are owed. His reason is purely the *chalufin* theory — the implicit sale — and not any protective *gezeirah*.

---

## Ma'aser Case

### Ma'aser Nothing

Rav Pappa now introduces a comparative case. *Hakol modim besafek ma'aser shepatur min hamatanot* — everyone agrees that in a case of doubtful *ma'aser beheima*, the *kohen* receives no *matanot*. The scenario: one is counting out one's animals and the tenth one — the *ma'aser* — gets mixed up with the others. Now two animals are indistinguishable, one being *ma'aser* and one not. Both must wait to develop a *mum* and then be eaten by their owner. The *kohen* comes seeking *matanot* from one of them.

### Claim Difference

The difference from the *safek bechor* case is fundamental. With a *safek bechor*, the *kohen* can argue *mishnei tzdadim* — from both sides. If you call it a *bechor*, give me everything; if not, give me the *matanot*. Either way, he has a legitimate claim. With *safek ma'aser*, the *kohen* has no comparable argument. If this animal is the *ma'aser*, the *kohen* has no right to it at all — *ma'aser* is owned by its owner and eaten by the owner with a *mum*. So the *Yisrael* can simply say: perhaps this is the *ma'aser* one, and there is no *ממה נפשך* argument available. The *kohen* cannot prove entitlement to either animal individually, and therefore receives nothing.

### Institution Fear

This seems obvious, and the Gemara asks: what is the *chiddush* of Rav Pappa's statement? One might have thought, the Gemara answers, that Rabbi Meir's position — obligating the *Yisrael* to give *matanot* even for a *safek bechor* — is not based on the principled *din* that the *kohen* has a legitimate *mimah nafshach* claim, but rather on a concern *delo tishtakach torat matanot* — that the institution of *matanot* should not fall into desuetude. People might become lax about giving *matanot* if they see that in doubtful cases one is exempt. On this reading, Rabbi Meir would obligate even when there is no strict legal basis — including in cases of *safek ma'aser* — as a protective measure to ensure *matanot* remain a living practice.

### Principle Debate

The Gemara rejects this reading of Rabbi Meir on the basis of the *seifa* of the later *mishnah*, which states explicitly that Rabbi Yosei grounds his exemption in the *chalufin* principle, and Rabbi Meir obligates. The structure of their debate presupposes that each is arguing from a principled *din* position. If Rabbi Meir's position were merely a protective ordinance, Rabbi Yosei's response — emphasizing the *chalufin* theory — would be non-responsive to Rabbi Meir's concern. One does not counter "we should protect the institution" with "but there was an implicit sale." The fact that Rabbi Yosei argues the *chalufin* point means Rabbi Meir's position must be a substantive claim about entitlement under the law.

Reciprocally, the Gemara also considers whether one might have thought Rabbi Yosei's *chalufin* argument was offered not as his genuine reasoning but as a rhetorical move aimed at convincing Rabbi Meir — and that Rabbi Yosei's own view, even without any *chalufin*, would exempt from *matanot* on *gezeirah* grounds. The explicit language of the later *mishnah* forecloses this as well: Rabbi Yosei's exemption is conditional on *chalifin beyad kohen*, and applies only when the *kohen* took something in exchange. Without exchange, Rabbi Yosei concedes *matanot* are owed.

The upshot, confirmed by the Gemara, is that the entire dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei — including its extension to *ma'aser* cases — is a debate *al pi din*, on the merits of the law itself. Rabbi Meir holds the *kohen* can claim from both sides and is therefore entitled to *matanot*. Rabbi Yosei holds that the implicit exchange constitutes a legal sale that severs the *matanot* obligation. Neither is animated by secondary protective concerns.

---

## Death Division

### Tarfon Reversal

The *mishnah* now reaches the case already anticipated: one of the two animals dies. Rabbi Tarfon says *yachloku* — they split. This is the position that prompted Rabbi Yochanan's reinterpretation of the *reisha*, since it is flatly inconsistent with Rabbi Tarfon's earlier statement that the *kohen* picks the nicer animal. If Rabbi Tarfon truly held in the *reisha* that the nicer animal is presumptively the *bechor* and belongs to the *kohen*, then when one dies, the outcome should be determinable: if the nicer one died, it was the *kohen*'s and the remaining one is the *Yisrael*'s; if the lesser one died, it was the *Yisrael*'s and the remaining one is the *kohen*'s. There would be no basis for splitting.

### Reversed Position

Rabbi Ami therefore says: *chazar bo Rabbi Tarfon* — Rabbi Tarfon reversed his position. His final ruling is *yachloku*, and the *reisha* represents an earlier view he subsequently abandoned. Rabbi Tarfon's operative position is thus that the two parties split what remains.

### Burden Proof

Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, says *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya* — the burden of proof rests on the one seeking to extract from another's possession. The *kohen* cannot prove that the one that died was the *Yisrael*'s, so the *kohen* is told: prove it, and if you cannot, receive the dead one.

### Two Analogies

The Gemara introduces two analogies to map the logical terrain. Rabbi Tarfon's position resembles the case of two people who each deposited an animal with a shepherd, one of the animals died, and now neither owner knows which of their animals survived. In that case, the shepherd holds both animals as a neutral third party. He can only say: here is the surviving animal, sort it out yourselves. Since neither claimant is in possession, there is no *hamotzi mechavero* — no one is extracting from the other's *reshut* — and they split.

Rabbi Akiva's position resembles the case of a single person who deposited an animal with a *ba'al habayit*, it became mixed with the *ba'al habayit*'s animals, and one died. There, the *ba'al habayit* is in possession of the surviving animal, and the depositor is trying to extract from that possession. The depositor bears the burden of proof, and if he cannot establish which survived, he must accept the dead one.

The difficulty is that the actual case in our *mishnah* does not map neatly onto either analogy. The animals were born in the *Yisrael*'s possession and remain there — this looks like the *ba'al habayit* scenario, in which case everyone should agree on *hamotzi mechavero*. What, then, is Rabbi Tarfon's basis for *yachloku*?

### Kohen Shepherd

Rava, and some say Rav Pappa, answer that everyone agrees on both basic models. In the pure shepherd case — neutral third party, no one has superior possession — everyone agrees on *yachloku*. In the pure *ba'al habayit* case — one party holds, the other seeks to extract — everyone agrees on *hamotzi mechavero*. The dispute arises only in a specific intermediate scenario: *bechatzer ba'al habayit ve'ro'eh kohen* — the animals are in the *Yisrael*'s yard, but the *kohen* is serving as the shepherd.

### Tarfon Theory

Rabbi Tarfon holds *aknoiye kamachni lei bechatzero* — by appointing this *kohen* as his shepherd, the *Yisrael* implicitly grants the *kohen* a degree of possession in the yard sufficient to acquire the *bechor* at the moment of birth. The reasoning: since it is understood that the *kohen*-shepherd will receive any *bechor* that is born, it is practically necessary and implicitly intended that the *kohen* be able to acquire it immediately even if he is not physically present. Thus the *Yisrael* effectively grants the *kohen* a partial right in the field for this purpose — *venicha lei deliavid mitzvah bemamonei* — the *Yisrael* wishes the *kohen* to perform a *mitzvah* through his property. Since both parties effectively have a stake in the animals, it resembles the shepherd case where neither has exclusive possession, and they must split.

### Akiva Counter

Rabbi Akiva counters: *kivan de'is lei pseida* — precisely because the *Yisrael* knows that in cases of doubt he may lose the benefit of the doubt, he would never implicitly grant the *kohen* rights to the field. He may intend to give the *kohen* a *bechor* when one is born, but he does not grant the *kohen* acquisition rights in the yard. Since the *kohen* has no formal *kinyan* in the field, all the animals remain in the *Yisrael*'s possession, and the *kohen* who comes to claim one is the *hamotzi* — the one extracting from another's domain — and bears the burden of proof.

---

## Animal Variations

### Gender Mix

The *mishnah* now repeats and elaborates the same *halachic* principles across a series of variations, with the underlying rules remaining constant throughout. If two sheep that have never previously given birth each produce a male, *shneihem lakohen* — the *kohen* receives both. If one produces a male and one a female, *hazachar lakohen* — the male goes to the *kohen*, straightforwardly.

### Multiple Births

If two sheep together produce two males and a female, one *bechor* certainly belongs to the *kohen* — since at least one of the animals bore a male first — but it is unknown which of the two males is the *bechor*. The positions of Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva apply as before. If the births produce two females and a male, or two males and two females, it is possible in each scenario that the female emerged first from each of the two animals, meaning the *kohen* might receive nothing at all. Since the *kohen* cannot establish his claim, *ein kan lakohen klum* — the *kohen* gets nothing.

### Prior Birth

Another scenario: one animal has previously given birth — meaning it has already had a *bechor* — and one has not. Together they produce two males. Since only the animal that has not yet had a *bechor* can produce a *bechor* now, one male certainly belongs to the *kohen* — but which one is unknown. Rabbi Tarfon says the *kohen* picks the nicer one; Rabbi Akiva says *meshamnim beineihem*, read as the *kohen* taking the lesser one. The *mishnah* obligates the retained animal in *matanot*; Rabbi Yosei exempts, for the reasons already analyzed — and it is here that the *mishnah* makes explicit what was earlier implicit, with Rabbi Yosei stating: *kol shechalifin beyad kohen patur min hamatanot*, wherever the *kohen* takes something in exchange, one is exempt. Rabbi Meir obligates. The same positions on the death of one animal follow: Rabbi Tarfon says *yachloku*, Rabbi Akiva says *hamotzi mechavero alav hara'aya*.

If the births yield a male and a female and one animal had previously given birth, the *kohen* gets nothing — since it is possible the male came from the animal that had already had a *bechor*, and the female from the one that had not.

### Repetition Reason

The Gemara asks the natural question: given that all these cases ultimately turn on the same principles, why does the *mishnah* bother to enumerate them all? Is it not simply a repetition of the same *halacha* applied to slightly different facts?

### Strength Proof

The Gemara answers: *tzericha* — each case is necessary. Without the full enumeration, one might think that in some configurations the physical qualities of the animals — their size, health, or vigor — could serve as evidence of birth order and thus resolve the doubt. For instance, in the case where one animal produced twins and the other a single birth, one might think the stronger male, presumably the single birth, could be identified as the *bechor* with enough confidence to award it to the *kohen* definitively. Rashi notes that this argument has some appeal: a single birth is typically more robust than a twin, and if one could identify the single-birth male as the healthier one, one might accept this as proof of its *bechor* status. Similarly, in the case where one animal had previously given birth and one had not, one might reason that the animal never before having given birth produces a healthier offspring, and therefore the healthier male is more likely to be the *bechor*.

Each scenario in the *mishnah* is therefore required to teach that Rabbi Akiva — and the *halacha* as a whole — does not employ such reasoning. No matter how suggestive the physical evidence, strength and healthiness cannot serve as probative evidence of birth order. The *tzericha* across all the scenarios collectively establishes this principle, ruling out in each configuration the argument that might have seemed most natural for using physical appearance to resolve the doubt.

---

---

# Bekhorot 20

## Baraita & Miscarriage

### Species & Age Thresholds

The daf opens five lines from the top of 20a, picking up a *baraita* that revisits and elaborates upon the themes of the *mishnah* concerning when a purchased animal — whose history is unknown — is presumed to be a certain *bechor*, a doubtful *bechor*, or certainly not a *bechor*.

The *baraita* begins: a goat (*ez*) that gives birth within its first year is definitively a *bechor* — *vadai lakohein* — and goes to the *kohen* to be brought as a *korban*. From that point onward, if it gives birth, the status is *safek*, doubtful. The *gemara* had addressed yesterday why we cannot simply assume that a birth after the first year is certainly not a firstborn — there is sufficient basis for doubt, so the *Yisrael* retains the animal but waits for it to develop a *mum* and redeems it at that point. Similarly, a sheep (*rachel*) that gives birth within two years is definitively a *bechor* and goes to the *kohen*; thereafter, it is *safek*. A cow (*parah*) that gives birth within three years is definitively a *bechor*; thereafter, *safek*. And a donkey (*chamora*) follows the same rule as a cow. The visual symmetry of the *baraita* is striking: the words *bat*, *vadai*, and *lakohein* line up in each clause with notable regularity.

### Donkey Exception

Rabbi Yosi be-Rabbi Yehuda dissents regarding the donkey, holding that the threshold is four years rather than three: *chamora bat arba shanim*. In his view, donkeys do not typically give birth before the beginning of their fourth year, and so a birth anywhere up to that point would still be the first. This in itself is a remarkable position, since one might have thought this was simply a matter of observable animal biology. The *baraita* then notes: *ad kan divrei Rabbi Yishmael* — up to this point is the position of Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that one determines *bechor* status based on the earliest age at which the animal could have a live birth.

### Tinuf Objection

When this was reported to Rabbi Yehoshua — notably, the *baraita* does not say simply that he responded, but that when it was reported *in his presence* he sent back a reply — he told those who reported it: go back and tell Rabbi Yishmael, *ta'ita*, you have erred. Rabbi Yehoshua reasons as follows: if an animal were exempt from *bechorah* only through a prior live birth, then you would be correct — a goat born in its first year certainly had no prior live birth, a sheep born in its second year similarly had none, and so on. But the accepted tradition is otherwise. *Siman havelad bibeheima daka tinuf* — for small grazing animals such as goats and sheep, the sign of a prior "birth" sufficient to exempt from *bechorah* is a *tinuf*, a pathological discharge indicating a miscarriage, not a live birth. For large animals such as cows, it is the *shilya* — a placenta — and for a woman, either a *shapir* (fetal sac) or placenta. The point is that an animal need not have had a prior live birth to be exempt; a prior miscarriage suffices. And if that is the case, then even a goat that gives birth in its first year — which is concededly its first live birth — may nonetheless have miscarried earlier, and that prior miscarriage would have already exempted it from *bechorah*. Rabbi Yishmael's confident *vadai lakohein* is therefore premature.

### YH's Reformulation

Rabbi Yehoshua then adds: *ve-ani ein ani omer kein* — and I personally do not say it exactly as I just reported. The tradition I received holds generally that a prior miscarriage raises doubt about firstborn status. My own *sevara*, however, is more precise about the timing. *Az she-tinfah be-shisha yoledet betoch shnatah* — a goat that miscarried within the first six months of its life could still give birth within the first year. *Rachel she-tinfah bi-shnatah yoledet betoch shtayim* — a sheep that miscarried in its first year could still give birth within the second year. This framing sounds nearly identical to the tradition he just reported, and the *gemara* will analyze carefully what the difference actually is.

### RA's Refusal

Rabbi Akiva then states: *ani lo bati lidei middah zo* — I have not arrived at this level of analysis. He is not engaging in the theoretical discussion about when miscarriages are possible and how they affect presumptions. His position is categorical: if you know for certain that the animal gave birth before — *kol she-yadu'a she-bikra* — then the *kohen* has no claim and you do not even need to wait for a *mum*. If it is certain that it has never given birth, it goes to the *kohen*. And if there is any doubt, *yochal be-mumo la-ba'alim* — the owner waits for a *mum* and eats it then. As we will see, Rabbi Akiva appears to be saying that in the absence of direct, certain observation, the case falls into the doubt category — he refuses to accept the theoretical demographic reasoning of Rabbi Yishmael about what is "certainly" a first birth.

---

## YI vs YH Debate

### Tinuf Exempts?

The *gemara* now analyzes the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua. The most obvious explanation is that they disagree about whether *tinuf* — a prior miscarriage — exempts from *bechorah* at all. *Leima be-tinuf poter kamifligi*: perhaps Rabbi Yishmael holds that miscarriage does not exempt, and only a live birth breaks the *bechorah* obligation, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds that miscarriage does exempt. This would make Rabbi Yehoshua's objection straightforward.

### Peter Rechem

The *gemara* immediately rejects this framing. If we had actually witnessed a miscarriage — *de-chazinan de-tanif* — everyone agrees that *tinuf poter*, that miscarriage exempts. The concept of *peter rechem*, the opening of the womb, cannot be limited only to live birth; any prior opening of the womb — including miscarriage — must disqualify the subsequent birth from *bechorah* status. The *gemara* takes this as axiomatic, and so it forces the debate into a more nuanced register. The question between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua is not whether miscarriage would exempt in principle, but rather: *ve-hacha be-chosheshin le-tinuf kamifligi* — to what extent must we be concerned that a prior miscarriage *may* have occurred? How much does that theoretical possibility create a *safek*? Everyone agrees that if a goat gave birth in its first year, it is certainly the first live birth. The question is whether the mere possibility of a prior miscarriage is substantial enough to remove that case from the category of *vadai bechor*.

### Consistency Issue

This reframing, however, generates a serious difficulty. Rabbi Yishmael seems to hold that such a possibility is simply not a significant concern — *ein chosheshin le-tinuf*. But this clashes with what was established at the end of yesterday's daf. Rava there concluded — *machvarta Rabbi Yishmael ke-Rabbi Meir svira lei* — that the best explanation of Rabbi Yishmael's position is that he holds like Rabbi Meir, *de-chaish le-miuta*, that he is indeed concerned for minority scenarios. That concern was what explained why, when a goat gives birth in its second year, Rabbi Yishmael treats it as *safek* rather than *vadai* not a *bechor*: since there is a small possibility that it is still the first birth, he does not write it off as certainly not a *bechor*. So Rabbi Yishmael pulls cases from the "certainly not" category into the middle *safek* category because of concern for the minority. By the same logic, he should pull cases from the "certainly is a *bechor*" category into the *safek* category as well, since there is a minority possibility of prior miscarriage. The asymmetry seems incoherent.

### Stringency Only

The *gemara* resolves this with a principle: *ki chaish le-chumra, le-kula lo chaish* — Rabbi Yishmael is concerned for the minority when it leads to *chumra*, to stringency, but not when it leads to *kula*, to leniency. This resolution invites reflection. When a goat gives birth in its second year, the natural conclusion would be that the majority have already given birth before, so this is *vadai* not a *bechor* — and the owner could simply eat it once it has a *mum*. Playing it safe and treating it as *safek* — keeping the animal, not giving it to the *kohen*, waiting for a *mum* — is the *machmir* approach, and that is where Rabbi Yishmael applies his concern for the minority. In the converse case, where the goat gave birth in its first year, the conclusion is that it is *vadai* a *bechor* — give it to the *kohen* and bring it as a *korban*. To say, "but perhaps there was a miscarriage, so it might not be a *bechor*," would be a *kula*, removing it from the category of definite *bechorah* and keeping it from the *kohen* and the altar. That leniency, Rabbi Yishmael does not apply.

It is worth flagging that the *gemara*'s categorization here is somewhat counterintuitive. One could argue that treating the animal as a *safek* rather than a *vadai bechor* is itself a form of *chumra* — after all, if one brings an animal to the altar that turns out not to be *kadosh*, that is *chullin ba'azarah*, a serious transgression. Treating it as *safek* would prevent that possibility. So one could reason that holding it back as a *safek* is actually the safer, more *machmir* path.

The answer lies in understanding the nature of the *chashah le-miuta* principle. According to the *gemara*'s framing — and this connects to a broader discussion in *Tosafot* — concern for the minority is a rabbinic overlay, not a biblical requirement. Biblically, one may and should follow the majority. Rabbinically, we sometimes play it safe. But the motivation for that rabbinic care is always protective *chumra* — caution against transgression. When the majority determination leads to the conclusion that this is a *bechor* and should go to the *kohen*, that is the correct and proper disposition of the animal. Introducing doubt to prevent that outcome is not playing it safe; it is depriving the *kohen* of his due and depriving the altar of the *korban*. The "play it safe" instinct therefore does not operate here, and Rabbi Yishmael gives the animal to the *kohen* without concern for the rare possibility of a prior miscarriage. That is the first resolution.

The *gemara* then offers a second answer: *ve-iba'it eima* — one could alternatively say that Rabbi Yishmael applies concern for the minority symmetrically, in both the *chumra* and *kula* directions. If so, why isn't he concerned about the possibility of miscarriage in the first-year case? This leads to the second reframing of the dispute.

### Rebirth Timing

*Ve-hacha be-mitanefet ve-chozeret ve-yoledet betoch shnatah kamifligi* — the debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua may actually concern a different question entirely: is it biologically possible for an animal to miscarry *and* give birth within the same year? Rabbi Yishmael holds: *mitanefet eina chozeret ve-yoledet betoch shnatah* — if an animal has miscarried, it will not go on to give birth within that same year. And therefore, *mi-de-olid vadai lo tanif* — from the very fact that it gave birth, we know with certainty that it did not miscarry this year. The possibility of a prior miscarriage, while real in principle, simply cannot apply in the very year of the observed birth. Rabbi Yehoshua, by contrast, holds *mitanefet chozeret ve-yoledet betoch shnatah* — that an animal can miscarry and then go on to give birth within the same year, and therefore the concern for a prior miscarriage remains real even in the case of the first-year goat birth.

This, then, is the *gemara*'s preferred reframing of the dispute: not a debate over whether miscarriage exempts, not a debate over concern for minority possibilities, but a biological-empirical disagreement about whether miscarriage and live birth can occur within the same gestational year.

---

## YH's Timing Rules

### Time Windows

Having established the broad contours of the dispute, the *gemara* now turns to Rabbi Yehoshua's own personal position — his *sevara* — which is distinct from the tradition he reported. His formulation: *az she-tinfah ba-shisha yoledet betoch shnatah* — a goat that miscarried within the first six months of its life can still give birth within the first year; *rachel she-tinfah bi-shnatah yoledet betoch shtayim* — a sheep that miscarried within its first year can give birth within the second year. This sounds very similar to the general tradition, except that Rabbi Yehoshua's own formulation adds a precise timing constraint — the miscarriage must have occurred within the first six months (for goats) or the first full year (for sheep) for the subsequent birth to fall within the relevant threshold period.

### Month Seven Case

The *nafka mina* between Rabbi Yehoshua's received tradition and his own *sevara* emerges in the following case: an animal that miscarried at the end of the sixth month — *she-tinfah be-sof shisha* — and then gave birth within the first year. The tradition simply says: be concerned about prior miscarriage. But Rabbi Yehoshua's own *sevara* specifies that the miscarriage must have occurred *within* the first six months for the scenario to work. If it miscarried at the end of the sixth month, was a subsequent birth in the first year actually possible?

### Ze'iri Principle

This is where Ze'iri's principle enters. Ze'iri rules: *ein tinuf pachot mi-shloshim yom* — after a miscarriage, an animal does not conceive (and in some formulations, does not copulate) for thirty days. Consider the implications for our case. If the goat miscarried at the beginning of the seventh month, it cannot conceive until the beginning of the eighth month. Goats require five months of gestation. So the earliest it could give birth would be the beginning of the thirteenth month — the second year. Therefore, if we hold like Ze'iri, a birth within the first year is impossible given a seventh-month miscarriage. The *nafka mina* is for a case where we have in fact been observing the animal: we see it miscarry late in the sixth month or early in the seventh, and then we see it give birth within the first year. How do we interpret what we saw?

### Gamara Distinction

The *gemara* draws a distinction between Rabbi Yehoshua's received tradition and his own *sevara* with respect to Ze'iri's principle. *Le-Gemara it lei de-Ze'iri* — according to his received tradition, they hold of Ze'iri's thirty-day rule. *Le-svara leit lei de-Ze'iri* — according to his own *sevara*, he does not hold of Ze'iri's rule.

The practical consequence: if we hold like Ze'iri, and we observed this goat miscarry late in the seventh month and then give birth within the first year, the mathematics make that biologically impossible if the miscarriage was genuine. Therefore, we re-read the observed facts: what we thought was a miscarriage was not a real miscarriage, and the birth within the first year is the genuine first birth — *chayav be-bechor*. That is the application of Ze'iri under the received tradition. If, however, we do not hold like Ze'iri — Rabbi Yehoshua's own *sevara* — then we accept the miscarriage as genuine and treat this birth as not a *bechor*.

The *gemara* then raises a second formulation of the same *nafka mina*: *ve-iba'it eima de-kulei alma it lehu de-Ze'iri* — one could say that everyone holds of Ze'iri's principle, and the dispute between the received tradition and the *sevara* is instead about *yoledes le-mikutain* — whether an animal can give birth within a partial month, i.e., whether the five-month gestation period must be five complete months. According to the received tradition, partial months do not count and the animal cannot give birth within the fifth month. According to his own *sevara*, it can. This too alters the arithmetic of the seventh-month miscarriage case. If we require five full months and Ze'iri requires a thirty-day wait, then a seventh-month miscarriage cannot produce a first-year birth; if partial months count, perhaps it can.

The *gemara* adds yet a third variation: *iba'it eima* — perhaps the dispute concerns the principle of *miktzat ha-yom ke-kulo*, the halakhic rule that a partial day counts as a full day. If, for instance, the animal miscarried one day into the seventh month, waited the Ze'iri-mandated thirty days, then began a five-month gestation, it could theoretically give birth on the last day of the first year. Does that last day count as a full fifth month of gestation? According to the received tradition, *lo amrinan miktzat ha-yom ke-kulo* for this purpose, so the scenario is impossible and the observed "miscarriage" must have been spurious. According to the *sevara*, *amrinan miktzat ha-yom ke-kulo*, the last day counts, so the miscarriage was genuine and the animal is not a *bechor*.

The underlying logic threading through all these formulations is the same: we are watching an animal whose behavior we have observed, and we are using our biological-halakhic principles to re-read the observed facts. If the scenario we witnessed is physically impossible given our principles, we reinterpret the evidence accordingly. The basic *pshat* of the received tradition and the personal *sevara* converge on the same essential concern — a prior miscarriage creates doubt about *bechorah* status — but diverge in the precise biological constraints that govern whether such a miscarriage-followed-by-birth scenario is even possible in the relevant time window.

---

## RA & Lactation

### Chalav Question

With the question of Rabbi Yehoshua's precise position clarified, the *gemara* turns to the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva, and the question of what would constitute a *vadai* not-*bechor* at the other end of the spectrum. Rabbi Chanina mi-Sura identifies the fulcrum: *chalav poter ika beinaihu* — the question that separates them is whether lactation exempts an animal from *bechorah* status. The scenario is as follows: the animal has not been observed to have given birth before, but it is visibly lactating when it delivers this offspring. Does lactation constitute sufficient evidence of a prior birth to classify this newborn as definitively not a *bechor*, not requiring even waiting for a *mum*?

Intuitively, one would expect lactation to be powerful evidence of prior birth. The question is whether the rare possibility of hormonal lactation without prior birth is substantial enough to generate a *safek*.

### Initial Proposal

The *gemara*'s initial attempt to frame the debate assigns the positions as one might expect: Rabbi Akiva holds *chalav poter* — lactation exempts, we go by the majority of animals that do not lactate unless they have given birth, *rov behemos ein cholvo ela im kein yaldu* — and therefore the lactating animal is presumed to have given birth before, and this newborn is *vadai* not a *bechor*. Rabbi Yehoshua, in this initial framing, holds that there is a *miut* — a minority of animals that lactate without prior birth — and therefore the case is *safek*.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this assignment. *U-mi chaish Rabbi Yehoshua le-miuta?* Is Rabbi Yehoshua really the one who is concerned for a minority? The *gemara* cites an explicit *mishnah*: a widow whose mother-in-law was pregnant when she last saw her does not need to be concerned that she has a brother-in-law she is unaware of before remarrying — and Rabbi Yehoshua explicitly rules *einah chosheshes*, she need not be concerned. The arithmetic there is striking: roughly half of pregnancies end in miscarriage, and of live births roughly half are male. The probability of a living brother-in-law is perhaps 45% — and yet Rabbi Yehoshua dismisses even this as a *miut* beneath concern. If he ignores a 45% possibility there, he can hardly be the one insisting on concern for the rare lactation-without-birth case here.

### Position Reversal

The *gemara* therefore reverses the attribution: *ela ippoich* — flip the positions. Rabbi Yehoshua holds *chalav poter* — lactation exempts; the animal is *vadai* not a *bechor*, and Rabbi Yehoshua is not concerned with the minority possibility of lactation without prior birth. Rabbi Akiva holds that lactation does not suffice to definitively exempt — even this produces only a *safek*, and one must wait for a *mum*. This, notably, fits Rabbi Akiva's general stance perfectly. His categorical position from the *baraita* was that anything short of absolute certain knowledge falls into the *safek* category. Here too, even the presence of lactation does not constitute the kind of absolute certainty Rabbi Akiva requires, so he treats it as *safek*. And the reversal is confirmed by an explicit *baraita*: *chalav poter divrei Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva omer chalav eino poter* — it is stated plainly in the *baraita*.

### Tosafot Resolution

This reversal, however, creates a new difficulty. If Rabbi Yehoshua is not concerned for the minority — not even a 45% possibility — why was he concerned earlier about the minority possibility that an animal giving birth in its first year had previously miscarried? There, his objection to Rabbi Yishmael was precisely that miscarriage might have occurred. That minority concern led him to treat first-year births as *safek*. But here he dismisses a majority-range concern with respect to lactation. The inconsistency is pointed.

*Tosafot* addresses this directly, and the resolution is conceptually significant. Rabbi Yehoshua, *Tosafot* explains, is genuinely not concerned for the minority when it comes to *issur ve-heter* — the domain of religious prohibition and permission. He would let a woman remarry, ignoring a 45% risk. In principle, he would also be willing to treat a first-year birth as a *vadai bechor* brought to the altar, ignoring the minority chance of prior miscarriage. That, from the *issur* perspective, is entirely coherent with his position on lactation.

Why then does Rabbi Yehoshua object to Rabbi Yishmael? Not because he is *chaish le-miuta* in the *issur* domain, but because of a different consideration entirely: *dinei mammonot*. When the *kohen* comes to claim the animal, the governing principle is *ha-motzi me-chaveiro alav ha-re'ayah* — the burden of proof falls on the one seeking to extract an object from another's possession. In *dinei mammonot*, the standard of proof required to transfer property is higher than the standard for *issur* determinations. Even a minority possibility that there was a prior miscarriage means the *kohen* cannot definitively prove his claim, and the *Yisrael* is entitled to retain the animal.

This bifurcation generates a tension of its own, which *Tosafot* himself flags: *u-mihu hi ktzat teima* — this is somewhat difficult. Can the same animal simultaneously have two different legal statuses? From the *issur* perspective — questions of whether one may shear it, work it, or bring it to the altar — one ought to treat it as a *vadai bechor*, and misusing it would theoretically incur lashes. From the *dinei mammonot* perspective, the *kohen* cannot extract it. *Tosafot* raises the possibility, without fully resolving it, that the *dinei mammonot* determination might actually govern the *issur* question as well — since the *kohen* cannot prove his claim, one holds on to the animal and treats it as *safek bechor*, waiting for a *mum*, and even the *issur* dimension is then shaped by that outcome. *Tosafot* on 68b formulates the tension explicitly: *le-inyan malkot be-gizah va-avodah u-le-inyan lehakrivo al ha-mizbe'ach chashiv vadai bechor* — for purposes of lashes if one shears or works it, and for purposes of bringing it to the altar, it has the status of *vadai bechor* — *de-azlinan basar ruba ve-chazakah*; but *le-inyan litno la-kohen yechasheiv safek*, for the purpose of the *kohen* extracting it, it is treated as doubtful. Whether these two determinations can coexist without one contaminating the other is precisely the *teima* that *Tosafot* acknowledges without definitively answering.

This is not merely a technical question in laws of *bechorah*. It reflects a broader and genuinely important conceptual issue: when the same fact-pattern is governed by two different halakhic frameworks with different evidentiary standards, can they yield different results, and if so, does one framework's conclusion constrain the other? The practical analogy is a debt dispute where *dinei mammonot* says one need not pay — yet one wonders whether one incurs *safek gezel* by withholding. There, we say the civil framework governs the *issur* of ownership; but in *bechorah*, the *issur* and the monetary claim are truly distinct categories, and it is less obvious that the civil outcome should determine the *issur* status.

---

## Multi-Gen Baraita

### Scenario Setup

The *gemara* introduces a new *baraita*: *tanu rabbanan: gedya she-yalda shalosh banos, ve-chol bnoseiha holidu — bnoseiha yaldu shalosh shalosh* — a doe-goat that gave birth to three daughters, and all of its daughters gave birth — each daughter gave birth to three more — all within one year. Since goats have a roughly five-month gestation cycle, it is biologically possible for a goat to become a grandmother within the first year. The conclusion: *kulan nichnasos la-dir le-hit'aser* — all of them enter the fold to be tithed under *ma'aser behemah*, the animal tithe applied to all animals born within a single year. The arithmetic yields twelve animals: three from the first generation of daughters, and nine from the second (three times three).

### Why Three-Three?

The *gemara* questions the choice of scenario. Why specify that each daughter had three offspring? *Tolid chada mineihu tlas ve-inach tarti tarti* — you could achieve ten animals (the minimum needed for *ma'aser*) with one daughter having three and the other two each having two: three plus five plus seven gives ten total, including the original mother — though one counts the mother? Actually: three daughters, then one has three and two have two each = three plus three plus two plus two = ten. The *gemara* answers: *aidi de-ika chada de-lo sagya bi-lo shalosh* — since at least one of them would need to have three, the *tanna* stated that all of them had three, for the sake of uniformity in presentation.

The *gemara* presses further: why do we need any of the daughters having three? *Lei-havu kulhu tarti* — if all three daughters each had only two, that gives three plus six = nine, and then *ve-teihadar ee ve-tolid bahadeihu* — the mother herself gives birth a second time, producing a tenth animal along with the grandchildren. That would require only two births per daughter and one additional birth by the original mother. Why didn't the *baraita* employ that simpler scenario?

### No Double Birth

The *gemara* draws an implicit inference: *leima kasavar* — perhaps the *baraita* implicitly holds that *yoledes vadai eina chozeret ve-yoledet betoch shnatah* — an animal that has had a live birth does not give birth again within the same year. The *baraita* did not employ the scenario of the mother birthing twice because the *tanna* assumed that a second live birth within the same year simply does not occur.

The *gemara* is careful not to overstate: *im timtza lomar metanefet chozeret ve-yoledet betoch shnatah* — one might still argue that after a *miscarriage* an animal can go on to give birth within the same year; that remains a live debate. But *aval yoledes vadai eina chozeret ve-yoledet betoch shnatah* — after a full, successful live birth, a second live birth within the same year does not occur. This is not the explicit subject of the *baraita*, but it is the implicit biological assumption that explains why the *tanna* chose the three-by-three scenario over the simpler double-birth-by-the-mother scenario. The *baraita* will be examined further in the next *daf*.

---

---

# Bekhorot 21

## Intro & Minority

### Daf Overview

Daf 21 is a relatively short daf, and part of the reason for its brevity lies in the massive *tosafot* that appears on 21b, under the heading *chalav*. That *tosafot* is essentially devoted to working out the general rule of whether we are concerned for minority possibilities in halachic reasoning — and it made the preceding daf shorter as well by extending the analysis there. Today's daf is compact not because the *gemara* lacks conceptual depth, but because the actual details of the cases described are particularly challenging to reconstruct, resulting in unusually large *Rashi* and *Tosafot* commentaries.

### Minority Possibilities

The overarching concern driving that lengthy *Tosafot* is the question of minority possibilities and how *chazakah* interacts with them — specifically, whether we are concerned about a minority scenario when a *chazakah* supports one direction, and whether the answer changes depending on whether the question tends toward *l'chumra* or *l'kula*. *Tosafot* attempts to resolve how we generally rule across these variables, and it is that extended analysis that gives the daf its particular character.

---

## Multiple Births

### First Birth Recap

The broader topic we have been tracking concerns what happens when a sheep or goat gives birth and one does not know the animal's prior history — specifically, whether one must assume it is a *bechor*, and whether one must be concerned that it may have previously miscarried. The *gemara* yesterday presented a *baraita* with a scenario in which *ma'aser behemah* could be taken from the offspring of a single goat all within one year.

### Three Generations

*Ma'aser behemah* applies only to animals born between one *Rosh Chodesh Elul* and the next. The *baraita* described a case in which a goat gave birth to three kids, each of those kids gave birth to three more kids, and since the gestation period for goats is five months, this sequence can indeed unfold within a single year — yielding three kids and nine grandkids, thirteen animals in total, from which *ma'aser behemah* is taken. The question that arose from yesterday's discussion was why the *baraita* did not simply describe the mother giving birth a second time. Why go to three generations?

### Sequential Births

The *gemara* resolved this: it is possible for an animal that has miscarried to give birth again in the same year. But the case at hand concerns a mother who first had live children — three kids — and so to have her give birth a second time within the same year would require two separate live births in a single year, which may not be possible. Therefore, the *baraita* constructs the scenario through the children having children, not through the mother producing a second litter. With this background established, we turn to the daf before us.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Dispute

### Tanna Kamma vs Shimon

Four lines from the top of 21a, the *gemara* cites Rabbi Shimon as saying: "I saw a goat give birth such that *ma'aser behemah* could be taken all within the same year" — which sounds like little more than a paraphrase of the *tanna kamma*'s position. The *gemara* therefore asks: *mai ika bein tanna kamma l'Rabbi Shimon* — what exactly distinguishes them? Both describe a scenario in which *ma'aser behemah* is possible within a single year.

### Ze'iri Doctrine

The *gemara* answers: *ika beinaihu d'Ze'iri* — the difference between them turns on the doctrine of Ze'iri. Ze'iri had stated that after a miscarriage, an animal cannot become pregnant again for thirty days. The *tanna kamma* holds of Ze'iri's position; Rabbi Shimon does not. But this raises an immediate difficulty: Ze'iri's principle addresses the waiting period after a miscarriage, and the *baraita* has not been discussing miscarriages at all. What relevance does Ze'iri have here?

### Rashi's Scenario

This is precisely why there is such a substantial *Rashi* and *Tosafot* on this passage. *Rashi*'s explanation — though he himself has reservations about it for technical reasons — is that the scenario involves counting the mother herself as one of the animals born within the year, not just the kids and grandkids as assumed yesterday. That is, the mother was born at the start of the year, became pregnant, gave birth to three kids, and those kids themselves then went on to give birth — producing three generations all within the same year.

### Gestation Timeline

Here is how the timeline works according to *Rashi*. Assume the mother is born on *Rosh Chodesh Elul*, which is *Rosh Hashanah l'ma'aser behemah*. Assume further — for reasons we will return to — that she cannot become pregnant during her first month of life. So she becomes pregnant on *Rosh Chodesh Tishrei*. With a five-month gestation, she gives birth on *Rosh Chodesh Adar*: *Tishrei, Cheshvan, Kislev, Tevet, Shevat* — birth on *Rosh Chodesh Adar*. Those three kids, if they also cannot become pregnant in their first month, must wait until *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*. Their five-month gestation runs: *Nissan, Iyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av* — bringing us to birth on *Rosh Chodesh Elul*, the very last day of the year, or even into the next year.

This is where Ze'iri enters. The one-month waiting period that Ze'iri mandates after a miscarriage is being applied here by analogy — or in one reading, literally — to the waiting period after birth. The question becomes: can the mother, having given birth on *Rosh Chodesh Adar*, become pregnant again and give birth a second time before the next *Rosh Chodesh Elul*? If she must wait a full month before conceiving again, she cannot do so. If she can conceive immediately, she might.

### Rashi's Concern

What troubles *Rashi* about this construction is that it seems to treat the mother differently from her offspring. The scenario requires the mother to wait a month before becoming pregnant, while the kids apparently do not. The asymmetry is difficult to justify. This is one of the reasons *Rashi* himself is uncomfortable with this reading, even as he presents it.

### Alternative Explanations

One resolution offered is that the requirement to wait a month is not absolute — it is the *tanna kamma*'s default assumption, but the kids could in principle have become pregnant within their first month. The scenario is constructed so that the mother did wait a month, producing the conditions for the dispute, while the kids became pregnant earlier than the one-month mark. This is technically permissible even if atypical, and this is what makes the scenario function.

The *gemara* goes on to offer multiple framings of what distinguishes the *tanna kamma* from Rabbi Shimon. The first is Ze'iri himself: the *tanna kamma* holds that an animal must wait a month after birth before conceiving again (*itai d'Ze'iri*); Rabbi Shimon does not (*leitai d'Ze'iri*). Given the timeline, if the one-month waiting period applies, the mother's second birth would fall on *Rosh Chodesh Elul* at the earliest — either still within the year or at the very boundary. If it does not apply, she could give birth earlier.

The second framing (*iba'it eima*): perhaps everyone agrees on Ze'iri's waiting period, but the dispute is whether an animal can give birth with less than five full months of gestation (*yoledet limkuta'in*). The *tanna kamma* holds that five full months are required, placing the second birth at *Rosh Chodesh Elul*; Rabbi Shimon holds that a birth can occur with less than five full months, allowing the second birth before *Rosh Chodesh Elul*.

The third framing (*ve'ee ba'isayma*): perhaps everyone agrees that five full months of gestation are required and everyone agrees on Ze'iri. The dispute is then about *miktzat hayom kekulo* — whether the final day of the fifth month counts as the complete last day of gestation. According to the *tanna kamma*, one does not say *miktzat hayom kekulo* in this context, meaning she cannot give birth until *Rosh Chodesh Elul* itself. According to Rabbi Shimon, one does say *miktzat hayom kekulo*, meaning she could give birth on the last day of *Av*, the 29th — while the year is still open. It is admittedly striking to apply a legal category like *miktzat hayom kekulo* to a biological reality, but that is how the *gemara* frames it.

The fourth framing (*ve'ee ba'isayma*): perhaps everyone agrees on all of the above, and the mother could indeed have given birth on the last day of *Av*. But then the *tanna kamma* says that second offspring cannot be counted for *ma'aser*, because the question arises — *mechusar zman nichnas l'dir l'hit'aser* — can one take *ma'aser behemah* on an animal that is not yet eight days old? That offspring, born on the last day of *Av*, would be only one day old on *Rosh Chodesh Elul*. Is it eligible for *ma'aser*? This fourth framing transitions us to an entirely new halachic discussion, which the *gemara* now takes up.

### Tosafot Calendar

*Tosafot* raises a pointed question about *Rashi*'s construction: the scenario depends on a precise five-month timeline that lines up exactly with the calendar. But what about *chaseirim* and *maleiim*, short and full months? And what about a *shanah me'uberet*, a leap year? A leap year adds an extra month, which would throw off the entire calculation. If the timeline *Rashi* constructs only works in an ordinary year, one might ask whether the scenario is actually achievable in practice.

### Leap Year Interpretations

*Tosafot* does not offer a fully direct resolution to this question. *Rashi* himself, in what appears to be an alternate version of his commentary, offers a different reading of the dispute that incorporates the *shanah me'uberet* concern. According to this reading, the *tanna kamma* merely requires that the relevant births occur before *Rosh Chodesh Elul* — which, in a leap year, is a wider window. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, says *betoch shenatah* — literally within twelve months. According to Rabbi Shimon, the scenario must be achievable within a strict twelve-month period. This is why Rabbi Shimon needs a more flexible understanding of gestation and waiting periods, whereas the *tanna kamma* can rely on the extended calendar of a leap year to make the scenario work. This reading ties the dispute back to whether *betoch shenatah* means a calendar year from *Elul* to *Elul*, which can expand with a leap year, or a literal twelve-month period.

*Rashi*'s various explanations of this *sugya* number at least three distinct versions, and the difficulties are significant enough that the scenario has resisted clean resolution across the *rishonim*. The large *Rashi* and *Tosafot* here are not the result of complex legal disputes but of a *gemara* whose underlying factual scenario is genuinely difficult to reconstruct. This happens occasionally when the *gemara* is very specific about a practical case and the details resist a clean reading.

---

## Mechusar Zman

### Young Animals

The final framing of the *tanna kamma*–Rabbi Shimon dispute introduced the question of whether an animal born just before *Rosh Chodesh Elul* — and therefore less than eight days old — can be sanctified as *ma'aser behemah* and counted toward the group from which *ma'aser* is taken. This question of *mechusar zman* — an animal that has not yet reached the minimum age for a *korban* — now becomes the focus.

### Baraita: <8 Days

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah says in the name of Rabbi Shimon — and *stam* Rabbi Shimon in the *gemara* refers to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai — that an animal which is *mechusar zman*, not yet eight days old, may nonetheless enter the pen for *ma'aser*: *mechusar zman nichnas l'dir l'hit'aser*.

### Bechor Comparison

Rabbi Shimon derives this position from an analogy to *bechor*: just as a *bechor* is sanctified with *kedushah* from the moment of its birth — even before it is eight days old and even though it cannot be brought as a *korban* until after the eighth day — so too *ma'aser* can be sanctified on an animal less than eight days old, and it is brought as a *korban* once it reaches the proper time. The formula is parallel: *kadosh lifnei zmano, v'karev l'achar zmano* — sanctified before its time, and offered after its time.

This is explicitly an exception to the general rule. Normally, the Torah states *miyom hashmini vahalah yeiratzeh l'hakriv korban laHashem* — only from the eighth day onward is an animal acceptable for offering — and *Chazal* understand this to mean that if one tries to sanctify an animal younger than eight days, the *kedushah* does not take effect at all. The exception is *bechor*, which is sanctified by its very identity as the firstborn the moment it is born. Rabbi Shimon argues that *ma'aser* shares this quality and therefore likewise applies before the eighth day.

### Korban Analogy

The *gemara* challenges: rather than deriving *ma'aser* from *bechor*, why not derive it from other *korbanot*, where sanctification of a *mechusar zman* animal is not effective? The *gemara* therefore moves to a classical comparison — to which category is *ma'aser* more properly analogous?

### Shared Properties

The *gemara* states that it makes more sense to compare *ma'aser* to *bechor* — *mistabra mibechor hava lei lemeilaf* — and lists four features shared by *bechor* and *ma'aser* that other *korbanot* do not share: *goel*, *mum*, *tmura*, and *achilah*.

### Goel & Mum

*Goel* means that neither a *bechor* nor *ma'aser* can be redeemed (*podeh*), even when they bear a blemish. A *bechor* with a *mum* is eaten by the *kohen*; *ma'aser* with a *mum* is eaten by the *Yisrael* — but neither can have its *kedushah* transferred through redemption. This feature is directly connected to the nature of their *kedushah*: it is tied to their identity as the first or as the tenth, and because it is not an abstracted, transferable sanctity, it cannot be removed.

*Mum* as a separate point highlights the flip side of the same principle. Since they cannot be redeemed, an animal with a blemish is simply eaten with that blemish — outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, without being brought as a *korban*. This is genuinely anomalous: a *korban* with *kedushat korban* and a blemish that ordinarily would have to be redeemed before it could be used — yet here it is eaten directly, without redemption. The rule in the *gemara* more broadly is that if an animal already had a *mum* before being sanctified, its *kedushah* is never *kedushat korban* but only *kedushat damim* — the value of its money, because it never had the capacity to be brought as a *korban*. The exception is *chutz min habechor min hama'aser*: for *bechor* and *ma'aser*, since the *kedushah* attaches by virtue of their identity as first or tenth, they receive *kedushat korban* even if the *mum* preceded the *kedushah*. This does not mean they are brought as *korbanot*; it means the character of their *kedushah* is full *kedushat korban*, and they are eaten outside the *Beit HaMikdash* even though they bear a blemish.

### Tmura

*Tmura* is the prohibition against substituting one animal for a sanctified animal. While *tmura* is forbidden across all categories of *korbanot*, by regular *korbanot* the substitution is effective — the *kedushah* expands and applies to the substitute animal as well. By *bechor* and *ma'aser*, *tmura* is not effective: the *kedushah* does not transfer. Again, this is a direct consequence of the identity-based nature of their *kedushah*. Because the sanctity of *bechor* is precisely its being the first, and the sanctity of *ma'aser* is precisely its being the tenth, the *kedushah* cannot extend to something that is not the first or the tenth. It is not an abstraction being instilled; it is an attribute inseparable from their particular identity.

### Achila

*Achila* is the fourth point. *Rashi* explains that this refers to the fact that *bechor* and *ma'aser*, when blemished, are eaten without first being brought as a *korban* — they are eaten outside the *Beit HaMikdash* entirely. This might seem to overlap with *mum*, but *Rashi* distinguishes them: *mum* addresses the rule established in the previous *perek* — that if an animal has a blemish before sanctification, the *kedushah* is ordinarily only of the monetary kind. *Achila* addresses the practical consequence: even with a *mum*, they are eaten rather than redeemed. All four properties point toward the same underlying principle — that *bechor* and *ma'aser* have identity-based *kedushah* rather than instilled *kedushah*, and that principle is what makes Rabbi Shimon's position coherent: if the *kedushah* can apply even when a *mum* precedes it, perhaps the *kedushah* can apply even when the animal has not yet reached the minimum age.

### Identity Kedushah

These four properties are deeply interconnected and all derive from the same source: the *kedushah* of *bechor* and *ma'aser* is not an abstract quality instilled by an act of the owner but is intrinsic to the animal's standing as first or tenth. It is worth noting that *ma'aser* occupies an interesting middle position in this regard — unlike *bechor*, it is the owner's act of counting that designates which animal is the tenth. The *kedushah* does not arise entirely without human action. And yet, once designated as the tenth, the *kedushah* is fully identity-based and cannot be transferred. It is a midpoint between naturally arising *kedushah* and deliberately instilled *kedushah*.

### Counter-Analogy

The *gemara* counters: *adaraba mikosham hava lei lemilaf* — perhaps one should rather derive *ma'aser* from regular *korbanot*. The four grounds offered are: *zachar* — *bechor* must be male, but *ma'aser* like other *korbanot* need not be; *kadosh* — *ma'aser* requires a human act of designation, as with regular *korbanot*, unlike *bechor* which is sanctified automatically; *b'matanos* — *bechor* is a *matnat kehunah* going to the *kohen*, whereas *ma'aser* like certain other *korbanot* is eaten by the owners; and the fourth, that *ma'aser* is not itself required to be a *bechor*, and indeed cannot be one. These are genuine similarities, though they feel less central than the four *bechor*-*ma'aser* parallels. Nevertheless, the *gemara* treats the comparison as four against four, leaving the analogy-based argument at a standoff.

### Gezeira Shava

Since the analogical argument cannot resolve the question definitively — either comparison could be argued — the *gemara* concludes that Rabbi Shimon actually learns the law through a *gezeira shava*. The word *ha-avarah* appears in the context of *ma'aser*: *yaavor tachat hashevet* — the animals pass under the staff. And the same root appears by *bechor*: *v'ha'avarta kol peter rechem* — you shall cause every opener of the womb to pass. This verbal linkage through *gezeira shava* ties *ma'aser* to *bechor* formally, even though the analogical comparison was inconclusive.

---

## Miscarriage Signs

### Miscarriage Definition

Returning to the central concern of the *masechta*, the *gemara* now addresses the question of how to identify whether what emerged from an animal constitutes a true miscarriage — with implications both for the mother's *tumah* status in the human case and for the *bechor* status of the next birth in the animal case. There are two distinct questions: first, was this in fact an aborted pregnancy rather than some other discharge? Second, even if it was an aborted pregnancy, was the fetus sufficiently developed that its miscarriage exempts the mother from *bechor* for the subsequent birth?

### Raba's Signs

*Heichi dami tinof* — how does one assess a miscarriage? *Amar Rava*: like the shepherds of Tzaltza say, *atzar chayuta*. *Rashi* explains this as meaning that the womb was somehow closed or constricted — *ne'etzar rachmah* — and the fetus dissolved within it, *venimok ha'ubar*. The term *chayuta* may mean the life of the fetus was somehow held back or squeezed out, and the result is what emerges from the animal. This describes the internal mechanism rather than the visual appearance of what one sees.

### Shmuel's Signs

Shmuel describes the appearance more directly: *bavu'ei dedama* — bubbles or clots of blood, a congealed and bloody discharge. This is a description of what one observes externally.

### Expert Consultation

The *gemara* then says: *vetzarich leharot lechacham* — it must be shown to a *chacham* for assessment. But the *gemara* immediately questions this: *chacham mena yada* — what does a Torah scholar in the *beit midrash* know about animal miscarriages? The answer is given by Rav Papa: *ro'eh chacham* — a shepherd who is an expert. When the *gemara* says to show it to a *chacham*, it means an expert in the relevant domain, not a *posek*. The conclusion is explicit: if you want to know whether an animal has miscarried, ask an expert shepherd, not a rabbi.

### Forty Days

Rav Chisda introduces the human parallel: *yetzirat havlad be'ishah arba'im yom* — fetal formation in a human woman occurs at forty days. The halachic significance of this threshold is twofold: if a woman miscarries before forty days, she does not become *teme'ah leidah*, as it is not considered a birth for these purposes; and in the context of *bechor*, if the miscarriage occurs before forty days it is not considered a prior birth and the next child remains a *bechor*, whereas if it occurs after forty days, the next child is exempt. The forty-day threshold is understood as the point at which the fetus has taken on enough form to be halachically recognized as a fetus. What exactly constitutes that formation is a matter of biological interest — the *gemara* seems to understand it in terms of the fetus taking on a recognizable shape, limbs acquiring some form — though the precise developmental biology involved is not fully resolved in the text.

### Animal Development

The question is then raised for animals: *ba'ei Rav Chisda — bevehemah bekammah* — what is the analogous threshold for animals? How much fetal development must there be for an animal's miscarriage to count as a prior birth and exempt the next offspring from *bechor*?

### Ze'iri 30 Days

Rav Papa responds to Abaye: *lav hainu deZe'iri* — is this not what Ze'iri meant when he said *ein nefalim pachot mishloshim yom*, there is no miscarriage with less than thirty days of development? That is, perhaps Ze'iri's statement means that a fetus of less than thirty days' development is not considered a *nefel* — and therefore does not exempt from *bechor*. This is a natural reading of Ze'iri's words, and it is worth noting that it is quite different from how Ze'iri has been understood throughout the preceding discussion, where his statement was read as meaning an animal cannot conceive again within thirty days after a miscarriage.

### Ze'iri Ambiguity

The *gemara* responds: *hahu lekabla itmar* — Ze'iri's statement was said regarding the waiting period after miscarriage, i.e., the animal does not conceive for thirty days afterward. That is the way we have been reading Ze'iri for the last two days. The reading Rav Papa now proposes — that thirty days refers to the minimum fetal development needed for the miscarriage to count — sounds more natural from the words themselves, but the *gemara* does not accept it as the correct interpretation of Ze'iri. And the *gemara* leaves unresolved the underlying question of how much fetal development is required in an animal for the miscarriage to create an exemption from *bechor*. This is a genuine *teku* — how much development is needed remains undetermined.

---

## Buyer Context

### Seller Type

Having discussed what assumptions can be made when an animal's prior birth history is unknown, the *gemara* now turns to a related question: to what degree can one rely on explicit or implicit statements made by the seller? Until now, the discussion assumed one bought from a non-Jew. The *gemara* now addresses the case of buying from a Jew.

### Rav: Silence=No Birth

*Amar Rav: bechor vadai.* Rav's position is that when one buys from a Jew and the seller says nothing, one can conclusively assume the animal has not yet had its firstborn, and the next birth is a *bechor* given to the *kohen*. The reasoning: *de'im itta debackera ishtabochei hava mishtabach lei* — if it had already given birth, the seller would have praised it as a selling point.

### Praise Inference

Why would a prior birth be a selling point? *Rashi*'s explanation is that the seller would have advertised: this animal has already given birth, so you do not need to worry about *bechor*. The animal is, in a manner of speaking, pre-*bechor*ed — the obligation has already been discharged. From the seller's silence we therefore infer that the animal has not yet given birth and the next birth is definitively a *bechor*.

### Health Benefit

*Tosafot* presents a different version of *Rashi*'s text and a different rationale for why a prior birth would be praiseworthy. According to *Tosafot*'s reading, the seller would advertise that the animal has already successfully survived pregnancy and childbirth — proving its capacity to bear young without risk to its life. An animal that has demonstrated this is thereby more valuable. From this angle, the seller's silence indicates he has no such track record to advertise, and the animal has not yet given birth.

### Shmuel: Safek

Shmuel disagrees: *bechor safek* — silence leaves the status uncertain. Nothing can be conclusively inferred from the seller's failure to praise the animal's prior birth history.

### Slaughter Assumption

Shmuel's reasoning: *lishchita ka ba'ei lei* — the seller may have assumed the buyer intended to slaughter the animal immediately, in which case its prior birth history is irrelevant and there would be no occasion to mention it. Indeed, once an animal is slaughtered it may not matter at all whether it had previously given birth, and if anything the prior birth might be a drawback — as one suggested, older animals that have already given birth can have tougher meat. Since silence can be explained by the seller's assumption that the buyer will slaughter, nothing can be inferred from that silence.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan takes the opposite extreme from Rav: *chullin vadai* — one can conclusively assume from the seller's silence that the animal has already given birth and is *chullin*. There is no *bechor* concern.

### Seller Warning

Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: *im issa d'lo bichra, kivan d'ika issura* — if the animal had not yet given birth, and there is therefore a potential *issur* that the buyer might stumble into by not recognizing the next birth as a *bechor*, then *udoi havai modi lei* — the seller would surely have warned the buyer. A responsible person selling an animal to someone who might unknowingly misuse a *bechor* would feel obligated to flag that concern. From the seller's silence, we conclude he has nothing to warn about — the animal has already given birth.

### Responsibility

The *gemara* notes that a *baraita* appears to support Rabbi Yochanan: we know that on four occasions during the year when it is common to purchase animals for slaughter, a butcher who sold the mother and then the child on the same day, or the child and then the mother, must announce this to subsequent buyers — so that the next person who slaughters does not violate *oso v'et beno*. If the butcher said nothing, *holech v'shochet v'eino nimna* — the buyer may proceed to slaughter without concern. Silence implies there is no problem. The *gemara* therefore entertains that this *baraita* supports Rabbi Yochanan and refutes both Rav and Shmuel.

The *gemara* deflects: *hasam b'mocher talyo miltasa, hacha b'lokeach talyo miltasa* — there the obligation falls on the seller, here it falls on the buyer. What does this mean?

### Verse Mandate

*Rashi*'s explanation is that in the case of *oso v'et beno*, there is a specific Torah-derived mandate requiring the seller to announce. *Rashi* understands this from a *pasuk* — *yom echad*, *yom hamiyuchad* — indicating a formal requirement to declare on those particular days. Where such a mandate exists, silence carries evidentiary weight. But in the *bechor* case, no such mandate falls on the seller; the responsibility to inquire belongs to the buyer. Therefore the seller's silence cannot be used to draw any inference, and the cases are distinguishable.

### Knowledge Duty

*Tosafot* offers an explanation grounded in practical reality rather than a formal verse. In the *oso v'et beno* case, the seller knows exactly what has occurred — he sold the mother earlier that day, he knows the buyer intends to slaughter tonight, and he alone possesses the relevant information. Given that he knows what is about to happen, the responsibility falls squarely on him to prevent the buyer from sinning. It is not a verse-derived rule; it is simply that the seller is the only one positioned to prevent the sin and has full knowledge of the facts.

### Mother/Child Case

The seller in the *oso v'et beno* case possesses clear and complete knowledge: he sold the mother, he knows the buyer plans to slaughter, he knows what the consequence will be. There is nothing that should make the buyer suspect a problem — why would the buyer assume the seller had already sold the mother or the child? The buyer has no particular reason to ask. Therefore, the obligation falls entirely on the seller who does have full knowledge.

### Buyer Responsibility

By contrast, in the *bechor* case, the seller's knowledge may be uncertain, the buyer's exposure to risk is not immediate, and there are many scenarios in which the animal's history would not create any problem at all — perhaps the animal is female, perhaps the buyer will wait for a *mum*. There is nothing that specifically heightens the seller's obligation to speak. On the other hand, the buyer has every reason to suspect that an animal of unknown history might not yet have given birth, and it is a straightforward question to ask. The responsibility accordingly falls on the buyer, and the seller's silence carries no evidentiary inference.

According to *Tosafot*, this distinction is not arbitrary but arises from the relative positions of knowledge and moral exposure. How much is it my responsibility, and how much is it buyer beware? The answer depends on: does the seller have full knowledge? Does the seller know the buyer is about to sin? Is the seller the only one who can prevent it? In the *oso v'et beno* case, all three conditions are met and the obligation is fully the seller's. In the *bechor* case, none of them are, and the obligation is the buyer's. This is a more compelling analysis than *Rashi*'s, which makes the distinction somewhat mechanical through appeal to a verse.

### Non-Jew Seller

We now return to the case of buying from a non-Jew. The implicit question is what one can infer from a non-Jewish seller's statements — both explicit and implicit. The prior discussion assumed one simply could not rely on a non-Jew's statement. The *gemara* now makes this explicit.

### Tosafot: Non-Jew

*Tosafot* engages the question directly. *Rashi*'s text, as *Tosafot* reads it, is that even if a non-Jewish seller explicitly praised the animal — saying it had already given birth — one cannot trust him, because he may be saying it merely to increase the sale price: *d'lehashbiach mekach d'oveid kochavim omer kein*. Furthermore, *Tosafot* adds, even if the non-Jew was not speaking with any mercenary intent — even *masiach lefi tumo*, speaking in passing without any agenda of answering a halachic question — *eino ne'eman*, he is still not trusted, because even an unintentional statement may be motivated by the desire to make his merchandise appear more valuable.

### Testimony Principles

This raises a broader halachic question about the reliability of testimony and the factors that affect it. Two distinct concerns emerge in the *gemara*'s framework. The first is intentional misrepresentation for profit: if someone stands to benefit from a statement, we discount it. The second is more subtle — whether someone who is not part of the halachic system fully appreciates the weight of the question being decided. Someone who does not understand what is at stake halachically may give a technically accurate answer without grasping its significance, or may be cavalier about details that would matter greatly to a *posek*.

### System Understanding

These concerns are heightened specifically in the context of non-Jewish sellers because of the dynamic between the Jewish halachic system and those outside it. Within the Jewish community, the mechanism of *areivut* — mutual responsibility — and *lifnei iver* — the prohibition against causing another to sin — create strong incentives for honesty in halachic matters. A Jewish seller who knows a buyer is about to stumble into a *bechor* situation is personally at risk of violating *lifnei iver* if he says nothing. He is not merely being honest for the buyer's sake; he is protecting himself from his own transgression. A non-Jewish seller has no such system of incentives, and that absence is part of what the *gemara* identifies as a reason for reduced reliability in this specific context. The question of whether these observations are framed as general statements about non-Jewish trustworthiness or as statements about the specific dynamics of Jewish–non-Jewish commercial relations in the context of halachic compliance is a matter of ongoing discussion.

---

## Large Animal Miscarriage

### Mishna: Clots

The *gemara* now presents the *mishna* of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: if a large domesticated animal — *behemah gassah*, i.e., a cow — expelled clots or clumps of blood, *harei zo tikkaver* — it must be buried — *peturah min habechorah* — and the mother is exempt from *bechor* for the next birth.

### Bechor Exemption

The burial requirement is stated alongside the exemption from *bechor*, and the combination raises an immediate question. On one hand, the next birth is exempt — this implies that what emerged is considered to have halachic standing as a fetus, as a prior birth. On the other hand, the *mishna* mandates burial, which normally applies to *neveilah* — a carcass that conveys *tumah*. So is this a formed fetus? And if it is, why would it need to be specified that it must be buried?

### Rabbi Chiyya

*Tani Rabbi Hiyya*: it does not cause *tumah* — *einah metammah lo bemaga velo bemassa* — neither through contact nor through carrying. It is therefore not *neveilah* in the conventional sense.

### Burial Paradox

The *gemara* immediately asks: if it does not cause *tumah* — meaning the fetus was not formed — then why must it be buried, and why is the mother exempt from *bechor*? If there is no fetus, there is no prior birth, and burial seems unnecessary.

### Burial Purpose

The *gemara* answers the first question: *kedei lefarsem she'niptarah min habechorah* — the burial is not because the clots constitute *neveilah*, but because burying them announces publicly that the mother has been discharged from the obligation of *bechor*. The act of burial is a declaration: this was treated as a birth, and therefore the next offspring is not a *bechor*.

### Tumah Paradox

But this answer creates the second problem: if the burial functions as a declaration that what emerged is a fetus — enough to exempt the mother — then why doesn't it cause *tumah*? A formed fetus that constitutes a *nefel* ought to convey *tumah* through contact and carrying.

### Bittul B'Rov

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *mishum bittul be-rov* — it is nullified in the majority. There is indeed a fetus present within the discharge. But the fetus is mixed together with a large quantity of non-fetal material — blood, fluid, and other matter from the womb — and in that mixture, the fetal matter loses its legal identity through *bittul be-rov*, nullification in the majority. Since the fetus cannot be identified as a distinct, present entity, it does not convey *tumah*.

### Lost Identity

The result is an unusual combination: there is a fetus here, sufficient to cause the mother's exemption from *bechor*, but the fetus has lost its identity in the surrounding material, and therefore does not cause *tumah*. It exists halachically for one purpose — exempting the mother — but has lost its distinct identity for another — conveying impurity.

### Rabbi Shimon

The *gemara* notes that Rabbi Yochanan is going according to his own reasoning (*ve-azda Rabbi Yochanan le-taameih*), since he had stated that Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon said the same thing. The parallel from Rabbi Shimon is drawn from a *mishna* about the placenta: *ha-shilya ba-bayit, ha-bayit tamei* — if a placenta is found in a house, the house is *tamei*, not because the placenta itself is the fetus, but because there is no placenta without a fetus — *she-ein shilya belo valad*. Rabbi Shimon, however, says: *valad nimok ad she-lo yatza* — the fetus dissolved before it emerged, and therefore does not cause *tumah*.
