### Eating vs. Touching

Shmuel adds one further specification: *v'hani milei b'achila, aval b'negi'ah leis lan bah* — the restriction on *tamei* consumption of *terumah chutz la'aretz* applies only to eating, not to touching. Even a person whose *tum'ah* is of the *yotzei migufo* variety may handle the *terumah* — kneading it, separating it, preparing it — as long as they do not eat it.

---

## Challah Example

### Niddah Challah Case

Avina states: *hilekhach niddah kotza challah* — a woman who is *niddah* and is making *challah* (which has the status of *terumah* outside *Eretz Yisrael*) may touch it, since the restriction is limited to eating. She cannot eat the *challah* herself even though she is married to a *kohen*, because she has *tumah yotzei migufo*. But she may handle it and give it to her minor son, who is a *kohen*. A young son who has not yet reached the age where seminal emission is a concern does not have *tumah yotzei migufo*, and may therefore eat it.

### Tosafot's Question

Tosafot raises a question about the specificity of this ruling: why is a minor son mentioned in particular? If the only issue is *tumah yotzei migufo*, any adult *kohen* who is currently in a *tahor* state — a man who has been to the *mikveh* after a *keri*, for instance — could eat it just as well. Tosafot suggests that perhaps the reason a minor is specified is connected to the quantity involved: *challah chutz la'aretz* is only a small amount, and perhaps the ruling was framed with that in mind, or perhaps there is a view that one should ideally give it to someone who has never had the relevant *tum'ah* at all. However, that reading is a stretch, and it is generally assumed that a minor is mentioned only as an example rather than as a *davka* requirement.

### Burn Alternative

If no minor is available — and more broadly, if there is no one available to eat the *challah* given the *tum'ah* situation — *shakla l'reish masa v'shadi b'tanura*: take it on a skewer and throw it into the oven to burn. This is the familiar practice of burning *challah chutz la'aretz* when it cannot be eaten: the piece separated as *challah* is placed in the oven and burned.

### Two Challot

But burning the *challah* is not the end of the process: *mefarsha challah achrisi, k'heichi d'lo tishtakkach toras challah v'ochla kohen gadol* — one separates a second piece of *challah* so that the institution of *challah* is not forgotten, and this second piece is eaten by an adult *kohen* who is *tahor*. The point is to ensure that the practice of *challah* being given to and eaten by a *kohen* — which is its essential meaning — remains visible and operative, not reduced entirely to the burning of an uneatable piece. Tosafot engages at length with the broader topic of *shtei challahs* — the two *challot* separated in areas of different halachic status relative to *Eretz Yisrael* — a topic that would require considerable time to develop fully.

---

## Woman on Boat

### Tamei Meis Question

The Gemara now presents a narrative. Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rami bar Chama were traveling together on a boat. Rav Amram stepped away momentarily. A woman approached the two remaining rabbis and asked: *tamei meit mahu sheyitbol v'yochal trumas chutza'aretz* — if someone is *tamei* from contact with the dead, may they immerse in a *mikveh* and eat *terumah chutz la'aretz*? The question carries a subtle difficulty: ordinarily, *tum'at meit* cannot be removed by *mikveh* alone — the full purification process requires the sprinkling of *parah adumah* ashes. So what good does immersion do here?

### Rav Nachman Response

Rav Nachman turned to Rami bar Chama and said: *v'chi haza'ah yesh lanu* — do we have the sprinkling of *parah adumah* ashes? The implication: since we do not have the ashes and cannot complete the purification of *tum'at meit* in any case, there is no reason to require waiting for nightfall after immersion either. In fact, the logic extends further: if we already permit *tamei* people to eat *terumah chutz la'aretz* (since only *tumah yotzei migufo* is restricted), and this person's *tum'ah* is *tum'at meit* rather than *yotzei migufo*, they may eat the *terumah* regardless.

### Rav Amram Ruling

Rami bar Chama counseled waiting for Rav Amram's return before issuing a ruling. When Rav Amram returned, he said in the name of Rav: *tamei meit tovel v'ochel b'trumat chutza'aretz* — one who is *tamei* from the dead immerses and may eat *terumah chutz la'aretz* without waiting for nightfall. The Gemara immediately adds: *v'leis hilchasa k'vasei* — and the halacha does not follow this ruling. A similar statement appears regarding *tamei sheretz*: one who became *tamei* through contact with a crawling creature immerses and may eat *terumah chutz la'aretz*, and again *v'leis hilchasa k'vasei*.

### Tosafot Interpretation

The question is: how does the Gemara mean that the halacha does not follow these rulings? One reading would be that the halacha requires waiting until nightfall after immersion. But Tosafot reads it very differently, in a manner consistent with everything we have established: *v'leis hilchasa k'vasei b'ha d'matriach tvilah — ella afilu tvilah lo ba'ei* — the halacha does not follow these rulings in the specific sense that they require immersion at all. One does not even need to go to the *mikveh*. If a person's *tum'ah* is not *tumah yotzei migufo* — and *tum'at meit* and *tum'at sheretz* are not — they may eat *terumah chutz la'aretz* without any intervention whatsoever. Rashi's reading, that one must wait for nightfall, is noted but rejected by Tosafot.

### Inherent Tumah Logic

The underlying logic of this position is captured in a remark made during the discussion. The land of *chutz la'aretz* is itself inherently tamei — *tum'at eretz ha'amim*, the *tum'ah* of the lands of the nations, is a well-known rabbinic concept. The practical upshot: requiring someone living outside *Eretz Yisrael* to purify themselves from *tum'at meit* before eating *terumah* would be entirely futile, since the moment they stepped back outside they would be *tamei* again. Tosafot reads Rav Nachman's rhetorical question — "do we have *haza'ah*?" — not as referring to the absence of *parah adumah* ashes in our time, but as referring to the absurdity of requiring someone in *chutz la'aretz* to travel to *Eretz Yisrael*, obtain sprinkling, and then return — only to immediately incur *tum'ah* again upon leaving. Restricting *terumah chutz la'aretz* to those with *tumah yotzei migufo* is the only logically coherent restriction given this reality.

---

## Year of Bechor

### Shana Beshana

The Gemara now transitions to a new Mishnah: *bechor ne'echal shana beshana* — the *bechor* must be eaten within a year, whether brought as a *korban* or eaten in the context of a *bamah*. A clarification is in order: the Torah elsewhere specifies that certain *korbanot* must come from animals less than a year old, and an animal that exceeds that age is rendered *pasul* as a *korban* because one of its criteria — its age — has not been met. The *bechor* is different. The Torah does not specify a maximum age for a *bechor* as a *korban*; what it specifies is the owner's personal obligation to bring or eat it within the year. Failure to do so does not *pasul* the animal — it simply means the owner was derelict in his obligation. He may still bring it afterward.

### Animal's Own Year

The Mishnah speaks of *blemish arising "within its year"* — using a possessive construction that implies the animal's own year, from birthday to birthday, rather than a calendrical year. Rav Yehuda citing Rav derives this from the verse: *lifnei Hashem Elokecha tochelenu shana beshana* — eat it before God year by year. Reading *shana beshana* as one year entering into another: *eizu shana shenichneset bachaverta* — which year goes into another year? It must be the animal's birthday year, because a birthday year, by definition, spans from one calendar year into the next. A calendar year does not go "into" another calendar year — when one ends, the other begins. A birthday year, however, intersects two calendar years. The possessive *shnato* — "its year" — thus refers to the twelve months from the animal's birth.

### Verse Derivation

The derivation is elegant: the doubled language *shana beshana*, if read straightforwardly as two separate calendar years, would imply only "every year." But read as one year entering into another, it points toward a year that bridges two calendrical periods — the animal's biographical year. That is how we know the obligation is measured from birthday to birthday rather than from the new year.

---

## School of Rav

### Two Calendar Years

The school of Rav (*debei Rav*) offers a different *derasha* from the same phrase *shana beshana*. Rather than reading it as pointing toward the animal's biographical year, they read it as teaching a new halacha about the span over which the *bechor* may be eaten as a *korban*: *yom echad beshana zu v'yom echad beshana zo* — one day in one calendar year and one day in another calendar year. That is, the *bechor* may be eaten across two different calendar years. This would be the case if it is brought on *erev Rosh Hashanah* — one day's eating in the outgoing year, another day's eating in the incoming year.

### Two Days One Night

This *derasha* teaches a new halacha: *limed al habechor shene'echal lishnei yamim velaylah echad* — the *bechor* is eaten over two days and the intervening night. Until now, it was not clear how long the *bechor* may be eaten. Some *korbanot* are eaten for only one day; others, like *shelamim*, for two days. The *derasha* of *shana beshana* — that it may span two calendar years — tells us it has the eating-period of a two-day *korban*. If it may be brought on *erev Rosh Hashanah* and eaten into *Rosh Hashanah*, it has an eating span that crosses two days.

### Linked to Shelamim

But if *debei Rav* uses *shana beshana* to establish the two-day eating period, where does Rav himself (who used that verse to establish the birthday-year measurement) derive the two-day eating period? The answer is from a different verse. When the Torah speaks about the *bechor* given to the *kohanim*, it says: *u'vesaram yihyeh lach, ke-chazeh hatenufah u'khe-shok hayamin* — the flesh will be yours, like the breast and the right thigh of the *shelamim*. The Torah explicitly equates the *bechor* with the breast and thigh of the *shelamim*. Since *shelamim* is the paradigmatic two-day *korban*, the equation teaches that the *bechor* is also eaten for two days and the intervening night: *hikisho hakatuv le-chazeh v'shok shel shelamim — mah halan lishnei yamim velaylah echad, af kan lishnei yamim velaylah echad*.

### Todah Objection

An objection is raised: the *shelamim* is not a monolithic category. The *todah* — the thanksgiving offering — is a type of *shelamim*, yet it is eaten for only one day and night. Perhaps the Torah's equation of the *bechor* with the breast and thigh of the *shelamim* should be understood more narrowly, and we should link the *bechor* to the *todah* rather than to the standard *shelamim*. If so, the eating period would be only one day.

### Lach Yihyeh Response

The response: *amar kra lach yihyeh* — the verse adds the phrase "it will be for you," which *hosif lach hakatuv havayah acheret* — the Torah grants to the recipient of the *bechor* an additional measure of ownership. This extra ownership indicates that the *bechor* is not like the *todah*, which is more restricted; it carries the more generous scope of the standard *shelamim*, and therefore it is eaten for two days and the intervening night.

---

---

# Bekhorot 28

## Bechor's First Year

### Intro & Overview

The daf opens three lines down from the top, with the word *ve-idach*, picking up a discussion that had been underway regarding the *mishna*'s ruling that a *bechor* must be brought within the first year — or, if it is a *ba'al mum*, eaten within the first year. As the *Gemara* in Rosh Hashanah makes clear, this does not mean the animal becomes *pasul* after the first year. Unlike other animals where the validity of the *korban* depends on the animal's age, the requirement here governs the obligation of the owners: they must bring it within the first year. This distinction prompted *Tosafos* to raise the question of whether *bal te'acher* — the prohibition against postponing one's *korbanos* for a year — would already cover this case. *Tosafos* resolves the difficulty by noting that, depending on how the calendar falls, one might not have three *regalim* occur within the animal's first year, and since *bal te'acher* is defined by the passage of three *regalim*, the independent obligation of the first year is not redundant. The essential point, however, remains: this rule is about the owner's obligation, not the animal's validity.

### Obligation vs. Validity

The *Gemara* derives this obligation from the *pasuk* of *shanah b'shanah* — "year by year." The ensuing discussion turns to what each side does with additional *pesukim*, since *shanah b'shanah* had already been used to teach that the *bechor* may be eaten for two days and the intervening night.

### Shlamim vs. Todah

The *Gemara* raises the question of why the eating period is two days and a night rather than one day and a night, as with a *todah*. One view holds that the comparison is to *shlamim*. Another position counters that the phrase *yiheyeh lach* — "it shall be yours" — implies something additional, and therefore the eating period extends like *shlamim* rather than *todah*. The opposing view responds that *yiheyeh lach* might not be teaching the duration of eating at all. Instead, it may be coming to teach us that even when the *bechor* develops a blemish, it is still given to the *kohen* — a novel principle that the *Gemara* notes is not found anywhere else in the *Torah*: *she-lo matzinu b'chol ha-Torah kulah*.

### Blemished Bechor Status

*Tosafos* explains why this phrase is deployed here with particular emphasis. Normally when we say "we haven't found this anywhere else in the Torah," it simply means the *pasuk* is teaching something new. But here the phrase is meant to convey something genuinely exceptional. The novelty is this: a *ba'al mum* — a blemished *bechor* — is eaten outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, without being redeemed, while retaining its *kedushah*, and is still given to the *kohen*. This is highly unusual; the only parallel is *ma'aser*. Because this *chiddush* is so fundamental, the *Gemara* argues that *yiheyeh lach* is needed to teach it, and cannot simultaneously be used to derive the two-day eating period.

The *Gemara* then presents the counter-response: the verse *u-vesaram yiheyeh lach* uses the plural form — "their flesh shall be yours" — which implies *echad tam v'echad ba'al mum*, whether unblemished or blemished, the *kohanim* receive it. From the plural *u-vesaram* alone one can derive that a blemished *bechor* is given to the *kohen* without redemption, thus freeing *yiheyeh lach* for another purpose. The reply to this is that *u-vesaram* simply refers to all *bechoros* of the Jewish people collectively, not to two distinct categories of blemished and unblemished animals.

### Two Days & Night

The discussion settles several foundational *halachos* of *bechor*. First, it must be brought within the first year, measured from the animal's birth rather than by the calendar year, and if brought after a year it remains *kosher*. Second, even with a blemish, the *kohen* eats it without redemption, outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, while its *kedushah* remains intact. Third, it is eaten for two days and the intervening night.

---

## Blemish & Extensions

### Mishna's Ambiguity

The *mishna* then addresses what happens when a *bechor* develops a blemish, and the question of how much time the owner retains. The *mishna* states: *nolad lo mum b'soch shnaso rashai l'kaymo kol shneim asar chodesh* — if the *bechor* develops a blemish during the first year, one may keep it for the full twelve months. The *mishna* then adds that afterwards one may keep it for thirty days. The precise meaning of this is ambiguous, and the *Gemara* sets out to clarify it.

### Two Readings

The *Gemara* presents two possible readings. The first reading: if the blemish develops during the year, one has the full twelve months — *and* an additional thirty days after the year ends. The second reading: if the blemish develops during the year, one has only until the end of the twelve months and no more. If the blemish develops after the year — meaning one had no choice but to wait — then one has thirty days from that point, and no more.

The logic strongly favors the second reading. If the blemish appears early in the year, say in the first month, there is no obvious rationale for granting an additional thirty days on top of the full year. The sensible principle is: one has until the end of the year, *or* thirty days from when the blemish developed, whichever comes later. The *Gemara* then introduces a *baraisa* to explore these readings further.

### Modern Practice

The *baraisa* introduces the modern context: *bechor b'zman hazeh* — nowadays, when the *bechor* cannot be brought as a *korban*. In this situation one has no choice but to wait for the animal to develop a blemish. Since the animal must wait for a *mum* in any case, the clock cannot begin running until one has both a blemish and the opportunity to present it to an expert for inspection.

### Waiting for Blemish

The *baraisa* states: *ad shelo nira lehar'oso lechacham* — before the animal has developed a blemish and there is someone available to inspect it — *rashai l'kaymo shtayim veshalosh shanim*, one may hold onto it for two, three years. *Tosafos* points out that this would be almost tautological if it simply meant the animal has no blemish yet, since there is nothing to do with it in any case. Rather, *Tosafos* understands the phrase to mean that even when a blemish has appeared, if no qualified expert is immediately available, one is not required to travel great distances or expend significant effort to find one. One may wait however long it takes — two or three years if necessary — until an expert becomes accessible. This is an important ruling: the obligation does not require extraordinary measures to arrange inspection.

### Hashavas Aveida

Once a blemish has developed and an expert is available, the *baraisa* distinguishes between two scenarios. If the blemish developed during the year: *rashai l'kaymo kol yud-bet chodesh*, one has until the end of the twelve months. If after the year: *eino rashai l'kaymo afilu yom echad*, technically one should not even have a single day, since the year has already passed. Nevertheless, *mipnei hashavas aveida leba'alim* — because of concern for returning loss to the owners — the rabbis granted thirty additional days.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

*Rashi* and *Tosafos* differ on what *hashavas aveida* means in this context. *Rashi* understands it as a case where no *kohen* is available to receive the animal. If one were required to *shecht* it immediately with no *kohen* available, the meat would rot and the *kohanim* would receive nothing. The thirty days therefore allow time to locate a *kohen*, protecting the *kohen*'s interests.

*Tosafos* describes a less extreme scenario. The *mishna* already provides that the *yisrael* gives the animal to the *kohen* after a month or two, so the *kohen* is presumably already in possession. The *hashavas aveida* concern for *Tosafos* is simply that the *kohen* may not need thirty pounds of meat at that very moment. Requiring immediate *shechita* would force him to absorb a needless loss. Granting thirty days allows the *kohen* to arrange the sale or consumption of the meat in a way that minimizes waste. This is accordingly a lower threshold — the *kohen* could *shecht* it right away, but the thirty days give him the opportunity to make the most of it.

### 15-Day Proof

The *Gemara* then introduces a proof case to resolve the ambiguity. A *baraisa* states: *nolad lo mum b'chamisha asar yom b'toch shnaso* — if the blemish developed with fifteen days remaining in the year — *mashlimin lo chamisha asar yom achar shnaso*, one receives those fifteen days plus an additional fifteen days after the year, completing the thirty. This case makes the principle clear. If the blemish had appeared early in the year, granting a year and thirty days would be excessive. If it appeared after the year, thirty days are granted from that point. If it appeared with fifteen days remaining, one receives fifteen days plus fifteen more. The operative rule is thus: thirty days from when the blemish developed, *or* until the end of the year, whichever comes later. *Shma mina* — this is the conclusion.

### Rabbi Eliezer

The *Gemara* notes that this ruling supports *Rabbi Eliezer*, who said: *notnin lo shloshim yom mishaa shenolad bo mum* — thirty days are given from the time the blemish develops. This formulation means that if the thirty days extends past the end of the year, one benefits from those days; if the year ends first, the year is the limit. This is precisely the principle established by the *baraisa*.

### Alt. Rabbi Eliezer

However, there is an alternative tradition of *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position. This version states: how do we know that if the blemish developed during the year, one receives thirty days *after* the year — i.e., a full year plus thirty days regardless? *Rabbi Eliezer* derives it from the phrase *shanah b'shanah*: "year by year." He asks, what constitutes a halachically significant "year" in some contexts? Thirty days — since we sometimes treat thirty days of a year as symbolically representing the entire year. Therefore *shanah b'shanah* implies two years, with the second "year" consisting of at least thirty days, granting everyone fundamentally a year and a month.

The *Gemara* challenges this position with the *baraisa*: if the blemish developed fifteen days before the end of the year, one receives *mashlimin* — the remaining fifteen days are completed up to thirty, not an entirely new thirty-day period. *Hashlama in, mi-hava lo* — making up the thirty days, yes; granting an additional thirty on top of a full year, no. This constitutes a *teyuvta* — a decisive refutation — of *Rabbi Eliezer*'s second formulation.

The practical upshot is this: nowadays, since the animal cannot be offered as a *korban*, one waits for a blemish to appear. Once it does, and an expert is accessible, the time allotted is until the end of the year or at least thirty days, whichever comes later — granted by the rabbis as a concession to prevent undue loss.

---

## Pre-Shechita Issues

### Before vs. After

The *Gemara* turns to the next *mishna*, which concerns what happens when a *bechor* is *shechted* before its blemish is inspected by a qualified expert. The *mishna* presents two positions. *Rabbi Yehuda* permits relying on an inspection conducted after the *shechita*: if the blemish is then determined to be genuine, the animal may be eaten. *Rabbi Meir* forbids it: *ho'il v'nishchat shelo al pi mumche assur* — since it was *shechted* without the ruling of an expert, it is forbidden regardless of what the post-*shechita* inspection reveals.

### Non-Expert Ruling

The *mishna* then presents a separate case: *mi she'eino mumche shera'ah es habechor v'nishchat al piv* — someone who is not a qualified expert examined the *bechor* and it was *shechted* on the basis of that examination. In such a case, *harei zeh yikaver* — the animal must be buried — and the person who gave the ruling must compensate the owner from his own assets for the loss caused by his unauthorized ruling. The *Gemara* notes that the instruction to bury it applies regardless of what a subsequent inspection might reveal. This is because the *Gemara* reads this ruling as consistent with *Rabbi Meir*'s position that *shechita* on the basis of an unauthorized ruling is entirely illegitimate.

### Eye vs. Body Blemish

*Rabba bar bar Chana* offers a key clarification. Regarding *dukin she'ba'ayin* — cataracts of the eye — *chulei alma lo pligi*, everyone agrees it is forbidden to rely on a post-*shechita* inspection, because such blemishes *mishtanin* — they change at or around the moment of death. A ruling made after *shechita* therefore cannot tell us what the eye looked like before. By contrast, *mumim she'beguf* — blemishes on the body — do not change at the moment of death, and a post-*shechita* inspection reliably reflects the animal's pre-*shechita* condition. The debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* therefore concerns only this latter category.

### Rabbi Meir's Gezeirah

*Rabbi Meir* holds: *gazrinan mumim she'beguf atu dokin she'ba'ayin* — we make a *gezeira* that if we permit reliance on post-*shechita* inspection for body blemishes, it will lead people to do the same in cases of eye cataracts, where it is invalid. Therefore *Rabbi Meir* prohibits even the legitimate cases.

### Rabbi Yehuda View

*Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees: *lo gazrinan mumim she'beguf atu dokin she'ba'ayin* — we do not extend the prohibition from one category to the other. Since body blemishes provide a reliable basis for ruling, we permit the post-*shechita* inspection in those cases without concern that it will be confused with the eye-blemish scenario.

One might ask why *Rabbi Meir* does not frame his concern differently — namely, as a *knas* against the irresponsible behavior of *shechting* without prior inspection, rather than as a *gezeira* against confusion between cases. Indeed, allowing someone to salvage the situation after the fact by inspecting post-*shechita* could be seen as encouraging the bad behavior of not seeking inspection beforehand. Yet the *Gemara* frames *Rabbi Meir*'s rationale as a *gezeira* about the slippery slope from body blemishes to eye blemishes, not as a penalty for procedural negligence.

### Slippery Slope

This distinction carries significant practical weight. The *Gemara* elsewhere establishes that *halacha k'Rabbi Meir b'gezeirotav* — we rule like *Rabbi Meir* when he makes a *gezeira*.

### Knas Analysis

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* notes that the language of the *mishna* — *ho'il v'nishchat shelo al pi mumche assur* — suggests that what is driving *Rabbi Meir* is the violation of procedure: the animal was *shechted* without an expert ruling. This language implies a *knas*, a fine for wrongdoing, rather than a *gezeira* designed to prevent confusion between cases. *Tosafos* draws a sharp distinction between the two: *b'gezeirotav velo b'knasav* — we rule like *Rabbi Meir* when he makes a *gezeira*, but not when he imposes a *knas*. Since the *Gemara* here frames the ruling as a *knas*, *Tosafos* concludes that we do not rule like *Rabbi Meir* in this instance. The question of whether *Rabbi Meir* is making a *gezeira* or a *knas* is therefore not only a matter of conceptual clarity but has direct implications for the *halacha*.

### Variability Question

The *Gemara* then raises a further question: when we say that *dokin she'ba'ayin* change after death, do we mean all such blemishes change, or only some?

### Witness Testimony

The practical stakes of this question concern the reliability of witness testimony. If all *dokin she'ba'ayin* change, then witnesses who testify that the blemish looked exactly the same before *shechita* as after must be lying — *shakrinei hinhu* — since we know that change is universal. In that case, a *chacham* could never accurately assess the pre-*shechita* state of the eye, and no reliable ruling could be made even with witness support.

### Some Change, Some Don't

However, if some change and some do not, then witness testimony can be trusted in the cases where no change occurred, and the *chacham* can issue a valid ruling based on what he observes combined with what the witnesses attest.

### Rabbi Yoshiya Demo

*Rabba bar bar Chana* reports: *sach li Rabbi Yoshiya demin Osha* — *Rabbi Yoshiya* of *Osha* told me: *bo va'arecha be-dukin she'ein mishtanin* — come, let me show you cases of *dokin* where the blemish does not change. The *Gemara* infers from this — *miklal de'ika demishtanei ve'ika delo mishtanei* — that some change and some do not, since he was pointing out specific cases as examples rather than demonstrating a universal phenomenon. This resolves the question: witnesses can be trusted, and *chacham* rulings can be made reliably in those cases where the blemish is known not to change.

This passage touches on a broader and genuinely striking question about the relationship between *halacha* and empirically observed facts. The *Gemara*'s willingness to declare witnesses unreliable — *lachushei sahadi* — if their testimony contradicts the received understanding of how *dokin she'ba'ayin* behave reflects a general disposition toward authoritative tradition over direct observation. This same issue surfaces in the *Rashba*'s *teshuvah* on the question of *treifos*: if witnesses attest that an animal survived a condition the *Gemara* classifies as fatal, does that revise the list of *treifos*? The *Rashba* holds that such testimony cannot be accepted, because accepting facts that contradict the statements of *Chazal* would undermine the authority of received tradition. This approach is not unique to *halacha*; the pre-modern world broadly privileged authoritative texts over empirical evidence — Galen's anatomical descriptions, for example, were presumed correct even when dissection seemed to suggest otherwise.

A related nuance also surfaces here: the combination of expert assessment and witness testimony. The *chacham* observes the blemish directly after *shechita*, while the witnesses attest that no change occurred. The expert's ruling depends not only on his own observation but on the reliability of testimony he cannot independently verify. This interplay of expertise and testimony — the expert sees what is present now, the witnesses supply the historical fact of continuity — raises interesting questions about the structure of authoritative rulings that will recur throughout the discussion that follows.

---

## Judicial Liability (III)

### Civil Errors

The *Gemara* now broadens its discussion to the larger question of judicial malpractice. The *mishna* presents the paradigm case: *dan et hadin zika et hachayav ve-chiyav et hazakai* — a judge who ruled that a liable party was exempt, or that an exempt party was liable. Similarly, he may have declared *tamei* what was *tahor*, or *tahor* what was *tamei*. In all such cases, *mah she'asa asuy* — what has been done is done. The ruling is not reversed. Nevertheless, *ve-yeshalem mibeito* — the judge must compensate the injured party from his own assets.

---

## Compensation Rates

### Quarter vs. Half

A *baraisa* specifies that compensation is not at the full value of the animal. Rather, one pays a quarter of the value for *behema daka* — small grazing animals — and half for *behema gasa* — cattle.

### Not Full Loss

The reason compensation falls short of the full loss is that the *bechor* situation involves inherent uncertainty. Nowadays the animal can only be *shechted* once it develops a *mum*, and it is possible the animal never develops a *mum* at all, or develops one only in old age after significant investment. The actual loss is therefore not equivalent to the full current value of the animal, which is why liability is capped at a fraction.

### Value Difference

*Rav Papa* explains the disparity between the two fractions by noting that cattle represent a far greater absolute loss than small animals — *zeh hefsed merubeh ve-zeh hefsed mu'at*. The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: if the only difference is the absolute magnitude of the loss, one should simply pay half of the relevant amount in each case, and the proportion should be identical. Merely pointing to the difference in absolute value does not explain why the rate itself — a quarter versus a half — differs.

### Grazing Discouragement

*Rav Huna bar Manoach* in the name of *Rav Acha* the son of *Rav Ika* offers the definitive answer: *mishum gezeirat megadlei behema daka nagu bah* — the lower rate for grazing animals reflects the rabbinic prohibition against raising small livestock in settled areas of *Eretz Yisrael*. Grazing animals strip vegetation entirely and can seriously damage the land when kept in one place. Because the institution of raising such animals is disapproved of, the compensation rate is reduced accordingly.

This explanation, however, contains an apparent difficulty: the person who suffers from the lower compensation is not the owner who raised the disapproved animals, but rather the *kohen* — who may well have received the animal legitimately. It is the *chacham* who pays less, and it is the *kohen* whose recovery is reduced. The person who bore no wrongdoing absorbs the consequence of a disapproved practice by someone else.

### Rashi Alt. View

This difficulty may explain why *Rashi* offers an alternative explanation. Rather than grounding the lower rate in the *gezeira* against raising small livestock, *Rashi* argues that the lower rate reflects the lower return on investment that *behema daka* yields in any case. By the time the animal eventually develops a blemish after years of maintenance and expense, the net benefit to the *kohen* would have been considerably less than its current market value suggests. Accordingly, the actual loss the *kohen* sustains is genuinely smaller for grazing animals than for cattle, making the lower proportion fair as a reflection of realistic diminished return. This reading also sidesteps the problem raised by the *gezeira* explanation, since it focuses on what the *kohen* would actually have received rather than on penalizing a practice for which he bears no responsibility.

---

## Grama & Garmi

### Garmi Definition

This brings the *Gemara* to the general principles of causation in damages. The well-known principle is *grama be-nizikin patur* — indirect causation in damages is exempt from liability. But there is a category identified with *Rabbi Meir* called *garmi*, which occupies an intermediate position: more direct than ordinary *grama*, though still not a fully physical act of damage in the classic sense. *Garmi* is distinguished from *mazik* — direct physical damage — on one end, and from remote *grama* on the other. The *Ramban* devoted an entire *kuntres* to analyzing the *garmi* cases in the *Gemara*, precisely because the line between categories is difficult to draw with precision.

---

## Judicial Liability (III)

### Purity Rulings

Returning to the *mishna*, the *Gemara* addresses the cases of *tima et ha-tahor ve-tiher et ha-tamei* — declaring something *tamei* that was *tahor*, or *tahor* that was *tamei*.

### What's Done Done

*Mah she'asa asuy* — what has been done is done — is straightforward in the civil case: money that has changed hands cannot be clawed back. But in the *tumah* and *tahara* cases, the phrase requires clarification. If a ruling was simply wrong, one would expect to reverse it. The *Gemara* will explain below how concrete physical actions were taken that make the ruling's effects irreversible.

### Mumche Exemption

However, the *mishna* qualifies the liability rule with a crucial exception: *im haya mumche le-veit din patur mi-leshalem* — if the judge was a court-authorized expert, he is exempt from paying. The *mumche le-veit din* status — which involves licensing, community recognition, and demonstrable expertise, as discussed in *Sanhedrin* — carries with it exemption from financial liability. Two possible rationales present themselves. The first is purely pragmatic: without such protection, no one would be willing to accept the responsibility of rendering rulings. The second, and perhaps more analytically compelling, rationale is that an expert of such recognized standing who makes an error is presumed to have committed not a negligent mistake but an *oness* — an unavoidable, unforeseeable occurrence for which liability is inappropriate.

---

## Grama & Garmi (II)

### Taking & Handing

The *Gemara* asks whether the *mishna*'s liability cases even constitute *garmi* or *mazik*, and *Rav Elazar* in the name of *Rav* explains. In the case of *mechayev et ha-zakkai* — obligating an exempt party — the *Gemara* posits a scenario of direct physical action: *kegon she-natal ve-natan be-yad* — the judge himself physically took the money from *Reuven* and handed it to *Shimon*. In this scenario, the judge is a direct *mazik* and liability is clear.

### Collateral Example

For the case of *zika et ha-chayav* — exempting the liable party — physical action is harder to construct, since simply declaring someone exempt involves no physical act. *Ravina* provides the scenario: *Reuven* held *Shimon*'s jewelry as collateral, worth the amount of the disputed debt. The judge ruled *Reuven* exempt, and to demonstrate the finality of his ruling, physically took the collateral from *Shimon*'s possession and returned it to *Reuven*. Since *Reuven* was not in fact exempt, the judge took something *Shimon* had legal rights to and removed it from his control. That is a direct physical damage, and the judge must compensate.

### Mixing Grain

In the case of *tima et ha-tahor* — declaring *tahor* things *tamei* — the direct action is constructed as follows: the judge takes a *sheretz* and physically throws it onto the *terumah* to prove his point, thereby actively making *tahor* produce *tamei*. This explains both the physical causation and the irreversibility signified by *mah she'asa asuy*.

### Mixing Proof

For the reverse case, *tiher et ha-tamei* — declaring *tamei* things *tahor* — the scenario is: *she'irvev im peirotav*, the judge mixes the questionable grain with the *kohen*'s *tahor terumah* to prove his ruling that it is *tahor*. When it turns out the grain was *tamei*, the entire mixture is now compromised. This explains both the physical action and the resulting loss: the *kohen* loses his *tahor terumah* because it has been irreversibly mixed with *tamei* produce.

### Ruling Binding?

This also illuminates the phrase *mah she'asa asuy* in the *tumah* context. The case of *tiher et ha-tamei* is particularly useful, because in that case alone it is not obvious what loss was caused by the ruling as such — the judge declared something *tahor*, and one might ask what financial harm that produces. The mixing scenario creates the loss and demonstrates the irreversibility. But it also raises a deeper question: does the judge's ruling have independent halachic force? If a *rav* rules something is *tahor*, does it actually become *tahor* for halachic purposes, such that another *rav* cannot simply overrule it? There is direct discussion in the *Gemara* about one rabbi overruling another in a *halacha* ruling. In the case of *tiher et ha-tamei*, however, the ruling cannot actually render something *tahor* if it is truly *tamei*, which is precisely why the mixing scenario is necessary to explain the mechanism of the loss.

---

## Judicial Liability (III)…

### Rabbi Tarfon Story

The *Gemara* now presents the famous story of *Rabbi Tarfon*. A cow was brought before him that was missing its uterus — whether congenitally or surgically removed was unclear. *Rabbi Tarfon* ruled it was a *treifa* and ordered it fed to the dogs, since one may not eat a *treifa*. The case was then brought before the sages at *Yavneh*, who ruled that an animal lacking a uterus is in fact not a *treifa* at all.

### Todos Evidence

The basis for the sages' ruling was the testimony of *Todos the doctor*, who stated: *ein parah ve-chazirah yotzet me-Alexandria shel Mitzrayim she-ein chotchin ha-em shelah bishvil she-lo teled* — no cow or pig leaves Alexandria of Egypt without its uterus having been surgically removed, so that the animals cannot breed outside the city, thereby preserving the Alexandrians' monopoly on their specialized breeds. Since these animals were known to survive the procedure and live productively, it was proven that the absence of a uterus is not a fatal defect. Notably, while the *Gemara* earlier was inclined to dismiss the testimony of witnesses when their account conflicted with received knowledge, here expert factual testimony is accepted and it reshapes the *halachic* ruling.

When *Rabbi Tarfon* heard the sages' ruling, he exclaimed: *chamorkha Tarfon* — there goes your donkey, *Tarfon* — implying that he now expected to have to sell his most valuable asset to compensate for the loss his erroneous ruling had caused.

### Akiva Response

*Rabbi Akiva* responded immediately: *Tarfon, atah mumcheh le-veit din, ve-chol ha-mumcheh le-veit din patur mi-leshalem* — you are a court-authorized expert, and any expert authorized by the court is exempt from liability. *Rabbi Tarfon*'s exemption from paying is therefore clear. What is striking, however, is that *Rabbi Tarfon* himself did not know this rule, and had to be reminded of his own status by *Rabbi Akiva*. There is something quite ironic in this: the same *Rabbi Tarfon* who possessed *mumche* status and was protected by it was unaware that his status carried this exemption. This raises a genuine question about what *mumche* status actually requires — it evidently signifies recognized expertise and communal authorization, but it does not require encyclopedic knowledge of every *halacha*, even *halachos* directly pertinent to the *mumche*'s own position.

---

## Error Categories

### Black-Letter Error

The *Gemara* adds that *Rabbi Tarfon* might in any case have been exempt on an entirely different and seemingly opposite basis. The principle of *toeh b'dvar mishna* holds that if a judge makes an error in a matter of obvious, black-letter law — something that is explicitly and clearly stated — the ruling is not considered a binding ruling at all. A *mishna* in *Chullin* lists a missing uterus among the conditions that do *not* make an animal a *treifa*, which means *Rabbi Tarfon*'s error was precisely this kind of blatant mistake.

### Judgment Error

By contrast, *toeh b'shikul hadaas* — an error in judgment — refers to a case where reasonable arguments exist on both sides, the general practice runs one way, but one could understand how a judge might have concluded otherwise. Such a ruling, even if wrong, is still binding as a ruling.

### Void & Exempt

The distinction carries a decisive practical consequence. A *toeh b'dvar mishna* ruling is treated as a non-ruling: *chozer*, it is reversed. And since it never constituted a valid ruling, no liability attaches to it. A *toeh b'shikul hadaas* ruling, by contrast, remains binding despite being wrong — *mah she'asa asuy* — and the judge must compensate for the resulting loss.

The rationale is subtle and worth pausing over. Why should a *wrong* ruling remain binding? Because although the outcome was incorrect, the process fell within the reasonable bounds of legitimate judicial reasoning. It is analogous to an appellate court's standard of review: not every error is reversed. Since the ruling was within bounds, it stands. But since it was in the end wrong, the judge bears financial responsibility for the harm it caused.

### Obvious Error

In *Rabbi Tarfon*'s case, however, the *mishna* in *Chullin* explicitly includes the missing uterus among non-*treifa* conditions. His error was not in judgment but in failing to apply a clear and explicit ruling. *Toeh b'dvar mishna* therefore applies, the ruling is void, and there is no liability.

### Both Extremes

The *Gemara* notes the remarkable paradox: *Rabbi Tarfon* is exempt from liability either because he is a *mumche* — one extreme of expertise — or because his error was so blatant as to constitute no ruling at all — the opposite extreme. Both routes lead to the same result.

### Indirect Causation

But a further complication arises. Even granting that it was not a binding ruling, *Rabbi Tarfon*'s statement still caused the animal to be fed to the dogs. (*Rashi* clarifies that *Rabbi Tarfon* did not literally feed it himself; rather, it was fed to the dogs on the basis of his ruling.) But if his pronouncement was technically a non-ruling, why did the owner's act of feeding it to the dogs flow from *Rabbi Tarfon*'s responsibility at all? The answer has to do with the structure of *grama*: if the statement is formally a ruling, one can argue that it directly caused the resulting action — the owner had no choice but to comply. If it was not a ruling, the causal chain becomes more attenuated. The owner acted on something that was not formally binding; the causal connection now looks more like indirect *grama*, for which the *Gemara* generally does not impose liability. This is a genuinely difficult point: the formalization of a statement as a ruling is what elevates the causal connection from *grama* to something more direct, yet the very same formalization also triggers the question of whether it was a legitimate ruling in the first place.

### Canonization

The *Gemara*'s discussion of *toeh b'dvar mishna* also raised a broader question among the *rishonim*: what texts and opinions are sufficiently authoritative that contradicting them constitutes a *dvar mishna*-level error? Are the opinions of the *Geonim* in this category, such that ruling against them would be *toeh b'dvar mishna*? This question led to extended discussion among the *rishonim* about which texts become canonized within *halacha* to the degree that they carry that status, and to what extent everything written after the *mishna* and *Gemara* falls into the category of *shikul hadaas* — reasoned judgment that may legitimately be contested.

---

---

# Bekhorot 29

## Judicial Liability Review

### Bad vs. No Judgment

The present daf opens by returning briefly to the major themes of daf 28, which centered on the question of judicial liability for legal malpractice. The discussion there explored a fundamental distinction: on one end of the spectrum, a ruling so defective that it cannot even be characterized as a *din* at all — provided the judge did not physically transfer funds — carries no liability; on the other end, a *mumche l'din*, a licensed and acknowledged expert judge, is likewise free from liability. These two exemptions bracket the middle ground where liability actually attaches.

### Kiblu Aleihu & Din Torah

This framework connects to a broader discussion found in Sanhedrin concerning the role of *kiblu aleihu* — the parties' acceptance of a particular individual as their adjudicator. Where the parties accepted the judge unconditionally, with no further stipulations, there would be no liability, as the ruling would not be characterized as a *to'eh* in any meaningful sense. However, where the acceptance was contingent — for instance, where the parties normally could not have gone before a single judge or a relative, but agreed to do so on the condition that the judge issue a genuine *din torah*, a binding halachic ruling — the full framework of error and liability still applies. That discussion, however, belongs to Sanhedrin and is not taken up here.

### Liability: Error vs. Aut…

A further ambiguity in the *mishnah* is worth noting before moving on. The case of the *bechor* established that a person who was not a recognized expert — an *eino mumche* — bore liability when his ruling led to an improper *shechita*. But the subsequent *mishnah*, which simply states that one who judges and errs must pay, does not specify that a mistake was actually made. By juxtaposition, the *mishnah* seems to suggest that even a correct ruling by an unauthorized judge triggers liability — as though the lack of authorization is itself the disqualifying factor, regardless of outcome. Yet the *gemara* here, like the *gemara* in Sanhedrin, engages at length with the question of *to'eh b'dvar mishna* versus *to'eh b'shikul hadaas* — error in black-letter law versus error in judgment — and the case of Rabbi Tarfon cited there is a clear instance of an actual mistake. So there remains some ambiguity: does liability follow from demonstrable error, or does the *mishnah* treat the absence of authorization as constructively equivalent to error, regardless of whether the ruling itself was correct?

---

## Ilo & Fee Structure

### Ilo Exception

With those questions noted, the *gemara* turns to an entirely different domain — the question of accepting payment for the performance of religious functions. The *mishnah* at the bottom of 28b states: *hanotel sachar lirot es habechorot* — one who accepts a fee for inspecting *bechorot* — *ein shochtin al piv*, one may not *shecht* on his ruling. The very fact that payment is involved renders his determinations suspect, even if he is otherwise expert. One might ask whether expertise alone is not sufficient to validate the ruling; but the *mishnah* makes clear that financial interest overrides the presumption of competence.

The *mishnah* then introduces an exception: *ke'ilo b'yavne* — like Ilo, the recognized *bechor* inspector in Yavne, whom the *chachamim* permitted to take four *issarot* for a small animal and six for a large animal, whether he ruled it *tam* or *ba'al mum*.

### Ilo's Piety

Rashi explains the exception briefly but pointedly: *ke'ilo hadar b'yavne dechasid hava v'lo nechshad bekach* — Ilo was so extraordinarily pious that there was no objective ground for suspicion that payment would influence his rulings. His personal character removed the concern that animates the general prohibition.

### Flat Fee Logic

The *gemara* first asks why the fee for a large animal exceeds that for a small one. The answer is straightforward: *hai nafish tirchei v'hai lo nafish tirchei* — one involves considerably more effort than the other. One might have assumed that since the inspection focuses on a specific suspected blemish rather than the whole animal, the size difference is irrelevant. Rashi explains otherwise: *gassa nafish tirchaihu l'hashlicha l'aretz l'chpota v'liros muma* — a cow must be brought to the ground and held down in order to examine the blemish properly, which is a substantially more demanding physical task. The differential fee reflects that differential effort.

The *gemara* then probes the logic of the flat fee structure. The payment seems justified when the ruling is *ba'al mum* — the owner gains a tangible benefit when the animal is declared blemished and permitted for slaughter. But why should the owner pay when the ruling goes against him, when the animal is declared *tam*? The *gemara* answers: *de'im ken ati l'michshdei* — if payment were only made upon a favorable ruling, people would suspect the inspector. They would say: *hai ba'al mum tam hu v'hai deka shari lei mishum agra* — this animal is really unblemished, but he declared it *ba'al mum* because he was being paid for the result.

### One Payment Takana

The *gemara* presses further: even with a flat fee, suspicion has merely shifted direction. Now one might say that when the inspector rules *tam*, people will suspect he is prolonging the process — that he declared it unblemished precisely so that the owner will bring the animal back repeatedly, generating additional inspection fees. The *gemara* responds: *chada zimna takinu lei rabanan, tarti zimnei lo takinu lei rabanan* — the same rabbinic institution that authorized Ilo's fee structure also stipulated that he may only be paid once per animal. The inspector receives one payment, regardless of how many subsequent inspections occur. With repeat-business incentive eliminated, the suspicion of ruling *tam* for financial gain collapses.

### Blemish Incentive

Yet this resolution creates its own paradox. If the inspector receives only one payment per animal and cannot be compensated for future inspections of the same animal, the incentive now runs in the opposite direction: he has every reason to declare *ba'al mum* on the first inspection, collect his single fee, and be done with it. Why bother ruling *tam* and being called back repeatedly, knowing that no further payment is forthcoming?

### Right of Refusal

Tosafot addresses this directly. The concern would be that even with one-time payment, people would suspect the *ba'al mum* ruling was motivated by the desire to avoid the burden of repeated inspections. Tosafot answers: *shelo chiyu hu chachamim lirot pa'am acheret* — the *chachamim* never obligated the inspector to examine the same animal a second time. The right of refusal always remains with the inspector. *Ela d'im ra'ahu hu d'ein yachol litol alav sachar* — only if he voluntarily agrees to inspect again is he barred from collecting an additional fee, but he is never compelled to do so. Therefore, no one can claim his *ba'al mum* ruling was motivated by the desire to avoid future effort, since he could simply decline any future inspection without consequence. Tosafot adds a second answer: we would not carry the suspicion that far in any case.

The broader point is that this entire carefully constructed system — flat fee, equal payment for *tam* and *ba'al mum*, one payment per animal — was in place only for Ilo, as a sanctioned exception. The general principle remains that accepting any fee for this function, however structured, is prohibited, because financial interest inevitably raises questions of objectivity.

---

## Payment Prohibitions

### Judges & Witnesses

The *mishnah* now extends this principle well beyond the specific case of *bechor* inspection. *Ha'notel sacharo ladun* — a judge who accepts payment for his rulings — *dinav betelin*, his judgments are nullified. *Leha'id* — if a witness accepts payment for testifying — *eduto betela*, his testimony is thrown out. The stakes here are plain: the entire institution of expert witness testimony — an enormously lucrative field in contemporary legal practice, where witnesses are retained precisely because they are expected to perform in a particular direction — is directly implicated by this principle.

### Parah Adumah Payment

The *mishnah* continues beyond the realm of adjudication and testimony: *lehazot ulekadesh* — if one accepts payment for sprinkling the ashes of *parah adumah* or for sanctifying the ashes by mixing them with well water — *meimav mei me'arah* — his water becomes like the water of a cave, i.e., it is not valid *mayim chayim* — and *afro efer mikleh* — his ashes are like ordinary fireplace ash. The purification process is entirely annulled.

### Subjective Functions

This is a striking expansion. The concern about payment for judgment and testimony can be understood through the lens of integrity and objectivity — money compromises the subjective determinations of judges and witnesses. But the preparation of *parah adumah* involves no such subjective determination. The functionary is simply performing a physical act of preparation; there is no ruling to be corrupted, no testimony to be distorted. Yet payment for this act is equally disqualifying. The *gemara* will generalize this principle across *mitzvot* broadly: one is never to accept payment for the performance of a *mitzvah*. The inclusion of *parah adumah* in the *mishnah* can be read as establishing precisely this point — that the prohibition is not limited to contexts where money might compromise judgment, but extends to the very mixing of *mitzvah* performance with monetary gain.

One might alternatively read the *mishnah* as *davka* these cases — judgment, testimony, and *parah adumah* — because they each involve a situation of dependency and power differential. In the case of *parah adumah*, one who requires purification is entirely dependent on another to perform the act; one cannot sprinkle the ashes on oneself. This power asymmetry, combined with the enormous rarity and value of *parah adumah* itself, creates conditions where financial incentive could be particularly corrupting or at least suspicious. That reading has considerable force. It is worth noting that the *gemara* does in fact generalize the principle to all *mitzvot*, but the more limited reading of the *mishnah* itself remains textually defensible.

### Kohen Expenses

Before turning to the *gemara*'s discussion of the Scriptural source, the *mishnah* introduces the case of a *kohen* who became *tamei* in the course of traveling to fulfill the *mitzvah* of testimony or adjudication. As a result, he can no longer eat his *terumah* and must purchase the more expensive *chulin* food instead. May he be reimbursed for this additional expense?

---

## Kohen Tamei Case

### Food Compensation

The *mishnah* rules that he may be fed and given drink and oil — that is, compensated for the additional costs incurred as a result of his *tumah*. The reimbursement covers only the differential expense caused by becoming *tamei* — the cost of *chulin* food in place of *terumah* — and not a general food allowance.

---

## Payment Prohibitions (II)

### Sechar Batel

The *mishnah* adds: if the witness or judge was elderly and could not travel unassisted, one pays for his transportation — *markivo al hachamor*, the donkey, equivalent to a car service today. And finally: *venosein lo secharo kepo'el* — one pays him his fee as a worker. The *gemara* will clarify that this means *sechar batelah* — payment for lost opportunity, for the time he took away from his regular occupation — not a fee for the service of judging or testifying itself. The distinction between time and service will occupy the *gemara* at length.

---

## Torah Teaching Sourc (II)

### Moshe's Example

The *gemara* asks: *mina hani mili* — what is the Scriptural source for the prohibition against accepting payment for these functions? Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: the verse states, *Re'eh limadeti etchem chukim umishpatim ka'asher tzivani Hashem Elokai* — Behold I have taught you statutes and judgments just as Hashem my God commanded me. The *gemara* derives: *ma ani bechinam af atem bechinam* — just as I, Moshe, taught you without payment, so too you must teach others without payment. The same way God taught Moshe freely, Moshe transmitted that teaching freely, and the chain must continue unbroken.

A *baraita* corroborates: just as I teach *bechinam*, so must you teach *bechinam*.

### Emet Kneh

The *baraita* immediately asks: how do we know that if one cannot find a teacher who will teach for free, one should nonetheless pay for learning? The answer: *talmud lomar emet kneh* — the verse says, "purchase truth." If the only available teacher demands a fee, one should pay. The supreme value of Torah study overrides the impropriety of the teacher's conduct; one does not decline an education because the teacher is behaving wrongly.

And conversely: how do we know that once one has paid for one's own learning, one should not argue that since one's own teachers charged, one is entitled to do the same? The verse continues: *emet kneh ve'al timkor* — purchase truth, but do not sell it. One may spend freely to acquire Torah; one may not charge to transmit it.

This formulation illuminates an important structural point. One might have thought that the principle against payment should generate a *takkanah* parallel to the one governing judgment and testimony — that Torah transmitted for payment is somehow *batel*, invalidated. Yet no such consequence is applied. Instead, the student is instructed to seek out free teaching and, when unavoidable, to pay without thereby legitimizing the practice. This asymmetry reflects the *gemara*'s recognition that *talmud torah* occupies a position of such supreme value that the normal enforcement mechanism — nullification — is suspended in order to preserve the institution of Torah study itself.

---

## Teachers & Official (III)

### Sechar Batel Principle

This raises the obvious question: how do we justify paying teachers, *rabbanim*, and full-time *dayanim* in practice? The answer turns on *sechar batelah* — compensation for lost opportunity, for the time one is not pursuing other work. The principle is that one may pay a judge, witness, or teacher not for the service itself but for the opportunity cost of their time. This is symbolized, however inadequately, by the nominal daily fee paid to jurors in civil courts, which is meant to represent time rather than expertise.

The *sechar batelah* framework has a significant structural implication: it would mean, in principle, that teachers and *dayanim* should be paid not according to the quality of their service, nor according to their seniority in their current role, but according to what they could have earned doing something else. A person who left a career in law or medicine to become a teacher would, on this model, receive a substantially higher salary than someone with no other marketable skills — not because the former is a better teacher, but because the value of what they gave up is greater.

### Community Funds

Tosafot addresses the problem of full-time judges and officials. The *gemara* in other contexts records that *dayanei gezeirot* — the permanent judges in Jerusalem — received salaries from the Temple treasury. How could this be, given the prohibition? Tosafot writes: *vein litmoah al dayanei gezeirot shebishchar hayu notlin schar mitrumat halishka* — one should not be astonished that these judges received payment from communal funds. The reason, Tosafot explains, is: *dekivan dechol askam haya al ze velo hayu oskim beshum melacha* — since this was their entire occupation and they had no other livelihood, *al korcham tzrichim lehitparnes* — they necessarily had to be supported. When someone devotes their entire professional life to a communal function and has no other income, the payment is not framed as a fee for services but as a living stipend enabling their dedication. The community's need for that institution overrides the formal concern about payment for *mitzvah* performance.

---

## Payment & Mitzvah (III)

### Talmud Torah Exception

A further question arises from the structure of the *mishnah*: we throw out the judgment, nullify the testimony, invalidate the *parah adumah* when payment is involved. Why do we not apply the same consequence to *talmud torah*? The *gemara* permits paying for Torah study when no free option is available, and does not say the Torah learned from a paid teacher is *batel*. This asymmetry demands explanation.

### Supreme Value

The answer lies in the supreme value of *talmud torah* itself. The concern that money might corrupt the integrity of a religious function is always present in principle, but the institution of Torah learning is so foundational that the normal enforcement mechanism — nullification of the act — is suspended. We allow what we do not approve of, because *talmud torah* transcends the ordinary calculus.

### Communal Necessity

The same logic applies, by extension, to supporting full-time teachers, *rabbis*, and *dayanim*. The societal need for dedicated, expert transmission of Torah and *halacha* is itself an overriding value, one that justifies departure from the strict theoretical framework. This is not merely *sechar batelah* — it is recognition that when someone devotes their entire working life to communal religious service, the community must sustain that person. As Tosafot frames it, this is not payment for doing a *mitzvah*; it is support for a person who has placed themselves entirely in service of the community's spiritual needs.

---

## Modern Application

### Rambam Critique

The Rambam has a well-known and sharp critique of those who draw on communal funds while engaged in full-time Torah study without performing direct communal service. The question of *kollel* stipends — whether Torah study alone, without a functional communal role, justifies communal support — is a distinct and contested matter. The Rambam's critique focuses specifically on this scenario and does not directly undermine the legitimacy of supporting those who perform actual teaching, rabbinic, or judicial functions for the community.

---

## Torah Teaching Sourc (II)

### Rashi's Limitation

Rashi, in his comment on *mina hani mili*, specifies that the Scriptural source and its derived prohibition apply to *hora'ah* — the giving of rulings — and to *talmud torah*, the transmission of Torah. This connects to the verse's subject matter: Moshe is speaking not abstractly but specifically about *chukim umishpatim*, statutes and legal norms, and teaching what the law requires. The link between *hora'ah* and *talmud torah* in this context is natural — both are transmission of the substance of *halacha* — and from there the *gemara* extends the principle to the full range of *mitzvot*. Whether this extension is logically necessary or whether it is better read as a *gezerat hakasuv* — a Scriptural decree whose extension is learned rather than derived — is a point of analysis, but the *gemara*'s practical application of the principle is not limited to teaching and ruling.

---

## Invalidation Gezerah

### vs. Shochad

The obvious question is: why is a separate principle needed at all? Is this not simply a case of *shochad* — bribery? The Torah already prohibits *shochad* and states explicitly that *ki hashochad ye'aver einei* — bribery blinds the eyes of the wise. Why is a distinct source necessary to invalidate paid judgments?

Tosafot responds that *shochad* is specifically payment from only one side, with an implicit or explicit expectation that the judge will exert himself on behalf of the paying party. The Rema notes that *shochad* is forbidden even when the judge takes it with the intent to remain objective, because the giving party's intent is that the judge will work harder for them. The cases in our *mishnah*, however, may involve payment from communal funds, payment shared equally by both parties, or a straightforward fee-for-services arrangement with no directional expectation. None of these constitute *shochad* in the technical sense. Yet the *mishnah* still invalidates the judgment.

### Why Throw Out

The question then is sharper: if it is not *shochad*, why throw out the judgment? The person may have ruled entirely correctly. The testimony may have been perfectly accurate. Why do we negate the result?

### Prevention Takana

The answer is that the invalidation is a rabbinic *gezerah* or *takkanah*, not a biblical consequence. The rabbis determined that no money should be involved in the processes of judgment, testimony, and — by extension — *parah adumah* preparation, and they established the nullification of the result as the enforcement mechanism. For *talmud torah*, they deliberately chose not to apply this enforcement, as the value of Torah study is too great to allow the prohibition to function as a barrier to learning. For the full-time judges supported by communal funds, they similarly allowed exceptions where the structural concern — that money might compromise integrity — does not in fact apply in the same way. The *gezerah* is not a response to demonstrated corruption but a prophylactic institution designed to keep money entirely out of these domains.

---

## Teachers & Official (III)

### Rosh's Position

Returning to the case of Ilo: Rashi explained Ilo's exception on the basis of his extraordinary personal piety — *dechasid hava v'lo nechshad bekach* — he was so pious that no suspicion could attach to him. The Rosh offers a structurally different reading. The Rosh argues that Ilo was permitted to receive fees not because of his personal character, but because he was a full-time *bechor* inspector. His situation parallels the *dayanei gezeirot* of Jerusalem — people who devoted their entire professional lives to this function and had no other livelihood. On this reading, the Rosh wants to connect the Ilo exception directly to the principle that Tosafot articulates about full-time communal officials, rather than making it a personal exception grounded in Ilo's *chasidus*.

---

## Payment & Mitzvah (III)

### Kohanim Model

A useful analogy for this entire structure is the *kohanim* themselves. The *kohanim* were designated teachers of Torah for Israel — this was among their primary roles — and they were supported by the entire community through *terumah* and other designated portions. They were not paid per class or per ruling; rather, the community sustained them so they could devote themselves to service. This is precisely the model that Tosafot's principle invokes: not *sechar batelah* in the narrow sense of compensating for a specific missed opportunity, but communal support for a life devoted to religious function. The payment is, in essence, a living stipend enabling dedication, not a fee for services rendered.

---

## Parah Adumah Details

### Preparation Payment

Having established the general principle, the *gemara* now engages a tension. The *mishnah* says that if one is paid to sprinkle or sanctify the *parah adumah* waters, the waters and ashes are invalidated. But a separate *mishnah* elsewhere states: *ha'mekadesh b'mei chatat u've'efer chatat harei zu mekudeshet* — one who gives the water or ashes of *parah adumah* as *kesef kiddushin* for betrothal, it works, even if he is a non-*kohen* Israelite. If one cannot derive benefit from these materials, how can they function as a medium of *kiddushin*?

Abaye resolves the tension: *kan bischar hava'ah u'milui, kan bischar haza'ah v'kiddush* — in one case the payment is for bringing the ashes or filling the containers, acts of preparation and effort; in the other case the payment is for the actual act of sprinkling or sanctification, the *mitzvah* act itself. Payment for preparatory effort — transporting the ashes, drawing and carrying the water — is entirely permissible; the *mitzvah* has not yet been performed and one is simply being compensated for physical labor. But payment for the *mitzvah* act itself — the sprinkling, the mixing — is what invalidates. The water used in *kiddushin* represents the value of the preparatory effort involved, which is a legitimate commodity.

### Teacher Preparation

This distinction maps naturally onto the case of teachers and *dayanim*. We are not paying them for the moment of teaching or the moment of ruling — which is the *mitzvah* act itself — but for the enormous investment of preparation that precedes it: the years of study, the preparation of lessons, the time spent in research, the effort of grading and review. That preparatory work is compensable, even if the act of transmission itself is not.

### Language Inference

The *gemara* notes that the resolution is supported by the precise language of the *mishnah*. The prohibitory clause says *lehazot ulekadesh* — to sprinkle and to sanctify — referring to the acts themselves. The permissive clause in the other *mishnah* refers to *mei chatat v'efer chatat* — the water and ash as objects, which implies their value derives from the effort involved in preparing and transporting them, not from the *mitzvah* act itself. *Shema mina* — this is a sound inference.

---

## Kohen Tamei Case (II)

### Tamei Override

Returning to the case of the *kohen* who became *tamei*: the *gemara* asks directly, *ihu gufeh heichi azil* — how was the *kohen* permitted to go and become *tamei* in the first place? A *kohen* is biblically prohibited from contracting corpse impurity. How did he incur *tumah* in the course of coming to testify?

### Blowing Debate

The *gemara* answers: *l'Beis HaPras d'rabbanan* — we are discussing a *beis ha'pras*, a field where a grave has been lost and the concern is only rabbinic. And as Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *minapeach adam Beis HaPras v'holech* — a person may blow in front of himself while walking through a *beis ha'pras*, sifting the dirt to check for chips of bone, and proceed step by step.

Tosafot identifies two ways to read this *gemara*. One reading: the fact that blowing allows one to traverse a *beis ha'pras* proves that the *tumah* concern there is only rabbinic. Since it is only rabbinic, a *kohen* may traverse it — even without blowing — for the sake of a *mitzvah*, specifically the *mitzvah* of testifying. He still contracts *tumah*, but since the prohibition is rabbinic rather than biblical, it yields to the *mitzvah* obligation. Alternatively, the *gemara* may mean that the *kohen* did in fact employ the blowing technique and traversed in that manner, and even so he became *tamei* — because while the blowing makes traversal permissible, it does not guarantee absolute purity; he still attains *tumah* status and therefore requires reimbursement for the additional food costs.

Either way, the key structural point is the same: *tumah* incurred via *beis ha'pras* is rabbinic, and it is therefore overridden by the *mitzvah* of testimony, even though the *kohen* will still be regarded as *tamei* thereafter for the purpose of his *terumah*.

### Different Tumah

The *gemara* then offers Rav Yehuda bar Ami's position: *Beis HaPras shenidosh tahor* — a *beis ha'pras* that has been trodden over is *tahor*, because any bone chips would have been pulverized by the foot traffic. This might suggest that in such a case the *kohen* would remain fully *tahor*, which would then undercut our *mishnah*'s premise that he became *tamei*. The resolution is that this statement proves the rabbinicity of the concern rather than establishing what happened in the *mishnah*'s case. The *mishnah*'s *kohen* traversed an untrodden area, became *tamei*, but was allowed to do so because the prohibition was only rabbinic and was overridden by the *mitzvah* of testimony.

The *gemara* adds a simpler alternative: *bish'ar tumos d'lo muzhar aleihu* — perhaps the *kohen* became *tamei* through a different type of *tumah* altogether, one that does not implicate the special prohibition against a *kohen* contracting corpse impurity. Contact with a *neveilah* or a *sheretz*, for instance, renders one *tamei* and prohibits eating *terumah*, but does not involve the specific biblical prohibition that applies to a *kohen* regarding the dead. In such a case, the *kohen* may have become *tamei* in a manner that was entirely permissible for him, yet still incurred the consequential expense of having to purchase *chulin* food.

---

## Sechar Batel Deep

### Rashi's Definition

The *mishnah*'s phrase *kepo'el batel* — as a worker who is idle — is amplified by the *gemara* as *k'poel batel shel osa melacha*, and Rashi provides the practical definition: how much would a person accept to take a day off from his job and not work? That amount — not the wage he would have earned working, but the lesser sum he would accept as sufficient compensation for the pleasure or inconvenience of a day of rest — is what he receives.

---

## Sechar Batel Deep (II)

### Batel Variables

This definition contains several variables that make it structurally complex. The amount a person would accept to take a day off depends on both how much they earn and how demanding their work is. As Rashi himself illustrates — using the example of someone who cuts precious stones — some of the highest-earning occupations are also the most refined and least physically burdensome. For such a person, the incentive to take a day off is low on both dimensions: the job pays very well and is relatively pleasant, so the threshold for accepting a day off is close to the full daily wage. By contrast, a laborer doing heavy construction work earns much less and would welcome the relief of a day off, so his *sechar batelah* would be substantially lower.

### Ethical Problem

The result is a structurally inequitable compensation system: those who could earn more elsewhere receive higher compensation for their time as judges or witnesses, while those at the lower end of the economic spectrum — who may actually need every dollar and cannot afford to take a day off — receive less. The system pays for the economic position of the individual rather than for any intrinsic value of their testimony or judgment.

### Tosafot Critique

Tosafot raises a pointed objection to Rashi's formulation. If one asks how much this person would accept to take a day off from their job and spend the day as a judge or witness, one is already partially paying for the act of judging or testifying — because being a judge involves effort, and that effort is factored into the amount the person demands. Tosafot insists that the correct baseline is how much the person would accept to take a day off and spend it on the beach — pure leisure, with no effort involved. Any amount above that baseline reflects compensation for the work of judging itself, which is forbidden. Therefore the only permissible payment is the leisure-value of a day away from work, not the cost of the day's labor spent in a different capacity.

---

## Teachers & Official (III)s…

### Sechar Batel Issues

The structural inequity of *sechar batelah* is worth dwelling on. The system as described means that a highly-paid professional who takes a day to testify receives far more compensation than a low-wage worker who does the same. Moreover, someone who is independently wealthy or whose other income does not depend on daily attendance — say, an investor who earns passively at night — faces the question of whether they are entitled to any *sechar batelah* at all. Prima facie, such a person may have no legitimate claim to compensation for time taken from work. The converse side of this — *emet kneh* — suggests that the community should not refuse to engage such a person if they will not perform the service without payment, since acquiring Torah and justice is worth any price. But whether that person is entitled to take the payment is a separate question.

### Beach Day Debate

Tosafot's position — that one must calculate *sechar batelah* relative to a day of pure leisure rather than a day of alternative work — carries significant practical implications. It would mean that the amount paid to any judge or witness should reflect only the value they place on leisure, stripped of any component that could be characterized as paying for the act of judging. This is a genuinely demanding standard, and it is one of the central debates in the application of *sechar batelah* as a compensatory concept.

---

## Payment & Mitzvah (III)…

### Doctors & Services

All of this bears directly on the question of how doctors can be paid. The Ramban — himself a physician — grapples with the question of whether a doctor performing the *mitzvah* of healing (*ve'rappo yerape*) is subject to the same prohibition against payment for *mitzvah* performance. The analysis mirrors the *parah adumah* distinction: one might argue that the physician is paid not for the act of healing itself but for all of the years of preparation, training, and expertise that preceded it. But that framework is strained when fees are calibrated to the complexity and duration of specific procedures — a three-hour surgery commands a different fee than a thirty-hour surgery — suggesting that the payment does in fact track the service itself, not merely the preparation.

---

## Modern Application (II)

### Doctor Dilemma

The doctor's situation illustrates the tension between the ideal of *mitzvah* performance without payment and the practical necessity of sustaining a healthcare system.
