This rests on the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: *kol talmid chacham she'omrim davar shmuah mipi ba'olam hazeh dovvot siftotav bakever* — any Torah scholar in whose name a teaching is repeated in this world, even after his death, his lips continue to murmur in the grave. The *Gemara* then cites Rav Yitzchak ben Birya, who finds this in the verse *v'chichech k'yayin hatov holech l'dodi l'meisharim doveiv siftei yesheinim* — your palate is like good wine flowing to my beloved, causing the lips of the sleeping to speak. Just as touching a cluster of ripe grapes causes the juice to run freely, so too the moment a Torah teaching is mentioned in a scholar's name, his lips begin to murmur again in the grave. David's prayer, then, was precisely for this: that his Torah be transmitted by name so that he would remain alive in both worlds at once. This is why Rav Sheshes was wounded so personally — had the teaching been transmitted in his name, his lips would have moved in the grave; robbed of the attribution, he was robbed of that immortality.

One might wonder: the phrase is *omrim davar shmuah mipi* — they say a teaching from his mouth — rather than simply repeating what he said. It seems clear that the *Gemara* understands this to mean saying it over specifically in his name, not merely repeating his idea without attribution.

### Hashavas Aveidah

Returning to the legal discussion: the underlying rationale for permitting orphans to sell *ma'aser behemah* is *hashavas aveidah*, the concern for preventing loss. When the animal is slaughtered, if there is more meat than the orphans can consume before it spoils, and they are unable to manage the situation as a capable adult might — salting the meat, arranging reciprocal hospitality, and so on — the entire financial value of the animal may simply be wasted. To prevent this, the Rabbis permitted the sale.

### Havla'ah & Orphans

The *braisa* presents two cases: first, *ma'aser behemah shel yetomim mochrin oso* — orphans may sell their *ma'aser behemah*. Second, for *ma'aser behemah* that has been slaughtered (*shesha'chato*), one may absorb its cost (*mavlio*) into the sale of the skin (*b'oro*), the fat (*uv'chelvo*), the sinews (*uv'gido*), and the horns (*uv'karnav*). In other words, one may price the non-meat parts at an inflated figure and include the meat as a free addition, thereby technically not selling the *ma'aser* meat at all.

### Abaye vs Rava

Abaye and Rava dispute the proper reading of these two clauses. Abaye reads them together: *ma'aser behemah shel yetomim mochrin oso b'havla'ah* — orphans may sell *ma'aser behemah*, but only using the technique of absorption. This implies that a normal adult may not use *havla'ah* at all — doing so would be too transparent a circumvention to be permitted. Rava objects that if that were the meaning, why would the text repeat the phrase *ma'aser behemah* a second time? The repetition signals a second, independent case. Rava therefore reads the *braisa* as presenting two distinct rulings: for orphans, outright sale (*k'darko*) without any workaround is permitted; for a normal adult who slaughters *ma'aser behemah*, absorption into the cost of the other parts is permitted.

### Lulav-Etrog Analogy

Abaye's position raises a difficulty from another *mishna*: one who purchases a *lulav* from a neighbor during *shvi'is* — where there is concern about transacting with produce that has *kedushat shvi'is* — may give the *esrog* as a gift. If the seller refuses to give it as a gift, Rav Yehuda rules that one may absorb the cost of the *esrog* into the price of the *lulav* (*mavli'a lo d'mei esrog b'lulav*). If *havla'ah* is permitted there, why should it be prohibited for an adult with *ma'aser behemah*? The *Gemara* answers: *hatam lo mukcha milta* — in the *lulav* case it is not so obvious, since the various components of the *arba'ah minim* are normally bundled together and the relative pricing is not transparent. *Hacha mukcha milta* — in the *ma'aser behemah* case it is entirely obvious: no one would genuinely pay thousands for the horns and sinews of a cow while receiving all the meat for free. The blatant artificiality of such an arrangement makes it impermissible for an ordinary adult, and Abaye therefore restricts *havla'ah* to the orphan case. Rava, reading the two clauses as separate rulings, allows orphans to sell outright and allows adults to use *havla'ah* — because for Rava the *braisa* is presenting two distinct leniencies, not one modified leniency.

---

## Biblical vs Rabbinic

### Tmura Context

Rava offers a proof for his position that orphans may sell *ma'aser behemah* outright. The relevant verse reads: *v'hayah hu u'tmurato yihiyeh kodesh lo yiga'el* — it and its exchange shall be holy, it shall not be redeemed. The verse invokes *tmura*, the act of exchanging one animal for another, transferring sanctity. This act is only possible *mechayim* — while the animal is alive. Once it is dead, *tmura* cannot take effect. The verse thus situates the prohibition within a context that is inherently limited to the animal's life. Accordingly, the restriction encoded in *lo yiga'el* — which Rava (following Rashi's reading) interprets as *lo yimacher*, cannot be sold — applies only while the animal is alive.

### Rabbinic Extension

The conclusion follows: biblically, the prohibition on selling *ma'aser behemah* applies only *mechayim*, while it is alive. Once it has been slaughtered, sale is biblically permitted. It is the Rabbis who extended the prohibition to cover the slaughtered animal as well, as a fence against the biblical prohibition of selling it alive (*gazru rabanan le'achar shechita atu lifnei shechita*). This rabbinic extension is qualified: it applies only to *davar ha'nishom mechayim* — something that was valued while the animal was alive, meaning the meat itself, which is the primary commodity of a living animal. The Rabbis did not extend their prohibition to parts that do not factor into the living animal's market value — the skin, fat, sinews, and horns. That is why the *havla'ah* technique works at all: the parts whose sale is absorbed into the transaction are not subject to the rabbinic restriction. Furthermore, in the case of orphans, the Rabbis waived even this extension of their own decree, permitting outright sale of the slaughtered animal, since the underlying biblical prohibition does not apply after *shechita*.

### Alternate Derivation

Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak holds the same substantive position as Rava — that orphans may sell outright — but derives it from a different verse. The Torah says (*Devarim* 12): *rak be'chol avat nafshecha tizbach ve'achalta vasar ke'virkat Hashem Elokecha* — with all the desire of your soul you shall slaughter and eat meat, as God has blessed you. This verse is understood in the context of a blemished *bechor* or *ma'aser*: once the animal bears a *mum*, you need not bring it as a *korban* but may slaughter and eat it. The phrase *ke'virkat Hashem Elokecha* — as God has blessed you — implies that the divine blessing comes specifically after slaughter. Since the animal is subject to various restrictions while alive, the blessing is manifest only once it has been slaughtered. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak derives from this that the post-*shechita* state is one of expanded permission — not merely eating but even selling is now included within the divine blessing. Selling from one's home is thus biblically permitted; only in the marketplace is it restricted, and that restriction itself is rabbinic.

### Bones Absorption

The *Gemara* raises a further question about *havla'ah*: the *braisa* mentions absorbing the cost of the meat into the skin, fat, sinews, and horns. What about bones? May one price the bones at an inflated value and absorb the cost of the meat there as well, or are bones too similar to the meat itself — or alternatively, too valueless — to serve as the vehicle for absorption?

### Sheep vs Cow

Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi dispute the question, one permitting *havla'ah* in bones and the other prohibiting it. The *Gemara* resolves their dispute by noting that they are not actually in disagreement: *ha b'daka ha b'gasa* — one is speaking of sheep and the other of cattle. Sheep bones are generally not used for anything and have no independent commercial value; absorbing the price of the meat into their cost would be transparently artificial. Cattle bones, on the other hand, are large, hard, and used in the production of bone vessels — there is a genuine market for them, and charging an elevated price for them can be done with a straight face. The *Gemara* adds that even if both sages are discussing cattle, they may simply reflect the practice in their respective locales: in one scholar's location, bones were regularly used for vessels, while in the other's they were not.

---

## Gezerah Shavah

### Verse Parallels

The *braisa* states the relevant prohibitions in full: by *bechor* the Torah says *lo tipadeh* — it shall not be redeemed; by *ma'aser* it says *lo yiga'el* — it shall not be redeemed; by *charamim* the Torah says *kol cherem lo yiga'el v'lo yimacher kodesh kodashim hu l'Hashem* — any *cherem* shall neither be redeemed nor sold, it is holy of holies to God. The question is: from where do we derive that *lo yiga'el* by *ma'aser* prohibits selling as well as redeeming?

### Rav Chanina Link

Rav Chanina says in the name of Rav, and Rav Dimi repeats this in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the verse uses the phrase *lo yiga'el* both by *ma'aser* and by *charamim*. By *charamim*, *lo yiga'el* stands alongside *lo yimacher* — selling and redeeming are juxtaposed and both prohibited. The *gezeirah shavah* links the two: just as by *charamim* the prohibition on redemption comes paired with a prohibition on sale, so too by *ma'aser* the prohibition on redemption carries with it a prohibition on sale. The *Gemara* confirms: *mah hallan mechira imo, af kan mechira imo* — the same way selling accompanies the redemption prohibition by *charamim*, it accompanies the redemption prohibition by *ma'aser*.

For this *gezeirah shavah* to function, the linking word must be *mufni* — unattached, available for the purpose of linking — rather than essential to its own context. If the word is needed in its own verse, it cannot serve as a free link; the comparison would then be merely analogical and subject to logical challenge. A truly extra word, by contrast, signals that its entire purpose is to establish the link, and logical critique cannot dissolve it.

### Ha'avarah Challenge

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: at least one side of the *gezeirah shavah* must be unattached. Can we establish that *lo yiga'el* is free — that is, extra — by *ma'aser*? One might have argued that the prohibition on redeeming *ma'aser* could have been derived from *bechor* via the verbal bridge of *ha'avarah* (passing over): both *bechor* and *ma'aser* use the language of *ha'avarah*, and since *bechor* cannot be redeemed, the same follows for *ma'aser* by analogy. If so, the explicit *lo yiga'el* by *ma'aser* is unnecessary and is thereby freed up to teach the prohibition on selling.

The *Gemara* tests whether the word is truly extra by *ma'aser* rather than by *charamim*, and whether the *ha'avarah* bridge genuinely makes the *ma'aser* restriction derivable without the explicit verse. The answer turns on whether each category possesses a unique feature that would defeat an inference from another category: *bechor* has automatic sanctity from birth (*kedushah merachem*), *ma'aser* sanctifies accidentally and symmetrically before and after (*kadesh lefanav ule'acharayiv*), and *charamim* apply to anything and everything. Because each has a distinctive stringency, one cannot straightforwardly derive one from another, and each needs its own explicit prohibition — unless we can find an exact verbal parallel that licenses the link without relying on logical analogy.

### Exact Phrase Link

The *Gemara* establishes that when there exists an exact verbal parallel, we prefer that link over an approximate analogy. *Lo yiga'el* appears identically by both *ma'aser* and *charamim*. *Lo tipadeh* by *bechor* means the same thing, but in different words. The principle derived from the school of Rabbi Yishmael is that even words with the same meaning can sometimes anchor a *gezeirah shavah* — the example being *uva hakohen* and *veshav hakohen* in the laws of *nega'im*, where both mean the same thing and the *gezeirah shavah* is nonetheless valid. However, the *Gemara* qualifies this: that principle applies *heicha de'lika dedami lei* — only when there is no more exact match available. Where an identical phrase exists, *mididami lei yalfinan* — we prefer to link through the exact match. Since *lo yiga'el* by *ma'aser* is identical to *lo yiga'el* by *charamim*, and that word is rendered extra by *ma'aser* through the *ha'avarah* connection to *bechor*, we link the two identical phrases and derive the prohibition on selling.

### Rava's Approach

Rava offers an entirely different approach, departing from the *gezeirah shavah* methodology. Following Rashi's reading, Rava argues that *lo yiga'el* by *charamim* is not the relevant word — the operative word is *lo yimacher*, the explicit prohibition on selling. And that word, Rava contends, is extra by *charamim*. Why? Because *charamim* presents two distinct states: while the animal is still in the owner's possession, it has the full status of *hekdesh* — *harei hein k'hekdesh l'chol divreihem*. Once it is transferred to the *kohen*, it loses all *kedushah* entirely and becomes *chullin* — *harei hein k'chullin l'chol divreihem*, as the *braisa* teaches, citing the verse *kol cherem b'Yisrael lecha yihiyeh*. Given this framework: if the *cherem* is still with its owner, it is *hekdesh*, and the owner has already divested himself of legal ownership — he cannot sell what is no longer his. If it has passed to the *kohen*, it is *chullin* — of course the *kohen* may sell it. In neither state is the explicit prohibition on selling doing any work. The word *lo yimacher* is therefore genuinely superfluous by *charamim*. *Im eino inyan l'charamim* — since it is not needed there — *tneihu inyan l'ma'aser*, apply it to teach the prohibition on selling *ma'aser*. And why *ma'aser* rather than *bechor*? Because *lo yiga'el* by *ma'aser* provides the connecting thread to *charamim*, whereas *bechor* uses *lo tipadeh*, a different formulation.

---

## Rav Ashi's Proof

### Tmura Logic

Rav Ashi takes the most direct interpretive route of all. Rather than constructing a *gezeirah shavah* or deriving the prohibition through an extra word, Rav Ashi reads *lo yiga'el* by *ma'aser* as simply meaning *lo yimacher* — it shall not be sold — by virtue of contextual logic alone. The proof: the verse says *v'hayah hu u'tmurato yihiyeh kodesh lo yiga'el* — it and its *tmura* shall be holy, it shall not be redeemed. *Tmura* — the transfer of sanctity through exchange — is only operative *mechayim*, while the animal is alive. Once it has been slaughtered, *tmura* is impossible. The verse's prohibition is thus embedded in a context that is inherently limited to the living animal.

### Alive vs Dead Logic

Now apply this to the literal meaning of *lo yiga'el*: if the word truly means "shall not be redeemed," then contextualizing it within *tmura* would yield the rule that redemption is prohibited only while the animal is alive, and once slaughtered it could be redeemed. But this is incoherent: redemption of a *korban* requires *ha'amadah veha'arachah* — the animal must stand before its assessors — and once slaughtered it cannot be redeemed regardless. The *Gemara* tests whether one might nonetheless say that while the animal lives its *kedushah* is stronger and therefore redemption is restricted, while after slaughter the *kedushah* weakens and redemption becomes available. The *Gemara* rejects this with a *kal vachomer* in the opposite direction: *u'mah mechayim d'alim l'mifas pidyon lo mifrak* — if even when the *kedushah* is strong and the animal is alive, when it has the power to extend to and take hold of new money, redemption is still prohibited; then *l'achar shechita d'lo alim l'mifas pidyon* — after slaughter, when the *kedushah* is weak and lacks the power to transfer — all the more so it cannot be redeemed. Stronger *kedushah* enables redemption; weaker *kedushah* forecloses it. A rule of "prohibited alive, permitted dead" makes sense for selling — it is a meaningful distinction — but makes no sense for redeeming. *Ela shma mina lo yiga'el lo yimacher hu* — we learn from this that *lo yiga'el* in this context means *lo yimacher*, shall not be sold.

### Why Use Lo Yiga'el

One might then ask: if the Torah means to prohibit selling, why does it write *lo yiga'el* at all? Why not simply say *lo yimacher*? The *Gemara* answers: *ei katav rachmana lo yimacher, hava amina zivuni hu d'lo mizdaban* — if it had only written "shall not be sold," one might have thought that the prohibition is limited to the act of sale proper, treating the animal as though it were mundane property. But regarding redemption — *aval mifrak mifrak* — one might naturally have assumed that redeeming *ma'aser* is permitted. After all, other *korbanot* can be redeemed, and redemption transfers the value to a sacred purpose; it does not profane the *kedushah* but rather fulfills it. *D'ayilu dmei l'hekdesh* — the money paid in redemption goes to a sanctified use. Had the Torah not explicitly prohibited redemption, one would have assumed it was permitted. Therefore, *l'hachi katav rachmana lo yiga'el* — the Torah writes "shall not be redeemed" precisely to close off that assumption, while the contextual logic of *tmura* teaches us that the word also prohibits sale. Both prohibitions — selling and redeeming — are communicated by the single phrase *lo yiga'el*, the one explicitly and the other through context.

The upshot of the entire sugya: *bechor* may be sold because the Torah's only restriction is *lo tipadeh*, prohibiting redemption without restricting sale; *ma'aser* may not be sold, because *lo yiga'el* means *lo yimacher*, but that prohibition is grounded in the context of *tmura* and applies only while the animal is alive. After *shechita*, the prohibition is rabbinic. It is that rabbinic character of the post-*shechita* restriction that allows the Rabbis to waive it for orphans, permitting them to sell outright to prevent financial loss — and it is that entire structure of biblical permission and rabbinic restriction that the *mishna* on which we opened presupposes.

---

---

# Bekhorot 34

## Bloodletting & Mum

### Intro: Blood Clot

The daf opens — or rather, continues — with the *mishna* from 33b, covering a case in which a *bechor* in the possession of a *kohen* has developed a blood clot (*dam*) and requires bloodletting in order to survive. The concern is that the act of letting blood may produce a *mum* — a permanent blemish — which would be halachically significant given the prohibition understood by *Chazal* from the verse *lo yihiyeh bo mum*: one may not make a *mum* in *kodshim*. The prohibition presumably applies only to a permanent *mum*, and so the debate turns on how to navigate the animal's medical need against the risk of creating such a blemish.

### R. Yehuda: Prohibit

Rabbi Yehuda takes the most stringent position: one may not perform bloodletting at all. His concern is that even if one intends to let blood only in a location that will not produce a *mum*, the anxiety and urgency of the moment will cause the person to inadvertently perform the procedure in a location where a permanent *mum* does result. To prevent this, Rabbi Yehuda rules that the animal must simply be left to die.

### Sages: Conditional

The *chachamim* take the opposite policy view. If one prohibits bloodletting entirely, they reason, the owner will abandon caution altogether and deliberately inflict a *mum* in order to be rid of the problem — and then slaughter the animal on that basis. Therefore, the *chachamim* permit bloodletting, but only in a location where no *mum* will result. If a *mum* does accidentally result, the animal may still not be slaughtered on that basis; the policy concern about what such permission would lead to remains in force.

### R. Shimon: Lenient

Rabbi Shimon is more permissive still. He allows bloodletting even in a location where a *mum* will or may result — the precise scope of his position will be clarified shortly. The *mishna* thus presents three views ranging from complete prohibition to significant latitude.

### Biblical Source

Underlying the entire debate is a biblical prohibition. *Chazal* derive from the verse *lo yihiyeh bo mum* a prohibition against making a *mum* in *kodshim*. It is worth noting that this verse is understood not as a descriptive statement but as a normative one: "there shall be no blemish in it" is read as "you shall not make a blemish in it." Naturally, only a permanent *mum* triggers the concern, which is why the location of the bloodletting matters so much.

---

## Baraita: Three Views

### R. Meir Position

A *baraita* now presents a parallel set of opinions, while adding important nuance. The *baraita* opens with the view of Rabbi Meir: *makizin lo et hadam bimkom she-eino oseh bo mum, ve-ein makizin lo et hadam bimkom she-oseh bo mum* — one may let blood only in a place where it will not make a *mum*, but not in a place where it will. This maps exactly onto the position of the *chachamim* in the *mishna*, as expected: the anonymous *chachamim* opposing Rabbi Yehuda in a *mishna* typically reflects the view of Rabbi Meir.

### Sages: No Slaughter

The *baraita*'s *chachamim* go one step further: one may let blood even in a location where a *mum* will certainly result (*af makom she-oseh bo mum*), but one may not slaughter the animal on the basis of that *mum* (*u-vilvad she-lo yishchat al oto mum*). This introduces a position that lies between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon — permitting the creation of the *mum* for medical purposes while retaining the policy restriction against *shechita* on that basis.

### R. Shimon: Allow

Rabbi Shimon in the *baraita* goes further still: *af nishchat al oto mum* — one may even slaughter the animal on the basis of the *mum* that was made in the course of the bloodletting procedure. This makes explicit what was only implied in the *mishna*: Rabbi Shimon not only permits making the *mum* but also permits *shechita* on its basis.

### R. Yehuda: Forbid All

Rabbi Yehuda's position in the *baraita* matches his *mishna* position precisely: *afilu met ein makizin lo et hadam* — even if the animal will die, one may not let blood at all, out of concern that it will lead to an impermissible *mum*.

The *baraita* thus clarifies the spectrum of opinion and, crucially, introduces an explicit debate about whether *shechita* on the basis of a medically-necessary *mum* is permissible.

---

## Terumah Comparison

### Comparison Intro

The *gemara* now records a teaching transmitted by Rabbi Eliezer to his son — and according to some, by Rabbi Chiyya to his son — comparing the debate of the *baraita* to a parallel dispute in an entirely different context: *ke-machloket kan kach machloket be-chavit shel terumah* — just as they debate here, so too they debate regarding a barrel of *terumah*.

### Terumah Setup

The case is as follows: a barrel of *terumah* wine has developed a doubtful *tumah* — it is uncertain whether it became *tamei*. This creates what amounts to the worst of all possible situations. If the *terumah* were definitively *tamei*, it could not be eaten or drunk, but one could derive benefit from it through its destruction — for example, by sprinkling the wine as an air freshener, a legitimate form of benefit that comes through consumption. If it were *tahor*, it could simply be eaten. But in a state of doubt, one can neither drink it (since it may be *tamei*) nor sprinkle it (since it may be *tahor*, and sprinkling would be an inappropriate use of *terumah* that is fit to eat). The barrel is thus completely unusable in its current state of doubt.

### R. Eliezer Terumah

Rabbi Eliezer says: *im haita bemakom haturpah yanichena bemakom hamutzna* — if it was in an exposed place, put it in a private place; if it was uncovered, cover it. Even though these actions will not change the barrel's status or resolve the doubt — the *terumah* will remain doubtfully *tamei* and unusable — Rabbi Eliezer maintains that one is obligated to protect it from further possible *tumah*. Since it might in fact be *tahor*, the duty to guard it remains in force.

### R. Yehoshua Terumah

Rabbi Yehoshua takes the pragmatic view: *im haita munachat bemakom mutzna yanichena bemakom haturpah* — if it was in a private place, move it to a public place; if it was covered, uncover it. The goal is to expose the *terumah* to conditions that will cause it to become definitively *tamei* — not directly through one's own action, but indirectly. Once it is definitively *tamei*, one can at least salvage something from the situation by using it in a permissible form of benefit through destruction.

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabban Gamliel takes neither approach: *lo yachadesh bah davar* — do nothing at all. One should neither protect the barrel nor expose it. Both courses of action may raise their own concerns, and since neither resolves the underlying problem, the correct policy is simply to leave the barrel alone.

### Correspondence

The *gemara* attempts to draw a correspondence between the two disputes. Rabbi Meir of the *baraita*, who permits bloodletting only where no *mum* results — addressing the animal's need while avoiding anything halachically problematic — is said to parallel Rabbi Eliezer, who protects the *terumah* without taking any questionable action. The common thread is: help the object at risk, but do nothing that crosses a halachic line. The *chachamim* of the *baraita*, who permit doing something halachically questionable (creating a *mum*) for the sake of salvaging the situation, parallel Rabbi Yehoshua, who permits the indirect exposure of *terumah* to *tumah* in order to make it usable. Rabbi Yehuda, who says do nothing and let the animal die, parallels Rabban Gamliel's hands-off approach.

### Objection 1: Direct/Indi…

The *gemara* immediately subjects this comparison to a battery of objections. The first: *dilma ad kan lo ka'amar Rabbi Meir hatam — dekavid beyadayim* — perhaps Rabbi Meir's restriction in the *bechor* case is specifically because one is performing a direct, hands-on act that may produce a *mum*. By contrast, in Rabbi Yehoshua's scenario with the wine, the *tumah* would come about only indirectly (*de-garma*) — the person merely exposes the barrel, and external agents cause the *tumah*. Perhaps, then, Rabbi Meir would actually agree with Rabbi Yehoshua by the *terumah* case, where only indirect action is involved.

### Objection 2: Facts/Urgen…

The second objection runs in the opposite direction: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer's protectiveness by the wine is specifically because the facts remain unresolved — *shema yavo Eliyahu ve-yitaharenu*, perhaps Elijah will come and clarify matters, and the doubt will be resolved. There is something unknown, so one must be cautious. But in the *bechor* case, the facts are not in doubt — if nothing is done, the animal will die within hours. Given that urgency, perhaps Rabbi Eliezer would permit even making a *mum* in order to save the animal, in line with the *rabbanan*.

### Objections 3-6

The *gemara* continues pressing the analysis from every direction, reversing the logic for each position in turn. The *rabbanan* of the *baraita* who permit making a *mum* may do so specifically because of the urgency — *de-ei shavik lei mayit*, if left alone it will die — and they might agree with Rabbi Eliezer in the *terumah* case, where the facts are uncertain and Elijah might yet resolve the doubt. By symmetry, Rabbi Yehuda's hands-off ruling in the *bechor* case may reflect only his concern about direct action (*bekavid beyadayim*), while in the *terumah* case — where exposure is only indirect — he might side with Rabbi Yehoshua. And Rabban Gamliel's inaction in the *terumah* case may be driven by the fact-uncertainty rationale (*shema yavo Eliyahu*), not by a general policy of non-intervention; in the *bechor* case, where the urgency is real and immediate, he might permit action in line with the *rabbanan*.

### Cases Not Parallel

The conclusion is clear: the two disputes are not genuinely comparable despite their surface similarities. The *bechor* case involves direct action under conditions of urgency with known facts; the *terumah* case involves indirect action under conditions of factual uncertainty with no urgency. These differences cut in opposite directions for each position, making it impossible to draw firm correspondences. The *gemara* adds a further and decisive point: *hacha bikrai peligi ve-hacha bikrai peligi* — in each case, the dispute is grounded in its own specific scriptural sources, which are distinct from each other, as will now be shown.

---

## Scripture: Mum B'Ba'al M…

### Assumption: Blemished

Turning to the scriptural underpinnings of the *bechor* debate, the *gemara* — in a teaching of Rav Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — proceeds from a foundational assumption: a *bechor* about to die from a blood clot is treated as if it already has a *mum*, as if it were a *ba'al mum*. The entire scriptural analysis that follows rests on this premise.

### Tosafot: Analysis

This assumption is not self-explanatory, and *Tosafot* addresses it directly. The animal does not display any visible *mum* — and a *mum* is by definition something visible. *Tosafot* suggests two possible approaches. One is that since the animal is effectively doomed — it cannot survive without bloodletting, and bloodletting will produce a *mum* — it is treated, in some sense, as already dead, and a dead animal has no *mum* in the ordinary sense. The other, and perhaps more workable, framing is not to say the animal is literally a *ba'al mum* but rather that it cannot be seen as a *tam* — a fully unblemished animal eligible for the altar. A *tam* animal is one that can actually be brought as a *korban*, but this *bechor* cannot realistically reach the *Beit Hamikdash* before dying; it will not survive. Therefore, while it may not technically carry a visible *mum*, it falls outside the category of *tamim*, and the relevant halachic analysis proceeds on that basis — essentially as an analogy to the case of making a *mum* in an animal that already has a *mum*, rather than a literal categorization.

### Debate Restated

With this framing in place, the *gemara* restates the core debate: Rabbi Meir prohibits making any *mum* in such an animal, even given its precarious state; the *chachamim* permit it, reasoning that since the animal is already effectively outside the category of *tamim*, creating a further *mum* causes no additional wrong.

### Textual Parallels

The scriptural basis for this dispute is now laid out. The *gemara* cites two precedents where everyone agrees (*hakol modim*) about the law. The first: *ha-kol modim be-mechameitz achar mechameitz she-hu chayav* — all agree that one who causes dough of a *mincha* offering to become *chameitz* is liable even if the dough had already become *chameitz* through someone else's action. The basis is that the Torah uses two distinct formulations: *lo teiafeh chameitz* (do not bake it as *chameitz*) and *lo teiaseh chameitz* (do not make it *chameitz*), signaling that each stage of the process constitutes an independent transgression. Even after the dough is already *chameitz*, a second person who bakes it is also liable, because the prohibition is about the act at each stage of the process, not merely about producing the final state. The second precedent: *ha-kol modim be-mesareis achar mesareis she-hu chayav* — all agree that one who castrates an animal (*mesareis*) after it has already been partially castrated by another is also liable. The Torah lists multiple forms of genital damage — *m'ruach, chasuach, nasuk, karus* — to indicate that each distinct act of mutilation constitutes a separate transgression, even if the animal was already sterile from an earlier act. In both cases, the point is that even when the critical state has already been achieved, performing a subsequent act in that same category carries liability.

### R. Meir: Act Focus

These two cases of universal agreement set up the contested question. The dispute, the *gemara* says, concerns specifically *ha-matil mum be-va'al mum* — making a *mum* in an animal that already has a *mum*. Here the views diverge. Rabbi Meir holds: *kol mum lo yiheyeh bo* — the verse "no blemish shall be in it" is understood as "you shall not make any blemish in it," with the word *kol* ("any") indicating that the prohibition applies regardless of whether a *mum* already exists. The act of making a *mum* is prohibited as an act, independent of what state the animal was already in.

### Sages: Result Focus

The *rabbanan* read the verse differently. The full verse begins *temimi yiheyeh le-ratzon* — "it shall be unblemished to be acceptable" — and continues *kol mum lo yiheyeh bo*. The *rabbanan* argue that the prohibition is conditional: it applies only when the animal is *tamim*, only when making a *mum* would move it from the state of being unblemished to the state of being blemished. If the animal is already not *tamim* — already ineligible for the altar — then making a *mum* in it does not violate this prohibition, because the relevant transition (*temimi* to *ba'al mum*) is not occurring.

### Act vs. Result

This is the fundamental conceptual divide. Rabbi Meir understands the prohibition as targeting the *act* of making a *mum*: the act is intrinsically prohibited in any animal with sanctity, regardless of its current condition. The *rabbanan* understand the prohibition as targeting the *result*: the prohibited outcome is the transformation of a *tamim* animal into a *ba'al mum*, and if that transformation cannot occur because the animal is already blemished, there is no prohibition.

### Grama Implication

This conceptual divide has a direct implication for *grama* — indirect action. If the prohibition is about producing the result, then causing the result indirectly is equally forbidden; both direct and indirect action equally bring about the prohibited state. This is why the *rabbanan*, according to this analysis, also prohibit *grama* when the animal is *tamim*: even if you wrap a piece of dough around the animal's ear so that a dog bites it off, you have still brought about the prohibited result, and the verse *kol mum* extends to cover indirect causation. Rabbi Meir, on the other hand, who frames the prohibition as being about the act itself, may not extend the prohibition to *grama* at all. If the problem is performing the act, then indirect causation — where one does not personally perform the act — would not be prohibited. These positions are, in this sense, two sides of the same coin: the *rabbanan* who permit making a *mum* in an already-blemished animal are also the ones who extend the prohibition to indirect action when the animal is *tamim*; Rabbi Meir, who forbids even blemish-upon-blemish, may not require the prohibition to reach indirect action.

---

## Scripture: Terumah

### Guarding Source

The *gemara* turns to the parallel scriptural basis underlying the *terumah* dispute, as reported by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and corroborated by Reish Lakish and Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha. The relevant verse is *va-ani hinei natati lecha et mishmeret terumotai* — "and I hereby give you the guarding of My *terumot*." The debate concerns whether this obligation of *shemirah* — guarding — extends to *terumah* whose status is in doubt.

### R. Eliezer: Dual

Rabbi Eliezer reads the verse as referring to two distinct categories of *terumah*, both of which must be guarded. The word *terumotai* is read in the plural — "My *terumot*" — indicating that the duty of guarding applies both to *terumah tehorah*, definitively pure *terumah*, and to *terumah teluyah*, *terumah* of doubtful status. Even when the *terumah* is of uncertain purity and cannot currently be used, the obligation to protect it from further *tumah* remains. Therefore, one must put it in a covered, protected place.

### R. Yehoshua: Singular

Rabbi Yehoshua reads the same verse through its written form. As noted, the word is actually spelled *terumati* — without a *vav* — which could be read as the singular: "My *terumah*." On this reading, the obligation of guarding applies only to *terumah* that is fully functional and beneficial to the *kohen* — that is, *terumah tehorah*. Doubtful *terumah*, from which no benefit can currently be derived, carries no guarding obligation. Since one need not guard it, one is free to expose it so that it becomes definitively *tamei*, after which some limited form of benefit can at least be extracted.

### Different Bases

This confirms the *gemara*'s earlier point: the two disputes — that of the *bechor* and that of the *terumah* — are not only different in their circumstances and policy logic, they are grounded in entirely separate scriptural sources with no textual connection to each other.

### Benefit Logic

Rabbi Yehoshua's position is then refined further. The phrase *natati lecha* — "I have given it *to you*" — is understood as the operative limiting condition. The obligation to guard *terumah* exists only insofar as the *terumah* is genuinely *lecha*, genuinely available to and beneficial for the *kohen*. Doubtful *terumah* that cannot be eaten or otherwise used is not, in any meaningful sense, *lecha* at this moment. Since you cannot benefit from it, you bear no obligation to guard it — and since no guarding obligation exists, the pragmatic course is to allow it to become definitively *tamei* so that some benefit can be recovered.

### Possibility Argument

Rabbi Eliezer counters: the doubtful *terumah* is still potentially *lecha* — it may yet prove to be *tahor*. One's current inability to benefit from it stems from ignorance of its true status, not from its actual condition. The object is possibly fit; therefore the guarding obligation remains. As the *gemara* phrases it: *shema yavo Eliyahu ve-yitaharenu* — perhaps Elijah will come and clarify the matter. The *terumah* might be *tahor*; that possibility is enough to sustain the duty of protection.

---

## Ruling: R. Shimon

### Rav Yehuda Ruling

With the theoretical analysis complete, the *gemara* turns to the practical *halacha*. Rav Yehuda cites a ruling in the name of Shmuel: *halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon* — the law follows Rabbi Shimon.

### Which R. Shimon?

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak immediately challenges this ruling with a pointed question: *hai Rabbi Shimon* — which Rabbi Shimon? There is a Rabbi Shimon in the *mishna* and a Rabbi Shimon in the *baraita*, and their positions are meaningfully different.

### If Mishna

If the ruling follows the Rabbi Shimon of the *mishna*, then the teaching is redundant. It is already well established elsewhere that Shmuel rules that *davar she-eino mitkavein* — an unintentional act — is *mutar*. Rav Chanan bar Ashi already transmits this ruling from Shmuel explicitly, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin teaches it without attribution to any particular case. A ruling by Shmuel that the *halacha* follows the Rabbi Shimon of the *mishna* would add nothing new.

### Rav vs. Shmuel

The *gemara* makes the broader *machlokes* explicit: Rav rules like Rabbi Yehuda — that is, an action likely to produce a prohibited consequence even unintentionally is forbidden — while Shmuel rules like Rabbi Shimon, permitting such unintentional acts. This is confirmed by Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi reporting in Rav's name that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda, and by Rav Chanan bar Ashi in Shmuel's name that it follows Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin transmits the same *machlokes* without a chain of names.

### Two Explanations

The *gemara* thus raises a conceptual question: the ruling attributed to Shmuel here is stated in the context of the *bechor* case, but what precisely is Shmuel saying? There are two distinct rationales that could underlie permission to make a *mum* in the *bechor* with a blood clot: either the animal's condition is treated as equivalent to already having a *mum*, making this a case of *mum* upon *mum* — which is what the earlier scriptural analysis established — or the act is permitted because one's intention is solely to let blood, not to create a *mum*, making this a case of *eino mitkavein*.

### Rashi Approach

Rashi takes a striking position. He holds that even where a *mum* will *certainly* result from the bloodletting, it can still be classified as *eino mitkavein*, because the person's purpose is surgical — to save the animal — and not to create a blemish. What appears to be a *pesik reisha* (an inevitable consequence) is reframed by Rashi as *eino mitkavein* because the agent's intent is categorically different from the prohibited act. This is reminiscent of the category of *melacha she-eina tzricha le-gufah* familiar from Shabbat: you know exactly what you are doing, but your purpose diverges entirely from the purpose that defines the prohibition. Rashi extends this concept beyond Shabbat, treating it as a form of *eino mitkavein* applicable here as well.

### Tosafot Distinction

*Tosafot* objects to this reading and draws a sharper distinction between the two texts. In the *mishna*, Rabbi Shimon says *af al pi she-hu oseh bo mum* — "even though it makes a *mum*" — while the *baraita* uses the phrase *bimkom she-oseh bo mum* — "in a place where it makes a *mum*." *Tosafot* argues that *bimkom she-oseh bo mum* means the *mum* is certain to result from the procedure. In that scenario, the only coherent explanation for why Rabbi Shimon permits it is the *mum*-upon-*mum* rationale: the animal is already treated as blemished, so creating an additional *mum* is not prohibited. The *mishna*, however, says only "even though it makes a *mum*" — which *Tosafot* reads as a case where a *mum* might result accidentally, not inevitably. That case is straightforwardly explained as *eino mitkavein* in the ordinary sense: one does not intend the blemish and it is not certain to occur.

### Must Be Baraita

This distinction is decisive. If the *mishna*'s Rabbi Shimon is simply relying on the principle of *eino mitkavein* — a principle Shmuel already endorses explicitly — then Shmuel's ruling would tell us nothing new by citing that Rabbi Shimon. The ruling must therefore be referring to Rabbi Shimon of the *baraita*, whose position goes further: he permits *shechita* on the basis of the *mum* that was created, without any policy-based restriction. Accordingly, Rav Yehuda's ruling in Shmuel's name is that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Shimon of the *baraita* — one may perform bloodletting even where a *mum* will certainly result, and one may subsequently slaughter the animal on the basis of that *mum*, without concern that such permission will be exploited. This is confirmed explicitly by Rav Sheshes the son of Rabbi Idi, who transmits the ruling in those precise terms: *halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon de-baraisa*.

---

## Nicking Ear

### Nicking Prohibited

A new *mishna* introduces a related but distinct case. If someone intentionally nicks the ear of a *bechor* — a classic form of *mum*, since cuts in the ear characteristically do not heal — he may never slaughter the animal on the basis of that *mum*. Unlike the bloodletting case, where making the *mum* was at least done out of medical necessity, here the person deliberately produced a *mum* in order to gain permission to slaughter the *bechor*. All agree that *shechita* on the basis of this deliberately inflicted *mum* is never permissible.

### R. Eliezer: Forever

Rabbi Eliezer goes further: the *bechor* is permanently disqualified. Even if a new, independent *mum* later appears on the animal — a blemish that had nothing to do with the owner's act — one may still never slaughter the animal. The prohibition extends to all future *shechita*, regardless of what blemish is invoked.

### Sages: Another Blemish OK

The *chachamim* disagree. Their position is that while one may never slaughter on the basis of the deliberately inflicted *mum*, if a new, independently occurring blemish subsequently appears, *shechita* on that basis is entirely permissible. The prohibition is limited to the product of the forbidden act; it does not color the animal's status in perpetuity.

### Deterrent Logic

The policy logic behind Rabbi Eliezer's position is clear. If the only consequence of deliberately creating a *mum* is that you cannot slaughter on the basis of that specific *mum*, there is no meaningful deterrent. The person might reason: if no one notices, I benefit; if they do notice, I lose nothing beyond what I already had. Making the disqualification permanent — so that the animal can never be slaughtered at all — creates a genuine disincentive.

### Question Severity

This prompts a challenge: does Rabbi Eliezer consistently impose such severe and permanent penalties? The question is sharpened by a contrasting case.

### Tzaraat Parallel

The *gemara* cites a case of *tzaraat* — a skin condition creating ritual impurity — in which someone intentionally excises the affected spot (*baheret*) in order to achieve *tahara*. Since the spot is no longer present, it cannot be evaluated by a *kohen*. Rabbi Eliezer rules: *le-ch'she-yivaled lo nega acher yitaher mimenu* — the person will only achieve *tahara* when a new *nega* appears and he is subsequently declared *tahor* from that one, at which point we assume the same process would have resolved the original spot. Notably, Rabbi Eliezer does *not* say the person is permanently impure; he allows one specific path to *tahara*, even if it may take a very long time. The *chachamim* in this context are actually stricter than Rabbi Eliezer: they say *tahara* is possible only if the condition spreads to cover the entire body (*ad she-tifrach be-kulo*) or, in *Tosafot*'s reading, if the remaining portion of the spot shrinks below the requisite minimum size — in either case, one would be *tahor* even were the excised portion still present.

### Rabbah Resolves

Rabbah bar Rav Yosef resolves the apparent inconsistency in Rabbi Eliezer's positions: *ki kanis Rabbi Eliezer be-mamono, be-gufo lo kanis* — Rabbi Eliezer imposes the permanent penalty when the transgression involves *property*; when it involves a person's *body*, he does not.

### Property vs. Body

Two considerations explain the distinction. First, a penalty of permanent bodily impurity would be an extraordinarily severe imposition on a person — too severe to serve merely as a policy deterrent. Second, the deterrence calculus differs: in the case of the *bechor*, if there is no permanent consequence to deliberately making a *mum*, the owner faces no real downside from the scheme. In the case of *tzaraat*, however, the prospect of remaining *tamei* indefinitely until a second *nega* appears — which may never happen — is already a severe enough deterrent without extending it to permanent disqualification.

---

## Formalism vs. Policy

### Rava Question

Rava presses the analysis further. Even granting the distinction between property and person, one still needs to account for the fact that the *chachamim* also shift positions between the two cases. In the *mishna* about the *bechor*'s ear, the *chachamim* say that a new independently-arising *mum* makes *shechita* permissible — a relatively lenient position. Yet in the *tzaraat* case, the *chachamim* are the strict ones, allowing *tahara* only under quite limited circumstances. How is the *rabbanan*'s position internally consistent?

### Different Approaches

The *gemara* answers that Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* are, at a foundational level, operating from entirely different jurisprudential frameworks. Rabbi Eliezer reasons from policy: what penalty, calibrated to the severity of the transgression and the practical realities of the case, will best deter future violations? The *chachamim* reason from legal formalism: when someone performs a prohibited act, the proper response is to negate that act — to treat it juridically as though it never occurred.

### Formalism: Negate

Under the *chachamim*'s formalist approach, the consequence of any prohibited act is that the act is voided. The law proceeds as though the person had not done what they did.

### Nick Negated

In the case of the deliberately nicked ear: the nick is treated as if it never happened. The *mum* is negated, juridically speaking. That means the only lasting consequence is that this particular *mum* is unavailable as a basis for *shechita* — since we treat it as nonexistent — but any other, independently arising *mum* is entirely independent of what the owner did and may be relied upon freely.

### Spot Still There

In the case of *tzaraat*: the excision is treated as if it never happened. The spot is deemed still present. This means the person's path to *tahara* must be one that would work *even if the original spot were still there*. That is why the *chachamim* require either that the condition spread to cover the whole body (which would produce *tahara* regardless) or that the remaining fragment shrink below the minimum size (which would equally mean the original spot, had it been present, was also subthreshold). In both scenarios, *tahara* is achieved through a process that is valid independently of whether the excised portion ever existed.

### Policy: Deterrent

Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, is not engaged in negating acts. He is asking: what is the appropriate deterrent, proportionate to the nature and stakes of the transgression? For property violations where the practical temptation is real and the downside of getting caught is otherwise negligible, a severe and permanent penalty is warranted. For violations affecting a person's body, where the suffering involved in an open-ended wait for another *nega* already creates significant deterrence, a lesser penalty suffices. This policy-sensitivity, rather than a formal rule about negating actions, drives all of Rabbi Eliezer's rulings in these cases.

---

---

# Bekhorot 35

## Bridegroom Tzara'as

### Yitaher Tenan Debate

The *daf* opens by completing the wrap-up discussion of *tzara'as* that began on 34b. *Ba'ei Rav Papa* — Rav Papa poses the question: *yitaher tenan o ve-yitaher tenan*? The *mishnah* rules that if a person cuts away a *nega* in order to prevent a *kohen* from declaring him *tamei*, he must wait until a second *nega* appears and runs its course, at which point he becomes *tahor* from the first as well. The question is how to read the text: does the *advent* of the second *nega* itself purify him from the first, or must he wait until he becomes *tahor* from the second before the first is resolved?

At first glance the question seems academic — either way, as long as the second *nega* is present he remains *tamei*. The *Gemara* therefore asks *le-mai nafka mina*, and the answer lies in a specific case.

### Chosson Tzara'as

The practical difference involves a *chosson* who develops a *nega*. As the *mishnah* in *Nega'im* teaches: *chosson she-nira bo nega*, a bridegroom who shows signs of *tzara'as* is given seven days before any ruling is issued — *notnim lo shiva yamim* — out of respect for his *simcha*. This deferral applies not only to him personally but even to his garments and his house. Similarly, *ve-chen ba-regel notnim lo kol yemei ha-regel*: for any person, if the *nega* appears during *yom tov*, the ruling is postponed until after the full seven days of the festival.

Now imagine that during this deferral period a second *nega* appears. If we read *yitaher tenan* — that the arrival of the second *nega* itself extinguishes the first — then from the moment the second spot appears, the person becomes *tahor* from the first, and we then defer examination of the second for the seven days of *sheva brachos*. During that window, he is actually *tahor*. But if we read *ve-yitaher tenan* — that he must first become *tahor* from the second before the first is resolved — then he never achieves *tahor* status during the wedding week, because the unresolved first *nega* keeps him *tamei* until the second has been purified. The two readings yield meaningfully different practical outcomes for the *chosson* during *sheva brachos*.

### First vs. Second Spot

The question is posed cleanly: *ei amart yitaher tenan*, the second spot's arrival itself grants *tahor* status from the first — *mi-kamaisa tihar lei*, and we then defer the second under *le-basraisa natrinan lei sheva yemei mishta*, giving the *chosson* a genuine period of *taharah*. *Ella ei amart ve-yitaher tenan*, then even without the *kohen* ruling on the second, he remains *tamei* from the first until the second is fully purified — *sof sof ke-ilu metamei lei le-basraisa, ha metamei ve-kaimi mi-kamaisa* — and the wedding week provides no relief. The *Gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

---

## Kansu Beno Acharav

### Son Fined Question

With the *tzara'as* discussion concluded, the *Gemara* returns to the central topic of *bechor*: the rabbinic fine imposed on one who intentionally inflicts a *mum* on a *bechor*. *Ba'ei minei Rabbi Yirmiyah me-Rabbi Zeira* — Rabbi Yirmiyah poses the question to Rabbi Zeira: *tzorem ozen be-bechor u-meis* — if a person punctures the ear of a *bechor* and then dies, *mahu liknos beno acharav*? Will the son be fined as well?

The ear is the paradigmatic example of an intentionally inflicted *mum* — it does not heal, and we will see shortly why it features so prominently in the *mishnah*. The underlying tension in the question is genuine: if the fine is understood primarily as a *knas*, a punishment directed at the transgressor, then once that person is dead, the rationale for the fine evaporates. On the other hand, one might argue that the purpose is societal — to create a disincentive for anyone who might contemplate deathbed manipulation, ensuring that heirs cannot benefit either. The *Gemara* approaches the question by comparing it to several parallel cases.

### Servant & Field Cases

The *Gemara* introduces two other situations in which the question of *kansu beno acharav* arises. The first: *mocher avdo le-kochavim u-meis* — if someone sells his Jewish slave to a non-Jew. Since such a slave is obligated in *mitzvot*, selling him to a non-Jew effectively strips him of the ability to fulfill them. *Chazal* therefore required the seller to redeem the slave at up to ten times the original sale price. If the seller dies, must the son redeem him? The *Gemara* reasons that in this case the answer may well be yes — not because of a general rule that fines pass to heirs, but because *be-chol yomo ve-yomo mafkei lei mi-mitzvot*: every single day the slave remains with the non-Jew he is prevented from performing *mitzvot*. The concern is for the welfare of the slave himself, not merely for punishing the seller. Because the rationale is remedial rather than punitive, it may apply even after the transgressor's death.

The second case involves one who deliberately plans his agricultural labor for *chol ha-mo'ed*. *Chazal* permitted working a field on *chol ha-mo'ed* only in cases of *davar ha-aved* — unavoidable financial loss — not when the person intentionally scheduled his work for that time. If such a person dies having done so, must his son refrain from planting? Here the *Gemara* suggests the son may be exempt — *keivan moachda be-mo'ada u-meis lo kansu beno acharav* — because the father had not yet even completed the transgression when he died. There was no act that concretely needed undoing. The *Gemara* itself acknowledges that framing these cases as *knas* is somewhat strained: in the field case, one could simply say the father never qualified for the *davar ha-aved* exception to begin with.

With these two cases before it — one where the son likely does bear consequences, one where he likely does not — the *Gemara* asks *hacha mai*: what about our case of the *bechor*? The father did perform a concrete act; but unlike the slave case, there is no ongoing victim requiring active remedy. The *Gemara* presents two framings. *Le-didei kansu rabanan* — perhaps the rabbis directed their fine at the person himself, and since he is gone, it cannot reach the son. *O dilma le-mamonei kansu rabanan* — alternatively, they made a statement not about the person but about the property: this animal can no longer yield benefit, and since the animal *ve-hai itei*, the property still exists, the restriction ought to travel with it to the heir.

### Abaye's Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves the question by citing a *mishnah* in the laws of *shemita*. *Sadeh she-nitnaksha ba-shevi'it* — a field from which one cleared thorns and thistles on *shemita* without actually working the soil may still be planted after *shemita*. But one who manured or penned animals in the field on *shemita* — thereby genuinely improving it — is fined and may not plant it after *shemita* either. *Ve-amar Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina*: *hetiva u-meis, beno zor'ah* — if the father fertilized the field and died, the son *may* plant it. *Alma le-didei kansu rabanan, livrei lo kansu rabanan* — we fine the person, not the son.

*Amar Abaye* anticipates the objection: the field case may not be fully analogous to the *bechor*, because by the field the fine is action-directed — we are telling the transgressor not to do this. By the *bechor*, one could argue more formalistically that the rabbis made a declaration about the object itself — the *mum* is treated as non-existent — which would naturally extend to the heir. Abaye does not press the distinction but rather embraces the comparison, and the *Gemara* treats the principle of *le-didei kansu rabanan, livrei lo kansu rabanan* as the operative rule across cases.

### Terumah Case

Abaye proceeds to extend the principle. *Tima taharotav u-meis* — here is the case discussed in *Gittin*: a person intentionally causes someone else's *terumah* to become *tamei* by casting a *sharetz* upon it, rendering it worthless. Ordinarily no payment is collected for such damage because *hezek she-eino nikar lo shmei hezek* — damage that is not visually apparent does not constitute actionable injury under biblical law. Yet if done intentionally, *Chazal* imposed liability. If the perpetrator dies, must his son pay? Abaye says: *lo kansu beno acharav* — the son does not pay. *Mai ta'ama*? Because *hezek she-eino nikar* is only a *rabbinic* fine — *knas de-rabanan hu* — and *didei kansu rabanan, le-vrei lo kansu rabanan*: they fined him, not his son.

One might ask whether policy considerations should override this conclusion — after all, a real person has suffered a real loss, and allowing the debt to die with the transgressor seems like an obvious loophole. The *Gemara* here is consistent in its approach: it categorizes these cases as *knas* and applies the general rule, leaving the harder policy questions to the side. The real analytical challenge — noted but not fully resolved here — is determining which situations qualify as *knas* in the first place, as opposed to *takanos* or corrections of substantive law, since that threshold determination governs everything that follows. The *sugya* in *Tosafot* and other *masechtos* develops this question further; for our purposes, the *Gemara* has established the principle firmly.

---

## Intentional Blemish Cases

### Quaestor Story

The *Gemara* now returns to the question of precisely what *le-da'ato* — intentionality — means when it comes to inflicting a *mum* on a *bechor*, and introduces a remarkable *mishnah*. *Maaseh be-zachar she-peruchav zekenim*: there was an incident involving a very old ram whose wool had never been sheared — as a *bechor* without a *mum* it could not be shorn — and was accordingly trailing and scraggly. *Ve-ra'ahu kastor echad*: a certain Roman official, a *quaestor* (a revenue and legal officer), encountered it and asked what was going on with this animal. The people told him, *bechor hu ve-eino nishchat ela im ken hayah bo mum* — it is a firstborn, and it cannot be *shechted* unless it has a blemish. The official then took a *pigum* — a pugio, a double-bladed Roman dagger — and *tzaram be-ozno*, punctured its ear. *U-va ma'aseh lifnei chachamim va-hitiru*: the case came before the Sages and they declared it permitted.

It is worth noting that the *pigum* — the instrument of piercing — lends its name to the paradigmatic act of inflicting a *mum* on a *bechor*: *pogem ozen shel bechor*. Whether the term derives from this story or simply reflects the ease with which an ear wound is inflicted and yet never heals is an interesting question in itself.

The first ruling — that the animal is *mutar* — seems straightforward if one frames it as: the non-Jew acted on his own initiative, nobody commissioned him, and therefore there is no *le-da'ato* on the part of the Israelite owner. The difficulty is that the non-Jew plainly understood what he was doing and why; he was acting deliberately to benefit the Jewish owner. *Rashi* attempts to address this by arguing that at the time the non-Jew acted he did not yet know that the *chachamim* would actually permit the *bechor* — he was, in Rashi's reading, uncertain about the legal effect of his action. This is admittedly difficult: why would he do it if he didn't believe it would help?

*Ve-achar she-hitiru, halach ve-tzaram be-oznei bechorot acherim* — after hearing the ruling, the quaestor went and started puncturing the ears of other people's *bechorot*. *Va-asru* — and then the Sages forbade it. Taken at face value, one might read the reversal as a policy measure: once a single permissive ruling leads to systematic exploitation, the policy itself must be retracted. But *Rashi* and the *Gemara* read it differently: the first act, whatever degree of awareness it involved, did not constitute an act performed with the specific knowledge that it would render the *bechor* permitted. Once the non-Jew heard the ruling and knew with certainty, each subsequent act was performed *le-da'ato* — with full knowledge of the legal effect — and therefore forbidden. The *Gemara* does not read this as a blanket prospective prohibition on all future cases of the same type; it is specifically the post-ruling acts that are forbidden because of the actor's now-certain intent.

The tension is real. If even the first act was being performed to benefit the Jewish owner, it is somewhat difficult to describe it as *shelo le-da'ato*. One way to resolve this — though the *Gemara* does not state it explicitly — is to distinguish between doing something that *benefits* another and doing something *at another's behest*. The first time the non-Jew acted, he was doing the Jew a favor; the Jew had not prompted him, had not hinted at it, had not expressed desire that it be done. After hearing the ruling, the non-Jew was effectively acting as the Jew's *shaliach*, and at that point the Jew's implicit desire becomes the operative factor.

### Children Tail Case

A parallel incident is then cited: *pa'am achat hayu tinokot mesachakim ba-sadeh ve-kashru zinvei telaim zeh ba-zeh* — some children were playing in a field and tied the tails of sheep together, *va-nifsaka zanavo shel echad me-hem* — and one animal's tail was pulled off. The animal turned out to be a *bechor*. *Ba ma'aseh lifnei chachamim va-hitiru* — the case came before the Sages and they permitted it, since the act was entirely unintentional. But *ra'u she-hitiru ve-holchu ve-kashru zinvos bechorot acheirim* — once they saw the first case had been permitted, they went and tied other *bechorot'* tails together, *va-asru*.

The same interpretive question arises: is this a prospective policy reversal, or is it only the second set of acts that are forbidden because the children now knew what effect their action would have? The *Gemara* adopts the latter reading, which sets up the concluding principle of the *mishnah*.

Both cases are needed — *tzericha*. Had the *Gemara* cited only the non-Jew's case, one might have thought that the first act was innocuous precisely because there was no concern it would be repeated: a freak occurrence by a Roman official would not lead to Israelites following suit. The novelty of the children's case is that allowing children to do something will very plausibly lead to repetition — *de-ati le-misrach* — because children, once told something is permitted, will do it again. On that logic, one might have argued the first case involving children should never have been permitted. Conversely, had the *Gemara* cited only the children's case, one might have thought Israelites would not follow the precedent of a non-Jew — *de-lo ati le-achlufi be-gadol* — so that non-Jewish acts would always remain in a category apart. *Tzericha*: you need both.

The *Gemara* also notes that the concern about children acting again carries a *chinuch* dimension — it is an *aveira* for a Jewish child to do this, and we do not want to habituate children to such behavior. No corresponding *aveira* concern applies to the non-Jew, which is why the initial permissive ruling presented no *chinuch* problem in that case.

### Intentionality Principle

*Zeh ha-klal: kol she-hu le-da'ato asur, shelo le-da'ato mutar* — this is the governing principle: done with awareness of the legal effect, forbidden; done without such awareness, permitted.

The *Gemara* asks what the principle comes to include beyond the stated cases. *Le-atuyei grama*: it includes even indirect causation. As the *Gemara* discussed on the previous *daf*, even if one creates the conditions for a *mum* to occur without directly inflicting it — the small *kre'ach-lach* made for dogs, for instance — if this was done intentionally, not only is the act itself prohibited but the resulting *mum* does not permit *shechita*. Conversely, *shelo le-da'ato mutar* includes even *masiach le-fi tumo* — speaking casually and offhandedly. If a Jew mentions to a friend, without directing his words at any non-Jew, that the animal has no *mum* yet, and a non-Jew overhearing the remark spontaneously acts — that too would be permitted, even though the earlier case of a direct response to a non-Jew was already permitted.

What is striking about this entire *sugya*, taken together, is the degree to which it points toward *policy* considerations rather than a pure *knas* framework. The concern with children repeating the act, the concern with non-Jews acting *as an agent* for the Jew, the focus on whether the Jew's intent to benefit is operative — all of this fits more naturally within a framework of protecting the institution of *bechor* from being systematically undermined. Yet the *Gemara* continues to frame the analysis in terms of *knas*, and that framing creates genuine tension with the conclusions it reaches.

### Kicking Analysis

Rav Chisda, citing Rav Katina, adds an important clarification about the case of a direct verbal response to a non-Jew: *lo shanu ela de-amar lei* — the first case is permitted only when the Israelite responded by saying the animal cannot be *shechted* unless it *has* a *mum*, using language that describes the existing condition. *Aval im amar lei ye'aseh bo mum* — but if the Israelite said "unless a *mum* is *made* in it," using the passive but clearly implying human agency, *ke-man de-amar lei zil avid bei mum dami* — it is as though he said to the non-Jew: go make a *mum*. In that case it would be forbidden even the first time.

*Amar Rava*: this distinction is rejected. *Mimela hu* — the passive voice is not an instruction; *na'aseh* can simply mean something that happens on its own, just as *hayah bo mum* describes a *mum* that exists. If the Israelite said "unless a *mum* comes to be in it," that is not a directive. Rava insists that only an unambiguous explicit instruction crosses the line.

The analogy to *amira le-akum* on *Shabbat* is apt here. On *Shabbat*, a Jew who describes his situation — "how dark it is in this room" — has not issued an *amira*; a Jew who says "it would be wonderful if someone turned on the light" has crossed into *remez* territory. The same distinction operates here. A passive construction describing a condition is not an *amira*; only language that functionally directs the non-Jew's action would constitute one.

The *mishnah* then addresses a case on the opposite end of the spectrum. *Haya bechor rodfo* — if a *bechor* ram was chasing a person, *be-ato ve-asah bo mum* — and the person kicked it defensively and in so doing created a *mum*, *harei zeh yishachet alav*: the animal may be *shechted*. *Amar Rav Papa: lo shanu ela she-be'at be-sha'at redifa* — this applies only if the kick occurred during the chase itself. *Aval achar redifa* — if after the ram stopped pursuing him the person kicked it out of residual anger, *assur*. The *Gemara* presents two formulations of this ruling. One version holds the post-chase kick is clearly problematic — one might argue the person was simply venting *tzaraosav*, remembering his suffering, rather than acting to create a *mum*, but *kah mashma lan* that we are still concerned his intent was to inflict a *mum*. The other version is that even a post-chase kick is permitted — *afilu achar redifa nami* — because *tzayreh hu de-madkar*: he is acting out of remembered pain and anguish, not to create a *mum*, and we are not concerned.

---

## Pre-Birth & Visibility

### Pre-Birth Blemish

*Amar Rav Yehuda: muttar le-hatil mum be-bechor kodem she-yetze le-avir ha-olam* — it is permitted to inflict a *mum* on a *bechor* before it has fully emerged into the world. This is another practical solution to the difficulty of managing a *bechor*, parallel to the early-period strategy noted by the *Rishonim* and later codified in the *Shulchan Aruch*. The idea here is that while the animal is still partially within the womb — before the majority of its head has emerged and it is considered halachically born — any blemish inflicted is not a prohibited act.

### Goat Ears, Sheep Lips

*Amar Rava*: the practical application depends on the species. For a *gadya* — a goat — one works with the *oznei*, the ears, since goats have long ears that protrude well before the majority of the head emerges. For an *imra* — a sheep — the ears are shorter, so one uses *bi-sfatei*, the lips, which similarly emerge before the head is fully born. A cut to the lip will not heal and constitutes a permanent *mum*. An alternate tradition — *ika de-amri* — holds that even a sheep's ear may be used if the animal happens to emerge sideways, *derech tzad nafak*, with the ears preceding the head. *Tosafot* reads *eima* here not as a permissive "one could say" but as a definitive description: if the birth happens to be sideways, the ears indeed come out first and may be used.

### Visible When Bleating

*Amar Rava*: if an animal has a blemish on the inside of its mouth that is not visible while it eats but becomes visible *pa'i* — when it bleats — *u-machzi*, and can be seen from the outside, *havei muma* — this constitutes a valid *mum*. The visibility standard for a *mum* is that it must be externally observable; the question is what counts as external when the blemish is technically internal.

*Rav Papa* responds that Rava is not introducing a new principle but explaining the *Gemara* — that is, providing the *peshat* of the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* lists among valid *mumim* the case of *ha-chitei ha-chitzonot she-nifgemu* — outer incisors that have been chipped — and *ha-penimiyot she-ne'ekru* — inner molars that have been completely extracted. The question is why extracted inner molars, which cannot be seen normally, count as externally visible. *Mai ta'ama de-ne'ekru havei muma? Mishum de-chi pa'i machzi* — because when the animal bleats, the absence of those molars becomes visible. That defines the outer visibility threshold: a blemish seen when the animal opens its mouth to bleat is considered sufficiently external to qualify.

---

## Witness Credibility

### Mishnah Framework

The *Gemara* now pivots to the equally consequential question of credibility: who may testify that a *mum* on a *bechor* occurred naturally and was not intentionally inflicted? The *mishnah* states: *kol ha-mumim ha-re'uyim lavo bi-dei adam* — for any blemish that could have been humanly inflicted, credibility is required. Blemishes that obviously could not have been produced by human agency — a supernumerary limb, congenital blindness, or the like — require no such testimony. For the rest: *ro'ei Yisrael ne'emanim, ro'ei Kohanim einam ne'emanim* — Israelite *ro'im* are believed, *kohanim ro'im* are not.

The *mishnah*'s formulation is itself ambiguous. *Ro'ei Yisrael* in construct form (*smichut*) means "shepherds of Israelites" — describing who the owner is. *Ro'im Yisra'elim*, by contrast, would describe the shepherd's identity. The *Gemara* notes that the *mishnah* actually uses both constructions — *ro'ei Yisrael* and *ro'im Kohanim* — and the textual variation will be at the heart of the *Gemara*'s debate.

### Yochanan Opinion

Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar dispute which reading is primary. One opinion reads the *mishnah* as going by the identity of the shepherd: *ro'ei Yisrael bei Kohanim ne'emanim* — even if the shepherd is employed by a *kohen*, if the shepherd himself is an Israelite he is believed. The rationale is that we are not concerned he will compromise himself for small incidental benefit — *legima lo chaishinan*, we do not worry that the *kohen* will reward him with a meal of *shechted bechor*. He has no sufficient stake to lie.

Conversely, *ro'ei Kohanim be-Yisrael einam ne'emanim* — a *kohen* shepherd employed by an Israelite is not believed. The *kohen* shepherd reasons: *keivan de-katarchana bei*, I have worked with this animal faithfully — surely when the time comes my master will give the *bechor* to me rather than to some other *kohen*. Since he anticipates receiving the animal, he cannot be trusted. Furthermore, *ve-hu ha-din Kohen le-Kohen*: a *kohen* testifying about a neighboring *kohen*'s *bechor* is equally untrustworthy, because *chashiyan le-gomlin* — we are concerned for reciprocity. Today I testify for your *bechor*; tomorrow you testify for mine.

### Shimon Opinion

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* disagrees with both the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Meir. He says: *ne'eman hu al shel chaveiro ve-eino ne'eman al shel atzmo* — one is believed to testify about another person's animal, and is not believed only about one's own. Whether you are an Israelite or a *kohen*, if you are testifying about someone else's *bechor* — even a family member's according to some readings — we do not worry about the small benefits that might flow to you. The concern of reciprocity and the concern of incidental reward (*legima*) are simply not weighty enough to override the basic presumption of credibility. You are disqualified only when it is your own sheep, because then you are a direct and immediate beneficiary.

### Owner Determines

The second major reading of the *mishnah* holds that the operative question is not who the shepherd is but who the *owner* is — that is, who benefits from the testimony. Under this reading: *ro'ei Yisrael she-hen Kohanim ne'emanim* — shepherds employed by Israelites, even if those shepherds are themselves *kohanim*, are believed. The *kohen* shepherd reasons: *lo shevik tzurba mei-rabbanan ve-yahiv li didi* — why would this Israelite owner give the *bechor* to me, a lowly shepherd, rather than to a distinguished *kohen*? He does not expect to benefit and therefore has no motive to lie.

*Ro'ei Kohanim ve-hen Yisrael einam ne'emanim* — shepherds of *kohanim*, even if those shepherds are Israelites, are not believed. Here, the *kohen* owner directly benefits from the testimony, and we fear the shepherd will be rewarded — *chashinan le-legima*. And *kol she-kein Kohen le-Kohen d'lo* — certainly one *kohen* cannot testify for another *kohen*'s *bechor*, because in that case we face *both* concerns simultaneously: *chashinan le-gomlin ve-chashinan le-legima* — both the reciprocity concern and the reward concern apply together.

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* then comes and says: both concerns are overstated. You may testify for another's animal entirely regardless of who you are and regardless of who benefits. Only self-testimony is excluded.

### Meir Opinion

Rabbi Meir then articulates a categorically different principle: *ha-chashud al ha-davar lo dano ve-lo me'ido* — anyone who is suspect regarding a matter may neither judge it nor testify about it. *Kohanim* as a class are suspect when it comes to *bechorot* — they have a systemic interest in the institution and have been known to take liberties. They cannot be trusted regardless of context, regardless of whether they are shepherds or bystanders, regardless of whether it is their own animal or a total stranger's. *Yisraelim* are not suspect as a class.

How does Rabbi Meir's position differ from the first reading of the *tanna kamma*, which also held that a *kohen* is not believed? The difference surfaces in the case of *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai*, who rules: *bechor be-veit Kohen tzarich shnayim min ha-shuk le-haid alav* — a *bechor* in the possession of a *kohen* requires two disinterested witnesses from the marketplace to establish that a *mum* occurred naturally. The *tanna kamma*'s concern with *kohanim* was circumstantial — based on possible reward or reciprocity. Two strangers with no connection to each other and no relationship with the *kohen* would, under the *tanna kamma*'s framework, adequately address both concerns. But Rabbi Meir, who distrusts *kohanim* categorically, would still refuse to accept two *kohanim* from the marketplace regardless of their independence, because the disqualification is not circumstantial but class-based. This is the precise *nafka mina* between the two positions.

---

## Safek Bechor Trust

### Owners Testify

*Keman azla ha de-amar Rav Chisda amar Rav Katina: safek bechor she-nolad be-Yisrael tzarich shnayim min ha-shuk le-haid alav* — a doubtful firstborn in the possession of an Israelite requires two witnesses from the marketplace. This ruling seems aligned with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kapusai, who consistently demands two disinterested strangers. *Rav Nachman* objects: he holds that even the *owners themselves* can testify — *ba'alim me'idin alav*.

Rav Nachman argues by analogy: *de-ai lo teima hachi, ma'aser le-Rabbi Meir mi me'id alav?* If we distrusted every possible beneficiary, then for *ma'aser behemah* — every tenth animal, which must be treated as *maaser* and whose *mum* permits ordinary consumption — nobody could ever testify, since any Israelite could one day have a *ma'aser* with a *mum* and would therefore be a potential future beneficiary of any testimony he gives today. The *Gemara* responds: *ma'aser vadai ne'eman*.
