The *gemara* offers an initial resolution: *ha begufa ha be'ayna* — the distinction is between the body and the eye. A *yavelet* on the eye is a full *mum* because it is far more disfiguring; a *yavelet* on the rest of the body falls into the middle category. The *Torah*'s ruling likewise refers to the eye. The *gemara* then challenges this: the *pasuk* says nothing of the kind — *kra stama ketiv*, it speaks without any qualification, making no distinction between the eye and the body. The first resolution is therefore rejected.

The *gemara* then proposes a second answer: *ha de'is bei etzem ha deleis bei etzem* — the distinction is not between eye and body but between whether the growth contains a bone or not. The *Torah*'s case of *yavelet* as a full *mum* involves a growth with a bone, which represents a genuine and serious deformity. Our *mishnah* about the eye and the later *mishnah* about the middle category both involve a *yavelet* without a bone — just a skin flap. In the eye, even a boneless skin flap is sufficiently disfiguring to be a full *mum*; on the body, a mere skin flap without a bone falls into the middle category.

---

## Yavelet Analysis

### Yavelet w/ w/o Bone

To summarize the framework emerging from the *gemara*: the *Torah*'s ruling that *yavelet* is a *mum* refers to a growth containing a bone — a genuine structural deformity. Both of our *mishnayot* are discussing a boneless growth, merely a skin flap (*tiltul*). Within that category, the *gemara* draws a further distinction between the eye and the rest of the body.

### Eye vs Body

The *gemara* then presses a further question: if the *yavelet* in question has no bone, is it really meaningful to say it is even a middle-category disqualification on the body? *Harei tiltul be'alma hu* — it is just a trivial skin flap; why should it matter at all? This touches on a deeper conceptual challenge that runs throughout the *perek*: how do we define *tamim*? Is the absence of a *mum* sufficient to render an animal *tamim*, or is *tamim* a separate, more demanding standard? And what kinds of conditions are even significant enough to enter the discussion — what makes something worth paying attention to in terms of disfigurement? Color variation, for instance, is presumably not enough to constitute a *mum*. So where does the skin flap fall?

The *gemara* brings a ruling of *Rabbi Eliezer*: *ba'alei hatiltulin pesulin be'adam u'ksherim bivehema* — people (*kohanim*) with skin flaps are disqualified for Temple service, but animals with them are entirely acceptable. This raises an apparent difficulty: if skin flaps are entirely acceptable for animals, how can our *mishnah* say they fall into the middle category? The *gemara* responds: *ela idi ve'idi be'einav* — both cases concern the eye. The question then becomes what distinguishes the two *mishnayot* when both deal with a skin flap on the eye.

One proposed distinction, reflecting the *girsa* in the text and the reading of Rashi: *ha beshachar ha belavan* — one case concerns the black of the eye and one concerns the white of the eye. A skin flap on the black of the eye is sufficiently disfiguring to be a full *mum*; one on the white of the eye is less so, placing it in the middle category. The *gemara* then raises a further objection: *ein mumim belavan* — there are, apparently, no *mumim* recognized in the white of the eye at all, which makes it puzzling to say the white-of-eye case even reaches the middle category. The reason for this categorical exclusion of the white of the eye is a matter of its own complexity; the *gemara* elsewhere seems to want to define the relevant *mum* of the eye — *tavlul be'eino* — quite narrowly.

### White of Eye

*Tosafot*, troubled by the principle *ein mumim belavan*, prefers a different *girsa*: instead of *ha beshachar ha belavan*, Tosafot reads both cases as being in the black of the eye — *idi ve'idi beshachar*. What then distinguishes the two cases? *Ve'amar Reish Lakish lo kashya ha de'it bei se'ar ha delait bei se'ar* — the distinction is whether hair is growing out of the skin flap. If hair grows from the flap, that is significantly more disfiguring — a full *mum*; if there is no hair, it is a lesser disqualification. The mechanics of how a skin flap with hair could grow from the eyeball are admittedly difficult to visualize, though the possibility was raised that some types of ocular tumors or growths, including papillomas, do occur on and around the eye in animals, and hair-bearing growths are apparently not unknown. In any case, Tosafot's reading preserves the consistent principle that the white of the eye is never the basis of a *mum*, while Rashi's *girsa* allows for at least some role for the white of the eye in the middle category.

The *gemara* also cites a *baraita* about the disproportionate size ruling: *gedola keshel egel* — if an eye is as large as that of a calf, or *keshel avaz* — as small as that of a duck, those extremes would be too large or too small. It should be noted that this *baraita* appears to be reading the *mishnah*'s formulation of *achat gedola ve'achat ketana* differently: the *mishnah* seems to refer to disproportionality between the two eyes of the same animal, whereas the *baraita* in the *gemara* seems to address absolute size — whether one eye is abnormally large or small compared to the norm — and then specifies how large or small would be too much. This may represent a genuine interpretive divergence between the *mishnah* and the *baraita*, and how we rule on that question remains unresolved.

Regarding the Sages' disagreement with Rabbi Yehuda on testicles, the *gemara* cites a *baraita* suggesting that even a testicle as small as a bean would not constitute a *mum* according to the Sages — implying they may not recognize any size disproportion of testicles as a *mum* regardless of degree.

---

## Tail Length

### Calf Tail Rule

The *mishnah* states: *zanav ha-egel she-eina maga'at l'arkov* — the tail of a calf that does not reach the *arkov*, the knee joint, is a *mum*. The Sages add: *kol marbit agalim kach hen* — this is the normal situation of all calves. *Kol zman sheheim magdilot hen nimtachot* — as they grow, the tail continues to stretch and lengthen. Rashi reads this not as a disagreement but as an agreement: the Sages are affirming that the normal developmental pattern is for the tail to reach and then extend beyond the knee joint as the animal grows, so an animal whose tail falls short of that range is outside normal and is therefore a *mum*.

### Joint Definition

The *mishnah* then asks: *eizu hi arkov?* — which knee are we speaking of? *Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos* says: *ba-arkov she-be'emtza ha-yarech* — the joint in the middle of the thigh, which corresponds to what we would call the knee, as opposed to the lower joint closer to the foot (which in bovines is higher up than a human ankle but is analogous to it). A *baraita* adds: *kaf ha-elyon ve'lo kaf ha-tachton* — the upper joint, not the lower one. *U'kenegdo be-gamal nikar* — and this joint is particularly visible and recognizable in camels.

---

## Wrap-Up & Middle

### Consensus Mishna

The *mishnah* now offers a wrap-up statement: *al elu mumim shochtin et ha-bechor u'psulei ha-mukdashin nifdin aleihem* — on all the *mumim* enumerated above, one may slaughter the *bechor*, and if such a condition occurred in other *korbanot*, they may be redeemed on account of it.

The *gemara* asks: why is this wrap-up statement needed at all? *Ha'tana lei reisha* — did we not already establish at the very opening of the *perek* that these *mumim* permit *shechita* of the *bechor*? The *gemara* answers: *seifa itzterich* — the necessary addition is the second clause: *u'psulei ha-mukdashin nifdin aleihem* — to inform us that the same standard applies to other *korbanot* as well, equating the *mum* of a *bechor* with that of other *kodashim*. The *gemara* then suggests even this is obvious: if we can slaughter on account of a *mum*, surely we can redeem on account of it. But that obviousness only holds if we assume the categories are the same across *bechor* and other *korbanot* — an assumption the *Torah*'s more detailed treatment of other *korbanot* might have led one to question.

The *gemara* concludes: *ela aidei de'tana shalosh osif* — the wrap-up *mishnah* is needed because in yesterday's discussion, the opinion of *Ila* added three additional *mumim* that the Rabbis said *lo shamanu* — we have no tradition about. And the subsequent *mishnayot* present rulings in the names of individual *Tannaim* — notably *Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos* — without explicit recorded disagreement. The wrap-up *mishnah* therefore comes to tell us that *de'kasasnehu be'chulehu* — despite all the individual attributions and earlier uncertainties, the ruling is consensus: all of these are agreed-upon *mumim* for purposes of both *shechita* of the *bechor* and redemption of other *korbanot*. The one explicit debate earlier in the *perek* was resolved when the later *Beit Din* accepted that position as well, so by now everything is in agreement.

### Middle Category

The *mishnah* now introduces a distinct and important intermediate category: *ve'elu she'ein shochtin aleihem lo ba'mikdash ve'lo ba'medinah* — these are animals upon which one may not slaughter, neither in the *Beit HaMikdash* nor outside it. This is the worst of all positions: the animal is not *tamim* enough to be offered as a *korban*, yet it lacks a sufficiently definitive *mum* to permit slaughter outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. One can do nothing with it.

---

## Transitory Blemishes

### White Spots

The first items in the middle category: *chavarur* — white spots in the eye — and *hamayim she'einan kvu'im* — water in the eye that is not fixed, meaning the condition is not permanent. Rashi explains *chavarur* as white spots on the eye. The underlying principle governing both cases can be generalized: any *mum over*, any transitory *mum*, falls into this middle category. While the condition persists, one cannot bring the animal as a *korban*; but because the *mum* may resolve, one may not slaughter it either.

### Inner Molars

The *mishnah* continues: *ve'hachittin hapnimiyot she'nifgemu aval lo she'ne'ekru* — the roots of the inner molars that were damaged or nicked but not completely uprooted. This is notable because the inner molars are not visible externally. This raises a question about whether the standard of *tamim* for bringing a *korban* is simply the mirror image of the absence of a *mum*, or whether it is an independent and more demanding requirement — one that may be triggered even by non-visible conditions. Alternatively, perhaps under certain circumstances these molars can be observed, or perhaps the standard of visibility for *korbanot* is different from that for *mumim* generally.

---

## Skin Conditions

### Scabs & Warts

The *mishnah* lists: *u'va'al garav u'va'al yavelet* — those with *garav* (scabs or hardened growths) or *yavelet* (warts or skin protrusions) — and *u'va'al chazazit* — another variety of wart or skin condition. All of these fall into the middle category: not a full *mum* permitting slaughter, but not acceptable for offering as a *korban*. As established in the earlier *gemara* discussion, these conditions on the body — as opposed to the eye — are insufficiently disfiguring to constitute a full *mum*, yet they prevent the animal from being *tamim*.

---

## Non-Blemish Issues

### Age Sick Smelly

The *mishnah* now introduces a categorically different set of disqualifications — not physical deformities at all, but factors relating to the animal's condition and history. *Zaken* — if the animal is very old; *ve'choleh* — or sick; *u'mezoham* — or smelly. These are not *mumim* in the conventional sense, but they render the animal inappropriate as a *korban*.

---

## Tumtum Analysis

### Tumtum Case

*Ve'tumtum* — the *tumtum* case: an animal whose genitalia are covered or concealed, making it impossible to determine the sex. Because we do not know whether it is male or female, it cannot be brought as a *bechor* — perhaps it is female — and it cannot be slaughtered outside the *Beit HaMikdash* either — perhaps it is male and retains the *kedusha* of a *bechor*.

### Androgynos Issue

*Ve'androgynos* — the *androgynos*: an animal that has both male and female genitalia. This too falls into the middle category according to the first view in the *mishnah*.

### Rabbi Yishmael View

*Rabbi Yishmael* dissents: *ein lecha mum gadol mizeh* — there is no greater *mum* than this. His position is that if the animal is male — as would be required for a *bechor* — and yet it also has female genitalia, that constitutes a major disfigurement and is a full *mum*. It would therefore be a *bechor* with a *mum*, and one could slaughter it accordingly.

### Sages' View

The Sages go even further in leniency: *eino bechor ela nigzaz ve'ne'avad* — it is not a *bechor* at all; one may shear it and work it. Their reasoning, apparently, is that the *androgynos* is not definitively male. There is a debate as to whether the Sages consider it to be of uncertain gender — possibly male or possibly female — or whether they regard it as a third, separate gender category entirely. This latter possibility has attracted attention well beyond the *beit midrash*, as there are those in contemporary discussions of gender identity who find it meaningful that the *gemara* devotes serious attention to *androgynos* as a possible third category.

---

## Skin Conditions (II)

### Garav Resolution

The *gemara* now takes up the tension raised earlier: *d'garav lo* — are we saying *garav* is not a *mum*? But *ve'haksiv garav b'Orayta* — the *Torah* explicitly lists *garav* as a *mum*! Similarly: *ve'chazazit* — is the *chazazit* not a *mum*? But the *Torah* says *yallefet*, and a *baraita* identifies *yallefet* with *chazazit mitzrit* — the Egyptian form of *chazazit*. How can our *mishnah* place them merely in the middle category?

The *gemara* resolves the *chazazit* tension first: *kan be'chazazit hamitzrit, kan be'chazazit d'alma* — the *Torah*'s *yallefet* refers specifically to the Egyptian *chazazit*, which is a severe, adherent condition. (Reish Lakish elsewhere notes that *yallefet* is named because *she'melapefet ve'holeches ad yom hamisa* — it clings and adheres until the day of death, a remarkably unpleasant image.) Our *mishnah*'s *chazazit* refers to a less severe variety that does not have the same character as the Egyptian form.

### Three Garav Types

The *garav* tension is more difficult. The *gemara* says: *garav agarav nami lo kashya, ha belach ha beyavesh* — the *Torah*'s *garav* that constitutes a full *mum* is dry, permanent, and non-healing; the *garav* in our *mishnah* that is only a middle-category disqualification is moist and can heal: *lach mitztaya, yavesh lo mitztaya*.

But the *gemara* challenges this: the *Torah* in *Devarim* says *yakecha Hashem be'shchin mitzrayim u'va'afolim u'vagarav u'vayallefet... asher lo tuchal lehirafeh* — it mentions *garav* together with the other Egyptian afflictions and says they cannot heal. Moreover, *cheres* — dry pottery-like skin — is also mentioned in that context, and if one form of the word is explicitly the dry type, the *garav* in the same verse should also be taken as unable to heal even if moist. How then can we say the moist *garav* heals?

The *gemara* resolves this by identifying three distinct types of *garav*. The *garav* mentioned among the *mumim* in the context of animal disqualifications is *yavesh bein mibifnim bein mibachutz* — dry on both the inside and outside, equivalent to *cheres*, like pottery. This is permanently non-healing and constitutes a full *mum*. The *garav* of our *mishnah*, which places it in the middle category, is *lach mibachutz umibifnim* — moist inside and out, and therefore capable of healing, placing it in the transitory-disqualification category. The *garav* mentioned in the verse about the Egyptian afflictions — identified by the word *sprouting* (*pore'ach*) used in the neighboring phrase *shchin ava'bu'ot* — is *yavesh mibifnim velach mibachutz*: dry on the inside and moist on the outside. Because it is dry on the inside, it cannot heal; this also constitutes a full *mum* upon which one may slaughter.

---

## Non-Blemish Issues (II)

### Three Exclusions

The *gemara* asks: *mena hani mili* — where do we derive the exclusion of old, sick, and smelly animals? A *baraita* answers from the threefold use of *min* ("from") in the verse: *min hatzon min hakesavim umin ha'izim* — from the flock, from the sheep, from the goats. Each *min* is understood as a limiting term, and the three exclusions correspond: *perat lezaken ulecholeh ulemizuham*.

The *gemara* notes that all three are necessary and none could be inferred from the others. Had the *Torah* excluded only the old (*zaken*), one might have thought sickness is different because the animal may recover — *delo hadar bari*; had it excluded only the sick, one might have thought old age is different because it is the normal condition of any living being — *dehainu orchia*. Had it excluded only two, one might have thought the smelly is different because it is not physically weakened — *delo kachish*; or conversely, had it excluded only the smelly because it is repulsive — *mishum dema'is* — one might have thought the merely old or sick are not so repulsive and therefore not excluded. Each of the three possesses a distinct character, and therefore all three exclusions are necessary.

### Sin-Related Animals

The *gemara* then derives the exclusion of animals involved in *aveira*: from the verse *adam ki yakriv mikem korban min habehema min habakar umin hatzon*, each limiting phrase is understood to exclude a different category. *Min habehema* — to exclude *rove'a ve'nirva'*, animals used in bestiality, whether as the active or passive party. *Min habakar* — to exclude *hane'evad*, an animal that was worshipped as an idol. *Umin hatzon* — to exclude *hamuktza*, an animal set aside for *avodah zarah* even without being actively worshipped. The additional *vav* of *umin hatzon* serves to exclude *hanogei'ach*, an animal that gored a person.

### Single Witness Rule

A question arises: animals used in bestiality or that gored someone are subject to the death penalty — they are to be stoned. Why is it necessary to say they may not be brought as *korbanot* if they should not even exist? The *gemara* answers: this is why the *mishnah* specifies *al pi ed echad o al pi ha-be'alim* — through one witness or through the owners' own testimony. Without two witnesses in a formal court proceeding, the animal does not acquire the legal status of *shor haniskal*. Even if the facts are known to one witness or to the owner, it does not become *assur behana'ah* without a formal adjudication with two witnesses. The animal is permitted for general use — it can be slaughtered and eaten — but it cannot be brought as a *korban*.

---

## Androgynos Dispute

### Rava's Question

The *gemara* now takes up the debate about *androgynos* in greater depth. *Bei Rava* — Rava raises a question: what exactly is Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning when he says *ein lecha mum gadol mizeh* — there is no greater *mum* than this? The question is not about the conclusion but about the conceptual basis.

### Male Status

*Michdi pshita lei* — is it obvious to Rabbi Yishmael that an *androgynos* is definitely male and that the female genitalia is his *mum*? Or does Rabbi Yishmael himself hold that there is doubt whether the *androgynos* is male or female? Under that second reading, Rabbi Yishmael's position would be a legal hedge: *im timtzo lomar bechor hu, harei mumo imo* — even if it turns out to be male, it has a *mum*, and either way you can slaughter and benefit from it. This is a coherent position regardless of the underlying gender question.

Abaye had proposed that the female genitalia should constitute a *charutz* — a crevice — and therefore a *mum*, based on the *Torah*'s enumeration of *o charutz* among the *mumim*. The *gemara* discussed at length whether *charutz* must be at a location of bone, as *shavur* (broken) is at a location of bone, or whether *charutz* can apply anywhere on the body. The *gemara* ultimately concluded that *charutz* requires a place of bone, and therefore the female genitalia of an *androgynos* — located where there is no bone — would not technically satisfy the definition of *charutz*.

Rava goes further: even without the comparison to *shavur*, one could not classify a crevice in a place of soft tissue as a *mum*, because the *Torah* separately needed to mention *garav* — which digs into the skin — to establish that it is a *mum*. If a skin-penetrating *garav* required a separate verse, how much more so would a crevice in soft tissue need one. By negative implication, *charutz* alone would not cover a soft-tissue location.

### Practical Difference

*Lemai nafka mina* — what practical difference does it make whether Rabbi Yishmael considers the *androgynos* definitely male or merely possibly male? The *gemara* offers two answers. First: *lemilkei alei mishum giza va'avoda* — if the *androgynos* is definitely male and merely has a *mum*, then the animal retains *kedushat bechor* until it is slaughtered. If the owner shears it or works it before slaughter, he transgresses. If it is only doubtfully male, one cannot administer lashes because perhaps it was never a *bechor* to begin with. Second, and more practically significant: *lemasvei le-kohen* — does the owner need to give this animal to a *kohen*? If it is definitively a male *bechor* with a *mum*, it must be handed over to the *kohen* who will then slaughter it. But if there is genuine doubt whether it is even male, the owner can say: you cannot prove it is a *bechor*, and I may keep and slaughter it myself.

### Torah Proof

The *gemara* attempts to determine Rabbi Yishmael's actual position from a source. *Rabbi Ilai* says in the name of *Rabbi Yishmael*: *androgynos bechor hu u'mumo imo* — an *androgynos* is a *bechor* and its blemish accompanies it. This sounds like an unequivocal statement that it is definitively male with a *mum*. The *gemara* resists this reading: *dilma im timtzo lomar kamar* — perhaps Rabbi Yishmael means even if you were to say it is a *bechor*, its *mum* comes with it, leaving open the possibility that he is not certain it is male.

The *gemara* then brings a stronger proof: the *Torah* uses the word *zachar* (male) twice in the relevant passages concerning *olah*. Since the *Torah* already established that an *olah* must be male, the second mention of *zachar* would be superfluous. From this we derive *lehotzi tumtum ve'androgynos* — to exclude the *tumtum* and the *androgynos*, which are not fully or definitively male. The question becomes: whose position does this *pasuk* fit?

### Legal vs Factual

It cannot fit the first *tana* of the *mishnah*, who considers *androgynos* a matter of doubt. As *Tosafot* explains, there is a critical distinction: the *Torah* may address factual doubts — situations where we humans do not know what the facts are — and tell us how to proceed. But if the question is not a factual uncertainty but a *halachic* definitional question — how do we legally categorize the entity known as *androgynos*? — then that is not a factual doubt for the *Torah* to resolve by telling us to treat it as a *safek*. The *Torah* defines categories; it does not tell us that an inherently ambiguous legal category should be treated as a doubt. So if the first *tana* says *androgynos* is a doubt, the *Torah* verse would not have been needed to tell us to exclude it — the doubt itself would resolve the question. Therefore, the verse cannot be directed at the first *tana*'s position.

Could it be directed at the last Sages, who say *androgynos* is a completely separate gender and not a *bechor* at all? The *gemara* considers this: if that were the case, one *pasuk* saying *zachar* should have sufficed to exclude a being that is categorically not male. Why would two mentions of *zachar* be needed? The *gemara* answers: *ve-gabei bechor tarti kra'ei ktivi* — there are in fact two mentions of *zachar* by *bechor* as well, *hazachar takdish* and *asher yihiye lecha hazacharim l'Hashem*. The reason two are needed, even for the Sages who say it is a completely separate gender, is that one mention of *zachar* might only exclude the opposite gender — the definitive female — while this middle category would not automatically be excluded by a single *zachar*. A second mention is needed to make clear that even this middle category is excluded.

### Final Analysis

The *gemara* thus does not conclusively establish that the two-*pasuk* proof points exclusively to Rabbi Yishmael. The argument that was thought to prove Rabbi Yishmael's position — that two *psukim* are needed only if we are excluding something that would otherwise have been considered definitively male — is answered by saying even a completely separate third gender might need two exclusionary *psukim* rather than one.

The upshot is as follows: the first position holds that the gender of an *androgynos* is in doubt — it may be male or female. The second position, Rabbi Yishmael's, holds either that it is definitively male with a *mum*, or at minimum that even if there is doubt, once it is male it has a *mum* — and either way it may be slaughtered. The third position holds it is a completely separate gender, neither male nor female, and it is not a *bechor* at all. What remains unresolved in the present discussion is whether Rabbi Yishmael's position entails a definitive claim that the *androgynos* is male, or whether he too acknowledges a doubt and merely adds that even under the more favorable assumption it has a *mum*.

One further point is worth noting regarding the framing of the *androgynos* analysis. The *gemara*'s discussion of whether the female genitalia constitutes a *charutz* reflects an implicit conceptual approach: female genitalia are understood as the absence of male anatomy — a *charitz*, a crevice, a lack — rather than as a positive presence of a different kind. This framing explains why the *gemara* never raises the mirror-image possibility of calling the *androgynos* a female with a *mum* (due to the presence of male genitalia). Once male genitalia are present, the animal cannot be classified as female; the only remaining questions are whether it is definitively male with a *mum*, possibly male, or a third category entirely.

---

---

# Bekhorot 42

## Androgynos Status

### Intro: Gender Categories

The daf opens in the middle of a rich discussion about two categories of indeterminate gender: *androgynos*, an individual possessing both male and female genitalia, and *tumtum*, an individual whose genitalia are covered over by a layer of skin and therefore undetectable. These are among the most fascinating discussions in the tractate, touching on questions of gender identity that resonate well beyond their technical halachic context.

### Three Positions

By way of review, three theoretical positions exist regarding the status of an *androgynos*. The first is that it is *safek zachar safek nekeiva* — not that any individual case is unknowable in fact, but that by its very nature the *androgynos* occupies an intrinsically indeterminate space between male and female. The second possibility is that it is a *zachar* with a *mum*, a male with a blemish — since it possesses female genitalia in addition to male. The third possibility is that it constitutes a third gender altogether, a *beriyah bifnei atzmah*, a category unto itself.

It is worth noting that the *Gemara* does not seriously entertain the possibility that an *androgynos* is a female with a *mum*. This reflects the assumption, shared by much of ancient society, that the presence of male genitalia is definitionally masculine; femaleness is understood as the absence of male genitalia, not as a positive category that can be "blemished" by the presence of male anatomy.

### Rav Chisda Position

The *Gemara* then turns to *tumtum*. The Mishnah records that *Chachamim* say an *androgynos* is definitively not a *bechor*, because it is an entirely third type of gender. *Amar Rav Chisda*: the entire debate concerns *androgynos* alone. But *aval be-tumtum divrei hakol safek hu ve-kadosh misafek* — a *tumtum* is agreed by all to be a mere doubt. Unlike the *androgynos*, whose very anatomy is hybrid, the *tumtum* is simply an animal or person whose genitalia are hidden under skin. The doubt here is a doubt in fact — each individual *tumtum* is either male or female, we simply do not know which. Rav Chisda therefore holds that no one could seriously categorize a *tumtum* as its own gender. It is a *safek zachar safek nekeivah*, and the applicable *halachot* are those of any ordinary doubtful case: it is treated as a doubtful *bechor*, not given to a *Kohen*, and a *Yisrael* eats it when it acquires a *mum*.

---

## Erech Pasukim

### Rava Challenge

*Amar lei Rava*: if that is true — if a *tumtum* is nothing more than a standard *safek* — then in the domain of *erchin*, when someone vows the *erech* of an individual, a *tumtum* should generate an obligation. The Torah's chart of valuations is keyed to gender and age; male and female carry different values. If a *tumtum* is simply one or the other and we do not know which, then presumably one should at least pay the male value out of *safek*. Why, then, does a *braita* at the top of 42a teach: *ha-zachar* — and *ve-lo tumtum ve-androgynos*? Both are excluded from the *parsha* of *erchin* entirely.

### Cross Out Tumtum

The *Gemara* responds: *sami mikan tumtum* — cross out the word *tumtum*. The *braita* lists *tumtum* and *androgynos* together, but that pairing is incidental; the *halacha* of exclusion from *erchin* really concerns only *androgynos*. The *Gemara* tries a second formulation as well. Perhaps one would think that while a *tumtum* or *androgynos* cannot be assigned the male *erech*, it should at least receive the female value, which is lower. The *Torah* responds by stressing *ha-zachar* and separately *ve-im nekeiva* — and *aval lo tumtum ve-androgynos*. Again, both are excluded. And again the *Gemara* says: *sami mikan tumtum* — cross it out. The *halacha* pertains to *androgynos* only.

### Male Value Default

This pattern — quoting *tumtum ve-androgynos* as a fixed pair and then erasing *tumtum* — recurs throughout the sugya, and it is genuinely troubling. *Tosafot* himself flags the problem. One might have said: even granting that a *tumtum* is a factual doubt, the *Torah* could legitimately assign it distinct *halachot* precisely because of the manner in which it is in doubt. This is not the same as saying it is a third gender. An individual who is biologically one or the other, but whose sex is impossible to determine in the present state — because determining it requires surgery that may have been considered dangerous — is in a situation that the *Torah* might well treat differently from a mere epistemic uncertainty. This is the concept of *ishtani*: since something about this individual is different, perhaps the *Torah* prescribes different *halachot* for them.

But Rav Chisda's position, as the *Gemara* understands it, is more radical than that. He is not merely saying the *tumtum* is a factual doubt; he is saying there would be no special *halachot* for this person at all, ever. A *tumtum* is treated identically to any other *safek* — no differently from a case where one simply did not know, from behind a curtain, whether an animal was male or female. Consequently, any *braita* that appears to categorically exclude a *tumtum* must be edited to remove the word. According to the *maskanah* where *tumtum* is crossed out, then: by *erchin*, one pays the male value out of *safek*, being *machmir* for the doubt. By *androgynos*, however, since the more plausible reading of this *braita* treats it as a *beriyah bifnei atzmah* — a third-category entity entirely — the *Torah*'s language of male and female simply does not encompass it, and one pays nothing.

---

## Shelamim Exclusion

### Shelamim Requirement

The *Gemara* continues with another attempted proof. The *pasuk* governing *shelamim* sacrifices states *im zachar im nekeivah* — whether male or whether female, one may bring it. The *braita* derives: *zachar vadai nekeivah vadai* — only a definitively male or definitively female animal qualifies. *Ve-lo tumtum ve-androgynos* — neither may be brought as a *shelamim*, even though either gender is individually acceptable.

This appears to be a strong proof that *tumtum* is not a *safek*. If it truly were merely a doubt between male and female — and either male or female may be brought as a *shelamim* — then one should be able to bring a *tumtum* as a *shelamim*, since it is certainly one or the other. Yet it is excluded. That exclusion implies something more than mere doubt.

### Second Crossing Out

The *Gemara* responds predictably: *sami mikan tumtum* — erase it. According to Rav Chisda, a *tumtum* may in fact be brought as a *shelamim*.

### Categorical vs. Safek

The force of excluding *androgynos* from *shelamim* lies in the *derasha*: *zachar vadai, nekeivah vadai* — the *Torah* demands a clear, known identity at the moment of *hekdesh*. One could admit that an *androgynos* is one or the other in some abstract sense, and still maintain that the *Torah* requires the owner to *know* which one it is at the time of the dedication. That is a coherent categorical exclusion independent of the *mum* framework.

This also clarifies why *androgynos* is more categorically excluded than a *ba'al mum*. If an animal had a blemish and was dedicated as a *korban*, the dedication takes effect — the animal becomes *kadosh* — even though it cannot be sacrificed. The category of *androgynos*, however, by contrast, is so removed from the valid categories that *kedushah* does not fall upon it even in a standard case of *temurah*. As Michael noted, this confirms that we are not dealing merely with a *mum*; we are dealing with something categorically excluded. And there is a further distinction: an *androgynos* might in some cases have its covered-over portion exposed, unlike a permanent irreversible *mum kavua*, which adds complexity to the *mum* analysis. Ultimately the *Gemara* accepts that for *shelamim*, the exclusion of *androgynos* is categorical, and the exclusion of *tumtum* — per Rav Chisda — is erased.

---

## Bird Sacrifices

### Neveilah Status

The *Gemara* adduces another *braita* regarding bird sacrifices. When a bird is brought as a *korban*, the act of *melikah* — severing the neck from the back — is what renders it fit. If the bird were categorically unfit as a *korban*, then the *melikah* would not constitute a valid act of *shechitah*, and the bird would be *neveilah*. Consuming *neveilah* renders one's garments *tamei*. The *braita* lists the categories of birds whose *melikah* produces *neveilah* because they cannot be valid *korbanot*: an animal that was used for bestiality (*haneer'va*), one that was set aside for *avodah zarah* (*hamuktzeh*), one given as payment to a *zonah* (*esnan*), one exchanged for a dog (*mechir kelev*) — and *tumtum ve-androgynos*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Birds

What makes this case particularly striking is that the *Torah* does not mention gender at all with respect to bird sacrifices. Regarding *shelamim*, the exclusion was derived from the phrase *im zachar im nekeivah* — and where the *Torah* specifies both genders, one can exclude that which fits neither. But birds are never characterized by gender in the *parsha* of *korbanot*. Why, then, should a *tumtum* or *androgynos* bird be excluded?

*Rabbi Eliezer* addresses this directly: *kol makom shene'emar zachar u-nekeivah, ata motzi tumtum ve-androgynos* — wherever the *Torah* says male or female, fine, then you exclude them. That is the *shelamim* case. *Ho'il ve-lo ne'emar bo zachar u-nekeivah, ein ata motzi tumtum ve-androgynos mibeinehen* — but since the *Torah* never mentions gender for birds, you cannot exclude them. Rabbi Eliezer therefore holds that an *androgynos* or *tumtum* bird may actually be brought as a valid *korban*. This is a very reasonable position. Notably, *Tosafot* adds that Rabbi Eliezer is not merely saying such a bird avoids *neveilah* status; he would hold it is actually a *kasher korban*.

According to the *tanna kamma*, however, even birds without gender specification are affected — *tumtum* and *androgynos* are excluded. For *shelamim*, the question is whether the *tumtum* fits one of the specified categories; for birds, the question is why gender matters at all when it goes unmentioned. In either case, the implicit message is that *tumtum* carries some independent ground for exclusion beyond a simple *safek*.

### Third Crossing Out

The *Gemara* again responds: *sami mikan tumtum*. Erase it. A *tumtum* bird may, according to Rav Chisda, be brought as a *korban* or at least cannot be categorically excluded on the basis of gender indeterminacy. The exclusion applies only to *androgynos*. One might note, as was observed during the shiur, that in the world of *korbanot* there exist independent grounds for exclusion — much as *neveilah*, *muktzeh*, and the others on the list are excluded not because of gender but because of their distinct intrinsic *psul*. One could have said that *androgynos* and *tumtum* are excluded on the same independent ground — their physical reality, whatever one calls it — without needing to say it is a gender category. But the *Gemara* follows Rav Chisda's extreme position and refuses to allow even that reasoning for *tumtum*.

---

## Temurah Status

### Five Categories

The *Gemara* now turns to *temurah*, the attempted exchange of sanctity from a *korban* to a non-sanctified animal. Although doing so violates a *lav*, the *temurah* takes effect, and the second animal acquires *kedushah* — provided it is not categorically excluded. A *ba'al mum* acquires *kedushah* even through *temurah*. But a categorically excluded animal does not. The *braita* records: *Rabbi Eliezer omer, ha-treifah ve-ha-kilayim ve-yotzei dofen tumtum ve-androgynos lo kedoshim ve-lo makdishim* — they do not become *kadosh* through *temurah* and cannot sanctify others through *temurah*.

*Ve-amar Shmuel*: *lo kedoshim bi-temurah ve-lo makdishim la'asot temurah* — to clarify: they do not acquire *kedushah* when *temurah* is attempted upon them, and if they somehow did possess *kedushah* (for instance, having been born from a *korban* mother), they cannot transmit that *kedushah* through *temurah* to something else. This double exclusion — *lo kedoshim, lo makdishim* — underscores the categorical nature of the disqualification. It is not a *mum*; it is a complete removal from the domain of *kedushah* as applied through *temurah*.

### Kedusha Rules

The *Gemara* here makes the conceptual point explicit. When an animal has a *mum*, it is still potentially within the world of *korbanot* — one could redeem it, the *kedushah* has effect, and *temurah* upon it works. But when an animal is categorically excluded — *treifah*, *kilayim*, *yotzei dofen*, or *androgynos* — the relationship to *kedushah* is entirely severed in this context. The *Gemara* adds that even if such an animal did acquire *kedushah* through birth from a *korban* mother, it still cannot propagate that *kedushah* through *temurah*. The mechanism of *temurah* simply does not operate upon categorically excluded animals.

And once again, *tumtum* appears on the list. And once again, this is plainly inconsistent with Rav Chisda's position. A *safek* animal that has a *mum* does not lose the ability to receive *kedushah* through *temurah*; it would be treated as any other *safek*. So *tumtum* cannot belong on this categorical list. The *Gemara* says: *sami mikan tumtum* — erase it. Cross out *tumtum* here as well.

### Text Emendation

But at this point the *Gemara* faces a difficulty. An earlier source enumerates exactly *five* categories: *treifah, kilayim, yotzei dofen, tumtum ve-androgynos* — five items. If one crosses out *tumtum*, only four remain. Saying "cross it out" to get from five to four seems like too crude a move. The *Gemara* therefore goes further: *afik tumtum ve-ayeil yatom* — remove *tumtum* and replace it with *yatom*, an orphaned animal. What is a *yatom* in this context? It is an animal born after its mother died, or one whose mother was not alive for its first seven days. The *pasuk* states *shivat yamim yihyeh tachat imo u-miyom ha-shemini va-halah* — the animal must have been with its mother for the first seven days; if the mother was not alive, it can never be brought as a *korban* at all. So *yatom* is a legitimate fifth category of categorical disqualification, and by replacing *tumtum* with *yatom*, the count of five is preserved, and the list becomes coherent. The text has required significant emendation — but the underlying principle is consistent: *tumtum* belongs nowhere on any list of categorical exclusions.

---

## Tannaitic Debate

### Rabbi Yishmael

Having worked through the proofs, the *Gemara* now asks: *leima kitannai* — perhaps the dispute between Rav Chisda and his challengers reflects an underlying debate among *tannaim*. The *Gemara* cites: *Rabbi Ilai* in the name of *Rabbi Yishmael* — *androgynos bechor hu u-mumo imo* — an *androgynos* is a *bechor* and its blemish accompanies it. This aligns with Rabbi Yishmael's position in our Mishnah: the *androgynos* is a definite male, the female anatomy constituting a *mum*, and therefore it may be slaughtered and eaten but may not be worked as a draft animal. It is a valid *bechor* with a *mum*.

### Chachamim View

*Ve-Chachamim omrim: ein kedushah chalah alav* — the Sages say: no *kedushah* falls upon an *androgynos* at all. It is a third gender, definitively not male, and therefore entirely outside the framework of *bechor*. One may work it; one need not bring it to the *Kohen*; the normal *halachot* of firstborn animals do not apply.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Then comes a third position, not found in our Mishnah: *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon* cites the *pasuk* of *ha-zachar takdish* — the male you shall sanctify. And he rules: *ve-chol makom she-ne'emar zachar eino ela le-hotzi tumtum ve-androgynos* — wherever the *Torah* says *zachar*, the intention is to exclude both *tumtum* and *androgynos*. At first glance this seems redundant with the *Chachamim*, who already say *androgynos* is categorically excluded. But Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda adds one word: *tumtum*. The *Chachamim* spoke only of *androgynos*; Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda explicitly extends the categorical exclusion to *tumtum* as well. If one were to cross out *tumtum* here, Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda would be saying nothing beyond what the *Chachamim* already say — *Rabbi Shimon Yehuda hainu rabbanan*. The only meaningful addition is the word *tumtum*. It therefore appears that the debate between *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda is precisely whether *tumtum* is a separate, excluded category or merely a *safek*.

### Clarification

The *Gemara* resists this reading. *D'chulei alma tumtum b'birya lo mesafkei* — nobody actually argues that *tumtum* is a third gender, a *beriyah* unto itself. Rather, the question is *zachar u-nekeivah hu d'mesafkei* — everyone agrees it is a *safek* between male and female; the question is whether and how that *safek* can be resolved. According to this clarification, the *tanna kamma* holds that *tumtum* is a *safek* and the *kedushah* of *bechor* applies *misafek*, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda is not saying *tumtum* is a third gender but rather that in the specific case where a *tumtum* urinates from the place where a female would urinate, that evidence suffices to determine it is female and exclude it — while the *tanna kamma* holds that even that evidence is insufficient, since the male organ may be displaced. The debate, in other words, is not over ontological categories but over evidentiary standards for a factual determination.

---

## Tumtum Evidence

### Both Are Doubtful

Having clarified that everyone agrees *tumtum* is a *safek zachar safek nekeivah*, the *Gemara* now addresses the question of determination. Each *tumtum* is one or the other in fact; the question is whether we can determine which. 

### Urine Tests

*Matil mayim b'makom zachrut* — if the urine exits from the place where male genitalia would normally be, *d'chulei alma lo pligi d'zachar hu* — all agree the animal is male. There is no conceivable mechanism by which a female animal's urine would exit from the anterior male location. *Ki pligi b'matil mayim b'makom nekeivut* — the dispute arises when the urine exits from the posterior, female location.

### Organ Displacement

*Mar savar chashinan shema nehepcha zachruto le-nechvuto* — one opinion holds: since the genitalia are covered over, we cannot know the orientation of the male organ. It may be folded back such that the opening points toward the rear. The urine exiting from the posterior location does not therefore prove female identity; the animal may be male with a displaced organ. *U-mar savar lo chashinan* — the other opinion holds that we are not concerned with this remote possibility. Normally, posterior urination indicates a female, and we apply normal assumptions.

---

## Case: Female Urination

### Rabbi Ila Ruling

The *Gemara* presents a concrete case. *Beheimah ha-matil mayim bi-mkom nekeivah* — an animal that was urinating from the posterior, female location — was a *tumtum* in which a question about *bechor* arose. *Rabbi Ila* (some versions read *Rabbi Elazar*) ruled: *chullin*, it is completely ordinary non-sacred — *lo safek* — not a *safek* at all. It is a definite *nekeivah* and therefore not a *bechor*.

### Yochanan Objection

*Tamah Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Yochanan was astonished at this ruling. *Man lo chash le-Tanna Kamma u-le-Rabbi Yishmael?* — How could he be unconcerned with the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yishmael? The Mishnah's opening statement treats *tumtum* as a *safek* — and nobody in the Mishnah disputed that. The *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yishmael both accept *tumtum* as a *safek zachar safek nekeivah*. Rabbi Ila's ruling — that posterior urination definitively resolves the question — seems to override this consensus entirely. How does one have the *chutzpah* to *pasken* against the Mishnah?

The *Gemara* asks: why did Rabbi Yochanan only mention the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yishmael? What about the *Rabbanan basrai* — the last opinion in the Mishnah, who say *androgynos* is a third gender? They also implicitly accept *tumtum* as a *safek*, as Rav Chisda explicitly stated. The *Gemara* answers: Rabbi Yochanan does *not* accept Rav Chisda's ruling — *lo sevira lei de-Rav Chisda*. He holds that the same *Rabbanan basrai* who say *androgynos* is its own category would also say *tumtum* is its own category, at least for the purposes of *korbanot*. Therefore Rabbi Yochanan cannot invoke them as additional support for the *safek* position.

### Chisda vs. Yochanan

The debate between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan is thus substantive and fundamental. Rav Chisda reads the Mishnah's opening *tumtum safek* statement as a unanimous ruling and cross-cuts every *braita* that treats *tumtum* as categorically excluded. Rabbi Yochanan reads the Mishnah differently: the *Rabbanan basrai*, who say *androgynos* is its own category, would extend that reasoning to *tumtum* as well. This reading preserves the integrity of all those *braitot* without erasure.

Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Rabbi Ila's ruling, then, is as follows: even if you disagree with Rav Chisda and follow the *Rabbanan basrai* regarding *androgynos* and *tumtum* as categorical exclusions, you are still adopting the position of only one of three *tannaim* in the Mishnah. The first two — the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yishmael — clearly treat *tumtum* as a *safek*. Who gave you the authority to *pasken* like the one minority position and permit a *bechor* on the basis of urine location, when the majority of the Mishnah's voices treat it as a *safek*?

The *Gemara* answers: *man shavak terei ve-avid ke-chad?* — that is exactly Rabbi Yochanan's point. Abandoning two Mishnaic positions to rule like the third is problematic. And this is not merely an abstract debate about consistency. We are talking about a *bechor*, which may or may not have the *kedushah* of a firstborn animal. Ruling definitively that it is *chullin* based on urination patterns, in the face of a Mishnaic consensus that treats it as a *safek*, requires serious justification.

It is worth pausing on what is conceptually at stake. Rabbi Yochanan is not saying that *tumtum* is definitively a third gender. He is saying that an animal that is biologically one or the other, but whose biology is currently unresolvable — and whose unresolvability is itself a function of its physical constitution — may appropriately receive distinct *halachic* treatment, particularly in the domain of *korbanot*. Whether this is "truly" a third category or merely a *halachic* proxy category for undetermined status is a question that remains open within *Tosafot*'s analysis. What is clear is that Rabbi Yochanan preserves the simple sense of all those *mishnayot* and *braitot* that categorically exclude *tumtum*.

### Resh Lakish Pesak

*Resh Lakish* offers a resolution that is strikingly practical. *Lo amru tumtum safek ela be-adam* — when the Sages said *tumtum* is a *safek*, they meant only by a human being. Why? *Ho'il ve-zachruto u-nekvuto bi-makom echad* — because in a human, the male and female genitalia are located in essentially the same area of the body, and therefore urination location does not disambiguate between male and female regardless of where it exits. But *aval bi-vehemah* — in an animal — *matil mayim bi-mkom zachrut zachar, matil mayim bi-mkom nekeva nekeva* — the male and female anatomies are in distinctly different locations, and urine exiting from the respective location is definitive. We are not concerned that the male organ is bent.

This is a *pesak halacha*, not merely a theoretical position. Resh Lakish is saying: follow Rav Chisda and treat *tumtum* as a *safek*, but then apply evidentiary reasoning to resolve that *safek* in animals based on urination location. This enables a ruling of *chullin* for a *tumtum* that urinates posteriorly in an animal without crossing into categorical exclusion or third-gender territory.

### Oshaya Challenge

*Matkif lah Rabbi Oshaya*: how can Resh Lakish rule with such confidence? *Ve-leicheish shema nehepcha zachruto le-nechvuto* — perhaps the male organ has bent over, and the urine is exiting from the rear even though the animal is male? Resh Lakish responds: should we follow *Rabbi Meir*, who is concerned with remote possibilities? This is not a likely scenario; normally we do not raise concerns about the improbable.

### Abaye Hanina

*Abaye bar Avin ve-Rav Hanina bar Avin* respond together: *afilu teima Rabbanan, ishtani ishtani* — even if one follows the *Rabbanan* who generally do not concern themselves with remote possibilities, here we must. This entire animal is biologically anomalous — its genitalia are covered over and the normal anatomical assumptions do not hold. When the body has departed from normal in one significant way, you cannot simply apply normal anatomical reasoning to it. *Ishtani ishtani*: since it is different, it is different — meaning that once something about an organism is abnormal, you must remain concerned about other anomalies in the same organ system. And therefore the question of whether the urine location proves anything remains genuinely unresolvable.

---

## Tumtum Evidence (II)

### Ishtani Principle

The *Gemara* then asks whether the *ishtani* principle — the idea that an anomalous body cannot be measured by normal biological assumptions — is itself a *tannaitic* debate. *Leima ishtani ve-lo ishtani tana'ei hi* — perhaps the question of whether anomalousness should extend our concerns from one bodily feature to another is the actual axis of the dispute in the *braitot* we have been examining. This sets up the transition to the practical domain of marriage law.

---

## Marriage Halachot

### Tumtum Marriage

*D'tanya*: if a *tumtum* marries a woman, the *kiddushin* are binding — *kidushav kidushin* — because he may be male, and at minimum it is a *safek kiddushin*. If a man marries a *tumtum*, likewise, the *kiddushin* are binding because the *tumtum* may be female. The *braita* continues: *ve-choletz ve-choltzin le-ishto* — a *tumtum* who is the sole surviving sibling performs *chalitzah* to his deceased brother's wife, because he may be male and subject to the obligation. And *choltzin le-ishto* — his brothers must perform *chalitzah* to his wife if he dies without children, because he may have been male and the marriage may have been fully valid.

*U-miyabeim et ishto* — additionally, a brother may perform *yibum* with his wife. The logic is: *miman nafshach* — either way it works out. If the *tumtum* was male, *yibum* is a positive obligation. If the *tumtum* was female, the *kiddushin* were never valid, and marrying the widow is simply a new marriage — there is no prohibition of *eshet ach* where there was never a valid marriage.

### Woman Marries Tumtum

The second *braita* addresses the reverse: *eshet tumtum choletzet ve-lo mistayabemet* — the wife of a *tumtum* who dies must undergo *chalitzah* but cannot be taken in *yibum*. The *chalitzah* is required because the *kiddushin* may have been valid. But unlike the first case, *yibum* is not permitted. Why the asymmetry?

### Saris Concern

The *Gemara* initially assumes the debate is rooted in *Rabbi Akiva*'s ruling that a *saris chamah* — a naturally sterile man — does not perform *chalitzah* or *yibum*. A *saris chamah* was never capable of having children, and since the obligation of *yibum* derives from the commandment to perpetuate the deceased brother's line, one who could never have had children is outside that framework. The *Gemara* proposes: the first *braita* that permits *yibum* holds that we do not suspect a *tumtum* of being a *saris* — we do not say *ishtani, ishtani*, that because the genitalia are covered, we should assume fertility is also affected. The second *braita* that forbids *yibum* holds that we do suspect sterility — *ishtani ishtani* applies, and since we are already dealing with a body that is anomalous in one respect, we are concerned about ancillary anomalies as well.

The *Gemara* ultimately rejects this framing, saying that actually all opinions may agree that we apply *ishtani ishtani*. The debate is rather about what *Rabbi Akiva*'s ruling implies for our case: one opinion holds that sterility — even if probable — does not eliminate the obligation of *yibum* (because *Rabbi Akiva*'s exclusion was limited to definite cases), while another holds that even a *safek saris* is sufficient to preclude *yibum*.

### Rabbi Yehuda View

*Ilima Rabbi Yehuda* — if this *braita* that forbids *yibum* reflects Rabbi Yehuda's position, there is a problem. For Rabbi Yehuda holds *vadai saris* — that a *tumtum* found upon investigation to be male is definitively sterile. *Harei zeh lo yachalotz mipnei she-hu ke-saris* — such a person does not perform *chalitzah* because he is treated as a definite *saris*, not merely a doubtful one. If that is so, then the *braita* that says *choletzet* — *chalitzah* must be done — cannot reflect Rabbi Yehuda's view, because Rabbi Yehuda would say the *chalitzah* is entirely unnecessary and meaningless: the man was definitively sterile and the *mitzvah* of *yibum* never applied.

### Rabbi Yossi View

*Ela Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Yehuda hi* — this *braita* reflects the position of *Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Yehuda*. *D'tanya: Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Yehuda omer, tumtum lo choletz shema yikara ve-yimatza saris chamah* — a *tumtum* does not perform *chalitzah* because perhaps when the covering is removed, he will be found to be a *saris chamah*. If one might ask: but there is another reason not to perform *chalitzah* — perhaps the *tumtum* turns out to be female! The *Gemara* responds: *shema ka'amar* — Rabbi Yossi is listing possibilities, not giving a single reason. *Shema yikara ve-yimatza nekeivah* — perhaps it will be found to be female, *ei nami zachar, nami shema yimatza saris chamah* — and even if it is found to be male, perhaps it will prove to be naturally sterile.

So according to Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Yehuda, there are two sources of concern that preclude *chalitzah* by the surviving *tumtum*: the possibility of being female, and the possibility of being sterile even if male. Neither is assumed to be definite — both are possibilities — but together they prevent confident performance of the *mitzvah*.

### Practical Differences

*Mai beinayhu* — what is the practical difference between Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the *tumtum* is a *definite saris*, and Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Yehuda, who holds it is only a *possible saris*? *Amar Rava: lifsol bi-mkom achim* — the difference manifests when there are other brothers present.

If this *tumtum* — the surviving sibling of the deceased — performs *chalitzah* to the deceased's wife, the question is whether that *chalitzah* has any force. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the *tumtum* is a definite *saris*: his *chalitzah* is completely meaningless, and other brothers retain the full option to perform *yibum*. According to Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Yehuda, the *tumtum* is only a possible *saris*: the *chalitzah* may have been valid, and therefore other brothers cannot perform *yibum* — the possibly-valid *chalitzah* has already precluded that option. They may, however, still need to perform *chalitzah* themselves to definitively free the woman, since we are not certain this *tumtum*'s *chalitzah* was fully effective.

*Ve-lachlotz she-lo bi-mkom achim ika beinayhu* — a second practical difference arises when there are no other brothers at all. If the *tumtum* is the sole surviving sibling and he is a definite *saris* (Rabbi Yehuda), then the widow requires no *chalitzah* whatsoever — the *mitzvah* of *yibum* never applied to this brother, and she is free. But if he is only a possible *saris* (Rabbi Yossi be-Rabbi Yehuda), and he might actually be obligated in *chalitzah*, then she does require him to perform it in order to be released.

---

## Final Summary

### Androgynos Options

To summarize the range of positions encountered throughout this daf: regarding *androgynos*, there are three distinct theoretical frameworks. The first holds that *androgynos* is intrinsically indeterminate — *safek zachar safek nekeivah* — not in the sense that any individual case is resolvable but that the category itself is defined by irresolvable indeterminacy, with only two genders acknowledged. The second holds it is a male with a *mum*, the female anatomy constituting a blemish that affects the *halachot* of *bechor* but not its fundamental identity. The third holds it is a third gender — *beriyah bifnei atzmah* — entirely outside the binary framework.

### Tumtum Options

Regarding *tumtum*, the picture is more nuanced. The first position, championed by Rav Chisda, holds that *tumtum* is a pure *safek* — each individual case is either male or female in fact, we simply do not know, and the applicable *halachot* are those of any ordinary doubt. This requires erasing the word *tumtum* from every *braita* that treats it as categorically excluded. The second position, associated with Rabbi Yochanan, holds that at least in the domain of *korbanot*, *tumtum* functions as an excluded category, whether because it is genuinely a third category or because its irresolvable factual indeterminacy (which is not epistemic but constitutive of its current state) warrants categorical treatment. The third position seeks to preserve the *safek* framing while allowing for empirical resolution — Resh Lakish's view that in animals, urination location definitively determines gender — though this is challenged by *Abaye bar Avin* and *Rav Hanina bar Avin* on the basis of *ishtani ishtani*, the principle that anomalous bodies cannot be measured by normal anatomical assumptions.

### Next Perek

All of these issues — the three positions on *androgynos*, the three positions on *tumtum*, and the *ishtani* principle — will be revisited in the next *perek*, where the *Gemara* returns to the topic of *mumin* specifically as it applies to human beings. The animal-based analysis of this *perek* provides the foundation; the human dimension, with its additional complexities, will be the subject of what follows.

---

---

# Bekhorot 43

## Mumim for Kohanim

### Opening & Scope

Daf 43 opens a new *perek*, *Mumim Ellu*, transitioning from the earlier discussion of blemishes in animals to the parallel category of blemishes in *kohanim*. The connection is organic: while the *masechta* is primarily concerned with the *bechor*, the issue of *mumim* naturally bridges to the priestly service. Although this is not strictly about the *bechor* in the narrow sense, the conceptual framework — what constitutes a disqualifying blemish — applies across both domains, and the Mishnah treats them together.

### Kohanim-Specific Blemish…

The Mishnah introduces a list of blemishes that are additional to those shared with animals — conditions that disqualify a *kohen* but have no exact parallel in the laws governing animal offerings. These include distinctive head shapes referred to as *kilyon*, *liftan*, and *makban*; deformities of the neck known as *shakut* and *shamut*; a condition called *skifat* affecting the back of the skull; and *ba'alei chatoteret*, those with a hunchback or dorsal growth. The Mishnah then addresses *kireach* — baldness — and records a dispute concerning whether a hunchback is disqualifying.

### Fixed vs. Transitory

The Mishnah opens with the principle that *mumim elu*, the blemishes enumerated in the previous *perek*, whether *kevi'in* (fixed) or *overin* (transitory), *poslin ba'adam* — disqualify a *kohen* from performing the *avodah*. The conceptual basis is clear: just as a *bechor* with a transitory blemish cannot be offered as a *korban* in the *Beis HaMikdash* at that moment, so too a *kohen* with even a transitory blemish may not serve. The parallel holds on both sides of the equation.

### Head Shape Blemishes

The Gemara provides anatomical descriptions of each unusual head shape. *Kilyon* — likely derived from the root meaning "to come to a point" — describes a triangular, pointed head, essentially the shape of an inverted cone. *Liftan*, the turnip, is the inverse: wide at the top and pointed at the bottom, a description that carries rather unflattering connotations. *Makban* — which shares its root with the *Maccabees*, from *makevet*, a hammer — describes what might be called a hammerhead configuration: a large skull, narrow neck, with the cranium protruding markedly both in front and behind, not unlike a hammerhead shark.

### More Physical Deformities

The condition *shakut* refers to a head that is slanted in the front, or alternatively, to a person whose neck is so short that the head appears buried or sunk between the shoulder blades. The Gemara clarifies *shakut* and *shamut* as two neck-related deformities: *shakut* is a neck that appears hidden, depressed; *shamut* is the opposite — thin and narrow, so that the head appears to protrude outward from the neck on both sides. *Skifat* describes a back of the head that is flattened or cut off, lacking the normal curvature; the Gemara invokes the folk expression *shakil pisa*, "a piece was removed," to capture how it appears. The *ba'al chatoteret* is the hunchback — the word *chatoteret* being the same used for a camel's hump — and it is this category that generates a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages.

### Baldness Debate

The Mishnah declares *kireach pasul* — a bald *kohen* is disqualified. What is the definition of *kireach*? The Mishnah says: *kol she'ein lo shita shel sei'ar mukefet me'ozen l'ozen* — one who lacks even a single row of hair encircling the head from ear to ear. The Gemara, as will be seen, will subject this definition to careful scrutiny, differentiating among various patterns of baldness and concluding that only particularly bizarre manifestations are problematic, not normal baldness.

### Visibility in Service

A natural question arises: many of these conditions — misshapen heads, hunchbacks — would have been partially obscured during *avodah*. *Kohanim* wore the *mitznefet*, and priestly garments covered much of the body. One might therefore wonder whether the concern is primarily visual — about what the people assembled in the *Azarah* see — or whether these are intrinsic disqualifications independent of visibility.

This question proves consequential. The Gemara, as will emerge, distinguishes sharply between a genuine *mum*, a condition that *machil avoda* (desecrates the service), and the categories of *she'eino shaveh bezera shel Aharon* and *marit ha'ayin*, which are lesser in halakhic force. The fact that many of the conditions in this Mishnah are inherently visual — head shapes, baldness, a visible dorsal growth — suggests that visibility is indeed a factor. Yet the Gemara does not limit these disqualifications to visible locations alone, which deepens the question. For now, the observation is worth carrying forward: are the *kohanim*-specific disqualifications limited to what would be seen by the people bringing *korbanot*, or do they extend beyond that?

One broader framework for understanding the entire category is that the *kohen* in the *Beis HaMikdash* occupies a role analogous in certain respects to the *keilim* of the *Mikdash* — not merely a functionary but a sanctified instrument of the service. The *Rambam*, in discussing the laws of *kohanim*, speaks of *klei hamikdash vehamishartim bo*, treating the priests and the vessels together. In *Zevachim*, the *kohen* must serve barefoot, his feet touching the floor of the *Azarah*, so that he connects to the *kedusha* of the *Beis HaMikdash*. Seen through this lens, the aesthetic demands placed upon *kohanim* reflect the same principle as the aesthetic demands placed upon the *menorah* and the *mizbe'ach* — objects used in the service must conform to a certain standard of wholeness and appearance. This framing is perhaps more satisfying than alternative explanations, and it will be developed further when the Gemara addresses the category of *nitraba bemitzvot*.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah

### Why Derive Lists

The Gemara opens with a structural question: why should we assume that the full list of *mumim* applying to animals also applies to *kohanim*, and vice versa? The *pesukim* in *Emor* list specific blemishes for animals brought as *korbanot*, and separately list blemishes that disqualify *kohanim*. There is significant overlap, but the lists are not identical. Why not treat each list as discrete and exhaustive for its own domain?

### Textual Gaps

The Gemara identifies the specific asymmetries. *Yabbelet* — a type of wart or skin growth — is written in the list of *mumim* for animals but is not mentioned in the Torah's list of blemishes for humans. Conversely, *dak* and *tavlul* — conditions involving the eye, specifically a line penetrating the pupil that mixes white and colored areas — appear in the Torah's list for humans but are not mentioned for animals. If the lists are distinct, *yabbelet* would not apply to *kohanim*, and the eye condition would not apply to animals.

### Garav & Yalefet Link

The Gemara resolves this through a *gezeira shava*. A *baraita* teaches: since *garav* and *yalefet* — two types of skin conditions — appear in both the human list and the animal list, this shared terminology creates a verbal link allowing us to apply each list to the other. The *gezeira shava* on *garav–garav* and *yalefet–yalefet* permits us to learn: whatever is written regarding blemishes for humans applies equally to animals, and whatever is written for animals applies to humans.

### Mufne Requirement

The Gemara raises the standard requirement for a valid *gezeira shava*: the linking words must be *mufne* — superfluous in their own context, freed from the need to carry independent meaning, so that they are available for the hermeneutical link. If the words were not superfluous, the *gezeira shava* would be subject to logical challenge. The Gemara demonstrates that *garav* is indeed superfluous, because the Torah could have written only *yalefet* and derived *garav* through a *kal v'chomer*: if the less severe skin condition (*yalefet*) constitutes a *mum*, certainly the more severe and visually repugnant *garav* does. Since the Torah wrote *garav* explicitly despite this *kal v'chomer*, it must be to render the word available for the *gezeira shava*.

### Asymmetric Learning

With the *gezeira shava* established, the Gemara explains why one could not simply reason by logic from one list to the other — which would have made the *gezeira shava* unnecessary. The reason is that logical inference is blocked in both directions, and because the *gezeira shava* must be *mufne*, the superfluous writing is justified.

### Animals on Altar

Why can one not learn humans from animals? *Sheken hu atzmo karev legabei mizbe'ach* — because the animal itself is placed upon the *mizbe'ach*. The aesthetics demanded of something offered on the altar may be held to a higher standard than what is demanded of a person who performs a service. Therefore, a longer or stricter list of *mumim* for animals might be justified by that distinctive quality, and one cannot straightforwardly apply the animal list to humans.

### Nitraba Bemitzvot

Conversely, why can one not learn animals from humans? *Sheken nitraba bemitzvot* — because a human being has more *mitzvot*. An animal has no *mitzvot* at all. This phrase requires interpretation, and on the surface it is challenging: the abundance of *mitzvot* does not obviously explain why a *kohen*'s appearance should be held to a stricter standard.

### Kodushat Kohanim

The Gemara later explains this through the concept of *kedushato meruba* — a greater intrinsic *kedusha*. Rashi understands this as a general statement about human sanctity through *mitzvot*. However, the commentary *Reishis Bikurim* offers an interpretation that is both more contextually precise and more theologically satisfying: *nitraba bemitzvot* refers specifically to the *mitzvot* of the *kehuna* — the priestly service in the *Beis HaMikdash*. On this reading, the heightened standard applied to *kohanim* flows from their specific sacred role as *meshartim*, servants, in the *Mikdash*, not from a generic statement about human beings and *mitzvot*. This reading aligns with the framework described above — the *kohen* as a sanctified instrument of the service, analogous to the *keilim* of the *Mikdash* — and limits the aesthetic concern appropriately to the *Beis HaMikdash* context. It would be a mistake to extrapolate from these *halachot* any general principle about the worth of persons with physical differences.

Importantly, these disqualifications do not prevent a *kohen* from receiving *terumah* or sharing in the *korbanot*. They exclusively limit actual participation in the *avodah*. This narrowness itself is significant.

### Why Repeat Words

The Gemara then asks a more refined question: granted that *garav* and *yalefet* must appear in both contexts to enable the *gezeira shava*, why was it necessary for the Torah to repeat the entire list in each context? One might imagine the Torah writing the full shared list only once, the distinctive *mumim* of each category separately, and then writing *garav* and *yalefet* in both places as the linking mechanism — without repeating everything.

The Gemara considers the various permutations. If the Torah wrote the full list only by humans and the linking words by animals: there are *mumim* distinctive to animals, such as *kalut* (fused hooves) and *chalut* (problems with the teeth roots), that have no parallel in humans — they could not have been included in a human-only list and then applied to animals. If the Torah wrote the full list only by animals and linked to humans: there are conditions distinctive to humans, such as *giben* (eyebrow deformity — one eyebrow or no eyebrows, which animals do not have) and *charum* (a flat or absent nasal bridge between the eyes, a condition that does not present in animals because their noses are positioned below their eyes), which would have been omitted.

What if the Torah wrote the shared conditions only once, wrote each distinctive list separately, and used *garav* and *yalefet* as the link? This is exactly the question posed — and the answer comes from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *kol parsha shene'emrah v'nishnis, lo nishnis ela bishvil davar shenischadesh bah* — any *parasha* that is stated and then repeated is repeated only for the sake of one new thing it introduces. The Torah does not need to justify every word of a repeated passage. If the Torah needed to introduce even one distinctive element in that passage, it would naturally restate the broader context without the reader being required to find independent significance in every repeated item. This is the school of *dibra Torah k'lashon bnei adam* — the Torah speaks in the manner of human language — associated with Rabbi Yishmael, as distinct from Rabbi Akiva's principle of *omnisignificance*, which would require every repeated letter and word to carry independent meaning.

The two schools represent a genuine and enduring divide in hermeneutics. Rabbi Akiva is *doresh kotzei osiyot* — he draws meaning from the very crowns atop the letters. Rabbi Yishmael counters: *afilu atah doresh bas u'vas kol hayom kulo eini shomeia lach* — even if you expound extra *vavs* all day, I will not accept it. It is worth noting that the *baraita* we recite each morning as part of the liturgy is Rabbi Yishmael's — the thirteen hermeneutical principles — yet that *baraita* introduces the *Sifra*, the halakhic midrash on *Vayikra*, which follows Rabbi Akiva's school. The relationship between the two approaches is not always a clean opposition.

Nachum Ish Gamzu, who had developed the approach of drawing meaning from the particle *et* — the same technique picked up by Rabbi Akiva — ultimately ceased applying it in one instance, stating *et Hashem elokecha tira peiresh*. Rabbi Akiva then took up that very exposition: *et Hashem elokecha l'rabot talmidei chachamim* — and indeed Nachum Ish Gamzu was Rabbi Akiva's own teacher. Rabbi Akiva in this sense inherited and extended the interpretive mantle.

### Rava's Question

The Gemara now turns to a separate but related question, posed by Rava. If through the *gezeira shava* we learn all the lists from one another, why did the Torah need to write the word *mum* in all three separate contexts — by *adam* (the *kohen*), by *kodshim* (other offerings), and by *bechor*? Given that the categories are linked, could the Torah not have written that a *mum* is disqualifying in only one place and derived the others through inference?

### Three Categories

Rava's answer is that each of the three categories is distinctive in a way that blocks inference from the others. *Mum ba'adam* — the disqualification of *kohanim* — might be thought distinctive *sheken nitraba bemitzvot*, by virtue of the particular priestly role. Since the *kohen*'s status is distinctive, one could not infer the disqualification of animals from humans. Conversely, animals placed on the *mizbe'ach* — *sheken atzma karev legabei mizbe'ach* — might be thought subject to a higher aesthetic standard, blocking inference from animals to humans. *Bechor* is distinctive because its *kedusha* attaches *meirechem*, from the moment of birth, and it is offered on the *mizbe'ach*; perhaps the demand is greatest there. *Kodshim* (other offerings) may have a greater *kedusha* in a different sense: as Rashi explains, the category of *kodshim* is broader, applying to both male and female animals across many types, whereas *bechor* is narrower; moreover, a *bechor* with a *mum* may be eaten outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, while other *korbanot* may not — indicating that the *kedusha* of ordinary *kodshim* in certain respects exceeds that of *bechor*.

The Gemara systematically considers whether any two of the three might suffice to establish the third. Each attempt fails because the paired categories share a feature the third lacks: *adam* and *kodshim* share *kedusha* that is in some sense intrinsic or broad; *bechor* and *kodshim* both go on the *mizbe'ach*; *adam* and *bechor* are both *kadosh* from birth in their respective ways. In each case, the third category could argue it is distinctive. *Tzrichi* — all three mentions are necessary.

The lesson of *Reishis Bikurim* applies here as well: when the Gemara speaks of *nitraba bemitzvot* as the distinctive feature of the human/priestly category, it is referring specifically to the *mitzvot* of service in the *Beis HaMikdash*, and the entire discussion of aesthetics and *mumim* is bounded by and makes sense within that particular sacred context. These concerns do not translate beyond the *Mikdash* setting. Whether a *ba'al mum* is disqualified on a *bamah* (private altar) during the period when *bamot* were permitted is a related question that warrants separate investigation, but the logic of the aesthetics concern suggests it would not apply there.

---

## She'eino Shaveh Category

### Rav Yochanan Drasha

Having established the *gezeira shava* that links the *mumim* lists, the Gemara now turns to the categories of blemishes unique to *kohanim* — the *yeser aleihem*, those conditions listed by the Mishnah that go beyond what applies to animals. The foundation for this expanded category is a *drasha* of Rabbi Yochanan. The verse in *Emor* reads: *kol ish asher bo mum mizerah Aharon lo yikrav lehakriv lechem elohav* — any man who has a blemish from the seed of Aaron shall not draw near to offer. Rabbi Yochanan reads this as: *ish sheshaveh bezera shel Aharon* — it must be a man who is similar to the typical members of Aaron's seed, the normative population of *kohanim*. The disqualification is not limited to those with a specific catalogued *mum*; it extends to anyone who does not fall within what we might call the normal distribution of the priestly community.

### Mum vs. She'eino

This is a striking reading. It moves the disqualification from the specific and catalogued to the statistical and distributional — not a formal blemish, but a significant deviation from the norm. The Gemara asks the obvious question: what is the practical halakhic difference between calling something a *mum* and placing it in this new category of *she'eino shaveh bezera shel Aharon*?

### Aseh Not Lo Ta'aseh

The answer is *mishum achulei avoda* — the difference lies in whether the *avodah* performed is retroactively invalidated. A *kohen* with a genuine *mum* who performs the *avodah* has *mum bo velo yechalel* — the verse establishes that performing the service constitutes *chillul*, desecration of the service, which means the *avodah* is *pasul*.
