As an aside, none of the complexities regarding the double portion of inheritance or the writing of a *harsha'ah* apply here, since those issues arose from a different kind of confusion. Here we are squarely back to *pidyon*.

### Death Within 30 Days

The *mishnah* then introduces a complication: *mes echad mehen betoch sheloshim yom* — one of the twins died, God forbid, within thirty days. Since the obligation to redeem only takes effect on day thirty, the father may argue to the *kohen* that perhaps it was his firstborn son who died. He is therefore exempt.

This is a striking point worth pausing on. One might expect that even under conditions of doubt — a *safek* — the father would be pressed to perform the *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben*. Yet the *mishnah* rules him exempt. This reflects a fundamental framing: the obligation of *pidyon haben* hinges not merely on the ritual dimension but on a civil liability, the enforceable debt of five *sela'im* owed to the *kohen*. And a civil obligation can only be enforced when it can be proven. Since the father can credibly deflect the claim, he is released. This is, as we will see, quite a pervasive feature of how the *gemara* understands this entire topic.

### Father Dies—Sons Obligat…

The next scenario: *mes ha'av vehabbanim kayamim* — the father dies while both sons survive. Now the question of self-redemption arises, since a son not redeemed by his father must redeem himself. But which son is obligated? Neither can be proven to be the *bechor*.

If one approaches this as a question of *mitzvah* performance alone — I am in doubt, therefore I ought to fulfill the *mitzvah* — the answer would seem obvious: each son should redeem himself as a matter of *safek mitzvah*. But the *mishnah* treats this as a civil matter. Under civil framing, I cannot prove that *you* are the *bechor*, and you cannot prove that *he* is the *bechor*. The *kohen* approaches one brother, who directs him to the other; he approaches the other, who directs him back. Each individual simply deflects the claim. A civil case can only be brought against one person at a time, and neither can be held individually.

### Rebbi Meir vs. Rebbi Yeh…

*Rebbi Meir* addresses the case where the father has died and the sons are debating whether to pay before or after dividing the estate. He says: *im nasnu ad shelo chalku nasnu* — if they gave the *pidyon* before dividing the estate, it stands; the money has already been given. *Ve'im lav, peturim* — but if the estate has since been divided and payment has not yet been made, they are exempt. The *gemara* will explore why division should matter, but Rebbi Meir's logic presumably rests on the idea that before division there exists some enforceable claim on the estate as a whole, even if no individual can be specifically targeted. After division, each brother stands alone with his portion, and each can deflect the claim.

*Rebbi Yehuda* takes the position: *nitchayvu nechasim* — the property itself becomes obligated. Even after the estate is divided, one may still collect from the property. At first glance this seems almost self-evident, but as we will see, the *gemara* is far from convinced that it is.

### Mixed-Gender Twins

The *mishnah* closes this section with the case of *zachar unekeivah* — a male and female born together. Here, *ein kan lakohen klum* — there is nothing at all for the *kohen*. Unlike the case of two males, where the obligation definitely exists and the only question is its identity, here there may be no obligation whatsoever. If the girl emerged first, she is the *bechor* and there is no *pidyon haben* obligation at all. The very existence of the debt is in question, not merely its assignment. Once again we observe how thoroughly the *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben* is intertwined with and dependent upon the underlying civil liability of the five *sela'im*.

---

## Father's Obligation Timi…

### Post-Day-30 Death Scenar…

The *gemara* opens by interrogating the timing of the father's death: *de'meis ha'av eimas* — when exactly did he die? The *gemara* proposes: *ileima de'meis achar sheloshim yom* — suppose he died after thirty days. By that point the obligation had already crystallized: on day thirty or shortly thereafter, the father became obligated in the five *sela'im*, and presumably a *shi'bud* — a lien — had already attached to his estate. The father then dies. Should it not follow that the *kohen* can collect from the estate regardless of whether the sons subsequently divide it?

Consider the analogy: if someone borrowed a hundred dollars from me and then died, and his sons divided the estate, my *shi'bud* persists. I can collect from either son's portion. The division of the estate does not dissolve a pre-existing lien. So if the father became obligated at day thirty, why does Rebbi Meir say division matters? *Ve'ishtabdu lehu nechasim* — the estate was already encumbered!

This leads the *gemara* to the alternative scenario: *ela de'meis betoch sheloshim yom* — rather, the father died within thirty days, before the obligation ever fell on him. In that case, the obligation arises for the first time with the sons themselves. There never was a lien on the father's estate because he was never obligated. If so, says the *gemara*, why should the pre-division state of the estate make any difference? Even before division, there is no lien: *de'azil legabei hai umadchei leh ude'azil legabei hai umadchei leh* — the *kohen* goes to one brother, is turned away, goes to the other, is turned away again. There is no lien because the obligation first came to rest on the sons and no individual son can be held. And therefore: *ki lo chelku nami* — even without dividing the estate, why should the *kohen* be able to collect? Each brother could push him off regardless.

### Liens Through Persons On…

This leads to a critical *gemara* principle, articulated by Rava in his rejection of the proposed reading. The principle is stated thus: *nichsei devar inish inun arevin beh* — a person's property stands as guarantor for him. This sounds like it empowers the creditor to go directly to the property. But Rava reads it in precisely the opposite direction: the property is the guarantor *for the person*, meaning the lien can only be exercised *through* the person's individual obligation. One cannot bypass the obligated individual and go directly to encumbered property. The property is not an independent source of liability; it is a conduit for the person's personal debt.

This is a counterintuitive principle, certainly by the standards of secular commercial law. In *halakha*, the paradigm is that you cannot proceed against a guarantor — an *arev* — without first establishing the claim against the principal debtor. The same logic governs liens: I cannot declare that I have a lien on this property and proceed to collect without first being able to name and confront the specific person who owes me the money. The *shi'bud* is not free-floating; it is tethered to the interpersonal obligation. And the ruling — *de-lo yidpeih min ha-arev techilah*, that you may not go directly to the guarantor first — is the accepted *halakha*. So too, if I cannot identify the obligated person and bring him before a court, I cannot exercise the lien.

### Two Yosef ben Shimons Pa…

Before Rava's rejection is explained, the *gemara* first floats a possible reading of the *mishnah* that would validate collecting from an undivided estate even where only the sons are obligated. Rabbi Yirmiya proposes: *zot omeret* — from the fact that collection is permitted pre-division, one can derive a principle through the case of two people in the same city who share the name Yosef ben Shimon.

The scenario is this: I have a promissory note stating that Yosef ben Shimon owes me money. When I attempt to collect, I discover — or he informs me — that there is another Yosef ben Shimon in town. Each claims the debt belongs to the other, and I cannot prove otherwise. Ordinarily, I would be unable to collect from either. But suppose these two Yosef ben Shimons were unwise enough to purchase a field together in partnership. Now I have an opening. *Ba'al chov goveh mehem* — the creditor may collect from the shared property. The reasoning: *de'amar leh ei bedidach masikna, manta didach kashakilna* — if you are the one who owes me money, I am taking your share; *ve'ei bechaverach masikna, manta dechaverach kashakilna* — and if it is the other one, I am taking his share. The two partners can then sort out among themselves who must compensate whom. The creditor knows that whoever holds the debt is a part-owner of this property, and so he collects from the property directly, leaving the internal accounting to the debtors.

This, Rabbi Yirmiya suggests, is precisely the structure of the *mishnah* before the estate is divided: the brothers are equal partners, one of them is definitely obligated, and the *kohen* can collect from the shared estate using the same logic. This would explain why Rebbi Meir allows collection pre-division even where the obligation falls on the sons, not the father.

### Loan Sale & Waiver Examp…

Rava, however, rejects this reading and insists that the lien-through-person principle forecloses the Yosef ben Shimon solution. To illustrate the depth of this principle, consider the following: if one person owes another money, the creditor can sell that loan to a third party. The sale is effectively a sale of the creditor's lien on the debtor's estate — that is the concrete property right being transferred. But suppose the original creditor, after selling the loan, then proceeds to be *mochel* — to waive — the underlying debt to the original debtor. The third-party purchaser of the loan is left with nothing. Why? Because the lien does not exist independently of the interpersonal obligation. The lien operates only through the creditor's personal claim against the debtor, and that is a relationship that is uniquely between those two parties. Once the original creditor dissolves that personal obligation — even if someone else has nominally purchased the right to collect — the lien collapses, because it was never anything other than an expression of that personal debt. There is no free-standing property right that persists once the underlying obligation is extinguished.

This is a striking feature of *halakhic* commercial law with significant practical implications, and the *gemara* acknowledges that workarounds must be constructed. But the baseline rule stands: you cannot go straight to the property, you must go through the person, and if you cannot identify or confront that person, you are stuck. The Yosef ben Shimon scenario therefore cannot serve as a model for our *mishnah*.

---

## Small Estate & Division

### Rava's Resolution

Having rejected the reading in which the father dies within thirty days, the *gemara* — through Rava — now establishes the correct framing of the *mishnah*: *le'olam she-meis achar sheloshim yom* — in fact, the father died after thirty days. The obligation therefore attached to the father, a lien came into existence on his estate, and the father subsequently died leaving two sons. Now the *kohen's* right to collect is clearly grounded: there was an enforceable debt with a lien, and it runs against the estate. The question Rebbi Meir is addressing is therefore not whether a lien exists — it does — but what happens to that lien when the estate is divided.

### Small Estate—Five Sela'i…

If the estate is large — *ve'i ika nechasim tuva* — then of course the *kohen* simply collects the five *sela'im* via the lien; there is no difficulty. *Ve'hacha be-mai askinan* — what case is the *mishnah* actually discussing? *Kegon d'leika ela chamesh sela'im* — the entire estate is worth exactly five *sela'im*. The father owed five *sela'im*, the estate is worth five *sela'im*, and the *kohen* has a lien on it. Before division, the *kohen* can take the entire estate. But what happens when the sons divide it and each brother walks away with two and a half *sela'im* worth of property?

### Half-Heir, Half-Purchaser

At this point the *gemara* invokes the ruling of Rav Assi: *u've-chulei alma is le-hu de-Rav Assi* — everyone in this debate operates within the framework of Rav Assi's principle. Rav Assi holds: *ha-achin she-chalku, mechtza yorshin u-mechtza lekuchot* — brothers who divide an estate are considered half heirs and half purchasers. That is, when two brothers split shared property — say, the north half goes to one and the south half to the other — the portion each receives is not fully his by right of inheritance. Half of it is treated as his natural inheritance, and the other half is treated as if he purchased it from his brother. This distinction matters enormously for what a creditor can collect and from whom.

The question of whether division retroactively defines each brother's share as always having been his — the issue of *yesh bereira* — bears on this, though Rav Assi's resolution is the operative one: split the difference, half and half.

### Torah Debt vs. Written L…

The *gemara* then layers on a second shared assumption: *u've-chulei alma, milveh ha-ketuvah ba-Torah lav ke-chetuvah bi-shtar damya* — everyone agrees that a debt mandated by the Torah does not carry the status of a debt written in a formal document, a *shtar*. This requires explanation. When a person borrows money and the transaction is memorialized in a *shtar*, that document creates a *shi'bud* — a lien — on all of the borrower's real property. A creditor holding a *shtar* can collect not only from the borrower directly but from property the borrower subsequently sold, because the lien attached at the moment the document was executed.

But what about an obligation that arises not from a contractual document but from the Torah itself — such as a tortfeasor's obligation to pay for damages, or a father's obligation to redeem his firstborn son? Is the fact that the Torah mandates this payment equivalent to a written *shtar*, generating a lien on real property? The *gemara* assumes that everyone in this dispute holds: no, it is not equivalent. A Torah-mandated obligation, without an accompanying document, does not by itself create a lien on property.

### Rav Pappa on Heirs & Buy…

The third shared assumption comes from Rav Pappa: *milveh al peh goveh min ha-yorshin ve-einah goveh min ha-lekuchot* — a verbal loan, not memorialized in a *shtar*, may be collected from the borrower's heirs but not from purchasers of his property. The logic is that heirs stand in the place of their father — they are a continuation of him, and so the personal obligation runs through them. But since there is no *shtar* creating a lien on the property, a third-party purchaser who acquired the property takes it free and clear of the creditor's claim.

Now line up all three assumptions. The father owed five *sela'im* as a Torah-mandated obligation — which, per assumption two, is not equivalent to a *shtar*. He died. The obligation can pass to his sons as heirs — per Rav Pappa, even without a *shtar*, heirs are collectible from. But now the sons divide the estate, and per Rav Assi, half of what each son holds is treated as if he purchased it from his brother, not as inheritance. Since there is no *shtar*, there is no lien on the purchased portion. Therefore, the *kohen* can only collect from each son's half-as-heir — that is, half of each son's two and a half *sela'im*, yielding only half of the total five *sela'im*.

---

## Full Five vs. Half Five

### Rebbi Meir: Five Only

With this framework in place, the *gemara* now articulates the actual dispute. *Uv'ha b'chamesh v'lo b'chatzi chamesh kamiflagi* — they are debating the phrase *chamesh v'lo b'chatzi chamesh*: five, and not half of five. Rebbi Meir holds that the five *sela'im* must be collectible as a unit. This reflects not merely a quantitative requirement but a formal, ritual dimension of the *pidyon haben* payment: the five *sela'im* function as an indivisible unit of redemption. If the only amount collectible from the divided estate is two and a half *sela'im* — half of five — then that is insufficient, and no payment at all is due.

*Tosafot* notes that Rebbi Meir's position does not necessarily mean a father in ordinary circumstances must hand over exactly five *sela'im* in a single transaction. If a father wishes to pay in installments, or to distribute the five *sela'im* among different *kohanim*, that may be permissible, since in those scenarios there exists an underlying enforceable debt of five *sela'im*. The issue here is that the total collectible amount, after applying all three assumptions, is only two and a half — a debt of that magnitude never existed. And since the civil liability never amounted to five, the *mitzvah* cannot be fulfilled.

### Rebbi Yehuda: Half Suffi…

*Rebbi Yehuda* appears to say the opposite: *chamesh v'afillu chatzi chamesh* — five, and even half of five suffices. The property is obligated — *nitchayvu nechasim* — even post-division, and one may collect whatever is available.

But this framing immediately raises a difficulty in the *gemara*.

### Baraita: Twenty Zuz Requ…

The *gemara* challenges the reading of Rebbi Yehuda from a *baraita*: *Rebbi Yehuda omer ha-achim she-chalku* — Rebbi Yehuda says that when the brothers have divided the estate, *im yesh asara zuz l'zeh v'asara zuz l'zeh, chayavin* — if each has ten *zuz* (recall that a *sela* is four *zuz*, so ten *zuz* is two and a half *sela'im*, i.e., half of the five), they are obligated. *V'im lav, peturim* — if not, they are exempt.

At first this seems to confirm that Rebbi Yehuda allows collection of half the redemption amount — ten *zuz* from each, twenty total, equals five *sela'im* spread across two brothers each paying half. But the *gemara* presses: if Rebbi Yehuda truly permits collecting less than the full five *sela'im*, why set the threshold at ten *zuz* from each? *Afillu pachot mi-asara nami* — even less than ten *zuz* should suffice, since he has abandoned the requirement of a full five. The fact that he specifies a minimum of ten from each means he requires a total of twenty *zuz* — five full *sela'im* — to be collectible. *Alma chamesh v'lo chatzi chamesh sevira lei* — it is clear, then, that even Rebbi Yehuda demands the full five.

### Full Five: Hidden Debate…

The *gemara* now reformulates the dispute cleanly: *ela d'chulei alma chamesh v'lo chatzi chamesh* — in fact, both Rebbi Meir and Rebbi Yehuda agree that the full five *sela'im* must be collectable. The debate is not about whether half suffices. Rather: *uv'ha b'Rav Assi u'Rav Pappa kamiflagi* — they are disputing the applications of Rav Assi's ruling and Rav Pappa's ruling, which together determine whether the full five *sela'im* can in fact be collected from the divided estate.

### Rebbi Yehuda's Hidden As…

Rebbi Meir accepts all three assumptions laid out above — no lien from a Torah obligation, heirs collectible but purchasers not, and post-division each brother is half heir and half purchaser — and therefore concludes that only half of five is collectible per brother, which means the full five cannot be extracted, which means the *kohen* gets nothing.

Rebbi Yehuda, who insists the property *is* obligated — *nitchayvu nechasim* — and collection is possible, must therefore reject at least one of those assumptions. Either he holds that a Torah-mandated obligation *does* create a lien equivalent to a *shtar*, in which case the purchased half of each brother's share is also encumbered and the full five can be extracted; or he rejects Rav Assi's half-and-half principle and holds that after division each brother is considered a full heir to his portion, again allowing collection of the full amount. By rejecting whichever assumption he rejects, Rebbi Yehuda is able to say that a full lien — *nishta'abdu nechasim* — persists on the entire estate even after division, and the *kohen* may collect the complete five *sela'im*.

---

## Alt Sugya via R. Yehuda

### Textual Variant: Rebbi Y…

The *gemara* notes: *ve'ika de'matni la a'seifa* — some versions of this sugya are taught starting not from Rebbi Meir's clause in the *mishnah* but from Rebbi Yehuda's. The analytical content is substantially the same, but the entry point differs. Instead of beginning with Rebbi Meir's statement that division renders the sons exempt and then asking why, the alternative version takes Rebbi Yehuda's statement — that the property becomes obligated, *nitchayvu nechasim* — as its starting point and interrogates that.

### Two Yosef—Purchase Eleme…

Starting from Rebbi Yehuda: when did the father die? If after thirty days — *ilei d'mita achar shloshim* — then the lien exists on the estate and of course the *kohen* can collect; that is unremarkable. And if after division, Rebbi Meir would presumably say the sons are exempt — but why? *Nishta'abdu nechasai!* The lien already existed! So the father must have died within thirty days — *ela betoch shloshim* — meaning the obligation first arose with the sons themselves.

But then: *ki silku amai michayeiv Rebbi Yehuda* — if they have divided the estate and there was never a lien from the father, how can Rebbi Yehuda say they are obligated? *Leizeil legabei hai u'lidchiyei u'legabei hai u'lidchiyei* — the *kohen* goes to one, is pushed off, goes to the other, is pushed off. How does Rebbi Yehuda justify collection?

*Amar Rebbi Yochanan: zot omeret* — Rabbi Yochanan says this implies the Yosef ben Shimon principle. In this version, however, the case is slightly different: *velakach echad mehen sadeh mechaveiro* — one of the brothers purchased a field from the other. Not simply a shared purchase as in the earlier version, but an actual sale between them. The creditor — the *kohen* — now approaches the purchasing brother and says: *ei de'didach maseikna, manta didach shakilna* — if you owe me the money, I take this field from you; *ve'ei de'chaverach maseikna, mesha'abda lei kamai d'idach* — and if your brother owes me, I have a lien that I can exercise against property he sold to you. Either way, I collect from this field. You two sort it out internally.

This is the mechanism by which Rebbi Yehuda, starting from the within-thirty-days scenario, could justify collection after division: because division functions like a purchase, each brother may find himself holding property either directly owed by him or subject to a lien through his brother's obligation.

### Rava Rejects Direct Prop…

Rava, however, rejects this analysis as well. *Michtei nechezei, nichsei de'var inish inun arvun beih* — the same principle applies: you may only approach the property through the person. Since the obligation cannot be assigned to any particular individual — each brother deflects it to the other — the creditor has no mechanism by which to exercise a lien, regardless of what passed between the brothers in dividing the estate. The lien, as always, can only be exercised through the personal obligation of a specific, identified debtor. *Ve'chol k'lishna kama* — and the rest of the sugya proceeds exactly as in the first version.

### Ritual Hinges on Civil L…

The conclusion, in both versions of the sugya, is that the correct reading of the *mishnah* requires the father to have died after thirty days, giving rise to a genuine lien on the estate. The subsequent dispute between Rebbi Meir and Rebbi Yehuda concerns whether that lien survives division in a form sufficient to collect the entire five *sela'im*, with the answer turning on which of the layered assumptions — Rav Assi's half-heir/half-purchaser principle, the non-equivalence of a Torah obligation to a *shtar*, and Rav Pappa's rule about heirs versus purchasers — one accepts or rejects.

The deeper conceptual point the *gemara* has established is this: the ritual obligation of *pidyon haben* is not free-standing. It derives from, and is entirely conditioned by, the civil obligation of the five *sela'im*. If the civil debt cannot be enforced — whether because no individual can be identified as the debtor, or because the lien cannot be exercised after division — then the *mitzvah* itself is unenforceable. At the same time, the obligation is not purely civil either: even Rebbi Yehuda, who insists that what is collectible may be collected, requires the full five *sela'im* to be available. A civil debt of two and a half *sela'im* would still be a debt and would still be owed, but the *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben* would not be triggered. The ritual framing imposes its own formal requirement — *chamesh v'lo chatzi chamesh* — even as its very existence depends on the underlying civil liability being enforceable.

---

---

# Bekhorot 49

## Two Wives, One Husband

### Two wives, two males

The daf begins with the mishnah on 48b, continuing the discussion of *pidyon haben* and the complications that arise when the identity of the *bechor* is uncertain. The mishnah opens with the case of *shtei nashim shelo bichru* — two wives of the same husband, neither of whom has yet given birth. Each wife now gives birth to a male; since each child is a potential firstborn, there would ordinarily be two obligations of *pidyon haben*. The husband gives ten *sela'im* to a *kohen* — five for each child, since a *sela* is equivalent to a *shekel*.

### Death within 30 days

The mishnah then introduces a tragic complication: one of the two boys dies within thirty days. Since the obligation of *pidyon haben* does not begin until the thirtieth day — as derived from the verse *ufduyav miben chodesh tifdeh* — a death within that window cancels the obligation for that child. The precise parameters of giving the money before day thirty will be addressed later in the daf, but the mishnah for now proceeds on the assumption that such early payment can be valid.

### One vs. two Kohanim

If the husband had given both payments to the same *kohen*, that *kohen* must return five *sela'im*, since only one child is now obligated. However, if he had given the payments to two separate *kohanim* without specifying which payment was for which child, he cannot recover from either one. Each *kohen* will simply claim that he received payment for the child who survived, not the one who died, and since the father himself did not know which payment corresponded to which child at the time of giving, neither *kohen* can be compelled to return anything. This outcome reflects the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya*: in civil matters, the burden of proof lies with the one seeking to extract money from another.

### Mixed gender births

The mishnah continues with further scenarios of uncertainty. If the two wives gave birth to a boy and a girl — or to two boys and a girl — and it is unknown which mother bore which child, there may be only one *bechor*, or possibly none at all. In the case of a boy and a girl where identity is confused, the father gives only five *sela'im* to one *kohen*, designating the payment for whichever boy turns out to be the firstborn. In the case of two girls and either one or two boys, it is entirely possible that each mother gave birth to a girl first, yielding no *bechor* at all. In that case, *ein kan lakohen klum* — the *kohen* receives nothing.

The underlying principle here is striking: the obligation of *pidyon haben* is treated entirely as a civil liability. If the debt cannot be established through civil procedure, there is no residual obligation to perform the *mitzvah* on its own. One might raise the objection that a father ought to give the money *matanah al menat lehachzir* — as a gift on condition that it be returned — in order to fulfill the ritual act of *pidyon* even without sustaining a financial loss. Indeed, there is a *gemara* elsewhere that holds that *matanah al menat lehachzir* does satisfy the *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben*. If that is so, one might argue that even where no civil liability can be established, the ritual act itself ought to be performed. The answer implicit in the mishnah is that without an underlying debt, there is no *mitzvah* at all — not even the ritual act. The *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben* is entirely a function of the civil obligation, and where that obligation cannot be sued for, the *mitzvah* simply does not exist.

### One experienced wife

The mishnah closes this section with a case of *achat bichra v'achat shelo bichra* — one wife who has previously given birth and one who has not — both married to the same man. Even if the identities of the children are confused, the wife who has never given birth has definitively produced a firstborn male. Therefore, regardless of which child is biologically hers, the father is obligated in *pidyon*. He gives five *sela'im* to a *kohen* for whichever boy turns out to be the firstborn of the previously childless wife. If one of the two boys then dies within thirty days, the father may recover the money from the *kohen*, since the child who died may have been the firstborn of the previously childless wife, removing the obligation. In the case of a boy and a girl born to these two wives — where identity is confused — the *kohen* receives nothing, because it is entirely possible that the previously childless wife gave birth to the girl first.

The mishnah also addresses the scenario where the father dies while the sons survive. Drawing on the preceding discussion, if the boys themselves seek to claim a double portion of the estate, each will argue that he is the *bechor*; but when the obligation to pay *pidyon* arises, each will argue the opposite. The *gemara* had addressed this tension previously, noting that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda debate the conditions under which the lien on the estate enables collection even after the estate has been divided.

---

## Two Wives, Two Men

### Setup: mixed paternity

The mishnah now turns to a more complex scenario: *shtei nashim shel shenei anashim shelo bicharu* — two wives of two different men, neither of whom has previously given birth. Each wife bears a male child, so each father is separately obligated in *pidyon haben*. However, the children have become confused, so neither father knows which child is his. Despite this confusion, each father knows that his wife has given birth to a firstborn male, and therefore each gives five *sela'im* — *zeh noten chamesh sela'im vezeh noten chamesh sela'im*.

### Single Kohen payment

If one of the children then dies within thirty days, one of the fathers is no longer obligated. But since the children's identities are confused, neither father knows whether it is his child who died. If both fathers had given their payments to the same *kohen*, the *kohen* must return five *sela'im* — that much is clear, since he is holding ten and is only entitled to five. The difficulty is: which father receives the refund? The *kohen* can push off each father individually, saying to each that perhaps the other father is the one owed the refund.

### Power of attorney

The *gemara* resolves this through the mechanism of *harsha'ah* — power of attorney. One father grants a power of attorney to the other, so that the second father can present himself to the *kohen* and say: you owe either me or the other father — and I hold the other father's power of attorney. Since the *kohen* indisputably owes five *sela'im* to one of the two, he cannot push off a claimant who holds power of attorney for both. This is the ruling of Shmuel: *be-bar harsha'ah* — the solution works through the instrument of power of attorney.

The introduction of *harsha'ah* prompts a broader discussion of its halakhic parameters. *Harsha'ah* is a challenging concept in *halacha* because *halacha* tends to operate with concrete, physical transfers rather than abstract legal instruments. The mechanism by which it functions is understood as a kind of transfer of title: when I give you my power of attorney, I am effectively transferring to you the ownership of the claims — the rights that others owe to me. Because this involves a conceptual transfer of title rather than a transfer of a physical object, there are limits.

The *Nehardei* — the scholars of Nehardea — rule: *lo katvinan adrachta a-metalteli* — we do not write a power of attorney (*adrachta* being the Aramaic equivalent of *harsha'ah*) on chattel; we write it only on real estate. The reason is as follows. If someone owes me money in the form of real estate — say, they are sitting on my land — I remain in conceptual control of that land even if they are physically present on it, because land cannot be hidden or moved. Chattel, however, can be taken away, concealed, and removed from my sphere of control. If a thief has taken my movable property and carried it off, I cannot sell it, I cannot consecrate it — it is outside my control. Since the *harsha'ah* mechanism depends on my being able to transfer something I control, I cannot transfer power of attorney over chattel that has left my possession.

The *gemara* then distinguishes: *hani mili heicha dechafrei* — this limitation applies where the other party is denying that he owes the money. If he denies the obligation, then the chattel in question is genuinely beyond my reach and I have no ability to transfer title to it. However, *aval heicha delo kafrei* — where the *kohen* is not denying the debt but only unclear as to whom he owes it, the situation is different. Here the *kohen* himself admits he owes five *sela'im* to one of the two fathers. Since he admits a debt exists — even if he does not know to whom — the money is considered conceptually accessible to the potential creditor, enough to enable a transfer of rights. Therefore, even though this involves chattel rather than real estate, the *harsha'ah* is effective.

*Tosafot* notes, both here and at length in Bava Kamma, that in practice the *Geonim* and *Rishonim* expanded the limits set by the *gemara*, developing the ability to write *harsha'ah* even where the other party denies the debt and even on chattel. This reflects a broader phenomenon in *dinei mamonot* where the economic realities of developing societies required *halacha* to adapt categories that had been formulated under more limited conditions. *Tosafot* attempts to explain on what grounds this expansion was halakhically justified. This is one illustration of a recurring tension in *halacha*: the tradition operates with concrete, physical categories, but modern economic and legal life requires instruments — corporations, intellectual property, abstract powers of attorney — that have no direct precedent in the *gemara*. How that gap is bridged in the post-*gemara* period is its own significant area of inquiry.

### Two Kohanim payment

If both fathers gave their payments to two separate *kohanim*, however, neither father can recover from either *kohen*. Each *kohen* will simply claim that the payment he received was for the surviving child, not the one who died, and since neither father can disprove this, neither *kohen* is compelled to return anything.

### Mixed genders, two men

The mishnah continues: if one wife bore a boy and the other a girl, and the identities are confused, the fathers are exempt — *ha'avot peturim* — because each father can say that perhaps his wife bore the girl, not the boy, and he has no *bechor*. However, the son who was born first to the wife who had never previously given birth knows that he is obligated in *pidyon haben*, even though he does not know who his father is. Since his paternity is in doubt but his status as a *bechor* is not, the *gemara* rules: *haben chayav lifdot et atzmo* — he must redeem himself when he reaches the appropriate age.

If there are two girls and one or two boys, with identity confused, then it is possible that neither mother bore a firstborn son — each may have given birth to a girl first. In that case the *kohen* receives nothing, the fathers give nothing, and the sons themselves cannot be certain they are firstborns.

This section of the mishnah is followed by a compressed presentation of the case where one of the two wives has previously given birth and the other has not. Since the mother who has never previously given birth has definitely produced a firstborn male, *ze shelo becherah ishto noten chamesh sela'im lakohen* — the husband of the previously childless wife gives five *sela'im* to the *kohen*. In the case of a boy and a girl where identity is confused, since it is possible the previously childless wife bore the girl first, *ein lakohen klum* — the *kohen* receives nothing.

A question arises regarding the sons themselves: if they reach the age of bar mitzvah and neither knows whether he is the *bechor*, can either be compelled to give *pidyon haben*? Since the *kohanim* cannot prove which son is obligated, neither can be sued, and therefore neither is obligated. This too reflects the governing principle: where the civil liability cannot be established, the *mitzvah* does not attach.

### Chattel vs. real estate

The preceding discussion of *harsha'ah* has already addressed the distinction between chattel and real estate in the context of transferring power of attorney. As noted, the *Nehardei* limit the writing of a formal *harsha'ah* to real estate precisely because real estate remains under the conceptual control of its owner even when another party occupies it, whereas chattel taken away or denied is beyond the owner's reach. The exception — where the other party admits a debt but disputes to whom it is owed — permits *harsha'ah* even on chattel, since the admission of the debt restores sufficient conceptual access to enable the transfer.

### Rav Huna's cases

The mishnah had ended the section on two wives of two separate husbands by stating only that if a boy and a girl are born and identity is confused, *ein kan lakohen klum*. Rav Huna adds a further case: *shenei zacharim u'nekeivah ein kan lakohen klum* — even two boys and a girl yields a case where the *kohen* receives nothing. In this scenario — two wives of two different husbands, neither of whom has previously given birth — each husband can claim that his wife bore the girl first and he has no obligation. It remains possible that the two boys were born to one mother and the girl to the other, and that the girl was the firstborn of the wife with no prior children.

The *gemara* then asks: why did the Tanna of the mishnah not include this case? The answer is that this case — two boys and a girl with *kohen* receiving nothing — is only applicable in the scenario of two wives of two different husbands. It does not arise in the case of one man and two wives, because if one man has two wives who each bore a child, one of them definitively bore a male firstborn — the obligation exists. The Tanna therefore omitted the two-boys-and-a-girl scenario because it has no parallel in the one-husband cases that preceded it, and the mishnah had already illustrated the principle with the simpler case of a boy and a girl.

---

## Death after 30 days

### Death before day 30

The next mishnah states the rule in its clearest form: *meis haben betoch shloshim yom af al pi she'nasan lakohen yachzir* — if the son died within thirty days, even though the money has already been given to the *kohen*, the *kohen* must return it. The *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben* does not take effect until the thirtieth day, and a death before that point means no obligation ever crystallized.

### Death after day 30

Conversely: *le'achar shloshim yom af al pi shelo nasan yiten* — if the child died after thirty days, even if the father has not yet given the money, he must still give it. One might think that since the child is now gone, there is no longer a living firstborn on whose behalf the *mitzvah* could be performed. The mishnah rules otherwise: once day thirty-one arrived, the father became obligated in *pidyon haben* at that moment. The subsequent death of the child does not undo an obligation that already took effect. The *pidyon* is thus not contingent on the child being alive at the time of payment; it became an irrevocable debt at the moment the thirty-day threshold was crossed.

### Shehecheyanu paradox

*Tosafot* raises a pointed question in this connection. The practice among *Ashkenazim* is to recite the *bracha* of *shehecheyanu* at *pidyon haben* — unlike at *bris milah*, where *Ashkenazim* do not recite *shehecheyanu* (though *Sephardim* do, and the reason *Ashkenazim* omit it at *bris milah* is itself difficult to explain). *Tosafot* then considers the scenario described by this mishnah: the child has died after thirty days, the father is still obligated to perform the *pidyon haben*, and he would, following this ruling, presumably still recite *shehecheyanu* — a blessing of thanksgiving over a joyous occasion — even as he mourns his deceased child. *Tosafot* acknowledges the painful irony of this situation without resolving it away.

---

## Day 30 status

### Rav Gidel ruling

What is the status of day thirty itself? Rav Gidel rules: *meis be'yom shloshim ke'yom she'lefanav* — if the child dies on day thirty, it is treated like the previous day, meaning the obligation has not yet taken effect. The verse says *miben chodesh* — from a month old — which Rav Gidel understands to mean that the child must have entered his second month, i.e., day thirty-one has begun.

### Rabbi Akiva doubt

Rabbi Akiva is uncertain about the status of day thirty. He rules: *im nasan lo yital* — if the father has already given the money to the *kohen*, the *kohen* need not return it, since day thirty may already be considered "a month old." *Ve'im lo nasan, lo yitein* — if the father has not yet given, he need not give. Rabbi Akiva's position is thus a pure *safek*: since day thirty is of ambiguous status, whoever currently holds the money retains it.

### Bamidbar derivation

The *gemara* asks: what is the basis for the rabbinic position? The answer is *gemiri chodesh chodesh mimisbar* — it is learned by analogy from the opening of Bamidbar, where it says *miben chodesh vama'alah*, counting from a month and above. The word "and above" indicates that the count begins only when the child has passed beyond a month — i.e., starting on day thirty-one. The same phrase appears in our context and therefore carries the same meaning.

### Two verses principle

Rabbi Akiva's uncertainty stems from a specific textual observation. The phrase "a month and above" appears not only in the context of the census in Bamidbar but also in the context of *erchin* — the system of valuations established in the Torah, where the value assigned to a person of one month and above is given. If the rule could have been derived from the Bamidbar census, why did the Torah need to repeat "and above" in the context of *erchin*? The principle *shnei kesuvim haba'im ke'echad ein melamdin* — two verses that come to teach the same thing do not generate a general rule — suggests that perhaps these two cases are exceptions rather than the norm. If they were the norm, one verse would suffice; the need for two verses implies they are anomalous, and the standard rule may therefore be that day thirty is already considered a full month.

The *gemara* then raises the counter-possibility: *aval legufaihu melamdin* — the principle that two verses cannot extend a rule to other areas does not prevent each verse from informing cases closely related to its own subject matter. The Bamidbar census of *bechorim* for the purpose of redeeming them with the *Leviim* is structurally similar to our *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben*, even though it was a unique historical event. Perhaps the Bamidbar verse may inform our *mitzvah* precisely because they share the same fundamental subject. Rabbi Akiva is therefore genuinely uncertain: *u'mishum hachi misapkinan lehu* — this unresolved doubt is why he treats day thirty as ambiguous and leaves the money in the hands of whoever holds it.

One additional observation: the *gemara* throughout this discussion takes it for granted that a month means thirty days. Given that an average lunar month is approximately twenty-nine and a half days, one might have thought the threshold was twenty-nine days. The *gemara* consistently rounds upward, reflecting the assumption that a full month counts as thirty days. Whether one could technically perform *pidyon haben* after exactly thirty twenty-four-hour periods, rather than waiting until halakhic day thirty-one, is a question addressed in the later *poskim*.

---

## Viability & mourning

### Rava's consensus

Rava introduces an important clarification: *hakol modim le'inyan aveilus yom shloshim ke'yom she'lefanav* — all authorities agree that for the purposes of *aveilus*, day thirty is treated like day twenty-nine, i.e., as still within the first month. This is because the rule *halakha ke'divrei ha'meikel be'avel* — in matters of mourning, we follow the lenient opinion — means that even Rabbi Akiva, who is uncertain whether day thirty already qualifies as "a month old" for *pidyon haben*, would agree to leniency in the context of *aveilus*. A parent whose child dies on day thirty would not observe *shiva*.

### Full-term babies

The *gemara* draws a distinction regarding viability. If a baby is known to be full-term, it is considered viable from the moment of birth, and even if it dies on the first day, the parents observe *shiva* and all the laws of *aveilus* apply. If, however, there is uncertainty whether the baby was full-term — for instance, whether it may have been a *neifel* — then the child must survive thirty days for viability to be established. If such a child dies before thirty days have elapsed, the parents do not observe *shiva*. If it survives to day thirty-one, it is established as viable and all *aveilus* obligations apply. The status of day thirty in this context is the subject of Rava's statement: all agree it is treated like the previous day, and parents would not observe *shiva*.

### Viability vs. mitzva

*Rashi* on the mishnah suggests that the reason *pidyon haben* does not apply until thirty days is because of the *neifel* concern — the child may not have been viable. *Tosafot* disputes this. The thirty-day requirement for *pidyon haben* is not a function of establishing viability; it is an independent halakhic rule derived from the verse *miben chodesh*. The evidence for this is that even a child known with certainty to be full-term and healthy — where there is no *neifel* concern whatsoever — cannot have *pidyon haben* performed before day thirty-one. The thirty-day wait for viability determination and the thirty-day threshold for *pidyon haben* are therefore two distinct halakhic categories that happen to share the same number, but operate on entirely different principles.

This distinction has practical consequences. One might think that since Rabbi Akiva treats day thirty as potentially satisfying the *pidyon haben* requirement, and yet Rava says all agree day thirty is like the previous day for *aveilus*, there could be a case where a *kohen* retains money for *pidyon haben* even as the parents do not observe *shiva* — because the two *halakhot* track different criteria. The thirty-day period for *aveilus* is about establishing viability in cases of doubt, and we are lenient there; the thirty-day period for *pidyon haben* is about when the *mitzvah* becomes operative, and Rabbi Akiva thinks that may already be day thirty.

---

## Father dies

### Before day 30

If the father dies before day thirty and the son, upon reaching adulthood, does not know whether his father performed *pidyon haben*, he operates under the presumption *be'chezkat shelo nifdah* — he should assume he has not been redeemed. It would be most unusual for a father to perform *pidyon haben* before day thirty, and in the absence of information to the contrary, the son must assume he is unredeemed and must redeem himself. This presumption holds *ad she'yavi ra'ayah she'nifdah* — until he can bring proof that he has been redeemed.

### After day 30

If the father dies after day thirty, the presumption reverses: *be'chezkat she'nifdah* — the son should assume that he has been redeemed. The father lived to see day thirty-one, the obligation took effect, and we assume he fulfilled it at the earliest opportunity. This assumption holds unless people inform him that he was not redeemed: *ad she'yomru lo shelo nifdah*.

### Types of proof

The mishnah uses different language in the two cases: in the first, the son must *bring proof* that he was redeemed; in the second, *people must tell him* he was not. Rashi explains the asymmetry: proof of the absence of an event is inherently difficult to produce. If a *kohen* says "I never received payment from your father," that is not necessarily conclusive evidence — there are many *kohanim*. Therefore, the mishnah does not ask for formal *ra'ayah* in the case of presumed redemption, but instead envisions a scenario such as the father having stated on his deathbed that he had never redeemed his son. That kind of testimony — not a formal evidentiary proof, but a credible statement about an absence — is what *yomru lo* encompasses.

---

## Son's redemption

### Dual obligations

The mishnah presents a case that arises in practice more often than one might expect: *hu lifdot u'beno lifdot* — a man who was never himself redeemed by his father now has his own firstborn son. He faces two obligations simultaneously: to redeem himself and to redeem his son. The question is one of priority.

### Self comes first

The mishnah rules: *hu kodem li'veno* — he takes care of himself first. The implication seems to be that his own *mitzvah* of redemption is the primary one, and his obligation to his son is secondary.

### Child comes first

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *beno kodmo* — his son comes first. The reason is *she'mitzvato al aviv* — the *mitzvah* of redeeming him was his father's *mitzvah*, and therefore his own redemption is derived from his father's obligation, not his own. *U'mitzvat beno alav* — by contrast, his *mitzvah* to redeem his son is his own primary *mitzvah*. Rabbi Yehuda therefore holds that the father's primary *mitzvah* is to redeem his son, and his own redemption is something he inherits, as it were, from the unfulfilled obligation of his own father. His son's *pidyon* therefore takes priority.

### Practical memory issues

A significant practical difficulty underlies all these cases: who will remember? If a father dies young, leaving an infant son who has never been redeemed, who will recall thirteen years later, when the boy reaches bar mitzvah, that he still needs to redeem himself? The *Acharonim* discuss various solutions, including fashioning a piece of jewelry or a bracelet that the child wears bearing some indication of his unredeemed status, so that when he reaches maturity the matter will not be forgotten. Beyond this, the question arises whether a *beit din* can act on behalf of a minor child and arrange his *pidyon* before he comes of age. Two possible grounds exist: first, since the *pidyon* is in the child's own interest, perhaps an agent can be appointed for him even though he is a minor; second, perhaps the community at large bears some responsibility to ensure *pidyon haben* is performed. This remains a debated question among the *poskim*.

### Artificial insemination

These questions about communal obligation and *beit din* intervention arise acutely in contemporary cases involving artificial insemination. Where the sperm donor is unknown — typically assumed to be non-Jewish — and the halakhic status of the donor as father is in doubt, the practical result is that the husband of the mother may not be considered the child's halakhic father for purposes of *pidyon haben*. There is no father to perform the *mitzvah*, and no one to remember it in thirteen years. Some *poskim* permit the *beit din* to appoint the mother's husband as agent — not as father, but as representative of the *beit din* or of the child — to perform the *pidyon haben* while the child is still young, before it is forgotten. Where the husband donates his own sperm for his wife, the question of whether he is considered the halakhic father for purposes of *pidyon haben* is more complex, and there is considerably more reason to regard him as fully the child's father in that case.

---

## Early redemption

### Rav's view

The *gemara* now addresses the case — implicit in the mishnah throughout — of *hapodeh et beno betoch shloshim yom*: a father who gives the *pidyon haben* money to a *kohen* before day thirty. The mishnah has assumed in various cases that such early payment can be valid. Now the *gemara* considers the precise parameters. Rav rules: *beno paduy* — the son is redeemed; the early payment is effective.

### Shmuel's view

Shmuel disagrees: *ein beno paduy* — the early payment does not work. The *gemara* clarifies that all authorities agree on two extreme cases. If the father gives the money and says it should take effect *now*, on day two or day ten, everyone agrees it does not work — the *mitzvah* has not yet begun. If the father gives the money with the stipulation that it take effect after thirty days, and the money is still in the *kohen*'s possession on day thirty-one, everyone agrees it works — it is as if the *pidyon* were performed on day thirty-one itself.

### Money must exist

The debate between Rav and Shmuel concerns a third scenario: the father gives the money within thirty days, designating it to take effect after thirty days, but by the time day thirty-one arrives, the money has already been spent. In this case, is there a valid *pidyon*? Rav says yes — the act was performed and the effect is merely postponed, and the fact that the money no longer exists on day thirty-one is irrelevant. Shmuel says no — if the money is gone by day thirty-one, it does not work.

### Kiddushin parallel

Rav supports his position by analogy to *kiddushin*: a man can betroth a woman today and specify that the *kiddushin* take effect in thirty days, and even if the ring has been spent or lost, the betrothal is valid. If splitting the act from the effect is permissible in *kiddushin*, it should be permissible here as well. Shmuel responds by distinguishing the cases. In *kiddushin*, the man could, if he chose, perform the *kiddushin* with immediate effect today — the thirty-day delay is purely his preference. Because he *could* have performed the act and its effect simultaneously right now, he is considered to be in control of the transaction, and he may legitimately separate the act from the effect. In *pidyon haben*, however, the father cannot perform the *pidyon* with immediate effect today — the *mitzvah* is not yet active. Since he has no present ability to perform the act now, he cannot be said to be "doing the act now" in any meaningful sense. Without that present ability, there is no valid act at all, and the designation of future effect cannot save it.

### Shmuel accepted

The *gemara* rules: *hilchasa kevasei de'Shmuel* — the *halakha* follows Shmuel. This is notable because the general principle is *kol heicha de'pleigi Rav u'Shmuel hilchasa ke'Rav be'isuri u'ke'Shmuel be'dinei* — we follow Rav in matters of *issur* and Shmuel in civil matters. Since *pidyon haben* might appear to be a matter of *issur*, one would expect the ruling to follow Rav. Yet the *gemara* rules like Shmuel — either because Shmuel's reasoning was more persuasive on its merits, or because the consensus among later authorities developed in that direction. It is worth noting that there appears to be a second, possibly interpolated, statement of this ruling in the *gemara* — the *halakhta* appears to be repeated, which is itself a textual indication that it may be a *Geonic* gloss rather than original *gemara* text. This is consistent with the observation that many of the *halakhta* rulings in the *gemara* were originally found in *Hilkhot Gedolot*, written in Aramaic and following the flow of the *gemara*, and were subsequently incorporated into the *gemara* text itself. Notably, the Rambam, Ramban, and Rosh all rule according to Rav — which may indicate that they regarded the *halakhta* here as precisely such a later gloss rather than authoritative *gemara*.

### Mishnah clarified

The *gemara* then reconciles Shmuel's ruling with the various mishnah cases that appear to assume early payment can be valid. Each time the mishnah speaks of money given before day thirty that is effective, Shmuel's position is that the money was still present on day thirty-one. The statement that if the father died within thirty days the son is *be'chezkat shelo nifdah* is similarly consistent: the proof that the *pidyon* was valid even though paid early would consist of showing that the money was still with the *kohen* on day thirty-one. All the mishnah's cases are thus harmonized with Shmuel's requirement that the money physically exist at the moment the *mitzvah* becomes operative.

---

## Self vs. son priority

### Tannaitic dispute

The *gemara* returns to the question of priority between self-redemption and son-redemption, now framing it as a full *baraita*: the Sages rule *hu kodem li'veno* — he redeems himself first; Rabbi Yehuda rules *beno kodmo* — his son comes first, since the *mitzvah* of his own redemption was his father's *mitzvah*, while the *mitzvah* of redeeming his son is his own primary *mitzvah*.

### Yirmiyah reframes

Rabbi Yirmiyah reframes the debate in a way that significantly alters its character. Rather than presenting it as a pure dispute over whose *mitzvah* takes conceptual precedence, he reframes it as a question of what happens when funds are limited: *hakol modim heicha de'leika ela chamesh sela'im* — all agree that if only five *sela'im* are available, the person redeems himself first.

### Limited funds

The reason Rabbi Yirmiyah gives is: *mitzvah didei adif* — his own *mitzvah* takes priority. This raises a fundamental conceptual question that the *gemara* does not fully resolve. Does "his own *mitzvah*" mean that the *mitzvah* of *pidyon haben* is, at its conceptual root, the *mitzvah* of the *child*, with the father acting on the child's behalf — in which case when this person was unredeemed, it was fundamentally *his* *mitzvah* that went unfulfilled? Or does it mean that even if the *mitzvah* is fundamentally the father's, nevertheless since an unredeemed status directly affects this person's own being and standing, he is entitled — analogous to *chayecha kodmin* — to attend to his own status before attending to his son's? These are two very different conceptual frameworks, and Rabbi Yirmiyah's language supports either reading.

### Lien theory

Rabbi Yirmiyah then identifies *eimas pligi* — when the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda actually disagree. The debate concerns a case where there are five *sela'im* in cash — *bnei chorin* — and a field sold by the father that carries a lien of five *sela'im* — *meshubadot*. The lien on the field exists because when this person was an infant, his father was obligated in *pidyon haben*, and *milveih hakesuvah ba'Torah k'kesuvah b'shtar damya* — a debt written in the Torah is treated like a debt recorded in a formal document, and therefore creates a lien on property the father then owned. That lien follows the property even after it was sold. However, the five *sela'im* cash was acquired after the father's death, so no lien from the son's *pidyon* obligation ever attached to it.

### No lien view

The Sages dispute the premise: *milveh hakesuvah ba'Torah lav k'kesuvah b'shtar damya* — a Torah-mandated obligation does not create a lien equivalent to a written document. No lien ever attached to the sold field. Therefore, the only funds available are the five *sela'im* cash, and a choice must be made between self-redemption and son-redemption. In this scenario, all agree the person redeems himself first: *hilkhakh mitzvah didei adif*.

### Mitzva status

The deepest question running through this entire discussion is the fundamental nature of the *mitzvah*: is *pidyon haben* at its root the father's *mitzvah* — with the son, should the father fail to act, merely inheriting a derived obligation — or is it fundamentally the son's *mitzvah*, with the father acting as agent on his behalf, so that the "real" obligated party is always the child? Rabbi Yehuda's formulation in the mishnah leans strongly toward the latter: *she'mitzvato al aviv*, your own redemption was your father's *mitzvah*, implying that the *mitzvah* is yours by right but was discharged by your father. The Sages' position, as articulated by Rabbi Yirmiyah, may reflect either the same understanding — in which case the priority of self-redemption is grounded in the analogy to caring for one's own needs first — or a fundamentally different one, in which the *mitzvah* is the father's and a person's own obligation to redeem himself is purely derivative, yet still takes priority because of the direct connection to his personal status.

---

---

# Bekhorot 50

## Pidyon HaBen Overview

### From Definition to Mitzv…

The tractate's opening sugyot addressed the definition of *bekhor* — the firstborn — and worked through a series of curious edge cases, including questions about dead fetuses. Having established what counts as a firstborn, the Mishnah now turns to the *mitzvah* itself: *pidyon haben*, the redemption of the firstborn son. This is not an unusual organizational pattern; *Mishnayot* frequently open with definitional questions before turning to the operative *mitzvah*. One practical note before entering the text: if the father is too poor to afford the redemption, a *Kohen* may give him the money as a gift, and the father may then return it to the *Kohen* — a mechanism that ensures the *mitzvah* can be fulfilled regardless of financial circumstance.

### Mishnah: Five Sela'im

The Mishnah, found at the bottom of 49b, opens: *chamesh sela'im shel ben* — five *sela'im* for the son. Notice immediately the terminological translation embedded in this phrase: the *shekel* of the Torah is here equated with the *sela*. The Torah's *shekel* is a silver *shekel* — *esrim gerah hashekel*, twenty *gerah* to the *shekel* — and this is understood to be identical with what the Mishnaic world called a *sela*. The Mishnah specifies further: *bemaneh Tzuri*, measured according to the Tyrian *maneh*, meaning the *sela* of Tyrian coinage.

### Shekel/Sela Equivalency

The Mishnah then enumerates the other Torah payments that share this same standard. *Sheloshim shel eved* — the thirty *kesef* paid when an ox gores a slave (Shemot 21:32). *Chamishim shel ones u'mefateh* — the fifty *shekel* paid by the rapist or seducer to the father of the girl. *U'me'ah shel motzi shem ra* — the hundred *kesef* paid by the man who libels his new wife by falsely claiming she was not a virgin, which is double the ordinary fifty. The Mishnah concludes: *kulam beshekel hakodesh* — all of these are reckoned in the holy *shekel*. The Torah itself defines this: *chatzi hashekel beshekel hakodesh esrim gerah hashekel* — the half-*shekel* offering is measured by the *shekel hakodesh*, which is twenty *gerah*. All of the Torah's *kesef* payments, when unspecified, refer to this same silver *shekel*, which is the *sela* of the Tyrian standard.

### Biblical Payment Amounts

Two foundational principles emerge from the Mishnah. First, the standard Torah *kesef* — *kesef stam* — means the *shekel*, which equals the *sela* of the Tyrian coinage. This identification is presumed throughout rabbinic literature. Second, the Mishnah notes that *kulam nitnin bekesef uveshaveh kesef* — all these payments may be made either in silver or in items of equivalent value — *chutz mishkalim*, with the exception of the half-*shekel* contribution to the Temple, which must be paid in actual silver, not merely in equivalent value. This exception will receive further treatment in the Gemara.

### Payment in Equivalent Va…

The operative *halachah* is therefore twofold: the Torah's use of *kesef* refers to the *shekel*/*sela* standard, and payment need not be in silver per se but may be discharged in any item of equivalent monetary value. The Gemara will now take up the task of translating what that *sela* actually represents in terms of contemporaneous coinage — a project that requires working through several layers of monetary equivalency.

---

## Monetary Conversions

### Maneh Tzuri & Coins

The Gemara opens by asking what exactly *maneh Tzuri* means. *Amar Rav Asi maneh shel Tzuri* — Rav Asi says it is the *maneh* of Tyre. This clarification helps primarily through contrast with other coinage systems. To understand the broader equivalency table: one *sela* equals four *dinarim*; a *dinar* is also called a *zuz*. These are all silver coins. The *maneh* is a larger unit: one *maneh* equals twenty-five *sela'im*, which means one *maneh* equals one hundred *zuzim* — this is the standard Talmudic equivalency familiar from many sugyot. Far below on the scale sit the copper *prutot*: one *sela* equals 768 *prutot*. To put this in perspective, this is the difference relevant to the famous dispute between *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* regarding *kiddushei isha*: *Beit Hillel* rules that a woman may be betrothed with even a *prutah*, while *Beit Shammai* requires a *dinar* — a ratio of roughly 1 to 196.

### Sela/Dinar/Maneh Ratios

The key relationships for *pidyon haben* are as follows. One *sela* equals four *dinarim*. Five *sela'im* — the Torah's requirement for *pidyon haben* — therefore equals twenty *dinarim*, or twenty *zuz*. The *maneh* of twenty-five *sela'im* means that one *sela* is one twenty-fifth of a *maneh*. When the Mishnah says the five *sela'im* are measured *bemaneh Tzuri*, it is situating the *sela* within this Tyrian coinage structure. The bottom line for *pidyon haben* in terms of silver coinage is twenty silver *dinarim*.

### Modern Silver Equivalence

The question of how this translates into modern terms has been addressed by *Rishonim* and later authorities. The standard understanding, following the *Chazon Ish*, is that one *shekel*/*sela* equals approximately 19.2 grams of silver — a figure derived from ancient barley-seed weight measurements (*she'orim*), which served as precise standards for weighing precious metals in antiquity. Five *shekalim* therefore equals approximately 96 grams of silver, or more precisely 95.85 grams.

### Dollar Equivalency

At current silver prices — approximately $29 per troy ounce, with 96 grams equaling roughly two and a half troy ounces — the five *shekalim* for *pidyon haben* comes to approximately $72–$75. This figure fluctuates, and there is some uncertainty about the $125 figure that is frequently cited; it likely reflects a period when silver prices were higher. For reference, one *shekel* comes to approximately $25 at that rate, meaning the fifty *shekel* payment for *ones* or *mefateh* would be approximately $1,250. One *prutah*, dividing the *shekel* value of roughly $25 by 800, works out to approximately 3 cents.

### Silver Price Fluctuation

This fluctuation in silver prices carries practical *halachic* implications. The Torah's *shekel* is understood to mean a specific weight of intrinsic-value silver — as if the Torah had said "five ounces of silver." Our money today does not carry intrinsic value, but silver still does, and so the redemption amount must track the silver market. This is not merely theoretical: Rabbi Willig recently required his agent for *mechiyas chametz* to bring more silver coins than in prior years, because the price of silver had risen, affecting the value needed to complete a valid kinyan. The fluctuation of silver prices thus has practical consequences for anyone performing *pidyon haben* or calculating the value of any Torah-mandated silver payment.

---

## Coinage Systems & Opinio…

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

The Gemara presents three Amoraic opinions on how to express the *pidyon haben* amount in contemporary coinage. *Rashi*'s interpretation of this passage is complex and will not be elaborated here; instead, the approach of *Tosafot* will be followed, as it offers a cleaner and more analytically satisfying account. According to *Tosafot*, these opinions are not debating which coinage standard to use in the abstract. Rather, they are answering a practical question: given that five *shekalim* equals twenty silver *dinarim*, and given that gold *dinarim* were the dominant high-value coins, what gold coin or combination of coins could a person present to discharge the *pidyon haben* obligation? The answer is complicated by the fact that the standard ratio of one gold *dinar* to twenty-five silver *dinarim* does not line up neatly with the twenty silver *dinarim* required — the standard gold coin is worth slightly more than what is needed.

### Gold/Silver Dinar Ratio

The key equivalency is this: one gold *dinar* equals twenty-five silver *dinarim*. Five *shekalim*, however, equals only twenty silver *dinarim*. So the *pidyon haben* amount is four-fifths of one standard gold *dinar*. One cannot simply hand a priest a standard gold *dinar*, because that would be overpaying. The Amoraim are therefore proposing various ways to express this amount in coinage that actually existed — coins whose denominational value was close enough to twenty silver *dinarim* to serve as a practical medium of payment.

### Rabbi Ami: Arabian Dinar

*Rabbi Ami* says *dinara arva'ah* — one Arabian *dinar* suffices. According to *Tosafot*, the Arabian gold *dinar* was worth not twenty-five but exactly twenty silver *dinarim*. This was a smaller gold coin than the standard, and its value happened to align precisely with the requirement for *pidyon haben*. Thus, according to Rabbi Ami, one may discharge the obligation by presenting a single Arabian gold *dinar* — no fractional calculation required.

### Rabbi Chanina: Syrian Is…

*Rabbi Chanina* proposes a different coinage: *istira sarsira*, a Syrian *istira*. The Gemara says *demizdabna tamanya bedinara* — eight Syrian *istirin* go for one gold *dinar*. Therefore one *istira* equals one-eighth of a gold *dinar*. Since a standard gold *dinar* is worth twenty-five silver *dinarim*, and one *istira* is one-eighth of that, five *istirin* equal five-eighths of a gold *dinar*. The calculation behind this is that the Syrian *dinar* had a different silver content — effectively it was a larger denomination, such that one gold *dinar* in Syrian coinage equaled thirty-two silver *dinarim* rather than twenty-five. Five-eighths of thirty-two is twenty. So five Syrian *istirin* — five-eighths of a Syrian gold *dinar* — yields exactly twenty silver *dinarim*, the required amount.

### Reconciliation of Opinio…

All three approaches, read according to *Tosafot*, arrive at the same practical conclusion: the *pidyon haben* obligation is twenty silver *dinarim*. In the standard coinage, this is four-fifths of a gold *dinar*. Rabbi Ami finds a coin — the Arabian *dinar* — whose denomination happens to equal exactly four-fifths of the standard, making it a single-coin solution. Rabbi Chanina works in Syrian coinage, where five *istirin* achieve the same result. The opinions differ not in their *halachic* requirement but in their identification of what actually circulating coin or combination of coins could serve as a practical vehicle for the payment.

---

## Rabbi Yochanan & 20 Zuz

### Hadrianic Dinar = 25 Zuz

Rabbi Yochanan says: *dinra hadreina tayreina sheifa demizdabna be'esrin vechamish zuzei* — a Hadrianic Tyrian *dinar* (*Rashi* reads this as referring to Hadrian; *Tosafot* suggests it may simply mean "circular" or similar) sells for twenty-five *zuzim*. This is the standard ratio: one gold *dinar* equals twenty-five silver *dinarim*/*zuzim*. Rabbi Yochanan is working with the standard coinage and asking how one arrives at the twenty *zuz* needed for *pidyon haben* from a coin worth twenty-five.

### Sixth Removal Method

The Gemara proposes: *dal mineihu shetuta* — remove a sixth. One-sixth of twenty-five is four and a fraction, so removing a sixth leaves approximately twenty-one minus a small fraction — not twenty. The Gemara objects: *hanei esrin vechad nechi danka havei* — that is twenty-one minus a sixth, not twenty.

### Corrected Calculation

The Gemara then tries: *ela dal shetuta vezuza* — remove a sixth and then one more *zuz*. But that yields slightly less than twenty, since one is removing more than a fifth. The Gemara objects again: *achti esrin nechi danka havei* — that is twenty minus a sixth, still not exactly twenty. The correct procedure, the Gemara concludes, is: *ela dal zuza* first — subtract one *zuz*, leaving twenty-four — *veshetuta*, and then remove one-sixth of twenty-four, which is exactly four. Twenty-four minus four equals twenty precisely. This yields *dehanei lehu esrin metkali bemetkali dedinra* — twenty *zuz* in the weight-equivalent of a *dinar*.

### Zuz Weight Expression

The resulting formulation — twenty *zuz* in the weight of a *dinar* — is the Gemara's way of expressing that *pidyon haben* requires an amount of silver equivalent to four-fifths of a standard gold *dinar*, reckoned by weight. The fondness the Gemara displays here for the fraction of a sixth, rather than the more obvious fifth, is notable; the roundabout method of subtracting one *zuz* and then a sixth of the remainder achieves the same result as a straightforward four-fifths calculation but expressed in terms of the fractional units the Talmud preferred. *Rashi* notes that the subsequent line converting twenty *zuz* into twenty-eight and seven-twelfths units of another currency may be a gloss.

---

## Biblical vs. Rabbinic Se…

### Rava: Torah Sela = 3.33

*Rava* now introduces a striking complication. *Sela d'Oraita tlata v'tilta havei* — the *sela* of the Torah was worth only three and one-third *zuz*, not four. The assumption throughout the preceding discussion has been a one-to-four ratio between the *sela* and the *dinar*/*zuz*, but Rava says this ratio reflects a later standard; the Torah's original *sela* was smaller.

### Gerah/Ma'ah Calculation

The proof proceeds as follows. The Torah says *esrim gerah hashekel* — the *shekel* is twenty *gerah*. The Targum translates *gerah* as *ma'ah*: *esrim ma'in*. And a *braita* teaches *shesh ma'ah kesef dinar* — there are six *ma'ot* in one *dinar*. Therefore one *shekel* equals twenty *ma'ot*. But if one *dinar* equals six *ma'ot* and the *shekel* equals twenty *ma'ot*, then the *shekel* equals twenty-sixths of a *dinar* — that is, three and one-third *dinarim*. Three and one-third times six equals twenty, which is internally consistent. But this means the original Torah *shekel* was not four *dinarim* but three and one-third.

If, however, we use the later standard of four *dinarim* per *sela*, then one *sela* equals twenty-four *ma'ot*, not twenty. This implies that at some later point the coinage was enlarged — the coins were made bigger — so that what had been twenty *ma'ot* in the Torah's system became twenty-four *ma'ot* in the later system. The ratio of *ma'ot* to *dinar* stayed fixed at six, but the *sela* grew from three and one-third *dinarim* to four.

### Yovel Redemption & Fundi…

The Gemara raises a challenge from a *braita* (possibly from the *Sifra*) concerning the *yovel* redemption of a dedicated field. The Torah states that a field of a *beit zera chomer se'orim* — a field sown with a *chomer* of barley — is valued at fifty *shekel* for the full forty-nine years until *yovel*. Dividing fifty *shekel* by forty-nine years, each year comes to one *shekel* plus one forty-ninth of a *shekel*. The *braita* teaches that one *sela shel kodesh* equals forty-eight *pundiyot*, and a *pundiyah* is a *ma'ah*. So one *sela* equals forty-eight *ma'ot*. But if the Torah's *shekel* were only twenty *ma'ot*, then forty-nine times one *shekel* and one *pundiyah* would yield forty-nine *shekel* plus forty-nine *pundiyot*; forty-nine *pundiyot* at the Torah rate of twenty *ma'ot* per *shekel* would give only a fraction of a *shekel*, not a whole additional *shekel*. The arithmetic of the *braita* seems to presuppose the larger, later standard of forty-eight *ma'ot* per *sela*. The extra *pundiyah* in the *braita* — *kilbon l'prutot* — reflects a minor rounding discrepancy, not a substantive difference. The point is that the *braita*'s calculation only works with the larger coin.

### Coinage Enlargement

The Gemara resolves this: *basar de'osfu aleihu* — after the Torah was given, the coinage was enlarged. The coins were made physically bigger. One might ask: if the coins changed, shouldn't we be bound by the silver weight at the time of the Torah, not the later standard? The Gemara's implied answer — which will be made more explicit — is that *Chazal* understood the Torah to permit a certain degree of incorporation of changed coinage into the system, provided the change moves upward (larger coins with more silver) and not downward. The Torah's original *sela* of three and one-third *dinarim* was the floor; the subsequent enlargement to four *dinarim* was absorbed into the operative standard. The *braita*'s arithmetic reflects the post-enlargement standard that became normative.

---

## Flexibility & Rav Ashi S…

### 'Yihyeh' Drasha

A *braita* provides the textual basis for this flexibility. The Torah says *esrim gerah yihyeh hashekel* — the *shekel* shall be twenty *gerah*. The word *yihyeh* — "shall be" or "it shall be" — is read as a superfluous term. *Minayin she'im ratzah lehosif yosif* — from where do we know that one may increase the number of *gerah* per *shekel*? *Talmud lomar yihyeh* — the word *yihyeh* implies that the standard is flexible upward.

### Minimum Gerah Standard

At the same time, there is a lower limit. *Yachol yifchos* — might one reduce below twenty *gerah*? *Talmud lomar hu* — the word *hu* ("it," in the phrase *esrim gerah hu*) establishes a fixed minimum. The *shekel* may be no less than twenty *gerah* — the original Torah standard is an inviolable floor. Thus: the Torah *shekel* may be enlarged by communal or governmental coinage changes but may never be reduced below the original biblical weight. When later authorities enlarged the coins, this was permitted under the *yihyeh* license. The new, larger *sela* of four *dinarim* became the operative standard, but the floor remains the Torah's original three and one-third.

### Rav Ashi's 17 Zuzim

This distinction between the old and new standards generates a remarkable anecdote. *Rav Ashi shadrei shitsar zuzei le-Rav Acha brei de-Rav Ina be-pidyon haben* — when Rav Ashi redeemed his firstborn son, he sent seventeen *zuz* to Rav Acha son of Rav Ina, who served as the *Kohen* recipient. The standard requirement, as established throughout the preceding discussion, is twenty *zuz*.

### Priest's Demand

*Shalach lei* — the *Kohen* sent back: *lishdar li mar tlata achrinei de'ika aleihu* — please send me the additional three *zuz* that you still owe me.

### Rav Ashi's Justification

Rav Ashi responded: *lishdar li mar tilta achrina de'osifi aleihu* — send me back the extra third that I already overpaid you. His reasoning: he was applying the original Torah standard of three and one-third *dinarim* per *sela*. Five *sela'im* at three and one-third *dinarim* each equals sixteen and two-thirds *zuz*. He had sent seventeen, which is actually one-third more than required under the old standard.
