*Ka mashma lan nehi d'ptirei b'sha'at avodah* — true, they are exempt when actually engaged in *avodah*, but *b'lo sha'at avodah chiyuvi mechayvei* — when they are not on duty, they are obligated. The *Kohanim* are not working every moment.

### Travelers Analogy

The analogy is to *holchei drachim* — travelers on *Sukkot*: *holchei drachim bayom pturim min hasukkah* — they are exempt during the day while traveling, since they cannot erect a *sukkah* on the road, *v'chayavim balailah* — but they are obligated at night when they stop and sleep. So too *Kohanim*: exempt while working, obligated during the hours they are home.

### Better Girsa

The side *girsa* of the *gemara* reads *bein bayom bein balailah* — the concern is about day and night, not about *ish v'ishto*. This is a superior reading: the question is whether the fact that *Kohanim* are never home during the day exempts them from the daytime requirement, just as travelers are exempt during the day. The answer is that just like travelers must dwell in the *sukkah* at night, *Kohanim* must do so in whatever hours they are not occupied with *avodah*. This *girsa* is clearly to be preferred.

### Women Exempt

The other dimension of the *ish v'ishto* reading is different: since women are exempt from *sukkah*, a man might argue that *teshvu k'ein taduru* — living as at home — is impossible without his wife, since she will not join him in the *sukkah*, and therefore he too should be exempt. This argument is never accepted as *halacha*.

### Rama's Justification

Yet interestingly, the *Rama* invokes a version of this reasoning to justify the *Ashkenazi* practice of not sleeping in the *sukkah*. The real practical reason, as anyone who has spent *Sukkot* in northern Europe will understand, is that the cold weather renders sleeping in the *sukkah* a case of *mitzta'er* — suffering — which halachically exempts one. But the *Rama* also offers the rationale that since *teshvu k'ein taduru* requires living with one's wife and the wife is exempt, the husband cannot fully achieve the required quality of dwelling. The obvious problem with this justification is that it would have always exempted married men from sleeping in the *sukkah*, which cannot be right. This demonstrates that the *girsa* suggesting *ish v'ishto* as the conceptual basis for the *sukkah* requirement is problematic, reinforcing the conclusion that the alternative *girsa* — *bein bayom bein balailah* — is the correct one.

### Girsa Problems

As for the inclusion of *Levi'im* and *Yisraelim* along with *Kohanim*: the *chiddush* applies to *Kohanim*, and *Levi'im* may be added because they too have *avodah*, while *Yisraelim* follow because one states all three together. The *gemara* assumes this grouping is not problematic — once one element of the list requires explicit mention, the entire formulation *Kohanim, Levi'im, v'Yisraelim* follows naturally.

---

## Tzitzit & Kohanim

### Tzitzit Obligation

*Hakol chayavin b'tzitzit* — everybody is obligated in *tzitzit* — with *Kohanim, Levi'im, v'Yisraelim* listed explicitly. Again, *pshita* — obvious. And again, *Kohanim itztricha lei* — you need to tell me specifically about *Kohanim*.

### Why Spell Out

Why would I have thought to exempt *Kohanim*?

### Shatnez Concern

The verse juxtaposes the prohibition of *shatnez* — the mixing of wool and linen — with the obligation of *tzitzit*: *lo silbash shatnez, gedilim ta'aseh lach* — do not wear *shatnez*, you shall make fringes for yourself.

### Exempt from Shatnez

The inference: *man d'lo ishtari kilayim legabei l'visho hu d'michayav b'tzitzit* — someone who is never permitted to wear *shatnez* is the one who is obligated in *tzitzit*. The law of *tzitzit* is conceptually linked to and conditioned by one's relationship to the *shatnez* prohibition.

### Kohanim Shatnez

*V'hanei Kohanim ho'il v'ishtari kilayim legabeihu* — and since *Kohanim* are permitted *shatnez* in the form of their *bigdei kehuna*, specifically the *avnet* (belt), which is a mixture of wool and linen — one might argue that since they have a general dispensation regarding *shatnez*, they should be outside the category of persons obligated in *tzitzit*.

### Avodah Exemption

The *gemara* resolves this: *nehi d'ishtari b'idan avoda* — true, they are permitted *shatnez* during their *avodah*, in the specific garments of their priestly service — *belo idan avoda lo ishtari* — but outside of *avodah*, *Kohanim* are not exempt from the laws of *shatnez*. They remain fully subject to the *shatnez* prohibition in their ordinary clothing, and therefore remain in the category of persons obligated in *tzitzit*.

### Outside Avodah

The principle is again parallel to the *sukkah* case: exemption during *avodah* does not create a general exemption from the *mitzvah*.

### Tzitzit Connection

There is a deeper dimension to note here. *Tzitzit* themselves have an inherent connection to the question of *shatnez*: the *techeilet* string of *tzitzit* is wool, and if attached to a linen garment, it would otherwise constitute a *shatnez* violation. The Torah's juxtaposition permits this. Furthermore, the blue of *techeilet* is also a primary color of the *bigdei kehuna*. 

### Priestly Concept

This has led some to suggest that *tzitzit* function as a kind of *bigdei kehuna* for *Yisraelim* — a way of maintaining, in everyday dress and in the wider world, something of the consciousness of divine service that the *Kohen* embodies in the *Beit HaMikdash*. If so, there is a certain irony in the fact that *Kohanim* might have been thought exempt from *tzitzit* precisely because they already have that garment — but the *gemara* insists they are obligated nonetheless.

---

## Tefillin & Kohanim

### Tefillin Obligation

*Hakol chayavin b'tefillin* — everybody is obligated in *tefillin* — with *Kohanim, Levi'im, v'Yisraelim* listed. *Pshita*. *Kohanim itztricha lei*.

### Why Explicit

Why might *Kohanim* have been thought exempt?

### Shel Yad vs. Shel Rosh

The verse states: *u'kshartam l'os al yadecha v'hayu l'totafos bein einecha* — you shall bind them as a sign on your arm and they shall be as *totafot* between your eyes. The *gemara* derives from here: *hakol d'isa b'mitzvah d'yad isa b'mitzvah d'rosh* — whoever is in the category of *tefillin shel yad* is also in the category of *tefillin shel rosh*, the two being linked by the verse's formulation.

### Chatzitzah Issue

The problem with *Kohanim*: during *avodah*, a *kohen* cannot wear *tefillin shel yad* because it would constitute a *chatzitzah* — an interposition — between the *bigdei kehuna* and the flesh.

### Direct Contact

The verse *v'yilbash al besaro* — "he shall wear it upon his flesh" — requires the *bigdei kehuna* to be in direct contact with the skin: *shelo yehei davar chotzetz beino l'vein besaro*. The *tefillin shel yad* sits on the arm, which is also where the sleeve of the priestly garment sits — so wearing *tefillin shel yad* during *avodah* is forbidden.

### One Doesn't Prevent

Since *Kohanim* cannot wear *tefillin shel yad* during *avodah*, one might conclude they are also exempt from *tefillin shel rosh*, given the linkage between the two. The *gemara* says: *ka mashma lan d'lo me'akvi adadi* — one does not prevent the other. As the *Mishna* teaches: *tefillin shel yad einah m'akeves shel rosh v'shel rosh einah m'akeves shel yad* — if one has only one, one puts on only one. Each *tefillin* is an independent obligation.

### Hair Area

But a further difficulty presents itself: *tefillin shel rosh* must be placed on the head, and the *kohen* wears a *mitznefet* — a hat — which covers his head. Where can *tefillin shel rosh* be placed? The *gemara* quotes a *Tanna*: *sa'aro hayah nir'eh bein tzitz l'mitznefet* — even on the *Kohen Gadol*, there was visible hair between the *tzitz* (the golden forehead plate) and the *mitznefet*. The *mitznefet* sat on the crown, the *tzitz* sat on the forehead, and in the strip of hair between forehead and crown — precisely where *tefillin* are placed — there was exposed space: *v'sham maniach tefillin* — there one places the *tefillin*.

### Hair Space

This is consistent with what we know from archaeology. The *tefillin* found in the Bar Kochba caves, like those in the Dead Sea Scrolls collection, are extremely small — they require very little space. Even a narrow band of visible hair between the *tzitz* and the *mitznefet* would suffice.

### Mitznefes Chatzitzah

The question of whether the straps of the *tefillin shel rosh* must lie directly on the head — or whether they could pass over the *mitznefet* — relates to the general laws of *chatzitzah* by *tefillin* straps. The placement described by the *gemara* places the *tefillin* itself in the exposed hair area; exactly how the straps are arranged in relation to the *mitznefet* is a further question that requires more detailed examination.

---

## Shofar & Kohanim

### Shofar Obligation

*Hakol chayavin bitkias shofar* — everybody is obligated in the blowing of the *shofar* — with *Kohanim, Levi'im, v'Yisraelim* listed. *Pshita*. *Kohanim itztarich lei* — you still need to tell me about *Kohanim*.

### Why Explicit

What reason might there be to exempt *Kohanim*?

### Daily Blasts

A first suggestion: the verse calls *Rosh Hashanah* a *yom teruah* — a day of blast. The implication might be: *man d'leis lei bitkiah ela chad yoma chayav* — those for whom there is a special blast on only one day are the ones obligated. But *Kohanim*, who hear ritual blasts regularly throughout the year — *ho'il v'isnhu bitkiah kol sha'ata*, as the verse says *u'tkatem bachatzotzros al olosaychem*, you shall blow trumpets over your offerings — are accustomed to ritual blowing and might be thought to stand outside this category. The *gemara* rejects this reasoning immediately: *mi dami? hasam chatzotzros, hacha shofar* — there is no comparison. There it is *chatzotzrot* — trumpets; here it is *shofar*. These are entirely different instruments with different halachic statuses, and familiarity with one does not affect obligation regarding the other.

### Yovel Connection

A more serious line of reasoning: the *Mishna* teaches that *Yovel* — the Jubilee year — is equivalent to *Rosh Hashanah* in its blowing and its *brachot*: *malchuyot, zichronot, v'shofrot*. This equivalence suggests a deep connection between the obligation to hear *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah* and one's relationship to the *mitzvot* of *Yovel*. If so, one might reason: *d'isa b'mitzvot Yovel isa b'mitzvot Rosh Hashanah, d'leis b'mitzvot Yovel leis b'mitzvot Rosh Hashanah* — those who are subject to *Yovel* obligations are subject to *Rosh Hashanah* obligations; those who stand outside *Yovel* obligations stand outside *Rosh Hashanah* obligations as well.

### Yovel Equality

The connection between *Yovel* and *Rosh Hashanah* through *malchuyot, zichronot, v'shofrot* is striking. *Zichronot* and *shofrot* seem naturally relevant to *Yovel*'s proclamation of liberty and renewal — but *malchuyot* as well, since the Jubilee represents a kind of cosmic reset, a re-proclamation of divine sovereignty over the land and over human freedom.

### Relevance Principle

The principle is clear: if *Yovel* and *Rosh Hashanah* share the same *tekiot* and *brachot*, there must be a category of persons to whom both apply simultaneously — and they are the ones upon whom the *shofar* obligation is primarily imposed.

### Yovel Exclusions

Now: *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* are excluded from certain *Yovel* laws. *Kohanim Levi'im mocherim le-olam v'go'alim le-olam* — they can sell and redeem their fields at any time. *Go'alim le-olam*: normally, a seller of land may redeem it only after two years, with the redemption value calculated by the years remaining until *Yovel*. *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* may redeem immediately — you buy from a *levi* knowing he may take it back the next day. *Mocherim le-olam*: even a sale made during the Jubilee year itself — which for an ordinary Yisrael is automatically nullified — remains effective if made by a *Kohen* or *Levi*. Rashi explains this to mean that the *Kohen* or *Levi* validly receives the sale price even though the field may still revert; it is not that the sale is treated as if it never occurred.

### Partial Inclusion

Given these exclusions from *Yovel* land laws, one might conclude that *Kohanim* and *Levi'im* are sufficiently outside the *Yovel* system to be exempt from *Rosh Hashanah* *tekiot* as well. Hence the need to specify *Kohanim, Levi'im, v'Yisraelim*.

### Enough Inclusion

The *gemara* responds: *nehi d'leis lehu b'shmitat parka* — true, they may be excluded from some of the *Yovel* land laws — *b'shmitat kesafim u'b'shiluach avadim mi-is lehu* — but they remain subject to the release of debts and the freeing of slaves at *Yovel*, along with the other *Yovel* obligations. Since they are included in enough of the *Yovel* structure, they remain within the category of persons subject to *Rosh Hashanah* *tekiot* as well.

### Textual Problem

One difficulty remains with the *gemara*'s phrasing: it mentions *shmitat kesafim* — the release of debts — in the context of *Yovel*. But the release of debts is a law of *Shemitah*, the seventh year, not of *Yovel*, the fiftieth year. According to all other sources, *Yovel* does not trigger debt release. *Tosafot* addresses this difficulty, and it raises genuine questions about whether our text accurately reflects what *Yovel* entails, or whether there are alternative interpretations of the phrase. We will continue the survey of *hakol* tomorrow.

---

---

# Arakhin 4

## Kohanim in Megillah

### Hakol Overview

The fourth *daf* of *Arakhin* continues the *gemara*'s extended treatment of the word *hakol* — "everyone" — and its companion phrase *kohanim levi'im v'yisrael*. Before returning to the primary themes of the *mishnah*, the *gemara* surveys a series of parallel *mishnayot* and *beraitot* that employ the same formulation, examining in each case why it was necessary to specify that *kohanim*, *levi'im*, and *yisraelim* are all included.

### Megillah Reading

Beginning two dots from the top of the *daf*, the *gemara* cites: *hakol chayavin bemikra megilla* — everyone is obligated in the reading of the *megilla* — *kohanim levi'im v'yisraelim*. The *gemara* immediately objects: *peshita* — is this not obvious? It answers: *lo, tzricha levatel avodatam* — no, it is necessary to teach that even the *kohanim* would interrupt their *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash* in order to hear the *megilla* reading. This is consistent with the ruling of *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: *kohanim b'avodatam v'levi'im b'duchanam v'yisrael b'ma'amadam* — even if the *kohanim* are in the midst of the Temple service, the *levi'im* are on their *duchan* singing, and the *yisrael* representatives are present at their *ma'amad* (the rotation of Israelites who attended the communal *korbanot* on behalf of the people) — nevertheless, *mevatlin avodatan u'va'in lishmoa mikra megilla*: they stop the *avoda* and come to hear the *megilla*.

### Pirsumei Nisa

This is a striking formulation, particularly given that *Rav Yehuda* spoke at a time when the *Beit HaMikdash* no longer stood, making the description entirely theoretical. Why paint so graphic a picture? Two considerations suggest themselves. First, to underscore the centrality of *pirsumei nisa* — publicizing the miracle — which is especially characteristic of *megilla* and *Chanukah*, as reflected in the *beracha* of *she'asa nissim l'avoteinu*. Unlike *Chanukah*, which is observed privately at night in one's home, *mikra megilla* is a markedly public *mitzvah*, performed in community and, in the primary sense recognized by the *gemara* and *mishnah*, during the day. The point, then, may be to emphasize that because *pirsumei nisa* demands collective public participation, everything else — even the *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash* — must yield.

A second consideration is historical framing. The miracle of the *megilla* occurred precisely during the period when the Second *Beit HaMikdash* was being rebuilt. One might thus have been tempted to frame the *nisa* of *megilla* specifically within the context of the Temple's restoration — reasoning that the Temple service, which the miracle enabled, should not be displaced by its commemoration. The *gemara* counters this framing dramatically: the very *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash* stands down for *mikra megilla*. Of course, the *nisa* of the *megilla* transcends any narrow connection to the Temple — it was a moment when the Jewish people as a whole, not merely their religion, faced annihilation — and therefore its commemoration cannot be circumscribed by Temple imagery alone.

### Zimun Obligation

The *gemara* then turns to: *hakol chayavin b'zimmun* — everyone is obligated in *zimmun* — *kohanim levi'im v'yisraelim*. Again the *gemara* asks *peshita*, and again it answers: *lo, tzricha* — the novel case is where *kohanim* are eating *kodashim*, their portions of the sacrifices. Let us first consider the case of three *kohanim* eating *korbanot* together — with bread, as required for *zimmun* — before introducing the question of combining with *yisraelim*.

### Kohanim Eating

One might have thought that *kohanim* eating *korbanot* would not make a *zimmun*. The *gemara* states: *salka da'atakh amina* — I might have thought — *akhlu otam asher kuppar bahem amar Rachmana*: the Torah teaches that when the *kohanim* eat the sacrificial portions, this achieves atonement for the *bnei yisrael* who brought the offerings. From this one might reason that the *kohanim*'s eating is not primarily a personal act of physical sustenance — it is, as it were, a ritual act, a consumption analogous to the altar's consumption, a representation of divine or sacrificial acceptance. If so, perhaps it is not appropriate to frame their eating in the terms that ground *birkat hamazon* — gratitude for one's own physical nourishment. Perhaps the *kohanim* eating *korbanot* should not even make a *beracha* at all.

To this the *gemara* responds: *v'achalta v'savata amar Rachmana* — the Torah says "you shall eat and be satisfied," and this applies equally here. Even if the conceptual framing of the *kohanim*'s eating is that of a ritual act — the altar consuming, atonement being achieved — the physical reality is that they are nourishing themselves, filling their bellies, deriving genuine benefit. That reality obligates them in *birkat hamazon*.

This raises a genuine question: is the *gemara*'s conclusion reframing how we understand the act of the *kohanim*'s eating — telling us to think of it also as personal sustenance, a form of payment or gift for their service — or is it leaving the ritual framing intact while saying that the derived benefit itself, independent of how we frame the act, creates the obligation? Either way, the point is established: the *kohanim* must recite *birkat hamazon*. And there is a profound dimension to this ruling, as one participant noted: it keeps the *kohanim* anchored in their humanity, preventing them — and the people — from regarding them as purely divine representatives who transcend ordinary human gratitude.

A textual note is worth flagging: the *gemara* speaks of *zimmun* rather than *birkat hamazon* as such, and the *psukim* it invokes seem more naturally to address the personal *beracha* than the communal *zimmun*. *Rabbeinu Gershom*'s text actually reads *beracha* where our text has *zimmun*, suggesting a variant tradition. In any event, the *gemara* transitions immediately to *zimmun* as a *tziruf* — a grouping — in the next clause.

There is also a practical question lurking here: *birkat hamazon* requires bread, and the primary sacrificial portions are meat. The answer may be that the eating of *menachot* — flour offerings that are among the *kohanim*'s portions — is included, though the *gemara* does not spell this out explicitly.

### Tziruf Principle

The *gemara* then addresses: *hakol mitztarfin lezimmun* — everyone can combine for *zimmun* — *kohanim levi'im v'yisraelim*. Again, *peshita*. The novel case: *lo tzricha dekachli kohanim teruma*, where the *kohanim* are eating *teruma* or *kodashim* — food a *zar* cannot eat — while the *yisrael* is eating ordinary *chullin*. One might have thought they cannot form a *zimmun* group, since *salka da'atakh amina*: if the *zar* wanted to share the *kohen*'s food, *lo matzi achil* — he cannot eat it. Perhaps they cannot be considered a joint eating. The *gemara* responds: although the *zar* cannot eat with the *kohen*, the *kohen* can eat with the *zar* — there is theoretical mutuality in one direction, and that suffices to create the *tziruf*.

This ruling has immediate practical implications. *Tosafot* raises the case of *milchigs* and *fleishigs*: if one person is eating dairy and another meat, they can still form a *zimmun*, since the dairy eater could wash out his mouth and in principle eat with the meat eater (though some hold the *zimun* leader should be the dairy eater, who is the one with theoretical ability to join). More complex is the case of hard cheese, where one follows the custom of waiting six hours — or someone with halakhic dietary restrictions versus merely physical intolerances such as lactose intolerance or gluten sensitivity. The general principle emerging from our *gemara* is: as long as at least one person can in theory eat with the others, *tziruf* is possible. But where no one can halakhically eat with anyone else, *zimmun* cannot be made. Whether purely physiological barriers — health conditions rather than halakhic prohibitions — have the same effect is a matter discussed in later *halacha*, but it is a serious possibility that they would equally preclude *tziruf*.

---

## Machatzit Hashekel

### Return to Mishnah

With these parallel cases completed, the *gemara* at last returns to our *mishnah*: *hakol maarichin* — everyone can make an *erech* vow — *kohen levi v'yisrael*. The structure has been almost chiastic: beginning with *hakol* in the *mishnah*, traversing all the parallel *hakol* formulations, and now returning to the *mishnah* itself. Why did the *mishnah* need to specify *kohen levi v'yisrael* in the context of *erchin*? *Peshita* — obviously anyone can be *maariach*! *Amar Rava lo nitzrecha ela l'Ben Buchri* — Rava says it is needed only to address the position of *Ben Buchri*.

### Ben Buchri Opinion

The *mishnah* in *Shekalim* (and elsewhere in *shas*) records: *amar Rabbi Yehuda he'id Ben Buchri b'Yavne she-kol Kohen she-shokel eino chotei* — Ben Buchri testified at Yavneh that any *kohen* who contributes the half-*shekel* has not sinned. The implication is that *kohanim* are not obligated to give; if they choose to contribute, they may do so without transgression, but it is optional. This testimony was given at Yavneh, the center of rabbinic reconstruction after the destruction of the Temple, where scholars gathered to record traditions of *Torah she-be'al peh*.

### Yochanan ben Zakkai

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai responds sharply: *lo chen* — that is not the *halacha*. Rather: *kol Kohen she-eino shokel chotei* — any *kohen* who does *not* contribute is sinning. It is not merely permitted; it is required. Why do *kohanim* think otherwise? *She-ha-Kohanim dorshim mikra zeh l'atzman* — they interpret a verse in their own self-interest: *v'chol minchat Kohen kalil tihyeh lo te'achel* — every flour-offering of a *kohen* must be entirely burned and may not be eaten. From this they reason as follows: the obligation of the half-*shekel* is to become a partner in the communal sacrifices. Among those communal sacrifices are the *omer*, the *shtei ha-lechem* of *Shavuot*, and the *lechem ha-panim* — all *menachot* that are eaten. If *kohanim* were to contribute the half-*shekel* and become part-owners of these communal *menachot*, their *minchat kohen* ownership would require those *menachot* to be burned entirely rather than eaten. And so, they say, *shelanu hem* — they would become ours — and such consecrated items could no longer be eaten. Out of concern for the integrity of the communal *korbanot*, they refrain from contributing.

This is a familiar human dynamic. As Rav Soloveitchik reportedly counseled: a rabbi must be the first to donate at an appeal and must always be present for *minyan* — because it is precisely the communal servant who is most tempted to reason that his service exempts him from communal obligation. The *kohanim* doring *mikra zeh l'atzman* is a paradigmatic example of self-interested exegesis that nonetheless has a surface plausibility.

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai dismisses this reasoning: *minchat kohen* applies only when a *kohen* is the complete owner, not when his ownership is a fractional share in a collective. And beyond that technicality lies a more fundamental principle.

### Tzibbur Concept

*Halacha* generally does not recognize a corporate entity in the modern legal sense — it knows partnerships, not corporations. Yet in a handful of contexts, it does operate with the concept of an abstract communal entity. One is *yorshim* who inherit an estate collectively. The other is the *tzibbur*: even if millions of individuals each contribute a half-*shekel*, the communal sacrifices are not owned by millions of fractional partners. They are owned by the *tzibbur* as a single abstract corporate entity. Therefore, even if *kohanim* contribute, their contribution dissolves into this corporate ownership — it does not create a personal partial ownership in the *kohen* that would redefine the *minchat kohen* status of the communal *menachot*. The *korban* belongs to the *tzibbur*, not to any individual, including *kohanim*.

### Excluding Kohanim

This brings us back to the question of *erchin*. *Salka da'atakh amina*: since the verse states *vechol erkecha yiheyeh beshekel hakodesh* — every valuation shall be in the *shekel* of the sanctuary — one might link *erchin* to *machatzit hashekel*. If *kol de'isa bishkalim isa be'erchin* — whoever is in the category of *shkalim* is in the category of *erchin* — and since *kohanim* (according to *Ben Buchri*) are not in the category of *shkalim*, one might conclude they are likewise excluded from *erchin*. Therefore the *mishnah* teaches: *kamashma lan* — even so, *kohanim* who undertake an *erech* vow are obligated to pay.

### Abaye Response

*Amar lei Abaye*: that verse — *vechol erkecha yiheyeh beshekel hakodesh* — is not intended to link *erchin* to *machatzit hashekel* at all. It comes for an entirely different *drasha*: *lechol erchin she'atah maariach lo yifchasu misela d'oraysa* — for all *erchin* valuations, the minimum unit of payment shall be one *sela* (shekel). Why is this needed? The Torah's smallest fixed *erech* is three *shekels* (for a female infant). So what does a minimum of one *shekel* contribute? The answer lies in *hasagat yad* — the sliding scale. The Torah provides that if the one who vowed cannot afford the assessed amount, the *kohen* shall reassess according to the vower's means. But this sliding scale has a floor: even in the most reduced circumstances, the minimum obligation is one *shekel*. That is what the verse teaches. It has no implications for who is or is not included in the *erchin* system.

*Abaye* then offers his own *hava amina*: the verse *upduyav miben chodesh tifdeh beerchecha* — you shall redeem them from one month onward according to your *erech* — uses the word *erech* in the context of *pidyon haben*. Since a male infant's *erech* (five *shekels*) matches the five-*shekel* cost of *pidyon haben*, there is a conceptual link. One might say: *kol de'ita bepidyon haben ita be'erchin* — whoever is in the *pidyon haben* category is in the *erchin* category. Since *kohanim* and *levi'im* do not redeem their own children (*pidyon haben* does not apply to them), they might also be excluded from *erchin*. Hence the *mishnah*'s ruling is necessary.

### Rava's Logic

*Amar lei Rava*: one cannot draw such far-reaching conclusions from the shared word *erech*, because this would lead to absurd results. The verse concerning the *ayil asham* — the guilt-offering ram — also uses the phrase *beerchecha*: *ve'et ashamo yavi l'Hashem ayil tamim min hatzon beerchecha*. If the shared word *erech* creates categorical linkage, one might say *kol de'ita be'erchin ita be'ayil asham* — whoever is in the category of *erchin* is required to bring the ram — and therefore *tumtum* and *androgynos*, who are excluded from *erchin* valuations, would also be exempt from bringing a guilt offering. That is clearly impossible: liability for sin cannot depend on indeterminate gender. Therefore the word *beerchecha* cannot bear so much categorical weight, and *Abaye*'s *hava amina* proves too much.

*Rava* (some say *Rav Ashi*) offers the correct *hava amina*: the verse states *vehe'emido lifnei hakohen* — you shall stand him before the *kohen* — referring to the person whose means are assessed for the sliding scale. The *kohen* plays the role of assessor and collector; the rest of *bnei yisrael* are those who make the vows. One might have thought these are categorically distinct roles — *velo kohen lifnei kohen*, a *kohen* does not stand before a *kohen* — and that a *kohen* therefore cannot occupy the role of vow-maker. This parallels *Ben Buchri*'s reasoning about *machatzit hashekel*: those who administer the Temple and those who fund it are different classes. *Kamashma lan*: the *mishnah* teaches that although the *kohen* plays the assessor's role, he can equally stand in the role of the vow-maker.

---

## Scope of Arak'in

### Braita Intro

Having resolved why the *mishnah* specifies *kohen levi v'yisrael*, the *gemara* turns to the next component of the *mishnah*: *hakol ne'erachim* — everyone can be the *object* of an *erech* valuation. What does this come to include? *Ne'erachim le'atuyei menuval u'mukat shechin* — it includes even a repulsive person covered with blemishes who would have no market value. This leads the *gemara* to a major *braita* that it quotes in full before analyzing clause by clause. *Detanu rabanan* — the sages taught in a *braita* — and the *braita* opens: *be'erkecha* — "according to the value" — *lehavi erech satum*, to include an unexplicated valuation.

### Erech Stum

The word *be'erkecha* teaches that even if a person said *erech* without specifying whose *erech* — simply "I will pay an *erech*" — the obligation is valid and binding. The vower has not rendered the pledge meaningless by failing to name the subject; we will see shortly what amount is owed.

### Complete Person

A second teaching from *be'erkecha*: *erech kulo hu notein velo erech evarim* — one pays the full *erech* of a person, not the *erech* of a limb. If someone says "I will pay the *erech* of that person's arm," he pays nothing. The word *erech* applies to a whole person and the Torah's fixed values correspond to whole persons. An *erech* of a limb has no legal force.

### Nefashot

From here the *braita* proceeds to a qualification. *Yachol she'ani motzi af davar she'haneshama tluyah bo* — one might think that even the *erech* of a vital organ, something life depends upon, is excluded. *Talmud lomar nefashot* — the Torah says "souls," indicating that anything upon which the soul depends counts. Therefore, if someone says "I will pay the *erech* of that person's heart," that is treated as if he pledged the entire *erech*, since the heart is a vital organ. The principle is asymmetric: ordinary limbs produce no obligation; vital organs produce the full obligation.

### Living Only

The *braita* continues: *nefashot velo hamet* — "souls," not a corpse. The *erech* of a dead person cannot be pledged — the obligation requires a living subject. *Hotzi hamet velo hotzi et hagoses* — perhaps one has excluded only a corpse but not a *goses* (a person in the final throes of death)? *Talmud lomar vehe'emid vehe'erich* — the *kohen* shall stand and evaluate. *Kol she'yeshno be'ha'amada yeshno be'ha'aracha* — whoever can be stood up is subject to valuation; *ve'chol she'eino be'ha'amada eino be'ha'aracha* — whoever cannot be stood up is not. A *goses*, halakhically, is not considered in the category of one who can be stood up, and is therefore excluded.

The *gemara* notes a slight redundancy: if we can already exclude a corpse from the principle that it cannot be stood up, why do we need *nefashot velo hamet* as a separate source? The *gemara* answers: we did not really need the verse to exclude the corpse — *kiri bei nefesh nefashot*, the plural form teaches other things, as the *gemara* proceeds to enumerate.

### Multiple Persons

*Davar acher nefashot*: *ein li ela echad she'he'erich echad* — I know only that if one person valued one other person, each individual pledge is binding. But what if someone said "I will pay the *erech* of *Reuven Shimon Levi Yehuda*," naming many people in a single utterance while using the word *erech* only once? One might think only a single *erech* payment is owed. *Talmud lomar nefashot* — the plural teaches that each named person creates a separate obligation, and all must be paid.

### Women Obligors

*Davar acher nefashot*: the Torah's formulation opens with *ish ki yafli be'erkecha* — "a man who articulates your *erech*" — establishing the paradigm of a man undertaking the vow. *Ein li ela ish she'he'erich bein ish bein isha* — I know only that a man can make an *erech* vow for a man or for a woman. But what of a woman who vows to pay the *erech* of a man, or of a woman? *Talmud lomar nefashot*: the word *nefashot* is read here as the subject — those who undertake the vow — as well as the object. Whether the vow-maker is male or female, the obligation is valid.

### Menuval Case

*Davar acher nefashot*, a third application: *lerabot menuval u'mukat shechin* — to include even the repulsive person and the one afflicted with boils who would fetch no price on the slave market and therefore would have no *damim* (market value). One might have thought: since the Torah links *neder* and *erech* — vowing and valuation — *kol she'yeshno be'erchin yeshno bedamim, ve'chol she'eino be'erchin eino bedamim* — only someone on the *erech* chart would have an actionable market-valuation pledge, and since a person without market value seems outside the system, perhaps there is no *erech* obligation either. *Talmud lomar nefashot*: souls — the fixed *erech* values apply to all living persons regardless of market worth.

The *gemara* explains the economy of these multiple *drashot* from a single word. Each of the earlier derivations — multiple persons, female vow-makers — could arguably have been deduced without a verse. *Shakul hu v'yavo'u kulam*: when there is no compelling reason to prefer one application of a verse over another, we say the verse encompasses all equally plausible teachings. The one application that genuinely required the verse is the *menuval u'mukat shechin* case, because there one might truly have reasoned that a person without market value falls outside the *erchin* system entirely. That is the distinctive *chiddush* the word *nefashot* comes to teach.

---

## Minimum Value

### Erech Satum

The *gemara* now analyzes the *braita*'s first clause: *be'erkecha lehavi erech satum* — the word *be'erkecha* includes an unexplicated valuation. *Mai erech satum*? What does an unexplicated *erech* obligate? *Detanya ha'omer erech satum alai* — if someone says "an unspecified *erech* is upon me" — *noten kepachot shebe'arachin*: he pays the minimum of all the *erchin* values.

### Three Shekels Min

*Ve'kamma pachot shebe'arachin*? What is that minimum? *Sheloshah shkalim* — three *shekels*. The Torah's fixed schedule yields a minimum of three *shekels* for a female infant between one month and five years. That is the floor. Why not simply pay the maximum of fifty *shekels*?

### Grab Principle

*Ve'eima chamishim*? The *gemara* invokes the principle: *tafasta merubbah lo tafasta, tafasta mu'at tafasta* — if you grab too much you do not have it, if you grab a little you keep it. When the amount of an obligation is uncertain, we assume the minimum. Any amount higher than three *shekels* would require explicit justification; the bare minimum is what the unspecified pledge obligates.

But perhaps the minimum should be one *shekel*, since the verse *vechol erkecha yiheyeh beshekel hakodesh* establishes that the sliding scale descends no lower than one *shekel*? The *gemara* responds: *hahu behasagat yad hu dechtiv* — that verse addresses *hasagat yad*, the reduced payment for one who cannot afford the standard amount. The normal minimum — for one who can pay — is three *shekels*. The one-*shekel* floor is a lower boundary for impoverished vow-makers only.

### Hasagat Yad

This raises a further question: if the verse establishing the one-*shekel* minimum is already derivable from first principles (since we would conclude the minimum is three *shekels* regardless), what new information does the verse convey? *Amar Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha*: the verse teaches that when someone makes an unexplicated *erech* pledge — *erech satum* — the obligation is *not* subject to the *hasagat yad* sliding scale. Why? *Kemeforash dami* — it is as though he stated the amount explicitly. The sliding scale operates because when a person names a specific subject — "the *erech* of *Reuven*" — there is someone to assess: if he cannot pay the full amount, the *kohen* can evaluate him according to his means, choosing among different "books of valuation," so to speak. But when no specific person is named, there is nothing to assess. The pledge translates directly to the fixed sum of three *shekels*. Saying "an *erech*" without a subject is tantamount to saying "three *shekels*" explicitly — and explicit pledges cannot be reduced by *hasagat yad*.

The practical consequence is significant: if such a person genuinely cannot afford three *shekels*, the debt to the Temple remains outstanding. There is no mechanism to reduce it below three.

The *gemara* then records an *ika d'amri* — an alternative version of *Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha*'s ruling — to the opposite effect: the *erech satum* is subject to *hasagat yad*. The *chiddush* here is precisely the reverse: one might have thought that because the unexplicated pledge is *kemeforash dami* — like an explicit amount — it is fixed and not reducible. The *kamashma lan* is that since the person did not in fact say three *shekels* explicitly but only said "*erech*," the *kohen* retains the latitude to assess the obligation downward according to the vower's means.

---

## Tumtum/Androgynos

### Gender Requirement

The *braita* also teaches that the verse *vehaya erkecha hazachar* — "and your valuation shall be for the male" — establishes that the *erech* system applies only to *zachar vadai* and *nekeva vadai*: definitively male and definitively female individuals. *Velo tumtum ve'androgynos* — a *tumtum* (one whose gender is indeterminate due to anatomical ambiguity) and an *androgynos* (one with characteristics of both sexes) cannot be the objects of a fixed *erech* valuation. One might further wonder: since the verse says *hazachar*, perhaps a *tumtum* who is not definitively male could nonetheless pay the female *erech* value — treating "not male" as equivalent to "female"? The verse answers this as well: *vehaya erkecha hazachar ve'im nekeva hi* — the Torah specifies both male and female explicitly, meaning *zachar vadai nekeva vadai*, definitively one or the other. There is no middle category in the *erchin* chart.

### Market Value OK

Nevertheless, *tumtum* and *androgynos* are not without halakhic valuation altogether. The *braita* teaches: *vehaya erkecha lerabot tumtum ve'androgynos ledamim* — the word *vehaya erkecha* comes to include *tumtum* and *androgynos* for purposes of *damim*, market valuation. Even though they cannot be the subject of a fixed *erech*, if someone says *damav alai* — I will pay this person's market value — the pledge is binding.

The *gemara* asks: why do we need a verse for this? Even a palm tree can be consecrated by declaring its value — *lo yehei ela d'mei dikla* — one can dedicate the value of any object to *hekdesh*. Why would we think that gender ambiguity could prevent a market valuation from taking effect?

### Nidon Bichvodo

*Amar Rava*: the verse comes to teach that *nidon bichvodo* — they are judged according to their honor. What does this mean? *Rashi* explains it as follows: within the law of *erchin*, we learned from the word *nefashot* that a vital organ represents the whole person — if one says "the *erech* of this person's heart," one pays the full *erech*, not a fractional amount. The question is whether this principle — that a vital organ stands in for the whole — extends also to market valuations. If someone says "I will pay the market value (*damim*) of this person's heart to *hekdesh*," do we assess the entire market value of the person, treating the heart as representing the whole? This is what *nidon bichvodo* means: the vital organ is assessed at the honor of the whole person's value.

The *hava amina* was: since we derive this principle from the laws of *erchin* — specifically from *nefashot* in that context — perhaps it applies only to persons who are in the *erchin* category. A *tumtum* or *androgynos*, excluded from fixed *erech* valuations, might not benefit from this principle, and if one said "the market value of this *tumtum*'s heart," one might have to assess only the heart in isolation rather than the whole person. The verse therefore teaches that *tumtum* and *androgynos* are *nidon bichvodo* for market valuations as well.

### Abaye Challenge

*Amar lei Abaye*: is it truly the case that anyone outside the *erchin* category is not *nidon bichvodo*? This seems demonstrably false. A *braita* teaches: *rosh eved zeh hekdesh* — if one says "the head of this slave is *hekdesh*" — *hu ve'hekdesh shutafin bo*: the person and *hekdesh* become joint owners of the slave. Similarly, *rosh eved machur lach* — "the head of this slave is sold to you" — creates a partnership.

### Body Part Values

The same principle applies to animals: *rosh chamor zeh hekdesh* — "the head of this donkey is *hekdesh*" — creates a partnership between the owner and *hekdesh*. The same for *rosh chamor machur lach*. However, *rosh parah machur lach* — "the head of this cow is sold to you" — means only the head itself: *lo machar ela roshah*. Why the difference? *Amar Rav Papa*: because in the butcher shops, a cow's head is sold separately — *de-hamizdavin reisha de-tora be-veit tavcha* — and therefore "head of a cow" denotes the literal head, not a representative share of the whole animal.

What emerges from these cases is that saying a body part does not in general cause the whole to be treated as represented — rather, it typically creates co-ownership. The vital-organ principle of *nidon bichvodo* thus stands in need of further analysis: does saying a vital organ truly assign the full value to one party, or does it create some form of shared ownership? And does this principle apply even outside the formal *erchin* context? These questions remain open as the *daf* concludes, and the *gemara* will continue the discussion on the following day.

---

---

# Arakhin 5

## Vital Organ Representati…

### Kevodo Chiddush

We pick up near the bottom of 4b, in the middle of the *drasha* concerning *tumtum* and *androgynous* — those of indeterminate gender — and their status in *arachin*. The *gemara* had established that they can be *maarich* (the subject who vows a valuation) but not *ne'erach* (the object of such a valuation). The question arose: why would one have thought to exclude them even from a simple *neder* (vow of market value)? After all, a person can vow the market value of a tree, and the tree's gender is plainly irrelevant.

The *gemara*'s answer is that the *chiddush* here is something more subtle. From the *parsha* of *arachin* we learn that even if you do not explicitly mention the whole person — even if you say only their heart, their lungs, or some other vital organ, referred to as *kevodo* — that designation is understood to represent the entire person. This principle is derived from *arachin* and extended to apply in cases of *neder* as well: if you vow to pay the value of someone's heart, you owe the full value of that person. One might have thought that the concept of *kevodo* — a vital organ representing the whole — is limited to those who fall within the formal category of *arachin*, thereby excluding a *tumtum* and *androgynous*. This *drasha* teaches otherwise: the principle that a vital organ represents the entirety applies to everyone when reckoning market value, not only to those formally within the *arachin* framework.

### Braita Contradiction

With that established, the *gemara* turns directly to challenge the principle itself. The preceding *amud* quoted an extensive *braita* stating that if someone says "the head of this slave" or "the head of this donkey I am donating to the *Beit HaMikdash*," it does not represent the whole — rather, it is as though the *Beit HaMikdash* and the donor are partners in the animal, each owning half. So which is it? Does a vital organ, when donated, represent the entirety or only a partial share?

The *gemara* sharpens the contradiction. One might think the distinction turns on whether the subject is formally within *arachin* — animals are not, humans are. But the *gemara* rejects this framing immediately: even by a slave, who *is* within the category of *arachin* (and for whom, therefore, the principle of *kevodo* should clearly apply), this same *braita* says that "the head of this slave" creates only a partnership, not full ownership by the *Beit HaMikdash*. The problem therefore is not about who falls within *arachin*; it is a direct contradiction between the principle of *kevodo* and the *braita*'s rule of partial ownership.

### Direct Cases Resolved

The *gemara* offers its first resolution: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. The distinction is between *kodshei mizbe'ach* (sanctity for the altar) and *kodshei bedek ha-bayit* (sanctity for the Temple treasury). Intuitively, one might have expected the reverse resolution: a *korban* is defined entirely by its identity as an offering, so it is either everything or nothing, and therefore a vital organ sanctified for a *korban* should represent the whole. Property and ownership, by contrast, can be divided, so one might have expected that designating a vital organ for the *Beit HaMikdash* treasury creates only partial ownership. The *gemara*, however, says the opposite. When designated as a *korban* for the altar, the vital organ represents only a part, yielding a partnership. When donated directly to the Temple treasury, the vital organ represents the whole.

The *gemara* does not leave the altar-side of this resolution unchallenged. It focuses on the *braita*'s case of a cow: if you say "the head of this cow is *hekdesh*," it literally means the head — because people actually sell the head of a cow separately in the market, so the word "head" here is meant literally, not as a representative designation for the whole animal. The *gemara* asks: but if we are saying that by a *korban* the head yields only a partnership, why is the effect limited to literally just the head? If the logic of *korban* sanctity is that it is all-or-nothing in nature, then designating a vital organ for a *korban* should cause the sanctity to spread throughout the entire animal — *tifshot kedusha bekulah*.

To demonstrate this, the *gemara* cites a *braita* (found on 89a): if someone says "the leg of this animal is an *olah*," one might think this makes the entire animal an *olah*. The verse teaches otherwise: *kol asher yiten mimenu la-Hashem yiheyeh kodesh* — only that which you give from it is holy, not the entirety. So a non-vital organ does not extend its sanctity to the whole. But what is done with an animal that now has one leg consecrated as an *olah*? The animal cannot simply be freed to non-sacred use, since the verse says *yiheyeh* — it retains its status. The resolution offered: sell the animal to someone who needs to bring an *olah* — say, a fellow who already has an *olah* obligation. He acquires the animal, sanctifies it in its entirety as an *olah*, and brings it. He pays the seller for everything except the leg, since the leg was not the seller's to sell; the money received for the rest is non-sacred. This is the position of Rabbi Meir.

Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon read the verse differently: *kol asher yiten mimenu la-Hashem yiheyeh kodesh* means that even a partial designation causes the whole to be sanctified. An *olah* is definitional — like a state that either fully obtains or does not. You cannot be partially an *olah*, just as one cannot be partially in a certain condition. Either the animal is a *korban* or it is not.

The *gemara* then synthesizes: even according to the view that partial designation does not spread to the whole, that is only when the designated limb is a non-vital organ — the leg. But if it is a vital organ, *davar she-neshamah teluyah bo*, all agree that the sanctity spreads to the entire animal. So we are back to the same difficulty: by a direct *korban*, a vital organ sanctifies the whole; by a direct donation to the *Beit HaMikdash*, a vital organ represents the whole. Where, then, does the *braita* fit — the one that says designating a vital organ yields only a partnership?

### Hybrid Category

The *gemara* provides the resolution: *lo kashya* — the distinction is not between *mizbe'ach* and *bedek ha-bayit*, but between *kedushat ha-guf* (intrinsic sanctity, where the thing itself is used) and *kedushat damim* (value sanctity, where the thing is sold and the proceeds are used). These pairs are often assumed to be synonymous — *kedushat mizbe'ach* with *kedushat ha-guf*, and *kedushat bedek ha-bayit* with *kedushat damim* — but they do not in fact coincide perfectly.

*Kedushat ha-guf* means the thing itself is being used, whether as a *korban* or as some direct donation like wood for the altar or a vessel for Temple service. *Kedushat damim* means the thing is sold and the money is used — whether donated to the Temple treasury or designated toward purchasing a *korban*. A third category emerges: *kedushat damim le-mizbe'ach* — I sanctify this animal (or this car, or this slave) such that the proceeds of its sale will go to fund a *korban*. This is neither pure *kedushat ha-guf* (the thing itself becomes a *korban*) nor pure *kedushat bedek ha-bayit* (a straight donation to the treasury). It is a hybrid.

The *gemara*'s answer: when the donation is direct to the Temple treasury, a vital organ represents the whole. When it is a direct *korban*, a vital organ represents the whole. But when it is this hybrid middle category — the value of the vital organ designated toward a *korban* — that is the one case in which the *braita* applies: you and the *Beit HaMikdash* are partners, and the vital organ does not represent the entirety. The logic of this middle category is admittedly difficult to articulate clearly. The *gemara* itself does not offer a conceptual explanation for why this intermediate position behaves differently from each of its two pure analogues.

### Blemished Animal Test

Abaye challenges Rava, who had articulated the above position. Rava himself had elsewhere ruled that if someone tries to sanctify a male, unblemished animal for its *damim* — meaning the proceeds should go toward an *olah* — the animal automatically receives an upgrade: it is treated as sanctified directly as a *korban* with *kedushat ha-guf*, since that is where it is headed anyway. If so, there is no middle category to speak of: whenever you try to sanctify a fit animal for the proceeds to go toward a *korban*, it immediately becomes an outright *korban*. You cannot inhabit the hybrid space at all.

The *gemara* offers a preliminary answer: the distinction is between sanctifying the whole animal and sanctifying only a single organ. If you designate only a vital organ toward a *korban*, we will not perform the double translation — first treating the organ as representing the whole, and then upgrading the whole from *kedushat damim* to *kedushat ha-guf*. We perform only one translation at a time. But Abaye pushes back: Rava himself asked in *Temurah* whether sanctifying a vital organ for its *damim* toward a *korban* undergoes the automatic upgrade. He raised it as an open question, not as a settled ruling.

The *gemara* then supplies the decisive answer: the automatic upgrade applies only to an unblemished animal, *betam*, one that is itself fit to become a *korban*. Here, in the cases we are discussing — a donkey, a slave, or a blemished animal — there can be no upgrade, since the thing cannot itself become a *korban*. The *braita* that established the partnership rule was precisely using such examples: the case of the donkey, the cow, the slave. In those cases, where the animal or person cannot be directly sanctified as a *korban*, and where you are therefore necessarily in the hybrid space of *kedushat damim le-mizbe'ach*, the vital organ does not represent the whole, and the result is a partnership.

This also clarifies the geometry somewhat: a direct donation to the *Beit HaMikdash* — even if it is just a check — gives the full value of the vital organ as the whole person's value. A direct *korban* sanctification, where the vital organ triggers *kedushat ha-guf*, gives the whole animal. But when neither upgrade is possible — you have something that cannot be a *korban* itself, and you want the *damim* to go toward a *korban* — you are in this middle space where only a partnership results.

### Unresolved Hybrid Cases

Before concluding, the *gemara* raises Rava's question (from *Temurah*) in its original form: *meirosh li le-gabei mizbe'ach mahu* — if I say "the value of my head toward the altar," do we reckon the full value of the person (*niddon bi-khvodo*) or only a partial value? Rava had noted the tension: in cases of pure monetary valuation (*damim*), we find that *kevodo* always applies, the organ representing the whole. But in cases directly for the *mizbe'ach*, we have never found *kevodo* applying in the hybrid sense. The question was left as *teiku* — unresolved. The *gemara* now clarifies: that question was asked before this *braita* was brought to bear. Now that the *braita* has been cited, we know the answer: this is precisely the hybrid case, and the result is a partnership, not full valuation.

The *gemara* then presents two further unresolved hybrid cases. Rava (or Rabbah — there is a textual question about the name) asks: *erchi alai le-gabei mizbe'ach mahu* — if someone says "my *erech* upon me toward the altar," what is the law? The word *erech* invokes the Torah's fixed valuation system, which was instituted for donations to the Temple treasury. What happens when someone tries to use that system but directs it toward a *korban*? Rava frames the specific question in terms of *haseig yad* — the Torah's sliding scale provision for *arachin*, allowing someone who cannot afford the fixed value to pay a reduced amount. Does this hybrid — *erech* directed toward the *mizbe'ach* — carry the sliding scale rules of *arachin*? Or, since contributions to the *mizbe'ach* are never on a sliding scale, do we apply the rule of a *korban* and require the exact fixed amount? *Teiku* — no answer.

Finally, Rav Ashi asks: *hikdish sdei achuza le-gabei mizbe'ach* — if someone sanctifies his *sdei achuza* (inherited ancestral field, whose redemption is governed by the Torah's fixed rules in the *parsha*) not for the Temple treasury but with the proceeds designated for *korbanot*, what is the law? Does he get the benefit of the Torah's special fixed redemption formula (*beit zera chomer se'orim ba-chamishim shekel kesef*), since this is after all a *sdei achuza*? Or, since contributions to the *mizbe'ach* are always redeemed at market value, does that rule apply instead? *Teiku* — no answer.

These unresolved cases are an almost natural outgrowth of the *gemara*'s recognition that *kedushat damim le-mizbe'ach* exists as a category at all. Once the *gemara* allows that one can sanctify something for its monetary value to be used toward a *korban* — rather than only sanctifying the thing directly — it opens the door to these hybrid constructs, combining the rules of one system (*arachin*, *sdei achuza*) with the destination of another (the *mizbe'ach*). The *gemara* leaves these configurations without resolution.

---

## Arachin Categories

### Less Than Month Old

With the complex *sugya* of vital organs set aside, the *gemara* returns to more straightforward questions of *erchin*. The next *mishna* states: *pachot mi-ven chodesh nidar aval lo ne'erach* — an infant less than one month old does not fall within the Torah's *arachin* framework (which begins at one month old with fixed valuations), but such an infant is *nidar*: if someone says "I will pay the market value of this infant," he is obligated to pay whatever the market value is.

### Erech Reinterpretation

A *braita* introduces a complication: what if you used the wrong word? You said *ha-maareich pachot mi-ven chodesh* — you used the word *erech*, the technical term for the Torah's fixed valuation, in reference to an infant less than one month old for whom no fixed *erech* exists. Rabbi Meir says: *noten damav* — you pay the market value. The Rabbis say: *lo amar klum* — you said nothing; there is no *erech* for this infant, so your statement is legally void and you owe nothing.

The *gemara* asks: what is the logic of the dispute? Rabbi Meir holds *ein adam motzi devarav le-vatala* — a person does not utter meaningless statements. Therefore, even if you said *erech*, since you presumably know that there is no *erech* for an infant under one month, what you really intended was market value (*damim*). The Rabbis hold that people do sometimes say things without halakhic content, and we interpret your words as literally as possible: you said *erech*, there is no *erech* here, you owe nothing.

Tosafot notes an important dimension to Rabbi Meir's position. One might think that Rabbi Meir is simply reinterpreting your words as a policy matter. But Tosafot emphasizes that this is connected to the broader principle operative in *arachin* and *hafla'ah* more generally — we care about your *da'at*, your underlying intent, not merely the words spoken. Rabbi Meir is therefore prepared to interpret the word *erech* contextually, giving it the meaning of *damim*, because we are attentive to what you were trying to achieve. Tosafot further notes that this is easier to apply here than in a case of outright error. If someone intended to say one thing and said something completely different — a complete mismatch between thought and speech — the statement is void entirely. But here it is not a complete error; it is a question of contextual meaning. You said *erech* in a context where *erech* cannot operate, and Rabbi Meir holds that in such a case we translate the term into the closest operative equivalent: *damim*.

### Vessel Erech

The *gemara* then asks: *ke-man azla ha de-amar Rav Gidel amar Rav* — who does the following ruling follow? Rav, citing Rav Gidel, taught: *ha-omer erech kli alai noten damav* — if someone says "the *erech* of this vessel is upon me," he pays its market value. A vessel does not appear anywhere in the Torah's *arachin* charts — the charts are for persons. So one might say that "the *erech* of my car" is legally meaningless, yielding zero. Rav says no: he pays market value. This clearly follows Rabbi Meir.

But the *gemara* asks: is this obvious? Perhaps even the Rabbis would agree here. The Rabbis might hold that by an infant under one month, the person genuinely made a mistake — he knew the word *erech* has a technical meaning and honestly thought that the charts extended to infants under a month. Given that error, his statement can be voided. But by a vessel, no one could seriously think that the Torah's fixed valuation charts apply to a car. Therefore, the Rabbis would agree that in this case, the person certainly knew there is no *erech* for a vessel and intended to obligate himself in the market value. The *gemara* rejects this: no, the Rabbis maintain consistently that we go by what you literally said, and if *erech* has no technical application, you said nothing. It is Rabbi Meir alone who makes the principled claim that *ein adam motzi devarav le-vatala* and interprets the term contextually to mean market value, whether by an infant or by a vessel.

### Ani's Animal

The *gemara* proceeds to a further case. *Ke-man azla ha de-amar Rav Gidel amar Rav* — the ruling that if someone says "I am sanctifying my fellow's animal," he must pay its value to the *Beit HaMikdash*. One cannot sanctify another person's animal — it is not his to sanctify. Yet Rav says the statement obligates him in the animal's market value. This clearly follows Rabbi Meir.

The *gemara* asks: didn't we already know this from Rav's earlier ruling about a vessel? Why do we need an additional ruling about another's animal? The *gemara* answers: one might have thought those cases are different. In the vessel case, the person knows with certainty that there is no *erech* for a vessel and consciously substituted market value for the inapplicable term. In the animal case, there is a more plausible alternative interpretation: the person may be saying, "if I can persuade the owner to sell it to me, I will sanctify it and bring it as a *korban*." We might therefore not interpret his statement as an immediate monetary obligation to the *Beit HaMikdash* but as a contingent intention to purchase and then sanctify. The *chiddush* is that Rabbi Meir goes even further: he interprets the statement to create a present, binding obligation to pay the animal's value to *hekdesh*, even though this is a significant stretch from the words "I am sanctifying another's animal." Rabbi Meir's principle that statements must be given halakhic meaning is applied even here, where the reinterpretation is not a simple contextual translation but a substantial extension of what was said.

### Alai Requirement

Rav Ashi qualifies the ruling: *ve-hu de-amar alai* — the rule that one who sanctifies another's animal must pay its value applies only if he included the word *alai* ("upon me"). Rashi explains the relevant formulation as *behemat chaveiro zu alai* — "my fellow's animal is upon me." The word *alai* creates a hook: even if we cannot give the statement the meaning of a direct sanctification (since the animal is not his), we can read *alai* as expressing a personal obligation. Without *alai*, however — if he simply said *harei zu* ("behold, this animal is a *korban*") — that is too far a stretch. A declaration that this specific animal is a *korban*, with no language of personal obligation, cannot be reinterpreted to mean a monetary obligation to pay its market value. Thus even Rabbi Meir's expansive principle has its limits: the initial statement must contain some linguistic foothold on which the reinterpretation can rest.

To summarize the arc of this *sugya*: Rabbi Meir's principle begins with the straightforward case of *erech* misapplied to an infant — a simple contextual reinterpretation of a technical term. It extends to a vessel — a slightly greater stretch since vessels are entirely absent from the *arachin* framework. It extends further to another's animal, where the reinterpretation moves from the vocabulary of sanctification to an obligation in monetary value. And it is qualified at last by Rav Ashi's requirement that the word *alai* be present to anchor the reinterpretation to something actually expressed.

---

## Non-Jews in Arachin

### Mishnah Dispute

The next *mishna* takes up the status of non-Jews (*ovdei kochavim*) in *arachin*. The *parsha* of *arachin* opens with the words *dabeir el Bnei Yisrael* — speak to the Children of Israel — which could suggest the entire system is limited to Jews. But separately, the *parsha* uses the word *ish* (a man, any man), which is inclusive. The question is how to distribute these two signals.

Rabbi Meir rules: a non-Jew is *ne'erach* — he can appear on the valuation charts as the object of an *erech* — but he is not *maarich*, meaning he cannot himself obligate in an *erech*. Rabbi Yehuda rules the reverse: a non-Jew is *maarich* — he can undertake the obligation — but he is not *ne'erach*, meaning he cannot be the object of an *erech*.

### Agreement Zone

Both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree, however, that *she-nodrim ve-nidrim* — non-Jews can obligate themselves through regular *nedarim* (vows of market value) and can be the object of such vows as well. The entire dispute is confined to the technical category of *erech* with its fixed Torah charts. Outside that narrow framework — for ordinary donations, market-value vows, and the like — non-Jews participate fully on both sides.

### Meir Analogy

The *braita* elaborates each position. Rabbi Meir explains why he allows the non-Jew to be *ne'erach* but not *maarich*: *mipnei she-ribah kasuv ba-ne'erachim yoseir mi-ba-maarichin* — the Torah's charts include a wider class of people as objects than as subjects. Specifically: a *cheireish*, *shoteh*, and *katan* — a deaf-mute, a mentally ill person, and a minor — all appear on the charts as objects (*ne'erachim*) but cannot themselves be subjects (*maarichin*), since they lack the requisite legal competence. Since the category of *ne'erach* is broader, we extend it to include non-Jews; since the category of *maarich* is narrower, we exclude non-Jews from it.

### Yehuda Analogy

Rabbi Yehuda makes the opposite argument: *mipnei she-ribah kasuv ba-maarichin yoseir mi-ba-ne'erachim* — there are people who can be subjects without appearing on the charts. Specifically: a *tumtum* and *androgynous* — persons of indeterminate gender — can be *maarichin* (they can obligate themselves in an *erech*) but are not *ne'erachim* (they do not appear on the charts, since the charts require determinate gender). Therefore the category of *maarich* is broader, and we extend it to non-Jews; the charts are more restrictive, and we exclude non-Jews from them. Rabbi Yehuda reasons that the Torah's fixed valuation charts are formal and exclusive — they exclude those of indeterminate gender, and by the same logic they exclude non-Jews — whereas the capacity to make an *erech* obligation is more open, extending to those of indeterminate gender and therefore to non-Jews as well.

### Rava Evaluation

Rava offers a striking evaluation: *hilchata de-Rabbi Meir mistabra, teimeh lo mistabra* — the legal ruling of Rabbi Meir (that non-Jews are *ne'erachim* but not *maarichin*) is correct, but his reasoning is unpersuasive. And conversely: *teimeh de-Rabbi Yehuda mistabra, ve-hilchesa lo mistabra* — Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is more logically compelling, but his ruling does not follow.

Why is Rabbi Meir's reasoning weak? Because his comparison to *cheireish*, *shoteh*, and *katan* is inapt. Those individuals are excluded from being *maarichin* because they lack *da'at* — the legal and cognitive capacity to make binding decisions. A non-Jew possesses full *da'at*; the analogy therefore does not hold. Why is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning stronger? Because his comparison to *tumtum* and *androgynous* is apt — these are persons of full competence who nonetheless appear on one side of the *arachin* framework and not the other, demonstrating that the Torah can allocate these categories asymmetrically without reference to cognitive capacity.

### Ezra-Nehemiah

Yet Rava rules like Rabbi Meir's *psak* — that non-Jews cannot be *maarichin* — on entirely different grounds. A verse from *Ezra-Nechemia*: *lo lachem va-lanu livnot beit Elokeinu* — "it is not for you and for us to build the house of our God." When the non-Jews of the land offered to participate in rebuilding the *Beit HaMikdash*, Nechemia refused, out of concern about the influence they might exert over the project. This demonstrates that there is some principled reservation about non-Jewish contributions to the *Beit HaMikdash*, even if the reservation is not absolute.

As Tosafot notes, this reservation is not total: the *mishna* itself states that non-Jews can make *nedarim* and donate market value to the *Beit HaMikdash*. But where the Torah is excluding non-Jews from *some* category of involvement in the *arachin* system, the *Ezra-Nechemia* story gives us reason to locate that exclusion on the giving side — they cannot be *maarichin* — rather than on the receiving side. This reasoning, external to the internal logic of the *arachin* charts, is what actually supports Rabbi Meir's *psak*, not his analogy to *cheireish*, *shoteh*, and *katan*. We will continue with this discussion on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Arakhin 6

## Non-Jews & Erech

### Non-Jews in Erech

The *daf* opens by continuing a discussion that began at the bottom of 5b: can non-Jews participate in the category of *erech*? Can they obligate themselves to pay an *erech*, and can they serve as the object of one? The *Gemara* had been inclined to suggest that if an exclusion is to be drawn, it should fall specifically on the giving of *erech* — and the basis for this inclination is a story and verse from the book of *Ezra*, in which non-Jewish contributions to the *Beit HaMikdash* were rejected at the outset of the building process out of concern that it would undermine the enterprise as a distinctly Jewish undertaking. As *Tosafot* notes, this does not warrant a sweeping exclusion: the *Mishnah* already states that non-Jews may give a *neder*, and whatever limitation exists pertains specifically within the domain of *erchin*.

### Ezra-Nehemiah Story

The story from *Ezra-Nechemia* is the textual anchor for this entire discussion. When the rebuilding of the Second *Beit HaMikdash* began, those who sought to contribute from outside the Jewish community were rebuffed. The concern was not merely theological abstraction — it was the vulnerability of the enterprise itself. The text describes the surrounding peoples working to weaken the hands of those who were building. In that charged climate, accepting outside contributions risked importing with them outside interests, outside influence, and ultimately outside ownership of what was meant to be an exclusively Jewish national undertaking. The *Gemara* will ultimately need to grapple with how much general policy can be derived from this singular historical episode.

### R. Yehuda: Erech Valid,…

The *Gemara* asks: since *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that a non-Jew can be *maarich* — can give an *erech* that takes effect — what does he do with the verse from *Ezra-Nechemia* that seems to prohibit accepting non-Jewish contributions to the *Beit HaMikdash*? The answer given is that of *Rav Chisda* in the name of *Rav Avimi*: *ve'erko nignaz* — even *Rabbi Yehuda* would agree that as a matter of policy the contribution should not be accepted. Nevertheless, if a non-Jew does set aside the money for an *erech*, the money becomes sanctified. The question then becomes: what does one do with it? The answer: it must be buried.

A note on terminology is appropriate here. The *Gemara*'s use of *ovdei kochavim* is almost invariably a later self-censorship; the original text would have read *goy* or *nochri*. In context, the concern is not limited to idolaters per se — it applies to all non-Jews, and the driving concern is the integrity of the *Beit HaMikdash* as a Jewish enterprise.

This is an interesting way of incorporating the policy concern within *Rabbi Yehuda*'s framework. He agrees that sanctity attaches when the money is set aside, but agrees as well that the practical outcome is burial rather than use. This is admittedly a waste. And it applies only to *erchin* — the *Mishnah*, as noted, permits *nedarim* from non-Jews.

### Me'ila Objection

The *Gemara* immediately presses this position. If the money is to be buried and will never be used by the *Beit HaMikdash*, there ought to be no violation of *meila* — the prohibition against misusing sanctified property. The underlying principle is that if something is sanctified but can never in any way be put to use, there is no *meila*: *lo nehenin velo moalin*. This is established in the *Mishnah* itself, which teaches that items such as the five *chatatot* that must be left to die, or money that is sanctified but must be thrown into the Dead Sea, are governed by this rule — they are rabbinically prohibited from benefit, yet no transgression of *meila* attaches to them.

If the *erech* money of a non-Jew is destined for burial, the same should apply. But this is contradicted by a *braita*: *bameh devarim amurim bekodshei mizbeach* — when does the rule of no *meila* apply to things sanctified by a non-Jew? Only for *kodshei mizbeach*, sacrificial offerings. *Aval bekodshei bedek habayit moalin bo* — if a non-Jew sanctified something for the Temple treasury, *meila* does apply. Since *Rabbi Meir* holds that non-Jews cannot even sanctify effectively, this *braita* must be reflecting *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position — and it states explicitly that *meila* applies. This refutes the burial conclusion.

### Rava: Unique Circumstance

*Rava* concedes the point. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position is that non-Jews can give an *erech*, the money becomes sanctified, and it would be used — which is in fact the straightforward reading of *Rabbi Yehuda*. What, then, does *Rabbi Yehuda* do with the *Ezra* story? *Rava* answers: *mishum rifyon yadayim hu* — that story reflects entirely unique circumstances. It cannot serve as the basis for general policy. The verse cited is explicit: *vayehi am ha'aretz merappim yedei am Yehuda umevahhalim otam livnot* — the surrounding peoples were actively working to weaken the hands of the Jews who were building the *Beit HaMikdash*. The entire venture was extraordinarily fragile, and those who offered to contribute may well have harbored ulterior motives — seeking to insert themselves into the process and use their contribution as leverage for manipulation. That concern was specific to those circumstances; it does not translate into a standing general rule.

With this, *Tosafot*'s observation becomes all the more pointed: even the opinion that does derive some policy from the *Ezra* story applies that policy narrowly — only to *erchin*, not to *nedarim*. The *Mishnah* is explicit that non-Jews may give a *neder*. So if one presses the question of what precisely distinguishes *erchin*, *Tosafot*'s answer is essentially that there is nothing uniquely disqualifying about *erchin* — but given that there are grounds for some concern, if any limitation is to be drawn, this is where it lands. That said, the simple reading of the *Gemara* we have just concluded, along with what follows at the top of 6a, suggests that the policy implications extend more broadly than *erchin* alone.

## Contributions: Beginning…

### Two Baraitot on Neder

At the top of 6a, the *Gemara* turns to a different type of contribution — not *erech* but *nedavah*, a vow or gift to the Temple treasury — which according to our *Mishnah* should present no problem at all. Yet even here, policy concerns emerge. One *braita* states that if non-Jews gave a *nedavah* to *bedek habayit*, the Temple maintenance fund, one accepts it. A second *braita* states that one does not accept it. How are these reconciled?

### Beginning vs. End

*Rabbi Ila* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *lo kashya — ha bitechilah ha besof* — there is no contradiction. It depends on whether the contribution comes at the beginning or the end of the process. The straightforward explanation, rooted directly in the *Ezra-Nechemia* narrative, is this: at the very beginning, when the foundation is being laid, the Jewish community must establish itself unambiguously as the owner and driver of the enterprise. The question of who is investing in the *Beit HaMikdash*, who owns the process, who is responsible for it — all of that must be settled firmly through Jewish commitment alone. Once the project is well underway, once the Jewish community's investment is beyond question, outside contributions can be absorbed without threatening that sense of ownership.

### Stringent at Beginning

The stringency at the beginning is sweeping. *De'amar Rabbi Assi amar Rabbi Yochanan: bitechilah, afilu mayim u'melach ein mekablin* — at the beginning of the process, even the most basic items — water and salt — are not accepted from non-Jews. It matters not at all how trivial or how essential the contribution might be; the principle of exclusive Jewish ownership of the enterprise is absolute at the outset.

### End: Specific/Generic

Once the process is well along, distinctions emerge. *Davar hamesuyam ein mekablin, davar she'eino mesuyam mekablin* — a specific, identified item is not accepted, but a generic contribution — money that is absorbed into the general fund — is acceptable. The logic is clear: a generic donation disappears into the collective and carries no identifying mark. A specific item, however, remains associated with its donor and introduces the very concern that drove the original rejection: an outside party now has a visible, named stake in the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Ama Chalya Oreiv

*Rav Yosef* offers an example of a *davar mesuyam*: the *ama khalya oreiv* — the spiked device, one *amah* by one *amah*, installed on the Temple roof to prevent birds from landing and contaminating the altar with its burning sacrifices. The spikes frightened away ravens and other birds that would otherwise be drawn by the smell of burning meat. The *Gemara* presumably selects this example to forestall a mistaken inference: one might have thought that only prestigious items — like the *Aron Kodesh* — would carry identifying weight. The *ama khalya oreiv* is relatively minor, yet it would still be identified as a non-Jewish contribution. Any specific item, regardless of its prominence, is in the same category.

### Reclamation Concern

*Rabbeinu Gershom* adds a further dimension to the rationale for rejecting specific items: the concern is not only about identification and prestige, but about reclamation. When a non-Jew donates something specific, there is a risk that he might later seek to reclaim it — either because he has a change of heart, because relations deteriorate, or simply out of self-interest. A generic monetary donation cannot be demanded back once absorbed into general funds, but a specific, identifiable object presents an ongoing vulnerability. The *Beit HaMikdash* should not be in the position of having to refuse such a demand, or worse, of losing something it has already integrated into its operations. This is also why, at the end of the process, even relatively minor specific items are rejected: the concern about future complications is independent of the item's importance.

### Royal Contribution

*Rav Yosef* raises a challenge: the *Gemara* in *Nechemia* records a letter from the king to *Asaf*, the keeper of the royal forest, directing him to supply timber for the construction of the *Beit HaMikdash*.
