This is a contribution at the very beginning of the building process — yet it was accepted. *Tosafot* notes the broader difficulty: the entire reconstruction under *Koresh* was carried out under royal directive and with royal support. *Tosafot* suggests that *Koresh* himself was in a special category, already singled out by prophecy in *Yeshayahu*. But here the contributor was not *Koresh* directly; it was *Asaf*, acting on royal command. How could such a contribution be accepted at the beginning of the process?

### Royal Cannot Reverse

*Abaye* resolves this: *shani malchusa d'lo hadra beih* — royal action is categorically different, because a king does not reverse himself. *Shmuel* stated this principle explicitly: if the king says he will uproot mountains, the mountains will be uprooted — *i amar malchusa akarna tura, akar tura v'lo hadra beih*. The maxim is well known: *Shmuel* was the *amora* who articulated *dina d'malchusa dina*, the rule that governmental law is binding law. *Shmuel* was also personally close to the Persian royal court.

What exactly is the concern that is being neutralized? *Rashi* indicates that the worry is not only about dramatic manipulation but about something more mundane: will this contribution turn out to be sincere and final, or will the donor later seek to take it back, creating complications and conflict? When the contribution comes by royal decree, there is no realistic concern that it will be reversed or reclaimed. Royal declarations carry the weight of institutional permanence. A king does not say "I changed my mind" and ask for the lumber back. That assurance removes the concern that makes outside contributions at the beginning of the process so fraught.

One might ask: does this not leave open a different concern — that the government, precisely because it has contributed, will now seek to influence or control the enterprise? The point is a sharp one, and it applies with equal or greater force to a royal contributor than to a private one. If anything, a government can manipulate a situation regardless of whether it has made a formal donation. The *Gemara*'s resolution, focused on the concern about reversal, does not address the manipulation concern directly — though it may be that royal contribution at the outset, made under the authority of a decree, is simply taken as a given that falls outside the ordinary policy framework.

## Non-Jew Terumah

### Non-Jew Separates

*Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav*: if a non-Jew separates *terumah* from his own grain grown in *Eretz Yisrael*, what is the status of that separation? The question presupposes the view that non-Jewish ownership of land in *Eretz Yisrael* does not remove its *kedusha* — a position with significant practical implications, including for the question of selling land to a non-Jew in a *shemita* year. Given that the grain carries inherent sanctity, is a non-Jew capable of actualizing it by performing the separation?

### Intent Investigation

The *Gemara* rules that the answer depends on an investigation: *bodkin oto* — one must examine what the non-Jew had in mind. *Im bedaat Yisrael hifrishah* — if he performed the separation with Jewish intent — meaning either that he did so at the direction of a Jew, or, as *Rashi* offers alternatively, that he intended it to work precisely as *terumah* works for Jews — then *tinaten lekohen*: it is genuine *terumah* and must be given to a *kohen*. A non-Jew, if the grain carries sanctity and he intends the separation in the Jewish sense, can effectively make *terumah* from his own produce.

### Ambiguous Terumah

If, however, his intent cannot be so confirmed, the situation becomes complicated. *Chayshinan shema belibo lashamayim* — we are concerned that when he said *terumah*, he may have meant something different. The word *terumah* appears in the Torah not only as the name for the priestly portion separated from grain, but also as the name for gifts given for the construction of the *Beit HaMikdash* — *zot haterumah*, the portion from which the *Mishkan* materials were gathered. If the non-Jew meant to give his grain as a donation to the Temple treasury, it is now *kodshei bedek habayit* rather than *terumah* in the agricultural sense. Since one cannot be certain which he intended, one faces an impasse: if it is *terumah*, it cannot be used for the Temple. If it is *kodshei bedek habayit*, it cannot be given to *kohanim* to eat. There is no way to use it appropriately in either direction, and so it must be buried.

One might wonder whether some creative solution could avoid the need for burial — perhaps having a *kohen* redeem it on a small coin, or finding some other mechanism to release it. The *Gemara* does not pursue such a path, and the ruling is that in the absence of clear intent, burial is required.

### Non-Jew Sanctity

This entire discussion raises a broader question about whether non-Jews can create *kedusha* that operates meaningfully within a Jewish legal framework. The natural assumption might be that someone outside the system cannot generate such effects. But the *Gemara*'s line of reasoning suggests otherwise. Non-Jews can bring *korbanot*, which requires sanctifying the animal. They can donate to the Temple treasury in ways that take effect. Once those capacities are established, the possibility that they can also separate *terumah* — particularly where the *kedusha* is already inherent in the grain and the non-Jew is in some sense merely actualizing it — is not a radical extension.

This is distinct from the question of whether such actions constitute *mitzvot* for the non-Jew, or whether the non-Jew accrues merit. The *Rambam* holds that even non-Jews who perform *mitzvot* are performing a meaningful act, if not at the same level as one who is commanded. But the question here is not about spiritual accounting — it is about legal efficacy. Can non-Jews generate *kedusha* that imposes real obligations and restrictions within *halacha*? The answer emerging from this *sugya* is yes, within defined parameters.

## Beam with God's Name

### Donation Conditions

The *Gemara* raises a case: a non-Jew donates a beam for the Temple — or, as *Rashi* indicates the *braita* implies, in a time when there is no Temple, for the synagogue — and on the beam he has written God's name, indicating that he is donating it for religious purposes.

### Cut Name, Use Rest

*Bodkin oto* — again an investigation is conducted. *Im amar bedaas Yisrael hifrashtiah* — if he says that he donated it in the manner that Jews donate things, intending it as a straightforward religious donation rather than as a formal act of sanctification, then *yigod* — one cuts out the section of the beam bearing the divine name, which carries *kedushat Hashem* and must be buried as *sheimos*, while the remainder of the beam may be used.

The fact that the text requires cutting out the name even in this case is itself significant: even a divine name written by a non-Jew apparently carries real *kedushat Hashem*, not merely a matter of propriety or respect. This is the apparent implication of the *braita*, and we will return to this point.

### Unclear Intent Buried

*Ve'im lav* — if he cannot confirm that he intended it the Jewish way — *teuna genizah* — the entire beam must be buried. The concern is *chayshinan shema belibo lashamayim*: perhaps he meant to formally sanctify the beam for religious use, in which case the beam carries *kedusha* of *hekdesh*. In the present era, when there is no functioning Temple, *hekdesh* that cannot be used — as we learned at the end of *Bechorot* — must be put away. There is nothing that can be done with it. If it might be *hekdesh*, it cannot be used for the synagogue; and since there is no Temple to which it could be brought, it must be buried.

This is particularly intelligible in the context of the ancient pagan world, where the standard form of religious donation was often not an animal sacrifice but the dedication of precious objects — literally placing valuables in the temple treasury as an act of religious devotion. We know, for example, of temple treasuries found in various ancient religious sites containing enormous accumulations of gold and other precious goods — dedicated, never to be sold or used, simply offered to the deity. In that world, a non-Jew who donates a beam without specifying that he means to do so "the Jewish way" very plausibly intended precisely such a formal, irrevocable sanctification. That is why the absence of a clear statement of Jewish-style intent triggers the concern and requires burial.

### Limited Sanctification

The *Gemara* then draws a further inference. The fact that the *braita* specifies a beam with God's name written on it implies that if there were no name on the beam, burial would not be required — the default assumption would not be that the non-Jew intended formal *hekdesh*. But the *Gemara* immediately pushes back: *hu hadin de'af al gav de'ein shem katav aleha nami bay genizah* — even without God's name, if the non-Jew cannot confirm Jewish intent, we would still be concerned that the donation might constitute *hekdesh* and burial would be required.

What, then, is the *chiddush* of specifying that God's name was written on the beam? *De'af al gav deshem katav aleha* — even with God's name on it, if the non-Jew explicitly states that he meant to give it in the Jewish manner, then the beam may be used — provided the section bearing the name is cut out. The name sanctifies only its immediate location: *shem she'lo bimkomo lav kadosh* — a divine name does not extend its sanctity beyond the space it physically occupies. Only that section requires burial; the rest of the beam is fully usable.

A supporting *braita* from *Masechet Sofrim* establishes this principle: if God's name was written on the handles of vessels or the legs of a bed, one cuts out and buries those specific parts. The vessel or bed itself is not sanctified throughout.

### Pagan vs. Modern

The question arises whether these concerns about a non-Jew's writing of *Shem Hashem* — and the possibility that an unclear donation constitutes *hekdesh* — remain relevant outside the context of the ancient pagan world. The parallel to a *Sefer Torah* written by a non-Jew, where *Shem Hashem* is treated as genuine *sheimos*, suggests that there is real *kedusha* at stake, not merely a question of respect. But when it comes to the concern about formal sanctification, the pagan context matters considerably. A non-Jew in the contemporary world who donates his car to a synagogue does not inhabit a world in which the default religious act is the irrevocable dedication of objects to a deity's treasury. The concern that his donation might constitute formal *hekdesh* is correspondingly attenuated. Whether contemporary *poskim* have addressed this distinction directly is a question worth pursuing.

## Tzedakah Money

### Mutar Lishnosah

*Rav Nachman* said in the name of *Rabbah bar Avuha*: *ha'omer sela zu litzedakah mutar lishnosah* — if one says "this coin is for *tzedakah*," one may switch it out, meaning one may use the coin for another purpose and give a different coin to *tzedakah*. The coin does not become sanctified to the point where it must be this specific coin; the obligation is to give the money, not to give this particular piece of currency.

### Self vs. Other

The *Gemara* initially considered whether this latitude extended only to the donor's own use — that perhaps one could use it for oneself but could not lend it to a third party. The reasoning behind this hypothetical distinction, as *Rashi* explains, is that one might naturally reserve in one's own mind the option to use the money oneself, while never having contemplated that others might draw on it.

### Borrow & Repay

This restriction was rejected. *Amar Rabbi Ami amar Rabbi Yochanan: bein la'atzmo bein la'acher* — it makes no difference whether it is used by the donor or lent to a third party. The fundamental principle is that designating money for *tzedakah* does not sanctify it the way *hekdesh* sanctifies Temple property. The obligation is to give the money, but the money itself retains a degree of flexibility. Whether one said *alai* — creating a personal obligation — or *harei zu* — setting aside the specific coin — the ruling is ultimately the same: one may borrow it and repay, as long as the *tzedakah* ultimately receives what is owed.

### Rava's Reasoning

*Rava* challenges a proposed distinction between the two formulations — *alai* versus *harei zu* — on policy grounds. *Adrabba ipecha mistabra* — the opposite of the proposed distinction makes more sense. If one says *harei zu*, designating this specific coin, one should actually be encouraged to go ahead and use it. Why? *Ki heichi d'lichayev b'achrayusa* — so that one will bear personal financial responsibility for it. If the coin remains as designated but the donor has not accepted a personal obligation, and the coin is lost, the *tzedakah* loses out entirely. But if the donor uses the coin and now owes the money, the debt remains regardless of what happens to the original coin. The *tzedakah* is thereby better protected. *Ella lo shna* — ultimately, the *Gemara* collapses the distinction: it does not matter which formulation was used, and the latitude to borrow and repay applies throughout.

The deeper question is what this ruling implies about the status of money designated for *tzedakah*. If it had no status at all, the various concerns and distinctions the *Gemara* entertains would not arise. But if it had the full status of *hekdesh*, one could not use it at all. The *Gemara* seems to describe something intermediate: the money has a status — an aspect of *neder*, a quality of being earmarked — yet that status comes with considerably more latitude than *hekdesh*. The *Rambam* famously emphasizes that *tzedakah* is a *neder* and that the designated money carries something like a *kedusha*, while also recognizing that it may be borrowed and repaid. Reconciling the status with the latitude is the ongoing challenge of the *sugya*.

### Neder Not Hekdesh

A *braita* is cited in support of *Rava*'s overall position: *neder tzedakah ve'ein hekdesh tzedakah* — *tzedakah* is like a *neder* but not like *hekdesh*. What does this mean? The *Gemara* clarifies: *tzedakah harei hi beval ta'acher* — a commitment to give *tzedakah* carries the force of a vow, such that failing to fulfill it within three *regalim* constitutes a transgression of *bal ta'acher*, just as delaying the fulfillment of a vow to bring a *korban* does. This has real practical implications: when a person commits to give at a communal appeal, the laws of *bal ta'acher* apply to that commitment. The exact conditions under which such a pledge constitutes a binding *neder* — as opposed to a mere expression of intention — is a subject for the tractate of *Nedarim*, but the principle that *tzedakah* can carry *neder* status is established here.

At the same time, *ve'eino kehekdesh* — it is not like *hekdesh*. *Hekdesh* places the object entirely off-limits: *assur lehishtamesh bo*. *Tzedakah*, by contrast, *shari lehishtamesh bah* — may be used, in the sense of borrowing. This unique hybrid — carrying the obligation structure of a *neder* while lacking the use-prohibition of *hekdesh* — captures the peculiar character of *tzedakah* money. It is perhaps best understood as a *neder* whose fulfillment is measured not by the fate of the specific object but by whether the *aniyim* ultimately receive what they are owed.

### Gabbai Control

*Tanu rabanan*: if one says "this *sela* is for *tzedakah*," the latitude to borrow and repay exists only *ad shelo ba'ah leyad gabbai* — until the money reaches the hands of the *gabbai*, the communal official responsible for collecting and distributing *tzedakah*. Once it is in the *gabbai*'s hands, *assur lishnotah* — it cannot be switched or used for another purpose. The reason is that when the *gabbai* receives the money, he acquires it on behalf of the *aniyim*. At that point it is their money. Whatever latitude existed before, based on the donor's continuing personal ownership and obligation, disappears once a third party has taken possession on behalf of the intended beneficiaries.

### R. Yannai Exception

The *Gemara* challenges this from practice: *Rav Yannai*, who served as a *gabbai*, would himself borrow from the *tzedakah* funds and later repay them. How could he do so once the money was in the *gabbai*'s hands?

The *Gemara* answers: *shani Rav Yannai denicha lehu la'aniyim* — the situation of *Rav Yannai* was different, because it was actually beneficial for the poor that he borrow the money. The mechanism is as follows: when the *tzedakah* coffers were depleted because *Rav Yannai* had borrowed from them, he bore personal responsibility to ensure the poor were fed. Faced with empty coffers and an outstanding obligation, he would go out and compel additional donations from the community — thereby generating more funds than would otherwise have been collected. The poor ultimately received more, not less, as a result of his borrowing. When the borrowing is genuinely in the interest of the *aniyim*, that implicit permission may be attributed to them, and the act is permitted.

This reasoning underscores how the entire framework of *tzedakah* money is calibrated around the welfare of the poor rather than around abstract categories of sanctity. The status of the money, whatever it is, exists to ensure that the *aniyim* are served. When a departure from the ordinary rules serves that same purpose better than rigid adherence would, the departure is endorsed.

## Synagogue Donations

### Jewish Donation

The *Gemara* now turns to specific donations made to a synagogue. *Yisrael she-nitnadev menora o ner le-beit haknesset* — if a Jew donated a candelabrum or a lamp to a synagogue, *assur lishnosah* — the synagogue may not reuse it for a different purpose. It is as though the item carries a form of *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic sanctity attached to the object itself — rather than merely *kedushat damim*, monetary value earmarked for a particular use.

### Mitzvah Reuse

*Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba* initially understood this prohibition to be absolute, applying even if the synagogue wished to repurpose the item for a different *mitzvah* purpose. *Rav Ami* corrected him in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: the prohibition applies only to *dvar reshut*, to uses unrelated to any *mitzvah*. For a *dvar mitzvah*, repurposing is permitted. The practical question of what constitutes a *dvar reshut* versus a *dvar mitzvah* in a synagogue context is left with some ambiguity, though Torah study or another religious purpose would clearly qualify.

### Non-Jew Limited

When the donor is a non-Jew, additional considerations apply. *Rabbi Assi* said in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: if a non-Jew donated a lamp or candelabrum to a synagogue — and here, notably, the *Gemara* implicitly accepts that such a donation was received, unlike the *Beit HaMikdash* context — *ad she-lo nishtaka sheim ba'aleha, assur lishnosah*. As long as the donor's name is still remembered in connection with the object, it may not be repurposed even for a *mitzvah* purpose.

### Name Forgotten

*Mishenishtaka sheim ba'aleha, mutar lishnosah* — once the donor's name has been forgotten, the synagogue may sell the item and apply the proceeds to other purposes. The operative concern is not intrinsic sanctity but rather the risk of the donor's complaint: as long as people remember that this is "John's candelabrum," using it differently would constitute a public insult to the donor. The donor — the non-Jew — may appear and ask what happened to his gift. Even if the donor himself always remembers, once the communal memory fades and the item is no longer identified with him in the public consciousness, the risk of offense has sufficiently passed.

The parallel to communal life is vivid and genuine. A synagogue that accepts a specific donated item enters into an ongoing relationship with the donor's identity. The familiar scenario — a major donor wishes to give a new *aron kodesh* to replace the one already bearing another family's name — is precisely the tension this *halacha* addresses. The *Gemara*, strikingly, assumes this concern applies only to non-Jewish donors. For Jewish donors, *lo payei* — the assumption is that a Jew gives wholeheartedly and would not complain. Whether that assumption is realistic in every communal context is another matter.

### Shazrik Case

The *Gemara* then presents a concrete case. *Shazrik the Taya* — a non-Jewish merchant — donated a lamp to a synagogue associated with *Rav Yehuda*. *Rechava* subsequently repurposed it for some other use. *Rava* was upset, holding that the repurposing was impermissible. A second version has the versions reversed — *Rava* made the change and *Rechava* objected. A third version has the synagogue's *chazanim* make the change, with both *Rechava* and *Rava* objecting.

The substantive dispute in the case is this: the one who permitted the change reasoned that since *Shazrik* was a traveling merchant, he was almost never in the city — *d'lo shechiah* — and the likelihood of his appearing and noticing the change was remote. The one who forbade it — or in the versions where multiple authorities objected, the shared ground — is that *zimnin d'mikla v'asi*, merchants do occasionally pass through, and one cannot count on him never seeing the change. The *halacha* therefore requires that as long as the donor could plausibly appear and recognize what was done with his gift, the donation must remain as it was received.

The section thus concludes with a subtle observation: whereas at the beginning of the *sugya* the *Beit HaMikdash* context led to a rule against accepting specific named items from non-Jews at all, the synagogue context apparently operates differently — donations are accepted, and the consequence is a set of ongoing obligations regarding their use. The concern about reclamation or complaint, managed in the *Beit HaMikdash* context by refusal, is managed in the synagogue context by ongoing attention to the donor's association with the gift.

## Goses & Execution

### Mishna Rule

The *Gemara* now arrives at a new *Mishnah*. *HaGoses v'hayotze lehareg lo nidar v'lo ne'erach* — a *goses*, a person who is actively dying and imminently terminal, and a *yotzei lehareg*, a person condemned to execution by a Jewish court, cannot be the object of a vow or an *erech*. As an object of a vow — *nidar* — this makes immediate sense: they have no market value; if sold as slaves they would fetch nothing. The *chiddush* lies in the ruling that they also cannot be the object of an *erech*, since *erech* is a fixed sum determined by age and gender, entirely independent of market value.

### R. Chanina View

*Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya* disagrees on the point of *erech*: he holds that they are *ne'erach*. His reasoning is straightforward — *mipnei shedamav ketzuvim* — the *erech* value is fixed by the Torah chart, and that chart does not require market value. The *goses* and the condemned are still men or women of a certain age; their place on the chart exists regardless of their condition or fate.

### R. Yosi View

*Rabbi Yosi* goes further: *noder u'maarich u'makdish, ve'im hizik chayav* — a *goses* and a condemned person can themselves make vows and commit to pay *erech*, can sanctify objects, and are liable for damages they cause. In other words, while they may not serve as objects of the vow or *erech* — since they lack the requisite status as subjects of valuation — they retain their full legal agency as actors. They can still do legally binding things. *Rabbi Yosi*'s position is not in direct conflict with the opening ruling: the *Mishnah* says they cannot be the object, and *Rabbi Yosi* confirms they can be the subject.

### Goses Analysis

The *Gemara* works through each case. For the *goses*: *bishlama goses lo nidar delav bar damim hu* — his exclusion from being the object of a monetary vow is clear, since he has no market value. *Velo ne'erach delav bar ha'amada veha'aracha hu* — and his exclusion from *erech* is derived from the verse at the opening of the tractate, which implies that the person must be capable of being stood up for valuation. Since a *goses* cannot stand, the technical condition for *erech* is not met.

### Condemned Analysis

For the condemned person: *bishlama lo nidar delav bar damim hu* — no market value, same as the *goses*. *Ela lo ne'erach amai lo* — but why can he not be the object of an *erech*? He can stand; the technical condition is met. The answer is from a *braita*: *minayin leyotze lehareg ve'amar erki alai shelo amar klum* — from where do we know that if a condemned person declares his own *erech* upon himself, it is not binding? *Talmud lomar kol cherem lo yipadeh* — "anything under the ban shall not be redeemed." The verse is read to mean that a person who is sentenced to destruction cannot be redeemed through any payment mechanism, and since *erech* is conceptually akin to a form of redemption, it does not apply.

One might think this exclusion applies even before the final verdict is rendered. *Talmud lomar min ha'adam* — the verse teaches *from people*, implying *not all people*. Only after the court issues its final judgment does the person lose the capacity to be the object of *erech*; prior to that, *erech* applies normally.

*Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya*, who holds that the condemned person *is* an object of *erech*, must find a different reading for *kol cherem lo yipadeh*. The *Gemara* provides one, drawn from *Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka*: since we find that some categories of heavenly death — those imposed by divine judgment rather than court verdict — can be mitigated through payment of *kofer*, atonement money (as in the case of the goring ox whose owner bears liability for the victim's death), one might have thought that the same principle applies to court-imposed execution. The condemned person might pay money to redeem himself from his sentence. *Kol cherem lo yipadeh* then teaches that no — a condemned person cannot pay *kofer* to escape execution. On this reading, the verse is about the prohibition of monetary redemption from the death penalty, not about *erech* at all, leaving *Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya* free to hold that *erech* applies.

### Atonement Principle

The *Gemara* refines this further. Perhaps the prohibition against *kofer* applies only to *mitot chamurot shelo nitna shegagatan lechapara* — the most severe categories of execution, for which even an unintentional violation carries no possibility of *korban* atonement. For less severe capital offenses — *mitot kalot shenitna shegagatan lechapara* — where an unintentional violation would be atoned for by a *korban*, perhaps there is a concept of monetary atonement even for the intentional offense, and *kofer* might be permitted. *Talmud lomar kol cherem* — "anything under the ban" — the word *kol*, "all," extends the prohibition to every form of court-imposed execution, regardless of its severity.

In the end, the substantive dispute between the *tanna'im* — whether the condemned person can be an *erech* — may rest less on the interpretation of *kol cherem* and more on a prior disagreement about whether a person's fixed value on the Torah chart can be set aside by any external circumstance. The one who says he cannot be an *erech* reads *kol cherem* as speaking directly to *erech* and redemption. The one who says he can be an *erech* reads it as speaking to *kofer* money, and finds the *erech* chart simply unaffected by the verdict of the court.

# Arakhin 7

## Execution & Obligations

### Rabbi Yosei's Position

The seventh daf of *Arakhin* opens its discussion on 7b, picking up from the *mishnah* dealing with special cases of *erech* — specifically, the status of a person who has been condemned to execution. The *mishnah* had raised the question from two directions: can such a person be the object of an *erech* vow, and can he be the subject — that is, can he himself incur obligations? It is the latter question that concerns us here.

*Rabbi Yosei omer nodeh u'ma'arich* — Rabbi Yosei holds that even a person condemned to execution can take a vow, can be the subject of an *erech*, and if he causes damage, he is liable. The *mishnah* thus appears to present a four-part list of legal acts: *neder* (vow), *erech*, *hekdesh* (sanctification), and *mazik* (causing damage).

### Debate on Damages

The *Gemara* presses immediately: the *tanna kamma* — *mi amar de'lo*? Who said he could not do these things? In fact, the *Gemara* clarifies, *ella be'nodeh u'ma'arich u'makdish kulei alma lo pligi* — regarding vows, *erech*, and sanctification, there is no real dispute. *Ki pligi be'im hizik* — the debate concerns only the case of damage: if this person who is about to be executed goes and damages someone's property, must he pay?

*Tosafot* notes that the textual basis for identifying this emphasis is the formulation of the *tanna*'s ruling — some manuscript traditions read *chayav leshalem* or *chayav betashlumin*, making explicit that it is the obligation of monetary compensation that is at issue.

### Compensation Obligation

The positions are now set out clearly. *Tanna kamma savar im hizik ein chayav betashlumin* — the first *tanna* holds that one condemned to execution does not have to pay compensation for damage he causes. *Rabbi Yosei savar im hizik chayav betashlumin* — Rabbi Yosei holds that he does. The *Gemara* then asks: *bemai kamifligi* — what is actually the underlying point of dispute?

## Debt & Heirs Debate

### Rav Yosef's Reframe

*Amar Rav Yosef bemilveh al peh vegoveh min hayorshim kamifligi* — Rav Yosef reframes the entire debate. The question is not whether the condemned person is a legal entity capable of incurring an obligation. Rather, it concerns whether a debt without a *shtar* — an oral debt, or in this case, a debt that arose from damage but for which no document was ever written — can be collected from the heirs.

The general principle is that when a loan is recorded in a *shtar*, the document creates a lien on property, and the creditor may collect from heirs or even from purchasers. An oral loan, however, lacks this documentary mechanism: it is not a matter of public record and no lien is thereby created. The question remains whether heirs are nonetheless liable — since they are, in some sense, a continuation of the debtor — even in the absence of a written instrument. When someone causes damage, no *shtar* accompanies that debt. So the question becomes: does that debt, which cannot be elevated by court proceedings because the person is about to be executed, pass on to his heirs?

### Oral Loan Collection

*Tanna kamma savar milveh al peh eino goveh min hayorshim* — the first *tanna* holds that an oral debt, meaning any debt without an accompanying writ, cannot be collected from the heirs. *Rabbi Yosei savar milveh al peh goveh min hayorshim* — Rabbi Yosei holds that although one may not be able to collect from purchasers, the heirs are a continuation of the father, and the debt may be collected from them.

This reframing has an important corollary. One might ask why the same question does not apply to the cases of *neder*, *erech*, and *hekdesh*, which were said to be undisputed. The clearest case is *hekdesh*: if the condemned person sanctified his property, ownership has already passed to the *Beit HaMikdash* at the moment of the declaration. There is no mere debt — the property already belongs to the *Beit HaMikdash*, and no question of collection from heirs arises. *Tosafot* argues that the same logic must extend, at least under certain conditions, to *neder* and *erech* as well: when property has been set aside for the fulfillment of the vow, it is already designated in a way that preempts the inheritance question. But when it is simply a debt without ownership having transferred — as in the case of damages — the question arises sharply.

### Torah-Inscribed Debt

*Rava amar dekulei alma milveh al peh eino goveh min hayorshim* — Rava offers a different framing. Everyone would agree, he says, that a plain oral debt cannot be collected from heirs. *Ve'hacha bemilveh haktuvah batorah kamifligi* — the dispute here concerns something categorically different: the obligation to pay for damage is not merely an informal oral commitment, but a debt explicitly mandated by the *Torah* itself. The question is whether this gives the obligation added legal weight — analogous perhaps to a *shtar* — entitling the creditor to collect from heirs even without a written instrument.

*Tanna kamma savar milveh haktuvah batorah lav ke'shtar dami* — the first *tanna* holds that being written in the *Torah* does not elevate the debt to the status of a *shtar*, and therefore it remains an uncollectable oral debt as far as heirs are concerned. *Rabbi Yosei savar k'katuv b'shtar dami* — Rabbi Yosei holds that it does carry that weight.

## Personal Injury Case

### Tosefta on Injury

The *Gemara* now introduces a parallel passage — not a *mishnah* but a *Tosefta* in *Bava Kamma* — that presents the same scenario with a different type of harm. *Hayotzei l'hareg*, someone going out to be executed, *v'chaval b'acherim*, if he injures others — *chayav*, he is liable. *V'acherim shechavlu bo pturim* — if others injure him, they are exempt.

### Cannot Stand Trial

*Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar omer af hu shechaved b'acherim patur* — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees and holds that even if the condemned person injures others, he too is exempt — *shelo nitan l'chazarat amidah b'din*, because he cannot be brought to stand in judgment. The logic is that once a person has been condemned to execution under Jewish law, there is a prohibition against delaying the execution — *einui hadin*. Unlike some legal systems where condemned persons may wait many years, *halacha* regards the prolonged deferral of an executed sentence as its own form of torment. Therefore, it is impermissible to delay the execution in order to bring the condemned person to a separate civil trial. Since he cannot stand trial, the debt — which remains at the oral level — cannot be elevated to a written one by court judgment, and therefore, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds, it cannot be collected from the heirs.

### Reframe to Heirs

*Michlal de'tanna kamma savar nitan l'chazarat amidah b'din?* — Does this imply that the *tanna kamma* of this *Tosefta* holds that the condemned person *can* be brought to a new trial? *Amar Rav Yosef bemilveh al peh goveh min hayorshim kamifligi* — Rav Yosef reapplies his earlier framework. No, everyone agrees the condemned cannot be taken to court. The significance of that agreement is this: if a court case could be held while he is alive, the court's ruling would transform the debt from an oral one into an official written record, and the question of heirs would be resolved. Since that is impossible, everyone accepts that the debt remains at the oral level. The dispute is therefore once again whether an oral debt — or, by Rava's reading, a debt whose source is in the *Torah* — can be collected from heirs at all.

*Tanna kamma savar milveh al peh goveh min hayorshim* — the first *tanna* holds that even without elevation through court proceedings, the oral debt passes to heirs. *V'Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar savar eino goveh min hayorshim* — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds it does not.

Rava once again offers the alternative framing: everyone might agree that a plain oral debt cannot be collected from heirs, and the debate is whether the *Torah*-inscribed obligation changes that. *Tanna kamma savar k'katuv b'shtar dami* — it does. *V'Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar savar lav k'katuv b'shtar dami* — it does not.

It is worth pausing on the broader point the *Gemara* is making. The surface reading of both the *mishnah* and the *Tosefta* suggests a debate about the condemned person's ongoing legal personhood — to what degree does a person who has had judgment passed against him retain the status of a legal actor? The *Gemara* firmly rejects that framing. It insists that the condemned person is entirely a legal entity, fully capable of incurring obligations. The only open question is the technical one of whether debts incurred by a person who subsequently dies — without having had time to produce a written instrument or undergo court proceedings — can be pursued against his heirs.

This is confirmed by the *Gemara*'s treatment of the converse question: why is it that if others injure the condemned person, they are exempt? Here, unlike the question of his obligations to others, *Rashi* does invoke the condemned person's specific legal status. *Rashi* offers two explanations. First, *de'ein lo damim* — he has no monetary value, in a sense, because he is about to be killed; the market-based component of damage assessment breaks down when the injured party is destined for imminent death. The second and more compelling explanation is *ve'omed hu lachavel* — he stands in a position of being killed, meaning there is a *halachic* mandate in place. The court is, as it were, already in the process of injuring him. Someone who injures him in the interim cannot be said to have acted against a person who has full protection of the court. It is specifically because the execution is by a Jewish court that this changes his legal status with respect to receiving compensation. But the *Gemara* confines this reasoning to the question of others' obligations to him — it does not allow this logic to diminish his obligations to others.

The *Gemara* then introduces a *braita* involving a case where someone digs an illegal well in a public domain, an ox falls in and dies, and the digger himself is killed. *Yorshei ba'al habor chayav leshalem dmei shor laba'alim* — the heirs of the well-digger must pay the owner of the ox. This appears to be a case where a debt for damage passes to heirs, which would conflict with the reading of the *mishnah* that denies such collection.

*Amar Rav Ila amar Rav, keshe'amad b'din* — Rav resolves the conflict: we are dealing with a case where the well-digger had already stood in court. Once a court ruling has been entered, the debt is no longer merely oral; it carries the weight of an official record and can be collected from heirs without question.

The *Gemara* objects: *vehargo ktani* — the text says the ox killed him! There was no time for a court case! *Amar Rav Adda bar Ahava, keshe'asa treifa* — it did not kill him outright. The ox dealt a fatal wound, and there was sufficient time for a court case before the man ultimately died.

The *Gemara* presses further: *ve'ha'amar Rav Nachman*, a *tanna* taught that what actually happened was that the man died and was buried simultaneously — the earth from the well's collapse became his grave. There is no room for a court case at all. The *Gemara* therefore resolves: *deyavti dayani apuma deveira* — the judges happened to be sitting right at the edge of the well. Their direct observation of the event functions like testimony, and they were able to issue a ruling before the man died. The resolution is strained, but the *Gemara* insists on it, clearly inclining toward the view that a *Torah*-inscribed debt, or an oral debt in general, does in fact pass to heirs.

## Sacrifice & Execution

### Einui HaDin Principle

The *Gemara* now turns to a *braita* that addresses a related but distinct aspect of the condemned person's legal status: his capacity to receive *kapparah* — atonement — and whether the obligation to bring sacrifices for him can or must be fulfilled. The concern throughout is *einui hadin*, the prohibition against delaying the execution once judgment has been passed.

### Sin Before Death

*Hayotzei l'hareg* — someone going out to be executed. If he had previously sinned *beshogeg* and was obligated to bring a *chatat* or *asham*, the *braita* rules that the sacrifice may be brought for him even while he is condemned. The *chatat* would otherwise become a *chatat shemetu ba'aleha* — a *chatat* whose owner has died — and would have to be put to death. The *asham* would have to wait to develop a *mum*. To avoid this, one brings the sacrifice on his behalf even as he walks to execution. This is consistent with the *Gemara*'s position that he remains a full legal entity.

However, *chata be'otah sha'ah ein nizkakin lo* — if he sins at that very moment, as he is being led to execution — say he impulsively eats *chelev* and thereby incurs a new obligation of *karet* — the *Gemara* rules that no one bothers to bring a sacrifice for that sin.

### Abaye's Challenge

*Amar Rav Yosef mipnei she'ein me'anin es dino* — the reason is that bringing a sacrifice would require a delay, and we do not delay the execution even for the sake of *kapparah*.

*Amar lei Abaye i hachi, afilu reisha nami* — Abaye presses: if the concern is any delay, then even the first case, where the sin occurred long before, should present a problem, since bringing the sacrifice takes time.

### Slaughtered Sacrifice

The *Gemara* resolves: the first case, *reisha*, refers specifically to *kegon shehayah zivcho zavuach be'otah sha'ah* — the sacrifice had already been slaughtered at the moment the report came that the man was being led to execution. The *kohanim*, with the slaughtered animal before them, asked whether to proceed with the sprinkling of the blood, and the answer is yes. There is no postponement whatsoever — the sacrifice is already in progress. But *aval ein zivcho zavuach* — if it had not yet been slaughtered — even for a sin of the past, one does not wait for it to be brought. Such a case becomes equivalent to having sinned at that very moment, and the sacrifice is not brought. The rule, therefore, is that any delay in execution for the sake of *kapparah* is forbidden; only when the sacrifice is already slaughtered is the completion of the process permitted.

## Pregnant Woman Execution

### No Delay for Birth

The *mishnah* now shifts to the case of a pregnant woman condemned to execution. *Ha'isha sheyatza l'hareg, ein mamtinin lah ad sheteled* — a pregnant woman who has been condemned is not held back until she gives birth. The principle of *einui hadin* governs here as well, and the fetus, being part of her body, does not create grounds for postponement.

### Exception in Labor

*Ha'isha sheyashva al hamashber, mamtinin lah ad sheteled* — once she is already sitting on the birthing stool, in active labor, the execution is postponed until after delivery.

### Fetus Independence

*Rashi* explains the reason for this exception: at the moment of active childbirth, the fetus acquires a form of independent identity. Even though full legal personhood requires actual birth — normally marked by the emergence of the head — there is an intermediate stage: the fetus in the process of being born is no longer entirely one with the mother. Since it is no longer simply part of her body, executing her at that moment would entail acting against a distinct entity. Rashi's reading here anticipates the *Gemara*'s own explanation, which we will see shortly.

One might alternatively explain the exception on entirely different grounds — that the extreme physical and psychological experience of childbirth itself negates any sense of *einui hadin*, or that no court would or should execute a woman in the midst of active labor on grounds of basic human dignity, *bizayon*. These explanations make no claim about the independent status of the fetus and remain plausible readings of the *mishnah*. But as the *Gemara* will make explicit, *Rashi*'s interpretation — that the fetus gains independent identity — is the *Gemara*'s own reasoning.

## Abortion & Fetus Status

### Pshita Gufa Hi

The *Gemara* now opens what is perhaps the most consequential discussion on the entire daf, generating its significance in just three words: *pshita gufa hi* — of course, it is her body.

The *mishnah* had stated that a pregnant woman condemned to execution is not held back until delivery. The *Gemara* says this is obvious: the fetus is simply part of her body, and executing her is executing her entirely. There is no independent entity present whose life requires separate consideration.

These three words carry enormous halachic import in the broader debate on abortion. The *Gemara*'s use of *pshita* — indicating that this should go without saying — has been read as a foundational statement about the ontological status of the fetus: it is part of the mother's body, not an independent life. This is not merely an exception created by the mandate of execution; the *Gemara* treats it as self-evident.

This stands in tension with another well-known *Gemara* in *Sanhedrin*, which discusses the case of a woman in labor whose life is endangered, and frames the fetus in terms of *rodef* — one who pursues another's life — suggesting that under ordinary circumstances the fetus cannot simply be removed, and that permission to do so requires the extreme justification of *pikuach nefesh*. If *pshita gufa hi* represents the rule, then the *rodef* formulation represents an extreme and exceptional description. If the *Sanhedrin Gemara* is the rule, then *pshita gufa hi* must be read as applying only in the narrow context of an execution mandate. This is the crux of the halachic debate on abortion.

The weight of *pshita* — the *Gemara*'s frame of presenting the permissibility as obvious — tilts toward the first reading: this *Gemara* presents the baseline, and the fetus is, at its core, part of the mother.

### Father's Interest

*Itztarich* — nevertheless, the *Gemara* says the ruling is needed. *Salka daitach amina*, I might have thought otherwise: *ka'asher yashit alav ba'al ha'isha* — the *Torah* states that if a fetus is accidentally killed in the course of an altercation, the responsible party must pay a fine to the father. *Mamona de'ba'al hu* — the fetus, in some sense, represents the father's financial interest, perhaps even his property. *V'lo lifsadei minei* — one might therefore argue that the father has a right to object to the execution of the fetus, demanding that the court wait until the child is born. The ruling of the *mishnah* is therefore needed to reject that claim.

### Both Shall Die

*Amar Rabbi Abbahu amar Rabbi Yochanan amar kra, u'metu gam shneihem* — they shall both die. This verse, in the context of adultery, is expounded: *l'rabot et havalad* — the word *gam* ("also") includes the child. Even the unborn child of an adulteress is included in the execution, thereby overriding any property claim the father might raise. The *Gemara* resolves a technical objection about the word *shneihem* ("both of them") by locating the derivation specifically in *gam*, attributed to Rabbi Yoshiya's interpretive tradition.

The significance of the *Gemara*'s framing here should not be understated. The *Gemara*'s maximum concern, in raising the possibility that the ruling needed to be stated, is the father's monetary interest in the fetus. It does not raise the fetus's own life as a competing claim. This too carries weight in the abortion discussion: the frame within which the *Gemara* articulates any possible objection is property rights, not the taking of a life.

## Labor & Abortion

### Fetal Abortion Practice

The *Gemara* continues: *yashva al hamashber* — when she is in active labor, execution is postponed. *Mai ta'ama* — why? *Keivan de'akar gufa achrina hu* — once the birth process has begun, the fetus has been "uprooted" and is already a separate entity. This confirms *Rashi*'s earlier explanation: not yet a full person, but no longer simply one with the mother.

The *Gemara* now introduces a ruling attributed to Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel that is striking in its directness. *Ha'isha hayotzei lehareg* — a woman condemned to execution. *Makkin osah keneged beis haherayon kedei sheyamus havalad techilah* — before executing her, one strikes her in the womb so that the fetus dies first.

### Nivul Ha-Meis

The reason given is *kedei shelo tavo lidei nivul* — to prevent *nivul hameis*, degradation of the corpse. The concern is that if the woman is executed while the fetus is alive, the fetus will continue to move and eventually die inside the corpse, which would be degrading to her body.

This ruling is remarkable on several levels. It is not merely permitting the incidental death of the fetus as a consequence of executing the mother. It mandates the direct abortion of the fetus for the sake of the mother's posthumous dignity. One might ask why, if the fetus is viable and near term, a cesarean could not be performed first. The *Gemara*'s implicit answer returns to *me'annin dino* — postponing execution is prohibited. Even a brief delay to save a viable life cannot be countenanced once the execution has been decreed. The father's claim has already been dismissed from the verse. The *Gemara* presents all of this as operating within the framework of *einui hadin*, however difficult that framework may be to accept.

### Order of Death

*Lememra de-hi kadma misa* — the entire concern presupposes that the mother dies first and the fetus survives her momentarily. But *ve-ha kaima lan de-vlad mayis breisha* — is there not a principle that the fetus dies before the mother?

The *Gemara* derives this from a *mishnah* about inheritance: *tinok ben yomo nochel u'manchil* — a child even one day old can inherit and bequeath. *Rav Sheshes* explains that this allows an infant born as his mother dies to inherit her estate and then bequeath it to his paternal half-brothers. But the *Gemara* notes that *davka ben yom echad* — this applies only to a born infant. *Aval ubar lo* — not a fetus. And the reason is not that a fetus lacks legal personhood, but rather that the fetus would always die first — *de-hu mayis breisha* — making it impossible for the inheritance sequence to operate. A son cannot inherit from his mother *ba'kever* — in the grave — if he is already dead.

The *Gemara* then reconciles this with the current ruling: *hani mili legabi misa* — this principle about the fetus dying first applies to natural death. *Aidi de-vlad zutra chayusei, ayal tipa de-malach ha-maves u-mechatech lehu le-simanin* — because the fetus's hold on life is more tenuous, the gradual process of natural dying affects the fetus first, cutting through its *simanim*. *Aval neherag, hi mesa breisha* — but in a violent death, instantaneous and total, this gradual process does not apply, and the mother may well die first, leaving the fetus alive momentarily inside the corpse.

The *Gemara* then notes an apparent contradiction: *v'havai uvda u'parkhas tlas pirchusei* — there were cases in natural death where the fetus was observed thrashing after the mother died. The *Gemara* dismisses this: *midi d'hava adnava d'lata'a* — this is like the tail of a lizard, which continues to move after being severed. Such movement does not indicate life.

## Cesarean on Shabbat

### Cutting Permitted

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: ha'isha sheyashva al hamashber u'meita b'Shabbat* — a woman in labor who dies on Shabbat. *Mevi'in sakin u'mekar'in et kreisah u'motzi'in et havlad* — one brings a knife, performs a cesarean section, and removes the fetus.

### No Melachah

The *Gemara* immediately questions why this needs to be stated: *mai avid, chatikhat basar hu* — what *melachah* is one performing? Cutting into a dead body is not *chavalah*, not a prohibited act of injury. It is simply cutting into flesh. There is no *chillul Shabbat* involved at all, and thus seemingly no novel ruling.

### Violate Shabbat

*Amar Rava lo nitzrecha ela l'havi sakin derech reshut harabim* — Rava explains: the ruling is needed for the case where one must carry the knife through a *reshut harabim*, thereby genuinely violating Shabbat. The ruling teaches that one may violate Shabbat to save the fetus.

*U'mai kamashma lan, d'midi sefeika mechalelinan Shabta* — and the *chiddush* is that we violate Shabbat even for a *safek*, an uncertainty, since the fetus may or may not survive the cesarean.

### Building Collapse

This, however, already seems obvious from a different *mishnah*: *mi shenafela alav mapolet* — if a building collapses on someone, *safek hu sham safek eino sham, safek chai safek meis* — we don't know if the person was inside, and don't know if he is alive — *mefakchin alav et hagal*, one clears the rubble even on Shabbat, despite all the accumulated uncertainty.

*Mahu d'teima: hatam hu d'it lei chazaka d'chiyuta* — one might have thought: there, the person had already established a status of life — *chazakah d'chiyuta* — and we therefore try to preserve it. *Aval hacha d'lo it lei chazaka d'chiyuta me'ikara, eima lo* — but the fetus has never established a status of recognized life. Perhaps we would not violate Shabbat for it. *Kamashma lan* — the ruling teaches that we do.

This formulation opens an important question. The phrase *chazakah d'chiyuta* can be understood in two ways. One reading emphasizes viability: the known-living person had demonstrated he was alive and viable; the fetus has not. On this reading, the ruling simply teaches that even uncertain viability justifies *chillul Shabbat*. The other reading emphasizes legal status: the born person is a recognized halachic person; the fetus is not yet. On this reading, the ruling teaches that even for an entity that has not yet attained full halachic personhood, Shabbat may be violated. Both readings flow from the text, and the question of how far this obligation extends — to a fetus of three months, or even one of less than forty days — is debated among the *rishonim*, with the *Ramban* in *Toras HaAdam* raising it explicitly. The practical *halacha* appears to be that one may violate Shabbat even for a very early-stage pregnancy where there is concern for the fetus's survival.

## Hair of Executed Woman

### Hair Permitted

The *mishnah* concludes with a brief ruling: *ha'isha sheneherga, nehenin bise'arah* — the hair of an executed woman is not subject to *issur hana'ah*. One may derive benefit from it. This stands in contrast to the immediately following ruling: *behema sheneherga, asurah behana'ah* — an animal that has been executed by a court is entirely forbidden for benefit.

### Woven Hair Only

The *Gemara* initially assumes this is about natural hair and raises an obvious question: is not the hair part of her body, which is a *meis* and therefore forbidden? *Amar Rav, be'oma'eret tenu se'ari leviti* — Rav explains that we are dealing with a case where the woman herself declared that her hair should be given to her daughter, thereby indicating it is not part of her body. The *Gemara* objects: *ilu amar tenu yadi leviti, mi yahavinan lah?* If she said give my hand to her daughter, we would not comply — that is clearly part of her body. One cannot simply declare that a limb is not one's body. So Rav clarifies: *be'pe'ah nochrit* — we are speaking of a wig, or more precisely, hair that has been woven into her own hair. Since it is not her natural hair, she has the ability to indicate that it is a separate article, like personal property.

### Apostate City Hair

This raises a parallel question: *ba'ei Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Chanina, se'ar nashim tzidkaniyot, mahu?* — Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Chanina raised the question of the hair of righteous women in an *ir hanidachas*, an apostate city. Those who did not sin must leave and abandon all their property, which is destroyed along with the city. The question is whether this woven-in hair is considered her body — in which case she takes it with her — or her property — in which case it must be left behind.

### Hanging by Peg

*Ve'amar Rava be'pe'ah nochrit kamiba'ya lei* — Rava clarifies that Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Chanina's question too is about the wig, not natural hair. *Ki ka miba'ya lei, detali besichas* — and specifically, his uncertainty concerned hair that was merely hanging by a peg, that is, a loosely attached wig, not hair tightly woven in. Where the hair is fully woven in, the *Gemara* treats it as part of the body by default; only if she explicitly says to give it elsewhere does it become categorized as property. The wig that simply rests on the head, attached loosely, occupies an intermediate status — that was Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Chanina's genuine doubt.

### Hair Doesn't Die

*Kashya lei leRav Nachman bar Yitzchak* — this entire discussion troubled Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, and he resolved it from a different direction. The *mishnah* juxtaposes the woman's hair with the case of an executed animal. *Dedumya debehema katani* — it is structured as a comparison: just as by the animal it is the body itself we speak of, so too by the woman we must be speaking of her body — her natural hair, not a wig.

*Ella amar Rav Nachman, zu misasah osartah ve'zu gmar dinah osartah* — the distinction is between the source of the prohibition. For the animal, the court's ruling itself — *gmar dinah* — creates the *issur hana'ah* from the moment the verdict is delivered, before the animal is even executed. The entire animal, including its wool, is encompassed by that ruling. For a human being, there is no *issur hana'ah* that attaches during her lifetime as a result of the verdict. The prohibition on deriving benefit from a human body arises only from death itself.

Why, then, does the prohibition of death not apply to her hair? *Rashi* draws out the implicit logic: hair does not die. The experience of death that creates *issur hana'ah* applies to living tissue. Hair, however, is in a sense already inert — new hair grows, but the hair shaft itself is not living tissue in the same biological sense. Death therefore does not occur to the hair, and the prohibition that stems from death does not apply to it.

This emerges as the *halacha*: the hair of a deceased woman is permitted for benefit, because hair does not share in the experience of the body's death, while the body of an executed animal is entirely forbidden, because the court's ruling — not merely death — is the source of its prohibition, and that ruling encompasses the entire animal from the moment it is issued.

*Hadran alach kol hame'arus* — what a *daf*.

# Arakhin 9

## Intro & Mishna

### Yesterday's Nida

We begin Daf 9 by picking up with the *mishna* at the bottom of 8b. For those who were present yesterday, the preceding *mishna* dealt with a woman whose *nida* status is uncertain — specifically the complex question of *petach betoch pitchai nida* — which represents one of the most mathematically demanding areas of *halacha*. This connects naturally to a well-known *mishna* at the end of the third *perek* of *Pirkei Avot*, which states: *kinim upitchai nida hen hen gufei halachot* — that *kinim* and *pitchai nida* are the very substance of *halacha*, genuinely difficult and requiring rigorous analysis. The *mishna* adds that *tkufot ugmatriot parparot lachochma* — questions of astronomical seasons and numerical calculations are more like spices, not as essential. This is worth noting both because it acknowledges the difficulty of yesterday's *mishna* and because the topic of *tkufot* touches directly on the *mishna* before us today.

### Rosh Chodesh Topic

Today's *sugya* concerns *Rosh Chodesh* and the permissible range of variation in the number of *malei* and *chaseir* months — full and lacking months — within a given year. This is another challenging piece of Talmudic reasoning, and the entire *gemara* on this *daf* will be devoted to it.

### Mishna Text

The *mishna* states: *ein pochin me'arba'a chodashim hame'ubarim bashana* — one may not have fewer than four full (*me'ubarim*, literally "pregnant") months in a year. The *mishna* continues: *velo nireh yeter al shmona* — and it did not appear appropriate, as the *gemara* will explain (*lo nireh lachachamim*), to have more than eight. So the range is: no fewer than four full months, no more than eight. This permitted variation — two on each side of the standard — is the entire focus of the *gemara* that follows.

### Lunar Structure

The underlying structure of the lunar calendar must be understood first. A lunar month is approximately 29 and a half days — slightly more, as *Rashi* notes. Since a month must be a whole number of days, months alternate between 29 and 30 days in order to approximate this 29.5-day cycle.

### Standard Year

In a standard Hebrew year, there are six months of 29 days (*chaseir*, lacking) and six months of 30 days (*malei*, full, also called *me'ubar*). This six-and-six structure perfectly represents the 29.5-day average.

### Permitted Range

The *mishna* permits a variation of two from that standard. You may have as few as four full months — two fewer than the standard six — and no more than eight full months — two more than the standard six. The *gemara* will explain why exactly this degree of variation is tolerable and why going beyond it is not.

### Secondary Cases

The rest of the *mishna* enumerates other cases following the same "no fewer than X, no more than Y" pattern, though the *gemara* does not analyze them in depth. The *shtei halechem* — the two loaves brought on *Shavuot* — may not be eaten fewer than two days after baking, nor more than three days after. The reasoning: one does not bake the *shtei halechem* on *Shavuot* itself, even though it is *Yom Tov*, because the baking does not override *Shavuot*. Therefore, in a standard year, it is baked on *erev Shavuot* — day one — and brought on *Shavuot* — day two. If *erev Shavuot* falls on *Shabbat*, then it is baked on *erev Shabbat* — day one — and brought on *Shavuot* — day three. Hence the range of two to three days.

The *lechem hapanim* — the showbread placed on the *shulchan* in the *Beit Hamikdash* — is not eaten fewer than nine days after baking, nor more than eleven. One does not bake the *lechem hapanim* on *Shabbat*. In the standard case, it is baked on Friday (day one), placed on the *shulchan* on *Shabbat* (day two), and eaten the following *Shabbat* (day nine, counting the day of baking as day one). How does one reach eleven? If the two days before *Shabbat* are the two days of *Rosh Hashanah* — which carries two days of *Yom Tov* even in *Eretz Yisrael* — then since one does not bake on *Yom Tov* for bread that will only be eaten nine days later, the baking is pushed back to *erev Yom Tov*, adding two days and yielding a total of eleven.

One should note a sharp question that arises here: if Thursday is *Rosh Hashanah*, then the following *Shabbat* would be *Yom Kippur*, on which eating the *lechem hapanim* would be problematic. The resolution is that the two-day *Rosh Hashanah* in the time of the *Beit Hamikdash* was structured differently from our own: the second day was the actual 1st of *Tishrei*, while the first day was the 30th of *Elul*. Accordingly, Thursday as the first day of *Rosh Hashanah* means it is the 30th of *Elul*, making *Yom Kippur* fall on *Shabbat* — not on the Friday immediately following. The question was very nearly perfect.

### Brit Milah Rules

A *katan* is not given a *brit milah* fewer than eight days after birth — the day of birth itself being counted as day one, so the *milah* occurs on the same day of the week one week later. The maximum is twelve days. How does one reach twelve? If a baby is born during *bein hashmashot* on Friday night — the twilight period between Friday and *Shabbat* — the *brit milah* cannot be performed on Friday, because perhaps he was born on *Shabbat* and Friday would be too early; nor on *Shabbat*, because perhaps he was born on Friday and a *brit* on any day other than the eighth does not override *Shabbat*. Therefore, the *brit* is performed on Sunday. Counting Friday as day one, *Shabbat* is day two, the following *Shabbat* is day nine, and Sunday is day ten. If that Sunday and Monday happen to be two days of *Yom Tov*, the *brit* cannot be performed then either, pushing it to day twelve. That is the range of eight to twelve.

---

## Why Not Nine?

### Rav Huna's Limit

The *gemara* opens its analysis by clarifying the *mishna*'s ambiguous phrase *lo nireh*. *Rav Huna* states: *lo nira lachachamim le'aber yeter al shmonah* — it did not appear proper to the Sages to have more than eight full months. This is the plain reading: the permissible range is four to eight.

### Nine Full Problem

The *gemara* immediately asks: *mai shna tisha delo* — why not nine? The answer: *de'im ken kadim asi sira tlata yomei* — because then the new moon would appear three days before *Rosh Hashanah*. The arithmetic is straightforward. The standard is six full months. If you have nine full months — three more than standard — you have pushed *Rosh Hashanah* forward three days relative to when the *molad* actually occurs. The new moon would thus be visible three days before *Rosh Hashanah*, making a mockery of the calendar: people would be observing *Rosh Hashanah* three days after seeing the new moon.

### Two Days & Leap

But the *gemara* presses further: if three days is clearly unacceptable, what about two extra full months — i.e., eight full months — which would push *Rosh Hashanah* two days past the *molad*? *Kadimati terei yomei* — you would still see the new moon two days before *Rosh Hashanah*. Is that acceptable?

### Mesharshiya Fix

The *gemara* answers by citing *Rav Mesharshiya*: *kegon shehayeta shana me'uberet* — we are speaking of a case where the year (or the previous year) was a leap year, a *shana me'uberet*. The significance of this is as follows: when a leap year is declared and an extra month is added, that extra month must represent a 29.5-day lunar cycle. But it can only be expressed as either 29 or 30 days. If the extra month is made 29 days, the calendar is effectively pulled back by half a day relative to where it would have been with a precise 29.5-day cycle. This half-day correction partially offsets the two-day error produced by the eight full months.

### Offset Correction

The practical result: what would have been a two-day discrepancy between *Rosh Hashanah* and the *molad* is reduced to one and a half days. Is a day-and-a-half error tolerable? The *gemara* acknowledges there is still a discrepancy — *lo adatei de'inshei* — but people are not paying close enough attention for an error of a day or a day and a half to be glaringly obvious. Three days would be unmistakable; a day and a half can pass unnoticed.

It is important to clarify what is meant by "correction" here. The system is not saying: if you have too many full months, simply add more lacking months. That would merely be restoring the six-and-six balance, which is what we started with. The question is how much deviation from six-and-six is permissible. The answer is that two days of deviation is permissible precisely because in a leap year scenario — where the extra month is made 29 days rather than 30 — the true discrepancy is only one and a half days, which falls within the range of human tolerance. There is no way to correct for the remaining half-day until the next leap year, since one cannot express a half-day difference through any single month's adjustment.

---

## Ulla Position

### Ulla Reformulation

*Ulla* offers a reformulation: *lo nira lachachamim lechaser yeter mishmona* — the Sages did not see fit to have more than eight *chaseir* (lacking) months. This is not a new ruling but a restatement of the *mishna*'s other limit — the minimum of four full months — expressed from the opposite direction. One cannot have fewer than four full months because that would mean having more than eight lacking months.

### Eight Lacking

The *gemara* explains why more than eight lacking months is problematic: *de'im ken lihavei saira tlata yomei* — the moon would then appear three days after *Rosh Hashanah*. Just as too many full months push *Rosh Hashanah* ahead of the *molad*, too many lacking months push *Rosh Hashanah* behind it. With nine lacking months — three more than the standard six — *Rosh Hashanah* would occur three days before the new moon actually appears.

Eight lacking months, by the same logic, would produce a two-day gap — *Rosh Hashanah* occurring two days before the new moon is visible. The *gemara* again applies *Rav Mesharshiya*'s correction: *kegon dehavya shana shelifneha meuberet* — if the previous year was a leap year, and this time the extra month was made 30 days (rather than 29), then the leap month pushed the calendar forward by half a day beyond the precise cycle. This partially offsets the two-day deficit, reducing it to one and a half days.

In this scenario, the situation is actually somewhat more tolerable than in the previous case. Here, *Rosh Hashanah* occurs before the new moon is visible. On the night of *Rosh Hashanah*, one looks up at the sky and sees — nothing. The old moon has set and the new crescent has not yet appeared. This is not as jarring as seeing a bright new moon the night before *Rosh Hashanah*, because the absence of the moon on *Rosh Hashanah* night can be explained: perhaps in *Yerushalayim* witnesses did see it, perhaps clouds obscured it elsewhere. *Savri itchazi itchazyei ve'anan lav adatin* — people assume it was seen and they simply did not notice. This explains why the *gemara* frames this case as more forgivable: a one-day-early *Rosh Hashanah* (where the sky is dark) is more easily rationalized than a one-day-late one (where a new crescent is already visible).

### Tolerance Rationale

This also clarifies the asymmetry between the two tolerance explanations offered. In the case of too many full months (eight *malei*), the new moon has already been seen for a day before *Rosh Hashanah* — this requires the weaker explanation of *lav adatei de'inshei*, that people are generally inattentive. In the case of too many lacking months (eight *chaseir*), the sky on *Rosh Hashanah* night is dark — this is explained by *savri itchazi*, a more natural and plausible rationalization. The *gemara* thus provides different but complementary justifications for why each direction of error remains within tolerable bounds, so long as the discrepancy does not exceed a day and a half.

A sharp question arises here: what happens if *beit din* finds itself already at the limit of eight *malei* or eight *chaseir* months, and the witnesses continue to arrive late? Can *beit din* simply declare the month on its own authority, without witnesses, to prevent the calendar from exceeding the permitted range? The *gemara* implies that in extremis, *beit din* may indeed do so — which is, of course, the basis of our fixed calendar today. The witnesses and their testimony are the preferred mechanism, and the system is largely self-correcting (a late declaration one month tends to be offset the following month), but when genuine correction is needed and the testimony cannot be relied upon, *beit din* acts on its own authority.

---

## Leap Year Dispute

### 30-Day Leap

At this point the *gemara* asks: *b'mai kamifligi* — what exactly is the dispute between *Rav Huna* and *Ulla*? After all, both seem to be saying the same thing — variation between four and eight — just from opposite ends. The *gemara* points to a dispute in a *baraita* about the length of the leap month. The first opinion: *kama ibur shana* — how long is the month added in a leap year? *Lamed* — 30 days.

### RSbG Flexible

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* says: it can simply be a *chodesh* — a month — meaning either 29 or 30 days, as with any other month.

### Seven vs Eight

This dispute is precisely what divides *Rav Huna* and *Ulla*. The entire argument for tolerating eight full months rests on the correction provided by a leap year whose extra month is made 29 days: that 29-day representation of a 29.5-day cycle pulls the calendar back half a day, reducing the apparent two-day error to one and a half days. But if the extra month of a leap year must always be 30 days — as the first opinion holds — then this half-day correction is never available. Making a 30-day month for the leap year pushes the calendar in the other direction. Accordingly, if the leap month is always 30 days, the maximum tolerable deviation is not eight full months but seven. Seven full months, combined with a 30-day leap correction pushing half a day forward, reduces the net error to half a day above one — that is, one and a half days — which is tolerable. But eight would produce a two-day error with no available correction, which is not. *Ulla*, who holds that the maximum is effectively seven full months (since eight can never be corrected), reads the *mishna*'s statement about not going beyond eight as referring to *chaseir* months — because only on that side of the equation does a correction mechanism exist in his framework.

Why does the first opinion require the leap month to always be 30 days? The *baraita* does not elaborate, though one might suggest it reflects a presumption that a standard month, by default, is 30 days — hence the terminology *malei* for a 30-day month and *chaseir* for a 29-day month. A 29-day month is the "lacking" one; when adding an extra month, one adds a full one. But the precise rationale is not discussed in the *gemara*.

---

## RH & Pesach

### Shavuot Fixed

The *gemara* now explores the relationship between *Rosh Hashanah* and *Pesach* through a *baraita*: *ein Atzeret chala ela b'yom hanaf* — *Shavuot* falls only on the day of the waving of the *omer*. This is self-evident: *Sefirat HaOmer* is counted for seven full weeks beginning with the waving, and *Shavuot* always falls on the fiftieth day — which is always the same day of the week as the second day of *Pesach* when one began counting. Add seven weeks to the second day of *Pesach* and you return to the same day of the week; *Shavuot* is structurally fixed to that day.

### RH Dates

The *baraita* continues: *Rosh Hashanah* falls only on *yom hanaf* — the same day of the week as the second day of *Pesach* — or on *le'or iburo* — the day following the 30th of *Nissan*, meaning the day after. In other words, *Rosh Hashanah* falls either on the same day of the week as the second day of *Pesach* or one day later — i.e., on the second or third day of *Pesach*.

### Math Proof

The arithmetic is straightforward. The first day of *Nissan* falls on the same day of the week as the second day of *Pesach* (since the 15th of *Nissan* is *Pesach*, and 14 days before is the 1st — both fall on the same day of the week). Between *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* and *Rosh Hashanah* are six months. On average, each month deviates from a perfect number of weeks by one and a half days (since months alternate between 29 and 30 days, averaging 29.5, while a full week is 7 days: 28 is 4 weeks, leaving 1.5 days). Six months times one and a half days equals nine days. Subtract one full week (seven days) and you are left with two days. *Rosh Hashanah* therefore falls two days after the day of *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* — which is the same as the third day of *Pesach*. If, however, one of those six months is a *chaseir* rather than a *malei* month, it pulls the total back by one day, landing *Rosh Hashanah* on the second day of *Pesach*. In our fixed calendar, those six months always consist of exactly three *malei* and three *chaseir*, producing a standard two-day offset — that is, *Rosh Hashanah* on the third day of *Pesach*.

### At Bash Gar

*Rashi* records a powerful mnemonic that captures this relationship and extends it across the entire Jewish calendar year. The device is *at bash gar* — an *at-bash* pairing of the days of *Pesach* with the holidays they correspond to:

The first day of *Pesach* corresponds to *Tisha B'Av* — they always fall on the same day of the week. The second day of *Pesach* is *Shavuot*. The third day of *Pesach* is *Rosh Hashanah* — as proven above. The fourth day of *Pesach* is *Kriat HaTorah*, meaning *Simchat Torah*: this follows because *Rosh Hashanah* (day 1 of *Tishrei*) is the third day of *Pesach*, and the eighth day of *Sukkot* falls on the same day of the week as *Rosh Hashanah*, so the ninth day — *Simchat Torah* — is one day later, which is the fourth day of *Pesach*. The fifth day of *Pesach* corresponds to *Yom Kippur*: *Rosh Hashanah* is the third day of *Pesach*, and *Yom Kippur* is ten days later — which lands on the fifth day of *Pesach* plus seven (one week), equaling the fifth day plus three, i.e., the fifth day of *Pesach* itself. The sixth day of *Pesach* is *Purim*, which can be derived by counting back from *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*. And to complete the picture: the seventh day of *Pesach* corresponds to *Yom Ha'atzmaut*.

---

## Acheirim Fixed

### 2nd or 3rd Only

The *baraita*'s limitation of *Rosh Hashanah* to the second or third day of *Pesach* — and not the fourth — creates a problem for both *Rav Huna* and *Ulla*. Even *Ulla*, who limits full months to seven, would allow one extra full month; if that extra full month falls in the six months between *Pesach* and *Rosh Hashanah*, it would push *Rosh Hashanah* a day forward to the fourth day of *Pesach*. And *Rav Huna* would permit two extra full months, potentially shifting *Rosh Hashanah* even further. So how can the *baraita* flatly restrict *Rosh Hashanah* to only two possible days?

### Four Days Only

The *gemara* resolves this: *ha mani acherim hi* — this *baraita* follows the position of *Acheirim*, elsewhere identified as *Rebbi Meir*. The *baraita* of *Acheirim* states: *ein bein atzeret l'atzeret v'ein bein Rosh Hashanah l'Rosh Hashanah ela arba'ah yamim bilvad* — between one *Shavuot* and the next, and between one *Rosh Hashanah* and the next, there are only exactly four days. *Acheirim* holds that the calendar is entirely fixed, with no permissible variation from the six-and-six norm. On this view, there are never extra *malei* or extra *chaseir* months — the calendar is precise — and therefore *Rosh Hashanah* can only fall on the second or third day of *Pesach*, corresponding to one lacking month or zero extra months in the intervening six.

### Four Day Math

The figure of four days follows from the mathematics of a perfect lunar year. A lunar month averages 29.5 days. Over twelve months, that yields 354 days. Dividing 354 by 7 gives 50 weeks and 4 days. So from one year to the next, the calendar advances exactly four days of the week. This is derived more simply as follows: each month deviates from an exact number of weeks by 1.5 days on average. Twelve months times 1.5 days equals 18 days. Subtract two full weeks (14 days) and the remainder is four. Hence the four-day shift from one *Rosh Hashanah* to the next.

*Acheirim*'s system is thus entirely fixed: the calendar never deviates from six *malei* and six *chaseir*, and the four-day rule always holds. This implies, as *Rav Adda bar Abba* points out to *Rava*, that *Acheirim* is teaching something significant: *d'lo ba'inan mitzva l'kadesh al pi re'iya* — we do not require, as an absolute necessity, that the month be sanctified through the testimony of witnesses. *Acheirim* holds that *beit din* will set the month correctly on its own authority when necessary, ensuring that the calendar never deviates. This is, of course, the very principle underlying our fixed calendar today.

### Adar Correction

But how does *Acheirim* handle a leap year?
