If the variation from one *Rosh Hashanah* to the next in a regular year is exactly four days, adding a leap month (*Adar Sheni*) will add more days. *Rav Mesharshiya* explains: *kegon shehayta shana me'uberet ibur shana lamed yom* — if it was a leap year and the extra *Adar* was made 30 days. According to *Acheirim*, this 30-day extra month, combined with what should be a standard year, would create a six-day gap from one *Rosh Hashanah* to the next. To correct this, *dal yarcha l'vadei yarcha* — one removes a month for a month: one of the subsequent 30-day months is made 29 days instead. This pulls *Rosh Hashanah* back by one day, from the third day of *Pesach* to the second day. This is precisely why the *baraita* says *Rosh Hashanah* falls on *yom hanaf* (the second day of *Pesach*) — this is the corrected scenario following a 30-day leap month. *Acheirim*'s system is thus not absolutely rigid in every single year, but it maintains strict control: deviations introduced by leap years must be immediately corrected in the months that follow, so that the gap between *Rosh Hashanahs* never exceeds five days. The key principle is that *beit din* will actively manage the calendar rather than waiting for witnesses to determine it.

---

## Ravina Objection

### Exact Cycle

*Ravina* raises a fundamental objection to the claim that the gap between one *Rosh Hashanah* and the next is always exactly four days. As *Rashi* notes — counting seven lines from the bottom of the relevant passage — the true gap between years is not four days precisely, but four days, eight hours, and 876 *chalakim*. A *chelek* is one 1080th of an hour, so 876 *chalakim* represents approximately 876/1080 of an hour — roughly 0.8 of an hour. The reason 1080 is used as the base unit is that it is highly divisible, allowing clean fractional representation. The total annual remainder beyond four days is therefore approximately 8.8 hours. This arises because the true lunar month is not exactly 29.5 days but slightly more, and the accumulated excess over twelve months, beyond the four-day figure, comes to this additional 8-plus hours.

### Long Cycles

These extra hours accumulate over time. Since the daily remainder beyond four days is roughly 8 hours, every three years the accumulated excess reaches approximately 24 hours — an additional full day. Every 30 years, the smaller fractional excess (the *chalakim* beyond the eight hours) likewise accumulates to an additional day. So over longer cycles, the gap between one *Rosh Hashanah* and the next is not always four days — sometimes it is five.

---

## Ravina Objection (II)

### Five Days Some

The *gemara* responds to *Ravina*'s objection: *keivan delaisa bechol shata lo kachashiv* — since this extra day does not occur every year, *Acheirim* did not count it. The statement that the gap is four days is meant as the standard case; in some years, the accumulated hours will indeed produce a five-day gap rather than four. *Acheirim*'s principle describes the norm, not an invariable rule.

---

## Shmuel Year

### 354 Days Base

*Shmuel* holds like *Rav Huna* — that the calendar may vary between four and eight full months — and his statement about the length of a lunar year confirms this. The calculation: twelve months times 30 days each gives 360 days, but since six of those months are *chaseir* and lose one day each, the true standard is 360 minus 6 equals 354 days. A perfect lunar year is 354 days.

### 352-356 Range

*Shmuel* states: *ein shenat levana pechuta mishlosh me'ot vachamishim ushnayim yom velo yeteira al shlosh me'ot vachamishim veshisha yom* — a lunar year is no fewer than 352 days and no more than 356. Two extra *malei* months add two days to the standard 354, yielding 356. Two extra *chaseir* months subtract two days, yielding 352. One extra of each cancels out, leaving 354. The range of 352 to 356 directly corresponds to the permissible variation of four to eight full months in a year.

### Nazir 354

A *baraita* tests this: if someone takes a vow of *nezirus* for the duration of a solar year (*kiyemot hachama*), he counts 365 days; if he vows for a lunar year (*kiyemot halevana*), he counts 354 days. But if a lunar year can be as long as 356 days, why does he not count 356 to be safe? The *gemara* answers: *binedarim halach achar leshon benei adam* — in matters of vows, one follows common speech and the majority of years. Most people, when referring to a lunar year, mean the standard 354-day year, and so that is the operative figure for purposes of *nedarim*.

---

## Rabbi's 9 Lacking

### Nine Lacking Act

The *gemara* records a striking historical incident: *ma'aseh ve'asa Rebbi tish'a chaseirim* — there was an incident in which *Rebbi* (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) implemented nine lacking months in a single year. This exceeded the stated limit of eight. Yet remarkably, *venira chodesh bizmano* — the new moon appeared precisely at the right time: *Rosh Hashanah* coincided exactly with the *molad*. *Rebbi* was astonished. How could nine lacking months have produced a perfectly timed *Rosh Hashanah*?

### Two Full + Leap

*Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi*, his son, offered the explanation: *shema shana me'uberet hayta* — perhaps last year was a leap year, and *ibur shana lamed yom* — the added month of that leap year was made 30 days. Furthermore, in the previous year, *asinu shenayim mele'im* — two extra full months had been declared. The result: last year's calendar was running two and a half days ahead. Two extra full months pushed *Rosh Hashanah* two days forward; a 30-day leap month (representing a true 29.5-day cycle) pushed it forward an additional half day. The cumulative error was two and a half days ahead of where the *molad* actually fell.

### 3 Lacking Fix

To correct this accumulated error, *Rebbi* declared nine lacking months in the current year — three more *chaseir* months than the standard six, rather than the usual maximum of two. Three extra lacking months pulled the calendar back by three days. *Da telasa levahadei telasa* — three against three: the three days of correction exactly offset the two-and-a-half-day excess of the previous year, with the slight remainder absorbed within the system's tolerance. *Vekam lei beduchta* — and the calendar was restored precisely to its correct position, which is why the new moon appeared exactly on *Rosh Hashanah*.

### RSbR Confirms

*Rebbi* responded to his son: *ner Yisrael, kein haya* — "Light of Israel, that is indeed what happened." The incident demonstrates two important principles. First, nine lacking months — while beyond the ordinarily stated limit — is permissible when correction of the calendar demands it; the limits of four to eight describe normal operation, not an absolute constraint in cases of deliberate calendrical correction. Second, the incident confirms *Rav Huna*'s position that a calendar can legitimately include two extra full months in a year, since *Rebbi* accepted last year's declaration of *shenayim mele'im* as valid. The parameters of 352 to 356 days, and the range of four to eight full months, reflect the real boundaries of the lunar calendar as it operates — boundaries that *Rebbi* himself navigated with mastery.

---

---

# Arakhin 10

## Intro: Trumpets & Instru…

### Opening Remarks

Daf 10 opens with the *mishna*, and the shift is immediately palpable — after the demanding material of the previous daf, involving *pitchei nida* and the calendar calculations of months, we now enter considerably more accessible and, as will become clear, remarkably relevant terrain. The topics of this *mishna* touch on questions that remain very much alive in Jewish practice today.

### Trumpet Blasts Range

The *mishna* opens: *Ein pochtin me-esrim v'achas teki'os ba-mikdash* — there would be no fewer than twenty-one trumpet blasts in the *mikdash*, and *v'lo mosifin al arba'im u-shmonah* — no more than forty-eight. These are not *shofar* blasts but *chatzotzrot* blasts, the priestly trumpets sounded in connection with the Temple service.

### Seven Sets Structure

To understand the range, one must recognize that every blast comes in a set of three: *tekiah*, *teruah*, *tekiah*. The minimum of twenty-one blasts thus represents seven such sets, and the maximum of forty-eight represents sixteen sets. What are the standard seven? One set accompanies the opening of the gates at the start of the day. Three sets are sounded at the *tamid shel shachar* — the morning daily offering — specifically during the three pauses in the Levitical song. And three sets accompany the *tamid shel bein ha-arbayim*, the afternoon daily offering. Those seven sets, representing twenty-one blasts, constitute the baseline for any ordinary day in the *mikdash*.

### Additional Days & Occasi…

The number expands on special occasions. On *Erev Shabbat*, two additional sets are sounded: one to signal the approaching *Shabbat* and give people in the fields time to cease their activities and return, and one at the precise onset of *Shabbat* itself — bringing the total to nine sets. On a *Yom Tov* with a *korban musaf*, three more sets are added, reaching twelve. Notably, when *Erev Shabbat* coincides with *Yom Tov*, those two additional *Erev Shabbat* blasts are still sounded, since work must cease before *Shabbat* even when *Yom Tov* immediately precedes it.

The maximum of sixteen sets — forty-eight blasts — is reached on *Sukkot*, where the special ritual of *nisuch ha-mayim*, the water libation, was accompanied by additional blasts: one when the upper gate was opened for the procession descending from the *Beit Hamikdash* to draw the water, one when the lower gate was opened, one when the water was drawn, and one when it was poured upon the *mizbeiach*. Those four extra sets, added to the twelve of an *Erev Shabbat Yom Tov*, yield sixteen sets on *Erev Shabbat* of *Sukkot* — forty-eight blasts in total. This is spelled out in the *mishna* in *Sukkah*.

### Harps & Flutes Numbers

The *mishna* continues with the musical instruments that accompanied the Levitical song. *Ein pochtin mishnei nevalim v'lo mosifin al shisha* — there would be no fewer than two lyres and no more than six. *Rashi* notes that the reason for these limits is not explained, and he candidly says *lo nitparesh ta'ama* — he does not know why. *Tosafot* likewise offers nothing, which is itself striking.

Regarding the flute: *ein pochtin mishnei chalilin v'lo mosifin al shneim asar* — no fewer than two flutes and no more than twelve. *Rashi* explains that the upper limit of twelve corresponds to the twelve special days per year on which the flute was played — which the *mishna* is about to enumerate. *Rashi* holds that the flute was played exclusively on those twelve days, and on no others. The *Rambam* implies a different reading: that flutes were played on other days as well, but perhaps on these twelve days the flute played in a solo capacity to distinguish them.

### Twelve Days of Flute

The *mishna* states: *u-vishneim asar yom ba-shanah ha-chalil makeh lifnei ha-mizbeiach* — the flute would play before the altar on twelve special days of the year. *Rashi* notes that the word *makeh* — literally "strikes" — refers to the tapping of the fingers over the holes of the flute, and hence the playing of the flute is described this way.

### Twelve Days Listed

What are the twelve days? *Shechitat ha-pesach rishon v'shechitat ha-pesach sheini* — the bringing of the *korban pesach* on the fourteenth of *Nisan* (*pesach rishon*) and on the fourteenth of *Iyar* (*pesach sheini*), *v'yom tov ha-rishon shel pesach* — the first day of *Pesach*, *u-v'yom tov shel atzeret* — *Shavuot*, and *u-vishmonat yemei ha-chag* — the eight days of *Sukkot*. That is eight days for the *shalosh regalim* plus two occasions of bringing the *korban pesach*, totaling twelve.

### Flute Days = Hallel Days

Bracketing the two days of *korban pesach* for a moment, the remaining ten days — the first day of *Pesach*, *Shavuot*, and all eight days of *Sukkot* — immediately call to mind the days on which *Hallel* is recited. The question that will drive the *Gemara*'s discussion is why only the first day of *Pesach* and all eight days of *Sukkot*, rather than every day of *Pesach* as well. The *Gemara* will make this connection explicit: the days on which the flute is played correspond to the days on which *Hallel* is recited — and the *Gemara* will analyze that correspondence in depth.

### Flute Materials & Players

The *mishna* adds that they would not use a copper flute — *v'lo haya makeh be-avuv shel nechoshet* — but rather a reed flute — *ella be-avuv shel kaneh* — because the reed produced a more beautiful, mellifluous sound. The *mishna* also states *v'lo haya machlit ella be-avuv yachidi*: the conclusion of the flute playing — the coda, as it were, the moment that brought closure to the musical passage — would be done with a solo flute. Although twelve flutes might be playing together, the final phrase was left to a single instrument alone, *mipnei she-hu machlit yafeh* — because it made for a beautiful ending.

### Musicians' Status

Who actually played the musical instruments? The *mishna*'s answer is striking: *v'avdei kohanim hayu* — they were the slaves of the *kohanim*. The primary mode of the Levitical musical service was, after all, *ikar shirah b'peh* — the song itself, which was vocal — and the instrumental accompaniment was not limited to *Levi'im*. That the slaves of the *kohanim* performed this function is surprising. While slaves of *kohanim* are considered part of the priestly household in certain respects — they eat *terumah*, for instance — one would not ordinarily imagine them playing a role inside the sacred precincts.

The *mishna* also mentions two Israelite families, from the places referred to as Pagrim and Tzipara, who came from the town of Ammaus. These families were of distinguished *yichus*, such that *kohanim* would marry their daughters — *mesi'in li-khuna*. The precise significance of this detail is worth noting: the point may simply be that they were families of recognized lineage and standing, whose proximity to the *kohanim* made their presence in the *mikdash* in a musical role intelligible — or it may be that the marital connection to *kohanim* gave them a more formal association with the priestly household. These two readings carry different weight: the former takes *mesi'in li-khuna* as merely a testimony to their *yichus*, while the latter treats it as the operative rationale for their participation.

### Rabbi Chanina: Levites

*Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos* offers a different position entirely: *Levi'im hayu* — the musicians were *Levi'im*. This is a simple factual assertion that pushes back on the assumption that it was non-*Levi'im* who filled this role. The question of who actually performed the instrumental music in the *Beit Hamikdash* thus remains genuinely contested, and one might wonder whether archaeology has shed any light on the matter.

---

## Tekiah-Teruah-Tekiah Unit

### Mishna vs. Rabbi Yehuda

The *Gemara* opens its analysis with the observation that *masnisin d'lo ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — the counting method of our *mishna*, which enumerates the blasts individually as twenty-one to forty-eight, does not follow the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*. A *baraita* records that *Rabbi Yehuda omer ha-pochet lo yifchos mi-sheva ve-ha-mosif lo yosif al shesh esrei* — the minimum is seven and the maximum is sixteen. This is in fact the same range as the *mishna*, except *Rabbi Yehuda* counts each set of *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* as a single unit rather than three.

### One Unit vs. Three Units

The conceptual dispute, then, is whether *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* constitutes one indivisible unit or three separate units. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *tekiah teruah u-tekiah chada hi* — it is one unit. The *Rabbanan* hold *tekiah l'chudei u-teruah l'chudei ve-tekiah l'chudei* — each of the three is distinct.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Proofs

What is *Rabbi Yehuda*'s reasoning? He draws on the grammatical tension in two *pesukim*. One verse says *u-tekatem teruah* — using the verb of *tekiah* to describe the act of *teruah*. Another verse says *teruah yitka'u* — using the verb of *tekiah* with *teruah* as its subject. The mixing of the verb associated with one sound with the noun of another, *Rabbi Yehuda* argues, reveals that these sounds are conceptually unified. If they were truly separate units, each would carry its own distinct verbal form. The intermingling of verb and noun across the two types of blasts demonstrates that *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* is a single composite unit — one sound with distinct internal components.

### Rabbanan's Proofs

The *Rabbanan* counter with a verse describing the gathering of the camp: *u-ve-hak-hil et ha-kahal titke'u ve-lo tari'u* — when assembling the congregation, one sounds a *tekiah* without a *teruah*. This shows that a *tekiah* can stand entirely alone, independent of a *teruah*. And if a *tekiah* can exist as a self-sufficient act, it must be considered a distinct unit. The *Rabbanan* further derive from the interplay of the same two verses that a *tekiah* precedes every *teruah* and a *tekiah* follows it — but they insist this is structural information about the sequence, not proof that the three constitute a single unit.

Why, the *Rabbanan* argue, would the Torah ever command performing half of a unit? *De-i salka dachtatich tekiah teruah u-tekiah chada hi, amar Rachmana avid palga de-mitzvah* — if *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* were one indivisible unit, then the Torah, by directing a *tekiah* alone for the gathering of the camp, would be instructing the performance of only half a unit.

### Yehuda's Reply

*Rabbi Yehuda* responds: *simana b'alma hu* — the lone *tekiah* for gathering the camp is not a formal ritual act at all. It is merely a signal, the equivalent of an announcement. Because it is not a halakhic sound in the full ritual sense, the fact that a *tekiah* can be used alone in that context does not prove that a *tekiah* is a self-contained halakhic unit. Only where we are dealing with something ritualized — a formally constituted act, not a loudspeaker — does the full composite of *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* apply, and there it is one unit.

### No Interruption Rule

The *Gemara* now turns to practical implications. The question is raised: *ke-man azla ha de-amar Rav Kahana* — whose position does *Rav Kahana*'s statement follow?

### Rav Kahana's Statement

*Rav Kahana* states: *ein bein tekiah le-teruah ve-lo klum* — there cannot be even the smallest interruption between *tekiah* and *teruah*. They must flow one into the other without any pause whatsoever — essentially in a single breath. The *Gemara* identifies this as following *Rabbi Yehuda*: if *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* is one unit, one sound, then any break within it is a disruption of the sound itself.

### Rabbi Yochanan Rosh Hash…

The *Gemara* then asks: is *Rav Kahana*'s statement not self-evident? Of course it follows *Rabbi Yehuda*. The answer is that it comes to exclude the position of *Rabbi Yochanan*, who said regarding *Rosh Hashana* that *shama tisha tekiyot be-tisha sha'ot ba-yom yatza* — if one heard the nine required blasts of *shofar* spread across nine different hours of the day, one has fulfilled the obligation.

### Rejection of Yochanan

One might have thought that *Rav Kahana*'s only intent was to rule out hearing the blasts hours apart — that is, to exclude *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position — while still allowing for a brief pause between *tekiah* and *teruah* within a single sequence. The *Gemara* rejects this: the phrase *ve-lo klum* — absolutely nothing — is too strong to allow even the slightest interruption. It establishes that the sounds must be literally continuous, not merely in proximity.

### Independent vs. Group Bl…

This analysis yields three distinct positions. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* is one unit — one sound — and there can be no interruption whatsoever between its components. According to the *Rabbanan*, the three are distinct units, but they form a group: they must cohere, there must be some proximity, though one may pause to take a breath between them. And the most extreme position, that of *Rabbi Yochanan* regarding *Rosh Hashana*, treats the nine blasts as completely independent sounds, such that one could hear them spread across nine different hours of the day and still fulfill the obligation. The *Rabbanan* clearly reject this final position. This same conceptual issue — whether the sequence is one sound, a group, or entirely independent units — applies equally to the trumpet blasts in the *Beit Hamikdash* as to the *shofar* on *Rosh Hashana*.

---

## Flute-Hallel Connection

### Gomair Hallel Principle

The *Gemara* now provides its analysis of why the flute is played specifically on these twelve days. *Hoil ve-yachid gomer bahen et ha-Hallel* — because it is on these days that an individual completes — *gomer* — the full *Hallel*. Both words in this phrase deserve attention and will generate important discussion shortly.

### Eighteen Hallel Days

*Rabbi Yochanan* says in the name of *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak*: there are eighteen days in the year on which an individual completes the *Hallel* — *shmonah yemei ha-chag*, the eight days of *Sukkot*, already mentioned in our *mishna*; *shmonah yemei Chanukah*, eight days of *Chanukah*; *yom tov ha-rishon shel Pesach*, the first day of *Pesach*; and *yom tov shel atzeret*, *Shavuot*. That yields eighteen.

The reason *Chanukah* appears here but not in our *mishna* is straightforward: the *mishna* deals with the special playing of instruments in connection with *korbanot*, and *Chanukah* has no special *korban* associated with it. The days of full *Hallel* and the days of the flute thus overlap substantially but do not map onto each other perfectly. There are also two days that the *mishna* includes — the bringing of the *korban pesach rishon* and *pesach sheini* — that do not appear in *Rabbi Yochanan*'s list, because the *Hallel* on those days was tied entirely to the act of bringing the *korban*. Without the *korban*, there is no corresponding *Hallel* obligation on those dates, and so those days have no relevance outside the *Beit Hamikdash*.

### Diaspora: Twenty-one Days

Outside of Israel, where second days of *Yom Tov* are observed, the number of full *Hallel* days rises to twenty-one: nine days of *Sukkot*, eight days of *Chanukah*, two days of *Pesach*, and two days of *Shavuot* — three additional days for the three *regalim* bringing the total from eighteen to twenty-one.

### Succos vs. Pesach

The *Gemara* now takes up the central question that the *mishna* already prompted: *mai shna de-chag d'amrinan kol yoma ve-yoma u-mai shna de-Pesach de-lo amrinan* — why is *Hallel* said every single day of *Sukkot*, while on *Pesach* it is said only the first day?

### Midrash: Egyptians Drown…

Before turning to the *Gemara*'s answer, it is worth noting the explanation most commonly taught: the *Midrash* records that when the Egyptians were drowning in the *Yam Suf*, the angels wished to sing *shira*, and God replied, *ma'aseh yadai tove'im ba-yam ve-atem omrim shira* — My creations are drowning in the sea and you would sing song? The argument then proceeds that if one does not say full *Hallel* on the seventh day of *Pesach* because of the Egyptian deaths, one certainly does not say it on *Chol Hamoed*, which is less distinguished than the seventh day itself. This *Midrash* raises its own conceptual questions — notably, *Bnei Yisrael* did sing *shira* at the sea. The point may be that we, removed from the direct experience of salvation, are positioned more like the angels than like the generation that witnessed it firsthand. But in any event, this is not what the *Gemara* says.

### Distinct Korbanot Logic

The *Gemara*'s answer is halakhic in character: *kol yoma de-chag chalukin be-korbanoteihem* — every day of *Sukkot* is distinct in its *korbanot*, since the number of bulls brought as *musaf* decreases each day — thirteen, twelve, eleven, and so forth, down through seven. *Pesach ein chalukin be-korbanoteihen* — on *Pesach*, the *korban musaf* is identical every day. Since there is no distinction among the days of *Pesach* as expressed in the *korbanot*, there is nothing to mark each day as a separate unit.

This answer, however, requires careful handling when applied to our practice today, since we no longer bring *korbanot*. One position would be that our *Hallel* is essentially a *zecher*, a memorial act linked to the *Hallel* that was once said in connection with the *korbanot*. That is, however, a position one would generally resist — we normally understand our *Hallel* as a response to the *kedusha* and significance of the day itself, not merely as a commemoration of a Temple-era practice. And in any case, such an explanation could not account for *Chanukah*, where full *Hallel* is said without any *korban* connection whatsoever. The more satisfying reading is that the difference in *korbanot* is a *siman* — an indicator of a deeper distinction — rather than the cause in itself.

### Pesach Unity vs. Succos…

What is that deeper distinction? *Pesach* was a process, a narrative. The *geulah* began with *Yetziat Mitzrayim* and culminated in *Kriat Yam Suf*. The entire seven-day period is one connected story — each day leads into the next, and the whole constitutes a single arc of redemption. On *Sukkot*, by contrast, the commemoration is *ki ba-sukkot hoshavti et Bnei Yisrael* — that God caused the Jewish people to dwell in *sukkot*. Sitting in a *sukkah* could have been commemorated on any single day of the year. There is no narrative that binds day two to day one, no progression by which each subsequent day is intelligible only in light of what preceded it. Therefore, if one wishes to observe *Sukkot* for eight days, each day stands as an independent commemoration. Each day of *Sukkot* is a separate unit; the entirety of *Pesach* is one unit.

### Bracha Wording Evidence

This distinction is not merely theoretical — it manifests in *halacha*. On *Shabbat Chol Hamoed Sukkot*, when the *haftarah* is concluded, one mentions *ve-al yom chag ha-Sukkot hazeh* — the specific day of *Sukkot* is acknowledged in the *beracha*. On *Shabbat Chol Hamoed Pesach*, however, one says only *ve-al yom ha-Shabbat hazeh* — the day of *Pesach* is not mentioned alongside it, because on *Pesach* the individual day does not carry a distinctive identity of its own. The day is part of *Pesach* as a whole, not a separately identifiable occasion. Similarly, a *she-hecheyanu* is recited on *Shemini Atzeret* — the last day of *Sukkot* — but not on the last day of *Pesach*, precisely because on *Sukkot* each day is a distinct unit warranting its own recognition, while *Pesach* is conceived as a single extended occasion.

### Yachid Gomair Phrase

Returning now to the phrase in the *Gemara* — *yachid gomer et ha-Hallel* — two aspects deserve attention. First, the word *gomer*, "completes," implies that on other days there is some partial form of *Hallel* being said. *Tosafot* is uncertain on this point. There are *Gemarot* that indicate a practice of saying a *chatzi Hallel* — an abbreviated *Hallel*, skipping certain sections — on days such as *Rosh Chodesh* and *Chol Hamoed Pesach*, though *Tosafot* raises the possibility that the *minhag* of saying even the partial *Hallel* on those days developed later and was not yet implied by this statement.

### Half-Hallel Bracha Dispu…

Second, the word *yachid* — "individual" — raises the question of whether there is a difference between an individual saying *Hallel* and a congregation saying *Hallel*. This has implications for whether one says *Hallel* at all on those lesser days when alone, and whether a *beracha* is recited on *chatzi Hallel*. The *beracha* on *chatzi Hallel* is a major debate. If the *minhag* to say it is later than the Talmudic period, and possibly not even directed by the *rabbanim* in a binding way, the question of making a *beracha* on a *minhag* becomes central.

In practice, *Ashkenazim* do recite a *beracha* on *chatzi Hallel*. When *Sefardim* say a full *Hallel*, the *beracha* is *ligmor et ha-Hallel*, echoing the language of *gomer et ha-Hallel*. When saying *chatzi Hallel*, *Sefardim* recite no *beracha* at all, and moreover say it only *be-tzibbur* — as a congregation — not in private. The *Ashkenazic* practice of reciting a *beracha* even when saying *chatzi Hallel* in private follows *Rabbeinu Tam*'s position, and the *pesak* is that even one saying it alone recites the *beracha* — though one should be aware that there are authoritative opinions to the contrary.

---

## Why Hallel: Kedusha & Mi…

### Shabbat Objection

The *Gemara* now presses further: *Shabbat d'chaluka be-korbanoseiha leimra* — *Shabbat* has distinct *korbanot* just as *Sukkot* does; why not say *Hallel* on *Shabbat*?

### Shabbat Not Moed

The answer: *lo ikri moed* — *Shabbat* is not called a *moed* in the manner of *Yom Tov*. Before one can say *Hallel*, the day must qualify as a *moed*.

### Soloveitchik Distinction

This raises a natural question: if *Hallel* is a response to *kedushat hayom*, is not the *kedusha* of *Shabbat* higher than that of *Yom Tov*? The *Rav* — *Rav Soloveitchik* — offers an elegant distinction here. He observes that on *Shabbat*, we welcome the *kedusha* into our space — we perform *Kabbalat Shabbat*, as though inviting God's sanctity into our week. On *Yom Tov*, particularly understood through the lens of *aliyah la-regel*, it is we who enter God's space. The absence of a *Kabbalat Yom Tov* parallel to *Kabbalat Shabbat* is telling. However different the qualities of *kedusha* may be, *Yom Tov* carries a more acute sense of directly standing before God, of entering a sacred realm — and perhaps that is what the *Gemara* means by *moed*, the sense of a special appointed encounter that is by its nature less regular than *Shabbat*.

### Rosh Chodesh: No Melacha…

The *Gemara* continues: *Rosh Chodesh d'ikri moed leima* — *Rosh Chodesh* is also called a *moed*, so why not say *Hallel* on *Rosh Chodesh*? The answer: *lo ikadesh be-asiyat melacha* — *Rosh Chodesh* was not sanctified through the prohibition of *melacha*. There is no formal *issur melacha* on *Rosh Chodesh*.

### Song & Kedusha Link

The source for this linkage between *Hallel* and the prohibition of *melacha* is a verse: *ha-shir yihiyeh lachem ke-leil hitkadesh chag* — the song shall be for you like the night sanctified for the festival. *Laila ha-mikudash le-chag taun shirah* — a night sanctified through the *chag*, which means sanctified through the prohibition of *melacha*, requires *shira*. *She-eino mekudash le-chag ein taun shirah* — when there is no such sanctification, *shira* is not required. This is a notably technical formulation — nothing here about miracles, history, or themes. The operative criterion is *kedushah* expressed through *issur melacha* in the context of a *moed*.

### Rosh Hashana & Yom Kippur

The *Gemara* presses further: *Rosh Hashana ve-Yom ha-Kippurim d'ikrei moed*, and *d'itkadesh be-asiyat melacha* — both *Rosh Hashana* and *Yom Kippur* are called *moed*, and both carry a prohibition of *melacha*. Why not say *Hallel* on those days?

### Midrash: Books of Life

The *Gemara* answers with a statement of *Rabbi Abbahu*: the ministering angels asked God, *mipnei mah ein Yisrael omrim shirah lefanecha be-Rosh Hashana u-ve-Yom ha-Kippurim* — why do Israel not sing before You on *Rosh Hashana* and *Yom Kippur*? God replied: *efshar melech yoshev al kisei ha-din, ve-sifrei chayim ve-sifrei meitim ptuchim lefanav, ve-Yisrael omrim shirah* — is it possible that the King sits upon the seat of judgment, with the books of life and death open before Him, and Israel should be singing?

### Lack of Simcha

What does this *Midrash* tell us? One reading is that *Hallel* is ultimately linked to *simchat haregel*, the mitzvah of *simcha* on *Yom Tov* — *ve-samachta be-chagecha* — and the anxiety of *Rosh Hashana* and *Yom Kippur* precludes the kind of *simcha* that *Hallel* requires. The *Gemara*, it should be noted, did not invoke *simcha* in its earlier reasoning. One possibility is that the *Gemara* is now adding a further dimension: even given the *moed* and *issur melacha*, there must also be *simcha*, and where there is profound concern about divine judgment, that *simcha* cannot be fully realized.

### Simcha on Rosh Hashana

This *Midrash* gives rise to an interesting dispute among the *Rishonim* and *Poskim*: is there a *mitzvah* of *simcha* on *Rosh Hashana* at all? One practical expression of this debate is whether it is permitted to fast on *Rosh Hashana*. Some permit it; others hold it is *assur* because there is a *mitzvah* of *simcha* that one would thereby be violating. A famous story is told of the *Beit Halevi* — *Rav Chaim Brisker*'s father — who said: "People call rabbis strict; I am a great *meikel*! Those who say one may not fast on *Rosh Hashana* — I say one may!"

### Ashkenazi vs. Sephardi

The tension is also visible in the divergence between *Ashkenazic* and *Sefardic* practice on *Rosh Hashana*. For *Ashkenazim*, the dominant tone is *eimas ha-din* — awe and fear before the divine judgment. The query of the angels — *heikha shira* — resonates deeply with this sensibility. For *Sefardim*, the *simcha* dimension is more prominent. The two approaches need not be seen as contradictory. Another *Midrash* captures the balance: God tells the angels that while an ordinary person coming before a judge dresses in mourning clothes to demonstrate humility, *Bnei Yisrael* — *lovshei levanim* — dress in white and come before God with confidence and joy. The confidence that one will be found meritorious does not eliminate all gravity; it means one does not go so far as to sing *Hallel*, which would be, in the language of the *Gemara*, going too far.

*Tosafot* notes that the *Midrash* asks why *Israel* does not sing — not why *we* do not sing — implying that the angels themselves do sing *Hallel* on *Rosh Hashana* and *Yom Kippur*. He cites a *piyut* unique to these days: *v'hachayot yishoreru u-cheruvim yefaeru* — the *chayot* will burst into song and the *cheruvim* will offer praise. Some questioned whether this *piyut* should be recited since it would imply that the angels do sing, but *Tosafot* affirms that indeed they do — the prohibition is on *Israel*, not on the heavenly host.

### Chanukah: Miracle Basis

The *Gemara* now addresses *Chanukah*: *la-Chanukah d'lo hachi ve-lo hachi ve-ka'amar* — *Chanukah* has none of these qualifications: it is not a *Yom Tov*, there is no *issur melacha*, it is not a *moed* in the formal sense. Why then is *Hallel* recited on *Chanukah*? *Ah, mishum nisa* — because of the miracle. This is a remarkable moment in the *Gemara*, because up until this point the entire discussion has proceeded without invoking the concept of miracle at all. The answer for *Chanukah* introduces the *nes* as a separate, independent basis for *Hallel* — and *Chanukah* in particular has the additional dimension of *pirsumei nisa*, the proclamation of the miracle, which makes the recitation of *Hallel* especially apt.

### Purim: Why No Hallel

The obvious next question: *Purim d'ika nisa leima* — *Purim* also has a miracle, so why not say *Hallel* on *Purim*?

### Outside Eretz Yisrael Lo…

*Rabbi Yitzchak* answers: *lefi she-eino omrim shira al nes she-be-chutz la-Aretz* — because one does not say *shira* over a miracle that occurred outside *Eretz Yisrael*. The miracle of *Purim* lacked the eternal significance that would warrant *Hallel*.

### Objection: Exodus Outside

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* immediately challenges this: *harei Yetziat Mitzrayim de-nes she-be-chutz la-Aretz hu* — the Exodus from Egypt was also a miracle that occurred outside *Eretz Yisrael*, and we do say *Hallel* for it. The same could be said for the wandering commemorated by *Sukkot*.

It should be noted here that the most natural response — that *Hallel* on *Pesach* has nothing to do with miracles and everything to do with *kedushat ha-yom*, as the entire earlier discussion established — is conspicuously not given. The *Gemara* at this point shifts into a mode where it treats the miracle as relevant to the question, which in turn creates tension with everything that preceded it. The *Gemara*'s handling of this is noteworthy.

### Before vs. After Entry

The *Gemara* answers with a *baraita*: *ad she-lo nichnesu Yisrael la-Aretz huchshru kol ha-aratzot lomar shirah* — before the Jewish people entered *Eretz Yisrael*, all lands were eligible, as it were, for the singing of *shira*. Since *Eretz Yisrael* had not yet assumed its full distinction over all other lands, miracles performed anywhere could warrant *shira*. But *mishe-nichnesu la-Aretz, lo huchshru kol ha-aratzot lomar shirah* — once they entered the land, events outside of *Eretz Yisrael* lost that status. The miracle of *Purim* occurred after the entry into the land, during *galut*, and is therefore subject to this diminishment.

### Megilla = Hallel

*Rav Nachman* offers an alternative approach: *kriotah zu hi Hallel* — the reading of the *Megillah* itself functions as the *Hallel* for *Purim*. The reading of the *Megillah* constitutes a highly articulate form of *pirsumei nisa* — a verbal proclamation of the miracle — and therefore serves the purpose that *Hallel* would otherwise serve. The *Meiri* draws out the practical implication: if one were in circumstances where the *Megillah* was unavailable, one would be obligated to say *Hallel* on *Purim* in its place.

### Rava: Still Subjects

*Rava* offers yet another explanation: *bishlama hatam halelu avdei Hashem ve-lo avdei Pharoh* — there, in the context of the Exodus and *Chanukah*, we sing *halelu avdei Hashem* — praise ye the servants of God — because the miracle brought about a real change in status. We are no longer the servants of *Pharoh*; the liberation was complete and lasting. But in the context of *Purim*: *halelu avdei Hashem ve-lo avdei Achashverosh* — praise ye servants of God and not servants of *Achashverosh*? That cannot honestly be said. *Akti avdei Achashverosh anan* — we are still subjects of *Achashverosh*. The miracle of *Purim* saved us from destruction but did not change our fundamental political condition. We remain in exile, subjects of foreign rulers.

### Chanukah Independence

By contrast, *Chanukah* represented a moment of genuine independence — the *Hasmoneans* threw off foreign domination and achieved actual sovereignty. The *nes* of *Chanukah* thus crossed the threshold where one can honestly say *halelu avdei Hashem ve-lo avdei* whoever came before. The *Purim* miracle, as wondrous as it was, left the Jewish people in the same unredeemed condition. In this sense, *Rava*'s answer converges thematically with the *chutz la-Aretz* reasoning: both point to a *nes* that was transformative but incomplete, a salvation embedded within the condition of *galut* rather than transcending it.

### Rav Nachman Reconciliati…

The *Gemara* reconciles *Rav Nachman*'s position — that reading the *Megillah* constitutes *Hallel* — with the *baraita* that states one does not say *shira* over a miracle in *chutz la-Aretz* after entering the land. *Rav Nachman* holds that we do in fact have an obligation to say some form of *Hallel* for *Purim*, fulfilled through the reading of the *Megillah*. The *baraita*'s restriction applies to the direct singing of *shira*; the *Megillah* reading satisfies the obligation through a different medium. He further argues that since the miracle of *Purim* occurred during *galut*, after *Churban ha-Bayit*, it falls under a different framework — *keivan she-galu chazru le-heteran ha-rishon* — returning, in a sense, to the pre-land status where miracles in *chutz la-Aretz* retain their significance. During the *galut* period, the *nes* in *chutz la-Aretz* was very much relevant and very much a reason for *Hallel*.

---

## Instruments: Materials &…

### Reed vs. Copper Flute

The *Gemara* turns to the practical details of the instruments. The *mishna* stated that a copper flute was not used — *lo haya makeh be-avuv shel nechoshet* — but only a reed flute, *be-avuv shel kaneh*, because the reed produced a superior sound.

### Chalil Etymology

*Rav Papa* observes that the *mishna* opens by calling the instrument a *chalil* and then shifts to calling it an *avuv*. He clarifies: *hainu chalil hainu avuv* — they are the same instrument. As for the name *chalil*, *Rashi* explains: *de-chali kalei* — because its sound is so sweet and mellifluous. The word *chalil* derives from an Aramaic term for sweetness.

### Ancient Reed Flute

A *baraita* elaborates on the instrument's history. *Abuv hayah ba-mikdash chalak* — the flute in the *mikdash* was smooth, *hayah dak* — thin, *shokana hayah* — made of reed, *u-mimot Moshe hayah* — and it had been passed down continuously from the time of *Moshe Rabbeinu* himself.

### Gold Plating Incident

At some point, a king — the identity is not specified — commanded that the flute be plated with gold to make it more beautiful. The result: *ve-lo hayah kolo areiv* — it no longer produced a pleasant sound. So *natlu et tzipuyo* — they removed the gold plating — *ve-hayah kolo areiv ke-mot she-hayah* — and the beautiful sound returned, just as it had been. The *drush* practically writes itself: the perfection of the original cannot be improved upon by later embellishment. What was fashioned from the time of *Moshe* had a quality that gilding could only diminish.

### Copper Cymbals History

*Tziltzal hayah ba-mikdash* — there were cymbals in the *mikdash*, *shel nechoshet hayah* — made of copper, *ve-hayah kolo areiv* — and they produced a beautiful sound. *Ve-nifgam* — at some point they were damaged. *Ve-shalkhu chakhamim ve-hevi'u umanin me-Aleksandrya shel Mitzrayim* — the Sages sent and brought master craftsmen from Alexandria in Egypt.

### Cymbals Repair Issue

*Ve-tiknuhu* — the artisans repaired the cymbals. *Ve-lo hayah kolo areiv* — but afterward the sound was no longer beautiful. So *natlu et tikuno* — they removed whatever the craftsmen had done — *ve-hayah kolo areiv ke-mot she-hayah* — and the beautiful sound was restored, exactly as it had been before.

### Incense Mortar

*Machteshet hayah ba-mikdash* — there was a mortar in the *mikdash* used *le-pitum ha-ketoret* — for grinding the spices of the incense — *shel nechoshet haytah, mimot Moshe haytah* — also of copper, also passed down from the time of *Moshe* — *ve-haytah mefattemet et ha-besamim* — and it would grind the fragrances effectively.

### Mortar Repair Failure

*Nitpagmah* — it was damaged. Again, *ve-hevi'u umanin me-Aleksandrya shel Mitzrayim* — the Alexandrian craftsmen were brought in — *ve-tiknuah* — and they repaired it. *Ve-lo haytah mefattemet ke-mot she-haytah* — but it no longer released the same quality of fragrance. The manner of grinding affects the release of aroma — much as crushing garlic one way yields a different flavor than crushing it another way — and the repair had altered something essential in the mortar's function. *Natlu et tikunah* — they removed the repair work — *ve-haytah mefattemet ke-mot she-haytah* — and it resumed working as it always had.

### Drush: Perfection Theme

All three episodes — the reed flute, the copper cymbals, and the incense mortar — follow the same pattern: an ancient vessel of surpassing quality, damage, an attempt at repair by the finest craftsmen of the age, failure of the repair to restore the original quality, and finally the removal of the repair to restore what was. The *drush* is rich. The perfection of what was fashioned in the time of *Moshe* cannot be replicated or improved by later human artistry, however skilled. The Alexandrian craftsmen were the best available — and still they could not match what was. There is something here about the irreducibility of the original, the impossibility of truly recovering through technical means what was once possessed organically, and the wisdom of recognizing when to simply restore rather than improve.

---

---

# Arakhin 11

## Temple Vessels

### Cymbals & Mortar

The Gemara on 10b, roughly twelve lines from the bottom of the page, opens with *elu shenei kelim* — these two vessels. The discussion concerns two instruments that were carried over from the First Temple: the cymbals and the mortar and pestle used to grind the aromatic spices. The previous lines had noted that these may even have dated back to the time of Moshe Rabbeinu, but the Gemara here clarifies: it was the reed flute that dated to Moshe Rabbeinu, while the cymbals and the mortar are identified as having been preserved from the First Temple. *Nishtayru miMikdash Rishon* — they remained from the First Temple. *Venispagmu* — they were damaged. *Velo haya lahem arucha* — and they were never truly able to be repaired; every attempt to fix them made them worse.

*Ve'alehem amar David* — regarding them, David said, *nechoshet memurat* or *nechoshet maruk*, a form of beaten or refined copper. And another verse says: *bichli nechoshet mutzav, shenayim chamudot* — copper vessels *mutzav*, meaning golden-looking or gold-plated, and they are two that are desirable.

### Vessel Value Dispute

*Rav veShmuel* dispute the interpretation of *mutzav shenayim*. One holds that *kol echad ve'echad shakol kishnayim shel zahav* — each one of the two vessels was worth as much as two of its weight in gold. Though they were copper, they were so perfectly crafted as to be worth twice their weight in gold. The other holds *sheneihem shekulim ke'echad shel zahav* — the two combined were worth as one of them in gold, meaning half their weight in gold.

In any case, this is a *drash* on the *pasuk* regarding these two copper vessels. The observation that copper instruments over a thousand years old remained usable is itself noteworthy, since copper corrodes over time.

*Tani Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef taught a *baraita* in accordance with the second position, that the two together were worth as one of gold. *Tanya*, Rav Natan says *sheniyim hayu* — they were doubled, meaning there were two of each, two of the grinders and two of the cymbals. The *Shita* switches the *girsa* to read *shenayim* simply as meaning there were duplicates. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel derives this with an *al tikrei*: do not read *shenayim* but rather *sheniyim*.

### Water Tunnel Lesson

The Gemara now returns to the theme that animated the discussion on the previous daf: sometimes attempting to fix something only makes it worse. *Tani Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*: *shiloach haya mekalach mayim be'issar* — there was a water system that funneled water into Yerushalayim, and the water poured through an opening the size of a small coin, *issar*. *Tziva hamelech vehirchivuhu* — the king ordered the opening widened, *kedai she-yirbu meimeiha*, so that more water would flow. *Ve'nistamu* — but the reverse occurred; less water came out, perhaps because widening the passage reduced the water pressure. *Ve'chazru lechomuto* — they restored it to its original dimensions, and the water flowed as it had before.

*Lekayem mah shene'emar*: the conclusion drawn returns to the verse cited yesterday: *al yithalel chacham b'chochmato ve'al yithalel gibor bigvurato* — let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his strength. The end of that *pasuk*, *ki im b'zot yithalel hamithalel haskel v'yadoa oti*, points to knowing God as the primary purpose of life, not worldly achievement. But the immediate moral here has a more practical register: if something isn't entirely broken, do not assume that your technology or ingenuity will improve it. Sometimes intervention makes things worse.

### Bells Excluded

*Vekhen Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer: hardulin lo haya b'Mikdash* — these *hardulin* were not present in the Temple. *Mai hardulin? Amar Abaye: tavla gurgadna* — Rashi identifies this as something like a bell. *Mipnei she-kolo arev* — because its sound was sweet or, according to another reading, *av*, deep and sonorous — *u'mearvev et hane'ima* — and it would interfere with the singing. The principle is that musical accompaniment should support the singing, not compete with it. Not every musical addition is beneficial; some sounds, even if rich in tone, can overwhelm the voice and undermine the *ne'ima*.

### Magrefa Instrument

The final line of 11b introduces another instrument: *amar Rabbah bar Shila amar Rav Matna amar Shmuel: magrefa hayta b'Mikdash* — there was a *magrefa* in the Temple. Normally *magrefa* denotes a shovel used for clearing ashes; Rashi takes the name literally, while Tosafot holds that the same name was applied to an instrument that merely resembled one. *Asara nekavim hayu bah* — it had ten holes. *Ve'chol echad ve'echad motzi asara minei zemer* — each hole produced ten different musical sounds. *Nimtzet kula motzia me'ah minei zemer* — the instrument in total produced a hundred types of sound. Rashi describes it as something like a square frame with ten holes, each connected to a tube resembling a flute with additional holes — not unlike an organ in structure. There was also a handle that extended from it, which may have been used to pump air through the mechanism.

*Be'matnita tana*: a *baraita* teaches that the instrument was one *ama* wide and one *ama* tall, with a handle emerging from it, and ten holes — but in this version, *kol echad ve'echad motzi me'ah minei zemer* — each hole produced a hundred sounds, and *nimtzet kula motzia elef minei zemer* — a thousand sounds in total.

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak ve'simanach: matnita guzma* — the *baraita* exaggerates. This is offered as a mnemonic to distinguish between the two versions. Rashi explains that it is the *derech* of the *baraita* to exaggerate, though one might observe that exaggeration seems more characteristic of *Amoraim* than of *Tannaim* — and in that sense Rashi's remark is itself somewhat surprising.

---

## Who Are Musicians?

### Three Positions

The Gemara turns to the question of who actually played the musical instruments in the Temple. This discussion connects to the physical location of the *duchan* — the platform on which the Levites stood to sing. The *duchan* was situated at the border between the *Ezrat Yisrael* and the *Ezrat Kohanim*, directly in front of the *Mizbeach*, within the *Azara* proper.

Three positions exist regarding the identity of the musicians who provided the instrumental accompaniment: *de'avdei kohanim hayu sham* — they were the servants of the *kohanim*; or they were full-status Levites; or they were Israelites from genealogically distinguished families (*meyuchas* families). The Gemara attempts to correlate these positions with the underlying dispute about the primary function of the musical service: *ikar shira b'peh* — the essence of the *shira* is vocal singing — or *ikar shira b'kli* — the primary service is with instruments.

*De'man de'amar avadim hayu, kasavar ikar shira b'peh* — if the real service is vocal, then the instrumental accompaniment merely sweetens the singing, *levasumei kala hu d'avida*, and it need not be performed by a Levite; even a servant could do it. *U'man de'amar Leviyim hayu, kasavar ikar shira b'kli* — the one who holds that only Levites may play holds that the instrumental service is itself primary. Rabbi Yossi, who requires *meyuchas* Israelites, presents a puzzle: if it is about the voice, servants should suffice; if about the instruments, Levites should be required. What middle ground justifies his position?

### Circular Logic

The Gemara resolves this with a striking observation: *le'olam kasavar ikar shira b'peh* — in truth, all opinions may agree that vocal singing is primary. The debate is not about the nature of the service itself, but about what assumptions people will draw from the *duchan*. *Bema'alin miduchan l'yuchasin ul'ma'asrot kamiflagi* — the dispute concerns whether we allow inferences from the fact that someone stood on the *duchan*.

This reasoning is admittedly circular. The identity of who is permitted on the *duchan* is being shaped by the assumptions we expect people to make from seeing who stands there — and those assumptions depend in turn on who we decide is permitted.

*Man de'amar avadim hayu, kasavar ein ma'alin miduchan lo l'yuchasin ve'lo l'ma'asrot* — if we allow servants, we must hold that no one draws inferences from the *duchan* regarding lineage or the right to receive *ma'asrot*. *Man de'amar Leviyim hayu, kasavar ma'alin miduchan bein l'yuchasin bein l'ma'asrot* — if only Levites are permitted, then people do draw such inferences, and we must restrict access accordingly so that *ma'asrot* are not misdirected. *U'l'man de'amar Yisraelim hayu, kasavar ma'alin miduchan l'yuchasin, ve'lo l'ma'asrot* — the position requiring distinguished Israelites holds that people draw genealogical inferences from the *duchan* but not inferences regarding Levitical entitlement to *ma'asrot*; therefore distinguished Israelites are sufficient, and Levites are not required.

One might resolve the circularity by saying the Gemara is describing not what we prescribe people to assume, but what people naturally assume in practice — and since perception is difficult to change, we must shape reality to match prevailing perception. In that framing, the practical constraints of public inference determine the requirements for who may stand on the *duchan*.

The Gemara's conclusion is that in principle all positions may agree: the fundamental service is vocal singing, and the instrumental accompaniment could theoretically be performed by anyone. The debate is entirely downstream, about what safeguards must surround that service given social inference patterns.

---

## Levite Singing Role

### Song Validity

Having established that the heart of the Temple music is vocal *shira*, the Gemara now asks a more fundamental question: where in the Torah do we find any basis for *shira* accompanying the *korbanot* at all? The basic Levitical function described in the Torah is carrying the components of the *Mishkan* and guarding the surrounding encampment. Once the Temple was built and there was no more carrying, the Levites took on the roles of *sho'arim* (gatekeepers) and *meshorerim* (singers), as is clearly documented in *Divrei HaYamim* — but what is the Torah-level basis?

The Gemara opens with the *baraita*: *hashir me'akev et hakorban* — the song prevents the *korban* from being valid if not performed. This applies primarily to the fixed communal *korbanot* — the morning and afternoon *Tamid*, and the *Musaf* — and it is done during the time of the *nisuch hayayin*, the pouring of the wine libation. The principle *ein shira ela al hayayin* — song is said only over wine — will be developed shortly.

Rabbi Meir holds that without the song one is not *yotzei*; the Sages hold one is. Tosafot raises a sharp objection: since *shira* is linked to the *nisuch hayayin*, and one who omits the *nisuch* entirely is still *yotzei* the *korban*, how can Rabbi Meir say that omitting the *shira* invalidates the offering? Tosafot therefore limits the statement: without the *shira* one is not *yotzei* the *nisuch hayayin* specifically, but one is *yotzei* the *korban* itself. This interpretation is technically forced by the language, but the question is powerful.

*Mai ta'ama deRabbi Meir?* The verse states: *venatati et haLevi'im netunim leAharon ulevanav mitoch Bnei Yisrael ulechaper al Bnei Yisrael* — I will give the Levites to Aharon and his sons from among Bnei Yisrael, to atone for Bnei Yisrael. Rabbi Meir reasons: *mah kapara me'akevet* — just as the atoning act (the sprinkling of blood) is indispensable to the *korban*, *af shira me'akevet* — so too the *shira* of the Levites, which is identified here as their participation in the *kapara*, is indispensable. The Levites' singing accompanies the *korban* and is thereby part of the atonement it achieves; if it is omitted, the *kapara* is incomplete.

The Sages respond: *hahu lechid-Rabbi Eliezer* — that verse is expounded for a different purpose, as Rabbi Eliezer teaches: *mah kapara ba-yom af shira ba-yom* — just as the *korbanot* are performed by day, the *shira* must also be performed by day. This is relevant because the *nesachim* (libations) that accompany a daytime *korban* may in certain circumstances be offered at night; the verse comes to teach that even then, the *shira* is performed only when the *nesachim* are done by day. But from this verse one cannot derive that *shira* is *me'akev*; it speaks only to timing.

### Torah Proofs

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: minayin le'ikar shira min haTorah?* How do we establish the very concept of *shira* accompanying the *korban* from the Torah? From the verse: *lesharet beshem Hashem Elokav kechol echav haLevi'im ha'omdim sham lifnei Hashem* — to serve in the name of Hashem his God, like all his Levite brothers who stand there before Hashem. The verse speaks of a Levite coming to serve in the Temple. What service involves invoking God's name? *Eizehu sherut she-beshem? Hevei omer zeh shira* — it must be the singing, which contains *pesukim* in which God's name is pronounced.

The Gemara asks: perhaps *lesharet beshem* refers to *nesiat kapayim*, the Priestly Blessing? The reply: another verse states *lesharto ulevarch bishmo* — to serve Him and to bless with His name — implying that serving and blessing with His name are two distinct acts. *Mikhlal de-Birkat Kohanim lav sherut hi* — the Priestly Blessing is therefore not categorized as *sherut* in the sense of service of the *korbanot*; it is a blessing directed toward Bnei Yisrael. The *sherut* that involves God's name is the *shira* of the Levites.

*Rav Matna amar mehacha*: from the verse in the *kelala* section: *tachat asher lo avadta et Hashem Elokecha besimcha uvtuv levav* — because you did not serve Hashem your God with joy and with goodness of heart. *Eizehu avoda she-besimcha uvtuv levav? Hevei omer zo shira* — singing, which, as Rashi notes, emerges from an inner feeling of love, joy, and gladness.

The Gemara challenges this derivation: perhaps *besimcha uvtuv levav* refers to Torah study? The verse in Tehillim says: *pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev* — the statutes of God are upright, they gladden the heart. The Gemara responds: yes, Torah is called *mesamchei lev* — it brings joy to the heart — but *tuv* it is not called. Tosafot objects: Torah is called *tov* throughout — *lekach tov natati lakhem*. Tosafot therefore qualifies: Torah is not called *tuv levav*, goodness of heart — that particular formulation belongs uniquely to *shira*. It is admittedly difficult to articulate a fully substantive distinction between the joy that *shira* brings and the joy that Torah brings. One might observe that both phenomena — Torah and *shira* — occupy a singular place in the world of *Chazal* as modes of direct engagement with the divine. Torah may be understood as listening to God, while *tefilla* and *shira* represent speaking to God. The Gemara here is deliberating between these two on the basis of which better embodies *simcha* and *tuv levav*, which suggests that the joy of *shira* carries a quality of gratitude and outward-directed expression that distinguishes it from the inward intellectual joy of Torah study. That nuance, however, is difficult to extract cleanly from the technical formulation.

### Joy & Service

The Gemara continues: perhaps *besimcha uvtuv levav* refers to the bringing of *Bikkurim*? For it is written *vesamachta bechol hatov* — you shall rejoice in all the goodness. The reply: *tov ikri, tuv levav lo ikri* — *Bikkurim* is indeed called *tov*, but not *tuv levav*. The concept of *tuv levav* — a goodness emerging from deep within — is reserved for *shira*. One could suggest that *Bikkurim* evokes gratitude, which might explain why it is called *tov*, but *shira* represents a more profound inwardness of joy that the formulation *tuv levav* uniquely captures.

Having said this, the Gemara — which one might call the *Breslov daf* — raises a related question: *Amar Rav Matna: minayin leBikkurim shete'unim shira?* Now that we have established that *shira* accompanies the *korbanot*, how do we know that *Bikkurim* also require *shira*? *Atya tov tov mehacha* — a *gezeirah shavah*: since *Bikkurim* uses the word *tov* and the verse about serving God with *tuv levav* (which we have identified as *shira* of the *korbanot*) also uses *tov*, we derive that *shira* accompanies *Bikkurim* as well.

### Song Over Wine

The Gemara immediately challenges: *amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan: minayin she-ein omrim shira ela al hayayin?* How do we know that *shira* is said only over wine? From the *mashal* in Shoftim, where the vine is asked to be king and replies: *hechadalti et tiroshi hamesameach Elohim va'anashim* — shall I leave my wine that brings joy to people and to God? We understand how wine gladdens people; how does it gladden God? *Mikan she-ein omrim shira ela al hayayin* — from here we learn that the singing in the Temple, which accompanies the wine libation, is how wine brings joy in the service of God. The *shira* is sung at the time of the *nisuch hayayin*, and in that sense wine and song are inseparable in the Temple service.

This principle has resonances beyond the Temple. The reason *Kiddush* is said over wine, the reason later *minhag* attached *Sheva Berachot*, *Birkat Erusin*, and *Birkat Brit Milah* to wine — even though the Gemara itself does not mandate wine for these — is the sense that wine elevates the ritual significance and adds a dimension of joy. Even where the Gemara does not require wine for these blessings, later practice associated them with wine precisely because wine carries this quality of sanctified joy.

But if *shira* requires wine, how can *Bikkurim* require *shira*? There is no wine brought with *Bikkurim*. The Gemara resolves this: *meshkachat lah ke-detanya Rabbi Yossi* — there is a way to find wine in *Bikkurim*. The verse says to bring *reshit pri ha'adama* — the first fruits — from which one might infer that only fruit is brought, not fruit juices. Yet if one brought grapes, one may press them into wine, as the extra word *tavi* allows the inclusion of classic liquids — wine and olive oil — as *Bikkurim*. Tosafot reads the *maskana* as *lechatchila*: one may bring wine as *Bikkurim*. Once *shira* accompanies *Bikkurim* when wine is present, the institution of *shira* for *Bikkurim* was established broadly. This does not mean *shira* is never said without wine in other contexts — *Hallel*, for example, is recited without wine — but it underscores wine's centrality to the formal *shira* of the Temple service.

---

## When Singing Require (II)

### Chizkiyahu Story

*Chizkiya amar mehacha* — from the following verse: *ve-Chananyahu sar haLevi'im yassur bemassa ki mevin hu* — Chananyahu the officer over the Levites will *yassur* regarding the burden, for he is understanding. The Gemara reads *al tikrei yassur ela yashir* — do not read *yassur* (he will direct) but *yashir* (he will sing). The word *bemassa* — in the burden — connects to the Levitical *massa*, the carrying, which is the Torah's own term for the Levites' service. In this reading, the verse tells us that the Levites sing, and links that singing to their defined *avodah*. Tosafot notes that there are explicit verses in *Divrei HaYamim* identifying specific Levitical families as *meshorerim*; one might simply quote those. But Tosafot explains that the earlier derivations are preferred because they connect *shira* to the concept of *avoda* rooted in the Torah itself — particularly through the word *massa* — rather than merely noting historically that Levites happened to sing. That connection gives *shira* the character of an obligatory *avoda* rather than an incidental practice.

*Bavati amar Rabbi Yochanan mehacha*: from the verse *la'avod avodat avoda ve-avodat massa* — to perform the work of work and the work of carrying. *Eizo avoda she-tzricha avoda?* What work serves another work? *Hevei omer zu shira* — it is the singing that serves the *avoda* of the *korbanot*. This derives directly from a Torah verse and identifies *shira* as a service that enables and accompanies another service.

*Rabbi Yitzchak amar mehacha: se'u zimrah, u'tnu tof, kinor na'im im nevel* — lift up song, give the drum, harp and lyre. Tosafot notes that the keyword *se'u* (lift up) echoes the word *massa* and thereby connects this verse about singing to the Levites whose defining Torah-term is *massa*.

*Amar Rav Papa Rav Yitzchak amar mehacha: hemmah yis'u kolam yaronnu big'on Hashem tzahalu miyam* — they lift their voices, they sing joyously to God's greatness, the waters burst forth. Again the keyword *yis'u* (they lift) links the singing to the Levitical *massa*.

*Ve-tanna maiti lah mehacha*: the *baraita* derives it from *ki avodat hakodesh aleihem ba-katef yis'u* — the sacred work is upon them, they shall carry on the shoulder. The Gemara asks: if the verse already says *ba-katef* (on the shoulder), why add *yis'u*? *Ein yis'u ela lashon shirah* — *yis'u* is the language of song. This is then linked back to the verse *se'u zimrah u'tnu tof*. The *baraita* is essentially connecting the same dots as the preceding *Amoraic* derivations, just anchored more firmly in the Torah text.

*Chananya ben akhi Rabbi Yehoshua omer mehacha: Moshe yedabber veha-Elokim ya'anennu ve-kol* — Moshe spoke and God answered him with voice. Since Moshe was a Levite, the Gemara reads this as God informing Moshe about the Levitical responsibility of *kol* and of song. Other authorities evidently found this derivation difficult; Rav Ashi therefore brings a verse from *Divrei HaYamim* directly: *vayehi ke-echad la-mehatzetzrim ve-la-meshorerim, le-hashmi'a kol echad* — the trumpeters and the singers were as one, making one unified sound. As Tosafot notes, this is the most explicit source, but its strength lies in direct attestation rather than in connecting *shira* to the Levites' foundational *avoda* in the Torah. *Rabbi Yonatan amar mehacha: ve-lo yamutu gam hem gam attem* — and they shall not die, neither they nor you. Just as the *kohanim* (you) perform a service at the *mizbe'ach*, so too the Levites (they) perform a service at the *mizbe'ach* — and that service is singing.

---

## Role Boundaries

### Death for Wrong Role

The Gemara now develops the implications of the verse *ve-lo yamutu gam hem gam attem* in a striking direction. *Tanya nami hakhi: attem be-shelahem, ve-hem be-shelakhem, be-mitah* — if the *kohanim* perform Levitical duties or the Levites perform priestly duties, they are *chayav mitah*. The case of a Levite doing priestly service is understandable: the *halacha* is *zar she-shimmesh be-mitah*, that a non-*kohen* who performs the Temple service is liable. But the verse now establishes the parallel: just as they are liable for doing your job, you are liable for doing theirs.

More striking still: *hem be-shelahem* — if Levites perform Levitical duties that are not their assigned role. The Levitical functions in *Divrei HaYamim* were family-specific: certain families were *sho'arim* and others were *meshorerim*. Performing the function assigned to a different Levitical family is not simply an administrative irregularity — it carries the status of *chayav mitah*. This is derived from the verse *ve-hazar ha-karev yumat*: *mai zar?* *Ilima zar mamash* — if it means literally a non-Levite, we already know that from elsewhere. *Ela lav, zar de'osa avoda* — it must mean one who is foreign to that particular service, even if a Levite. Performing the role you were not assigned makes you a *zar* with respect to that service.

Rav Soloveitchik, in his *Shiurim Lezecher Abba Mari*, develops this point into a broader philosophical distinction between *kohanim* and *Levi'im*. A *kohen* is defined by his personal status — *kehuna* is a matter of who he is. A Levite, by contrast, is defined by his *avodah* — by the role to which he is assigned. His identity in the Temple context is constituted by his job, not the reverse. This is why a Levite who performs a different Levitical function is a *zar* relative to it: the assignment is not incidental to his Levitical identity but constitutive of it. Among the *kohanim*, by contrast, we never find a parallel prohibition against performing a priestly function outside one's specific assignment — because for *kohanim*, all priestly functions flow from a unified personal status.

### Crossing Roles Story

*Maaseh be-Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya she-halach le-sayei be-agafat daltot* — there was an episode involving Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, who was a Levite and a singer, and who went to assist with the closing of the Temple gates. *Matza'o Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada encountered him. *Amar lo: beni, chazor le-achorecha, she-atah min ha-meshorerim, va-ani min ha-sho'arim* — my son, go back; you are among the singers, and I am among the gatekeepers. One must not perform the role belonging to the other.

---

## Role Boundaries (II)

### Assisting Debate

The Gemara draws on this episode to address the question of whether *assisting* in another Levitical role triggers the same concern as performing it. The *baraita* rules: *meshorer she-shiyeir, ve-sho'er she-shorer, einam be-mitah ela be-lav* — a singer who performs gating duty, or a gatekeeper who performs singing duty, is not *chayav mitah* but transgresses a prohibition. Abaye rules more stringently: *naktinan, meshoreir she-shiyeir beshel chaveiro, be-mitah* — our ruling is that a singer who performs a gatekeeper's duty is in fact liable, like a non-Levite doing Levitical service.

The Gemara notes that this is a dispute of Tannaim; the episode of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada reflects this underlying disagreement. Rabbi Yehoshua may have believed that assisting was permissible; Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada corrected him because he held otherwise. *Mai lav be-ha kamiflagi: de-mar savar mitah hi ve-gazru bah rabanan* — one opinion holds the underlying transgression is *chayav mitah*, and therefore the Sages made a safeguard prohibiting even the act of assisting, lest it lead to actually performing the role. *U-mar savar lav hi, ve-lo gazru bah rabanan* — the other holds it is only a prohibition, and no safeguard against assisting was decreed.

The Gemara then suggests an alternative: *de-kulei alma lav hi* — perhaps everyone agrees it is merely a prohibition, and the debate is only whether we decree against *assisting* when the transgression is a simple *lav*, not *mitah*. One holds that the Sages did make such a decree; the other holds they did not. Importantly, the Gemara takes it as given that merely assisting is not itself the transgression — it is only a question of rabbinic safeguard. This is a qualitatively different analysis from the case of two people jointly performing a *melacha* together.

---

## When Singing Require (II)

### Free-Will Offerings

*Ba'ei Rabbi Avin*: now that we have established that *shira* accompanies *korbanot*, the question is which *korbanot* require it. The assumption is that obligatory communal *olot* — the *Tamid* and the *Musaf* — are accompanied by *shira*. Rabbi Avin asks: *olat nidvat tzibur, te'unah shirah o einah te'unah shirah?* Does a voluntary communal *olah* require *shira* or not?

The case in question is the *olat kaitz ha-mizbe'ach*: a communal fund existed from which *olot* were brought on slow days in the Temple when no *korbanot* were being offered, so as to keep the *mizbe'ach* active. This was a communal *olah* drawn from communal funds, but it was not obligatory and had no fixed time. Does *shira* accompany it?

The Gemara cites the verse *oloseichem amar Rachmana* — the Torah uses the plural, *your olot*. Does this plurality indicate *achas olas chova ve'achas olas nedava* — both the obligatory and the voluntary — or does *oloseichem* simply mean the entirety of the Jewish people's obligatory *olot*, without extending to free-will offerings?

*Ta shema*: from the episode of Chizkiyahu, *vayomer Chizkiyahu le'haalos ha'olah la-mizbe'ach u'veit heichel ha'olah heichel shir Hashem veha-chatzotzrot* — Chizkiyahu directed that the *olah* be brought to the altar, and when the offering began, so did the singing and the *chatzotzrot*. The verse implies deliberation before this decision. If this were a standard obligatory *olah*, why was there consultation? It seems he was deliberating about a non-standard case. *Ela lav de'olas nedava* — it must have been a voluntary offering, and the deliberation concluded that *shira* and *chatzotzrot* accompany even a voluntary communal *olah*.

### Offering Identity

However, the identification of Chizkiyahu's offering remains unresolved. *Amar Rav Yosef: lo, olas Rosh Chodesh hava* — it was the *Rosh Chodesh olah*, and the deliberation concerned whether *Rosh Chodesh* had been properly established that day. Abaye objects: *ve-chasiv beyom shisha asar lachodesh harishon* — the verse explicitly states it was the sixteenth of Nissan, the second day of Pesach — so it cannot have been *Rosh Chodesh*.

*Ela amar Rami brei de-Rav Yeiva: keves haba im ha'omer ka mibaya lei* — it was the lamb accompanying the *Korban Omer*, and his question was whether *Rosh Chodesh* had been established in time for the *Omer* to be brought. But since this was the sixteenth of Nissan — the second day of Pesach — one would expect the timing of *Rosh Chodesh* Nissan to have been resolved long before. The Gemara asks: *ve-leichezi Pesach heicha avi, matza heicha achal* — when did they bring the *Korban Pesach*? When did they eat *matza*? These events would have anchored the calendar unambiguously.

*Ela amar Rav Ashi: midi de-hava a-shlicha de-tzibura de-mimloch* — the deliberation was not about calendrical uncertainty but about the formal ritual procedure. Just as the *shliach tzibur* performs a ritual act of requesting permission from the community before representing them — a practice still observed on *Yom Kippur* before *Musaf* — so too Chizkiyahu performed a formal consultation before bringing the *olah* on behalf of the community.

The Gemara concludes: *hashta de-asis le-hacha, afilu teima olas chova* — now that we have this explanation, one could equally read the verse as referring to an obligatory *olah*, where the deliberation was simply the customary ritual of communal consultation before representative sacrifice. If so, the story of Chizkiyahu does not prove that *shira* accompanies a *nidvat tzibur* — and the question raised by Rabbi Avin remains unresolved, to be addressed in the continuation of the *sugya*.

---

---

# Arakhin 12

## Shirah Without Korban

### Shirah Basic Principle

The *gemara* on the bottom of 11b has been laying out the basic principle governing the *shirah* of the *levi'im*: one performs it in conjunction with an *olat chovah* of the *tzibur* — that is, the *temidim* and the *musafim*. The question under discussion is whether one would also perform it for a communal *olah* that is a free-will offering. To address this, the *gemara* introduces a *braita* that will serve as the focus of the remainder of the discussion.

### Meritorious Days Braita

The *braita* opens with the view of Rabbi Yosi: *megalgelin zechut l'yom zakai v'chovah l'yom chayav* — good things happen on meritorious days and bad things on inauspicious ones. The *braita* then offers evidence for the second half of this principle. When the First *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed, it was *Tisha B'Av* — the same day the spies returned with their report, which is presumably the original reason it was designated a *yom chayav*. It was also *motzei Shabbat*, a Sunday, and *motzei shevi'it*, the first year of the *shemita* cycle. The coincidence of those latter two details seems to carry its own ominous resonance as the beginning of a new era of *galut*, even if not directly tied to the notion of *yom chayav*.

### Temple Destruction Story

The *braita* continues: it was the cycle of *Yehoyariv* among the *kohanim*, and the *kohanim* and *levi'im* were standing on their *duchan* and singing *shirah*. One might note that it is slightly unusual to say the *kohanim* were on the *duchan* — that platform is really associated with the *levi'im* — but the *braita* includes them. The *shirah* they were singing was *vayashov aleihem et onam u'vera'atam yatzmitem* — "God will return upon them their iniquity; in their evil He will cut them off." The words that were coming out of their mouths were remarkably — even chillingly — apt for the moment. And they did not even complete the verse, *yatzmitem Hashem Elokeinu*, before the enemies came and conquered them. The *braita* concludes: *v'chen bashniyah* — the same thing happened in the Second *Beit HaMikdash*, which was also destroyed on *Tisha B'Av*, on a Sunday, in the first year of the *shemita* cycle.

### No Tamid Problem

The *gemara* now raises its central question: *hai shirah mai avidetei?* — what was this *shirah* doing there at all? Normally one performs *shirah* in conjunction with the *tamid* or the *musaf*. But it was *Tisha B'Av*, so there was no *musaf*. And as for the *tamid* — *b'Yud-Zayin b'Tammuz batel hatamid*: already from the 17th of Tammuz, under siege and without sufficient animals, they had ceased to bring the *korban tamid*. How could *shirah* have been performed without it?

The *gemara* suggests: perhaps it was *d'olat nedavah* — perhaps a single animal happened to be available, not enough to maintain the regular *tamid* (which requires a sheep), but they found a calf — *ben bakar krei b'alma hu d'isrami lehu* — and brought a free-will communal *olah*. If so, this would constitute proof that *shirah* may be performed even when the *olah* is not the fixed obligatory one. The *gemara* then asks: but *v'tisbarah* — does this reasoning really hold up? If they lacked sufficient animals for the *tamid*, how did they happen to have an animal for a free-will *olah*? The *gemara* answers: *ha lo kashya* — that is not difficult. The *tamid* requires a specific species; a *ben bakar*, a calf, cannot serve as the *tamid* and might well have been available.

### Duchan Refutation

However, Rava (and some say Rav Ashi) raises a deeper objection: *v'tisbarah* — does this even cohere? The *shir shel yom* for Sunday is *la'Hashem ha'aretz u'mlo'ah*, yet they were singing *vayashov aleihem et onam*, which is the Wednesday *shirah*. The whole thing was already out of order. *Ailaya b'alma hu d'nafal lehu b'pumaihu* — Rashi explains this as a *kinah*, a dirge: it simply fell from their mouths, not as a proper *shir shel yom* but as an almost instinctive lament for what was about to befall them. At this stage, the *gemara* initially understands this to mean they were not even performing the official *shirah* of the *levi'im* at all — they were simply anticipating the destruction.

But the *gemara* immediately rejects this reading: *v'ha omdin al haduchan katani* — the *braita* explicitly states they were standing on the *duchan*, which indicates they were performing official *shirat levi'im*. The fact that they sang the wrong *shir* might mean they erred, but they were still engaged in formal *shirah*.
