For there is a further consideration: the *chomesh* appears in additional contexts beyond these two — for *ma'aser*, for a *beheimah tehorah*, for a *beheimah temei'ah*, and others. When a law appears in far more than two places, *ein melamdin* — one cannot derive a general principle from any of them — because the very multiplicity of instances demonstrates that each context required its own explicit statement, and none of them are generating a broad rule.

A *baraita* is cited in support of Rava's conclusion, though it reaches the same result through a different path: *bemichsat erkecha — hikisho hakatuv le'erchin*. The verse links *sdei mikneh* to the language of *erech* — and just as *erachin* carries no *chomesh* (one who vows an *erech* and pays the prescribed amount adds nothing), so too *sdei mikneh* carries no *chomesh*.

## Goring Ox/Slave Case

### Slave: Fixed 30 Shekalim

The *mishna* takes up the case of *shor muad*: *echad shehemit et hana'eh sheba'avadim o et haka'ur sheba'avadim — noten shloshim sela*. Whether the goring ox killed a highly valuable slave or a slave of the lowest worth, the owner pays thirty *sela*, no more and no less. The Torah fixes the compensation at thirty *shekalim* regardless of the slave's market value. If the slave was worth one hundred thousand on the market, thirty is a *kula*; if the slave was worth one *shekel*, thirty is a *chumra*.

The *mishna* contrasts this with the case of a free person: *hemit ben chorin — noten shivyo*. When an ox kills a free person, the owner pays *kofer*, ransom — calculated according to what that individual would have fetched on the slave market. That calculation is variable.

The *mishna* adds: *chaval b'zeh u'v'zeh noten nezek shalem* — if the ox injured (rather than killed) either a slave or a free person, the owner pays full damages in both cases, without any fixed schedule.

### Tame vs. Muad Ox

The *gemara* focuses on this last clause — *chaval b'zeh u'v'zeh noten nezek shalem* — and asks: *b'muad in, b'tam la*? Does this apply only to a *shor muad*, a forewarned goring ox, but not to a *shor tam*, one with no prior history of goring? If so, the *mishna* would appear to conflict with the view of Rabbi Akiva, who holds: *af tam she'chaval be'adam meshalem beyoter nezek shalem* — even a *shor tam* that injures a person pays full damages, not merely half damages.

### Muad Context Explains

The *gemara* resolves this: *afilu teima Rabbi Akiva — hu hadin de'afilu shor tam nami*. The *mishna* is consistent with Rabbi Akiva; a *shor tam* is equally subject to the rule of full damages for injuring a person. Why, then, does the *mishna* speak of a *shor muad* rather than a *shor tam*?

Because the earlier part of the *mishna* — the case of killing a slave with a fixed thirty-*shekel* payment, and killing a free person with a variable *kofer* — is a case that *only* arises with a *shor muad*. A *shor tam* that kills a person is entirely exempt from monetary liability; no *kofer* or payment of thirty *shekalim* applies. *D'v'muad hu de'mishkachat lah, v'tam lo mishkachat lah* — those laws are found only in the case of a *shor muad*, not in the case of a *shor tam*. Since the *mishna* needed to introduce the category of *shor muad* for the killing cases, it carries that language into the injury clause as well — even though the injury clause itself would equally encompass a *shor tam*.

## Sexual Offenses: Fixed/F…

### Offense: Fixed 50 Sela

The final *mishna* of the chapter: *echad she'anas u'mefateh gedola she'bakehunah ve'et haktana she'be'Yisrael — noten chamishim sela'im*. Whether the man raped or seduced a woman of the highest standing — a grown woman from the priestly families — or the most minor girl from ordinary Israelite stock, he always pays fifty *sela*. The *mishna* notes the *lehakeil ulehachmir* dynamic: for the person who violated a woman of high status and thereby caused enormous damage and humiliation, the fixed fifty *sela* may be a *kula* relative to her true loss; for the person who violated a woman of low status, it may be a *chumra*.

### Boshet/Pgam Variable

The *mishna* then adds: *ve'haboshet ve'hapgam — hakol lefi hamevayesh ve'hamitbayesh*. The *boshet* — the shame and humiliation — and the *pgam* — the diminishment of her bodily value, in particular the loss of her virginity — are *not* fixed. These are assessed according to the status of both parties: the person who committed the offense and the person who suffered it. A high-status perpetrator violating a high-status victim may carry a different calculus of humiliation than a low-status perpetrator violating a low-status victim.

### Rav Zeira Objection

This raises an obvious question: if there are variable additional damages on top of the fifty *sela*, why did the Torah bother fixing fifty *sela* at all? Perhaps the fifty *sela* was meant to cover everything — *amar Rachmana chamishim sela'im mikol milei* — God said fifty *sela'im* and that should cover the entire obligation. Why do we then add *boshet* and *pgam* on top?

The *gemara* presents the version of this question attributed to Rav Zeira: *yomru ba'al bat melachim chamishim ba'al bat hedyotot chamishim* — it will be said that the man who violated a princess pays fifty and the man who violated a commoner pays fifty? Such an equation seems unjust, and it is this apparent inequity that motivates the need for variable additional damages.

Abaye challenges Rav Zeira: if this reasoning is sound, the same problem would arise with the case of the slave. *Eved nokeiv margaliyot shloshim eved oseh ma'aseh machat shloshim* — an ox that kills a slave who bores pearls pays thirty, and an ox that kills a slave who does ordinary needlework also pays thirty? We are entirely comfortable with that fixed rate; the same should apply here.

The *gemara* therefore sets aside Rav Zeira's first formulation and substitutes a more refined question attributed to him: *ilu ba'u aleha shnayim echad shelo kedarka ve'echad kedarka — yomru ba'al pgumah chamishim ba'al shlemah chamishim*? Suppose two men violated her, one in an atypical manner (which did not technically break her hymen) and then one in the normal manner. The second offender has violated a woman who was already subjected to a prior violation. Rashi explains that the first man, by violating her in an atypical manner, has already subjected her to profound humiliation even while she technically remains a virgin. By the time the second offender arrives, the humiliation she suffers is arguably less acute — yet he too would pay the same fifty *sela*? Does the fixed payment not fail to track the actual damage in such a case?

### Rava Resolution

Abaye responds to this reformulation as well: *gabei eved nami limru — eved bari shloshim eved mukeh shechin shloshim*. Even in the case of the slave: an ox that kills a healthy slave pays thirty, and an ox that kills a slave afflicted with boils pays thirty. The fixed payment applies regardless of condition. So too here.

Rather, says Abaye, citing the verse: *tachat asher inah* — "because he humiliated her." The Torah states that a man who rapes a virgin must marry her *lo tihyeh le'isha tachat asher inah* — she shall be his wife because of what he did to her, the *inui*. This *inui*, the suffering he caused, is what the fifty *sela* is meant to address. *Tachat asher inah miklal de'ika boshet u'pgam* — the phrase *tachat asher inah* implies that there are other elements *beyond* the *inui*: namely *boshet* and *pgam*. The fifty *sela* covers the *inui* — the core offense of the violation; the *boshet* and *pgam* are additional obligations addressed separately.

Rava offers an alternative resolution: *amar kra ve'natan ha'ish hashochev imah* — "and the man who lay with her shall give." The verse specifies that the payment is for the act of lying with her — *hana'at shchiva chamishim*, the fifty *sela* is for the physical act itself. *Miklal de'ika milta achriti* — this implies there are other matters beyond the act for which additional payment is owed. *U'mai nihu boshet u'pgam* — and those additional matters are *boshet* and *pgam*. The fifty *sela* and the variable additional damages thus address distinct aspects of the offense: the fixed payment covers the act of violation itself, while *boshet* and *pgam* cover the shame and bodily diminishment that accompany it.

---

---

# Arakhin 18

## Poverty Timing

### Tanna Kamma & R. Yehuda

The *daf* begins on 17b, picking up a *machlokes* in the *Mishnah* about the *din* in *erchin* concerning the poor person's discount. Ordinarily, the *Torah* assigns a fixed amount when one declares an *erech* — a donation to the *Mikdash* based on the fixed price schedule for different age ranges. However, when the pledger cannot afford the fixed amount, the *kohen* assesses what the person can actually pay. The dispute in the *Mishnah* centers on *when* one must be poor in order to qualify for this reduced assessment. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that one must be poor both at the time the *erech* is declared and at the time of payment. Rabbi Yehuda, however, holds that one must be poor for the *entire interval* from the declaration until the payment in order to qualify for the discount.

### Vehu Source

The *Gemara* seeks the source for Rabbi Yehuda's position. The proposed source is the word *vehu* — "and he" — which appears in the relevant *pasuk* and which Rabbi Yehuda reads as indicating that the condition must persist across the entire interval. The *Gemara* then proceeds to examine every other instance in the *Torah* where the word *vehu* appears, asking whether Rabbi Yehuda would apply the same interval-spanning logic in each case.

### Shebuot Ha'edut

The case under examination at the opening of our *daf* is *shevu'at ha'edut* — the oath of testimony. If a litigant claims that someone possesses information relevant to his court case and that person denies it, the litigant may compel that person to take an oath declaring that he knows nothing. However, this mechanism only applies if the person is a *kosher* witness. The *Gemara* asks: following Rabbi Yehuda's logic, would *vehu* require that the potential witness be *kosher* for the entire interval from the moment he allegedly witnessed the event until the moment he would give testimony in court?

### Witness Disqualifications

A *Braisa* is then cited that enumerates cases of disqualification. If a man knew testimony before becoming someone's son-in-law and then became that person's son-in-law — thereby rendering himself *posul le'edus* for that case — or if he was able to hear and speak and became deaf-mute, or was sighted and became blind (Rashi notes there is a special *gezeiras hakasuv* that a blind person is *posul le'edus*), or was sane and became insane, then in each of these cases he is invalid and cannot be compelled to take *shevu'as ha'edut*. So far, this appears consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's requirement of uninterrupted qualification.

### Temporary Disqualificati…

However, the *Braisa* continues with more difficult cases. Suppose the person was *kosher* at the time he witnessed the event, then became disqualified — for instance, he became someone's son-in-law, or became a deaf-mute, or went blind, or became insane — and then the disqualification was removed: his son-in-law status ended because the daughter died, or he regained his hearing and speech, or his sight was restored, or he recovered his sanity. In all such cases, the *Braisa* rules *kosher* — the litigant may compel him to take the oath. The *Braisa* states the general principle: *kol shetechilaso v'sofo b'kashrus* — whenever the beginning and the end are in a state of qualification, the person is valid. This appears to pose a direct challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's position, since the person was not *kosher* throughout the entire interval.

### Gezeirat Hakasuv

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty: *shani hatam*, the case of *shevu'as ha'edut* is different, because there is a special *gezeiras hakasuv*. The *pasuk* reads *o ra'ah o lo yagid* — the Gemara deduces from the juxtaposition: *b're'iyah v'hagadah talah rachmana milta*. The *Torah* specifically anchors the obligation to two moments — the act of witnessing (*re'iyah*) and the act of testifying (*hagadah*) — and only those two moments are halachically decisive. This is a particular scriptural decree unique to *shevu'as ha'edut*, and therefore one cannot draw any general inference about the word *vehu* from this case.

### Vehu & Specification

Since the rule in *shevu'as ha'edut* is derived entirely from the special *gezeiras hakasuv* of *o ra'ah*, the word *vehu* is freed from that context and must be teaching something else. The *Gemara* cites a *Braisa*: if someone sees a large group of people and says to all of them collectively, "I make all of you take an oath — if any of you knows testimony relevant to my case, come forward," one might have thought they are all thereby obligated. The word *vehu* — "and *he* is a witness" — teaches that one must specify the individual: the obligation of *shevu'as ha'edut* cannot be triggered by addressing a group indiscriminately. However, one might then think that even saying "whoever among you knows" is also insufficient specification. Therefore, the word *ed* after *vehu* teaches that if one does indicate "whoever among you," that is sufficient — what is prohibited is only addressing the group as a collective whole, but singling out any individual, even by implication, is adequate.

---

## Korbanot vs Erchin

### Korban Metzora Rules

The *Mishnah* then states: *aval b'korbanos eino kein* — but for *korbanos*, the rule is not the same. The interval-based poverty assessment that governs *erchin* does not apply to *korbanos*. This refers specifically to *korban metzora*, which is the only *korban* that follows a tiered structure — the *korban oleh v'yored* — where a wealthier person brings a different offering than a poor person. For *korban metzora*, wealth is assessed solely at the moment of bringing the offering; one does not look at any prior interval. The *Mishnah* gives two illustrative cases: if one's father died and left a substantial inheritance, or if one has a ship at sea worth tens of thousands, neither of these counts toward the wealth assessment.

### Inheritance Case

The *Gemara* asks on the first case: *aviv meis v'hiniach lo ribo* — why state this? If your father is wealthy but you are not, is it not obvious that you are poor and cannot be assessed as wealthy? Rav Papa clarifies: the case must be discussing a father who is *goses* — in the final stages of dying. One might have thought that since *rov gosesin lemita* — virtually all *gosesim* die imminently, to the point where the *Gemara* notes that the correct formulation is essentially *kol gosesin lemita*, as a *goses* by definition is irreversibly dying within days — we should treat the inheritance as already effectively in the son's possession. The *Gemara* teaches *ka mashma lan* that we do not; we assess only what is presently in one's actual possession.

### Ship Rental Income

The second case — a ship at sea generating tens of thousands in income — similarly seems obvious: your assets are simply inaccessible. Rav Chisda clarifies that the case is one where the ship is rented out to others and the tens of thousands refer not to cargo but to rental fees owed to the owner. The *Gemara* then asks: but does the person not in fact have the rental income? The *Gemara* answers: *schirut eina mishtalemet ela levasof* — rental fees were not payable until the conclusion of the rental period. Since the fees are not yet due, the person does not presently have them and cannot be assessed as wealthy on their account.

One might ask whether it matters that the fees will eventually accrue: if someone is legally owed money right now and could in theory pursue it immediately, should that not count as current wealth? The answer is that the present case involves fees that are not actionable until the end of the rental period — they simply have not come due yet. The related question of what the law would be for fees that are currently actionable but simply uncollected remains less clear, and the *Gemara* does not directly resolve it here. Note that the rule *schirut eina mishtalemet ela levasof* is itself a matter of *machloket* in other contexts, and the present ruling follows the opinion that rental payments accrue only at the end of the term.

### Boat Ownership Value

The *Gemara* then raises a further point: even if the rental fees are not yet owed, the owner still holds title to the boat itself. Should not the value of the boat as an asset render him wealthy?

### R. Eliezer Tools

The *Gemara* answers: *ha mani* — whose opinion does our *Mishnah* follow? It is that of Rabbi Eliezer, as we learn from a later *Mishnah* in the tractate: Rabbi Eliezer holds that when assessing a person's wealth for these purposes, we do not count a farmer's plow-animals or a donkey-driver's donkey. Rabbi Eliezer's principle is that the primary tools of one's livelihood are not included in the wealth assessment — we do not strip a person of the means by which he earns his living. Accordingly, the boat, as the owner's instrument of income, would similarly be excluded under Rabbi Eliezer's position, and the *Mishnah* reflecting that view would not count the ship's value toward the assessment.

---

## Age-Based Pricing

### Age of Valued Person

The *Mishnah* now turns to the mechanics of how *erchin* valuations are calculated. The *Torah* provides a price schedule based on age, and the *Mishnah* establishes that it is the age of the person being valued — the *ne'erach* — that determines the applicable price, not the age of the person making the pledge. The *Mishnah* illustrates: if a younger person (*yeled*, meaning here an adult between twenty and sixty) pledges the *erech* of an older person (*zaken*, meaning over sixty), he pays the price for the *zaken*; and if an older person pledges the *erech* of a younger person, he pays the price for the *yeled*.

### Gender Determines Price

Similarly, the *Mishnah* states: *ha-erchin be-ne'erach* — the *erchin* valuation follows the person being assessed. If a man pledges the *erech* of a woman, he pays the price for a woman; if a woman pledges the *erech* of a man, she pays the price for a man.

### Time of Pledge

The *Mishnah* further rules: the valuation follows the moment the pledge was made, not the moment of payment. If someone pledged the *erech* of a person who was under five years old at the time, and by the time of payment that person had already turned five — or was between five and twenty at the time of pledge and turned twenty before payment, or was under sixty and turned sixty before payment — in each case the pledger pays based on the age category at the *time of the pledge*, not at the time of payment.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The *Gemara* introduces a *Braisa* that explains why this rule requires a scriptural source. The *Torah* elsewhere establishes a *hekesh* between *erchin* and other *nedarim* — specifically, *damim*, the type of vow where one pledges the market value of a person as opposed to the fixed *erech* schedule. From this *hekesh* we derive two laws: first, that when a person must sell property to fulfill a *neder*, we do not force him to travel to the city to obtain a higher price — he may sell locally, *margalit l'kalim*, the easiest way. Second, that if the *neder* concerned a limb that is indispensable to life — such as one's head — the entire value of the person is owed, *lidon b'chvodo*.

One might have thought to extend the *hekesh* further and conclude that just as with *nedarim* the obligation is assessed at the time of payment, so too with *erchin* the valuation should follow the time of payment. After all, a *neder* of market value is assessed based on what the person is worth at the time he pays, not at the time he made the vow.

### Keerkecha Yakum

The *Gemara* therefore cites the *pasuk*: *k'erkecha yakum* — "as your *erech*, so shall it stand." The word *k'erkecha* teaches that the *erech* is fixed at the moment the pledge is made: *eino noten ela bizman ha-erech*. The *erech* valuation, unlike a *neder*, does not shift with changing circumstances at the time of payment. This is why our *Mishnah*'s rule, though it might initially have appeared counterintuitive given the *hekesh* to *nedarim*, follows the time of the pledge.

---

## Boundary Age Cases

### Thirtieth Day Rule

The *Mishnah* now addresses what happens at the boundary points between the age categories. The age categories for *erchin* are: under thirty days (for which there is no *erech* at all), thirty days to five years, five years to twenty years, and twenty years to sixty years, and above sixty. The *Mishnah* rules: *yom shloshim k'lemata heimena* — the thirtieth day itself counts with the prior period (i.e., below thirty days), not with the period that begins at thirty days. In practice, the thirty-first day is the first day of the next period.

### Birthdays with Younger

The *Mishnah* similarly rules that the fifth birthday and the twentieth birthday each count with the younger period. So the fifth birthday itself is still assessed at the lower rate, and only the day *after* the fifth birthday enters the higher category. The same applies at twenty.

### Shishim Pasuk Source

The *Mishnah* derives this principle from the *pasuk*: *v'im ben shishim shana v'ma'ala* — "and if he is sixty years and above." The *Mishnah* reads this as teaching that only from above sixty — meaning, the day after the sixtieth birthday — does one enter the higher (or in this case, lower-priced) category. The sixtieth birthday itself therefore counts with the younger period. This is read as a *chumra*: since the price drops at sixty, counting the birthday with the younger, higher-priced period means paying more.

### Binyan Av

From this ruling regarding the sixtieth birthday, the *Mishnah* makes a *binyan av* extending the same principle to all of the other age boundaries: just as the sixtieth birthday counts with the prior period, so too the twentieth and fifth birthdays count with their respective prior periods. However, the *Mishnah* immediately raises an objection to this *binyan av*: the sixty-year boundary goes with the younger period *lechumra* — you pay a higher price. But the twenty-year and five-year boundaries go with the younger period *lekula* — the younger price is lower. One cannot derive a general rule of "always count the birthday with the prior period" from a case where doing so is a *chumra* and then apply it to cases where doing so is a *kula*. Perhaps the correct rule is simply that the birthday always goes *lechumra*.

The *Mishnah* therefore abandons the *binyan av* approach and instead invokes a *gezeirah shavah*. Each of the relevant *pesukim* uses the word *shana* — "year." Since *esrim shana* and *shishim shana* both contain the word *shana*, we apply a *gezeirah shavah*: just as by the sixtieth year the word *shana* indicates that the birthday counts with the prior period, so too by the twentieth year and the fifth year the word *shana* carries the same implication. The *gezeirah shavah* thus extends the rule symmetrically, applicable both *lehachmir* and *lehakeil*, independent of which direction the price moves.

### Thirty Days Gap

This approach, however, leaves the thirty-day threshold unaddressed. There is no word *shana* associated with the thirty-day boundary, and therefore the *gezeirah shavah* cannot reach it. The *Gemara* acknowledges that we need a *binyan av* to extend the boundary rule from the year-based categories to the thirty-day threshold.

### R. Eliezer Month+Day

Rabbi Eliezer dissents from the *Tanna Kamma*. He holds that one day past the birthday is not sufficient; rather, one needs *chodesh v'yom echad* — a full month and a day beyond each birthday. According to Rabbi Eliezer, the applicable thresholds are: one month and a day, five years and a month and a day, twenty years and a month and a day, and sixty years and a month and a day.

The *Gemara* then introduces a further complication regarding the *gezeirah shavah* itself. The words *shana shana* that serve as the basis for the *gezeirah shavah* — appearing in *ben shishim shana* and *ben esrim shana* — raise the question of whether they are *mufneh*, free from other *derashos*. If they are not *mufneh*, the *gezeirah shavah* is vulnerable to challenge. However, the *Gemara* notes that *shana shana yitirei ketivi* — the words are in fact written as free, and furthermore, the structural symmetry of the *pesukim* supports this reading. Since the fifth birthday appears as both an endpoint (*v'ad ben chamesh shanim*) and a starting point (*miben chamesh*), the two instances of *shana* are equally balanced — *ishtaklelu* — and therefore neither can be *darshen*'d in the other direction. Rabbi's principle of *ad v'ad bichlal* (that every instance of *ad* includes the endpoint) would not apply here, because the same word is pulled equally in both directions. Consequently, even according to Rabbi, the *Mishnah*'s ruling stands.

Regarding the *tzara'at* discussion that arises in the context of *merosho v'ad raglav* — the *Gemara* explains that the head and feet are treated as separate regions from the body, either because the diagnostic criteria (*simanim*) for a *nega* on the head differ from those on the body (*shani simanim degufo misimanim derosho*), or alternatively because of the verse *lechol marei einei hakohen* — the assessment covers everything visible to the *kohen*'s eye, and certain areas of the head and feet are not ordinarily exposed to easy inspection.

### Chodesh Gezeirah

The source for Rabbi Eliezer's requirement of a month and a day beyond each age boundary is derived from a *Braisa*: *ne'emar kan lemalah v'ne'emar lehan chodesh ulemalah* — the word *lemalah* ("and above") appears both in connection with the year-based age categories and in the formulation *miben chodesh ulemalah* for the thirty-day threshold. Rabbi Eliezer applies a *gezeirah shavah*: just as the thirty-day period begins only from a month and a day after birth, so too all other age periods begin only from a month and a day beyond their threshold.

The *Gemara* challenges: why not read the *gezeirah shavah* the other way — just as the thirty-day threshold requires only one day above the threshold, so too all other thresholds require only one day? The *Gemara* responds: *im ken gezeirah shavah mai ahani* — if that were the intended reading, there would be no need for a *gezeirah shavah* at all, since we could derive "one day above each threshold" from straightforward reasoning (*misvara*). The *gezeirah shavah* must therefore be coming to teach us something beyond what reason alone would suggest — namely, a full month beyond each threshold, not merely one day.

---

## Mei'et L'Et

### Mei'et L'Et Contexts

The *Gemara* now cites a *Braisa* that collects multiple halachic domains where time is measured precisely — *mei'et le'et* — meaning that we count exact intervals from the moment an event occurred, rather than using calendar-year cutoffs. The *Braisa* lists: the year specified for *kodashim* (sacrificial animals of a certain age), the year for houses in walled cities, the two years for a *sedeh achuza*, the six years of a *eved ivri*, and — as the *Gemara* will discuss — sons and daughters. In each case, the operative measurement is a full interval from the triggering event, not a partial year counted as a full one.

Rashi reads *mei'et le'et* as measuring down to the exact hour — *oto yom v'ota sha'ah*. The Rambam, however, holds that we measure only by the day and not by the hour. The *Kesef Mishneh* notes this *machloket* and suggests that the majority view among the *Rishonim* follows the Rambam.

### Kodashim Full Year

For *kodashim*, the source is the phrase *keves ben shnato* — "a lamb in its year." The *Gemara* expounds: *shnato shelo* — its own year, meaning a full twelve months from its birth, and not *shana l'minyan olam*, not a calendar year measured from Rosh Hashanah. Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives this from the possessive form of the word.

### Walled City Year

For houses in walled cities, the *pasuk* states *ad tom shnat mimkaro* — "until the completion of the year of his sale." The word *mimkaro* — "of his sale" — indicates a year measured from the date of the sale itself, not from the New Year.

### Field Redemption

For the two-year restriction on redeeming a *sedeh achuza*, the *pasuk* states *b'mispar shnei t'vuot yimkar lach* — "according to the number of harvests shall it be sold to you." Rashi explains that *t'vuot* implies multiple harvests and is not limited to exactly two. The significance is that two calendar years could only ever include two harvests, but two full years measured from the time of sale can sometimes encompass three harvests — if the sale occurred partway through an agricultural cycle. This demonstrates that the measurement must be two full years *mei'et le'et*, not two calendar years.

Regarding leap years: these *halachot* are expressed in terms of years, not months, and therefore a full year is counted inclusive of any extra month added in a leap year. By contrast, *avelut* — which is twelve months — runs for twelve months regardless of whether the year is a leap year.

### Hebrew Servant Six Years

For the *eved ivri*, the *pasuk* states *shesh shanim ya'avod u'vashvi'it yetzei lachofshi chinam* — "six years shall he serve, and in the seventh he shall go free." The *Gemara* reads the *pasuk* with an alternative punctuation: "six years shall he serve, and in the seventh" — meaning that there are times when the service will extend into the seventh calendar year. This is only possible if we measure six full years from the date servitude began, because a six-year calendar count would always end within the sixth year and never reach into the seventh. The fact that the *Torah* implies the servant sometimes works into the seventh year proves that we count six full years *mei'et le'et*.

### Mei'et L'Et Dispute

The final entry in the *Braisa* — "sons and daughters" — requires explanation: to what *halacha* does it refer? Rav Gidel in the name of Rav says it refers to *erchin*: when determining whether a child has reached a new age category for the purposes of an *erech* pledge, we measure from the child's actual birth date, not from the calendar year. Rav Yosef, by contrast, says the reference is to the examples in *Perek Yotzei Dofen* — the chapter in Tractate *Niddah* dealing with when a boy or girl becomes halachically an adult (*gadlut*). According to Rav Yosef, it is *bar* and *bat mitzvah* — reached at thirteen and twelve years respectively — that is measured *mei'et le'et* from the child's birthday, not from Rosh Hashanah.

### Abaye Resolution

Abaye intervenes and asks Rav Yosef: do you disagree with Rav? Rav Yosef replies: not at all — *ana amri chada v'hu amar chada*, I cited one example and he cited another, and we both agree that the *halacha* is *mei'et le'et* in both cases. Abaye confirms that this is indeed the more sensible reading: *hacha nami mistabra*. For if they were truly in dispute — if the one who says *erchin* did not hold *mei'et le'et* for *Perek Yotzei Dofen*, and vice versa — it would be difficult to reconcile with the explicit statement of Rav, cited elsewhere, that *hilchata be-kula pirka me'et le'et* — the ruling throughout the entirety of *Perek Yotzei Dofen* is *mei'et le'et*. Since Rav himself stated this about the *perek*, and Rav is also the one cited by Rav Gidel as saying *erchin* is *mei'et le'et*, clearly Rav holds both. Rav Yosef and Rav Gidel were each giving *pshat* in the *Braisa*, not asserting an exclusive ruling.

### Opinion Consistency

The *Gemara* then asks: why did the one who cited *erchin* not cite *Perek Yotzei Dofen* as his example, and why did the one who cited *Perek Yotzei Dofen* not cite *erchin*? The answer is *dumya de-hanach* — each sought an example that was parallel to the other cases listed in the *Braisa*. All of the other cases in the *Braisa* — *kodashim*, walled-city houses, *sedeh achuza*, *eved ivri* — have explicit *pesukim* from which *mei'et le'et* is derived. *Erchin* similarly has a scriptural basis for *mei'et le'et* and therefore fits naturally alongside those cases. Bar and bat mitzvah, by contrast, appear to be derived from reasoning (*misvara*) rather than from a direct *pasuk*; Tosafot notes that the *Gemara* never actually supplies an explicit verse for *erchin* being *mei'et le'et*, and suggests that the thirty-day threshold — for which *mei'et le'et* is clearer — extends by inference to the other *erchin* categories.

The one who cited *Perek Yotzei Dofen*, on the other hand, did not use *erchin* because the *Braisa*'s language of *ben u-vat* — "son and daughter" — does not naturally describe *erchin*, which uses the language of *zachar v'nekevah* — "male and female." The more natural reading of *ben u-vat* is *bar mitzvah* and *bat mitzvah*, the domain where a son and a daughter become adults. Each *amora* therefore chose the example that best fit both the language of the *Braisa* and the pattern of derivation.

---

## Gender Value Differences

### Age 60 Gender Gap

A notable observation closes the *perek*. The *Gemara* asks: *mai shna nekeva de-chi mizkana kaima atilta* — why is it that when a woman ages past sixty, her *erech* remains relatively high compared to her prior value, whereas *mai shna zachar de-lo kaima atilta* — for a man, the drop in *erech* at sixty is far steeper? In concrete terms: the *erech* of a woman between twenty and sixty is thirty *shekalim*, and at sixty it drops to ten — a threefold decrease. The *erech* of a man between twenty and sixty is fifty *shekalim*, and above sixty it drops to fifteen — more than a threefold decrease. The proportional decline for men is sharper than for women. And this is worth noting alongside the broader picture: even a younger woman's *erech* is lower than a man's in the same age range, so this is not a simple question of relative honor.

### Old Age Proverbs

Chizkiyah answers with a popular saying: *amri inshi, saba be-veita pacha, savta be-veita sima be-veita* — people say, "an old man in the house is a burden in the house; an old woman in the house is a treasure in the house." The *erech* schedule reflects economic and social utility: the type of work associated with women — domestic labor, cooking, serving — remains productive and valuable into advanced age. The type of labor associated with men, being more physically demanding, loses value more sharply with age. Rashi explains the underlying logic in these terms. The Torah's fixed valuation schedule, counterintuitive as it may seem in some respects, tracks observable social realities as understood in the context of the time.

With this, we conclude *Perek HaSheg Yad*.

---

---

# Arakhin 19

## Weight Donation

### Pledging Weight

We begin a new *perek* today — Daf 19a — and with it a shift in focus. Although we are still in *Masechet Arakhin*, this *perek* is less concerned with *erchin* proper and deals instead with more traditional *nedarim*: the various ways a person may donate money to the *Beit HaMikdash*. The opening *Mishnah* states: *ha'omer mishkali alai* — if someone says "my weight is upon me," pledging their body weight to the *Beit HaMikdash*, then *noten mishkalo*, they must give their weight. And the *Mishnah* adds: *im kesef kesef, im zahav zahav* — if silver, then silver; if gold, then gold. The *Gemara* will clarify precisely what this means.

### Yarmatya Story

The *Mishnah* then introduces a narrative: *maaseh be'imo shel Yarmatya* — a story involving the mother of someone named Yarmatya, a figure of apparent importance. The mother declared *mishkal biti alai* — the weight of my daughter should be upon me. She went up to Jerusalem, they weighed her daughter, and the court required her to give that weight in gold. The reason this story is brought — and why gold specifically was demanded — will become clear from the *Gemara*'s discussion below.

### Hand Weight Method

The *Mishnah* continues with a further case. If someone says *mishkal yadi alai* — I want to donate the weight of my hand — Rabbi Yehuda says: you fill a barrel completely with water and insert the arm until *marpeko*. *Rashi* understands *marpeko* as the shoulder; *Tosafot* understands it as the elbow, and *Tosafot*'s reading fits more smoothly across the relevant *sugyas* in *Shas*. You observe how much water is displaced, then take donkey flesh, bones, and sinews — *besar chamor va'atzamot vegidin* — and displace the same amount of water. The density of donkey flesh is assumed to be approximately equal to that of human flesh, so you weigh the donkey material needed to reach the same displacement, and that is the weight owed to the *Beit HaMikdash*.

Rabbi Yosi objects: *heich efshar lechaven basar keneged basar, gidim keneged gidim, atzamot keneged atzamot?* — How is it truly possible to match muscle for muscle, sinew for sinew, bone for bone in exact proportion? Rather, says Rabbi Yosi, *shammin et hayad kamah hi re'uyah lishkol* — we simply estimate approximately how much the hand would weigh. The *Mishnah* thus presents both approaches, and the *Gemara* will develop the dispute further.

---

## Conditional Pledges

### Silver vs. Gold

The *Gemara* opens by asking: *mai im kesef kesef?* — what does the *Mishnah* mean when it says "if silver, silver; if gold, gold"? Rav Yehuda explains: *peireish kesef kesef, peireish zahav zahav* — if you specified that you want to give silver, you must give silver; if you specified gold, you must give gold. The *Gemara* immediately objects: *peshitah* — that is obvious. What new information does the *Mishnah* convey?

The answer is that the *Mishnah* is teaching by implication: *ta'ama depeireish, ha lo peireish patar nafshih bechol dehu* — the reason you must give the specified metal is because you specified it. Had you not specified, you could give your weight in any substance — or rather, in nearly any substance, as Rachba qualifies. Rachba teaches: *ba'asra detakli kufra, patar nafshih afilu bekufra* — in a locale where pitch or tar is sold by weight, you may discharge your obligation by giving your weight in pitch. The substance need not be a precious metal; it must simply be something sold by weight in your locale.

### Pitch & Onions

The *Gemara* again objects: *peshitah* — why shouldn't pitch work if it is sold by weight? The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzerichah de'ika detakal ve'ika dekayal* — the novelty is in a case where some merchants sell pitch by weight and others sell it by volume. One might have thought that since not all merchants sell it by weight it cannot qualify; the teaching tells us it is nonetheless sufficient.

Rav Papa then adds a parallel ruling: *ba'asra detakli shamchei, patar nafshih afilu beshamchei* — in a place where onions are sold by weight, you may discharge your pledge by giving your weight in onions (*shamchei*, as *Rashi* explains, meaning *betzalim*, onions). Again the *Gemara* challenges: *peshitah*. And again the answer identifies the novelty: *debasar deshakli shadu trei platei* — the typical practice when selling onions was to weigh them out and then throw in two or three extra as a bonus, like a baker's dozen. One might have thought that since the transaction is not purely by weight — given the extra portion added — the substance is no longer considered *sold by weight*. The *Gemara* teaches that it nonetheless qualifies.

### Wealthy Assessment

The *Gemara* now returns to the story of Yarmatya's mother. It asks: *maaseh listor?* — is the story coming to contradict what we just said? We explained that if you do not specify a substance you may give anything sold by weight. Yet in the story, Yarmatya's mother did not specify, and the court required her to give gold. The *Gemara* resolves this with *chasuri mechasra vehachi kasani* — our text of the *Mishnah* is incomplete, and here is what it should have read: *ve'im adam chashuv hu, af al gav delo peireish, lefi kevodo amdinan* — if the person is a person of great means, then even if they did not specify, we assess what would be fitting for someone of their standing. The story of Yarmatya's mother is thus brought to illustrate this principle: she was a wealthy woman, she said merely that she was pledging her daughter's weight, and because of her stature the court assessed that the appropriate payment was gold.

---

## Height & Limbs

### Height Rods

The *Gemara* now takes up a related question. Rav Yehuda asks: what is the *din* if one says *komasi alai* — I want to donate my height? The ruling is: *nosein sharvit she'eino nichpaf* — you must give a rod of the appropriate substance equal to your height, and the rod must be thick enough that it cannot bend. However, if one says *melo komasi alai* — the fullness of my height — then *nosein sharvit hanichpaf*, you may give even a flexible rod.

The *Gemara* challenges this from a *Tosefta*: the *Tosefta* explicitly states that whether you say *komasi alai* or *melo komasi alai*, in both cases you must give a rigid rod — *sharvit she'eino nichpaf*. The *Gemara* resolves this by saying that Rav Yehuda follows the *shita* of Rabbi Akiva, as indicated by the phrase *dedayek lishnei yeseira* — Rabbi Akiva pays close attention to every extra word and interprets it as introducing a meaningful distinction.

We know this principle from a *Mishnah* in *Bava Batra*, in *perek* on selling a house (*perek hamocher et habayit*): *velo et habor velo et hadus* — when selling a house or field, the sale does not automatically include cisterns or cellars, even if the deed specifies dimensions. Rabbi Akiva rules, moreover, that if the seller must now pass through sold land to reach his retained cistern, he must purchase a path back from the buyer — because the path is not assumed to be included in what was retained. The *Chachamim* disagree, holding that since the cistern was not sold, the path necessary to access it was implicitly retained as well.

The part relevant to our case is *modeh Rabbi Akiva bizman she'amar lo chutz me'elu she'ein tzarich likach lo derech* — Rabbi Akiva concedes that if the seller said "I am selling my field with the exception of the cistern," he does not need to repurchase the path, even though he normally would. Why? Because he did not need to specify the exception — under the ordinary rule the cistern is not included. Since he specified it anyway, *alma keivan delo tzarich veka'amar litfuyei milta ka'ati* — since he did not need to say it and he said it regardless, he must have been adding something, and what he was adding was his retention of the path as well. From this we see Rabbi Akiva's general interpretive method: any extra word a person uses carries legal weight.

Applying this to our case: *hacha nami keivan delo tzarich veka'amar litfuyei milta ka'ati* — here too, the person did not need to say *melo komasi*; the ordinary formulation *komasi* would have sufficed. Having added the word *melo*, he must have intended to give something different — namely, the more lenient option of a flexible rod.

### Teiku Cases

The *Gemara* then raises a series of unresolved questions. *Iba'ya lehu*: what is the *din* if someone says *omdi* — my stature? What if they say *rochvi* — my breadth? What about *yeshivati* — the space I occupy when seated? What about *ovyi* — my width? Or *heikefi* — my circumference? The *Gemara* leaves all of these at *teiku* — unresolved. These edge cases may simply be too rare to require definitive resolution.

---

## Limb Weight

### Displacement Method

We now return to the question of how to weigh a specific limb. The *Gemara* quotes a *baraita*: *tanu rabbanan* — if someone pledges *mishkal yadi alai* or *mishkal ragli alai* — the weight of their hand or foot — Rabbi Yehuda rules as follows. Fill a barrel with water. For the hand, insert the arm *ad ha'atzil*, until the elbow. For the leg, insert it *ad ha'arkuva*, until the knee. Then take donkey flesh, bones, and sinews, and displace that same volume of water — *noten letocho ad she'titmalei*. The donkey material used to achieve equivalent displacement is then weighed, and that is the amount owed.

The *baraita* acknowledges: *ve'af al pi she'ein re'ayah la'davar zecher la'davar* — even though there is no *pasuk* that proves this method, there is a *pasuk* in *Yechezkel* that alludes to it: *asher besar chamorim besaram* — their flesh is like the flesh of donkeys. This verse is taken to confirm that donkey flesh is a reasonable analogue for human flesh in density, making it a valid substitute for this measurement.

Rabbi Yosi objects, as in the *Mishnah*: *hei efshar lechaven basar keneged basar, gidim keneged gidim, atzamot keneged atzamot?* — Can one truly replicate the exact proportional composition of muscle, sinew, and bone? Rabbi Yehuda responds: *umdana* — you estimate where necessary. Rabbi Yosi presses the point: *ad she'umdana yamodu et hayad* — once you have to estimate anyway, simply estimate the total weight of the hand directly, without the elaborate donkey-flesh procedure. Rabbi Yehuda's position, in turn, is *kama de'efshar avdinan bah* — we do everything possible to be precise, and only where an exact match is impossible do we rely on estimation.

### Hand Definition

The *baraita* states that for the hand one inserts the arm *ad ha'atzil*, until the elbow. The *Gemara* challenges this from a *Tosefta* in *Masechet Yadayim*: *kidush yadayim veraglayim bamikdash ad haperek* — when a *kohen* sanctifies his hands in the *Mikdash*, he sanctifies until the *perek*, the wrist. This implies that the halakhic definition of *yad* is only until the wrist, not the elbow.

The *Gemara* resolves this: *binedarim halach achar lashon benei adam* — in *nedarim* we follow not formal halakhic definitions but ordinary speech. When people in those times used the word *yad*, they meant the entire arm up to the elbow, and therefore a pledge using the word *yad* is interpreted accordingly.

But the *Gemara* then asks whether the assumption itself is correct — is it really true that *deoraita* the definition of *yad* extends only to the wrist? After all, regarding *tefillin*, the *pasuk* says *yadcha*, and a *baraita* (*Tana devei Menashe*) teaches: *yadcha zo kiboret* — the Torah's use of *yad* by *tefillin* refers to the bicep. No one wraps *tefillin* on the hand itself; it goes on the upper arm. So the *Gemara* revises its assumption: *deoraita kiboret kulah* — the Torah's definition of *yad* actually extends all the way to the end of the bicep.

The principle *binedarim halach achar lashon benei adam* now works in the opposite direction. Previously, *lashon benei adam* was *machmir* relative to the halakhic definition — people say *yad* and mean more than the wrist. Now it is *mekil* — because the halakhic definition extends to the end of the bicep, while *lashon benei adam* stops at the elbow.

As for the earlier ruling about hand-washing in the *Mikdash* going only to the wrist: *vekidush yadayim veraglayim bamikdash hilchata gemiri lah* — that is a special transmitted tradition, not an expression of the Torah's general definition of *yad*, and does not affect our analysis.

### Foot Definition

Parallel to the hand, the *baraita* states that for the foot one inserts *ad ha'arkuva*, until the knee. The *Gemara* challenges this from a *davar* in the laws of *aliyah leregel*. The *Gemara* derives from the word *regalim* — the pilgrimage festivals, which contains the word *regel* — that *prat lebaalei kabin*: those who walk on wooden feet, i.e., amputees with prosthetics, are exempt from the obligation to appear in Jerusalem and bring the *olat reiyah*. This implies that the definition of *regel* relevant to this *mitzvah* is the foot alone, not the entire leg up to the knee.

The *Gemara* resolves this the same way: *binedarim halach achar lashon benei adam* — in *nedarim* we follow how people speak, and people refer to the entire lower leg up to the knee as their *regel*. It is only for the purpose of *aliyah leregel* that the Torah's narrower definition applies.

### Chalitza Anatomy

The *Gemara* then asks whether it is really accurate that the Torah's definition of *regel* is limited to the foot alone. Is there not the case of *chalitza*, where the *pasuk* reads *vechaltzah na'alo me'al raglo* — she removes his shoe from his *regel* — and a *tanna* teaches that if the *chalitza* shoe was tied anywhere below the knee, the *chalitza* is *keshera bedieved*? This seems to indicate that the Torah's definition of *regel* extends all the way up to the knee, not merely the foot.

The *Gemara* responds: *shani hatam de'amar me'al raglo* — by *chalitza* the *pasuk* adds the word *me'al*, "from above the foot," and it is this extra word that comes to include the calf. One might then ask: if *me'al* expands the definition, why not extend it above the knee as well? The *Gemara* answers: *me'al velo me'al deme'al* — "above," but not above that which is above the foot. The word *me'al* adds one extension above the foot — the calf — but not a second extension beyond that, which would include the thigh. The thigh therefore does not qualify for *chalitza*.

Rav Papa then derives an anatomical observation from this *sugya*. Rav Sheshet notes: *shma mina hai istavira ad ara nachit* — one can infer that the ankle bone extends all the way down to the ground. His reasoning: if the ankle bone ended before reaching the ground, then the ankle itself would be *me'al* the foot, and the calf would be *me'al deme'al*, leaving the calf outside the valid range. Since the *Mishnah* permits *chalitza* up the entire length of the calf, it follows that the ankle must descend all the way to the floor, placing the calf — not the ankle — as the single extension *me'al* the foot.

Rav Ashi disagrees: *afilu teima mafsek pasik* — even if you say the ankle bone does end before the ground, the rule is *kol de'bahadei kara ke'kara dami* — whatever occupies the same horizontal plane as the foot is considered part of the foot. Therefore the ankle, though not physically continuous to the ground, counts as part of the foot because it enters the same horizontal plane. The calf is then *me'al* the foot, and the thigh is *me'al deme'al* — and therefore invalid for *chalitza*.

---

## Limb Value

### Slave Market Value

The *Mishnah* now addresses a related but distinct case: *de'mei yadai alai* — I pledge the *value* of my hand to the *Beit HaMikdash*, not its weight. The *Mishnah* rules: *shamin oso kama hu shaveh be'yad u'velo yad* — we assess how much he is worth with a hand, how much without, and the difference is the value of the hand. The *Mishnah* notes this is *chomer binedarim mi'be'erchin* — more stringent in *nedarim* than in *erchin*, because saying *erech yadi* — the *erech* of my hand — obligates nothing, since *erchin* only applies to a limb *she'ha'neshama teluya bo*, a limb without which one cannot live. *Demai*, by contrast, assigns real monetary value to the limb.

The *Gemara* asks: *heichi sham'inan* — how precisely do we carry out this assessment? Rav Ada says: *omden oso omed shel nezikin* — we assess him the same way we assess for tort damages. In a *nezikin* case where someone's hand was severed, the assessment involves estimating what the person would have been worth on the slave market with the hand, versus what they are worth now without it, and the difference is the hand's value. This appears to be simply the plain reading of the *Mishnah*.

Abaye challenges this: *mi dami?* — are the cases truly comparable? *Hasam gavra zila hu, hacha gavra shvi'ach hu* — in the *nezikin* case, the person stands before us as he currently is, namely without a hand, and we estimate his value *with* the hand. In the *nedarim* case, the person currently *has* the hand, and we must estimate what he would be worth *without* it. Abaye's concern is that the direction of estimation matters: even if we accept that estimating upward from an incomplete state is reliable, we cannot assume the same reliability when estimating downward from a complete state.

Abaye therefore proposes a different method: *omden kama adam rotze litein be'eved ha'oseh melacha be'yad achat le'oseh bi'shtei yadayim* — we assess how much more a buyer would pay for a slave who works with both hands versus one who works with only one. One might ask: is this not essentially the same as going to the slave market and comparing the prices of people with and without a hand? The *Gemara* raises exactly this point: if we are talking about a slave who is actually missing a hand, *hainu hach* — that is the same method as Rav Ada's. Rather, Abaye specifies: *yado muchtevet lerabo rishon* — we are dealing with a case where one hand of the slave is sold to a different master. One person therefore owns the entire slave except one hand. The differential in market value between owning a complete slave versus owning this slave-minus-one-hand yields, according to Abaye, a more precise and less speculative measure of that hand's value than estimating the price of someone who has lost the hand entirely.

### Assessment Scenarios

The *Gemara* then enters a series of *sha'alot* posed by Rava regarding estimation in *nedarim*. The first: suppose someone had their hand severed and their value was already assessed for *nezikin* purposes — and then they say *demai alai*, pledging their value to the *Beit HaMikdash*. Can that prior assessment be used for the *nedarim* obligation? *Mi amrinan ha amduhu chada zimna* — do we say it has already been assessed once, and that is sufficient? *O dilma shani umdena devei asara me'umdena devei tlata* — or perhaps the two assessments are categorically different, since for *nezikin* a *beit din* of three suffices, while for *nedarim* the *Mishnah* in *Sanhedrin* requires a *beit din* of ten. If so, the assessment performed for *nezikin* cannot discharge the requirement for *nedarim*.

A follow-up question: assuming it does matter that the *nedarim* assessment requires ten — *amar demai alai ve'amduhu vechazar ve'amar demai alai mahu* — if someone was already assessed with a *beit din* of ten for a prior *neder*, and then makes the same *neder* again, do we require a new assessment? *Hacha vadai amduhu bei asara* — this time he certainly was assessed by ten, so perhaps it counts again. *O dilma shevach beini uveini* — or perhaps his value has changed in the intervening period, so the first assessment can no longer serve for the second *neder*.

Yet another question: *amar demai alai velo amduhu vechazar ve'amar demai alai* — if someone made a pledge of their value, was never assessed, and then made the same pledge again before any assessment occurred, must they now be assessed twice? This question probes whether the assessment is purely fact-finding — in which case one determination of the value serves for both *nedarim* — or whether it constitutes a distinct component of the *mitzvah* of *nedarim*, requiring a separate act for each *neder*. *Hacha vadai b'chad zimna amdinan* — perhaps one assessment clearly suffices since the value will be identical. *O dilma keivan d'v'zeh achar zeh nadar trei zimnei amdinan* — or perhaps since two separate *nedarim* were taken, two separate assessments are required.

A further extension: *amar shnei damai alai b'vat achat* — what if someone says "twice my value should be upon me," taking both pledges simultaneously? *Hacha b'vat achat nadar b'vat achat amdinan* — perhaps since it was said at one moment, one assessment suffices. *O dilma keivan d'ka'amar shnei k'zeh achar zeh dami* — or perhaps since the person said *two*, it is legally treated as if the *nedarim* were taken one after the other, requiring two assessments.

### Self-Assessment

Finally, the *Gemara* asks: *amduhu me'elav mahu* — what if a person was assessed entirely on their own initiative, not in connection with any *neder*, simply out of curiosity as to their slave-market value, and ten people were present — does this count for a subsequent *neder*? *Mi amrinan ha amid me'elav v'ka'i* — do we say the value is already established? *O dilma ba'inan kavana l'umdana* — or do we require that the assessment be performed with specific *kavanah* for this *neder*? If specific *kavanah* is required, this strongly suggests that assessment is itself part of the *mitzvah* of *nedarim*, not merely a factual inquiry.

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve at least this final question from a *Mishnah*: *damai alai v'met lo yitnu yorshim she'ein damim l'metim* — if someone pledged their value and then died, the heirs need not pay, because *ein damim l'metim* — there is no way to assess the value of a dead person. One might suggest: even if we require *kavanah* for a formal assessment, at least we know that every living person is worth some minimum value on the slave market. The *Gemara* notes *mi ika gavra d'lo shaveh arba zuzei* — is there anyone not worth at least four *zuzim*? So why not make the heirs liable for four *zuzim* as a kind of *umdana me'elav*, an informal assessment derived from general knowledge?

The *Gemara* rejects this proof. *Amduhu me'elav nachit l'umdana* — a person who had their value assessed, even informally, has at least undergone an act of assessment. *Damai alai lo nachit l'umdana* — someone who merely pronounced *demai alai* has performed no assessment whatsoever. General knowledge that no person sells for less than four *zuzim* is not equivalent to an *umdana*. Even if we were to hold that no specific *kavanah* is required, an affirmative act of assessment is still necessary — and that was never done here. Accordingly, the *Gemara* leaves all of these questions unresolved.

---

---

# Arakhin 20

## Arachin vs Nedarim

### Definitions

The Mishnah on this daf continues the comparison between *arachin* and *nedarim*. To recall the basic framework: *arachin* are the special vows for which the Torah provides its own fixed pricelist, whereas *nedarim* — in the sense used here — are individual vows in which one pledges the value of a person or object as assessed on the slave market or the open market. The Mishnah opens with the declaration *chomer be'arachin mibinedarim* — in the following respects, *arachin* are stricter than *nedarim*.

### Death Cases

The first case: *ha'omer erchi alai umet yitnu hayorshin* — if one takes a pledge to give one's *erach* to the *Beis Hamikdash* and then dies, the heirs must still pay. By contrast, if one said *damai alai* — "my value is upon me," which is *lashon neder* — and then dies, the heirs do not pay: *she'ein damim lemetim*, because dead people cannot be evaluated. Dead persons are not sold on the slave market, and it is the value of a living person that is required. There is also the consideration that a dead body is *assur be-hana'ah*, forbidden for benefit, rendering any such evaluation categorically inapplicable.

### Life-Dependent Limbs

The Mishnah continues: *erach yadi ve'erach ragli alai lo amar klum* — if one says "I wish to pledge the *erach* of my hand or of my foot," this is a meaningless statement and nothing is owed. By contrast: *erach roshi ve'erach kivedi alai noten erach kulo* — if one says "I wish to pledge the *erach* of my head or of my liver," one must give the full *erach* of the whole person. The *klal* is stated explicitly: *davar she'haneshama teluya bo noten erach kulo* — any limb upon which one's life depends obligates the full *erach*. Hand and foot, by contrast — *ein haneshama teluya bo* — one can live without them, and the pledge is therefore meaningless in the context of *arachin*.

### Half-Value Pledges

The Mishnah then addresses partial pledges. *Chatzi erchi alai noten chatzi ercho* — if one says "I pledge half of my *erach*," one gives half of the Torah's fixed valuation. But *erach chatzi alai noten erach kulo* — if one says "the *erach* of half of me," one must give the entire *erach*, for the same reason: one cannot live without half one's body, making this a *davar she'haneshama teluya bo*.

Turning to the parallel rules for *nedarim*: *chatzi damai alai noten chatzi damav* — pledging half one's value means paying half one's value. Yet *dmei chatzi alai noten dmei kulo* — pledging "the value of half of me" requires giving the full value, since the same principle of *davar she'haneshama teluya bo* applies: *ze haklal davar she'haneshama teluya bo noten dmei kulo*. This rule applies equally to *arachin* and to *nedarim*.

It is worth noting that yesterday's Mishnah established an important asymmetry: by *nedarim*, pledging the value of a limb *she'ein haneshama teluya bo* — such as a hand or a foot — does require payment of that limb's actual value, whereas by *arachin*, such a pledge is entirely meaningless and nothing is owed.

### Another's Value

The Mishnah addresses a further case: *ha'omer ercho shel ploni alai* — one who pledges the *erach* of another person. *Met hanoder vehanidar yitnu hayorshin* — if both the pledger and the one whose *erach* was pledged die, the heirs must still pay. By contrast, in a *neder* of *damav shel ploni*: if the pledger dies, the heirs still pay; but if the one whose value was pledged dies — *met hanidar lo yitnu hayorshin she'ein damim lemetim* — the heirs do not pay, again because there is no way to evaluate the value of someone already dead.

### Nedarim Strictures

The Gemara then cites a *Baraisa* that presents the reverse list: *chomer binedarim mibe'arachin* — the ways in which *nedarim* are stricter than *arachin*. *She'ha-nedarim chalin al behemah chaya va-of* — *nedarim* can apply to domestic animals, wild animals, and birds, whereas *arachin* apply only to human beings. Additionally, *nedarim* do not have the *heseg yad* discount that applies to *arachin*: if a person is too poor to afford the *arach* listed in the Torah, the *kohen* evaluates how much that person can afford, and that reduced amount suffices — *mah she'ein ken be-arach*. No such concession applies to *nedarim*; regardless of one's means, the full value must be paid.

The *Baraisa* then restates the corresponding rules in which *arachin* are stricter, replicating the substance of our Mishnah: *erchi alai va-met yitnu yorshin* — the heirs pay the *erach*, whereas *dami alai va-met lo yitnu yorshin* — the heirs do not pay the *neder* value — *she'ein damim le-metim*.

---

## Oral Loans Analysis

### Oral Loan Collection

The Gemara fastens onto that last line of the *Baraisa* — that one who pledges *erchi alai* and then dies leaves the heirs obligated to pay — and asks: *shema mina milveh al peh goveh min ha-yorshin*? Can we derive from here that an oral loan — one made verbally with witnesses but without a written contract — may be collected from heirs? The Gemara's reasoning is that the *arach* obligation involved no formal contract; the person merely stated verbally that he wished to make the pledge. If the *Beis Hamikdash* can nevertheless collect from heirs, does this not establish that oral monetary obligations are likewise heritable?

### Torah-Written Status

The Gemara immediately deflects this inference: *shani hacha de-milveh kesuvah ba-Torah hi* — this case is different, because the obligation is written in the Torah. Even though no individual contract was drawn up, the *arach* is not strictly an oral loan in the relevant sense, since the Torah itself records the obligation. One therefore cannot derive any ruling about ordinary oral loans from this case.

### Baraisa Challenge

The Gemara then pivots to the other side of the *Baraisa*: since *dami alai va-met lo yitnu yorshin* — when the pledge was a *neder*, the heirs do not pay — might one not infer from here that *milveh al peh* cannot be collected from heirs? The Gemara responds: no, because the reason the heirs do not pay in the *neder* case is a technicality — *she'ein damim le-metim*. The evaluation cannot be performed because the person is dead. The implication, then, is striking: the distinction in the Mishnah between *arachin* and *nedarim* appears to be purely technical. *Arachin* carry a fixed price, so heirs can pay without any evaluation. *Nedarim* require evaluation of a living person — and once that person is dead, the evaluation is impossible. Had the evaluation already been completed before death, the heirs would seemingly be obligated to pay even in the *neder* case.

One might ask whether we truly require a formal *ha'amada bedin* — a court ruling — in every case. In practice, if no one is contesting the obligation, one simply pays and that is the end of it. If, however, the pledger has second thoughts and questions whether the *neder* was validly contracted, the matter goes to court, which rules on its validity. The Gemara's discussion assumes that for purposes of creating a heritable obligation, such a court ruling is what triggers the lien on the property.

The Gemara then attempts a further inference: *shema mina milveh ha-katuv ba-Torah ke-katuv be-shtar dami* — perhaps one can prove from here that a monetary obligation written in the Torah has the status of a written contract, a question that was itself subject to a *machloket* in Masechet Bechorot. The Gemara declines this inference as well.

### Court Lien

The Gemara resolves the difficulty with an *okimta*: *hacha be-mai askinan ke-she'amad be-din* — we are dealing with a case where the person not only stated the pledge verbally but subsequently appeared in court, and the court ruled that his statement constituted a valid *arach* obligation. Once the court has so ruled, the obligation acquires the status of *ke-katuv be-shtar dami* — it is as though it were written in a contract — and the heirs are therefore bound. The mere verbal pledge, before any court ruling, may still retain the status of *milveh al peh*. Thus no general inference about oral loans can be extracted.

### Two Evaluations

The Gemara then challenges this answer: if the *ha'amada be-din* is what makes the obligation heritable even in *neder* cases, why does the Mishnah say the heirs do not pay in the *neder* case? Once the pledger has appeared in court and the court validated his *neder*, should the heirs not be obligated?

The answer is that *nedarim* require two distinct steps: the court must evaluate whether the obligation was validly contracted (*ha'amada be-din*), and then a separate evaluation of the value of the person whose *damim* were pledged must be carried out. *Dami alai mechusar umdana* — the *neder* pledge remains deficient until that second evaluation has been performed. By contrast, *erchi alai lo mechusar ve-lo klum* — once the court has ruled that the *erach* pledge was valid, no further evaluative step is needed, because the Torah itself supplies the valuation. Accordingly, the *seifa* of the Mishnah dealing with *damav shel ploni alai* comes to teach a precise point: *de-keivan de-amad be-din ishtabdu nikhsei* — once the court has ruled on the obligation, a lien is immediately created on the property. The subsequent evaluation of the pledgee's value merely reveals retroactively the amount of that lien; the lien itself existed from the moment of the court's ruling.

---

## Limbs & Meaningless

### Hand/Foot Cases

The Gemara turns to the Mishnah's case of *erach yadi ve'erach ragli alai* — pledging the *erach* of one's hand or foot — which the Mishnah had ruled *lo amar klum*, a meaningless statement under *arachin*. This stands in contrast to pledging the *erach* of one's head or liver, which requires full payment.

### Rav Gidel Ruling

*Amar Rav Gidel amar Rav ve-noten dameha* — Rav Gidel in the name of Rav rules that one who says *erach yadi ve'erach ragli* must give the value of the hand or foot. This appears to contradict the Mishnah's ruling of *lo amar klum*. The Gemara resolves the tension: the Mishnah reflects the position of the *Rabbanan*, who hold *adam motzi devarav le-vatalah* — people do sometimes make meaningless statements, and this is one such case. Rav Gidel's ruling reflects the view of Rabbi Meir, who holds *ein adam motzi devarav le-vatalah* — people do not normally make meaningless statements. Therefore, according to Rabbi Meir, if one said *erach yadi*, one must have meant to pledge the hand's monetary value (*damim*), and must pay accordingly.

The Gemara then asks: but Rav Gidel himself had already told us about this *machloket* between Rabbi Meir and the *Rabbanan*. What does his new ruling here add? The reference is to an earlier statement of Rav Gidel: *ha'omer erech kli zeh alai noten damav* — one who says the *erach* of a vessel should be upon him must pay the vessel's value. Everyone knows that *arachin* do not apply to vessels; therefore, according to Rabbi Meir, since the person knew this, he must have intended the pledge as a *neder* and must pay the vessel's value.

### Vessel Distinctions

One might have thought that the vessel case and the limb case are distinguishable. In the vessel case, everyone knows that *arachin* do not apply to *kelim*, so when someone says *erech kli zeh*, we confidently assume he intended it as a *neder* for its market value — *gamar ve'amar le-shem damim*. In the limb case, however, one might argue that the person simply made an error: he may have assumed, by analogy with pledging the *erach* of one's head or liver, that pledging the *erach* of one's hand or foot was equally valid — *savar ki heichi de-ika erech roshi ve-erech kveidi, ika nami erech yadi ve-erach ragli*. In that case, he never intended to pledge the hand's monetary value at all — *aval damim lo ka'amar*. Rav Gidel therefore comes to teach us that even in this limb case, Rabbi Meir holds *ein adam motzi devarav le-vatalah*: the person must have intended to pledge the actual value of his hand or foot. The *Chachamim*, by contrast, hold that people do sometimes speak loosely, and the pledge is therefore meaningless.

---

## Life Dependency Rule

### Nefashot Source

The Mishnah had stated *erach roshi ve'erach kveidi noten erach kulo* — pledging the *erach* of one's head or liver requires paying the full *erach*. The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama*? The answer: *nefashot ka'amar Rachmana* — the Torah's passage concerning *arachin* employs the word *nefashot*, invoking a person's life. This grounds the rule that any limb upon which one's life depends obligates the full *erach*.

### General Principle

The Mishnah then states the *klal*: *davar she'haneshama teluya bo — kulo*. The Gemara asks what this general rule comes to teach beyond the cases already explicit in the Mishnah — the head, the liver, and pledging half the body.

### Leg Application

The Gemara answers: *le-atuyei min ha-arkuvah ulema'lah* — the general rule comes to include the leg cut off above the knee, which is likewise something one cannot live without and thus constitutes a *davar she'haneshama teluya bo*. This was itself the subject of a *machloket* in Masechet Chullin in the chapter of *Elu Trefot* regarding whether loss of a leg above the knee renders an animal a *trefah*, but this Gemara clearly adopts the position that it does — and accordingly, pledging the *erach* of one's whole leg (not merely up to the knee) requires paying the full *erach* of the entire person.

### Half Distinction Rule

The Mishnah's formulation regarding partial pledges — *chatzi erchi alai noten chatzi ercho*, *erach chatzi alai noten erach kulo* — is then examined through a *Baraisa*. The first position in the *Baraisa* simply restates the Mishnah: pledging half one's *erach* requires paying half one's *erach*. However, Rabbi Yossi beRabbi Yehuda rules: *loke ve-noten erech shalem* — one receives punishment and must pay the full *erach*. The Gemara asks: *loke amai*? What transgression warrants lashes? No prohibition was violated. Rav Pappa explains that *loke* here does not mean literal lashes but rather that one is "punished" in the sense of being required to pay the full *erach*. The reason for this *gezeirah*: *gezeirah chatzi erchi atu erech chatzyi* — since *erach chatzyi* (the *erach* of half of me) obligates the full *erach*, and people can easily confuse that formulation with *chatzi erchi* (half of my *erach*), Rabbi Yossi beRabbi Yehuda rules *mi-derabanan* that either formulation requires full payment. And why does *erach chatzyi* itself require the full *erach*? *Havei davar she'haneshama teluya bo* — half of one's body is something one cannot live without.

The Gemara then addresses the parallel *neder* case: *chatzi damai alai noten chatzi damav*; *dmei chatzyi alai noten dmei kulo*. The Gemara asks: how do we know this rule of *davar she'haneshama teluya bo* applies to *nedarim* as well? The answer lies in the *pasuk*: *neder be-erkecha nefashot la-Hashem* — the *pasuk* juxtaposes the language of *neder* and *erech*, creating a *hekesh* that allows us to derive the rule for *nedarim* from *arachin*. The Gemara notes that the *klal* stated in the Mishnah for *nedarim* serves the same function as the *klal* for *arachin*: both come *le-atuyei min ha-arkuvah ulema'lah*, to include the leg above the knee as a *davar she'haneshama teluya bo* — applicable equally to both categories.

---

## Vessel Pledge Dispute

### Vessel Half-Value

The Gemara now cites a *Baraisa* returning to the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *Chachamim* regarding vessels. *Ha-ma'arich chatzi erech kli* — one who takes an *erach* pledge of half the value of a vessel: *Rabbi Meir omer noten damav* — Rabbi Meir rules one must pay half the vessel's value, treating the pledge as a *neder*. *Ve-Chachamim omrim lo amar klum* — the *Chachamim* rule it is a meaningless statement.

### Rava Discussion

When Rava fell ill, Abaye and a group of *Rabbanan* came for *bikur cholim*, and they occupied themselves with this *Baraisa*. They noted: *bishlama Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir's position is entirely consistent and easy to understand. He holds *ein adam motzi devarav le-vatalah*, and accordingly *lo shna kulo ve-lo shna chetzyo*: it makes no difference whether you pledged the whole vessel's value or half — in either case you must pay. But what is the position of the *Rabbanan* of this *Baraisa*? The Gemara observes that the *Baraisa* must be making a meaningful distinction between pledging half the value and pledging the whole value. If the *Rabbanan* here were the same *Rabbanan* who hold that pledging even the whole vessel's *erach* is meaningless, there would be no reason to formulate this *Baraisa* specifically around the half-value case. The fact that "half" is specified must mean that the *Rabbanan* here hold that pledging the full vessel's value does have effect — only the half-value pledge is meaningless.

### Combined Positions

The resolution offered jointly by Rava and Abaye: *rabbanan de-hacha ke-Rabbi Meir savri lei ve-savri lah ke-Rabbi Shimon* — the *Rabbanan* of this *Baraisa* hold like Rabbi Meir on one *machloket* and like Rabbi Shimon on another. They hold like Rabbi Meir in that *ein adam motzi devarav le-vatalah* — people do not make meaningless statements — and this is why pledging the whole vessel's value is treated as a valid *neder*.

### Rabbi Shimon View

At the same time, they hold like Rabbi Shimon, who rules *she-lo hitnadev ke-derech ha-mitnadvim* — a pledge is only binding if it was made in a normal manner of pledging. *Kulei orchei le-mitnadvei* — it is entirely normal for people to pledge the full value of an object; *palgei lav orchei le-mitnadvei* — pledging half the value of something is not the normal way people make donations to the *Beis Hamikdash*. Accordingly, the half-value pledge is not a valid *neder* at all. Tosafot raises a question here: when exactly is pledging half the value of something not normal? Tosafot therefore prefers to emend the reading throughout this passage from "half the value of a vessel" to "the value of half a vessel" — meaning the value of a broken vessel, which is essentially worthless rubble. Pledging the value of worthless rubble to the *Beis Hamikdash* is plainly not a normal manner of making a donation, and Rabbi Shimon's principle therefore excludes it.

---

## Nedarim/Nedavot

### Object Obligation

The Gemara moves on to the next Mishnah, which shifts from *arachin* altogether and now compares *nedarim* and *nedavot* — two modes of donating animals or objects to the *Beis Hamikdash*. The Mishnah opens with two cases: *shor zeh olah* — "this ox should be a *korban olah*"; *bayit zeh korban* — "this house should be *korban*." The Mishnah teaches that by saying *korban* about something that cannot itself be brought as a *korban*, such as a house, the object is sanctified with *kedushat bedek ha-bayit* — it goes to the temple treasury. If the ox then dies or the house collapses, the pledger is *patur mi-lishalem* — exempt from paying — because all he pledged was this specific object, not a personal monetary obligation. This is the classic distinction between a *neder* formulated as *harei zu* (this object) and one formulated as *harei alai* (it is upon me): the former changes the status of the object; the latter creates a personal *chiyuv* on the pledger.

### Mishnah Reread

Rabbi Chiya bar Rav interprets the Mishnah's language carefully: the case of *shor zeh alai olah* — "this ox should be upon me as an *olah*" — where the Mishnah says the pledger remains liable even if the ox dies, should not be read too literally. Rabbi Chiya bar Rav says: *lo shanu ela de'amar dmei shor zeh alai olah* — this applies only if one said "the value of this ox should be upon me." If one simply said "this ox should be upon me," the intent is *alai lehavio* — it is upon me to bring this animal, but not to replace it if it dies.

### Zeh vs Alai

The Gemara challenges this interpretation from a *Tosefta*. The *Tosefta* distinguishes three formulations. First, *shor zeh olah*: the ox itself becomes *hekdesh*, with *kedushat haguf*, and one can violate *me'ilah* by deriving benefit from it; if it dies or is stolen, the pledger owes nothing further. Second, *shor zeh alai olah*: again the ox itself is *hekdesh* and *me'ilah* applies, but now — since the word *alai* was used — if it dies or is stolen, *chayav be-achrayuto*, the pledger must pay its full value. Third, *dmei shor olah*: the ox itself is *chullin* and there is no *me'ilah* concern; if it dies or is stolen, the pledger is not liable for this specific ox — *eino chayav be-achrayuto* — but is liable for its value — *aval chayav be-achrayut damav* — since what was pledged was a monetary value, not a specific animal.

### Tosefta Challenge

The Gemara attempts to apply the same *okimta* to the *Tosefta* as Rabbi Chiya bar Rav applied to the Mishnah: that *shor zeh alai* in the *Tosefta* should also be read as *dmei shor zeh alai*. But this is more difficult here, because the *Tosefta* itself goes on to discuss a case where *dmei* is stated explicitly — and if both the second and third cases of the *Tosefta* refer to pledging the "value," the distinction between them collapses.

The Gemara therefore offers a more elaborate *okimta*: the second case — *reisha* — is where one said *yakdish ha-shor le-damav*, sanctifying the ox itself for its monetary proceeds, which both designated the specific ox as *hekdesh* and imposed a personal obligation to pay its value.
