The third case — *seifa* — is where one said *le-ch'she-yavo damav yikdashu*: when its value arrives — meaning, when I sell this ox, those proceeds will automatically become *hekdesh*. Accordingly, *eino chayav be-achrayuto* means the pledger does not owe the value of a whole live animal if it dies or is stolen; but *aval chayav be-achrayut damav* means that whatever proceeds the animal does fetch upon sale — even as a carcass — must go to the *Beis Hamikdash*.

---

## House Rental Case

### House Plague

The Gemara cites a *Baraisa* about a house rental situation: *ha-maskir bayit le-chaveiro ve-nitnaga* — one who rents a house to another person, and the house then contracts *nega'im* — the biblical plague that requires condemnation and eventual demolition. Even after *chalto kohen* — the *kohen* has formally condemned the house — the landlord may say *harei shelcha lefanecha*: the house is before you, as it was when I rented it to you. The tenancy was contracted for this specific house, and however unfortunate its fate, the landlord has technically delivered what was promised. However, *nitzo chayav le-ha'amid lo bayit*: once the house is actually demolished, the landlord is obligated to provide the tenant with another house to live in.

### Rent Hekdesh

The *Baraisa* continues with a separate case: *hikdisho ha-maskir* — the landlord was *makdish* the house after renting it out. In that circumstance, *hadar bo ma'aleh sechar le-hekdesh* — the one living there makes the rent payments to *hekdesh*. The Gemara asks: how can the tenant continue to live there at all? If the house itself is *hekdesh*, any benefit derived from it constitutes *me'ilah* — misuse of consecrated property. And once *me'ilah* has been committed — *ein me'ilah achar me'ilah* — the *kedushah* is removed from the object, so why would subsequent rent payments go to *hekdesh* at all?

### Future Value Problem

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting the *Baraisa*: *de'amar le-ch'she-yavo sachar yikdash* — the landlord did not consecrate the house itself, but rather declared that whenever the rent payment arises, it should automatically become *hekdesh*. The house itself remains *chullin*; the tenant derives no forbidden benefit from it. Whatever rent is paid flows directly to *hekdesh* by virtue of the landlord's prior declaration.

This leads to the same question that arose earlier in the passage: *va-ha ein adam makdish davar she-lo ba la-olam* — how can one be *makdish* a rent payment that has not yet been paid and does not yet exist? One cannot consecrate something that has not yet come into the world.

### Rabbi Meir Future

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: ha mani? Rabbi Meir hi* — Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers: this *Baraisa* follows the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who holds *adam makdish davar she-lo ba la-olam* — a person can be *makdish* something that does not yet exist in the world. An alternate tradition records this same exchange as between Rav Papa and Abaye, or between Rami bar Chama and Rav Chisda. In either formulation, the questioner asks: *ke-man? Ke-Rabbi Meir?* — are you saying this *Baraisa* follows Rabbi Meir? And the response is: *amar lei, be-ela ke-man?* — of course; who else would it follow?

---

---

# Arakhin 21

## Confiscation & Erchin

### Beis Din Confiscation

The twenty-first daf of Arakhin opens a new topic: when is *beis din* permitted to confiscate property in order to compel someone to fulfill an obligation to the *beis hamikdash*? With this question the *mishnah* inaugurates a fresh subject, though one that retains a thematic connection to the preceding *perek* through its focus on *erchin* — vows of personal valuation.

### Erchin vs. Chatas/Asham

The *mishnah* states: *chayvei erchin memashkenin osan* — one who is liable for an *erach* may have property confiscated as *mashkon*, as collateral, until the debt is paid. By contrast, *chayvei chataos va'ashamot ein memashkenin otan* — one who owes a *korban chatas* or a *korban asham* is not subject to confiscation. The distinction requires explanation.

### Benefit Principle

Rashi articulates the underlying principle most explicitly: wherever a person stands to benefit from fulfilling an obligation, we assume he will do so voluntarily and confiscation is unnecessary. The *chatas* and the *asham* are brought for specific transgressions, and the *kapparah* — the atonement — they confer is a powerful personal incentive. The *erach*, by contrast, is a wholly voluntary pledge; precisely because no automatic benefit drives fulfillment, *beis din* must intervene. One might argue the reverse — that a voluntary commitment reflects genuine desire, while a compelled obligation resembles an unwanted parking fine that one endlessly defers. The *mishnah* sets that argument aside: the operative criterion is not the voluntariness of the original undertaking but whether the person has something to gain from following through.

### Olos & Shlamim

The *mishnah* continues: *chayvei olos ushlamim* — one obligated to bring an *olah* or a *shelamim* — is likewise not subject to confiscation. This prompts an immediate observation: does an *olah* not also provide *kapparah*, atoning for the neglect of a positive commandment (*bitul aseh*)? Rashi on the *mishnah* addresses this directly. Even though the *olah* carries a measure of atonement for *bitul aseh*, *hoil velo chova hi aleha lo chashiv lah kapparah* — since this *kapparah* is not one the person is strictly required to seek, the *mishnah* does not treat it as *kapparah* in the operative sense. The atonement is incidental rather than the driving purpose of the obligation, and therefore does not suffice as an incentive to guarantee fulfillment.

### Coercion & Consent

The *mishnah* then introduces a striking qualification: *af al pi she'ein miskafer lo ad sheyirtzeh* — even though a person cannot receive atonement through the *olah* until he wills it. What, then, can *beis din* do? *Kofin oto ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* — the court may apply coercive pressure until the individual declares, "I want to bring it." The coercion is legitimate; what cannot be compelled is the internal consent, which must ultimately be voiced.

### Gittin Analogy

The *mishnah* appends a parenthetical remark that on its surface seems unrelated to the foregoing: *ve'chen ata omer be'gittei nashim kofin oto ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* — the same rule applies to divorce. Wherever *beis din* rules that a man is obligated to divorce his wife, the court may exert pressure until he declares of his own volition that he wishes to give the *get*. If *beis din* coerces him but he never voices consent, the *get* is a *get me'useh* — a coerced document — and not *kasher*. But once he pronounces the words *rotzeh ani* in response to legitimate *beis din* coercion, the *get* is valid. The *mishnah*'s juxtaposition of these two cases underscores that the same conceptual structure governs both contexts: compulsion that terminates in freely voiced consent is juridically effective, while compulsion without that voiced consent is not.

---

## Exceptions: Nazir & Metz…

### Rav Pappa Exceptions

The *gemara* records the following statement: *amar Rav Pappa pe'amim she'chayavei chata'ot memashkenin otam* — Rav Pappa declares that there are cases in which even one who owes a *chatas* may have property confiscated. And conversely, *chayavei olot ein memashkenin otam* — there are cases where one obligated to bring an *olah* is nonetheless exempt from confiscation. These are exceptions to the *mishnah*'s general framework in both directions.

### Chatas Nazir

The case where confiscation is applied to a *chatas* is the *chatat nazir* — the sin-offering brought by a *nazir* upon completing or terminating his *nezirut*. A *nazir* is required to bring three *korbanot*: a *chatas*, an *olah*, and a *shelamim*. The *chatat nazir* is notable because it is not brought in response to any specific sin, and therefore does not carry the *kapparah* that would normally motivate compliance. The *nazir* does, however, stand to gain substantially: the completion of his *nezirut* restores his right to drink wine and to come into contact with the dead.

### Three Korbanos Requirement

Why, then, does the *gemara* permit confiscation for the *chatat nazir* despite this benefit? The answer lies in the rule that *de'keivan de'amar mar im gile'ach al achat mi'shloshtan yatza ve'im nizrak alav echad min ha'damim hutar ha'nazir lishtot yayin u'letamei le'metim* — since, as the Sages taught, once the *nazir* has shaved his head and the blood of any one of the three *korbanot* has been sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach*, he immediately regains the right to drink wine and to become *tamei* from the dead. He need not bring all three first. The three *korbanot* may be brought in any order, and upon the *zerika* of the first one, his restrictions are lifted. At that point, the remaining two *korbanot* represent obligations from which he gains nothing further. Therefore, *u'pashia velo mayti* — we are concerned that once he has recovered his freedoms, he will be negligent and simply not bring the remaining offerings. Hence confiscation is warranted even for the *chatas*.

### Olat Metzora

The converse exception — an *olah* for which confiscation is *not* applied — is the *olat metzora*, the burnt-offering of a person afflicted with *tzara'at*. A *metzora* must bring three *korbanot*: an *asham*, a *chatas*, and an *olah*. The *gemara* teaches that in this case confiscation is unnecessary because the *metzora* cannot regain his full *taharah* until all three are brought.

### Olat Yoledet Rejected

Before reaching the *olat metzora*, the *gemara* initially proposes *olat yoledet* — the *olah* brought by a woman after childbirth — as the paradigmatic case of an *olah* exempt from confiscation. The reasoning would be as follows: a *yoledet* brings both an *olah* and a *chatas*; she is motivated to bring the *chatas* because it grants her the right to eat *kodshim*; and since the *olah* must be brought before the *chatas*, her incentive to bring the *chatas* carries the *olah* along with it. The *gemara*, however, dismisses this example. *De'akdamei kra?* — is the sole basis for requiring the *olah* first merely that the *pasuk* lists it first? *Ve'hamar Rava le'mikra hikdima hakatuv* — Rava has already established that the *Torah* placed the *olah* before the *chatas* in the *pasuk* only for the purpose of its reading order, not to determine the order of offering. In practice, the *yoledet* may bring the *chatas* first, receive her right to eat *kodshim* immediately, and then owe the *olah* as a residual obligation from which she gains nothing. That would suggest confiscation should actually apply, making the *olat yoledet* a poor example of an *olah* exempt from confiscation.

### Braita: Metzora Tahara

The *gemara* therefore turns instead to the *olat metzora*, supported by a *braita*: *Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yehuda ben Beroka omer* — Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beroka teaches: *keshem she'chatato ve'ashamo ikavto, kach olato ikavto* — just as the *chatas* and the *asham* of the *metzora* are indispensable for his *tahara*, so too is his *olah* indispensable. All three *korbanot* are required before the *metzora* fully regains his status. Because none of the three can be dispensed with, the *metzora* retains his incentive to bring the *olah* just as much as the other two, and therefore confiscation is unnecessary.

---

## Coercion & Consent

### Baraita: Yakriv Oto

The *gemara* now examines the *mishnah*'s rule of *kofin oto ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* through the lens of a *baraita*. The *baraita* cites the *pasuk* regarding the *olah*: *im olah korbano min habakar zachar tamim yakrivenu el petach ohel moed yakriv oto* — if his offering is an *olah* from the cattle, a complete male, he shall bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting; *yakriv oto* — he shall offer it. From the phrase *yakriv oto*, the *baraita* derives *melamed she'kofin oto* — it teaches that we may apply compulsion.

### Lirtzono Limit

One might have read this as licensing total compulsion, even completely against the person's will. The *pasuk* forecloses this: *lirtzono lifnei Hashem* — according to his will, before God. The apparent tension is resolved: *kofin oto ad she'yomar rotzeh ani* — we coerce him until he says he wants to do it. The compulsion is the mechanism; the voiced consent is the indispensable conclusion.

### Shmuel: Olah Needs Da'at

*Amar Shmuel: olah tzricha da'at, shene'emar lirtzono* — Shmuel states that an *olah* requires the consent of the owner, as the *pasuk* says *lirtzono*.

### Gemara Questions Shmuel

The *gemara* immediately presses: *mai kamashma lan?* What is Shmuel adding beyond what the *mishnah* already teaches? The *mishnah* itself already stated that the *olah* requires *lirtzono* — the person must be willing — deriving this from the same *pasuk*. Is Shmuel merely repeating the *mishnah*?

### Donated Animal Consent

The *gemara* answers: *lo tzricha — d'parish lei chavrei* — Shmuel's statement is necessary for a case where someone else has donated an animal to fulfill another person's *olah* obligation. One might have thought that *da'at* is required only when it is the owner's own animal, since he might resist parting with it. But when a friend donates an animal on his behalf, who would ever refuse? He is not losing anything. *Ka mashma lan: zimnin delo nicha leih lechapurei bemidi delav dideih* — Shmuel teaches that there are indeed people who do not wish to receive atonement through something that is not their own. Therefore consent is required even in that case.

### Ula vs. Shmuel

A *baraita* cited earlier distinguishes between the *chatas* and the *olah* with respect to consent: for a *chatas* or *asham* donated by one person for another, *leda'at yatza, shelo leda'at lo yatza* — if the beneficiary consents, the obligation is fulfilled; if not, it is not. But for an *olah* or *shelamim* donated by one person for another, *bein leda'at bein shelo leda'at yatza* — whether or not the beneficiary consents, the obligation is fulfilled. This appears to challenge Shmuel, who requires *da'at* for an *olah*.

*Ula*, however, reads the *baraita* differently. *Lo chilku bein chatat le'olah* — the distinction the *baraita* draws between *chatas* and *olah* is not about whether consent is required at all, but specifically about *when* it is required. According to Ula: a *chatas* requires *da'at bish'at hafrasha* — at the moment of designation; an *olah* does not require *da'at* at that stage. But *bish'at kapara* — at the time of actual offering — *idi ve'idi leda'at yatza shelo leda'at lo yatza* — for both the *chatas* and the *olah*, the obligation is fulfilled only with consent, not without it.

Shmuel and Ula are thus in direct disagreement, and the *gemara* notes: *upliga de'Ula* — Shmuel disputes Ula. Shmuel holds that an *olah* requires *da'at bish'at hafrasha* at the time of designation. Ula holds it does not require *da'at* at designation but does require it at the time of offering. They are, as it were, mirror images of each other on this question.

### Baraita Challenge

The *gemara* then raises a challenge from a second *baraita* that appears to apply the consent requirement uniformly to all four *korbanot* — *chatatav ve'ashamo olato ushlamav shel ploni alai* — pledging any of the four on another's behalf, with *leda'at yatza, shelo leda'at lo yatza* applying across the board. If taken at face value for both the time of designation and the time of offering, this *baraita* challenges both Shmuel and Ula.

### Time Distinction

The resolution is that neither Shmuel nor Ula is in fact contradicted. *Shmuel mokmi lah bish'at hafrasha* — Shmuel reads the second *baraita* as referring solely to the time of designation, which is consistent with his view that an *olah* requires *da'at* at that stage. *Ula mokmi lah bish'at kapara* — Ula reads it as referring to the time of offering, consistent with his view that both *chatas* and *olah* require *da'at* at that stage. Rav Pappa then observes that the two *baraitot* are not in contradiction with one another either: *ha bish'at kapara, ha bish'at hafrasha* — one addresses the time of offering, the other the time of designation. Each *amora* assigns the two *baraitot* to the two different time-points in the reverse order, yet each achieves internal consistency.

---

## Gittin & Moda'a

### Rav Sheshet: Moda'a

The *mishnah*'s parenthetical remark about *gittei nashim* now receives sustained *gemara* treatment. *Amar Rav Sheshet: hai man de'masar moda'a a'gitta, moda'ei moda'a* — one who makes a *moda'a* concerning a *get*, that *moda'a* is valid. A *moda'a* is a formal declaration, made before two witnesses prior to entering into a legal transaction, that the transaction is being performed under duress. As a mechanism applicable to any contract, it can in principle invalidate the agreement. Rav Sheshet rules that a *get* is subject to this same mechanism.

### Bittul Moda'ot

The *gemara* initially regards this ruling as self-evident — *pshita*. The substantive question is therefore: *lo tzricha — de'ansuha ve'irtzei* — what if he was coerced and then went ahead and gave the *get* anyway? One might have thought that the act of giving the *get* itself constitutes a *bittul*, a nullification, of any prior *moda'a*. *Mahu de'teima bitulei batlei* — perhaps his subsequent action demonstrates that he intended to nullify the *moda'a*. Rav Sheshet teaches that this is not so: the act of giving alone does not nullify the *moda'a*.

### Saying Negates Duress

The proof is textual and structural. *De'im ken litnei ad she'yiten* — if the act of giving were sufficient to negate the *moda'a*, the *mishnah* should have stated: *kofin oto ad she'yiten* — we coerce him until he gives the *get*. *Mai ad she'yomar?* — why does the *mishnah* say we coerce him until he *says* "I want to give it"? *Ad de'mevatlei le'moda'ei* — because only the explicit verbal declaration *rotzeh ani* is sufficient to nullify any prior *moda'ot*. The act of giving without that declaration does not accomplish this, and the *get* would remain invalid. The explicit voiced consent is thus doing precise legal work: it is not only the *halachically* required expression of will but the instrument that cancels any prior declaration of duress.

### Beis Din Procedure

Tosafot identifies this *gemara* as the source for the established custom of *bittul moda'ot* in *get* procedure. Before a *get* is given, *beis din* requires the husband to explicitly nullify any *moda'ot* he may previously have made, and to declare that he will never place a *irur* — a challenge — on the validity of the *get*. Additional procedures accompany this, including *beis din*'s annulment of any *neder* the husband may have taken that might have prevented the *get* from taking legal effect. The *gemara*'s analysis thus has direct practical consequence: it is the conceptual foundation for the procedural safeguards that *batei din* employ to ensure the integrity of the *get* even where the giving occurs under *beis din* compulsion.

---

## Shum HaYetomim

### Overview

The *gemara* now transitions to a new *perek*: *shum ha-yetomim* — the appraisal and sale of orphans' property. The connection to the preceding material lies in the broader theme of *beis din*-administered confiscation and debt collection: just as *beis din* may confiscate property to enforce obligations to the *beis hamikdash*, so too does *beis din* administer the sale of an estate when a father dies leaving both property and outstanding debts, with heirs who are minors below *bar mitzvah*. In such a case, *beis din* assesses the land, establishes an opening bid, and conducts a thirty-day auction, with proceeds going to satisfy the father's creditors.

### Auction Periods

The *mishnah* establishes: *shum ha-yetomim shloshim yom* — the auction period for orphans' property is thirty days. The first Tosafot in this *perek* raises the obvious question: is this procedure not identical to *beis din*'s general practice of selling any debtor's land? Tosafot answers that the *mishnah* specifies orphans because one might have thought that *beis din* should allow a longer period to maximize bids on their behalf — *kamashma lan* that the procedure is identical to any other debt collection.

The exception is *hekdesh*: when a person has consecrated land to the *beis hamikdash* and the temple treasury must convert it to cash, the auction period is sixty days — *mishum ha-hekdesh shishim yom*. In both cases, the *mishnah* requires: *umachrizin ba-boker uva-erev* — announcements are made every morning and every evening throughout the auction period.

### Morning & Evening

The *gemara* asks: *mai shna baboker uva'erev?* — why specifically morning and evening? *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav: bish'at hotza'at po'alim uvish'at hachnasat po'alim* — we announce at the time workers are going out from work and at the time workers are coming in to work. This is, in effect, rush hour — the times when people are moving through public spaces and the announcement will reach the widest audience.

### Worker Inspection

The *gemara* then offers a more specific explanation. *De'ika denicha lei lemizban, amar lehu lepo'alim: azilu sayeru li ar'a* — there are wealthy buyers who, at the time workers are leaving, can instruct their employees: go and survey that field for me. This is why the evening announcement matters: employers can dispatch their workers, while still on the clock or with overtime compensation, to inspect the property being auctioned. The morning announcement serves the complementary purpose: *denidkar de'amar lehu, nizil venishaylinhu* — so that the employer will remember to ask his workers what they found out about the land, allowing him to follow through on a potential purchase. A *baraita* confirms this explanation and restates the thirty-day and sixty-day periods along with the morning-and-evening announcement requirement.

### Baraita: Announcement

The *baraita* then specifies the content of the announcement itself: *sadeh ploni besimaneha uvimetzareha* — this particular field, identified by its *simanim* (distinguishing markers) and its *metzarim* (borders), so that potential buyers know precisely what is being offered. This is followed by two further pieces of information.

### Kol Harotzeh

*Kach hi yafah vekach hi shumah* — this is the quality of the field and this is its assessed value. Rashi explains *yafah* as a productivity rating: *kach vekach hi osah tevuah* — how much grain the field can be expected to yield per season. The *shumah* is the valuation established by *beis din*, which functions as the opening bid. The auction then opens: *kol harotzeh likach yavo v'yikach* — whoever wishes to buy should come and do so.

### Widow vs. Creditor

The formula continues: *al menat litein l'isha b'ktubata u'l'ba'al chov b'chovo* — on condition of giving the proceeds to the widow for her *ktuba* or to the creditor for his debt. The *gemara* asks why this specification is necessary. The answer is that different buyers are motivated by different beneficiaries. *D'ika denicha lei b'ba'al chov d'meikel b'zuzei* — there are buyers who specifically prefer to purchase when the recipient is the creditor, because a professional creditor is an expert in evaluating coinage and will accept a wider range of coins, including worn or debased ones that other recipients might refuse.

### Payment Flexibility

Conversely, *v'ika denicha lei b'isha d'shakla al yad al yad* — there are buyers who prefer to give the payment to the widow, because widows were often willing to accept payment *al yad al yad* — in installments, a little at a time. A buyer who lacks the full purchase price in hand but can pay over time finds it advantageous to know that the beneficiary is someone willing to accommodate installment payments. By specifying both the widow and the creditor in the announcement, *beis din* ensures that the broadest possible range of potential bidders is informed and motivated — maximizing the proceeds for the benefit of all parties owed.

---

---

# Arakhin 25

## Intro: Arachin & Makdish…

### Masechet Overview

Today's *daf* is 25, though we pick up from the bottom of 24b, where we enter a new *perek* beginning with *ein makdishin*. It is worth stepping back to appreciate the full scope of *Masechet Arachin*. The tractate is not limited to the laws of *arachin* — the fixed valuations of persons — but rather addresses the entire latter half of *Parshat Bechukotai*, covering a range of subjects. The tractate begins with *erech*, but then moves into the second major topic of that parasha: the laws governing one who is *makdish* a *sadeh*, a field, during the *yovel* period — how such a field is redeemed, and what occurs when *yovel* arrives. Indeed, the very end of *Bechukotai* deals with *temura*, which is the subject of the next tractate. This is not a digression; rather, the full subject of *Masechet Arachin* is the range of different *hakdashot* — donations to the *beit hamikdash* — discussed at the close of *Parshat Bechukotai*.

### Hakdashot Structure

The tractate thus encompasses multiple forms of consecration and dedication to the *beit hamikdash*. What unifies them is their source in the concluding passages of *Bechukotai*, even if the tractate's name is drawn, as with many tractates, from the opening topic. With that context established, we turn to the *sugyot* at hand.

---

## Rav vs Shmuel: Yovel Year

### Mishna: Sanctify Fields

The *mishna* had stated that one may not be *makdish* a *sadeh* within two years of the *yovel*, because the *Torah* says *al pi hashanim hanotarot* — based on the remaining years. The Gemara, however, based on analysis of a *baraita* and the positions of Rav and Shmuel, revised that reading. Rather than a prohibition, what the *mishna* means is that it would be very unwise to be *makdish* within two years of *yovel*. The system works as follows: fifty *shekel* is the base value for a field planted with a *chomer* of barley seed — a *chomer seorim* — and this amount is divided proportionally over forty-nine years. That proportional deduction, *girua*, applies when there are more than two years remaining. Once fewer than two years remain, the *girua* no longer applies, and the full flat fifty *shekel* is charged. On this point, Rav and Shmuel agree. Their *machloket* concerns a different question: what is the law if someone is *makdish* a *sadeh* during the *yovel* year itself?

According to Shmuel, if one is *makdish* a *sadeh* during the *yovel* year, the sanctification does not take effect — it is not *kadosh*. According to Rav, the sanctification is valid and the person pays the full fifty *shekel*.

### Baraita: No Sanctify Yov…

The *gemara* now challenges Rav's position from a *baraita*. We read: *makdishin bein lifnei hayovel bein achar hayovel* — one may sanctify a field whether before *yovel* or after *yovel* — *uvesha'at hayovel atzmo lo yakdish* — but during the *yovel* year itself one shall not sanctify — *ve'im hikdish einah kedushah* — and if one did sanctify, it does not take effect. This appears to be a straightforward ruling like Shmuel's: just as *yovel* causes the field to revert to the *kohanim* and effects all manner of change, if one attempts to be *makdish* during *yovel* itself, it accomplishes nothing.

How does Rav respond? *Amar lecha Rav*: when the *baraita* says *einah kedushah*, it means *einah kedushah begirua* — it is not sanctified with a *girua* deduction — *aval kadosh venoten chamishim* — but it is indeed sanctified, and one pays the full fifty *shekel*. The reasoning is that the *yovel* year is the end of one cycle and the beginning of the next, so there is nothing to deduct — one pays full freight from the outset of a new cycle.

The *gemara* challenges this interpretation: if *einah kedushah* in the *baraita* really means "not sanctified with a *girua*," then the opening clause — *makdishin lifnei hayovel* — must mean *kedushah lege'al begirua*, that sanctification before *yovel* entails a *girua* deduction. But that cannot be, because both Rav and Shmuel agree — *de'amri tavaihu* — that *ein makdishin lege'al begirua pachat mishtei shanim*: within the last two years there is no *girua*, and yet the sanctification is still valid. So we are back where we started: the *mishna* says sanctification during *yovel* is invalid, and Rav says it is valid. What does Rav do with this *baraita*?

### Rav's Hermeneutic

Rav responds: *ha mani rabanan hi* — this *baraita* follows the position of the *Rabbanan* — *va'ana de'amri kirebbi* — and I follow *Rebbi*. For *Rebbi* holds the principle *de'amar rishon rishon bikhlal shevi'i shevi'i bikhlal*: when the *Torah* specifies a range from one point to another, both endpoints are included. This principle was discussed earlier in the tractate in the context of the verse *miyom harishon ad yom hashvi'i* — does "from the first until the seventh" include days one and seven? *Rebbi* says yes: endpoints are inclusive.

Applying this to our case: the verse says *ve'im mishnat hayovel yakdish sadehu* — from the year of *yovel*. According to Rav, following *Rebbi's* hermeneutic, this means including the *yovel* year itself — *ushnat hayovel bikhlal*. Therefore, the sanctification takes effect on the *yovel* year itself. The *baraita* that says otherwise follows a different hermeneutic, not *Rebbi's*. Rav is free to follow *Rebbi*, and on that basis holds that sanctification during *yovel* is valid and the full fifty *shekel* is paid.

### Years Calculation

The *gemara* now raises a fascinating arithmetic question. If, according to Rav, sanctification can begin during the *yovel* year itself — meaning the *yovel* year is the first year of the new cycle — then the total period over which the sanctity operates is fifty years: the *yovel* year itself plus the next forty-nine. If we are dividing fifty *shekel* proportionally over the number of remaining years, and sanctification on the *yovel* year itself means fifty years remain, then the rate should be exactly one *shekel* per year — fifty divided by fifty. Yet we know from the *mishna* we are about to read that *Rebbi* himself rules *noten sela upundyon leshana* — one *sela* and one *pundyon* per year — which reflects a division by forty-nine, not fifty.

*Rebbi* himself says it is one *sela* and a *pundyon* — a *pundyon* being one forty-eighth — so that forty-nine times one and one forty-eighth yields fifty plus a small remainder (for the money-changer). But according to Rav's reasoning, based on *Rebbi's* hermeneutic that *yovel* itself is included, should it not be a division by fifty, yielding exactly one *shekel* per year? The *gemara* asks: *pundyon mai avidteih* — why does the *pundyon* exist at all?

### Yovel as Year One

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking a different *tannaitic* dispute: *Rebbi keRebbi Yehuda sevira leih* — *Rebbi* holds like *Rabbi Yehuda*, who says *bishnat chamishim ola lechan ulechan* — the fiftieth year, the *yovel* year, counts toward both cycles. It is not merely year fifty of the previous cycle; it is simultaneously year one of the next cycle. If the *yovel* year itself is year one of the next cycle, then even if sanctification begins at the start of *yovel*, the count runs from year one through year forty-nine of that same cycle — only forty-nine years — because *yovel* is one, the following year is two, and so on. The division is therefore by forty-nine, which yields *Rebbi's* figure of one *sela* and a *pundyon* per year.

There is even a conceptual elegance to this alignment: if the *yovel* year is also considered the first year of the following cycle, then it makes intuitive sense that the laws governing the next fifty years — including the capacity to be *makdish* — can already take hold during *yovel* itself. The *gemara* notes: *shnat hachamishim shana zu vezu* — the fiftieth year is simultaneously this and that.

The *gemara* then extends the analysis to Shmuel's position. According to Shmuel, who holds that one cannot be *makdish* during the *yovel* year, if we were to combine Shmuel with *Rabbi Yehuda's* position that *yovel* counts as year one of the next cycle, the result would be troubling: since *yovel* — year one — is off limits, only years two through forty-nine are available, meaning only forty-eight years remain. Dividing fifty by forty-eight yields one *sela* and two *pundyos*, not the one *sela* and one *pundyon* that *Rebbi* rules. Therefore, *al karchach d'Shmuel* — we must say that according to Shmuel, *Rebbi* holds like the *Rabbanan*, who say that the *yovel* year does not count as year one of the next cycle. Year one begins only after *yovel* concludes, leaving exactly forty-nine years — yielding the familiar *sela* and *pundyon*.

The net result of the discussion: everyone agrees the division is by forty-nine. According to Rav, one achieves this by holding that *yovel* is year one (so counting begins at *yovel* itself and runs forty-nine years). According to Shmuel, one achieves it by holding that *yovel* is year zero — the first usable year comes only after *yovel* — again leaving forty-nine years. In theory, one could combine positions to produce a division by fifty or a division by forty-eight, but neither of those is *Rebbi's* ruling.

---

## No Partial Years: Whole…

### Baraita: Full Year Units

The *gemara* continues. *Ta shema* — come and hear: *ve'lo goalin achar hayovel pachat mishana* — one cannot redeem after *yovel* in units less than a year. At first glance this is puzzling: why should there be any restriction on redeeming immediately? The *Torah* seems to permit redemption at any time from the outset. So what does it mean that one cannot redeem in less than a year after *yovel*?

The *gemara* explains that *b'shlama l'Shmuel* — according to Shmuel, this makes reasonable sense: since one cannot be *makdish* during the *yovel* year itself, the entire process of sanctifying and redeeming does not begin for a full year from the start of *yovel* — it begins only after *yovel* concludes. The statement "one cannot redeem less than a year after *yovel*" is thus an indirect way of saying the whole process is suspended during the *yovel* year itself. It is an unusual formulation, but it works.

*Ella l'Rav* — but according to Rav, who holds that sanctification during *yovel* is valid, why would one be unable to redeem within a year of *yovel*? *Mi savar achar yovel mamash?* The *gemara* rejects the literal reading. *Mai achar yovel? Be'emtza yovel* — it just means in the middle of any cycle, a normal case. *Achar yovel* simply denotes "sometime during a cycle," not specifically in the year immediately following *yovel*.

### Full Years Rounding

The real meaning of the *baraita*, according to Rav, is this: if one is *makdish* a field at some point during the cycle and then seeks to redeem it, one cannot calculate the remaining time in units smaller than a full year. *Dechol kamma delo malya lishana lo migra lei* — if a year has not yet been completed, one cannot deduct it. When counting the number of years that have passed since *yovel* in order to determine how much has been deducted from the fifty *shekel*, one counts only complete years. Conversely, when counting the number of remaining years, one rounds up: a fraction of a year counts as a full year remaining. In short, all calculations are done in whole-year units, always to the benefit of *hekdesh*.

### Verse Source

The *gemara* proceeds to ask: what does the *baraita* add that we did not already know? *She'ein mechashevin chodashim im hahekdesh* — that one does not count months when dealing with *hekdesh* — is already stated explicitly in the *mishna*. The *gemara* responds: *mah ta'am ka'amar* — the *baraita* is providing the rationale. Why may one not redeem in units less than a year? Because *she'ein mechashevin chodashim im hahekdesh* — when it comes to *hekdesh*, one reckons by years, not months. The two statements reinforce each other. The *tanna* derives this from the verse: *vechishev lo hakohen et kesef al pi hashanim hanotarot* — the *kohen* calculates the money based on the remaining *years* — *shanim ata mechashev ve'ei ata mechashev chodashim*: you count by year units, not month units.

### Months for Hekdesh Benef…

One might ask: is it ever possible to count months? The *tanna* continues: *minayin she'im ata rotze la'asot chodashim leshana ose?* How do we know that if you wish to count months toward a year, you may do so? The *gemara* asks what case this addresses. The answer: *kegon de'akdesha bepalga de'arba'in vetamnei* — suppose the field was sanctified when forty-eight and a half years had already elapsed in the cycle, meaning there is a year and a half remaining. Recall the rule: if fewer than two full years remain until *yovel*, there is no *girua* and the full fifty *shekel* is charged. Now, if one rounds up the remaining time to two years, the owner is still in the *girua* zone and pays less. If one rounds down to one year remaining, the owner pays the flat fifty *shekel* — which is more. Rounding down here benefits *hekdesh*. In such a case, the *tanna* teaches from the verse *vechishev lo hakohen* — the *kohen* will calculate for him in whatever manner — *mikol makom*, broadly — meaning the calculation can run either way so long as it serves *hekdesh's* interest.

The principle is thus: whole year units only; normally one rounds up when counting years remaining (benefiting *hekdesh*); but in cases where rounding down benefits *hekdesh* — as in the scenario with a year and a half remaining — that too is permitted.

---

## Field Measure & Rocks

### Chomer Barley Seed

Turning now to the *mishna* itself, the *Torah* states: *ve'im misedei achuzato yakdish ish laHashem vehaya erkecha lefi zaro zera chomer seorim bachamishim shekel kasef* — if one sanctifies a field of one's inheritance, the valuation is fifty *shekel* for a field planted with a *chomer* of barley seed. This is the standard: fifty *shekel* for the acreage corresponding to the planting of a *chomer seorim*, and everything is proportional from there. For the full forty-nine years until *yovel*, one pays fifty *shekel* for that acreage. If it is two and a half times that acreage, or a quarter of that acreage, the calculation is proportional.

### Crevices & Rocks

The *mishna* then introduces a complication. *Hayu sham neka'im amukim asara tefachim* — if there are deep crevices in the field, more than ten *tefachim* deep — a *tefach* being roughly three to three and a half inches, so ten *tefachim* is approximately three feet — *o sela'im gevohim asara tefachim* — or rocks more than ten *tefachim* tall — *ein nimdadim imah* — they are not counted toward the acreage of the field. One cannot plant in a deep narrow crevice or on top of a tall rock, so these areas are excluded from the calculation based on the fixed Torah rate of fifty *shekel* per *chomer seorim*. Instead, they are assessed separately at market value. The entire field is still sanctified; it is simply that the unplantable portions are not measured according to the Torah's fixed rate.

The *gemara* will also note the converse: if the crevice or rock is less than ten *tefachim*, it is counted with the field even if that specific spot cannot technically be planted. The ten-*tefachim* threshold is the standard measure distinguishing a separate domain from what is considered part of the surrounding area.

One might ask whether a drought or change in conditions affects the valuation — whether a parched and unusable field would receive a deduction. That question is not addressed in the *mishna* here; it concerns the intrinsic nature of the field, not temporary conditions.

The *mishna* continues: *hikdishah shtayim veshalosh shanim lifnei hayovel* — if one sanctified the field two or three years before *yovel* — *noten sela upundyon leshana* — one gives one *sela* and one *pundyon* per year. A *sela* is a *shekel*, and a *pundyon* is one forty-eighth of a *sela*, so forty-nine times one and one forty-eighth yields fifty *shekel* plus a small increment to cover the money-changer. This was already mentioned above in connection with *Rebbi's* ruling.

### Seed vs Harvest

A *baraita* clarifies the precise meaning of the *chomer seorim* measure. *Kor zera velo kor tevuah* — it is a *kor* (equivalent to a *chomer*) of seed, not a *kor* of produce. That is: the field must be large enough to plant a *kor* of barley seed in it, not large enough to produce a *kor* of barley. This is a crucial distinction, because one seed produces many times its weight in grain; a field large enough to produce a *kor* would be vastly smaller than one large enough to plant a *kor*. Since the *Torah's* measure is the planting amount, this results in a larger field — and since a larger field means a lower per-unit cost of redemption, this interpretation is more favorable.

*Mapolet yad velo mapolet shevarim* — the seed is spread by hand, not by ox. The practice of placing a bag of seed on an ox and making a small hole in it so that the seed scatters as the ox walks back and forth results in a denser distribution of seed than hand-spreading. Hand-spreading uses more seed per unit area — or equivalently, a given amount of seed covers more ground when scattered by hand. Again, this results in a larger field and therefore benefits the person redeeming.

*Tani Levi*: *lo me'aveh velo medak, ela beinoni* — neither overly thick nor overly thin seed, but average seed. This specification is notable in itself. One might have assumed that some fixed, well-known measure had long been standardized, like a foot of measurement. But the fact that the *gemara* must describe the seed in these terms — not this kind, not that kind, but average — suggests that in the era of the *gemara*, there was no single universally known standard, and the calculation would have required actual measurement in practice.

### Why Excluded

The *gemara* asks: why are rocks and deep crevices excluded from the field measurement at all? They were part of the field that was sanctified. Let them be sanctified and assessed using the same proportional system — fifty *shekel* per *chomer seorim* — as the rest of the field. If everything follows the same rate, why distinguish them at all?

One possible answer is that these areas might not reach the minimum measure of a *beit kor* on their own. The *gemara* rejects this, however, based on a *baraita*: the verse says *zera chomer seorim bachamishim shekel* — fifty *shekel* for a *chomer* — but one might think that only a full *chomer*-sized field is subject to this law. The *baraita* asks: *minayin lerabot letach, vechatzi letach, se'ah, vetarkav, vechatzi tarkav* — how do we know it applies to smaller measures such as a half-*chomer*, a *se'ah*, a *tarkav*, or even half a *tarkav*? The answer: *talmud lomar sadeh mikol makom* — the *Torah* says "a field," without restriction, meaning any size is subject to the proportional rate. So size alone cannot be the reason rocks and crevices are excluded.

*Amar Mar Ukva bar Chama*: *hacha benekikim melei mayim, dela benei zeri'ah ninhu* — we are speaking here of crevices that are filled with water and are simply not plantable. Since the entire measure of *zera chomer seorim* is about planting, an area that cannot be planted is categorically excluded from the calculation. The *gemara* notes that this interpretation is consistent with the parallel to rocks: *deika nami dekatani dumya desla'im* — the *mishna* puts crevices in the same category as rocks, and the issue with rocks is, of course, that nothing can be planted on them. *Shema mina*.

*Ei hachi* — if so, asks the *gemara*, why are smaller rocks and shallower crevices included? They also cannot be planted. The *gemara* answers: *hanu niganay de'ara mikeru* — those are considered mere "puddles of the ground" (in the case of shallow water-filled depressions) or *shidlay de'ara mikeru* — "backbones of the ground" (in the case of low rocky protrusions). In other words, below the ten-*tefachim* threshold, one takes a macro view: minor irregularities are considered part of the field even if this particular patch cannot technically be planted. At a certain scale, one does not measure every centimeter and ask whether that precise spot can hold a seed. Only features that are sufficiently large — ten *tefachim* tall or deep — are treated as genuinely separate from the surrounding field.

An interesting question, not resolved in this *sugya*, is what happens if a low-lying but unplantable feature takes up a very large percentage of the field. At what point does a feature that is technically below the ten-*tefachim* threshold nevertheless demand separate treatment because of its extent? Similarly, what is the minimum size for a field to be considered a "field" at all, such that the Torah's fixed valuation applies? The *gemara* does not address these questions here.

---

## Deduction & Installments

### Deduction Always

A *baraita* addresses a question left ambiguous in the *mishna*: when exactly does the deduction based on remaining years apply? Specifically, suppose the field was sanctified on year one of the cycle and has been sitting idle in the possession of *hekdesh* for many years — either because *hekdesh* has been working the land and collecting income from it, or because *hekdesh* has been lazy and nobody has been earning anything from it. When the owner now comes to redeem it, does the redemption price reflect the number of remaining years from the time of the original *hekdesh*, or from the present moment of redemption?

The *baraita* teaches: *venigra me'erkecha af min hahekdesh* — you deduct the years that have elapsed even if they elapsed while the field was in the possession of *hekdesh*. *She'im achla hekdesh shana o shtayim* — if *hekdesh* farmed it for a year or two — *inami lo achla ela shehayta lefanav* — or even if *hekdesh* did nothing with it and it simply sat there — *noten sela upundyon leshana* — you still pay one *sela* and a *pundyon* for each remaining year calculated from the moment of redemption. The logic is that the current value of the field is determined by the number of years remaining until *yovel*, and that is precisely the time of redemption. An earlier, higher valuation at the moment of *hekdesh* does not fix the redemption price.

### No Payment Plans

The *mishna* then rules: *ve'im amar hareini noten davar shana beshana* — if the owner says, "Let me work out an installment plan, paying a portion each year" — *ein shomin lo* — this is not permitted. The entire amount must be paid at once, *kulo ke'echad*.

The owner's incentive to redeem is acute: if the field is not redeemed before *yovel*, it is lost to the family entirely. If *hekdesh* has already sold it to a third party and the owner has not redeemed it, the *Torah* states *lo yiga'el od* — the owner is out of the picture — *vehayah hasadeh betzeito bayovel kodesh laHashem kisdeh hacherem lakohen tihye achuzato* — the field goes to the *kohanim* at *yovel*. Given this pressure, one can easily imagine an owner desperate to redeem but unable to marshal the full sum. Nevertheless, the *Torah's* language — *vechishev lo hakohen et kesef* — the *kohen* shall calculate the money — implies the full amount, *kulo ke'echad*, not in portions.

A *baraita* confirms this derivation: if the owners say *harenu notnim davar shana beshana* — we will pay a certain amount per year — *she'ein shomin lahem* — one does not listen to them. *Talmud lomar, vechishev lo hakohen et kesef* — the verse teaches that the *kohen* calculates the money as a single payment.

### Fifth for Owners

Both the owner and any other person are entitled to redeem the field. *Echad ba'alim ve'echad kol adam* — both the owner and any other person — may redeem it. The difference: *shehaba'alim notnim chomesh vekol adam eino noten chomesh* — the owner must add a *chomesh*, a fifth, on top of the redemption value, while any other person does not. This is somewhat counterintuitive — like the inverse of a pawnshop, where one buys back one's own item at a premium rather than a discount.

The logic appears to be this: when a person is *makdish* their own inherited field to the *beit hamikdash*, the act carries considerable spiritual and symbolic weight. If the very same person then turns around and buys it back, that somewhat undermines the power of the original donation. The *chomesh* is therefore not simply a financial surcharge; it is an acknowledgment that buying back what one gave is a step that diminishes the initial act of largesse, and the additional payment compensates for that diminishment. If a third party redeems it, no such concern applies — the *hekdesh* is simply liquidating an asset, and the third party pays the market equivalent with no surcharge.

It follows that the owner has a strong incentive to redeem the field before *yovel* — and to do so personally — but at a higher price. One might ask: could the owner engineer a workaround by having a third party redeem it and then transferring the field back? The *mishna* addresses precisely this question next.

---

## Redemption & Yovel

### Owner Redeems

The *Torah* spells out the case explicitly: *ve'im ga'ol yigal et hasadeh hamakdish oto veyasaf chamishit kesef erkecha alav vekam lo* — if the one who sanctified the field redeems it, adding a fifth to the valuation price, it remains his. The *mishna* states this as its first case: *hikdishah uge'alah* — if the owner sanctified and then redeemed it — *einah yotzah miyado bayovel* — it does not leave his possession at *yovel*. He paid the *chomesh*, he redeemed it, and he keeps it. That is the best outcome.

### Son Redeems

*Ge'alah bno* — if the owner's son redeemed it — *yotzah le'aviv bayovel* — it reverts to the father at *yovel*. Remarkably, this is an even better financial arrangement for the owner: the son pays the redemption price without the *chomesh* (since he is not the one who was *makdish*), and at *yovel* the field returns to the father. The son functions as a form of legal continuity of the father — not as a stranger, but as an extension of the father's own identity in the halakhic sense.

### Other Redeems

*Ge'alah acher o echad min hakrovim* — if a stranger, or even a relative who is not the son, redeemed it — *uge'alah miyado* — and even if after that person redeemed it the original owner purchased it from him, so that the field is now in the owner's hands — *yotzah lakohanim bayovel* — it still goes to the *kohanim* at *yovel*. The chain of redemption has been broken. The field was not redeemed from *hekdesh* by the owner or his son, and that is the operative fact. The subsequent transfer from the third-party redeemer back to the owner changes nothing.

The consequence is stark: if one wants to keep the field in one's family, one must either redeem it personally — paying the *chomesh* — or have one's son redeem it.

### Priest Redeems

*Ge'alah echad min hakohanim ve'harei hi tachat yado* — if one of the *kohanim* redeemed the field from the *beit hamikdash*, and then *yovel* arrives while it is still in his possession — *lo yomar ho'il vehia yotzei lakohanim bayovel veharei hi tachat yadi harei hi sheli* — that *kohen* may not simply say: since it is going to the *kohanim* anyway, and it is already in my possession, it is mine. *Ella yotzei mitachat yado umitchaleket lechol echav hakohanim* — rather, it must leave his possession and be divided equally among his fellow *kohanim*. The *mishna* does not specify which *kohanim* receive the division; the *gemara* will address this.

Left open by the current *mishna* is the case where nobody redeems the field and it remains sanctified in the hands of *hekdesh* when *yovel* arrives. The *Torah's* language — *ve'im lo yigal et hasadeh ve'im machar et hasadeh le'ish acher* — might suggest that going to the *kohanim* requires two conditions: the owner did not redeem it, and *hekdesh* sold it to someone else. What happens if neither condition is met — if it simply remained with *hekdesh*, unsold and unredeemed? That question will be the subject of a later *mishna*.

---

## Son vs Other: Baraita

### Not to Son Exception

The *gemara* now brings a *baraita* to clarify the precise scope of "other." *Im lo yigal et hasadeh ve'im machar et hasadeh le'ish acher* — if it is sold to another person — *le'acher velo laben* — to another, but not to the son. The *baraita* teaches that when the field passes out of *hekdesh* into the hands of someone other than the son, the owner's ability to reclaim the field through the *yovel* mechanism is lost. The son is an exception precisely because he represents continuity with the father.

### Brother Continuity

The *gemara* asks: perhaps the brother should enjoy the same status as the son? The word *ish* in the verse — "a man" redeems — is very broad and would include the brother. So the question is whether *acher* — "other" — excludes the brother as much as it excludes the son.

The concept underlying the son's special status is *continuity*: the son is not truly "other" relative to the father; he is a legal extension of the father's presence. The brother too, by the laws of *yibbum* — levirate marriage — is considered a continuation of the deceased brother. *Lehakim shem achiv* — he perpetuates his brother's name and inherits his brother's property. Does the brother's *yibbum*-based continuity earn him the same standing as the son?

### Son Higher Status

The *gemara* resolves the question: *klum yesh yibbum ela bemakom she'ein ben* — *yibbum* only applies in the absence of a son. The entire institution of *yibbum*, in which a brother stands in for a deceased man, is contingent on the absence of a son. If a son exists, there is no *yibbum*. This means the son's claim to continuity is categorically prior to and stronger than the brother's. *Ha'yesh ben, ein yibbum* — where there is a son, there is no *yibbum*.

The *gemara* adds: *vetipok leih dehacha tarti vehacha chada* — could one not have given the simpler answer of two against one? The son has two independent sources establishing his status as a continuation of the father: the case of *yi'ud* (where the *Torah* explicitly gives the son the right to convert a transaction involving an *amah ivriyah* into a *kiddushin*), and the case of *eved Ivri* (where the son-master continues the master's relationship with the slave). The brother has only one: *yibbum*.

The *gemara* responds that this quantitative argument, while valid, is actually circular: *mishum de'eved Ivri mehai pircha nami hu denafka* — the case of *eved Ivri* is itself established only through the very same logical argument about son versus brother that we are now making. We know the son, not the brother, maintains the master-slave relationship in *eved Ivri* only because we have already derived that the son has greater continuity status than the brother — based on the principle that *yibbum* only applies when there is no son. So the "two against one" argument cannot be invoked independently; both cases rest on the same underlying logic.

---

## Daughter & Wife Questions

### Daughter Preserves Field

*Ba'ei Rava bar Avuha*: if a daughter redeems the field from *hekdesh*, does it preserve the field for the father? That is, will the field revert to the father at *yovel*, as it does when the son redeems it?

### Daughter Yibbum Status

The question turns on which framework is more applicable to the daughter. On one hand, *keivan delinyan yibbum ben ubat kiyadadi patrei* — for the purpose of *yibbum*, a son and a daughter are treated identically: either one exempts the widow from *yibbum* because the father's memory and lineage are considered preserved. If that framework applies here, then the daughter should count as continuity just as the son does, and the field should revert to the father at *yovel*.

### Daughter as Other

On the other hand, *keivan delinyan nachalah, bat bimkom ben ke'acher damya* — when it comes to inheritance, a daughter's standing is lower than a son's; a daughter inherits only in the absence of sons. If the inheritance hierarchy is the relevant framework, then the daughter is categorically "other" vis-à-vis the son, and she does not represent continuity in the way the son does.

The *gemara* resolves the question from a *baraita*: *kol shehu acher bimkom ben* — whoever is considered "other" relative to a son — *veha nami bimkom ben ke'acher damya* — and the daughter too is considered "other" relative to the son. This reflects the underlying structure of the patrilineal inheritance system, in which legal continuity runs through the male line. The daughter, for all that she shares certain attributes of continuity with respect to *yibbum*, occupies a lower position in the inheritance hierarchy, and it is that hierarchy which is determinative here.

### Woman's Sanctification

*Ba'ei Rami bar Chama*: if a woman was *makdish* a field, who plays the role of the son — who represents continuity such that, if they redeem it, the field reverts to her at *yovel*? There are two candidates: her husband and her son.

The case for the husband: *ba'al mukim lah shekein yarshah* — the husband establishes continuity because he inherits from her. Moreover, he inherits first — before the son — in cases where both are present.

The case for the son: *shekein notel baraui kevemuchzak* — the son inherits what is "raui," what was owed to her but not yet in her possession at the time of her death. If she dies, is divorced, and then her father dies, the inheritance from her father passes down to her son. The husband, by contrast, inherits only what was already in her possession at the time of death. The son's inheritance is more expansive — it has a character of ongoing continuity rather than a one-time transfer.

One can frame the distinction conceptually: when a husband inherits from his wife, it has the quality of a transfer — the property passes from her domain to his. When a son inherits from his mother, it has the quality of continuity — the property flows through her to him as an extension of her line.

### Unresolved: Husband vs S…

The *gemara* leaves this question unresolved: *teiku*. We do not know whether it is the husband or the son who functions as the operative "continuity" figure for a woman who was *makdish* a field.

---

## Within Two Years & Pries…

### Within Two Years

*Ba'ei mineih Rami bar Chama meRav Chisda*: if a field was sanctified less than two years before *yovel* — in which case we know the owner pays the full fifty *shekel* with no *girua* deduction — does that field still go to the *kohanim* if not redeemed by *yovel*? One might think not: the *Torah* juxtaposes the going-to-*kohanim* with *venigra me'erkecha*, the deduction mechanism. Perhaps only fields subject to *girua* — proportional deduction — are subject to the *yovel* transfer to *kohanim*. A field sanctified within two years, where no *girua* applies, might be a different category.

### Redeemable Goes to Pries…

*Amar leih mai da'atach* — Rav Chisda asks: what exactly are you thinking? The concern is that the verse *venigra me'erkecha* implies that fields subject to deduction go to the *kohanim*. *Debat girayon hi* — only something eligible for deduction goes to the *kohanim*; *delav bat girayon lo* — something not eligible for deduction does not.

Rav Chisda rejects this. *Adaraba* — on the contrary. The operative verse is *im lo yigal hasadeh vehayah hasadeh betzeito bayovel* — if the field is not redeemed, it goes to the *kohanim* at *yovel*. The criterion is not eligibility for deduction but eligibility for redemption. *Ve'hai nami bat geulah hi* — any field that is capable of being redeemed goes to the *kohanim* if it is not redeemed. A field sanctified within two years is perfectly capable of redemption — it simply costs the full fifty *shekel* with no discount. Therefore it absolutely goes to the *kohanim* if not redeemed.

### Priest Possession Rule

A *baraita* then addresses the case raised in the *mishna*: *ga'al echad min hakohanim* — one of the *kohanim* redeemed the field. Can he keep it? *Lo yomar ho'il veyotzei lakohanim bayovel veharei hi tachat yadi harei hi sheli* — he cannot argue: since it is going to the *kohanim* at *yovel* and it is already in my possession, it is mine. *Ella yotzei mitachat yado umitchaleket lechol echav hakohanim* — it must leave his hands and be divided among all his brother *kohanim*.

### Inheritance Principle

The *baraita* explains the underlying principle by asking: *minayin lesdeh sheyotzei lakohanim bayovel vega'al echad min hakohanim minayin shelo yomar* — how do we know the *kohen* who redeemed it cannot simply keep it? *V'din hu* — he might reason as follows: *b'shel acherim ani zoche* — I receive a portion in a field that belongs to others entirely; *b'shel atzmi lo kol shekein* — how much more so should I keep a field that is already in my possession? But *talmud lomar achuzato* — the verse says *achuzato*, his inheritance. The field must be like one's own ancestral inheritance to be retained. *Achuza shelo ve'ein zo shelo* — it must be truly his; and this field, which he purchased from *hekdesh*, is not his ancestral inheritance. Therefore he has no special claim to it, and it is divided equally among the *kohanim*.

### Next: Nobody Redeems

The one scenario not yet addressed — neither in the *Torah's* explicit language nor in the *mishnayot* discussed so far — is the case in which nobody redeems the field and it simply remains in the possession of *hekdesh*, still sanctified, when *yovel* arrives. The *Torah's* formulation — *ve'im lo yigal et hasadeh ve'im machar et hasadeh le'ish acher* — might be read as requiring two conditions: the owner did not redeem it, and *hekdesh* sold it to someone else. What happens if only the first condition is met — the owner did not redeem it, but *hekdesh* never sold it either, and the field remains in *hekdesh* in a sanctified state when *yovel* strikes? That question, and its resolution, will be the subject of the *mishna* taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Arakhin 26

## Mishnah: Field at Yovel

### Torah's Silence

The *daf* begins at the bottom of 25b, where the *mishnah* addresses a case that the *Torah* itself does not explicitly resolve. The *Torah* discusses a scenario in which someone is *makdish* a *sdeh achuza* — a field of ancestral inheritance — and that field is subsequently redeemed or sold. If the owner redeems it himself, the matter is concluded cleanly. If someone else purchases it from *hekdesh*, then when the *yovel* arrives, the field passes to the *kohanim*. But what happens if *hekdesh* simply sits on the field and nothing occurs — no owner redemption, no sale to a third party? The *Torah* provides no explicit ruling for this case, and it is precisely this lacuna that the *mishnah* addresses.

### R. Yehuda Pays

*Higia yovel velo nigal* — the *yovel* arrives and the field has not been redeemed by anyone. According to Rabbi Yehuda, *hakohanim nichnasim letocha venosnim et dameha* — the *kohanim* enter and take possession of the field, but they must pay money for it. The reasoning is as follows: had someone purchased the field from *hekdesh*, that transaction would have transferred the *kedusha* from the field to the money. But here, no such transaction occurred. The field has been sitting in the possession of *hekdesh* the entire time, and so it still carries its *kedusha*. The *kohanim* do receive the field, but since the *kedusha* has never been transferred, they must pay money in order to remove it.

Several details remain unclear according to Rabbi Yehuda. What is the applicable price — the fixed fifty *shekel* per *beis chomer se'orim*, which diminishes as the *yovel* approaches, or the market value? The simple inference from the *Gemara*'s comparison to sanctifying a house, as we will see, suggests market value. It is also not entirely clear whether the *kohanim* have any choice in the matter, or whether they are compelled to take possession and pay. These questions are left open.

### R. Shimon No Pay

Rabbi Shimon agrees that the *kohanim* acquire the field when the *yovel* arrives, but disagrees that they must pay. In his view, *nichnasim velo nosnim* — they enter without payment. Even though the field has remained in *hekdesh* and technically still carries its *kedusha*, that *kedusha* is extinguished by virtue of the transfer to the *kohanim*, without any monetary exchange being required.

### R. Eliezer Waits

Rabbi Eliezer adopts an entirely different position: *lo nichnasim velo nosnim* — the *kohanim* neither enter the field nor pay any money. His fundamental premise is that the *Torah* provides rulings only for two specific scenarios: either the owner redeems the field and retains it, or someone else purchases it from *hekdesh*, in which case when the *yovel* arrives, the field goes to the *kohanim*. If neither of these conditions has been satisfied — if the field simply remained in the possession of *hekdesh* without being purchased by anyone — then the *Torah* does not address the outcome. The field simply stays as *hekdesh*.

### Abandoned Field

So what becomes of this field? The *mishnah* says it is called *sdeh retushin* — an abandoned field — *ad hayovel hasheni*, until the second *yovel*. Rabbi Eliezer's position, in other words, is that the matter defers. The *Torah* provides for two scenarios; if neither has yet occurred, the field awaits a future cycle in which one of them might. Over the course of this second fifty-year period, the owner or a third party can still redeem or purchase the field, after which the normal laws will apply.

If the second *yovel* also passes with no redemption, the field is called *retushei retushin* — the abandoned of the abandoned — and the same logic extends: *ad hayovel hashlishi*, until the third *yovel*, and so on indefinitely. *Le'olam ein hakohanim nichnasim letocha ad sheyigalena acher* — the *kohanim* never acquire the field unless and until someone else redeems it, at which point the *Torah*'s provision regarding the next *yovel* becomes applicable.

A practical question arises: once a subsequent cycle begins, how does one calculate the redemption price? Presumably the cycle resets, so that at fifty years' distance from the next *yovel*, one again pays the full fifty *shekel*, diminishing as the *yovel* approaches.

The discussion also surfaces the question — which the *Gemara* will take up at length — of what happens if the original owner himself redeems the field during the second or a later cycle. Does he retain his status as the ancestral owner and therefore get to keep the field? Or has the passage of the first *yovel* without redemption irrevocably altered his standing, such that he is now treated like any random purchaser, meaning the field would pass to the *kohanim* at the next *yovel*?

---

## R. Yehuda Analysis

### Sanctified House

The *Gemara* now turns to the underlying reasoning of each opinion. *Mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Yehuda* — what is the basis for Rabbi Yehuda's requirement that the *kohanim* pay? The answer is *gamar kodesh kodesh mi-makdish bayit*: Rabbi Yehuda derives the rule through a *gezeira shava* from the case of one who sanctifies his house. The *Torah* states, *ve-ish ki yakdish et beito kodesh l'Hashem ve-he'ericho ha-kohen bein tov u-vein ra ka'asher ya'arich oto ha-kohen ken yakum* — a man who sanctifies his house must have it valuated by the *kohen*, and the redemption proceeds by paying that assessed value. The *kedusha* is removed through payment. Rabbi Yehuda applies the same principle here: *mah le-halan bi-damim*, just as the *kedusha* of a sanctified house is dissolved through monetary payment, *af kan bi-damim*, so too here the transfer to the *kohanim* requires the payment of money.

The *Gemara* notes that if this analogy to the sanctified house is the operative source, the amount would naturally be market value, since that is how the *kohen*'s valuation of a house works.

### Kodesh Transfer

The broader principle emerging from Rabbi Yehuda's position is that *kedusha* attaches to an item and cannot simply evaporate. It must be displaced through a formal act of valuation and monetary exchange. The field remained *kadosh* throughout its time in *hekdesh*; for the *kohanim* to receive it as a secular holding, that *kedusha* must transfer to the money they pay, which itself then becomes *kadosh*.

---

## R. Shimon Analysis

### Korbanot Parallel

The *Gemara* asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not instead derive the rule from the *kivsei ha-atzeret* — the lambs of *Shavuot*. These are *korbanot* that are *kodesh*, yet the *kohanim* consume them without any monetary payment. The answer is that Rabbi Yehuda employs the principle *danin kodshei bedek habayit mi-kodshei bedek habayit* — we derive the law of items sanctified for the *Temple Treasury* from other items sanctified for the *Temple Treasury*, not from *kodshei mizbeach*, items consecrated for the altar. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, argues for the comparison to *korbanot*: *mah le-halan be-chinam*, just as the *kohanim* receive those offerings without payment, *af kan be-chinam*, the same applies here.

### Kodesh Consumption

However, there is a significant conceptual asymmetry between the two cases. When *kohanim* eat a *korban*, they consume it while it retains its *kodesh* status — within the *Beit HaMikdash*, subject to the restrictions of *notar*, *tumah*, and so on. It is consumed *as hekdesh*, not after being converted into something secular. By contrast, a field that is acquired by *kohanim* for ongoing agricultural use is no longer being used *as hekdesh* — it becomes a secular holding. One works the field without restriction, employs non-*kohanim*, and ignores the constraints that would attend actual *kedusha*.

This is the conceptual problem with Rabbi Shimon's position: in every other case, either the item was never *kodesh* to begin with, like *pidyon haben* money or *reishit hagez*, or it was consumed under strict *kedusha* conditions, like *terumah* and *korbanot*. Here we are positing something that begins as *kodesh* but transitions into fully secular use — and Rabbi Shimon maintains that no monetary transfer is required to effect that transition.

---

## R. Yehuda Analysis (II)

### Treasury vs Altar

The *Gemara* now presents the full dialectic regarding why each opinion cannot simply borrow the other's proof. The question is posed: why does Rabbi Shimon not derive from the sanctified house — *neilef mi-makdish bayit* — that payment is required? His answer is *danin davar she-matanah la-kohanim mi-davar she-matanah la-kohanim* — we learn from things that are given to the *kohanim* to other things that are given to the *kohanim*. The field sanctified by *achuza* that goes to the *kohanim* at *yovel* should be compared to other *matanot kehunah*, all of which the *kohanim* receive without payment: *terumah*, *korbanot*, *pidyon haben*, *reishit hagez*. In every instance, the *kohanim* receive what is due them without having to pay for it.

The reason Rabbi Shimon rejects the comparison to *makdish bayit* is that a sanctified house goes to the *Temple Treasury*, not to the *kohanim* as their personal *matanah*. Its proceeds fund the operating expenses or structural repairs of the *Beit HaMikdash*. Rabbi Yehuda, in turn, refuses the comparison to *korbanot* because *kodshei bedek habayit* — items consecrated to the Temple Treasury — must be redeemed through money in order to become usable, and one does not derive that rule from *kodshei mizbeach*, altar offerings, where a fundamentally different mechanism is at work.

The crux of the debate, then, is this: Rabbi Yehuda insists on deriving from items that share the *hekdesh le-bedek habayit* structure, where monetary exchange is required to release the *kedusha*. Rabbi Shimon insists on deriving from items that share the *matanah la-kohanim* structure, where the *kohanim* simply receive without payment. Each has a legitimate formal basis; neither can simply be dismissed.

---

## R. Eliezer Analysis

### Only If Sold

The *Gemara* turns to Rabbi Eliezer. *Amar Rabbah: mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Eliezer?* Rabbah explains that Rabbi Eliezer derives his position directly from the *pasuk*. The verse states: *ve-im lo yigal et hasadeh hamakdish oto* — if the one who sanctified it does not redeem it — *ve-im machar et hasadeh le-ish acher* — and *hekdesh* sells it to another person — *lo yigal od* — then the owner can no longer redeem it, and it will pass to the *kohanim* at *yovel*.

Rabbah reads this as a telescoped derivation: *amar kra ve-im lo yigal et hasadeh... lo yigal od* — by connecting the opening clause (*not redeemed*) with the closing clause (*shall not be redeemed further*), the verse teaches that if nobody purchased it at all, the entire middle scenario — the transfer to the *kohanim* at *yovel* — simply does not apply. The provision for the field passing to the *kohanim* at *yovel*, according to this reading, is contingent on it having first been sold to someone.

### Abaye Objects

Abaye is sharply critical of this method. *Sakina charifa mafseqa kra'ei?* — Are you taking a sharp knife and splitting the *pasuk*? You cannot simply lift the opening phrase, skip over the entire middle of the verse, and attach it to the closing phrase. The *pasuk* is a structured unit; you cannot splice it with scissors and tape. The *drasha* of Rabbah is therefore rejected.

Before moving to Abaye's alternative, it is worth pausing over the observation raised by *Tosafot*. *Tosafot* asks why anyone finds Rabbi Eliezer's position surprising in the first place: the *psukim* straightforwardly discuss what happens *if* the field is sold — *ve-im machar* — which naturally implies that if it is not sold, the provision does not apply. Rabbi Eliezer may simply be reading *pshat*. The problem, as *Tosafot* acknowledges, is that the *Gemara* — both Rava and Abaye — insists that the *Torah* must be actively speaking to this scenario, not merely leaving it in silence. There must be a *drasha* that locates Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in the text, not merely an argument from the *Torah*'s omission.

### Lo Yiga'el Drasha

Abaye therefore proposes an alternative *drasha*: *ta'ama de-Rabbi Eliezer ke-detanya* — the reason is as found in a *baraita*. The verse says *lo yiga'el* — it shall not be redeemed. One might have thought this means the owner can never redeem it in any capacity, not even as an ordinary person would redeem a random field. The *baraita* therefore teaches: *talmud lomar od* — the word *od* (*anymore*, or *in the same manner as before*) qualifies the prohibition. It does not mean the owner is entirely excluded; it means he cannot redeem it *ke-moshe hayetah* — in the same way it used to be redeemable, whereby he would redeem it and retain it in his ancestral holdings. But *aval nigelet she-tehei lefanav ke-sdeh miknah* — he can certainly redeem it as an ordinary person redeems any field, using it until the next *yovel* without any claim to permanent ancestral ownership.

---

## Lo Yiga'el Od

### Field to Kohanim

The *Gemara* now asks when exactly the scenario described by this *baraita* applies. If it is during the first *yovel* cycle — the same cycle in which the owner originally sanctified the field — then what is the difficulty? That is the normal rule of a *sdeh achuza*: the owner redeems it and keeps it. There would be no need for the verse to tell us he cannot redeem it "as before." The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ela pshita*, we must be talking about *yovel sheni* — the second *yovel* cycle, and only according to Rabbi Eliezer, since for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon there is no second cycle — the *kohanim* already took the field at the first *yovel*.

The *Gemara* initially takes this as the explanation of the *baraita* — that according to Rabbi Eliezer, if the owner redeems the field in the second cycle, he does not retain ancestral status and the field passes to the *kohanim* at the next *yovel*, just as any purchased field would. The *baraita* therefore reflects Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that original-owner status belongs exclusively to the first cycle.

But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this: *vetisbara* — does this really make sense? Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon also have to account for the word *od* in the verse. You cannot confine the *drasha* to Rabbi Eliezer. The *baraita* must have a broader application that works across all opinions. Therefore the *Gemara* proposes a completely different scenario for the *baraita*: *hacha be-mai askinan* — what we are really dealing with is *besadeh sheyatzah la-kohanim ve-hikdisha kohen* — a field that transferred to the *kohanim* at *yovel* and was subsequently sanctified by one of the *kohanim* who received it.

The scenario runs as follows. The original owner sanctifies his *sdeh achuza*. A third party — James — redeems it from *hekdesh* and uses it until the *yovel*. At the *yovel*, the field passes to the *kohanim* — say, to Joe. Joe is now the effective ancestral owner of this plot. Joe then sanctifies the field. Now the original owner — whose *sdeh achuza* this once was — seeks to redeem it.

### Original Owner Rights

The question is: can the original owner, when redeeming a field that was once his but has since become the *kohen*'s ancestral holding, claim any special status? One might argue that the *Torah*'s declaration *lo yigal od* — he shall not redeem it any further — bars him entirely, meaning he cannot touch the field at all. The *baraita* teaches that this would be an overreading. The word *od* narrows the prohibition: he cannot redeem it *ke-moshe hayetah* — in the way he once could, such that it would revert to being his ancestral plot. But he can certainly redeem it like a random purchaser, using it until the next *yovel*. The *kedusha* does not act as a total barrier against him.

### Two Phrases Needed

The *Gemara* then asks why both phrases — *lo yiga'el* and *la'asher kanahu* — are necessary, given that they seem to be making the same basic point about the loss of original-owner status. The answer is that each covers a case the other would not.

### Status Never Returns

Had the *Torah* stated only *lo yiga'el* — ruling that the original owner loses his redemptive status when he comes to actively buy it back — one might reason as follows: there, his loss of status makes sense because the field does not revert automatically. He is attempting an affirmative act of purchase, and evaluated purely in present terms, he is no longer the ancestral owner. But in the case of a *sdeh miknah* — where the field *does* revert automatically to the ancestral owner at *yovel* — maybe the automatic character of the reversion invokes the original ancestral order, and the original owner could claim that the *yovel* should restore everything to its primordial state, including his ownership.

Conversely, had the *Torah* stated only *la'asher kanahu* — that when a purchased field reverts at *yovel* it goes to the most recent ancestral holder, not the original one — one might argue: that makes sense because I am claiming something for nothing, without paying; naturally my claim is weak.
