But when I am actually paying money to redeem the field after Joe sanctified it, perhaps my original status should reassert itself, since I am acting in the way an owner would act by paying for the redemption.

Therefore both phrases are required. *Lo yiga'el* rules out the case where the original owner pays to redeem but seeks to retain ancestral standing. *La'asher kanahu* rules out the case where the reversion is automatic and one might argue that the original order is being restored. And the word *od* is essential in *lo yiga'el*, because without it one might read the prohibition as absolute — totally excluding the original owner from any use of the field, even as a random purchaser. *Od* clarifies that the prohibition is specifically against redeeming it in the manner he once could, with full ancestral retention; he retains the ordinary rights of any person.

The upshot is elegant and firm: once the original owner loses the field to the *kohanim*, he has no special status. The *kohanim* become the new ancestral holders. If the original owner wishes to use the field, he is entitled to do so as any other person would, by paying for the redemption and occupying the field until the next *yovel* — at which point it reverts not to him but to the *kohanim*, who are now the *ba'alei ha-achuza*.

This principle receives further reinforcement from a second *baraita* on the verse *la'asher kanahu me'ito la'asher lo achuzat ha'aretz* — the field reverts to the one from whom it was purchased, to the one who holds the ancestral claim. One might have thought this refers to the *gizbar*, the Temple treasurer, since he is the one from whom the buyer technically purchased it. The verse clarifies: it goes to the one who holds the ancestral claim in the land. Yet if that is all the verse intends, why does it need to say *la'asher kanahu* — the one from whom it was purchased? Because it must address the case of *sadeh sheyatzah la-kohanim u-machrah kohen* — a field that transferred to Joe as *kohen*, which Joe then sold to David, who sanctified it and had it redeemed by yet another party. In that scenario, the original owner might argue that he is the true ancestral holder and the field should return to him. The verse counters: *la'asher kanahu* — it goes to the one most recently constituting the ancestral owner, meaning Joe. The original owner has no claim whatsoever.

---

## Second Yovel Status

### Second Cycle Question

With the analysis of *lo yiga'el od* complete, the *Gemara* raises the question that has been lurking since the *mishnah*: *ke-va'alim be-yovel sheni ka'acher damu o lo* — according to Rabbi Eliezer, when the original owner seeks to redeem the field in the second *yovel* cycle, are they treated like any other person (*acher*), or do they retain their ancestral owner status?

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this by applying the same *baraita* just analyzed. The argument runs: *lo yiga'el* — it shall not be redeemed — one might think this means it cannot be redeemed at all, not even as an ordinary field. The *drasha* of *od* teaches that it can be redeemed, but only in the manner of a *sdeh miknah* — that is, without the right to keep it at *yovel*. When would owners be in the position of being able to redeem but not retain? If we are speaking of the first *yovel* cycle, there is no difficulty — the normal rule of *sdeh achuza* applies and they simply redeem and keep. So we must be speaking of the second cycle, and only according to Rabbi Eliezer, since for Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon there is no second cycle. The *Gemara* concludes: *ushma mina* — this shows that according to Rabbi Eliezer, *ba'alim be-yovel sheni ka'acher damu* — the original owners in the second cycle are treated as strangers, and the field will pass to the *kohanim* at the next *yovel*.

### Baraita Evidence

But the *Gemara* immediately objects: *vetisbara* — can this reasoning really stand? Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon also need to account for the word *od*. You cannot simply declare the entire *drasha* relevant only to Rabbi Eliezer. The *drasha* of *od* must serve a function within all opinions. Therefore the *baraita* must be reinterpreted, as already argued, as referring to the case of the *kohen* who sanctified a field that came to him at *yovel*, and the original owner seeking to redeem it — a case perfectly applicable under all three opinions.

Accordingly, the *Gemara* concedes that the earlier attempt to resolve the question from the *baraita* fails. A different *baraita* is then cited explicitly: *Rabbi Eliezer omer ga'alah ba'alim be-yovel sheni, yotzei la-kohanim be-yovel* — Rabbi Eliezer says that if the owners redeem it during the second *yovel* cycle, it goes to the *kohanim* at the subsequent *yovel*. This would definitively answer the question: the owners have lost their status; in the second cycle they are treated like any other purchaser.

### Mishnah Language

But Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: *ha nan lo tenan hachi* — that is not what our *mishnah* says. The *mishnah* states that Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *kohanim* never take possession of the field *until an other person* (*acher*) redeems it. The implication of *acher* — another — is that the owner is not included in the category of those whose redemption triggers the transfer to *kohanim*. If the owner redeems it, presumably he keeps it, in every cycle. So the *mishnah* appears to contradict the *baraita*.

Rav Ashi responds: *ba'alim be-yovel sheni ka'acher damu* — by the time the second cycle arrives, the owners themselves have become the functional equivalent of *acher*, a stranger. The *yovel* passed without the field reverting to them, which is itself a signal that they are no longer in the halachic category of original owner. So when the *mishnah* says the *kohanim* get it only when *acher* redeems it, that includes the original owners in the second cycle — because by then, they are *acher*. The *mishnah* and the *baraita* are consistent.

### Competing Versions

The *Gemara* closes with an alternative formulation: *ika de-amri* — there are those who say the *baraita* was reported in the opposite version. In this second version, *Rabbi Eliezer omer ga'alah be-yovel sheni eina yotza la-kohanim be-yovel* — if the owners redeem it in the second cycle, it does *not* go to the *kohanim*; the original owner retains his status. Ravina then notes that this version is consistent with our *mishnah*, since the *mishnah*'s use of *acher* implies that the owner is distinct from the stranger, and the owner's redemption produces a different outcome.

Rav Ashi counters that the *mishnah* alone is insufficient to settle the question, since the *mishnah*'s language is ambiguous: *iy matnitin, hava amina ba'alim be-yovel sheni ka'acher damu* — even from the *mishnah* one might argue that in the second cycle the owners are already considered *acher*. The resolution would have required the explicit *baraita*, but since there are two versions of that *baraita* — one saying the field does go to *kohanim*, the other saying it does not — the question remains unresolved.

This is the *Gemara*'s conclusion, and it is a striking one. The fundamental question of whether the original owner retains any ancestral status during a subsequent *yovel* cycle, according to Rabbi Eliezer, is left entirely open — *gemara de-avda kizeh ve-kizeh*. Two versions of the *baraita* exist, pointing in opposite directions, and the *mishnah* alone cannot adjudicate between them.

---

---

# Arakhin 27

## Son Purchases Father's F…

### Scenario Setup

The mishnah presents the following scenario: *halokeach sadeh me-aviv u-meis aviv* — someone purchased a field from his father and then his father died, after which he sanctified the field. The question is how to classify that field's status for purposes of redemption. Is it a *sdei miknah*, a purchased field, because it was originally acquired through purchase? Or is it a *sdei achuza*, an inherited field, because had the son never purchased it, he would have inherited it regardless? The mishnah rules *harei hi k'sdei achuza* — it is treated as an inherited field — and the son therefore enjoys the full rights of an owner to redeem it and retain it when the *yovel* arrives.

Before turning to the more complex case in the mishnah, it is worth noting a fascinating *Rambam* and *Ra'avad* bearing on the earlier portion of the chapter. The mishnah had established that if the original owner did not personally redeem his field from *hekdesh* but instead bought it from a third party who had redeemed it, he loses the field when *yovel* arrives, since he was not the first to redeem it from the Temple treasury. The *Rambam*, however, rules the opposite: if someone else redeemed the field and the original owner subsequently purchased it from that person, the owner retains it when *yovel* comes. The *Ra'avad* objects sharply — this contradicts an explicit mishnah. He then adds, however, that upon consulting various manuscripts, he actually found a version of the mishnah that reads as the *Rambam* does. This exchange illustrates how much of this area of *halacha* remains underdeveloped in the *gemara*, given its practical irrelevance in later generations.

### Father Dies After Sancti…

The mishnah then turns to a harder case: *hikdisha ve-achar kach meis aviv* — he purchased the field, sanctified it, and only afterward did his father die. At the moment of sanctification, the son's relationship to the field was that of a purchaser alone; his father was still alive and the son had not yet inherited anything. Later, when *yovel* arrives, the field would naturally fall into the category of an inherited field since his father has since died. The question is: which moment determines the field's classification — the moment of sanctification or the moment of *yovel*?

### Rabbi Meir's Opinion

*Rabbi Meir* rules *harei hi k'sdei miknah* — it is treated as a purchased field. At the moment the son sanctified it, he had not yet inherited it, and therefore the determinative classification is that of a purchased field.

### Rabbi Yehuda & Shimon

*Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* rule *harei hi k'sdei achuza* — it is treated as an inherited field. They derive this from the verse: *im misdei miknato asher lo misdei achuzato* — "if from a purchased field that is not from his inherited field." The phrase is apparently redundant: of course a purchased field is not an inherited field. The Torah must therefore be pointing to a case where a field could be both purchased *and* inherited. The exclusion — *sdei she-einah re'uya lihyot sdei achuza*, a purchased field that is not in line to become inherited — carves out the scenario before us. Since this son was in line to inherit the field, it is treated as inherited.

A natural question arises: would *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* take this reasoning to its logical extreme and rule that even if the *yovel* arrived while the father was still alive, the field would revert to the son as a *sdei achuza*? That cannot be correct. If the son purchased the field from his father, sanctified it, and then *yovel* hit while the father was still living, logic demands the field revert to the father — it is his ancestral portion. To rule otherwise would allow a son to purchase a field from his father, sanctify it, and then reclaim it as his own *sdei achuza* even though he only ever held a lease-like interest for the remaining years until *yovel*. The ruling of *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* must therefore be limited to cases where the father has in fact died before *yovel* arrives. The verse's exclusion applies only to that case: the son was in line to inherit and has now actually inherited; we therefore treat the field as *sdei achuza*.

It is also worth considering the practical difference between the two opinions. If the father has died by the time *yovel* arrives, and the field is classified as a *sdei miknah* per *Rabbi Meir*, then it reverts to the original owner — the father — and passes to all of the father's heirs. If the son has brothers, the field will be divided among them all. By contrast, according to *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon*, since the son is treated as the field's owner by virtue of *sdei achuza*, he retains it entirely at *yovel*. This underscores the real *chiddush* of their position: it is not necessary that the son would have inherited the entire field himself. Even if he was merely one of several heirs, his status as an heir-in-line is sufficient to designate him as the owner for purposes of *sdei achuza*.

### Kinyan Peiros Debate

The *gemara* proposes that the underlying dispute between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* may reflect the broader legal debate over *kinyan peiros k'kinyan haguf*: whether ownership of produce alone is legally equivalent to full ownership of the corpus. The relevance here is as follows. When the son purchases the field from his father in a period when *yovel* is operative, the purchase is effectively a lease for the remaining years until *yovel* — the son does not acquire outright title, only the right to work the land and benefit from its produce. This is *kinyan peiros*. Now, is that functionally equivalent to owning the land itself?

If *Rabbi Meir* holds *kinyan peiros k'kinyan haguf dami* — that the produce-lease is treated as full ownership — then even before the father dies, the son already has a status equivalent to full title. His first relationship to the land was therefore as a full owner, and when he sanctifies it, you might classify it as a *sdei miknah* based on that full-title-equivalent acquisition. A verse is then needed even for the simpler case — father dies, then son sanctifies — because without the verse one might have said that the prior purchase-as-title precludes *sdei achuza* status.

*Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon*, by contrast, would hold *kinyan peiros lav k'kinyan haguf dami* — the lease-purchase is not equivalent to full title. The son never had real title until his father died; at that point he first acquires genuine ownership, and any subsequent sanctification is obviously that of an inherited field. No verse is needed for the simple case. The verse's work is reserved for the harder case: where the son sanctified the field while still holding only his lease — while the father still lived — and the father died afterward. Only in that case does one need a scriptural basis to say we treat it as *sdei achuza*.

### Hermeneutic Analysis

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* rejects this framework. In truth, he says, *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* may agree that *kinyan peiros k'kinyan haguf dami* in other contexts. The difference here is purely hermeneutic. The verse could have been written simply: *im mi-sdei miknato asher lo sdei achuza* — "if from a purchased field that is not an inherited field." That formulation alone would have excluded the case of father-dies-then-sanctifies, since in that scenario the field is also an inherited field. What is the additional mem in the phrase *mi-sdei achuzato* — "from his inherited field" — teaching? It is teaching *sdei she-einah re'uya lihyot sdei achuza* — not merely a field that is not currently inherited, but a field that is not even in line to become inherited. The additional mem pushes us to the further case: purchased, then sanctified, then father dies. *Maidei mi-sdei achuzato* — what is the purpose of the word *mi-*? To exclude a field that, though purchased at the time of sanctification, was in line to become an inherited field. And that is precisely this case.

The *gemara* concludes, then, that the debate between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* is driven by hermeneutics — by which case each sage requires the verse to address — rather than by a direct consequence of the *kinyan peiros* debate.

The mishnah closes this section with a statement about purchased fields generally: *sdei miknah einah yotzah la-kohanim ba-Yovel* — a sanctified purchased field does not go out to the *kohanim* at *yovel*, but returns to its original owner. The reason given is *she-ein adam makdish davar she-eino shelo* — a person cannot sanctify something that is not fully his. Since a purchase in the *yovel* era is really only a lease for the years remaining until *yovel*, the buyer never owned the land outright. He cannot therefore cause it to leave the possession of the original owner. At *yovel*, it reverts.

The mishnah then states: *ha-kohanim ve-ha-Levi'im makdishim le-olam ve-go'alim le-olam* — the *kohanim* and *Levi'im* may sanctify and redeem at all times, both before and after *yovel*. This is derived from the verse in *Behar* concerning the cities of the *Levi'im*: *ge'ulat olam tihyeh la-Levi'im* — permanent redemption rights belong to the *Levi'im*. The *gemara* will explore what this means in the context of fields. The *gemara* notes: *bishlama go'alin itztarich* — the ruling that they may redeem is clearly necessary, *le-afukei mi-Yisrael de-lo parkei*, to exclude an ordinary Israelite who does not have that ongoing redemption right. The precise contours of what *go'alin le'olam* entails — whether it refers to redeeming from *hekdesh* directly, or whether it also allows the *kohen* or *Levi* to force a repurchase from a third-party buyer, and whether the *kohen* who sanctified retains priority over other *kohanim* — are left as open questions by the *gemara*.

---

## Redemption Without Jubil…

### No Jubilee Effects

When *yovel* is not operative, the fixed-rate valuation chart of the Torah — fifty *shekel* for a given acreage for the full cycle — no longer applies, since that rate is calibrated to the number of years remaining until *yovel*. With no *yovel*, the framework collapses and market value takes its place. The question then becomes how to determine that market value.

When *yovel* is operative, two powerful forces shape the redemption of a sanctified field: the fixed rate locks in the price, and *yovel* itself functions as a deadline — if the owner does not redeem by *yovel*, the field transfers to the *kohanim*. When *yovel* is not operative, neither force applies. The owner retains an indefinite right to redeem the field as long as it remains in *hekdesh*'s possession. If *hekdesh* sells it to a third party, the owner must negotiate with that buyer — there is no *yovel* to force a reversion. This is, as the *gemara* puts it, essentially how we treat property today: if one sanctifies one's field, one may attempt to buy it back before anyone else does, and if *hekdesh* has already sold it to another, one must deal with that buyer directly. The one remaining distinctively Torah-law feature is that if the owner wishes to repurchase from *hekdesh*, he must add a *chomesh* — a fifth. That obligation persists even when *yovel* is not in force.

One might ask: if there is no *yovel*, does the category of *sdei achuza* even apply? The answer is no — without *yovel*, there is no *sdei achuza* framework. Sanctifying a field when *yovel* is not operative is effectively treated as a standard dedication of movable property, except for the *chomesh* obligation.

The *Tosafot* make an important point about the historical setting of this mishnah. If there is no *Beit HaMikdash* at all, then while one can technically sanctify property — since sanctity is a metaphysical status and the Torah's categories do not disappear merely because there is no institution to collect — *Tosafot* notes that *hekdesh* in that case has no practical financial interest, and the entire mechanism of redemption reduces to a purely symbolic act. One would simply redeem on a *perutah* to remove the *kedushah*. There would be no bidding war. The mishnah's scenario — with its competitive auction and financial stakes — therefore must describe a period when there is a *Beit HaMikdash* but no *yovel*. That is precisely the period of the Second Temple, during which *yovel* did not apply because the majority of the Jewish people were not settled on the Land in accordance with their tribal portions.

### Owner's First Bid Right

The mishnah establishes: *omer lo petach atah rishon* — we say to the owner, make the first offer. The rationale is that since the owner must add a *chomesh* to whatever he bids, he will ultimately contribute more to the Temple treasury than any other bidder at the same base price. By inviting him to enter the bidding first, *hekdesh* maximizes the likelihood of receiving his augmented contribution.

In practice, a savvy owner will discount his bid to account for the eventual *chomesh* — bidding less than he would otherwise be willing to pay, knowing the *chomesh* will bring it up to his true ceiling. This exposes him to being outbid. The dynamics are thus genuinely those of an auction, not a simple assessment. The *gemara* identifies two reasons to want the owner involved in the bidding. *Chada de-aydi de-chaviva lei tfei hu parik lei* — first, because the field is personally dear to him, he may be willing to pay more than a disinterested third party. *Ve-od mitzvat geulah ba-adon* — and further, the Torah itself establishes that the owner has the first right and obligation to redeem what he has sanctified; the bidding process gives that right procedural expression. Beyond both of these, there is the concrete financial consideration: *she-ha-be'alim notnim chomesh ve-chol adam einam notnim chomesh* — the owner adds a fifth while everyone else does not.

### Poor Quality Field Case

A striking episode is recorded in the mishnah. Someone sanctified a field *mipnei ra'atah* — on account of its poor quality. The field was so unproductive that it was not worth the expense of working it. By sanctifying it, the person made a gesture of piety at essentially no personal cost. When told *petach atah rishon* — make the first offer — he offered a trivial amount. *Rabbi Yose* says that the amount he offered was the value of an egg — *harei sheli be-beitzah* — on the basis that *hekdesh nifdeh be-kesef u-ve-shaveh kesef*, that *hekdesh* may be redeemed with monetary equivalents, not only with coin. The court accepted his offer: *higatanu* — deal. And the consequence: *nimtza mafsid et sadehu lefanav* — he wound up paying for his trivial field and being stuck with it anyway.

The point of the episode is dual. First, it confirms that redemption is a bidding process and not a unilateral assessment by *hekdesh*. Second, and more significantly, it establishes that the court does not merely invite the owner to bid — it pressures him to bid. *Hekdesh* must not become a dumping ground for worthless property.

### Fifth Addition Requireme…

The *gemara* explores the precise mechanism of the owner's obligation to add a *chomesh*. The *tanna kamma* of the case holds that the owner must bid at least an *issar*, because an *issar* contains at least four or more *perutot*, meaning that when the *chomesh* — which is technically one quarter of the principal, such that the principal becomes four-fifths of the total — is calculated on an *issar*, the result is at least a *perutah*. One cannot add a *chomesh* of less than a *perutah*, since that is the minimum denomination for a valid halachic transaction. *Rabbi Yose*, however, holds that even if the bid is only a *beitzah* — an egg — whose fifth would fall below a *perutah*, it is still valid: *hekdesh nifdeh be-kesef u-ve-shaveh kesef*, even a non-monetary equivalent of minimal value suffices to redeem *hekdesh*. The *gemara* confirms that the dispute cannot concern whether equivalents are acceptable in principle — that is agreed upon by all. The debate is specifically whether one may redeem *hekdesh* when the *chomesh* that results would be less than a *perutah*.

The case therefore works as follows: *stama de-rabbanan de-amar ke-issar* — the anonymous rabbinic position requires at least an *issar* to ensure a valid *chomesh*. *Rabbi Yose* permits even a *beitzah*. In either case, if the owner makes even that minimal offer and the court accepts it, *nimtza mafsid* — he is left having paid something trivial and having retrieved his worthless field. The *gemara* confirms that the court does not merely suggest: *kofin* — they compel him. Or more precisely, per one reading: first they suggest, *omer lo petach atah rishon*, and if he declines, *kofin* — they coerce. The policy is clear: *hekdesh* refuses to absorb property it cannot use, and the obligation falls back on the owner.

---

## Auction Mechanics

### Bids Set Price

The mishnah now describes the full auction. One bidder offers ten *sela*, another twenty, another thirty, another forty, another fifty. The field is awarded to the highest bidder. But what happens if the winning bidder backs out? The *gemara*'s insight, and that of the mishnah itself, is that each bid functions not merely as an offer but as a *designation of value*. When the fifty-*shekel* bidder makes his offer, he has, in some objective sense, established the value of the field at fifty. If he then backs out, *hekdesh* can only recover forty from the next bidder. The fifty-*shekel* bidder has caused a loss of ten *shekel* and must make up that difference. *Memashkenin minichasav ad eser* — the court seizes assets to collect the ten-*shekel* gap.

### Backing Out Penalties

The principle applies uniformly at every level. If the forty-*shekel* bidder backs out, he pays ten — the difference between his bid and the thirty-*shekel* bid below him. If the thirty-*shekel* bidder backs out, he pays ten. If the twenty-*shekel* bidder backs out, he pays ten. Each backing-out causes a loss of ten, and each is responsible for exactly that gap. This structure serves as a powerful deterrent against frivolous or strategic bidding — entering the auction solely to drive up the price for others. Every bid is binding, and the bidder remains liable for the gap his withdrawal creates even if others above him have already withdrawn and been assessed their own penalties.

### Initial Bidder Backs Out

The case of the initial ten-*shekel* bidder who backs out is handled differently. Since there is no lower bid to serve as the floor, the court sells the field at market value — *mochrin oto be-shavyo* — and the ten-*shekel* bidder pays the difference between market value and ten. *Ve-nifra'in mi-shel eser et ha-motar* — the surplus above ten is collected from him.

---

## Owner vs. Other Bidd (II)

### Owner's Fifth Advantage

The mishnah turns to competition between the owner and other bidders. When the owner and another bidder both offer twenty, *ha-be'alim kodmim mipnei she-hem mosifim chomesh* — the owner takes precedence because he will add a fifth. His effective payment is twenty-five, whereas the other bidder's payment is twenty. *Hekdesh* receives more from the owner.

### Non-Owner Bids Higher

Things become more complex when a non-owner bids higher than the owner. Say the owner bids twenty and another bidder says twenty-one. The non-owner's higher bid designates the value at twenty-one, yet the owner still wins the auction since his twenty plus his *chomesh* of five yields twenty-five, which is more than twenty-one. But because the non-owner's bid has set the price at twenty-one, the owner does not pay based on his own initial offer of twenty. He pays twenty-one — the price set by the competing bid — and then adds his *chomesh* calculated on his original bid of twenty, yielding a total of twenty-six. *Ha-be'alim notnim esrim ve-shesh.*

This is a striking consequence. The owner entered the auction prepared to pay twenty plus the *chomesh* — twenty-five total. Because another bidder said twenty-one, the owner is now committed to twenty-six. He wins, but at a higher cost than he anticipated. The rule is clear before one enters the auction: all bids are binding, bids set prices, and the owner's *chomesh* is calculated on his own bid regardless of what price has been set by another bidder's offer.

### Equivalence Point

The mishnah traces through successive increments. At twenty-two, twenty-three, and twenty-four offered by the non-owner, the owner still wins — paying twenty-seven, twenty-eight, and twenty-nine respectively — since his twenty plus five still outpaces the non-owner's offer. When the non-owner reaches twenty-five, the owner's twenty plus five equals exactly twenty-five — a tie — and the owner still receives the field since the tie goes to him, with his total payment now thirty. At this point the mishnah notes: *she-ein mosifin chomesh al iluyo shel zeh* — the *chomesh* is calculated only on the owner's own bid, not on the non-owner's higher offer.

### Owner's Final Offer Opti…

When another bidder reaches twenty-six, the owner's twenty plus five is now only twenty-five — strictly less than twenty-six — and the owner can no longer claim the field on the strength of his original bid alone. At this point the mishnah affords the owner an option: *im ratzu ha-be'alim notnim shloshim ve-echad ve-dinar* — if the owner wishes, he may submit a final offer of thirty-one and a fraction, which is equivalent to revising his base bid to approximately twenty-six, yielding a total that exceeds twenty-six. If he elects to do so, *ha-be'alim kodmim* — he takes the field. If not, *omer lo harei hi shelcha* — the field goes to the twenty-six bidder.

The mishnah's structure implies that outside of this final option, the auction is essentially a sealed-bid, single-round process — what one might call a silent auction. The owner is the one party who retains the right to a final counteroffer after the other bids are revealed.

---

## Auction Mechanics (II)

### Sequential vs. Simultane…

*Rav Chisda* introduces a critical distinction. The mishnah states that when the fifty-*shekel* bidder backs out, he pays ten; when the forty-*shekel* bidder backs out, he pays ten; and so on down to the twenty-*shekel* bidder, each paying ten. *Rav Chisda* asks: why does the forty-*shekel* bidder pay the full ten between his bid and the thirty-*shekel* bid below him? If the fifty-*shekel* bidder had also backed out, should he not share responsibility for that gap?

*Rav Chisda*'s answer is *lo kashya — kan be-vat achat kan be-zeh achar zeh*: there is no contradiction, because the two scenarios are different. If the fifty-*shekel* bidder backed out first — sequentially — and was assessed his ten-*shekel* penalty and departed, the auction then proceeds as if he were never there. The forty-*shekel* bidder now stands as the high bidder and bears full responsibility for the gap between his bid and the next. His backing out therefore costs him the full ten between forty and thirty. But if both the fifty and forty-*shekel* bidders back out *simultaneously*, their responsibilities overlap. Both bear responsibility for the gap between forty and thirty, since either one of them, had he remained, would have covered that gap. In the zone of overlap, liability is divided equally — *mishalshin beineihem*. The fifty-*shekel* bidder thus pays ten for the exclusive gap between fifty and forty, and then five for his half of the shared gap between forty and thirty — fifteen in total. The forty-*shekel* bidder pays five for his half of the gap between forty and thirty.

The *gemara* initially attempts to read the mishnah as describing separate auctions, each with only one bidder at a given level, in order to avoid the question of shared liability. But this reading is forced and ultimately abandoned. The text *nifra'in mi-shel asarah* — "collected from the ten-*shekel* bidder" — implies there are others in the same auction, not that he is the sole participant. *Rav Ashi* confirms that the resolution is *Rav Chisda*'s: sequential withdrawal and simultaneous withdrawal are governed by different rules, and a *baraita* that states *mishalshin beineihem* is describing the simultaneous case while the mishnah's straight ten-*shekel* penalty describes sequential cases.

---

## Owner vs. Other Bidd (II)

### Ma'aser Sheni Comparison

The *gemara* raises a challenge from the laws of *ma'aser sheni*. In our mishnah, *hekdesh* gives the field to the owner when the owner and another bidder are tied at the same base amount — precisely because the owner's *chomesh* will result in a higher total payment to the treasury. The fifth, in other words, is treated as a decisive factor. The *gemara* then cites a *baraita* about redeeming *ma'aser sheni*: if the owner offers one *sela* and another person offers one *sela* and an *issar*, the other person's bid wins — *mipnei she-mosif al ha-keren* — because he has added more to the principal. The owner's *chomesh* is not taken into account as a tiebreaker; the higher principal wins outright.

The *gemara* resolves this by pointing to a fundamental structural difference. *Hacha de-chumsha rivcha de-hekdesh hu, chumash adif* — in our case of a sanctified field, the *chomesh* that the owner adds goes to *hekdesh*. *Hekdesh* has a direct financial interest in receiving the *chomesh*, and so naturally it factors the fifth into its calculation of who offers more. By contrast, with *ma'aser sheni*, *karna tefei parik shapir, chumsha lo ichpat lan* — the fifth that the owner adds to redeem his *ma'aser sheni* accrues only to himself; he takes both the redeemed value and the money he spent to Jerusalem to eat. The institution receiving the redemption money has no stake in whether the owner adds more or less. Therefore, in the *ma'aser sheni* context, only the principal matters, and a higher principal wins regardless of what *chomesh* the owner might add.

---

---

# Arakhin 28

## Field Valuation & Auction

### Market Value Today

Today's daf is 28, and we begin from the bottom of 27b. We are in the middle of discussing what happens nowadays — when there is no fixed value assigned to a field — in determining how to assess it. This question is interesting, because one could in principle also raise it regarding a *sedei mikneh*, a purchased field, to which the Torah also assigns no fixed value. Yet there the situation is less clear: the value of a *sedei mikneh* might in fact be fixed, albeit proportional to the years remaining — it is simply that what happens at *yovel* is different. The *pesukim* are not entirely clear on this point.

The question before us is: nowadays, when *yovel* no longer applies, when there is no fixed value and *yovel* has no operative effect, and a sale is a sale and a *hekdesh* is a *hekdesh* — how does one determine the market value of a field that has been consecrated and must be redeemed? The scenario, as Tosafot points out, presupposes that there is a *beit hamikdash*, but no *yovel* — which was precisely the situation throughout the entire Second Temple period. Tosafot further notes that nowadays, since there is no *beit hamikdash* and therefore no financial interest in redemption, the entire purpose of the transaction is simply to remove the *kedushah*, and one would redeem it for a *perutah*.

One might add that today people are so far removed from the act of being *makdish* that it is an open question whether such a declaration even carries full halakhic force. On the one hand, the wrong word renders an act of *hekdesh* ineffective — it is a matter of formal speech. On the other hand, as was noted at the very beginning of this *masechet*, in matters of *hafla'ah*, one's inner intention is highly significant. Whether someone who has learned the relevant *halachot* — through *yeshiva* study or *Daf Yomi* — is in a different category is an interesting question left unresolved.

### Assessment vs. Auction

The *mishnah* presents two methods for determining value. One is a standard assessment: appraisers determine the market value. The other is an auction — apparently something like a silent auction — in which a competitive bidding process is used in the hope of achieving a price higher than the baseline market rate. The owner is not merely invited to participate; he is compelled to do so. There are multiple reasons for this: there is a *mitzvah* for the owner to redeem his own field; if no one else wants the field, at least someone will buy it; and once the owner enters the auction process, he becomes liable to add a *chomesh*, a fifth. So the owner is drawn into the auction on all of these grounds.

### Owner's Fifth Advantage

What follows from this are some remarkable rules about who "wins" the auction. It is not simply the highest bidder in the ordinary sense. Because the owner adds a *chomesh* on top of his base bid, a higher base bid by a competitor may nonetheless be defeated by the owner — since the owner's base bid, once the fifth is added, produces a higher total that the *hekdesh* will ultimately receive. This means the owner must enter the auction knowing the rules thoroughly. Whatever base bid he makes may be escalated — against his initial expectations — and he should be prepared for that eventuality before going in.

### Case Law Philosophy

One might ask why the *mishnah* does not simply state the general principle: treat the owner's bid as though it were twenty percent higher, and award accordingly. The answer is that the *mishnah* has an even more striking rule — if someone bids twenty-one and the owner bids twenty, we award it to the owner and force him to accept the higher bid as his base. The *mishnah*, in other words, does not abstract to a general principle; it articulates concrete cases.

This reflects something important about the development of Talmudic discourse. The Torah is almost entirely case law. The *mishnah* is also largely case law, though occasionally one finds the construction *zeh kelal* — "this is the rule" — which represents a move toward abstraction. The Gemara then always asks: *zeh kelal l'atuyei mai*, what does this inclusive rule come to add? But perhaps a *zeh kelal* is not always coming to include a new case; sometimes it is the *mishnah* itself stepping back from the concrete and attempting to articulate the abstract. As one moves further into the Amoraic period, abstraction becomes progressively more prominent.

### Owner Coercion

A natural question arises about the owner's liability once he is drawn into the auction process. Can he withdraw without penalty if he finds the final price beyond his means? The answer, based on the language throughout the *mishnah*, is that he apparently cannot — *mamashknin oto*, we seize from him. He is stuck. What happens in the extreme case where the owner has no assets whatsoever — whether the *hekdesh* would then turn to the next bidder or treat the obligation as an outstanding debt — is not resolved, though presumably *hekdesh* would act in its best financial interest in such circumstances.

---

## Equal Bids Problem

### Ishtakach Gavra

We are now approximately seven lines down in the wide section of the daf. The Gemara presents the following case: someone other than the owner bids twenty-five, and the owner bids twenty. We know that the owner's twenty becomes twenty-five once the *chomesh* is added. So we award it to the owner, and now use the outsider's twenty-five as the base, making the owner's total obligation thirty. But the Gemara is dissatisfied with this reasoning when the bids are exactly equal at the base level. The Gemara asks: why can the owner not say *ishtakach gavra b'chariki* — I have a man standing in my place? If this outsider bid twenty-five and my twenty, once my fifth is added, also becomes twenty-five, they are effectively identical. There is no basis for preferring me over him, and I should be able to say: take the other fellow.

The Gemara finds this argument compelling. Contrary to what one might have thought was the *chiddush* of the *mishnah* — that we always push the owner to produce the maximum amount — the Gemara draws a line here. If the owner's bid plus his fifth equals exactly the outsider's bid, we would indeed go to the outsider. The *chiddush* of the *mishnah* must therefore be a case where the owner bid slightly more than twenty.

### Rava's Resolution

The Gemara therefore reads the *mishnah* as describing a case where the owner bid twenty and a *dinar* — a *dinar* being a quarter of a *shekel*. The owner bid twenty and a bit; once his *chomesh* is added, the total exceeds twenty-five, and the owner genuinely wins. The outsider's twenty-five then becomes the base, yielding thirty as the owner's total payment.

### Fraction Precision

The Gemara then raises an objection: if that is the case, why does the *mishnah* not say so explicitly — *v'litnei dinar*, let it state "and a dinar"? The answer given is *v'lo dak*, the *mishnah* is not being precise. But this is a surprising answer, since the entire *halakha* hinges on that extra amount. The Gemara then points out that the *mishnah* does in fact mention a *dinar* at its conclusion — in the rule that the owners may bid thirty-one and a *dinar* — demonstrating that the *mishnah* is not averse to mentioning fractions. Rava therefore reformulates: the owner bid twenty and a *perutah* — a penny — and the *mishnah* simply rounds and omits it.

This remains somewhat unsatisfying, since the legal outcome depends entirely on that marginal addition. But the Gemara's conclusion is clear: if the bids are truly equal — twenty producing twenty-five with the *chomesh*, meeting the outsider's twenty-five exactly — we would give it to the outsider, and the *mishnah*'s case is one where the owner's bid, however slightly, exceeded that threshold.

---

## Assessment Reinforcement

### Rabbi Yehuda's Condition

The Gemara continues. The *mishnah* has stated that the *chomesh* is based on the owner's own bid, not the higher bid of the outsider. However, Rabbi Yehuda qualifies this: *lo shanu ela shelo nishom hekdesh b'shlosha* — this is only true when *hekdesh* did not have the field independently assessed by a panel of three. Rashi explains that the *chiddush* of specifying three is that the general rule requires *hekdesh* to assess with ten — a principle derived in Sanhedrin. But if there was at minimum an assessment by three, that assessment has binding force.

### Ten vs. Three

What does this mean practically? If someone else bids twenty-two and there is an independent assessment also arriving at twenty-two — thereby reinforcing the higher bid — and the owner bid only twenty, then while the owner still wins the field (since his twenty plus the *chomesh* exceeds twenty-two), his *chomesh* is now based not on his own bid of twenty but on the reinforced base of twenty-two. This is the principle that Rav Chisda had in mind: when an independent assessment supports the outsider's higher bid, the owner's fifth must be calculated on that higher figure.

Questions naturally arise. What if the independent assessment was higher than the outsider's bid — would the owner be bound by that even higher figure? What if the assessment is lower? Rashi's framing suggests the assessment must reinforce the outsider's bid specifically, but the Gemara does not address these edge cases explicitly. Also left unaddressed is the scenario the *mishnah* implies but never states: what happens when all bids come in below the market price? Presumably *hekdesh* is not bound by such bids — like a minimum bid in a standard auction — but this is not spelled out.

### Shammai vs. Hillel

The Gemara brings a *baraisa* in support: *Beit Shammai omerim mosifin u-Beit Hillel omerim ein mosifin* — Beit Shammai says that the owner must add his fifth based on the higher bid, while Beit Hillel says he does not. The Gemara immediately asks: what is the case? If *hekdesh* made no independent assessment, what is Beit Shammai's reasoning for applying the *chomesh* to the higher bid? The Gemara finds this difficult. It concludes that the *baraisa* must be speaking about a case where an independent assessment was made — only then does Beit Shammai's position become intelligible.

### Gemara Resolution

This, however, raises a new problem: if Rav Chisda's ruling — that the *chomesh* is based on the independently assessed figure — represents Beit Shammai's position, since when do we rule like Beit Shammai? The Gemara offers two resolutions. The first is that the *baraisa* is speaking of a case *without* assessment, and Beit Shammai is simply being stringent in requiring the owner's fifth to be based on the higher bid even without an independent assessment. The second is to reverse the positions entirely — *v'eiphach* — with Beit Shammai saying *ein mosifin* and Beit Hillel saying *mosifin*, so that Rav Chisda would align with Beit Hillel. But this second reading is rejected, because if Beit Shammai were the lenient party, the rule would have been listed among the well-known *kulei Beit Shammai* and *chumrei Beit Hillel*.

The Gemara therefore settles on the first explanation: the *baraisa* concerns a case without assessment, and Beit Shammai is stringent. In the end, this *baraisa* neither supports nor contradicts Rav Chisda, since Rav Chisda's principle specifically concerns the case *with* independent assessment — a case the *baraisa* is not addressing.

---

## Owner's Final Option

### Last Chance Reading

The *mishnah* presents a final case: someone bid twenty-six, while the owner bid twenty. The owner's twenty plus the *chomesh* of five yields only twenty-five, which does not match the outsider's twenty-six — so the outsider wins. But the *mishnah* adds: *im ratzu haba'alim b'shloshim v'echad v'dinar*, if the owners wish, they may bid thirty-one and a *dinar*. How is thirty-one and a *dinar* derived? A fifth of twenty-six is five and a *dinar* (since there are four *dinars* in a *shekel*), and twenty-six plus five and a *dinar* is thirty-one and a *dinar*. Exactly what the *mishnah* says.

The plain reading of the *mishnah*, then, is that even after the outsider has won the bidding, the owner is given one last chance. We turn to him and say: if you wish, you may now bid twenty-one — which, with your *chomesh*, will exceed the outsider's twenty-six and yield a total of thirty-one and a *dinar*, in which case you would win. This seems to reflect the principle of *mitzva d'ba'alim*, the preferential standing of the owner, extended all the way to a final option after the auction has nominally concluded.

### Rav Sheshet Reinterprets

The Gemara, however, does not read the *mishnah* this way. Rav Sheshet introduces the word *me'ikara* — from the outset. The Gemara reads the *mishnah* as saying: if the owners had *originally* made a higher bid — specifically, a bid of twenty-one — then the resulting calculation of thirty-one and a *dinar* follows automatically from the rules already established. The case of twenty-one as the owner's initial bid plus the outsider's twenty-six yields the owner's victory, with the base set at twenty-six, yielding thirty-one and a *dinar*.

The Gemara also raises the question of the *dinar* directly: *v'dinar mai avidtei* — why the extra *dinar*? If the owner's bid stays at twenty and he is simply given a last option to match the outsider's twenty-six, then the total should be thirty-one even — not thirty-one and a *dinar*. The *dinar* only appears because the *chomesh* is calculated on twenty-one (the owner's original bid), and a fifth of twenty-one is five and a *dinar*. This arithmetic works only if the owner's original bid was twenty-one, not twenty.

### Bid Timing Dispute

The straightforward reading of the *mishnah* is that the owner is given a post-hoc opportunity: you didn't bid high enough, but we are now giving you one last chance to say twenty-one, and if you do, the math will yield thirty-one and a *dinar* and you will win. The Gemara's introduction of *me'ikara* takes that away: no such last-chance option exists. You must have made that higher bid initially. If you bid twenty, and the outsider bid twenty-six, the twenty-six wins and you have no recourse.

As the *Shita Mekubetzet* notes, quoting Tosafot at 126, 16, what is the *chiddush* of this last rule if all it does is reiterate the earlier principle? The entire force of the *mishnah*'s conclusion seems to be the grant of a final option to the owner. But the Gemara, with the insertion of *me'ikara*, reads that away entirely. The *chiddush* evaporates, and we are left with a mere restatement. This is indeed a striking observation, and the tension between the plain sense of the *mishnah* and the Gemara's reading remains.

---

## Cherem Intro

### Cherem vs. Hekdesh

We turn now to the top of 28a, and to the next *mishnah*. As we move through the final section of *Parshat Bechukotai*, we progress from *erchin* to *sdei achuzah* to *sdei mikneh* and now arrive at *cherem*. The term *cherem* differs meaningfully from *hekdesh*. *Hekdesh* is a positive act: one is granting property to a recipient — the *hekdesh* institution. *Cherem*, by contrast, is focused on removal from oneself: one is declaring something off-limits, banned. This difference in emphasis is not merely semantic; it will shape the legal analysis that follows.

### Kisedei Hacherem

The textual basis for *cherem* in this context comes from two places in the Torah. First, from the verse near the end of *Bechukotai* describing a field that was consecrated but not redeemed: *vehaysa hasadeh betzeiso bayovel kodesh l'Hashem kisedei hacherem lakohein tihyeh achuzaso* — the field, upon the *yovel*, shall be holy to God, like a field of *cherem*, and shall become the possession of the *kohen*. Within this context, the Torah introduces the phrase *kisedei hacherem*, "like a field of *cherem*." Second, in the portion of Korach, where the gifts of the *kohanim* are enumerated, it says: *kol cherem b'Yisrael lecha yihiyeh* — all *cherem* in Israel shall be yours. So *cherem* goes to the *kohanim*, and we are now going to analyze what that entails.

One should note that the term *cherem* appears in multiple contexts with somewhat different resonances. In the narratives of Yehoshua and the city of Ai, *cherem* meant a total ban — nothing could benefit from it, everything was forbidden. Elsewhere, the verse says *kol cherem kodesh kodashim hu l'Hashem*, it is holy of holies to God. Whether *cherem* goes to *bedek habayit* or to the *kohen* will itself be a matter of discussion in the Gemara, though several *pesukim* clearly indicate *kol cherem lecha yihiyeh* — it goes to the *kohen*.

### Cherem Categories

The *mishnah* introduces the laws of *cherem*: a person may declare *cherem* over some of his flock, some of his cattle, some of his servants, some of his female servants — all Canaanite slaves — and some of his inherited fields. The prefix *mem* in each case — *mitzono*, *umibakaro*, *umiavadav* — is critically important, as the Gemara will emphasize. If, however, he attempts to make all of an entire category *cherem*, the *mishnah* records the ruling of Rabbi Eliezer that it does not take effect.

---

## Cherem Limitations

### Rabbi Eliezer Partial

Rabbi Eliezer's position is that *cherem* can only operate on a portion of one's property within a given category. If one attempts to declare all of his fields, or all of his slaves, or any complete category *cherem*, it simply does not take effect. At first glance, this is surprising. We might have expected that since the declaration of *cherem* operates through formal speech to transfer a metaphysical status, it should make no difference whether the quantity is partial or complete. Yet Rabbi Eliezer says otherwise.

There is an analogy to *terumah*, where one may give as little as one kernel or as much as everything minus one kernel — but it must be separated from something, meaning there must be *shirayim*, a remainder. However, *terumah* is conceptually different: the Torah frames it as taking an offering from one's produce, presupposing a larger whole from which a portion is set aside. *Cherem*, by contrast, is more akin to writing a check directly to the *beit hamikdash* — not a taking-from but a direct designation. Despite this conceptual difference, Rabbi Eliezer applies the same limitation.

### Moral Argument

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah draws out the broader moral and *derech eretz* lesson: if even toward the Most High (*gavoha*) a person is not permitted to declare all of his property *cherem*, how much more so should a person be protective of his own property in general — *al achas kamah v'chamah she'adam chas al nechasav*. The lesson is not merely about *cherem* as a formal institution but about proper comportment with one's resources. Do not give away everything even to a worthy cause; one has obligations to oneself.

This teaching is worth contextualizing. It is no coincidence that around the time of the *mishnah*, there were well-known examples of individuals donating all their property to institutions and becoming destitute. The Gemara is clear that this is not the desired model. One continues to maintain oneself, thereby remaining a productive member of society — and *only from that position* can one also help the *beit hamikdash* and the poor. Becoming one of the *aniyim* through excessive generosity defeats the purpose.

The question Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's formulation raises is one of hierarchy: is giving to the *beit hamikdash* of greater value than giving to *tzedakah* for the poor? The *kal v'chomer* — if you cannot give everything to the *beit hamikdash*, how much more so you cannot give everything to the poor — implies that the *beit hamikdash* stands higher in the hierarchy. Rashi indeed reads it this way, and that is also how the Gemara ultimately understands it, though one might have thought the reverse: the *beit hamikdash* has ample resources, whereas the poor urgently need support. Regardless, if that is the hierarchy, the *kal v'chomer* is meaningful.

One must be careful about the scope of Rabbi Eliezer's rule. It is not a general prohibition on giving away all of one's property. If a person declares all of his property *hekdesh* to *bedek habayit* — using the term *hekdesh* rather than *cherem* — that does take effect. The limitation on effectiveness applies specifically and technically when one employs the term *cherem*. As for whether the act was advisable — that is a separate question; the rabbis may counsel against it, but the act stands.

### Mikol Asher Lo

The Gemara asks: where is this derived from? The *baraisa* teaches: *mikol asher lo* — from all that is his — *velo kol asher lo* — not everything, but from all. The verse in *Bechukotai* reads: *ach kol cherem asher yacharim ish l'Hashem mikol asher lo, me'adam u-vehema u-misdei achuzato* — every *cherem* that a man dedicates to God from anything of his, whether person, animal, or his inherited field, is not sold or redeemed; it is holy of holies to God. The *baraisa* reads *mikol asher lo* as "from all" — implying some but not all — *me'adam* as "from [some of] his people [i.e., slaves]" but not all of them, *mibehema* as "from [some of] his animals" but not all, and *misdei achuzato* as "from [some of] his inherited field" but not all.

One might object: perhaps this is merely a behavioral instruction — do not declare all *cherem* — but if you did so, it would nonetheless take effect. The answer is the word *ach*, which the *baraisa* reads as a limiting particle: it does not always take effect, and if one declares an entire category *cherem*, it does not take effect. This is the ruling of Rabbi Eliezer.

The Gemara then adds that all three formulations — the limitation on chattel, on slaves, and on fields — are necessary: *tzrichi*. The reason is that each category might have yielded a different inference without the others. One might have thought that the prohibition is on giving away all one's property across categories, but giving away all of one single category would be acceptable. The verse therefore specifies each category separately to make clear that even all within a single category is impermissible. Conversely, one might have thought that since slaves (*adam*) and fields (*sdei achuzah*) are each essential for livelihood in an agricultural society, the Torah naturally limits *cherem* on them — you simply cannot manage without field labor and without land — but chattel (*metaltelin*), the loss of which does not threaten basic survival, could be given away entirely. Therefore the verse must also address chattel explicitly.

---

## Analysis of Limitation

### Necessity Analysis

The Gemara now probes why it is that one cannot make *cherem* of an entire category. It begins by examining the distinction between types of property. Regarding slaves (*adam*) and fields (*sdei achuzah*), the argument is relatively intuitive: in a pre-industrial agricultural society, both are absolutely essential for livelihood. One cannot manage without labor, and one cannot manage without land. But these two grounds are distinct — you cannot work someone else's land if you have no slaves of your own, and you cannot deploy slaves productively if you have no land. Hence, *ha chayuso v'ha chayuso* — both are essential for survival, each in its own right.

Regarding chattel (*metaltelin*), the Gemara acknowledges that chattel does not carry the same necessity — if one retains slaves and land, one could theoretically survive without one's movable property. Nevertheless, the verse limits even that. All three must be stated.

### Ownership Principle

The deeper structural principle underlying much of this discussion is that *cherem* operates only on things one fully owns. *She'ein adam machrim davar she'eino shelo* — a person cannot declare *cherem* on something that is not truly his. This principle does not come from a specific *derasha* alone but reflects the foundational logic of *cherem* as a complete transfer. If one does not have full and unconditional title, the act of *cherem* has nothing to fully operate on.

### Exclusions Listed

The *mishnah* — which effectively parallels the *baraisa* cited earlier — enumerates explicitly what cannot be made *cherem*: one's children, one's Hebrew slaves (*avdo veshifchato haivriyim*), and a purchased field (*sedei miknato*). Hebrew slaves, whether male or female, are not fully owned — they function more as indentured servants, with a legally bounded term and personal status that precludes complete ownership. Similarly, a *sedei miknah* during the period of *yovel* is in effect a lease, not an outright purchase. The remaining years of use can be transferred, but true title to the land reverts at *yovel*, meaning the "owner" does not hold it unconditionally. Therefore *cherem* cannot apply.

It is worth contrasting this with *hekdesh*: one *can* declare a *sedei miknah* as *hekdesh*, because in doing so one is simply consecrating the years of use until *yovel*, and that functional right is genuinely one's own. *Cherem*, however, demands the kind of full, absolute ownership — like one has over a *Canaanite* slave — that a *sedei miknah* does not represent.

The Gemara also raises the case of a minor daughter (*bito ketana*): can one declare her *cherem*? After all, a father can sell his daughter. The answer is no, for the same reason that applies to Hebrew slaves. When a father sells his daughter, she becomes an *amah ivriyah* — a Hebrew bondswoman — which is a form of indentured servitude, not outright ownership as property. The underlying reason is not merely the duration but the nature of the transaction itself: selling one's daughter into *amah ivriyah* status is not a transfer of property in the full sense; it is not real ownership.

### Permanent Sale Test

The Gemara derives the *mechkar* principle — the test of permanent salability — from the word *behemah* in the verse. Just as an animal can be sold outright and permanently, so too, only things that can be permanently sold can be made *cherem*: *mah behemah yesh lo reshut limkor leolam, af kol sheyesh lo reshut limkor leolam*. What is the quality of "permanent"? It must be something over which one has complete and irrevocable title to sell. This excludes Hebrew slaves, children, and purchased fields — none of which can be sold with permanent, unconditional effect.

The Gemara notes that this framing through *leolam* — permanence — is a natural way of articulating the rule, though arguably the more fundamental point is that Hebrew servitude is not ownership as property at all, not merely a question of duration.

---

## Kohen/Levi Cherem

### Kohanim Cannot

The *mishnah* continues: *hakohanim vehaLeviyim ein machrimim* — *kohanim* and *Levi'im* cannot make *cherem* — according to Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara begins its analysis: the case of *kohanim* is understandable — *shecharmeihem shelahem*, the *cherem* goes to the *kohanim* anyway. Since a *kohen* is entitled to receive *cherem* property, his own act of declaring something *cherem* is meaningless from a practical standpoint: he is effectively giving to himself. One could argue that he might wish to designate the property to a different *kohen*, or that a *kohen* recipient who is reluctant to accept direct charity might accept *cherem* more readily, but the operative logic is that since *cherem* reverts to him anyway, the act lacks the defining character of a genuine transfer.

### Shimon's Logic

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *kohanim hein machrimim* — *kohanim* can in fact declare *cherem*. His reasoning is that since the *cherem* goes to the *kohanim* in any event, the act is still meaningful — the *kohen* can designate which *kohen* receives it, and the sanctity of the *cherem* designation itself has independent significance. However, Rabbi Shimon concedes that *Levi'im* cannot make *cherem* of land — as we will see below — and can only make *cherem* of chattel.

### Leviyim Inheritance

The reason *Levi'im* cannot make *cherem* of their inherited land is derived from the verse: *ki achuzat olam hi lahem* — it is an eternal inheritance to them. When the Torah establishes the cities of the *Levi'im*, it characterizes their holdings as an *achuzat olam*, a permanent inheritance that cannot be divested. If the *Levi'im* attempt to declare their *sdei achuzah* as *cherem*, this permanent designation by the Torah overrides and nullifies the act.

### Rabbi's Compromise

Rabbi (Rebbi) offers what appears to be a compromise: *nir'in divrei Rabbi Yehuda bekarka'ot* — it seems to me that Rabbi Yehuda is right regarding land, and *divrei Rabbi Shimon bemataltelin* — Rabbi Shimon is right regarding chattel. At first reading, Rebbi appears to be splitting the difference between two positions. By land, Rabbi Yehuda prevails — *Levi'im* cannot make *cherem* of their inherited land due to *achuzat olam*. By chattel, Rabbi Shimon prevails — *Levi'im* can make *cherem* of movable property since they do not retain it.

### Gemara Reinterprets

The Gemara, however, will not allow this reading to stand. From the fact that the *mishnah* records Rebbi saying that Rabbi Yehuda seems right by land and Rabbi Shimon seems right by chattel, the Gemara infers: *michlal*, the implication is that Rabbi Shimon himself maintained that *Levi'im* can declare *cherem* even on *karka* — land. Otherwise, Rebbi's statement would not constitute a compromise but merely a redundant agreement.

But how can that be, given the verse *ki achuzat olam hi lahem*? The Gemara therefore reinterprets Rebbi's statement: *hachi ka'amar* — this is what Rebbi is actually saying. He is not offering a compromise; he is offering an *interpretation* of Rabbi Shimon. When Rabbi Shimon said *Levi'im* can make *cherem*, he surely meant only chattel — he could not have meant land, given the clear force of *achuzat olam*. Therefore Rebbi is saying: it seems to me that even Rabbi Shimon himself would agree with Rabbi Yehuda regarding land; his position that they can make *cherem* was never meant to extend there. The apparent dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on land was never a real one — *af Rabbi Shimon lo nechelak ela bemataltelin*, even Rabbi Shimon disputed only regarding chattel.

This is a striking reinterpretation. Rather than a compromise between two tannaitic authorities, Rebbi is read as collapsing a dispute entirely — arguing that once one examines the underlying sources, Rabbi Shimon's position was never as broad as it appeared, and *bishlama karka* they would agree, *aval bemataltelin modeh lo*. The question left open is what the *halacha* would be for a *Levi* seeking to make *hekdesh* rather than *cherem* of his *achuzah*, or seeking to make *cherem* of fields other than his ancestral *arei haLevi'im* — fields that are not subject to the *achuzat olam* designation. The analysis here addresses primarily the *sdei achuzah* of the *Levi'im*, and generalizing beyond that may require additional reasoning.

---

## Cherem Distribution

### Designating Kohen

Rabbi Chiya bar Abin establishes the rule for chattel *cherem*: *hachrim metaltelin, nosen le-chol kohen she-yirtzeh* — one who makes chattel *cherem* may give it to any *kohen* he wishes. This was already implicit in the earlier discussion, where the argument against *kohanim* making *cherem* rested precisely on the fact that they are entitled to receive it — which presupposes that the dedicator gets to choose the recipient. The textual basis is the verse in the portion of Korach: *kol cherem b'Yisrael lecha yihiyeh* — all *cherem* in Israel shall be *to you*, with *lecha* in the singular suggesting that an individual *kohen* can be designated. This parallels *terumah* and *maaser*, where the owner may choose which *kohen* or *Levi* to give to.

### Land Goes to Mishmar

However, a different rule governs *cherem* of fields: *sadosav nosen le-kohen sheba-oso mishmar* — his fields go to the *kohen* who belongs to that *mishmar*, the priestly rotation serving that week. He does not get to designate a specific *kohen* of his choosing. The textual basis is the phrase *kisedei hacherem* in *Bechukotai*: when describing how a field that was consecrated and not redeemed passes to the *kohanim* at *yovel*, the Torah says it goes like a *sdei hacherem* — like a field of *cherem*. This comparison suggests that *sdei hacherem* and the fields returning at *yovel* share the same distribution rule.

### Yovel Analogy

That rule is: the fields that go to the *kohanim* at *yovel* are distributed to the *mishmar* serving during the *yovel* — assumed to mean the *mishmar* working on *Yom Kippur* of the *yovel* year, since *yovel* is proclaimed with the *shofar* on *Yom Kippur*. By the *gezerah shavah* of *la-kohen / la-kohen*, derived from the law of *gezel ha-ger* — theft from a convert who dies without heirs — the Gemara establishes that *cherem* property likewise goes to the *mishmar* of the *kohen* on duty at the relevant time. In *gezel ha-ger*, the money and the atoning sacrifice (*asham gezeilos*) are brought together, and the *kohen* officiating that week receives both — establishing the principle that it is the *mishmar* on duty at the time that receives the designated property.

### Yovel on Shabbat

A question is then posed: what if *Yom Kippur* of the *yovel* year falls on *Shabbat*? Since *Shabbat* is the changeover day for the priestly *mishmarot*, two *mishmarot* are both in a sense "on duty" — one completing its week and one beginning. Which one receives the fields? Rabbi Chiya bar Ami in the name of Chofna rules: *nitnat lamishmar hayotzei* — it goes to the outgoing *mishmar*, the one that had been serving that week. The logic, as the Gemara will develop, is that the outgoing *mishmar* was already present and serving at the onset of the *yovel* year, giving it greater claim.

### Yovel Timing Dispute

The Gemara supports this ruling by connecting it to a broader *tanna'itic* debate about when *yovel* takes effect. The *baraisa* states: *echad Yovel ve-echad Shevi'is*, both *yovel* and *shemitah* annul simultaneously. This requires explanation: *shemitah* annuls debts at the *end* of the seventh year — *miketz sheva shanim ta'aseh shemitah* — while *yovel* might seem to begin at *Yom Kippur*. Yet the *baraisa* says they happen together. The Gemara is struck: the verse explicitly says *beyom haKippurim ta'aviru shofar bechol artzechem* — the *shofar* of *yovel* is sounded on *Yom Kippur*. How then can *yovel* and *shemitah* annul at the same moment if *yovel* begins on *Yom Kippur* and *shemitah* ends at the close of the forty-ninth year?

The answer is: *ha meni Rabbi Yishmael beno shel Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka hi* — this *baraisa* follows the view of Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that *yovel* takes effect from *Rosh Hashanah*, not *Yom Kippur*. The Gemara in *Masechet Rosh Hashanah* discusses this at length. According to this view, beginning on *Rosh Hashanah* of the fiftieth year, one may no longer enslave servants — their personal freedom is initiated — but they do not physically depart until *Yom Kippur*, when the *shofar* is sounded. Since the effective beginning of *yovel* is *Rosh Hashanah*, it coincides with the very moment that *shemitah* ends. Both take effect in the transition from the forty-ninth year to the fiftieth.

The relevance to our question about the *mishmar*: because *yovel* already begins in earnest on *Rosh Hashanah* — ten days before *Yom Kippur* — the *mishmar* that was serving on and around *Rosh Hashanah* has a temporal claim to the *yovel* period that predates the *Yom Kippur* changeover. It was already present at the onset of the *yovel* year. This lends weight to awarding the fields to the outgoing *mishmar* when *Yom Kippur* happens to fall on *Shabbat*.

### Abbahu's Question

The sugya closes with a challenge raised by Rabbi Abbahu, as reported by Chizkiyah bar Biloti. If chattel *cherem* goes to a *kohen* of the dedicator's choosing, while *cherem* of fields goes to the *mishmar*, how can one maintain this distinction when the verse explicitly links them together — mentioning land and chattel in the same passage? The same *pasuk* encompasses *adam, behemah*, and *sdei achuzah* together. How can we treat chattel differently from land?

Rabbi Abbahu's answer is: *la tannai de-makkish u-de-la makkish* — it depends on which *tanna* one follows: whether the *tanna* who links (*makkish*) chattel to land, or the one who does not. We have already encountered this dispute in the context of the *Levi'im* — whether the verse's mention of *metaltelin* and *karka* together creates a genuine halakhic equation between them. The *tanna* who does not create the *hekkesh* is free to distinguish: chattel *cherem* goes to a designated *kohen*, while *cherem* of fields follows the *mishmar*. This is a satisfying resolution that ties together the earlier dispute about *Levi'im* with the present question about *cherem* distribution.

What has also been made explicit in this closing passage is something that was implicit throughout: the *kohanim* of the *mishmar* serving at *yovel* are the ones who receive the fields that return at *yovel*. This point, which has been in the background of several discussions, is now formally articulated — and with it, the Gemara's treatment of *cherem* and its connections to *yovel*, the priestly rotation, and the laws of sanctified property is substantially advanced.

---

---

# Arakhin 30

## Yovel Sale Debate

### Mishnah Context

The *mishnah* on this *daf* deals with the *halachot* of redeeming one's field — the *sadeh achuza* — during the period of *yovel*. The Torah in *Parashat Behar* establishes that a seller possesses both the right and ultimately the obligation to repurchase his ancestral field, but only after the buyer has had a minimum of two years of unimpeded use. That two-year period is not merely a practical threshold — the seller is actually prohibited from exercising his right of redemption during those first two years. With that framework in place, the *gemara* introduces an *itmar*, a dispute between the *Amoraim*, concerning a more specific and provocative question.

### Rav's View

*Itmar hamokher sadehu bishnat hayovel atzmah* — what is the *halacha* if someone attempted to sell his field during the *yovel* year itself, the very year in which all ancestral fields revert automatically to their original owners? *Rav amar mechura ve-yotza*: Rav holds that the sale does go through, but that *yovel* then immediately kicks in, causing the field to revert to the seller. The practical consequence is striking: the buyer has paid money, the sale was binding, and a moment later the field returns to the seller. The seller keeps the money. It is, in effect, a case of buyer beware — a valid transaction that is instantly undone by the operation of *yovel*.

### Shmuel's View

Shmuel disagrees sharply. *Einah mechura kol ikar* — the sale never took effect at all. In Shmuel's view, a *sadeh achuza* simply cannot be sold during a year whose entire legal purpose is to return ancestral fields to their owners. The very concept of *yovel* is incompatible with a sale taking effect.

### Kal Vachomer

Shmuel's reasoning is articulated as a *kal vachomer*: if a field that has already been sold goes back to its owner at *yovel*, then how much more so should a field that is being sold at that very moment simply not be sold at all? The *gemara* acknowledges that this is not a technically precise *kal vachomer* in the classical sense — a proper *kal vachomer* applies the identical law in both cases — but the intuitive force of the argument is clear. The entire logic of *yovel* is to restore fields to their owners; it would be internally contradictory for a sale to succeed during the very year that embodies that principle.

### Challenge to Rav

The *gemara* asks: would Rav simply reject this type of *kal vachomer* reasoning? *U-le-Rav lo amrinan kal vachomer ki hai gavna?* To test the point, the *gemara* adduces a parallel case where everyone agrees such logic applies.

### Daughter Example

*Yachol yimkor adam et bito keshe-hi na'arah?* — Could a father sell his daughter as a Hebrew slave once she has already reached the status of *na'arah*, twelve years and a day with signs of maturity? She goes free automatically upon reaching that status if she was already sold. The *gemara* presents a *kal vachomer*: if the fact that she was already sold is sufficient to trigger her freedom — since one cannot retain ownership over a *na'arah* — then certainly a father cannot initiate a new sale of her once she has reached that age. This *kal vachomer* has the same structure as Shmuel's argument: if the condition causes release when already in force, it should certainly prevent a new transaction from taking effect. Since everyone accepts this *kal vachomer* in the daughter case, one might think Rav should accept the same reasoning for *yovel*.

### Field vs. Daughter

The *gemara* rejects the analogy. *Hatam lo hadra mi-zavna, hacha hadra mi-zavna.* In the case of the daughter, once she reaches the age of *na'arah*, she exits her father's control permanently and becomes a person in her own right — there is no future window in which he can sell her again. The logic of preventing the sale is therefore compelling. The field, by contrast, is always within the seller's sphere; even if he cannot sell it during *yovel*, he will be able to sell it again after *yovel* is over. The seller never loses fundamental control over the field, and therefore the argument that *yovel* should categorically prevent the sale from taking effect is not as forceful. This distinction allows Rav to accept the *kal vachomer* regarding the daughter while rejecting an analogous inference regarding the field.

---

## Biblical Sources

### Baraita Proof

With the theoretical debate in place, the *gemara* attempts to adduce proof. It cites the relevant *pesukim* from *Behar*, beginning with *bemispar shanim achar hayovel tikneh me'et amitecha* — according to the number of years after the *yovel* you shall purchase from your fellow. The *gemara* then turns to a *braita* that derives from these verses several rules: *achar hayovel shanim tikneh* teaches that one may sell immediately after *yovel* for the full fifty years; *muflag min hayovel minayin* — how do we know one may also sell in the middle of the cycle? From the phrase *l'fi rov hashanim u-l'fi me'at hashanim*, whether there are many years or few, a sale may occur at any point in the cycle. The *braita* then states explicitly: *u-vishnat hayovel atzmah lo yimkor* — do not sell during *yovel* itself. *Ve-im machar einah mechura* — and if one did sell during *yovel*, it is not a valid sale.

### Rav's Reinterpretation

This *braita* appears to prove Shmuel's position. However, the *gemara* reports Rav's response: *einah mechura l'mispar shnei tvuot aval mechura hi ve-yotza*. Rav reinterprets the *braita* as teaching not that the sale was void entirely, but that it was not valid with respect to the two-year entitlement. Under normal circumstances, a buyer is guaranteed a minimum of two years of unimpeded use before the seller can force redemption. Rav's reading of the *braita* is that selling during *yovel* does not grant the buyer those two years — the sale takes effect and *yovel* immediately causes the field to revert, but the buyer cannot claim the two-year use period.

### Two-Year Rule

This interpretation forces a conceptual reexamination of the two-year rule. Until now, one would naturally understand it as a *limit* on the seller's right to redeem — he may not exercise his right of *geulah* for the first two years. But Rav's reading suggests an alternative understanding: the two-year period is itself an *entitlement* that attaches to any valid purchase. Any buyer is owed a minimum of two years. This is a genuinely surprising idea, one that would not have been expected from the plain reading of the *halacha*.

### Pre-Yovel Purchase

To probe this further, the *gemara* raises the following challenge against Rav: if the sale during *yovel* was truly valid, why shouldn't the buyer be entitled to hold the field for two full years after *yovel* concludes? The *gemara* then invokes a *braita*: *achal shana achat lifnei hayovel* — if a buyer had one year of produce before *yovel*, *mashlimin lo shana acheret achar yovel* — he is entitled to one additional year after *yovel* to complete his two years. Why, then, if the sale on *yovel* itself was valid, would we not give him two full years after *yovel*?

### Use vs. Opportunity

The *gemara* resolves this by drawing a distinction. *Hatam nachit l'achila* — in the case of the pre-*yovel* purchase, the buyer actually began using the field; he had at least one year of produce. *Hacha lo nachit l'achila* — in the case of a sale on *yovel* itself, he never began using it at all. The instant the sale took effect, *yovel* caused it to revert. Since he never entered into actual use of the field, he does not acquire the entitlement to complete two years. The entitlement is triggered not by the mere fact of purchase but by having actually begun to use the property.

This distinction is significant beyond the narrow question of Rav versus Shmuel. It reveals an unexpected dimension of the two-year rule: it is neither a pure procedural limit nor a simple purchase entitlement, but something that crystallizes through the act of actual use.

---

## Slave Comparison

### Two Teachings

The *gemara* now reports that Rav Anan identified two parallel teachings of Shmuel on related topics. *Tartei* — two teachings. The first is the one already discussed: that a sale of a *sadeh achuza* during *yovel* does not take effect.
