### Legal Duty vs. Gift

The fundamental distinction, then, is between a pure gift — where the recipient must want what is offered — and the execution of a legal duty, right, or conditional obligation, where the physical act of transfer may be sufficient regardless of the other party's subjective willingness. In the latter category, the definition of "giving" may not require the other person to actively accept; it may require only that the money come into their physical domain. That is the conceptual foundation of the entire debate, and the Gemara leaves it without a definitive resolution.

---

## House Definition

### Basic Definition

The Mishnah now turns to the question of what properties qualify for the laws of *batei arei chomah*. The principle is: *kol shehu lifnim min hachoma harei hu k'batei arei choma* — anything located within the walls of a walled city has the same status as a house in a walled city. The category is not limited to residential dwellings; a store, a storage facility, or any other structure located within the walls is included. The sole explicit exclusion is *chutz min hasados* — fields are excluded. A field, as a piece of land used primarily for agricultural cultivation, does not fall within the category of *bayis*.

### Baraita Examples

A *baraita* elaborates on the inclusive scope of *bayis*. The verse says *asher ba'ir* — "that is in the city" — which expands the category beyond literal houses. Accordingly, *batei badim* (leather-processing houses), *batei merchatzos* (bathhouses), *migdalos* (towers, apparently used for housing birds), *shovachim* (dovecotes), *boros*, *shichin*, and *me'aros* (various types of wells, cisterns, and caves) are all included. These are all either man-made structures or man-modified spaces with some kind of defined, non-agricultural function.

### Fields Debate

The Mishnah records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah. Rabbi Meir reads *asher ba'ir* expansively to include even fields, reasoning that anything within the city walls falls under the category. Rabbi Yehudah reads the word *bayis* as a limiting qualifier: only things that are *dumya de'bayis* — similar in character to a house — are included, and a field is fundamentally different in character from a house and is therefore excluded.

### Swamps & Rocky Ground

The Gemara (in the name of Rav Chisda citing Rav Katina) sharpens the dispute: the real point of contention between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah concerns *chulasit umetzulah* — hard, rocky terrain that cannot be planted, and swampy ground. A *baraita* records that Rabbi Meir considers these to have the status of *batim* (like houses), while Rabbi Yehudah considers them to have the status of *sados* (like fields). The reframing implies that even Rabbi Meir would agree that genuinely plantable agricultural land is excluded; his expansive ruling applies only to land that, while not structurally built upon, is also not suitable for cultivation. Conversely, even Rabbi Yehudah might agree that fully constructed non-residential structures are included. The debate turns on this middle category of land that is neither cultivated nor built upon. Rashi suggests that according to Rabbi Meir, such terrain is classified as *bayis* because materials from it can be harvested for building construction — drawing it closer to the *bayis* category. The simpler reading, however, may be that *sadeh* (field) and *bayis* (house) represent conceptual opposites, and this intermediate category simply does not fit the definition of *sadeh*.

---

## House in Wall

### Mishnah Position

A further definitional question arises regarding a house physically built into the city wall itself. The Mishnah records a dispute about whether such a house qualifies as a house in a walled city.

### Views Compared

Rabbi Yehudah holds that a house built into the wall is not considered a *bayis be'arei chomah*. Rabbi Shimon holds that the outer wall of such a house serves a dual function — it is simultaneously the outer wall of the dwelling and the city wall — and this dual service does not disqualify the house. The house is still considered part of the walled city.

### Rachav's Story

The Gemara notes that both opinions derive from the same verse — the episode of Rachav, who sheltered the Israelite spies and lowered them through a window: *vatoredem bachevel bead hachalon ki veitah bechir hachoma uvachoma hi yoshavet* — her house was in the wall of the city, and she dwelt in the wall. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: u'sheneihem mikra echad darshu* — both Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon derive their positions from this single verse.

Rabbi Shimon reads the verse in its plain sense: Rachav's house was in the wall, and she is described as a resident of the city — therefore such a house is included. Rabbi Yehudah, by contrast, reads the verse as evidence to the contrary: *bechoma hi yoshavet velo be'ir choma* — she was dwelling *in the wall*, not *within the walled city*. To dwell within the walled city, one's entire house must be contained inside the wall; a house that is itself part of the wall is not the same as a house situated inside. Rachav's case thus illustrates the excluded category.

---

## City Criteria

### Wall Independence

The Gemara establishes that for a city to qualify as a *ir chomah*, its wall must be an independent structure. The Mishnah formulation *ir shegagoteha chomatah* — a city whose rooftops (or more precisely, whose house walls) constitute its surrounding wall — does not qualify. The wall must exist as a freestanding entity, not merely as an aggregate of the exterior sides of the buildings within.

### Joshua Timeline

A second requirement: the wall must date from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun*. This temporal criterion will be examined more closely in the Gemara. The simple sense is that the *kedushah* of *Eretz Yisrael* begins from the time of *Yehoshua*'s conquest, and it is that original sanctification which determines a city's status. Later walls do not confer the status; and conversely, as we will see, a city that *had* a wall from the time of *Yehoshua* but no longer has one today retains its status.

### Population Minimum

There is also a minimum population structure required: *shalosh chatzerot shel shenei batim mukafet choma miyemos Yehoshua bin Nun* — three courtyards, each containing at least two houses, all surrounded by a wall from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun*. What we call streets, they called courtyards — enclosures around which houses were built. Fewer than three such units of settlement may constitute a hamlet or a handful of dwellings but does not rise to the level of a *ir*, a city.

### City Examples

The Mishnah provides examples: *Katzra Hayeshana shel Tzipori*, *Chakra shel Gush Chalav*, *Yodfat Hayeshana*, *Gamla*, *Gedud*, *Chadid*, *Ono*, and *Yerushalayim* — and anything similar. Many of these cities are also mentioned in *Ezra-Nechemya* among the communities resettled upon the return from exile. The Mishnah uses the word *kegon* — "such as" — implying that the list is not exhaustive. The examples may be intended to show that even quite small localities can carry the status of a walled city, provided the structural criteria are met.

---

## Wall Requirements

### Wall vs. Roof

The *Tanna* in a *baraita* states: *choma* — a wall — *velo shur igar*, not a *shur igar*, which is Aramaic for "wall of a roof." This echoes the Mishnah's exclusion of a city whose house walls form its perimeter. The Gemara adds: *saviv* — the wall must surround the city — *perat leTverya sheyama chomatah*, which excludes Tiberias, where the *Kinneret* serves as one of its boundaries. Since Tiberias is not completely surrounded by a constructed wall — one side is defined by the sea — it does not meet this criterion. The Gemara in *Masechet Megilla* separately discusses Tiberias's status and concludes it may be treated differently from other cases of *mukafet choma miyemos Yehoshua bin Nun*.

### Historical Status

*Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Yosi* derives from the verse *asher lo choma* — "that has a wall" — an additional principle: *af al pi she'ein lo achshav vehaya lo kodem lachen* — even if the city does not have a wall now, if it had one previously, its status is preserved. The present absence of a wall is irrelevant; what matters is whether it originally possessed a wall. Conversely, a wall constructed after the time of *Yehoshua* does not confer the status. The same rule applies in the laws of *Megilla*.

### Torah Text Variants

The textual basis of this *drasha* is a *ketiv/kri* phenomenon in the Torah. The word *lo* in the phrase *asher lo choma* is written with an *alef* — which ordinarily means "no" or "not" — but is read as if written with a *vav*, meaning "that has." This dual reading supports the *drasha*: a city that *has* a wall (*lo* with *vav*) and a city that does *not* have one now (*lo* with *alef*) but once did — both are treated as walled cities.

Rashi understood the word to be written as *lo'a* — with both a *vav* and an *alef* — making the double meaning graphic. *Tosafot* disputes this, citing *chumashim meduyakim* (precisely corrected Torah scrolls): *ksiv lo be'alef u'krei bevav* — it is written with an *alef* but read with a *vav*. The pronunciation is identical in either case. According to *Tosafot*, the *drasha* is not based on an unusual spelling but on a *masorah* — a transmitted interpretive tradition — that the word carries both implications simultaneously. This is not the only place where Rashi and *Tosafot* appear to have worked from texts that differ in small orthographic details.

### Geographic Specificity

The *baraita* specifies the geographic locations of the listed cities: *Gamla baGalil*, *Gidud be'Ever Yarden*, *Chadid*, *Ono*, and *Yerushalayim biYehudah*. Abaye reads this as indicating geographic extent — up to *Gamla* in the *Galil*, up to *Gidud* in *Ever Yarden*, implying that no further walled cities are recognized beyond those points. Rava offers a more economical explanation: the geographic specifications exist to distinguish these cities from other towns of the same name. *Gamla baGalil* — only the *Gamla* of *Galil*, not the various other places called *Gamla* that may have existed. Similarly *Gidud be'Ever Yarden* — only that particular *Gidud*. Cities without problematic name-twins needed no such qualification.

---

## Jerusalem Exception

### Jerusalem Question

Having listed *Yerushalayim* among the examples of walled cities, the Gemara asks: *BiYerushalayim mi machlita?* Since when do the laws of *batei arei chomah* apply to *Yerushalayim*? A *baraita* records that among the ten special enactments (*asara devarim ne'emru biYerushalayim*) pertaining to *Yerushalayim*, one is *ein bayis chalat bah* — a house in *Yerushalayim* does not become permanently transferred (*chalut*) under these laws.

### Ten Things

The list of ten things said about *Yerushalayim* thus explicitly negates one of the core consequences of *batei arei chomah* law.

### National Property

The underlying rationale is that *Yerushalayim* is not the possession of any individual tribe. It is, in a meaningful sense, national property — owned collectively by *Klal Yisrael* as a whole, not assigned to any tribe as *nachalah*. The laws of *batei arei chomah* presuppose that the house sits within a *city of tribal inheritance* — a city firmly within a tribe's assigned territory. Rashi frames it similarly: the permanent transfer contemplated by these laws requires an initial ownership that is itself grounded in the concept of *achuza*, ancestral inheritance. Since *Yerushalayim* is not any tribe's *achuza*, the full framework does not apply. There are indeed traditions about precisely where the tribal boundary between *Yehudah* and *Binyamin* ran through the city — and even through the *Beis Hamikdash* itself — but the implication of this *baraita* is that even though *Yerushalayim* falls within the geographic region of those tribes, it is not *possessed* by them in the way that generates *achuza* obligations.

### Example vs. Application

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan: ki Yerushalayim demukafes choma miyemos Yehoshua bin Nun* — Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by saying that the Mishnah used *Yerushalayim* as an illustrative example of what a walled city looks like, not as an actual application of these laws. Any city *like Yerushalayim* — *ki Yerushalayim* — that is surrounded by a wall from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun* would have this status, but *Yerushalayim* itself does not: *d'ilu Yerushalayim ein bayis chalut bah, v'ilu hacha habayis chalut bahen*. This is an admittedly uncomfortable interpretive move — citing as a paradigm example a case to which the rule does not itself apply.

### Two Jerusalems

Rav Yosef proposes an alternative: just as there are, according to a tradition he cites elsewhere, two places called *Kadesh*, there might be two places called *Yerushalayim*. The *Yerushalayim biYehudah* mentioned in the Mishnah might be a different *Yerushalayim* — a smaller locality in *Yehudah* bearing the same name, to which the laws of *batei arei chomah* do apply normally.

---

## First vs. Second Kedusha

### Limited List Question

A *baraita* now raises a fundamental challenge to the Mishnah's short list. *Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi* opens by asking: *lama manu chachamim es elu?* — why did the Sages list these particular cities? The *baraita* then addresses the question of which historical moment determines a city's status as a *batei arei chomah*.

### Second Kedusha View

The first position in the *baraita*: when the returning exiles came up in the time of *Ezra*, *matzu elu v'kidshum* — they found these cities and sanctified them. The implication is that these are the *only* cities that carry the status of *batei arei chomah*, because the sanctification of the land by *Yehoshua* had lapsed and the relevant status had to be freshly granted in the time of the Second *Beis Hamikdash*.

### Kedusha Lost Theory

The theological underpinning of this position is stated explicitly: *kedushah rishonah kidshah l'sha'atah v'lo kidshah l'asid lavo* — the first *kedushah*, the sanctification of the land at the time of *Yehoshua*, was operative only for its own era. When the *Beis Hamikdash* was destroyed, the *kedushah* was lost. It needed to be actively reinstated in the time of the Second *Beis Hamikdash* — and only the cities resanctified during Ezra's return now carry the status. This means the Mishnah's short list is essentially complete: only these cities qualify.

### First Kedusha View

The second position in the *baraita* — also attributed to Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi — asks the same opening question but draws a diametrically opposite conclusion. *V'chi elu bilvad hayu?* — were these the only walled cities that existed? The verse in the Torah speaks of *shishim ir kol chevel Argov* — sixty cities, all *betzuros* (fortified), just in the region of *Argov* in *Ever HaYarden* alone! There were vastly more walled cities than this handful. So why list just these?

The answer: *shekeshe'alu bnei hagolah matzu elu v'kidshum*. When the *baraita* uses the word *kidshum* here, the Gemara interrupts: you already said there is no need to resanctify — they already have their status from *Yehoshua*! The answer is that *kidshum* here means not that they resanctified them but that they *listed* them — *m'na'um*. They catalogued these as examples of what a walled city looks like. *V'lo elu bilvad* — and not only these, but any city about which you have a transmitted tradition (*masores b'yadcha me'avosecha*) that it was surrounded by a wall from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun* — *kol mitzvos halalu nohagos bah* — all these laws apply to it, *mipnei shekedushah rishonah kidshah l'sha'atah v'kidshah l'asid lavo* — because the first sanctification was permanent and was never lost.

### Resolution Attempt

The Gemara notes the problem directly: we now have two statements attributed to Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi that flatly contradict each other on the central question of *kedushah rishonah*. The Gemara offers two resolutions. First, *trei tannai aliba d'Rabi Yishmael* — these represent two *tannaim* who disagreed about what Rabbi Yishmael actually held. Second, one of the attributions may be in error: *chad mineihu Rabi Elazar b'Rabi Yosi amrah* — one of the two *beraisos* was actually said by Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Yosi, not Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi.

---

## Limited List Analysis

### Rabbi Elazar Proof

The attribution to Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Yosi is especially apt because he is on record regarding precisely this issue. The *baraita* cited earlier — where Rabbi Elazar derives from *asher lo choma* that even a city that currently lacks a wall retains its status if it had one from the time of *Yehoshua* — makes clear that Rabbi Elazar holds by the *kedushah rishonah* view. For him, it is the original *Yehoshua*-era wall that establishes permanent status, with no need for resanctification at Ezra's return.

### View Attribution

With this identification, the Gemara assigns the two *beraisos* to their respective positions: the first *baraita* (which understands the Mishnah's limited list as complete, based on Ezra's resanctification) reflects the *kedushah shniyah* view; the second *baraita* (which treats the Mishnah's list as merely illustrative, with the true scope going back to all of *Yehoshua*'s walled cities) reflects the *kedushah rishonah* view, identified with Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Yosi.

---

## Kedusha Connection

### Conceptual Link

It is worth pausing to appreciate why the status of *batei arei chomah* should be connected to the concept of *kedushah* at all. One might have expected these laws to be purely dependent on whether *yovel* is operative — a calendrical and demographic question about whether the tribes are settled in the land. The connection to *kedushah* is not self-evident. Yet this Gemara makes clear that the status of walled cities is indeed tied to the question of *kedushah rishonah* versus *kedushah shniyah*, perhaps because the laws of *batei arei chomah* are intertwined with the *yovel*, and the practice of *yovel* is itself understood to be a function of the *kedushah* of the land.

### Keilim Parallel

There is another dimension to walled city status that is easily overlooked: the *mishnah* in *Masechet Keilim* that enumerates the graduated levels of holiness within *Eretz Yisrael*. That *mishnah* is typically discussed in the context of *tumah* and *taharah*, not real estate law. Yet it reveals that every walled city in *Eretz Yisrael* carries the status of *machaneh Yisrael* — the camp of Israel, the outermost of the three camps that structured the *midbar* encampment around the *Mishkan*. In the structure of the *midbar*, the *machaneh shechina* was the *Mishkan* itself, the *machaneh leviyah* surrounded it, and the *machaneh Yisrael* was the broader camp of the entire people. In *Eretz Yisrael*, *machaneh shechina* maps to the *Beis Hamikdash*, *machaneh leviyah* maps to the *Har HaBayis* (the Temple Mount), and *machaneh Yisrael* maps not merely to *Yerushalayim* but to every walled city. A *metzora* was to be sent outside the *machaneh Yisrael* — not outside *Eretz Yisrael*, but outside the walled city. This is why the three *metzora'im* in *Tanakh* are found sitting outside the city gates, not in some distant wilderness.

### Place-Based Status

This parallel in *Keilim* is significant because there the holiness in question is clearly about *makom* — a sanctity of place — rather than simply the agricultural or fiscal sanctity of the soil that normally drives the *kedushah rishonah/shniyah* debate. When the Gemara here ties *batei arei chomah* status to that same *kedushah* question, it is therefore connecting it to the holiness of place, the status of a walled city as a defined sacred precinct within the broader land. This also illuminates the connection to *Megilla* law: the obligation to read the *Megilla* on the fifteenth of Adar in *mukafet choma miyemos Yehoshua bin Nun* cities, rather than on the fourteenth, draws on this same concept of the walled city as a distinct sacred category. The status-determining moment — whether *Yehoshua*'s conquest or Ezra's return — is therefore not merely about when the soil became obligated in *terumot* and *maasros*, but about when a place acquired its defining identity as a walled sacred enclosure.

---

## Ezra Parallel Evidence

### Sukkot Verse

The Gemara now examines the prooftext offered by those who hold *kedushah rishonah kidshah l'sha'atah v'lo kidshah l'asid lavo*. The verse in *Nechemiah* describes the celebration of *Sukkot* upon the return from exile: *kol hakahal hashavim min hashvi sukkot vayeshvu bassukkot ki lo asu miyemos Yehoshua bin Nun kol ken benei Yisrael vattehi simcha gedola me'od* — the entire assembly that returned from captivity made *sukkot* and dwelt in them, for from the days of *Yehoshua bin Nun* until that time the Jewish people had not done so like this, and the joy was very great. This verse is read as connecting Ezra's generation to *Yehoshua*'s, suggesting that something analogous to the original conquest and settlement was being repeated in Ezra's time.

### Gemara Response

The Gemara immediately challenges the literal reading of this verse: *efshar ba David velo asu sukkot?* Is it possible that throughout the entire reign of David HaMelech there was no proper celebration of *Sukkot*? The verse cannot literally mean that no one observed *Sukkot* between *Yehoshua* and *Ezra*. Something else must be meant by the comparison.

### Returns Compared

The Gemara's interpretation: *makish bi'atam biymei Ezra livi'atam biymei Yehoshua* — the verse draws a parallel between the return in Ezra's time and the original entry in *Yehoshua*'s time. The parallel is halachic in import: just as the entry under *Yehoshua* entailed *manu shmittin veyovelot vekidshu arei chomah* — the counting of *shmitah* and *yovel* cycles and the sanctification of walled cities — so too the return under *Ezra* involved the same: a reinstatement of *shmitah*, *yovel*, and the sanctification of *arei chomah*. This confirms the view that the second *kedushah* was a genuine fresh sanctification, parallel in structure and legal force to the first.

### Inheritance Verse

A further prooftext: the verse in *Devarim* — *vehevi'acha Hashem Elokecha el ha'aretz asher yarshu avotecha viyrishtah* — "and Hashem your God will bring you to the land that your fathers inherited, and you shall inherit it." *Makish yerushat'cha liyrushat avotecha* — your inheriting is equated with your fathers' inheriting. Just as the fathers' original inheritance involved *bechidush kol haddevarim hallalu* — the fresh institution of all these matters (including *shmitah*, *yovel*, and the sanctification of walled cities) — so too the return from exile constitutes a new inheriting with a corresponding fresh sanctification.

---

## First Kedusha Defense

### Joshua Comparison

The Gemara now asks on behalf of the opposing view — *kedushah rishonah kidshah l'asid lavo* — why Ezra's return is compared to *Yehoshua*'s entry if not to indicate a fresh sanctification. The answer given: the comparison to *Yehoshua* is made for a different reason entirely, unrelated to sanctification of the land or walled cities.

### Yetzer Hara Removed

The comparison is meant to highlight the spiritual achievement of Ezra's generation. There is a well-known tradition that when the returnees came back to *Eretz Yisrael* at the time of the Second *Beis Hamikdash*, they prayed to have the *yetzer hara* of *avoda zara* removed — the burning drive toward idolatry that had caused the destruction of the First Temple. Their prayer was answered, and that *yetzer hara* was destroyed. The verse's comparison to *Yehoshua* is thus about spiritual merit and the conquest of the inner *yetzer*, not about reinstating *kedushah*.

### Joshua Critique

This framing contains an implicit critique of *Yehoshua*. If Ezra's generation was able to destroy the *yetzer hara* of *avoda zara* — thereby protecting *Klal Yisrael* from the catastrophe that led to the First Temple's destruction — why didn't *Yehoshua* do the same? He entered the land, he had at least as great a *zechut*, and yet he left this *yetzer* in place, allowing it to plague the Jewish people for centuries.

### Spelling Criticism

The Gemara identifies this criticism as embedded in the text itself: throughout *Tanakh* the name is spelled *Yehoshua* with a *hei*, but in the verse comparing Ezra's celebration of *Sukkot* to what was done *miyemos Yehoshua*, the name is spelled *Yeshua* — without the *hei*. *Vehainu dekakapi kari lei Yehoshua* — this orthographic anomaly is read as a subtle rebuke. The abbreviated spelling signals criticism: *Bishlama* one can understand why *Moshe* did not pursue this, *d'lo havei zechuta d'Eretz Yisrael* — he was outside the land and lacked that particular merit. But *Yehoshua*, who entered the land and possessed that merit, could have done it — *amai lo ba rachamei?* Why did he not pray for the removal of the *yetzer hara* of *avoda zara*?

---

## Summary & Implications

### List Interpretation

The debate about *kedushah rishonah* versus *kedushah shniyah* comes back to the most practical question raised by the Mishnah's short list. Is that list — *Gamla baGalil*, *Gidud be'Ever Yarden*, *Chadid*, *Ono*, and *Yerushalayim* (plus their neighbors) — essentially complete? Or is it merely a set of examples, with the real scope extending to all cities that possessed walls from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun*?

### Scope Implications

If one holds *kedushah shniyah* — that only the cities resanctified in Ezra's return carry the status — then the Mishnah's list is nearly complete. Only the handful of cities that were part of the resettlement under *Ezra* and *Nechemya* retain the laws of *batei arei chomah*. The vast number of walled cities from *Yehoshua*'s conquest — including the sixty fortified cities of *Argov* alone — lost their status at the destruction of the First Temple and were not renewed. If, however, one holds *kedushah rishonah* — that the original sanctification by *Yehoshua* was permanent — then the Mishnah's list is merely a sampling. Any city that can be shown by tradition to have been surrounded by a wall from *Yehoshua*'s time retains its full status as a walled city for all the relevant laws, and the true list is vastly larger.

### Debate Unresolved

This debate remains open. The full implications — for *batei arei chomah* law, for *Megilla* reading, and for the broader question of the halachic status of walled cities throughout *Eretz Yisrael* — will be taken up in the next shiur.

---

---

# Arakhin 33

## Kedusha Rishona/Shniya

### Cities Listed in Mishna

Today's daf is 33a, the penultimate daf of the masechta. We pick up, however, at the very bottom of 32b. The *mishna* had listed the cities governed by the laws of *batei arei chomah* — houses in walled cities — and those cities were primarily ones mentioned in *Ezra Nechemiah*. This raises an obvious question: what about all the cities from the time of *Yehoshua*? What is the explanation for this restricted list?

### Rabbi Ishmael's Braitas

The *gemara* had presented two *braitos* in the name of Rabbi Ishmael b'Rabbi Yose. The first holds that the *mishna*'s list is merely a sample, and of course the full roster from the time of *Yehoshua* is included. The second holds that the list is essentially complete — or nearly so — because the operative framework derives from the time of *Ezra*, not *Yehoshua*.

### Kedusha Frameworks

These two positions reflect a fundamental *machlokes*. Do we go by the first *kedusha* of *Eretz Yisrael* from the time of *Yehoshua* — *kedusha rishona kidsha l'sha'ata v'kidsha l'atid lavo*, meaning the first sanctification was effective both for its time and for all future time — or do we say that *kedusha* lapsed at the destruction of the *Beis Hamikdash* and we go by the second *kedusha* established at the time of *Ezra*, following the position that *kedusha rishona lo kidsha l'atid lavo*?

### Sanctity of Place

Beyond its importance as a general *machlokes*, what is fascinating here is that this dispute is being translated not merely into terms of soil and agricultural sanctity, but into issues of *makom* — the sanctity of place itself. The *gemara* speaks of cities being formally sanctified as *arei chomah*, which bears some resemblance to the *kedusha* of *Yerushalayim* and *kedushas hamikdash*. This is a striking dimension of the concept.

### Megilla Parallels

This also has significant bearing on *Megilla*. Why does *masechta Megilla* connect the status of *mukaf chomah* to *mukaf chomah mi'yemos Yehoshua bin Nun*? One explanation is that *Chazal* generally prefer to employ prefabricated *halakhic* models — if a *halakha* needs to be articulated, it is conceptually cleaner to apply an existing model, even if it is not a perfect fit. A similar phenomenon appears at the beginning of *Gittin*, which uses the geographic definition of *Eretz Yisrael* established for *trumos u'maasros* when discussing the transmission of a *get*, even though that particular definition is not strictly germane to the *gittin* question.

### Megilla & Purim

There is, however, a deeper dimension to the *Megilla* connection that deserves attention — and since *Purim* is approaching, it bears mention. The *gemara* in *Megilla* suggests that tying *megilla* reading to cities *mukaf chomah* from the time of *Yehoshua* is a way of giving *kavod* to *Eretz Yisrael*. The whole problem of *megilla* is that it commemorates a *nes* that occurred *b'chutz la'aretz*. Perhaps, then, the choice of connecting *megilla* to *mukaf chomah mi'yemos Yehoshua* is not only about the historical period of *Yehoshua* per se, but about drawing on the model of the *kedusha* of *batei arei chomah* — finding, at the very moment when everything is centered on exile and *chutz la'aretz*, a way to anchor the celebration in the *kedusha* of *Eretz Yisrael*. Of course, this is complicated by the fact that the law also applies to cities in *chutz la'aretz* that were *mukaf chomah mi'yemos Yehoshua bin Nun*, such as *Shushan* — but the connection is nonetheless striking.

---

## Reinheritance Question

### Pesach Inheritance

The *gemara* now challenges the position that everything follows the *kedusha* from the time of *Yehoshua*. A verse in *Devarim* states: *asher yarshu avosecha v'yirashta* — the land that your fathers inherited, you will inherit. This seems to imply that the return from exile constitutes a new act of inheriting the land — in other words, a resanctification. How can one maintain that everything flows from the original *kedusha* of *Yehoshua* if the verse describes a fresh inheritance upon return?

### Repossession Model

The *gemara* resolves this with a careful reading: *kivan d'yarshu avosecha yarashta at* — once your fathers inherited it, you have already inherited it. The verse does not describe a new inheritance at all. Rather, returning from exile means repossessing the inheritance of your forefathers. You are not *reinheriting*; you are reclaiming what was already yours. The question of whether the operative *kedusha* is the *kedusha rishona* or *kedusha shniya* is precisely the question of which framework governs that repossession.

---

## Shemita/Yovel Status

### Yovlos Nullified

The *gemara* now asks: *u'mi manu shmitin v'yovlos* — is it really true that they counted *shmitos* and *yovlos* during the second *Beis Hamikdash*? According to the *braita* that holds they resanctified the land in the time of *Ezra* and restarted the *shemita* and *yovel* cycle, the implication is that such counting was indeed in effect during the second *Beis Hamikdash*. But this requires scrutiny.

The *gemara* notes — as was discussed on the previous daf — that already when the tribes of *Reuven*, *Gad*, and half of *Menashe* were exiled by *Sancherev*, even before the exile of the remaining tribes of *Eretz Yisrael* proper, the *yovlos* were nullified: *batlu yovlos*.

### Kol Yoshveha Aleha

The *gemara* proceeds to the *drasha* that underlies this principle. The verse states: *u'krasem dror ba'aretz l'chol yoshveha* — you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. The operative phrase is *l'chol yoshveha*: *yovel* applies only *b'zman she'kol yoshveha aleha* — when all its inhabitants are upon it. This means when the Jewish people as a whole, each tribe in its proper ancestral portion, fully possesses the land. If even a fraction of the tribes has been exiled, *yovel* is no longer *noheig*.

A further *she'ela* arises: perhaps if all twelve tribes were present but intermixed — not dwelling in their ancestral tribal allotments — *yovel* would still apply? The verse therefore adds *yoshveha*, indicating that they must dwell upon it as they should, *k'tikunan*, each in the proper place. *Yovel* requires not merely the presence of all tribes but their proper, ordered settlement.

### Ezra's 40,000

Given this standard, the *gemara* asks how *yovel* could have been instituted at the time of *Ezra*. The verse records that *kol ha'kahal k'echad* — the entire community that made the ascent from *Bavel* — numbered forty-two thousand six hundred and sixty persons. If *yovel* was already nullified by the loss of the Trans-Jordan tribes, and if even a partial exile suffices to suspend it, how could forty thousand returnees — representing at most two tribes, *Yehuda* and *Binyamin* — have reinstated *yovel*?

### Yovel for Shemita

Rav Papa bar Yitzchak resolves this: *manu yovlos l'kadesh shemita* — they did not practice *yovel*, but they designated *yovel* years in order to sanctify *shemita*. *Shemita* does not require the presence of all twelve tribes; it requires a valid *kedusha* of the land and a properly calibrated agricultural cycle. So while the practices of *yovel* were not observed, the *beis din* — the same central authority that sets *Rosh Chodesh* and *ibbur* — designated the fiftieth year as the *yovel* year. This was a calendrical act, not a substantive one. The year was named and counted as *yovel* without the associated *yovel* practices being observed.

This framework requires clarification on two levels. First, can *shemita* exist at all without *yovel*? Second, if the *yovel* year is not designated, does the cycle collapse because one ends up with forty-nine-year cycles rather than fifty-year cycles, throwing off the entire *shemita* count? The *gemara* here seems to be working from the premise that you need *yovel* at least to maintain the integrity of the calendar — the fifty-year cycle — in order for *shemita* to remain properly aligned.

The conceptual structure being proposed is thus: there can be a formal designation of a *yovel* year by the *beis din* without the actual *yovel* practices, similar to how the *beis din* sets *Rosh Chodesh* without any agricultural consequence. This designation has *halakhic* significance as a calendrical act even when the substantive laws of *yovel* are not operative.

---

## 50-Year vs. 49-Year

### Rabbis' 50-Year

The *gemara* refines Rav Papa's answer by distinguishing between the positions of the *rabbanan* and Rabbi Yehuda on the structure of the *yovel* cycle. The *rabbanan* hold that *shenat chamishim eina min haminyan* — the fiftieth year does not count as year one of the next cycle. There is thus a genuine fifty-year cycle: forty-nine working years, then the *yovel* year, then the new cycle begins with year one. Under this view, the designation of the *yovel* year matters enormously for the calendar, because without it one would count seven-year *shemita* cycles within an incorrect framework.

### Rabbi Yehuda 49-Year

Rabbi Yehuda holds that *shenat chamishim ola lechan u'lechan* — the fiftieth year counts as both the last year of the old cycle and the first year of the new one. There is therefore no break year between cycles; the cycle is effectively forty-nine years. Under Rabbi Yehuda's view, the designation of a *yovel* year has no calendrical significance, since the count proceeds on seven-year cycles regardless. The *gemara* therefore challenges Rav Papa's answer: according to Rabbi Yehuda, why would anyone bother designating *yovel* years if they do not practice *yovel* and the *yovel* designation has no effect on the calendar? Could they not simply observe *shemita* without any reference to *yovel*?

### Shemita Independence

The *gemara* responds that Rav Papa's answer is indeed not consistent with Rabbi Yehuda's view. According to Rabbi Yehuda, if one is not practicing *yovel*, there is no reason to designate the year at all — the seven-year *shemita* cycles proceed independently. The resolution the *gemara* offers is simply that Rav Papa's position aligns with the *rabbanan* and not with Rabbi Yehuda.

### Shemita Today

This discussion yields an important implication: the *gemara*'s treatment here strongly suggests that *shemita* does not require *yovel* to be operative. Under the *rabbanan*, the only reason to designate a *yovel* year is calendrical — to maintain fifty-year cycles. But the practice of *shemita* itself does not appear to require *yovel*. Under Rabbi Yehuda there is not even a calendrical reason needed, and *shemita* proceeds entirely independently.

This has direct bearing on the question of whether *shemita* today is *d'Oraisa* or *d'rabbanan*. *Tosafos*, based on a *gemara* in *Gittin* discussing *Hillel*'s *takana* of *pruzbul*, raises the question of how *Hillel* could enact a *takana* that circumvents even a nominal *mitzvah min haTorah*. The *gemara* there seems to suggest that the relevant obligations were already only rabbinic in force. Some *Rishonim* read that discussion to mean that without operative *yovel*, *shemita* — or at least certain aspects of it such as the nullification of debts — does not apply *d'Oraisa*. Others read the *gemara* differently, limiting the rabbinic character specifically to *shmiyas kesafim*, the release of monetary debts, which is conceptually most parallel to *yovel*'s land-reversion provisions, while holding that the agricultural restrictions of *shemita* retain biblical force. This is a question with direct practical relevance — Rav Kook's *heter mechira* rested in part on the assumption that *shemita* is only *d'rabbanan* today.

One further point: this *gemara* implies that during the second *Beis Hamikdash* they designated *yovel* years and therefore observed fifty-year cycles. Yet the *Rambam* states that today we operate on forty-nine-year cycles. The question of exactly when and how this shift occurred — from the fifty-year framework of the second *Beis Hamikdash* period to the forty-nine-year framework of today — is itself an open question, compounded by the *Rambam*'s famous reliance on *mesorah* from the time of the *Geonim* to establish the current *shemita* year. The *Rishonim* are not fully in agreement on when exactly the year falls.

---

## Yovel in First Temple

### Jeremiah & Slaves

The *gemara* now asks a different question: can one really say that *shmitin v'yovlos* were not kept even toward the end of the first *Beis Hamikdash* period? A verse from *Yirmiyahu* — speaking at the end of the first *Beis Hamikdash* — records him exhorting the people: *tishalchu ish et achiv ha'ivri asher yimacher lach* — send free the Hebrew slave. The formulation in *Yirmiyahu* is *miketz sheva shanim*, at the end of seven years.

### Six vs. Seven Years

This raises an immediate textual difficulty. The verse elsewhere states *v'avadcha shesh shanim* — the slave works six years and is freed at the beginning of the seventh. What then does *Yirmiyahu* mean by commanding release at the end of seven? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this: *shesh l'nimkar v'sheva l'nirtza* — six years applies to the ordinary case of a sold slave, while seven years applies to the slave who had his ear pierced and thus extended his service beyond the initial six. The earliest the *yovel* could free such a slave is year seven of his service. *Yirmiyahu* is thus referring to the case of the *nirtza* slave who is freed at *yovel*, which could fall in year seven. Reading the verse this way implies that *yovel* was operative during *Yirmiyahu*'s time — long after *Sancherev*'s exile of the Trans-Jordan tribes.

### Sarcastic Rebuke

The *gemara* deflects this implication by proposing that *hahu b'tochecha ksiv* — that verse is written as *mussar*, as a rebuke. *Yirmiyahu* was not issuing a practical directive about what the people should currently be doing. Rather, he was sarcastically reproaching them, asking whether they had ever fulfilled this *mitzvah* in the past. The exhortation was about their prior failures, not a command for the present.

### They Listened

The *gemara* immediately challenges this reading: *v'ha ksiv vayishmeu vayishallachu* — but the verse says they listened to him and actually released the slaves. This demonstrates that *Yirmiyahu* was speaking about something they could and did act upon in the present, not merely lamenting the past. The rebuke interpretation cannot be sustained in light of their actual response.

### 12 Tribes Restored

The *gemara* therefore accepts that *yovel* was indeed *noheig* at the end of the first *Beis Hamikdash* period and turns to reconcile this with the earlier principle that *yovel* requires *kol yoshveha aleha*. The answer, offered in the name of Rav Nachman, is both bold and striking: *Yirmiyah hechziran v'Yoshiyahu ben Amon malach aleihem* — *Yirmiyahu* undertook a special mission and gathered representatives of all twelve tribes, bringing them back to settle in their ancestral lands, and *Yoshiyahu* ruled as king over all twelve tribes.

Some *Rishonim* hold that one does not need a majority of each tribe — a small representative group from each tribe is sufficient. The proof that *Yirmiyahu* accomplished this comes from *Yechezkel*, who, writing after the *churban*, says: *ki hamocher el hamimkar lo yashuv* — the seller will no longer return to what he sold. This implies that before the *churban*, sellers did return to their ancestral land — that *yovel* was operative. As the *gemara* notes, it would be strange for a *navi* to lament the passing of something that had already been nullified since the time of *Sancherev*. Therefore, *yovel* must have been reinstated, which establishes that *Yirmiyahu* must have restored representatives of all twelve tribes.

Evidence that *Yoshiyahu* ruled over those beyond *Yehuda* and *Binyamin* comes from a verse recording that *Yoshiyahu* traveled through *Beis El* — a city belonging to the kingdom of *Yisrael*, not *Yehuda*. His presence there would be inexplicable unless he had governance over those territories. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds a further proof from *Hoshea*: *gam Yehuda shat katzir lach b'shuvi shevut ami* — the *drasha* reading *katzir* as *katzin*, a ruler, indicating that *Yehuda* would exercise governance over *Yisrael*.

This leaves an outstanding question regarding the second *Beis Hamikdash*. The *gemara* has now resolved the apparent *yovel* at the end of the first *Beis Hamikdash* period through *Yirmiyahu*'s restoration of tribal representatives. But the *gemara* also makes clear that during the second *Beis Hamikdash*, *yovel* was not practiced. This creates a difficulty for *Hillel*'s *takana* regarding the walled city house — a *takana* apparently responding to a practical situation of sellers going into hiding to avoid having to return the house. *Tosafos* addresses this, suggesting that perhaps even in the time of the second *Beis Hamikdash* there were small representatives of all twelve tribes: *mikol shevet v'shevet chavru miktatan*. This answer is in some tension with the *gemara* itself, which emphasized the small number of returnees with *Ezra* and the impossibility of *yovel* under those conditions. Some *Rishonim* accordingly propose that *Hillel*'s *takana* addressed a *d'rabbanan yovel* — a rabbinic-level framework without *d'Oraisa* force — that was operative during the second *Beis Hamikdash* period.

---

## Unwalled City Houses

### Hybrid Status

We turn now to the second major topic of the *daf*: the status of houses in unwalled cities, *batei hachatzeirim*. One might have assumed that such houses enjoy neither the privileges of *batei arei chomah* nor the full protections of agricultural fields — or perhaps that they simply follow the rules of fields. The *mishna* surprises us: *nosnim lahem kol ha'yafeh she'b'vatei arei chomah v'kol ha'yafeh she'b'sadot* — we give them every favorable feature of houses in walled cities and every favorable feature of fields.

Concretely, this means: the house in the unwalled city can be redeemed immediately (*nigalim miyad*), like a house in a walled city. It may be redeemed at any point during the twelve-month period, *k'vatim*, as houses are redeemed. And it goes out at *yovel* and is redeemable at proportional cost during the remaining years, *k'sadot*, like fields. The only period during which the seller cannot force redemption is year two — the gap between the two categories, as we will clarify below. So the seller retains the right to force redemption during year one, and again from year three onward, and also recovers the property at *yovel*. It is a remarkable consolidation of privileges.

Conceptually, this can be understood as the Torah's analog to a housing initiative: a house in a walled city is expensive urban real estate, perhaps more transitory in character, more commercial, and therefore subject to more limited protections. But a house in a village outside the metropolis is connected to one's farmland and ancestral inheritance — the very concept of *nachalah* the Torah is so insistent upon. One can sell one's field and still live somewhere, but giving up a village home is more existentially significant. Hence the Torah provides even broader protections for these houses than for either category alone.

### Sedeh Achuza

The *gemara* traces the derivation. The verse says *al sedei ha'aretz yeichashev* — it shall be reckoned as a field of the land — which alone would suggest treating the unwalled city house simply like a *sadeh*. The *gemara* reads this as a *hekesh* to *sedeh achuzah*: just as *sedeh achuzah* goes out at *yovel* and may be redeemed proportionally during the remaining years, so too *batei chatzerim* go out at *yovel* and are subject to proportional redemption. So far this tracks the simple *pshat* of the verses.

But the *gemara* then asks: perhaps like *sadeh achuzah*, these houses cannot be redeemed within two years? To this, the verse says *geulah tihyeh lo* — he has a right of redemption — which the *mishna* reads as affirming all redemption rights, including the right to redeem immediately, *miyad*, as one redeems a house. And conversely, once we have granted the seller all the favorable features of both categories, one might have supposed that the property should perhaps not revert at *yovel* — the verse therefore explicitly states *v'vayovel yetzei*, affirming that *yovel* reversion applies.

### Hekdesh Redemption

The *gemara* then asks a pointed question: *mai ka'amar* — what was the point of that last concern? If we have already established through the *hekesh* to *sedeh achuzah* that it goes out at *yovel*, why was there any *hava amina* that it would not?

### Sanctified Houses

Rav Huna answers: *lo nitzrecha ela b'makdish bayis b'vatei chatzerim* — the teaching is necessary specifically for the case where someone *sanctifies* his house in an unwalled city — rendering it *hekdesh* — and someone else (*acher*) redeems it from *hekdesh*. Now *yovel* arrives in year two. The dilemma is sharp: into which category do we place this?

If we treat it like a house in a walled city, then after the first year has passed the buyer (*lokeiach*) gets it permanently — *chalit lei lokeiach*. If we treat it like *sedeh achuzah*, then when *yovel* hits it goes to the *kohanim* — *nafka l'Kohanim* — not back to the original owner. Either way, the original owner would not recover his house. The verse *v'vayovel yetzei* therefore comes to teach that even in this scenario, sitting between the two categories, the property returns to the original owner. This is a privilege that transcends both frameworks.

### Levite Redemption

The *gemara* then asks: *menalan* — from where do we know that *hekdesh* does not simply revert to the owner without a redemption payment? The proof comes from the laws of *Levi'im*. A *Levi* has enhanced rights when it comes to selling his property — *geulat olam tihyeh l'Levi'im*, he may always redeem — yet when he sanctifies his property as *hekdesh* and it returns to him, he has a diminished right — *hura kocho b'hekdesho* — because *hekdesh* does not exit without a *pidyon*. If even a *Levi*, with all his expanded rights in property transactions, must give money to transfer the *kedusha* when his sanctified property is returned to him, then certainly an ordinary *Yisrael* — whose general rights are more limited — must do the same. The principle: *hekdesh yeitzei b'lo pidyon* — *hekdesh* does not exit without redemption.

The *gemara* then traces the derivation by the *Levi'im* themselves from the verse *va'asher yiga'al min ha'Levi'im v'yatza mimkar bayis v'ir achuzato ba'yovel* — what he redeems from the *Levi'im* goes out at *yovel*. One might have thought *yatza mimkar* means all property a *Levi* sold — including slaves, movable property, and documents. The verse therefore specifies *bayis*, house, limiting the category to landed property. And the formulation *mimkaro*, from his selling — things he sold to another person — exit at *yovel* automatically, but things he *sanctified* do not exit automatically. For those, redemption money is required: *mimkaro yotzei b'chinam v'ein hekdesh yotzei b'chinam*.

### Hekdesh Principle

When *Abaye* expressed this principle — that we do not want *hekdesh* to appear to exit without some formal transfer — he framed it in terms of appearances, *shelo yomru hekdesh yeitzei b'lo pidyon*. Based on the verse, however, it is not merely a matter of appearances. It is a substantive rule: the *kedusha* of *hekdesh* must be formally transferred through *pidyon*. No property exits *hekdesh* without that mechanism.

### Hekdesh Stays

The *gemara* notes that Rav Huna's analysis argues with the position of Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Yehoshua holds: *kulam hayu b'chlal v'nasan ha'kesef v'kam lo* — the general rule is that one gives money to acquire from *hekdesh* and thereby obtains it. The verse by *sedeh achuzah* — *ve'hayetah ha'sadeh b'tzeitah ba'yovel kodesh la'Hashem ke'sedeh ha'cherem* — specifies that it goes to the *kohanim* only because *David* had already redeemed it from *hekdesh* first. *Sadeh hu de'prakei v'nafka l'Kohanim* — it is specifically the field that was redeemed by someone else and thereby exits *hekdesh* that goes to the *kohanim*. But property still sitting in the possession of *hekdesh* — *hanach k'dakai kaimi* — stays exactly as it was. *Hekdesh* retains it indefinitely until someone redeems it. *Yovel* does not dislodge property from *hekdesh* at all; it simply remains there until a *pidyon* occurs.

### Second Year Gap

Rav Papa then applies this principle to the unwalled city house scenario. The teaching *v'vayovel yetzei* is necessary precisely for the case where someone sells his house in an unwalled city and *yovel* arrives in the second year — the gap between the two categories. *L'mai medamit lei* — into which framework does it fall?

If it is treated like *batei arei chomah*, then after the first year has passed, the buyer gets it permanently even at *yovel*. If it is treated like *sedeh achuzah*, then the seller cannot recover it — the buyer is entitled to make up any year that fell within *yovel*, *hashlamah ba'ei*. The verse *v'vayovel yetzei* therefore teaches that neither framework applies in this year-two gap: the property returns to the seller, and the buyer receives no right of extension. A *braita* is cited in support of Rav Huna's position, and the *gemara* notes it constitutes a contradiction to Rabbi Yehoshua's view: if someone sanctifies a house in an unwalled city and *yovel* arrives without redemption, *chozer l'be'alim ba'yovel* — it returns to the owner. This contradicts Rabbi Yehoshua's position that *hekdesh* remains in *hekdesh* until actively redeemed.

---

## Unwalled City Criteria

### Two/Two Minimum

Having established the laws of *batei hachatzeirim*, the *gemara* turns to their definition. The *mishna* states: *shnei chatzeiros shel shnei batim* — even if a settlement has a wall, if it consists of only two streets with two houses each, it does not qualify as a walled city — *harei hen k'vatei chatzeirim*. It retains the status of an unwalled settlement regardless of its physical wall.

The *braita* derives this from the verse's phrasing. The verse says *batei hachatzeirim* — houses of the unwalled cities — and then adds the apparently redundant phrase *asher ein lahem chomah saviv* — which do not have a wall around. One would have assumed from context that these cities lack walls. The redundancy therefore teaches: *af al pi she'yesh lahem chomah k'mi she'ein lahem chomah* — even if they have a wall, they are treated as though they have none. The *drasha* then identifies two houses (*batim*) and two courtyards or streets (*chatzerot*) as the minimal threshold below which even a walled city does not count.

### Size Over Walls

This ruling applies even to a settlement that is *mukaf chomah mi'yemos Yehoshua bin Nun* — walled from the time of *Yehoshua*. The physical wall is simply not determinative if the settlement does not meet the minimum population and structural threshold. The *gemara* also asks: could the minimum be even lower — one house and one street? The derivation from *batim chatzerot* (both in the plural, with *batim* adding a count beyond what *chatzerot* alone would imply) establishes that two houses per two streets is the minimum, and anything below that, regardless of walls, is treated as *batei chatzerim*.

The question of whether an existing wall might elevate a small settlement's status if it later grows is implicitly addressed: the status is fixed based on the historical condition at the time of *Yehoshua* or *Ezra*, as one follows based on the earlier *machlokes*. Subsequent development does not alter the classification.

### Historical Status

A final point: the *gemara* notes that *af al pi she'ein lo achshav* — even if the settlement no longer has [the wall] now — the determinative factor is what it had at the time of *Yehoshua* or *Ezra*. The classification is entirely backward-looking. This has obvious resonance with the laws of *megilla*, where the question of which cities read on the fifteenth versus the fourteenth of *Adar* similarly turns on their ancient walled status — a point the *gemara* notes is apposite precisely as *Purim* approaches.

---

## Levite Inheritance

### Israelite Inherits

The *mishna* now addresses the interaction of Levitical status with Levitical land. The first case: a *Yisrael* who inherits from his maternal grandfather, a *Levi*, now holds Levitical land but is not himself a *Levi*. The *mishna* states *eino go'el k'seder hazeh* — he does not redeem according to the [special Levitical] arrangement.

### Levite Inherits

The converse: a *Levi* who inherits from his maternal grandfather, a *Yisrael*, now holds non-Levitical land but is himself a *Levi*. Again, *eino go'el k'seder hazeh* — he does not redeem according to the Levitical arrangement.

As the *gemara* will demonstrate, these two rulings appear to contradict the *mishna*'s conclusion, which establishes a two-criteria requirement. The *gemara* therefore rereads *eino go'el k'seder hazeh* as *eino go'el ella k'seder hazeh* — he redeems only in the manner of an ordinary *Yisrael*, not with Levitical privileges. The double negation is resolved into a positive limitation: with only one of the two criteria, one is treated as a *Yisrael*.

### Rabbi's Requirement

The *mishna* concludes: *ad she'yehei Levi b'arei haLevi'im* — *divrei Rabbi* — one must be both a *Levi* and the land must be Levitical land to exercise the special perpetual redemption rights. The verse states *ki batei arei haLevi'im hi achuzatam* — the houses of the cities of the *Levi'im* are their inheritance — linking both the person (*Levi'im*) and the land (*batei arei*) as joint conditions.

The *gemara* then asks how Rabbi derives that the *person* must be a *Levi*. The proof is from *va'asher yigal min ha'Levi'im* — "whoever redeems from the *Levi'im*" — which emphasizes the identity of the seller, not merely the land. Furthermore, one might have thought that a *Levi* can force back land sold to another *Levi*, since both have superior rights — *shezeh yafeh kocho v'zeh yafeh kocho*. The verse *ha'Levi'im* teaches that the right applies regardless of who purchased the land — even from another *Levi*, the seller may always redeem. But then *min ha'Levi'im* — "from the *Levi'im*" and not all *Levi'im* — excludes those who are not fully legitimate members.

### Mamzer Exclusion

The *drasha* of *min ha'Levi'im v'lo kol ha'Levi'im* — from the *Levi'im* but not all *Levi'im* — excludes the *ben Levi mamzer* and *netin*. This is a notable ruling: a *mamzer* who is a *Levi* retains his *Levi* status in most halakhic contexts — he receives the second *aliya*, he receives *ma'aser rishon* — but here, the perpetual redemption right of *geulat olam* is denied to him. The rationale is that the special Levitical right is keyed to the full identity of membership in the *shevet*, and a *mamzer*, whose lineage is compromised in the halakhic sense, does not possess that full identity.

### Chachamim's View

The *Chachamim* disagree with Rabbi's position: *ein devarim halalu amurim ella b'arei Levi'im af al pi she'eino Levi* — the special redemption rights follow the land, not the person. So long as the property in question is Levitical land — land within the cities of the *Levi'im* — the perpetual redemption right applies, regardless of whether the current owner is personally a *Levi*. The land-type alone determines the *halakha*.

---

## Levite City Structure

### City Layout

The *mishna* establishes that one may not convert a *migrash* into a field, nor a field into a *migrash*, nor extend the city into the *migrash*, nor rezone part of the city as *migrash*. The Torah describes the structure of Levitical cities as having the city itself, surrounded by a *migrash* — a thousand-*amah* radius of open, park-like space — and beyond that another thousand-*amah* radius of planting fields. This layout must be preserved.

### Rabbi Elazar

Rabbi Elazar ben Menachem clarifies that these restrictions apply only to *arei haLevi'im* — the cities of the *Levi'im* — where the Torah explicitly prescribes the city's layout. For cities of ordinary *Yisrael*, the rules are flexible: *osim sadeh migrash o migrash sadeh* — one may convert a field to park space or park space to field, and the city may expand outward into what was previously *migrash*.

### No Destruction

However, even for non-Levitical cities, one restriction remains: *v'lo ir migrash* — one may not demolish part of the city and rezone it as open park space. The reason given is *shelo yachrivu et arei Yisrael* — lest they destroy the cities of *Yisrael*. The *mishna* thus preserves at minimum a prohibition against the deliberate dismantling of established settlements. One might ask: if the city has been abandoned anyway, does it matter whether the structures stand empty or are repurposed as open ground? The *halakha* nonetheless maintains that the act of demolishing and converting is prohibited, imposing a floor beneath which urban degradation cannot be deliberately accelerated.

### Geulat Olam

The *mishna* then states: *hakohanim v'haLevi'im mocherim l'olam u'goalim l'olam* — *kohanim* and *Levi'im* may sell at all times and redeem at all times. This formalizes what was implied throughout the prior discussion: the perpetual right of redemption applies to all Levitical property, without the one-year limit applicable to walled city houses or the two-year limit applicable to fields. The source is *geulat olam tihyeh la'Levi'im*.

### Lo Yimacher

The *gemara* closes by addressing the verse's phrase *u'sdeh migrash areihem lo yimacher* — the field of their *migrash* shall not be sold. The question arises: does *lo yimacher* mean a literal prohibition on selling? If so, it would contradict the principle of *geulat olam*, which presupposes the possibility of sale.

The *gemara* resolves this: *lo yimacher* does not mean they cannot sell. Rather, it means *lo yeshaneh* — the structure may not be *changed*. *Levi'im* may sell their property and their buyers may hold it — and the *Levi'im* always retain the right to redeem it. But the underlying structure of the Levitical city — its spatial layout of city, *migrash*, and fields — must remain intact. The prohibition is not on the transaction, but on structural alteration. Sales occur; redemptions occur; but the essential character of the *arei haLevi'im* endures unchanged.

---

---

# Arakhin 34

## Levite Redemption Rights

### Mishna Intro

Daf 34 opens at the bottom of 33b, with the final line of the *mishna*. The *mishna* has concluded its treatment of houses in unwalled cities and the structure of the cities of the *leviim* — including the conversion of parks to fields and the preservation of that urban arrangement. It now closes with a statement about the *leviim*'s rights of sale and redemption: the *leviim* may sell at all times, and — more significantly — they may redeem at all times. The perpetual right of redemption, *geulat olam*, means that whatever they sell, they may redeem from the very outset. Unlike a *sedeh achuza* of an ordinary Israelite, where the seller must wait until the third year before redeeming, and unlike a house in a walled city, where the right of redemption lapses after one year, a *levi* retains the right to redeem continuously, right up through the *yovel*.

### Geulat Olam Fields

A *baraita* is introduced: *Geulat olam tihyeh laleviim* — an eternal redemption shall belong to the *leviim*. The *Gemara* asks: what does this teach? It proceeds to identify three distinct *chiddushim* conveyed by this phrase, each addressing a different situation in which one might have thought the *levi*'s right to redeem would be curtailed.

The first *chiddush* concerns fields. The verse concerning a *sedeh achuza* of an ordinary Israelite states *mispar shenei tevuot yimkor lach* — the field is sold for a number of years' worth of produce, and *Chazal* derive from this that the seller must wait at least two years before redeeming. One might have thought that this restriction applies equally to a *levi*'s field. Therefore the *Torah* teaches *geulat olam tihyeh laleviim* — the *levi* may redeem even from the very beginning, without any waiting period.

The second *chiddush* addresses sanctification. By a standard *sedeh achuza*, the verse states *veyatza hasadeh b'yovel kodesh l'Hashem kesedeh ha-cherem* — if the Israelite sanctified the field and someone else redeemed it from *hekdesh*, then at *yovel* the field passes to the *kohanim*. One might have thought this rule applies equally when a *levi* sanctifies his field and an Israelite redeems it from *hekdesh* — that at *yovel* it would go to the *kohanim* and be lost to the *levi* entirely. Therefore the *Torah* teaches *geulat olam tihyeh laleviim*: the *levi* retains the perpetual right to redeem.

What precisely happens in this latter scenario is not spelled out explicitly in the *Gemara*. If the *Torah* is not directing the field to the *kohanim*, one must conclude that the field remains in the hands of the person who redeemed it from *hekdesh*, and the *levi* retains the right to redeem it from him. Alternatively, it is conceivable that at *yovel* the field passes to the *kohanim*, and the *levi* would then have the right to redeem it from them. This possibility is not foreclosed, though it would represent a considerable stretch of the principle, since the *geulat olam* is framed as an override of what the *Torah* would otherwise prescribe. The *Gemara* does not resolve these details — and indeed, much of this area of *halacha* was not practiced and has not received the detailed treatment one finds in the great *masechtot* of *kodashim*. Accordingly, many of the particulars remain unspecified.

One further question left open is whether this right of redemption is inheritable. The *Gemara* had discussed previously whether the rights are limited to the *arei ha-leviim* specifically, and whether they attach to the *levi* personally or to the city's status. One opinion required both — that the seller be a *levi* and the property be in an *ir leviim*; the other required only that the property be in an *ir leviim*. Whether a *levi*'s son could inherit his father's right to redeem — a question distinct from whether a completely unrelated *levi* could redeem another *levi*'s field — remains an interesting open question that the *Gemara* does not address.

### Geulat Olam Houses

The third *chiddush* concerns houses in walled cities. The verse states *ve-kam ha-bayit asher ba-ir asher lo chomah litzmitut* — if a house in a walled city is not redeemed within the year, it passes permanently to the buyer. One might have thought this rule applies to a *levi*'s house in a walled city as well, such that after the year the house is lost forever. Therefore the *Torah* teaches *geulat olam tihyeh laleviim*: even after the year has passed, the *levi* may redeem. And notably, unlike the case of a house in an unwalled city — where the *Gemara* elsewhere grappled with a gap period between the second year and certain transitional stages — here the *Gemara* understands the rule to be unqualified: across the board, regardless of what year it is, the *levi* may always redeem.

### Walled City Problem

Having stated this third *chiddush*, the *Gemara* pauses to ask a sharp question. The first two *chiddushim* — regarding fields and sanctification — are perfectly comprehensible: the scenarios are real and the *chiddushim* meaningful. But the third raises a difficulty. *Bishlama hani tarti lachai* — the first two are fine, but as for *battei arei chomah* for *leviim*, how would a *levi* ever come to have a house in a walled city in the first place? This problem requires resolution, and the *Gemara* immediately turns to it.

## Walled City Definition

### Cities of Refuge

To understand why a *levi*'s owning a house in a walled city is problematic, the *Gemara* cites a *baraita* from Maseches Makkos. The *baraita* states that the *arei miklat* — the cities of refuge — may not be made too small, for the accidental killer who is exiled there must have adequate provisions and must remain within its boundaries; a tiny village would be insufficient and would force him to venture out. Nor, however, may the *arei miklat* be major metropolises. Rashi explains that in a very large city — like a great urban center — it is impossible to track the movements of everyone within; the *goel ha-dam* could too easily slip in undetected and kill the inadvertent killer. Therefore the *arei miklat* must be *arim beinoniyot* — medium-sized towns, neither too small nor too large.

The implicit corollary, though not stated explicitly in the *baraita*, is that *arei miklat* must be unwalled: walls are the hallmark of major fortified cities. This means that if the *levi* cities served as *arei miklat*, as they did according to the account in Yehoshua, they would by definition be unwalled. And if they are unwalled, how could a *levi* ever have a house with the legal status of a *bayit b'ir chomah* — a house in a walled city?

### Wall Precedence

Rav Kahana says: *lo kashya* — this is not difficult. There are two distinct scenarios: one where the wall preceded the settlement (*hukaf u-levasof yashav*), and one where the settlement preceded the wall (*yashav u-levasof hukaf*). His suggestion is that a *levi* city could have first been designated as a city and then had a wall built around it afterward. But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this resolution.

### Non-Jewish Walls

The *Gemara* objects: does a wall built after settlement even count as a wall (*mi havei chomah*)? A *baraita* is cited: the verse *ve-ish ki yimkor beit moshav ir chomah* — when a man sells a house in a walled city — means specifically a city that was *hukaf u-levasof yashav*, walled first and then settled. A city settled first and then walled does not qualify. The *baraita* continues: one might think that even if Jews built the wall after the conquest of the land, that should suffice to confer the status of *ir chomah*. The *Gemara* responds with a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *chomah* is used here in the context of walled-city laws, and the same word *chomah* appears in the description of the sixty walled cities in *Ever HaYardem* that were conquered. Just as there the walls were built by non-Jews, so too here, the qualifying wall must be one built by non-Jews.

### Pre-Conquest Standard

A further refinement follows. One might propose that the non-Jewish wall need not predate the conquest — perhaps a non-Jewish wall built *after* the Israelites entered the land would also qualify. The *Gemara* again applies the same *gezeirah shavah*: just as by the cities in *Ever HaYarden* the wall predated the Israelite arrival, so too here, the wall must have preceded the conquest. The upshot is stark: the only cities that carry the *halacha* of *battei arei chomah* are those that, at the time of Yehoshua's conquest, already had walls built by non-Jews, and in which the walls had preceded the city's settlement — walls that stood for generations before the city grew up within them.

This tightens the problem considerably. The *arei miklat* were designated at the time of Yehoshua; the only *batei arei chomah* are cities walled in the time of Yehoshua. So how could there exist a city that was simultaneously designated as an *ir miklat* — which requires being unwalled — and also qualifies as an *ir chomah*? One might suggest *Yericho* as a candidate, since it did famously have a wall that then fell. But the *Gemara* does not pursue this line.

### Refuge Then Walled

Rav Yosef son of Rav Sala Chasida, speaking before Rav Pappa, offers a resolution: *kegon she-naflu lahem hen u-migresheihem* — it is a case where a city and its surrounding *migrash* fell to the *leviim* by lot. The word *naflu* here does not mean that the walls fell; it means that the city fell to them by lottery when the *arei miklat* were being assigned. In other words, in the random assignment of *arei miklat* among the *levi* cities, a city happened to be chosen that had a wall — one that had been walled by non-Jews before settlement, and thus qualified as an *ir chomah*. Since an *ir miklat* must not be a walled city, the plan would have been to knock down the wall. The *Gemara* notes that the *migrash* perimeter was maintained, but the wall surrounding it was slated for demolition.

### Wall Knockdown

Rav Ashi clarifies why the *pasuk*'s ruling is still necessary even within this scenario. One might have thought: until the wall is actually knocked down, if a *levi* sells his house during that interim period, the house would carry the full status of a house sold in a walled city and would be forfeited permanently after the year. Therefore the *Torah* teaches *geulat olam tihyeh laleviim* — even during that transitional window, before the wall has been demolished, the *levi* retains the right to redeem his house at any time.

It is worth noting that Tosafos raises a pointed question here: we have established that for the purposes of *battei arei chomah*, the status of a walled city is fixed from the time of Yehoshua and does not change even if the wall subsequently falls down. If so, it would seem that once the wall is knocked down, the house would *still* retain the *ir chomah* status — in which case the scenario of the interim period before demolition would have been a perfectly natural answer to the original question. For some reason, the *Gemara* does not pursue that argument. Tosafos flags the difficulty, but the *Gemara* chooses to present the ruling through Rav Ashi's narrower formulation.

## Sanctified Kohen Fields

### Non-Levitical Field

The *Gemara* now introduces a new *baraita*: *kisdeh ha-cherem lakohen tihyeh achuzato* — it shall be to him like a *cherem* field belonging to a *kohen*. This formulation echoes a *Gemara* encountered earlier in the tractate almost word for word, but it is being revisited here in the context of *kohanim* and *leviim*, since the preceding discussion concerned their special rights regarding fields and sanctification.

To situate the discussion properly, it is necessary to distinguish two categories of permanent *kohen* fields. The first is the *arei ha-leviim* — the cities of the *leviim*, with their surrounding fields, which are the subject of the *geulat olam* rule. That case is already resolved: if a *levi* or *kohen* sells or sanctifies property in the *arei ha-leviim*, the right to redeem is always retained and the property does not pass permanently to others.

The second category is a field that a *kohen* received permanently, but *not* by virtue of the *arei ha-leviim*. How does such a situation arise? An Israelite could declare a field *cherem*, whereupon it passes to the *kohanim*; or an Israelite could sanctify his *sedeh achuza*, another Israelite redeems it from *hekdesh*, and then at *yovel* it is distributed to the *kohanim*. In either case, the *kohen* now holds a field permanently — it will not revert to any prior owner — but it is not part of the *arei ha-leviim*. This is the *kohen*'s *sedeh charmo* (his field acquired through a *cherem*), and it constitutes its own legal category.

The *baraita* now asks: if a *kohen* sanctifies this *sedeh charmo*, what is the result? One might have thought the answer is obvious from analogy to the *arei ha-leviim* rule. But the *baraita* signals that a distinct treatment applies, and the question is precisely what law governs sanctification of a *kohen*'s permanent field that falls outside the *arei ha-leviim* framework.

### Kohen's Claim

At *yovel*, a *sedeh achuza* of an ordinary Israelite that was sanctified and not redeemed is distributed among the *kohanim*. When a *kohen* sanctifies his own *sedeh charmo*, the question arises whether the same fate befalls it. And here the *kohen* advances a claim: the verse states *vehaya hasadeh betzeito ba-yovel kodesh l'Hashem kesedeh ha-cherem* — at *yovel* the field becomes sanctified to God like the *cherem* field and goes to the *kohanim*. But the *kohen* argues: *v'harei hi tachat yadi* — it is already in my hands. It will go to *kohanim* at *yovel* regardless; I am a *kohen*; I should simply retain it.

He frames this as a logical argument: *beshel acherim ani zocheh, besheli lo kol sheken* — if I am entitled to receive a share in other people's fields when they are distributed at *yovel*, how much more so should I simply retain a field that was originally my own.

The *Torah* responds by teaching the parallel to the *sedeh achuza* of the Israelite: just as the Israelite's sanctified field, when redeemed by another and then reaching *yovel*, leaves his hands and is distributed equally among all the *kohanim*, so too the *kohen*'s *sedeh charmo* that he sanctified leaves his hands and is distributed equally among his fellow *kohanim* — *yotzei miyado u-mitchalek le-echav ha-kohanim*. He has no special status with respect to that field.

This parallel serves an important structural purpose. It places in sharp relief the fundamental distinction between the *kohen*'s *sedeh charmo* and the *arei leviim*. Property in the *arei leviim* — whether sold or sanctified — is subject to *geulat olam*: the *levi* or *kohen* can always redeem, and it does not transfer permanently. The *sedeh charmo* — though it is the *kohen*'s permanently, and though it did not originate in the *arei leviim* — is treated for purposes of sanctification exactly like the *sedeh achuza* of an ordinary Israelite.

### Cherem Comparison

The *baraita* asks: why does the verse invoke the imagery of a *sedeh ha-cherem* when it speaks of what happens to the Israelite's sanctified *sedeh achuza* at *yovel*? The connection seems to go in the direction of the *cherem* field teaching something to the *sedeh achuza*. But *harei zeh ba lilamed ve-nimtza lamed* — the *cherem* field appears to come to teach yet ends up being taught. The *hekesh* — the Scriptural analogy — runs in both directions, or rather, the verse connects the *kohen*'s *sedeh charmo* to the Israelite's *sedeh achuza*: *makish sdeh charmo l-sdeh achuza shel Yisrael*. The law governing each is identical. Just as the Israelite's *sedeh achuza* that was sanctified, redeemed, and then reached *yovel* leaves his control and is divided among the *kohanim*, so too the *kohen*'s *sedeh charmo*, if sanctified, leaves his control at *yovel* and is divided equally among all the *kohanim*. The *kohen* who held the field has no greater share than any of his colleagues.

### Group vs Individual

The *Gemara* then returns to scrutinize the *kohen*'s argument. His reasoning was: since I receive a share of other people's fields at *yovel*, I should certainly receive my own field in its entirety. The *Gemara* objects: *mi dami* — are these comparable? *Hatam zocheh be'alma* — there, you receive a portion as part of a group; you are one of many *kohanim* who together inherit the distributed field. *Hacha ka shakil lei* — here, you want to take the entire field for yourself alone. Being entitled as a member of a group of a thousand to a fractional share of another's field is no basis for claiming sole individual ownership of your own field. The argument fails on its own terms.

### Korbanot Analogy

Rami bar Chama notes that despite the refutation, the *baraita*'s ruling remains necessary, because without it a *kohen* could have constructed a different argument. The verse states *ve-ish et kodashav lo yihiyu* — a man's sanctified offerings belong to him. This means a *kohen* who brings a *korban* to the *Beit HaMikdash* may declare himself the officiant for that offering and thereby retain the priestly portions. One might argue by analogy: just as a *kohen* can sanctify his *korban* and still benefit from it by performing the *avodah*, so too a *kohen* who sanctifies his field should be entitled to stand at the receiving end when the field is distributed at *yovel*.

The *Gemara* rejects this analogy: *mi dami? Kodashav lav birshuto, hacha birshuto* — your sacrificial portions are not yours in the ordinary sense of ownership; here, the field is fully yours. At first glance this seems to argue *in favor* of the *kohen*'s claim — the field started as his, so he should have greater rights, not fewer. But the *Gemara*'s point is more precise: by *korbanot*, the entitlement to benefit from the offering is grounded in having performed the *avodah*. The *kohen* brings his animal, performs the service, and by virtue of that service receives the meat. There is a functional basis for his receipt.
