Here, by contrast, once the *kohen* has sanctified the field, there is nothing that entitles him to be the one who receives it at the other end. His prior ownership provides no operative claim once he has removed the field from his domain through *hekdesh*. The analogy to *korbanot* therefore cannot sustain his argument.

### Acharit Olam

Rav Nachman identifies a final, more fundamental argument that required the *Torah*'s explicit ruling to refute. The verse states *ka-achuzat olam hi lahem* — it is an eternal inheritance for them — referring to the *leviim* and *kohanim* with respect to their *arei leviim*. One might have reasoned as follows: since the *leviim* and *kohanim* have the principle of *geulat olam* operative for their *arei leviim*, perhaps that same principle should extend to everything they hold permanently — including the *sedeh charmo* and other fields they receive through *cherem* or through distributions at *yovel*. After all, these too are their permanent inheritance. If the *acharit olam* — the eternal inheritance — is the basis for *geulat olam* in *arei leviim*, should it not equally apply to all things they hold permanently?

Therefore the *Torah* teaches: *achuzato in, cherem lo* — the special rights of *geulat olam* apply to their genuine ancestral inheritance, the *arei leviim*, and not to property acquired through *cherem* or through the *yovel* distributions. Fields that *kohanim* receive permanently through *cherem* or similar mechanisms have the same legal status as a *sedeh achuza* of an ordinary Israelite. If sanctified, they leave the *kohen*'s control at *yovel* and are distributed equally among all the *kohanim*.

This final point brings the *perek* to a clean and satisfying conclusion. The organizing distinction throughout has been between the *arei leviim* — the true, Divinely allocated inheritance of the tribe — and everything else that *kohanim* and *leviim* may come to hold permanently. Only the former carries the privilege of *geulat olam*. All else follows the ordinary rules applicable to any Israelite's *sedeh achuza*.

*Hadran alakh ha-mocher sadehu, ve-slik lah Masekhet Arakhin.*

# Temurah 2

## Temurah Overview

### Masechet Overview

Masechet Temurah, like many of the tractates toward the end of Seder Kodashim, spans approximately thirty *daf* — roughly a month of study. What makes *Temurah* particularly fascinating, especially at its outset, is the phenomenon it describes: a halachic act that is simultaneously a transgression and an effective legal deed. This tension is not merely academic; it drives virtually every discussion in the *masechet* and invites a broader inquiry into how the Torah relates prohibition to halachic consequence.

### Prohibition & Effect

The opening *mishnah* is grounded in a pair of *psukim* at the end of *Parshat Bechukotai* — the same section of Torah that underlies Masechet Erchin. On one hand, the Torah states *lo yachalifenu velo yamir oto tov bera o ra betov*: one may not attempt to exchange or substitute a sanctified animal. This is a clear negative prohibition. Yet the very next phrase reads, *ve'im hamir yamir behema behema, vehaya hu utmurato yihye kodesh*: if one nonetheless proceeds to do so, both the original animal and the substituted animal become *kadosh*.

This is a striking feature of *temurah*. One might have expected the Torah to simply ignore an act done in violation of its own command — if you murder someone, the physical reality remains, but here we are dealing with halachic status, which the Torah itself assigns. What actually happens in *temurah* is not a clean transfer: the *kedushah* does not leave the first animal. Rather, the owner attempted to move it, violated a prohibition, and now finds himself with two sanctified animals instead of one. The halachic impact of his transgression is thus real, even if it did not achieve everything he intended.

This dynamic is what makes *Temurah* so distinctive. Much of the *masechet* is devoted to analyzing the *effect* of *temurah* — when does it apply? What is the status of the second animal? Can it be brought as a *korban*? — and one can easily lose sight of the fact that every single case under discussion involves someone who transgressed a negative prohibition and is liable for *malkot*. The *mishnah* puts this front and center from the very first line, both to acknowledge it and, in a sense, to bracket it: we will spend most of our time analyzing the consequences of the act, setting aside — though never forgetting — the sin that occasioned them.

### Hakol Memirin

The *mishnah* opens: *hakol memirin, echad anashim ve'echad nashim* — everybody can perform *temurah*, whether men or women. Immediately, the *Gemara* flags a linguistic difficulty. The phrase *hakol memirin* — "everybody performs *temurah*" — sounds as though the act is permitted *l'chatchila*, which it plainly is not. The *mishnah* itself then adds *lo she'adam rashai lehamir*: a person is not permitted to do this. So what exactly does the word *memirin* mean?

The *Gemara* is pointed in its response: *tishbera* — does it really make sense to think *hakol memirin* means it is permitted? Even without the clarification in the *mishnah*, the *pasuk* itself says *lo yachalifenu velo yamir oto*. The apparent contradiction is not between two clauses of the *mishnah*; the prohibition was never in question.

### Act Effectiveness

The genuine question, as the *Gemara* frames it, is what the term *memirin* actually means. The answer is provided by Rav Yehuda: *hakol matpisin b'temurah* — everybody's act of *temurah* is effective. The word *memirin* does not describe permitted conduct; it describes effective conduct. When the *mishnah* says *hakol memirin*, it means: whoever performs *temurah*, their act will take hold. The *kedushah* will indeed attach to the second animal. And to complete the picture: *lo she'adam rashai lehamir* — you are not permitted to do it — and *vesofeg et ha'arba'im* — you receive forty lashes for having done it.

This framing sets the agenda for the *masechet*: the word *memirin* is about efficacy, not permission.

## Sin vs Metaphysics (III)

### Core Question

Once we understand that *temurah* is both prohibited and effective, a deeper question arises: what is the relationship between those two facts? Is the halachic effect — that the second animal becomes *kadosh* — a natural metaphysical consequence of any act of *temurah*, independent of whether that act is sinful? Or is it specifically a consequence of having sinned — a kind of divine penalty imposed by the Torah on one who transgresses?

Put differently: if the act of *temurah* were not a violation at all, would the *kedushah* still transfer? Are the natural metaphysical laws of *kedushah* such that an attempt to move it from one animal to another always results in the second animal becoming sanctified, even as the first retains its status? Or is it only because the Torah wishes to punish the transgressor — you tried to do this, and now you will suffer the consequence of having two *kadosh* animals — that the second animal becomes sanctified at all?

This question will recur across several subsequent discussions and is one of the animating conceptual tensions of the entire *daf*.

## Heir Ownership

### Heir Question

The *Gemara* now turns to parse the word *hakol* in the *mishnah*. Since men and women are explicitly mentioned later in the *mishnah*, the word *hakol* — "everybody" — must be coming to include someone not otherwise obvious. *Hakol le'atuyei mai?* What does "everybody" add? The *Gemara* answers: *le'atuyei yoresh* — it comes to include an heir.

The background assumption is that only the owner of a *korban* can perform *temurah*. The question is how to define "owner." If a person dies and his son inherits the sacrificial animal, is the son considered the owner? He will bring the *korban* on his father's behalf, but he did not originally sanctify it. Can he perform *temurah* on it? And correlatively, if the *temurah* were performed, would it take effect?

One might also ask whether he would be liable for *malkot* — after all, if he is not the owner, his act is entirely meaningless, and he would not even have transgressed. But the *Gemara*'s primary focus here is on the question of efficacy.

### Rabbi Meir

A *baraita* records the dispute directly: *yoresh somech, yoresh mamir, divrei Rabbi Meir* — an heir performs *semichah* and can perform *temurah*, in the view of Rabbi Meir. These are linked propositions: *semichah*, the laying of hands on the sacrifice, can only be performed by the owner of the *korban*. If I ask a friend to bring my *korban* to the *Beit HaMikdash* on my behalf, he may do so, but he does not perform *semichah* — only the owner does. Rabbi Meir holds that an heir becomes, in effect, the new owner of the inherited *korban*. He therefore does *semichah* when bringing it, and he is similarly positioned to perform *temurah*, the beginning of the process.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *yoresh eino somech veyoresh eino mamir* — the heir does not perform *semichah* and cannot perform *temurah*. In Rabbi Yehuda's view, the heir is not the owner; the true owner remains the deceased father. The heir will bring the *korban*, but the personal ownership required for *semichah* and *temurah* is simply absent.

What is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning? *Yalif techilat hekdesh misof hekdesh* — he derives the rule for the beginning of the process (*temurah*) from the end of the process (*semichah*). Just as an heir cannot perform *semichah* at the conclusion of the *korban*'s life cycle, so too he cannot perform *temurah* at its inception. *Temurah* is called the "beginning" here because, for the substituted animal, this act of *temurah* was what first brought it into *kedushah*. Conversely, *semichah* is the "end" — the culmination of the owner's personal involvement. Since Rabbi Yehuda holds that an heir cannot perform *semichah*, he likewise holds that he cannot perform *temurah*.

### Three Korbano

But how does Rabbi Yehuda know that an heir cannot perform *semichah*? The *Gemara* derives it from the word *korbano* — "his *korban*" — which appears three times in the context of *shlamim* in the Torah. Each appearance of *korbano* is understood to convey a distinct exclusion in the context of *semichah*.

The first exclusion: *korbano velo korban oved kochavim* — "his" means his, not that of a non-Jew. A non-Jew can bring a *korban* and sanctify animals, and we will discuss this at length. But the non-Jew's *korban* does not receive *semichah* — not by the non-Jew himself, and the *kohanim* do not perform *semichah* on his behalf either. The more familiar *drasha* derives the exclusion of non-Jews from *semichah* from the phrase *daber el bnei Yisrael* — *bnei Yisrael somchin velo ovdei kochavim somchin*. Here we have an additional dimension: even if we set aside the non-Jew's own inability to perform *semichah*, the *kohanim* also cannot stand in for him. His *korban* simply does not receive *semichah* at all.

The second exclusion: *korbano velo korban chavero* — his, and not his friend's. If Reuven asks Shimon to bring his *korban* for him, Shimon cannot perform *semichah* on it. The importance of this is conceptual: *semichah* expresses a deeply personal connection between the owner and his animal, emphasizing that this *korban* is truly his. Some understand *semichah* as a symbolic act in which the owner identifies with the animal as his substitute; even without adopting that position fully, *semichah* communicates personal ownership and connection. When someone else brings my *korban*, that connection is absent, and *semichah* is therefore inappropriate.

The third exclusion: *korbano velo korban aviv* — his, and not his father's. This is where the heir is excluded. The inherited *korban* remains, in some fundamental sense, the father's — and it is not sufficiently the son's own for *semichah* to apply.

### Partnership Ownership

Rabbi Meir, who holds that an heir *can* perform *semichah*, reads the third instance of *korbano* differently. For him, it is inclusive rather than exclusive: *lerabot kol ba'alei chovrin l'smicha* — it comes to include all members of a partnership *korban*. If three people jointly purchase and sanctify an animal, each one is a co-owner, and each must perform *semichah*. The word *korbano* conveys that every owner — each *ba'al* in the partnership — performs *semichah* on his *korban*.

One might then ask: does Rabbi Meir need to use one of the three instances of *korbano* for the heir and the other for the partnership? The *Gemara* addresses this. Rabbi Meir argues that the exclusions of a non-Jew and a friend actually derive from a single *pasuk*, since both cases reduce to the same question: can someone who is not the owner perform *semichah*? The non-Jew's *korban* is brought by *kohanim* who are not its owner; a friend bringing my *korban* is not its owner. Since they share the same underlying logic, one *pasuk* covers both. This frees up the second *pasuk* for the heir, and the third for the partnership.

What does Rabbi Yehuda do with the partnership case? *Ba'alei chovrin l'smicha leit lei* — he does not accept that partners perform *semichah* at all. The reasoning is consistent with his overall position: when multiple people own the *korban* jointly, no single individual has that intense personal connection to the animal that *semichah* demands. It is a more corporate relationship, and therefore *semichah* does not apply. Alternatively, the *Gemara* offers a second approach: Rabbi Yehuda could hold that partners do perform *semichah*, deriving it together with the heir from two separate *psukim*, while combining the non-Jew and the friend under a single *pasuk* — exactly as Rabbi Meir did, but arriving at a different allocation.

## Women & Temurah

### Women Inclusion

Having established that *hakol* in the *mishnah* comes to include the heir, the *Gemara* turns to the explicit inclusion of women in the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states *echad anashim ve'echad nashim* — the laws of *temurah* apply equally to men and women. The difficulty is that the entire *parsha* of *temurah* in the Torah is written in the masculine form. As the *baraita* states: *lefi she'kol ha'inyan kulo eino medaber ela bi'leshon zachar* — the entire passage is written in the male gender, as in *lo yachalifenu* and *lo yamir oto*, with masculine grammatical forms throughout. Since the Torah generally uses the masculine as its default, one might not automatically know whether women are included.

### Hamir Yamir

The source for including women is the doubled expression *hamir yamir*: if *temurah* is performed, both animals are *kadosh*. The doubled form functions as an inclusive device, extending the prohibition and its effect beyond the literal address of the *pasuk*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who does not include the heir through this language, the doubling of *hamir yamir* comes entirely to include women. According to Rabbi Meir, who derives the inclusion of the heir from *hamir yamir*, the inclusion of women comes from the additional word *ve'im* — the conjunction at the beginning of *ve'im hamir yamir*, which he treats as a separate inclusive particle. Rabbi Yehuda, for his part, does not attach independent halachic weight to the *vav* of *ve'im*, and so he does not need it.

Both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree that women are included in *temurah*.

### Exclusion Logic

This raises a philosophical question that the *Gemara* does not let pass: if the entire Torah is written in *lashon zachar* and we always interpret that as including women unless explicitly excluded, why would we have needed a special verse to include women in *temurah* at all? What possible basis could there have been for excluding women from a negative prohibition?

The *Gemara* responds by citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, and the same ruling appears as a *tannaic* teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *ish o ishah ki ya'asu mi'kol chatot ha'adam* — if a man or a woman commits any of the sins of humanity, the Torah explicitly equates women and men for all punishments in the Torah. Nevertheless, a potential basis for exclusion can be constructed.

The *Gemara* suggests: one might have thought that this principle of equating men and women applies only to prohibitions that are uniform — that apply equally at the individual and communal level. *Temurah*, however, is specifically excluded from communal application: *ein hatzibur veha'shutfin osin temurah* — neither communal *korbanot* nor partnership *korbanot* can have *temurah* performed on them. *Temurah* is uniquely the domain of the private, fully individual *korban*. Since in some sense not everyone is included — groups and partnerships are excluded — perhaps women too might have been excluded from the prohibition and its effect. The verse therefore comes to teach that they are not.

## Heir Ownership (II)

### Communal vs Partnership

It is worth noting here a point of distinction between *korban tzibur* — a communal sacrifice representing all of *Klal Yisrael* — and a *korban shutfin*, a partnership sacrifice of a small group. These are different categories. The earlier discussion comparing *semichah* and *temurah* in the context of ownership was primarily about whether one is considered the owner at all. The exclusion of *shutfin* from *temurah* is not precisely the same as saying they are not the owners; rather, it reflects a different quality of ownership — not the intense personal relationship that *temurah* requires. This is an important nuance: the discussion of ownership for the purposes of *semichah* and the discussion of what kind of *korban* is eligible for *temurah* are related but not identical considerations.

## Women & Temurah (II)

### Speech Act

There is a further reason the *Gemara* considers why women might have been excluded. Rashi records an alternative *girsa* of this passage, one that identifies a distinct *chiddush* in *temurah*: unlike virtually all other prohibitions for which one receives *malkot*, the prohibition of *temurah* is violated through speech alone. No physical action is required — one simply declares the exchange, and the prohibition is transgressed. Ordinarily, a purely verbal transgression does not carry *malkot*; *temurah* is exceptional in that it does. Because *temurah* is such an anomaly in this respect, one might have entertained the possibility that it is anomalous in other ways as well — perhaps in ways that would affect who is subject to it.

### Rashi's Girsa

Rashi acknowledges that this remains an odd *hava amina*: the general principle is that wherever the Torah does not explicitly exclude women, the use of *lashon zachar* does not suffice to exclude them. Still, the *Gemara* is trying to articulate what *kind* of reasoning one would have needed to overcome in order to include women — and the double novelty of *temurah*, both as a violation that takes effect despite being prohibited and as a violation achieved through speech alone, provides at least a theoretical basis for questioning the default inclusion.

## Sin vs Metaphysics (III)

### Minor Case

The *Gemara* now returns to the central conceptual question. Rami bar Chama poses the following: *katan mahu she'yamir* — can a minor perform *temurah*? The case requires careful framing. As the *Gemara* immediately specifies, if the minor has not yet reached *onot nedarim* — the age, approximately one year before *bar* or *bat mitzvah*, at which the Torah recognizes a child's capacity to make vows and effect *hekdesh* — there is no question at all. If he cannot create *kedushah* in the first place, he obviously cannot perform *temurah* on an animal that cannot be "his *korban*." One might argue that there is a difference between creating *kedushah* and transferring *kedushah* that already exists, but the practical point remains: without ownership of the *korban*, there is no basis for *temurah*.

### Minor Punishment

The genuine question concerns a minor who *has* reached *onot nedarim* — one who understands the significance of *hekdesh* and vows and is within a year of *bar* or *bat mitzvah*. Such a child can sanctify animals; the Torah recognizes his capacity to do so based on the principle of *mufla ha'samuch le'ish*, derived from the verse *ki yafli neder*. Given that he can create *kedushah*, perhaps we should say: *mide'akdushei makdish, amurei nami mameir* — since he can effect *kedushah*, he can also perform *temurah*. That would follow if *temurah* is understood as a natural extension of the power to sanctify, a metaphysical capacity.

On the other hand: *keivan de'lav bar onshin hu, tmurah nami lo mitfsa* — since he is not yet subject to punishment, the *temurah* will also not take effect. If the effectiveness of *temurah* is tied to the transgression — if it is, in some sense, the Torah's response to sin — then a child who is not yet *bar onshin* should not be able to trigger that response, even if he has the underlying *kedushah* capacity.

### Minor Metaphysics

The *Gemara* leaves the question unresolved, and then introduces a conditional follow-up: *im timtza lomar katan avid temurah* — if we were to say that a minor can perform *temurah*, perhaps that is specifically because he is *de'ati likhlal onshin* — because he will eventually become an adult and enter the category of punishment. Even within the model that ties *temurah*'s effect to sin, the minor is not entirely outside that framework; he stands on its threshold. His *temurah* might work because the concept of *temurah* as a sinful act is relevant to him, even if not yet applicable in practice.

## Non-Jew Case

### Non-Jew Setup

This conditional leads directly to the parallel case of the non-Jew: *oved kochavim mahu she'yamir* — can a non-Jew perform *temurah*? The *Gemara* notes that a non-Jew does have the power to sanctify. The *baraita* derives this from the double expression *ish ish* — "any man" who brings a *korban* — understood as inclusive of non-Jews, who may make *nedarim* and *nedavot* like Jews. So he has *kedushah* capacity. Yet he is not merely not yet subject to the laws of *temurah* — he will never be. He is categorically outside the prohibition. The question is whether this categorical exclusion also removes the metaphysical efficacy of his act.

## Sin vs Metaphysics (III)…

### Frameworks

At this point the *Gemara* draws out the two frameworks clearly. One way to understand the question is in terms of *temurah* as a consequence of a sinful act. On this model, a minor's *temurah* might still work because, even though he personally has not sinned, the act itself belongs to the category of sin — a category that will eventually be relevant to him. A non-Jew, by contrast, cannot even in principle transgress this prohibition, so the framework of sin is entirely foreign to his situation.

The second way to frame the question is not about sin at all, but about membership in the *parsha* — in the halachic category. Many halachic acts require the performer to belong to a certain category. *Shechita*, for instance, requires a Jew; a minor can perform it validly, but a non-Jew cannot. This has nothing to do with whether there is a *mitzvah* on the Jew and not the non-Jew — it is about being within the *parsha*, the framework of the relevant halachot. On this reading, the minor who will become an adult is within the *parsha* of *temurah*, and therefore the metaphysics of *temurah* apply to him; a non-Jew who stands permanently outside the *parsha* is beyond its reach. The underlying question — whether *temurah*'s effect is about sin or about the metaphysics of *kedushah* — remains the animating concern.

## Non-Jew Case (II)

### Weaker Kedusha

Rava now attempts to bring a *tannaic* source to resolve the question. The *baraita* states: *kodshei ovdei kochavim lo nehenin ve'lo mo'alin* — the sanctified animals of non-Jews, while genuinely sanctified, do not carry the same weight of *kedushah* as those of Jews. Two immediate consequences follow. First, one does not benefit from them in a halachically significant sense at the biblical level. Second, one does not transgress the biblical prohibition of *me'ilah* — the violation of sanctified property — with respect to them.

### Kedusha Implications

The *baraita* continues with further implications of this diminished *kedushah*: *ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul notar ve'tamei* — one does not incur liability for *pigul* (improper intention in the offering), *notar* (leftover sacrificial meat), or *tumah* (ritual impurity). These are all severe prohibitions precisely because they represent an affront to the full sanctity of a *korban*. The underlying logic of the *baraita* is that the sacrifices of non-Jews, while accepted and brought on the altar, carry a lesser degree of *kedushah*, and therefore the full constellation of sacrificial prohibitions does not apply to them.

And flowing from this: *ein osin temurah* — one cannot perform *temurah* on the *korban* of a non-Jew. There is the answer, at least technically. The question Rami bar Chama raised — can a non-Jew perform *temurah*? — appears to be answered: no.

### Nesachim

The *baraita* adds: *ve'ein mevi'in nesachim aleihem* — non-Jews do not bring *nesachim*, the drink offerings of wine, flour, and oil. Rashi, however, notes that the straightforward reading creates a difficulty, since in practice *nesachim* are indeed brought together with the *korban* of a non-Jew. He therefore understands the statement to mean that non-Jews cannot bring *nesachim* separately — that is, they cannot bring *nesachim* in connection with their animal on a day other than when the animal itself is offered. Whereas a Jewish owner may, under certain conditions, link his *nesachim* to a prior offering on a later day, for the *korban* of a non-Jew the *nesachim* must be brought together with the sacrifice itself.

### Shimon & Yosi

The *baraita* then records a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosi. Rabbi Shimon is the source of all the above leniencies regarding the *kedushah* of non-Jewish sacrifices. Rabbi Yosi, however, disagrees: *bechulan ani ro'eh lehachmir* — in all of these matters I rule stringently. Rabbi Yosi holds that the *korban* of a non-Jew carries full *kedushah*. The *baraita* then qualifies the scope of the dispute: *bamah devarim amurim? Be'kadshei mizbe'ach* — this debate pertains to *kadshei mizbe'ach*, sacrifices offered on the altar. *Aval be'kadshei bedek ha'bayit, mo'alin bahen ke'din me'ilah* — with regard to sanctifications dedicated to the Temple treasury, everyone agrees that *me'ilah* applies in full. Thus, the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosi is limited to altar-offerings, with Rabbi Shimon holding they carry diminished *kedushah* and Rabbi Yosi holding they carry full *kedushah*.

For our purposes, at least according to Rabbi Shimon, the explicit statement *ein osin temurah* settles the technical question: there is no *temurah* on the *korban* of a non-Jew.

### Non-Jew for Jew

Yet the *Gemara* notes that this answer, while technically satisfying, does not fully resolve the conceptual question that Rami bar Chama was pursuing. When the *baraita* states that *temurah* does not apply to the *korban* of a non-Jew, it presumably refers to the standard case: the non-Jew sanctified the animal for himself — *hikdish oved kochavim le'hitkaper oved kochavim*. In that scenario, the *kedushah* is the weaker variety associated with a non-Jew's own sacrifice, and the inability to perform *temurah* may simply reflect the insufficiency of that *kedushah*, not any ruling about the relationship between sin and halachic effect.

The genuine question Rami bar Chama is asking, however, is a different one: *behikdish oved kochavim umitkaper be'Yisrael* — what if a non-Jew sanctified an animal as a *korban* for a *Yisrael*? This is possible: one may sanctify an animal to serve as the *korban* of another, such that the *makdish* is the non-Jew and the *mitkaper* — the one on whose behalf atonement is made — is a Jew. In that case, we might suppose the *kedushah* is full and equivalent to that of any Jewish *korban*, since it is dedicated to a Jewish purpose within the Temple's primary framework. Now, with full *kedushah* in place, can the non-Jew who did the sanctifying perform *temurah*? If *temurah*'s effect depends on the power of *kedushah*, the answer should be yes. If it depends on the transgression — on being within the framework of a sin — the answer should be no, since the non-Jew is categorically beyond the reach of that prohibition.

This is the genuinely unresolved question with which the *daf* concludes, and the discussion will resume in the subsequent session.

# Temurah 3

## Temurah Basics

### Masechet Overview

Masechet Temurah opens with the straightforward biblical prohibition: *lo yachlifenu velo yamir oto* — one may not transfer or substitute a consecrated animal. Yet, as becomes immediately apparent, the *masechet* devotes the overwhelming bulk of its attention not to the prohibition itself but to its consequences. The Torah states: *ve'im hamir yamir behemah bivehemah vehayah hu utemurato yihyeh kodesh* — if one attempts the exchange, the *kedusha* is not removed from the first animal, and the second animal also becomes *kadosh*. In many cases, that second animal may even be brought as a *korban*. The central drama of the *masechet*, then, is what happens after someone has violated the prohibition — what are the legal effects of that transgression?

### Why Do It?

This raises an immediate question: why would anyone attempt *temurah* in the first place? Nobody in their right mind would do so. The transgressor violates a prohibition, yet accomplishes nothing: the first animal retains its *kedusha*, and if one wished to sanctify the second animal, one could do so directly. The entire scenario seems to presuppose either genuine foolishness or, more plausibly, someone who knows the act is prohibited but does not appreciate its legal futility.

### Sin & Lashes

Does this lack of awareness about the consequences affect one's liability for *malkus*? It does not. To incur lashes, one must willfully transgress a prohibition — but one need not fully understand the legal consequences of that transgression. A person who knows that substitution is forbidden, yet does it anyway while remaining unaware that it will leave the first animal *kadosh* and render the second *kadosh* as well, has still willfully violated the *lav* and is liable. The transgression consists simply in uttering the words of substitution; no physical act is required. That alone constitutes the violation.

### Torah's Reason

This brings into focus a deeper question about the nature of the prohibition. If someone were to say, "I simply want the second animal to become *kadosh* as well, without intending to remove the *kedusha* from the first," that would not constitute *temurah* at all. *Temurah* is defined specifically as the *attempt to substitute* — to remove *kedusha* from the first animal and transfer it to the second. The Torah's prohibition targets this attempt. Even though the attempt fails on its own terms, the Torah forbids the very act of trying to replace one *korban* with another.

### Sin vs Effect

This leads to a fundamental question that animates much of the discussion: is the consequence of *temurah* — that both animals become *kadosh* — a *punishment* imposed because of the sin, or is it simply the natural legal *consequence* of having applied *kedusha* to the second animal? The *gemara* frames this question sharply: what if the person who performed *temurah* committed no sin?

## Temurah & Sin

### Minor's Temurah

The *gemara* explores this through two cases. First: a minor. A child who is within approximately one year of *bar* or *bat mitzvah* and who understands what he or she is doing has the capacity to create *kedusha*. If such a minor utters the formula of *temurah* — declaring that this non-*korban* animal should stand in place of the *korban* — has the minor sinned? Not in a full halachic sense. Does the second animal nevertheless become *kadosh*? This question goes to the heart of whether *temurah*'s effect is about sin or about the act. The *gemara* leaves this as an unresolved question.

### Non-Jew Case

The second and more pointed case is that of a non-Jew. A non-Jew can sanctify an animal and bring it as a *korban* — the *halacha* accepts this. But for a non-Jew, there is no concept of sin with respect to *temurah* at all, in a qualitatively different sense than a minor. Can a non-Jew perform *temurah*? The *gemara* notes that this question is, in a sense, moot: one of the established *halachot* governing the status of *mukdashei akum* — animals sanctified by non-Jews — is that *temurah* cannot be performed on them. The question therefore cannot be tested in the simple form in which it was posed.

### Rav Abahu

But the *gemara* then refines the question. *Ki kamibaya li behekdesh akum miskaper beyisrael* — the real question is when a non-Jew sanctifies an animal for a Jew to use as his *korban*. In such a case, the non-Jew provides the animal, but it is the Jew's *korban*. So who is the relevant party for *temurah*: the one who sanctified (*makdish*), or the one for whom the *korban* is being brought (*miskaper*)?

To resolve this, the *gemara* cites the principle of Rav Abahu in the name of Rav Yochanan: *hamakdish mosif chomesh* — the one who sanctifies an object is the one who must add the *chomesh* (the additional fifth) when redeeming it. Anyone else who redeems *hekdesh* pays only the market value. This establishes that in the *chomesh* context, we follow the *makdish*, not someone else. However: *umiskaper oseh temurah* — by contrast, when it comes to *temurah*, it is the *miskaper*, the one for whom the *korban* is being brought, who is considered the owner and who can perform *temurah*. If I sanctify my animal for another Jew to use as his *korban*, it is now his *korban*, and he — not I — would be in a position to perform *temurah* (and thereby transgress).

A parallel case is cited: *hatorem mishelo al chavero tovat hana'ah shelo* — if one takes *terumot u'ma'asrot* from one's own grain in order to exempt a friend's grain, the *terumah* and *ma'aser* so separated belong to the one who did the separating, not the friend. So the one who separated gets to designate which *kohen* receives it, not the friend whose grain was also covered. This illustrates how these roles of *makdish* and *miskaper* are parsed differently in different contexts.

### Hybrid Case

Returning to the *sha'aleh*: if a non-Jew sanctified the animal, but it is now being used as a Jew's *korban*, do we say it is a fully valid *korban Yisrael* such that the Jew can now perform *temurah* on it? Or does the fact of the non-Jewish sanctification leave the animal at a lesser level of *kedusha*, one that cannot be the subject of *temurah* even when the *miskaper* is a Jew?

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this from Rav Abahu's ruling, but the attempt fails. The *gemara* responds: *hasam hu dekasi mikoach yisrael* — in Rav Abahu's case, a Jew sanctified the animal for another Jew, so it began with a Jew and ends with a Jew. *Vehavlei techilato vesofo beyad yisrael.* Therefore it was obvious that the *korban* retained its full Jewish *kedusha* and only the question of ownership needed to be resolved. *Aval hacha hacha kamibaya li* — but in our case the entire question is whether we require that the animal remain in the domain of someone capable of performing *temurah* from beginning to end. The *gemara* concludes: *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

It is worth pausing on what has happened here. The original question — does *temurah* require sin, and thus can a minor or non-Jew perform it? — has been substantially reframed. The question about the non-Jew, specifically in the hybrid case, has shifted away from the person of the non-Jew and toward the *kedusha* of the animal. The *gemara* is no longer asking about whether sinfulness is required for *temurah*'s effect, but rather whether the level of *kedusha* imparted by a non-Jew's sanctification is the type of *kedusha* upon which *temurah* can operate. That question remains open.

Rashi, it is worth noting, comments that although the *gemara* left the minor's case as an open question, he understood the conclusion to be that a minor cannot perform *temurah*. If that is correct, it implies that some connection to sin is indeed required for *temurah*'s effect. But if a minor can perform *temurah*, the relationship between sin and the act of *temurah* remains genuinely unresolved.

## Non-Jew Sanctity

### Mukdashei Akum

Having been drawn into the subject by the discussion of the non-Jew's *korban*, the *gemara* now turns to a sustained analysis of *mukdashei ovdei kochavim* — animals sanctified as *korbanot* by non-Jews. The *braita* states: *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — one may not derive benefit from such animals, yet one does not transgress the biblical prohibition of *me'ilah*. This captures the intermediate status of these *korbanot*: they possess genuine *kedusha* yet at a diminished level, such that while benefit is rabbinically prohibited, the biblical *me'ilah* violation is not triggered.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — how do we derive that there is no *me'ilah* for a non-Jew's *korban*? The verse states: *nefesh ki tim'ol ma'al vechata'ah bishgagah* — if a *nefesh* transgresses *me'ilah* in error. From the word *nefesh*, a *gezeirah shavah* is made to *terumah*, where the verse uses the same language of sinning, and in the context of *terumah* it is written *bnei Yisrael*. The *gemara* concludes: the limitation to *bnei Yisrael* applies equally here, meaning only things sanctified by Jews carry the full *me'ilah* liability. A non-Jew can sanctify a *korban* — this is indeed a significant *chiddush* — but the *kedusha* of that *korban* does not carry the same set of legal consequences.

### Temurah Exclusion

In this same context, the *braita* states: *ve'ein osin temurah* — one cannot perform *temurah* on animals sanctified by a non-Jew. The derivation: the prohibition *lo yachlifenu velo yamir oto* appears at the end of a *parsha* that opens *Daber el bnei Yisrael*. Since the *parsha* of *temurah* is contextualized within a framework addressed to *bnei Yisrael*, the same limitation applies — only *bnei Yisrael*, not non-Jews.

## Non-Jew Sanctity (II)

### Two Drashot

A second derivation for the exclusion of non-Jews from *temurah* is offered: *de'itkesh temurah behemah le'ma'aser behemah* — *temurah* is *hekesh*'d to *ma'aser behemah*. The Torah discusses *temurah* in the general case and then specifically in the context of *ma'aser behemah*, as both passages use the same language of *lo yachlifenu velo yamirenu*. *Ma'aser behemah* is in turn linked to *ma'aser dagan*, and by *ma'aser dagan* it is written *ki et ma'asar bnei Yisrael asher yarimu l'Hashem* — specifically *bnei Yisrael*.

The two derivations address, in effect, different aspects of the exclusion. The first *drasha* — from the opening of the *parsha* — excludes the *person* of the non-Jew: a non-Jew's act of *temurah* has no legal force. The second *drasha* — through the chain of *hekesh* — focuses on the *kedusha* of the animal itself: an animal whose sanctification derives from a non-Jew does not possess the category of *kedusha* upon which *temurah* can operate. This distinction becomes practically relevant in the hybrid case discussed earlier: when a non-Jew sanctifies an animal for a Jew, the person of the non-Jew is no longer the operative party, but the *kedusha* imparted by the non-Jew may still be of the lesser type. That is the precise question that was left as *teiku*.

### Nesachim

The *braita* further states: *ve'ein mevi'in nesachim aleihem* — one does not bring *nesachim* with the *korbanot* of non-Jews. Yet: *vekorbano ta'un nesachim divrei Rabbi Shimon* — his *korban* does require *nesachim*. The apparent tension is resolved as follows: the non-Jew himself cannot be the provider of the *nesachim*; they come instead from the *tzibbur*. Rashi, citing another *gemara*, interprets this differently and removes the bracketed word *aleihem*, understanding that a non-Jew can in fact bring *nesachim* for his own *korban*, but unlike a Jew's *nesachim* which may come days after the *korban*, a non-Jew's *nesachim* must accompany the *korban* directly. The derivation: *debar el bnei Yisrael* — the verse introducing *nesachim* begins with *ezrach*, a citizen, meaning a Jew: *mevi nesachim ve'ein oved kochavim mevi nesachim*. Yet the *korban* itself requires *nesachim*, derived from *kacha ta'asu* — so shall you do.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi takes a stringent position: *ro'eh ani bechulah lehachmir* — he would apply full *kedusha* status to all *korbanot* of non-Jews, including *me'ilah*, *pigul*, *notar*, *tumah*, and *temurah*. His reasoning: the verse from which we derive that a non-Jew can sanctify a *korban* — *ish ish mipnei Yisrael asher yakriv korbano lashem* — explicitly concludes with *lashem*, dedicated to God. The dedication is to God with full force, and therefore carries full *kedusha* consequences.

### Types of Kedusha

Even the first opinion, which grants lesser status to a non-Jew's *korban*, limits that lesser status to *kodshei mizbe'ach* — animals brought on the altar as acts of worship. *Aval bekodshei bedek habayit* — if a non-Jew simply donates money or property to the *Beit HaMikdash*, that carries full *kedusha* and full *me'ilah* liability. How do we know? Because the derivation that limited *me'ilah* was based on a *gezeirah shavah* to *terumah*, and *terumah* is *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic *kedusha*, the kind that defines the identity of the object. *Kodshei bedek habayit*, by contrast, is *kedushat damim* — a monetary *kedusha*, a property transfer. The limitation derived from *terumah* applies only when the sanctification is of the *terumah*-type — intrinsic and identity-defining — not when it is a straightforward property donation to the Temple treasury.

## Lav Shein Bo Maase

### General Principle

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *kol lo ta'aseh she-ba-Torah, asah bo ma'aseh chayav, lo asah bo ma'aseh patur* — all negative prohibitions in the Torah: if one performed an act in violating them, one is liable to lashes; if no act was performed, one is exempt. This is the general principle of *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh*, and it is well established. The *gemara* now introduces it because the *masechet* is about to address one of the unusual features of our *mishnah*: the ruling that one who performs *temurah* incurs lashes — despite the fact that *temurah* consists entirely of a verbal act.

### Temurah Exception

Is the principle of Rav truly absolute? The *gemara* challenges immediately: *ve-harei meimar* — but consider *temurah*! It is a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — there is no physical act — yet our *mishnah* says *lo she-hu rashai lehamir, ela she'im hemir mumar, vesoveg et ha-arba'im* — you are not permitted to perform *temurah*, but if you did, it takes effect, and you receive forty lashes. That is a case of a purely verbal transgression resulting in lashes.

### Attribution

Rav's response: *hamani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — our *mishnah* follows the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh lokin alav* — that even without a physical act, lashes apply. The inference to Rabbi Yehuda's position comes from a *sugya* elsewhere concerning *notar*: two *tannaim* each exempt *notar* from lashes but for different reasons. Rabbi Yehuda's reason is *hatra'at safek* — the warning is doubtful, because when one is warned not to leave meat over, the transgression does not occur until hours later. Rabbi Yehuda does not cite the absence of an act as the reason for exemption, which implies that for him, absence of an act is not, by itself, a sufficient ground for exemption. Hence Rabbi Yehuda would agree that a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* can still carry lashes.

### Resolution

But this raises a difficulty: was not the beginning of our *mishnah* — the passage about heirs and who can perform *temurah* — established as *not* following Rabbi Yehuda? Rabbi Yehuda holds that an heir cannot perform *smicha* and cannot perform *temurah*, while our *mishnah* includes the heir as someone who can. How then can one part of the *mishnah* follow Rabbi Yehuda while another contradicts him?

The *gemara* resolves this: *hai tanna savar lei k'vosei b'chada u-falig lei b'chada* — the author of our *mishnah* agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point (*lav she'ein bo ma'aseh lokin alav* — lashes apply even without an act) and disagrees with him on another (the heir's status). This is entirely standard: a *tanna* may selectively adopt another *tanna*'s ruling on one issue without accepting the full range of that *tanna*'s positions.

## Exceptions

### Three Exceptions

Rav Idi bar Avin transmitted in the name of Rav Yitzchak, who transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, in the name of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili: *kol lo ta'aseh she-ba-Torah, asa bo ma'aseh lokei, lo asa bo ma'aseh patur* — the general principle is confirmed. But *chutz* — three exceptions: *min ha-nishba* — one who takes a false oath, *u-memir* — one who performs *temurah*, and *u-mekalel chaveiro ba-shem* — one who curses another with God's name. In all three cases, lashes apply despite the absence of a physical act.

Tosafot notes that there are arguably additional exceptions — *eidim zomemim* (false witnesses) and *motzi shem ra* (defamatory accusation) — but these are qualitatively different. There, while the transgression consisted of words, those words were aimed at real-world consequences: a person could have been executed on the basis of the testimony or the accusation. The speech was, in effect, a form of action with direct this-worldly impact. The three cases enumerated by Rabbi Yosi HaGlili are the more striking exceptions precisely because the words had no such direct real-world consequence: one performed *temurah* verbally, one took a vain oath, one uttered a curse. These are genuinely the hard cases for the principle.

### Shvuat Shav

The first exception: a false oath of *shvuat shav*. This is an oath that is utterly in vain — classically, swearing to something universally known to be true (or false). No purpose is served; the words themselves constitute the offense.

### Shvua Derivation

Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Meir: *ki lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa shemo lashav* — God will not cleanse one who takes His name in vain. From this the *gemara* derives a crucial structure.

### Courts & Kaparah

*Beit Din shel ma'alah ein menakin oto* — the heavenly court will not cleanse such a person. *Aval beit din shel matah malkin u-menakin oto* — but the earthly court can lash this person and thereby cleanse him. This reflects a deep understanding in *Chazal* that lashes are not merely punitive but serve as *kaparah* — they atone and restore the transgressor to a clean slate. The weight of *shvuat shav* is so great — which is why Jewish practice has historically avoided even truthful oaths — that without earthly intervention, the heavenly court will not forgive. But when *beit din* acts, the lashes function as a mechanism of atonement that restores the person's standing.

Rav Pappa asked: perhaps we should simply read *lo yenakeh* as meaning the person is never cleansed at all? The *gemara* responds: if so, the verse should have written simply *lo yenakeh* and stopped there. The explicit mention of *Hashem* indicates that *God*, on His own, will not cleanse — but the human court, acting through its authority, can do so.

### Shvuat Sheker

The *gemara* turns to *shvuat sheker* — a false oath about something that is not obviously vain. How do we know that *shvuat sheker* also incurs lashes? Rabbi Yochanan, now in his own name, notes that the verse repeats *lashav* twice: once in *lo tisa et shem Hashem Elokecha lashav* and once in *ki lo yenakeh Hashem et asher yisa shemo lashav*. *Im eino inyan lishvuat shav* — since one repetition suffices for the case of a vain oath, the second comes to teach us: *tnehu inyan lishvuat sheker* — apply it to a false oath as well, *delokei* — that lashes apply there too.

### Shvuat Sheker

But what type of *shvuat sheker* does this refer to? Rav Pappa presses the question. If the false oath concerns the future — "I swear I will not eat" — and then one eats, the act of eating is itself the violation: *hatam hama'aseh avid* — there, an act was performed. That is not a case of *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* at all; the act of eating is the transgression of the *shvuah*. What about the other direction: one swears "I will eat this loaf today," and then does not eat it? A *gemara* in *Shvuot* records that both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree no lashes apply here, but for different reasons: Rabbi Yochanan because it is a *lav she'ein bo ma'aseh* — the violation was through inaction — and Reish Lakish because it is *hatra'at safek* — the warning is doubtful, since when warned, one has hours remaining before the transgression occurs, so the warning is not *samuch l'ma'aseh*, not juxtaposed to the act itself. For a valid *hatra'ah*, the warning must immediately frame the person's awareness that they are sinning now; a warning given long before the moment of transgression does not achieve that psychological immediacy.

### Future Oaths

So where do lashes apply for *shvuat sheker*? Rav Abahu answers: *b'achalti v'lo achalti* — when one swears about the past. "I ate" or "I did not eat." There, the focus is not on any future performance but on the speech act itself — the words of the oath are where the wrong occurs, just as in *shvuat shav*. And just as *shvuat shav* incurs lashes because the transgression inheres in the act of speaking, so too a *shvuat sheker* that is past-oriented, where the lie occurs at the moment of utterance, incurs lashes.

The *gemara* asks: why do we distinguish past-oriented *shvuat sheker* from future-oriented? Rava answers: *d'pishit kra sheker duma l'shav* — the verse equates *sheker* to *shav* by repeating *lashav* twice. *Ma shav l'shavar af sheker l'shavar* — just as *shav* involves something wrong in the present moment of speech, so too the *sheker* that incurs lashes must be the kind that is false at the very moment of utterance, i.e., past-oriented.

### Reconciliation

A *braita* then threatens to complicate matters. It describes *shvuat bituy* — a future-oriented oath of "I will not eat this loaf," which one then violates by eating — as the paradigmatic case for which one incurs lashes and, if violated inadvertently, brings a sliding-scale *korban*. By contrast, *shvuat shav* — where the violation is in the utterance itself — incurs lashes but the unintentional case is exempt from a *korban*. The *gemara* asks: does each of these formulations, by saying "this is the case," implicitly exclude the past-oriented *shvuat sheker* from lashes? If so, this would contradict our principle.

The *gemara* resolves the difficulty. The phrases *zo hi* — "this is the one" — are not intended to contrast with the past-oriented case at all. Rather, *mishum deka'ei lehaba memait lehaba* — since the *braita* is discussing future-oriented oaths throughout, its contrasts are internal to the future-oriented category. The contrast is between a future oath violated by an act (one swore not to eat and then ate — lashes apply) and a future oath violated by inaction (one swore to eat and then did not — no lashes). The past-oriented case is simply not in view; there is no implication whatsoever that it is exempt. With that resolved, the principle stands: a *shvuat sheker* about the past incurs lashes, because the speech act of swearing falsely is itself the violation.

### Speech as Action

This brings into relief the underlying principle that unifies all three exceptions: in each case, speech functions as a sufficient act. For *shvuat shav* and past-oriented *shvuat sheker*, the words of the oath are themselves the transgression — the speech act is where the wrong occurs. For *temurah*, similarly, the verbal declaration of substitution is the transgression. These are not cases of pure inaction; they are cases where the action is the speech itself. That is what distinguishes them from a future-oriented oath violated by inaction, where the expected act never occurred and thus there is no actionable performance to anchor the lashes. Where the speech is the act — where the wrong inheres in the words at the moment of their utterance — lashes apply even without any accompanying physical act.

---

---

# Temurah 5

## Abaye-Rava Debate Intro

### Fundamental Question

One of the most famous debates in all of Talmudic literature — known even to those who have never studied *Masechet Temurah* — opens at the bottom of daf 5b. It is the *machlokes* of Abaye and Rava concerning a deceptively simple question: if the Torah says "do not do" something, and a person goes ahead and does it anyway, does that act have a halachic effect?

It is important to clarify what kind of effect is at issue. No one disputes the physical, this-worldly consequences of a prohibited act — if a person steals, the money is in his pocket; if someone is murdered, the victim is dead. Nor is the question about punitive consequences, such as whether food cooked on Shabbos becomes forbidden in *hana'ah* (a position some *amoraim* hold but which we do not rule). The question concerns purely halachic or metaphysical change — a change in status — that results from an act the Torah has forbidden.

A useful illustration: a *kohen* is forbidden to marry a *gerushah*. If he does so, should the *kiddushin* take effect? On one hand, he violated the Torah's prohibition; on the other, a *lav* (negative prohibition) is less severe than an *issur kares* — everyone agrees that a marriage to a man's sister or to a married woman produces no *kiddushin*. The question is whether violating a *lav* is sufficient to prevent the halachic effect from taking hold.

### Abaye Position

Abaye holds: *im avid, mahani* — if you did it, it works. Even in violation, the act takes halachic effect. His proof is logical: *amai loki?* — why would the offender receive lashes? If a *kohen* tried to marry a *gerushah* but the *kiddushin* never took effect, then in what sense did he commit a transgression? You cannot receive lashes for a mere attempt. The fact that the Torah prescribes lashes implies that the prohibited act was realized — meaning it was effective.

### Rava Position

Rava holds: *im avid lo mahani* — if you did it, it does not take effect. His reasoning flows from an internal logic: if the entire act was in violation of the Torah's will, why should the Torah allow it to produce a halachic result? And as for lashes — *mishum de'avar ameimra deRachmana*, because he transgressed the word of God. According to Rava, lashes are imposed not because the act succeeded halachically, but simply because the person defied the Divine command. The transgression is the attempt itself, independent of whether the forbidden effect materialized.

With these two positions in place, the *Gemara* proceeds through a series of cases. In each, either Abaye or Rava will appear to be contradicted, and each will explain why the case before him is an exception to his general rule. One might wonder at the end whether the debate matters at all if every case can be explained away — and the *Gemara* will eventually identify one or two cases where the disagreement is genuinely operative. But this pattern, where a sweeping principled debate is followed by mutual concessions to the facts, is itself a classic Talmudic phenomenon.

---

## Rapist/Divorce Case

### Ones Shegeirash

The *Gemara* opens its first challenge with the case of *ones shegeirash* — a rapist who divorces the woman he was compelled to marry. The Torah requires that a man who rapes an unmarried woman marry her, and that once married, he may not divorce her (*lo yuchal leshalchah*). It must be acknowledged that these laws are deeply foreign to contemporary sensibilities; they can only be understood against the ancient social reality in which a woman who had been violated was frequently abandoned by her family and society, and the Torah sought at minimum to ensure she would have the security of marriage. The father or the woman may refuse, but assuming they do not, the marriage stands — and the man is thereafter forbidden to send her away.

If he nonetheless divorces her, the *braisa* states: *im Yisrael hu, machazir ve'eino lokeh* — if he is a non-*kohen*, he must take her back and does not receive lashes.

### First Version

The *Gemara*'s first framing of the challenge focuses on the lashes question. According to Rava — who says that transgressing a Divine command brings lashes even without the act being effective — why does this man not receive lashes? If we frame the matter as: he divorced her, and *kol yamav* teaches that the divorce cannot be allowed to stand permanently, then the reason he avoids lashes is that his divorce was not fully effective. But that reasoning works only for Abaye, who requires the act to be effective before lashes apply. According to Rava, the lack of a full effect should be irrelevant — he should still be lashed for transgressing.

### Rava's Mitzvah Answer

Rava responds: *shani hatam de'amar kra kol yamav* — there it is different, because the verse says *kol yamav*, "all his days." Tosafot explains that the correct framing is not about the incompleteness of the divorce but about a *mitzvas asei*: the Torah's statement of *kol yamav* creates an affirmative obligation to remarry, and that positive commandment counteracts the negative prohibition, thereby exempting him from lashes. This is the principle of *lav ha'nitak la'asei* — a negative prohibition that is linked to a corrective positive commandment does not result in lashes, because the positive act of rectification takes precedence.

The *Gemara*'s initial framing — which treated the avoidance of lashes as flowing from the divorce not being fully effective — was a somewhat confusing way to arrive at what is ultimately a straightforward answer: the positive *mitzvah* to remarry overrides the lashes. The *Gemara* does arrive there, but not before exploring the tension in how to read the interaction between the prohibition, the effect of the *gerushin*, and the obligation to restore the marriage.

### Lishna Achrina

A second version of the challenge (*lishna achrina*) reframes the issue. Here the *braisa* reads: *im Yisrael hu, machazir ve'eino lokeh; ve'im kohen, lokeh ve'eino machazir* — if a non-*kohen*, he remarries and is exempt from lashes; if a *kohen*, since he cannot remarry a *gerushah*, he receives lashes. This version focuses not on the lashes question but on the very fact that he remarries — which presupposes that the *gerushin* took effect. The Torah said do not divorce, he divorced, and it worked. This seems to support Abaye directly.

Yet the *Gemara* frames the challenge as *tiyuvta de'Abaye* — a difficulty for Abaye, not for Rava. Why? Tosafot addresses the apparent inversion: because the *Gemara* takes for granted that *gerushin* by its very nature takes effect — analogous to death, which severs the marriage without any halachic act of the wife. Since it is assumed from the outset that the divorce works (even according to Rava), the *Gemara* shifts focus to the *mitzvah* to reverse it. The obligation to remarry suggests the Torah refuses to allow the effect to be permanent — and this appears more aligned with Rava's view that violations are not meant to produce lasting halachic change. So the challenge to Abaye is: does not this case show that the Torah resists the permanence of a forbidden act's effect?

### Abaye on Kol Yamav

Abaye's response is: *shani hatam d'rachmana amar kol yamav* — there it is different, the Torah explicitly said *kol yamav*, and that creates an obligatory exception. As a general rule, Abaye maintains that forbidden acts do produce full and lasting effect. Here the Torah specifically intervenes to say otherwise. But that raises a question: if the Torah simply says *lo yuchal leshalchah*, that already means he may not divorce her. Why add *kol yamav*?

Abaye explains: *i lav de'amar Rachmana kol yamav, hava amina issura hu de'avid lei, i ba'ei lehader ve'i ba'ei lo lehader* — without the phrase *kol yamav*, one might have thought that reversing the divorce was his option, not his obligation. If he chose to remarry, his original act would lack a lasting effect and he would escape lashes; if he chose not to, he would be lashed. The Torah therefore said *kol yamav* to establish not an option but a binding obligation to remarry — regardless of his preference.

### Rava on Kol Yamav

Rava explains *kol yamav* differently. Without that phrase, he would have known from his own general principle that the divorce cannot be fully effective, and that the man would be obligated to reverse it. But he would also have concluded that lashes still apply, since the prohibition on divorce stands independently. The phrase *kol yamav* therefore comes to do more than merely obligate the remarriage — it transforms the case into a *lav she'nitak la'asei*, a negative prohibition attached to a positive corrective commandment: *l'shavyei l'ones lo ta'aseh she'nitak la'asei, d'ein lokin alav* — to establish that in the case of the rapist, the prohibition is of the type linked to a *mitzvas asei* and therefore carries no lashes.

---

## Terumah Bad-Good

### Terumah Mishna

The *Gemara* moves on to a cleaner set of examples drawn from the laws of *terumah* and *ma'aser*. The Torah states *mikol chelbo* — from all of its fat you shall take *terumah*, meaning from the best of the grain. The implication is that *terumah* must be taken from the superior portion — *chelbo in, geru'in lo* — not from inferior grain. It is worth noting that the violation here is not a classic *lav* in the form of an explicit negative prohibition; it is rather a departure from the prescribed manner of performing the *mitzvah*. Nonetheless, as Rashi and Tosafot note, Abaye and Rava debate not only explicit prohibitions but any act performed contrary to the Torah's direction — including *mitzvas asei* violations.

The *Mishnah* teaches: *ein tormin min hara al hayafa* — one may not take *terumah* from inferior grain upon superior grain, *ve'im taram, trumato trumah* — but if one did, it takes effect.

### Challenge to Rava

This is presented as *tiyuvta deRava*: the act was done contrary to the Torah's directive, yet it takes halachic effect. According to Rava's principle that violations do not produce halachic effects, this *terumah* should be null.

### Rava's Drasha

Rava responds: *shani hatam keRabbi Ila'i* — there it is different, based on a *drasha* of Rabbi Ila'i. The verse states, *velo tise'u alav chet beharimchem et chelbo mimenu* — "you shall not bear sin upon it when you take its fat from it." Rabbi Ila'i infers: if even when done improperly the *terumah* were not effective, why would there be a *chet*, a sin? If the act produced no halachic result, there would have been nothing to sin about. Therefore, *mikan* — from here we learn — that even when taken from the inferior upon the superior, it does take effect. That is why the Torah can say you will have sinned.

There is an important internal tension here, which Tosafot raises: Rabbi Ila'i's *drasha* appears to simply restate Abaye's logic — that an act only constitutes a *chet* if it was effective. How can Rava, who rejects that logic, rely on this *drasha*? Tosafot resolves this by reading the *drasha* differently: it is not the mere fact that the Torah calls it a *chet*, but the redundancy and emphasis of the verse that signals a special case. The Torah went out of its way to underscore that this particular act constitutes a sin precisely because — unlike the general rule — it does have an effect. The emphasis marks it as an exception, not as a universal principle.

### Abaye's Reading

According to Abaye, who already knows that violations produce effects, why does this verse need to say *velo tise'u alav chet*? *I lav de'amar Rachmana velo tise'u alav chet, hava amina avid mitzvah min hamuvchar* — without it, one might have thought that taking from the best on the best is simply the ideal (*l'chatchila*), but that taking from the inferior on the superior, while not ideal, does not rise to the level of *chet*. The verse therefore teaches us that it is not merely a failure to fulfill the *mitzvah* in the best manner — it is an actual sin.

---

## Species-to-Species Terum…

### Species Rule

The next case involves taking *terumah* from one species of produce on a different species. The Torah states: *kol cheilev yitzhar v'kol cheilev dagan v'tirosh reishitam* — all the fat of the oil, and all the fat of the grain and wine, their *reishit* you shall give. By separating the species into distinct phrases — oil on one side, grain and wine on the other — the Torah implies that each species must give *terumah* from within itself: grain on grain, wine on wine, oil on oil. The principle: *leitein cheilev lazeh v'cheilev lazeh* — the "fat" designation applies to each species separately.

The *Mishnah* teaches: *ein tormin mimin al she'eino mino* — one may not take *terumah* from one species upon a different species, *ve'im taram, ein tromaso trumah* — and if one did, it does not take effect. Here the violation renders the act null. This seems to validate Rava's position: *alma lo mahani*, and therefore *tiyuvta de'Abaye*.

### Challenge to Abaye

According to Abaye's principle that violations still produce halachic effects, this case is a direct counterexample — a case where acting improperly yields no *terumah* at all.

### Abaye's Reishitam

Abaye responds: *shani hatam, de'amar kra reishitam* — there it is different, because the verse says *reishitam*, "their first," using the possessive plural. This extra word teaches that the *reishit* must be appropriate to each species individually — *reishit lazeh v'reishit lazeh*. Each species must have its own distinct *terumah*, and if taken from the wrong species it is entirely invalid. This is an explicit Scriptural ruling that overrides his general principle, making this an exception.

Rabbi Ila'i is also cited here: *reishit o reishitam* — the word *reishitam* (rather than simply *reishit*) indicates that each species must have its own separate *terumah* and nothing else will suffice.

### Rava's Reading

Rava has a different account of why *reishitam* is necessary. According to Rava, the general principle already tells him that a violation does not produce effect — he did not need *reishitam* to know that cross-species *terumah* fails. So what does *reishitam* add?

The initial verses group *tirosh* (wine) and *dagan* (grain) under a single instance of the word *cheilev* — *v'kol cheilev dagan v'tirosh*. Without *reishitam*, one might have thought that since wine and grain share a single *cheilev* designation, one could take *terumah* from wine upon grain or vice versa. Similarly, within the category of grain — wheat and barley — since they are subsumed under one word, one might have thought you could take wheat *terumah* on barley. But the *halacha* is that only wheat on wheat and barley on barley is valid.

The word *reishitam* comes to clarify: even within the grouped phrase, every species retains a separate identity, and *terumah* may only be taken from a species upon itself. This is not because violations fail — that Rava already knew — but because the initial phrasing might have suggested these species were interchangeable for purposes of *terumah*, and *reishitam* corrects that impression.

A second formulation makes the same point more succinctly: *tirosh vedagan dechada chelev kesiv behu* — since wine and grain share one *cheilev*, one might have thought *sarim mehai ahai*, you could take from one to the other. *Kesav Rachmana reishitam* — the Torah therefore added *reishitam* to establish that each species is entirely separate.

---

## Consecrated Animals

### Charamim Case

The *Gemara* now turns to the laws of *charamim* and *bechor*, cases involving consecrated animals that cannot be redeemed. The Torah states regarding *cherem* property belonging to *kohanim*: *lo yimacher velo yiga'el* — it shall not be sold and shall not be redeemed. The item retains its *kedushah* until it is physically transferred to the *kohen*. The question is: if one attempts to redeem the *cherem* — transferring the *kedushah* onto money — does it take effect?

The *Mishnah* rules: *charmei kohanim ein lahem pidyon ella notnim l'kohein* — there is no redemption; it must be physically given to the *kohen*. Attempting to redeem it is ineffective: *alma lo mahani*, and therefore *tiyuvta de'Abaye*.

### Hu Emphasis

Abaye responds: *shani hatam de'amar Rachmana kodesh kodashim hi* — there it is different, because the verse says *kodesh kodashim* with the word *hu* (or *hi*) — "it is holy of holies." This word, *b'havayaso yehei*, teaches that the item must remain exactly as it is. Its status cannot be altered. The reason the redemption fails is not Rava's general principle that violations lack effect — it is the specific Scriptural word that anchors the *kedushah* in place. Therefore it is an exception.

### Rava on Hu

Since Rava already knows from his general principle that violations fail, he does not need *hu* for that purpose. What then does *hu* teach? *L'ma'utei bechor* — to exclude the case of a *bechor*.

The *Gemara* cites a *baraisa*: by *bechor* the Torah says *lo tifdeh* — it shall not be redeemed. The *bechor* has intrinsic sanctity by virtue of its being the firstborn, so the *kohen* cannot transfer that *kedushah* elsewhere. But unlike *cherem*, no verse forbids selling a *bechor*. The *halacha* is therefore that a *kohen* may sell his *bechor* if it has developed a *mum* (blemish). *Hu* thus draws the line: the prohibition on selling applies to *cherem* and *ma'aser*, but not to *bechor*. The word *hu* limits the scope of *lo yimacher velo yiga'el* — it cannot be extended to *bechor* by analogy.

Additionally, the *Gemara* digresses briefly to note how *ma'aser* relates to *bechor* on this point. The Torah says by *ma'aser*: *lo yiga'el*. Since the same phrase appears by *cherem*, and *ma'aser* and *bechor* are frequently linked, one might have concluded that just as *ma'aser* cannot be redeemed, it also cannot be sold — and the same should apply to *bechor*. The word *hu* forestalls this: *ma'aser* indeed cannot be sold (*lo chai velo shachut, lo tam velo ba'al mum*), but *bechor* retains the leniency of being sold when blemished.

### Bechor Case

The *Gemara* then challenges from *bechor* directly. The *Mishnah* states: *yesh lahem pidyon ultemuroteihem pidyon, chutz min habechor umin hama'aser* — all other sacrifices can be redeemed if blemished, as can their *temurot*, except for *bechor* and *ma'aser*, which cannot be redeemed. This again suggests that violation is ineffective — *alma lo mahani*, and *tiyuvta de'Abaye*.

### Abaye on Hem

Abaye responds: *shani hatam de'amar Kra hem, kodesh hem* — there it is different, because the verse says *hem*, "they are holy." *Be'havayatan yehu* — they retain their *kedushah* as is. As before, Abaye argues that this is not a general consequence of violation, but a specific Scriptural declaration. The word *hem* anchors their sacred status, making the failed redemption an exception rather than evidence for Rava's principle.

### Rava on Hem

Since Rava already knows redemption fails, he uses *hem* to derive a different *halacha*: *hem krevim ve'ein temuratam kreivah* — only the *bechor* and *ma'aser* themselves are brought as *korbanot*; their *temurot* are not brought, even though the *temura* of other sacrifices can be. The underlying reason is that the *kedushah* of *bechor* and *ma'aser* is inseparable from the physical identity of the animal — it was the firstborn, or it was the tenth. That reality cannot be relocated to a different animal. Even when the *kedushah* of *temura* extends to a second animal through the act of exchange, that second animal does not become a *bechor* or *ma'aser* in any meaningful sense, and therefore cannot be offered.

A question arises for Abaye: if he used *hem* to teach that the *kedushah* cannot be removed, where does he derive the rule that the *temura* of *bechor* and *ma'aser* cannot be brought? Abaye derives it from a different verse: *im shor im kesev la'Hashem hu* — whether an ox or sheep, it is designated to God. *La'Hashem kari* — only what was originally designated to God is brought, and the *temura*, not having been the original animal, is excluded.

Rava then derives from *hem* yet another *halacha*: *ain olim mevatlin zeh et zeh* — bloods of sacrifices that go on the *mizbe'ach* do not nullify one another. If the blood of a *bechor* or *ma'aser* became mixed with the blood of other sacrifices, the principle of *bittul* does not apply, and the blood is placed on the *mizbe'ach* regardless. *Hem* teaches that their identity persists even when commingled.

Abaye, who needed *hem* for a different purpose, derives *ein olim mevatlin* from the verse in Yom Kippur: *ulekach midam hapar umidam hasa'ir* — the *Kohen Gadol* takes from the blood of the ox and the blood of the goat. Since the blood of the ox greatly exceeds the blood of the goat, why is the goat's blood not nullified? *Mikan la'olim she'ein mevatlin zeh et zeh* — here we see that bloods designated for the *mizbe'ach* do not nullify one another, as per Rabbi Yoshi'a's reading that the two bloods are mixed together. Rava, however, does not read the verse this way: *hatam mizeh bifnei atzmo umizeh bifnei atzmo*, following Rabbi Yonatan's view that each blood is applied separately, so no mixing and no opportunity for *bittul* arises from that verse.

---

## Consecrated Animals (II)

### Maaser Case

The challenge from *ma'aser* follows naturally. The Torah states *lo yiga'el* — it shall not be redeemed. The same *Mishnah* that excludes *bechor* also excludes *ma'aser* from redemption, even with a blemish. Abaye's response: *de'alif evra evra mibechor* — the case of *ma'aser* is linked to *bechor* through a *gezerah shavah*. By *ma'aser* the Torah uses the root *ya'avor* (*kol asher ya'avor tachat hashavet*), and by *bechor* a parallel root of passage (*ha'avarta kol peter rechem*). This linguistic link draws the laws of *ma'aser* directly from *bechor*, and since we have already established that *bechor* is an exception — where Abaye acknowledged that a special verse (*hem*) prevents the redemption from taking effect — the same exception carries over to *ma'aser* by extension.

---

## Out-of-Order Terumah

### Order Violation

The *Gemara* turns now to a case that is in some ways the most conceptually direct of all the examples. The Torah states *mele'atcha vedim'acha lo te'acher* — you shall not delay your *mele'atcha* (read as *bikkurim*) and your *dim'acha* (read as *terumah*). This is interpreted to mean: do not take the later one before the earlier one — do not take *terumah* before *bikkurim*, and do not take *ma'aser* before *terumah*.

### Mishna Language

The *Mishnah* states: *hamakdim — af al pi shehu belo ta'aseh, ma she'asa asui* — if one went out of order, even though it constitutes a violation of a *lo ta'aseh*, what was done is done. What is striking about this case — and about the parallel formulation in the laws of *temura* — is that the conceptual tension is explicitly articulated in the language of the *Mishnah* itself: you are forbidden to do it, yet if you did, it takes effect. This is Abaye's principle stated in so many words.

### Challenge to Rava

The *Gemara* presents this as *tiyuvta deRava*: here the Mishnah explicitly says the act takes effect despite the violation. According to Rava's principle, it should not.

### Rava's Mikol

Rava responds: *shani hatam de'amar kra mikol matnoteichem tarimu* — there it is different, because the verse says "from all of your gifts you shall take (*tarimu*)." The word *mikol* — "from all" — teaches that even when taken out of order, the *terumah* is still effective. The Torah went out of its way to indicate that this act produces valid *terumah*, which means it is an exception to the general rule.

### Abaye on Obligation

According to Abaye, who already knows violations take effect, why is this verse necessary? The *Gemara* explains through an exchange that Rav Pappa had with Abaye directly.

### Rav Pappa

Rav Pappa raised a challenge to Abaye's teaching. Abaye had ruled that if a *Levi* comes to a farmer in the field before the grain has been threshed, piled, and processed into a *kri* (the requisite stage at which *terumot uma'asrot* obligations take hold), and asks for his *ma'aser* early, the farmer may give it and it takes effect — even though *terumah* has not yet been taken. This is a significant *chiddush*, as the *kohen* would receive a smaller share (since the *ma'aser* is taken off a larger pre-*terumah* base). Rav Pappa asked: if this works in the field before piling, should it not also work at the threshing floor once the grain has been piled — let the *Levi* also get his *ma'aser* there ahead of *terumah*?

### Obligation Timing

Abaye responded: *alecha amar kra mikol matnoteichem tarimu* — regarding this case the verse says "from all your gifts you shall take." This tells us that at the stage when the obligation of *terumot uma'asrot* has already kicked in — once the grain has been fully processed and piled, reaching the stage of *digun* — the *kohen*'s claim to *terumah* is active, and the *Levi* cannot preempt it. *Marbe ani et hakri* — I include the case of the piled grain as obligated; *umotzi ani et hashibolim* — and I exclude the case of the bundles in the field, *she'eino bechlal digun*, which has not yet reached the stage of obligation. The verse *mikol matnoteichem tarimu* thus serves Abaye not to confirm that violations take effect, but to define the boundary of when the *terumah* obligation is operative — and to establish that once that threshold is reached, it cannot be circumvented by the *Levi*'s early claim.

---

## Kohen Gadol-Widow

### Kiddushin Effect

The final case considered in this section concerns a *kohen gadol* who marries an *almanah* (widow). The Torah states: *almanah u'gerushah lo yikach* — a *kohen gadol* shall not take a widow or divorcee. Does *kiddushin* take effect if he does so?

The general rule, derived from the principle *kol makom she'yeish kiddushin v'yeish aveirah, havlad holeich achar hapagum*, is that when *kiddushin* is effective despite a prohibition, the child follows the stigmatized party — meaning the child is *pasul* (*chalal*) but not a *mamzer*. The severe *issurei arayos* — *kares*-level prohibitions such as incest or adultery — produce no *kiddushin* at all, and the child is a *mamzer*. But the case of a *kohen gadol* with an *almanah* or a regular *kohen* with a *gerushah* is at a lower level of severity, and *kiddushin* does take effect. The child becomes *pasul* for *kehunah*, but the marriage registers.

### Challenge to Rava
