The *braisa* explicitly states *yeish kiddushin* — there is *kiddushin* in this case. This is a direct challenge to Rava: why does the forbidden act take effect?

### Rava's Zaroh

Rava responds: *shani hacha, de'amar kra lo yechalel zaro* — it is different here, because the verse says "he shall not profane his seed." Tosafot explains that the doubled language — *lo yechalel* rather than simply *lo yechel* — signals a special Scriptural emphasis that the act is effective. From this additional formulation, Rava learns that the *kiddushin* does register, making this a Scripturally mandated exception to his general principle.

### Abaye on Zaroh

According to Abaye, who already knows violations take effect and thus did not need the verse to establish validity, the doubled language *lo yechalel* serves a different purpose. *Echad lo v'echad lah* — it teaches that the forbidden union affects both the child and the woman. Not only does the child born of this union become a *chalal*, but the woman herself becomes a *chalalah*. The practical significance is considerable: an *almanah* is only forbidden to a *kohen gadol*, not to a regular *kohen*. But once she engages in a prohibited *issurei kehunah* union, the act of forbidden cohabitation transforms her into a *chalalah* — making her forbidden even to an ordinary *kohen*. The verse thus extends the consequence of the prohibition to both parties. Notably, the *kohen gadol* himself is not thereby rendered *pasul* in any new way. The *Gemara* will continue with additional proofs and counter-proofs in the next *amud*.

---

---

# Temurah 6

## Abaye vs. Rava Debate

### Core Debate Setup

The daf for today continues the foundational debate between Abaye and Rava concerning whether a prohibited act nonetheless takes *halachic* effect. Abaye's principle — *ei avid mahani* — holds that even a violation produces its intended *halachic* consequence, while Rava's principle — *ei avid lo mahani* — holds that acting in violation prevents any such effect. The Gemara proceeds by testing this debate against a series of cases, each of which initially appears to vindicate one side, only for the other side to produce a scriptural or logical counter.

### Blemished Animal Case

The Gemara opens with the case of one who sanctifies a blemished animal for the altar: *hikdish ba'al mum l'gabbei mizbe'ach*. The Torah states *kol asher bo mum lo takrivu* — anything with a blemish you shall not offer up. As the Gemara will later explain at length, this prohibition is understood to encompass not merely placing the animal on the altar but the initial act of sanctification itself. A Mishnah is cited: *hamakdish ba'al mum l'gabbei mizbe'ach, af al pi she'hu b'lo ta'aseh, mah she'asa asuy* — if one sanctifies a blemished animal for the altar, even though he acts in violation, what is done is done. The sanctification takes effect.

### Abaye's Position

This *Mishnah* seems to encapsulate Abaye's position: *ei avid mahani*. Even a prohibited act produces its *halachic* result. The force of this proof is considerable — we have not merely a theoretical principle but a direct *Mishnaic* ruling that the sanctification holds despite the prohibition.

### Rava's Response

The Gemara raises this as a *tiyuvta d'Rava* — a refutation of Rava. Rava responds: *shani hatam d'amar kra*, there it is different because we have a special verse. The verse states *u'l'neder lo yeratzeh* — it will not be acceptable as a vow offering. Rava's reading is precise: the verse must say that it will not be acceptable as a *korban* because the sanctification did take hold. Had the sanctity not taken effect at all, there would be no need to specify that it cannot be brought as an offering — it would simply be an ordinary animal. The very necessity of the verse implies that the sanctification succeeded, and it then adds the further restriction that the animal may not be brought to the altar. Thus Rava concedes the effect here, but attributes it to a special scriptural teaching rather than to any general principle.

Abaye, in turn, requires the verse for a different reason. Without *u'l'neder lo yeratzeh*, one might have thought: since the sanctification takes effect (*ei avid mahani*), and the animal is now *kodesh*, perhaps it may still be brought as a *korban*. The verse therefore comes to teach that although the sanctity holds, the animal remains prohibited from being offered. Each Amora thus uses the verse, but for opposite purposes: according to Rava, the verse is the source of the exceptional ruling that the sanctification works at all; according to Abaye, the verse is needed only to forestall the conclusion that the animal may now be sacrificed.

---

## Temple Treasury Case

### Mirror Case Intro

The Gemara now examines what amounts to the mirror image of the previous case. The earlier discussion concerned sanctifying a blemished animal *for the altar* — an animal unfit for a *korban* being designated as one. Now the Gemara turns to sanctifying an unblemished animal *for the temple treasury* (*bedek ha-bayit*) — an animal perfectly fit to be a *korban* being diverted to a different sacred purpose instead. This case is structurally parallel but ethically somewhat less acute: whereas sanctifying a blemished animal for the altar is doubly inappropriate (the animal is unfit and the designation is wrong), sanctifying an unblemished animal for the *bedek ha-bayit* is merely a misallocation of a perfectly serviceable animal.

### Applied to Treasury

The verse at the top of 6a reads: *nedavah ta'aseh oto u'l'neder lo yeratzeh* — make it a donation, it will not be accepted as a vow offering. The first half of the verse addresses a blemished animal: present it as a donation to the treasury, not as a *korban*. By implication, the reverse is also true: an unblemished animal should be designated as a *korban*, not given to the treasury. This implicit prohibition is what *Chazal* derive, and a corresponding teaching is cited: *hamakdish tmimim l'bedek ha-bayit, af al pi she'hu b'lo ta'aseh, mah she'asa asuy* — if one sanctifies unblemished animals for the treasury, even though he acts in violation, what is done is done. Here too, the designation takes effect. The Gemara again raises this as a *tiyuvta d'Rava*.

### Unified Verse Analysis

Rava answers by pointing to the unity of the verse. The explicit half of the verse — prohibiting blemished animals for the altar while permitting them for the treasury — was already resolved: the verse had to specify that the sanctification takes effect despite the prohibition. Now the implicit reverse — prohibiting unblemished animals for the treasury — is derived from the same verse: *mimakom shenisrabu ba'alei mumim l'gabbei mizbe'ach nisrabu tmimim l'bedek ha-bayit*. Since the explicit prohibition, though violated, nonetheless produces *halachic* effect (as established by the verse), the same logic applies to the implicit prohibition derived from the same verse. The two cases are inseparable: whatever the verse teaches about the explicit case applies equally to the implicit one. Rava thus accounts for both rulings without abandoning his general principle; both are exceptional cases grounded in a single scriptural source.

---

## Practical Examples

### Challenge to Debate

With each case having been either explained away by a special verse (according to Rava) or accounted for naturally (according to Abaye), the Gemara raises the obvious challenge: now that you have answered every one of these cases with these answers, what exactly do Abaye and Rava disagree about? This is a recognizable pattern in the Gemara, where an apparently sweeping principled debate ultimately yields very little *nafka mina* once the individual cases are examined. A comparable example appears in the second *perek* of Pesachim, where the debate between *Chizkiyah* and *Rabbi Abbahu* over whether *lo tochal* means only "do not eat" or also "do not derive benefit" proceeds through every applicable case until the Gemara similarly asks: what then is the difference?

A student raises the case of a *kohen* who marries a *grushah* in violation of his priestly status — does the marriage take effect? The answer is yes, the marriage does take effect. The Gemara yesterday employed a special verse to reconcile this with Rava's position. The personal and social consequences of such a marriage are notable: the man incurs *malkos*, the child is a *chalal*, and at the societal level the *kohen* is effectively stripped of his active priestly standing for as long as he remains in the marriage — as close to non-*kohen* status as is possible without formally losing the designation. A *chalal* is one who has lost his *kehunah* standing; a *chalalah* may not marry a *kohen*.

### Theft & Change

The Gemara next considers the case of theft (*gezel*): *lo tigzol* — do not steal. If one steals wood and fashions it into vessels, or steals wool and makes it into garments, the ruling (*ha-gozel etzim ve-asaan keilim, tzemer ve-asaan begadim, meshalem ki-sh'at ha-gezeilah*) is that he pays the value of what he stole at the time of the theft — he does not return the finished goods. He has in some sense acquired the transformed object. This appears to be a *tiyuvta d'Rava*: the prohibited act of theft produced a *halachic* consequence, namely a form of ownership.

### Quasi-Ownership Rights

The *halachic* mechanism underlying this case merits attention. When one steals an object, certain authorities understand that at the moment of theft the thief acquires a form of quasi-ownership known as *kinyanei gneivah* or *kinyanei gezeilah*. He does not hold full legal title — the object is not *de jure* his — but he has *de facto* control, and this creates limited rights in the object. One well-known consequence: if someone borrows an object without permission, he must compensate the owner for use. But if he stole it, his *kinyanei gezeilah* means he need not pay for the use during the period of possession; he need only return or compensate for the object itself.

Now, when the object changes — when the thief transforms the stolen wood into vessels — ownership of the transformed object may be understood in one of two ways. Either the act of transformation itself constitutes an act of acquisition, rendering it his through the force of that physical change; or the act of change does not independently confer ownership, but rather removes the final connection between the new object and its original owner. On this second understanding, what actually makes it the thief's is the *kinyanim* he acquired at the moment of theft — those rights were always there, but the object retained a residual connection to the original owner so long as it remained identifiably the same thing. Once the transformation is complete, only the thief's original rights remain, and the object becomes fully his. The relevance to the Abaye–Rava debate now becomes clearer: if *ei avid mahani*, then the act of theft — itself a violation — can confer those initial quasi-ownership rights, and the subsequent change ripens them into full ownership. If *ei avid lo mahani*, then the theft confers no such rights, and the question of subsequent change becomes legally irrelevant.

### Pledge Seizure

The Gemara turns next to the case of seizing a *mashkon* — a pledge or collateral — without permission. The creditor has a right to a pledge, but only through the proper legal channels: either the debtor willingly hands it over or *beis din* authorizes its seizure. If the creditor walks into the debtor's home and takes the *mashkon* on his own initiative, he has acted in violation. The question is whether his possession of the *mashkon* nonetheless carries any legal standing.

### Daily Return Rule

The Torah mandates daily return of certain pledges — a cloak taken as collateral must be returned each night. The double language of *hashev tashiv* — "you shall surely return" — extends this obligation to the case of a *mashkon* seized without permission. Rava cites this as his special verse: *shani hatam d'amar kra hashev tashiv*. Had the Torah not said this, one might have concluded: the creditor acted outside the law by seizing the *mashkon* unlawfully, and since he acted outside the law, perhaps the daily return obligation no longer applies. The verse therefore comes to tell us that even a *mashkon* seized in violation must be returned daily — and the implication of that ruling is that the creditor retains possession (and his associated rights) every alternate period.

Abaye, who would have said the creditor retains rights even without the verse, needs *hashev tashiv* for a different reason. Had the Torah not said it, one might have thought: since the initial act was in violation, *ei avid mahani*, the creditor does have rights, but there is no *mitzvah* to return it. He may keep it as long as he likes. The verse comes to teach that even though the initial seizure was unlawful, the creditor must now return it daily. This is a striking Gemara: without it, we would have intuitively sided with Rava — one who marches into a debtor's house and takes his property unlawfully should surely have no legal standing. Yet the Gemara teaches otherwise, and the framework of *kinyanei gezeilah* and *ei avid mahani* explains why.

### Change & Ownership

Regarding Tosafos's brief observation here: when one steals an object and it subsequently undergoes *shinui* — a significant change — the question of whether the thief thereby acquires title is, as Rashi notes, a question whose emphasis lies on the limits of that principle. Tosafos reads the case somewhat differently and will be addressed more fully below.

### Pe'ah Case

The Gemara considers the agricultural case of *pe'ah* — the corner of the field left for the poor. The Torah states *lo techaleh pe'at sadecha be-kotzrecha* — do not cut the *pe'ah* when you harvest. Alongside the positive obligation to leave the corner, there is a *lo ta'asei* against harvesting it. A Mishnah teaches: the *mitzvah* of *pe'ah* is ideally fulfilled from the standing grain; if one did not do so, he may designate it from the bundled grain; if not then, from the winnowed pile (*kari*), up until the grain has been smoothed over (*meiruach*). After *meiruach*, he takes *ma'aser* first and then gives *pe'ah* to the poor — this because at that stage the grain has become obligated in *terumos u-ma'asros*. *Pe'ah* given before *meiruach* is exempt from *ma'aser*; after *meiruach*, the *ma'aser* must be separated first so that the poor receive their *pe'ah* free of obligation.

### Double Language

Rabbi Yishmael goes further, ruling that one must still give *pe'ah* even after the grain has been turned into dough — even after a *shinui* that might have terminated the obligation. Rashi reads the emphasis of this ruling as falling on Rabbi Yishmael's position: even after significant change, the *pe'ah* obligation persists, suggesting *ei avid lo mahani* — your act of harvesting did not successfully terminate the obligation. The *tiyuvta* here falls on Abaye.

Abaye responds with the double language of *ta'azov ta'azov* — "you shall surely leave" — appearing twice in the verses concerning gifts to the poor. This extra language teaches that even where one would otherwise find a way to escape the obligation (through *shinui* or through the technique of ownerless declaration), the doubled language forecloses that escape and insists on fulfillment.

### Ownerless Vineyard

Rava, who already holds that one cannot escape obligations through violation, uses the doubled *ta'azov* differently. He derives from it an additional *halacha*: *yesh lach aziva acheret k'zo* — there is another "leaving" like this one. The case is *mafkir karmo*: one who declares his vineyard ownerless (*hefker*) at night, then rises at dawn and retakes possession before harvesting. A *baraita* teaches that in such a case he is still obligated in all the agricultural gifts to the poor (*peret*, *olelot*, *shichecha*, and *pe'ah*), because the double language prevents this technical *hefker* from serving as an exemption. However, he is exempt from *ma'aser*, because by *ma'aser* no such doubled language exists. The *pe'ah* case is thus somewhat unlike the others in this series: the other cases involve *halachic* acts whose *halachic* status is in question — sanctifying, divorcing, seizing, stealing — whereas the *pe'ah* case is closer to the question of whether the doer benefits from his sin (*chotei niskar*). The harvesting itself does not generate a *halachic* change of status in the grain; it simply raises the question of whether the *mitzvah* is terminated by the violation, which sits somewhat more awkwardly in the framework of Abaye and Rava.

---

## Shinui Koneh Debate

### Real Difference Found

After exhausting the list of cases and finding that each has been answered by a special verse or textual argument, the Gemara poses the question directly: *be-mai paligi?* — what do Abaye and Rava actually disagree about? The answer given is *be-shinui koneh* — the question of whether change confers ownership on the thief. This case, drawn from the discussions in Bava Kamma, is presented as one where the debate is not driven by a *pasuk* but by *sevara* — pure legal reasoning. There, the question of whether a *gazlan*'s act of transformation of the stolen object gives him title is a genuine dispute not resolved by any particular verse, and it is therefore a proper arena for the principles of Abaye and Rava to operate. If *ei avid mahani*, the theft confers quasi-ownership rights that the *shinui* then ripens; if *ei avid lo mahani*, the theft confers no such rights and the *shinui* is legally ineffective. So, after this entire discussion, the actual *nafka mina* of the debate between Abaye and Rava reduces to this one relatively obscure question in Bava Kamma.

---

## Ribit Case

### Ribit Question

The Gemara introduces the case of *ribit ketzutzah* — explicit, fixed interest on a loan — as another arena for the Abaye–Rava debate. Rav Acha the son of Rava poses the question to Rav Ashi: now that you have answered all those answers, what is the *nafka mina* between Abaye and Rava? He suggests that they disagree regarding *ribit ketzutzah*. The case is arresting in its structure: unlike *gezel*, where property is taken against the owner's will, *ribit* is a contractual arrangement entered into willingly by both parties. The lender charges fixed interest; the borrower agrees to pay it. Yet the entire arrangement violates a *lo ta'asei*. The question is whether the contractual obligation thus created is binding or whether the violation strips it of legal force.

### Elazar vs. Yochanan

Rabbi Elazar holds that *ribit ketzutzah yotzah bedayanim* — fixed interest is extracted by the courts; the courts will compel return of the interest. *Avak ribit* — the "dust of interest," referring to indirect forms of financial advantage that are rabbinically prohibited but not explicit biblical *ribit* — does not come out through the courts (*einah yotzah bedayanim*). Rabbi Yochanan holds that even *ribit ketzutzah* does not come out through the courts: *afilu ribit ketzutzah einah yotzah bedayanim*. This dispute maps directly onto the Abaye–Rava debate: if *ei avid mahani*, the contract is binding, and if binding, the interest need not be returned; if *ei avid lo mahani*, the contract lacks force and the courts may demand the money back.

### Interest Verses

The Gemara then examines what verses each position relies upon. Rabbi Yitzchak explains Rabbi Yochanan's position: a verse in Yechezkel states *be-neshech natan ve-tarbit lakach ve-chai lo yichyeh* — he gave his money at interest, took back increase, and shall not live. The Gemara reads this as *le-chayim nitan ve-lo le-hashavon* — the consequence of *ribit* is that it endangers the lender's life, but it does not create an obligation of repayment. The money is not considered stolen; no *hashavah* — return — is mandated.

Rav Adda bar Ahava derives the same conclusion from a different verse: *ve-yareta me'Elohecha Ani Hashem*, said in the context of *ribit* laws — the consequence is *mora*, fear of divine judgment, but not legal repayment. Rava derives it from yet another verse in Yechezkel: *ha-to'evot ha'eleh asah, mot yumot, damav bo yihyeh*, followed by a description of the wicked son who is a murderer. From the juxtaposition, *hukshu malvei ribit le-shofchei damim* — lenders of *ribit* are compared to murderers. Just as a murderer's act cannot be undone — *mah shofech damim lo nitan le-hishiv* — so too *ribit* once collected need not be returned: *af malveh ribbis lo nitan le-hishiv*.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains Rabbi Elazar's position: *de'amar kra ve-chai achicha imach* — the verse says "your brother shall live with you." This is understood as: *ahadar lei ki heichi de-nichi imach* — return it to him so that he can get along with you. There is thus a separate *mitzvah* to restore the relationship by giving back the interest.

### Binding Contract

What is particularly striking here is that even according to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that *ribit* must be returned, the legal basis is not that the contract was void from the start or that the money is considered stolen. Rather, the contract is fundamentally binding — the lender is contractually entitled to the interest — but a separate *mitzvah* of *ve-chai achicha imach* imposes an obligation to return it as a moral-*halachic* gesture. This reading has concrete *halachic* consequences: the Gemara in Bava Kamma establishes that if the lender dies, his sons are not obligated to return the *ribit*. A debt arising from a void or stolen transaction would bind the heirs; an obligation arising from a separate *mitzvah* imposed personally on the transgressor does not. The sons inherit money to which their father was contractually entitled, and the personal *mitzvah* to restore harmony — *ve-chai achicha imach* — did not pass to them.

This means that both sides effectively agree that the *ribit* contract is binding as a matter of monetary law, which reflects the approach of Abaye. The fact that *ribit* laws appear in the *Shulchan Aruch* in *Yoreh Deah* (the realm of *issur ve-heter*) rather than in *Choshen Mishpat* (monetary law) — though the *Rambam* places them in *Hilchos Malveh Ve-Loveh* — reflects precisely this ambiguity: the prohibition is ritual in character, but the underlying transaction remains a binding contract. The broader principle, that a contract entered into in violation of a Torah prohibition is nonetheless enforceable, finds support across the *Rishonim*. The case of *esnan zona* — where the Torah grants *esnan* status even to payment made in exchange for relations with one's mother, the most severe of *arayos* — illustrates that even a transaction embedded in the gravest violation is recognized as a form of payment and not merely a gift.

One might ask whether *beis din* would enforce such a contract by compelling performance. The cases discussed here generally involve situations where the party holding the money willfully fulfills (or refuses to fulfill) the terms; no one would dream of summoning *beis din* to collect *ribit*. Whether *beis din* would actively enforce a contract made in violation of Torah law is a separate question, and one with significant implications.

---

## Shinui Koneh Debate (II)

### Rava's Statement

The Gemara returns to the core question: *ve'ela be-mai paligi, be-shinui koneh*. Rashi explains the connection: earlier in the *sugya*, the case of a thief who transforms the stolen object was raised. In Bava Kamma there is an actual debate about whether *shinui koneh* — whether the change confers title on the thief. That debate is not resolved by any verse; it is a pure question of *sevara*. According to Abaye — *ei avid mahani* — the original act of theft generates *kinyanei gezeilah*, and the subsequent *shinui* completes the acquisition. According to Rava — *ei avid lo mahani* — the theft generates no such rights, and the *shinui* therefore cannot transform a nullity into ownership. It is here, in this case in Bava Kamma, that the debate between Abaye and Rava has genuine, verse-independent traction. The weight of evidence throughout the *sugya* points substantially toward Abaye's position — case after case is ruled in accordance with *ei avid mahani*, and even the *ribit* analysis ultimately converges on the bindingness of the contract. Yet the Gemara, with characteristic economy, locates the actual operative difference in this one obscure corner of *dinei geneivah*.

---

## Lishna Achrina

### Alternative Version

The Gemara introduces at this point the formulation *lishna achrina* — an alternative version — before restating the conclusion about *ribit ketzutzah* and *shinui koneh*. This phenomenon deserves attention. The *lishna achrina* in our *masechta* is not merely an occasional textual variant; it is a recurrent feature that signals something linguistically distinctive about *Temurah*.

### Rashi's Analysis

Rashi, in his commentary here, identifies the *lishna achrina* as a specimen of *lashon Yerushalmi* — the language of the Yerushalmi. He notes: *ela zeh Yerushalmi ve-zeh Bavli* — one version is Yerushalmi and one is Bavli. The two versions are functionally identical in content — *uvein hai lishna le-lishna de-shami'a lei be-shinui koneh leika midi*, there is no substantive difference between them regarding *shinui koneh* — but their linguistic character differs.

### Scholarly Background

This observation is illuminated by the standard scholarly introduction to the Talmud, Strack and Stemberger's *Introduction to the Talmud and Midrash*, which surveys the linguistic and grammatical peculiarities of certain tractates. Five tractates — Nedarim, Nazir, Me'ila, Kerisot, and Tamid — differ from the rest of the Bavli in a range of linguistic and grammatical features, a phenomenon already noted by Tosafos. These tractates are characterized by what the authors call "extraordinary" or linguistically anomalous material, and the *lishna achrina* sections of Temurah fall into the same category.

### Temurah's Status

Temurah itself is specifically identified as belonging to this group by virtue of its *lishna achrina* passages, which exhibit not merely terminological differences but grammatical peculiarities characteristic of Palestinian Aramaic rather than standard Babylonian Aramaic. Rashi's identification of this language as *Yerushalmi* thus reflects a genuine philological reality.

The scholarly debate over the origin of this phenomenon is itself instructive. One view, associated with Yitzchak Halevi, proposes that these tractates were genuinely more studied in *Eretz Yisrael* than in Bavel, based on geonic testimony that Nedarim was not taught after *Yehudai Gaon*. On this account, the tractates were transmitted and shaped largely in a Palestinian milieu, and their language reflects that environment. The more commonly accepted contemporary view holds that the difference is one of editorial geography within Babylonia itself: while most of the Bavli was redacted in Sura under *Rav Ashi*, these linguistically unusual tractates were redacted in *Pumbedita* or *Nehardea*, whose Aramaic dialect approximates Palestinian Aramaic more closely. On this understanding, the language is Babylonian in provenance but reflects a regional dialect that sounds more "Palestinian" to the ear. The existence of parallel *sugyot* placed side by side — one in each dialect — is itself evidence of a redactional process in which independent transmissions were assembled rather than harmonized.

---

## Tosafos Question

### Other Cases

Before proceeding, Tosafos raises a question on 6a: now that the Gemara has explained away all the cases and located the *nafka mina* in *shinui koneh*, why does the Gemara not suggest other cases where the debate would have practical traction? Could one not propose, for example, cases where a person took an oath not to perform some otherwise-permitted act and then violated it?

### Oath & Divorce

Tosafos addresses this with a distinction between natural violations and imposed violations. The paradigm case Tosafos raises is: a man swore not to divorce his wife and then proceeded to do so — *nishba she-lo legaresh et ishto ve-achar kach avar ve-geirsha*. Should we say that according to Rava the *get* is invalid, since he acted in violation? Tosafos answers that this type of case does not fall within the scope of Rava's principle. The act of divorce is not inherently prohibited; the man himself artificially imposed a prohibition upon it through his oath. Where the violation arises not from the nature of the act but from an external constraint the person created, Rava would agree that the act takes effect. Rava's principle applies only where the Torah itself prohibits the act as such — where the violation is *natural* to the action — not where the person has constructed his own prohibition on top of an otherwise permissible deed.

Tosafos also raises the question of cases like redeeming a *bechor* or *cheirem* objects — whether there would be a *nafka mina* there — but notes a complication about whether lashes (*malkos*) would apply, which affects how cleanly those cases can serve as examples.

---

## Blemish Prohibitions

### Five Prohibitions

The Gemara now examines in detail the *halachos* of sanctifying a blemished animal, which was mentioned in passing earlier in the *sugya* and which has structural parallels to *temurah*: in both cases, one performs a prohibited act of sanctification that nonetheless takes *halachic* effect. A *baraita* teaches: *hamakdish ba'alei mumim l'gabbei mizbe'ach, over mishum chamisha sheimos* — one who sanctifies animals with a blemish for the altar transgresses five separate prohibitions.

### Verse Derivation

The derivation proceeds as follows. The verse *kol asher bo mum lo takrivu* appears to prohibit bringing such animals. A second verse, *iveres o shavur o charutz o yabeles lo takrivu eileh l'Hashem*, also prohibits bringing blemished animals. Since the Torah uses *lo takrivu* twice, each instance is interpreted separately. The first (*kol asher bo mum*) is taken to mean *lo takdishu* — do not sanctify; the second (*iveres o shavur*) is taken to mean *lo tishchatu* — do not slaughter. Thus the first two prohibitions are: (1) do not sanctify a blemished animal, and (2) do not slaughter it as a sacrifice. The verse then adds *ve-isheh lo sitnu meihem* — do not give it as a fire offering. The word *meihem* (from them) extends the prohibition from burning the full set of *eimurim* (innards burned on the altar) to burning even a part: (3) do not burn all of it; (4) do not burn even part of it. Finally, (5) *al ha-mizbe'ach* — do not place it upon the altar — is read as a prohibition against *zerikos dam*, sprinkling the blood, since that is what goes upon the altar.

### Blood Reception

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda adds a sixth prohibition: *af kabbalas ha-dam* — even receiving the blood (the step immediately preceding sprinkling). He reads an additional verse as prohibiting this distinct Temple service.

### Dual Meanings

The derivation that *lo takrivu* means both "do not sanctify" in one verse and "do not slaughter" in another is arrived at by exclusion: each verse is redundant if interpreted identically to the other. *Kol asher bo mum lo takrivu*, if understood as "do not slaughter," would merely duplicate *iveres o shavur lo takrivu*. Conversely, *iveres o shavur lo takrivu*, if understood as "do not sanctify," would duplicate *kol asher bo mum lo takrivu*. Therefore the two instances must carry distinct meanings: one refers to the initial act of designation (*kedushat ha-guf*) and the other to the Temple service of slaughter.

### Burning Portions

The dual prohibition regarding burning — both the whole and the part — is derived from the single phrase *ve-isheh lo sitnu meihem*. The word *isheh* refers to the burning of *eimurim* on the altar; the word *meihem* ("from them") extends the prohibition from the totality to any portion. Without *meihem*, one might have thought only a complete burning was prohibited, or conversely that only a partial burning was prohibited; the phrase encompasses both.

### Blood Sprinkling

The prohibition of blood sprinkling is derived from *al ha-mizbe'ach* — upon the altar. Since the blood is what is placed upon the altar in the Temple service (*zerikos dam*), this phrase generates a distinct prohibition against sprinkling the blood of a blemished animal.

### Scapegoat Extension

The verse concludes *l'Hashem*, and this phrase is used to extend the prohibition of sanctifying blemished animals to the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* — the scapegoat sent to *Azazel* on Yom Kippur. One might have thought that since the scapegoat is not brought to the altar and is not a burnt offering, the prohibitions of the altar service do not apply to its sanctification. The word *l'Hashem* extends the prohibition of sanctifying a blemished animal even to this designation, since the *sa'ir* too is consecrated "to God" in the broad sense.

---

## Altar vs. Outside

### Outside Slaughter Ban

The Gemara now raises a tension between the extension of the prohibition to the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* and a different *halachic* domain: the laws of *shechutei chutz*, the prohibition of slaughtering sacrifices outside the Temple (*Beis HaMikdash*). The Torah states *el pesach ohel moed lo hevi'o, le-hakriv korban l'Hashem* — one who did not bring the animal to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to offer it as a *korban* to God incurs liability for *shechutei chutz*.

### For God Clause

One might have thought that *kodshei bedek ha-bayit* — animals sanctified to the temple treasury — are also subject to *shechutei chutz*, since there are sources that call such animals a *korban* (*va-nakrev et korban Hashem*, said in the context of the Midian booty). The Gemara resolves this by noting that *shechutei chutz* applies only to things *ra'uy le-fesach ohel moed* — fit to be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, i.e., proper *korbanos* for the altar. Things not fit for the *ohel moed* are exempt. And as Rashi notes, animals sanctified to *bedek ha-bayit* are by definition blemished animals — since sanctifying unblemished animals to the treasury is itself a violation — and blemished animals are not fit for the altar. Therefore they are exempt from *shechutei chutz* by reason of their unfitness.

### Scapegoat Exclusion

The Gemara then asks: having excluded *kodshei bedek ha-bayit* by the qualifier *ra'uy le-ohel moed*, what of animals that are technically fit — unblemished — but are not brought as conventional *korbanos* on the altar, such as the *parah adumah* and the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach*? One might still include these in *shechutei chutz* since they are unblemished. The Gemara answers: *talmud lomar l'Hashem* — "for God." Only things that are fully and exclusively designated *la-Hashem* are subject to *shechutei chutz*. The *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach*, which is sent *la-Azazel*, is not fully designated *la-Hashem* in this sense; nor is the *parah adumah*, which is burned outside the Temple in a procedure oriented differently from the normal service. These are therefore excluded.

### Context Direction

This creates an apparent contradiction. In the context of sanctifying blemished animals, the phrase *l'Hashem* was used to *include* the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* — one who sanctifies a blemished animal as the *sa'ir* transgresses the prohibition. But in the context of *shechutei chutz*, the same phrase *l'Hashem* is used to *exclude* the *sa'ir* — one who slaughters it outside the Temple does not incur *shechutei chutz* liability. How can the same phrase include in one context and exclude in another?

Rava resolves the contradiction: *ha ke-di'ita ve-ha ke-di'ita* — each case fits its own context, and *l'Hashem* acts in the direction required by the surrounding logic. By *shechutei chutz*, before we encounter *l'Hashem*, the criterion already established is *ra'uy le-pesach ohel moed*. Given that criterion, the natural inclination is to include the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach*, which is unblemished and in principle fit. *L'Hashem* comes to counter that inclination and exclude: since the *sa'ir* is not fully dedicated to God's service on the altar, it is outside the scope of *shechutei chutz*. By the laws of sanctifying blemished animals, the operative term in the verse is *isheh* — a fire offering on the altar. Given that term, the natural inclination is to exclude the *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach*, since it is never burned on the altar. *L'Hashem* comes to counter that inclination and include: since the *sa'ir* is nevertheless consecrated within the framework of divine service, the prohibition of sanctifying it with a blemish applies. The phrase *l'Hashem* in each case moves against the default assumption established by its immediate context: including where one would have excluded, and excluding where one would have included.

---

---

# Temurah 7

## Se'ir HaMishtale'ach

### Opening Remarks

The discussion on daf 7 continues a line of inquiry that is only somewhat related to the masechta's central theme of *temurah*. The unifying thread is the concept of sanctity one ought not to confer — and which, once conferred, takes effect regardless. Specifically, the *gemara* is occupied with the prohibition against sanctifying as a *korban* an animal that bears a blemish. The prohibition will, before long, explicitly invoke *temurah* as well. We pick up at the bottom of 6b.

### Lottery Requirement

The *gemara* states: *ta'ama de-katav kra la-Hashem* — the reason one may not designate a *se'ir hamishtalea'ach* that is blemished is because the verse explicitly adds the word *la-Hashem*, which serves to include this case. The question immediately arises: had the verse not added *la-Hashem*, one might have supposed a blemished *se'ir hamishtalea'ach* would be permitted. But how could that be? The principle is *ein ha-goral kove'a ela be-davar ha-ra'uy* — the lottery over the two Yom Kippur goats is valid only if both animals are fit to serve in either capacity. Since one of the two goats may emerge from the lottery as the one designated *la-Hashem*, both must be unblemished at the outset. How then could we ever have entertained the thought that a blemished goat is acceptable?

The *gemara*'s answer is that without the explicit verse, one might have thought the blemished goat is technically ineligible but that no negative prohibition has been violated — perhaps the entire procedure would simply have been invalid from the start, and there would have been no occasion for transgression. The verse therefore comes to teach that not only is such a designation invalid, but that one actively transgresses in making it. Although the *gemara*'s precise reasoning on this point is somewhat elusive, the upshot is clear: without the verse, one might have thought that since a blemished animal is categorically excluded from the lottery, the prohibition never applies in the first place. The verse tells us otherwise.

### Chananya HaMitzri

Rav Yosef offers a different answer: this ruling follows the position of *Chananya HaMitzri*, who maintains that *afilu dam be-kos me'akev chaveiro mishtafek lo* — even if the blood of the *korban la-Hashem* has already been collected in the vessel, you may bring a replacement for the *se'ir la-Azazel* should it have died. According to *Chananya HaMitzri*, the collected blood remains valid and does not become *dachui* (rejected). If so, one might imagine a scenario in which the replacement goat is designated directly as *la-Azazel* without going through the lottery again, since we know from the outset that it will serve only in that capacity — in which case we might have thought that such a goat could bear a blemish.

The *gemara* pushes back: even granting *Chananya HaMitzri*'s position that the blood is not rejected, one cannot infer that no new lottery is required. *Dilma mayti u-magril* — perhaps you bring two new goats and conduct the lottery again. The one that falls *la-Hashem* is set aside and eventually redeemed when it acquires a blemish, while the blood from the original *korban* is used. Under this reading, even the replacement goat destined *la-Azazel* must be fit for the altar, since we do not know which will emerge from the lottery as *la-Hashem*. The original *hava amina* is thus not resolved by *Chananya HaMitzri*.

Rav Yosef therefore revises his answer: this ruling follows the view of Rabbi Shimon, who states explicitly in a *baraisa*: *met echad mehen mevi chaveiro belo hagrala divrei Rabbi Shimon* — if one of the two goats dies, you bring a replacement without a new lottery. According to Rabbi Shimon, there are scenarios in which the replacement goat is directly designated *la-Azazel*. One might therefore have thought that in such a case, a blemished animal would either be permitted or at least not constitute a punishable transgression. The extra word *la-Hashem* comes to teach that even a directly designated *se'ir la-Azazel* must be unblemished, and one who designates a blemished animal violates a prohibition.

### Rava's Scenario

Rava offers yet another scenario that does not depend on any disputed position. *Kegon shehumam bo bayom* — suppose the lottery has already been conducted, designating one goat *la-Azazel*, and that goat then acquires a blemish on that same day. It cannot be used in its current state. The procedure is to transfer the *kedusha* off the blemished goat onto money, and then reassign that *kedusha* to a replacement. Everyone agrees no new lottery is required in this case, because the replacement's sanctity derives from the original designated animal rather than from a fresh designation.

In this scenario, one might have thought no prohibition is violated when the replacement itself bears a blemish, since the one designated *la-Hashem* is already clearly established. *Keivan d'itparesh l'shem lo laki* — once the other goat is explicitly set aside as *la-Hashem*, surely the *la-Azazel* replacement stands in no danger of being confused with it, and therefore perhaps no transgression occurs if it has a blemish. *Ka-mashma lan* — the verse teaches that you do nonetheless transgress when you transfer that *kedusha* onto a blemished replacement. Rava thus provides an independent scenario in which a new lottery is unnecessary, and where the prohibition against a blemished *se'ir la-Azazel* must be explicitly derived.

### Sanctity Transfer

It is worth noting that Rava's formulation assumes we already know, prior to the verse's teaching, that a blemished animal is objectionable for this purpose. The verse's contribution is specifically to establish that one incurs lashes — that the act constitutes a punishable violation — even in a case where the animal's role as *la-Azazel* has been unambiguously established. The broader principle established across all three scenarios is that transferring *kedusha* to a replacement for a designated *la-Azazel* animal does not require a new lottery, yet does not exempt one from the prohibition against conferring sanctity on a *ba'al mum*.

---

## Catching Blood

### Rabbi Yose Position

The *gemara* proceeds to an expansion of the prohibition's scope. We read: *mishum Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda af kabbalat hadam* — Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda adds that even the *kabbalat hadam*, the catching or receiving of the blood, constitutes a violation. Those familiar with Zevachim will recall the four principal acts of the sacrificial service: *shechita* (slaughter), *kabbala* (receiving the blood), *holacha* (conveying the blood to the altar), and *zerikat hadam* (sprinkling the blood). The preceding discussion had established that one transgresses by sanctifying, slaughtering, sprinkling, and burning a blemished animal. Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda now argues that catching the blood is equally prohibited.

### Rhetorical Verse

The *gemara* asks: what is the source for this view? *Amar kra: u-ma'uach ve-chatut ve-natua'ch ve-karut lo takrivu elu la-Hashem* — the verse enumerates various categories of genital mutilation and declares: you shall not bring these to God. This *lo takrivu* could serve as the basis for prohibiting *kabbalat hadam*. The *tanna kamma*, who does not hold that catching the blood is prohibited, must use this verse for something else — specifically, as a source for the prohibition against sprinkling the blood. But the *gemara* points out that the prohibition against sprinkling was already derived from the phrase *al ha-mizbe'ach lo ta'alu*, "you shall not cause to ascend upon the altar." Why is the additional *lo takrivu* needed?

The *gemara* answers for the *tanna kamma*: *orcha dikra d'mishtaei hachi* — this is simply the rhetorical manner in which the verse speaks. The *lo takrivu* in this context is not establishing a new prohibition; rather, given that the verse is enumerating particularly repugnant physical mutilations, the phrase "you shall not bring these to God" functions as something closer to a moral declaration than a legal prohibition. The *Shita Mekubetzet* explains that the verse, dealing with mutilated genitalia, takes the tone of the verse in Malachi — *hakrivehu na le-pachatecha* ("present it to your governor") — expressing that this is simply not the sort of thing one brings before God. It is a statement of moral inappropriateness rather than a new *lav*.

This explanation is admittedly striking. Throughout the preceding *sugyot*, the *gemara* has derived separate prohibitions from each instance of *lo takrivu*. To now dismiss one instance as merely rhetorical requires explanation, and the *Shita Mekubetzet*'s answer — that the surrounding context of mutilation lends the phrase a different character — is the *gemara*'s considered response.

### Non-Jew Source

The *gemara* continues: since even Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda cannot use the verse about mutilated animals (it too is merely rhetorical in its context), from where does he derive that *kabbalat hadam* is prohibited? *Nafka lei mei-ha: u-miyad ben nechar lo takrivu elu la-Hashem* — the verse states that you may not accept blemished animals even from non-Jews. This verse, as *Tosafos* notes, is itself revealing: its plain meaning presupposes that one may ordinarily accept *korbanos* from non-Jews (a principle derived elsewhere from the phrase *ish ish*), and only prohibits accepting blemished ones. The question then is why the verse needs to specify *lo takrivu* in this context. The answer, according to Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda, is that this phrase is superfluous — it would have been obvious that blemished animals cannot be accepted from non-Jews, since they cannot be accepted from anyone — and therefore the verse's additional *lo takrivu* must be teaching something new: that *kabbalat hadam*, the receiving of the blood, is also among the prohibited acts.

### Non-Jew Standards

The *tanna kamma* disagrees. For the *tanna kamma*, the verse prohibiting acceptance of blemished animals from non-Jews is not superfluous at all, because there is a genuine *hava amina* that non-Jews might be held to a different standard. The *gemara* explains: *ho'il ve-lo nitztavevu Bnei Noach ela mechusrei evarim* — the Noahide laws that govern sacrificial practice for non-Jews prohibit bringing animals that are lacking a limb, but do not restrict non-Jews to the same level of unblemished perfection required in the *Beit HaMikdash*. On their own altars, non-Jews sacrifice under a more lenient standard. One might therefore have thought: *lo shena be-mizbe'ach didu ve-lo shena be-mizbe'ach didan* — just as a non-Jew may bring a blemished (though not limb-deficient) animal on his own altar, perhaps he may bring it in the *Beit HaMikdash* by the same standard. *Ka-mashma lan* — the verse teaches that once an offering is brought in the *Beit HaMikdash*, our standards apply regardless of who is bringing it. The standards of the Temple are determined by the Temple's sanctity, not by the donor's national affiliation.

This principle invites a broader reflection. There is something significant in the idea that the *kedusha* of the *Beit HaMikdash* imposes its own normative standard irrespective of the donor. The *mikdash* is not merely a site of individual worship but a space with its own claims. A blemished animal that would be acceptable to God on a private altar becomes unacceptable when brought into that particular space.

One further consequence of this debate is worth noting: since the *tanna kamma* must use the verse about non-Jews to address the *hava amina* of differential standards, and Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda uses it instead for *kabbalat hadam*, the two are locked in a dispute about what the verse's *chiddush* is. For Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda, the differential standards problem is resolved from the verse about mutilated animals — though that verse's *lo takrivu* is admittedly rhetorical — and the verse about non-Jews is genuinely superfluous, teaching the prohibition on *kabbalat hadam* for Jews. For the *tanna kamma*, the mutilated animals verse teaches nothing new (it is rhetorical), and the non-Jew verse is needed to address the differential standards problem.

### Alternative Version

The *gemara* now presents *lishna achrina* — a second, parallel version of this debate. As noted in connection with Aramaic dialect patterns, these alternative versions appear to stem from an independent source tradition, likely of *Eretz Yisrael* provenance, and were preserved and incorporated together rather than one being selected over the other. The substantive positions are the same.

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda states: one transgresses even through *kabbalat hadam*. His source: the verse *u-ma'uach ve-chatut... lo takrivu eleh* — from which he derives *kabbalat hadam*. The prohibition against sprinkling he derives from the verse *al ha-mizbe'ach*. The *rabbanan* use the *al ha-mizbe'ach* verse for sprinkling as well, and must therefore explain what they do with the *lo takrivu* from *u-ma'uach ve-chatut*.

### Private Altar

In this version, the *rabbanan* use the *lo takrivu* from the verse about mutilated animals not merely as a rhetorical flourish but to prohibit bringing a blemished animal even on a *bamat yachid*, a private altar, during the periods when such altars were permitted. This is the *chiddush* of that verse according to the *rabbanan*: even outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, even at a time when an Israelite was permitted to maintain a private altar, the prohibition against offering blemished animals applied.

Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda also needs this verse for *bamat yachid* — and indeed he uses it for that purpose as well. He derives *kabbalat hadam* from the verse about non-Jews, which in his view is superfluous since it would be obvious that blemished animals accepted from non-Jews in the *Beit HaMikdash* are prohibited. The *rabbanan* counter that the verse about non-Jews is not superfluous, since without it one might have reasoned that Noahides operate by their own lenient sacrificial standard (*ein metzuvin ela mechusrei evarim*) even within the *Beit HaMikdash*. The verse is needed to clarify that the *Beit HaMikdash* imposes a single standard. In the end both versions converge on the same fundamental debate, presented through slightly different angles.

---

## Reish Lakish

### Birth vs. Later

With all of the above established — the prohibition extended to private altars, to non-Jews, and to multiple stages of the service — Reish Lakish poses a foundational challenge. *Shema lo shaninu ela be-tam she-nasa ba'al mum* — perhaps the entire prohibition applies only when an animal began its life unblemished and subsequently acquired a blemish. If the animal was a *ba'al mum* from birth, *dikla be-alma hu* — it is like a palm tree; why should its sanctification be treated any differently than the sanctification of an object that can never serve as a *korban*?

The question has genuine force. If an animal has borne a blemish since birth, it is, at the moment of sanctification, entirely outside the category of sacrificial animals. Sanctifying it for the altar would presumably produce only *kedushah* destined for *bedek ha-bayit* (the temple treasury), not *kedushat ha-mizbeach* at all. How then does the prohibition — which seems to presuppose that you are perverting something with genuine sacrificial potential — apply?

### Rashi's View

Rashi explains the distinction psychologically. Technically, one might acknowledge that by the time a person sanctifies the animal it has a blemish regardless of when the blemish appeared. But an animal born without a blemish carries a history of potential — it was once in the category of the fit, and therefore sanctifying it in its blemished state is experienced as a perversion of that potential, a wasted opportunity. By contrast, an animal born with a blemish was never in the category of the sacrificially relevant, and sanctifying it is no more a perversion than sanctifying a car or a palm tree. According to Rashi, then, the question of whether the prohibition applies is about how the act is perceived and evaluated, not about a formally different legal category.

### Tosafot's View

*Tosafos* is troubled by Rashi's approach. If the animal has a blemish at the moment of sanctification, it is hard to see — on Rashi's own terms — why the history of the blemish should matter. *Tosafos* therefore reads Reish Lakish's question as directed not at the prohibition against *sanctifying* a blemished animal, but at the prohibition against *offering* one. The distinction hinges on a well-known principle discussed in Bechorot: when an unblemished animal is sanctified and subsequently acquires a blemish, its *kedushah* retains the character of *kedushat ha-mizbe'ach* — altar sanctity — even though it cannot be brought. The sanctity was, at the moment it took hold, the sanctity of something fit for the altar. But when an animal already bearing a blemish is sanctified, the *kedushah* that takes hold is never *kedushat ha-mizbe'ach* to begin with, since the animal was unfit at the defining moment.

*Tosafos* therefore understands Reish Lakish's challenge thus: the prohibition against offering a *korban* with a blemish applies to an animal that genuinely had *kedushat korban*, which then became unfit. If the animal was sanctified while already blemished, it never had *kedushat korban* at all. Offering it is more akin to bringing *chullin la-azara* — bringing non-consecrated produce into the Temple precincts — than to offering a disqualified *korban*. That may be some form of prohibition, but not the specific prohibition against offering a blemished *korban*.

### Birth Defects

Rabbi Chiya bar Rav Yosef challenges Reish Lakish's proposed limitation directly from the scriptural text. The list of disqualifying conditions enumerated in the relevant passage includes *sarua* and *kalut* — a *sarua* is an animal with disproportionate limbs, and a *kalut* is one with undivided hooves. Both are birth defects, congenital conditions present from the animal's first moment of life. Yet they appear in the very same *parasha* from which we derive the prohibitions against sanctifying and offering blemished animals. This demonstrates that the prohibition explicitly encompasses animals that were *ba'alei mumim* from birth.

### Temurah Limitation

Reish Lakish accepts this but shifts his position. *Shema lo shaninu ela be-temurah* — perhaps the prohibition includes congenitally blemished animals, but only in the context of *temurah*. The connection to *temurah* is significant and direct: a *mishna* in Bechorot establishes *chomer be-temurah mi-bezevach* — a stringency of *temurah* over ordinary sanctification — in that *kedushah* fully takes hold on a *temurah* animal even when it bears a permanent blemish. Normally, as discussed above, an animal with a blemish that is sanctified never acquires *kedushat ha-mizbe'ach*. The exception is *temurah*, where the Torah's own mechanism of sanctification transfers full *kedushah* from the original animal to its replacement regardless of whether the replacement is blemished — derived from the verse *ra be-tov o tov be-ra*, indicating that the exchange applies even when the substitute animal is inferior. In a *temurah* scenario involving a congenitally blemished animal, then, the full *kedushat ha-mizbe'ach* is genuinely at stake, and the prohibition would apply for that reason.

Reish Lakish therefore proposes: the cases where a congenitally blemished animal is included in the prohibition are those where real *kedushat ha-mizbe'ach* is conferred — namely, *temurah*. Outside of *temurah*, when you sanctify a congenitally blemished animal, no genuine altar sanctity is created, and perhaps no punishable prohibition applies.

### Rabbi Yannai Vote

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *lo shemia lach ha de-amar Rabbi Yannai* — have you not heard what Rabbi Yannai taught? *Nimnu ve-gamru* — they convened, deliberated, and voted conclusively: *ha-makdish ba'al mum legabei mizbe'ach over mishum chamisha shemot* — one who sanctifies a blemished animal and offers it transgresses on account of five separate prohibitions. If Reish Lakish's limitation to *temurah* were correct, the count would rise to six, since *temurah* itself would add a sixth prohibition to the five. The fact that only five are enumerated — without *temurah* in the count — demonstrates that the prohibition applies even to animals with congenital blemishes outside the *temurah* context.

### Offensive Nature

The *gemara* then addresses Reish Lakish's residual conceptual objection: granted that the prohibition applies, why should it? If the animal never acquires *kedushat ha-mizbe'ach*, in what sense is this categorically different from sanctifying a palm tree?

The answer is: *dikla lav zila milta, min eitzim hu* — a palm tree is not degrading; it is simply wood, categorically irrelevant to sacrifice. But an animal with a blemish is different. *Ve-keivan de-chazi le-tami ve-akdishei le-mumi mechayev* — since unblemished animals of the same species are eligible for sacrifice, the act of sanctifying one that is blemished stands in vivid contrast to what could and should have been done. The alternative is manifest. There is something *zila milta* — something that carries a sense of offense or desecration — about the act, precisely because the right choice was so evidently available.

According to Tosafos, the same logic extends to the act of offering: though the animal technically lacks *kedushat korban*, it was sanctified as if for sacrificial use and is being presented as an *olah*. Even if the *kedushah* never reached the level of *kedushat korban*, the act of bringing it retains a quality of offense that the prohibition captures. This represents a notably non-formalist dimension of the halachic analysis: the prohibition is not grounded solely in the animal's technical legal status but in the experiential and religious character of the act itself.

The *gemara* then presents *lishna achrina* of this resolution, which conveys the same point with slightly different phrasing: *de-dakla be-mina lo laki* — for a palm tree, since no specimen of its kind can serve as a sacrifice, there is nothing offensive about sanctifying it; but *l'afukei ba'al mum, keivan de-ika be-mina laki* — for a blemished animal, since unblemished animals of its species can and should be brought, the choice of a blemished one is inherently offensive and the prohibition applies. As with all instances of *lishna achrina* in this *sugya*, the two versions are substantially equivalent and reflect parallel textual traditions that the editors of the *gemara* chose to preserve in full.

---

## Nesachim & Treasury

### Rava's Extension

Rava now draws an important and somewhat surprising inference from the preceding conclusion. *Ha-shta de-amarta ta'ama de-ba'al mum de-laki mishum de-bziya milta hi* — now that the rationale for the prohibition has been established as the offensive character of the act rather than any technical quality of the *kedushah* conferred, Rava proposes: *afilu makdish lei li-dmei nesachim nami laki* — even if one sanctifies a blemished animal not for direct sacrificial use but in order to use its monetary proceeds for *nesachim* (wine offerings), one transgresses.

The logic is that once the prohibition is grounded in the offensive and unseemly nature of the act rather than in the formal legal quality of the *kedushah*, it extends to any use of a blemished animal within a sacrificial or temple context. Even if you are not attempting to bring the animal itself as a *korban* but only to benefit from its proceeds for sacrificial ends, there is something inherently degrading about employing a blemished animal in the orbit of the Temple service.

Rashi himself flags the difficulty in this inference. He notes in his commentary: *afilu akdesho li-dmei nesachim, de-hashta leika bizayon kol kach* — if you sanctify it for wine offerings, it is not so obviously a *bizayon*, since one does not bring sheep for wine offerings in the first place, and furthermore you are using only the proceeds rather than the animal itself. And yet the conclusion is that one still transgresses. This means the prohibition extends even where the *bizayon* rationale is, by Rava's own framing, considerably attenuated. The *gemara* appears to accept this despite the tension.

### Nedava Verse

The *gemara* then cites a *baraisa* that teaches: *nedava ta'aseh oto u-le-neder lo yiratzeh* — the verse states that you may make the blemished animal a *nedava* (a free-will gift) but it shall not be accepted as a *neder* (a vow-offering). In the standard halachic vocabulary of *Chazal*, the distinction between *neder* and *nedava* turns on whether one says *harei alai* (imposing an obligation on oneself) or *harei zo* (directly designating the animal). The verse therefore must be read through a different lens in this context.

The *baraisa* reads the verse as distinguishing between two modes of temple dedication: giving the animal to *bedek ha-bayit* (the temple treasury) versus bringing it as a *korban* on the altar. *Nedava ta'aseh oto* — you may make it a gift, meaning you should dedicate it to the temple treasury. *Le-neder lo yiratzeh* — it shall not be accepted as a sacrifice, meaning *ritzuy* (divine acceptance) only applies when it is an offering on the altar, which is inappropriate for a blemished animal.

The *baraisa* then derives that this applies both to a *nedava* and to a *neder* in the conventional sense: whether one said *harei zo* or *harei alai*, a blemished animal may be dedicated to the temple treasury but may not be designated as a sacrifice. *Talmud lomar u-le-neder* — the verse includes the *neder* case explicitly. Conversely, *talmud lomar nedava* — the mention of *nedava* teaches that even a direct designation (*harei zo*) cannot be used for the altar. The verse is thus read to cover both directions: the blemished animal may and should go to the treasury, and cannot go to the altar regardless of how the dedication was framed.

### Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi

The *baraisa* records a dispute regarding a related but distinct question. *Tanna kamma* does not restrict *lo yiratzeh* to the animal itself but appears to extend the prohibition to using its proceeds in a sacrificial context — including, following Rava's extension, sanctifying a blemished animal for *nesachim*. *Rebbi*, by contrast, holds: *birtzos gufo ha-kasuv medaber* — the verse is speaking about the body of the animal itself; the prohibition applies only when one attempts to use the blemished animal itself as a sacrifice. *Aval bi-dmei nesachim lo laki* — but if one sanctifies it merely to use the proceeds for wine offerings, one does not transgress.

The *gemara* therefore understands the debate between *tanna kamma* and Rebbi as a dispute over the scope of Rava's extension: whether the prohibition encompasses the use of proceeds for sacrificial purposes, or whether it is limited to bringing the animal itself. Rava had argued for the broader reading based on the *bizayon* rationale; Rebbi's position restricts the prohibition to cases where the degrading act is direct — where the blemished animal is itself being presented as a sacrifice. *Tosafos* observes that in many other contexts, the *gemara* treats the sanctification of animals for their proceeds as unproblematic, which lends support to Rebbi's more restrictive reading.

### Unblemished for Treasury

The word *oto* in the verse (*nedava ta'aseh oto*) is now examined. A limiting word in the Torah typically carries a *chiddush* of exclusion. Here the *baraisa* derives: *oto ta'aseh nedava, ve-ee ata oseh temima nedava le-veit ha-bedek* — this blemished animal you may designate for the temple treasury, but you may not designate an unblemished (*temima*) animal for the treasury. Just as a blemished animal may only go to the treasury and not the altar, an unblemished animal may only go to the altar and not the treasury. Each category has its proper domain, and crossing those domains is itself a violation.

### Positive & Negative

The *baraisa* continues: *mikan amru, ha-makdish temimim le-veit ha-bedek over be-aseh* — one who sanctifies an unblemished animal for the temple treasury transgresses a positive commandment, namely the positive implication of *nedava ta'aseh oto* — a blemished one you shall dedicate, implying that an unblemished one should not be dedicated this way.

The *baraisa* then asks: from where do we derive not only a positive violation but also a negative prohibition? *She-ne'emar: va-yidaber Hashem el Moshe lemor* — the verse introducing this passage says "God spoke to Moses *lemor*." The *gemara* records that Rebbi himself was asked by Bar Kappara: *mai mashma* — what is the implication of this? The answer: *le-mor* is read as *lav ne'emar* — a *lav* (prohibition) was stated about these matters. In the school of Rebbi they say: *lav emur* — a prohibition was said in connection with this passage.

The *Shita Mekubetzet* addresses the obvious question: does this mean that every *parasha* introduced with *va-yidaber Hashem el Moshe lemor* carries an implied negative prohibition? He explains that the principle applies specifically where a positive obligation already implies something should not be done — where, in other words, we know from a positive formulation that a certain act is wrong — and the introductory phrase *va-yidaber Hashem el Moshe lemor* serves to indicate that this implied prohibition carries the force of a formal *lav*, subject to lashes. Rashi emphasizes this as a very local *drasha*; how precisely its scope is limited to this context rather than applying universally remains a difficult question, though it is treated throughout as operative here.

---

## Five Transgressions

### Burning Parts

Rava raises the question of whether burning part of the limbs of a blemished *olah* and burning all of them constitute one transgression or two. The *gemara* had established five prohibitions for one who sanctifies and offers a blemished animal: sanctifying, slaughtering, sprinkling the blood, burning part, and burning all. The verse *ve-isheh lo takrivu mehem* — do not bring a fire-offering from them — forbids even a partial burning. The question is whether these final two — partial and complete burning — produce two separate sets of lashes.

### Abaye's Principle

Abaye holds: *ein lokin al lav she-be-chlelot* — a generic prohibition (*lav she-be-chlelot*), one that encompasses multiple distinct acts within a single formulation, does not produce multiple sets of lashes. A *lav she-be-chlelot* is a *lav* broad enough to include more than one type of prohibited act, and the halachic consequence is that one does not receive separate *malkot* for each included act. In the present case, the prohibition against offering even part of the limbs (*mehem*) is itself a subset of the prohibition against offering all of them; one is subsumed within the other. Abaye therefore maintains that only one set of lashes applies.

### Five or Four

This leads to an apparent contradiction with the enumeration of five transgressions cited from Rabbi Yannai's ruling. If Abaye is correct that the last two prohibitions (burning part, burning all) collapse into one, then only four transgressions incur lashes, not five. The *gemara* tries several resolutions.

One suggestion is that the five apply to different people: the five prohibitions describe different ways in which different individuals might transgress, and no single person necessarily incurs all five. The *gemara* rejects this: the text says *over* (singular — one person transgresses), implying the count refers to a single individual.

Abaye then proposes a textual revision: remove the prohibition of burning part from the count and substitute *kabbalat hadam* (catching the blood) as the fifth prohibition. But the *gemara* objects: *kabbalat hadam l'Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda it lei, le-tanna kamma leit lei* — catching the blood is only a prohibition according to Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda; the *tanna kamma* does not hold this view, and the count of five belongs to the *tanna kamma*. *Kashya* — this remains a difficulty.

The *lishna achrina* of this discussion preserves the same essential problem: even if one reads the *sof* of the passage as reflecting the view of Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda (who includes *kabbalat hadam*), the *reisha* reflects the *rabbanan* (who do not include it) — and yet the number five is stated. According to Abaye, the correct count for the *rabbanan* should be four, not five. The *gemara* concludes *tiyuvta de-Abaye tiyuvta* — this is a decisive refutation of Abaye's position. The text establishes that burning part and burning all do produce separate transgressions, contrary to Abaye's principle as applied here.

---

## Kohanim Temurah

### Mishna Introduction

The *gemara* now introduces the opening *mishna* of the next section. *Ha-kohanim memirim be-shelahem ve-Yisrael memirim be-shelahem* — kohanim may perform *temurah* on their own animals and a Yisrael may perform *temurah* on his. The *mishna* then enumerates a set of important qualifications.

### Chatat & Asham

*Ein ha-kohanim memirim lo be-chatat ve-lo be-asham* — kohanim may not perform *temurah* on a *chatat* or *asham*, even though a kohen who brings such an offering on behalf of a Yisrael is entitled to eat its meat. One might have thought that since the kohen has a proprietary interest in the meat, he has sufficient standing to perform *temurah* on the animal. The *mishna* teaches otherwise: however significant the kohen's share in the *korban*, he is at all times offering the *korban* of the Yisrael, not his own. The Yisrael remains the *ba'al ha-korban*, and only a *ba'al ha-korban* may perform *temurah* on his own sacrifice. The kohen cannot perform *temurah* on what belongs to another.

### Bechor Principle

The *mishna* adds a more striking ruling: *ve-lo ba-bechor* — a kohen may not perform *temurah* on a *bechor*, even though the *bechor* is given to him as an outright gift. This is a genuine *chiddush*. In the case of the *chatat* and *asham*, one can understand why the kohen is not the owner: he never held title to the animal. But a *bechor* is given to the kohen entirely — he brings it, he benefits from it, and there is no sense in which the Yisrael retains any ongoing claim. Yet the *mishna* holds that even here the kohen cannot perform *temurah*. The reason: the *kedushah* of the *bechor* took hold *be-veit be'alim* — in the house of the original owner, at the moment of birth, while the animal still belonged to the Yisrael. The location and moment of *kedushat korban* define the ownership context of the sacrifice for all subsequent purposes, including *temurah*.

### Akiva's Response

Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects to this logic. *Mipnei mah ein memirim ba-bechor?* — why should a kohen not perform *temurah* on a *bechor*? He distinguishes: I understand the rule regarding *chatat* and *asham*, because *she-ein zochim bahen be-chayeihen* — the kohen has no legal entitlement to the animal while it is still alive. The *korban* is entirely the Yisrael's throughout the sacrificial process, and the kohen's benefit comes only after the offering. But *tomar ba-bechor she-zochim bo be-chayav* — in the case of the *bechor*, the kohen acquires the living animal itself; he receives it while it is alive and he is the one who brings it to the *Beit HaMikdash*. Surely that living animal is now *his* sacrifice?

Rabbi Akiva responds with a verse: *ve-lo kvar ne'emar, ve-haya hu u-temurato yihiyeh kodesh* — the Torah states that "it and its *temurah* shall be holy." The principle embedded in this verse is that *temurah* takes place wherever the original *kedushah* took hold. *Heichan kedushah chala alav?* — where did the *kedushah* of the *bechor* first apply? *Be-veit be'alim* — in the owner's house, at birth. Therefore *af temurah be-veit be'alim* — the act of *temurah* also belongs to the context of the owner's house, that is, to the original Yisrael owner. The source of the *kedushah* determines who may perform *temurah*, and since the *bechor*'s *kedushah* is rooted in the Yisrael's ownership, only the Yisrael can be the subject of a *temurah* act. The discussion of this *mishna* and the *gemara*'s analysis of it will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Temurah 8

## Kohen Ownership of Bechor

### Ba'al HaKorban Definition

The Gemara on daf 8 opens by resuming the analysis of who is considered the *ba'al hakorban* — the owner of the sacrifice — for purposes of performing *temurah*. The general rule is that the *kohen*, despite eating the meat of a *chatat* or *asham*, is not the owner of that offering; it belongs to the individual for whom it provides atonement. The *kohen* may eat the flesh, but it is the Yisrael who brought the *korban*, and only the Yisrael who can perform *temurah*. When a *kohen* brings his own *korban*, of course, he is the owner and performs *temurah* accordingly.

### Mishnah Position

The focus of the Mishnah, and now of the Gemara's discussion, concerns the *bechor* — the firstborn animal. The Mishnah appears to reflect the position of Rabbi Akiva, over the resistance of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, that the *kohen* is not the owner of the *bechor*. When a Yisrael possesses a *bechor*, the animal must be given to a *kohen*, who then brings it as a *korban* and eats its meat. Yet the *kohen* is not considered the *ba'al hakorban*. He receives it, as the Gemara will later articulate, *mishulchan gavo'ah* — as one eating from God's table — just as he eats the meat of a Yisrael's *chatat* or *asham* without being that *korban*'s owner. According to this position, it is the Yisrael who can perform *temurah* prior to transferring the animal to the *kohen*; once it is in the *kohen*'s possession, no one performs *temurah* at all.

### Bechor's Intrinsic Kedushah

This raises a striking point worth pausing on. A *bechor* is fundamentally different from every other *korban*: it is never actively sanctified by a person. Its *kedushah* arises automatically by virtue of being the firstborn. One might have imagined, therefore, that no one could perform *temurah* on a *bechor*, since *temurah* would naturally be associated with the one who instills the *kedushah*. The Mishnah itself uses the phrase *chalah alav* — the sanctity took effect — in the owner's house, establishing that the Yisrael in whose possession the *kedushah* first took hold is the relevant party for *temurah*, even though no deliberate act of sanctification was performed.

### Owner vs. Sanctifier

The deeper principle at stake here, already established by the Gemara earlier in the tractate, is that the performer of *temurah* is not the one who instilled the *kedushah* but the one for whom the *korban* operates — the *ba'al hakorban* in the functional sense. Even when one person consecrates an animal as a *korban* on behalf of another, it is the beneficiary who performs *temurah*, not the one who pronounced the consecration. Given this principle, one might have expected the *kohen* to be the *ba'al hakorban* of the *bechor*, since the animal is ultimately brought by him and serves, in a sense, for his benefit. Rabbi Akiva's position, however, maintains that the *kohen* is nonetheless not considered the owner, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri appears to dispute this. The Gemara now proceeds to examine this question at length.

---

## Bechor Sales & Beit HaMi…

### Bechor Sale Conditions

The Gemara opens this discussion by citing a Mishnah from Maseches Ma'aser Sheni: *bechor mochrin oto tam chai uva'al mum chai veshachut* — a *bechor* may be sold unblemished while alive, and if it is blemished, it may be sold alive or slaughtered. The one case excluded is an unblemished animal after it has been slaughtered in the *Beit HaMikdash*. Once the *korban* has been offered, its meat may not be treated as an ordinary commercial commodity; the flesh of *kodashim* is to be eaten by its proper recipients, not sold in the marketplace. But prior to that — while the animal is alive — the *kohen* may sell it, even to another *kohen* who will be the one to bring it to the *Beit HaMikdash* and eat its meat.

### Redemption vs. Sale

The Torah states regarding the *bechor*, *lo yipadeh* — it may not be redeemed. Since its *kedushah* was never instilled through a human act, it cannot be dissolved through a human act either; there is no mechanism for transferring its sanctity to money and rendering the animal ordinary. But the prohibition is specifically against redemption, not against sale. A *bechor* can be sold. If blemished, it retains its identity as a *bechor* with all accompanying restrictions but may be sold to anyone, eaten by *kohanim* and their households when unblemished, and by anyone once it bears a permanent blemish (*mum kavua*). The Gemara notes further that the *kohen* may even use a *bechor* as *kesef kiddushin* — as a means of betrothing a woman. This is significant because the ability to effect *kiddushin* with an object is a strong indicator of full ownership. While one might argue that selling rights to an object merely transfers *tovas hana'ah* rather than actual ownership, using something to betroth a woman demonstrates that the object is genuinely and fully one's property.

### Kiddushin Test

The point about *kiddushin* is worth dwelling on. The Gemara and its commentators sometimes use the question of whether an object may serve as *kesef kiddushin* as a litmus test for ownership. Can a *kohen* say, *harei at mekudeshes li be'bechor zeh* — "you are hereby betrothed to me with this *bechor*"? If he can, the animal is unambiguously his property, not merely an entitlement or a right. The Mishnah's ruling that he may sell it suggests as much, but the explicit mention of *kiddushin* reinforces the point.

### Time Period Distinction

The key distinction in this entire discussion is introduced by Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: *lo shanu ela bizman hazeh* — this ruling applies only nowadays, in the absence of the *Beit HaMikdash*.
