The reason is that *de'ho'il ve'is lei le'Kohen zechiyah begavei* — nowadays the *kohen* has effective and comprehensive ownership of the *bechor*, because even an unblemished animal will never be brought as a *korban*. Since there is no *Beit HaMikdash*, the animal must wait until it develops a blemish before being eaten, and in the interim it is unambiguously the *kohen*'s property to manage, sell, or use as he sees fit.

But *aval bizman she'Beis HaMikdash kayam* — when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands, the situation is different. An unblemished *bechor* is headed for the altar. The *kohen* receives this animal and brings it as a *korban*, but in doing so he is acting, as it were, *mishulchan gavo'ah* — just as a *kohen* who eats the meat of a Yisrael's *chatat* is eating from God's table and is not considered that *korban*'s owner, so too a *kohen* who brings a *bechor* in the time of the *Beit HaMikdash* is not considered its owner. Consequently, *ein mochrin oso tamim chai* — an unblemished *bechor* may not be sold, because the *kohen* does not have the ownership rights that would authorize such a sale.

### Time Period Challenge

The Gemara immediately challenges this position. Rava cites the very Mishnah that permits selling the *bechor* unblemished and alive. The Mishnah also refers to a situation where the animal is *tam veshachut* — unblemished and slaughtered — as a case where sale is prohibited. But, Rava argues, when does the scenario of an unblemished *shechutah* arise? Only when there is a *Beit HaMikdash* and the animal is actually brought as a *korban*. The Mishnah is therefore implicitly set in the time of the *Beit HaMikdash*, and yet it permits selling the *bechor* unblemished while alive — which would contradict Rav Nachman's position.

### Mishnah Context

The Gemara deflects this challenge. The Mishnah, it explains, need not be read as contrasting the case of unblemished-alive against unblemished-slaughtered in order to teach that the latter is forbidden. Rather, the Mishnah is discussing the present time, *bizman hazeh*, and the *chiddush* is precisely that even nowadays, when an unblemished animal cannot be brought to the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *kohen* may sell it. The scenario of unblemished-slaughtered simply does not arise nowadays; there is no altar, no *korban*, and therefore no case to discuss. The Mishnah's formulation — focusing on cases available in the present — tells us something meaningful about today's law without implying anything about the status of a *kohen* vis-à-vis an unblemished *bechor* when the *Beit HaMikdash* stood.

---

## Pasuk Analysis & Proof

### Bayit Aleinu Proof

The Gemara now presses the question more sharply with a *braita* citing the verse about *bechor*: *lo tipadeh* — it may not be redeemed — from which the inference is drawn that while it may not be redeemed, it may be sold. Rav Mesharshiya asks: in what context is this *braita* operating? If we say it is discussing the present time, the verse itself concludes — *ve'es damam tizrok al ha-mizbe'ach, ve'es chelbam taktir* — "their blood shall be sprinkled on the altar and their fat shall be burned." This reference to the altar and the offering makes clear that we are discussing the time of the *Beit HaMikdash*, where the *bechor* is actually being brought as a *korban*. And in that context, the *braita* teaches that the *bechor* may be sold. This appears to prove Rav Nachman wrong — it seems that even when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands, and the unblemished *bechor* is to be brought as a *korban*, it may nonetheless be sold by the *kohen*, which would imply that the *kohen* is its owner.

### Pasuk Interpretation

The Gemara resolves this by reading the verse in two parts, each applying to a different scenario. The beginning of the verse — *lo tipadeh*, it may not be redeemed but may be sold — refers to a blemished animal. A blemished *bechor* cannot be redeemed, since *bechor* admits no redemption regardless, but it may be sold. The end of the verse — sprinkling the blood on the altar, burning the fat — refers to an unblemished animal that is brought as a *korban*. On this reading, the *drasha* permitting sale applies only to the blemished case, not to the unblemished one. The *braita* therefore offers no proof that an unblemished *bechor* in the time of the *Beit HaMikdash* may be sold, and Rav Nachman's position stands undisturbed.

This reading is internally elegant. What type of *bechor* would its owner wish to redeem? Precisely one that has a blemish — a *kohen* with a blemished *bechor* might prefer to redeem it for money and use the proceeds freely. The verse therefore addresses that very impulse: even if your *bechor* has a blemish, you cannot redeem it; you may sell it, but you may not redeem it. The unblemished *bechor*, by contrast, is headed for the altar.

---

## Taruva Case

### Mixed Identity Setup

The Gemara introduces a *braita* involving a *ta'aruva* — a case of mixed identity. A *kohenes* gave birth to a son, but the infant was mixed up at the hospital with the newborn son of her *shifchah* — her slave woman. The children grow up without knowing which of the two is the *kohen* and which is the slave belonging to the *kohen*. This uncertainty creates a series of unusual *halachic* situations.

Once they reach maturity, the first step is *meshachrerin zeh es zeh* — they free one another. Each one writes a document of manumission declaring that if I am the master and you are my slave, you are hereby freed, and they do so mutually. This resolves the question of personal status as between the two of them, though the one who was in fact the slave is now a freedman rather than a *kohen*.

Before the freeing takes place, both may eat *terumah*: one is a *kohen*, the other is an *eved* of a *kohen*, and both categories permit consumption of *terumah*. However, when they go to the threshing floor to receive their *terumah*, they receive only a single portion. There is a concern about giving *terumah* directly to the *eved* of a *kohen* independently, since this could create the impression that he is a *kohen* himself. They therefore go together as a pair and receive one combined allocation.

### Waiting for Blemish

The more analytically interesting scenario concerns a *bechor* that one of these two individuals owns. If he were known to be a *kohen*, he would keep the *bechor*, bring it as a *korban* when it is unblemished, and eat it. If he were known to be a slave, he would have to give it to a *kohen* — specifically his master. But since neither knows which he is, the *halacha* is *yiru ad sheyistavu veyochlu bemuman* — the animal grazes until it develops a blemish, and then it is eaten with the blemish.

Why this resolution? Once the animal has a blemish, the question of bringing it as a *korban* no longer applies. It becomes a straightforward question of monetary ownership, governed by the principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* — the burden of proof lies with the one seeking to extract from another's possession. Neither of the two individuals can prove that the other is the *kohen* entitled to the animal, and therefore neither can be compelled to hand it over. Without the blemish, however, the question is not merely monetary. An unblemished *bechor* in the time of the *Beit HaMikdash* must be brought as a *korban*, and only the *kohen* who owns it may do so. Since we do not know who is the *kohen*, the animal cannot simply be brought by any *kohen* who steps forward.

### Seizure Argument

The Gemara draws a significant inference from this case. Why, it asks, does the *Beit HaMikdash* not simply send its treasurer to seize the animal and ensure that it is brought as a *korban*? After all, if the *kohen* is not truly the owner of an unblemished *bechor* — if he merely holds the right to bring it but the *bechor* fundamentally belongs to God — then the *Beit HaMikdash* should be able to compel its offering. The very fact that we instead allow these two individuals to retain the animal until it develops a blemish demonstrates that the *kohen* does have genuine ownership rights over his *bechor*, even while it is unblemished. Because one of the two individuals may be the *kohen* owner, the *Beit HaMikdash* cannot simply appropriate the animal.

### Nowadays Response

The Gemara declines this proof. It maintains that the *braita* is discussing the present time, *bizman hazeh*, and that the *chiddush* of the case is not the ruling to wait for a blemish — since nowadays every *bechor* must wait for a blemish anyway — but rather the monetary *halacha* that follows. Everyone today waits for a blemish; that is simply the baseline. The novel teaching of this *braita*, according to the Gemara, is that since each of the two individuals might be the *kohen*, neither is obligated to give the animal to the other. The principle of *hamotzi mechavero alav haraya* operates in their favor: no other *kohen* can come and demand the animal either, since each of the two will declare, "I am the *kohen* and this animal is mine." Tosafos makes explicit what the Gemara is implying: the *chiddush* here is purely monetary, not the instruction to wait for a blemish.

The Gemara even offers a second formulation (*lashon acher*) to reinforce this reading. Nowadays, the *braita*'s instruction to "let it graze until it develops a blemish" is unremarkable — that is what one does with every *bechor*. The novel point is that these two individuals of uncertain identity may collectively prevent any other *kohen* from claiming the animal. Each can say to a third-party *kohen*: "I may be the *kohen* owner; you cannot take this from me."

It is worth appreciating the intellectual texture of this exchange. The attempt to prove from the *ta'aruva* case that the *kohen* is the owner of his unblemished *bechor* was elegant: if the *kohen* were not the owner, the *Beit HaMikdash* would simply seize the animal and ensure it was brought. The Gemara's response — that we are in fact discussing the present time and the *chiddush* is merely monetary — is technically adequate but, as the Gemara itself acknowledges, less sweeping. The *hava amina* (the initial assumption) powerfully illustrates what it would mean to say the *kohen* is not the owner: his personal preference to wait for a blemish would be legally irrelevant, and the *Beit HaMikdash* would simply take what it regards as its own.

---

## Ir HaNidachat

### Ir HaNidachat Principle

The Gemara turns to yet another case in its ongoing effort to resolve the question of *kohen* ownership. An *ir hanidachat* — an idolatrous city whose inhabitants were led to worship *avodah zarah* — is subject to a special law requiring the destruction of all its property. The Torah specifies *shlalah* — its booty — indicating that what must be destroyed is the private property of the city's inhabitants. Excluded, however, is *shlal shamayim* — things that belong to Heaven. Sacred objects such as *Sifrei Torah*, *mezuzos*, and sanctified animals do not belong to the city and are therefore not destroyed with it.

### Bechor Status Question

A *braita* cites Rabbi Shimon, who derives from a separate word in the verse — *behemtah*, "its animals" — that *bechor* and *ma'aser behemah* are excluded from the destruction of the *ir hanidachat*. The *drasha* reads: its animals are destroyed, excluding the animals of *bechor* and *ma'aser*. The Gemara asks: in what context is this *braita* operating? An *ir hanidachat* requires a *beis din* of seventy-one, which functioned only when the *Beit HaMikdash* stood. We are therefore squarely in the world of the *Beit HaMikdash*. Furthermore, if the *bechor* in question were blemished, it would be so thoroughly the *kohen*'s property that it would seemingly be destroyed together with the rest of his belongings — why would we need a special verse to exclude it? The Gemara therefore concludes that we must be discussing an unblemished *bechor*, one that in theory would be brought as a *korban*.

And here the proof: if the unblemished *bechor* requires a special verse to establish that it is *shlal shamayim* and not *shlal ha-ir*, that verse was necessary precisely because one might have thought the *bechor* belongs to the *kohen* who owns it and is therefore part of the city's property to be destroyed. This *hava amina* — this initial assumption that would require exclusion — implies that the *kohen* does have genuine ownership rights over his unblemished *bechor* even in the time of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

### Kedushah Prevents Trade

The Gemara again finds a way out. It insists that the *braita* is discussing a blemished *bechor* after all. The question then becomes: why was a special verse needed? If the *bechor* has a blemish and the *kohen* can eat it freely, is it not simply his property, subject to destruction like any other? The answer is that even a blemished *bechor* is not treated as entirely ordinary property. The Mishnah establishes that all sanctified animals whose blemishes have been redeemed may be sold in the marketplace and weighed out by the pound as *chullin*, except for *bechor* and *ma'aser behemah*, which are not redeemed and retain an element of *kedushah* in the way they are handled. Even with a blemish, they cannot be sold in the open marketplace like ordinary meat. Their *kedushah* continues to express itself, preventing them from being treated as fully *behemtah* — as completely ordinary animals. Therefore the word *behemtah* in the verse excludes them: since they do not function as ordinary *behemtah*, they are not included among the city's ordinary property to be destroyed.

On this reading, the verse was not needed because the *kohen* is the owner; it was needed because the *bechor*'s *kedushah*, even after a blemish, renders it categorically distinct from normal property. Rav Nachman's position remains intact.

---

## Ashám & Me'ilah

### Kodashim Kalim Position

The Gemara now brings another challenge, this time from the laws of *me'ilah* — trespass against God. The Torah describes a situation where someone is entrusted with his fellow's property and falsely denies it under oath, committing *ma'al b'Hashem* — a trespass involving God's name. The inclusion of the phrase *l'Hashem* beyond the plain meaning of the oath's sanctity prompted a *drasha*: the verse comes to include *kodashim kalim* — lighter sacrifices — which are owned by their bearers yet possess a dimension of divine sanctity. This is the classic position of Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who teaches *l'rabot kodashim kalim she'hem mamon ba'alim* — the lighter sacrifices are the property of their owners, and one who falsely denies holding his fellow's *shelamim* has committed *ma'al b'Hashem*.

### Ben Azzai Limit

A variant tradition (*acherim omrim*) limits the inclusion to *shelamim* alone, and then Abba Yosi ben Dosai transmits a further restriction in the name of Ben Azzai: only *bechor* — and not all *kodashim kalim* — is truly owned in this sense.

### Bechor Distinction

Why would Ben Azzai exclude *shelamim* and *ma'aser* while retaining *bechor*? Rashi explains that *shelamim* carry numerous ritual trappings — *semichah*, *tenufah*, the bringing of *nesachim* — that continuously emphasize its status as a *korban* and distance it from the owner's sphere of personal property. *Ma'aser behemah* carries the restriction of *lo yimacher* — it may not be sold — which similarly marks it as something other than fully owned property. *Bechor* alone lacks these extra encumbrances and restrictions. There is no *semichah*, no *tenufah*, no libation, and no prohibition on sale. It is therefore the one *korban* that Ben Azzai regards as sufficiently the owner's property to fall under the *ma'al* category.

### Context Analysis

Having cited Ben Azzai's position, the Gemara immediately asks the standard pair of questions: what time period and what state of the animal are we discussing? Since *shelamim* is mentioned as a contrast case, we are clearly in a context where animals are being brought as *korbanos* — i.e., the time of the *Beit HaMikdash*. And if we are discussing blemished animals, the case is not comparable to *shelamim* in the way the *drasha* requires. We must therefore be discussing an unblemished *bechor* in the time of the *Beit HaMikdash*. And the very fact that Ben Azzai considers it *mamon ba'alim* in that context would appear to prove that the *kohen* is the owner of his unblemished *bechor* even when it would be brought as a *korban*.

### Chutz La'aretz Answer

Abaye responds with the third avenue of escape that has now entered the discussion: *l'olam b'tam u'be'bechor b'chutz la'aretz* — granted that it is unblemished and granted that there is a *Beit HaMikdash*, but we are discussing a *bechor* that arose outside of *Eretz Yisrael*. Rabbi Shimon, as noted earlier, holds that *bechor* in *chutz la'aretz* is ideally left to develop a blemish before being brought — or consumed — since *bechor* and *ma'aser behemah* are linked to the agricultural and communal life of the Land. *Bedi'eved*, if an unblemished *bechor* from *chutz la'aretz* is brought to the *Beit HaMikdash*, it is offered. But *lechatchila*, it should wait for a blemish, much like the situation *bizman hazeh*. In such a case, the *kohen* is effectively the owner, because the animal is not headed to the altar; hence it is *mamon ba'alim*, as Ben Azzai teaches.

This completes the set of three defenses available to Rav Nachman's position: the animal has a *mum*; or it is *bizman hazeh*; or it is in *chutz la'aretz*.

---

## Yochanan vs. Akiva

### Yochanan's Challenge

The Gemara at last returns to the Mishnah itself — the debate between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva with which the entire discussion began. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri challenges Rabbi Akiva: I understand why a *kohen* cannot perform *temurah* on a *chatat* or *asham* brought by a Yisrael — *she'harei ein zachin bahem b'chayeihem*, because the *kohen* has no rights whatsoever to those animals while they are alive. He merely eats the meat after *shechitah*. But *chomer b'bechor she-zachin b'chayav* — what do you say about a *bechor*, where the *kohen* has genuine rights to the animal while it is still alive? How can you say he cannot perform *temurah*? The argument is that the *kohen*'s living ownership of the *bechor* — the fact that this animal is actually his while it breathes — distinguishes it fundamentally from a *chatat* or *asham*.

### Chutz La'aretz Resolution

Abaye responds, applying the framework already established: the discussion in the Mishnah concerns a *bechor* in *chutz la'aretz*, where Rabbi Shimon rules that one should ideally wait for a blemish. In *chutz la'aretz*, the *kohen* is the owner, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri correctly observes that the *kohen* has rights to the living animal. The question of whether he may therefore perform *temurah* is precisely what Rabbi Akiva disputes, even there, based on the *pasuk* about *beis ba'alim*.

### Debate Reframing

The Gemara then steps back to reflect on how this debate maps onto a broader *tannaitic* dispute. A *braita* formulates the rule as follows: *bechor b'veis ba'alim osim temurah, b'veis kohen ein osim temurah* — for a *bechor* in the owner's house, *temurah* is performed; once it is in the *kohen*'s house, *temurah* is not performed. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees and says: once the animal comes into the *kohen*'s possession, no one performs *temurah*.

At first glance, these positions might seem identical — after all, if only the owner can perform *temurah* and the animal is now with the *kohen*, the owner no longer has it and clearly cannot act. The Gemara therefore re-reads the *Tanna Kamma*: *b'veis kohen hu oseh temurah ve'ein ba'al oseh temurah* — once it is in the *kohen*'s house, the *kohen* performs *temurah*, and the original owner may not. This is the position aligned with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that the *kohen* is the owner of his *bechor* and may perform *temurah*. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar then takes the position of Rabbi Akiva: once the *kohen* has it, no one performs *temurah*, because the *kohen* is not the owner and the original owner has relinquished possession.

The Gemara concludes simply: *ha Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, ha Rabbi Akiva* — the two positions in the *braita* parallel the two positions of the Mishnah exactly. This entire discussion of whether the *kohen* is the owner of his *bechor*, and all the attempts to prove it from *bayit aleinu*, *ta'aruva*, *ir hanidachat*, and the *me'ilah* case, ultimately circle back to that foundational Mishnaic debate, which remains in the form of a *machloket* between these two Tannaim, with the resolution anchored to the case of *chutz la'aretz* and the opinion of Rabbi Shimon.

---

## Sale Restrictions

### Kohen-to-Kohen Only

Having explored the theoretical dimensions of *kohen* ownership, the Gemara pivots to an eminently practical question. Rav Chisda rules: *lo shanu ela kohen le-kohen, aval kohen le-Yisrael assur* — the ruling permitting a *kohen* to sell his *bechor* applies only when he sells it to another *kohen*, but it is prohibited to sell it to a Yisrael.

### False Blemish Risk

The reason, explains Rav Chisda, is the concern of *dilma azil Yisrael ve-shadi bei muma* — lest the Yisrael who now possesses an unblemished *bechor* go and inflict a blemish on it himself. The Yisrael has every incentive to do so: without a blemish, the animal cannot be eaten; with a blemish, it can be consumed. If the Yisrael creates the blemish artificially, that is itself a transgression. But the further concern is that when he brings the animal to a sage to have the blemish certified, he will claim *bechor zeh natun li Kohen be-mumo* — "this *bechor* was given to me by the *kohen* already bearing this blemish" — thereby deflecting suspicion and falsely implicating the *kohen* in the transgression.

### Ruling Safeguard

The Gemara raises a counterargument: would a sage actually rule in favor of the Yisrael under these circumstances? Rav is cited: *ein ro'in bechor le-Yisrael ela im ken Kohen immo* — sages will not render a ruling on a *bechor* in a Yisrael's possession without the *kohen* being present. This rule exists as a broader safeguard against *kochot* withholding *bechor* from *kohanim* — since a Yisrael might claim falsely that he received it back from a *kohen*, sages require the *kohen* to be present and to testify directly. If the *kohen* is present, the sage can ask directly when the blemish arose — before or after the sale — and the scheme of blaming the *kohen* for an artificially induced blemish collapses.

### Mar Zutra Story

The Gemara illustrates the texture of these concerns with a brief narrative. Mar Zutra visited the household of Rav Ashi and was invited to eat. Meat was brought before him, and those present told him it was the meat of a *bechor* — considered especially healthful — and he should partake. Mar Zutra asked how they had obtained *bechor* meat, since they were not *kohanim*. They replied that a certain *kohen* had sold them his *bechor*.

### Purchase Defense

Mar Zutra challenged them, asking whether they did not accept the ruling of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua that it is prohibited to purchase a *bechor* from a *kohen* — because it resembles *kohen hamisaye'a b'veis hagranot*, a *kohen* who volunteers his services at the threshing floor in order to secure his priestly gifts. They replied: *danan mizban kazavninan* — but we paid for it. We actually purchased this meat; there was no gift, no favor, no implicit exchange. Why should a straightforward commercial transaction be prohibited?

### Discount Concern

Mar Zutra then pivoted to a second challenge, citing the Mishnah that requires a Yisrael to raise his *bechor* for thirty days (small animals) or fifty days (large animals) before transferring it to the *kohen*. If a *kohen* offers to relieve the Yisrael of that financial burden and take the animal early, the Yisrael may not hand it over — because such a favor from the *kohen* would constitute an implicit exchange for the *bechor* he is about to receive. Mar Zutra's point was that even when a Yisrael transfers a *bechor* to a *kohen* to which the *kohen* is legally entitled, if that transfer is entangled with a favor received from the *kohen*, it is inappropriate. A fortiori, one might argue that a purchase from a *kohen* is similarly suspect if the price is artificially low.

The response is that the *Mishnah*'s case is obviously problematic — the favor and the *bechor* are directly linked, with the *kohen* doing a service and the immediate benefit being the receipt of the *bechor*. A straightforward purchase is entirely different.

### Profit Motive

The Gemara finally addresses the underlying concern about a discounted sale: *mouzil kohen gabei* — perhaps the *kohen* sold the meat at a discount, hoping that the Yisrael would in turn give him his future *bechor* in exchange. This is the *maris ayin* concern — not that the transaction is prohibited on its face, but that a below-market price signals an implicit deal and creates the appearance of impropriety. The Gemara's response is pithy and psychologically astute: *butzina tav mikara* — a small gourd now is worth more than a large gourd later; a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. A *kohen* who is selling his *bechor* will extract as much money as he can in the present transaction and will not reduce his price on the speculative hope that this same Yisrael will someday give him a *bechor* in return. The profit motive of the immediate sale rules out any assumption of a discounted exchange.

With this practical resolution, the daf concludes its long and intricate examination of the *kohen*'s relationship to the *bechor* — from the theoretical question of ownership and *temurah*, through the time-sensitive distinctions between the era of the *Beit HaMikdash* and the present day, and finally to the concrete commercial regulations governing how a *kohen* may and may not dispose of the sacred property entrusted to him.

---

---

# Temurah 9

## Types of Temurah

### Sheep & Cattle

The ninth daf of *Temurah* opens with a new *mishna* that returns us to the core concerns of the tractate after an interlude on *bechor*. The *mishna* begins: *memirin min hatzon al habakar, min habakar al hatzon* — one may effect a *temurah* exchange from sheep to cattle or from cattle to sheep. It bears repeating that the capacity to perform *temurah* is not a commendable one; the act constitutes a transgression. Nonetheless, it is effective, and the *mishna* establishes that the exchange need not involve animals of the same species. If one has a sheep designated as an *olah*, one may attempt to exchange it with a cow, even a cow not suited to that particular *kedusha*.

### Male & Female

The *mishna* continues: *min hazcharim al hanekeivot, umin hanekeivot al hazcharim* — from males to females and females to males. This holds even where the type of *kedusha* conferred upon the animal is inappropriate for its gender. If, for example, one has a female animal that has been sanctified with the *kedusha* of an *olah* — a category ordinarily requiring a male — the *temurah* is nonetheless effective. What becomes of such an animal in practice, given the mismatch between its sex and its designated sanctity, is a matter the *Gemara* will address later.

### Blemished Animals

The *mishna* goes on: *min hatmimim al ba'alei mumim* — from unblemished animals to blemished ones. This case requires some clarification. As a general rule, an animal that already possesses a *mum* at the time of its sanctification cannot acquire *kedushat korban* — *kedushat haguf* — since it is, in a sense, an improper object for sanctification, no different in principle from consecrating a piece of furniture. The *kedusha* that attaches to such an animal is only *kedushat bedek habayit*, which pertains to the Temple maintenance fund rather than to sacrifice.

However, when an animal is first sanctified in an unblemished state and subsequently develops a *mum*, it retains full *kedushat korban*. It cannot be brought as a *korban* due to its blemish, but its sanctity as a *korban* remains intact. From such an animal, *temurah* is applicable: the *kedusha* that resided in the original animal now passes to the second one, even if that second animal also carries a *mum*. The verse states, *vehaya hu utemurato yihye kodesh* — it and its *temurah* shall be holy — and this takes effect regardless. The *mishna* also mentions the reverse: *min ba'alei mumim al hatmimim* — from blemished to unblemished — which, while perhaps seeming like a beneficial exchange, is equally an act of *temurah*.

### Prohibition Verse

The *mishna* cites the source verse: *lo yachalifenu velo yamir oto tov bera o ra betov* — one shall not exchange it nor transfer it, good for bad or bad for good. The *mishna* then poses a question of interpretation: what constitutes a case of *tov bera*, good for bad? Rashi understands the first term in the verse as referring to the non-sanctified animal being offered in exchange — one is attempting to replace a bad animal (the sanctified one) with a good one. Tosafot read it in the opposite direction. Following Rashi, the *mishna* answers that *tov bera* refers specifically to *ba'alei mumim shekadam hekdesham et muman* — animals whose sanctification preceded the onset of their blemish. That is, *temurah* from a blemished animal is only operative when the animal's *kedusha* was established prior to its blemish.

## Blemish Case

### Rashi Position

The *mishna*'s formulation raises a sharper question about the case of an animal that was sanctified first and then developed a *mum*. Such an animal possesses full *kedushat korban*, yet one is supposed to redeem its value and use those proceeds to purchase a replacement *korban*. If one instead takes a healthy unblemished animal and declares *zeh tachas zeh*, one has committed the transgression of *temurah*. But given that redemption is both permitted and obligatory in such a case, is there a way to transfer the *kedusha* directly to another animal without incurring the prohibition?

### Blemish Timing

The answer depends, according to several *rishonim*, on the precise framing of the act. The *Minchas Chinuch* states in passing, and the *Shita Mekubetzes* develops more fully, that one may in principle transfer the *kedusha* directly to another animal when the original has a *mum*, provided one frames the act correctly. If one says "I am exchanging A for B," that is *temurah* — one has transgressed and incurs *malkut*. If one says "I am redeeming this blemished animal and placing its *kedusha* upon B," that is *pidyon* and is precisely what one is required to do.

The conceptual distinction is not merely semantic. When one frames the act as exchange, the focus rests on the new animal — one prefers it and wishes it to take the place of the original. When one frames the act as redemption, the focus rests on the original: the animal already has a problem and one is removing its *kedusha* and relocating it. The *Shita Mekubetzes* goes further still and suggests the distinction may be expressed even physically: if one places one's hands on the new, unblemished animal and declares *zeh tachas zeh*, that is *temurah*; if one places one's hands on the animal bearing the *mum* — even using the identical words *zeh tachas zeh* — that constitutes *pidyon*, not *temurah*, since one is initiating the act from the seat of the *kedusha* and removing it outward.

### Redemption Strategy

The irony of the situation is worth noting. *Temurah* with a blemished animal is in a certain sense a strange category, because the entire point of having a *korban* with a *mum* is that one is *obligated* to transfer the *kedusha* elsewhere. The prohibition is not against the outcome — transferring the *kedusha* to another animal — but against the manner in which the transfer is framed and initiated.

If the animal never had *kedushat korban* to begin with — because the *mum* preceded the sanctification — then no act of *temurah* is relevant at all. The question of what effect, if any, such a declaration would have in that scenario is an interesting one left for further analysis. Presumably it would also fail to constitute a valid *pidyon*, since there is no *kedushat korban* to redeem.

### Intent & Words

This leads to a broader principle regarding the relationship between *temurah* and *pidyon*. If an animal has no *mum* and one attempts to "redeem" it onto another animal using the language of redemption, that would presumably still constitute *temurah*, since *pidyon* is not a relevant or legitimate category for an unblemished *korban*. The distinction between framing an act as *temurah* versus *pidyon* is operative only where *pidyon* is itself an applicable and appropriate course of action — that is, where the original animal genuinely has a *mum* and is due for redemption. Outside of that context, the attempt to transfer *kedusha* directly to another animal is *temurah* by definition. This point, while not exhaustively analyzed in the early sources, will resurface in a more extreme form at the end of the *Gemara*.

## Gemara Derivation

### Abaye's Duality

The *Gemara* asks *mena hani mili* — where is all of this derived? The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: the verse in *Vayikra* states *lo yachalifenu velo yamir oto tov bera o ra betov v'im hamer yamir behemah b'vehemah vehaya hu utmurato yihye kodesh* — if one exchanges *behemah b'behemah*, animal for animal. The word *behemah* is entirely generic, and from this the *baraita* derives that all the combinations enumerated in the *mishna* — sheep for cattle, cattle for sheep, sheep for goats, goats for sheep, male for female, female for male, blemished for unblemished, unblemished for blemished — are all subsumed under *behemah b'behemah*. 

The *baraita* then asks: might one think *temurah* applies even when the blemish preceded the sanctification — *yachol afilu kadam mum lehekdesham*? The *Gemara* answers that the verse therefore specifies *tov bera o ra betov* — the language of *tov* and *ra* is interpreted technically, in the sense of unblemished and blemished in a *korban* context, and is used to exclude the case where the animal was already *ra* — blemished — at the moment of its sanctification.

The question then becomes how to derive this exclusion from the language of the verse. Abaye explains: the verse could have said simply *tov bera o ra bo* — good for bad, or bad for it — since having already established the first animal as "bad," the implication of "good" in the second case would be understood. The explicit repetition of the word *tov* — *ra betov* — is therefore a redundancy. That redundancy is the textual hook: *shema minah*, infer from it that the origin animal must possess an element of *tov*. Concretely: *tov me'ikara oseh tmurah, ra me'ikara ein oseh tmurah* — only an animal that was good at the outset, that was unblemished at the time of sanctification, is subject to *temurah*. If it was bad — *ra* — from the outset, its *kedusha* was never *kedushat haguf* and it falls outside the domain of *temurah* entirely.

### Rava's Position

Rava offers a somewhat different analysis. He observes that in fact both uses of the word *tov* in the verse are in some sense redundant — *travaihu tov yateira mi'asrei*. The verse could have simply said *lo yachlifenu velo yamir tov bera o ra bo* and dispensed with both explicit *tov* references. Why, then, are both needed? Rava answers that one extra *tov* is needed to establish that even *tov betov* — even exchanging a good animal for another good animal — carries lashes. The verse could not have left this to inference, since it requires an explicit source for lashes to be imposed. The second extra *tov* then teaches *tov me'ikara*, that the original animal must have been unblemished at the time of sanctification.

### Kal va-Chomer

Abaye challenges Rava's need for an explicit verse prohibiting *tov betov*. The argument seems obvious: *kal vachomer* — if exchanging a good animal for a bad one, which might appear to be an improvement, still incurs lashes, then certainly exchanging good for good, where no improvement is even being attempted, should incur lashes as well. Why does Rava require a verse for that?

Rava responds with the principle *ein onshin min hadin* — one does not impose lashes on the basis of a *kal vachomer* alone. A *kal vachomer* may establish the prohibition in principle, but for lashes to be imposed, the prohibition must have an explicit textual source.

Abaye, however, counters that this is not a genuine *kal vachomer* at all. The argument *mi gara tov mera* — is *tov betov* any worse than *tov bera*? — suggests that *tov betov* is not a separate inference derived from *tov bera* but rather is already included within the same statement. The principle that one may not exchange even for something "better" already encompasses, by definition, the case of exchanging for something equivalent. Just as a prohibition against harming something includes a prohibition against simply not improving it, the inclusion of *tov betov* in the prohibition follows not as a separate *kal vachomer* but as an implicit component of the original rule. Abaye draws an analogy to the case of a full sister in the laws of *arayot*, where a *kal vachomer* from a half-sister is needed and yet the question arises whether this is genuinely a *kal vachomer* or merely implicit in the original prohibition — the *Gemara* elsewhere resolves such cases by treating them as distinct enough to require explicit sources.

### Redundancy Resolution

Having established Rava's position that both extra *tov* references are necessary, and that according to Abaye the *tov betov* prohibition is implicit rather than derived by *kal vachomer*, the *Gemara* still needs to resolve why, according to Abaye, the verse contains an extra *tov* at all if *tov betov* is already implicit. The answer is precisely what Abaye himself stated at the outset: the extra *tov* is not there to teach *tov betov* as a new case but rather to teach *tov me'ikara* — to signal that the animal originating the *temurah* must have possessed an element of *tov* at the time of its sanctification. Once you say you cannot do bad for good, you know that "bad for good" refers to animals that were at least once good — because if the animal started blemished, it was never in the domain of *tov* at all, and the prohibition never touches it.

## Exchange Cases

### Hachlif Case

The *Gemara* now turns to the *baraita*: *lo yachlifenu beshel acherim velo yamiru bo beshel atzmo* — do not exchange it with another person's animal, and do not transfer it on your own. The case of exchange with another person involves a scenario in which one party holds a sanctified *korban* and another holds an unsanctified animal, and they attempt to swap — the sanctified animal passing to one party and the unsanctified animal, now absorbing the *kedusha*, passing to the other. The one who controls the sanctity — the owner of the *korban* — is the one who would incur *malkut*. The verse *velo yamiru bo* covers the separate case where both animals belong to the same individual and that person declares one to be the substitute of the other.

### Two Prohibitions

The *Gemara* asks why both prohibitions are necessary. Could the verse not have stated only *lo yachlifenu* — do not exchange — and left *lo yamiru bo* to be understood by inference? The answer depends on which case is considered more obviously prohibited. One possibility is that when both animals belong to the same person, the act is more obviously a real and meaningful act of exchange, since the individual has full control over both, and therefore *lo yamiru bo* is the more obvious case. One might have supposed that *lo yachlifenu* — exchange with another — could escape prohibition since the actor does not fully control the other party's animal. To preclude that reasoning, the *Torah* states both.

Conversely, it could be argued the other way: perhaps one would have thought that when both animals are mine, I am not truly exchanging but merely extending the *kedusha* — declaring that the second animal shall also carry the *kedusha* of the first without removing it from the first. If that were permitted, the second prohibition would be needed to clarify that even this constitutes a transgression.

This is indeed what some *rishonim* appear to conclude from the *Gemara*: that even a mere attempt to extend *kedusha* — not to replace one sanctified animal with another, but to add *kedusha* to a second animal without removing it from the first — is also considered *temurah*. This is a striking position, since the entire intuitive conception of *temurah* was that it represents an attempt to replace one *korban* with another. Rabbeinu Gershom, however, reads the *Gemara* differently, and his version of the text is more persuasive. His text reads *detzavuyei matzi makdish lehu* — that one has the capacity to sanctify both of them — not that one is actually in the process of sanctifying both. According to Rabbeinu Gershom, the *Gemara* is saying only this: since both animals belong to me, and I have the inherent ability to sanctify both independently, one might have thought the act should be interpreted charitably — that what I really intended was to sanctify the second animal through my own independent power, and therefore perhaps I should not incur lashes. *Ka mashma lan* — the *Torah* teaches that no such charitable reinterpretation applies; the act is one of exchange and lashes follow.

This reading is far more coherent, since it does not require positing a novel category of *temurah* never encountered elsewhere. The contrast with the case of exchange with another person is also illuminated by Rabbeinu Gershom's reading: there, the question is how I have the power to affect another's *korban* at all; here, I do have the power — but that power does not redefine the act I actually performed.

### Matfis Concept

The *Gemara* now examines the case of exchange with another person's animal more closely. *Hai beshel acherim heichi dami* — what exactly is the scenario? If my *korban* is being exchanged for Michael's unsanctified animal, then while I control the *kedusha* I wish to transfer, I do not control Michael's animal — and the verse teaches *ish ki yakdish et beito kodesh l'Hashem*, from which the rule is derived: *mah beito birshuto af kol birshuto* — just as one's house must be in one's possession, so too any sanctification must be of something in one's control. So how could I sanctify Michael's animal?

Conversely, if Michael's *korban* is being exchanged for my unsanctified animal, then I control the object receiving the *kedusha*, but I do not control the *korban* — and therefore how could I transfer the *kedusha* of Michael's *korban* onto my animal?

This raises the technical distinction between *makdish* and *matpis*. *Makdish* refers to direct sanctification — I impose new *kedusha* on something. *Matpis* — from the root *tofes*, to grasp — refers to transferring or extending an existing *kedusha*: I cause something to become *kadosh* by latching it onto, grabbing onto, the *kedusha* that already inheres in another object. The *Gemara* resolves the case by stipulating that the scenario of *lo yachlifenu* is one where the owner of the *korban* — Michael — has publicly announced: *kol harotze lehamir b'vehemti yavo veyamir* — whoever wishes to use my animal for *temurah* is welcome to do so. By granting this permission, Michael enables another person to perform the act of *matpis* — to grab the *kedusha* of his *korban* and transfer it — and that person may then do so and will incur *malkut*.

### Permission Cases

This leads to a fascinating observation: *temurah* is not categorically limited to the owner of the *korban*. The owner has, by default, the exclusive capacity to exercise the act of *temurah*, because only the owner is in full control of the sanctity. But that capacity can be delegated. If the owner makes it known — whether through an explicit declaration or through circumstances that make his consent clearly evident — that others may use his animal for *temurah*, then others can perform a valid act of *temurah* on his animal. The comparison to *terumah* is instructive: just as an owner may authorize others to separate *terumah* from his grain by declaring *kol harotze litrom yavo veyitrom*, so too an owner may authorize others to perform *temurah* on his *korban*.

The observation that such an announcement is itself a violation of *lifnei iver* is noted, but it does not prevent the act from taking effect — a principle already explored in earlier discussions in this tractate regarding the relationship between prohibited intent and the efficacy of the resulting act.

All of this reinforces Rabbeinu Gershom's reading of the earlier passage. The *Gemara*'s central concern throughout the discussion of exchange with another's animal is the question of power and control: does the actor have the capacity to do what he is attempting to do? This is precisely the contrast Rabbeinu Gershom identified in the case where both animals belong to the same person — there the question was not one of capacity but of how the act should be characterized, and the *Torah* teaches that it is still *temurah* regardless.

## Multiple Animals

### Mishna Positions

A new *mishna* presents the question of exchanges involving unequal numbers of animals. *Hamemir echad bishnayim ushnayim be'echad* — what if one takes a single sanctified animal and declares two unsanctified animals to be in its stead? Or takes two sanctified animals and designates one as their replacement? The *mishna* rules that this is indeed an act of *temurah*: it takes effect, lashes are incurred, and the *kedusha* attaches to the receiving animals. The same applies to one for a hundred or a hundred for one.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon disagrees. *Ein memir ela echad be'echad* — *temurah* is only valid when performed one for one. His source: *vehaya hu utmurato yihye kodesh* — "it and its *tmurato*" — all terms in the singular. Just as *hu* is singular, so the *temurah* object must be a single animal. This derives from the equivalence between the sanctified animal and its *temura*: *mah hu meyuchad af hi o tmurato meyuchadet*.

### Behemah Debate

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* that the word *behemah b'vehemah* — generic animal for animal — is the source for the *Rabbanan*'s position allowing one for multiple, since *behemah* can denote a plurality of animals, as evidenced by the verse using *behemah rabah* to refer to many animals. Rabbi Shimon responds: *behemah rabah ikrei* — "many animals" may be called *behemah* when explicitly modified by a term indicating plurality. But *stam* — an unqualified *behemah* — does not refer to many; it refers to one. The word *tzon*, by contrast, can on its own denote a flock of many.

### Shimon's Strategy

The *Gemara* observes that in the *mishna*, Rabbi Shimon grounded his position in the word *hu* — in the phrase *hu utmurato*, both the sanctified animal and its *temura* are singular — rather than in the word *behemah*. But the *baraita* presents his position as based on the word *behemah*. The *Gemara* resolves this: initially, Rabbi Shimon argued from *vehaya hu utmurato* — the singular *hu* and the singular *temura*. When he saw that the *Rabbanan* were latching onto the word *behemah* and arguing that it could connote plurality, he responded by fighting on their terrain: even from *behemah b'vehemah* I can derive my position, since *behemah* unmodified is singular. This was a tactical shift — using the *Rabbanan*'s own prooftext against them.

## Sequential Exchanges

### Reish Lakish

Having established that according to Rabbi Shimon only a one-to-one exchange is valid, the *Gemara* turns to the question of what that limitation encompasses. Reish Lakish rules that Rabbi Shimon concedes that one may perform *temurah* sequentially and repeatedly from the same original animal: I have my one *korban*, I declare this one to be its *temura*, I incur lashes — but the original *korban* remains, its *kedusha* untouched. I may then perform another act of *temurah* from that same original animal, and so on. Each act is a valid one-to-one exchange. The reasoning: *kedusha rishona d'hekdesh l'heichan halchah* — where has the original *kedusha* gone? It remains in the original animal, so why should its capacity for *temurah* be exhausted?

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. *Keshem she'ein memirin shnayim be'echad kach ein memirin ve'chozrin u'memirin* — just as one may not do two animals at once in exchange for one, so too one may not return and do it a second time sequentially. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the limitation Rabbi Shimon imposes on *temurah* means not merely that each individual act must be one-to-one, but that the original animal may be the source of only one *temurah* act in total.

Both a *baraita* supporting Rabbi Yochanan and a *baraita* supporting Reish Lakish are cited. The *baraita* supporting Reish Lakish derives from the verse *vehaya hu utmurato* — *afilu meah b'meah* — even one hundred sequential acts, each one-to-one, are permitted according to Rabbi Shimon, as long as each individual exchange is singular.

### Kedusha Transfer

The debate between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan turns on a fundamental question: is Rabbi Shimon's limit purely formal — one animal at a time — or substantive — one act of *temurah* per original animal? For Reish Lakish, since the *kedusha* of the original animal is never diminished by an act of *temurah*, the capacity for further *temurah* from that animal logically persists. For Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Shimon's *derashah* from the singular *hu* carries a stronger implication: the original animal is entitled to one and only one *temura*, and any further attempt is outside the scope of the Torah's provision. It is worth noting that the principle *ein temura osah temura* — that a *temura* animal cannot itself generate a further *temura* — is a separate rule agreed upon by all, and is not at issue in this debate, which concerns only sequential acts of *temurah* from the original sanctified animal itself.

## Asham Case

### Compound Question

Rabbi Avin poses a compound question that takes the debate to a new level. He asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds one may not return and perform *temurah* a second time from the same animal, consider the following: one sets aside an *asham*, performs *temurah* once with it — so the question of a second *temurah* is now germane — then the *asham* develops a *mum* and is redeemed onto a second animal. The second animal's *kedusha* is therefore derivative of the first. That second animal is then lost, another *korban* is brought in its place, and the second animal is subsequently found. Under the applicable *halacha*, an *asham shenitkapru ba'aleha be'acher* — an *asham* whose owner has already achieved atonement through a replacement — does not die as a *chatat* would under analogous circumstances; it is instead redirected and becomes an *olah*. Its *kedusha* transforms from *kedushat asham* to *kedushat olah*.

The question Rabbi Avin is asking is whether one may now perform *temurah* with this animal. The animal is different from the original in two respects: it is a physically different animal, since the *kedusha* was transferred due to a *mum*; and it carries a different *kedusha*, since it has transformed from *asham* to *olah*. Does either or both of these differences constitute sufficient novelty such that it is no longer bound by Rabbi Yochanan's rule that one may not return and perform *temurah* again?

### Abaye's Response

Abaye challenges Rabbi Avin's framing. *Mai ka mibaya lei* — what exactly is the question? Why present a compound case that involves two distinct variables simultaneously? If the question concerns a physically different animal carrying derivative *kedusha*, that case can be asked cleanly: the original *asham* develops a *mum* and is transferred to a second animal — *shnei gufim vekedusha achas*. Does the change in physical body constitute sufficient novelty? And if the question instead concerns whether a transformation of the *kedusha* itself provides sufficient novelty, ask that case cleanly: the original *asham* itself becomes an *olah*, no second animal involved — *kedusha acheres b'oso guf*. Why conflate both issues into a single complicated scenario?

### First Lishna

In the first version of the *Gemara*'s presentation, Rabbi Avin's compound question is addressed together. Abaye's rejoinder is that Rabbi Avin should have asked each component independently. The *Gemara* suggests that if one concludes *shnei gufim vekedusha achas* does not permit a further *temurah* — because the *kedusha* is the same *kedusha* upon which *temurah* was already performed once, *mishum d'vaha kedusha itamer bah* — then the question escalates: what if it is *shnei gufim ushnei kedushos*, both a new physical animal and a transformed *kedusha*? The *Gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

### Second Lishna

A second version of the passage presents the questions separately. Rav Avin asks Rabbi Yochanan two distinct questions. First: the original *asham* develops a *mum* and the *kedusha* is transferred to a second animal — same *kedusha*, different body — *mahu sheyachzor veyamir*, may one now perform *temurah*? Second: the original *asham* is found after another has been brought in its place and the *kedusha* transforms from *asham* to *olah* — same body, different *kedusha* — *mahu sheyachzor veyamir*?

Abaye, in the second version, notes that one of these two sub-questions is more obvious than the other, and that this is what shaped Rav Avin's inquiry. The case of *guf echad b'kedusha acheres* — the same physical animal but a transformed *kedusha* — is the more serious and uncertain question, because there one can genuinely argue that the transformation of the *kedusha* from *asham* to *olah* represents a new identity. The case of a new physical animal bearing derivative *kedusha* is, by contrast, more likely to be governed by the original *kedusha*'s exhausted capacity for *temurah*, since the *kedusha* is fundamentally unchanged. If one concludes that even derivative *kedusha* in a new body is still bound by the original limitation — *kol b'oso kedusha ein chozer u'meimer* — then the more pressing question becomes whether the same body with a genuinely new *kedusha* changes the picture. The *Gemara* concludes: *teiku*. In both versions, the questions remain unresolved.

### Teiku Resolution

The *teiku* is apt given the nature of Rabbi Shimon's *derashah*. Rabbi Shimon's position is derived from the singular *hu* in *vehaya hu utmurato*. The question of how literal a reading to adopt — whether *hu* tracks the physical object, the identity of the *kedusha*, or both — is precisely what these unresolved questions probe. If one takes a maximally literal approach, *hu* refers to this specific physical body with this specific *kedusha*, and any change in either element might in principle allow a fresh *temurah*. The *Gemara* declines to resolve how far that logic extends.

## Fifth Addition

### Yehoshua Rule

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states: *hekdesh rishon mosif chomesh, v'ein hekdesh sheni mosif chomesh* — one adds a fifth when redeeming the original sanctification, but not when redeeming a derivative one. The background: the *Torah* mandates that one who redeems something one has sanctified must add a fifth of its value. The question is whether that obligation applies when one redeems not the original sanctification but a *kedusha* that was derived from it through transfer.

### Rav Pappa

Rav Pappa explains Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's reasoning. The verse states: *ve'im hamakdish yigal et beito, veyasaf chamishit kesef erkecha alav vekam lo* — if the one who sanctified it redeems his house, he shall add a fifth. The operative word is *hamakdish* — the one who directly sanctified. *Makdish velo matpis* — the verse speaks of the one who directly installed the *kedusha*, not the one who latched onto or transferred an existing *kedusha*. When I sanctified my property directly, I am *hamakdish* and must add a fifth upon redemption. But when the *kedusha* in question arrived at its current object through *hatfasah* — by being transferred or extended from the original sanctification — then I am merely *matpis* with respect to that object, not *makdish*, and the obligation to add a fifth does not apply.

### Asham Redemption

Rabbi Avin then applies this rule to the *asham* case. If one separated an *asham*, it developed a *mum*, one added a fifth and redeemed it onto a second animal, that second animal was then redeemed and transferred, the *asham* was brought from a third replacement, and the original *asham* — now with transformed *kedusha* from *asham* to *olah* — is to be redeemed: does one add a fifth? Here the animal has become different in both ways — it is a physically different animal from the original, and its *kedusha* has transformed from *asham* to *olah*. Perhaps because of both these changes, this should be treated as an original *kedusha* requiring the addition of a fifth rather than as a derivative one exempt from that requirement. The *Gemara* is just reaching Abaye's response to this question as the *daf* concludes, leaving the resolution for the discussion that continues into the next *amud*.

# Temurah 10

## Asham & Pidyon Chomesh

### Rav Avin Shiala

The *daf* opens by picking up from a discussion established the previous day regarding the laws of *pidyon* and the *chomesh* — the added fifth. The ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had established that when one redeems a sanctified object, the obligation to add a fifth applies only to the person who directly sanctified that object, not to one who redeems something to which *kedusha* was merely transferred. To illustrate: if one sanctified his Ford and then redeemed it onto his Camry, and now wishes to redeem the Camry, he does not add a fifth — because the Camry's *kedusha* is derivative, not direct.

Against this backdrop, Rav Avin poses a complex question. The case runs as follows: one designated an *asham* to atone for himself (*hifrish asham le-hitkaper bo*), and that animal developed a *mum* — a blemish. One is permitted to redeem a blemished *korban*, and in doing so one adds a fifth. (This requires a brief clarification, since one might assume the *chomesh* obligation applies only to *kadshei bedek habayit*, temple treasury sanctifications, not to *kadshei mizbe'ach*. However, the *Gemara* derives from the verse *ve-im mibehema asher lo yakrivu mimena korban l'Hashem* — an animal from which no *korban* may be brought — that even when redeeming a *korban* that became blemished, one adds a fifth. The point is therefore surprising but well-established.) So: one redeemed the blemished *asham* onto another animal (*ve-chilalo al chavero*) in a lawful act of *pidyon*, adding a fifth in the process. Then, having subsequently achieved atonement through a different *asham* (*ve-nitkaper be-asham acher*), the original animal — now in the second body — became released from its *asham* identity and was designated instead as an *olah* (*ve-nitak zeh le-olah*), exactly as in the complex case discussed the previous day. Now this second animal develops a blemish. The question (*mah hu she-yosif alav chomesh*) is: does one add a fifth when redeeming it?

Two considerations pull in opposite directions. On one hand, the *kedusha* of this second animal is derivative — the *chomesh* was already added once when the first animal was redeemed — and therefore no further fifth should be required. On the other hand, this is not merely a straightforward transfer of *kedusha* from one body to another; the *kedusha* has actually transformed from that of an *asham* into that of an *olah*. Perhaps this transformation constitutes something sufficiently new that one would treat it like the first time and add a fifth.

### Abaye's Breakdown

Abaye interjects: why pose such a layered question? The case contains two distinct variables — two separate bodies with one *kedusha*, and a transformation from one type of *kedusha* to another within the same *kedusha*. Each could be asked independently. If the question is about two bodies sharing the same *kedusha* (*shtei gufe mi-kedusha achas*), ask it without the complication of the *asham*-to-*olah* transformation — ask *tivaya belo nitkaper*. If the question is about whether a *kedusha* transformation within the same body constitutes something new (*shtei kedushos ve-guf echad*), ask it without the *mum* — ask *tivaya belo mum*.

Rav Avin replies with the same principle invoked in analogous cases: *chada mi-go chada ka-mivaya lei* — he is building one question on top of the other. He knows that in the simple version of each question the answer might seem obvious, so he deliberately compounds the variables. The logic proceeds: if you would say that transferring to a second body but maintaining the same *kedusha* does not trigger a new *chomesh* (*mishum de-hahi kedusha itosef be-chada zimna* — because a fifth was already added when this *kedusha* was in its first incarnation), then what if it is not only a different body but a transformed *kedusha* — from *asham* to *olah*? Does that qualify as something new? The *Gemara* concludes: *teiku* — the question stands unresolved.

### Rashi's Distinction

There is, however, something textually puzzling here. Abaye frames the first component as a genuine question, yet the established *halacha* is simply that one does not add a fifth upon redeeming the second body. What would the uncertainty even be?

Rashi resolves this by drawing a distinction between the ordinary case of transferring *kedusha* and the case at hand. Normally, when *kedusha* is transferred from one animal to another, it is an equivalent exchange — the *kedusha* moves from one object to another of comparable status. But in Rav Avin's case, the first animal had a *mum* and thus could not be brought as a *korban*. The second animal onto which the *kedusha* was transferred was unblemished and *could* be brought as a *korban*. The impact of the *kedusha* has therefore qualitatively changed: the first animal was unfit for the altar, the second is fit. Perhaps this difference is enough to treat the second animal as something genuinely new, such that a *chomesh* would be added upon its redemption. This is the first stage of uncertainty. Layered onto that — even if one says the change in fitness does not suffice, what if the *kedusha* also changed in character from *asham* to *olah*? That is the second, compounded question.

### Rav Papa Version

The *Gemara* then presents a *lishna achrina* — an alternative version of the same question — attributed to Rav Papa rather than Rav Avin. Rashi consistently identifies the *lishna achrina* formulation as *lashon Yerushalmi*, an Eretz Yisrael Aramaic idiom; the *Gemara* on 6b uses this designation, and whether it literally derives from a Yerushalmi on *Kodashim* — of which there is none — remains a point of discussion.

The substance of Rav Papa's version parallels Rav Avin's: one designated an *asham* (*hifrish asham le-hiskaper bo*), it developed a blemish (*ve-humam*), was transferred to a second animal (*ve-chilalo al acher*), a fifth was added (*ve-hosif bo chomesh*), atonement was achieved through a different *asham* (*ve-niskaper be-asham acher*), and the second animal became designated as an *olah* (*ve-nitak ze le-ola*). Now the second animal is blemished — does one add a fifth (*mahu she-yosif alav chomesh*)?

Abaye again responds: which component is being asked? If the question concerns whether a transformed *kedusha* within the same body — the *asham*-to-*olah* conversion — counts as something new (*kedusha acheres be-oso guf*), why complicate the case with a *mum* at all? And if the question is about a different body sharing the same *kedusha* (*guf echad be-osah kedusha* — in the peculiar idiom, "one body" meaning a second, derivative body), why introduce the transformation?

### Kedusha Transformation

The *Gemara* proceeds to work through both stages of the question. The first stage: does transferring to a second body with the same *kedusha* occasion a new *chomesh*? The second stage: even granting that in such a case no new fifth is required because the *chomesh* was already added once for this *kedusha*, what happens when the animal is not only in a different body but the *kedusha* itself has been transformed — from *asham* to *olah*? When is a *kedusha* considered old and when new?

The text here presents genuine difficulty in establishing the precise *girsa*, and the reading of the *Shita Mekubetzet* is followed because it renders the *lishna achrina* parallel to the first version. The operative question in the final stage is whether one says *kol be-osah kedusha eino mosif chomesh* — as long as it is the same *kedusha*, even in a separate body, no further fifth is added — or whether a genuinely new *kedusha* type, such as the transformation from *asham* to *olah*, breaks that chain and occasions a fresh obligation. The *Gemara* concludes once again: *teiku*.

---

## Makdish vs. Michaper

### Core Question

With the *asham* cases behind us, the *Gemara* turns to a fundamental question posed by Rami bar Chama — a question that strikes at the heart of several *mishnayot* treated earlier in the *masechta*: who is considered the *ba'al ha-korban*, the halachic owner of a *korban*, when one person sanctifies and another benefits?

In the context of *bedek habayit*, the question does not arise. Sanctifying something for the temple treasury is simply transferring its value; there is no ongoing personal relationship between the donor and the object. But a *korban* is different. A *korban* stands in an intermediate state: it is holy, yet it continues to relate to its owner. This is the basis on which Rabbi Yose HaGlili considers *kodshim kalim* to be *mamon ba'alim* — property of the owners. The relevant question for present purposes is not whether it rises to the level of civil ownership enforced in *dinei mamonot*, but rather: within the *halachot* of *korbanot* themselves — specifically the *chomesh* and *temurah* — who is designated the owner?

The case Rami bar Chama addresses is: I sanctify my animal to serve as a *korban* for Charlie — say, his *olah* or his *chatat*. This *korban* will satisfy Charlie's halachic obligation. But the animal was mine, and I was the one who performed the act of *hekdesh*. If the animal later develops a *mum* and must be redeemed, who adds the fifth? And if someone attempts to perform *temurah* with it, whose act carries the halachic effect? This is Rami bar Chama's question: *makdish mosif chomesh o mitchaper mosif chomesh* — does the sanctifier add the fifth, or the one for whom atonement is achieved?

### Makdish Chomesh

The answer to the first part comes directly from a scriptural verse: *ve-im hamakdish yigal et beito* — if the sanctifier redeems his house. The Torah, when specifying who adds the fifth, does not use the language of *im ha-ba'alim* — the owner — which might have opened a theoretical question of who the owner is. Instead, it designates the person by his role as *makdish*. Thus the *makdish* — the one who performed the act of sanctification — is the one who adds the fifth. The *pasuk* is formulated for a house, but the designation applies broadly: the *makdish*, not the *mitchaper*, adds the *chomesh*.

### Temurah Ownership

The second question follows: *makdish oseh temurah o mitchaper oseh temurah* — does the *makdish* or the *mitchaper* perform the act of *temurah*? This is a genuinely fascinating question, and in some ways a strange one. The entire institution of *temurah* is that one attempts to transfer *kedusha* from one animal to another — an act that is prohibited and yet, paradoxically, effective. The *temurah* takes hold even though the person has no right to do it. Given that the act is meaningful only insofar as the person is treated as having the standing of ownership, the question of who holds that standing — *makdish* or *mitchaper* — becomes acute.

### Rava Tzibur Proof

Rava addresses the *temurah* question and argues that if ownership for purposes of *temurah* were determined by who performed the *hekdesh*, a serious problem would arise. The *Gemara* has established that *temurah* cannot be performed with a *korban tzibur* — the communal sacrifices such as the *tamid*. But it is at least theoretically possible for a *korban tzibur* to have been sanctified by a single individual (*kegon de-shavu shaliach le-akdoshei*). If ownership for *temurah* were determined by who sanctified, then such a *korban* — sanctified by an individual — would be classified as a *korban yachid* for these purposes, and *temurah* would take effect upon it. But we know that *temurah* does not apply to *korbanos tzibur*. The only way this exclusion makes sense is if the classification of a *korban* as communal or individual is determined not by who sanctified it but by whom it atones for — the *tzibur* or the individual. The same logic applies to *korban shutfin*: the *korban* of partners is defined by who benefits, not by the mechanics of how it was sanctified. Since these categories exclude *temurah* based on the beneficiary's identity, it follows that ownership for the purposes of *temurah* is defined by the *mitchaper*, not the *makdish*.

### Nazir Braisa

A further proof is adduced from a tradition of Rav Nachman in the name of Rav Huna, citing a *braisa* on the verse regarding the *nazir*: *korbano l'Hashem al nizro, milvad asher tasig yado* — his *korban* to God for his *nezirut*, beyond what he can afford. The phrase *asher tasig yado* — that which he can afford — typically introduces a sliding scale of obligation, as in *Erchin*. But there is no such sliding scale for a *nazir*'s *korban*; a poor *nazir* does not substitute lesser animals. The *braisa* therefore interprets the phrase differently: it refers not to poverty but to whether the *nazir* paid for the *korban* himself or whether others sanctified it on his behalf (*she-hifrishu lo acherim*). This is actually a remarkable teaching, because the very possibility that someone else can sanctify a *korban* to work for another person is not self-evident. One would naturally have assumed that a *korban* requires the owner to sanctify his own animal. The Torah's explicit address of this case (*milvad asher tasig yado*) establishes that such a *korban* is valid — a person may sanctify their animal as another's *korban*.

### Temurah Universal

With the principle established that someone else can sanctify a *korban* on one's behalf, the *Gemara* considers what additional teaching this *pasuk* might convey. The *Gemara* initially suggests the *pasuk* teaches that *temurah* applies equally whether you sanctified the *korban* yourself or whether another sanctified it for you. The verse's parallel phrasing — *mah ke-shehu hifrish mishelo oseh temurah, af ke-she-hifrishu lo acherim oseh temurah* — would then be teaching that the *mitchaper* retains the ability to perform *temurah* regardless of who performed the *hekdesh*. This reading would directly support the conclusion that for *temurah*, the operative party is the one for whom the *korban* works.

The *Gemara* then walks this back: perhaps the *pasuk* is only teaching the basic validity of the *korban* when sanctified by another, which was genuinely non-obvious. Without the explicit verse, one would have said *gzeirat hakatuv hi* — the Torah's essential conception of a *korban* requires the owner to sanctify his own animal (*korvano mididei hu de-mechaper, mid-achrina lo*). The verse teaches that this is not so. This reading softens the direct proof for the *mitchaper* governing *temurah*, though Rava's earlier proof from *tzibur* and *shutfim* remains strong.

### Final Ruling

The *Gemara* resolves the question with a tradition cited by Rav Avin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *makdish mosif chomesh u-mitchaper oseh temurah* — the *makdish* adds the fifth; the *mitchaper* performs *temurah*.

This conclusion warrants a closer look at its internal logic, particularly regarding the question of who redeems the *korban* when it develops a *mum*. The *Gemara* only asked which of the two parties adds a fifth — but by asking this question, it presupposes that either of them could in principle redeem the animal. If only one party could redeem it, asking which one adds the fifth would be superfluous. Thus implicit in the *Gemara*'s question is the assumption that when I sanctify an animal for James, both I and James are in a position to redeem it if it develops a *mum*. If I am the one who redeems it, I add the fifth as the *makdish*. If James redeems it, he does not add the fifth. And yet, despite the fact that both of us can redeem it — and therefore both of us might have been imagined to have the standing to perform *temurah* — only James, as the *mitchaper*, has the power to effect a *temurah*.

There is a further irony here worth noting. The acts of *pidyon* (redemption) and *temurah* are closely related, and yet there is a subtle conceptual distinction between them. When I redeem a *korban*, I am removing the *kedusha* from this object and placing it on another. When I perform *temurah*, I designate the second animal and declare it as the replacement for the first — the directionality is reversed. The difference can seem almost terminological, yet it has profound consequences: one is a permitted act when the animal has a *mum*, and the other is a *lav*. And now it emerges that they may even have different *ba'alim*: the *makdish* redeems, while the *mitchaper* performs *temurah*. The *Gemara* does not address whether the identity of who can redeem it should be the same as who can perform *temurah*, and this remains a point for further investigation.

### Trumos Parallel

In characteristic Talmudic fashion, the *Gemara* appends a third related ruling to round out the discussion. Rabbi Yochanan's statement as transmitted by Rav Avin includes: *torem mishelo al shel chaveiro* — if I separate my *terumot u-maasrot* from my own grain in order to exempt your grain, then *tovas hana'ah shelo* — the right to direct which *kohen* or *levi* receives those *terumot u-maasrot* belongs to me. The scriptural basis is *et kol ma'asar tevuascha ve-nasata* — "the tithe of your grain you shall give." Since the *terumot u-maasrot* physically derive from my grain, even though they exempt yours, I retain the allocation rights. This parallels the *korban* case: just as the *makdish* controls the *chomesh* and the *mitchaper* controls the *temurah*, so too in the domain of *trumos u-maasrot* the sanctifier's ownership controls the dispensation of what was sanctified.

---

## Limbs & Fetuses

### Mishnah Text

The *Gemara* now takes up the next *mishna*: *ein memirin lo evarin be-ubarim* — one may not perform *temurah* with limbs exchanged for fetuses, *ve-lo ubarim be-evarin* — nor fetuses for limbs, *ve-lo ubarim ve-evarin bi-shleimim* — nor fetuses or limbs for whole animals, *ve-lo shleimim bahen* — nor whole animals for them.

### Behemah Requirement

The most straightforward case to understand is the exchange involving whole animals on one side and a partial animal on the other. The *korban* stands on one side; on the other, one presents the leg of a sheep and declares this leg as the exchange for that *korban*. Can *temurah* take effect? We have established that *temurah* can exchange a sheep for a goat, a cow for a sheep, one animal for a hundred or a hundred for one. But what of a partial animal?

The exclusion derives from the verse's formulation: *behemah be-vehemah* — an animal for an animal. The requirement is for a whole *behemah*, not a limb, not a fetus. Even if one can validly sanctify a limb, and even if one can sanctify a fetus, the act of *temurah* requires *behemah be-vehemah*. A leg is not a *behemah*; a fetus is not a *behemah* in the requisite sense. Therefore, *shelemim be-evarin* — a whole animal exchanged for a limb — does not work. Nor does the reverse: if I sanctified a fetus (assuming that was effective) and now try to exchange it for a whole yearling sheep, *temurah* does not take effect because the fetus is not *behemah be-vehemah*. Once these cases are settled, it follows all the more obviously that a limb for a limb, a limb for a fetus, or a fetus for a limb — all of these fail doubly.

### Rabbi Yosef Challenge

Rabbi Yosef challenges this with a case from the *halachot* of sanctification generally: *velo be-mukdashim, ha-omer raglah shel zo olah, kulah olah* — when it comes to sanctified animals, if someone says "the leg of this animal is an *olah*," one cannot limit the sanctity to the leg; the entire animal becomes an *olah*. If that is so, Rabbi Yosef argues, then *af ke-she-yomar raglah shel zo tachat zo, tehei kulah temurah tachteiha* — if one says "the leg of this animal shall be in exchange for that *korban*," it is as if one has sanctified the leg, which sanctifies the whole animal, and therefore the whole animal should stand as *temurah*.

The logic can be sharpened: the effect of *temurah* is that an attempt to transfer *kedusha* from A to B results in B becoming sanctified even though the transfer itself is forbidden. If I attempt a *temurah* from a *korban* to a leg, the effect is to sanctify the leg. And if sanctifying a leg sanctifies the whole animal, then the whole animal becomes *kodesh* through this attempted *temurah* — indeed, the *lav* of *temurah* would presumably have been transgressed as well, not merely the sanctification effect.

---

## Ubar Kedoshah Dispute

### Bar Padda Position

The *Gemara* now examines the underlying dispute about whether *kedusha* can take direct effect on a fetus. Bar Padda states plainly: *ein kedusha chala al ubarim* — sanctity does not take direct effect on fetuses. If one attempts to sanctify a fetus directly, the act is ineffective. When the animal is born, it does not emerge with the status of something directly sanctified; it has only the derivative status of *vlad kodashim* — offspring of sacred animals — which carries different *halachot* than an animal directly sanctified.

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *kedusha chala al ubarim* — sanctity does take direct effect on fetuses. He supports this from a case he himself articulates: if one sanctified a pregnant *chatat* and it gave birth (*hikdish chatat me-uberet ve-yalda*), one may use either the mother or the offspring to achieve atonement (*ratza bah mitchaper, ratza be-vlad mitchaper*). Under Bar Padda's view, the offspring would be a *vlad chatat*, which carries the ruling of *mitah* — it must be left to die, as one of the five categories of *chatat* that may not be brought. But Rabbi Yochanan holds that the fetus was directly sanctified when the mother was sanctified, making the offspring a full-fledged *chatat* in its own right.
