The situation then parallels one who designates two animals simultaneously for one *chatat* obligation: one may select which to bring, and the other is treated as a backup, left to graze until it develops a *mum* and can be redeemed.

### Ubar Independence

A *lishna achrina* formulates Rabbi Yochanan's conceptual position more explicitly through the phrase *ubar lav yerech imo* — a fetus is not merely a limb of its mother. The fetus has genuine independent existence and identity. This principle is the conceptual foundation for everything Rabbi Yochanan maintains: because a fetus is not simply part of the mother, it can be the subject of independent *hekdesh*, can have its own *kedusha*, and when I sanctify a pregnant animal, the mother and fetus each receive their own distinct *kedusha* rather than the fetus being subsumed under the mother's. Rashi's formulation essentially unifies the two expressions of Rabbi Yochanan's position: the fetus can be left over as an independent entity (*im shiyaro meshuyar*), and it is not merely a limb of its mother.

### Why Both Cases

The *Gemara* notes that two distinct cases must be stated to fully express Rabbi Yochanan's position. The first case is where one attempts to sanctify the fetus directly, without reference to the mother. The second is where one sanctifies the pregnant animal as a whole, with the *kedusha* applying to the entire package. Each case contains a *chiddush* that the other might not convey.

Had one only stated the case of sanctifying the pregnant mother as a whole, one might have concluded that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only there — because the mother is fit for sanctification in her own right (*de-imei chazya le-gufei*), and it is the power to sanctify the mother that extends and enables the sanctification of the fetus (*migu de-nachas kedusha alah, nachas nami le-vlad*). But if one attempts to sanctify the fetus directly, without the mother's sanctification empowering the act, perhaps even Rabbi Yochanan would agree that the fetus cannot be directly sanctified. The first case therefore teaches that Rabbi Yochanan holds the fetus can be sanctified even entirely on its own terms.

Conversely, had one only stated the case of directly sanctifying the fetus, one might have thought Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only there — because in that case the person is explicitly and exclusively focusing on the fetus (*mishum de-kamafish kedusha al ha-vlad*), and the concentrated intention may be what gives the act effect. But when one sanctifies the whole package including the mother, one might have thought that even Rabbi Yochanan would interpret the *kedusha* as resting on the mother and treating the fetus as a component of her rather than as an independent entity. Both cases are therefore necessary.

---

## Fetus & Bechor

### Bechor Scheme

The *Gemara* now cites a *mishnah* that asks: *keitzad maarimin al ha-bechor* — how does one employ a legal stratagem to avoid the *bechor* obligation? The case: one has an animal that is *mavakeret* — pregnant for the first time, meaning the birth will be a firstborn for both the mother and the species — and one declares: *mah she-be-me-eha shel zo olah* — whatever is in this animal's womb is an *olah*. If the fetus is born male, it emerges as an *olah* and the *bechor* obligation does not take effect, since *bechor* requires that both the mother and offspring be non-sacred at the moment of birth. By preemptively sanctifying the fetus, one removes it from the reach of *bechorah*. If female, the animal is redeemed and the proceeds go toward an *olah*.

### Bechor Proof

This *mishna* appears to constitute a direct proof for Rabbi Yochanan's position. The text speaks of directly sanctifying the fetus — not the mother, only the unborn offspring — and the *mishna* treats this as effective. *Alma kadosh ubar* — evidently a fetus can be sanctified. Herein lies the difficulty for Bar Padda.

### Damim vs. Guf

Bar Padda resolves the challenge: *ki matnita hi bi-kdushat damim* — the *mishna* is not speaking of *kedushat ha-guf*, the intrinsic sanctity that confers the identity of a *korban* upon the animal. It is speaking of *kedushat damim* — value sanctity, by which the animal's monetary proceeds are dedicated toward sacred purposes. One is not saying "this fetus is itself an *olah*"; one is saying "the value of this fetus should go toward an *olah*." The difference is crucial: *kedushat ha-guf* confers upon the animal a *korban* identity that cannot apply to a fetus according to Bar Padda, since a *korban* identity must inhere in a living animal. But *kedushat damim* requires only that the object have monetary value and can be sold — conditions a fetus satisfies. Therefore, Bar Padda can maintain his position: the *mishna*'s stratagem works not because the fetus has been made a *korban*, but because it has been sanctified for its value.

---

## Damim Kedusha

### Damim Bechor Q

The *Gemara* raises an immediate challenge to Bar Padda's resolution: *mi alim kedushat damim de-mapka lei mi-bechora* — is *kedushat damim* really strong enough to exempt from *bechorah*? If the sanctity is not an identity sanctity — if it does not make the fetus a *korban* but merely dedicates its proceeds — has anything really changed about the animal's status that would deflect the *bechor* obligation?

### Blemish Precedent

The answer is yes, and a proof is adduced from a *mishna*: *kol ha-kodashim she-kadam mum kavua le-hekdeshan ve-nifdu* — all sacred animals whose permanent blemish preceded their sanctification and were then redeemed. When an animal is blemished before being sanctified, the *kedusha* that takes effect can only be *kedushat damim* — the blemish prevents *kedushat ha-guf* from taking hold, since such an animal can never stand as a *korban*. Its sanctification is entirely one of value, akin to sanctifying a car toward sacred proceeds.

### Before/After Pidyon

The *mishna* states that such animals, once redeemed (*nifdu*), are *chayavim bi-bechora u-matnot* — they are subject to the *bechor* obligation and to the priestly gifts (*zeroa, lechayayim, ve-keiva*). They are treated as complete *chullin*, because when only *kedushat damim* was involved and the *kedusha* was removed, nothing of the *kedusha* remains. This contrasts sharply with an animal that was first sanctified with *kedushat ha-guf* and then redeemed after developing a *mum*: in that case, a residue of *kedusha* persists and the animal remains forbidden for shearing and labor even after redemption. But an animal whose sanctity was only ever *kedushat damim* from the start is completely freed upon redemption.

The critical implication, however, is found in the *ta'ama* — the reasoning. The *mishna* says these animals are *chayavim* in *bechorah* after redemption. The qualification "after redemption" (*la-achar she-nifdu*) implies: *kodem she-nifdu piturim* — before redemption, they are exempt from *bechorah*. Even though the *kedusha* is only *kedushat damim*, it is sufficient to suspend the *bechor* obligation.

### Fetus Damim Apply

This precedent answers the *Gemara*'s challenge squarely: *alma dealim kedushat damim de-mapka lei mi-bechorah* — you see that *kedushat damim* is indeed powerful enough to exempt from *bechorah*. Bar Padda's resolution therefore holds. When the *mishna* in *Ketziyas Bechor* describes the stratagem of sanctifying the fetus before birth to avoid *bechorah*, it is referring to *kedushat damim*. This form of sanctification can apply to a fetus, requires no *korban* identity, and nonetheless carries the halachic force to displace the *bechor* obligation. Bar Padda's view that *kedusha* cannot take direct effect on a fetus as a *korban*-identity is thus fully consistent with the *mishna*'s ruling.

### Avodah Restriction

A second challenge is pressed against Bar Padda's resolution. The *mishna* states that when one declares the fetus an *olah* in the manner of the *bechor* stratagem, *muteret be-giza va-asura ba-avodah* — the mother may be shorn but may not be worked. If the sanctification of the fetus only creates *kedushat damim*, why should the mother be prohibited from labor? *Kedushat damim* does not impose the prohibitions of shearing and labor that attend *kedushat ha-guf* — it is merely a dedication of monetary value. The prohibition of *avodah* (labor) seems to presuppose a genuine *korban* identity.

Bar Padda responds: the prohibition on *avodah* applies even to animals with only *kedushat damim*. The proof comes from a *mishna* (*yotzin le-chullin le-gozez ve-la-avod*) about animals that are released entirely to *chullin*. This ruling — that after complete redemption of a *kedushat damim* animal one may shear and work it — implies by the converse that before redemption one may not shear it and may not work it. *Ta'ama mishum de-nifdu* — it is permitted *because* they have been redeemed; *kodem she-nifdu asurin ba-avodah* — before redemption they are forbidden for labor. Thus *alma kedushat damim asurin ba-avodah*: even value-sanctity imposes the work prohibition.

### After Redemption OK

The contrast is instructive. Once a *kedushat damim* animal is redeemed, the *kedusha* is entirely removed and the animal is fully *chullin* — it may be shorn and worked without restriction. This is precisely the distinction that separates *kedushat damim* from *kedushat ha-guf*: an animal that was sanctified with *kedushat ha-guf*, developed a *mum*, and was subsequently redeemed retains a residual prohibition on shearing and labor even after redemption, because the body-sanctity leaves an indelible mark. No such mark remains when the original sanctity was only of value. Before redemption, both types share the prohibition on *avodah*; after redemption, only *kedushat ha-guf* leaves its trace. The *daf* continues with these themes in the next session.

---

---

# Temurah 12

## Sanctifying Skin

### Abaye's Question

The daf opens by completing the series of questions that grew out of the previous discussion about sanctifying a limb or part of an animal. The *gemara* at the bottom of 11b records that Abaye posed the following question to Rabba, his teacher: if one sanctifies only the skin (*ora*) of an animal — without sanctifying the animal as a whole — may one put the animal to work? The *shita mekubetzet* notes that this question may apply even according to Rabbi Yosi, who generally holds that sanctifying a part of an animal causes the whole to become sanctified, since the skin is never itself offered as a *korban* and therefore may occupy a conceptually distinct status. But regardless of which *tanna* the question is framed under, the basic issue is this: given that only the skin is sanctified, does working the animal constitute a prohibited use of sanctified property?

### Fetus Analogy

The *gemara* brings a proof: *ta shma* — if one sanctifies the fetus of an animal, the mother is permitted for shearing but forbidden for work, because working weakens the fetus (*d'kachish ubar she'bah*), whereas shearing has no effect on the fetus. The implicit suggestion is that the same logic would apply to the case of the skin: working might affect the skin, and therefore be forbidden, while shearing would not.

### Rabbinic vs Biblical

Rav Yosef, however, pushes back. He suggests that the prohibition on working the mother when only the fetus is sanctified may be only *m'derabanan* — of Rabbinic origin — since the act of working is not technically directed at the sanctified object itself. If so, the case of the fetus cannot serve as a proof for whether working an animal whose skin alone is sanctified is *biblically* prohibited, since the fetus case may itself only be Rabbinic. This is the thrust of Abaye's question: what is the biblical status?

### Working Impact

The counter-argument is then raised: if the prohibition in the fetus case is only Rabbinic, why did the Rabbis not extend the decree to shearing as well? The answer is that the Rabbis issued a *gezeira* specifically because working weakens the fetus, whereas shearing does not. Since shearing causes no harm to the fetus, there was no reason to include it in the decree. The parallel to the skin case is left somewhat open. Rashi explains that working an animal can affect the skin — *avoda machish lei l'ora* — though precisely why working would impact the skin more than shearing is not fully developed in the *gemara*. One plausible reading is that a yoke placed on the animal directly presses against the hide. Regardless, the *gemara* has established that the question of the skin parallels the fetus question structurally, and that the proof from the fetus case is inconclusive because the entire prohibition there may be Rabbinic.

---

## Unsanctified Fetus

### Fetus Status

The *gemara* continues with Abaye now addressing a new set of questions to Rav Yosef. The case: the mother was sanctified as a *shelamim* while the fetus was not sanctified — either because Rabbi Yochanan permits one to explicitly exclude the fetus when sanctifying the mother, or because the animal was not yet pregnant at the time of sanctification and we hold that *vladei kodashim* only become sanctified at birth. The mother is then *shechted* inside the Temple as a *korban*. The question Abaye poses: has one transgressed the prohibition of *chullin ba-azarah*?

### Act vs Result

The question is conceptually sharp. The physical act of *shechita* was performed on the mother, not on the fetus. Yet the *halachic* effect of *shechita* — rendering the animal *shechted* — applied to the fetus by virtue of its being inside the mother. The fetus was not sanctified, so it is *chullin*. The act of *shechita* was not performed on it, but the result of *shechita* was. Is it the act or the result that determines whether one has performed *shechita* on *chullin* inside the *Beis HaMikdash*?

### Pasuk-Based Answer

Rav Yosef responds not by resolving the conceptual question directly, but by citing the *pasuk*. The verse from which the prohibition of *chullin ba-azarah* is derived states that if the place is far from you, *then* you may slaughter there — implying that non-sanctified animals are to be slaughtered outside the Temple. But in this case, the mother was a *shelamim* and *had* to be slaughtered inside the Temple. Since the *shechita* was required to occur in the Temple, one cannot be said to have violated the prohibition. As Rashi frames it: *lo yachol lishchot behemah zo ela ba-azarah* — this animal could only be slaughtered in the Temple. The *Torah* prohibits only what could have been done elsewhere. This answers the question on a technical level without directly adjudicating whether it is the act or the result of *shechita* that is legally operative.

### Reversed Fetus

Abaye then presents the mirror image of the previous case. Here the mother is *chullin* and the fetus is a *shelamim* — sanctified directly, as Rabbi Yochanan permits — and the mother is *shechted outside* the Temple. The act of *shechita* was performed on the mother, which is *chullin*, but the result rendered the fetus — a *korban* — effectively slaughtered. Has one violated the prohibition of *shechitas kodashim bachutz*, slaughtering sanctified animals outside the Temple? Again, the same conceptual tension arises: the act was performed on the *chullin*, not on the *kodashim*, but the *kodashim* was in practice slaughtered.

### Fit for Mishkan

Rav Yosef again answers by *pasuk*, this time citing the verse *v'yevi'um la-Hashem* — bring them to God — which implies that the prohibition of *shechitas kodashim bachutz* applies only to something fit to be brought as a *korban* at the *ohel moed*. The fetus, while still *in utero*, was not yet fit to be brought as a *korban*. Therefore, one is exempt on technical grounds. An alternate formulation of the same principle is stated directly: *ra'uy l'pesach ohel moed chayavin alav bachutz* — only what is fit for the entrance of the *ohel moed* triggers the prohibition. In both cases, Rav Yosef sidesteps the fundamental question of whether it is the act or the result of *shechita* that matters, answering instead with a limiting principle: neither case meets the threshold for a violation.

---

## Derivatives Rule

### Overview

Having concluded the discussions that grew out of the opening *mishnayot* of the *masechet* — who may perform *temurah*, on which animals, including questions about fetuses and limbs — the *gemara* now turns to a series of *mishnayot* that are grouped together by structural similarity rather than by direct subject matter. These *mishnayot* share a common theme: a secondary or derivative status does not generate a further secondary status of the same kind. *Temurah* is one of the cases in this list, which is why it appears in this *masechet*, but the series includes topics ranging from *terumah* and *chametz* to *mikvaot*, *mei chatat*, and *beit ha-peras*.

### Meduma

The first case is *meduma* — a mixture of *terumah* and *chullin* that is not *batel* because the ratio is less than one in a hundred. If a unit of *terumah* falls into fifty units of *chullin* and the mixture is forbidden, and then one unit from that mixture falls into another fifty units of *chullin*, how much *terumah* is in the second mixture? One could reason that the unit drawn from the first mixture was entirely forbidden and should be treated as entirely *terumah*, thereby making the second mixture forbidden as well. But the *mishnah* rules: *ein hameduma medama'as ela lefi cheshbon* — the mixture does not render the next batch forbidden except in proportion. Only the actual fraction of *terumah* in the unit drawn from the first mixture counts; you calculate the math and determine whether the second mixture still has enough *terumah* to be forbidden.

### Mechometz

The same formulation applies to *mechometz* — a mixed yeast (containing both *chullin* and *terumah* yeast) that falls into dough and causes fermentation. Normally, the fact that a small amount of something causes fermentation — and thereby exerts an effect on the dough — could prevent *bitul* even if the quantity is below the usual threshold. But the *mishnah* says: *ein hamuchometz mechametz ela lefi cheshbon*. It is only according to proportion: you examine how much of the yeast is actually *terumah*, and only if the *terumah* portion alone could have caused fermentation does it matter.

### Drawn Water

Similarly, *mayim she'uvim* — drawn water — invalidates a *mikvah* if three *lugin* of it enter before the *mikvah* has reached forty *se'ah*. The *mishnah* states that this too operates *lefi cheshbon* — according to proportion or calculation. The precise meaning of this phrase will be unpacked in the *gemara*.

### Mei Chatat

*Mei chatat* — the waters of purification prepared from the ashes of the *parah adumah* — cannot make other water into *mei chatat*. The only valid preparation is ashes placed with water; one cannot take an existing mixture of *mei chatat* and use it to sanctify fresh water. This case is structurally closest to *temurah*: just as a *temurah* derives its sanctity from the original *korban* and cannot pass that sanctity to yet another animal, so too the *mei chatat* mixture, however potent, cannot transmit its status to additional water without the original ingredients — *eifer* and water.

### Beit Ha-peras

A *beit ha-peras* — a field plowed over a grave, which scatters bone fragments and creates a zone of potential *tum'ah* — does not make another field into a *beit ha-peras*. The designation requires a grave having been plowed over in that location; a field contaminated by proximity to an existing *beit ha-peras* does not acquire the status independently.

### Double Terumah

*Terumah* cannot be taken twice from the same grain. If one separated *terumah* once, a second attempt to separate *terumah* from the same produce does not produce valid *terumah*. The act of designation has already been performed; the product of an attempted second *hafrashat terumah* does not acquire *terumah* status.

### Temurah Rule

Finally, *temurah* cannot make *temurah*, and a *vlad kodashim* — an animal born from a sanctified animal — cannot make *temurah*. The *mishnah* records this as the position of the *chachamim* in their debate with Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yehuda holds that once a *vlad kodashim* is born, it can perform *temurah*; the *chachamim* respond that only what was directly sanctified — the original *hekdesh* — can create *temurah*, not what derived its sanctity through birth. Some manuscripts include the additional phrase that *temurah* itself also cannot make *temurah*, underscoring that the principle applies to both forms of derivative sanctity.

The conceptual unity of the list is now visible. *Temurah* sanctity derives from the original *korban*; a *temurah* cannot pass its sanctity forward to yet another animal. A *vlad kodashim*'s sanctity derives from its mother; it too cannot perform *temurah*. The pattern mirrors what we saw with *beit ha-peras*, *mei chatat*, and the others: a derivative status does not generate a further degree of the same status. That structural parallel is why these *mishnayot* are grouped together in this *masechet*, even though most of them do not directly concern *temurah*.

---

## Meduma Debate

### Sages Position

Having laid out the list, the *gemara* now examines each case in turn. On the question of *meduma*, Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the *mishnah*'s ruling that *meduma* affects the next mixture only in proportion is *not like Rabbi Eliezer* — *de-lo k'Rabbi Eliezer*. The position of the *chachamim* is that you follow the actual mathematics.

### Rabbi Eliezer Strict

The proof text is a *mishnah* in *terumah*: if a *se'ah* of *terumah* fell into fewer than a hundred [units of *chullin*] — so that it is not *batel* — and the whole became *meduma*, and then a unit from that *meduma* fell elsewhere, what is the status of that second mixture? *Rabbi Eliezer omer: medame'a k'terumah vadai* — Rabbi Eliezer says it is treated as pure *terumah*, as though the unit that fell into the second mixture was entirely *terumah*. The entire mixture having been forbidden, Rabbi Eliezer treats each unit extracted from it as if it were fully *terumah*, making the second mixture forbidden at the same ratio as if actual *terumah* had fallen into it. This is a stringent position: the forbidden status of the first mixture has, in effect, been transferred in full to each unit that exits it. This echoes the general principle of *chatichah na'aseis neveilah* found in *hilchos kashrus* — the whole piece becomes intrinsically forbidden — though there it operates on a Rabbinic level and the analogy is not exact, since in the *meduma* case everything is *min b'mino* and the amount is less than one in sixty.

### Sages Proportional

The *chachamim* reject this. *She'ani omer se'ah shenaflah hi she'altah* — I apply the logic that the very *se'ah* that fell in is the same one that fell out. Or, in a simpler formulation, the mixture is forbidden only proportionally, and when you take a unit from it, only the proportional fraction of *terumah* within that unit is considered to have fallen into the second mixture. The second mixture therefore has far less than a problematic amount of *terumah* and is *batel*. The *gemara* here does not simply identify the anonymous *mishnah* as being against Rabbi Eliezer — it also illuminates the debate fully, demonstrating exactly how the *chachamim*'s principle of *lefi cheshbon* is expressed in that *mishnah* in *terumah*.

---

## Yeast Fermentation

### Yeast Mixture Case

The *gemara* turns to *mechometz*. Rabbi Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the ruling about *mechometz* in our *mishnah* is also not like Rabbi Eliezer. The relevant case: yeast made of *chullin* and yeast made of *terumah*, mixed together, fell into a batch of dough. Neither the *chullin* yeast alone nor the *terumah* yeast alone was sufficient to cause fermentation; only together did they have that effect. The amount of *terumah* yeast is below one in a hundred, so it would ordinarily be *batel*. But the fact that yeast causes fermentation — exerts a tangible effect on the dough — can prevent *bitul*. The question is whether the *terumah* yeast, by participating in the fermentation even though it could not have done so alone, is considered to have had its impact and is therefore not *batel*.

### Rabbi Eliezer Yeast

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *achar acharon ani ba* — I follow the last one. If the two yeasts fell in sequentially rather than simultaneously, the second one to fall in is the one that tipped the scales and caused the fermentation to occur. If that was the *terumah* yeast, the dough is forbidden. If the *terumah* fell in first, before it had anything to combine with, it had no effect at that moment and is therefore *batel*. Rashi's analysis of a *gemara* elsewhere extends this: even if the two fell in simultaneously, as long as the *terumah* yeast was not the first to fall, it is considered to have participated in the fermentation and creates a problem.

### Sages Yeast

The *chachamim* disagree: *bein shenaphal b'techilah bein shenaphal b'sof* — regardless of whether the *terumah* yeast fell in first or last, *l'olam eino oser ad sheyehei bo k'dei l'hachmitz* — it is never forbidden unless the *terumah* yeast alone was sufficient to cause fermentation. This is the principle of *ze v'ze gorem*: when two causes together produce an effect but neither would have done so independently, the *chachamim* hold that *ze v'ze gorem mutar* — the involvement of the forbidden item does not render the result forbidden, since it could not have acted alone.

### Cheshbon Meaning

What, then, does *lefi cheshbon* mean in the context of *mechometz* in our *mishnah*? According to Tosafot's reading — which is the more straightforward approach, as opposed to Rashi's more complex interpretation — it means: examine the yeast mixture and determine what fraction of it is *terumah* yeast. Only if that *terumah* fraction, taken on its own, would have been sufficient to cause fermentation does it prevent *bitul*. If the *terumah* yeast needed the *chullin* yeast to accomplish anything, then *lefi cheshbon* it is insufficient and the *terumah* is *batel*.

---

## Drawn Water

### Three Log Rule

The *mishnah* states that drawn water invalidates a *mikvah lefi cheshbon*. To understand this, it is necessary to recall the basic rule: three *lugin* of *mayim she'uvim* — water that has been drawn in a vessel — invalidates a *mikvah* that has not yet reached forty *se'ah* of valid water. By way of orientation, a *revi'it* is a quarter of a *log*, and the standard *revi'it* used for *kiddush* is approximately three and a half ounces; a *log* is therefore roughly fourteen ounces, and three *lugin* amounts to approximately forty-two ounces — somewhat more than three standard cups. This relatively modest quantity, falling into an incomplete *mikvah*, invalidates it.

The standard practice in modern *mikvaot* addresses this concern by maintaining two connected bodies of water: a sealed pit containing forty *se'ah* of collected rainwater, connected through a small opening to a separate pool in which people actually immerse. Because the rainwater pit was already a complete, valid *mikvah* before the second pool was added, any amount of piped water added to the second pool cannot invalidate — the connection to the kosher *mikvah* saves it. The pipes themselves are not considered *keilim* — receptacles — because they lack a bottom; they simply channel water through continuously without holding it. The pit in the ground is similarly not a *kli* because it is in the ground, not a detached vessel. When the *mikvah* is cleaned and the water replaced, care must be taken regarding residual water, a point that becomes halachically significant and will be addressed below.

The question now is what *lefi cheshbon* means in this context. A natural reading would parallel the *meduma* case: if water from an invalidated *mikvah* overflows into a second *mikvah*, only the proportional fraction of drawn water in that overflow is considered *she'uvim*, not the entire overflow. But the *gemara* understands the phrase differently. The attribution comes first.

### Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the *mishnah*'s rule is *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*. The source is a *Tosefta* in Mikvaot: *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov omer* — a *mikvah* that already contains twenty-one *se'ah* of rainwater may have the remaining nineteen *se'ah* filled by drawing water with a vessel from one's shoulder and pouring it into the *mikvah*, provided the water runs along the ground before entering — and it is nevertheless valid. The reasoning: *she-ha-rubah metaheret bi-revi'it u-ve-hamshachah* — the majority [of kosher water] combined with the drawn water running along the ground (*hamshacha*) renders the *mikvah* valid. 

The key condition is twofold: first, the majority of the forty *se'ah* must already consist of kosher rainwater — at least twenty-one *se'ah*. Second, the drawn water may not be poured directly into the *mikvah* but must run along the ground before entering, making it somewhat more "natural" and less directly a product of human conveyance. The underlying principle appears to be that what invalidates a *mikvah* is not an intrinsic flaw in the water itself but rather the manner in which the *mikvah* is constituted — if the foundational majority of water was rainwater and the drawn water merely supplemented it through a process that was not entirely direct, the *mikvah* retains its character as a naturally formed body of water rather than a manufactured one.

### Opposing View

This being an implicitly lenient ruling — drawn water in the minority, combined with *hamshacha*, is permitted — one might assume the *Rabbanan* take a stricter position. The *gemara* initially considers this inference: *mikhlal de-rabbanan savri* that *hamshacha* would not work here and any drawn water, even if in the minority, would invalidate. But then Ravin arrived from Eretz Yisrael and reported in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the opposing position is actually *more* lenient: *she-hu ve-she-shichu kulo tahor* — even if one drew all of the water in this manner it would be valid. If so, our *mishnah* cannot be identified as lenient relative to the *Rabbanan*, since the *Rabbanan* are more lenient still. The *gemara* therefore concludes that this reading leaves the *mishnah* attributable to neither the *Rabbanan* nor Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov — *lo Rabbanan ve-lo Rabbi Eliezer*.

### Rava Vessels

Rava therefore offers a different interpretation: *lefi cheshbon kelim* — "according to calculation" means according to the *number of vessels*. This shifts the entire frame of analysis.

### Yosef ben Choni

The source is a *Tosefta*: the *chachamim* rule that three *lugin* of drawn water invalidate a *mikvah* regardless of how many vessels the water was distributed among — whether it fell in from two vessels, three vessels, four, or five, it does not matter. Yosef ben Choni disagrees: *bi-shnayim u-vi-shelosha kelim posel et ha-mikvah, be-arba ve-chamisha ein posel et ha-mikvah* — two or three vessels invalidate, but four or five do not.

Why should the number of vessels matter? The logic appears to be that the *psul* of *mayim she'uvim* is not a flaw in the water's composition but a consequence of the *mikvah* having been formed through deliberate human effort. What constitutes a "meaningful act" of drawing? Only when each individual act of pouring contributed a significant quantity — at least a *log* per vessel. If the three *lugin* were spread across four or five vessels, each act contributed less than a *log* and was therefore not a halachically significant act of formation. The aggregate still totals three *lugin*, but no single act of drawing was substantial enough to leave its mark on the *mikvah*'s character. This reading assumes roughly equal distribution across vessels, though the *mishnah* does not spell this out explicitly.

*Lefi cheshbon*, then, according to Rava, means: do not automatically say that any three *lugin* of drawn water invalidates; calculate according to the number of vessels and the significance of each individual act.

### Practical Application

The ראב"ד — Rav Avraham bar David — is cited (via the *Tosefot Yom Tov*) as ruling in accordance with Yosef ben Choni, and draws an important practical inference: when one empties a *mikvah* to clean it, removing the water with a vessel, some residual water inevitably remains — splashing back from the bucket, dripping on the floor. This water may technically be *mayim she'uvim* and might accumulate to three *lugin* on the floor before new rainwater fills the *mikvah*. The ראב"ד rules that there is no concern, since in the course of cleaning, the water falling back was spread across many removals — each removal contributed only drops, not a *log* per vessel. Thus even if the residual water on the floor exceeds three *lugin* in total, it was never drawn three *lugin* at a time, and according to Yosef ben Choni it does not invalidate. Some *poskim*, however, are *machmir* and make a small hole in the cleaning bucket so that the water is never fully "held" — and thus never technically *she'uvim* — even as it is removed.

A separate and significant halakhic question addressed in passing is whether *hamshacha* can be performed on the *majority* or even the entirety of the water in a *mikvah*. This was a pressing practical question for communities that could not obtain rainwater easily. Tosafot, finding that the implication of even one *gemara* line suggesting *kulo* — the entire *mikvah* — conflicts deeply with numerous *mishnayot* in *Taharot*, reads that line restrictively, arguing that it can only mean cases where forty *se'ah* of valid rainwater are present somewhere in the mixture regardless. The *Rishonim* debated this extensively, and the question of how we rule (*posken*) depends both on the correct textual reading and on reconciling this passage with the *mishnayot* in Seder Taharot — a tractate that, lacking a *gemara*, relies on analysis of the *mishnayot* themselves, the *Tosefta*, and the incidental citations of those passages in the *Bavli* and *Yerushalmi*.

---

## Mei Chatat Rule

### Basic Rule

The *mishnah* states: *ein mei chatat osim mei chatat* — *mei chatat* cannot make *mei chatat*. The mixture of water and ashes of the *parah adumah* cannot serve as a source for preparing new *mei chatat*; one cannot simply add the existing mixture to fresh water and thereby sanctify the fresh water. The valid preparation requires introducing ashes (*eifer*) to water — not *mei chatat* to water.

### Attribution

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: this ruling is not like Rabbi Shimon — *d'lo k'Rabbi Shimon*.

### Rabbi Shimon Lenient

A *Tosefta* in Parah records the dispute: *hikdim afar l'mayim pasul* — if one puts the ashes in the vessel first and then adds the water, it is invalid. Rabbi Shimon holds that it is valid: *Rabbi Shimon machshir*. Note that the text here uses *afar* (dirt) rather than *eifer* (ashes), because the same *gezeira shava* connects the *parah adumah* to the *sotah* ritual, where the verse uses *afar*. Rabbi Shimon notes: is this really "dirt"? No, it is ashes. The Torah used the word *afar* in the context of the *parah adumah* in order to create a *gezeira shava* with the *sotah* verse — *ne'emar kan afar, ve-ne'emar lehan afar* — "dirt" is mentioned both here and there. Just as for the *sotah* the ideal procedure is water first and then dirt, the same ideal applies for *parah adumah*. But the *gezeira shava* cuts both ways for Rabbi Shimon: just as the *parah adumah* permits ashes before water (as Rabbi Shimon will now establish), so too the *sotah* permits dirt before water. Either order is acceptable.

### Verse Analysis

The question then is: how does Rabbi Shimon know that ashes-before-water is valid for *parah adumah*? *Trei krayi ksivi* — two separate formulations are written. One phrase is *v'natan alav mayim chayim el keli* — the simple reading of this *pasuk* is: take the ashes, then put water on them into a vessel — implying ashes come first. The other reading draws on only the end of that same verse: *mayim chayim el keli* — living water into a vessel — which implies the water must be the first thing to enter the vessel. Rabbi Shimon reads both phrases as independently valid options: either put the ashes first and then the water (*v'natan alav*), or put the water first into the vessel (*mayim chayim el keli*). Either is acceptable.

### Sages Water First

The *chachamim* insist on water first, deriving this from *mayim chayim el keli* and treating it as the definitive instruction (*seifa de-kra davka* — the end of the verse determines). As for *v'natan alav* — "and he put upon it" — they read *alav* not as a statement of sequence (ashes first, then water on top), but as an instruction about mixing: *le-arvan* — you must mix them well together. The word *alav* merely ensures thorough combination, not a specific order. How do the *chachamim* know that water-first is the definitive rule? *Mima matzinu be-chol makom machshir lemala* — from the general principle that the *machshir*, the activating ingredient, is put on top. Since for *sotah* it is explicit that the water is the base and the dirt is placed upon it, the same structure governs *parah adumah*: water first, ashes on top.

It is notable that Rabbi Shimon's reading is arguably the more straightforward *pshat* of the verse, yet the *chachamim* reinterpret *alav* as referring to mixing rather than sequence. The *gemara*'s attribution of our *mishnah* as opposing Rabbi Shimon emphasizes the aspect of *matan eifer* — the ashes must be added to the water — which implies the water precedes the ashes, contrary to Rabbi Shimon's permissive ruling.

---

## Beit Ha-peras

### Mishnah Position

The *mishnah* states: *ein beit ha-peras oseh beit ha-peras* — one *beit ha-peras* does not create another *beit ha-peras*. The *gemara* immediately identifies this as not like Rabbi Eliezer — *matnitin de-lo ke-Rabbi Eliezer*.

### Rabbi Eliezer

The source *mishnah*: *Rabbi Eliezer omer beit ha-peras oseh beit ha-peras* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that a *beit ha-peras* can make another field into a *beit ha-peras*. The scenario is that a field was already plowed over a grave — creating a *beit ha-peras* — and then that field was plowed further into a neighboring field.

### Definition

The fundamental rule of *beit ha-peras* is established by a *braita*: *ha'choresh et ha-kever oseh beit ha-peras milo ma'ane me'ah amah* — one who plows over a grave creates a *beit ha-peras* of a full *ma'ane*, one hundred *amot* (approximately 150 feet). This is the assumed radius of scatter: when a grave is plowed over, bone fragments may have been dispersed up to a hundred *amot* in the direction of plowing, and *kohanim* may not traverse the field. If the grave was at the edge of the field, the *beit ha-peras* extends a hundred *amot* in each direction of plowing. The *gemara* notes that on this underlying rule — that plowing from a *beit ha-peras* into a neighboring field contaminates that neighboring field up to a hundred *amot* — even the *Rabbanan* seem to concede, as Rav Dimi reported in the name of Reish Lakish: *shalosh sadot u'shtei ma'anot* — three fields and two *ma'anot*, meaning the contamination radiates outward to the adjacent fields in the direction of plowing. The *Rabbanan* apparently agree that the second field is affected.

### Tosafot Interpretation

Tosafot resolves the apparent inconsistency: the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Rabbanan* is not actually about the immediately neighboring field — both agree it is impacted. The debate concerns the *third* field. If the *beit ha-peras* status of the second field is treated as a genuine, independent *beit ha-peras* in its own right, then plowing from it into a third field would create yet another *beit ha-peras* — and so on, potentially without limit. This is what Rabbi Eliezer holds: *beit ha-peras oseh beit ha-peras*, meaning the second field's status is primary and self-generating, capable of producing further generations of *beit ha-peras*. The *chachamim* say no: the second field's impurity is derivative of the original plowed grave; it is a *beit ha-peras* only in a secondary sense and cannot in turn make a third field into a *beit ha-peras*. The chain stops at the first remove.

This is the structural parallel that places this case in the list: just as *temurah* cannot make *temurah*, and a *vlad kodashim* cannot make *temurah*, because derivative sanctity does not generate further derivative sanctity — so too a *beit ha-peras* created by proximity to an original *beit ha-peras* cannot produce yet another *beit ha-peras*. The *machlokes* between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Rabbanan* here is therefore precisely analogous to the *machlokes* about *temurah*: does a derivative status become primary and self-perpetuating, or does it remain secondary and terminate there?

---

---

# Temurah 13

## Terumah Achar Terumah

### Intro to Two Terumot

The *mishna* on 13a introduces a rule that has a superficially similar structure to several laws discussed earlier in the tractate but is actually making a distinct point: *ve'ein trumah achar trumah* — one cannot take a second *terumah* after the first has already been taken from the same produce.

### Terumah vs. Temurah

This rule is importantly different from the prohibition against daisy-chaining *temurah*. The *temurah* prohibition is that one cannot take a *temurah* from a *temurah* — that is, one cannot take A, make it a *temurah* of B, and then take C as a *temurah* of that derived B. The chain cannot extend beyond one remove from the original sanctified animal. But *temurah* does permit making multiple exchanges from the same original source: one may take A, designate B as its *temurah*, and then designate C as a *temurah* as well, as long as each exchange starts from A. That is not daisy-chaining — it is always returning to the original. *Terumah*, by contrast, prohibits doing the act twice even from the same original source: once *terumah* has been taken from a pile of grain, it cannot be taken again.

### Rabbi Eliezer Position

The *gemara* identifies the source for this rule in a debate recorded in a *mishna* elsewhere. The case involves *shutfim* — partners in a field — who take *terumah* from their jointly owned produce sequentially, without coordinating with one another. This is the interesting test case: a single person taking *terumah* twice from his own produce is so obvious as not to need discussion. But partners acting independently create a genuine ambiguity. Rabbi Eliezer rules that *trumat shneihem trumah* — both *terumot* are valid. His logic is apparently that we interpret each partner as having taken *terumah* on his respective half of the shared produce.

### Rabbi Akiva Position

Rabbi Akiva rules *ein trumat shneihem trumah* — neither works. This is the *mishna*'s position, and the *gemara* therefore attributes our *mishna* to Rabbi Akiva rather than to the *tanna kamma*, since it disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer on this point.

### Rashi Interpretation

Rashi explains Rabbi Akiva's view as follows: when the second partner goes ahead and takes *terumah* again after the first already did, this demonstrates retroactively that he was not satisfied with what his partner had done. And if the second partner did not want the first partner taking *terumah* on his behalf, then by symmetry we can assume the same was true in reverse. Both of them, it turns out, did not consent to the other's act. The mutual presumption of rejection invalidates both.

### Tosafot Interpretation

Tosafot disagrees with Rashi's reading and offers what is in some ways the simpler interpretation of Rabbi Akiva: the first *terumah* is valid, and the second is void. This is consistent with the plain reading of our *mishna*, which says *ein trumah achar trumah* — there is no *terumah* after *terumah*, implying the first stands and the second accomplishes nothing. On Tosafot's reading, the first partner's act is presumed to have been done with the other's agreement, and once it is done, any subsequent attempt by the second partner is simply meaningless.

### Chachamim Position

The *chachamim* offer a third position that introduces the concept of proper measure. *Im taram harishon kashiur* — if the first partner took the standard amount (roughly two percent, the average that the Rabbis identify as appropriate), then *ein trumat hasheni trumah* — the second one's act has no effect. The first was done correctly, it stands, and the second adds nothing. But *ve'im lo taram kashiur* — if the first partner did not take the appropriate measure, taking instead the minimum permissible amount of one sixtieth, then *trumat hasheni trumah* — the second one's act is effective. According to Rashi, this means that taking a stingy amount signals dissatisfaction with the first *terumah*, and the second partner's subsequent act then validates itself. Whether this means the first is entirely nullified or merely supplemented is somewhat unclear, but the underlying logic seems to be that insufficient performance by the first creates the opening for the second.

---

## Temurah Osah Temurah

### Temurah Prohibition

After the digression about *terumah*, the *mishna* returns to the direct discussion of *temurah*: *ve'ein temurah osah temurah* — a *temurah* cannot generate a further *temurah*. The *gemara* derives this from the verse, which says *be'temurato* — its exchange, meaning the exchange of the original sanctified animal — *velo temurat temurato* — not the exchange of the *temurah* itself. The Torah permits *temurah* only with respect to the original sanctified animal, not with respect to something whose *kedushah* is itself already derivative.

### Vlad Cannot Temurah

The *mishna* links this to a parallel rule: *ve'ein ha-vlad oseh temurah* — the offspring of a *korban* cannot generate a *temurah* either. The common thread between the two cases is the distinction between primary and derivative *kedushah*. A *temurah* has derivative *kedushah* because it acquired its sanctity by being exchanged for the original. A *vlad* has derivative *kedushah* because it was born to a sanctified mother. In both cases, the chain of sanctity has moved one step away from the original act of consecration, and the Torah does not permit *temurah* to be performed from that derived position.

### Rabbi Yehuda Exception

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees specifically with respect to *vlad*, drawing on the verse *yihiyeh* — it shall be — which he reads as expanding the category of *temurah* to include offspring. In his view, one cannot make a *temurah* from a *temurah*, but one can make a *temurah* from a *vlad*, since the *vlad* possesses a legitimate form of *kedushah* even if it is derivative. The Rabbis, by contrast, read *yihiyeh* as a source for a different expansion: *lerabot shogeg ke-mezid* — to include even an unintentional act of *temurah*.

### Temurah Binding Force

This introduces a broader theme that recurs throughout the tractate: *temurah* is more binding in certain respects than an original act of consecration. If one accidentally designates the wrong animal — say, one intended to designate a black cow but mistakenly referred to a white one — an original *hekdesh* would be *ta'os* and would not bind. But *temurah* takes hold even where there is a certain element of error, because the verse *yihiyeh* comes to ensure its binding force even in cases of *shogeg*. This is one of several contexts in which *temurah*, paradoxically, is more forceful than a deliberate primary consecration.

---

## Excluded Objects

### Birds Menachot

The next and final *mishna* of this *perek* turns to a systematic catalog of what is excluded from *temurah*. The *mishna* opens: *ha-ofot veha-menachot ein osin temurah* — bird sacrifices and *menachot* cannot perform *temurah*. The reason is that the Torah uses the word *behemah* — it says *behemah bivehemah*, specifically restricting *temurah* to domesticated livestock. A bird is not a *behemah* in the relevant sense, and *menachot* are certainly not livestock. Furthermore, since the verse says *behemah bivehemah*, both the original sanctified animal and the object of exchange must be a *behemah*. This presumably excludes birds from being either side of the transaction.

### Tzibur Shutfim

The *mishna* continues: *ha-tzibur veha-shutfim einam osim temurah* — communal sacrifices and jointly owned sacrifices cannot perform *temurah*. The *mishna* derives this from the verse *lo yachalifenu velo yamir* — you shall not exchange it or substitute it — where the verb is in the singular. *Yachid oseh temurah* — only an individual can perform *temurah*; *ve'ein tzibur ve-shutfim osim temurah* — not the community and not partners. A *korban tamid* or *musaf*, brought on behalf of the entire community, cannot be subject to *temurah*, nor can a *korban* that two individuals own jointly.

### Bedek Habayit

The *mishna* adds: *kodshei bedek ha-bayit einam osim temurah* — items sanctified for the Temple treasury do not perform *temurah*. The underlying principle, as has been noted throughout this chapter, is that *temurah* requires *kedushat haguf* — genuine intrinsic *korban*-sanctity, the kind that attaches to an animal designated for the altar. An animal consecrated for the treasury has only *kedushat damim*, and even in the middle cases — such as a blemished animal whose proceeds are designated to purchase a *korban* — the status is insufficient for *temurah*.

### Rabbi Shimon Maaser

Rabbi Shimon adds a distinctive methodological point. He does not dispute the conclusions just stated, but he derives them differently. The Torah, in *Bechukosai*, states the prohibition of *temurah* once generally, and then, a few verses later, repeats the prohibition specifically in the context of *ma'aser behemah*. *V'harei ma'aser bichlal haya* — *ma'aser* was already included in the general prohibition, so why was it singled out? *Lomar lecha* — to serve as a paradigm. *Mah ma'aser korban yachid* — just as *ma'aser* is a private individual's *korban*, *yatzu korbanos tzibur* — communal sacrifices are excluded. *U'mah ma'aser korban mizbe'ach* — and just as *ma'aser* is an altar sacrifice, *yatzu korbanos bedek ha-bayit* — gifts to the treasury are excluded. Rabbi Shimon thus reads the Torah's repetition of *temurah* by *ma'aser* not as redundant but as providing the halachic model for all subsequent exclusions.

---

## Maaser Paradigm

### Korban Definition

The *gemara* opens with a *braita* that presses the *tanna kamma*'s position: *yachol yehu kodshei bedek ha-bayit osim temurah* — one might have thought that items dedicated to the Temple treasury would also be subject to *temurah*. The *braita* derives their exclusion from the word *korban*: since the Torah links the prohibition of *temurah* to a *korban*, and items dedicated to the treasury are not called a *korban*, they are excluded. But the *gemara* immediately challenges this: is it really true that treasury items are not called *korban*?

### Shechutei Chutz

Another *braita*, in an entirely different context, shows that the word *korban* can indeed encompass treasury items. That *braita* concerns the prohibition of *shechutei chutz* — slaughtering a *korban* outside the Temple precincts, which incurs *karet*. The verse formulates the prohibition in terms of one who failed to bring his animal *el pesach ohel mo'ed*. The *braita* notes that one might have thought the prohibition extends even to animals sanctified for the treasury, since such animals are also called *korban*, citing the verse *vanakrev es korban Hashem* — and we brought the offering of God — a passage from after the war with Midian where the officers' gift to the treasury is explicitly called *korban Hashem*. However, the *braita* concludes that the actual exclusion of treasury items from *shechutei chutz* comes not from the word *korban* but from the phrase *lo hevi'o el pesach ohel mo'ed* — since treasury items would not normally come to the *ohel mo'ed* in the first place (either because they have a blemish or because they are not animals fit for the altar at all), one is not liable for slaughtering them outside the Temple.

The upshot of citing this *braita* is clear: if the word *korban* were on its own insufficient to exclude treasury items in the context of *shechutei chutz* — requiring the *gemara* to find another source — how can the *tanna kamma* of the *temurah* discussion use the word *korban* to exclude them there?

### Korban Hashem

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction by observing that it is not *korban* simpliciter that includes treasury items, but specifically *korban Hashem* — with the divine name attached as a modifier. *Korban Hashem ikri* — when it appears with that qualifier, it may refer to a gift. *Korban l'Hashem lo ikri* — but plain *korban*, or even *korban l'Hashem*, does not extend to treasury gifts. The occurrence in the Midian passage uses the distinctive formulation *korban Hashem*, which the *gemara* treats as an exceptional usage. The standard term *korban*, on its own, does not encompass *bedek ha-bayit*.

### Resolution

With this in hand, the *gemara* identifies the underlying dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the *rabanan*. *Ha Rabbi Shimon ha rabanan* — the two *braitot* represent two positions. The *rabanan* hold that *korban stam* does not include treasury items, and therefore the word *korban* in the *temurah* verse is sufficient to exclude them. Rabbi Shimon holds that *korban* could in principle encompass *bedek ha-bayit* and is therefore insufficiently precise to serve as the basis of exclusion. For that reason, Rabbi Shimon must derive the exclusion of treasury items from the paradigm of *ma'aser*, and cannot simply rely on the word *korban*.

---

## Maaser Repeated

### Rabbi Shimon Paradigm

The *gemara* now cites a *braita* that spells out Rabbi Shimon's position fully. The *braita* asks: *lama ne'emar* — why does the Torah need to state the prohibition of *temurah* a second time by *ma'aser*? *V'halo kvar ne'emar lo yachalifenu velo yamir oso tov be-ra* — the general prohibition was already stated earlier. *Lefi she-ne'emar lo yachalifenu* — since the general statement might have been read to apply whether the *korban* is individual or communal, whether it is a sacrifice for the altar or a gift to the treasury, therefore the Torah singles out *ma'aser* as the paradigm. *Mah ma'aser korban yachid vekorban mizbe'ach* — since *ma'aser* is a private individual's sacrifice and is specifically an altar offering — *ve-davar she-ba be-chovah* — and it is something that comes through an obligation, a point we shall return to shortly — *ve-davar she-eino be-shutfus* — and it is not jointly owned — so too all *temurah* must meet all of these conditions. This is Rabbi Shimon's full derivation.

The *rabanan* who do not use *ma'aser* as their paradigm derive the same exclusions from different sources: the singular verb excludes communal and partnership sacrifices, and the word *korban* excludes treasury gifts. What remains unclear is whether the *rabanan* agree with the additional requirement of *ba be-chovah* — that the *korban* must come through an obligation — or whether that exclusion is unique to Rabbi Shimon's paradigm.

### Rebbi Alternative

Rebbi offers an alternative explanation for why the Torah repeats the *temurah* prohibition by *ma'aser*. His position is introduced with the phrase *lama yatzas ma'aser min ha-klal* — why was *ma'aser* singled out from the general rule? His answer: *lidon bi-tmurat shemo uvi-tmurat gufo* — because *ma'aser* has a special *halakha* that involves two distinct types of exchange, and the Torah repeats the *temurah* verse by *ma'aser* in order to clarify that both apply.

The reference is to a well-known *halakha* in *ma'aser behemah*, discussed at length in *Bechoros*. When an animal owner counts his animals through a gate to separate the tenth as *ma'aser*, if he miscalls the count and declares the ninth "ten" or the eleventh "ten," those animals also acquire *kedushah*. This is *tmurat shemo* — not an exchange of the body of the animal, but a misapplication of the name. The animal called "ten" in error acquires a status similar to *temurah*, but through the mechanism of naming rather than through the physical act of exchange. Normal *temurah*, by contrast, is *tmurat gufo* — an exchange of the body itself.

Rebbi's point is that since *ma'aser* has this distinctive feature of *tmurat shemo*, one might have thought that the introduction of this new category displaces the older category: perhaps *ma'aser* is now governed exclusively by the rules of *tmurat shemo* and is no longer subject to the standard rules of *tmurat gufo*. The Torah therefore repeats the *temurah* prohibition by *ma'aser* to clarify that *ma'aser* retains *tmurat gufo* as well. Both regimes apply simultaneously.

### Shemo vs. Gufo

The *gemara* then elaborates the practical differences between *tmurat shemo* and *tmurat gufo*, and the analysis is worth following carefully.

*Tmurat shemo kriva, tmurat gufo einah kriva* — if one performs *tmurat shemo*, calling eleven "ten," that animal becomes a *shelamim* and is brought as a *korban*. If one performs *tmurat gufo*, a standard *temurah* of *ma'aser*, the resulting animal is not brought as a *korban*. The reason connects to the previously learned principle that *tmurat ma'aser* and *tmurat bechor* are uniquely not brought as *korbanot*. What makes *bechor* and *ma'aser* different from other *korbanot*? Their identity is defined not by an act of consecration but by a reality — this animal was the firstborn, this was the tenth out of the gate. When *temurah* is performed with such an animal, the resulting *temurah* inherits the *kedushah* of *ma'aser* or *bechor* without actually being the tenth or the firstborn. It possesses the *kedushah* without the defining reality, and consequently it is not brought as a *korban*. *Tmurat shemo*, by contrast, produces a *shelamim*, not a *ma'aser*, and a *shelamim* is of course brought as a *korban*.

### Eligibility Diff

Further differences follow. *Tmurat shemo nigelet* — the animal that arose from *tmurat shemo* can be redeemed if it acquires a *mum*. Since it became a *shelamim*, the ordinary rules of *shelamim* apply, and a blemished *shelamim* may be redeemed. *Tmurat gufo einah nigelet* — the animal that arose from *tmurat gufo* cannot be redeemed. Since it is *kedushat ma'aser*, and the Torah says *lo yiga'el* — *ma'aser* cannot be redeemed — a *temurah* of *ma'aser* retains that prohibition. One waits for it to acquire a *mum* and then eats it outside the *beit ha-mikdash*, rather than redeeming it.

A further distinction: *tmurat gufo chalah al davar ha-ra'uy ve-al davar she-eino ra'uy* — a proper *temurah* takes effect whether the substitute animal is blemished or unblemished. The *halakha* of *temurah* generally is that even if you attempt to exchange a sanctified animal for a blemished one, the exchange takes real effect: the blemished animal acquires genuine *kedushat mizbe'ach*, even though it cannot actually be brought as a *korban*. *Tmurat shemo einah chalah ela al davar ha-ra'uy bilvad* — the exchange of name, calling the eleventh "ten," only takes full effect when that animal is unblemished. If the animal designated by the erroneous count has a *mum*, it is not treated as a proper *shelamim* with intrinsic *kedushat ha-guf*; it has only *kedushat damim*, like any blemished animal that is consecrated to the altar. Rashi clarifies that this does not mean the animal acquires no sanctity at all, only that it never achieves real intrinsic altar-sanctity and must be sold with the proceeds going toward a *korban*.

The elegance of Rebbi's formulation lies in lining up these two parallel categories — calling eleven "ten" versus exchanging bodies — and showing precisely where the analogy holds and where the two regimes diverge. In the case of *tmurat shemo*, one has effectively created an original act of consecration as a *shelamim*; all the *halakhot* of an original *shelamim* designation follow from that. In the case of *tmurat gufo*, one has the special and peculiar category of *temurah* with all its distinctive stringencies and limitations.

---

## Ba'ah Bechovah

### Ba'ah Definition

The *braita* that spells out Rabbi Shimon's paradigm introduces a requirement that has not been previously explained: the *korban* must be *davar she-ba be-chovah* — something that comes through obligation. Only when a *korban* is an obligatory offering — something that one has taken upon oneself as an obligation — is it subject to *temurah*.

### Leftover Money

One might wonder what is excluded by this criterion, since most *korbanot* are either fixed obligations or voluntary pledges. The *gemara* explains: the case excluded is *olat ha-ba'ah min ha-motarot* — an *olah* that arises from leftover money. When one sets aside funds for a *chatat* and the *chatat* ends up costing less than anticipated, the remaining money must be used for an *olah*. Similarly, when an *asham* is rendered unnecessary because the owner brings a different *asham* to atone, the original *asham* transforms into an *olah*. In both cases, the *olah* was not the result of any deliberate, intentional act of consecration; it arose as a byproduct of an accidental circumstance. Because this *olah* was never consciously undertaken as an obligation, it is considered *lo ba be-chovah* and is therefore excluded from *temurah*.

---

## Ba'ah Bechovah (II)

### Rabbi Eliezer

The *gemara* then notes an apparent tension. The criterion of *ba be-chovah* — that it requires an individual's *korban* — leads us to ask which opinion holds that leftover money produces an individual *korban* in the first place. The answer is Rabbi Eliezer, who rules that *motarot* go toward a *nidvat yachid*, a personal voluntary *korban*. However, the *gemara* points out that a *braita* explicitly records Rabbi Eliezer himself as ruling *oseh temurah* — that this *olah* from leftover money *can* perform *temurah*.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon, therefore, agrees with Rabbi Eliezer on one point and disagrees on another. *Savar lah kavateih be-chada u-falig aleih be-chada* — he agrees that the leftover money goes toward an individual *korban*, but he disagrees that such an *olah* can perform *temurah*. Rabbi Shimon holds that because the *olah* was not consciously and intentionally undertaken, it is excluded from *temurah* by virtue of the *ma'aser* paradigm, which requires *ba be-chovah*. This is also where the practical significance of Rabbi Shimon's paradigm approach becomes manifest: until this point, the exclusions Rabbi Shimon derived from *ma'aser* were identical to those the *rabanan* derived from other verses. But the requirement of *ba be-chovah* represents a novel *halakha* — one that the *rabanan* may not share, and one that only emerges because Rabbi Shimon is reading *ma'aser* as the governing model.

---

## Asham to Olah

### Setup Scenario

With this discussion in place, the *gemara* revisits a conceptual puzzle raised on an earlier *daf* — a scenario involving an *asham* whose *temurah* eventually transforms into an *olah*. The case: one sets aside an *asham*, performs *temurah* with it, and then separately brings another *asham* to fulfill the obligation, at which point the original *asham* transitions into an *olah* according to the relevant *halakha*.

### Double Temurah

The question now reframed: can one perform a second *temurah* with that animal after its transformation? This was the question that generated extended discussion on the earlier *daf*, based on Rabbi Yochanan's reading of Rabbi Shimon that one may not perform *temurah* twice with the same animal. But the *gemara* now notes a complication: according to Rabbi Shimon himself, this *olah* that arose from an *asham* should not be eligible for *temurah* at all, since it is an *olah ha-ba'ah min ha-motarot* and is excluded as *lo ba be-chovah*. The earlier discussion, therefore, presupposed a position — that this *olah* can perform *temurah* — that is actually Rabbi Eliezer's position, not Rabbi Shimon's.

### Same Kedusha

The *gemara* therefore reframes the question: *aliba d'man* — according to whom is this question even relevant? One would need to find a *tanna* who holds both that one cannot perform *temurah* twice with the same animal (Rabbi Shimon according to Rabbi Yochanan) and that an *olah* arising from an *asham* can perform *temurah* (Rabbi Eliezer's position). Rabbi Avin's question thus becomes a hypothetical: if such an opinion were to exist, what would the answer be? *Be-shnei gufin bi-kedushah achas mai* — if the *kedushah* is the same but the body changes — that is, if the animal acquires a *mum* and the *kedushah* is transferred to a replacement — is performing *temurah* on that replacement considered a second *temurah* or a first?

### Different Kedusha

*Ve-im timtzo lomar* — and if you were to say that scenario is limited (because it is the same *kedushah* passing through a different body, which counts as "twice"), the question extends further: what if the *kedushah* itself changes? In our case, the animal began as an *asham* and transformed into an *olah* — two distinct categories of *kedushah* in a single body. Would performing *temurah* after such a transformation be considered a second *temurah* on the same animal, or a first *temurah* on what is effectively a newly categorized entity?

### Unresolved Tivai

The *gemara* leaves this unresolved: *tibai*. This term functions identically to the more familiar *teiku* — the question stands unanswered. It is worth noting, as the *gemara* makes clear, that there may be no *tanna* who actually holds both of the presuppositions necessary to make this question practically relevant. Yet the *gemara* pursues it anyway — a striking illustration of how the *gemara* sometimes presses conceptual questions for their own intrinsic interest, independent of whether any concrete *halakha* turns on them. With this *tibai*, the chapter concludes: *Hadran alach ha-kol memirin* — we complete the first *perek* of Temurah.

---

---

# Temurah 15

## Nazir Sacrifices

### Abaye's Question

The daf begins six lines down on 14b, where Abaye poses a question against a *baraita* that had been cited in the course of a broader discussion about the differences between *korbanot tzibur* and *korbanot yachid*. That earlier discussion had led the *Gemara* to quote a lengthy *baraita* based on the verse *u'minchatam u'niskeihem*, which catalogued the various *korbanot* that could be brought on *Chol HaMoed*. Among the words of that verse, *nidreichem u'nidvoteichem* — "your vows and your free-will offerings" — was understood to cover all voluntary sacrifices, leaving the remaining words of the verse to cover obligatory ones. The *baraita* used one set of words to include the *korbanot* of a *nazir*, reading *u'shalmeichem* as referring to *shalmei nazir*.

Abaye's challenge is pointed: why derive the *shalmei nazir* from that word at all? If the *shalmei nazir* are in the category of *neder u'nedavah*, they are already covered by *nidreichem u'nidvoteichem*. And if that is so, the remaining word would be better used to include *shalmei pesach* — the *shlamim* brought to accompany the *korban pesach* so that one may eat *al hasova*, satisfied, before consuming the *pesach* itself. The *shalmei pesach* carries a more genuinely obligatory character, since the requirement to eat *al hasova* is itself grounded in obligation. The *shalmei nazir*, by contrast, originates entirely in a voluntary act — the person chose to undertake *nezirut*, and that initial choice was a *neder*.

### Neder vs. Obligation

This is not merely a narrow question of *parshanut* but opens onto a broader issue: are the *korbanot* of a *nazir* to be categorized as *neder* or as *chovah*? On one hand, once a person has accepted *nezirut*, the sacrifice is obligatory — there is no choice about whether to bring it. On the other hand, the entire structure of *nezirut* began with an act of will, with a *neder*, and perhaps that originating character defines the *korbanot* as belonging to the *neder* category throughout.

The *Gemara* brings a *baraita* to demonstrate that the *korbanot* of a *nazir* are indeed considered *neder u'nedavah*: *zeh haklal — kol she'neder u'nedavah kariv b'vamat yachid, v'she'eino neder u'nedavah eino kariv b'vamat yachid*. The rule governing what may be offered on a private altar (*bamas yachid*), in the era before the *Beit HaMikdash* was built, is that only free-will sacrifices may be brought there — obligatory sacrifices, including an individual's *chatat*, may not. The *Gemara* then cites the *Mishnah*: *hamenachos v'hanezirus krevim b'vamat yachid* — *minchot* and the *korbanot* of *nezirut* may be brought on a *bamas yachid*. This is the view of Rabbi Meir, and it shows that *nezirut* sacrifices fall into the *neder u'nedavah* category.

The *Gemara* then considers the other side: could there be an opinion that *nezirut* sacrifices are *not* considered *neder u'nedavah*? One response is simply *samei mikan nezirus* — cross out the word *nezirus* from the *Mishnah* — implying that perhaps others disagree with Rabbi Meir on this classification. But Abaye is not satisfied. He insists that the categorization of *nezirut* as *neder* is supported not merely by rabbinic sources but, as we are about to see, by a careful reading of *pesukim*.

### Private Altar Rule

The *baraita* establishes the general principle: free-will offerings may be brought on a *bamas yachid*, while obligatory ones may not. Crucially, the *Mishnah* cited by the *Gemara* places *nezirut* offerings firmly in the free-will column by ruling that they are valid on a private altar. This ruling by Rabbi Meir anchors the discussion. Even if we were to cross out the word *nezirus* and acknowledge that there may be other views, the structural logic remains: the question of whether *nezirut* constitutes a *neder* or a *chovah* is precisely what determines whether its offerings may be brought on a *bamas yachid*.

### Avshalom's Vow

To prove from *pesukim* that *nezirut* is treated as a *neder*, Abaye points to the story of Avshalom. The verse in Shmuel reads: *vayomer Avshalom el hamelech — elcha na va'ashalem es nidri asher nadarti l'Hashem b'Chevron* — "I must go and fulfill the vow I made to God in Chevron." The rabbis understand Avshalom to have been a *nazir olam*, a *nazir* for life, whose practice was to bring his *korbanot* and shave his hair every thirty days. And the verse explicitly calls this a *neder*.

The *Gemara*'s initial reading of the verse is that Avshalom was heading to Chevron to *offer* his *korbanot* there — that is, to bring his *nazir* sacrifices on a *bamas yachid* in Chevron. This would directly prove that *nezirut* offerings were treated as *neder u'nedavah*, permissible on a private altar. At that time, the central *Mishkan* was in Givon, not in Chevron, so Avshalom's bringing his *korbanot* in Chevron could only be explained if those offerings were of the *neder* type.

The verse, however, includes an important detail that complicates this reading. As Michael pointed out from the full *pasuk*: *ki neder nadar avdecha b'shivti b'Geshur* — "the vow I made while I was in Geshur." Avshalom came from Geshur. So if the vow was made in Geshur, why does the verse say he is going to fulfill it *b'Chevron*? One answer offered is *lo ikar nidro* — the verse does not mean that Chevron is where he undertook the *nezirut*, but rather that *asher nadarti l'Hashem b'Chevron* means he is going to Chevron to fulfill it there. This maintains the original inference: he is bringing his *korbanot* on a private *bamah* in Chevron.

### Chevron Clarified

The *Gemara* offers a second interpretation: *lo l'Chevron ela l'havi kevasim miChevron* — he was not going to Chevron to bring the *korbanot*, but to obtain the animals there. Chevron was known for fine sheep, and he would fetch the lambs there and then bring his offerings in Givon. The *Gemara* notes that this reading is actually compelling on its own terms: *hachi nami mistabra* — it makes good sense. If he was going to bring on a *bamas yachid*, why travel to Chevron at all? He could bring them right there in Yerushalayim.

This raises an interesting implicit question: does the *Gemara* here assume that Yerushalayim already held some elevated status even before the *Beit HaMikdash* was built? Perhaps — it may simply mean that there is no point *schlepping* when you could bring it immediately where you are. But the implication may also be that Yerushalayim already occupied a higher position in the spiritual hierarchy, even in the era of *heter bamos*.

The *Gemara* then pushes back on the "going to fetch lambs" reading: *asher nadarti l'Hashem b'Chevron* should read *miChevron mibayei* — if the intention were that he was obtaining animals *from* Chevron, the verse should have said something like "from Chevron," not "in Chevron." So the *Gemara* returns to the plain reading: *ella l'olam l'akruvei hu d'azil* — he was truly going to Chevron to bring the offering. And the question of why not in Yerushalayim is answered: *keivan shehutra bamos, kol heichah d'ba'ei makri* — once private altars were generally permitted, there was no inherent preference of one location over another. In a period of *heter bamos*, every location was, in principle, equally valid. There was no hierarchy of place for offerings that were permissible on a *bamas yachid*. Whatever personal reason Avshalom had for preferring Chevron, there was no *halachic* reason to prefer Yerushalayim.

The *Gemara* thus concedes the point. The plain reading of the *pesukim* supports Abaye's position: Avshalom brought his *nazir korbanot* in Chevron, on a private *bamah*, and this is entirely consistent with the rule that *neder u'nedavah* type offerings may be brought on a *bamas yachid*. The *nezirut* sacrifice is accordingly classified as *neder*, not *chovah*, and Abaye's challenge to the *baraita* stands. No satisfactory answer emerges for why the word *ushalmeikem* should be used to derive the *nezirut korban* rather than the *shalmei pesach*.

The *Gemara* then turns briefly to the question of what is meant by *miketz arba'im shanah* — the forty-year marker in the Avshalom episode. It cannot refer to forty years of David's reign, since the rebellion occurred earlier. A *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Nehorai citing Rabbi Yehoshua explains that the forty years are counted from when Israel first asked for a king. Breaking it down: ten years of Shmuel's leadership on his own, one year of joint leadership of Shmuel and Shaul, two years of Shaul's sole reign, and then thirty-six or thirty-seven years of David's reign, arriving at forty from the start of the monarchic process. The variation in the count — whether thirty-six or thirty-seven — is the subject of considerable textual discussion in both Rashi and Tosafot, but the essential point is that the forty years mark from the very beginning of the institution of kingship, lending the episode of Avshalom's rebellion a wider resonance: barely a generation into the experiment of monarchy, and already its dangers were manifest.

---

## Chattat Rules

### Individual Chattat

The *Gemara* now transitions to a *Mishnah* dealing with the category of *chataot* that must be left to die. The reason this subject arises here is directly connected to the overarching framework of *Temurah*: the opening *Mishnah* of the tractate enumerated the differences between *korbanot tzibur* and *korbanot yachid*, one of which was the capacity to make a *temurah*. The present discussion asks whether the *halacha* of *chataot* that must die also differs along these lines.

The *Mishnah* states: *chatat hayachid shekiperu ba'aleha — meisa*. If a person designated an animal as his individual *chatat*, it was lost, he brought a replacement to atone, and then the original was found — the original must be left to die. It has no further use; it cannot be offered.

### Communal Status

The *Mishnah* then draws a contrast: *v'shel tzibur einah meisa* — a communal *chatat* in analogous circumstances does not die. It is instead left to graze (*tir'eh*) until it develops a blemish (*mum*), at which point it can be redeemed. The question of what is done with the proceeds is left somewhat open in the *Mishnah* itself. Rashi understands the animal to graze until redeemed, though the precise application of the redemption money is a matter worth exploring.

Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *tamus* — the communal *chatat* must also die, just like the individual one. This is the *machloket* in the *Mishnah*.

### Five Categories

Rabbi Shimon, who appears to be the *tanna kamma*, explains the principled basis for distinguishing communal and individual *chataot*. He begins from the five categories of *chatat* that must be left to die: *(1) vlad chatat* — an offspring of a *chatat*; *(2) tmuras chatat* — an animal exchanged for a *chatat*; *(3) meisu ba'aleha* — the owners died; *(4) niskapru b'acher* — the owners were atoned for through another animal; *(5) avar shnasah* — it passed its first year.

Rabbi Shimon observes that three of these five categories simply never occur with a communal *chatat*. A *tzibur chatat* is always male, so there can never be a *vlad chatat*. A *tzibur* cannot make a *temurah* — as established in the framework of this entire tractate — so there can never be a *tmuras chatat*. And a *tzibur*, as a corporate entity, never truly dies, so there is never a case of *meisu ba'aleha*. Since three of the five categories are structurally inapplicable to a *tzibur*, Rabbi Shimon argues that the entire framework of the five categories was formulated with the *yachid* in mind. The remaining two categories — *niskapru b'acher* and *avar shnasah* — are also, therefore, said only of the *yachid*, not the *tzibur*.

Rashi explains Rabbi Shimon's logic as follows: the rule that five categories of *chatat* must die is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*. Clearly that *halacha* was stated with reference to the *yachid*, because by the *tzibur* only two categories could ever occur, not five. A *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* articulated in the framework of five cannot simply be exported to a different context where the framework collapses, and you cannot apply the individual's *halachot* to the *tzibur* at all.

### Found Before

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* that seems to generate a surprising complication. The verse *im keves yavi korbano lechatas* is expounded: if you sanctify an animal as a *chatat*, it is lost, you sanctify a replacement, and then the original is found still alive — from where do we know that you may bring whichever one you choose? The verse says *yavi* — you shall bring — emphasizing your agency, indicating you may select either. But perhaps you should bring both? The verse later says *yivienah* in the singular — just one, not two.
