The second animal then has the status of a *chatat shekiperu ba'aleha b'acheres* — and the *baraita* records a dispute about what becomes of it.

Rav Hamnuna reports: Rabbi Yehuda says *tireh* — let it graze; Rabbi Shimon says *tamus* — let it die. This is deeply puzzling. In the *Mishnah*, both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon seemed to agree that an individual *chatat shekiperu ba'aleha* must die, differing only about the communal case. Yet here Rabbi Yehuda says the individual *chatat* should graze, and after reversing the names the *Gemara* finds Rabbi Shimon in the same position. How can either of them contradict what the *Mishnah* implies?

### Timing Issue

The *Gemara* resolves the difficulty with a crucial distinction: *kan ba'avudah bish'as hafrashah, kan ba'avudah bish'as kaparah*. The two sources are addressing different situations based on *when* the original animal was found. The *Mishnah*'s ruling — that the *chatat* must die — applies when the original was found *after* the replacement had already been offered. In that case, atonement has been fully achieved through the second animal, and the first is entirely displaced; it is *chatat shekiperu ba'aleha*, and it must die. The *baraita*'s ruling, by contrast, applies when the original was found *before* the replacement was offered. In that situation, both animals are simultaneously available candidates. When the owner then proceeds with the replacement and sets aside the original, that original does not necessarily have to die — there is a difference in its status because it was never fully superseded.

The logical asymmetry here is difficult to articulate neatly, since the case *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — but the general structure can be seen: when both animals are simultaneously present and a conscious choice is made, the rejected one retains some vestigial standing that it lacks when it was simply displaced after the fact.

An alternative resolution proposed by the *Gemara* is that even if both texts deal with animals found *bish'as hafrashah*, they can be reconciled by noting that Rabbi Yehuda himself holds different positions depending on whose underlying framework he is following. When Rabbi Yehuda in the *Mishnah* says *tamus*, that is according to the opinion of Rabbi — who rules that even if the original is found before the replacement is brought, it must die. When Rabbi Yehuda says *tireh* in the *baraita*, that is according to the *Rabbanan*, who rule that finding it before the replacement has been offered saves it from the status of mandatory death. The underlying dispute between Rabbi and the *Rabbanan* over this precise timing question thus accounts for the apparent inconsistency in Rabbi Yehuda's rulings across the two texts.

---

## Ein Tzibur Meisa

### Rav Papa Ruling

With the individual *chatat* framework now clarified, the *Gemara* turns to the communal case. A *baraita* cited by Rabbi Yossi introduces the verse from Ezra describing the return of the exiles to Eretz Yisrael: *verabim mehakohanim vehaleviyim verashei ha'avos hazkenim*... They brought burnt offerings: *parim shenem asar, eilim tish'im v'shisha, kevasim shiv'im v'shivah, tzfirei chatat shenem asar*. Twelve oxen and twelve he-goats — the oxen as *olot*, the goats as *chatat* — followed by the statement *hakol olah l'Hashem*, which Rava reads not as a general expression of offering but in its technical sense: all of it was burnt as an *olah*. How could the *chatat* goats be burnt as an *olah*? Rava explains: *mah olah einah nechelet, af chatat einah nechelet* — just as an *olah* is not eaten, so too this *chatat* was not eaten. These were *chataot hanisrafot*, burnt outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, of the type associated with *par helam davar shel tzibur* — the communal sin-offering brought when *Beit Din* ruled incorrectly and the community transgressed on the basis of that ruling.

The twelve oxen and twelve he-goats correspond to the twelve tribes. The sin for which they were atoning was *avodah zarah* — the *pasuk* in *Bamidbar* in *Parshas Shelach*, *v'im me'einei ha'eidah ne'esta lishgagah*, connecting to a *shgagah* committed by the entire community in matters that represent *kol mitzvos Hashem*, understood by the *Gemara* to refer to *avodah zarah*. Specifically, as Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel, this was for the *avodah zarah* committed in the time of Tzidkiyahu, in the final period of the first *Beit HaMikdash*.

The *Gemara* now raises its central question: if one were to hold that a *chatat tzibur shekiperu ba'aleha* must die — the position of Rabbi Yehuda in the *Mishnah* — then one would presumably also hold that a *chatat tzibur shemeisu ba'aleha* must die. But here, the original sinners — those who worshipped *avodah zarah* in the time of Tzidkiyahu — were dead by the time of Ezra's return, some seventy years later. Yet they brought the *chatat*. This would seem to require us to say that even when the *ba'alim* of the *tzibur* have died, the *chatat* does not die with them. Tosafot asks a sharp question: the very structure of the *Mishnah* takes for granted that *meisu ba'aleha* never applies to a *tzibur*, since a *tzibur* never dies. What was the *havah amina* that it might? Tosafot answers: the *Mishnah*'s assumption may only have been that *meisu ba'aleha* does not apply so long as *some* of the original members remain. The question posed here is whether even when *all* the original members have been replaced — as may have been the case by Ezra's time — the *tzibur* is still considered the same entity.

Rav Papa rules: *afilu man de'amar chatat tzibur shekiperu ba'aleha meisah* — even one who holds that a communal *chatat* whose *ba'alim* were atoned elsewhere must die — *chatat tzibur shemeisu ba'aleha einah meisah* — that same authority would never say the communal *chatat* dies when its *ba'alim* die.

### Corporate Entity

The reason is: *ein tzibur meisa*. A community does not die. The *Gemara* notes that the better textual reading is *ein tzibur meisa* — treating the community as a single entity — rather than *ein tzibur meisin* — which would treat it as a collection of individuals. The conceptual point is precisely this: the *tzibur* is not a set of specific persons. It is a corporate entity, and that entity persists regardless of whether its membership has changed. כלל ישראל remains כלל ישראל across generations, even if not a single original member survives.

The *Gemara* asks: where does Rav Papa derive this principle? One suggestion is the verse *tachas avosecha yiheyu vanecha* — your children take the place of your fathers, indicating continuity. The *Gemara* immediately rejects this: if that were the basis, then even an *individual* should benefit from the same continuity, with his children able to bring his *chatat* after his death. That is obviously not so. Children do not allow a deceased individual's *chatat* to survive.

### Rosh Chodesh Proof

The *Gemara* proposes a stronger basis: the ongoing practice of bringing *chataot* for *Rosh Chodesh* and the *musafim* from *trumat halishka*, the funds collected in *Nissan* from all of Israel. By the time *Rosh Chodesh Iyar* arrives — or *Pesach*, or any subsequent *musaf* — some contributors will have died. Yet the *chatat* of the *musaf* is brought without any concern that a portion of its ownership has lapsed. *Ve'amar Rachmanah mitrumat halishka* — the Torah says to bring it from *trumat halishka* — and we do not say that those whose coins funded the animal have died and therefore the *korban* is a *chatat shemeisu ba'aleha*. This demonstrates the principle of *ein tzibur meis* in a regular, recurring context.

The limitation of this proof is acknowledged: it demonstrates only that when *some* contributors have died, the *tzibur* is still considered intact. It does not prove that the principle holds when the *majority* — let alone *all* — of the original members have died.

### Ezra's Return

The *Gemara* therefore returns to the Ezra episode in an attempt to demonstrate the principle in a more extreme case. The verse reads: *verabim mehakohanim vehaleviyim verashei ha'avos hazkenim asher ra'u et habayit harishon beyasdo zeh habayit bochim bekol gadol verabim bitru'ah*. There were many priests, Levites, and elders who had seen the *first* Beit HaMikdash with their own eyes who were now witnessing the founding of the second. They wept bitterly at the contrast. This shows that there *were* survivors from before the *churban* — people alive at the time of Tzidkiyahu's *avodah zarah* who were still present at Ezra's return. Thus, the *Gemara* now considers whether the whole case of Ezra's *korbanot* might simply reflect continuity through surviving members rather than proving anything about a fully replaced community.

### Crying vs. Shofar

The verse concludes: *ve'ein ha'am makirim kol tru'at hasimcha lekol bechi ha'am* — the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful *shofar* blasts from the sound of the weeping, because the weeping was so loud it overwhelmed the rejoicing. The *Gemara* reads this as evidence that the weepers — those who had witnessed the first *Beit HaMikdash* — were a *majority*, since only a majority could drown out the joy of those who had no such memory.

This is a striking conclusion given the seventy-year gap. The *Gemara*, however, concedes that this inference is difficult to sustain. As we know from other episodes — the spies, for example — one does not need a numerical majority to overwhelm a crowd emotionally. A small number of older eyewitnesses could easily reduce an entire assembled community to tears. The *Gemara* ultimately cannot resolve the difficulty fully: it cannot definitively prove the principle of *ein tzibur meis* for cases where the majority, let alone the entirety, of the original members has been replaced.

Nevertheless, the *Gemara* remains committed to the principle. And practically speaking, the narrow case that *was* proven — from *Rosh Chodesh* and *musaf* — is sufficient for virtually all real applications. When dealing with a *chatat* animal still alive, the *tzibur* whose *ba'alim* have partially turned over is the standard case, and for that the *Rosh Chodesh* proof holds.

---

## Horaat Sha'ah

### Intentional Sins

The *Gemara* then presses an underlying difficulty in the Ezra narrative. The *avodah zarah* committed in the time of Tzidkiyahu was not *b'shogeg* — it was not accidental. It was willful, deliberate transgression. Normally a *chatat* can only be brought for an unintentional sin. How then could the returning exiles bring a *chatat* for intentional *avodah zarah*?

### Special Exception

Rabbi Yochanan answers: *horaat sha'ah* — it was a temporary exception, a one-time dispensation that does not reflect the ordinary *halacha*.

### Purpose

The purpose of this *horaat sha'ah* deserves attention. The act of bringing *korbanot* upon returning from exile was not merely ritualistic. It was a symbolic break from the past, a public acknowledgment of the sins of the first *Beit HaMikdash* era and a declaration of intent: we take responsibility, and things will be different now. This is precisely what the prophets had called for at the close of the first *Beit HaMikdash* period, when *avodah zarah* was among the gravest failures of the generation of Tzidkiyahu.

The *Gemara* confirms this reading with the observation that the twelve oxen and twelve goats, corresponding to the twelve *shevatim*, structured the *korban* as one of *par helam davar shel tzibur* — brought on behalf of the entire community. And the extra animals — ninety-six rams and seventy-seven sheep — whose precise correspondence is not explained, were also part of this *horaat sha'ah*. The *Gemara* simply notes *horaat sha'ah* and does not try to account for every detail.

There is an additional conceptual layer here. By accepting the designation of *horaat sha'ah*, the *Gemara* technically undermines some of the earlier proof for *ein tzibur meis*. If the entire act was a special exception, one cannot draw standard *halachic* inferences from it. The *Gemara* does not press this point, and one might argue that even within a *horaat sha'ah*, the very act of taking communal responsibility for past sins implies a strong sense of continuity. If the community could simply say "that was a different generation, we bear no connection," there would be no basis for the statement of responsibility at all. The act of *horaat sha'ah* itself is premised on the idea that this community is continuous with the one that sinned.

---

## Torah Transmission

### Complete Person

The *Gemara* concludes the daf with a *Mishnah* from Sotah cited in the context of lamenting the greatness that has been lost. The *Mishnah* states: *mishemet Yosef ben Yoezer ish Tzereda v'Yosef ben Yochanan ish Yerushalayim, batlu ha'eshkolot* — when Yosef ben Yoezer and Yosef ben Yochanan died, the *eshkolot* ceased. These figures lived in the earliest pre-*Tannaitic* period, even before the *Zugot*. What is an *eshkol*? The *Gemara* glosses it as *ish shehakol bo* — a person in whom everything is found.

Rashi's definition is worth pausing over. The three qualities Rashi identifies are: *Torah, yirat chet, u'gemilut chasadim* — Torah knowledge, a deep fear of sin, and acts of lovingkindness. The precision of this triad is instructive. Intellectual mastery of Torah is necessary but not sufficient; one can possess vast *talmudic chachmah* without the accompanying *yirat chet* — that genuine religiosity, humility, and sense of standing before God that keeps knowledge from becoming merely cerebral. Nor is the inner dimension alone enough; *gemilut chasadim* insists on responsibility toward other people. A complete person integrates all three.

### Lost Halachot

The *Gemara* then introduces an apparent challenge to the notion that the period from Moshe until Yosef ben Yoezer was one of perfect Torah transmission. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *shloshet alafim halachot nishtakchu b'yimei evlo shel Moshe* — three thousand *halachot* were forgotten during the mourning period following Moshe's death. If so, the generation immediately after Moshe was already imperfect. How can we describe that period as one of learning Torah *k'Moshe Rabbeinu*?

### Mesorah Standard

The *Gemara* resolves the question with a crucial distinction: *ahani d'ishtakach ishtakach* — those that were forgotten were forgotten; *u'd'gamir havu g'miri k'Moshe Rabbeinu* — but those that were retained and transmitted were preserved with complete faithfulness, exactly as Moshe himself had received and taught them. The standard being invoked here is not omniscience but fidelity of transmission. To learn Torah *k'Moshe Rabbeinu* means to be a perfect conduit of the *mesorah* — to pass on what one received without alteration, without substitution, without the intrusion of one's own reconstructions.

This points to a distinction that the *Gemara* will develop further in subsequent discussion: the difference between *mesorah* — perfect preservation of received tradition — and the use of one's own intellect to recover or reconstruct what may have been lost. The great figures from Moshe until Yosef ben Yoezer excelled at the former. What changed after Yosef ben Yoezer was not that *halachot* were necessarily forgotten or that Torah learning collapsed, but that the chain of perfectly faithful transmission was no longer maintained at the same standard. The discussion of this distinction will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Temurah 16

## Eshkolot & Decline

### Glory & Eshkolot

The daf picks up from the bottom of 15b, where the Gemara had quoted *pesukim* relating to the return of the Jewish people and the building of the second *Beit HaMikdash* — how they wept, remembering the glory of the first *Beit HaMikdash* — alongside the concluding *pasuk*, *gadol yihiyeh kevod habayit ha'acharon min harishon*, that the glory of the latter house would ultimately surpass that of the former. From there, the Gemara transitions into quoting a *Mishnah* in Sotah that likewise reflects on the greatness of earlier generations, citing Yosef ben Yoezer Ish Tzeredah and Yosef ben Yochanan Ish Yerushalayim as the last of the *Eshkolot* — those who possessed everything within them.

### Eshkolot Definition

Rashi explains that *Eshkolot* — literally "clusters," like a cluster of grapes — is expounded by the Gemara as *ish shekol bo*, a person who is complete: possessing *Torah*, *Yirat Chet*, and *Gemilut Chasadim*. The Gemara now focuses on the *Torah* dimension, asserting that after these two figures, nobody learned *Torah* through them the way one learned through Moshe Rabbeinu — meaning, apparently, that they transmitted it with perfect fidelity. The Gemara proceeds to challenge this claim.

### Righteous Man & Goat

The Gemara cites the *Baraita*: *lo hayah bahem shum dofi* — from the time of Moshe until Yosef ben Yoezer died, the *Eshkolot* had not even the slightest *dofi*, no defect of any kind. *Mikan va'eilach hayah bahem shum dofi* — from that point onward, there were problems.

But what exactly is the *dofi* in question? The Gemara clarifies that the issue here is not primarily the *Torah* transmission dimension; it concerns the *Eshkolot*'s behavior, character, and *shmirat mitzvot*. To illustrate, the Gemara cites a *Baraita*: *ma'aseh bechasid echad shehayah gone'ach milibo* — there was a righteous individual who suffered from chest pains. Doctors were consulted, and they prescribed that each morning he drink freshly milked warm milk — that is, milk drawn directly from the animal while still at body temperature. To facilitate this, he tied a goat to his bedpost and would draw milk from it each morning.

The following day his friends came to visit, and when they saw the goat they exclaimed: *listim mezuyan betoch beito ve'anu nichnasim levakro*? — "There is an armed robber inside his house, and we are coming to visit him?" The prohibition against raising small grazing animals — sheep and goats — in the settled areas of the Land of Israel was well known, since such animals devastate the ground, cropping the grass to its roots and causing serious harm to the land. The friends were not moved by the man's medical need, and according to the Tosefta's version of the story, they left.

After he died, they examined his entire record and found that the only transgression in his life was this one goat — *velo matzu bo avon ela shel osah ez bilvad*. And he himself acknowledged as much on his deathbed: *she-avarti al divrei chaverai* — I violated the ruling of my colleagues, *she-ein megadlin behemah dakah be-eretz yisrael*. What is striking is the way he frames the transgression: not as an intrinsic sin, but as a violation of a rabbinic policy and the authority of his colleagues. One might question whether a *pikuach nefesh*-adjacent need might have warranted an exception, or whether the issue was more a matter of the precedent and policy implications of keeping an animal in one's home rather than grazing it on open land.

### Chasid Stories

The Gemara then notes: *kol heicha de'amar ma'aseh bechasid echad* — whenever a story mentions a *chasid*, it was either Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava or Rabbi Yehuda berabi Ilai. This creates a difficulty, because those Rabbis lived many generations after Yosef ben Yoezer. If after these two *Eshkolot* there could be no one without *dofi*, how can such later figures be held up as exemplars of near-perfect conduct? The Gemara is suggesting that even after Yosef ben Yoezer and Yosef ben Yochanan, individuals existed whose only failing was something as minor as this one goat — *shum dofi* in the meaningful sense, then, hardly applied to them.

### Dofi Smichah

Rav Yosef resolves the tension: *dofi shel smicha ktani* — the *dofi* referred to in the *Baraita* is not about personal observance or *Yirat Chet* at all. In those respects, great figures continued to exist even after that generation. The *dofi* pertains specifically to the realm of *Torah* transmission and *halacha* — and in particular it refers to *smicha*. Here *smicha* does not mean rabbinic ordination, but rather the earliest recorded disputes among the *zugot* concerning whether one may perform *smicha* — the laying of hands — on an animal sacrifice brought on *Yom Tov*. This controversy, which persisted across many generations of the *zugot*, only began after Yosef ben Yoezer and Yosef ben Yochanan. Before them, no debates in *halacha* arose; the transmission was perfect. The *dofi* was, therefore, the emergence of *halachic* debate — not a failure of moral character.

The Gemara anticipates an objection: Yosef ben Yoezer himself was a party to the original *smicha* controversy. The response: *ki plig bah besof shnei* — that controversy arose only at the very end of his life, *debatzer liba*, when the sharpness of transmission had already begun to erode. Until that point, the transmission had been flawless.

---

## Transmission Debate

### Forgetting View

This brings the Gemara to a broader question that was lurking throughout: why are there so many debates recorded in the Talmud? This critique was famously leveled by the Karaites, who argued that the sheer volume of disagreement in the *Talmud* demonstrates that *Torah shebe'al peh* rests on a faulty transmission — and if the *masorah* is unreliable, it cannot be trusted at all. One response available to the Rabbis is to note that the vast majority of basic *halachic* parameters are universally agreed upon, and that the debates concern only a subset of questions.

The approach implied by a number of *Gemarot*, including the present one, is more direct: debates arose because things were forgotten. This is reinforced by the well-known statement about Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel — *mishe-rabu talmidei Beit Shammai uBeit Hillel shelo shimshu kol tzarchan* — that when students did not attend sufficiently to their teachers and did not absorb the tradition fully, disputes proliferated. The entire narrative arc of this Gemara — which is building toward the *chamesh chataot hameitot* of our *Mishnah* — presses this theme: had things been transmitted perfectly, there would have been no debates.

### Rambam's View

The Rambam emphatically rejects this position. Both philosophically and as a response to the Karaite challenge, he insists that the transmission was always perfect: nothing that was *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* was ever forgotten or disputed. In his view, all *halachic* debates arise not from forgotten traditions but from the application of received principles to new cases — the clarification of parameters that were never explicitly transmitted in the first place. This is a powerful and intellectually coherent position. Even granting perfect transmission of every received *halacha*, enormous tracts of *halachic* reality remain unaddressed, and it is in navigating that territory that debates inevitably emerge.

The difficulty, of course, is that the present Gemara appears to cut directly against the Rambam, framing debates as products of forgetting. The Rambam's approach is also notably in tension with *Rashi*'s reading of the earlier passage, which interprets the debates that arose after Moshe's death as attempts to recall forgotten *halachot*.

### Gadol Yihiyeh

One may ask whether the surface nostalgia of this entire *sugya* — its lament for the great transmission that eroded — contains a hidden subtext. The *pasuk* that opened the *sugya*, *gadol yihiyeh kevod habayit ha'acharon min harishon*, suggests that the "latter house" ultimately surpasses the first. Elsewhere the Gemara weighs in clearly on the relative merits of received transmission versus creative intellectual engagement: Rabbi Akiva, who derived and developed, is preferred to Rabbi Eliezer, who essentially received and transmitted. One might wonder whether beneath the apparent mourning over forgotten *halachot* lies an implicit acknowledgment that *Torah shebe'al peh* — in its fullest form — is not merely retrieval but creation, and that perhaps the intellectual vitality of later generations represents its own kind of *gadol yihiyeh*. This reading may press beyond what the text explicitly supports, but the tension is present.

---

## Forgetting & Retrieval

### 3000 Halachot Lost

The Gemara now turns to the theme of forgetting and retrieval in full. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *shloshet alafim halachot nishtakechu bimei evlo shel Moshe* — 3,000 *halachot* were forgotten during the mourning period after Moshe's death.

The people turned to Yehoshua and said: *she'al* — go and ask God, retrieve what we have lost. Yehoshua replied: *lo bashamayim hi* — it is not in heaven. After Moshe, the process of divine supplementation of *Torah* is closed.

They then turned to Shmuel and said: *she'al*. He replied: *eileh hamitzvot* — these are the commandments God gave to Moshe; they are complete, and no prophet may innovate thereafter. The principle *she'ein navi rashai l'chadesh davar mei'ata* — that no prophet after Moshe may add to *halacha* — applies here as well. Even if one wished to frame the request not as innovation but as recovery, the answer *lo bashamayim hi* forecloses it.

Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha then notes: *af chatat shemetu ba'aleha nishtakecha bimei evlo shel Moshe* — the *halacha* regarding a *chatat* whose owners died was among the things forgotten during that mourning period. The alternate textual reading, cited by the *Shita Mekubetzet*, replaces *shemetu* with *shenitkapru ba'aleha*, tying the forgotten *halacha* directly to the dispute in our *Mishnah* — whether the *chatat* of a *tzibur* that brought another *korban* must die or may graze.

One might wonder how *halachot* could be forgotten during a mourning period of only forty days, particularly *halachot* about relatively rare scenarios such as a *chatat shemetu ba'aleha*. The answer may lie in how rarely such cases arose in practice — a *halacha* that was never applied during the forty years in the wilderness might simply never have been internalized in a way that survived the upheaval of Moshe's death. Beyond that, the people were profoundly dependent on Moshe, much as they had been during the episode of the golden calf when he was absent only briefly. The trauma of his death, and the grief of mourning, could have been enough to disrupt even memories that were held.

They then turned to Pinchas and said: *she'al*. He responded: *lo bashamayim hi*. They turned to Elazar and said: *she'al*. He responded: *eileh hamitzvot she'ein navi rashai l'chadesh davar mei'atah*. It is notable that the Gemara groups these four figures into two pairs, each pair giving a different formulation of the refusal. Yehoshua and Shmuel — political leaders who also had prophetic capacity — gave the *lo bashamayim hi* answer. Elazar and Pinchas — whose primary role was as *Kohen Gadol* and communicators of divine will through the *Urim VeTumim* — gave the second answer. The people may have hoped that those who wore the *Urim VeTumim*, whose very function was to ask God's guidance in critical moments, might succeed where the political leadership had not. Yet the answer is the same: from this point forward, *halacha* cannot be retrieved from Heaven.

### Yehoshua's Loss

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: at the moment Moshe was about to depart to *Gan Eden*, he said to Yehoshua — *she'al mimeni kol sefeikot sheyesh lach* — ask me whatever questions or doubts you have. Yehoshua responded: *Rebbi, kelum hinachticha sha'ah achat vehalachti lemakom acher* — "My teacher, have I ever left your side even for a moment? Did you not yourself write of me: *umesharto Yehoshua bin Nun na'ar lo yamish mitoch ha'ohel*? I never left the tent of Torah. I have nothing to ask."

*Miyad tashash kocho shel Yehoshua* — immediately Yehoshua's intellectual strength was sapped. *Venishtakechu mimenu shalosh me'ot halachot* — he forgot 300 *halachot*, *venoldu lo sheva me'ot sefeikot* — and 700 doubts arose for him.

Rashi explains the punishment in interpersonal terms: *she'hitzta'er Moshe Yehoshua be'atzmo shehayah gadol kamohu* — Yehoshua pained Moshe by essentially declaring himself Moshe's equal, "I have everything I need from you." To someone on his deathbed, the appropriate response is not confidence but need, not self-sufficiency but expression of dependence. Yet one may also read a deeper moral in Yehoshua's failure: the Gemara elsewhere warns that *ba'al ga'avah*, arrogance, causes one's *Torah* to be forgotten. Even if Yehoshua's statement was factually accurate at that moment, a disposition of humility demands that one never consider oneself complete — that one seize every opportunity to learn. The very last moment with one's teacher is not the moment for declarations of self-sufficiency.

The loss was especially irreversible because, as God later told Yehoshua: *lomar lach ee efshar* — I cannot tell you what was forgotten. *Lo bashamayim hi* now applied in full. The moment of Moshe's final teaching had passed, and with it the last window for this kind of recovery. Yehoshua was told instead: *lech u'tordan b'milchama* — direct their energies toward war, which was in any event the next stage of the national mission. The people, furious that their *halachot* had been lost and demanding from Yehoshua what he could not supply, needed to be redirected — and the conquest of the land was at hand.

It should be noted that the 3,000 *halachot* forgotten during the mourning for Moshe and the 300 forgotten because of Yehoshua's response are not contradictory traditions; they describe different moments and different losses.

### 1700 Hermeneutics Lost

The *Baraita* then adds a further dimension: *elef u'shva me'ot kalin v'chamurin, u'gezeirot shavot, v'dikdukei sofrim nishtakechu bimei evlo shel Moshe* — 1,700 instances of *kal v'chomer*, *gezeirot shavot*, and *dikdukei sofrim* were forgotten during the mourning for Moshe.

This is a striking formulation. *Kal v'chomer* and *gezeira shava* are the foundational hermeneutical tools of *Torah shebe'al peh* — the very instruments of rabbinic legal reasoning. The Gemara here frames even these as part of the *masorah*, as something transmitted and then forgotten, rather than as exercises of independent creative intellect. Indeed, the overriding thrust of this *sugya* is to present the entire enterprise of *Torah shebe'al peh* as essentially an act of retrieval.

What are *dikdukei sofrim*? Rashi (cited in the context of *Rabbeinu Gershom*) explains that *dikdukei sofrim* refers to the practice of organizing *halachot* into counted groups — *sefirot sefirot* — as, for example, the five *chataot hameitot*, or the thirteen things said about such-and-such topic. The role of the *sofrim* was apparently to take the existing data and organize it, to assign it a number and pull it together. What was forgotten was the content that would have permitted this organizing to be done — so the categories and counts could not be reconstructed. Rashi adds the phrase *she'adayin lo tzirfum* — things that had not yet been pulled together — suggesting that the *dikdukei sofrim* represented the one dimension of the rabbinic enterprise that was not pure transmission but involved an act of organization. Even that was lost.

The full weight of the Gemara's framing here is that the rabbinic tools most associated with intellectual creativity — *kal v'chomer* most of all, since it famously requires no *mesorah* — are being cast as part of the received tradition. The implication is that even rabbinic derivation, on this reading, is ultimately a form of recovery rather than innovation.

Rabbi Abahu then announces the resolution: *hechiziran Osniel ben Kenaz mitokh pilpulo* — Osniel ben Kenaz recovered all of them through his sharpness. The reference point is the verse in which Kalev offered his daughter in marriage to whoever could conquer *Kiryat Sefer*, and Osniel ben Kenaz, his brother, won her. The name *Kiryat Sefer* — a city of the *sofrim*, of counting — is read as a reference to the *dikdukei sofrim* that had been lost, and Osniel's conquest of it through *milchama* is read as his recovery of the lost tradition through the *milchamta shel Torah*, the battle of intellectual engagement.

### Achsah & Provision

The Gemara now digresses on the figure of Achsah, Kalev's daughter given to Osniel in marriage. Why was she called *Achsah*? *Shekol haro'ah otah ko'eis al ishto* — because anyone who saw her became angry at his own wife, so striking was her beauty.

The narrative then turns to the *pasuk*: *vayehi b'vo'ah vatasteihu lish'ol mei'et aviha sadeh* — when she came to Osniel, she enticed him to ask her father Kalev for a field. *Vatitznach mei'al hachamor* — she lowered herself, or in the Gemara's reading, she brayed, from the *chamor*. The Gemara reads *vatitznach* as a kind of complaint. Rava said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak: she said to Osniel — *mah chamor zeh keivan she'ein lo ma'achal b'avuso miyad tzo'ek* — just as a donkey, when it has no food in its trough, immediately cries out, *kach ishah she'ein lah tevu'ah b'tokh beitah miyad tzo'eket* — so too a wife who has no grain in her house immediately cries out. In short: we are about to start a life together, and someone must attend to practical provision.

She then goes to her father and says: *tnah li bracha ki eretz hanegev netatani* — give me a blessing, for you have given me a dry land. The Gemara reads this allegorically: *bayit shemenugav mikol tova* — a house emptied of all good. *Adam she'ein bo ela Torah bilvad* — a man who has nothing but *Torah* alone. What, she says to her father, have you given me? *Gulos mayim* — springs of water? She is saying: a *talmid chacham* is all well and good, but who puts food on the table?

Kalev's response — *vayiten lah Kalev et gulos eliyot v'et gulos tachtiyot*, he gave her the upper and lower springs — is also read allegorically. The Gemara reads his reply as: *mi shekol razei elyonim vetachtiyot*, the one who knows all the secrets of the upper and lower worlds — that is, this great *talmid chacham*, your husband who was able to restore what was lost from the time of Moshe — *yevakesh mimenu mezonos*, from him you should seek your sustenance.

Two readings of this response emerge in the *Rishonim*. Rashi, citing *Eishes chayil hayesah k'oniyot socheir*, reads it as a reassurance: if your husband is a *talmid chacham*, you need not worry — God will provide. *Rabbenu Gershom* takes a sharper tone: you have been given a man who knows the secrets of heaven and earth; is that not enough? Must you also ask for material comfort? You should know where your priorities lie.

The contrast between wife and husband here is pointed. Achsah is presented as a strong, practical figure — she is the *eishes chayil* who looks after her household, presses her father for what the family needs, and refuses to be satisfied with abstractions. Osniel is the scholar who restored 1,700 lost traditions through *pilpulo* and who, as we will shortly see, turned to God for what he truly needed. Both perspectives are given their due.

### Osniel Genealogy

The Gemara pauses to address a genealogical question. The *pasuk* calls Osniel *achi Kalev* — brother of Kalev — and refers to him as *ben Kenaz*. This would imply that Kalev too was *ben Kenaz*. Yet we know that Kalev is consistently called *ben Yefunneh* in the *Torah*. The Gemara resolves this: *mai Yefunneh? She'pannah me'atzat meraglim* — Yefunneh is not a proper name but a description, meaning "the one who turned away from the counsel of the spies." His real patronymic is *ben Chetzron*, as attested by the verse *v'Kalev ben Chetzron holid et Azuvah* in Divrei HaYamim. Rava explains: *chorgei d'Kenaz hava* — Kalev was Kenaz's stepson. Kalev's mother remarried Kenaz, and Osniel was born of that union. Thus Osniel and Kalev were half-brothers — Osniel was *ben Kenaz* in the literal sense, and Kalev was *ben Kenaz* only through his mother's remarriage.

### Osniel's Prayer

The Gemara identifies Osniel ben Kenaz with Yavetz, mentioned elsewhere in *Divrei HaYamim*. *Hu Osniel hu Yavetz* — they are the same person. His real name was Yehudah achi Shimon. He was called *Osniel* because *she'annao El* — God answered him. He was called *Yavetz* because *ya'atz v'ribbetz Torah* — he advised and spread *Torah* throughout Israel.

The proof that God answered him is drawn from the *pasuk*: *vayikra Yavetz l'Elohei Yisrael lemor* — Yavetz called out to the God of Israel. The prayer that follows is read by the Gemara not in its *peshat* sense as a request for land and territory, but as a *talmid chacham*'s prayer for the conditions necessary to sustain his learning.

*Im barech tevarcheni* — bless me, *baTorah*. *V'hirbita et gevuli* — expand my borders, *b'talmidim*, with students. *V'hayetah yadcha immi* — and Your hand should be with me, *she'lo yishtakach talmudi mi'libbi*, that my Torah should not be forgotten from my heart — echoing the central theme of this entire *sugya*. *V'asita mera'ati* — the word *mera'ati* is read as *merei'im*, friends: *she'yizdamnu li rei'im kamoti*, that I should have colleagues like myself. *L'vilti otzvi* — that the *yetzer hara* should not seduce me, *she'lo yasgiveni yetzer hara mi'lishnot*, into straying from my path, into abandoning *Torah* for other pursuits or priorities.

Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi offers an alternative reading. Rather than reading the prayer as entirely about *Torah*, he reads it as a prayer for both spiritual and material sustenance: *piryah verivyah* — that God bless him with many children; *b'vanim uvevanot* — sons and daughters; *bemassa umattan* — success in commerce, to provide for them; and health sufficient to pursue his responsibilities. This reading acknowledges the practical dimension that Achsah had pressed: a *talmid chacham* who understands his obligations to his household prays not only for Torah but for the means to fulfill his domestic responsibilities.

In both readings, the prayer ends the same way: *im atah oseh ken mutav* — if You do this, it is good, and if not, *hareini holech benisisi lishol* — I will go down in anguish to the depths. The passion here is remarkable. This is not a polite petition; it is a declaration that the life he has committed to is everything — and without divine support to sustain it, there is nothing.

*Vayavei Elohim et asher sha'al* — God gave him what he asked.

The Gemara closes this passage with a parallel *pasuk*: *rash ve'ish tichachim nifgashu, me'ir einei sheneihem Hashem* — a poor man and a man of substance encounter one another; God illumines the eyes of both. In the first reading, this refers to a student who comes to his *rebbi* and says: *lamdeni Torah* — teach me Torah. If the *rebbi* teaches him, *me'ir einei sheneihem Hashem* — God illumines both. If he refuses, *ashir varash nifgashu ose chulam Hashem* — God can reverse their fates: *mi she'asa chacham laze oseh oto tipeish, tipeish laze oseh oto chacham* — whoever was made wise will become foolish, and whoever was not will take his place. In the second reading, the *pasuk* applies to a poor person who insists on fulfilling his duty to provide for his household and seeks help from the wealthy — if he is helped, good; if refused, God can reverse their fortunes. In both cases the moral is the same: insist on your proper priorities, press them from God and from people, and do not waver.

---

## Five Deaths Debate

### Five Deaths Listed

The Gemara now returns to the *halacha* that lies at the center of the *Mishnah*. Rabbi Shimon states: *chamesh chata'ot metot* — there are five types of *chatat* that must be left to die when they arise in the case of an individual: *velad chatat* — the offspring of a *chatat*; *tmurat chatat* — a *temura*, an exchange made on a *chatat*; *chatat shemetu ba'aleha* — whose owners died before it was offered; *chatat shenitkapru ba'aleha* — whose owners achieved atonement through another offering; and *chatat she'avra shnata* — that has passed its first year.

### Three Don't Apply

Three of these five cannot arise in the case of a *tzibur*. A communal *chatat* is never female, so there can be no *velad chatat* of a *tzibur*'s offering. The *tzibur* cannot perform *temura*, as we have established. And the *tzibur* does not die — so *chatat shemetu ba'aleha* has no communal application. These three are therefore exclusively *yachid* scenarios.

### Group Unity Logic

Given that three of the five apply only to the *yachid*, Rabbi Shimon argues that the other two — *chatat shenitkapru ba'aleha* and *chatat she'avra shnata* — must likewise apply only to the *yachid*. The logic is *yilamed satum min hameforash*: the unexplicated cases are learned from the explicated ones. Since the five form a unified group, and three of them can only operate in the context of an individual, the entire group is understood to apply only to the *yachid* and not to the *tzibur*.

### Rav Natan: One Lost

Reish Lakish complicates this further by introducing the dimension of transmission. He suggests that the *mesorah* was actually for four *chataot* to die, not five. The fifth was uncertain — they knew there were four, they knew one could graze, but they did not know which was which. Rather than leave one unassigned, they extended the ruling to all five. The point about five forming a unified group still holds: since those four that had to die could only have been stated in the context of a *yachid* — the communal scenarios simply do not exist for enough of them — the entire *halacha* was said *beyachid*.

Rav Natan goes further still, to the opposite extreme: the *mesorah* was in fact for only one *chatat* to die. The rest were to graze. Four were lost, and since they did not know which of the five was the one, they extended the ruling to all of them.

### Double Forgetting

The Gemara then asks: even granting Rav Natan's position, might they not have at least remembered whether the one that dies was in the category that applies only to a *yachid*, or in the category that applies to both *yachid* and *tzibur*? The answer is: *trei shchiach shchu* — they forgot two things. Not only did they forget which specific *chatat* had to die; they also forgot whether it belonged to the group that applies exclusively to a *yachid* or the group that applies to both. Two layers of forgetting compounded one another.

Nevertheless, a resolution is still available. The *mesorah* that four had to graze — whatever its relationship to the five — was at minimum stated in a context where not all four could exist for a *tzibur*. At most two of the four could apply *betzibur*. Since those four form a unified group, and some of them apply only *beyachid*, the entire group of four must have been stated *beyachid*. And once we establish that the four that graze are a *yachid* matter, it follows that the one that dies is also a *yachid* matter. Therefore the entire *halacha* of *chamesh chataot meitot* applies only to the *yachid* and not to the *tzibur*.

### Transmission Problem

The full force of this *sugya* now comes into view. The *halacha* of *chamesh chataot meitot* is generally cited as a paradigmatic case of *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — a law transmitted directly from Sinai. Yet the Gemara has now shown that even this *halacha* was subject to the problems of transmission and forgetting. Whether the number was five, four, or one; whether it applied to *yachid* alone or also to *tzibur* — these were not questions about application to new cases, but questions about the transmission itself. The Gemara that began with the glory of perfect transmission and the *Eshkolot* who sustained it ends by demonstrating, case after case, that transmission was in fact vulnerable — that forgetting occurred, that debates arose from that forgetting, and that even foundational *halachot l'Moshe miSinai* were among the casualties.

This is, to put it directly, powerful evidence against the Rambam's position that disputes in *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* never occurred. The entire trajectory of this daf — from the mourning for Moshe through Yehoshua's loss, through the 1,700 forgotten hermeneutical traditions, through Osniel's recovery, and finally through the uncertainty at the heart of *chamesh chataot meitot* — is a sustained meditation on the fragility of transmission and the centrality of that fragility to the nature of *Torah shebe'al peh*.

---

---

# Temurah 17

## Kodshim vs. Temurah

### Mishnah Setup

The daf begins by picking up on the *mishnah* at the bottom of 15b. After a fascinating *gemara* on *halacha lemoshe misinai* and *mesorah*, the discussion returns to a direct analysis of *temurah* — but characteristically, it does so within a comparative framework. Just as earlier material contrasted *korbanos tzibur* with *korbanos yachid*, this *mishnah* compares *temurah* to direct sanctification. Since *temurah* involves attempting to transfer *kedusha* onto another animal, it is natural to ask: in what ways does this resemble, and in what ways does it differ from, an original act of sanctification? The *mishnah* frames this as a two-directional comparison: *chomer bekodshim mibetemurah vechomer betemurah mibekodshim* — there are respects in which sanctification carries greater weight, and respects in which *temurah* carries greater weight.

### Sanctify > Temurah

The first set of cases establishes where direct sanctification has greater weight. *Hakodshim osin temurah ve'ein temurah osah temurah*: sanctified animals can generate a *temurah*, but a *temurah* cannot generate a further *temurah*. The *kedusha* cannot be daisy-chained; only the original animal, not its *temurah*, can serve as a source for the act.

Furthermore, *hatzibur vehashutfim makdishim aval lo memirim*: the community and partners can sanctify but cannot perform *temurah*. This addresses both the animal and the act. The *tzibur* acquires its communal *korban* through sanctification using communal funds; partners sanctify jointly even if only one partner utters the words. But neither the *tzibur* nor *shutfim* can perform *temurah*, and a *korban tzibur* or *korban shutfim* cannot be the subject of *temurah*.

Additionally, *umakdishim ubarim ve'eivarim aval lo memirim*: fetuses and limbs can be sanctified, but *temurah* cannot be performed from them, or to them. As established in an earlier *sugya*, the Torah's language of *behemah bibehemah* requires that the act begin with a whole *behemah* and conclude with a whole *behemah*.

### Temurah > Sanctify

Now the *mishnah* turns to the ways in which *temurah* carries greater weight: *shehakedusha chalah al ba'al mum kavua ve'eino yotzei lechulin legazez vela'avod*. The printed text reads *shehakedusha chalah*, but as the *hagahot habach* notes, the correct reading should be *shehatemurah chalah* — for this clause describes the greater weight of *temurah*, not of sanctification generally.

The underlying principle is this: if one sanctifies an unblemished animal directly and it subsequently develops a blemish, it cannot be offered as a *korban* and must be redeemed. After redemption, however, a residual *kedusha* remains — the animal may not be shorn or worked, because it was once in a state of *kedushat haguf*. By contrast, if one directly sanctifies an animal that already has a blemish, the animal never attains *kedushat haguf* in the first place. Since it was never fit to be a *korban*, the act is analogous to sanctifying one's woodpile or one's car: it produces only *kedushat damim*, monetary sanctity, and upon redemption no residual *kedusha* remains.

*Temurah* operates differently. The Torah states *vehayah hu utemurato yihyeh kodesh* — the exchanged animal becomes *kodesh* just as the original. This applies even if the animal designated as *temurah* already had a blemish. The pasuk *ra betov o tov bera* — one cannot switch good for bad or bad for good — and the ruling of *chazal* that this refers to blemished animals, teaches that even when *temurah* is attempted onto a blemished animal, the *kedusha* takes effect in full, as *kedushat haguf*. Accordingly, when this blemished *temurah* is eventually redeemed, a residual *kedusha* remains, just as with any animal that possessed *kedushat haguf*. Here, then, *temurah* is weightier: the *kedusha* takes hold even where direct sanctification would not have produced *kedushat haguf* at all.

## Shogeg kemezid

### Position Statement

The *mishnah* continues: *Rabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda omer, asah shogeg kemezid betemurah velo asah shogeg kemezid bemukdashin*. Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda holds that by *temurah*, unintentional action is treated like intentional action, but this principle does not apply to original sanctification. The *gemara* will spend considerable effort unpacking what precisely this means, as will be seen below. The basis offered is the pasuk *yihyeh kodesh* — the word *yihyeh* is read as an amplification that extends the effect of *temurah* even to unintentional cases.

## Excluded Animals

### R. Eliezer Statement

*Rabbi Eliezer omer: hakilayim vehaterifa vehayotzei dofen vehatumtum veha'androgynos lo kedoshim velo makdishim*. Although the *mishnah* has just established that *temurah* takes effect even on a *ba'al mum*, Rabbi Eliezer teaches that certain categories are treated more severely — or more precisely, differently — than a *ba'al mum*: a crossbred animal (*kilayim*), a mortally wounded animal (*treifa*), one born by Caesarean section (*yotzei dofen*), and animals of uncertain or mixed gender (*tumtum* and *androgynos*). None of these become sanctified through *temurah*, and none of them can serve as the source of *temurah*.

This does not mean, it should be noted at the outset, that these animals cannot be sanctified at all. What is excluded is *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic sanctity, the sanctity of an animal designated for the altar. They can still be subject to *kedushat damim*, monetary sanctity, much like sanctifying a car or a woodpile. But *kedushat haguf* is foreclosed to them. Nor can they serve as the source from which *temurah* is generated, since *temurah* can only flow from something that already possesses *kedushat haguf*. The *gemara* will explore all of this further below.

## Shogeg kemezid (II)

### Lokeh vs. Kadosh

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ameih deRabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda?* What is the reasoning? The answer is that the Torah says *yihyeh kodesh* — this amplified language extends the law to unintentional cases as well.

But the *gemara* then asks: *heichi dami shogeg kemezid?* What exactly are the cases? Before examining them, a fundamental question must be posed. Anyone glancing at this passage in the *gemara* will notice an abundance of textual variants, parenthetical corrections, and notational marginalia. This reflects a genuine interpretive dispute about what Rabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda is even teaching.

*Temurah* has two dimensions: there is the prohibition against performing the act, and there is the effect — the second animal becomes sanctified regardless. The first dimension involves the actor's culpability; the second concerns the mechanics of *kedusha*. The critical question is: which dimension does Rabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda's statement address? Is he saying that *shogeg kemezid* means one receives *malkot* even for an unintentional act of *temurah* — a remarkable *chiddush* given that lashes ordinarily require *mezid*? Or is he saying that the *effect* of *temurah*, the sanctification of the second animal, takes hold even in cases of error?

The textual evidence for this ambiguity is explicit. *Tosafot* notes: *ve'ika sefarim degarsi gabei tmura lokeh gabei kodshim lo lokeh* — some texts read the ruling in terms of lashes — while other versions read *gabei tmura kadish vegabei kodshim lo kadish* — the ruling is about whether sanctification takes effect. According to *Tosafot*, two major *ba'alei hatosafot* adopted these two readings consistently: Rabbeinu Shimshon (Rav Shimshon miShantz) and Rabbeinu Baruch. Each either worked from a different *girsa* of the *gemara* or interpreted the same text in fundamentally different ways, and their respective readings pervade their treatment of all the cases that follow.

### Olah/Shelamim Case

The *gemara* cites Chizkiya's analysis first: *kasavar shemutar lehamir* — the actor believed the act of *temurah* was permitted. According to the version where lashes are at stake: *gabei tmura laki, gabei kodshim lo laki* — by *temurah* one receives lashes, while by *kodshim* one does not. The comparison to *kodshim* is meaningful because there is in fact a way to incur lashes for an act of sanctification: the prohibition of *hamakdish ba'al mum* — sanctifying a blemished animal — is a *lav*, and the *gemara* has established elsewhere that when a speech-act (*dibbur*) has a legally operative effect, one can receive *malkot* for it. So the comparison is between two scenarios where a verbal act of sanctification produces lashes: one via *temurah*, one via directly sanctifying a *ba'al mum*. The *chiddush* is that *temurah* generates lashes even when the actor believed the act was permissible — a form of *shogeg*.

The alternative *girsa* — *gabei tmura kadish gabei kodshim lo kadish* — raises a difficulty. If the issue were about the *effect*, why would *omer mutar*, believing it to be permitted, prevent the act from taking effect by direct sanctification? If someone tries to sanctify an animal thinking it is permitted, the animal is sanctified. *Omer mutar* has no obvious bearing on whether the *kedusha* takes hold. This reinforces the reading that the debate in this passage concerns lashes, not effect.

Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan offer a different paradigm: *kasavar lomar tmuras olah ve'amar tmuras shelamim* — the person intended to designate an animal as a *temurah* for his *olah* but said *temurah* for his *shelamim*, or vice versa. What emerged from his mouth differed from what was in his mind. In ordinary sanctification, the rule is *kedusha betaos lo kedusha* — a speech-act of *hafla'ah* that does not match the speaker's intent does not take effect. The words must express the actual intent; *devarim shebelev einam devarim* does not apply here, and the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is resolved in favor of Beit Hillel: an erroneous designation does not take effect. But by *temurah*, the word *yihyeh kodesh* extends the effect even to this case of verbal error. This answer clearly concerns the *effect* of the act, not lashes — the question is whether the designation takes hold despite the discrepancy between intent and utterance.

The logic, moreover, is coherent: when creating *kedusha* from scratch, the speech-act must be precise and complete, since the act itself generates the sanctity. But *temurah* operates differently — the *kedusha* already exists in the source animal, and the act merely transfers it. It requires less perfection in execution for a transfer to succeed. Just as *temurah* takes effect on a *ba'al mum* in a way that direct sanctification does not, so too it takes effect even in a case of verbal error.

### Black/White Case

The same principle governs the next case: *kasavar lomar lishachor ve'amar lalavan* — one intended to say "I am exchanging for the black animal" but said "the white one." Again, the question is whether the discrepancy between intent and utterance prevents the act from taking effect. The two *girsa'ot* again appear: by *temurah*, it either takes effect (*kadish*) or one receives lashes (*laki*); by *kodshim*, it does not. The case most naturally concerns the question of effect, since the issue is squarely about *kedusha betaos*, whether a mistaken designation has legal force.

### Stipulation Case

Rabbi Yochanan adds a further case: *be'omer tetzei zu vetikanes zu* — the person explicitly stipulates that he wants this animal to exit its sanctity and that one to enter it in its place. In other words, he makes the effectiveness of the *temurah* conditional on the original animal's *kedusha* being transferred away. This is a surprising case. One might think such a stipulation could limit the act — after all, the person is explicitly stating he does not want the *kedusha* to take hold unless the condition is met. And yet *yihyeh kodesh* teaches that the designation takes effect regardless. The *gemara* records this as a distinct case, apparently because the person's explicit stipulation represents a particular form of misunderstanding about the act's mechanics.

### Pre-intent Case

Rav Sheshet presents yet another scenario: *be'omer ekaneis le-bayit zeh ve-akdish ve-amir mida'ati* — someone says in advance, "When I enter that house I intend to sanctify" or "I intend to perform *temurah* intentionally," and then goes in and does so *shelo mida'ato* — without conscious intention at the moment of the act. Rashi understands the person as a *ba'al machshavot*, a distracted or absent-minded individual whose head is elsewhere; he had previously declared his intention, but at the moment of execution his attention had wandered and the act was performed on autopilot.

By *temurah*, the advance declaration of intent frames the subsequent act, and lashes apply (or the effect takes hold, depending on the *girsa*); by *kodshim*, since the person was not consciously intending the act at the moment, there is no consequence.

*Tosafot* offers an alternative reading: the person makes a *tnai*, a formal condition — "when I enter this house, let this animal become a *temurah*" (or "let it be sanctified") — and then when he actually walks into the house, he has completely forgotten the stipulation and is simply going in for a drink of water. The condition was met, but he was wholly unaware of it at the time. On this reading, whether the *kedusha* takes effect is the natural question, since the condition was satisfied independently of his consciousness. But why would the mere forgetting of a *tnai* prevent the effect in a case of direct *kodshim*? This puzzle reinforces the view that Rav Sheshet's case is primarily about lashes — the question is whether one is culpable for *malkot* when one was not consciously willing the transgression at the moment it occurred.

Stepping back, these cases appear to reflect two different lines of analysis: some answers treat the *chiddush* as concerning lashes, others as concerning the effect. Different *amora'im* may have understood Rabbi Yose berabbi Yehuda's statement differently, and the underlying dispute between the *ba'alei hatosafot* is really a dispute among the *amora'im* themselves. If the *chiddush* concerns lashes, then something deeply unusual is being asserted — that one can receive *malkot* even without full willfulness — and the *gemara* works hard to limit such cases as narrowly as possible. If the *chiddush* concerns effect, then the *gemara* is explaining why *temurah* can succeed even where a direct act of sanctification would fail, on the reasoning that transferring existing *kedusha* requires less precision than creating it from nothing.

## Excluded Animals (II)

### Shmuel Position

Having concluded the discussion of *shogeg kemezid*, the *gemara* turns back to Rabbi Eliezer's list of excluded animals. The *gemara* cites the *baraita* of Rabbi Meir: *ume'achar she'einan kedoshim heich makdishim?* If these animals cannot become sanctified, how could they ever serve as the source of *temurah*? This observation underscores that the exclusion is comprehensive — they cannot receive *kedushat haguf* through *temurah*, and there is equally no direct route to *kedushat haguf* through ordinary sanctification. The only exceptional scenarios in which such an animal might acquire *kedushat haguf* are: (a) an animal was sanctified while unblemished and then became a *treifa*; (b) a fetus was sanctified in utero and then born by Caesarean section; or (c) the mother was sanctified and then gave birth to such an animal, so that the offspring derived its *kedushat haguf* from the mother — and this third case holds only according to Rabbi Yehuda, who maintains that offspring of *kodshim* can perform *temurah*.

Shmuel, however, stakes out a strikingly different position: *hamakdish et hatreifa tzricha mum kavua lifdota alav* — if one sanctifies a *treifa*, the animal requires a formal *mum kavua* (a fixed blemish) in order to be redeemed. The necessity of a blemish for redemption implies that the animal has attained *kedushat haguf*, not merely *kedushat damim*. Shmuel thus appears to hold that directly sanctifying a *treifa* does confer *kedushat haguf*.

### Rav Oshaya

Rav Oshaya rejects this position directly: *eina ela ke-makdish eitzim va'avanim beva'alei mumin* — sanctifying such an animal is like sanctifying wood and stones in the case of *ba'alei mumin*. The act produces only *kedushat damim*, monetary sanctity, not *kedushat haguf*. Given that a *treifa* is worse than a *ba'al mum* in terms of its fitness to be brought as a *korban*, and we already know that directly sanctifying a *ba'al mum* does not produce *kedushat haguf*, it follows all the more that sanctifying a *treifa* cannot do so either. The practical consequence of *kedushat damim* is that the sanctity can be removed through a simple act of redemption without requiring a formal *mum*.

The *gemara* challenges Shmuel's position from the *mishnah* that states: *kol hakodashim shena'asu treifa ein podim osam lefei she'ein podin et hakodashim leha'achilan laklavim* — all sanctified animals that became *treifa* cannot be redeemed, since one may not redeem *kodshim* merely to feed them to dogs. The *gemara* notes: *ta'ama shena'asu* — the scenario in the *mishnah* is that they *became* *treifa* after sanctification. This implies: *ha hayu mei'ikara* — if it was a *treifa* from the start, one *could* redeem it, which would support Shmuel. But the *gemara* deflects this: perhaps that *tanna* holds *kol heicha delo chazi legufah lo nachsa lei kedushat haguf* — wherever an animal cannot be used as a *korban*, *kedushat haguf* does not descend upon it at all. So the *mishnah* does not demonstrate Shmuel's view; it reflects a different authority.

Indeed, the *gemara* presses further: Shmuel himself explained Rabbi Eliezer's statement as meaning *lo kedoshim bitemurah velo makdishim la'asot temurah* — they cannot become *kodesh* through *temurah* and cannot generate *temurah*. But from Rabbi Meir's *baraita* it is evident that they cannot become *kodesh* through direct sanctification either. Shmuel is ultimately driven to say that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Meir represent one opinion, and that he himself disagrees with them — holding that these animals *can* receive *kedushat haguf* through direct sanctification. Implicitly, Shmuel reads Rabbi Eliezer's ruling as a minority view, and maintains the opposite position.

### Category Distinction

Having laid out the controversy, Rav Pappa asks the pointed question: *mai ta'ama deRabbi Eliezer?* What is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for treating these animals so differently from a *ba'al mum*? The answer proposed is: *kebehemah teme'ah* — Rabbi Eliezer compares them to a non-kosher animal. Just as a non-kosher animal is categorically ineligible to serve as a *korban* and cannot attain *kedushat haguf* whether through direct sanctification or *temurah*, these animals too, since they cannot be brought as *korbanos*, are placed in the same categorical exclusion.

Rav Pappa then turns to Rava and asks: *veharei ba'al mum* — why are these treated differently from a *ba'al mum*? After all, even a *ba'al mum* cannot be offered as a *korban*. Rava answers: *ba'al mum karev be-mino* — other animals of the same category and type are indeed brought; the *ba'al mum* is still a sheep or an ox, just one with a defect. These other animals, by contrast, are viewed as belonging to a categorically different grouping altogether. The comparison to a non-kosher animal is apposite precisely because the same categorical othering applies.

### Psul Guf Analysis

Rava sharpens his reasoning: *mah behemah teme'ah psula guf, af go psula guf* — just as a non-kosher animal is disqualified by something intrinsic to its identity (*psul guf*), these animals too are disqualified by an intrinsic quality of their body. *Ba'al mum*, by contrast, is categorized as *psulei chisaron* — a disqualification of lacking, of deficiency, not of essential identity.

It is worth noting what the *gemara* does *not* mean by this. The distinction is not purely physical — that is, it is not simply that a *ba'al mum* has something physically missing while these others are whole. The *gemara* will immediately challenge that reading. Rather, the conceptual distinction is between an animal that is viewed as intrinsically of a different type versus an animal that is essentially the same type but happens to be lacking in some respect.

### Challenge to Rava

The *gemara* challenges this immediately: *amar lei Rav Ada leRava, velo saru'a vekalut katav beparasha* — the Torah lists *saru'a* (an overgrown limb) and *kalut* (fused hooves) among the *mumim*. These are not cases of physical lacking; they are cases where the body has something extra or something differently configured. Yet they are categorized as *ba'alei mumin*, the class Rava is claiming is defined by *psulei chisaron*. So the definition of *ba'al mum* cannot be reduced to physical lacking.

In defense of Rava's conceptual approach: the intent is not that every *mum* involves the physical absence of something, but rather that *ba'alei mumin* are conceptually framed as animals that are essentially of the same type as fit *korbanos* but fall short in some respect — they do not quite meet the standard, yet they belong to the same genus. The excluded categories, by contrast, are framed as categorically other, regardless of whether the "otherness" is physically observable. For *kilayim* and the gender-ambiguous animals (*tumtum* and *androgynos*), this categorization is readily understood; for *yotzei dofen*, Rashi notes that in people's minds a Caesarean birth placed the animal in an entirely different category — so unusual was it that the animal was perceived as wholly other.

### Behemah Tmeia

The *gemara* then acknowledges the remaining difficulty: what about *treifa*? An animal that has a hole in its lung is still a sheep; it has not changed species or category. Rava's first formulation — that these are *psulei guf* in the sense of being categorically other — does not straightforwardly apply to *treifa* in the way it does to *kilayim* or *tumtum*. This is why the *gemara* challenged only on *treifa* and not on *yotzei dofen*.

Rava therefore offers a complementary answer for *treifa*: *behemah teme'ah asura ba'achilah, vetreifa asura ba'achilah, le'apukei ba'al mum demutar ba'achilah* — a non-kosher animal cannot be eaten, a *treifa* cannot be eaten, whereas a *ba'al mum* may be eaten after redemption. The *treifa* is thus excluded not because it is categorically of a different type like a non-kosher animal, but because it shares with the non-kosher animal the decisive characteristic of being forbidden for consumption. This ineligibility to be eaten places it in the same functional category as *behemah teme'ah*, and on that basis it receives the same exclusion from *temurah* and *kedushat haguf*.

The full picture that emerges from Rava is: the excluded animals differ from *ba'al mum* for one of two reasons. Some are categorically viewed as a different type of creature altogether (*kilayim*, *tumtum*, *androgynos*, *yotzei dofen* in the popular imagination). Others — specifically *treifa* — are not categorically different but are excluded by analogy to *behemah teme'ah* on account of their inability to be eaten. Either way, they stand apart from *ba'al mum*, which is ultimately still the same type of animal, merely lacking in some quality that the *beit hamikdash* demands.

## Vlad Shelamim

### Mishnah on Vlad

The daf concludes with the opening of a new *perek*: *elu kodshim shevladosem vetmurosem keyotzei bahen* — the following *kodshim* whose offspring and *temurot* have the same status as themselves and may even be offered as *korbanos*. The *mishnah* begins with *shelamim*: *vlad shelamim vetemurasan, vladan vladan vlad vladan ad sof kol ha'olam, harei hen shelamim* — the offspring of a *shelamim*, its *temurah*, and all subsequent generations of offspring to the end of time are themselves *shelamim*. They require the full treatment of *shelamim*: *semicha*, the wine and flour libations (*nesachim*), and the waving of the breast and thigh (*tenufat chazeh veshok*). They are treated as *shelamim* in every respect. The one limitation that follows from earlier *halachot* is that a *temurah* cannot itself generate a further *temurah* — *ein temurah osah temurah* — but for the chain of offspring, *vlad vevladei vladan ad sof kol ha'olam*, there is no such restriction.

### End of Time

The *gemara* asks: *keivan detanya vladan vevladei vladan, lamma li ad sof kol ha'olam?* If the *mishnah* already teaches that the ruling applies to children and grandchildren, why add "until the end of time"? Surely this is superfluous. The *gemara* answers: *shema leih leRabbi Eliezer de'amar vlad shelamim lo yikrav shelamim* — the phrase is addressing Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that the offspring of a *shelamim* cannot itself be offered as a *shelamim*. Our *tanna* is responding with pointed emphasis: not only do I disagree regarding the children, as I would not concede even that to you, but I extend the ruling to grandchildren and all subsequent generations to the end of time. The exaggerated formulation signals that the *mishnah* is deliberately rejecting Rabbi Eliezer's position in the strongest possible terms. The underlying intuition Rabbi Eliezer might invoke — that later generations are like lower-quality copies of an original, progressively less identical to their source — is explicitly repudiated.

### Zachar Source

The *gemara* proceeds to identify the scriptural basis: where do we know that a *temurah* or offspring of a *shelamim* may be offered as a *korban*? A *baraita* derives this from the verse regarding *shelamim*: *im zachar im nekeivah* — whether male or female. Since the verse could have simply stated the relevant law without specifying gender, the specification must be coming to include additional cases. The word *zachar* comes to include the *vlad* — even an offspring of a *shelamim* may be brought.

One might have thought to derive this from a *kal vachomer*: if a *temurah*, which was not itself gestated within a *korban*, can be brought, then certainly a *vlad*, which was, should be brought. But the *kal vachomer* can be deflected: the *chiddush* of *temurah* is that it applies across all categories of *kodshim*, whereas *vlad* is only possible with female animals, which do not include all categories of *korbanos* (there is no *vlad* from an *olah*-male or an *asham*). Since *vlad* does not apply universally, perhaps it should not be brought. The verse *im zachar* therefore comes explicitly to include the offspring.

### Nekeivah Source

The verse's mention of *nekeivah* then addresses *temurah*: *kodesh yekadash* — the word *nekeivah* (or the grammatical phrase in which it appears) comes to include the *temurah* of a *ba'al mum* and the *vlad* of a *ba'al mum*. Without this derivation, one might have thought that since a *ba'al mum* cannot itself be brought as a *korban*, its offspring or *temurah* should equally be restricted. The verse teaches otherwise — even these attain the status and can, in terms of their inherent *kedusha*, be treated as *shelamim*, though how far this extends (whether they can actually be offered) remains a subject for further analysis.

### Word Gender Debate

A brief but pointed exchange between Rav Safra and Abaye addresses the assignment of the *derashos*. Rav Safra asks: *ipcha mana?* Why derive the *vlad* from *zachar* and the *temurah* from *nekeivah*? Why not reverse the derivations — learn the *temurah* from *zachar* and the *vlad* from *nekeivah*?

Abaye initially understands the question as asking why the *alef-mem* (*im*) prefixes are not learned cross-contextually, but Rav Safra clarifies: *hachi ka'amina lach* — that was not his question. Of course the *im* modifying *zachar* will be learned in conjunction with *zachar*, and the *im* modifying *nekeivah* will be learned in conjunction with *nekeivah*. The real question is about the original assignment: why is *zachar* the source for *vlad* and *nekeivah* the source for *temurah*, rather than the reverse?

Abaye answers: *vlad lashon zachar mashma, temurah lashon nekeivah mashma* — the word *vlad* is grammatically masculine, so it is naturally derived from the masculine term *zachar*; the word *temurah* is grammatically feminine, so it is naturally derived from the feminine *nekeivah*. The derivation follows the grammatical gender of the rabbinic term, not the biological sex of the animal in question. The discussion of the precise import of each derivation — specifically regarding whether the offspring and *temurah* of a *ba'al mum* can actually be offered as a *korban* — will be taken up in the following daf.

# Temurah 19

## Toda: Children & Substit…

### Mishna 22 Introduction

Mishna 22 opens by examining the status of the child and *temurah* of animals sanctified as *korbanot* — specifically, whether they may themselves be brought as offerings. The preceding material established that by *shelamim*, the child and *temurah* carry the same status as the parent and may be brought, with certain limited exceptions for children. We now turn to the *toda*, the thanksgiving offering, which is a subcategory of *shelamim*.

The *mishna* teaches: *vlad toda* — the child of a *toda* — and *tmurasah*, its *temurah*, and *vlad vlada*, the child of its child, and so on *ad sof kol hadoros*, until the end of all generations — *harei elu k'toda bilvad she'ein te'unim lachem*: these are treated in every respect like a *toda*, with the single exception that they do not require bread. Unlike the fuller *shelamim* procedure — which includes *smicha*, *nesachim*, and *chazeh v'shok* — the *toda* ordinarily also requires forty loaves of bread. Its derivatives, however, are brought without that bread.

One notable feature of this *mishna* is the absence of any debate. The position of Rabbi Eliezer — encountered earlier — which holds that the children of certain *korbanot* are not brought, does not appear here. As will become clear, the *gemara* uses precisely this absence to press the inquiry into what Rabbi Eliezer's position really is and why it does not apply in the case of *toda*.

### Toda Law Sources

The *gemara* asks *m'nan hani mili* — where do we know this? The *tanna'im* derive the law from a close reading of the relevant *pesukim*. The *pasuk* concerning *shelamim* uses the verb *yakrivenu*, and the *pasuk* concerning *toda* reads *im al toda yakrivenu* — "if it is for a *toda*, bring it." The *gemara* proceeds through a series of derivations:

If one designated a *toda* and it was lost, and he designated a replacement, and then the original was found, we know from the phrase *im al toda* — understood broadly — that either one may be brought. The question then is: which of them requires the bread? From the word *yakrivenu* — the singular form — we learn *achas v'lo shtayim*: one, not two. Only one of the two is brought with bread; the other is brought without.

Having established the law for *chalifin* — the exchange case — the *gemara* then asks how we extend the rule to include children and *tmuros* as well. The answer is that the additional phrase *v'im al toda* introduces further cases. Once again, the question is raised: perhaps these should also require bread? The *gemara* answers from the phrase *al zevach hatoda* — bread accompanies the *toda* sacrifice itself, *toda te'una lachem*, not the child, not the *temurah*, and not the *chalifa*. The one that was not ultimately brought has the status of a *chalifa* and does not require bread.

### Bread Exclusion Explained

It is notable that the *gemara* derived the law of *toda* from a separate *pasuk* rather than simply extending the general rule established for *shelamim*. The derivation is necessary in part because it establishes not just that these derivatives are brought, but also that they are brought *without* bread. *Tosafot* raises the broader question of whether the general rule is that derivatives may be brought unless there is a specific reason to exclude them, or vice versa. The impression is that the default is to bring them unless excluded — yet *toda* still required its own derivation, particularly to resolve the bread question.

Why would the bread requirement fall away for the derivative? A useful conceptual framework places the *toda* somewhere between the generic *korbanot* — *shelamim* and *olah*, which are non-specific — and the more singular *korbanot* such as *chatas* and *asham*, which are bound to a particular transgression. A *toda* is by its nature a response to a specific experience of divine deliverance. It has an individual identity, a specific narrative behind it. Only when the *toda* itself is brought does the full expression of that particularity — embodied in the bread — apply. The derivative shares the *toda*'s *kedusha* but not its singular, personal occasion, and therefore its more distinctive characteristic, the bread, is not carried over. That said, it does not become a generic *shelamim* in every sense: it retains the *toda*'s stricter eating schedule of one day and one night, rather than the two days allowed for *shelamim*.

The question of why Rabbi Eliezer's position does not generate a debate here is what drove the *gemara* in the preceding discussion to reframe his position. Had Rabbi Eliezer's view been a principled objection to ever bringing derivatives, it would apply to *toda* as well. The *gemara* therefore concluded that his position rests on a *gezeira* that does not apply to *toda* because *toda* is uncommon — *lo shechicha*, and therefore *lo gazru*. This reading renders Rabbi Eliezer's position considerably more limited in scope.

---

## Olah: Gender & Derivativ…

### Olah Chain Structure

The *mishna* turns next to the *olah*, the elevation offering. Unlike the *shelamim* or *toda*, the *olah* must be male. This constraint makes the discussion of children and derivatives considerably more complex, since one cannot simply speak of the child of an *olah* — female offspring cannot be brought as an *olah* at all, and even male offspring of a female *olah* pose difficulties. The discussion therefore focuses on what happens when sanctity travels through the chain via *temurah* and then through offspring.

The *mishna* states: the *temurah* of an *olah*, or the *vlad* of a *temurah* — note that it is the child of the *temurah*, not the child of the *olah* itself, since the *temurah* can be female — along with the child's child, and all subsequent descendants *ad sof kol haolam*, all carry the status of an *olah*. Wherever along the chain a male appears, that animal may be brought as an *olah* — *harei elu k'olah* — and is subject to the full procedure: *hafshat v'nituach v'kalil l'ishim*, flaying, dissection, and complete burning on the *mizbeach*.

What then of the females along the chain?
